name: Competitor corporate political activity
definition: CPA towards the EPA by other companies in the same industry, proxied by lobbying expenditures, which the authors use to measure the ongoing exchange of information between firms and the EPA.

name: Regulatory enforcement
authors_terms: ["regulatory enforcement", "enforcement actions", "EPA fines", "probability of being fined"]
definition: Enforcement actions taken by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency against facilities, measured as whether a facility incurs an EPA fine in a given year.

name: Risk of significant harm
authors_terms: ["toxicity", "risk of significant harm", "potential harm", "level of facilities' toxicity"]
definition: The potential severity of a firm violating the law, proxied by the toxicity of chemicals processed by the facility, following the literature on EPA fines.

name: Geographic proximity to competitors
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity", "co-location", "distance to the closest lobbying competitor"]
definition: The distance between a facility and the closest facility owned by an industry competitor that has a lobbying relationship with the EPA; geographic proximity lowers the cost of obtaining private information about rivals.

name: Production standardization
definition: The degree to which a rival's production process is close to the industry standard, in this context the similarity of the toxic chemicals a facility uses as inputs relative to the rest of the industry.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: The intensity of competition in an industry, with higher price competition and lower margins, measured by changes in industry-level net imports.

name: Performance relative to industry peers
definition: A firm's performance relative to its industry peers, measured as Returns on Assets relative to the SIC-4 level average.

name: Stakeholder conflict
definition: The sum of SMO-initiated conflict against the focal firm, including protests, boycotts, or lawsuits. Pre-acquisition, conflict is the yearly sum of the acquirer's and target's conflict, while post-acquisition it is the combined firm's annual conflict.

name: Offsetting stakeholder relationships
definition: An offsetting relationship occurs when, at the time of deal announcement, one of the firms brings cooperative stakeholder relationships while the other brings conflictual relations. An acquisition involving firms with offsetting relationships prompts stakeholders to evaluate if their disparate pre-acquisition strategies aimed at previously separate firms will be effective with a combined entity post-acquisition.

name: Issue alignment
authors_terms: ["issue alignment", "issue-aligned offsetting relationships", "offsetting relationships: similar issues", "issue peers"]
definition: An acquisition involving firms with offsetting stakeholder relations is more likely to prompt a reset effect if conflictual and cooperative stakeholders engaged the firm on the same or similar issues before that deal. Issue alignment makes the promise of the firm changing more credible because one of the combining firms already cooperates with stakeholders on an issue of interest to the conflictual stakeholder.

name: Relational alignment
authors_terms: ["relational alignment", "relationally aligned offsetting relationships", "offsetting relationships: socially proximate", "social proximity"]
definition: Relational alignment between the cooperative and conflictual stakeholders brought by the parties to the deal enhances the odds that the conflictual stakeholders will favor the certainty of cooperation that is offered by those stakeholders. To the extent that the acquirer and target have offsetting relationships with stakeholders that previously cooperated with one another, the combined firm might benefit from the advocacy of newly gained cooperative stakeholders due to relational embeddedness.

name: Stakeholder field fragmentation
definition: Fragmented fields, where little consensus exists among stakeholders, are characterized by distinct clusters of disconnected stakeholders working on their preferred solutions to an issue. A field is defined as being fragmented if SMOs that never cooperate with firms have no ties to (or do not cooperate with) SMOs that do cooperate with firms.

name: CEO agreeableness
definition: Individuals high in agreeableness tend to be described as soft-hearted, selfless, sincere, humble, and helpful, and a salient characteristic is their suppression of self-focused tendencies and elevated consideration of others' interests.

name: CEO conscientiousness
definition: Conscientiousness is a personality dimension associated with scrupulousness, diligence, and orderliness; individuals high in it tend to be reliable, careful, punctual, hardworking, persevering, and well-organized, and adhere closely to moral obligations.

name: CEO neuroticism
definition: Neuroticism, or emotional instability, is a personality dimension associated with anxiety, impulsivity, and a sense of vulnerability; a key characteristic of more neurotic individuals is their tendency to experience and express negative affect.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Unrelated diversification is a manifestation of agency costs: CEOs pursue a level of diversification beyond what is optimal for shareholders, and industries that fall under different two-digit SIC codes are considered unrelated.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured with accounting-based and market-based indicators, all adjusted by industry averages at the two-digit SIC level.

name: CEO compensation
definition: CEO total compensation, used as the dependent variable to examine pay-for-performance through interaction effects.

name: Solo founding
authors_terms: ["solo founder", "solo-founded ventures", "solo founding", "solo-founded", "found the company alone"]
definition: The choice to found a new venture alone rather than with one or more co-founders; a company is solo-founded when it has only one founder.

name: New venture performance
definition: The success of a new venture, measured by whether the startup achieved a successful exit (IPO or acquisition), a metric the authors describe as encapsulating one of the main goals of new ventures.

name: Breadth of experience
authors_terms: ["broad experience", "breadth", "breadth of experience", "broad experience across multiple functional domains"]
definition: The extent to which a founder has worked across multiple functional areas, consistent with prior work that discusses breadth as functional diversity across different skill domains.

name: Depth of experience
authors_terms: ["deep experience", "depth", "deep experience within one functional domain", "specialization"]
definition: The extent to which a founder has accumulated significant expertise (years of experience) within a single functional domain.

name: T-shaped skills
definition: The combination of deep and broad experience - that is, broad experience in multiple domains (the horizontal bar of the 'T'), while at the same time having deep experience in one particular domain (the vertical bar).

name: Industry relatedness of founding team human capital
authors_terms: ["industry relatedness of founding team human capital", "industry relatedness", "inside knowledge", "insider startups", "outsider startups", "pre-entry industry experience"]
definition: We define industry relatedness of founding team human capital as the distance in human capital space between the startup industry and the prior industry of the founding team. Higher employee mobility from industry j to industry i reflects greater similarity in how the two industries value human capital.

name: Startup failure
definition: Startup failure is measured with a dummy variable equal to 1 if all establishments affiliated with the startup's firm identifier no longer appear in the data or contain any employment in the following year.

name: Startup employment growth
definition: We use the standard measure of firm growth based on employee headcount (including the founding team) and aggregate across all establishments affiliated with the startup's firm identifier.

name: Startup firm size
definition: The model implies that the average outsider startup entrepreneur will have a higher z than the average insider startup entrepreneur, resulting in a faster growth and larger size, conditioning on survival.

name: Startup acquisition
definition: If the underlying technical idea may create enough value for potential acquirers, entrepreneurs may exit by seeking an acquisition.

name: Industry specificity of knowledge
definition: If more of the open positions in an industry are filled by workers who are already employed in that industry, it suggests that industry requires skills, knowledge, and relationships that are not typically held by industry outsiders.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Involuntary successions included CEO departure due to death, illness, job performance, and personal issues. CEO dismissal was coded as one if the CEO departed for poor job performance or undisclosed personal issues, and zero otherwise.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Our working definition of corporate reputation is a perceptual evaluation of the firm's overall appeal in the eyes of particular evaluating audiences. Corporate reputations are thought of as relatively stable, long-term, and collective perceptual judgments of the firm as a whole.

name: CEO awards
definition: CEO awards are typically conferred by prominent business publications (e.g., Business Week, Forbes, etc.) on executives who are judged to be exceptionally capable (e.g., 'CEO of the Year'). These awards reflect strong positive views of the CEO's human capital and are powerful signals of CEO capability or even 'star' status.

name: CEO media coverage
definition: We conceptualize media coverage as an indicator of CEO prominence. Media coverage increases general awareness of CEOs and the strategies they set for their firms.

name: Pre-succession firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["historical market return", "pre-succession firm financial performance", "firm performance"]
definition: A firm's performance is a key signal that evaluators interpret, and poor results can generate an expectation that change at the firm is needed. Historical market return is measured as the mean change (in fractional terms) in the market value of equity during the three prior years.

name: Temporal distance
authors_terms: ["temporal distance", "temporal (time zone) distance", "difference in time zones"]
definition: Temporal distance, or difference in time zones, is a particularly important feature on digital platforms that connect users globally. It reduces the time overlap of participation in synchronous interactions.

name: User interactions
definition: Interactions between users on the platform, measured for this study as the number of votes and unique views that flow within a region-region dyad on a given day. Views are conceptualized as a type of knowledge seeking and votes as a type of knowledge engagement or curation.

name: Knowledge popularity
authors_terms: ["knowledge popularity", "popular vs. niche category", "popular communities", "niche communities", "popular categories", "niche categories"]
definition: Popular vs. niche category is defined based on the number of posts associated with each programming language tag in the sampling period, so that communities differ in how many users subscribe to and contribute to them.

name: Content representation shuffling
authors_terms: ["shuffling content representation", "shuffle the representation of data", "shuffling of content representation"]
definition: Facilitating interactions based on dynamic, value-creating activities, so that platforms essentially 'shuffle' the representation of data rather than ordering content only by posting time.

name: Ethnic integration
authors_terms: ["ethnic integration", "integration across ethnic boundaries", "integration within organizations"]
definition: Integration describes the degree to which diverse actors are connected through collaborative ties that cross identity boundaries. Integrated organizations exhibit a network configuration where any skilled worker has an equal likelihood of interacting and collaborating with any other skilled individual in the organization, regardless of their ethnic or cultural background.

name: Ethnic diversity
definition: Diversity refers to the heterogeneity of individuals within the organization along dimensions such as ethnic and cultural background, reflecting the range of knowledge and perspectives available; it denotes the mere coexistence of different identities and capabilities, but does not, in and of itself, imply interaction or collaboration.

name: Economic value of innovation
authors_terms: ["economic value of innovation", "patent value", "patent monetary value", "value of innovation"]
definition: The value of innovation for a patent, deflated to 1982 dollars, constructed from the abnormal stock return around the patent's grant date, scaled by the patent's ex ante probability of grant and multiplied by the firm's market capitalization just prior to grant; summing these patent-level values yields the firm's total real economic value of patents.

name: Innovation complexity
definition: The complexity indicator is the Shannon entropy of the shares of a firm's patent subclasses across global technology domains; it equals 0 if all of a firm's subclasses lie in a single cluster and increases as the firm's subclasses spread more evenly across multiple technological domains.

name: PPP payment model
authors_terms: ["user-pay contracts", "user-pay payment mechanisms", "PPP payment systems", "government-pay contracts"]
definition: The contractual allocation of demand risk, most visible in the choice between two broad payment structures: in government-pay contracts the public authority compensates the private partner and bears most demand risk, while in user-pay contracts the private partner is paid directly by users and is the residual claimant on project revenues.

name: Legal specificity
authors_terms: ["legal specificity", "specificity of PPP laws", "degree of legal specificity", "number of provisions"]
definition: The extent to which PPP laws specify what actors need to do, in terms of procedures, timelines, formulas, and contingencies.

name: PPP-specific law
definition: Bespoke legislation explicitly designed to govern public–private partnership arrangements, intended to offer greater clarity and credibility than general procurement law.

name: Institutional constraints on government
authors_terms: ["institutional constraints on government", "political constraints on the government", "checks and balances", "POLCON"]
definition: The political environment, in particular institutional constraints on the executive branch of government, conditions how much specificity is needed to achieve credibility; where checks and balances are weak, governments enjoy greater leeway in transactions with private entities and the risk of governmental opportunism is heightened.

name: Social class background
authors_terms: ["social class background", "social class", "class background", "lower social class background", "higher-class background"]
definition: Social class background, defined as parents' relative socioeconomic standing as reflected by income, education, and occupational attainment. It is captured by parents' education, occupation, and income, which together constitute an individual's formative class experience.

name: CEO initial compensation
authors_terms: ["initial compensation", "initial CEO compensation", "initial pay", "starting compensation", "initial salary"]
definition: Initial compensation is a critical mechanism through which boards signal how they value a newly appointed CEO; boards often use initial compensation as a key strategic tool to entice talented CEOs and to reflect initial assessments of fit and anticipated performance.

name: CEO current compensation
definition: Pay-for-performance ties CEO pay directly to firm outcomes; whereas initial pay reflects CEOs' anticipated performance potential at their new firm, pay-for-performance sensitivity captures how boards perceive and respond to actual performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured using industry-adjusted total shareholder returns (TSR), a market-based performance measure commonly used in corporate governance studies measuring firm performance.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Dismissal represents the most severe form of board sanction and reflects a judgment that performance has fallen substantially short of expectation to warrant leadership change.

name: ESG ownership
authors_terms: ["ESG ownership", "ESG (signatory) institutional ownership", "institutional pressure from ESG investors"]
definition: The cumulative proportion of ownership by ESG investors, where ESG investors are defined as institutional investors that joined the UN PRI before the current holding year and are considered to represent institutional pressure for environmental performance.

name: Pollution outsourcing
authors_terms: ["pollution outsourcing", "Scope 3 upstream emission", "outsourcing pollution to suppliers"]
definition: Firms' transfer of institutionally incompatible polluting activities out of their organizational boundary by buying polluting inputs from suppliers rather than making them in-house; it is measured as Scope 3 upstream emissions, that is, GHG emissions caused by activities of the firm but stemming from the firm's suppliers.

name: Scope 1 direct emissions
definition: GHG emissions that are generated directly by the firm's production activities, that is, emissions directly controlled by the firm.

name: Scope 1 + 3 emissions
definition: The sum of Scope 1 direct emissions and Scope 3 upstream emissions, which the authors use to capture the total carbon footprint of the entire value chain and which provides, in their words, a cleaner estimation of pollution outsourcing.

name: Access to green technologies
definition: The extent to which a firm can gain access to environmental technologies through the coordination of its ESG investors, proxied by whether a firm's ESG ownership is green-technology-intensive; it captures the firm's capacity to develop cleaner production.

name: Investor purview of suppliers
authors_terms: ["investor purview of suppliers", "ESG investors' purview encompasses the firm's suppliers"]
definition: The number of suppliers that a firm's ESG investors invest in while also having ownership in the focal firm; the larger this number, the greater the expected purview of ESG investors in terms of the focal firm's supply chain network.

name: Self-perception of ability
authors_terms: ["perceived ability", "self-perception of ability", "self-perceived ability", "perception of ability to deal with challenges", "perceived ability to deal with challenges", "self-perceptions of ability"]
definition: Entrepreneurs' perceptions of their own ability to deal with challenges that may arise as they develop their business ideas. The authors describe it as a particular form of self-belief, an individual's belief in their ability to perform certain actions.

name: Strategic decision-making training approach
authors_terms: ["training on strategic decision-making", "entrepreneurship training program", "training conditions", "evidence-based approach", "theory-and-evidence-based approach"]
definition: Training that teaches entrepreneurs to improve their strategic decision-making through a deductive experimentation logic, delivered in one of two conditions: an evidence-based approach that emphasizes iterative experimentation and rapid hypothesis testing to refine the business model, or a theory-and-evidence-based approach in which entrepreneurs additionally develop a theory-of-value to articulate hypotheses, design tests, and interpret evidence.

name: Information access speed
authors_terms: ["information access speed", "speed of information access", "faster information access", "data velocity"]
definition: We focus on information access speed, defined as the time between when information becomes available and when decision-makers can observe and use it. Increasing information access speed need not alter the information set itself; rather, it reduces frictions in detecting the availability of existing information.

name: Information acquisition
authors_terms: ["information acquisition", "less, more targeted information acquisition", "information gathering", "less information acquired"]
definition: Faster information access can enable the identification of more relevant and targeted information, even when holding the informativeness of the information constant, allowing decision-makers to ultimately require less information overall. This shifts information acquisition toward fewer, more targeted tests before a final decision is reached.

name: Decision speed
definition: We argue that when faster information access improves the targeting of information acquisition, it can reduce decision time by enabling earlier resolution of uncertainty ... If faster access allows more informative signals to be observed earlier, it can resolve uncertainty sooner and accelerate the decision.

name: Decision quality
definition: In this section, we empirically investigate Hypothesis 3 on how the speed of information access affects decision quality, focusing on the outcomes related to quality of care and patient satisfaction.

name: Access to decision-relevant information
authors_terms: ["greater access to decision-relevant information among lower-level team members", "information access", "greater access to and standardized information in the new EHR"]
definition: EHRs increase decentralization by providing greater access to information and rendering information in a more standardized form, and by standardizing processes by embedding decision rules and routines into the system itself.

name: Decentralization
authors_terms: ["decentralization", "degree of decentralization present in the care team"]
definition: Decentralization refers to the formal or de facto distribution of decision-making authority down the hierarchy, away from central authority.

name: Team familiarity
authors_terms: ["team familiarity", "mutual understanding of members", "experience working together"]
definition: Mutual understanding among team members represents team members' mutual understanding of each other's backgrounds, preferences, and habits. It is commonly referred to as 'team familiarity' and reflected in the degree to which team members have worked with one another in the past.

name: Mutual understanding of task-related processes
authors_terms: ["mutual understanding of task-related processes", "task-related process knowledge", "common training"]
definition: Task-related process knowledge includes the general organizational practices and strategies through which to carry out the tasks. Such processes are not task-specific but rather hold across a variety of (albeit similar) tasks.

name: Mutual understanding of the problem-solving context
authors_terms: ["mutual understanding of the problem-solving context", "mutual understanding of the patient context", "contextual understanding"]
definition: A third type of mutual understanding reflects knowledge about the context in which coordinated problem-solving activities take place. In a hospital, the context is defined by the patient's condition, which specifies the immediate problem to be addressed, constrains the feasible set of actions, and shapes the urgency of choice.

name: Generative AI assistance
authors_terms: ["GAI assistance", "availability of GAI assistance", "GAI availability", "generative artificial intelligence", "ChatGPT introduction"]
definition: Individuals being assisted by artificial intelligence tools in the innovation process.

name: Original innovation
authors_terms: ["original (software) products", "original innovation", "new add-ons", "new product introductions", "rate of original software product introductions"]
definition: We refer to the development of completely new products (i.e., products that have not existed on the market before) as 'original innovation'.

name: Original innovation by new developers
authors_terms: ["new developers", "newly entering developers", "extensive margin", "new add-ons introduced by new developers"]
definition: An add-on is considered an add-on by a new developer if the focal developer has not introduced any add-ons before; the extensive margin is more new developers starting to develop original products.

name: Generational innovation
authors_terms: ["generational innovation", "improvements to existing products", "updates", "number of updates"]
definition: Improvements to existing products (e.g., software updates) that consist of refinements to previously introduced products.

name: Scope of knowledge domains
authors_terms: ["scope of knowledge domains", "broader set of knowledge domains", "category count", "efficient recombination"]
definition: The extent of knowledge that original products draw on, that is, the number of different domains whose knowledge elements are combined in a product.

name: Novelty
authors_terms: ["novelty", "original but not truly novel", "similarity to previous products"]
definition: The degree to which a product diverges from existing products; an innovator may launch a product that is original but not necessarily novel, as it may be very similar to other existing products on the market.

name: Anti-SLAPP laws
definition: Laws that prevent Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation, i.e., retaliatory lawsuits filed against critics who have spoken against the plaintiff in a public forum. They aim to protect public participation by deterring lawsuits intended to silence critics, thereby lowering the perceived legal risks and costs for activists and increasing the risk of activism firms face.

name: Institutional corporate social performance
definition: The tangible outcomes of firms' activities and initiatives in 'promoting social welfare outside firms' formal boundaries' (Acharya et al., 2022: 312). It reflects actual performance along dimensions of interest to activists, involving stakeholders such as local communities and society at large who do not engage in regular economic exchange with the firm.

name: Media coverage of corporate social irresponsibility
authors_terms: ["media coverage of CSI", "media coverage of corporate social irresponsibility", "CSI coverage in the media"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's irresponsible practices, such as human rights violations and environmental damage, are widely reported in the media; when a firm's irresponsible practices are widely reported in the media, it becomes harder for the firm to manage its public image and easier for activists to credibly frame it as morally culpable.

name: Results similarity
definition: Results similarity is how patents that belong to the same patent family or disputes between the same litigants are evaluated in different countries; it captures the degree of similarity in win rates across countries for parallel patent cases involving the same patent families or litigants.

name: Geographic concentration of patent litigation
authors_terms: ["litigation concentration", "geographic concentration", "geographic concentration of their patent litigation cases"]
definition: The extent to which the infringement lawsuits are concentrated within a handful of countries, as opposed to being dispersed among a large number of countries.

name: Number of patent infringement cases filed in a country
authors_terms: ["number of cases", "number of litigation cases the firm files in that country", "number of patent cases filed by a firm in individual countries"]
definition: The number of cases that each corporate family files in that country-year.

name: Firm-country assets
authors_terms: ["firm-country assets", "proportion of assets the firm has in a country"]
definition: A gauge of a country's relative importance within the firm's business operations: the focal firm's assets in the focal country divided by its total assets 1 year before the focal year.

name: Firm-country competitors
authors_terms: ["firm-country competitors", "number of competitors the firm encounters in a country"]
definition: The intensity of competition encountered by the focal firm in the focal country, measured by counting the number of Fortune Global 500 entities that operate in the firm's top five industries and have a presence in the same focal country.

name: Excess CEO returns
definition: The financial returns from the CEO's firm-related wealth and compensation that exceed the financial returns of shareholders. The authors argue that CEO returns in excess of shareholder returns are an appropriate measure of the agency costs inherent in financial alignment arrangements.

name: External board social capital
definition: Social capital that directors access through board interlocks; boards positioned at the center of the board interlock network offer beneficial external social capital, such as strategic opportunities, and expose directors to the normative pressures of the corporate elite.

name: Internal board social capital
definition: A type of social capital constituted by the degree of shared networking experience among independent directors on the same board; it may allow directors to more effectively monitor CEOs and their financial alignment with shareholders and exposes them to monitoring norms.

name: CEO power
definition: The capacity of powerful CEOs to bring about their preferred outcomes, which may alter the normative pressures to follow managerial preferences; a multidimensional construct measured with complementary power dimensions.

name: Institutional investor monitoring
definition: Powerful monitors affecting norm enforcement from outside the board; institutional investors have lobbied to restrain managerial autonomy and are concerned with the structure and level of CEO pay.

name: De alio entry
authors_terms: ["de alio entrants", "de alio producers", "de alio status", "lateral diversifier", "diversifying entrants"]
definition: Diversifying entrants coming from other industries; the authors refer to them by the Latin term de alio, a term meaning literally 'from another,' in contrast to new startup (de novo) entrants.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: The rate of mortality at the organizational level is defined as the probability of mortality in an infinitesimally small interval. Mortality events collapse across all ending events that resulted in the demise of a unique organization, including cessation of production, bankruptcy and acquisition by another firm.

name: Organizational age
definition: Years the firm has spent in automobile production; ecological models concern the relationship between organizational age and the probability of death.

name: Preproduction period
definition: For would-be de novo automobile producers who built a prototype, incorporated the concern, or listed themselves as a producer in an industry directory prior to production, the time elapsed between these activities and production is defined as the preproduction period.

name: Organizational population density
definition: Contemporaneous organizational population density indicates the total number of producer organizations in the population in a year.

name: Origin-industry transferable skills and knowledge
authors_terms: ["relevant specialized transferable skills and knowledge", "core competence", "skills and knowledge", "origin industry"]
definition: Strategic management theory emphasizes the skills and knowledge held by firms as a result of their successful operation in origin industries or populations, and assumes that these skills and knowledge are transferable and that different origin industries equip firms with systematically varying levels of potential advantage.

name: Business dissolution
definition: Business survival is the outcome measure of the study; the authors record exits when businesses shut down, and treat business dissolution as the appropriate measure for situations in which interfirm collaboration plays a central role in business strategy.

name: Partner dissolution
definition: One of the two situations in which dependence on a partner may cause problems: cases in which a partner shuts down its business, so that the collaborating business usually loses access to capabilities that were the purpose of the collaboration.

name: Partner new partnership formation
authors_terms: ["partner adds a new partner", "partner forms a collaborative agreement with a new partner", "partners form new partnerships"]
definition: The second situation in which dependence on a partner may cause problems: cases in which a partner forms a collaborative agreement with a new partner, whether of the same type or of a different type from the existing relationship.

name: Business new partnership formation
authors_terms: ["business adds partner", "form a new collaborative relationship", "businesses that formed new relationships"]
definition: Forming a new collaborative relationship after a partner has shut down or has added a new partner; the authors argue a business may be able to overcome the problems caused by the loss or deemphasis of a partner by forming a new partnership with another firm.

name: Partner divestiture
authors_terms: ["partner divestiture", "partner sold its hospital software systems business"]
definition: Partner divestiture is the sale of a business partner as an ongoing business to new ownership; it might disrupt collaborative links, but the new ownership will often preserve collaborative linkages.

name: Recent competitive experience
authors_terms: ["recent competitive experience", "mean duration of an organization's competitive relationships in recent times", "recent exposure to rival"]
definition: The mean duration of an organization's competitive relationships in recent times, measuring how much experience the organization has had per relationship recently.

name: Distant-past competitive experience
authors_terms: ["distant competitive experience", "experience in the more distant past", "distant-past experience"]
definition: The mean duration of an organization's competitive relationships in the more distant past, which is more likely to have taught now-outdated lessons.

name: Rivals' recent competitive experience
authors_terms: ["rivals' recent competitive experience", "mean duration of the competitive relationships experienced by an organization's rivals in recent times"]
definition: The mean duration of the competitive relationships experienced by an organization's rivals in recent times, which makes those rivals more potent competitors.

name: Rivals' distant-past competitive experience
authors_terms: ["rivals' distant competitive experience", "mean duration of the competitive relationships experienced by an organization's rivals in the distant past"]
definition: The mean duration of the competitive relationships experienced by an organization's rivals in the distant past; such rivals are more likely to have learned outdated lessons and so should be weaker competitors.

name: Variance in durations of competitive relationships
authors_terms: ["variance in the durations of an organization's competitive relationships", "variance in competitive experience"]
definition: The variance in durations of an organization's relationships, gauging whether an organization's relationships have been coincident or whether they have been spread among different cohorts of rivals.

name: Organizational viability
definition: The authors state the hypotheses in terms of effects on 'viability,' which they operationalize as organizational failure rates.

name: Fund family size
authors_terms: ["fund family size", "size of the fund family", "log-size", "size in assets"]
definition: One of the four interrelated factors of the growth system: the size of the fund family in assets. Fund family size is measured as the natural logarithm of the sum of the net assets in the family's funds.

name: Product-line breadth
definition: One of the four interrelated factors of the growth system: the number of funds in a fund family.

name: Expense subsidization
authors_terms: ["expense subsidization", "subsidization of fund expenses", "subsidized expenses", "strategic pricing"]
definition: Expense subsidization is a form of strategic pricing: by reducing its charges for services performed, the fund family lowers its short-term return in order to raise fund yields and thereby attract new shareholders. It is measured as the proportion of the fund family's net assets that are subsidized.

name: Product performance
authors_terms: ["product performance", "financial performance of the family's funds", "net yield", "fund performance"]
definition: Product performance is the investment performance of the fund (the 'gross yield') minus the expenses charged by the fund family to manage the fund, which here are reduced by subsidization. Money market fund yield measures return to the shareholder perfectly since money market funds do not have capital gains.

name: Search outcomes
authors_terms: ["coefficients in the dynamic growth system", "growth system coefficients", "time-varying coefficients", "outcomes of search"]
definition: The time-varying coefficients of the fund family's growth system equations, which in each time period represent the outcome of a search process oriented towards growth. If their values improve, in the sense that greater economies of scale and scope and a stronger link between product performance and size are achieved, the risk of failure should decrease.

name: Cumulative search
authors_terms: ["CUMSEARCH", "cumulative amount of search", "amount of search over time", "cumulative search"]
definition: The amount of search over time, measured as the cumulative sum of the search component of the forecast error, which reflects the cumulative contribution of search behavior to changes in the growth system coefficients, independent of error in the growth system.

name: Risk of failure
authors_terms: ["risk of failure", "hazard rate", "risk of exit", "mortality", "failure rate"]
definition: The hazard rate of exit from the money market fund industry, i.e. the risk that a fund family fails, estimated with a log-linear hazard model.

name: Related diversification
authors_terms: ["related diversification", "related diversifiers", "relatedness measured in the traditional (Rumelt) way", "RELATED"]
definition: Firms classified as Related or Dominant under Rumelt's (1974) diversification categories, as opposed to firms classified as Unrelated. The sample firms were classified according to Rumelt's diversification categories (Single-business, Dominant-business, Related-business and Unrelated-business).

name: Strategic relatedness
authors_terms: ["strategic relatedness", "'strategic' relatedness", "our structural indicators of relatedness"]
definition: 'Strategic relatedness' between two markets, in the sense that they value nontradeable, nonsubstitutable assets with similar production functions, is a requirement for diversification to yield super-normal profits in the long run. A measure of relatedness should consider not only whether the underlying SBU-level assets of a firm are related, but also whether these assets are a potential source of competitive advantage.

name: Profitability
definition: The profitability of the sample firms, measured as return on sales (ROS).

name: Leveraged buyout
definition: A transaction in which the change in capital structure was the primary goal rather than a secondary consequence of other events; the typical LBO pushed debt to total capital ratios to over 90 percent and generally took a public firm private.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Defined as company sponsored R&D plus contract R&D divided by company sales; R&D intensity has been shown to be a reliable archival measure of managers' commitment to innovation and a firm's long run growth.

name: Change in R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["LBO related change in R&D", "change in R&D intensity", "LBO induced change in R&D intensity"]
definition: The change in R&D intensity from the 3 years before the buyout to the 3 years after the buyout.

name: Firm size
definition: Size is measured as the natural log of company sales.

name: Diversification
definition: Our proxy for diversification is a dummy variable which equals one if the firm operates in five or more 4-digit SIC industries and zero otherwise.

name: Post-LBO divestiture
definition: Divestiture activity was measured by a dummy variable that equals one if the firm sells off 10 percent or more of its assets in the three post-LBO years and zero otherwise.

name: Management buyout
definition: If we found any evidence that the pre-LBO management took an equity stake in the buyout (i.e., the LBO was a management buyout [MBO]), we set the MBO dummy variable equal to one.

name: Hostile takeover threat
definition: If we found evidence of hostile threats in the 3 years before the buyout, the hostile takeover dummy variable was set equal to one.

name: Change in performance
definition: Performance is measured by the change in cash flow divided by sales, where cash flow is defined as operating income before depreciation.

name: Corporate restructuring
definition: Corporate restructuring is defined as a period of multiple divestitures for larger multiproduct firms where at least 10 percent of the asset base of such firms was divested.

name: Diversification strategy type
definition: Firms are placed into four corporate strategy types—dominant business, related-constrained business, related-linked business, and unrelated business—in the pre- and postrestructuring periods. Related-linked firms are a 'between' category with aspects of both related and unrelated diversification, which may create inconsistent control system problems.

name: Diversification scope
authors_terms: ["level of diversification", "total diversification", "diversified scope", "entropy measure of diversification"]
definition: Total level of diversification (DT) is formed by adding the two components of the entropy measure, related diversification (DR) and unrelated diversification (DU). Related diversification is defined as the diversification arising from operating in 4-digit segments within a 2-digit industry group, and unrelated diversification as the diversification arising from operating between 2-digit industry groups.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D spending", "risk taking as measured by R&D intensity"]
definition: R&D intensity, the dependent variable, was the firm's reported spending on R&D per $1000 of sales. Increased R&D spending may indicate more risk taking while increased levels of diversification may indicate less risk taking.

name: Equity share inequality
authors_terms: ["initial division of equity", "division of ownership", "ownership structure", "unequal division of ownership"]
definition: The initial division of equity share between partners at the start of the venture, indicated by three types of ownership structure. Unequal division of ownership gives the majority holder greater power to dictate terms, and this power manifests itself in renegotiation of joint venture contracts.

name: Foreign investment restrictiveness
authors_terms: ["foreign investment climate of the host country", "restrictive foreign investment policy", "host-country restrictions on inward foreign investment"]
definition: The foreign investment climate of the host country, represented by a dummy variable that classified the host country as either 'restrictive' or 'nonrestrictive,' depending on the country investment policies reported in two publications designed for U.S. investors. Governments pursuing indigenization policies monitor the activities of foreign ventures and erect bureaucratic hurdles that make it more difficult to alter terms once the investment is in place.

name: Prior renegotiation
authors_terms: ["incidence of prior renegotiation of the joint venture contract", "prior renegotiations"]
definition: The occurrence of previous renegotiations of a joint venture contract's ownership terms. Renegotiation of a joint venture contract, like many acts, is easier if it has been done before.

name: Joint venture instability
authors_terms: ["joint venture instability", "change in the ownership structure of the joint venture", "hazard rate", "renegotiation of joint venture contracts"]
definition: Joint venture instability is represented here as a change in the division of equity between joint venture partners, not necessarily as termination of the joint venture. The unit of analysis is the joint venture contract rather than the joint venture itself.

name: Formality of strategic planning
authors_terms: ["formality of planning", "formalized strategic planning", "formal planning", "planning formality", "formal planners", "non-formal planners"]
definition: Bank presidents were asked to categorize their planning efforts for the previous five years according to the degree to which sophisticated written documentation emanated from the planning effort. Written documentation is identified as a major dimension of the move toward formal planning in small firms.

name: Financial performance
definition: Bank performance measured on the four performance goals consistently identified by bank presidents: profit margin, return on assets, loan growth and return on equity. Banks were ranked within relative-size groups and the ranking converted into a percentile for each performance measure during each year.

name: Emphasis on strategic decision-making dimensions
authors_terms: ["degree of emphasis in bank's strategic decision-making process", "six dimensions of strategic decision-making", "six basic dimensions of strategic management"]
definition: The degree to which the bank's strategic decision-making incorporated six basic dimensions of strategic management commonly espoused in the literature, solicited regardless of the formality of the planning process.

name: Managerial motivation
authors_terms: ["managerial motivation", "motivation to manage", "bureaucratic managerial orientation", "managerial motivation as measured by the MSCS"]
definition: Bureaucratic orientation is conceptualized in terms of Miner's (1965, 1977, 1978a) role-motivation theory of managerial effectiveness within hierarchic systems. When the subscale scores are combined into a single index, it reflects the overall positive versus negative trend of the responses to the 35 scorable items, and thus provides a measure of the extent to which an individual is motivated to fulfil the role requirements specified in the theory of managerial effectiveness.

name: Type of entrepreneur
authors_terms: ["type of entrepreneur", "craftsman-opportunistic dimension", "opportunistic orientation", "craftsman entrepreneur", "opportunistic entrepreneur"]
definition: Different types of entrepreneurs could be isolated. One such type is the craftsman entrepreneur characterized by narrowness in education and training, low social awareness and involvement, a feeling of incompetence in dealing with the social environment, and a limited time orientation. In contrast, opportunistic entrepreneurs exhibited breadth in education and training, high social awareness and involvement, confidence in their ability to deal with the social environment, and an awareness of, and orientation to, the future.

name: Type of firm
authors_terms: ["type of firm", "rigid-adaptive dimension", "adaptive pattern in the firm", "rigid firm", "adaptive firm"]
definition: The more the individual fitted the craftsman model, the greater the likelihood that the firm itself would be rigid in nature; the greater the degree of fit with the opportunistic model, the more probable it was that the firm would be changing and adaptive. Interviews were used to classify the firms along the rigid-adaptive dimension in accordance with the working definitions.

name: Entrepreneur status
definition: The entrepreneurial sample consisted of 38 individuals who had founded, and still were associated with, business enterprises located in the state of Oregon. Comparisons were made with managerial samples from large business firms constituted from the second author's files.

name: Employee strategic salience
authors_terms: ["employee strategic salience", "strategic salience of employees", "strategic salience"]
definition: The extent to which employees are portrayed as central to a firm's purpose, strategy, and value creation in shareholder-directed narratives.

name: Human capital-intensive industries
authors_terms: ["human capital-intensive industries", "labor-capital share ratio", "labor composition", "R&D intensity"]
definition: Industries in which employees often possess specialized skills, possess tacit knowledge, and engage in adaptable organizational routines, making them especially valuable in sustaining the firm's competitive advantage.

name: Labor market tightness
definition: The scarcity of skilled workers facing firms, which increases the strategic value of human capital as firms face greater challenges in attracting and retaining talent.

name: Executive short-termism
definition: A short-termist propensity among executives at the helm of firms in capital markets to meet quarterly earnings targets.

name: Product market uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty in the firm's product market, which the product-market-fluidity variable captures as the competitive threat for a particular firm and the risk of changes in its product market.

name: Reputation
definition: The verbal definition of 'reputation' is the 'public's perception of the decision maker's ability.' In the model, each agent's perceived likelihood of being 'smart' is publicly observable, namely, reputation.

name: Herding
definition: In this study, herding is defined as a decision maker 'doing what everyone else is doing, even when their private information suggests otherwise.'

name: Signal correlation
definition: The partial correlation between two smart agents' signals is ρ (termed as 'signal correlation') where 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1; it is the correlation among true experts' private signals, and a unique feature of the reputational herding mechanism.

name: Industry knowledge breadth
definition: A dimension of managerial knowledge breadth reflecting career experience across multiple industries, that is, the number of industry knowledge domains a manager's career has spanned. Industry experiences reflect knowledge of industry-specific attributes critical for value creation, such as technologies, growth trajectories, and norms.

name: Firm knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["firm knowledge breadth", "multifirm experience", "experience across different firms"]
definition: A dimension of managerial knowledge breadth reflecting career experience across multiple firms, where firms are viewed as distinct knowledge domains within a broader industry-level knowledge domain. As managers move across firms they gain knowledge about each firm and build cognitive structures that encompass links between these domains.

name: Functional knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["functional knowledge breadth", "experience across multiple functions", "cross-functional knowledge"]
definition: A dimension of managerial knowledge breadth reflecting career experience across multiple functions (e.g., finance, sales, R&D), accumulating knowledge and skills in each functional domain and understanding their operational connections.

name: Strategic foresight
definition: Strategic foresight is the ability of managers to predict how their actions will create a competitive advantage. The authors capture managers' ability to predict long-term investor response to firms' strategic initiatives.

name: Preannouncement stock purchases
authors_terms: ["Stock Trading", "stock purchases", "managers' trading activity in their firms' stock", "insider trading"]
definition: Managers' purchases of their firms' stock ahead of the firms' new product introduction announcements. Such trading is strictly regulated but reflects managers' foresight about the firm's prospects; purchases involve a commitment of personal capital and ensue based on the conviction that the firm's prospects are strong.

name: Financial market volatility
definition: Environmental uncertainty in financial markets, expressed largely through higher volatility of asset prices; when asset prices are volatile, investors face greater uncertainty about the future direction of these prices and how the market will react to company announcements.

name: Residential proximity
definition: The distance between employees' homes, that is, proximity in a nonwork setting. The authors argue it operates primarily through social mechanisms that lower search costs and the social component of execution costs.

name: Inventor collaboration
definition: Whether a pair of inventors listed on a given patent application form a collaboration, measured through coinventorship on the patent application.

name: Divisional affiliation
definition: Whether a pair of inventors belongs to the same product division. The companies organize research scientists and engineers within product divisions that correspond to musculoskeletal treatment areas (e.g., knees, hips).

name: Gender homophily
definition: Whether the two inventors in a pair are of the same gender. Because informal interactions outside of work often follow homophily, the authors expect residential proximity to matter more for same-gender pairs.

name: Internal knowledge reuse
definition: The extent to which a patent draws on the firm's existing intellectual property and is maintained over time. The authors interpret closer inventors tapping in-house knowledge as reuse rather than radical recombination.

name: Invention novelty and breadth
definition: How novel and broad-reaching a patent's knowledge recombination is, indicated by the originality and generality metrics.

name: Time constraints
definition: Time constraints are externally imposed conditions that can be layered onto strategic decision-making to varying degrees; they can amplify the cognitive strain associated with strategic decision-making because decision-makers must deal with complexity and uncertainty in a shorter timeframe.

name: LLM use
definition: Decision-makers' use of a large language model, conceptualized as an artifact capable of providing interactive external representations rather than merely predictions.

name: Breadth of mental representations
definition: Breadth captures categorical diversity of a mental representation (e.g., value to customer, industry structure).

name: Depth of mental representations
definition: Depth reflects the within-category detail (e.g., large domestic market, large international market).

name: Consensus of mental representations
definition: Consensus captures the similarity to the crowd's representation; a high level of consensus indicates a high alignment with the wisdom of the crowd or close agreement with a typical member of the audience that is decisive for success (e.g., investors).

name: Strategic foresight accuracy
authors_terms: ["strategic foresight", "strategic foresight accuracy", "accuracy of strategic foresight"]
definition: Strategic foresight is the ability to predict strategic outcomes, which depends on how effectively decision-makers utilize environmental cues to update their mental representations.

name: Predicted market reactions
authors_terms: ["predicted market reactions", "Predicted CAR", "predictions of market reactions"]
definition: Predictions of the stock market reaction to an acquisition announcement formed by extrapolating from historical transaction outcomes and their incoming cues. The authors generate them with machine learning models that serve as empirical analogues for managerial representations or mental models.

name: Market reactions to acquisition announcements
definition: The stock market reaction to an acquisition announcement, measured as the cumulative abnormal return to the acquirer's stock surrounding the announcement date.

name: Prediction error
definition: The distance between the observed outcome and the predicted value, i.e., the absolute difference between the actual CAR and the Predicted CAR for a transaction, representing the level of surprise and encompassing both positive and negative deviations.

name: Deal completion time
definition: The length of the deal closure phase of an acquisition, that is, the period between the public announcement of an intended transaction and the formal completion date when the deal becomes legally effective.

name: Ex ante deal selection
definition: The ex ante choice of which targets and transactions managers pursue, informed by predictions of market reactions; managers may pursue targets expected to elicit positive market reactions and avoid those likely to generate negative ones.

name: M&A deal termination
authors_terms: ["terminated acquisition", "deal termination", "termination of an announced acquisition", "Post-Termination"]
definition: The termination of an announced acquisition; the paper studies announced M&A deals that ultimately do not close.

name: Target-related divestitures
authors_terms: ["target-related business divestitures", "divesting units in industries/sectors related to the intended target firm", "divesting related units"]
definition: Whether the focal firm undertakes divestitures in a given year in industries/sectors related to the intended target firm. Relatedness is measured by the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code.

name: Resource complementarity
authors_terms: ["Resource Complementarity Motive", "target's resources are more complementary to the bidder's existing resources"]
definition: The degree of complementarity between the firm's existing assets and the target's resources.

name: Target rejection
authors_terms: ["Target Rejection", "deal termination was caused by target rejection"]
definition: Deal termination caused by target-related resistance, including target management or board rejection, target shareholder rejection, disagreement on transaction price, or inability to agree on management terms.

name: Opportunity cost of complementary resources
definition: The opportunity cost of the resources tied up in the focal business; high opportunity costs mean the firm's existing complementary assets cannot be easily or profitably redeployed elsewhere in the organization.

name: Distance to acquisition target
authors_terms: ["Distance to Acquisition Target", "distance from the bidder's core operations", "distance from the bidder's primary business"]
definition: The distance between the previous target business and the acquirer firm's primary business.

name: Demand surge
authors_terms: ["demand surge", "end-customer demand surge", "increase in the number of potential buyers", "positive demand shock"]
definition: We view a demand surge as an increase in the number of potential buyers of a good. In periods marked by unexpected surges in consumer demand, those possessing scarce resources are positioned to profit.

name: Wholesale price
definition: The wholesale value, that is, the price at which the dealership could sell a particular vehicle in the national wholesale market.

name: Retail price
definition: The retail price (selling price) at which the vehicle is sold to the buyer.

name: Intermediary margin
authors_terms: ["intermediary margin", "dealer margin", "dealer profit margin", "dealer percentage margin"]
definition: The intermediary margin is the profit realized by the intermediary scaled by the retail price.

name: Dealer dollar profit
authors_terms: ["dealer dollar profits", "per vehicle gross profit", "dealer profits"]
definition: The difference between the retail and wholesale value gives rise to the per vehicle gross profit.

name: Intermediary dispensability
definition: If lambda = 0, the intermediary is said to be indispensable, because there can be no direct trade between the buyer and the seller. For lambda in (0,1), the intermediary is dispensable.

name: Market thickness
definition: We define 'thick' markets as those in which a large volume of the good is potentially for sale; in 'thin' markets, by contrast, the aggregate market size is small.

name: Resource reallocation across business lines
definition: Suppose an intermediary allocates a fixed amount of capital across two business lines; every deviation of this period's dollar allocation to a business line relative to last period's allocation creates a reallocation cost.

name: Vehicle age
definition: The age of the vehicle at the time of sale; young used cars are those of age less than or equal to three years, and old cars are those above three years.

name: Dealer-make match
authors_terms: ["Dealer-Make Match", "same-make dealers", "dealers selling their own makes"]
definition: A variable equal to one if the dealer is selling a used vehicle of its own make and zero otherwise.

name: New Japanese car supply
authors_terms: ["reduction in the supply of new Japanese cars", "reduced availability of new Japanese cars", "missing new cars", "new Japanese cars were very hard to find"]
definition: The March 2011 tsunami caused a dramatic short-term reduction in the supply of new Japanese cars, so that new Japanese cars were very hard to find.

name: Post-acquisition period
definition: This time variable indicates whether the observation is in a year after the acquisition event. It is coded one if the year is sometime after the acquisition year and zero if it is in the acquisition year or any year prior.

name: Inventor innovation performance
authors_terms: ["innovation performance", "meaningful innovation performance", "# Citations", "inventor forward citations", "inventor productivity"]
definition: To measure the meaningful innovation performance of inventors, the authors focus on the quality (i.e., impact) of inventions by observing forward citations, the three-year forward citation count for an inventor's patents generated in year t.

name: Inventor knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["Inventor Knowledge Breadth", "generalist", "breadth of knowledge", "knowledge diversification", "knowledge specialization"]
definition: This variable represents the extent to which an individual inventor is a generalist; it is considered the inverse of knowledge specialization. Inventor knowledge breadth is one minus the inventor specialization value, that is, a fraction that lies between zero and one, where one indicates a fully knowledge-diversified inventor with the most breadth and zero indicates a fully knowledge-specialized inventor.

name: Inventor knowledge distance
authors_terms: ["Inventor Knowledge Distance", "technological distance", "knowledge distance", "High Inventor Knowledge Distance"]
definition: This variable is the (preacquisition) distance between the acquirer inventor's knowledge and the knowledge brought in by the acquired firm; it is measured at the dyad level prior to the acquisition and varies each year. The degree of distance (or dissimilarity) in patents held between the acquirer inventor and target firm is measured at the inventor-target dyad level for each year before and after the acquisition.

name: Continuation of patenting
definition: This is a dummy based on whether the acquiring firm inventor who patented for the firm prior to the acquisition continued to patent for the firm after the acquisition or not.

name: Firm patenting in new technology classes
authors_terms: ["Proportion of New Classes", "patenting in new classes", "new classes"]
definition: This is calculated as the proportion of patents in classes where the acquiring firm did not patent prior to the acquisition but did so after the acquisition.

name: Demand shock
authors_terms: ["demand shock", "weather-driven demand shock", "predicted demand", "demand spurred by the weather event"]
definition: The estimated demand for electric vehicles following extreme weather events; demand is the predicted sales for BEVs, PHEVs, and HEVs in a country based on the effect of extreme weather events, and the authors refer to this predicted demand as the 'demand shock.'

name: Adoption of radical technology
authors_terms: ["users' adoption of the radical version of the technology", "BEV demand", "BEV sales"]
definition: Users' adoption of the radical version of an emergent technology, which in this setting is the fully electric vehicle (BEV) that requires not just new components but also an architectural innovation relative to the dominant internal combustion vehicle technology.

name: Adoption of hybrid technology
authors_terms: ["users' adoption of the hybrid version of the technology", "demand for hybrid products", "PHEV demand", "HEV demand"]
definition: Users' adoption of the hybrid versions of the emergent technology - plug-in (PHEV) and non-plugin (HEV) hybrids that combine features of the old and new technology and serve as gateway technologies with lower switching costs.

name: Hub firm entry
authors_terms: ["hub firms' entry", "firm entry into a country's electric vehicles market", "market entry"]
definition: Entry by a hub automotive firm into a country's electric vehicle technology market in a particular year; hub firms play a crucial role in providing the core technology and in orchestrating the emergent technology's ecosystem.

name: Availability of complement providers
authors_terms: ["complementor bottlenecks", "complement providers", "complementors", "charging stations", "potential complementor firms", "complementary (EV related) startups"]
definition: Presence of upstream and downstream complement providers in a country market, such as component partmakers, specialized repair shops, public charging stations, and EV-related startups; scarcity of such complements presents an ecosystem bottleneck for value creation and value capture.

name: Product market overlap
authors_terms: ["product market overlap", "product market distance", "overlap between firm's global portfolio and country product market characteristics"]
definition: Overlap between the electric vehicle model segments (and subsegments) that a firm has experience producing and the segments and subsegments commercially available in a country; the lower the overlap, the larger the product market bottleneck a firm experiences with commercializing products.

name: Time since entry
definition: The key independent variable for estimating the change in firms' postentry product portfolios and investments in complements is time since entry in a country's EV market, counted from the year of entry.

name: Post-entry portfolio shift toward radical technology
authors_terms: ["shift of hub firms' product portfolios toward the more radical version of the emergent technology", "proportion of hybrids in firm's local electrics portfolio", "firms' investments in radical products"]
definition: The postentry evolution of a firm's local electric vehicle product portfolio toward the more radical version of the technology, away from hybrid products; hybrid products could serve as initial gateways but portfolios will likely evolve toward the radical version.

name: Investments in complements
authors_terms: ["investments in complements", "complementor firm acquisitions", "acquisitions of complementor businesses"]
definition: Postentry investments by a firm in complements for the emergent technology in a country market; firms may vertically integrate by investing in complements subsequent to market entry, thereby building reliable value chains for the emergent technology.

name: Local commitments in the legacy technology
authors_terms: ["firms' local commitments in the legacy technology", "legacy market position", "local operating revenue in fossil fuel autos", "local human capital in the legacy technology"]
definition: A firm's local commitments in the legacy fossil-fuel vehicle technology in a country market, in the form of market position and human capital, which can present strategic bottlenecks such as cannibalization concerns and adjustment costs.

name: Crisis response
authors_terms: ["airline responses", "crisis response", "responses to the crisis", "responded more strongly"]
definition: The strength of an airline's response to the COVID-19 crisis through adjusting its fleet, measured by the number of aircraft stored, retired (scrapped), or sold. Storage, retirement, and sales have different implications for immediate costs and future capacity.

name: State policy stringency
definition: A factor calculated based on the strictness of state lockdown policies that restrict people's mobility, updated monthly. It is the most important variable indicating the extent of the crisis.

name: 9/11 crisis experience
definition: An indicator of whether the airline was a U.S. airline in operation on September 11, 2001, capturing prior exposure to a demand-loss crisis that was concentrated in the United States.

name: Financial crisis experience
definition: An indicator of whether the airline was headquartered in a high-GDP-per-capita nation and in operation on January 1, 2008, capturing prior exposure to the 2007/2008 demand-loss crisis.

name: Peer crisis response
authors_terms: ["crisis response by other airlines", "imitation", "mimetic learning", "actions of other airlines in the region"]
definition: The sum of aircraft subject to the same action in the same region in the previous month, capturing the actions of peer airlines that a focal airline may imitate.

name: Regional crisis severity
authors_terms: ["stringency in the region", "crisis observation by the focal airline", "regional stringency"]
definition: The average stringency in nations in the same region in the previous month, capturing the severity of the crisis observed nearby.

name: Wedge between control and cash-flow rights
authors_terms: ["wedge between control rights and cash-flow rights", "wedge between a parent's control and cash-flow rights", "difference between control and cash-flow rights", "excess control rights", "control premium"]
definition: The wedge is the difference between control and cash-flow rights of a subsidiary's parent in the subsidiary. Control (or voting) rights are the legal entitlements granted to exert influence on the subsidiary's decisions, and cash-flow rights are the percentage of the subsidiary's return that can be attained by the parent.

name: Relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "extent of relatedness of the subsidiary to the firm"]
definition: Relatedness relies on inferring interdependence and synergy potential from resource flows; the relatedness of any two subsidiaries increases with the degree of overlap in the mix of their inputs, weighted by the importance of each market to the firm. Thus, the relatedness of a subsidiary to its firm is a function of the input similarity between its business and other businesses in which the firm operates as well as how prominent each of these businesses is for the firm.

name: Multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact", "extent of a firm's multimarket contact with rivals in the industry in which the subsidiary operates"]
definition: Multimarket contact is the percentage of sales from markets (i.e., industries) in which the firm faces multimarket rivals. The measure takes the value of zero for subsidiaries facing no multimarket rivals and is greater if a firm has significant sales in markets in which many incumbent firms are also in the focal market.

name: Homing strategy
definition: The decision to produce a complementary product for a single platform or for multiple platforms (multihoming). Following the shock, three alternative strategic choices for game developers became viable: single homing, sequential multihoming, and simultaneous multihoming.

name: Breadth of console experience
authors_terms: ["Breadth of Unique Consoles", "breadth of experience in programming for various specific platforms", "experience in developing games for a broader variety of consoles"]
definition: Experience in developing different games for different consoles enables developers to learn about the distinctive features and requirements of each console, leading to fungible capabilities that can be applied toward developing the same games for multiple platforms.

name: PC game development specialization
authors_terms: ["PC Specialization", "specialization in developing videogames for PCs"]
definition: Producing games for a PC involves developing capabilities in computer languages such as C or C++ (high-level languages); because these languages are console-/platform-agnostic, they facilitate porting to multiple consoles, so developers with experience in PC games enjoyed broader, more fungible capabilities.

name: Console-specific programming specialization
authors_terms: ["Console-Specific Programming Specialization", "console-specific programming", "console-specific assembly language programming"]
definition: Developers without PC programming experience typically specialized in particular console architectures using assembly language that was specific to the CPU/architecture of a given console ('coding to the metal'), which led to narrower but deeper programming capabilities.

name: Licensed game title
definition: Games based on a movie or franchise license (e.g., Harry Potter or the NFL). Such games exploit film tie-ins, cartoon or comic characters, or sports leagues and incur high fixed costs from license fees.

name: Cult genre specialization
definition: Specialization in games based on stories, puzzles, music, or party games, which often enjoyed a highly devoted, cult-like following and did not necessarily feature or require the highest level of graphic fidelity or processing speed.

name: Franchise system acquisition
definition: New owners of franchise systems, because they were not party to the original franchise agreements signed by franchisees, may be less constrained by the same set of franchisee expectations (entitlement constraints) compared with current system owners.

name: Royalty fee increase
authors_terms: ["Royalty Fee Increase", "increase in royalty fees", "raise royalty fees"]
definition: Our dependent variable is Royalty Fee Increase, a binary variable that equals one if the annual royalty fee increased from one year to the next and zero if it decreased or remained unchanged.

name: Multiunit franchising emphasis
definition: Although most franchise systems employ multiunit franchising, some rely on it more heavily than others. One measure of a franchise system's emphasis on multiunit franchising is whether it offers so-called 'area development agreements'; the variable is thus a proxy for a franchise system's strategic intent regarding multiunit franchising.

name: Fraction of recently added franchise units
authors_terms: ["Newness Rate", "recently added units", "fraction of younger units"]
definition: The greater the fraction of younger units in a franchise system overall, the less likely that franchisees will retaliate against fee increases, so entitlement constraints will be less binding in franchise systems with a greater fraction of recently added units.

name: Inventor CEO status
authors_terms: ["inventor CEO", "CEO inventor status", "inventor CEO status", "CEO's inventor background"]
definition: Inventor CEOs have experiences in successfully developing at least one patent; management research often defines inventors as individuals who have developed at least one such patent.

name: Strategic change
definition: Strategic change involves a firm altering its competing domains or manners of competition within existing domains, and often entails significant adjustments in how resources are distributed across key areas.

name: CEO liberalism
definition: Liberals emphasize progress, openness to change, and diversity of thought, in contrast with conservatives, who value stability, the status quo, and cognitive closure; political ideologies reflect fundamental beliefs and values that are intrinsic to CEOs.

name: CEO career variety
definition: CEO career variety is defined as an 'array of distinct professional and institutional experiences an executive has had prior to becoming CEO'; it captures the work experiences of a CEO in various industries, firms, and functional areas.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Industry dynamism refers to 'the magnitude of change in a firm's industry and market conditions'; a dynamic industry is characterized by instability, turbulence, and low predictability.

name: Protestant imprinting
authors_terms: ["Protestant imprinting", "Protestant influence when a state was admitted to the Union", "Protestant imprinting process", "Protestant imprint"]
definition: The religious preferences of a state's founding residents, which were left as institutional imprints at the time the state was admitted to the Union and have endured. I specifically focus on the difference between Protestants versus other major religious groups, with a defining feature of Protestantism being a strong focus on equality.

name: Female representation in firm leadership
authors_terms: ["female representation in firm leadership", "female representation in corporate leadership", "number of female executives", "number of women senior leaders", "female representation in the leadership teams"]
definition: The presence of women in the senior leadership of firms; the authors measure it with the number of women senior leaders and note that women are still relatively underrepresented in C-suite positions.

name: Constitutional focus on equality
authors_terms: ["constitutional focus on equality", "state institutions", "state constitutions' emphasis on equality issues", "equality focus of state constitutions"]
definition: The state-level institutional emphasis on equality, measured by the difference between the number of words in a state constitution addressing suffrage, initiative, and representation (categories 1-3) and those addressing state powers and executive authority (categories 4-5), divided by the total number of words.

name: Historical Catholic immigration
definition: The average number of immigrants from countries with predominantly Catholic populations (e.g., France, Ireland, Italy, Poland, and Spain) settling in a state, which the authors argue acted as a counter-imprinting force against the Protestant imprint.

name: Opponent ability
authors_terms: ["higher-ability opponents", "higher-ability (as compared with lower-ability) opponents", "ability differences", "competing against higher-ability opponents"]
definition: The ability level of the opponents a contestant faces in a contest; contestants near the division threshold face opponents of similar ability in the lower division but opponents of significantly higher ability in the upper division.

name: Contestant performance
definition: The expected performance of contestants in crowdsourcing contests, measured by the point score earned from submitted solutions in the contest.

name: Motivational orientation
authors_terms: ["achievement-based motives", "economic-based motives", "motives to participate in crowdsourcing contests"]
definition: The distinction between economic-based motives, which are primarily extrinsic and linked to financial gains and career advancement, and achievement-based motives, which are driven by the desire to test skills, gain recognition in the community, or pursue intellectual or creative fulfillment.

name: Gender
