definition: The gender of the contestant; the authors contrast female and male coders.

name: Contest experience
authors_terms: ["contest experience", "experience in competing in crowdsourcing", "repeated participation"]
definition: Contest experience, defined as repeated participation in crowdsourcing contests, measured by the number of prior competitions.

name: Top performance
definition: Achieving a score placing the contestant in the top 5% of all participants in the specific SRM.

name: Coder ability rating
definition: Topcoder's ability rating, which determines the division assignment; contestants with an ability rating below the threshold compete in the lower division, whereas contestants with an ability rating above the threshold compete in the upper division.

name: Firm-specific industry effects
definition: We define FSIE as the extent to which a firm's business performance is shaped by industry-level factors rather than idiosyncratic firm-level factors. This construct captures the relevance of industry investment opportunities for the firm's capital allocation decisions, helping us predict which firms are more likely to strategically conform to (or deviate from) an industry-comparing logic.

name: Conformity to an industry-comparing logic of capital allocation
authors_terms: ["Conformity", "Conformity to an industry-comparing logic of capital allocation", "AVA", "Relative Value Added by Allocation (AVA)"]
definition: Conformity measures the extent to which a firm's capital allocation across its business units aligns with an industry-based benchmark.

name: Acquired worker status
definition: Individuals who join the acquiring firm as part of a startup acquisition, purchased along with the other assets of the target firm, as opposed to workers who are organically hired from the external labor market.

name: Turnover
definition: The worker-level outcome of leaving the acquiring firm; the main measure counts departures in which the worker is no longer employed at the acquiring firm and is employed at another firm for higher wages.

name: Prior job tenure
authors_terms: ["prior job tenure", "prior tenure", "length of prior tenure"]
definition: The number of quarters the individual was employed by her prior employer before joining the acquirer, which is the target firm for acquired workers and the previous employer for regular hires.

name: Founder retention
authors_terms: ["Founders Retained", "preservation of the founding team", "founder retention"]
definition: A binary indicator equaling one if all the founders remain employed with the acquirer in the year prior to the focal year.

name: Structural separation of the target firm
definition: A dummy variable equaling one if the acquired establishment remains as a stand-alone entity in its preacquisition location three years after the acquisition, and zero (integration) if it is moved to, or absorbed by, the acquirer's headquarters establishment.

name: Founders' human capital
authors_terms: ["founders' human capital", "human capital", "human capital of founders"]
definition: The quality of the venture's founders in terms of their experience, expertise, education and commitment, about which firms have a strong knowledge or informational advantage over investors in traditional IPOs and in the SPAC sector.

name: Uncertainty language about founders' human capital
authors_terms: ["uncertain language - S1 human capital", "uncertainty expressed in relation to the founders and their human capital"]
definition: The amount of uncertainty expressed in the section of the firm's S-1 prospectus that discusses the SPAC founders and their human capital (the management team section).

name: Uncertainty language about the acquisition target
authors_terms: ["uncertain language - S1 acquisition of a target", "uncertainty expressed in the proposed business section"]
definition: The amount of uncertainty expressed in the section of the firm's S-1 prospectus about performance factors that relate to the acquisition of a target (the proposed business section).

name: Uncertainty language about the SPAC vehicle
authors_terms: ["uncertain language - S1 SPAC vehicle", "uncertainty expressed in the risk factors section", "uncertainty about the investment in the SPAC vehicle"]
definition: The amount of uncertainty expressed in the section of the firm's S-1 prospectus about the risks associated with SPACs as a vehicle (the risk factors section).

name: IPO completion
authors_terms: ["IPO completion", "securing financing through an IPO", "successfully completing an IPO"]
definition: Our dependent variable is IPO completion, which we coded one when a SPAC's attempt to go public resulted in a successful IPO completion, and zero when the attempt failed.

name: Shareholder litigation threat
authors_terms: ["threat of shareholder litigation", "threat of being sued", "industry peer litigation", "litigation threat"]
definition: The threat of shareholder litigation that arises from lawsuits levied against industry peers, operationalized as the frequency of securities class action lawsuits filed against a firm's industry peers. Managers are believed to observe their industry peers when assessing their own risk of being sued.

name: Investment horizon
authors_terms: ["corporate investment horizons", "investment horizon", "asset durability", "horizons of firms' new capital investments"]
definition: The investments firms make in different initiatives have varying horizons; by definition all investments incur immediate costs to produce benefits later, but they differ in how quickly those benefits are realized. Firms can forgo profits today to invest in strategies that build future competitive advantages or maximize short-term profits by investing in incremental projects that produce smaller but faster returns.

name: Investor horizon
definition: The total length of time that a shareholder is expected to hold a security. Investors who hold stocks for relatively short (long) periods of time and thus churn their portfolios quickly (slowly) are seen as having short (long) investment horizons.

name: CEO future focus
authors_terms: ["CEO future focus", "CEOs' temporal focus", "future-focused CEOs", "future temporal focus"]
definition: Temporal focus is a subdimension of temporal orientation that refers to the allocation of attention to the past, present, and future, which is widely considered a stable tendency among individuals. Individuals with a strong future focus tend to make decisions that steadfastly align with long-term priorities.

name: Competition from a traditional knowledge platform
authors_terms: ["competition from Google Maps", "Post Google Entry", "competitive entry", "platform competition"]
definition: The indicator variable Post Google Entry equals one for each quarter after Google Maps has formally entered a given country and zero otherwise and captures whether the OpenStreetMap community in a given country is in competition with Google Maps.

name: Contributions from pre-entry contributors
authors_terms: ["pre-entry contributors", "contributions from pre-entry contributors", "individual contributions from pre-entry contributors"]
definition: Individual-level contributions from those who became active before the entry of a competitor.

name: Contributions from newly recruited contributors
authors_terms: ["newly recruited contributors", "contributions from newly recruited contributors"]
definition: Group-level contributions from the cohort of first-time contributors to the platform in a given time period.

name: Ideology-based attachment
definition: By ideology, we refer to a strong belief in the core tenets of open source, that everyone has the opportunity to contribute knowledge to the platform and that the resulting knowledge is made freely available.

name: Social-interaction-based attachment
definition: Contributors often form strong bonds with other contributors and these bonds positively affect their motivation to contribute; contributors in countries where mechanisms for social interaction are present will develop significant attachment based on social interaction in comparison with their counterparts in countries where these do not exist.

name: Standing-based attachment
definition: Contributors are motivated by and derive benefits from having a high standing in the community; contributors of high standing may enjoy high status in the community so that other members may defer to them and they may leverage their standing in an open source community into career opportunities.

name: CEO risk propensity
definition: 'risk propensity is defined as an individual's current tendency to take or avoid risks. It is conceptualized as an individual trait that can change over time and thus is an emergent property of the decision maker.' It is a behavioral inclination, more malleable than dispositional traits but more stable than transient states.

name: Exploration tendency
authors_terms: ["firm's tendency to explore in product development", "tendency to explore versus exploit", "exploration tendency"]
definition: Exploration involves relying on new knowledge, whereas exploitation entails refining and leveraging existing knowledge; the two are conceptualized as contradictory activities resting at two ends of a continuum, with firms engaging in both to different extents. Exploration and exploitation are studied here by means of product development via the firm's internal organization.

name: CEO tenure
definition: A CEO's tenure defines the amount of time the individual has spent in the firm's CEO position since being appointed as the CEO.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality indicates whether the CEO holds the position of chairperson of the board of directors.

name: CEO origin
definition: Prior research distinguishes inside CEOs who were appointed from within the firm from outside CEOs who were hired after spending their recent career in other firms.

name: Exploration experience
authors_terms: ["firm's exploration experience", "experience with exploration", "accumulated exploration experience"]
definition: The firm's accumulated experience with exploration in product development; a firm that has previously focused on exploration features routines that support subsequent exploration, and such experience is likely to be self-reinforcing. It can be considered a primary constraint on the firm's capacity to explore.

name: Competitive pressure
definition: Competitive pressure corresponds to the number of competitors that the firm encounters in its product markets; it imposes competitive threats to the firm's position in these markets and makes competitive interactions more visible and consequential.

name: Production focus
authors_terms: ["Production Studio Focus", "production studio focus", "studio focus", "focus in film production", "level of focus/diversification in distribution"]
definition: Producer (distributor) focus estimates are used as independent variables in the movie-level model in a decade-specific measure that captures the average of these similarity coefficients over all pairs of movies in the studio portfolio leading to the release of the focal movie (to allow for temporal variation in focus).

name: Distribution focus
definition: Producer (distributor) focus estimates are used as independent variables in the movie-level model in a decade-specific measure that captures the average of these similarity coefficients over all pairs of movies in the studio portfolio leading to the release of the focal movie (to allow for temporal variation in focus).

name: Movie profitability
definition: We use return on investment (ROI) as our dependent variable. ROI is calculated as the ratio of domestic box office revenues minus production costs divided by production costs.

name: Strategic focus
definition: A firm's focused strategy as opposed to diversification; operationalized in the film industry by production studio focus and distributor focus.

name: Multipoint contact in product markets
authors_terms: ["multipoint contact in product markets", "degree of multipoint contact (MPC) in product markets", "multipoint contact"]
definition: By multipoint contact in product markets, we refer to the situation in which a firm and a rival meet each other in more than one product market.

name: Expansion into rival's technological areas
authors_terms: ["technological expansion", "degree of firm i's expansion into rival j's technological areas", "expansion into the rival's technological areas"]
definition: We use the term 'technological expansion' to describe the entry of a firm into areas of technological development that it had not previously pursued; by technological areas, we refer to the specific areas of technological research and development in which a firm is already involved.

name: Relative market share
authors_terms: ["relative market share", "firm's market share relative to a rival's", "relative capacity"]
definition: We calculated each firm's market share using the ratio of a firm's total sales over the industry's total sales in a given year. We then constructed Relative market shareijt as firm i's market share minus rival j's market share.

name: Relative technological status
authors_terms: ["relative technological status", "technological status relative to a rival's", "relative capability"]
definition: A firm's status in areas of technological development reflects the firm's capability to produce high-quality or influential technological knowledge. Relative technological statusijt is firm i's Euclidean normalized eigenvector centrality at year t minus rival j's Euclidean normalized eigenvector centrality in year t.

name: VC industry specialization in the syndicate
authors_terms: ["VC industry specialization in the syndicate", "VC syndicate specialization", "specialist VC firms", "industry specialization"]
definition: The degree to which the VC firms in the investment syndicate are specialized in a particular industry, reflecting the commercialization knowledge and specialized networks that specialist VC firms accumulate through industry-focused human capital and more active hands-on engagement.

name: Start-up patenting hazard
authors_terms: ["hazard of patenting", "start-up's innovative outcomes", "start-up patents after VC investment", "time to first patent after VC investment"]
definition: The rate at which a start-up applies for a patent after VC investment; patents are not just a signal of innovation, but a necessary resource and milestone in the innovation process, especially in biotechnology.

name: Research environment development
authors_terms: ["research environment", "well-developed research environment", "less developed research environment", "country research environment"]
definition: The richness of the start-up's research environment in terms of resources relevant to its innovation process; the more patents within a given research or scientific field in a country, the more resources (scientists, universities, or government institutions) for innovation there are in that country.

name: Entry into the incumbent's own identity category
authors_terms: ["entry of new organizations into the same category", "number of organizations founded in the incumbent's category", "same-category entries"]
definition: When new entrants claim the same category-based identity as an incumbent, they encroach on its identity-based niche, creating a competitive threat by increasing the number of firms that consumers in that niche will consider.

name: Entry into other identity categories
authors_terms: ["entry of new organizations into other categories", "number of organizations founded in other categories", "other-category entries", "growth of other categories"]
definition: New entrants into a field can pose a categorical identity threat if they join categories that are distinct from the incumbent's category.

name: Entry outside ancestral categories
authors_terms: ["new entrants outside ancestral categories", "number of organizations founded outside ancestral identity categories", "entrants that do not clearly fit in the shared identity schema"]
definition: New organizations that locate outside the ancestral categories of the shared identity schema, so that the degree of overlap these organizations have with an incumbent's identity-based niche is hard to assess and the extent of categorical identity threat may also be unclear.

name: Identity-deepening actions
authors_terms: ["identity-deepening tactics", "identity-deepening actions", "within-niche product proliferation", "depth or product versioning"]
definition: Identity-deepening actions develop and enrich an organization's identity-based resources within the parameters of its identity category's template. Our review of the literature shows that within-niche product proliferation is a common method.

name: Identity-extending actions
definition: Identity-extending actions attempt to enhance an organization's identity by adding features that will be recognized and valued across categories. These enhancements can increase capabilities of the organization to compete with organizations outside its niche, but, as a special case, by creating appeal on the basis of identity.

name: Identity-affirming actions
definition: Identity-affirming tactics highlight an organization's membership in a particular category, typically by emphasizing its adoption of the category's distinguishing features. Through identity-affirming tactics, organizations strengthen their distinguishing features and/or make them more salient to their audiences.

name: Positive emotionality of product names
authors_terms: ["beer name positive emotionality", "positively charged names", "positive emotions conveyed by product names"]
definition: The level of positive emotion conveyed by the words of a product's name, measured as the percentage of words in a name that are positively charged.

name: Negative emotionality of product names
authors_terms: ["beer name negative emotionality", "negatively charged names", "negative emotions conveyed by product names"]
definition: The level of negative emotion conveyed by the words of a product's name, measured as the percentage of words in a name that are negatively charged.

name: Consumer appeal
definition: Aggregated evaluations by online reviewers are seen as a manifestation of the collective product appeal in an industry. Actual appeal is a function of intrinsic appeal and engagement by producers.

name: Perceived product authenticity
definition: Audiences see a craft organization as authentic when its actions and behavior on the frontstage match the audience expectations about that producer's true self on the backstage.

name: Valuation accuracy
definition: The extent to which an individual's valuation or an agreed-upon market price matches the true value of the underlying asset; the authors measure whether a price or an offer to trade matches true value, which also allows identifying misvaluation.

name: Similarity of valuation errors
authors_terms: ["common error", "correlated errors", "increasingly similar valuation errors", "conformity of errors"]
definition: The extent to which valuation errors are correlated rather than idiosyncratic: 'The higher the common error component, the greater is the similarity of errors across market participants.'

name: Market experience
authors_terms: ["experience in the market as trading progresses", "trading experience", "observe others and interact"]
definition: The degree to which market participants observe other participants and interact in the market as trading progresses over successive trading periods.

name: Social ambiguity
definition: The extent to which an individual is unsure as to whether he or she shares a common understanding of the situation in which he or she is placed; it refers to social expectations about the socially appropriate way to behave, such as the right technique to price an asset.

name: Price bubbles
definition: Trade in high volume at prices that are considerably at variance from intrinsic [true] value; operationally, persistent deviations of prices from true values above 0.10 on a scale of 0.00-1.00.

name: Investment flexibility
definition: Flexibility allows the revision of investments prior to their completion as more is learned about the investment's potential and uncertainty dissipates. In this study it takes the form of piloting a television program while retaining the option to terminate its development.

name: Project type
definition: Projects classified into two types, high-type and low-type, based on both the uncertainty inherent in project outcomes and the information revealed after the experimental phase. High-type projects have a lot of uncertainty about their final outcomes and generate significant information about the specific type of uncertainty that puts project outcomes at risk; low-type projects fail one or both criteria.

name: Project termination
definition: Termination is the revision of an investment by cancelling the project at the interim stage rather than continuing it to completion; it is the form revision often takes under flexibility.

name: Subsequent resource allocation
definition: The decision made by the owner of a resource to allocate that resource to a project after the experimentation decision has been made but before new information on the quality of the project is available due to that experimentation.

name: Project performance
definition: Project-level outcomes that reflect whether the final project output itself is of higher or lower quality, distinct from other costs related to experimentation such as monitoring, administrative, or opportunity costs.

name: Superstar resources
definition: Resources for which moving from a very high allocation to a slightly lower allocation can greatly affect project outcomes, much like superstar individuals and firms perform better than their second-best peers.

name: Scientist mobility
definition: Mobile scientific personnel carry fine-grained information about firms' technological activities; scientists that migrate from one firm to another are likely to be informed and have knowledge about the underlying R&D resources and activities of the firms.

name: R&D alliance formation
definition: The likelihood that two ventures in the biotechnology industry engage in an R&D alliance with each other; the dependent variable is dyadic and dichotomous and equals one for realized alliances and zero for unrealized alliances between two ventures in year t.

name: Relational ties
authors_terms: ["relational ties", "prior ties", "direct and indirect ties", "absence of ties"]
definition: Prior direct and indirect (shared third-party) interfirm relationships between prospective partners; prior direct and indirect relationships provide firm access to significant information about prospective collaborators' R&D resources and activities.

name: Geographic colocation
definition: Physical closeness that allows for frequent interactions and effective exchange of information between firms and engenders connectedness within a local institutional and cultural fabric.

name: Category spanning
definition: A startup's degree of category spanning is determined by how infrequently its own category labels have previously been used to simultaneously label any single organization. Intuitively, this measure will be higher for startups classified by many previously unrelated categories, and lower for startups assigned to categories that frequently coincide.

name: Relatedness between entrant and incumbent
definition: A startup's degree of relatedness to the incumbent is determined by the percentage of shared industry categories.

name: Audience valuation of incumbents
authors_terms: ["audience valuations for related incumbents", "investors' assessments of incumbents", "cumulative abnormal returns", "stock reactions", "CAR"]
definition: We use stock reactions to capture investors' assessments of incumbents. As a forward-looking measure embodying investors' expectations of future earnings, the stock returns are not a measure of actual performance but rather investors' evaluations of the present value of the company based on estimated future cash flows.

name: CSR uniqueness
authors_terms: ["CSR uniqueness", "uniqueness in CSR strategy", "uniqueness of CSR strategies", "cross-category uniqueness in CSR", "unique CSR strategies"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's CSR strategy differs from the average portfolio of CSR positions observed in its industry in each given year; a high value indicates that the firm's CSR strategy follows a pattern of cross-category performance that differs from the average pattern observed in its industry.

name: Market value
definition: The market value of the firm, calculated as the market value of common stocks (i.e., number of stocks outstanding times stock price) plus the total debt outstanding.

name: Overall CSR performance
authors_terms: ["overall CSR performance", "Total CSR Score", "aggregate CSR performance"]
definition: The overall CSR performance of the firm, which proxies for the company's overall stakeholder orientation and is obtained by aggregating the firm's categorical CSR scores across all eight CSR categories observed in the data set in each year.

name: Industry materiality of CSR categories
authors_terms: ["materiality", "number of material CSR categories", "material categories", "Number Material Categories"]
definition: A stakeholder-related issue is considered material to firms in an industry when it has the potential to bring about significant financial impact to these companies; the number of such material categories varies across industries and constrains firms' degrees of freedom in CSR positioning.

name: Oil and gas extraction
authors_terms: ["oil-related sectors", "Oil & Gas Extraction", "oil and gas companies", "treated sectors"]
definition: Firms in oil-related sectors, defined as extractive industries closely related to oil, formally those with SIC equal to 13.

name: Post-shock period
definition: A dummy that equals one for the first fiscal year ending after April 20, 2010 (the day on which the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded) and zero for the last fiscal year ending before this same date.

name: Legacy technology orientation
authors_terms: ["legacy technology orientation", "legacy technology orientation linked to analog photography"]
definition: A firm's relative emphasis on resources aligned to a legacy or incumbent technology. The authors theorize that it privileges corporate strategy decisions centered around the legacy technology and imposes inertia.

name: New technology acquisitions
authors_terms: ["new technology acquisitions", "likelihood of making new technology acquisitions"]
definition: Acquisitions in which a firm acquires a target possessing digital photography resources and products.

name: Legacy technology divestitures
definition: Divestitures in which the divested units or assets were based on the legacy technology, that is, analog (silver-halide based) photography.

name: New technology alliance experience
definition: The cumulative number of alliances made by a firm for technological or product-related knowledge sharing with partners or joint development of technology- or product-related resources linked to digital photography.

name: Partial acquisition integration
authors_terms: ["partial approach to acquisition integration", "partial integration", "partial autonomy"]
definition: An approach in which the acquirer selectively integrates a subset of the target's new technology resources while granting operational autonomy to other target resources that are not complementary or synergistic with its internal resources.

name: Product market survival
authors_terms: ["product market survival", "likelihood of product market survival"]
definition: Whether a firm survived in the digital camera product market, where exit is assessed using the three types of exit of Josefy et al. (2017): operations failure, ownership failure and solvency failure.

name: Negative status contrast of a new CEO
authors_terms: ["Negative status contrast of new CEO", "negative status contrast"]
definition: The extent to which the new CEO is of lower status than the predecessor. It equals old CEO status minus new CEO status when the new CEO's status is below the old CEO's, and equals zero otherwise.

name: Positive status contrast of a new CEO
authors_terms: ["Positive status contrast of new CEO", "positive status contrast"]
definition: The extent to which the new CEO is of higher status than the predecessor. It equals new CEO status minus old CEO status when the new CEO's status exceeds the old CEO's, and equals zero otherwise.

name: Acquisitiveness of new CEOs
definition: The rate at which a new CEO announces acquisitions early in the CEO's tenure. As each CEO can make multiple acquisition announcements during the observation window, they are conceived as point processes and the rate of transition from the Kth acquisition to the K+1th acquisition is estimated.

name: Bold and visible acquisitions
authors_terms: ["bolder and more visible deals", "unrelated acquisitions", "big acquisitions"]
definition: Acquisitions that are bolder and more visible than others. Prior research indicates that not all acquisitions are equally bold and visible; related acquisitions are often considered less bold and visible than diversifying acquisitions, and larger acquisitions are more grandiose than smaller ones.

name: Stock market reaction to new CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["Market reaction to new CEO announcement", "market reaction to new CEO appointment"]
definition: The market's evaluation of the new CEO, measured as cumulative abnormal returns. Abnormal returns capture that part of a stock price that is not anticipated by statistical predictions based on normal returns for a stock.

name: Legacy of the predecessor CEO
authors_terms: ["Legacy of predecessor CEO", "media's positive evaluation of old CEO legacy"]
definition: The net positive influence the outgoing CEO had over the firm, reflecting the accumulated reputation for quality of the CEO during the CEO's tenure, measured through content analysis of news items in the print media.

name: Epistemic motivation
authors_terms: ["epistemic motivation", "the drive to learn and hold well-informed views of the world", "process accountability"]
definition: Epistemic motivation is defined as the drive to learn and hold well-informed views of the world (Kruglanski 1989, Amit and Sagiv 2013). The level of epistemic motivation that a person experiences at any moment results from both dispositional and situational factors, and the most widely studied situational driver is process accountability, which is also the preferred way to experimentally induce epistemic motivation.

name: Construal level
authors_terms: ["construal levels", "high construal levels", "level of abstraction", "abstract thinking style"]
definition: Construal levels, or the levels of abstraction with which individuals engage in information processing (Trope and Liberman 2010), represent a cognitive tool. People at a higher construal level process information in a way that is abstract, schematic, and decontextualized, capturing superordinate characteristics of targets, whereas at a lower construal level people attend to more specific, contextualized characteristics of targets.

name: Problem formulation comprehensiveness
definition: Problem formulation comprehensiveness refers to the number of nonredundant, relevant causes of a problem that organizational actors identify, such that the entire problem space is canvassed as much as possible, given the limits of human rationality (Baer et al. 2013). Strategic problem formulation is considered comprehensive when all symptoms characterizing a problem can be explained by a set of underlying causes, such that each cause explains at least one of the symptoms.

name: Social exposure
definition: Efforts by organizations to draw attention to their products so that they enjoy growth in popularity. In the model these are observable differences that increase social exposure for products.

name: Popularity rate
definition: The rate at which products experience the event of becoming popular, modelled as a function of the time since the product was released.

name: Extinction rate
definition: The rate at which popular products experience the event of falling into obscurity, modelled as a function of the time since the product became popular.

name: Popularity-based competition
definition: Competition among products that are popular at the same point in time: rather than including products in the competition matrix solely on the basis of overlap in product space, a product is included only while it is within its time period of being a hit.

name: Cannibalization
definition: Competition that a multiproduct organization generates among its own products; competitive effects within an agency are 'cannibalization'.

name: Efficacy belief
definition: Employees' beliefs about the likelihood with which they can attain innovation rewards, influenced by impressions of their own task efficacy; efficacy beliefs stem partly from beliefs about their own general cognitive aptitude, task-specific beliefs about skillfulness, and beliefs about the level of difficulty of a particular innovation challenge. The more capable an employee believes the employee to be, the greater the anticipated probability of success.

name: Innovation choice
definition: Employees' choice to work on the creative problem solving necessary for commercial development, as opposed to continuing with routine work; whether employees choose to innovate depends on whether they consider it worth their while.

name: Resource-allocation regime
definition: Tunnels refer to regimes that select candidates once and furnish them with the resources they need at the outset, so that everyone who begins the development process also completes it, successful or not. Funnels select more than once, disbursing tranches of resources at each stage, so that successive filtering occurs along the development process.

name: Enabling technology
definition: Building on Teece (2018a), we define enabling technologies as (1) pervasive, (2) novel and improvable, and (3) supportive to spawn complementary innovations.

name: Public-private R&D relationship
authors_terms: ["public-private relationship", "public-private R&D relationship", "private firm's relationships with the public sector"]
definition: We define a public-private relationship to exist for a patented invention if a federal interest statement is included in the patent document, indicating that a tie between a public agency and a for-profit firm existed to exchange resources (e.g., financial, infrastructure, or research support) and to create a mutually desired R&D outcome (i.e. the patented technology).

name: Grant
definition: Grants are direct financial subsidies given to a firm by a public funding agency as an investment toward an objective specified by the agency. Grants allow considerable latitude, and the grant recipient (i.e., the firm) often defines the scope of work because there are no legally binding requirements to achieve results.

name: Contract
definition: A contract is a binding agreement between a buyer and a seller to provide goods or services in return for compensation. In government contracts with private firms, the contracting agency is looking to procure a good or a service that will be of direct benefit to the government.

name: Cooperative agreement
definition: Cooperative agreements (agreements for short) are public-private relationships in which firms and public agencies agree to work side by side toward a mutual objective. In agreements, federal employees often are substantially involved in the execution of the work and participate closely in performing the work side by side with the private firm.

name: Science agency partner
definition: Science agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF), the NIH, and the National Institutes for Standards and Technology (NIST) are science focused (Ergas 1987), and their goal is to provide the scientific freedom for private firms to pursue their own research goals.

name: Mission agency partner
definition: Mission agencies are defined as programmatic agencies with the goal of achieving practical goals; that is, they focus on an agency's mission. Mission agencies including the DOD and NASA are, conversely, generally built to support a national externality, for example, national security or space travel.

name: Partial price regulation
authors_terms: ["partial or incomplete regulation", "partial price-ceiling regulation", "price-ceiling regulation", "regulation"]
definition: Firms that operate in regulated submarkets also tend to participate in horizontally related, unregulated submarkets within a product market, leading to a case of partial or incomplete regulation. Regulation-driven repositioning is defined as how firms respond to regulation using positioning strategies.

name: Repositioning
definition: Repositioning refers to the movement of firms from their current location toward a more beneficial location. The authors consider repositioning as the set of actions that firms undertake to improve their competitive position, such as reallocating resources to submarkets where they can be used most profitably.

name: Price
definition: To facilitate easy comparison of prices across products containing 500-mg and 650-mg dosage strengths, the authors normalize product prices to price per 500-mg tablet.

name: Ability to shift demand
authors_terms: ["ability to shift demand", "demand shifting", "marketing intensity", "marketing proxy"]
definition: Firms put costly effort into shifting demand across intraindustry boundaries to mitigate the impact of regulations that threaten their profits. The authors expect that firms with greater investments in demand shifting, proxied by marketing intensity, can more effectively influence the prescription behavior of physicians toward their branded products.

name: Submarket regulation status
definition: In a market consisting of unregulated submarkets alone, firm profitability is not constrained by a firm's presence in a specific submarket. But when one of the submarkets is regulated, then the prospect of increasing profitability substantially is limited to unregulated submarkets.

name: Rice culture
authors_terms: ["rice culture", "rice vs. wheat culture", "rice-wheat farmland ratio", "rice culture similarity", "rice region"]
definition: Rice culture can be characterized by several attributes with the core cognitive process of holistic thinking; it is formulated through the requirements of rice farming, which needs extensive labor and irrigation collaboration.

name: Direction of cultural difference
authors_terms: ["cultural difference", "cross-cultural acquisitions", "asymmetrical effects of cultural differences", "rice target + wheat acquirer"]
definition: The effect of cultural differences is also asymmetrical at the subnational level, and the influence of the difference between rice and wheat culture depends on whether the acquisition is between a wheat acquirer and a rice target or vice versa.

name: Post-acquisition performance improvement
authors_terms: ["post-acquisition performance improvement of targets", "target's ROA improvement"]
definition: The post-acquisition performance improvement of targets is measured using the improvement of the target's return on assets (ROA) from one year before to one year after the acquisition.

name: Wheat acquirer's experience with wheat targets
authors_terms: ["wheat acquirers' experience with wheat targets", "prior experience with wheat target for wheat acquirer", "intracultural experience"]
definition: We expect wheat acquirers to be better able to learn from their prior wheat targets and use the knowledge gained to improve a focal target's performance; it is one of the four types of cultural experience the authors contrast (intracultural experience).

name: Rice acquirer's experience with rice targets
authors_terms: ["rice acquirers' experience with rice targets", "prior experience with rice target for rice acquirer", "intracultural experience"]
definition: Rice acquirers may not be able to effectively learn from their prior experience with rice targets despite being in the same culture, because holistic thinkers' knowledge is tacit and embedded in context.

name: Wheat acquirer's experience with rice targets
authors_terms: ["wheat acquirers' experience with rice targets", "prior experience with rice target for wheat acquirer", "cross-cultural experience"]
definition: Wheat acquirers may have difficulty articulating and codifying the knowledge embedded in rice targets because the tacit knowledge of rice culture is embedded in the interrelationships among contextual factors.

name: Rice acquirer's experience with wheat targets
authors_terms: ["rice acquirers' experience with wheat targets", "prior experience with wheat target for rice acquirer", "cross-cultural experience"]
definition: Rice culture acquirers may be capable of generating new tacit knowledge by aligning the explicit knowledge in wheat culture through learning by doing and then applying the new knowledge to the focal target.

name: Intrinsic speed capability
authors_terms: ["intrinsic speed capabilities", "firm speed", "firm slowness", "Slowness", "speed capabilities of the focal firm"]
definition: Intrinsic speed capabilities capture the ability of firms to execute investment projects faster than competitors at the same cost. Firms lacking these capabilities (slow firms) realize revenue streams later and risk being preempted by faster competitors.

name: Valuable complementary assets
authors_terms: ["valuable complementary assets", "complementary supporting assets", "valuable supporting assets", "LNG tankers"]
definition: A set of valuable supporting assets that are especially relevant for the development of the focal project; if deployed to the focal project, the performance of the focal project is likely to be enhanced, benefitting both the partner firm and the focal firm.

name: Alliance choice
authors_terms: ["decision to partner or go it alone", "alliance over autonomous project development", "alliances versus autonomous project development", "choosing to enter the market for alliances", "joint venture"]
definition: The choice of whether to engage in an investment project through internal, or autonomous, development versus through a partnership with another firm; the authors frame it as the decision of whether to enter the market for alliances or not.

name: Partnering with a fast partner
authors_terms: ["partner with fast partner firms", "Fast Partner", "partnering with fast partner firms", "obtaining a partnership with a fast partner firm"]
definition: Choosing as collaboration partner a firm that is intrinsically fast: partner firms are categorized as fast or slow based on their realized values of Slowness, where a negative value indicates a fast partner firm.

name: Risk of quality liability
authors_terms: ["risk of quality liability", "risk of medical malpractice liability", "MML risk", "liability risk"]
definition: The risk that liability costs will occur; it is jointly determined by the firm's endogenous choice of quality and the exogenous probability that a product or service failure gives rise to a lawsuit, as determined by the liability regime under which the firm operates.

name: Prevention expenditure
authors_terms: ["prevention expenditure", "investment in quality", "investment in prevention", "hospital medical expenditure per patient"]
definition: Expenditure on prevention, such as upgrading the product or service, purchasing advanced equipment, training employees, and reforming operational procedures; investment in quality lowers the probability of liability lawsuits.

name: Nonprofit status
definition: Nonprofits are precluded from distributing earnings to individuals or organizations such as members, directors, or trustees, and are precluded from raising equity, relying on revenue, private donations, and government subsidies to cover expenses; their objective function contains a smaller profit and a larger (nonprofit) quality component.

name: Reputation for quality
definition: Reputation serves as an important signal of organization competence and trustworthiness, because stakeholders rely on an organization's past record to forecast its future quality; a good reputation is a valuable asset that is sustainable only through a continuous effort to invest in reputation.

name: Platform certification
authors_terms: ["certification", "selective promotion of complements and complementors", "social performance badges", "badging program", "FCE badge"]
definition: Another important way to govern complementor quality and diversity is for the platform to use selective promotion of complements and complementors, which includes certification. After receiving a certification for a specific product, a complementor will learn how valuable that product is relative to the other products in its portfolio.

name: Product portfolio reorientation
authors_terms: ["portfolio reorientation", "postcertification portfolio reorientation", "reorient their product portfolio", "portfolio composition", "loan portfolio composition"]
definition: Complementors typically offer a range of products on a platform, which we refer to as the complementor's portfolio of products. We expect that, after receiving a selective promotion or other types of certification by the platform, complementors will reorient their product portfolio to align with the dimension certified.

name: Additional certifications
authors_terms: ["additional badge received", "additional certifications", "multiple certifications", "more than one badge"]
definition: However, multiple certifications may have a less positive effect by causing the complementor to reorient its product portfolio across several dimensions. In the limit, if certification is provided for every dimension represented in the complementor's portfolio of products, the complementor will have no incentive to reorient its portfolio.

name: Portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["portfolio concentration", "portfolio concentration ratio", "specialization", "specialist complementors", "concentrated loan portfolios"]
definition: We propose the degree of the complementor's specialization - a supply-side factor - as a second limit to portfolio reorientation. Specialist complementors, those with product portfolios in only one or a few sectors, will thus have to search extensively to offer more quality products in the same sector to meet the increased demand from customers.

name: Diffuse organizational knowledge environment
authors_terms: ["diffuse organizational knowledge environment", "diffuse organizational knowledge structure", "diffuse structure", "high within low across diversity"]
definition: A knowledge environment in which knowledge in a given technological area can be seen as diffuse throughout the firm, depicted as high levels of within-team knowledge diversity and low levels of across-team knowledge diversity.

name: Concentrated organizational knowledge environment
authors_terms: ["concentrated organizational knowledge environment", "concentrated knowledge environment", "concentrated team knowledge diversity structure", "low within high across diversity"]
definition: A knowledge environment where knowledge can be characterized as concentrated, in the sense that teams hold unique knowledge relative to other teams in the firm, depicted as low levels of within-team knowledge diversity and high levels of across-team knowledge diversity.

name: High within-team and high across-team knowledge diversity
definition: An organizational knowledge environment indicator for firm-years where within-team knowledge diversity is above the 75th percentile and across-team diversity is above the 75th percentile of their underlying distributions.

name: Innovation quality
definition: Forward citations are an accepted measure of innovation output, acting as a proxy for the economic value created by the patented innovations.

name: Team contribution inequality
authors_terms: ["more unequal team contributions to their innovation output", "inequality in innovation quality", "forward citation Herfindahl", "concentration of a firm's forward citations"]
definition: The dispersion of innovation outcomes across a firm's teams; under a diffuse structure the authors expect greater inequality across teams with respect to innovation quality, and the measure captures the concentration of a firm's forward citations among its patents in a focal year.

name: Within-team knowledge diversity
definition: The degree to which an average production team inside the firm has individuals who differ among themselves with respect to the knowledge embodied in their prior technical experience.

name: Across-team knowledge diversity
definition: The degree to which an average production team inside the firm differs from other teams with respect to the knowledge embodied in the aggregate technical experience of the team's inventors.

name: Within-team coordination
authors_terms: ["within-team coordination", "within-team coordination costs", "within-team collaborative experience", "shared team processes"]
definition: Coordination through jointly shared prior experience: a longer history of shared production experience by members of a production team allows for the emergence of routines and processes for coordination, thereby muting the negative effect of dissonant cognitive frameworks and work processes.

name: Cost of across-team knowledge access
authors_terms: ["cost of knowledge accessibility across teams", "accessibility of knowledge across teams", "team geographic dispersion", "geographic dispersion"]
definition: Firm characteristics that hinder the ease of across-team knowledge flows, such as geographic dispersion when the firm's inventors are spread across multiple locations, would reduce the positive effect of a concentrated team structure.

name: Within-firm external-to-team knowledge use
authors_terms: ["within-firm external-to-the-team knowledge", "utilization of knowledge within the firm but outside of the team", "firm nonteam self-citation ratio"]
definition: The utilization of knowledge within the firm but outside of the team generating a given patent, capturing the volume of knowledge flowing inside the firm from one team to another distinct team.

name: Privatization
definition: Privatization is 'the deliberate sale by a government of SOEs or assets to private economic agents'; in privatization, the state expects to sell its ownership in an SOE to private owners, and government ownership is being converted into private ownership.

name: Firm innovation
definition: Following existing research, the authors use patent data to measure firm innovation, focusing on invention patents, the only type of patents at the SIPO that require substantive examination and comparable to patents filed in other countries.

name: Owner-manager interest alignment
authors_terms: ["interest alignment between firm owners and managers", "owner-manager interest alignment", "TMT shareholding"]
definition: After privatization, interests of managers become better aligned with those of firm owners: managerial ownership links managers' financial outcomes with those of shareholders and bonds managers' preferences and actions with those of shareholders.

name: Shareholders' interest alignment
authors_terms: ["interest alignment between controlling and minority shareholders", "shareholders' interest alignment", "intercorporate loans"]
definition: By way of privatization, principal-principal conflicts are ameliorated, and improved interest alignment between controlling and minority shareholders, in turn, facilitates firm innovation, as new owners in privatized firms have a clear goal of maximizing returns on investment consistent with that of other previous minority shareholders.

name: Perceived deservingness of own allocation
authors_terms: ["perceptions of the allocation one deserves", "perceptions of a fair offer to oneself", "escalation of deservingness under secrecy (EDS)", "minimum acceptable offer (MAO)"]
definition: The absolute amount of the reward expected by an individual as fair for oneself; the mere presence of a peer who is receiving an unknown allocation should inflate the notion of what is considered fair in an interaction with a superior.

name: Presence of a peer with a secret allocation
authors_terms: ["mere presence of a peer", "noncompeting peer", "PUG aware"]
definition: A noncompeting peer is operationalized as a peer respondent whose actions do not influence the allocation outcome of the focal respondent, even if both are dealing with the same offeror; in the PUG aware condition respondents knew another respondent was being engaged but not the magnitude of the offer to that respondent.

name: Transparency of the allocation to a peer
definition: The degree of information a respondent has about the offer amount made to the peer respondent, manipulated in four ways: full secrecy (no information), partial secrecy (information on the offeror's past offers to past respondents), risk (the exact range of possible offer amounts to the peer) and transparency (the exact offer amount to the peer).

name: Willingness to accept an allocation
authors_terms: ["willingness to accept", "likelihood to accept the job offer", "accept or reject the offer"]
definition: The respondent's reported willingness to accept the offer made to oneself, reported on a Likert scale in the scenario studies.

name: Perceived fairness of the offer
definition: The participant's subjective sense of fairness of the amount offered to them; the authors note that the central process in EDS is an escalated perception of what is considered a fair allocation to oneself.

name: Data breach
authors_terms: ["data breach", "technological failure", "digital failure", "failure experience", "PII-related data breach"]
definition: The most prevalent outcome of cyberhacking is a data breach, whereby data are exposed to an unauthorized party. In this study the breaches are PII-related events involving the loss of personally identifiable information such as medical and credit card information, personal addresses, and social security numbers.

name: Unrelated divestiture
authors_terms: ["unrelated divestiture", "divestitures of unrelated subsidiaries", "divesting unrelated subsidiaries"]
definition: Divestitures of unrelated units enable the standardization of technological systems by removing subsidiaries with dissimilar practices, thereby harmonizing practices and routines across the remaining subsidiaries.

name: CTO turnover
authors_terms: ["CTO turnover", "replacement of the CTO", "top management turnover", "CTO dismissal"]
definition: The replacement or laying off of the firm's chief technology officer, or of a senior executive holding a similar responsibility, following a failure event; the authors treat it as a social-political response to failure.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["aspiration-performance feedback", "performance-aspiration gap", "historical aspiration performance", "social aspiration performance", "performance-aspiration levels"]
definition: An organization's willingness to learn and undertake exploratory steps to improve performance rather than simply refine existing practices depends on its performance-aspiration levels. These aspiration levels may be benchmarked to the organization's own historical performance, or emerge from vicarious learning and social comparison with industry peers.

name: Popularity of a management concept
authors_terms: ["popularity of a keyword", "popularity of a focal concept", "future popularity", "popularity in year t"]
definition: The popularity of a keyword in a given year, measured by the count of articles in that year that include the keyword. The authors use the yearly frequency of each distinct HBR keyword as the popularity of the corresponding management concept.

name: Affiliation with popular concepts
authors_terms: ["affiliation with popular others", "affiliation with popular concepts", "affiliating with popular others"]
definition: A concept A is affiliated with concept B if discussion about concept A mentions concept B; this can occur even if concepts A and B are not similar. Operationally, the authors sum the popularity of the keywords with which the focal keyword is mentioned in the previous period.

name: Similarity to popular concepts
authors_terms: ["local crowding", "similarity to other popular concepts", "being similar to other popular concepts"]
definition: Whether a concept is positioned in an already crowded space, that is, whether there are several similar and popular concepts in its vicinity. The authors measure it as the sum of the similarity-weighted popularity of the keywords that were used together with the focal keyword in the previous year.

name: Combination with similar concepts
authors_terms: ["combination with similar concepts", "similarity between the elements a concept combines", "combining similar elements"]
definition: The extent to which a keyword is mentioned together with keywords that are similar to it, i.e., whether it combines similar or very different elements. The authors measure it as the average Jaccard similarity between the focal keyword and all the keywords with which it is ever mentioned.

name: National diversity
authors_terms: ["national diversity", "national diversity of a workforce", "diversity whole crew"]
definition: The extent to which the members of a unit originate from different national (regional) backgrounds. The authors argue that national diversity reduces cohesiveness and increases the potential for conflict among workers.

name: Workforce experience
authors_terms: ["workforce experience", "experience accumulated by workers", "average experience of the whole crew", "crew experience"]
definition: The experience accumulated by the workers of a unit, which the authors associate with positive returns for performance at the level of individuals and teams.

name: Ship performance
authors_terms: ["ship performance", "operational performance of a unit", "a unit's performance", "voyage duration"]
definition: The operational performance of a unit, proxied by the reduction in time to perform a given task; measured for each ship as the time taken to reach Asia.

name: Standardization of work practices and procedures
authors_terms: ["standardization", "standardization of work practices and procedures", "standardization of ship design and work procedures"]
definition: The consistency and reproducibility of work practices, procedures and ship designs, which the authors argue magnifies the returns from workforce experience and softens demographic differences.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below aspiration", "performance shortfall", "declining performance", "performance relative to historical (social) aspiration"]
definition: Firm performance relative to historical (social) aspiration refers to current performance minus historical (social) aspiration. The authors refer to performance below aspiration as declining performance (or performance shortfall).

name: Strategic change
definition: The extent of year-on-year change in the overall allocations of corporate resources across key strategic dimensions, such as leverage, overhead, advertising, and R&D expenditure.

name: Product diversification
definition: Product diversification involves sales expansions into new product segments, markets, and technology bases.

name: Geographic diversification
definition: Geographic diversification represents sales expansions into new geographic segments, which often involve political and economic risks; cross-cultural business models; and interactions with highly diverse customers, suppliers, and competition.

name: Product bright spot
definition: The greatest increase in percentage sales in a product segment among the firm's respective diversified portfolio.

name: Geographic bright spot
definition: The greatest increase in percentage sales in a geographic segment among the firm's respective diversified portfolio.

name: Exposure to policy reversal
authors_terms: ["Treated firm", "firms whose market activities are directly affected by the policy reversal", "firms affected by the license cancellation"]
definition: The treatment group comprises firms who held at least one license that was ordered to be cancelled by the Supreme Court, that is, firms whose market activities are directly affected by the reversal of a previously adopted market-expanding policy.

name: Operational performance
definition: The authors' outcome of interest is operational performance and specifically network-service quality, measured with technical network performance indicators reported at the firm-region level. Network service quality is traditionally a crucial differentiator among telecom firms and is significant to each firm's overall strategic success.

name: Patriotic rhetoric
authors_terms: ["patriotic rhetoric", "firm's use of patriotic rhetoric", "corporate flag-waving"]
definition: Statements that signal the firm's commitment to act in line with the national interest.

name: Nationalist sentiment
definition: A widespread 'sense of national consciousness [. . .] exalting one nation above all others and placing primary emphasis on promotion of its culture and interests as opposed to those of other nations or supranational groups.'

name: Overseas involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement in overseas markets", "overseas involvement", "the level of a firm's international operations", "involvement overseas"]
definition: The level of a firm's international operations, which varies with the importance of foreign operations for the organization and thus with its dependence on resources held by overseas actors.

name: Firm performance
definition: Following prior research, we measure our dependent variable - that is, firm performance - using the firm's return on assets in a given year.

name: Business input in regulatory design
authors_terms: ["business participation", "business input", "input from other businesses", "notice and comment", "VCCI clauses"]
definition: Comments and suggestions on draft regulations provided by firms through a public notice-and-comment consultation; in this study eight clauses were altered as a result of business participation and are referred to as the 'VCCI clauses.'

name: Awareness of business participation in regulatory design
authors_terms: ["learning about the participation of fellow firms", "endorsement experiment", "learning that businesses advised the decision"]
definition: Learning that fellow small and medium enterprises had participated in the regulatory design process behind the changes being judged, as opposed to learning that the changes were advised by chemical and labor safety experts; this manipulation assesses the participation spillover mechanism.

name: Perceived benefit of the regulatory change for business performance
authors_terms: ["positive change for business performance", "good for business", "most suitable for successful business operations"]
definition: A firm's belief that a regulatory change represents a positive change for business performance; elicited by asking respondents which clause version was most suitable for successful business operations.

name: Perceived benefit of the regulatory change for worker safety
authors_terms: ["positive change for society", "safer for workers", "provides the greatest protection to your employees"]
definition: A firm's belief that a regulatory change represents a positive change for society in the form of greater protection of workers; elicited by asking respondents which clause version provided the greatest protection to their employees.

name: Acceptance of the revised regulatory change
authors_terms: ["see a regulatory change as positive", "selection of the revised clause", "acceptability"]
definition: Whether the respondent views the revised version of a draft regulation clause as positive for either business performance or society; measured by whether the revised clause was selected over the original version.

name: Legitimacy of government's regulatory authority
definition: Firms' belief that government regulation is intended to protect workers, communities and the environment rather than to extract informal fees from business; an association of regulations with bribe extraction signals doubt about the intentions behind state regulation.

name: Discriminatory customer preferences against Israel-related passengers
authors_terms: ["Customer Attitudes", "customer preferences against traveling with Israel-related passengers", "discriminatory customer preferences for Israel-related passengers"]
definition: Customer Attitudes measures negative assessments of Israel-related passengers by airline customers.

name: Discriminatory customer preferences against Jewish passengers
authors_terms: ["Customer Kosher Interests", "Customer Kosher Interest (CKI)", "kosher interest", "customer preferences against traveling with Jewish passengers"]
definition: Customer Kosher Interests measures positive assessments of Israel-related passengers by international airline customers.

name: Discriminatory owner tastes
authors_terms: ["State-Owned Doesn't Recognize", "State-Owned Doesn't Recognize (SODR)", "owner tastes against serving Israel-related customers", "owner tastes against serving Jewish customers"]
definition: We classify majority state-owned airlines located in countries not recognizing Israel as owners potentially preferring not to serve customers associated with Israel.

name: Online route map treatment of Israel
authors_terms: ["Route Map Treatment", "Route Map Treatment (RMT)", "online route map treatment of Israel"]
definition: We observe the treatment of Israel on an international airline's online route map and categorize that treatment either as an Israel embracer (Route Map Treatment = 3), avoider (Route Map Treatment = 2), or denier (Route Map Treatment = 1).

name: Kosher meal options on online in-flight menus
authors_terms: ["Kosher Meal Options", "Kosher Meal Options (KMO)", "kosher meal options on online in-flight menus"]
definition: We observe whether an international airline inflight menu lists kosher meal options at its company website or at wanderbat.com.

name: Membership in a major international airline alliance
authors_terms: ["Alliance", "Star, OneWorld, or SkyTeam alliances", "major international alliances"]
definition: We observe whether an international airline is listed as a member of either the Star, OneWorld, or SkyTeam alliances.

name: Labor market flexibility
authors_terms: ["labor flexibility", "flexible labor", "labor rigidity", "employment protection law rigidity", "EPL", "employment protection"]
definition: We say that labor is flexible if the adjustment cost of reducing labor from period 1 to period 2 (cL) equals 0 and rigid if that adjustment cost equals c. Empirically the rigidity of labor is measured with a country's employment protection law rigidity, the OECD employment dismissal protection index, which measures cross-country differences in the difficulty of dismissing workers.

name: Factor substitutability
definition: The parameter alpha in the model measures the efficiency of the high elasticity of substitution technology relative to the low elasticity of substitution technology, and is proxied at the industry level by measures of factor substitutability sigma. Industries with high substitutability are those in which laborers can be replaced by machinery or vice versa.

name: Entry
definition: In building the panel, firms are coded as entrants if their date of incorporation is the same as the publication year, and all other firms are classified as incumbents.

name: Labor-capital ratio
authors_terms: ["labor-capital ratios", "capital-labor ratios", "capital intensity", "labor-intensive strategy", "assets per employee"]
definition: The relative use of labor and capital in a firm's production strategy; firms may be expected to exhibit higher labor-capital ratios when labor is flexible and it is relatively easy to substitute capital with labor. Capital intensity is calculated as the log ratio of assets over employees.

name: Corporate group affiliation
definition: Following Belenzon et al. (2013), a corporate group is defined as a collection of at least two legally distinct firms of which one is a controlling ultimate shareholder of the other or others. Firms are classified as group affiliates if they have a controlling parent company, are a parent company of another firm, or have the same controlling shareholder as at least one other firm; firms with no equity ties to other firms, or with missing ownership information, are classified as stand-alones.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: Demand is initially uncertain: demand is high with probability one half and low with probability one half, and the parameter Delta captures the magnitude of the uncertainty shock. Empirically uncertainty is measured by the media Economic Policy Uncertainty Index from Baker et al. (2016), computed as a function of the number of terms in local newspapers that indicate economic policy uncertainty.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age measures how long a firm has been in existence and is used to characterize how labor-capital ratios evolve over a firm's life cycle, that is, how firms exploit factor substitutability as they grow.

name: Platform algorithmic recommendation
authors_terms: ["recommended by the platform's algorithm", "platform recommendations", "Recommended (Rec)", "platform algorithmic recommendations"]
definition: The platform uses a machine-learning algorithm to assess each applicant and score the applicant on a zero-to-one scale in terms of the applicant's fitness for that specific job. All applicants who score a 0.50 or above at the time of their applications are automatically recommended by the platform, resulting in a 'recommended' flag being added to their profile at all stages of the hiring process.

name: Applicant viewing
authors_terms: ["viewing an application", "probability of view", "which applicants' CVs to view"]
definition: The first step of the hiring process, in which the employer selects which applicants' CVs to view from the pool of applicants.

name: Applicant interviewing
authors_terms: ["interviewing", "probability of interview | view", "which applicants to interview"]
definition: The intermediate step of the hiring process in which the employer selects which of the viewed applicants to interview; interviews are conducted on the platform and mostly involve the exchange of written messages between the firm and potential employees.

name: Applicant hiring
authors_terms: ["hiring", "probability of hire", "which applicant(s) to contract with for the job"]
definition: The final decision of the hiring process, in which the employer selects which applicant(s) to contract with for the job, often on terms proposed by the applicant(s).

name: Submarket size
authors_terms: ["market size", "submarket demand", "the market for similar jobs on the platform"]
definition: The size of the market (or relevant submarket), measured by the number of job postings in the submarket; the larger the number of firms offering similar jobs on the platform and the larger the number of similar jobs being offered, the lower the bargaining power of any individual firm.

name: Firm experience on the platform
authors_terms: ["firm experience", "number of prior jobs it filled on the platform", "employer's prior experience"]
definition: The extent to which the firm has transacted on the platform, measured as the number of previous jobs the employer has filled on the platform.

name: Institutional specialization
authors_terms: ["institutional specialization", "institutional specialists", "consistent conformity to an institutional logic"]
definition: Organizations engage in a form of institutional specialization, i.e., they consistently demonstrate conformity to an institutional logic identified by their stakeholders; they consistently deliver products or services that conform to the logic-based expectations of one particular audience.

name: Firm survival
definition: For the purpose of this study, I focus on a firm-level outcome that is critical to all firms in the population: I model differences in survival rates. Firms enter the risk set at the date they sign their first contract and are assumed to have failed when they have been inactive for at least three years.

name: Logic contrast
authors_terms: ["logic contrast", "contrast between institutional logics", "industry-level logic contrast"]
definition: Like categories, institutional logics may be seen as varying in contrast: when a logic has high contrast, stakeholders typically perceive firms as being mostly associated with (or dissociated from) the logic. At the industry level, contrast decreases when the proportion of noninstitutional specialists increases.

name: Termination capability
authors_terms: ["termination capability", "TC", "capability to terminate failing investments", "capability to detect and discontinue unsuccessful innovation investments"]
definition: A firm-level capability to detect and discontinue unsuccessful innovation investments; the term 'capability' refers to a heterogeneously distributed firm-level behavior pattern that leads to superior performance.

name: Partner workload
authors_terms: ["ventures per general partner", "ventures per partner", "number of ventures invested relative to the number of VC professionals", "intensity of workload"]
definition: The workload borne by general partners, which is a function of the number of ventures in a portfolio; in firms where GPs are overly burdened, each venture receives less of a GP's effort and attention, and evaluations of the ventures may be less accurate.

name: Support staff relative to partners
authors_terms: ["pyramid", "ratio of support members to partners", "number of support members in the VC firm relative to the GP's"]
definition: The support available to VC partners as they make investment decisions, captured by the number of support members relative to high-level members; division of labor between GPs and support functions could help ease the burden on GPs.

name: VC firm experience
definition: The total number of ventures in which the VC firm invested in the study period; prior experience could improve the accuracy of evaluations leading to termination decisions.

name: Investment specialization
authors_terms: ["VC's industry focus", "specialist VC firms", "industry specialization", "specialized experience"]
definition: The extent to which a VC firm concentrates its investments in a narrow set of industries; a focused investment strategy may enable a firm to better comprehend the subtler, industry-specific cues to assess the progress of its investments and terminate at the right time.

name: Management of successful investments
authors_terms: ["policies with respect to successful investments", "tendency to continue or terminate successful investments", "term capability-successful investments"]
definition: The firm's investment policy with respect to ventures that eventually succeed, i.e. its tendency to continue or terminate such investments.

name: VC firm performance
definition: The long-run performance of the venture capital firm, measured as the proportion of successful exits in its portfolio or as fund-level internal rates of return.

name: Knowledge proximity to a target CPU
authors_terms: ["knowledge space proximity to a target CPU", "knowledge relevance", "knowledge proximity to target CPU"]
definition: How close an organization is in knowledge space to areas associated with a 'target' CPU, mapped based on the patenting behavior of computer manufacturers that use the CPU.

name: Knowledge consistency
authors_terms: ["knowledge consistency", "consistent strategy in knowledge space", "consistently build knowledge in an R&D area"]
definition: Building knowledge in a particular area consistently over time; measured by comparing an organization's patent portfolio in the current year to its portfolio in previous years.

name: Knowledge generalism
definition: The extent to which an organization spreads its research across areas of knowledge space associated with CPUs other than the target CPU, rather than focusing on one area.

name: New-supplier technology adoption
authors_terms: ["adopting a CPU from a different supplier", "technology adoption", "new-supplier technology adoptions", "technical change"]
definition: An organization's adoption of a CPU from a supplier that it does not already use, which the authors treat as a major, nontrivial technical change.

name: Craigslist entry
definition: Craigslist's staggered entry into local markets, which provides an exogenous change in competitive intensity for classified ads for the incumbent newspapers.

name: Content differentiation
definition: The distance in editor-type space between a newspaper and its competitors; the measure is between 0 and 1, where identical sets of editor types give 0 and no overlap in editor types gives 1.

name: Cost-cutting
definition: Newspaper-level cost-cutting proxies on both sides of the market, constructed from editor and news-service data because annual cost expenditures are unavailable.

name: Reader heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["reader heterogeneity", "customer heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of reader preferences", "market-level reader heterogeneity"]
definition: Market-level heterogeneity of reader preferences for news content, constructed from historical voting patterns and demographic data on race and ethnicity; reader heterogeneity increases as the measures increase in value.

name: Sister firm experience
authors_terms: ["sister experience", "sister newspapers that have already been affected by Craigslist", "sister firms"]
definition: For a newspaper that experiences Craigslist's entry in year t, whether any of its sister firms have already faced the same challenge prior to year t.

name: Newspaper survival
definition: Whether a newspaper firm continues to offer daily editions, and whether it still exists at all, as of 2014.

name: Low strategic response
authors_terms: ["outlier (low response)", "low response", "deviation from the appropriate differentiation and cost-cutting strategies", "do not respond to Craigslist's entry"]
definition: Being in the bottom decile of all newspapers based on how responsive they are to Craigslist's entry, in terms of both differentiation and cost-cutting.

name: Contentious discourse
authors_terms: ["discourse", "contentious public discourse", "public discourse", "discourse supporting the legitimacy of a controversial strategy", "level of discourse surrounding metacompetition"]
definition: Public discourse among social actors in support of an approach to competing; contentious public discourse in support of controversial strategies serves as a tactic to improve their viability.

name: Carrying capacity
definition: The environment's potential to support organizations of a given strategy.

name: Organizational growth rate
authors_terms: ["organizational growth", "growth rates", "size", "observed change in size", "monthly proportionate change in rank"]
