definition: The observed change in size of an organization following a strategy from time t to time t+1; greater carrying capacity manifests as greater prospects for organizational growth.

name: Logic of competition
definition: A system of principles in a given context that determines who can compete, how they compete, on what criteria they succeed or fail, and what are the consequences of success or failure.

name: Interdependence between activities
definition: Interdependencies exist where the efficiency of one activity depends on another activity, where positive interdependencies are the joint benefits to performing activities together, sometimes called complementarities (Milgrom and Roberts 1990), and negative interdependencies are the joint costs of performing activities together, sometimes referred to as coordination costs (Gulati and Singh 1998).

name: Firm scope reduction
authors_terms: ["refocusing", "REFOCUS", "reduction in firm scope", "reduction in the scope of a firm's activities", "reduction in firm activity scope", "change in the scope of a firm's activities"]
definition: We study the implications of interdependence during periods of stability, when activity scope is constant, and turbulence, when there is a reduction in the number of activities performed by the firm.

name: Activity-level performance
authors_terms: ["activity-level performance", "productivity", "TFPQ", "total factor productivity in quantities", "anchovy productivity"]
definition: For the purposes of testing for the effects of a change in activity scope on interdependence effects, productivity-based measures of performance will generally be superior to market- and accounting-based measures of activity-level performance, because productivity-based measures filter out accounting allocations and market fluctuations.

name: Organizational rigidity
definition: If there are any negative interdependencies and firms are rigid in the sense that they are not able to instantaneously adapt in the short run (Hannan and Freeman 1984), but are adaptable in the long run, activity performance will improve over time.

name: Parent software installed base
authors_terms: ["parent-installed base", "installed base of games for the compatible parent console", "software installed base of the compatible parent generation", "SW installed base"]
definition: The installed base of games for the parent generation proxies all games that could potentially be used with the new console. We also create the software installed base of the compatible parent generation IB SW j 1 1 t .

name: Hardware demand
authors_terms: ["hardware demand", "demand for new hardware", "demand for the new generation"]
definition: Demand for a new console generation, measured by a console's market share of market potential and the market share of the outside good. Backward compatibility implies that the installed base of games for the parent generation can still be used with the new console, which increases demand for new hardware.

name: Software supply
authors_terms: ["software supply", "supply of new software titles", "software variety"]
definition: Software supply is expressed by the variety of different game titles Njt available for a specific platform.

name: Console age
authors_terms: ["console age", "age of the new technological generation"]
definition: Age of the console (months). The startup phase is usually characterized by a low number of available game titles for the new generation, and as more titles for the new console become available, consumers will buy the console for its supply of new games rather than for the existence of a large installed base of outdated games.

name: Technological progress between generations
authors_terms: ["technological progress", "relative improvement of CPU to parent console", "technological leap between generations"]
definition: We derive IMPR CPU j1 j 1 as the percentage improvement of the CPU speed compared to the CPU speed of the compatible parent generation. An old game will be a worse substitute as the technological frontier is pushed out.

name: Major record label
definition: Major record labels specialize in releasing music targeted at large groups of consumers and have traditionally utilized high-cost, high-promotion approaches aimed at commercializing music products with broad expected market appeal and high revenue potential.

name: Independent record label
definition: Independent record labels employ lower-cost approaches; for example, forgoing attempts to obtain radio airplay, allowing them to release products expected to appeal to smaller, niche groups of consumers.

name: Leveraging previously successful artists
authors_terms: ["selectivity", "leveraging already-successful artists", "share of already-successful artists", "leverage previously-successful artists"]
definition: Greater selectivity, i.e., increasing the extent to which record labels leverage prior success, reduces the costs of discovery and increases the certainty of revenues. The authors measure the extent to which record labels leverage previously-successful artists for their music releases within a year, in essence the extent to which organizations are shifting away from 'discovery' of new-to-the-world artists.

name: Number of music releases
authors_terms: ["number of music releases", "number of albums released", "number of new music products released", "release volume"]
definition: The number of albums released by a music organization, by year and by label type (i.e., independent labels versus major labels).

name: Music release success
authors_terms: ["success of releases", "current success", "relative success in the Billboard top 200 or top 50", "chart success"]
definition: Outcomes are measured using data from the weekly Billboard top 200 and Billboard top 50 rankings; the number of weekly appearances in these rankings provides a relative measure of success based on U.S. sales ranks.

name: Formal control
definition: Formal control refers to 'officially sanctioned (usually codified) institutional mechanisms, such as written rules, standard operating systems, and procedural directives-visible, objective forms of control'. In the context of strategic initiative teams, formal behavior control entails the establishment of explicit rules, procedures, and policies for strategic initiatives, whereas formal outcome control entails deadlines, goals, and cost budgets.

name: Informal control
authors_terms: ["informal control", "informal behavior control", "informal outcome control", "informal clan control"]
definition: Informal control refers to 'unwritten, unofficial, less objective, uncodified forms of control'. Informal behavior control is a noncodified but deliberate attempt by which managers influence the means to achieve desired ends, and informal outcome control is directed at the results of behavior.

name: Degree of exploration
definition: The degree of exploration is 'the degree to which controlled tasks draw on existing internal knowledge (lower exploration) versus knowledge that is new to the firm (higher exploration)'.

name: Initiative team performance
authors_terms: ["initiative team performance", "performance of strategic initiative teams", "performance of growth initiatives"]
definition: Initiative team performance is evaluated as the extent to which a number of goals and objectives were achieved by the growth initiative, on a seven-point scale from 'very unsuccessful' to 'very successful'.

name: Corporate spin-off
definition: Spin-offs are a type of divestiture in which a divesting ('parent') firm separates one of its divisions or business units into a new, publicly traded company by distributing shares in the new entity (the 'spin-off firm') pro rata to its existing shareholders.

name: Capital allocation efficiency
authors_terms: ["efficiency of capital allocation decisions", "efficiency of capital allocation", "efficiency of managers' capital allocation decisions", "sensitivity of capital expenditures to investment opportunities"]
definition: The efficiency of capital allocation decisions is defined as the sensitivity of capital expenditures to investment opportunities; positive (negative) coefficients indicate alignment (misalignment) between segments' capital allocation decisions and segments' investment opportunities.

name: Segment capital expenditures
definition: The capital investments made by business units in diversified firms, measured by their capital expenditures and scaled by the segment's total assets.

name: Investment opportunities
definition: The investment opportunities in the industries in which business units operate, typically represented by the median Tobin's q of single-business firms operating in the same Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code; this variable measures the investment opportunities available to the individual business units operated by the firms in the sample.

name: Time since spin-off
authors_terms: ["time", "After", "After 1", "After 2", "After 3", "years after the completion of a spin-off"]
definition: The time elapsed since the completion of a spin-off, captured by indicators for the first, second, and third years after completion relative to the three years before completion.

name: Pre-spin-off diversification
authors_terms: ["number of businesses", "number of segments", "#Segments", "diversification", "pre-spin-off diversification levels"]
definition: The number of businesses in which the divesting firm operated prior to the completion of the spin-off; the magnitude of the attentional gain produced by a spin-off is argued to be contingent on this number.

name: Political campaign contributions
authors_terms: ["Campaign Contributions", "financial campaign contributions to elected politicians", "political campaign contributions"]
definition: The monthly sum of political campaign contributions made by a firm's top management team and political action committee to state politicians.

name: Stakeholder contestation in regulatory hearings
definition: The degree of opposition from organized stakeholders that participate in regulatory agency policy-making processes, operationalized as the number of intervenors that participated in a firm's rate reviews.

name: Regulator experience
definition: The extent of regulators' prior experience in office, which determines their information processing capabilities in scrutinizing stakeholder evidence and claims.

name: Time to reappointment
authors_terms: ["Time to Reappointment", "length of time until reappointment of the regulator"]
definition: The length of time remaining before regulators' reappointment dates, which determines their responsiveness to the policy ideals of elected political institutions.

name: Industry potential for interdependency
authors_terms: ["interdependency", "industries' potential for interdependency", "potential for interdependency in activities", "industry-level interdependency"]
definition: Interdependencies are high when the value of conducting one or more activities in a particular manner depends on how other activities are conducted. Industries' potential for interdependency is a latent construct, which is theoretical in nature; it cannot be directly observed and is inferred from variables that are observed and directly measured.

name: Industry average profitability
definition: MeanQ is defined in LRL as log Qit, which is the natural log of the average Qit within each four-digit SIC code industry. The authors also describe it as the industry average profitability that is predicted to peak at moderate levels of an industry's potential for interdependency.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The firm-level profitability ln(Qit), referred to as LogQ; Qit is the ratio of the market valuation of the firm to the value of tangible assets, commonly referred to as Tobin's q.

name: Patent effectiveness
definition: Industries vary in the effectiveness of patents as a means of capturing and protecting the competitive advantages of new or improved processes and products.

name: Carbon goal announcements
definition: In response, some firms have started to aim for carbon neutrality (eliminate or offset (mostly) direct firm emissions, scope 1 and 2) or net-zero emissions (additionally eliminate upstream and downstream scope 3 emissions and only offset emissions that cannot be eliminated). We collectively refer to such announcements as carbon goal announcements.

name: Cumulative abnormal stock returns
definition: This study applies the Fama and French four-factor model and regresses each firm's stock returns on the relevant market index as well as the size, value, and momentum factor over the estimation period t - 255 to t - 11 relative to the event day t = 0. Intercept alpha i is the abnormal return (AR) of stock i on day t, and CAR is computed for each stock over event windows of varying lengths.

name: Business impact
definition: The most common concern in news coverage related to transition risk is the business impact topic. It includes a variety of transition risk concerns that could impact businesses (e.g., climate legislation, carbon taxes), and henceforth we refer to signals about the business impact in media coverage simply as business impact.

name: Current emissions volume
definition: Investors can proxy the potential for transition risk reduction by considering the firm's existing emissions volume in the relevant scopes. Consistent with prior literature, we use emissions as a proxy for transition risk.

name: Announcement timing
definition: Announcement timing measures the number of days since the first carbon goal announcement by any firm within the same industry.

name: Personal absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["absorptive capacity", "personal absorptive capacity", "inventor experience", "experience in a field", "interpersonal absorptive capacity"]
definition: We define interpersonal AC as individual experience in a field that benefits from close geographical proximity to a living inventor in that same field. We measure this one type of AC as the pertinent and prior experience and 'personal absorptive capacity' of a firm's inventors.

name: Geographic proximity to a living coinventor
definition: Identification comes from observing citation likelihood in regions around still-living coauthors (where the external source of interpersonal knowledge remains available or still turned 'on') relative to local citations in regions around the deceased inventor (where the source of interpersonal knowledge becomes unavailable).

name: Interpersonal knowledge flow
definition: This is possible if one accepts the convention that a citation between patents correlates with some type of knowledge transfer and can provide an empirical (although admittedly quite noisy) proxy for the flow of interpersonal knowledge from one inventor to another.

name: Recency of inventor experience
authors_terms: ["more recent experience", "newer capacity", "recent AC", "recently gained experience", "age or recency of a firm's AC"]
definition: If AC increases with experience and learning, then it will be strongest for recently gained experience and learning. The advantage of absorptive capacity will be greater when that capacity is newer.

name: Multidisciplinary knowledge
authors_terms: ["multidisciplinary technologies", "knowledge that spans multiple disciplines", "multiple-technology knowledge", "complex knowledge"]
definition: The assumption is that multidisciplinary technologies are newer, more complex, and difficult to transfer. Knowledge that is more difficult to transfer should benefit more from absorptive capacity because the recipient will be better able to comprehend at least part of the original context.

name: Within-firm knowledge flow
authors_terms: ["within-firm knowledge flows", "internal knowledge diffusion", "within-firm knowledge diffusion", "knowledge transfers within firms"]
definition: Knowledge flows within firms should localize less and be less sensitive to individual absorptive capacity. We measure within-firm knowledge diffusion as citations from a patent within the same firm.

name: Termination costs
definition: Employment protection legislation refers to the legal and regulatory measures designed to enhance job security by making employee terminations costly for employers. The Portuguese severance pay reform of 2011 reduced these costs for newly hired workers.

name: Startup hiring
authors_terms: ["Hired by startup", "being hired by a startup rather than an established firm", "startup hires", "startup joiners"]
definition: The probability that a new hire joins a new venture (defined as a firm five years old or younger) rather than an incumbent firm.

name: Gender
definition: The gender variable, measured and reported by Quadro de Pessoal, identifies individuals as a woman or a man but does not identify additional genders; it refers to the gender reported in the identification documents used in Portugal.

name: Entrepreneurial experience
definition: Whether the focal employee was a startup owner at any point during the five years preceding the hiring year.

name: Industry female representation
authors_terms: ["industry female representation", "industries with greater female representation", "female-dominated industries"]
definition: The percentage of female employees in the industry where the employer operates during the hiring year.

name: Industry female representation in startups
authors_terms: ["industry female representation in startups", "industries with greater female representation in startups"]
definition: The percentage of female employees among all startup employees in the industry where the employer operates during the hiring year.

name: Local manager hiring
definition: Local manager hiring (LMH) refers to decentralizing hiring decisions to local business unit managers, rather than relying on the headquarters' human resource department to make decisions. Under LMH, local managers are responsible for sourcing, interviewing, and selecting candidates based on their understanding of team needs and local operating conditions.

name: Individual productivity
definition: A worker's productivity is the sum of two independent components, where generic ability and the matching quality of a worker with a particular position are captured separately. Individual productivity was measured using each worker's average monthly sales and their product-return probability.

name: Productivity variance
definition: The dispersion in productivity among those newly hired through LMH. The authors argue that LMH increases the dispersion of hiring outcomes: while some units benefit from strong matches, others suffer from costly hiring mistakes.

name: Manager information precision
authors_terms: ["information precision", "precision of the local manager's information", "local information", "local knowledge"]
definition: The precision of the local manager's information, which includes an improved ability to evaluate an applicant's fit for a position. Repeat customer share and manager tenure proxy the precision of managers' local information.

name: Incentive alignment
definition: The degree to which the local manager's interests are aligned with the firm's interests; the bias parameter k measures the degree of misalignment between the local manager's incentives and the firm's interests. Pretreatment store sales and distance to the regional headquarters proxy alignment between managerial and firm incentives.

name: Recruiting opportunity cost
definition: A local manager incurs an opportunity cost for spending time on hiring rather than on performing directly productive work, such as sales. Busyness, measured as the ratio of active customers to store personnel, captures the opportunity cost of managers' recruiting time.

name: Manager welfare
definition: The manager's welfare from LMH, which the authors argue falls as the manager's opportunity cost for time spent on hiring rises. It is assessed through store managers' self-reported overall job satisfaction.

name: Store sales
definition: Store-level productivity was measured as total monthly sales generated by all store staff.

name: Employee job satisfaction
definition: Self-reported overall job satisfaction of nutritionists (store employees), collected in the before, during, and after experiment surveys. In the pre- and post-RCT surveys the authors asked store managers and nutritionists about their overall job satisfaction.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: Geographic proximity not only increases the chance of a serendipitous interaction, but also lowers the cost of a scheduled one. When colocated, joint execution costs are also lower, as coordination, monitoring, and the transfer of complex information can all rely on more frequent, face-to-face interactions.

name: Search costs
definition: In this context, search costs are defined as the frictions scientists incur in finding new collaborators and collaboration opportunities. A reduction in search costs should therefore induce an increase in the probability of collaboration between two labs and possibly shift over time the collaboration portfolios of the scientists affected.

name: Joint execution costs
definition: Joint execution costs include the cost of face-to-face meetings, coordination, monitoring, and transfer of complex information between teams of scientists. The first effect of a reduction in joint execution costs is, as in the case of search costs, an increase in the probability of collaboration.

name: Collaboration between labs
authors_terms: ["collaboration", "joint research", "probability of collaboration", "number of collaborations", "rate of collaboration"]
definition: Collaboration across labs is a rare event, and only 0.4% of all lab pairs collaborate in any given year, receiving on average 0.20 citations per lab-pair-year.

name: Knowledge space similarity
authors_terms: ["proximity in knowledge space", "similarity in keywords", "similarity in cited references", "cosine similarity between vectors of cited references (or keywords)", "overlap in the references they cite"]
definition: Cited references and keyword data are then used to create measures of proximity in knowledge space between the labs. Research agendas can be mapped into knowledge space using keywords and cited references.

name: Low-impact research output
authors_terms: ["lower-quality projects", "left tail of the outcome distribution", "selection effect", "projects at the low end of the distribution"]
definition: On the one hand, lower execution costs locally may induce scientists to engage in marginal, lower-value projects. Conditional on an idea being developed, this should lead to an increase on the left tail of the outcome distribution.

name: High-impact research output
definition: On the other hand, if scientists can improve a project more efficiently when colocated (e.g., through additional face-to-face meetings, better knowledge transfer, team coordination, etc.), this leads to the expected value of colocated projects being higher for any underlying idea quality.

name: Franchisee management
definition: The organizational form (e.g., company management, franchising) used to manage an outlet, which varies from site to site within dual-distribution chains. Dual distribution is a firm's simultaneous use of a vertically integrated channel and a contractually based channel to distribute and sell its goods or services.

name: Room-night price
authors_terms: ["price", "average price charged for one room-night", "room-night prices"]
definition: The average price charged for one room-night by each hotel in each monthly observation.

name: Brand quality tier
authors_terms: ["brand quality", "quality tiers", "upper tiers", "lower tiers", "upper quality tier brands", "lower tier brands"]
definition: Dual-distribution brands are found in four STR-defined quality categories: upper upscale, upscale, midscale, and economy. The first two are combined as the 'upper tiers' and the latter two as the 'lower tiers.'

name: Price-based brand externality
definition: A brand externality is said to exist when the attributes of one unit of a brand's good or service affects demand for the brand as a whole. In the context of multioutlet branded chains, the presence of a price-based brand externality implies that the prices chosen by managers at one outlet will affect demand at other same-brand outlets.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was measured by number of employees and is empirically treated both categorically and log linearly in the data analysis. A cutoff of 250 employees was utilized in categorical analyses.

name: Performance-contingent compensation
authors_terms: ["performance-contingent contracts", "individual performance based", "output based", "group performance based", "pay-for-performance"]
definition: Contracts that compensate individual performance rather than hidden behaviors and attributes, or that base pay on the performance of the project, organizational unit or firm rather than on seniority.

name: Engineer talent and ideas
definition: An engineer's ability, skill and performance: education-related ability measures, the uniqueness of technical skills, and correlates of the possession of valued skills and information such as awards, patents and publications.

name: Engineer effort
definition: Variance in effort levels and in the composition of effort may also greatly affect performance in R&D. Yet, effort in R&D is often as difficult to assess as individual ability, skill, and information.

name: Yearly salary
definition: The engineer's yearly salary, modeled as a function of tenure, experience, engineer type, location, firm size and various performance, ability, skill and effort measures.

name: Contract risk
authors_terms: ["contract risk", "perceived contract risk", "risk of job loss", "bankruptcy likelihood", "layoff likelihood"]
definition: Performance contingent contracts should involve greater risk for employees. This contract risk was measured in part as the perceived risk of job loss through bankruptcy or layoff.

name: Strategic group membership
definition: A strategic group is defined as a set of firms competing within an industry on the basis of similar combinations of scope and resource commitments.

name: Performance level
definition: Performance is treated as a multi-dimensional concept, so several performance measures are considered, reflecting the multi-dimensional nature of performance; the study examines levels of performance, levels of risk exposure and levels of risk-adjusted performance.

name: Risk exposure
definition: The level of risk-taking associated with a strategy; different strategies might result in different levels of performance but may entail different risk exposure, so risk measures were obtained by calculating the standard deviation about the temporal mean of each performance measure for each period of stable strategic group structure.

name: Risk-adjusted performance
definition: Performance considered from a risk-return perspective, obtained by dividing average firm performance for each of the three indicators by their respective standard deviation.

name: Frequency of communication
authors_terms: ["frequency of communication", "frequency of interaction", "technical communication frequency"]
definition: How often researchers on a project communicate technically with other projects; respondents were asked to report their technical communication with other projects only and were told not to include written and/or social communication.

name: Centrality of communication
authors_terms: ["centrality", "location within the communication network", "centrality of communication"]
definition: Centrality is therefore defined as the position (in this study the project) within the network at which communications are directed; in other words; more central projects receive greater numbers of communications while less central projects receive fewer.

name: Project performance
authors_terms: ["project performance", "technical performance of the projects", "successful project performance"]
definition: The dependent variable was project performance as perceived by multiple observers, the top managers who were responsible for and familiar with the projects and who evaluated the technical performance of the projects.

name: Age of project participants
definition: The age of project members; the median age of the project members was 42 years and age is used as an explanatory variable for the frequency and centrality of communication.

name: Educational attainment of project participants
definition: The education of project members, described by the degrees they had received (of the 146 researchers, 51 had doctoral degrees, 58 master's and 37 bachelor's degrees), and used as an explanatory variable for the frequency and centrality of communication.

name: Intrinsic valuation ratio
authors_terms: ["intrinsic valuation ratio", "intrinsic value to book ratio", "V/B", "market to book ratio", "M/B", "valuation ratio"]
definition: Value is a rationally determined or economic estimate based on the expected cash stream of a firm discounted by a factor which incorporates inflation and the nondiversifiable risk of the firm. The ratio of intrinsic value to the book value of a firm's equity (V/B) is represented in this study by the market price to book ratio (M/B).

name: Return on Equity
definition: Return on Equity is represented by the ratio of year-end net income (after interest, after taxes) to year-beginning equity. Value is only created when the rate of return (ROE) exceeds the corresponding cost of the investment (KE).

name: Cost of Equity
definition: The discount factor applied to the firm's expected cash stream; as specified by CAPM, the discount factor can be determined by Cost of Equity = Risk-free Rate + Systematic risk (equity risk premium).

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth", "growth in dividends per share", "growth in sales", "growth in earnings per share", "growth in assets", "growth in equity per share"]
definition: Growth in five measures, dividends per share, sales, earnings per share, assets and equity per share, are included in this study; each measure reflects the average annual growth rate over the past three years.

name: Technology policy
definition: An aggressive technology policy, defined by the authors as a preemptive, long-range strategy for technological innovation.

name: Concentration of technical specialists
authors_terms: ["concentration of technical specialists", "concentration of specialists", "concentration of technical and engineering group(s)"]
definition: The concentration of technical specialists in the organization, which the model proposes is promoted by an aggressive technology policy and in turn supports the preinnovation conditions necessary for radical process adoption.

name: Innovation champion
definition: The presence of an innovation champion for a particular technology, the first preinnovation condition in the differentiated model.

name: Technology-organization congruence
definition: The degree of fit between a particular innovation and an organization based on the opinion of key organization members of the technology on several important attributes.

name: Market dominated growth strategy
authors_terms: ["market dominated growth strategy", "(market dominated) growth strategy"]
definition: A growth strategy dominated by market concerns, one of the strategy and size variables of the incremental innovation half of the differentiated model.

name: Diversification
definition: Product diversification policy, one of the strategy and size variables of the incremental innovation half of the model.

name: Organization size
definition: Organization size, measured as the natural logarithm of the number of year-round employees.

name: Traditional structural arrangements
definition: The known organization structure dimensions, complexity, formalization, and centralization, which the authors describe as the structural arrangements of the incremental innovation half of the model.

name: Complexity
definition: One of the known organization structure dimensions named by the authors (complexity, formalization, centralization); organization size significantly accounts for 61% of the variance in complexity.

name: Formalization
definition: One of the known organization structure dimensions named by the authors (complexity, formalization, centralization).

name: Centralization
definition: One of the known organization structure dimensions named by the authors (complexity, formalization, centralization).

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["new product introduction", "new product (service) introduction", "introduction of new products"]
definition: New product (service) introduction, the innovation outcome of the incremental innovation half of the differentiated model.

name: Incremental process innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["incremental process adoption", "incremental innovation", "incremental departures from existing process technology"]
definition: Adoption of incremental departures from existing process technology, the incremental outcome in the differentiated model.

name: Radical innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["radical process adoption", "adoption of radical process innovation", "radical process and packaging innovation adoption", "radical packaging adoption", "adoption of radical packaging innovation"]
definition: Adoption of radical process and packaging innovation: innovation that incorporates technology which is a clear, risky departure from existing practice, new to the adopting unit and to the referent group of organizations.

name: Frequency of communication
authors_terms: ["frequency of communication", "frequency of communication among the principal investigators"]
definition: The principal investigators reported the frequency of communication with other principal investigators; based on their responses they were classified into high, moderate and low frequency of communication levels.

name: Centrality in communication network
authors_terms: ["project centrality", "centrality of communication", "aggregate centrality of communication"]
definition: The position of a particular project within the communication network; projects to which most communications are directed will have more information useful to the problem's solution.

name: Diversity of communication
authors_terms: ["diversity of communication", "diversity of the principal investigator's contacts", "aggregate diversity of communication"]
definition: Not only the frequency of the principal investigator's contact, but also the diversity of his/her contact plays a major role in the success of innovation, because the researcher needs to be aware of the interests of different groups and their potential contributions to his project.

name: Formality of communication
authors_terms: ["formality of communication", "amount of written communication", "aggregate formality of communication"]
definition: The formality of communication among the principal investigators, expected to have a negative impact on problem solving since the more formal the communication the less frequent its rate.

name: Interproject cohesiveness
authors_terms: ["interproject cohesiveness", "cohesiveness of the communication network", "network cohesiveness"]
definition: Social interaction between the research personnel of several projects may result in more cohesive communications; such a cohesive communications system built within a network of interactive projects will produce greater degrees of innovation as compared with networks of projects with lower degrees of cohesiveness.

name: Project success
authors_terms: ["project success", "success of technological innovation", "aggregate success of the projects", "network success"]
definition: Multiple measures were used to evaluate the success of each project; the principal investigators, the program directors, and the project monitors were independently asked to indicate the success of the project.

name: Need recognition
definition: Recognition by organizational members of a need for change, usually triggered by the emergence of a performance gap, i.e., a problem or opportunity. In this study the existence of an organizational need for the practices was captured through a surrogate measure, the complexity of the software development environment.

name: Means recognition
definition: Recognition of a technological means that promises to enhance organizational performance; means recognition reflected simply whether or not the respondents were familiar with a practice (a yes-no response).

name: Management attitude toward the innovation
authors_terms: ["management attitude toward a particular process innovation", "favorable management attitudes", "top management attitude", "management support"]
definition: The attitude of an organization's 'power elite' toward a particular process innovation; innovation invariably requires the reallocation of scarce organizational resources and without the active support of management it is unlikely such allocations will occur. It was measured by having the software managers characterize each of the practices along a Likert-like scale on six items.

name: Organizational receptivity toward change
authors_terms: ["receptivity toward change", "member receptivity toward change", "organizational receptivity toward change"]
definition: The general receptivity toward change held by an innovating organization's members, which has been found to be an important determinant of innovation success. The four items used addressed the degree to which an organization was flexible and continually adapted to change, examined its most basic assumptions, searched for fresh ways of looking at problems, and dealt with new problems and tasks constructively.

name: Process innovation use
authors_terms: ["use of modern software practices", "innovation success", "use of process innovations", "use of the practices", "process innovation"]
definition: The extent to which modern software practices (method improvements in task and managerial behaviors) have been incorporated into task behaviors, i.e., the extent to which each practice was currently applied within the software group.

name: Process innovation type
authors_terms: ["technical process innovation", "administrative process innovation", "technical and administrative innovations", "technical and administrative process innovations"]
definition: Modern software practices are directed at two quite distinct behaviors: methods or procedures for designing and developing software, and methods or procedures for managing these technical activities; these distinct behaviors respectively transpire within an organization's technical and administrative cores.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: Entrepreneurship is a multidimensional concept encompassing the firm's actions relating to product-market and technological innovation, risk taking, and proactiveness. An entrepreneurial firm is one that engages in product-market innovation, undertakes somewhat risky ventures, and is first to come up with proactive innovations, beating competitors to the punch.

name: Innovation
definition: One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship: the firm's product-market and technological innovation.

name: Proactiveness
definition: One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship: being first to come up with proactive innovations, beating competitors to the punch, rather than imitating their moves.

name: Risk taking
definition: One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship: the extent to which the firm undertakes somewhat risky ventures rather than being highly risk averse.

name: Locus of control
definition: A personality characteristic of the leader; the more internal the executive, that is, the more he feels he has control over his environment and his destiny, the more entrepreneurial his behaviour. If he believes that outcomes influencing his life are principally due to chance or to elements beyond his control, he is much less likely to take risks or to be innovative and proactive.

name: Centralization
definition: The extent to which decision making power is centralized, or arrogated, in the hands of one or two top administrators.

name: Environmental scanning
definition: Engaging in much scanning of the environment to discover important challenges and opportunities; in Simple firms it is the leader's knowledge of the environment, that is, of customer wants, sources of supply, and competitor strategies.

name: Technocratization
definition: The use of technocrats such as scientists and engineers in creating product and technological innovations; it also reflects the extent to which leaders are frequently in touch with scientists, engineers or even marketing experts.

name: Explicitness of product-market strategy
authors_terms: ["explicitness of strategy", "explicitness of product-market strategy", "explicit and well articulated product-market strategy"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's product-market strategy is explicitly articulated and formally elaborated; where strategies are clear and well articulated they draw attention to the big picture: the distinctive competence of the firm, its ultimate mission, its business scope, and present and future target markets.

name: Strategic integration
definition: The extent to which an established strategy tends to guide decision making and is resistant to change.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environments in which customer tastes, product-service technologies, and competitive weapons often change unpredictably.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: The extent to which the firm's markets are hostile; ease of entry makes markets hostile and the small size of firms leaves them susceptible to threats from competitors.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: The diversity of the firm's market; because product-market innovations are common in such firms, managers often find themselves dealing with a rather diverse array of customers, that is, with a heterogeneous market.

name: Organizational structure
definition: The structural configuration of the firm, ranging from mechanistic (centralized, restricted hierarchical communication, high integration, low differentiation, tight formal controls) to organic (delegation of authority to lower level personnel, technocratization, scanning, differentiation, open internal communication).

name: Differentiation
definition: The extent to which the firm is highly differentiated, so that diverse contingencies posed by the environment require individuals and departments with very different abilities; it provides the mix of skills necessary to develop innovative ideas.

name: Internal communication
definition: The extent of extensive and open internal communication among organizational members so that they can work jointly on complex innovative projects.

name: Organizational age
definition: Age refers to the number of years since the organization established production facilities for the product lines covered in this study. The organizations studied were divided into a group of older and a group of younger organizations.

name: Mechanistic structure
definition: Structure refers to the pattern of the relationships among various activities or subsystems within an organization designed to attain organizational objectives effectively. Taken together, studies suggest four structural dimensions-complexity, formalization, centralization and integration-which also reflect the concept of organic and mechanistic patterns.

name: Operations technology adaptability
definition: Operations technology refers to the techniques an organization uses in its workflow activities (producing and distributing the output) or equipping and scheduling of activities in the workflow. Adaptability refers to the degree of flexibility in operations technology.

name: Indigenous technical capability
definition: Indigenous technical capability refers to the degree of indigenous capability in developing new products.

name: Technological innovation
definition: Innovation is defined here as the number of technological changes in products and processes during one year.

name: Organizational size
definition: Size refers to the number of workers in the organization.

name: Supplier component importance
authors_terms: ["supplier component", "supplier component of the task environment", "raw material suppliers", "equipment suppliers"]
definition: The task environment refers to individuals, organizations, and other social systems that are external to the organization but directly affect the formulation and attainment of its objectives; the supplier component is one of its components.

name: Government component importance
definition: The task environment refers to individuals, organizations, and other social systems that are external to the organization but directly affect the formulation and attainment of its objectives; the government component is one of its components.

name: Customer component importance
definition: The task environment refers to individuals, organizations, and other social systems that are external to the organization but directly affect the formulation and attainment of its objectives; the customer component is one of its components.

name: Competitor component importance
definition: The task environment refers to individuals, organizations, and other social systems that are external to the organization but directly affect the formulation and attainment of its objectives; the competitor component is one of its components.

name: Technology component importance
definition: The task environment refers to individuals, organizations, and other social systems that are external to the organization but directly affect the formulation and attainment of its objectives; the technology component is one of its components.

name: Centralization
definition: Within a software development group, centralization and formalization pertain to the amount of discretion given analysts and programmers in performing assigned duties as members of a project team. In a highly centralized group, most of the decisions regarding project planning, control and selection of development methods would be made by the group's management.

name: Formalization
definition: Within a software development group, centralization and formalization pertain to the amount of discretion given analysts and programmers in performing assigned duties as members of a project team. In a highly formalized group, software standards are specified that dictate the procedures to follow in many of the activities comprising software development.

name: Organizational innovation
definition: An organizational manipulation, i.e., extent of centralization and formalization, may facilitate or impede innovative behavior depending on specific innovation-organization interactions, in this case innovation phase, innovation compatibility with organizational members and the organizational interest served by the innovation. Innovation is a multi-phased process: initiation of an innovative idea or proposal; adoption of an innovation as represented by an organizational mandate for change; and implementation of the innovation such that it becomes ingrained within organizational behaviors.

name: Technical innovation
authors_terms: ["technical innovations", "technical MSP", "MSP directed at the technical core", "incompatible technical innovations"]
definition: MSP directed at the technical core (such as top down development, structured design and structured review) generally require analysts and programmers to adopt radically new behaviors; as analysts and programmers have tended to not welcome such change these technical innovations are classified as being incompatible with the technical core. As the first three MSP are techniques employed in designing and developing software, they were classified (by the author) as being technical innovations.

name: Administrative innovation
authors_terms: ["administrative innovations", "administrative MSP", "MSP directed at the administrative core"]
definition: The opposite reaction has been observed from the administrative core regarding the administrative MSP (such as chief programmer team, configuration management and unit development folder) with software managers generally expressing very favorable attitudes. As the latter three MSP are management mechanisms, they were classified as being administrative innovations.

name: Mechanistic overlay
definition: Pierce and Delbecq suggest that this paradox might be resolved by instituting organizational 'overlays'—that is, complementing an organic organization with a mechanistic overlay, such as a structured decision body. The presence of a mechanistic overlay was identified by whether analysts/programmers were maintained as fixed teams, i.e., a formal structure existed through which innovations could be channeled, or were assigned to new projects on an as-needed basis.

name: Organic overlay
definition: Pierce and Delbecq suggest that this paradox might be resolved by instituting organizational 'overlays'—that is, complementing a mechanistic organization with an organic overlay, such as a venture group. The presence of an organic overlay was identified by the existence of a formal group whose organizational role was to search for methods to improve the software development process and introduce these methods throughout the software group, i.e., a venture group.

name: Political orientation of management
authors_terms: ["political orientation", "political orientation of management", "business and political orientations", "business-political orientation"]
definition: Managers of SOEs must be concerned both with managing the business and with managing public support. The greater the relative emphasis on managing public support, the stronger is the political orientation in our terminology; the greater the relative emphasis on managing the business, the stronger is the business orientation.

name: External orientation of management
authors_terms: ["external orientation of management", "internal and external orientation", "internal versus external managerial orientation"]
definition: An organization may concentrate primarily on its own needs and goals with little effort to study and respond to the requirements of outside publics, or it can focus on, and respond to, the needs and concerns of its major publics. Movement along the axis from B to C implies a greater relative emphasis on the public and a stronger external orientation of management.

name: External orientation in business management
authors_terms: ["external orientation in business management", "external orientation in managing the business"]
definition: The external orientation of management in managing the business, that is, whether in managing the business top management focuses on the needs of the enterprise or on the needs of the customers.

name: External orientation in political management
authors_terms: ["external orientation in political management", "external orientation in managing public support"]
definition: The external orientation of management in managing public support; the authors hypothesize that management with an external orientation in managing the business is also likely to have an external orientation in managing public support.

name: Sales goal emphasis
authors_terms: ["sales goals", "profit-sales goals", "emphasis on sales rather than profit goals"]
definition: The likelihood that the enterprise will emphasize sales rather than profit goals.

name: Prices relative to costs
authors_terms: ["relative prices", "low prices relative to costs", "high prices"]
definition: The likelihood that the enterprise's strategy will be characterized by relatively low prices.

name: Goal stability
authors_terms: ["stability of goals", "unstable goals", "instability in its goals"]
definition: Instability in the enterprise's goals, expected from frequent shifts in priorities following the political mood.

name: Goal and policy clarity
authors_terms: ["clarity of goals and policies", "general and vague goals"]
definition: The likelihood that the enterprise's objectives and policies will be general and vague rather than specific and clearly stated.

name: Regularity of performance evaluation
definition: The likelihood that performance evaluation will take place at irregular intervals.

name: Timing of support cultivation
authors_terms: ["strategy over time in cultivating public support", "cultivating support prior to action", "ask for support before acting"]
definition: The likelihood that management will ask for support before acting on a new plan, rather than acting first and cultivating support during or after implementation.

name: Top management background
authors_terms: ["background of top-management", "top managers from public enterprises"]
definition: The likelihood that top managers will come from public rather than private enterprises.

name: Gatekeeper presence
definition: Gatekeepers are those key individuals who are both strongly connected to internal colleagues and strongly linked to external domains; they are individuals in the communication network who are capable of understanding and translating contrasting coding schemes.

name: Project performance
definition: A subjective measure of the overall technical performance of a project, based on managers' informed judgements using criteria such as schedule, budget, and cost performance, innovativeness, adaptability, and the ability to cooperate with other areas of the organization.

name: Project task characteristics
authors_terms: ["project task characteristics", "locally defined tasks", "universally defined tasks", "task characteristics"]
definition: In R&D settings, tasks can differ along several dimensions, including time span of feedback, specific vs. general problem-solving orientation, and generation of new knowledge vs. utilization of existing knowledge and experience; the task categories form a universal (research) to local (technical service) task dimension.

name: External communication
definition: Extra-organizational (i.e. external) communication is the sum of the reported communication to professional and operational areas.

name: Project funding change
authors_terms: ["change in project funding", "project funding changes", "mean absolute change", "mean absolute percent change", "adjusted funding"]
definition: Recommended and actual funding decisions for applied research projects at the several points in the budget cycle, and the changes in those funding levels between decision points; mean absolute changes 'establish the average magnitude of actual dollar changes in project funding between decision points'.

name: Organizational level
definition: The hierarchical position of the participants in the decision; individuals involved are 'in different organizational levels, organizational units (at the same hierarchical level), and/or geographic locations'.

name: Budget cycle phase
definition: The stages of the budget cycle; 'the cycle is divided into several phases in which the budget is developed, refined, apportioned, and reallocated among research projects'.

name: Project size
definition: The funding level of a project, distinguished by the authors as smaller (lower funded) versus larger (higher funded) projects; 'the size of project is an important variable in determining the extent of relative change in project funding'.

name: Prior project funding information
authors_terms: ["prior project funding information", "prior project funding levels", "previous changes", "prior changes"]
definition: Earlier funding levels and earlier changes made in the cycle; the authors examine 'if these changes are related to prior project funding levels or to changes made by other entities'.

name: Final allocation
definition: 'Final allocation (13) consists of the released program following reallocation by all entities.'

name: Total research budget
definition: The total research funds available in the cycle; 'changes in total research budget generally are beyond the control of the hierarchical entities studied in this analysis'.

name: Student achievement growth
authors_terms: ["achievement growth", "changes in student achievement levels", "pre- to post-test achievement changes", "project success"]
definition: Pre- to post-test gains in achievement scores, measured by the Comprehensive Test of Basic Skills and used as the basic criterion measure in the study as an indicator of achievement growth; also used as the measure of the success of the program.

name: Parent satisfaction with decisional participation
authors_terms: ["parental groups' expectations concerning decisional participation levels", "satisfaction with current decisional participation levels", "decisional dissatisfaction"]
definition: The condition of decisional participation as experienced by parents, indexed by the absolute differences between the number of decisions in which each person currently participated and those in which he or she wished to participate, so that a higher score indicates greater dissatisfaction.

name: Teacher satisfaction with decisional participation
authors_terms: ["teacher expectations concerning decisional participation levels", "teacher satisfaction with their current state of decisional participation", "decisional dissatisfaction"]
definition: The condition of decisional participation as experienced by teachers, indexed by the absolute differences between the number of decisions in which each person currently participated and those in which he or she wished to participate, so that a higher score indicates greater dissatisfaction.

name: Teacher predisposition to accept change
authors_terms: ["personal predispositions of teachers to accept change", "willingness to accept change", "personal factors of teachers", "individual characteristics of teachers"]
definition: Those personal factors of teachers which have been associated with the willingness to accept change and innovation, examined through authoritarianism, interpersonal trust and job involvement.

name: Organizational health
authors_terms: ["organizational health", "organization health", "manageable tension levels and high commitment levels"]
definition: Organizational conditions of manageable tension levels and high commitment levels in the organization; two indicators of organizational health were gathered in the study.

name: Perceived teacher autonomy
authors_terms: ["perceptions and preferences of teacher autonomy", "perceived current teacher autonomy levels"]
definition: An indication of perceived current teacher autonomy levels derived from ranking how a series of role performers—including school principals, superintendents, the community, and the teacher herself—currently influenced daily teaching activities; the higher the rank, the more autonomous the teacher was perceived.

name: Attitudes toward the school system
authors_terms: ["attitudes", "attitudinal differences", "attitude toward the school system, performance contracting and the school principal"]
definition: Semantic differential scales yielding three general factors of meaning: the individual's judgement concerning the desirability of various school system issues, the judgement concerning the current existence of each condition, and its importance.

name: Violent traumatic event in the community
definition: Events in the organization's community that can profoundly influence organizational members' psychological states by instigating negative emotions: violent traumatic events such as mass shootings and domestic terrorism. They are sudden, place specific, and personally meaningful to decision-makers.

name: Performance below aspirations
definition: Performance relative to aspirations, where organizational members classify performance as unsatisfactory using aspiration levels as minimally acceptable performance goals; a negative attainment discrepancy is performance falling short of those aspirations.

name: Performance above aspirations
definition: Instances where performance exceeds expectations, coded as the score differential between the team of interest and their opponent when performance exceeds aspirations.

name: Risk-taking
definition: The pursuit of uncertain actions aimed at closing the performance-aspiration gap; in the NFL context the risky option for the team in possession is to 'go for it' on fourth down rather than punt or attempt a field goal.

name: Decision-maker tenure in the community
authors_terms: ["decision-maker tenure in the community", "community tenure", "tenure in the respective area"]
definition: The decision-maker's length of residence in the community affected by a violent traumatic event, which shapes the strength of social-psychological connection and identification with victims.

name: Geographic proximity to the violent event
authors_terms: ["proximity to the site of violence", "geographical proximity", "distance between a team and a violent traumatic event"]
definition: The decision-maker's (organization's) geographic closeness to a violent traumatic event, which increases the salience of the event and the intensity of the psychological reaction to it.

name: Promotion focus
definition: A promotion focus causes an individual to seek to achieve ambitious goals, aspirations, and growth; its relative activation can be situationally altered, with negative emotions associated with a relative abandonment of promotion focus.

name: Prevention focus
definition: A prevention focus orients an individual to preserve the status quo and to prevent significant losses; negative emotions are positively associated with prevention focus.

name: Scout experience with other divisions
authors_terms: ["scout experience with other divisions", "experience gained with other divisions", "experience with other divisions"]
definition: Experience resulting from a scout's sustained engagement in divisions other than the focal one, measured as the number of new products previously launched by divisions other than the one associated with the focal project, using knowledge from startups found by the focal scout.

name: New product launch
authors_terms: ["new product launch", "launch of a new product based on external knowledge"]
definition: The culmination of the external knowledge integration process in the focal division in the launch of a new product based on external knowledge.

name: Startup technological similarity
authors_terms: ["startup technological similarity", "similarity of a startup's technology to the ones of startups the focal division previously engaged with"]
definition: The similarity between the focal startup's technology and that of startups that the focal division worked with earlier, measured as the extent of overlap between a startup's patents and those of startups previously selected by the focal division, in terms of patent classes.

name: Division product-market overlap
authors_terms: ["division product-market overlap", "product-market overlap between the divisions with which a scout has gained experience and the focal division"]
definition: The overlap in product market between the focal division and those with which the focal scout gained experience, calculated using yearly data on each division's product lines and market segments via the Jaccard index.

name: Founders leading the market discussion
authors_terms: ["founders leading the market discussion", "founder leading discussion", "leading the market discussion"]
definition: The extent to which market discussion changes in response to a change in founder discussion; it captures whether founders introduce new frames into the market.

name: Founders following the market discussion
authors_terms: ["founders following the market discussion", "founder following discussion", "following the market discussion", "listening"]
definition: The extent to which founder discussion changes in response to a change in market discussion; it captures whether founders align with prevailing themes.

name: Introducing new products
definition: New products are material artifacts, concrete physical outputs that embody the founder's imagined opportunities in a tangible form; we conceptualize new products as tools for communication - where founders' imagined opportunities intersect with evolving market needs.

name: Market attention
definition: Market attention is captured by the organic traffic to the startup's website each quarter; 'organic traffic' refers to visits that come to a website via unpaid search results and it is associated with future revenues and market value.

name: Time since founding
definition: Time is the quarterly progression of the startup, with the first quarter in which a startup is observed (i.e., the quarter of its founding) coded equal to 0 and variables centered at their grand mean.

name: Stakeholder political ideology
definition: Political ideologies are philosophies regarding 'how society should be governed' (Jost et al., 2009) and reflect individuals' closely held values. U.S. politics is starkly divided along ideological lines between proponents of liberalism (i.e., liberals) on the one hand, and proponents of conservatism (i.e., conservatives) on the other.

name: Purpose of business beliefs
authors_terms: ["purpose of business beliefs", "beliefs regarding the purpose of business", "perceived purpose of business", "corporate purpose"]
definition: Conservatives tend to view the purpose of business as focusing on activities related to its core functions so as to generate profits. In contrast, liberals tend to believe that businesses have an additional responsibility to pursue behaviors that promote societal well-being and refrain from activities that harm societal well-being, even when this approach negatively affects business functioning.

name: CEO sociopolitical activism
authors_terms: ["CEO activism", "CEO sociopolitical activism", "ideologically aligned CEO activism", "ideologically misaligned CEO activism", "non-activism on the part of the CEO"]
definition: CEO activism refers to public stance-taking by CEOs on politically polarized issues. Through participating in interviews with the media, coming together to sign petitions, and buying op-ed space in prominent newspapers, CEOs have taken stands on topics such as police reform, guns, LGBT rights, climate change, voting restrictions, and abortion.

name: Stakeholder response to CEO activism
authors_terms: ["intention to pursue employment", "intention to buy product", "purchase intentions", "stakeholder responses to CEO activism"]
definition: Stakeholders' favorable or unfavorable response to a firm's CEO activism, expressed as their intention to form a relationship with the firm - job seekers' intention to pursue employment and consumers' intention to buy the firm's products.

name: Stakeholder violation intensity
authors_terms: ["violation intensity", "stakeholder violation intensity", "intensity of stakeholder violations"]
definition: Violation intensity is the severity and visibility of a firm's stakeholder-related misconduct, theorized as the aggregate intensity of a firm's recent stakeholder violations.

name: Employee turnover
definition: Employee turnover, defined as employees voluntarily severing their employment ties; the authors measure employee departures as the count of all employee job spells at each company that have end dates in a given calendar year, excluding internal job moves.

name: Violation breadth
definition: Violation breadth refers to the geographic span of stakeholder harm; it is defined as the geographic dispersion of stakeholder violations across an organization's operational footprint.

name: Violation interval
definition: Violation interval captures the temporal proximity of successive violations - the temporal spacing between successive incidents of stakeholder misconduct.

name: Violation novelty
definition: Violation novelty reflects the extent to which current violations differ categorically from past violations - that is, whether violations occur within new domains or affect previously unaffected stakeholder groups.

name: Consumer sales
definition: Our dependent variable, sales, captures the total U.S. dollar (USD) amount of marijuana products sold by dispensaries to consumers each month.

name: Market-stigmatized group concentration
authors_terms: ["market-stigmatized groups", "concentration of market-stigmatized groups", "percentage of Black residents (Black)"]
definition: We introduce the construct of market-stigmatized groups - social groups marked by stigmatizing labels, where the content of these labels is similar to the content of labels used to stigmatize markets. We contend that in stigmatized markets, the effectiveness of stigma management strategies in attracting consumer patronage is contingent on the concentration of market-stigmatized groups that are in geographic proximity to the organization.

name: Distancing strategy
definition: Distancing strategies reduce an organization's perceived association with the stigmatized market through tactics such as concealment, straddling multiple markets, reframing, and highlighting identity discrepancies. By reducing perceived association with the stigmatized market, distancing decreases public scrutiny and penalties.

name: Displaying strategy
definition: Displaying strategies, by contrast, deliberately emphasize the organization's association with the stigmatized market by openly describing products and practices in relation to the market's stigma. This transparency can habituate audiences to the market's stigma, reducing the stigma's perceived deviance and fostering social acceptance that normalizes the market over time.

name: Hispanic resident concentration
definition: The inclusion of Hispanic residents (Hispanic) allows us to test the theory's application to a group whose connection to the market stigma is less straightforward. While historically linked to the marijuana market, studies suggest Hispanics do not face the same level of disproportionate arrest for marijuana-specific offenses in the current context.

name: Asian American resident concentration
definition: The inclusion of Asian American residents (Asian) serves as a theoretically grounded comparison group. While Asian Americans experience social stigma, the content of this stigma (e.g., the 'perpetual foreigner' stereotype) is distinct from that associated with the marijuana market.

name: Knowledge bridging
definition: Knowledge bridging refers to an acquirer absorbing knowledge from its target's prior alliance partners, without requiring direct collaborative ties between the acquirer and those partners. In knowledge bridging, the acquirer leverages relational assets inherited from the target to access new-to-firm knowledge from the target's prior partners.

name: Target–partner prior alliance
definition: Whether the source of knowledge is a firm that formed an alliance with the target in the decade preceding its acquisition, as opposed to a similar firm with a comparable knowledge base with whom the target had no alliance. The acquirer is predicted to absorb more new-to-firm knowledge from a prior partner of its target than from a similar firm with whom the target had no alliance.

name: Target–partner knowledge absorption
authors_terms: ["target's knowledge absorption from the partner", "T–P knowledge absorption", "the target's absorbed knowledge from the partner"]
definition: The extent to which the target has absorbed knowledge from a prior partner during their alliance, which indicates the strength of its relational assets with that partner. These relational assets, once inherited by the acquirer, enable the acquirer to access knowledge from the partner.

name: Acquirer–partner knowledge base relatedness
definition: The extent to which the acquirer and the target's prior partner operate in similar knowledge domains and file patents in similar technology classes. Greater knowledge base relatedness between the acquirer and the partner provides the acquirer with generic absorptive capacity in the partner's knowledge domain.

name: Acquirer–partner business relatedness
definition: The relatedness between the business domains of the acquirer and the target's prior partner, which affects the competitive tension among firms on product markets. The greater the relatedness between the business domains of the acquirer and the partner, the more likely the partner will see the acquirer as a rival.

name: Target post-acquisition autonomy
definition: Target autonomy refers to the extent to which a target firm's structure and processes are maintained as an independent organization after its acquisition.

name: Identification of rising stars
authors_terms: ["identification of rising stars", "rising stars", "early identification of rising stars"]
definition: Rising stars are competitors that are currently peripheral (i.e., ignored by other firms in a market) that later grow to become prominent (i.e., widely recognized as a threat within that market). Conceptually, a rising star is a peripheral competitor that later grows to become prominent.

name: TMT varied firm experience
authors_terms: ["varied firm experience", "prior firm affiliations", "experience across firms"]
definition: Varied firm experience (i.e., prior experience at other firms) weakens relational investment in familiar or proximate competitors, thereby encouraging deviant attention to peripheral competitors.

name: TMT deep firm experience
authors_terms: ["deep firm experience", "firm tenure", "tenure at the focal firm"]
definition: Deep firm experience (i.e., longer tenure at the focal firm) increases investment in relational beliefs and assumptions, making it harder to redirect attention and spot rising stars.

name: TMT varied industry experience
definition: Varied industry experience (i.e., prior experience in other industries) is expected to inhibit identification of rising stars primarily by reducing expertise and in turn inhibiting foresight.

name: TMT deep industry experience
authors_terms: ["deep industry experience", "industry tenure", "tenure in infrastructure software"]
definition: Deep industry experience builds a more comprehensive, nuanced understanding of the industry and its competitive logic that helps to generate the foresight needed to identify rising stars.

name: Attention to peripheral competitors
authors_terms: ["attention to peripheral competitors", "attention to the periphery", "deviance"]
definition: Identifying rising stars requires (a) deviance - that is, attention to peripheral competitors in general; and (b) accurate evaluation of which peripheral competitors will grow to prominence.

name: Broadening stakeholder governance
authors_terms: ["broadening stakeholder governance", "broadened stakeholder governance", "extending governance rights to contracted stakeholders", "stakeholder governance"]
definition: Building on prior work, we conceptualize broadening stakeholder governance exclusively as extending residual control rights to contracted stakeholders.

name: Residual value available to equity stakeholders
authors_terms: ["residual value available to equity stakeholders", "residual value", "residual surplus", "net profit margin"]
definition: These dynamics can be aggregated in a stylized model that captures the relationship between the value created by broadening stakeholder governance, the value of claims made by contracted stakeholders, and the residual value (i.e., profits) left to equity stakeholders after contracted claims are satisfied.

name: Distribution of governance rights
authors_terms: ["distribution of governance rights", "wider distribution of governance rights", "stakeholder diversity", "count of stakeholders with governance rights", "Blau index of stakeholder diversity"]
definition: Together, the number of stakeholders with governance rights and the evenness of the distribution can be understood as the extent to which governance rights are widely distributed. When governance rights are more widely distributed, reaching decisions or consensus becomes more costly.

name: Contracted stakeholder governance rights
authors_terms: ["supplier representation", "employee representation", "a given contracted stakeholder's governance rights"]
definition: As contracted stakeholders gain a larger share of governance rights, value tends to become more widely distributed, reflecting stakeholders' stronger voice in decisions and firms' efforts to sustain collaboration over time. We calculated supplier representation and employee representation as the percentage of governance rights allocated to suppliers and workers, respectively.

name: Contracted stakeholder claims on firm resources
authors_terms: ["claims made by contracted stakeholders", "contracted claims", "supplier fixed claim", "worker fixed claim", "draw on firm resources"]
definition: Contracted stakeholders derive benefits through claims that the firm is legally obligated to fulfill before any remaining profits are paid to equity holders. These measures capture how firm resources are allocated to input costs and labor expenses, reflecting stakeholders' financial and economic demands.

name: Coordination costs
definition: Broadening stakeholder governance may increase coordination costs by broadening the heterogeneity of voices and perspectives to be aligned. Computing the total duration of annual meetings in minutes for each year enabled us to quantify the time spent on internal coordination activities among various stakeholders with residual control rights.

name: Firm maturity
definition: We measured firm maturity as the number of years that the firm had operated as either a conventional firm, a worker cooperative, or a multistakeholder cooperative.

name: Firm-specific investments
definition: Increasing contracted stakeholders' control rights is likely to increase their willingness to make firm-specific investments. Contracted stakeholders' firm-specific investments give them the motivation to negotiate increased rewards; otherwise they may face the risk of holdup because such investments are firm-specific, and thus have lower value outside the focal firm.

name: Economic crisis
authors_terms: ["economic crisis", "moments of economic crisis", "regions in recession"]
definition: Economic crisis can be understood as unanticipated significant downturns in the economy. During such moments, firms face scarce external resources and reduced profitability.

name: Organizational survival
authors_terms: ["firm survival", "organizational survival", "firm closure", "lower odds of closure"]
definition: Survival may be the best measure [of firm performance], since stakeholders have an interest in the organization's continued existence. Because our theorizing focuses on the firm's persistence as an organization that provides value to stakeholders, treating all exit modes as loss of survival is conceptually appropriate.

name: CEO lower social class origin
authors_terms: ["social class origin", "lower social class origins", "lower-class origins", "social class origins"]
definition: One significant individual difference between CEOs is their social class origin, which encompasses childhood experiences with scarce versus abundant resources (Kish-Gephart & Campbell, 2015; Kraus et al., 2012), and refers to 'a person's perceived place in an economic hierarchy' (Liu et al., 2004: 9).

name: CEO greedy behavior
