definition: We define greedy behavior as the relentless pursuit of material resources (Haynes, Campbell & Hitt, 2017) combined with the feeling that one never has enough (Seuntjens et al., 2016). In the CEO context, such a pursuit means putting in effort to engage in negotiations with the board to set compensation and perks beyond what would be a 'fair exchange for the CEO's human and social capital, institutions of governance, or the market for managerial talent' (Haynes et al., 2017: 557).

name: Internal CSR
authors_terms: ["internal CSR", "internal CSR behavior", "internal corporate social responsibility"]
definition: Internal CSR refers to 'the enactment of CSR-related change initiatives and corporate policies, such as adopting and implementing a policy to increase water and energy efficiency' (Hawn & Ioannou, 2016: 2572). Internal CSR is distinct from external CSR, which involves 'public and highly visible initiatives and patterns of communication'. It includes policies and actions aimed at improving the well-being of stakeholders within the scope of the CEO's control.

name: Resource insecurity mindset
definition: We define the resource insecurity mindset as a heightened perception that current and future resources are likely to be scarce and uncertain, leading to increased watchfulness and greater reactivity to environmental cues that indicate a threat to one's current and future material wellbeing, as well as an awareness that resource scarcity and uncertainty affect everyone's well-being.

name: CEO job insecurity
definition: The dismissal of industry peers has been identified as a critical factor shaping CEOs' perceptions of job insecurity in large public organizations (Connelly et al., 2020). Such dismissals can trigger spillover effects, heightening concerns among remaining CEOs about their own job security (Connelly et al., 2020; Shoss, 2017).

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: Overconfident individuals tend to overestimate their abilities, control over their environment, and knowledge (Burkhard et al., 2023). These individuals, including CEOs, also tend to be overly optimistic about future positive outcomes (Malmendier & Tate, 2005).

name: CEO philanthropy toward vulnerable populations
authors_terms: ["philanthropy toward vulnerable populations", "CEO philanthropy", "personal philanthropy", "charities aimed at helping the less fortunate"]
definition: Our focus is on philanthropic actions directed toward those in need; CEOs from lower social class origins are expected to be more inclined to participate in charities aimed at helping the less fortunate in ways that require personal resources - both financial and time - on the part of the CEOs themselves.

name: Feedback incorporation
definition: The degree to which firms' changes to the game reflected the preceding user-community feedback, operationalized as the textual similarity between firm update announcements and user reviews during Early Access.

name: Community unrepresentativeness
definition: The degree to which the market-segment distribution of each game's reviewers does not overlap with the overall customer base on Steam.

name: Post-launch revenue
definition: Base-game sales revenue during the first six months post-launch after leaving Early Access, used to operationalize commercial performance for each new game.

name: Positive within-community evaluations
definition: How much the users who provided feedback enjoy and positively rate the product, measured as the proportion of positive reviews within the initial feedback community.

name: CVC knowledge obsolescence
definition: The declining relevance of a firm's knowledge base as technological domains evolve; a firm's knowledge base may become isolated from the core of technological progress. For a venture's partner, it is the knowledge obsolescence of the CVC investor (its parent firm).

name: Venture innovation performance
authors_terms: ["venture's innovation performance", "venture innovation", "innovation outcomes", "venture's subsequent innovation performance"]
definition: The venture's innovative output operationalized with patent-based measures: the annual number of patent applications captures the volume of inventive activity, and the annual number of patent citations captures the technological impact and knowledge spillovers of the venture's patents.

name: Market competition faced by the CVC's parent firm
definition: The extent of competition faced by the CVC's parent firm in its own industry, which shapes the pressures confronting knowledge-obsolete CVCs.

name: IVC network prominence
authors_terms: ["IVC network prominence", "network prominence", "prominence of coinvesting IVCs"]
definition: The position an independent venture capitalist holds in the network of syndicate relationships, a function of both its direct and indirect ties; prominent IVCs occupy central positions in syndicate networks and have superior information about coinvestors.

name: Female director appointment
definition: The number of newly appointed female director(s) within a focal firm in year t. A female director is considered newly appointed if she did not serve on the board in the previous year but joined in the current year.

name: CEO pay raises
definition: The log difference in CEO total compensation between year t and year t+1, adjusted for industry variations by subtracting the corresponding industry-level raises.

name: Token status of newly appointed female director
authors_terms: ["token status", "token status of newly appointed female director(s)"]
definition: A dichotomous indicator of whether the newly appointed female director(s) joined a board that previously had no women; a woman is a token when there were no women on the board before the appointment.

name: Female board representation relative to industry norms
authors_terms: ["at or above industry norms on diversity", "female board representation relative to industry norms"]
definition: A comparison of the focal firm's female board representation with the average female board representation in the focal firm's primary industry.

name: CEO gender
definition: Whether the firm's chief executive officer is male or female.

name: Male directors' interlocking directorships
definition: The difference between the total number of external board seats held by male directors and female directors, divided by the number of male directors in the focal firm, capturing male directors' structural embeddedness in elite networks.

name: Male directors' membership instability
authors_terms: ["male directors' membership instability", "membership instability of male directors"]
definition: The degree to which male board membership changes over time, computed as one minus the stability index that assesses how consistent group membership remains over time.

name: CEO political party affiliation
authors_terms: ["CEO political party affiliation", "political party affiliation", "party affiliation", "CEO Republican Party affiliation"]
definition: The CEO's political party affiliation is defined as the CEO's support for a specific political party. The authors note that political party affiliation and political ideology are closely related but distinct, and that party affiliation can also serve as a salient social identity.

name: Competitive repertoire conformity
definition: Competitive repertoire conformity is the extent to which CEOs shape their firms' portfolio of competitive actions to resemble (vs. differ from) other firms in the industry.

name: Industry CEO political composition
authors_terms: ["industry's CEO political party affiliation", "presence of Democratic CEOs in the industry", "concentration of Democratic CEOs in the industry", "political composition of CEOs in the focal firm's industry"]
definition: The industry's CEO political party affiliation is the ratio of the number of Democratic-leaning CEOs in the focal firm's industry to the number of Republican-leaning CEOs (excluding the focal firm CEO's party affiliation), so that higher values indicate a higher concentration of CEOs who prefer the Democratic Party.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors measure firm performance in two ways to capture both the firm's long- and short-term financial performance: long-term investor value appropriation (LIVA) and net income.

name: CEO psychopathy
authors_terms: ["CEO psychopathic tendency", "CEO psychopathic deviate", "CEO Pd", "psychopathy", "corporate psychopathy"]
definition: Psychopathy is built on the triarchic conceptualization consisting of disinhibition (impulse control deficits), boldness (social dominance, emotional resilience, fearlessness, and venturesomeness), and meanness (aggressive resource seeking without regard for others). With higher levels of psychopathy, sensitivity to threat is lower and sensitivity to reward is higher.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "distance from aspiration (below)", "performance shortfalls", "negative aspiration gap", "performance below historical aspirations"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's actual performance falls below its aspiration level; the authors use the historical aspiration level of a firm's past performance in terms of return on assets (ROA, measured as annual profits divided by assets) as the reference point.

name: Performance above aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance above aspirations", "distance from aspiration (positive)", "positive performance discrepancy", "performance above historical aspirations"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's actual performance exceeds its aspiration level, defined against the historical aspiration level of a firm's past return on assets.

name: Organizational risk-taking
definition: Risk-taking is a multidimensional construct including expenditures associated with uncertain returns—specifically, capital investments and foreign operations. Capital investments entail substantial upfront costs and uncertain long-term payoffs, whereas foreign operations expose firms to political, regulatory, economic, and cultural risks.

name: Negative attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["negative attainment discrepancy", "performance below aspirations", "performance below historical aspiration", "performance below social aspiration"]
definition: Performance that is below the aspiration level - that is, negative attainment discrepancy - represents failure, and the general postulation is that as the intensity of negative attainment discrepancy increases, firms are motivated to increase their search efforts. It is measured as a spline, equal to the difference between firm performance and the corresponding historical or social aspiration level when performance falls short of that level, and zero otherwise.

name: R&D search
authors_terms: ["R&D search", "problemistic R&D search", "problem-driven R&D search", "R&D search intensity"]
definition: R&D search remains the most commonly assumed behavioral consequence of problemistic search, and R&D intensity captures a firm's commitment to developing its innovative capabilities; the authors use this factor as a measure of R&D search.

name: Firm founding period
definition: The timing of a firm's founding relative to the regulatory punctuation of the 1991 pro-market reforms, distinguishing firms that originated in the pre-reform period from those that originated in the post-reform period.

name: Founding industry protection
authors_terms: ["protected industries", "more protected industries", "protectionist policies", "import penetration ratio"]
definition: Industry-level variation in the protectionist policies associated with a firm's founding industry, captured by the import penetration ratio, which reflects both tariff- and nontariff-based import barriers; industries with lower than median import penetration are classified as more protected and vice versa.

name: Category spanning
definition: Category spanning of a restaurant: the number of cuisine categories offered by the restaurant and the average distance between those categories, where the average distance is based on cosine similarity for pairs of categories in a yearly co-occurrence matrix.

name: Exposure to a new organizational form
authors_terms: ["new organizational form", "gourmet food trucks", "number of GFTs", "city density of GFTs"]
definition: An organizational form is a codified, socially embedded, and sanctioned identity perception that is shared by external audiences; the authors focus on gourmet food trucks, a new form that presents category spanning as a distinctive feature of its products, and measure audience exposure to it through the number of GFTs in a metro-year.

name: Audience evaluation
authors_terms: ["Rating", "average yearly Yelp customer rating", "evaluations of spanning", "spanning appeal"]
definition: The audience's evaluation of a restaurant, measured as the average yearly Yelp customer rating of a brick-and-mortar restaurant in the seven metropolitan areas, aggregated from individual ratings ranging from 1 for 'completely dissatisfied' to 5 for 'completely satisfied.'.

name: Attribute similarity with the new form
authors_terms: ["share salient attributes", "attribute similarity", "low price segment", "price positioning"]
definition: Transfer of the new form's theory of value is facilitated when the forms share salient attributes, because these common attributes make it more plausible that understandings about one type of organization will be useful to evaluate another type of organization.

name: Corporate research
authors_terms: ["corporate research", "industrial research", "research undertaken at private firms", "corporate researchers", "corporate scientists", "papers written by corporate researchers"]
definition: Applied research undertaken by scientists in private firms; the study observes it through published scientific papers written by corporate researchers on flat-panel-display technologies.

name: University research
authors_terms: ["university research", "academic research", "university-based research", "university researchers", "academic scientists", "papers written by university researchers"]
definition: Applied research undertaken in university laboratories; the study observes it through published scientific papers written by university researchers on flat-panel-display technologies.

name: Citation by firm-based scientists
authors_terms: ["cited by firm-based scientists", "citations by industrial researchers", "citation by a company's scientists"]
definition: The number of citations a scientific paper receives from scientists working in industrial firms; the study assumes that the more frequently a given paper is cited by a company's scientists, the greater its relevance to the R&D activities pursued by that company.

name: Citation by foreign firms
authors_terms: ["citations by foreign researchers", "cited by foreign firms", "citations by industrial researchers housed in R&D facilities located outside the author's country of residence"]
definition: Citations to an article by industrial researchers housed in R&D facilities located outside the author's country of residence.

name: Time lag to foreign citation
authors_terms: ["time lag for citation from abroad", "cited abroad more quickly", "speed at which academic and corporate articles were cited by foreign researchers"]
definition: The average number of years between the publication date of an article and its citation by industrial researchers outside the author's country.

name: National innovation system
authors_terms: ["national innovation system", "national institutional structures", "national environment", "institutions and policies that guide university-based scientists"]
definition: A national innovation system is comprised of resources and institutions, built through interactions among a country's research organizations, that domestic firms harness to successfully commercialize innovations; the relevance of a country's academic research depends considerably on the institutions and policies that guide university-based scientists.

name: Legal environment
definition: Whether a corporation's state of incorporation has adopted an other-constituency statute, which codified into law the right of boards to consider stakeholder interests in their decision making.

name: Industry regulatory environment
authors_terms: ["industry regulatory environment", "industry regulation", "more highly regulated industries", "heavy regulation"]
definition: Organizations operating within highly regulated industries have a context that reinforces accountability to public concerns and heightens the importance of maintaining legitimacy vis-a-vis the public and the government.

name: Company size
definition: Organizational size is an important determinant of corporate responsiveness to the legal and normative environment influencing stakeholder representation; by virtue of their size, large organizations are more visible and hence subject to greater attention from such external constituencies as the state, the media, professional groups, and the general public.

name: Stakeholder representation on boards of directors
authors_terms: ["stakeholder representation on boards", "proportion of stakeholder directors on a board", "presence of stakeholder directors"]
definition: The proportion of stakeholder directors on a board, computed by dividing the number of nonshareholder stakeholder directors by the total number of directors on a board. The presence of stakeholder directors on corporate boards is one of the most direct means through which firms can reflect stakeholder interests in corporate governance and policy decision making.

name: Stakeholder representation on board committees
authors_terms: ["stakeholder representation on key board committees", "proportion of stakeholder representation on each committee"]
definition: For each of the four major board committees-audit, compensation, executive, and nominating-the numbers of public and private stakeholder directors on the committee divided by the total number of directors on the committee.

name: Stakeholder-oriented board committees
authors_terms: ["stakeholder committee", "board committees oriented to nonshareholder stakeholder issues"]
definition: A committee with a stakeholder orientation, such as a public policy, social responsibility, or contributions committee, typically given the responsibility of reviewing the firm's compliance with regulations, evaluating corporate donation policies and practices, and addressing other areas of social and ethical concern.

name: Prior success with an existing IT
authors_terms: ["success with e-filing", "prior success with e-filing", "process gains from e-filing", "strategic benefits from e-filing"]
definition: We developed questionnaire items assessing the extent to which use of an existing IT had resulted in two kinds of benefits: (1) improvement in the company's processes and (2) strategic benefits. The greater companies' process gains or strategic benefits from e-filing, the greater their success with e-filing was considered to be.

name: Threat-opportunity framing
authors_terms: ["threat/opportunity framing", "issue definition/labeling", "framing the new ITs as an opportunity"]
definition: Issue definition/labeling of the new ITs measured using threat/opportunity framing, which is the extent to which managers frame a phenomenon as an opportunity for, rather than a threat to, their company.

name: Effect certainty
definition: Effect certainty, which is the extent to which managers feel certain about how a phenomenon will affect their company.

name: Response certainty
definition: Response certainty, which is the extent to which managers feel certain that they know what actions to take in response to a phenomenon.

name: Perceived similarity of new ITs to the existing IT
authors_terms: ["perceived similarity of the new ITs to e-filing", "perceptions of similarity between e-filing and the new ITs"]
definition: Perceived similarity of the new ITs to e-filing was measured using an item asking respondents to indicate the extent to which they perceived e-filing technology as similar (1 = extremely dissimilar, 7 = extremely similar) to each of five new ITs.

name: Experience with the existing IT
authors_terms: ["amount of experience with e-filing", "amount of the company's experience with e-filing"]
definition: The amount of experience with e-filing was measured as the percentage of returns filed electronically by the company in the previous tax-reporting year (1993-94).

name: Proactive information seeking
authors_terms: ["proactive information seeking about new ITs", "proactive information seeking about the new ITs"]
definition: Proactive information seeking about new ITs was measured as the average of responses on a seven-point scale to four items assessing the extent to which a company kept in touch with the IRS on developments in information technologies for return filing, monitored what ITs its competitors were adopting or developing, monitored developments in IT that might potentially affect its business, and surveyed its customers.

name: Strategic issue interpretations
authors_terms: ["strategic issue interpretations", "managers' interpretations of the new ITs", "interpretations of the new ITs"]
definition: Strategic issue interpretations are meanings that are ascribed to a strategic issue as a product of managers' "sensemaking" about the issue (Weick, 1995). In this research the new ITs constituted the strategic issue, and interpretations were assessed with threat/opportunity framing, effect certainty, and response certainty, which capture distinct aspects of managers' interpretations.

name: Strategic proactivity
authors_terms: ["business strategy proactivity", "strategic proactivity", "proactivity of business strategy"]
definition: I therefore defined strategic proactivity as a firm's tendency to initiate changes in its various strategic policies rather than to react to events.

name: Approach to the natural environment
authors_terms: ["approaches to the natural environment", "natural environmental approaches", "corporate natural environmental postures"]
definition: These classifications are based on making distinctions along a continuum ranging from the most reactive postures to the most proactive ones. The specific characterization of each type of posture may be based on firms' use of either traditional or modern approaches to improving their natural environmental performance.

name: Industry R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "industry R&D intensity", "R&D intensity of a U.S. manufacturing industry"]
definition: R&D intensity was defined as R&D investment expressed as a percentage of net sales averaged for each industry.

name: Industry political sensitivity
authors_terms: ["politically sensitive industries", "political influence factors", "government-mandated import restrictions"]
definition: A firm's industry may be politically sensitive, a condition often accompanied by the presence of import protection, as is the case in the auto and steel industries.

name: Entity newness
authors_terms: ["new entity", "new companies", "acquired versus new firm status"]
definition: A variable was included to represent whether direct investments were new companies (1) or acquired (0).

name: Japanese parent's product experience
authors_terms: ["product experience of Japanese firm", "experience with the product", "Japanese firms make similar products in Japan"]
definition: Whether any Japanese parent of an entity produced a product in Japan that was similar to the entity's product or products in the United States.

name: Partial ownership structure
definition: A partially owned firm is either an existing company that has had a substantial amount of stock purchased by a Japanese company or a start-up in which substantial amounts of stock are held publicly or privately by individuals.

name: Joint venture structure
definition: A joint venture is a manufacturing firm and separate legal entity, with a Japanese parent or parents and a U.S. or non-U.S. parent or parents, established in the United States; joint ventures are those in which one or more Japanese parents own between 5 and 95 percent of the equity.

name: Total ownership structure
definition: Ownership of between 95 and 100 percent of equity was considered total ownership.

name: Contemporaneous strategy report
authors_terms: ["time 1 strategy", "current strategy", "time 1 strategy assessment", "the validated time 1 measure"]
definition: A hospital's current strategy was assessed with a procedure based on the Miles and Snow (1978) typology of generic strategies. During the first wave of data collection, in 1984, CEOs indicated the type to which their hospital was currently most similar.

name: Retrospective strategy account
authors_terms: ["retrospective account", "retrospective measure of time 1 strategy", "retrospective reports"]
definition: As part of the second wave of data collection, in 1986, each CEO was asked to identify the hospital's business strategy of two years ago (time 1), using the same strategy typology.

name: Acquisitions
definition: A mode of firm growth in which firms acquire other firms, offering immediate entrance to a new market, a larger share of a market served currently, or both. The authors frame acquisitions as an alternative to internal development and to R&D investment.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Firm R&D intensity, defined as total R&D expenditures divided by total sales, adjusted for average industry R&D intensity. It represents a firm's investment in R&D inputs relative to its size.

name: Patent intensity
definition: The total number of patents a firm holds divided by its annual sales. Patents reflect a firm's intention to commercialize a product idea and are described as one of the most direct measures of innovative output available.

name: Corporate political strategy
authors_terms: ["corporate political involvement", "political strategy", "leaders, followers, and free riders", "political activity"]
definition: We used Yoffie's (1987) typology of free riders, followers, and leaders to classify firms in terms of their relationship to escape clause petitions.

name: Strategic dependence
authors_terms: ["strategic dependence", "dependence on the sales of a product for which a petition has been filed", "dependence on a product that is the subject of a petition"]
definition: Yoffie (1987) suggested that firms depending on the sales of an affected product have a strong incentive to seek import relief. More diversified firms can compensate for loss in income in one division by increasing income in another division unaffected by imports.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Bourgeois defined slack as "a cushion of excess resources available in an organization that will either solve many organizational problems or facilitate the pursuit of goals outside the realm of those dictated by optimization principles".

name: Firm size
definition: We defined size as the absolute size of corporate resources available for political action, including financial assets as well as chief executive officer (CEO) expertise (Salamon & Siegfried, 1977).

name: Washington office presence
authors_terms: ["maintenance of a Washington office", "presence of a Washington office", "Washington offices"]
definition: The presence of a Washington office shows that a firm has had sufficient resources in the past to invest in trying to influence the political process.

name: Industry structure
authors_terms: ["industry structure", "number of firms in an industry", "membership in an industry with a small number of firms"]
definition: Our third hypothesis suggests that the structure of an industry affects the cost and benefits a firm can expect when seeking import relief through political means.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "corporate diversification strategy", "Rumelt's categories of corporate diversification strategy", "strategic type", "strategy category"]
definition: The corporate diversification strategy a firm pursues, classified using Rumelt's (1974) categories of corporate diversification strategy; these strategy groups displayed significant differences in financial characteristics.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Systematic risk is the result of investors' expectations about the future volatility of a firm's total return relative to the market as a whole.

name: Outsider board representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of outsiders on its board", "proportion of outside directors", "percentage of outsiders", "majority of outsiders", "outside dominance"]
definition: The proportion of outside members on a board of directors, where outside directors did not currently hold, nor had they previously held, management positions within the company for which they were serving as director.

name: Corporate illegal acts
authors_terms: ["illegal acts", "illegal activities", "commission of illegal acts", "involvement in illegal activities"]
definition: The total number of instances in which firms were found guilty in litigated cases, were parties to nonlitigated consent decrees, or were involved in unsettled cases in which the court found substantial merit to the charges against the cited firms.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["dual leadership", "unitary leadership", "single individual serving in the roles of CEO and chairman", "CEO/chairman"]
definition: The arrangement in which a single individual serves in both the chief executive officer and board chairman roles, as opposed to firms in which two separate individuals hold these positions.

name: Medical department presence
authors_terms: ["presence of a medical department", "in-house medical departments", "medical departments"]
definition: The presence within the firm of an in-house medical department, one of the two influential groups the authors see as relevant to the adoption of employee health innovations.

name: Union presence
definition: Unions can be seen as an external formal organization that routinely and predictably represents workers' interests.

name: Organizational complexity
definition: Complexity in the firm implies an increase in the variety of elements (whether tasks to be performed or types of performers or subunits) being dealt with.

name: Urban location
authors_terms: ["urban location", "firm location", "size of the community in which an organization is located"]
definition: Access to informational systems can be limited by an organization's location or its community context; cities were found to be more likely sites for innovation than rural areas.

name: Firm size
definition: In this study size will be defined as the number of employees in the firm.

name: Program adoption
authors_terms: ["program adoption", "adoption of employee assistance/alcoholism programs", "adoption of in-house programs"]
definition: Program adoption was defined in the questionnaire as the existence of a formal program consisting of either written procedures, a special office, or a coordinator for employees with emotional, personal, alcohol or drug problems.

name: Insurance coverage adoption
authors_terms: ["insurance adoption", "provision of insurance coverage for alcoholism treatment", "special insurance coverage"]
definition: Insurance adoption was indicated if the firm's basic insurance plan specifically covered reimbursement for alcoholism treatment.

name: Prior insurance adoption
authors_terms: ["prior insurance adoption", "prior insurance adoption as an explanatory variable"]
definition: A dummy variable coded 1 if insurance was adopted prior to program adoption, and 0 otherwise.

name: Boundary spanning activity
definition: The strategic activities in which the owner/operators engage manifest themselves as boundary spanning activities; the entrepreneur occupies the boundary spanning role, mediating between internal and external forces, and his boundary spanning activity represents both the perception of the aspects of the environment for which action is necessary and the commitment of organizational resources.

name: Integrative complexity
definition: Individuals who can discriminate among a wide variety of stimuli possess a larger potential for information processing, which increases their capacity for boundary spanning activity; integrative complexity is one of the two measures of information processing capability.

name: Intolerance of ambiguity
definition: The tendency to perceive ambiguous situations as sources of threat; the situations may be new, complex, or insoluble. As such, this definition represents the "content" dimension of information capability.

name: Financial performance
definition: Performance of the small business organization, measured by net addition to retained earnings, current sales, and the gross economic benefits accruing to ownership.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Diversification was defined in the questionnaire as "the manufacture of new products and services using significantly different inputs from existing products and services, and/or selling to new industries." Firms themselves decided whether they had diversified over the specific period.

name: Return on total assets
definition: The first ratio attempts to measure the total after-corporate tax return on the total capital invested in a firm by shareholders and lenders.

name: Return on equity
definition: The second ratio is a measure of the return on shareholders' equity in a firm; it is a measure of the success of management in managing a firm on behalf of its shareholders.

name: Business risk
definition: The coefficient of variation of EBIT measures operating or business risk, or the sensitivity of the firm's earnings stream to changes in sales, output and input prices relative to average EBIT.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The level of debt financing is measured by the proportion of a firm's investment in its assets financed by debt, and by the extent of usage of interest bearing debt in financing assets.

name: Growth rate
definition: G is the compound rate of growth in assets over the period; growth is compared across the two groups for assets, sales, earnings, market capitalization and the profitability ratios.

name: Turnover
definition: Total assets turnover (TO) as mentioned in the prediction statement; exact definition not provided in the card.

name: Firm size
definition: Average firm size over the period, measured by assets (A), used as an explanatory variable.

name: Comprehensiveness of strategic decision processes
authors_terms: ["comprehensiveness", "comprehensiveness of strategic decision processes", "comprehensive decision process", "analytic comprehensiveness", "integrative comprehensiveness"]
definition: The extent to which an organization attempts to be exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions. It is a measure of rationality and involves the thorough canvassing of alternatives, surveying a full range of objectives, weighing costs and risks, searching for information, and making detailed plans.

name: Organization performance
definition: Because organization performance is a complex variable that can be measured many ways, the measures used in this study address only the firm's most commonly acknowledged goal-economic performance. Two distinct measures of financial performance that reflect the strategic process literature's frequent reference to the importance of balancing efficiency and effectiveness were selected.

name: Comprehensiveness of strategic decision processes
definition: The extent to which an organization attempts to be exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions; it is presented as a measure of rationality.

name: Organization performance
authors_terms: ["organization performance", "economic performance", "average after-tax return on assets", "percentage change in gross sales"]
definition: Organization performance is assessed with two measures of economic performance: average after-tax return on assets during the most recent five years, used to assess how efficiently firms managed their resources, and percentage change in gross sales during the same period, included as a measure of long term viability or effectiveness.

name: Regulatory uncertainty
definition: Regulatory uncertainty is the unpredictable changes in regulations, not merely increasing regulation, that create the regulation's uncertainty; it is associated with the actions of governmental agencies that create and enforce regulations.

name: Customer uncertainty
definition: Customer uncertainty is associated with changes in product demand and is typically reflected in sales. Regulatory uncertainty creates it by increasing customers' awareness of a real or potential problem with the product and their uncertainty over the safety and quality of products offered for sale.

name: Competitor uncertainty
definition: Competitor uncertainty is associated with market structure. Regulatory actions may control rates charged or establish performance standards and thereby control market entry and the number of competing firms.

name: Less risky strategic alternatives
authors_terms: ["less risky strategic alternatives", "strategies that have more predictable outcomes", "adaptation strategies"]
definition: Relative to invention, other strategic choices are lower in uncertainty, and as uncertainty increases decision makers will select adaptation strategies based on the increasing likelihood of being able to predict their outcomes. The less risky alternatives examined here are diversification, outsiders on the board, board size, and joining trade associations.

name: Invention
definition: Invention of new products is an inherently uncertain undertaking fraught not only with the risk of failure early in the process, but throughout as the invention is tested, developed, and brought to market.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["organizational size", "size of firm", "firm size", "larger firms", "smaller firms"]
definition: Large organizations should have greater slack because they have greater sales, more capital and human assets, and consequently a greater capacity to absorb the uncertainties posed by regulation, and so should be more able to engage in long term risky inventions as well as less risky alternatives.

name: Diversification
definition: Diversification represents a prevention strategy that attempts to exert direct control over the environment by spreading the risk to the firm from any single product market.

name: Outsiders on the board of directors
authors_terms: ["outsiders on the board", "percentage of outsiders on the board", "proportion of outsiders"]
definition: Increasing the proportion of outsiders on the board should allow for more indirect control over the environment through better forecasting of what otherwise would be unpredictable behavior by critical elements of the focal organization's task environment.

name: Board size
definition: Increased board size, which may result from adding outsiders to an existing board without replacement or from adding more outsiders or a combination of insiders and outsiders, increases the representation of important external constituent groups and enables an organization to maintain greater direct control over its external dependencies.

name: Trade association memberships
definition: Organizations may join together into trade associations in order to forecast changes or to exert indirect control over their environment by amplifying the influence of any single firm in pending legislation or in negotiating with regulatory bodies.

name: Relative market power
authors_terms: ["relative power", "relative market power", "power ratio (POW)", "bilateral market power"]
definition: Market power resides in the bilateral relationships between buyer and seller, and power relationships become important only when distributed asymmetrically among market participants.

name: Merger strategy type
definition: Each merger is classified by the FTC according to the primary strategic relationship between the acquiring and acquired firm; five primary merger strategies are identified: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension, and conglomerate.

name: Prospecting orientation
authors_terms: ["Miles and Snow strategic types", "defenders", "prospectors", "prospecting", "defending", "relative new product activity", "defender-like", "prospector-like"]
definition: The key dimension underlying the typology is the rate at which an organization changes its products or markets. Defenders are organizations that engage in little or no new product/market development; prospectors attempt to pioneer in product/market development.

name: Business performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "profitability", "return on investment", "ROI", "cash flow", "cash flow on investment", "CFOI", "market share change"]
definition: Profitability (return on investment) is the most conventional measure of current business performance. Cash flow indicates the extent to which the company currently is reaping more money than it is putting into the business. Market share change indicates the growth of the business and its fitness for the future.

name: Product life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["product life cycle stage", "life cycle stage", "mature industry", "growth industry"]
definition: Product life cycle stage was one of the two environmental variables included in the study; the present study used PIMS data on businesses in the growth and maturity stages of the life cycle.

name: Industry product innovation
authors_terms: ["industry new product innovation", "industry innovation", "innovative industry", "noninnovative industry"]
definition: Industry innovation was the second environmental variable included in the study, classifying industries according to the extent to which industry revenues come from recently introduced products; noninnovative and innovative industries were contrasted and those with moderate innovation scores were excluded.

name: Product R&D intensity
definition: Resources a business spends on product research and development, as a percentage of sales.

name: Marketing expense intensity
definition: Marketing expenses (sales force, promotion, and marketing administration), as a percentage of sales.

name: Forward vertical integration
definition: The extent to which a business moves into stages downstream of production, tending to handle its own selling, warehousing, and distribution.

name: Backward vertical integration
definition: Vertical integration toward stable, inexpensive sources of raw materials.

name: Fixed asset intensity
definition: The capital intensity of a business, relating its gross assets to its employees.

name: Employee productivity
definition: Value added per employee, an indicator of the productivity of a business's workforce.

name: Capacity utilization
definition: The extent to which a business uses its productive capacity.

name: Compensation rates
definition: Average compensation rates for a business's employees, considered relative to competitors.

name: Direct costs
definition: The overall direct costs of a business, considered relative to competitors.

name: Process R&D emphasis
definition: The portion of a business's total R&D expenditures devoted to process improvements.

name: Price level
definition: The prices of a business's offerings, considered relative to competitors.

name: Product quality
definition: The quality of a business's offerings, considered relative to competitors.

name: Customer service
definition: The service a business provides to customers, considered relative to competitors.

name: Economic orientation
definition: The profit or nonprofit orientation of an organization, proposed by Rushing as a strategic contingency that strongly influences macro level organizational behavior. The study examined the relationship between an organization's economic orientation and the perceived power relationships among those responsible for its strategic decision making.

name: Perceived power of the medical staff
authors_terms: ["perceived power of the medical staff", "power position", "perceived ability to influence organizational goals"]
definition: The amount of influence respondents felt the medical staff was actually able to exert on their hospital's organizational goal-setting process.

name: Perceived power of the board of trustees
authors_terms: ["perceived power of the board of trustees", "power position", "perceived ability to influence organizational goals"]
definition: The amount of influence respondents felt the board of trustees was actually able to exert on their hospital's organizational goal-setting process.

name: Perceived power of the hospital administrator
authors_terms: ["perceived power of the hospital administrator", "power position", "perceived ability to influence organizational goals"]
definition: The amount of influence respondents felt the hospital administrator was actually able to exert on their hospital's organizational goal-setting process.

name: Organizational size
definition: There has been controversy regarding the appropriateness, dimensionality, and psychometric properties of common size metrics; given these disparate positions, multiple measures of size will be used, with both number of employees and sales relied on as size metrics.

name: Successor origin
authors_terms: ["inside/outside succession", "successor type", "inside versus outside succession", "inside succession", "outside succession"]
definition: An inside successor is a person promoted from within the executive span of the predecessor; and outside succession occurs when the newly appointed CEO was not in the predecessor's span.

name: Stock exchange listing
definition: The hypothesis relies on an assumption that presence on different exchanges provides some evidence of size heterogeneity.

name: Private ownership
definition: Three central factors are used here as the basis for differentiating public and private ownership: trading or lack of public trading of the stock, top management's financial stake in the firm, and the autonomy of top management.

name: Sales growth rate
authors_terms: ["growth in sales", "rate of growth in sales"]
definition: Growth in sales is the least squared growth rate for sales over the previous five years, 1974 through 1978.

name: Consistency of sales growth
authors_terms: ["consistency of the growth rate", "consistent growth in sales"]
definition: The consistency of the growth rate is the mean square of the error term.

name: Emphasis on sales growth
authors_terms: ["importance on growth in sales as a decision criterion", "importance of growth in sales"]
definition: The CEO's perception of how important a role potential growth in sales played, on average, in the five key decisions he had identified earlier in the interview.

name: Emphasis on consistent sales growth
authors_terms: ["importance on consistency of sales growth as a decision criterion", "importance on consistency of sales"]
definition: The CEO's perception of how important a factor consistency of sales had been, on average, in the specific key decisions.

name: Emphasis on near-term earnings
authors_terms: ["importance on near-term earnings", "near-term earnings as a decision criterion"]
definition: The CEO's opinion of the importance that forecasts of near-term earnings had on the specific decisions he had earlier identified as important.

name: Tax-minimizing accounting policies
authors_terms: ["accounting policies oriented more toward minimizing taxes", "accounting policies predicated more on reducing taxable income"]
definition: The index measuring this characteristic was developed from the CEO's description of the accounting policies. It was comprised of policies on inventory valuation (LIFO versus FIFO), depreciation, and attitude toward decisions to expense or capitalize investments.

name: Cash-flow-oriented pricing policy
authors_terms: ["pricing policies that enhance cash flow rather than growth in sales", "pricing policies aimed at maximizing internally generated cash flow"]
definition: Their pricing policies are aimed at maximizing internally generated cash flow rather than growth.

name: Reliance on subjective judgment in decisions
authors_terms: ["reliance on subjective judgment in its crucial decision making", "subjective factors such as quality, fashion, design, or appearance"]
definition: greater likelihood that the crucial decision making will center on subjective factors such as quality, fashion, design, or appearance.

name: Asset turnover
definition: Asset turnover (sales/asset book value).

name: Labor intensity
authors_terms: ["ratio of labor to sales", "ratio of production and clerical personnel to sales", "ratio of hourly employees per dollar of sales"]
definition: The ratio of hourly (i.e., non exempt) employees per dollar of sales.

name: Capital constraints on decisions
authors_terms: ["constraints on the ability to raise capital", "capital constraints"]
definition: The importance of constraints on the ability to raise capital as a consideration in the firm's major decisions.

name: Formalization
authors_terms: ["formal, written policies and processes requiring formal, written documentation", "formalization of the management process", "formalization of planning"]
definition: fewer formal, written policies and processes requiring formal, written documentation.

name: Participativeness
authors_terms: ["participativeness", "management styles with wider extremes of participativeness"]
definition: Participativeness was measured with an instrument developed by Likert (1967) to characterize the firm's management style as System I, II, III, or IV.

name: Management formal education
definition: An index of formal education was developed for each second-level manager consisting of one point for each year of postsecondary education plus one point for each academic degree.

name: Administrative and professional personnel ratio
authors_terms: ["ratio of administrative and professional personnel to sales"]
definition: The ratio of administrative and professional (i.e., exempt) personnel to sales.

name: Emphasis on cash flow and long-term profitability
authors_terms: ["cash flow and long-term profitability", "greater importance placed on cash flow and long-term profitability", "greater cash flow in the short-term"]
definition: greater importance placed on cash flow and long-term profitability, even at the sacrifice of near-term earnings or steady growth in earnings per share.

name: Outsider-based strategic planning
authors_terms: ["outsider-based strategic planning", "OBSP", "in-depth SBDC consulting", "outsider-based, small firm strategic planning"]
definition: Strategic planning in the small firm carried out with the participation of outsiders such as consultants, lawyers, accountants, bankers and board members; the assistance rendered by SBDC consultants in in-depth SBDC cases provides a logical operationalization of outsider-based, small firm strategic planning.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "net profit before taxes over sales (NPOS)", "return on sales (ROS)"]
definition: A dimension of small firm effectiveness measured as net profit before taxes divided by sales (profitability) in the comparison of OBSP firms with RMA firms, and as return on sales in the multivariate operationalization.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["growth", "percentage increase (decrease) in total sales", "growth in sales"]
definition: Improvement in the firm's sales, measured as the percentage change in total sales between matching pre- and post-OBSP time periods.

name: Productivity
definition: Small firm productivity measured as sales per employee (total sales divided by number of employees).

name: Employment growth
authors_terms: ["increase in number of employees", "number of full-time equivalent employees (FTEs)", "social responsibility dimension"]
definition: Increase in the number of full-time equivalent employees, used in this study to reflect the social responsibility dimension of small firm effectiveness.

name: Small firm effectiveness
definition: Organizational effectiveness, which is a multivariate phenomenon; in this study effectiveness generally was operationalized as a multivariate phenomenon, comprising growth, profitability, productivity and employment.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: The strategy by which a large firm's component businesses are related to one another, characterized by categories from single business to unrelated business; this study distinguishes related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated strategies. In related-constrained firms all component businesses are related to each other, whereas in related-linked firms only one-to-one relationships are required.

name: Return on assets
definition: A 5-year average (1973-1977) return on assets (ROA) defined as net income after taxes but before extraordinary items divided by total assets. ROA was chosen because it reflects a return more directly under the control of management.

name: Accounting determined risk
definition: Risk is considered as the variability of returns, measured by the standard deviation of the ROA figure across the 5-year time period. Other risks, such as the risk of bankruptcy or the risk to management of a takeover, are not explicitly considered.

name: Grand strategy
definition: grand strategy was defined as the major plan of action for achieving the sales and earnings goals for an industrial firm as a whole (rather than a product, division, or market segment).

name: Relative strategic importance of organizational functions
authors_terms: ["relative strategic importance of organizational functions", "functional importance", "critical functional areas", "relative importance of organizational functions"]
definition: managerial perceptions of relative strategic significance (to effective implementation of the grand strategy being pursued) of 55 key result areas grouped into 7 functional categories.

name: Type of production system
definition: Type of production system was measured by using Woodward's (1965) classification scheme. Her scheme is less abstract than others and is appropriate for manufacturing firms.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["perceived environmental uncertainty", "PEU", "managerial perceptions of environmental uncertainty"]
definition: PEU was measured with Miles and Snow's (1978) instrument. It includes 6 scales (total of 25 items) to measure major dimensions of an industrial firm's environment.

name: Organizational performance
definition: High performance samples contained only firms that performed well in both sales growth and profitability. Low performance samples performed poorly according to both criteria.

name: Concerted structural change
definition: Change must be concerted, that is, variables of uncertainty reduction, differentiation, and integration must change together to maintain a complementary alignment.

name: Dramatic structural change
definition: This second aspect of the quantum view postulates that change should occur either in dramatic jumps or not at all. Firms showing very great (or no) changes therefore may be outperformed by firms that change gradually and incrementally.

name: Variability of structural change
authors_terms: ["standard deviations along the variables", "larger standard deviations"]
definition: Firms will be expected to be in one of two states: one in which the variables do not change, or one in which they change a great deal, so that samples pursuing such a strategy will show substantial standard deviations along the variables.

name: Change in uncertainty reduction devices
definition: Uncertainty reduction devices may comprise staff information seeking and processing services, formal structural devices such as delegation of authority and formal policies, programs, and procedures, and interpersonal devices such as consultative decision making.

name: Change in differentiation devices
definition: Organizations must respond to the more diverse contingencies brought about by an uncertain or diverse environment by employing differentiation devices such as decentralization, differentiation of operating styles, and the use of technocrats.

name: Change in integration devices
definition: The coordinative difficulties caused by increased differentiation will require more use of integrative devices, such as participative management, sophisticated control systems, computerized information and budgeting systems, and the use of committees.

name: Strategic planning
definition: Strategic planning is defined here as the systematic process of determining the firm's goals and objectives for at least three years into the future and developing the strategies that will govern the acquisition and use of resources to achieve these objectives.

name: Abnormal stock returns
definition: The residual, u, which is the security-specific component of R,, can be viewed as the return on security j in excess of that expected from acquiring a diversified portfolio of equivalent risk. In this sense, returns are adjusted for risk, and u, may be considered an abnormal return.

name: Systematic risk
definition: In the context of equation (2), b; is a measure of the sensitivity of a security's rate of return relative to market fluctuations.

name: System level technology
authors_terms: ["system level aspects of technology", "system level technology", "system level technology measure", "degree of computerization", "rate of technological change"]
definition: System level aspects of technology, i.e., the rate of technological change and the degree of computerization (extent of computer use in clerical functions and presence of an in-house computer), which represent the activities of the coordinative, service, and control functions of the organization rather than the production process itself.

name: Mass production technology
authors_terms: ["work flow level technology", "degree of mass production", "degree of use of mass production techniques", "degree of automation"]
definition: A work flow level aspect of the transformation technology based on Woodward's scale of production continuity; because many firms used a mix of the different categories, a weighted average of the relative importance of each category was computed as an index of the degree of use of mass production techniques.

name: System level organization structure
authors_terms: ["system level measures of organization structure", "system level structural variables", "structure of the total organizational system"]
definition: Three major dimensions of system level structure have been identified in prior research: (1) differentiation or specialization (horizontal and vertical), (2) formalization, and (3) decentralization; staff ratios also are aspects of the structure of the total organizational system.

name: Work flow level organization structure
authors_terms: ["work flow level measures of organization structure", "work flow level structural variables", "work flow-level structure"]
definition: Structural indicators considered as being more closely related to the work flow or core technology itself, namely the maintenance staff, the span of first line supervisors, and the operating decisions component of decentralization.

name: Employee share ownership
authors_terms: ["number of shares owned", "stockholdings", "financial ownership", "the amount of stock held", "capital invested"]
definition: The scope of an employee's financial ownership of the plant, that is, the number of shares an employee owns in the organization.

name: Employee ownership status
definition: The status of being an owner of the plant, which the purchase effort created for workers, managers and members of the surrounding community; the authors contrast stockholders and nonstockholders.

name: Perceived personal ownership
authors_terms: ["perception of ownership", "psychological or felt ownership", "perceives himself as an owner", "considers themselves owners"]
definition: The extent to which an employee perceives himself or herself as an owner of the firm.

name: Perceived labor-management partnership
definition: The belief that a psychological labor-management partnership exists in the enterprise, i.e., that employees and management are equal partners.

name: Desired influence over decision making
authors_terms: ["desired control", "desired personal influence", "preferred distribution of influence", "preferences for a distribution of power"]
definition: The distribution of influence over the company's decisions that respondents believe should exist, assessed issue by issue for employees as a group, the union, and management.

name: Preference for power equalization between labor and management
definition: The preference for an even distribution of power between labor and management; a difference in power preferences for management and union indicates a lack of interest in power equalization.

name: Occupational interest group
authors_terms: ["occupational interest groups", "interest group membership", "blue-collar, white-collar, middle managers, top managers"]
definition: Occupational positions such as labor and management or blue-collar, white-collar, and managerial, which specify interest groups that exist within a firm and have different definitions of the appropriate distribution of control.

name: Diversification
definition: The degree of diversification of the company's product strategy, placed among Wrigley's (1970) strategic categories; the authors use 'strategy' to denote this degree of diversification.

name: Divisionalization
definition: The degree of divisionalization of organization structure, measured on an ordinal scale ranging from low for functional, through geographically divisional, then product divisional, to highest for product and geographically based divisional structures.

name: Vertical span of control
authors_terms: ["vertical span of control", "number of levels in the core work flow hierarchy"]
definition: A greater vertical span of control, defined as the number of levels within the core workflow hierarchy, is implied by interposing an additional, divisional, level between the chief executive and the peripheral business units.

name: Lateral span of control
authors_terms: ["lateral span of control", "chief executive's lateral span of control"]
definition: It often is assumed that a greater number of specialist staff officers report to the chief executive at the head office, thus increasing his lateral span of control.

name: Company size
authors_terms: ["size", "size of companies", "annual sales", "capital employed", "number of employees"]
definition: The size of the company, captured by the three strongly intercorrelated measures of capital employed, annual sales and number of employees.

name: Number of operating sites
definition: The number of separate sites operated by a company, which can create a complexity and difficulty of coordination and control of its own kind.

name: Geographical dispersion of operations
authors_terms: ["geographical dispersion", "dispersion of major site locations", "geographic dispersion of sites"]
definition: The wide geographical separation of the company's major site locations.

name: Perceived environmental pressure
authors_terms: ["perceived environmental pressure", "perceived environmental pressures", "environmental hostility", "environmental turbulence"]
definition: Five scales were developed for environmental pressure or hostility perceived by interviewees; perceived rather than some other objective levels of external pressure are of concern here.

name: Fit between strategy and structure
definition: A scalar measure of the match between the strategy and structure scales was devised which incorporates the assumptions implicit in the strategy/structure school.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "measures of performance", "return on capital employed", "ROI", "growth"]
definition: Performance measured by average return on capital employed (ROI), growth in profits and ROI, and growth in capital employed, sales, and numbers employed.

name: Variability of return on capital employed
definition: The variability of return on capital employed, measured by the standard deviation of ROI alongside its four-year average.

name: Type of business
definition: Whether the company's operations are in service industries, in manufacturing, or combine both manufacturing and service activities.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["market share", "market strength", "market dominance", "share of most important market"]
definition: Market share, rank (inversely), and dependence on largest customers are treated together as a cluster of variables expected to reduce the hostility of environmental pressures; competitive pressure is likely to be inversely related to the market dominance of the company.

name: Core technology
authors_terms: ["core technology", "process core technology", "small batch or unit core technology", "continuous process technology"]
definition: The core technology is the primary or central transformation process used by the organization to convert inputs into outputs. The core technology is seen as one of the major shaping factors in the organization, but supportive activities, such as purchasing, personnel, and shipping, are viewed as "intervening technologies."

name: Buffering response
definition: The use of part-time and temporary workers is viewed as a buffering, coping response whose purpose is to protect and isolate the technical core from environmental influences as suggested by Thompson (1967) and Litterer (1963).

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: Perceived environmental uncertainty, as used in this study, has three components: (1) the lack of information regarding the environmental factors associated with a given decision making situation; (2) unpredictability of the outcome of a specific decision in terms of the amount of the organization's losses if the decision was incorrect; (3) inability to assign probabilities with any degree of confidence with regard to the effect of environmental factors on the success or failure of the decision unit performing its function.

name: Organization size
definition: In this study, size will refer to the average number of full-time people the organization had available to do its work during 1976. This definition represents the most commonly used approach in research.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size is one of the two principal explanatory variables of the study; the authors discuss the relationship of organizational size to the various aspects of specialization.

name: Task scope
definition: Task scope is a technology indicator, distinguished from other concepts such as specialization, vertical differentiation and horizontal differentiation. Among retail stores, the task scope measure classes the sale of services as offering more variety to the customer than does the sale of goods in the same sense that, among public agencies, more extensive involvement with clients offers more variety than does less extensive involvement.

name: Complexity
definition: Complexity is the number of types of knowledge, discussed by the authors as occupational specialization. The idea of specialization is distinguished from, among other concepts, task scope, vertical differentiation and horizontal differentiation.

name: Horizontal differentiation
definition: Horizontal differentiation is the number of departments or divisions, one of the two very different empirical referents that have been used for structure.

name: Organizational environment
definition: The organizational environment can be broken down into its internal and external environment, and the two key dimensions of complexity and stability are used to provide a measure of organizational environment.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: The simple-complex dimension is viewed as dealing with the degree to which the factors in the decision unit's environment are few in number and are similar to one another in that they are located in a few components.

name: Environmental instability
definition: The static-dynamic dimension is conceived of as the extent to which factors in the decision unit's environment remain stable over time.

name: Long-range planning completeness
authors_terms: ["completeness of the long-range planning process", "planning completeness", "planning process completeness"]
definition: Based on the normative requirements of planning, three ordinal classes of planning completeness were identified: firms with plans in Class 1 do basically no formal long-range planning, those in Class 2 do engage in some long-range planning, and those in Class 3 have a reasonably sophisticated long-range planning process.

name: Use of uncertainty-reducing methods
authors_terms: ["uncertainty-reducing methods", "uncertainty reduction methods", "consultants and computer models"]
definition: One way in which organizations might attempt to reduce uncertainty in their environment is to use a type of formal planning system; another possibility is to utilize outside consultants and predictive models.

name: Open systems approach to planning
definition: Open systems approaches to planning are measured by more participation of lower organization levels, more upward flows of information, and more public information.

name: Planning process development
authors_terms: ["planning process development", "length of time that the planning process had been in use"]
definition: The length of time that the formal long-range planning process had been in use.

name: Long-range planning time span
authors_terms: ["long-range planning time span", "planning horizon", "planning time span"]
definition: The time span of the long-range plan, which the authors expect to be shorter for organizations that plan in a dynamic environment.

name: Planning review frequency
definition: The frequency with which the plan contains procedures for anticipating or detecting differences between the plan and actual performance and for preventing or correcting these differences.

name: Immediacy and tangibility of planning goals
definition: Whether planning premises support more immediate and tangible goals, as opposed to longer-range and intangible goals.

name: Administrative turnover
authors_terms: ["turnover of department heads", "departmental turnover", "administrative change", "succession", "administrative turnover"]
definition: Departmental turnover was defined as the number of different persons occupying the department head position during the period 1954 to 1974.

name: Paradigm development
definition: The concept of paradigm development expresses the extent to which members of a field share beliefs about the field's problems, content, and procedures. Paradigm development can indicate a department's potential for disagreement and, hence, for managing interdependence.

name: Resource interdependence
authors_terms: ["resource interdependence", "pooled interdependence for resources", "resource scarcity", "resource scarcity index"]
definition: Because the study is concerned with resource availability relative to size, a resource scarcity index was derived by taking the rank difference between each department's rank on size and rank on grants; this index classifies departments according to their pooled interdependence for resources.

name: Task interdependence
authors_terms: ["task interdependence", "interdependence of teaching activities", "interdependence in teaching activities"]
definition: Interdependent tasks require coordination and can create unpredictability and conflict; in university departments, teaching duties become interdependent when courses are prerequisites to others and must be coordinated. Such differences can be characterized as differences in task interdependence.

name: Turbulence of historical period
authors_terms: ["turbulence", "years of turbulence", "periods of change", "historical periods", "turbulent times", "turbulent period"]
definition: Periods of change, whether growth or decline, force a greater number of decisions on organizations; the 20 years were divided into two groups of 10 each, one set labeled 'years of turbulence' and the other set 'years of normalcy.'

name: Form of administrative position
definition: The head is appointed for an indefinite term unless removed by death, resignation, or a two-thirds vote by the faculty. The chairperson serves for a specific term, usually three years, which can be aborted by death and resignation and extended by a vote of renewal at the end of the term.

name: Risk taking propensity
authors_terms: ["risk taking propensity", "propensity for risk taking", "general risk taking propensity"]
definition: The perceived probability of receiving the rewards associated with success of a proposed situation, which is required by an individual before he will subject himself to the consequences associated with failure, the alternative situation providing less reward as well as less severe consequences than the proposed situation.

name: Entrepreneurial status
authors_terms: ["entrepreneur", "major owner and manager of a business venture who is not employed elsewhere", "owner-managers"]
definition: An entrepreneur is a major owner and manager of a business venture who is not employed elsewhere; respondents were selected who very recently had made the decision to become owner-managers.

name: Momentum in strategy and structure
authors_terms: ["momentum", "continuous change", "continuity in the direction of change", "simultaneous continuity", "pervasive momentum"]
definition: Momentum is expected to be a dominant factor in organizational evolution; that is, reversals in the direction of change in variables of strategy and structure are expected to be relatively rare. A variable changes continuously over two consecutive transition periods if its transition score is greater than or equal to four for both periods, or else less than or equal to four for both periods.

name: Reversal in the direction of change
definition: A variable is said to have had a reversal (e.g., from an increase to a decrease or vice versa) from the former period to the latter when its change is not continuous across two consecutive transition periods. Sequences are called revolutionary if there are significantly many simultaneous reversals in the variables.

name: Interdependence among strategy and structure elements
authors_terms: ["interdependencies among variables of organization and strategy making", "multivariate interdependencies", "integral relationships", "gestalts"]
definition: There are integral relationships among environmental, organizational, and strategy-making variables, so that changes (or stability) in the variables tend to occur together in order to maintain an appropriate balance or configuration. Such multivariate interdependencies tend to manifest gestalts, that is common configurations of mutually reinforcing elements of strategy, structure and environment.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The authors state that 'Performance was also measured'; performance changes between periods are described as improvements, declines, or no-change ratings.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: One of the environmental variables measured; the authors write that 'The environmental variables that were measured were: dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity of the markets.'

name: Environmental hostility
definition: One of the environmental variables measured; the authors write that 'The environmental variables that were measured were: dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity of the markets.'

name: Market heterogeneity
definition: One of the environmental variables measured; the authors write that 'The environmental variables that were measured were: dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity of the markets.'

name: Scanning
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'scanning' among these variables, whose definitions and scales are available from the senior author.

name: Controls and communication system effectiveness
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'controls and communication system effectiveness' among these variables.

name: Centralization of authority for strategy making
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'centralization of authority for strategy making' among these variables.

name: Delegation of routine authority
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'delegation of routine authority' among these variables.

name: Technocratization
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'technocratization' among these variables.

name: Resource availability
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'resource availability' among these variables.

name: Organizational differentiation
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'differentiation' among these variables.

name: Top management tenure
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'tenure (years in office) of top management' among these variables.

name: Prevalence of traditions
definition: One of the structural or organizational variables included; the authors list 'the prevalence of traditions' among these variables.

name: Proactiveness
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Risk taking
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Product-market innovation
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Analysis
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Multiplexity
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Integration
definition: One of the strategy-making variables measured; the authors write that 'Strategy making was described by: proactiveness, risk taking, product-market innovation, analysis, multiplexity, integration, futurity, consciousness of strategies, adaptiveness, and industry expertise.'

name: Futurity
