name: Discretion over work decisions
authors_terms: ["discretion over work", "autonomy in work decisions", "hierarchy of authority"]
definition: The discretion that job occupants have over decisions about their own work, measured by the hierarchy of authority; Perrow makes a critical distinction between organizational power and work discretion.

name: Emphasis on efficiency
authors_terms: ["emphasis on efficiency", "efficiency as a system goal", "efficiency of operation"]
definition: The emphasis placed by organizational decision-makers on the efficiency of operation as a system goal; the routinization of the work-flow allows for the efficient handling of large numbers of clients at low cost, efficiency thereby becoming a system goal.

name: Emphasis on staff morale
authors_terms: ["emphasis on morale", "morale as a system goal", "morale of the staff"]
definition: The emphasis placed by organizational decision-makers on the morale of the staff as a system goal, one of the four goals presented to respondents in paired comparisons.

name: Emphasis on new programs
authors_terms: ["emphasis on the development of new programs", "development of new programs or services", "new programs as a system goal"]
definition: The emphasis placed by organizational decision-makers on the development of new programs or services as a system goal, akin to the idea of innovation.

name: Emphasis on quality of client service
authors_terms: ["emphasis on quality", "quality of client service", "quality of service"]
definition: The emphasis placed on the quality of client service as a product goal, contrasted with the quantity of clients served; respondents were asked whether the organization placed greater emphasis on the quantity of clients served or on the quality of client service.

name: Emphasis on effectiveness
definition: The emphasis placed on the effectiveness of client services, one of the four goals presented to respondents in paired comparisons.

name: Technical communication network structure
authors_terms: ["structure of the technical communication network", "technical discussion network", "three forms of technical communication networks"]
definition: The structure of the technical communication network of the laboratory, investigated in three forms: technical discussion, critical incident information, and new research ideas.

name: Formal organizational structure
definition: The pattern of formal organizational relationships in the laboratory; the work group consists of a first-line supervisor and those reporting to him.

name: Informal organization
definition: The structure of the informal organization; that is, the pattern of friendships and social relations among members of the laboratory.

name: Technological gatekeepers
authors_terms: ["technological gatekeepers", "sociometric stars", "key positions in the communication network"]
definition: Individuals who occupy key positions in the communication network of the laboratory; that is, those to whom others in the laboratory most frequently turn for technical advice and consultation.

name: Use of the scientific and technological literature
authors_terms: ["scientific and technological literature", "technical reading habits", "professional and scientific periodicals"]
definition: Such formal media as the scientific and technological literature, that is, the technical periodicals to which members subscribe or which they read regularly, including journals published under the sponsorship of scientific and engineering societies.

name: Use of external information sources
authors_terms: ["informal contact with members of the scientific and technological community outside of their own laboratory", "personal friends outside the laboratory as sources of information", "contact with members of other organizations"]
definition: Contact with members of the scientific and technological community outside of the laboratory, including the use of technical friends and personal friends outside the organization as sources of information.

name: Technical information flow into the laboratory
definition: The flow of technological and scientific information both into and within the research and development laboratory.

name: Status in the laboratory
definition: The presence of prestige or status hierarchies in a social system; in these laboratories the status differential is exemplified by possession of the doctorate degree.

name: Organizational slack
definition: It is the difference between the payments required to maintain the organization and the revenue obtained from the environment, and is the source of resources for the organization.

name: Economic orientation
definition: Economic orientation is defined, in this study, as the degree of preference that an organization has for low costs.

name: Frequency of trial of new drugs
authors_terms: ["frequency of trial", "frequency of trial of new drugs"]
definition: Frequency of trial of new drugs was measured by responses to a questionnaire on drug use.

name: Promptness of trial of new drugs
definition: The raw score for promptness of trial was the elapsed time in days between the date of market release of a drug and the date of first purchase.

name: Hierarchical differentiation
authors_terms: ["hierarchical differentiation", "vertical division of labor", "the proliferation of supervisory levels", "number of levels of supervision"]
definition: Hierarchical differentiation is the proliferation of supervisory levels in an organization; it is described as increasing vertical division of labor in a bureaucracy.

name: Functional differentiation
authors_terms: ["functional differentiation", "horizontal division of labor", "the proliferation of subunits", "number of divisions"]
definition: Functional differentiation is the proliferation of subunits in an organization, described as horizontal division of labor.

name: Decentralization of decision-making authority
authors_terms: ["decentralization of authority", "delegation of authority", "centralization of decision-making authority", "decision-making authority"]
definition: The extent to which authority to make decisions is centralized in the head of an organization rather than delegated among his subordinates; decentralization is the delegation of decision-making authority to lower levels.

name: Accessibility of rules
authors_terms: ["formal rules", "written regulations", "accessibility of the rules", "written and formalized rules"]
definition: The extent to which organizational regulations are written and formalized, that is, accessible to all members of the organization. The presence of written rules governing promotions was used as the indicator of accessibility.

name: Rules that determine decisions in advance
authors_terms: ["rules that partly determine decisions in advance", "rules that remove decisions from the managerial hierarchy", "examinations"]
definition: Regulations that set criteria according to which decisions are to be made and thereby remove decisions from the managerial hierarchy; a promotion rule based on examination scores is the example given.

name: Rules allowing discretion to top managers
authors_terms: ["rules and practices that allow much discretion to top managers", "rules that centralize authority in the managers", "evaluations"]
definition: Rules and practices that centralize authority in the managerial hierarchy by allowing top managers wide discretion in making decisions, such as weighting personal evaluations in promotion decisions.

name: Division of labor
definition: Division of labor refers to the distribution of individuals among the structural parts, in contrast to structural differentiation, which means the number of structural parts that exist.

name: Industry size
definition: Industry size refers to the number of production personnel in each industry; since administrative personnel exist to solve problems of coordination among production personnel, the measure of industry size is the total number of craftsmen, operatives, and laborers in each industry.

name: Relative number of administrative personnel
definition: Relative number of administrative personnel refers to the ratio between the number of administrative personnel and the number of production personnel.

name: Managerial hierarchy
definition: Managerial personnel represent coordination through managerial hierarchy; since the managerial hierarchy exerts its coordinative functions primarily through hierarchical authority and supervision, the relative number of managerial personnel in an industry indicates the extent to which coordination is achieved through these mechanisms.

name: Formal communication structure
definition: Clerical personnel are concerned with paper work and communication, so the relative number of this group is indicative of the development of files and the degree to which production activities are regularized and standardized through formal written specifications and communications.

name: Professional authority
definition: For professional personnel the primary coordinative mechanism is professional authority; the relative number of professional personnel reveals the extent to which status and authority are legitimated on the basis of knowledge and technical skills.

name: Subenvironment certainty
authors_terms: ["certainty of the relevant subenvironment", "subenvironmental certainty", "certainty of the subenvironment"]
definition: Three indicators of subenvironmental certainty were used: the rate of change of conditions over time in the subenvironment, the certainty of information about conditions in the subenvironment at any particular time, and the modal time span of definitive feedback from the subenvironment on the results of subsystem behavior. Each of these environments can range from highly dynamic to extremely stable.

name: Relevant subenvironment
definition: In dividing tasks, the organization is also ordering its environment into three sectors: the market subenvironment, the technical-economic subenvironment, and the scientific subenvironment. Each major subsystem was seen as coping with its respective segment of the total external environment.

name: Time span of definitive feedback
authors_terms: ["modal time span of definitive feedback", "time span of definitive feedback", "modal time required to get definitive feedback"]
definition: One of the three indicators of subenvironmental certainty: the modal time span of definitive feedback from the subenvironment on the results of subsystem behavior.

name: Formalized structure
definition: Structure here refers to those aspects of behavior in organizations subject to pre-existing programs and controls, that is, the extent of pre-existing programs and controls.

name: Interpersonal orientation
authors_terms: ["interpersonal orientation", "task-social dimension", "task-oriented interpersonal orientations", "social interpersonal orientations"]
definition: A cognitive and affective orientation toward the objects of work, which is manifested in a person's interpersonal style; the objects can be either people or inanimate tools and instruments, and the concern of members with them tends to polarize along a task-social dimension.

name: Time orientation
authors_terms: ["time orientation of members", "time orientations of subsystem members", "dominant time orientation"]
definition: A production subsystem that received feedback about its efforts on an almost daily basis could be expected to have members with a short-term orientation, whereas a research unit coping with a subenvironment where feedback might occur only on the completion of a project lasting well over a year would be apt to have members with a more long-term orientation.

name: Goal orientation
definition: The fourth attribute that subsystems were expected to develop in relation to their subenvironments was the goal orientation of members: marketing managers could be expected to be more concerned with customer and competitor actions, while production executives would be more oriented toward the operation of equipment and the actions of suppliers.

name: Differentiation
definition: Differentiation is defined as the state of segmentation of the organizational system into subsystems, each of which tends to develop particular attributes in relation to the requirements posed by its relevant external environment. Differentiation includes the behavioral attributes of members of organizational subsystems.

name: Requisite integration
definition: What March and Simon have identified as the felt need for joint decision-making, or what is here termed the degree of requisite integration: whether task characteristics make it possible for subsystems in an organization to operate independently of each other, or require continual collaboration in making decisions before a given subsystem may act.

name: Integration
definition: Integration is defined as the process of achieving unity of effort among the various subsystems in the accomplishment of the organization's task.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["overall performance", "relative economic performance", "total performance of the organization"]
definition: Overall performance in coping with the external environment; in the organizations studied it seemed desirable to use the conventional financial data used by management as measures of performance.

name: Integrative devices
definition: Many organizational systems develop integrative devices in addition to the conventional hierarchy: coordinating departments, task forces, and cross-functional coordinating teams are emerging to achieve coordination.

name: Effectiveness of integrative devices
authors_terms: ["effective integrative devices", "effective integrative subsystems", "effectiveness of these devices"]
definition: The extent to which integrative devices function effectively in achieving integration between differentiated subsystems; in organization I, with the most effective integration, the integrative subsystem was consistently intermediate in structure and orientation, whereas other organizations had integrative subsystems that were only moderately intermediate or intermediate to a very limited extent.

name: Environmental demands for differentiation and integration
authors_terms: ["environment requires both a high degree of subsystem differentiation and a high degree of integration"]
definition: The environmental conditions of the industry studied, particularly the importance of innovation, seemed to require organizations to achieve a high degree of both differentiation and integration.

name: Intermediacy of integrative subsystem attributes
authors_terms: ["intermediate position of integrative subsystems", "intermediate between those found in subsystems"]
definition: The orientations of members of the integrative subsystem are intermediate between those found in the subsystems they are to coordinate, and the structure of the integrative subsystem is intermediate between those of the basic subsystems being linked.

name: Influence attributed to integrative subsystem
authors_terms: ["influence attributed to integrative subsystem", "perceived to have high influence in decision making"]
definition: The members of effective integrative subsystems would be perceived by other organizational members as having high influence in decision making relative to the members of other subsystems.

name: Basis of integrators' influence
definition: Influence can be based either on professional expertise or on hierarchical authority; influence based on hierarchical position is not appropriate where professional judgment is required for decisions related to coordination.

name: Perceived rewards for a superordinate goal
authors_terms: ["perceived basis of rewards", "rewarded for the achievement with others of a superordinate goal", "basis of evaluation"]
definition: Effective integrators were expected to perceive that they were being rewarded for the achievement with others of a superordinate goal; the criteria by which personnel were being evaluated indicated to them the basis on which they were being rewarded.

name: Total perceived influence
definition: Another factor related to effective integrative devices would be a high total amount of perceived influence in the organization.

name: Locus of influence relative to knowledge
authors_terms: ["locus of influence", "sufficient degree of influence to resolve interdepartmental conflicts at the level where the most knowledge is available"]
definition: A sufficient degree of influence to resolve interdepartmental conflicts at the level in each subsystem where the most knowledge about subenvironmental conditions was available.

name: Confrontation mode of conflict resolution
authors_terms: ["confrontation", "confrontation as the typical mode of conflict resolution", "problem-solving modes of conflict resolution"]
definition: One of five possible modes of resolving conflict identified by Blake and Mouton: win-lose power struggle, smoothing over, withdrawal, compromise, or confrontation; organizations placing greater emphasis on confrontation or problem-solving modes of conflict resolution would have effective intergroup relations.

name: Centralization
authors_terms: ["degree of centralization", "centralization of power", "distribution of power", "participation in decision making", "hierarchy of authority"]
definition: The degree of centralization in an organization may be defined either as the degree of participation in decision making or the degree of reliance on the hierarchy of authority. Participation in decision making represents how much the occupants of various positions participate in decisions about the allocation of resources and the determination of organization policies; hierarchy of authority refers to decisions involving the work associated with each social position.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization represents the use of rules in an organization. Job codification is a measure of how many rules define what the occupants of positions are to do while rule observation is a measure of whether or not the rules are employed.

name: Complexity
definition: We interpret complexity to mean at least three things: the number of occupational specialities, the professional activity, and the professional training.

name: Degree of bureaucratization
definition: The degree to which an organization or organizational segment shows the dimensions of the bureaucratic model. "Organizations considered bureaucratic are thought to have these dimensions present to a high degree; nonbureaucratic organizations, in these terms do not show these dimensions."

name: Task routinizability
authors_terms: ["type of task", "Type I tasks", "Type II tasks", "uniform or routinizable tasks", "nonuniform or difficult to routinize tasks"]
definition: The extent to which the task of an organizational segment deals with uniform events and traditional skills and is easily routinized. Type I tasks are "uniform, easily routinized tasks"; Type II tasks are "nonuniform and difficult to routinize," requiring social or creative skills.

name: Hierarchical level
definition: The position of an organizational member in the vertical hierarchy, distinguishing executive from nonexecutive levels. "Different types of behavior and interpersonal relationships are expected at different hierarchical levels and these differences would appear to influence the structure."

name: Job skill level
authors_terms: ["technology", "highly skilled crafts", "unskilled and semiskilled jobs", "department A", "department B", "mass production characteristics"]
definition: The technology of the job: department A includes jobs that represent highly skilled crafts, in which an individual must apply difficult skills to produce a whole or almost a whole, highly complex product; department B includes jobs that are primarily unskilled and semiskilled, composed of automatic and semiautomatic tasks where the employee performs very little creative work.

name: Desire for high-quality work
authors_terms: ["desire to produce high-quality work", "concern about the quality of their products", "needs to produce high-quality work"]
definition: The need to produce high-quality work and concern about the quality of one's products, inferred from an individual content analysis made of each interview.

name: Work involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement and interest in their work", "need to learn more", "interest in their actual jobs"]
definition: Involvement and interest in one's work; one measure of involvement in the kind of work is the extent to which the individual expresses a desire to learn more about his particular job or jobs within the same family of jobs.

name: Emphasis on money
authors_terms: ["emphasis on the importance of money as a reward", "potency of the need for money", "money as being the thing they like best about the company", "need for wages"]
definition: The emphasis an individual places on money as a reward, expressed as the degree of potency of the need for money and as the extent to which money is reported as what the employee likes best about the company.

name: Maturity of needs
authors_terms: ["needs allied to the \"infant\" side of the model", "mature predispositions", "model of personality growth", "needs for variety and challenge", "relative independence"]
definition: Human beings in our culture are hypothesized to develop from infants to adults along dimensions such as passivity to increasing activity, dependence to relative independence, shallow to deeper interests, few to many ways of behaving, short to longer time perspective, subordinate to equal or superordinate position, and lack of awareness of self to awareness of and control over self. Employees in a work world requiring behavior nearer the infantile side of the model should view themselves as having more needs allied to the infant side than to the mature side.

name: Sense of self-worth
authors_terms: ["sense of self-worth", "low sense of self-worth", "many abilities to offer", "nothing much to offer"]
definition: The sense that one has many abilities to offer that are very important to one's company or any other company, as opposed to the sense of having nothing much to offer except a few abilities learned on the job.

name: Spoiled work
authors_terms: ["spoiled work and extra operations", "spoilage of work"]
definition: The amount of spoiled work and extra operations in a department, compared with the standard the department defines for itself at the beginning of each month.

name: Self-blame for errors
authors_terms: ["willingness to blame themselves for their errors", "blame other departments for the cause of errors, waste, and scrap"]
definition: The willingness of employees to see errors as resulting from their own haste rather than blaming other departments for errors, waste and scrap.

name: Friendships at work
authors_terms: ["friendships that endure", "close friendships", "enduring friendships within the plant"]
definition: The close and lasting friendships employees form while working in the plant.

name: Creative activity outside the plant
authors_terms: ["creative and productive outside the organization", "creative activities", "noncreative activities"]
definition: Activities outside the plant that require more skill and are viewed by people as challenging, as opposed to activities that do not require much creative thought and permit an individual to be passive, quiet, and alone.

name: Absenteeism and turnover
definition: Absenteeism, turnover and transfer, which the framework treats as informal activities by which employees leave the situation when they cannot actualize themselves.

name: Upward mobility and organizational involvement
authors_terms: ["desire to become executives", "involved in the objectives and survival of the organization", "desire for upward mobility", "involvement in the company's problems"]
definition: The desire to become an executive and to be involved in the objectives and survival of the organization, including wanting information about the company and having suggestions to improve one's responsibility.

name: Desire to unionize
authors_terms: ["desire to unionize", "formalize the informal groups in the form of trade unions"]
definition: The desire of employees to formalize informal groups in the form of trade unions.

name: Board size
authors_terms: ["board size", "board size squared", "total number of board positions"]
definition: The number of individuals serving on a board of directors, which the authors argue may be either positively or negatively associated with strategic change; measured as the total number of board positions.

name: Board tenure
authors_terms: ["board tenure", "average board member tenure", "maximum number of years that a board member could sit on the board"]
definition: The average length of time board members have served on the board: low-tenure boards have a less rich information base for recommending strategic change, while high-tenure boards are likely to be more rigidly committed to the strategic status quo.

name: Board member age
authors_terms: ["board member age", "average age of board members", "average board member age"]
definition: The average age of the members of a board, where older members are argued to be more risk averse but also to have greater confidence and experience, implying a possible nonlinear relationship with strategic change.

name: Occupational heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["occupational heterogeneity", "occupational heterogeneity squared", "group heterogeneity", "board member occupational heterogeneity"]
definition: The extent to which board members' occupational experiences vary widely; heterogeneous boards are more likely to generate a broad array of strategic options, but at very high levels the drawbacks of conflicts may impede acting on those options.

name: Board business orientation
authors_terms: ["business orientation", "proportion of board members from business occupations", "business leaders on boards"]
definition: The extent to which board members' occupations are of a business or legal nature; business leaders are expected to represent the business interests of the organization and to be particularly receptive to the need for adaptive change.

name: Board attention to strategic issues
authors_terms: ["attention to strategy", "board attention to strategic issues", "attention to strategic vs. nonstrategic issues"]
definition: The degree to which the board devotes its attention and time to strategic rather than nonstrategic issues; boards that spend more time on strategic issues are proposed to be more familiar and aware of the question of strategic change.

name: Comprehensiveness of board evaluation process
authors_terms: ["comprehensiveness of CEO evaluation", "comprehensiveness of a board's evaluation process"]
definition: The degree to which the board evaluates top management performance; boards that engage in comprehensive evaluations of the CEO are likely to be and see themselves as well informed about the strategic direction of the organization.

name: Board power
authors_terms: ["board power", "relative power of the board over the CEO"]
definition: A relational construct: the relative power of the board over the CEO, measured with multiple behavioral and structural indicators of the board-CEO relationship.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "changes in the scope of the firm", "proportional change in product/services"]
definition: Change in the scope of the firm, operationalized as changes in the hospital's product/service portfolio: the growth or decline in products/services from 1985 to 1990, expressed as a proportional change from the services originally offered in 1985.

name: Strategic difference between focal firm and director home firms
authors_terms: ["difference between the strategy of the focal firm and the strategy of manager-director home companies", "non-directional difference", "squared difference scores"]
definition: The non-directional difference, or the absolute value of the difference, between the focal firm's strategy and manager-director home company strategies. The authors argue that board members perceive a greater need for change in the current strategy if it diverges from their home firm strategies.

name: Outside succession
authors_terms: ["outside succession", "outside CEO succession", "selecting an outsider as the new CEO"]
definition: Hiring a new CEO from outside the organization. The authors argue that boards may use outside CEO succession as an initial step in the process of implementing strategic changes that make the focal firm more strategically similar to their home companies.

name: Director home firm strategy
authors_terms: ["strategy of manager-director home companies", "corporate strategy of a manager-director's home firm", "average diversification of director home companies"]
definition: The corporate strategy of a manager-director's home firm, where the director serves as an executive. It can be viewed as an important indicator of their attitudes and beliefs about strategy, because directors involved in formulating or implementing a strategy tend to develop attitudes that validate it.

name: New CEO's prior employer strategy
authors_terms: ["strategy of the outside successor's prior firm", "strategy of the new CEO's prior employer", "prior experience with the chosen strategy"]
definition: The corporate strategy of the firm where the outside successor previously worked as a top manager, which indicates that the new CEO has prior experience with the strategy the board favors for the focal firm.

name: New CEO's board tie firm strategy
authors_terms: ["strategy of firms where the new CEO serves as outside director", "strategy of the new CEO's board ties"]
definition: The corporate strategy of firms where the new CEO serves as an outside director. The authors argue that CEOs who serve as outside directors can learn about the efficacy of different approaches to strategic change by observing first-hand the consequences of management decisions at other firms.

name: Focal firm strategy
authors_terms: ["focal firm's strategy following outside succession", "focal firm's new corporate strategy", "diversification strategy prior to succession"]
definition: The corporate strategy of the focal firm, indicated by its level of product market and geographic diversification, assessed following outside succession while controlling for the prior value so that the models estimate change in strategy.

name: Focal firm performance
definition: Firm performance at the focal firm, measured with accounting- and market-based indicators. Poor firm performance may amplify the effect of strategic differences on outside succession, because it empowers the board and justifies its involvement in management selection.

name: Director home firm performance
authors_terms: ["home firm performance", "performance at manager-director home firms", "apparent success of their home firm strategies"]
definition: The apparent success of a manager-director's home firm strategy, indicated by performance at the director's home company. Boards are more likely to consider adopting the strategies of other organizations when those strategies are associated with favorable outcomes.

name: Director home firm tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure of manager-directors", "director home firm tenure", "tenure of manager-directors at their home firms"]
definition: The number of years a manager-director has been employed at their current home company. Tenure in an organization is associated with psychological commitment to the status quo, including commitment to the organization's current strategy.

name: Learning from foreign parents
authors_terms: ["learning from the foreign parents", "Current Knowledge learned from Foreign Parents", "knowledge acquired from foreign parents", "IJV learning"]
definition: The IJV's learning from its foreign parents, i.e. grafting: adding to an organization's knowledge base by internalizing knowledge not previously available to it. Measured as the extent to which the IJV has learned new technological expertise, new marketing expertise, product development, managerial techniques, and manufacturing process from its foreign parents.

name: IJV performance
definition: The IJV's performance in specific areas (increasing business volume, increasing market share, achieving planned goals, and making profits) together with the general performance of the IJV as evaluated by the Hungarian parent, foreign parents, and the IJV general manager.

name: Trust between parents
authors_terms: ["trust between an IJV's parents", "Trust Between Parents", "level of trust"]
definition: A willingness to risk vulnerability and the confidence that another party, not under your control, will refrain from exploiting your vulnerabilities. What matters most is the partners' overall confidence in one another's trustworthiness.

name: Relative absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["absorptive capacity relative to its foreign parents", "relative absorptive capacity"]
definition: One firm will be better able to learn from another when it is familiar with the type of new knowledge offered by the teacher firm, when the organizations have compatible norms and values, and when they have similar operational priorities or 'dominant logics'.

name: Prior knowledge from foreign parents
authors_terms: ["Prior Knowledge from Foreign Parents", "relevant prior knowledge", "prior learning"]
definition: The knowledge the IJV has previously acquired from its foreign parents, which is expected to make its current learning efforts more effective.

name: Cultural compatibility of parents
authors_terms: ["Cultural Compatibility", "cultural compatibility of an IJV's parents"]
definition: The extent to which the parents' cultures are compatible, so that the IJV's managers can understand the norms and values implicit in the acquired know-how; it is measured by reverse scoring items on the extent to which cultural misunderstandings and cultural differences have been issues in the IJV.

name: Business relatedness of IJV and foreign parent
authors_terms: ["Relatedness of IJV's and Foreign Parent's Businesses", "business relatedness"]
definition: The similarity of business objectives and strategic resources of the foreign parent and the IJV, used as a proxy for shared dominant logics.

name: Organizational flexibility and adaptability
authors_terms: ["IJV Flexibility", "Flexibility and Adaptability", "organizational flexibility and creativity"]
definition: The extent to which the IJV organization is flexible, adapting to change, creative, and rewards performance, an organizational structure or process thought to facilitate the assimilation of knowledge from the foreign parent.

name: Formal goals and objectives
authors_terms: ["Formal Goals", "formal goals and objectives", "written business goals and plans"]
definition: The IJV's use of explicit written goals and business plans, which help focus the attention of the parents and the IJV on potentially useful knowledge to be transferred.

name: Specialization of parents' roles
authors_terms: ["Specialization by Foreign and Domestic Parents", "specialization of parents' roles"]
definition: The extent to which the foreign parent(s) provides technology to the IJV while the domestic parent provides the manufacturing capability.

name: Management support by foreign parents
authors_terms: ["Management Support by Foreign Parents", "managerial involvement by foreign parents", "contributions of management support"]
definition: The degree to which the foreign parent(s) contribute sales/marketing support, managerial resources, administrative support, emotional support, training, and time to the IJV.

name: Training by foreign parents
authors_terms: ["Training by Foreign Parents", "Education and Training by Foreign Parents"]
definition: The extent to which managers in the IJV were given education and training by the foreign parents, providing a vehicle for transferring both explicit and tacit knowledge.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: The degree to which the IJV's business strategy emphasizes differentiation rather than cost leadership, through new products, promotion and advertising, a broad product line, customer service, trained personnel, and influence over distribution channels.

name: Training and personnel development competence
authors_terms: ["Training Competence", "competence in training and personnel development"]
definition: The IJV's ability to train and develop its own personnel, which can help performance by adapting and disseminating new knowledge learned from foreign parents and by helping managers develop new skills.

name: International strategy
authors_terms: ["international corporate strategy", "international strategy", "global strategy", "multidomestic strategy", "global companies", "multidomestic companies"]
definition: International corporate strategy is defined as the way in which the organization positions itself with regard to the global business environment and creates and sustains competitive advantage across national boundaries. The paper focuses on the distinction between global and multidomestic strategies.

name: Acquisition entry mode
definition: If an equity mode of entry into a foreign market is chosen, the issue of whether to acquire an existing local firm (acquisition) or to set up a completely new plant (greenfield investment) has to be decided.

name: Headquarters control
authors_terms: ["level of control", "control mechanisms", "control exercised by headquarters", "control by headquarters"]
definition: The level of control exercised by headquarters by means of the different types of control mechanisms is the first element of the headquarters-subsidiary relationship. The key aspect of the headquarters-subsidiary relationship is the way in which headquarters ensures that subsidiaries are working towards common organizational goals.

name: Expatriate presence
definition: The second element of the headquarters-subsidiary relationship that is studied is the level of expatriate presence in subsidiaries. Expatriates can perform many roles in the headquarters-subsidiary relationship, among them control and knowledge transfer.

name: Local responsiveness
authors_terms: ["level of local responsiveness", "local responsiveness", "local production, local R&D and adaptation of products and marketing to local conditions"]
definition: The final element studied is the level of local responsiveness - in terms of local production, local R&D and adaptation of products and marketing to local conditions - that headquarters allows to the subsidiary.

name: Headquarters-subsidiary relationship
definition: The headquarters-subsidiary relationship can be seen as a classic control problem, whose attributes are similar to principal-agent relationships; its key aspect is the way in which headquarters ensures that subsidiaries are working towards common organizational goals. It is examined through the level of control, the level of expatriate presence and the level of local responsiveness.

name: Subsidiary tenure under headquarters ownership
authors_terms: ["time for which subsidiaries had been under ownership of headquarters", "length of ownership", "time the subsidiary has been under headquarters ownership"]
definition: The time for which subsidiaries had been under ownership of headquarters at the time of the study, calculated as the year of data collection minus the year of establishment for greenfields and minus the year in which the current owner had acquired them for acquisitions.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Strategy is conceptualized as a 'second order' construct that is composed of all three 'first order' strategic dimensions (marketing differentiation, innovative differentiation and low cost), on which a firm can score low or high; its effects are denoted 'utility' effects and result from the fit of the particular offering to the particular needs of the market segment addressed.

name: Firm assets and capabilities
authors_terms: ["firm assets", "idiosyncratic firm assets", "resources and capabilities", "firm specific effects", "efficiency effects"]
definition: Resources are those tangible (or intangible) assets that are tied semi-permanently to the firm; available idiosyncratic assets resulting from strategic factor market imperfections and/or internal processes constrain strategy choice, and in this research they were determined to include organizational, marketing and technical capabilities.

name: Industry forces
definition: Industry forces affect the sustainability of above average performance against bargaining and against direct and indirect competition; they comprise barriers to entry, bargaining power of buyers, power of suppliers, threat of substitutes and competitive rivalry, referring to the particular situation confronted by each firm in its major market served.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm success is treated as a two-dimensional phenomenon, where market performance reflects the external firm accomplishments in the market place, and profitability the internal to the firm economic rents stemming from its strategic activities.

name: Market performance
definition: Market performance reflects the external firm accomplishments in the market place and was measured with market share, absolute sales volume, increase in market share and sales, all relative to competition.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability represents the internal to the firm economic rents stemming from its strategic activities and was gauged with perceptual items reflecting return on equity, profit margin and net profits relative to competition.

name: Revenue performance
definition: An industry standard performance measure, given as revenues per room. Heightened demand should increase hotels' occupancy or allow hotels to hike their prices, or a combination of both, and all these possibilities increase revenues.

name: Presence of larger hotels
authors_terms: ["FRA GTSZ", "fraction of firms in the market that are larger", "fraction of larger hotels in a market"]
definition: The fraction of firms in the market that are larger (greater in size) than the focal hotel. For the largest hotel in a market FRA GTSZ is zero while for the smallest hotel it is equal to one.

name: Presence of chain affiliated hotels
authors_terms: ["FRA HAIN", "fraction of chain affiliated firms", "fraction of chains"]
definition: The fraction of chain affiliated firms in the market, which can be based upon either the count of competitors or the count of rooms in the market.

name: Chain affiliation
definition: Brand affiliation, or chain affiliation in the lodging setting, is a signaling mechanism for quality; firms create brands to signal higher unobserved quality.

name: Establishment size
definition: The physical size of an establishment in rooms. Large hotels are typically more luxurious than small hotels and therefore will charge higher prices per room because they have more features.

name: Rural location
definition: Whether a hotel's market is rural rather than suburban or urban. Rural economic activity is more homogenous, so rural hotels' actions to inform customers are likely to easily extend to other hotels in the immediate vicinity.

name: Size similarity to market
definition: Degree to which an establishment's size is similar to the sizes of other hotels in the same market; higher values indicate greater similarity in size.

name: Chain affiliation similarity to market
definition: Degree to which an establishment's chain affiliation status is similar to the chain affiliation statuses of other hotels in the same market; higher values indicate greater similarity in chain affiliation.

name: Top manager age
definition: The age of a hospital's top manager, suggested to be negatively associated with his/her receptivity to change and innovation; with advancing age, managers may become less flexible from a cognitive standpoint in adapting to new ideas and practices.

name: Top manager organizational tenure
definition: The length of a top manager's tenure in the organization; top managers with long tenure are likely to have obligations to existing organizational constituencies that have vested interests in the status quo.

name: Top manager education
authors_terms: ["director's possession of a graduate degree", "education", "highly educated"]
definition: The level of a top manager's education; in theory highly educated individuals may engage in more boundary spanning and may possess greater ability to handle the complex information processing that change efforts entail.

name: Prior exposure to TQM
authors_terms: ["director's prior TQM exposure", "prior exposure to TQM", "prior exposure"]
definition: A manager's previous exposure to an innovation, which may be an indicator of his/her propensity to adopt that innovation in the future; VHA hospital directors who have managed a hospital with an innovation may be inclined to adopt that innovation at other hospitals that they subsequently manage.

name: Adoptions among structurally equivalent hospitals
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of previous adoptions among hospitals with a similar level of service complexity", "cumulative adoptions within service complexity categories"]
definition: Potential adopters are mostly likely to be influenced by adopters to whom they are structurally equivalent, that is to whom they share a similar social role or social position within a network; within VHA, hospital directors would be influenced by the adoption decisions of those directors who manage hospitals with comparable levels of service complexity as their own.

name: Adoptions in patient referral network
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of previous adoptions among hospitals with which it has a patient referral relationship", "cumulative adoptions within patient referral networks"]
definition: According to the cohesion model, direct communication linkages provide potential adopters with ongoing information about the innovation that induces them to adopt; a greater number of adoptions within a patient referral network will translate into greater normative pressures for potential adopters to adopt a management innovation such as TQM.

name: Demonstration-site adoption in referral network
authors_terms: ["previous adoption of TQM by a hospital within its patient referral network that served as a demonstration site", "demonstration-site status"]
definition: Under conditions of high visibility, the demonstration of an innovation can facilitate the innovation's diffusion, particularly among those potential adopters who can observe the demonstration through their usual interactions with the adopters participating in the demonstration.

name: Private-sector TQM adoptions in local community
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of private-sector hospitals in its community that have adopted TQM", "prevalence of adoptions among private-sector hospitals"]
definition: Potential adopters may be inclined to imitate adopters whose goals or activities they perceive to be more certain or legitimate than their own; such mimetic processes can be expected to apply to VHA hospital directors vis-a-vis the local health care delivery networks in which their hospitals are embedded.

name: Innovation adoption
definition: For purposes of the questionnaire, TQM adoption was defined as a decision by the hospital director (whether the director responding to the survey or a predecessor) to put into practice each of the three TQM principles: a focus on customer satisfaction, a commitment to continuous quality improvement, and an emphasis on empowering employees to identify opportunities to improve quality.

name: Organizational ownership
authors_terms: ["organizational ownership", "ownership status", "state vs. private ownership", "ownership structure"]
definition: Organizational ownership was defined as a dummy variable that was coded 0 to indicate a privately owned firm and 1 to indicate an SOE; there were no firms with hybrid ownership structures in the sample.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: Competitive intensity (RIVALRY) was measured using the Herfindal index, based on market share data providing annual market statistics on over 300 product groups in the manufacturing sector.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was measured in terms of return on sales (ROS) and return on investment (ROI), two commonly used indicators of profitability, complemented by an indicator of operational efficiency (OPEFF) measured as a ratio of cost of goods sold to sales.

name: Breakthrough inventions
definition: Breakthrough inventions are those foundational inventions that serve as the basis for many subsequent technological developments; in this research radicality is technological rather than user- or market-based.

name: Exploration of novel technologies
authors_terms: ["novel technologies", "technologies that are new to the organization"]
definition: Novel technologies are technologies that are new or unfamiliar to the firm (i.e., they are technologies in which the firm lacks prior experience), even though they possibly have existed in the industry before.

name: Exploration of emerging technologies
definition: Emerging technologies are leading-edge technologies that are recent or new to the entire industry (as distinct from older, mature technologies).

name: Exploration of pioneering technologies
authors_terms: ["pioneering technologies", "technologies that build on no prior technologies"]
definition: Pioneering technologies are technologies that have no technological antecedents (i.e., they represent technologies that do not build on any existing technologies).

name: Alliance proactiveness
authors_terms: ["alliance proactiveness", "ALLPRO", "proactiveness of a firm with regard to forming alliances"]
definition: The extent to which an organization engages in identifying and responding to partnering opportunities; the authors conceptualize it 'in terms of efforts to identify potentially valuable partnering opportunities, and to initiate preemptive actions in response to identified opportunities.'

name: Market-based firm performance
definition: Firm performance defined in terms of sales growth, market share, product development, and market development, following Venkatraman and Ramanujam's conceptualization of market performance.

name: Perceived technological dynamism
definition: Technological shifts that threaten the continued relevance of existing competencies and increase the potential pay-off for firms that can form links with partners that possess new and complementary competencies.

name: Perceived market dynamism
definition: Environments in which customer needs are evolving rapidly, so that the potential value of tapping into external resource pools to develop products and services that keep pace with demand changes may be substantial.

name: Perceived competitive dynamism
definition: Rapidly transforming competitive landscapes that present potential opportunities for firms to reengineer their affiliations and undertake structural changes in their networks so as to improve their positions therein.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the organization, measured as the logarithmic transformation of sales.

name: Strategic alliances with providers of new technology
authors_terms: ["strategic alliances", "total number of strategic alliances", "alliance intensity"]
definition: The number of strategic alliances a traditional pharmaceutical firm has entered into with providers of biotechnology. Interfirm cooperation between incumbents and new entrants allows the incumbent to adapt to radical technological change.

name: Exploration alliances
definition: Alliances motivated by organizational learning, entered with the goal of discovering or developing a new service or product, allowing partners to share tacit knowledge such as basic R&D. They permit the incumbent to build new upstream value chain activities.

name: Exploitation alliances
definition: Alliances motivated by access to complementarities, in which the incumbent leverages existing complementary assets and the new entrant provides the new technology while the incumbent commercializes it; partners exchange explicit knowledge.

name: Complementary assets
definition: Assets, particularly when specialized to the commercialization of an innovation, whose ownership determines who will benefit from that innovation; incumbents with downstream value chain activities specific to commercializing a new technology may be able to adapt to radical technological change.

name: New product development
definition: Firm-level innovation, following Schumpeter's definition of innovation as commercialized invention: only when approval is granted and the product has been commercialized can one count this product as new product development.

name: Firm performance
definition: An incumbent's financial performance, measured so as to capture the reward the firm obtains for bringing innovative products to market.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: The term entrepreneurial orientation (EO hereafter) captures the organizational processes, methods, and styles used to implement the start-up's founding strategy (Lumpkin and Dess, 1996; Miller, 1983). EO is the entrepreneurship defined at the firm level rather than at the individual level.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: In RBV, technological capabilities define the roots of a firm's sustainable competitive advantage, since the capabilities comprise patents protected by law, technological knowledge, and production skills that are valuable and difficult to imitate by competitors. They comprise technological knowledge, trade secrets, know-how generated by R&D and other technology-specific intellectual capital (Dollinger, 1995).

name: Financial resources invested during the development period
authors_terms: ["financial resources invested during the development period", "financial resources invested"]
definition: Financial resources invested during the development period can be a source of sustainable competitive advantage, since a start-up that invested disproportionately more financial resources during the period is likely to accumulate a larger stock of strategic assets than peer ventures that lacked financial resources during the development period (Dierickx and Cool, 1989).

name: Partnership-based linkages
definition: Partnership-based linkages are cooperative, bilateral relationships in which partners give and take resources and maintain long-term ties. Partnership-based linkages with external actors can be defined as cooperative bilateral relationships with environmental constituents.

name: Sponsorship-based linkages
definition: Sponsorship-based linkages are unilateral relationships as the sponsor commits unilateral support to a business venture without receiving explicit rewards.

name: Start-up performance
definition: After interviewing top managers and considering prior studies on venture performance, we measure it by sales growth—the sales volume of years 1998 and 1999 subtracted by the sales volume of years 1996 and 1997.

name: CEO founder status
definition: Whether or not the IPO firm's CEO is also its founder. Founder CEOs, relative to nonfounder CEOs, are viewed as representing greater managerial uncertainty to the investment banker.

name: Unretained wealth
authors_terms: ["unretained wealth", "IPO underpricing", "underpricing", "wealth retention", "money left on the table"]
definition: IPO underpricing, viewed as the wealth the initial shareholders fail to retain when the initial offer price is less than the first-day stock closing price; it represents both wealth creation for first-day investors and unretained wealth for the initial shareholders who sold their equity to the investment banker.

name: Investment banker market share
authors_terms: ["investment banker market share", "IPO market share of the investment banker", "share of the IPO market"]
definition: Summing the value of the IPO deals underwritten by the investment banking firm during the sample period and dividing this figure by the total value of all IPO deals completed during this same period.

name: Proportion of insiders on the board of directors
authors_terms: ["proportion of insiders on the board of directors", "proportion of inside directors", "proportion of insiders", "board composition"]
definition: The ratio of board members currently serving as firm officers to total board members.

name: Social interaction
definition: Social interaction refers to the extent of social relationships between the focal firm and the customer.

name: Relationship quality
definition: Relationship quality refers to the extent that this interaction is marked by the development of goodwill trust and expectations of reciprocity.

name: Customer network ties
definition: Customer network ties denote the extent to which the key customer provides the focal firm access or introductions to a broader set of customers.

name: Knowledge acquisition
definition: External 'business' knowledge, i.e., knowledge of products, markets, and technology, rather than 'organizing' knowledge, acquired by the young firm through its key customer relationship; an organization learns if any of its units acquires knowledge that it recognizes as potentially useful to the organization.

name: New product development
authors_terms: ["new product development", "number of new products developed"]
definition: The number of new products, services, or technologies the firm has developed specifically as a result of the key customer relationship.

name: Technological distinctiveness
definition: The extent to which the firm's technology, defined as 'the company's technological skills and knowledge as well as the products, services, and processes based on these skills and knowledge,' is a source of competitive advantage for the firm.

name: Sales cost efficiency
definition: Efficiency gains from knowledge acquired in the key customer relationship demonstrated as a reduction in the sales costs of the young technology-based firm.

name: Social capital
definition: Relational resources embedded in relationships; the paper focuses on how social capital in a young firm's relationship with its key customer affects the firm's ability to acquire new knowledge and exploit it for product development, technological distinctiveness, and reduced sales costs.

name: Knowledge exploitation
definition: The exploitation of acquired knowledge for competitive advantage through new product development, technological distinctiveness, and sales cost efficiency; the paper focuses not explicitly on the knowledge exploitation process but rather on its results.

name: Corporate units
authors_terms: ["corporate units", "company-owned units", "corporate-owned units", "number of corporate units"]
definition: Establishments owned and operated by the franchiser, in which managers face monitoring and weak profit incentives that channel their effort toward the refinement of existing routines.

name: Franchised units
definition: Restaurants run by independent owner-operators, who operate with strong incentives to maximize the performance of their unit and tend to search more broadly and adapt to local conditions.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["environmental heterogeneity", "geographic dispersion", "heterogeneous markets", "varied local market conditions"]
definition: The extent to which a chain encounters varied local market conditions requiring local adaptation, because uniform operating procedures cannot optimize performance across diverse locations.

name: Mean performance
authors_terms: ["mean performance levels", "mean growth", "mean performance", "growth rates", "mean growth rate"]
definition: The mean level of chain performance, measured here as sales growth, reflecting the efficiency and adaptation benefits that a chain realizes from its mix of governance structures.

name: Reliability of performance
authors_terms: ["reliability of performance", "stability", "stabilizing growth", "stability benefits", "reduction in risk"]
definition: The stability of chain performance over time and space, where successful exploitation decreases the variability of firm performance as behavior becomes routine while exploration offers highly uncertain returns.

name: Entry barriers
authors_terms: ["entry barriers", "barriers to entry", "high barriers to entry"]
definition: Entry barriers are key industry structural characteristics that impact business performance; the most important entry barriers are economies of scale, capital requirements, and product differentiation.

name: Economies of scale
definition: Economies of scale typically result from advantages associated with large firm size that facilitates lower costs per unit of output and higher efficiency, and are strongly related to firm size as indicated by asset levels per establishment.

name: Capital requirements
definition: Capital requirements is the primary absolute-cost advantage which can serve as an important barrier to entry; its importance is reflected by the amount of funds needed to establish an efficient capital-intensive production process associated with mass production techniques.

name: Product differentiation
definition: The degree of product differentiation within an industry is an important type of entry barrier influencing interindustry profitability differences; product differentiation advantages of established firms are strongly related to heavy advertising or other sales promotion efforts.

name: Industry life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["stage of the industry life cycle", "industry life cycle stage", "life cycle stage"]
definition: Stage of the industry life cycle captures components of industry growth and industry evolution, with growth rates closely corresponding to certain life cycle stages.

name: Competitive scope breadth
authors_terms: ["venture strategy", "breadth of competitive scope", "competitive scope", "broad-scope strategy", "narrow-scope strategy"]
definition: Venture strategy is the breadth of competitive scope of the venture's product/market offerings relative to its competitors.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability of the new venture, measured by return on sales, described by the authors as the most commonly used measure of profitability in prior new venture studies.

name: Shareholder wealth creation
definition: Shareholder wealth creation is the increase in shareholder wealth for publicly held ventures, tied to share price appreciation and dividends over the years following the IPO.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth is one of the two most appropriate performance goals for new ventures along with profitability.

name: Pre-entry radio experience
authors_terms: ["radio experience", "experience producing (home) radios", "prior radio production", "experience producing radios"]
definition: Experience in radio production prior to the start of the TV industry, which the authors argue influenced both a potential entrant's TV R&D productivity and when it became a potential entrant. For each of the 265 radio producers they measure this experience on three dimensions: firm size, the type of radios produced, and the number of years the firm produced radios.

name: Entry likelihood
authors_terms: ["likelihood of entry into the TV industry", "probability of TV entry", "entry into the TV industry"]
definition: Whether a firm that produced radios before the start of the TV industry entered the television receiver industry; 56 of the 265 radio producers did so.

name: Entry timing
definition: How early a firm entered the TV industry, modelled as the annual hazard of entry, i.e. the probability of firm entry in a year for firms that had not yet entered.

name: Exit hazard
definition: The hazard of a firm exiting the industry in year t assuming it has survived up to year t.

name: Market share
definition: The firm's share of the U.S. television receiver market, measured in 1951-53 and 1959-60 for monochrome sets and in 1970 for color sets.

name: Innovation rate
definition: The innovations a firm generates per year, comprising major product innovations and process innovations in TV set manufacturing; the annual rate for each firm is its number of innovations divided by the number of years it was a TV set producer for which innovation data were available.

name: CEO external directorate networks
authors_terms: ["CEO external directorate networks", "external directorate networks", "executive external networks", "external directorship ties", "CEO external linkages"]
definition: Executives' external directorship ties, i.e. outside corporate board seats held by the CEO, which convey strategic benefits such as reduced uncertainty surrounding resource dependencies, access to strategic information and legitimacy and status. The ties are properties of the individual executive and cannot be easily traded or transferred, although their benefits may extend to the firm.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "CEO rewards", "chief executive pay levels"]
definition: The rewards paid to the chief executive, measured as a two-indicator construct comprising total cash compensation and long-term compensation.

name: Firm diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm must contend with a broader array of buyer, supplier, competitor and other groups; the scanning and information-processing demands faced by diversified firms are significantly greater than those encountered by single or dominant-business entities, and diversification imposes an elevated need for a diversity of resources.

name: Strategic similarity
definition: Strategic similarity is a multi-dimensional concept. To foreshadow our empirical analysis, we will measure strategic similarity on three dimensions, including customers, geographic markets, and competition.

name: Resource redeployment to target
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment to the target", "redeployment to targets", "resource redeployment to a business"]
definition: Resource redeployment is the use by a target or acquirer business of the other businesses' resources, where redeployment may involve physical transfer of resources to new locations or sharing resources such as R&D facilities and distribution systems without physical transfer.

name: Resource redeployment to acquirer
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment to the acquirer", "redeployment to acquirers", "resource redeployment to a business"]
definition: Resource redeployment is the use by a target or acquirer business of the other businesses' resources, where redeployment may involve physical transfer of resources to new locations or sharing resources such as R&D facilities and distribution systems without physical transfer.

name: Target asset divestiture
authors_terms: ["divestiture of the target's resources", "divestiture of the target's assets", "target asset divestiture"]
definition: Asset divestiture is the partial or complete sale or disposal of physical and organizational assets, shut down of facilities, and reduction of work forces of target or acquirer businesses.

name: Acquirer asset divestiture
authors_terms: ["divestiture of the acquirer's resources", "divestiture of the acquirer's assets", "acquirer asset divestiture"]
definition: Asset divestiture is the partial or complete sale or disposal of physical and organizational assets, shut down of facilities, and reduction of work forces of target or acquirer businesses.

name: Resource asymmetry
authors_terms: ["resource asymmetry between target and acquiring business", "resource asymmetry of target to acquirer"]
definition: Resource asymmetry is the extent of asymmetry between the resources of the target and the acquirer, measured with four items including product innovativeness, manufacturing know-how, commercial dynamism, and product quality.

name: Alertness
authors_terms: ["alertness", "similarity in alertness", "proactive attentiveness to market information"]
definition: We define alertness as the firm's proactive attentiveness to market information. The possession and continuous updating of private information allows alert banks to make more accurate assessments of price trends, and to quote market-leading prices.

name: Speed of response
authors_terms: ["speed of response", "similarity in speed of response", "responsiveness to market volatility"]
definition: We define speed of response as the ability of a firm to act quickly to seek information when market volatility is high.

name: Country of location
authors_terms: ["country of location", "being located in the same country", "shared country of location"]
definition: Banks located in a country may potentially provide customers with country-specific information, which may not be globally available, and customer banks wanting to deal a particular country's currency may include banks in that country more easily in their consideration sets.

name: Time zone of location
authors_terms: ["time zone", "located in the same time zone", "shared time zone"]
definition: As the currency market is most active during daylight hours in each of these time-zones, it is likely that banks located in the same time-zone will compete with each other for the same customers to a greater extent than with banks in other time zones.

name: Location in a primary cluster
definition: The regional agglomeration of currency trading banks in the three primary clusters may provide spillover benefits from superior information to firms located in them. As a result, banks located in any of the three primary clusters are likely to be substitutes in customer banks' consideration sets.

name: Extent of direct competition
authors_terms: ["extent of direct competition", "market microstructure", "similarity in customer profiles", "structural equivalence", "competitive overlap"]
definition: We calculated the extent to which bank pairs are in direct competition with each other by creating measures of structural equivalence (similarity in their customer profiles) between them based on their patterns of ties with all 4088 customer banks in this market. A high correlation between a pair of banks on their customer profiles indicates that the banks compete directly for business from many of the same other customer banks.

name: Market orientation
definition: Market oriented firms 'seek to understand customers' expressed and latent needs, and develop superior solutions to those needs' (Slater and Narver, 1999:1165); the distinguishing characteristic is system-wide attention to markets throughout the organization.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: Entrepreneurship refers to the pursuit of new market opportunities and the renewal of existing areas of operation (Naman and Slevin, 1993).

name: Innovativeness
definition: Innovativeness is present when the implementation of new ideas, products, or processes is encouraged (e.g., Hurley and Hult, 1998).

name: Organizational learning
definition: Organizational learning refers to the generation of new insights that have the potential to reshape behavior (Huber, 1991).

name: Positional advantage
authors_terms: ["positional advantage", "higher-order positional advantage", "higher-order factor of positional advantage"]
definition: The positional advantage that the four capabilities give rise to is thought to be rare, valuable, and difficult to imitate; it is a latent, intangible construct to which the four capabilities collectively contribute rather than cause.

name: Return on investment change
definition: Five-year average change in return-on-investment, used as an SBU-level performance indicator.

name: Income change
definition: Five-year percentage change in income, used as an SBU-level performance indicator.

name: Stock price change
definition: Five-year percentage change in stock price, used as a firm-level performance indicator.

name: Line extension
definition: A brand extension is a product that uses the brand name of an existing brand (e.g., Honey Nut Cheerios or Country Crisp Corn Flakes); in marketing parlance the paper considers line extensions rather than brand extensions into completely new product categories.

name: Advertising cost of new product introduction
authors_terms: ["cost of advertising", "marketing expenditures", "fixed marketing expenditures", "advertising expense", "cost of introducing new products"]
definition: The firm must spend money on advertising and other marketing activities (e.g., promotions and slotting allowances) to get consumers to try the product, and these expenditures are both sunk and fixed. Advertising is the single largest marketing expense of introducing a new product.

name: Fixed cost of new product introduction
authors_terms: ["fixed cost of product introduction", "fixed entry costs", "fixed cost effect", "F_t"]
definition: Managers must make sunk and fixed investments to get consumers to try new products; these expenditures during period t are denoted by F_t and called the fixed cost of product introduction (e.g., advertising).

name: Market size
authors_terms: ["market size", "dollar size of the market", "market size effect", "lagged market size"]
definition: The dollar size of the market at time t is given by M_t; the variable profits from a new product that come from existing consumers switching to it are called the market size effect.

name: Expected market growth
authors_terms: ["expected market growth", "expected growth in the market size", "market growth effect"]
definition: The expected growth in the market size from period t-1 to t is denoted g; variable profits from a new product due to the growth in market size are called the market growth effect.

name: New product entry
definition: A manager would choose to introduce a new product i during the next period, t, if its expected profits are greater than zero.

name: Spatial preemption
definition: Managers can credibly preempt outside entry by introducing brand extensions prior to anticipated demand growth; preemption is credible only if it is subsequently costly for managers to withdraw their products.

name: Partner-venture business relatedness
definition: The task-related context refers to partner–venture business relatedness, that is, to the nature of business activity undertaken by a stand-alone firm, the JV partner, vis-à-vis that undertaken by the venture in which it participates.

name: Partner-partner business relatedness
authors_terms: ["partner-partner business relatedness", "PPRELATED", "business relatedness between JV partners"]
definition: One dimension of the partner-related context refers to partner–partner business relatedness, that is, to the nature of business activity undertaken by a firm vis-à-vis that undertaken by its JV partner.

name: Previous JV experience
definition: Expectations about JV performance are also influenced by a firm's accumulated learning about managing JVs, that is, by the magnitude of its JV experience.

name: Similarity in partners' relative firm size
definition: Another influence on JV performance refers to partners' relative firm size, that is, to the nature of administrative protocols (systems and procedures) engaged by a firm vis-à-vis that of the protocols engaged by its JV partner.

name: National cultural relatedness
definition: Cultural relatedness refers to the nature of work-related 'mental programs' (Hofstede, 1991) of a firm vis-à-vis that of the work-related program of its JV partner.

name: Host country political risk
definition: Political risk refers to the risk that political forces will cause drastic changes in a country's business environment so as to affect corporate profitability.

name: Firm-level competition
authors_terms: ["firm-level competition", "level of competition facing the firm", "LOCOMP", "HICOMP"]
definition: The relative efficiency of a firm's resources can be deduced from the level of competition encountered by the firm (Richardson, 1959).

name: Shareholder value creation
authors_terms: ["shareholder value creation", "JV-based value creation", "abnormal return", "cumulated abnormal returns"]
definition: Shareholder value is created for JV partners when capital markets expect these firms' ventures to contribute to the firms' rent stream (Sakullelarasmi, 1991).

name: Competitive advantage over local firms
authors_terms: ["competitive advantage over local firms", "competitive advantage at the line of business level", "R&D Difference", "R&D intensity", "home-based competitive advantage"]
definition: The competitive advantage possessed by the line of business relative to local firms, which the authors argue makes greenfield investment the most efficient mode because home-based knowledge can be transferred without dealing with incompatible routines. It is operationalized by the relative intensity of spending on R&D.

name: Diversified entry
authors_terms: ["diversified entry", "diversified foreign investment", "entry in a new line of business", "corporate diversification"]
definition: Entry into a line of business in which the firm does not yet compete, which the authors describe as the clearest example of resource-seeking foreign direct investment because the diversifying firm seeks expertise it does not yet possess.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Differences in work-related attitudes and values between the investing firm's home country and the host country, which the authors say pose a risk for postacquisition integration and for managing a joint venture partner.

name: International sales experience
authors_terms: ["prior international sales experience", "international sales", "international experience", "preinvestment experience"]
definition: General, indirect preinvestment knowledge of foreign markets gained through exporting or through prior investments in other countries, which may make firms more confident in setting up a greenfield entry.

name: Foreign entry mode
definition: The way a firm enters a foreign market through direct investment, examined by the authors as three kinds of entry modes: greenfield investments, acquisitions, and joint ventures.

name: Entry sequence
authors_terms: ["sequence of entry", "sequential entry", "early entries", "subsequent entries", "first entry"]
definition: The position of an entry in a firm's sequence of investments in the host country: the firm's earliest observed entry (Sample A), a first entry into a different line of business (Sample B), or a further investment in a line of business where an investment has already taken place (Sample C).

name: Firm prior entry mode
authors_terms: ["First Firm Mode Acquisition", "First Firm Mode Joint Venture", "prior entry mode choices", "path dependency"]
definition: The mode of entry the firm first used at the firm level, which the authors argue may shape the mode used in a subsequent line of business because firms try to apply the learning from prior experience in similar choices.

name: Line of business prior entry mode
authors_terms: ["First LOB Mode Acquisition", "First LOB Mode Joint Venture", "path dependency within a line of business"]
definition: The mode of entry first used in a given line of business, which the authors expect to shape the modes of subsequent entries in that same line of business.

name: Strategic orientation
