definition: A firm's (division's) position on a continuum of 'orientation towards change' that subsumes the Miles and Snow strategic types, where Prospectors represent a strong orientation towards change and Defenders a weak orientation.

name: Hierarchical position
definition: An employee's level in the organization's hierarchy, which the authors argue is an indicator of managerial discretion: rather than discretion 'ending' at the upper echelon, it is likely to flow down the hierarchy, albeit with greater and greater restriction.

name: Base salary
definition: The compensation level component of the pay package: total base salary paid to an employee.

name: Bonus pay
definition: The incentive component of the pay package: total bonus pay received by an employee.

name: Pay mix
definition: The risk-exposure component of the pay package, computed as the degree of leverage, defined as the ratio of bonus to base pay.

name: Top executive tenure
authors_terms: ["production head tenure", "tenure of the top executive", "tenure of the production head", "job tenure", "years in office"]
definition: The number of years a production head has held the position of studio head, used to locate the stage of the executive life cycle.

name: Product line experimentation
authors_terms: ["product line experimentation", "experimentation", "product line changes", "changes in the mix of films"]
definition: Changes made from year to year in the mix of products (film genres) released by the organization; it is treated as a key source of managerial learning about the business and its markets.

name: Financial performance
definition: The financial outcome of the studio's slate of productions, taken as an indicator of how much the top manager has learned.

name: '.com' name change
authors_terms: ["'.com' name changes", "'.com' corporate name change announcements", "adding a '.com' to their names", "'.com' suffix"]
definition: A corporate name change in which the firm adds a '.com' suffix to its name, which identifies the firm with the internet and sends a signal to shareholders about the universe in which the firm competes.

name: Stock price reaction
definition: The direction of the stock price (up or down) following an announcement, which serves as an indicator of shareholder approval or disapproval.

name: Trading volume change
authors_terms: ["changes in trading volume", "trading volume", "trading activity", "abnormal trading activity"]
definition: The level of trading activity, which serves as an indicator of the announcement's impact and the general level of interest in the firm's actions.

name: Strategic name change
authors_terms: ["strategic name changes", "name changes that are accompanied by other strategies", "name change type", "image-only name changes"]
definition: Name changes that were preceded by internet-related acquisitions, closings of retail outlets, and alliances with other internet firms, as opposed to name changes for which no such activity could be detected ('image only').

name: Acquisition strategy orientation
authors_terms: ["consolidation-oriented acquisitions", "diversification-oriented acquisitions", "overlapping business units", "nonoverlapping business units", "defense-defense acquisitions", "defense-civilian acquisitions"]
definition: The authors compare two strategic responses to industry decline: diversification-oriented acquisitions, operationalized as acquisitions of businesses with nonoverlapping assets that increase corporate scope, and consolidation-oriented acquisitions, operationalized as acquisitions of firms with overlapping assets that narrow corporate scope.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["performance of acquisitions", "abnormal stock market returns", "normalized operating cash flows", "postacquisition cash flow return on assets"]
definition: Performance of acquisitions measured at the transaction level by risk-adjusted abnormal stock market returns, an ex ante measure of expectations, and by ex post pretax operating cash flows normalized by the market value of assets.

name: Industry decline
authors_terms: ["declining industries", "decline phase", "growth phase", "periods of growth", "periods of decline"]
definition: Industries that are suffering a decline in demand; in the U.S. defense sector the paper contrasts the growth period of the late 1970s through the mid-1980s with the sharp cutbacks and restructuring of the post Cold War decline period.

name: Corporate focus
authors_terms: ["focus", "corporate scope", "focused firms", "number of business units", "single-segment and multisegment firms"]
definition: The scope of the firm: focused firms are firms with narrower scope, i.e. firms active in fewer business units, whereas diversified firms operate in a larger number of business units.

name: Firm valuation
definition: Tobin's q, which is defined as the ratio of the market value of the firm's assets to their replacement value, is a stock (as opposed to a flow) measure of the economic value of the firm.

name: Corporate governance system
definition: Corporate governance concerns the mechanisms which suppliers of financial resources use to obtain an appropriate return on their investment. Two corporate governance systems have evolved in the developed world: the 'market-based' system of the United States and the United Kingdom, and the 'bank-based' system often associated with Japan and Germany.

name: Investment bandwagon behavior
authors_terms: ["investment bandwagon", "bandwagon behavior", "capacity expansion bandwagon behavior", "herd behavior", "hop on an investment bandwagon"]
definition: Investment bandwagon behavior is the tendency to invest in capacity when rivals are investing. Firms tend to poorly time their capacity expansions by investing when their rivals are investing, often leading to excess capacity and poor returns.

name: Capacity expansion
definition: The incidence of capacity expansion is a firm's discrete addition of capacity in a product-market, either by adding a new greenfield plant or by expanding one or more of its plants' production capacity by more than 5 percent; de-bottlenecking is excluded because it is not a major, discrete investment.

name: Rivals' capacity expansion
definition: The degree to which rivals invest simultaneously in a product-market during an observation year, measured either as the percentage of the number of rivals that invested or as the percentage of total capacity added simultaneously by rivals.

name: Free cash flow
definition: Free cash flow is included as an indicator of a firm's propensity to expand; agency costs, especially the residual loss associated with value-destroying projects, are greatest when firms earn significant free cash flow and have few significant investment opportunities.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["alliance scope", "vertical scope", "scope of alliance activities", "broad alliance scope", "pure R&D alliances"]
definition: The extent to which the partners combine multiple and sequential functions or value chain activities within the alliance, such as R&D, manufacturing and/or marketing; pure R&D alliances are of more narrow scope than mixed-activity R&D alliances.

name: Alliance governance
definition: The organizational form or governance structure used to organize the alliance, ranging from contractual alliances to the more protective equity joint venture.

name: Competitive overlap
authors_terms: ["competitive overlap", "product market competition", "market overlap", "geographic market competition", "geographic overlap"]
definition: The extent to which alliance partners are direct competitors, captured by two complementary measures: product market and geographic market competition.

name: Market leadership
definition: Whether a firm is a leading technology company, a highly subjective and multifaceted issue that is tied to the possession of firm-specific resources such as human capital, training programs, suppliers and distributors.

name: Technology overlap
authors_terms: ["technology overlap", "overlap in partner capabilities", "technological overlap", "overlap in partner firms' areas of technological expertise"]
definition: The extent of overlap among partner firms' areas of technological expertise, thought of as a continuum from no areas of expertise in common to completely overlapping areas of technological expertise.

name: Proximal technological experience
authors_terms: ["proximal technological experience", "proximal experience", "technological experience within the focal therapeutic area"]
definition: Our distinction between proximal and distal technological experience defines the set of knowledge elements with respect to a focal new product. Proximal experience facilitates local search, while distal experience enables more global search. Proximal Technological Experience counts those patents assigned to the same therapeutic area as the new product introduction.

name: Distal technological experience
authors_terms: ["distal technological experience", "distal experience", "technological experience that is not closely linked to the focal product introduction"]
definition: Technological experience that accumulates within the firm, but that is not closely linked to the focal product introduction, may be considered more distant. Distal Technological Experience counts those patents assigned to other therapeutic areas.

name: Proximal product-market experience
definition: Product-market experience is decomposed into Proximal Product-Market Experience and Distal Product-Market Experience in order to distinguish the experience that accumulates within the focal therapeutic area from that which accumulates in other areas. Proximal experience gives the firm access to specific customers, established distribution channels, and area-specific reputations.

name: Distal product-market experience
definition: Some of the assets that a firm needs are more general, and develop as a function of a broad portfolio of product-market activities. A firm's distal product-market experience tends to develop a general understanding of potential customer needs.

name: New product success
definition: The initial sales level is an appropriate indicator of new product success in the pharmaceutical industry, where a primary objective is to maximize the revenues associated with the fixed costs of product development and launch. We expect new product introductions to be more successful when a firm possesses superior technological knowledge, combinative capabilities, and complementary assets.

name: Relatedness of technological competencies
authors_terms: ["related competencies", "relatedness in competencies", "relatedness of technological competencies", "related technological competence", "relatedness"]
definition: A target subsidiary possesses a related technological competence to the extent that its technologies and technical expertise fall in the same areas as those required by a focal new product development team.

name: Spatial distance
definition: Spatial distance is the distance in miles between subsidiaries; a focal team and a subsidiary may be less likely to interact to the extent that the spatial distance between them is large.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance is the extent to which the national cultures of the countries in which subsidiaries are located differ, which includes differences in power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, individualism, and long-term orientation between national cultures.

name: Cross-border interaction
definition: Whether interactions take place across national borders; a focal team and a subsidiary should be less likely to interact and exchange technological competencies to the extent that they represent different national cultures and countries.

name: Formal proximity
definition: At the dyadic level, the formal organization links two subsidiaries to the extent that they are formally grouped together and report to the same superior in the organizational hierarchy.

name: Informal relations
authors_terms: ["informal relations", "established informal relation", "informal cross-subsidiary relations", "informal linkage"]
definition: We define informal cross-subsidiary relations as continuous work-related informal relations between individuals from two subsidiaries; they are grounded in norms, habits, and personal reciprocity rather than authority based on a formal hierarchy.

name: Technological competence transfer
definition: Technological competence transfers include the transfer of technical advice and technologies embodied in existing artifacts, such as software or hardware.

name: Assignment of R&D responsibility to a foreign subsidiary
authors_terms: ["assignment of new R&D responsibilities", "PROB-R&D", "probability of assigning R&D responsibility to an existing foreign subsidiary"]
definition: Our theoretical predictions focus on the assignment of new R&D responsibilities to existing subsidiaries that had no R&D activities in the previous year.

name: Host country R&D magnitude of other firms
authors_terms: ["total magnitude of R&D", "total R&D expenditure by other same industry firms", "host country R&D by other firms", "scale of R&D"]
definition: We focus on two characteristics of the host country R&D activities of other firms in the same industry as the focal subsidiary; the total magnitude and the interfirm dispersion of R&D. Greater R&D expenditure by other firms would, on average, produce a more abundant and diverse supply of technical knowledge which might potentially spill over.

name: Interfirm dispersion of R&D
authors_terms: ["interfirm dispersion of R&D", "dispersion of other firms' R&D", "R&D dispersion"]
definition: While the magnitude of R&D refers to the total amount of R&D being done by other firms, dispersion refers to the distribution of R&D expenditure across firms.

name: Local market focus
authors_terms: ["local market focus", "proportion of the subsidiary's revenues derived from local sales", "subsidiary local/total sales"]
definition: The greater the proportion of its revenues that a subsidiary derives from sales within the host country, the more locally focused the subsidiary would be expected to be. As such, local market focus can be regarded as a valid indicator of the subsidiary's capacity for local utilization of its technical knowledge.

name: MNC ownership stake in subsidiary
authors_terms: ["MNC's ownership stake in the subsidiary", "ownership stake", "ownership control"]
definition: We argue that the extent of the MNC's ownership stake in the focal subsidiary is likely to be a key driver of its ability to appropriate the latter's knowledge. In a context of shared ownership, the MNC is likely to be at least partly constrained by the economic stakes of other owners in appropriating the subsidiary's knowledge for its own use.

name: Increase in MNC ownership stake
authors_terms: ["recent moves to increase the ownership stake further", "increase in the MNC's ownership stake"]
definition: We predict both a 'stock' and a 'flow' level connection between ownership stake and the probability of assigning R&D responsibilities to the focal subsidiary. In other words, when assigning R&D responsibilities to a foreign subsidiary, we predict that corporate executives would prefer to have as high an ownership stake as feasible, based not only on historical decisions regarding ownership but also on recent moves to increase the ownership stake further.

name: Cross-border intrafirm trade
authors_terms: ["magnitude of intrafirm trade", "cross-border intrafirm trade between the parent and its foreign subsidiaries", "intrafirm trade/total sales"]
definition: As indicators of the MNC's ability to transfer subsidiary-level knowledge throughout the MNC, we focus on two properties of the MNC: the extent of cross-border intrafirm trade between the parent and its foreign subsidiaries, and the number of existing subsidiaries with R&D responsibilities within the MNC's global network.

name: Number of existing foreign R&D units
authors_terms: ["number of existing foreign R&D units", "count of the MNC's foreign subsidiaries which already have R&D responsibilities", "number of existing R&D units within the MNC's global network"]
definition: Our focus on the second indicator, the number of existing R&D units within the MNC's global network, rests on the premise that, up to a point, MNCs with a larger number of preexisting foreign R&D units are more likely to have the absorptive capacity to transfer and utilize any subsidiary's knowledge on a global basis.

name: Knowledge utilization capacity
authors_terms: ["MNCs capacity for both local and global utilization", "capacity for local utilization", "capacity to appropriate the subsidiary's knowledge for global use", "internal capacity to utilize the subsidiary's newly acquired knowledge both locally and globally"]
definition: We propose that the likelihood of a given subsidiary being assigned R&D responsibilities would be positively associated with the MNCs capacity for both local and global utilization. The probability that a subsidiary would be assigned R&D responsibilities is likely to be higher when the parent MNC has a more developed internal capacity to utilize the subsidiary's newly acquired knowledge both locally and globally.

name: Subsidiary innovation
definition: Subsidiary innovatory performance is measured as the number of successful semiconductor patents applied for by the subsidiary in a given year t.

name: MNC technological richness
authors_terms: ["MNC technological richness", "technological richness of the MNC", "network technological richness"]
definition: Technological richness of the MNC or host country is an indicator of the total innovative knowledge that resides within the MNC or the host country network (and is potentially available to the subsidiary to utilize in innovation).

name: Host country technological richness
authors_terms: ["host country richness", "technological richness of the host country", "country richness"]
definition: Technological richness of the MNC or host country is an indicator of the total innovative knowledge that resides within the MNC or the host country network (and is potentially available to the subsidiary to utilize in innovation).

name: MNC technological diversity
authors_terms: ["MNC technological diversity", "technological diversity of the MNC"]
definition: This variable captures the breadth of the technological knowledge contained in the MNC or the host country.

name: Host country technological diversity
authors_terms: ["host country diversity", "technological diversity of the host country"]
definition: This variable captures the breadth of the technological knowledge contained in the MNC or the host country.

name: Knowledge linkages to the MNC
authors_terms: ["subsidiary knowledge linkages with the MNC", "knowledge linkages to the MNC", "subsidiary linkages to the MNC"]
definition: We use the instance of a citation by the subsidiary to another subsidiary (in the MNC) or firm (in the host country) to indicate a 'knowledge linkage' between the two.

name: Knowledge linkages to the host country
authors_terms: ["subsidiary knowledge linkages with the host country", "knowledge linkages with the host country", "linkages to the host country"]
definition: We use the instance of a citation by the subsidiary to another subsidiary (in the MNC) or firm (in the host country) to indicate a 'knowledge linkage' between the two.

name: Local context experience
authors_terms: ["experience in its local context", "domestic experience", "experience in the domestic Japanese market", "local experiences", "experience in 'Old Japan'", "experience in 'New Japan'"]
definition: Firms acquire this capability through experience in specific contexts. This study contrasts the effects of participation in local and foreign contexts for pharmaceutical innovation.

name: Foreign context experience
authors_terms: ["experience in foreign contexts", "overseas experience", "experience overseas", "experience in foreign markets"]
definition: Experiences in overseas markets for Japanese firms differ fundamentally from that in their home market. Those markets will employ distinct routines for pricing, doctor demand, and clinical trials.

name: Contextual proximity
authors_terms: ["proximity between the home and foreign countries", "proximity between countries", "proximate foreign contexts", "isomorphism between their contexts"]
definition: Proximity between countries is measured as the degree of isomorphism between their contexts, or institutional environments. Proximity is therefore really cognitive/cultural similarity that enables and sustains trust.

name: Innovative capability
authors_terms: ["capabilities", "innovative capability", "the capabilities of the firm", "core competence"]
definition: The literature defines resources as the stocks of strategic assets (valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable) that are owned or controlled by the firm, and capabilities as the capacity of the firm to deploy these resources for competitive advantage. The core competence of pharmaceutical firms in Japan is discovery of new drugs.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["age of the firm", "duration of its experience in the pre-1981 domestic context in Japan"]
definition: The age of each of these 38 firms is computed using the first year of discovery of any new drug as the birth year for the firm.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["corporate diversification", "diversification by Japanese firms out of ethical pharmaceuticals", "corporate operations outside the focal industry", "diversified markets"]
definition: We find that diversification by Japanese firms out of ethical pharmaceuticals into chemicals and OTC products significantly reduces the beneficial impact of proximate foreign contexts.

name: Technological exhaustion
definition: The state of working in a well-exploited technological domain, i.e., in domains where current inventive efforts build on many preceding inventions and the potential for further recombination declines.

name: Science search
authors_terms: ["science search", "search across the science base", "intensity of science search"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's search crosses the technology-science boundary; firms search the science base to overcome the limitations of their current technology base and to gain access to a more heterogeneous resource base.

name: Geography search
authors_terms: ["geography search", "breadth of geography search", "international research presence"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's search efforts span national boundaries; firms search across geographical boundaries to expand their technology base and to solve local technological problems.

name: International product-market presence
authors_terms: ["international product-market presence", "international product-market change", "international product market footprint"]
definition: The breadth of a firm's presence in international product markets; as a firm's international product market presence broadens it is likely to promote the broadening of its international research presence.

name: Innovativeness
definition: The innovative performance of the firm, the productivity of its innovation efforts as reflected in its innovation output.

name: Centralization of R&D decision authority
authors_terms: ["centralization of R&D activity", "centralized R&D organization structure", "centralization of R&D decision-making authority", "R&D organization structure"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's research is conducted within a centralized corporate function with authority relations at the corporate level rather than exclusively within divisions or business units. In the centralized structure a single executive in charge of the firm's research reports directly to a corporate-level executive; in the decentralized structure research is conducted exclusively within divisions and R&D directors report to division general managers; hybrids combine the two.

name: Centralization of R&D funding authority
authors_terms: ["centralization of R&D funding", "R&D budget authority", "corporate-level control of R&D funding"]
definition: The source of research funding within large firms, which can be the business units, corporate headquarters, or some combination of the two; the degree to which R&D budget authority is centralized at corporate headquarters.

name: Level of innovative impact
authors_terms: ["level of impact", "overall impact", "citations received", "level of innovative impact"]
definition: The number of subsequent innovations that a firm's innovations affect; generic or non-specific knowledge is more likely than product-specific knowledge to produce innovations that affect a large number of future innovations.

name: Breadth of innovative impact
definition: The extent to which a firm's innovations have relevance for technical applications in a broader range of technological areas; the more diverse the technologies citing a patent, the broader is the impact of that patent.

name: Organizational breadth of search
authors_terms: ["organizational breadth of search", "breadth of search in organizational space"]
definition: The extent to which a firm looks outside its own organizational boundaries for innovations on which to build, searching over previous innovations developed by other organizations and independent inventors rather than building narrowly on its own previous innovations.

name: Technological breadth of search
definition: The extent to which a firm builds on innovations from a diverse rather than a narrow set of technological areas; firms that build on innovations from a more diverse range of areas can be understood as searching more broadly, whereas firms searching fewer, more closely related areas are searching more narrowly.

name: Category scope
definition: The breadth of application categories in which the product or firm competes; at the product level the number of application categories in which a given product is classified and at the firm level the number of application categories in which the firm has a product classified.

name: Platform scope
definition: The breadth of computing platforms in which the product or firm competes; at the product level the number of computing platforms that a product is classified under and at the firm level the number of computing platforms under which the firm has at least one product classified.

name: Product scope
authors_terms: ["product count", "dimension of scope at the firm level"]
definition: A dimension of scope at the firm level measured as the number of products that the firm has on the market.

name: Niche scope
definition: An additional dimension of scope at the product level, the number of niches, defined as the intersection of category and platform, in which the product is classified.

name: Category integration
definition: The range of application categories a particular product incorporates, such that firms that tend to offer products integrated over multiple categories have greater category entropy.

name: Platform focus
definition: The range of computing platforms on which a particular product is offered, such that firms that tend to offer each product across several platforms have greater platform entropy (less focus).

name: Change in product variety
authors_terms: ["changes in product variety", "adjustments in product variety", "new product entry", "product extensions"]
definition: Adjustments in firm-level product variety strategies, as measured by entry into new products, application categories, computing platforms, and category/platform combinations.

name: Firm survival
definition: Continued appearance of the firm in The Software Catalog: Microcomputers; survival is a necessary condition for positive profits and exit directly measures poor performance.

name: Product survival
definition: Continued appearance of the product in The Software Catalog: Microcomputers; survival is a necessary condition for positive profits and exit directly measures poor performance.

name: COO presence
definition: Our interest is in the presence of the COO role, in which an executive other than the CEO has been assigned to oversee all, or essentially all, internal and operational (i.e., shorter-term) affairs. We are not interested in the presence of the COO title, per se.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Highly dynamic industries are particularly taxing, due to large information-processing demands and the potential need for quantum changes in strategy. Dynamic industries include those that exhibit rapid growth, unstable growth, and technological intensiveness.

name: Organizational task demands
authors_terms: ["organizational task demands", "extraordinary organizational task demands", "internal task demands"]
definition: The characteristics of the organization also affect the nature and magnitude of the CEO's workload in ways that can lead to the decision to have a COO. Heavy demands exist in firms that are large, highly diversified in a related manner, heavily engaged in acquisitions, and when the CEO also serves as board chairman.

name: CEO professional limitations
authors_terms: ["the CEO's own limitations", "professional limitations", "limiting experiences", "repertoires which limit their capabilities"]
definition: CEOs who are personally ill-equipped to manage internal operations will tend to have COOs to fulfill that role. Limiting experiences include a background in finance/law, no firm-wide operating experience (as COO), and recent arrival from outside the firm.

name: Organizational performance
definition: For our performance measures, we used return on assets (ROA), a common accounting-based performance indicator, and market-to-book value of common equity (MTB), which reflects the stock market's assessment of the health and prospects of the firm.

name: Market valuation
authors_terms: ["market valuation of the firm", "market returns", "market performance", "cumulative abnormal daily stock returns (CAR)"]
definition: The dependent variable is market valuation of the firm, operationalized as the cumulative abnormal daily stock returns (CAR) observed at the time of the downsizing announcement. According to Cascio (2002), the effectiveness of management actions is ultimately judged on the criterion of the attractiveness of stock returns generated to investors.

name: Level of downsizing
definition: Downsizing can be defined as an intentional, permanent, and systematic reduction of an organization's workforce. The level of downsizing was operationalized as the percentage reduction in total employees in the firm as announced in the Wall Street Journal.

name: Reallocation strategy
definition: A reallocation strategy refers to specific decisions regarding those to be laid off or which departments will be reduced. Low reallocation suggests wide, sometimes shallow, across-the-board cuts in the number of employees, whereas high reallocation indicates deep, selective or focused reductions targeting specific units or functions.

name: Disengagement incentives
definition: Disengagement incentives are offered to employees to entice them to voluntarily leave the organization. Such incentives include extraordinary cash payments, additional credit for time employed (increasing retirement benefits), and the extension of existing salary or other benefits (e.g., health insurance) normally halted upon termination.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technological uncertainty", "industry uncertainty", "exogenous uncertainty", "uncertainty about the value of a growth opportunity"]
definition: Technological uncertainty is the exogenous uncertainty surrounding the value of a growth opportunity in technology exploration, which raises the value of the underlying growth option. In the empirical setting it is measured as the monthly standard deviation of the returns of a biotechnology industry index.

name: Equity alliance divestiture
definition: Divestiture is the termination of an equity alliance in which the pharmaceutical firm exits a biotechnology partnership, which the authors treat as one form of option exercise.

name: Equity alliance buyout
definition: Acquisition (buyout) is the termination of an equity alliance in which the pharmaceutical firm acquires a majority stake of the biotechnology partner, which the authors treat as one form of option exercise.

name: Portfolio technological distance
authors_terms: ["portfolio distance", "portfolio correlation", "correlation among outcomes of options", "technological distance between a focal alliance and the portfolio of other alliances"]
definition: Portfolio distance approximates the potential for sub-additive portfolio effects and is measured as the distance between equity partners in a pharmaceutical firm's alliance portfolio, obtained by taking one minus the ratio of common technological domains among partners.

name: Firm-partner technological distance
authors_terms: ["partner distance", "technological distance between the firm and an alliance", "fungibility of resources"]
definition: Partner distance approximates super-additive effects and is measured by one minus the ratio of common technological domains of the pharmaceutical firm and one of the partners in its portfolio divided by the total number of technological domains of the pharmaceutical firm; lower values suggest a higher possibility of redeploying assets from the pharmaceutical firm to the biotechnology partner.

name: Correlation among project outcomes
authors_terms: ["correlations among the outcomes of the projects", "correlation between an ongoing options portfolio", "correlations between the underlying assets", "uncertainty correlation"]
definition: Correlations among the outcomes of the options held in a firm's portfolio; when option investments in a portfolio are competitive, option investments are duplicated and overlap with one another, which makes the portfolio sub-additive. In the case of technology-based alliances, uncertainty correlation may be seen as the technological distance between them.

name: Fungibility of shared resources
definition: A resource is fungible or redeployable if it can be used by the target, either by a physical transfer of the resource or by a resource sharing without physical movement. Fungibility represents a firm-level capability that enables a firm to benefit from redeployment of existing capabilities to new endeavors, thus reducing the cost of each investment.

name: Portfolio option value
authors_terms: ["sub-additive value of the portfolio", "super-additive value of the portfolio", "portfolio effect (PE)", "value of a portfolio of real options"]
definition: The value of a portfolio of real options relative to the value of the options if they were independent (i.e., not part of the same portfolio); the change in the value of the portfolio is referred to as the portfolio effect (PE), which may be negative (sub-additive) or positive (super-additive).

name: Academic quality
authors_terms: ["academic quality", "adjusted citation count", "citation count measure of academic quality"]
definition: The quality of published research as judged by the academic community, for which the number of citations an article receives is taken as an objective measure; while citation counting is not a perfect measure of academic quality, it is objective, readily observable, and highly correlated with other measures.

name: Practical relevance
definition: We conceptualized relevance as a construct that applies to a particular study to the extent that an appropriately defined community of practitioners judges it to be interesting and justified.

name: Interestingness
definition: Consistent with Davis (1971), we define research as interesting based on the extent to which it challenges assumptions or extends knowledge that is based on these assumptions, whether such assumptions are expressed as part of a formal theory or represented in the way people behave on a daily basis.

name: Justification
definition: A judgment about research being justified in the sense that its claims are well supported by evidence; interesting research will not be seen as high quality by academicians or relevant to practitioners unless it is also supported by evidence.

name: Perceived environmental performance
authors_terms: ["perceived performance", "environmental record", "environmental performance relative to competitors", "perceived performance gaps", "perceived unsatisfactory performance"]
definition: Respondents' assessment of how well their firm has done on environmental protection compared with other organizations in their industrial sector, used as the performance feedback signal that champions monitor.

name: Leader commitment to environmental initiatives
authors_terms: ["leaders' commitment to environmental initiatives", "champions' individual commitment", "champions' environmental commitment", "commitment to environmental protection"]
definition: The championing executive's individual commitment and effort towards environmental initiatives, which the model treats as being adjusted in response to performance feedback.

name: Expectancy of success
authors_terms: ["expectancy of success", "expectancy to achieve their initial goal"]
definition: Leaders' perceived probability of attaining their initial goal; in control theory this expectancy acts as a 'watershed', separating further efforts from the abandonment of effort.

name: Upper echelons' strategic commitment to environmental initiatives
authors_terms: ["strategic commitment", "strategic commitment to environmental initiatives by the upper echelons", "perceived strategic commitment by the upper echelons"]
definition: The collective strategic commitment of the upper echelons to environmental initiatives; the upper echelons serve as a collective repository of organizational knowledge and norms for action and formulate new strategic directions.

name: Diffusion and integration of environmental responsibilities among organizational members
authors_terms: ["diffusion and integration of environmental responsibilities among organizational members", "integration of environmental responsibilities among organizational members"]
definition: The extent to which environmental responsibilities are diffused and integrated among organizational members, including the spread of environmental values through the organizational layers.

name: Structural formalization of environmental responsibilities
authors_terms: ["structural formalization of environmental responsibilities", "perceptions of formalization", "degree of formalization of environmental responsibilities"]
definition: The degree to which environmental responsibilities are formalized within the organization's structure, i.e. the creation of formal functions and departments to address environmental issues.

name: Diversification
definition: A change from reporting one business segment to reporting two or more in the Compustat database.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Current year R&D expense divided by assets.

name: Technological specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization of knowledge assets", "technology breadth", "breadth of technology", "less specialized knowledge assets"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's patent portfolio is concentrated across patent classes and industries. Greater specialization appears as a lower value for the Technology Breadth index.

name: Financial performance
definition: The two measures of financial performance are Return on Assets and Tobin's q.

name: Extent of diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm's diversification is related, defined using a Herfindahl index based on segment assets in the first year after diversification.

name: Mode of diversification
definition: Whether a firm diversifies through acquisition/merger or through internal growth.

name: Share leadership
definition: A firm that has the highest market share in its 4-digit SIC code, using revenue data for the year just prior to diversification.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "market value of the firm shares", "firm performance"]
definition: The market value of the firm shares is the dependent variable of the value models; the paper examines how ownership structure influences firm value.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership concentration", "percentage of common shares held by shareholders that own significant shares"]
definition: The percentage of common shares held by shareholders that own significant shares; concentrated ownership may produce both a monitoring effect and, at very high levels, an expropriation effect.

name: Insider ownership
authors_terms: ["insider ownership", "percentage of common shares held by insiders"]
definition: The percentage of common shares held by insiders (managers); rising insider ownership may align interests with shareholders (convergence of interest) or entrench insiders at intermediate levels.

name: Market cycle
authors_terms: ["market cycle", "market cycles", "high-equity market cycles", "low market cycle", "equity market cycles"]
definition: Prior studies have argued that, during high-equity market cycles (hereafter we will use market cycles for simplicity), managers, with shareholder support, will pursue aggressive strategies such as mergers and acquisitions. During low market cycles, however, cautious shareholders might induce managers to scale back their merger plans.

name: Acquirer performance
definition: First, we define performance as cumulative abnormal retums (CARs) to the acquirer surrounding the date of the acquisition (Singh and Montgomery, 1987). CARs have been found to be correlated with ex post measures of acquisition performance (Sirower, 1997).

name: Intra-industry diversification
definition: The strategy of firms that operate in more than one market niche within the same industry. Almost all previous studies examined firms whose business activities span more than one industry; intra-industry diversification had been a hitherto neglected strategy.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm profitability", "firm performance", "rate of return before tax (ROA)"]
definition: Whether strategies of diversification are associated with organizational performance; in this study measured as rate of return before tax, which OSFI defined in the general insurance industry as net income before taxes divided by average capital, surplus, and reserves.

name: Multi-market contact
definition: Multi-market contact (MMC) is the extent to which a firm's market niche dispersion corresponds to that of other firms (Greve and Baum, 2001). Diversification engenders multi-market contact between firms, which in turn provides the opportunity for firms to dampen the effects of market forces by exercising mutual forbearance.

name: Firm similarity
definition: Similarity between two firms in cultivating the same locations of industry resource space; the authors argue that when two firms of similar size deploy resources in similar market niches they are more likely to receive feedback from the same stakeholders and cultivate the same pool of input factors.

name: Relatedness weighted diversification
definition: Related diversification refers to the 'relatedness' of market niches as revealed by patterns of strategic behavior: 'related' means that there is a very close consistency between the market niches served by competitors. The effect of a firm's portfolio diversification on its performance depends on the degree of market niche overlaps with other insurers.

name: Human resource education
authors_terms: ["technical education", "education level", "human resource education levels", "level of education"]
definition: Better educated human resources are expected to result in more productive human capital; the level of education is a proxy for employee cognitive skills (e.g., absorptive capacity) and a motivational need for achievement.

name: Pre-employment screening tests
definition: Screening tests during the hiring process offer the potential for superior foresight in evaluating human resources that are well suited for the firm's specific environment.

name: Human resource training
authors_terms: ["human resource training", "investments in human resource training", "training", "development"]
definition: Training is an investment that speeds the flow of both codified and tacit knowledge into the stock of human capital.

name: Human capital deployment to learning activities
authors_terms: ["deployment of human capital to learning activities", "human capital deployment", "human resource deployment", "deployment"]
definition: Firms that both (a) deploy more personnel to learning activities, and (b) encourage workers to allocate a greater percentage of time to learning activities, should increase learning by doing performance.

name: Prior industry experience of newly hired human resources
authors_terms: ["prior industry experience", "prior experience variable", "prior firm-specific experience"]
definition: The prior experience variable measures whether firms require experience for hiring and the degree to which employees have previous experience in their production area, semiconductor manufacturing, and unrelated manufacturing.

name: Human resource turnover
definition: The operator turnover variable is the average annual percentage of full-time equivalent (FTE) operators that are replaced.

name: Learning by doing performance
authors_terms: ["learning by doing", "learning by doing performance", "learning performance", "rate of learning"]
definition: Learning by doing refers to the observed phenomenon of manufacturing costs falling as manufacturing experience increases.

name: Market expansion logic
authors_terms: ["market expansion", "market expansion logic", "growth through market expansion"]
definition: Growing by extending the market for an existing set of products; a managerial growth logic, i.e. a belief that defines what is perceived to be the set of feasible expansion paths for a firm.

name: Product expansion logic
authors_terms: ["product expansion", "product expansion logic", "growth through product expansion"]
definition: Growing by developing new products for existing markets; a managerial growth logic that defines what is perceived to be the set of feasible expansion paths for a firm.

name: Financial slack
authors_terms: ["financial slack", "available financial slack", "financial resource slack", "'liquid' financial resources"]
definition: Resources in excess of what is needed for a firm to meet its current commitments and support current sales levels; a dynamic quantity representing the difference between the resources currently possessed by a firm and the resource demands of the current business.

name: Human resource slack
authors_terms: ["human resource slack", "slack in human capital", "'sticky' human resources"]
definition: Slack in human resources, which is relatively sticky because much of the value of human capital is context-dependent and is therefore more closely tied to the nature of existing organizational routines than is the value of financial resources.

name: Short-term sales growth
authors_terms: ["2-year cumulative percentage growth in sales", "short-term sales growth", "rate of short-term sales growth"]
definition: The 2-year cumulative percentage growth in sales during the year that the narrative was written and the year following the narrative year.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "previous acquisition experience", "accumulation of tacit experience", "learning-by-doing"]
definition: The acquiring firm's accumulated experience from prior acquisitions; firms might learn how to manage acquisition processes by simply doing more of the same, thereby tacitly forming and refining organizational routines that directly impact the performance of subsequent acquisitions.

name: Knowledge codification
definition: The degree to which knowledge accumulated through previous acquisition experiences is articulated and codified into ad hoc tools, manuals, and information systems; it is the process of deliberately creating and refining these tools rather than their usefulness as repositories of memory.

name: Post-acquisition integration level
authors_terms: ["level of integration", "degree of integration", "extent of functional integration"]
definition: The extent to which the functions of the acquired unit are linked to, aligned with, or centralized in, the equivalent functions of the acquiring organization.

name: Acquired top management team replacement
authors_terms: ["replacement of top management", "replacement", "top management turnover", "managerial replacement"]
definition: The degree to which pre-existing resources within the acquired firm are replaced with the equivalent resources of the acquirer, or simply dismissed; chief among these resources is the human and social capital embedded in the acquired firm's employees, particularly in its top management team.

name: Acquired firm resource quality
authors_terms: ["resource quality", "quality of the assets of the acquired firm", "pre-acquisition performance of the acquired firm", "pre-acquisition quality of the acquired firm's resource endowment"]
definition: The quality of the acquired firm's pre-acquisition resource endowment, assessed through the performance level of the target bank prior to the acquisition and used as a moderator of the impact of top management replacement.

name: Acquisition economic performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "economic performance of the acquisition", "change in ROA"]
definition: The variation in the acquiring firm's overall performance, measured as the deviation from competitors' long-term variation in return on assets.

name: Intangible organizational elements
authors_terms: ["intangible organizational elements", "intangible core elements (resources)", "strategic organizational element (resource)", "intangible elements"]
definition: In this study we use the construct of strategic organizational element (resource) to refer to a special type of element which is unique, imperfectly imitable, nontransferable and aims to improve the productivity of the organization independently or through a process of interacting with other elements. This study focuses on six intangible elements: managerial capabilities, human capital, perceived organizational reputation, internal auditing, labor relations, and organizational culture.

name: Managerial capabilities
definition: The managerial capabilities or skills that the top management team possesses; attaining superiority in a competitive market requires that the organization's top management possesses a broad set of complementary skills, such as technical, human, and conceptual skills.

name: Human capital
definition: The education, work experience, and competence of the organization's members; the educational level of employees is a source of labor productivity and economic growth for the organization and the nation.

name: Perceived organizational reputation
definition: Whereas organizational reputation refers to outsiders' beliefs about what distinguishes an organization, we use the term perceived organizational reputation to mean top management's view of the outsiders' beliefs about the organization.

name: Internal auditing
definition: Internal auditing is a process that examines and evaluates the functioning of the organization. It is an ongoing process of comparing actual performance with standards or expectations, based on relevant indexes, in order to improve the organization's achievements.

name: Labor relations
definition: Labor relations are the relationships between the management team and the employees and/or their representatives. Organizations with positive labor relations are likely to obtain high benefits from their employees.

name: Organizational culture
definition: Organizational culture refers to the 'underlying values, beliefs, and principles that serve as a foundation for the organization's management system as well as the set of management practices and behaviors that both exemplify and reinforce those basic principles'.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "performance of the organization", "organizational performance measures"]
definition: The performance of the local authority, evaluated by two measures of financial performance (self-income ratio and collecting efficiency ratio), the employment rate, a measure of municipal development, and internal migration.

name: Business strategy type
definition: Business strategy is concerned with how businesses achieve competitive advantage. Miles and Snow identified four archetypes of how firms define and approach their product-market domains and construct structures and processes: Prospectors, Defenders (differentiated between Low Cost Defenders and Differentiated Defenders), Analyzers and Reactors.

name: Marketing strategy type
definition: Marketing strategy is the set of integrated decisions and actions by which a business expects to achieve its marketing objectives and meet the value requirements of its customers. The authors derive from the clustering of marketing activities a taxonomy of four marketing strategy types: Aggressive Marketers, Mass Marketers, Marketing Minimizers and Value Marketers.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Performance is a multidimensional construct that is influenced by both the level of analysis and strategy type. The authors focus on profitability and market performance (i.e., sales and market share effectiveness) because they are widely recognized as two of the most important indicators of financial performance.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: The focal independent variable is whether or not an establishment is foreign owned, assessed by identifying the ultimate parent of the establishment and its home nation.

name: Regulatory strictness
definition: The authors measure the degree to which the different facilities in our sample are regulated by counting the number of performance criteria with which each facility must comply.

name: Waste generation
definition: Byproducts for which no internal or external user can be found must be reported to federal authorities as waste; the authors create a value for waste generated at the facility level by summing the toxicity-weighted chemical waste generated by the facility in each year.

name: Waste processing
definition: The firm can process the material it reports as waste through recycling, energy recovery, or treatment; the measure captures the amount of waste processed by the facility on and offsite.

name: Onsite waste processing
definition: The authors estimate the relative degree to which each facility processes its waste onsite, measured as the amount of waste processed onsite by the facility (log of the sum of all toxicity-weighted pounds burned, recycled, or otherwise treated).

name: Home country energy prices
definition: The price of oil should approximate the relative price of important environmental factors; high oil prices also often result from government taxes on oil and thus often represent attempts to encourage resource conservation.

name: Home country waste processing
authors_terms: ["RELATIVE RECYCLING", "the extent to which a country engages in waste processing"]
definition: The extent to which a country engages in waste processing, measured by the percentage of glass and cardboard recycled in each country.

name: Exporting activity
definition: Exporting has been traditionally regarded as the first step to entering international markets, serving as a platform for future international expansions; it provides fast access to foreign markets with little capital investment required.

name: Foreign direct investment activity
definition: FDI is an internationalization mode that enables firms to minimize transaction-related risks through internalizing markets for proprietary asset exchange and to leverage location-based advantages; it requires a greater level of resource commitment in foreign countries than exporting and is more difficult to reverse.

name: Alliances with local partners
authors_terms: ["alliances with local partners", "joint ventures with local firms", "J-L equity joint ventures"]
definition: Alliances formed in the internationalization process with partners from the host country; a local partner represents a primary source of local knowledge, being familiar with the needs and tastes of local consumers, local competitors and local contacts.

name: Alliances with home country partners
authors_terms: ["alliances with home country partners", "joint ventures with other Japanese firms", "J-J equity joint ventures"]
definition: Alliances formed in the internationalization process with partners from the firm's home country; such partners hold fewer local knowledge benefits because, as foreign investors themselves, they usually do not have full access to local resources.

name: Firm performance
definition: Parent firm profitability is the dependent variable for all models; the performance of Japanese firms is measured using accounting-based measures, return on assets (ROA) and return on sales (ROS).

name: Financial leverage
definition: Since the pivotal point is the degree of leverage, we use financial leverage to examine the capital structure. Financial leverage is defined as the ratio of debt to equity.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Most relevant among these characteristics is environmental dynamism, defined as the rate and the instability of environmental change. Environmental dynamism is the product of several forces operating at one time.

name: Firm economic performance
definition: Performance is a multidimensional construct ... thus any single index may not be able to provide a comprehensive understanding of the performance relationship relative to the constructs of interests. Therefore it is important to look at multiple indicators.

name: Business reconfiguration
definition: At the most general level, we define reconfiguration to be the change of resources within an organization. In this study, we consider reconfiguration to be greater when organizations retain fewer product lines and/or add more product lines over time.

name: Target product line retention
definition: Our dichotomous dependent variable in this study was the retention or disposal of a target's product line by the acquirer.

name: Target-acquirer resource overlap
authors_terms: ["overlap of acquirer and target resources", "resource overlap", "focal line overlap", "complementary line overlap", "category overlap"]
definition: The greater the overlap of acquirer and target resources, the more likely that acquirers will retain targets' resources and their own resources; resource deepening is the retention of product lines that overlap with current product lines.

name: Target-acquirer resource distinction
authors_terms: ["resource extension", "distinction", "target line distinction", "acquirer line distinction", "target category distinction", "acquirer category distinction"]
definition: Resource extension involves retaining product lines that are distinct from a firm's current product lines, and thus represents pathbreaking change.

name: Target status
definition: Firms in the panels that were acquired by other firms; the authors tracked the firms and found which had been acquired by 1995.

name: Acquirer status
definition: Firms in the panels that themselves undertook acquisitions; the authors found which firms had pursued acquisitions by 1995.

name: Strategic group membership
definition: A strategic group represents a collection of firms within an industry that differs systematically from firms outside the group along certain strategic dimensions. Strategic groups are subsets of an industry separated by mobility barriers that limit movement across groups.

name: Reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "reputation for product/financial quality", "reputation for financial stability and product quality", "composite reputation measure", "favorable and publicly recognized standing"]
definition: Reputation has been defined as the knowledge about a firm's true characteristics and the emotions towards the firm held by stakeholders of the firm. The authors expand the definition of a group's reputation as 'favorable and publicly recognized standing' to include knowledge of the true characteristics of strategic groups.

name: Personal lines orientation
authors_terms: ["Personal vs. commercial lines (PPERS)", "proportion of personal lines business"]
definition: The division of products primarily sold to individuals (e.g., home owners, private passenger auto) and those sold to businesses (e.g., ocean marine, fidelity, workers compensation, commercial multi-peril).

name: Property lines orientation
authors_terms: ["Proportion of property lines (PPROP)", "proportion of property lines business"]
definition: Property exposures, i.e. direct and associated indirect losses suffered by the primary policyholder, as one of the three major types of financial loss exposures covered by property/casualty insurers.

name: Financial lines orientation
authors_terms: ["Proportion of financial products (PFNAN)", "proportion of business derived from financial lines"]
definition: Products dealing with financial exposures resulting from the failure of others, such as fidelity coverage, surety and performance bonds, mortgage guaranty, and credit insurance.

name: Product line diversification
authors_terms: ["Diversification (DIVER)", "extent of firm diversification across lines of business"]
definition: The number of lines an organization chooses to offer, as well as the relative emphasis placed on each line, reflecting strategic choices with implications such as reduced portfolio risk.

name: Firm size
definition: Size can influence organizational market power, flexibility and strategic response to environmental concerns, and is expected to influence scope of operations due to potential economies of scale and scope.

name: Ownership form
authors_terms: ["Ownership form (OWNER)", "stock and nonstock ownership forms", "mutual and stock"]
definition: The insurance industry is dominated by two major forms of ownership: mutual and stock. Mutual insurers combine the owner and policyholder roles, while stock insurers clearly demarcate owner/investor and policyholder functions.

name: Firm age
definition: Age is an important factor in determining scope of operations in that insurers acquire customers, credibility and capacity to sell multiple product lines over time, and is strongly correlated with reputation and firm survival.

name: Distribution system
definition: The method of product dissemination into their target market(s), representing a crucial competitive strategic decision; the 'American agency' (or 'indirect') system channels products through independent agents and/or brokers, while 'direct writers' use exclusive agents, salaried employees, and/or mass merchandising techniques.

name: Reinsurance use
definition: Reinsurance is the transfer of all or a portion of a particular risk by a primary insurer to another insurer or insurers, which further spreads the risk and reduces exposure to extraordinary losses.

name: Financial leverage
definition: Strategic use of financial leverage by insurers can magnify potential returns obtained through underwriting operations and commensurate investment activities.

name: Investment strategy
definition: Investment strategies represent organizational choices of acceptable risk/return relationships, with investment earnings offsetting (supplementing) underwriting losses (profits).

name: CEO founder status
definition: Whether the CEO is also the firm's founder; the indicator is set to 1 for founder-managed firms and 0 for nonfounder-managed control firms.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm financial performance", "stock performance", "holding period stock returns"]
definition: The stock market valuation of a firm is the present value of future expected cash flows to its shareholders. A stock-based performance measure was used as the financial performance indicator in the current study.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm, operationalized as the natural logarithm of the firm's market capitalization.

name: Firm age
definition: The natural logarithm of the difference between the year the firm enters the sample and the year of the firm's incorporation.

name: Work-life program extensiveness
authors_terms: ["work-life programs", "work-life initiatives", "work-life benefits", "extensiveness of its work-life program", "composite work-life index (WLI)"]
definition: Work-life programs are initiatives adopted by organizations to help employees manage the interface between their paid work and other important life activities, including family (Lobel, 1999).

name: Share of professional employees
authors_terms: ["percentage of professionals", "percentage of professional employees", "large numbers of professionals"]
definition: Professionals have been defined as an organized body of experts who apply some form of specialized, theory-based knowledge to a set of complex problems (Webster, 1999). Firms employing larger numbers of professionals are more likely to adopt extensive work-life programs because the expense, value, and scarcity of professionals help to justify the programs' costs and challenges.

name: Firm-specific skills
authors_terms: ["firm-specific skills", "investments in workers' firm-specific skills", "career ladders"]
definition: Worker skills are firm-specific when they are highly unique to the setting (Cappelli, 1997). When firm-specific skills are needed to conduct work effectively, the firm must make training investments so workers can develop specific skills.

name: Share of female employees
authors_terms: ["percentage of women", "percentage of female employees", "largely female workforce"]
definition: Because primary responsibility for homemaking and childcare tasks falls on women (Shelton and John, 1996), female employees face particularly strong work-family conflicts (Greenhaus and Parasuraman, 1999).

name: Firm productivity
definition: For the public for-profit firms in the data base, we used a standard measure of productivity: the logarithm of sales per employee (Huselid, 1995; Pritchard, 1992).

name: Industry cluster location
definition: A cluster is a group of firms from the same or related industries located geographically near to each other; firms in Toronto comprise the industry cluster in this study.

name: Managerial network centrality
authors_terms: ["Managerial Centrality", "centrality in the managerial network", "managerial tie network"]
definition: Centrality measures the involvement in the network: the extent to which an actor is deeply involved in network relations. The managerial network is the network of informal ties among firm executives.

name: Institutional network centrality
authors_terms: ["Institutional Centrality", "centrality in the institutional network", "institutional tie network"]
definition: Centrality measures the involvement in the network: the extent to which an actor is deeply involved in network relations. The institutional tie network is the network of formal ties between firms.

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: Innovation is the development and implementation of new ideas to solve problems. It entails the development of new products or services as well as new administrative systems.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is the outcome hypothesized to be enhanced by centrality in the managerial and institutional networks.

name: Strategic group size
authors_terms: ["size", "company size", "size-defined strategic groups", "size-defined strategic groups of an industry", "large-size strategic group", "small-size strategic groups"]
definition: Strategic groups are identified a priori in terms of company size, size being the volume of deposits at the end of 1994, and three groups are distinguished: large, medium and small.

name: Degree of competitive response
authors_terms: ["degree of response", "greater degree of response", "response", "competitive response", "reaction"]
definition: A 'competitive response' is a discernible and observable competitive movement of counterattack (to an initial competitive action), undertaken by a company with respect to one or more competitors to defend or better its position. The degree of response is the extent to which the entities of one strategic group respond to the competitive actions of another.

name: Speed of response
authors_terms: ["speed of response", "response speed", "speed of competitive responses", "slower speed of response"]
definition: This indicates the time that a company takes to respond to the action of a competitor; it is defined as the average delay time, in days, of the responses of an entity to the actions of its competitors in a year.

name: Ex ante aggressiveness expectation
authors_terms: ["conjectural variation", "ex ante expectations", "expectations of aggressiveness", "expected aggressiveness", "expected competition"]
definition: Conjectural variation reflects the expectations that agents have of the different strategic behaviour of entities, and is generated through time as a function of past experience through a process of adaptative expectations; it can be viewed as a reflection of a strategic asset, namely the reputation of a firm, which here relates exclusively to the aggressiveness of firms in responding to changes in rivals' policies.

name: Industry factors
definition: Industry effects measured through executives' perceptions of industry structure, built from Porter's industry analysis framework and Scherer's reviews of empirical findings in industrial organization economics. A factor analysis of the 16 survey items produced three independent industry factors used in the hypothesis tests.

name: Industry maturity
definition: One of the three independent industry factors into which Porter's five factors reduced empirically, labeled by the researchers on the basis of its underlying component variables.

name: Entry barriers
definition: One of the three independent industry factors into which Porter's five factors reduced empirically, labeled by the researchers on the basis of its underlying component variables.

name: Competitive power
definition: One of the three independent industry factors into which Porter's five factors reduced empirically, with rivalry, the threat of substitutes, power relative to customers, and power relative to suppliers collapsing into this single variable.

name: Financial performance
definition: Overall financial performance was measured using three survey questions (and a Likert-type 1-5 scale), addressing 3-year profitability, sales growth, and overall financial performance.

name: Audit committee affiliated director proportion
authors_terms: ["proportion of affiliated directors serving on the audit committee", "audit committee affiliated director proportion", "audit committee composition"]
definition: The proportion of directors serving on the firm's audit committee who are affiliated with the firm or its management under Securities and Exchange Commission criteria, as opposed to independent, outside directors.

name: Institutional investor equity holdings
authors_terms: ["institutional holdings", "institutional investor equity holdings", "percentage common stock held by institutional investors", "the extent of firms' equity held by institutional investors"]
definition: The extent of a firm's equity held by institutional investors, which the authors treat as an external monitoring force in the corporate community.

name: Bankruptcy filing
authors_terms: ["incidence of bankruptcy", "bankruptcy status", "bankruptcy reorganization filing", "incidence of a bankruptcy reorganization filing"]
definition: Whether the firm filed a bankruptcy reorganization petition during the study period.

name: Prepackaged bankruptcy filing
authors_terms: ["prepackaged bankruptcy", "prepackaged filing", "prepackaged plan", "prepackaged bankruptcy petition filing"]
definition: A specialized Chapter 11 filing in which the firm negotiates a reorganization plan with its creditors prior to the actual bankruptcy filing.

name: Time in reorganization
authors_terms: ["length of time spent in reorganization", "time spent in a Chapter 11 reorganization", "length of time in reorganization"]
definition: The length of time a bankrupt firm spends in a Chapter 11 reorganization, measured in days.

name: Acquirer abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "stock market performance of the acquirer", "change in market value of acquiring firms"]
definition: The stock market performance of the acquirer at the announcement of the acquisition, assessed with event study methodology as the abnormal return generated as a result of the acquisition announcement.

name: Acquisition of online firms by offline firms
authors_terms: ["acquisitions of online firms by offline firms", "offline firms acquiring online firms"]
definition: Acquisitions in which an offline firm, an organization that operates largely outside of electronic markets and networks, acquires an online firm that pursues an Internet-based business model or has fully adopted an Internet-based market strategy.

name: Acquisition of online firms by online firms
authors_terms: ["acquisitions of online firms by online firms", "online firms acquiring other online firms"]
definition: Acquisitions of online firms by other online firms, which may be driven by the desire to increase the customer base, an advantage to the acquirer's and the target's businesses.

name: Timing of acquisition relative to the stock market correction
authors_terms: ["stock market correction in March 2000", "Pre March 2000", "after March of 2000", "timing of the acquisition"]
definition: The period before and after the March 2000 stock market correction, which introduced significant uncertainty into financial markets and led to a dramatic reduction of financial and human resources available to online firms and to lower competition and pace of development in the online business.

name: New CEO outsiderness
authors_terms: ["new CEO outsiderness", "successor outsiderness", "outsiderness", "insider vs. outsider CEO"]
definition: The underlying construct of successor origin is conceptualized as a continuum of new CEO 'outsiderness,' which is conceptually defined as the extent to which a new CEO brings different leadership style, knowledge, skills, and perspective to a firm based on his or her previous experience in other firms and industries.

name: Post-succession firm performance
authors_terms: ["post-succession firm performance", "post-succession firm performance change", "subsequent firm performance"]
definition: Post-succession firm performance change, measured as a composite of the standardized change in a firm's operational performance indicators (industry-adjusted ROA and ROS) and a market-based performance indicator (industry-adjusted TSR) from the time of succession until 3 years later; the change rather than the absolute measure is used.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Turbulence refers to instability, or difficult-to-predict changes in the environment.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence refers to the ability or capacity of the environment to permit organizational growth.

name: Pre-succession firm performance
authors_terms: ["pre-succession firm performance", "pre-succession adjusted firm performance", "poor pre-succession firm performance"]
definition: A composite measure constructed by summing the standardized (Z-score) average growth (or decline) in a firm's industry-adjusted ROA, ROS, and TSR for 2 years before the succession event occurred.

name: Post-succession strategic change
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategy changes from the last year of the previous CEO's tenure (t-1) to the end of the year that follows the succession year (t+1).

name: Post-succession senior executive team change
authors_terms: ["post-succession senior executive team change", "senior executive team change", "post-succession senior executive team turnover"]
definition: The senior executive team is defined as all executives who report directly to the CEO (the CEO is not included in the count of senior executive team); post-succession senior executive team change is the overall percentage of change in teams, computed as the average of the percentages of team entries and exits following the CEO succession.

name: Nonprofit status
definition: Society treats profit making and non-profit organizations differently because profit making institutions act in their own self-interest while non-profit organizations act in society's interest and not their own self-interest; it follows that they should respond to government differently, based upon their different long-term relationships.

name: Private ownership
authors_terms: ["privately owned organizations", "publicly owned organizations", "ownership structures", "private ownership", "public ownership"]
definition: Organizations vary in their ownership structures from privately owned to publicly owned: private ownership includes business firms of all types whether ownership shares are closely or widely held, while public ownership refers to ownership by the government, such as some public corporations or state universities.

name: Perceived impact of influence strategies
authors_terms: ["influence strategies", "influence preference strategies", "political influence strategies", "external interorganizational responses"]
definition: Organizational actions in response to regulations directed externally in attempts to influence the form of the authorizing legislation, the form of implementing regulations, and the form of enforcement practices; the present study analyses external interorganizational responses under conditions of vertical interdependence.

name: Perceived impact of information influence strategies
authors_terms: ["information strategies", "information based influence strategies", "direct influence methods"]
definition: Direct influence methods include the information strategies of submitting technical reports, making personal visits, giving testimony and contacting colleagues.

name: Perceived impact of pressure influence strategies
definition: Indirect influence strategies include the pressure strategies of letter-writing campaigns, seeking third-party organizations and third-party individuals to exert influence and media campaigns.

name: Organizational size
definition: Regulations impose an unequal burden on organizations of different sizes if written and administered uniformly, and regulations that impose different requirements generally increase the frequency of contacts between government regulators and the larger and more visible organizations while reducing the frequency of contacts for the smaller ones.

name: Resource dependence
definition: The theory of power dependence argues that power is a function of dependence and dependence is due to the availability and value of alternative outcomes; dependence in this study is operationally measured as the proportion of financial resources controlled by regulations to the total financial resources available to the organization at the same time.

name: Fear of retaliation
