authors_terms: ["fear of retaliation", "organizational fear of retaliation by regulatory agencies", "fear of regulatory agency retaliation"]
definition: Organizational decision makers respond to their objective situation based on their perception of that situation and more importantly their perceptions of the government's willingness to actually deny the outcome alternatives to the organization; if regulators are perceived to respond vigorously to enforce regulations, organizational decision makers should perceive a power imbalance.

name: Merger relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness of merging firms", "merger relatedness", "merger types", "merger strategies"]
definition: The degree to which the acquiring and acquired firms share unifying product and market features. Mergers are grouped into four categories based on the FTC's categorization: product concentric; horizontal and market concentric; conglomerate; and vertical.

name: Acquiring firm stockholder value appreciation
authors_terms: ["appreciation in stockholder value of acquiring firms", "changes in stockholder value", "abnormal returns", "value created by the merger"]
definition: The change in the wealth position of the acquiring firm's stockholders associated with a merger, measured as the firm's stock returns in excess of expected (normal) returns.

name: Acquired firm stockholder value appreciation
authors_terms: ["appreciation in stock value", "premiums", "stock returns of acquired firms"]
definition: The change in the wealth position of the acquired firm's stockholders associated with a merger, measured as abnormal stock returns.

name: Signals of commitment to diversify
authors_terms: ["announcements or moves of the acquiring firm which signal entry into the corresponding market", "commitment to diversify and enter a new market", "related strategic moves by the acquiring firm to enter a new industry"]
definition: Announcements or moves by which the acquiring firm signals its entry into the corresponding (target) market, which the paper argues may lead the capital market to capitalize the value created from synergy well ahead of the acquisition.

name: Abnormal returns to the acquiring firm
authors_terms: ["abnormal return", "cumulative abnormal return (CAR)", "change in the acquiring firm's stock price"]
definition: The deviations of a firm's actual stock returns from the returns expected under the market model around a discrete event date; a statistically significant positive CAR indicates that the event has had a positive economic impact on the value of the firm.

name: Organizational innovativeness
definition: When a firm is described as 'innovative' it generally means that the firm frequently develops (or adopts) innovative products, programs, or services for its own use and/or to sell. In the present study innovation was operationalized as the number of innovation 'items' (products, programs and services) firms had adopted and/or developed.

name: Top management team average age
authors_terms: ["average age", "average age of the members of the top management team"]
definition: The average age of the members of the top management team.

name: Age heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity among team members with respect to age", "age heterogeneity"]
definition: Diversity of top management team members with respect to age. For interval variables with a theoretically fixed zero point such as age, heterogeneity is measured by the coefficient of variation (the standard deviation divided by the mean).

name: Average organizational tenure
definition: The average organizational tenure of members of the top management team.

name: Tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of team members with respect to tenure", "tenure heterogeneity"]
definition: Diversity of top management team members with respect to their organizational tenure, measured for interval data by the coefficient of variation.

name: Average education level
authors_terms: ["average education level", "education level attained", "attained education level"]
definition: The average education level attained by members of the top management team, assuming attained education level is correlated with cognitive ability.

name: Education curriculum heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity with respect to the education curricula", "heterogeneity with respect to education major"]
definition: Diversity among top management team members in the types of curricula (major fields studied) they completed, because curriculum choices correspond to personalities, attitudes and cognitive styles.

name: Functional background heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity among team members with respect to their functional background experiences", "functional heterogeneity", "functional diversity"]
definition: Diversity among top management team members with respect to the functional areas in which they have had most of their experience, since managers with differing functional histories differ in attitudes, knowledge and perspectives.

name: Golden parachute size
authors_terms: ["size of the golden parachute", "dollar size of golden parachutes", "size of compensation", "contracted payments in years of salary"]
definition: The dollar size of golden parachutes provided for top management expressed in terms of the number of years' compensation of top executives as reported in the proxy statement.

name: Golden parachute coverage
definition: The number of executives covered by golden parachute contracts, an indicator of how far the protection is distributed within a company.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["average absolute tenure of the top executives", "top executive tenure", "key executive tenure"]
definition: The average absolute tenure of the top executives of the company, reflecting the human asset investment of the executives and the related hazard of loss of employment.

name: Relative top management tenure
authors_terms: ["relative executive tenure vis-a-vis outside directors", "relative tenure of top management teams"]
definition: The tenure of top management teams relative to outside directors, measuring the information asymmetry between top management and the board.

name: Management stock ownership
authors_terms: ["stock ownership by management", "percentage of stock owned by the management team", "management-owned stock"]
definition: The percentage of stock owned by the management team, which increases the degree of congruence between top management interests and those of stockholders and indicates top management team incentives.

name: Non-management stock ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of stock ownership not owned by management", "blocks of stock ownership greater than 5 percent"]
definition: The level of concentration of stock ownership not owned by management, measured as the sum of all blocks of stock ownership greater than 5 percent, which constrains the ability of top management to influence the board.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of outside directors on the board", "outside directors"]
definition: The proportion of outside directors on the board, which indicates the relative potency of outside versus inside directors in protecting shareholder interests.

name: Inside director representation on the compensation committee
authors_terms: ["proportion of inside directors sitting on the executive compensation committee", "proportion of company executives in the executive compensation committee"]
definition: The proportion of inside directors sitting on the executive compensation committee, the committee generally responsible for initiating and reviewing compensation packages for key executives, including the ratification of golden parachutes.

name: Prior takeover threat
definition: A prior threat of takeover experienced by the firm, measured conservatively as an actual transfer of more than 5 percent of the firm's total stock to a potential acquirer and the filing of a 13D statement with the SEC at least a year in advance of adoption of the golden parachute.

name: Board size
definition: The size of the board of directors, which has been related to its complexity in decision-making and whose effect on board-management relationships may be complex and not monotonic.

name: Top management group heterogeneity
definition: Homogeneity is an aggregate level index of interpersonal similarity along one, or several, dimensions. Heterogeneity is a group-level index of the degree of similarity between members of a group.

name: Short-term performance
definition: Measures which assess the stewardship of the top management or how efficiently the firm utilizes its resources to produce a profit; since the period considered is usually brief these measures can be interpreted as indicators of how well fitted the firm is to present conditions.

name: Expected long-term performance
authors_terms: ["adaptability-based measures of performance", "expected long-term performance", "long-term performance"]
definition: Measures based on the prevailing price of the firm's stock; the stock price can be thought of as all the firm's future earnings discounted back to the present, and as such it is the best estimate we have of the adaptability of the firm.

name: Industry competition
definition: Real competition exists only when a firm attempts to increase sales or market share at the expense of competitors; during these periods market shares are likely to be less stable than during periods when competition is mild.

name: Environmental change
definition: Change here refers to variations in the set of environmental constraints on a firm's behavior that are of sufficient magnitude and duration to necessitate alteration of the firm's strategy if optimal performance under the new conditions is to be realized.

name: National culture
definition: Culture is herein defined by country cluster as follows: North American-U.S. and Canada; Anglo-U.K.; northern European-Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria; Latin European-France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal; and Nordic-Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland. Country clusters, based on previous crossnational research which attributes similar managerial values and beliefs to similarities in national culture, may serve as a better indicator of culture.

name: Latin European culture
authors_terms: ["Latin European managers", "Latin European", "Latin European cluster", "Latin Europeans"]
definition: Latin European managers prefer to avoid uncertainty which can result in more centralized and formalized organization structure, i.e. bureaucracy. Laurent (1983) has demonstrated that Latin European managers prefer clear-cut job descriptions, clear hierarchical lines, and centralized decision-making.

name: Strategic issue interpretation
authors_terms: ["interpretation of strategic issues", "interpreting strategic issues", "issue interpretations"]
definition: Strategic issues by their very nature are ill-defined, and their potential impact is uncertain. As these events are thus subject to perception and interpretation, multiple meanings are possible.

name: Threat interpretation
authors_terms: ["interpret the issue as a threat", "interpretations of 'threat'", "threat"]
definition: Threat and opportunity interpretations derive from perceptions of issues as negative or positive, as potential losses or gains, and as uncontrollable or controllable.

name: Crisis interpretation
authors_terms: ["interpret the issue as a crisis", "as a crisis", "crisis"]
definition: Crisis interpretations derive from the perceived value of possible loss, probability of loss, and time pressure. Crisis is similar to threat in terms of being perceived as negative, as not controllable, and as a potential loss, yet differs from threat in terms of perceived probability and magnitude of that loss and time pressures.

name: Strategic response
authors_terms: ["strategic response", "responses to strategic issues", "strategic behaviors", "proactive behavior"]
definition: Behavior is considered to be proactive when actions are taken to effect change, in the environment or in the organization, and reactive when simply responding to change. Different interpretations trigger different decision processes and different behaviors.

name: Cognitive strategic group structure
authors_terms: ["cognitive strategic groups", "group structure", "cognitive groups", "cognitively group their competitors"]
definition: Strategists' perceptions of their competitors' strategies characterized by a group structure, rather than each firm's strategy being perceived as unique or all firms' strategies being perceived as similar.

name: Shared strategic group structure
authors_terms: ["widely shared", "shared strategic groups", "commonality of group membership", "shared sense of group structure"]
definition: Strategic group structure widely shared by strategists within an industry, rather than each strategist holding unique perceptions of strategic group structure.

name: Competitive strategy dimensions
definition: The bipolar dimensions, or constructs, that strategists use to organize, simplify and interpret the strategies of competitors; they are elicited from each informant rather than imposed by the researcher.

name: Profitability
definition: Firm profitability, measured as return on assets, used to examine the correspondence between cognitively derived strategic groups and economic outcomes.

name: Firm survival
definition: Whether a focal bank holding company remained independent or was acquired after the executive assessments, and, if acquired, what type of firm made the acquisition.

name: Strategic group membership
authors_terms: ["core firms", "core group of firms", "core members", "group membership"]
definition: The position of a firm within a strategic group; the authors distinguish core firms that are tightly associated and define the basic 'recipe' of a strategic group from secondary group members and from transient, misfit and idiosyncratic firms.

name: Innovativeness
definition: The extent to which a firm is innovative; the authors hypothesize that core firms will vary in terms of innovativeness.

name: Referent status
authors_terms: ["key referents", "serve as referents", "dominate external views of the industry"]
definition: The role of a firm as a key reference point for other members of the industry and its tendency to dominate outsiders' views of the industry; the authors hypothesize that core firms will serve as key referents and tend to dominate external views of the industry.

name: Strategic capabilities
definition: The product of the history of strategic choices and resource commitments made by the firm, representing what the firm has come to learn how to do and possibly embedded in tacit organizational routines; they are the fundamental source of a firm's competitive advantage.

name: Strategic groups
definition: Groups of firms in an industry that have similar strategic capabilities.

name: Strategic blocks
definition: A strategic block is a set of firms that are connected more densely to each other than to other firms in the industry.

name: Complementarity of strategic block
definition: The composition of a block in terms of the strategic groups its members come from: a pooling block has all firms from the same strategic group, while a complementary block has each member from a different strategic group.

name: Prominence within strategic block
definition: The extent to which one or more firms in a block play a focal and central role, ranging from a star structure in which all firms are tied to one firm to a fully connected clique.

name: Strategic linkages
definition: Commitments among major multinational competitors, including mergers, acquisitions, equity partnerships, joint ventures, technology licensing and development agreements, supply agreements, manufacturing collaborations, and marketing agreements, in which the partners continue to compete with each other.

name: Ties across strategic blocks
definition: The linkages that connect firms belonging to different strategic blocks within the network of linkages in an industry.

name: Relative dominance of strategic capabilities
definition: Relative dominance increases if the firms in a group possess those strategic capabilities that firms in all the other groups desire, and for which there are few substitutes.

name: Relative size
definition: The extent to which the firm has economies of scale and scope, and its relative resource endowment, both financial and managerial.

name: Relative market share
definition: The firm's presence in different markets, reflecting capabilities such as knowledge of consumer attitudes, sales and distribution channels, brand name and reputation, and relationships with local institutions.

name: Breadth of product line
definition: A product market capability reflecting whether the firm is present in every market segment rather than specializing in a particular segment.

name: Relative technological sophistication in manufacturing
definition: The firm's use of advanced manufacturing technologies such as robots and other production and assembly equipment, relative to the industry.

name: Relative organizational capability
definition: The firm's management ability in different spheres, such as manufacturing operations, human resource practices and product development.

name: Relative labor cost
definition: A location-based capability of the firm, since automobile production is labor-intensive and differences in labor cost can be of considerable significance.

name: Wholly-owned entry mode
definition: The organizational form the firm chooses for its diversifying moves, specifically whether entry is attained via a wholly-owned venture rather than a collaborative arrangement with another firm. The dependent variable distinguishes own entry from joint venture or affiliate.

name: Firm-specific assets
definition: Firm-specific assets such as implicit knowledge, organized teams and assets whose continued maintenance is necessary for one party's other businesses, which create contractual and sharing difficulties in joint ventures. For financial services firms these include a branch network of retail outlets, specific human capital and brandname capital.

name: Firm size
definition: The scale of the society, treated as a proxy for the general availability of resources; the authors argue that the general availability of resources promotes wholly-owned ventures at least up to the level of the largest (i.e., national) societies.

name: Accumulated reserves
definition: Accumulated reserves, i.e. assets minus debt and deposit liabilities, representing each society's relative availability of funds for investment.

name: Product financial risk
definition: The level of financial risk carried by a new product market, indicated by whether the product involves extending credit. Risk aversion was expected to encourage collaboration, hence risk sharing, particularly where products appeared to carry high levels of financial risk.

name: Product fixed cost
definition: Whether a product requires a particularly large initial fixed investment, which the authors expected to favour collaborative rather than wholly-owned entry.

name: Product market regulation
authors_terms: ["FSA REG", "1986 Financial Services Act", "regulatory restrictions", "regulated products", "markets covered by the restrictions of the 1986 Financial Services Act"]
definition: Whether a product is covered by the restrictions of the 1986 Financial Services Act, which required sellers of selected products, including investment advice, general insurance and pension plans, to opt for either 'tied' or 'independent intermediary' status, the former being essentially collaborative arrangements.

name: Pre-deregulation profitability
definition: Pre-diversification profitability, assumed to proxy the potential of the core business to generate returns and hence the opportunity cost of extending the scope of the enterprise.

name: Board control
definition: The degree to which the board of directors fulfils its control responsibilities; the board is the primary internal control mechanism to better align the different interests of shareholders and top management. Effective control requires that directors have sufficient incentive and are free from collusion or domination by the CEO.

name: CEO compensation
definition: CEO compensation is composed of three elements: base salary, bonus, and long-term or deferred income. Total cash compensation is the sum of salary and bonus, and is the measure used by most studies of CEO compensation.

name: Strategy-making process capability
definition: Firms able to develop and accumulate several different process skills into a complex strategy-making 'capability' - the simultaneous use of multiple processes of strategy-making. Firms can develop skill in several modes over time, resulting in varying levels of strategy-making 'capability'.

name: Perceived firm performance
definition: Perceived performance was conceived as a multidimensional construct, following the work of Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1986): five dimensions of performance were postulated - Current Profitability, Growth/Share, Future Positioning, Quality, and Social Responsiveness.

name: Firm size
definition: As the number of employees hired by the firm grows, the distance between top managers and organizational members increases; the strategy-making process becomes less centralized and more complex.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: A munificent environment allows for the accumulation of slack resources by the firm and should provide the organization with both the opportunity and resources for innovation; it represents the conceptual opposite of environmental hostility.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: A turbulent environment is one that is both dynamic and complex - it changes both frequently and unpredictably, and embodies many inter- and intraorganizational linkages.

name: Command strategy-making mode
definition: Each mode reflects a pattern of interaction between the roles performed by the top managers and organizational members and represents a resource or skill set available to the firm; Command is one of the five strategy-making process modes developed by Hart (1992).

name: Symbolic strategy-making mode
definition: Each mode reflects a pattern of interaction between the roles performed by the top managers and organizational members and represents a resource or skill set available to the firm; Symbolic is one of the five strategy-making process modes developed by Hart (1992).

name: Rational strategy-making mode
definition: Each mode reflects a pattern of interaction between the roles performed by the top managers and organizational members and represents a resource or skill set available to the firm; Rational is one of the five strategy-making process modes developed by Hart (1992).

name: Transactive strategy-making mode
definition: Each mode reflects a pattern of interaction between the roles performed by the top managers and organizational members and represents a resource or skill set available to the firm; Transactive is one of the five strategy-making process modes developed by Hart (1992).

name: Generative strategy-making mode
definition: Each mode reflects a pattern of interaction between the roles performed by the top managers and organizational members and represents a resource or skill set available to the firm; Generative is one of the five strategy-making process modes developed by Hart (1992).

name: Ownership dilution
definition: Firms with a diluted ownership structure, as reflected by a large number of shareholders.

name: First-generation ownership
definition: Current first-generation majority owners of the firm.

name: First-generation executives
definition: Current first-generation senior executives of the firm.

name: Founder involvement
authors_terms: ["FOUNDERS", "original founders who are still partners or shareholders"]
definition: Original founders who are still partners or shareholders.

name: Firm age
definition: The age of the firm; mature firms are contrasted with younger firms.

name: Managerial function diversity
definition: The range of managerial functions currently operated by the firm.

name: Sole responsibility concentration
authors_terms: ["SOLE", "high proportion of managerial functions which are the sole responsibility of one person"]
definition: The proportion of managerial functions that are the sole responsibility of one person.

name: Managerial delegation
authors_terms: ["MANINDEX", "high levels of delegation of managerial functions to individuals"]
definition: The level of delegation of managerial functions to individuals.

name: Management planning
definition: The presence or extent of management planning; the text only gives the variable name in the hypothesis.

name: Professional advisor interaction
authors_terms: ["PLANPROF", "regular and frequent meetings with professional advisors"]
definition: Regular and frequent meetings with professional advisors such as banker, accountant and lawyer.

name: Business contact interaction
authors_terms: ["PLANBUS", "regular and frequent meetings with customers and suppliers"]
definition: Regular and frequent meetings with customers and suppliers.

name: Management training
authors_terms: ["MANTRAIN", "management has undergone some form of management training"]
definition: Whether management has undergone some form of management training.

name: External finance diversity
authors_terms: ["FINANCE", "financial investment from a large number of sources"]
definition: Financial investment received from a large number of sources, not including overdraft facilities from banks.

name: Production control technology
authors_terms: ["PRODUCTION", "non-manual control technology for the major manufactured product lines"]
definition: Non-manual control technology for the major manufactured product lines.

name: Production equipment age
definition: The age or maturity of the firm's production equipment.

name: Administrative technology sophistication
authors_terms: ["CSADMIN", "sophisticated technology in the control of the administration base"]
definition: The use of sophisticated technology in the control of the administration base.

name: Prosperous market location
authors_terms: ["LOCATION", "located in the prosperous and buoyant markets of the south of England"]
definition: Firms located in the prosperous and buoyant markets of the south of England (East Anglia, South East and South West).

name: Government training scheme use
definition: Whether the firm has taken advantage of government training schemes.

name: Government grant use
definition: Whether the firm has taken advantage of government grants.

name: Product line diversity
authors_terms: ["PRODUCT", "wide number of major product lines or major service groups"]
definition: The number of major product lines or major service groups.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["NEWPRODUCT", "introduced a large number of new major product lines or major service groups during the previous year"]
definition: The number of new major product lines or major service groups introduced during the previous year.

name: Revenue concentration
authors_terms: ["REVENUE", "high percentage of sales revenue accounted for by the major product line or service group"]
definition: The percentage of sales revenue accounted for by the major product line or service group.

name: Customer base diversity
definition: The diversity of the firm's customer base.

name: New customer acquisition
authors_terms: ["NEWCUSTOMERS", "added significant numbers of new customers over the previous year"]
definition: The number of significant new customers added over the previous year.

name: Supplier base diversity
authors_terms: ["SUPPLIERS", "purchase goods and services from a wide number of suppliers"]
definition: The number of suppliers from which the firm purchases goods and services.

name: New supplier acquisition
authors_terms: ["NEWSUPPLIERS", "becoming more diverse and wider in scale"]
definition: The extent to which the firm's supplier base is becoming more diverse and wider in scale.

name: Customer geographic reach
authors_terms: ["DISTCUSTOMERS", "sell the majority of their products and services in nationwide or overseas markets"]
definition: The extent to which the firm sells the majority of its products and services in nationwide or overseas markets rather than local or regional markets.

name: Supplier geographic reach
definition: The extent to which the firm is not exclusively supplied by local suppliers.

name: Competitor number
definition: The number of direct competitors faced by the firm.

name: Small firm growth and performance
definition: Three measures of size are used as surrogates for presumed growth: sales turnover, trading profit, and total number of employees. Performance is measured by the owner-manager's scoring of his firm's profit performance against the market.

name: Product innovativeness
authors_terms: ["product innovativeness", "degree of innovativeness", "level of product innovation", "newness to the market", "newness to the firm", "level of innovation"]
definition: The extent to which the new product changes the customer's habits or usage patterns indicates the degree of product innovativeness. Three dimensions of product innovativeness are developed: newness to the market, newness to the firm, and Booz, Allen & Hamilton's innovativeness scale.

name: Interfirm cooperation
authors_terms: ["cooperating firms", "number of firms involved", "cooperative strategies", "strategic alliances", "cooperative ventures"]
definition: Strategic alliances or cooperative ventures are new cooperative organization forms through which firms exchange resources for mutual benefit given functional specialization and a scarcity of resources. In this study the number of firms involved in the product introduction distinguishes a single firm from multiple cooperating firms.

name: Strategic linkage
definition: Vertical linkages occur when firms cooperate across different levels of the value-added chain whereas horizontal linkages are across the same level; vertical linkages are distribution or outsourcing arrangements, while horizontal linkages include R&D consortia, patent swaps, technology transfers, and joint ventures.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of the firm", "small firm", "large firm", "mixed-size firms"]
definition: Firm size is coded from membership in the Fortune 500 or Fortune International 500 (large) versus otherwise (small), with mixed cases being those with at least one firm in each firm size category.

name: Technology type
authors_terms: ["Type B industries", "Type M industries", "product type", "technology fusion"]
definition: Type M (mechatronics) products are essentially assembled from mechanical and electronic components, while Type B (biotechnology, pharmaceutical, and chemical) products are the result of genetic engineering and biochemistry and are created at the molecular level.

name: Industry match
authors_terms: ["agreement between the firm's industry and the product's industry", "MATCH", "cross-industry product offerings"]
definition: The agreement between the firm's industry and the product's industry. Firms associated with an industry outside an existing product's industry are likely to offer more innovative products than firms within the industry.

name: Interindustry cooperation
definition: Agreement or accord between the cooperating firms' industries, coded as intraindustry versus interindustry cooperation.

name: Progression of time
definition: Time (competitive imitation, intensification of competition, and knowledge accumulation) renders nearly all advantages obsolete, and increasingly innovative products are introduced in a shorter time interval. It is measured by the month in which the product was introduced.

name: Cross-national cooperation
authors_terms: ["crossnationally cooperating firms", "nationality of the firm", "Triad region", "NATION"]
definition: Cooperation between firms of different national origin; new products introduced by single firms or cooperating firms from the same country are likely to be more innovative than those introduced by cross-nationally cooperating firms.

name: Outside institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["outside institutional stockholdings", "stock ownership by outside institutions", "institutional ownership", "institutional stockholdings"]
definition: The percent of a firm's stock held by outside institutions-banks and trust companies, pension funds, savings and loan associations, insurance corporations, and mutual fund management institutions. Firms with high institutional ownership of stocks are classified as dispersed-involved.

name: Capital structure
authors_terms: ["capital structure", "debt-capital ratio", "long-term debt-to-capital ratio", "long-term debt as a percent of the firm's total capital"]
definition: The firm's capital structure, one of two specific domains of institutional investors' potential influence, represented by the debt-capital ratio.

name: Financial performance
definition: A firm's financial performance as captured by four measures: percent return on assets, percent return on equity, price-earnings ratio, and percent of total stock return.

name: Executive stock ownership
authors_terms: ["stock ownership by executives", "corporate executives' shareholdings", "executive stock ownership", "management ownership"]
definition: The percent of a firm's stock held by its corporate executives. Greater stock ownership by executives increases the power of the internal constituency and decreases the power of the external constituency in influencing firms' strategies.

name: Family ownership
authors_terms: ["stock ownership by non-executive individuals or family owners", "family owners' shareholdings", "family ownership"]
definition: The percent of a firm's stock held by non-executive individuals or family owners, who do not manage the firm and can also be regarded as external owners.

name: Insider-institutional ownership
definition: The percent of a firm's stock held by insider-institutions (e.g. employee stock ownership plans, union funds), which are managed by professional fund managers but have contractual relationships with the firm.

name: Strategic group heterogeneity
definition: Under the strategic management model, groups represent firms pursuing strategies in imitation of successful entrepreneurial firms that represent 'ideal types'; such groups should be heterogeneous, with firms showing various degrees of commitment to an ideal strategic form.

name: Strategic configuration
authors_terms: ["strategic configuration", "strategic group membership (GROUP)", "strategic groups", "strategic position", "strategic configurations"]
definition: Groups of firms in a host market with distinct strategic configurations, established empirically as firms with common strategic positions and interpreted from their loadings on 'ideal firm' components.

name: MNE global size
authors_terms: ["global MNEs", "global sales (GLOBAL)", "firm size", "world wide sales", "potential market power"]
definition: The overall size of the parent multinational, indicated by period-average worldwide sales; parent MNE size may indicate the potential for resource availability in the United States.

name: DFP experience
authors_terms: ["use of DFP in other markets (ODFP)", "other DFP in the U.S. (ODFPUS)", "experience-oriented variables", "resources related to DFP skills"]
definition: The proven skills to use direct foreign production in one market or for one product, which the authors argue MNEs will carry over to other markets or products.

name: Host market resource commitment
authors_terms: ["US sales to global sales ratio (USRAT)", "dependency on the U.S. auto market", "strategic resource focus on the U.S. market", "resource commitment"]
definition: The firm's relative commitment of resources to the host market, expressed as the ratio of U.S. sales to global sales and described as a measure of strategic resource focus on the U.S. market.

name: Internalization level
authors_terms: ["level of internalization", "direct foreign production (DFP)", "structural form", "internalization decision", "market versus hierarchy"]
definition: The structural decision for a single host market, focusing on the level of internalization to be used in that market, based on the need for a governance structure to best fit the firm's market strategy and firm-specific resources to the environment.

name: Host market performance
definition: Firm performance in the host market, measured as the annual percentage increase in market share in the market for foreign autos in the United States.

name: Strategic orientation
definition: The typology of strategic orientations adopted from Miles and Snow (1978): Prospectors aggressively seek growth opportunities through product and market development and innovation; Defenders adopt and protect narrow and stable domains and are internally-oriented and efficient; Analyzers exhibit characteristics of both Prospectors and Defenders; Reactors do not follow a consistent strategy.

name: Amount of senior management compensation
definition: The overall level of pay provided to senior managers, which tends to be large in high-discretion contexts to reduce managerial risk.

name: Outcome-based compensation plans
authors_terms: ["outcome-based compensation plans", "outcome-based pay", "incentive plans", "type of compensation"]
definition: Compensation plans designed to reward managers for their performance; outcome-based pay can reduce monitoring costs when appropriate managerial behaviors are difficult to determine.

name: Proportion of outcome-based cash compensation
authors_terms: ["proportion of outcome-based cash compensation", "mix of pay", "proportion of pay tied to performance"]
definition: The share of managers' cash compensation that is tied to performance outcomes, i.e. the mix of pay.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["environmental change", "environmental uncertainty", "environmental period", "deregulation", "high discretion environmental periods"]
definition: The level of uncertainty and managerial discretion conferred by the environment; deregulation increased environmental uncertainty, upset established patterns of behavior and enhanced managerial discretion.

name: Venture outcome assessment
definition: Outcomes represent events that reflect venture members' assessment of performance over time. Positive (negative) outcomes reflect venture members' assessment of performance above (below) their aspiration levels.

name: Action persistence
authors_terms: ["action persistence", "persistence", "continue with a course of action", "continuation events"]
definition: Entrepreneurs may continue with a course of action despite experiencing negative outcomes; this type of 'action persistence' is often required to overcome the resistance most ventures encounter from naysayers within and outside the organization.

name: Plan change
definition: When a resource controller or CIP entrepreneur stated plans or outcome criteria that were different from the past, it was coded as a shift.

name: Corporate sponsors' involvement
definition: When corporate sponsors were behaviorally involved in an event, it was coded as such; SP is the monthly count of the number of times corporate sponsors were involved. Besides their resource allocation role, sponsors perform other roles such as mentor, champion and critic.

name: External environmental change
definition: When an event involved a change in the activities occurring external but reported as relevant to CIP (including changes in competitors' technology and industry structure), it was coded as an environmental event.

name: Ambiguity
definition: While uncertainty implies imperfect knowledge about the causal relationships between means and ends, ambiguity implies imperfect knowledge of which ends are worth pursuing. Ambiguity is enhanced if entrepreneurs are not able to compare the different approaches in order to conclude which one will eventually be successful.

name: Competitive posture
definition: Competitive posture is a component of organizational strategy that encodes theories of action regarding the competitive advantages that its managers value, and toward which they allocate its resources.

name: Efficiency orientation
definition: By emphasizing efficiency through high volume and speediness of return preparation and through policies that keep costs down, a firm can charge a lower price for its services and attract those taxpayers who might otherwise bypass these services because of high costs.

name: Service quality orientation
definition: By stressing features of tax-return preparation that reflect a more personal touch, a firm captures customers who are willing to pay more for the quality of the service they receive.

name: Issue interpretation
authors_terms: ["managerial interpretations", "issue interpretations", "strategic issue diagnosis", "assessments of the impact of a technological innovation"]
definition: Strategic issue diagnosis refers to those activities and processes by which data and stimuli are translated into focused issues (i.e., attention organizing acts) and the issues explored (i.e., acts of interpretation); the interpretations that emerge from strategic issue diagnosis influence subsequent commitment to, and investment in, electronic filing.

name: Effect significance
definition: The extent to which managers expect implementation of electronic filing to have a significant impact on the marketplace.

name: Effect valence
definition: The extent to which managers frame electronic filing as an opportunity for the firm to gain competitive advantage.

name: New technology capability commitment
definition: The extent to which there is a commitment to strengthening or acquiring the capabilities that firms need to adopt electronic filing.

name: New technology adoption
authors_terms: ["new technology adoption", "adoption of new technology", "adoption of electronic filing"]
definition: The extent to which the firm uses electronic filing.

name: Mental model change
authors_terms: ["succession in mental models", "change in mental model", "change in mental maps", "map change"]
definition: The key construct for the analysis is a change in mental model or map, which the authors believe is basic evidence of managerial learning. They identify change systematically as changes in concepts, relationships, and map structures.

name: Organizational renewal
definition: Organizational renewal requires that a firm's top managers make timely adjustments in their mental models following significant changes in the environment. The Chicago and North Western engaged in radical restructuring during a period of radical environmental change and continues to be a viable company today, whereas the Rock Island showed steady decline until it went bankrupt in the mid-1970s.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: A munificent or benign environment; significant weaknesses appear in failing firms long before bankruptcy but go unaddressed because the environment remains munificent, and growth can hide 'a multitude of sins', so that a favorable environment permits firms to enjoy profitability in spite of managers' outdated mental models.

name: Detection of environmental change
authors_terms: ["noticing", "problem sensing", "detect a substantial change in their organizations' environments"]
definition: Problem sensing, the cognitive processes of noticing and constructing meaning about environmental change so that organizations can take action. Delays in the succession of mental models may occur if managers fail to detect a substantial change in their organizations' environments.

name: Organizational learning process
authors_terms: ["unfreezing, change, and refreezing", "unlearning", "single loop learning", "double loop learning"]
definition: Learning characterized by unfreezing, change, and refreezing: old beliefs are discarded to make way for new understandings, new understandings are achieved often via experimentation, and changes in mental models are solidified. Low level or single loop learning is reflected in changes in behavior, while higher level or double loop learning involves unlearning and a restructuring of mental models.

name: Acquisition status
definition: Companies that were acquired in a merger or acquisition (the experimental group) as opposed to a matched sample of companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity during the observation period (the control group).

name: Top management turnover
authors_terms: ["top management turnover", "top management team turnover rate", "management turnover"]
definition: The percentage of turnover among the top management teams, computed at each of 5 years following the date of the merger in the experimental group, or the time of initial observation in the control group.

name: Acquisition relatedness
authors_terms: ["type of merger or acquisition", "type of acquisition", "related merger or acquisition", "unrelated merger or acquisition"]
definition: The primary economic relationship established between the parent firm and the target firm, grouped into the FTC categories of horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated acquisitions.

name: Executive seniority
authors_terms: ["very senior top managers", "management level", "very senior executives", "colleagues of somewhat lesser rank"]
definition: The rank of a member of a target company's top management team, distinguishing very senior executives (presidents, CEOs, or chairmen of the board) from colleagues of somewhat lesser status such as vice-presidents and other officers.

name: Time to turnover
definition: The elapsed time between the acquisition and the departure of a member of the target company's top management team.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: Hostile environments are characterized by precarious industry settings, intense competition, harsh, overwhelming business climates, and the relative lack of exploitable opportunities. Non-hostile or benign environments, on the other hand, provide a safe setting for business operations due to their overall level of munificence and richness in investment and marketing opportunities.

name: Organicity
definition: Organicity is the extent to which organizations are structured in organic versus mechanistic manners; the higher the organicity index, the more organic the firm's structure.

name: Strategic posture
authors_terms: ["strategic posture", "entrepreneurial-conservative orientation", "entrepreneurial strategic posture", "conservative strategic posture"]
definition: Strategic posture can be broadly defined as a firm's overall competitive orientation. A firm's entrepreneurial-conservation orientation is indicative of its strategic posture, demonstrated by the extent to which top managers are inclined to take business-related risks, to favor change and innovation in order to obtain a competitive advantage, and to compete aggressively with other firms.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is measured as a subjective, weighted average index obtained by multiplying top managers' satisfaction with their firm's performance on each of nine financial performance criteria by the importance the firm attaches to that criterion.

name: Competitive tactics
authors_terms: ["business practices and competitive tactics", "overall business strategy"]
definition: The firms' reliance on various business practices and competitive tactics, assessed by the extent to which respondents agreed that various statements were descriptive of their firms' current overall business strategy.

name: Buyer purchasing behavior
definition: The behavior of buyers in a market, described by variables guiding the interviews: perceived purchasing risks, competing technologies perception, suppliers selection criteria, product purchasing criteria, purchasing tactics, purchased products, evaluation of suppliers, expected improvements on key purchasing criteria, and customers' reactions to improvements.

name: Market segments
authors_terms: ["market segments", "segments", "groups of customers having similar purchasing behaviors"]
definition: Groups of customers having similar purchasing behaviors, defined for each industry by an ascendant hierarchical cluster analysis on the set of variables describing buying behavior.

name: Key purchasing criteria
authors_terms: ["key purchasing criteria", "components of the offers which bear value for the customers"]
definition: Components of the offers which bear value for the customers.

name: Differentiation sources
definition: Differentiation sources can be defined as components of the offers which bear value for the customers (key purchasing criteria), on which current offers are not optimal.

name: Industry-wide differentiation sources
definition: Valuable potential differentiation sources common to the majority of the segments of the industry.

name: Segment-specific differentiation sources
definition: Valuable potential differentiation sources specific to particular segments of the industry.

name: Defendability from imitation
authors_terms: ["defendable from imitation", "risks of imitation", "probability of imitation by other competitors"]
definition: The extent to which a differentiation source found can be defended against imitation by competitors, evaluated through the experts' forecast probability of imitation and the means to defend from such imitations.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: We defined differentiation as a position in which the offer of a given competitor has some valuable distinctive characteristics (except from price) for the customers.

name: Relative product quality
authors_terms: ["product relative quality", "relative product quality index", "product quality index"]
definition: The relative quality of the firm's products compared to the best competitors', one of the ten variables describing the firm's position on differentiation criteria.

name: Product environment
authors_terms: ["'product environment' index", "firm's position on delivery times, technical services and other services"]
definition: The product (or service) environment (delivery time, peripheral services, relations, etc.); in the firm survey it is an index combining the firm's position on delivery times, technical services and other services.

name: Product innovation
definition: Product innovation, one of the ten variables describing the firm's position on differentiation criteria in the firm survey.

name: Profitability
definition: The firm's performance evaluated through profitability: return on sales, return on investment and a profitability index.

name: Market share gain
definition: The firm's performance evaluated through market share variation.

name: Order of entry
definition: A measure of order of entry which identifies three categories-namely, pioneers, early followers and late entrants.

name: Scale of entry
authors_terms: ["scale of entry", "scale of the business at its point of entry"]
definition: Variables primarily concerned with establishing the scale of the business at its point of entry, which, in ecological terms, reflects the difference between generalism and specialism.

name: Relationship to parent firm
definition: Variables describing the level and types of resources that a new business has available to it by virtue of its ownership characteristics, including the size and the diversity of the parent firm's activities, the possibility of buying materials or selling output internally, and the opportunity to share existing production facilities or distribution channels.

name: Ongoing competitive strategy
definition: Variables measuring the ongoing competitive position of the business, all measured relative to competitors, including marketing expenditure, product quality and customer support services, price and direct manufacturing costs.

name: Long-term performance
definition: The market shares and profitability of the three entrant groups, used as the performance measures in the comparison of entrant types.

name: Strategic restructuring
authors_terms: ["restructuring", "strategic restructuring", "modes of restructuring", "major changes in strategy and organization"]
definition: For this study, restructuring will refer to major changes in strategy and organization in response to changing environmental conditions; the three modes identified for liberal arts colleges are adding business programs, adding graduate programs, and moving from single sex to coeducation.

name: Environmental change
authors_terms: ["changing environmental conditions", "common environmental changes", "market-based pressures for change"]
definition: The market environment faced by these colleges was altered by several significant trends: a major shift in the life goals of potential students, increasing specialization in the labor market, and an expected dramatic decline in the population of traditional college age students.

name: Endowment
definition: A relatively small endowment is one of the organization-level conditions that may increase the perceived need for strategic change, but simultaneously place a severe resource constraint on the organization's ability to engage in modes of restructuring that attempt to expand product offerings or reach new students.

name: Debt
definition: A high level of debt is one of the organization-level conditions that may increase the perceived need for strategic change, but simultaneously place a severe resource constraint on the organization's ability to engage in modes of restructuring that attempt to expand product offerings or reach new students.

name: Reputation for premium quality
authors_terms: ["reputation for premium quality", "a reputation for delivering a premium product or service", "selectivity"]
definition: A reputation for delivering a premium product or service (relevant for higher education and other types of organizations) could diminish the perceived need for strategic restructuring but enhance the ability of an organization to successfully offer new products or reach new customers.

name: Organizational size
definition: Size can be considered another proxy for resource endowment: larger organizations may have a lessened need to change, while their greater resource endowment suggests that they are more likely to be able to change.

name: Organizational age
definition: The 'rigidity of aging' notion stresses the ossification of older organizations, whereas the 'fluidity of aging' notion stresses the likely growing lack of 'fit' between an aging organization and its environment.

name: Regional economic growth
definition: During the time frame of this study, the Northeast region was declining economically and demographically (exacerbating the need for restructuring), while the West/Southwest was growing.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: The first and most direct performance outcome is organizational death; survival is an overarching goal of colleges as well as other organizations.

name: Enrollment growth
authors_terms: ["yearly enrollment", "proportional change in enrollment", "proportional increases in enrollment"]
definition: Enrollment is a widely accepted measure of organizational health among colleges.

name: Operating margin
definition: Operating margin, which captures financial viability, is measured as: (operating revenue-operating expenses)/operating revenues.

name: Firm risk
authors_terms: ["firm risk", "organizational (and managerial) risk", "riskiness of the firm", "risky firms"]
definition: Differences in firm risk are associated with differences in the cost of using incentive compensation, since it can influence managers' willingness to accept compensation contracts that include a risk-bearing component.

name: Long-term incentive compensation
definition: LTI compensation includes grants of multiyear performance incentives, such as performance shares, performance units, and restricted stock.

name: Noncash incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["noncash incentives", "proportion of a CEO's total wealth change comprised of noncash incentives", "proportion of CEO total compensation derived from noncash sources"]
definition: A more complete calculation of a CEO's wealth that is 'at risk' in that it includes the dollar value of LTIs as well as the gain/loss attributable to the shares of stock held by the CEO, expressed relative to total wealth change.

name: CEO equity holdings
authors_terms: ["CEO equity holdings", "equity stakes", "managerial stock holdings", "percentage of a firm's equity held by the CEO"]
definition: The magnitude of the existing equity positions held by CEOs in their firms, which may influence their willingness to accept further risk-bearing.

name: Board monitoring
authors_terms: ["board monitoring", "monitoring by boards of directors", "level of monitoring", "governance structures"]
definition: The level of monitoring provided by the firm's board of directors, as represented by the proportion of outside directors, outside directors' stock ownership, the presence of a major nonboard member blockholder, and the separation of the CEO and board chairman positions.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["corporate diversification", "level of corporate diversification", "strategic complexity", "complex corporate strategy"]
definition: A widely accepted characterization of a firm's strategy is its level of corporate diversification; complex corporate strategies are costlier for boards of directors to monitor, although at the highest levels of diversification financial oversight becomes more straightforward.

name: Drug discovery productivity
authors_terms: ["drug discovery productivity", "research productivity", "research output", "drug discovery efforts"]
definition: The productivity of drug discovery as measured by counts of 'important' patents, where an 'important' patent is one that was granted in two of the three major jurisdictions: Japan, Europe, and the U.S.A.

name: Firm-specific disciplinary expertise
authors_terms: ["firm-specific expertise in particular disciplinary areas", "unique disciplinary expertise", "excellence in a discipline"]
definition: Expertise in a scientific discipline (such as pharmacology, medicinal chemistry or molecular biology) that builds on a foundation of largely tacit experience held by a disciplinary group embedded within a particular firm.

name: Component competence in disease areas
authors_terms: ["component competence in particular disease areas", "'local' competence", "local knowledge and ability in particular areas"]
definition: Tacit or proprietary knowledge about particular disease areas developed over time by groups of disciplinary specialists working together.

name: External boundary spanning
authors_terms: ["the ability to access new knowledge from outside the boundaries of the organization", "the ability to span the boundaries of the firm", "flow of information across the boundaries of the firm", "links to the wider scientific community"]
definition: The ability of the firm to encourage and maintain an extensive flow of information across its boundaries, reaching outside the organization for knowledge generated elsewhere.

name: Internal knowledge integration
authors_terms: ["the ability to integrate knowledge flexibly across disciplinary and therapeutic class boundaries within the organization", "flow of information across the boundaries between scientific disciplines and therapeutic classes within the firm"]
definition: The ability of the firm to integrate knowledge across both disciplinary and disease area boundaries within the firm.

name: Centralized resource allocation
authors_terms: ["use of a 'dictator' to allocate resources", "resource allocation within research controlled by a single individual", "management by committee"]
definition: The degree to which resource allocation within research is controlled by a single individual, as opposed to being decentralized and managed through a governing committee.

name: Executive departure
definition: Departure was defined as the proportion of executives present at the time of the acquisition who had departed by the end of the second postacquisition year. The executives of interest were officers of the acquired firm who either held a title above the rank of Vice-President or were inside directors, or both.

name: Postacquisition performance change
definition: Performance Change was calculated as the average within rater difference between performance at t = 4 and performance at t = 0. Thus, negative values imply performance declines, while positive values imply improvement.

name: Preacquisition performance
definition: Expert informants rated the profitability of the acquired firm at the time the deal was made on a 7-point scale anchored 'very poor' and 'very good.'

name: Postacquisition performance
definition: Expert informants rated the profitability of the acquired firm four years after the deal on a 7-point scale anchored 'very poor' and 'very good.'

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: Relatedness is often defined as the extent to which acquired and acquiring firms serve similar customers or utilize similar production processes. In the present study, the authors consider three categories of relatedness, based on product/market similarities between the acquirer and the acquired firm.

name: Top management team status bestowal
definition: Acquirers may mitigate the negative status effects of an acquisition by bestowing status (officerships and/or directorships) on some executives from acquired firms; these status-bestowed executives may feel little or no status decline, maintaining a high degree of morale and effectiveness.

name: Executive seniority
definition: Executives who held any of five titles were classified as 'More-Senior': Chairman, Vice-Chairman, President, CEO, and COO; the remainder were classified as 'Less Senior.' The senior-designated titles correspond to executives who are at the very top of corporate decision making.

name: Organizational form of production
authors_terms: ["organizational status of the production", "organizational form", "independent production", "internal production", "studio production", "studio films", "independent films"]
definition: The organization and management of production: studio films were made by employees of large organizations working under long-term contracts, while independent productions came from small, entrepreneurial firms that sometimes were created in order to carry out individual projects.

name: Production cost
authors_terms: ["production cost", "cost of production", "cost of independent productions"]
definition: The cost of producing a film, tracked for each project from the initial acquisition of rights through shipment of a final print.

name: Economic performance of film projects
authors_terms: ["market performance", "economic performance", "box office performance", "performance", "gross revenues", "margin of revenue over cost", "cashflow"]
definition: Performance of a film as reflected in gross revenues, the most fundamental indicator of the audience appeal of a film, and in the margin of gross revenues over production cost, which controls for production expenditures and permits examination of market responses to characteristics of films that are less readily priced and purchased.

name: Variability in market performance
authors_terms: ["variance in market performance", "variability in the audience appeal of films", "greater variance in performance"]
definition: The dispersion of a film's market performance, which serves solely as a measure of variability in the audience appeal of films and is not treated as an analysis of risk.

name: Board involvement in strategic restructuring
authors_terms: ["strategic board involvement", "board involvement in strategic restructuring", "board strategic involvement"]
definition: The extent of board pressure or involvement in the decision to restructure or acquire business units, measured as a factor of survey items.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["ratio of outside board members to total board members", "outside director representation", "board structure"]
definition: The ratio of outside directors to total board members; outside directors are those with no personal or professional relationship with the firm other than as directors.

name: Outside director equity ownership
authors_terms: ["board equity holdings of outside directors", "outside director equity", "outside director ownership"]
definition: Equity interests of outside directors, operationalized as the sum of their equity holdings divided by common shares outstanding.

name: Top management team equity ownership
authors_terms: ["top management team equity", "managerial equity holdings", "top management team equity ownership"]
definition: Equity interests of top management team members, operationalized as the sum of their equity holdings divided by common shares outstanding.

name: Emphasis on strategic controls
authors_terms: ["strategic controls", "strategic control usage", "emphasis on strategic controls"]
definition: Strategic controls describe both the quality of the relationship between corporate and business levels and the depth of understanding of business unit operations by corporate managers, requiring more open and subjective evaluation than financial controls.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["mean top management team tenure", "top management team tenure"]
definition: The mean number of years in which individuals were a member of the top management team.

name: Top management team organizational tenure
definition: The mean number of years in which individuals were employed by the firm.

name: Board tenure
definition: The mean number of years in which individuals served on the board of directors.

name: Board tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["board tenure heterogeneity", "heterogeneity in board member tenure", "variance in mean board tenure"]
definition: The dispersion of board member tenure, operationalized as the coefficient of variation of board tenure.

name: Top management team tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["top management team tenure heterogeneity", "heterogeneity in top management team tenure"]
definition: The dispersion of top management team member tenure, operationalized as the coefficient of variation of top management team tenure.

name: Top management team education level
authors_terms: ["education level of the top management team", "top management team educational level"]
definition: The average number of years of education of top management team members, an indicator of their knowledge and skill base.

name: Insider ownership
definition: Ownership of firm shares by insiders, the corporate decision makers; agency theory arguments suggest that when corporate decision makers own shares, their interests are aligned more closely with those of nonmanagerial shareholders.

name: Change in insider ownership
authors_terms: ["increases in insider ownership", "change in insider ownership", "change in managerial share ownership"]
definition: Increases or decreases in insider share ownership during the 1980s; firms in which insider share ownership increased during the 1980s should have restructured more than firms where it did not.

name: Blockholder ownership
definition: Ownership by blockholders, owners of 5 percent or more of a firm's shares, who have enough shares to influence corporate policy through the voting process and have both the incentives and the power to ensure that managers operate the firm efficiently.

name: Blockholder buy-in
authors_terms: ["buy-in by a blockholder", "acquisition of a block of shares", "blockholder buy-in"]
definition: The acquisition of a block of shares in a previously diffusely-held firm during the 1980s.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: Shares managed by institutions on behalf of third-party investors; institutions buy, sell, and sometimes vote on behalf of their clients, but do not own the shares directly.

name: Change in institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["increases in institutional ownership", "change in institutional ownership"]
definition: Increases or decreases in the level of institutional ownership during the 1980s; firms wherein the level of institutional ownership increased during the 1980s should have undertaken more restructuring than other firms.

name: Corporate restructuring
definition: Corporate restructuring comprises radical changes in firms' business portfolios or financial structures; following Bowman and Singh (1990), the authors define corporate restructuring to include both portfolio restructuring and financial restructuring.

name: Portfolio restructuring
definition: Portfolio restructuring involves changes in both the size and the mix of businesses of diversified firms.

name: Financial restructuring
definition: Financial restructuring takes cash out of managers' hands and returns it to shareholders by increasing dividends and by issuing new debt and paying out the proceeds, thereby reducing managers' ability to overexpand and overdiversify; the authors measure it in terms of increases in cash payments to shareholders and bondholders and in terms of reductions in inward investment.

name: Cumulative victories in certification contests
authors_terms: ["cumulative victories", "accumulated victories", "log of victories", "wins", "victories in certification contests"]
definition: Victories in certification contests legitimate organizations and validate their reputation because of the taken for granted axiom that winners are 'better' than losers. A winner was defined as an organization whose product was awarded the first prize in an event.

name: Reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "favorable reputation", "reputations of organizations", "reputation of individual organizations"]
definition: Reputation becomes an outcome of the process of legitimation; legitimation means not only the normative justification of organizations but also the cognitive validation of an entity as desirable, proper, and appropriate in a widely shared system of beliefs and norms.

name: Exit rate
definition: An exit was defined as bankruptcy, cessation of operations, or withdrawal by an organization, and mergers were not defined as exits. The exit rate of organizations was defined as the probability of an organization experiencing an event in the interval from t to t + s given that an organization was at risk at time t.

name: Organizational origin
authors_terms: ["startup organizations", "lateral entries", "de novo organizations", "pre-existing organizations that have entered the industry"]
definition: Lateral entries are pre-existing organizations established in another industry that have entered the industry in question. Startup organizations are de novo organizations.

name: Certification contests
definition: I use the term 'contest' to denote a yardstick competition in which performances are ranked. Such certification contests are social tests of products and organizations wherein the technical criteria chosen to evaluate performance are themselves the outcomes of institutional processes.

name: Market share
definition: By market share, we mean a firm's share of total industry sales, which is an important indicator of its market performance.

name: Business survival
definition: By business survival, we mean that a firm's business continues to operate in the industry. The survival predictions address business dissolution rather than sale of an ongoing business to a new owner.

name: First-to-market innovation introduction
authors_terms: ["among the first to introduce", "first to market"]
definition: Introducing a product that incorporates an incremental innovation within the first 12 months that the innovation is available in the market.

name: Incremental innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["adopting the innovation", "Adopt: year 2 or 3", "Adopt: year 4 plus"]
definition: Introducing a product that incorporates an innovation more than a year after the innovation became available in the market.

name: Total innovation introductions
definition: The number of times that a firm either was among the first to introduce or adopted an incremental innovation, combining the first to market and adoption variables; used as a variable in the survival analysis.

name: Competitive density
authors_terms: ["Competitors: first to market", "Competitors: total introductions", "the number of competitors that offered similar products", "competitive density"]
definition: The number of competitors that offered similar products during each year after the firm introduced an incremental innovation.

name: Second source entry rate
authors_terms: ["second source entry", "rate of second source entry into a focal community", "entry rate of second sources", "rate at which communities gain second source support"]
definition: The rate at which firms enter a technological community as second sources, that is, by copying an existing microprocessor design rather than designing an original one; second sourcing is treated as one particular type of organizational support.

name: Number of second sources in focal community
authors_terms: ["number of second sources in that community", "community density", "number of community members", "density of community members"]
definition: The number of firms belonging to a community, including both the sponsor and the second sources; it is the density of the focal community whose effect on entry is predicted to be nonmonotonic.

name: Number of communities in the market
authors_terms: ["number of other communities in the market", "community density", "number of technological communities in the market other than the focal community"]
definition: Community density at the market level, defined as the number of technological communities in the market other than the focal community.

name: Second source support outside focal community
authors_terms: ["number of second sources outside the community", "number of second sources supporting other communities", "second source support for other communities"]
definition: The extent of organizational support, in the form of second sources, that other communities in the market have attracted.

name: Architectural innovation
authors_terms: ["architectural innovation", "communities based on architectural innovations", "RISC technology"]
definition: Architectural innovation has been described as the reconfiguration of an established system to link together existing components in a new way; the basic scientific knowledge underlying the technology has not changed. Communities whose primary design was based on RISC technology are treated as communities based on an architectural innovation.

name: Community dominance
authors_terms: ["community dominance", "installed sales base", "community's sales in the previous quarter", "dominance"]
definition: In the economics of standards literature dominance is generally equated with the number of products sold that are compatible with a given standard; here it is captured by a community's installed sales base and by its sales in the previous quarter.

name: Time since last innovation
authors_terms: ["time since innovation", "shorter the time since a community has last innovated"]
definition: The time elapsed since a community last introduced a product that is technologically superior to its previous products; the rate at which a community improves its own products is a signal to prospective supporters that the community is viable.

name: Executive evaluation of a technological collaborative opportunity
authors_terms: ["evaluation of the opportunity", "top executive assessments of technological collaborative opportunities", "attractiveness of technological collaborative opportunities"]
definition: Each executive was asked to rate both the attractiveness of the relationship and the probability that they would pursue such a relationship. The study evaluates managerial, economic, and cognitive explanations for why top executives consider technological collaborative opportunities more or less attractive.

name: Significance of the technology to strategy
authors_terms: ["significance of the technology to current strategy", "significance of the technology to the company's strategy"]
definition: The attractiveness of collaborative efforts to develop technology will increase with the significance of the technology to strategy up to a point and then decrease as concerns over proprietary control build.

name: Existing skill capability of the firm
authors_terms: ["existing skill capability of the firm to develop this technology", "perceived strengths and weaknesses"]
definition: If executives believe that the firm has the technological skills (perceived strength), logic suggests that they will be less likely to consider a cooperative relationship to develop technology; if they think the firm has some of the skills and knowledge required but lacks specific capabilities, they are more likely to consider a technological cooperative relationship.

name: Life cycle phase of the technology
definition: If the technology is in an early stage of its life cycle, firms may see great potential in the use of a cooperative relationship to develop the technology; in maturity, when market uncertainties are resolved, acquisitions or licensing may be preferred.

name: Compatibility of operating and management styles
authors_terms: ["compatibility of operating and management styles", "compatibility of management styles"]
definition: The compatibility of operating and management styles of the company and the potential partner (potential opportunity or threat); similarity in partner values and methods of conducting business activities allow for easier merging of efforts.

name: Number of other potential partners
authors_terms: ["number of other potential partners", "number of capable partners"]
definition: The smaller the number of capable partners for a desired relationship, the lower the bargaining power of the firm relative to any given potential partner; the larger the number of other potential partners the more attractive a potential technological collaborative opportunity becomes.

name: Asset-specific investments required
definition: The need to invest in assets specific to the cooperative project and of limited value outside the relationship can lead to higher switching or exit costs for the firm.

name: Relative information advantage
authors_terms: ["relative information advantage", "information relative to partner", "distribution of information between technology partners"]
definition: The distribution of information between technology partners is likely to be skewed toward one partner over the other; an informational disadvantage pertaining to the technology in question can lead to excessive transaction costs, and relationships where the firm has little or most of the pertinent information should be less attractive than opportunities where the information is more equally shared.

name: Favorability of the potential partner's cooperative history
authors_terms: ["favorability of potential partner's cooperative history", "cooperative history of the potential partner"]
