definition: The cooperative history of the potential partner may give some measure of the opportunistic potential of that partner and decrease the need for extensive monitoring and contracting efforts.

name: Capacity for learning from the relationship
authors_terms: ["capacity for learning from the relationship", "potential to learn from the relationship", "ability of the firm to absorb"]
definition: A primary factor in a firm's ability to develop technology-based competencies from a cooperative venture is the potential to learn from that relationship, contingent upon both the transparency or openness of the partner's skills and the ability of the firm to absorb them.

name: Learning by doing required by the technology
authors_terms: ["learning by doing", "importance of learning by doing of the technology"]
definition: The acquisition of skills associated with tacit technologies requires hands-on experience or 'learning by doing' and will be more difficult to learn than technological skills that can be transferred via documented routines.

name: Potential for broad corporate application of the technology
authors_terms: ["potential for broad corporate application of the technology", "potential for broad application"]
definition: The value of the technical competencies gained will hinge upon the perceived likelihood of applying such skills on a corporate basis rather than to a narrow product line or market.

name: Potential for gaining patent protection
authors_terms: ["potential for gaining patent protection", "ability to patent protect the technology"]
definition: From a legal basis, patent restrictions may limit the overt copying of technology and allow the developing firms the opportunity to reap the benefits of the technological advantage; government patent policies create barriers to imitation and provide a source of competitive advantage.

name: Availability of technological substitutes
authors_terms: ["availability of technological substitutes", "probability of substitution of a technology"]
definition: The probability of substitution of a technology is often hard to predict; technological change may be evolutionary or revolutionary, and revolutionary changes may provide technologies that meet the same customer needs but are based on a completely different technological base.

name: Potential for decreasing development risk
definition: According to risk theory, actions that increase the probability of success will have value; companies may through technological collaboration gain valuable experience and skills which lower development risk and thus improve the probability of success.

name: Expected cost for developing the technology
authors_terms: ["total expected cost for development", "expected cost for developing the technology"]
definition: Given a limited amount of money to invest in R&D, the higher the expected cost to develop a technology, the more attractive collaborative technological relationships would be to top executives, and a collaborative relationship can be thought of as a series of options where the firm can stop buying subsequent options contingent on the outcomes of the collaboration.

name: Contingency of cost commitments on outcomes
authors_terms: ["contingency of cost commitments on outcomes", "degree to which cost commitments for a technology can be made contingent on outcomes"]
definition: For a given expected cost for development, a technological collaborative relationship that allows those costs to be committed incrementally contingent on positive income outcomes will be more attractive than those in which costs must be committed up front.

name: Increased exposure to related market opportunities
authors_terms: ["increased exposure to related markets", "potential for related market opportunities"]
definition: Companies may through technological collaboration develop strong working relationships and gain valuable experience and skills which increase their exposure to related market opportunities; the knowledge obtained through the partnership increases the number of future options available to the firm.

name: Executive level in the hierarchy
authors_terms: ["level of the executive", "number of levels between them and their firm's CEO"]
definition: Executives were asked to report the number of levels between them and their firm's CEO. The further the executive was from the CEO, the higher the number.

name: Dominant functional experience
definition: Executives were asked to denote their primary work experience by marking one of five categories: engineering and R&D, general management, finance and accounting, marketing, or other.

name: Industry tenure
authors_terms: ["industry tenure", "length of time the top executive has been in the industry"]
definition: The number of years the executive had worked in the firm's primary industry; executive experience in an industry can influence the type of information that is focused upon when evaluating technological collaborative opportunities.

name: Executive cognitive limitations
definition: Although individuals may intend to evaluate information rationally, they are not able to incorporate all the information available in their decision model due to cognitive limitations; executives can be predicted to apply simplified decision models.

name: Information dimensions used in evaluation
authors_terms: ["number of available informational dimensions", "type of information used", "number of significant factors"]
definition: An assessment of what information top executives actually utilize in their evaluations can give a more accurate description of managerial decision making than academic theoretical prescriptions; top executives will use a limited number of available informational dimensions.

name: Strategic type
authors_terms: ["Miles and Snow's (1978) strategic type", "strategic type", "organization's strategy"]
definition: Miles and Snow's (1978) typology of organizations along a strategic continuum: Defenders produce a limited set of products directed at narrow market segments; Prospectors constantly exploit new product and market opportunities; Analyzers combine elements of both Defenders and Prospectors; Reactors are a 'residual' set of organizations that pursue an inconsistent mix of entrepreneurial, engineering, and administrative choices.

name: Championing alternatives
definition: The persistent and persuasive communication of strategic options to upper management.

name: Synthesizing information
definition: The interpretation and evaluation of information, which affects top management perceptions; the function is integrative in that it combines ambiguous and diverse data and interprets it within a given strategic context.

name: Facilitating adaptability
definition: Fostering flexible organizational arrangements.

name: Implementing deliberate strategy
definition: Managerial interventions that align organizational action with strategic intentions.

name: Middle management strategic involvement
authors_terms: ["middle management strategic involvement", "involvement in strategy", "strategic involvement"]
definition: The level and type of middle managers' strategic activity; the relative mix or emphasis placed on each of the four roles constitutes the nature of middle management involvement in the strategy process.

name: Peer departures
authors_terms: ["number of departing peers", "NDP", "peer exits", "number of peer departures"]
definition: The main explanatory covariate counts the number of firms exiting a particular market segment in any given year. Departures of peers are the shared driver of both imitation and resource release in the model.

name: Market segment exit
authors_terms: ["market segment transition", "position move", "abandon its segment", "change in market segment position"]
definition: The propensity of a firm positioned in a market segment to abandon that segment for a different market segment. Change in market segment position marks observations in which a firm's mid-niche falls in different market segments between two consecutive years and in which that firm's niche midpoint changes between two consecutive years.

name: Niche overlap density
authors_terms: ["firm niche overlap density", "FNO", "crowding", "extent of competitive intensity experienced by the firm"]
definition: The count of firms whose niches overlap at least partly with the niche of a focal firm; it measures the extent of competitive intensity experienced by the firm.

name: Market center position
authors_terms: ["position in the market center segment", "market center segment (MCS)", "position in the market center"]
definition: The market center segment is the area of the market where resources are most concentrated and competition is most intense; it lies between the mean of the lower niche bounds of the four largest firms and the mean of the upper niche bounds of these firms in a given year.

name: Peripheral segment position
authors_terms: ["position in either periphery", "position in the low and high periphery", "low periphery (economy cars)", "high periphery (luxury and sports cars)"]
definition: The two peripheral market segments are the area surrounding the center: the low periphery comprises the area between the low end of the market and the low end of the market center, and the high periphery falls within the high end of the market center and the high end of the market.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The ratio of the annual production of the four largest firms to total industry output.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: The rate at which U.S. automobile manufacturers fail; the authors test whether position in the market segments matters not only for position moves but also for survival chances.

name: Overlapping institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["overlapping ownership", "overlapping institutional ownership", "number of overlapping owners", "percentage owned by overlapping owners", "ownership overlap"]
definition: Owners who simultaneously hold stakes in both the acquirer and the target firms; the acquiring and target firms thus share some of the same owners.

name: Acquirer shareholder gains
authors_terms: ["acquirer gains", "shareholder gains", "M&A shareholder gains", "M&A returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Cumulative abnormal returns, or the returns over the event window minus the normal returns, which represent the expected returns if the event had not taken place, weighted by the market value of the acquiring firm.

name: Corporate governance
authors_terms: ["corporate governance", "corporate governance mechanisms", "monitoring and incentive alignment", "bundling effect of strong corporate governance"]
definition: Corporate governance mechanisms may moderate the impact of heterogeneous ownership by constraining its adverse effects on M&A outcomes; the authors consider three aspects of monitoring (board independence, board size, and board leadership structure) and two aspects of incentive alignment (managerial ownership and options compensation).

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below the aspiration level", "low performance", "performance shortfall"]
definition: Decision makers evaluate the level of performance through comparison with an aspiration level, which is influenced by the past performance of the firm and the performance of its peers; firms initiate problemistic search when the performance is below the aspiration level. Performance is operationalized as ROA minus the social aspiration level.

name: Firm size
definition: Organizational size as an indicator of low (perceived) risk of failure, and firm size is measured as the logarithm of the total fleet of the firm, measured as a count of ships.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risky actions that reposition the firm relative to its competitors; the dependent variable used to assess risk taking is the number of used ships acquired during the focal year.

name: Positional rigidity
definition: Defined as the similarity between the new resources acquired and the current stock of resources; positional rigidity is displayed if the firm acquires new resources for the same uses as its existing resources.

name: Order of market entry
authors_terms: ["order of entry", "order of market entry", "entry timing", "first-moving", "pioneering", "early-mover advantages"]
definition: The order in which firms entered each national market, distinguishing the pioneer, the second entrant, the third entrant and late followers. The authors argue that the position a firm achieves in terms of the isolating mechanisms is determined by entry timing.

name: Switching costs
definition: The concept of switching costs refers to all the costs that a consumer has to bear when he or she changes the current provider.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance as captured by the two performance measures used in the empirical tests, market share and profitability (EBITDA). Given the availability of data on both market share and profitability, the authors use both variables in their empirical tests.

name: Pro-market reforms
authors_terms: ["pro-market reforms", "extent of pro-market reforms", "reform index", "extent of reforms"]
definition: Pro-market reforms in emerging economies are a process with an initial set of changes in laws and regulations to strengthen the functioning of markets followed by subsequent changes that reinforce the original changes.

name: Sustainability of superior profits
authors_terms: ["sustainability of superior profits", "sustained superior performance", "persistence of superior profits", "profit persistence"]
definition: We define sustainability of superior profits as the ability of firms to sustain financial performance that is above the industry norm across time periods.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are collections of 'firms in a wide variety of industries, with a significant amount of common ownership and control, usually by a family'.

name: Foreign firm affiliation
definition: Emerging economy subsidiaries of foreign firms (i.e., foreign firm affiliates) had access to tangible and intangible resources of the foreign firm as a whole, which provided advantages that were not easily matched or substituted by domestic firms prior to reform initiation.

name: Investment in R&D
definition: R&D investments facilitate the development of technological innovations and innovation capabilities.

name: Investment in marketing and advertising
authors_terms: ["investment in marketing and advertising", "marketing and advertising investment", "greater investments in marketing and advertising"]
definition: Investment in marketing and advertising helps differentiate products and creates brand identity.

name: Analogical transfer
authors_terms: ["analogical transfer", "transfer performance", "knowledge transfer", "performance on the target transfer task"]
definition: Knowledge transfer is defined in psychology as the ability to extend what has been learned in one context to new contexts and as 'how knowledge acquired in one situation applies (or fails to apply) in other situations'. Analogical transfer in problem solving entails reaching the solution to one problem based on experience with a previous, analogous problem.

name: Variation in the source situation
authors_terms: ["variation in an initial management situation", "source task variation", "task variation", "exposure to variation on the source task"]
definition: Task variation was manipulated through changes to the employees managed by experimental group participants in decision trials 6-13 of the production team source task; two of the employees were changed at decision trial 6 and changed back to the original employees at decision trial 14, exposing decision makers to a slightly altered variation of the production team task.

name: Performance on the source problem
authors_terms: ["performance on an initial management source problem", "higher performance outcomes on an initial managerial source problem", "performance on the production team source task"]
definition: Performance on the simulation task was calculated from the score participants received after each decision trial for the performance of their team; on the source task the individual decision trial data were averaged to compute mean performance across three trial blocks.

name: Knowledge of the source problem
authors_terms: ["knowledge of the underlying structural relations of the source task", "knowledge levels of an initial management source problem", "knowledge of the source situation"]
definition: Knowledge of the underlying structural relations of the source task was assessed using 12 questionnaire items derived directly from the underlying equations of the simulation, to which participants responded true or false; an overall knowledge score was computed by taking the sum of correct answers to the 12 items.

name: Systematic search
authors_terms: ["systematic search strategy", "systematic hypothesis testing strategy", "VOTAT (vary one thing at a time)"]
definition: Systematic search involves unconfounded changes made to decision variables within each block of trials; an unconfounded change is one in which only one variable at a time is changed within a decision trial, allowing the participant to test the effect of a change in a single variable by holding the other variables constant.

name: TMT functional diversity
authors_terms: ["TMT functional diversity", "functional diversity of a top management team", "team functional diversity", "TMT functional background diversity"]
definition: The degree to which TMT members differ with respect to their functional backgrounds.

name: Cognitive conflict
definition: Cognitive conflict exists when group members disagree about the content of the tasks, including differences in viewpoints and ideas.

name: Affective conflict
definition: Affective conflict exists when there are interpersonal incompatibilities among group members, often reflected by tension and animosity.

name: Organizational innovation
definition: Organizational innovation involves generating and implementing new ideas or behaviors, including new products, services, process technologies, organizational structures, or administrative systems.

name: Competitive uncertainty
definition: Competitive environment determines the extent to which a firm is affected by its competitors, customers, and suppliers.

name: Institutional support
definition: The extent to which administrative institutions provide support for firms in order to reduce the adverse effects of an inadequate institutional infrastructure.

name: Host country de facto property rights protection
authors_terms: ["de facto property rights protection", "host country property rights institutions", "property rights protection"]
definition: Clearly specified and well-functioning property rights allow firms to use, transform, and sell their offshored services, and utilize them in economic activity and trade. The paper distinguishes these de facto practices from formally adopted property rights regulations, noting that notwithstanding the formal adoption of property rights regulations, governments frequently fail to implement these policies altogether, delay or partially implement adopted policies, or support de facto departures from formal rules.

name: Related international property rights experience
authors_terms: ["related experience", "similarity weighted experience measure", "firm's related experience"]
definition: For each firm the authors capture the home country and its network of global subsidiaries and construct a similarity weighted experience measure in the home and host countries compared to the target host country. The numerator captures the extent of operations in a country, while the denominator captures the similarity of the country with the target host country; the final measure is the average value of experience across all other countries.

name: Host country location choice
authors_terms: ["likelihood of locating its offshored information services in a host country", "foreign investment by a firm in a greenfield project in the information services sector", "entry decision"]
definition: The main dependent variable is foreign investment by a firm in a greenfield project in the information services sector, a binary measure that takes the value of '1' if a firm made an investment in a new greenfield project in a host country in a given year, and '0' otherwise.

name: Alliance value creation
definition: The objective of a research alliance is to create value (in the form of new knowledge or cross-learning among partners) beyond what scientists and firms would yield separately. The joint output depends on the combination of partner attributes, which may include strengths building upon strengths or the strengths of one partner substituting for the other partner's shortcomings.

name: Firm publishing capability
authors_terms: ["firms' publication capabilities", "corporate publishing", "publishing capabilities", "firms' stock of publications"]
definition: Publishing capability denotes the ways firms deploy their knowledge capital to signal expertise and preferences for the 'open' science regime. Publications indicate a firm's willingness to abide by the norms of reciprocation and full information disclosure and signal a firm's research quality.

name: Scientist publishing capability
authors_terms: ["university scientists' publication capabilities", "scientists' publishing capabilities", "faculty publications"]
definition: Publishing capability denotes the ways university scientists deploy their knowledge capital to signal expertise and preferences for the 'open' science regime, in which the scientific merit of a discovery is decided by the research community through peer review and citations.

name: Firm patenting capability
definition: Patenting capability denotes the ways firms deploy their knowledge capital to signal expertise and preferences for the 'commercial science' regime. Patents signal to other market participants the strength of a firm's proprietary knowledge and technical expertise in a field.

name: Scientist patenting capability
authors_terms: ["university scientists' patenting capabilities", "scientists' patenting expertise", "faculty patents"]
definition: Patenting capability denotes the ways university scientists deploy their knowledge capital to signal expertise and preferences for the 'commercial science' regime. In academia, patents indicate that a scientist's ideas have useful marketable applications and are often perceived as a 'symbol of commercial savvy'.

name: Firm knowledge specialization
authors_terms: ["breadth of a firm's knowledge base", "knowledge diversification", "specialization", "diversity or 'breadth' of knowledge"]
definition: Specialization implies that an innovator's knowledge is concentrated in a narrow territory of the knowledge space, and diversity or 'breadth' of knowledge indicates familiarity with a broad range of scientific or technological components. By patenting or publishing in a narrower or a broader territory of the knowledge space, firms convey the breadth of their knowledge base.

name: Scientist knowledge specialization
authors_terms: ["knowledge-diversification index of the university scientists", "focused expertise", "broader expertise", "knowledge specialization"]
definition: Specialization implies that an innovator's knowledge is concentrated in a narrow territory of the knowledge space, while diversity or 'breadth' indicates familiarity with a broad range of scientific or technological components. Scientists convey the breadth of their knowledge base by publishing in a narrower or a broader territory of the knowledge space.

name: Alliance management capability
definition: Helfat et al. (2007: 66) define alliance management capability as a 'type of dynamic capability with the capacity to purposefully create, extend, or modify the firm's resource base, augmented to include the resources of its alliance partners.'

name: New product development capability
definition: New product development capability is commonly defined as organizational routines that purposefully reconfigure the organizational product portfolio. A new product development capability is reflected in organizational routines that structure innovation processes aimed at reconfiguring the firm's product portfolio.

name: Competitive advantage
definition: A firm is said to have a competitive advantage when it enjoys greater success than current or potential competitors in its industry, suggesting that superior firm performance serves as a key indicator of competitive advantage.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism refers to the volatility and unpredictability of the firm's external environment (Miller and Friesen, 1983).

name: Interfirm knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["interfirm knowledge transfer", "interfirm transfer of technological capabilities", "interfirm knowledge transfers", "technological overlap", "cross-citation rate", "convergent development"]
definition: The extent to which a firm is acquiring technology-based capabilities from its alliance partner, reflected in higher rates of citation of the partner's patents in the firm's new patents and in higher technological 'overlap' between the partners.

name: Prealliance technological overlap
definition: The extent of overlap between partners' technological portfolios before the alliance; substantial prealliance overlap between partners' technological portfolios should enhance their capacity to absorb new competencies from one another.

name: Equity joint venture structure
authors_terms: ["equity joint ventures", "equity arrangements", "shared equity by partner firms", "EQUITY"]
definition: Alliances in which ownership in a separately incorporated entity is shared by the partner firms, held to be a more effective vehicle for the transfer of tacit knowledge between the partners.

name: Unilateral contract-based alliance
definition: Contract-based alliances such as licensing agreements in which technology is exchanged for cash payments and is more tightly 'packaged', creating fewer opportunities for interfirm knowledge transfer than bilateral contractual arrangements.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D investment relative to the firm's size, used as a proxy for absorptive capacity; R&D investment is a necessary (although not necessarily sufficient) condition for the creation of absorptive capacity.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm, based on sales; larger firms have more diverse technological portfolios and therefore are more likely to possess technology that is relevant to the alliance.

name: Japanese nationality of partner firm
definition: Whether the alliance partner is a Japanese company, reflecting the asserted greater 'intent to learn' of Japanese firms in alliances with U.S. firms.

name: Magnitude of change in technological overlap
authors_terms: ["absolute value of changes in technological overlap", "ABSDCRSS"]
definition: The absolute value of the pre- to post-collaboration change in partners' technological overlap, capturing the strength of change in either a convergent or a divergent direction.

name: Alliance participation
definition: Whether a pair of firms is an alliance partner pair as opposed to a pair of nonallying firms matched over the same time period.

name: Pace of technological change
authors_terms: ["pace of technological change", "rapid pace of technological change", "frequent introduction of new production processes and products"]
definition: The rate at which an industry introduces new products and processes, reflected by the average time between new product or process introductions. The pace and nature of technological change in different industries help explain why distinctive patterns of knowledge sharing coexist.

name: Private knowledge sharing
authors_terms: ["private knowledge sharing", "private channels of communication", "private, cross-company communication", "private-unrestricted know-how trading", "knowledge sharing"]
definition: Knowledge sharing is defined as the transfer of useful know-how or information across company lines. Access to knowledge can occur either through public channels or through private channels: e-mail, the telephone, face-to-face meetings, visits to other companies' fabrication plants (fabs), consortia or benchmarking studies.

name: Home country
authors_terms: ["home country", "U.S. semiconductor industry", "Japanese counterparts", "respondents from U.S. companies"]
definition: The country in which the employee works, the United States or Japan, taken to reflect institutional differences between the two countries in the intellectual property right regime and the employment system.

name: Training in information control
authors_terms: ["training in information control", "training on how to control sensitive information"]
definition: Whether the respondent's company provided training on how to control sensitive information, which is predicted to make the respondent more hesitant to provide requested information.

name: Rewards for conference presentations
authors_terms: ["rewards for presenting papers at professional conferences"]
definition: Whether the respondent's company included paper presentations at professional conferences in pay or promotion decisions, which the authors treat as active encouragement of external knowledge diffusion.

name: Capability heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["capability heterogeneity", "heterogeneity in the participating firms' capabilities"]
definition: Capability heterogeneity is defined here as the breadth or diversity of technological capabilities that firms possess.

name: Skill-sharing motive
authors_terms: ["skill-sharing motive", "skill-sharing", "gain access to the complementary knowledge of other participants", "complementary knowledge sharing", "learning-based R&D cooperation"]
definition: These learning-based arguments imply that a key objective of cooperative R&D is complementary knowledge or skill-sharing among participants, where complementary knowledge is defined as knowledge that, in combination, yields better R&D results. This learning effect is likely to be large for firms whose motivation is skill-sharing.

name: Cost-sharing motive
authors_terms: ["cost-sharing motive", "cost-sharing", "scale-based R&D cooperation", "share fixed costs among participants and realize economies of scale in R&D", "avoid wasteful duplication of research by dividing the tasks among participants"]
definition: Past economic theoretical research focuses on three primary motivations for cooperation: fixed cost-sharing among R&D participants, the realization of economies of scale in R&D, and the avoidance of 'wasteful' duplication, which are scale-based motives implying that the principal purpose of cooperative R&D is to set cost-sharing rules.

name: Relative importance of the skill-sharing motive
authors_terms: ["RELATIVE", "relative importance of the skill-sharing motive vis-a-vis the cost-sharing motive"]
definition: RELATIVE represents the relative importance of the skill-sharing motive vis-a-vis the cost-sharing motive and is defined as the difference of these two constructs.

name: Project size
definition: PJTSIZE is the total project budget, in real terms as of the project's first year.

name: Project-related R&D spending
definition: Project-related R&D spending is a firm's R&D spending in project-related areas including its outlays in the R&D consortium and additional R&D conducted at the firm's labs.

name: Own operating experience
authors_terms: ["own operating experience", "own experience", "Organizational Experience", "Own Operating Experience"]
definition: The level of operations of a hotel chain, represented by the number of units it has operated in the past; it is a discounted sum of the units (hotels or motels) operated in the past, discounted to account for antiquation or decay of knowledge.

name: Geographic generalism
definition: The extent to which a chain operates across many geographic markets, operationalized as the number of the nine census regions that the chain operates in. Geographic generalists have heterogeneous inputs to the learning process and their units have heterogeneous learning needs.

name: Industry operating experience since entry
authors_terms: ["Industry Operating Experience Since Entry", "industry's operating experience", "industry operating experience"]
definition: The operating experience of other organizations in the industry accumulated during the focal organization's life, a discounted accumulation of all the units other chains have operated during the focal chain's life.

name: Industry competitive experience since entry
authors_terms: ["Industry Competitive Experience Since Entry", "industry's competitive experience", "industry competitive experience"]
definition: The industry's competitive experience accumulated during the focal organization's life, a discounted sum of the number of hotel chain failures in the history of the industry since the organization's entry.

name: Industry operating experience at entry
authors_terms: ["Industry Operating Experience at Entry", "industry experience at the time of the organization's entry"]
definition: The level of the industry's accumulated operating experience at the time the focal organization entered the industry, computed as the discounted accumulation of industry mass from the industry's first year to the year before the organization's entry.

name: Industry competitive experience at entry
definition: The level of the industry's accumulated competitive experience (past failures in the industry) at the time the focal organization entered, defined like the industry experience at entry variable but substituting the number of failures in a year for the industry mass.

name: Organizational failure rate
authors_terms: ["rate of failure", "risk of failure", "chain failure", "hazard rate of failure"]
definition: Chain failure occurs when the chain ceases to operate at least three units; it is modeled as the instantaneous rate of failing, the limiting probability of a failure between t and t + Dt given that the chain was operating at t.

name: Political heterogeneity of founding teams
authors_terms: ["political heterogeneity", "politically heterogeneous founding teams", "political composition", "political homophily"]
definition: Founding teams were classified as politically homogeneous if all founders were registered with the same party and heterogeneous if registered with different parties, considering only Democrats and Republicans; the sample was restricted to firms in which the political views of all founders could be identified as either Democrats or Republicans.

name: Founding team formation
authors_terms: ["team formation", "founding team composition", "team formation likelihood", "joint new venture formation"]
definition: The dependent variable 'observed' is set to 1 for teams in the authors' dataset and 0 for randomly constructed counterfactual teams, allowing an assessment of the extent to which various types of heterogeneity independently predict the formation of a real team over a synthetic one.

name: Startup performance
definition: Performance is measured in the main model by the probability of closure, and in alternative models it is assessed by the (log) total amount of funding, the (log) number of employees, the probability of the startup being acquired, and CrunchBase rank.

name: Political affiliation
definition: To assess the founders' political attitudes, the authors used political registration data from L2, a data platform providing information on the voter registration of over 210 million US citizens; founders were identified as registered Democrats or Republicans.

name: Executive communication of growth strategies
authors_terms: ["communication of growth strategies", "communicated growth strategies", "Growth Strategies", "managerial communication about growth strategies"]
definition: As top executives discuss strategies for firm growth - defined here as expanding firm revenue and profitability - the information they provide may be consistent or inconsistent with their firm's previous strategic trajectory.

name: Analyst curiosity
definition: Curiosity is a fundamental response to cognitive arousal (Silvia, 2012; Wojtowicz & Loewenstein, 2020) that has been studied rigorously for decades, reflecting the 'desire to know, to see, or to experience that motivates exploratory behavior, information seeking, and learning' (Lievens et al., 2022).

name: Analyst analytical focus
definition: Analytical thinking represents the degree to which individuals become more formal and logical in their thinking about a situation (Boyd & Pennebaker, 2015). Defined as 'a deliberate mode of thought wherein complex concepts are deconstructed into more manageable components and their interrelations' (Jordan et al., 2019).

name: Analyst evaluation
authors_terms: ["analyst evaluations", "analyst stock ratings", "forecasted stock prices", "Price Forecast", "Analyst Rating"]
definition: Differences in what executives communicate about their strategies significantly influence how analysts cognitively process the information these managers provide, how they interact with managers, and ultimately their guidance to the market about firms' future prospects. To test Hypotheses 2a, 2b, 2c and 3a, 3b, we use two dependent variables capturing analyst evaluations: analyst stock ratings and forecasted stock prices.

name: Price-earnings ratio
definition: Analyst expectations regarding a firm's growth positioning become reflected in the evaluations made by analysts (Bradshaw, 2004) that they publish to the market, for example as evidenced in their guidance to the market regarding the firm's predicted price-to-earnings (PE) ratio in 12-months.

name: Dividend yield
definition: We examine a different dimension of a firm's strategic positioning - the degree to which analysts have incorporated an expectation for the firm to be a reliable producer of cash returns to investors in the form of dividends into their cognitive schemas.

name: CEO activism
authors_terms: ["CEO activism", "CEO sociopolitical activism", "CEO message supporting gun rights", "CEO support for gun rights"]
definition: CEO activism—business leaders speaking out on social and political issues unrelated to their core business. In the experiment, it is a social media message from the CEO supporting gun rights.

name: Consumer product choice
authors_terms: ["chose Bean Brigade coffee over the bonus payment", "purchase", "purchasing behavior", "buycott", "boycott"]
definition: Our main dependent variable is an indicator for whether a subject chose Bean Brigade coffee over the bonus payment in the second survey. Because the choice is real and incentive compatible, it measures an actual purchase decision rather than a stated intention.

name: Consumer agreement with CEO activism
authors_terms: ["views on gun laws", "views on federal gun laws", "gun policy views", "consumers who agree with a CEO's activism", "consumers who disagree with a CEO's activism"]
definition: To condition our analyses on participants' gun policy views, we asked if they believed gun policy in the United States should be stricter, should be less strict, or is about right. Those who favor stricter gun laws disagree with a CEO supporting gun rights, while those who favor less-strict gun laws agree with him.

name: Purchase observability
authors_terms: ["purchase observability", "public vs. private purchase", "observable to another person (public)", "visibility of a purchase"]
definition: Purchase observability—the extent to which others see a purchase. In the experiment, subjects in the public condition were told that their choice and information about Bean Brigade would be shared with their study partner.

name: Importance of the CEO's values
authors_terms: ["the beliefs and values of Bean Brigade's CEO", "CEO Values"]
definition: In a follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of several factors in their choice between the coffee and bonus, including the beliefs and values of Bean Brigade's CEO.

name: Expressing one's own values
authors_terms: ["expressing their own beliefs and values", "Expressing My Values"]
definition: In a follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of several factors in their choice between the coffee and bonus, including expressing their own beliefs and values.

name: Partner's reaction to the choice
authors_terms: ["how their partner would react to their choice", "Peer Reaction"]
definition: In a follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of several factors in their choice between the coffee and bonus, including how their partner would react to their choice.

name: Perceived product quality
authors_terms: ["the likely quality of Bean Brigade's coffee", "coffee's perceived quality"]
definition: In a follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of several factors in their choice between the coffee and bonus, including the likely quality of Bean Brigade's coffee.

name: Constituency-building attitudes
authors_terms: ["constituency-building indices", "attitudes toward corporate political activity", "attitudes toward the corporation"]
definition: Shareholder attitudes captured by the three indices—credibility, legitimacy, and shareholder involvement—that the authors describe as vital components of an effective constituency-building effort.

name: Corporate management credibility
definition: Shareholder attitudes concerning the credibility of corporate management.

name: Legitimacy of corporate political activism
definition: Shareholder attitudes concerning corporate political activism in general.

name: Shareholder involvement in corporate political activities
definition: Shareholder attitudes concerning their own involvement and participation in the political activities of the corporation.

name: Exposure to corporate public policy communications
authors_terms: ["exposure to public policy information", "information exposure", "exposed to corporate communications on public policy issues"]
definition: Shareholders who had been exposed to public policy information from any corporate source, as opposed to shareholders who had not been exposed to such information.

name: Formal and extensive constituency program
authors_terms: ["formal and extensive constituency program", "well-developed program", "Corporation I membership"]
definition: Corporation I had a well-developed, 5-year-old program that communicated extensively and regularly with shareholders concerning public policy issues.

name: Shareholder subgroup characteristics
authors_terms: ["number of shares held", "tenure as a shareholder", "employment status with the corporation"]
definition: Three subgroup characteristics relevant to the hypothesis: number of shares held, tenure as a shareholder, and employment status with the corporation.

name: Innovative efficiency
definition: The degree to which innovative outputs exceed what would typically be expected from a given level of R&D inputs; the relationship between innovation inputs and outputs, rather than innovative outputs alone.

name: Technological opportunity
definition: The extent of basic scientific knowledge in the field, with a market reference-that is, a function of the degree to which the market seeks or accepts product changes; R&D is relatively inexpensive where land is fertile.

name: Recent major technological change
definition: The presence of major technological changes in the products offered by the business or its major competitors during recent years; early in a technological era progress is very slow and expensive.

name: Market share
definition: The scale of the business, used as an indicator of size in the absence of data on absolute size.

name: Product line breadth
definition: The relative breadth of the product line of the business, the business-level analogue of diversification.

name: Relative innovative experience
definition: The recent innovation rate of a business relative to those of its competitors, an indicator of the firm's innovative adeptness and an innovation experience curve.

name: R&D volatility
definition: The stability and persistence of R&D spending; volatility is argued to harm innovative efficiency through lab morale, assimilation, team integrity, and uneven leadership.

name: Forward integration
definition: In-house selling and servicing for a business unit, which aids in the gathering of market intelligence and the astute introduction of new products.

name: Auxiliary services to customers
definition: The degree of ongoing product-related service provided by a business to its customers, such as installation, repair, and customer education, which keeps the business aware of customer problems.

name: Interdivisional sales
authors_terms: ["interdivisional sales", "sales to sister units", "percentage of sales derived from within the corporation"]
definition: The percentage of sales a business derives from within the corporation, which should make market intelligence and customer ties fluid and abundant in a way that aids the research effort of the seller unit.

name: Fixed asset intensity
definition: The capital intensity of the production process, expected to create rigidities that hamper innovation, although robots and programmable machinery could be versatile.

name: Plant and equipment newness
authors_terms: ["plant and equipment newness", "newness of plant and equipment"]
definition: The newness of a business's plant and equipment, where newer assets may be designed to accommodate emerging shifts or variations in raw materials and market preferences.

name: Worker unionization
authors_terms: ["unionization", "unionization rate", "percentage of workers who are unionized"]
definition: The percentage of a business's workers who are unionized; union work rules and seniority systems are generally thought to stymie flexibility and adaptation.

name: Board insider representation
authors_terms: ["INSIDER1", "INSIDER2", "INSIDER3", "percentage of directors who are insiders", "insider status", "inside directors", "affiliated directors"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's board of directors who are current employees (INSIDER1), current or former employees (INSIDER2), or current employees, ex-employees, employees of a customer or supplier, employees of the firm's investment bank or corporate counsel, and employees of its parent company or a subsidiary (INSIDER3).

name: Board stock ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock owned by a board", "percentage of total stock outstanding that their boards of directors own", "director stock ownership"]
definition: The percentage of total stock outstanding that members of a firm's board of directors own, measured as shares owned by directors divided by total shares outstanding.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "book value of total assets", "rank within the Fortune 500", "FORTUNE"]
definition: The size of the firm, measured by the book value of total assets and by its rank within the Fortune 500 based upon sales volume.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "ROA", "ROE", "operating income divided by sales", "excess value ratio", "EXCESS"]
definition: How well a firm performs financially; the excess value ratio measures the difference between the total market value of a firm (market value of equity and book value of debt) and the book value of its assets normalized by sales, that is, the value premiums or discounts the market accords to each firm.

name: Financial leverage
authors_terms: ["financial leverage", "debt", "interest-bearing debt divided by total assets"]
definition: Financial leverage was measured by interest-bearing debt divided by total assets.

name: Golden parachute adoption
definition: Golden parachutes are a management perquisite that allow covered managers to voluntarily resign and collect substantial remuneration after a triggering event, usually a hostile takeover; for this study a golden parachute is narrowly defined as a guarantee of severance pay after a triggering event related to a change in control, even in cases of voluntary termination.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The organizational outcome examined as the antecedent of the choice of successor type; the authors note that the number of corporate performance measures that could serve as dependent variables is almost infinite and select two representative measures, an investor return and an accounting return.

name: Accounting return
authors_terms: ["accounting return", "average return on equity", "return on equity", "ROE"]
definition: One of the two broad categories into which measures of financial performance fall; in this research it is represented by average return on equity for the three years prior to succession.

name: Investor return
authors_terms: ["investor return", "common stock performance", "end-of-the-month closing stock prices"]
definition: One of the two broad categories into which measures of financial performance fall; in this research it is represented by a metric derived from end-of-the-month closing stock prices for the three years prior to succession.

name: CEO successor origin
authors_terms: ["inside/outside succession", "successor type", "outside succession", "inside succession", "choice of successor types"]
definition: Inside successors are promoted from within the executive spans of their predecessors; outside successions occur when newly appointed CEOs were not in their predecessors' spans.

name: Contingency variable
definition: A contingency variable is significant to the degree that businesses that differ on that variable also exhibit major differences in how strategic attributes or actions are associated with performance. Contingency variables are usually thought to be environmental; businesses have little or no control over them and they therefore form the contexts in which businesses must develop strategies.

name: Strategic attributes
definition: A reasonably complete set of strategic attributes, drawn from those prominent in past PIMS studies, was used as the independent variables whose associations with performance are examined within each contingency split.

name: Business performance
definition: Business performance was measured as Return on Investment (ROI); the use of four-year averages helped to minimize its accounting-related limitations.

name: User sector
definition: The dichotomy between consumer- and industrial-product settings; the fundamental differences between the two sectors seem to concern buyer dispersion, buyer needs and knowledgeability, and demand uncertainty.

name: Stage of product life cycle
authors_terms: ["stage of product life cycle", "stage of life cycle"]
definition: Stage of product life cycle: many facets of the business seem to depend on it, including production technology, buyer criteria, capital intensity, the nature of competition, and others.

name: Technological change
definition: Whether an industry has undergone a recent major technological change, because major technological changes lead to redistribution of market shares among competitors and raise different issues of resource allocation and competitive weapons.

name: Purchase frequency
authors_terms: ["purchase frequency", "purchase infrequency", "frequency with which end users purchase products"]
definition: The frequency with which end users purchase a business' products; purchase frequency determines buyer criteria and knowledgeability and affects the lumpiness of demand, and so may affect the nature of competition.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Rate of concentration in an industry, typically presumed to determine the degree of opportunity for collusion; it may reflect the nature of competition, but not much about how value is added or buyers' needs.

name: Industry imports
definition: Level of imports in an industry, a useful although not ideal indicator of world wide competition; import levels indicate something about the nature of competition but not necessarily about buyer needs or ways in which value is added.

name: Market share instability
authors_terms: ["share instability", "market share instability", "instability of market shares"]
definition: The degree to which market shares in an industry are unstable, which indicates rivalry to some extent; exogenous shocks like imports or product innovations and conditions that break oligopolistic bargains can destabilize shares.

name: Demand instability
definition: Instability of primary demand, which should have major effects on the nature of competition because competitors will fight hard to cover fixed costs during slow times, and should affect outcomes of various fixed asset strategies.

name: Dollar importance to customers
authors_terms: ["dollar importance", "dollar importance to customers", "dollar importance of products"]
definition: The dollar importance of products to customers, which affects their tendencies to bargain for favorable prices: if a product represents a large portion of a customer's dollar purchases, the customer will make a point of becoming very knowledgeable about the product and about alternative suppliers.

name: Product differentiability
definition: The degree to which a product can be differentiated: an undifferentiated product requires firms to attend primarily to cost and capacity considerations, whereas a product that can be highly differentiated opens up many more avenues of competition.

name: Organizational life-cycle stage
authors_terms: ["life-cycle stages", "organizational life cycle", "stages of the organizational life cycle", "stage-of-life-cycle groups"]
definition: Models of life-cycle stages presuppose that there are regularities in organizational development and that these regularities occur in such a way that the organizations' developmental processes lend themselves to segmentation into stages or periods of time. The three stages used here are organizational inception and mobilization, growth, and maturity.

name: Technical efficiency priority
definition: The technical efficiency priority is defined as concern for maximization of organizational efficiency. Individuals hold technical efficiency as a priority when they (1) were concerned with efficiency, (2) sought short term, quantifiable criteria for evaluating decisions, (3) sought high levels of accomplishment, and (4) held maximization of organizational efficiency as a personal value.

name: Organizational coordination priority
definition: The organizational coordination priority can be defined as concern for the long-term integration of total organizations. Individuals held organizational coordination as a priority when they were concerned with cooperation and coordination, or integration, of their total organizations, and were concerned with building organizational synergy.

name: Political support priority
definition: The political support priority is defined as concern on the part of top-level managers for maintaining individual power and support and the commitment of subordinates. Individuals have political support as a priority when they are concerned with maintaining the commitment and support of subordinates, with their suggestions and attitudes, and with how subordinates accept their decisions.

name: Business-level strategy
definition: Strategy variables were chosen by measuring parts of strategy. Seventeen variables were classified into four broad theoretical dimensions of strategy: cost efficiency, asset parsimony, differentiation, and scale scope.

name: Environment
definition: The overall measure of environment used in this study was a discrete variable with eight categories representing business units' environments. Every business unit was classified into one of eight categories according to its pattern on 17 environmental components representing characteristics of market structures.

name: Business performance
definition: The criterion variable in the study is return on investment (ROI).

name: Resource sharing among SBUs
authors_terms: ["resource sharing", "resource sharing with other SBUs", "operating synergy", "sharing of functional resources"]
definition: Operating synergy refers specifically to sharing of functional resources by two or more SBUs within a single firm. It is measured as the extent to which focal SBUs share functional facilities like sales forces or manufacturing plants with all other SBUs in their corporations, weighted by the importance of each function for the SBU's strategy.

name: SBU effectiveness in implementing strategy
definition: The effectiveness with which a business unit implements its chosen strategy, measured as a comparison between actual performance and a priori expectations rather than on an absolute scale, and weighted across performance dimensions by their relative importance for the SBU.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: The generic basis for developing a strategic advantage over competition: a strategy of differentiation implies creating something that is perceived industrywide as being unique, whereas a strategy of overall cost leadership requires aggressive construction of efficient-scale facilities and cost minimization.

name: Organizational familiarity
authors_terms: ["organizational familiarity", "general manager's years with firm", "general manager's years on current job"]
definition: The longer an individual has worked for an organization, the more familiar that person is likely to be not only with its products, markets, and technologies, but also with its people, standard operating procedures, and culture.

name: Subjectivity in bonus assessment
authors_terms: ["subjectivity in bonus assessment", "reliance on subjective as opposed to formula-based approaches", "extent of reliance on subjectivity"]
definition: The extent to which a general manager's bonus is determined on the basis of a purely subjective assessment by the manager's superior rather than through a strict formula such as a percentage of the SBU's operating profit, or by some combination of the two.

name: Determination of bonus pool
authors_terms: ["determination of bonus pool", "bonus pools", "linking the bonus to the performance of an entire cluster of SBUs"]
definition: Bonus pools can be based on divisional (SBU) performance, total corporate performance, or some mix of the two, and each arrangement sends different signals in terms of interdivisional cooperation.

name: General manager's job satisfaction
definition: The general manager's satisfaction with the overall job context, assessed as satisfaction with the current job, career progress made in this organization up to now, and chances for career advancement in this organization in the future.

name: Structural integration
authors_terms: ["structural integration", "integration", "integrative liaison devices", "use of liaison devices"]
definition: Structural integration refers to liaison devices such as coordinative committees and task forces.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization is the use of formal procedures and job descriptions, cost and quality controls, specialists, and professional technocrats.

name: Centralization of authority
authors_terms: ["centralization of power for making decisions", "centralization", "decentralization of authority"]
definition: Centralization places most of the onus of decision making on top executives, taxing their cognitive abilities and imposing significant time constraints on them; decentralization divides decision making tasks into more manageable bits.

name: Structural complexity
definition: Complexity is a structure's breadth, height, and clerical intensity, related to number of operating sites, vertical span of control, ratio of clerical to total personnel, and level of specialization.

name: Rationality in strategy making
definition: Systematic, analytical decision making that includes analysis of decisions, future orientation and planning, explicitness of strategy, and systematic scanning of the environment.

name: Interaction in strategy making
definition: Decision making viewed as an outcome of political and social processes in which bargaining, politicking, and consensus-building come to bear on decisions.

name: Assertiveness in strategy making
definition: Assertiveness concerns levels of risk taking and the reactiveness or proactiveness of decisions.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "relative profitability", "growth in net income", "return on investment"]
definition: Performance is multifaceted and was indexed by long-term profitability relative to the industry average, average annual growth in net income, and average return on investment over the previous five years.

name: Complex innovation
authors_terms: ["complex product innovation", "innovation", "innovativeness", "research and development expenses as a percentage of sales"]
definition: Firms that must often perform complex innovations face complex administrative tasks in which structure alone is insufficient and interactive and rational decision making must complement it.

name: Firm size
definition: Size is measured by number of employees; larger firms have many managers, departments, and contingencies.

name: Revenue acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition of advertising revenues", "acquisition of revenues", "station revenue acquisition", "performance", "relative station performance"]
definition: The relative percentage change in yearly acquisition of advertising revenues in a station's market was the measure of its performance. The measure indicates how well a station performed in acquiring resources relative to the other stations within its market.

name: Number of interorganizational linkages
authors_terms: ["number of linkages", "number of resource linkages", "number of interorganizational linkages"]
definition: Interorganizational linkages are voluntary ties with other organizations. To measure numbers of linkages, we assigned a value of 1 to each reported resource exchange and a value of 0 where no resource exchange was reported, and summed across all exchanges.

name: Interorganizational linkage complexity
definition: Complexity of linkages is not a product of their location in a particular cell, but of their distribution among cells: the wider the distribution, the more complex the interorganizational linkages of a commercial television station.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Aldrich and Mindlin (1978) defined uncertainty as existing when relationships between organizations are unpredictable. Market uncertainty (M1) was measured by the absolute percentage change in advertising expenditures within a market from the prior year.

name: Market scarcity
definition: Environmental scarcity refers to the quantity of resources available to a group of competitors. Scarcity is, therefore, a function of the amount of advertising expenditures and the number of competing stations in a market.

name: Market complexity
definition: In this research, we measured market complexity in terms of demographic characteristics of populations. Market complexity (M3) was measured on the basis of demographic distributions of age, education, and wealth within a market's Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area.

name: Transactional form
definition: the term refers to the vertical economic arrangements between manufacturers, wholesalers, and dealers. Exchanges may occur between parties owned by one organization, between a series of independently owned and managed organizations, or on a contractual basis between two independently owned organizations; these three transactional forms are respectively called corporate, conventional, and contractual networks.

name: Dealer dependence
definition: The extent to which a dealer relies upon the manufacturer, measured from the dealers' side of the relationship; power-dependence relations between organizations are based on the exchange of resources.

name: Manufacturer influence
definition: A measure of each manager's perception of the manufacturer's influence over the strategic decisions of the dealership, used as a measure of power.

name: Environmental linkages
definition: Linkages with other organizations, relationships with customers and elites, degree of establishment in a domain, and organizational size; in Hypothesis 2a these are joint programs, industry contacts, number of employees, number of customers, number of years in business, and market share.

name: Abnormal shareholder returns
definition: Abnormal returns are returns to stockholders above what shareholders would expect to receive on the basis of market risk; the abnormal return to the stock is the difference between the actual return and the normal return, and it does not result from overall movements of the market but rather from events specific to a firm.

name: Top management compensation
authors_terms: ["salary and bonus", "changes in CEOs' salaries and bonus levels", "percentage changes in salary and bonus figures", "annual cash compensation"]
definition: Compensation to the top corporate executive consisting of salary payments and bonus awards; salary payments distributed over a given year are based on a board's perceptions of the previous year's performance, whereas bonus awards at the end of a year represent the board's perception of performance in that year.

name: Overall market movements
authors_terms: ["overall market movements", "overall market performance", "overall market movements, or systematic risk"]
definition: Movements of the overall stock market, which the time-event method corrects for; the study contrasts a bear market year, in which the Standard and Poor's 500 stock index was down 11.5 percent, with a bull market year, in which the index was up by 25.8 percent.

name: Corporate merger
definition: A combination of two firms into one corporation; unlike stockholder diversification, management actions may alter the underlying risk profiles of the combining businesses.

name: Merger strategy relatedness
authors_terms: ["merger strategies", "merger type", "relatedness of merging firms", "degree of relatedness"]
definition: Following Lubatkin's (1983) classification scheme, four types of merger are distinguished: single-business mergers, including mergers between businesses that are either horizontally or market-concentrically related; vertical mergers; related mergers, involving businesses that share related production or marketing technologies; and unrelated mergers.

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: The component of a security's risk that varies unsystematically with general economic movements; such sources of risk are specific to a firm and do not equally affect the returns of all securities.

name: Systematic risk
definition: The source of variability that stems from market-wide trends, since to some extent all corporate securities move in the same direction as the economy; scholars call it systematic risk because it cannot be diversified away.

name: Total risk
definition: Total risk is defined as the total variability in a security's returns; it is the combination of the unsystematic variability and the systematic variability.

name: Market conditions
definition: General economic conditions in which mergers occur: during economic downturns, or bear markets, most companies face some combination of reduced cash flows, few growth opportunities, and uncertain future cash returns, whereas bull markets are periods of growth.

name: Leverage
definition: Leverage is defined as the book value of a firm's long-term debt divided by the book value of its total assets.

name: Implementation approach
definition: Rule-bound behavior was operationally defined as compliance with the standard technical specifications, and autonomy as customizing those guidelines through the adoption of unique, plant-specific characteristics.

name: Safety performance
authors_terms: ["safety outcomes", "safety records", "safety of nuclear power plants", "unsafe events", "events attributable to human error"]
definition: Reports of unsafe events, which the NRC receives in the form of license event reports, are one of the main methods that nuclear power plants and the regulatory agency have for assessing safety.

name: Capacity utilization
definition: Capacity ratings show the percentage of electric power that a nuclear power plant has generated in a particular period in comparison with the amount that it could generate given its overall capacity.

name: Externally induced innovations
definition: Innovations adopted by nuclear power plants in response to external pressures or requirements, as stated in the prediction.

name: Stage of growth
definition: Stages are described as a configuration of organizational design variables representing a firm's response to the sets of dominant problems it faces at sequential times. The particular problems faced at a given time appeared to be strongly associated with a venture's position in a particular stage of growth.

name: Strategic positioning problems
authors_terms: ["strategic positioning factor", "strategic positioning", "position in a new product-market segment", "development of a new product or technology application"]
definition: Factor 5 includes a firm's position in a new product-market segment and the development of a new product or technology application and is therefore a strategic positioning factor.

name: Sales and marketing problems
definition: Factor 2, which includes such concerns as meeting sales targets, attaining profit and market-share goals, penetrating new geographic markets, and maintaining the quality of product support and customer service, is related to critical requirements for success in the marketplace and can be interpreted as a sales and marketing factor.

name: People problems
definition: Only two variables, attracting capable employees and management depth and talent, load on factor 3, which can be termed a people construct.

name: Production problems
definition: Factor 4, which also includes only two variables, the ability to produce in volumes adequate to meet demand and the development of a network of reliable vendors and suppliers, is a production construct.

name: Organizational and administrative problems
definition: The first factor, which loads heavily with problems related to internal administrative systems and concerns-management information systems, cost control, financial information systems, and the general level of red tape-is an organizational-administrative construct.

name: External relations problems
definition: The two problems that loaded on the last factor were securing financial resources and backing and acquiring key outside advisers or board members, which makes this an external relations factor.

name: Change in automaticity
authors_terms: ["change in automaticity", "magnitude of change in automaticity", "technological change"]
definition: The magnitude of change in automaticity was measured as the percentage of change from 1973 to 1981 in a plant's manufacturing-equipment automaticity scores. Automaticity was measured by Amber and Amber's (1962) scale of automaticity, which indicates the extent to which machines replace human energy, dexterity, diligence, judgment, and evaluation of the manufacturing process.

name: Production system development
definition: Our measure of production system development followed the logic of Woodward's (1965) original technical complexity scale, which has been widely used to measure the extent of production system development. Production systems set broad limits on the extent or rate of technological change.

name: Complexity
definition: Complexity referred to the degree to which labor was divided on the basis of specialized knowledge, as indicated by the percentage of professional and technical employees. Complexity in this sense is not just a number of jobs in an organization or boxes on an organization chart; it is directly related to organizational awareness of performance problems and solutions to them.

name: Decentralization of strategic decisions
definition: Decentralization referred to the locus of decision-making authority within a plant, and items measuring decentralization were divided into two classes of variables that captured fundamental differences in types of decisions: strategic and line-operating. Strategic decisions are decisions pertaining to the basic goals, policies, and practices of an organization.

name: Decentralization of line-operating decisions
definition: Decentralization referred to the locus of decision-making authority within a plant; line-operating decisions are operating decisions, those having to do with the functioning of a production system, and are typically made at the production-head level.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization was defined as the extent to which activities were prescribed in an organization. Formalization leads to both structural and communicative rigidities that thwart organizational attempts to change technologies once problems have been identified.

name: SBU effectiveness
definition: SBU effectiveness measured along a multiplicity of dimensions rather than on any single dimension, using the degrees of importance of each dimension for an SBU as weights, and in the form of a comparison between actual performance and a priori expectations rather than on an absolute scale.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Porter (1980, 1985) identified two generic ways in which an SBU can gain a sustainable competitive advantage over other firms in its industry: low cost and differentiation; the author measured competitive strategy in terms of SBUs' intended trade-offs between becoming the cost leader and achieving differentiation.

name: Budget evaluative style
authors_terms: ["budget evaluative style", "budgetary emphasis", "emphasis on meeting a budget"]
definition: A continuous variable whose values depend on the amount of emphasis that meeting budgetary goals receives during the ongoing process of evaluating the performance of an SBU's general manager.

name: Decentralization
definition: The amount of decisionmaking authority that is delegated to an SBU's general manager by corporate superiors; decentralization between a corporate office and general manager was considered, but decentralization within an SBU was not.

name: Locus of control
authors_terms: ["locus of control", "internal locus of control", "external locus of control", "internal-external control"]
definition: Internal control refers to an individual's perceiving events, whether positive or negative, as a consequence of his or her own actions and thereby as potentially under personal control; external control refers to perceiving positive and negative events as unrelated to personal behavior and therefore beyond personal control.

name: Fit between administrative mechanisms and strategy
definition: The degree of fit (or, more accurately, misfit) for any given SBU, measured as the euclidean distance between that SBU's scores on the administrative mechanisms and the scores of its ideal type, identified on the basis of the focal SBU's strategy; the distance variable represents the multivariate fit of each SBU with the relevant ideal profile and takes into account the overall effect of deviation on all the administrative mechanisms simultaneously.

name: Golden parachute adoption
authors_terms: ["golden parachutes", "golden parachute adoption", "adoption of golden parachutes"]
definition: Golden parachutes involve a renegotiation of top-management compensation contracts to include very sizable payments to be made in the event of a takeover.

name: Takeover threat
definition: We measured takeover threat conservatively as actual transfer of ownership of more than 5 percent of the total stock of a firm to a potential acquirer and the filing of 13D statements with the SEC at least a year before acceptance of a golden parachute proposal.

name: Board size
definition: The size of a board reflects the complexity of the organization it serves. As a board grows, so does the spectrum of interests it represents.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of outside directors", "percentage of external directors", "percentage of outside directors"]
definition: The proportion of outside directors on a board, which managerialists use to evaluate the relative potency of outside and inside directors in board decision making.

name: CEO relative tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure vis-a-vis board members' tenures", "CEO relative tenure", "CEO tenure relative to outside director tenure"]
definition: CEO tenure vis-a-vis board members' tenures, which appeared to be a good proxy for CEO influence.

name: Management stock ownership
authors_terms: ["management stock ownership", "stock owned by top management", "proportion of stock owned by a top management team"]
definition: The extent of top management's stock ownership reflects the degree of congruence between the interests of stockholders and those of top management.

name: Nonmanagement stock concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of stock ownership in nonmanagement hands", "shares owned by groups other than management", "blocks of stock ownership greater than 5 percent"]
definition: The concentration of stock in the hands of a few outsiders gives them significant voting power that limits management influence on matters requiring board-level decisions.

name: Structural complexity
definition: Measures of structural complexity included the level of functional specialization and the professional qualifications of the officeholders.

name: Formalization
definition: I measured formalization of procedures using the abbreviated scale of formalization developed by Inkson and colleagues (1970), adopting the same scoring procedure they used.

name: Centralization of decision making
authors_terms: ["centralization", "centralization of operating decisions", "centralization of strategic decisions", "decentralization"]
definition: The extent of the centralization of decision making was measured with a subset of decision items originally developed by Pugh and colleagues (1968) to measure centralization and subsequently used by Inkson and coauthors (1970) to represent organizational autonomy. Each decision item is scored on a 5-point scale indicating, in an ascending order, the hierarchical level at which the decision is made.

name: Perceived environmental pressures
authors_terms: ["perceived environmental pressures", "perceived constraints", "perceived competition", "perceived constraints and competitive pressures"]
definition: Perceived constraints resulting from interactions with other organizations (financial institutions, trade unions, buyers, governments, etc.) in an environment as well as perceived competitive pressures, in prices, promotion, product quality and variety, in organizations' markets were the focal points of study.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence and scarcity refer to the objective condition of an environment and were measured with objective industry-demand data.

name: Technological inflexibility
authors_terms: ["inflexibility of technology", "technological inflexibility", "automaticity mode", "operations technology", "explicitness of technology"]
definition: Highly automated production processes, particularly if equipped with special purpose machinery, reflect relatively inflexible operations technologies.

name: Organizational size
