definition: Size was measured as the logarithm of the number of employees in a firm.

name: Intergroup mobility
definition: Movement of a firm from one strategic group to another; cluster analytic assignment of a firm to a different group than it had been in during the prior year defined a membership shift.

name: Industry economic decline
definition: Economic decline is one of the three periods of industry economic conditions (stability, growth, and decline) identified by two indicators, capacity change and capacity utilization. During decline, capacity levels leveled off and capacity utilization was low.

name: Strategic group similarity
authors_terms: ["similar groups", "dissimilar groups", "relatively similar groups", "adjacent groups", "less similar groups"]
definition: The degree to which strategic groups resemble one another on the group-defining variables; group 2 more nearly resembled group 1 and group 3 than groups 1 and 3 resembled each other.

name: Comprehensiveness
definition: The extent to which an organization attempts to be exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions.

name: Change in comprehensiveness
definition: Change in a firm's overall comprehensiveness over the years since the original studies; a positive change score indicates that a firm became more comprehensive and a negative score that it became less so.

name: Change in organizational size
definition: Change in the number of full-time employees from the original study to the present study, measured as a percentage increase or decrease.

name: Change in executive-team intrafirm tenure
authors_terms: ["change in executive-team intrafirm tenure", "change in executive-team members' intrafirm tenure", "change in team tenure"]
definition: Change in the average number of years executive-team members have worked in their firm, computed by subtracting the average reported in the earlier study from the average reported in the present study.

name: Executive-team continuity
definition: The proportion of a firm's executives whom the CEO identified in the present study who had also been identified in the first study; the higher the proportion, the more continuity in an executive team.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "average after-tax return on assets adjusted for extraordinary items"]
definition: Economic performance measured as average after-tax return on assets adjusted for extraordinary items for the years since the original studies.

name: Environmental stability
definition: The stability or instability of an industry's environment, as determined by Dess and Beard (1984) using multiple objective measures; the paint and coatings industry was highly stable and the forest products industry was unstable.

name: Head-to-head competition intensity
authors_terms: ["head-to-head competition", "intensity of head-to-head competition", "direct head-to-head competition", "competitive intensity"]
definition: Head-to-head competition is competition between firms that both serve the same routes as significant competitors; intensity refers to the proportion of a firm's routes that are served also by a given competitor.

name: Indirect board interlocking intensity
definition: An indirect interlock occurs when two firms have directors or executives who are also on the board of a third firm; intensity refers to the proportion of a firm's indirect board interlocks that are with a given competitor.

name: Competitive uncertainty
definition: Organizational uncertainty is derived from failure to understand a task environment and from interdependence with elements of the task environment; government regulatory agencies generate information that reduces uncertainty, so the withdrawal of regulation increased it.

name: Distance between headquarters
authors_terms: ["distance between competitors' headquarters", "geographic proximity of corporate headquarters", "great circle distance"]
definition: The great circle distance, the shortest distance over the surface of the globe, between the cities housing the headquarters of the firms in each dyad.

name: Financial dependence
definition: A firm's dependence on outside sources of capital, indicated by its debt and performance levels; the greater the need for the resource an element provides, the greater the tendency to manage the dependence.

name: Financial interlocking
authors_terms: ["financial interlocking", "direct board interlocks with financial institutions", "proportion of direct board interlocks to financial institutions"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's direct board interlocks with financial sector institutions such as banks, investment companies, or insurance firms.

name: Profit performance
definition: A firm's average before-tax return on stockholders' equity over five years.

name: Industry financial dependence
authors_terms: ["overall industry financial dependence", "overall industry dependence", "dependence of one sector on another"]
definition: The dependence of an industry as a whole on the financial sector, which increased over the study period as the airlines' debt ratios rose and internally generated funds fell short of capital needs.

name: Organizational foundings
definition: We defined organizational founding as the formal incorporation date of an organization because we saw incorporation as a clear signal from an organization's founders that they planned to maintain it as an ongoing entity. The frequency of foundings, the dependent variable in this study, was the number of voluntary social service organizations founded every quarter during the period between January 1970 and December 1982.

name: Prior foundings
definition: One of the ecological dynamics affecting new founding levels is the previous level of foundings in the population; research on the ecological dynamics of organizational foundings has suggested that founding levels have curvilinear relationships with previous levels of foundings.

name: Prior disbandings
definition: Disbandings are the other population dynamic included in ecological dynamics, that is, the previous levels of disbandings in the population, and founding levels have been argued to have curvilinear relationships with previous levels of disbandings.

name: Population density
definition: Density was defined as the total number of organizations alive at a given time in the population.

name: Institutional environmental change
authors_terms: ["institutional changes", "institutional environmental changes", "major institutional changes", "Opportunities for Youth", "Provincial Restraint"]
definition: In the context of effects on this population, two major institutional changes occurred during the period of observation. From 1971 to 1975, termed the Opportunities for Youth period, the creation of new voluntary social service organizations was legitimated in Canada and socially accepted as the preferred way to deal with social problems; from 1976 to 1981, the Provincial Restraint period, fiscal restraint was the watchword and more emphasis was placed on improving the productivity of existing organizations than on creating new ones.

name: Organizational form
definition: Specialist organizations have characteristics specialized to suit specific environmental features, and generalist organizations have features adapted to a broad range of environmental conditions. One important aspect of this distinction in organizational form is the number of different domains in which organizations operate: specialists operate in single domains and have narrow niches; generalists operate in multiple domains and have broad niches.

name: Information-processing structure of the top management team
authors_terms: ["information-processing structure of top management teams", "capacity of an organization's top management team's information-processing structure", "top-management-team information processing", "information-processing capacity"]
definition: We operationally defined the information-processing structure of top management teams during strategic issue interpretation using the dimensions of participation, interaction, and formalization (Duncan, 1974). Structural characteristics such as high levels of participation and interaction and a low level of formalization facilitate a high level of information processing (Galbraith, 1973) and foster extensive use of information (Daft & Lengel, 1986).

name: Strategic domain orientation
authors_terms: ["organizational strategy", "strategic pattern", "domain offense", "domain defense", "domain-offensive strategy", "domain-defensive strategy"]
definition: We viewed organizational strategy in terms of the strategic patterns Miles (1982) described: domain defense and domain offense. According to this conceptualization, the type and extent of service and product offerings, the population served, relations with others in a market, and the success criteria used reflect a firm's strategic pattern.

name: Positive-negative issue label
authors_terms: ["positive-negative dimension", "label the situation as something positive", "positive label", "negative label"]
definition: The interpretation of a strategic issue is often represented by general labels such as 'opportunity' or 'threat.' These labels capture top managers' beliefs about the potential effects of environmental events and trends (Edelman, 1977) and set in motion processes that move an organization in a particular direction (Dutton et al., 1983). Three continua represent these labels: positive-negative, gain-loss, and controllable-uncontrollable.

name: Gain-loss issue label
authors_terms: ["gain-loss dimension", "label the situation as a potential gain", "label the situation as a potential loss"]
definition: The interpretation of a strategic issue is often represented by general labels such as 'opportunity' or 'threat.' Three continua represent these labels: positive-negative, gain-loss, and controllable-uncontrollable.

name: Controllable-uncontrollable issue label
authors_terms: ["controllable-uncontrollable continuum", "feel it can manage the situation instead of the situation managing it"]
definition: Several researchers investigating stress (e.g., Averill, 1973) have argued that people also see threats as uncontrollable. Likewise, opportunities are seen as distinguished by a high degree of controllability (McCrae, 1984). Thus, we also used the controllable-uncontrollable continuum as a dimension differentiating interpretations of strategic issues.

name: Variable usage
authors_terms: ["variable usage", "information usage", "extent to which the CEO uses variables for interpretation"]
definition: Variable usage is the quantity of data about a situation that an organization's participants gather and use for interpretation (Daft & Macintosh, 1981). The amount of data gathered reflects the perceived level of understanding of a situation (MacKay, 1969).

name: Organizational response time
authors_terms: ["response time", "conversion time", "time to conversion", "speed of response"]
definition: The amount of response time that precedes conversion to for-profit status. The speed of an organization's response relative to that of other organizations with which it competes for resources reflects inertia.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age is the number of years an organization has been in operation; as organizational habits form with age, organizations become increasingly bureaucratized and traditional ways of doing things become entrenched.

name: Organizational size
definition: The scale of an organization; large firms are more likely to be formalized and bureaucratic than small firms and tend to have complex structures that can constrain adaptability.

name: Tightness of system coupling
definition: The overall tightness or looseness of coupling between different spheres within an organization, which influences its ability to overcome inertial forces. In a tightly coupled structure, change in one unit requires adjustment by many more units.

name: Resource utilization
definition: When an organization is prepaid for the resources it offers, the level to which those resources are used has a direct effect on the organization's slack: as utilization increases, resources decrease, which increases vulnerability to environmental change and motivation to respond.

name: Physician case load
definition: The efficiency with which an HMO uses its physicians; because HMO clients pay in advance, the higher the physician case load, the less slack an HMO will generate.

name: Federal qualification
definition: Federally qualified HMOs agree to provide a specific array of services and to make them available to all members whenever they are needed, and face additional pressure to perform well.

name: Physician availability
definition: Physicians represent a key input to HMOs because there is no substitute for their skills; physician availability is a measure of the opportunities an environment presents to an organization.

name: Market saturation
definition: Market saturation indicates the potential for future demand; if a market is highly saturated, the benefit of obtaining the few new customers available is unlikely to outweigh the costs of pursuing growth.

name: Competitive pressure
definition: New entrants into a market bring new capacity, the desire to gain market share, and often substantial resources, and the entry of new HMOs into a market increases competition in that market.

name: National chain membership
authors_terms: ["membership in a chain", "chain membership", "national HMO chains"]
definition: National HMO chains are organized as semiautonomous, geographically diversified profit centers; HMOs that belong to a national chain must report their growth and profits to the chain's headquarters.

name: For-profit HMO prevalence
authors_terms: ["percentage of for-profit HMOs", "presence of for-profit HMOs in a state"]
definition: As the proportion of for-profit HMOs increases, so does their acceptance by the industry and the public; the existence of for-profit providers in a health care market exerts pressure on nonprofit providers to behave more like for-profit entities.

name: Supportive state legislation
definition: Some states have made conversion more difficult by rigorously scrutinizing conversion requests, while others have statutory provisions that explicitly allow a nonprofit HMO to become a for-profit business corporation; the existence of a state statute is an indication that a process has become institutionalized.

name: Relatedness of entered market
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "unrelatedness", "degree of unrelatedness", "closeness of an entered market"]
definition: The closeness of an entered market to an entrant's core markets; the more related the new market is to the entrant's core markets, the more likely its excess physical and knowledge-based resources can reduce operating costs there and the fewer complementary resources are needed.

name: Internal funds and leverage
definition: Funds generated internally and the ability to raise low-risk debt; low financial leverage usually indicates the availability of internal funds, because firms with internal funds do not need to borrow and low leverage implies a low risk of default.

name: Stock price
authors_terms: ["stock price", "high stock price", "cost of equity capital"]
definition: The level of a firm's stock price relative to its own past level, which reflects the cost of equity capital: the higher the value, the cheaper it is for a company to use stock as a medium of exchange.

name: Industry concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration ratio", "four-firm concentration ratio", "concentration of an entered industry"]
definition: The extent to which sales in an entered industry are concentrated among a few large firms; the threat of retaliation is high in a concentrated industry in which the incumbents tend to be a few powerful firms who are very protective of their market share.

name: Industry growth rate
authors_terms: ["growth rate", "growth rate of an entered industry", "sales growth"]
definition: The expected rate of growth of an entered market, approximated by the growth rate of sales in the entered industry one year prior to the entry year.

name: Mode of entry
definition: The way a firm enters a new market; two modes of entry are considered, direct entry and acquisition.

name: Accommodativeness of crisis policy statements
authors_terms: ["accommodative signal", "defensive signal", "presentations of corporate policy", "declarations of corporate policy"]
definition: By an accommodative signal, we mean a statement in which management accepts responsibility, admits to the existence of problems, and takes actions to remedy a situation. A defensive signal is a statement in which management insists that the problems do not exist, tries to alleviate doubts about the firm's ability to generate future revenue, and takes action to resume normal operations rapidly.

name: Crisis type
definition: Crises differ in at least two important respects: first, in their effects on any victims they might have; and second, in what can be plausibly said about their causes. Accidents have identifiable victims and responsibility can plausibly be denied; the victims of a scandal are less identifiable than the victims of an accident and responsibility for a scandal is hard to deny; in terms of effects on victims and deniability, product safety and health incidents lie somewhere between accidents and scandals.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: The abnormal, or excess, return is the part of a return not anticipated by a statistical or economic model; it is the deviation of the actual return from the model's predictions.

name: Decision speed
definition: Decision duration is "the time between the first reference to deliberate action, such as scheduling a meeting or seeking information, to the time in which a commitment to act was made." Because decision duration reflects the slowness of a decision, the scale was reversed so that high values reflect fast decisions.

name: Number of alternatives
authors_terms: ["number of alternatives", "alternatives simultaneously considered", "simultaneous consideration of multiple alternatives"]
definition: The number of alternatives that were simultaneously considered in making the strategic decision studied, as identified and discussed by the CEO.

name: Board experience
definition: Board experience was measured as the principal component of the average board member's tenure on the board, average age, and average years of working experience in the focal industry.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The authors note that the three most common ways of measuring organizational performance are profitability, sales growth, and stock appreciation; since the hospitals studied were not publicly traded, this study relied on the first two measures.

name: Environmental velocity
definition: Environmental velocity reflects both the pace of change in an environment and the predictability of the changes that occur; high-velocity environments are those in which changes in demand, competition, and technology are rapid and discontinuous.

name: Discretionary cash
definition: Cash resources, a fully fungible asset that firms can apply with full discretion; unlike specific assets, cash has wide potential uses and underscores the need for a corporate office to pool and allocate it.

name: Multidivisional form adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of a multidivisional, or M-form, organizational structure", "adoption of an M-form structure", "announcement of the intention to adopt an M-form structure"]
definition: Adoption of a multidivisional structure, in which subsidiaries return cash to the parent, which pools it and then redistributes it to the subsidiaries to optimize returns.

name: Diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm is active in different businesses; measured as the number of different four-digit SIC codes in which first-tier subsidiaries were active and, alternatively, as the investment level in nonvertical subsidiaries.

name: CEO compensation
definition: CEO compensation consisted of two components, cash and executive stock options. Cash compensation included salary, bonuses, and deferred amounts.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["company performance", "firm performance", "market return", "return on average assets"]
definition: To avoid the biases inherent in using either method alone, we used both an accounting-based and a market-based measure of performance in this study. Both measures were based on rates of return to facilitate comparisons to each other, to previous research, and to the measure of compensation.

name: Unique decision making
authors_terms: ["unique decision making", "unique decisions", "unique decision making measure"]
definition: Expenditures on the decision variables consist of both a common component, representing a response to environmental forces faced by an industry as a whole, and a unique component, representing attempts to outmaneuver the competition or responses to environmental forces unique to a firm. The absolute size of a residual provides information to evaluators because it signals how much a CEO's behavior differed from general industry trends.

name: Competitor dependence
definition: The extent to which a competitor relies on the markets affected by an action.

name: Action irreversibility
authors_terms: ["irreversibility of an action", "action irreversibility", "irreversibility of a competitive move"]
definition: Clearly, some actions are easier to change or reverse than others, since there are multiple sources of irreversibility: economic, institutional, organizational, psychological, and political.

name: Likelihood of nonresponse
definition: The estimated probability that an action would not provoke retaliation from a given competitor.

name: Response delay
definition: The length of time a responding competitor took to react to an action.

name: Likelihood of a matching response
authors_terms: ["likelihood of a matching response", "matching response", "matching move"]
definition: The estimated probability that a responder would imitate an action.

name: Price move
definition: A competitive move that is a price change; since price changes directly affect a business's bottom line, it is much easier to estimate their impact on the profits of both an attacker and a defender than it is to estimate the impact of other types of competitive moves.

name: Market share change
definition: Increases and decreases in share for each attacking and responding airline, calculated as a percentage of total passengers.

name: Competitive role
definition: A firm's position in a competitive exchange: all initiators and quick responders in a contest are likely to benefit at the expense of slow responders and nonresponders.

name: Complexity of vertical integration
authors_terms: ["complexity of vertical integration", "complexity inherent in patterns of vertical integration", "complex patterns of vertical integration", "fully integrated firms"]
definition: Patterns of vertical integration in which there are a large number of vertical links between products create complexity because these links imply interdependencies that must be coordinated. Complexity is decreased if a firm's diversification is constrained to products in adjacent stages of production because there are relatively few cognitive problems in coordinating and managing noncore products that are very closely related to a firm's center of gravity.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Systematic risk, or 'beta' in Lintner's (1965a,b) and Sharpe's (1964) capital asset pricing model (CAPM), is the risk most relevant to shareholders. Systematic risk is the portion of a stock's return variance that is systematically related to general economic conditions, such as business cycles.

name: Bankruptcy risk
definition: Creditors assume the risk of default on the loans made to a firm. This risk is also called bankruptcy risk because loan default triggers bankruptcy (Altman, 1983).

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Two characteristics of a firm's product-market environment influence intrinsic business risk: environmental turbulence, or volatility, and demand growth and decline. Changes in industry structure and competition that cause some product markets to have volatile returns over time create environmental turbulence.

name: Environmental growth
authors_terms: ["environmental growth", "environmental growth rate", "demand growth and decline"]
definition: Two characteristics of a firm's product-market environment influence intrinsic business risk: environmental turbulence, or volatility, and demand growth and decline. Environmental growth should lower the risks of shareholders and creditors because it encourages high volume and capacity utilization, which in turn protects even the most vulnerable firms from economy-wide trends, such as business cycles.

name: Countercyclical hiring
definition: Countercyclical hiring is defined as hiring that is conducted by an individual company during downturns in the economic environment of its predominant industry. Specifically, it is hiring that takes place during downturns before there is a clear upturn in general economic activity in a company's predominant industry.

name: Human resource planning for avoiding personnel shortages
authors_terms: ["avoiding personnel shortages", "human resource planning for avoiding shortages of qualified personnel"]
definition: Forecasting shortages of critical personnel and planning for their future supply are basic activities in human resource planning. Companies that can accurately forecast demands for and supplies of personnel should make greater countercyclical hiring investments than other companies because they possess more information on future needs.

name: Link between human resource planning and strategic planning
authors_terms: ["human resource planning's link with strategy", "link between the human resource and strategy-planning processes"]
definition: When human resource planning and strategic planning are linked, hiring is more likely to serve a strategic purpose. With stronger links between the human resource and strategy-planning processes, companies should be well positioned to benefit from countercyclical hiring.

name: Availability of high-quality applicants
authors_terms: ["applicant quality", "availability of high-quality applicants during downturns"]
definition: Companies that hire during downturns generally face less competition for high-quality applicants. By hiring applicants of better quality through countercyclical hiring, companies can replace lower-quality employees.

name: Importance of affirmative action
definition: Many companies have affirmative action goals of increasing the number of female and minority managers and professionals. Since qualified individuals in these groups are often in short supply, it may be difficult to hire them during economic upturns.

name: Maintaining regular age distributions
authors_terms: ["regular age distributions", "maintaining regular age distributions of employee groups"]
definition: Concerns over age distributions may serve as a stimulus for countercyclical hiring as gaps (shortages) or bulges (excesses) in age cohorts may result from discontinuities associated with procyclical hiring.

name: Development and career planning
authors_terms: ["development and career planning", "employee development and career planning"]
definition: Taking an investment perspective, companies can hire some high-potential employees during downturns and place them in training programs with the expectation that their future productivity will offset the costs of countercyclical hiring. Companies committed to development are less likely than others to discontinue such programs during downturns.

name: Financial performance
definition: Regardless of the expected future benefits of countercyclical hiring, companies must have sufficient resources to trade present costs for more uncertain future benefits. In general, profitable companies are more likely than poorer performers to have the resources to make countercyclical hiring investments.

name: Importance of costs
definition: Decline in a company's need for employees should accompany a decline in demand for its goods and services. Obvious financial costs are associated with a strategy of hiring when there is no compelling or immediate demand for additional employees.

name: Risk aversion
definition: Whether the type and level of risk will deter investments in countercyclical hiring was expected to depend on the risk aversion of decision makers. Countercyclical hiring carries with it the risk of selection error and the risks of forecasting when an upturn will occur.

name: Constraints on human resource forecasting accuracy
authors_terms: ["inaccurate human resource forecasting", "lack of human resource forecasting", "constraints on the accuracy of human resource forecasting"]
definition: Companies vary in their human resource forecasting capabilities. Some have little experience in this area and have not developed capabilities, and others have substantial expertise; the accuracy of human resource forecasting also varies across industries.

name: Focus on customer segments
authors_terms: ["focus on customer segments", "degree of focus on customer segments"]
definition: A focus on customer segments encourages service businesses to segment the general market carefully and tailor their services to meet the needs of selected customer segments.

name: Focus on internal capabilities
authors_terms: ["focus on internal capabilities", "degree of focus on internal capabilities"]
definition: A focus on internal capabilities implies that firms produce and deliver products (goods and services) that share some unique factor of production, whether a management or distribution system, a product or process technology, or plant and equipment.

name: Focus on geographic regions
authors_terms: ["focus on geographic regions", "degree of focus on geographic regions"]
definition: The potential benefits of geographic focus arise from understanding, responding to, and taking advantage of varying environmental conditions across geographic areas.

name: Firm performance
definition: ROE adjusted for industry and systematic risk, industry-adjusted market-to-book value of equity, and Jensen's alpha were the performance measures. I adjusted performance measures where necessary to account for the relationship between risk and return and for differences in firms' performance owing to their participation in different industries.

name: Associate membership program establishment
definition: Associate membership in a national union provides individuals with an opportunity to affiliate with the union, independent of any union-employer bargaining relationship; individuals pay reduced membership fees to gain access to a set of union-provided benefits. To be considered relevant to the study, a program had to have a special membership category for those not covered by a collective bargaining agreement, be open to workers who were not merely the union's retired members, involve a union with a majority of its members in private industry, and offer benefits directly to such members.

name: Union membership growth
definition: Membership change was measured as the percentage change in a union's membership between 1983 and 1987; the hypothesis refers to unions with low membership growth.

name: Scope of union strategies
authors_terms: ["scope of strategies", "broader scope of strategies", "strategic scope"]
definition: The degree to which a union stressed collective bargaining alone or several strategies, including bargaining, organizing, and political activities; high scores indicated a reliance on a broader scope of strategies.

name: Union size
definition: Size, measured as the logarithm of union membership (in thousands) in 1985; the authors viewed size as a proxy for such organizational variables as slack resources, specialization, and expertise.

name: Knowledge worker organizing
definition: Knowledge workers can be defined as those who exercise considerable autonomy and judgment; knowledge worker organizing was the proportion of a union's National Labor Relations Board certification elections that were held in prospective professional and/or technical and office, clerical, and other white collar collective bargaining units between 1977 and 1985.

name: Supporters in failed representation campaigns
authors_terms: ["lost prospects", "large numbers of supporters in failed representation campaigns"]
definition: Workers who supported unionization in a failed campaign to institute a union at their workplace; measured as the logarithm of the number of votes cast for a union in failed union certification campaigns.

name: Construction sector jurisdiction
authors_terms: ["construction sector", "building construction industry", "primary jurisdiction in construction"]
definition: A union's primary jurisdiction, coded 1 for unions with a primary jurisdiction in construction and 0 otherwise; the authors argue that construction unions face negative synergy and negative reputational carryover effects from associate member programs.

name: Centralization of decision making
definition: The degree to which a union limited staff and rank-and-file member participation in policy decisions; highly centralized structures make it easier for leaders to direct an innovation's implementation in the face of resistance to change from lower levels.

name: AFL-CIO committee participation
authors_terms: ["participation in the AFL-CIO Committee on the Evolution of Work", "membership on the AFL-CIO Committee on the Evolution of Work"]
definition: Whether a union's leaders participated in the AFL-CIO Committee on the Evolution of Work, whose 1985 report recommended establishing new categories of membership for workers not employed in an organized bargaining unit.

name: CEO succession
authors_terms: ["CEO succession", "change in leadership", "appointment of a new CEO"]
definition: A change in leadership, that is, the appointment of a new CEO, marking the start of a period of analysis.

name: Concentration of power
definition: Concentration of power for making strategic and routine decisions; one of the structural dimensions of structure and process.

name: Information processing
definition: The factor that encompasses the intelligence systems (controls and internal communication networks) and intended rationality (environmental scanning, analysis, long planning horizons, and multiplex perspectives) dimensions.

name: Structural complexity
definition: The structural dimension that encompasses interunit differentiation and the use of technocrats.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: A decision-making-process dimension comprising risk taking, proactiveness, innovativeness, and adaptiveness.

name: Organizational integration
definition: The codification of and complementarity among elements of strategy, and the presence of unifying traditions.

name: Organizational change
authors_terms: ["absolute change", "change in virtually all dimensions of structure and process"]
definition: Absolute change, change in either a positive or a negative direction, in virtually all aspects of organizations.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The performance context in which a succession decision occurs, taken as both return and risk, since low levels of return and high levels of risk can each be interpreted as unsatisfactory outcomes; risk refers to the level of uncertainty associated with an organization's cash flow.

name: Outsider CEO selection
definition: The selection of a successor to the chief executive from outside the organization; the authors defined an outsider as any successor with less than two years of service in the firm he or she headed.

name: Incumbent CEO disposition
definition: An incumbent's disposition indicates the influence that the incumbent may have on director allegiances and values and on director expectations and attributions; it is captured by the association a former CEO retains with the firm after succession, with dismissal representing the case in which all officership and directorship connections are severed.

name: Heir apparent
authors_terms: ["heir apparent", "presence of an heir apparent", "president title"]
definition: The presence of an heir apparent is a second indicator of the sociopolitical construct of director allegiances and values, and is measured by an individual in the firm other than the incumbent CEO holding the title 'president', a title generally reserved for individuals who are expected to become CEO.

name: CEO-chair duality
definition: The number of titles held by an incumbent, which may be associated with incumbent power, another sociopolitical construct; it concerns whether the outgoing CEO also held the title of chairperson at the time of a succession.

name: Managerial succession
definition: The exit of the president or of another manager of an organization. When a manager of a small telephone company left, he took along a great deal of tacit operational and organizational knowledge.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: Organizational failure, which the authors call a fundamental standard of organizational performance: an organization ceased to operate.

name: Duration since succession
authors_terms: ["duration since succession", "elapsed duration since the most recent succession event", "time elapsed since succession"]
definition: The time elapsed in years since the most recent succession event; organizations that have experienced succession and survived rebuild internal processes and external relations over this period.

name: Organizational age
authors_terms: ["organizational age", "age", "timing of succession in the organizational life cycle"]
definition: Organizational age measured in years since founding, which captures where in its life cycle an organization experiences succession.

name: Variance in R&D intensity across lines of business
authors_terms: ["variance in R&D intensity", "variance of R&D intensity", "similarity in R&D resource allocations", "consistency in R&D resource allocations"]
definition: The variance of R&D intensity (R&D expenditures divided by sales) across the lines of business of a diversified firm, used as a measure of the difference or dispersion in resource allocations; low variance indicates resource allocation similarities.

name: Variance in capital intensity across lines of business
authors_terms: ["variance in capital intensity", "variance of capital intensity", "similar capital requirements"]
definition: The variance of capital intensity (capital expenditures divided by sales) across the lines of business of a diversified firm, used as a measure of the difference or dispersion in resource allocations.

name: Corporate financial performance
authors_terms: ["industry-adjusted return on assets", "industry-adjusted ROA", "corporate financial performance"]
definition: Corporate financial performance measured as return on assets (ROA), adjusted for industry influences by subtracting a weighted average of the ROA of the firm's dominant four-digit industry (excluding the firm's own figures) from firm ROA.

name: Organizational design
authors_terms: ["organizational structures and management systems", "organizational design", "organizational arrangements", "structures and systems"]
definition: An acceptable definition of organizational design has to include coverage of both structure and systems, and there is a developing convergence upon a definition of design as having three essential elements: the vertical and horizontal structures of roles and responsibilities, decision systems, or policy and resource allocation mechanisms, and human resource systems, such as recruitment, appraisal, and compensation.

name: Organizational structure
authors_terms: ["vertical and horizontal structures of roles and responsibilities", "structural dimensions"]
definition: The vertical and horizontal structures of roles and responsibilities, commonly analyzed in terms of the extent of differentiation, the criteria of differentiation or basis for grouping activities, and the extent of integration.

name: Decision systems
authors_terms: ["decision systems, or policy and resource allocation mechanisms"]
definition: Policy and resource allocation mechanisms; Miller's survey identified three dimensions of decision systems: rationality, interaction patterns, and assertiveness. Rationality is the extent to which decisions and resource allocations are the product of careful analysis, systematic scanning of markets for problems and opportunities, and methodical planning and articulation of strategies; interaction is the degree to which decision making is individual and directive or collective and consensual; assertiveness covers the extent to which an organization engages in reactive or proactive behavior and is prepared to assume risk.

name: Human resource systems
authors_terms: ["human resource systems, such as recruitment, appraisal, and compensation"]
definition: Human resource systems, such as recruitment, appraisal, and compensation; significant dimensions are the extent to which control is based on a bureaucratic or a clan form of appraisal and the criteria used for recruitment, career development and compensation.

name: Archetypal coherence
definition: Archetypal coherence comes from the consistent relationship between an interpretive scheme and an organization's structures and systems; organizations tend to operate through structures and systems that are manifestations of a single, underlying interpretive scheme. An archetype is a set of structures and systems that consistently embodies a single interpretive scheme.

name: Archetypal inertia
definition: Organizations are characterized by convergence toward a prevailing archetypal form and inertia and tend to remain within the assumptions of the existing archetype; conservatism marks normal organizational development. A track is the temporal association of an organization with one or more archetypes.

name: Inductive configuration approach
definition: The historically dominant approach focuses on empirical classification of organizations in order to define inductively a set of configurations appropriate to a given context; it concentrates on maximizing internal validity while sacrificing generalizability.

name: Deductive configuration approach
definition: An approach that uses a particular theoretical perspective for both defining groups and predicting their relative performance; deductively derived configurations apply broadly and are not dependent on particular industry contexts.

name: Organizational configurations
definition: Commonly occurring clusters of attributes of organizational strategies, structures, and processes.

name: Consistency of configurations over time
authors_terms: ["different numbers of configurations over time", "consistently define four configurations in a given industry over time"]
definition: The extent to which a configurational approach defines a stable set of configurations over multiple time periods, as opposed to capitalizing opportunistically on random variation in a given time period and producing different numbers of configurations across periods.

name: Configuration type
definition: A given industry has four distinct and internally homogeneous configurations: entrepreneurs/r-specialists, who pursue new opportunities in a narrow domain; prospectors/r-generalists, who pursue new opportunities across a broad domain; defenders/K-specialists, who efficiently exploit existing opportunities in a narrow domain; and analyzers/K-generalists, who efficiently exploit existing opportunities across a broad domain.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance was measured with five variables representative of previous studies of the configurations-performance linkage.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence is resource-carrying capacity, the extent to which environmental resources are available and accessible to firms.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism is the amount of turbulence and instability in an environment; it refers to changes that are difficult to predict in terms of both frequency and direction and thus can increase environmental uncertainty for organizations.

name: Relatedness to core skills
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "product diversification", "horizontal, related, and vertical expansions", "cognitive distance", "proximity"]
definition: Distinctions of diversification type correspond to varying degrees of an expansion's cognitive distance from a firm's base, with horizontal being more proximate than related, and related more proximate than unrelated; expansions are beneficial if they are relatively proximate to a firm's current skills.

name: Expansion location
definition: Organizations' expansion projects can be implemented at home or abroad; differences in economic development, regulatory traditions, political infrastructure, and memberships in economic blocks all may increase the riskiness of foreign expansion, and firms that expand globally encounter different customs, traditions, and beliefs about management.

name: Expansion mode
definition: The form in which expansion projects are implemented; takeovers and new ventures are profoundly different diversification alternatives, homegrown expansion being embedded in the accumulated skills of a firm while acquired expansion expends major resources for subsequent amalgamation with the acquired firm's stock of know-how.

name: Expansion ownership structure
definition: Organizations can undertake expansion alone or share ownership with strategic partners; shared equity and control engenders more unfamiliarity than solitary diversification, and the added uncertainty of incomplete control and ambiguity render partly owned expansions risky.

name: Longitudinal learning
definition: Learning can also be gained temporally, from a firm's cumulative experiences, or the process of doing; the stream of a firm's diversification decisions endows it with cumulative skills, so expansions will face a better fate if the firm has been a successful diversifier before.

name: Expansion success
definition: The longevity of expansion projects and the learning process that accompanies them was interpreted as signaling success; ventures liquidated relatively early were viewed as less successful than enduring ones, and the duration of a venture can be construed as a measure of process.

name: Strategic task needs
definition: The degree to which the realization of intended synergies depends on the sharing or exchange of critical skills and resources; the successful sharing or exchange of the critical skills and resources that form the foundation for value creation.

name: Organizational task needs
definition: The degree to which acquisition synergies depend on the preservation of a unique, context-specific set of organizational capabilities; the preservation of any unique characteristics of an acquired firm that are a source of key strategic capabilities.

name: Multiculturalism of the acquirer
definition: A multicultural organization tolerates and even encourages cultural diversity, and is therefore more likely to allow an acquired firm to retain its own values, beliefs, and practices than is a less multicultural organization that uses culture as a powerful control system emphasizing conformity.

name: Power differential
authors_terms: ["power differential", "power differential between the two organizations"]
definition: The extent to which there can be a unidirectionality of influence from acquirer to target, possible when the acquirer is significantly larger than its acquisition, a situation creating a power differential between the two organizations; measured as the difference in size of the two organizations in number of employees.

name: Compatibility of acquisition visions
definition: The extent to which the acquirer and the acquired organization had compatible ideas about the goals each was trying to achieve through the acquisition and the means to achieve those goals; the degree to which the target has a vision of essential actions and outcomes in the acquisition that is compatible with the acquirer's.

name: Level of integration
authors_terms: ["level of integration", "integration design", "level of integration chosen"]
definition: The degree of postacquisition change in an organization's technical, administrative, and cultural configuration; integration design choices sit on a continuum from autonomy to absorption, and levels of integration can range from low to high.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "amount of acquisition experience", "previous experience with acquisitions"]
definition: Managers' previous experience with acquisitions, which may influence how they make integration design decisions.

name: Acquiring organization size
authors_terms: ["organization size", "size of an organization", "size of the organizations"]
definition: The size of the acquiring organization, which provides an experiential background that may influence managers' perceptions of situational variables and their use of that information; size differences between the combining organizations are discussed as a source of power.

name: Industry classification
definition: The industry context in which managers operate, distinguished here between service and manufacturing industries, which may influence managers' integration design decisions.

name: Strategic decision-making pace
authors_terms: ["pace of strategic decision making", "decision-making pace", "decision speed", "strategic decision-making pace", "speed of decision making"]
definition: A pivotal aspect of strategic decision-making activities, the pace at which they occur; the speed at which executives move through the intelligence, design, and choice activities of strategic decision making.

name: Cognitive ability
definition: The level of intellectual capability brought to a decision; it manifests itself in an individual's cognitive complexity or information-processing skills.

name: Use of intuition
definition: Intuition refers to the nonconscious ability to code, sort, and access the meaningfulness or relevance of the outcomes of past decisions efficiently; it is an ability to learn from or draw upon experience.

name: Tolerance for risk
definition: High tolerance for risk appears to be associated with high tolerance for ambiguity and a willingness to decide, and tolerance for risk, rather than risk seeking or risk averseness, appears to be associated with psychological flexibility.

name: Propensity to act
definition: High energy and activity levels have been associated with ambition, impatience, and decisiveness; intrinsically motivated executives probably bring greater energy levels, action orientations, and decisiveness to the strategic decision-making process.

name: Centralization of decision-making structures
definition: Centralization refers to the concentration of authority or decision-making power in a firm; the more centralized an organization, the less authority has been delegated by top executives.

name: Formalization of decision-making structures
definition: Formalization refers to the extent to which firm policies, job descriptions, organization charts, plans, and objective-setting systems are articulated explicitly, usually through written communications.

name: Business relatedness
authors_terms: ["business relatedness", "related acquisitions", "unrelated acquisitions", "relatedness of the acquisitions"]
definition: An acquisition was judged related when at least 70 percent of the acquiring firm's revenues came from a business area that was related by product, market, or production process to a business of the acquired firm; otherwise it was judged unrelated. The authors argue that familiarity with the industry lets acquirers of related distressed targets better uncover hidden problems and synergies.

name: Prior acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "prior acquisition experience", "experience of an acquirer"]
definition: The number of acquisitions made by an acquiring firm during the four years prior to the purchase of a focal acquired firm. Some prior acquisition experience is argued to provide valuable lessons for top managers, improving target selection skills and knowledge of when to withdraw and what resources are needed.

name: Relative firm size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "the ratio of acquired firm size to acquiring firm size", "relative firm sizes"]
definition: The ratio of the acquired firm's revenue to the acquiring firm's revenue. The authors argue the relationship may be curvilinear: distressed targets may need to be large enough relative to their acquirers to ensure sufficient attention from top management, but acquirers may still need to be significantly larger than the targets to ensure necessary slack is available.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The success of the acquisition of interest, rated by a panel of academic evaluators on a seven-point scale ranging from 1, very unsuccessful, to 7, very successful. The measure focuses directly on how successfully an acquisition was implemented rather than on the postacquisition performance of the acquiring firm as a whole.

name: Equity-based alliance governance
authors_terms: ["equity based", "mode of alliance", "use of equity", "equity alliances", "nonequity alliances"]
definition: The governance structure of an alliance classified by its use of equity ownership; equity alliances are equity joint ventures or minority equity investments, whereas nonequity arrangements involve no sharing or exchange of equity and are more akin to arm's-length market exchanges on the market-to-hierarchy continuum.

name: Joint R&D component
authors_terms: ["shared R&D component", "R&D component", "presence of R&D", "R&D alliances"]
definition: The presence of a shared research and development component in an alliance, covering basic R&D, product development, or elements of both; alliances with an R&D component are argued to have higher transaction costs than those that do not involve joint R&D.

name: Prior alliances between partners
authors_terms: ["repeated ties", "number of prior alliances", "prior alliances", "history of alliances"]
definition: The number of prior alliances two firms have had with each other; repeat alliances are treated as the factor most likely to produce interfirm trust between the partners.

name: Prior equity alliances between partners
authors_terms: ["repeated equity ties", "prior equity alliances", "prior equity-based ties", "repeated equity"]
definition: The number of prior equity alliances between two parties, including both the situation in which there are only prior equity alliances and that in which there have been mixed alliances.

name: Prior nonequity alliances between partners
definition: The number of prior nonequity alliances between two parties in the absence of any other ties; it does not include situations with mixed alliances.

name: International alliance
authors_terms: ["international alliance", "firms of different nations", "domestic or international"]
definition: An alliance among firms of different nationalities; firms are expected to trust domestic partners more than international partners because more and better information is available about domestic firms and the reputational consequences of opportunism are greater in a domestic context.

name: Multilateral alliance
definition: An alliance among more than two firms; multilateral alliances are argued to pose larger organizational problems and a heightened possibility of stalemates and conflicts than bilateral alliances.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was defined as average income growth during the five years prior to the measurement.

name: International interdependence
definition: Managing international interdependence is defined as the degree to which the performance of functional activities is coordinated or integrated among units located in different countries. International interdependence increases as an organization performs more of its activities in multiple international locations and those locations are coordinated or integrated.

name: Locus of control
definition: The locus of control dimension derives from Rotter's (1966) distinction between the internal and external control of reinforcement; the concept refers to individuals' perceptions about their control over events in life. A manager with an internal locus of control essentially sees outcomes as a result of personal initiatives; at the other extreme, the manager with an external locus perceives events as beyond his or her control.

name: Information-gathering style
definition: Sensation and intuition are alternate orientations toward information gathering. Sensing individuals are "detail persons" who prefer to use rules, regulations, and standardized procedures, whereas intuitive types tend to perceive problems as a whole, seeing integrative meanings and relationships rather than discrete details.

name: Information evaluation style
definition: The feeling and thinking information evaluation orientations are different approaches individuals use in making judgments. Feeling types tend to emphasize the personal and emotional content of decisions; thinking types evaluate information on the basis of formal systems of reasoning and process information analytically and impersonally.

name: Functional experience
definition: The breadth of a CEO's career experience across functional areas. The CEO in a firm with extensive international interdependence must understand the overall pattern of resource deployment for core functional activities, an understanding more likely developed when CEOs have a broad base of organizational experience.

name: International responsibility
definition: An understanding of international interdependence would presumably develop through direct responsibility for managing international functions and through international experience.

name: International experience
definition: Time spent on overseas assignments, through which managers increased their knowledge of international networks and developed informal information networks among managers.

name: CEO–interdependence fit
definition: A fit between international interdependence and CEO characteristics. The distance-effectiveness index compares the consistency of a CEO's characteristics, given a particular international interdependence state, to the ideal profile; as distance increases, fit decreases.

name: Leveraged buyout
definition: A leveraged buyout involves a swap of equity for debt; the group undertaking an LBO typically raises cash by issuing bonds and then uses that cash to buy the firm's stock, replacing its stockholders with bondholders and transforming the firm from a public to a private entity.

name: Debt
definition: By definition, a leveraged buyout is associated with an increase in debt; the change in debt is the difference between the total debt-to-equity ratio of a firm one year after its LBO and one year prior to it.

name: Management stockholdings
definition: The ratio of the value of management-owned shares or share equivalents (sometimes referred to as 'shadow stock') to total capitalization (total debt plus total equity); managers' stockholdings align their interests with those of the principals.

name: Emphasis on efficiency goals
authors_terms: ["efficiency goals", "emphasis on efficiency goals", "increased emphasis upon efficiency goals"]
definition: A scale containing three items - profitability, profit growth, and cash flow - measuring the emphasis placed on efficiency goals; the authors also refer to an increased emphasis upon financial criteria as efficiency goals.

name: Emphasis on growth and market share goals
authors_terms: ["growth goals", "growth and market share goals", "sales growth", "market share"]
definition: A two-item scale containing sales growth and market share, where the higher the score the greater the importance of these criteria as goals; under a pre-LBO governance structure managers are expected to emphasize sales growth, market share, and the like.

name: Diversified scope
authors_terms: ["diversified scope", "diversification", "reduction in scope", "Herfindahl index of diversification"]
definition: The extent of a firm's diversification, measured with a Herfindahl index of diversification; a reduction in scope occurs as the firm divests itself of diversified activities and refocuses on its strategic core.

name: Decentralization
definition: Decentralization, one way of releasing organizational efficiencies below the level of top management, allows individuals who are close to operations and the market to make decisions; it is measured as the extent to which operating decisions and strategic decisions are shared with lower-level managers rather than being the sole responsibility of the executive office.

name: Hierarchical complexity
definition: Organizational waste and inefficiency expected to exhibit itself in excessive organizational slack, in a tendency to add personnel and hierarchical layers, resulting in a higher 'head count', a 'taller' structure, and smaller spans of control than are optimal.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "change in performance", "labor productivity", "return on sales"]
definition: Change in performance was measured by the difference between the labor productivity of a firm one year after and one year prior to its LBO; labor productivity was measured by earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) over total labor costs, and the change in return on sales (EBIT/total sales) was also measured.

name: Industry information-processing load
definition: The information-processing load associated with an industry reflects the quantity and nature of relevant information and determines the difficulty of analyzing the competitive impact of an industry event. It depends on the multiplexity of information, the presence of simultaneous signals that compete for attention in the industry's environment.

name: Abnormal stock market returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "prediction error", "market value impact", "stockholder wealth creation"]
definition: The abnormal return is the difference between the actual return during the event period and the return predicted using the market model. The prediction error is assumed to represent the market value impact of the announcement.

name: Change in CEO salary
authors_terms: ["changes in CEO salary", "change in CEO compensation", "salary change"]
definition: Changes in CEO salary were measured as the percentage change in salary and bonus between a past and a present year; percentage change rather than the dollar amount of change was used because the former adjusts for salary differences across individuals.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm-specific performance is a measure of current compensation relative to the firm's past performance, and in this study firm performance was measured as net profit, return on equity, and earnings per share of common stock.

name: Relative firm performance
definition: Relative performance is performance judged in relation to concurrent industry-relative or market-relative performance; several relative performance measures can be computed: an intrafirm effect (measured over time), an industry effect, or an across-firms effect.

name: Firm size
definition: The second factor represents scale, and its highest factor loading is sales; sales was the net sales of a firm before extraordinary revenues.

name: Simplistic strategy-making process
authors_terms: ["simplicity", "simplistic strategy-making process", "simplicity as a strategy-making process", "simplicity in strategy making"]
definition: An overemphasis on the very things that made an organization successful in the first place, an 'overwhelming preoccupation with a single goal, strategic activity, department or worldview' that develops a value system and decision-making processes reflecting 'highly constrained values and strategies.' Simplicity suggests lack of variety and a narrow focus based on a small set of constraints and closely defined goals.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "sales growth", "profitability and return on investment", "overall company performance"]
definition: Executives assessed their organization's performance over the past five years relative to competitors on sales growth, profitability and return on investment, and overall company performance.

name: Stage of organizational development
definition: The phase an organization has reached in its development, identified by respondents as pre-start-up, start-up, accelerated growth, steady growth, stability, or decline; coherent stages of an organization's life cycle can be identified and performance varies in each phase.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism is characterized by uncertainty resulting from rapid growth, shifting trends, and frequent changes in customers' tastes or competitive tactics.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: Environmental heterogeneity is characterized by a wide array of customers and competitors and diversity in the type of marketing and production methods needed to cater to the different segments of a market.

name: Participative strategy-making process
definition: A strategy-making process including variables that clearly indicate a participative management style, such as business planning involving everyone in the organization and consensus and cooperation across departments and functional areas.

name: Innovative strategy-making process
definition: A strategy-making process characterized by innovation, risk taking, and entrepreneurship, including being very dynamic and entrepreneurial, encouraging experimentation, and willingness to take risks.

name: Adaptive strategy-making process
definition: An external orientation toward adapting to customer needs and responding to supplier feedback and environmental cues, including continually adapting based on feedback and spending time with customers and key stakeholders.

name: Performance group
definition: A set of firms whose performance levels are statistically indistinguishable from those of other firms in the group but are distinguishable from the performance levels of firms in other performance groups.

name: Performance group membership stability
authors_terms: ["stability of performance group membership", "stability of membership", "stability of the performance groups"]
definition: The degree to which firm memberships in performance groups persist over time; a high level of stability in performance group membership over time would indicate the presence of mobility barriers, and low stability would indicate that mobility barriers are not present in a significant fashion.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance levels obtained by firms; the central theme in the strategic groups literature is that strategic group membership has performance consequences, that is, strategic groups are characterized by performance levels that differ from the performance levels obtained by other strategic groups.

name: Board power relative to CEO
authors_terms: ["the power of a firm's board in relation to its existing CEO", "relative board power", "relative CEO/board power"]
definition: The extent of board influence over the CEO selection process relative to that of the incumbent CEO, reflected in CEO duality, relative tenure, board independence and outside director ownership. The authors argue that the relative power of the two parties predicts whose preferences for a new CEO are realized.

name: Change in CEO characteristics
authors_terms: ["change in CEO characteristics", "change in leader characteristics", "changes in fundamental top manager characteristics"]
definition: Demographic dissimilarity between an old and a new CEO; observing such dissimilarity (change in leader characteristics) is taken to indicate change in leader attitudes and behavioral tendencies.

name: CEO-board demographic similarity
authors_terms: ["CEO-board demographic similarity", "similarity between a new CEO and existing board members", "demographic similarity between a CEO and existing board members"]
definition: Demographic similarity between a firm's CEO and its board members, assessed by aggregating measures of the similarity of all CEO-board member dyads.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured both by a market-based measure (excess stock returns) and an operating measure (return on assets); higher values reflect better performance, and the variables are inverted in the interaction measure so that higher values reflect lower performance.

name: Outside succession
definition: Successor origin, indicating whether the new CEO was hired from outside the organization rather than promoted from within.

name: Cognitive conflict
definition: When conflict is functional, it is generally task oriented and focused on judgmental differences about how best to achieve common objectives. This type of conflict is called cognitive conflict (Amason & Schweiger, 1994).

name: Affective conflict
definition: When conflict is dysfunctional, it tends to be emotional and focused on personal incompatibilities or disputes. This type of conflict is called affective conflict (Amason & Schweiger, 1994).

name: Decision quality
definition: A perceptual measure of relative decision quality was used because an objective measure of the quality of a single decision is difficult to isolate.

name: Understanding of the decision
definition: The understanding measure gauged how similarly team members understood the rationale for their decision.

name: Commitment to the decision
definition: Commitment is important because it reduces the likelihood that a particular decision will become the target of cynicism or countereffort.

name: Affective acceptance
definition: To do this, team members must maintain affective relationships that allow them to work together effectively.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The degree of industry concentration, which is an indicator of the level of competition in an industry; high concentration implies high levels of competitive interdependence, which limits the range of competitive actions.

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: An indicator of barriers to industry entry that has an important impact on both industry profitability and firm behavior; a firm in a capital-intensive industry is generally committed to a course of action as capital intensity often creates rigidity.

name: Industry growth
definition: Industries experiencing rapid growth provide greater market opportunity and competitive variation and consequently, greater managerial discretion.

name: Demand instability
definition: Demand volatility, which results in an expanded set of options for key executives, reducing inertial tendencies.

name: Product differentiation
definition: Product differentiability, generally measured as industry advertising intensity, forms an important basis for competition in an industry; industries characterized by high differentiation offer more avenues for competition and exhibit a wider range of competitive actions.

name: CEO firm tenure
definition: The number of years a CEO had served in a firm; longer firm tenures have been associated with restricted information processing, increased cognitive rigidity, and commitment to established organizational policies and practices.

name: CEO educational level
definition: An indicator of an individual's various cognitive orientations; researchers have equated a high attained level with greater capacity for information processing and receptivity to innovation.

name: CEO throughput functional orientation
definition: The extent to which a CEO's functional background lies in throughput functions (production, process R&D, and accounting), which is regarded as an important indicator of the types of knowledge and cognitive biases top managers bring to their jobs.

name: CEO functional heterogeneity
definition: The variety of functions to which the CEO has been exposed during the length of his or her career, reflecting the breadth (or narrowness) of the individual's functional perspective.

name: Firm performance
definition: A composite measure of firm performance built from three financial measures of performance (return on sales, return on equity, and return on assets) standardized within each firm's industry and averaged.

name: CEO characteristics
authors_terms: ["CEO characteristics", "observable managerial characteristics", "observable background characteristics", "demographic characteristics"]
definition: Observable managerial characteristics such as tenure, education, and functional background, which represent key proxies for a CEO's cognitive orientation and knowledge base with important implications for strategic decision making.

name: Emphasis on franchising as expansion strategy
authors_terms: ["relative emphasis of a firm on expansion through franchising", "strategy", "expansion through franchising", "the degree to which a firm emphasizes franchising as its organizational form"]
definition: The predictor variable in this study was the relative emphasis of a firm on expansion through franchising, measured as the ratio of the number of new franchised outlets established to the number of new company-owned outlets established for the period prior to the one under study.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth", "growth in the number of franchised and company-owned outlets", "rate of growth in the number of outlets of a franchise system"]
definition: Growth was defined as the logarithm of the change in the number of outlets in a system from 1983 to the year under investigation.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["survival", "likelihood of survival", "survival of the franchise system"]
definition: The dependent variable survival was defined as the existence of the organization in the year under investigation.

name: Market domain overlap
definition: Market domain refers to the set of markets in which a firm operates; market domain overlap measures the potential for competition at the firm level, aggregating the overlap of a focal firm's market domain with the market domains of all other firms.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact measures the potential for mutual forbearance at the firm-market level, that is, one market in a firm's market domain; as multimarket contact between a focal firm and another firm increases, the likelihood that they will behave aggressively toward each other decreases.

name: Market entry rate
authors_terms: ["rate of market entry", "entry rate", "route entry rate", "market entry"]
definition: The rate at which a firm enters new markets; market entry provides a useful theoretical proxy for the intensity of rivalry, with higher entry rates meaning more intense rivalry.

name: Market exit rate
authors_terms: ["rate of market exit", "exit rate", "route exit rate", "market exit"]
definition: The rate at which a firm exits markets it currently serves; market exit provides a valuable proxy for the intensity of rivalry, the more intense the rivalry the higher the rate of defensive or conciliatory market exit.

name: Market density
definition: Market density is the number of firms operating in the market; when density is low an increase signals legitimacy and encourages entry, while at high density a crowding or competitive effect dominates.

name: Market dominance
definition: A firm's sphere of influence includes all markets in which it has the largest market share; the greater the number of firms with spheres of influence, the more prevalent reciprocal subordination and superordination, and thus mutual forbearance, become.

name: Market concentration
definition: Concentration in a market, a feature of oligopoly theory in which coordination derives from market concentration, small numbers of sellers each with market power.

name: Related diversification
definition: The strategy of related diversification enables firms to exploit economies of scope; related firms are identified by traditional measures such as Rumelt's categories or the entropy index.

name: Strategic relatedness
definition: Strategic relatedness is the degree to which competence in building the same class of strategic asset could add to competitive advantage in both markets, measured with a portfolio of indicators rather than only common inputs.

name: CM-form organizational structure
definition: In the centralized multidivisional (CM-form) organizational structure, the corporate center of a diversified firm exercises centralized strategic and financial control over the divisions and also intervenes in their operating decisions.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability is defined as return on sales (ROS).

name: Purchase infrequency
definition: The requirement for, and the ease with which, a relationship with customers can be built over time; goods purchased infrequently tend to involve bigger financial expenditures, so manufacturers must demonstrate superior quality and invest in after-sales support to induce trial.

name: Distributor-directed marketing
definition: The extent to which a manufacturer focuses its marketing and sales efforts on distributors or other intermediaries rather than on end users, as opposed to marketing directed at a large number of often less sophisticated end users.

name: Procedural rationality
definition: The extent to which the decision process involves the collection of information relevant to the decision and the reliance upon analysis of this information in making the choice. The term 'procedural' focuses on the decision-making process and distinguishes the construct from more global conceptions of rationality.

name: Political behavior
definition: Intentional acts of influence to enhance or protect the self-interest of individuals or groups. Two key ideas underlie the political dimension: people in organizations have differences in interests, and they try to influence decision outcomes so that their own interests will be served.

name: Strategic decision effectiveness
definition: The extent to which a decision achieves the objectives established by management at the time it is made. Effectiveness is conceptualized on the basis of managers' own goals because the intent was to examine managers' capacity to influence organizational outcomes through strategic choice.

name: Environmental instability
definition: The extent to which market demand and technology are rapidly changing in a given industry. When instability is high, demand fluctuates dramatically and new technologies are introduced at a rapid pace; when it is low, neither demand nor technology changes much over time.

name: Environmental favorability
definition: The extent to which environmental conditions subsequent to a decision favor the choice that was made. It is included to capture the influence of the environment on decision effectiveness.

name: Quality of decision implementation
definition: The competence with which the steps are taken to execute the strategic decision. It is included because of the potentially significant influence of implementation on the final effectiveness of strategic decisions.
