name: Insider equity ownership
authors_terms: ["insider equity ownership", "insider stock ownership", "equity ownership by corporate insiders", "insider share ownership", "level of equity ownership"]
definition: The degree of equity ownership of a firm held by its corporate insiders, who are the firm's top executives and the members of their boards of directors.

name: Corporate risk taking
authors_terms: ["corporate risk taking", "firm risk taking", "corporate risk-taking behavior", "risk taking"]
definition: We defined corporate risk taking as the analysis and selection of projects that have varying uncertainties associated with their expected outcomes and corresponding cash flows. The unpredictability in a firm's income stream is a result of its risk-taking behavior.

name: Blockholder equity ownership
authors_terms: ["equity ownership by blockholders", "blockholder share ownership", "blockholders' stock ownership", "large equity blockholders"]
definition: The level of equity ownership by blockholders, which the authors treat as large external shareholders whose stakes may have a contemporaneous or lagged impact on corporate risk taking.

name: Institutional equity ownership
authors_terms: ["equity ownership by institutional investors", "institutional ownership", "ownership by institutional investors"]
definition: The level of equity ownership of a firm held by institutional investors, who own substantial equity and for whom it is in their best interests to encourage firm strategies that capitalize on growth opportunities.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: Existence of growth opportunities, which firms may have because of valuable internal resources or locations in attractive industries; Tobin's q, defined as the market value of a firm standardized by the replacement cost of its assets, can represent the existence of growth opportunities, with q's in excess of unity indicating firms whose value is largely driven by growth opportunities.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["chief executive compensation", "CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "executive pay", "total compensation"]
definition: CEO pay is often viewed as consisting of (1) cash compensation and (2) long-term compensation, in the form of stock options, performance plans, restricted stock, and other long-term incentive plans; total compensation equals the sum of cash and long-term pay.

name: Number of businesses managed
authors_terms: ["number of businesses managed", "number of businesses", "a simple count of businesses", "number-of-businesses"]
definition: The number of businesses a firm manages, argued to raise the range and complexity of the nonroutine, strategic decisions a CEO must make and thus the amount of information that must be processed.

name: Conglomerate diversification strategy
definition: A diversification pattern in which top executives focus primarily on managing internal capital markets and run their businesses by the numbers through arm's-length financial control systems, as opposed to related diversifiers, which use strategic control systems requiring in-depth knowledge of business-level operating issues.

name: Top management team size
authors_terms: ["top management team size", "TMT size", "size of the dominant coalition"]
definition: The size of the top management team; increasing the size of the dominant coalition can reduce the number of decisions that must be made and monitored by the CEO and thus the information-processing demands confronting the CEO.

name: Capital investment activity
definition: Annual capital equipment expenditures divided by sales, an activity-based measure that captures the magnitude of consequential, nonroutine decisions made by a top executive in the recent past.

name: R&D activity
definition: Annual R&D expenditures divided by sales; high levels of R&D activity are typically associated with higher technological uncertainty, more sophisticated and differentiated products, more specialized personnel, and higher levels of intrafirm technology pooling.

name: Postentry performance
authors_terms: ["postentry performance", "postentry survival", "postentry sales growth", "postentry market share growth"]
definition: Postentry survival, growth in sales, and market share were used in this research to evaluate the performance of entrant businesses.

name: Fixed asset intensity in the entered industry
definition: The capital investment required to put in place one or more optimally sized plants; the greater this investment, the higher the incremental costs new entrants bear.

name: Selling intensity in entered industry
definition: Selling and distribution expenses per unit of sales in the destination industry.

name: Advertising intensity in entered industry
definition: Advertising expenditures per unit of sales in the destination industry.

name: Research and development intensity in entered industry
authors_terms: ["research and development intensity", "R&D intensity", "intensity of research and development"]
definition: R&D expenditures per unit of sales in the destination industry.

name: Seller concentration in entered industry
definition: High seller concentration is a situation in which a few incumbents have large market shares; it was measured as the combined market shares of the top four firms in the destination industry.

name: Scale of entry
definition: The scale at which entry is made; large-scale entry is often associated with large capital investment and was measured as the dollar sales made during an entrant's first year of operations.

name: Industry growth rate
definition: Industry shipments in 1982 over industry shipments in 1977.

name: Functional dissimilarity between parent firm and entered industry
definition: The difference in advertising, R&D, and fixed asset intensity between entered industry and entering firm.

name: Product relatedness
definition: The relatedness between an entrant business and the other business of its parent firm.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance is determined by the degree to which there are differences in the cultural characteristics common to the headquarters market and the market of the foreign subsidiary, and it is defined so as to reflect the difference between the cultures of the two countries in which the principal and agent are located.

name: Lateral centralization
definition: With lateral centralization a foreign subsidiary has worldwide responsibility for a complete set of value-adding activities associated with a specific product or product line; decision making is not centralized at headquarters but dispersed laterally throughout the organization, with responsibilities for the sets of value-adding activities for different products or product lines carried out at different subsidiary locations.

name: Parent commitment
definition: Parent commitment is the psychological identification of a foreign manager with headquarters.

name: Agency problem
definition: The agency problem arises from incongruence between the goals of principal and agent and because of difficulty in monitoring or verifying agent behavior; in the headquarters-foreign subsidiary relationship it is determined by information asymmetries and goal incongruence.

name: Senior management pay mix
definition: Senior management pay mix is the proportion of senior subsidiary management's total compensation paid through incentive-based forms rather than fixed salary.

name: Market positioning
definition: Market positioning is the extent to which the pay level of the subsidiary was above or below that of competitors.

name: Subsidiary pay mix
definition: Subsidiary pay mix is the percentage of total compensation paid by the subsidiary through incentive-based compensation forms to all employees.

name: Salary adjustment criteria
authors_terms: ["salary adjustment criteria", "senior management salary adjustment criteria"]
definition: Salary adjustment criteria concern the basis for evaluating senior subsidiary management performance for salary adjustments; the construct reflects the reward alignment for the nonincentive compensation component and is the aggregate percentage of the salary adjustment criteria given to regional and corporate performance.

name: Incentive alignment
definition: Incentive alignment is the degree to which a compensation system is designed to induce a subsidiary's management to make decisions that are in the best interests of headquarters.

name: Perceived subsidiary effectiveness
definition: Perceived subsidiary effectiveness is the desired outcome expected by the principal, defined by the performance dimensions a principal expects, since subsidiaries can be evaluated on a wide range of performance dimensions.

name: Corporate political involvement
authors_terms: ["political involvement", "corporate political involvement", "political activity", "corporate political strategy"]
definition: Corporate political strategies are a pattern in a stream of managerial decisions that represent an integrated set of activities within a firm intended to produce public policy outcomes favorable to the firm's economic survival and continued success. For the present study, corporate political involvement entails a firm's activities aimed at achieving sector-specific policy outcomes, such as trade policy for a single industry.

name: Relative firm size
authors_terms: ["relative size in the industry", "market share", "firm size"]
definition: The relative size of a firm provides one indication of its incentive to participate in providing a collective good for its industry. In Olson's framework, the returns from a collective good will increase with firm size.

name: Related business diversification
definition: Related diversification implies that synergy can be realized across business units through economies of scope or the sharing of resources and capabilities across businesses. A firm that operates wholly in a single line of business or that has a high degree of vertical integration or related diversification is likely to anticipate greater benefits from a sector-specific public policy than a firm with a wide range of unrelated business.

name: Dedicated organizational political units
authors_terms: ["dedicated organizational political units (structures)", "dedicated in-house political relations unit", "Washington, DC, office"]
definition: The organizational structure of interest dedicated to politics is a firm's Washington, DC, office. The hierarchy, or organizational structure, is the formal segmentation of work into roles, such as production and marketing.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Organizational slack is the cushion of actual or potential resources that allows an organization to alter strategies in response to internal or external pressures for adjustment. The present study adopts Singh's (1986) view that a firm requires a certain level of resources to engage in political actions.

name: Import penetration
authors_terms: ["import penetration", "share of imports in the U.S. market", "heightened competitive pressures from foreign imports"]
definition: Heightened competitive pressures from foreign imports, which is analogous to an increase of supply in the domestic market. It is expected that firms will undertake political strategies in an attempt to rectify supply increases from foreign firms (i.e., imports).

name: Domestic demand
authors_terms: ["domestic demand", "level of domestic steel demand", "domestic consumption"]
definition: Changes in consumption in the domestic market, particularly downward swings in domestic demand. Low levels of consumption—which decrease the demand in the domestic market—should trigger firms' political involvement.

name: Strategic human resource practices
definition: Strategic HR practices are those that are theoretically or empirically related to overall organization performance. Seven practices are consistently considered strategic HR practices: internal career opportunities, formal training systems, appraisal measures, profit sharing, employment security, voice mechanisms, and job definition.

name: Internal career opportunities
authors_terms: ["internal career opportunities", "internal career ladders", "internal labor markets"]
definition: The first practice, internal career opportunities, refers to the use of internal labor markets. In other words, organizations can choose to hire predominantly from within or from outside.

name: Formal training systems
definition: The second practice, training systems, refers to the amount of formal training given to employees. Organizations can provide extensive formal training or rely on acquiring skills through selection and some socialization.

name: Results-oriented appraisal
definition: Appraisals can be based on results or behavior. Behavior-based appraisals focus on the behaviors of individuals necessary to perform the job effectively, whereas results-oriented appraisals focus merely on the consequences of those behaviors.

name: Profit sharing
definition: Fourth, profit-sharing plans, which tie pay to organizational performance, have been seen as an integral part of a strategic HR system. Profit sharing was measured as the extent to which employees received bonuses based on an organization's profit.

name: Employment security
definition: The degree to which employees are given employment security has many strategic implications. Employment security was conceptualized as the degree to which an employee could expect to stay in his or her job over an extended period of time.

name: Employee voice
definition: Sixth, voice mechanisms, both formal grievance systems and participation in decision making, have emerged as key factors. Employee participation, or voice, was defined as the degree to which employees were allowed to have input into their work and the degree to which the organization valued their input.

name: Job definition
authors_terms: ["job definition", "job description", "broadly defined jobs", "tightly defined jobs"]
definition: Finally, the degree to which jobs are tightly or narrowly defined is important. Tightly defined jobs are those in which the employees know the content of their jobs exactly; the job is limited in scope, and incumbents do not perform duties that are not considered part of the job.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "return on average assets (ROA)", "return on equity (ROE)"]
definition: The current study incorporated two financial measures important to the banking industry as dependent variables: return on average assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE). The financial measures were obtained from the Sheshunoff Bank Search database.

name: Business strategy
authors_terms: ["organization's strategy", "firm strategy", "strategic contingency", "rate of product/market innovation", "innovation"]
definition: The organization's strategy is considered to be the primary contingency factor in the SHRM literature. Following previous contingency interpretations of Miles and Snow's theory, the strategic contingency variable was defined as rate of product/market innovation.

name: Employment system fit
authors_terms: ["configurational fit", "ideal-types fit", "contingent ideal-types fit", "contingent hybrid-types fit", "similarity to the ideal employment system"]
definition: We computed the measures of configurational fit that assessed the similarity of an organization to an ideal profile using the mathematical models presented by Doty and associates. Ideal-types fit was operationally defined as the additive inverse of the deviation between a real organization's employment system and the ideal employment system that the organization most closely resembled.

name: Human resource system
authors_terms: ["human resource systems", "HR systems", "bundles of HR practices", "systems of HR practices", "internally consistent systems"]
definition: Internally consistent systems, or bundles, of human resource practices; the authors argue firms should create a high degree of internal consistency, or fit, among their HR activities.

name: Human-capital-enhancing human resource system
definition: Human-capital-enhancing HR systems-those with such features as selective staffing, selection for technical and problem-solving skills, comprehensive training, training for technical and problem-solving skills, developmental and behavior-based performance appraisal, group incentives, and salaried compensation-focus on skill acquisition and development.

name: Administrative human resource system
definition: Administrative HR systems (i.e., selection for manual skills, policies and procedures training, results-based performance appraisal, hourly pay, and individual incentives) are consistent with the requirements of a cost strategy focused on standardizing processes, reducing errors, and maximizing production efficiency.

name: Operational performance
definition: Each plant's current performance relative to other firms in its industry in terms of product quality, employee morale, on-time delivery, inventory management, employee productivity, equipment utilization, production lead time, and scrap minimization.

name: Customer alignment
definition: One of three stable performance factors revealed by factor analysis; customer alignment is represented by items such as product quality and on-time delivery.

name: Employee productivity
definition: One of three stable performance factors revealed by factor analysis; employee productivity is represented by items such as employee morale and employee productivity.

name: Machine efficiency
definition: One of three stable performance factors revealed by factor analysis; machine efficiency is represented by items such as equipment utilization and scrap minimization.

name: Manufacturing strategy
definition: Manufacturing strategy was measured by items that operationally defined potential competitive priorities in manufacturing, including cost, quality, and flexibility; researchers have typically focused on three primary manufacturing strategies: cost, quality, and flexibility.

name: Cost manufacturing strategy
definition: The cost dimension was made up of items dealing with low labor, material, and unit costs.

name: Quality manufacturing strategy
definition: The quality factor was comprised of virtually every quality-related item on the list (e.g., dependability, product performance).

name: Flexibility manufacturing strategy
definition: Flexibility refers to a firm's agility, adaptability, and responsiveness; factor analysis produced two distinct dimensions of flexibility, delivery flexibility and scope flexibility.

name: Human resource value
authors_terms: ["human resource value", "HR value", "the degree to which a company values employees as a specialized asset"]
definition: The degree to which a company values employees as a specialized asset, captured as variance in the degree to which firms consider employees important to business. A firm's strategy, mission statement, and operating practices should reflect that value.

name: Organization-based rewards
authors_terms: ["organization-based rewards", "organization-based compensation programs", "organization-based employee rewards", "firm-based employee rewards"]
definition: Compensation systems based on organizational performance (such as stock options and profit sharing) that link all employees to a firm and its mission, thus encouraging collective action. Employers can design such systems for all employees or for only management teams.

name: Organizational survival
definition: A dependent variable reflecting long-term performance: all firms still in business at year-end 1993 were coded as survivors. Survival status is not easily determined, so several steps were taken to assure correct identification of survivors.

name: Perceived market potential
authors_terms: ["perceived potential of the firm", "investor reaction", "initial performance", "perceived market potential"]
definition: The perceived potential value of a firm as judged by initial investors, measured by the amount of the stock price that is above and beyond book value and by the ratio of initial stock price to book value.

name: Progressive HRM practices
authors_terms: ["progressive HRM practices", "high performance HRM practices", "HRM systems", "HRM practices"]
definition: Conceptually, such practices can be classified in terms of their impact on employees' skills and ability, motivation, and the way that work is structured. Taken as a whole, the seven practice items provide a reasonably broad reflection of the progressive HRM practices that have been identified in the literature.

name: Organizational advancement opportunities
authors_terms: ["organizational advancement opportunities", "internal labor markets", "employment security", "promotion opportunities"]
definition: Internal labor markets for employee promotions and the provision of employment security are also forms of work structure that have been held to positively affect firm performance; the available data were used to create two alternative indicators of organizational advancement opportunities.

name: Complementarity among HRM practices
definition: Complementarities, or synergies, among a firm's HRM practices can have an additional and positive effect on firm performance; the returns from investing in progressive HRM practices are enhanced to the degree a firm invests in such practices at a uniform (and high) level throughout.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["perceptual measures of organizational performance", "perceived organizational performance", "perceived market performance", "perceptions of performance"]
definition: Perceptual measures of organizational performance that are relative, or benchmarked, in the sense that they are derived from questions asking informants to assess organizational performance relative to the performance of industry competitors.

name: Early retirement program announcement
authors_terms: ["announcement of an early retirement program", "early retirement program announcements", "offering early retirement"]
definition: Offering early retirement is an increasingly popular way to terminate the 'lifetime' wage contract between employer and employee, and it is used as a human resources strategic response to changes in the business environment; day 0 is defined as the announcement day of such a program.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market's reaction", "market reaction", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: Stock market reactions depend on investors' perceptions of an event's positive or negative effects on the value of a firm; the market reaction to these announcements can be interpreted as investors' unbiased estimate of the announcement's incremental effect on firm financial performance.

name: Institutional rationale for the workforce reduction
definition: If a reason was provided for the early retirement program, it typically was either cost cutting in response to decline, or broader corporate restructuring; organizational downsizing is either 'reorientation' or 'convergence,' convergence being a defensive reaction to decline focusing on internal efficiency through cost cutting.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: Prior firm performance was assessed with the firm's profit margin in the year of the announcement and two years prior, and with abnormal stock returns in the year preceding the announcement, over the period days -240 to -20.

name: Percentage of employees offered the program
authors_terms: ["percentage of employees offered the program", "percentage of employees eligible for an announced program", "percentage of employees involved"]
definition: The percentage of employees eligible for an announced early retirement program, which ranged from programs that rounded to 0 percent up to those including 33 percent of a firm's employees.

name: Strategic isomorphism
definition: Organizational isomorphism is defined as the resemblance of a focal organization to other organizations in its environment; strategic isomorphism is the similarity of a focal organization's strategy to the strategies of other organizations in its industry. Isomorphism is conceptualized here as a state, the similarity among a set of organizations at a given point in time.

name: Regulatory endorsement
authors_terms: ["regulatory endorsement", "regulatory assessment of total capital", "absence of regulatory enforcement actions"]
definition: Regulatory endorsement is the acceptance of an organization by the state agencies that formally regulate it. Regulators evaluate commercial banks by examining banks' financial capital and by examining them on-site.

name: Public endorsement
definition: Public endorsement is the acceptance of an organization by the general public. It is measured from articles in the print media using content analysis, since media influence and reflect the values of a culture.

name: Acquisition intensity
definition: The extent of a firm's participation in acquiring businesses, captured by the number of acquisitions completed and the percentage of sales acquired.

name: Divestiture intensity
definition: The extent of a firm's selling of business units, captured by the number of divestitures made and the percentage of sales divested.

name: Strategic controls
definition: Strategic controls entail the use of long-term and strategically relevant criteria for the evaluation of business-level managers' actions and performance.

name: Financial controls
definition: Financial controls entail objective criteria such as return on investment (ROI) in the evaluation of business-level managers' performance.

name: Internal innovation
authors_terms: ["internal innovation", "internal firm innovation", "internal development of innovation"]
definition: Internal innovation refers to the development and introduction of new products and processes.

name: External innovation
definition: External innovation is the acquisition of innovation from outside, such as acquiring firms with new products or processes.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "market share in excess of what one would expect", "premium that cannot be explained simply on the basis of price"]
definition: The difference between a firm's predicted market share in each year and its realized market share, a premium that cannot be explained simply on the basis of price. The measure calculates relative performance in competition, advantage in a highly standardized market.

name: Technology adoption lag
authors_terms: ["technology adoption lag", "whether and when to adopt the new generation", "delaying innovation", "the faster a firm adopts a new generation of technology"]
definition: The delay between the appearance of a new generation of technology and a firm's adoption of it; incumbents face the decisions of whether and when to adopt the new generation, and delaying innovation may carry a penalty.

name: Technology leadership relative to local rivals
authors_terms: ["higher innovativeness", "the proportion of local rivals that are at least one technology generation behind it"]
definition: The extent to which a firm has adopted newer generations of technology than the other firms in its niche; a firm benefits from adopting new technology to the extent that it is differentiated within its niche, and those adopting before their local rivals may capture a variety of benefits.

name: Technology lag relative to local rivals
authors_terms: ["lower innovativeness", "the proportion of local rivals that are at least one technology generation ahead of it"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's local rivals that are at least one technology generation ahead of it. Advantages from moving early need not be symmetrical with disadvantages of moving late.

name: Differentiation within a niche
authors_terms: ["differentiation within a niche", "average distance in resource space from others in the same niche"]
definition: A firm's average distance in resource space from the other firms in its own niche. Strong performers distance themselves in resource space as much as they can from local rivals, and differentiation matters most within a niche.

name: Differentiation across niches
authors_terms: ["differentiation across niches", "average distance in resource space from firms in other niches"]
definition: A firm's average distance in resource space from firms outside its own niche; with respect to competitors outside the niche, what matters is the structural relationship among niches, not how distant the firm is from nonlocal rivals.

name: Niche change
definition: A firm's move from one niche cluster to another between two years, whether through action or inaction. Firms that switch niches may incur costs such as loss of valuable niche-specific experience, increased uncertainty in a new environment, and costly investment in new capabilities.

name: Niche tenure
definition: The length of a firm's continuous experience in the same niche. Niche tenure reflects learning about niche conditions in general, and the longer a firm accumulates experience in a particular niche the more it can reduce uncertainty and develop valuable, specialized assets.

name: Niche density
definition: The number of firms in a firm's niche. Ecological theory suggests that organizations in more densely populated environments are less successful, and the more competitors a firm has the more difficult it becomes to steer rivalry away from perfect competition.

name: Munificence growth
definition: Munificence generally means a high ratio of resources to the number of rivals competing for them; the authors focus on growth in munificence, positive change in munificence over time that makes a niche structurally favorable.

name: Stable rivals in a niche
authors_terms: ["stable rivals", "proportion of rivals in a firm's niche during period t that were also in its niche during period t - 1"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's niche contains a stable set of rivals from period to period. As local rivals become more familiar, managers grow increasingly able to accurately gauge the intentions of their competition and to make appropriate decisions.

name: Density of other niches
authors_terms: ["density of other niches", "aggregate density of other niches"]
definition: The number of firms in the market outside a given firm's niche, a measure of marketwide competition that complements niche density. The authors argue that performance will rise or fall not with higher density in other niches, but with the relationship of its focal niche with other niches.

name: Prior original design sponsorship
authors_terms: ["firms that have previously created one or more designs", "firms that have pioneered previous designs", "former sponsors", "existing sponsors"]
definition: There are two possible sources of new designs: new entrants and firms that have previously created one or more designs. Once a firm introduces a design, it remains bound to it, so subsequent products share at least some technical compatibility with its initial design.

name: New design introduction
authors_terms: ["new designs", "original designs", "proliferation of new designs", "technological variation"]
definition: An important source of technological variation is the proliferation of new designs, each of which represents a potential technological trajectory for an industry; each introduced design is supported by a community of organizations that have a stake in the design.

name: Technological community density
authors_terms: ["density of technological communities", "density of design communities", "density of sponsor communities", "number of communities"]
definition: The density of design communities was operationally defined as the number of designs currently in the market and was updated quarterly; the density of sponsor communities was measured as the number of sponsors in the market and was updated quarterly. At low levels of density legitimation processes dominate, causing founding rates to rise, whereas at high levels of density competition dominates and founding rates fall.

name: Sponsor entry rate
authors_terms: ["rate of sponsor entry", "entry rate of sponsors", "entry rate of new sponsors"]
definition: Sponsors are firms that design and produce an original microprocessor. Entries were defined as occurring when a firm first put a product into production.

name: Second-source density
authors_terms: ["density of second sources supporting existing communities", "number of second sources", "second-source support"]
definition: Second sources are firms that copy an existing microprocessor design. A large number of second sources in the market may imply that there are large numbers of customers locked in to existing designs, creating poor opportunities for entrants sponsoring new designs.

name: Emergence of a dominant technological community
authors_terms: ["dominant design", "dominant technological community", "dominant-design community", "market concentration", "market share of the largest community"]
definition: The emergence of a dominant design signals the emergence of a dominant-design community, since the design forms the center of the community. Emergence of a dominant design was coded as a dummy variable after a single technological community achieved a 50 percent or greater market share, and concentration was captured by the market share of the largest community.

name: Specialist sponsor entry
definition: The emergence of a dominant design or, correspondingly, an increase in concentration might lead to an increase in the number of sponsors whose designs cater to specialist applications; such entrants serve the high end of the market, in which performance has the highest priority.

name: Adverse environmental conditions at founding
authors_terms: ["environmental conditions at founding", "adverse environmental founding conditions", "adverse founding conditions", "environmental adversity at founding", "high-adversity environments", "adverse environmental conditions at founding"]
definition: The environmental conditions that prevail at the time an organization is founded. Adverse founding conditions are conditions such as high organizational density, high competitive intensity, and political turmoil that are expected to have persistent effects on organizational mortality rates.

name: Founding density
authors_terms: ["density at founding", "founding density", "density at the time of founding"]
definition: Density at the time of founding is the number of organizations in a population when an organization is founded. Periods of high density are likely to be characterized by resource scarcity and tight niche packing.

name: Competitive intensity at founding
authors_terms: ["competitive intensity at founding", "age-based competitive intensity", "competitive intensity based on the experience of competitors", "aggregate age of competitors"]
definition: Competitive intensity at founding is the competitive pressure generated against a new organization by its competitors in the year of founding. Older organizations generate stronger competition because they fit their environment better than younger organizations.

name: Political turmoil at founding
authors_terms: ["political turmoil at founding", "years of political turmoil", "periods of political turmoil"]
definition: Political turmoil reflects an environmental discontinuity in that it alters links between social groups and societal resources. Newspapers founded during years of political turbulence are usually established for specific political purposes and therefore become irrelevant once the political crisis is resolved.

name: Organizational mortality rate
authors_terms: ["organizational mortality rate", "mortality rate", "death rate", "initial mortality rate", "asymptotic mortality rate", "asymptotic death rate"]
definition: The instantaneous rate at which organizations in a population fail at a given organizational age. Following Makeham's law, the mortality rate is decomposed into an initial mortality rate, an asymptotic death rate, and the speed with which the asymptotic death rate is reached.

name: Organizational age
definition: The age of an organization, that is, the time elapsed since its founding. Research on a wide variety of organizations has shown that mortality rates tend to decline with organizational age, an effect Stinchcombe labeled the liability of newness.

name: Organizational niche overlap density
definition: The overlap density of an organization is the aggregate of the resource overlaps of its organizational niche with those of all other population members; it estimates the potential competition faced by the organization.

name: Organizational niche nonoverlap density
definition: Nonoverlap density is the aggregate of the resource nonoverlaps; it is an estimate of the number of organizations whose resource requirements do not overlap with those of the focal organization.

name: Organizational niche differentiation
definition: Organizational niche differentiation refers to the degree of resource nonoverlap among potential competitors, and is measured as nonoverlap intensity, the sum of an organization's ratios of organizational niche nonoverlaps to overlaps with all other potentially competing population members.

name: Institutional embeddedness
definition: Institutional embeddedness refers to connections between a population and its institutional environment; the authors operationally define it as relational density, the number of formal relations between the members of a population and key institutions in the population's environment, where key institutions refer to government agencies and community organizations.

name: Organizational founding rate
definition: The likelihood that organizing attempts result in successful foundings, measured as the yearly numbers of nonprofit and for-profit day care center foundings that occurred in each organizational niche in each of Metropolitan Toronto's six constituent cities.

name: Profit orientation
definition: Profit orientation is the dimension along which the competitive orientations and social legitimacy of organizations in the nonprofit and for-profit sectors differ; it adds a behavioral dimension to the operational definition of the organizational niche, since niches are defined both by where organizations are located and how they are expected to behave within the resource space.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
definition: Corporate entrepreneurship is defined here as consisting of innovation aimed at business creation and venturing, and strategic renewal; a review of the literature by Guth and Ginsberg concluded that corporate entrepreneurship has two dimensions: innovation aimed at business creation and venturing, and strategic renewal.

name: Innovation
definition: As a component of corporate entrepreneurship, innovation is a company's commitment to creating and introducing products, production processes, and organizational systems.

name: Corporate venturing
definition: Venturing means that the firm will enter new businesses by expanding operations in existing or new markets.

name: Strategic renewal
definition: Strategic renewal refers to revitalizing the company's operations by changing the scope of its business, its competitive approach, or both; strategic renewal also means building or acquiring new capabilities and then creatively leveraging them to add value for shareholders.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["ratio of outsiders on a company's board", "outsider ratio", "representation of outside directors", "outside directors' board representation"]
definition: The representation of outside directors on a board; a high ratio of outside directors on a board can expand the base of expertise from which a firm's CEO can draw, enhance objectivity in board deliberations, strengthen the system of corporate checks and balances, and increase directors' independence.

name: Outside director stock ownership
authors_terms: ["stock ownership by outside directors", "outsider equity ownership", "outside directors' stock ownership"]
definition: Outside directors' equity interest in the company; outside directors who hold ownership interests will be motivated to monitor a CEO and will thus become more involved with a firm's operations.

name: Executive stock ownership
definition: The percentage of a company's total stock held by its senior executives, defined as vice presidents and those in higher offices.

name: Long-term institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["long-term institutional stock ownership", "long-term institutional investors", "long-term ownership"]
definition: Ownership by institutional investors with long investment horizons, including mutual, pension, and retirement funds whose managers may be primarily interested in improving their portfolios' long-term value.

name: Short-term institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["short-term institutional stock ownership", "short-term institutional owners", "short-term institutional investors"]
definition: Ownership by institutional investors with short investment horizons, such as investment banks and private funds, whose managers are evaluated quarterly and usually focus on maximizing their portfolios' annual performance.

name: Technological opportunities
authors_terms: ["technological opportunities", "perceived technological opportunities", "level of perceived technological opportunities"]
definition: Technological opportunities are defined as executives' perceptions of ability to support and generate growth opportunities through product and process innovations; industries with high levels of perceived technological opportunities are usually characterized by rapid and frequent product and process technology introductions and high levels of R&D spending and patenting.

name: International joint venture longevity
definition: Longevity was defined as the number of years a venture persisted.

name: International wholly owned subsidiary experience
authors_terms: ["international wholly owned subsidiary experience", "experience with international wholly owned subsidiaries"]
definition: Experience with international wholly owned subsidiaries was measured as the number of previous such affiliates a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.

name: Domestic joint venture experience
authors_terms: ["domestic joint venture experience", "experience with domestic joint ventures"]
definition: Experience with domestic joint ventures was measured as the number of previous such affiliates a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.

name: International joint venture experience
authors_terms: ["international joint venture experience", "previous international joint venture experience"]
definition: Experience with international joint ventures was measured as the number of previous such affiliates a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance has been defined as "the sum of factors creating, on the one hand, a need for knowledge, and on the other hand, barriers to knowledge flow and hence also for other flows between the home and the target countries." Cultural difference scores unavailable from Hofstede's published work were obtained via personal communication with that author.

name: Collaborative know-how
definition: A construct that measures the extent to which firms have skill in identifying, negotiating, managing, monitoring, and terminating collaborations. It is a complex, multifaceted construct that can be thought of along four fundamental phases of a collaboration cycle: identifying and selecting potential collaborators, negotiating the terms and structure of an agreement, monitoring and managing an ongoing collaboration, and terminating a collaboration.

name: Collaborative experience
definition: Collaborative experience involves many aspects of a firm's collaborative history; it is determined not only by the frequency with which a firm has collaborated with other firms, but also by the intensity, longevity, and types of the collaborations. The construct should reflect all previous experiences of a firm in interfirm collaborations.

name: Tangible collaborative benefits
definition: Tangible benefits are strategic and financial: generating additional profits, improving market share, and sustaining competitive advantage, for instance.

name: Intangible collaborative benefits
definition: Intangible benefits are learning or knowledge-based: learning specific skills and competencies, learning about interfirm cooperation, and learning how to behave cooperatively; or, in an emerging area of interest to both scholars and practitioners, simply learning how to learn from collaborations.

name: Multinational diversity
definition: Multinational diversity is the number of different national settings in which a firm operated at the time of an expansion; it was measured by the number of countries in which the firm had established subsidiaries at the time of the expansion.

name: Product diversity
definition: Product diversity was measured by the number of three-digit Standaard Bedrijfs Indeling (SBI) codes in which the firm was active at the time of the expansion.

name: Foreign entry mode
authors_terms: ["mode of foreign entry", "start-up or acquisition", "whether ventures are set up from scratch or whether they are acquired"]
definition: When a firm expands into a foreign market by establishing a local subsidiary, it has to decide whether to start a new venture or acquire an existing local company. A venture was called an acquisition if it entailed the takeover of another company (or one of its business units) in which the Dutch firm did not previously have an ownership stake; it was called a start-up if it was a subsidiary newly established by the Dutch firm, alone or with one or more partners.

name: Product relatedness
definition: An expansion was coded as horizontal if it took place within the same three-digit SBI category as the core activities of the firm, as related if it took place within the same two-digit SBI category but not in the same three-digit category, as vertical if it took place within the firm's value-added chain, and as unrelated if none of the other three categories applied.

name: Degree of internationalization
definition: A firm's degree of internationalization reflects its dependence on foreign markets for customers and factors of production, and the geographical dispersion of this dependence.

name: CEO long-term pay mix
authors_terms: ["long-term pay mix", "percentage of CEO compensation paid in long-term forms", "CEO long-term compensation"]
definition: Long-term pay mix was the proportion of total compensation paid in long-term forms (e.g., stock options, restricted stock, and long-term incentive plans) and was calculated as long-term compensation divided by total compensation.

name: CEO compensation level
authors_terms: ["level of CEO pay", "total level of its CEO's compensation", "CEO compensation level"]
definition: CEO compensation level was measured as the logarithm of the total of all forms of compensation granted during 1992.

name: Top management team size
authors_terms: ["TMT size", "top management team size", "executive team size"]
definition: TMT size refers to how many people comprise the top management team.

name: CEO duality
definition: Duality describes the situation in which an executive holds both the CEO and chairperson of the board positions.

name: Board size
definition: Board size was the number of members of a board of directors.

name: Board outsider representation
authors_terms: ["board structure", "proportion of outsiders on a board", "representation of insiders on the board"]
definition: Board structure was the proportion of board members who were outsiders. Insiders were executives of a firm who also served on the board of directors, and outsiders were board members not otherwise employed by the firm.

name: Network size
definition: The size of an organization's network of direct ties, i.e. the number of organizations in the focal organization's consortium.

name: Network heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["network heterogeneity/homogeneity", "enrollment heterogeneity in network", "tuition heterogeneity in network", "homogeneous networks", "social similarity within a network"]
definition: The degree of social dissimilarity among the organizations in a focal organization's network; the authors measure it as the dispersion of members' enrollments and tuition charges.

name: Network age
authors_terms: ["network age", "older networks", "age of a network tie"]
definition: The age of a network tie, which the authors describe as a defining characteristic of tie strength, measured as time since a consortium's founding.

name: Adoption of core adaptive change
authors_terms: ["professional program adoption", "adoption of professional programs", "first-time adoption", "adapt their core features"]
definition: The adoption of undergraduate professional programs, a mission-redefining curricular change that responds to environmental change.

name: Number of adopters in network
authors_terms: ["number of adopters in network", "number of prior adopters", "number of its network ties adopting some practice"]
definition: The number of colleges in a focal college's association that had previously adopted a specific program.

name: Previous adopters' size
authors_terms: ["adopters' size", "mean size of previous adopters", "larger network contacts"]
definition: The size (enrollment) of the network contacts that had previously adopted the practice in question.

name: Previous adopters' prestige
authors_terms: ["adopters' prestige", "prestige of earlier adopters", "more prestigious network contacts"]
definition: The prominence or status of the network contacts that had previously adopted the practice, captured by their reputational ranking scores.

name: Previous adopters' performance
authors_terms: ["adopters' performance", "performance outcomes obtained by early adopters", "responses have been more successful"]
definition: The performance outcomes that prior adopters of a practice within the focal organization's network obtained with that response.

name: Similarity to previous adopters
authors_terms: ["similarity to previous adopters", "enrollment similarity to adopters", "tuition similarity to adopters", "similarity between a focal organization and prior adopters"]
definition: The similarity between the focal organization and previous adopters of a practice within its network, inferred from enrollment and tuition similarity.

name: Performance below aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below aspiration level", "budget deficit", "substandard performance", "financial distress"]
definition: Substandard performance relative to aspirations, inferred when a focal college suffered a budget deficit in a given year.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact refers to firms' engaging each other simultaneously in more than one distinct product and/or geographic market. It is a property of the relationship between two firms, not of markets or industries.

name: Initiation of multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["initiation of multimarket contact", "creating multimarket contact", "come into multimarket contact"]
definition: The creation of multimarket contact between a pair of firms, explicitly taking into account which (if either) firm in a given dyad acted to create the multimarket contact.

name: Expansion of multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["expansion of multimarket contact", "expand its level of multimarket contact"]
definition: An increase in the level of multimarket contact between airline i and competitor j after multimarket contact has been established between them.

name: Number of markets served
authors_terms: ["number of markets served", "number of routes served", "number of routes"]
definition: The number of markets in which a firm operates; firms serving many markets are more likely to exhibit multimarket contact because they are likely to encounter competitors in multiple markets, given the sheer number of markets in which they operate.

name: Market entry rate
authors_terms: ["market entry rates", "entries into competitor j's routes", "market entry"]
definition: The number of entries a firm makes into additional markets; as firms enter additional markets they come into contact with new competitors and reencounter firms they already meet in other markets.

name: Market capacity
authors_terms: ["market capacity", "average route capacity", "capacity of the markets served"]
definition: The munificence of markets: high-capacity markets are those sufficiently munificent to sustain large numbers of competitors, whereas low-capacity markets may be viable operating environments for only a few competitors.

name: Competitor size
definition: The size of a competitor, one of the firm traits (such as size, prestige, and success) that affect the likelihood that a firm's actions and practices will be imitated; large, high-performing firms are likely targets of imitation because their success signals that they have done something right to gain access to resources and to satisfy constituents.

name: Competitor operational performance
authors_terms: ["performance of competitor j", "airline operational performance", "passenger load factor", "high-performing firms"]
definition: The operational performance of a competitor; large, high-performing firms are likely targets of imitation, and imitation of firms with superior access to resources may also satisfy firms' quests for legitimacy.

name: Multimarket contact among other firms
authors_terms: ["frequency-based imitation", "extent to which other firms in their industry engage in multimarket contact", "average multimarket contact in other dyads", "frequency-by-trait-based imitation"]
definition: The prevalence of multimarket contact among other firms in the industry, which is the basis for frequency-based imitation: as multimarket contacts among firms increase, others are more likely to observe such behavior, come to believe in its competitive value, and strive to develop multimarket contacts of their own.

name: Prior multimarket contact experience
authors_terms: ["experiential learning", "average MMC with competitors other than j", "number of firms other than competitor j with which firm i has engaged in multimarket contact"]
definition: The extent of a firm's own prior experience with multimarket contact with firms other than the focal competitor; organizations are routine-based, experiential learning systems that adapt incrementally to past experience, and the more experienced a firm becomes with a particular strategy, the more likely it will be to use the strategy again.

name: Selective search
definition: The intentional targeting of specific competitors for the creation and expansion of multimarket contact: if firms experienced in multimarket contact targeted each other for creation and expansion of such contact, there would be strong evidence of the intentional pursuit of multimarket contact designed to capitalize on mutual forbearance.

name: Foreign expansion
authors_terms: ["foreign expansion", "expansion into foreign markets", "expand into foreign countries", "expansion activities in foreign countries"]
definition: Expansion of the chain's operations into countries outside the United States; such expansion exacerbates direct monitoring problems and renders the ownership incentive found in franchising attractive.

name: Specific knowledge
authors_terms: ["specific knowledge", "knowledge that is costly to transfer to agents"]
definition: Knowledge that is costly to transfer to agents (Jensen & Meckling, 1995); for retail and service firms it can be time-consuming and thus costly to effectively communicate a large repository of detailed knowledge to outlet managers.

name: Outlet-level asset specificity
authors_terms: ["outlet-level asset specificity", "asset specificity in a firm's outlets", "franchisee investments in specific assets"]
definition: Assets that would be difficult for a potential franchisee to exploit after termination of a franchise agreement, including signage, specialized equipment, and a unique building design.

name: Capital scarcity
definition: The degree to which a firm confronts a shortage of capital, reflected in its ability to secure funds from both internal and external sources.

name: Expansion through franchising
authors_terms: ["expansion through franchising", "reliance on expansion through franchising", "emphasis on growth through franchising versus company ownership"]
definition: The relative importance of franchising and company ownership in a chain's expansion; the percentage of total growth achieved through franchising.

name: Focal firm resource-sharing opportunities
authors_terms: ["resource-sharing opportunities", "economies of scope", "strong resource-sharing opportunities with the focal market", "markets served (strong resource sharing)"]
definition: The set of markets that offer strong resource-sharing opportunities with a focal market is defined as those markets that share an end-city (origin or destination) with the focal market; such routes can share important ground resources and common flight segments within a hub-and-spoke network. Resource-sharing opportunities across markets are an antecedent of economies of scope.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact occurs when firms encounter the same rivals in multiple markets; when firms compete with each other in several markets their competitive behavior may differ from that of single-point rivals.

name: Efficiency
definition: Efficiency, defined as the ability of a firm to produce a given level of output with fewer inputs and resources (or greater output with a given level of resources), is an important predictor of competitive advantage within a market or industry.

name: Intensity of rivalry
definition: The intensity of rivalry experienced by a focal market-unit is determined by the competitive interaction with focal-market rivals and is commonly reflected in decreased prices for the services provided by a firm.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability represents the ability of a firm to obtain revenues above costs; it is a combined result of efficiency and intensity of rivalry.

name: Rivals' resource-sharing opportunities
authors_terms: ["rivals' resource-sharing opportunities", "rivals' noncontact markets served", "strong resource-sharing opportunities available to rivals from markets not served by a focal firm"]
definition: The resource-sharing opportunities available to rivals from markets not served by a focal firm, defined as the markets served by focal-market rivals but not by the focal firm that have strong resource-sharing opportunities with the focal market.

name: Number of issues in dispute
authors_terms: ["number of issues in dispute", "the more issues in dispute", "multiple issues"]
definition: Each docket sheet contained numerical codes indicating what a dispute was about; the authors counted the number of different codes to determine the number of issues in dispute.

name: Speed of dispute resolution
authors_terms: ["speed of resolution", "the timeliness with which outcomes are reached", "elapsed time"]
definition: Sheppard (1984) argued that one measure of efficiency is the timeliness with which outcomes are reached. The authors subtracted the filing date from the resolution date to obtain the speed of resolution.

name: Legal representation
authors_terms: ["legal representation", "plaintiff legal representation", "defendant legal representation", "number of lawyers involved"]
definition: The agents who dominate at the Chancery are the lawyers involved in the cases; a large amount of legal representation communicates important information to one's opponent and to the court.

name: Type of settlement
definition: Who determines an outcome: the third party or the disputants. A decision imposed by the Chancery reflects low decision control by the disputants; a settlement negotiated by the disputants reflects high decision control on their part.

name: Corporate documentation
authors_terms: ["documentation", "corporate documentation", "docket entries", "plaintiff documents", "plaintiff proportion of documents"]
definition: Docket entries comprise all materials placed into the court record by the parties in the dispute, as well as the court's rulings, opinions, and orders. The documentation presented by each disputant can be seen as the exercise of process control.

name: Outcome favorability
authors_terms: ["outcome favorability", "favorableness of the outcome", "whether a given party has won or lost its case"]
definition: Perhaps the most obvious outcome to examine is whether a given party has won or lost its case. The favorableness of the outcome one receives can be seen as reflecting the satisfaction criteria suggested by Sheppard (1984).

name: Compliance with the third-party decision
definition: Whether disputants accepted unfavorable outcomes from the third party, or whether they initiated actions to overturn the decisions; in this context, whether losing parties appealed the Chancery verdict to the Delaware supreme court.

name: Organization size
definition: Size was the total assets of a firm for the year in which a dispute was filed.

name: Competitive activity
authors_terms: ["total competitive activity", "newly created competitive actions", "relative total competitive activity"]
definition: Total competitive activity was defined as the total number of new competitive moves a firm carried out in a given year.

name: Action timing
definition: Action timing is defined as the time elapsed between the actions carried out by a firm and those carried out by a rival.

name: Action repertoire simplicity
definition: Action repertoire simplicity is defined as a firm's propensity to concentrate on carrying out a narrow range of action types in a given year, as opposed to a broad range of action types.

name: Leader-challenger action dissimilarity
definition: Leader-challenger action dissimilarity is defined as the degree to which leaders and challengers differ in the actions they carry out.

name: Market share gap erosion
authors_terms: ["market share gap erosion", "erosion of market share gap", "loss of market leadership"]
definition: Erosion or loss of market leadership was measured as the continuous change in the market share gap in a given year between leader and challenger.

name: Leader dethronement
definition: Turnover in market leadership within a leader-challenger-pair-year was defined as leader dethronement.

name: Stakeholder relationships
definition: The paper focuses on five major stakeholder areas important to firm operations-employees, the natural environment, workplace diversity, customers and product safety, and community relations-and rates firm actions toward each of the five groups in the KLD database.

name: Employee relations
authors_terms: ["employee relations", "how a firm manages its employees"]
definition: A range of theory and some empirical evidence suggest that how a firm manages its employees can affect its financial performance; HR practices may lower turnover and absenteeism, improve productivity, and increase worker commitment and effort.

name: Natural environment
authors_terms: ["the natural environment", "concern for the natural environment", "environmental responsiveness"]
definition: Several different arguments have been advanced as to why concern for the natural environment could enhance firm financial performance, including lower compliance costs, greater efficiencies, ecofriendly products, and improved image and stakeholder loyalty.

name: Workforce diversity
definition: Lack of diversity may cause higher turnover and absenteeism from disgruntled employees, whereas diversity may enhance the ability of a firm to attract the best talent from the labor pool and to relate to a broad customer base.

name: Product safety and quality
authors_terms: ["product safety/quality", "customers/product safety", "positive customer perceptions about product quality and safety"]
definition: Positive customer perceptions about product quality and safety may lead to increased sales or decreased costs associated with stakeholder relationships.

name: Community relations
definition: The effects of community relations on financial performance are less clear; recent work suggests that companies are reorienting corporate community relations to fit broader strategic plans, and that community involvement is often seen as creating a competitive advantage.

name: Firm strategy
definition: When we refer to firm strategy, therefore, we are discussing strategic resource allocation decisions, such as the mix of capital and labor (capital intensity), rather than broader strategy typologies such as those developed by Porter (1980) and Miles and Snow (1978).

name: Cost efficiency
definition: Cost efficiency measures assess the degree to which costs per unit of output are low.

name: Asset parsimony
definition: Asset parsimony highlights the degree to which assets per unit of output are few.

name: Differentiation
definition: Differentiation, as discussed by Hambrick (1983), broadly captures a firm's attempts to differentiate itself from its rivals using a variety of marketing and marketing-related activities.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance was operationally defined as return on assets (ROA), computed as the ratio of operating income to total assets.

name: Customer service performance
authors_terms: ["customer service performance", "published customer service levels", "levels of service", "customer service indicators"]
definition: The quality of service the water companies provide to their customers, monitored by the regulator (OFWAT) through published indicators of levels of service. Each year all the companies are required to report to OFWAT on the quality of the delivery of their services in terms of these seven indicators.

name: Relative profitability
definition: The posttax profits available for distribution to shareholders (net income), expressed in relation to the book value of shareholders' equity and relative to the sector average for the same period.

name: Shareholder returns
definition: The returns (dividend payments and capital gains) received by shareholders, measured relative to the sector-average return for the same period.

name: Easily decoupled ethics program practices
authors_terms: ["easily decoupled practices", "easily decoupled ethics program practices", "policy communications", "ethics policy communications"]
definition: An easily decoupled structure or policy provides the appearance of conformity to external expectations while making it easy to insulate much of the organization from those expectations; taken by themselves, ethics policy communications are more easily decoupled than are other ethics program practices.

name: Integrated ethics program practices
authors_terms: ["integrated practices", "integrated ethics program practices", "ethics-oriented performance appraisals"]
definition: Integrated structures and policies affect everyday decisions and actions; decisions are made in light of these policies, and people occupying these specialized structures have the confidence of and regular interaction with other departments and their managers. Practices like ethics-related performance appraisals integrate ethics expectations into regular organizational activities because they make concern for ethics part of employees' formal role identities.

name: Management awareness of the USSC guidelines
authors_terms: ["management awareness of USSC guidelines", "awareness of the USSC guidelines"]
definition: The more that key decision makers are aware of the USSC guidelines' stipulations and incentives, the more we should find an organization implementing at least the easily decoupled elements of ethics programs.

name: Negative media attention
definition: Critical media attention prompts organizations to respond in ways that will preserve or restore their legitimacy, and may not correspond to genuine organizational problems.

name: Conference Board ethics meeting attendance
authors_terms: ["presence at Conference Board ethics meetings", "company attendance at the Conference Board's annual ethics meetings", "company attendance at Conference Board ethics meetings"]
definition: The Conference Board is a high-profile business association whose annual ethics meetings emphasize practices like ethics communications; a company's attendance at these meetings is treated as exposure to a standard-setting influence.

name: Top management commitment to financial and strategic concerns
authors_terms: ["top management commitment to financial and strategic concerns", "management's commitment to financial and strategic performance", "top management's concern for financial and strategic matters"]
definition: Business executives are expected to be committed to the financial, strategic, and operational success of their organizations, which entails an instrumental interest in ethics programs.

name: Top management commitment to ethics
authors_terms: ["top management commitment to ethics", "top management's commitment to ethics", "management's commitment to ethics", "executive commitment to ethics"]
definition: Top managers may be committed to ethics for its own sake, expressing concern for integrity, fair treatment of others, and 'doing the right thing' for its own sake, and not merely for instrumental benefits.

name: Senior HRM executive presence
authors_terms: ["senior HRM executive", "senior human resource executive", "vice president of HRM who reported to the CEO", "having a senior HRM executive reporting to the CEO"]
definition: Whether the firm had a senior HRM executive on its top management team—that is, a vice president of HRM who reported to the CEO.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["long-term firm performance", "longer-term firm performance", "stock price growth", "earnings performance"]
definition: Long-term performance of the firm after its initial public offering, assessed with market-based measures; the authors state that market-based measures are the most prevalent and relevant firm performance measures in the IPO literature and supplement stock price with earnings per share.

name: Rate of growth
authors_terms: ["rate of growth", "rate of change", "motion", "change in sales"]
definition: The firm's pace of change, operationalized as the percentage change in sales over periods following the initial public offering; the authors describe rate of change, or motion, as a contingency variable drawn from inertia concepts.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "company size", "size measured as number of employees"]
definition: Company size, measured as the number of employees at the time of the offering; the authors note that according to the structural inertia model firm size should be associated with the form of inertia that results in being at rest.

name: Top management team diversity
definition: The extent to which a top management team is heterogeneous with respect to members' demographics and cognitions.

name: Debate
definition: An open discussion of task-related differences and the advocacy, by different top management group members, of differing approaches to the strategic decision-making task.

name: Decision comprehensiveness
definition: The extent to which organizations attempt to be exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions.

name: Company financial performance
authors_terms: ["company performance", "firm performance", "organizational performance", "TMT performance", "increased firm profitability and sales"]
definition: Following previous TMT research, the authors conceptualized TMT performance as increased firm profitability and sales.

name: Age diversity
definition: Although age diversity may capture experiences and perspectives relevant to the workplace, those experiences constitute a small portion of the total set of experiences and perspectives age diversity captures. Thus, age diversity is less job-related than the other three demographic variables.

name: Company tenure diversity
definition: Of these demographic variables, functional, education-level, and tenure diversity are generally classified as more job-related because they largely capture experiences, information, and perspectives relevant to cognitive tasks.

name: Education level diversity
definition: Of these demographic variables, functional, education-level, and tenure diversity are generally classified as more job-related because they largely capture experiences, information, and perspectives relevant to cognitive tasks.

name: Functional background diversity
definition: Of these demographic variables, functional, education-level, and tenure diversity are generally classified as more job-related because they largely capture experiences, information, and perspectives relevant to cognitive tasks.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty diversity
definition: PEU diversity is the degree to which TMT members differ in their perceptions about the level of uncertainty in their company's external business environment.

name: Group diversification
definition: The extent to which a business group is diversified across unrelated (two-digit ISIC) industries. The authors measure it as a count of the number of industries in which a group is involved, including the industries of all group members, even those not in the sample.

name: Firm performance
definition: The profitability of a firm, measured as firm return on assets (ROA), defined as [net income + interest x (1 - tax rate)]/[total assets], where an average tax rate is estimated for each firm.

name: Group affiliation
authors_terms: ["group affiliation", "group membership", "affiliation with a diversified business group"]
definition: Membership of a firm in a business group, formally defined in Chilean regulation: a group is a set of companies which present such a sort of relationships and linkages in their property, management, administration, or credit responsibilities, that there is ground to believe that the economic and financial decisions of those companies are guided by or subordinated to the shared interest of the group.

name: Institutional development
definition: The extent to which markets in an economy are characterized by the presence of specialized intermediaries and by low costs of transacting; the authors note that a time trend serves as a reliable proxy for several changes in this institutional context.

name: Downsizing
definition: Employment downsizing, or "strategically laying off employees during times of economic stress"; it was considered the main strategic outcome of downsizing and was measured in terms of changes in the logarithm of a firm's number of employees.

name: Industry decline
authors_terms: ["industry decline", "industry-specific factors", "contractation of a firm's industry", "change in industry decline"]
definition: Measures of decline at the industrial and national level that can be analyzed as antecedents of downsizing, denoting a need to change; operationalized as an index of an industry's real output in the three countries between 1993 and the measurement point expressed as a percentage of the 1993 level.

name: National reform environment
authors_terms: ["country effects", "country-specific, systemic factors", "systemic differences between individual countries"]
definition: Country-specific, systemic factors: although the three countries share a common background as parts of the FSU, their approaches to reform following the break-up of the USSR have been distinctively different, and restructuring strategies may be affected by such systemic factors.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: Managerial equity ownership has been identified as a crucial aspect of managerial willingness to implement strategic change; the greater the extent of managerial stockholding, the more likely managers adopt strategies consistent with maximizing stockholder wealth, though managerial shareholding may also create entrenchment.

name: Institutional share ownership
definition: Ownership of voting shares by institutional investors such as banks, investment funds, and foreign companies; outside shareholders may be powerful enough to press managers to raise shareholder value, especially when outside ownership is concentrated in the hands of institutional investors.

name: Outside individual share ownership
authors_terms: ["outside individual share ownership", "outside private individuals", "dispersed, minority shareholders"]
definition: Ownership of voting shares by outside private individuals; dispersed, minority shareholders have few incentives to become involved in managerial monitoring, although some individuals may accumulate significant blocks of shares and invest in enterprise control.

name: Public expropriation hazards
definition: Risks arising from the ability of a host country's institutional environment to credibly commit to a given policy or regulatory regime, taking the form of regulatory or tax policy shifts or, at the extreme, outright expropriation of private sector assets.

name: Private expropriation hazards
authors_terms: ["private expropriation hazards", "technological leakage", "free riding on brand name and reputation"]
definition: Risks that arise when conducting transactions with other firms in the host country, because an opportunistic joint venture partner may divert the revenue stream of the joint venture away from the multinational; the categories developed in the literature are technological leakage and free riding on brand name and reputation.

name: Equity ownership level
authors_terms: ["level of equity ownership", "ownership position", "percentage of equity ownership", "level of equity control"]
definition: The percentage of equity ownership chosen for the host country operation; by increasing the percentage of equity held by host country partners, multinationals can partially alleviate the knowledge disparity and organizational rigidity they face.

name: International experience
definition: The capabilities developed in a firm's sequence of foreign investment activities; experience is measured by a firm's foreign investment activity in a given host country, in a given industry, and in countries other than the focal host country.

name: Keiretsu and sogo shosha affiliation
authors_terms: ["sogo shosha partners", "sogo shosha as primary partner", "sogo shosha as secondary partner", "keiretsu membership", "keiretsu without sogo shosha"]
definition: Membership in a business group through which a firm can benefit from the experience of other firms: a sogo shosha equity partner provides extensive knowledge of foreign markets, and membership in a horizontal keiretsu gives firms access to information pooled among member firms.

name: Internalization of technology development
authors_terms: ["undertake joint or independent R&D", "internalize a transaction", "make, buy, or ally", "involved in or independently pursue new compound development activities"]
definition: The choice to acquire new product technology by collaborating with a research institute (joint) or by developing it in-house (independent) rather than transferring (buying) it from a research institute.
