The authors state that the decision to undertake either joint or independent technology development rather than buy technology from a research institute is the outcome examined.

name: Number of potential technology suppliers
authors_terms: ["number of potential suppliers of new product technology", "number of suppliers", "suppliers"]
definition: The number of research institutes that, from 1985 up to the decision year, were listed in the MPH records as involved in the research for other approved compounds in the same therapeutic category. A large number of potential suppliers of research is argued to reduce the possibility of opportunism and of small-numbers bargaining hazards.

name: Number of rivals in the therapeutic category
authors_terms: ["number of rivals", "number of rivals producing compounds in the same therapeutic category"]
definition: The number of firms that, from 1985 to the decision year, were listed in the MPH records as producers of other compounds in the same therapeutic category. As the number of firms with experience in a therapeutic area increases, it is easier for a research institute to switch to another firm and research results can be appropriated by another firm.

name: Regional industry competitiveness
authors_terms: ["highly competitive region", "the level of competition in the region in which a firm is located", "the competitiveness of their local industry"]
definition: The level of competition of the pharmaceutical industry in the province-level region in which a firm is located, reflecting the presence of many other strong firms and of strong local research institutes. Firms in the same region compete for resources from local governments and research institutes.

name: Therapeutic category experience
authors_terms: ["experience in same therapeutic category", "experience producing other compounds in the same therapeutic category", "technological expertise"]
definition: A firm's technological expertise gained from having produced another compound in the same therapeutic category as the focal compound. Framed by the authors either as related capabilities and knowledge or, following transaction cost logic, as lower uncertainty surrounding the transaction.

name: Technical uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technical uncertainty", "me-too drug", "level of innovativeness of a drug"]
definition: The technical ease with which a compound can be developed; compounds that other firms have already developed and commercialized are easier to reverse-engineer than globally new compounds, and much of the uncertainty has been removed, with production processes publicly disclosed.

name: Prior independent development experience
authors_terms: ["experience in independent development", "prior experience in independent development"]
definition: Capabilities developed as a result of previous experience in independent R&D: whether the firm had been recorded as the sole research organization for a compound in any therapeutic category prior to the focal compound's development.

name: Importance of business groups in an economy
authors_terms: ["importance of business groups", "importance of business groups relative to the size of an economy", "importance of business groups in an economy"]
definition: A business group is a "collection of firms bound together in some formal and/or informal ways"; the study considers groups active in a wide variety of industries, operating under somewhat unified entrepreneurial guidance, and falling short of a fully integrated organizational structure. Importance is assessed relative to the size of the economy.

name: Market failure in factor markets
authors_terms: ["market failure", "market imperfections", "market failure view", "underdeveloped financial markets"]
definition: Economists assume that diversified business groups can only exist in the absence of a well-functioning market and regard them as functional substitutes for allocation failures in the markets for production inputs; groups step in where the market does not work or is not allowed to work.

name: Vertical social relationships
authors_terms: ["vertical pattern of relationships in a society", "vertical social relationships", "power distance", "vertical or hierarchical societies"]
definition: A social order characterized by vertical relationships is based on a patrimonial concept of authority and on inheritance rules that favor eldest sons, and members of a firm owe obedience and personal loyalty to its patrimonial figurehead. Economic sociologists assume such patterns of authority are relatively stable over time and resilient to foreign pressure.

name: State autonomy and size
authors_terms: ["state autonomy", "state size", "autonomy and size of a state"]
definition: Autonomous states are those free from socially rooted demands and from struggles among class or group interests, and for control and accountability reasons they generally prefer to deal with only a few entrepreneurs as their private sector agents; a second version of late-development theory attributes a key role even to states that cannot act autonomously.

name: Asymmetries in foreign trade and investment
authors_terms: ["asymmetries in foreign trade and investment", "asymmetric foreign trade and investment", "asymmetries in trade and investment", "unbalanced outward and inward flows"]
definition: Asymmetric situations are those in which only some (local) entrepreneurs and firms have access to domestic and foreign resources simultaneously, and they arise when outward and inward foreign trade and investment flows are unbalanced. Symmetric high-high or low-low configurations do not produce cross-border limits to resource access.

name: Industry relatedness
definition: The degree to which the merging firms operate in the same or similar industries. "The anticipated progress is most likely to occur if the merging firms operate in the same or similar industries."

name: Vertical relatedness
authors_terms: ["vertical relatedness", "forward or backward vertical integration", "up- or downstream relationship"]
definition: An up- or downstream relationship between the merging firms, such that outsourcing to the target represents forward or backward vertical integration of the acquirer.

name: Control and reward policy similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity in the control and reward policies of merging firms", "management control and reward policies", "organizational fit"]
definition: The degree to which an SOE's policies for controlling and rewarding its management are in line with Western firms' business standards, so that fewer adjustments in the SOE are necessary. "Organizations with similar structures, cultures, systems, procedures, and so forth are expected to have lower integration costs."

name: Investment intensity in transformation
authors_terms: ["investments in the transformation of an acquired state-owned enterprise", "investment intensity", "investments made by an acquirer in a privatized firm"]
definition: The financial investments an acquirer makes in transforming an acquired SOE to Western competitive standards. "The intensity of transformation apparently required to lift a target SOE to Western performance standards suggests the need for substantial investment by the acquirer."

name: Government-imposed employment guarantees
authors_terms: ["employment guarantees", "number of employees an acquirer must retain", "postprivatization conditions"]
definition: A government condition requiring the acquirer to retain a given number of the acquired SOE's employees after the privatization acquisition.

name: Retained government ownership
authors_terms: ["retained ownership by a privatizing government", "continued government ownership", "government ownership", "partial government ownership"]
definition: The share of a privatized firm that the selling government continues to hold after the privatization acquisition.

name: Country risk
definition: The risk of foreign direct investment caused by the political and economic conditions of the host country, including transfer, economic, and political elements.

name: Postprivatization performance
authors_terms: ["postprivatization performance", "performance of a formerly state-owned enterprise", "postmerger performance"]
definition: The performance of an acquired state-owned enterprise after its privatization acquisition, assessed as sales growth, return on assets, and performance relative to premerger levels.

name: Intangible resources
authors_terms: ["intangible resources", "intangible, knowledge-based resources", "intangible resources of a firm"]
definition: Intangible resources like technology and brand loyalty are particularly important sources of sustainable competitive advantage. Intangible, knowledge-based resources are identified through R&D and advertising intensities.

name: Financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources of a firm", "financial resource variables", "liquidity and leverage ratios"]
definition: Indicators of liquidity and the level of debt carried by a firm reflect the availability of capital raised. Firms with more cash and more debt-carrying capacity can better finance their investments and expect to show higher performance.

name: Group-level intangible resources
authors_terms: ["intangible resources of other firms in the same business group", "group-level intangible resources", "group-level productive resources"]
definition: The weighted averages of the R&D and advertising intensities of other firms associated with the same business group, which generate spillover benefits for a focal affiliate.

name: Group-level financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources of other firms in the same business group", "group-level financial resource variables"]
definition: The weighted averages of the liquidity and leverage ratios of other firms in the same business group, reflecting the groupwide availability of financial resources for a focal affiliate.

name: Financial resource provision to affiliates
authors_terms: ["financial resources a business-group-affiliated firm provides to affiliated companies", "outflow of capital", "supply of debt guarantee", "equity investment to affiliates"]
definition: Capital outflows in the form of debt guarantees and equity participation provided by a firm to other affiliates in its business group.

name: Financial resource reception from affiliates
authors_terms: ["financial resources a business-group-affiliated firm receives from affiliated companies", "inflow of capital", "reception of debt guarantee", "equity investment from affiliates"]
definition: Capital inflows in the form of debt guarantees and equity participation that a firm receives from other affiliates in its business group.

name: Internal sales to affiliates
authors_terms: ["sales to affiliates", "internal selling", "sales to and purchases from affiliated companies"]
definition: The amount of sales to affiliated companies divided by the total sales of a firm, used to measure internal trade.

name: Internal purchases from affiliates
authors_terms: ["purchases from affiliates", "internal purchase", "sales to and purchases from affiliated companies"]
definition: The amount of purchases from affiliated companies divided by the total sales of a firm, used to measure internal trade.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability is used as an indicator of firm performance; economic performance is calculated as a firm's return on invested capital, defined as the sum of net income before tax plus interest payments, deflated by total assets.

name: Market context
authors_terms: ["emerging market context", "developed market context", "emerging and developed markets", "emerging market firms", "developed market firms"]
definition: Variation between developed and emerging markets is likely to occur as a function of differences in norms, resources, and infrastructures; the relative economic and social stability in developed countries promotes the development and acceptance of rules of exchange, whereas economic and sometimes social instability in emerging markets produces ambiguity and uncertainty regarding the rules of exchange.

name: Partner financial assets
definition: The financial resources of a potential partner; given poorly developed financial markets, weak institutions for distribution of capital, and volatility in emerging market countries, capital generally has low availability and high cost, and partners that are financially healthy and require less capital and financial investment from a developed market firm are preferred.

name: Partner technical capabilities
definition: The partner's technological know-how, including cutting-edge technology and the sophisticated information hardware and software from which an emerging market firm can learn in order to build its own technological capabilities.

name: Partner managerial capabilities
definition: The partner's managerial capabilities and know-how, including modern management concepts, techniques, and processes such as decentralization of authority, from which a firm can learn and which can compensate for its own deficits.

name: Partner intangible assets
definition: Intangible resources such as a potential partner's strong positive reputation and legitimacy, which bestow important advantages to firms in the form of enhanced capabilities to attract and retain customers, suppliers, business partners, and financial resources.

name: Partner willingness to share expertise
authors_terms: ["willingness to share expertise", "willingness of a potential partner to share its capabilities"]
definition: The partner's willingness to share its expertise and, perhaps, to make special efforts to help its partner acquire capabilities, such as working in tandem to develop an adequate absorptive capacity before knowledge is transferred.

name: Complementary capabilities
definition: Capabilities of a partner that are complementary to the focal firm's resources and capabilities and that can be integrated to create synergy, since resources may be more valuable, rare, and difficult to imitate when used in combination.

name: Market knowledge and access
authors_terms: ["market knowledge/access", "local market knowledge and access", "market knowledge and access"]
definition: Access to customers and channels of distribution and better knowledge of the customers, local markets, local culture, and idiosyncratic local government policies and regulations that a local partner can provide.

name: Unique competencies
definition: Rare competencies of a potential partner that can be leveraged in an alliance to gain a competitive advantage and that the focal firm may also wish to learn in order to enhance its own resource endowments.

name: Alliance partner attractiveness
authors_terms: ["attractiveness of the firm described as a partner", "probability that the respondent would recommend an alliance with the firm described"]
definition: Executives rated each of the 30 potential partners described in the cases on the attractiveness of the firm described as a partner and on the probability that they would recommend an alliance with that firm.

name: Resource commitment to technology transfer
authors_terms: ["resource commitment to technology transfer", "commitment to technology transfer", "technology transfer", "technology"]
definition: The transfer of superior technological knowledge and specialized technical staff to a local subsidiary, representing a firm's commitment to technology transfer.

name: Early entry
authors_terms: ["early entry", "timing of entry", "early mover", "order of entry"]
definition: The timing of entry into a foreign market, specifically whether the firm enters earlier than its rivals.

name: Perceived economic performance
definition: The perceived economic performance of a joint venture, assessed by the partner's evaluation of the venture's economic performance.

name: Strategic importance
definition: An investment in a particular local market is considered strategically important when it is consonant with the primary focus and function of a firm's global strategy.

name: Parental control
definition: The extent of a foreign parent's control over a joint venture, reflecting the parent's ability to safeguard proprietary technology and manage local operations.

name: Supporting local infrastructure
definition: The availability of supporting local infrastructure, which includes complementary or co-specialized assets such as distribution networks, local human capital, and legal systems for intellectual property protection.

name: Employee retention likelihood
definition: The likelihood of retaining employees, representing the level of employee satisfaction and motivation.

name: Overall satisfaction
definition: The overall satisfaction of the joint venture partner with the venture.

name: Ties with managers at other firms
authors_terms: ["ties with top managers at other firms", "ties with managers at other firms", "ties with other managers", "business ties", "personal ties possessed by a firm's top managers with top managers at other firms"]
definition: Top managers' personal relationships with executives at other firms, decomposed into relationships with buyers, suppliers, and competitors.

name: Ties with government officials
authors_terms: ["ties with government officials", "ties with officials", "personal ties with government officials"]
definition: Top managers' personal connections with government officials, designated as connections with political leaders at various levels of the government, officials in industrial bureaus, and officials in regulatory and supporting organizations such as tax bureaus, state banks, and commercial administration bureaus.

name: Firm performance
definition: As a multidimensional construct, firm performance can be measured both financially and strategically; the authors measured both dimensions with return on assets and market share.

name: Ownership type
definition: A hallmark of transition economies is the coexistence of non-state-owned and state-owned enterprises (SOEs); Chinese firms are differentiated according to their ownership types.

name: Business sector
definition: The sector in which the firm operates, distinguishing manufacturing firms from service firms; service businesses in general are more relationship-intensive and rely more on external resources.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size has long been found to be an important factor affecting firm survival and performance; smaller firms typically need to rapidly establish ties with other organizations in order to gain legitimacy.

name: Industry growth
definition: The growth of the industry in which a firm operates; a fast-growing industry may offer most of its firms an opportunity to expand, whereas a slow-growing industry is likely to be more competitive and saturated.

name: Management HRM values
authors_terms: ["management HRM values", "management values regarding human resource management (HRM)", "beliefs of management regarding the importance of human resources and people as a source of competitive advantage"]
definition: The beliefs of management regarding the importance of human resources and people as a source of competitive advantage.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: An organizational strategy that differentiates a firm's products from those of competitors on the basis of the products' intrinsic characteristics, rather than purely on the basis of price.

name: Speed of firm activities and services
authors_terms: ["speed", "speed of firm activities and services for internal and external customers"]
definition: The emphasis a firm places on speed in its activities and in services for internal and external customers, reflecting flexibility, rapid decision making, and a strong customer orientation.

name: High-involvement HRM strategy
definition: An HRM approach characterized by high employee participation, extensive training programs, and broad job designs, in contrast to a traditional HRM strategy characterized by low participation, limited training, and highly specialized jobs.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors' perceptual, largely market-focused measure of organizational performance, including public image and goodwill, growth rate of sales or revenues, product (or service) quality, long-run profitability, financial strength, and employee productivity.

name: Market niche attractiveness
authors_terms: ["attractiveness of a market niche", "attractiveness of an area", "benefit (B) to firm i from locating in an area j"]
definition: An organization's choice of a branch location is analyzed as a market niche entry decision; the benefit to a firm from locating in an area is a function of the number of people, own branches, and competitors in the focal area and of the number of own branches in neighboring areas, and an organization chooses the area that maximizes this benefit.

name: Organizational density in a market niche
authors_terms: ["organizational density of a market niche", "branch density", "head office density", "densities of different forms of bank offices"]
definition: The densities of different forms of bank offices in each area, calculated by counting all banks and branches operating per area per year.

name: Size-weighted organizational density
authors_terms: ["summed bank sizes", "size-weighted density of organizations in the niche"]
definition: The density of branches each weighted by the number of branches owned by the branch's firm and summed by area.

name: Own office presence in the area
authors_terms: ["own offices, same area", "a bank's own offices in the same area"]
definition: A count of all offices (banks or branches) of the same bank in a given area.

name: Own office presence in neighboring areas
authors_terms: ["own offices, neighboring areas", "its own offices in neighboring areas"]
definition: A count of all offices of the same bank in areas adjacent to a focal area.

name: Multipoint competitor presence
definition: A count of the number of offices in an area owned by banks that a focal bank had contact with in two or more areas.

name: Single-point competitor presence
definition: A count of all offices in the area owned by banks that the focal bank had contact with in just one area.

name: Organizational size
definition: An organization's size, measured as its number of branch offices; levels of both experience and strategic opportunities are argued to differ depending on an organization's number of branches.

name: Work-family human resource bundle
authors_terms: ["work-family bundle", "work-family human resource bundles", "bundles of work-family policies", "work-family policies", "work-family cluster groupings"]
definition: A work-family bundle can be defined as a group of complementary, highly related and, in some cases, overlapping human resource policies that may help employees manage nonwork roles. The bundle approach is less focused on specific components and is more focused on the extent to which the policies are highly related and interactive in a way that suggests an organization-level approach or philosophy.

name: Firm-level performance
authors_terms: ["firm-level performance", "organizational performance", "market performance", "profit and sales growth"]
definition: We used three dependent variables in this study to reflect firm-level performance. Two of these, organizational performance and market performance, are the perceptual measures of firm performance assessed relative to that of other firms doing the same kind of work.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size has been one indicator of the extent to which a firm concedes to institutional demands, with larger firms expected to be more affected by such pressures. Firm size was the logarithm of total employees.

name: Firm age
definition: Younger firms tend to be more concerned with mere survival than older, more established firms. Firm age was the natural logarithm of 1991 minus the founding year.

name: Proportion of women employed
authors_terms: ["proportion of women", "percentage of women", "percentage of women in core positions"]
definition: In the case of work-family policies, a key assumption is that they are a salient need and reflect an important value system for women; the extent to which a firm employs women is expected to be related to its adoption of work-family policies. The proportion of women was measured as the percentage of women in core positions.

name: Innovation
definition: Innovation was a composite measure computed by adding standardized values of R&D spending and number of patents. R&D spending was used as a proxy for innovation, including both projects under development and innovations not publicly disclosed, while patents represent only a subset because a firm can choose other legal forms to protect its intellectual property.

name: CEO short-term compensation
definition: Short-term pay for executives consists of the base salary and a short-term bonus tied to performance objectives of one year or less and is paid in the form of cash.

name: CEO long-term compensation
definition: Long-term pay for executives consists primarily of stock options and other forms of equity-based compensation tied to achieving objectives over periods ranging from three to five years.

name: Management fashion life cycle
authors_terms: ["life cycle", "life span", "length of its life cycle", "number of years in the fashion's life cycle", "number of years it took the fashion to peak"]
definition: Whenever possible, life cycle was computed as the difference between the year an article was first published on a fashion and the year in which publications on the fashion first dropped to zero. The life span of a management fashion was measured either as the number of years it took the fashion to peak or as the number of years in the fashion's life cycle.

name: Year of fashion introduction
authors_terms: ["the year in which a fashion emerged", "the year in which a management fashion was introduced", "year of introduction"]
definition: The year in which a fashion emerged or was introduced into the management domain, operationalized as the year an article was first published on a fashion.

name: Difficulty of implementation
authors_terms: ["difficulty in implementation", "difficulty of implementing it", "difficult to implement"]
definition: Difficulty in implementation assessed the degree to which implementation of a fashion in organizations is difficult.

name: Broadness
definition: Broadness assesses the degree to which a fashion targets (or affects) specific people, project teams, or departments (narrow) as opposed to an entire organization (broad), consistent with a systems perspective.

name: Burden of implementation on management
authors_terms: ["burden of implementation on management", "degree to which responsibility for its implementation resides with upper management"]
definition: Burden of implementation on management focuses on whether successful implementation of a fashion demands more effort, responsibility, and persistence from upper management than from those lower in an organization's hierarchy.

name: Radicalness
definition: Degree of radicalness represents the degree to which a fashion encourages divergence from established management thinking.

name: People orientation
definition: People-oriented was based on Abrahamson's (1997) explanation of normative rhetoric; it represents the degree to which a fashion addresses the needs, concerns, and motivations of an organization's staff.

name: Production orientation
definition: Production-oriented represents the degree to which a fashion focuses on enhancing the output and productivity of an organization, and is drawn from Abrahamson's (1997) explanation of rational rhetoric.

name: Fear induction
definition: Fear-inducing relates to the degree to which a fashion is likely to create apprehension, anxiety, and consternation among the members of an organization.

name: Management seen as blameless
definition: Management seen as blameless represents the degree to which a fashion represents management as responsible for the creation of organizational ills that have given rise to the need to adopt the fashion.

name: Management fashion prevalence
authors_terms: ["prevalence", "degree of implementation", "interest in a fashion", "number of articles penned regarding a specific management fashion", "penetration"]
definition: The number of articles penned regarding a specific management fashion is an imperfect proxy for degree of implementation, but it certainly measures interest in a fashion; fashion discourse and adoption have been empirically shown to coevolve.

name: Trade balance
definition: Trade balance was included as an indicator of overall global competitiveness.

name: Corporate profits
definition: Corporate profits were included as a benchmark of organizations' financial health.

name: Per unit labor costs
authors_terms: ["per unit labor costs", "labor costs", "high labor costs"]
definition: Per unit labor costs were included as evidence of efficiency.

name: Management consulting industry revenues
authors_terms: ["management consulting industry revenues", "management consulting industry's revenues"]
definition: Data were gathered on management consulting industry revenues to potentially gain greater insight into the degree to which management fashion implementation may indeed be supply-driven.

name: Mergers and acquisitions
definition: Information was collected on the number of mergers and acquisitions in each year of the study period to reflect structural alterations.

name: Foreign market revenue exposure
authors_terms: ["foreign market revenue exposure", "foreign revenue exposure", "proportion of revenue exposure", "percentage of foreign revenue exposure"]
definition: The proportion of firm revenue that is exposed to the risks of being derived from a specific foreign location. The more a firm relies on a foreign market for revenues, the more it can be exposed to international risk there.

name: Host country risk
authors_terms: ["host country risk", "country risk", "economic and political riskiness of the country entered", "foreign country risk"]
definition: Countries vary in characteristics that directly affect the risk of doing business; country risk is the economic and political riskiness of a specific country entered.

name: Entry mode commitment
authors_terms: ["entry mode commitment", "entry mode", "mode of entry", "commitment to the foreign location"]
definition: The degree of resource commitment to a foreign location, as evidenced by the entry mode chosen: entry modes vary in the complexity and commitment of resources they involve, and, therefore, in risk.

name: Number of countries entered
authors_terms: ["number of countries entered", "number of foreign markets entered", "breadth of a venture's foreign entry strategy", "geographic diversification"]
definition: The count of the number of foreign markets in which each firm operated in its sixth year, representing the breadth of a venture's foreign entry strategy.

name: Resource-based sequencing
authors_terms: ["resource-based sequencing", "resource-sequencing", "resource-based sequencing of a firm's resource development decisions", "resource-based development path", "sequential development of resources and capabilities"]
definition: The sequencing of a firm's resource development decisions over time, consisting of (1) utilizing excess capacity, followed by (2) international economies of scale, followed by (3) development of dynamic capabilities, followed by (4) utilizing excess capacity, followed by (5) innovation.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["firm growth", "change in sales", "change in employees", "change in total assets"]
definition: Growth of the firm measured through increments to its size; following Penrose, change in sales, change in employees, and change in total assets are treated as important measures of growth.

name: Product innovation strategy
definition: A reflection of a firm's commitment to developing and marketing products that are new to the firm and/or the market.

name: New technology venture performance
definition: Performance of the venture relative to its principal competitors, composed of five financial and four market performance measures combined into a single variable.

name: Dysfunctional competition
definition: The extent to which the competitive behavior of firms in a market is opportunistic, unfair, or even unlawful.

name: Institutional support
definition: The extent to which administrative institutions (such as government departments) provide support for firms in order to reduce the adverse effects of the inadequate institutional infrastructure in the transition process.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: The degree of change and unpredictability of a market environment.

name: Strategic alliances for product development
definition: Cooperative agreements such as licenses, R&D agreements, and joint ventures with other firms to develop and market new products.

name: Political networking
definition: A firm's allocating resources to cultivate relationships with government officials, banks, and administrative and other regulatory agencies.

name: Heterogeneity of inputs and demands
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in inputs and demands", "heterogeneity of inputs and demands", "heterogeneity of the production process", "heterogeneity of inputs", "heterogeneity of demands"]
definition: The number and diversity of potential inputs available to combine within an industry's production system and the diversity of demands made on that system; the combination of heterogeneous inputs and demands increases the value of modularity.

name: Use of modular organizational forms
definition: The degree to which an industry's production system substitutes loosely coupled organizational components for tightly integrated, hierarchical structures, through contract manufacturing, alternative work arrangements, and alliances.

name: Availability of industry standards
definition: The existence of formalized standards in an industry, which reduce specificity and provide a form of embedded control that reduces search, monitoring, and enforcement costs, thus allowing firms to efficiently exchange with multiple partners.

name: Rate of technological change
authors_terms: ["technological change", "rate of technological change", "high-speed technological change", "TFP growth"]
definition: The rate at which technology progresses in an industry, measured as total factor productivity growth, which shortens product life cycles and makes innovation the primary driver of competition.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The degree of rivalry in an industry, where industries with numerous firms that are relatively equal in terms of market share typically have high rivalry and competitiveness.

name: Top management team international work experience
authors_terms: ["international work experience", "breadth of international work experience"]
definition: International work experience is considered one of the most broadening elements of executives' backgrounds, since it typically complements and expands on the role played by other experiences.

name: Top management team educational heterogeneity
definition: Top management team educational heterogeneity provides an indicator of the diversity of skills and cognitive processes, as well as the basic knowledge, embedded in a TMT.

name: Top management team functional heterogeneity
definition: Functional diversity captures the breadth of skill sets and network resources available to TMTs.

name: Top management team firm tenure heterogeneity
definition: Firm tenure heterogeneity is relevant to global strategic posture because differences in tenure have been shown to influence the degree to which TMT members use their networks to provide advice on international markets.

name: Global strategic posture
definition: Global strategic posture reflects the degree to which a firm depends on foreign markets for customers and factors of production and the geographical dispersion of these markets and factors.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty is a consequence of environmental factors that generally result in a lack of the information needed to assess means-ends relationships, make decisions, and confidently assign probabilities to their outcomes.

name: Human capital of partners
authors_terms: ["human capital", "human capital embodied in partners", "human capital of partners"]
definition: The human capital embodied in the partners, formed by education from the best institutions and the most experience as partners in a particular professional service firm, and representing a firm's most important resource.

name: Leveraging of human capital
definition: The leveraging of partners' human capital, in which partners work with associates to transfer tacit knowledge and in which the partners' knowledge and capabilities are leveraged while associates gain tacit and firm-specific knowledge.

name: Service diversification
definition: Diversification of a professional service firm into new services, which offers opportunities to share knowledge across service areas and to achieve economies of scale and scope.

name: Geographic diversification
authors_terms: ["geographic diversification", "geographic market diversification", "diversification into new geographic markets"]
definition: Diversification of a professional service firm into new geographic markets, which provides the opportunity to learn about new clients, new service markets, and potential new resources.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable in the study, firm performance, defined as the ratio of net income to total firm revenue.

name: Collaboration in foreign market entry
definition: The extent to which firms collaborate with local firms in the host markets they enter; when collaborating for the purpose of market access, firms may license local firms, offer international franchises, or form strategic alliances or joint ventures with them, rather than internalizing operations.

name: Performance in foreign markets
authors_terms: ["performance in that market", "performance in foreign markets", "firm performance"]
definition: Firm performance in each foreign market entered, examined with two objective measures: profitability and sales growth, because transaction costs have direct implications for both profitability and sales growth.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity is commonly used as a proxy for the firm-specific advantages gained from research and development activities; proprietary knowledge gained from R&D is often ill codified, complex, and surrounded with uncertainty.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: Advertising expenditures generate firm-specific assets in the form of brand recognition and product differentiation, and like technological advantages they obsolesce over time, requiring continuous reinvestment in advertising.

name: Learning effectiveness
definition: Learning occurs when people develop "knowledge about action-outcome relationships and the effect of the environment on these relationships"; to the extent that members of an organization can produce desired outcomes, they can be said to have developed specific operational knowledge, or competence. Operational knowledge allows an organization to respond effectively to environmental conditions, making this a useful construct for approximating adaptive capacity.

name: Goal autonomy
definition: This construct represents the extent to which a project team was granted autonomy with respect to goals, roles, and authority structures. When goal autonomy is high, managers do not specify goals, talent allocations, or lines of authority.

name: Supervision autonomy
definition: This scale was developed to assess the extent to which a project team was granted autonomy with respect to operating activities; to the extent that a group has high supervision autonomy, it will enjoy greater local discretion, which permits greater heterogeneity in day-to-day activities.

name: Degree of exploration
definition: This measure captures how, and in what ways, newness manifested itself in a project - whether in the product, technology, resources employed, or markets sought. It allows an overall assessment of how exploratory a project is across a number of dimensions.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["network position", "centrality", "in-degree centrality", "centrality of an organizational unit's network position"]
definition: Network position, a unit's location in an interunit network, describes its access to knowledge. An organizational unit's network position reveals its ability to access external information and knowledge.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: Organizational units differ in their ability to assimilate and replicate new knowledge gained from external sources; Cohen and Levinthal (1990) labeled such ability absorptive capacity. R&D investment is a necessary condition for the creation of absorptive capacity.

name: Business unit innovation
definition: Innovation is one of the two dependent variables in the study, measured at the business unit level. Because units may specialize in different industries and have different strategic priorities, innovation was adjusted and expressed as an innovation achieved rate.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Performance is one of the two dependent variables in the study, measured at the business unit level. It was adjusted for unit differences and expressed as a profitability achieved rate.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age was defined as the number of days that a fund family had been in existence; the natural logarithm of age was used because the difference between age 365 days and age 565 days is not the same as the difference between age 1,000 days and age 1,200 days.

name: External connections
authors_terms: ["external connections", "formal external connections", "external linkages", "linkages with other organizations"]
definition: We measured the external connections of a mutual fund family by counting the number of subadvisors it used. We focused on subadvisors because they provide access to managerial resources, and their use represents an approach that differs from the use of in-house managers.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "probability of product innovation", "introduced a new mutual fund"]
definition: Product innovation occurred when a given product offered in a particular year had not previously been offered. A mutual fund family was defined as having introduced a new mutual fund if it entered any of the 33 mutual fund categories maintained by Morningstar.

name: Recruitment from competitors
authors_terms: ["recruitment from competitors", "recruiting talent from rivals", "recruitment of talent from competitors"]
definition: To analyze the probability of recruitment from competitors, we created a dummy variable coded 1 when a focal fund family recruited a portfolio manager employed in a stock fund in another fund family. A recruitment event includes only moves in which a portfolio manager changed fund families and also changed advisors.

name: Recruit industry tenure
definition: The industry tenure of recruits was the number of days a recruit had served as a portfolio manager in the open-ended mutual fund industry.

name: Prior employer performance
authors_terms: ["competitor fund performance", "short-term performance of the rival organizations", "performance of the organizations from which recruits are hired"]
definition: We measured competitor fund performance (the performance of the competitor from which a recruit originated) as the percentile ranking of that fund's latest annual performance among all other funds with the same investment objective.

name: Prior employer size
authors_terms: ["competitor fund size", "size of the organizations from which recruits are hired"]
definition: Competitor fund size was the total net asset value of the fund at which a recruit last worked. If a recruit had worked for multiple funds, we added up their net asset values.

name: Prior employer age
authors_terms: ["competitor fund age", "age of the organizations from which recruits are hired"]
definition: Competitor fund age was the number of days in which the fund that had last employed a recruit had been in existence.

name: Recruit characteristics
definition: Expertise, a multidimensional construct, can be inferred from recruits' industry tenure and immediate past performance and from the size and age of their previous employers.

name: Manager sharing
authors_terms: ["shared/dedicated manager", "shared manager", "resource sharing", "sharing managers", "dividing a manager", "dedicated manager"]
definition: Organizations allocate product-level staff in one of two ways: they attempt to exploit accumulated product knowledge by sharing managers and professionals over existing and new product lines, or they dedicate staff to developing knowledge in new product areas.

name: Current related managerial experience
definition: Current related experience is found among managers who are working on products related to the given product-line extension at the time of the product's introduction.

name: Previous related managerial experience
definition: Prior related experience resides among the managers who are currently working on unrelated products but who have worked on products related to the extension at some point in their career.

name: Unrelated managerial experience
definition: Managers who work and have worked solely on unrelated projects possess unrelated experience.

name: Task complexity
authors_terms: ["task complexity", "complexity of a product-line extension", "high-complexity extensions", "low-complexity extensions"]
definition: High-complexity extensions imply increased search for solutions, difficulty in predicting the outcome of a decision, and high variety in the number and types of tasks faced; low-complexity extensions are characterized by known outcomes and little search and variety in the problems encountered.

name: Erosion of professional dominance
authors_terms: ["erosion of professional dominance", "professional dominance", "decline in the hegemony of the medical profession"]
definition: The erosion of professional dominance, which assessed the 'main effect' of the impact of changes in governance, logics, and actors in the field of health care, was a dummy variable coded 1 for years following the major shift in 1965. It refers to the period in which the profession-dominated logic and governance structures eroded and were succeeded by reshaped institutional governance arrangements.

name: Governmental involvement
authors_terms: ["governmental involvement", "government involvement", "expansion of governmental regulatory functions"]
definition: This variable, which captures the expansion of governmental regulatory functions in the field of health care, was measured by the number and types of health-related regulatory bodies operating in various capacities at the federal level.

name: Fragmentation of dominant actors
authors_terms: ["fragmentation of dominant actors", "fragmentation within the medical profession", "increase in the number of recognized specialties"]
definition: To measure fragmentation within the medical profession, the author collected data on the number of specialties and subspecialties in existence each year of the study period. The growth of specialties is described as an indicator of the erosion of the dominant profession's authority and control.

name: Public attention logics
authors_terms: ["public attention logics", "increasing public attention", "public voice in the institutional logics"]
definition: As an indicator of the movement toward a greater public voice in the institutional logics of health care (that is, the consumer health movement), the number of popular magazines devoted to health-related issues was tracked.

name: Founding rate of identity-based associations
authors_terms: ["identity-based associations", "identity associations", "founding rate of identity-based associations"]
definition: Identity-based associations are field-authorized professionals and occupational groups, primarily professional or organizational associations that make claims on the field that are based on professional standing or expertise. The founding rate of these associations is one of the two dependent variables of the study.

name: Founding rate of advocacy-based associations
authors_terms: ["advocacy-based associations", "advocacy associations", "founding rate of advocacy-based associations"]
definition: Advocacy associations are formed on the basis of advocacy or claims making on behalf of 'interested' roles in the field, such as patient advocacy groups, foundations or groups for support of disease prevention or research, or national initiatives for health promotion. The founding rate of these associations is one of the two dependent variables of the study.

name: Population growth of identity-based associations
authors_terms: ["growth in the number of identity-based associations", "population density", "cross-effects of populations"]
definition: Density (the linear term) was calculated as cumulative yearly sums of foundings minus failures for the entire community as well as for each population of identity-based and advocacy-based associations; growth in the number of identity associations is captured by this population variable.

name: Population growth of advocacy-based associations
authors_terms: ["growth in the number of advocacy associations", "population density", "cross-effects of populations"]
definition: Density (the linear term) was calculated as cumulative yearly sums of foundings minus failures for the entire community as well as for each population of identity-based and advocacy-based associations; growth in the number of advocacy associations is captured by this population variable.

name: Firm risk
authors_terms: ["firm risk", "performance uncertainty", "firm performance uncertainty", "uncertainty over performance outcomes", "uncertainty in firm outcomes"]
definition: Firm risk is uncertainty over performance outcomes, that is, uncertainty in firm outcomes that makes the connection between agent effort and observed outcomes weaker.

name: Unsystematic firm risk
authors_terms: ["unsystematic risk", "unsystematic firm risk", "firm-specific risk", "idiosyncratic firm risk", "unsystematic market risk (sigma)", "epsilon"]
definition: The first risk component, known as unsystematic risk or epsilon, captures the degree of variation in a firm's performance (as reflected in its income stream or stock returns) that can't be explained by overall market trends.

name: Systematic firm risk
authors_terms: ["systematic risk", "systematic firm risk", "market risk", "systematic market risk (beta)", "beta"]
definition: The second component, systematic risk or beta, captures the amount of variation in firm performance outcomes that mirrors concomitant changes taking place in the overall market.

name: Performance-contingent pay
authors_terms: ["pay mix", "performance-contingent compensation", "compensation risk bearing", "contingent pay", "variable pay", "risk sharing"]
definition: The reliance on performance-contingent pay, or compensation risk bearing, is the degree to which a portion of a CEO's income is linked to firm performance; it is measured as pay mix, the proportion of variable pay in the total pay package.

name: CEO compensation level
authors_terms: ["total CEO compensation", "total pay", "compensation level", "amount of pay"]
definition: The total amount of pay received by a chief executive, combining cash and noncash forms of income.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measured firm performance using total stock returns over the five years of the study; total stock return includes the appreciation of stock price over the period plus dividends paid.

name: Executive functional position
authors_terms: ["functional position", "executive functional position", "functional responsibilities", "functional department", "functional area"]
definition: For each individual in the survey, the company provided information on the functional department, broken out by the category that the employee worked in (such as finance, marketing, and so forth); the authors viewed each executive's current responsibilities solely as indicative of a functional position's criticality or potential power.

name: Strategic resource allocation
authors_terms: ["strategic resource allocations", "strategic contingency variables", "actions and resource allocation decisions", "strategic contingencies", "resource allocation choices"]
definition: Strategy is characterized as the pattern resulting from a stream of resource allocation decisions, comprised of a firm's resource allocation choices in research and development, marketing, diversification, capital investments, and international markets; in general, the larger the value of a strategic resource allocation variable, the greater a firm's dependence on the functional area corresponding to that allocation variable.

name: CEO-executive functional similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity to CEO functional background", "CEO-executive functional similarity", "CEO same", "functional similarity"]
definition: An executive's functional position that is similar to the functional background of a firm's CEO; the similarity variable was coded 1 to signify such similarity, otherwise 0.

name: Hierarchical proximity to the CEO
authors_terms: ["proximity", "hierarchical proximity", "levels closest to the level of the CEO", "executive rank", "hierarchical rank"]
definition: The level an executive occupies relative to the level of the CEO; particular executives are afforded greater opportunity to interact with their CEO by virtue of their rank, and higher-level executives are most likely to have an organizationwide orientation that overlaps that of the CEO.

name: Human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "education and work experience", "managerial experience, education, functional expertise, and tenure"]
definition: Examples of relevant human capital include managerial experience, education, functional expertise, and tenure; in this study human capital was measured as executives' levels of education and work experience.

name: Cash compensation
definition: Cash compensation for the executives in the sample was computed as the sum of base salary and annual bonus; the authors focus on cash compensation because it typically creates less uncertainty for executives than contingent pay schemes and is thus preferred by them.

name: Negative spread
definition: The difference between the strike price of executives' options and the market price of a stock; the greater the negative spread that has resulted from a fall in the price of a stock, the greater the perceived loss.

name: Option repricing
definition: Option repricing occurs when a board of directors elects to either adjust the exercise price (also known as the strike price) of an executive's existing options downward, or to cancel an executive's existing options and grant him or her new options with a lower strike price.

name: Institutional stock ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional stock ownership", "institutional ownership", "stock ownership by institutional investors"]
definition: The percentage of outstanding voting shares owned collectively by all institutions, at the beginning of the period of study.

name: CEO stock ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO stock ownership", "CEO ownership", "percentage ownership of the CEO"]
definition: The percentage of outstanding voting shares owned by a firm's CEO, at the beginning of the period of study.

name: CEO structural power
definition: Power that comes from a CEO's formal organizational position or positions and from organizational structures and rules that protect the CEO from outside influence; sources and exercise of power are context-specific.

name: CEO and firm visibility
definition: The visibility of the repricing event, increased by two factors: the size of the firm and the amount of compensation the CEO receives.

name: Market feedback
authors_terms: ["market feedback", "market feedback favoring PA-firms", "differential survival rate", "differential growth rate"]
definition: The market as a selection environment provides feedback about firms' actions by detecting firms that are substandard; when the market favors firms with a certain organizational form over others, that feedback furnishes a clue about how firms should be structured.

name: Adoption of a new organizational form
authors_terms: ["adoption of a PA-form", "adoption of the partner-associate structure", "PA-form adoption"]
definition: Adoption of the partner-associate form, a governance structure in which partners participate in important strategic decisions and take the profits from operations while associates receive the command and guidance of partners and usually fixed annual salaries.

name: Network ties to adopting organizations
authors_terms: ["total number of direct ties", "total ties to adopters", "number of ties to adopters"]
definition: The total number of direct ties that accountants at a focal firm have with accountants working for adopting (PA-) firms; networks function as information conduits and as channels that embody conformity pressure.

name: Proportion of adopters in network
authors_terms: ["exposure to the adoption norm", "proportion of adopters among other firms with which a focal firm has a network tie"]
definition: The proportion of adopters among the firms with which a focal firm's accountants have network ties, capturing the conformity pressure that adopters and nonadopters in the network exert on the focal firm.

name: Adoption among similarly sized firms
authors_terms: ["percentage of adopters among similarly sized firms", "size similarity", "percentage of PA-form adopters among firms having a size similar to that of a focal firm"]
definition: The percentage of PA-form adopters among firms of a size similar to the focal firm, summarizing the average behavioral pattern of the reference group on which the focal firm anchors its interpretation of market responses.

name: Adoption among geographically proximate firms
authors_terms: ["percentage of adopters among geographically proximate firms", "locational proximity", "propinquity"]
definition: The percentage of PA-form adopters among firms that are geographically proximate to a focal firm; neighboring firms are windows through which a focal firm makes sense of its environment.

name: Firm mortality
definition: For each firm-year observation, our dependent variable, failure, was coded as 1 if the firm exited the market in a given year, and as 0 otherwise.

name: Life cycle phase
authors_terms: ["life cycle phase", "growth phase", "mature phase", "pretransformation growth phase", "posttransformation mature phase"]
definition: Our theoretical framework distinguishes between the growth phase, or the period in an industry's history from the time of the industry category's commercialization till the transformation of barriers to entry, and the mature phase, or the subsequent years.

name: Firm age
definition: For each year of a firm's existence, age was calculated as the number of years since the time of industry entry. Population ecologists have noted the vulnerability of young organizations to selection processes... Since the accumulation of competitive resources and capabilities happens over time, age is positively related to survival.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was measured as the asset size listed in the Thomas Register for each year of a firm's existence. Empirical findings from evolutionary studies in both ecology and economics indicate that mortality rates decline with increased size.

name: Order of entry
authors_terms: ["order of entry", "chronological sequence of entry", "chronological time of entry", "timing of entry"]
definition: For order of entry, we adapted Suarez and Utterback's (1995) measurement, the logarithm of rank of entry, where rank is measured by the year in which a firm entered an industry relative to the time of commercial introduction.

name: Population density
definition: We measured relative density, defining it as the density in a particular year divided by the peak density observed in an industry. The peak density was used as the divisor since it represents the carrying capacity of a market, or the number of firms sustainable in the market given its resource base.

name: Installed base
definition: The number of users or current installations of the technology, assessed relative to competing technologies. A large installed base extends the range of a user's network, increases the value of the user's training in the particular technology, and attracts more developers of complementary technologies.

name: Availability of complementary goods
authors_terms: ["availability of complementary goods", "complementary goods", "lack of complementary goods"]
definition: The availability, relative to competing technologies, of the associated set of goods that a technology requires to be desirable to customers, such as software for computers and videotapes for VCRs.

name: Learning orientation
authors_terms: ["learning orientation", "investment in learning", "investment in continuous learning processes", "failure to invest in continuous learning"]
definition: The degree to which a firm invests in technology development and learning relative to competitors and emphasizes learning or the development of new capabilities. Through such investment, firms expand their knowledge and skill bases and improve their absorptive capacity.

name: Timing of entry
authors_terms: ["timing of entry", "entry time", "timing of market entry"]
definition: The timing of the entry of a new technology into the market, which can be important to the likelihood of its being adopted as a standard.

name: Technological lockout
definition: A situation in which a firm finds itself unable to develop or competitively sell products to a particular market because of technology standards.

name: Relay CEO succession
definition: A relay CEO succession is one in which a new CEO came from within the firm in question and had been his or her predecessor's heir apparent; the firm identifies an heir apparent well in advance and uses the interval between designation and promotion to groom the heir for the top job.

name: Number of internal candidates
definition: Internal candidates were defined as current executives of a firm (other than the incumbent CEO) whose position was executive vice president (EVP) or higher.

name: Presuccession firm performance
definition: Firm performance before the succession, measured as a composite of return on assets, return on sales, and the ratio of market value to the book value of shareholders' equity averaged over the three years prior to succession.

name: Postsuccession firm performance
definition: Firm performance after the succession, measured with the same procedure applied to corresponding data for the three years after a succession occurred.

name: Presuccession strategic instability
definition: Firm strategic instability is the extent to which a firm's strategy has changed over time; it is conceptually and operationally the opposite of Finkelstein and Hambrick's (1990) concept of strategic persistence.

name: Postsuccession strategic instability
definition: Postsuccession strategic instability was measured in a similar fashion to presuccession strategic instability, with corresponding data for the three years after a succession.

name: Presuccession industry instability
definition: Industry instability is defined as the level of the unpredictability of changes in industry-specific factors over time.

name: Postsuccession industry instability
definition: Postsuccession industry instability was measured similarly to presuccession industry instability, with corresponding data for the three years after a succession.

name: Demographic distance from team members
definition: Demographic distance is defined as focal individual i's dissimilarity to his or her team on a given variable; for the categorical characteristics it is the squared proportion of team members with the same background subtracted from 1. An individual's overall distance from the rest of the team is the average of the standardized distances on the four demographic characteristics.

name: Executive turnover
authors_terms: ["likelihood of exit", "hazard of exit", "exit from the team", "exit rate"]
definition: The dependent variable in the event history framework was the instantaneous rate of individual exit from a top executive management team, defined as the probability of a manager experiencing exit between t and t + dt, conditional on being at risk for the event at time t.

name: Top management team power vis-à-vis the board of directors
authors_terms: ["team power", "relative executive management team power", "top executive management team power"]
definition: Members of or groups in an organization derive power from being able to deal with the critical issues that the organization faces, and power basically derives from asymmetry in the information and knowledge of an executive management team and a board of directors.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational performance was measured as yearly gross return on sales (ROS) and as the difference in ROS from year t - 1 to year t, so that both the absolute level of and the change in a firm's performance are included.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: To capture firm diversification, the authors calculated a Herfindahl index (that is, the sum of squared proportions) on the spread of firm turnover in ten different activities; heavy reliance on a few activities (low diversification) raises the Herfindahl index, so subtracting the index from 1 yields a positive measure of diversification.

name: Firm-level competitive intensity
definition: For firm-level competitive intensity, the authors subtracted each firm's yearly net turnover growth rate from those of its four Big Five competitors combined; crowding occurs, and competitive pressures are most severely felt, when a focal company's growth lags behind that of its major competitors.

name: Product-line structure
definition: A structure that groups positions according to the type of product (or service) that occupants of the positions help the organization produce; an organization establishes an administrative system to coordinate and control the work of those individuals whose job positions are connected to the production of a product or service.

name: Professional service quality
authors_terms: ["professional service quality", "service quality", "quality of professional services"]
definition: The extent to which professionals met the needs and expectations of patients.

name: Clinical innovation
definition: The extent to which professionals developed new ideas for improving patient care.

name: Professional development
definition: The extent to which individuals had opportunities for developing knowledge and skills for their careers.

name: Job satisfaction
definition: An employee's general satisfaction with his/her job.

name: Project termination
definition: The termination of a new product development project, which the authors model as a dynamic process that involves if and when terminations occurred during the two-year period of the study.

name: Management advocacy
definition: Expressing support for the project and assigning it a higher priority; higher scores indicate that a project was strongly supported and given a higher priority by management.

name: Performance judgments
definition: Judgments about the likelihood that a project will achieve its technical and commercial objectives; a higher score indicates that a respondent perceived the project as more likely to achieve its technical and commercial objectives.

name: Emerging technology
definition: The speed at which the science and technology being used in the new product development project was emerging in the general scientific community; a higher score indicates that the focal area of science and technology knowledge was rapidly developing.

name: Technical and business experience
definition: The experience a firm had in commercializing such a product and the experience a firm had with the science and technology germane to the project being assessed; higher scores indicate more experience.

name: Resource investment
definition: The magnitude of the resource commitment made to a project; a higher score indicates a greater resource investment in the project.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity (R&D expenditures/sales) is used as an indicator of knowledge intensity, which refers to the extent that knowledge is a key factor of production. R&D in progress is an important source of information asymmetries when evaluating a firm's prospects.

name: Lockup agreements
definition: A lockup agreement, which grants a preferred bidder benefits should a rival emerge, tells potential rival bidders that their bids will be unwelcome while helping the favored bidder should a bidding war occur. Lockup agreements may be considered as signals of target managers' intentions to oppose any rival bidders that might emerge.

name: Bidding wars
definition: A bidding war is defined here as a situation in which more than one party issues a formal bid. Bidding wars are dramatic public contests over a firm's scope and boundaries.

name: Management buyouts
definition: A management buyout may represent an opportunity for managers to pay a small premium for their firm and realize large gains that were not apparent to the market. A transaction was coded as an MBO if news accounts confirmed that management's bid was not a defensive response to another bid and that management would have gained control of the firm if their bid succeeded.

name: Industry experience
definition: For the purposes of this research, we defined a stock of organizational knowledge as the years of industry experience and education of a firm's TMT members and knowledge workers and as the diversity of the information and knowledge this group holds.

name: Education
definition: For the purposes of this research, we defined a stock of organizational knowledge as the years of industry experience and education of a firm's TMT members and knowledge workers and as the diversity of the information and knowledge this group holds.

name: Functional heterogeneity
definition: The diversity of the information and knowledge a firm's TMT members and knowledge workers hold, as reflected in their functional backgrounds.

name: Number of direct contacts
definition: One of the most common measures of an individual's set of social relations is the number of people to whom he or she is directly connected.

name: Network range
definition: Network range refers to the scope of different types of contacts contained in TMT and knowledge worker networks.

name: Tie strength
authors_terms: ["strength of ties", "strength of network ties", "strength of a tie"]
definition: The strength of a tie refers to the nature of a relational contact. Closeness, long duration, and frequent contact are characteristics of strong ties.

name: Climate for risk taking
authors_terms: ["climate for risk taking", "climate that stresses risk taking"]
definition: We examined two aspects of organizational climate: the extent to which organizations encourage risk taking versus control, and the extent to which organizations emphasize team behaviors versus individual behaviors. Organizational climate is defined as the collective attitudes and beliefs of employees about the manner in which they perform their daily jobs.

name: Climate for teamwork
definition: We examined two aspects of organizational climate: the extent to which organizations encourage risk taking versus control, and the extent to which organizations emphasize team behaviors versus individual behaviors.

name: Knowledge creation capability
definition: Following Nahapiet and Ghoshal (1998), we defined and measured an organization's knowledge creation capability as the extent to which TMTs and knowledge workers have access to one another and other stakeholders, are capable of combining information and knowledge into new knowledge, and perceive value from the exchange and combination process.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["number of new products and services", "number of new products or services", "level of innovation"]
definition: A firm's level of innovation has often been defined and measured as the number of new products or services it generates in a given period.

name: Certification with a management standard
definition: Certification is a fundamentally public act because it entails submitting to an independent and public audit; it allows organizations to communicate the use of a set of standard practices. Certification occurs at the facility level.

name: Physical distance to potential buyers
definition: The geographic distance from a facility to its nearest major buyer. Distance reduces information transfer through its direct effect on transfer costs and by its association with other restricting factors.

name: Foreign location of potential buyers
authors_terms: ["foreign buyers", "potential buyers located in foreign countries", "international supply relationships"]
definition: The degree to which facilities in an industry sell to buyers outside of the United States. The authors argue that information asymmetries should be especially high in international supply relationships.

name: Ongoing vertical relationships with buyers
authors_terms: ["ongoing vertical relationships", "vertical relationship", "vertically integrated buyer", "industry vertical relationship"]
definition: The term vertical relationship captures both vertical integration and long-term contracts between suppliers and buyers. Such relationships occur more frequently when suppliers or buyers need to invest in relationship-specific assets and therefore cannot easily switch to new exchange partners.

name: Environmental management system
definition: An EMS requires a company to develop environmental objectives and policies, provide training and documentation, delegate responsibilities, and perform internal performance audits.

name: Environmental performance
definition: The extent of pollution generation relative to other facilities in an industry, estimated as the deviation between observed and predicted waste generation given a facility's size and industry sector.

name: Wholly owned foreign subsidiary entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rate of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries", "WOFS entry rate", "adoption of the WOFS form"]
definition: The entry rate of new wholly owned foreign subsidiaries was taken as a measure of the adoption of the WOFS form, which was the dependent variable. The focus in this study was on the rate at which wholly owned foreign subsidiaries entered Community I.

name: WOFS density in same industry and home country
authors_terms: ["WOFS density", "within-form (WOFS) densities", "Community I (same industry and home country)"]
definition: WOFS density was measured by the total number of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries from the same home country in the same industry (Community I) in the previous year.

name: WOFS density in same home country
authors_terms: ["home-country WOFS density", "Community II (same home country, different industries)"]
definition: Home-country WOFS density was measured as the total number of subsidiaries from the same home country but in different industries (Community II) in the previous year.

name: WOFS density in same industry
authors_terms: ["industry WOFS density", "Community III (same industry, different home countries)"]
definition: Industry WOFS density was measured as the total number of such subsidiaries in the same industry but from different home countries (Community III) in the previous year.

name: Joint venture density
authors_terms: ["cross-form (JV) density", "number of joint ventures in that community"]
definition: Joint venture (cross-form) density was measured as the total number of foreign joint ventures in Community I in the previous year.

name: Local acceptance of the WOFS form
authors_terms: ["local acceptance of the WOFS form in the host country", "public acceptance of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries", "host country receptiveness"]
definition: Local acceptance of the WOFS form was coded from the index of People's Daily, China's official newspaper. We then used the number of articles endorsing wholly owned foreign subsidiaries published in People's Daily in the previous year as a proxy for local acceptance of the WOFS form in the host country.

name: Relative product cost
definition: A fund's production costs relative to its competitors', reflected in expense ratios, which are well publicized and are a key input into consumer decision making. The authors treat inefficiency in this sense as a potential trigger for practice adoption.

name: Relative fund performance
definition: A fund's performance measured against the mean performance of all funds in its product category; poor performance relative to competing funds causes serious concern given its transparency and direct relation to consumer purchases of mutual fund shares.

name: External money management contracting
authors_terms: ["contracting to independent professional money management firms", "establish external contracts", "switch from in-house to external money management", "external contracting"]
definition: The decision to continue to make (i.e., manage funds in-house) or to buy (i.e., establish a contract with an independent professional money management firm) money management services.

name: Growth fund category
definition: The product category of a fund: growth funds invested more narrowly and aggressively in speculative companies that promised more rapid appreciation of principal, in contrast to conservative, broadly diversified stock funds.

name: Boston location
definition: Whether a mutual fund was located in Boston, the origin of the trustee logic; Boston-based funds tended to be more conservative and were especially resistant to the new performance logic.

name: New York location
authors_terms: ["New York-based funds", "located in New York", "New York funds"]
definition: Whether a mutual fund was located in New York, which was the epicenter of the performance logic promulgated by funds and money management firms located mainly in New York.

name: Horizontal relational governance
authors_terms: ["relational governance of horizontal ties", "horizontal relational governance", "horizontal ties"]
definition: Relational governance mechanisms are interfirm cooperative arrangements based on informal rules and unwritten codes of conduct that affect the behavior of firms when they are dealing with others. Horizontal ties are those involving SMEs located in the same industry segment or producing complementary products.

name: Vertical relational governance
authors_terms: ["relational governance of vertical ties", "vertical relational governance", "vertical ties"]
definition: Relational governance mechanisms are interfirm cooperative arrangements based on informal rules and unwritten codes of conduct that affect the behavior of firms when they are dealing with others. Vertical ties involve SMEs specialized in sequential activities of a particular supply chain.
