name: Sourcing of collective resources
authors_terms: ["sourcing of collective resources", "collective sourcing", "provision of collective resources"]
definition: Firms pool their common needs to collectively source a broad set of scale-efficient resources, such as export infrastructure (e.g., roads and ports), aggregate market information, and even governmental support (e.g., promotion of products in foreign markets).

name: Manufacturing productivity
authors_terms: ["manufacturing productivity", "production efficiencies", "manufacturing productivity gains along a supply chain"]
definition: Firms may attain manufacturing productivity (e.g., inventory and delivery efficiencies) if they coordinate their sequential activities and jointly develop competencies to manage their supply chain.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "rates of product innovation", "joint product innovation"]
definition: SMEs interested in jointly developing new products can mutually deploy resources and cospecialize their knowledge through recurrent simultaneous interaction; by combining distinct and complementary resources, SMEs can collectively achieve rates of product innovation that would be unattainable individually.

name: Access to global markets
authors_terms: ["access to global markets", "improved access to global markets", "export performance"]
definition: Such efficiencies in turn enhance SMEs' access to global markets, enabling firms to seek, find, and supply international clients.

name: Size relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["aspiration level for size", "size relative to aspiration level", "size below aspiration level", "size above aspiration level", "size goals"]
definition: An aspiration level is 'the smallest outcome that would be deemed satisfactory by the decision maker' (Schneider, 1992: 1053). Managers form an aspiration level for size through social comparison with similar organizations, and the difference between actual size and that aspiration level determines growth-seeking behavior.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below aspiration level", "loss ratio increase", "aspiration level for the loss ratio", "low performance"]
definition: A goal consists of an aspiration level on a measurable organizational outcome; the realized outcome on a goal variable is called performance for goal variables that measure firm profitability. When an organization falls below the aspiration level of a goal variable, decision makers initiate problemistic search for actions that may produce outcomes above the aspiration level.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm growth is the ratio of next-period and current-period size, and firm growth rate is this ratio minus 1.

name: Director interlocks
definition: Two firms are said to be connected by a director interlock when a person affiliated with one firm sits on the corporate board of the other firm.

name: Reputational penalties
authors_terms: ["reputational penalties", "decline in market value", "significant reputational penalties", "spillover effects"]
definition: Reputational penalties arising from allegations of financial reporting fraud, which I empirically defined as decline in a firm's market value as a result of fraud allegations.

name: Audit committee chair in associated firm
authors_terms: ["audit committee chair in the firm", "audit chair of associated firms"]
definition: An interlocking director holds the position of audit committee chair in the associated firm; the audit committee's charter is to provide independent oversight over the firm's accounting functions and assure the objectivity of the firm's financial statements.

name: Governance committee chair in associated firm
authors_terms: ["governance committee chair in the firm", "corporate governance chair of associated firms"]
definition: An interlocking director holds the position of corporate governance committee chair in the associated firm; corporate governance committees are responsible for developing and recommending governance principles to corporate boards.

name: Audit committee chair in accused firm
authors_terms: ["audit committee chair in an accused firm", "audit chair of accused firm"]
definition: An interlocking director holds the position of audit committee chair in an accused firm and may be viewed as more responsible than other directors for failing to detect the alleged financial reporting fraud.

name: Governance committee chair in accused firm
authors_terms: ["governance committee chair in an accused firm", "corporate governance chair of accused firm"]
definition: An interlocking director holds the position of governance committee chair in an accused firm and may be attributed more responsibility for potential lapses in these firms' governance practices.

name: Independent board chair
authors_terms: ["independent board chair", "independent chairs", "independence of board chair"]
definition: Board leadership structure in which a firm's CEO is not also its board chair; when a firm's CEO is also its board chair, board vigilance is weakened.

name: Proportion of independent directors
authors_terms: ["proportion of independent directors", "proportion of independent directors in an associated firm"]
definition: The number of independent directors divided by the total number of directors in an associated firm, where an outside director is classified as independent if the firm's proxy statement did not identify the director as having any direct or indirect business relationship with the firm.

name: Ownership of independent directors
definition: The total percentage of shares held by all the independent directors in an associated firm; independent directors holding equity stakes are expected to promote investors' interests because their personal wealth is tied to investors' wealth.

name: Pressure-resistant institutional investor ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership of pressure-resistant institutional investors", "ownership by pressure-resistant institutional investors", "pressure-resistant institutional investors"]
definition: The total percentage of shares held by public pension funds and professional investment funds, which are more effective monitors because of their independence from top executives.

name: Ownership of inside directors
authors_terms: ["ownership of inside directors", "inside directors' ownership", "insiders' ownership"]
definition: The total percentage of shares held by all inside directors (including the CEO) in an associated firm.

name: TMT intrapersonal functional diversity
definition: Intrapersonal functional diversity is defined as the average breadth of functional experience within TMT members; it gauges the extent to which TMT members are narrow functional specialists or broad generalists.

name: TMT dominant functional diversity
definition: Heterogeneity in the functional areas in which each TMT member has served the longest, that is, the functional area in which each TMT member has spent the most time.

name: TMT member colocation
definition: TMT member colocation is defined as the proportion of TMT members who work at the same physical address.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: The degree to which an absence of pattern, unpredictability, and unexpected change characterize a firm's competitive context.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was calculated as ROA, captured as annual income before extraordinary items and discontinued operations divided by net assets, with the corresponding industry-average ROA subtracted from each firm-level measure.

name: Dispositional optimism
authors_terms: ["dispositional optimism", "optimism", "entrepreneurs' optimism", "entrepreneurs' level of dispositional optimism"]
definition: Generalized expectancies for experiencing positive outcomes; individuals high in optimism exhibit confidence in a way that is both broad and diffuse, and it encourages them to approach challenges with enthusiasm and persistence.

name: Entrepreneurial experience
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial experience", "experience in starting new ventures", "previous experience in starting new ventures", "number of previous ventures founded"]
definition: Experience acquired through having started multiple new ventures; individuals possessing such experience are often described as habitual or repeat entrepreneurs.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamic environments are characterized by unpredictable and rapid change, which increases uncertainty for individuals and firms operating within them.

name: New venture performance
definition: Growth is often cited as the most important performance indicator of new venture success; the authors use two different objective measures of growth, revenue growth and employment growth.

name: Analyst appraisals
authors_terms: ["analyst appraisals", "negative analyst appraisals", "relatively low earnings forecasts", "negative stock recommendations"]
definition: Analysts' assessments of a firm, defined here as relatively low earnings forecasts or negative stock recommendations. Analysts' earnings forecasts and stock recommendations significantly influence trading behavior and stock market valuations.

name: Formal board independence
definition: A board's contractual, or 'formal,' independence from management, defined as the proportion of directors who lack contractual ties to their firm. The agency logic equates formal independence with a board's capacity to exercise control over management.

name: Actual board control
authors_terms: ["actual board control", "board control of management", "board monitoring and control of management"]
definition: The board's actual tendency to control management decision making on behalf of shareholders. Behavioral theory and evidence suggest that boards must be both formally and socially independent from management to objectively control management decision making.

name: CEO social influence over the nominating committee
authors_terms: ["CEO social influence over a nominating committee", "CEO-committee ties", "CEO's social influence over the board"]
definition: A CEO's a priori social influence over the nominating committee of the firm's board, indicated primarily by the proportion of committee members with friendship ties to the CEO. When committee members have social connections to the CEO they are reluctant to circumvent the CEO's preferences regarding board candidates.

name: CEO verbal impression management about board control
authors_terms: ["CEO verbal impression management about board control", "verbal impression management", "CEO attestations of board decision control"]
definition: The extent to which CEOs engage in verbal impression management directed toward analysts about the board's propensity to control management decision making, attesting to their boards' tendency to monitor and control management on behalf of shareholders.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated institutional ownership", "dedicated ownership", "level of ownership by dedicated shareholders"]
definition: Dedicated institutional investors acquire concentrated equity positions in a few firms and have extended investment horizons. The term refers to the level of ownership, or number of shares held, by this class of owner.

name: Transient institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["transient institutional ownership", "transient ownership", "level of transient ownership"]
definition: Transient institutional investors tend to acquire less concentrated equity stakes in a dispersed portfolio of firms and have a shorter investment horizon. The term refers to the level of ownership, or number of shares held, by this class of owner.

name: Strategic competitive actions
definition: Strategic competitive actions entail significant commitments of specific, distinctive resources and are difficult to implement and reverse.

name: Tactical competitive actions
definition: Tactical actions are 'designed to fine-tune strategy; they involve fewer and more general resources than strategic actions, are easier to implement, and are often more reversible.'

name: Foreign parent resource provision
authors_terms: ["foreign parent resource provision", "resource provision", "resource contribution", "foreign parent resource contribution"]
definition: The extent to which a joint venture received support from its foreign parent in areas such as product technology, operations technology, operations support, sales/marketing, administrative support, and training. Foreign parents can provide both critical resources and influence on how resources are deployed, and resource provision is viewed as distinct from decision influence.

name: Foreign parent decision influence
definition: The degree of influence the foreign parent has over specific areas and issues of joint venture management, such as financing, product and process technology, operations, sales/marketing, management decisions, administrative support, and pricing. Resource provision and decision influence are viewed as two different forms of foreign parent involvement.

name: Joint venture market performance
definition: A multiple-item survey measure of how key managers in the Hungarian parent, key managers in the foreign parent, and the respondent rate the performance of the joint venture, together with an aggregate rating of performance across seven activities.

name: Knowledge acquisition from foreign parent
definition: An index of the knowledge that a joint venture has acquired from its foreign parent, appraised with the frame 'to what extent have you learned from your foreign parent' across technological expertise, marketing expertise, product development, foreign cultures and tastes, managerial techniques, and production processes.

name: Transition phase
authors_terms: ["transition phase", "phase of the transition process", "early phase", "late phase"]
definition: A dichotomous indicator of the phase of a country's economic transition in which a joint venture operates, distinguishing an early phase with weak institutions, undeveloped factor markets, and a limited capacity for learning from a late phase with relatively stronger institutions, developed factor markets, and an enhanced capacity for learning.

name: Firm specialization
definition: The breadth of the market segments in which a firm operates: "Specialists concentrating their business in a few industry segments have a deep understanding of these segments' operations... Generalists have access to a wide range of market segments and a broad knowledge of their entire industry." The authors' measure approaches 0 for a bank underwriting in all seven market sectors (a generalist) and approaches 1 for a bank concentrated in few sectors (a specialist).

name: Structural holes
definition: The extent to which a firm's network partners are otherwise disconnected from one another: "A high value of structural holes meant that a bank's network contained a large proportion of otherwise disconnected partners; thus, the bank was located in an open network." The authors also describe it as the degree of a bank's network openness, measured with Burt's network efficiency measure.

name: Market share
definition: An investment bank's share of the value of public offerings underwritten in a period, used as the indicator of bank performance: "market share reflects banks' ability to earn underwriting fees that contribute to the return on their financial assets, and consequently their profitability."

name: CEO certification
definition: By a 'certification contest,' we mean a competition in which actors in a given domain are ranked on the basis of performance criteria that key stakeholders accept as credible and legitimate.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors assessed both the immediate and longer-term effects of CEO certification on performance; for longer-term performance they used both an accounting and a market measure to assess annual performance from 1992 through 1996.

name: CEO compensation
definition: Because CEO compensation takes a wide variety of forms, the authors used CEOs' total direct compensation as their measure.

name: Public ownership
authors_terms: ["public ownership", "publicly traded professional service firms", "public corporation", "public agencies"]
definition: Ownership of a firm by outside investors, so that the firm is traded publicly; the comparison is with a firm that has no outside owners (exclusive insider ownership).

name: Firm performance
definition: Overall agency performance, measured by the firm's growth rate; faster growth is often an indication of greater efficiency, and in the sample of publicly traded agencies growth rate and profitability were highly correlated.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of an agency, measured as the logarithm of global revenue adjusted to 1982 dollars.

name: Creativity
definition: Creativity refers to the originality of an ad campaign as expressed both in its artistic conception and its approach to positioning the clients' product; producing high levels of creativity is dependent on highly skilled individuals and is a distinct strategic position or choice.

name: Firm exit
definition: A firm's having ceased operations in the disk drive industry, excluding firms that were acquired; exit from the industry was concomitant with a cessation of industry-related innovative activity for diversified firms.

name: Knowledge diffusion
definition: The subsequent use of a firm's technology by other firms, tracked via the citations a patent receives from firms other than the one holding the patent.

name: Firm age at patenting
authors_terms: ["firm age at the time of a patent", "age of the innovating firm", "older firm"]
definition: The age of the innovating firm at the time of the patent application; older firms have higher stocks of private knowledge because they have stored past learning in behavioral rules and routines.

name: Internal knowledge base reliance
authors_terms: ["internal focus", "a patent's internal focus", "localized search", "building on its prior innovations"]
definition: The degree to which an innovation builds on the innovating firm's own prior innovations rather than on the knowledge of others; such innovations are closely bound within the routines and culture of the innovating firm.

name: Inventor team size
authors_terms: ["number of inventors", "team of inventors", "size of the team"]
definition: The number of inventors listed on a patent application, used as an indication of the size of the team involved in the innovative research being patented.

name: Technological diversity
authors_terms: ["range of technologies combined", "diversity of technologies", "range of technologies drawn upon"]
definition: The degree to which a patent draws upon a wide range of technological areas, captured by counting the number of citations a patent makes within each of the three-digit patent classes.

name: Response speed
definition: We model the rivalry of MNE dyads as an unfolding and continuous sequence of actions between the two firms in all the country markets where both compete. Response speed derives from the time between a rival's initiating action and the firm's response.

name: Home-host country distance
definition: The geographic distance between an MNE's home and a given host country will constrain the MNE's capability to act in that country and thereby slow its response.

name: Home-initiating country distance
authors_terms: ["home-initiating country distance", "geographic distance between an MNE's home country and the initiating country"]
definition: We focus on the geographic distance between an MNE's home country and the initiating country where a rival's attack has taken place. We argue that when an attack occurs in a geographically distant country, the MNE's awareness of the action as well as its motivation to respond swiftly are hampered.

name: Host government constraints
definition: We define government constraints as rules and regulations that hinder MNEs' entry and daily operations. We propose that host government constraints hinder the motivation and capability of an MNE to respond to rivals' attacks.

name: Home government constraints
definition: Building on the awareness-motivation-capability framework, we develop the notion that a 'safe backyard,' well protected by an MNE's home government, increases the MNE's motivation and capability to respond in host countries.

name: Subsidiary control
definition: Subsidiary control refers to the strength of the link between an MNE's headquarters and its subsidiary in a given host country (we assume that headquarters control is uniformly strong in the home country). Conceptually, subsidiary control captures the efficiency and effectiveness of information flows between headquarters and subsidiaries as well as the extent to which MNE headquarters can dictate the operating and strategic decisions of its foreign-based subsidiaries.

name: Initiating country importance
authors_terms: ["initiating country importance", "strategic importance of the initiating country"]
definition: In Hypothesis 6 we propose that the strategic importance of an initiating country increases an MNE's awareness of an attack and enhances its motivation to respond quickly.

name: Response location
authors_terms: ["within-country response", "response occurrence in the country of attack"]
definition: There are several reasons to believe that the speed of an MNE's response to an attack will be faster in the initiating country (the country where the action occurred).

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact occurs when firms encounter the same rivals in multiple markets.

name: Ownership form
definition: Ownership forms, defined as different structures of property rights, differ in residual control and income rights; the two prevalent forms studied are company ownership and franchising.

name: Market concentration
definition: The most commonly used measure of market concentration is the Herfindahl index, which is defined as the sum of the squared shares of the firms in a given market.

name: Room price
authors_terms: ["price per room per night", "average price for a hotel room", "room price"]
definition: The average price for a hotel room charged by an establishment; lower prices reflect more intense rivalry.

name: Rivals' price
authors_terms: ["rivals' price per room per night", "prices of the rivals", "rivals' prices"]
definition: The average price the rival hotels in the same market charged.

name: Revenues per available room
authors_terms: ["revenues per unit of capacity", "revenues per available room", "RevPAR", "performance"]
definition: Management scholars and industry practitioners frequently use revenues per unit of capacity as a performance measure, especially in industries with high fixed costs, such as the airline and hotel industries.

name: Royalty fee rate
definition: Our variable indicated the royalty fee per brand as a percentage of revenues.

name: MNC project investment
authors_terms: ["project count", "project investment", "project finance investment", "MNC investment project announcements", "announced investment projects"]
definition: Project investment, also described as project finance investment, is defined as direct investment using a legally independent project company financed by equity from a sponsoring firm or syndicate of sponsoring firms, and by nonrecourse debt. The dependent variable, project count, is the count of project investments announced by foreign-domiciled MNCs for developing country i in year t.

name: MNC electoral expectations
authors_terms: ["expectations", "MNC electoral expectations", "likelihood of reelection", "likelihood that a right-wing party candidate will prevail", "electoral expectations"]
definition: The framework's three rows define different MNC expectations (expressed as 'lambda') regarding the likelihood that a right-wing party candidate will prevail, ranging from zero to one. Expectations takes on three possible values related to three expected electoral outcomes MNCs might consider: a value of 1 indicates MNC expectations that right-wing parties and policies will prevail, -1 indicates expectations that left-wing parties and policies will prevail, and 0 indicates there is no clear MNC expectation of either.

name: Incumbent party partisan orientation
authors_terms: ["right-wing incumbent", "partisan orientation of incumbents", "partisan orientation of the incumbent party"]
definition: The columns of the framework define the partisan orientation of an incumbent party seeking to retain office in a general election. The DPI sets criteria for incumbent and challenger partisan orientation with left-wing, centrist, right-wing, and other classifications based primarily on content analysis of party titles and secondarily on content analysis of party platforms and historical commitments to investor (right-wing and centrist) versus worker (left-wing) interests.

name: CEO attention to a new technology
authors_terms: ["CEO attention", "attention to optics", "CEO attention to optics", "attention"]
definition: Attention refers to what managers pay attention to during periods of change; given the overwhelming amount of (often conflicting) information available, what managers pay attention to should affect a firm's strategic direction. It is captured as the emphasis on a theme relative to other themes.

name: Organizational incentives to invest in a new technology
authors_terms: ["organizational incentives", "incentives to invest", "incentives to adopt a new technology", "incentives to invest in optics"]
definition: Dependence on an existing customer base can create powerful incentives to invest in new technologies if such technologies are demanded by the customers or if action is required to preempt competition or create user switching costs. When a firm depends on a set of customers for its profits, the organizational incentives to invest in new technologies are higher if those customers are interested in the new technology.

name: Prior related capabilities
authors_terms: ["prior related capabilities (experience)", "prior related competence", "optical product experience", "capabilities (experience)"]
definition: Prior related competence can be thought of as accumulation of experience in an affiliated domain. Capabilities in the optical product-market are a construct that is primarily a function of time and can be meaningfully measured by the cumulative number of years of experience in a particular arena.

name: Firm investment in a new technology
authors_terms: ["investment in optical technologies", "investment in that technical domain", "optical patenting", "response to technical change"]
definition: The dependent variable is a measure of investment in a new technology, the extent to which a firm responded to optical technologies at a given time.

name: Number of related acquisitions since last restructuring
authors_terms: ["number of related acquisitions since last restructuring", "number of related acquisitions", "related acquisitions"]
definition: A count of the number of horizontal, vertical, and related diversified acquisitions made since the year of a firm's most recent restructuring; in the case of organizational restructuring, the count variable was reset to 0.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors measured firm performance through return on assets (ROA), which is the least sensitive to biases due to changes in leverage or bargaining power caused by acquisitions among accounting measures of profitability.

name: Organizational restructuring
definition: Organizational restructuring refers to recombination of existing subunits that leaves the scope of the firm unchanged, and is fundamentally different from portfolio restructuring, which refers to changes in the scope of a firm.

name: Number of related acquisitions between last two restructurings
authors_terms: ["number of related acquisitions between last two restructurings", "total number of related acquisitions between last two restructurings"]
definition: The total number of related acquisitions a firm had undertaken between its most recent restructuring and the one prior to that (i.e., between the last two restructurings).

name: Acquisition intensity
definition: The narrowness of the time interval in which a sequence of acquisitions is undertaken; attempting to integrate a given number of acquisitions in a shorter period of time is likely to lower the degree and quality of integration.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: Experience a firm accumulates as it repeatedly performs acquisitions, which routinizes the search process and allows the firm to decide on and implement a suitable course of action with less cognitive effort.

name: Restructuring experience
definition: Experience with organizational restructuring, which may benefit integration at the level of an acquirer as a whole, enabling it to recombine subunits and unlock untapped synergistic potential more efficiently and effectively.

name: Social status
definition: Status is defined as the prestige granted a firm because of its position in a social structure rather than merely its observed performance. It functions as a signal of quality that affects how focal firms and the activities in which they engage are perceived.

name: Partner structural holes
authors_terms: ["bridging structural holes", "unconstrained ego networks", "network constraint", "structural closure"]
definition: A firm bridges a structural hole in its network if it connects two otherwise unconnected firms. Such partners can create and extract more value for themselves but are exposed to less intense social control and norm enforcement than firms in structurally closed networks.

name: Entrant category
authors_terms: ["entering commercial bank", "comanager commercial bank", "entering firms", "incumbent investment banks"]
definition: Potential collaborators are either entering firms (commercial banks that set up investment banking subsidiaries to enter the corporate bond market) or incumbent firms (investment banks). Exclusion implies that incumbent firms disfavor collaborating with entering firms compared to collaborating with incumbent firms, even though the potential collaborator firms are otherwise similar in their attributes.

name: Collaboration likelihood
definition: The choice of which potential partner firm an incumbent lead manager bank collaborates with on a bond issue. Favoring entering firms over otherwise similar incumbent firms is inclusion; disfavoring them is exclusion.

name: Integration depth
definition: Integration depth is a basic strategic choice regarding the degree of structural and resource reconfiguration of an acquiring and acquired firm. It reflects the degree of change in structural relationships between a target and an acquirer and ranges from minimal to complete.

name: Integration speed
definition: Integration speed concerns the length of time the resources of the two organizations are disrupted during integration.

name: Top management team turnover
definition: Top management team turnover is the loss of managers of the combined firm during integration; managers represent potentially valuable resources in the combined firm that may be lost during integration.

name: Market focus
definition: Market focus is the extent to which management remains attentive to customer needs during integration.

name: Internal reorganization goal achievement
definition: The achievement of the intermediate goal of internally reorganizing combined firms' operations, realized by consolidating operations (e.g., asset rationalization and elimination of redundancies) and encouraging coordinated exchange of knowledge and information.

name: Market expansion goal achievement
definition: The achievement of the intermediate goal of market expansion, realized by leveraging coordinated market activities to increase the acquirer's market share, products offered, geographic markets served, customer markets served and/or effective selling of one firm's products to the other's customers.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: Acquisition performance is conceptualized as long-term abnormal stock returns to an acquirer, the deviation of actual stock performance from the performance expectations investors would have had in the absence of an acquisition, net of the premium paid by an acquirer.

name: Attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["attainment discrepancy", "performance relative to aspirations", "performance feedback", "performance relative to aspiration level"]
definition: The difference between actual performance and aspiration level is called 'attainment discrepancy'; a negative attainment discrepancy is performance below aspiration level. An aspiration level is 'the smallest outcome that would be deemed satisfactory by the decision maker'.

name: Acquisition hazard
authors_terms: ["acquisition hazard rate", "probability of an acquisition", "acquisition activity", "acquisitions", "acquisition announcements"]
definition: Because the authors were interested in firms' intentions to engage in acquisition activity (irrespective of whether the announced acquisitions were completed or how many acquisitions were announced by a focal firm), they coded announcements of one or more acquisitions during a year as an event.

name: Organizational slack
definition: The presence of slack resources (e.g., unused capacity, employees, unexploited opportunities, and financial resources) enables firms to increase search, which generates opportunities for change. Bourgeois (1981) identified three different categories of organizational slack: absorbed, unabsorbed, and potential.

name: Distance from bankruptcy
authors_terms: ["distance from bankruptcy", "proximity to bankruptcy", "financial distress", "Altman's Z-score", "distance from bankruptcy variable"]
definition: A firm that is experiencing significant operational and financial trouble and is on the verge of bankruptcy is said to be in financial distress. Altman's (1983) Z-score is an indicator of how far a firm is from bankruptcy: a high Altman's Z indicates that a firm is not at risk of bankruptcy, whereas a low score indicates that a firm is on the verge of bankruptcy.

name: Preexisting prestige
authors_terms: ["preexisting prestige", "quantity of preexisting prestige", "preexisting stock of prestige", "preexisting prestige index"]
definition: The total preexisting stock of prestige a firm possessed, formed from the number of prestigious executives, prestigious outside directors, and prestigious VCs in place at any given point in time.

name: Scarcity of preexisting prestige
definition: The inverse-coded preexisting prestige index; a higher score indicates that a firm had a relative lack of preexisting prestige.

name: Urgency
definition: The inverse of the number of months remaining until the IPO registration date; higher values indicate greater urgency, so that urgency grows as the final year counts down.

name: Prestigious hiring
authors_terms: ["final-year enhancement", "prestigious hiring", "number of prestigious executives and directors hired", "final-year prestigious hiring"]
definition: The number of prestigious executives and outside directors hired by a firm in a period during the year prior to its IPO; an individual is treated as prestigious if he or she possessed any of the indicators of prestige.

name: Personal prestige
definition: Whether a hired executive was prestigious, that is, possessed any of the indicators of prestige.

name: Executive compensation
authors_terms: ["cost of hiring an executive", "total compensation", "executive compensation"]
definition: The total compensation paid to an executive hired during the year prior to IPO, equal to the sum of annual salary, bonus, all other compensation, and the value of stock options granted.

name: Technical experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["technology solution provider technical experiential diversity", "provider technical experiential diversity", "technical experiential diversity"]
definition: The technical experiential diversity of a client's technology solution provider refers to its breadth of experience with different technological innovations.

name: Organizational experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["technology solution provider organizational experiential diversity", "provider organizational experiential diversity", "organizational experiential diversity"]
definition: The organizational experiential diversity of a technology solution provider refers to the breadth of its experience with different types of client firms.

name: Marketing intensity
authors_terms: ["client firm's marketing intensity", "marketing intensity", "a client's marketing intensity"]
definition: Marketing intensity is a market-based conceptualization of absorptive capacity; it exposes a firm to consumer trends and competitor activities and sensitizes it to external developments, enhancing its ability to utilize external knowledge in the pursuit of innovations.

name: Innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["client firm innovation adoption", "client innovation adoption", "innovation adoption"]
definition: A client firm's innovation adoption reflects the extent to which it offers new technology services, and by implication, the degree to which it has been able to overcome the adoption challenges, or knowledge hurdles, associated with the innovation.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Firms that compete in multiple markets will be more likely to cooperate, because a competitive attack in any one market may draw responses in all other jointly contested markets; the punishment for deviations from collusive behavior would increase with the number of markets in which rivals meet.

name: Service quality
definition: A critical dimension of a firm's competitive strategy, alongside price; in the airline industry, 'on-time performance provides a good measure of service quality, which varies across carriers and routes.'

name: Scheduled flight time
authors_terms: ["scheduled flight times", "scheduled time for a flight", "flight schedule length"]
definition: The time window airlines schedule for a flight; the authors use the scheduled time for a flight as a dependent variable because scheduling longer flight times reduces costs by reducing the need to invest as much in on-time performance and also reduces demand.

name: Contact market concentration
definition: The level of concentration of the routes on which multimarket contacts occur, measured with the Herfindahl index; firms are expected to fear retaliation in less competitive contact markets more, because there are more profits to be lost if rivals cut prices or increase quality in these markets.

name: Recruitment of technologically distant scientists
authors_terms: ["technologically distant scientists", "distant scientists", "recruitment of distant scientists", "hiring distant scientists", "number of distant scientists"]
definition: I define technologically distant scientists as those who possess knowledge outside their firm's existing technological boundaries. Recruitment is identified as a person filing a patent for firm x and then subsequently filing a patent for firm y.

name: Significant technological repositioning
definition: I define significant technological repositioning as the introduction of novel recombinations of far-flung knowledge elements. This study examines conditions in which recruitment results in significant technological repositioning-that is, knowledge combinations that fall outside a firm's existing technological boundaries.

name: Distribution of innovative productivity
authors_terms: ["distribution of innovative productivity", "asymmetries in a firm's innovative productivity", "power asymmetries", "centralization of patenting among incumbent scientists"]
definition: Distribution of innovative productivity refers to the degree to which the innovative productivity in firm y centered on one or a few key scientists. When the innovative productivity of a firm is concentrated in one or a few scientists, power asymmetries are likely to emerge.

name: Technological breadth
authors_terms: ["technological breadth", "breadth of an organization's existing technological knowledge", "technological scope", "technological diversity", "technological base"]
definition: The breadth of an organization's existing technological knowledge, measured as the dispersion of a firm's patents across technological fields. Firms that develop broader technological platforms also develop broader expertise.

name: Breadth of knowledge
definition: By breadth of knowledge, we mean the extent to which an individual possesses knowledge of a variety of different business areas important for starting and running a firm.

name: Prior leadership experience
definition: Leadership involves the use of noncoercive influence to direct and coordinate the activities of the members of an organized group toward the accomplishment of group objectives; a founder's prior leadership experience is measured as the highest position attained in a previous work activity.

name: Sector-specific labor requirements
definition: Because different businesses have different technical and market characteristics, they require different numbers of employees to staff and run them. The sector-specific labor requirements of a business opportunity capture the average employment size of newly founded firms in the industry in which the opportunity is pursued.

name: Job creation
authors_terms: ["job creation", "employment count", "employment counts", "jobs created for others"]
definition: Our dependent measure captures the total employment count of a newly founded firm in a given year, that is, jobs created for individuals besides the founders.

name: Branching policy
authors_terms: ["branching policy", "state branching policy", "state policy regulating bank branching", "restrictiveness of state policy regulating branching"]
definition: State-level policy stipulating whether banks in a state can establish branch offices outside of their headquarters location; laws sanction three primary types of branching: unit banking, statewide branching, and limited statewide branching.

name: Geographic dispersion of bank locations
definition: The extent to which banks rely on outlying locations, capturing growth achieved by the dispersed strategy.

name: Bank location size
authors_terms: ["bank location size", "size of individual bank locations", "average bank location size"]
definition: The average size of a bank's locations, meant to capture bank growth achieved by the centralized strategy, whereby banks establish large branches without necessarily expanding geographically.

name: Transportation infrastructure
authors_terms: ["transportation infrastructure", "transportation technology", "technological infrastructure", "nonurban (i.e., rural) roadway mileage"]
definition: The advancement of a state's transportation technology, in particular nonurban roadway mileage, which helped bank headquarters coordinate and inspect local branches.

name: Urbanization
definition: The degree to which a state's population is concentrated in cities.

name: Business competition
definition: The degree of competition among banks in a state.

name: Agrarian presence
authors_terms: ["agrarian presence", "cultural resistance", "local agrarianism", "actors with an agrarian logic"]
definition: The presence in a state of actors with an agrarian logic who promote community-oriented banking and resist banks' geographical expansion.

name: Environmental regulation stringency
authors_terms: ["country environmental stringency", "stringency of a country's environmental regulations", "stringency of industrial environmental regulation"]
definition: The stringency of a country's regulation of industrial pollution. In the context of environmental and other social institutions, the central institutional characteristic is institutional stringency: the degree to which firms are expected to limit the pollutant emissions that result from their operations.

name: Corporate investment in a host country
definition: The likelihood and magnitude of a firm's investment in a given country in a given year; investment is a censored continuous variable because it cannot take negative values.

name: Institutional distance from home country
authors_terms: ["institutional distance vs. home", "institutional strength (home country)", "distance between a country's environmental institutions and those of a firm's home country"]
definition: The distance between the environmental institutions of a focal country and those of an automaker's home country, where environmental institutions comprise the regulative and normative aspects of a country's institutions for environmental protection.

name: Institutional distance from prior experience countries
authors_terms: ["institutional distance vs. prior experience", "institutional strength (prior experience country)", "those of the countries in which the firm has previously invested"]
definition: The distance between the environmental institutions of a focal country and the weighted average of the environmental institutions of the countries in which the firm has previously invested.

name: Environmental capabilities
definition: A firm's ability to carry out its productive activities in ways that limit damage to the natural environment; environmental capabilities constitute the utilization of bundles of resources and routines that allow a firm to minimize its environmental impact.

name: TMT board control
authors_terms: ["TMT board membership", "TMT board control", "TMT director representation", "percentage of TMT board members", "TMT board member control"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's board made up of top management team members, particularly executives who were actively involved with the business at the time of the IPO.

name: Post-IPO performance
definition: A market-based measure of firm performance after an initial public offering, assessed as the returns earned by investors over the 24 months beginning on the second day of trading.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: The extent to which a firm existed in an environment of sustained growth, estimated as five-year industry sales growth.

name: Market dynamism
definition: High variation in demand for industry outputs.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: The presence of frequent industry innovations.

name: Technical complexity
definition: The degree to which esoteric technical requirements characterize industry conditions, requiring a firm to have a greater array of knowledge to participate fully in the industry.

name: Product diversity
definition: The diversity of products offered within an industry, another aspect of external complexity.

name: Geographic dispersion
definition: The physical dispersion of the operations of the firms included in the industries represented in the sample, a dimension of environmental complexity.

name: Founding branching policy
authors_terms: ["founding branching policy", "founding branching law", "statewide banking", "founding legal environment"]
definition: The state branching law in force at a bank's time of founding. Regulations were divided into three categories: full statewide banking (no geographic restrictions on locations), unit banking (banks limited to one location), and limited statewide banking (branching permitted but restricted).

name: Bank acquisition propensity
authors_terms: ["bank acquisition", "propensity to engage in acquisitions", "grow by acquisition", "acquisition activities"]
definition: Whether a bank acquired another bank in a given year. The authors relate their hypotheses to the propensity to engage in acquisition, rather than its frequency, in a given year.

name: Founding transportation infrastructure
authors_terms: ["founding transportation infrastructure", "founding technology environment", "transportation technology", "extent of highway development"]
definition: The development of roadways in a state at the time of a bank's founding, which the authors treat as one of two manifestations of modernization processes; it reflects the expansion and quality of highways available for coordinating and monitoring outlying bank locations.

name: Founding urbanization
definition: The level of urbanization in a state at founding, that is, the degree to which its population is concentrated in cities.

name: Founding Grange membership
authors_terms: ["founding Grange membership", "presence of agrarian social movement organizations", "Grange presence"]
definition: The presence of the National Grange of the Patrons of Husbandry, an agrarian activist organization that resisted large-scale commercial banks, in a state at the founding of a bank, measured as national Grange family members per state.

name: Founding agrarian presence
definition: The presence of actors holding agrarian beliefs in a state at founding, which constrained banks' geographical expansion and fostered locally oriented banks.

name: Founding Progressive presence
authors_terms: ["founding Progressive presence", "presence of Progressive political support", "Progressive presence at founding"]
definition: The presence of Progressivism, a general spirit of reform that opposed the concentration of power in large corporations and financial interests, in a state at the time of a bank's founding.

name: Enrollment management adoption
authors_terms: ["enrollment management", "enrollment management structure", "initial adoption of the enrollment management structure"]
definition: Enrollment management is both an organizational structure and a set of accompanying practices. The structural aspect involves the consolidation of various administrative functions that have the potential to affect enrollments and tuition revenues, facilitated by a new administrative position charged with overseeing them both.

name: Faculty power and professionalism
authors_terms: ["power and professionalism of internal elites", "powerful and professionalized faculties"]
definition: Power and professionalism are the two main ingredients in Selznick's recipe for avoiding goal displacement and value attenuation; organizations are predicted to be at lower risk of adopting value-subverting management innovations when the internal elites who stand to be affected by them are relatively powerful and highly professionalized.

name: Admissions personnel power and professionalism
authors_terms: ["power and professionalism of admissions personnel", "powerful and professionalized admissions personnel"]
definition: Power and professionalism are the two main ingredients in Selznick's recipe for avoiding goal displacement and value attenuation; colleges are proposed to be less vulnerable to enrollment management adoption to the extent that admissions personnel are empowered and demonstrably committed to the values of their profession.

name: Tuition independence
authors_terms: ["autonomy from enrollment pressures", "less dependent on tuition as a source of revenue", "tuition independence", "lower dependence on tuition as source of revenue"]
definition: Colleges with significant nontuition revenue streams (e.g., from endowment and grant income) are relatively autonomous from enrollment pressures; lower dependence on tuition as a source of revenue is a telling indicator of a college's relative autonomy.

name: Student drawing power
authors_terms: ["student drawing power", "geographic dispersion of its student body", "national 'drawing power'"]
definition: Two telling indicators of a college's relative autonomy from enrollment pressures are: (1) lower dependence on tuition as source of revenue and (2) geographic dispersion of its student body. Colleges with national 'drawing power' are predicted to be at lower risk of enrollment management adoption.

name: Prior adoption of professional programs
definition: During the 1970s and 1980s, a majority of liberal arts colleges adopted professional degree programs in response to changing student degree preferences and enrollment and budgetary pressures. These changes were critical ones because they were manifestly inconsistent with these colleges' traditionally espoused values.

name: Presidential tenure
definition: Longer experience in a college (and, more specifically, as its president) is expected to make a leader more attuned to institutional values and commitments, more aware of organizational complexities and interdependencies, and more wary of new management innovations that offer easy solutions to perennial problems.

name: Presidential migration from prior adopters
authors_terms: ["president from school with enrollment management structure", "presidential migration", "migrated from previous adopters"]
definition: Schools are more likely to adopt enrollment management when they are led by presidents who have worked at another institution that has previously adopted the structure; such leaders should be less normatively opposed to the change and more likely to see it as an 'appropriate' administrative device.

name: Field-level prevalence of enrollment management
authors_terms: ["cumulative prior adoption of enrollment management at the field level", "prevalence at the field level"]
definition: The overall percentage of liberal arts colleges that had adopted the enrollment management structure as of time t-1; the neoinstitutional literature suggests that the mere prevalence of a structure or practice is strong evidence of its cultural acceptability.

name: Direct competitor adoption of enrollment management
authors_terms: ["percentage of direct competitors previously adopting the enrollment management structure", "more of its direct competitors have adopted the structure"]
definition: A college's group of direct competitors is defined as the five other schools that had the highest degree of geographic overlap and were also within one standard deviation of a focal school on tuition similarity and selectivity similarity.

name: Competitor tuition discounting
authors_terms: ["mean tuition discount rate of direct competitors", "direct competitors are heavily engaged in tuition discounting"]
definition: Tuition discounting is the core practice of enrollment management: colleges strategically allocate financial aid to maintain desired enrollment levels and meet financial goals. Hypocrisy 9 uses the mean tuition discount rate of a focal college's direct competitors.

name: Status position
definition: An organization's position in the overall status hierarchy of its field; organizational sociologists have noted a strong tendency toward 'middle-status conformity' that appears to be driven by the social insecurity and 'status anxiety' of organizations that occupy positions in the middle of a status hierarchy.

name: Time period
definition: The late period was defined as the latter half of our 20 year study period (1997-2006).

name: Defensive institutional work
authors_terms: ["defensive institutional work", "defensive institutional statements", "defensive institutional efforts", "fieldwide defense", "fieldwide defensive efforts"]
definition: Purposive action to minimize disruptions via rhetoric that counters assertions of negative events or inappropriate practices or that otherwise communicates reassuring information regarding the ongoing activities of organizations within an impacted field. In this context, such efforts communicate reassuring information about the safety of one or more railroad companies or the overall field.

name: Accidents at other firms
authors_terms: ["others' accidents", "accidents in the field", "accidents at other firms"]
definition: A count of the number of accidents (in hundreds) involving other firms, and not the focal firm, during a prior year. Railroads are required to report all accidents that result in fatalities, significant injuries, or damage above an established value, including derailments, hazardous material spills, and impacts with pedestrians or motorists.

name: Field issue scrutiny
authors_terms: ["issue scrutiny across the field", "fieldwide scrutiny", "scrutiny of safety-related issues across the field"]
definition: Scrutiny refers to ongoing, obtrusive, and critical attention to particular organizational activities coming from customers, stockholders, board members, regulators, the press, and other members of the public. The field-level variable is the ratio of negatively toned articles about safety for all companies excluding the focal firm to total articles about any issue.

name: Firm issue scrutiny
authors_terms: ["issue scrutiny at the focal firm", "scrutiny of safety-related issues at the focal firm"]
definition: Ongoing, obtrusive, and critical attention to a focal organization's activities; measured as the ratio of negatively toned articles about safety for the focal firm to total articles about any issue pertaining to it.

name: Core similarity
authors_terms: ["core similarity", "similarity between stricken organizations and potential responders", "core attributes"]
definition: Organizations share relatively central, enduring, and salient attributes with stricken firms, such as major product lines and a prominent brand image. In the railroad industry, the provision of passenger service is one of the most prominent and distinguishing attributes, and a higher value on the interaction of passenger service revenue with accidents at other passenger service providers indicates greater core similarity with accident-prone firms.

name: Similarity of experience with externally induced accidents
authors_terms: ["similarity of experience with accidents that could involve external forces", "similarity involving accidents that could be driven by forces outside direct organizational control"]
definition: Similarity based on characteristics not believed to be directly responsible for the disruptions, namely experience with accidents whose causes could have arisen at least in part through forces outside of direct organizational control, such as collisions between rail equipment and pedestrians or motorists. A higher value on the interaction reflects more accidents across the field that could involve external forces combined with increases in the firm's own experience with similar accidents.

name: Substitution threat
authors_terms: ["substitution threat", "threat from potential substitutes", "threat of substitution"]
definition: The threat that rivals will create alternative innovations drawing on alternative knowledge bases to perform the same function as the focal innovation, thereby eroding the sustainability of the firm's competitive advantage.

name: Imitation deterrence
authors_terms: ["imitation deterrence", "propensity to deter imitation", "deterrence inclination", "patent litigation"]
definition: The extent to which the firm sponsoring an innovation acts to deter rivals from creating innovations that build on the same knowledge base, in this setting by initiating patent infringement lawsuits.

name: Commercial value
definition: The extent to which an innovation is already embodied in saleable products and generates commercial value in the form of current profits.

name: Innovation development stage
definition: The phase of an innovation's life cycle between discovery, development and market introduction, during which uncertainties about the innovation's viability, technical superiority and scope of applicability gradually diminish.

name: Knowledge novelty
authors_terms: ["novelty of the knowledge", "pioneers novel knowledge", "new mechanism"]
definition: The extent to which the knowledge base underlying an innovation has not been utilized before in a product class, so that its elements, combinations and cause-effect relationships are yet to be fully understood.

name: Formal board independence
authors_terms: ["formal board independence", "formal independence", "change in formal independence"]
definition: Directors are classified as independent if they do not have employment, family, or business relationships with the firm that they serve as directors; board independence can be viewed as a multidimensional construct consisting of two distinct dimensions, formal independence and social independence.

name: Social board independence
definition: Social independence is typically conceptualized and measured as the existence of informal ties between directors and management or demographic similarity between them, which can contribute to 'similarity-attraction bias' and impair directors' ability to impartially evaluate management.

name: Positive media coverage
authors_terms: ["positive media coverage", "positive coverage", "favorability of media coverage"]
definition: The positive valence of a firm's press coverage, captured simultaneously with negative valence rather than coded as a single bipolar dimension because positive and negative valence are distinct constructs rather than opposite ends of a continuum.

name: Negative media coverage
definition: The negative valence of a firm's press coverage, captured simultaneously with positive valence rather than coded as a single bipolar dimension because positive and negative valence are distinct constructs rather than opposite ends of a continuum.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: A dummy variable coded 1 if the reason for departure given in ExecuComp was 'resigned.'

name: CEO compensation level
definition: CEO compensation level includes CEO salary, short-term bonus, and the value of long-term incentive grants made in a particular year.

name: At-risk compensation
authors_terms: ["at-risk compensation", "contingent compensation", "proportion of at-risk pay", "variable compensation"]
definition: Following prior research, at-risk compensation is measured as the proportion of total compensation consisting of long-term incentive pay.

name: Political pluralism
definition: An institutional arrangement wherein the political orientations of national and subnational policy makers differ, in such a way that one political party may dominate the national government while a political party with an ostensibly incompatible creed governs certain subnational units.

name: Organizational expansion
authors_terms: ["branch expansion", "expansion", "organizations' decisions to expand in a subnational unit"]
definition: A bank's expanding in a state in a particular year, represented as a count of the number of branches opened annually by each bank in each of the 24 states.

name: Reduction in political competition
authors_terms: ["reduction in political competition", "political competition in a subnational unit", "voter loyalty"]
definition: The extent to which political competition in a subnational unit is curtailed, measured as the number of years the incumbent ruling party had ruled the state continuously.

name: State ownership
authors_terms: ["state ownership", "state-owned firms", "organizations owned by or dependent on a government"]
definition: Whether a government entity had a majority ownership share in a particular bank; organizations owned by or dependent on a government will normally be unable to take advantage of many opportunities offered by pluralism.

name: Proportion of business from focal state
authors_terms: ["proportion of business from focal state", "the proportion of an organization's total business coming from that subnational unit", "situational embeddedness"]
definition: The ratio of a bank's branches in a focal state to its total number of branches in all states in a particular year.

name: Disapproval
definition: Disapproval refers to the negative social evaluations of firms brought to public attention. It is the expression of criticism directed at a firm's activities, values, or behavior.

name: Stigma dilution
authors_terms: ["stigma dilution", "stigma dilution across categories", "stigma dilution across industry categories", "stigma dilution across customer categories"]
definition: Stigma dilution is the process whereby category straddlers associated with a stigmatized category dilute stakeholder attention, moving it away from that stigmatized category by forming multiple categorical associations.

name: Category saliency
definition: Salient organizational categories (stigmatized or not) are those that industry stakeholders systematically use to classify firms.

name: Current option wealth
authors_terms: ["current wealth", "current option wealth", "accumulated current wealth", "risk bearing", "endowed wealth"]
definition: Current wealth is the accumulated cash value of the CEOs' options (option wealth at time t) that is at risk of loss when pursuing prospective wealth. The accumulated cash value of stock options is likely to be immediately endowed into calculations of personal wealth.

name: Prospective option wealth
authors_terms: ["prospective wealth", "prospective wealth within CEOs' stock options", "prospective gains"]
definition: Prospective wealth reflects potential increases to the options' cash value, over and above their current cash value, if the firm's stock price were to increase in the future (potential increases in wealth between time t and t + n). Prospective wealth is the potential additional wealth that an agent estimates could be realized, over and above the current cash value of stock options, due to future increases in a firm's stock price.

name: Strategic risk taking
definition: Strategic risk taking is measured through the strategic risks the literature argues reflect such risk: R&D expense, capital expenditures, and long-term debt. A higher score for this variable is interpreted as greater risk taking.

name: Availability of hedging instruments
authors_terms: ["CEO hedging", "availability of hedging instruments", "active risk management", "hedging"]
definition: Hedging is an example of active risk management that describes the process of making investments protecting one's wealth against adverse price movements. The authors use measures of cost and ease of hedging through the purchase of put options as a proxy for actual CEO hedging.

name: CEO vulnerability
definition: Agent vulnerability derives from severe threats to endowed wealth, for instance due to possible dismissal that involves the loss of current income as well as depressed future earnings resulting from a tarnished reputation in the executive labor market. Conceiving of employment risk as a proxy for vulnerability.

name: Founding team embeddedness in the financial logic
authors_terms: ["embeddedness in the financial logic", "financial embeddedness", "financial founders", "financial directors"]
definition: Measures of a founding team's embeddedness in the financial logic were financial backgrounds, banking backgrounds, and corporate board backgrounds; those backgrounds are assumed to influence the cognitive structures of founders so that they give greater primacy to financial considerations than do other founders.

name: Founding team embeddedness in the community logic
authors_terms: ["embeddedness in the community logic", "community embeddedness", "community directors", "community-oriented founders"]
definition: The measure of a founding team's community embeddedness was the proportion of directors who listed some involvement in volunteer community boards, whether social, civic, professional, or economic.

name: Entrepreneurial success
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial success", "likelihood of a founding team reaching the point of establishment", "establishing a bank", "bank establishment"]
definition: Entrepreneurial success is defined as the likelihood of a founding team reaching the point of establishment, that is, the odds of a founding team establishing an organization.

name: Economic turbulence
definition: Economic perspectives took a sharp turn for the worse in September of 2008; the measure of turbulence, crisis, is a dummy variable with a value of 1 for banks not established or withdrawn by August of 2008, since banks that were still in the process of being established as of September of 2008 were much less likely to get established.

name: Logic diversity in founding teams
authors_terms: ["highly embedded in both financial and community logics", "diverse teams", "diverse founding boards", "diversity of logics", "logic complexity"]
definition: Founding teams highly embedded in both financial and community logics, that is, diverse teams; founding teams could be strongly or weakly enmeshed in those logics independently of one another, and teams could be strongly embedded in both, or in neither.

name: Information technology capital
definition: Information technology (IT) capital-personal computers, servers, networks (e.g., the internet) and associated software. IT capital has two contrasting effects, an electronic brokerage effect and an electronic integration effect.

name: Narrowly valuable assets
authors_terms: ["narrowly valuable assets", "narrowly valuable physical and R&D capital"]
definition: Narrowly valuable assets are transaction-, user-, use-, or usage-specific. They have the potential to increase revenues and/or decrease costs in a relatively small set of economic exchanges.

name: Broadly valuable assets
authors_terms: ["broadly valuable assets", "broadly valuable relational and organizational capital"]
definition: In contrast to narrowly valuable assets, broadly valuable assets can reduce costs and/or increase revenues in a wide variety of economic contexts. Examples of such broadly valuable assets include relational and organizational capital.

name: Vertical integration
definition: The level of a firm's vertical integration, assessed by the input-output interdependencies between a firm's primary segment and its secondary segments.

name: Product-market diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm's output is distributed across different product markets, captured by horizontal complementarity and by the entropy measures of related and unrelated diversification.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance, which the authors measure using return on assets, or pretax income divided by total assets.

name: Geographic proximity to industry peers
authors_terms: ["firm proximity", "proximity", "proximity to other companies that perform related R&D", "proximity to industry peers"]
definition: Proximity to other companies that perform related R&D; the measure is computed from the distances between a focal firm and all other firms at time t, weighted by the patent productivity of those other firms.

name: Innovative performance
definition: A firm's innovation performance, modeled with two dependent variables: the citation-weighted impact of its nanotechnology patents and the number of patents that introduce new combinations of technological domains.

name: Intraorganizational network cohesion
authors_terms: ["cohesion", "network cohesion", "cohesive networks", "cohesiveness of intraorganizational collaboration network", "clustering"]
definition: The overall level of clustering in a firm's network of inventors, capturing the extent to which inventors' collaborators also collaborate with one another; cohesive networks are highly connected with many redundant ties.

name: Intraorganizational network inefficiency
definition: Inefficient networks have low connectivity and diffuse information slowly, fostering innovation by creating opportunities for brokers to join disconnected network areas and by facilitating parallel problem solving.

name: CEO career variety
definition: The array of distinct professional and institutional experiences an executive has had prior to becoming CEO; it encompasses the breadth of work experiences an executive has engaged in over the course of his or her career prior to becoming a CEO.

name: Strategic dynamism
definition: Strategic dynamism refers to the magnitude of change in a firm's allocation of resources and priorities over time.

name: Strategic distinctiveness
definition: Distinctiveness (or strategic nonconformity) refers to how much a firm's profile differs from the profiles of other firms, or its industry's central tendencies, at any given point in time; it reflects the degree to which a firm adheres to, or conversely ignores, prevailing industry norms.

name: TMT membership change
definition: TMT membership change concerns the extent to which the composition of a given TMT differs over time.

name: TMT heterogeneity
definition: TMT heterogeneity is the extent to which a group of senior executives is characterized by diversity in backgrounds, experiences, and outlooks.

name: VC centrality
authors_terms: ["VC centrality", "centrality of a young firm's VC investors", "central VC investors", "centrality"]
definition: The centrality of a young firm's VC investors captures the investors' position in the overall VC syndication network, and therefore their desirability and network reach. The core features of third parties are captured by centrality—that is, by the extent to which the third party is connected to well-connected others.

name: VC proximity
authors_terms: ["VC proximity", "geographically local VC investors", "proximity", "geographically more proximate VC investors"]
definition: Geographic proximity between the young firm and its VC investors captures the familiarity and strength of the immediate tie, because more proximate investors are likely to interact more frequently with a young firm; thus they have a closer and more influential relationship.

name: Corporate investment relationships
authors_terms: ["corporate investment relationships", "CVC relationships", "corporate ties", "number of corporate venture investors", "corporate partners"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the number of corporate venture investors that participated in a given round of a young firm's funding.

name: Secrecy defenses
authors_terms: ["secrecy defenses", "trade secret defenses", "strength of trade secret protection", "secrecy defense"]
definition: Trade secrets represent an exclusive source of protection for a diverse range of intellectual property—from knowhow, to recipes, to customer lists—as long as firms actually keep them secret. Strong trade secret regimes make corporate relationships more likely, because trade secrets are an agreeable defense for both the young firm and the corporation.

name: Timing defenses
definition: Forming relationships at a later stage in a venture's development (termed a 'timing defense') makes corporate relationships more likely: as young firms mature, their innovations become harder to imitate and misappropriate, thus reducing the likelihood of detrimental shifts in power.

name: Business group diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification of a business group", "business group diversification"]
definition: The number of industries in which a business group is involved, with industries defined at the two-digit NIC level.

name: Business group international sales
authors_terms: ["international sales of a business group", "group international sales"]
definition: The sum of international sales (in ten million rupees) of all firms that belong to the same group, not including the focal firm.

name: Industry segments served
authors_terms: ["industry segments served", "number of industries a firm serves"]
definition: A count of the number of industries that a firm serves in each year; the Nasscom directories list the industries (commonly referred to as 'verticals') each firm serves.

name: Foreign markets served
authors_terms: ["foreign markets served", "range of foreign markets served"]
definition: The number of foreign regions that a firm serves, with firms classified according to the geographic regions they serve rather than individual countries.

name: International sales
definition: International sales figures come directly from firm entries in the Nasscom directories, where firms report both their total sales and their export (or international) sales.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm productivity, measured as sales per employee, is a measure of how much a firm is able to charge its clients for its services, which in turn reflects its relative profitability.

name: New deregulation
definition: The deregulation of the telecommunications sector in India, which began in 1999 and gained significant momentum in 2000, had a dramatic effect on increasing the number of competitors in the Indian software industry.

name: Indirect competitor links
authors_terms: ["indirect competitor links (ICL)", "indirect links to the focal firm's competitors", "indirect ties to rivals", "second-order links to rivals", "indirect links to competitors"]
definition: Firms can be exposed to competitors when their first-order partners establish second-order paths to their rivals; the authors define rivals as firms operating in the same industry based on their primary six-digit Global Industry Classification Standard code.

name: Strategic experience
authors_terms: ["strategic experience", "strategic knowledge", "Eastern European experience", "experience in Eastern Europe"]
definition: Based on the behavioral theory of the firm, the authors define strategic knowledge as the information and know-how embodied in a firm's accumulated experience with a strategic issue, which they operationalize as foreign experience in Eastern Europe.

name: Tie termination
definition: Pruning refers to dissolving interlocks, and the authors argue that such an action is more likely as the firms to which directors connect the focal firm increasingly create paths to rivals.

name: Tie formation
definition: Grafting refers to creating new interlocks by appointing directors that establish new links to other firms.

name: Network closure
definition: Firms can safeguard strategic knowledge by seeking to embed themselves in a closed, dense network in which social monitoring is more prevalent and knowledge diffusion is more circumscribed.

name: Failure concentration
authors_terms: ["failure concentration", "distribution of failures within an organization", "concentration of failures"]
definition: The distribution of failures within an organization refers in essence to the distribution of the locations of those failures; failures are concentrated in their origin when they primarily involve a particular unit or even a specific individual, and dispersed when each involves different units or individuals.

name: Failure rate
definition: The organization's failure rate, measured as the average risk-adjusted mortality rate across CABG surgeries performed at the hospital during each two-year period, with higher values reflecting a worse patient survival rate.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size provides decision makers with contextual information regarding concentrated failures; larger organizations have greater structural differentiation, more subunits, and more employees compared to their smaller counterparts, and thus more locations in which failures could potentially arise.

name: Performance above aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance above the aspiration", "performance exceeds this aspiration level", "distance between performance and aspiration level"]
definition: The discrepancy between performance and aspiration when performance increases above the aspiration level; organizations performing far above aspirations are able to use slack or excess resources in order to thoroughly explore their environment.

name: Performance below aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below the aspiration", "performance drops below the aspiration level", "performance decreases (in absolute value) below the aspiration level"]
