definition: The discrepancy between performance and aspiration when performance falls below the aspiration level; decision makers at organizations performing far below the aspiration level are motivated to repair the gap and are able to direct resources to more thoroughly explore their environment.

name: Probability of making a subsequent acquisition
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of making a subsequent acquisition", "probability of making a subsequent acquisition", "acquisition likelihood", "subsequent acquisitions"]
definition: The dependent variable of this study was the hazard rate of a firm in the sample making a subsequent acquisition following the focal acquisition.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: We measure acquisition performance based on the stock market response using the 'cumulative abnormal return' (CAR). We call this variable Acquirer Market Returns to reflect accurately the construct it captures.

name: Historical aspiration level
definition: We similarly measured historical aspiration levels by taking an exponentially weighted moving average of the CARs of prior acquisitions.

name: Social aspiration level
definition: We measured the social aspiration level by the average acquirer market returns of all acquisitions made by all other banks in the state in which the focal bank derives the largest amount of deposits during the year prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Acquisition performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["acquirer market returns relative to aspiration levels", "acquisition performance relative to aspiration levels", "relative acquirer market returns"]
definition: Acquirer market returns relative to the aspiration level is the difference between the acquirer market returns of the focal acquisition and the aspiration level; the authors split this variable into a part below the aspiration level and a part above it using a spline function.

name: Acquisition performance relative to historical aspiration level
authors_terms: ["acquirer market returns relative to historical aspiration", "Acquirer Market Returns below Historical Aspiration", "Acquirer Market Returns above Historical Aspiration"]
definition: Acquirer Market Returns below Historical Aspiration was set to 0 when the acquirer market returns of the focal acquisition is above the historical aspiration level and equals the difference between the acquirer market returns of the focal acquisition and the historical aspiration level when the acquirer market returns of the focal acquisition is below the historical aspiration level.

name: Acquisition performance relative to social aspiration level
authors_terms: ["acquirer market returns relative to the social aspiration level", "Acquirer Market Returns below Social Aspiration", "Acquirer Market Returns above Social Aspiration"]
definition: To test Hypothesis 2, we created two variables of acquirer market returns relative to the social aspiration level using the same method used to create the relative performance measures for the historical aspiration level.

name: Variability in acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquirer market returns variability", "variability in acquisition performance", "performance variability"]
definition: This variable captures the degree to which the acquirer market returns of a bank's prior acquisitions vary, and was measured by the standard deviation of the acquirer market returns of all acquisitions made prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Leadership defense
authors_terms: ["leadership defended", "staying ahead", "remaining in the lead", "avoiding dethronement"]
definition: Whether or not the boat that was ahead at the start of the upwind leg is the first to round the windward mark, thus remaining in the lead at the end of the leg.

name: Action imitation
definition: Imitation of the follower's tactical moves; it captures similarity between the sequences of leader and follower actions over time.

name: Positioning imitation
definition: The similarity between leader and follower competitive positions; in a business context it can broadly be thought of as imitation of the competitive strategy of the follower.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Unpredictability defined as the amount of disorder or turbulence in the flow of opportunities such that there is less consistent similarity or pattern; the term uncertainty is used to refer to the unpredictability of environmental contingencies affecting performance.

name: Leader initial advantage
definition: The initial performance advantage of the leader over the follower at the start of the competitive interaction; a leader with a strong initial advantage, such as high market share, may become isolated in competitive interactions.

name: Follower capability advantage
authors_terms: ["follower capability advantage", "capability advantage of the follower", "capability advantages of the follower"]
definition: The extent to which the follower is better able to execute its competitive strategy than the leader, i.e. holds a capability advantage over the leader.

name: Organizational status
definition: Status is an organization's relative position in a hierarchical social order. It is directly tied to the firm's pattern of affiliations and indirectly tied to its past behavior.

name: Corporate illegality
definition: The illegal act examined was the use of illegal loan recovery practices by the commercial banks and their agents, that is, loan recovery harassment, the 'non-observance of Reserve Bank guidelines on engagement of recovery agents by banks'.

name: Decline in historically referenced reputation for quality
authors_terms: ["decline in historically referenced reputation for quality", "fall short of its historical reputation for quality"]
definition: A decline in a bank's reputation for quality relative to its own historical reputation, defined through a spline function of the difference between a bank's reputation for quality and its own past reputation.

name: Decline in socially referenced reputation for quality
authors_terms: ["decline in socially referenced reputation for quality", "reputation for quality falls short of those of its peers"]
definition: A decline in a bank's reputation for quality relative to its social reference points, that is, relative to the reputations of its status bracket peers, defined through a spline function of the difference between a bank's reputation for quality and the reputations of its peers.

name: Associates' reputation for integrity expectations
authors_terms: ["reputation for integrity expectations of associates", "integrity expectations", "reputation for integrity"]
definition: Reputation for integrity is the use of ethical means to deliver a given level of quality; a bank's associates' expectations about integrity are inferred from the reputation for integrity of the BSE500 firms associated with the bank.

name: Organizational resistance to institutional pressure
authors_terms: ["resistance to the smoking ban", "resistance", "active resistance", "organizational resistance"]
definition: Institutional resistance is defined, following Lawrence (2008: 171), as 'attempts of actors to impose limits on institutional control and institutional agency.' In this study it is the active resistance of small bars to the smoking ban.

name: Residential stability
definition: Residential stability is the relational dimension of community social cohesion: in communities where the turnover of residents is relatively low, the relational facet of cohesion is more likely to develop through connections built over time among residents, producing a latent relational infrastructure.

name: Kinship
definition: Kinship is the sentiment, sense, or feeling that bonds residents to a specific place - community - and generates commitment and a responsibility for the residents to take care of it.

name: Resistance in neighboring communities
authors_terms: ["contiguity effect", "level of resistance in neighboring communities", "resistance in neighboring municipalities"]
definition: The contiguity effect is the influence of neighboring communities: the level of resistance in the communities surrounding the focal community, with the weight of these neighboring municipalities exponentially diminishing with distance from the focal municipality.

name: Employee-experienced performance-oriented HR systems
definition: A set of internally consistent HR practices that develop employee work-related skills and motivation and provide opportunities for their utilization.

name: Employee-experienced maintenance-oriented HR systems
definition: A set of internally consistent HR practices that protect employment security and status equality, the so-called 'iron rice bowl'.

name: Domain-relevant skills
definition: The factual knowledge and the technical skills required in a given domain, which determine what employees can do in the creative process.

name: Employee creativity
definition: The generation of novel and useful ideas.

name: Aggregate employee creativity
definition: The mean of the firm's core knowledge employees' creativity evaluations done by their supervisor, formed through an additive composition model.

name: Firm ownership
definition: Whether a firm is a privately owned enterprise (POE) or a state-owned enterprise (SOE).

name: Firm innovation
definition: The development and launch of new products.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: A subjective evaluation of a firm's overall quality which is ascribed by various audiences. Corporate reputation is 'corporate' not only in the obvious sense that it applies to business firms, but also in the sense that it represents a gestalt evaluation of a whole (i.e., corporate) entity.

name: Earnings misses
authors_terms: ["earnings misses", "failed stakeholder exchanges", "number of earnings misses"]
definition: These events occur when a firm reports quarterly profits that fall short of the 'consensus estimate' which prevails at the time of the announcement. When a firm fails to deliver the specific currencies that a constituency expects at a given time, a failed stakeholder exchange can be said to have occurred.

name: Firm earnings reliability
authors_terms: ["historical reliability", "firm earnings reliability", "history of making its earnings estimates", "track record"]
definition: The firm's past success in satisfying the stakeholder in question, captured as the number of quarters in which a firm made its earnings estimates in the three years prior to the focal year.

name: Earnings guidance
definition: The practice whereby a firm actively participates in forming analysts' quarterly earnings estimates by providing public and explicit earnings guidance.

name: Media coverage
definition: The extent to which the firm receives attention from the business media, which shapes whether an earnings miss attracts attention and enters the consciousness of reputational arbiters.

name: Peer earnings reliability
authors_terms: ["peer firm reliability", "peer earnings reliability", "comparison to peer firms"]
definition: The extent to which other surveyed firms within the firm's industry met their quarterly earnings estimates, reflecting how common earnings misses are among the firm's industry peers.

name: Institutional context
definition: The larger institutional context in which failed exchanges occur, which shifts profoundly over time; over the study period firms, analysts, investors and the business press all became increasingly focused on quarterly earnings expectations.

name: Formalized succession processes
authors_terms: ["formalized succession processes", "formalized succession planning processes", "formalized CEO succession planning processes"]
definition: 'Formalized succession processes' refer to the systematic, formalized processes designed to collect and analyze relevant information to promote comprehensive and systematic succession planning outcomes.

name: CEO influence in succession planning
definition: CEO influence in succession planning is the degree of influence the CEO holds in the succession process, measured by asking about the amount of influence the CEO had versus that of the board.

name: Consideration of multiple successor candidates
authors_terms: ["consideration of multiple successor candidates", "multiple successors", "consideration of more than one CEO successor candidate"]
definition: Multiple successors is whether the board is considering more than one successor as a replacement for the CEO; considering multiple candidates allows for direct comparisons of candidates over time and reduces the likelihood of adverse selection.

name: Likelihood of internal successor
authors_terms: ["likelihood of internal successor", "likelihood of having an internal successor candidate"]
definition: Likelihood of internal successor is the level of confidence that, if the current CEO stepped down, the next CEO would be chosen from the internal pool of candidates; the hiring of an internal successor is one way to judge succession planning effectiveness.

name: Time to permanent successor
authors_terms: ["time to permanent successor", "expected time required to name a permanent CEO"]
definition: Time to permanent successor is the amount of time that it would take to identify and name a permanent successor if the CEO stepped down today.

name: Use of external help
authors_terms: ["use of external help", "use of external/third party help"]
definition: Use of external help is whether the company is using external help in the succession process; third-party succession planning experts can increase decision efficacy by serving as an additional information source.

name: Voluntary standard adoption
definition: We utilized a count of new LEED-certified buildings in an MSA-year as our dependent variable of LEED adoption.

name: Regional market logic
authors_terms: ["market logic", "regional market logic", "strength of the market logic"]
definition: A market logic valorizes economic efficiency, profits, and self-interest; the authors created a factor composed of six items to capture the strength of the market logic in each MSA-year.

name: Regional community logic
authors_terms: ["community logic", "regional community logic", "strength of the community logic"]
definition: A community logic has norms of group membership, trust, and reciprocity rather than economic profitability and self-interest; the authors measure its regional strength with an established measure of community social capital.

name: Economic incentive policies
authors_terms: ["government economic incentive policies", "economic incentive policies", "public policy"]
definition: The authors measured economic incentive policies as the implementation of public policies that supported the adoption of LEED, such as tax refunds and rewarding of government contracts based on LEED.

name: Technology-focused social movement organizations
definition: A TSMO is a form of specialized SMO that exclusively focuses on supporting the development and adoption of a specific technology to advance its social goals; the USGBC has been the dominant TSMO in green building.

name: Market intermediaries
definition: Market intermediaries are economic agents that help buyers and sellers to transact; in the case of green building, intermediaries are real estate professionals (e.g., architects, project managers, real estate agents) who become LEED Accredited Professionals.

name: Environmental entrepreneurs
definition: Individuals who create new, often for-profit, ventures that help address environmental challenges; regional green building suppliers can be conceptualized as hybrid organizations that blend a community and market logic.

name: Economic distance
authors_terms: ["economic distance", "economic distance between a home country and a host country", "level of economic development of the host country relative to that of the home country"]
definition: Economic distance is the level of economic development of the host country relative to that of the home country; it often reflects differences in factor costs (such as wages) and in technological capability, both important factors affecting FDI decisions and performance. It was measured as the difference, in U.S. dollars, in the real per capita gross domestic product (GDP) between Singapore and a host country in the first year of an FDI.

name: FDI hazard rate
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of an FDI", "hazard rates of FDIs", "survival of foreign direct investments"]
definition: The dependent variable was the hazard rate of an FDI; the study rests on the assumption that 'survival is an indicator of affiliate success,' so that a lower hazard rate means a higher chance of FDI survival.

name: Entry mode
definition: When a firm expands into a foreign market through direct investment, it has to decide whether to establish a new venture from scratch (create a 'greenfield') or to acquire at least part of the equity of an existing local company (make an acquisition).

name: Prior entrepreneurial experience
authors_terms: ["prior entrepreneurial experience", "prior start-up experience(s)", "multiple founding experiences"]
definition: Founder CEOs with prior entrepreneurial experience are serial founders who have participated in multiple start-up activities, as opposed to founder CEOs for whom the focal firm is their only 'child' and legacy. In the sample, 45% of the founder CEOs had prior entrepreneurial experience.

name: Number of cofounders
definition: The total number of founders at a firm's inception, capturing whether the founder CEOs initiated their companies on their own or in collaboration with one or more cofounders. An increase in founding members decreases the CEO's control over the firm and distributes the spotlight among founders.

name: Core founder status
definition: 'Core founders' are those who initiated the founding activities and led the organization at the inception stage. The authors follow Wasserman (2017) and use initial CEO status to define the core founders in the sample.

name: Time as a private firm
authors_terms: ["time as a private firm", "private-year ratio", "length of time a firm was private"]
definition: The length of time a firm operated as a private firm before its IPO. During the private firm stage the organization is small and members maintain a family-like relationship, and the founder's vision and values are heavily reflected in the organization.

name: Voluntary founder CEO succession
authors_terms: ["voluntary founder CEO succession", "time to voluntary founder CEO succession", "voluntary succession"]
definition: An event during the sample period in which a founder CEO was succeeded by a new CEO after an IPO and when the succession event was voluntary in nature.

name: Negative media reaction
authors_terms: ["negative media reactions", "negative media coverage", "negative coverage", "Negative Media Reaction"]
definition: Media reactions are soft external performance feedback cues that are difficult to quantify and may simultaneously include both positive and negative feedback elements. Negative media reactions to an acquisition announcement are the negative assessments of the focal acquisition contained in press coverage of it.

name: Subsequent acquisition spending
definition: The total value of all large acquisitions announced during the 365 days following the focal acquisition. It captures the nuance in the range of acquisitions a firm can undertake, including willingness to pursue further acquisitions, the number of deals, the size of targets and aggressiveness in completing deals.

name: CEO past focus
definition: A temporal focus disposition reflecting the extent to which individuals characteristically direct their attention to the past; a past focus is associated with reflection on the past and the repeated use of past memories in decision making.

name: CEO future focus
definition: A temporal focus disposition reflecting the extent to which individuals characteristically direct their attention to the future; a future focus is associated with thinking primarily concerned with future events, making long-term plans, and frequently considering what the future holds.

name: Female TMT appointments
authors_terms: ["female TMT appointments", "female appointments into top management teams", "female executives who represent new additions to the TMT"]
definition: Counts of female executives who represent new additions to the top management team in a given year.

name: Male TMT appointments
definition: Counts of male executives who represent new additions to the top management team in a given year.

name: TMT change orientation
definition: A TMT's tendency to experiment, promote novel ideas, and depart from established organizational practices.

name: TMT risk-taking propensity
authors_terms: ["TMT risk-taking propensity", "risk-taking propensity", "TMT willingness to take risk"]
definition: The TMT's generalized preference for strategic alternatives with higher risk, given an expected return (or a lower need for assurance of success before committing to a given strategy).

name: TMT female incumbency
authors_terms: ["TMT female incumbency", "female incumbency", "the presence of women on the TMT to which females are appointed"]
definition: The presence of women on the TMT to which females are appointed, measured as the total number of women on a TMT lagged by one year, i.e., in a year preceding the year in which a new appointment occurred.

name: Relative size of the cohort of incoming TMT appointees
authors_terms: ["size of the cohort of new TMT appointees", "size of the incoming cohort of appointees", "(relative) size of the cohort of incoming TMT appointees"]
definition: The number of new TMT appointees relative to the number of TMT incumbents in a given year.

name: R&D investment
definition: Discretionary firm expenditures that reflect explicit executive decisions to engage with innovation as a capability making and capability building strategy, notably by investing in scientists and engineers, but also in new R&D labs or internal product development.

name: M&A activity
definition: M&A represent a capability buying and resource-picking strategy that requires substantial financial resources and carries considerable risk.

name: Within-founder experience variety
authors_terms: ["within-founder experience variety", "experience variety", "the number of founders with a variety of firm experiences", "founders with a variety of firm experiences"]
definition: Within-founder experience variety captures experience variety originating from a founder's frequent job changes across organizations before creating their startup. In other words, founders who individually acquired a variety of firm experiences can replace the variety distributed across the team.

name: Prior shared experience
authors_terms: ["shared experience", "prior shared experience", "shared experience of founders transitioning from the same industry incumbent"]
definition: The shared experience of founders transitioning from the same industry incumbent is the number of years the team worked together in the same incumbent firm right before creating the startup.

name: Startup failure
definition: Startup failure is a relevant measure of performance for young firms; the variable is coded 0 in any year the startup is alive and 1 the year the startup fails.

name: Change in Demo Day sunshine
authors_terms: ["Sunnier", "daily change in Demo Day sunshine", "change in Demo Day sunshine", "daily change in sunshine"]
definition: The difference between the number of hours of actual sunshine realized on a Demo Day and that on the previous day. The authors describe it as an incidental contextual factor that is unrelated to the focal startup.

name: Investment decision
definition: The dependent variable Demo day funding takes a value of 1 if a startup secures a Demo Day funding round and 0 otherwise. In the experiment, two facets of the investment decision are captured: investment attractiveness and investment amount.

name: Startup maturity
definition: A startup's age is a proxy of its maturity: the time elapsed (in months) between the startup's founding date and its Demo Day date. All else being equal, the younger a startup, the greater the level of uncertainty associated with it.

name: Founders' human capital
definition: Information about entrepreneurial experience and educational attainment used as a proxy for founders' human capital; individuals possess substantial human capital if they have attained a post-graduate degree or have had a prior entrepreneurial experience.

name: Investor mood
definition: The mediation variable, Mood, reports mood valence based on participants' scores on the PANAS-SF instrument.

name: TMT industry experience variety
authors_terms: ["TMT industry experience variety", "TMT experiential variety", "experiential variety", "industry experience variety"]
definition: The number and spread of qualitatively different industry experiences across team members; it captures the 'batches' of information content, knowledge, and unique network ties available within and across team members from accumulated prior work in different industries.

name: Calibrated repertoire complexity
definition: The extent to which the complexity of a focal firm's competitive repertoire aligns with the level of complexity attained by industry top performers; deviations in either direction from this standard result in lower calibration levels.

name: Calibrated repertoire consistency
definition: Occurs when the composition of a firm's competitive repertoire shifts to the same degree as top performers' repertoires over time; it does not capture the conformity of the underlying pattern of actions between a focal firm and top performers.

name: Firm performance
definition: Measured with return on assets, which is appropriate for measuring overall financial performance because it captures the efficiency by which the firm uses its assets to generate revenues above the costs of operations.

name: Firm market performance
definition: Market-based firm performance, which the authors characterize as a forward-looking measure reflecting brighter future growth prospects; they argue controlling families appoint family members to boards of higher performing firms to provide opportunities to build human and reputational capital.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Reputation is defined as a collective judgment of observers regarding an entity's qualities, reliability, and generalized favorability.

name: Intragroup board interlock centrality
authors_terms: ["intragroup board interlock centrality", "intragroup interlock centrality", "intra-group board interlock centrality", "centrality within the business group"]
definition: Membership of a business group-affiliated firm in a network of firms with varying degrees of centrality, where some are core members and others are peripheral, captured in terms of intragroup board interlocks.

name: Financial distress
authors_terms: ["financial distress", "signs of distress", "signs of potential failure"]
definition: A firm state in which net income is negative and which the authors describe as being subject to a higher risk of bankruptcy, constituting a stigmatizing association of failure.

name: Number of existing family directors
authors_terms: ["number of existing family directors", "presence of other family members on the board", "excess number of family members on the board"]
definition: The count of existing family members already serving on a focal firm's board, which the authors argue triggers perceptions of nepotism stigma.

name: Family member board appointment
authors_terms: ["appointment of family members to the board of directors", "family director appointments", "family member board appointment"]
definition: The appointment of a member of the controlling family to a board position of a business group-affiliated firm, compared with the appointment of nonfamily inside directors.

name: Family generation
authors_terms: ["later- versus earlier-generation family members", "generation of family members", "later generation", "earlier generation"]
definition: The generation of the family member, where the first and second generations of the family are treated as the 'earlier generation' and family members beyond the second generation are classified as part of the 'later generation.'

name: Relational embeddedness
authors_terms: ["relational embeddedness", "VC joint collaboration experience", "VC prior collaboration", "joint collaboration experience", "prior collaborative experience", "shared collaboration experience"]
definition: Relational embeddedness is conceptualized in terms of the existence of prior relationships; it arises from a history of interactions or repeated direct ties, and is a function of how often the various members of a group have previously collaborated. In the VC context, relational embeddedness is a function of how often the various members of the VC syndicate have previously coinvested in start-ups.

name: Acquisition exit
definition: In an acquisition, a start-up is purchased outright by another company that assumes a controlling ownership stake. An acquisition exit corresponds to a focused success outcome.

name: IPO exit
definition: In an IPO, a large fraction of ownership is sold on public markets, enabling any investor to purchase shares. An IPO exit corresponds to a broadcast success outcome.

name: CEO political ideology divergence
authors_terms: ["CEO political ideology divergence", "divergence of the CEO's political ideology from the national political climate", "divergence"]
definition: The divergence of the CEO's political ideology from the national political climate is the absolute difference between the CEO's liberalism index and the political affiliation of the president; it captures the conflict a CEO experiences when leading an organization in an environment perceived to be at odds with their deeply held beliefs.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity represents a firm's investment in future products and services adjusted for firm sales and is one of the most commonly studied manifestations of firm-level search behavior.

name: Retention of earnings
definition: Retained earnings are the self-funding mechanism by which managers use the returns the firm has generated to fund future operations, providing relatively cheaper financing, greater discretion and control, and simplicity and certainty under threat.

name: Vested stock options
authors_terms: ["CEO vested stock options", "vested stock options", "vested (i.e., unexercised but exercisable) option value"]
definition: The value of vested stock options is the unexercised but exercisable option value, which executives view differently than unvested options because the endowment effect leads them to treat the vested option as an owned asset whose value correlates with firm performance.

name: Industry regulation
definition: The nature of regulation often both prescribes and proscribes firm action, limiting search behavior and restricting strategic options; regulation generally imposes formalization and standardization and reduces complexity and uncertainty, signifying less managerial discretion.

name: Executive job demands
definition: All aspects of top executives' jobs that require continuous physical and psychological effort, considered a fundamental feature of top executives' objective job environment; executive job demands include both quantitative (workload, time pressure) and qualitative (organizational politics, role ambiguity, role conflict) dimensions.

name: Overall innovation
definition: A firm's overall innovation, captured by combining exploratory and exploitative innovations, which compete with one another for limited innovation resources.

name: Share of exploratory innovations
authors_terms: ["share of exploratory innovations", "share of innovations that are exploratory"]
definition: The share of a firm's innovations that are exploratory, calculated as exploratory innovations divided by the sum of exploratory and exploitative innovations after standardization.

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: Innovation that generates new knowledge and develops new products for emerging customers.

name: Exploitative innovation
definition: Innovation that builds on existing knowledge and extends current products for existing customers.

name: TMT variety
authors_terms: ["variety in executives' gender, age, and tenure", "horizontal variety in top executives' gender, age, and tenure", "TMT variety"]
definition: Horizontal variety in top executives' gender, age, and tenure, which reflects the variety in their knowledge, experience, and cognition.

name: Controlling climate
definition: A climate that emphasizes systematic management and control, in which employees are given clear goals, evaluated by well-established performance standards, and expected to follow clearly articulated rules and regulations.

name: Innovative climate
definition: A firm climate that values the development of new products, services, technologies, and processes and encourages employees to experiment with new ideas for exploration.

name: Employees' education
definition: The abilities and skills that employees acquired through their formal education, which constitute their general human capital and reflect mental abilities useful in a broad range of settings.

name: CEO social conservatism
definition: Social ideology is the extent to which individuals respect and conform to traditional norms and practices.

name: CEO economic conservatism
definition: Economic ideology reflects individuals' stance on competitive versus cooperative interactions with others.

name: Intuitive strategic decision-making
definition: The degree of reliance on experience-based intuition in strategic decision-making.

name: Cooperative strategic decision-making
definition: The degree to which shared goals promote cooperation in strategic decision-making.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
definition: CE encompasses innovation (introduction of new products, processes, and organizational systems or methods), strategic renewal (revitalization of operations by changing the business scope and competitive approaches), and corporate venturing (creation of businesses in existing or new fields, markets, or industries, either internally or externally).

name: Anticipated development help
authors_terms: ["development help", "personalized development help", "anticipated development help", "big fish"]
definition: The share of an established firm's excess development resources that the focal entrepreneur expects to receive; such help is personalized, late-stage product development support that is limited by the attention the established firm has available and is rationed in rank order among peers.

name: Anticipated market access
definition: An established firm's ability to act as a gatekeeper that regulates access to buyers; unlike development help this resource is not personalized to individual needs and is scalable across many entrepreneurs.

name: Resource needs evolution
definition: As entrepreneurs gain experience, their resource needs shift from internal resources (upstream resources such as development help) to external ones (downstream resources such as market access).

name: Competition-induced resource uncertainty
authors_terms: ["competition-induced resource uncertainty", "resource uncertainty due to competition", "resource uncertainty"]
definition: The uncertainty created by anticipated competition from peers in the entrepreneur's market, which makes it important to have a differentiated product and thus to secure personalized resources from a partner.

name: Tie formation
definition: Whether a developer (entrepreneur) and a publisher (established firm) formed a tie to collaborate on a PS2 game or games in focal year t.

name: Initial stock market reaction magnitude
authors_terms: ["magnitude of the market reaction", "magnitude of the stock market reaction", "magnitude of expectancy violation", "absolute value of negative CAR[-1,0]"]
definition: The magnitude of expectancy violation refers to the significance of the stock market reaction (i.e., the absolute value); it reflects the degree to which stakeholders perceive that the focal decision violates their expectancies.

name: Reactive positive strategic noise
definition: Strategic noise refers to any news releases controlled and sent by a firm around the time of a decision announcement, but these releases are 'neither intended to clarify nor are causally related to the initial event'. Reactive positive strategic noise is the count of positive strategic noise items released after the focal event has become publicly known.

name: Reactive negative strategic noise
definition: Strategic noise refers to any news releases controlled and sent by a firm around the time of a decision announcement, but these releases are 'neither intended to clarify nor are causally related to the initial event'. Reactive negative strategic noise is the count of negative strategic noise items released after the focal event has become publicly known.

name: Entrepreneurial team formation strategy
authors_terms: ["formation strategies", "dual formation strategy", "interpersonal attraction strategy", "resource-seeking strategy"]
definition: The interpersonal-attraction strategy is a relational search process by which founders take advantage of their close and immediate network (e.g., family and friends), where homophily and attraction govern the initiation of cofounder ties; the resource-seeking strategy reflects a rational search process within a more distributed network for cofounders who have complementary knowledge and skills. A dual formation strategy combines more than one type across the two strategies.

name: Transactive memory systems
definition: 'The collective system that individuals in a close relationship use to encode, store, and retrieve knowledge'; a specific type of team mental models, they include both a structural component that reflects the links between individual memories which create a collective knowledge network, and transactive processes to enable encoding, storing, and retrieving of team members' memories.

name: Early entrepreneurial success
definition: Initial milestones that are critical for early success and survival of new ventures, such as raising initial funds, winning entrepreneurial competitions and entering prestigious accelerator programs, and cumulating initial profits from sales of the product.

name: Overall investment experience
authors_terms: ["VC overall investment experience", "overall investment experience", "general investment experience"]
definition: VCs' learning obtained from experience investing in ventures similar to the venture in crisis, giving them greater confidence in their ability to control their investments and the outcome of venture lawsuits.

name: Focal venture experience
authors_terms: ["VC focal venture experience", "venture-specific experience", "experience with the focal venture"]
definition: VCs' experience with the specific focal venture, which gives them in-depth knowledge, trust, and identification with the venture and reduces uncertainty about it.

name: Prior lawsuit experience
authors_terms: ["VC lawsuit experience", "own prior lawsuit experience", "VCs' own prior lawsuit experience"]
definition: VCs' experience with their own internal lawsuits, crises similar to those of the ventures, which can produce identification and learning that affect how they respond to venture lawsuits.

name: Defendant lawsuit experience
authors_terms: ["VC defendant experience", "prior lawsuit experience as a defendant", "defendant experience"]
definition: Whether the VC's role in a past lawsuit was as a defendant, which the authors argue is more negative and makes VCs focus more on uncertainty, duration, costs, and possible negative outcomes.

name: Settlement lawsuit experience
authors_terms: ["VC settlement experience", "prior prejudgment lawsuit settlement experience", "settlement experience"]
definition: VCs' experience with lawsuits that were settled prior to trial, which the authors argue teaches VCs that they can control the outcome of lawsuits and can produce post-traumatic growth.

name: Post-lawsuit follow-on investment
authors_terms: ["VC investment after lawsuit", "continued investment", "follow-on investment", "post-lawsuit investment"]
definition: A dichotomous outcome coded as one if the VC firm invested in the first round following the filing of the first venture lawsuit and zero if the VC firm did not invest in that round.

name: Patent litigation accusation
authors_terms: ["litigation event", "accused firm", "accused of patent infringement", "patent infringement litigation"]
definition: A patent-holding firm files an infringement complaint against another firm; the firm accused of infringing the patent is the defendant. Firms that do not undergo litigation have not initiated lawsuits nor been sued.

name: Novel innovation output
definition: The number of a firm's novel drugs in a given therapeutic class approved by the FDA subsequent to the litigation event. Drugs considered novel by the FDA include those utilizing new molecular entities, as well as those containing new combinations of existing molecular entities that offer significantly better treatment or much lower side effects than existing drugs.

name: Knowledge recency
definition: The recency of the knowledge in the litigated patent, reflected in a smaller difference between the grant dates of a focal patent and the patents it cites.

name: Knowledge heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["knowledge heterogeneity", "heterogeneous knowledge", "heterogeneity of the knowledge in the litigated patent"]
definition: Heterogeneous knowledge components differ considerably in their underlying attributes and involve scientific principles from different disciplines, in contrast to homogeneous knowledge whose components show important similarities and overlap in their function.

name: Litigated patent scope
authors_terms: ["knowledge scope", "scope of the litigated patent", "scope of the patent"]
definition: The number of claims in a patent, each of which identifies fundamental and distinct features of the new art, reflects the scope of knowledge in the patent.

name: Post-succession firm performance
authors_terms: ["Post-Succession Firm Performance", "post-succession performance", "appointing firm's subsequent performance"]
definition: The appointing firm's performance following the appointment of a CEO, measured with return on assets.

name: Length of executive experience
definition: The length of a CEO's experience captures the cumulative time that the CEO has spent in executive positions during their career.

name: Breadth of executive experience
definition: The breadth of a CEO's experience refers to the variety of firms in which the CEO has accumulated executive experience prior to the appointment as CEO in the current firm.

name: Corporate misfit
definition: We define corporate misfit as the extent of incongruence between the CEO's corporate background and fundamental characteristics of the appointing firm.

name: Negative stakeholder sentiment
definition: In line with Dorobantu, Henisz, and Nartey (2017), we define negative stakeholder sentiment as the unfavorable view or opinion of the firm's stakeholders that connotes opposition toward the appointment of a CEO.

name: Outside CEO appointment
definition: A dummy variable, Outside CEO, which took a value of 1 if the newly appointed CEO was not employed by the firm prior to the appointment as CEO and a value of 0 otherwise (hence, considered an inside CEO).

name: Board chair Communist Party membership
authors_terms: ["Party membership", "Communist Party membership", "CCP membership", "Party-member board chair"]
definition: Following a growing number of empirical studies that consider political party affiliation or donations as an indication of ideological orientation, the authors suggest that, on average, a CCP member board chair will exhibit behavioral patterns that are consistent with Maoist communist ideology.

name: Patent applications
definition: Patent applications are the total number of invention, utility, and design patent applications submitted by the firm, and are used as a common indicator of innovative development.

name: Patent infringement
authors_terms: ["patent infringement", "likelihood of patent infringement", "violate other firms' patent rights"]
definition: Patent infringement is whether the firm experienced a patent infringement lawsuit as the defendant in a given year that resulted in conviction.

name: Board chair age
definition: The authors expect a decay of Maoist ideological influence by age: the younger a Party member's age, the less likely he or she would have been directly imprinted with Maoist ideology.

name: Board chair educational attainment
definition: The authors posit that a higher level of educational attainment, especially university or above, helps to resist or reduce the impact of Maoist ideology on innovation activity.

name: Presence of older Party-member directors in a region
authors_terms: ["older Party-member directors", "older Party-member corporate directors", "presence of older Party-member directors"]
definition: Measured as the percentage of older Party-member corporate directors out of the total number of Party-member directors of all listed firms in the province where a focal firm is headquartered; older Party members are those who reached age 18 before 1978 (born before 1960) and are most likely to have been imprinted with Maoist ideology in their formative years.

name: Alliance performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["alliance performance", "alliance performance feedback", "alliance performance relative to the aspiration level", "performance that falls short of the aspiration level"]
definition: Managers compare a focal alliance's performance with an aspiration level: performance that falls short of the aspiration level is considered a failure, while performance that exceeds it is considered a success; alliance performance feedback is measured based on the social aspiration level.

name: Subsequent acquisition likelihood
authors_terms: ["the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition", "changing from an alliance to an acquisition", "the likelihood that a firm will turn to acquisitions"]
definition: The unobserved hazard rate for a firm that used an alliance at t to change to an acquisition at t+1.

name: Number of alliance partners
definition: Alliance partner number represents the total number of partners that participated in the focal alliance.

name: Partner alliance experience
authors_terms: ["partner alliance experience", "partners' prior alliance experience", "perceived capability of partners", "alliance experience of partners"]
definition: Partner alliance experience represents the perceived alliance capabilities of the partners in an alliance.

name: Alliance performance variability
authors_terms: ["alliance performance variability", "variability in alliance performance", "consistency of performance"]
definition: Alliance performance variability represents the degree to which a focal firm's past alliance performances fluctuated.

name: Novel business model design
definition: Companies establishing a novelty-oriented business model focus on innovation and hope to win customers over by providing superior use value; novelty involves introducing new combinations of products and services, creative methods to generate revenue, and new ways to connect providers, customers, and partners.

name: Efficient business model design
definition: Efficiency-oriented companies build transaction-based, scalable business models to remove market imperfections.

name: Lock-in business model design
definition: Lock-in refers to a company's attempts to create switching costs to ensure the retention of customers and other business model participants.

name: Complementarity business model design
definition: Complementarity emphasizes products, services, and technologies that are provided to add value to the core offering.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: A strategy that seeks a position increasing customers' willingness to pay by delivering unique products in new ways.

name: Low-cost strategy
definition: A strategy whose basis is scaling advantages or learning curve effects; the paper refers to low-cost strategy and low-cost position.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The degree of competition, or competitive threat, in the firm's industry; high levels of competition may allow firms to capture less of the overall value created by a business model.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is a key contingency affecting a firm's ability to acquire and exploit resources efficiently; the paper calibrates firm size using the number of employees.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured as Tobin's Q, the ratio of a firm's market value to its total assets; higher values indicate higher performance.

name: Configurational complexity of complementary design elements
definition: Complexity is commonly considered as the number of elements in the configuration multiplied by the number of interactions between them; because all design elements interact with each other, complexity here refers to the number of elements in the configurations.

name: Benefit corporation legislation
definition: A new legal form, the benefit corporation, adopted across U.S. states; BCL imposes significantly fewer requirements on businesses than the B Corp certification, and many observers have raised concerns regarding its legal ambiguity, lax requirements for incorporation, and the lack of audits to verify organizational commitment to the legislation's stated goals.

name: Legislative strength
definition: Legislative strength is defined as the degree of unambiguous requirements and strict enforcement standards which characterize state mandates.

name: Legislative scope
definition: Legislative scope is defined as the extent of those mandates' regulative requirements; legislation is broader in scope when it addresses more criteria.

name: Initial certification
definition: Initial B Corp certifications are the count of newly certified B Corps in each state-year, constructed by assigning each B Corp to its home state and aggregating them by year.

name: Recertification
definition: Retaining rigorous voluntary certifications (i.e., recertification) provides a means of ongoing verification that organizations' practices meet or exceed the requirements of broad sustainability legislation; firms must generally actively recertify (i.e., enter a new certification spell) to maintain their B Corp status.

name: Corporate sustainability norms
definition: Corporate sustainability norms are measured as the reversed, normalized count of ESG concerns attributable to public companies headquartered within each Census division; higher scores indicate 'cleaner' corporate sustainability norms.

name: Product failure
authors_terms: ["product failure", "experience of product failure", "product failure-related exit", "adverse event"]
definition: In line with Maslach (2016: 717), the authors define product failure-related exits as products being removed from the market because they ostensibly do not meet predefined technical or usage requirements; they define product failure as a product not meeting predefined technical or usage requirements, and an adverse event involves a malfunction of a medical device due to technical or user errors.

name: Product market reentry
definition: The authors focus on whether firms persist, that is, reenter product markets after a prior exit; reentry serves as an outcome of successful local search and their measure of persistence following failure. They recorded product market reentry whenever a business unit offered a product in a market where it did not offer a product in the previous year but did have offerings in prior years.

name: Corporate proximity
definition: Corporate proximity is multidimensional: the first dimension, hierarchical proximity, is the distance between the corporate office and its business units in terms of vertical structure or 'layers'; the second, geographic proximity, is the spatial distance between the business unit and corporate headquarters; and the third dimension, cognitive proximity reflects the extent to which headquarters and business units share similar types of experiences.

name: Product market age
authors_terms: ["established product markets", "established product market", "age of the product market"]
definition: Established product markets are those that are more mature, having existed for a relatively long period, and stand in contrast to product markets that are new and in a nascent stage; they are operationalized using the age of the product market based on the FDA Premarket Notifications and Premarket Approval databases.

name: Cause of product failure
authors_terms: ["technical error-driven product failure", "cause of the product failure", "technical errors", "user errors"]
definition: Technical errors involve defects of the product or the underlying technology (e.g., flawed design or defective parts), whereas user errors involve failure caused by the usage of the product (e.g., nonadherence to instructions, poor maintenance).

name: Severity of product failure
authors_terms: ["severe product failure", "severe product failures", "severity of the failure"]
definition: Severe product failures are those that cause significant harm; that is, are associated with serious injury or death.

name: Entrepreneurial entry
authors_terms: ["whisky distillery foundings", "entrepreneurial entry", "organizational foundings", "organizational founding rates"]
definition: This variable captures entrepreneurial entry by aggregating all new distilleries founded each year in a given county.

name: Social movement mass
authors_terms: ["social movement mass", "mass mobilization", "mass-driven private politics", "membership base", "STL member proportion"]
definition: A broad membership base, or social movement mass, is thus seen as an important resource for social movements employing private politics to delegitimize an organizational form (Sine & Lee, 2009). To aspiring entrepreneurs, the cost of social disapproval will increase with the mass of the opposing social movement.

name: Political elite mobilization
authors_terms: ["political elite mobilization", "elite mobilization", "elite-driven public politics", "backing of social elites"]
definition: Under certain circumstances, the backing of social elites, defined as 'a small social group that occupies the command posts of key societal institutions' (Yue, 2015: 1961), can be critical to social movement contestation (Jenkins & Perrow, 1977). We therefore expect the tactic of elite mobilization to be crucial to social movements using a public politics strategy.

name: Ancestral populations
definition: As evidenced by Greve and Rao (2012), newly founded organizations can 'inherit' such taken-for-grantedness from their predecessors, even decades after the latter have exited the scene. Larger ancestral populations are expected to locally endow whisky distilling with a higher level of cognitive legitimacy (Suchman, 1995).

name: Incumbent countermobilization
definition: National-level incumbent countermobilization seeks to undercut social movement efforts in the political sphere through lobbying efforts (Meyer & Staggenborg, 1996). Countermobilization provides aspiring entrepreneurs with greater assurance that more favorable regulatory frameworks, as well as direct political support, might be available in the future (Tolbert et al., 2011).

name: Resource idling
authors_terms: ["resource idling", "temporary idling of resources", "extent of idling", "idling resources", "a rig becomes 'stacked'"]
definition: The temporary idling of resources is a common way that firms manage resources to address changing market environments. A driller's rig becomes 'stacked' when its drilling operations are suspended or even completely deactivated by disassembling the rig and placing it into storage.

name: Firm capabilities
authors_terms: ["capabilities", "intrinsic speed capabilities of drilling", "a driller's drilling speed"]
definition: A 'capability' refers to a firm's ability to perform a set of tasks in routine activity. In this industry, a driller's speed of drilling wells reflects the efficiency of its internal routines and processes, technical competency of its engineers, coordination among crew members, and its managerial ability to quickly deploy its people and resources without increasing costs.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: We measured demand uncertainty as the percentage difference of realized demand compared to the predicted level at a given month t. It captures the degree to which industry oil demand diverged from the level of demand that would have been predicted based on historical information.

name: Reliance on human capital
authors_terms: ["reliance on human capital", "human capital reliance", "reliance on automation"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's operations depend on human labor rather than automated technologies; the authors determined whether the focal rig being considered for idling is the traditional type that is fully human operated, as opposed to automated.

name: Performance shortfalls
definition: The extent to which a firm's performance falls below its aspirational level; the authors calculate it as the difference between actual ROA and a firm's aspirations if the firm's ROA was lower than or equal to its aspirations and zero otherwise.

name: R&D intensity
definition: The intensity of a firm's investment in research and development, examined as a response to performance shortfalls. R&D search is one of the most frequently examined responses in the BTOF literature, and the authors examine the influence of performance shortfalls on R&D intensity.

name: Philanthropic donation intensity
definition: The intensity of a firm's philanthropic giving, used to capture CSR search because firms seem to view philanthropic donations as easy-to-implement CSR solutions. Corporate donations contribute valuable resources to society and are therefore highly desired and praised.

name: Shared belief in the effectiveness of R&D
authors_terms: ["shared belief in the effectiveness of R&D", "shared belief in R&D"]
definition: A belief in the effectiveness of a particular response reflects decision-makers' cognitive efforts to anticipate the outcomes that each specific response might generate before choosing between responses; here it is a collective belief in the contribution of R&D practices to firm performance.

name: Shared belief in the effectiveness of CSR
authors_terms: ["shared belief in the effectiveness of CSR", "shared belief in CSR"]
definition: A collective belief in the contribution of CSR practices to firm performance, reflected in sentences that explicitly mention causal linkages between CSR and firm performance.

name: R&D-performance correlation
definition: Evidence supporting belief in the effectiveness of R&D, based on the linkage (correlation) between the response and a firm's performance, observed either in the firm's own past or among industry peers.

name: CSR-performance correlation
definition: Evidence supporting belief in the effectiveness of CSR, based on the linkage (correlation) between CSR ratings and a firm's performance, observed either in the firm's own past or among industry peers.

name: Firm–stakeholder dialogue
definition: Firm–stakeholder dialogue is an ongoing 'structured interactive and proactive process' that facilitates the exchange of information between firms and their stakeholders through direct (unmediated) two-way communication. Participation in stakeholder dialogue is the result of a choice to be proactive, whereas in its absence firms default to a reactive stance.

name: Improvement in stakeholder evaluations
authors_terms: ["improvements in a stakeholder's evaluation of a firm", "the evolution of a stakeholder's evaluation of a firm", "changes in stakeholders' evaluations of firms"]
definition: A stakeholder's actions toward a firm or statements about it reflect the stakeholder's evaluation of the firm, and the authors code whether that evaluation has improved over time. The dependent variable takes the value 1 if a stakeholder's evaluation of a firm has improved from one observation to the next, and 0 otherwise.

name: Information availability
authors_terms: ["information availability", "availability of media information", "the availability of information"]
definition: Information availability is a firm-level construct describing the amount of information that exists about a firm. It captures how much stakeholders know about a firm.

name: Thematic ESG content of media information
authors_terms: ["thematic content", "information content", "thematic ESG content", "level of emphasis on ESG issues", "media ESG content"]
definition: Thematic content is a time-varying construct that reflects the extent to which information available about a firm focuses on ESG issues. It captures what stakeholders know about a firm.

name: Information reliability
definition: Information reliability is a country-level construct defining the extent to which media information can be trusted. It captures how much stakeholders trust the media that informs them.

name: Category heterogeneity
definition: Intra-category coherence refers to the degree of heterogeneity that a set of products exhibits within a focal category; a category exhibits low heterogeneity when actors frame their products by mobilizing similar sets of vocabularies, claims, identities, or other cultural resources, and high heterogeneity when they mobilize dissimilar sets of cultural resources.

name: Category distinctiveness
definition: Inter-category coherence refers to the similarity between a focal category and its related categories, making it either more or less distinctive; a focal category is less distinctive when actors mobilize cultural resources that other actors in related categories mobilize too, and is more distinctive when they mobilize cultural resources that mainly belong in their focal category but not in others.

name: Category viability
definition: The extent to which actors and their audiences collectively use a category to position and assess products; a category is and remains viable when it is repeatedly and actively used.

name: Entrepreneur gender
authors_terms: ["gender", "entrepreneur gender", "gender composition of entrepreneurial units", "proportion of women entrepreneurs"]
definition: The gender of the entrepreneur or entrepreneurial unit leading the venture; in the archival study it is operationalized as the proportion of women entrepreneurs in the entrepreneurial unit, and in the experiments it is manipulated as a female or male entrepreneur pitching an otherwise identical venture.

name: Venture novelty
definition: New ventures vary substantially in novelty, with some providing groundbreaking products and services that defy existing market categories and spark radical transformations, yet others only refining what has been existing or making marginal improvements to common practices.

name: Venture norm violation judgments
definition: Venture norm violation judgments capture implicit evaluations of the extent to which new ventures violate the socially constructed system of beliefs, logic, prototypes, and practices in relevant industries.

name: Social approval forecasting
definition: Social approval forecasting is an implicit sociocognitive activity in which investors leverage a heuristic of social cues inherent in a venture to anticipate the extent to which it will gain endorsement from peer investors.

name: Funding support
authors_terms: ["venture funding support", "funding support", "funding likelihood", "funding amount", "financial valuation of the deal"]
definition: The funding that investors provide to a venture, measured both as whether an investment is made and as the amount or valuation of the deal received.

name: Venture gender type
definition: The gender typing of the industry the venture operates in, that is, whether the venture caters to an industry whose workforce is dominated by men (male-typed ventures) or by women (female-typed ventures).

name: General human capital
authors_terms: ["general human capital endowments", "general human capital", "generalist founders"]
definition: General human capital endowments involve concept-based schooling that equips individuals with broad-based knowledge and skills that are of use across settings.

name: Specific human capital
authors_terms: ["specific human capital endowments", "specific human capital", "specialist founders"]
definition: Specific human capital endowments typically relate to knowledge of one's domain, such as the industry or profession (vocation) within which a founder has studied and worked.

name: New firm performance
definition: Our dependent measure is the yearly sales revenues generated by a new firm - a common outcome in research on new firm performance; achieving sales indicates that a firm attracted customers and met market demand through its offerings.

name: Favorable industry setting
authors_terms: ["most favorable industry settings", "favorable industry setting", "most favorable industries"]
definition: Industry settings with the highest rates of growth during an economic crisis, in which the characteristics of the crisis are expected to be attenuated and founders face fewer crisis-specific challenges.

name: Unfavorable industry setting
authors_terms: ["most unfavorable industry settings", "unfavorable industry setting", "most sharply declining industries"]
definition: Industry settings with the highest rates of decline during an economic crisis, in which the challenges associated with a crisis are in full force.

name: Selection consistency
authors_terms: ["selection consistency", "consistency in organizational selection", "selection consistency by organizations"]
definition: The extent to which an organization selects similar ideas.

name: Idea variety
definition: The degree to which ideas diverge in their contents.

name: Churn among external contributors
definition: The amount of churn among external contributors, that is, the degree to which new contributors (newcomers) join and established contributors (incumbents) leave.

name: Cohesion among external contributors
definition: The degree to which externals outside the organization are connected, for example, through social interactions in the form of commenting on and refining each other's work.

name: Self-selection
definition: External contributors' decisions to continue sharing their ideas.

name: Distance from selected ideas
authors_terms: ["distance from selected ideas", "distance from organizational selection", "dissimilarity between a focal idea and its closest selected idea"]
definition: The dissimilarity between a focal idea and its closest selected idea.

name: Number of previous contributions
authors_terms: ["number of previous contributions", "number of participations", "number of submissions made"]
definition: The number of prior submissions made by a contributor.

name: Public–private collaboration
definition: Collaboration in which one partner is a for-profit business and the other is an organization with a public mission, defined to include governmental institutions, academic institutions, and other nonprofit and nongovernmental organizations. In the case of multipartner collaboration, mixed partner types are coded as a public–private collaboration.

name: Innovation task effectiveness
definition: Whether a task progresses to the next stage in the innovation process. Effectiveness is measured based on whether the drug progresses to the consecutive phase of drug development for the corresponding indication.

name: Innovation task efficiency
definition: The costs in terms of time to achieve the desired progress, where efficiency is achieved when resources expended for reaching an outcome are minimized and time is the resource focused on in this setting.

name: Innovation stage
definition: The stage of the innovation process through which a drug-development task proceeds; drug development goes through five stages, each with its own practices, performance criteria, and risk profile, with early stages (discovery and preclinical) involving higher technological uncertainty than clinical stages (phases 1, 2, and 3).

name: Technological novelty
definition: The degree to which the underlying technology in the focal drug-development task has been employed in the industry before, with novel technologies characterized by greater uncertainty due to a limited preexisting knowledge base and lack of industry experience relative to a more established technology.

name: Provisional spaces
definition: Small-scale, easily accessible settings in a geographic community where market pioneers temporarily conduct experimentation with an innovation's applications before dedicated organizations emerge. They disseminate community-specific knowledge about an innovation's possible applications and give rise to a proto-form.

name: Highbrow provisional spaces
definition: Provisional spaces whose cultural status is highbrow - taken for granted as sophisticated, artistic, intellectual, and prestigious - such as opera houses, symphony orchestra theaters, legitimate theaters, concert halls, resort centers, and playhouses.

name: Lowbrow provisional spaces
definition: Provisional spaces whose cultural status is lowbrow - viewed as simple, entertaining, sensuous, and vulgar - such as dime museums, burlesque houses, dance halls, penny arcades, storefronts, and airdomes.

name: First organizational founding
authors_terms: ["founding of the first dedicated organization", "first movie theater of any kind", "founding of its first movie theater"]
definition: The instantaneous rate of a community experiencing the founding of its first organization of a new form since 1896, where the form may be of any kind; communities that had not experienced any movie theater founding by 1927 are treated as censored.

name: First highbrow-form founding
authors_terms: ["first movie house or palace", "highbrow form of movie house and movie palace"]
definition: The instantaneous rate of a community experiencing the founding of its first highbrow movie theater, i.e., a movie house or movie palace; the two forms are combined because both are more highbrow than nickelodeons.

name: First lowbrow-form founding
definition: The instantaneous rate of a community experiencing the founding of its first lowbrow movie theater, the nickelodeon - a movie theater with admission prices of only a nickel.

name: Community insider status
definition: The authors introduce the social structure of insiders (i.e., firms affiliated with at least one network community) and outsiders (i.e., firms not affiliated with any network community). Community insiders are expected to have an edge in information acquisition and resource exchange.

name: Number of network community affiliations
definition: Community structure in the context of interorganizational relationships refers to the existence of groups of firms that are more densely connected internally than with the rest of the network; the number of community affiliations counts how many such communities a focal firm is affiliated with.

name: Firm performance
definition: VC firm performance is captured by the exit outcomes of portfolio companies; VC firms usually make profits via IPO or M&A exits, and the ratio of successful exits serves as an appropriate measure of VC firm performance.

name: Institutional development
definition: Institutional development indicates the extent to which formal institutions reduce the barriers to doing business.

name: Predecessor-successor professional experience differential
definition: A construct that captures how different the new CEO is from the departing CEO with respect to professional experience, a core characteristic of CEOs' human capital. Professional experience includes a history of involvement in one or more functional areas of expertise and activities such as work in other firms or industries or companies located in foreign countries.

name: Successor insiderness
authors_terms: ["insider-outsider distinction", "whether the successor is an insider", "insider"]
definition: The insider-outsider distinction captures the new CEO's social capital within the firm, thus indicating the likelihood that organizational processes and relationships will be altered. Insiders possess more internal social capital than outsiders, so insiders are more likely to be familiar with processes, norms, and accepted behaviors and have established working relationships with other decision-makers.

name: Competitive attacks received
authors_terms: ["competitive attacks", "total attacks", "rival firms' competitive attacks against the focal firm"]
definition: The total number of competitive attacks in the post-succession year in which the focal firm was the intended target. A competitive attack is only coded as such if the focal action can be classified into one of the eight types of competitive actions established in prior studies.

name: Predecessor retention as board chair
authors_terms: ["retaining the predecessor to serve as board chair", "predecessor serving as the board chair", "predecessor stayed as chair"]
definition: A human and social capital preservation strategy in which the predecessor continues to have a presence in the firm by serving as chair post-succession, so that the firm's existing human capital and social capital are not completely lost and the disruptive effects of human and social capital changes are reduced.

name: Host country sentiment toward the deal
authors_terms: ["host country sentiments toward deal", "sentiment toward a deal", "host country sentiments toward the deal"]
definition: Host country stakeholders' socially constructed and collectively shared attitudes and emotional dispositions toward the acquisition deal itself, captured as sentiment valence in the situated discourse about price premium, synergies, and the winning versus losing framing of the deal.

name: Host country sentiment toward the acquirer
authors_terms: ["host country sentiments toward acquirer", "sentiment toward an acquirer", "sentiments toward the acquirer"]
definition: Host country stakeholders' attitudes and emotional dispositions toward the acquiring firm, aroused by discourse about the acquirer's strategic motives, management experience, and post-acquisition integration.

name: Host country sentiment toward inward investments
authors_terms: ["host country sentiments toward inward investments from China", "sentiments toward inward investments from home country", "sentiments toward the investments from China"]
definition: Host country stakeholders' attitudes and emotional dispositions toward the broader phenomenon of inward investments from the acquirer's home country, triggered by past collective sentiment experiences and by categorization of acquisitions by nation.

name: Sentiment volatility toward the deal
authors_terms: ["sentiment volatility toward a deal", "host country sentiment volatility", "volatility of the host country social sentiment toward the deal"]
definition: The fluctuations of sentiments toward the deal across time, describing sentiment experiences reflected in the rapid changes in the intensity of valence of opinions and expressions of thoughts about the deal.

name: Sentiment volatility toward the acquirer
authors_terms: ["sentiment volatility toward an acquirer", "volatility of the host country social sentiment toward the acquirer"]
definition: The fluctuations across time of host country sentiments toward the acquiring firm, describing rapid changes in the intensity of valence of opinions about the acquirer.

name: Sentiment volatility toward inward investments
authors_terms: ["sentiment volatility toward inward investments from China", "volatility of the host country social sentiment toward the inward investments from home country"]
definition: The fluctuations across time of host country sentiments toward inward investments from the home country, describing rapid changes in the intensity of valence of opinions about those investments.

name: Sentiment wavelength toward the deal
authors_terms: ["sentiment wavelength toward a deal", "sentiment wavelength toward deal", "host country sentiment wavelength"]
definition: The spatial period of a sentiment wave cycle, or the time distance between two adjacent peaks, signifying how fast sentiments toward the deal are regulated from ups and downs to ups again.

name: Sentiment wavelength toward the acquirer
authors_terms: ["sentiment wavelength toward an acquirer", "sentiment wavelength toward acquirer"]
definition: The time distance between two adjacent peaks in the sentiment waveform for the acquiring firm, capturing how fast sentiments toward the acquirer change from a peak to a trough and back to another peak.

name: Sentiment wavelength toward inward investments
authors_terms: ["sentiment wavelength toward inward investments from China", "sentiment wavelength toward inward investments from China"]
definition: The time distance between two adjacent peaks in the sentiment waveform for inward investments from the home country, capturing the speed of alternation between positive and negative sentiments about those investments.

name: Sentiment augmentation between acquirer and deal
authors_terms: ["sentiment augmentation between acquirer and deal", "sentiment augmentation between an acquirer and a deal"]
definition: How one type of sentiment in the current period influences another, related type of sentiment in the subsequent period; specifically, the spillover augmentation effect of sentiments toward the acquirer on sentiments toward the deal subsequently.

name: Sentiment augmentation between inward investments and deal
authors_terms: ["sentiment augmentation between inward investments from China and deal", "sentiment augmentation between the inward investments and the home country to the deal"]
definition: The spillover augmentation effect whereby sentiments toward inward investments from the home country in one period influence sentiments toward the deal in the subsequent period.

name: Acquisition completion
definition: Whether an announced cross-border acquisition deal is completed, which the authors treat as an indication of host country legitimacy for the foreign entity's strategic action.

name: Failure complexity
authors_terms: ["failure complexity", "accident complexity", "complexity of prior failure experience", "complexity of past serious accidents"]
definition: We adopt Haunschild and Sullivan's (2002) definition of failure complexity as a function of the heterogeneity of the causes of the failure, such that complex failures involve interactions between more organizational routines and subsystems.

name: Failure culpability
definition: Culpability is defined as the degree to which an organization or its members are considered to be responsible for causing the failure.

name: Routine relatedness
definition: Our fourth and final set of independent variables were yearly indicators for relatedness in routines; that is, how related the routines involved in an accident were to the dominant routines used across the entire firm.
