name: Knowledge depreciation
definition: Organizational learning theory holds that the retention of knowledge learned through experience over time is usually imperfect, such that some organizational knowledge is lost as time progresses - a process referred to as 'knowledge depreciation.' Such knowledge depreciation is the inverse of knowledge retention; it represents the loss of organizational knowledge over time.

name: Safety performance
authors_terms: ["safety performance", "current performance", "improvement in organizational safety performance"]
definition: Following the tradition in empirical organizational learning work, we operationally define learning in our context as improvement in organizational safety performance, where safety performance is tracked using a count of the number of employee days that a firm's employees missed work due to mining injuries during a year.

name: Accident experience
authors_terms: ["accident experience", "serious accident experience", "all accident experience", "past failure experience"]
definition: The first set of independent variables were counts of a firm's prior experience with serious accidents, where a 'serious' accident is defined as an accident that results in at least one fatality or permanent disability.

name: Quality shareholder industry holdings
authors_terms: ["QS industry holdings", "QS industry shareholdings", "QS industry investment", "focused concentration"]
definition: QS industry shareholdings denote the concentration of shareholdings focused within an industry, and this carries information because QSs have deep knowledge about firms and industries.

name: CVC funding termination
definition: Termination of CVC funding means the withdrawal of CVC funding for a venture that was previously funded.

name: Quality shareholder industry concentration
definition: QS industry concentration describes the extent to which QS shareholdings are dispersed among many industries or concentrated within a few.

name: Market heat
definition: Market heat is the degree to which it is desirable to venture into an industry; hot markets are characterized by readily available capital, high customer demand, and promising market opportunities.

name: Industry-specific knowledge
definition: A high level of industry familiarity means that the decision-maker understands the industry's customers and suppliers, its buying cycles, technical aspects of the industry's products and services, and the partners active within the industry.

name: CEO attentional vigilance to exploration
authors_terms: ["attentional vigilance", "vigilance of CEO attention to exploration", "CEO attentional vigilance to exploration"]
definition: Ocasio (2011: 1287) has defined attentional vigilance as 'the process by which individuals sustain concentration on a particular stimulus.' A high level of attentional vigilance is a state in which a constant amount of attention is distributed evenly over time (e.g., a year), whereas a low level of attentional vigilance means that CEO attention fluctuates during the same time period.

name: Firm exploration
authors_terms: ["exploration", "rate of exploration", "explorative product introductions", "brand new products"]
definition: Exploration includes the creation of new outcomes by means of activities including experimentation and search, while exploitation involves the improvement and extension of existing outcomes. Because exploration is viewed as a reflection of firm-level efforts to create outcomes beyond their existing market and technological domains, the introduction of brand new products with no prior versions is considered a measure of exploration.

name: Financial performance below aspiration levels
authors_terms: ["financial performance below aspiration levels", "underperformance", "ROA - Aspiration Level < 0"]
definition: A spline function of the discrepancy between the return on assets (ROA) and aspiration levels, where the aspiration level is the linear combination of the historical aspiration level and the social aspiration level; the negative attainment discrepancy variable indicates firms with financial performance below aspiration levels.

name: Employee satisfaction in explorative units
authors_terms: ["employee satisfaction in explorative units", "satisfaction level of employees in explorative units with the firm"]
definition: Employee satisfaction indicates the degree to which employees positively evaluate their employer (Spector, 1997). The level of employee satisfaction with their firm is increased when the firm provides a work environment that supports what employees value in their job (Locke, 1976).

name: CEO paranoia
definition: Relatively stable tendencies toward suspiciousness, feelings of ill will or resentment, mistrust, and belief in external control or influence; paranoia is a dispositional trait appearing "on a spectrum from normality to pathology" and engendering "feelings of mistrust and suspicion, whether of a particular person, a group of people, or an entire organization." The authors focus on subclinical levels of the trait.

name: Lobbying breadth
definition: Lobbying breadth is defined as the number of government agencies and pieces of legislation targeted for information exchange; it indicates the amount of unique governmental entities targeted for lobbying influence and thus information provision.

name: Competitive actions
definition: A count of the number of competitive actions taken by a firm in a year, with fewer indicating more avoidance and more actions indicating engaging with external entities with aggressive actions.

name: Regulatory ruling severity
definition: The paranoia-relevant cue of regulatory rulings captures the result and severity of a regulatory process exacted on a firm using the penalty amount, in millions of U.S. dollars, for assessed rulings.

name: Rival attacks
definition: The paranoia-relevant cue of rival attacks is captured by counting the number of competitive actions in RavenPack with the caveat that the focal CEO or firm is the target of the action rather than the initiator of the action.

name: Peak displayed anger
authors_terms: ["peak displayed anger", "director peak displayed anger", "peak anger", "displays of anger"]
definition: The strongest display of anger expressed by a board member within their comments on a given agenda item; the peak, or maximum level, of emotions displayed is what influences observers' summary assessment of an interaction.

name: Peak displayed happiness
authors_terms: ["peak displayed happiness", "director peak displayed happiness", "peak happiness", "displays of happiness"]
definition: The strongest display of happiness expressed by a board member within their comments on a given agenda item; peak displayed emotions are processed rather than the average or general state of all stimuli.

name: Discussion duration
definition: The duration of the discussion on a given agenda item.

name: Focused influence
definition: Influence that is direct in nature and occurred in the boardroom exchange between director and top manager, indicated when the top manager responds to the board member's request by making a promise or offering concessions.

name: Diffuse influence
definition: Influence achieved through the overall board via majority vote, indicated when the director's change initiative received majority support.

name: CEO abusive leadership
definition: CEO abusive leadership is characterized by a CEO's sustained display of nonphysical, aggressive (non)verbal behaviors toward subordinates. It differs from other negative CEO traits by manifesting as direct and hostile actions toward subordinates.

name: TMT behavioral integration
definition: TMT behavioral integration comprises the collaborative efforts of TMTs in pursuit of shared goals, and provides a comprehensive portrayal of vital TMT processes and dynamics. It captures not only social and emotional TMT tendencies but also task-oriented and behavioral propensities.

name: Philanthropic corporate social responsibility
definition: Philanthropic CSR is not mandated by law, nor is it inherently designed for immediate economic gain; it provides a clear signal of the organization's genuine altruistic engagement to its broader stakeholders, shows an empathetic understanding of societal needs, and demonstrates the CEO's commitment to maintaining positive relations with external stakeholders.

name: Organizational innovation
authors_terms: ["organizational innovation", "percentage of sales generated from new products"]
definition: Organizational innovation is here defined as percentage of sales generated from new products.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational performance is here defined as return on assets (ROA).

name: Corporate social responsibility of partners
definition: Engaging in voluntary corporate actions that have a positive impact on stakeholders (e.g., customers, employees, investors, and local communities), and that are in line with the going social expectations so that they are considered moral.

name: Corporate social irresponsibility of partners
definition: Engaging in corporate actions that cause harm to stakeholders (without appropriate actions to rectify this harm), and that are considered immoral as they fall below the threshold of what is socially expected.

name: Alliance formation
definition: Whether an alliance between two firms was realized or not; operationalized as a dichotomous variable that takes the value of '1' if an alliance is realized in a given year, and '0' otherwise.

name: Geographical proximity
definition: Geographical proximity describes whether or not a potential partner is located in the same geographical area as the focal firm (i.e., same location).

name: Media coverage
definition: The extent of potential partners' media exposure; the number of unique articles in which a firm is mentioned in a given year in major news outlets.

name: Rival common ownership in rating agency
authors_terms: ["rival-MSCI CIO", "common ownership with a rating agency", "rivals' institutional investors have in a rating agency", "common ownership in MSCI"]
definition: Common institutional ownership among a target firm's industry rivals and MSCI, the rating agency.

name: ESG rating
authors_terms: ["MSCI ESG rating", "target firm's ESG rating", "ESG rating"]
definition: The target firm's ESG rating issued by the rating agency.

name: ESG media controversies
authors_terms: ["ESG media controversies", "rival ESG media controversies", "target firm ESG media controversies"]
definition: Reputational threats faced by firms based on their ESG activities as reflected in media coverage of ESG controversies.

name: ESG awards
authors_terms: ["ESG awards", "rival ESG awards", "target firm ESG awards"]
definition: External awards for a firm's social, ethical, community, or environmental activities, which can alter a firm's ESG reputation by increasing its social standing relative to non-winners.

name: Product diffusion
definition: Our hypotheses pertain to the diffusion of board games. We use ownership data from Board Game Geek to measure diffusion: the dependent variable counts the number of owners two years after a board game's release.

name: Network product
authors_terms: ["network products", "collectible network games (CNGs)", "board games with collectible components"]
definition: While standalone products exclusively offer standalone value, network products can also provide some standalone value (e.g., a single-player campaign included in an online multiplayer video game). Network value entails the benefits a consumer derives from other users adopting and using the same product.

name: Product novelty
definition: Departure from familiar designs can disrupt a consumer's evaluation schemas and upend their ability to discern whether a product matches their preferences. As a result, novel products tend to primarily appeal to a small subset of consumers - so-called innovators and early adopters - while later adopters apply a more cautious 'wait-and-see' approach.

name: Promoting early adoption
authors_terms: ["promoting early adoption", "frontloading a product's demand", "Kickstarter success"]
definition: Firms can employ various tactics to promote early adoption, including offering preorders, facilitating early access, and launching crowdfunding campaigns. Frontloading a product's demand via, for example, preorders or a crowdfunding campaign can help to create the impression of a large user base.

name: Competition intensity
definition: Competition intensity - the number of similar products entering the market around the same time as a focal product - is especially detrimental for network products, given their reliance on users to create value.

name: Competition from a hit product
authors_terms: ["hit competition", "competition from a hit product", "type of competition"]
definition: Due to their outsized popularity, hit products often dominate consumers' attention, making it harder for competing products to gain a foothold in the market. This is particularly problematic for network products that require large and engaged user bases.

name: Product failure risk
authors_terms: ["failure risk", "risk of failure", "risk of commercial failure"]
definition: The risk that a new product fails commercially. The authors examine a product's failure risk as a key attribute that drives the risk of escalating commitment and the importance of its preemption through buy.

name: Contract manufacturing
definition: The external-market governance choice in which a firm pays a contract manufacturer to take responsibility for interpreting and translating a provided design into the final product, in contrast to CMT/make.

name: Core products
definition: Products that form the basis of a firm's competitive advantage and are central to a brand's identity; they tend to produce stronger ownership and are more prone to escalating commitment.

name: CEO political partisanship
definition: We define CEO political partisanship as the strength of identification with political and ideological groups. Political scientists have often described this identity component of ideology as political partisanship, which is defined as the strength of an individual's identification with an ideological group.

name: CEO political ideology
definition: Political ideology is defined as 'widely shared and deeply held beliefs regarding how a society ought to be structured'. Political ideology exists on a spectrum, with the left and right dimensions being synonymous with liberalism and conservativism, respectively.

name: Corporate misconduct
definition: Corporate misconduct is defined as 'activities and actions that organizational members engage in to deceive or swindle investors or other key stakeholders'.

name: Perspective taking
definition: Perspective taking is the cognitive process by which individuals 'adopt others' viewpoints in an attempt to understand their preferences, values, and needs'. Perspective taking refers to attending others' 'viewpoint, thoughts, motivations, intentions, and/or emotions'.

name: Moral foundations
definition: Moral foundations here refer to the degree of self-righteousness and convictions animating a person's own moral beliefs and worldview.

name: Patent stock
authors_terms: ["patent stock", "patent stocks", "number of patents", "possession of patents"]
definition: A venture's extant stock of patents, a particularly relevant quality-signaling resource and 'narrative ingredient' for new entrepreneurial ventures; a patent is an exclusive legal right granted if an invention is evaluated as novel, nonobvious, and useful.

name: Narrative distinctiveness
definition: The degree to which a narrative's content is distinctive from the content of a prototypical narrative in its category (in this study, the venture's industry).

name: Industry hotness
authors_terms: ["industry hotness", "hot industries", "cold industries", "hotness of their industry"]
definition: The degree to which an industry attracts attention from entrepreneurs and entrepreneurial resource providers.

name: Patent breadth of impact
authors_terms: ["patent breadth of impact", "breadth of impact", "patent stocks with a broader impact"]
definition: The degree to which a venture's patent stock has been cited by a diverse array of other patents, i.e. patents that influence a diverse array of subsequent patents are perceived to be particularly valuable.

name: Patent intensity
definition: The degree to which the possession of patents is common (vs. rare) in a given industry.

name: Uniplex technology closure
authors_terms: ["uniplex technology closure", "within-network uniplex closure", "triadic closure within a technology network"]
definition: Situations in which open transitive triads close within a technology network. The authors differentiate between situations in which open transitive triads close within a technology network (i.e., uniplex technology closure) or across technology networks (i.e., multiplex technology closure).

name: Multiplex technology closure
authors_terms: ["multiplex technology closure", "cross-network multiplex closure", "transitive collaborations across incumbent and emergent technology networks"]
definition: Transitive collaborations across incumbent and emergent technology networks; situations in which open transitive triads close across technology networks.

name: Emergent technology expertise asymmetry
authors_terms: ["asymmetry in the emerging technology expertise", "differences in expertise with mAbs patents", "knowledge asymmetry between firms"]
definition: The asymmetry between two unconnected firms in their level of technological expertise in the emerging technology, considered as a nodal attribute. The authors consider the level of technological expertise in the emerging technology as a nodal attribute to assess the role of knowledge asymmetry between firms.

name: Emerging technology tie formation
authors_terms: ["emerging technology alliance", "tie formation in the emergent technology network", "mAbs alliance"]
definition: Formation of a direct R&D alliance tie between two organizations in the emergent technology (mAbs) network; the emergent technology network is comprised of ties formed to codevelop and transfer knowledge on a new technology that represents a groundbreaking industry change.

name: Issue settlement
authors_terms: ["issue settlement", "judicial or legislative settlement", "marriage equality decision", "settlement of an issue", "issue settlements"]
definition: Settlement of an issue transforms the institutional landscape by providing authoritative guidance about legitimate organizational behavior. In this setting, judicial or legislative decisions regarding same-sex marriage during the 2004-2015 period are treated as issue settlements.

name: Collective action framing
authors_terms: ["collective action frames", "firm's collective action frames (relative to individual action frames)", "use of collective action frames"]
definition: Activism relies on collective action frames that articulate 'action-oriented sets of beliefs and meanings that inspire and legitimate the activities and campaigns of a social movement'; these frames are agentic and contentious, problematizing and challenging existing authoritative views. The authors contrast them with individual action frames, which characterize social issues as business or workplace concerns and tout the firm's own actions using economic rationales.

name: Executive liberal political ideology
authors_terms: ["BOD and CEO's liberal political ideology", "liberal executives", "executive ideology"]
definition: Liberal managers take a more optimistic view of human nature, which drives them to place importance on social change, social justice, and equality in outcomes; liberal managers are more likely to support social liberalization policies such as LGBTQ rights.

name: Industry political conservatism
definition: If the political orientation of a firm's industry is predominantly conservative, whether for ideological or strategic reasons, collective action frames will deviate significantly from their peers' frames or strategic silence; such industries orient their political giving toward conservative politicians.

name: State political conservatism
definition: Deviations between public opinion and social liberalization policies are greater in states where residents and politicians are predominantly conservative, which the authors gauge from the average ideology score of political candidates in the state.

name: Issue-aligned advocacy organizations
definition: Advocacy NGOs seek to change existing institutions through tactics such as public information campaigns, lobbying, litigation, and private politics; the presence and activities of NGOs proximate to firms increase the pressures firms feel to comply with standards espoused by such organizations or participate in their issue-related activities.

name: Merger partner ownership type
definition: A merger occurs when firms cease to exist and are subsumed into a combined entity. We defined a merger between two family firms as family–family merger, a merger between a family firm and a nonfamily firm as family–nonfamily merger, and a merger between two nonfamily firms as nonfamily–nonfamily merger.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family firms are defined as those owned by a family, involving two or more family members.

name: Job security
definition: We measured job security as 1 minus the percentage reduction in the number of employees dismissed in the combined organization in the years after the merger.

name: Post-merger performance
definition: We captured post-merger performance as the merged firm's return on assets (ROA). As an indicator of how profitable a company is relative to its total assets, ROA is an established measure of performance.

name: Vicarious experimentation
authors_terms: ["vicarious experimentation", "learning by being imitated", "extent of vicarious experimentation"]
definition: An innovator's learning by being imitated, in which an imitator's copy is a near-clone that functions as a quasi-experimental treatment while the innovator's original is the control. The innovator learns by observing the imitator's choices and outcomes and comparing them to its own.

name: Next-generation product quality
authors_terms: ["sequel quality", "quality of the innovator's next-generation product", "quality of the sequel game"]
definition: The quality of the next-generation product released by the innovator, measured with the average critics' rating scores of the innovator's sequel game.

name: Imitator prominence
definition: Imitators' market prominence, a critical external factor shaping the success of vicarious experimentation: prominent imitators generate more available and higher-quality information through increased visibility, comprehensiveness, and reliability.

name: Tacit knowledge loss
authors_terms: ["loss of tacit product-specific knowledge", "retention of tacit knowledge", "tacit knowledge"]
definition: Tacit knowledge encompasses the understanding developed through the creation and refinement of a product, including insights about design, technical constraints, and customer preferences; it is a form of absorptive capacity specific to the vicarious experiment. It is vulnerable to erosion, for example when the product development unit changes.

name: Government corruption scandal disclosure
definition: Government corruption scandals involve public outcry over the abuse of power by politicians for personal gain. Operation Carwash is the scandal setting: a Brazilian police investigation launched in 2014 that revealed a bribery scheme involving politically appointed board members, state-owned firms, and private companies.

name: Corporate-nonprofit partnership
definition: Corporate-nonprofit partnerships are collaborative relationships in which both parties combine complementary resources to achieve shared goals. They are reciprocal relationships that arise when the net benefits to both the firm and nonprofit are positive.

name: Direct scandal taint
definition: Firms directly involved in a scandal are those directly implicated in Operation Carwash. The paper distinguishes firms that remained untainted, those directly tainted due to their involvement in the scandal, and those indirectly tainted.

name: Indirect scandal taint
definition: Firms indirectly tainted are those associated with the scandal by virtue of state ownership and politically connected boards. These connections, though lawful, came to be perceived as more corrupt after Operation Carwash.

name: Trade association
definition: Trade associations are nonprofit business and professional associations that can claim to advance public interests, yet they are not solely public serving and instead pursue partisan objectives to represent their members' interests rather than broader social benefits.

name: Education and research nonprofit
definition: Education and research nonprofits include nonprofit universities, research institutes, think tanks, and educational foundations that aim to serve society by offering impartial analyses that can influence public policy.

name: Nonprofit political capital
definition: Nonprofit political capital consists of relationships with political actors that can help nonprofits achieve their goals. Nonprofits can build political capital by fostering cooperative political relationships, which enable them to advocate more effectively for policy changes or expand their services.

name: Novelty-centered business model design
authors_terms: ["novelty-centered business model design", "design novelty", "business model novelty", "business model innovation"]
definition: Novelty-centered business model design refers to new ways of conducting economic exchanges among various participants. It can be achieved, for example, by connecting previously unconnected parties, by linking transaction participants in new ways, or by designing new transaction mechanisms.

name: Efficiency-centered business model design
definition: Efficiency-centered business model design refers to the measures that firms may take to achieve transaction efficiency through their business models. It aims at reducing transaction costs for all transaction participants.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "market value of equity", "stock market value", "perceived venture performance"]
definition: A firm's stock market value reflects the market's expectations of future cash flows to shareholders, and can be viewed as a measure of perceived venture performance.

name: Environmental resource munificence
definition: We define munificence as the extent to which the environment supports growth. In this paper, munificence refers to the scarcity or abundance of critical resources required to create and implement business model designs.

name: Interunit tie weakness
authors_terms: ["weak interunit ties", "tie weakness", "weak ties", "interunit tie weakness"]
definition: Interunit relations are regularly occurring informal contacts between groups of people from different operating units in an organization. Weak interunit ties are infrequent and distant relationships, and maintaining a weak tie is significantly less costly than maintaining a strong one.

name: Project completion time
authors_terms: ["project completion time", "completion time", "time to project completion"]
definition: Time to project completion is the number of months from the start of concept development to the time of market introduction for a given project (or time to the end of the study period or cancellation for on-going and canceled projects, respectively).

name: Knowledge complexity
definition: When such complex forms of knowledge are considered, the instrumental benefits of weak ties are called into question. One of the main dimensions of complex knowledge is its level of codification, and another important dimension of knowledge complexity, especially in product development tasks, is the extent to which the knowledge to be transferred is independent or is an element of a set of interdependent components.

name: Knowledge codification
definition: By codification I mean the degree to which the knowledge is fully documented or expressed in writing at the time of transfer between a subunit and the receiving project team in another subunit. Knowledge with a low level of codification corresponds closely to the concept of tacit knowledge.

name: Knowledge dependency
definition: The extent to which the knowledge to be transferred is independent or is an element of a set of interdependent components. When the knowledge to be transferred is dependent, the software module functions in conjunction with other components.

name: Direct ties
definition: The number of direct ties maintained by a firm, i.e., the number of the focal firm's direct collaborative partners in the interfirm network.

name: Indirect ties
authors_terms: ["indirect ties", "number of indirect ties", "reach in the network"]
definition: The number of indirect ties maintained by the firm, the firms it can reach in the network through its partners and their partners, excluding its direct ties.

name: Structural holes
authors_terms: ["structural holes", "connections between partners", "degree of connectivity between a firm's partners"]
definition: Gaps in information flows between alters linked to the same ego but not linked to each other; a structural hole indicates that the people on either side of the hole have access to different flows of information.

name: Innovation output
definition: The innovation output of the firm, measured as its patenting frequency, the number of patents received in a given year.

name: Domain change
authors_terms: ["organizational change", "diversifying", "change in organizational structures and activities", "change in domain", "diversification"]
definition: Change in one or more dimensions of an organization's domain. Organizational form is encompassed by domain, meaning the claims an organization stakes out for itself in terms of the clients it serves, the goods and services it produces, and the technologies it employs.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is measured in two ways: net worth, a stock variable that assesses a firm's capital adequacy, and net income, a flow variable that assesses the profitability of each period's operations.

name: Organizational failure
definition: The rate at which organizations disappear through involuntary exit; three types of exits were grouped together under organizational failure: mergers explicitly labelled as FHLBB- or FSLIC-supervised, outright liquidations, and mergers of firms with zero or negative net worth.

name: Relatedness of new activities
authors_terms: ["related diversification", "unrelated diversification", "relatedness", "degree to which new activities are related to existing competences"]
definition: What distinguishes related from unrelated diversifying is the extent to which each dimension of an organization's domain must be altered to accommodate new activities.

name: Size-localized market density
definition: A count of thrifts, newly founded or established, that were active in the market above the 5-percent threshold and that were within a size-localized window around the focal firm's size.

name: Large-firm market density
definition: One of the two measures of successful-firm market density: the number of large savings and loan associations (those in the top quartile for size, measured as assets) operating in the product market above the 5-percent threshold in each period.

name: Profitable-firm market density
definition: One of the two measures of successful-firm market density: the number of highly profitable savings and loan associations (those in the top quartile for return on assets) operating in the product market above the 5-percent threshold in each period.

name: Rate of entry into new markets
authors_terms: ["rate of entry into a new market", "market entry", "diversification"]
definition: The instantaneous rate of entry into a new market, the hazard rate of change, defined as the probability of organizational change (entry into a new market) between times t and t + dt, given that the firm under study has not yet entered the market in question at time t.

name: Potential entrant size
authors_terms: ["being a large potential entrant", "potential entrant size", "top quartile for organizational size"]
definition: Whether a potential entrant is a large organization, indicated by a dummy variable for being in the top quartile for organizational size.

name: Potential entrant profitability
authors_terms: ["highly profitable potential entrants", "potential entrant profitability", "top quartile for profitability"]
definition: Whether a potential entrant is a highly profitable organization, indicated by a dummy variable for being in the top quartile for profitability (return on assets).

name: Insider director ratio
authors_terms: ["insider ratio", "ratio of inside directors to total directors", "inside-director ratios"]
definition: The insider ratio was calculated as the number of employee directors divided by the total number of board members.

name: CEO-board chair duality
authors_terms: ["CEO-board-chairman duality", "dual position of CEO and board chairman", "separation of the CEO and board chair positions"]
definition: CEO-board-chairman duality is a binary variable, coded as one if a CEO was also chairman of the board, and zero otherwise.

name: CEO tenure relative to board tenure
definition: Several studies have hypothesized an effect for relative tenure (i.e., the tenure of board members relative to the CEO's tenure) on board power. The authors hypothesize about the CEO's tenure relative to the board's (average) tenure.

name: Directors' stock ownership
authors_terms: ["directors' stock ownership", "stock ownership held by board members"]
definition: Directors' stock ownership was measured as the percentage of total common equity owned by non-CEO directors.

name: CEO-new director demographic similarity
authors_terms: ["demographic similarity between the CEO and new directors", "CEO-new-director similarity"]
definition: Similarity between a new director and the CEO on particular demographic attributes: functional background, age, educational level, and insider/outsider status.

name: Board-new director demographic similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity between existing board members and new directors", "board-new-director similarity"]
definition: Similarity between a new director and existing board members, assessed by aggregating similarity measures of all board-member-new-director dyads.

name: CEO-board demographic similarity
authors_terms: ["demographic similarity between the CEO and the board", "CEO-board similarity"]
definition: Demographic similarity between the CEO and other board members, assessed as similarity in functional background, age, educational level, and insider/outsider status.

name: CEO total compensation
definition: Total compensation comprises base salary, annual bonus, and the total value of long-term incentives granted in a given year (Crystal, 1984).

name: Contingent CEO compensation
definition: Compensation contingency was calculated for each year as the total value of long-term incentive grants divided by total compensation.

name: Institutional control
authors_terms: ["public and private control", "type of organizational control", "public control"]
definition: The classification of institutions of higher education as public or private. The authors argue that public and private organizations face different institutional expectations: there are different expectations for different types of organizations, with dependence on different sources of support viewed as an appropriate difference between the two types of organizations.

name: Dependence on public sources of support
authors_terms: ["dependence on public sources of support", "dependence on public funding", "dependence on governmental appropriations"]
definition: The proportion of an institution's total revenues derived from sources of support treated as public: government appropriations and government grants and contracts, with government grants treated as technically a public source of support.

name: Dependence on private sources of support
authors_terms: ["dependence on private sources of support", "dependence on private funds", "dependence on private gifts"]
definition: The proportion of an institution's total revenues derived from sources conventionally associated with private status: gifts and grants from private sources and self-generated funds, that is, tuition, fees, and endowment income.

name: Public-funding administrative offices
authors_terms: ["public-funding offices", "number of offices with primary responsibility for the management of public-funding sources"]
definition: The number of administrative offices and positions with primary responsibility for dealing with sources of public funding, selected from the list of coded administrative positions as having major responsibility for managing relations with external sources of financial support.

name: Private-funding administrative offices
authors_terms: ["private-funding offices", "number of offices with primary responsibility for the management of private-funding sources"]
definition: The number of administrative offices and positions with primary responsibility for the management of private-funding sources, selected from the list of coded administrative positions as having major responsibility for managing relations with external sources of financial support.

name: Institutionalization of dependency relations
definition: A central premise of this approach is that dependency relations can, over time, become socially defined as appropriate and legitimate; in the institutional environment there are normative understandings of appropriate and inappropriate organizational dependency patterns.

name: Dependence on external sources of support
definition: The environment is conceptualized in terms of other organizations with which the focal organization engages in direct exchange relations; increasing dependence on exchange relationships produces administrative differentiation as organizations create offices and positions to manage these relationships.

name: Administrative differentiation
definition: Increasing dependence on exchange relationships produces administrative differentiation as organizations create offices and positions to manage these relationships. The magnitude of dependency predicts administrative differentiation when the relations are not institutionalized.

name: Unit centrality
definition: how closely the purposes of a unit match the central mission of its institution. Although centrality is defined as a continuum, for research purposes it is useful to characterize units as core or peripheral.

name: Internal resource allocations
authors_terms: ["resource allocations", "internal resource allocations", "budgetary change", "budget allocations", "relative change in a unit's share of the general budget"]
definition: the relative share of internal institutional resources acquired by a unit, especially money, space, and campus location. The present research focuses on one important aspect of resource allocations - the relative change in a unit's share of the general budget.

name: Environmental power
authors_terms: ["environmental power", "tapping external academic resources", "tapping external financial resources"]
definition: the relative ability of a unit to bring in outside resources that are critically needed by the institution. A unit realizes this form of power when the rest of the institution recognizes both the organization's motivational investment in the resources that the unit can acquire (criticality) and the relative ability of the unit to bring in needed resources from the environment (substitutability).

name: Institutional power
definition: the unit's relative influence within the institution, independent of its environmental power.

name: Resource negotiation strategies
definition: strategies used by unit heads to acquire resource allocations, particularly in negotiating budgets. In the present study, the strategies surveyed included how much a unit head used each of the strategies listed in Table 1 in negotiating the unit's annual budget allocation.

name: Executive migration
authors_terms: ["executive migration", "movement of top managers across organizations", "interfirm movement of executives"]
definition: The movement of top managers between organizations, which the author terms executive migration.

name: Product-market entry
authors_terms: ["product-market entry", "entry into new product markets", "entry into a new product market", "strategic change"]
definition: The event of a firm entering a product market that is new for it; the paper operationalizes strategic change as entry into a market that was new for a particular semiconductor firm.

name: Executive functional background
definition: The functional background of the top manager determines how well situated he or she is to provide input into organizational decisions, including strategic decisions.

name: Executive formal rank
definition: Formal hierarchical position is an indication of authority and power in a manager's former firm and may indicate how much authority he or she brings to the new position.

name: Executive industry experience
authors_terms: ["industry experience", "industry tenure", "years of experience in the semiconductor industry"]
definition: Managers' industry experience may reflect their level of expertise and the influence they could be expected to have in helping mold their new firm's strategy.

name: Prior firm size
authors_terms: ["prior firm size", "relative size of the organization the executive came from"]
definition: The amount of influence managers have may be influenced by the size of the organization that they come from.

name: Top management team tenure
definition: The organizational tenure of team members has been shown to have important effects on the way teams function; the paper measures it as the average organizational tenure of the entire top team.

name: Top management team tenure diversity
authors_terms: ["top management team tenure heterogeneity", "TMT tenure diversity", "tenure diversity", "tenure heterogeneity"]
definition: The level of heterogeneity or homogeneity of the top management team tenure distribution; it leads to a propensity to maintain the strategic status quo.

name: Top management team size
authors_terms: ["top management team size", "TMT size", "size of the top management team"]
definition: The size of the top management team is likely to have a negative effect on the amount of influence that a newly recruited executive will have in the focal organization.

name: Geographic distance
definition: The geographic distance between a newly founded hotel and established hotels, measured as a Euclidean distance using hotels' positions within the Manhattan street-avenue grid.

name: Size distance
authors_terms: ["size distance", "similarity to established hotels in product space", "size"]
definition: The difference in size (number of rooms) between a newly founded hotel and its neighboring established hotels, computed as a Euclidean distance at the time of the focal hotel's founding.

name: Price distance
definition: The difference in average advertised daily room rate (in constant dollars) between a newly founded hotel and its neighboring established hotels, computed as a Euclidean distance at the time of founding.

name: Product distance from incumbents
authors_terms: ["product offerings", "product space", "product dimensions", "product attributes", "similarity in product space"]
definition: The extent to which a newly founded hotel's product attributes differ from those of established hotels; product space is multidimensional, and size and price are the two product dimensions examined here.

name: Conformity to normative TQM adoption
authors_terms: ["conformity to the normative pattern of quality practices", "conformity in TQM adoption", "conformity to the normative pattern of implementation"]
definition: Conformity by a hospital to the normative pattern of quality practices implemented by other TQM adopters; conformity to normative adoption can involve the selection of quality practices most commonly used by other adopters, or the adoption of standard and accepted approaches to TQM.

name: TQM adoption timing
authors_terms: ["time of TQM adoption", "late adoption", "time of adoption"]
definition: The time of TQM adoption, which divides early and late adopters; institutional theory holds that the motivation for adopting shifts from internal, efficiency concerns to external, legitimacy concerns over time as the practice becomes institutionalized.

name: Alliance ties to prior adopters
authors_terms: ["alliance ties to adopters", "ties to alliance partners who had adopted TQM", "number of alliance partners having adopted TQM"]
definition: Membership in a strategic alliance, a contractual arrangement between hospitals for the provision of goods and services, which affords close, multiplex network ties that facilitate the flow of information between hospitals connected to each other.

name: System ties to prior adopters
authors_terms: ["system ties to adopters", "number of other system members having adopted TQM", "ties to fellow system members who had adopted TQM"]
definition: Membership in a hospital system, which binds hospitals together under common ownership and is frequently characterized by high levels of informal and formal communication between member organizations.

name: Organizational legitimacy
definition: By conforming to normative TQM adoption an organization's quality program will be taken for granted as legitimate, apart from evaluations of its impact on work outcomes; accreditation by the JCAHO imparts significant institutional legitimacy.

name: Organizational efficiency
definition: We defined efficiency broadly, as institutional theorists have, and use the term synonymously with the internal workings of the organization; it covers the perceived impact of TQM on costs, errors, turnover and satisfaction as well as archival profitability and productivity.

name: Financial interlock
authors_terms: ["financial interlocks", "ties with financial firms", "industry of sending firm", "financial ties"]
definition: Whether the broken tie was with a financial institution rather than a nonfinancial firm; the authors argue that financial institutions are more likely than nonfinancial firms to have both the incentive and the power to have their ties reinstated.

name: Ownership control
definition: Whether a firm is under family or management control (that is, the type of ownership); management-controlled firms are generally more vulnerable to external control because their ownership is more easily subject to change.

name: Multiple interlock
definition: A multiple interlock (interlocking firms share two or more directors) as opposed to a single interlock (firms share one director).

name: Board size
authors_terms: ["board size", "the size of the board", "smaller the board"]
definition: The number of directors on a firm's board in a given year.

name: Interlock duration
definition: The number of years that a tie had existed prior to its disruption.

name: Business relationship with the financial firm
definition: Whether the industrial firm had a known business relation with the financial institution with which the tie was disrupted, including the financial's being in any way involved in the firm's public offering of stocks or bonds.

name: Financial representation on the board
authors_terms: ["number of representatives of financial institutions on the board", "number of financials' representatives on a board", "number of financial representatives"]
definition: The number of representatives of financial institutions on the board at the time of the tie disruption, examined to see if an increase in the number of financial directors increases their power.

name: Capital dependence
authors_terms: ["change in the firm's debt ratio", "debt ratio", "dependence on financial institutions", "capital-dependent"]
definition: A firm's dependence on financial institutions for capital, captured by the change in the firm's debt ratio; firms that become capital-dependent are more likely to add a financial director to their board.

name: Direct reconstitution
authors_terms: ["direct reconstitution", "directly reconstituted", "reconstituting a broken tie with the same firm"]
definition: Reconstituting a broken tie with the same firm; the authors argue it is most likely when the sending firm is in a position to exercise power over the receiving firm.

name: Functional reconstitution
definition: The process of reestablishing a tie with a different firm in the same industry as the previous tie, rather than reestablishing the tie with the same firm.

name: Technical complexity
authors_terms: ["technical complexity", "production-process complexity", "technical complexity of the plant's production process", "technical complexity of the quality-control function", "quality-control complexity"]
definition: The technological sophistication and degree of predictability of a production system. A second aspect of technical complexity is tapped by the technical complexity of the quality-control function, which is generally closely integrated with the production process.

name: Structural complexity
definition: An aspect of complexity whose elements or subdimensions are horizontal differentiation of tasks among different occupational positions or organizational subunits, vertical differentiation into distinct hierarchical levels, and spatial dispersion of subunits or members of an organization.

name: Administrative intensity
definition: The size of the administrative component relative to the rest of the organization's population.

name: Organizational decline
authors_terms: ["organizational decline", "tendency toward organizational decline", "tendency toward decline"]
definition: A downturn in organization size or performance that is attributable to change in the size or qualitative nature (shape) of an organization's environmental niche.

name: Family ties of outside directors
authors_terms: ["family members of the company executives' families among their outside directors", "family of management", "management's family members"]
definition: Outside board members who are related to the company's managers, and who might have been selected for this reason, may feel more inclined to support publicly the proposals of their family-member executives.

name: Reciprocity arrangements of outside directors
definition: Outside directors may experience pressure when their board position is subject to an informal arrangement in which executives and outside directors reciprocate favors by sitting on each others' boards.

name: Contractual links of outside directors
authors_terms: ["outside directors who are contractually linked to the company", "contracts with the company", "directors who had contracts with the company"]
definition: Outside directors who have established transactions with the company or who represent external contractors may consider their board membership as an instrument for securing their own contract rather than for promoting stockholders' interests.

name: Outside director proportion
authors_terms: ["proportion of outsiders", "proportion of outside directors", "relative independence"]
definition: The board's relative independence, or the proportion of outside board members; effective board governance presumes that board members engage in a critical assessment of management's performance.

name: Outside director equity holdings
authors_terms: ["outside directors' stockholdings", "outside directors' equity holdings", "average amount of equity held by the board's outside directors"]
definition: Outside directors' stockholdings in the company are expected to promote their identification with stockholders' interests and to reinforce the directors' critical assessment of management's performance.

name: Outside directors' executive experience
authors_terms: ["outside directors who have executive experience", "outside director-executives", "directors with executive experience"]
definition: Outside directors who hold executive positions in other companies could contribute to governing performance because they can draw on their own expertise and experience as strategic decision makers.

name: Greenmail payment
authors_terms: ["paying greenmail", "private repurchase of company stock at a premium", "greenmail"]
definition: A company's private repurchase of a block of its stock from a minority stockholder at a premium above the market price; boards that allow management to pay greenmail at stockholders' expense prove ineffective in governing management's performance and protecting stockholders' interests.

name: Federal funding
authors_terms: ["federal funding", "federal funds", "federal money", "ESEA funding", "nonESEA federal funding"]
definition: School district revenue from federal programs, including the ESEA, the NDEA, Federal Vocational Programs, School Lunch monies, and direct federal aid through Public Laws 815 and 874; taken to embody the most complex and fragmented set of demands on the local district.

name: State funding
definition: Total revenue received by the district directly from the state, taken to embody the least complex and most integrated set of demands on the district.

name: Local funding
definition: School district revenue derived from local sources, including the property tax, the parent government funding (local city or county), and revenue from other school districts, assumed to involve diverse but less formally structured interests.

name: State centralization of education
definition: Wirt's measure of the programmatic authority of the state department of education, based on content analyses of state law covering items such as accreditation, textbook, and attendance requirements.

name: Administrative complexity
definition: The complexity of the district's administrative component, reflected in the number of administrative positions and administrative expenditures, which mirrors environmental complexity and buffers the technical work of the district from external demands.

name: Instructional complexity
authors_terms: ["instructional roles", "instructional staffing", "teaching positions", "instructional expenditure", "technical work of the district"]
definition: The complexity of the district's instruction, its technical work, which the authors argue should not be much affected by environmental complexity.

name: ESEA federal funding
definition: Federal funds linked to the recent reforms of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA).

name: Non-ESEA federal funding
definition: All federal funds other than those linked to the ESEA reforms, comprising older federal programs such as NDEA, vocational education, School Lunch monies, and direct federal aid through Public Laws 815 and 874.

name: Corporate diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["strategy", "previous strategy", "corporate strategy", "diversification strategy", "single and vertically integrated strategy", "dominant and related strategy", "unrelated and conglomerate strategy"]
definition: For the purposes of this study, Rumelt's typology of strategy was reduced to three categories because of the theoretical similarities among the categories; strategy was thus classified as being single and vertically integrated, dominant and related, or unrelated and conglomerate.

name: Career specialization of the former CEO
authors_terms: ["CEO career specialization", "CEO specialization", "career specialization", "core specialist", "administrative specialist", "environmental specialist", "internal focus", "external focus", "internal/external focus"]
definition: Because the relationship between a CEO's institutional experience and specific functional career specializations had not been well defined empirically, a typology was developed for this study: CEO career specialization was defined as having a core, an administrative, or an environmental focus.

name: Career specialization of the successor
authors_terms: ["successor's specialization", "career specialization of the CEO chosen as the successor", "new CEO will tend to be a core specialist", "administrative specialist", "environmental specialist"]
definition: The former CEO's specialization and the successor's specializations were identified in each of the 370 cases of CEO successions; the successor's specialization uses the same three-category typology of core, administrative and environmental specialists.

name: Functional specialization
definition: Functional specialization was divided into production, sales, management, finance, and law and was based on the CEO's education and career positions.

name: Institutional experience
authors_terms: ["institutional specialization", "institutional experience", "company experience", "industry experience", "generalist experience", "multiple-industry experience"]
definition: Institutional specialization measured the institutional experience of a CEO using three categories: company experience (CEOs who had spent their entire working lives in one company), industry experience (CEOs who had spent their entire working lives in one industry but more than one company), and generalist experience (CEOs who had spent their working lives in a number of industries and companies).

name: Institutional environment fragmentation
authors_terms: ["fragmentation in institutional decision making", "fragmented institutional environment", "fragmentation of institutional decision making", "structure of the institutional environment"]
definition: The structure of the institutional environment, conceived as the number of competing authorities and the relative distribution of power among them. The critical issue for isomorphism concerns this structure, which previous thinking has implicitly assumed to be centralized but which the authors believe should be treated as a variable.

name: Interorganizational linkages
definition: Lateral linkages that organizations build with other subordinate organizations when the institutional environment is fragmented, rather than relying solely on directives from above. Measured as the number of enterprise exchange partners a cooperative had in the past year for both supplies and sales.

name: Interorganizational linkages outside the basic functional activity
authors_terms: ["interorganizational linkages with organizations outside the basic functional activity", "linkages outside the basic functional area"]
definition: Exchanges with other organizations outside the basic functional activity assigned to the organization, such as agricultural production; in a fragmented environment the superordinate organization cannot exercise firm control and organizations produce for sectors other than the assigned one. Measured as enterprise exchange partners for nonagricultural purchases and sales.

name: Competition among similar organizations
definition: Competition between organizations conducting similar activities. In a fragmented institutional environment a single plan often cannot be generated and nonduplicated functions are less likely to be allocated, so organizations are given more freedom to pursue activities outside any assigned function.

name: Administrative component
authors_terms: ["administrative component", "administrative ratio", "size of the administrative component"]
definition: The administrative structures organizations set up in response to multiple and conflicting environmental demands; these structures sometimes handle purely symbolic activities and at other times play a more rational, procedural and technical role. Organizations respond to many external agencies making demands by having more administrators.

name: CEO cash compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "CEO salary and bonus", "short-term CEO compensation"]
definition: The cash compensation (salary and bonus) paid annually to CEOs; the paper deals only with this component of CEO remuneration and its determinants.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the corporation, typically indexed by sales, assets, or number of employees; the CEO's job in a large firm is thought to be more complex and to carry more responsibility than in a smaller firm, and large firms may have an increased ability to pay.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The economic performance of the firm; because the CEO is the individual responsible for the overall performance of the organization, rewards should be contingent on this criterion.

name: Industry
definition: Industry membership, which compensation consultants observe is associated with industry-wide differences in top-management salaries, some industries having adopted conventions of paying higher or lower than others independent of organizational characteristics.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["term in the job", "term as CEO", "tenure in office"]
definition: The length of time an individual has served as CEO, a human capital variable that may affect potential compensation either through human capital factors or ability to manage the compensation-setting process.

name: Number of vice presidents
authors_terms: ["number of vice presidents", "number of VPs", "players in the tournament"]
definition: The number of agents who can be thought of as being in the tournament for the CEO's job; in this paper the participants in this tournament are defined to be those currently serving as vice president.

name: CEO-VP compensation gap
authors_terms: ["gap between CEO and average VP compensation levels", "difference between CEO and average VP compensation levels", "prize"]
definition: The difference between the CEO's salary and bonus and the average compensation of the vice presidents, which tournament theory treats as the prize whose size should grow with the number of contestants.

name: Vice president compensation
authors_terms: ["average salary of top VPs", "average salary of executive officers", "average VP salary"]
definition: The average compensation of the firm's vice presidents, computed for the top-ranked vice presidents and for the group of executive officers identified under SEC reporting regulations as having significant responsibility.

name: Compensation committee member compensation
authors_terms: ["average salary of compensation committee", "highest salary on compensation committee", "salary level of members of the compensation committee"]
definition: The salary level of the outside directors who serve on the corporation's compensation committee, who are frequently CEOs of other firms and may anchor their judgments about the focal CEO's pay in their own salaries.

name: Outside director compensation
authors_terms: ["average salary of outside directors", "highest salary of outside director", "salary levels of outside members of the board of directors"]
definition: The salary levels of outside members of the board of directors who are executives in other firms, which should be related to CEO compensation if social comparison processes are operating.

name: State ownership
definition: State-owned firms are owned by governments. Their managers have less autonomy than managers of other ownership types due to external rules, such as civil service policies and rigid, hierarchical reporting requirements to government controllers.

name: Publicly traded ownership
definition: Publicly traded firms issue shares that are traded on stock exchanges. Public ownership increases the financial resources available to the firm through greater risk sharing among many owners, and the firm has relative autonomy in tapping the equity market.

name: Privately held ownership
definition: Privately held firms are not owned by governments and do not have shares traded on stock exchanges. Ownership is typically concentrated in few residual risk bearers, reducing the financial resources available.

name: Firm growth
definition: Growth: the average annual growth rate of an organization's size.

name: International scope
definition: The international breadth of a firm's operations, measured as the number of countries in which a firm had operations.

name: Domestic market dominance
authors_terms: ["domestic market dominance", "domestic market position", "share of the domestic market"]
definition: The market share of a firm in its home country, measured as the number of rigs a firm had in its domestic market divided by the total number of rigs in the firm's domestic market.

name: Product-line scope
definition: The breadth of a firm's product line, measured as the number of rig types in a firm's fleet. Four types of rigs existed in the industry: barges, jack-ups, drillships, and semisubmersibles.

name: State-owned customers overseas
authors_terms: ["state-owned customers overseas", "affinity for state-owned customers overseas"]
definition: The propensity of a firm to have state-owned customers overseas, measured as the number of rigs overseas contracted to state-owned customers divided by the number of rigs a firm had operating overseas.

name: Customer-base stability
definition: The propensity of a firm to enter into long-term contracts with customers, measured as the firm mean of the proportion of years in a rig's life it was contracted to the same customer.

name: Advanced technology
definition: The propensity of a firm to employ high-cost, complex technology, measured with a dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm had a drillship rig or semisubmersible rig in its fleet, and 0 otherwise.

name: Top-management-team tenure
authors_terms: ["team tenure", "managerial tenure", "top-management-team tenure", "executive-team tenure", "organizational tenure", "tenure in the company"]
definition: The organizational tenure of top-management-team members, which is argued to affect (and serve as an approximation for) the team's commitment to the status quo, its informational diversity, and its attitudes toward risk; measured as the mean number of years of employment in the firm of team members in year t.

name: Strategic persistence
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategy remains stable over time.

name: Strategic conformity
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategy conforms to the central tendency of the entire industry.

name: Performance conformity
definition: The extent to which a firm's performance is similar to the average for the industry.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: The latitude of action available to top executives; a means of accounting for differing levels of constraint facing different top-management groups, determined here by environmental sources (industry) and organizational sources (size and slack).

name: Technological discontinuity
definition: Innovations that dramatically advance an industry's price vs. performance frontier; Tushman and Anderson (1986) defined a technological discontinuity as an order-of-magnitude improvement in the maximum achievable price vs. performance frontier of an industry.

name: Competence-enhancing discontinuity
definition: A competence-enhancing discontinuity builds on know-how embodied in the technology that it replaces.

name: Competence-destroying discontinuity
definition: A competence-destroying discontinuity renders obsolete the expertise required to master the technology that it replaces.

name: Era of ferment
definition: A breakthrough innovation inaugurates an era of ferment, characterized by two distinct selection processes: competition between technical regimes and competition within the new technical regime; this period of substantial product-class variation and uncertainty ends with the emergence of a dominant design.

name: Era of incremental change
authors_terms: ["era of incremental change", "period of incremental technical change", "retention period"]
definition: After a dominant design emerges, technological progress is driven by numerous incremental innovations; an era of incremental change persists until it is ended by another technological discontinuity.

name: Dominant design
definition: A dominant design is a single architecture that establishes dominance in a product class; it marks the end of the era of ferment and reduces variation and uncertainty in the product class.

name: Technological variation
definition: Variation is reflected in the number of variants of old and new technology competing in the market; the era of ferment is expected to be characterized by a high rate of variation.

name: Appropriability regime
authors_terms: ["regimes of high appropriability", "regimes of low appropriability"]
definition: High appropriability exists where a firm is able to build a thicket of patents around a technology and control its diffusion via strategic licensing decisions; in regimes of low appropriability, rivals appropriate some of these returns via imitation.

name: Timing of the sales peak
authors_terms: ["sales peak", "point at which sales of the new technology peak"]
definition: The point in time at which sales of all versions of the new technology peak; the authors contend the emergence of a dominant design enables sales to take off.

name: Position relative to technical performance frontier
authors_terms: ["frontier of technical performance", "industry performance frontier", "state of the art"]
definition: The frontier of technical performance is the maximum value of the key performance parameter achieved in a given year; dominant designs are expected to lie behind it at the time they become dominant.

name: Origin of the dominant design pioneer
definition: A firm was classified as an incumbent with respect to a given discontinuity if it entered the industry before the discontinuity; otherwise it was classified as a newcomer.

name: Technical progress
definition: The total performance improvement over the lifetime of a technology, decomposed into advance from the discontinuity, the era of ferment, and the era of incremental change.

name: External attention
definition: Attention to the external environment, formed by combining output attention and input attention.

name: Internal attention
definition: The number of sentences referring to owners, employees, and top managers.

name: Output attention
definition: The number of sentences referring to customers or general economic factors affecting demand.

name: Input attention
definition: The number of sentences referring to creditors and suppliers.

name: Firm survival
definition: Whether the firm eventually filed for bankruptcy or survived; each bankrupt firm was matched with a surviving firm closely positioned in size and scope of activities and in the same environment five years prior to the bankruptcy.

name: Transaction costs
authors_terms: ["transaction costs", "difficulty in allocating adjustment costs", "difficulty of agreement with the supplier on the allocation of costs", "interunit conflict"]
definition: We defined transaction costs as the difficulty experienced by the assembly division in reaching agreement with its suppliers on the allocation of adjustment costs. Difficulty in reaching interunit agreement on cost allocation specifically measures the intensity of bargaining over adjustment costs.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "asset uniqueness", "supplier asset specificity", "supplier asset specialization"]
definition: We measured the construct in terms of the uniqueness of the supplier's technical labor skills and manufacturing equipment for producing the product delivered to the assembly division.

name: Preselection investment in technology
authors_terms: ["preselection investment in technology", "supplier preselection investment in new technology", "supplier technology investment"]
definition: Our hypothesis for supplier technology investment requires that the investment be made in order to increase the supplier's chances of selection. If the investment was made for other reasons, the proportion of nonredeployable assets is likely to be small.

name: Supplier market competition
definition: Since the availability of competitors makes it easier for the buyer to switch suppliers, it raises the credibility of a buyer's threats to terminate the relationship. The more credible the threat of termination, the less the supplier should haggle with the buyer over adaptation costs.

name: Governance form of supply relationship
authors_terms: ["profit centers", "component manufacturing divisions", "outside suppliers", "market suppliers", "relational contracting"]
definition: Supply relationships with component manufacturing divisions occur between units operated as profit centers within the corporation, while relationships with outside suppliers strongly resembled MacNeil's (1978) concept of relational contracting, in which supplier expectations of a long-term, exclusive relationship attenuate short-term conflict over cost allocation.

name: Institutional linkages
authors_terms: ["institutional linkages", "institutional relations", "institutional ties", "institutional attachments", "purchase of service agreements (POSAs)", "site-sharing arrangements (SSAs)"]
definition: An institutional linkage is defined here as a direct and regularized relationship between an organization and an institution in the organization's environment. Institutions are defined as government or community constituents in the organization's task environment that possess either communitywide and uncontested social acceptance or legislative and administrative authority in the organization's domain.

name: Organizational mortality
authors_terms: ["organizational mortality", "mortality rate", "failure", "risk of failure", "likelihood of survival"]
definition: A CCSO was defined to have failed on the earliest date of closing reported in the MCSS archives or Directory listings. CCSO mortality was modeled using r(t), the instantaneous rate of mortality.

name: Competition
definition: The differential ability of organizations to obtain scarce resources under competitive conditions is argued to determine which organizations survive. If an increase in population density increases mortality, this indicates competition; conversely, if mortality rates decline as density increases, then there is evidence of mutualism.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age was defined as the number of years since a CCSO was founded. Younger organizations are assumed to confront a liability of newness that increases their vulnerability to mortality.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size was defined as the maximum capacity specified in a CCSO's annual operating license. Licensed capacity is highly correlated with many aspects of organizational size, including enrollment, number of qualified and unqualified program staff, and size of physical facilities, playground, and equipment inventory.

name: Strategic generalism
definition: Investigation of the distinction between generalism (broad adaptive capacity in diverse conditions) and specialism (high growth rates in a limited set of conditions) has been an important research agenda in population ecology. The generalism of CCSO strategies was measured by the number of age ranges served by CCSOs.

name: Profit orientation
definition: In the community of child care service organizations of this study, the distinction between nonprofit and for-profit organizations is critical because it reflects the organization's mission and values. Nonprofit child care has been increasingly perceived as more socially acceptable than for-profit child care.

name: Organizational transformation
authors_terms: ["organizational transformation", "age-range entry and exit", "age-range changes", "fundamental or core changes"]
definition: Age-range entry and exit are proposed to represent fundamental or core changes for day cares. To change the age range(s) it can serve, a day care must submit to reinspection by provincial authorities and obtain a new license.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured by comparing a firm's performance, measured as annual sales growth, to average sales growth for the semiconductor industry. Because many semiconductor manufacturers are willing to operate at a low level of profitability while building market share, sales are a better indicator of performance than profits.

name: Chief executive dismissal
authors_terms: ["chief executive dismissal", "dismissal of the chief executive", "firing"]
definition: Chief executive dismissal, measured on an annual basis for each firm, was coded 1 if a dismissal occurred, and 0 otherwise. Great care was taken to identify and differentiate between dismissal and voluntary succession or retirement.

name: Top management dismissal
authors_terms: ["top management dismissal", "top manager dismissals", "dismissal of top managers", "scapegoating"]
definition: Top managers were defined as all executives reporting to the chief executive. Top management dismissal was measured on an annual basis for each firm, coded 1 if any top manager was dismissed, and 0 otherwise.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of inside members of the board of directors", "proportion of insiders on the board"]
definition: Board composition measured the proportion of inside members of the board of directors. The higher the proportion of insiders on the board, the higher the probability that the board will be dominated by the company's management.

name: Board loyalty
authors_terms: ["board loyalty", "proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive"]
definition: Board loyalty measured the proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive. Board members appointed during the incumbent chief executive's tenure are more likely to be individuals with whom the chief executive feels comfortable and who feel some loyalty to the chief executive for their appointments.

name: Insider loyalty
authors_terms: ["insider loyalty", "proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive who were insiders"]
definition: Insider loyalty measured the proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive who were insiders. Board loyalty may be especially intense when the board members appointed by the current chief executive are insiders.

name: Ownership dispersion
definition: Ownership dispersion was measured as the converse of ownership concentration. It was operationalized as one minus the proportion of total firm ownership held by the four largest owners.

name: Chief executive ownership
authors_terms: ["chief executive ownership", "chief executive's ownership position", "stock ownership by the chief executive"]
definition: Chief executive ownership was measured as the proportion of total firm ownership held by the chief executive. Organizational ownership is a source of power that can be used either to support or prevent the dismissal of the chief executive.

name: Chief executive power
authors_terms: ["chief executive power", "powerful chief executives", "power and influence"]
definition: Chief executive power is a function of the composition and loyalty of the board of directors and the ownership configuration of the organization.
