If the chief executive is powerful, it is unlikely that he or she will acquiesce to dismissal efforts, even during periods of poor performance.

name: Successor origin
definition: Successor origin, measured for each firm each time a succession event occurred, was coded 1 if the successor was from outside the organization, and 0 otherwise. An insider is a person promoted from within the firm; an outside succession occurs when a newly appointed chief executive is appointed from outside the firm.

name: Top management board membership
authors_terms: ["board membership", "proportion of top managers who were members of the board of directors"]
definition: Board membership measured the proportion of top managers who were members of the board of directors. Top managers who are also board members have more influence over the chief executive.

name: Top managers appointed by the chief executive
authors_terms: ["appointed by the chief executive", "proportion of top managers appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive"]
definition: Appointed by the chief executive measured the proportion of top managers appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive. Chief executives may be especially reluctant to dismiss managers whom they personally have either appointed or promoted.

name: Ownership form
authors_terms: ["mutual and stock savings and loan associations", "organizational form", "ownership structure"]
definition: Two organizational forms of savings and loan association that differ in their ownership rights and the allocation of control between managers and owners. Mutuals are owned by depositors with limited ownership and voting rights, whereas stocks are owned by stockholders with freely alienable residual claims and external monitoring through stock markets and the market for corporate control.

name: Competition
definition: Interpopulation and intrapopulation competition that intensifies as the density of organizations relying on similar resources increases, exhausting resources and raising mortality. Density, or the number of existing organizations in a population, was used as a measure of competition, computed locally and nonlocally for each type of financial intermediary.

name: Environmental variability
definition: Environmental variability, or the variance of a series around its mean, constrains organizational diversity by complicating the problem of reliable performance. Organizations need excess resources to sustain reliable performances in the face of environmental variability.

name: Deregulation
definition: The deregulation of the SLA industry from 1980 onward, which dramatically altered the asset powers, opportunities, and incentives of SLA managers to take risks.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: The end of the organization, defined by the rule that the organization ends when it ceases to carry out routine actions that sustain its structure, maintain flows of resources and secure the allegiance of its members. Disbandings were defined as the liquidation, forced merger, or voluntary merger of SLAs.

name: Size-localized competition
authors_terms: ["size-localized competition", "localized competition in terms of size", "D,size"]
definition: Competition among organizations that depends on their similarity in organizational size: organizations compete most intensely with organizations of similar size, because large and small organizations depend on different mixes of resources.

name: Geographically localized competition
definition: Competition among hotels located close to one another, which is traded off against the agglomeration economies and economies of geography that draw hotels to cluster in particular hotel districts.

name: Price-localized competition
authors_terms: ["price-localized competition", "localized competition in terms of price"]
definition: Competition among hotels that depends on similarity in price, since service-level segmentation makes patterns of resource use specialized to regions of the price distribution.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: Failure was defined as the cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors; changes in name or ownership were not included as failures because the organization itself continued to provide transient-hotel services.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size is conceptualized in terms of scale of operations and measured as total assets, in millions of dollars.

name: Domain change
authors_terms: ["organizational change", "domain shift", "diversification", "expansion into nontraditional markets", "change in organizational form"]
definition: Organizational change is conceptualized as shifts in an organization's activity set or strategic domain and is operationalized as diversification into new product markets. Diversification--the development of new products or services, often for new client groups and frequently requiring the implementation of new administrative, production, or distribution technologies--is one way in which organizations can change their domains and hence transform their core structures and activities.

name: CEO influence over the board
authors_terms: ["CEO influence", "CEO's influence over the board", "CEO power", "influential CEOs"]
definition: The CEO's influence over the board, measured with multiple indicators. We draw on power, impression management, and institutional perspectives to explain why and under what conditions the decoupling of LTIP adoption and use exists, in particular the ability of powerful CEOs to enhance their legitimacy while minimizing risk in their compensation contracts.

name: Long-term incentive plan adoption
authors_terms: ["LTIP adoption", "adoption of a long-term incentive plan", "adoption of LTIPs"]
definition: In this study, the adoption of a long-term incentive plan refers to the introduction, identifiable as an announcement in proxy statements for purposes of gaining shareholder approval, of a relatively comprehensive incentive program that includes a performance plan.

name: LTIP use
authors_terms: ["LTIP use", "actual use of LTIPs", "implementation", "use (i.e., make any grants under)"]
definition: The adoption of an LTIP does not guarantee that it will be used at all: a board may announce a new LTIP and then make trivially small grants under the plan or no grants at all. Use refers to the actual making of grants under an adopted plan.

name: LTIP grant magnitude
authors_terms: ["magnitude of LTIP use", "size of LTIP grants as a proportion of total compensation", "magnitude of subsequent grants"]
definition: The magnitude of LTIP use, i.e., the size of LTIP grants as a proportion of total compensation.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: Prior firm performance, measured by one market-based and one accounting-based variable, each lagged by one year.

name: Time of LTIP adoption
authors_terms: ["time of adoption", "later date of LTIP adoption", "late adopters", "early adopters"]
definition: A continuous measure of time of adoption, with values ranging from 1, when adoption was in 1972, to 19, when adoption was in 1990, distinguishing early from late adopters.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: The uncertainty surrounding the underlying parameters used to price securities and the ability of banks to place them, which arises when analysts do not agree on the amount of risk associated with a security. It was much greater in the non-investment-grade debt market than in the investment grade market during the period of the study.

name: Reliance on prior exchange partners
authors_terms: ["reliance on previous exchange partners", "prior exchange relations", "repeat exchange", "enduring exchange relations"]
definition: The tendency of actors, under uncertainty, to restrict their range of possible exchange partners to those with whom they have had prior interactions, relying more on previous partners and cultivating enduring exchange relations.

name: Status-based homophily
definition: The tendency for exchange relations to be formed among actors of roughly equivalent status, which follows from actors generally avoiding exchanges with those of lower status. The authors state that we therefore should observe greater status-based homophily in the formation of exchange relations under conditions of uncertainty than under conditions of certainty.

name: Status
definition: An attribution on which actors rely to make inferences about the quality of market products when quality cannot be directly observed, which derives not only from past demonstrations of quality but from the status of the actor's exchange partners. A focal bank's status is a positive function of the number and status of the banks that appear in lower, nonmanagement bracket positions than it.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["market concentration", "market share", "domination of the market by the high-status banks"]
definition: The extent to which offerings are concentrated in the hands of the higher-status banks; a decline in status-based homophily implies greater market concentration, since the higher-status banks become much less reluctant to expand their market share.

name: Cesarean section use
authors_terms: ["primary cesarean section rate", "cesarean section rate", "cesarean use", "cesarean deliveries"]
definition: The dependent variable was the hospital's primary cesarean section rate. This primary rate measure excludes cesareans performed because of a prior cesarean, called repeat cesareans.

name: Measured patient risk
definition: Measured risk characteristics are those that may be directly responsible for a cesarean section, including labor complications or an infant's birth weight. Measured risks used for this study include labor complications and low fetus weight.

name: Inferred patient risk
definition: Inferred risk characteristics indirectly indicate that a woman or her baby might be at risk for a cesarean section and include such factors as the woman's age and whether she has previously given birth. Inferred risk characteristics for this study included age (under 18 or over 34) and birthing experience (first birth or sixth or more), called parity.

name: Hospital structural characteristics
authors_terms: ["hospital characteristics", "hospital types", "structural features of a hospital"]
definition: We capture these constraints and incentives by simultaneously characterizing hospitals according to three structural features: ownership, patient contract, and teaching status. These three characteristics are foundational structural features of a hospital rather than management practices. They cannot be changed without changing the charter of the hospital, and they set the constraints within which managers must operate, thereby also shaping the incentives and interests facing a hospital.

name: Hospital ownership charter
definition: Ownership is the three types of charters for incorporating a hospital: for-profit, nonprofit, or government.

name: Patient contract basis
definition: Patient contracts refer to whether the hospital operates on a fee-for-service (FFS) or prepaid insurance basis. Since health maintenance organizations (HMOs) accrue profit or surplus from giving less expensive care to their members, they thus will have a financial incentive to find less expensive alternatives to surgical deliveries.

name: Teaching status
definition: Teaching status indicates whether a hospital is accredited for training medical personnel in affiliation with a medical school. Teaching hospitals were defined as members of the Council of Teaching Hospitals (COTH), a common definition of a major academic teaching facility.

name: Cesarean treatment standard
authors_terms: ["hospitals' standards for cesarean treatment", "standards for managing risk with cesareans", "a hospital's standard for treating risky pregnancies"]
definition: We created a z-score representation of the difference between these proportions, which generates a linear scale of hospitals' standards for cesareans by normalizing the difference in proportions with the standard deviation of the proportion at risk. Lower scores indicate that fewer risky patients are treated relative to the proportion at risk; higher scores indicate that more are treated.

name: Institutional uncertainty
authors_terms: ["institutional uncertainty", "uncertainty in institutional standards", "institutional standards are uncertain", "uncertain prevailing institutional standards"]
definition: We propose that institutional standards are insufficient for constraining practice when they are uncertain. When institutional standards are uncertain, however, they will be unable to constrain actions completely.

name: R&D alliances
authors_terms: ["R&D ties", "number of research and development alliances", "collaborative R&D activity"]
definition: The number of research and development ties a firm has captures the extent of its involvement in the core activities of the industry. The number of a firm's R&D alliances reflects its network profile for the purposes of exploration.

name: Non-R&D collaborations
authors_terms: ["non-R&D network activity", "ties of each type (other than R&D)", "non-R&D ties"]
definition: We used the disaggregated number of ties for each stage of the product life-cycle (see Table 1) to capture the non-R&D network activity in which firms are involved. We view these efforts as a way to exploit R&D discoveries and thus as a complement to R&D networks.

name: Network portfolio diversity
definition: The range of ties that a firm is engaged in at any given time reflects a firm's portfolio of collaborative activities.

name: Collaboration experience
authors_terms: ["network experience", "collaborative R&D experience", "non-R&D network experience", "experience at managing ties"]
definition: Collaborative R&D experience at time t was measured as the time since inception of a firm's first R&D alliance. Non-R&D network experience at time t, an additional measure of experience at managing ties, is the time since inception of a firm's first tie for any purpose other than R&D.

name: Central connectedness
definition: Centrality is a measure of how well connected, or active, a firm is in the overall network. We contend that firms with more experience have more ties and that the ties they have provide more central connectedness.

name: Firm growth
definition: We indexed growth in two ways. We used the reported number of employees at time t + 1 as a measure of size. We also created a dummy variable, public, that takes on the value of 1 if the firm is publicly traded at time t + 1 and 0 otherwise.

name: Park development
authors_terms: ["park development", "development of parks", "development of the park"]
definition: The parks around the falls are institutions that, by protecting the area from commerce, reorganized the incentives of tourist organizations and increased the resources hotels rely on; their development is measured by the accumulated, depreciated value of past capital investments in each park.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: Hotel failure occurs when the hotel ceases operation, but not when it changes ownership or changes name; failure is modeled with the instantaneous rate of failing, the limiting probability of a failure between t and t + t given that the hotel was operating at t.

name: Organizational founding rate
definition: For founding, the dependent variable is the number of foundings in a year in one of the hotel subpopulations at Niagara Falls.

name: Subpopulation density
authors_terms: ["own density", "population density", "density within the focal hotel's subpopulation"]
definition: Population density is the number of organizations in the population; own density is density within the focal hotel's subpopulation, and it is expected to operate through legitimation and competition.

name: Rival subpopulation density
definition: The density of the other hotel subpopulation, the population on the other side of the border.

name: Founding density in own subpopulation
authors_terms: ["own founding density", "founding density in the hotel's subpopulation"]
definition: Density at the time of the focal organization's founding, measured within the focal hotel's own subpopulation.

name: Founding density in rival subpopulation
definition: Density at the time of the focal organization's founding, measured in the rival subpopulation across the border.

name: Recent failures in own subpopulation
authors_terms: ["own failures at t-1", "failures in the previous period in the own subpopulation"]
definition: The number of recent failures in the focal hotel's own subpopulation in the previous period, which signals that the environment may be less hospitable but also liberates resources.

name: Recent failures in rival subpopulation
authors_terms: ["other failures at t-1", "failures in the previous period in the other subpopulation"]
definition: The number of recent failures in the rival subpopulation in the previous period; both signaling and resource implications of past events are expected to extend across the border.

name: Organizational age
definition: Age is the time since the hotel's founding; because of disagreement about age dependence in organizational mortality, its effect is estimated with a piecewise exponential model in which baseline rates are estimated for preselected age periods.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size usually decreases failure and may represent slack resources and economies of scale; for Niagara Falls hotels the number of rooms best explained failure.

name: Hotel type
definition: Lodging firms are classified by the naming strategy of the firm: house, hotel, motel and inn, with firms that do not use any of these naming strategies classified as other; the public associates different characteristics with these terms and selects or avoids establishments on the basis of their interpretation of the terms.

name: Distance to the falls
authors_terms: ["distance to the falls", "proximity to the falls"]
definition: The Euclidian distance in miles between the hotel and the falls; proximity to relevant attractions should help hotels.

name: Distance to competitors
definition: The average of the Euclidian distance in miles between the focal hotel and all other hotels that existed in the year; for hotels on different sides of the Niagara River, distances were calculated by way of the major bridge.

name: Hotel agglomeration
definition: The number of other hotels within a half-mile of the focal hotel; locating within a cluster of similar organizations may reduce tourists' search costs.

name: Calendar time
definition: Calendar time is the year of the observation minus 1885; it captures trends in the failure rate that are a function of historical time.

name: Own-side park development
definition: Accumulated, depreciated value of past capital investments in the park on the same side of the border as the focal hotel subpopulation.

name: Other-side park development
definition: Accumulated, depreciated value of past capital investments in the park across the border from the focal hotel subpopulation.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: Failure is defined as the cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors, and changes in name or ownership are not counted as failures because the organization itself continued to provide transient-hotel services. The failure rate of Manhattan hotels was estimated using the instantaneous rate of failure.

name: Chain affiliation
definition: Chains are collections of service organizations, doing substantially the same thing, that are linked together into a larger organization; the component organizations focused on are hotels affiliated with hotel chains. A chain can be linked to its components through ownership, franchise agreement, or other types of contracts or agreements.

name: Chain local operating experience
authors_terms: ["local experience", "initial local experience", "incremental local experience", "chain's operating experience in Manhattan"]
definition: To measure the initial and ongoing knowledge transfer from a chain to its components, variables were created based on chains' accumulation of operating experience in Manhattan, which corresponds to the cumulative output measure of experience used in the organizational learning literature. A hotel chain's operating experience in Manhattan is a function of the number of component hotel-years it operated in Manhattan during its past history.

name: Chain nonlocal operating experience
authors_terms: ["nonlocal experience", "initial nonlocal experience", "incremental nonlocal experience", "operating experience outside Manhattan"]
definition: To measure the strategic constraint imposed by a chain on its components, variables were created based on chains' accumulation of operating experience outside Manhattan. A hotel chain's operating experience outside Manhattan is a function of the number of component hotel-years it operated outside Manhattan during its past history.

name: Chain market power in the local market
authors_terms: ["market power", "number of rooms controlled by its chain in Manhattan", "Manhattan rooms"]
definition: Large chains are more powerful in the market for inputs, which is a local source of economies of scale; chains with a strong presence in Manhattan should be able to buy advertising, food, subcontracted labor and other inputs cheaper and might be able to collude successfully on prices. All of these advantages of market power should be a function of how many rooms a chain controls in Manhattan.

name: Market power diffusion
authors_terms: ["market power diffusion", "number of hotels controlled by its chain in Manhattan", "number of Manhattan components"]
definition: Market power may be a negative function of the number of units over which the chain's rooms in Manhattan are spread; if the market power is divided among many component hotels, it will be diluted. Collective action is also more costly when more actors have to be coordinated.

name: Name concentration
authors_terms: ["name concentration", "reputation", "names linking them to the component"]
definition: Chains that provide a reputation benefit to their Manhattan components can be differentiated from those that do not by looking at whether the chain gives other components names that link them with the Manhattan component, which is a necessary condition for building a reputation that benefits the Manhattan component. Name concentration is the percentage of a hotel chain's components that had the same name as the focal component.

name: Presence of independent hotels
authors_terms: ["independent hotel density", "independent hotel mass", "other-type density and mass"]
definition: Independent hotel density and independent hotel mass were measured, respectively, as the total numbers of independent hotels and the total number of rooms in independent hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year; each independent hotel's own rooms were subtracted from the total mass.

name: Presence of component hotels
authors_terms: ["component hotel density", "component hotel mass", "other-type density and mass"]
definition: Component hotel density and component hotel mass were measured, respectively, as the total numbers of component hotels and the total number of rooms in component hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year; each component hotel's own rooms were subtracted from the total mass.

name: CEO hubris
definition: We use Webster's Dictionary definition of hubris as "exaggerated pride or self-confidence, often resulting in retribution." In our perspective, hubris infects extremely confident managers who highly estimate their ability to extract acquisition benefits and consequently pay large premiums.

name: Recent acquiror performance
authors_terms: ["recent organizational success", "recent acquiror performance", "recent performance of the acquiring firm"]
definition: Recent organizational success, which the authors argue fosters CEO hubris because success is readily attributed to the leader and reinforces the CEO's confidence and preexisting beliefs.

name: Media praise for the CEO
authors_terms: ["media praise for the CEO", "recent media praise", "favorable article about the CEO"]
definition: Favorable, nationally distributed press commentary about the CEO, which the authors argue reinforces the CEO's confidence and increases the likelihood that the CEO is infected with hubris.

name: CEO self-importance
definition: Self-importance may be an aggregate construct, intersecting with or even composed of other personality traits such as self-esteem, narcissism, and need for power; the most revealing manifestation of CEOs' self-importance is their pay relative to the other executives in their firms.

name: Acquisition premium
authors_terms: ["acquisition premium", "premium paid for an acquisition", "takeover premium"]
definition: Acquisition premiums, defined as the ratio of the ultimate price paid per target share divided by the price prior to takeover news, are major statements by acquiring managers of how much additional value they can extract from the target firm.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["the consolidation of the board chair and CEO positions", "the board-chair/CEO combination", "CEO is also board chairman"]
definition: Board vigilance is weaker when the CEO is also board chairman than when the posts are separated; this duality is expected to allow a board-chair-CEO to advance and endorse personal preferences relatively unchecked.

name: Proportion of inside directors
authors_terms: ["percentage of inside directors", "proportion of inside directors", "percentage of insiders on the board"]
definition: A greater proportion of insiders, representing a lack of board independence, is expected to heighten CEO discretion; inside manager-directors are more beholden to the CEO for their positions and thus are more likely to endorse the CEO's initiatives.

name: Outside director stockholdings
definition: Board vigilance of the CEO is weakened when outside board members have little financial stake in the company, when their stockholdings are small.

name: Subsequent acquiror performance
authors_terms: ["subsequent performance of the acquiring firm", "postacquisition performance", "shareholder returns"]
definition: Firm performance measured as cumulative abnormal security returns, where a positive abnormal return indicates that the security market has revised upward its expectations of future returns from the security and a negative return indicates that the market has lowered its expectations for the firm.

name: Corporate charitable contributions
definition: Charitable contributions are a type of discretionary expenditure, because it is difficult to measure and thus know what benefits these expenditures accrue to the firm.

name: Time period
definition: I studied charitable contributions in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota in 1979-81 and 1987-89, and the purpose of the current study was to see if the bases for giving changed between the two periods.

name: Dependence of sales on consumers
authors_terms: ["percent sales to consumers", "dependency of industry sales on consumers", "SALESCON", "market position"]
definition: To measure a firm's dependency on household or consumer sales, I asked company representatives to estimate the percentage of sales that went to households or consumers, and where there were missing data I substituted an indicator based on the industry's dependency on consumer sales.

name: Labor intensity
authors_terms: ["labor intensity", "labor intensities", "ratio of employees to total assets", "LABINT"]
definition: To derive a measure of labor intensities, I computed the average number of employees and the average value of firms' total assets and then divided the former by the latter.

name: Network ties to local philanthropic leaders
authors_terms: ["network ties to local philanthropic leaders", "proximity to the elite", "elite proximity", "social network ties", "ELITPROX", "embeddedness"]
definition: Companies gave more if their CEO, top executives, or board members had extensive network ties to a cadre of local businesspeople promoting corporate giving and corporate social responsibility; a firm's executives were thought to be more embedded in the leaders' network if a larger percentage of the philanthropic leaders cited the firm.

name: Firm performance
definition: This measure of performance is more valid because it standardizes earnings and makes comparisons within size and industry categories; it is based on after-tax net income and ratios rather than pretax net income and raw scores.

name: Firm size
definition: The natural log of employees averaged across 1979-81 and 1987-89 was the indicator of firm size.

name: Large outside investor ownership
authors_terms: ["large outside investor", "large outside shareholder", "outside interest", "LGINVEST", "investor control"]
definition: The presence of a large single shareholder (whether inside or outside) makes management more accountable; large outside interests include a person, a family group, or a corporation owning a substantial stake in the company.

name: CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["percent of stock owned by the CEO", "manager-owner", "owner-manager", "CEO"]
definition: Because of the weak coupling between contributions and performance, it is not in an owner's business interest to give money to charity; charitable contributions are more likely under conditions of managerial autonomy.

name: CEO birthplace in headquarters community
authors_terms: ["CEO's birthplace", "CEO was born in the headquarters community", "BIRTHPL"]
definition: Although the CEO's birthplace had no effect in my earlier analysis, both institutional theory and theories that view contributions as serving managerial utility would hypothesize that it should affect giving in both periods.

name: Change in firm performance
authors_terms: ["changes in performance", "decline in performance", "APERFORM", "decline in earnings"]
definition: Crises such as a decline in earnings call into question managerial authority, and when crises arise the value of these expenditures is open to question.

name: Change in firm size
definition: Downsizing calls into question managerial authority, and management of firms that are downsizing are under much greater scrutiny and will be held more accountable for their actions.

name: Change in large outside investor ownership
authors_terms: ["changes in outside ownership", "ALGINVEST", "came under the control of a large outside shareholder"]
definition: Among firms that came under tighter shareholder scrutiny or owner control, e.g., a large outside investor came to own the firm, giving should have decreased.

name: Change in CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["changes in ownership", "ACEO", "CEO increased his or her ownership of stock"]
definition: Among firms in which the CEO increased his or her ownership of stock, giving should have decreased.

name: Prior adoption frequency
authors_terms: ["frequency imitation", "frequency-based imitation", "number of other firms using IBanker", "frequency of use by others"]
definition: With frequency-based imitation, organizations tend to imitate actions that have been taken by large numbers of other organizations; it is precisely the large number of other organizations enacting a practice that enhances legitimacy or endows a practice with a taken-for-granted status.

name: Traits of prior users
authors_terms: ["trait imitation", "trait-based imitation", "traits of other firms", "size of other firms", "success of other firms", "profitability of other firms"]
definition: In trait-based imitation, organizations may also selectively imitate practices that have been used by some subset of other organizations; we focus on two traits of the other firms using a given investment banker: their size and success.

name: Acquisition premiums paid by prior users
authors_terms: ["outcome imitation", "outcome-based imitation", "average past premiums", "maximum premium", "minimum premium", "very high premiums", "very low premiums"]
definition: An acquisition premium is a measure of how much one firm pays to acquire another firm; the premium is expressed as the percentage difference between the target company's stock price prior to the announcement of the acquisition and the price per share paid by the acquiring firm. With outcome-based imitation, organizations use the outcomes that occur after other organizations use a practice or structure to determine whether they should adopt.

name: Contextual uncertainty
definition: General environmental uncertainty has been criticized as an amorphous construct, so we chose two measures, each of which captures an important source of uncertainty: transaction uncertainty, which is uncertainty about the acquisition target, and partner uncertainty, which represents uncertainty about prior performance of an investment banker.

name: Investment banker selection
authors_terms: ["which investment banking firm(s) the acquirers selected", "whether an acquiring firm will use IBanker", "likelihood of a given investment banking firm being selected"]
definition: The dependent variable is which investment banking firm(s) the acquirers selected to advise them on the acquisition.

name: Railroad foundings
definition: The dependent variable is the number of railroad charters granted by the legislature each year; a railroad's charter date provides a good approximation of its founding date.

name: Public capitalization policy regime
authors_terms: ["public capitalization", "public capitalization policy regime", "public capital contributions", "state capitalization"]
definition: The regime under which American state and local governments actively promoted early industries, using public funds to help found private organizations; it extends from the industry's beginning to 1871, when Massachusetts legislation curtailed public capitalization.

name: Pro-cartel policy regime
definition: The pro-cartel regime extends from the year after rate regulation legislation, 1872, to 1896; cartels dampened competition by fixing prices, allocating or 'pooling' traffic among railroads, and pooling profits.

name: Antitrust policy regime
definition: The antitrust regime begins with the Supreme Court enforcement of the Commerce and Sherman acts in 1897; antitrust prohibits cartels designed to halt competition and thereby enlivens competition.

name: Periods in economic history
authors_terms: ["periods in economic history", "five major periods in economic history"]
definition: Economic historians have argued that during the century examined, the American economy went through five economic periods, marked by wars and depressions.

name: Density
definition: As an industry approaches the environment's carrying capacity, foundings decline because demand is being filled by existing firms; density has a curvilinear effect on foundings and is modeled with a quadratic in which the first term represents legitimacy and the second term represents competition.

name: Prior-year foundings
definition: Foundings in one year stimulate foundings in the next by signaling to prospective entrepreneurs that the time is right, but very high numbers of foundings in one year may exhaust available capital, so prior foundings typically show an inverted U-shaped effect.

name: Prior-year failures
definition: Recent failures foster new foundings because each creates a fund of floating resources available for new ventures, although massive numbers of failures signal a pernicious environment.

name: British economic growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the British economy", "British capital market", "vitality of the British capital market"]
definition: The vitality of the British capital market, which states and localities tapped by issuing guaranteed railroad bonds in British sterling; transport historians note that in several periods the American rail industry appears to follow the fortunes of the British economy.

name: U.S. economic growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the U. S. economy", "U. S. capital market", "vitality of the U. S. capital market"]
definition: Population ecologists and industrial organization theorists alike expect the availability of capital to have a positive effect on foundings; following ecologists, the authors measure capital market vitality by economic growth in the previous year.

name: Network size
definition: In railroading, a firm's prospects depend on the number of destinations available in the whole network; in such industries mass, or total industry size, may have a positive effect on foundings net of the effect of density.

name: Capital accumulation
definition: In industries characterized by high fixed costs, capital accumulation reduces production costs for incumbents, thereby making it difficult for new entrants to compete; it is measured as the cumulative capitalization of the industry.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Concentration may encourage foundings by partitioning markets into mass and specialist segments, or may serve as a barrier to entry because prospective entrants perceive the presence of large firms to undermine their likelihood of success.

name: Intraindustry ties
authors_terms: ["intraindustry ties", "intraindustry linkages", "intraindustry interaction", "intraindustry importation", "trade association ties"]
definition: Intraindustry ties, or linkages to entities operating within the same competitive field, facilitate interaction among managers who face the same contingencies.

name: Extraindustry ties
definition: Extraindustry ties, or linkages to entities operating outside of the firm's competitive field, by contrast, should increase managers' ability to formulate strategies that deviate from common practice in the industry.

name: Strategic conformity
definition: Strategic conformity is the degree to which the firm's business strategy profile adheres to central tendencies of the industry. It is the extent to which the firm adheres to the average, or typical, strategy of the industry.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance was measured as the firm's average return on assets (ROA) in years t+2 and t+3. A common gauge of organizational profitability, ROA captures the degree to which management has effectively deployed firm assets; thus, it is useful in assessing the performance implications of business strategies.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Prior research suggests that a host of factors contributes to environmental dynamism and uncertainty, with perhaps the most commonly cited including: innovation, technological discontinuity, demand instability, supply instability, competitive rivalry, and market growth.

name: General human capital
authors_terms: ["general human capital", "formal education", "prior work experience", "management experience", "supervisory experience"]
definition: Skills, such as formal education and prior work experience, that are useful across a wide range of occupational alternatives.

name: Specific human capital
authors_terms: ["specific human capital", "human capital specific to the current venture"]
definition: Education, training, or experience that has a limited scope of applicability; it creates value in a particular business context but does not have relevance in alternative occupations.

name: Psychic income from entrepreneurship
definition: The personal satisfaction the entrepreneur derives from self-employment.

name: Switching costs
authors_terms: ["switching costs", "cost of switching to alternative occupations", "cost of switching"]
definition: The costs inherent in the act of switching between two alternative occupations, reflecting efforts and expenses of job searches and retraining and the psychic costs of uncertainty, excluding differences in returns in those occupations.

name: Economic performance of the venture
definition: The economic returns to the entrepreneur for both the financial and human capital invested in the venture.

name: Threshold of performance
definition: The level of performance below which the dominant organizational constituents will act to dissolve the organization.

name: Entrepreneurial exit
definition: The entrepreneur's decision to discontinue or stay in business; the venture is expected to be discontinued when economic performance falls below the threshold level of performance.

name: Specificity of human capital ratio
definition: The proportion of an entrepreneur's human capital that is specific to the current venture relative to general human capital, reflecting greater specificity in the mix of skills.

name: Dependence on organizations with different ideologies
authors_terms: ["dependence", "dependence on organizations with different ideologies", "resource dependency", "short-term debt owed to banks", "dependence on capitalist organizations"]
definition: An organization's resource dependency on another can result in asymmetric power relations: the more dependent the focal organization is on the other organization, the more power the latter will have, and it can use this imbalance to force the focal organization to conform to a variety of demands.

name: Cost of ideology
authors_terms: ["cost of ideology", "economic cost of not hiring labor", "economic cost of maintaining its ideology", "economic incentive of hiring labor"]
definition: The economic cost of not hiring labor is the difference between the marginal revenue that an additional unit of labor would bring and the cost of that unit of labor; the income that a kibbutz loses by not hiring labor.

name: Ideological adherence
definition: The term adherence describes the strength of an actor's devotion to an ideology; an organization's adherence to its ideology is a function of the adherence of its participants and of ideological heterogeneity among them.

name: Conformity to exchange partner ideology
authors_terms: ["practices will reflect the ideology of the other", "ideological conversion", "ideological isomorphism", "isomorphic pressure"]
definition: The extent to which an organization's practices reflect the ideology of another organization, as when a focal organization's dependence on an exchange partner with a different ideology results in its doing something that is not fully consistent with its own ideology.

name: Implementation of the self-labor principle
authors_terms: ["self-labor", "implementation of the tenets of its ideology", "implementation of the organizing principles of an ideology", "application of the principle of self-labor", "exercise of ideology"]
definition: The extent to which a kibbutz follows the principle of self-labor, an operational organizing principle of kibbutz socialist-Zionist ideology holding that kibbutzim should rely only on the labor of their members and should not employ hired labor.

name: Performance relative to social aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to the social aspiration level", "share - average share", "relative performance"]
definition: The social aspiration level is based on the contemporary performance of a reference group of organizations; here, the reference group is all other organizations in a market, specified according to industry convention, and the aspiration level is set to their mean performance. The relative performance measure is defined as share minus the social aspiration level.

name: Performance relative to historical aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to the historical aspiration level", "share - historical aspiration level", "relative performance"]
definition: The historical aspiration level gradually accommodates to the current performance of the firm, specified as an exponentially weighted moving average of experienced performance. The relative performance measure is defined as share minus the historical aspiration level.

name: Market position change
authors_terms: ["format change", "market position change", "risky organizational change", "all changes"]
definition: A change in market position, in this setting a change of radio station format, which has serious and uncertain consequences for the station's economic performance and is therefore an appropriate outcome for a study informed by the theory of risk-taking behavior.

name: Observed local market changes
authors_terms: ["market change, local", "changes seen in the market", "format changes by other stations in the local market"]
definition: The observation of market changes by competitors in the station's local market, which provide information by giving managers an opportunity to learn about the market structure through the experience of others.

name: Observed nonlocal market changes
definition: Market changes by competitors observed in other markets in which the focal corporation had stations, except changes in the focal market and by its own stations, so that local learning is augmented by nonlocal learning.

name: Prior market position change
authors_terms: ["station change, local", "changes done by the station", "recent experience with change"]
definition: The organization's own recent experience of making a market position change; based on their experience, organizations develop routines for responding to environmental stimuli, and they are likely to reuse old solutions to problems.

name: Nonlocal prior market position change
authors_terms: ["station change, nonlocal", "changes done by other organizations in the same corporation", "nonlocal momentum"]
definition: Market position changes recently made by other organizations in the same corporation; changes done in one unit organization can be routinized at the corporate level and repeated in other unit organizations.

name: Anticipated interdependence
definition: Our usage of interdependence focuses on the partners' anticipation of the extent of complexity in decomposing tasks and the degree to which it will entail ongoing mutual adjustment and adaptation to accomplish joint tasks, which is akin to Teece's discussion of 'coupling.'

name: Hierarchical governance structure
definition: The governance structure of the alliance is the formal contractual structure participants used to formalize it. We depart from prior efforts here by presenting a typology of alliance structure that defines three distinct types of alliance governance structures—joint ventures, minority investment, and contractual alliances—and the magnitude and specific types of hierarchical controls typically present in each of them.

name: Technology component in alliance
definition: R&D alliances included those that encompassed a technology component in the agreement. They could involve exchange, unilateral transfer, sharing, or co-development of technology or elements of all the above.

name: Appropriability regime strength
definition: The strength of the appropriability regime of an industry is the degree to which firms are able to capture the rents generated by their innovations. In a tight appropriability regime, firms can retain the profits they earn from their proprietary resources, while in a loose regime, these profits are subject to involuntary leakage or spillovers to other firms.

name: Interfirm trust
definition: Researchers have argued that although expectations of trust ultimately reside with individuals, it is possible to think of interfirm trust in economic transactions. Trust between alliance partners at the time of an alliance formation should address both coordination-cost and appropriation concerns and thus reduce the need for hierarchical controls in the alliance.

name: Technical legitimacy
authors_terms: ["technical legitimacy", "normative endorsement of technical staff and programs", "technical form of legitimacy", "technical approbation"]
definition: Technical legitimacy is focused on aspects of core technology, including normative support for staff qualifications, training programs, work procedures, and quality assurance mechanisms.

name: Managerial legitimacy
authors_terms: ["managerial legitimacy", "normative endorsement of managerial staff and programs", "managerial form of legitimacy", "managerial approbation"]
definition: Managerial legitimacy involves normative support for organizational mechanisms such as personnel management, accounting practices, and the rules of conduct and structure of the administrative staff.

name: Organizational survival
definition: Organizational survival refers to the continued existence of a hospital organization; exit events included dissolutions, acquisitions by other hospitals, transformations into other organizational forms, and equal-status mergers.

name: Centralization of sector funding decisions
authors_terms: ["sector funding decisions", "centralized funding decisions", "centralization", "centralized regulatory and funding controls"]
definition: The extent to which sector funding decisions are more highly centralized, as in the era of federal involvement.

name: Formalized organizational interdependence
authors_terms: ["formalized organizational interdependence", "increased levels of formalized organizational interdependence", "interdependence", "widespread provider linkages", "formal linkages"]
definition: The extent to which organizations are linked through formalized relations such as multihospital systems and contractual arrangements.

name: Density-dependent effects
definition: Density-dependent effects subsume cognitive legitimation and competition and are captured by organizational density and squared density terms in the survival models.

name: Normative legitimation
definition: Normative legitimacy places emphasis on normative rules that introduce a prescriptive, evaluative, and obligatory dimension into social life.

name: Organizational age
authors_terms: ["organizational age", "age", "time since the founding of a hospital"]
definition: Organizational age was operationalized as the time since the founding of a hospital.

name: Niche specialization
authors_terms: ["niche specialism", "niche generalism", "market niche", "specialist hospitals", "general hospitals", "scope of market niche"]
definition: The scope of a hospital's market niche, distinguishing general hospitals from specialists such as children's, orthopedic, TB, and maternity hospitals.

name: Mission-regime conformity
authors_terms: ["conformity of its mission with that of the overarching institutional regime", "match between mission and logic", "mission and the logic of the overarching institutional regime"]
definition: The correspondence between an organization's mission, indicated by ownership status, and the logic of the overarching institutional regime.

name: Coverage mismatch
definition: A firm that participates in a given industry but does not draw attention from industry specialists can be described as suffering from coverage mismatch. The coverage mismatch of a firm is greater to the extent to which the analysts who specialize in the industries in which a firm participates fail to cover the firm.

name: Excess value
definition: A firm's excess value is the extent to which its market value exceeds the imputed value of its divisions; it indicates the relative discount or premium attached to a firm's stock price.

name: Profitability
definition: To tap economic performance, the authors followed common practice and used the division's and the firm's return on assets (ROA), the ratio of its earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to its assets.

name: Expected profitability
authors_terms: ["expected profitability", "prospects of future earnings", "expected profitability of a division"]
definition: As an indicator of expected profitability of a segment, the authors employ the median ratio, taken over all single-segment firms in the corresponding industry, of a firm's total value or capitalization to its sales; a high value indicates that the stock market sees the industry as having superior prospects.

name: Firm investment in a division
authors_terms: ["firm's investment in a division", "expenditure on research and development (R&D)"]
definition: As a measure of a firm's investment in a segment, the authors used its expenditure on research and development (R&D).

name: Intersegment relatedness
definition: Standard economic reasoning suggests that a pair of businesses should be under the same corporate roof when there is something complementary about their resources, capabilities, or market positions such that they are more valuable when combined in the same firm than as separate entities. A firm is more likely to de-diversify when its existing profile of businesses does not possess economies of scope.

name: Division size relative to other divisions
authors_terms: ["segment's percentage of the firm's total sales", "larger is a division relative to others", "size and age"]
definition: Accounts of the de-diversification wave suggest that firms retain their core operations but divest peripheral businesses, and it seems reasonable to expect that firms will be least willing to part with their largest and oldest operations. As a measure of the centrality of a segment to a firm, the authors took the segment's percentage of the firm's total sales.

name: Division age relative to other divisions
authors_terms: ["segment's age", "older is a division relative to others", "size and age"]
definition: To the extent that organizational identity tends to be preserved, it seems reasonable to expect that firms will be least willing to part with their largest and oldest operations. As a measure of the centrality of a segment to a firm, the authors took the segment's age.

name: Divestiture of a division
definition: Divestiture refers to instances in which a firm has exited a 3-digit industry.

name: Prevalence of adoption in status group
authors_terms: ["percent of program adoptions by school selectivity group", "prevalence of adoption of recycling programs in a school's status group", "social comparison processes"]
definition: The extent to which schools within each of four status groups have adopted a recycling program; schools that are highly selective share common elements that lead them to define each other as peers and look to each other for cues about how to respond to institutional pressures.

name: School selectivity
definition: Schools that are highly selective share many common elements that lead them to define each other as peers and look to each other for cues about how to respond to institutional pressures, competing for the same kinds of talented students and sharing similar degrees of media visibility.

name: Public school status
authors_terms: ["public school", "public or private", "state versus privately generated budgets"]
definition: Public schools are those whose resources are mostly tied to state rather than privately generated budgets, and which are therefore more closely tied to state governments than private schools.

name: Environmentally related major
definition: An official major related to environmentalism offered by a college or university; schools with such majors may have students that are more likely to get involved in environmental activism on campus.

name: SEAC affiliation
authors_terms: ["Member of SEAC", "student environmental group membership in the SEAC", "connections to the SEAC"]
definition: Whether a student environmental group was affiliated through official membership with the Student Environmental Action Coalition, a national social movement organization that provided resources and support to student environmental groups.

name: Status-creation staffing
authors_terms: ["status creation", "recycling programs staffed with new full-time recycling coordinator positions", "full-time recycling coordinator positions"]
definition: A staffing form in which a job description for a role is worked out in the abstract, with corresponding rights and duties and in relation to other roles, and this vacancy is filled by recruitment; in this setting, staffing a newly adopted recycling program by creating a new full-time recycling coordinator position.

name: Role-accretion staffing
authors_terms: ["role accretion", "recycling duties given to an existing facilities employee"]
definition: A staffing form in which various rights and duties are added in small bundles to the estate of a given person; in this setting, staffing a newly adopted recycling program by giving recycling duties to an existing facilities employee as an additional obligation.

name: Recycling program adoption
authors_terms: ["recycling program adoption", "adoption of recycling programs", "authorized recycling programs"]
definition: Adoption by a college or university of an authorized recycling program, that is, a program formally sponsored and funded by a school's administration.

name: New knowledge creation
authors_terms: ["new knowledge created", "creation of new knowledge", "innovation achieved through the creation of new knowledge"]
definition: Technological innovation achieved through the creation of new knowledge de nouveau, that is, the extent to which extensive new technical knowledge had to be created by the firm's technical experts during the research and development period.

name: Knowledge synthesis
authors_terms: ["synthesis of existing knowledge", "knowledge synthesis", "innovation created by knowledge synthesis"]
definition: Technological innovation created by knowledge synthesis, in which existing technical knowledge is combined (synthesized) in unique ways to create a new product.

name: Technological innovation
definition: Technological innovation is defined as a technology new to a given organization or to a given industry; the degree of innovativeness is regarded as an initial condition of the new venture.

name: Waiting time to first product shipment
authors_terms: ["waiting time to first product shipment", "speed with which first products reach the marketplace", "number of months from founding to first product shipment"]
definition: The number of months from its date of founding that it takes a new organization to ship its first product for revenues.

name: Semiconductor industry experience of the founding team
authors_terms: ["semiconductor industry experience", "average number of years of semiconductor industry experience on the founding team"]
definition: The average number of years of semiconductor industry experience on the founding team obtained prior to founding the current new venture, defined as years spent as an employee of a merchant producer of semiconductor devices.

name: Prior start-up experience
authors_terms: ["previous start-up experience", "prior experience in a start-up company"]
definition: Prior experience of the founding managers in a start-up company, calculated as the proportion of founding managers who had previously worked in a start-up firm during its first twelve months after founding.

name: Prior joint work experience
definition: The extent to which members of the founding team had worked together in a prior employment setting, calculated as the proportion of entrepreneurs who had worked with any of the others prior to founding the new venture.

name: Manufacturing position in the founding structure
authors_terms: ["manufacturing position in the founding organizational structure", "manufacturing and marketing position"]
definition: The presence of a manufacturing position, that is, formalized functional expertise in manufacturing, in the founding organizational structure of the new venture.

name: Marketing position in the founding structure
authors_terms: ["marketing position in the founding organizational structure", "manufacturing and marketing position"]
definition: The presence of a formalized marketing position in the founding organizational structure, which should facilitate identification of relevant market data and lead users to inform product development and marketplace requirements.

name: Financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources", "monthly expenditures", "rate of spending during the development period"]
definition: The amount of capital a new venture has available to spend during the development period, measured as the rate of monthly expenditures.

name: Venture capital ownership
authors_terms: ["proportion of venture capital ownership", "proportion of the firm owned by venture capital investors"]
definition: The proportion of the firm owned by venture capital investors during the first year of the new venture's life.

name: Outside investor representation on the board
authors_terms: ["proportion of outside investors on the board of directors", "ratio of outsider investors to total members on the board of directors"]
definition: The proportion of members of the board of directors who were outside investors, traced from founding to the date of the interview.

name: Number of competitors
definition: The number of competitors in the market; for a new venture, a munificent environment would be characterized by a market with few competitors, so that greater numbers of competitors decrease environmental munificence.

name: Mimetic isomorphism
authors_terms: ["mimetic isomorphism", "cohort's average waiting time", "average number of months to first shipment for all other companies founded in the same year"]
definition: The behavior of mimicking or modeling other organizations in the environment, which occurs when organizations face high levels of uncertainty; measured as the average number of months to first shipment for all other companies founded in the same year as the focal organization.

name: Tied-to firm acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["acquisitions by the tied-to firms", "prior acquisitions completed by firms that are tied to a focal firm through director ties", "number of acquisitions by the tied-to firms"]
definition: The number of acquisitions completed by firms that are tied to a focal firm through director ties, i.e., firms on whose boards the focal firm's inside directors sit.

name: Focal firm acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["number of current acquisitions by the focal firm", "number of acquisitions completed by the focal firms", "focal-firm acquisitions"]
definition: The number of acquisitions completed by the focal firm in the selected year.

name: Horizontal acquisitions by tied-to firms
definition: Acquisitions in which the two-digit industry code of the acquiring (tied-to) firm matched that of the acquired firm.

name: Horizontal acquisitions by the focal firm
authors_terms: ["current horizontal acquisitions by the focal firm"]
definition: Acquisitions by the focal firm coded as horizontal because the two-digit industry code of the acquiring firm matched that of the acquired firm.

name: Vertical acquisitions by tied-to firms
definition: Acquisitions by tied-to firms coded as vertical because the industry of the acquiring firm either sold more than 5 percent of its output to or received more than 5 percent of its input from the industry of the acquired firm.

name: Vertical acquisitions by the focal firm
authors_terms: ["current vertical acquisitions by the focal firm"]
definition: Acquisitions by the focal firm coded as vertical according to the input-output criterion between the acquiring and acquired firm's industries.

name: Conglomerate acquisitions by tied-to firms
definition: Acquisitions by tied-to firms that were neither horizontal nor vertical, i.e., acquisitions of unrelated firms.

name: Conglomerate acquisitions by the focal firm
authors_terms: ["current conglomerate acquisitions by the focal firm"]
definition: Acquisitions by the focal firm that were neither horizontal nor vertical.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["network centrality", "access to private information", "number of ties"]
definition: Network centrality is having many director ties to other firms; it is calculated as the sum of ties for all inside directors of a firm, minus any duplicated ties.

name: Similarity of focal and tied-to firms
authors_terms: ["similar conditions", "focal and tied-to firms are similar", "dissimilar"]
definition: The extent to which a focal firm and a tied-to firm are subject to similar internal or external conditions; the test contrasts tied-to firms that are banks with tied-to firms that are not banks.

name: Timing within the 1980s merger wave
definition: Whether an observation falls early or late in the 1981-1990 period; the sample was split between 1986 and 1987, right after the peak of the 1980s merger wave.

name: Industry of tied-to firm acquisitions
authors_terms: ["industries in which the tied-to firms are acquiring"]
definition: The industries in which the tied-to firms are acquiring other firms.

name: Industry of focal firm acquisitions
authors_terms: ["industries in which the focal firms are acquiring"]
definition: The industries in which the focal firms are acquiring other firms, classified by whether the tied-to firms also acquired in that industry.

name: Prior focal firm acquisition activity
definition: The number of acquisitions completed by the focal firm in years preceding the current year.

name: Business sales
definition: Business sales is the annual sales revenue achieved by a business in a particular product market, which is equivalent to corporate sales for a single-business firm. It is used as the measure of commercial success and therefore of business size.

name: Business age
definition: Business age is the length of time that a firm has sold goods in a particular product market.

name: Entrant type
authors_terms: ["start-up firms", "diversifying entrants", "start-up firm and diversifying-entrant dummy variables"]
definition: Many entrants are existing firms that already operate businesses in other product markets and are diversifying by entering a new market, while other entrants are start-up firms formed to enter a product market. Entry by start-up firms and diversifying entrants represents two forms of experiments by which new capabilities are introduced into a product market.

name: Business dissolution
definition: Business dissolution refers to single business corporations that shut down and multibusiness corporations that shut down a single business and includes both voluntary liquidation and involuntary bankruptcy. Dissolution is likely to destroy some of the new capabilities that a business introduced to the product market.

name: Business divestiture
definition: Business divestiture refers to single-business corporations that are sold and multibusiness corporations that sell single businesses to new owners. When a business is sold, capabilities are transferred to a new owner and continue to be part of commercial practice.

name: Planning time
definition: Planning corresponds to the percentage of time that was spent on the predevelopment phase (i.e., from the start of the project to the development of basic product requirements).

name: Supplier involvement
authors_terms: ["supplier involvement", "supplier involvement in stages of the development process"]
definition: Supplier involvement in stages of the development process was measured by whether suppliers were involved in each of the stages of the product development process and was calculated as the number of stages in which suppliers actually participated.

name: Computer-aided design usage
authors_terms: ["CAD usage", "use of computer-aided design", "more designers using computer-aided design (CAD)"]
definition: CAD usage was measured by the percentage of design engineers on the product development team (electronic, mechanical, and manufacturing process) who used computer-aided design systems when designing on the project.

name: Project overlap
definition: Project overlap was measured by the sum of the overlaps (in months) across the six phases described above of the product development project, divided by the total development time.

name: Multifunctional team
definition: Multifunctional team was measured by whether personnel from specific functions were involved on the product development team during the various stages of product development.

name: Reward for schedule attainment
authors_terms: ["reward for schedule attainment", "reward for schedule", "rewards for schedule"]
definition: Reward for schedule attainment was measured by a 5-point Likert scale asking whether the product development personnel were rewarded for meeting the schedule deadlines during the course of the project.

name: Design iterations
authors_terms: ["design iterations", "number of design iterations", "multiple design iterations"]
definition: Number of design iterations was measured directly by asking how many iterations occurred in the development of the product, with an iteration defined as a redesign of at least 10 percent of a product's parts.

name: Testing time
definition: Test corresponds to the percentage of time that is spent on testing the designs.

name: Time between milestones
definition: Time between milestones was measured by first asking the respondent group to provide the number of formal milestones for the project, with a milestone defined as an officially scheduled project review point, and then asking the average time (weeks) between these milestones during the project.

name: Power of the project leader
authors_terms: ["power of the project leader", "project leader power", "powerful project leaders", "powerful leaders"]
definition: Power of the project leader was measured by asking the respondent group where in the SBU hierarchy the project manager reported.

name: Development time
definition: Development time for each development project corresponds to its duration relative to the average development time of all projects in its industry segment.

name: Agency explanation in LTIP announcements
definition: An agency theory explanation of a new LTIP holds that the primary objective of executive incentive plans is to maximize shareholder wealth by aligning the interests of management (as agent) with the interests of shareholders (as principal); boards adopting CEO incentive plans to control executive behavior by aligning executive pay more closely with shareholders' interests use this logic.

name: Human resource explanation in LTIP announcements
authors_terms: ["HR explanation", "human resource management explanation", "HR-based explanation", "HR-management explanation", "HR logic"]
definition: A human resource explanation highlights as an important organizational objective the ability of an organization to attract and retain scarce managerial talent; from this perspective the board adopts CEO incentive plans to compete with other firms for scarce leadership talent and to raise potential total compensation levels.

name: Dual explanation in LTIP announcements
authors_terms: ["both explanations", "agency and HR explanations", "dual explanations", "dual character"]
definition: The possibility that both an agency and an HR explanation may be used in the same LTIP announcement, which the authors associate with periods of transition in which LTIP explanations have a 'dual character' and reflect the integration of declining and emerging perspectives.

name: Timing of LTIP adoption
authors_terms: ["time of adoption", "date of LTIP adoption", "year of adoption", "later adopters"]
definition: The position of the LTIP adoption in time within the 1976-1990 study period, coded from 1 (adoption in 1976) to 15 (adoption in 1990), used to capture changes in the institutional context of CEO compensation explanations.

name: CEO-board demographic similarity
authors_terms: ["demographic similarity", "CEO-board similarity", "similarity in functional backgrounds", "educational background similarity", "age similarity"]
definition: Similarity between the CEO and the board along demographic attributes such as functional background, educational degree and affiliation, and age; demographic similarity provides a salient basis for psychological group membership and in-group bias.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "performance context", "total stock returns", "return on assets"]
definition: The firm's performance context, which constrains the plausibility of LTIP explanations: organizations need to select explanations that are plausible in light of current firm performance.

name: Board power over the CEO
authors_terms: ["board power", "power of the board", "board control over management"]
definition: The board's power relative to the CEO, which enhances the board's independent monitoring capacity and curtails managerial entrenchment; it is examined through separation of the CEO and board chair positions, the portion of the board composed of outsiders appointed before the CEO, CEO tenure, and relative stock ownership of the board and CEO.

name: CEO power over the board
authors_terms: ["power of the CEO", "CEO power over the board", "managerial power"]
definition: The CEO's power relative to the board of directors, reflected in holding both the CEO and board chair positions, long CEO tenure, a large portion of outsiders appointed after the CEO, and low relative director stock ownership; it allows CEOs to signal that they deserve minimal board interference in managing corporate affairs.

name: Balance of power between the board and the CEO
authors_terms: ["balanced distribution of power", "power is relatively balanced", "intermediate levels of board power"]
definition: A situation in which power is relatively balanced between the CEO and the board, so that both parties may be sufficiently powerful to influence the content of LTIP explanations.

name: Organizational founding
definition: Organizational foundings increase the supply of jobs and thus increase demand for labor; in response, employees in established organizations often transfer into newly founded enterprises.

name: Organizational dissolution
definition: Organizational dissolutions or disbandings increase the available labor supply and therefore directly increase entry into surviving organizations, to the extent that these organizations can and wish to accommodate employees from dissolved firms.

name: Merger activity
definition: Many organizations disappear through merger rather than through outright dissolution, and other firms in an industry experience the merger of two or more firms as similar to, but less disruptive than, the dissolution of a firm.

name: Acquisition
authors_terms: ["acquisition", "acquisitions", "own merger", "acquisition of one or more organizations"]
definition: Merger will have different effects on the demographic composition of two sets of surviving organizations: nonmerged organizations and organizations that acquire other organizations.

name: Managerial entry
definition: I coded entry into a firm as occurring in the calendar year in which a manager's name was first recorded in the list of executives for that firm.

name: Managerial exit
definition: I coded exit from a firm as occurring in the calendar year after which a manager's name last appeared in the list of executives for that firm.

name: Mean firm tenure
definition: The central tendency of firms' length-of-service profiles, examined as mean firm tenure.

name: Tenure dispersion
authors_terms: ["dispersion of tenure", "tenure dispersion", "standard deviation of tenure", "coefficient of variation"]
definition: The simple dispersion of social actors along the tenure distribution, measured using the coefficient of variation of individual employees' years of tenure.

name: Organizational size
definition: Large organizations are subject to bureaucratic rigidity, are more likely to develop internal labor markets that reduce personnel flux, and tend to pay more and offer more comprehensive benefits than small organizations.

name: Organizational age
definition: Age, measured in years, controls for the variety of transformations that organizations go through over the course of their lives; older organizations tend to be less flexible than young organizations.

name: Ecological processes
definition: The outcomes examined in research in organizational ecology are generally organizational populations' vital rates: rates of organizational birth, dissolution, and merger. The vital processes of employing organizations-birth, dissolution, merger, and acquisition-create and destroy large numbers of jobs, thereby altering labor-market structures and driving individual employees across organizational boundaries.

name: Personnel flows and tenure distributions
authors_terms: ["personnel flux", "personnel flows", "rates of organizational turnover and ... organizations' tenure distributions"]
definition: 1 propose that organizational ecology, the context within which organizations operate and the dynamics of that context, influences rates of organizational turnover and thereby affects organizations' tenure distributions.

name: Farm winery founding rate
authors_terms: ["founding rate of farm wineries", "state-level farm winery founding rate", "farm winery founding rate", "farm winery foundings"]
definition: The rate at which farm wineries are founded in a state in a given year; it is the dependent variable in the event-count models of specialist organization proliferation.

name: Farm winery density
authors_terms: ["state-level farm winery density", "farm winery density", "form-specific density"]
definition: The number of farm wineries ever to operate in a particular state in a given year, regardless of how long, obtained by breaking up the total winery count by organizational form.

name: Niche volume
authors_terms: ["volume of the new niche", "volume of wine imports", "niche formation"]
definition: The volume of a new niche created by changes in consumer preferences; the authors capture this niche creation process by the volume of wine imports.

name: Market concentration
definition: The degree to which the wine market is concentrated, measured by the share of the total market accounted for by the largest four firms.

name: Direct institutional support
authors_terms: ["direct institutional support", "existence of state farm winery laws", "farm winery laws"]
definition: A supportive institutional environment for farm wineries, specifically the existence of state farm winery laws that offer excise tax benefits and reduced licensing fees for operators of wineries below a certain size.

name: Mass-production winery density
definition: The form-specific density of mass-production wineries, obtained by breaking up the total winery density count by organizational form.

name: Centralization
definition: The concentration of decision making at the top of the organization.

name: Vertical differentiation
definition: The number of formally designated job levels from the direct workers to the chief executive, i.e. the height of the vertical hierarchy.

name: Horizontal differentiation
authors_terms: ["horizontal differentiation", "horizontal division of labor", "role specialization", "functional specialization"]
definition: The number of functions to which a full-time employee was assigned, i.e. the division of work into specialized positions.

name: Formalization
definition: The availability of organization charts, written operating instructions, written terms of reference or job descriptions, written policies, and a workflow or production schedule.

name: Work satisfaction
definition: Satisfaction refers to the difference between an individual's expectations and his or her perceptions; it is measured as the evaluative reaction of the employee to his or her current work.

name: Promotion
authors_terms: ["promotion", "promotions", "staffing of senior positions by recruiting internally"]
