definition: One of the two staffing processes for senior positions, in which positions are filled by recruiting internally, through promotion. In law firms, associates progress up the job ladder and are made partners.

name: Lateral entry
definition: The staffing of senior positions by recruiting externally, through lateral entry. Lateral entry is the mirror image of promotion and its ease, relative to promotion, is inversely related to the openness of the internal labor market.

name: Differentiation
definition: Increasing differentiation, the division of labor within a firm, implies increasing specialization; it determines whether the skills a lawyer develops are general and transferable between firms or firm specific.

name: Proportion of lawyers in litigation
definition: The specialty singled out by the authors because litigation skills are more transferable between firms than are skills associated with office practice, and because clients want well-known litigators, usually a partner.

name: Law firm growth
definition: As organizations grow, more employees are required and the problem of staffing partnership positions increases; growth is measured as the difference between size in the current year and size in the prior year, divided by the size in the prior year.

name: Partner-to-associate ratio
authors_terms: ["partner-to-associate ratio", "ratio of partners to associates", "grade ratios"]
definition: The partner-to-associate ratio in a law firm is a rough estimate of the amount of profits generated for partners to share, with lower ratios being associated with greater profits.

name: Partner exits
definition: The number of partners who leave the firm in a current year. In graded-position systems vacancies caused by exit should be positively related to promotion, while in graded-personnel systems exits should be unrelated to promotion.

name: Major client linkages
authors_terms: ["number of major clients", "number of clients", "client linkages", "number of linkages"]
definition: The number of links between a law firm and major corporate clients, measured as the number of corporations listing the law firm as its outside counsel or listing a member of the law firm on its board of directors. Either relationship usually reflects a close and substantial linkage.

name: Addition of major clients
authors_terms: ["addition of major clients", "adding clients", "change in linkages", "changes in clients"]
definition: The change in the number of client linkages from one year to the next. Adding clients is correlated with growth and should have effects similar to it.

name: Political activity
definition: Pfeffer defined organizational politics as actions undertaken to acquire, enhance, and use power to obtain preferred outcomes in situations having dissensus on choices; the study focuses on political activities that reflect the use of nonbureaucratic and particularistic criteria.

name: Interdependence
definition: Interdependence arises when an organization's technology and environment increase the need for internally differentiated work units and accomplishing tasks requires cooperation among these work units.

name: Consensus on decision preferences
authors_terms: ["consensus", "consensus on the desired characteristics for a new dean", "consensus among organizational participants"]
definition: Agreement among faculty members on the attributes to be desired in a new dean; high scores indicate more consensus on the desired characteristics for a new dean.

name: Task specialization
definition: A measure of task specialization, as contrasted with a measure of differentiation, is intended to capture the prevailing level of skill specialization among faculty members.

name: Heterogeneity in faculty training
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity", "heterogeneity in faculty training", "heterogeneity in the institutions providing training"]
definition: Heterogeneity in the institutions providing training reflects the extent to which a college's faculty members have potentially dissimilar views about how teaching and research should be conducted.

name: Centralization of decision-making authority
definition: Centralization vests more decision-making authority in specific hierarchical levels; it is measured by the distribution of decision-making authority across five hierarchical levels.

name: Corporate profitability
definition: Profitability of the nonfinancial corporation involved, used as an operational indicator of the balance of power and influence between it and a financial corporation.

name: Identical tie
definition: A broken interlock that has been replaced with a new tie in the same direction between the same pair of firms.

name: Directional interlock
definition: An interlock in which individual A, who is a full-time executive with corporation X, also sits as an outside director on the board of Y, so that intercorporate influence flows in the direction of the interlock.

name: CEO stock ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock owned by the CEO or president", "CEO stock ownership", "stock ownership of the CEO"]
definition: The percentage of voting stock in the company owned by the CEO or president, which indicates the degree to which the CEO was also the owner of the company.

name: Individual shareholder ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock owned by the single largest individual shareholder other than the CEO", "ownership by the largest individual shareholder"]
definition: The percentage of voting stock owned by the single largest individual shareholder other than the CEO, indicating the degree to which management was controlled by a dominant individual interest.

name: Corporate shareholder ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock owned by the single largest corporate stockholder", "percentage of stock owned by the largest corporate investor"]
definition: The percentage of voting stock owned by the single largest corporate stockholder, indicating the degree to which management was controlled by a dominant corporate interest.

name: Family group ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock owned by the single largest family group", "family ownership", "family group ownership"]
definition: The percentage of voting stock owned by the single largest family group, identified by immediate kin relationships among officers, board members, or individuals holding more than 5 percent of the company's stock.

name: Ownership pattern
authors_terms: ["patterns of ownership", "managerial firm", "agency firm", "entrepreneurial firm", "partnership firm"]
definition: The combination of CEO stock ownership with the presence or absence of a dominant outside individual, corporate or family interest, yielding the 'Managerial Firm', 'Agency Firm', 'Entrepreneurial Firm' and 'Partnership Firm' patterns of ownership.

name: Corporate contributions to charity
authors_terms: ["total tax-deductible cash contributions", "corporate contributions to charity", "corporate giving"]
definition: Tax-deductible charitable contributions given by companies to private nonprofit organizations that serve some public good; generally these have been unilateral transfer payments.

name: Enlightened self-interest rationale
authors_terms: ["rationalized contributions as enlightened self-interest", "rationalization as enlightened self-interest", "rationalizations justifying contributions as enlightened self-interest"]
definition: A rationale stating that corporations give to charity because they believe it is in the long-term interests of the business community to do so and not because it will bring direct, immediate benefits to the firm.

name: Social proximity to the philanthropic elite
authors_terms: ["CEO's social proximity to the elite", "elite-network index", "corporate-elite factor score"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's CEO and executives were in direct contact with a local philanthropic elite, indicated by the number of citations a firm received from philanthropic leaders and by the number of boards and clubs shared with those leaders.

name: Organizational isomorphism
definition: Organizations within the same population possessing similar characteristics; a high degree of variance among organizations in a particular cluster for a particular organizational attribute reflects a low level of isomorphism, and vice versa.

name: Interorganizational collective type
authors_terms: ["collective strategy typology", "interorganizational collectives", "population collectives", "collective strategy framework"]
definition: The collective strategy framework divides interorganizational field relations exhaustively into four distinct idealized types of population collectives: confederate, conjugate, agglomerative, and organic, based on the cross-classification of direct versus indirect relations and commensalistic versus symbiotic relations.

name: Goal multiplexity
authors_terms: ["goal multiplexity", "number of different identified service areas"]
definition: The number of different identified service areas pursued by the organization.

name: Internal specialization
definition: The sum of specialized functions identified in the organization.

name: Decision-making centralization
definition: The level at which decisions are made for each of a broad range of decisions occurring within the organization.

name: Formalization
definition: The degree of role specification of different policies and procedures in the organization.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership type", "type of control", "ownership structure", "owner-controlled firms", "management-controlled firms", "ownership distribution"]
definition: Firms are called owner-controlled when there is a single equity holder who controls as little as 5 percent of the voting stock; when there is no equity holder with at least 5 percent of the stock, the firm is called a management-controlled firm.

name: Monitoring and incentive alignment
authors_terms: ["monitoring", "incentive alignment", "monitoring index", "monitoring and incentive alignment", "monitoring activities"]
definition: Monitoring is defined as the direct or indirect observation of the agent's effort, or behavior, over some period of time; incentive alignment is defined as the degree to which the reward structure is designed to induce managers to make decisions that are in the best interests of stockholders.

name: CEO compensation risk
authors_terms: ["compensation risk", "pay risk", "risk in CEO pay policies", "risk-related features of the executive compensation package"]
definition: The relative risk to the CEO of the firm's compensation policies, assessed by a composite scale combining three dimensions: variability, downside risk, and long-term orientation.

name: Influence of the CEO on pay
authors_terms: ["influence exercised on CEO pay by the chief executive officer", "CEO influence"]
definition: One of the actors whose relative influence over CEO compensation is assessed; the authors argue that in management-controlled firms the CEO and other actors under his or her command are more likely to be influential than principals in setting executive compensation.

name: Influence of outside consultants on pay
definition: Outside consultants are among the parties identified as influencing CEO pay; consultants may be used to create the appearance of a rational pay-determination process and are typically hired by management.

name: Influence of major stockholders on pay
definition: Major stockholders are among the parties whose relative influence over CEO compensation is assessed; the significant equity holder who has the interest to exercise influence on CEO compensation also has the power to do so in owner-controlled firms.

name: Influence of the board of directors on pay
definition: The board of directors is one of the parties whose relative influence over CEO compensation is assessed; the board will represent the owners' interests because in owner-controlled firms owners are more influential in the selection of board members.

name: Influence of the compensation committee on pay
definition: The compensation committee is among the parties whose relative influence over CEO compensation is assessed; compensation committees will be selected by management and will represent the interests of the constituency that chose them.

name: Influence of the chief compensation officer on pay
definition: The chief compensation officer is one of the actors whose relative influence over CEO compensation is assessed; the authors argue the influence of the compensation official is likely to be lower in management-controlled firms because of the dominant role of the CEO.

name: Industry-specialized assets
authors_terms: ["specialized assets", "industry-specialized assets", "specialized supporting assets", "assets to which a new good is specialized"]
definition: Following Teece (1986), the supporting products required for successful commercialization are referred to as assets to which a new good is specialized, or simply specialized assets. Such assets are often difficult to replicate quickly, so many firms that could imitate a product cannot undertake necessary improvements or distribute and service it.

name: Potential rivalry
authors_terms: ["potential rivals", "potential rivalry", "number of firms possessing industry-specialized assets", "number of multiple-subfield incumbents"]
definition: The rivalry to secure the value of specialized assets is captured by the number of potential rivals, defined as the number of multiple-subfield incumbents during the year before a subfield emerged. Such firms were those participating in at least two subfields of the imaging industry.

name: Threat to core products
definition: An incumbent of a threatened subfield is one whose core products face partial substitution by the goods of an emerging subfield; a member-of-threatened-subfield variable was coded as 1 if the potential entrant participated in a threatened subfield and 0 otherwise.

name: Entry probability
definition: Whether a firm that manufactured imaging systems during the year before a new subfield emerged entered the new subfield at any subsequent time. If it did, the entry variable was coded as 1; otherwise it was coded as 0.

name: Entry waiting period
definition: The number of years an industry incumbent waited before entering an emerging subfield, with the count starting at 1 for a firm that entered during the first year; right-censored cases are incorporated by the event-time models.

name: Structural differentiation
authors_terms: ["structural differentiation", "differentiation of the new hierarchical overlay"]
definition: The new hierarchical overlay may be differentiated from the existing structure by establishing (a) a director of project management and (b) a department of project management. Structural differentiation is also indicated by placement of unit management under the supervision of a new administrative hierarchy rather than under the control of the existing nursing hierarchy.

name: Dual authority
definition: Matrix programs may develop dual authority relationships in which lower-level managers from the original hierarchy ("shared subordinates" or "two-boss managers") are supervised by officials from both hierarchies ("matrix bosses"). Such relationships are designed to increase the influence and power of the new hierarchy to coordinate activities across the old hierarchy.

name: Decision-making influence
definition: Managers in the new hierarchy may be responsible for administration, budgeting, and policymaking activities in addition to coordinating local-level personnel. Such influence is required to maintain the quality of local decisions.

name: Dual support systems
definition: The new hierarchy may develop its own set of administrative support systems: strategic planning, budgeting, information processing, employee appraisal, and career ladders.

name: Internal diffusion
definition: As matrix programs develop, they may encompass more of the organization's activity (e.g., a greater number of personnel, departments, product lines, or geographical areas).

name: Temporal coverage
definition: As matrix programs develop, they may also become permanent rather than temporary, cover any or all work shifts, and cover weekend as well as weekday hours.

name: Matrix complexity
authors_terms: ["matrix complexity", "program complexity", "level of matrix complexity", "scale of complexity"]
definition: Matrix programs vary in terms of the structural and administrative elements that build upon one another to form more dense grids; the degree to which the new and existing forms of departmentalization become blended and balanced is variable. The complexity score is a valid scale that measures the progression toward increasingly complex coordination.

name: Program age
definition: According to these authors, matrix programs typically evolve through a set of stages reflecting the hierarchical ordering of matrix elements; the level of matrix complexity is thus associated with program age.

name: Program survival
definition: Researchers also suggest that matrix programs that develop incrementally through these stages enjoy greater survival prospects than fully implemented matrix programs. Full-scale implementation may be too radical a change for the existing structure of social and political arrangements; the resultant conflict will lead to matrix devolution or termination.

name: Task diversity
authors_terms: ["task diversity", "diversity", "diversity among the organizational elements relevant for hospital decision making"]
definition: Task diversity, i.e., "the number of elements relevant for decision-making," increases the number of decision-making points in the organization and causes problems of coordination (e.g., number of departments and product lines).

name: Task uncertainty
definition: Task uncertainty was defined as the amount of information that must be acquired and processed during task performance and was viewed as a function of changing technologies, markets, and scientific knowledge.

name: Market demand
authors_terms: ["demand", "changes in industry sales", "changes in unit sales", "percentage changes in unit sales"]
definition: The availability of untapped demand for a product or service; the authors argue that excess demand establishes a baseline condition that will attract critical resources for organizing and should increase the likelihood of new-firm survival. It is measured as a three-year average of percentage changes in unit sales for the entire minicomputer-producer population.

name: Competitive concentration
authors_terms: ["competitive concentration", "percentage changes in concentration ratios", "four-firm unit sales concentration ratios"]
definition: Competitive concentration, calculated in terms of such factors as the percentage of sales, plant capacity, or distribution channels controlled by the largest four or eight competitors, provides a summary indicator of both the strength and intensity of competitive rivalry. Concentration, and especially changes in concentration, signals the extent to which a few firms are increasing or decreasing their control of critical resources.

name: Market breadth
definition: Firms address broad or narrow market segments depending on the range or variety of resources they try to exploit; market-specializing organizations concentrate on exploiting a relatively narrow band of available resources, while generalists address broad or multiple market segments.

name: Market aggressiveness
definition: Where market breadth refers to the range and variety of available resources that a firm seeks to control, the aggressiveness/efficiency dimension expresses the depth and rapidity of resource-acquiring activities in either broad or narrow market domains. The aggressive firm seeks to acquire and control as many resources as possible as quickly as possible, while the efficient firm seeks to protect an established position by husbanding scarce organizational resources.

name: Early survival
authors_terms: ["survival", "early survival", "likelihood of survival", "surviving their early years"]
definition: A firm was coded as surviving if it remained an independent producer of minicomputers from birth through the end of the study; all other firms were coded either as failures or acquisitions. The authors explore the likelihood of an organization's surviving its start-up years.

name: Founding environmental period
authors_terms: ["environmental period", "period of founding", "environmental period of founding", "period during which the semiconductor firm was incorporated"]
definition: The period during which the semiconductor firm was incorporated. The semiconductor industry's development was divided into four periods: the Military Market (1958-1966), the Commercial Market (1967-1973), Price Competition (1974-1979), and the Custom Market (1980-1985).

name: Founder functional background
authors_terms: ["entrepreneur background", "previous functional experience of the founder", "entrepreneur's functional background"]
definition: The primary functional experience of the entrepreneur, prior to starting the new firm, within the areas of research, design, and development; manufacturing and production; or marketing, sales, and customer service.

name: Research and development functional importance
authors_terms: ["research and development", "the research and development function", "research and development importance"]
definition: The relative importance of research and development as one of the three major line or operating functions found in most semiconductor manufacturers.

name: Manufacturing and production functional importance
authors_terms: ["manufacturing and production", "the manufacturing and production function", "manufacturing and production importance"]
definition: The relative importance of manufacturing and production as one of the three major line or operating functions found in most semiconductor manufacturers.

name: Marketing and sales functional importance
authors_terms: ["marketing and sales", "the marketing and sales function", "marketing and sales importance"]
definition: The relative importance of marketing and sales as one of the three major line or operating functions found in most semiconductor manufacturers.

name: Functional importance of a subunit
authors_terms: ["functional importance", "importance of functions", "submit importance", "relative importance of functional areas"]
definition: The relative importance or status of an organizational function within the firm, reflected in the resources devoted to it, shared perceptions of its importance, and its representation in the top-management structure.

name: Change in functional importance from founding
authors_terms: ["change in patterns of functional importance", "difference score", "change from founding functional importance"]
definition: The absolute value of the difference between each organization's measure of founding functional importance and current functional importance for each of the three functional areas and for each of the three measures.

name: Organizational performance since founding
definition: The extent to which sales growth has been poor relative to the overall industry in a given year, accumulated over the life of the organization.

name: Organizational age
definition: The number of years since the organization was incorporated.

name: Entrepreneur tenure
definition: The proportion of the firm's lifetime that the entrepreneur had worked in the firm.

name: Managerial ownership at founding
authors_terms: ["ownership", "ownership control at founding", "managerial ownership at founding"]
definition: The proportion of firm ownership initially held by members of the founding group.

name: Task uncertainty
definition: Task uncertainty was defined as the presence of task difficulty and/or variability. Tasks are difficult to the extent they are unclear, incompletely understood, give rise to problems, and necessitate time spent in problem solving; variability refers to the extent tasks are different from day to day, involve different issues each time, involve frequent exceptions, and involve different methods or steps from day to day.

name: Horizontal dependence
definition: Work-unit dependence exists when task performance is related to (and thus dependent on) actions or outcomes occurring outside the unit; it is operationalized as the extent to which resources or information from outside sources are deemed necessary inputs at the beginning, middle, or completion of a work process. Such sources may consist of other units inside or outside the organization (horizontal dependence) or higher levels within the organization (vertical dependence).

name: Conflicting contingencies
definition: Patterns of context in which the design implications of the two contingency factors conflict and hence are problematic; conflicting contingencies increase the likelihood that design will deviate from the demands of either task uncertainty, dependence, or both.

name: Overall work-unit design
authors_terms: ["overall design", "organic design", "mechanistic design", "overall pattern of design"]
definition: The gestalt or configuration of the design dimensions. A negative score on overall design indicates a design that is predominantly mechanistic; conversely, a positive score indicates a predominantly organic design.

name: Design consistency
authors_terms: ["consistently mechanistic or consistently organic designs", "internally consistent pattern of design", "inconsistent pattern of design"]
definition: The degree to which a unit's design forms an internally consistent pattern; a mixed or hybrid strategy is internally inconsistent because member behaviors are structured mechanistically to handle some activities (unit tasks) but organically to handle others (external communication).

name: Design deviation
definition: The extent to which each unit deviates from a pattern of design known to produce high performance under similar contextual conditions; the composite measure reflects deviation across all design dimensions simultaneously.

name: Unit efficiency
definition: Measures of unit efficiency consisted of the amount of output produced per full-time equivalent position, with relevant output criteria developed for each unit type.

name: Corporate donation size
authors_terms: ["size of the donation", "corporate contributions", "size of the gift", "donative transfer", "amount of corporate contributions"]
definition: The size of the donation made by corporate donor i to nonprofit donee j, measured on the nonprofit's report of the amount of corporate contributions it received from each publicly held firm.

name: Philanthropic elite regard for nonprofit
authors_terms: ["ELITE PREFS", "well regarded by the local philanthropic elite", "opinions of the philanthropic elite"]
definition: How highly the corporate philanthropic elite regarded a nonprofit; the more leaders recognized an NPO and thought it essential and outstanding, the higher its score.

name: Corporate executives' integration into elite circles
authors_terms: ["PROX TO ELITE", "corporate-elite integration", "direct contact with the local elite", "proximity of the company's executives to the elite"]
definition: How well a firm's executives were integrated into elite circles, indicated by whether philanthropic leaders personally knew an officer or board member of the firm and by the number of clubs and boards a firm's CEO shared with members of the elite.

name: Giving officer regard for nonprofit
authors_terms: ["OFFICER PREFS", "preferences of the giving officer", "recognition and regard"]
definition: Whether a firm's giving officer recognized a nonprofit, felt it provided very essential services to the community, and regarded it as having achieved extraordinary accomplishments.

name: Network giving officers' regard for nonprofit
authors_terms: ["OFFICER NETS/OFFICER PREFS", "opinions of those in the networks of donation officers"]
definition: The aggregate attitudes toward nonprofit j of donation officers linked to the donation officer of firm i.

name: Prior funding by giving-officer network peers
definition: The number of officers in other firms, known by the donation officer of firm i, whose firm gave money to nonprofit j in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift.

name: Prior funding by CEO network peers
definition: The number of CEOs who share club and board memberships with the CEO of firm i whose firm gave money to nonprofit j in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift.

name: Prior corporate funding of board-interlocked nonprofits
definition: The number of nonprofits that interlock with nonprofit j and that received a gift from corporation i in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift.

name: Prior funding by indirectly linked giving-officer peers
definition: The 1980 gifts of companies linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donor i in the officer network.

name: Prior funding by indirectly linked CEO peers
definition: The 1980 gifts of companies linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donor i in the CEO network.

name: Prior corporate funding of indirectly interlocked nonprofits
definition: The 1980 gifts received by nonprofits linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donee j in the nonprofit network.

name: Materiality of the investment tax credit
authors_terms: ["amounts of ITC", "most material", "MTLTY", "amount of ITC included in the current year's calculation of net income"]
definition: The extent to which the investment tax credit is significant relative to earnings; the amount of ITC included in the current year's calculation of net income on the financial statements stated as a percentage of total net income in the current year.

name: Income variability with negative mean
authors_terms: ["percentage change to income that is highly variable over time and on average negative", "percentage changes in the earnings per share", "ASPR"]
definition: Changes to reported income characterized by high variance and a negative mean; managers are assumed to want to avoid variation around the level of reported income considered normal for their firm.

name: Firm size
definition: The firm's total assets stated relative to the median total assets of all sample firms in the same year, so that the measure is comparable cross-sectionally and across inflationary years.

name: Managerial control
definition: Firms in which stockholders are relatively less influential, so-called managerially controlled firms, in which the separation of ownership and management leads to incentive problems.

name: Debt covenant restrictions
definition: Managerial actions are proscribed by debt convenants, which limit the amount of dividends, the amount of additional debt, and may even require costly renegotiation of debt contracts if reported income goes below a certain amount.

name: Incentive compensation plans
definition: Bonus plans based on reported net income that do not adjust computation of the bonus for accounting changes, giving managers an incentive to increase bonus income by adopting the flow-through method.

name: Institutional environment change
authors_terms: ["changes in the institutional environment", "end of the prohibition of the FTM by the APB in 1964", "generally accepted accounting principles"]
definition: Longitudinal variation in the institutional environment, specifically the key event regarding regulation of accounting for the ITC, the end of the prohibition of the FTM by the APB in 1964.

name: Interstate Commerce Commission regulation
authors_terms: ["subject to regulation by the Interstate Commerce Commission", "ICC"]
definition: Companies subject to the jurisdiction of the Interstate Commerce Commission, which regulated the rates charged in two monopolistic industries and required companies subject to its regulation to use the FTM on financial statements.

name: Federal Power Commission regulation
authors_terms: ["subject to regulation by the Federal Power Commission", "FPC"]
definition: Companies subject to the jurisdiction of the Federal Power Commission, which regulated the rates charged in two monopolistic industries and required companies subject to its regulation to use the FTM on financial statements.

name: Institutional imprinting
authors_terms: ["institutional imprinting", "imprinted in favor of the DM", "LATE"]
definition: A theory of institutional imprinting in which crucial choices must be made at important junctures of change in the institutional environment; firms that did not adopt the FTM in 1964 can be regarded as being imprinted in favor of the DM.

name: External auditor affiliation
authors_terms: ["Big Eight firms that voted for Pronouncement #2", "external auditor", "ADTR"]
definition: Whether the firm's external auditor is one of the four Big Eight accounting firms that voted for the APB pronouncement prohibiting the FTM; external auditors advise firms and lend practices legitimation and expert authorization but usually do not impose preferred practices.

name: Investment tax credit variance
authors_terms: ["high variance over time in the amount of ITC", "coefficient of variation of capital expenditures", "VCE"]
definition: High variance over time in the amount of ITC on the firm's financial statements, taken to create uncertainty, so that firms with higher variance would be more likely to conform to prevailing practice.

name: Top management team turnover
definition: The entry of new personnel to the top-management team from both inside and outside the organization, which may lead to conformity as a result of the increasing professionalization of management and exposure to a common cognitive base.

name: Flow-through method adoption
definition: Recording the full amount of the credit against income taxes payable in the income statement in the year of the investment, so that net income is increased by the full amount of the credit in that fiscal year.

name: Performance relative to analyst expectations
authors_terms: ["unexpected earnings per share", "differences between actual and expected earnings per share", "differences from expectations", "unexpected EPS"]
definition: Performance measured as the difference between actual performance and the board of directors' expectations, proxied by the mean of financial analysts' forecasts of earnings per share. A positive value denotes performance greater than analysts' predictions, a negative value represents performance less than predictions.

name: CEO turnover
definition: The incidence of turnover of chief executive officers in 1983, in which the departing (i.e., incumbent) CEO is under the age of 64, thus avoiding the potentially confounding effects of retirement.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal security returns", "abnormal stock returns", "stock price performance"]
definition: That part of the return that is unanticipated by a statistical or economic model of anticipated, normal returns; it represents the actual return minus the normal or predicted return. A positive abnormal return reflects performance that exceeds the market's expectations, and a negative abnormal return reflects performance that fails to meet expectations.

name: Return on assets
definition: One of the accounting ratios, which are measures of profitability and efficiency tracked by internal and external evaluators of the firm to assess the firm's health, used to represent selectively determined accounting-based bonus plans. For each ratio the authors evaluated the firm's performance relative to its industry counterparts.

name: Return on equity
definition: One of the accounting ratios, which are measures of profitability and efficiency tracked by internal and external evaluators of the firm to assess the firm's health, used to represent selectively determined accounting-based bonus plans. For each ratio the authors evaluated the firm's performance relative to its industry counterparts.

name: Profit margin on sales
definition: One of the accounting ratios, which are measures of profitability and efficiency tracked by internal and external evaluators of the firm to assess the firm's health, used to represent selectively determined accounting-based bonus plans. For each ratio the authors evaluated the firm's performance relative to its industry counterparts.

name: Earnings per share
definition: One of the accounting ratios used to represent selectively determined accounting-based bonus plans, obtained from IBES; the mechanical measure compares current earnings per share with the prior year's, evaluated relative to the firm's industry counterparts.

name: Organizational change
definition: The authors examined three kinds of organizational change: brand-portfolio changes and product-line changes, which are changes in diversification, and change in land ownership status.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size is measured as storage capacity expressed in thousands of gallons.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age is measured as the number of years of continuous existence.

name: Prior change experience
authors_terms: ["number of preceding changes of the same kind", "experience", "repetitive inertia"]
definition: The authors measure the organization's experience with each particular kind of organizational change through the number of preceding changes of the same kind, arguing that having undergone a change means that such change is part of the organization's repertory.

name: Time since last change
authors_terms: ["log duration since the last event of the same kind", "duration since last change"]
definition: The time elapsed, measured in years, since the last organizational change of a kind.

name: Environmental variation
definition: Three measures of environmental variation based on level of wine consumption: uncertainty of change, frequency of change, and amplitude of change.

name: Organizational disbanding
definition: Organizational disbanding is the ultimate stage of unpreparedness, the converse of survival; the event under consideration in the second set of analyses is winery disbanding.

name: Land acquisition
definition: Land acquisition indicates that a non-vineyard-owning winery has acquired land; in disbanding analyses, it is coded 0 until the first such event and 1 thereafter.

name: Leadership instability
authors_terms: ["leadership instability", "leadership stability", "systemic pattern of frequent succession"]
definition: Leadership instability in an organization can be defined in terms of the rate of succession in the CEO position over a specified time period; it emphasizes succession frequency as a systemic organizational attribute rather than serial independent events.

name: CEO power and influence over the board
authors_terms: ["CEO power and influence vis-a-vis the board", "CEO power/influence over the board", "CEO power over the board"]
definition: In not-for-profit organizations power is more appropriately manifested in the ability of the CEO to influence key decisions within the organization and by the control of the CEO over the selection of board members who are sympathetic to the CEO's strategic orientation or style of management.

name: CEO-board employment contract
authors_terms: ["formal employment contract between the board and the CEO", "written CEO-board employment contract", "CEO contract"]
definition: The board-CEO employment contract is a contractual agreement between the board of the hospital and the CEO it hires to manage the institution.

name: Board size and heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["board size and heterogeneity", "governing board size", "occupational heterogeneity of board members", "internal vs. external focus of the board"]
definition: The board size and heterogeneity factor was defined by governing board size, diffusion of board member selection responsibility, and occupational heterogeneity of board members; large, representational boards are more outwardly focused and less concerned with internal policy making and control.

name: Corporate representation on the board
authors_terms: ["board members with corporate affiliation", "corporate representatives", "number of board members whose occupation was corporate executive"]
definition: The number of board members occupationally classified as corporate executives; these individuals are more likely to be sympathetic to the strategic orientations of top management in complex organizations.

name: Medical staff representation on the board
authors_terms: ["medical staff representation on board", "members from the active medical staff", "board representatives from the hospital's medical staff"]
definition: The number of board members who are physicians with active staff privileges at the hospital; such representatives are likely to hold views in opposition to those of the management of the hospital.

name: Organizational life-cycle stage
authors_terms: ["life-cycle stage", "organizational life-cycle stage", "growth, decline, stability, and instability"]
definition: Four stages have been identified in this literature: growth, decline, stability, and instability. Growth and decline are often conceptualized as those sets of conditions in which a substantial increase or decrease in an organization's resource base occurs over a specified period of time.

name: Strategy abandonment
authors_terms: ["strategy abandonment", "abandonment of an organizational product-market strategy", "abandonment", "format change"]
definition: Abandonment is observed as the cessation of some activity or structural feature of the organization. Strategy abandonment occurs as part of a replacement decision in which one strategy is abandoned and another adopted.

name: Contagion of strategy abandonment
definition: Contagion is viewed as a form of interorganizational learning that occurs because uncertainty causes decision makers to use social comparison to evaluate the practices of their organization. A strategy is evaluated less positively the more other organizations abandon it, leading to contagion of abandonment.

name: Corporate contact
authors_terms: ["corporate contact", "corporate links", "other stations in the corporation", "corporate reference group", "corporate contacts"]
definition: In geographically distributed industries, such as radio broadcasting, one corporation can own a number of local units competing in different markets. Even if their decisions are formally independent, other units of the corporation are likely to be an important reference group because of frequent contact among decision makers, leading to contagion of strategy abandonment within the corporation.

name: Market contact
authors_terms: ["market contact", "market contacts", "organizations in the markets in which the corporation competes"]
definition: In geographically distributed industries, it is easier to observe the actions of organizations in markets in which the corporation is represented, because news of their actions is spread through intracorporate contacts. The organizations that are salient because they compete with other units of the corporation are here called market contacts.

name: Direct competitor
authors_terms: ["direct competitor", "direct competitors of the focal organization", "market contacts in the focal market"]
definition: Competitive influences are important for organizations using the same strategy in the same market, i.e., the direct competitors of the focal organization. They are coded as the market contacts in the focal market.

name: Corporate size
authors_terms: ["size of the corporation", "corporate size", "number of radio stations it owned", "size of its corporation"]
definition: Corporations differ in the number of organizational units they hold, leading to differences in the sizes of their respective reference groups. Units of large corporations have large reference groups, which subjects them to more contagious influence.

name: Market size
authors_terms: ["market size", "market rank", "large market", "size of the market"]
definition: Large markets are frequently hubs of information that receive news about changes in strategy sooner than other locations, as there is a larger number of contacts outside of the market; centrality in the information structure causes higher susceptibility to contagion.

name: Corporate contact
authors_terms: ["corporate contact", "corporate contacts", "corporate sister organizations", "common corporate ownership"]
definition: When two organizations have a common corporate ownership there is at least the possibility of high communication between them, and they may in fact be governed by one decision-making center.

name: Market contact
definition: When corporations span several markets, then a unit organization may get information about the actions of the competitors of its corporate sister organizations in other markets.

name: Direct competitor
authors_terms: ["direct competitor", "direct competitors", "competitors operating in the same market"]
definition: Direct competitors are organizations that are closely watched but are also engaged in competition with the focal organization over resources, and this interdependence is likely to enter the decision making.

name: Adoption of a new market position
authors_terms: ["adopt a new market position", "adoption of a new market position", "market position entry", "entry into that position", "adopt Soft AC"]
definition: This study examines how existing organizations in an industry come to adopt a new market position in a differentiated market. Mimetic adoption of newly innovated market positions may be the heuristic that allows managers to act in the face of uncertainty.

name: Ownership change
definition: Change in top management introduces new interpretations of the situation and allows the current position to be evaluated by managers who are less committed to it because they did not decide it. Such reevaluation of the strategy with fresh eyes is a likely consequence of ownership change.

name: Recent format change
authors_terms: ["recently changed its market position", "recent format change", "recent change"]
definition: Inertia is also temporarily weakened when the organization has just implemented a change. The effect may decay over time, so that a change event is more likely to spawn new change shortly after it occurred.

name: Transferable knowledge
authors_terms: ["knowledge that can be transferred to a new market position", "knowledge that proves to be transferable", "knowledge hurdle"]
definition: Organizations in some market positions may possess knowledge that proves to be transferable to a certain new position, while other market positions leave the organization less fit to change to this position.

name: Board control over management
authors_terms: ["board control over management", "board control", "board independence", "board passivity", "low control", "high control"]
definition: The paper's overall concept capturing the extent to which a firm's board displays a relatively enduring orientation toward board control (high control) or board passivity (low control). It is an aggregate of five visible indicators of board structure, strategy and policy: the ratio of outside to inside directors, board leadership structure, diversification, total compensation, and compensation contingency.

name: Participation in increased outsider ratio
authors_terms: ["participation in increased outsider ratio", "participation in increasing the outsider ratio", "increases in the ratio of outside to inside directors"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently raised the ratio of outside to inside directors, which the authors treat as indicative of increased board control over management.

name: Participation in decreased outsider ratio
authors_terms: ["participation in decreased outsider ratio", "experience with decreasing the outsider ratio", "decreases in this measure"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently lowered the ratio of outside to inside directors, which the authors treat as indicating greater board passivity in monitoring management.

name: Participation in CEO-board chair separation
authors_terms: ["participation in CEO/board chair separation", "separating the CEO and board chair positions"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently separated the CEO and board chair positions, which the authors treat as greatly increasing the board's capacity to control management decision making.

name: Participation in CEO-board chair combination
authors_terms: ["participation in CEO/board chair combination", "combining the CEO and board chair positions"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently allocated the CEO and board chair positions to the same individual, a structure the authors associate with greater CEO control over the board.

name: Participation in decreased corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["participation in reduced diversification", "reduced corporate diversification", "decreased corporate diversification"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently overseen reduced corporate diversification, which the authors treat as an indication of greater shareholder representation and lower managerial control over board monitoring activity.

name: Participation in increased corporate diversification
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently overseen increased corporate diversification, which the authors treat as reflecting managerial interests and board passivity.

name: Participation in decreased total CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["participation in reduced total CEO compensation", "decreased total compensation", "decreasing total CEO compensation"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently reduced the level of CEO total compensation, which the authors treat as a visible indicator of greater board independence from management.

name: Participation in increased total CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["participation in increased total compensation", "increasing total CEO compensation"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently increased the level of CEO total compensation, which the authors treat as reflecting board passivity and CEO entrenchment.

name: Participation in increased CEO compensation contingency
authors_terms: ["participation in increased compensation contingency", "increased CEO compensation contingency"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently made CEO compensation more contingent on firm performance through long-term incentive grants, which the authors treat as a primary mechanism by which boards protect shareholder interests.

name: Participation in decreased CEO compensation contingency
authors_terms: ["participation in reduced compensation contingency", "decreased compensation contingency"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently reduced the contingency of CEO compensation on firm performance, which the authors treat as reflecting limited board monitoring of management.

name: Subsequent appointments to low-control boards
authors_terms: ["appointments to boards with low control over management", "change in appointments to low-control boards", "additions/subtractions in appointments to boards with low control over management"]
definition: The net change in the number of board appointments held by a director at firms whose boards display a relatively enduring orientation toward board passivity (low control over management). The authors examine it separately for additions and subtractions to assess director selection and retention.

name: Subsequent appointments to high-control boards
authors_terms: ["appointments to boards with high control over management", "change in appointments to high-control boards", "additions/subtractions in appointments to boards with high control over management"]
definition: The net change in the number of board appointments held by a director at firms whose boards display a relatively enduring orientation toward board control over management (high control). The authors examine it separately for additions and subtractions to assess director selection and retention.

name: Participation in increased board control over management
authors_terms: ["participation in increased board control", "moved to increase board control over management", "increased board control over management"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently moved to increase board control over management, as indicated by changes in board structure, strategy or policy. The authors argue that powerful boards can perpetuate or increase their control over management by appointing individuals with prior experience in asserting board control.

name: Participation in decreased board control over management
authors_terms: ["participation in decreased board control", "moved to decrease board control over management", "decreased board control over management"]
definition: A director's prior experience on boards that have recently moved to decrease board control over management, as indicated by changes in board structure, strategy or policy. The authors argue that powerful CEOs may sustain CEO control by selecting directors whose experience on other boards reflects board passivity toward management.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
definition: The variation in team members' characteristics; we rely on demographic conceptions of the group, according to which the executives' functional backgrounds, educational experiences, and firm tenures serve as proxies for their perspectives, beliefs systems, and networks and affiliations.

name: Action propensity
definition: The firm's relative tendency to undertake competitive actions.

name: Strategic significance of actions
definition: The firm's relative use of strategic rather than tactical initiatives; strategic moves involve large outlays, long time-horizons, great departures from the status quo, and are difficult to reverse.

name: Noteworthiness of actions
definition: The amount of attention a move receives from industry observers and analysts.

name: Scope of actions
definition: The extent of the firm's operations that are affected by the moves.

name: Action execution speed
definition: How quickly the firm implements its actions.

name: Response propensity
definition: The firm's relative tendency to respond to competitors' actions.

name: Noteworthiness of responses
definition: The amount of industry attention accorded a response.

name: Scope of responses
definition: The extent of the firm's operations that are affected by its response.

name: Response generation speed
definition: The time taken to formulate and announce a response to a competitor's action.

name: Response execution speed
definition: The amount of time taken to implement an announced response.

name: Performance improvement
authors_terms: ["overall performance improvements", "performance improvement", "growth in market share", "growth in profits"]
definition: The firm's improvement in performance, measured as changes in market share and in profits.

name: CEO-director presence
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors", "proportion of the board composed of CEO-directors", "outside directors currently also serving as chief executive at another Fortune or Forbes 500 company"]
definition: Outside directors who are themselves CEOs of other large corporations, who may play a pivotal role in determining whether a board has a passive or an active orientation. The authors measure their presence as the number of outside directors currently also serving as chief executive at another Fortune or Forbes 500 company divided by the total number of outsiders on the board.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "increased board activism and control over top management", "board control", "internal corporate control"]
definition: The degree to which boards act independently of top management's preferences, as opposed to serving as rubber stamps or tools of management. While it is difficult to observe and measure directly, a number of structural variables have been used to assess differences in levels of board independence across organizations, and the authors also examine changes in diversification and compensation contingency that are thought to reflect greater board independence.

name: Home-company board independence experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced an increase in board independence at their home companies", "CEO-directors' experience with increased board independence at their home companies"]
definition: The extent to which the CEO-directors sitting on a board have themselves experienced an increase in board independence at the companies they run as CEOs. The authors measure it with separate variables for each dimension of change: separation of the CEO and board chair positions, increases in the ratio of outside to inside directors, increases in demographic distance from the board, reductions in unrelated diversification, and increases in compensation contingency.

name: CEO and board chair separation
authors_terms: ["separation of the CEO and board chair positions", "separation", "CEO duality"]
definition: Allocation of the CEO and board chair positions to separate individuals rather than uniting both roles in one person; separation is argued to enhance the board's independent monitoring capacity, whereas CEOs holding both positions possess greater formal authority and heightened informal power over board members.

name: Board outsider ratio
authors_terms: ["ratio of outside to inside directors", "increased outsider ratio"]
definition: The ratio of outside to inside directors on the board; increases in the ratio are viewed as reflecting increased board independence from management because outsiders are better positioned to evaluate managerial performance impartially.

name: CEO-board demographic distance
authors_terms: ["demographic distance between the CEO and the board", "CEO-board similarity", "increased dissimilarity"]
definition: Demographic dissimilarity between board members and top managers, which should minimize bias and enhance independence and objectivity in decision control activities; the authors measure it as CEO-board similarity across functional background, education and age.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: The extent to which the firm operates in largely unrelated businesses; top managers have personal incentives to diversify beyond the level at which shareholder wealth is maximized, to enhance their personal power, compensation and status while stabilizing income streams and minimizing employment risk, so shareholders and boards favoring shareholder interests should favor lower levels.

name: Compensation contingency
definition: The extent to which CEO compensation is contingent on future firm performance, through long-term incentives such as stock options, performance shares or restricted stock, thereby aligning the interests of CEOs with the preferences of shareholders.

name: CEO-director separation experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced a separation of the CEO and board chair positions at their home companies"]
definition: CEO-directors on a board who have experienced a separation of the CEO and board chair positions at their home companies, whether by losing both positions, only the CEO position, or only the board chair position.

name: CEO-director outsider-ratio experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced increases in the ratio of outside to inside directors at their home companies"]
definition: CEO-directors on a board who have experienced increases in the ratio of outside to inside directors at their home companies.

name: CEO-director demographic-distance experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced an increase in demographic distance from the board at their home companies"]
definition: CEO-directors on a board who have experienced an increase in demographic distance from the board at their home companies.

name: CEO-director diversification-reduction experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced a reduction in unrelated diversification at their home companies"]
definition: CEO-directors on a board who have experienced a reduction in unrelated diversification at their home companies, thus sacrificing their personal preferences for risk reduction, power and status.

name: CEO-director compensation-contingency experience
authors_terms: ["CEO-directors who have experienced an increase in compensation contingency at their home companies"]
definition: CEO-directors on a board who have been subjected to greater compensation contingency at their home companies.

name: Long-term incentive plan adoption
authors_terms: ["LTIP adoption", "long-term incentive plan (LTIP) adoption", "symbolic LTIP adoption", "substantive LTIP adoption"]
definition: We defined LTIP adoption as the addition of a new performance plan that aimed at providing multiyear performance incentives, such as performance shares or performance units, to a CEO's compensation contract. A substantive LTIP adoption is one in which firms adopted and also announced grants under the plan, and a symbolic LTIP adoption is one in which firms adopted an LTIP in a particular year but did not announce grants of any of the incentive vehicles included under the plan.

name: Agency explanation
definition: This example illustrates what Zajac and Westphal (1995: 288) called the 'agency explanation,' which they suggested is the most frequently used explanation for LTIPs adopted in the 1980s. The agency logic emphasizes explicitly how LTIPs promote shareholder interests by tying CEO compensation more closely to shareholder wealth.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction", "excess stock returns", "mean cumulative excess returns"]
definition: We followed standard event study methodology in measuring stock market reactions to LTIP adoption with excess stock returns, or the cumulative difference between a firm's observed return and its expected return during a specified period surrounding adoption.

name: CEO and board chair separation
authors_terms: ["CEO/board chair separation", "separation of the CEO and board chair positions", "CEO/board-chair separation"]
definition: Institutional investors and advocates of board reform have pressured firms to separate the CEO and board chair positions as a means of improving board monitoring and control of management decisions. Given that the board chair is nominally responsible for monitoring and evaluating CEO decision making, uniting both roles in one person represents a formalized conflict of interest.

name: Outside director ratio
authors_terms: ["ratio of outside to inside directors", "outsider ratio", "increased outsider ratio"]
definition: With respect to outside directors, stockholder groups such as the California Public Employee Retirement System (CALPERS) and other large pension funds have consistently advocated increases in the ratio of outsiders to insiders as a source of increased board control over top management.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional ownership", "ownership by institutional investors", "equity held by pension funds, banks and trust companies"]
definition: Institutional investors represent an important subgroup of owners who typically hold significantly larger equity stakes in corporations than do individual shareholders. One important implication of holding such large equity stakes is that for dissatisfied institutional investors, the option of 'exit' (i.e., selling the stock) is somewhat more difficult and costly, hence leading to the greater exercise of 'voice' (Hirschman, 1970; Jensen, 1989; Kim and Ocasio, 1995).

name: Structural board independence
authors_terms: ["structural board independence", "change in structural board independence", "structural board independence from management"]
definition: Structural board independence is defined by those aspects of formal position and informal social structure that can potentially reduce the extent to which directors are socially or professionally beholden to the CEO. This definition incorporates both formal and informal sources of structure in CEO-board relationships, while excluding other possible sources of power such as ownership and tenure that do not clearly indicate both structure and independence.

name: Ingratiation
definition: Ingratiation encompasses a set of influence tactics that serve to 'increase one's attractiveness in the eyes of [another] person'. Jones (1964) and Jones and Wortman (1973) identified four different kinds of ingratiation behaviors: opinion conformity, other-enhancing communications, or flattery, self-enhancing communications, and favor doing.

name: Persuasion
definition: Persuasion involves the application of reason or logic to 'convince a target that the agent's request or proposal is feasible and consistent with shared objectives'. Yukl and Tracey's definition referred to the use of 'logical arguments and factual evidence' to exercise influence, and Kipnis and Schmidt referred to the use of 'reason and logic to gain compliance'.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: According to several theoretical perspectives, including managerialist and agency theory, top managers have personal incentives to pursue corporate diversification beyond the level at which shareholder wealth is maximized. Given that a major objective of unrelated diversification is to stabilize corporate earnings, diversification reduces these career risks while also stabilizing the CEO's personal income.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "total CEO compensation", "level of CEO compensation"]
definition: The CEO's total compensation includes base salary, short-term bonus awards, and the total value of long-term incentives granted in a given year. Both economic and behavioral perspectives on corporate governance suggest that CEOs' and shareholders' preferences diverge on the level and form of CEO compensation.

name: Compensation contingency
definition: Compensation contingency was calculated as the total value of long-term incentive grants divided by total compensation. Long-term incentives such as stock options or performance shares represent a primary mechanism by which corporate boards effect incentive alignment, and by making pay contingent on future firm performance they add uncertainty to a CEO's compensation.

name: International expansion
authors_terms: ["international expansion", "establishment by a supplier of its first plant in a foreign location", "foreign direct investment", "supplier entry"]
definition: The establishment by a supplier of its first plant in a foreign location, a form of expansion commonly referred to as foreign direct investment.

name: Cumulative entry by current buyers
authors_terms: ["number of current buyers entered", "number of transplanted current buyers", "entry by current buyers"]
definition: The number of a supplier's current domestic buyers that have entered the foreign market as of a given year, where a current buyer is one for which the supplier manufactured at least one component for direct sale in Japan.

name: Cumulative entry by potential buyers
authors_terms: ["number of potential buyers entered", "entry by potential buyers", "transplanted potential domestic buyers"]
definition: The number of a supplier's potential domestic buyers, that is, firms in the home-country industry to which the supplier does not sell goods, that have entered the foreign market as of a given year.

name: Cumulative entry by competitors
authors_terms: ["number of competitors entered", "prior competing entrants", "entry by competing suppliers"]
definition: The number of a focal supplier's domestic competitors that have already entered the foreign market, where two suppliers are competitors if the lists of components they manufacture contain at least one component in common.

name: Cumulative entry by non-competing suppliers
authors_terms: ["number of non-competing suppliers entered", "non-competing domestic suppliers that have entered the foreign market"]
definition: The number of non-competing domestic suppliers that have entered the foreign market, where two suppliers are non-competing if there is no overlap between the lines of components they manufacture.

name: Time since first current buyer entry
authors_terms: ["time since at least one current buyer entered"]
definition: The number of years elapsed since the earliest entrant among a supplier's current buyers established its first plant in the United States or Canada.

name: Time since first potential buyer entry
authors_terms: ["time since at least one potential buyer entered"]
definition: The number of years since the first potential buyer of a supplier expanded into the foreign market.

name: Time since first competitor entry
authors_terms: ["time since at least one competitor entered"]
definition: The number of years since the first competing supplier of a focal supplier expanded into the foreign market.

name: Time since first non-competing supplier entry
authors_terms: ["time since at least one non-competing supplier entered"]
definition: The number of years since the first non-competing supplier of a focal supplier expanded into the foreign market.

name: Technological crowding
definition: Organizations occupy crowded technological positions when many other firms concentrate in their areas of technological specialty and so are undifferentiated from them. Technological crowding is therefore much like an organization-specific measure of competitor density: it reflects the degree to which the technological focus of a firm is shared by many other organizations.

name: Technological prestige
definition: Firms accrue technological prestige by developing path-breaking technological advances, defined as such because they become the foundation for imitation and elaboration by other firms. In the patent network, a prestigious innovator is a firm with a patent portfolio that is highly cited by other innovators.

name: Technological overlap
definition: Two organizations occupy overlapping technological positions when their patent portfolios cited the same antecedent patents, i.e., when the two firms were structurally equivalent in the citation network. Two patents are structurally equivalent when they cite the same antecedent inventions.

name: Technology alliance formation
authors_terms: ["strategic technology alliances", "technology development and/or exchange alliances", "alliance formation rate"]
definition: Strategic alliances are contractual asset pooling or resource exchange agreements between firms. In this study an alliance had to satisfy two criteria: both of the firms in the agreement must have been semiconductor producers, and the deal must have been to exchange or develop technology.

name: Interlock partner acquisitions
authors_terms: ["acquisitions by interlock partners", "number of prior acquisitions completed by its interlock partners", "acquisitions completed by the focal firms' interlock partners"]
definition: Acquisitions completed by the firms tied to the focal firm through its directors. The authors collected data on acquisitions by inside directors' sent ties, outside directors' received ties and neutral ties, and combined the influential sent and received tie acquisitions into a single variable.

name: Focal firm acquisitions
authors_terms: ["number of acquisitions completed by the focal firm", "number of current acquisitions completed by focal firms"]
definition: The number of acquisitions completed by the focal firm during the sampled year. The authors restricted the sample to 'traditional' acquisitions, in which one existing firm buys a controlling interest in another existing firm.

name: Firm size
definition: Size was measured by the sales of the focal firm at the end of the year prior to the sampled year, log-transformed to correct for skew.

name: Network centrality
definition: The authors chose simple degree centrality, the number of interlock ties to other firms, because it best captures the number of information sources available to a firm. It was calculated as the number of sent ties, minus any duplicated ties.

name: CEO membership in business associations
authors_terms: ["CEO membership in Business Council or Business Roundtable", "association membership", "council or roundtable membership"]
definition: Whether the CEO of the focal firm was a member of the Business Council and/or the Business Roundtable, which the authors treat as an alternate source of information about acquisitions.

name: Business press coverage
authors_terms: ["business press articles", "recent business press coverage of mergers and acquisitions", "business press"]
definition: The number of articles dealing with mergers and acquisitions in Business Week, Fortune, and Forbes, which the authors expect to represent the amount of relevant business press information about acquisitions available to directors.

name: Interlock partner industry similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity", "industry similarity", "degree of similarity between the focal firm and its interlock partners"]
definition: The degree of similarity between the focal firm and its interlock partners, based on the primary industry in which the firm does business, with both focal firms and interlock partners classified according to 2-digit SIC codes.

name: Rule density
definition: Rule density, as in models of organizational populations, can be defined as the number of rules in a given organizational rule population at a given time.

name: Rule birth rate
authors_terms: ["rate of rule birth", "rule production", "birth rate", "rate of rule production"]
definition: A rule is born when a new rule document is put in force in an organization. The birth rate is the number of new rules born per year.

name: Rule suspensions
definition: A rule suspension (rule death) occurs when the rule is removed and no successor version of the rule is put in place.

name: Problem supply
authors_terms: ["supply of problems", "problem supply", "differential supply of problems", "stock of problems"]
definition: Organizational rule production is driven by experiences with organizational problems. Organizations create new rules when they encounter problems that are not yet covered by existing rules and when these problems are fairly recurrent, consequential, or salient; the supply of problems sets limits on organizational rule production.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: The absorption and sorting mechanisms are likely to be weakened when many new problem sources emerge in a problem area, a situation termed turbulence.

name: Adjacent state prohibitions
authors_terms: ["number of state-level prohibitions in adjacent states", "number of local prohibitions", "adjacent state prohibitions", "number of adjacent states with prohibition"]
definition: For each state, the number of state-level prohibitions in force in adjacent states, which the authors call the number of local prohibitions.

name: Nonlocal state prohibitions
authors_terms: ["nonlocal prohibitions", "number of nonlocal state prohibitions in force", "nonlocal prohibition variable"]
definition: The total number of state-level prohibitions in force each year minus the number of local prohibitions for the focal state, created to avoid confounding nonlocal with local effects.

name: Founding rate
definition: The dependent variable is the number of brewery foundings in each state in each year, modeled at the level of the brewing industry in a state.

name: Mortality rate
definition: A firm-specific instantaneous mortality rate is estimated assuming that the mortality rate of an organization declines with the natural logarithm of age.

name: Urban location
authors_terms: ["breweries located in large urban centers", "large cities", "very large cities", "rural areas"]
definition: The location of a brewery or founding in a large city (250,000 to 500,000 people), a very large city (greater than 500,000 people), or a rural area (cities of less than 250,000).

name: Change in prohibition status of adjacent state
authors_terms: ["any change in the prohibition status of an adjacent state", "environmental reversal", "changes in the prohibition status of adjacent states"]
definition: Changes in the prohibition status of adjacent states can be viewed as reversals in environmental conditions for breweries operating in a focal prohibition-free state.

name: Time since environmental change
authors_terms: ["time elapsed since a change in the prohibition status of an adjacent state", "clock denoting the elapsed time"]
definition: The greater the time elapsed since a change in the prohibition status of an adjacent state, the lower the mortality rate of breweries.

name: Organizational age
authors_terms: ["organizational age", "age of the firm", "age of the brewery", "older breweries"]
definition: Organizational age may mediate the impact of the enactment of prohibition in adjacent states; the older the organization, the more inertial its routines and structures.

name: Heterogeneity of causes of prior errors
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of prior causes", "prior accident heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of causes", "homogeneity of prior causes", "heterogeneous accident causes"]
definition: Some firms have heterogeneous experience in that their accidents and incidents ("errors") are caused by a large number of different factors, which are likely to interact in complex ways. Some firms have more homogeneous experience, with errors caused by a small number of similar factors.

name: Accident and incident rate
authors_terms: ["accident and incident (event) rate", "subsequent error rate", "accident rate", "error rate"]
definition: An accident is an occurrence in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or in which the aircraft received substantial damage; an incident is an occurrence other than an accident which affects or could affect the safety of operations. The rate is calculated as the number of accidents plus incidents per 100,000 departures.

name: Operator errors
definition: Errors attributed to the operator, i.e. the pilot, rather than to other causes; the authors argue that heterogeneity reduces the tendency to blame the operator (the pilot) and measure the number of pilot errors reported for each airline for each year.

name: Repetition of error causes
authors_terms: ["the number of prior causes of a given type", "repetition of the same accident causes", "number of prior causes of each type"]
definition: Repetition of the same accident causes found with homogeneous error experience, which is likely to make those causes salient and thus aid in learning and reduce subsequent error rates of that same type.

name: Same-type error rate
authors_terms: ["subsequent rate of errors of that same type", "subsequent causes of that same type"]
definition: The rate of subsequent errors that share the same cause type as an organization's prior errors; the authors model the number of each of the 23 causes each airline experienced in a given year as a function of the number of prior causes of each type experienced by that airline.

name: Organizational form
definition: Specialist organizational forms depend on a narrow range of environmental resources for survival.
