Their formal structure, patterns of activity, and normative order are different from generalist organizations, which depend on a wide range of environmental resources; generalists are more complex forms because their larger resource space and broader range of products mean they have to deal with a wider range of issues.

name: Driver governance misalignment
authors_terms: ["Driver Misalign", "driver misalignment", "degree to which carrier i's governance of its driver force deviates from the prescriptions of transaction cost economics"]
definition: The degree to which a carrier's governance of its driver force (its reliance on company drivers versus owner-operators) deviates from the level prescribed by transaction cost economics. It is operationalized as the absolute value of the residual from a model predicting reliance on company drivers.

name: Profitability
definition: An accounting measure that represents annual return on assets for each carrier i in year t. It is calculated by dividing annual earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation expense by total assets.

name: Adaptation in driver governance
authors_terms: ["adaptation", "rate and amount of organizational change", "organizational change", "adjustment"]
definition: The rate and amount of organizational change in the governance of a particular transaction, i.e., movement toward the level of driver integration prescribed by transaction cost economics. Firms with small adjustment costs adapt quickly and completely, whereas firms with large adjustment costs delay adaptation.

name: Asset specificity
definition: The degree of specific investment associated with a transaction; an asset is specific to a particular transaction if its value in its next-best use and user is less than its use in this transaction. Investments in durable, idiosyncratic assets raise the cost of altering or abandoning the activities in which these assets are used.

name: Contractual commitments
authors_terms: ["deep contractual commitments", "formal contractual commitments", "informal commitments", "contractual commitment"]
definition: Long-term contractual commitments that constrain an organization from switching to an alternative trading partner or organizational form until the contract expires, unless it pays appropriate compensation to break it. Informal commitments, such as normative standards and political coalitions, also constrain organizations and raise adjustment costs.

name: Kibbutz founding rate
authors_terms: ["kibbutz founding rate", "founding rate", "number of kibbutzim founded in a region in a year"]
definition: The dependent variable is the number of kibbutzim founded in a region in a year. Regions are ten-by-ten kilometer map-grid squares, and regions are included in years in which they were part of Palestine, Israel, or occupied by Israel.

name: Capitalist organization density
definition: Capitalist organizations in the economy, measured as the number of corporations; the authors argue for a society-wide competition between kibbutzim and corporations, so corporation density is available only in aggregate.

name: Alternative settlement forms
authors_terms: ["settlement types that represent alternatives to its organizational control over community relations", "moshavim", "development towns"]
definition: Settlement forms that represent alternatives to the kibbutz's organizational control over community relations. The moshav employs traditional forms of consumption with nuclear families in their own homes, and development towns are government-planned communities whose social life was defined mainly by family, community, and religious values.

name: Sephardic immigration
authors_terms: ["proportion of Sephardic immigrants", "percentage of immigrants from Africa and Asia", "flow of Jewish immigrants who favor traditional forms of community governance"]
definition: Sephardic immigrants from Asia and Africa were culturally less partial to the kibbutz than Ashkenazi immigrants from Europe, and were prominently represented in alternative settlement types; kibbutz founding is expected to decrease as the proportion of such immigrants increases.

name: Opportunities to provide order
authors_terms: ["opportunities to provide defense, settlement, and absorption", "opportunities to provide order"]
definition: The social needs that the kibbutzim took on themselves - absorption of immigrants, settlement, and defense - and which constituted opportunities for order provision: a rapidly growing Jewish population, the threat of political violence, and the desire to win territory contested by Jews and Arabs.

name: State institutional capacity
definition: Operationalized as the size of the state bureaucracy; relying on the size of the bureaucracy as the indication of state institutional capacity reflects Weber's argument that bureaucracy is the foundation of authority for the modern state.

name: Establishment of the State of Israel
authors_terms: ["Israeli state", "establishment of the State of Israel", "campaign to delegitimize the kibbutz"]
definition: The formation of the Israeli state and the onset of its campaign to delegitimize the kibbutz, which stripped kibbutz members of honorific labels such as pioneer and volunteer and attacked the legitimacy of the organizational form.

name: Early community establishment
authors_terms: ["early establishment", "early-established communities", "communities established before the era of auto and air travel", "degree of early business establishment"]
definition: The degree to which a community's corporate establishment dates from the early part of the twentieth century, before the era of auto and air travel that began after 1920. Communities established when intercity travel was difficult are expected to have imprinted locally focused networks.

name: Local intercorporate network connections
authors_terms: ["local network connections", "local connections", "locally focused networks", "percentage of local connections", "local received ties"]
definition: At the community level, the number of direct connections between local companies compared with the total number of direct network connections; at the organizational level, the count of local received ties, i.e., officers of other corporations sitting on the focal firm's board.

name: Exclusive upper-class club presence
definition: The existence in a community of the most exclusive upper-class social clubs, which are the most exclusive meeting grounds of the elite and a primary socialization institution for the upper class.

name: Commercial bank presence in a community
authors_terms: ["presence of commercial banks", "number of banks headquartered"]
definition: The number of commercial banks headquartered in a community, which act as local connecting institutions because banks are central nodes of local intercorporate networks and their boards are locally oriented.

name: Arts and culture organization presence
authors_terms: ["arts and culture organizations", "arts and cultural organizations", "nonprofits"]
definition: The number of arts and culture nonprofit organizations in a community, which are the type of nonprofit organization most associated with the cohesiveness of local elite networks.

name: Prominent firms' local network orientation
authors_terms: ["prominent firm percent local connections", "degree of local connections made by prominent firms", "prominent firms' percent local connections"]
definition: A community-level profile of the propensity of prominent firms (the largest 25 percent of firms in each community by sales) to create local received connections, expressed as the percentage of local received connections held by this group.

name: Network connectivity
authors_terms: ["connectivity", "network connectivity", "degree of connectivity of the network between audience members and candidate organizations", "reachability"]
definition: Connectivity defines the threshold of candidates' acceptance by signaling their inclusion as members, and reflects the existence of a relational pathway connecting as many members of the community as possible. Higher connectivity of the system should reduce ambiguity about organizational action and foster consensus on the rules that specify what types of agents are allowed to exist.

name: Repeated ties
definition: Repeated ties occur when a producer organization repeats its exchange of a film with a distributor organization. Repeated interactions highlight candidates' exemplariness by signaling preferred audiences' interactions among accepted candidates.

name: Audience turnover
authors_terms: ["audience turnover", "turnover of audience members", "heterogeneity of audience members"]
definition: Audience turnover is a structural feature of audiences that affects the stability of consensus or the lack thereof; as members leave and are replaced, new members have more difficulty learning established norms and are more likely to change them.

name: Exit rate
authors_terms: ["exit rates", "failure", "exit of producer organizations", "hazard of exit"]
definition: Analyzing failure, or exit rates, is a typical strategy to test ecological theories; the dependent variable is exit rates of feature film producer organizations from the market. Organizations can exit in many different ways, including disbanding, bankruptcy, merger, or acquisition.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["level of institutional ownership", "ownership by pressure-resistant institutional investors", "ownership power of institutional investors"]
definition: The level of ownership by pressure-resistant institutional investors, which include public pension funds, mutual funds, endowments, and foundations. The authors argue that these investors are likely to have sufficient power to change corporate governance practices.

name: CEO ingratiation
definition: Ingratiation comprises specific social influence tactics that serve to enhance one's interpersonal attractiveness and gain favor with another person, including other-enhancement or flattery, opinion conformity, and favor rendering.

name: CEO persuasion
definition: Persuasion involves the use of reason or logic to convince others that certain actions, positions, or policies are in their own best interests.

name: Outside director ratio
authors_terms: ["outsider ratio", "ratio of outside to inside directors", "increases in the portion of the board composed of outside directors"]
definition: The ratio of outside directors to inside directors on the board, reflecting a board structure reform that increases the board's independence from management.

name: CEO/board chair separation
authors_terms: ["separation of the CEO and board chair positions", "CEO/board chair separation"]
definition: Separation of the CEO and board chair positions, such that the CEO does not occupy both roles, a governance reform thought to increase the board's willingness and ability to challenge the CEO.

name: Independent board nominating committee
authors_terms: ["creation of an independent board nominating committee", "independent board nominating committees"]
definition: Creation of a board nominating committee made formally independent of management, either by creating a new nominating committee composed entirely of outside directors or by removing the CEO and other inside directors from the existing committee.

name: CEO compensation level
authors_terms: ["level of CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "annual total direct compensation"]
definition: The size of the CEO's pay package, which CEOs seek to maximize and which shareholders are presumed to benefit from containing.

name: CEO compensation risk
authors_terms: ["compensation risk", "CEO compensation risk", "proportion of total direct compensation consisting of long-term incentive pay"]
definition: The extent to which CEO pay is made contingent on firm performance through the use of long-term incentives such as stock options or restricted stock.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["corporate diversification", "level of corporate diversification", "product market diversification"]
definition: Product market diversification beyond the level at which shareholder wealth is maximized; executives tend to prefer higher levels of diversification than shareholders.

name: Structural holes
definition: The more network partners, otherwise not connected to one another, that are linked to the focal firm through bridging ties, the more structural holes the focal firm spans. An open network, which is rich in structural holes, enables firms to receive information about business opportunities available in different parts of the network.

name: Status accumulation
definition: Status accumulation refers to a firm's ability to augment its social standing by forming cooperative relationships with prominent network partners. The higher the position of an organization in a social system, as a function of its privileged affiliations, the higher is its status.

name: Market performance
definition: Market performance pertains to a firm's ability to generate financial resources, such as revenues, as a result of collaborative activities with its partners. Market performance refers to the firm's ability to earn revenues and hence enhance its financial position.

name: Financial resource need
authors_terms: ["financial resource needs", "financial resources", "need for financial resources"]
definition: When the costs of technology development or sales are high, the financial resource needs of new firms may outstrip the funding capabilities of many types of investors. Forming investment relationships with established firms can be attractive because these firms are especially rich sources of capital.

name: Complementary resource need
definition: New firms rarely own all of the resources necessary for the development and commercialization of their products, so new firms that need complementary resources (e.g., manufacturing, a sales force, and branding) can potentially use funding relationships to harness such resources from investing corporations.

name: Manufacturing resource need
definition: New firms in highly capital-intensive industries are likely to require greater manufacturing assets to commercialize their products. Manufacturing resources are often expensive and slow to create, important to operational success, and uniquely available from corporations.

name: Marketing resource need
definition: If the advertising intensity in the industry is high, product commercialization is likely to be marketing-intensive and require the joint exploitation of marketing resources and new technology.

name: Patent defense
definition: A patent gives the holder the right to exclude others from the use of the invention covered by the patent and allows the holder to prosecute others who infringe, and so is an effective means of protecting some parts of the venture's product invention.

name: Secrecy defense
definition: Trade secrets offer an exclusive source of protection to a diverse range of intellectual property, from know-how to recipes to customer lists, as long as the firm keeps them secret; both the use of improper means to discover trade secrets and the use of improperly discovered trade secrets are illegal.

name: Timing defense
definition: New firms may protect their technology resources and themselves more broadly by timing their corporate relationships to coincide with later funding rounds, when the firm's technologies, products, and strategic agendas are more mature and so more defensible.

name: Corporate investment relationship
definition: The entrepreneur's decision to enter a corporate investment relationship is an equity relationship in which the agreement includes an equity purchase of a portion of a private, new entrepreneurial firm by another company that is typically larger, older, more established, and publicly traded.

name: Knowledge-base decomposability
authors_terms: ["level of decomposability", "near-decomposability", "decomposability of a knowledge base", "knowledge-base structure"]
definition: The structure of a firm's knowledge base is the set of couplings between its elements of technical knowledge, and it varies along a continuum from fully decomposable, through nearly decomposable, to non-decomposable. In a nearly decomposable knowledge base some elements are more densely connected with each other than with other elements, allowing clusters to be distinguished, but at the same time there are some couplings that connect clusters to one another.

name: Usefulness of inventions
definition: Useful inventions are conceived fairly broadly, as those that directly solve important techno-economic problems and thus create economic value directly or serve as the basis for further solutions of techno-economic problems. The frequency with which a patent is cited is taken as a crude proxy of its usefulness in driving technical change.

name: Knowledge-base malleability
authors_terms: ["malleability", "capacity for change", "extent of change in structure"]
definition: A knowledge base's capacity for change is its malleability, which the authors argue should be determined by its decomposability. Knowledge bases that are conducive to exploring, evolving, and absorbing new knowledge should demonstrate changes in their patterns of coupling over time.

name: Non-local pre-founding experience
authors_terms: ["non-local wine industry pre-founding experience", "non-local pre-founding experience", "non-local wine industry experience"]
definition: Non-local pre-founding experience is formal wine industry education and employment in other wine-producing countries (e.g., France, Italy, the U.S., or Australia).

name: Local pre-founding experience
authors_terms: ["local wine industry pre-founding experience", "local pre-founding experience"]
definition: Local wine industry experience accrues in the focal organizational population: in the current context, the Israeli wine industry.

name: Organizational form at founding
definition: Kosher and non-kosher wine production represent two distinct organizational forms, separated by a semistrict form boundary and held in place by founding ideology or organizational inertia, so that a winery's organizational form results from decisions taken at founding.

name: Organizational size
definition: The number of bottles a producer turns out in a vintage; larger size improves survival chances because size is advantageous in scale-driven investments in production and distribution.

name: Product quality
definition: A producer-level assessment of the quality of a winery's wines; favorable quality ratings are valuable in their own right and allow producers to be taken seriously by quality-oriented consumers.

name: Socio-demographic distance between venture capital firms
authors_terms: ["socio-demographic distance", "distant ties", "geographic distance", "industry distance", "geographic proximity", "industry specialization", "distance"]
definition: The authors measured the socio-demographic distance between venture capitalists on two dimensions: geography and industry. They assume as a baseline that (local) relationships more commonly form among actors close in socio-demographic space.

name: Syndicate tie formation
authors_terms: ["co-investment relationship", "syndicate relationship", "probability of a tie", "presence or absence of the ijth link"]
definition: In all models, the authors estimated the probability that lead VC firm i chooses syndicate partner j to participate in the setting of target company z, so that the presence or absence of the ijth link in z is the dependent variable.

name: Fashionable settings
authors_terms: ["fads and fashions", "fashionable settings", "market heat", "region heat", "industry heat"]
definition: A particular class of settings can become especially fashionable for reasons external to the organizations participating in them; a surge in the popularity of an activity—a fad or fashion—often provides a point of first contact between actors.

name: Setting risk
authors_terms: ["level of risk", "level of uncertainty", "lower-risk settings", "relational risk"]
definition: Settings vary in their level of inherent uncertainty, and the hosts issuing the invitations to these uncertain settings will prefer to restrict attendance to familiar and trusted partners.

name: Setting size
authors_terms: ["syndicate size", "number of participants", "number of members", "larger settings"]
definition: Each member's contribution in multilateral exchange, and therefore the actor's influence on the success of the joint initiative, declines with the total number of confederates.

name: Density of prior relationships among setting participants
authors_terms: ["density of connections among the participants", "prior interaction among syndicate members", "prior partners", "trusted associates"]
definition: The authors anticipate that having a number of friends and trusted colleagues in a group will mitigate the perceived risk of interacting with a stranger.

name: Media attention to a boycott
authors_terms: ["media attention", "level of media attention", "amount of media coverage", "number of newspaper articles related to the boycott"]
definition: High levels of media attention to a boycott translate as high levels of a movement's threat against the target organization; the media is both an indicator of the potential for consumers to support a boycott and a conduit of negative images and grievances brought by activists against the company.

name: Sales decline
authors_terms: ["decline in sales", "decline in sales revenue", "sales decline"]
definition: Declines in sales revenue represent a potential deterioration of a firm's competitive advantages; Boycotts highlight problems inherent in companies that are already suffering losses in sales revenue and the boycott becomes the impetus that executives needed to make corrections in their course of action.

name: Reputation decline
authors_terms: ["decline in reputation", "reputation decline", "perceived decline in reputation"]
definition: Declines in reputation represent a potential deterioration of a firm's competitive advantages; firms experiencing a perceived decline in reputation may view the threat of boycott as an additional signal that the company is losing credibility or legitimacy in the eyes of important stakeholders.

name: Corporate concession to boycotters' demands
definition: A concession, according to the criteria of the coding process, is a recognition by the corporation of the boycotters' demands and a public expression of conformity to those demands; the criterion excludes responses to boycotts that are attempts by the target to demobilize the activists without making any real changes.

name: Corporate orientation toward activism
authors_terms: ["orientation toward activism", "activism resistance", "activism proneness", "activism-resistant firms", "activism-prone firms", "imputed identities"]
definition: Activism-proneness and activism-resistance are loosely constituted cognitive categories that inform observers' heuristic expectations about how observed companies are likely to respond when confronted with a contentious practice. We coded a company's perceived orientation toward activism by using archival media reports describing each firm's responses to activists' efforts targeting them on other contentious social movement issues.

name: Adoption of domestic partner benefits
authors_terms: ["domestic partner benefits", "benefit adoption", "domestic partner health benefits"]
definition: Levi Strauss became the first firm listed on the Fortune 500 to extend healthcare benefits to employees' same-sex 'domestic partners.' Data on the date of domestic partner benefit adoption were taken from data provided by the Human Rights Campaign.

name: Activist employee group presence
authors_terms: ["GLBT employee groups", "activist groups", "employee activist groups", "affinity groups composed of GLBT workers"]
definition: The spread of domestic partner benefits coincided with the emergence of affinity groups composed of GLBT workers, who are widely credited for lobbying companies to adopt the benefits. We modeled the presence of activism inside organizations with a time-varying covariate reflecting the formation of GLBT employee groups.

name: Prior adoptions in the organizational field
authors_terms: ["prior adoption by companies in the organizational field", "adoptions in the wider population", "adoption events in a firm's environment", "prior adopters"]
definition: Prior adoption by companies in the organizational field is a form of evidence used in making these claims. But the evidentiary value of those adoptions is often filtered by the imputed identities of the adopting companies.

name: Benchmarking attention network
definition: Corporate benchmarking involves assessing the practices of other organizations with the intention of learning from them. The benchmarking data were taken from responses to the manager survey, in which respondents were asked to name two or three other employers to which they compare their health benefits.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) refers to a company's performance on a range of social and environmental issues over time.

name: Firm niche overlap density
authors_terms: ["firm niche overlap density (FNO)", "crowding in the firm's niche", "niche overlap density"]
definition: Firm niche overlap density is the count of firms whose niches overlap with the niche of the focal firm, and it captures crowding in the firm's niche and the extent of competitive pressures experienced by the firm.

name: Segment density
authors_terms: ["segment density (SN)", "number of firms operating in its market segment", "commensalistic mutualism"]
definition: Segment density is the number of firms operating in each of the market segments; because legitimacy and collective identity are collective goods shared by all firms in a market segment, mutualism is theorized to unfold at this level.

name: Market segment transition
authors_terms: ["move to a different market segment", "position move between market segments", "segment-to-segment transition", "change in market segment position"]
definition: A position move between market segments is a specific instance of organizational change; the event that defines the transition rate is a change in market segment position, which occurs when a firm's mid-niche falls in different market segments between two consecutive years and the firm's niche midpoint changes between those years.

name: Cross-border alliance formation
authors_terms: ["cross-border strategic alliances", "cross-border alliance formation", "access to cross-border alliances"]
definition: The alliances studied here include equity joint ventures, joint production arrangements, joint sales and marketing arrangements, exclusive supply arrangements, joint R&D, and joint financial investment, including a foreign firm's purchase of a Korean firm's shares.

name: Political network ties
definition: Political ties are helpful for securing access to a key market resource, namely, cross-border strategic alliances with multinational firms.

name: Choongchung regional origin
authors_terms: ["born in the central-western region of Choongchung", "CEO or chairman from the Choongchung region"]
definition: Elites from the western Choongchung region were peripheral players, being neither systematically favored nor disfavored, during the time of generals Chun and Roh and during the administration of Kim Young Sam.

name: Gangwon regional origin
authors_terms: ["born in the northeastern region of Gangwon", "CEO or chairman from the Gangwon region"]
definition: The Gangwon region in northeastern Korea is a largely rural area with only a small percentage of the country's population.

name: Jeolla regional origin
authors_terms: ["born in the Jeolla region", "the Jeolla network"]
definition: Another network that was often discriminated against because of its traditional position outside of Korean political power is the Jeolla network, which was associated with Kim Dae Jung.

name: Daegu-Kyungpook High School network
authors_terms: ["attended Daegu's Kyungpook High School", "the Daegu-Kyungpook High School network"]
definition: One of the most important networks in recent decades has been the Daegu-Kyungpook High School network, which was closely affiliated with the military generals Roh and Chun, who nominated allies from the same city and often the same high school for key finance and law enforcement positions in the finance, trade, and construction ministries.

name: Busan High School network
authors_terms: ["attended Busan High School", "the Busan High School network"]
definition: The Busan High School network is notable for its subregional rivalry with the elites from Daegu.

name: Federation of Korean Industries officer tie
authors_terms: ["served as an officer of the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI)", "former official of the FKI"]
definition: The Federation of Korean Industry (FKI) is South Korea's leading business interest group, and its membership and leadership have historically been drawn to a significant extent from the Busan region.

name: North Korea birth origin
definition: While South Korea was ruled by military generals, a person born in North Korea simply was not part of the mainstream elite structure based on regional networks, and only some (such as the head of Hyundai) overcame this outsider status.

name: Former government official tie
authors_terms: ["former minister", "mid-ranking bureaucrat or higher", "prior ministerial experience"]
definition: Throughout the first two regimes, those seizing power often not only replaced but even punished numerous elites who had served in any prior administrations.

name: New product introduction frequency
authors_terms: ["product frequency", "frequency of new product introductions", "number of new product introductions"]
definition: We measured product frequency as the number of new industrial robots introduced by each sample firm each year. To qualify as new, each product had to differ in technical or physical characteristics from the producing firm's previous products.

name: Product innovativeness
authors_terms: ["product innovativeness", "innovativeness of new product introductions", "innovativeness of these introductions"]
definition: We measured product innovativeness annually for each firm as the improvement in those product design characteristics that were important to users, which is a well-established method.

name: Firm's exclusive search
authors_terms: ["a firm's exclusive search", "exclusive exploration", "exclusive exploitation", "head-start search"]
definition: We measured a firm's exclusive exploration (firm uses for the first time, rivals have never used) as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were neither in its own or its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases nor in its rivals' knowledge bases in the current year. We measured the firm's exclusive exploitation as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its rivals' but were in its own past five years' knowledge bases.

name: Rivals' late exploration
definition: We measured rivals' late exploration as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its rivals' but were in the firm's own past five years' knowledge base and were used in the current year by both.

name: Rivals' exclusive search
authors_terms: ["rivals' exclusive search", "rivals' exclusive exploration", "rivals' exclusive exploitation", "catch-up search"]
definition: We measured rivals' exclusive exploration (rivals use for the first time, focal firm has never used) as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the firm's rivals' current-year patents that could not be found in the rivals' past five years' technological knowledge bases nor in the focal firm's knowledge bases in the current year or earlier. We measured rivals' exclusive exploitation as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in rivals' current-year patents that were in the rivals' but not in the focal firm's past five years' knowledge bases and were not used by the focal firm in the current year either.

name: Firm's late exploration
authors_terms: ["a firm's delayed search", "firm's late exploration", "late exploration"]
definition: We measured the firm's late exploration as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were in rivals' knowledge bases during the past five years but not in the firm's knowledge base and were used in the current year by both.

name: Synchronous search
definition: We measured synchronous exploration as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its own nor in its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases but were used in the current year by both. We measured synchronous exploitation as the proportion of those prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that could be found in its own and in its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases and were used again in the current year by both.

name: Economic values in executive decision making
authors_terms: ["economic values", "economic value set", "emphasis on economic values"]
definition: The economic value set represents a strongly held belief that profit and other quantifiable indicators of progress (e.g., sales growth, cost control) are important decision-making criteria. Executives who emphasize economic values assign the highest priority to profitability and other numerical indicators of progress in their decision making.

name: Stakeholder values in executive decision making
authors_terms: ["stakeholder values", "stakeholder value set", "emphasis on stakeholder values"]
definition: Rather than predominantly emphasizing profit maximization, the stakeholder perspective suggests that executives should consider and balance the needs of multiple stakeholder groups, including employees, customers, environmental constituents, and the broader community. The stakeholder perspective focuses less on quantifiable or economic-based outcomes and more on relationships with constituencies.

name: Autocratic leadership
authors_terms: ["autocratic leadership", "autocratic leadership style", "perceptions of autocratic leadership"]
definition: Autocratic leadership connotes a tough-minded leader who assumes full responsibility for decision making and policy. Autocratic leadership goes beyond decision making and involves what may be perceived as attempts to dominate or force values and opinions on followers; autocratic leaders are not concerned with building relationships with followers.

name: Visionary leadership
definition: Leaders viewed as visionary are perceived as providing a sense of mission or purpose and articulating a vision that challenges the status quo and is based in powerful imagery and a sense of purpose. They also have great sensitivity to the environment of their firms and use that sensitivity to articulate their visions.

name: Followers' extra effort
definition: Followers' perceptions of a leader relate to their willingness to expend extra effort for the leader and the organization, including a willingness to make personal sacrifices to realize the vision.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors conceptualize firm performance as a broad phenomenon, combining sales and return on investment to capture a more general concept of internally controlled organizational performance, assessed relative to close competitors so that exogenous industry and environmental influences are partly controlled.

name: Investment tie formation
authors_terms: ["vertical investment tie", "investment tie", "new tie", "formed a tie"]
definition: These vertical investment ties involve professional investors (e.g., venture capital firms, private equity firms, and corporations) investing in ventures, providing capital and advice in exchange for equity.

name: Founder direct tie
authors_terms: ["founder direct tie", "founders' direct ties", "direct tie with the founder(s)"]
definition: Founders are likely to have relevant personal ties gained through a lifetime of education, employment, and previous entrepreneurial endeavors; potential partners with ties to a founder are likely to benefit from any information they may previously have acquired about the founder's abilities and the relevance of those abilities to the new organization.

name: Founder indirect tie
authors_terms: ["founder indirect tie", "founders' indirect ties", "founder's indirect tie"]
definition: A new organization and a potential partner may still acquire accurate information about each other if a founder of the new organization has a tie with one of the potential partner's partners (i.e., the potential partner and the founder both have previously worked with a common partner).

name: Founder entrepreneurial human capital
definition: Entrepreneurial human capital is a team's skills and knowledge related to identifying opportunities and launching a venture.

name: Founder managerial human capital
definition: Managerial human capital is a team's skills and knowledge related to leading and growing a venture.

name: Investor status
authors_terms: ["investor's status", "status of the partnering organization", "affiliation-based status"]
definition: Status is determined by an organization's prior network partners; affiliation-based status is a 'multifaceted and encompassing' signal, reflecting and summarizing the detailed and varied information available to an organization's network partners.

name: Human capital-status similarity
authors_terms: ["human capital ENT / status similarity", "human capital MAN / status similarity", "human capital / status similarity"]
definition: The similarity between a venture's founders' human capital and an investor's status; new organizations whose founders have higher human capital will form ties primarily with high-status partners, leaving new organizations whose founders have less human capital to form ties primarily with low-status partners.

name: Organizational accomplishments
definition: A new organization's accomplishments (e.g., releasing products or receiving awards) signal the progress that a new organization has already made in resolving the market, technology, and organizational challenges that it faced initially.

name: Accomplishments-status similarity
authors_terms: ["accomplishments PRODUCT / status similarity", "accomplishments AWARD / status similarity", "accomplishments / status similarity"]
definition: The similarity between organizational accomplishments and investor status; high-accomplishment new organizations will seek and primarily form ties with high-status partners, leaving low-accomplishment new organizations primarily to form ties with low-status partners.

name: Venture age
definition: Age is the number of years that a venture had existed at the time of the focal investment round; as a new organization ages, potential partners increasingly judge it by its accomplishments rather than by its founders' ties and human capital.

name: Developed direct tie
definition: Partners that have already formed a direct tie with the new organization; such developed direct ties are likely to provide privileged access to nuanced, inside information that reveals more about the new organization's current capabilities, resources, and progress.

name: Developed indirect tie
definition: Through its initial network position, a new organization is also likely to develop indirect ties, which may provide access to the same privileged information as developed direct ties, as the common partner connecting a new organization and a potential partner may be willing to share its inside information.

name: Developed status similarity
definition: A new organization's initial network position confers a status position on the new organization; this developed status, obtained through the organization's own history of prior network affiliations, is likely to be interpreted as a better signal of a new organization's future potential than its founders' ties and human capital and recent organizational accomplishments.

name: Recruitment as a benchmarking partner
definition: Recruitment involves the process that led Global Financial to formally visit some organizations as benchmarking partners.

name: Influence on benchmarking teams
authors_terms: ["influence", "impact on the recommendations forwarded by benchmarking teams", "perceived influence", "best practice citations"]
definition: Influence speaks to the impact of benchmarking partners on the recommendations forwarded by benchmarking teams.

name: Board interlock
definition: The tie formed when executives or directors of one firm sit on the board of another; a board interlock equals 1 if Global Financial's senior executives and inside board members served on a firm's board, that firm's executives served on Global Financial's board, or Global Financial's outside board members served on that firm's board.

name: Spatial proximity
definition: A cohesive tie based on physical closeness: interaction and influence fall off with distance, and spatially proximate firms are also likely to share cultural understandings about business strategy and managerial techniques.

name: Executive migration tie
authors_terms: ["executive migration", "management ties based on executive migration", "migration-based ties", "management tie"]
definition: The tie formed when a manager moves from one firm to another; executive migration provides a high-capacity conduit for the transfer of organizational practices.

name: Competition
definition: An indirect form of equivalence that links rivals through common relations to third parties; in business, the sharpest rivalries occur when organizations compete for the same customers.

name: Corporate prestige
definition: Social status is defined as the esteem and respect that actors enjoy within some social community; much research points to the imitation of prestigious firms due to their visibility, possession of putative secrets of success, and broader standing as leaders.

name: Environmental social movement organization membership
authors_terms: ["environmental group membership", "Sierra Club membership", "SMO strength", "social movement organization strength"]
definition: State-level membership in an environmental social movement organization, which the authors use to capture the size and strength of the movement; membership reflects the size and strength of the Sierra Club more accurately than other measures such as the number of Sierra Club chapters in a state.

name: Wind energy entrepreneurial activity
authors_terms: ["nascent entrepreneurial activity", "entrepreneurial activity in wind energy", "entrepreneurial activity in this sector"]
definition: Nascent entrepreneurial activity: attempts by entrepreneurs to found new ventures in new sectors. In this setting it is measured by registration with FERC by an entrepreneur or entrepreneurial team, which signals intent to build but does not necessarily mean that the facility will become operational.

name: State regulatory environment
definition: The number of regulatory policies adopted by a state that promoted renewable energy and energy conservation, which taps the degree to which a state's regulatory environment is supportive of renewable energy.

name: Availability of land with high-quality wind
authors_terms: ["availability of land with high-quality wind flows", "available windy land", "wind availability", "availability of natural resources"]
definition: The number of acres of available land in each state that had wind quality rated at a wind class greater than 3 (wind speeds greater than 6.4 meters/second).

name: Human capital with relevant technological expertise
authors_terms: ["human capital", "technical workers", "skilled human capital", "human capital with related technological expertise"]
definition: The number of people in each state employed in technical fields relevant to wind energy technology.

name: Shortages of state-level electricity generating capacity
authors_terms: ["shortages of state-level electricity generating capacity", "capacity shortages", "net electricity imports"]
definition: The degree to which a state is unable to generate sufficient electricity to meet electricity demand, proxied by the amount of net electricity imports into a state.

name: Firm innovation
authors_terms: ["fi rm-level innovation", "organizational innovation", "innovation", "patenting activity", "innovative intensity of fi rms and industries"]
definition: The outcome of interest is firm-level innovation in knowledge-intensive industries, measured as a yearly count of patents assigned to the firms; patents are a commonly used measure of the innovative intensity of firms and industries.

name: Proximity to other firms
authors_terms: ["proximity to other fi rms", "proximity f", "localized geographic density", "physical proximity to similar fi rms", "propinquity"]
definition: The extent to which a firm is physically located near other companies in the same industry, which is expected to increase firm-level innovation through local labor pools, social-network spillovers, and learning by hiring.

name: Proximity to public research organizations
authors_terms: ["proximity to PROs", "proximity p", "proximity to public-sector research organizations", "proximity to public research organizations"]
definition: The extent to which a firm is located near public research organizations, including universities, research institutes, and teaching hospitals, which are producers of technical personnel and cutting-edge scientific knowledge.

name: Global network centrality
authors_terms: ["global centrality", "centrality in the global interorganizational network", "global power centrality"]
definition: A firm's global position refers to its location in an industry-wide network of collaborative relations and contractual ties, irrespective of partners' geographic locales; a central position in such a network facilitates innovation.

name: Local network centrality
definition: A firm's position in a structure comprising interorganizational ties connecting all partners located in the same region as the focal firm; in agglomerated areas, an active local network connects those who share both a physical and structural space.

name: Family ties in the inner circle
authors_terms: ["family relationships", "family ties", "percentage of family members", "family members in the inner circle"]
definition: Family relationships include primary family members and close kin of the key leader. Because of the Confucian ideology, which puts a strong emphasis on family piety and obligations, family executives interact with the key leader on the basis of role obligation, and such relationships tend to be characterized by unconditional trust and protection.

name: Prior social ties in the inner circle
definition: Prior social relationships, or familiar persons, such as former friends and colleagues, have had stable interpersonal contact in social or work-related contexts other than the current inner circle and have built mutual trust. They interact with the key leader under the norm of reciprocity.

name: Common-identity ties in the inner circle
definition: Executives with common identity have not had personal contact before but share a common identity, such as being from the same hometown. The key leader tends to deal with them in a utilitarian way but has some depersonalized affection toward them.

name: Business group performance
definition: Return on assets is used to gauge business group performance; it takes into account the efficiency of using the firm's assets and hence reflects a firm's profitability.

name: Market-oriented institutional transition
definition: Taiwan has experienced large-scale institutional changes since 1987, ranging from economic liberalization to political democratization, a change so significant that scholars labeled it the Great Transition. The authors coded the 1988-1996 period as the post-transition period and the 1973-1986 period as the pre-transition period.

name: Institutionalized female leadership
definition: The degree to which female leadership is institutionalized in the parent firm: the proportion of years that a progeny firm's parent had any women partners before the founder left to found the progeny firm.

name: Institutionalized female subordination
authors_terms: ["institutionalized female subordination", "female subordination", "women in subordinate positions"]
definition: Institutionalized female subordination occurs when a firm's routines result in women's perpetual occupancy of lower-ranked positions; it is measured as the proportion of years that a parent firm had women associates.

name: Social contact with women in leadership positions
authors_terms: ["social contact with women partners", "social contact with women in leadership positions"]
definition: The number of years the founder worked when there were also women partners in the parent firm.

name: Social contact with women in subordinate positions
authors_terms: ["social contact with women associates", "social contact with women in subordinate positions"]
definition: The number of years the founder worked when there were also women associates in the parent firm.

name: Founder's former rank
authors_terms: ["founder's former rank", "founder's former position", "former associate", "former partner", "lower-ranked member"]
definition: The position the founder occupied in the parent firm; law firms have two positions, associates and partners, and the type and volume of routines transferred should vary by the founder's former position in the parent firm.

name: Similarity of organization of work
authors_terms: ["similarity of organization of work", "difference in leverage ratios", "leverage ratio"]
definition: The extent to which a progeny law firm's organization of work resembles its parent firm's, captured by the associate-to-partner ratio (the leverage ratio), the central organizing principle in law firms.

name: Organizational genealogy
definition: Whether a firm is a progeny firm, founded by a founder who left a parent firm, or a de novo firm that has no parent firm; the lineage that creates the organizational genealogy is meaningful if the transfer of routines distinguishes progeny from de novo firms.

name: Promotion of a woman into partnership
authors_terms: ["promote a woman into a leadership position", "having a woman in a partner position", "making a woman partner"]
definition: The likelihood that a law firm promotes a woman to partner, modeled as the risk of a firm partnering a woman for the first time.

name: Reported corporate deviance
authors_terms: ["reported deviance", "organizational deviance", "deviant act", "the Skandia scandal", "corporate deviance"]
definition: Organizational behaviors that deviate from societal norms. The authors argue that a single act of organizational deviance will affect legitimacy if it leads to contagion of judgment from the culpable organization to others that audience members see as related.

name: Withdrawal from transactions
authors_terms: ["withdrawal from transactions", "withdrawal of transactions", "avoidance", "withdrawal of business", "net loss of business"]
definition: Transaction partners can respond to loss of legitimacy by avoidance, a culturally typical reaction to stigmatization of a social actor. Avoidance is an 'exit' strategy rather than a 'voice' strategy and is easy to choose because it is inexpensive.

name: Organizational form similarity
authors_terms: ["organizational form", "same form", "within-form contagion", "similarity of organizational form"]
definition: Organizational forms are formally defined as externally imposed social identities formed by a set of diagnostic characteristics and expected values on these characteristics. Organizational form affects generalization because forms are categories of presumed similar organizations, so an action performed by one member of an organizational form can be inferred to be likely by other members.

name: Size similarity
definition: Skandia's size was a salient characteristic of the firm and may have evoked an image of a privileged 'establishment' of large organizations; the authors investigated size as a similarity characteristic that led to the transfer of legitimacy loss.

name: Real estate holdings
authors_terms: ["real estate holdings", "real estate business", "percentage of real estate holdings"]
definition: The reported misallocation of apartments made the real estate business a central characteristic of the deviance, so firms owning real estate are expected to be judged closer to the scandal. The percentage of real estate holdings is measured relative to the total assets held by each parent corporation.

name: Status
definition: Status is audiences' beliefs about the quality of goods or services provided by a given organization. It influences markets by causing a preference for the higher-status organization, holding constant the objective quality, which is imperfectly known to audience members.

name: IGO connections
definition: IGOs represent concrete, formal, and relatively durable expressions of mutually aligned intentions in regard to future and ongoing interactions in a given domain among signatory nations, their firms, and citizens; IGO connections is hence an observable if imperfect indicator of mutually favorable intentions among states.

name: Export dependence
definition: A significant macro structural relation among nation states is the pattern of dependence among them; the authors focus on the host country's export dependence on the transnational's home country, which indicates state-on-state sanctionability.

name: Immigration links
definition: Another significant macro structural relation among nation states is the pattern of immigration and resulting links of common ethnicity among them.

name: Relative host market performance
authors_terms: ["relative host market performance", "relative host market local sales", "relative host market sales", "foreign market performance"]
definition: The authors measured a transnational's relative host market performance using its relative host market local sales, contending that a measure more closely related to the market provides a direct comparison of the success of transnationals in competition with each other.

name: Proportion of WCTU members
authors_terms: ["proportion of WCTU members in a state", "WCTU membership proportion", "WCTU membership"]
definition: The normative pressure created by the Woman's Christian Temperance Union in a state, based on the presence of dues-paying members pledged to abstain from alcohol and to proselytize abstention among others. It is measured as the annual number of dues-paying members of local chapters (unions) in each state divided by the total state population.

name: Number of AMA members
authors_terms: ["number of AMA members", "AMA membership", "proportion of AMA members"]
definition: The number of American Medical Association members in a state, used to capture the amount of resources available for lobbying and temperance endorsement, in contrast to the WCTU membership proportion measure, which gauged normative influence.

name: Prohibition laws in adjoining states
authors_terms: ["percentage of adjoining states with prohibition laws", "percentage of all counties in adjoining states that had enacted state and county prohibition laws", "prohibition percentage of surrounding states"]
definition: The extent of prohibitory legislation in states adjoining a focal state, which the authors argue created pressure on residents of the focal state to conform to growing acceptance of temperance values. It is measured as the percentage of all counties in adjoining states that had enacted state and county prohibition laws.

name: Scientific temperance instruction
definition: A WCTU tactic, adopted in 1879, that called for the classroom study of the nature of alcoholic drinks and narcotics and their effects upon the human system, and which the WCTU sought to embed into public and private school curricula through legal mandates at the state level.

name: Prohibition regulation
definition: Laws that made the sale and transport of liquor within state boundaries illegal, which the WCTU pursued at federal, state, and local levels through its Committee on Temperance Legislation.

name: Brewery failure
definition: The disbanding of individual breweries as the temperance movement delegitimated alcohol production and consumption and reduced demand for breweries' products.

name: Soft drink firm foundings
authors_terms: ["soft drink firm foundings", "soft drink producer foundings", "foundings of soft drink producers"]
definition: The creation of new soft drink manufacturing organizations, which the authors argue arose as the WCTU's tactics created demand for alcohol substitutes, inspired entrepreneurs, and made resources available.

name: Environmental performance
definition: To gauge environmental performance, we followed Berrone and Gomez-Mejia (2009) and weighted on-site emissions using the Human Toxicity Potential (HTP) factor developed by Hertwich and colleagues (2001), which measures toxicity in terms of benzene equivalence (for carcinogens) or toluene equivalence (for noncarcinogens).

name: Family control
definition: We classified an organization as a family firm if family members owned or controlled at least 5 percent of the voting stock.

name: Local roots
definition: To gauge local roots, we first considered the average distance of the firm's subsidiaries from its headquarters, weighted by the relative importance in terms of employment that each subsidiary had in the geographical zone where it was located.

name: Family CEO status
definition: The family CEO status measure was a dummy variable that assumed the value of 1 if the CEO belonged to the family that controlled the firm, and 0 otherwise.

name: CEO duality
definition: The situation in which the same individual was both CEO and board chair was a dummy variable, CEO duality, coded 1 if the CEO held both positions, and 0 otherwise.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: The CEO stock ownership variable measured the CEO's percentage of ownership in the firm.

name: Commitment to self-regulation
authors_terms: ["disclosed", "committed to self-regulate", "commit to adopting internal compliance auditing", "self-regulatory commitments", "pledges to self-regulate"]
definition: A facility's representation, made through voluntary disclosure of a regulatory violation under the U.S. EPA Audit Policy, that it has adopted formal internal compliance procedures and has committed to maintaining them in the future to prevent subsequent violations.

name: Regulatory compliance
definition: A facility's compliance outcomes as recorded by regulatory inspectors, capturing whether a facility is found to be in compliance with the Clean Air Act when inspected.

name: Direct regulatory threat
authors_terms: ["direct regulatory threat", "regulatory threats", "explicit enforcement threat", "coercive pressure"]
definition: An explicit enforcement threat conveyed by the EPA when it targets particular facilities through Compliance Incentive Programs, notifying them of its concern about possible non-compliance and warning that failure to review and disclose puts the facility at risk of being prioritized for scrutiny.

name: Facility-level regulatory surveillance
authors_terms: ["heavily monitored facilities", "heavy regulatory monitoring", "regulatory surveillance", "routine inspections"]
definition: The intensity of routine regulatory monitoring directed at an individual facility, reflected in the number of Clean Air Act inspections the facility receives, as distinct from explicit threats of punishment.

name: Field-level regulatory surveillance
definition: The intensity of regulatory inspection activity directed at all facilities in an industry, which sends a normative message about expectations in the field and signals that competitors are being watched too.

name: Compliance experience
authors_terms: ["superior compliance experience", "compliance histories", "superior compliance histories", "regulatory experience"]
definition: A facility's history of navigating its regulatory environment, reflected in its compliance routines and indicated by its record of compliance violations and enforcement actions.

name: New market category legitimacy
definition: Legitimation is an outgrowth of producers' claims and audiences' assessments, making the new market category more comprehensible by clarifying its meaning and associated identity codes and making it more attractive and real. Because traditional density-based indicators could not be used, the authors used widespread commercialization and consumer adoption of a new market product as an indicator of legitimacy, and they locate the legitimation of satellite radio in 2002.

name: Distinctiveness of identity claims
authors_terms: ["identity claims", "collective identity", "distinctive organizational identities", "who we are", "what we do"]
definition: An individual organization's identity consists of claims about its central, distinctive, and enduring attributes as well as its rightful membership in a particular market category. Member organizations need to navigate between their shared sameness with other category members and their individual distinctiveness from other members.

name: Distinctiveness of linguistic framing
definition: One linguistic device that bridges diverse elements or domains is the metaphor, which frames the unfamiliar in terms of the familiar to make it more understandable and often more attractive. Linguistic framing can index an organization's gradient of membership through qualifying terms, differentiating category members.

name: Distinctiveness of affiliation announcements
definition: Entrepreneurial organizations select and publicize their partnerships; before legitimation, affiliation announcements emphasize features of the partnership that denote the category's feasibility and appeal, whereas following legitimation they emphasize features of the partnership that distinguish firms within the category.

name: Firm-specific audience attention
definition: Audiences are 'collections of agents with an interest in a domain and control over material and symbolic resources that affect the success and failure of the claimants in the domain.' Once a category is legitimated, audiences should refocus their attention away from the category as a whole and toward the individual organizations within it.

name: Democratic similarity
authors_terms: ["similar democratic governance structures", "democratic variability", "democratic similarity", "similarity in terms of political systems"]
definition: The similarity of the democratic governance structures of the states in a group, measured as the divergence of their polity scores; similar democratic governance is argued to smooth interaction and support shared understandings, making affiliation easier.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: The physical proximity of states, a proxy for similarity on hard-to-measure state characteristics such as cultural and religious dimensions and a basis for contact and communication between citizens that should smooth affiliations between their states.

name: Interstate conflict
authors_terms: ["armed confl ict", "recent dyadic wars", "states in confl ict"]
definition: Conflict between two states, indicated by whether they have recently been in armed conflict with each other; conflicts make affiliations harder to maintain but also valuable to the states involved.

name: Dyadic trade
authors_terms: ["trade", "average dyadic trade", "trade extensively with each other"]
definition: The extent to which two states trade with each other, which signals economic codependence and increases both conflict and the potential benefits of conflict resolution, and therefore the value of bridges between them.

name: Dyadic IGO ties
authors_terms: ["numerous dyadic IGO ties between them", "average dyadic IGO ties within group", "crowding of IGO connections between two states"]
definition: The strength of the existing IGO ties between the states of a group, defined for a dyad as the number of IGOs in which the two states share a membership; crowding of such ties is interpreted primarily as direct competition for supplying the same affiliation.

name: External IGO affiliations
authors_terms: ["IGO ties to third parties outside the focal group", "average IGO memberships outside group", "IGO affi liations beyond the membership group"]
definition: Members' IGO memberships that do not create ties among the focal group of states, representing diffuse competition for the limited relational capacity of states.

name: NGO participation
authors_terms: ["NGO participation by the citizens of a state", "average NGO memberships", "memberships in NGOs"]
definition: The participation of a state's citizens in non-governmental organizations, a key indicator of an internationalist orientation that legitimates international relations through international organizations.

name: Democracy level
authors_terms: ["level of democracy of a state", "average democracy", "democratic governance structures"]
definition: The level of democracy of a state's governance structures, argued to identify states whose governance is isomorphic with IGOs and that view IGO affiliation as more legitimate.

name: IGO founding rate
definition: The rate at which intergovernmental organizations are founded; an IGO is treated as founded in the year it actually began operations.

name: IGO failure rate
definition: The rate at which IGOs disappear, defined as ceasing to exist outright or being merged into another IGO, but not as being replaced by a new IGO.

name: Acquisition premium
authors_terms: ["acquisition premium", "the premium paid for an acquisition"]
definition: The premium paid for an acquisition; as acquiring firms pay higher acquisition premiums it becomes increasingly difficult to create sufficient value, so the magnitude of the premium reflects the strength of the acquirer's desire to acquire the target.

name: Organic growth relative to peers
authors_terms: ["relative social organic growth", "organic growth relative to its peer firms"]
definition: The three-year organic growth of the focal bank in the sample minus the average three-year organic growth of its peer banks, where peer firms are all the banks in existence that operated in all the states in which the focal bank operated in a given year.

name: Organic growth relative to past growth
authors_terms: ["relative historical organic growth", "organic growth relative to its past organic growth"]
definition: An acquirer's current level of organic growth relative to its past level of organic growth, where the past level is an exponentially weighted moving average of the acquirer's organic growth in the past.

name: Acquisition dependence relative to peers
authors_terms: ["relative social acquisition dependence", "acquisition dependence relative to its peer firms"]
definition: The three-year acquisition dependence of a focal bank in the sample minus the average three-year acquisition dependence of all the banks that also operated in the states in which the focal bank operated.

name: Acquisition dependence relative to past levels
authors_terms: ["relative historical acquisition dependence", "acquisition dependence relative to its past acquisition dependence"]
definition: The difference between an acquirer's current year's acquisition dependence and its historical level of acquisition dependence, which was measured in the same way that historical organic growth was created.

name: Acquirer acquisition experience
definition: The acquirer's own experience with past acquisitions, measured as the discounted sum of the number of intraindustry acquisitions that a bank in the sample made since 1988.

name: Advisor acquisition experience
definition: The acquisition experience of the financial advisor of the focal acquisition, measured by the discounted sum of the number of bank acquisitions that the advisor advised between 1988 and the focal acquisition.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risk taking is conceptualized as financial outlays for investment categories that are known to have highly uncertain returns; the size of an acquisition premium is also treated as an expression of risk taking.

name: Recent firm performance
authors_terms: ["recent performance", "objective performance", "recent firm performance", "total shareholder returns", "return on assets"]
definition: A firm's recent performance provides a CEO with a strong cue about his or her own capability, as well as that of the entire organization, thus affecting risk-taking behaviors. Poor performance engenders hesitance and self-doubt, while high performance stimulates eagerness and a sense of potency.

name: Recent social praise
definition: Social praise, in the form of flattery, applause, and acclaim, tends to buoy one's sense of capability. On the contemporary business scene, social praise for individual CEOs comes in various forms, notably in media accounts of CEOs' talents and in awards bestowed by prominent media outlets.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissism is the degree to which an individual has an inflated sense of self and is preoccupied by having that self-view continually reinforced. It is a personality dimension on which all individuals can be placed.

name: Early support for the failing technology
authors_terms: ["enter with plasma", "early plasma supporters", "firms initially supporting the losing technology", "supporting plasma"]
definition: Early entrants whose first five years of flat panel patenting were 80 percent or more in plasma technology, i.e., firms that bet on the technology that later lost the competition.

name: Early support for the winning technology
authors_terms: ["enter with LCD", "early LCD supporters", "firms supporting the winning technology initially", "share LCD at entry"]
definition: Early entrants whose first five years of flat panel patenting were 80 percent or more in LCD technology (Enter with LCD, the omitted category), or, on the continuous measure, the ratio of LCD patents to all flat panel display patents in the early entrant's first five years in the industry.

name: Early simultaneous support for both technologies
authors_terms: ["enter with both", "early supporters of both technologies", "technological generalists", "early hedgers"]
definition: Early entrants with ratios of LCD to all flat panel patents between the two extremes, classified as Enter with both, i.e., firms that invested in both LCD and plasma at entry.

name: Late entry after uncertainty resolution
definition: Firms whose first flat panel display patent was after 1982, that is, after the emergence of LCD as the dominant technology.

name: Knowledge growth in the winning technology
authors_terms: ["LCD patents", "new knowledge created in the winning technology", "knowledge growth", "knowledge creation in the winning technology"]
definition: New knowledge created in the winning technology, proxied by the annual count of LCD patents the firm applied for and later received.

name: Reinvestment in the reemerging technology
authors_terms: ["plasma patents", "reinvest", "pursuing plasma during its reemergence", "invest in plasma"]
definition: Whether the firm had any plasma patents in a given year during plasma's renaissance, used to capture willingness to reinvest in the previously failed technology when it reemerges.

name: Complementary assets
authors_terms: ["complementary assets", "relevant complementary assets", "upstream complementary assets", "downstream complementary assets"]
definition: Relevant complementary assets may be either upstream, relating to design and manufacturing (such as component parts for the final product), or downstream, related to commercialization (such as brand name and distribution networks); they increase the incentives for generating new knowledge in the winning technology.

name: Size of the failed investment
authors_terms: ["size of the failure", "scale of the failure"]
definition: The magnitude of the failure, which must be large enough to be visible in the organization yet not so large that it results in organizational failure or comprehensive management turnover.

name: Failure-driven inertia
authors_terms: ["inertia", "observed inertia", "inertial effect of prior failure", "inertial response to failure"]
definition: The inertial response to failure: reduced effort and ability to generate new knowledge in the winning technology following an initial failed technological investment, driven by managers' updated expectations.

name: Similarity of prior institutional experience
definition: The level of similarity between the regulatory institutional environments in which a multinational has prior home- and host-country experience and the regulatory institutional environment of the target host country. Similar institutional experiences afford firms a more precise ability to predict and mitigate new institutional conditions.

name: Foreign subunit survival
authors_terms: ["subunit survival", "time to failure", "survival of the subsequent foreign subunit investment"]
definition: Survival of a foreign subunit investment, analyzed as the time to failure event, where a firm's exit from Brazil driven by financial underperformance, difficulty securing capital, lack of understanding of local institutions, or related situations counts as failure.

name: Breadth of institutional experience
definition: The amount of dispersion according to types of host-country regulatory experience prior to entering Brazil.

name: Depth of institutional experience
definition: The frequency of each of the six regulatory dimensions summed across countries that exactly matched the regulatory environment in Brazil, based on the fraction of replication of Brazil's regulatory environment and the depth within each replicated dimension.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family ownership is defined by government as all those mills in which a particular family has undivided property rights over the mill's assets.

name: Family ownership stage
definition: The three family stages are founding-family-controlled and managed firms (first stage), ownership and management by extended family (second stage), and ownership by extended family members who are not involved in the firm's management (third stage).

name: Loss of family control
authors_terms: ["loss of control", "loss of family control", "give up family control", "relinquishing family control", "joining the cooperative"]
definition: An olive oil mill was coded as '1' on this variable whenever it voluntarily decided to change status from being a privately owned independent firm to being a cooperative, an exclusive agreement that transfers power from the mill owners to the coop governance structure.

name: Probability of organizational failure
authors_terms: ["probability of failure", "probability of organizational failure", "performance hazard"]
definition: Performance hazard concerns the potential for negative consequences associated with a decision choice, one manifestation of which is the probability of organizational failure or threats to survival, 'the worst case scenario'.

name: Attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["attainment discrepancy", "distance from the aspiration level", "target achievement", "historical target achievement", "referent-target achievement", "performance target"]
definition: Because the extent to which an organization meets its performance target cannot be measured directly, the authors used two common proxies to measure the distance between performance and target, or attainment discrepancy.

name: Venturing risk
definition: Venturing involves the search for alternative routines and opportunities when the firm is unhappy with the status quo; the search for new approaches may raise organizational performance but also increases the chance of unexpected outcomes, causing variance in performance.

name: Procurement relationship performance
authors_terms: ["a manufacturer's performance in the procurement relationship", "buyer's satisfaction with the exchange relationship", "manufacturer's performance in economic exchanges"]
definition: The manufacturer's performance in the procurement relationship, measured as the buyer's satisfaction with the exchange relationship.

name: Joint dependence
definition: The sum of dependence between actors in the relationship, which operates through a logic of embeddedness.

name: Manufacturer's dependence
definition: The manufacturer's dependence on the supplier, measured with items reflecting the magnitude and concentration of exchange, the availability of alternative sources of exchange, and the magnitude of transaction-specific investments.

name: Supplier's dependence
definition: The supplier's dependence on the manufacturer, measured with items reflecting the magnitude and concentration of exchange, the availability of alternative sources of exchange, and the magnitude of transaction-specific investments.

name: Manufacturer's dependence advantage
definition: The manufacturer's dependence advantage is the supplier's excess dependence on the manufacturer, net of the manufacturer's dependence on the supplier.

name: Supplier's dependence advantage
definition: The supplier's dependence advantage is the manufacturer's excess dependence on the supplier, net of the supplier's dependence on the manufacturer.

name: Joint action
definition: The degree of dyadic cooperation and coordination across a wide array of organizational activities, such as design, cost control, and quality improvement, including bilateral solutions to relational and operational problems.

name: Interorganizational trust
definition: The expectation that another organization may be relied upon to fulfill its obligations, to behave predictably, and to act and negotiate fairly even when the possibility of opportunism is present.

name: Quality of information exchange
authors_terms: ["quality of information exchange", "quality of information transfer"]
definition: The level of detail, timeliness, and accuracy that characterizes the information exchange between the exchange partners.

name: Scope of information exchange
definition: The scope of information exchange, in terms of the types of information exchanged between the partners.

name: Firm performance relative to aspiration levels
authors_terms: ["relatively low firm performance", "firm performance is relatively low", "below aspiration levels", "performance below the firm's historical average and below the average performance of competitors"]
definition: Firm performance is evaluated relative to aspiration levels jointly influenced by the firm's prior performance and the performance of competitors. Concern about strategy is generally low above aspiration levels and generally high below them.

name: Pluralistic ignorance
authors_terms: ["pluralistic ignorance", "underestimate the extent to which fellow directors share their concerns", "difference between directors' concern about strategy and directors' perception of others' concern"]
