definition: Pluralistic ignorance is a situation in which virtually all members of a group privately reject group norms, practices, or policies, or have concerns about them, but believe that virtually all other group members accept them. It is typically defined at the group level as the extent to which group members underestimate the degree to which others share their concerns.

name: Outside directors' concern about corporate strategy
authors_terms: ["directors' concern about strategy", "concern about the viability of the current corporate strategy", "private concern about strategy"]
definition: Directors' private concern about the appropriateness or viability of the firm's current corporate strategy, especially when firm performance is relatively low.

name: Perceived concern of fellow directors
authors_terms: ["directors' perception that other board members are concerned about strategy", "perceived concern of other board members", "perception of others' concern"]
definition: A director's perception of the extent to which other board members are concerned about the firm's current corporate strategy.

name: Expressed concern about corporate strategy
authors_terms: ["expressed concern about strategy", "expressed concern about corporate strategy", "tendency for outside directors to express their concerns about corporate strategy"]
definition: The extent to which outside directors have voiced or expressed concern about the firm's current corporate strategy in board meetings.

name: Density of personal friendship ties among outside directors
authors_terms: ["density of personal friendship ties among outside directors", "density of friendship ties", "friendship ties among outside directors"]
definition: The density of personal friendship relationships among outside directors, measured as the number of such ties between outside directors divided by the number of possible ties.

name: Demographic homogeneity among outside directors
authors_terms: ["demographic homogeneity among outside directors", "demographic homogeneity of the board", "homogeneity in educational affiliation, gender, and functional background"]
definition: The level of similarity among outside directors on salient demographic characteristics, including functional background, primary industry of employment, gender, and educational affiliation.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "subsequent strategic change", "change in corporate strategy", "change in product market diversification and geographic diversification"]
definition: Change in key dimensions of the firm's corporate strategy, examined as change in product market diversification and geographic diversification.

name: Prior exchange relations
authors_terms: ["prior relations", "prior exchange experience", "direct ties to the distributor", "repeated exchange", "prior interactions", "number of direct ties"]
definition: The depth of repeated exchange linking a film's production team to its distributor; because production companies are ephemeral, the authors track them by decomposing each team into its constituent principals (producer(s), writer(s), a director, and actors) and counting their prior dealings with the same distributor.

name: Film budget
definition: The film's budget or negative cost, which the authors treat as the most meaningful 'price' in exchanges between producers and distributors and as a mechanism through which the principals involved in a film can extract rents from distribution companies.

name: Post-exchange resource allocation
authors_terms: ["post-exchange resource allocation", "allocation of resources", "allocate larger shares of those resources", "scarce resources"]
definition: Resources that one party allocates to a trading partner after the exchange, at its own discretion and without compensation, to the benefit of the other party; in this setting, the resources devoted to promoting a film and the attractiveness of the date on which it is released.

name: Box office performance
authors_terms: ["box office performance", "box office sales", "box office receipts", "ticket sales"]
definition: The box office sales of the film, described as the most direct measure of film performance and as the critical measure of success, particularly because ancillary revenues correlate highly with theatrical sales.

name: Organizational growth
definition: We used the growth and decline in expenditures of community based nonprofit organizations as our performance measure.

name: Organizational status
definition: We conceptualized status as the prestige or esteem that actors in the environment attributed to an organization as they passed judgment on its value. Status is one dimension of an organization's reputation in an organizational field.

name: Ties to urban elites
authors_terms: ["ties to urban elites", "ties to local urban elites", "elite use/support of the organization", "ties to the elite"]
definition: In the surveys of local elites, we asked respondents which nonprofits they supported personally with donations, volunteer work, consulting, board memberships, etc. In a subsequent question, we asked them which nonprofits they or their families had used in the last couple of years.

name: Interorganizational network centrality
authors_terms: ["interorganizational network centrality", "network centrality", "Bonacich centrality", "interorganizational exchange network"]
definition: We used Bonacich's (1972) measure of network centrality because it best captured the idea of social capital as used in this paper. Ego's centrality was weighted by the centrality of those to which ego was tied.

name: Nonprofit type
authors_terms: ["donative vs. commercial", "Donative _ commercial", "organizational form", "organizational inputs", "nonprofit type"]
definition: Two different logics drive the acquisition of resources among charities: a donative logic in which nonprofits depend on donations and grants, which is based on relationships, a shared sense of mission, and trust, and a commercial logic in which nonprofits depend on fees and earned income, which is based on price, quality, and consumer choice.

name: Change in reliance on donations and volunteers
authors_terms: ["change in the percent of gifts/grants", "change in the percent of employees/volunteers", "became more donative"]
definition: We computed change scores for the percentages of funding that came from private gifts/grants and the percentage of employees/volunteers. We subtracted percentages in 1980 from percentages in 1988 and percentages in 1988 from percentages in 1994.

name: Change in reliance on fees and employees
authors_terms: ["change in the percent of fees/sales", "increase in reliance on fees/sales", "became more commercial", "became more dependent on fees/sales"]
definition: We computed change scores for the percentages of funding that came from fees/sales. We subtracted percentages in 1980 from percentages in 1988 and percentages in 1988 from percentages in 1994.

name: Community symbiosis
authors_terms: ["community's symbiosis", "community symbiosis", "community supplier symbiosis", "community purchaser symbiosis", "symbiotic organizational populations"]
definition: The extent to which a local community is characterized by the presence of organizations that either supply goods to (supplier symbiosis) or purchase goods from (purchaser symbiosis) instruments producers.

name: Community commensalism
definition: The extent to which a community is characterized by the presence of organizational populations that are similar to instruments manufacturing in terms of the markets they serve or the suppliers from which they acquire inputs.

name: Founding rate
authors_terms: ["founding rate", "rate of instruments manufacturing company foundings", "organizational foundings"]
definition: The rate at which new instruments manufacturing companies are founded in a community; organizational foundings are defined as those autonomous establishments present only in the second year of a two-year period.

name: Probability of first foundings
authors_terms: ["initial foundings", "first foundings", "probability of the first foundings"]
definition: The probability that a community that had no instruments manufacturers at the beginning of the observation period experiences its first foundings of instruments manufacturing companies.

name: Local density of instruments manufacturers
authors_terms: ["local density of instruments manufacturers", "number of instruments manufacturers", "local density"]
definition: The count of instruments manufacturers in a community, defined as the count of all establishments, both autonomous units and branches, of the focal population.

name: Geographic distance
authors_terms: ["geographic distance", "geographical distance", "nonlocal density weighted by geographic distance"]
definition: The distance in geographical space between a community and instruments manufacturers located elsewhere, which creates friction in the transfer of information across space.

name: Unrelated dominant population
authors_terms: ["unrelated dominant population", "dominant population unrelated to instruments manufacturing", "community's dominant population"]
definition: A community's dominant organizational population, defined as the population with the largest share of resources in the area, weighted by the degree to which it lacks symbiotic and commensalistic ties to instruments manufacturing.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissism is a coherent but multifaceted personality dimension that can be defined as the degree to which an individual has an inflated sense of self and is preoccupied with having that self-view continually reinforced. Its chief manifestations include feelings of superiority, entitlement, and a constant need for attention and admiration.

name: Strategic dynamism
authors_terms: ["strategic dynamism", "strategic flux", "degree of change in an organization's strategy"]
definition: Strategic dynamism, or the degree of change in an organization's strategy, is a central construct in the study of strategic management.

name: Acquisition frequency
definition: Acquisitions, particularly large acquisitions, are among the most visible initiatives a CEO can take; by their very nature, acquisitions represent quantum action and are attention-getters.

name: Acquisition size
authors_terms: ["size of acquisitions", "aggregate size of acquisitions", "strategic grandiosity"]
definition: Acquisitions, particularly large acquisitions, are among the most visible initiatives a CEO can take; by their very nature, acquisitions represent quantum action and are attention-getters.

name: Performance extremeness
authors_terms: ["extreme performance", "performance extremeness", "big wins or big losses"]
definition: The tendency of narcissistic CEOs to deliver extreme performance, or big wins or big losses, as reflected in the firm's absolute difference from the industry average level of performance.

name: Performance fluctuation
definition: Wide swings in performance, or instability, from one period to the next, measured as the magnitude of the annual performance swing for each firm.

name: Social movement protest event
definition: Protest demonstrations-or protests for short-capitalize on the outsider status of individuals and movements that choose to use them; they are the organized, collective, and public expression of discontent and a more radical means of influence available to stakeholders mostly shut out from institutionalized channels of change.

name: Investor reaction to protest
authors_terms: ["investors' reactions", "abnormal stock price returns", "cumulative abnormal return (CAR)", "negative reaction by investors"]
definition: The cumulative abnormal return (CAR) is a standard measure of stock price return in event studies that allowed the authors to estimate fluctuation in stock price as it deviates from the expected return, based on exogenous market fluctuation.

name: Protest size
definition: One of the most common indicators of threat is protest size, typically measured by the number of participants; larger protests also have a greater impact on their targets because of their ability to disrupt the target's routine activities.

name: Organizational strength of the movement
authors_terms: ["organizational strength of the movement", "number of organizations sponsoring a protest event", "SMO involvement"]
definition: Another traditional indicator of threat is the organizational strength of the movement; when multiple organizations collaborate to sponsor a protest, they draw on a larger resource base, which allows them to coordinate more effectively every aspect of the event.

name: Labor or consumer issues
authors_terms: ["labor or consumer issues", "protests relating to labor or consumer issues", "critical stakeholder groups"]
definition: Issues relating to resource flows that are critical to the firm's survival may be particularly damaging to investors' confidence; protests relating to labor or consumer issues should be more troublesome to investors, given that they signal an underlying discontent with two stakeholder groups central to organizational survival.

name: Consumer boycott
definition: Protests accompanied by consumer boycotts may constrain future revenue and directly threaten profitability.

name: Institutionalized organizational practice
authors_terms: ["institutionalized programs, policies, or practices", "institutionalized features of the organization", "highly institutionalized practices or policies"]
definition: Protests related to deep-seated issues involving the institutionalized policies and practices of a corporation may generate stronger investor reactions than protests dealing with temporary or situational organizational problems; highly institutionalized practices or policies are costly to repair and may not have easy solutions.

name: Media coverage of the protest
authors_terms: ["media coverage", "level of media coverage", "national media coverage"]
definition: Intensified media coverage amplifies investors' attention and focuses it on negative aspects of a corporation's behavior and is a proxy for information about the value of a firm in the absence of firm-generated data.

name: Past media attention to the firm
authors_terms: ["past media attention", "past media attention to a firm", "past media coverage"]
definition: Past media attention to a firm has already significantly molded investors' perceptions of the target firm and may thus actually protect firms from further reputational damage because firms that have been scrutinized in the past already have their public 'warts' exposed.

name: Financial performance
definition: Firms with strong financial performance may also have excess cash flow to buffer them from potential costs from protests; companies with poor financial performance should face greater scrutiny by investors and be more likely to experience retreat by investors when an attack is made against the firm.

name: MPPC membership
definition: Membership in the Motion Pictures Patents Company (MPPC), the trust formed in 1909 that pursued market control in the early film industry. Membership functioned as an institutional link among members, joining not just their experience but also their patents and prior claims to legal protection.

name: Firm mortality
definition: Exit of a firm from the population, with firms assumed to die as of the release date of their last film. Mortality was coded as a dependent variable set to 0 in each month a firm remained alive and 1 in the month the firm died.

name: MPPC market control
authors_terms: ["market control by the MPPC", "MPPC market share", "competitive intensity exerted by the MPPC"]
definition: The competitive intensity exerted by the MPPC during its period of effective market control. The authors propose that the MPPC was able to use compensatory fitness to enhance its competitive intensity in addition to increasing members' viability.

name: Litigation filed by the MPPC
authors_terms: ["litigation filed by the MPPC", "lawsuits brought by the MPPC", "Plaintiff"]
definition: Lawsuits and related legal actions that the MPPC initiated against other firms. There were lawsuits to enforce licensing agreements, frequent seizures of licensed films being shown in unlicensed theaters, and frequent litigation alleging patent violations.

name: Litigation against the MPPC
authors_terms: ["lawsuits against the MPPC", "litigation filed against the MPPC", "countersuits naming the MPPC as defendant", "Defendant"]
definition: Lawsuits in which the MPPC was named as defendant, brought by independent firms and eventually joined by the federal government. These countersuits initially met with little success, but the MPPC softened its anti-competitive tactics in response to the legal pressures.

name: Framing of the MPPC
authors_terms: ["framing", "patent framing", "trust framing", "shift in how the MPPC was framed"]
definition: The perception of the MPPC in the legal environment, captured as a shift from a view emphasizing the pooling of patents to a view labeling the MPPC an illegal trust. The authors propose that this shift in how the MPPC was framed will undercut its competitive intensity.

name: Feature-length film production
definition: Production of feature-length films, which the AFI defined as four reels or longer, while shorts were typically only one reel. The dependent variable equals the number of feature-length films made in each month by each firm.

name: Termination of investment
definition: The decision by a VC firm to stop investing in a venture; a VC-venture investment relationship was coded as terminated if the VC firm did not appear in any of the subsequent investment rounds or if the focal round was also the final round of financing for the venture.

name: Successful exit
definition: The hazard of a successful exit for a venture at time t. IPOs and acquisitions were considered successful exit events because they are the two attractive exit options for VC investors.

name: Rounds of financing
definition: The number of rounds of financing a venture received from each VC firm; two or more consecutive rounds listed within a 90-day period were aggregated and treated as a single round.

name: Intraorganizational politics
definition: Political processes through which organizational members pursue their own interests and negotiate support for their deals; such processes tend to become more prevalent as organizations grow in size, authority is delegated to more members, and the organizational structure becomes more complex.

name: Co-investor pressure
definition: Pressure from co-investors in a syndicate that increases as the number of co-investors that join the syndicate grows, because the relationships between co-investors become more complex and severing the investment tie may involve more penalties for each VC.

name: VC firm status
authors_terms: ["high-status (elite) VC", "social status", "centrality in the co-investment network", "elite status"]
definition: A VC firm's social status, measured by its centrality in the co-investment network; high-status organizations are subject to less pressure to comply with investment norms than their low-status counterparts.

name: Fund age
definition: The difference between the focal round year and the fund vintage year.

name: Political opportunities
authors_terms: ["political opportunities created by the weakening of incumbents' power", "vulnerability to external pressures", "changes in the political opportunity structure"]
definition: Political opportunities for change created in a university in terms of the agency power structure among its institutional agents after political democratization. Public universities came to have such opportunities by losing a powerful incumbent who would otherwise champion the traditional appointment system.

name: Organized power of challengers
authors_terms: ["organized power of challengers", "having challengers with organized power", "organizing of challengers"]
definition: The degree to which challengers who want social change can organize themselves into sustainable interest groups, which gives them stronger bargaining power and makes them harder for incumbents to penalize. In Korean universities, the organizing of professors as challengers was achieved through the founding of faculty councils.

name: Explicit conflict tactics
authors_terms: ["tactic of explicit conflict", "explicit political conflicts", "explicit conflict tactics"]
definition: A movement tactic of engaging in explicit conflicts through open confrontation, involving harassment, obstruction, coercion, and threatened or actual violence that have detrimental effects on the welfare of incumbents. Specific examples include picketing, demonstrations, sit-ins, strikes, street rallies and marches, boycotts, public protests, violence, and physical clashes.

name: Field-level institutional pressure
authors_terms: ["field-level institutional dynamics", "institutional pressure for change at the field level", "density of adopters", "institutional isomorphism"]
definition: Field-level dynamics that indicate the extent of pressure from other organizations within an organizational field, reflecting institutional isomorphism. It was measured by the diffusion of direct voting systems among Korean universities.

name: Presidential selection system change
authors_terms: ["replacing an existing organizational practice with a new alternative", "adoption of a direct voting system", "replaced the appointment system with a direct voting system"]
definition: Whether or not a given university replaced the appointment system with a direct voting system. Changing the governance mechanism of an organization is a core change because it requires adjustments such as reallocating resources, redistributing decision-making rights, and realigning with external constituencies.

name: Technology novelty
authors_terms: ["novel technologies", "risky novel technologies", "green technologies", "established technologies", "brown technologies", "green fuels", "brown fuels"]
definition: Facilities using green fuels (biomass/biogas, geothermal, small hydro, solar, and wind) were categorized as using novel technologies, while facilities using brown fuels (fuel oil, natural gas, coal, waste natural gas, nuclear, other waste, and 'other') were categorized as using established technologies.

name: Founding rate
definition: Founding is understood as an arrival process, wherein each newly founded independent power plant is an addition to the unit of analysis—here, the state.

name: Founding heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["founding heterogeneity", "technological heterogeneity of foundings", "heterogeneity of foundings", "organizational diversity"]
definition: The heterogeneity of foundings in California and New York every six months between 1980 and 1992, measured with an index that captures the probability that randomly sampled pairs of firms being founded in a given period will have different forms.

name: State financial support
authors_terms: ["state financial support", "avoided costs", "sectorwide tax credit", "tax credit"]
definition: Regulations that lower economic entry barriers for an entire sector by increasing state financial support, such as avoided-cost rates and tax relief for independent power generators.

name: Favorable court rulings
authors_terms: ["court rulings that uphold laws favoring the new independent-power sector", "Supreme Court decision", "favorable court rulings"]
definition: Court rulings that uphold laws creating a new sector are interpreted as endorsements of that sector and thus lower the risks of entering it.

name: Sector density
definition: The number (density) of organizations operating in a sector, which shapes shared definitions of the sector as economically viable.

name: Media coverage
definition: Media mentions indicate the extent to which a sector is considered legitimate; positive media attention both increases its status as a credible site for business and reflects the development of knowledge about the sector.

name: Trade association establishment
definition: Collective actors, such as professional and trade associations, are major sources of normative institutions and can provide form-specific normative support.

name: Propensity for nonlocal syndicate ties
authors_terms: ["propensity for nonlocal ties", "proportion of nonlocal syndicate ties", "nonlocal syndicate ties", "level of risk and uncertainty in a bank's portfolio of syndicate ties"]
definition: The proportion of a bank's syndicate ties initiated in each year that were nonlocal, i.e., the number of nonlocal ties formed in a given year divided by the number of new ties formed in the same year; a syndicate tie is nonlocal when, in all prior observation years, the focal bank was separated from the partner by a path length greater than two.

name: Performance relative to historical aspirations
authors_terms: ["historical aspiration performance", "performance relative to historical aspirations", "relative historical performance"]
definition: The value of the performance metric at t minus its historical aspiration at t, where the historical aspiration level is a weighted moving average of an organization's own experienced performance; historical performance feedback indicates a trend, whether an organization's performance is improving, worsening, or stable over time.

name: Performance relative to social aspirations
authors_terms: ["social aspiration performance", "performance relative to social aspirations", "relative social performance"]
definition: The value of the performance metric minus its social aspiration, where the social aspiration level is based on the current performance of other banks in the network (initially their mean performance, and in finer-grained specifications the performance of size- or role-similar banks); social performance feedback provides a benchmark level, whether an organization's performance is currently above, below, or similar to its peers.

name: Market share
definition: A performance metric adopted for its salience in the investment banking industry, where underwriting fees and margins are relatively constant across the industry.

name: Network status
definition: A performance metric based on a bank's position in the syndicate network; an investment bank's network status is a function of the number and the status of the banks with which it forms underwriting syndicates, and the status of these partners is in turn a function of the number and status of their syndicate partners.

name: Internal selection
definition: Internal selection is an event in which a firm's managers proactively remove a product from the market before it becomes obsolete, an act that frees resources to develop new technologies. Internal selection is proactive and exploratory, since managers use forecasts of future environmental demands to remove products that remain viable today.

name: Partial external selection
authors_terms: ["partial external selection", "partial selection", "partial external selection events"]
definition: Partial external selection occurs when the environment kills a product but leaves its host firm alive. It is the case in which a firm survives, but the economic performance of the focal product is so poor that it is forced from the market.

name: Full external selection
authors_terms: ["full external selection", "full external selection events", "organizational failure"]
definition: Full external selection occurs when a product dies because the environment kills the entire organization in which it resides. It is therefore both a product-level and firm-level occurrence, and the authors assess it both as product-level events and as organizational failure rates.

name: New product introduction
definition: Search comes in numerous forms, but the authors focus on new product development, a vital mode of search in high-velocity settings, one that catalyzes organizational learning and creates relationships between past and future selection events.

name: Cumulative internal selection
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of internal selection events in a firm's past", "cumulative internal selection", "cumulative number of selection events across a firm's life"]
definition: The cumulative number of selection events across a firm's life taps its potential for selection-based learning; it is the sum of the products that were internally selected out of the firm's portfolio over its life, with more distant events discounted.

name: Cumulative partial external selection
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of partial external selection events in a firm's past", "cumulative partial external selection", "cumulative partial selection"]
definition: A firm's cumulative historical experience with partial external selection is the discounted sum of partial external selection events in its past, measured in the same way as cumulative internal selection. By definition, the cumulative number of partial selection events in a firm's past increases monotonically across time.

name: Client exchange manager exit
authors_terms: ["exit of exchange managers from client firms", "exit of marketing managers", "exit"]
definition: The exit of a client firm's exchange managers, which jeopardizes relationship-specific skills and knowledge and severs the social relations that reinforce ongoing buyer-seller relationships.

name: Agency exchange manager exit
authors_terms: ["exit of exchange managers from professional service firms", "exit of account services managers", "exit of creative managers", "exit of other boundary-spanning managers"]
definition: The exit of exchange managers from a professional service firm, which creates uncertainty about that firm's intentions and ability to meet its clients' needs and severs social relations that convey trust and a willingness to accommodate clients.

name: Client exchange manager promotion
authors_terms: ["promotion of exchange managers in client firms", "promotion of marketing managers"]
definition: Promotion of exchange managers within a client firm to positions with broader responsibilities, which can pull them away from exchange relationships and lead them to develop preferences about current and potential exchange partners.

name: Agency exchange manager promotion
authors_terms: ["promotion of exchange managers in professional service firms", "promotion of account services managers"]
definition: Promotion of exchange managers within a professional service firm; newly promoted managers take time to gain experience and acclimate to their new roles, diverting attention away from exchange partners and diminishing the firm's capacity to serve them.

name: Organization size
definition: Size of the focal organization, measured as annual gross revenue for both clients and agencies in the focal year. Large organizations tend to be more bureaucratic, formalized, rigid, and impersonal, with more specialized jobs, than small firms.

name: Number of market ties
authors_terms: ["number of market ties", "number of exchange partners", "roster of clients"]
definition: The number of clients listed by an agency each year or the number of agencies used by a client each year; the number of exchange partners is a reflection of a firm's strategy and capabilities for managing market relationships.

name: Market tie dissolution
definition: A market tie that exists in year t but not in year t+1; dissolution is defined conservatively as completely severed ties between exchange partners.

name: Oppositional religiosity
authors_terms: ["MSA bio-oppositional religiosity", "regional oppositional religiosity", "proportion of adherents of religious denominations that morally oppose a controversial industry"]
definition: The proportion of a region's population made up of adherents of religious denominations that perceive a controversial industry as immoral and oppose it. The higher this proportion, the more likely the region is to be an unfavorable place for starting and running businesses in the controversial industry.

name: Oppositional religiosity of neighboring regions
authors_terms: ["MSA neighbor bio-oppositional religiosity", "proportion of neighboring regions with oppositional religiosity higher than that of a focal region"]
definition: The proportion of a focal region's neighboring regions whose oppositional religiosity to a controversial industry is higher than that of the focal region.

name: Religious social movement mobilization
authors_terms: ["mobilization by religious activists against a morally controversial industry", "MSA religious anti-biotherapeutics mobilization", "religious social movements"]
definition: Mobilization by religious activists against a morally controversial industry in a region, taking the form of social movement events such as protests, letter-writing campaigns, demonstrations, and bans targeting the industry and its participants.

name: Organizational entry rate
authors_terms: ["organizational entry rates", "MSA firm entry rate", "firm entry rates"]
definition: Organizational entry into a regional industry consists of both entrepreneurs founding new firms and pre-existing diversifying companies launching new subsidiaries, with entrepreneurship usually contributing a substantially greater number of new entries in regional clusters. New firm entry is a key to cluster formation and growth.

name: Venture capital investment
authors_terms: ["MSA VC biotherapeutics investments", "venture capital investments in biotherapeutics in an MSA", "venture capital investments into biotherapeutics"]
definition: The U.S. dollar amount invested by venture capitalists in the biotherapeutics firms in a region each year, a proxy for investors' willingness to contribute financial resources and for fixed initial setup costs.

name: Government research grants
authors_terms: ["MSA NIH grants", "grants given by the National Institutes of Health"]
definition: The U.S. dollar amount of grants given by the National Institutes of Health to firms and research organizations in a region each year.

name: Top bioscience universities
authors_terms: ["MSA universities with top bioscience", "universities with top bioscience programs"]
definition: The number of universities in a region with biotechnology-relevant graduate programs, used as a proxy for an MSA's scientific resources and for coordination effects with universities.

name: Non-oppositional religiosity
definition: A yearly proportion of the adherents of denominations that were either neutral or supportive of biotherapeutics in a given year.

name: Quality of nursing care
authors_terms: ["quality of care", "quality of nursing care", "performance", "subunit quality", "workgroup performance"]
definition: Quality of nursing care as assessed by the Rush-Medicus Nursing Process Monitoring Methodology; it evaluates nursing processes, including assessment, planning, intervention, and evaluation of patient care.

name: Technology uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty is the degree to which work to be performed is difficult to understand and complex.

name: Technology instability
definition: Instability is the degree to which unpredictable fluctuations in work techniques and practices occur.

name: Technology variability
definition: Variability is the degree to which workers must engage in many different tasks.

name: Vertical participation
definition: Vertical participation is the degree to which supervisors and subordinates consult together concerning job-related tasks and decisions that must be made.

name: Horizontal participation
definition: Horizontal participation is the degree to which individuals are involved with peers in decision making and defining tasks.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization is the extent to which rules, procedures, and instructions exist and are used.

name: Fit between instability and vertical participation
definition: Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure; for each value of a technology variable there is a best value of structure in terms of high performance.

name: Fit between variability and horizontal participation
definition: Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure; for each value of a technology variable there is a best value of structure in terms of high performance.

name: Fit between uncertainty and formalization
definition: Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure; for each value of a technology variable there is a best value of structure in terms of high performance.

name: Task difficulty
definition: Task difficulty refers to knowledge of cause-effect relationships; it is the analyzability component of task uncertainty, which we labeled task difficulty.

name: Interunit interdependence
definition: The degree of policy and procedural interdependence between focal units and other units as indicated by changes that other units induced in focal units.

name: Boundary-spanning activity
definition: Interactions with members of other units, measured by the frequency of and time spent in such interactions; a mechanism that coordinates relations between units.

name: Participation in decision making
definition: The level of unit members' participation in decision making, measured by the frequency of participation in four decisions and by influence in changes in methods initiated by subordinates.

name: Autonomy
authors_terms: ["autonomy", "discretion at the point of task execution", "independence of action"]
definition: The degree of autonomy of unit members, that is, independence of action generally and independence in handling nonroutine decisions.

name: Commitment to nuclear power
authors_terms: ["commitment to nuclear power", "investment in nuclear technology", "investment in nuclear power", "nuclear investment"]
definition: Utilities with high investments are described as more committed because they allocate more resources toward safely managing their plants than other utilities do. Commitment to nuclear power was calculated as one minus the ratio of nonnuclear power generation to the total energy output of a utility, a measure of the utility's reliance on nuclear power to satisfy energy demand.

name: Earnings growth
authors_terms: ["prior earnings growth", "earnings growth", "prior financial performance", "record of earnings growth"]
definition: The growth in earnings potentially available for additional safety investments and expenditures.

name: Plant reliability
definition: Plant reliability was measured as the ratio of total hours of operation to the total hours a plant could have operated if it had not experienced a forced shut-down.

name: Safety violations
definition: Deviations from predetermined technical specifications are considered violations and signal a plant that is potentially less safe than if specifications were followed. The NRC classified the most severe conditions as a severity 1 violation; severity levels 2, 3, and 4 were also classified major violations, and severity levels 5 and 6 were classified minor violations.

name: Disruptive intergroup conflict
authors_terms: ["intergroup conflict", "disruptive conflict", "conflict levels", "high- and low-conflict organizations"]
definition: Conflict is here defined as disruptive when it becomes sufficiently intense to adversely influence organizational performance.

name: Intergroup strong ties
authors_terms: ["outgroup, or external, strong ties", "strong ties between groups", "external strong ties"]
definition: Strong ties are frequent contacts that almost invariably have affective, often friendly, overtones and may include reciprocal favors; strong ties were defined as involving contacts occurring six or more times in an average week, and external strong ties are those between groups.

name: Intragroup strong ties
authors_terms: ["internal strong ties", "within-group strong ties", "ingroup strong ties"]
definition: Strong ties are frequent contacts that almost invariably have affective, often friendly, overtones and may include reciprocal favors; internal strong ties are those occurring within groups.

name: Network configuration
authors_terms: ["network configuration", "configurations of contacts", "sociometric structure", "configuration of contacts", "structure of group relations"]
definition: The pattern of contacts among groups in an organization; the second part of the article examines the sociometric structure of high- and low-conflict organizations in order to explore the proposition that the configurations of contacts will differ in high- and low-conflict organizations.

name: Resistance to greenmail
authors_terms: ["corporate resistance to greenmail", "resistance to greenmail", "the probability that a company had resisted greenmail"]
definition: The probability that a company resisted a challenging stockholder and refrained from paying greenmail under an imminent threat for control. A greenmail transaction is a private repurchase of a block of stock from a dissident stockholder who poses an explicit or potential threat to top management's control position.

name: Outside directors' equity-to-compensation ratio
authors_terms: ["outside directors' equity ownership relative to their cash compensation for board membership", "the ratio of outside directors' equity divided by their cash income from board compensation", "outside directors' average equity ratio"]
definition: The ratio resulting from dividing outside directors' average equity ownership by their fixed board compensation, proposed as a more comprehensive measure of the incentives influencing outside directors when they weigh the interests of stockholders and management than the absolute size of their holdings.

name: Heterogeneity in outside directors' equity holdings
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in outside directors' equity holdings", "variation in the size of the outside directors' stakes", "variation in outside directors' equity holdings"]
definition: The distribution of equity holdings among a board's outside directors. Given two boards whose outside directors on the average own similar stakes, a board with equal distribution of equity holdings among outside directors is expected to be more vulnerable to free-riding and less active in monitoring top management than a board with highly concentrated equity ownership.

name: Average tenure of outside directors
authors_terms: ["average length of tenure of a board's outside directors", "outside directors' average tenure"]
definition: The average length of tenure of a board's outside directors, where a director's tenure is the total number of years the director has served on the board.

name: Heterogeneity in outside directors' tenure
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in the lengths of outside directors' tenures", "variation in outside directors' tenure", "diversity in their tenures"]
definition: The distribution of tenure lengths among a board's outside directors. Directors who joined a board at similar dates are more likely to interact and form cohorts, whose cohesiveness may increase pressures for conformity and impede the exploration of multiple alternatives.

name: Heterogeneity in outside directors' occupations
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in the occupations of its board's outside directors", "diversity in outside directors' principal occupations", "occupational diversity"]
definition: Diversity in the principal occupations of a board's outside directors, which may promote the airing of different perspectives and reduce the probability of complacency and narrow-mindedness in a board's evaluations of executive proposals.

name: Top management equity-to-compensation ratio
authors_terms: ["top management's equity interests", "top management's equity ratio", "the size of top management's equity interests"]
definition: Top managers' equity interests in a company-as reflected in the dollar value of stock and options owned by the top three executives divided by their income from salary and cash bonuses-reflecting their personal economic incentive to promote the value of the firm and pursue stockholders' interests.

name: Scope of service
definition: Scope of service refers to the degree to which workers view their clients comprehensively; systems high in scope employ workers who take a holistic approach to intervention, use a detailed theoretical framework for diagnosis, and assume numerous intervention roles.

name: Intensity of service
definition: Intensity refers to the amount of time committed to individual clients; services can be very concentrated or nonintensive.

name: Client volitional status
authors_terms: ["client status", "clients' volitional status", "involuntary clients", "percentage of involuntary clients"]
definition: Client status refers to whether the clients of a system enter it voluntarily or involuntarily; when clients are in a system involuntarily, the community is mandating behavior change, which makes therapeutic relationships difficult to establish and such systems must usually be bureaucratic.

name: Coordination
definition: In this article the terms cooperation and coordination are used interchangeably, subsuming coordination under cooperation as a specific form of cooperative activity; the study defined coordination as the use of cooperative methods and differentiated between those used by workers and administrators.

name: Conflict
definition: Conflict is conceptualized as an organizational behavior that occurs and reoccurs during the life of a service delivery system, occurring between individuals and organizations as organizations strive to maximize their control over their dependency on the collective, or as an oppositional process in which one party attempts to change, block, or impede the activities of another.

name: Centrality
definition: Centrality, a measure of power and dominance in interorganizational service delivery systems, is conceptualized as the degree to which a core agency controls client flow.

name: Differentiation
definition: As in single organizations, differentiation in interorganizational structures refers to the degree to which a system is functionally specialized.

name: Service complexity
definition: Whereas differentiation refers to specialization of function, complexity refers to specialization of service, that is, the variety and mix of services a system encompasses.

name: Dissolution of an interorganizational relationship
authors_terms: ["dissolution", "dissolution of the relationship", "likelihood of dissolution", "auditor switching", "severing of exchange relationships"]
definition: The severing of a dyadic interorganizational exchange relationship; the dissolution of an auditor-client relationship was defined as a change in the identity of the client's auditor, except when the change followed a merger or acquisition of the incumbent auditor, a cessation of the auditor's practice, or a merger of the client firm.

name: Change in resource fit
authors_terms: ["change in resource fit", "changes affecting resource fit", "changes in the components of resource fit"]
definition: The fit between one organization's resource needs and another's resource provision, relative to an opportunity set. The research measured changes in the components of resource fit - the changing needs of clients and the changing resources of auditors - rather than resource fit directly.

name: Change in resource requirements
authors_terms: ["change in resource requirements", "changes in clients' resource needs", "changing needs of the clients"]
definition: A reduction in the ability of exchange partners to satisfy resource requirements may result from increases in one organization's resource requirements. For a client, the resource needed from an audit firm is external verification, and the verification task is more demanding the more complex the audit situation.

name: Change in resource provisions
authors_terms: ["change in resource provisions", "changing resources of the auditors", "auditors' resource provisions"]
definition: The capabilities of an audit firm consist of both general auditing expertise and knowledge of issues pertaining to a particular institutional setting, and prior research has noted considerable variation among auditing firms with respect to industry expertise.

name: Change in the set of alternative exchange partners
authors_terms: ["change in the set of alternative exchange partners", "client's set of alternatives", "opportunity set"]
definition: The set of alternatives is composed of the audit firms that can provide some degree of the relevant resource, which consists of both general accounting and industry-specific expertise; all auditors that operate in a client's industry constitute its set of alternatives.

name: Individual attachment
definition: Sources of individual attachment include personal skills, knowledge, and interpersonal relationships; specific organization members constitute the repository of such assets. Individual attachment reflects the prior history of learning and socialization by individuals during their involvement in exchange activities, and it accrues over the period of time the particular organizational representatives are involved in exchange activities rather than with the duration of the relationship.

name: Structural attachment
definition: Sources of organizational attachment include the formalization and standardization of exchange arrangements, such as the establishment of policies and procedures for managing interorganizational transactions; the collectivity, rather than specific individuals, is the repository of these assets. Structural attachment reflects the history of organizational investments made since the formation of the interorganizational relationship and increases as the duration of the relationship increases.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["investor reactions", "market reaction", "abnormal returns", "mean cumulative prediction errors (MCPEs)", "stock price changes"]
definition: The difference between the actual returns and the normal returns is a security's prediction error, or abnormal return; these prediction errors are averaged across firms on each day and accumulated over test intervals to provide mean cumulative prediction errors.

name: Permanent replacement information
authors_terms: ["announcements of the dismissals of key executives containing information about permanent replacements", "firing and permanent replacement announcements", "subsequent appointment announcements"]
definition: Firing announcements are classified by whether they carry information about a permanent replacement for the departing executive; the authors distinguish departure-only, appointment-only, and combined departure and appointment announcements.

name: Successor origin
authors_terms: ["successor origin", "inside and outside succession", "insider and outsider", "inside successor", "outside successors"]
definition: Whether an announced replacement comes from inside or outside the firm; the authors use a strict definition of insider and outsider: outsiders have had no previous employment with a company or any of its subsidiaries.

name: Raider control challenge
definition: Companies challenged by one of eight notorious raiders that had obtained 5 percent or more of the outstanding equity and whose management the raider had publicly challenged; competitors are companies in the same industry grouping as a targeted company, and control companies are publicly traded companies nearest in size to the target companies.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: A company's performance before a raider's appearance, measured as its monthly market-adjusted return, defined as the simple excess return for any company's performance compared to the value-weighted market index for that month, and cumulated over intervals before the 13D filing.

name: Top management turnover
authors_terms: ["top management turnover", "officer turnover", "officer and director turnover"]
definition: Turnover among a company's top executives; the authors established annual and cumulative turnover rates for three categories of officers and directors, including officers, the top executives without positions on their employer's board.

name: Director turnover
definition: Turnover among the members of a company's board of directors, including inside directors, who hold executive positions, and outside directors, who do not hold executive positions in the company on whose board they sat.

name: Age heterogeneity
definition: The dispersion of top management team members' ages within a team. The authors argue that age dissimilarity can result in major differences in beliefs and value systems, affecting integration and cohesion.

name: Organizational tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity on organizational tenure", "heterogeneity on organizational tenure"]
definition: The dispersion of top management team members' tenure within the organization. Heterogeneity on organizational tenure suggests that team members differ in their sets of experiences within an organization and bring varied cognitive perspectives to issues.

name: Team tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity on team tenure", "heterogeneity on team tenure"]
definition: The dispersion of the lengths of time team members have worked together on the top management team. Group tenure similarity is likely to heighten integration and cohesion.

name: University prestige heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in the prestige of the university attended", "heterogeneity on university prestige"]
definition: The dispersion of the prestige of the universities attended by top management team members. The prestige of the university an individual attended is a strong indicator of social class in Japanese society and among managers.

name: Top management team turnover
definition: Turnover occurs when a director's appointment is not renewed. Turnover was examined at both the individual and organizational levels.

name: Technological discontinuities
definition: Discontinuous shifts in an organization's technological environment; when such shifts occur, existing competencies and decision-making processes may no longer match environmental conditions.

name: Environmental jolts
definition: Dramatic shifts in the environment for firms and for industries as a whole, such as regulatory changes. Environmental jolts may be associated with changes in executive team structure and processes.

name: Reorientations
definition: Tushman and Romanelli (1985) defined a reorientation as simultaneous changes in strategy, structure, power, and control systems. Reorientations are discontinuities in the life of a firm.

name: CEO succession
definition: A change in the firm's chief executive; new CEOs often initiate sweeping changes in direction and alter standards of performance for their teams.

name: Time since reorientation
authors_terms: ["time since reorientation", "time since last reorientation", "time since a reorientation has occurred"]
definition: The number of years between consecutive reorientations; in the year a reorientation occurs, time since reorientation is reset to 0.

name: Time since environmental jolt
authors_terms: ["time since environmental jolt", "time since last environmental jolt", "time since an environmental jolt has occurred"]
definition: The number of years elapsed since any of the identified environmental jolts had occurred, set equal to 0 in the year an external jolt occurred.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The number of years a given person was CEO; when a change in CEO (or top executive) occurred, CEO tenure was set back to 0 in that year.

name: CEO experience with reorientations
definition: The total number of reorientations in which a given CEO was present and in the CEO role. Reorientations that occurred while the person was on a firm's executive team but not the CEO were not counted.

name: Executive team change
authors_terms: ["team change", "change in the composition of a senior team", "fluctuation", "entries", "exits"]
definition: Team-level composition and change: change in an executive team is measured by counting in each year the number of executives who were not on the team the previous year and the number of executives who were listed in the prior year but not in the current year.

name: Executive team heterogeneity
definition: The relative heterogeneity (or homogeneity) of an executive team's demographic characteristics, here captured by the coefficient of variation in team tenure and functional heterogeneity.

name: Mean executive team tenure
authors_terms: ["mean team tenure", "mean executive team tenure", "team tenure"]
definition: Mean executive team tenure captures how long members of an executive team have been together, and is a useful proxy for intragroup processes such as the extent of scanning and external communication.

name: Integrated manufacturing
authors_terms: ["integrated manufacturing", "advanced manufacturing technology (AMT)", "total quality management (TQM)", "just-in-time (JIT) inventory control"]
definition: The core thrust of integrated manufacturing is that advanced manufacturing technology (AMT), total quality management (TQM), and just-in-time (JIT) inventory control can work synergistically to create a streamlined, high-quality production system that transforms raw materials into finished products, uninterrupted by logistical impediments.

name: Task characteristics of knowledge work
authors_terms: ["task characteristics of knowledge work", "task uncertainty", "task interdependence", "knowledge work"]
definition: The transition from touch labor to knowledge work has been discussed in terms of task uncertainty, which increases with the complexity, variety, and unusualness of tasks, and task interdependence, or the need for individuals to rely on or collaborate with others to complete work.

name: Compensation system
definition: At their root, compensation systems represent a network of contingent promises for reward and the basis for an inducements-contribution exchange. There are three dimensions upon which rewards may be contingent: performance, job content, and personal characteristics.

name: Individual incentives
definition: In conventional factories, rewards are primarily administered to individuals for individual performance; individual incentives are the compensation practice that explicitly rewards performance output per se through, for instance, piece-rate pay and incentives.

name: Group incentives
definition: Aggregate incentives are based on the assumption that task uncertainty, interdependence, and complexity require cooperation among employees; team-based rewards promote an environment in which individuals' goals are intertwined.

name: Hourly wages
definition: Within the category of job-contingent rewards, the most common mode of compensation in manufacturing plants is the hourly wage rate; to ensure continuity, employees are paid for their time on the job.

name: Salary
definition: Placing employees on salary eliminates distinctions between sectors of employment, signaling that production workers are viewed as equal partners in the operation, and is intended to engender a climate of professionalism conducive to cooperation.

name: Seniority-based pay
authors_terms: ["seniority-based pay", "seniority-based compensation", "pay based on company seniority"]
definition: In the traditional factory, the most prevalent form of person-contingent pay is that based on company seniority; seniority-based compensation rewards loyalty to a firm and experience at a minimum.

name: Skill-based pay
definition: With skill-based pay, employees are rewarded for learning new jobs and developing a broad array of talents.

name: Organizational inertia
authors_terms: ["sources of inertia", "organizational inertia", "structural inertia", "sources of organizational conservatism"]
definition: Once in place, administrative systems, such as compensation systems, are notoriously intractable; as systems become institutionalized, precedents tend to become normative standards of behavior, and managerial preferences, values, traditions, and other sources of organizational conservatism may mitigate the administrative alignments dictated by new technology.

name: Individual-level characteristics
authors_terms: ["individual-level characteristics", "individual characteristics of top managers", "individual context", "personal attributes"]
definition: Personal attributes of top managers; at the individual level, personal attributes explain, in part, why different people exposed to the same situation perceive it differently. In this study the individual context is represented by top managers' experience, role, and type of education.

name: Executive level
definition: A manager's level in the organization and its top management team; the information available to and used by decision makers varies with their level in both an organization and its top management team, and higher-level managers are those most responsible for interpreting issues involved with aligning an organization's strategy, structure, and environment.

name: Position tenure
definition: Experience in a given position: the number of years a respondent had been in a current position; less experienced managers are less inclined to recognize the strategic and political implications of associated organizational issues.

name: Institutional tenure
definition: The number of years a respondent had been at his or her present institution; individuals with long tenures in an organization have vested interests in the status quo and hence are more likely to interpret issues as having more strategic implications for their organizations.

name: Academic background
definition: A respondent's area of formal education, used as a surrogate for his or her knowledge and skill base; because of differences in personal values, cognitive preferences, and specialized knowledge, members of different specializations are expected to use different cognitive models in interpreting an issue.

name: Information-processing capacity
definition: The perceived formality, interaction, and degree of participation among the top managers involved in executive decision processes in an institution; teams with strong information-processing capacity are more likely to perceive an organizational issue as controllable because they have a sense of mastery over the issues they confront.

name: Political activity
definition: The extent of political activity in an institution, a political environment being characterized by changing goals and preferences represented by shifting coalitions, by the push and pull of different interests, and by information use that supports positions or discredits others.

name: Top management team identity
authors_terms: ["identity", "identity held by a top management team", "organization's identity", "strong identity", "group identities"]
definition: A top management team's beliefs about various facets of its organization's cultural values; an organization's identity is defined as what its members believe to be central, enduring, and distinctive about the organization, and such perceptions serve as a reference point for gauging the importance of issues.

name: Organization-level characteristics
definition: Organization-level features, in this study size, type, and ownership, that provide a social setting and architecture affecting perceptions of organizational issues and that form an organization-level context for interpretation.

name: Organization size
definition: The size of the institution, an organization-level factor that creates inertial forces; managers in large organizations often have severe difficulties contemplating or effecting change and large organizations have more elaborate structures and greater diversity among the units top management oversees.

name: Organization type
definition: The type of the institution, reflecting its level of specialization and the range or type of products and services it provides; the type and ownership of an organization set parameters defining what information is important and what is to be ignored during interpretive processes.

name: Organization ownership
definition: Whether ownership of the organization is public or private; ownership provides a social setting that affects perceptions of organizational issues, and managers in publicly owned organizations must more often address the concerns of multiple and diverse stakeholders.

name: Strategic interpretation
authors_terms: ["strategic interpretation", "strategic interpretations of organizational issues", "interpretation of an issue as strategic"]
definition: An issue was defined as strategic if it (1) could alter an institution's position in the market, (2) could significantly affect the whole institution, and (3) could affect the institution's goals and missions.

name: Political interpretation
authors_terms: ["political interpretation", "political interpretations of organizational issues", "interpretation of an issue as political"]
definition: An issue was defined as political if it (1) involved influence attempts among individuals and groups, (2) generated conflict over control of the issue, and (3) was associated with bargaining, compromise, and negotiation among top administrators over its meaning.

name: Issue content
authors_terms: ["issue content", "content of the issue", "characteristics or content of the issue"]
definition: Interpreting an organizational issue is a function not only of the different contexts in which knowledge of that issue is manifested, but also of the content of the issue itself; here it is represented by six issues that were deemed important to managers in institutions of higher education.

name: Group-level context
definition: Group characteristics of a top management team that are not aggregates of individual-level descriptors, including its information-processing structure, its political activity, and its members' shared sense of identity, which are systematically related to the interpretation of organizational issues by individual members of the team.

name: Functional diversity
authors_terms: ["functional diversity", "work history diversity", "diversity of members' work histories"]
definition: The extent to which members of a top management team differ in the functional backgrounds they bring to the team; the authors also refer to it as the diversity of members' work histories.

name: Team tenure
authors_terms: ["team tenure", "length of time the members of a group have been together"]
definition: The length of time the members of a group have been together.

name: Organizational scanning
definition: Organizational scanning refers to the acquisition of information about an environment by organization members and the subsequent communication of relevant information.

name: Performance monitoring
definition: Performance monitoring refers to the ongoing gathering of real-time information about the effectiveness of an organization's operations in fulfilling goals and the requirements of stakeholders.

name: Centralization
definition: The centralization of decision-making authority, a structural characteristic that directly affects the extent to which executives notice environmental information; in highly centralized organizations lower-level members are not involved in important decision making.

name: Perceptual accuracy of environmental instability
authors_terms: ["perceptual accuracy", "congruence", "match between environmental instability and managers' perceptions of environmental instability"]
definition: Perceptual accuracy, or congruence, is the match between perceived environmental characteristics and objective environmental characteristics; the instability congruence score captures how closely a team's perceived instability matches its industry's actual instability.

name: Perceptual accuracy of environmental munificence
authors_terms: ["perceptual accuracy", "congruence", "match between environmental munificence and managers' perceptions of environmental munificence"]
definition: Perceptual accuracy, or congruence, is the match between perceived environmental characteristics and objective environmental characteristics; the munificence congruence score captures how closely a team's perceived munificence matches its industry's actual munificence.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Environmental instability reflects unpredictable change or variability in an organization's environment.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence is the availability of resources and extent to which an environment supports sustained stability or growth.

name: Perceived environmental instability
definition: Top managers' perceptions of the degree of unpredictable change or variability in their firm's environment, assessed with Likert-type questionnaire items based on the work of Duncan (1972) and Bourgeois (1985).

name: Perceived environmental munificence
definition: Top managers' perceptions of the availability of resources and the extent to which the environment supports sustained stability or growth, assessed with questionnaire items developed by the author.

name: Director sex
definition: Director sex was measured as a dichotomous variable, with 0 representing women and 1 representing men. The authors treat sex as distinct from directors' experience-based characteristics.

name: Board committee membership
authors_terms: ["committee membership", "odds of committee membership", "membership on a given board committee", "standing committees of corporate boards"]
definition: These subgroups of directors are critical structures for the conduct of a board's work since each is chartered with specific authorization, strategic, and oversight duties contributing to the board's total corporate governance task. Each of these committees contributes in a specific way to the overall governance task of a board of directors.

name: Experience-based director characteristics
definition: The experience-based director characteristics investigated in this study were director type (insider or outsider), board tenure, occupation (business or nonbusiness), business interlocks (directorships of other corporate boards), and nonbusiness interlocks (directorships of noncorporate institutions such as social, cultural, educational, and religious organizations).

name: Director type
definition: Inside directors have day-to-day familiarity with company performance, and outside directors are valued for their objectivity and independent judgment. Inside directors are defined as all current or former employees of a company or its subsidiaries and all relatives of such persons, and all other directors are defined as outsiders.

name: Board tenure
definition: Tenure on a board was measured in years. Generally, directors who have served on a board for several years are valued for their business experience and their familiarity with company- and industry-specific factors.

name: Director occupation
definition: Occupation was measured as a dichotomous variable, with directors whose primary employer was a corporation, financial institution, or law firm classified as holding business occupations and all other directors categorized as holding nonbusiness occupations. Directors whose primary occupation is business are valued for their business experience.

name: Business interlocks
authors_terms: ["business interlocks", "corporate directorships", "business interlocks (directorships of other corporate boards)"]
definition: Business interlocks were defined as the total number of concurrent directorships of other corporations or financial institutions a director held; directors who are members of several corporate boards are valued for their business experience.

name: Nonbusiness interlocks
authors_terms: ["nonbusiness interlocks", "noncorporate directorships", "nonbusiness interlocks (directorships of noncorporate institutions)"]
definition: Nonbusiness interlocks were defined as the total number of concurrent directorships or trusteeships of political, cultural, educational, religious, or other nonprofit institutions a director held; directors who serve on other nonbusiness boards are valued for their experience with a wide network of contacts.

name: High Performance Work Practices
authors_terms: ["High Performance Work Practices", "systems of High Performance Work Practices", "work practices", "practices scales"]
definition: Human resource policies and procedures, including comprehensive employee recruitment and selection procedures, incentive compensation and performance management systems, and extensive employee involvement and training, that can improve the knowledge, skills, and abilities of a firm's employees, increase their motivation and enhance retention; the paper adopts the U.S. Department of Labor (1993) designation High Performance Work Practices.

name: Employee turnover
definition: The level of turnover within each firm, which includes both voluntary employee departures (quitting) and involuntary ones (firings); the author assumes that low rates of turnover are preferred to high rates.

name: Organizational productivity
definition: Organizational productivity, measured by the logarithm of sales per employee, a widely used single index that can also be used to estimate the dollar value of returns for investments; the author notes that productivity is not synonymous with profitability.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: Firm-level financial performance, for which the author distinguishes measurements of accounting profits from economic profits: economic profits represent the net cash flows that accrue to shareholders and are represented by capital (stock) market returns, whereas accounting profits reflect an historical perspective; both a market-based and an accounting measure are used.

name: Internal fit
authors_terms: ["internal fit", "complementarities or synergies among High Performance Work Practices", "fit as moderation", "fit as matching"]
definition: Internal fit is the first of the complementarities described by Baird and Meshoulam (1988); their primary proposition was that firm performance will be enhanced to the degree that firms adopt human resource management practices that complement and support each another.

name: External fit
authors_terms: ["external fit", "alignment of a firm's system of High Performance Work Practices with its competitive strategy"]
definition: A second form of complementarity, Baird and Meshoulam's (1988) external fit, occurs at the intersection of a firm's system of HRM practices and its competitive strategy.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Porter (1985) provided the dominant typology of competitive strategies in the business policy literature; the types specified are cost leadership, differentiation, and focus.

name: Functional background
authors_terms: ["functional background", "functional area work experience", "functional work histories", "proportions of total years of experience in each of the functional areas"]
definition: "Functional background" refers to an executive's past work experience in jobs within functional areas of organizations. Operationally, the set of proportions of an executive's total years of work experience occurring in each functional area defines the executive's functional background.

name: Perceived environmental change
authors_terms: ["changes executives perceive in their organizations' environments", "changes in an organization's environment", "perceived environmental changes"]
definition: The changes an executive perceives in his or her organization's environment, studied as perceived changes rather than perceived steady state conditions. It is measured as the number of important changes the executive reported in each environmental sector.

name: Perceived effectiveness change
authors_terms: ["changes executives perceive in their organizations' effectiveness", "changes in the organization's effectiveness"]
definition: The changes an executive perceives in his or her organization's effectiveness, studied as perceived changes rather than perceived steady state conditions, and grouped into categories of organizational effectiveness.

name: Selective perception
definition: What executives take cognizance of, what they note, what they do heed out of all that they might heed.

name: Reward linkage of the perceptual area
definition: The extent to which the connection between cognitively directed, functionally related actions and intrinsic or extrinsic rewards associated with such actions is reliable and conceptually and temporally short and where the rewards are highly salient.

name: Organizational size
definition: Large organizations are more visible and receive more attention from regulators, the media, and the public, and they are therefore held to higher standards of institutional compliance than smaller organizations.

name: Female employee representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of female employees", "percentage of an organization's employees who were women"]
definition: Organizations' female employees are a constituency that has been identified as important in driving responsiveness to work-family problems. Organizations that have a high proportion of female workers are more dependent on the constituency that traditionally makes the strongest demands for work-family accommodations and should therefore be more responsive.

name: Female manager representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of women in management positions", "percentage of an organization's managers who were women"]
definition: A possible mitigation to the effectiveness of female employees as a constituency is the fact that they often have less power in organizations than their male counterparts. The proportion of women in management positions may better capture the dependence of the organization on women.

name: Public sector
definition: Public sector organizations are responsive to social welfare concerns because of their goal of delivering social service and because they are not held to exclusively economic standards of performance.

name: Work-family program diffusion in the organizational field
authors_terms: ["proportion of other organizations within an organization's industry adopting work-family policies and programs", "degree of work-family program diffusion", "control"]
definition: The legitimacy of norms and practices within an organizational field increases with the degree of their diffusion in the field. Organizations that fail to meet the level of work-family responsiveness of their organizational field suffer damage to their reputations.

name: Attentiveness to other organizations' practices
definition: Attentiveness to other organizations' policies and practices allows a focal organization to compare itself to the standards of the organizational field and make necessary adjustments.

name: Countervailing power
authors_terms: ["countervailing power", "unemployment rate for women in the organization's industry"]
definition: If the dependence of organizations on constituents is balanced with dependence of the constituents on the organization, the likelihood of resistance to pressures for institutional conformity increases. Organizations are less responsive to the work-family demands of employees when the employees making those demands face a high unemployment rate.

name: Technical benefits from work-family responsiveness
authors_terms: ["benefits from work-family responsiveness", "problems when employees with young children miss work"]
