definition: For some organizations, work-family programs do much to solve the internal problems of organization and production. Organizations that have greater problems than others when parents miss work because of problems with their children receive a greater benefit from work-family programs.

name: Responsiveness to work-family issues
authors_terms: ["responsiveness to work-family issues", "level of responsiveness to institutional pressures for employer involvement in work-family issues", "strategic response to institutional pressure"]
definition: Responsiveness to work-family issues is the degree of organizational compliance with institutional pressures for employer involvement in work-family issues, coded into ordered strategic responses ranging from acquiescence, compromise and avoidance to defiance (Oliver, 1991).

name: Downside risk
authors_terms: ["downside risk", "root lower partial moment", "RLPM", "lower partial moment", "downside outcomes", "failure to perform at an aspired-to level"]
definition: Downside risk is measured as a function of the magnitude of performance shortfalls relative to an aspiration level; the lower partial moment refers to the inclusion of only the left-hand (downside) tail of the returns distribution in the calculation.

name: Financial performance
definition: The authors focus on a profitability measure of performance, using return on assets: return on equity and return on assets are two common accounting-based measures of performance, and the study used average ROA over the five-year period as the return measure.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack resources accumulate during periods of performance and provide a cushion allowing organizations to maintain more stable aspirations when faced with performance variability than would be possible without slack resources.

name: Returns variability
authors_terms: ["returns standard deviation", "standard deviation of returns", "variability measures of risk", "variance measures of risk"]
definition: Operational measures of risk reflecting variability in accounting or stock returns; such variability measures fail to differentiate upside and downside outcomes.

name: Timely feedback
definition: By timely feedback, we mean information that allows the investor to stay up to date on the performance of a venture. This information will be on both the good and bad consequences of decisions.

name: Investor influence
definition: Influence refers to the extent to which individuals affected by a decision can directly affect the outcome of the decision.

name: Procedural justice
definition: Procedural justice concerns the fairness of the formal procedures used to make decisions. According to procedural justice theory, individuals perceive as just those decision-making procedures that provide assurance that their self-interests are protected.

name: Trust in the entrepreneur
authors_terms: ["trust in an entrepreneur", "trust in the entrepreneur", "trust"]
definition: Venture capitalists' assessment of the extent to which they believed a CEO to be honest, sincere, and trustworthy.

name: Decision commitment
authors_terms: ["commitment to decisions", "decision commitment", "commitment to the entrepreneur's decisions"]
definition: The extent to which venture capitalists supported the strategic directions taken by the CEOs.

name: Investor monitoring
definition: The extent to which the investors sought additional performance reports and documentation.

name: Propensity to reinvest
authors_terms: ["propensity to reinvest", "willingness to invest in the venture", "investing"]
definition: Whether investors had taken or would take every opportunity to invest in the venture.

name: Outcome-based incentive plan
definition: Outcome-based control involves relatively little managerial supervision of employees, reliance on straightforward, objective measures of performance, and use of compensation schemes that are based on these outcome measures. At the research site the plan was a bonus program paying a base wage plus a cash bonus when quarterly sales exceeded a prespecified goal.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Outcome-based incentive plans are expected to have both short- and long-term effects on organizational performance; the authors used two short-term measures, store sales and profitability per square foot, and one long-term measure, customer satisfaction.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The intensity of the competition faced by a retail store, constructed from the number and type of competitors in its trade area; stores with a higher value on competition were located in more intensely competitive areas.

name: Upscale customer profile
definition: The construct of upscale customers was measured in terms of income, age, college education, and employment characteristics; an upscale store's trade area had a higher median household income, an older population, and larger percentages of both college-educated and white-collar individuals.

name: Supervisory monitoring
definition: A behavior-based control in place at all stores prior to the implementation of outcome-based compensation, which continued to be used even after the implementation, was sales managers' supervision and monitoring of sales consultants' efforts.

name: Social similarity between CEO and compensation chair
definition: Social capital viewed as based on social similarity, the shared affiliations or activities that indicate "how" one knows someone; the authors assess it as overlap between the backgrounds of a firm's CEO and the chair of its compensation committee.

name: CEO global social status
authors_terms: ["CEO absolute or global status", "CEO global status", "absolute social capital"]
definition: CEO absolute or global status, that is, social capital relative to structurally equivalent others (other CEOs), reflecting the extent and prestige of an individual's social resources.

name: Compensation chair global social status
authors_terms: ["compensation chair's global status", "compensation committee chairs of higher social status than other compensation committee chairs"]
definition: The absolute status of the chairperson of the compensation committee relative to other compensation committee chairs, reflecting the extent and prestige of that individual's social resources.

name: Local social status
authors_terms: ["local status", "status relative to the compensation committee chair", "relative social capital"]
definition: Relative social capital in the dyad: an individual's status compared to that of the other member of the CEO–compensation chair dyad, evaluated with a status index standardized on the full sample so that a CEO scoring higher than his chair is in fact higher in raw status.

name: Relational social status
authors_terms: ["relational status", "status pairings", "high-status CEO paired with a low-status compensation chair"]
definition: The relationships of a CEO and a compensation chair to their respective groups and to the other member of a dyad, captured by pairing the CEO's status relative to other CEOs with the chair's status relative to other compensation chairs.

name: CEO compensation
definition: The compensation paid to the firm's chief executive officer; the study's dependent variable is the CEO's cash compensation (base and bonus).

name: Private company ownership
definition: Chinese organizations are classified into three types: state (federal)-owned, privately owned, and collective-hybrids, enterprises typically owned by local governments that produce products for competitive markets. Private companies do not have the institutional protection of government ownership that state-owned and collective-hybrid companies do.

name: Importance of business connections
authors_terms: ["business connections are more important to their success", "importance of a connection", "importance of personal connections"]
definition: All Chinese managers will use guanxi, but these connections will be seen as even more important by those with less structural support.

name: Connections as defense against threats
authors_terms: ["defense against threats", "protect against threats", "reliance on connections as a defense against threats"]
definition: Those who rely on their business connections as a substitute for a stable rule of law would be expected to see them as primarily defensive, that is, as needed to help them face fundamental threats, such as expropriation and extortion.

name: Government connections
authors_terms: ["connections with individuals who hold positions in government", "government connections", "connections in government", "good connections in government"]
definition: Private-company managers will use personal connections to government officials to substitute for the government protection that state-owned and collective-hybrid companies secure structurally, via government ownership.

name: Trust in connections
definition: Private-company executives will seek to build relationships that are deeper in trust (closer guanxi) than those sought by executives with structural protection; this depth of relationship should be reflected in reports of greater trust in connections among those who most depend on them for protection.

name: Nonreciprocated gift giving
definition: Although guanxi often involves the exchange of gifts, these gifts are viewed as investments in the relationship; gift giving is expected to cultivate connections.

name: Employment variability
definition: The degree of variation in organizational employment levels over time. It was measured with the coefficient of variation in number of employees, standardizing variation units across firms of all sizes, because organizations avoid employment variability by controlling both downward and upward variability.

name: Short-term bonus pay
authors_terms: ["short-term bonuses", "bonus-to-base ratio", "short-term bonus pay", "degree of emphasis on short-term bonus pay"]
definition: The extent to which an employee group's pay is based on short-term bonuses, measured as the organization-level emphasis on short-term bonus pay. Bonus pay was typically a function of individual and business performance combined.

name: Long-term incentives
definition: The extent to which pay is tied to the long-term performance of the organization, operationally the average number of employees eligible for performance-based payments that would not be available to those employees during the next year.

name: Nationalism norms
definition: A condition of mind among members of a nationality, for whom loyalty and pride and belief in their nationalism is foremost; nationalism promotes norms of conduct and sets expectations for conformity to these norms. In Finland nationalism comprised values, principles, and beliefs, foremost among them the belief that use of the Finnish language was paramount for the establishment of a national identity.

name: Language of publication
authors_terms: ["language of publication", "Finnish-language newspapers", "Swedish-language newspapers", "language of publication chosen by a newspaper at the time of founding"]
definition: The language in which a newspaper was published at the time of founding. During the period of Finnish nationalism, Finnish was institutionally favored as the appropriate language for newspaper publication, so the language of publication is the organizational characteristic strongly mandated by the nationalism norm.

name: Organizational founding rate
definition: The instantaneous probability that the population experiences the birth of a new newspaper organization; founding is defined as the start of a newspaper's publication, and the data are coded as a single series of repeatable events since the population experiences multiple foundings.

name: Local language composition
authors_terms: ["Swedish-speaking city", "predominantly Swedish-speaking locales", "language spoken by locale", "numbers of Finnish and Swedish speakers in each city"]
definition: The language composition of a locale, that is, the relative presence of Swedish and Finnish speakers in a given city; potential readership, indicated by the number of Finnish or Swedish speakers in each locale, is the most important indicator of newspaper demand.

name: Partner reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "partner reputation", "management reputation", "product quality reputation", "financial performance reputation"]
definition: Reputation is a latent construct that may vary with the stakeholder queried about it; for this study the stakeholder of principal interest was a partner in an alliance, and reputation was operationally defined as the perceptions of the representative of a respondent firm of its partner's characteristics. Reputation can reflect an alliance partner's characteristics in the areas of management, product quality, and financial position.

name: Prior affiliation between partners
definition: Affiliation, broadly defined as prior market contact, is suggested to affect alliance success: it allows a firm to know a partner better and should build trust between partners and a mutual understanding of how the companies work together. Prior relationship between partners was measured as the extent to which the two firms had a prior affiliation as customer and supplier, competitors, or partners of another type.

name: Shared decision making
authors_terms: ["shared decision making", "degree of shared decision making", "mutual involvement"]
definition: The degree to which partners invest in and are involved in the relationship; a high level of mutual involvement in the strategic decision making of the alliance acts as both a signaling and a monitoring mechanism by establishing and building trust and commitment, and the ability to appropriate the knowledge resident in a partner requires close involvement in an alliance and its decision-making processes.

name: Similarity between alliance partners
authors_terms: ["similarities between partners", "strategic similarities", "similarities in strategic content", "similarities in organizational processes", "organizational fit", "strategic fit"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's capabilities and processes are similar or related to those of its alliance partner, measured on a range of organizational attributes. Exploratory factor analysis supported two types of similarities: in strategic content and in organizational processes, paralleling the distinction between strategic and organizational fit.

name: Alliance outcomes
authors_terms: ["alliance outcomes", "alliance performance", "alliance success", "sustained benefits to partner firms", "initial satisfaction", "satisfaction"]
definition: The primary alliance outcome measure was a three-item scale reporting performance as perceived by a partner organization in the alliance, reflecting overall satisfaction with the alliance, the degree to which it has met the goals of the partner, and its contributions to the partner's core competencies. A second outcome measure, initial satisfaction, asked partners to assess their level of satisfaction in the first year of an alliance.

name: Administrative form of an alliance
authors_terms: ["administrative form", "joint equity position", "alliance form", "equity or nonequity"]
definition: The administrative form of an agreement may indicate the motives of the partner companies and have a considerable impact on the outcomes expected; it was measured by joint equity position. If equity in the relationship and outcomes were shared to any extent by the partners, the alliance was coded 1; if one partner maintained all equity and proceeds were shared by some predetermined contractual method, the alliance was coded 0.

name: Performance context
definition: A firm's performance relative to a referent benchmark that decision makers use in judging the level of firm performance. When performance exceeds the referent, decision makers have little incentive to entertain risk; when performance falls short of the referent, they may accept greater risk.

name: Realized credit risk
definition: The observed downside risk resulting from operational policy choices about the degree of risk acceptable when extending credit. Realized credit risk results when managers accept loans and other investments that have a higher probability of borrower delinquency or default.

name: Realized interest-rate risk
definition: The realized downside risk resulting from interest-rate policy decisions. When managers accept higher levels of interest-rate risk, they either intentionally or mistakenly mismatch the repricing of the firm's assets and liabilities so that the interest rate paid on liabilities rises faster than the interest earned on assets.

name: Realized liquidity risk
definition: A measure of the ability of a firm to meet its debt obligations. Liquidity risk results when costless assets (such as cash on hand) are unavailable to satisfy those obligations; hence, it is a threat to firm solvency.

name: Recoverable slack
definition: Slack refers to the excess resources available to a firm. Recoverable slack represents excess expenses relative to rival firms and comes closest to reflecting the concept of 'X-efficiency'.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Within the S&L industry, ownership structure is distinguished by a firm's charter: savings and loans can be chartered as either stock (shareholder-owned) or mutual (depositor-owned) institutions. The two forms differ in the sharing of the costs and benefits of monitoring.

name: Leverage
definition: Leverage represents a firm's amount of debt financing relative to its equity financing. Debt incurs a fixed cost of capital, so highly leveraged firms have strong incentives to prefer investments promising higher payoffs and exhibiting higher risk.

name: Regulatory supervision laxity
definition: The degree to which regulatory oversight of S&Ls was lax. Where regulatory supervision was lax, S&Ls could pursue riskier strategies; regulatory supervision may substitute for ownership control when regulation prescribes limits on strategic and operational choices.

name: State regulation
definition: Whether an S&L is chartered through state rather than federal regulatory offices. During the period of the study, state-chartered institutions generally enjoyed more liberal limits on their investment powers than federal S&Ls, and the type of charter can affect the nature of a firm's operating activities and the assets in which it invests.

name: Operating performance
definition: Firm performance captured through operating cash flow, which is measured as the ratio of operating cash flows to total assets and more closely reflects the actual operating performance of a firm than ROA.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity taps the information-processing demands that largely result from heterogeneity in an organization's primary domain.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Instability focuses on the degree of unexpected change that occurs in a task environment.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence was an index that assessed the availability of external resources to support growth.

name: Centralized control over goal formation
authors_terms: ["centralized control", "centralization of goal formation", "centralized goal formation"]
definition: Centralized control taps which level had the most authority (i.e., the vertical locus of authority) over goal formation for six union activities; activities included organizing, bargaining, and politics.

name: National union size
definition: National union size is an index based on a union's membership, total assets, and total annual dues receipts.

name: Industrial diversity
definition: Industrial diversity assesses the breadth of industries, defined in terms of two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, in which a union actively sought new members from 1986 to June 1990.

name: Average local size
definition: Average local size taps the human resource and political capacity of local unions and is measured as the natural logarithm of average local size.

name: Elaboration of representative structures
authors_terms: ["representative structures", "representative systems", "elaboration of national union representative structures"]
definition: The representative structure comprises the constitutionally recognized bodies and offices empowered to make decisions and the formal (e.g., elections) and informal (e.g., caucuses) channels for members' influence.

name: Bargaining unit capacity
definition: Potential bargaining unit capacity captured the extent to which a union's primary jurisdiction could generate locals with members who were able to participate in decision making and willing to pay for the costs of representative structures.

name: Membership heterogeneity
definition: Membership heterogeneity is an index that measured diversity in three member attributes: race, gender, and white-collar/blue-collar employment.

name: Administrative structural differentiation
definition: Administrative structural differentiation assessed the degree of departmentalization, divisionalization, and specialization within an administrative system.

name: Administrative rationalization
definition: Administrative rationalization assessed the degree to which tasks were standardized, formalized, and coordinated among units and information was clearly communicated to union personnel.

name: Concentration of decision making
authors_terms: ["concentration of decision making", "dispersion of decision making"]
definition: Concentration of decision making tapped the degree to which decision making and influence were shared throughout a union.

name: Pay anomaly
authors_terms: ["pay anomaly", "payment anomalies", "pay anomalies", "deviations from the going rate", "comparison pay anomalies"]
definition: Deviations from the going rate, the compensation level typically paid by similar firms to comparable individuals occupying similar posts, which the authors term payment anomalies. The time t pay anomaly experienced by executive i is the deviation of actual pay from the estimated comparison level of pay.

name: Change in executive cash compensation
authors_terms: ["changes in executive cash compensation", "subsequent-period pay changes", "changes in compensation", "cash compensation awards", "t + 1 changes in executives' cash compensation"]
definition: Changes in executive i's cash compensation between time t and time t + 1. The dependent variable is the logarithmic change in cash compensation, where the payments compared are the actual cash compensation reported at times t + 1 and t.

name: Work-family responsiveness
definition: The degree to which a company has adopted a broad range of family-supportive benefits and policies designed to help employees manage their work and family lives. It is measured both as an overall level of responsiveness and as specific forms of response.

name: Percentage of female employees
authors_terms: ["percentage of women in an organization's workforce", "percentage of female employees on a firm's current payroll"]
definition: The percentage of women employed by the company at the time of the survey, reflecting the organization's dependence on female labor.

name: Growth in female representation
authors_terms: ["growth in the percentage of women in their labor forces", "change in the percentage of employees who were women"]
definition: The change in the percentage of employees who were women over the five years preceding the survey.

name: Top management team composition
definition: Whether the top management group includes at least one member who is a woman or who has had personal experience with issues such as dual-career parenting, single parenting, or elder care.

name: Industry
authors_terms: ["the industry that the company operated in", "industry-level institutional effects"]
definition: The industry sector in which the company operates, used to capture industry-level institutional effects on work-family responsiveness.

name: Geographic region
authors_terms: ["geographic region in which his or her company operated", "regional differences"]
definition: The region of the country in which the company operates, reflecting region-level institutional pressures such as state legislation, regional media attention, and imitation among neighboring organizations.

name: Employee information gathering
authors_terms: ["employee-information-gathering measure", "procedures for obtaining information about employees' needs and concerns"]
definition: The extent to which a company has organizational procedures for gathering information about its employees, such as employee surveys and exit interviews.

name: Issue salience to HR executives
authors_terms: ["salience of work and family issues", "salience of the increased presence of women", "salience of changes in the structure of families"]
definition: The relative salience of work and family issues in the minds of human resource executives, reflected in what workforce changes they mention as having most affected their firms.

name: Perceived productivity impact
authors_terms: ["perceived productivity impact", "beliefs about the likely impact of changing demographics on productivity"]
definition: Human resource executives' judgments about how likely the growing number of dual-career couples and single employees with dependents is to affect workforce productivity, absenteeism, turnover, relocation refusals, and commitment if not responded to adequately.

name: Managerial interpretation of work-family issues
authors_terms: ["managerial interpretations", "strategic issue interpretation", "issue interpretation variables", "managers' sense-making activities"]
definition: The active processing of information about work and family issues by managers: whether these issues are noticed by key decision makers and whether managers perceive them as likely to affect the organization's functioning if not addressed.

name: Within-team dissent
definition: Team members try to alter the course of discussion by expressing divergent opinions as to the implications of facts and information or the proper course of action; dissent provides information to the decision process.

name: Perceived loyalty
definition: The belief that an individual might hold that others in a decision process will not do him or her harm or take advantage should an opportunity arise to do so; the characteristic of disinclination toward opportunism.

name: Perceived competence
definition: The belief that the other individuals in a decision process are competent in their professed areas of expertise; the extent to which team members are perceived as being skillful and reliable in performing their jobs.

name: Decision quality
definition: The quality of the strategic decision, measured against organizational goals and assessed in terms of the information used, fit with current strategy, financial responsibility, and contribution to overall effectiveness.

name: Decision commitment
authors_terms: ["decision commitment", "commitment to decisions", "team member commitment to decisions"]
definition: Team members' effort toward decision implementation; the extent to which team members are willing to stick with the decision through implementation and exert effort to see it implemented.

name: Stakeholder power
definition: Stakeholder power exists where one social actor, A, can get another social actor, B, to do something that B would not have otherwise done.

name: Stakeholder legitimacy
definition: Stakeholder legitimacy is a generalized perception or assumption that the actions of an entity are desirable, proper, or appropriate within some socially constructed system of norms, values, beliefs, and definitions.

name: Stakeholder urgency
definition: Stakeholder urgency is a multidimensional notion that includes both criticality and temporality, with a stakeholder claim considered to be urgent both when it is important and when delay in paying attention to it is unacceptable.

name: Stakeholder salience
definition: The degree to which managers give priority to competing stakeholder claims.

name: CEO values
definition: Values that shape levels of selectivity and intensity through their influence on what dominates an individual's perceptual field and demands mental focus.

name: CEO other-regarding values
definition: Values at the other-regarding-system-centered end of a continuum, emphasizing benefit to others and the larger social system rather than profit maximization.

name: Cumulative stakeholder attributes
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of the stakeholder attributes", "cumulative attributes"]
definition: The cumulative number of the stakeholder attributes of power, legitimacy, and urgency perceived to be present.

name: Corporate performance
definition: The outcomes of corporate activity, considered through corporate social performance variables and corporate financial performance variables.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: A firm's social performance, measured across a wide variety of stakeholders; in this study, the KLD dimensions of employee relations, community relations, environment, and products.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: Accounting-based financial performance measured with return on assets and return on equity.

name: Pollution prevention technologies
authors_terms: ["pollution prevention technologies", "pollution prevention", "product and process adaptation"]
definition: Structural investments in operations that involve fundamental changes to a basic product or primary process; they reduce or eliminate pollutants by using cleaner alternatives than those currently in place.

name: Pollution control technologies
authors_terms: ["pollution control technologies", "pollution control", "end-of-pipe and remediation technologies"]
definition: Structural investments that treat or dispose of pollutants or harmful by-products at the end of a manufacturing process, either immediately or later, leaving the original product and process virtually unaltered.

name: Environmental management systems
definition: Infrastructural investments that affect the way manufacturing is managed, such as formalizing procedures for evaluating environmental impacts, stakeholder involvement, employee training, environmental departments, and cross-functional coordination.

name: Manufacturing performance
definition: Plant-level manufacturing performance, traditionally assessed using at least four factors: cost, quality, speed (delivery), and flexibility performance.

name: Environmental performance
definition: Environmental performance has been based on the quantity of pollutants released from a plant, either as measured by a third party or as reported to the federal government; here it is the total environmental release and transfer of hazardous pollutants.

name: Perceived strategic uncertainty
definition: Daft and colleagues proposed that only when perceived uncertainty (complexity and rate of change) was deemed important to a firm's goal attainment would the phenomenon actually create strategic uncertainty in environmental sectors for top managers; their multiplicative construct combines rate of change plus complexity, weighted by importance.

name: Environmental scanning frequency
definition: The frequency with which participants collected or received information about each of the seven environmental sectors, measured on a five-point scale; scanning is the first step in the managerial problem-solving sequence and an indispensable activity in the strategic management process.

name: Perceived source accessibility
definition: Accessibility was defined as "the ease with which you can acquire this information at reasonable to no cost, and the extent to which you are readily aware of where to get the information."

name: Scanning of personal sources of information
definition: Modes of scanning, or sources of information, are defined by the nature and acquisition of data; personal sources involve direct communication with other individuals either within or outside of the organization.

name: Scanning of impersonal sources of information
definition: Impersonal sources include documents like internal reports and externally generated documents such as newspapers and government reports.

name: Scanning of external sources of information
definition: An internal source is within the organization; an external source is outside it.

name: Scanning of internal sources of information
definition: An internal source is within the organization; an external source is outside it.

name: Environmental sector
definition: An organization's environment can be divided into two distinct strata, with the distinction based upon the directness of influence on operations and upon organizational goal attainment: the task environment involves sectors in which there is direct interaction with the organization, and the general environment includes sectors with indirect interaction with the organization.

name: Perceived rate of change
definition: Rate of change was defined as "the frequency and speed of change that you see in the trends, issues and conditions in each environmental sector."

name: Perceived environmental complexity
definition: Complexity was defined as "the number and diversity of events occurring in environmental sectors outside the operations of your company," a measurement focused on heterogeneity.

name: Perceived importance of environmental sector
definition: Respondents were asked: "How important do you consider each environmental sector to be in accomplishing your company's goals?" Perceived importance is a component, together with rate of change and complexity, of the composite strategic uncertainty construct.

name: Venture creation decision
definition: An outcome variable that indicates whether or not an individual has made the decision to start a venture.

name: Arrangements scripts
definition: Arrangements scripts are the knowledge structures individuals have about the use of the specific arrangements that support their own performance and expert-level mastery in a given domain.

name: Willingness scripts
definition: Venture willingness is commitment to venturing and receptivity to the idea of starting a venture; willingness scripts are the knowledge structures that underlie (inform) this commitment.

name: Ability scripts
definition: Venture ability consists of the knowledge structures or scripts that individuals have about the capabilities, skills, knowledge, norms, and attitudes required to create a venture.

name: Individualism
definition: Individualism represents a preference for acting in the interests of the self and immediate family as opposed to the interests of the group or collective.

name: Power distance
definition: Power distance refers to the acceptance of inequality in power and authority between individuals in a society.

name: Cultural values
definition: Cultural values concern the way human societies organize knowledge and social behavior into a fairly consistent set of cognitive orientations that reflect a broad tendency to prefer certain states of affairs over others.

name: Cognitive scripts
definition: Experts possess knowledge structures, or scripts, about particular domains; an expert script is comprised of highly developed, sequentially ordered knowledge germane to a specific field and can be defined as an action-based knowledge structure.

name: Incumbent CEO power
definition: Following Pfeffer (1981), power is defined as a store of potential influence through which events can be affected and the motivation to use that influence to bring about desired outcomes. Incumbent CEO power is an index of the three most widely used measures of CEO power: stockholdings, duality, and tenure.

name: Outside director power
definition: Outside directors are board members who are not officers of the firm on whose board they serve and have never been its officers; outside director power is an index built from the percentage of outside directors on the board and outside ownership.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured with return on assets (ROA), a commonly used and well-understood measure that is particularly appropriate for manufacturing firms, and with shareholder returns.

name: Heir apparent promotion
authors_terms: ["heir apparent promotion", "promotion to the CEO position", "promotion"]
definition: One of the two competing terminal outcomes of heir apparent tenure: the heir apparent is promoted to the CEO position. An heir apparent faces three possibilities at any given point during his or her tenure - promotion, exit, and continuation in the present position.

name: Heir apparent exit
definition: One of the two competing terminal outcomes of heir apparent tenure: the heir apparent exits the firm, which by definition is unexpected and violates the rule of a relay succession.

name: Heir apparent company tenure
authors_terms: ["company tenure", "heir company tenure", "heir apparent company tenure"]
definition: The number of years the heir apparent was employed in the firm at the time he or she became the heir apparent, which also creates a fine-grained distinction between insider and outsider heirs apparent.

name: Heir apparent director status
definition: Whether the heir apparent is also a member of the firm's board of directors; just as CEO duality can be used as a measure of CEO power, directorship can be used as an indicator of heir apparent power.

name: Institutional activism
definition: Activism refers to actions taken by institutional investors to pressure managers; in other words, it is the means by which institutions engage in political ploys to leverage their ownership power. The most common actions are public announcements, shareholder proposals, direct negotiations with managers, and proxy contests.

name: R&D inputs
definition: R&D inputs was computed as the total expenditures in research and development expressed as a percentage of sales.

name: R&D outputs
definition: R&D outputs was the number of new products announced by a firm in a year.

name: Form of institutional activism
definition: Proxy-based activism included instances initiated through the formal proxy machinery, including shareholder proposals and proxy contest initiations. Non-proxy-based activism included public announcements or instances of negotiation reported in the press.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: Firms with profitable growth opportunities may experience a "demand-pull" impetus for appropriate R&D investments.

name: High-technology industry R&D underinvestment
authors_terms: ["hi-tech R&D", "high-technology industry that has underinvested in R&D"]
definition: Hi-tech R&D was a dummy variable that took on a value of 1 for firms in high-tech industries with firm R&D intensity below the industry average, based on the primary two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code, and 0 otherwise.

name: Activist institutional ownership
definition: Ownership by other activist institutions (typically pension funds like CalPERS) can leverage activism, as the actions of one activist institution are likely to be supported by other activist institutions.

name: Board independence
definition: Independent directors lack business relationships that pose a conflict of interest and are therefore expected to provide better oversight.

name: Productive efficiency
definition: Productive efficiency was estimated with data envelopment analysis; the paper states that productivity is a critical indicator of competitive advantage and is the article's focus.

name: Air and water pollution control investment
authors_terms: ["air pollution", "water pollution", "air and water pollution equipment", "air and water pollution control plant", "spending on air and water pollution equipment"]
definition: Air pollution was the ratio of each utility's air pollution plant value to total plant value; water pollution was the ratio of each utility's water pollution plant value to total plant value. These variables captured utilities' investment exposure to different types of pollution control requirements.

name: Waste pollution control investment
authors_terms: ["waste pollution", "waste pollution equipment", "solid waste requirements", "solid waste pollution expenditures"]
definition: Waste pollution was the ratio of waste pollution plant value to total plant value, capturing utilities' investment exposure to solid waste pollution control requirements.

name: Monitoring understandings
definition: In applications of an emergent style, monitoring understandings gauges progress in terms of team members' experiential learning—that is, how their project focus, knowledge, and skills are developing as they interact with others and with the product itself.

name: Monitoring milestones
definition: The planned style of monitoring, in which interim goals, schedules, and tests offer managers clear indications of a project's progress; milestones ideally convert a project strategy into analyzable technical, budgetary, and time-related objectives.

name: Information gathering
definition: Applying an emergent style, team members evaluate their project by gathering information from external sources; this is a potentially vital boundary-spanning activity through which teams gauge organizational support and manage others' impressions of the project.

name: Formal review
definition: A planned approach entails more systematic evaluation, or formal review, in which reviewers act as gatekeepers who determine whether a project will contribute significantly to its firm's product portfolio, is ready for transfer from R&D to manufacturing, or should be terminated.

name: Participative control
definition: An emergent style of control that offers teams the freedom to challenge existing ideas and solve problems regarding product design and their own tasks, building trust and enabling team members' roles to evolve over time.

name: Directive control
definition: A planned style of control in which project and senior managers provide teams guidance and support and remain closely involved in project details so as to finish on time, within budget, and according to the initial plan and design.

name: Emergent project management style
definition: An emergent style involves facilitating team members' creativity, flexibility, and improvisation; advocates view product development as inherently ambiguous, helping innovation emerge from the bottom up, so that monitoring, evaluation, and control are loosely coupled activities.

name: Planned project management style
definition: A planned style provides managerial discipline and direction; its proponents presume that product development is more predictable and rational, best managed as a top-down process in which monitoring, evaluation, and control activities appear tightly coupled within a systematic cycle.

name: Project innovation
definition: The facet of project performance that includes building technical knowledge and achieving commercial objectives: a successful project both contributes technical knowledge that enhances the product and future R&D efforts and produces a final product capable of attaining its projected market share.

name: Project efficiency
definition: The facet of project performance concerned with keeping projects on time and within budget, so that projects remain on schedule and within projected cost levels.

name: Project uncertainty
definition: Technical and commercial forms of project uncertainty, both deemed a function of familiarity: technical uncertainty concerns team members' familiarity with the science and technology used and the division's expertise, and commercial uncertainty concerns the firm's experience commercializing products like the developing product.

name: Project performance
definition: Project performance is multifaceted, encompassing the need for innovation and efficiency: a successful project both contributes technical knowledge that enhances the product and future R&D efforts and produces a final product capable of attaining its projected market share, while remaining on time and within budget.

name: Professional finance association foundings
authors_terms: ["professional finance association foundings", "foundings of professional finance associations", "creation of professional associations"]
definition: Professional finance association foundings, the dependent variable, was defined by the first year that a professional finance association was in existence. The establishment of a professional association is a specific way in which an occupation can formalize its identity, make claims about its occupational status, and participate in the governance of a field.

name: Decline of the regulatory logic
authors_terms: ["decline of the regulatory logic", "decline of a regulatory logic", "deinstitutionalization of the regulatory logic", "erosion of the regulatory logic"]
definition: One of the main characteristics of the field of finance after the passage of Depression era regulations was the concentration of financial assets in commercial banks; the erosion of the regulatory logic that segregated the field of finance by organizational form is tracked through the decline in market concentration for financial intermediaries. The deinstitutionalization of the regulatory logic opened up opportunities for actors to make claims that challenged the regulatory framework enacted in the 1930s.

name: Rise of the market logic
authors_terms: ["rise of a market logic", "rise of the market logic", "market logic", "retail-oriented market logic"]
definition: A market logic that emphasized retail-oriented financial services competition and a blending of previously segregated organizational forms began to be constructed. A key aspect of the emergence of the more retail-oriented market logic has to do with how financial actors have focused increasing attention on customer service, innovation, and competition.

name: Growth of expert financial knowledge
authors_terms: ["growth of expert financial knowledge", "growth of financial knowledge", "growth rate of portfolio management knowledge", "financial knowledge", "abstract body of expert knowledge"]
definition: A key resource that enables occupations to make credible claims about professionalism is connection to an abstract body of expert knowledge; the growth of financial knowledge and the ascendancy of financial economics as a subfield provided an important foundation for the professionalization of various financial occupations. The growth rate of portfolio management knowledge tracks the percentage of articles published in the Journal of Finance that focused on portfolio management.

name: Pace of change
authors_terms: ["pace of change", "rapid pace of change", "speed at which change takes place", "rate at which design arrangements become decoupled"]
definition: The speed at which change takes place during a transition; the authors state that 'the speed at which change takes place is seen as integral to the change track followed' and measure it through the amount of change activity in a period.

name: Completion of radical organizational transition
authors_terms: ["reorientation", "completion of a radical transition", "successful reorientation", "executive office archetype status"]
definition: An organization's attainment and retention of a new archetypal configuration; in this study an NSO had to achieve, and maintain until 1996, executive office archetype status, having started from a position outside the embryonic executive office archetype.

name: High-impact organizational elements
definition: Organizational elements that 'have an important functional and symbolic role in the effective functioning of an organization'; in this paper the high-impact element examined is the organization's decision-making structures.

name: Linearity of change
authors_terms: ["linearity of the change process", "nonlinear manner", "linear transition", "linear process"]
definition: The degree to which change unfolds as an ordered, consistent process rather than through the introduction and subsequent withdrawal of changes; the authors contrast the normative linear view of change with evidence that radical change is characterized by delays, reversals, and oscillations.

name: Radical organizational transformation
definition: A shift from one archetypal configuration to another, or a transition from a design that can be identified with no single archetype to one that has clear archetypal status.

name: Specialization
definition: The degree to which an organization was differentiated in terms of administrative, technical, and support roles.

name: Formalization
definition: The extent to which an organization made use of formal plans, policies, and procedures, and the degree of engagement with formal monitoring, evaluation, and communication systems.

name: Centralization
definition: The location of decision-making authority in the organization, in particular whether professional staff rather than volunteers make key decisions; measured through the locus of final decision-making responsibility, the number of hierarchical levels involved in decisions, the number of decisions made by professional staff, and the number of decisions in which volunteers have no input.

name: Stock option exercise
authors_terms: ["decision to exercise stock options", "stock option exercise", "exercise of stock options"]
definition: The CEO's decision to exercise stock options; the authors measure it as whether the CEO of a sample company had exercised stock options during a focal year.

name: CEO equity ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO equity", "CEO ownership", "percentage of shares owned by a CEO"]
definition: The percentage of shares owned by a CEO (net of options exercised during the year), used as the preexisting level of CEO ownership that moderates the effect of exercise.

name: Change in CEO equity
authors_terms: ["change in CEO equity levels", "changes in CEO ownership", "change in CEO equity"]
definition: The difference in a CEO's equity ownership percentage between 1995 and 1996.

name: Reduction in CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["reduction in CEO equity", "reduction of CEO ownership levels", "ownership retrenchment"]
definition: A negative change in CEO equity from 1995 to 1996, coded with a dummy variable, that moderates the relationship between option exercise and subsequent performance.

name: Subsequent firm performance
authors_terms: ["subsequent firm performance", "subsequent financial performance", "firm market performance", "accounting performance"]
definition: Firm performance following the exercise decision, measured with one market-based measure (annualized market performance for three years) and one accounting-based measure (average return on assets over the subsequent three years).

name: Intrafirm CEO succession
definition: A succession in which an executive with firm tenure of at least two years has been promoted to the CEO position.

name: Intraindustry CEO succession
definition: A succession in which the successor CEO had firm tenure of less than two years but had industry tenure of at least two years in the same four-digit industry that the hiring firm was in; succession from within a firm's industry but from outside the firm.

name: Presence of an heir apparent
definition: The executive who holds the most senior formal position in a firm's hierarchy (below the CEO) and who has the opportunity to access the task of the CEO; identified as any officer who was the only person in the firm holding the title of president or of COO or both and who was at least five years younger than the incumbent CEO.

name: Number of nonheir inside directors
definition: The total number of executives, other than a firm's current CEO and heir apparent, who were also members of the board of directors.

name: Prior strategic persistence
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategy remains stable over time.

name: Number of similarly sized and larger firms in the industry
authors_terms: ["number of similarly sized and larger firms in an industry"]
definition: The number of firms in a focal firm's primary industry whose sales in the year prior to succession were equal to or larger than half of the focal firm's sales.

name: Industry strategic homogeneity
definition: The extent to which the strategic resource allocations of different firms within an industry follow the same pattern; an absence of strategic variance among firms.

name: Firm strategic conformity to industry central tendencies
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategy adheres to the central tendencies of its industry; an absence of difference from other firms in the industry.

name: Work-family initiatives
authors_terms: ["work-family initiatives", "work-family human resource initiatives", "work-family policies", "work-family human resource decisions"]
definition: Work-family initiatives include any human resource program or policy previously identified in relevant scholarly literature as having the potential to alleviate employees' work and family conflicts; they fall into three main categories: dependent care, family stress programs, and flexible work arrangements.

name: Shareholder returns
authors_terms: ["shareholder returns", "share price reaction", "excess return", "cumulative excess returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Excess (abnormal) returns are calculated as the difference between the actual firm return and the firm's expected value around the announcement of a work-family initiative.

name: High-technology industry
definition: A high-technology industry was defined as one "in which the number of research and development workers was at least 50 percent higher than the average proportion of all industries surveyed [by the Bureau of Labor Statistics]".

name: Proportion of female employees in an industry
authors_terms: ["proportion of female employees", "proportion of women in an industry"]
definition: The proportion of female employees, expressed as a percentage, within an industry one year prior to a work-family announcement.

name: Industry unemployment rate
authors_terms: ["industry unemployment rate", "unemployment rate in a firm's industry"]
definition: The industry-level unemployment rate one year prior to a work-family announcement, identified through the three-digit SIC code and expressed as a percentage.

name: Legitimation of work-family initiatives
definition: Legitimation is the point at which adoption of work-family initiatives reaches a critical mass, so that a firm's adopting the initiative signals legitimacy to constituents; 1981 was used to define the periods before and after legitimation.

name: Discontinuous change
definition: Discontinuous changes are shifts in organizational domains (such as technology) that are infrequent, episodic, and intentional, unlike incremental changes that are ongoing, evolving, and cumulative. The general term 'change' is used to refer to a system of discontinuous changes in one or more organizational domains.

name: Latent errors
definition: Latent errors are deviations from procedures and policies that may have adverse consequences of organizational significance. By themselves, latent errors are neither necessary nor sufficient to produce adverse organizational outcomes.

name: Work-inherent risk
definition: Risk is a basic and 'indigenous source' of adverse consequences that is embedded in work activities; high-risk work is inherently more error-prone than low-risk work and errors in high-risk activities have a greater potential for producing adverse consequences.

name: CEO stock option compensation
definition: Stock option plans give executives the rights to purchase shares of stock at some future time at a prespecified price; because executives incur no cash outlay until they exercise options, they experience less downside risk than with equity.

name: CEO equity ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO equity ownership", "CEO equity", "equity ownership", "executive equity ownership"]
definition: The percentage of firm equity owned by a CEO, measured as the fraction of firm equity a firm's CEO retained after its IPO.

name: Investor valuation of IPO firms
definition: Investor valuation captures the premium that investors place on a firm's assets; investors tend to reward encouraging prospects with higher premiums.

name: Organizational size
definition: Larger organizations should have more resources than smaller ones and are more likely to adopt many programs simply because they can afford to do so. Also, larger firms may have more concern with showing legitimacy because they have greater public visibility, resulting in greater normative and coercive pressures from the environment.

name: Perceived drug problem
authors_terms: ["perceptions of drug problem", "perceived extent of drug problem", "perception of drug problem", "perceive a drug problem"]
definition: If managers already perceive a drug problem at their organization, they are more likely to adopt a drug-testing program or an EAP to gain a sense of control over this issue.

name: Union presence
definition: The authors state that unionized work sites have been found to be more likely than nonunionized locations to have drug-testing programs, and that even if only some of the workforce at a work site is unionized, these relationships should still hold, since treating unionized and nonunionized employees differently might affect morale.

name: Employee turnover
definition: Work sites with high turnover may find that the costs of EAPs or drug-testing programs are not worth the benefits since employees don't remain in the organizations for very long.

name: Percentage of male employees
authors_terms: ["percentage of male employees", "proportion of male employees", "predominately male workforces"]
definition: Some research suggests that workplaces where the majority of employees are male may be more likely to drug-test in response to commonly held suspicions that men are more likely to use drugs.

name: Workplace substance abuse prevention program adoption
authors_terms: ["workplace substance abuse programs", "adoption of drug-testing programs and EAPs", "Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs)", "drug testing"]
definition: The major ways organizations have responded is (1) by detecting the presence of illegal drugs through drug testing and (2) by having Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), which are formal programs that assist employees with personal problems that may be affecting their work-related behaviors.

name: Institutional adoption density
authors_terms: ["density", "industry densities", "labor market density", "proportion of organizations in their industries or in their local labor markets that have adopted"]
definition: If enough organizations in the same geographical area have drug-testing programs or EAPs, organizations without them may feel mimicry pressure to also adopt these programs. This statement implies organizations are more likely to adopt if other firms in their local labor market have already adopted, or if most firms in their industry have adopted.

name: Positive media discourse
authors_terms: ["positive discourse", "positive discourse about substance abuse treatment", "positive discourse about drug testing", "positive words"]
definition: The implication is that the more positive words in an article abstract, the more positive in tone the discourse. It was change in the tone of discourse over time that we expected to be related to adoption rates.

name: Negative media discourse
authors_terms: ["negative discourse", "negative discourse about EAPs", "negative discourse about drug testing", "negative words"]
definition: Negative discourse might discourage managers at organizations that don't have these practices from adopting. For this study, the content categories examined were 'positive' and 'negative'.

name: Adoption period
authors_terms: ["period effects", "period of adoption", "early, middle, and late periods of adoption", "early or late period"]
definition: We predict that the period of adoption (early or late) moderates the effects of strategic choice and institutional factors on the probability of the adoption of programs addressing substance abuse.

name: Cumulative implemented employee suggestions
authors_terms: ["cumulative employee suggestions", "cumulative suggestions", "cumulative number of implemented employee suggestions", "implemented suggestions", "suggestion-based knowledge", "cumulative knowledge pool comprised of written employee suggestions"]
definition: Employee suggestions implemented under gainsharing, accumulated over time, which the authors treat as a stock of explicit organizational knowledge produced by the deliberate transformation of tacit employee knowledge into written suggestions.

name: Unit production costs
authors_terms: ["cost per unit produced", "unit costs", "unit production costs", "production costs", "plant operational performance"]
definition: Plant operational performance measured as the cost per unit produced, based on the total costs of production divided by the number of standard units produced.

name: Knowledge depreciation
authors_terms: ["knowledge depreciation", "organizational forgetting", "depreciation of suggestion-based knowledge", "depreciation factor (lambda)"]
definition: The decline over time in the value of knowledge contained in previously implemented employee suggestions, such that knowledge acquired in the past has less effect on organizational performance than more recently acquired knowledge.

name: Attention
definition: Organizational researchers increasingly recognize that choice under uncertainty involves two distinct actions: selection of a subset of firms to focus attention on, and evaluation of the relative merits of their competing offerings. Attention determines where market actors focus their cognitive efforts because both individuals and organizations have limited attentional capacities.

name: Widely available attention
authors_terms: ["widely available attention", "available attention", "widely available actions", "cumulative media attention", "turnover on the first day of an IPO"]
definition: We distinguish between recent and what we have termed 'widely available actions,' which are actions that, because of either their extremity or pervasiveness, are likely to be salient at the individual level and to become magnified and socially reinforced at the collective level.

name: Recent attention
authors_terms: ["recent attention", "recent actions", "daily turnover lagged by one day", "daily media attention lagged by one day"]
definition: To the extent the information conveyed by recent actions influences market actors, information cascades are operating; the unfamiliar also draws attention, so recent stimuli can also attract attention because of their potential novelty.

name: Positive evaluation
definition: In addition to allocating attention, another cognitive task actors perform in uncertain environments is evaluating, which requires drawing conclusions about often unobservable attributes, such as underlying firm or product quality. Evaluations are based on interpreting cues about a firm itself as well as on evaluations made by others.

name: Widely available positive evaluation
authors_terms: ["available evaluations", "widely available positive evaluations", "cumulative positive media coverage", "degree of underpricing"]
definition: Widely available prior evaluations can serve as 'quasi-prior beliefs': the more available prior evaluations are, the easier it is to categorize recent evaluations as consistent or inconsistent with them, and they become part of the memory content accessed in processing information to form new evaluations.

name: Recent positive evaluation
authors_terms: ["recent positive evaluations", "recent evaluations", "daily return lagged by one day", "daily positive media coverage lagged by one day"]
definition: When the subject is unfamiliar, evaluators are especially uncertain about the accuracy of their assessments; thus, they will be likely to look at the assessments of others when deciding what to do, and their opinions are likely to be easily influenced by the recent evaluations offered by others.

name: CEO charisma
authors_terms: ["CEO charisma", "charismatic leadership", "top management team perceptions of CEO charisma", "strategic charismatic leadership"]
definition: Top management team members' perceptions of their CEO's charismatic leadership, measured with a refinement of a larger instrument developed by Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Moorman, and Fetter (1990). High interrater agreement and scale reliability justified combining individual managers' responses into a single measure of charisma for each CEO.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "perceived organizational performance", "stock return", "return on assets", "return on equity", "return on sales", "sales growth"]
definition: Firm performance operationalized through both primary and secondary sources and objective and perceived modes of assessment, because accounting- and market-based measures may suffer from measurement and controllability issues and may not converge to represent the same construct.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: An objective measure of environmental uncertainty, firm risk, that may be interpreted as the collective assessment of uncertainty by stock market participants rather than the assessment of managers.

name: Team member status
definition: Status is defined as position within a social structure that confers rights, prestige, or honor upon an individual according to various ascribed and achieved criteria. The authors measure status as social prestige, the esteem, respect, or approval granted by an individual or a collective for performance or qualities they consider above the average.

name: Newness of team members
authors_terms: ["newness of team members", "newcomers", "newcomers index", "entry of newcomers", "introduction of newcomers"]
definition: A newcomer was defined as an individual who was new to the industry and not as new to a firm, to team work, or to other members of the organization because the authors intended to capture the risk-taking and search dimensions of explorative action. Individuals were considered new if they had not been employed in the industry before 1926.

name: Newness of team member combinations
authors_terms: ["newness of combinations of team members", "new combinations", "new combinations index", "recombination of team members"]
definition: The new combinations index scored dyadic combinations according to the level of newness each one involved. A combination was considered new if it had never been employed in the industry before 1926.

name: Hierarchical layers in organizational structures
authors_terms: ["hierarchical layers", "organizational structures", "hierarchical structures", "one-layer structure", "two-layer structure", "three-layer structure"]
definition: Hierarchy consists of structures in which individuals are arranged in a cascade of authority and communication relations. The authors analyze three scenarios: one-layer structures, in which the CEO is responsible for designing the different teams; two-layer structures, in which the CEO oversees the various projects and project managers control team design; and three-layer structures, in which a layer of middle managers exists between the CEO and the project managers and team design is the joint responsibility of project managers and liaison middle managers.

name: Team mechanisms
definition: In this study, we examine the relationships of both a conceptually pure team process (communication) and an emergent state (cohesion) with team and organizational performance. We refer to these jointly as team mechanisms to reflect the broadened IPO model (Ilgen et al., 2005).

name: Communication
definition: Communication is a key team process, as it clarifies 'how' a team interpersonally orchestrates its work to get things done and perform effectively.

name: Cohesion
definition: Cohesion is an affective, psychological state that reflects the shared commitment, attraction, and team pride that emerges from the experiences and interactions among team members.

name: Team interdependence
definition: Interdependence is defined as the extent to which contextual features outside an individual and his or her behavior (i.e., tasks and outcomes) define a relationship between entities as collective, so that one entity should affect and be affected by the other (Campion et al., 1993; Stewart & Barrick, 2000; Wageman, 2001). A team with high interdependence is often referred to as a 'real team,' whereas teams with low interdependence are more commonly labeled 'working groups' (Katzenbach & Smith, 1993).

name: Team performance
definition: Studies in the small groups literature have only focused on team performance as a reflection of team effectiveness. Team performance was assessed with CEO ratings on Kirkman and Rosen's (1999) six-item measure.

name: Organizational performance
definition: This study captured measures of team performance and the ultimate criterion, organizational performance. Organizational performance was captured with the year following survey administration so that a lagged objective measure of firm performance could be examined.

name: Procedural justice
definition: In a strategic alliance setting, I define procedural justice as the extent to which the strategic decisionmaking process and procedures that impact each party's gains and interests are impartial and fair as perceived by the boundary spanners representing each party in an alliance.

name: Distributive justice
definition: In the specific setting of strategic alliances, I define distributive justice as the extent to which interparty sharing of the rewards from cooperation is fair in view of each party's contribution, commitment, and assumption of responsibility.

name: Interactional justice
definition: In a strategic alliance setting, I define interactional justice as the extent to which interpersonal treatment and information exchange between boundary spanners representing each party are fair.

name: Alliance performance
definition: Alliance performance is measured in this study by asset turnover (sales revenues divided by total assets).

name: Goal differences between alliance parties
authors_terms: ["goal differences between parties", "differences in the strategic goals", "goal disparity"]
definition: Partners generally gauge cooperation risks and returns from goal differences between parties; differences in the strategic goals underlying each party's strategic alliance formation hamper their perception and commitment toward the favorability of collective gains.

name: CEO transformational leadership
definition: According to Bass (1985), transformational leadership comprises four primary behaviors: idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration.

name: Dyadic goal importance congruence
definition: The similarity between CEO and individual VP perceptions about the importance of specific goals to the organization.

name: Within-team goal importance congruence
authors_terms: ["within-team goal importance congruence", "withinteam goal importance congruence"]
definition: The similarity of perceptions about the importance of specific organizational goals among all members of a TMT (including the CEO).

name: VP attitudes
definition: Follower attitudes, such as job satisfaction, organizational commitment, and satisfaction with one's leader.

name: VP performance
authors_terms: ["VP performance", "individual VP performance", "CEOs' ratings of individual VP performance"]
definition: CEOs rated the performance of each VP using an 11-item scale; items assessed four primary aspects of performance: task performance, communication, teamwork, and leadership.

name: Organizational performance
definition: In the preliminary survey, the credit union CEOs identified ROA as the most commonly used measure of organizational performance in the industry.

name: Perceived goal importance
authors_terms: ["goal importance", "goal importance ratings", "perceptions of the importance of specific goals"]
definition: The extent to which a respondent believes a specific goal is an important one to which the organization is devoting time and effort.

name: Relational governance
definition: Relational governance is defined here as a set of informal norms that affect the behavior of partners when they are dealing with each other; such codes of conduct emerge from the values and agreed-upon processes found in social relationships.

name: Contract completeness
definition: When using formal mechanisms, parties specify several verifiable contingencies, such as inputs and outputs, the level and timing of actions, task and review processes, performance benchmarks, procedures for dispute resolution, and even penalties for noncompliance; the more explicit and detailed such specifications are, the more a contract is said to be complete.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Bilateral governance is an efficient option when either party (or both) has made idiosyncratic investments-that is, acquired assets that are partnership-specific and have lower values in other relationships. Such specificity raises behavioral uncertainties.

name: Complexity
definition: Complexity arises from the difficulties of managing large numbers of subparts, organizational routines, and process steps in the production of goods; as the numbers of parts and multistage processes increase, the quantity and diversity of the information involved increase with it, making the integration of the various production tasks more cognitively difficult and costly to synchronize.

name: Negotiation efficiency
definition: Negotiation costs are those incurred as firms adapt to new circumstances; these costs are often seen as the 'bargaining and haggling' involved in the essentials of an exchange, such as price, delivery, and product specifications. Negotiation efficiency is the reverse of these costs.

name: Production efficiency
definition: By production coordination, the authors mean the handling of the organizational complexity inherent in decomposing production tasks and managing their interdependent parts across firms. The performance evaluation of a supply chain often involves inventory turns and timely delivery of goods.

name: Negative earnings surprise
authors_terms: ["negative earnings surprise", "reported earnings below consensus forecasts", "earnings surprise", "reported earnings"]
definition: The consensus forecast for a particular firm is the average quarterly earnings forecast among all analysts who cover the firm, and an earnings surprise is the difference between the consensus forecast and the actual quarterly earnings reported by the company.

name: Diversifying corporate acquisition announcement
definition: Acquisitions are coded as 'diversifying' when the primary two-digit SIC code of the acquiring firm does not match that of the acquired firm. The prevailing view among academic researchers and members of the financial community is that unrelated or diversifying acquisitions tend to have negative implications for shareholder interests.

name: Executive favor rendering toward analysts
authors_terms: ["favor rendering", "personal and professional favors", "executive favor rendering", "grant favors"]
definition: Top executives can perform a range of personal and professional favors for security analysts by drawing on their social contacts, status, knowledge, and personal experience, for instance by helping analysts acquire critical information about recent developments in an industry environment or by putting them in contact with personnel of buyer and supplier firms.

name: Personal access to top executives
authors_terms: ["personal access to top executives", "executive access", "access to top executives", "personal access"]
definition: There is considerable evidence that security analysts highly value frequent, timely access to top executives. Such access is perceived to be valuable in generating timely, insightful, and accurate company reports, and it enhances an analyst's stature with his or her clients.

name: Analyst influence on investor behavior
authors_terms: ["analyst's influence on investors", "indicators of analyst influence on investor behavior", "All-America status", "size of the analyst's employer"]
definition: There is evidence from the finance and accounting literatures that two analyst characteristics represent strong indicators of an analyst's influence on investors: selection as a member of the 'All-America Research Team' by the magazine Institutional Investor, and the size of the analyst's firm.

name: Analyst stock downgrade
authors_terms: ["downgrade", "downgrades", "negative recommendation", "downward change from the previous recommendation"]
definition: We created a dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal analyst's most recent stock recommendation involved a downward change from the previous recommendation.

name: Awareness of another analyst's loss of favors or executive access
authors_terms: ["awareness of another analyst's loss of favors or executive access", "aware of another instance in which an analyst had lost executive favors or personal access"]
definition: We used a survey scale to determine whether analysts were aware of another instance in which an analyst had lost executive favors or personal access to top executives after downgrading a focal firm's stock.

name: Depth of human and social capital
authors_terms: ["depth of human and social capital", "depth", "service tenure"]
definition: The depth of human and social capital refers to the profundity of a directors' expertise, knowledge, skills, and social networks.

name: Breadth of human and social capital
authors_terms: ["breadth of human and social capital", "breadth", "breadth of jurisdiction"]
definition: The breadth of directors' human and social capital refers to the extent of the skills, expertise, and social networks (i.e., connections and relationships) they possess. Depth denotes focused human and social capital, breadth refers to the range or scope of human and social capital.

name: Deterioration of human and social capital
authors_terms: ["deterioration", "deterioration of human and social capital", "human and social capital deterioration"]
definition: The authors expect that the resources government officials accumulate in office are the most valuable immediately after the officials leave public service and deteriorate over time, as other powerful individuals retire, are replaced, or feel less obligated to respond and as the deep knowledge about key issues and the inner workings of government also deteriorates.

name: Opposition party in power
authors_terms: ["opposition party in power", "party in power", "change in power"]
definition: Whether the political party in control of the executive branch and the Congress is not the political party with which the former government official is affiliated.

name: Outside directorship appointment
authors_terms: ["joined board", "joining a board as an outside director", "outside directorship"]
definition: A former government official joining the board of a U.S. public corporation as an outside director.

name: Supply chain disruption impact
authors_terms: ["disruption impact", "supply chain disruption impact", "the impact of a supply chain disruption"]
