definition: Supply chain disruption impact captures the extent to which a disruption had (direct or indirect) negative effects on a focal firm.

name: Buffering
definition: Buffering is external to a current relationship, as it is an effort to reduce a firm's exposure to the current exchange partner and to mitigate the detrimental consequences of disturbances that the relationship may confer.

name: Bridging
definition: Bridging is internal to a current relationship, as it is an effort to manage resource dependencies by enlarging a firm's influence over them.

name: Dependence on exchange partner
authors_terms: ["dependence on exchange partner", "dependence on the exchange partner", "dependence"]
definition: Dependence on an exchange partner implies that a firm needs to maintain the relationship with the partner to achieve its desired goals.

name: Supply chain disruption orientation
definition: We define supply chain disruption orientation as a firm's general awareness and consciousness of, concerns about, seriousness toward, and recognition of opportunity to learn from supply chain disruptions.

name: Trust in the exchange partner
definition: Trust in an exchange partner can be described as an expectation or a belief that the exchange partner will honor its commitments (is credible) and has good intentions (is benevolent).

name: Prior experience with supply chain disruptions
authors_terms: ["prior experience", "prior experiences with supply chain disruptions"]
definition: Prior experience is conceptualized as the number of supply chain disruptions a focal firm has faced during the past 12 months (before a specific supply chain disruption) and in the same product line as the specific supply chain disruption.

name: Social identification with the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["CEO social identification with the corporate elite", "identification with the corporate elite", "social identification"]
definition: Social identification reflects the degree to which people define themselves in terms of their membership in a social category. A premise of our theoretical perspective is that the corporate elite is a meaningful social category with which CEOs may identify.

name: Provision of social support to fellow CEOs
authors_terms: ["provision of social support", "provide social support", "social support provided to fellow CEOs"]
definition: Social support includes the provision of moral or emotional support, such as expressing confidence that a person's problem can be resolved or mitigated, and informational support, which involves providing specific advice, referrals, or other information on how to effectively address the problem.

name: Receipt of social support from fellow CEOs
authors_terms: ["receipt of social support", "received social support", "social support from fellow CEOs"]
definition: Moral and informational support that a CEO receives from fellow CEOs who have experienced a similar problem, aggregated across help providers; such support is expected to reduce the extent to which individuals manifest depressive mood and anxiety in the face of personal stressors.

name: Severity of personal problems
authors_terms: ["personal problems", "personal difficulties", "severity of a CEO's personal problems"]
definition: A personal problem refers to the subset of problems that have the potential to produce significant psychological or emotional distress and that therefore may evoke empathic concern in others; the most common ones for which CEOs received social support were marital discord, discord in relations with a child, and health problems of a loved one.

name: Depressive mood and anxiety
definition: Symptoms of depressive mood and anxiety that individuals manifest in the face of potential stressors in their personal lives and that reduce the emotional energy and cognitive attention available for discretionary behaviors at work.

name: CEO overall effectiveness as a corporate leader
authors_terms: ["CEO overall effectiveness as a corporate leader", "leader effectiveness", "effectiveness as a corporate leader"]
definition: A survey measure of a CEO's overall effectiveness as a leader, based on the evaluations of independent directors, for whom evaluating CEO performance is a primary role and a CEO's effectiveness as a leader is a primary component of his/her performance.

name: Mentoring of lower-level managers
definition: Mentoring of lower-level managers is a discretionary interpersonal leadership behavior; the leader-member exchange literature suggests that mentoring enhances leaders' effectiveness by promoting positive social exchange relationships with subordinates.

name: Encouragement of lower-level managers
authors_terms: ["encouraging lower-level managers", "providing encouragement to a lower-level manager"]
definition: In providing encouragement to a lower-level manager, a CEO recognizes the manager's contributions to their firm and expresses confidence in the manager's future as an executive.

name: Seeking input from lower-level managers in strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["seeking input from lower-level managers in making strategic decisions", "participative decision-making style"]
definition: A participative decision-making style in which a leader regularly seeks input from subordinates in the process of making decisions.

name: Seeking information about strategy implementation progress
authors_terms: ["seeking information from lower-level managers about their progress on implementing corporate strategies", "monitoring role"]
definition: Seeking information from managers about their progress in implementing corporate strategies is an important aspect of the CEO monitoring role.

name: Soliciting advice and counsel from outside directors
authors_terms: ["soliciting advice and counsel from outside directors on strategic issues", "advice seeking from board members"]
definition: CEOs who regularly solicit advice and counsel from outside directors on strategic issues are more likely to develop corporate strategies that enhance firm performance; such interactions are a primary form of board involvement in strategic decision making.

name: Interpersonal leadership behaviors
authors_terms: ["interpersonal leadership behaviors", "discretionary interpersonal behaviors", "interpersonal behaviors at work"]
definition: Five discretionary interpersonal behaviors that have been posited to promote leader effectiveness in the organizational behavior and strategy literatures on leadership: mentoring lower-level managers, encouraging lower-level managers, seeking input from lower-level managers in making strategic decisions, seeking information from lower-level managers about their progress on implementing corporate strategies, and soliciting advice and counsel from outside directors on strategic issues.

name: Intraorganizational ethnic diversity
definition: Intraorganizational ethnic diversity is conceptualized as the degree of ethnic category variability in an organization.

name: Community ethnic diversity
definition: The ethnic makeup of the local community served by an organization, measured with the same variability index as organizational diversity.

name: Demographic representativeness
definition: The degree to which the ethnic diversity of organizations is representative of the relevant community demography, labeled here as demographic representativeness.

name: Civility toward service recipients
definition: Civility, or treating others with dignity and respect, resembles other prosocial workplace behaviors in that it includes subtle behaviors that an organization may neither require nor formally recognize.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "quality of services", "use of resources", "quality of care"]
definition: The performance of health care organizations as rated by the official regulator, comprising the overall quality of services provided and the effective use of resources.

name: Participation process mentoring
definition: Guidance from an experienced fellow director to a first-time director regarding normatively acceptable forms of outside director involvement in board deliberations.

name: Director gender
definition: Dichotomous distinction between first-time directors who are women and those who are men, coded 1 if the focal director was a woman.

name: Director racial minority status
definition: Dichotomous distinction between first-time directors who are racial minorities and those who are white, coded 1 if the focal director was a racial minority.

name: Presence of a female incumbent director
authors_terms: ["the presence of a female incumbent director on a board", "the presence of a woman incumbent director"]
definition: Whether there was a woman among the incumbent directors of the focal board.

name: Presence of a racial minority incumbent director
authors_terms: ["the presence of a racial minority incumbent director", "the presence of an incumbent who is a racial minority"]
definition: Whether there was a racial minority among the incumbent directors of the focal board.

name: Additional board appointments
authors_terms: ["board appointments", "subsequent board appointments", "appointments to additional boards"]
definition: The number of board appointments acquired by a focal first-time director at other firms in the population.

name: Director decision control behavior
definition: The extent to which outside directors engage in behaviors that fail to recognize the primacy of firm managers, and especially the CEO, in strategy formulation.

name: Structural holes in the knowledge network
authors_terms: ["structural holes of a researcher's knowledge elements in the knowledge network", "structural holes measure in the knowledge network"]
definition: The extent of disconnectedness among knowledge elements tied to a focal knowledge element, averaged over the knowledge elements in a researcher's knowledge portfolio; it suggests the extent to which combinatorial opportunities in a knowledge element's egocentric knowledge domain have not yet been exploited.

name: Degree centrality in the knowledge network
authors_terms: ["degree centrality of a researcher's knowledge elements in the firm's knowledge network"]
definition: The number of knowledge elements tied to a focal knowledge element, averaged over the knowledge elements in a researcher's portfolio; it indicates the knowledge element's combinatorial potential with other knowledge elements.

name: Structural holes in the collaboration network
authors_terms: ["structural holes in a firm's collaboration network", "structural holes measure in the firm's collaboration network"]
definition: The extent to which a researcher's network contacts are disconnected, computed from the constraint measure in the firm-wide collaboration network of researchers.

name: Degree centrality in the collaboration network
authors_terms: ["degree centrality in the firm's collaboration network", "researcher degree centrality"]
definition: The number of direct network contacts, or collaboration partners, that a researcher had in the firm's collaboration network.

name: Exploratory innovation
authors_terms: ["exploratory innovation", "number of new knowledge elements explored"]
definition: The number of the knowledge elements that were explored, advanced, and incorporated into a focal researcher's inventions and were new to the firm's extant stock of knowledge; it measures the extent of exploration in a researcher's inventive activities.

name: Leader charisma
definition: Charisma is a 'symbolic leader influence rooted in emotional and ideological foundations'; such leaders are exceptionally expressive and inspiring and use charismatic leadership tactics that predict leader emergence and prototypicality.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "performance signals", "firm performance", "country-level economic performance", "state of the economy", "performance cues"]
definition: If the economy is healthy (e.g., high GDP growth and low inflation, which impact the labor market), electors reward the incumbent or his or her party, in the case of an incumbent not running again. If the state of economy is poor, voters punish the incumbent, or his or her party, and vote for the challenger.

name: Clarity of performance signals
authors_terms: ["clarity of performance signals", "attributional ambiguity", "strong performance signals", "performance signal", "clear performance signals", "ambiguous performance signals"]
definition: The clearer the performance signal, whether positive or negative, the less likely charisma will matter for leader evaluation and selection; under conditions of attributional ambiguity (i.e., when performance signals are unclear), observers will mostly rely on inferential processes.

name: Leader selection
definition: Note that we use the term 'selection' in a broad sense to include leader selection and re-selection (for incumbents) in cases of contests or retention at the helm of an organization or institution.

name: Organizational status
definition: We use Bonacich and Lloyd's (2001) eigenvector-like measure of centrality for non-reciprocal ties based on the cumulative diffusion networks of new composers over the previous 25 years. This measure of centrality captures two dimensions of status: visibility and social recognition.

name: Individual status
definition: We create a similar measure for musical director status, using Bonacich and Lloyd's (2001) centrality scores in the inter-director diffusion network of new composers, where the nodes are musical directors in charge of concert programming decisions.

name: Alignment
definition: The first form, alignment, refers to the proximity of an organization to its peers across a range of attributes. Consistent with prior research, we note that the motivation for alignment comes from an organization's need to look like its peers and thereby avoid penalties.

name: Conventionality
definition: The second form, conventionality, refers to the selective adoption of highly salient and expected attributes. The organization that exhibits conventionality stands out relative to its peers by overemphasizing certain widely recognizable features in its offering.

name: Contagious disease mortality
authors_terms: ["Spanish Flu mortality", "mortality due to a contagious disease outbreak", "mortality due to a contagious disease outbreak in a community"]
definition: Mortality caused by a contagious disease outbreak in a community; the authors study the Spanish Flu, a contagious disease transmitted person to person whose harm is attributed to infected individuals. It is measured as municipality Spanish Flu mortality per 1,000 individuals, adding mortality attributed to Spanish Flu and pneumonia because some Spanish Flu cases had pneumonia as the final cause of death.

name: Retail cooperative founding
authors_terms: ["foundings of cooperatives", "foundings of retail cooperatives", "founding of a cooperative association", "formation of retail cooperatives"]
definition: Foundings of retail cooperatives, non-profit community organizations that were general grocery stores organized on cooperative principles. The authors use them as their indicator of community organizing efforts and of resilience, because forming a cooperative is a community-level collective action problem.

name: Civic capacity
authors_terms: ["civic capacity", "organizational diversity", "diversity of nonprofits", "diverse non-profit sector"]
definition: The community's capacity to create a diverse stock of non-profits, encompassing experienced founders and workers, dense social connections, and trust of others. A more diverse stock of non-profits leaves a community with significant civic capacity that makes it adaptive in handling many kinds of community needs.

name: Weather shock
definition: Spring frost, a weather shock attributed to nature that damaged crops; unlike the Spanish Flu it did not produce fatalities, but it led to economic hardship and is expected to induce shared storage and insurance solutions.

name: Timing reproduction
authors_terms: ["timing reproduction", "Reproducing the timing of organizational actions", "Reproduction"]
definition: Following Cohen (2007), we define timing reproduction as the extent to which the timing of organizational actions in a specific routine performance is similar to its previous performances.

name: Effective routine performance
authors_terms: ["effective routine performance", "effectiveness of routine performance", "routine effectiveness", "performance effectiveness"]
definition: Our focus on effective performance is consistent with research distinguishing between routine effectiveness based on assessments of outcome quality, and routine efficiency based on the utilization of resources, such as time and costs. In our setting, effectiveness is evaluated through indicators of customer satisfaction.

name: Multiplicity in the timing of routine performances
authors_terms: ["multiplicity in the timing of routine performances", "multiplicity of the performative aspects", "variability in routine performances", "historical consistency of action timing"]
definition: Multiplicity of the performative aspects—manifested in variability in routine performances—is one of the core observations in routine dynamics research. Timing-based patterning, however, occurs only to the extent that action timing is recurrent, i.e., consistent across routine performances.

name: Outsider bureaucratic experience
definition: Participants' bureaucratic experience—the knowledge of organizing that they have obtained by working in organizations characterized by cultural and coordinative structures that favor formal design—is likely to influence individual orientations toward adherence to formal routine design.

name: Co-present point of view on the routine
definition: Participants' perspective on the routine is also affected by their co-presence, and the resulting ability to observe and attend to the interdependent actions of other participants.

name: Different performance conditions
authors_terms: ["different performance conditions", "differences in the performance conditions", "holidays"]
definition: Differences in the performance conditions refer to recognizable differences in some aspects of the environment in which the routine is performed.

name: Proportion of agency workforce
authors_terms: ["proportion of the agency workforce", "proportion of agency workers", "use of an agency workforce", "use of agency temps"]
definition: The number of agency workers divided by the total workforce in each store; the authors use it as the measure of how much a store relies on agency temps.

name: Workplace identification
authors_terms: ["workplace identification", "identification of the regular workforce with the workplace", "identification of employees with their workplace", "workplace identification of the regular workforce"]
definition: 'Workplace identification' describes the degree to which employees define themselves as members of their group and experience a sense of oneness with, or belonging to, a group. It also captures the extent to which a workplace is valued and meaningful to its members.

name: Store-level business performance
authors_terms: ["store-level business performance", "store-level performance", "business performance", "business outcomes", "store-level sales and service quality"]
definition: The business outcomes of the store, examined specifically as store-level sales and service quality.

name: Shared instrumental values
authors_terms: ["shared instrumental value", "sharing an instrumental value of using agency workforce", "shared instrumental values", "shared vision"]
definition: 'Shared instrumental value' refers to communicating the 'business case,' or why a strategic direction is believed to be an effective means to a desirable end state; in this context it includes explaining to the regular workforce why having an agency workforce was necessary or at least important for the stores and its stakeholders.

name: Social integration practices
definition: Practices for managing differences such as social events with coworkers, bringing family members to work events and celebrations, or sharing information about personal lives across different groups, which blur the social identity boundary across different races and statuses in the workplace.

name: Job security threat
definition: The prior-research explanation that regular employees believe that agency temps may replace them, i.e., a job security threat.

name: Opportunities for advancement
definition: The competing explanation that agency temps may reduce regular employees' opportunities for advancement, i.e., a professional threat.

name: Firm strategic nonconformity
authors_terms: ["strategic nonconformity", "firm strategic nonconformity", "nonconformist strategies", "strategic behaviors that deviate from their industries' norms"]
definition: Strategic behaviors in which a firm deviates from its industry's norms, potentially involving unique investments in marketing or research and development, unusual strategic asset deployments, innovative use of capital, or aggressively using acquisitions to grow and enter new markets.

name: CEO demographic atypicality
definition: A CEO's personal distinctiveness arising from demographic attributes that are rare among CEOs; the authors define minority status as the CEO being either a woman or a person of color.

name: CEO self-promotion
definition: CEOs' own efforts to attract positive media attention, through which they push themselves and their stories into public view by becoming regular sources for journalists' stories.

name: CEO celebrity
authors_terms: ["CEO celebrity", "degree of celebrity attainment", "degree of CEO celebrity"]
definition: The degree to which a CEO elicits positive emotional responses from a broad public audience; conceptualized here as an ordinal construct with discrete gradations referred to as noncelebrities, B-list celebrities, and A-list celebrities.

name: Brokerage structure inequity
authors_terms: ["brokerage structure inequity in knowledge recombination opportunity", "brokerage knowledge recombination inequity", "structural inequity", "inequity in knowledge recombination opportunity"]
definition: We define brokerage knowledge recombination inequity as the disproportionately higher recombination opportunities available to the broker for the alter firms' knowledge use than those available to the alter for the broker's knowledge use because of the broker occupying a favorable structural position.

name: Brokerage decay
definition: A brokerage triad remains stable when it exhibits no change in composition and relationships from one time period to the next (i.e., when neither of the two existing broker-alter ties dissolves and the triad stays open). We operationalize Decay as 1 for the year in which the triad status quo changes and thus brokerage decays.

name: Broker-alter geographic distance
authors_terms: ["Broker-alter geographic distance (in thousand miles)", "geographic distance", "geography", "broker-alter spatial proximity"]
definition: We use the term 'geography' to refer to the spatial distance between two firms. Geographic distance is the distance between the broker firm and each of its two alter firms.

name: Investor funding decision
authors_terms: ["investment decisions", "funding a venture", "investors' funding", "investment attractiveness", "amount invested", "expected investment"]
definition: We operationalized respondents' investment decisions using three measures (Huang & Pearce, 2015). The first, Investment Attractiveness, captures the response for the attractiveness of the investment opportunity using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (definitely unattractive) to 5 (definitely attractive).

name: Previous venture outcome
authors_terms: ["past entrepreneurial outcome", "previous entrepreneurial outcome", "previous venture outcome", "past failure", "past success"]
definition: The answers reflect entrepreneurial outcomes as perceived by investors; that is, the previous venture was either a failure or a success.

name: Entrepreneurial skill cue
authors_terms: ["additional skill cue", "credible skill cue", "information about entrepreneurial skill", "skill cue"]
definition: The award concerns the individual entrepreneur rather than the venture's ultimate outcome and is an important cue of that person's entrepreneurial skill.

name: CFO function-based language incongruity
authors_terms: ["CFO function-based language incongruity", "function-based language incongruity", "role incongruent language"]
definition: The incongruity that occurs when a CFO exhibits linguistic attributes (high optimism, risk-taking, promotion focus, and future focus) that are inconsistent with the expectations bankers hold of the CFO's functional role. The authors describe it as a within-role incongruity arising from the mismatch between the individual's exhibited linguistic pattern and the expectations of that individual's particular functional role.

name: Number of covenants
authors_terms: ["number of covenants", "number of debt contract covenants"]
definition: The number of covenants used in a debt contract; covenants require the borrower to maintain certain accounting measures of financial health, and a contract with more covenants gives the lender more stringent control over the borrower.

name: Corresponding CEO language
definition: The linguistic pattern of the CEO measured on the same four dimensions used for the CFO (optimism, risk-taking, promotion focus, and future focus), capturing whether the CFO's language is consistent with the broader social context of the organization.

name: Media sentiment positivity
definition: The positivity of sentiment toward the borrowing firm expressed in business news articles, which shapes bankers' sentiment toward the firm and their interpretation of the CFO's incongruent language.

name: Employee disability status
authors_terms: ["receiving service from a person with a disability", "receiving service from an employee with disabilities", "employment of people with disabilities", "receiving service from a cashier with a disability", "service from a person with a disability"]
definition: Disability is a complex construct that incorporates a plethora of conditions, encompassing physical, mental, sensory, learning, neurological, and other differences. The studies vary whether customers receive service from an employee with a disability (hearing disability in Studies 1 and 2; also using a wheelchair in Study 2) versus an employee without disabilities.

name: Contact quality
definition: In our service context, service (transaction) satisfaction - that is, the customer's assessment of a specific service encounter - is quality. Contact quality is operationalized as service satisfaction in the retail setting.

name: Competence stereotypes
definition: Stereotypes are defined as socially shared sets of beliefs about traits and behaviors of members of a social group. People with disabilities are viewed as less competent (i.e., low performing, more absent, dependent, and helpless) than people without disabilities.

name: Warmth stereotypes
definition: Stereotypes are defined as socially shared sets of beliefs about traits and behaviors of members of a social group. People with disabilities are viewed as warmer (i.e., capturing gentlehearted, nonegoistical, and saintlike) than people without disabilities.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Customer-based corporate reputation is defined as the customer's overall evaluation of a firm based on his or her reactions to the firm's goods, services, communication activities, interactions with the firm and/or its representatives or constituencies (such as employees, management, or other customers) and/or known corporate activities.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR is well established in the literature and refers to discretionary organizational responsibility for its impact on society. Since employment of people with disabilities benefits these individuals and society, it can be perceived as a specific CSR initiative.

name: Sincere CSR motives
authors_terms: ["sincere CSR motives", "sincere motives", "value-driven and other-oriented CSR initiatives"]
definition: Customers process available information to infer the CSR motives of the company for the initiative; two primary attributions are sincere and pro-social versus egoistic and self-serving motives. Customers approve value-driven and other-oriented CSR initiatives.

name: Egoistic CSR motives
definition: Two primary, though variably labeled, attributions are sincere and pro-social versus egoistic and self-serving motives. Customers disregard or even boycott self-oriented, egoistic initiatives.

name: Disability-job fit stereotypes
definition: Individuals hold stereotypes about what a person with a specific disability can do well and not as well. This impression is compared to what individuals know, or think they know, about requirements for specific jobs, and based on this, individuals hold specific disability-job fit stereotypes.

name: Subordinate category spanning
definition: Companies were considered to be in the subordinate category spanning (SubCS) condition when they were assigned to more than one subordinate category but only one basic category. A nested category is a subordinate category that is included within a basic category through an 'is-a' relationship and shares certain features with its basic category while adding some information.

name: Firm valuation
definition: We use the term valuation to refer to the investors' assessment of a firm's economic value relative to other firms. The company's valuation is the pre-money value, which is the value prior to receiving a capital infusion.

name: Perceived inter-category congruence
definition: Congruence is defined as a feeling of harmony between elements. From an information processing perspective, congruence depends on an impression of harmony between cues from different categories, in other words, cues that 'go well together'.

name: Investor expertise
definition: Expertise, defined as a 'high level of domain-specific knowledge', affects how individuals understand and use categories. An investor's expertise is a lead investor's past experience in the target company's primary basic industry.

name: Across-domain thinking
definition: To manipulate perceived congruence, the authors built on research showing that when individuals are asked to cognitively bridge separate domains together, they are induced to rely on a relational thinking, that is, 'inferential processes constrained by the relational roles that entities play rather than the specific features of those entities'.

name: Between-group pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["between-group pay dispersion", "BGPD", "job-based horizontal pay dispersion", "pay dispersion between job groups", "the pay-level differences between employees with different jobs in different groups"]
definition: Between-group pay dispersion is the pay-level differences between employees in the same job level but in different job groups. The authors conceptualize it as a job-based form of horizontal pay dispersion, whose bases lie in internal job evaluation and external labor market value differences between job groups.

name: Within-group pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["within-group pay dispersion", "WGPD", "explained WGPD", "explained within-group pay dispersion", "pay dispersion within a job group"]
definition: Within-group pay dispersion refers to the pay-level differences between employees with the same job within a group. In the authors' research context it is mainly based on legitimate, person-related factors such as productivity-relevant employee inputs and human capital, and is therefore used as a proxy for explained WGPD.

name: Distributive justice climate
authors_terms: ["distributive justice climate", "distributive justice perceptions", "shared perceptions of distributive justice"]
definition: Distributive justice climate is defined as employees' shared perceptions of high fairness regarding the distribution of organizational resources like pay.

name: Intergroup helping
definition: Intergroup helping is a form of affiliative organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) that is cooperative and directed toward out-group colleagues inside the organization.

name: Voluntary turnover rates
definition: Voluntary turnover rates capture the organization's workforce stability, that is, the rate at which employees voluntarily depart. The authors compute each store's voluntary turnover rate as the number of departing employees who left their stores voluntarily divided by the total number of employees working in the store in January 2018.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "store performance", "objective organizational performance", "subjective organizational performance"]
definition: Organizational performance is the store's overall effectiveness, assessed with both an objective indicator (the extent to which the store's first half-year goal was met) and a subjective, multidimensional assessment by store managers of the store's overall productivity and effectiveness.

name: Dismissal rate
definition: 'Employee dismissal' is defined as termination due to poor task performance, lack of integrity, violation of rules and policies, behavior that disrupts the work unit, or other similar reasons with a plan for later replacement.

name: Layoff announcement rate
definition: 'Layoffs' are planned workforce reductions that eliminate certain positions to lower costs. At the unit level, announcements of upcoming changes, such as layoffs, serve as warning signs that jobs are at risk.

name: Voluntary turnover rate
definition: 'Voluntary turnover' events, unlike other exit events, are not initiated by the organization and arise when current employees choose to leave the organization.

name: Human capital flow quality
authors_terms: ["human capital flow quality", "quality of human capital outflows", "human capital quality", "leaver performance", "higher leaver performance", "high-quality workers"]
definition: Consistent with previous literature, we identify 'high-quality workers' as those whose job performance is relatively higher than that of their peers. We index 'human capital quality' using average performance ratings for the unit, thereby defining high-quality workers as those whose performance is above the unit's average.

name: Hiring rate
definition: Although we do not theorize about the effects of hiring on subsequent voluntary turnover, due to the interdependence of human capital inflows and outflows, we included hiring rates in our analysis to ensure we take into account this interdependence.

name: Structural embeddedness
definition: 'Structural embeddedness' refers to economic exchange in patterns of ongoing relations between network actors; applied here, an EE is structurally embedded within the larger EE network to the extent that it maintains ongoing relationships and engages in resource exchanges with other EEs who are themselves connected.

name: Corporate density
definition: 'Corporate density' is defined as the number of public companies in a region, which the authors treat as an important sociocognitive force within the EE.

name: Religiosity
definition: 'Religiosity' is defined as religious orientation and involvement and is typically measured as the level of religious participation and membership in a given region; the authors treat it as a primary source of social interaction within communities.

name: New venture creation
authors_terms: ["new venture creation", "new business establishments", "local entrepreneurial activity"]
definition: New venture creation is the creation of new ventures in an EE, a key indicator of local entrepreneurial activity, operationalized as the total number of new business establishments in each MSA.

name: Firm status
definition: Status reflects an actor's position within 'a socially constructed, intersubjectively agreed-upon and accepted ordering or ranking ... in a social system'. Status hierarchies are often bounded by horizontal categories, such as industries, so a firm's market identity is defined at the intersection of its vertical status position and horizontal industry membership.

name: High-status insider misconduct prevalence
authors_terms: ["high-status insiders' misconduct", "high-status insider breaches", "the prevalence of high-status insiders' transgressions"]
definition: The extent to which other high-status firms in the focal firm's own industry have previously been involved in similar misconduct. The prevalence of high-status insiders' misconduct connotes a potential problem endemic to the industry that is worthy of public concern, increasing the newsworthiness of the current high-status firm's transgression.

name: High-status outsider misconduct prevalence
authors_terms: ["high-status outsiders' misconduct", "high-status outsider breaches", "the prevalence of high-status outsiders' transgressions"]
definition: The extent to which high-status firms outside the focal firm's industry have previously been involved in similar misconduct. Multiple transgressions by high-status firms in a different industry more likely lead to an industry-based explanation the media cannot use to explain the focal actor's transgression.

name: Misconduct scandalization
definition: Scandals are 'publicized transgressions that run counter to established norms'; they arise when actors engage in behaviors that transgress social norms and values in disruptive ways, and their behaviors are brought into the public forum, typically by the media. Misconduct is scandalized only if it is widely publicized by a mediating institution, such as the press.

name: Misconduct publicization
definition: Publicization is the process through which organizational misconduct-relevant allegations make their way into the public domain, i.e., the process whereby misconduct enters the public sphere through the media.

name: Community homogeneity
definition: At the community level, social identification relates to the extent to which the community forms a homogeneous whole - that is, whether community members share a common social identity - or whether, conversely, it is partitioned into subgroups that coalesce based on various attributes.

name: Local embeddedness of the offending organization
authors_terms: ["local embeddedness of the offending organization", "Catholic Church embeddedness", "embeddedness of the offending organization in the community"]
definition: We conceptualize the local embeddedness of an organization within a local community as a function of the degree to which organizational members have ties to the community and the strength of such ties.

name: Community social connectedness
definition: We define community social connectedness as the degree to which the community provides opportunities for social interaction that allow for the circulation of information across social groups.

name: Predecessor-candidate racial similarity
definition: We argue that racial similarity between predecessors and leader candidates is a necessary precondition for evaluators to confuse two leaders in memory, and that this confusion drives leader transference.

name: Predecessor performance
authors_terms: ["predecessor performance", "prior coach's win-loss record", "team winning percentage"]
definition: Evaluators will assume that the predecessor's personality was well-suited for the leadership role if they performed well, and detrimental if they performed poorly. In Study 1 it is measured as the prior coach's win-loss record, which reflects the objective team winning percentage for the season leading up to the new coaching appointment.

name: Leader selection
definition: Succession events involve decisions about who to hire for a leadership role; leader selection is the decision of evaluators, such as board members and human resource managers, about which candidate to appoint to the vacated role.

name: Transference
definition: We introduce racial transference as a bias in which evaluators falsely assume that a leader candidate has the same personality traits and leadership potential as a racially similar predecessor. We used false alarms as the measure of transference, a score that refers to the probability of erroneously recognizing traits of the predecessor as traits of the candidate.

name: Cross-industry mobility
definition: A voluntary job move in which an executive changes industry, that is, moves to a firm belonging to a different industry category than the origin firm. The authors conceptualize cross-industry moves as a two-way process comprising candidate-side judgments and audience evaluations.

name: Executive compensation
definition: The executive's total compensation, used as the dependent variable in all core regressions and measured with ExecuComp data item TDC1, winsorized and log-transformed.

name: Industry status difference
authors_terms: ["industry-status differences", "status differences between an executive's origin and destination industries", "status leap", "status leak", "industry status"]
definition: The difference in social standing, or prestige, between the industry an executive leaves and the industry the executive joins; a status leap is a move to a higher-status industry and a status leak a move to a lower-status industry. Industry status refers to the social standing or prestige accorded to a particular type of business, originating from the vertical connection of categories through status hierarchies.

name: Women's representation in senior management
authors_terms: ["women's representation in senior management", "representation of women in senior management", "proportion of women partners", "women's representation at the top", "gender diversity in senior management"]
definition: Women's representation in senior management alludes to the demographic composition of the top managerial ranks; it indicates that the firm has relatively more women in top positions compared to industry peers where gender diversity at senior levels is exceedingly low.

name: Engagement with internal diversity practices
authors_terms: ["engagement with internal diversity practices", "engagement with diversity practices", "organizational attention to diversity practices"]
definition: The extent to which a firm prioritized and implemented a comprehensive set of internal diversity practices that require a substantial allocation of resources, time, and effort. A firm's attention to diversity becomes evident when it prioritizes and allocates resources to initiatives and practices aimed at addressing diversity issues.

name: Job offers to junior women
authors_terms: ["number of jobs offered to junior women", "job offers extended to women at entry levels", "number of full-time job offers extended to women candidates"]
definition: The number of full-time job offers extended to women candidates for the entry-level associate position, where each job offer is based on a discrete, independent selection decision for a candidate.

name: Women's representation on diversity and hiring committees
authors_terms: ["substantive representation of women on the diversity and hiring committees", "women on diversity and hiring committees", "women's substantive representation on these committees"]
definition: Substantive representation entails the appointment of a significantly higher proportion of women across ranks to the diversity and hiring committees; having critical mass across these decision-making bodies gives women the formal responsibility, assigned power, and authority to monitor the diversity and employment-related decisions of the firm.

name: Entrepreneur gender
definition: Gender is described as one of the most potent explanatory variables studied in entrepreneurship; entrepreneurs in the studies were categorized as women or men.

name: Interdependent self-construal
definition: 'Interdependent self-construal' refers to a view of the self that is defined by one's close relationships (Cross et al., 2011). Individuals with higher interdependent self-construals answer the question 'Who am I?' in terms of their important relationships (e.g., friend, coworker).

name: Interpersonal attraction
authors_terms: ["interpersonal attraction", "interpersonal attraction strategy", "interpersonal attraction selection strategy"]
definition: Women entrepreneurs are likely to select cofounders by focusing on cofounder qualities that promote cohesive relationships (e.g., trustworthiness, familiarity, liking) - a selection strategy known as 'interpersonal attraction'.

name: Resource seeking
definition: Women entrepreneurs are likely to choose cofounders with a heightened focus on the skills, knowledge, or experience of their potential cofounder - a selection strategy known as 'resource seeking'.

name: Legitimacy
definition: 'Legitimacy' is defined as the extent to which the actions of a venture and founder are deemed appropriate by evaluators operating within a socially constructed system of norms.

name: Trust violation
definition: An event or act that erodes trusting beliefs and confidence in a trustee; in this setting it arises when a shipbroker, instead of matching the focal firm with a cargo owner, matches the focal shipowner-operator with another shipowner-operator and in turn matches the latter with the cargo owner.

name: Spatial embeddedness
definition: 'Spatial embeddedness' captures collocation, or the embeddedness of both partner firms in the same space.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: A joint history of formal dyadic relationships between a focal firm and its broker partner, highlighting that a formal interfirm relationship is 'by definition an a-spatial concept'.

name: Focal firm-broker tie reinitiation
authors_terms: ["focal firm-broker tie reinitiation", "tie reinitiation", "repeat tie formation", "tie persistence", "repatronage"]
definition: The hazard that the focal firm reinitiates a tie with a broker firm (i.e., experiences an event) conditional on the existence of a prior tie between the focal firm and the broker.

name: Participation in a knowledge-sharing gathering
authors_terms: ["participation in the gathering", "participation in the intervention", "having participated in the intervention", "post-participation dummy"]
definition: Whether one or more entrepreneurial ecosystem architects from a county attended an in-person, connectedness-related gathering designed to foster cross-county sharing of tacit knowledge.

name: New business foundings
definition: Registration occurs when a founder formally establishes a venture as a legal entity by filing paperwork with a governmental authority; the authors refer to instances of registration as foundings.

name: Community improvement organizations
authors_terms: ["community improvement organizations", "community improvement and business associations", "community improvement associations"]
definition: Local chambers of commerce and voluntary associations aiming to improve local economies, whose presence is treated as reflecting a community's social capital.

name: Economic inequality
definition: The level of income inequality within a county, which the authors argue drives generalized social trust and thereby shapes the absorption of knowledge spillovers.

name: Formal collective membership
authors_terms: ["formal collective focus", "formal collective membership", "shared departmental membership", "disciplinary department"]
definition: Formal foci are organizational units such as departments or divisions, in which membership to the unit is assigned as a term of employment.

name: Semiformal collective membership
authors_terms: ["semiformal collective focus", "semiformal collective membership", "shared center membership", "research center membership"]
definition: Semiformal foci are organizational units that are administratively afforded but voluntarily joined. Semiformal foci take a variety of forms, including task committees, voluntary project teams, and advisory groups.

name: Formal bridging membership
definition: Formal bridging memberships occur when one individual is assigned to more than one functional department; for both memberships to qualify as formal, the employee must hold reporting and responsibility in both.

name: Semiformal bridging membership
definition: Semiformal bridging memberships occur when the individual is a full member in one department and is allowed to join a second department on a voluntary basis; this membership does not include the full set of duties and responsibilities inherent in a formal membership.

name: New work-related collaboration tie
authors_terms: ["new work-related collaboration", "new tie formation", "new collaborative tie", "coauthoring publications", "applying together for grants"]
definition: The unit of focus is the new tie created between individuals i and j in year t, in the two activities of coauthoring publications and applying together for grants, both of which are central to the work of knowledge creation.

name: Individual productivity
definition: Employees' overall productivity, comprising both individual output and collaborative work, measured as yearly counts of publications authored and grants proposed.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: Organizational mortality was modeled in terms of the instantaneous mortality rate: q is the probability of organization j dying between t and t + dt, and the rate r for j is allowed to vary as a function of age t.

name: Density of magneto companies
authors_terms: ["density of magneto companies", "magneto density", "local density", "nonlocal density"]
definition: Density of the nonstandardized companies using the primitive magneto power technology, measured for each organization with a local term (the number of magneto companies in its geographic area) and a nonlocal term (the number of geographically distant magneto companies).

name: Density of common-battery companies
authors_terms: ["common-battery density", "density of common-battery companies", "standardized, common-battery companies"]
definition: Density of the standardized organizations that used the common-battery power technology, in which all telephones in the system were necessarily standardized to the same power level.

name: Density of multi-exchange companies
definition: Density of companies that operated multiple exchanges in communities more than 30 miles apart, taken as the indirect measure of the adoption of line loading in the transmission system.

name: Density of single-exchange companies
definition: Density of companies operating in only one community, or in geographically adjacent communities within a 30-mile radius, i.e., firms without the loaded transmission system.

name: Technological standardization
definition: A systemic technology is made up of more elemental systems, some of which, referred to here as uniform, cohere on the basis of similarity throughout. This is the case with the telephone power system, which must be standardized to the same power level, so that standardized organizations can work together in the same technological system.

name: Technological differentiation
definition: Other elemental systems, referred to here as differentiated, cohere on the basis of complementary differences among components. The telephone transmission system is a differentiated technology; local service and long-distance technologies work together due to their complementary differences.

name: Use of temporary workers
authors_terms: ["temporary workers", "use of temporary workers", "temporary job", "employment externalization"]
definition: Temporary workers are hired and managed by the employing firm rather than by an outside agency and correspond to externalization by reducing the duration of employment.

name: Use of independent contractors
authors_terms: ["independent contractors", "use of independent contractors", "externalization of administrative control"]
definition: Independent contractors correspond to externalization of administrative control and often plan and control their own work.

name: Fringe benefit costs
definition: Fringe benefits are a component of total compensation that is likely to differ significantly between internal and external workers and yields few tangible outputs for the firm.

name: Firm-specific training
definition: Firm-specific training in skills and procedures unique to the firm can be provided only by the firm and involves investing time and other organizational resources in an employee.

name: Variability in employment levels
authors_terms: ["variability in organizational employment levels", "variation in employment", "variation in employment needs"]
definition: Variability in organizational employment levels means that organizations have highly variable employment needs and must continually adjust the size of their workforce.

name: Unionization
definition: Unionization refers to the percentage of workers in an establishment covered by collective bargaining agreements.

name: Government oversight
authors_terms: ["government oversight of affirmative action", "government oversight of employment", "government involvement in monitoring affirmative action practices"]
definition: Government oversight refers to government scrutiny of employment practices, especially affirmative action oversight for firms required to file EEO-1 reports.

name: Bureaucratic employment practices
authors_terms: ["bureaucratization in employment practices", "bureaucratized employment practices", "bureaucratic employment practices"]
definition: Bureaucratic employment practices are practices that ensure that competent, stable, and reliable people are hired and promoted and that make it easier to exercise control over employees.

name: Establishment size
definition: Establishment size is the number of employees at the establishment.

name: Multiple-site organization
authors_terms: ["multiple-site organizations", "multiple-establishment firm", "being part of a multiple-site firm"]
definition: Being part of a multiple-site organization means the firm has other divisions or subsidiaries located outside of the establishment's SMSA.

name: Interpersonal complexity
definition: Jobs high in interpersonal complexity require high levels of interpersonal skill, are typically interdependent with other jobs, and involve high levels of interaction with incumbents of other jobs.

name: Informational complexity
definition: Informational complexity refers to the extent to which jobs involve complex information and are difficult to monitor.

name: Technical complexity
definition: Technically complex jobs often involve both high skill levels and multiple types of skill.

name: Attribute centrality
definition: A dimension's centrality is the average absolute correlation between that dimension's attribute ratings and the ratings of the attributes for all other dimensions. A high DC score means that a dimension is, on average, highly correlated with the other 12 dimensions and is thus central to the correlational structure of the perceived attribute space in the industry.

name: Category association
definition: A dimension's category association is the average absolute correlation between that dimension's attribute ratings and the ratings on the seven self-categorization items. A high CA indicates that a dimension's attribute ratings, on average, are highly correlated with the seven industry categories.

name: Industry model category membership
definition: Organizations in the same category are perceived as comparable and thus form a cognitively plausible market order, so that rivalry within model categories is greater than rivalry between categories.

name: Interfirm rivalry
definition: The authors define rivalry as occurring when one firm orients toward another and considers the actions and characteristics of the other in business decisions, with the goal of achieving a commercial advantage over the other.

name: Category representativeness
definition: Representativeness is defined in the cognitive literature as distance from a category's central tendency; firms close to the category means on defining attributes are representative of the category and should be perceived as core members, while firms that are distant from the attribute means should be perceived as peripheral.

name: Organizational size
definition: Size is a salient and predictive organizational attribute, and size differences are considered to be a major factor in economic rivalry.

name: Outbound rivalry
definition: The number of other firms within the same category that a respondent cited as a rival, standardized by the number of other firms in the category.

name: Inbound rivalry
authors_terms: ["RIVIN", "defined as a rival by other firms"]
definition: The number of other firms within the same category that cited the respondent's firm as a rival, standardized by the number of other firms in the category.

name: Internal labor market practices
definition: Personnel systems within organizations having internal job ladders and other arrangements conducive to long-term employment. In the ideal-typical ILM, ladders are fairly long with few dead-ended jobs, jobs are not concentrated at the bottom, most jobs above the bottom are closed to external entrants, and links between jobs are clearly specified.

name: Job in a promotion ladder
authors_terms: ["job in a promotion ladder", "job in an ILM"]
definition: Whether a particular job is part of a formal promotion ladder. The analyses pertain to formal promotion ladders among jobs as described by employers and U.S. government job analysts, not to the career movements of individuals.

name: Firm-specific skills
definition: Skills acquired on the job that are specific to the establishment and give rise to skill gradients that demarcate career paths. ILMs are said to emerge because they reduce the potential costs of turnover and opportunism that employers face when workers' skills are firm-specific.

name: Establishment size
authors_terms: ["establishment size", "total establishment size", "total number of workers"]
definition: The total number of workers in the establishment; size is claimed to be a pre-eminent determinant of ILMs because large bureaucratic organizations specialize and small firms lack the resources and skill specialization that are preconditions for promotion ladders.

name: Linkage to a larger organization
authors_terms: ["linkages to a larger organization", "linked establishments", "branch establishments"]
definition: Whether the establishment is part of a larger organizational entity, such as a plant or branch office, rather than an autonomous firm; establishments linked to a larger entity are expected to develop bureaucratic procedures and formalized promotion and transfer arrangements.

name: Unionization
definition: Whether any portion of the establishment's line workforce was unionized. Unions are argued to bargain for job ladders, internal bidding systems, company-sponsored training programs, and seniority rights when members' skills are firm-specific.

name: Technology
definition: The modal technology of the establishment. Interdependent tasks in continuous process technologies make skill transmission between senior and junior workers important, whereas craft production is thought to involve general human capital.

name: Industry sector
definition: The industry sector in which the establishment is located, used as a proxy measure for the tangibility of the organization's outputs. Institutional sectors include state and social-overhead-capital activities (transportation, communication, finance, education, health care, culture).

name: Establishment gender composition
definition: The percentage of women working in the jobs analyzed by the Employment Service in each establishment.

name: Job gender composition
authors_terms: ["all-male jobs", "jobs held exclusively by women", "sex composition"]
definition: Whether a job is held exclusively by women or exclusively by men, based on Employment Service staffing schedules and job analyses.

name: Job size
definition: The number of incumbents in a job, which reflects the job's position among the rungs of a ladder; positions in which many individuals are employed often serve as key jobs that define promotion and wage ladders.

name: Information-oriented job tasks
authors_terms: ["jobs oriented principally toward information", "complex informational skills", "DOT measures of 'data' and 'things'"]
definition: The complexity of workers' informational and technical duties, operationalized by job ratings on the DOT measures of data and things. Jobs dealing primarily with information are expected to have fewer firm-specific assets than jobs dealing with things.

name: Managerial and production occupational composition
authors_terms: ["percentage of workers in managerial and production occupations"]
definition: The percentage of an establishment's workers in managerial and production occupations, based on three-digit DOT codes; such workers are thought to monopolize firm-specific skills and internal promotions.

name: Professional, technical, clerical, and service occupational composition
authors_terms: ["percentage of workers in professional, technical, clerical, and service occupations"]
definition: The percentage of an establishment's workers in professional, technical, clerical, sales, and service occupations, based on three-digit DOT codes; such workers' skills are more general and transferable across establishments.

name: Occupational type of job
authors_terms: ["occupational type", "professional and technical jobs", "line production jobs"]
definition: The occupation of a job, based on three-digit DOT codes, used to distinguish managerial and production jobs from professional, clerical, sales, and service jobs.

name: Bottom-level position in a ladder
definition: Whether a job is on the bottom level of its promotion ladder.

name: Openness to external entry
authors_terms: ["entered from outside the establishment", "open to outsiders"]
definition: Whether a job can be entered from outside the establishment. A job was considered open to outsiders if it was at the bottom of a promotion ladder or, for jobs above the bottom, if the employer stated that outsiders could be hired.

name: Future mobility prospects of a job
definition: Whether a job that is in a ladder has additional mobility opportunities, i.e., is not dead-ended at the top of a ladder.

name: Job title proliferation
authors_terms: ["fragmentation", "job-title proliferation", "proliferation of detailed job titles", "excess division of labor"]
definition: The extent to which organizations use detailed job titles to describe work roles, making finer distinctions among jobs than are required simply on the basis of job content. It is measured by comparing an organization's administrative titles to an independent expert's classification of jobs.

name: Organizational size
definition: The scale of the enterprise. A large body of research regards organizational scale as the principal determinant of the division of labor; as organizations grow, they increasingly specialize and differentiate activities, vertically as well as horizontally.

name: Production technology
definition: The modal technology of the enterprise, classified into categories derived from Woodward: unit or craft, batch, mass, and process, with additional categories for service and extractive technologies. Establishments using batch and mass production technologies attempt to make unskilled workers as replaceable as possible.

name: Firm-specific skills
authors_terms: ["firm-specific skills", "level of technical skill", "highly trained workers"]
definition: The extent to which work roles depend on skills that are specific to the firm. Vertical distinctions are often used within skilled occupational roles requiring learning by doing, and the measures of technical skill and the percentage of non-entry-level jobs tend to capture the effects of firm-specific skills.

name: General human capital
authors_terms: ["general human capital", "general skills", "general training", "average training time (specific vocational preparation, SVP)"]
definition: The relative importance of general skills in an organization, captured by the net effect of the average training time (SVP) measure, controlling for the level of manual skills and the percentage of workers in non-entry-level jobs. Workers whose training is general are likely to move frequently across firms, which diffuses work arrangements and job structures across organizations.

name: Internal labor market
authors_terms: ["internal labor markets", "internal labor market arrangements", "promotion hierarchies"]
definition: Firms whose workers are difficult to replace implement promotion hierarchies, even in the absence of skill gradients among specific jobs, to reduce turnover and ensure harmony among workers; such hierarchies can be viewed as an efficient incentive mechanism or as a subtle control device.

name: Professional, technical, and managerial worker share
authors_terms: ["professional, technical, and managerial (PT&M) occupations", "PT&M workers", "percentage of workers in professional, technical, and managerial occupations"]
definition: The proportion of an organization's workforce in professional, technical, and managerial occupations. The power and autonomy that professionals command may allow them to solidify their organizational positions by differentiating work along lines dictated by occupational specialties, and status gradations have the greatest significance among these highest status occupations.

name: Gender composition of the workforce
authors_terms: ["percent female", "gender composition", "gender mix", "percentage of female employees", "sex ratio"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's employees who are female. When women constitute a trivial percentage of the workforce they tend to be concentrated in stereotypical roles, whereas when the gender mix is relatively balanced the authors expect organizations to use separate labels to preserve the customary segregation of work by sex.

name: Personnel specialization
authors_terms: ["personnel specialists", "specialized personnel role or function", "personnel specialization", "personnel function"]
definition: The presence of a specialized personnel role or function in the organization. In larger enterprises the duties of personnel specialists were more likely to include the specification of job requirements and titles.

name: Unionization
definition: Whether an enterprise's line workers are covered by collective bargaining. Unions represent a constituency affecting job structures: industrial unions have attempted to make members irreplaceable by acceding to the proliferation of detailed administrative job titles, whereas craft unions have generally resisted managerial attempts to define the nature of the task.

name: Institutional sector
authors_terms: ["public sector", "social overhead capital industries", "institutional sectors", "industry sector"]
definition: The industrial location of the organization, especially the public sector and social-overhead-capital industries. Organizations often adopt highly bureaucratic procedures because this enhances their legitimacy in the eyes of constituents, and bureaucratization occurs most when the output of a set of organizations cannot easily be measured.

name: Industry average organizational size
authors_terms: ["average size of enterprises in the organization's industry", "large organizational co-actors", "average firm size"]
definition: The average size of enterprises in the organization's industry, used as a proxy for the tendency toward isomorphism within organizational fields. When most enterprises within a field are large, they are more likely to engage in regularized and systematic exchanges that foster a more similar lexicon of job titles across organizations.

name: Market environment complexity
authors_terms: ["market scope", "complexity and diversity of an organization's market environment", "environmental complexity"]
definition: The breadth and diversity of the organization's market environment. Open systems perspectives posit that organizations confronting complex environments are favored when they adapt through internal complexity, labeling boundary-spanning jobs according to the particular parts of the environment with which they deal.

name: Sales worker share
definition: The proportion of an organization's workers employed in sales jobs. The authors expect enterprises with a large contingent of sales personnel to exhibit more fragmentation, since product, market, or geographical distinctions are often used to distinguish sales personnel.

name: Craft and skilled workforce
authors_terms: ["craft workers", "skilled workers", "craft technology", "general skills or training"]
definition: Whether an enterprise's production workers command substantial general skills or training, as indicated by reliance on craft technology or unusually high average training time. The bargaining power of such workers depends on keeping skills general rather than firm-specific and on retaining control over job assignments.

name: Threat-distinctive issue characteristics
definition: Issue characteristics that are consistent with threat and discrepant from opportunity; such characteristics are distinctive and should lead to strong inferences.

name: Opportunity-distinctive issue characteristics
definition: Issue characteristics that are consistent with opportunity and discrepant from threat; such characteristics are distinctive and should lead to strong inferences.

name: Ambiguous issue characteristics
definition: Nondistinctive issue characteristics that are consistent with both concepts and discrepant from neither.

name: Neutral issue characteristics
definition: Nondistinctive issue characteristics that are neither consistent nor inconsistent with either concept.

name: Perceived threat
authors_terms: ["inferences about the presence of a threat", "perceived threat", "threat inferences"]
definition: An inference about the presence of a threat; one of the two dependent variables of Study 2.

name: Perceived opportunity
authors_terms: ["inferences about the presence of an opportunity", "perceived opportunity", "opportunity inferences"]
definition: An inference about the presence of an opportunity; one of the two dependent variables of Study 2.

name: Threat concept fit
authors_terms: ["threat ratings", "how well the characteristic fits your understanding of a strategic issue that is a THREAT"]
definition: How well an issue characteristic fits a manager's conception of a threat.

name: Opportunity concept fit
authors_terms: ["opportunity ratings", "how well the characteristic fits your understanding of a strategic issue that is an OPPORTUNITY"]
definition: How well an issue characteristic fits a manager's conception of an opportunity.

name: Bargaining without a bargaining law
authors_terms: ["bargaining without a law", "bargaining without being covered by a law", "CBNOLAW", "bargaining without law coverage"]
definition: A bargaining relationship not covered by a protective law, in which unions use economic and political power tactics to compel the city to bargain and must rely on their power to maintain the relationship. If subunits are able to maintain such a bargaining relationship, they are expected to receive greater resource allocations than nonbargaining subunits.

name: Bargaining under a bargaining law
authors_terms: ["mandated relationship", "bargaining in mandated relationships", "bargaining under a law", "CBLAW"]
definition: A relationship in which a state law gives employees the right to negotiate and requires the employer to deal with the employees' representative, removing the public employer's right to refuse to participate in bargaining. Given equivalent economic sources of power, a subunit bargaining in a mandated relationship increases its power relative to the employer to a greater extent than subunits bargaining without a law.

name: Bargaining with interest arbitration available
authors_terms: ["arbitration available by law", "bargaining with arbitration available", "compulsory interest arbitration", "CBARB"]
definition: A second type of mandated relationship, created by an arbitration law, in which cities and unionized police officers must submit unresolved negotiating disputes to an arbitrator whose award is binding on the parties. When economic sources of power are controlled for, a subunit bargaining with arbitration available increases its power relative to the employer to a greater extent than subunits bargaining without arbitration.

name: Resource allocations to the police department
authors_terms: ["resource allocations to the police department", "allocations to police departments", "police department resource allocations"]
definition: The allocation of financial and human resources to the police department, constructed from data on police department expenditures, total city expenditures, and full-time police employment. Because bargaining increases the subunit's relative power, its claims on the organization's allocation of monetary resources are also expected to increase.

name: Total city expenditures
definition: The overall city budget, used to examine overall city budgets and assess possible responses to the cost pressures generated by bargaining relationships.

name: Submit power
definition: Subunit power within organizations is defined as the capacity of a subunit to influence the behavior of other subunits (Hickson et al., 1971; Hickson et al., 1981; Astley and Sachdeva, 1984).

name: Control over structural conditions
authors_terms: ["control over structural conditions", "control over strategic contingencies", "control over contingencies"]
definition: The structural conditions of coping with uncertainty, centrality, and substitutability prevalently proposed in the literature as the main sources of power; the theory proposes that subunit power is derived from control over contingencies that are strategic for the activities of other subunits and the organization as a whole.

name: Coping with uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty is defined as 'lack of information about future events so that alternatives and their outcomes are unpredictable'; coping is defined as the effective dealing with uncertainties, and the ability of subunits to cope with and reduce uncertainties for other subunits constitutes a source of intraorganizational power.

name: Centrality
definition: Subunits interconnected with many other subunits are considered to have more control over flows in the task, social interaction, or communication networks and, therefore, are potentially more powerful. Pervasiveness is the extent to which a subunit's activities are linked to the workflow of others.

name: Nonsubstitutability
definition: A subunit is regarded as nonsubstitutable when no alternatives are available to its activities and function.

name: Golden parachute adoption
definition: Contracts between the executive and the employer that provide for additional compensation should a change in control or ownership occur.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm; larger firms are considered less likely to become takeover targets because their size makes them more expensive to acquire and because size increases differentiation and structural complexity.

name: Owner control
definition: Whether the firm is owner-controlled, i.e., at least 5 percent of the stock is beneficially owned by an individual or organization, as opposed to management-controlled with dispersed shareholders.

name: Takeover susceptibility
definition: Factors that make a takeover significantly more or less likely; a firm whose assets are undervalued by the market is more susceptible to takeover.

name: CEO external reputation
authors_terms: ["external reputation", "CEO reputation", "number of corporate boards on which the CEO serves"]
definition: A CEO's social reputation and standing, indicated by the number of other corporate boards of directors on which the CEO serves, which may give the CEO leverage in bargaining with the board.

name: CEO relative tenure on the board
authors_terms: ["CEO's relative tenure", "CEO relative tenure", "board tenure of the CEO relative to the board's average tenure"]
definition: The CEO's board tenure relative to the board's average tenure; a CEO with long tenure compared to the board may leave the board feeling less expert and more obligated.

name: Outside directors appointed after the CEO
authors_terms: ["appointment of outside directors", "percentage of the board that is composed of outside directors appointed after the CEO", "number of outsiders appointed after the CEO"]
definition: The percentage of the board composed of outside directors appointed after the CEO joined the board; such directors were likely selected with the CEO's hand and may feel reciprocity and obligation toward the CEO.

name: CEO board tenure
definition: The length of the CEO's tenure on the board of directors.

name: Interorganizational linkages
authors_terms: ["interorganizational linkages", "affiliation with a political party", "party affiliation", "party-affiliated papers", "linked organizations"]
definition: The interorganizational linkage examined in this study was affiliation with a political party. Papers linked with political parties constitute the group of organizations with interorganizational linkages for this study.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Failure was defined as the permanent cessation of a newspaper's publication.

name: Organizational transformation
definition: Transformation was defined as the occurrence of a change in one or more of the following areas: content, coverage, editor in chief, language, layout (including frequency of publication), location, merger, publisher, or responsible editor.

name: Multiple transformations
definition: If more than one attribute was altered in the same issue (both frequency of publication and coverage, for example), the event was coded as a multiple-attribute change.

name: Environmental shocks
definition: Environmental shocks or disturbances were represented by a set of seven period-effect dummy variables. During environmental shock periods, change may be deep, fast-paced, and discrete.

name: Insider ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership by insiders", "insider ownership", "management stock ownership", "proportion of all outstanding shares held by all officers and directors"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's outstanding shares held by its officers and directors. Managers' and boards' stock ownership aligns their interests with those of stockholders, and their resistance to takeovers decreases with increasing stock ownership.

name: Golden parachute contract
definition: Contracts that provide compensation to one or more executives of the firm if their employment is terminated following a change in control, typically including several years' salary and often provisions to accelerate stock options and benefits.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["concentrated ownership", "ownership concentration", "percentage of shares held by all large blockholders"]
