definition: The percentage of shares held by all large (5 percent or more) blockholders. To the extent that ownership is concentrated in a small number of hands, the free-rider problem of monitoring management is lessened.

name: Insider board dominance
authors_terms: ["proportion of insiders on the board", "insider board dominance", "percentage of directors that were executives of the firm"]
definition: Inside directors are board members who are also executives of the firm; insider board dominance is the proportion of the board that such insiders constitute. The authors assume insiders can be presumed to be rubber stamps for management initiatives.

name: Interlock network centrality
definition: A firm's position in the interlock network described in terms of its centrality: more central firms are those that are tied to a greater number of other firms. Greater centrality gives a firm social capital and indicates its status and integration into the corporate elite.

name: Ties to prior adopters
authors_terms: ["ties to adopters", "interlocks with other firms that have already adopted", "ties to other adopters"]
definition: The number of the focal firm's interlock partners that had previously adopted a poison pill. Conceptually the measure captures the firm's access to direct information about the merits of adoption.

name: Industry prevalence of adoption
authors_terms: ["prevalence of adoption in a firm's industry", "prevalence of adoption by 2-digit SIC industry"]
definition: The percentage of firms in a firm's primary industry that had adopted a poison pill as of the beginning of the current quarter, where primary industry is defined by the 2-digit category in which the firm made most of its sales.

name: Poison pill adoption
authors_terms: ["poison pill adoption", "rate of poison pill adoption", "shareholder rights plan adoption"]
definition: The adoption by the board of directors, without shareholder approval, of a device that raises barriers to takeover; the pill is issued as a dividend and entitles its holder to buy shares at a deeply discounted rate should a takeover attempt occur without board approval.

name: Takeover risk
authors_terms: ["risk of takeover", "risk of receiving a tender offer", "risk of becoming subject to a tender offer", "hazard rate of a tender offer", "vulnerability to takeover"]
definition: The unobserved hazard rate at which a firm becomes subject to a tender offer, assumed to depend on the firm's individual characteristics as well as on factors that affect all firms in the risk set in similar ways.

name: Market-to-book ratio
definition: The ratio of the stock market value of the firm's outstanding common shares to the accounting (book) value of this equity, taken as a measure of how the market evaluates the firm and its management.

name: Return on equity
definition: A more immediate measure of corporate performance than market-to-book; firms earning higher returns are expected to be subject to less risk of takeover if takeovers discipline underperforming firms.

name: Cash flow
definition: Organization theory treats high cash flow as a cushion and buffer, while agency theorists argue that large cash flows increase managerial discretion and can be tapped after a takeover to pay off debt financing used to fund it.

name: Debt
definition: Taking on substantial debt is the most credible way for managers to bond a promise to pay out cash flows and thus reduces managerial discretion; firms laden with debt provide less post-takeover free cash flow to service takeover debt.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizations become increasingly rigid and incapable of adaptation with age as routines become set, political coalitions fall into place and the power structure crystallizes, so that under significant environmental change rigid organizations become out of sync with their environment.

name: Workforce tenure
definition: Firms that encourage loyalty through internal labor markets build more tenured workforces that are more highly paid, so that without growth to bring in new recruits at lower wages firms are saddled with high and increasing average wages.

name: Employment growth
definition: Expansion of the firm's workforce, computed as a percentage change in employment for each year; the use of deferred compensation is most feasible for firms experiencing sustained growth.

name: Family control
definition: Family-controlled firms are those in which a single individual or family maintains ownership of a significant block of the firm's stock, a situation in which the family can monitor management closely and can veto unwanted bids.

name: Bank control
definition: The view that financial institutions filled the breach in control caused by the managerial revolution by dominating decision making in many firms through controlling substantial blocks of stock or by placing representatives on the board of directors.

name: Board interlocks
authors_terms: ["interlocks", "interlocking boards of directors", "intercorporate network ties", "ties sent by banks"]
definition: Interlocks with banks and other firms rarely effect power relations; rather they provide firms with access to information and, potentially, resources, and indicate a firm's central position in the intercorporate power structure.

name: Organizational level
authors_terms: ["organizational level", "organizational hierarchy", "organizational position", "managerial position in the organizational hierarchy"]
definition: The hierarchical position occupied by an executive: Level 1 plant manager (highest authority in a manufacturing plant defined as a cost center), Level 2 divisional CEO (lowest level with profit-center responsibility), Level 3 group CEO (responsibility for multiple divisional profit centers), and Level 4 corporate CEO (highest authority in the corporation).

name: Executive compensation
authors_terms: ["level of executive compensation", "total compensation", "total executive compensation"]
definition: The level of compensation for an individual executive, measured as total compensation, or the sum of salary, annual bonus, and the authors' valuations for stock options, performance plans, phantom stock, and restricted stock.

name: Managerial power
definition: Extrapolating from Finkelstein's definition of managerial power, the authors define power as the ability of managers to influence or exert their will or desires on the remuneration decisions made by the board of directors, or perhaps the compensation committee of the board.

name: Executive performance
authors_terms: ["executive performance", "performance", "accounting return on assets", "stock market return"]
definition: The performance of an executive, typically measured by the performance of the unit managed by that executive; the authors use accounting return on assets and the firm's stock market rate of return, and for group, division, and plant managers a segment return on assets.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "formation of interfirm strategic alliances", "entering an alliance", "probability of the announcement of an alliance"]
definition: Any voluntarily initiated interfirm cooperative agreement that involves exchange, sharing, or codevelopment, and it can include contributions by partners of capital, technology, or firm-specific assets.

name: Strategic interdependence
definition: Strategic interdependence between organizations describes a situation in which one organization has resources or capabilities beneficial to but not possessed by the other. Firms with differing capabilities (belonging to different niches) are likely to share greater interdependence than firms with similar capabilities.

name: Prior direct ties between firms
authors_terms: ["repeated ties", "number of past alliances between two firms", "prior alliances", "prior direct ties", "prior relational ties"]
definition: The relational component of social structure is made up of the direct relationships within which a firm is embedded; prior ties create a strong social connection between organizations, which in turn leads to future interactions.

name: Common third-party ties
authors_terms: ["common third-party ties", "common ties", "third-party ties", "common third partners", "indirect ties"]
definition: A shared contact of a dyad (i,j) is any firm in direct contact with both firms i and j. Two such firms are likely to have access to more information about each other than two firms with no such connection.

name: Network path distance between firms
definition: The shortest distance between two firms in an alliance network, which should affect the likelihood of their forming an alliance.

name: Time elapsed since prior alliance
authors_terms: ["duration", "time elapsed since the prior alliance", "time elapsed since a last alliance"]
definition: How much time has passed since the initiation of the last alliance two firms entered; organizations have short memories, engaging in the activities of the recent past, and the likelihood of an action diminishes as the time elapsed since the last similar action increases.

name: Work/family programs
definition: Programs and policies employers provide in the work/family area, such as direct provision of day care on site or off-site, employer financial subsidies to pay for day care, donations to local day-care facilities in return for slots, full-time work/family staff, work/family workshops during the working day, day-care referral systems, elder-care referral systems, and flexible hours.

name: Female share of the workforce
authors_terms: ["female", "percentage of the establishments' core employees who were women", "gender composition of the workforce"]
definition: The percentage of the establishment's core employees who are women; the higher the fraction of core employees who are women, the greater the need and demand for work/family programs is expected to be.

name: Work/family-related workforce difficulties
authors_terms: ["labor force concerns", "difficulties which are attributable to family issues", "workforce problems"]
definition: The actual difficulties establishments experience as a result of their employees' family situations, identified in four separate areas: tardiness or absenteeism, turnover, recruitment difficulties, and refusal to relocate; also the establishment's expectation of how difficulties associated with work/family conflicts will evolve.

name: Internal labor market
definition: ILMs are systems of formal rules that structure the employment relationship and, as such, signal bureaucratization or rationalization; in this paper an ILM signifies the formalization of the employment relation.

name: High-commitment work systems
authors_terms: ["high-commitment work systems", "high-performance work systems", "high-commitment organizations", "high-commitment employment systems"]
definition: Work systems that seek to improve productivity by drawing on the ideas and commitment of the labor force to a much greater extent than is typical under traditional employment systems; commitment is the employees' willingness to engage themselves and offer their ideas and knowledge with a degree of authenticity that is not enforceable and therefore requires a substantial element of volunteerism on the part of the workforce.

name: Termination policies and benefits
authors_terms: ["termination policies and benefits", "termination policies and benefit plans", "employer-based termination policies and benefits"]
definition: Employer-based termination policies and benefit plans are privately financed policies and benefits that establish compensation agreements for employee terminations; they usually include one or more of severance pay, transition assistance, and advance notification and can be considered integral components of internal labor markets.

name: Severance pay
definition: Severance pay, the most common form of termination benefit, is the continuing payment of a predetermined wage or salary for a specified period of time after termination.

name: Transition assistance
definition: Transition assistance is outplacement and/or retraining assistance to terminated workers.

name: Advance notification
definition: Advance notification describes a formal personnel policy that assures employees of advance written notice of a pending job loss due to lack of work.

name: In-house training
definition: One key indicator of the importance of firm-specific skills in organizations is the location of skill training, in particular, the presence of in-house training; firms that sponsor their own training programs are more likely to have internal labor markets based on long-term employment relations.

name: Managerial and professional employee concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of managerial and professional employees", "percentage of managers", "percentage of professionals"]
definition: The concentration of managerial and professional-technical employee groups in an organization, argued to affect the provision of termination benefits to salaried workers through status competition, institutional legitimacy, and firm-specific training investment.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The extent to which product market sales are concentrated among a small number of firms; firms in concentrated product markets are seen as more able to establish the market stability, insulation, and long-term planning necessary to develop and manage employment security arrangements.

name: Firm size
definition: The scale of the firm; large firms generate the organizational resources, planning flexibility and stability, and technical expertise necessary for the development of internal labor markets and formal employment security and termination policies, and have greater visibility in public affairs and government relations.

name: Union presence
definition: The extent to which employees in an establishment are covered by collective bargaining; unions have been central political forces in the development and management of employment security agreements in the workplace.

name: Regulatory presence of government
definition: A set of industries from which regulatory presence can be inferred; firms in highly regulated industries are argued to be more responsive to government and public interest group demands.

name: Government market presence
authors_terms: ["government market presence", "government purchase", "strength of government presence"]
definition: The strength of government presence as a major market regulator and consumer of industry output, measured as industry output sold to government divided by total industry output.

name: Recent workforce reduction
definition: Previous experience in managing workforce reductions or plant closings; employment security and termination policies and benefits are probably more likely to be found in firms that have some previous experience in managing workforce reductions or plant closings.

name: Organizational change
authors_terms: ["organizational change", "changes in content", "changes in the frequency of publication"]
definition: The authors drew on the institutional aspects of this population to define two categories of key organizational changes: changes in content, particularly changes between general and specialized content, and changes in the frequency of publication, for example a weekly paper changing to a daily newspaper.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Organizational failure was defined as the voluntary and permanent cessation of publication.

name: Organizational age
definition: The age of the organization, used to test the prediction that the probability of organizational change decreases with the age of the organization.

name: Elapsed time since change
authors_terms: ["elapsed time since the occurrence of the change", "duration clocks", "change clocks", "time since last change"]
definition: Two duration clocks record the elapsed time since a particular type of organizational change occurred (a clock recording time since last content change and a clock recording time since last frequency change).

name: Repetitive momentum of change
authors_terms: ["repetitive momentum", "cumulative change variables", "number of prior changes of the same type", "frequency dependence"]
definition: Another form of inertia (momentum) results when organizations develop modification routines and change operations through processes established over time; types of changes made in the past are especially likely to be repeated in the future.

name: Life cycle timing of change
authors_terms: ["early occurrence of a change", "position of the sequence of changes in an organization's life cycle", "timing of the change within the organization's life cycle"]
definition: The probability of an organizational change is not just dependent on frequency and recency but also on the position of the sequence of changes in an organization's life cycle, so that sequences of changes initiated early should trigger a stronger tendency for additional change.

name: Corporate borrowing
authors_terms: ["corporate borrowing", "level of borrowing", "debt financing", "total debt financing", "level of debt financing"]
definition: The amount of debt financing initiated by a firm in a given year; the paper is concerned not with the firm's level of debt financing per se but with a decision to borrow at a particular time.

name: Expected return on borrowing
authors_terms: ["expected return on borrowing", "ERB", "extent to which the expected returns exceed the cost of funds", "extent to which it \"pays\" for firms to borrow"]
definition: The comparison between a firm's anticipated future earnings and its cost of capital; corporations will borrow funds only when their expected returns exceed the cost of capital.

name: Retained earnings
authors_terms: ["retained earnings", "available internal funds", "internal funds", "availability of funds"]
definition: The amount of internal funds left after a corporation has paid its stock dividends for the year.

name: CEO functional background
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation of the CEO", "finance CEO", "CEOs from financial backgrounds", "employment background of the person identified as being in control of the firm"]
definition: The employment background of the person identified as being in control of the firm; CEOs with previous positions exclusively in finance and/or accounting were coded as finance CEOs.

name: Financial representation on the board
authors_terms: ["financial representation on the board of directors", "presence of a representative of a financial institution on the firm's board", "financial representation"]
definition: The presence on the borrowing firm's board of directors of a representative of a financial institution, viewed as an important monitoring mechanism by bank hegemony and agency theorists.

name: Employee stock ownership plan
definition: Establishing ESOPs can provide additional funds to the firm, directly or indirectly; by issuing stock to its employees, the firm's management can raise capital while maintaining control over the firm's operations, and many large corporations establish ESOPs to take advantage of the accompanying corporate tax credits.

name: Firm risk
definition: The riskiness of the IPO firm; the authors state that cross-sectional variation in firm risk is associated with the costs of using incentive compensation, since it can influence managers' willingness to accept compensation contracts that include a risk-bearing component.

name: Executive stock option use
authors_terms: ["use of stock options", "stock options", "presence or absence of options"]
definition: Whether stock options were used to compensate the top management group; the authors state that for their sample the decision to offer stock options to top managers is a major decision made by the board of directors.

name: Top management equity ownership
authors_terms: ["managerial equity holdings", "top management equity ownership", "managerial stock ownership", "equity stakes held by top managers"]
definition: The percentage of the IPO firm's equity held by the top management group, based on the individuals in the top management group and their equity holdings before the IPO as explicitly identified in the IPO registration statements.

name: Noncash incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["noncash incentive portion of top managers' total compensation", "percentage of total executive compensation derived from noncash sources"]
definition: The percentage of total executive compensation derived from noncash sources, which captures the amount of a manager's total income that is at risk because it includes the gain or loss attributable to the shares of stock held by the manager, as well as options held.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["percentage of outside directors", "ratio of the number of outside directors to total directors"]
definition: The proportion of the board made up of outside directors; outside directors are seen by Fama (1980) and Fama and Jensen (1983) as professional referees and experts in internal organizational control.

name: Outside owner-director representation
authors_terms: ["percentage of outside director-owners", "proportion of outside owner-directors"]
definition: The proportion of outside directors who are also shareholders; outside directors who are also owners would seem likely to be more vigilant in their monitoring role.

name: Non-board blockholder presence
authors_terms: ["major non-board-member blockholder", "presence of a shareholder with large equity holdings"]
definition: The presence of a shareholder with large equity holdings who, for whatever reason, is not on the board but is a blockholder; such large-scale owners are more likely to be keen monitors of managerial behavior.

name: Venture capital backing
definition: Whether the IPO firm is financed by venture capital; venture capitalists are also likely to engage in active monitoring.

name: CEO and board chairman role separation
authors_terms: ["separate CEO and board chairman positions", "CEO/chairman variable"]
definition: Whether the CEO position is separated from the chairman of the board position; the presence of an outside board chairman who is not also CEO can represent an additional monitor of managerial behavior.

name: Presence of coercive organizations
authors_terms: ["coercive organizations such as the state or foreign multinationals", "presence of the state or of foreign multinationals in the economy", "resource dependence on powerful organizations"]
definition: The presence in a country's economy of coercive organizations, the state and foreign multinationals, which control critical resources and sanction the behavior of dependent organizations; dependent organizations are likely to adopt patterns of behavior sanctioned by the organizations that control critical resources.

name: Country knowledge base
authors_terms: ["the country's knowledge base in the areas of quality and production management", "scientific and technical knowledge about operations, engineering, manufacturing, or quality", "availability of knowledge about production management"]
definition: The availability in a country of knowledge about production management and of professional personnel with a technical background; the adoption of ISO certification, like other quality and organizational practices, depends on this availability.

name: Cohesion in trade networks
authors_terms: ["cohesive trade relationships", "cohesion in trade", "cohesive trade ties between countries", "strongly related in terms of trade"]
definition: Intense trade relationships between pairs of countries produce cohesion, and firms in trade-cohesive countries are likely to have similar numbers of certificates because of similar customer requirements, shared patterns of behavior, and imitation under uncertainty.

name: Role equivalence in trade
authors_terms: ["role equivalence", "role-equivalent trade relationships", "role equivalence in trade"]
definition: Two actors are said to be role equivalent to the extent that they have similar kinds of relationships with third parties; in this study a relation is the export or import of a particular type of product and a role set is a country's total exports and imports by reference to each type of good.

name: ISO 9000 certification
authors_terms: ["ISO 9000 quality certification", "number of ISO 9000 certificates", "quality certification"]
definition: The number of ISO 9000 quality certificates awarded to firms in a country; the ISO 9000 standards were developed as a set of international standards and guidelines that serve as the basis for establishing quality management systems at manufacturing and service firms, and certificates are awarded to quality processes within the organization rather than to products or services.

name: Ingratiation toward the CEO
authors_terms: ["ingratiation", "ingratiatory behavior", "interpersonal influence behavior", "ingratiation toward the CEO", "other-enhancement", "flattery", "opinion conformity", "favor rendering"]
definition: Ingratiation is a pattern of interpersonal influence behavior that serves to 'enhance one's interpersonal attractiveness' or 'gain favor' with another person; it comprises three distinct behaviors: opinion conformity, other-enhancement or flattery, and favor rendering.

name: Board appointment
definition: Appointment of the focal top manager to a board at another firm, either a board (x_j) on which the manager's CEO serves as an outside director or a board to which the CEO is indirectly connected through a fellow CEO-director on the nominating committee.

name: Elite undergraduate degree
authors_terms: ["degree from an elite undergraduate institution", "elite undergraduate degree", "top ranked college"]
definition: Holding a Bachelor's degree from a top ranked (elite) college or university, as designated in prior research on the corporate elite.

name: Elite MBA degree
authors_terms: ["MBA degree from an elite graduate school of business", "elite MBA"]
definition: Holding an MBA degree from a prominent (elite) graduate school of business.

name: Exclusive social club membership
authors_terms: ["membership in a prestigious social club", "member of an exclusive social club"]
definition: Membership in one or more of the most exclusive social clubs in the U.S., as designated in prior research on the corporate elite.

name: Upper-class background
authors_terms: ["indications of an upper-class status", "listed in the Social Register", "attendance at an exclusive preparatory school", "upper class origins"]
definition: Indications of an upper-class background, such as being listed in the Social Register or having attended an exclusive preparatory school.

name: Demographic minority status
authors_terms: ["demographic minority status", "minority status with respect to ethnicity and/or gender", "demographic minorities", "ethnic minorities and women", "demographic majority status"]
definition: Minority status with respect to ethnicity and/or gender; in the study, demographic dissimilarity from the CEO is effectively equivalent to having minority status, as all CEOs in the sample were white males.

name: Organizational rationalization
definition: Rationalization denotes the integration of formalized roles and rules around unified sovereignty, entailing the construction of nonprofits as 'actors' with clear identities.

name: Organizational professionalism
authors_terms: ["organizational professionalism", "organizational professionalism index", "staffed and managed by paid personnel"]
definition: The index of organizational professionalism is a sum of five variables ... to measure the level of organizational professionalism ... This index captures variation among nonprofits based on the fundamental volunteer-based and staffed distinction, the use of volunteers in service delivery, and the extent of executive leadership.

name: Professional credentialism
authors_terms: ["credentialism", "professional degree", "credentialed professionals", "cognitive knowledge bases of professionalism"]
definition: Professional authority and legitimacy lead to claims to technical expertise, typically acquired in the educational system. The interviews provided data on the educational backgrounds of both paid and volunteer executive directors, which we assigned to one of three categories.

name: Professional training and development
authors_terms: ["professional training and development", "professional training", "training and development"]
definition: Two dummy variables for training and professional development measure whether nonprofit managers, staff, and volunteers attend workshops or conferences to further hone their skills.

name: Management training
authors_terms: ["management development training", "management training", "management-related workshops or classes"]
definition: Nonprofit leaders who are more immersed in management training are more familiar with administrative ideas and practices that circulate in other sectors.

name: Substantive professional training
definition: Training and development in substantive areas, differentiated from management-related workshops or classes such as executive programs in nonprofit strategy or board governance.

name: Organizational hybridity
definition: Hybrids are organizations 'whose identity is composed of two or more types that would not normally be expected to go together'; empirically, hybrid organizations were defined as any firms that combined more than one industry category.

name: Hybrid form frequency
authors_terms: ["form frequency", "hybrid frequency", "rarity", "density", "common", "frequency with which a particular form or combination is encountered"]
definition: The frequency with which a particular form or combination is encountered in the Dun Reference Book, measured in 1,000s. Some hybrids are so common that they take on an idiomatic status, while others entail infrequent combinations that may challenge taxonomic schemata.

name: Categorical ambiguity
definition: Ambiguity results from the difficulty in knowing what implicit features of a hybrid organization's identity apply in any given context. Ambiguous businesses were defined as firms that were assigned a residual category in addition to one or more explicit industry categories.

name: Industry boundary violation
definition: Boundary violations occurred when hybrids contained unrelated lines of business, i.e., crossed the institutionalized industry boundaries of the classification system.

name: Credit coverage
definition: Whether an enterprise received coverage (a credit assessment) from a Dun correspondent; in 20 percent of the cases in the Reference Book an enterprise received no credit coverage from a Dun correspondent.

name: Credit rating
definition: The evaluation of an enterprise's credit-worthiness applied by Dun correspondents; during the postbellum period firms were ranked into seven credit categories ranging from A1 to 3.5.

name: Rating system ambiguity
authors_terms: ["ambiguity", "ambiguous rating system", "ambiguity of the rating system", "ambiguity score"]
definition: An ambiguous rating system is one with overlapping categories such that the categories do not have unique contents. Ambiguity is measured from the perspective of the brokerage firms that choose the set of categories, not from the interpretations of investors.

name: Conflict of interest
definition: A conflict of interest arises when parties are 'interdependent and have competing goals.' For a rating organization, conflicts of interest arise from relationships with the producers of the products it rates, such as underwriting relationships in equity research.

name: Organizational perceived quality
authors_terms: ["perceived quality", "organizational quality", "quality", "a focal actor's perceived quality"]
definition: An organization's quality as perceived by market actors, i.e., its propensity toward reliable performance and accountability. When a potential partner's quality is unobservable, difficult to observe, or expensive to observe, judgmental methods that leverage observable indicators of quality are used in evaluations.

name: Organizational size
definition: The size of the organization, measured by the total amount of capital raised by the fund; because of their reliability, high survival chances, and esteemed market standing, large organizations are likely to be perceived by market actors as higher quality than small organizations.

name: Organizational experience
definition: An organization's experience, measured by the number of funds it has previously raised; with experience organizations learn, develop routines, refine processes, implement correctives, and improve performance, and inexperienced organizations encounter skepticism from potential partners.

name: Organizational status
authors_terms: ["firm status", "organizational status", "Bonacich centrality", "status in the industry co-investment network"]
definition: An organization's status, operationalized as its Bonacich centrality in the private equity co-investment network; affiliations with high-status actors are useful indicators of otherwise difficult-to-observe quality.

name: Broker reputation
authors_terms: ["placement agent reputation", "a broker's reputation", "a placement agent's reputation"]
definition: A broker's reputation for consistently representing actors of high quality, which is a valuable intangible asset that enables the broker to realize future rents on the brokerage position and to influence market actors' quality perceptions.

name: Broker representation
authors_terms: ["representation by a placement agent", "the likelihood that a broker represents an organization", "represented by a placement agent"]
definition: The likelihood that a broker (a placement agent) represents a focal organization (a venture fund) in a brokered exchange.

name: Care logic
definition: A care logic highlights physicians' clinical skills used to treat patients and improve the health of the community.

name: Science logic
definition: A science logic focuses on knowledge of diseases built through research and innovative treatments.

name: Relative emphasis of care over science logic
authors_terms: ["relative balance between care and science logics", "relative emphasis of the care logic over the science logic", "relative attention to care versus science"]
definition: The relative attention to care versus science each year, captured as a ratio of the frequencies of care to science.

name: Interprofessional jurisdictional competition
authors_terms: ["growth of public health schools", "number of accredited schools of public health", "jurisdictional competition with rivals"]
definition: Competition from alternative professions whose jurisdiction is closely related to the established profession, an indicator of the relative size and of the relative resources and influence of the rival profession.

name: Intraprofessional differentiation
authors_terms: ["growth in the number of medical schools", "number of medical schools", "differentiation in the missions of medical schools"]
definition: Increasing the size of the population of medical schools, and the differentiation within it, which increases the likelihood that alternate logics will compete for attention.

name: Professional contestation over medical education
authors_terms: ["contestation within the profession", "calls for reform of medical education", "professional contestation"]
definition: Calls for reform of medical education that come from members within the profession and reflect a segment in the profession advocating for higher priority of their interests and values.

name: Public attention to managed care
authors_terms: ["public discourse about managed care", "public attention to managed care", "volume of discourse about managed care"]
definition: The volume of public talk and attention to managed care, used to capture the exogenous managerial market logic in healthcare.

name: Flattery
definition: Ingratiation involves two forms of behavior: flattery, or 'other enhancement,' and opinion conformity, or verbal statements that validate the opinion held by another person, in an attempt to gain favor with him or her.

name: Opinion conformity
definition: Ingratiation involves two forms of behavior: flattery, or 'other enhancement,' and opinion conformity, or verbal statements that validate the opinion held by another person, in an attempt to gain favor with him or her.

name: Sophisticated flattery
authors_terms: ["sophisticated forms of flattery", "subtle forms of flattery"]
definition: Relatively subtle forms of flattery that are less likely to be recognized or interpreted as ingratiation by the influence target and more likely to be accepted as genuine expressions of admiration; they are relatively 'non-obvious,' 'skillful' and 'refined,' and 'operate insidiously.'

name: Sophisticated opinion conformity
authors_terms: ["sophisticated forms of opinion conformity", "subtle forms of opinion conformity"]
definition: Relatively subtle forms of opinion conformity that are less likely to be recognized or interpreted as ingratiation by the influence target and thus more likely to engender social influence.

name: Board appointment at another firm
authors_terms: ["board appointments", "board appointment where alter serves on the nominating committee"]
definition: Dichotomous measures indicate whether the focal manager (or director) was appointed to a particular board where the CEO (or fellow director) served on the nominating committee at the time of the survey.

name: Vocational background
authors_terms: ["vocational background", "a background in politics, law, or sales"]
definition: People with similar behavioral dispositions and skills are drawn to similar occupations in 'a process involving a matching of self and occupation'; politics, law, and sales are fields in which interpersonal influence tactics are particularly instrumental to task accomplishment.

name: Upper-class background
definition: Members of the upper class acquire social status from birth (i.e., they are born into high-status families), and upper-class culture features a normative preference for subtlety in interpersonal communication and an aversion to blunt or especially direct forms of communication.

name: Fund typicality
authors_terms: ["fund typicality", "typicality of an organization's identity", "organizational conformity", "organizational nonconformity", "atypicality", "conformity signaled by an organization's identity"]
definition: Identity is defined as a fund's correspondence to the central tendency of a specified reference set of other hedge funds; typical funds have a high level of correspondence to the resulting central tendency, and atypical funds do not. Typical funds have combinations of attributes that are similar to an average, hypothetical fund of the same style, while atypical funds do not.

name: Fund performance
definition: Performance is a fund's returns.

name: Audience evaluation
definition: Audience evaluation is measured by capital flows into and out of a fund on behalf of investors (i.e., investment). Capital flows refer to increases, by way of additional investment, and decreases, by way of capital redemption or divestment, in the amount of invested capital in a fund.

name: Grape price
authors_terms: ["average price of raw materials", "price for grapes", "price paid for grapes"]
definition: The average price that a house pays for the raw materials it uses in its Champagne production in a given year, used as a proxy for the costs of grapes that a house purchases.

name: Family CEO
authors_terms: ["family CEO", "family management", "CEO is a descendant of the founder"]
definition: Firms whose CEO is a descendant of the founder by either blood or marriage.

name: Village density
authors_terms: ["village density", "relative density of houses in the various villages"]
definition: The number of Champagne houses in the village relative to the village's population (measured in hundreds).

name: Newcomer
definition: The extent to which a Champagne house was a relatively late entrant, measured with a proxy for lateness of entry.

name: Corporate group ownership
authors_terms: ["corporate group", "larger corporate group", "part of a larger corporation"]
definition: Whether a Champagne house belongs to a larger corporate group.

name: Listed group ownership
authors_terms: ["listed", "listed on the Paris stock exchange", "publicly owned financial groups"]
definition: Whether the group that owns the house is listed on the Paris stock exchange.

name: Supermarket brand supply
authors_terms: ["supermarket brands", "supplying Champagne for supermarket brands", "supermarket labels"]
definition: The total number of supermarket brands a house supplied in a given year, a practice viewed as a norm violation.

name: Foreign winemaking subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["foreign subsidiaries", "winemaking subsidiaries abroad", "subsidiaries outside of France"]
definition: The cumulative increase in the number of winemaking subsidiaries a house owned outside of France between 1998 and 2007.

name: Vineyard acquisition
authors_terms: ["vineyards acquired", "acquisition of vineyards", "cumulative number of hectares purchased"]
definition: The cumulative number of hectares of vineyard purchased by each house in Champagne during the sample period.

name: Local norm violation
authors_terms: ["local norms", "norm violations", "violations of local norms", "peripheral actors", "deviations from local norms"]
definition: These expectations represent the category's local norms: social agreements about what type of behavior is appropriate and desirable. Members who do not meet the expectations associated with operating within their category will experience a drop in their moral legitimacy.

name: Niche width
authors_terms: ["niche width", "width of the fundamental niche", "number of distinct genres", "niche breadth"]
definition: The width of an organization's niche refers the level of variance in environmental resources within the region bounded by these points. In this context it is represented by the number of distinct taste positions that each film targeted.

name: Audience size
authors_terms: ["audience size", "number of audience members", "size of the consumer audience"]
definition: The number of audience members an organization attracts. By targeting a broader array of taste positions, an organization increases the sheer number of audience members that it is able to reach.

name: Appeal
definition: The appeal audiences experience for the organization's offerings, assessed as the overall appeal of each film to audiences. Clear fit with taste preferences results in greater appeal among targeted audience members.

name: Audience consensus on fit
authors_terms: ["audience consensus on fit", "consensus about genre classification", "consensus in genre classifications", "clarity of generic identity"]
definition: The extent to which audience members clearly perceive an organization's fit with targeted taste positions; organizations that clearly establish themselves will experience a high level of agreement in audiences' perceptions about their fit with targeted positions.

name: Individualistic identity orientation
definition: In an organization with an individualistic identity orientation, members view the organization as an individual entity characterized by organizational traits that distinguish it from other entities; the emphasis is on maximizing the organization's own welfare (e.g., status).

name: Relational identity orientation
definition: In an organization with a relational identity orientation, members view the organization as an inter-entity partner and characterize it as having traits that connect it dyadically to particular stakeholders; the emphasis is on enhancing the welfare of particular others and on maintaining these relationships.

name: Collectivistic identity orientation
definition: In an organization with a collectivistic identity orientation, members view the organization as part of a larger collective and as characterized by traits that connect it to a larger whole; the emphasis is on maximizing the welfare of the larger group.

name: Organizational form
authors_terms: ["organizational form", "professional service firms", "classic production-based firms", "production-based companies"]
definition: Organizational forms broadly describe organizations that rely similarly on their material and social milieu and are hierarchically nested with increasingly specified subforms; the material and social milieu confronting professional service firms is markedly dissimilar from that confronting more classic production-based business firms.

name: Client type
authors_terms: ["client type", "type of clients served", "kind of clients served", "organizational subforms"]
definition: Because client relationships are so important among professional service firms, a crucial distinction among them is the kind of clients served, including corporations, families and individuals, and nonprofit organizations, public agencies, and citizens' groups.

name: Cooperative structure
definition: Co-ops are created to benefit a particular collective, which may be the suppliers, customers, or workers, and a particular group of stakeholders jointly owns the company; the social milieu surrounding co-ops mandates their relating to both external and internal stakeholders based on collectivistic principles.

name: Identity orientation purity
definition: The extent to which individuals viewed their organization as having a pure orientation of any type; purity scores range from 0, where the corresponding identity orientation received the maximum possible composite percentage score while the other two received the lowest possible score, to 300, where it received the lowest score while the other two received the maximum.

name: Economic development pressure
authors_terms: ["economic development pressure", "pressure to develop the economy", "pressure to commercialize temples to develop the economy", "ranking of the GDP growth rate"]
definition: The pressure that local government officials face to develop the local economy, which the authors argue increases their tendency to target Buddhist temples as a means of generating revenue. It arises from a tournament-based promotion system in which officials compete on measurable objectives such as GDP growth.

name: Free Entrance Movement strength
authors_terms: ["Free Entrance Movement", "strength of the Free Entrance Movement", "monk-led resistance movement"]
definition: A collective resistance movement launched by religious leaders calling on prominent Buddhist temples to abandon admission fees and open their doors freely to the public. Its strength in a region is reflected in the number of nationally prominent temples that no longer charge admission.

name: Admission fee
authors_terms: ["admission fee", "entrance fee", "ticket price", "level of admission fee"]
definition: The price charged for admission to a temple, which is the primary source of revenue for commercially operated temples and the target of the Free Entrance Movement. The price is set by the local government rather than by the temple itself.

name: Parliamentary connections to the central government
authors_terms: ["parliamentary connections", "political ties to the central government", "appointment of the abbot to the national NPC or CPPCC"]
definition: Ties created when a temple's abbot holds a position in the National People's Congress or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference at the central government level. Such connections give temples a top-down channel for reporting local government pressure to the central government.

name: Internet penetration
authors_terms: ["Internet penetration rate", "Internet development", "development of the Internet"]
definition: The development of the Internet as a bottom-up information channel that the central government uses to monitor public opinion and that gives the public a way to voice grievances and coordinate collective action.

name: Temple commercialization
authors_terms: ["temple commercialization", "commercialization of temples", "commercial activities of temples"]
definition: The extent to which a temple has been transformed into a commercial enterprise, captured by non-admission-fee-related commercial activities as well as by the admission fee. The authors measure it to capture the controversy surrounding temple commercialization from different angles.

name: Black metal cover image colorfulness
definition: A compound measure of the colorfulness of a cover image, representing a linear combination of the image's Weighted saturation and Color entropy components, simultaneously capturing the intensity and distribution of colors in the cover image.

name: Reference group cover image colorfulness
authors_terms: ["Median non-black metal image colorfulness per year", "non-black metal bands' choices on colorfulness", "past color choices of non-black metal bands"]
definition: The colorfulness of the cover images of non-black metal bands, the reference group that black metal bands observe and position themselves against.

name: Black metal cover image contrast
definition: The degree of difference in luminance between the dark and bright areas of a cover image; an image ranks high in contrast when the perceived difference between bright and dark areas is pronounced (e.g., a black/white image), while an image ranking low in contrast features proximate shades of the same color.

name: Reference group cover image contrast
authors_terms: ["Median non-black metal image contrast per year", "non-black metal bands' decisions about contrast"]
definition: The contrast of the cover images of non-black metal bands, the reference group that black metal bands observe and position themselves against.

name: Stigmatization of black metal
definition: A process whose defining function is the exclusion of actors who may threaten a community through the spread of perceived social disorder; in this context it is captured by the public outcry and social pressure on the genre in the form of negative newspaper coverage.

name: Commercialization of black metal
authors_terms: ["commercialization", "increasing global commercial success of black metal", "Number of commercial Norwegian black metal releases per year"]
definition: The growing commercial success and acceptability of the genre, captured by the number of commercial Norwegian black metal releases per year, an indicator of the degree to which a genre is becoming acceptable or prevalent in the record industry and in heavy metal.

name: Content purity
authors_terms: ["Pure black metal band", "perceived purity", "pure black metal bands", "hybrid bands"]
definition: The degree to which musical content reproduces musical and/or ideological canons, dividing bands into 'pure' bands that hew to black metal conventions and 'hybrid' bands that draw on other genres.

name: Lead user idea-generation method
authors_terms: ["lead user (LU) process", "LU method", "LU methods", "LU idea-generation methods", "lead user idea-generation process"]
definition: The lead user process collects information about both needs and solutions from users at the leading edges of the target market, as well as from users in other markets that face similar problems in a more extreme form. It involves four major phases, including pyramid networking to identify lead users both in the target market and in 'advanced analog' markets.

name: Commercial potential of product ideas
definition: The commercial potential of a funded idea is assessed with a New Product Idea Description Form that includes projected company sales/market share from the new idea in year 5, novelty of ideas, originality/newness of customer needs, potential for proliferating into an entire product line, probability of business success, and global market potential.

name: Rate of major new product line generation
authors_terms: ["rate of major product line generation", "rate of major new product line generation", "major new product lines"]
definition: The overall rate at which the organization generates major new product lines, where major product lines are operationalized as those that were separately reported upon in divisional financial statements.

name: Organizational fit
definition: The compatibility of an idea with key organization-fit criteria, namely the fit of the idea with existing divisional distribution channels, manufacturing capabilities, and divisional strategic plans.

name: Intellectual property protection
authors_terms: ["protectable by patent or other means of intellectual property protection", "intellectual property protection"]
definition: The degree to which an idea can be protected by patent or other means of intellectual property protection.

name: Cost of idea generation
definition: The money and time consumed to generate ideas forming the basis for funded projects, assessed as person days of idea development time and as the total cost per funded project using internal 3M data on average costs of professional development personnel.

name: New firm entry
definition: Firm entry not only affects supply but also demand for the product because product improvements, expanded distribution, and increased consumer awareness of brand quality through promotional activities are key ways in which entering firms seek to differentiate themselves.

name: Price decline
definition: Changes in price are the rate at which the average price of the product innovation falls over time; the authors fit an exponential time trend to the annual price series for each innovation and take the estimated exponential coefficient as their measure of changes in Price.

name: Sales takeoff time
authors_terms: ["sales takeoff time", "takeoff times", "time to sales takeoff", "sales takeoff"]
definition: For most new products, the 'takeoff' point is clear because it corresponds to the first large increase in sales. Takeoff times are identified by a statistical procedure that distinguishes consecutive intervals using the annual percentage change in sales.

name: Temporal exploitation
authors_terms: ["temporal exploitation", "recency", "recency in recombination", "median age of knowledge"]
definition: Temporal exploitation is the creation of new knowledge through a recombinant process that emphasizes recency; recency is the extent to which history does not matter in knowledge creation.

name: Temporal exploration
authors_terms: ["temporal exploration", "time spread", "time spread in recombination", "interquartile range of knowledge"]
definition: Temporal exploration is the creation of new knowledge through recombination of older knowledge obtained by examining a wider time spread. Time spread measures the extent to which history matters in the process of knowledge creation.

name: Impact on knowledge creation
authors_terms: ["impact", "impact on future knowledge creation", "total number of citations", "technological impact"]
definition: Patent citations have been considered to be an excellent measure for technological impact and performance; the total number of citations a patent receives is used as an indicator of impact on future knowledge creation.

name: Age of technical field
authors_terms: ["age of the technical field", "age of the technology class", "class age"]
definition: The age of the technical field in which an invention is found, measured as the number of years since the USPTO established the three-digit patent class to which the patent belongs.

name: Market segmentation
authors_terms: ["market segmentation", "tendency of the market toward segmentation", "tendency of a market toward segmentation"]
definition: Technologies vary on the degree to which markets for them can be segmented; the degree to which markets lend themselves to segmentation depends largely on customers' willingness to trade off different attributes (e.g., cost, functions, reliability, size).

name: Patent effectiveness
authors_terms: ["effectiveness of patents", "patent effectiveness", "effectiveness of intellectual property protection"]
definition: The effectiveness of patents as a mechanism to appropriate the benefits of innovation, i.e. the strength of legal rights of protection against imitation, which research has shown varies across technologies.

name: Complementary assets in marketing and distribution
authors_terms: ["complementary assets in marketing and distribution", "importance of complementary assets", "complementary assets in marketing"]
definition: Alternative barriers to imitation, such as specialized manufacturing, a distribution system, or after-sales support, that cannot be easily imitated because they result from a process of learning-by-doing; specialization creates asset specificity that makes it important to bring both assets under the control of a single firm.

name: New firm formation
authors_terms: ["firm formation", "new firm formation", "exploitation through firm formation"]
definition: The founding of a new firm to exploit a technology: firm formation is defined as occurring in a given year if the invention was licensed to a for-profit firm that did not exist as a legal entity in the previous year.

name: Centralization of decision making
definition: Centralization of decision making reflects the locus of authority and decision making and refers to the extent to which decision making is concentrated in an organization.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization is the degree to which rules, procedures, instructions, and communications are formalized or written down.

name: Connectedness
definition: Connectedness concerns the overall pattern of a unit's social network in terms of density; it is the structural dimension of informal social relations among individuals within units.

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: Exploratory innovations are radical innovations designed to meet the needs of emerging customers or markets; they require new knowledge or departure from existing knowledge.

name: Exploitative innovation
definition: Exploitative innovations are incremental innovations designed to meet the needs of existing customers or markets; they build on existing knowledge and reinforce existing skills, processes, and structures.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance of organizational units was measured through internal corporate records by a unit's average profitability from 2003 up to one year after the measurement of exploratory and exploitative innovation.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism refers to the rate of change and the degree of instability of the environment.

name: Environmental competitiveness
definition: Environmental competitiveness is the extent to which external environments are characterized by intense competition; it refers to the degree of competition reflected in the number of competitors and the number of areas in which there is competition.

name: Task programmability
definition: The information characteristic of a task concerning the knowledge of the transformation process. If the task can be programmed, then behaviors are explicitly defined and readily measured; as task programmability decreases, behaviors are more difficult to use as the basis of the control strategy because they are less clearly specified.

name: Behavior measurement
authors_terms: ["behavior measurement", "behavior measures", "amount of behavioral measurement", "information systems"]
definition: Behavior measures (e.g., budgeting systems, quantitative measures) improve information about behaviors, and are an alternative to outcome control. In this setting the construct is measured by the physical limitations on the observation of salespeople by management.

name: Cost of outcome measurement
authors_terms: ["cost of outcome measurement", "cost of measuring outcomes", "cost of the outcome measurement system"]
definition: Outcome measurement is a cost component of outcome based control; here the cost of outcome observation depends upon the cost of the outcome measurement system rather than on the inherent measurability of the outcome.

name: Outcome uncertainty
definition: In agency theory, outcome is assumed to be a function of employee behaviors and random effects such as competitor actions, government policies, and weather; such effects introduce uncertainty such that appropriate behaviors can lead to good or bad outcomes, and when outcome control is used the employee bears risk.

name: Control strategy
authors_terms: ["behavior based control", "outcome based control", "control strategy", "behavior based vs. outcome based control"]
definition: Control is operationalized in terms of behavior based vs. outcome based reward structures. Outcome based rewards are pay plans in which at least a portion of the compensation is based upon outcomes, generally sales, for which the employee is personally responsible; behavior based rewards are pay plans in which pay is salary or hourly rate.

name: New venture performance
authors_terms: ["new venture performance", "performance", "return on assets (ROA)", "compounded average sales growth"]
definition: The performance of new ventures, for which there is no commonly accepted set of performance variables or methods of evaluation; the authors adopt two measures, return on assets and compounded average sales growth over the three years prior to the IPO.

name: Early entry
authors_terms: ["early or late market entry", "year of incorporation", "first mover advantages", "strategic timing"]
definition: Whether the new venture entered the telecommunications equipment industry early after deregulation rather than later; year of incorporation was used to indicate early or late market entry.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: The strategic advantage a firm seeks, whether to emphasize cost leadership or differentiation strategies; differentiation means reconfiguring technology to provide unique value to the customer.

name: Strategic target scope
authors_terms: ["strategic target", "scope of activities", "narrow strategic target", "broad strategic target"]
definition: The strategic target of the new venture's strategy, i.e., whether new entrants should serve a broad market segment or whether they should, instead, focus on narrowly defined niches of demand.

name: Cooperative business strategy
definition: Whether cooperative business strategies such as joint ventures, exclusive distributer arrangements, supplier arrangements, etc. were used.

name: Relative R&D investment
definition: The resources allocated to technology activities; average relative R&D spending was the ratio of the most recent three year average R&D spending to average sales.

name: Cooperative technology strategy
definition: Cooperative technology arrangements such as R&D contracted externally by sub-contracting firms, cooperative R&D with competitors, or cooperative R&D with key customers or suppliers.

name: Investment in advanced manufacturing technologies
authors_terms: ["advanced manufacturing technologies (AMT)", "AMT investment", "flexible automation", "investment in individual technologies"]
definition: Design-based AMTs focus on the design of products and processes. Manufacturing-based AMTs focus on the actual manufacturing and physical transformation of the product. Administrative-based AMTs are used primarily to track operations inputs and outputs.

name: Manufacturing involvement in strategy
definition: The degree to which managers and executives closely tied to manufacturing take a proactive role in developing the business strategy of the organization, i.e. the involvement of the manufacturing function in the strategic processes of the business unit.

name: Plant-level performance
authors_terms: ["plant-level performance", "performance improvements at the plant level"]
definition: Plant-level performance is assessed in terms of profit and growth, each rated as the plant's position with respect to competitors.

name: Time lag between investment and performance measurement
definition: The authors expect a learning curve and a lag period associated with AMTs, so that performance improvements following AMT investment are delayed; the lag examined here is the two-year interval between the 1994 investment data and the 1996 performance data.

name: Ph.D. founder representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of founders with Ph.D.", "Ph.D.-holding entrepreneurs on the founding team", "proportion of Ph.D.s on the founding team", "founders' professional-education background"]
definition: I computed the proportion of founders with Ph.D. as an indicator of the professional-education background of the founders in a firm. Compared to most other types of educational programs (e.g., M.D., M.B.A., or B.A.), Ph.D. training stands out in the intensity of members' socialization of professional values and identity.

name: Open science adoption
authors_terms: ["open-science strategy", "adoption of open science", "open-science technology strategy", "open-science practice"]
definition: Open science is a policy that allows a firm's research personnel to do basic science research and publish the results in academic journals. Its core idea is at odds with the definition of technology as private property, a notion widely accepted by for-profit firms.

name: Technological appropriability risk
authors_terms: ["high-appropriability-risk technological environment", "appropriability risk", "technology niche density", "technology crowding"]
definition: Appropriability is the extent to which a firm can protect its intellectual property from being imitated by its competitors, and it is an important dimension of a biotech firm's technological environment. Appropriability risk is thus associated with the characteristics of a firm's technological niche: in densely populated niches, the risk of being scooped is higher, as there are more potential imitators.

name: Isomorphic pressure
authors_terms: ["isomorphic pressure for adopting open science", "isomorphic pressure (IP)", "institutional environment"]
definition: An increase in the number of firms adopting open science helps make the practice more popular and create pressure for the nonadopting firms to conform. This measure captures isomorphism among firms that are close competitors to each other.

name: Performance relative to the aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance", "performance relative to the aspiration level", "point spread"]
definition: Performance was measured as the difference between current performance (i.e., the offensive team's score) and the aspiration level (i.e., the opponent's score plus one point). When performance is below the aspiration level the relationship between performance and risk taking is negative such that risk taking increases as performance worsens; when performance is above the aspiration level the relationship is also negative such that risk taking decreases as performance improves.

name: Aspiration level
definition: The aspiration level refers to the 'smallest outcome that would be deemed satisfactory by the decision maker' (Schneider 1992, p. 1053) or the borderline between perceived success and failure (Greve 2003b).

name: Organizational risk taking
definition: A decision is risky to the extent that its potential outcomes vary and that at least some of those outcomes represent losses (March and Shapira 1992, Shapira 1995, Sitkin and Pablo 1992, Slovic 2000). An organization is risk seeking to the extent that its decision makers are willing to put resources at stake on such choices.

name: Within-period momentum
definition: Within-period momentum thus refers to a trend in which performance within a period is systematically moving toward or away from the aspiration level. Momentum is defined as a systematic and sustained trajectory in performance over time in which performance is either increasing (i.e., positive momentum) or decreasing (i.e., negative momentum) as a result of successive positive or negative outcomes in a row.

name: Across-period momentum
definition: Across-period momentum refers to a trend in which performance targets are either met or not met for multiple periods in a row.

name: Availability of within-period feedback
authors_terms: ["availability of within-period feedback", "within-period feedback", "within-period performance feedback"]
definition: Feedback about performance within a given performance period, not to mention within-period momentum, is not always available; this is particularly true early in a performance period. Within-period feedback will be more readily available because it will be more recent than across-period feedback and more salient because it will be deemed more relevant to the target for the period at hand.

name: Change adoption
authors_terms: ["change adoption", "degree of adoption of the change initiative", "likelihood of change adoption", "degree of institutionalization of each change project"]
definition: We measured the outcome of the change agent's initiative as the degree to which the organization had adopted it after 12 months of implementation.

name: Tie strength to fence-sitters
authors_terms: ["strong ties to potentially influential fence-sitters", "mean tie strength to fence-sitters", "closeness to fence-sitters"]
definition: We label 'fence-sitters' as organization members who are ambivalent toward the change and have the potential to influence change adoption. Tie strength is defined as a combination of the amount of time, the emotional intensity, the intimacy (mutual confiding), and the reciprocal services which characterize the tie, and we measured mean tie strength to fence-sitters as the average tie closeness with members of that subgroup.

name: Tie strength to resistors
authors_terms: ["strong ties to potentially influential resistors", "mean tie strength with resistors", "closeness to resistors"]
definition: We label 'resistors' as those organization members who have a negative attitude toward the change and have the potential to influence change adoption. Tie strength is defined as a combination of the amount of time, the emotional intensity, the intimacy (mutual confiding), and the reciprocal services which characterize the tie, and we measured mean tie strength to resistors as the average tie closeness with members of that subgroup.

name: Divergence from institutional status quo
authors_terms: ["degree of change divergence", "divergence from the institutional status quo", "divergent organizational changes"]
definition: An important dimension along which organizational change initiatives vary is the extent to which they break with the existing institutions in a field of activity, which are defined as patterns of acting and organizing that have become so taken for granted that actors perceive them as the only possible ways of acting and organizing.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entry", "hazard of entering a geographical market", "new market entry", "opening a new branch"]
definition: Market entry by bank i into postal area j in period t is captured by a dummy variable, which equals one if the bank opens a new branch. We analyze entries into new markets, that is, branch openings in markets where the focal bank does not have a branch.

name: Multimarket contact density
definition: We calculate multimarket contact density for each bank-target postal area-month triplet by summing the multimarket contact (the number of postal areas it comes into contact with outside of the target market) of the focal firm with each of the incumbents in the target market. We scale this sum by the number of incumbents in the target market.

name: Large bank branch density
authors_terms: ["Big Four bank branch density", "density of large banks", "number of large bank branches operating in the target market"]
definition: Density of local banks in a target market is calculated as the total number of branches. In some models the counts are separated into strategic groups, so that the density of large (Big Four) bank branches is measured separately from the density of other bank branches.

name: Strategically similar bank density
authors_terms: ["density by strategic group", "number of strategically similar competitors", "density of banks of their own kind"]
definition: Because ecological proximity corresponds to strategic similarity, we expect density dependence to be most clear when estimated for density by strategic group. In these models we separate density counts into strategic groups.

name: Islamic bank density
authors_terms: ["density of incumbent Islamic banks", "Islamic bank branch density", "incumbent Islamic bank density"]
definition: The number of branches of incumbent Islamic banks operating in the target market, which the authors argue shapes the legitimacy of the Islamic bank subform in that market.

name: Strategic similarity
authors_terms: ["strategic similarity", "strategically similar", "strategic similarity of multimarket competitors", "strategic groups"]
definition: Research on strategic groups has long argued that firms are more likely to recognize their mutual interdependence with other firms that follow similar strategies. Banks follow different strategies by targeting retail customers, small and medium companies, or corporate clients, and by developing different capabilities because of their scale and scope of operations.

name: Bank organizational subform
definition: We classify Islamic banks, which have a very different business model, into a separate group. These banks differ in their operations from their conventional counterparts in at least two respects, relying on interest-free financial instruments and being barred from financing activities forbidden in Islam.

name: Distance to target market
authors_terms: ["distance from closest branch", "distance to the target market", "distance from the focal firm's existing markets"]
definition: We calculate distance from closest branch as the minimum of the geodesic distances between the target postal area and all other postal areas in which the bank operated a branch in a given month.

name: Market centrality
authors_terms: ["market centrality", "centrality in the resource space", "Share of town in national GDP"]
definition: We proxy a given target market's centrality in the resource space with the share of its town in national gross domestic product (GDP). Central markets are at the hub of information flows and are central in the decision-making landscape.

name: Local legitimacy of Islamic banking
authors_terms: ["Islamist towns", "religiously conservative towns", "local differences in legitimacy of Islamic banks", "preexisting cognitive legitimacy across locations"]
definition: Because audiences of many organizational forms are local, the degree of hospitality for organizational forms varies across locations, and any preexisting differences in cognitive legitimacy across locations should moderate the relationship between rival density and likelihood of firm entry. We code towns that consistently voted for Islamic political parties as Islamist towns.

name: Writer observable quality
definition: The writer's observable quality, which the buyer observes before disclosure and which helps her to assess the idea's average value before learning about its specifics; empirically it is measured by the number of the writer's major writing credits in the previous five years.

name: Likelihood of a later-stage sale
authors_terms: ["likelihood of a spec sale", "likelihood of a later-stage sale", "sale stage", "spec"]
definition: The stage at which an idea is sold: the writer sells an idea to a studio either as a storyline (a pitch, an earlier-stage sale) or as a complete script (a spec, a later-stage sale).

name: Movie performance
authors_terms: ["movie's expected performance", "performance", "box office revenues", "gross return on investment"]
definition: The performance of a movie conditional on release, used to compare the quality of ideas sold as specs and pitches because released movies have comparable degrees of uncertainty and revenue reflects the total size of the pie.

name: Intermediary representation
definition: Having an intermediary of some sort (agents, managers, and sometimes lawyers), which is more or less the norm in Hollywood; the paper focuses on association with one of the five biggest agencies.

name: Idea quality
authors_terms: ["idea's quality", "average quality of specs", "average quality of pitches"]
definition: The quality of the idea underlying a sale; the authors proxy it with the likelihood of release because the degree of uncertainty is comparable within each subsample.

name: Idea price
definition: The reported price of a sale, which consists of a front-end payment, roughly the price for two drafts and a polish, and a credit bonus paid only if the movie is produced; PRICE is defined as the amount of the front-end payment.

name: Buyer willingness to meet
authors_terms: ["buyer decides whether to meet the writer", "buyer's meeting decision", "meets the writer for a pitch"]
definition: The buyer's decision at Stage 2, after observing the writer's observable quality and his choice of sale stage, of whether to meet the writer; she updates her belief about the idea's deviation from average value according to the writer's strategy and Bayes' rule. Getting buyers to listen is challenging because the costs of evaluating an idea can be substantial, and there is often significant legal risk over the unauthorized use of the disclosed knowledge.

name: Patent thicket density
authors_terms: ["patent thicket", "density of patent thickets", "triples of mutually blocking firms"]
definition: Patent thickets arise when many patents are filed concurrently and patent claims are not clearly delineated, resulting in multiple overlapping claims. The density of patent thickets in a technology area is measured by the number of triples of mutually blocking firms.

name: Patent thicket insider status
definition: Within a given technology area the authors distinguish between firms that are part of patent thickets (insiders) and firms that are outside the thickets (outsiders). Outsiders patent technology that is not closely related to the core technologies of the thicket but that is still patented in the same technology area.

name: Patent portfolio size
authors_terms: ["patent portfolio size", "size of an applicant's patent portfolio", "size of patent portfolio"]
definition: An applicant firm with a large portfolio presents a more credible threat of retaliatory opposition or will find it easier to apply simultaneously for multiple patents than a firm with a small portfolio.

name: Concentration of rivals' patent ownership
authors_terms: ["concentration of patent ownership", "concentration of patent holdings", "concentration of rivals' granted patents"]
definition: The measure captures the public good effect and is constructed as the Herfindahl index of the concentration of rivals' granted patents in a technology area, if these patents were applied for in the same year as the focal patent.

name: Patent opposition
definition: For each granted (focal) patent the authors observe whether an opposition was filed within the statutory period of nine months after the grant date; an opposition can lead to rejection, amendment or complete revocation of the opposed European patent.

name: Customer input
