definition: The comments customers leave on a project page; customers can only comment on projects that they have invested in. Such involvement allows customers to gather information, monitor project progress, and influence product development.

name: Funding success
authors_terms: ["funding success", "cumulative amount of funding", "likelihood of a successful campaign", "new funding"]
definition: The amount of funding a project has received, and whether a project's final funding amount is greater than or equal to its goal.

name: Individual project creator
definition: Whether a project was created by an individual or by a team, determined by counting the first singular and plural personal pronouns in the project description.

name: Project revisions
definition: The changes creators make to project descriptions during the campaign; at the end of a campaign the project page cannot be changed any more.

name: Distant funding experience
authors_terms: ["distant funding experience", "distance of commenting customers", "weighted distance of commenting customers"]
definition: The distance of commenting customers in terms of funding experience, resembling measures such as content distance, which calculate distance based on previous experience.

name: Accelerator participation
definition: Accelerators are financial organizations that invest in cohorts of start-up companies, usually in exchange for equity. After selecting a cohort of companies, accelerators run limited-duration programs that offer mentorship from industry experts, weekly educational programming, and coworking spaces.

name: Venture closure
definition: Closed is a binary variable with 1 indicating that a company is no longer active and 0 indicating that a company is still operational. A company is coded as inactive if it is indicated as 'closed' on any of the data sources, its website cannot be found, or its social media accounts or any traces of presence on the internet have not been updated in a year.

name: Time to closure
authors_terms: ["time-to-close", "how quickly companies go out of business", "faster time-to-close"]
definition: For companies with explicit closing dates reported in any of the databases, an additional variable, time-to-close, is calculated as the company age when it goes out of business.

name: Funding received conditional on closure
authors_terms: ["funding amount", "log of funding amount", "raise less money", "less funding"]
definition: External financing is based on the funding amount obtained by the companies in U.S. dollars. Hypothesis 2 concerns the log of funding amount for a company conditional on the company shutting down, that is, how much accelerator companies have raised at the time they go out of business.

name: Funding ratio
definition: Here I propose a 'funding ratio,' defined as FR = (Average Funding | Closed) / (Average Funding | Acquired). Using an acquisition as a successful outcome, the funding ratio is a measure of whether companies that eventually succeed receive more funding than companies that eventually shut down.

name: Ranking of the diagnosis specialty
authors_terms: ["rank of the diagnosis/ admitting specialty", "rank of the diagnosis specialty", "diagnosis specialty rank"]
definition: The rank of the diagnosis (admitting) specialty, obtained by mapping the patient's main DRG code onto the USNWR specialties and matching the hospital-specialty to the USNWR rankings based on the month of admission.

name: Ranking of the procedure specialty
authors_terms: ["rank of the procedure specialty", "procedure specialty rank", "procedure-specialty rank"]
definition: The rank of the specialty in which a nondiagnosis procedure is performed, mapping the procedure code DRG to the USNWR specialties in the same manner as the main diagnosis.

name: Nondiagnosis specialty procedure
authors_terms: ["nondiagnosis specialty procedures", "procedures performed in nondiagnosis specialties", "cross-specialty procedures", "cross-specialty ties"]
definition: Procedures performed in nondiagnosis specialties during a patient's stay; this is a dyadic phenomenon modeled as a bipartite (two-mode) graph linking two specialties within a given hospital.

name: Rank position tier
definition: Where a subunit is positioned in the overall (external) hierarchy of the rankings; the authors split specialties into those ranked in the top 10, those ranked 11 to 30, and those ranked 31 to 50.

name: Occupational prestige of a specialty
definition: The prestige of a professional's specialty, a particularly salient factor in determining task boundaries in medical settings, with some specialties consistently found to be above average in physician prestige surveys and average compensation.

name: Extrinsic reward cue
authors_terms: ["extrinsic reward cues", "extrinsic incentives", "Cash treatment", "Support treatment", "cash cue", "support cue", "monetary reward cue", "in-kind rewards cue"]
definition: "Each of our treatments stresses only one component of the grant that all awardees receive, either the £5,000 cash award or the one-to-one support." 'Extrinsic rewards' are traditionally defined as contingent, ex post rewards; they can take a monetary or nonmonetary form.

name: Full application submission
authors_terms: ["submitted a full application", "sorting into the applicant pool", "who applies", "opts in", "opts out"]
definition: "Those candidates whose EOI passes the first assessment are then invited via email to proceed to the second round of the application process, which involves completing a full application form that asks the applicants to explain in more detail their venture, past experiences, and current needs."

name: Money orientation
definition: "We used the software program Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) to create measures of self- and other-orientation ('I' and 'They'), orientation to interact with others ..., and money orientation (e.g., cash, bill, revenue) based on this field."

name: Prosocial orientation
definition: "We focus on DICTION's word lists related to prosocial references in text, such as 'collectives,' 'cooperation,' and 'exclusion.'"

name: Prosocial focus of the proposed venture
authors_terms: ["less prosocial/more money-oriented projects", "target beneficiaries belong to a disadvantaged group", "social challenge"]
definition: "We created a dummy variable indicating whether the target beneficiaries belong to a disadvantaged group such as minority groups or persons with disabilities, or whether they belong to more general groups such as adults and/or children."

name: Application effort
definition: "We therefore examine multiple measures of application effort: not just the application success rate but also whether the application is complete, whether it is submitted on time, and the word count in the text responses in the full application."

name: Application success
authors_terms: ["application success rate", "successful in obtaining a grant", "selection into the grant program", "grant winners"]
definition: "The committee of grant managers uses a standardized set of criteria to evaluate each full application (e.g., the expected social impact of the venture and the clarity of goals and outputs) and decides on the grant winners."

name: Self-promotion
definition: "Designed to augment one's status and attractiveness, self-promotion includes pointing with pride to one's accomplishments, speaking directly about one's strengths and talents, and making internal rather than external attributions for achievements."

name: Social venture performance
authors_terms: ["social entrepreneurial performance", "social entrepreneurial outcomes", "performance outcomes", "social entrepreneurial success"]
definition: "We use the detailed application materials and end-of-grant survey ... to examine relevant measures of the start-up venture type (such as the target beneficiary) and social entrepreneurial performance outcomes at the end of the one-year program."

name: Positive status shock
authors_terms: ["positive status shock", "status gain", "positive change to their status", "status change"]
definition: An exogenous shock in the attribution of status, namely the release of the first edition of the Michelin Guide for Washington, DC, in the fall of 2016, which elevates included restaurants to the elite of the industry. The authors describe it as a sudden and positive increase in status that can trigger insecurity pressures.

name: Self-presentation modification
definition: An organization's actions on the ceremonial and material aspects of its offering in an effort to better align with its perception of its audience's expectations and to qualify as legitimate members of the elite group. In this setting it is observed as changes to menu attributes.

name: Prior standing
authors_terms: ["prior standing", "high standing prior to a positive status shock", "standing of an actor prior to the shock"]
definition: The standing an organization enjoyed prior to the status shock, based on evaluations from prominent local critics and awards that contributed to its position long before the new hierarchy arrived.

name: Negative product market shock
authors_terms: ["public health advisory (PHA)", "negative shock to existing products", "negative product market shock", "idiosyncratic events for a specific drug"]
definition: PHAs are idiosyncratic events for a specific drug, allowing the authors to identify the effects of a shock to existing products that are distinct from other firm-specific or industry-wide developments; the authors argue that PHAs represent negative shocks to the profitability of warned drugs.

name: External R&D acquisition
definition: The model predicts that firms will find it optimal to undertake acquisitions in the same therapeutic area from other firms in an effort to replace the affected drug; the post-PHA R&D investments are primarily comprised of 'external' R&D (acquisitions) rather than 'internal' R&D (new initiations).

name: Internal R&D project development
authors_terms: ["internal R&D", "internal new project initiations", "trial initiations", "project suspensions", "internal pipeline decisions"]
definition: Firms' in-house pipeline investments: 'internal' R&D (new initiations), tracked as drug project initiations, trial initiations, suspensions and temporarily held projects at the firm and firm-therapeutic area level.

name: R&D expenditures
definition: R&D expenditures scaled by total assets; affected companies increase their investment in R&D to replace the PHA-affected drugs, and for the average firm in the sample R&D spending averages roughly 59% as a percentage of total assets.

name: Commercialization capital
authors_terms: ["commercialization capital", "downstream assets", "sunk commercialization investments", "excess downstream assets"]
definition: Commercialization capital includes investments in manufacturing and distribution centers in the supply chain, advertising and relationships with industry leaders (i.e., physicians) for marketing, and scientists for postmarketing research; it is specialized and not transferable across therapeutic areas, so it becomes underutilized after a PHA.

name: Internal R&D pipeline strength
authors_terms: ["internal pipeline", "late-stage project pipeline", "pipeline strength", "R&D portfolio strength"]
definition: The strength of the firm's internal development pipeline (its late-stage projects); firms with weaker pipelines will find it optimal to acquire a project from the seller, and the incentive for a firm to acquire new projects externally depends on the strength of the firm's internal development pipeline.

name: Physician promotion payments
authors_terms: ["promotion payments", "payments to physicians", "financial connections between firms and physicians", "physician connections"]
definition: Pharmaceutical firms frequently make monetary or in-kind payments to physicians for promotion of their drugs; these payments are used as a measure of downstream assets to illustrate how the redeployment of such assets may occur.

name: Social skills training
authors_terms: ["social skills training", "social skills treatment", "the two-hour interactive training session"]
definition: A two-hour training session that introduces entrepreneurs to social skills in business, with the objective of equipping them with a collaborative attitude toward interactions with peers who were previously unknown to them and teaching them how to communicate effectively about business issues.

name: Collaborative perception of interactions
authors_terms: ["collaborative perception of interactions", "perceived interactions as more collaborative"]
definition: The extent to which entrepreneurs perceive their interactions during the training program as collaborative rather than competitive.

name: Information exchange
definition: The amount of information entrepreneurs exchange during interactions with peers.

name: Relationship formation
definition: The number of new relationships entrepreneurs formed with other participants from the same training group after the program ended, measured by whether they had spoken over the phone or met in person and naming those individuals.

name: Skill complementarity of relationships
definition: Skill-complementary business relationships are those that connect an entrepreneur with another entrepreneur who possesses a management skill that the focal entrepreneur wants to learn.

name: Ethnic concentration of relationships
definition: The level of concentration of the newly formed relationships across ethnic groups, computed with Herfindahl indexes over an entrepreneur's portfolio of relationships.

name: Business performance
definition: The entrepreneurs' businesses' self-reported monthly profits in the month previous to each survey, a standard measure of performance for small businesses in developing economies.

name: Licensee product market competition
authors_terms: ["competition in licensee product markets", "licensee product market competition", "Licensee PMC", "product market competition"]
definition: The degree of competition in the product markets that license the innovator's technology; it is determined as the weighted-average degree of competition across the licensee product markets associated with an innovator industry, using the fraction of licensing deals made that year between the innovator industry and each licensee product market as a weight.

name: Technology market innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation in markets for technology", "technology market innovation", "innovation"]
definition: An innovator generates an innovation that can be licensed to the firms competing in the product market. Empirically, innovation is measured by citation-weighted patent counts, which capture both the quantity and the quality of firms' innovative output.

name: Licensing exclusivity
definition: The innovator's choice between licensing the innovation to one product market firm only (targeted licensing) or to both firms (market-wide licensing); under targeted licensing the innovator can commit to license to only one firm, for example by granting exclusive use of the innovation to that firm.

name: Innovator product market competition
authors_terms: ["Innovator PMC", "competition in the innovator product market", "innovator product market competition", "product market competition"]
definition: The degree of competition in the product market of the innovator industry, i.e., between firms that innovate; in the benchmark scenario without a market for technology this is the competition between innovating firms that are themselves the product market rivals.

name: Corporate purpose
definition: We conceive of corporate purpose broadly as a company's 'reason for being'; the measure captures 'a set of beliefs about the meaning of a firm's work beyond quantitative measures of financial performance.' The study measures the strength of these beliefs (purposefulness) rather than the content of purpose.

name: Public ownership
definition: Public listing enables a firm to raise capital from many investors, whose shares are traded on public exchanges. The liquidity of these shares in turn creates an ownership structure that is more fluid over time, in contrast to the limited liquidity of private markets.

name: Owner commitment
authors_terms: ["owner commitment", "committed owners", "commitment level of its owners"]
definition: Greater owner commitment entails a longer ownership duration, which in turn promotes greater engagement, 'a collaborative approach between owners and leadership'; commitment also brings soft information and mitigation of free-rider problems inside the firm.

name: Hedge fund ownership
authors_terms: ["hedge fund ownership", "percentage of outstanding shares held by hedge funds", "hedge funds"]
definition: We measure hedge fund ownership as the percentage of outstanding shares held by hedge funds. Hedge funds have a higher cost of capital, targeting 15%-20% investment returns, and are likelier to seek investments with large and relatively fast payoffs, and are used as a proxy of less commitment.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated relative to transient investors", "long-term investors", "dedicated investors"]
definition: Dedicated (transient) investors exhibit more (less) concentrated holdings and longer (shorter) holding periods, thereby, by definition, exhibiting a stronger (weaker) commitment to the firm.

name: Private equity ownership
definition: Because of the contractually determined and limited fund lifetime, PE owners typically have a five- to six-year horizon when investing in the firm, and therefore exhibit less commitment relative to other private market owners.

name: CEO background
authors_terms: ["background of the CEO", "CEO joined in lower ranks", "CEO tenure at company"]
definition: The first category of organizational features is background of the CEO, specifically overall tenure at the company and whether he or she was promoted from the lower ranks of the organization or brought from the outside.

name: CEO pay structure
authors_terms: ["structure of CEO compensation", "Pay gap relative to salaried ranks", "CEO total compensation"]
definition: The second category is the structure of CEO compensation, specifically the relative pay of the CEO versus the median salaried worker.

name: CEO incentive structure
authors_terms: ["incentive structure of the CEO", "Number of margin incentives", "Number of nonmargin incentives"]
definition: The third category is the incentive structure of the CEO, specifically whether his or her incentives are based on cost and profit margin measures or on growth and nonmonetary measures, such as employee satisfaction, customer retention, and other longer time horizon activities.

name: Employee compensation and benefits
authors_terms: ["compensation structure and benefits offered to employees", "Benefits Index", "ESOP", "Bonus as % comp"]
definition: The fourth category covers the compensation structure and benefits offered to employees, measured with a benefits index, an employee stock ownership plan indicator, and the share of salaried compensation that is variable.

name: Repositioning
definition: Repositioning is changing one's categorical position over time. The authors use book synopses to calculate the extent to which an author attempts to reposition, measured as the distance between the focal book's predicted position in label space and the positions of the author's previous books.

name: Label mismatch
authors_terms: ["label mismatch", "mismatch between the producer's positioning and the audience's labels"]
definition: For producers attempting to reposition within the market's category structure, a label mismatch arises as a producer's offerings are labeled by audiences differently than what the producer intends. It is calculated as the mean squared distance between the observed label vector of a book and the label vector predicted from the producer's synopsis.

name: Audience attention
definition: Attention is the extent to which audiences notice and evaluate an offering; the authors measure it with the count of users who rate a book, since readers who rate a book typically have enough awareness and familiarity with it to evaluate it.

name: Audience appeal
definition: Appeal is the perceived attractiveness of an offering to audiences; the authors capture the appeal that a book has generated with the numerical ratings users assign to books and with the count of five-star ratings, the latter distinguishing books with a relatively rare level of positive appeal.

name: Repeat readership
authors_terms: ["repeat readership", "repeat audience members", "prior exchange or consumption experience"]
definition: Repeat readership is the proportion of a focal book's readers who have had prior experience with an author, assessed by whether each reader has completed a book by that same author prior to the focal book.

name: Spatial proximity between matched entrepreneurs' business locations
authors_terms: ["spatial proximity", "average proximity to assigned peers", "average peer proximity", "peer proximity", "colocation"]
definition: The average proximity of the focal entrepreneur's business to their three assigned discussion partners' businesses. Using the geographic coordinates of entrepreneurs' businesses, the authors calculate the straight-line distance in kilometers between each dyad and convert it into proximity with an exponential distance decay function.

name: Tie maintenance
authors_terms: ["tie maintained", "sustaining a relationship", "sustain ties", "staying in touch"]
definition: Whether two matched entrepreneurs sustained their relationship after the networking event, defined at the dyad level as equal to one if the entrepreneurs spoke on the phone or met in person since the previous survey and zero otherwise.

name: Adoption of managerial best practices
authors_terms: ["management practices score", "managerial best practices", "management best practices", "learning"]
definition: Managerial best practices are sequences of tasks that often require adaptation or customization to each particular business. The measure is the proportion of 27 managerial best practices, defined by McKenzie and Woodruff (2017), that an entrepreneur uses.

name: Entrepreneur performance
definition: The performance of the entrepreneur's business, measured with two measures common in research on firms in developing economies: monthly profits and a performance index.

name: Supply portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["supply portfolio concentration", "SPC", "concentration into a regional", "scope of collaboration"]
definition: One of the most important decisions a firm makes in managing its supplier base is its degree of 'supply portfolio concentration' (SPC); that is, whether to concentrate its input purchases in a small number of suppliers versus spreading them among many suppliers.

name: Regional-to-major cooperation
authors_terms: ["regional-to-major cooperation", "cooperation from the regional to the major", "regional's cooperation with the major"]
definition: Cooperation by an airline with another is measured as the number of times the former accepts to reschedule some of its flights to make a landing time slot available to the latter during a GDP.

name: Major-to-regional cooperation
authors_terms: ["major-to-regional cooperation", "cooperation from the major to the regional", "major's cooperation with the regional"]
definition: Cooperation by an airline with another is measured as the number of times the former accepts to reschedule some of its flights to make a landing time slot available to the latter during a GDP.

name: Externalities between regional partners
authors_terms: ["externalities between regionals", "externalities between a major's regional partners", "positive externality"]
definition: Externalities arise because connecting flights on a given local route are more likely to depart on time if the regional operating the other local route helps the major to land its hub-to-hub flights on time.

name: Industry-university collaboration experience
definition: Firms' successful experience in collaborating with universities, captured by joint patents and joint publications, which reflects know-how, tacit knowledge, social connections and trust and constitutes an inimitable complementary asset.

name: Technology commercialization
definition: Commercialization is the step in which a firm converts invention into innovation, competitiveness and long-term performance, requiring complementary assets to convert innovation into sales and profits.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: Corporate R&D investment helps develop firms' absorptive capacity to learn from universities, benefiting organizations beyond directly creating in-house innovation.

name: Industry science dependence
definition: Some industries are more dependent on basic science (and university research) than others, reflecting industry heterogeneity in how closely technologies develop from basic science.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: The effectiveness of collaborations with universities hinges on geographic proximity because of tacit know-how, difficulties in codifying knowledge, and necessary interpersonal communications and mutual trust.

name: Technological complementarity
definition: Universities' and firms' innovations can complement each other in creating commercializable inventions; complementary technologies are those necessary for patentability.

name: Refund bonus offer
authors_terms: ["refund bonus", "refund bonuses", "offer of refund bonuses", "bonus offer"]
definition: Under a refund bonus extension, entrepreneurs offer investors refund bonuses in the event of unsuccessful fundraising; if the investment threshold is not reached, investors receive a refund of their investment and a refund bonus.

name: Fundraising success
authors_terms: ["fundraising success", "rate of fundraising success", "successful funding", "funding success"]
definition: A fundraising campaign is successful when the amount of capital raised reaches a prespecified threshold; in the experiment projects required both investors to invest in order to be developed (i.e., to be successfully crowdfunded).

name: Project quality
authors_terms: ["project quality", "good quality projects", "bad quality projects", "project type"]
definition: The entrepreneur and, respectively, his project can be one of two types: bad (B) or good (G), with a good project being more profitable. In the experiment, if both investors invest in a good quality project they earned a $3 return on their $1 investment, whereas if both investors invest in a bad quality project they each lose their $1 investment.

name: Investment decision
definition: After receiving private signals about the project, investors simultaneously and independently decide whether to invest their unit of capital in the project or in the outside option. In each round investors make two binary decisions: whether to invest a unit of capital ($1.00 in the experiment) into two projects offered by two entrepreneurs, and they could invest in zero, one, or two projects.

name: Product differentiation
definition: The reaction of consumers, that is, market performance, is affected by differentiation between the new product and these reference sets that consumers assign to the producer. Our main independent variables of interest are the metrics that track product differentiation (∆Xij) of newly released music from reference levels of audiences.

name: Within-artist differentiation
authors_terms: ["within-artist differentiation", "within-artist references", "deviation of the focal product from past profile of the artist", "∆WithinArtist"]
definition: Within-artist differentiation is based on references from products released by the focal producer in the past. The comparison of the focal product with past releases of the producer allows us to track within-artist differentiation.

name: Proximal-peer differentiation
definition: Proximal-peer differentiation is based on references from products released by close contemporaries of the focal producer. Audiences develop reference levels that build on their consumption of products by peers that are proximal to the focal producer (here, similar genre affiliations).

name: Dominant-design differentiation
definition: Dominant-design differentiation is based on references from products that establish a domineering position in the market. It is the product differentiation of the focal product from the dominant design, that is, the most successful contemporary music on the market, regardless of the genre.

name: Genre label differentiation
definition: A change in sonic attributes does not necessarily align with genre shifts, but a new genre label that is different than past genre affiliations of the focal artist or the popular chart-topper in the market serves as a clear communication that helps in managing audience expectations.

name: Artist tenure
definition: Artists with longer (shorter) tenure in the cultural sphere, possessing a larger (smaller) portfolio, are presumed to have more (less) market knowledge.

name: Radio airplay
authors_terms: ["radio station plays", "focal album plays", "plays on radio stations", "Focal_Plays"]
definition: To assess audience response to new music releases, we track the number of radio plays each album receives. The cumulative number of plays garnered by the songs on a newly released album j by artist i in the 52 weeks since its release on the radio station k becomes our dependent variable.

name: Critic ratings
definition: Critic ratings are the scores given by reviewers; for a newly released album j by artist i, Rating_kij is the score given by critic k.

name: Revenue
definition: The revenues private sector firms earn in a vaccine market; LnRevenue measures the logged value of monthly revenue (in domestic currency units plus one) of a firm in a market for a month.

name: Product variety
definition: The number of stock-keeping unit (SKU) types a firm offers in a vaccine market; the window of opportunity triggered by reduced competition from the PSUs can incentivize some firms in the private sector to increase their product variety in the market to serve heterogeneous customer preferences and pre-empt competition.

name: Domestic firm status
definition: Whether a private sector firm operating in the Indian vaccine markets is domestic or foreign; the authors construct the variables DomesticFirm and ForeignFirm to identify domestic and foreign firms operating in the Indian vaccine markets.

name: Reduction in competition from the public sector
authors_terms: ["reduction in competition from the public sector", "PSUs' supply disruption", "supply shock", "suspension of the PSUs"]
definition: The sudden reduction in supply from public sector organizations that private sector firms face in the affected vaccine markets; the surprising suspension of the three PSUs' production licenses following the GMP-related stipulations serves as the source of a sudden reduction in competition for private sector firms in the Indian vaccine markets.

name: Political alignment
authors_terms: ["political alignment", "political pluralism", "politically not-aligned states", "politically aligned states"]
definition: Political pluralism is an institutional arrangement in which the political party ruling at the state government level is different from that ruling at the national government level; politically not-aligned refers to states in which the political affiliation of the state government (where the firm is located) differs from that of the federal government.

name: Product variety
authors_terms: ["product variety", "product portfolio size", "product breadth", "portfolio size", "number of products"]
definition: Product variety (product portfolio size, product breadth) is the mass/number of products a firm offers; it increases the probability that switching consumers buy from the firm. Empirically it is directly measured by the number of products of a publisher in a market segment in a given release year.

name: Customer retention
authors_terms: ["investment in customer retention", "consumer retention", "retention", "investment in consumer retention"]
definition: A higher investment in customer retention induces consumers in the firm's customer base to repurchase one of the firm's products with a higher probability; empirically retention is proxied by the number of updates to a video game on Steam.

name: Market value
authors_terms: ["value of a market", "market value", "value of a market segment", "segment value"]
definition: The parameter v can be interpreted as the value of the market: if v is larger, the decrease in buying probability from a higher price is smaller, resembling markets that are more valuable. Empirically the value of a market segment is approximated by the price of the game.

name: Consumer heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["degree of consumer heterogeneity", "heterogeneity", "consumer heterogeneity", "degree of heterogeneity in consumers' preferences"]
definition: The parameter β can be interpreted as the degree of consumer heterogeneity: if β tends to infinity, the distribution of how consumers buy products becomes almost uniform and prices only play a minor role, representing consumers who are highly heterogeneous in their tastes.

name: Managerial prosocial preferences
authors_terms: ["prosocial preferences", "managerial prosocial preferences", "prosociality", "CEO prosocial preferences", "prosocial preferences of managers"]
definition: A person's prosocial preferences is a multidimensional construct that encompasses being fair, loyal, and moral in interpersonal relations, and it can be both an innate trait that remains stable across time and situations and a state influenced by the situation or the desire to care for a specific group of people.

name: Anticipatory guilt
definition: Guilt is an intense negative emotion that arises from failing to live up to one's moral standards and self-identity, especially when one's behavior has caused interpersonal harm that could have been avoided; antecedent guilt is the anticipation of that emotion and is treated as a key component of prosocial cost.

name: Exit threshold
definition: The minimum level of firm performance managers are willing to accept before choosing to exit; managers often have the discretion to set higher or lower thresholds based on their preferences.

name: Risky investments
authors_terms: ["risky investments", "less risky investments", "aggressiveness of firm financial investments", "conservative investments", "firm risk taking"]
definition: Investment choices whose dispersion of potential outcomes exposes the firm to the risk of falling below the exit threshold; whereas lower exit thresholds are usually thought to encourage high-variance investment, managers who set them out of concern for employees may instead pursue a strategy that maximizes the minimum potential payoff.

name: Harm to employees
authors_terms: ["severity of harm", "harm to employees", "anticipation of less harm to employees", "severity of the harm that exiting causes employees"]
definition: The severity of the harm that exiting causes employees; in situations where the harm is more severe, prosocial managers will perceive a greater violation of their prosocial preferences and experience greater anticipatory guilt.

name: Firm exit
definition: Firm-level exit is a terminal, nonreversible decision that halts firm operations and affects all employees indiscriminately; the authors proxy for exits based on a firm being delisted from Compustat, and examine divestitures as partial exits.

name: Chinese import competition
authors_terms: ["Chinese import competition", "negative industry shock", "increasing Chinese import competition", "ΔIC"]
definition: A well-established exogenous industry-level shock that increases firm exits, calculated for each four-digit SIC code as the change in imports from China from the previous year divided by initial absorption measured as the sum of U.S. industry shipments and Chinese imports minus U.S. exports.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Vertical integration involves organizational decisions about the types of value chain activities to be conducted within the firm rather than through markets, and such decisions have important implications for firm efficiency and outcomes. Vertical integration unifies the ownership of interdependent stages of production within a single firm.

name: Innovation quantity
definition: The quantity dimension of the rate of innovation, which the authors argue vertical integration increases because internal organization reduces the transaction cost of knowledge exchange and facilitates component recombination. It is measured as the combined patent counts of the acquirer and the target.

name: Innovation quality
definition: The quality dimension of the rate of innovation, which the authors argue vertical integration increases along with quantity. It is measured with patent forward citations of the acquirer and the target.

name: Systemic innovation
definition: A systemic innovation is a combination of multiple interdependent, oftentimes distinct, knowledge components, requiring significant coadjustment to other parts of a large system.

name: Autonomous innovation
definition: An autonomous innovation combines relatively independent knowledge domains connected with standardized interfaces, requiring little simultaneous modification. Autonomous innovation features relatively independent components connected with standardized interfaces or modular designs.

name: Organizational slack
definition: A cushion of actual or potential resources which allow an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for adjustment or to external pressures for change in policy, as well as to initiate changes in strategy with respect to the external environment.

name: Absorbed slack
definition: Tied up with current operations, absorbed slack, which amounts to excess costs in organizations, is not easy to redeploy.

name: Unabsorbed slack
authors_terms: ["unabsorbed slack", "free cash flow at the discretion of the managers"]
definition: Unabsorbed slack, which corresponds to currently uncommitted resources, is more easily redeployed elsewhere, allowing for greater managerial discretion.

name: Firm performance
definition: Managers were asked to identify their firms' relative performance, as compared with close competitors, based on profitability (after-tax return on assets) and market position. In Study 2 firms' total pre-tax profits were used because this is one of the most important measures of performance that managers focus on.

name: Strategic emphasis on innovation
authors_terms: ["Innovation", "the importance of innovativeness to a firm's strategy", "relative R&D intensity", "a strategy based on innovation"]
definition: The strategic importance of innovativeness to the firm will manifest itself not in absolute R&D intensity of the firm, but rather in the R&D intensity of the firm relative to others in its industry. Firms that invest in R&D at a much higher rate than their competitors are most likely trying to compete on the basis of innovativeness.

name: Leverage
definition: The authors equate financial slack with low leverage: financial slack is defined with 'low leverage' and the need for financial slack manifests itself in a relatively low leverage ratio. Leverage is computed by dividing the book value of debt by the total market value of the firm.

name: Profitability
definition: The variable Profitability controls for firm-level accounting profitability, as measured by return on assets (i.e., operating income before depreciation divided by the book value of assets).

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable used to test Hypothesis 3, which examines the performance implications of a mismatch between strategy and capital structure, was the firm's market-to-book ratio. The authors feel firm-level market-to-book is best considered a holistic proxy for performance, corresponding closely to Tobin's q.

name: Focal acquisition premium
definition: Focal acquisition premium was measured by the percentage difference between the actual price paid to a target firm and the market price of the target before the acquisition event. Acquisition premiums, the percentage difference between the final per share price paid to the target firm and the target's prior share price, have averaged 25-40 percent and often exceeded 100 percent.

name: Directors' average prior premium experience
authors_terms: ["average prior premium", "directors' average prior premium", "average prior premium experienced by directors"]
definition: The average premium previously experienced by directors across various boards should therefore reflect the premium that they tend to support prior to discussions about the focal premium. It was calculated as the grand mean of all premiums experienced by a focal board of directors across all boards, including the focal board, during the prior 48-month period.

name: Demographic homogeneity
definition: The degree of similarity among directors on salient demographic characteristics, which tends to increase interpersonal trust and promote open communications among group members. In the present study, demographic heterogeneity is also expected to exacerbate group polarization bias by reducing effective communications among directors.

name: Acquisition experience of minority viewpoint directors
authors_terms: ["minority expertise", "acquisition experience of minority viewpoint directors", "acquisition expertise of the minority"]
definition: The acquisition experience of the subgroup of directors who support the position held by less than half of directors, relative to that of the majority. Minority expertise was calculated as the average number of acquisitions experienced by minority viewpoint directors 48 months prior to the focal decision divided by the average number of acquisitions experienced by the majority in the same time period.

name: Board influence
definition: The extent to which boards can influence strategic decisions through monitoring and advising management; the extent to which outside directors influence strategic decisions through monitoring and advising management can vary across companies.

name: Vertical pay gap
definition: The authors define tournament incentives as the vertical pay gap between the CEO's compensation and the average compensation of the firm's top managers not including the CEO.

name: Securities class action lawsuit
authors_terms: ["securities class action lawsuit", "securities lawsuits", "filing of a class action lawsuit"]
definition: Under Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, securities class action lawsuits are filed by shareholders against a defendant firm in response to allegedly fraudulent and deceptive behavior. Securities class action lawsuits are generally attributable to top executives because they are directly responsible for disclosing information to shareholders.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: This is an objective categorical measure that reflects both the number of fundamentally different businesses in which a firm operates and the extent to which sales are evenly distributed among those types. Unrelated diversification arises from operating between two-digit SIC industry groups, with total firm sales as reference.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: The authors suggest that environmental uncertainty is an appropriate indicator of external influences that introduce randomness into managerial promotion tournaments, and they measure it as a composite index of dynamism and complexity.

name: Group affiliation
authors_terms: ["group affiliation", "business group", "affiliated with groups", "group membership", "membership in a group"]
definition: A business group is a set of firms which, though legally independent, are bound together by a constellation of formal and informal ties and are accustomed to taking coordinated action. Group affiliation marks the firms that belong to such a group rather than being unaffiliated.

name: Firm profitability
definition: We use a version of return on assets (ROA)—operating profit divided by total net assets—as our measure of profitability.

name: Within-group similarity of profitability
authors_terms: ["within-group similarity of profitability", "profit rates that move together", "returns within groups are similar to one another"]
definition: Regardless of whether group membership is costly or beneficial in total, membership seems certain to impose costs and benefits that are shared by members; equity crossholdings will ensure that costs and benefits are borne together, so that members of a given group exhibit profit rates that move together.

name: Entry timing
definition: We measure entry year as the calendar year in which a firm was established, as recorded in the NBS database. Entry timing distinguishes new entrants from incumbent firms.

name: Firm productivity
definition: The productivity index measures the proportional difference between the productivity of firm i in year t relative to the hypothetical firm in the base year. It is a multilateral index of output and inputs (labor, material, and capital) relative to industry averages.

name: Firm exit hazard
definition: Exit is a dichotomous variable that records the exit event when a given firm identifier at time t does not reappear in the database at time t + 1. New entrants' higher exit hazard reflects their survival disadvantage when productivity is controlled for.

name: Institutional barriers
definition: Institutional barriers are the hindrance in the institutional environment that prevent the market selection mechanism from functioning properly. They can result from inadequate institutional infrastructure, institutional voids, or institutional susceptibility such as excessive regulatory requirements and requests for bribery.

name: Alliance portfolio size
definition: We measure APS as the number of manufacturing alliances in which the focal firm is involved. Since the impact of an alliance may not be immediately felt on performance measures, we measure alliance portfolio as the cumulative number of manufacturing alliances that the focal firm has entered into in three years prior to the year in question.

name: Innovation performance
definition: Patent data has been used to measure innovation performance in the past literature and is considered a valid measure of innovation activity. Our measure of innovation performance is the number of granted patents filed by a firm in year t and is weighted by five-year forward citations.

name: Financial performance
definition: We measure financial performance using net income. This is based on past accounting literature, which suggests net income as a reliable indicator of the performance of the firm.

name: Vertical integration
definition: In our sample, VI firms engage in both design and manufacturing activities in-house while VS firms engage only in design activities in-house. We measure vertical integration using a dummy variable. Specifically, the variable takes a value of 0 if the firm engages in design only and a value of 1 if the firm engages in both design and manufacturing (referred to as fabrication in the industry).

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay dispersion", "pay dispersion among R&D employees", "pay dispersion in R&D groups", "horizontal pay dispersion"]
definition: Pay dispersion, which is defined as the degree to which pay is differentiated among employees within organizations, is recognized as a key decision area in organizational human capital management for its effects on the quality of organizational workforces and motivation.

name: Firm innovation performance
definition: In accordance with previous studies, we measured firm innovation as the annual number of successful patent applications by a firm. In the high-technology industry, patenting inventions is not only prevalent, but also recognized as a critical performance outcome.

name: Firm growth opportunities
definition: Firms undertake unique sets of investments and projects to achieve growth, and employees form expectations regarding their firm's future performance. When employees believe that their firm has greater growth opportunities, then they are more optimistic about their firm's future performance.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack refers to firm financial resources that are not committed to any specific activities.

name: Codified human resource slack
authors_terms: ["codified HR slack", "codified HR slack, be it general or specific"]
definition: Excess workers carrying knowledge that is easily separated from its source, i.e., knowledge whose transfer and replication is easy and therefore independent of whether it is general or specific to a given organization.

name: Tacit and general human resource slack
authors_terms: ["tacit and general HR slack", "tacit and generic HR slack"]
definition: Excess workers whose knowledge is tacit and therefore not readily transferred, but also general in the sense of being constructed upon knowledge available in the 'market' and not entirely specialized to a particular work setting.

name: Tacit and specific human resource slack
authors_terms: ["tacit and specific HR slack", "tacit and firm-specific HR slack"]
definition: Excess workers carrying knowledge that is both tacit and specific to a work context, whose usefulness is confined to the boundaries of a particular work setting and which takes prolonged employment to accrue.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance at the plant level", "gross profits", "plant profitability"]
definition: Performance at the plant level, computed as gross profits, which measure the residual value appropriated by a manufacturing plant after netting all expenses, except for taxes.

name: Competitive pressures
definition: A time-variant variable that proxies for the extent to which a focal maquiladora was disrupted by the availability of cheaper Chinese products.

name: Standardized operations
definition: A proxy for the extent to which maquiladoras' operational choices rely on more or less standardized workflows and tasks, distinguishing contract plants from focused plants.

name: Parent firm performance
definition: The performance of the parent firm, which in this setting is captured by the total number of years a firm remained active in automobile production; the authors use the annual firm hazard of exit as the dependent variable and interpret its inverse, the survival probability, as the parent's performance.

name: Spinout activity
definition: The founding of a start-up by a former employee of an incumbent firm within the same industry. In this article a spinout event takes the value of 1 in the year that the spinout was incorporated at the corresponding parent-year pair.

name: Spinout-parent distance
authors_terms: ["spinout-parent distance", "technological and marketing capabilities distance", "distance between the spinout opportunity and the parent's core", "product distance"]
definition: The technological and marketing capabilities distance between the parent and the spinout, operationalized as the log of the Euclidean distance between the characteristics of the most advanced automobile model at the parent in the spinout year and the characteristics of the first automobile model that the spinout introduced upon founding.

name: Severe disagreement resolution through spinout
definition: Spinout events that followed severe disagreement at the parent, defined in the broadest possible way to include management disputes, 'strategic disagreements,' rejections of new ideas and subsequent departure of the proposing employee(s), personal clashes and quarrels, and in general all the instances where the departure of the spinout founder from the parent firm occurred in nonamicable terms.

name: Hierarchical rank of departing employee
authors_terms: ["hierarchical role", "rank of the departing employee", "hierarchical level", "top executive", "employee"]
definition: The hierarchical role of the exiting employee at the parent firm, grouped into three distinct categories: employee for entry-level employees up to but excluding managerial level titles, manager to include sales, production, and marketing managers and job titles that included the term manager except for general manager, and top executive to include the rest of the executive positions, starting with general manager all the way to the founders themselves.

name: Job search
authors_terms: ["job search", "searchers", "stayers", "willingness to engage in job search"]
definition: Executives who agree to share their résumés and be interviewed by the search consultant for a position are classified as 'searchers' (D = 1), and 'stayers' (D = 0) are those that turn down the invitation. The decision studied is whether executives, when approached by a leading search firm about becoming a candidate for a position elsewhere, accept or decline the offer.

name: Current position attractiveness
authors_terms: ["relative attractiveness of one's current position", "attractiveness", "attractive positions"]
definition: The attractiveness of one's current position relative to jobs elsewhere, which is approximated by the value of the current job because the value of the open position is unknown at the point of contact. One of the reasons why positions may be attractive is compensation, another measure of attractiveness for executives is the financial performance of the firm, and firms with more positive reputations in the business world may represent more attractive jobs.

name: Uncertainty of current job prospects
authors_terms: ["uncertainty associated with one's current job", "uncertainty in one's current role", "uncertainty about future prospects"]
definition: Given the standard assumption that individuals are risk averse, if prospects for exploitation in their current role are less certain, that role is also less valuable. Uncertainty is measured with tenure in one's current employer, where greater tenure should be associated with better information and greater certainty about future prospects, and with shocks such as a recent merger or acquisition that make prospects in the current role less certain.

name: Career breadth
definition: The breadth of an executive's experience, measured with an index of the changes in his or her roles (changing industry, changing segments within the financial industry, changing occupations). The more focused one's career has been, the more focused the set of likely opportunities elsewhere are, so executives with broader, less focused experience are likely to learn more from search.

name: Strategic type
authors_terms: ["strategic type", "strategic types", "Miles and Snow's strategic types", "Defenders, Analyzers, Prospectors and Reactors"]
definition: Miles and Snow (1978) proposed a typology of strategic types based for the most part on the organization's orientation toward product-market development. They suggested four strategic types: Defenders, Analyzers, Prospectors and Reactors.

name: Entrepreneurial mode of strategy making
definition: In the Entrepreneurial mode as defined by Mintzberg (1973), strategy making is characterized by active search for new opportunities. Power is centralized in the hands of the chief executive, dramatic forward leaps are made in the face of uncertainty, and growth is the dominant goal of the organization.

name: Adaptive mode of strategy making
definition: The Adaptive mode of strategy making, as defined by Minzberg (1973), reflects a division of power among members of a complex coalition and clear goals do not exist. Solutions to existing problems are reactive rather than a proactive search for new opportunities, and disjointed decisions are made in incremental, serial steps.

name: Planning mode of strategy making
definition: Analysts play a major role in the Planning, the third strategy-making mode suggested by Mintzberg (1973). Assessment of the costs and benefits of competing proposals is systematically analyzed, and decisions and strategies are integrated.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Level of performance was operationalized by several measures. The two executives evaluations of performance, for which the data are more complete, were used as surrogates for all performance measures.

name: Strategy-making mode
definition: Mintzberg (1973) suggested three modes of strategy-making: the Entrepreneurial, the Adaptive and the Planning. Mintzberg thus laid emphasis on the process by which strategies emerge, rather than on their content.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was operationalized as the total sales in 1986 dollars.

name: Profit center size
authors_terms: ["profit center size", "PC size", "profit center sales", "PC sales"]
definition: Profit center size was operationalized as the total sales in 1986 dollars.

name: Relative profit center size
definition: Relative size is defined as profit center size divided by firm size.

name: Firm profitability
definition: ROE was selected as the measure of corporate performance, following previous research.

name: Cash compensation
definition: Cash compensation is defined as salary and bonus.

name: Compensation mix
authors_terms: ["bonus as a percentage of cash compensation", "bonus as a percentage of total cash compensation", "bonus ratio", "the ratio of bonus to salary", "salary mix", "the composition of pay"]
definition: The composition of pay (i.e. salary vs. bonus) and the ratio of bonus to salary; the bonus as a percentage of total cash compensation.

name: Firm tenure
definition: Firm tenure was operationalized as the number of years in the firm.

name: Job tenure
definition: Job tenure was operationalized as the number of years as the PCM of that particular profit center.

name: Age
definition: Age was measured as chronological age.

name: Education
definition: Education was measured as the number of years completed in school.

name: Scientific capability
definition: One of the two components of absorptive capacity distinguished by Arora and Gambardella (1994): the ability to evaluate external technology, which depends on a firm's upstream research capability. Firms with stronger scientific capabilities have greater ability to evaluate external technology, are more selective, and focus on fewer but more valuable external technologies.

name: Technological distance
authors_terms: ["Investor-partner technological distance", "technological distance (or proximity)", "technologies in areas that are new to the corporate investor"]
definition: Technological distance is associated with what Lane and Lubatkin (1998) have defined as relative absorptive capacity, a learning dyad-level construct based on the distance between the knowledge base of recipient and contributing organizations. It is measured by whether the technological areas covered by the partner firm are new for the corporate investor.

name: Pipeline pressure
authors_terms: ["Investor's pipeline pressure", "the proportion of early-stage drugs within the pipeline of a corporate investor"]
definition: Within a corporate investor's research pipeline, the number of drugs in the early stages of development (preclinical and Phase 1) divided by the sum of its total number of drugs in all stages of development. A larger value indicates a greater proportion of early-stage drugs and a greater likelihood of developing a late-stage pipeline gap.

name: Corporate venture capital investment
definition: The theoretical framework considers CVC as a 'wait and see' investment under conditions of uncertainty used to defer making larger commitments such as those associated with MFT transactions (i.e., R&D alliances, licenses and acquisitions). CVC investments are analogous to call options, giving the corporate investor the right but not the obligation to defer larger commitments of resources to the future.

name: Licensing post-CVC
authors_terms: ["license post-CVC", "licensing post-CVC", "exercise the option by licensing"]
definition: The exercise of the CVC option by increasing commitment with the technology supplier through an MFT transaction such as a license. In the second stage the authors examine the time to the occurrence of a licensing transaction between the corporate investor and partner firm starting from the year of the CVC investment.

name: Value of the partner's technology
authors_terms: ["Value of partner's technology", "value or quality of a partner firm's technology", "value of the underlying technology"]
definition: As a proxy for the value or quality of a partner firm's technology, the authors use the implied partner valuation obtained from its financing history. The valuation includes the expected future cash flows from the partner's technology.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty refers to the limited knowledge held by CVC investors about the future payoffs of the underlying technology. Development uncertainty serves as a proxy for exogenous uncertainty specific to technological subfields.

name: Firm exploration
authors_terms: ["Extent of Firm Exploration", "firm exploration", "exploration at the component level", "extent of explorative search"]
definition: This metric captures a team's tendency to search for technological solutions that are more or less distant from the baseline technical setup defined by the FIA; components based on unexplored industry-level knowledge belong to this explorative category.

name: Firm performance
definition: We take the best rank classification attained by either of a team's two drivers in each race as representing the team's performance in that race, and then average these performance scores across all races in the season, so that teams with lower averages outperform those with higher averages.

name: Magnitude of environmental change
authors_terms: ["Change in Technical Regulations", "magnitude of environmental change", "magnitude of the environmental regulatory change", "magnitude of such change"]
definition: The magnitude represents the size of the discontinuity of a new (technological) paradigm, and we conceptualize the magnitude of environmental change to be either incremental or radical.

name: Regulatory enforcement actions
definition: Regulatory enforcement involving the use of external pressure or mandates to require specific organizational changes; the PHMSA issues corrective orders and other directives when pipeline operators are deemed to have violated regulatory standards, and in many cases these orders are accompanied by monetary penalties.

name: Regulatory collaboration
definition: Voluntary efforts intended to exchange information about regulated activities or share other related knowledge between regulators and regulated organizations; their collaborative nature makes reciprocal knowledge sharing likely, meaning that organizations may learn directly from regulators while regulators also learn about participating organizations.

name: Performance problems
authors_terms: ["rate of performance problems", "organizational performance outcomes", "organizational failures", "accidents", "accident rate"]
definition: The organization's overall rate of performance problems following enforcement actions, which past research in regulated settings often measures through the rate of organizational failures such as accidents, incidents, injuries, and other negative events.

name: Compliance efforts
definition: The frequency or intensity of organizational efforts to comply with external mandates and to increase other compliance-related investments following enforcement actions; a focus on specific actions ensures that compliance arises through active organizational changes rather than through unintentional shifts.

name: Regulatory visibility
definition: The preexisting transparency of an organization's practices to regulatory agents, through a greater volume of prior inspections, investigations, site visits, or other similar monitoring efforts.

name: Social visibility
definition: The broader transparency of an organization's practices to a wider array of stakeholders, such as communities, suppliers, consumers, and other parties, that are indirectly affected by organizational performance in regulated settings.

name: Political engagement
definition: The ability of organizations to buffer or protect against future regulatory changes through lobbying, advocacy, or other efforts to shape their political or regulatory environment.

name: Foreign entry mode
authors_terms: ["foreign entry mode", "entry-mode choice", "choice between a joint venture and a wholly owned subsidiary", "subsidiary ownership"]
definition: From the institutional perspective, it could be argued that entry mode represents an organizational form appropriate for the firm's motivation to gain legitimacy in the relevant environments under the conditions of uncertainty. The dependent variable represents foreign entry mode, defined as a dummy variable, and coded 0 for a wholly owned subsidiary and 1 for a joint venture.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "parent's firm- and product-specific knowledge", "R&D intensity", "parent firm R&D intensity"]
definition: Asset specificity refers to durable investments that cannot be redeployed to alternative uses and by alternative users without a sacrifice of productive value. Research of entry-mode choice based on the transaction-cost theory has used R&D intensity as a proxy for asset specificity.

name: Host-country experience
authors_terms: ["parent's host-country-specific experience", "parent experience in the host country", "country-specific experience"]
definition: In our study, parent experience refers to the amount of local knowledge a parent firm accumulates through its subsidiary in a host country. Once foreign firms have accumulated local experience and obtained the necessary local knowledge and access in a host country, their dependence on local partners becomes less critical, and hence, they may exercise full control over the new subsidiaries.

name: Regulative institutional pressures
authors_terms: ["regulative pillar", "regulatory domain", "state influences", "regulative settings of the host-country environment"]
definition: The regulative pillar refers to rules and laws that exist to ensure stability and order in societies. The elements of the regulatory domain include laws and rules that construct and constitute the grounds of organizational and industry action as well as ensure stability and order in societies.

name: Normative institutional pressures
authors_terms: ["normative pillar", "normative domain", "cultural influences", "normative pressures imposed by the local people"]
definition: The normative domain refers to shared understandings and meanings, or the "logic of appropriateness" (March 1981), that are embodied in the form of national culture, value, norms, and belief systems in a given country. The more restrictive the normative domain, the more the multinational enterprises must accommodate institutional expectations and conform to social expectations.

name: Mimetic entry
definition: Mimetic isomorphism (DiMaggio and Powell 1983) results from the behavior of organizations that seek guidance from the experiences of other organizations in comparable situations when facing uncertainty. Hence, we postulate that multinational enterprises pursue mimetic behavior in choosing the mode of entry.

name: Historical norm
definition: Historical norm goes beyond this amount of experience and captures the cognitive constraint imposed upon the organizational decision maker once such past experience is institutionalized. In all, historical and inertia factors lead to institutional persistence; that is, firms repeat what they have been doing in the past.

name: Category contrast
definition: A category is high contrast if it features clear-cut boundaries, implying that there is wide agreement about the distinctive organizational form and capabilities required to be a legitimate member of that category. Low-contrast categories are characterized by greater uncertainty and contestation concerning their distinctive features, which produces ambiguity about which specific organizational form and capabilities are required in that category.

name: Technological entry
authors_terms: ["technological entry", "technological entries", "entry", "entering a new technological category"]
definition: An organization 'enters' a technology category when it is granted a patent in a technology class in which it had no prior patents. Technological entry events represent critical junctions in the history of an organization that may profoundly affect both its capabilities and its identity vis-a-vis external audiences.

name: Entry patent performance
definition: The performance consequences of each entry event, which patent data make it possible to measure for each entry patent. We measure patent performance by counting a patent's Forward citations, an indicator that innovation research has found to be correlated with patents' technological impact and economic value.

name: Entrant type
authors_terms: ["de novo organizations", "de alio organizations", "de novo entrants", "de alio entrants", "entry type", "de novo", "de alio"]
definition: We build on the well-understood distinction between de novo organizations (entering the categorical space for the first time) and de alio organizations (entering with a preexisting categorical affiliation). An organization is a de novo or a de alio organization in relation to the category considered at each point in time.

name: Sovereign credit ratings
definition: Risk ratings of sovereign government creditworthiness published by major credit-rating agencies. Higher (more positive) ratings indicate assessments of less risk associated with lending and investment, while lower (more negative) ratings indicate the opposite.

name: Crisis-induced industry turbulence
definition: By crisis the authors mean a generally short period of unexpected and notably unfavorable shift in the external environment organizations face; by industry turbulence a more protracted state of environmental volatility and generally unfavorable drift in key factors critical to the success and survival of firms in the industry. The phrase crisis-induced turbulence summarizes the dynamic market conditions in the period 1997-1998 and contrasts with stable industry conditions in the period 1987-1996.

name: Industry incumbency
authors_terms: ["incumbency", "industry incumbency", "incumbent agency", "positioning as an industry incumbent"]
definition: Expert positioning as an industry incumbent, rather than as a newcomer. In stable environments incumbency confers several 'first-mover' advantages, including those related to learning, reputation, and preemption of ratings business with preferred sovereigns.

name: Regional focus
authors_terms: ["regional focus", "focus", "regional specialization", "specializing in specific geographic regions"]
definition: Agency positioning as a specialist in a certain segment of the industry, rather than as a generalist with expertise across all industry segments; here it is the degree to which an agency specializes in rating sovereigns from a given geographic region.

name: Industry rivalry
definition: The degree of rivalry experts face in any one industry segment; in this case the number of firms operating in a given national market segment, that is, the number of agencies publishing ratings for a sovereign in a year.

name: Top management team age
authors_terms: ["age", "mean team age", "average age of a top management team", "low executive age"]
definition: An individual's age is expected to influence strategic decision-making perspectives and choices. Research has suggested that flexibility decreases and rigidity and resistance to change increase as people age.

name: Age heterogeneity
definition: Diversity of age is expected to increase the variety of perspectives on strategic issues facing a firm, thus stimulating the consideration of change. The benefits of increased age diversity will be greater at moderate levels and will taper off the more heterogeneous in age a top management team becomes.

name: Organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure", "mean team organizational tenure", "low organizational tenure", "average organizational tenure"]
definition: Higher commitment to the status quo and to the values of a firm are likely to be associated with long organizational tenure. In addition, long tenure increases understanding of organizational policies and procedures and perhaps reluctance to change such structures.

name: Organizational tenure heterogeneity
definition: Organizational tenure, by defining an individual's cohort membership, indicates experiences, perspectives, and values. Thus, a team's heterogeneity in organizational tenure should lead to diverse opinions and stimulate consideration of changes in strategy.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["team (executive) tenure", "top management team tenure", "mean team executive tenure", "average tenure of a top management team"]
definition: Long average group tenure results in decreasing levels of overall communication because group members feel they can anticipate other members' viewpoints and increased specialization occurs. We thus expected that long-tenured groups will become increasingly resistant to changes in strategic direction.

name: Team tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["tenure heterogeneity", "team executive tenure heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of team tenure"]
definition: Heterogeneity of team tenure indicates that the various members of a top management team have been promoted at different times, suggesting that new and different perspectives on the strategic vision for the firm have been added.

name: Educational level
authors_terms: ["educational level", "mean team educational level", "level of education"]
definition: Level of education reflects an individual's cognitive ability and skills. High levels are associated with high capacity for information processing and ability to discriminate among a variety of stimuli.

name: Science and engineering specialization
authors_terms: ["academic specialization in science and engineering", "science specialization", "academic training in the sciences", "educational specialization"]
definition: Selection of a curriculum of study reflects an individual's cognitive style and personality, and the curriculum pursued shapes perspectives and outlooks. Certain academic fields are more oriented toward change than others; for example, science and engineering are concerned with progress, invention, and improvement.

name: Educational specialization heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["educational specialization heterogeneity", "educational curriculum heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of educational curriculum"]
definition: Heterogeneity of educational curriculum within a team is likely to broaden perspectives on strategic decision making.

name: Corporate strategic change
authors_terms: ["corporate strategic change", "strategic change", "change in corporate strategy", "absolute change in diversification level"]
definition: This inquiry examined the link between top management teams and corporate strategic change, defined as absolute change in diversification level. Absolute change in the level of corporate diversification, the measure used in this study, is an accurate reflection of strategic change.

name: Diversification of knowledge resources
authors_terms: ["VC diversification", "diversification of knowledge resources", "diversification of knowledge assets", "scope of a VC firm's knowledge stocks"]
definition: The breadth of the industries in which a venture capital firm invests, which in this context reflects the diversification of its knowledge resources; the authors note that in other work on diversification the owner may contribute a wide range of resources, while 'VCs do not; they contribute only knowledge resources.'

name: VC firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "percentage of investments ... that ultimately resulted in a successful outcome", "IPO success rate"]
definition: Performance is measured by the percentage of investments made by a VC firm in the focal year that ultimately yielded an IPO event, an IPO being the liquidity event that allows VC firms to realize returns and the ultimate goal for most venture capitalists when they invest.

name: Investment stage
authors_terms: ["investment stage", "stage of investment", "stage of development of the portfolio company"]
definition: The stage of the investment round is an assessment of how advanced the portfolio company is in its development. Early stage investments are characterized by relatively higher uncertainty, while late stage investments are characterized by relatively lower uncertainty.

name: Co-investing
definition: VC firms partner through coinvestment with other VC firms; co-investing provides a way for VCs to leverage the knowledge assets of their syndicate partners, so that they can achieve efficiencies in evaluating and developing portfolio companies without developing all of the deep expertise in-house.

name: Involvement
definition: High levels of involvement and participation create a sense of ownership and responsibility, out of which grows a greater commitment to the organization and a growing capacity to operate under conditions of autonomy. In high-involvement systems the social definition of reality is created by individuals in an inductive manner, and the contrast between agents and subjects is generally much lower.

name: Consistency
definition: Effectiveness in these firms appears to spring from normative integration or consistency: the collective definition of behaviors, systems, and meanings in a integrated way that requires individual conformity rather than voluntary participation. Its root is the concept of normative integration, or the pervasiveness of a consensual system of behavioral control.

name: Adaptability
definition: Adaptability is the capacity for internal change in response to external conditions; the psychiatric term alloplastic describes the capacity to change in response to external conditions without abandoning one's underlying character. An effective organization must develop norms and beliefs that support its capacity to receive and interpret signals from its environment and translate these into internal cognitive, behavioral, and structural changes.

name: Sense of mission
definition: A mission provides purpose and meaning, and a host of noneconomic reasons why the organization's work is important; a sense of mission defines the appropriate course of action for the organization and its members. Both of these factors reflect and exemplify the key values of the organization.

name: Organizational effectiveness
definition: The multidimensional nature of the concept requires that effectiveness be defined by a complex of stakeholders, who may hold differing, incompatible, and changing criteria. Effectiveness is measured here through subjective ratings of performance relative to similar firms and through objective measures of profitability and growth.

name: Medical marijuana legalization
authors_terms: ["Medical marijuana", "medical marijuana laws", "legalization of marijuana for medical purposes"]
