definition: Medical marijuana laws officially establish the reclassification of marijuana as a medicine and its legalization for medical purposes.

name: Alcohol sales
definition: State-level sales of alcohol in millions of U.S. dollars; the dollar amount of sales - which is the quantity of a good consumed times its price - is able to capture the value that individuals attach to its consumption and their willingness to pay for it.

name: Tobacco sales
definition: State-level sales of tobacco in millions of U.S. dollars; the dollar amount of sales - which is the quantity of a good consumed times its price - is able to capture the value that individuals attach to its consumption and their willingness to pay for it.

name: Patient registration system
authors_terms: ["Medical marijuana registry", "patient registration system", "compulsory registration policies"]
definition: Compulsory registration policies restrict access to marijuana by ensuring that marijuana use is limited to consumers with medical needs (i.e., 'patients').

name: Health safety attribute
definition: Legalization challenged taken-for-granted judgments of marijuana as an unhealthy and dangerous 'vice' by emphasizing its safe consumption and potential health benefits - henceforth named the 'health safety' attribute.

name: Marijuana consumption
authors_terms: ["proportion of people consuming marijuana", "proportion of state residents that made use of marijuana"]
definition: The proportion of state residents that made use of marijuana (individuals 12 years or older).

name: Parent hostility
definition: The degree to which an incumbent firm disapproves of the spawning of a spin-out from within its ranks. The authors define hostility as an attitude rather than as a behavior.

name: Time to breakeven
definition: The number of full months between a firm's founding and the first time its costs equaled its revenues. It captures a firm's progress toward profitability and thus toward survival.

name: Product differentiation
definition: The degree to which the spin-out focuses on other products than the parent.

name: Network development
definition: The degree to which a spin-out establishes new ties outside the parent's immediate network.

name: Evaluative schema clarity
authors_terms: ["clarity of evaluative schemas", "clear evaluative schemas", "clearer schemas", "schema clarity", "Jaccard measure", "clarity of critics' evaluative schemas"]
definition: We propose that the similarity in the language used to describe wines within each quality band reflects the clarity of its critics' understanding of what quality means for that varietal in that year. When the descriptive words in the tasting notes for wines of similar quality are themselves more similar, one may infer that the Wine Spectator critics have a clearer schema of what quality is in that varietal category.

name: Pricing variability around expected levels
authors_terms: ["pricing variability around expected levels", "list price variability around expected levels", "variance around expected list prices", "pricing order"]
definition: Here, predictability is reflected in list prices that more accurately and systematically reflect the information that will ultimately shape consumer valuations. We employ a multiplicative heteroscedasticity, or variance function model, to assess the impact of quality schemas on list price variability around expected levels.

name: Prior critical coverage
authors_terms: ["prior critical coverage", "prior coverage", "producers that have not yet received coverage", "Producer's first review"]
definition: By not providing coverage to a producer, critics have effectively placed that producer outside of the quality-oriented segments of the market. Prior reviews provide a producer with direct exposure to how critics have perceived products and what dimensions have been emphasized.

name: Producer reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "low-reputation producers", "reputation for poor product quality", "producer reputation"]
definition: As negative ratings accumulate, a producer develops a reputation for poor product quality. Producers with superior reputations for product quality tend to charge higher prices for their wines.

name: Niche width
authors_terms: ["niche width", "generalist producers", "producers whose reviews are spread across a range of product categories"]
definition: To calculate each producer's niche width, we use Simpson's (1949) index of diversity, which measures the diversity of a distribution over a set of discrete categories. Producers that work across categorical boundaries run the risk of incurring penalties related to consideration, valuation, and experience accumulation.

name: Knowledge valuation
authors_terms: ["knowledge valuation", "valuation of knowledge", "valuing knowledge", "value internal and external knowledge"]
definition: How do managers value knowledge possessed by members of their own organization and how do they value the knowledge possessed by outsiders? After the acquisition, Fresh Choice executives reduced their valuation of Zoopa's knowledge and, consequently, their attempts to acquire and use that knowledge.

name: Internal competition
definition: Organizational boundaries demarcate an arena within which competition for promotions, status, and salaries occurs. Internal competition occurred at Fresh Choice because of its internal labor market and promotion-from-within policies, and at Xerox through senior management successions and layoffs.

name: External competition
definition: Managers are motivated to learn from external competitors because they fear being outcompeted in the marketplace, and they can learn and borrow without facing the status costs of validating a direct competitor.

name: Knowledge availability
definition: Insiders are physically proximate and more likely to communicate, so their knowledge is cheap and readily accessible, while legal and technological (security) barriers shroud competitor knowledge and prevent easy access to it. The difficulty of accessing external knowledge makes it scarce and unique, which heightens its perceived value.

name: Status implications of knowledge use
authors_terms: ["status implications of knowledge use", "status costs", "social costs"]
definition: When people value an insider's knowledge, they often gain little in the way of personal self-enhancement, and instead face the prospect of legitimating a direct competitor for organizational rewards. Managers actually gain status by using external contacts and knowledge.

name: Credit for knowledge use
definition: People seem to receive differential credit depending on whether they are using ideas from inside or outside of the company; managers receive more status, a higher bonus, and are given more credit for effort and creativity when they learn from outsiders rather than from insiders.

name: Effort attributed to the learner
definition: The effort respondents attributed to a manager who implemented services learned from an insider versus from an external competitor.

name: Creativity attributed to the learner
definition: How creative respondents rated a manager who implemented services learned from an insider versus from an external competitor.

name: Competence attributed to the learner
definition: How competent respondents rated a manager who implemented services learned from an insider versus from an external competitor.

name: Promotion likelihood
definition: How likely respondents were to promote a manager who implemented services learned from an insider versus from an external competitor.

name: Bonus awarded
definition: The bonus respondents allocated to a manager who implemented services learned from an insider versus from an external competitor.

name: External knowledge source
definition: Knowledge that originates outside the manager's own organization, in contrast to knowledge possessed by insiders. Managers cannot scrutinize the ideas of outsiders as closely, so the flaws of external ideas are less visible, and the difficulty of accessing external knowledge makes it scarce and unique.

name: Technological progress
authors_terms: ["technological progress", "investment in monitoring and adopting technological innovations", "monitoring technological innovations", "adopting technological innovations"]
definition: Two different constructs were used to operationalize the concept of technological progress: monitoring technological innovations and adopting technological innovations. Monitoring is the level of investment in evaluating new technologies and new ideas, and screening ideas suitable for use by the SBU; adopting is the level of integration of ideas and technologies in new products and processes, and how close the SBU is to the state of the art in its main line of activity.

name: Strategic type
authors_terms: ["Miles and Snow's strategic typology", "strategic types", "strategic archetypes", "defenders", "prospectors", "analyzers"]
definition: Miles and Snow's strategic typology comprising four strategic archetypes—defenders, prospectors, analyzers, and reactors—was used in this research; the high-tech industries can be differentiated into distinct strategic types along the entrepreneurial and engineering dimensions. Each SBU was categorized by its manager into one of the strategic types.

name: Short-term success
definition: The first two performance dimensions—profitability level and generating orders—are used in this research as 'short-term' dimensions measuring the results of past activities which do not determine future prospects. Profitability level is how well the business unit meets its financial objectives and how well it is doing relative to similar business units, and generating orders is how well the business unit is doing in achieving sales objectives and creating future orders.

name: Long-term success
authors_terms: ["long-term success", "long-term dimensions", "generating new opportunities", "preparing the infrastructure for the future"]
definition: The other two dimensions—generating new opportunities and preparing the infrastructure for the future—are used as 'long-term' dimensions which determine the SBU's ability to survive in the long run. Generating new opportunities is how successful the unit is in opening new opportunities for new products and for new markets, and preparing the infrastructure for the future is whether the business unit has the scientific and technological knowledge, equipment and facilities required for the development and production of future products.

name: Performance below aspiration level
definition: Member firms trigger R&D search when their performance is below an aspiration level. We measured firm performance below the aspiration level by using the spline function of the discrepancy between firm performance and the aspiration level.

name: R&D search
authors_terms: ["R&D search", "R&D search intensity", "R&D search behavior", "R&D expenditures"]
definition: To test H1a, H1c, H2a, and H2c, we adopted a member firm's R&D expenditures as our dependent variable to measure its R&D search. Member firms - in R&D intensive industries - often adopt R&D search behavior when their performance is below the aspiration level because R&D investments are a key vehicle to gain competitive advantages, respond to environmental changes, and facilitate long-term growth.

name: Prevalence of underperforming firms
authors_terms: ["prevalence of underperforming firms", "prevalence of underperforming member firms", "group-level cognitive accessibility of performance"]
definition: To test H1a, we measured the prevalence of underperforming member firms, which were defined as member firms with ROA below their aspiration level. We calculated the ratio of the sales aggregation of underperforming firms to the entire group sales to create a variable, Prevalence of Underperforming Firms, representing the group-level cognitive accessibility of performance.

name: Group-level managerial attention to performance
definition: To measure group-level managerial attention to performance and R&D, we first identified keywords related to performance, which included (financial) performance, profit, profitability, liability, sales, and cash. Using an automated analytic tool in R for the Korean language, we counted the frequency of those keywords in an individual letter and normalized it with the total number of words in the letter.

name: Prevalence of R&D intensive firms
authors_terms: ["prevalence of R&D intensive firms", "prevalence of R&D firms", "group-level cognitive accessibility of R&D"]
definition: To test H2a, we computed the sales-weighted ratio of R&D intensive firms to all the member firms in a business group to generate a variable, Prevalence of R&D Firms, indicating the group-level cognitive accessibility of R&D.

name: Group-level managerial attention to R&D
definition: Keywords for R&D included R&D, research, technology development, technology commercialization, technology innovation, and patent. Using an automated analytic tool in R for the Korean language, we counted the frequency of those keywords in an individual letter and normalized it with the total number of words in the letter.

name: Matrix structure
authors_terms: ["matrix structure", "matrix organization", "matrix organizations", "matrix firms", "matrix design", "matrixed firms"]
definition: A firm's internal use of a matrix structure is defined as formal structures characterized by dual (or multiple) authority relationships and lateral influence and communication. Matrix structures constitute a multiple command system, wherein each activity has two or more lines of command.

name: Multilateral alliance
definition: Multilateral alliances are partnerships in which a firm must interact with multiple partners; they are those alliances that involve more than two partners.

name: Partner unfamiliarity
authors_terms: ["partnerships with new partners", "alliances with new (previously unfamiliar) partners", "alliances with unfamiliar partners", "alliances with new partners"]
definition: Establishing an alliance with a new partner entails significantly more risks and uncertainties compared with collaborating with a familiar, repeat partner. Such partnerships are those involving partners with which the firm had no previous partnership history.

name: Alliance diversity
authors_terms: ["diverse alliances", "partner diversity", "functional alliance diversity", "alliances with diverse partners", "diversity"]
definition: Such diversity could entail partner diversity in terms of geographic location or industry affiliation, and functional alliance diversity, such as partnerships that combine different functions in the alliance scope, including research and development (R&D), production, and marketing.

name: Nondominant power position
authors_terms: ["nondominant power position", "nondominant power position ... equal or inferior power", "nondominant power"]
definition: Partnerships in which the firm occupies a nondominant power position are those in which the firm will hold equal or inferior power compared with its alliance partners.

name: Nonequity alliance
definition: Nonequity deals are the purely contractual arrangements, in contrast to the more determinate equity-based partnerships, which require companies to formalize the partners' roles and responsibilities, governance structures, and joint decision-making processes at the inception of the relationship.

name: Complex alliance
definition: We define complex alliances as those that engender multifaceted and intricate collaboration challenges, in line with the classic view of complex organizations. Such alliances include those that have multiple partners, those that are geographically or functionally diverse, and those in which a focal firm occupies a noncontrolling ownership position.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "abnormal stock returns", "stock market reactions", "stock market returns"]
definition: We regard abnormal stock returns as an expression of investors' expectations regarding the performance of the focal alliance.

name: Unemployment duration
authors_terms: ["duration of unemployment", "unemployment duration", "founder's duration of unemployment"]
definition: The length of time an individual has spent in unemployment; the authors argue that the level of need is not uniform across necessity entrepreneurs but instead increases with time spent in unemployment, and treat duration of unemployment as a key marker of the level of need experienced by an individual.

name: Industry-specific experience
definition: Experience that develops due to prior work in an industry setting; the knowledge involved 'is neither firm-specific nor general, but rather unique to the industry in which it was obtained' and would lose its value if a founder creates a firm in a different industry.

name: Attractiveness of the opportunity landscape
authors_terms: ["attractiveness of the opportunity landscape", "relative attractiveness of the opportunity landscape", "attractiveness of external opportunities", "opportunity landscape"]
definition: The attractiveness of external industries relative to the founder's home industry; if external industries are performing better than the individual's home industry, the opportunity landscape exerts pull-effects, and it can also exert push-effects by driving the founder away from a lower-performing home industry.

name: Industry choice
authors_terms: ["industry choice", "industry-choice decision", "re-enter their home industry", "creating a firm in the home industry", "'what business should I be in?'"]
definition: The decision about which industry a founder locates his or her new venture in - described by the authors as one of the most fundamental strategic decisions that entrepreneurs face, that is, 'what business should I be in?'; the paper compares creating a firm in the founder's home industry with creating one in an external industry.

name: External mobility
authors_terms: ["external moves", "external mobility", "external job moves", "external cross-firm moves", "cross-firm moves", "external voluntary moves", "external involuntary moves"]
definition: Employees can build their careers either by moving into a new job within their current organization or else by moving to a different organization. The paper studies these 'external' cross-firm moves and contrasts them with 'internal' moves within organizations.

name: Internal mobility
authors_terms: ["internal moves", "internal mobility", "internal job moves", "moves within organizations", "promotion"]
definition: One way that people can achieve the twin goals of vertical mobility and horizontal fit is through moving jobs within organizations, either being promoted or moving laterally into a different position.

name: Involuntary turnover
authors_terms: ["involuntary turnover", "external involuntary moves", "involuntary external moves", "involuntary mobility"]
definition: In some cases, people may move because their prior job has ceased to exist, as happens with involuntary turnover. External moves were coded involuntary when respondents reported that they moved because of 'position eliminated,' 'company, office, workplace or plant closed,' 'discharged or fired,' or 'left by mutual agreement'.

name: Change in job responsibilities
authors_terms: ["responsibilities", "changes in responsibilities", "increases in responsibilities", "change in responsibility", "upward progression"]
definition: Although some technical specialists can progress through their careers without managing anyone, the authors believe that size of units managed provides the most general measure of responsibilities for executives: the more individuals that someone manages in any field, the greater the span of activities that they can affect. They complement this with the hierarchical rank that the job title reflects.

name: Change in pay
authors_terms: ["pay", "earnings", "changes in pay", "increases in pay", "pay increases", "log earnings"]
definition: Respondents reported their total earnings in their first year in each job; pay is analyzed as the difference in log earnings between the first year of one job and the first year of the next, for consecutive jobs.

name: Change in job function
authors_terms: ["function change", "change in function", "changing function", "change of function", "functional shift", "change in job function"]
definition: Mobility allows people to change their job function, which, similar to occupation, defines the kinds of tasks that individuals carry out day to day. Functional changes therefore represent the most substantial way in which people can change their horizontal fit with their job.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Reputation 'can be defined as a subjective evaluation of a firm's overall quality relative to its peers'; it is amassed and depleted through temporal 'flow' sequences, and the models are specified as models of reputational change by including the prior year's ranking.

name: Downsizing
definition: 'Downsizing has been defined as the intentional reduction of personnel in an effort to improve efficiency or effectiveness.'

name: Short-term stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction", "market reaction to downsizing", "excess returns", "excess market returns"]
definition: 'One particular performance measure that seems quite likely to moderate a downsizing's reputational effect is the stock market's initial reaction to it (i.e., the 'excess returns' [Brown & Warner, 1985] associated with it).' It 'measures the change in a specific firm's stock price, net of broader market movements, during a short window of a few days surrounding an event.'

name: Profitability change
authors_terms: ["recent changes in a firm's performance", "change in profitability", "profitability change", "performance change"]
definition: 'We measured change in profitability as the difference between return on book assets in the downsizing year (t) and in the prior year (t - 1).'

name: Prior reputation
definition: The firm's reputation in the previous year: 'good reputations are sticky and enduring assets amassed through a history of making and meeting commitments', and 'prior ranking is measured in the previous year.'

name: Downsizing prevalence
definition: 'Prevalence is the percentage of firms in the sample that had downsized in prior years (including between 1977 and 1985).'

name: Audience type
definition: The two groups of reputation granters whose rankings Fortune ascribes, stock analysts and peer firm executives: 'analysts' roles culturally constitute them as shareholder representatives', whereas 'executives' roles are much more complex; executives are simultaneously embedded in multiple institutional domains.'

name: Information technology investment
definition: Investment in information technology (IT) and implications for firm performance are central issues in the IT payoff literature. IT investment was measured as the ratio of dollar investment in IT to sales.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance, the dependent variable, was measured as Tobin's q. Tobin's q incorporates a market-based measure of firm value, which is forward looking, risk adjusted, and less vulnerable to changes in accounting practices and, hence, is considered appropriate for measuring the performance impact of IT investments.

name: Level of diversification
definition: The level of diversification is the extent to which a firm's activities are spread across multiple businesses. Total diversification (TD) measures the extent of a firm's operations in different industries, whether related or unrelated, and is equal to the sum of the two diversification measures—RD and UD.

name: Related diversification
definition: Related diversification involves operating businesses in industries that are related to each other and, therefore, offers opportunities to share operating assets and capabilities as well as financial resources. Related diversification (RD) measures the extent of a firm's operations in different industries within the same two-digit Standard Industry Classification (SIC) code.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Unrelated diversification involves operating businesses in industries not related to each other and, consequently, presents opportunities to share financial resources and a relatively limited set of opportunities to share operating assets and capabilities. Unrelated diversification (UD) measures the extent of a firm's operations in different two-digit SIC codes.

name: External involvement
authors_terms: ["external involvement", "involvement with and dependence on its external environment", "response to external regulation", "cooperative interorganizational involvement", "external orientation"]
definition: The greater a hospital's involvement with and dependence on its external environment through regulation, cooperative interorganizational activity, and external sources of funding.

name: Hospital size
definition: The scale of a hospital's operations; the high volume of business or number of patients in large hospitals means they will incur more total costs than small ones and are likely to have more decentralized and professional management.

name: Hospital efficiency
definition: The extent to which a hospital uses its facilities efficiently, indicated by high occupancy rates and by the length of patients' stays adjusted for severity of illness.

name: Adoption of cost containment policies
authors_terms: ["adoption of cost containment policies", "policy adoption", "number of cost containment policies"]
definition: The number of cost containment policies a hospital claimed to have implemented; affirmative responses were considered to indicate only the adoption of policies, since a policy that has been implemented at all must first have been adopted.

name: Chief administrator board representation
authors_terms: ["chief administrators on their governing boards", "chief administrator on board"]
definition: Whether a hospital's chief administrator serves on its governing board, which gives administrators potential influence over board decisions and thus over policy adoption.

name: Physician board representation
authors_terms: ["physicians on their governing boards", "physicians on board"]
definition: The share of a hospital's governing board made up of physicians, whose micro concern for individual patients' needs is expected to make them resist formal cost containment policies.

name: Strategic differentiation
authors_terms: ["strategic differentiation", "strategic differentiation of new entrants vis-à-vis the exemplar", "distance between the characteristics of the new product and the exemplar"]
definition: New entrants' level of strategic differentiation vis-à-vis the exemplar, calculated by comparing the features of an entrant game and those of the exemplary hit game. The distance between the characteristics of the new product and the exemplar is argued to be critical in audience judgment and evaluation.

name: Entrant market performance
authors_terms: ["market performance of new product entrants", "entrant performance", "game sales", "entrant sales"]
definition: The market performance of new product entrants, measured by inflation-adjusted, aggregate U.S. dollar sales (logged) of a console video game.

name: Critics' evaluation
definition: Professional critics provide ratings of games, adjudicate quality, and help consumers sort through different offerings. Consistent with the theory that categories emerge around exemplars that serve as benchmarks, the measure is the relative improvement of a new release over the exemplar.

name: Proto-category evolution
definition: The temporal dynamic of proto-category evolution, captured by the time lapsed since the exemplary hit game's release, which moves a proto-category from early to more developed phases.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was measured as industry-adjusted average performance for the two years prior to a succession event. Performance for a given two-year period was measured by comparing a firm's two-year sales growth to the average sales growth for the semiconductor industry for the same two years.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of insiders on a board", "proportion of inside board members"]
definition: Board composition was measured as the proportion of inside members on a board of directors. Boards with a high proportion of insiders are expected to choose a chief executive who poses a minimal threat of disruption.

name: Insider ownership
authors_terms: ["inside ownership", "firm ownership by insiders", "proportion of ownership by insiders"]
definition: Inside ownership was the proportion of total firm shares held by individuals employed by the organization. Ownership is a source of power that can either reinforce or undermine successor choices.

name: Insider ownership concentration
definition: Inside ownership concentration was the proportion of total firm shares held by the four largest inside owners. If ownership is concentrated in the hands of relatively few insiders, they may be in a position to influence the selection process actively.

name: Outside successor selection
authors_terms: ["inside or outside succession", "successor origin", "outside succession", "choice of an inside or outside successor"]
definition: The dependent variable of interest was whether a chief executive successor came from inside or outside an organization. An inside successor was defined as a manager or employee promoted from within a firm and an outside successor as any other individual.

name: Offshore R&D outsourcing
definition: A governance mode of R&D offshoring in which firms perform R&D activities overseas through relationships with independent third parties, i.e., buying R&D services from other firms, public administrations, universities or organizations abroad.

name: Offshore R&D insourcing
definition: A governance mode of R&D offshoring in which firms perform R&D activities overseas via foreign-based affiliates; it takes value 1 when the firm acquires R&D services from an affiliate or captive center.

name: Innovation performance
definition: Innovation measures innovation performance; it is a dichotomous variable that takes value 1 when the firm has achieved a product or process innovation. The authors distinguish these innovation results as outputs from R&D activities as inputs.

name: Sales growth
definition: We use growth in sales to analyze firm growth. We obtain this continuous variable by dividing the difference between sales figures in year t and year t - 1 by the sales figures in year t - 1.

name: Extensiveness of practice implementation
definition: Extensiveness measures the degree of practice implementation; it assesses change in degree and is conceptually distinct from similarity.

name: Similarity of practice implementation
definition: Similarity measures how alike these implementations are to previous versions of the practice; it assesses change in kind, and the authors use the term similarity for the construct Ansari et al. (2010) call fidelity.

name: Time of adoption
definition: The year of adoption of an individual plan, used as a predictor variable that reflects the gradual field-level effects of diffusion over the analysis period.

name: Media coverage
definition: Media coverage is the number of articles per year that mention the terms 'golden parachutes' or 'employee retention plans,' and the authors consider it a proxy for overall information availability about the practice.

name: Court cases against the practice
definition: Federal and state court cases in which a challenge to golden parachutes was the central issue of the lawsuit, excluding cases in which parachutes were a mere incidental aspect and cases that were eventually ruled in favor of the golden parachute plan.

name: Firm visibility
definition: The visibility of an adopting firm, assessed by the number of times the firm is mentioned in the news media.

name: Takeover exposure
authors_terms: ["takeover exposure", "presence of a takeover bid", "takeover activity"]
definition: Firms differ in terms of their exposure to hostile bids for a change in control; the measure identifies whether a firm was subject to either takeover speculation or an actual tender offer.

name: CEO origin
authors_terms: ["outsider CEO", "having an outsider CEO", "CEOs hired from the outside versus inside"]
definition: Whether the CEO was hired from the outside versus from the inside of the firm, identified from biographical sources, newspaper searches, and the firm's own historical proxy statements and annual reports.

name: Female
definition: Female was coded 1 if the executive was female and 0 otherwise.

name: Speed of advancement
authors_terms: ["speed of advancement", "speed to the top", "time to the top"]
definition: It is defined as how long it takes an individual from the beginning of their career to secure a top executive job. We measure speed of advancement by the number of years between the year the executive entered the labor market and the year when she or he was appointed to the focal position.

name: Intra-firm mobility
definition: We capture intra-firm mobility with company tenure and measure it as the proportion of an executive's career spent in their focal organization before assuming their current executive position.

name: Number of female executive incumbents
authors_terms: ["number of female executive incumbents", "number of women executives", "number of incumbent women in the executive ranks"]
definition: To investigate whether women's advantage over men is a function of the number of women executives currently in the executive ranks of the company, we examine the companies that were present in the Fortune 100 list in both 2001 and 2011 and perform within-company analyses using the number of female executive incumbents in the year 2001 as a proxy for whether there were women at the top.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: We employ Wood's (1991, p. 693) definition of CSP as 'a business organization's configuration of principles of social responsibility, processes of social responsiveness, and policies, programs, and observable outcomes as they relate to the firm's societal relationships.' CSP is a composite construct that captures firm-level motivations, processes, and outcomes on environmental, human rights, and labor issues.

name: Stakeholder interactions with sociopolitical actors
authors_terms: ["stakeholders' interactions with sociopolitical actors", "CSP stakeholders' interactions with sociopolitical actors"]
definition: The collective interactions of CSP stakeholders with sociopolitical actors in a country, which the authors argue indicate the collective power of stakeholders in an issue network to influence all firms in a given country on an issue. Sociopolitical actors include individuals or organizations that influence formal rules and those that can influence informal rules.

name: Stakeholder heterogeneity
definition: The diversity of stakeholder organizational forms (e.g., government actors, IGOs, labor unions, NGOs, and community organizations or residents) and issue interests (e.g., environmental versus human rights issues) of stakeholders in the CSP network active in a country-year. The authors argue that heterogeneous stakeholder support suggests that an institutional expectation has diffused more widely.

name: Interstakeholder group conflict
authors_terms: ["interstakeholder group conflict", "relative disagreement between the heterogeneous stakeholder groups"]
definition: The degree to which conflictual interactions between heterogeneous stakeholder groups exceed the baseline level of conflictual interactions within groups, used as a proxy for the positions stakeholder groups take on an issue. Where stakeholder-group positions on an issue are in disagreement, firms are more likely to take a wait-and-see stance.

name: Proselytizing stakeholder actions against firms
authors_terms: ["proselytizing stakeholder actions against firms", "direct action against firms by proselytizing CSP stakeholders"]
definition: Direct conflictual actions against firms (e.g., protests or boycotts) taken by proselytizing stakeholders, which the authors define as actors within an issue network who organize and champion information about an alternative means of engaging with environmental and social challenges. Such actions attune managers in that country to the issue's urgency.

name: Proselytizing stakeholder density
authors_terms: ["proselytizing stakeholder density", "density of cooperative interactions between proselytizing CSP stakeholders"]
definition: The relative density of cooperative interactions among proselytizing stakeholders, calculated as a ratio of the density of cooperative interactions among all actors in the country. Dense networks of cooperative relations between proselytizing stakeholders reduce free riding and make repeated collective action more likely.

name: Similar innovations
authors_terms: ["similar drugs", "similar innovations", "number of similar drugs", "presence of similar drugs"]
definition: Innovations building on the same knowledge base as the focal innovation; in the pharmaceutical context, drugs that apply the same mechanism of action as the focal drug and are available in the same therapeutic class.

name: Potential substitutes
definition: Innovations that build on alternative knowledge bases to achieve comparable functionality; in the pharmaceutical context, the distinct mechanisms of action underlying drugs in the focal drug's therapeutic class.

name: Scientific publication rate
authors_terms: ["rate of publication about its drug in the top medical journals", "top medical publications on drug", "rate of scientific publication"]
definition: For each drug-year observation, the number of articles about that drug that the innovating firm published in the top medical journals in that year, used to position the innovation in the marketplace.

name: Scientific publications about similar innovations
authors_terms: ["top medical publications on similar drugs", "scientific publications about similar drugs", "scientific papers about similar innovations"]
definition: Scientific articles about drugs other than the focal drug that have the same therapeutic use and build on the same mechanism of action; by reinforcing outside parties' familiarity with these alternative innovations they increase the pressure on a firm to assert the uniqueness of its own innovation.

name: Scientific publications about potential substitutes
authors_terms: ["top medical publications on potential substitutes", "scientific publications about potential substitutes", "scientific articles about potential substitutes"]
definition: Scientific articles about drugs building on mechanisms of action other than the focal drug's mechanism; they help consolidate a collective understanding about these alternative technologies, which has a compound effect on the viability of an innovation.

name: Appropriability
authors_terms: ["appropriability", "appropriability of profits due to a firm's innovations", "appropriability strategy", "strength of appropriability"]
definition: Appropriability refers to the degree to which a firm captures the value created when it introduces innovations. The industrial organization literature typically models appropriability as the extent to which firms can limit other firms from imitating its innovations.

name: Firm economic performance
authors_terms: ["economic performance", "firm performance", "market valuation of a firm's R&D assets", "Tobin's q"]
definition: As a forward-looking measure of firm performance, Tobin's q captures two fundamental components of innovation and appropriability: the contribution of a firm's intangible assets to its market value and the firm's ability to earn supranormal rents from its tangible and intangible assets. Tobin's q is defined as the ratio of a firm's market value to the firm book value of its total assets.

name: Preemptive patenting
definition: Preemptive patenting is defined as the patenting of a substitute technology before rivals to deter entry. The incumbent may have no intention of commercializing those inventions, and by building what is sometimes called a 'patent fence,' it can preempt R&D rivals by foreclosing their ability to introduce substitutes and compete with its 'core' innovations.

name: Threat of entry by R&D competitors
authors_terms: ["threat of entry", "threat of entry by R&D competitors", "threat of entry by technology rivals"]
definition: Without a threat of entry, as when the probability of entry by R&D competitors is null, the expected profits from preemption (gross of patenting and R&D costs) would be null, and the incumbent would have no incentive to introduce a substitute before potential rivals. The presence of a threat of entry is measured using the percentage of R&D projects that the R&D unit initiated to respond to specific R&D projects of competitors.

name: Market power
definition: A standard industrial organization result is that in asymmetric oligopolies characterized by firms competing on output and linear demand, the Lerner index of market power is a positive function of a firm's market share and the degree of collusion in the industry, as conjectured by the firm, and a negative function of the elasticity of demand. A firm's market share is computed as the fraction of total industry sales captured by the firm in its primary business segment.

name: Drastic innovation
authors_terms: ["drastic innovation", "drastic nature of innovation", "drastic technological innovation", "radical innovation"]
definition: An innovation is defined as drastic if it makes the incumbent's technology obsolete. A drastic technological innovation involves methods and materials that are completely novel to both the firm and the industry, as opposed to the outcome of activities that incrementally improve existing products and processes.

name: R&D intensity
definition: The R&D stock variable is computed as the cumulated stock of past deflated R&D expenditures using a 15 percent depreciation rate. This is divided by the book value of total assets, giving the ratio R&D/assets.

name: Workforce downsizing
authors_terms: ["workforce downsizing", "employee downsizing", "workforce downsizing", "workforce reductions", "employee reductions", "workforce reductions", "employee downsizing", "downsizing"]
definition: Employee downsizing has been defined as the planned reduction in jobs and personnel (Cascio 1993).

name: Firm performance
definition: Return on assets (ROA), measured as operating income (before depreciation, interest, and taxes) divided by total assets, is the most widely used firm performance variable in management research, including research that has examined the performance consequences of downsizing.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity is widely used as an indicator of industry differentiation (e.g., Hambrick and Finkelstein 1987).

name: Industry growth
definition: Industry Growth. Similar arguments can also be made in the context of market growth, an industry characteristic that features prominently in industrial organization and strategic management literature (Porter 1980). Demand growth has been associated with greater market opportunity and competitive variation (e.g., Datta and Rajagopalan 1998), providing managers and employees with more discretionary opportunities.

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: Another important industry characteristic is capital intensity, a measure of the relative investment in fixed assets in an industry.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Industry Dynamism. Finally, industry dynamism has also been postulated to have an important effect on the nature of competition, defining the extent to which a firm faces an environment that is predictable and stable or changing and uncertain.

name: Competitors' prior entry
authors_terms: ["competitors' prior entry", "prior entry by competitors", "prior entry by the firm's direct competitors"]
definition: Competitors' prior entry was measured as the number of a firm's competitors that had previously entered a particular market.

name: Direct encounters between competitors
authors_terms: ["direct encounters between a firm's competitors", "competitors' direct encounters", "direct encounters"]
definition: Direct encounters between a firm's competitors indicated how often a firm's direct competitors also previously encountered one another in at least one common market segment. The variable indicates the extent to which a firm's direct competitors also compete with each other.

name: Asymmetric multimarket competition
authors_terms: ["asymmetric multimarket competition", "asymmetric multimarket contact", "multimarket contact between a firm's competitors"]
definition: Following Gimeno (1999), we refer to this situation in which competitors have a small foothold in each other's key market as 'asymmetric multimarket competition,' in contrast to symmetric multimarket competition, according to which both players are largely dependent on the same segment. It is in the situation of asymmetric multimarket contact that mutual forbearance is likely.

name: Symmetric multimarket competition
authors_terms: ["symmetric multimarket competition", "symmetric multimarket contact", "symmetric contact between a firm's competitors"]
definition: Symmetric multimarket competition is the situation in which both competitors are largely dependent on the same segment. Mutual forbearance is unlikely to occur when two multimarket competitors depend heavily on the same segment.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entry", "imitative market entry", "mimetic entry", "likelihood of entering the same market"]
definition: A market entry event was defined as a firm starting to produce an ingredient in a therapeutic category that it had not served before. In Study 2 a market entry move was defined as the first direct investment made by a Taiwanese company in a particular geographic market.

name: Alliance capacity constraint
authors_terms: ["capacity constraint", "alliance capacity", "carrying capacity", "unique number of co-investors", "number of partners in the existing alliance portfolio"]
definition: First, the capacity of a firm to manage and sustain alliance relationships is finite. The larger the number of partners in its existing alliance portfolio, the harder it will be to add additional partners, due to increasing marginal costs of alliance management.

name: Potential inter-partner rivalry
authors_terms: ["inter-partner rivalry", "rivalry effect", "potential rivalry", "competitive rivalry between partners"]
definition: Second, if the desired partner type happens to be a part of the existing alliance portfolio, then competitive rivalry between partners may also impede access to the desired partner that possesses the desired capabilities. As a result of inter-partner rivalry, the new partner may be forced to guard against potential knowledge spillover to its competitor in the alliance portfolio as opposed to providing uninhibited commitment towards the success of the new business practice.

name: New business practice adoption
authors_terms: ["add-on deal adoption", "add-on deals", "adoption of a new business practice", "likelihood of adoption of a new business practice that requires new alliances"]
definition: Add-on deals thus represent a novel business practice (requiring a new set of capabilities and alliance partners) and we investigate whether its adoption is aided or impeded by the existing alliance portfolio of the focal PE firm. What matters is that the new business practice must require the firm to develop new capabilities and 'activity systems' ... to serve its existing product market.

name: New market segment entry
authors_terms: ["new sector", "new market segment", "sector exploration", "exploratory moves", "new business practice adopted in a new market segment"]
definition: Therefore, conditional on the adoption of a new business practice, one can expect the new business practice to focus on a market segment that is hitherto unrepresented in the firm's alliance portfolio. A new vertical, by definition, is devoid of past alliance portfolios (or more generally, past ties) that can potentially impose rivalry effects on partners who can facilitate the adoption of a new business practice.

name: Attractiveness of the new business practice
authors_terms: ["attractiveness of the new business practice", "environmental regime", "regime (post crisis)", "regime change around financial crisis"]
definition: Thus, when environmental changes make the new business practice more attractive (and the construction of new alliance portfolios more valuable), the effect of the capacity constraints on the addition of new partners should relax. The post-crisis regime reflects a period of skepticism on the part of banks to lend to PE firms for large LBOs, which accentuated the tendency of PE firms to participate in add-on deals.

name: Distant search
authors_terms: ["distant search", "search distantly", "search beyond these domains", "new subclasses"]
definition: Distant search can be considered 'long jumps' on the landscape. It requires the inventor to change her choices along more interdependent dimensions, going beyond her existing capabilities to adapt to solutions with scientific principles that are new to her.

name: Change in technological opportunities
authors_terms: ["Change in Technological Opportunities", "reduction of technological opportunities", "reduced technological opportunities", "decline in technological opportunities", "reduction in opportunities in her domain"]
definition: We examine the reduction of technological opportunities as a trigger of career concern driving the inventor to engage in distant search. Technological opportunities usually reduce in ways external to the individual inventor.

name: Relative productivity
authors_terms: ["Relative Productivity", "relatively more productive", "relative productivity within the firm"]
definition: The inventor's job at the firm is more secure when she is relatively more productive at generating inventions compared to other inventors in the firm. In this scenario, she has a greater 'buffer' of other inventors within the firm with lower productivity.

name: Stardom
definition: Stars are more likely to create path-breaking inventions boosting firm performance. They exert disproportionate influence over firms' research programs, and their areas of expertise determine firms' directions of commercialization efforts.

name: Firm-specific experience
definition: The inventor with greater firm-specific experience in creating new technologies, that is, inventive experience within the current firm, has a higher opportunity cost of switching to another firm. As she invents within the firm, she tends to build up firm-specific knowledge over time.

name: Knowledge interdependence with the firm
authors_terms: ["Interdependence", "interdependence between the inventor's and the firm's knowledge", "interdependence with the firm"]
definition: Knowledge that an inventor possesses can be more modular and generic, such that it is applicable on a 'standalone' basis across settings and firms. Or, it can be interdependent with other knowledge components within the firm's portfolio, such that its application requires joint utilization with them for it to be useful.

name: Consensus on differentiation strategy
authors_terms: ["strategic consensus", "consensus on differentiation strategy", "consensus on a differentiation strategy"]
definition: Strategic consensus is defined as the level of agreement among senior managers concerning the emphasis placed on a specific type of strategy; the characterization of strategic types includes both the ends (goals) and typical means for achieving those ends.

name: Consensus on low cost strategy
authors_terms: ["strategic consensus", "consensus on low cost strategy", "consensus on a cost leadership strategy"]
definition: Strategic consensus is defined as the level of agreement among senior managers concerning the emphasis placed on a specific type of strategy; the characterization of strategic types includes both the ends (goals) and typical means for achieving those ends.

name: Business unit performance
definition: We used a three-dimensional conceptualization of performance consisting of effectiveness, efficiency, and adaptiveness. Effectiveness involves the degree to which organizational goals are reached, efficiency considers the relationship between organizational outputs and the inputs required to reach those outputs, and adaptiveness reflects the ability of the organization to adapt to changes in its environment.

name: Market-related dynamism
definition: The construct of market-related dynamism is conceptualized as the frequency of major market-related changes. It is a key component of the multidimensional construct of environmental uncertainty and concerns the market from which the business unit derives its largest amount of sales.

name: Interorganizational cooperation
authors_terms: ["cooperation", "reciprocal cooperation", "level of cooperation between two organizations", "joint cooperation", "pattern of cooperation"]
definition: The dependent variable is the level of reciprocal cooperation between two organizations; a pattern of reciprocal cooperation is a situation in which the two parties both tend to repeatedly pick the cooperative choice on continuing exchanges. Cooperation is a multidimensional phenomenon that includes four domains: flexibility, information exchange, shared problem solving, and restraint in the use of power.

name: Relationship extendedness
authors_terms: ["extendedness", "extendedness of a relationship", "anticipated open-ended future interaction", "anticipated future interaction", "open-endedness of future interaction"]
definition: The extendedness of a relationship is the degree to which the parties anticipate that it will continue into the future with an indeterminate end point. The more strongly a party expects that a relationship will continue in the future and that its end point is indeterminate, the higher is the extendedness of that relationship.

name: Frequency of contact
authors_terms: ["frequency of contact", "frequency of interaction", "frequency of delivery"]
definition: The relevant interactions are those exchanges in which two firms can or must cooperate or defect; foremost of these is the exchange of actual goods, or the delivery of supplies. Frequency of contact is embodied in product deliveries.

name: Performance ambiguity
definition: Performance ambiguity occurs when it is hard for a player to evaluate the outcomes or products received from another party.

name: Repetitive exploitation
definition: Repetitive exploitation occurs when a firm repeats its existing designs for its existing products. It corresponds to March's description of exploitation as 'production,' 'efficiency,' 'implementation,' and 'execution'.

name: Incremental exploitation
authors_terms: ["incremental exploitation", "the creation of new designs for existing products"]
definition: Incremental exploitation happens when a firm creates new designs for its existing products. It corresponds to March's (1991: 71) description of exploitation as 'refinement,' 'choice,' and 'selection.'

name: Relative emphasis on incremental exploitation
authors_terms: ["proportion of incremental exploitation", "relative effort distribution", "emphasis of incremental exploitation over repetitive exploitation"]
definition: The impact of exploitation on exploration is a function of a firm's relative effort distribution between incremental and repetitive exploitation, i.e., the relative levels of effort and attention devoted to the two types of exploitation.

name: Exploration
definition: The development of new products aimed at entering new product-market domains; exploration involves learning around new product-market domains.

name: Exploration speed
authors_terms: ["exploration timing", "firms' responsiveness to environmental changes", "how quickly a firm is to explore a new market segment"]
definition: When firms explore environmental changes is a reflection on how proactive and responsive firms are in the transition from exploitation to exploration; the measure captures how quickly a firm is to explore a new market segment.

name: Community membership turnover
definition: Membership turnover is the extent to which the community comprised distinct firms in year t compared with the previous year. Moderate membership turnover reduces 'lock-in' effects by opening up and updating a community's knowledge base, without imposing the costs and risks associated with excessive turnover.

name: Firm movement across network communities
authors_terms: ["movement across network communities", "prior community affiliations", "mobility across communities"]
definition: The direct effect of membership updating arises when a firm moves across different network communities over time, thus gaining exposure to the heterogeneous knowledge and resources of those communities.

name: Within-community coreness
definition: The extent to which a firm occupies a core location in its network community. A core firm is strongly embedded by virtue of holding multiple ties to many firms, both central and less central, in the network community; a peripheral firm is weakly embedded because it holds fewer ties to other community members.

name: Global network reach
definition: Global network reach is defined as the average shortest distance (geodesic) between any two actors in a focal network, based on inverted network distance, or network reach. Greater global network reach indicates that firms in the network can generally reach one another through shorter network paths.

name: Invention productivity
definition: Invention refers to the 'development of a new idea or an act of creation' in a product or service space. We captured the invention productivity of firms using the counts of their successful patent applications.

name: Knowledge homogeneity within network communities
authors_terms: ["homogeneity of knowledge within network communities", "knowledge heterogeneity", "homogeneous knowledge stocks"]
definition: Increased connectivity among actors within a network community and the resultant information flows between them can homogenize the knowledge stocks and flows inside the community, while a substantial degree of knowledge heterogeneity can still be preserved across different communities.

name: Dedicated alliance function
authors_terms: ["dedicated alliance function", "dedicated strategic alliance function", "alliance function"]
definition: One important way that organizations can capture, integrate, and disseminate alliance-management know-how is through the creation of a separate, dedicated organizational unit charged with the responsibility to capture prior experience, which the authors refer to as a 'dedicated alliance function.' It is measured as a position to manage or coordinate all alliance-related activity in the firm.

name: Alliance experience
authors_terms: ["alliance experience", "cumulative alliance experience", "cumulative number of alliances"]
definition: Alliance experience, which has often been used as a proxy for a firm's alliance capability, was measured by taking a count of each firm's alliances over a 10-year period from 1988 to 1997.

name: Abnormal stock market returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock market gains", "abnormal stock market returns", "percentage abnormal stock gains", "abnormal returns"]
definition: The first measure of alliance success was determined on the basis of incremental value creation, measured in terms of abnormal stock market gains following alliance announcements. The excess returns reflect the daily, unanticipated movements in the stock price for each firm over the event period.

name: Long-term alliance success
authors_terms: ["long-term alliance success", "overall longterm success with alliances", "managerial assessments of long-term alliance performance"]
definition: Following prior studies, the authors used a survey instrument to collect managerial assessments on the performance of every alliance formed by each firm during the 1993-97 time period, using a number of survey items including the extent of harmony between alliance partners, the extent to which the parent firm meets its alliance objectives, the extent to which the alliance enhances the competitive position of the parent firm, and the extent to which the parent firm acquires critical skills or capabilities from its alliance partner.

name: Market share
definition: Our dependent variable is a firm's market share, calculated as its number of active mobile cellular connections over the total number of active mobile connections in a country.

name: Demand window
definition: DWs are understood as 'a new type of demand, a major shake-up in local demand or a business cycle', often resulting in an upsurge of consumer demand for a product category in an industry; they are pronounced changes in demand conditions.

name: Technological window
definition: TWs have been described as situations in which a new technology appears on the market, progressively rendering the previous dominant technology obsolete due to its lower technical performance; it is the introduction of a new technology in an industry that requires new knowledge for firms to be able to exploit its potential.

name: Depth of international experience with demand windows
authors_terms: ["depth of IE with DWs", "IE with DWs (depth)", "depth of international experience with demand windows"]
definition: Experience depth refers to the repeated exposure of a firm to a certain type of challenge over time, in our case the accumulated exposure to a specific type of window (i.e., either a DW or a TW). We define the concept of a firm's depth of IE with a specific type of window of opportunity as the combination of countries, including the home country, in which it has accumulated operational experience with that type of window until a given point in time.

name: Depth of international experience with technological windows
authors_terms: ["depth of IE with TWs", "IE with TWs (depth)", "depth of international experience with technological windows"]
definition: Experience depth refers to the repeated exposure of a firm to a certain type of challenge over time, in our case the accumulated exposure to a specific type of window (i.e., either a DW or a TW). We define the concept of a firm's depth of IE with a specific type of window of opportunity as the combination of countries, including the home country, in which it has accumulated operational experience with that type of window until a given point in time.

name: Breadth of international experience with demand windows
authors_terms: ["breadth of IE with DWs", "IE with DWs (breadth)", "breadth of international experience with demand windows"]
definition: Breadth of experience refers to the variety of experience and represents the diversity of knowledge that a firm has to tackle a certain type of challenge. A firm's breadth of IE with DWs therefore pertains to the degree of variety in its IE with the different classes of DWs.

name: Breadth of international experience with technological windows
authors_terms: ["breadth of IE with TWs", "IE with TWs (breadth)", "breadth of international experience with technological windows"]
definition: Breadth of experience refers to the variety of experience and represents the diversity of knowledge that a firm has to tackle a certain type of challenge. A firm's breadth of IE with TWs pertains to the variety of its experience with the various technological changes in an industry in multiple countries, which we conventionally call 'classes' of TWs.

name: Acquisition premium
definition: A premium is the percentage spread between the trading price of the target's stock before the announcement of the acquisition and the price per share paid by the acquiring firm.

name: Network partner premium diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of network partners' premiums", "partner premium heterogeneity", "variation in partner premiums"]
definition: When a firm has network partners who have made acquisition decisions of varied quality, this variance presents firms with unique information, increases the salience of the acquisition experiences, and encourages a more deliberate, thoughtful conversation among board members.

name: Network partner acquisition size diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of the size of network partners' acquisitions", "partner acquisition-size diversity", "partner acquisition size heterogeneity"]
definition: Firms should learn more about how to negotiate and put together a deal when their partners have experiences with deals of diverse sizes.

name: Network diversity
authors_terms: ["network diversity", "diversity of a focal firm's network", "unique network information"]
definition: Network diversity means firms have access to unique information about the premium experiences of their partners and their partners' partners.

name: Network partner industry diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of network partners' industries", "partner industry heterogeneity", "industry diversity"]
definition: Another type of diversity potentially present in a firm's relationships with its network partners is diversity in the world-views of these other firms. Both the literature on organizational demography and upper-echelons theory suggest that diverse organizational characteristics such as industry and size are associated with diverse organizational experiences.

name: Network partner size diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of network partners' sizes", "partner size heterogeneity"]
definition: Organizational size offers another measure of partners' experience and has been considered an important characteristic in other work on interorganizational networks. Large companies have different constraints in acquisitions than small companies, and the constraints and issues should be clearer if a focal organization has exposure to both types of firms.

name: Network multiplexity
definition: One way to look at this is through relationship multiplexity, or the tendency for two or more different relationships to occur together.

name: Partner diversity
definition: The diversity of a focal firm's network partners' characteristics and experiences, including their premiums, acquisition sizes, industries, and sizes.

name: R&D project stage
authors_terms: ["stage of project", "stage of the R&D process", "innovation stage", "commercialization stage"]
definition: R&D projects evolve over stages. The events prior to new product launches, such as project initiation, progress, and other events that imply a project has not yet reached a successful outcome, represent an innovation stage, and new product introduction marks the beginning of the commercialization stage of an R&D project.

name: Shareholder wealth effect
authors_terms: ["wealth effects", "wealth created", "shareholder wealth", "shareholder value creation", "market response"]
definition: The wealth created by an R&D project announcement, measured as the excess returns to the announcing firm's stock; stock prices move upward when the new or unanticipated information suggests positive incremental cash flows, and conversely they move downward when the information is negative.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: Industry R&D intensity is often taken as an indicator of the technological opportunity in an environment, that is, the degree to which a firm's market demands or accepts product innovations.

name: Relative firm R&D intensity
definition: Organizations within an industry often differ in technological capability, that is, they differ in their R&D activity and spending relative to other firms in the same industry. Relative firm R&D intensity measures the degree to which the firm overspends or underspends its competitors.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration, the degree to which product markets are dominated by a small number of firms, is often employed to operationally define appropriability, the degree to which firms are able to internalize the benefits of R&D efforts that yield new products.

name: Relative sales growth
authors_terms: ["relative firm growth rate", "relative sales growth", "sales growth"]
definition: A firm's sales growth scaled by its dominant industry growth rate, because investors judge the growth potential of a firm in the context of its industry; low-growth firms are those that grow more slowly than their industry averages.

name: Firm size
definition: Size is measured by firm sales. Scholars have argued that the innovative potential of an organization is related to its size, and that size is also related to the response of the capital markets to R&D announcements.

name: Founder assessment of venture prospects
authors_terms: ["founder's positive assessment of the venture", "positive assessment of the prospects of the venture", "founder's self-assessment of the prospects of the venture", "founders' assessments of the ventures"]
definition: Because obtaining external financing is costly, 'founders assess the potential of their new ventures to determine whether or not to seek external capital,' and they 'are more likely to select as candidates for financing those ventures that they perceive to have higher market growth, and less industry and price competition.'

name: Objective venture development
authors_terms: ["objective measures of the venture's performance", "objective information about the venture", "objective verifiable indicators of venture development"]
definition: Observable information about the venture that financiers use instead of founders' perceptions, because 'financiers do not select ventures on the basis of the founders' perceptions, but instead seek observable sources of information about the performance of the new ventures.'

name: Seeking external financing
authors_terms: ["sought external funds", "seek financing for external capital", "decision of founders to seek financing for external capital"]
definition: Stage 1 of the financing process, 'defined as the decision of founders to seek financing for external capital'; 'Stage 1 is defined as the decision of founders to seek financing for external capital.'

name: Receipt of external financing
authors_terms: ["received funds from an external source", "awarded capital from external sources", "receipt of capital from external sources for the first time"]
definition: Stage 2 of the financing process, 'the decision of investors to provide capital to those ventures that sought external financing'; the first financing event is 'the first time the venture is awarded capital from external sources, where external sources include any provider of capital who was not a member of the founding team.'

name: Environmental litigation exposure
authors_terms: ["environmental litigation", "likelihood of environmental litigation", "likelihood of becoming a lawsuit defendant", "environmental wrongdoing"]
definition: The paper investigates 'the determinants of the likelihood that a firm violates an environmental law and gets penalized for doing so.' The authors use a conditional measure of environmental performance, litigation exposure, that is the product of an assessment by the EPA.

name: Board size
definition: Board size is the sum of all corporate directors at the end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement.

name: Directors affiliated with industrial firms
authors_terms: ["fraction of directors in peer firms", "fraction of industrial firm executives serving on the board of directors", "directors serving in industrial firms"]
definition: The fraction of directors in peer firms is the sum of all corporate directors who are active executives in other industrial firms, a category that excludes consultants, lawyers, financiers, academics, politicians, members of the clergy and the military, and private investors. The authors argue that these directors are more likely to side with management in tolerating poor environmental performance.

name: Director reputation
authors_terms: ["directorships per director", "number of directorships held by corporate directors", "director reputation capital"]
definition: The extent of outside director service is both a signal of a director's knowledge and experience and a proxy for a director's reputation capital. Directorships per director is the average number of directorship posts held by a corporate director and proxies for director reputation.

name: Inside ownership
authors_terms: ["inside ownership", "fraction of equity ownership held by officers and directors as a group", "fraction of common stock owned by officers and directors"]
definition: The fraction of common stock owned by officers and directors has often been used as a proxy for the incentives of insiders to protect the firm's interests. Inside ownership is the fraction of common stock owned by officers and directors as a group.

name: Community environmental preferences
authors_terms: ["environmental preferences", "revealed environmental preferences of the community", "community's interest in environmental issues"]
definition: The authors obtained an estimate of the community's interest in environmental issues in each state by measuring the environmental preferences of its population, a measure of revealed preference defined as the number of paying members of major U.S. environmental and conservation organizations per 1000 state residents.

name: Congressional environmental voting record
authors_terms: ["voting record", "environmental voting record of the Congressional delegation", "voting record of each state's Congressional delegation on environmental issues"]
definition: The authors measure stakeholder pressure emanating from political/legislative actors by the voting record of each state's Congressional delegation (members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate) on environmental issues, where voting records capture the percentage of times that members of Congress voted for an environmental measure.

name: Regulatory stringency
authors_terms: ["regulatory stringency", "pressures exerted on a firm by a state's regulatory environment", "level of toxic emissions released in states where the firm operates"]
definition: Regulatory stringency is a proxy for the pressures exerted on a firm by a state's regulatory environment, based on a state's toxic emissions. The authors assume that greater amounts of toxic emissions in states where a firm operates are associated with a lower level of regulatory stringency facing that firm.

name: Diversification
definition: A firm diversifies by adding a new business line to a corporation that already includes at least one other distinct business line that serves a different customer base or solution in the market.

name: Organizational authenticity signals
authors_terms: ["organizational authenticity", "authenticity signals", "high organizational authenticity", "low organizational authenticity", "disinterestedness"]
definition: Authenticity is an identity characteristic indicating that a firm is what it claims to be, an organizational identity feature that communicates to its customers that it is committed to them. Signals of authenticity are inferred from displays of disinterestedness, that is, a willingness to forgo short-term rewards in order to fulfill commitments.

name: Perceived commitment to customers
authors_terms: ["perceived commitment", "perceptions of commitment", "commitment to customers", "commitment concerns"]
definition: A firm is viewed as committed to its customers when that firm is willing to act in a consistent way, even if such a line of action may be at odds with the firm's (at least short-term) material benefit. Perceptions of commitment are based on ascertaining a firm's intentions, which are often hidden behind mental states.

name: Likelihood of selection
authors_terms: ["likelihood of selection", "likelihood of referral", "selection as exchange partner", "selection rates"]
definition: The likelihood that an audience selects the firm as an exchange partner; in the experiments it is the therapists' or customers' likelihood of referring a patient to, or buying from, the focal firm.

name: Forecasting ability
authors_terms: ["forecasting ability", "forecasting competence", "interest rate forecasting ability", "forecasting skill"]
definition: The firm's ability to forecast the future; in this study, a money market fund's ability to forecast changes in short-term interest rates. Forecasting competence is measured through the relationship between a firm's investments and subsequent market trends that affect the value of those investments.

name: Economic surplus
definition: The surplus generated for the firm by a competence: in order to identify any activity, including forecasting, as a distinctive competence, the activity must be shown to contribute to an economic surplus for the firm. The total economic surplus generated by forecasting ability is measured as the effect of the forecasting ability measure on gross yield (yield before the expense ratio is deducted).

name: Net yield
authors_terms: ["net yield", "yield paid to the MMMF's investors"]
definition: The difference between the gross return on an MMMF's portfolio and its expense ratio, which is the yield that is paid to the MMMF's investors.

name: Fund size
definition: Each fund's size, or total net assets (TNA), measured for each month in millions of U.S. dollars and converted to a constant-dollar figure by dividing it by the consumer price index at the time of the observation.

name: Incentive alignment
authors_terms: ["incentive alignment", "managerial incentives", "alignment of an agent's and a principal's interests"]
definition: Alignment of an agent's and a principal's interests can be achieved through contracts that make the agent's compensation contingent on outcomes of his or her performance that are desired by the principal.

name: Monitoring
definition: Monitoring is defined as observation of an agent's effort or outcomes that is accomplished through supervision, accounting controls, and other devices. It is expected to prevent managers from making decisions that have a negative impact on principals, independent of incentive alignment.

name: Term in office
authors_terms: ["term in office", "term of office", "CEO tenure", "long-term agents", "short-term agents"]
definition: A manager's tenure with a firm; the essential difference between the long-term and short-term conditions was the assignment of responsibility for prior decisions, so that long-term CEOs had made the earlier poor research and development investment decisions and short-term CEOs had not.

name: Profit-maximizing investment
authors_terms: ["profit-maximizing strategy", "profit-maximizing investments", "investment in the newly created SBUs", "decisions more consistent with the welfare of the principal"]
definition: The level of investment in the newly created SBUs, whose profit growth was predicted to be the result of the research and development expenditure; this was the 'profit-maximizing strategy.'

name: Escalation of commitment
