definition: Decision makers become trapped in previous courses of action in order to justify their actions as correct, so they are likely to continue to misallocate resources. It was measured as the investment in the previously poor choices that were made in the earlier periods, the 'escalation-level' decision.

name: CEO power
definition: The extent to which the focal CEO dominates the new director appointment process, reflected in the CEO's tenure, number of board appointments, ownership and board chair status. The authors argue that a CEO with greater influence over new director appointments is more capable of appointing a favored new director.

name: New director's prior experience with other demographically similar CEOs
authors_terms: ["prior experience with other similar CEOs", "prior experience working as an outside director with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO", "prior interlock ties to other similar CEOs", "prior ties to other similar CEOs"]
definition: The extent to which a new director has previously worked as an outside director with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO. The authors argue that such prior experience leads the focal CEO to perceive a new director as socially more acceptable.

name: New director's demographic difference from the CEO
authors_terms: ["new director's demographic difference from the CEO", "new directors' demographic difference from the CEO", "demographic difference between a new director and the focal CEO"]
definition: The extent to which a new director differs from the focal CEO on salient demographic characteristics such as gender, ethnicity, age, highest degree earned, Ivy League background, functional background and industry of employment.

name: CEO compensation
definition: The total compensation received by the focal CEO, including salary, bonus, options, and grants made in a given year. The determination of CEO compensation is characterized as an ill-structured decision that involves complex attributions about firm performance.

name: Initial feedback
definition: Initial feedback is the feedback achieved early on in the search process during the first few trials.

name: Average feedback
authors_terms: ["average feedback", "average performance so far", "sustained high levels of performance"]
definition: Average Feedback is the average of all payoffs that an individual has received until that trial.

name: Immediate feedback
definition: Immediate Feedback is a binary variable and is coded as 1 if the prior trial improved the status quo and found a better performing alternative, and 0 if the prior trial failed to improve upon the status quo.

name: Satisficing
definition: Individuals satisfice - that is, individuals continue to search for solutions until their aspirations are met rather than continuing to search until they achieve some globally optimal solution.

name: Search distance
definition: We identify the best-performing alternative found by the subject in any of the prior trials and measure how many attributes are changed relative to it in the current trial.

name: Trial number
authors_terms: ["Trial number", "later rounds", "later in the search effort", "later stages of the search process"]
definition: Trial number controls for the number of used trials to account for the limited resources available for searching (i.e., trails remaining within an assignment).

name: Coupling of labor codes and labor practices
authors_terms: ["coupling", "tighter coupling", "coupling of labor codes of conduct and labor practices", "labor practice improvement"]
definition: Legitimacy structures are more tightly coupled when they are associated with changes in organizational practices that more closely align practices with institutional demands; in this context that means improvement in compliance with codes of labor conduct. Larger values of the improvement measure indicate greater improvement and thus an increase in coupling between labor practices and labor codes of conduct.

name: High-powered productivity incentives
authors_terms: ["high-powered productivity incentive structures", "high-powered incentives", "piece-rate payment", "piece-rate (or piecework) payment"]
definition: In response to the global value chain's intense efficiency demands, some suppliers adopt incentive structures, ranging from cash bonuses to gift prizes, to promote low-cost, high-volume production. Some rely on high-powered incentives like piece-rate (or piecework) payment, compensating workers for each unit produced.

name: Certified management systems
authors_terms: ["certified management systems", "certification to management system standards", "management system standards certification", "certification"]
definition: A management system is "the way in which an organization manages the inter-related parts of its business in order to achieve its objectives," and firms that implement a management system standard can seek certification from a third-party auditor attesting that they adhere.

name: Workers' unions
definition: Among worker participation practices, unions have been the most important formal channel for worker participation in management processes; unions can play an effective communication role that facilitates dialogue between managers and workers and enables workers to help improve production processes and rectify issues.

name: Similarity of economic conditions
definition: A three-item construct measures the degree of similarity in economic conditions between the MNC's home and host market environments.

name: Similarity of regulatory environments
authors_terms: ["regulatory environment", "similarity of regulatory environments", "laws and regulations"]
definition: A four-item construct describes the extent to which the laws and regulations between home and host markets are similar.

name: Technological intensity and velocity
definition: A three-item scale assesses the technological intensity and velocity of the industry in which the MNC operates.

name: Similarity of customs and traditions
definition: A three-item scale measures the extent of similarity in customs and traditions between home and overseas markets.

name: Similarity of customer characteristics
definition: A four-item construct describes the homogeneity of customers in home and host markets.

name: Similarity of marketing infrastructures
definition: A five-item scale assesses the degree of similarity in the MNC's home and host marketing infrastructures.

name: Similarity of product life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["stage of product life cycle", "PLC stage", "similarity of the firm's PLC stage"]
definition: A single-item construct measures the degree to which the focal product or product line is in the same life cycle stage in the MNC's home and host markets.

name: Similarity of competitive intensity
definition: A three-item construct taps the degree of similarity in competitive intensity in the MNC's home and host markets.

name: International marketing strategy standardization
authors_terms: ["international marketing strategy standardization/adaptation", "degree of marketing program standardization", "marketing strategy standardization"]
definition: International marketing strategy is viewed as a second-order construct incorporating product, pricing, distribution, and promotion decisions. The scale describes the degree to which the elements of marketing strategy are standardized in pursuing markets abroad.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: Performance is viewed as a multidimensional, higher-order construct comprising three dimensions: sales performance, financial performance, and customer performance.

name: Strategy fit
definition: The 'coalignment' or 'fit' between strategy (conceptualized as the degree of marketing program standardization) and its environmental context; the strategic fit paradigm asserts the necessity of maintaining a close and consistent linkage between the firm's strategy and the context within which it is implemented.

name: Stock market reaction of innocent firms
authors_terms: ["negative spillovers", "Innocent RM CAR", "cumulative abnormal return", "guilt by association"]
definition: The stock market valuation response of innocent (non-accused) firms surrounding the event day when a peer RM firm is accused of misconduct by an SEC enforcement action, which captures the spillover of the accusation event.

name: Corporate misconduct accusation
definition: The authors use the terms 'accused' and 'offending' as shorthand for a firm accused by regulators of misconduct on a given date, and 'innocent' as shorthand for a firm not accused by regulators of misconduct on that given date.

name: Chinese origin of innocent firms
authors_terms: ["Chinese innocent", "innocent Chinese RM firms", "innocent firm's country of origin"]
definition: The spread of guilt by association to innocent RM firms following a specific instance of RM misconduct would hit innocent Chinese RM firms harder than innocent non-Chinese RM firms, even when the accused RM firm is not Chinese.

name: Chinese origin of accused firms
definition: When the offending RM firm is Chinese, evaluators' causal reasoning would lead them to see the offense as attributable to the firm's 'Chineseness' more than its 'RM-ness,' weakening the typical inductive generalization by which other RM firms would suffer guilt by association.

name: Similarity between innocent and accused firms
definition: A higher degree of similarity between a base (the offending firm) and a target (the innocent firm) is expected to lead to greater generalization from the base to the target; innocent RM firms that share more properties with the accused RM firm would be judged even more harshly.

name: China-related media tenor
authors_terms: ["China-related media tenor", "negative media coverage of China and Chinese businesses", "anti-Chinese media coverage"]
definition: Media tenor captures the relative proportion of positive to negative media articles about China and Chinese businesses; the lower the value of media tenor, the greater the proportion of negative articles.

name: Organizational commitment
definition: Following Mowday et al. (1982), we define commitment as the belief in and acceptance of organizational goals and values, a willingness to exert effort on behalf of the organization, and a desire to maintain organizational membership.

name: Commitment to the IJV
authors_terms: ["commitment to the IJV", "the IJV management team's commitment to the IJV"]
definition: Following Mowday et al. (1982), we define commitment as the belief in and acceptance of organizational goals and values, a willingness to exert effort on behalf of the organization, and a desire to maintain organizational membership. The authors measure this commitment separately for the IJV, the foreign parent, and the local parent.

name: Commitment to the local parent
definition: Following Mowday et al. (1982), we define commitment as the belief in and acceptance of organizational goals and values, a willingness to exert effort on behalf of the organization, and a desire to maintain organizational membership. The authors measure this commitment separately for the IJV, the foreign parent, and the local parent.

name: Commitment to the foreign parent
definition: Following Mowday et al. (1982), we define commitment as the belief in and acceptance of organizational goals and values, a willingness to exert effort on behalf of the organization, and a desire to maintain organizational membership. The authors measure this commitment separately for the IJV, the foreign parent, and the local parent.

name: Target of commitment
definition: In this investigation, the target of commitment (the JV, the local parent, or the foreign parent) was a repeated measures factor in that we had three observations of commitment per team, one for each target.

name: Procedural justice
authors_terms: ["procedural justice", "procedural justice in IJV decision-making", "perceived fairness"]
definition: Procedural justice concerns the impact of procedure independent of outcomes; thus, measures of procedural justice focus on processes that do not involve direct control over decision outcomes. Procedural justice theory focuses on how decisionmaking procedures affect those who have a stake in, but limited control over, the outcome of the decision.

name: Decision control
authors_terms: ["decision control", "control over decision-making", "control over the strategy-making process"]
definition: Control is the process by which one entity influences the behavior and output of another entity. Respondents were asked to indicate the extent to which the parents or the IJV controlled the strategy-making process.

name: Debt
definition: Lenders safeguard their investment with market governance: the rigid rules of the debt contract. Debt subjects managers to high-powered incentives because failure to adhere to the contract can result in financial distress, bankruptcy, and even organizational demise.

name: Bank debt
definition: Banks tend to have more concentrated holdings, allowing them to renegotiate debt contracts more easily if the client firm encounters financial difficulties. The close monitoring, ability to exercise administrative discretion and to be forbearing in the face of performance shortfalls makes the governance of bank debt more akin to a hierarchy than a market.

name: Bond debt
definition: Bond holders rely on the rigid rules of the debt contract because they have no alternative. As bonds are generally diffusely held, individual bondholders lack the incentive to monitor the firm, and it is costlier for joint action by bondholders to renegotiate debt contracts.

name: R&D intensity
definition: If a firm pursues an R&D-intensive strategy, the investments it makes in entering a new market will likely be knowledge intensive, highly specific, entail considerably uncertain. Investments in R&D also tend to be characterized by distant and highly uncertain payoffs.

name: Firm value
definition: Our dependent variable, performance, was measured using the firm's market-to-book ratio. This measure, which closely corresponds to Tobin's Q, is appropriate because it incorporates both current performance and also expectations of future cash flows.

name: Diversification
definition: Both product and international diversification have the potential to generate economic rents from leveraging critical resources and capabilities across multiple markets. Diversification into multiple product and geographic markets has been the focus of much research in strategy and international business.

name: Change in diversification
authors_terms: ["changes in diversification", "increases in diversification", "decreases in diversification", "Delta1 diversification"]
definition: Once we had measures of product and international diversification, we then computed measures of change in diversification. The variable Delta1 diversification is the year-to-year change for each type of diversification, computed as difference between the focal year and the previous year.

name: Centralization of decision-making authority
definition: We studied centralization of decision-making authority, i.e., the nearness of decision making authority to the topmost level of the organization's hierarchy.

name: Organizational effectiveness
definition: Organizational effectiveness subconstructs are numerous; in the reviewed studies effectiveness was measured in nonratio terms (productivity), in ratio terms (efficiency), or as a combination of the two.

name: Effectiveness subconstruct
definition: Whether effectiveness is assessed as productivity, effectiveness measured in nonratio terms (e.g., output), or as efficiency, effectiveness measured in ratio terms (e.g., output divided by input).

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Environments that are turbulent, i.e., fast-changing and unpredictable.

name: Organizational size
definition: The size of the organizations studied, assessed in the analyses by the average number of employees in the organizations used in each sample.

name: Average size of the units of analysis
authors_terms: ["average size of the units of analysis", "average size of sample units", "average size of units of analysis"]
definition: The average number of employees in each sample's units of analysis; if the level of analysis was the organization, this equaled organizational size, and if it was the subunit, the average size of the organizations containing the subunits was used as organizational size.

name: Professionalization
definition: The extent to which a sample's units of analysis are staffed predominantly by professionals, people whose jobs require them to have years of specialized schooling.

name: Industrial sector
authors_terms: ["industrial sector", "manufacturing versus service", "percent of units in manufacturing"]
definition: Whether the organizations studied produce primarily goods or services, assessed by examining the percent of each sample's units of analysis that were manufacturing organizations (or that were within manufacturing organizations for subunit level studies).

name: Similarity of data sources
definition: Whether centralization and effectiveness data were collected from the same type of source: institutional sources include key-informant interviews and analyses of archival materials, survey sources include interviews and questionnaires administered to a large percentage of organizational members.

name: Relativity of effectiveness standard
authors_terms: ["relativity of effectiveness standard", "relative effectiveness", "absolute standards of effectiveness"]
definition: Whether effectiveness was assessed in absolute terms or relative to the effectiveness of other organizations in the same industry (including assessments standardized with respect to industry, or single-industry samples).

name: Award-winning status
authors_terms: ["winning a prestigious award", "getting an award", "prizewinning", "award-winning books", "status shock", "receipt of a prestigious literary prize"]
definition: The receipt of a prestigious book prize, which is a form of public recognition that judging panels bestow on the new books they view as the best in a given year and which constitutes a dramatic shock to the status of a book.

name: Audience fit with evaluators' tastes
authors_terms: ["fit with evaluators' tastes", "predicted rating", "how predisposed a reader is to viewing a book favorably", "audience shift", "predicted fit with audience members' tastes"]
definition: The fit between the underlying features of a candidate and the preferences of the evaluator. The authors argue that high-status actors who make it into the consideration set should on average have a lower level of fit with evaluators' tastes than their lower-status peers, and they measure how predisposed a reader is to viewing a book favorably.

name: Increase in popularity
authors_terms: ["popularity", "increase in popularity", "proportional increase in popularity", "rate of increase in popularity", "growth in audience size"]
definition: Popularity denotes the prevalence or number of prior adoptions of a product, apart from whether the item is liked. The authors focus on the increase in popularity, arguing that both the absolute level and the rate at which popularity is achieved may in themselves be considered unattractive.

name: Perceived quality
authors_terms: ["ratings of perceived quality", "book ratings", "quality ratings", "readers' ratings", "ratings of the book in terms of quality"]
definition: The assessment of a book's quality by readers; the authors view a reader's evaluation of a book in a review as corresponding to the second stage of the two-stage evaluation process.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["suppliers' environmental uncertainty", "cost fluctuation", "environmental uncertainty", "suppliers' cost fluctuation"]
definition: The buyer's optimal choice of the risk-sharing parameter is related to the supplier's environmental uncertainty, measured as cost fluctuation. Following Kawasaki and McMillan (1987) and Asanuma and Kikutani (1992), the authors use the variance of the suppliers' operating costs as the measure for the suppliers' cost fluctuation.

name: Risk aversion
definition: Suppliers are the agents and are assumed to be risk averse; risk aversion is denoted by the Arrow-Pratt measure of absolute risk aversion. The more risk averse the supplier is, the larger the risk premium it requires to take on risk.

name: Moral hazard
definition: The buyer's capability to drive cost down measures how difficult it is for the supplier to reduce costs and can be interpreted as a proxy for the supplier's moral hazard. The more capable the supplier is of reducing costs, the less willing the buyer is to absorb risk, since it fears the supplier's opportunism.

name: Risk absorption
definition: A risk-sharing parameter measures how cost overruns and underruns are allocated between buyer and supplier: if it is 0 the contract is fixed priced and cost-related risk is borne by the supplier, while if it is 1 the contract is cost-plus and cost-related risk is borne by the buyer. The parameter is close to 1 when the standard deviation of the supplier's profit is low relative to the standard deviation of the supplier's cost; in this case the buyer absorbs risk.

name: Organizational status change
authors_terms: ["organizational status changes", "change in organizational status", "changes of organizational status", "privatization"]
definition: The study covers organizations which underwent changes in their organizational status within government or which crossed the public-private boundary, including moves from control by a government department to trading fund or public corporation status and changes of ownership from public to private or vice versa.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance measured using a set of standard financial ratios; the specific ratios studied were intended to reflect the quality of management in terms of the efficient use of working capital, fixed assets and profitability.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability measured as the percentage return on capital employed (ROCE).

name: Fixed asset turnover
authors_terms: ["turnover to average net fixed assets employed per annum", "sales to fixed assets", "sales or output/net fixed assets"]
definition: Turnover to average net fixed assets employed per annum, one of the six financial ratios studied.

name: Stocks to turnover
authors_terms: ["stocks (including work in progress) to turnover", "stocks/sales", "stocks ratio"]
definition: Stocks, including work in progress, relative to turnover; the authors initially state that a decline in this ratio indicates an improvement in performance, but later note that the direction of change in the stocks ratio signalling improvement or deterioration is not clear.

name: Debtors to turnover
definition: Debtors relative to turnover; the authors state that a decline in this ratio indicates an improvement in performance, but later note that the direction of change in the debtors ratio signalling improvement or deterioration is not clear.

name: Labor's share in costs
authors_terms: ["labor's share in costs", "wages to expenditure ratio"]
definition: Labor's share in costs, measured as the wages to expenditure ratio; a fall in the ratio implies a 'labor shake out' and a movement towards market clearing.

name: Value added per employee
authors_terms: ["value added per employee", "change in value added"]
definition: Value added per employee, approximated as (P+I+W)/N in the absence of detailed information on the costs of purchases.

name: Organizational structure
authors_terms: ["organizational structure", "organic and mechanistic structures", "organizational design", "type of structure", "architecture"]
definition: Relying on static rules, specialized jobs, and hierarchical distribution of responsibilities, mechanistic structures foster blueprinted and decidedly efficient patterns of information processing among individuals. In contrast, the highly interactive mechanisms associated with organic structures enhance individuals' reliance on communication and interdependence.

name: Information gathering
definition: The gathering component of information processing reflects the amount of work-related information compiled by an individual.

name: Information interpretation
definition: Interpretation is the process through which an individual gives meaning to information, or makes sense of its importance. Interpretation reflects the significance and importance individuals assign to a given information element.

name: Information synthesis
definition: Synthesis refers to the ability to develop linkages and understand interconnections among different information. Synthesis reflects understanding of the interrelationships of different information elements (i.e., assessment of how different information relate to one another).

name: Problem solving orientation
authors_terms: ["problem solving orientation", "comfort with problem solving", "orientation toward problem solving"]
definition: We conceptualize problem solving orientation as a multifaceted concept reflecting: (1) sense of responsibility for organizational performance; (2) sense of confidence in his/her ability to solve problems; and (3) willingness to resolve problems.

name: Safety performance
authors_terms: ["safety performance", "motor carrier safety", "performance on disclosed metrics"]
definition: These metrics can be classified as measuring safety performance, as opposed to safety outcomes, because they capture individuals' safety behaviors that are aggregated to the organization level.

name: Time elapsed since IDP implementation
authors_terms: ["Occasion", "the passage of time since the start of the CSA program", "time elapses from the start of an IDP"]
definition: Our key measure of interest is the passage of time since the start of the CSA program, which we denote as Occasion. A one-unit increase in Occasion corresponds to a six-month passage of time.

name: Organizational size
definition: We measure our moderating variable Size as the natural logarithm of the total power units reported by a motor carrier from its most recent MCS, a biennial survey completed by all carriers operating in the United States.

name: Initial safety performance
authors_terms: ["initial performance", "poor initial performance", "safety performance at the start of an IDP"]
definition: The authors focus on organizations' initial performance at the start of an IDP, capturing it with the between-subjects random intercept of the growth model, where positive values indicate that a carrier had worse safety performance than average in December 2010.

name: Rate of improvement in safety performance
authors_terms: ["rate of change", "rate of improvement", "rates of change on disclosed metrics"]
definition: The rate at which an organization's performance on disclosed metrics changes over time; the authors model it as the change in a carrier's safety score for a one-unit (six-month) increase in Occasion immediately after the start of the CSA program.

name: Degree of tapering in rates of change
definition: We define tapering as the difference between an organization's rate of change on disclosed metrics at a point in time well after the start of an IDP vis-a-vis the same organization's rate of change on disclosed metrics immediately after rollout of an IDP. An organization that improves its performance initially but then sees its rate of improvement slow or reverse direction will exhibit positive tapering.

name: Goal difficulty
authors_terms: ["goal difficulty", "assigned goal difficulty", "difficult versus easy assigned team goals", "difficulty of the performance or outcome goals"]
definition: A key determinant of the motivation of both individuals and teams is the difficulty of the performance or outcome goals toward which they are striving. Teams in the difficult-goal condition were assigned a goal of 75 points for each session, and teams in the easy-goal condition were assigned a goal of 10 points per session.

name: Monetary incentives
definition: When the receipt of incentive pay is contingent upon goal attainment, rational decision makers will clearly prefer to minimize risk taking whenever possible, so that they can maximize their chances of getting the reward. Every team was offered a monetary incentive of $15 in one of the two experimental sessions, and receiving the incentive was contingent on the team's achieving its assigned goal for that session.

name: Team efficacy
definition: Teams possessing greater confidence in their ability to perform should be more willing than others to undertake risky strategies, because they believe they can implement them successfully. Prior to each session, team efficacy was measured by asking members of the team to discuss, come to agreement about, and indicate on a single questionnaire the team's level of confidence in its ability to achieve each of a series of scores.

name: Strategic risk
definition: We define risk in terms of its general (dictionary) meaning as the possibility of suffering harm or loss in pursuit of a desired outcome. From the planning maps completed by each team at the beginning of each session, we calculated the strategic risk variable.

name: Tactical implementation
definition: Successful goal implementation can also be influenced by the tactics used to attain the goals. Once a strategy is chosen, the best way to guarantee a payoff is to implement it effectively.

name: Team performance
definition: Performance was measured using a scoring system derived from analyses of pillbox attacks and tank losses in a previous study and from the analysis of the teams' performance in the pilot sessions for the present study. Teams received points for each pillbox destroyed and penalties for each tank lost, both scaled according to the difficulty level of the target.

name: Expertise
definition: Expertise is the skills and knowledge accumulated through prior investments in learning within a domain. Integrating insights from human capital and cognitive psychology, the authors treat expertise as reflected in a wide range of markers, each acquired in different ways.

name: General expertise
authors_terms: ["general expertise", "passive markers of expertise", "general or passive markers of expertise"]
definition: Elite education and tenure represent general expertise indicative of broad endowments of ability and prior training/experience. This marker of expertise is correlated with selection of individuals based on their underlying attributes and their development during medical school.

name: Deliberate practice expertise
authors_terms: ["deliberate practice", "specialized expertise", "deliberate practice markers of expertise"]
definition: Specialized expertise gained through deliberate practice, the process through which agents build expertise by repetitiously and deliberately performing prescribed tasks. In medicine these markers are specialty board certification and task-specific experience gained through repeated performance of specific procedures.

name: Organizational expertise
authors_terms: ["organizational expertise", "organizational prevalence of expertise", "high organizational expertise"]
definition: The effect of organizational prevalence of expertise, represented by the proportion of physicians within a hospital who possess a marker of expertise.

name: Organizational deliberate practice expertise
authors_terms: ["organizational deliberate practice expertise", "high organizational expertise (deliberate practice)"]
definition: The proportion of physicians within an organization who possess markers of deliberate practice expertise, obtained by aggregating only physicians possessing those markers.

name: Speed of adoption of new practices
authors_terms: ["adoption rates of new information", "speed of response to new information", "faster adoption", "change in stenting"]
definition: The speed with which individuals change their practices in response to new information; the authors propose that higher levels of expertise will result in a swifter response to new organizational guidelines, observed here as the change in stenting behavior after the release of the guideline.

name: Shared subunit membership
authors_terms: ["same unit", "same subunit", "same division and site", "own subunits"]
definition: The membership of submitter and evaluator in the same subunit of the firm, defined as the intersection of a product division and a geographic location. The authors expect that a shared identity between two individuals will lead the evaluator to have a biased assessment in favor of the idea.

name: Idea approval
definition: Our dependent variable is a dichotomous variable, approval, with a value of one indicating that the initial evaluator decided that the idea merited further consideration and a value of zero denoting that the evaluator rejected the idea.

name: Evaluator subunit tenure
authors_terms: ["evaluator tenure", "tenure within those subunits", "organizational and subunit tenure"]
definition: The strength with which an individual comes to identify with an employer or one particular subunit of the organization should increase over time, so one would expect in-group biases to grow stronger with organizational and subunit tenure.

name: Subunit size
authors_terms: ["subunit size", "size of their subunits", "submitter subunit size"]
definition: Holding constant the total number of contacts that any particular individual has, the probability that two individuals have a direct relationship decreases with group size; people also find larger groupings less salient.

name: Submitter subunit status
authors_terms: ["submitter subunit stature", "submitter subunit R&D status", "status of those subunits", "standing within the firm"]
definition: People treat status as a signal of quality, so one might expect evaluators to have more favorable beliefs about the probable quality of ideas and innovations emerging from parts of the organization with higher standing within the firm.

name: Process and product component mix
authors_terms: ["Process-Product Mix", "mix of process and product components", "having both process and product components"]
definition: The extent to which the firm's innovation portfolio contains an even mix of process and product components, rather than consisting of pure process or pure product components. It captures the presence of both types of components in the portfolio but does not indicate the level of integration between them.

name: Process-product integration
authors_terms: ["integration", "process-product integration", "higher levels of integration between process and product components"]
definition: Integration refers to how closely coordinated and jointly conducted the process innovation and product innovation processes are; highly integrated process and product components are developed with key parameters of both being developed together, creating dependencies and co-specialization between them.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: The firm's financial performance, captured by its profit margin, that is, the returns the firm obtains from its innovations.

name: Production capacity
definition: A scale-based appropriation mechanism in the form of the firm's downstream production capacity: extensive production capacity in place incentivizes large-volume production and signals to rivals the speed at which the firm could flood the market.

name: Access to markets
authors_terms: ["Access to Markets", "access to multiple geographic markets", "market presence"]
definition: A scale-based appropriation mechanism in the form of commercialization capabilities in multiple geographic markets, which allows the firm to sell its products at greater volume and spread out the fixed costs of innovation.

name: Innovative productivity
authors_terms: ["innovative productivity", "R&D expense per unit of innovation", "R&D Per Patent"]
definition: The firm's rate of generating innovations relative to the organizational inputs it expends; lower innovative productivity means a higher R&D expense per unit of innovation.

name: Political risk
authors_terms: ["political risk", "political risk in the project's host country", "political risk in the host country"]
definition: Political risk refers to the extent to which governments can interfere with a firm's or an alliance's operations by changing government policies, altering the terms of contractual agreements, or hindering in the enforcement of such agreements. Political risk in a country is a function of the type and strength of its institutions and is high where weak checks and balances afford politicians and regulators ad hoc discretion to interpret or change policies and regulations.

name: Lead firm country knowledge
authors_terms: ["country knowledge", "a firm's country knowledge", "lead firm's country knowledge"]
definition: Knowledge of a particular country's institutions is a firm-level resource accumulated through past experience. Knowledge of a country's key political stakeholders and their identity, preferences, and predisposition to act opportunistically allows a firm to develop a careful plan to protect its operations from political interference.

name: Lead firm political influence
definition: The ability of a firm to deter and mitigate political interference, which may come from its presence in the country and the threat to not invest in the country in the future. Political influence reflects the dependence of the host-country government on the firm's home country.

name: Alliance country knowledge
definition: The combination of partners' knowledge of a country's institutions and key stakeholders, which enhances the alliance's overall understanding of the country and how it works. One firm may have knowledge of the jurisdiction of a particular agency, another of the local government in a certain region, and yet another of the country's judicial processes.

name: Alliance political influence
definition: The political influence of the group of partners selected by the lead firm, which, together with their knowledge, is needed to protect the alliance's operations in the host country. A firm leading an alliance in a country with high political risk is likely to select a group of firms that, together, equip the alliance with knowledge of and influence in that country.

name: Lead firm selection
authors_terms: ["probability of a bank being selected as the lead firm", "becoming the lead firm", "selection of the lead firm"]
definition: The selection of the bank that leads the formation of the multipartner alliance and coordinates its activities, which involves analysis at the firm level and is driven by the suitability of candidate banks for the target project.

name: Syndicate selection
authors_terms: ["syndicate formation", "probability of a syndicate being selected to finance a project"]
definition: The lead firm's choice of one group of partners over other groups for a given project, made by comparing the combination of resources alternative groups of partners provide and their respective coordination costs.

name: Interorganizational diversity
definition: Following Harrison and Klein, diversity refers not just to the differences among members but also to the distribution of differences among the members of a unit. It is a unit-level, compositional construct that captures how syndicates differ in the distribution of the differences among their members across one or more dimensions.

name: Repeat client proportion
authors_terms: ["Repeat Client Proportion", "proportion of Repeat Clients", "Repeat Clients", "client retention", "customer retention"]
definition: Repeat Clients equals Transactions minus New Clients, so Repeat Client Proportion is the share of client visits accounted for by repeat clients. The authors treat the outcome of client-retaining activities, i.e. client retention, as what differentiates the performance of practices.

name: Revenue per transaction
definition: Total fees for services per quarter divided by transactions, so that the estimated relationship can be interpreted as an average revenue curve.

name: Expense per transaction
definition: Total expense for professional services per quarter divided by transactions, so that the estimated relationship can be interpreted as an average cost curve.

name: Practice profitability
definition: Practice performance, which the authors investigate as indicated by the Revenue/Expense ratio. It is the net effect of client retention on revenues and costs.

name: Preventive medicine approach
authors_terms: ["Lab Services/Transaction", "preventive medicine approach", "preventive care", "early disease detection", "preventive medicine"]
definition: Practices which engage in a high degree of testing associated with early detection are considered as engaged in a preventive medicine approach, measured as practices with a high level of outside lab expenditures and inside lab supplies per transaction. Lab expenditures are necessary to diagnose and anticipate the problems that might adversely affect the long-term well-being of pets.

name: Boarding services
definition: Ancillary activities such as behavior training, animal boarding, and dog grooming, which provide an opportunity for standardization but must be specialized to the idiosyncratic nature of the pet; boarding is an activity with complex search qualities that also has some experience qualities.

name: Practice scale
definition: The volume of business, or total transactions (client visits), which the authors argue is the dominant source of competitive advantage for delivering services with search qualities.

name: Competition from chain entrants
authors_terms: ["Far West region", "new forms of competition", "new types of entrants", "large pet franchisers", "multiple-practice chains"]
definition: Competition from large multiple-practice chains and pet supply superstores that are entering and consolidating the industry. The authors proxy it with the Far West region, because the franchisers had established a competitive presence there before other regions.

name: Alignment with the preferred functional demand
authors_terms: ["alignment with the preferred contextual functional demand", "function-environment fit", "fit between dominant functional demand and the preferences of the environment", "preferred configurational design"]
definition: In a suboptimal equifinality situation, one function (or consistent set of functions) will be emphasized over the other(s), and the context will be structured in such a way as to favor this function. The fit between dominant functional demand and the preferences of the environment can vary across organizations.

name: Deviation from the preferred configuration
authors_terms: ["deviation from the ideal", "deviation from the preferred configuration type", "misfit", "distance from the more ideal type"]
definition: The extent to which an individual organization's configuration deviates from the environmentally preferred configuration type across all independent variables; the greater the configuration's degree of deviation from the ideal, in terms of function and design, the more severe the misfit penalty.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is captured with return on sales (ROS), return on equity (ROE), return on assets (ROA), and average profitability (profit), each measured using net revenue of the organization prior to disbursement to providers as the denominator.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: 'Pricing' is one of the six Ketchen et al. (1993) strategy categories used to define organizational configurations in this study and is operationalized as advertising intensity.

name: Continuing medical education intensity
definition: 'Research and development' is one of the strategy categories used to define organizational configurations and is operationalized as continuing medical education intensity.

name: Procedural efficiency
definition: 'Production and operations capacity' is one of the strategy categories used to define organizational configurations and is operationalized as procedural efficiency.

name: Practice type
definition: 'Scope of activities' is one of the strategy categories used to define organizational configurations and is operationalized as practice type.

name: Fee-for-service ratio
definition: 'Distribution' is one of the strategy categories used to define organizational configurations and is operationalized as the fee-for-service ratio.

name: Nonmedical revenue ratio
definition: 'Production and operations capabilities' is one of the strategy categories used to define organizational configurations and is operationalized as the nonmedical revenue ratio.

name: Organization size
definition: Organization size is one of the three expansiveness variables; expansiveness is defined as the size and scale of the organization in terms of employees, buildings, types of organizations, and geographic locations. Typically, larger size is used to facilitate economies of scale and other efficiencies.

name: Physical size
definition: Physical size is one of the three expansiveness variables used to develop the organizational configurations, representing the level of tangible resources and physical capacity available to the focal organization.

name: Geographic dispersion
authors_terms: ["geographic dispersion", "number of clinics", "number of separately operating clinics"]
definition: Geographic dispersion is one of the three expansiveness variables used to develop the organizational configurations, capturing the number of separately operating clinics that are part of a single organization.

name: Management contracting
definition: Management contracting is one of the three alliance or relational structure components used to derive the organizational configurations; the relational component resides in relationships between the organization and other firms.

name: Horizontal interorganizational relationships
authors_terms: ["horizontal relationships", "horizontal relationships with other medical practices"]
definition: Horizontal relationships with other medical practices is one of the three alliance or relational structure components used to derive the organizational configurations.

name: Vertical interorganizational relationships
definition: Vertical relationships with hospitals is one of the three alliance or relational structure components used to derive the organizational configurations.

name: Top management team structure
authors_terms: ["team structure", "TMT structure", "top management team structure", "team characteristics"]
definition: Following prior research, we define 'team structure' to encompass multiple dimensions related to both the demographic composition and structure of a firm's top management team. Specifically, our measure considers the: tenure, age, diversity, size, and ownership of a firm's top management team.

name: Operating performance
definition: We use each firm's 3-year, post-IPO return on assets (ROA) to capture operating performance (ROAPost).

name: Founder CEO leadership
definition: We use the Management section of each firm's final registration statement to identify whether each firm has a founder CEO. In the model, Founder is an indicator variable that takes the value of one if the firm has a founder-CEO at the time of IPO.

name: Founder CEO control
authors_terms: ["control", "the extent of the founder CEO's control of the firm", "equity blockholder", "Non-Blockholder"]
definition: We exploit variation in the degree of control that the founder has in the firm by dividing the sample of founder-led firms into two mutually exclusive groups, based on whether the founder-CEO is included as one of the firm's equity blockholders when the firm goes public (i.e., retains at least 5% equity ownership in the firm).

name: Client firm status
definition: An organization's status is defined as 'a socially constructed, intersubjectively agreed-upon and accepted ordering or ranking of individuals, groups, organizations, or activities in a social system.' In the current business environment, an organization's status encapsulates its social position relative to peers on valued characteristics such as quality and financial performance as well as other dimensions that are widely seen as desirable.

name: Audit fees
definition: Our dependent variable is the natural log of the annual audit fees an organization pays its auditor.

name: Media attention
definition: We used the client's level of past media coverage to measure the attention the firm might be expected to receive in the future. This measure captured the potential for negative and positive attention.

name: Industry restatement history
authors_terms: ["number of restatements in industry", "history of restatements in the industry", "restatements in the client's industry"]
definition: We counted the number of adverse (i.e., income-reducing) restatements caused by a misapplication of the Generally accepted accounting principles in each two-digit primary Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code. Negative events (i.e., restatements) are more common in certain industries, raising the perceived risk of conducting an audit.

name: Stigmatized industry
definition: We identified stigmatized industries using a binary variable coded as one if the client firm belonged to any of the following primary two-digit SIC codes: alcohol (12), gambling (16), tobacco (20), firearms (21), military (26), or nuclear power (28). Some industries (e.g., gambling and firearms) are widely seen as unsavory.

name: Auditor bargaining power
definition: The ability to act on this desire depends on the bargaining power that the supplier enjoys relative to the buyer. For the supplier to charge the buyer a premium, they must also be the more powerful party in the exchange relationship.

name: Stakeholder prior beliefs
authors_terms: ["stakeholders' prior beliefs", "prior beliefs about the target organization", "beliefs about the mine", "prior belief"]
definition: Beliefs about the net benefits and costs associated with a specific mine; such beliefs are private until revealed through statements and actions and can be updated. "Whereas some stakeholders believe that the mine in question is a ''good mine'' that will provide high economic benefits without harming the environment, others believe that the same mine is a ''bad mine'' yielding low economic benefits and incurring high environmental costs."

name: Stakeholder reaction
authors_terms: ["stakeholders' reactions", "stakeholder reaction", "reaction after a critical event"]
definition: A stakeholder's reaction to a critical event, captured as the updating of beliefs: the change in a stakeholder's belief from the day before the critical event to the day of the reaction, i.e., the difference between the stakeholder's prior belief and the stakeholder's posterior belief.

name: Peer stakeholder reactions
authors_terms: ["prior reactions of peer stakeholders", "reactions of peer stakeholders", "reactions of other stakeholders"]
definition: The reactions of peer stakeholders--those in similar domains of activity--which reveal those stakeholders' private beliefs and which a focal stakeholder weighs more heavily than the reactions of stakeholders in other domains.

name: Aggregate stakeholder prior beliefs
authors_terms: ["aggregate stakeholder prior beliefs", "histories of negative stakeholder relations", "histories of positive stakeholder relations", "history of the target organization's relations with its stakeholders"]
definition: Investors infer stakeholders' prior beliefs about the target organization from stakeholders' past actions and from the history of the organization's relations with its stakeholders. "They are likely to be negative, on average, for firms with histories of negative stakeholder actions, such as protests, boycotts, and negative statements."

name: Aggregate stakeholder reactions
authors_terms: ["aggregate stakeholder reactions to critical event", "stakeholders' reactions following the critical event"]
definition: The aggregate of stakeholders' positive and negative reactions to the critical event, which provide additional new information that investors use to update their assessment of stock value.

name: Stakeholder media visibility
definition: A stakeholder-level measure of past media attention, which prior studies emphasize is a good indicator of the amount of information available about a target or an event and is also an indicator of a stakeholder's relevance in public discourse.

name: Stakeholder status
definition: A stakeholder's position in the stakeholder network constructed from the source-verb-target triplets, measured as Bonacich eigenvector centrality, reflecting their access to information and the likelihood that other stakeholders would pay attention to their reactions.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "daily abnormal stock returns", "abnormal market returns"]
definition: The difference between the predicted and the observed stock prices for a given firm on a given day, computed using an event study methodology in which normal returns are estimated with a market model.

name: Critical event
definition: Stakeholder-initiated actions targeting an organization with the intention of drawing public and organizational attention to activities and practices that the initiating stakeholder deems inappropriate, illegal, or illegitimate; in the data, events that signal large negative changes in a stakeholder's prior beliefs.

name: Network information accuracy
definition: The amount of overlap between the network structure as perceived by key organization members and the objective network structure.

name: Degree centrality
definition: Degree centrality is measured as the total number of confirmed knowledge exchange relations each organization has in the objective network.

name: Domain similarity
definition: The degree to which organizations have the same services, clients, and skills.

name: Outsourcing of upstream activities
authors_terms: ["outsourcing rate of upstream activities", "rate of patent filing outsourcing", "degree to which a firm outsources patent filing activities", "average share of outsourced patent applications"]
definition: The degree to which a firm has its upstream activities (patent filing) processed externally rather than in-house. In the setting, this is the firm-year rate of patent filing outsourcing, i.e., the share of a firm's patent applications that were filed by external patent professionals.

name: Downstream performance
authors_terms: ["downstream performance", "downstream (litigation) performance", "ability to detect competitors for proactive litigation", "rate of detected competitors"]
definition: We thus conceive of downstream performance as the firm's ability to identify competitor patents and litigate against third parties' IP rights, relative to the firm's effort invested into IP.

name: Upstream knowledge base similarity
authors_terms: ["upstream similarity", "knowledge base similarity", "similarity between internal and external upstream activities", "similarity between the knowledge bases underlying upstream activities performed internally and externally"]
definition: A crucial construct in Hypothesis 2 is knowledge base similarity between internally and externally sourced upstream activities. Our similarity index is a refined measure of the extent to which firms are making and buying the same things-which is the case if the similarity between internally and externally processed patents in terms of technology is high.

name: Human capital
definition: Human capital is defined as the knowledge, skills, and abilities residing with and utilized by individuals.

name: Organizational capital
definition: Organizational capital is the institutionalized knowledge and codified experience residing within and utilized through databases, patents, manuals, structures, systems, and processes.

name: Social capital
definition: Social capital is defined as the knowledge embedded within, available through, and utilized by interactions among individuals and their networks of interrelationships.

name: Incremental innovative capability
definition: Incremental innovative capability is defined as the capability to generate innovations that refine and reinforce existing products and services.

name: Radical innovative capability
definition: Radical innovative capability is the capability to generate innovations that significantly transform existing products and services.

name: Number of competitors
definition: The argument is that when a firm faces many competitors, its strategic position is vulnerable. Resources are squeezed, profits are stressed, and even survival is threatened.

name: Market stage
definition: Markets evolve through several configurations of attributes or stages. Initially, emergent-stage markets arise and are small, new, and characterized by a lack of product clarity; eventually markets mature and, in contrast to emergent and growth-stage markets, mature-stage markets are more stable as demand approaches saturation.

name: Innovative strategy
authors_terms: ["innovative strategy", "pioneering technical strategies", "technically innovative strategies", "degree of innovation", "innovation"]
definition: Technically innovative strategies demand a high level of competence in basic technology and so require substantial resources. Innovative technology rarely works initially, and often takes a long time, if ever, to become viable.

name: Top management team size
authors_terms: ["top management team size", "team size", "size of the top management team", "large top management teams"]
definition: Large top management teams are likely to have more extensive connections and relationships with potential partnering organizations than small ones. Since alliances are usually sought after, orchestrated and negotiated at the highest levels of the organization, there is a greater chance that one or more executives will have the time to devote to alliance formation when the team is large.

name: Previous industry employers of the top management team
authors_terms: ["number of previous industry employers of top management team members", "number of previous semiconductor employers", "previous employers"]
definition: Top management teams whose members have worked for many firms within an industry are more likely to have connections with firms that are potential alliance partners than teams whose members have worked for only a few firms within the industry.

name: Previous job level of the top management team
authors_terms: ["previous employment in high-level jobs", "previous jobs held by members of the top management team", "mean previous job title", "high-level previous jobs"]
definition: Top managers who have held high-level jobs at other firms are likely to know the people who are making alliancing deals. They will, thus, be more aware of alliance opportunities, better able to assess the risks associated with specific partners, and more likely to have already built up relationships with members of the prospective partners.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["strategic alliance formation", "rate of alliance formation", "product development alliances", "formation of strategic alliances"]
definition: This article focuses on product development alliances, which are both common and important in the semiconductor industry. They are defined as interorganizational arrangements in which the partnering firms combine engineering and other personnel for the joint design of new products that at least one partner will sell.

name: Strategic similarity
definition: This paper defines strategic similarity as a firm-level construct representing the extent to which a firm's strategic position resembles the strategic positions of other firms competing in its market at a particular point in time. Strategic similarity is a covering term representing firm differences, isomorphism, etc.

name: Firm performance
definition: This paper defines performance as the net flow of resources through a firm. Performance is a covering term representing competitive advantage, survival, social and economic fitness, etc.

name: Corporate responsibility performance
definition: CRP is conceptualized as the broad array of strategies and operating practices that a company develops in its efforts to deal with and create relationships with its numerous stakeholders and the natural environment.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: The firm's financial performance; the authors measure it with Tobin's q, mainly because of its ability to capture the value of long-term investments like intangible investments.

name: Innovation
definition: The firm's capability for generating new technology, products, and improved processes, which is costly for competitors to copy and can become a source of competitive advantage.

name: Human capital
definition: The accumulation of human capital through human resource practices: the measurement of job satisfaction, training programs, profit-sharing programs and employee participation, and the introduction of indicators to seek information about employees.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Corporate reputations are representations of public opinion about a firm, and such opinions depend on a firm's success in meeting the expectations of those stakeholders.

name: Organizational culture
definition: This intangible has four dimensions: involvement, consistency, adaptability, and mission.

name: Industry growth
definition: Growth sectors are defined as those two-digit SIC code sectors in which the growth in sales is larger than the yearly mean for all sectors in the corresponding country; industry growth is a proxy of munificence.

name: Knowledge tacitness
definition: Tacitness is a feature of knowledge that requires "the observance of a set of rules which are not known as such" to those following them. Tacit knowledge is that which is not amenable to well-articulated representation.

name: Foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["foreign direct investment", "foreign rather than domestic investment", "propensity to invest abroad", "expand abroad"]
definition: The establishment of a wholly or partly owned production facility by a firm in a foreign location (rather than a domestic location).

name: Transfer-based learning
definition: Experiential learning that accrues as firms repeatedly engage in an activity; in this setting the relevant experience is with prior technology transfers. Past transfers develop a "discipline of practice" that creates more efficient replication routines.

name: Time-based learning
definition: As a firm uses a technology over time (even absent repeated transfers), it may gain insight into how to deploy and transfer the technology; this is a matter of gaining an introspective understanding of the technology in a process akin to learning-before-doing.

name: Antitakeover amendment proposal
authors_terms: ["antitakeover amendments", "corporate charter antitakeover amendments", "supermajority amendments", "classified board amendments", "supermajority and classified board amendments"]
definition: Supermajority amendments and classified boards are nonoperating defensive measures that require stockholder approval and involve no direct effect on share price paid by potential acquirers; they are intended to restrict the transfer of managerial control.

name: Stockholder wealth
definition: The wealth of stockholders is the object of the empirical focus: the effect of the announcement of new information related to the proposal of antitakeover amendments on the wealth of stockholders.

name: Board control
authors_terms: ["board control", "greater board control", "independent board control", "board of director control of management"]
definition: Prevailing perspectives on board control of management suggest that boards exercise greater control to the extent that they openly criticize, and otherwise actively seek to directly influence the content of, the strategic initiatives proposed by a firm's CEO.

name: CEO social identification with the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["CEO social identification with the corporate elite", "identification with the corporate elite", "CEO elite identification", "socially identified with the corporate elite"]
definition: A person can be said to be strongly socially identified with a particular social group to the extent that being a member of that group is an important part of his/her self-definition.

name: Strategic help provided
authors_terms: ["strategic help provided", "strategic help-giving", "strategic help", "help on strategic matters"]
definition: The authors use 'strategic help' to refer to assistance that one CEO provides to another CEO that supports the recipient's ability to make strategy-level decisions for his/her firm; strategic help provided is the amount of such assistance a focal CEO gives to other-firm CEOs.

name: Strategic help obtained
authors_terms: ["strategic help obtained", "difficulty in obtaining strategic help", "strategic help solicited but not received"]
definition: Strategic help obtained refers to the strategic help a focal CEO succeeds in getting from other corporate leaders; the authors measure a focal CEO's difficulty in obtaining strategic help from other CEOs.

name: Friendship tie
definition: Prior executive leadership research indicates that the presence or absence of friendship ties is a highly contextually salient factor with important implications for how a focal CEO categorizes, and ultimately behaves toward, particular other-firm leaders.

name: Demographic dissimilarity
definition: Similarity or dissimilarity on demographic aspects such as functional background, educational background, and age, which prior research identifies as highly contextually salient factors with important implications for how a focal CEO categorizes, and ultimately behaves toward, particular other-firm leaders.

name: R&D expenditure volatility
authors_terms: ["compact, significant changes in R&D expenditure", "significant, compact changes in R&D spending", "significant, compact increases in R&D spending", "R&D expenditure volatility"]
definition: We suggest that a compact, significant change in firm-level R&D expenditure can be an indicator that a firm is adapting to an important (and infrequent) change in the value of its competitive advantage. We also posit that compact, significant changes in R&D spending are beneficial to the firm, regardless of the direction of the change.

name: Exploratory R&D
definition: Extant research defines exploitation activities as those in which the firm leverages its existing knowledge base, while exploration involves the search for new knowledge in domains that are relatively distant from the firm's core base of knowledge. Firms pursuing exploratory R&D will create knowledge in a wider range, so that their R&D displays broad technological scope.

name: Highly cited patent creation
authors_terms: ["highly cited patent", "creation of highly cited patents", "breakthrough innovation"]
definition: A highly cited patent is judged to be more 'valuable' than a patent that has received relatively few citations from other patents over time. The technology management literature has often characterized successful exploratory R&D processes as leading to breakthrough innovation, most widely operationalized as the creation of highly cited patents.

name: R&D-related outputs
authors_terms: ["firm R&D-related outputs", "R&D-related outcomes", "firm-level innovative performance", "patented knowledge", "new product releases"]
definition: We also examine the relation between this specific form of R&D expenditure volatility and multiple proxies of R&D success and firm performance, including the amount of patented knowledge, new product releases, and stock-market based firm performance. Based on the knowledge creation and innovation literature, we measure R&D-related output in four ways.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured using a well-known proxy for Tobin's q (Chung and Pruitt, 1994). Tobin's q is defined as the ratio of the market value of a firm to the replacement cost of its assets.

name: Earnings underperformance relative to industry peers
authors_terms: ["firm earnings underperformance relative to industry peers", "earnings underperformance relative to industry", "downside risk of earnings underperformance"]
definition: The notion of risk in the behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert and March, 1963) has been operationalized as a lower partial moment (LPM) of the firm's earnings underperformance relative to target (Miller and Leiblein, 1996; Miller and Reuer, 1996). We posit that the firm's earnings benchmark is the average return on assets of the industry within which the firm competes from the previous year.

name: Antimanagement shareholder resolutions
authors_terms: ["antimanagement shareholder resolutions", "antimanagement resolutions", "antimanagement resolutions sponsored by investor rights activists"]
definition: Governance-related resolutions brought by investor rights activists challenging the management of errant companies; typically they offered a rival slate of directors or asked shareholders to disapprove management proposals deemed inimical to shareholders' interests.

name: Analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["number of analysts following an organization", "scrutiny by financial analysts", "coverage by analysts", "monitoring by financial analysts"]
definition: Financial analysts are independent professionals who serve current and potential investors by scrutinizing the performance of corporate managers. As watchdogs, analysts conduct independent research on the competitive position of a company and issue forecasts of its earnings prospects.

name: Board interlocks with prior adopters
authors_terms: ["board interlocks with prior adopters", "direct ties with prior adopters", "cohesion"]
definition: Board interlocks connect a focal organization with other organizations and structurally embed it in an intercorporate network; interlocks with prior adopters are direct ties through which information and norms about what is desirable and appropriate are transmitted.

name: Adoption by industry peers
authors_terms: ["number of adopters in a focal firm's industry", "adoptions by peers sharing the same two-digit SIC code", "structural equivalence"]
definition: Mimetic influence transmitted between structurally equivalent organizations: firms that have similar roles and share similar relations with the environment, defined here as firms sharing the same two-digit SIC code. The larger the number of competitors that have adopted an investor relations department, the greater the likelihood that other firms in the industry will establish such a department.

name: Investor relations department
authors_terms: ["investor relations department", "investor relations office", "boundary-spanning structure", "boundary-spanning unit"]
definition: Such departments consist of an office led by a manager or director, or a vice-president, and occupy a central place in the organizational chart. From an institutional perspective they may be viewed as attempts to incorporate socially valued models of the relationship between a corporation and its investors.

name: Accommodation response
definition: Accommodation consists of admitting that the allegations are true, or initiating an action, usually by implementing some change in a firm's organization-wide policies, to assist its overseas factory workers.

name: Denial response
definition: In our context, denial is a dismissal of the allegation, most often in the form of a denial that a problem exists or has existed with the firm's labor practices and contractors.

name: Defiance response
definition: In our context, defiance is when a firm challenges the assertion that it needs to take additional action and forcefully questions its portrayal as an unsympathetic or 'bad' company.

name: Decoupling response
definition: We found firms using a decoupling strategy, in which the firm implements a corrective action in response to specific allegations by distancing itself from the source of the problem, such as suspending or terminating a contract with a specific factory.

name: Normative legitimacy with the public
authors_terms: ["normative legitimacy with the public", "legitimacy with the public", "normative legitimacy", "firm legitimacy with the public", "legitimacy in the public mind"]
definition: We concentrate on organizational legitimacy, and in particular an organization's normative legitimacy, which stresses moral obligations and conformance with societal values. Normative legitimacy is acceptance of an organization's values by an audience—in our case, the public.

name: Investor perceptions of the firm
authors_terms: ["investor perceptions of the firm", "investor perceptions", "perceptions of the firm within the investment community", "stock market reaction", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: The dependent variable for investor perceptions of the firm is the market valuation of the firm, operationalized as the cumulative abnormal daily stock returns (CAR) observed after an accusation.

name: Finance functional background of corporate elites
authors_terms: ["finance corporate elites", "functional background experiences in finance", "corporate elites' functional background experiences"]
definition: Corporate elites whose dominant functional background experience is in finance (or accounting and law). Individuals with dominant functional experiences in finance typically perceive firms as a collection of return-generating assets that need not be associated with a single line of business, and are therefore more likely to emphasize growth through diversification and acquisitions.

name: Finance functional background among executive directors
definition: Executive directors (executives who also serve on the board) with a dominant functional background experience in finance. Because their wealth, particularly human capital, is tied to the corporation, finance executive directors are expected to prefer greater corporate diversification and more acquisitions than finance non-executive directors.

name: Finance functional background among non-executive directors
authors_terms: ["finance non-executive directors", "finance non-executive elites", "finance nonexecutive directors"]
definition: Non-executive (outside) directors with a dominant functional background experience in finance. Compared with executives, they do not face the same employment risk nor receive the same perks of public attention and prestige, and are more likely to act in accordance with director-role expectations and protect shareholder interests.

name: Finance functional background of the CEO
definition: A chief executive officer with a dominant functional background experience in finance. Individuals occupying the CEO role are likely to gain the most from diversification, benefiting most directly from the social perquisites of growing scale and scope and having the lowest level of personal wealth diversification.

name: Finance functional background among non-CEO corporate elites
authors_terms: ["finance non-CEO corporate elites", "finance non-CEO directors", "finance non-CEO elites"]
definition: Finance corporate elites who are not the CEO, i.e., all other executive and non-executive directors with finance backgrounds.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification level", "high levels of diversification", "highly diversified", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification"]
definition: The degree to which a firm operates across multiple business segments, measured with the entropy measure of diversification, which takes into consideration both the number of segments each firm operates in as well as the importance of each segment. Highly diversified firms are those whose degree of related and unrelated diversification were one standard deviation above the mean level of diversification.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: The amount of acquisition activity undertaken by the firm, measured in total dollar amounts per year (sum of all acquisitions per year).

name: Business process specificity
definition: We define the extent of business process specificity as the degree to which critical business processes of one firm are specific to the requirements of the other firm in an interorganizational relationship. Specialized business processes include context-specific processes for new product introduction, customer service, inventory management, and quality control.

name: Domain knowledge specificity
definition: We define the extent of domain knowledge specificity as the degree to which critical areas of knowledge of a supplier firm are specific to the requirements of a buyer. Domain knowledge specificity refers to an organization's ability to access and deploy a specific body of prior knowledge in an interorganizational relationship.

name: Physical-asset specificity
definition: In vertical relationships, suppliers often make relationship-specific investments in the form of tangible assets such as plant and machinery and in location choices that are advantageous in working with a specific buyer. An example given is a garment supplier that invested in a tunnel-shaped ironing machine specifically for a retailer that ordered garments to be shipped hung in wardrobe boxes.

name: Site specificity
definition: The location of manufacturing plants and warehouses also reflects the relationship-specific investments made by suppliers in vertical relationships. Suppliers can choose to locate their manufacturing plants in places that are particularly advantageous for supplying a particular focal firm or locate them so that they are equally useful for supplying multiple retailers; in the former case, site specificity is high.

name: Quasi integration
definition: We define the level of quasi integration as the degree of linkage between a supplier and a dominant buyer. The structural dimension, quasi integration, reflects the extent to which the activities of a supplier firm are linked to a retailer.

name: Joint decision making
definition: We define the level of joint decision making as the degree to which a supplier firm and its dominant buyer jointly make decisions about key issues in the relationship. The process dimension, joint decision making, reflects the supplier's level of participation in decision making in its relationship with the retailer.

name: Founder gender
definition: The gender of the venture's founder(s). The authors contrast female-founded ventures with male-founded ventures and code the variable one for female founders and zero for male founders.

name: Employee labor
authors_terms: ["Employee Labor", "employee labor imbalance", "hours worked", "labor supply", "extra labor"]
definition: The volume of labor employees supply to the venture for a given pay. The authors argue that, relative to male-founded startups, ventures founded by women will elicit a lower amount of employee labor for equal pay, leading to an employee labor imbalance.

name: Perceived unfairness of the request
authors_terms: ["Request is Unfair", "perceived unfairness", "fairness of the request"]
