definition: The perception that a founder's request for additional labor lacks sufficient justification. By violating widely held beliefs that working for a female-led company is less demanding, female founders' requests for additional work may be perceived as unfair and unjustified.

name: Perceived work difficulty relative to expectations
authors_terms: ["Work is Harder than Expected", "perceived work difficulty", "harder than anticipated"]
definition: The perception that the work demands exceed what the employee anticipated. An increase in labor demand from a female founder will violate employees' expectations of workload and trigger the perception that working for a female-led startup is more difficult or more demanding than anticipated.

name: Discontinuous jump
authors_terms: ["discontinuous jump", "temporal separation", "discontinuous jumps between exclusive periods of exploration and exploitation"]
definition: This conceptualization of a temporal transition describes it as discontinuous jumps between exclusive periods of exploration and exploitation. A discontinuous jump is conceptualized as a discrete switch between exclusive periods of exploration and exploitation.

name: Incremental transition
authors_terms: ["incremental transition", "gradual and progressive changes between exploration and exploitation"]
definition: According to this perspective, a temporal transition is a series of incremental transitions with varying combinations of exploration and exploitation, where firms remain effectively ambidextrous over time.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable in this study is Tobin's Q. A market-based value such as Tobin's Q is considered particularly useful in ambidexterity research since the market-based value reflects both short-term performance and long-term performance prospects.

name: Firm resources
definition: The scale-free property of resources indicates that the value of resources is assumed to not be reduced as a result of the sheer magnitude of firm operations over which they are applied; in contrast, non-scale-free resources are subject to opportunity costs and are limited in usable quantity. Firm resources are measured by considering both technological and financial resources.

name: Proximity to knowledge
authors_terms: ["proximity to knowledge", "proximity to the world's knowledge", "proximity of a country to the rest of the world's knowledge", "proximity to the distribution of knowledge worldwide"]
definition: The proximity of a country to the worldwide distribution of knowledge, measured by the aggregate distance of the focal country from that spatial distribution. It is framed as a function of both geographic distance and the worldwide spatial distribution of knowledge.

name: Proximity to markets
authors_terms: ["proximity to markets", "proximity to the world's markets", "proximity of a country to the rest of the world's markets"]
definition: The proximity of a country to the worldwide distribution of markets, measured by the aggregate distance of the focal country from that spatial distribution; markets are operationalized by PPP per capita GDP.

name: Proximity to resources
authors_terms: ["proximity to resources", "proximity to the world's resources", "proximity of a country to the rest of the world's resources"]
definition: The proximity of a country to the worldwide distribution of resources, measured by the aggregate distance of the focal country from that spatial distribution. A country's resources are defined as all tangible immobile production resources residing in a country, including the labor force, natural resources, and raw materials.

name: MNE location choice
authors_terms: ["MNE location choice", "the likelihood of a country being chosen as an MNE's investment location", "choice of a country as an MNE location"]
definition: The selection of a country as the location for an investment by a multinational enterprise. Firms are assumed to select locations with the greatest expected profitability, and the dependent variable equals one if a country was chosen for investment by a firm and zero for the countries not chosen.

name: Own knowledge endowment
authors_terms: ["own knowledge", "a country's own endowments of knowledge", "R&D investment in the focal country"]
definition: The knowledge resources residing in the focal country itself, measured for the focal country by the $ value of R&D investment in that country.

name: Own market endowment
authors_terms: ["own markets", "a country's own endowments of markets", "PPP per capita GDP of the focal country"]
definition: The market resources residing in the focal country itself, operationalized for the focal country by PPP per capita GDP.

name: Own resource endowment
authors_terms: ["own resources", "a country's own endowments of resources", "size of the labor force of the focal country"]
definition: The tangible immobile production resources residing in the focal country itself, including the labor force, natural resources, and raw materials; in the analysis measured by the potential size of the focal country's labor force.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the investing MNE, measured by the number of employees.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["sales per employee", "a broad measure of firms' performance"]
definition: A broad measure of the performance of the investing MNE, measured by sales per employee.

name: Dyadic collaborative density
authors_terms: ["relative collaborative structure", "relative collaborative density", "dyadic combination of collaborative density", "relative collaborative environments"]
definition: Collaborative density, reflected in the collaborative structure in an organization, is defined as the number of realized relationships in a group relative to the number of possible relationships. The dyadic approach compares this relative collaborative density of the hiring firm and of the losing firm for each mobility event.

name: Knowledge spill-in to the hiring firm
authors_terms: ["spill-ins", "knowledge spill-ins", "knowledge flow from the losing firm to the hiring firm"]
definition: Knowledge flows to the new (hiring) employer of the knowledge of a prior (losing) employer following an employee's move: new hires open up opportunities for knowledge spillovers from a prior employer to a new employer. In the study, any citation of one firm's patented knowledge by the other firm following a move, after accounting for past knowledge exchanges, likely reflects such flows.

name: Knowledge spill-back to the losing firm
authors_terms: ["spill-backs", "knowledge spill-backs", "knowledge flow from the hiring firm to the losing firm"]
definition: Knowledge flows back to the prior (losing) employer of the knowledge of the new (hiring) employer following an employee's move, that is, spillovers from a new employer to a prior employer. By maintaining old ties, new hires may provide their prior employers with access to the new employers' knowledge.

name: Broad knowledge spill-in
authors_terms: ["Types II and III knowledge", "broader knowledge", "firm-wide knowledge", "knowledge that the mobile employee is not directly involved in developing"]
definition: Spill-ins of the losing firm's knowledge that the mobile employee was not directly involved in developing, that is, knowledge developed by the collaborators of the mobile employee (Type II) and knowledge developed by other firm members (Type III), rather than the mobile employee's own knowledge.

name: Broad knowledge spill-back
authors_terms: ["Types II and III knowledge", "broader knowledge", "firm-wide knowledge", "knowledge that the mobile employee was not directly involved in developing"]
definition: Spill-backs of the hiring firm's broader, firm-wide knowledge that the mobile employee was not directly involved in developing (knowledge developed by others in the new firm) to the losing firm, as opposed to the mobile employee's own knowledge.

name: Technological process change
definition: In this paper we treat technical complexity and systemic shift as distinct aspects of technological process change.

name: Technical complexity
definition: Following this argument, we use the term "technical complexity" to refer to the relative novelty or sophistication of new equipment and its technical features.

name: Systemic shift
definition: This kind of process change, which we label systemic shift, can result from the introduction of conversion processes based on unfamiliar technical principles, such as thermal forming instead of mechanical shaping of metal parts, or on unfamiliar relationships among process operations, such as the integration of discrete manufacturing steps into a continuous production flow (Tushman and Anderson 1986).

name: Project size
authors_terms: ["project size", "size of the introduction project", "initial capital investment", "number of machines"]
definition: It is also possible that the magnitude of the introduction task, in terms of the initial capital investment (Eisner and Strotz 1963; Zaltman et al. 1973) or the number of machines involved (Bright 1958; Myers and Marquis 1969), affects the difficulty of introducing new technology by placing increased demands on a relatively fixed level of factory resources.

name: Preparatory search
definition: During the preparatory phase preceding introduction, users have the opportunity to examine, modify, and even "reinvent" both the new technology and relevant aspects of the receiving organization (Rice and Rogers 1980; Van de Ven 1986).

name: Joint search
definition: Interorganizational interaction or "joint search" has been shown to be a critical input in technical research projects (Allen and Cohen 1969; Allen 1977) and new product development (Imai, Nonaka and Takeuchi 1985). It can also be an important mechanism for problem solving at the plant level.

name: Functional overlap
definition: Another approach for increasing the manufacturing unit's real-time adaptability is to link relevant functions within the organization to create overlapping subsystems or multifunctional teams for dealing with the introduction (Landau 1969; Gerwin 1981a).

name: Introduction success
definition: This study takes into account both aspects of project success by examining the amount of disruption following introduction as well as intermediate-term benefits associated with the new technology.

name: Introduction disruption
definition: Disruption is expressed as the length of time required to complete the introduction; i.e. to solve the major problems associated with using the new technology.

name: Operating improvement
definition: The level of operating benefits derived by the user is also an indicator of the organization's ability to identify and respond to problems in introducing technology (Rice and Rogers 1980; Voss 1988).

name: Domain identity focus
authors_terms: ["focused domain identity", "focus of the domain identity", "identity focus of the U.S. television domain", "identity framing"]
definition: When audiences share similar perceptions about the characteristics of the new domain, they will develop a code that forms the basis of the identity of this domain. New domains with a focused and stronger identity are more likely to make sense of complicated social phenomena and to reduce the ambiguity that characterizes an emergent organizational form.

name: Density of identity-matching candidates
authors_terms: ["density of organizations whose identity matches the identity of the new domain", "density of de alio radio stations", "density of stations coming from radio broadcasting", "candidate matching"]
definition: The social validation of a new organizational form depends on the match between identity of the domain and density of candidate organizations bearing specific identities. Legitimate candidates are candidates whose identity matches the perceived identity of a domain.

name: Density of non-matching candidates
authors_terms: ["density of organizations whose identity does not match the identity of the new domain", "density of de novo stations", "de novo density"]
definition: Marked candidates (i.e., candidates whose identity does not match the perceived identity of a domain), by creating confusion in the perception of audiences, threaten the identity of a domain and its appeal.

name: Organizational entry
definition: Form emergence is modeled as a stochastic process that generates event counts of organizational entries; the aggregate number of entries of commercial television stations (Entry) in each semester from 1940 to 1960 is the dependent variable used in the study.

name: Customer demand
definition: The DDI model contends that innovation and technological change respond to customer demand. Customer demand is a function of customer preferences: as customers' tastes, income levels, and budget constraints change, so do their preferences, shifting the demand curve and promoting technological change and innovation.

name: Investment in incremental innovation
authors_terms: ["incremental innovation", "fulfillment", "the decision to invest in innovation", "customer request fulfillment"]
definition: Incremental innovation is defined as an innovation that preserves the market for the existing product; in this setting a customer request is fulfilled when the firm invests in the requested feature change.

name: Product complexity
definition: Complexity is presented as a function of the number of information cues a firm must process, the strength of interdependencies among those information cues, and the changes in the relationships among these information cues over time. Product complexity is measured at the time the request was received.

name: Change complexity
authors_terms: ["change complexity", "the complexity of change", "nature of change"]
definition: The complexity of change also has an impact on innovation investment: innovations that are complex - ones that span multiple elements of the product - create a unique set of behavioral challenges.

name: Standardization of innovation
definition: A fulfilled request was either standardized into the next release or customized for the customer making the request. While customization only generates returns from the customer who requested the feature, standardization diffuses the innovation across the customer base.

name: Core organizational change
authors_terms: ["core change", "core organizational change", "format change", "market position change", "change"]
definition: The organizational core consists of the organization's goals, forms of authority, technology, or marketing strategy. Market position changes are core changes because they change the organization's relationship with its customers and cause changes throughout the organization.

name: Market share
definition: The dependent variable is the market share of each station, the 12+ Metro audience share. It shows the average proportion of all listeners over 12 tuned in to the focal station during the broadcast week.

name: Multimarket corporation ownership
authors_terms: ["multimarket corporation", "branches of large organizations", "branch stations", "unitary organizations"]
definition: An indicator of whether the station was owned by a multimarket corporation, defined as an entity owning three or more stations; such branch units of large organizations are interdependent with other branches and less responsive to their local environment.

name: Prior performance
definition: The station's performance before the change, entered as the lagged share. The lagged share is expressed as a deviate from the mean share in the market, so the coefficient estimate shows the effect of having pre-change performance different from the market mean.

name: Environmental shareholder activism
definition: Investors can exert pressure through shareholder activism demanding managerial actions such as the reassessment of organizational practices and the disclosure of information. We measure environmental shareholder activism as the number of environment-related shareholder proposals a company faces in a given year.

name: Disclosure of climate change risks
authors_terms: ["disclosure of climate change risks", "voluntary disclosure of climate change risk information", "climate risk information"]
definition: Companies are asked to disclose information on three types of climate change risks: (a) regulatory risks, (b) physical risks, and (c) other risks. Our main dependent variable, disclosure of climate change risks, counts how many of these three climate change risks the company discloses (i.e., it ranges from 0 to 3).

name: Institutional investor sponsorship
definition: We also distinguish between environmental shareholder activism exerted by institutional investors - investors who tend to hold large stakes and actively monitor the companies they invest in - and by noninstitutional investors, who are often smaller, individual investors.

name: Institutional investor time horizon
authors_terms: ["institutional investors' time horizons", "long-term institutional investors", "short-term institutional investors", "churn rate"]
definition: 'Transient' investors tend to hold companies' stocks on a short-term basis (e.g., driven by speculation motives), while long-term investors hold stocks for a longer period of time, taking a vested interest in the companies' long-term success.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market response", "stock market valuation", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: Abnormal returns capture stock returns in excess of the 'normal' returns that are predicted by an asset pricing model. The CARs are then obtained by summing up the daily abnormal returns across all days during the relevant time interval.

name: Internal research
authors_terms: ["internal research", "in-house research", "investments in internal research", "in-house research investments"]
definition: Research in a radical technology performed by the incumbent's own research unit; because archival data on firms' internal research expenditures for specific technology regimes are not available, the authors proxy it with firms' patent grants and scientific publications in the regime.

name: Contract research
definition: Contract research involves an incumbent firm outsourcing a given R&D project and/or licensing a specific intellectual property (IP) with the goal of adding new knowledge to the firm.

name: Research alliances
definition: Incumbents frequently engage in bilateral research alliances, where they partner with new entrants or universities to jointly pursue research in radical technologies; partners jointly pool their resources to discover new technological solutions.

name: Technology acquisitions
definition: Acquisitions of start-ups are another important way incumbents invest in radical technologies; through acquisitions, firms can internalize and build on new knowledge developed by technology start-ups.

name: Initiation of drug development
authors_terms: ["development", "initiation of drug development", "initiation of preclinical trials", "product development"]
definition: The decision to initiate product development following research investments, observed as the initiation of preclinical trials, which the authors describe as the gatekeeper between research and commercialization.

name: Technological regime disruptiveness
authors_terms: ["disruptive technological regime", "sustaining technological regime", "radical technological regime"]
definition: The extent to which a radical technological regime does not conform to the incumbents' existing business model in terms of how they generate revenues and appropriate profits; gene therapy represents a disruptive regime and monoclonal antibodies a sustaining one.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use return on assets (ROA) as our dependent variable in line with the existing literature, calculated as income before extraordinary items divided by total assets.

name: Uncertainty
definition: We define uncertainty based on the difficulty in predicting the focal firm's outcomes. More precisely, we focus on variability of firm performance, because greater variability reflects lower predictability and therefore higher uncertainty.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["network centrality", "degree centrality", "centrality in interlocking directorate networks"]
definition: Network centrality refers to a central position within network relationships. We calculate degree centrality as the number of interlock ties a firm has with the other firms; it effectively measures the connectedness of an actor in a network and is related to 'information volume'.

name: Structural holes
definition: Structural holes refer to the lack of ties between different parts of a network, reflecting the degree of redundancy in social networks. An ego-network rich in structural holes provides two benefits: information and control.

name: Private target ownership
authors_terms: ["private ownership", "private target", "target ownership", "private vs. public targets"]
definition: Whether the acquired target is privately held or publicly listed. Acquirers are typically less aware of the existence of private targets because those targets are less visible and transparent to the investment community than public targets, and are therefore more difficult to locate as exchange partners and to value.

name: Acquirer abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["acquirer abnormal returns", "acquirer returns", "cumulative average abnormal return (CAAR)"]
definition: We estimate acquirer abnormal returns using an event study methodology. The cumulative average abnormal return (CAAR) has been calculated following the standard approach described by McWilliams and Siegel (1997: 628-629).

name: Acquisition diversification
authors_terms: ["Diversifying acquisition", "acquisition outside their core business", "diversification purposes"]
definition: An acquisition made outside the acquirer's core business. Compared to outsiders, industry insiders can more easily identify private targets because of higher business proximity, and an acquirer that buys a firm outside its core business runs a greater risk of overvaluing the target's assets.

name: Acquisition experience in the target industry
authors_terms: ["Acquirer M&A experience in target industry", "acquisition experience", "acquirer acquisition experience"]
definition: Acquisition experience provides opportunities for the acquirer to improve its skills in screening potential targets with refined selection criteria, and to price more accurately new targets based on prior experience. Acquirers lacking acquisition experience in the targeted industry are likely to have a narrower search and run a higher risk of adverse selection when dealing with private firms than with public firms.

name: Target international scope
authors_terms: ["Target international scope", "target's geographic scope", "geographic scope of the target"]
definition: The geographic scope of the target's activities. Information asymmetry, search costs, and valuation difficulties are likely to increase if targets have geographically dispersed activities, since firms have a lower ability to evaluate distant assets, particularly if they span multiple national settings.

name: Target intangible assets
definition: Intangible assets are information-based assets that include employees' know-how, company reputation, intellectual property rights, trademarks, etc. The knowledge held by the seller on the assets' quality is more difficult to communicate and to verify, which increases the likelihood of ex ante misrepresentation.

name: Target age
definition: The level of evaluative uncertainty is also associated with the target's age. There is a clear association between firm age and the extent and quality of information available on the firm: longstanding firms produce more objective data about their operations, whereas new firms have little objective data to disclose to prospective investors.

name: Target choice fit
definition: The fit between an acquirer's actual choice between a public or private firm and what the discrete choice model predicted that it should do.

name: Multihoming
definition: A complementor's decision to provide its products or services on multiple platforms. Multihoming to a new platform requires a complementor to adapt its offerings to the structure of the interdependencies of the ported platform.

name: Performance on the home platform
authors_terms: ["complementor's performance on the home platform", "performance", "Installed repositories"]
definition: Usage by other complements is an important performance outcome for complements available in ecosystems in the absence of a price mechanism. The authors operationalize a complementor's performance as the extent to which its software package was used on a software development platform.

name: Interdependencies on the home platform
definition: In the context of open-source software, interdependencies are reflected in dependency relationships, as a program often depends on other programs, whose functionalities the focal program builds on to deliver its own functionalities.

name: Similarity to other complements
definition: The extent to which the upstream packages used by a focal complement by a focal month overlapped with the upstream packages most frequently used by all the other complements in the relevant domains of use. It ranges from zero to one, with higher values denoting higher levels of similarity.

name: Organizational assimilation of innovations
definition: Assimilation is defined here as an organizational process that (1) is set in motion when individual organization members first hear of an innovation's development, (2) can lead to the acquisition of the innovation, and (3) sometimes comes to fruition in the innovation's full acceptance, utilization, and institutionalization.

name: Contextual attributes
definition: Contextual attributes influence organizational assimilation of innovations: characteristics of environments, organizations, and leaders each account for unique variance in assimilation.

name: Enacted environment
definition: Organizations do not merely respond to preordained environmental conditions but actively create the environments they inhabit through processes of attention and choices of markets, products, and services. When aggregated, patient and physician admission and referral choices mapped the unique geographic market served by each organization.

name: Organizational context
definition: Hospital size, structural complexity, and market strategy are the organizational attributes examined as antecedents of assimilation.

name: Leadership attributes
definition: Administrators and physicians share power in hospitals, and both are potential sponsors of innovations in medical technology; those who allocate resources can influence adoptions of innovative equipment.

name: Innovation attributes
authors_terms: ["innovation attributes", "attributes of innovations", "innovation variables", "innate attributes of innovations"]
definition: Innovations have certain inherent characteristics that influence their adoptability and are relatively invariant across settings.

name: Innovation-decision attributes
definition: Certain factors affecting the assimilation of an innovation are unique to the evaluation of that particular innovation within that particular organization; they are attributes arising from the interaction of innovations and contexts.

name: Urbanization
definition: Urbanization was measured in terms of average population density within a hospital's enacted service area.

name: Affluence
authors_terms: ["affluence", "income growth", "average increase in median family income"]
definition: Income growth within a hospital's enacted service area, measured as the average increase in median family income between 1960 and 1970.

name: Federal health insurance reliance
authors_terms: ["federal health insurance", "proportion of Medicare and Medicaid recipients"]
definition: The proportion of Medicare and Medicaid recipients within a hospital's enacted service area.

name: Organizational size
definition: Hospital size was measured in terms of the number of patient beds, using a logarithmic transformation to adjust for curvilinearity.

name: Structural complexity
definition: Complexity was measured in terms of the availability of 24 distinct medical services; since those services required either separate structural subunits or specialized staff members, the number available in a hospital reflects horizontal differentiation.

name: Market strategy
authors_terms: ["market strategy", "aggressiveness in developing new services and penetrating new markets"]
definition: Market strategy was measured by pooling the judgments of experts concerning the aggressiveness with which hospitals pursued new markets.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "tenure of the chief executive officer", "years of service"]
definition: The tenure of the chief executive officer, measured in years of service.

name: CEO education
definition: The CEO's educational level, measured using an index combining years of graduate and undergraduate education and degrees received.

name: Recency of medical education
authors_terms: ["recency of medical education", "median age of hospital's active medical staff"]
definition: Physicians who received their medical training recently are most likely to have been exposed to state-of-the-art technology and to seek its adoption in their hospitals; the variable was measured in terms of the median age of the members of each hospital's active medical staff.

name: Risk
authors_terms: ["risk", "level of risk of injury, death, or malpractice liability"]
definition: One relatively invariant characteristic of particular pieces of medical equipment is the level of risk of injury or death to which they expose patients and the concomitant risk of malpractice litigation to which they expose physicians who use them.

name: Skill requirements
authors_terms: ["skill", "manual skill or specialized training requirements", "skill required to use an innovation"]
definition: A characteristic likely to influence adoptability uniformly is the degree of manual skill or specialized medical training required to use an innovation.

name: Observability
definition: The degree to which the results of using the innovation are visible to organizational members and external constituents.

name: Compatibility
definition: An innovation's compatibility with the tasks and experiences of potential users, the most widely investigated aspect of the fit between innovation and organization; in the case of medical equipment the primary criterion is the presence on the medical staff of physicians practicing a specialty appropriate for using the equipment.

name: CEO advocacy
authors_terms: ["CEO's advocacy", "CEO champions or opposes adoption", "influential support"]
definition: The extent to which an organization's CEO champions or opposes adoption; the authors defined CEO's advocacy as influential support.

name: Technological unfamiliarity
definition: The primary independent variable in my analysis is the degree to which an invention is in an unfamiliar area of technology. The intuition behind this measure is that when there is more recent and frequent innovative activity concentrated in an area of technology, there is greater accumulation of technological knowledge to guide subsequent search.

name: Obviousness from overlooked counterfactuals
authors_terms: ["obviousness", "teach away", "Rejected for obviousness, teach away", "overlooking counterfactuals"]
definition: I use the term obviousness to refer to the extent to which an innovation is a predictable outcome of applying prior knowledge. In the patent context, the phrase 'teach away' means that prior art actually advised against the technological direction in a focal invention.

name: Ultimate claim allowance
definition: The dependent variable is the likelihood that a claim is ultimately allowed. Reversals of obviousness rejections provide a window on cases when examiners may have initially overestimated obviousness.

name: Participation in strategic planning
definition: We therefore take participation in strategic planning, in line with the dictionary (C.O.D., 1976), to be 'the process of taking part (with other persons) in the process of strategic planning'.

name: Interest groups participating
definition: Interest groups participating (P1), one of the three variables defining the dimensions of participation; it is a nominal recording of activity which omits any notion of depth of commitment or involvement.

name: Communication in the planning process
definition: Degrees of communication in the planning process (P2), one of the three variables defining the dimensions within which participation is measured.

name: Involvement in strategic decision making
definition: Involvement in strategic decision making (P3), one of the three variables defining the dimensions within which participation is measured.

name: Clear statement of objectives
definition: An effective system will focus on the objectives, clarify these and keep them in view throughout the planning process.

name: Integration of the planning function
definition: A strategic planning process can only be effective if the plans and analyses become the focus of the strategic decision making of the organization.

name: Catalytic action of the planning function
definition: Planning will be more effective if planners stimulate other participants to think strategically.

name: Richness of formulation
definition: An effective system will explore a wide range of possible futures rather than concentrating solely on a single history extrapolated one.

name: Depth of evaluation
definition: In evaluating a plan multiple criteria including several financial measures and measures associated with other resources will be used by an effective system; reliance on a single measure such as payback may cause important aspects to be overlooked.

name: Treatment of uncertainty in evaluation
definition: The evaluation of plans should take account of the uncertainty in estimates of demand forecasts, costs, economic environment and other exogenous variables.

name: Resources planned
definition: Organizations are dependent on a number of resources, including finance, manpower, raw materials and equipment, and strategic planning should consider them all.

name: Data used
definition: It is important that adequate data are available for planning; insufficient data can lead to unnecessary approximation or complete gaps in the planning process.

name: Iteration in process
definition: As the plans develop through the planning cycle, information will emerge that is relevant to previously completed parts. An effective system will recognize its relevance and cause appropriate modifications to be made.

name: Assumptions made
definition: Planning is necessarily based on assumptions. These must be explicit so that unrealistic and inconsistent assumptions are avoided.

name: Quantification of goals
definition: An effective system will quantify goals where this is appropriate and recognize qualitative goals.

name: Control measures
authors_terms: ["E11", "control measures (responsiveness to uncertainty)", "extent of control measures"]
definition: A static plan rapidly becomes valueless in times of change. An effective system will include a feedback mechanism leading to modifications of the plans.

name: Feasibility of implementation
definition: An effective system will anticipate barriers to the implementation of any given plan and avoid them, remove them, or accept that they cannot be surmounted.

name: Public sector non-profit organization
authors_terms: ["public sector, non-profitmaking organizations (PSNPOs)", "public organizations", "public sector, non-profitmaking organizations"]
definition: The public sector, non-profitmaking organizations (PSNPOs) in the sample, organizations (a) to (c), with the nationalized industry included in the complementary set; these organizations were accountable to a wider constituency than were the private organizations.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "average R&D intensity", "risky long-term expenditures", "risk aversion (as measured by R&D intensity)"]
definition: The central dependent variable, serving as a surrogate for risk aversion, is average R&D intensity—consolidated R&D expense divided by net sales revenue. R&D intensity has been used as a surrogate measure for risk aversion by researchers from both industrial organization and strategic management.

name: Division financial incentives
authors_terms: ["emphasis on division financial results (both short- and long-term) as the dominant incentive control scheme", "emphasis on division financial performance incentive", "emphasis on financial incentives", "division financial incentives"]
definition: Financial controls frequently are implemented, at least partially, through the use of performance-based incentive compensation schemes for division managers. Incentive compensation schemes based on financial performance are designed to reward managers for maximizing the desired performance criteria.

name: Short-term division financial incentives
authors_terms: ["emphasis on division annual (short-term) financial performance as the dominant incentive scheme", "emphasis on annual (short-term) division return on investment performance", "short-term incentives"]
definition: Because of the tendency in the more diversified firms to use divisional return on investment as the dominant criterion for incentive compensation for rewarding division managers, short-run profit maximizing behavior (e.g., maximizing ROI) among division managers can emerge. Division profit accountability implies that earnings, resources and career prospects of division managers are dependent on their ability to meet the specified ROI objectives.

name: Long-term division financial incentives
authors_terms: ["emphasis on long-term financial performance incentives", "longer-term incentives", "long-term incentives"]
definition: Longer-term incentives based on financial criteria are risky for division managers because they can be influenced by factors outside their control. Zajac (1987) proposed that longer-term incentives based on evaluation of financial performance over a five-year period might reinforce a longer-term outlook.

name: Constraints on the application of resources
authors_terms: ["constraints on the application of resources", "constraints on resources", "constraints on the application of resources toward innovation"]
definition: Constraints on the application of resources refer to the conditions in the firm, the external regulations, and the national context that impact on the firm's innovation.

name: Abundance of external knowledge
authors_terms: ["abundance of innovation-relevant external knowledge", "abundance of external knowledge", "external abundance of knowledge", "availability of knowledge external to the firm"]
definition: The extent to which external knowledge relevant to innovation is available; this knowledge represents the potential technological search space.

name: Innovative performance
authors_terms: ["innovative performance", "innovative performance of firms", "radical innovation", "incremental innovation"]
definition: Two proxies reflect the construct 'innovative performance of firms': one variable represents a firm's innovation turnover pertaining to new products (radical innovation), and a second variable indicates the turnover from incremental innovation (incremental innovation), which consists of new modified products or processes from previous innovations.

name: External search breadth
authors_terms: ["external search breadth", "search breadth", "breadth of the knowledge search"]
definition: 'The number of external sources or search channels that firms rely upon in their innovative activities' (Laursen and Salter, 2006: 4-5).

name: External search depth
authors_terms: ["external search depth", "search depth", "depth of the knowledge search"]
definition: 'The extent to which firms draw deeply from the different external sources or search channels' (Laursen and Salter, 2006: 4-5).

name: Board monitoring
authors_terms: ["board monitoring", "monitoring by boards of directors", "vigilant board monitoring", "board oversight"]
definition: The board's exercise of its oversight function, which 'should be able to ensure that something stupid is not being done' and which constrains managers' opportunities to pursue self-serving strategies. The authors measure it through board characteristics and an aggregate factor-analysis measure of board monitoring.

name: Institutional shareholder monitoring
authors_terms: ["monitoring by institutional investors", "monitoring by institutional shareholders", "institutional ownership concentration"]
definition: Institutional shareholders have a vested interest in monitoring M&A deals because M&As affect shareholder value; large institutional shareholders, due to the size of their holdings, have more to lose and thus greater incentives to monitor, but they also are more likely to gain access to and receive special attention from management.

name: M&A performance extremeness
authors_terms: ["M&A performance extremeness", "performance extremeness", "M&A extremeness", "less-extreme M&A returns"]
definition: How extensively a particular M&A deal affects shareholder wealth: 'big gains and big losses' measured as the absolute value of the dollar-adjusted abnormal returns, irrespective of whether the effect is value-creating or value-destroying.

name: Buyer-supplier tie density
authors_terms: ["buyer-supplier density", "intragroup buyer-supplier ties", "density of intragroup buyer-supplier ties", "BSD"]
definition: Buyer-supplier density measures intragroup buyer-supplier ties. Density is the ratio of buyer-supplier relationships to the number of potential ties among affiliates in a given year, and greater density means a higher number of direct and indirect ties among affiliates.

name: Market development
authors_terms: ["market development", "market development of the institutional environment", "market-based institutions", "market-oriented infrastructure"]
definition: The market development of the institutional environment is the degree to which a country possesses market institutions that businesses need for commercial activity.

name: Group innovativeness
definition: Patents record innovative activity as much as or more than they do innovative success, and the authors use Taiwan patent data to measure the innovative activity of business groups. The dependent variable is the aggregate patent application counts by all affiliates of each group over a two-year period following each of the five years for which BGT provided data.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in residential mortgage lending", "reliance on the traditional S&L strategy of residential mortgage lending"]
definition: We defined strategic change in terms of change in residential mortgage lending from year to year. Residential mortgage lending constitutes the historic core business of thrifts and the alteration of this business represents a significant change in strategy.

name: Dynamic strategic fit
authors_terms: ["dynamic strategic fit", "deviation from the contingency model of change", "dynamic misfit"]
definition: The comparison of actual and necessary strategic change determines the degree of dynamic strategic fit, which should then influence subsequent organizational performance. Organizations that deviated from our model's prediction of dynamic strategic fit (i.e., changed more or changed less than our model prescribed) experienced negative performance consequences.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "subsequent performance", "financial performance and survival chances"]
definition: We employed two separate measures of organizational performance. First, we used ROA at time t + 1... Our second performance measure was organizational failure.

name: Cost of funds
definition: S&Ls whose cost of funds (i.e., the funds used to make subsequent loans) is high will be disadvantaged relative to those whose input resource costs are lower.

name: Reliance on borrowed funds
authors_terms: ["reliance on borrowing from governmental and other nondepositor sources of funds", "percentage of borrowed funds", "dependence on borrowed funds"]
definition: Given that depositors generally represent the cheapest form of funds, one can extend this logic to suggest that S&Ls relying more heavily on other sources of funds, e.g., governmental sources, are at a competitive disadvantage, in terms of the cost of input resources.

name: Return on mortgage portfolio
authors_terms: ["rate of return on its mortgage portfolio", "return on mortgage lending", "portfolio management skills"]
definition: If an S&L's portfolio management skills are high (as evidenced by a high rate of return on its mortgage portfolio), then maintaining or even expanding its reliance on the traditional strategy of residential mortgage lending may be appropriate. If an S&L's portfolio management skills are low (as evidenced by a low rate of return on its mortgage portfolio), this implies an operational deficiency that puts that S&L at a competitive disadvantage.

name: Emphasis on fixed-rate mortgages
authors_terms: ["emphasis on fixed rate mortgages", "degree to which the S&L's loan portfolio is heavily weighted towards fixed-rate (vs. adjustable rate) mortgages"]
definition: Another prominent organizational resource difference that would suggest that an S&L needs to move away from its traditional mortgage business is the composition of the mortgage portfolio itself, i.e., the degree to which the S&L's loan portfolio is heavily weighted towards fixed-rate (vs. adjustable rate) mortgages.

name: Net worth
authors_terms: ["net worth", "decline in net worth", "poor prior performance"]
definition: An overall measure of a resource deficiency that may stimulate needed change is the financial situation of the organization, as indicated by poor prior performance... For S&Ls, a common indicator of overall performance is net worth.

name: Local competitor mortgage lending
authors_terms: ["an S&L's local competitors' reliance on residential mortgage lending", "percentage of competitor assets in mortgages", "imitation of geographic competitors"]
definition: One central feature that may affect the propensity of organizational adaptation is the competitive environment of a local area. Organizations often look to local competitors for cues regarding the appropriateness of potential strategic changes.

name: Interest rates
authors_terms: ["interest rates", "macroenvironmental variable interest rates", "average prime rate"]
definition: Macroenvironmental factors, i.e., those that affect all organizations in the population, clearly can also affect the desirability of strategic change over time... The late 1970s and early 1980s were particularly turbulent times for S&Ls, driven largely by the dramatic and unprecedented increases in interest rates.

name: Homogeneous group size
authors_terms: ["group size", "homogeneous group size", "size of the all-White work group", "size of the all-male Innovation Team", "all-male board size", "all-White board size"]
definition: Size is a fundamental and visible attribute of any organizational group or team. We propose that the size of a homogeneous group can play an important role in shaping (i) the way it is perceived, (ii) whether it will subsequently be diversified, and (iii) how aggressively decision makers pursue its diversification.

name: Perceived fairness of the selection process
authors_terms: ["perceived fairness of the homogeneous group's selection process", "perceived fairness of the process used to select the members", "perceived fairness of the original all-male Innovation Team's selection process"]
definition: People tend to perceive an organization's selection process as 'fair' when it shows no bias against particular applicants and as 'unfair' when bias exists.

name: Perceived diversity
authors_terms: ["perceived diversity", "perceived diversity of the original group", "the homogeneous group's perceived diversity"]
definition: Objective diversity focuses on the presence of differences within a group, whereas perceived diversity is defined by whether people recognize and are aware of those differences. Perceived diversity is also driven by subjective factors, such as motivated reasoning and self-serving biases.

name: Diversity-related impression management concerns
authors_terms: ["diversity-related impression management concerns", "perceived diversity-related impression management concerns faced by the homogeneous group"]
definition: Impression management describes efforts by individuals, groups, or organizations to ensure that they are perceived in a positive light. Impression management concerns arise when there is reason to worry that outside parties may have a negative perception of a group or organization that could harm it in some way.

name: Perceived influence of a newly added underrepresented member
authors_terms: ["perceived influence wielded by the underrepresented candidate", "perceived influence a woman would wield if she were added", "potential for a new addition to influence the group"]
definition: An individual group member's influence within a group and over group outcomes generally diminishes in larger groups relative to smaller groups. We therefore predict that for larger homogeneous groups, a newly added member who is demographically underrepresented will be expected to wield less influence.

name: Diversification of a homogeneous group
authors_terms: ["likelihood of selecting an underrepresented candidate", "decisions to diversify", "diversity-related hiring decisions", "whether a woman was added to the board"]
definition: We expect each of these perceptions to influence diversity-related hiring decisions, such that decision makers will be more prone to diversify larger homogeneous groups than smaller ones.

name: Observed prevalence of homogeneity relative to chance
authors_terms: ["likelihood of observing homogeneity", "underrepresentation of large homogeneous boards", "percent difference between the observed and expected proportions of all-male boards"]
definition: If decision makers disproportionately react to a lack of diversity in larger homogeneous groups, but not smaller ones, and if they respond by working especially hard to diversify larger homogeneous groups, then we should see a relative scarcity of large homogeneous groups compared with expectations.

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay dispersion", "wage dispersion", "horizontal wage dispersion", "intraclass dispersion", "pay compression"]
definition: The dispersion of pay within the same organizational echelon or core group of employees, in contrast to vertical pay dispersion, the spread of pay across organizational echelons. Dispersion is neither inherently functional nor dysfunctional; situational contingencies determine its strategic effectiveness.

name: Individual incentives
authors_terms: ["individual incentives", "individual incentive systems", "individual financial incentive systems", "paying for individual performance"]
definition: Formal individual financial incentive systems that pay for individual performance; such systems are normatively accepted and their use is argued to make pay dispersion appear legitimate and motivation enhancing.

name: Work interdependence
definition: The degree to which employees must rely on one another to accomplish work; the authors argue that work interdependence is the implicit key to the effectiveness of pay compression.

name: Workforce performance
authors_terms: ["workforce performance", "intermediate workforce performance", "intermediate outcomes", "workforce performance including productivity and safety"]
definition: Intermediate organizational outcomes of employee performance behaviors; employee performance is the intermediate outcome or the path through which compensation strategies affect organizational performance.

name: Foreign partner equity stake
authors_terms: ["foreign equity stake", "foreign partner's equity stake in the IJV", "the foreign partner's percentage of ownership in the IJV"]
definition: The foreign IJV partner's equity contribution to the IJV. As an IJV partner's relative bargaining power will increase with its equity stake, a higher equity stake should increase an IJV partner's ability to convert its equity into board representation.

name: Foreign partner board representation
authors_terms: ["foreign board representation", "the proportion of IJV board members from the foreign partner", "representation on the IJV board"]
definition: The dependent variable is the proportion of IJV board members from the foreign partner; the number of board members appointed by the foreign partner divided by the total number of members on the IJV board.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: Environmental volatility refers to the volatility of the external conditions faced by a firm that are outside its control and difficult to anticipate (Dess and Beard, 1984; Kumar and Seth, 1998).

name: Competitive overlap
authors_terms: ["competitive overlap", "overlap in the markets served by both partners"]
definition: The extent to which the IJV partners compete with each other; the authors consider competitive overlap between partners as a factor that can affect the internal role of IJV boards.

name: Board monitoring effectiveness
authors_terms: ["the effectiveness of internal board monitoring in the IJV host country", "board monitoring effectiveness"]
definition: How effectively boards monitor management within particular countries, that is, the effectiveness of the internal role boards serve.

name: Market growth
definition: The level of growth in the IJV's market, which affects the importance of the external role of the board for the IJV partners; one important dimension of environmental munificence is market growth.

name: Coordination needs
definition: Coordination needs, which exist when top executives must jointly process information to resolve interdependencies among different parts of their firms.

name: Related diversification
definition: Related diversification requires top executives to take an active role in resolving reciprocal interdependencies, coordinating resource exchanges, and leveraging core competencies across business areas.

name: Number of businesses
authors_terms: ["number of businesses", "number of product-market areas", "number of a firm's businesses"]
definition: In related diversifiers, larger numbers of businesses increase the operational interdependencies that the TMTs must address. In unrelated diversifiers, larger numbers of businesses add to the amount of information that top executives must consider to make informed decisions about investment flows in their firms' internal capital markets.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Technology is another source of coordination needs; here, we considered both R&D spending and capital investment activity, which represent critical long-term commitments. As either capital investment or R&D activity increases, the number of investment projects grows and/or the size and complexity of the average project increases.

name: Capital investment intensity
definition: Here, we considered both R&D spending and capital investment activity, which represent critical long-term commitments. Since coordination activities associated with old investments may have become routine events handled by lower-level employees, we considered new capital investment, which involves nonroutine decisions that likely require executive attention.

name: Firm size
definition: Larger firms are more structurally complex than smaller ones and have subunits that are more specialized and differentiated. So as firms become larger, they become more difficult to manage, and top management teams play a more important role in coordinating their activities.

name: Number of vice presidents
definition: Coordination needs will be greater in firms with more vice presidents. Employing more VPs has definite costs, both monetary and procedural, because larger groups are more difficult to integrate.

name: CEO pay gap
authors_terms: ["CEO pay gap", "pay gap", "gap size", "across-ranks pay gap"]
definition: This study examined the CEO pay gap, defined as the difference between a CEO's compensation and the average pay of other top management team members.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance, the dependent variable in Hypotheses 7 and 8, was measured by annual return on assets (ROA), which was obtained from COMPUSTAT.

name: CEO pay
authors_terms: ["CEO pay", "CEO compensation", "total cash compensation", "absolute compensation", "change in compensation"]
definition: The total cash compensation paid to a firm's chief executive officer. The authors argue that understanding the determinants of CEO pay requires focusing on both absolute compensation and change in compensation.

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure was measured by the number of years an individual had been the CEO of a given company. The authors treat tenure as a proxy for CEOs' ability to exercise influence over boards of directors.

name: Stock returns
definition: Returns to stockholders were measured by abnormal stock returns, operationally defined as the difference between actual and expected returns, Rit - E(Rit).

name: Firm size
definition: Measured by the natural logarithm of the number of a firm's employees.

name: Firm risk
definition: Risk that a firm depends for its earnings on high-risk operations that are vulnerable to changes in underlying economic fundamentals; calculated by one-year stock market betas.

name: Extent of strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "strategic reorientation", "extent of strategic change enacted during a turnaround"]
definition: In developing a measure of the extent of strategic change enacted during a turnaround, the authors wanted to capture both types of strategic change examined in the past: (a) changes in a firm's domain or portfolio of businesses and (b) changes in competitive decisions at the product-market level. Management actions viewed as either changes in a firm's domain or changes in competitive decisions at the product/market level were included on the list of changes in strategy.

name: Firm performance during downturn
authors_terms: ["level of firm performance during the firm's downturn", "extent of firm decline", "extent of the firm's performance decline"]
definition: Extremely poor performance creates pressure for management to change a firm's strategy, if the firm has sufficient resources; a declining firm with extremely poor performance is expected to have more extensive strategic problems than a firm suffering a milder downturn. The extent of a firm's decline was measured as the lowest annual return on investment achieved by the firm during its downturn.

name: Industry growth during downturn
definition: Industry growth or decline during a firm's downturn was measured as the GNP-deflated annual growth rate in a firm's industry's shipments during the last 3 years of the firm's performance downturn. If a firm's main industry is growing concurrent to the firm's decline, the need for strategic change increases.

name: Favorable industry events
authors_terms: ["favorable events in a firm's main industry that facilitate recovery", "contribution of industry events"]
definition: The extent that a firm's decline is corrected by external events reduces the need for strategic change. Survey responses provided data on what contribution managers thought industry changes made to their performance turnarounds.

name: CEO replacement
authors_terms: ["replacement of the firm's CEO", "CEO replacement", "CEO had been 'replaced' as part of the turnaround"]
definition: Previous researchers undertaking case studies of turnaround attempts have asserted that recovery from decline is often facilitated by replacing the CEO and other top managers, because new top managers bring new understandings of the firm's environment and lack personal commitments to previous firm policies and practices.

name: Slack financial resource depletion
authors_terms: ["depleted slack financial resources", "slack financial resource depletion", "accumulation of debt"]
definition: The level of firm resources at the time of the turnaround attempt may affect a declining firm's capacity to implement strategic change, because continued decline destroys resources over time, reduces slack resources and may increase organizational rigidity and managerial paralysis. Slack financial resource depletion was measured as the firm's highest debt to asset percentage during its downturn; firms with lower values have relatively greater access to financial resources through further borrowing.

name: Firm diversity
definition: Managers whose firms offer the widest array of products and services in the most markets have the greatest number of potential domains that can be emphasized or deemphasized; therefore diversity increases managerial discretion to implement change. The level of firm diversity was assessed using the entropy measure.

name: Firm size
definition: The effect of firm size on the capacity to implement strategic change is less established: small firms are often portrayed as flexible and large firms as inertial, but others assert that large organizations may be able to control their environments through superior resources and market power. Firm size was measured as a firm's sales revenue for the first year of the firm's downturn.

name: Antitrust holdup
definition: I define antitrust holdup in this context to be any action taken by an antitrust authority that reduces or delays the intended benefits of a proposed merger. Levels of antitrust scrutiny that involve investigations, monitoring and/or competitive curbs, dissolved mergers, asset divestments and preventions represent antitrust holdup.

name: Industry global competitiveness
authors_terms: ["global competitiveness of an industry", "trade balance", "net exporter status", "net importer status"]
definition: The 'global competitiveness of an industry' refers to the world competitiveness of a national industry: e.g., Japan is globally competitive in auto manufacturing. The underlying assumption is that the more an industry is a net exporter the more competitive it is.

name: Antitrust institutional mission
definition: An institution's mission-an articulation of vision, values, and goals-plays a primary role in the business-government interface because it sheds light on the priorities and direction of an antitrust authority.

name: Antitrust institutional capability
definition: An institution's capability-grounded in held resources and competencies-plays a primary role in the business-government interface because it gives some evidence as to what an antitrust agency can attain.

name: Antitrust institutional autonomy
definition: An institution's autonomy-the degree to which it is immune from political pressures-plays a primary role in the business-government interface, as it reflects how much an antitrust agency must take into account other political actors.

name: Institutional competence of antitrust jurisdictions
authors_terms: ["Institutional Competence", "overall commitment of national antitrust agencies to sound antitrust procedures", "commitment to antitrust principles and procedures"]
definition: The actual reporting from antitrust jurisdictions in the OECD's annual reports allows a convenient proxy of a jurisdiction's commitment to antitrust principles and procedures: average number of pages devoted to each antitrust jurisdiction over the 1992-2000 period.

name: Corporate political pressure
authors_terms: ["merging firms' political pressure", "political pressure", "political strategy tactics", "corporate political strategy"]
definition: 'effective political strategies' are 'defined as the overall theme, and incumbent tactics, that businesses take to shape their non-market environment in order to "encourage policymakers to be more responsive to the interests of business"'.

name: Effectiveness of corporate political pressure
authors_terms: ["more effective", "increase the probability of obtaining antitrust approval", "effective political strategies"]
definition: The source of antitrust holdup might be more difficult to predict when authorities consider non-competition issues as public interest criteria; yet by targeting an agency's non-competition mission merging firms increase the probability of obtaining antitrust approval.

name: Local newspaper scarcity
authors_terms: ["local newspaper scarcity", "scarcity of local newspapers", "the growing scarcity of local newspapers"]
definition: The scarcity or abundance of local newspapers reflects the overall strength of accountability journalism in each community because the collectivity of local newspapers constitutes a key policing mechanism in local governance.

name: Community social connectedness
authors_terms: ["community social connectedness", "social connectedness", "community social connectedness of a community"]
definition: Community social connectedness represents the dense interlocking network of relationships between local people in a community, characterizing the socio-cultural aspect of local communities.

name: Scale of organizational wrongdoing
definition: In our theoretical framework, the scale of organizational wrongdoing represents the overall severity of organizational wrongdoing as a prevalent social issue in a community. Organizational wrongdoing is any illegitimate action from an ethical, regulatory, or legal standpoint.

name: Internal organizational wrongdoing
definition: Internal organizational wrongdoing refers to illegitimate actions associated with internal stakeholders and systems, such as employee relations and corporate governance.

name: External organizational wrongdoing
definition: External organizational wrongdoing indicates illegitimate actions related to external stakeholders and operations, including customers, local communities, and the natural environment.

name: Managerial compensation
definition: Managerial compensation is the pay of top management team members. Because German company law does not require the reporting of individual compensation packages, the study uses the average compensation of top management team members, which the authors argue is essentially interchangeable with CEO compensation in the German context.

name: Relative education level
authors_terms: ["relative education level", "relative difference score", "education level difference", "relative education level difference"]
definition: Relative differences in education level between the CEO and the supervisory board chair are the simple difference between CEO education and board chair education, taking positive values when the CEO's level of education is higher and negative values when it is lower. If the CEO's level of education is relatively high vis-à-vis the board chair, the chair may be more likely to defer to the CEO's knowledge and status, leading to higher levels of compensation.

name: Same educational specialization
definition: Educational specialization was assessed for the highest obtained university degree and categorized into arts, sciences, engineering, business and economics, and law. Having the same educational specialization may highlight similarities and create language compatibility, making educational differences particularly salient.

name: Relative tenure
definition: Relative tenure is calculated as the simple difference between CEO tenure and board chair tenure, measured in years. If CEO tenure is comparatively long, the board chair may feel less expert and may be more likely to defer to the CEO's demands for higher compensation.

name: Role empathy
authors_terms: ["role empathy", "having a former CEO as board chair", "similar role experiences", "board chair is former CEO"]
definition: A former CEO serving as chair of the supervisory board may exhibit what the authors call role empathy, a form of similarity attraction: having experienced the demands of the CEO position and the problems of dealing with the board, such chairs should be more likely to empathize with the current CEO.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Ownership concentration is measured with a Herfindahl index, calculated by squaring the share each owner has of the total ownership and summing those squares. The German context is marked by much higher levels of ownership concentration than the United States, and powerful owners have incentives to monitor the board and top management.

name: Board compensation
definition: Board compensation is the average compensation of supervisory board members for each firm, reported in thousands of DM; supervisory board members are compensated equally in Germany. Theoretical arguments about the norm of reciprocity imply that management may extract greater pay raises from boards that themselves have received a pay raise.

name: Entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry
authors_terms: ["entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry", "entry tenure"]
definition: An individual foreign firm's entry tenure in a host country refers to the time elapsed since the firm was founded in the host country. Since multiple foreign firms may exist in an industry and they may have entered at different time periods, for the purpose of our study, we focus on the entry tenure of foreign firms at the industry level, defined as the average of all individual foreign firms' entry tenure in an industry.

name: Domestic firm productivity
authors_terms: ["productivity of an individual domestic firm", "domestic firms' productivity"]
definition: FDI spillovers to domestic firms in emerging markets are reflected in productivity increases for the latter.

name: Export intensity of foreign firms
authors_terms: ["export intensity of foreign firms in an industry", "foreign firms' market focus", "export market focus"]
definition: Export intensity of foreign firms in an industry was measured as the sum of foreign firms' export sales divided by the sum of their total sales. Foreign firms with an export market focus emphasize exploiting the resource endowments of the host country to meet demands of overseas markets.

name: Intangible asset intensity of foreign firms
authors_terms: ["intangible asset intensity of foreign firms", "foreign firms' asset composition"]
definition: Intangible asset intensity of foreign firms in an industry was measured as the sum of foreign firms' intangible assets divided by the sum of their total assets. Firms with substantial intangible assets have greater information asymmetry between insiders and outsiders.

name: Rhythm of foreign firms' entry pattern
authors_terms: ["rhythm of entry pattern of foreign firms", "rhythm of foreign firms' entry pattern"]
definition: In a 'rhythmic entry pattern,' foreign firms enter an industry in a constant and stable pace-for example, a couple of foreign entrants every year. In contrast, in an 'irregular pattern,' foreign entries are concentrated in a few time periods, followed by long periods with no foreign entries.

name: Barriers to imitation
authors_terms: ["barriers to imitation", "height of the barriers to imitation"]
definition: Barriers to imitation, or 'the restraining or obstructing of imitation by competitors,' can be created by information asymmetry between a firm with competitive advantage and its competitors and/or the causal ambiguity of the focal firm's competitive advantage.

name: Firm effects
definition: Firm effects capture the unique firm characteristics which influence the variation in strategies and performance outcomes across industries and firms.

name: Industry effects
definition: Industry effects refer to attributes common to an industry. Shared industry characteristics such as market structure and imitation of strategies lead to convergence of core strategies and performance among firms in the same industry and differences across industries.

name: Core strategies
definition: Key resources that are valuable, rare, nonsubstitutable, and difficult to imitate are termed core resources, and the strategies based on them are core strategies. The dependent variables for core strategies were developed for technology and marketing resources.

name: Business performance
definition: The performance outcome of the firm, for which the authors used return on assets as the measure of business performance.

name: Geographic distance
definition: The distance between the two firms in a dyad, calculated from the zip codes of their headquarters. The authors argue that firms' information disadvantages and their risk of adverse selection tend to rise with the geographic distance between exchange partners.

name: R&D alliance formation
definition: R&D alliances are formal agreements between independent firms who exchange, share, or codevelop specific resources related to R&D to reach a common goal. The dependent construct is the likelihood that a dyad of two firms forms an R&D alliance in a given year.

name: Prior ties
definition: Prior ties between the exchange partners offer firsthand information on each others' resources and prospects, so they can directly reduce information asymmetries. Prior collaborations can reduce firms' information disadvantages in different areas as well as the risk of adverse selection.

name: Product market relatedness
definition: Whether the two firms in a dyad operate in the same product market or in different industries. Previous studies have focused on the product market relatedness of firms as an inverse proxy for information costs as well as the risk of adverse selection.

name: Technological resource similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity in technological resources", "dissimilarity of technological resources", "technological knowledge"]
definition: The extent to which the two firms possess similar underlying technological resources. The authors argue that the information costs and risk of adverse selection experienced by distant prospective partners are a function of the similarities (or dissimilarities) of the firms' underlying technological resources.

name: Geographic proximity of research collaborators
authors_terms: ["average team distance", "team distance", "colocated teams", "local ties", "distant partners", "proximity"]
definition: Distance is conceptualized as a dichotomous rather than a continuous variable, reflecting the idea that the probability of face-to-face interaction falls rapidly beyond a given distance. A publication is coded 1 if its average team distance falls within 50 miles, and these are referred to as 'colocated teams'.

name: Scientific impact
definition: Paper citations capture the impact of research in wider scientific communities, and the dependent variable is a count of citations received by a paper from other scientific papers.

name: Technological impact
definition: A research paper may not create private value for a firm unless the firm applies the research to a patented technology. If a paper is cited by a patent, this is interpreted as evidence of a link between the knowledge contained in the publication and the invention covered by the patent.

name: Scientific prestige
authors_terms: ["prestige", "high-status scientists", "high-prestige institutions", "status in the scientific community", "partner prestige", "firm prestige"]
definition: Prestige in the scientific hierarchy is an important principle that stratifies position, career paths, and contact networks in scientific milieux. An institution was identified as high-prestige if it was ranked among the most highly cited institutions in molecular biology and genetics.

name: Ownership structure of chain-affiliated and independent units
definition: Chain-affiliated units include company-owned establishments (affiliated with a brand and owned by the brand itself) and franchisee-owned establishments (affiliated with a brand but owned by a franchisee), while independently owned establishments are not affiliated with a brand or chain.

name: Skill-enhancing HR practices
authors_terms: ["skill-enhancing HR practices", "ability or skill-enhancing HR practices", "selection and training"]
definition: Ability or skill-enhancing HR practices (e.g., selection and training) that promote employee knowledge, skills, and abilities to perform job tasks.

name: Motivation-enhancing HR practices
authors_terms: ["motivation-enhancing HR practices", "motivation-enhancing practices", "wages, benefits, and job security"]
definition: Motivation-enhancing HR practices (e.g., wages, benefits, and job security) that foster the organizational commitment of employees.

name: Opportunity-enhancing HR practices
definition: Opportunity-enhancing HR practices (e.g., employee discretion) that provide opportunities for employees to use their skills effectively and contribute to operational decision making.

name: Concentration among generalist firms
authors_terms: ["concentration among generalists", "concentration levels among generalists", "generalist concentration", "resource concentration in the general mass market"]
definition: Concentration among the large generalist firms that compete with each other to occupy the center of the market. It is measured as the variability in the distribution of firms with respect to either film production or film distribution in a given year.

name: Founding of specialist firms
authors_terms: ["foundings of specialist firms", "specialist foundings", "founding events of specialists", "Producer Foundings", "Distributor Foundings"]
definition: The number of new firms founded as specialist producers (or as specialist distributors) in the population during a given month.

name: Strategic specialization
authors_terms: ["specialist firms", "specialists", "specialist strategy", "strategically specialized organizations", "strategically specialized firms"]
definition: A focused strategy in which a firm engages only in the creation of feature films (specialist producer) or only in activities that ensure films are available to potential exhibitors (specialist distributor), rather than integrating production and distribution as generalist producer-distributors do.

name: Participation in genre creation
authors_terms: ["creation of film genres", "creation and transformation of film genres", "participation in the creation of film genres", "early genre production"]
definition: Participation in the production or distribution of films within a genre in the first year that genre appeared among feature-length films. Firms that produced or distributed films in a genre during its first appearing year are treated as having innovated.

name: Managerial construal level
authors_terms: ["construal level", "managers' construal", "more abstract-oriented managers", "more concrete-oriented managers"]
definition: Managers with more abstract (i.e., higher) construal will tend to view situations in a broad, schematic, and less contextualized manner that focuses on its superordinate characteristics. Those with more concrete (i.e., lower) construal will embrace a more detailed and highly contextualized view of a situation, capturing its subordinate and highly specific features.

name: Organizational control mechanisms
