authors_terms: ["organizational control mechanisms", "outcome-based controls", "process-based controls", "outcome controls", "process controls"]
definition: Organizational control systems represent the different management practices used within an organization to ensure employees behave in a manner consistent with a particular set of goals or objectives. Outcome and process control mechanisms represent opposite ends of a continuum.

name: Exploratory learning
definition: Employees are freer to seek out diverse and unusual knowledge from outside the organization. In this way, a team of employees may be more likely to draw upon and use knowledge that is new to the organization than that which is already known and established.

name: Exploitative learning
definition: Because employees will draw more upon the firm's already existing knowledge, use of more process-based controls will engender more precise and conservative forms of search.

name: Effectiveness of identified solutions
definition: Overall effectiveness (hereafter, effectiveness) is determined by how well the solution delivered by the project team of employees addresses the problem in a comprehensive and enduring manner.

name: Efficiency of identified solutions
definition: Efficiency is determined by the extent of resources expended to achieve the solution, including those associated with labor, financial, and other firm resources.

name: Competitive crowding
authors_terms: ["competitive crowding", "niche crowding", "crowding", "competitive crowding of the niche"]
definition: Competitive crowding refers to the density of actors who occupy similar niche positions. Occupants of crowded niches are argued to be less effective in accessing valuable information or building effective networks.

name: Niche status
definition: The status of a niche varies with the extent to which it offers access to colleagues who are in positions of influence in the organizational hierarchy. Certain niches are high status because the activities that define them confer privileged access to those in positions of power and influence in the organization.

name: Niche diversity
authors_terms: ["niche diversity", "diversity", "diversity of employees' niches", "functional diversity", "rank diversity", "level diversity"]
definition: A niche's diversity gauges the extent to which it provides access to employees in different functional areas and hierarchical levels of the organization. Diverse niches unite a diverse array of participants and therefore serve as gateways to a range of information and relationships with others of different rank, expertise, or social capital profiles.

name: Individual attainment
definition: The rewards employees garner inside organizations; the paper considers how niche properties help to understand the variation in discretionary rewards managers allocate to employees. It tests the hypotheses with two complementary measures of individual attainment: annual bonus and performance rating.

name: Geographic distance between acquirer and target
authors_terms: ["geographic distance", "geographic proximity", "distance between acquirers and newly public targets"]
definition: In this paper, we consider geographic distance as a proxy for information asymmetry and start from the assumption that the risk of adverse selection will be greater for distant acquirers compared to proximate ones, all else being equal.

name: Venture capitalist backing
authors_terms: ["Target IPO VC backed", "VC backing", "venture capitalist backing", "backing by a venture capitalist"]
definition: The first IPO characteristic we investigate is whether the target had financial backing by a venture capitalist (VC) at the time of its initial public offering.

name: Investment bank reputation
authors_terms: ["Target IPO IB reputation", "investment bank reputation", "reputation of the lead underwriter", "underwriter reputation"]
definition: The second IPO characteristic we examine is the reputation of the lead underwriter for the target's initial public offering.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: Underpricing is defined as the selling of shares below their market value, and underpricing is determined by the difference between the IPO's offer price and the stock's closing price on the first day of trading.

name: Geographic bias in acquisition activity
definition: We then calculated a measure of geographic bias, defined as the mean geographic distance between alternative acquirers and the IPO target less the geographic distance between the actual acquirer and the IPO target.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "value of a digital startup", "value of digital startups", "startup value"]
definition: The outcome of interest in this study is firm value of a digital startup. Unlike public firms, market-based valuation measures are not applicable to privately held startups.

name: Open source collaboration
definition: We conceptualize OSC as a specific type of open collaboration in which the innovation or production activities center on the development or use of OSS. We use the total number of public repositories the digital startup has on GitHub to represent overall OSC.

name: Inbound open source collaboration
authors_terms: ["inbound OSC", "inbound openness", "receiving side of the innovation process"]
definition: In inbound OSC, knowledge flows from outside-in in which participants absorb external software innovations from the open source community. In inbound OSC, the mechanism for value creation is knowledge reuse.

name: Outbound open source collaboration
authors_terms: ["outbound OSC", "outbound openness", "giving side of the innovation process"]
definition: In outbound OSC, knowledge flows from inside-out in which participants contribute their own software innovations to the open source community. In outbound OSC, knowledge sharing is the value creation mechanism.

name: Venture maturity stage
authors_terms: ["venture stage", "stage of venture maturity", "stages of venture maturity"]
definition: Kazanjian (1988) proposes a stage-of-growth model with four distinctive stages: conception, commercialization, growth, and stability. Since our primary interest is in new ventures as opposed to established firms, we follow Fisher et al. (2016) and focus on the first three stages of Kazanjian's model in our theoretical development.

name: Educational heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["educational heterogeneity", "education heterogeneity", "founding team's educational heterogeneity", "diversity of the founding team's formal education"]
definition: "Given that education is an important dimension that helps shape individuals' knowledge (Delmar and Shane 2006), the diversity of the founding team's formal education gives us insight into the subject matter and level of knowledge acquired from such an education."

name: Entrepreneurial experience
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial experience", "prior founding experience", "founding experience", "prior entrepreneurial experience"]
definition: "Whereas education is associated with declarative knowledge, prior entrepreneurial experience is associated with tacit knowledge. Past experience molds how individuals direct their attention and process critical information."

name: Breakthrough innovation
definition: "We followed existing conventions (Ahuja and Lampert 2001) and considered breakthrough innovations as patented inventions in the top 1% of patents in terms of forward citations (i.e., the number of citations a patent receives)."

name: Founder-CEO duality
definition: "...we consider one key factor of the decision-making structure, duality (which occurs when the founder is also the CEO), as a representation of the structural power (Finkelstein 1992) that shapes the founding team members' ability and motivation to affect the innovative direction of the new venture."

name: New venture's stage of life
authors_terms: ["stage of life", "firm's stage of life", "life cycle of new ventures", "startup stage", "growth stage"]
definition: "The initial startup stage is described as the period in which the main problems facing technology-based ventures are to create innovations and secure funding." "...we consider the growth stage as the period in which the firm experiences at least 10% growth in the number of employees as reported in BioScan."

name: Novel innovation
definition: Novel innovations are defined as new technologies that are unrelated to those that the firm is currently manufacturing (i.e., there are no technological predicates).

name: Incremental innovation
definition: Incremental innovations are defined as technologies that build upon and modify existing technologies very similar to those with which the firm has experienced repeated failure in the past.

name: Failure in novel innovation
authors_terms: ["failure in novel innovations", "adverse events in novel innovations", "negative feedback from novel innovations"]
definition: An adverse event is a product-caused event that leads to serious injury or death. Such events proxy failure because they indicate if a device has technological problem(s).

name: Failure in incremental innovation
authors_terms: ["failure in incremental innovations", "adverse events in incremental innovations"]
definition: An adverse event is a product-caused event that leads to serious injury or death. Such events proxy failure because they indicate if a device has technological problem(s).

name: Managerial relatedness
authors_terms: ["managerial relatedness", "managerial dimension of relatedness", "managerial (corporate level) dimension of relatedness"]
definition: A dimension of relatedness, considered a corporate level construct, that refers to 'similarities in organizational structure, management processes, dominant functions, succession paths, and management beliefs and values'. It focuses on leveraging vertical stage competencies across different industries and products.

name: Product relatedness
definition: The input, distribution, and technological similarities between a diversified firm's businesses determine its degree of product relatedness, which is the degree to which the new industry is related to the core industry in terms of resources, technologies, and distribution channels.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors do not define firm performance conceptually; they measure it with both return on sales and return on assets to assure comparability with previous studies.

name: Center of gravity
definition: Galbraith proposed that different stages in the vertical chain represent different 'centers of gravity' because they face very different managerial problems and tasks; the center of gravity is the initial success stage whose lessons influence a firm's values, business lessons, management systems, succession path, organization, and mind-sets.

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation", "strategic type", "strategic posture", "Prospector", "Defender", "Miles and Snow typology"]
definition: In this study, strategy was viewed as being implied from behavior rather than stated by management, and strategic orientation was conceptualized as a continuum with Prospectors and Defenders occupying the two extremes.

name: Coalignment
definition: Coalignment was conceptualized using the systems approach, which defines it as the degree of correspondence to an externally specified ideal profile. As this correspondence to the theoretically/empirically derived ideal profile increases, organizational performance should also increase and vice versa.

name: Top executive characteristics
authors_terms: ["managerial characteristics", "executive characteristics", "top executive profiles", "managerial profile", "Profile P", "Profile D"]
definition: In this study, strategic orientation was classified using the Miles and Snow typology and demographic variables were used to derive top executive profiles.

name: Organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["company tenure", "tenure in the company", "tenures in the organization"]
definition: This variable was operationalized by counting the number of years that the executive had served in the organization.

name: Position tenure
definition: This variable was operationalized by counting the number of years that the executive had served in the position.

name: CEO age
definition: Age was measured as the chronological age of the CEO.

name: CEO level of education
definition: To operationalize this measure, a coding scheme was devised whereby each year of college education was added to a base score of 12 (for example, bachelor's degree = 12+4=16, masters degree = 12+6=18, etc.).

name: Functional background
authors_terms: ["functional background", "output oriented functions", "throughput oriented functions", "output experience", "throughput experience"]
definition: Functional background was coded as a categorical variable to reflect output or throughput experience. Output experience included backgrounds such as marketing and product research and development while throughput experience included backgrounds in finance, engineering and manufacturing.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Since no single measure effectively captures the performance outcomes of different strategic types, several researchers have suggested that financial measures must be used in conjunction with market based measures.

name: Return on investment
definition: The most conventional measure of business performance, this indicator evaluates the rate of return on total assets utilized in the company. It is a measure of management efficiency in resource deployments.

name: Market share
definition: It captures the effectiveness of an organization's strategy or 'the success of a business' products and programs in relationship to those of its competitors in the market' (Ruekert and Walker, 1987: 19).

name: Abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal return", "abnormal returns", "abnormal profits", "abnormal rates of return"]
definition: Abnormal return can best be described as the difference between actual return and the competitive return, i.e. the return just sufficient to maintain capital investment. The behavior of total return is assumed to approximate the behavior of abnormal returns.

name: Persistence of abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["persistence of abnormal returns", "persistence of return", "persistence of profitability", "convergence process"]
definition: Persistence is a relative term; for public policy and strategic purposes the speed of the convergence process is the more important issue. The closer any of the roots are to 1.00, the more persistent the abnormal profits.

name: Strategic and market factors
definition: The strategic variables/market conditions whose influence on the convergence process is examined are industry concentration, market share, rate of return, vertical integration, marketing expenditure intensity, and whether entry or exit has occurred in the market. Factors that decrease the persistence of the return series promote competition, and factors that increase the persistence of return hamper competition.

name: Market share
definition: Firms with a large share may seek to take part of their supranormal profits in the form of avoiding uncertainty. They use their market power to obtain more stable and persistent profits.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Scholars have theorized that a high level of concentration permits easier (less costly) collusion. Collusion, in turn, suppresses internal competition and limits the inflow of resources.

name: Vertical integration
definition: A vertically integrated firm has better control over both supply and demand. The competitive pressures associated with dealings with upstream and downstream firms, hence some of the forces that tend to eliminate abnormal returns, are reduced.

name: Marketing expenditure intensity
definition: One view asserts that marketing expenditures create brand loyalty through product differentiation. This insulates a firm from competitive forces and results in more persistent returns.

name: Market entry
definition: New entry is not required for competition; existing firms may expand output and/or copy the strategies of a successful firm in the market to bring return back to its competitive level. Both entry and exit barriers can be hypothesized to slow the convergence process.

name: Market exit
definition: The decision to cut back on output may be quite difficult for management to undertake. Exit may thus be a useful mechanism to facilitate the convergence of return back up to its long-term rate.

name: Prior profitability
definition: Firms starting out with the highest and lowest profitability levels have a greater than expected probability of remaining in their initial grouping. This suggests differing convergence patterns based on the level of return.

name: Stock return
definition: The notion of market efficiency implies that the price of the stock reflects all anticipated information about profitability contained in ROI. Only the unanticipated component of ROI should exhibit an association with changes in stock prices.

name: Existing knowledge base
authors_terms: ["knowledge base", "existing knowledge base", "knowledge possession", "local knowledge contributions", "prior knowledge"]
definition: The stock of knowledge a prospective partner already possesses; the authors argue that a firm's propensity to seek new knowledge depends on its ability to monitor, search for and apply new knowledge to its existing knowledge base, and in this study it is captured by the local partner's contributions in management, marketing, and technology.

name: Knowledge search
authors_terms: ["knowledge search", "knowledge-seeking behavior", "knowledge seeking decisions", "search for management skills", "search for marketing skills", "search for technology"]
definition: The search by a prospective partner for knowledge it considers lacking but vital for the fulfillment of its strategic objectives; in this study it is the local firm's decision to seek transfer of a specific type of knowledge (management, marketing, or technology) from a foreign partner.

name: Tacit and embedded knowledge
authors_terms: ["tacit knowledge", "embedded knowledge", "tacit or embedded knowledge", "tacit and embedded knowledge"]
definition: Tacit knowledge is defined by its inherent nature, i.e., it is noncodified; embedded knowledge is typically defined by proxy, namely by its idiosyncrasies and its inseparability from the organizational routines it is a part of. Both terms describe knowledge that is not easily diffused across firm boundaries.

name: Governance mode
authors_terms: ["governance mode", "governance structure", "knowledge transfer vehicles", "equity joint venture", "contractual venture"]
definition: The prospective partners in ICVs seek either to establish independent entities known as equity joint ventures (EJVs) or agreements regarding joint development, comanufacturing and the like, known as contractual ventures (CVs).

name: SBU effectiveness
definition: The effectiveness of the strategic business unit, which serves as the dependent variable in the study. The authors state that the measurement procedures and the reliability and validity of this variable are reported in Govindarajan (1988).

name: Competitive strategy
authors_terms: ["competitive strategy", "SBU competitive strategy", "'low-cost' strategy", "'differentiation' strategy", "low cost-differentiation framework"]
definition: The way an SBU competes within its chosen industry. 'Porter (1980) identified two generic ways in which an SBU can gain sustainable competitive advantage over other firms in the industry: "low cost" and "differentiation".' A low-cost strategy emphasizes being the low-cost producer; a differentiation strategy is based on creating and offering a product perceived industry-wide as unique.

name: R&D functional experience
authors_terms: ["functional experience in research and development", "experience in R&D", "years of experience ... research and development"]
definition: Experience accumulated by the SBU general manager in the research and development function, measured as the total years of experience in that area, counting all jobs.

name: Marketing functional experience
authors_terms: ["functional experience in marketing/sales", "experience in marketing", "years in marketing"]
definition: Experience accumulated by the SBU general manager in the marketing/sales function, measured as the total years of experience in that area, counting all jobs.

name: Manufacturing functional experience
authors_terms: ["functional experience in manufacturing", "experience in production", "production/engineering experience"]
definition: Experience accumulated by the SBU general manager in the production/engineering (manufacturing) function, measured as the total years of experience in that area, counting all jobs.

name: Finance functional experience
authors_terms: ["functional experience in finance/accounting", "experience in finance and accounting", "years in finance/accounting"]
definition: Experience accumulated by the SBU general manager in the finance/accounting function, measured as the total years of experience in that area, counting all jobs.

name: General management experience
authors_terms: ["experience in general management", "years in general management"]
definition: Experience accumulated by the SBU general manager in general management, measured as the total years of experience in that area, counting all jobs.

name: Industry familiarity
definition: 'Each respondent was asked to indicate the length of experience in current and closely related industries (counting all jobs).' The authors argue that effective strategy implementation implies an appropriate coalignment between the SBU and its industry setting.

name: Locus of control
definition: 'Locus of control refers to Rotter's (1966) concept of internal versus external control of reinforcement.' At one end of the internal-external continuum are those who perceive effort to be largely instrumental in attaining success; at the other end those who ascribe little or no value to initiative.

name: Information-gathering style
definition: The sensing-intuition continuum: 'The sensing-intuition functions are viewed as paired opposites on the information-gathering continuum.' Sensing types attend to details, facts and routine; intuitive types focus on meanings and relationships and on hypothetical possibilities.

name: Information-evaluation style
definition: The thinking-feeling continuum: 'The thinking-feeling functions are identified as paired opposites on the information-evaluation continuum.' Thinking persons process information in an analytical, logical fashion; feeling types focus on human interactions and on the emotions and feelings of the individuals involved.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "baseline profitability", "return on total sales", "return on sales"]
definition: Profitability (which we define in terms of return on sales) is a relative measure of the flow of capital that the firm has available to convert into new stocks. Thus, the profitability ratio measure is a signal of the business's competitive success, in the sense that its customers' willingness to pay is greater than its cost of products.

name: Business scale
definition: We conceptualize business scale in terms of sales revenue and business scope in terms of product lines and product sub-sectors. Sales, which reflect commercial success, provide a common conceptually appropriate measure of business scale because they reflect current stock of resources with realizable value.

name: Business scope
authors_terms: ["business scope", "related scope", "scope", "product line breadth", "number of sub-sectors"]
definition: We define business scope in terms of the firm's variety of offerings (i.e., product lines, product sub-sectors) within an industrial sector. In our approach, the product line scope and sub-sector scope of a business provide measures of related and/or semi-related diversification because we focus on product-related proliferation within a specified industrial sector.

name: Long-term business survival
definition: Long-term business survival is the length of time following a baseline point before a business shuts down. We consider both types of business dissolutions to be business failure, including closure of a single-business firm and dissolution of a focal business by an ongoing corporation.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: Acquisition activity refers to the extent to which a firm engages in acquisitions, as discussed by the authors when hypothesizing a positive relationship with survival.

name: Multinationality
authors_terms: ["multinationality", "international dispersion of foreign subsidiaries", "dispersion of foreign subsidiaries across different countries", "dispersion of FDI"]
definition: Multinationality is the dispersion of foreign subsidiaries across different countries, measured by counting the number of countries in which a firm had foreign subsidiaries.

name: International joint venture investment
definition: International joint ventures entail lower initial capital outlays than wholly owned investments and allow firms to focus on core capabilities, access partners' skills, and facilitate market entry. A firm's investment in IJVs was measured as the log of 1 plus the number of equity joint ventures formed abroad or with a foreign partner during 1985-89.

name: Downside risk
authors_terms: ["downside risk", "income stream risk", "bankruptcy risk", "downside conceptualization of risk"]
definition: Downside risk is a probability-weighted function of below-target performance outcomes; in contrast to variance-based measures of risk that incorporate the entire distribution of firm performance, downside risk focuses solely on organizational outcomes below some target value.

name: Structural homophily
authors_terms: ["structural homophily", "similarity in prominence", "similarity in network position"]
definition: The similarity between the network positions of the two members of a dyad, capturing whether firms of comparable prominence partner with one another. The authors hypothesize that the likelihood of a new shortcut between two firms increases with the similarity in prominence between those firms.

name: Network prominence
definition: A more structural indicator of the attractiveness of a potential partner is its prominence in the alliance network, because firms with more extensive histories of alliance formation are more likely to form future alliances. Differential levels of network involvement introduce and reinforce systemic reputational differences that affect firms' visibility and attractiveness.

name: Shortcut formation
definition: The less common ties that span locally embedded clusters; shortcuts were defined as the alliances between firms belonging to different clusters. Because shortcuts serve as bridges spanning the structural holes across clusters, their use suggests access to less familiar contexts than partners residing within the same cluster.

name: New entrant alliance formation
authors_terms: ["new entrant", "nonembedded firms", "potential new entrants", "attaches to an incumbent firm"]
definition: Alliance formation between firms at risk of entering the main component ('nonembedded firms' or 'potential new entrants') and firms embedded in the main component. The authors argue that nonembedded firms seek admission to the network and prefer embedded partners that are advantaged by the current network structure.

name: Deal size
definition: Little attention has focused on the number of parties contracting in an alliance, which we will term 'deal size.' The variable Deal size indicates the number of partners represented in each alliance formed.

name: Nonembedded deal
definition: An alliance deal that includes firms that are not members of the main component of the alliance network, as opposed to deals whose members are all already members of the main component. Such deals admit nonembedded firms to the main component.

name: Alliance management capability
authors_terms: ["alliance management capability", "collaborative capability", "capability to manage any individual alliance", "alliance management know-how"]
definition: We conceptualize alliance management capability as a multidimensional construct that comprises three distinct skills, or dimensions: coordination, communication, and bonding. We develop the notion of alliance management capability to denote specifically a firm's capability to manage the post-formation phase of an individual alliance.

name: Coordination skill
authors_terms: ["coordination", "coordination dimension", "coordination aspect of alliance management capability", "coordination ability"]
definition: Alliance management capability entails a firm having an ability to coordinate and manage the interdependence between partners. It involves the ability to identify and build consensus about task requirements in a given alliance, the nature of the associated interdependence between partners, and the specification of working procedures for task execution.

name: Communication skill
authors_terms: ["communication", "communication dimension", "communication aspect of alliance management capability", "communication ability"]
definition: Alliance management capability entails a firm having the necessary know-how and skills to credibly convey relevant knowledge and information about itself to the partner in a timely, accurate, and complete manner. Communication refers to 'the formal as well as informal sharing of meaningful and timely information between firms'.

name: Bonding skill
authors_terms: ["bonding", "bonding dimension", "bonding aspect of alliance management capability", "bonding capabilities", "social bonding"]
definition: The bonding dimension of alliance management capability entails a firm's ability to develop strong bonds with partners by consistently providing instrumental or expressive value to them. Close personal bonds involve extensive and repeated contact between the concerned entities, coupled with elements of affect and interpersonal liking.

name: Joint action
definition: The need for joint action by partners will vary across different alliance situations; the greater the joint efforts taken by the partners to manage their focal activities, and/or the more one partner becomes involved in activities that are traditionally considered the other's responsibility and vice versa, the greater their ability to compete successfully with the marketplace. We measured the extent of joint action by assessing how closely partners work together to accomplish various tasks or activities.

name: Fulfillment of strategic goals in an alliance
authors_terms: ["fulfillment of its strategic goals", "goal fulfillment", "fulfillment of key strategic goals"]
definition: One of the most widely used ways to assess firm performance as a result of any given alliance is the study of the extent to which a firm attains some of its main strategic goals in a given relationship.

name: Customer knowledge acquisition
authors_terms: ["customer knowledge acquisition", "access to customer knowledge", "valuable customer knowledge"]
definition: Key informants in each company were asked about the extent to which their firm had received valuable customer knowledge from the partner.

name: Firm performance
definition: We collected information on firm performance by asking respondents to report how well their firm had performed during the last three years relative to other partner firms of that vendor in terms of sales growth, profitability, return on investment, and ability to build customer loyalty.

name: Partner status in the vendor's network
authors_terms: ["partner status", "status conferred by a vendor", "firm's partner status in the vendor's network", "preferred partner status"]
definition: In 2005, we collected secondary information on the status conferred by a vendor on the focal firm from vendors' online partner directories that are updated annually. Partner status varies between 1 (no formal status) to 4 (highly preferred partner).

name: Use of common naming
definition: A naming strategy in which components are named in a manner that identifies them with each other and the overall chain. A component that shares a common name is linked to the chain and to its other components rather than to its local market.

name: Use of local naming
authors_terms: ["local naming strategy", "local naming", "own local name concentration"]
definition: An alternative naming strategy in which components' names identify them with their locations, rather than with the chain. Adaptation to local market conditions, even on a dimension such as the name, can allow components to avoid the perception of chains as large, cold, impersonal bureaucracies.

name: Own commonly named component failures
authors_terms: ["own commonly named failures", "failures of a chain's own commonly named components"]
definition: The failure of one or more of a chain's own components that are named in common with the chain. A nursing home was defined as failing in the year it was de-licensed by the Ministry of Health.

name: Own locally named component failures
authors_terms: ["own locally named failures", "failures of a chain's own locally named components"]
definition: The failure of one or more of a chain's own components that are named locally rather than in common with the chain. Component failures are salient, unambiguous indicators of poor performance that provide a chain with information about what not to do.

name: Others' commonly named component failures
authors_terms: ["others' commonly named failures", "failures of other chains' commonly named components"]
definition: The failures of commonly named components experienced by chains other than the focal chain, which may discredit the common naming strategy in the eyes of the focal chain's decision makers.

name: Others' locally named component failures
authors_terms: ["others' locally named failures", "failures of other chains' locally named components"]
definition: The failures of locally named components experienced by chains other than the focal chain. Failure of other chains' locally named components would have the opposite effect to failure of their commonly named components.

name: Chemical relatedness
authors_terms: ["chemical relatedness", "chemical relatedness between a firm's home industry and a target industry", "similarities in the regulated toxic chemicals used in different industries"]
definition: An additional dimension of relatedness that captures similarities in the regulated toxic chemicals used in different industries, which the authors argue is distinct from product-market and technological relatedness. The skills and capabilities needed to deal with chemical challenges in a firm's home industry are especially useful in a new industry that uses highly similar regulated toxic chemicals.

name: Target industry regulatory sanctions
authors_terms: ["target industry regulatory sanctions", "regulatory sanctions", "industry environmental fines"]
definition: Fines and penalties imposed by the regulatory agencies on firms that fail to meet emission standards for regulated toxic chemicals, measured at the level of a target manufacturing industry.

name: Diversification entry
authors_terms: ["diversification", "likelihood of diversification", "likelihood that a firm will diversify into that target industry"]
definition: A firm's entry into a four-digit SIC industry in which it had no operating facility before 1998; the dependent variable captures whether a given firm-industry combination was realized during the 1998-2003 period.

name: CEO restricted stock value relative to reference point
authors_terms: ["restricted stock value relative to the reference point", "relative restricted stock value", "negative deviation from prior CEO restricted stock values", "positive deviation from prior CEO restricted stock values", "negative deviation context", "positive deviation context"]
definition: The paper considers how compensation values compare with the prior year's values, that is, whether compensation values are higher or lower than the prior year values. A negative deviation exists when the CEO's current restricted stock value is less than its previous value, and a positive deviation when it is greater.

name: CEO restricted stock value
authors_terms: ["absolute value of restricted stock", "absolute levels of restricted stock", "CEO restricted stock value"]
definition: Restricted stock is stock shares with sale restrictions of linear payoff function. The CEO restricted stock value was measured as the aggregate market value of restricted stock held by the CEO at fiscal year end.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D spending is generally conceptualized as a risky organizational decision involving highly uncertain investments that may or may not pay off over the long term. R&D intensity was measured as R&D investments in millions of U.S. dollars divided by the firm's annual sales.

name: CEO duality
definition: Duality characterizes CEO power and authority; it is regarded as reflecting CEO power, which allows CEOs to pursue actions consistent with shareholders' interests or engage in self-interest satisfaction. CEO duality is dummy-coded 1 if the CEO also holds the position of board chairperson.

name: Board vigilance
definition: Board vigilance represents the board's influence and monitoring level. A vigilant board generally constitutes a larger number of non-management outside directors who also have greater ownership of the firm in terms of shares and stock options.

name: Attention allocation
authors_terms: ["attention allocation", "decision to allocate attention", "allocating attention to a problem"]
definition: Attention allocation involves the focusing of time and effort on a stimulus. We focus on deliberate decisions to allocate attention to solving particular problems, as manifested by whether or not an individual posts a response to a problem in an online discussion forum.

name: Provider-problem expertise matching
authors_terms: ["provider - problem expertise matching", "expertise matching", "provider - problem expertise match"]
definition: Prior research suggests that a provider who can offer expertise that more closely matches the expertise required by a focal problem will be more likely to decide to allocate attention to that problem. Our measure of expertise matching was constructed by capturing how similar the keywords in the provider's expertise description were to the keywords in the focal problem.

name: Problem length
definition: Longer problems take up more space on the screen, dominating a provider's field of vision and crowding out other stimuli. To measure problem length, we counted the number of words in each problem posted to the forum.

name: Problem breadth
definition: Broader problems are more likely to touch on a domain of expertise of interest to a provider, offering a hook that captures the provider's attention. To measure problem breadth, we computed the extent to which there was variety in the domains of expertise addressed in the problem.

name: Problem novelty
definition: More novel problems can attract attention as a result of distinctiveness effects. Our measure of problem novelty captures how different the focal problem is from problems previously posted to the forum.

name: Problem crowding
authors_terms: ["problem crowding", "number of concurrently posted problems", "competing problems", "concurrent problems"]
definition: A central feature of the context that can be expected to influence the allocation of attention to a focal problem is problem crowding, in the form of the number of other problems concurrently posted to the forum.

name: Activist confidence in tone
definition: Confidence in tone is the articulated quality of being certain of one's abilities or of having trust in oneself, one's plans, or the future one predicts; a high clout score indicates that the author is speaking from the perspective of high expertise and is confident. The authors propose that activist investors who convey their concerns and demands with high confidence in their letters are likely to be perceived as more knowledgeable and competent by the firm's other shareholders.

name: Campaign success
definition: We measure campaign success by how successful activists are in having their demands met. Campaign success is measured as the number of demands that the target firm agreed to divided by the total number of demands issued by the activist.

name: Activist prior campaign success
authors_terms: ["activist prior campaign success", "prior campaign success", "activist campaign success"]
definition: We assess activist prior campaign success, including all campaigns launched in the previous three years. In line with our dependent variable, activist prior campaign success is operationalized as the number of demands met divided by the total number of demands made.

name: Multiple activists
authors_terms: ["multiple activists", "multiple activist engagement", "number of activists engaged in the campaign"]
definition: In the majority of campaigns, a firm is targeted by only one activist investor; however, other activist investors can also take a stake in the target firm after a lead activist has launched the campaign. When multiple activists have taken a stake in the target firm, it represents a different informational context than that of a solo-activist campaign.

name: Ship jumping
definition: The phenomenon of jumping ship, which we define as exit prior to an impending failure.

name: Firm failure
definition: Failed banks are public and private Texas banks that received FDIC intervention between 1 January 1985 and 31 December 1990; for each failed bank a matching non-failed bank was identified based upon geographic proximity and bank asset size.

name: Employment consequences
definition: The consequences that executives stigmatized by failure incur that affect their careers, measured as two dependent variables: demotion and city change, both of which represent penalties from an employment perspective.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
definition: Start-ups initiated by founders with relevant prior work experience but no financial or ownership links to their prior employer. The authors exclude spinoffs, that is, firms started with the involvement of the established firm.

name: Inventor-assessed patent value
authors_terms: ["patent value as assessed by the inventor", "assessed value of the invention", "high patent value as assessed by the inventor", "value of the patented knowledge"]
definition: The value of the patented knowledge as perceived by the focal inventor; the authors define this value as the inventor's estimate of the general monetary worth of the patent in the market.

name: Firm-assessed patent value
authors_terms: ["patent value as assessed by the firm", "value as assessed by the parent firm", "high patent value as assessed by the firm"]
definition: The value of the patented knowledge as assessed by the parent firm. If the firm believes that the invention is promising, and products or services based on this invention can reach a larger market, it is likely to invest in protecting the patent in multiple jurisdictions.

name: Internal commercialization
authors_terms: ["internal commercialization of the patent", "used internally for commercial purposes", "internal use of the focal patent"]
definition: Whether the incumbent firm uses the knowledge that the inventor created and that now resides within its boundaries, that is, whether it is developing and marketing products or services using the knowledge that the inventor initially created.

name: Patent licensing
authors_terms: ["patent licensing", "licensing of the focal patent", "licensed out by the incumbent firm to third parties"]
definition: Whether the incumbent firm licensed the patent to third parties; a licensee obtains access to the technology because it hopes to commercially exploit it.

name: Patent interdependence
authors_terms: ["patent interdependence", "interdependent with other patents held by the firm", "interdependence with other patents"]
definition: Whether the inventor's patent is interdependent with other patents held by the firm. Knowledge tends to diffuse throughout the organization, and various knowledge components residing in the firm are potentially interdependent, so the complementary ingredients may be necessary to utilize the focal knowledge.

name: Technological breadth
authors_terms: ["number of technological domains", "technological breadth", "classified in more technological classes"]
definition: Knowledge that is broader and covers multiple technological domains requires more complementary resources for its exploitation. A patent that covers multiple technological domains, even if not employed by the firm, likely overlaps with other patents that this firm holds.

name: Informal competition
authors_terms: ["informal competition", "competition from informal (unregistered) firms", "practices of competitors in the informal sector"]
definition: Competitive pressure from informal firms, defined as firms that 'produce and sell legal goods and services, yet they remain unregistered with government authorities, allowing them to avoid legal requirements such as taxes and regulations'; the authors rely on the definition of informal firms as 'businesses that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services.'

name: New product development
authors_terms: ["new product development", "NPD", "introduced new products or services", "upgraded an existing product line or service"]
definition: Activities that represent some level of newness in the firm's offerings (a totally new product/service and a new version of an existing product/service) relative to continuing to sell existing products.

name: Formal competition
authors_terms: ["formal competition", "competition from other formal firms", "obstacle level presented by formal competitors"]
definition: Competition from other formally registered firms, described as 'another significant issue vying for attention' in the firm's competitive context; formally registered firms are more likely to see other formally registered firms as closer rivals.

name: Irregular payment prevalence
authors_terms: ["irregular payments", "prevalence of irregular payments to regulatory officials", "bribery", "irregular 'additional payments or gifts'"]
definition: The prevalence in the institutional environment of the nonmarket response of engaging in corruption activities, which include activities such as bribes and irregular payments to government officials.

name: Regulatory optimism
definition: The level of optimism formal firm managers have about the regulatory environment, i.e., respondents who rate the regulatory environment more optimistically than predicted by industry, country, and amount of time dedicated to addressing regulations.

name: Hierarchical similarity
definition: The similarity between an ideator's and an evaluator's positions in the organizational hierarchy, which provides specific cues about an ideator and may distort evaluators' decisions. Individuals on a similar hierarchical level face similar challenges regarding their tasks, sources of pressure and career aspirations, and are therefore more likely to empathize with one another.

name: Idea evaluation
authors_terms: ["idea evaluation", "idea selection", "favorable idea evaluation", "overvaluation of ideas"]
definition: Evaluators' assessment of proposed ideas in the crowdfunding contest; the main dependent variable, Idea selection, captures whether or not an evaluator invested any money into a given idea.

name: Lateral closeness
definition: The degree of lateral closeness, that is, the horizontal dimension of the organizational structure, measured as the horizontal proximity between any given creator–evaluator pair. From smaller to larger units, the organization was structured into departments, business units, and divisions.

name: Idea novelty
definition: Novel ideas differ more from existing solutions than more conventional ideas, and their value is harder to assess. It is measured with the content distance between the proposed idea and previous innovation projects at Alpha.

name: Hierarchy-based homophily
definition: A form of homophily for which organizational hierarchy is the source, leading to preferential idea evaluation based on hierarchical similarity. It represents a source of identification: it elicits feelings of liking and 'sharing the same fate' among hierarchical peers, based on the assumption of similar roles, pressures, and career trajectories in an organization.

name: Ownership structure
authors_terms: ["ownership structure", "ownership configuration", "ownership conditions", "externally-controlled firms", "management-controlled firms", "ownership category"]
definition: In this paper we focus on the two contrasting ownership configurations most prevalent in prior research on large firms: (1) the externally-controlled firm, which has at least one major shareholder who is not a manager; in this firm, shareholder vigilance is presumed great; (2) the management-controlled firm, which has no single major shareholder; thus shareholder vigilance is presumed minimal.

name: CEO pay change
authors_terms: ["change in CEO pay", "CEO pay raises", "pay adjustments", "Δ CEO Pay", "annual percentage changes in CEO pay"]
definition: We examine annual percentage changes in CEO pay, much as any employee thinks of 'raises', rather than examining the absolute level of CEO pay in a given year. This approach is particularly suited to our focus on pay adjustments.

name: Change in firm sales
authors_terms: ["change in sales", "Δ Sales", "change in size", "change in corporate sales"]
definition: Change in sales in year t (using net revenues as reported in COMPUSTAT) was calculated by dividing the increase (or decrease) in sales from year t - 1 to t by firm sales for the year t - 1.

name: Change in economic returns
authors_terms: ["change in economic returns", "profitability", "return on equity (ROE)", "Δ ROE", "changes in profitability"]
definition: Profitability was assessed as return on equity (ROE), a measure used in several earlier studies of CEO pay. Because ROE could be negative, change in ROE could not be computed as a proportion; hence, the increase (or decrease) in ROE from year t - 1 to t served as the measure.

name: Shareholder returns
authors_terms: ["shareholder returns", "stock return measures", "Δ Shareholder returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Shareholder returns were computed by dividing the sum of the change in stock price and dividends paid during the year by the stock price at the beginning of the year.

name: Industry CEO pay change
authors_terms: ["change in industry pay", "Δ Industry pay", "change in CEO pay in the industry", "industry pay trends", "industrywide pay trends"]
definition: Industry pay was determined by averaging the pay of all CEOs in each respective industry sample each year. Change in industry pay was calculated by dividing the increase (or decrease) in industry pay from year t - 1 to t by the level of industry pay for the year t - 1.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Tenure as CEO was measured as the number of years an individual had been chief executive as of year t. To the extent that an executive's power, mobility, and motives evolve over his or her tenure, a dynamic, time-based examination of CEO pay would seem essential.

name: Internal CEO succession
authors_terms: ["new insider CEO", "new CEOs promoted from within the firm", "internal arrivals to the CEO job", "internally promoted CEOs"]
definition: New insider CEOs were CEOs for whom year t was their first year in the position, but not in the firm.

name: External CEO succession
authors_terms: ["new outsider CEO", "new CEOs hired from outside the firm", "outside hires", "externally hired CEOs"]
definition: New outsider CEOs were new to the firm entirely in year t.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["external stock concentration", "continuous measure of stock concentration", "percent of stock held by the single largest nonofficer shareholder", "continuous measure of ownership dispersion"]
definition: As a partial exploration, limited by the data available, we examined the effects, on CEO pay, of a continuous measure of stock concentration: the percent of stock held by the single largest nonofficer shareholder. This is not the only potentially relevant concentration measure that could be used, but it is most analagous to our categoric scheme, simply without a cutoff.

name: Demand variation
definition: The magnitude of variation in demand, which the authors conceptually and empirically distinguish from its predictability. In the airline setting it is the fluctuation over time of demand for flights between two given cities.

name: Strategic flexibility
definition: Flexible firms employ production technologies and organizational procedures to enable quick reaction to environmental change. In the airline industry flexibility is achieved by being able to change route capacity quickly through the reassignment of different types of airplanes, captured by the number of different aircraft types an airline operates.

name: Market entry
definition: Entry into a new market is defined as an airline offering their service on a route for the first time; the dependent variable for each carrier-route combination takes value zero as long as the airline has not yet entered the market and value one in the month of market entry.

name: Demand unpredictability
definition: The share of demand variation that is not driven by recurring patterns such as seasonality and overall trends; the authors call the share of demand variation driven by those factors predictable, while other changes in demand patterns are not so easily explained and will therefore be labeled unpredictable.

name: Creative imaginativeness
definition: 'Creative imaginativeness' is the cognitive skill to envision something that cannot be or is not currently being observed for the purposes of novel, original, artistic, or innovative creation.

name: Social imaginativeness
definition: 'Social imaginativeness' is a cognitive skill with which one envisions something that cannot be or is not currently being observed for the purposes of taking the perspective of others, seeing and feeling the world from another's frame of reference, or reading the desires, intentions, beliefs, and emotions of others.

name: Practical imaginativeness
definition: 'Practical imaginativeness' is a cognitive skill to envision something that cannot be or is not currently being observed for the purposes of planning, organizing, analyzing, or managing information, resources, or projects.

name: New venture idea quantity
definition: Generating ideas represents the diverging aspect of the creative problem-solving process and consists of generating as many new venture ideas as possible.

name: New venture idea quality
definition: We view idea quality as ideas possessing novelty and usefulness; consistent with prior research, idea quality was viewed as the combination of originality and feasibility.

name: Family-to-work conflict
definition: Defined as the extent to which one's work responsibilities are made more difficult by family responsibilities, FWC can refer to any situation, positive or negative, that distracts a person from his or her job that occurs away from work, such as care for a sick parent, a divorce, the purchase of a home, or the birth of a child.

name: Decision-making comprehensiveness
definition: Strategic decision-making comprehensiveness refers to the extent to which firm leaders seek out and process information from the external environment in order to make high-quality, informed strategic decisions. It pertains to the amount of exhaustiveness and inclusivity in searching for information using 'multiple approaches, multiple courses of action, and multiple decision criteria in evaluating and selecting alternative courses of action.'

name: Job engagement
definition: Job engagement represents a 'relatively enduring state of mind referring to the simultaneous investment of personal energies in the experience of performance of work' and holistically accounts for individuals' simultaneous investment of cognitive, emotional, and physical energy into their work roles.

name: Firm performance
definition: Objective data on firm financial performance was obtained from the consortium in the form of a standard accounting-based measure, return on assets (ROA).

name: Replicating unit restocking performance
authors_terms: ["replicating unit performance", "nonpilot performance", "focal store performance", "nonpilot store performance"]
definition: The performance metric - specifically meant to measure the overall efficacy of the new restocking practice - was the errors in the end-of-night reconciliation process to identify out-of-stock items. Missedscan captures the restocking team's ability to execute its overall task: ensuring that items are where they belong and that out-of-stock items are promptly reordered.

name: Template unit performance
authors_terms: ["template unit performance", "template experience", "pilot performance", "pilot store performance", "Lagged pilot missedscan"]
definition: The prior performance of the district pilot store, which is disclosed at the beginning of the week along with all the other district stores' missedscans. Templates act as outside models by which prospective replicating units can observe a new practice in action.

name: Own experience
authors_terms: ["own experience", "learning from own experience", "experiential learning", "own prior performance", "Lagged own missedscan"]
definition: Implementing a new practice triggers experiential learning and performance related to the practice improves as employees learn what problems exist and how to solve them. Lagged own missedscan captures the extent to which a store's prior week restocking performance can be used to predict this week's performance.

name: Performance relative to the template
authors_terms: ["Worse pilot", "performance superior to template performance", "superior relative performance", "perceived quality of the template's performance"]
definition: Worse pilot is an indicator variable equal to 1 if the focal store's restocking performance is better - that is, fewer missedscan errors - than that of its pilot, and equals 0 otherwise. The perceived quality of the template's performance is distinguished most easily by comparing last week's raw performance values for a district's pilot and nonpilot stores.

name: Density of de novo producers
authors_terms: ["density of de novo firms", "de novo density", "N°(t) to record de novo producers"]
definition: The number of organizations in a market that were founded to pursue the focal activity, i.e., de novo entrants, which the authors argue possess perceptually focused identities because they operate mainly in the focal market.

name: Geographic agglomeration of producers
authors_terms: ["density of geographically agglomerated producers", "density of each geographic agglomeration", "geographic agglomeration"]
definition: The number of producers of a market located in a geographic place with an identity related to the activity, such as the Boston Area (Route 128), California, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

name: Geographic agglomeration of de novo producers
authors_terms: ["density of geographically agglomerated de novo producers", "Bay Area de novo firms", "California de novo firms"]
definition: The number of de novo producers of a market that are also located in a geographic place with an identity related to the activity, combining the accretion and the attention-narrowing processes.

name: Product density
definition: The total number of products of a particular kind on the market in any given year, offered as the alternative basis for collective identities to be built around products rather than organizations.

name: Organizational founding rate
definition: The rate at which new organizations enter the focal production activity, modeled as the count of array producers entering the market per quarter.

name: Organizational mortality rate
definition: The rate at which organizations in the focal activity disband or exit to another industry, expressed as the instantaneous disbanding/exit rate for a firm.

name: Establishment of an organizational form
authors_terms: ["establishment of an organizational form", "form emergence", "form status", "become an organizational form"]
definition: A potential external identity code becomes an organizational form when it is codified, socially embedded, and sanctioned and taken for granted by outsiders, so that it applies to multiple organizations and persists over time.

name: Perceived-latent interdependence deviation
authors_terms: ["deviation between perceived and latent interunit interdependence", "perceptual error in the assessment of interunit task interdependence", "perceived-latent interdependence deviation"]
definition: The deviation between the unit manager's perceived interunit task interdependence and the latent (optimal feasible) interdependence of the same dyadic interface; the authors describe it as perceptual error in the assessment of interunit task interdependence.

name: Optimal-observed integration mode deviation
authors_terms: ["deviation between optimal and observed integration modes", "optimal-observed integration mode deviation"]
definition: The deviation between the mode of integration theoretically predicted (optimal) for a dyadic unit interface and the mode of integration actually observed for that interface.

name: Dyadic coordination performance
definition: A dependent variable that refers to the quality of coordination between interdependent units at the dyadic level of analysis; it is ostensibly a dimension of performance but is exclusive to the dyadic unit interface.

name: Latent interunit task interdependence
definition: Latent interdependence is the potential inherent interunit task interdependence and is defined as the optimal feasible interdependence, based on either actual task precedence constraints or optimality in task interrelationships.

name: Perceived interunit task interdependence
authors_terms: ["perceived interdependence", "operational assumptions of interunit task interdependence"]
definition: Each unit manager's recorded perception of interunit interdependence for each dyadic interface, ranging from no interdependence to pooled, sequential, and reciprocal interdependence, which revealed the manager's operational assumptions on interunit task interdependence.

name: Observed modes of integration
definition: The modes of integration actually in use for a dyadic unit interface, including standard operating procedures, databases and hierarchy, electronic/paper routing, phone/individual meetings, liaisons, and meetings with multiple staff including temporary teams.

name: Optimal modes of integration
authors_terms: ["optimal modes of integration", "theoretically predicted (optimal) modes of integration"]
definition: The modes of integration theoretically predicted as optimal for a dyadic unit interface, identified based on the interdependence level of that interface and the graduated sequence of modes of integration.

name: Information processing patterns of integration
definition: Network characteristics that describe and operationalize the information processing patterns of integration across functional units, including directional connectivity, openness, reciprocity, multiplexity, isolate levels, and centrality.

name: Technology convergence
definition: Technology closeness is related to whether the technological competences required in one submarket can be leveraged across submarkets, thus affecting the degree to which industry incumbents can respond to disruption by entrants from the technology side.

name: Market convergence
definition: Market closeness is related to whether the customer competences required in one submarket can be leveraged across submarkets, thus affecting the degree to which industry incumbents can respond to disruption by entrants from the market side.

name: Continued fab operations
authors_terms: ["continued plant operations", "success", "likelihood to exit or reposition through fab closure"]
definition: The success of industry incumbents or entrants in this paper corresponds to continued plant operations in a submarket - not survival at the industry level in general.

name: Incumbent status
definition: Industry incumbents are operationalized - in line with their higher inertia compared to entrants - as firms that own more than one fab in the industry. Industry incumbents (entrants) are characterized by less (more) flexibility in adjusting to changes in the industry structure.

name: Technological competences
definition: Technological competences refer to the ability to use certain technologies to bring a product or service into existence, such as capabilities involved in developing and manufacturing products by using certain process technologies.

name: Customer competences
definition: Customer competences refer to the ability to address different customer needs with these offerings, such as capabilities involved in developing product features, developing market applications, and understanding customers' needs.

name: Debt ratio
definition: Building from existing work in finance, the authors use the amount of a firm's outstanding debt as a measure of financial constraint and resource pressure. Higher levels of debt (as opposed to equity) suggest that the firm has already exhausted available avenues to acquire further capital and faces a more binding resource constraint.

name: Small institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["small institutional ownership", "small, transient institutional ownership", "transient investors"]
definition: Institutions with short-term orientation and high portfolio turnover; the authors define small institutional ownership as the sum of institutional shares with less than five percent of a firm's outstanding shares. Their limited equity share permits quick selling in response to negative news.

name: Block institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["block institutional ownership", "block investors", "large investors with long-term orientation"]
definition: The total percentage of firm shares owned by investors with more than five percent of a firm's outstanding shares. Block institutional investors provide careful monitoring of portfolio firms' operations and attenuate negative market reactions to missing the performance target.

name: Performance target aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["aggressive performance targets", "aggressiveness of performance targets", "upward striving", "downward striving"]
definition: Consistent with previous literature in finance and accounting, the authors impute the aggressiveness of performance targets by comparing them with realized outcomes; an earnings target above the realized value is considered an upward-striven, aggressive performance target, whereas a target below realized performance reflects downward striving.

name: Tie strength
definition: Strong ties imply frequent interaction and the rendering of reciprocal favors, whereas weak ties indicate infrequent interaction lacking affective content. Tie strength is measured as the closeness and interaction frequency of a relationship between two parties.

name: Bridging ties
definition: Bridging ties, social ties spanning between disconnected networks, facilitate opportunity identification by providing nonredundant information restricted within each network. Bridging ties have been conceptualized as nonredundancy.

name: Individualism-collectivism
definition: The IC dimension has to do with the perception of the self and its positioning vis-a-vis other members of society and other social groupings. Collectivist cultures do not separate the individual from his/her respective groups, whereas individualist cultures cherish the individual and his/her aspirations.

name: Opportunity recognition
definition: Opportunity identification is a cognitive process through which individuals strive to connect the dots between changes, events, and trends so as to come up with new product or service ideas.

name: Strategy uniqueness
definition: They classify strategy uniqueness as the (dis)similarity of a firm's strategy relative to other firms in its primary SIC industry (Litov et al., 2012).

name: Dedicated institutional investor influence
definition: Investors with large, long-term holdings concentrated in a few firms are called dedicated investors (Bushee, 1998; Eccles, Ioannou, & Serafeim, 2014; Porter, 1992). Dedicated institutional investors are characterized by a low portfolio turnover and focused portfolio holdings. They actively manage their investments by following a long-term investment strategy (Shi et al., 2017).

name: Hard-to-value industry
definition: The context of a firm is hard to value if the firm is affiliated with an industry in which evaluators have great difficulties to find a consistent firm valuation (Humphery-Jenner, 2014).

name: Stakeholder investment
authors_terms: ["stakeholder investments", "investments in stakeholders", "investments in primary and secondary stakeholders", "stakeholder management"]
definition: The firm's investments in its stakeholder groups, which the authors measure with Sustainalytics' proprietary aggregate scores. A company is evaluated according to about 200 points of information that cover the four main primary stakeholder groups (capital providers, employees, customers and suppliers) and two major secondary ones (local communities and environmental groups).

name: Firm performance
definition: Financial performance is operationalized using the industry-adjusted ROE lagged one year (ROEaj), defined as net income over total firm equity to control for possible industry effects on firm performance. Two alternative definitions of performance are used: high performance (P) and very high performance (Y).

name: Industry differentiation
authors_terms: ["industry differentiation", "level of differentiation in the firm's industry", "low differentiation industries", "high differentiation industries"]
definition: The level of differentiation among competitors in the industry in which the firm competes, which the authors argue mediates the firm's effort to differentiate itself through above-average stakeholder investments. The potential of stakeholder management to differentiate a firm is arguably higher in an otherwise minimally differentiated industry.

name: Firm innovation
definition: The extent to which the firm differentiates itself through innovative products rather than through stakeholder investments. Companies with superior, highly innovative products need offer little other reason for customers to choose them, whereas less innovative firms are able to differentiate themselves by investing in stakeholders above industry average levels.

name: National legal system
definition: The country's comparative legal and institutional context, which shows significant differences across countries in the level of adoption of stakeholder-oriented policies and the levels of legal enforcement. European corporations have significantly higher corporate social responsibility levels than U.S. corporations, driven partly by tougher EU regulation that requires higher standards.

name: Exchange value uncertainty
definition: A situation in which there is uncertainty about the value of future exchanges with a certain actor, whether or not there is a propensity to act opportunistically.

name: Willingness to switch exchange partners
authors_terms: ["willingness to exchange with new partners", "willingness to switch", "movement out of committed relationships", "social mobility", "propensity to switch partners"]
definition: The buyer's decision to accept an offer from a seller other than the incumbent seller with whom the buyer transacted in the previous period; the authors treat this decision as equivalent to movement out of an ongoing exchange.

name: Commitment to exchange partner
definition: The creation of committed relationships means repeated, long-term exchanges among the same actors, which establish an expectation of future exchange and a history of past exchange.

name: Partner cooperation
authors_terms: ["willingness to cooperate", "sellers' propensity to cooperate", "delivery of high quality", "cooperation"]
definition: Sellers' propensity to act cooperatively, i.e., to deliver high quality, the counterpart of opportunism, which committed relationships and repeated exchange are expected to curtail.

name: Contract enforcement
definition: A formal mechanism that promotes exchange among strangers; in the experiment the contract automatically forces sellers to deliver high quality whenever they choose low quality, a type of contract referred to in the legal literature as specific performance.

name: Contract use
authors_terms: ["use of contracts", "choice of contracts", "adopt formal contracts", "contract offered"]
definition: The buyer's voluntary choice to offer a formal contract to the seller in a given exchange; because the contract holds for a single period only, buyers are free to change their use of contract enforcement across experimental rounds.

name: General trust
definition: General trust refers to the expectation that people in general will not act opportunistically even when they have the opportunity to do so; it is independent of contractual provisions or controls in an exchange and is a personal trait.

name: Knowledge-based trust
definition: Knowledge-based trust refers to the expectation that familiar people, i.e., people with whom an individual has interacted in the past, will not act opportunistically; it is trust that emerges from experience with a particular exchange partner.

name: Firm wrongdoing
authors_terms: ["firm wrongdoing", "a firm's wrongdoing", "the magnitude of a firm's wrongdoing", "product recalls"]
definition: Wrongdoing is defined as firm behaviors that place a firm's stakeholders at risk and violate stakeholders' expectations of societal norms and general standards of conduct. In this study product recall announcements are treated as an example of negative violations of social expectations, and the magnitude of a firm's own wrongdoing is captured by the number of toys it recalls.

name: Industry wrongdoing
authors_terms: ["industry wrongdoing", "the magnitude of wrongdoing in a firm's industry", "wrongdoing by other firms in its industry"]
definition: Wrongdoing committed by the focal firm's peers: firms belonging to industries whose members engage in wrongdoing can suffer from negative spillovers and may be perceived as being "guilty by association."

name: Tenor of media coverage
authors_terms: ["tenor of media coverage", "the tenor of media coverage about a firm"]
definition: The media frame stories and influence stakeholders' perceptions about firms through their use of positive or negative language. Following prior research, the authors measure the tenor of media coverage about a focal firm as the relative prevalence of positive over negative articles, feedback, or words.

name: Technical actions
definition: Actions that have the potential to address the causes of wrongdoing and thus attract the media and stakeholders' attention to the internal processes of a firm.

name: Ceremonial actions
definition: Actions that have the potential to positively alter impressions about the firm and deflect media and stakeholders' attention away from the causes of wrongdoing; they do not directly address the cause of a recall but instead highlight positive characteristics of a firm.

name: Institutional barriers to growth
definition: A change that lowers institutional barriers to growth facilitates the scale-up of a firm after entry. Institutional barriers to growth are frequently due to industrial policies that create an uneven playing field by directing resources toward established firms, state-owned firms, and foreign-invested firms (leaving fewer resources for growing ventures).

name: Human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "human capital index", "higher human capital individuals", "lower human capital individuals"]
definition: High human capital individuals are individuals who possess the productivity-enhancing skills, connections, and knowledge. Individuals with higher human capital are those with greater productivity-enhancing skills and knowledge.

name: Entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurship", "rate of entrepreneurship", "likelihood of founding", "propensity for entrepreneurship"]
definition: The decision to pursue entrepreneurship can be thought of as the choice between staying in the labor market versus entering entrepreneurship, based on the potential earnings in the labor market and the potential earnings in entrepreneurship.

name: Firm size
definition: To test Hypothesis 3, I measure firm size by latest employees, which is measured in the most recent year the firm was still in operation and logged to reduce skew.

name: Industry growth
authors_terms: ["industry growth", "industry growth rate", "growth rate of the industry", "high growth industries", "low growth industries"]
definition: An industry's growth rate has been a key component of market attractiveness for both new ventures and established firms, even to the point of being the sole measure of market attractiveness of the Boston Consulting Group's product portfolio matrix. Growth has served as an indicator of disequilibrium, a condition favorably associated with entry and as an indicator of industry evolution.

name: Strategic breadth
authors_terms: ["strategic breadth", "breadth of strategy", "breadth", "broad breadth strategy", "focus strategy", "focus strategies"]
definition: The ventures were classified into one of four groups based on the narrowness or broadness of their strategy and on the growth rate of the industry segment each had entered. Strategic breadth was measured with five survey items: range of products, broadness of markets, number of market segments, number of customers, and number of distribution channels.

name: Return on sales
definition: Return on sales, one of the two objective performance measures used in the study; the authors state that profitability measures have been widely used in studies which assessed small firm and new venture financial performance.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["sales growth", "sales growth rate", "sales growth rates", "changes in sales"]
definition: Sales growth rate, one of the two objective performance measures used in the study; 'changes in sales' was reported as overwhelmingly the most popular operationalization of new venture performance.

name: Scale of entry
authors_terms: ["large scale entry", "scale of entry", "larger, more aggressive scale", "large, more aggressive scale", "aggressive entry"]
definition: Entering on a large, more aggressive scale by which the entrant may be able to both signal its commitment to the market and erect barriers to entry which make the segment less appealing, no matter how attractive the growth rate.

name: Capital from outside investors
definition: Capital attracted from outside investors such as venture capitalists, who consider high growth markets to be more attractive targets for investment.
