name: New product development
definition: Investment in product development; in earlier high growth stages there is a higher rate of technological change in product design, consequently ventures would be expected to invest more heavily in product development.

name: Patents and proprietary knowledge
authors_terms: ["ownership of patents or other proprietary knowledge", "patents", "proprietary processes", "patent/proprietary positions"]
definition: Ownership of patents or other proprietary knowledge; patents are described as a logical outgrowth of investment in product development in high growth stages.

name: Innovation in manufacturing processes
definition: Emphasis on innovation in manufacturing processes; as the industry growth rate slows and the industry becomes mature, investment would shift to process design.

name: Specialty products
definition: A prescription to new ventures pursuing focus strategies has been to develop specialized products and to compete in market segments which require high levels of customer service.

name: Customer service
definition: Competing in market segments which require high levels of customer service, a prescription associated with focus strategies.

name: Premium pricing
definition: Specialty products are often associated with premium pricing policies, thus allowing the venture to compete less on the basis of cost.

name: Low-cost concern
definition: Emphasis on competing on the basis of low cost; new ventures adopting a focus strategy may have difficulty competing on cost since they would typically lack economies of scale.

name: Advertising and promotion expenses
authors_terms: ["advertising and promotion expenses", "advertising and promotion expense"]
definition: Since firms competing through broader strategies would be expected to have a wider range of products, more channels of distribution to manage, more segments and customers, and broader markets, it seems reasonable that there would be a positive relationship between broad strategic breadth and advertising and promotion expense.

name: Top management marketing expertise
authors_terms: ["dominance of marketing expertise in their top management team", "top management marketing expertise"]
definition: Marketing expertise would be expected to be an important competency for developing additional channels of distribution.

name: New channels of distribution
authors_terms: ["developing new channels of distribution", "new channels of distribution", "new channels"]
definition: Additional channels of distribution would likewise increase advertising and promotion expense and are expected to be part of broadly defined strategies.

name: Brand identification and name recognition
authors_terms: ["brand identification and name recognition", "brand name identification and name recognition", "brand ID"]
definition: Emphasis on brand identification and name recognition would enhance the new venture's ability to market multiple products in numerous market segments.

name: Forward integration
definition: Like advertising and promotion, forward integration is a means by which firms achieve closer contact and communication with their markets.

name: Control board chair orientation
definition: A board chair exhibits a control orientation when he or she views monitoring, evaluating, and disciplining the CEO to be fundamental attributes of his or her working relationship with the CEO.

name: Collaboration board chair orientation
definition: Consistent with Sundaramurthy and Lewis's (2003) definition of a collaboration governance approach, a board chair exhibits a collaboration orientation when he or she views advising and guiding the CEO, and/or reducing the CEO's job demands to be fundamental attributes of his or her working relationship with the CEO.

name: Past firm performance
authors_terms: ["past performance", "past firm performance", "prior firm performance", "lagged performance"]
definition: Both articles argued that past performance determines a board's optimal leadership arrangement, but their arguments produce conflicting predictions as to the performance effects of the control and collaboration orientations. It is at the extreme levels of past performance that the board chair orientations become most impactful.

name: Profitability growth
definition: The dependent variable of interest is profitability growth, operationalized using two common measures: growth in return-on-assets (ΔROA) and growth in return-on-sales (ΔROS).

name: Financial resources
definition: Available funding has received little attention in the RBV, but represents a critical tangible financial resource. Financial resources, in the form of funds that are allocated to a task or project, are associated with the highest levels of fungibility.

name: Brand resources
definition: The names that a firm attaches to its products in order to attract and retain consumers can also represent a useful intangible brand resource. Each brand is typically developed to create a stronger tie or association between a target customer group and products that are offered by a firm within a well-defined category, so managers have some, but not unfettered, flexibility in how they can build upon and extract more value from these resources.

name: Human resources
definition: Employee talents have been given considerable emphasis as a key form of human resource; this embedded aptitude or talent among employees, typically reflected in a pattern of their professional accomplishments, often represents a resource that fulfills the criteria of RBV. Employees who demonstrate higher levels of talent are likely to be somewhat specialized, restricting their applicability to a well-defined area of expertise.

name: Managerial experience
authors_terms: ["managerial experience", "experience", "experience as a producer", "producer experience", "prior experience"]
definition: The ability of managers to generate value from the use of resources stems from the experience that they have accumulated in managing these over time. Experience provides a manager with the opportunity to develop deeper knowledge about the nature of the resource, the various benefits it can offer, and the best possible manner in which it can be deployed.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "box office revenue", "total box office revenue"]
definition: We used the total box office revenue generated from the U.S. release of each film as the indicator of financial performance. Although this does not include revenues from other sources, the U.S. box office revenue is the most widely used indicator of financial success for a film in Hollywood.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["environmental uncertainty", "parametric uncertainty", "level of uncertainty", "level of information", "information quality"]
definition: Changing environmental conditions, which Williamson (1985) defines as 'parametric uncertainty' and the authors refer to as environmental uncertainty; such uncertainty limits an organization's ability to plan ahead and causes information asymmetry between the Manager and Workers about the nature of the tasks.

name: Team skill heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["team heterogeneity", "skill specialization", "Worker heterogeneity", "team composition", "team selection", "distance between positions"]
definition: The degree of horizontal differentiation in team knowledge, which the Manager controls through the selection of Worker specializations; the Manager selects the team heterogeneity (θ1, θ2) before knowing the exact tasks to be completed.

name: Delegation of decision rights
authors_terms: ["delegation", "delegation of authority", "allocation of decision rights", "organizational structure", "centralized organization", "decentralized organization"]
definition: The choice of whether the Manager retains the right to reallocate (switch) tasks or delegates that right to the Workers; in a decentralized organization Workers make the task allocation decision by voting to switch tasks or not.

name: Deliberative thinking
definition: The use of slower, more reflective cognition requiring conscious effort and motivation to reach a decision, which Stanovich and West (2000) define as 'system 2' thinking.

name: Risk tolerance
definition: Individuals' attitudes toward risk, which are intimately linked to various economic behaviors; entrepreneurs and managers roughly share risk preferences and generally take more risk than the rest of the population.

name: Project performance
definition: Project performance is a subjective measure of how well a project team is performing relative to the level expected of it, given the particular technical activities on which the team was working. Managers considered, but were not limited to, criteria including schedule, budget, and cost performance; innovativeness; adaptability; and the ability to cooperate with other areas of the organization.

name: Locus of influence over technical details of project work
authors_terms: ["influence over the technical details of their project work", "technical content of project work", "influence over the detailed technical work of engineers", "influence over technical content"]
definition: One of the broad areas of decision making in which both project and functional managers are supposed to be involved: technical decisions regarding project work activities and solution strategies. It is the degree to which project and functional managers are seen to influence the direction or clarification of technical details and solution strategies.

name: Locus of influence over salaries and promotions
authors_terms: ["influence over their salary increases and promotions", "locus of influence over salaries and promotions", "influence over organizational rewards"]
definition: One of the broad areas of decision making in which both project and functional managers are supposed to be involved: the determination of salaries and promotional opportunities. It is the degree to which project and functional managers are seen to control engineers' chances for salary increases and promotions.

name: Locus of influence over personnel assignments
authors_terms: ["influence over personnel assignments", "locus of influence over personnel assignments", "influence over project assignments"]
definition: One of the broad areas of decision making in which both project and functional managers are supposed to be involved: the staffing and organizational assignments of engineers to particular project activities. It is the degree to which project and functional managers are seen to influence engineers' having been selected to work on the project.

name: Locus of organizational influence
authors_terms: ["locus of organizational influence", "perceived locus of organizational influence", "organizational influence", "influence in the overall organization"]
definition: The relative power of project and functional managers within the organization at large, as perceived by the engineers in matrix relationships; managers affect the behaviors and motivations of subordinates not only through leadership directed within the project group but also through their organizational influence outside the project.

name: Layoffs
authors_terms: ["layoffs", "massive layoffs", "number of laid-off workers", "policy-induced layoffs", "laid-off workers"]
definition: Massive layoffs from bankrupt state-owned firms, which reduced the social wellbeing of many citizens and could pose a threat to social stability; measured as the logged number of laid-off workers from the SOEs that went bankrupt in a given year in a province.

name: New industry entry
authors_terms: ["new industry entry", "entry into new industries", "new unrelated industries", "firms' diversification", "unrelated diversification"]
definition: The number of new unrelated industries a firm entered, i.e., industries present in the firm's industry portfolio at t+3 but not at t based on 2-digit SIC codes.

name: Closeness to retirement
authors_terms: ["closeness to retirement", "retiring governor", "retiring party secretary", "career stage", "on one's last political term"]
definition: Provincial-level officials are required to retire at the age of 65 and their political careers are structured as the number of political terms, so that a leader on the last political term approaches retirement and, lacking promotion prospects, prioritizes a peaceful transition to retirement.

name: Collective action intensity
authors_terms: ["collective action intensity", "intense collective actions", "intensity of collective actions", "collective actions"]
definition: The number of instances of labor protests and strikes that took place in the focal province each year; labor mobilization has been the most frequent type of collective action that led to social instability in China in recent years, and the higher the number of such incidents in a province, the more likely the provincial state will respond by prioritizing the social stability goal.

name: Socialist imprint
authors_terms: ["socialist imprint", "socialist legacy", "imprinted with the market mechanisms"]
definition: Firms that had IPOs in the early stage of the market transition were more imprinted with the socialist legacy than those in the later stage, giving them a stronger orientation toward acquiescing to government demands; measured as the number of years between 1990 and the year a firm had an IPO, reverse coded.

name: Industry regulation
definition: Firms operating in highly regulated industries depend on government policies and government-controlled resources for their daily operation and survival, and the government has great power over them as it can alter the rules of the game and shape their competitive environment.

name: Human resource slack
definition: HR slack refers to the accrual of employees in excess of what is required for a firm to maintain its current level of operation; it is defined as employees in excess of a firm's current business requirements.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack represents the accrual of financial resources in excess of a firm's typical holdings at a given level of operations, and is liquid and easily deployed for different purposes.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in a firm's client mix"]
definition: We define strategic change based on compositional changes in a firm's client mix. Strategic change refers to modifications in the orchestration of resources made to improve an organization's alignment with the external environment.

name: Change in human capital investment
authors_terms: ["change in human capital investment", "changes in human capital investment", "human capital investment"]
definition: Human capital reflects the KSAs of a firm's workforce, and firms accumulate human capital through acquisition (i.e., hiring) or internal development; human capital investment is the per-employee financial allocations that a firm makes to salaries, bonuses, and training. The measure of change in human capital investment represents the year-over-year difference in this value.

name: Firm performance
definition: Tobin's q provides a measure of the difference between a firm's market value and the replacement cost of its assets, and captures the value added through resource management as it reflects the premium the capital market will pay for the portfolio of assets possessed by the firm.

name: Departmental influence on strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["influence", "influence on strategic decisions", "departmental influence", "influence on strategic decision making", "intraorganizational influence"]
definition: Influence was defined as '... the ability to affect the outcome of the decision'.

name: Internal organizational power bases
authors_terms: ["power bases", "internal organizational power bases", "internally derived sources of influence", "internal sources of influence", "internal organizational factors"]
definition: Data were also gathered on the composition of each department's influence on strategic decisions attributable to internal organizational factors as represented by the five power bases of Shukla (1977) and Shukla and Leifer (1979). The power bases are position, expert, resource, political and miscellaneous power.

name: Environmental interaction
authors_terms: ["environmental interaction", "boundary spanning roles", "interorganizational boundary spanning", "environmentally derived sources of influence", "environmental sources of influence"]
definition: Environmental interaction was measured in terms of interorganizational boundary spanning using Jemison's (1979b) instrument, which identified three common boundary spanning roles: information acquisition and control, domain determination and interface, and physical input control.

name: Technology
definition: Technology, as used here, refers to the internal organizational processes by which utility is created for the organization's clients. These internal activities will create different demands upon (and thus different interdependencies among) the various departments in the course of their work.

name: System openness
authors_terms: ["open system", "more closed system", "more open system", "environmental interactions"]
definition: Some organizations deliberately try to eliminate outside interference in an attempt to rationalize their internal operations. In contrast, other organizations choose to have or are forced to have a more open system in which their environmental interactions are greater.

name: Economies of scale
authors_terms: ["economies of scale", "scale economies", "firm-specific scale economies", "marginal benefits from increasing their size", "interfirm differences in economies of scale"]
definition: Consistent with conventional usage, we define economies of scale as the marginal improvement in efficiency that a firm experiences as it incrementally increases its size—i.e., the slope of the relationship between a firm's size and its efficiency. Interfirm differences in the slopes of these efficiency frontiers represent interfirm differences in economies of scale.

name: Relative market share
definition: A fund family's relative market share is defined here as the difference between its market share and the industry-wide average market share of all fund families at the same point in time.

name: Fund family age
definition: Family age is included in the second-step model as a predictor of relative market share and as the moderator of both measures of firm-specific scale economies; the paper predicts that as a firm ages, its firm-specific scale economies will become less important as a predictor of its market share relative to competitors.

name: Board independence
definition: Board independence is assessed based on two elements of board structure: the proportion of independent outsiders on the board and the separation of the CEO and chair roles. Agency theory claims that outside board members act as monitors of the managers, reducing the managers' ability to act opportunistically.

name: Separation of CEO and chair roles
authors_terms: ["separation of the CEO and chair roles", "separation", "CEO-chair separation", "separate the roles of CEO and chair"]
definition: One of the two elements of board structure through which board independence is assessed: the separation of the CEO and chair roles, which allows more objective assessment of the performance of the CEO and thus more effective monitoring by the board.

name: Institutional investor new purchase decision
authors_terms: ["new purchase decisions", "Buy", "an investor's decision to add a firm to its portfolio"]
definition: An investor's decision to add a firm to its portfolio that it did not own in the previous quarter. Focusing only on new purchases clearly reveals the preferences of investors and clarifies the causality of the hypothesized relationship by separating the decision to invest in a firm from the possibility of subsequent attempts by investors to compel changes in a firm they already own.

name: Block-holding
definition: A dimension of institutional investors' trading strategy describing the sizes of stakes institutional investors typically take; institutional owners vary in average size of their investments in firms.

name: Turnover
definition: A dimension of institutional investors' trading strategy describing how long institutional investors hold stock; institutional owners vary in the length of time that they usually hold their investments in their portfolios.

name: Institutional investor legal type
definition: Institutional owners are categorized into distinct legal types according to how they are organized and registered; each legal type encounters different institutional pressures that lead to different professional practices.

name: Performance above aspirations
authors_terms: ["above-aspiration performance", "performance above aspirations", "performance above historical aspirations", "performance above social aspirations", "above historical aspirations", "above social aspirations"]
definition: Performance above historical aspirations is the difference between actual performance and aspiration levels when performance exceeds aspirations and is '0' otherwise; the authors followed the same approach to construct their measures of performance above social aspirations and performance below social aspirations, using spline functions.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: a 'personality trait that combines grandiosity, attention seeking, an unrealistically inflated self-view, a need for that self-view to be continuously reinforced through self-regulation, and a general lack of regard for others'

name: Acquisition activity
definition: The number of acquisitions made by a firm in a given year that led to a majority ownership of the target firm. Acquisitions often require a significant reconfiguration of firm resources and are widely studied as a major type of risky organizational change driven by firms' performance relative to aspirations.

name: Breadth of recombination
definition: The extent to which a patent combines multiple classes or subclasses, i.e., what we call the breadth of recombination. It captures the number of USPTO categories being recombined by the focal patent, as indicated by the patent class listed on each patent that the focal patent cites.

name: Organizational recombination experience
definition: The organization's experience with equivalent inventive search. It captures the number of previous instances of the same recombination by the assignee organization, derived from the number of previous patents filed by the focal organization that featured the exact same combination of USPTO classes as the focal patent until the year prior to that when the focal patent was filed.

name: Organizational focus
definition: By focus, we mean a limited diversity of simultaneous search by the organization, such that it commits to one or relatively few types of recombinant projects each year, where each type of recombinant project involves the same set of technological components. It is measured as the extent of concentration on a limited set of recombination types in a given year.

name: Inventive impact
definition: The noteworthiness of innovation-oriented ideas as indicated by their future influence, i.e., knowledge that has been retained and built upon as technology continues to evolve. It is measured by the number of forward citations received by the focal patent.

name: Market identity order
authors_terms: ["market identity order", "interspersion", "ordering of operas in a seasonal opera repertoire", "repertoire ordering"]
definition: The observed ordering of the operas in a seasonal repertoire relative to the ordering that minimizes the conventionality differences between adjacent operas. Holding the size and composition of the opera repertoire constant, a higher market identity order indicates more interspersion in an opera repertoire, whereas a lower market identity order indicates less interspersion in an opera repertoire.

name: Season-ticket sales
definition: The percentage of available tickets that are sold as season tickets, used to measure the appeal of opera companies to season-ticket holders, an audience that prefers conventional performances.

name: Opera critic coverage
authors_terms: ["Opera critics coverage", "critical attention", "critical coverage", "appeal to opera critics"]
definition: Whether a particular opera performed by a particular opera company in a particular year gets critical attention from any of the nine most prominent newspapers covering classical music. Getting attention from opera critics is important because it increases awareness of an opera company and moves the company, its artists, and directors up in the opera status hierarchy.

name: Property-rights protection
definition: The formal protection of property by law, which reduces the risk of infringement and expropriation and lowers the cost for contracting. In China, the property law was the first of its kind in modern history that grants formal protection of private property and, consequently, strengthens the property-rights regime substantially.

name: Private ownership
definition: Firms that are majority owned or ultimately controlled by private entities or individuals, as opposed to state-owned enterprises that are majority owned or ultimately controlled by the government or its agencies. Compared with SOEs, private firms lacked formal or informal institutional protection of their property.

name: Resource investment
authors_terms: ["resource investment", "investment in building resources", "firms' investment in both intangible and tangible assets"]
definition: Firms' investment in building assets, in both tangible and intangible assets, which property-rights protection is argued to encourage by enhancing expected value appropriation from the resource and lowering the uncertainty surrounding appropriability.

name: Intangible asset investment
definition: Intangible assets broadly include knowledge and skills, organizational and personnel resources, and various types of intellectual property rights, and they are an important source of firm capabilities and competitive advantage.

name: Tangible asset investment
authors_terms: ["tangible assets", "fixed assets", "Fixed assets", "investment in tangible assets"]
definition: According to China's accounting standards, fixed assets include buildings, machines, machinery, transportation vehicles, other equipment and instruments, and tools that firms can use for more than one year and are related to firms' production and operation.

name: External equity financing
definition: Equity financing obtained from external investors; strengthening property-rights protection secures equity investors' value appropriation from their investment by reducing the chance of value expropriation by the focal firm and lowering the contracting cost in equity investment.

name: Long-term debt financing
definition: Debt financing obtained from creditors in the form of long-term debt, which excludes short-term debt (less than one year) because short-term debt is used for firms' temporary financial needs rather than resource investment purposes.

name: Organizational founding rate
definition: Entries are assumed to be a realization of an arrival process, and the dependent variable takes on only integer values. The paper studies founding rates in the Dutch accounting industry at the population and the subpopulation levels of analysis.

name: Local density
definition: The authors created focal provincial density and focal provincial density squared to estimate the impact of processes of legitimation (through the linear effect) and competition (through the squared effect) at the province level.

name: National density
authors_terms: ["NationalDensity", "NationalDensity2", "density-dependence processes measured at the national level", "national density"]
definition: The influence of density-dependence processes measured at the national level of analysis, accounted for with a linear and a squared term.

name: Neighboring density
definition: The influence of neighboring subpopulations was measured by a variable computed as the sum of the density values of neighboring provinces; the variable is meant to capture the influence from these areas.

name: Local population age
authors_terms: ["ProvAge", "age of the local population", "age of the industry at the province level", "local evolutionary time", "local evolutionary clocks"]
definition: A variable that measures the age of the industry at the province level, used to test the temporal dimension of organizational heterogeneity and as the local evolutionary time with which founders' geographical origin is interacted.

name: National population age
authors_terms: ["IndustryAge", "age of the national population", "age of the entire industry", "national evolutionary clock"]
definition: A similar variable at the national level that controls for the age of the entire industry and is compared with the age of the subpopulation.

name: Interlocal mobility of professional accountants
authors_terms: ["interlocal mobility", "migration of professional accountants", "Neighboring Founders", "Distant Founders", "movements of professionals from neighboring and more distant provinces"]
definition: The movement of professional accountants across provinces, established by tracking whether in the year before the foundation of a new venture the founder worked in any of the neighboring provinces or in more distant provinces. The migration of individuals across geographical areas is an important micromechanism for the spreading of new organizational forms.

name: Intralocal mobility of professional accountants
definition: Founders who, in the year before the foundation of a new venture, worked within the same geographical area.

name: Current economic conditions
authors_terms: ["current economic conditions", "good economic times", "bad economic times", "prosperous times"]
definition: Current economic conditions were gauged using the seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rate.

name: Workforce entry economic conditions
authors_terms: ["workforce entry economic conditions", "economic conditions at workforce entry", "entering the workforce during an economic boom", "begin their careers in prosperous times"]
definition: Consistent with past research, economic conditions at workforce entry were measured using the annual unemployment rate in the year each CEO earned his or her highest degree.

name: CEO misconduct
definition: Like other scholars, we define corporate misconduct as behavior that is illegal, violates collectively agreed upon norms, or directly harms employees or shareholders.

name: Managerial entrenchment
definition: Managerial entrenchment provisions are arrangements that thwart corporate control; managers adopt MEPs, which grant them further insider power that may be used for long-term projects or for private benefits.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR encompasses a large array of voluntary and explicit attempts of corporations to integrate social and environmental concerns in their long-lasting interactions with their stakeholders, through activities differentiated from those that reflect the social responsibilities of government.

name: Internal CSR
definition: Internal CSR reflects an inward-looking perspective and involves substantive actions targeting those internal stakeholders upon which the firm relies on developing intangible resources that are critical for business success.

name: External CSR
definition: External CSR reflects communication patterns and highly visible public initiatives intended to influence external audiences to generate public endorsements of the firm, its management, and its practices.

name: Shareholder value
authors_terms: ["shareholder value", "firm value", "corporate shareholder value", "firm financial performance"]
definition: Shareholder value has been approached by means of Tobin's Q, which is obtained by dividing the sum of the company's market equity value plus book value of debt by the overall amount of assets.

name: Varieties of capitalism
authors_terms: ["varieties of capitalism (VOC)", "institutional setting", "Liberal Market Economies (LMEs)", "Coordinated Market Economies (CMEs)"]
definition: Countries cluster into distinct institutional settings; Hall and Soskice's framework distinguishes Liberal Market Economies from Coordinated Market Economies, with LMEs relying on market coordination and CMEs on nonmarket coordination.

name: Performance below aspiration
authors_terms: ["performance (when it is below the aspiration)", "ROA-Aspiration (below aspiration)"]
definition: The performance variable is calculated as performance minus the aspiration, but only for those observations where performance is below the aspiration, and is set to zero when performance is above the aspiration. Its values are negative when performance is below the aspiration, with lower (more negative) values indicating poorer performance and higher (less negative) values indicating an improvement in performance toward the aspiration from below.

name: Organizational change
definition: The framework applies to any category of activity that is relevant to a particular dimension of organizational performance and which may require, or at least is not excluded from, consultation with the board; for simplicity the authors refer to changes in these activities more generally as 'organizational change'. In this setting it is operationalized as service line divestitures.

name: Board size
definition: Board size is measured through the number of members on the hospital's governing board.

name: Board turnover
definition: Turnover is measured through the percent of the board that has turned over since the prior year.

name: Board equity ownership
authors_terms: ["board equity ownership", "board equity held", "board equity holdings"]
definition: Board equity ownership is measured through the percent of the hospital's equity that is held, on average, by each board member. When board equity ownership is high, directors have a stronger motivation to review changes proposed by the management team and to ensure that these proposals best serve shareholder interests.

name: Social comparison pressure from online rankings
authors_terms: ["online rankings of donations", "ranked as low donor", "not recognized as donor", "social comparison pressure from the rankings"]
definition: Online rankings generated strong social comparisons across corporations. The rankings provided aggregate and comparative information, promoted good role models, and exposed 'laggards.'

name: Internet coverage of corporate donation
authors_terms: ["the amount of Internet coverage on corporate donation", "number of Internet articles on corporate donation", "online articles on corporate donations"]
definition: The volume of information released online is likely to drastically overtake that in traditional media, and the large amount of online information and discussion on corporate donations may rivet public attention on corporate giving.

name: Traditional media coverage of corporate donation
authors_terms: ["coverage of corporate donations by traditional media", "articles on corporate donation in traditional media"]
definition: To compare the effects of online versus traditional media, the authors measured the total number of articles on corporate donation published in the major nationwide newspapers each day during the same observation period.

name: Speed of corporate donation
authors_terms: ["speed of donation", "hazard rate of donation", "speed of firm response", "speed of response"]
definition: Since we posit that speed is critical to firm response to Internet activism, we used event history analysis to examine the speed of donation. The dependent variable is the hazard rate of donation.

name: Private ownership
definition: State-controlled firms are those where the dominant shareholder is the state, while private firms are those where the dominant shareholder is private individuals.

name: Real estate industry
authors_terms: ["firms in a culpable industry", "real estate firms", "the real estate industry"]
definition: As described above, the real estate industry came under attack because of its potential culpability and extraordinary wealth.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: As a general assessment of a firm's character and approval rating, corporate reputation is conferred externally. Even a good reputation can be lost if audiences withdraw their approval after a critical event.

name: Executive political status
authors_terms: ["political status of top executives", "national-level political appointment", "provincial-level political appointment", "national PC/CPPCC delegate", "provincial PC/CPPCC delegate"]
definition: Given the importance of government control over resources and the prevalence of government intervention in business in transitional markets, top executives seek political office to secure favorable treatment of their firms, as well as to garner personal power.

name: Corporate image vulnerability
authors_terms: ["public image vulnerability", "image vulnerability", "vulnerability characteristics", "corporate opportunity structure"]
definition: In the Chinese context, characteristics that render corporate image more vulnerable include private ownership, potential culpability, and high social and political standing. These can be characteristics that make firms more vulnerable to attack, or circumstances that make firms more open to change.

name: Balance dimension of ambidexterity
authors_terms: ["balance dimension of ambidexterity", "BD", "balance of exploration and exploitation"]
definition: The dimension of organizational ambidexterity that corresponds to a firm's orientation to maintain a close relative balance between exploratory and exploitative activities; a higher level of BD means a closer match in the relative magnitude of exploratory and exploitative activities.

name: Combined dimension of ambidexterity
authors_terms: ["combined dimension of ambidexterity", "CD", "combined magnitude of exploration and exploitation"]
definition: The dimension of organizational ambidexterity that corresponds to the combined magnitude of a firm's exploratory and exploitative activities. It reflects the idea that exploratory and exploitative processes are not necessarily in fundamental competition and can be supportive of one another.

name: Firm performance
definition: CEO-rated firm performance over the last 12 months in terms of sales growth, profit growth, market share growth, operational efficiency, cash flow from market operations, and market reputation.

name: Organization size
definition: The authors state that a firm's size is strongly indicative of the resources it possesses at its immediate disposal, with larger firms tending to have a larger pool of resources to draw upon than smaller firms.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: The extent to which an environment supports the sustained growth of a firm; in a munificent (as opposed to scarce) environment there are many growth opportunities to pursue and abundant resources with which to pursue them.

name: Exploration
definition: Exploration involves searching for new knowledge and opportunities; in this study it is framed as a firm's orientation with regard to the introduction of new products/markets.

name: Exploitation
definition: Exploitation pertains to the refinement of existing competencies; in this study it is framed as a firm's orientation with regard to the improvement of existing products/markets.

name: Local knowledge base volume
authors_terms: ["volume of the local-knowledge base", "local knowledge volume", "volume of local-knowledge bases"]
definition: A key characteristic of a subunit's knowledge is the volume of knowledge kept in each of its knowledge bases. The likelihood of linkages arising between extra-unit knowledge and a given local-knowledge base should increase with the volume of the local-knowledge base, because a large local-knowledge base presents a larger target to extra-unit knowledge than a narrow local-knowledge base.

name: Local knowledge specialization
definition: Another important characteristic of a subunit's knowledge is its degree of specialization, the degree to which local knowledge does (or does not) overlap with knowledge offered by other subunits of the organization.

name: Knowledge codification
authors_terms: ["codification of knowledge", "level of codification of a knowledge base", "codification of local knowledge"]
definition: Codification allows organizations to retain lessons drawn from past experiences and apply this knowledge quickly when similar situations arise, and it helps organizations process new incoming knowledge faster because it facilitates and speeds up the establishment of linkages between old and new knowledge. Organizations frequently convert tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge through codification, articulating their knowledge and storing it in a number of forms, including abstract formulas, written text, images, prototypes, and technologies.

name: Extra-unit knowledge base volume
authors_terms: ["volume of the extra-unit knowledge base", "extra-unit knowledge volume", "size of the extra-unit knowledge base"]
definition: As the extra-unit knowledge base expands in volume, more linkages between local and extra-unit knowledge can arise, and chances increase that it includes elements that can elaborate, contradict, or strengthen elements of the local-knowledge base. All else being equal, large extra-unit knowledge bases are relevant for more things than small extra-unit knowledge bases.

name: Informal interunit relations
authors_terms: ["informal relations", "informal relations with peer or supervising subunits", "informal networks"]
definition: Informal relations help participants learn about others' operations, promote the development of transactive memory, and lead to greater familiarity with the operations performed in other parts of the organization than formal relations, such as formalized exchanges of budget reports, could. Such familiarity can raise the awareness of knowledge seekers about the potential availability of relevant knowledge in other units, and it can make providers of knowledge more aware of the relevance of their knowledge to the operations performed in other units.

name: Knowledge outflows
authors_terms: ["outflows of knowledge", "intensities of knowledge outflows", "horizontal outflows of knowledge", "vertical outflows of knowledge"]
definition: When a focal subunit sends knowledge to other units, it provides clues about its own operations and thereby helps other units to form assessments about what might be relevant to its own operations. The more knowledge the focal unit sends to others, the more other units learn about it, thereby raising their awareness of the potential relevance of their knowledge for the focal subunit.

name: Knowledge inflows
authors_terms: ["inflows of knowledge", "horizontal and vertical knowledge inflows", "knowledge flows"]
definition: Knowledge flows are understood as the aggregate volume of know-how and information transmitted per unit of time. The two dependent variables of this study are the horizontal and vertical knowledge inflows into a given knowledge base of a subunit.

name: Pressures for local responsiveness
definition: Pressures for local responsiveness arise because a multinational corporation must respond to contingencies that can differ quite dramatically between the multiple environments in which it operates, including differences of customer tastes, government regulations, or resource characteristics.

name: Pressures for global integration
definition: Pressures for global integration arise mainly from organizational opportunities to exploit commonalities across locations, including the pooling of similar activities in order to reap economies of scale.

name: Process concurrency
definition: Process concurrency refers to the degree of simultaneity in the design engineering and manufacturing engineering efforts; there is no concurrency when manufacturing engineering starts work only after design engineering signals it has completed its work, and total concurrency occurs when both functions start at the same time.

name: Process formality
definition: Process formality refers to existence of an overall organizational process and structure for the project; it represents the degree to which rules, policies, and procedures govern the product development work activities, typically via structured processes for managing the project such as phase/gate systems.

name: Process adaptability
definition: Process adaptability refers to flexibility during the project to meet emerging circumstances, and represents discretion available to the project management.

name: Technology novelty
definition: The newness of the technology to be developed can be a major source of uncertainty in product development; the product development literature describes technology novelty in terms of the degree of familiarity with the given technology or degree of change in the technologies relative to products previously developed or manufactured by the company.

name: Product technology novelty
definition: Product technology novelty was measured by the degree to which product modules, the product architecture, and product technologies overall were new to the firm at the start of project execution.

name: Process technology novelty
definition: Process technology novelty was measured by the degree to which manufacturing stages, the process layout, and manufacturing technologies overall were new.

name: Operational outcome achievement
authors_terms: ["operational outcomes", "achievement of operational objectives", "operational performance outcomes"]
definition: The operational task outcomes are reflected by the achievement of the project operational objectives (product quality, unit cost, and time-to-market); these objectives are set in place at the start of project execution and the degree of achievement of these objectives is evaluated at the end of project execution.

name: Product quality achievement
authors_terms: ["product quality", "achievement of the product quality target"]
definition: From an operational perspective, product quality typically refers to the technical performance and reliability of the product relative to specifications; the product quality targets set by the development organization must meet customers' needs and generate a high level of value for a new product to be successful in the marketplace.

name: Unit cost achievement
authors_terms: ["unit cost", "achievement of the unit cost target"]
definition: Achievement of the project's unit cost objective; the pricing strategy and product unit cost jointly determine a new product's short- and long-term profitability.

name: Time-to-market achievement
definition: The firm's ability to get to market with a new product at the time the firm wants to enter the market, regardless of whether that represents being first to market or not; time-to-market means the approximate date for which first customer shipment was planned.

name: Market outcomes
definition: External performance measures capture marketplace outcomes such as product sales, customer satisfaction, profitability, and market share, and so reflect the market success of the given new product development effort; here two market outcomes are considered: relative sales and customer satisfaction.

name: Customer satisfaction
definition: Customer satisfaction refers to the perceived level of overall customer satisfaction with the new product.

name: Relative sales
definition: Relative sales refers to the extent to which the product achieves the sales objectives set for the project.

name: External uncertainty
definition: Two sources of task-specific external uncertainty are considered: market newness (the degree to which the firm is familiar and has experience with the target market for the new product), and environmentally caused disruption (the degree to which events external to the development effort impact it).

name: Market newness
definition: Market newness is the degree to which the firm is familiar and has experience with the target market for the new product.

name: Environmentally caused disruption
definition: Environmentally caused disruption is the degree to which events external to the development effort impact it.

name: Trust-based governance
definition: In our context, trust-based governance is the use of trust to support ex post revisions to an incomplete contract between independent parties. Trust is defined as the confidence held by one party in its expectations of the behavior and goodwill of another party regarding business actions.

name: Task performance
definition: A 13-item scale measures performance on the outsourced R&D task, with four dimensions including the expected contribution of the technology to the client's product performance, a comparison of actual performance to goals and objectives, adherence to timelines, and the creativity and innovativeness of the technology.

name: Client task-related skills
definition: Assessing and interpreting the supplier's actions and being able to agree on the nature of profitable revisions depends squarely on the extant knowledge that the client possesses about the tasks in question, as well as the knowledge gained by the client during execution. The scale measures task-related client skills present at the outset of the engagement.

name: Teachability of task skills
definition: Skills are less teachable (more tacit) to the extent that they require face-to-face communication or direct experience with the task to be transferred. Teachability makes it easier for one party to learn task-related skills from the other party in a timely and accurate manner.

name: Colocation of parties
definition: Colocation refers to the physical proximity of the parties engaged in the collaborative effort; in R&D engagements, critical human assets can be colocated.

name: Parallel task execution
definition: Parallel task execution involves the client and supplier engaging in identical or overlapping tasks, with no competition implied between the two programs.

name: Firm success
definition: Firm success was a proxy for entrepreneurial success, the respondents being owners or founders; for publicly listed firms, profitability and growth rate more precisely reflect firm success than size and firm age.

name: Political appointment
authors_terms: ["political appointment", "attained political appointment", "desire to seek political appointment", "PC or PPCC membership"]
definition: Political appointment is one form of political connection, usually achieved through appointment to national or local legislative entities; in China, political appointments are through PC or PPCC memberships.

name: Proself motive
definition: The proself motive captures orientations toward achieving financial and competitive success for the company; it drives entrepreneurs to benefit their companies and themselves.

name: Prosocial motive
definition: The prosocial motive captures desires to address social problems and to shape better social policies; it drives entrepreneurs to benefit the collective and the broader society.

name: Human resource scarcity
authors_terms: ["human resource scarcity", "scarcity in human resources", "scarce human resources"]
definition: The origin of innovation—departure from up-or-out—rests with the human resources it required of large corporate law firm offices. Up-or-out required offices to acquire junior lawyers straight out of elite law schools. That requirement ultimately contributed to a scarcity of these lawyers.

name: Organizational prestige
definition: Organizations with prestige have the legitimacy to act as initial and early adopters (Rogers, 1983). Initial innovators, especially, and early adopters use their prestige or status to pull off being different by creating and disseminating new technical rationales. Their status allows them to experiment with or try innovations that have not been legitimized.

name: Senior attorney track adoption
authors_terms: ["senior attorney track", "adoption of the senior attorney track"]
definition: At the very end of 1982, Davis, Polk, & Wardell (Davis Polk), a highly regarded "silk-stocking" firm located principally in New York, innovated by creating a track for associates who did not make partner and would not go up again for partner. Their status would be that of continuing, or "permanent," salaried employees who would not receive draws on the firm's profits like those of partners.

name: Staff attorney track adoption
authors_terms: ["staff attorney track", "adoption of the staff attorney track"]
definition: A second innovation occurred in late 1985. The second largest firm in the country, Jones, Day, Reavis, & Pogue (Jones Day) of Cleveland, pioneered the practice of hiring lawyers as permanent employees with no chance to make partner. They were on the "staff attorney track."

name: Diffusion window
authors_terms: ["early diffusion window", "late diffusion window", "early adopters", "late adopters"]
definition: We created a time variable in order to distinguish early from late adopters of the senior and staff attorney tracks. ... The two variables for year divide our observations into early and late diffusion windows.

name: Interim CEO status
authors_terms: ["interim CEO", "interim succession", "interim period", "firm with interim succession"]
definition: An 'interim succession episode' occurs when a firm is unable to transition directly from an outgoing to a new CEO and thus resorts to an 'interim' CEO to lead the firm until a permanent successor is appointed. The interim period begins from the moment at which the interim appointment is announced and continues until the board finds a permanent successor, either by promoting the interim CEO or by appointing a new one.

name: Income-increasing earnings management
definition: We define 'earnings management' as the discretionary choices that corporate executives make using within-GAAP accounting methods to influence firm earnings performance. The higher the value of discretionary accruals, the greater the extent of income-increasing earnings management.

name: Interim CEO promotion
authors_terms: ["interim CEO promotion", "promoted to the permanent position", "promotion"]
definition: Promotion of the interim CEO to the permanent CEO position, that is, the interim CEO being appointed the permanent CEO of the firm.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "outside director ratio", "ratio of outside directors on the board"]
definition: Board independence is captured by the presence of independent outside directors, who provide more effective monitoring mainly because they have fewer conflicts of interests than inside or affiliated directors.

name: Board ownership
authors_terms: ["board ownership", "board ownership profile", "percentage of shares held by the board"]
definition: Higher board ownership increases the alignment of interests between directors and shareholders, since directors have a larger stake in the company; ownership is also a major source of power as a result of the associated voting rights.

name: Board financial or accounting expertise
authors_terms: ["board financial or accounting expertise", "financial or accounting expertise"]
definition: The financial or accounting expertise of the board, i.e., the relevant knowledge that directors need in order to effectively monitor a manager's behavior by evaluating whether reported earnings contain a managed component.

name: Board nonbusyness
definition: When the board directors are busy serving on multiple boards, they will have less time for the focal firm, and its governance may be weakened; a busy director is defined as one who holds three or more directorships.

name: Analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["analyst coverage", "analyst monitoring", "external monitoring by financial analysts"]
definition: Analysts act as informational intermediaries in the capital market and thus double as external checks on corporate executives; greater analyst coverage suggests that executives' activities will come under closer scrutiny from this group of industry experts.

name: Technical capital
definition: Technical capital represents a firm's capabilities in creating new technology, products, and processes; it is an asset-stock that adds value, is accumulated over time, and is difficult to trade across markets.

name: Commercial capital
definition: Commercial capital represents the supporting or complementary assets that a firm needs to commercialize new technologies and obtain rents from them, such as manufacturing facilities and service and distribution networks.

name: Social capital
definition: Social capital represents the firm's prior relationships with other firms and provides it with information and status benefits.

name: Linkage formation
definition: Collaborative arrangements between independent firms to share resources on an ongoing basis; the paper counts the new technical collaborative linkages formed by a firm with other firms in the sample in any year.

name: Important inventions
definition: Critical, path-breaking ideas: technological development that is radical, marked by significant discontinuities rather than smooth progress along innovation avenues.

name: Capital deficiency
authors_terms: ["capital-poor firms", "firms lacking technical, commercial, and social capital", "poorly endowed firms"]
definition: Firms that were below the median on all three forms of capital (technical, commercial, and social) for that year.

name: PE backing
definition: A situation where a private equity (PE) firm has an equity ownership stake in an acquirer. As the sample contains publicly listed acquirers, PE equity ownership is only partial and never 100 percent.

name: Announcement returns
definition: The acquirer's cumulative abnormal return, estimated from five days before to five days after the announcement. Using this methodology, the authors capture the market's confidence about whether a deal creates value.

name: Target information environment
authors_terms: ["target information environment", "target bad WB info", "target bad ICRG info", "poor information environment"]
definition: The quality of the information environment of the target, captured by measures that proxy both information disclosure and the regulatory aspects required to render it effective, including the riskiness of the country, government effectiveness, and corruption.

name: PE backer's local experience and networks
authors_terms: ["PE firms' experience and networks", "# PE backer deals target country", "prior deals by PE firms in the target country", "prior-local-deals variable"]
definition: The experience and networks that a PE backer gains from prior deals performed in the target country. Access to this experience and these networks can enable an acquirer to successfully identify and evaluate a foreign target and can signal to the market that information problems can be overcome.

name: Financial advisor experience
authors_terms: ["# deals fin. advisors", "# deals most exp. fin. advisors", "experience of the engaged advisors"]
definition: The experience of the financial advisors that the acquirer engages, reflecting that PE firms frequently buy and sell companies and have experience with, and access to, a wide range of financial advisors.

name: Change in operating performance
definition: The acquirer's change in earnings, measured as the change in earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) from the year of the acquisition to the year after, and the EBIT change until three years after the deal.

name: Structural holes
definition: Burt (1992) explains the value of structural holes as stemming from the ability of an actor to obtain and meld together diverse, nonredundant information from partners not directly connected to each other. The measure captures the extent of nonredundancy in a firm's network, where higher values of efficiency signify a network high in structural holes.

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: We measured firm innovativeness as the logged value of Trajtenberg's (1990) citation-weighted patent count formula, where pi is the number of patents granted to firm i, and ci represents the number of citations to firm i's patents. Citation-weighted counts of patents capture both the rate and impact of innovation simultaneously.

name: Broker country corporatism
authors_terms: ["corporatism", "focal firm corporatism", "the degree of corporatism in the focal firm's country", "broker corporatism"]
definition: Corporatism is a sociopolitical, nonmarket institution concerned with the organization of interest groups in society, which can take varied forms based on communitarian principles at one extreme and individualism at the other. Corporatism varies across countries and ranges from low (e.g., the United States, United Kingdom) to high (e.g., Japan, Germany).

name: Partner country corporatism
authors_terms: ["partner corporatism", "the degree of corporatism in the countries of the focal firm's alliance partners", "partners' corporatism"]
definition: We measured the degree of corporatism of the focal firm or its alliance partners based on the country in which each firm carried out the bulk of innovative activity as indicated by the location of the majority of its patents' inventors. To aggregate partner corporatism as an ego-network variable, we calculated the average country-level corporatism for the portfolio of each focal firm's alliance partners.

name: Combination of broker and partner country corporatism
authors_terms: ["combinations of focal firm and partner corporatism", "HH", "LL", "HL", "LH"]
definition: To test H3A and H3B, we split broker and partner corporatism at the median and created four categories capturing the different combinations of focal firm and partner corporatism-both high (HH), both low (LL), high focal firm and low partners' corporatism (HL), and low focal firm and high partners' corporatism (LH).

name: Discussion of entrepreneurial issues
authors_terms: ["discussion of entrepreneurial issues", "board attention to entrepreneurial issues", "board discussion of entrepreneurial issues", "discussion of firm opportunities"]
definition: We defined entrepreneurial issues following Miles and Snow's definition of 'the entrepreneurial problem,' as the 'choice of product-market domain' (1978: 24). Per this definition, a board that discusses entrepreneurial issues discusses new products or new markets.

name: Board tenure variance
definition: A board's heterogeneity or homogeneity of tenure means the degree of shared tenure its members have. Conversely, heterogeneity in tenure should lead to diversity in experiences and opinions and 'stimulate consideration of changes in strategy.'

name: Board functional background heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["board functional background heterogeneity", "functional background heterogeneity", "board functional heterogeneity"]
definition: Functional experience shapes and frames how managers view and approach issues and the kind of solutions with which they are familiar. Boards whose members have heterogeneous functional backgrounds can bring a greater breadth of knowledge and different approaches to problem solving, which in turn can make them more likely to generate alternatives and to 'acknowledge new ideas and discuss them.'

name: Proportion of output-oriented directors
authors_terms: ["percent output function", "proportion of directors with output-oriented backgrounds", "percentage of directors with functional output-oriented backgrounds"]
definition: Directors whose primary functions are output-oriented-that is, focused on products-are occupied full-time with evaluating product-market issues, and as a result they are more likely than directors with other primary functions to focus on new entrepreneurial issues.

name: Board firm/industry background heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["board firm/industry background heterogeneity", "board firm/industry heterogeneity", "firm/industry background heterogeneity"]
definition: The industry in which managers have experience can also impact their cognitive biases and their framing of problems and solutions. In the case of a board, three sets of cognitive frames relate to an individual's general level of knowledge about the firm the board belongs to and its industry: industry outsider, industry insider, and firm insider.

name: Faultline strength
definition: Faultlines are 'hypothetical dividing lines that may split a group into subgroups based on one or more attributes' (Lau & Murnighan, 1998: 328). Faultlines between subgroups become stronger as more attributes within each subgroup line up in the same way.

name: Board meeting informality
authors_terms: ["board meeting informality", "meeting informality", "meeting formality/informality", "board meeting formality"]
definition: The context of a board's meeting-its degree of formality or informality-can shape the board's attention in a way that either enhances or constrains the discussion of entrepreneurial issues. Formal meetings will be more tightly planned, structured, and managed and will have detailed, comprehensive agendas.

name: Human capital losses
authors_terms: ["human capital losses", "voluntary turnover rates", "human capital depletion", "resource depletion", "voluntary turnover", "quit rates"]
definition: Human capital losses are the depletion of accumulated human capital, marked by voluntary turnover or quit rates. The authors note that the literature has emphasized human capital accumulations but has ignored the risks of resource depletion.

name: Workforce performance
authors_terms: ["workforce performance", "workforce productivity", "accident rates", "intermediate dimensions of workforce performance"]
definition: Workforce performance is an intermediate dimension of organizational performance, defined by the authors as workforce productivity and accident rates. Productivity is sales per employee; accident rates are employee accidents per employee.

name: HRM investments
definition: The authors follow prior researchers and view HRM investments as a substitutable set of practices that contribute directly and indirectly to human capital accumulations. Such practices increase the value, rareness, and inimitability of the workforce and the costs of human capital depletion.

name: Financial performance
definition: The authors define distal financial performance as return on assets (ROA) and profit, the primary construct of interest in strategic management and strategic HRM research. Financial performance lies at the end of the process model, distal from human capital losses.

name: Financial fraud
authors_terms: ["financial fraud", "commitment of financial fraud", "commitment of financial fraud"]
definition: Financial fraud occurs when managers take actions that deceive investors or other key stakeholders. It often involves corruption, lying about facts, failure to disclose material information, falsifying information about the firm's performance, or covering up systematic problems.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated institutional ownership", "dedicated institutional investors", "dedicated owners", "dedicated ownership"]
definition: Porter (1992) described dedicated owners as being those who maintain large, long-term holdings concentrated in a small number of firms. These owners have incentive to monitor executive behavior and are able to understand rich and complex information about firms in which they invest.

name: Takeover defense provisions
definition: We can view the extent to which executives are exposed to the market for corporate control by looking at the firm's takeover defense provisions. External expectations to perform that arise from the market for corporate control are likely to be less dogged when managers enjoy more and better takeover protections.

name: Analyst recommendation pressure
authors_terms: ["analysts' recommendation pressure", "pressure from security analysts' recommendations", "analysts' pressure", "earnings pressure from analysts' recommendations"]
definition: External expectations from financial analysts may come in two forms. First, sell recommendations reduce a firm's stock price, and therefore, impose external pressure on managers to take action so that the firm's performance bounces back. Second, buy recommendations also introduce external pressure because managers are likely to feel the burden of high earnings expectations when analysts are recommending their stock to capital markets.

name: Environmental responsiveness strategy
authors_terms: ["proactive environmental responsiveness strategies", "proactive environmental strategy", "environmental responsiveness", "ENVSTRGY", "corporate environmental strategies"]
definition: Corporate strategy in the business/natural environment domain: 'companies were considered proactive only if they exhibited a consistent pattern of environmental practices, across all dimensions relevant to their range of activities, not required to be undertaken in fulfillment of environmental regulations or in response to isomorphic pressures within the industry as standard business practices.' In addition to consistency across dimensions, proactive firms 'should have exhibited a consistent pattern of such voluntary actions over time.'

name: Organizational capabilities
authors_terms: ["firm-specific organizational capabilities", "organizational capabilities", "CAPABLTY", "competitively valuable organizational capabilities"]
definition: 'Organizational capabilities are the coordinating mechanisms that enable the most efficient and competitive use of the firm's assets-whether tangible or intangible.' The competitive advantage of these capabilities 'stems from their elusive nature based on social complexity and deep embeddedness in organizations'; they are path dependent, causally ambiguous and lack an identifiable owner.

name: Competitive benefits
definition: Competitive outcomes perceived to flow from organizational capabilities; the proactive companies perceived 'lower costs of processes/inputs/products, innovations in processes/products/operating systems, improved corporate reputation, and relationships with a wide range of stakeholders.'

name: Family involvement
definition: A family firm is defined by a family's involvement in ownership and governance and a vision for how the firm will benefit the family, potentially over generations. Because family firms are owned, and typically managed by, family members, they have greater liberty to act unilaterally and idiosyncratically than nonfamily firms.

name: R&D investment
definition: R&D investment is the ratio of a firm's R&D expenditures to sales in year t adjusted by subtracting median industry-level R&D expenditures to sales in the same year. Since R&D investments generally do not yield payoffs immediately, the authors consider this variable to be an indication of a firm's long term economic orientation.

name: R&D variability
authors_terms: ["R&D variability", "variability of R&D investments", "variability of investments in R&D", "logged variance in R&D investments"]
definition: The variability of R&D investments is captured by y. If y is negative, variability decreases; if positive, variability increases.

name: Aspiration gap
authors_terms: ["aspiration gap", "gap between aspirations and performance", "negative aspiration gaps", "performance below aspirations"]
definition: As goal-directed systems, organizations use comparisons of performance to aspirations as a feedback mechanism; divergences between a firm's current performance and both its historical performance and the performance of its competitors are useful indicators of aspiration gaps. As negative discrepancies between a firm's performance and either its historical performance or the performance of competitors widen, decision makers are more likely to perceive gaps between current performance and aspirations.

name: CEO total pay
authors_terms: ["CEO total pay", "CEO pay level", "chief executive pay"]
definition: Total pay is simply the combined amount of compensation an executive receives. We gauged CEO pay level as the logged value of total compensation.

name: CEO long-term pay structure
authors_terms: ["CEO pay structure", "CEO long-term pay structure", "long-term pay structure"]
definition: Pay structure is the relative proportion of pay received in contingent, long-term forms (i.e., stock, stock options, etc.).

name: TMT pay level
authors_terms: ["TMT member pay level", "TMT member total pay", "TMT pay level"]
definition: Top management team (TMT) compensation is the pay of top executives apart from their chief executive officer (CEO); total pay is simply the combined amount of compensation an executive receives.

name: TMT external alignment
authors_terms: ["external alignment", "TMT external alignment", "TMT long-term pay structure", "TMT member long-term pay structure"]
definition: External alignment refers to the degree to which the structure of TMT member compensation takes into account the interests of shareholders.

name: TMT internal alignment
definition: The degree to which TMT member pay is internally consistent with characteristics of the firm, and specifically the degree to which TMT members' total pay was similarly a reflection of CEO pay and the managerial demands facing their firms. Greater alignment (i.e., positive covariance) between CEO total pay and organizational demands and TMT member pay.

name: Firm performance
definition: Return on assets is a widely used measure of firm performance in the literature on executive compensation and corporate governance because it indicates the efficiency with which a firm employs its current asset base.

name: Minority state ownership
authors_terms: ["minority state ownership", "minority state equity", "minority stakes", "state minority ownership", "minority state capital"]
definition: In several countries, the state instead participates in the ownership of corporations as a minority shareholder. If governments are minority shareholders, then they relinquish control of SOEs to other owners holding majority stakes.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors employ two measures of performance. Their first measure, return on assets, corresponds to net profits over total assets in a given year; their second measure, market-to-book, computed as the total market value of stocks divided by the book value of equity, is an indicator of future return on equity and hence incorporates future market expectations about firm-level performance.

name: Fixed investment
authors_terms: ["fixed investment", "capital expenditures", "investment in long-term fixed assets", "fixed asset investments"]
definition: The authors propose that minority equity stakes improve firm performance by promoting capital expenditures (investment in long-term fixed assets). They measured fixed investment as the ratio of a firm's yearly capital expenditures to its initial stock of fixed capital (observed at end of the previous year).

name: Constrained opportunity
authors_terms: ["constrained opportunity", "constrained investment opportunity", "financially constrained firms with investment opportunities"]
definition: We define firms with constrained opportunity as those that have a valuable investment opportunity but are at the same time limited in their ability to attract long-term funding.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["membership in business groups", "pyramidal business group", "group affiliates", "group membership"]
definition: Business groups - that is, collections of firms under the same controlling entity - provide their affiliates with resources flowing through internal capital markets. A firm was considered a member of a group when it was controlled by an owner or owners who controlled other firms in the data set.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "development of local institutions", "institutional improvements", "mitigation of voids"]
definition: The authors argue that the positive effect of minority state ownership is reduced when institutional improvements progressively attenuate or mitigate voids, and that as institutions develop, the positive effect of those stakes should decline. They measure institutional development with variables related to the capital, product, and labor markets.

name: Top management compensation
authors_terms: ["top management pay", "management compensation", "highest management compensation", "top management compensation"]
definition: Management compensation was measured as the salary, bonus, and other miscellaneous earnings of a company's highest-paid director. The authors use the term top management pay because the data collected are not for CEO pay per se; in the United Kingdom only data for the pay of the highest-paid member of a company's board were available over this time period.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["proportion of outsiders on the main board", "proportion of outside directors", "proportion of nonexecutive directors", "proportion of directors who were not executives of the firm"]
definition: The mix of inside and outside directors was measured as the proportion of directors who were not executives of a company on its main board. A low proportion of outside directors suggests poor monitoring capabilities.

name: Corporate performance
definition: The performance variable was total shareholder return, reflecting share price appreciation and dividend yield and calculated as the proportional change in a company's return index.

name: Remuneration committee existence
definition: Deliberation about and the determination of top management pay is often delegated to a subgroup of the main board termed the remuneration or compensation committee. The remuneration committee variable was defined as a dummy variable equal to one if a company reported the existence of such a committee in its annual report and to zero otherwise.

name: Remuneration committee outsider representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of nonexecutives on a remuneration committee", "proportion of outside directors on the remuneration committee"]
definition: The authors also calculated the proportion of nonexecutives on a remuneration committee, a similar measure to that used by Daily and colleagues (1996).

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality exists when a firm's CEO also serves as the chairman in the board of directors. Holding the highly symbolic position of board chair would provide the CEO with a wider power base and locus of control.

name: Relative organizational performance
definition: A firm-specific measure of accounting performance is used here to compare current performance to past performance. Using this procedure, substandard performers will have negative scores, while high performing firms will have positive scores.

name: Innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption (adopt/nonadopt)", "adoption of organizational innovations", "decision to join an R&D collaborative"]
definition: In the present study, attention centers upon the adoption of organizational innovations, i.e., the implementation of new ideas, procedures and structures in the management of the firm. The decision for a firm to join either MCC, SPC or COS constitutes the dichotomous adoption measure.
