name: Adoption timing
definition: For each of the three collaboratives, "early adopters" are core organizers of the embryonic collaborative, whose participation at development meetings preceded, and was instrumental to legal formation. "Late adopters" comprise the second wave of members, who typically followed the early adopters by 10 to 19 months, after formal incorporation of the collaborative.

name: Technological convergence
definition: By convergence, we refer to a process through which lagging firms from developing countries narrow the disparity between their own technologies and those at the global technological frontier. We use two indicators to assess whether firms from technologically lagging developing countries close technological gaps with leading firms from developed countries; specifically, we distinguish between two types of technological convergence: Quantitative Convergence and Qualitative Convergence.

name: Learning from technologically successful peers
authors_terms: ["Learning from Technologically Successful Peers", "Degree of Learning from Technologically Successful Peers", "technologically successful peers"]
definition: We define technologically successful peers as those that (1) share similar environmental, geographic, and cultural traits with the focal firm; (2) operate in the same industry as the focal firm; and (3) have achieved a certain degree of success in converging to the global technological frontier, having effectively closed the technological gap with leading firms from advanced countries prior to the focal firm. As an indicator of whether a firm learns from technologically successful peers, we measure the extent to which the focal firm cites - that is, builds upon and extends - the patents of technologically successful peers.

name: Technological proximity of successful peers
authors_terms: ["Learning from Technologically Proximal Successful Peers", "technologically proximal successful peers", "technologically distal successful peers", "technological proximity"]
definition: We qualify our analysis by adding a more disaggregated technological dimension and reconceptualize technologically successful peers as either technologically proximal or technologically distal to the focal firm. To assess whether laggards more effectively close the technological gap when they learn from technologically proximal successful peers, we measure the technological similarity between the focal laggard and the successful peers it cites in its patents.

name: Market expansion
definition: Market expansion represents a strategic decision to replicate the firm's existing business model in new markets. Market expansion initiatives usually require substantial investment in new infrastructure, place added demands on firm attention, and change the firm's scale and structure.

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure is measured as the number of years since a founder started a cable operation or an agent was hired into the chief executive position by a specific organization. Tenure has explanatory power because it captures the combined effects of consequential variables such as a CEO's task knowledge, motivation, and power.

name: Market complexity
definition: Market complexity broadly refers to the dissimilarity of market elements and the extent of their interconnectedness. Extant conceptualizations of market complexity emphasize the heterogeneity and density of markets served by the firm.

name: CEO founder status
definition: Many firms are led by founders, who constitute a subset of the broader category of owner CEOs because they typically own a significant percentage of the firms they lead. Whereas agent CEOs face concerns about job security but not loss of investment capital, owner CEOs bear financial risk but not the threat of dismissal.

name: Early-mover status
authors_terms: ["early mover", "early-mover acquisition", "early movers in acquisitions", "early-mover variable"]
definition: Acquirers that conduct their acquisitions in the beginning of an industry wave of transactions, as opposed to acquirers whose acquisitions occur later in the industry acquisition wave.

name: Combined announcement returns
authors_terms: ["combined abnormal returns", "combined announcement returns", "total shareholder returns", "total market value-added", "net announcement returns"]
definition: The total market value-added (combined abnormal returns) for the transaction as a whole rather than the acquirer's value-added, i.e., a weighted combination of the target's and the acquirer's announcement returns.

name: Acquirer announcement returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns to acquirers", "acquirer announcement returns", "acquirers' returns", "shareholder returns"]
definition: The portion of the acquisition's value-added that the acquiring firm retains for itself, measured as the industry-adjusted announcement period returns of the acquirer.

name: Strategic pioneer
definition: Early-mover acquirers that act in manners consistent with having superior information, as opposed to early movers that moved early by luck or happenstance; the profile is an early-mover acquisition of a related target in an expansionary industry financed primarily with cash.

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: Whether the acquirer and the acquired firm operate in the same industry, one of the most widely researched issues regarding acquisition success.

name: Industry cycle
definition: The industry context in which an acquisition wave occurs, classified as either an expansionary or a contractionary merger wave.

name: Cash financing
authors_terms: ["form of financing", "form of payment", "cash financing", "stock financing", "cash payments"]
definition: The medium of exchange used to finance the acquisition, which is linked to the presence of information asymmetry; managers with informational advantages that enable them to acquire undervalued targets choose to finance such acquisitions with cash.

name: Dual director presence
authors_terms: ["dual directors", "Firm Has Dual Director", "firm has dual director"]
definition: Dual directors are directors who simultaneously serve on the boards of parent and spinoff firms that are separated in corporate spinoffs. A parent firm's right to appoint its own representatives to its spinoff firm's board gives the parent firm power by affording it a voice in the spinoff firm's decision-making and strategy-setting processes.

name: Average parent-spinoff pair performance
authors_terms: ["average performance of a parent-spinoff firm pair", "Value-Weighted Returns", "value-weighted stock market returns of parent-spinoff firm pairs"]
definition: One of the unique features of corporate spinoffs is that it is possible to measure both the average and individual performance of the parent and spinoff firms involved in these deals. Value-Weighted Returns is defined as the value-weighted, average annual stock market returns of the parent and spinoff firms, weighting each firm's independent stock market returns by its relative size.

name: Parent firm performance
authors_terms: ["Parent Annual Stock Returns", "parent firm performance", "stock market returns of parent firms"]
definition: The performance of the divesting parent firm, measured as its annual stock market returns over the four post-spinoff years.

name: Spinoff firm performance
authors_terms: ["Spinoff Annual Stock Returns", "spinoff firm performance", "stock market returns of spinoff firms"]
definition: The performance of the newly independent spinoff firm, measured as its annual stock market returns over the four post-spinoff years.

name: Spinoff firm's sales dependence on its parent firm
authors_terms: ["Share of Sales", "Large Share of Sales", "share of sales a spinoff firm makes to its parent firm", "sales dependence"]
definition: The share of sales a spinoff firm makes to its parent firm. When a spinoff firm makes a large share of its sales to its parent firm, dual directors would be expected to have both the ability and the motivation to improve the parent firm's outcomes at the expense of the spinoff firm.

name: Communist ideological imprint
authors_terms: ["communist ideological imprint", "ideological imprint", "ideological imprinting", "communist ideological imprinting"]
definition: An ideological imprint is ideology formed through past events that serves as an information filter persistently affecting individuals' decision making; in this setting it reflects socialization and indoctrination by the Communist Party-led government of China during entrepreneurs' early, formative periods. Private entrepreneurs who joined the CPC prior to establishing their new ventures thus have an ideological imprint that reflects communist beliefs and are likely to rely on Chinese government communications for acquiring and interpreting information.

name: Internationalization
definition: Internationalization occurs when a corporation engages in 'the process of increasing involvement in international operations . . . both inward and outward' (Welch and Luostarinen, 1988: 36). The authors examine inward internationalization by attracting foreign capital and outward internationalization by investing in an overseas economy, which they describe as two fundamentally different processes that together reflect overall sentiments toward internationalization.

name: Political involvement
authors_terms: ["political involvement", "served as a delegate to the PC or CPPCC"]
definition: Political involvement is an important type of direct interaction with the government in which a firm's leader becomes a delegate to either of the two legislative bodies in China: the People's Congress (PC) or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC).

name: Government appropriation of firm profits
authors_terms: ["government appropriation", "rate of subsequent government appropriation of a firm's profits", "various fees to be shared with the government", "relational fees"]
definition: Government appropriation refers to government officials pursuing private gain through practices such as appropriating firms' profits, measured as the ratio of firms' profits taken by the government in a given year as 'various fees to be shared with the government', which Li, Meng, and Zhang (2006) termed 'relational fees'.

name: Government-created industry social network involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement in government-created industry social networks", "government-created industry social networks", "membership in the Association of Private Entrepreneurs (APE)"]
definition: Government-created industry social networks are government-backed membership associations such as the Association of Private Entrepreneurs (APE), established as a common strategy to informally monitor entrepreneurs; they give Chinese entrepreneurs an opportunity to obtain information about government policies and new international business opportunities encouraged by the government through frequent exchanges of business ideas and knowledge with colleagues.

name: National economic policy encouraging internationalization
authors_terms: ["post-2001 economic development plan", "10th Five-Year National Economic and Social Development Plan", "national economic policy encouraging internationalization", "post 2001"]
definition: The Chinese government implemented the '10th Five-Year National Economic and Social Development Plan' in 2001, explicitly encouraging foreign cooperation: both inward foreign investments and exploration of international markets, framing the need for internationalization as an economic necessity.

name: Regional FDI intensity
definition: Regional FDI intensity captures the abundance of foreign investors in the entrepreneurs' region; local governments play an increasing role in attracting foreign direct investment, which ratifies and endorses foreign cooperation, and it was calculated by the value of total FDI over the local GDP yearly.

name: Overoptimism in expectations
definition: Individuals are considered to be overly optimistic when they overestimate the likelihood that their nascent activity will result in an operating venture or when they overestimate the future sales and employment of their new ventures.

name: Formal business planning
definition: A business plan was defined as something that 'usually outlines the markets to be served, the products or services to be provided, the resources required-including money-and the expected growth and profit for the new business.' Formal business planning was determined to be present when nascent entrepreneurs responded that they had a business plan and that the current form of the plan was 'formally prepared.'

name: Financial projections
definition: The undertaking of financial projections was represented by a dichotomous variable based on whether projected financial statements, such as income and cash flow statements or break-even analysis, had been developed.

name: Venture operation
definition: Entrepreneurs self-reported whether the startup was an operating business in follow-up phone interviews; those who reported the existence of an operating business, and who did not abandon the operating business at a future date, were coded as operating.

name: First-year venture sales
definition: Entrepreneurs who were involved in a start-up that had completed its first full year of operation were asked what sales or revenue was achieved in the first full year of operation.

name: First-year venture employment
definition: For numbers of employees, entrepreneurs who were involved in a start-up that employed a nonowner employee were asked to provide the number of nonowner employees hired in full-time and part-time capacities.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "CEO's time in office", "time in the job", "time-in-job", "present-position tenure"]
definition: CEO tenure is the total number of years a specific individual has held the chief executive officer position with a company. The authors treat it as the CEO's time in office, which is argued to follow a life cycle of learning and later rigidity.

name: Firm inventiveness
definition: Invention is the creation of new and potentially valuable knowledge; a patent is a tangible embodiment of invention, and companies' patent activities provide an invention 'scoreboard' in invention-intensive industries. The authors measure firm inventiveness as the number of patents a firm successfully files.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: Technological dynamism is the rate of change in and the unpredictability of new technologies, an especially important component of environmental dynamism for firms in invention-intensive industries. It springs from uncertainties surrounding the economic and social feasibility of new technologies that are largely outside the control of a firm.

name: Corporate reputation
authors_terms: ["corporate reputation", "reputation", "public's assessment of corporate reputation", "reputation assessments of the general public"]
definition: A collective representation of a firm's past actions and results that describes the firm's ability to deliver valued outcomes to multiple stakeholders; it incorporates the relative standing and desirability of an organization compared with other organizations.

name: Stock market return
authors_terms: ["stock market return", "stock market returns", "total stock market return", "cumulative total return"]
definition: Stock market returns are commonly considered the firm financial performance measure most closely associated with shareholder value.

name: Earnings volatility
authors_terms: ["financial earnings volatility", "earnings volatility", "financial volatility", "financial performance volatility"]
definition: A firm's financial earnings volatility, measured by calculating the standard deviation of each firm's return on assets (ROA) over the past 10 years; creditors tend to favor stability and consistency in firms over maximizing share price.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: Corporate social performance refers to the extent to which a firm's actions attend to the needs and interests of stakeholders beyond simply its investors.

name: Shareholder rights protection
authors_terms: ["shareholder rights protection", "shareholder rights", "shareholder protections", "Protecting Investors index"]
definition: The level of minority shareholder rights protection against expropriation by corporate insiders, based on the presence or absence of representative shareholder rights provisions covering disclosure to shareholders, director liability, and shareholders' ability to file and pursue lawsuits against insiders.

name: Creditor rights protection
definition: The parts of the World Bank's 'Getting Credit' index that are directly related to creditor rights, such as whether secured creditors are paid first when a debtor is liquidated and whether they can enforce a security right outside of court following the creation of a security interest.

name: Labor rights protection
authors_terms: ["labor rights protection", "labor rights", "worker groups' rights", "core labor standards"]
definition: Labor rights measured based on each country's ratification of the ILO's two 'core' standards on collective bargaining and freedom of association, which are directly related to labor's ability to participate in the governance of the firm.

name: Target manufacturing productivity
definition: A firm's manufacturing productivity measured by the productivity index developed by Caves, Christensen, and Diewert (1982) and later modified by Aw, Chung, and Roberts (2003); the level of the target's capability captures how much stronger or weaker it is compared to the acquirer.

name: Acquisition likelihood
authors_terms: ["Acquisition", "probability of a potential target being acquired"]
definition: The probability that a given acquiring firm acquires a given potential target plant in a given year; all plants existing at time t are considered potential acquisition targets by a given acquiring firm.

name: Geographic market newness
definition: Whether the target operates in a geographic region where the acquirer has no existing presence, as opposed to the acquirer's existing markets; geographic regions are treated as distinct markets.

name: Acquisition capability
definition: A buyer's capability to identify, evaluate and integrate acquisition targets, which lowers the information and integration costs of acquisition; the authors use geographic diversification and prior acquisition experience as measures of general acquisition capabilities.

name: Style turbulence
definition: We define style turbulence as the amount of unpredictable changes-from year to year-in the popularity or 'size' of a style (i.e., in the number of patents granted within that style).

name: Function turbulence
authors_terms: ["function turbulence", "turbulence in product functionality", "turbulence in product function"]
definition: We conceptualize function turbulence as unexpected changes in the number of utility patents in these subclasses.

name: Time period
definition: The analysis segments each style's annual number of granted patents into successive five-year panels, and the period variable orders these panels so that the time trend in style turbulence can be estimated.

name: Financial slack
definition: Unabsorbed slack consists of resources that are currently uncommitted and are readily available for redeployment within firms, with cash resources representing the most easily redeployable resources. Financial slack is the excess cash resources firms hold compared to industry and country norms.

name: Human resource slack
definition: Absorbed slack consists of resources that are already tied to current operations but may be recovered, with more managerial effort and time; HR, accounts receivables and overhead expenses are examples. HR slack is stickier than financial slack and therefore more difficult to reallocate in the short term.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance outcome of a firm's slack resources, measured as gross profit on total assets, where gross profit is revenue minus the cost of making a product or providing a service before deducting overhead, payroll, tax, and interest payments.

name: Creditor rights
definition: Creditor rights refer to the legal rights of creditors against defaulting debtors; when these rights are strong, creditors have more power to force repayment, seize collateral assets, and/or gain control over the firm.

name: Employee rights
definition: Labor protection laws, which aim to protect employees from exploitative employers, differ considerably across countries in the power of unions, the costs of firing employees and the social insurance provided against unemployment and sickness. Employment laws regulate individual employment conditions, including alternatives to the standard employment contract, flexibility of working conditions, and termination of employment.

name: Congressional stock purchase disclosure
authors_terms: ["public disclosure of Congressional stock purchases", "senator stock purchase public disclosures", "disclosure of senator stock purchases"]
definition: The disclosure date, which may be up to 45 days after the actual trade, is the first date information of the stock purchase becomes public. The stock trade disclosure form reveals the name of the company, a range of stock value, and whether the trade was conducted by a member of Congress, jointly with a spouse, or individually by a spouse or child.

name: Abnormal returns
definition: Our outcome variable is cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), calculated with the Fama-French four-factor model surrounding the public disclosure date of the stock.

name: Congressional committee jurisdiction
authors_terms: ["senator committee jurisdiction", "Congressional committee with jurisdiction over the firm", "industry jurisdiction"]
definition: Our independent variable of industry jurisdiction is a dichotomous measure equaling 1 if the senator was on a committee with direct jurisdiction over a firm's primary industry within the past 3 years, and a 0 otherwise.

name: Lobbying the senator's legislative proposal
authors_terms: ["lobbying the senator's legislative proposal", "lobbying the senator's legislation", "lobbying the senator"]
definition: We capture lobbying the senator's legislative proposal utilizing the number of bills that the focal firm lobbied in the past 3 years that were sponsored or co-sponsored by the senator who purchased the stock.

name: Congressional testimony
authors_terms: ["Congressional testimony", "firm representative testimony before the congressional member purchasing a stock", "committee testimony"]
definition: Congressional testimony is the number of times a focal firm's representative testified before the senator in a hearing over the last 3 years.

name: Campaign contributions
authors_terms: ["campaign contributions", "PAC contributions alignment", "political contributions to the senator's political action committee"]
definition: Our variable PAC contributions alignment is calculated as the total amount of political contributions made by the focal firm to the investing senator's political action committee in the past 3 years.

name: Financial restatement
definition: Financial misrepresentation is a category of corporate misconduct that involves a violation of 'generally accepted accounting practices' (GAAP in the U.S.) by agents of publicly listed organizations to project more desirable performance. Filing of a restatement after financial misrepresentation results in loss of social approval.

name: New foundation board ties
authors_terms: ["new ties to foundations' boards", "number of new ties to foundations' boards", "new independent foundation board ties", "ties to foundations' boards"]
definition: A firm's CEO serving as a director on an independent foundation's board of trustees is a natural way to create such affiliations. A trustee's responsibilities primarily involve providing and refining vision, high-level strategic planning, and connecting to for-profit firms, and tend to include fewer fiduciary, due diligence, or management activities.

name: Corporate philanthropy
authors_terms: ["corporate philanthropy", "existing corporate philanthropy", "corporate foundation or giving program"]
definition: A firm's support for social responsibility; a major way in which firms engage in corporate philanthropy is through corporate foundations and giving programs.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: A firm's reputation reflects a pattern of behavior and is seen by external evaluators as a sign of adherence to such norms and as a baseline for assessing its actions.

name: Media tenor
definition: Because media provides a 'forum for what constitutes a good firm', positive coverage by media represents favorable public opinion and has been shown to play a significant role in shaping social approval among diverse stakeholder groups, including investors.

name: Individual human capital
definition: Human capital is the result of any investment in 'activities that influence future real income [of people] through the imbedding of resources in people'; for our purposes, such resources could be any individually resident knowledge or skill that is likely to create value for the individual's employer.

name: Parent firm size
authors_terms: ["parent size", "size of the parent", "log parent size", "log parent employment"]
definition: We analyze how parent size affects an individual's propensity to form spinouts and how that effect changes with the individual's level of human capital; parent size is the size of the parent at a given time, measured as the (log) number of employees at the parent establishment.

name: Within-industry spinout formation
authors_terms: ["within-industry spinouts", "WSOs", "spinouts in the parent's industry", "WSO formation"]
definition: If spinouts are formed in the parents' industry (hereinafter 'within-industry spinouts' or 'WSOs'), parents are direct competitors to these spinouts. We identify WSOs as spinouts that have the same 4-digit NAICS code as their parent.

name: Industry distance between parent and spinout
authors_terms: ["distance", "industry distance", "distance between the spinout industry and the parent industry", "related and unrelated out-of-industry spinouts"]
definition: We divide spinouts into WSOs, related OSOs or OSO-Rs (those at a close 'distance' to the parent industry), and unrelated OSOs or OSO-Us (those at a larger distance). The relevance of inherited knowledge to the performance of the spinout is likely to decrease with distance from the parent industry.

name: Spatial proximity
definition: Spatial proximity is the physical closeness of peers: each team was randomly assigned to a workstation within the bootcamp's large, open office space. The distance between individuals i and j is calculated as the shortest walkable route between each workstation in meters, and participants are assumed to walk around the 5-ft boundary wall.

name: Prior ties
authors_terms: ["prior ties", "prior connections", "prior knowing tie", "existing ties", "existing connections"]
definition: Within and outside organizations, individuals have ties to existing collaborators, advisers, and friends. At the bootcamp, prior connections are measured from participants' responses to the prebootcamp roster-based network survey asking them to select the people they know or know of.

name: Peer interaction
authors_terms: ["social interaction", "interact with their proximate peers", "knowing", "advice", "digital messaging"]
definition: The dependent variables measure whether individual i has a social interaction with a peer j. The authors measure three types of social interactions at the bootcamp: (a) if a participant knows, (b) seeks advice from, or (c) digitally communicates with a peer j outside his or her team.

name: Team performance
authors_terms: ["team performance", "quality of their product prototypes", "quality of such teams' final software prototypes"]
definition: The quality of a team's submitted project; all teams developed a prototype application for the Indian wedding industry, and performance is measured with the double-blind evaluations of the team projects submitted on Friday of the first week.

name: Performance of proximate teams
authors_terms: ["peers' team performance", "performance of nearby teams", "average performance of its nearby peers"]
definition: The average Team performance of the N most proximate teams to a focal team, where N is 4, 8, and 16.

name: AI exposure
authors_terms: ["AI exposure", "exposure to generative AI", "AI task exposure"]
definition: The extent to which AI impacts the tasks performed by a worker, assigned at the occupation level from Felten et al.'s language modeling AI exposure scores.

name: Labor market participation
definition: Participation is defined as the intensity with which a worker engages in the labor market by allocating effort toward seeking work; in this setting it is measurable via job applications, referred to as bids.

name: Horizontal positioning
definition: Horizontal positioning is defined as how a worker allocates effort across different work domains or categories.

name: Vertical positioning
definition: Vertical positioning is defined as how a worker allocates effort across segments of work that differ in economic value within a given domain.

name: Freelancer skill-level
definition: Freelancers' demonstrated skill-level, defined as the level of task complexity and expertise associated with the jobs those freelancers have historically contracted on the platform.

name: Share value
authors_terms: ["share value", "value of a firm's shares", "firm value", "perceived value of those shares"]
definition: Given that each share costs exactly the same, when the shares of a given firm are in higher demand than those of another firm it reflects differences in the perceived value of those shares. In other words, the number of shares demanded reflects the value placed on those shares.

name: Firm size
definition: SIZE is the log of total dollar book assets for 1991, summing the liabilities and equity values.

name: Variance of profitability
authors_terms: ["variance of profitability", "variability of profitability", "variance of intra-industry rates of return on assets", "uncertainty of environment", "historic uncertainty in the environment of the firm"]
definition: VAR is the variance of intra-industry rates of return on assets for 1991. In the absence of a time series of firm profitability, we employ this measure to capture the uncertain environment of the firm.

name: Debt leverage
definition: LEV is the percentage of total liabilities to total assets in 1991. The presence of debt suggests valuable connections through banks (and other lending enterprises).

name: Profitability
definition: ROA is return on assets for 1991. The authors use ROA rather than return on equity (ROE), since equity was a fictional notion during the communist regime.

name: Market share
definition: MKTSH is the percentage of sales of the individual firm relative to total sales of all firms in its industry in 1991. Larger market shares in an industry allow firms to enjoy certain monopolistic advantages such as elevation of prices above costs.

name: Number of rivals
authors_terms: ["number of rivals", "number of competitors", "number of firms in the industry", "rivalry", "COMP"]
definition: COMP is the log of the number of firms in the industry of the firm in 1991. Higher barriers to entry are associated with fewer competitors in the industry, so the number of firms in the industry reflects barriers to entry in the firm's market.

name: Managerial efficiency
definition: MQUAL is a dummy variable with a value of one when revenue per employee in 1991 is above median for firms in the industry, otherwise zero. It captures the knowledge underlying efficiency, or the ability to put organizational resources to their most productive use.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: MNGR is the log of insider ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero insider ownership, otherwise zero. Direct domestic sales represent insiders' holdings, since other domestic buyers could not easily acquire shares without the help of incumbent managers.

name: Restituent ownership
definition: Restituents are the original owners prior to the Communist takeover; OLD is the log of restituent ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero restituent ownership, otherwise zero. Restituents bring in new knowledge and skills into the firm that will be important for the firm's future competitiveness in a market economy.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: FOR is the log of foreign ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero foreign ownership, otherwise zero. Foreign owners bring in new knowledge and skills into the firm that will be important for the firm's future competitiveness in a market economy.

name: Government ownership
definition: GOVT is the log of government ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero government ownership, otherwise zero. Ties to the government give the firm greater competitive advantage over those with no such ties, since the government becomes an important source of institutional knowledge.

name: Dismemberment
authors_terms: ["dismemberment", "broken/dismembered unit", "dismembered component of a larger parent firm", "DISMEM"]
definition: DISMEM is a dummy variable with a value of one if the firm is a piece of a firm broken into multiple firms, and zero if it is the original unbroken firm. Units privatized separately from the original firm have lost critical resources and knowledge related to administrative heritage as well as its external networks with the state.

name: Corporate social initiative participation
authors_terms: ["participation in a corporate social initiative", "CSI participation", "CSI Participant", "employee participation in CSI"]
definition: Employees of the firm are offered the opportunity to participate in consulting projects with an explicit social impact goal, through an initiative the authors refer to as corporate social initiative (CSI). The distinguishing feature of such an initiative is that it has an explicitly stated social impact objective, and from the employees' perspective it aims to make a bigger difference to society compared with the commercial activities of the firm.

name: Employee retention
authors_terms: ["employee retention", "retention likelihood", "likelihood of leaving the firm", "employee departure"]
definition: Improved employee retention is a key strategic outcome for most firms, and the authors' indicator captures whether an individual has left the firm or is still with the firm as of the end of the study period. They also distinguish leaving by choice from being asked to leave.

name: CSI project duration
authors_terms: ["CSI Days", "duration of the participation", "length of the CSI experience", "project length"]
definition: The length of an employee's participation in a corporate social initiative project; in this setting projects ranged from short term (e.g., one month) to long term (e.g., six months), and duration is measured as the total number of days a participant billed to CSI projects.

name: CSI project location
authors_terms: ["CSI in Emerging Market", "emerging market location", "location of the CSI project"]
definition: The location in which the CSI project was based; projects could be based in developed countries such as the United Kingdom or in developing economies such as Tanzania, and the authors focus on whether the participation involved working in an emerging market.

name: Venture capital funding
authors_terms: ["venture capital investment", "venture capital funding", "securing venture capital", "VC investment"]
definition: Our dependent variable is venture capital investment, coded as a binary variable set to 1 in the year(s) that a firm received funding.

name: Patent hybridization
authors_terms: ["hybridization via patenting", "product hybridization", "hybridizes by patenting outside of its home category", "category spanning through patenting"]
definition: This indicates the degree to which a firm is focused on science or technology, as well as when it hybridizes by patenting outside of its home category. Patents may variously draw on scientific versus technological expertise and focus on general versus focused applications.

name: Top management team hybridization
authors_terms: ["TMT hybridization", "hybridize their top management team", "category mixing at this level", "management hybridization"]
definition: In addition to hybridizing at the product level, a start-up may also span between science and technology by altering the composition of its top management team (TMT). Top managers thus directly signal their organization's identity and provide a link to other key markers such as product focus.

name: Collaboration hybridization
authors_terms: ["collaboration hybridization", "hybridize by collaborating", "cross-category collaborations", "spanning categories through collaboration"]
definition: While product and management team hybridization affect fairly central identity markers, collaborations are more likely viewed as peripheral activities relative to the core of an organization's identity.

name: Firm founding category
authors_terms: ["science start-up", "technology start-up", "the category in which a firm starts", "category of origin", "starting category"]
definition: We distinguish between start-ups that originate in science (e.g., spinouts from academic labs) and those that originate in technology (e.g., firms created by high-technology entrepreneurs).

name: Expansion into new technical subfields
authors_terms: ["expansion into a new subfield", "expansion into new technical subfields", "expand", "expansion effect"]
definition: We dated expansion as the year when a firm began to manufacture imaging systems in the new subfield. The focus of this paper will be on what we refer to as spillback effects-the effects of expansion into a new technical subfield on performance in a firm's existing business.

name: Expansion failure
authors_terms: ["expand and exit", "failed expansion", "unsuccessful expansion", "expansion and must exit from it"]
definition: We consider expansion to have failed if the firm withdraws from the new subfield. If an imaging operation was shut down, either through a firm failing or dropping the product line, we recorded the exit as a dissolution.

name: Survival in the base subfield
authors_terms: ["survival", "continued survival in its base subfield", "continued participation", "length of participation"]
definition: In addition to market share, we examine the length of a firm's continued participation in the base subfield, which we refer to as survival.

name: Subsequent market share in the base subfield
authors_terms: ["subsequent market share", "subfield dollar revenue market share"]
definition: We refer to the market share attained in its base subfield by a pre-introduction incumbent after the emergence of a new subfield as "subsequent market share". We examine levels of a firm's market share in its base imaging business or businesses at several intervals after the emergence of a new technical subfield of the industry.

name: Industry-wide market share
authors_terms: ["prior industry-wide market share", "industry share", "pre-introduction industry market share"]
definition: A pre-introduction incumbent's prior industry-wide market share was calculated as its percentage of overall industry sales during the calendar year before the emergence of the new subfield.

name: Subfield market share
authors_terms: ["prior subfield market share", "base subfield share", "subfield market share", "subfield strength"]
definition: Each incumbent's prior subfield market share was recorded for the year before the emergence of a new subfield. While focusing operations on one area may enhance performance within it, this concentration may deprive such specialists of the broad experience and skills necessary to cope successfully with the challenges of a radically changing industry.

name: Entry timing
authors_terms: ["waiting period", "wait before entry", "how early a firm expanded", "expansion waiting periods", "timing of expansion"]
definition: The spillback effects may also depend on the timing of expansion into new subfields. How early a firm expanded into a new subfield was measured by the number of years between the emergence of the subfield and the expansion of the firm.

name: Prior expansion experience
authors_terms: ["number of past expansions", "the more times a pre-introduction incumbent has expanded in the past", "learning from expansion"]
definition: Spillback benefits will tend to increase as a firm and its managers learn how to realize them. Each time a firm successfully expands, it is likely to develop new routines for incorporating benefits across businesses in multiple subfields.

name: IT competency
definition: We conceptualize IT competency as the extent to which a firm is knowledgeable about and effectively utilizes IT to manage information within the firm. IT competency is conceptualized as a higher-order construct consisting of three domains represented by first order factors: IT knowledge, IT operations, and IT objects.

name: IT knowledge
definition: In this study, IT knowledge is conceptualized as the extent to which a firm possesses a body of technical knowledge about objects such as computer based systems.

name: IT operations
definition: For this study IT operations are conceptualized as the extent to which a firm utilizes IT to manage market and customer information.

name: IT objects
definition: For this study the conceptualization of IT objects represents computer-based hardware, software, and support personnel.

name: Organizational learning
definition: At a very basic level it is the process by which new knowledge or insights are developed by a firm. Organizational learning is conceptualized as a higher-order construct composed of five first-order factors representing information acquisition, information dissemination, shared interpretation, declarative memory, and procedural memory.

name: Information acquisition
definition: This is the process by which firms actively seek out and gather useable information.

name: Information dissemination
definition: Information dissemination is the extent to which the information that is obtained by an organization is shared between its functional units, through formal and informal channels.

name: Shared interpretation
definition: This refers to the presence of consensus among organizational members with regard to the meaning of information.

name: Declarative memory
definition: Declarative memory contains knowledge of facts and events.

name: Procedural memory
definition: Procedural memory contains knowledge about routines, processes, and procedures.

name: Firm performance
definition: Together the four performance measures are summated to provide a global indicator of how well a firm is performing relative to direct competitors.

name: Patent effectiveness
authors_terms: ["patent effectiveness", "strength of patent protection", "effectiveness of patent protection"]
definition: We use the term patent effectiveness to mean strength of patent protection. A variety of factors may drive the effectiveness of patents, including increases in length or breadth of protection, greater codifiability of knowledge, decreases in costs of application, and costs of disclosure; because we cannot empirically distinguish among these, we use effectiveness as a summary measure.

name: Specialized complementary assets
authors_terms: ["specialized complementary assets", "complementary assets", "complementary manufacturing assets", "specialized manufacturing capability"]
definition: Manufacturing and marketing assets required for commercializing an innovation are often not generic; instead, they are specialized to the innovation and thus have limited alternative uses. They are difficult to imitate because they result from the interaction of people from different parts of a firm's organization and are built over long periods of time.

name: Licensing propensity
definition: The available measure of licensing is not based on actual licensing deals but on firms' willingness to invest in R&D with the intention to license; it is the percentage of the unit's R&D projects undertaken with the objective of earning licensing revenues.

name: Patent propensity
definition: The percentage of product and process innovations for which the unit applied for patents in the period 1991-1993 in the United States, computed as a weighted average of product and process patent propensities.

name: Licensing conditional on patenting
authors_terms: ["probability of licensing conditional on patenting", "share of licensing in patented innovations", "licensing conditional on patenting"]
definition: The probability of licensing conditional on patenting, which the authors also call the share of licensing in patented innovations. It relates to the two propensities through the identity that the elasticity of the probability of licensing equals the elasticity of the conditional probability plus the elasticity of patenting.

name: Net licensing payoff
authors_terms: ["VL - Vs", "net licensing payoff", "licensing payoffs relative to not patenting"]
definition: The payoff to a firm if it patents and licenses a given innovation (VL), taken relative to the payoff if the firm keeps the innovation secret and does not license it (Vs).

name: Net patenting payoff
authors_terms: ["Vp - Vs", "patenting and not licensing payoffs relative to not patenting"]
definition: The payoff to a firm if it patents but does not license a given innovation (Vp), taken relative to the payoff if the firm keeps the innovation secret and does not license it (Vs).

name: Familiarity of category labels
definition: Familiarity implies the use of elements that by invoking existing understandings facilitate comprehension. The authors conceptualize familiarity in terms of the density of the semantic network of the words that make up a category label.

name: Creativity of category labels
definition: Creativity implies the recombination of elements that evoke surprise or curiosity. The authors conceptualize creativity in terms of the overlap between the semantic networks of the words that make up a category label.

name: Category label adoption
definition: The degree to which a category label is taken up and used by industry stakeholders in an emerging industry; the authors measure the level of a category label's adoption in a given year by counting the number of press releases that used the category label at least once.

name: Egalitarianism
definition: Egalitarianism is defined as 'the belief that all people are of equal worth and should be treated equally in society'; it is manifested in intolerance of abuses of market and political power and support for protecting less powerful actors, and it is a polar position in the egalitarianism/hierarchy dimension of the Schwartz framework, which specifies a society's orientation with respect to legitimate modes of exerting power.

name: Egalitarianism distance
authors_terms: ["egalitarianism distance", "sheer egalitarianism distance", "signed egalitarianism distance", "predicted egalitarianism distance"]
definition: The difference in terms of cultural egalitarianism between the home and host markets; the greater this difference, the greater the adjustments the firm will have to make in order to engage effectively with its stakeholders. The hypothesis focuses on sheer distance, whatever the direction of entry on the egalitarianism/hierarchy dimension.

name: Foreign direct investment flows
definition: Foreign direct investment, or a strategic investment that involves control; the authors examine the choices of organizational populations about the scope of their expansion to different international destination markets by looking at their aggregate foreign direct investment decisions.

name: Resource sharing with employees
definition: Organizations in more egalitarian cultures practice greater sharing of resources, which may be material, such as compensation or benefits; doing so reflects a view of all corporate constituencies as moral equals.

name: Executive-to-worker pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["less egalitarian compensation structures", "payment levels", "differentials between levels", "CEO-to-average-worker pay ratio"]
definition: Less egalitarian compensation structures are characterized by more payment levels and greater differentials between levels.

name: Firm size
definition: Organizational size may be considered as a proxy for the amount of slack resources available to a firm; larger organizations generally possess more slack resources, which favor adaptation to changing circumstances. A related argument holds that organizational size increases market power, lowering the barriers to entry in any market.

name: Profitability
definition: More competent firms should have higher expected profitability from the operation in any additional market and, therefore, should be the first to respond to environmental changes stimulating entry. More profitable organizations are expected to be favored by the possession of slack resources that increase the probability of successful entry and reduce the likelihood of failure.

name: Proximity to the objective market
definition: Proximity is a measure of potential entrant capability; entrants with closer headquarters are more able to better control activities, may be known to customers, and may have better knowledge of objective markets. Given that proximity increases the knowledge of markets, the option to wait may not be so valuable, and first-mover advantages and strategic factors may compel firms to quickly enter a new market.

name: Multimarket experience
authors_terms: ["experience in managing operations across markets", "previous multimarket experience", "number of markets in which a firm operates", "degree of previous diversification"]
definition: Previous multimarket experience may serve to build capabilities, to create effective routines and to accumulate knowledge about how to manage operations across markets. Firms with greater accumulated experience in managing operations across markets should exhibit a greater likelihood to enter more quickly into new geographical markets.

name: Rivalry in core geographical markets
authors_terms: ["extent of competition in core markets", "rivalry in the core market", "rivalry in the core geographical markets"]
definition: By core geographical markets, the authors refer to those markets in which the firm has been traditionally operating and that constitute the main source of revenues and profits. Rivalry in the core market may be an indicator about the extent to which the central activities of the firm are threatened and the need to look for new locations in which to develop these activities.

name: Actual rivalry in the objective market
authors_terms: ["actual rivalry", "current rivalry in the objective market", "concentration"]
definition: Actual rivalry is frequently measured through the use of concentration indexes. High levels of concentration may be used as a proxy for high profit expectations, while oligopoly theory suggests that a smaller number of firms may facilitate coordination practices directed to deter entry.

name: Potential rivalry in the objective market
definition: Potential rivalry should be disincentive to new entry; different arguments indicate that the number of potential entrants may influence competitive actions. As the number of potential entrants increases, the probability of entry and that incumbents discipline new entrants both increase, making entry less attractive.

name: Intensity of demand in the objective market
authors_terms: ["intensity of demand", "demand potential", "deposits per inhabitant", "density of population"]
definition: A higher intensity of demand will lead to higher expected profits in the market. Intensity of demand and market growth are also variables frequently considered in the literature.

name: Market growth in the objective market
definition: Entry timing decisions fundamentally depend on the level of market potential and its evolution (demand growth) over time. A higher rate of market growth can lead to excess, higher expected profits and easier entry, while the attractiveness of entry would be reduced by the larger queue of potential entrants.

name: Speed of entry
authors_terms: ["speed of entry", "timing of entry", "entry timing", "timing of the entry decision"]
definition: The objective of the analysis is to shed light on the factors that have determined the decision of a firm to enter or not into a new geographical market and, given the former, the variables affecting the timing of the entry decision.

name: System-level revenue subgroup representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of revenue functional subgroup managers in the system-level executive team", "Revenue Subgroup (SL)", "revenue functional subgroup at the system level"]
definition: The revenue functional subgroup focuses on achieving financial viability by improving revenues from services offered, optimizing contract agreements with insurance companies, and enhancing reimbursement rates. The paper theorizes about the proportion of managers in this functional subgroup within a system's executive management team.

name: Hospital-level revenue subgroup representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of revenue functional subgroup managers in the hospital-level executive team", "Revenue Subgroup (HL)", "revenue functional subgroup at the hospital level"]
definition: The revenue functional subgroup focuses on achieving financial viability by improving revenues from services offered, optimizing contract agreements with insurance companies, and enhancing reimbursement rates. The paper theorizes about the proportion of managers in this functional subgroup within a hospital's executive management team.

name: System-level medical mission subgroup representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of medical mission functional subgroup managers in the system-level executive team", "Medical Mission Subgroup (SL)", "medical mission functional subgroup at the system level"]
definition: The medical mission functional subgroup is focused on a commitment to provide accessible quality care for patients. The paper theorizes about the proportion of managers in this functional subgroup within a system's executive management team.

name: Hospital-level medical mission subgroup representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of medical mission functional subgroup managers in the hospital-level executive team", "Medical Mission Subgroup (HL)", "medical mission functional subgroup at the hospital level"]
definition: The medical mission functional subgroup is focused on a commitment to provide accessible quality care for patients. The paper theorizes about the proportion of managers in this functional subgroup within a hospital's executive management team.

name: Insured pricing
authors_terms: ["insured pricing", "Insured Price to Medicare Ratio", "commercial pricing", "insured rate"]
definition: The dependent variable is the median pricing of a hospital's basket of reported shoppable services by CPT class for commercial payers. It is operationalized as the Insured Price to Medicare Ratio, using the commercial rate as the numerator and the hospital-adjusted Medicare reimbursement rate as the denominator.

name: Generalized trust
authors_terms: ["generalized trust", "trust one has in an unknown other", "trust that is not specific to another party"]
definition: Generalized trust is the trust one has in an unknown other (Nannestad 2008). It is not specific to a counterparty and originates from a broader context.

name: External sourcing
authors_terms: ["external sourcing", "degree of external sourcing", "bought-in materials and services"]
definition: A firm's degree of external sourcing, or the extent to which it relies on external versus internal parties.

name: Economic downturn
definition: A sudden and drastic economic downturn, which requires firms to be flexible and adjust; we use the context of the Great Financial Crisis to better understand the mechanisms through which generalized trust operates.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measure performance in two ways: return on assets (ROA) and return on sales (ROS). We use earnings before interest and taxes for returns, total assets for assets, and operating revenue for sales.

name: Task environment complexity
definition: We define the collection of task problems as the task environment, which provides external sources of information to the organization. Task environments are categorized as simple or complex, a simple one being both decomposable and concentrated, a complex one being either nondecomposable or dispersed.

name: Organizational form
authors_terms: ["organizational form", "simple organizational form", "complex organizational form", "organizational design"]
definition: Organizational form can be characterized in terms of organizational authority structure and resource access structure. A simple organizational form consists of nonoverlapping communication channels such as a team or a simple hierarchy with a segregated resource access structure, whereas a complex form is composed of complex and overlapping communication channels such as a matrix structure with a nonsegregated resource access structure.

name: Complexity match
authors_terms: ["complexity match", "match between task environment and organizational form", "level of complexity match"]
definition: Level of complexity match between organizational form and task environment, with 1 = low and 2 = high. The authors create more general match categories because of the scarcity of the real data.

name: Level of substandard operating conditions
authors_terms: ["level of substandard conditions", "number of substandard conditions", "substandard operating conditions"]
definition: Operating conditions are defined as a substandard state of the organization with respect to information uncertainty (such as missing information and incorrect information) or agent malfunction (such as agent unavailability, communication channel breakdown, and agent turnover) or both. The level of substandard conditions is the number of such conditions occurring during the crisis.

name: Type of substandard operating condition
authors_terms: ["type of substandard conditions", "information uncertainty", "agent malfunction", "joint substandard conditions"]
definition: Substandard conditions are categorized into two major groups, information uncertainty and agent malfunction; the authors also examine cases when there are joint substandard conditions where both may occur simultaneously.

name: Organizational restructuring during crisis
authors_terms: ["organizational restructuring", "restructuring", "shift of organizational form during crisis"]
definition: Shift status of organizational form during crisis as compared with usual organizational form, with 0 = no shift and 1 = shift. Organizations in the corporate world may restructure under certain situations, and the authors examine the relative value of such restructuring when organizations move from usual to crisis conditions.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational performance can be characterized in a number of ways, including accuracy and timeliness in decision making, market share, and stakeholder perceptions; given that decision making is the core of organizational operations, the ability of an organization to accurately understand a problem and provide an appropriate solution becomes critical. The authors measure organizational performance in usual and crisis conditions.

name: Interdependence within research program
authors_terms: ["interdependence within the research program", "interdependence of a patent within a research program", "interdependence of the patent within its research program"]
definition: The independent variable is the interdependence of the focal patent with the other patents in the same research program within the firm's research portfolio. The premise behind the measure is that subclasses assigned to a patent represent the knowledge components comprising the patent, and the extent of shared knowledge components between two patents represents their interdependence.

name: Interdependence across research programs
authors_terms: ["interdependence across research programs", "interdependence of a given patent in a research program with patents that are in the other research programs"]
definition: The interdependence of a given patent in a research program with patents that are in the other research programs in the firm's portfolio; it captures the extent to which knowledge components of the patent are combined with subclasses of patents in other research programs.

name: Extent of external competition
authors_terms: ["extent of external competition", "extent of competition", "number of competitors"]
definition: The extent of external competition, which the authors measure as the number of other firms that have at least one patent in the same therapeutic area as the focal patent, weighted by the number of each firm's patents in the same therapeutic area.

name: Termination of a patented invention
definition: We use termination to refer to the firm giving up the intellectual property rights on a patented invention through nonpayment of periodic renewal fees. This is distinct from expirations that occur at the end of the 20-year patent term, and abandonments at the application stage.

name: Board political connections
authors_terms: ["corporate political activity (CPA)", "political capital", "political connections", "board political connections", "political connection"]
definition: A firm has a political connection when a company board member holds or held a position in the political establishment - the country's parliament, state legislatures, or a major political party - or has been a close professional associate of a politician (chief of staff, head of campaign committee, etc.). Political capital and CPA are used interchangeably with political connections if a general line of argumentation applies to that specific form of CPA.

name: Transient persistence
definition: Transient persistence λ i is the percentage of firm-specific returns in any period t - 1 that systematically remains in period t, and 1 - λ i is the convergence speed of firm-specific returns. Firm-specific returns are the deviation of a firm's return on assets from the industry mean.

name: Profit volatility
definition: Volatility is the second intertemporal performance metric the study examines and was measured by the standard deviation of ROA for each firm on forward-rolling windows of varying lengths; persistence and volatility are interdependent.

name: Hotel failure
definition: Failure was defined as the cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors. Changes in a hotel's 'doing-business-as' name, its brand affiliation, or ownership were not included as failures because the property continued to provide hotel services.

name: Size-localized competition
authors_terms: ["size-localized competition", "size distance", "localized competition in the size dimension"]
definition: Baum and Mezias argued that a smaller 'size distance' between a hotel and other properties in the market (i.e., too many properties of roughly the same size) should lead to size-localized competition. Size may provide value to some customers, particularly among those who prefer small establishments, and size provides economies of scale and scope for properties.

name: Geographic localized competition
authors_terms: ["geographically localized competition", "geographic-based localized competition", "geographical distance", "location-based competition"]
definition: Geographically proximate firms will likely share a need for the same resources, and thus, will be more intense competitors. The localized competition argument is weighed against the benefits of hotel 'clusters' and of proximate demand generators.

name: Price-point localized competition
definition: Baum and Mezias argued that price-point acts as a proxy for a set of hotel characteristics. Mid-price hotels may exhibit the lowest price-point distance from other properties in the market and feel the greatest effects of localized competition from both luxury and economy hotels.

name: Corporate venture capital funding
definition: CVC refers to the practice of established firms taking a minority equity stake in privately held entrepreneurial ventures (Gompers and Lerner, 1998). By receiving CVC funding, new ventures not only obtain financial capital but also complementary assets from their corporate investors.

name: Complementary asset specificity
authors_terms: ["specialized complementary asset requirement", "specificity of complementary asset requirements", "asset specificity", "specialized complementary assets"]
definition: Complementary assets vary in their specificity. Specialized complementary assets are tailored to a particular use, whereas generic complementary assets may be deployed for alternative uses without much alteration (Teece, 1986).

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty is conceptualized as the level of unpredictability in particular industries. Environmental uncertainty is a relatively broad construct that is arguably proxied somewhat incompletely with a sole measure.

name: New venture performance
authors_terms: ["new venture performance", "performance of new ventures", "venture performance"]
definition: We assessed the performance of new ventures in terms of their ability to exit through an initial public offering (IPO). In addition, we assessed the performance of new ventures by observing whether they survived or failed due to bankruptcy or ceasing operations.

name: Generational product innovation
definition: An improvement of an established product that results in substantial functional and technical advances within a technological regime. It is an approach to enhancing generative appropriability and is prevalent in the digital economy because software-based products allow continual improvement over the product lifecycle.

name: Customer adoption
authors_terms: ["customer adoption", "customers' adoption", "adoption of the product", "near-term demand"]
definition: Customers' adoption of the product in the near term, which the authors describe as overall market demand for and adoption of the product. It is measured by the number of unique users that engage with the app on a specific day in the focal country market.

name: Market position
definition: A product's standing in the market. In digital platforms, mobile app ranking lists capture the market positions of different apps based on their recent demand, rewarding popular apps with salient market visibility and a trendy appeal; a market-leading position means the product has attained a top ranking.

name: Technological legacy
definition: The distance between the present version of the product and its foundational technological roots. The authors draw on the idea that a firm's legacy in old technology constrains its ability to adapt to new product generations because of technological transitions and existing customer relationships.

name: Formal intellectual property protection
definition: As discussed in Hall, Helmers, Rogers, and Sena (2014), there are two forms of intellectual property protection: formal intellectual property protection (FIPP) and informal intellectual property protection (IIPP). FIPP mechanisms include legal tools such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrecy, and FIPP is the primary form of protection available to early-stage ventures prior to launch.

name: Experimentation
definition: I define experimentation as the process of disclosing an incomplete product to (at least part of) the target market to gather customer feedback prior to the completion of product development. This definition is consistent with the Lean Startup, where experimentation is embodied in the notion of a 'minimum viable product'.

name: Uncertainty
definition: Variance measures market uncertainty, that is, the accuracy of the venture's 'view' of the market. For more novel products it is more difficult to identify and understand the relevant market segment, so product novelty is mainly a proxy for market uncertainty, whereas AI is primarily a proxy for technical uncertainty.

name: Competition
definition: The risk of imitation is higher in more 'crowded' markets, and the threat of imitation is higher when a venture operates in a market niche with high competition. Competition is measured based on the number of firms building similar products.

name: Launch
definition: Launch is the circulation of the finished product, coded from evidence such as a 'formal launch' or 'official launch' rather than the testing qualifiers. The survey confirmed that launch is a qualitatively distinct moment: unlike testing, launch is primarily about marketing.

name: New CEO functional background
authors_terms: ["functional background", "functional backgrounds of new CEOs", "selection of functional backgrounds of new CEOs"]
definition: The functional background of a new CEO is the functional subunit from which the new chief executive is selected, as identified by the CEO himself among technical, production, sales, marketing, finance, operations, medical, journalism, and legal backgrounds. The authors treat the selection of new CEOs' functional backgrounds as the outcome of contests for control among contending factions of the firm's dominant political coalition.

name: Strategic contingencies
authors_terms: ["strategic contingencies", "structural contingencies", "corporate strategy and structure", "resource dependencies"]
definition: According to the structural contingencies model, positions of power flow to groups best able to meet the critical problems and contingencies faced by the organization in its environment. The authors measure the strategic contingencies facing the corporation by corporate strategy and structure, and argue that resource dependencies and structural contingencies are historically situated social constructions that are themselves the subject of conflict between contending factions.

name: Foreign import intensity
definition: The import variable is the amount of imports divided by total output in each industry, by 4-digit SIC code. The authors treat increasing foreign competition as a new strategic contingency facing U.S. manufacturing firms during the 1980s and early 1990s.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Return on assets, measured as the return on firm assets and adjusted for the industry average, was used as a measure of firm performance. The authors expect firm performance to shape which functional background is favored in CEO selection and to moderate the effect of imports.

name: Industry isomorphism
authors_terms: ["isomorphism", "industry-level mimetic effects", "isomorphism in the functional background of new CEOs"]
definition: Isomorphism in the functional background of new CEOs is captured by the proportion of CEOs with technical and production, sales and marketing, and finance and legal backgrounds within each industry. Institutional theory posits the role of coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures in leading to isomorphic tendencies in organizational characteristics within an industry.

name: Annual fluctuations in functional backgrounds
definition: The effects of annual trends and fluctuations in the functional backgrounds of new CEOs were captured by calculating the proportion of CEOs with technical and production, sales and marketing, and finance backgrounds for each year. The variable captures annual variations in the rate of selection of functional backgrounds for each year and offers a measure of which subunit may be more in fashion during any particular period.

name: Prior CEO functional background
authors_terms: ["prior CEO", "immediate predecessor", "functional backgrounds of the last two CEOs", "backgrounds of previous CEOs"]
definition: The political dynamics of the CEO succession process were captured by the functional backgrounds of the last two CEOs in office, which measure the stability in power of functional subunits in the firm across generations of CEOs. The authors use the background of the immediate predecessor to assess the entrenchment of power at the corporate level.

name: Second prior CEO functional background
authors_terms: ["second previous CEO", "second prior CEO", "two generations of predecessor CEOs"]
definition: The authors examine how the backgrounds of the two past incumbents influence the background of new CEOs in order to test for long-term entrenchment of functional subunits. The background of the second previous CEO measures whether intraorganizational power persists across multiple generations of CEOs.

name: Stock market impact of R&D announcements
authors_terms: ["stock market impact", "wealth effects of R&D project announcements", "stock price impact", "excess returns"]
definition: The wealth created by the R&D project announcements was operationalized as the excess returns resulting from the conventional event study methodology (Brown and Warner, 1985; McWilliams and Siegel, 1997).

name: Actions involving government agencies
authors_terms: ["actions related to governmental agencies", "actions involving government agencies", "actions related to government agencies"]
definition: Actions related to governmental agencies are captured by government approval or the mention of patents. Actions related to governmental agencies are accessible to investors from sources other than managers.

name: Government approval
definition: Actions related to governmental agencies are captured by government approval or the mention of patents; the example given is a firm that voluntarily submitted test data to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for approval before marketing.

name: Patent mention
definition: The mention of patents is one of the actions related to governmental agencies; patents reflect scientific accomplishment and may contribute to the intangible assets of the firm resulting from R&D efforts only in high-technology industries.

name: Product substitution goal
definition: Managerial intentions or beliefs are indicated by a goal of product substitution, a technical goal disclosed in the R&D announcement.

name: Market share increase intention
authors_terms: ["intention to increase market share", "market share intentions", "aggressive market share intentions"]
definition: Managerial intentions or beliefs are indicated by the intention to increase a firm's market share at the expense of competitors.

name: Growing market belief
definition: Managerial intentions or beliefs are indicated by a growing market mentioned, a belief about market estimates that is known only to management.

name: Diversification goal
definition: Managerial intentions or beliefs are indicated by a diversification goal. The value creation potential of diversification is uncertain, and hence, even when disclosed, it may not lead investors to revise their estimates of firm value.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: Industry R&D intensity is operationalized as the ratio of industry R&D expenditures (sum of R&D expenditures of firms in the industry) to sales (sum of firms' sales in the industry) over the last 3 years prior to the announcement.

name: Firm size
definition: Size is operationalized as the log transformation of total sales of the firm for the 3 years prior to the announcement.

name: Negative performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["negative performance relative to aspirations", "negative PRA", "performance below aspirations"]
definition: PRA is normally calculated as firm performance minus aspirations; the paper calculates separate variables for negative and positive PRA, measuring negative PRA as zero if PRA is positive, and equal to PRA if it is negative.

name: Positive performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["positive performance relative to aspirations", "positive PRA", "performance above aspirations"]
definition: PRA is normally calculated as firm performance minus aspirations; the paper calculates separate variables for negative and positive PRA, measuring positive PRA as zero if the PRA is negative, and equal to the PRA if it is positive.

name: Community orientation
definition: A community orientation is an orientation toward affiliation, engagement, and local social relationships; community banks exemplify the community-oriented firm, being locally owned and managed, smaller in size, operating within a limited geographic area, and pursuing both financial and community goals.

name: Risk-taking
definition: We measure risk-taking using credit risk, which refers to the risk that a borrower defaults on any type of debt by failing to make required payments.

name: Small business lending
definition: Small business loans serve as the measure of community investment; they include commercial and industrial loans with principal less than or equal to $1 million, which are typically extended to small firms, and not secured by farm or nonresidential properties.

name: Enterprise liability
definition: The doctrine of enterprise liability refers to the propensity of legal systems to pierce the corporate veil and hold an entire group liable for the losses incurred by one of its affiliates. Enterprise liability can thus be conceptualized as an exception to the general rule of limited liability.

name: Asset partitioning
authors_terms: ["asset partitioning", "finer asset partitioning", "coarser asset partitioning", "number of subsidiaries"]
definition: Asset partitioning refers to the extent to which the assets controlled by a single ultimate owner are divided into multiple legally independent entities. Finer asset partitioning occurs when assets under common control are divided into a greater number of legally independent entities.

name: Subsidiary decision-making autonomy
definition: Groups grant their subsidiaries decision-making autonomy, that is, the level of autonomy granted to a subsidiary by its corporate parent.

name: Industry downside risk
definition: Industry downside risk is computed using data from Standard & Poor's CRSP/Compustat as the share of firms in an industry (three-digit SIC) that experience 'failure': an annual drop of at least 50% in revenues.

name: Corporate group investment
definition: Investment is the annual change in a group's fixed assets; we examine investment as an outcome of weaker enterprise liability.

name: Corporate group growth
definition: Growth is the percentage change in revenues for corporate group i operating in country c between year t-1 to t, averaged over the sample period.

name: Corporate group failure
definition: A group is said to experience failure if it exhibits a decline in annual revenues of more than 50% (within country and industry) at some point during the sample period.

name: Headquarters monitoring of subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["headquarters' ability to monitor subsidiaries", "group factors related to a parent's control over its subsidiaries"]
