definition: The authors argue that an observing CEO will perceive a liberal-leaning referent CEO's adoption of a CSR executive position as fully congruent with the latter's ideology and unsurprising, whereas a conservative-leaning referent CEO's adoption is perceived as incongruent and therefore highly salient and thought-provoking. The key independent variable is computed as a count of prior industry adoptions in which each adoption is first multiplied by the prior adopter CEO's ideological conservatism.

name: Shareholder CSR pressure
authors_terms: ["shareholder CSR proxy proposals", "shareholders' CSR-oriented proxy proposals", "shareholder pressure"]
definition: Measured as the number of shareholder resolutions urging management to increase their firm's engagement in CSR issues in a given year. These proposals are widely used by shareholders to bring attention to social issues and to show disapproval of current actions, and such pressures should raise the salience of CSR issues inside the company.

name: Institutional equivalence
definition: CEOs who lead institutionally equivalent firms - that is, those in the same industry and geographic community - are likely to have greater awareness of each other's decisions and political values and to be especially attentive to (and puzzled by) their peers' ideologically-incongruent decisions. Firms that were both industry and community (headquartered in the same state) peers were considered institutionally equivalent.

name: Corporate illegality
definition: We define illegal corporate behavior as unlawful activities of members or agents of a firm, engaged in primarily for the firm's benefit. Our definition includes both intentionally and unintentionally illegal acts.

name: Seriousness of illegality
authors_terms: ["seriousness", "seriousness of an illegal corporate act", "seriousness of a violation"]
definition: We used Clinard and colleagues' (1979) three-point scale, which rates violations as ranging from somewhat serious to very serious. Somewhat serious violations (coded 1) were fairly short in duration, not repeated, affected few individuals, and did not result in major losses for those individuals.

name: Multiple convictions
definition: We created a variable representing the number of additional convictions a firm received in the same year as its initial conviction, or during the five-year post-conviction period.

name: Conviction history
definition: We operationally defined subsequent convictions as those occurring after an initial one—either during the five-year post-conviction period that we used to measure performance in the rest of the study, or in any year after that period until 1983.

name: Type of illegality
definition: The sample included four types of illegality (Baucus & Near, 1991): discrimination, per se antitrust, product liability with punitive damages, and other violations.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["longer-term financial performance", "performance", "accounting returns", "stockholder returns", "return on assets", "return on sales"]
definition: By longer-term performance, we refer to accounting and market returns measured over the period one through five years after a conviction, in contrast to returns over a few days or weeks.

name: Protest participation
authors_terms: ["protest participation", "number of participants", "participation in pro-LGBTQ protest", "protest activity"]
definition: The main variable coded from newspaper sources for protest participation is a measure of the estimated number of participants in each pro-LGBTQ event.

name: Multiaudience affiliated organization presence
authors_terms: ["multiaudience AFOs", "organizations that span categories", "organizations with both inside and outside audiences", "multiaudience organizations", "bridging organizations"]
definition: Organizations with both inside and outside audiences seek support from a mix of LGBTQ and non-LGBTQ customers/clients or owners/managers.

name: Inside-audience affiliated organization presence
authors_terms: ["inside-audience AFOs", "inside-audience organizations", "single-audience AFOs", "organizations focused on an inside audience"]
definition: An organization with an inside audience will be owned or managed by LGBTQ people and have primarily or exclusively LGBTQ customers, clients, or patrons.

name: Social movement organization presence
definition: We define SMOs as organizations listed as 'movement,' 'political, social and support,' 'political and legislative,' 'multipurpose and pride,' 'education, antidefamation, antiviolence, self-defense,' and 'community centers.'

name: Business domain
definition: We classify organizations as businesses by following the list of categories described as commercial organizations in table 3 of Negro et al. (2013). Businesses in the GyP include organizations that offer a broad variety of goods and services, such as restaurants and cafés, bars and clubs, hotel accommodations, bookstores, food stores, office supplies, and real estate agencies.

name: Uniqueness
authors_terms: ["uniqueness", "uniqueness of the technology to be sourced", "rarity"]
definition: When there is a small number of existing firms from which a resource can be procured, as can arise when the resource is rare or somehow specific to the exchange, higher switching costs and increased opportunism on behalf of the provider can occur. Uniqueness is captured in three items that assess the degree to which the technology in question is uncommon in the industry, or the degree to which competitors had fundamentally similar technology.

name: Barriers to imitation
authors_terms: ["barriers to imitation", "difficulty of imitation", "inimitability", "tacitness or social complexity"]
definition: Barriers to imitation (such as tacitness or social complexity) pose information transmission problems between the source and sourcing firms, creating information asymmetry and information costs. Barriers to imitation is measured by three items questioning the perceived difficulty of imitating or reverse engineering the technology.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty associated with the technology to be sourced", "technological uncertainty", "technical and commercial uncertainty"]
definition: Conditions of high uncertainty make it difficult to write, execute, and monitor contractual arrangements. Initial confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the authors' overall construct of technological uncertainty had two dimensions: commercial uncertainty and technical dynamism.

name: Commercial uncertainty
definition: The first dimension relates to the uncertainty associated with product design and the market's acceptance of those products and processes. Commercial uncertainty is evaluated with five items that assess the degree to which managers were confident the technology would meet technical and/or commercial expectations.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: The second dimension relates to the uncertainty of whether the underlying technology will be of ongoing value in the midst of a changing technological environment. Dynamism is captured in two items that assess the length of time for which the technology was anticipated to be valuable, or the length of its life cycle.

name: Perceived threat of opportunism
authors_terms: ["perceived threat of opportunism", "threat of opportunism", "potential for opportunism"]
definition: Transaction cost theory is grounded in the notion of bounded rationality and the potential for opportunistic behavior on the part of some individuals or firms. Threat of opportunism includes three items that assess the degree to which managers perceived that there was a risk of being taken advantage of, or the likelihood of partners and suppliers behaving dishonestly if given an opportunity, and the amount of oversight that would be required in the exchange.

name: Potential for sustainable competitive advantage
authors_terms: ["perceived potential for a sustainable advantage", "potential for sustainable advantage", "potential for sustainable competitive advantage"]
definition: Technological resources that are hard to acquire or imitate are more likely to provide their owner with a sustainable competitive advantage and above-normal economic rents. Potential for sustainable competitive advantage is measured in three items that capture the degree to which managers felt the technology would differentiate the firm, or the degree to which managers felt that competitors would be able to reap similar strategic benefits within a short period of time.

name: Governance mode
authors_terms: ["governance mode", "sourcing mode", "acquisition as opposed to a licensing agreement", "market control or hierarchical control"]
definition: Organizations have three basic options for acquiring technological know-how, and the study focuses on the two extremes of the external sourcing continuum: market contracting through licensing versus the use of firm hierarchy through acquisition. Governance mode was coded as a dichotomous variable (0 = license agreement, 1 = acquisition).

name: False positive rewards
definition: When pay and performance are not in sync, low-performance contributions may be rewarded; these are 'false positive' rewards. Measured at the firm level, false positives are the number of a firm's rewarded patents whose value is below the average value of patents in the same technological class, divided by all of a firm's patents.

name: False negative rewards
definition: When pay and performance are not in sync, high-performance contributions may be overlooked; these indicate 'false negative' rewards. Measured at the firm level, false negatives are the number of a firm's nonrewarded patents whose value is above the average value of patents in the same technological class, divided by all of a firm's patents.

name: Corporate scientists
authors_terms: ["corporate scientists", "inventors with a taste for science", "corporate inventors"]
definition: Industrial inventors with a taste for science, that is, inventors who work for for-profit firms but embrace a traditional view in which scientists are driven by a desire to resolve challenges and gain recognition from their peer community. The authors label this group of industrial inventors 'corporate scientists.'

name: Time devoted to R&D work
authors_terms: ["R&D Working Hours", "working hours dedicated to creative R&D activities", "effort in research activities"]
definition: The number of weekly working hours that the inventor dedicated to creative R&D activities during the project that led to the patented invention.

name: Interactions with R&D colleagues
authors_terms: ["Interactions with R&D Colleagues", "interactions with peers in the R&D department", "communication and interactions with colleagues in the R&D department"]
definition: The relative frequency of communication and interactions with colleagues in the R&D department, compared with interactions with colleagues in other departments.

name: Firm patent stock
authors_terms: ["Firm Patents", "firms that own many patents", "firms with many patents"]
definition: The firm's stock of patents as computed from the survey; observed reward decisions about many patents reveal false rewards as a consistent pattern.

name: Acquisition rate
definition: We define acquisition rate as the number of acquisitions that acquirers carry out over a given time period, for example, as the average yearly acquisition rate over three years.

name: Variability of acquisition rate
authors_terms: ["variability of the acquisition rate", "acquisition rate variability", "variability of the rate"]
definition: Acquisition rate variability refers to the variability of the acquisition rate over the same time period as the acquisition rate. Variability of the acquisition rate is a measure of the sequencing of individual acquisitions in an acquisition program.

name: Acquirer performance
authors_terms: ["acquirer performance", "excess market returns", "abnormal market value changes"]
definition: Our primary dependent variable is acquirer performance. As our main performance measure, we used excess market returns to acquirer shareholders, examined over longer time periods because of the focus on the performance effects of an entire acquisition program rather than individual acquisitions.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: Acquisition experience is a proxy for a firm's acquisition capability and was measured as the number of acquisitions carried out prior to our window of observation.

name: Acquirer size
definition: Beyond earlier acquisition experience, an acquirer's size helps alleviate the potentially negative effects of acquisition rate and its variability on performance: larger size commonly means more resources, and often also increased specialization of structures and processes for managing acquisitions.

name: Acquisition program scope
authors_terms: ["acquisition program scope", "breadth of the acquisition program scope", "scope of the acquisition program"]
definition: We determined acquisition program scope as a change in the acquiring firm's two-digit SIC code portfolio during our period of observation; the more a firm's SIC code portfolio expands by acquiring firms from unrelated industries, the broader its acquisition program scope.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["vertical integration", "degree of integration", "degree of total integration", "internal transfers"]
definition: A measure of the degree to which vertical transfers occur between lines of business within a single company, called the degree of integration. The authors measured a line of business's internal flow of goods relative to the goods exchanged in the open market.

name: Forward vertical integration
authors_terms: ["forward vertical integration", "degree of forward integration", "internal downstream transfers"]
definition: Defined as the ratio of the dollar value of internal downstream transfers to total sales (external sales plus transfers out of the line of business). A high degree of forward vertical integration through internal transfers can reduce costs by guaranteeing adequate outlets for a firm's outputs, reducing price distortions caused by powerful dealers or distributors, and providing access to information about upstream profits and manufacturing processes.

name: Backward vertical integration
authors_terms: ["backward vertical integration", "degree of backward integration", "internal transfers received"]
definition: Defined as the ratio of the dollar value of internal transfers received by the line of business to the cost of sales. A high degree of backward vertical integration through internal transfers can create economies by ensuring adequate supplies, reducing cost distortions from monopolized inputs, and providing access to information about input costs and manufacturing processes.

name: Operating costs
authors_terms: ["costs", "ratios of several types of expenditures to sales", "cost variables"]
definition: The ratios of several types of expenditures to sales that vertical integration is expected to reduce: R&D, media advertising, other selling expenses, general and administrative expenses, and production costs. Vertical integration should reduce these expenditure-to-sales ratios because it eliminates expenditures specific to market transactions, reduces common cost inputs shared by two stages of production, and may allow an optimal production technology with shared facilities and overlapping R&D efforts.

name: Advertising intensity
authors_terms: ["media advertising to sales ratio", "media advertising expenditures/sales", "media advertising expenses"]
definition: A line of business's media advertising to sales ratio, one of the five cost variables used as dependent variables. Sales was the sum of internal downstream transfers and market transactions.

name: Other selling expense intensity
authors_terms: ["other selling expenses to sales ratio", "other selling expenses/sales"]
definition: A line of business's ratio of other selling expenses to sales. Other selling expenses consisted mainly of wages for salespeople and promotional expenditures.

name: R&D intensity
definition: A line of business's ratio of R&D expenditures to sales, one of the five cost variables used as dependent variables. The Federal Trade Commission database does not separate process and product R&D.

name: Production cost intensity
authors_terms: ["production costs to sales ratio", "cost of sales/sales", "production costs"]
definition: Production costs were measured using the ratio of cost of sales to sales. Under the rules of full absorption accounting, cost of sales includes payroll, raw material, factory depreciation, and rental expenses incurred in the manufacturing of a product.

name: General and administrative expense intensity
authors_terms: ["general and administrative expenses to sales", "overhead costs to sales ratio", "overhead expenses", "overhead costs"]
definition: Overhead expenses were measured as the line of business's ratio of general and administrative expenses to sales.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "reported operating income/sales", "market-based operating income/market-based sales", "return on sales", "profit margins"]
definition: Two profit margin variables were used as dependent variables: reported operating income over sales and market-based operating income over market-based sales. In both variables, income was pretax, pre-interest expense income from operations for a line of business.

name: Industry demand uncertainty
definition: The predictability of demand in the industry of each line of business, measured from data on shipments recorded in the Annual Survey of Manufacturers. Demand stability was measured as the R-squared derived from regressing industry sales from 1972 through 1976 against a time variable (year 1 through year 5).

name: R&D investment intensity
definition: R&D intensity refers to the degree at which a firm devotes its financial resources to research and development given its stock of resources. It is typically calculated as the level of investments divided by the firm's sales, assets, or number of employees.

name: Managers' firm tenure
authors_terms: ["managers' firm tenure", "top-level managers' firm tenure", "firm tenure of managers", "managers' tenure in the firm"]
definition: During their tenure in the firm managers become knowledgeable about the firm's resources and develop a cognitive framework about the unique opportunities for the firm and what its strategy should be. Top-level managers' firm tenure is calculated as the average number of years managers have spent in a particular firm.

name: Shared team-specific experience
authors_terms: ["shared team-specific experience", "shared team-specific management experience", "shared experience at the upper ranks"]
definition: Shared team-specific experience in the top management team refers to accumulated knowledge of each other's skills, limitations, and idiosyncratic habits. It is essential for managers functioning together because teamwork at the upper ranks involves taking risks on behalf of the firm, committing to certain strategic actions under uncertainty, and winning or losing as a team.

name: Functional background heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["functional background heterogeneity in the top management team", "heterogeneity of functional background in the top management team", "TMT functional heterogeneity"]
definition: Functional background heterogeneity refers to representation in the top management team of various business functions such as marketing, operations, and finance.

name: Board outsider representation
authors_terms: ["ratio of outsiders on the board", "the ratio of outsiders", "board outsiders ratio", "board outsider composition"]
definition: Board independence can be greatly improved by separating the CEO and board chairperson duties, and by including independent outside members in the board, who are more likely to question the decisions made by the CEO and other executives. The ratio of outsiders is calculated as the proportion of outside (i.e., non-executive) directors who were appointed before the current CEO took office.

name: CEO-chair separation
authors_terms: ["separation of CEO and chair duties", "separation of CEO and board chairperson duties", "separate CEO-chair"]
definition: Separation of the CEO and board chairperson duties is a form of increased board independence, since board independence can be greatly improved by separating the CEO and board chairperson duties and by including independent outside members in the board.

name: Technological preadaptation
authors_terms: ["technological preadaptation", "preadaptation", "relevant transferable skills and knowledge", "stock of relevant skills and knowledge potentially available for new uses"]
definition: We develop the notion of technological preadaptation to describe the firm's accumulation, without anticipation or foresight of subsequent uses, of skills and knowledge. In biology, preadaptation refers to cases when the feature of an organism proves by chance to be useful, or preadapted, for performing a function other than the one for which it developed or was originally selected.

name: Leverage of preadaptation
authors_terms: ["leverage", "using preadaptation", "the extent to which firms actually build on these skills and knowledge in new domains", "the extent to which firms draw upon their technological preadaptation"]
definition: There is an important distinction between having a pool of 'relevant specialized transferable skills and knowledge' potentially available for other applications than the original ones and being able to leverage relevant skills and knowledge to generate innovations; 'having' preadaptation (i.e., availability of relevant skills and knowledge) is distinct from 'using' preadaptation. The variable measures the extent to which firms actually leverage their prior experience in a different domain.

name: Technological performance
authors_terms: ["technological performance", "firm performance in technological terms", "patent impact", "value of a firm's innovative output"]
definition: Our dependent variable measures a firm's technological performance by gauging the quality of its patenting activity, that is, the number of citations its patents receive from subsequent patents filed by other firms. The number of citations a patent receives from other patents is a more precise measure of technological performance and a better estimate of the focal patent's true value.

name: TC-enhanced entry mode fit
authors_terms: ["Fit firms", "Fit", "TC-enhanced mode choice", "TC-enhanced international entry mode choices", "TC-enhanced predicted modes", "Non-fit firms"]
definition: International entry mode decisions incorporating previously established variables, as well as transaction cost variables, are referred to as TC-enhanced mode choices. Fit firms are those that used the entry mode prescribed by the enhanced TC model (i.e., firms that the model correctly classified), while Non-fit firms are those that chose entry modes inconsistent with the model's prediction.

name: Entry mode performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "overall exchange performance", "performance of the vertical integration mode", "perceptual measures of firm performance"]
definition: Performance was measured with subjective measures of 'overall exchange performance rather than governance costs,' because firms may be unwilling or unable to provide objective financial measures. Williamson (1991) suggests that TC performance may include cost savings and/or increased revenues.

name: Entry mode choice
authors_terms: ["entry mode choice", "mode of entry", "joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries"]
definition: Entry mode choice examines the percentage of ownership, for example wholly owned vs. joint venture modes. As in previous TC-based entry mode studies, the authors examined two modes of entry: joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries.

name: Asset specificity
definition: One of the central tenants of TC theory is that the specificity of the assets employed in a transaction has a significant impact on the efficiency (TCs) of alternative governance structures. Specific assets are investments made that have less value outside the specific transactional relationship.

name: Behavioral uncertainty
definition: Behavioral uncertainty arises from the potential for free riding, dissemination, and shirking from a potential partner firm. Behavioral uncertainties increase TCs because of (1) the need to monitor partners and (2) the potential costs associated with enforcing agreements.

name: Economic uncertainty
definition: Economic uncertainty arises from political instability, economic fluctuations, currency changes and/or other volatility in a firm's environment.

name: Platform gatekeeping
authors_terms: ["platform gatekeeping", "gatekeeping", "platform access control", "lapse in platform gatekeeping"]
definition: Platform gatekeeping is a prominent policy for governing platform access, defined as a set of predetermined acceptance criteria that control what (complement) or who (complementor) is allowed on a platform. The study focuses on an exogenous lapse of platform gatekeeping, an externally caused weakening in gatekeeping that grants platform access to complementors who are otherwise rejected.

name: Knowledge sharing among complementors
definition: Knowledge sharing among complementors is an interaction driven by agents' competitive and cooperative incentives; when complementors are less burdened by competitive pressure, they are more likely to cooperatively exchange knowledge, such as users' needs or preferences. Knowledge sharing is more likely when agents are more cooperative than competitive.

name: Knowledge complexity
definition: Knowledge complexity is the degree of interdependence inherent in the subcomponents of knowledge. A complementor's knowledge complexity characterizes her mastery of knowledge of heavily interdependent subcomponents, and complex knowledge and associated innovations are difficult for competitors to imitate.

name: Knowledge routineness
definition: Knowledge routineness represents the degree to which knowledge is being applied repetitively, and the limited functional variability regarding the application of the knowledge. Because knowledge of high routineness is more commonly seen or repetitively used, it is easier to transfer and learn and the resulting innovation is easier to imitate.

name: Competition
authors_terms: ["competition", "intensity of competition", "amount of competition (n)", "number of competing products"]
definition: The intensity of competition from other firms' products, which is a function of how many competing products are on the market, n. The authors assume that as competition increases, prices fall, so the threshold condition for exit rises and the threshold condition for entry is less likely to be met.

name: Product exit
definition: The authors define a product exit as the first year that the product drops out of the dataset. Product exit is not 'failure,' but part of a carefully honed strategy of the firm; products should exit markets when marginal revenue is less than marginal cost.

name: Product entry
authors_terms: ["product entry", "product introduction", "launch new products", "incidence of entry"]
definition: A firm launches a product when it has a new model that results in positive profits. Once a firm has entered the market, it becomes at risk for entry into any niche and remains at risk for all time periods that it still has a printer on the market.

name: Product scale
authors_terms: ["quantity of a product sold (q)", "scale", "scale economies", "market share"]
definition: The scale, or how many printers of a particular model are shipped, q. Because economies of scale decrease cost for a product already on the market, for a given price a lower-cost product is more likely to survive, so the hazard of exit falls.

name: Product innovativeness
authors_terms: ["more innovative products", "innovative products", "product innovation", "performance of laser printers"]
definition: Consumers are willing to pay for product innovations, so an innovative firm may command a higher price for its product, and process innovations allow firms to decrease costs; both imply that innovative products have a higher threshold for exit. Printer performance is characterized by speed, measured by pages per minute, and resolution, measured by dots per inch, and firms innovate along both a top frontier of product innovation and a bottom mass-market frontier.

name: Firm innovative capacity
authors_terms: ["innovative capacity", "innovativeness of the firm (i)", "innovative activity of the firm", "stock of knowledge"]
definition: The firm's innovative capacity, i, which enters the marginal cost of a product in the authors' framework; innovative capacity increases the firm's ability to generate new products. The authors use patents to measure the innovative activity of the firm.

name: Brand strength
authors_terms: ["strong brands", "strong product brands", "brand equity", "strong laser printer brands"]
definition: Firms with strong brands, measured as high brand equity, are able to capture higher price premiums on brand extensions into nearby product classes than are those firms without such strong brands. Strong-brand firms are also likely to have more economies of scope (or less diseconomies of scope) than weak-brand firms, because brand equity spills over to new products and lowers advertising and channel costs.

name: Buyer's idiosyncratic investments
authors_terms: ["buyer's idiosyncratic investments", "supplier-specific investments", "buyer's specific investments", "idiosyncratic investments", "credible commitments", "pledges"]
definition: Consistent with transaction cost economics, we define idiosyncratic investments as investments specific to a relationship, which are difficult or expensive to transfer to another relationship without losing their value.

name: Architectural interdependence
authors_terms: ["architectural interdependency", "architectural interdependence", "significance of the interface between the component and the vehicle"]
definition: The extent to which the interface between the supplier's component and the assembled vehicle is critical to the buyer's product performance in its downstream market.

name: Task complexity
authors_terms: ["task complexity", "complexity and customization of the component"]
definition: The extent to which there is not a known procedure that specifies the sequence of steps to be followed in performing the task (of designing and producing the component).

name: Supplier size
definition: The absolute size of the supplier firm; the authors treat larger firms as having become so by virtue of achievement, which suggests a generalized competence on the part of a larger component maker and reflects accomplished economies of scale.

name: Supplier market share
authors_terms: ["supplier's market share", "supplier's share of the market for the component"]
definition: The supplier's share of the market for the component being sourced; a high market share is a reflection and a consequence of the superiority of the assets, skills, and capabilities of the supplier.

name: Volume unpredictability
definition: The inability to forecast accurately the volume (quantity) requirements in the relationship.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: The inability to forecast accurately the technical or design requirements for the component exchanged within the relationship.

name: Upstream market concentration
authors_terms: ["upstream market concentration", "concentration of supply of a component", "concentration of upstream market"]
definition: The concentration of supply of a component, used to assess how thin the supply market is: a concentrated supply market means there are few real players, hence input markets are thin, and buyers need protection against opportunism.

name: Resource standardization
authors_terms: ["standard resources required to produce component", "standardization of the resources needed", "how widespread are the resources needed to supply a component"]
definition: How widespread are the resources needed to supply a component. If a component can be produced using standard capabilities, that is, resources any supplier might be expected to have, then many more of the nominal players are really eligible suppliers than would be the case if the component demands rare resources that only a few suppliers might possess.

name: Relationship scope
authors_terms: ["scope of the overall supply relationship", "overall business relationship", "overall business done with this supplier"]
definition: The extent to which a given supply relationship occurs within the context of a larger overall business relationship, assessed by the number of distinct components the supplier provides to the buyer.

name: Relationship age
authors_terms: ["age of the overall supply relationship", "age of the relationship", "older relationship"]
definition: The length of time the buyer's firm has done business with the supplier altogether; the authors reason that an older relationship is itself an asset which the decision maker would hesitate to jeopardize.

name: Supplier reputation
authors_terms: ["supplier's market reputation", "supplier's performance reputation", "reputation for performance in supply relationships"]
definition: The supplier's marketwide reputation for performing well in its relationships with business partners; a reputation, once developed, can be an asset much too valuable to put at risk by behaving opportunistically.

name: National institutional context
definition: The institutional environment within which transactions are located, in which the need for transaction-specific safeguards, such as credible commitments, varies systematically; the main import of culture is that it serves as a check on opportunism.

name: Codified knowledge utilization
authors_terms: ["codified knowledge", "amount of codified knowledge obtained and used by the team", "amt. codified knowledge", "electronic documents", "knowledge utilization"]
definition: Codified knowledge is knowledge recorded in written documents and obtained through the firm's electronic database systems. 'Knowledge utilization' in this paper refers to the process of obtaining and using knowledge from documents and people outside the team.

name: Personal knowledge utilization
authors_terms: ["personal knowledge", "amount of personal knowledge obtained and used by the team", "amt. personal knowledge", "advice from colleagues", "knowledge utilization"]
definition: Personal knowledge takes the form of expertise held by individuals who do not belong to the team and is obtained through interpersonal networks. 'Knowledge utilization' in this paper refers to the process of obtaining and using knowledge from documents and people outside the team.

name: Team task experience
authors_terms: ["team's level of task experience", "team task experience", "team experience"]
definition: The measure captures the overall level of the team's experience in the area of the task, i.e., how much experience the sales team had with the solution and methodologies described in the proposal prior to the start of the sales proposal.

name: Task competitiveness
authors_terms: ["task competitiveness", "number of competitors", "no. of competitors", "number of competing consulting firms"]
definition: Assuming that a team confronts a more competitive task situation to the extent that more firms are bidding for the same contract, the authors measure task competitiveness as the number of competing consulting firms that a focal team faces when bidding for a new client contract.

name: Bidding performance
authors_terms: ["task-unit performance", "contract won", "chances of winning the bid", "winning bids"]
definition: At Centra, a sales bid was classified as a win when the client signed a letter of intent to hire the firm, or as a loss when the client decided not to hire the firm. The dependent variable is coded 1 if the team was successful in securing the contract or 0 if it was lost.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance when below social aspiration", "performance when below historical aspiration", "negative performance feedback", "performance below the aspiration level"]
definition: The aspiration level serves as a key reference point for evaluating firms' performance: performance below the aspiration level is, subjectively, equated with failure. The greater the performance gap below the aspiration level, the more motivated the firm is to engage in risk taking.

name: Performance above aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance when above social aspiration", "performance when above historical aspiration", "positive performance feedback", "performance above the aspiration level"]
definition: The aspiration level serves as a key reference point for evaluating firms' performance: performance above the aspiration level signals success. When performance rises above the aspiration level, managers are relieved from the pressures of addressing immediate problems and become motivated to focus on developing durable, proprietary assets.

name: Bribery expenditure
definition: 'Bribery' is defined as the offering or receiving of any undue reward to influence the actions of an official or other person in charge of a public or legal duty. Bribery is an example of deviant risk taking, namely risky undertakings with illegal and/or unethical actions.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity reflects a firm's efforts to build its long-run innovative capabilities. R&D is an example of aspirational risk taking: risky actions taken by a firm to sustain its competitive advantage and fulfill its long-term aspirations.

name: Legal development
definition: The development of legal institutions has direct implications for the containment of illegal behaviors such as bribery, as well as for the protection of intellectual property rights resulting from R&D activities.

name: Industry competition
authors_terms: ["industry competition", "level of competition", "competition level of an industry"]
definition: The level of competition can affect the perceived difficulty of reaching corporate goals and performance aspirations. High competition in a crowded industry - as indicated by low industry concentration - reduces scale economies and survival chances for all firms.

name: Country-of-origin agglomeration
definition: Recent studies have examined country-of-origin agglomeration, namely, clustering of firms from the same country in a foreign location.

name: Non-Korean foreign firm agglomeration
definition: Agglomeration of non-Korean foreign firms; non-Korean firms refer to non-Korean foreign firms, and Chinese firms are excluded from this category because they are not subject to the liability of foreignness and may behave differently from foreign firms in location choice.

name: Location choice
definition: For location choice, we use a dummy variable at the firm level, which is coded as one if a Korean firm i in industry s established a subsidiary in region j in year t, and zero otherwise.

name: Regulatory burden
definition: To capture regulatory burden that MNEs face in a host country, we resort to an exogenous diplomatic shock between MNEs' home and host countries that intensifies diplomatic tensions and increases regulatory burden for MNEs in the host country.

name: Firm size
definition: Empirically, absent a precise measure of resource endowment, we focus on the size of MNEs; large firms may muster more financial, technological, and reputational resources, all of which contribute to their bargaining power and relationship building with the government.

name: Subnational institutional quality
definition: Some regions have higher institutional quality as they allow the market principles to dominate, limit government interference in the market, respect the rule of law, and protect property rights.

name: Strategy coupling
authors_terms: ["strategy coupling", "degree of coordination or coupling among strategies", "tight coupling", "loose coupling", "coupling of the redesign and IT strategies"]
definition: The degree of coordination or coupling among a redesign project's work process strategy and its IT strategy. Tight coordination of redesign and IT strategies eliminates redundant resources and effort, enabling the leveraging of IT investments across business units, whereas loose coordination allows judgment at the operational level in determining and acquiring IT resources as the redesign project unfolds.

name: Process innovation
definition: We categorize redesign projects as process innovations when they produce radically new configurations of assets and activities. We refer to first-mover process innovation as process inventions and the second-movers' copied design as process imitations.

name: Project performance
definition: Traditionally, project performance has been defined as adherence to predictions regarding cost, schedule, and technical specifications. More recently, project performance has been described subjectively by measuring client satisfaction.

name: Sell-off experience
authors_terms: ["experience with sell-offs", "count of prior sell-offs", "10-year count of sell-offs", "restructuring experience"]
definition: Prior sell-off activity from which absorptive capacity and explicit knowledge can be developed; the absorptive capacity view of learning pertains more to sell-offs than spin-offs because sell-offs provide more of the conditions necessary for accumulating experience benefits, assimilating knowledge, and codifying routines and standardized procedures. Experience was measured as the count of prior restructuring events made during the 10 years before the focal restructuring.

name: Spin-off experience
authors_terms: ["experience with spin-offs", "count of prior spin-offs", "recent experience with spin-offs", "restructuring experience"]
definition: Prior spin-off activity, which is most relevant in its short-term and recent form because spin-offs typically occur infrequently and offer fewer opportunities for developing repetitive routines and the explicit knowledge that supports absorptive capacity. Experience was measured as the count of prior restructuring events made during the 10 years before the focal restructuring.

name: Sell-off adoption
definition: Use of a sell-off as the mode of the focal corporate restructuring event; a sell-off, also known as a divestiture, arises when assets are sold from one firm to another in exchange for cash and/or securities.

name: Spin-off adoption
definition: Use of a spin-off as the mode of the focal corporate restructuring event; a spin-off occurs when a firm distributes on a pro rata basis all the shares it owns in a subsidiary to its own shareholders, creating a separate, publicly traded firm from the spun-off assets.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance was measured as the ROA and mean earnings per share (EPS) for each of the five years after the year of the focal restructuring event; using both measures reflects the multidimensional aspects of financial performance.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "independent director proportion", "proportion of independent directors"]
definition: Board independence is assessed by the degree to which the board comprises people who are not otherwise affiliated with the company through employment or economic exchange relationships.

name: Board size
definition: Board size is the count of the members of the board of directors at the beginning of the year.

name: CEO power
definition: The degree to which a CEO wields power, following Finkelstein's (1992) measure, which described four elements of CEO power: structural, ownership, prestige, and expert power, of which the authors include the first three.

name: Financial distress
definition: The degree of financial distress of each firm at the beginning of each sample year, measured using the Ohlson bankruptcy prediction index; higher levels of the index indicate greater likelihood that the firm will declare bankruptcy during the upcoming year.

name: Firm failure
definition: A firm is coded as having failed if it was delisted from the stock exchange on which it was traded for reasons other than acquisition and the authors can find evidence that it has ceased conducting business.

name: Board informal hierarchy clarity
authors_terms: ["clarity of the informal hierarchy of a firm's board of directors", "board informal hierarchy", "board membership inequality", "informal hierarchy based on directors' deference for each other"]
definition: A tacit hierarchical order that forms among the directors on a board on the basis of the deference they give and receive; its clarity increases with the degree of differentiation in that deference, so that an ambiguous hierarchy exists when directors receive similar levels of deference and a clear one when they differ considerably.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Each firm's financial performance, measured by return on assets; accounting measures such as ROA are considered to reflect the influence of internal management better than market-based measures, which are more subject to exogenous economic factors.

name: CEO informal hierarchy rank
authors_terms: ["the CEO's rank in the informal hierarchy", "CEO has highest informal rank"]
definition: Whether the CEO of the focal firm has the highest rank in the informal hierarchy of its board; if the CEO has the highest rank, he/she has an enhanced capacity to influence other directors to yield substantially to his/her points of view.

name: Board rank composition
authors_terms: ["the rank composition of a board", "directors' ranks on average", "middle-ranking board"]
definition: Whether a board is mainly composed of individuals who are low-, middle-, or high-ranking in the corporate community, based on the average rank of the board's directors.

name: Board size
authors_terms: ["board size", "the size of the board", "the total number of directors on a board"]
definition: The total number of directors on a board; retrieving a rank order may be cognitively taxing for directors on a big board, making it harder for the informal hierarchy to guide their interactions.

name: Past firm performance
definition: A firm's prior financial performance, which provides feedback and serves as a cue for directors to determine what and how much strategic activity is called for; poor past performance may indicate a crisis at the top and often leads to conflict.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Volatility in an industry; highly dynamic industries are characterized by frequent, relatively unpredictable changes in their business environment, in which firms often find quick decisions critical to their performance.

name: Ethnic group relation to perpetrator
authors_terms: ["ethnic group membership", "coethnic", "ethnic rivals", "rival ethnic groups", "non-rivals", "shared versus rival ethnicity", "ethnic identity"]
definition: Membership in the institutionalized ethnic groups that make up Kenyan society: Kukuyu investors are coethnic with the corrupt brokerage and the market's governance regime, the Luo and Kalenjin are rival groups that challenge the Kukuyu for political and economic power, and other groups are non-rival.

name: Fraud victimization
authors_terms: ["fraud victimization", "client of the corrupt brokerage", "financial loss", "victims"]
definition: All Nyaga clients were victimized to some degree, as their assets were frozen by the regulator until they transferred their accounts, but about 25 percent of Nyaga clients also experienced direct financial losses when the corrupt brokerage stole cash and/or shares from their accounts.

name: Post-fraud market participation
authors_terms: ["future participation in the market", "continued market participation", "level of market participation post-fraud", "avoidance of the market", "account inactivity"]
definition: The investor's continued participation in the market after the fraud; the authors interpret account inactivity as avoidance of the market because the investor effectively surrendered his or her assets when the regulator froze all Nyaga accounts.

name: Ethnic affiliation of chosen intermediary
authors_terms: ["type of intermediary chosen", "choice of each of the four types of intermediaries", "another Kikuyu intermediary", "non-Kikuyu intermediary"]
definition: The social and professional category of the intermediary a victim chose as his or her new agent: each of the 35 intermediaries available during the weeks between regulatory intervention and the telecom IPO was categorized as a Kukuyu or non-Kukuyu stockbrokerage or commercial bank, with same versus different defined in relation to the corrupt Kukuyu stockbrokerage.

name: Perceived trustworthiness of chosen intermediary
authors_terms: ["integrity-based preferences for each type of intermediary", "perceived integrity of the intermediary", "most trusted type of intermediary"]
definition: The integrity- and competence-based trustworthiness that victims of a group attribute to a type of intermediary; the authors read each group's integrity-based preferences for each type of intermediary from victims' choices and match those preferences to the level of post-fraud investing enacted through each type.

name: Regulatory uncertainty
authors_terms: ["regulatory uncertainty", "uncertainty in the regulatory environment", "perceptions of regulatory uncertainty"]
definition: Regulatory change that creates potential uncertainty for decision makers in small organizations arises from both new legislation and unpredictable changes in current regulations. Uncertainty in the regulatory environment, seen as resulting from variation in the way the federal government and other third-party payers influenced the physicians' organizations, was measured with two items.

name: Competitive uncertainty
authors_terms: ["competitive uncertainty", "uncertainty in the physicians' environment", "perceptions of competitive uncertainty"]
definition: Two attributes of uncertainty in the physicians' environment were assessed: complexity and dynamism. Complexity was assessed by asking the physicians to what extent the types of health-care provider firms with which their practices competed directly had changed during the last six months.

name: Intraorganizational managerial adaptation
authors_terms: ["intraorganizational managerial responses", "boundary-spanning activities", "managerial-level adjustments within themselves"]
definition: Four items represented managerial responses that used an organization's present resources and were typically boundary spanning. Boundary-spanning activities represent the least costly strategy for small firms because they can be undertaken at the managerial level without disrupting the central operating procedures of a company.

name: Interorganizational managerial adaptation
authors_terms: ["interorganizational managerial responses", "managerial-level collaboration", "reciprocal exchanges at the managerial level"]
definition: The two managerial linkages included represented simple exchanges in which an organization attempts integration while preserving autonomy. Examples of reciprocal exchanges at the managerial level include pooling resources to lobby federal agencies, mounting public awareness campaigns to enlist consumer support, and engaging in joint ventures with noncompetitors like suppliers and clients.

name: Intraorganizational technical adaptation
definition: Three items typified technical-level responses involving alterations in actual services provided and representing changes in an organization's technical core designed to retain latitude and flexibility by increasing excess capacity. Small firms may attempt differentiation by changing their product mix, emphasizing particular products or services, or changing production schedules.

name: Interorganizational technical adaptation
authors_terms: ["interorganizational technical responses", "technical-level interdependencies", "interorganizational adaptation at the technical level"]
definition: Transactions at this level are not simple exchanges in which individual firms can maintain distinct identities. Instead, technical interdependencies often blur organizational boundaries, even to the point of merger.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty as the broad uncertainty in the physicians' environment encompassing regulatory and competitive uncertainty.

name: Corporate performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations (corporate unit)", "corporate performance-aspiration gap (below aspirations)", "corporate performance below aspirations"]
definition: Performance below aspirations equals 0 for all observations in which the performance (at the corporate level) of the focal firm is greater than its aspirations; for all other observations, it equals the difference between the performance and aspirations.

name: Business unit performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations (business unit)", "business unit performance-aspiration gap (below aspirations)", "business unit performance below aspirations"]
definition: Performance below aspirations equals 0 for all observations in which the performance (at the business unit level) of the focal firm is greater than its aspirations; for all other observations, it equals the difference between the performance and aspirations.

name: Corporate performance above aspirations
definition: Performance above aspirations is defined symmetrically: it is 0 when the performance is below the aspirations and equals the performance-aspiration gap when performance falls above the aspirations.

name: Business unit performance above aspirations
definition: Performance above aspirations is defined symmetrically: it is 0 when the performance is below the aspirations and equals the performance-aspiration gap when performance falls above the aspirations.

name: New product introductions
authors_terms: ["new product introductions", "number of new phones introduced", "rate of new product introductions"]
definition: Our dependent variable is new product introductions as measured by the number of new phones introduced during each quarter in a year. A mobile phone qualifies as 'new' if at least one of its design characteristics differs from those of the firm's previous products.

name: Business unit importance
authors_terms: ["BU importance", "strategically significant business units", "business unit share of operating income"]
definition: BU importance is measured as the ratio of business unit operating income to the firm's overall operating income of the firm, and it captures the relative importance of the business unit in corporate performance.

name: Business unit experience
definition: BU experience is measured as the cumulative number of prior mobile phones introduced by the business unit; this variable reflects the relative experience of the business unit.

name: Patent grant over knowledge claimed in a publication
authors_terms: ["patent in force", "grant of a patent over knowledge claimed in a publication", "gene patent grant"]
definition: The event in which the patent paired with a publication is granted, so that the knowledge disclosed in the paper is subject to formal legal intellectual property rights; patent in force is a dummy equal to 1 for all years after a patent was granted and 0 prior to patent grant.

name: Follow-on public knowledge production
authors_terms: ["annual citations", "rate of follow-on publications", "follow-on public knowledge stream", "public knowledge production"]
definition: Contributions to the public knowledge stream building on a focal gene paper, measured as the annual number of citations a gene paper receives.

name: Patent scope
definition: Following Lerner (1994), the number of national classes in which a patent was categorized.

name: Patent strength
definition: The number of claims a patent contains, which captures its strength: claims are the legal articulation of the boundary of the property rights, with the principal claim defining the essential, novel features of an innovation.

name: Patent assignee sector
authors_terms: ["public assignee", "private assignee", "all public assignees", "all private assignees", "patent assignee"]
definition: Whether the patent owner (assignee) is from the public (academic or government) sector or from the private sector, defined as a pharmaceutical, biotechnology, or other private sector corporation.

name: Patent thicket density
authors_terms: ["patent thicket", "thicket of patents", "gene patent 1", "gene patent 2 to 4"]
definition: A patent thicket is an overlapping set of patent rights requiring those seeking to commercialize new technology to obtain licenses from multiple patentees; measured as the number of patents claiming the same set of (gene) knowledge inputs.

name: Patent ownership fragmentation
definition: We measured fragmentation as the number of owners in a patent thicket; the patent-gene fragmentation index weights gene fragmentation, computed as the Herfindahl index of the shares of a gene held by each individual owner, across all the genes claimed by a patent.

name: Commercial relevance of patented genetic knowledge
authors_terms: ["usefulness of patented knowledge", "commercial relevance", "disease gene", "OMIM gene", "cancer gene"]
definition: The immediate usefulness and potential for commercialization of the knowledge in a patent-paper pair, proxied by whether a focal gene is linked to a specific human disease at the time of its patent grant.

name: Shock to managerial resource stock
authors_terms: ["Manager death", "negative shock to its stock of managerial resources", "shocks to resource stocks", "supply-side shock"]
definition: The unexpected death of a manager in a unit creates an exogenous, negative shock to a unit's managerial resource stock that is unlikely to be correlated with other determinants of a firm's resource allocation decisions. These indicators represent exogenous shocks to units' resource stocks.

name: Shock to firm managerial resource stock
authors_terms: ["Firm manager death", "negative shock to its stock of managerial resources"]
definition: A firm-level variable indicating firms that lose a manager to unexpected death in any unit, representing an exogenous shock to the firm's stock of managerial resources.

name: Outward redeployment of managers
authors_terms: ["Outward redeployment", "redeployed out of a focal unit"]
definition: We refer to a worker leaving an establishment as Outward redeployment; it is measured as workers who switch employment between establishments of the same firm between the end of 1 year and the end of the following year.

name: Inward redeployment of managers
definition: We refer to a worker joining an establishment as Inward redeployment; each inward redeployment necessarily has a matching outward redeployment.

name: Unit opening
definition: Any opening is an indicator variable for a firm having opened at least one establishment in a year. An establishment is identified as new in the first year it appears in RAIS, which is also the first year it has any employees.

name: Unit closing
definition: Any closing is an indicator variable for a firm having closed at least one establishment in a year. An establishment is identified as closed in the last year in which it has employees.

name: Firm technology intensity
definition: In this paper, the terms 'high technology,' 'technology intensive,' and 'R&D intensive' are used interchangeably; technology intensity was measured as the ratio of annual R&D expenditures to sales.

name: CEO bonus
definition: CEO short-term incentives were measured using the CEO's annual bonus, the year-end incentive linked to profitability indicators during the preceding year.

name: CEO total incentives
authors_terms: ["total incentives", "CEO total incentives", "CEO bonus and long-term pay", "total variable compensation", "combination of short- and long-term incentives"]
definition: Total incentives were calculated by adding CEO annual bonus and long-term income, so that they represent the CEO's total variable compensation.

name: Financial results
definition: Financial results represent more immediate assessments of a firm's ability to generate profits for shareholders; each firm's financial results were measured using its annual return on equity (ROE).

name: Invention resonance
definition: The first dimension of innovation quality reflects an invention's ability to stimulate subsequent inventions: the degree to which one observes a 'ripple effect' as an invention stimulates subsequent inventions. The authors refer to this dimension of innovation quality as 'invention resonance.'

name: Science harvesting
definition: The second dimension of innovation quality reflects evidence that an innovation that builds on basic scientific research tends to produce breakthrough technologies and discontinuous technological shifts, a process the authors call 'science harvesting.'

name: Market performance
authors_terms: ["firm market performance", "market expectations for future performance", "market-to-book ratio", "subsequent performance", "long-term performance"]
definition: Because innovation is a set of future-focused activities and processes whose value must be assessed over the long term, the authors use the market value of the firm to assess the market's expectations of firms' long-term innovation returns.

name: CEO incentive alignment
definition: The degree to which CEO incentives are aligned with financial results and behavioral indicators of innovation quality, captured by interactions of CEO bonus with financial results and total incentives with invention resonance and science harvesting.

name: Regional community density
definition: Regional community density is defined as the number of organizational communities in a specific region (a province or equivalently autonomous region and municipality city).

name: Geographic proximity to the nearest community
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity", "geographic proximity to the nearest community"]
definition: Geographic proximity captures the spatial distance between a focal community and the nearest neighboring community.

name: Domain overlap with the nearest community
authors_terms: ["domain overlap", "domain overlap with the nearest community"]
definition: Domain overlap captures a focal community's industry specialization relative to the nearest community; the authors define it as the extent to which the focal community's major industries correspond to those of the nearest community.

name: Community growth
authors_terms: ["community growth", "growth of organizational communities", "growth in terms of a zone's annual sales revenues"]
definition: To examine the effects of intercommunity relationships on community growth, the authors estimate models of growth in terms of a zone's annual sales revenues.

name: Locus of control
authors_terms: ["locus of control", "internal locus of control", "external locus of control"]
definition: Locus of control reflects individuals' generalized perceptions of the degree to which they control, or are controlled by, their environment (Rotter, 1966). 'External' individuals tend to believe that the outcomes of a strategy are beyond their control, whereas 'internals' tend to view their fate as primarily under their control.

name: Perceived managerial discretion
definition: The degree to which participants believed they had discretion over specific strategic organizational issues. The notion that discretion can be exercised or created only to the extent it is perceived.

name: Objective discretion
authors_terms: ["objective discretion", "high and low discretion contexts", "expert determined discretion", "objective levels of discretion"]
definition: Situations for which the panel of industry experts unanimously determined that the participant would typically either have, or not have, the discretion to act successfully. Situations possess characteristics which hinder or facilitate one's ability to act.

name: Managerial power
authors_terms: ["managerial power", "power", "perceived power", "power others ascribe to them"]
definition: Managerial power is defined as the ability to influence others. A manager must be recognized by others as powerful in order to influence these others.

name: CEO gender
definition: CEO gender is a dummy variable of 1 if the CEO was female and 0 if male.

name: Acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["acquisition activity", "number of acquisitions", "acquisition spending", "firm acquisition strategies"]
definition: We captured two distinct measures of firm acquisition strategies: number of acquisitions and acquisition spending.

name: Scrutiny
definition: High scrutiny contexts - or situations in which others are closely observing CEO and firm actions - likely attenuate the gender-based differences in acquisition activity, while low scrutiny contexts likely enhance those differences.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Industry dynamism reflects the level of industry instability and is marked by high turbulence, unpredictable changes, and heightened pressure and scrutiny from external stakeholders on firm decisions.

name: Media coverage
definition: Although media coverage represents scrutiny from others outside of the firm, it is a firm-specific source of scrutiny that serves as a barometer of the public attention individual firms receive.

name: Relative board power
definition: CEOs can vary substantially in the degree to which they face scrutiny from the board of directors. Powerful boards hold more control over the CEO in shaping firm-level decisions than do less powerful boards.

name: Competing extra-organizational affiliations
authors_terms: ["competing extra-organizational affiliations", "extra-organizational affiliations with organizations that compete with one another", "extra-organizational affiliations"]
definition: Specifically, we point to a hidden but common constellation: two coworkers have extraorganizational affiliations with organizations that compete with one another. If individuals A and B are employed by Organization 1 and if A has an affiliation with Organization 2 and B has one with Organization 3, we suggest that if Organizations 2 and 3 compete with each other, A and B's collaboration on behalf of Organization 1 will decrease.

name: Intraorganizational collaboration
definition: In line with prior research, we operationalize collaboration by studying passes between teammates. Measuring the number of times a player passes the ball to a teammate captures well his willingness to collaborate.

name: Identification with the extra-organizational affiliation
authors_terms: ["identification with the extra-organizational affiliation", "identification with the national team", "identification"]
definition: If people identify with the organization with which they have an (extra-)organizational affiliation, it affects how they perceive others. The authors suggest that the two colleagues need to strongly identify with the external organizations to which they are affiliated so that the competition between those organizations affects the colleagues' relationship.

name: In-person encounter
authors_terms: ["in-person encounter", "directly encountered a club teammate as a direct opponent", "encountering a coworker in a competitive activity"]
definition: Encountering a coworker in a competitive activity heightens one's categorization of that coworker as an outgroup member and as a competitor whose identity conflicts with one's own.

name: Government affiliation
definition: Government affiliation is established through administrative linkages with various levels of governments and is described by the authors as a unique type of administrative connection and a highly relevant characteristic of firms in China.

name: External innovativeness
definition: External innovativeness refers to the level of new products introduced by nearby or neighboring firms, in terms of vertically and horizontally related firms in the region where a focal firm is located.

name: Firm innovation performance
definition: The authors measure innovation performance as the log of a firm's yearly output of new products, where new products are those certified by the local government as new to the Chinese market.

name: Contractual governance with explicit targets
authors_terms: ["contractual governance forms with explicit targets", "governance by targets", "target-setting", "performance contract based on targets"]
definition: Contractual governance arrangements in which partners agree explicit performance targets within a performance contract; here, Local Area Agreements specifying targets for selected key performance indicators. The authors argue that explicit targets furnish the goal clarity and credible commitment required for the pursuit of shared objectives.

name: Target intensity
definition: High levels of target stretch or intensity, defined as the degree of improvement from a given baseline required to attain a specific target.

name: Partner diversity
definition: The degree of sectoral heterogeneity in the organizations represented on the executive board of a cross-sector partnership; gauged by a Blau index denoting the relative share of organizations from the public, private, and nonprofit sectors.

name: Partnership capabilities
authors_terms: ["partnership capabilities", "collaborative capability", "accumulated partnership capabilities", "administrative capacity", "managerial capability"]
definition: Capabilities are the high-level practices used to coordinate the productive activities of organizations. In this study partnership capabilities comprise the accumulated experience of the partnership, the administrative capacity available to it, and the managerial experience of the chief executive responsible for its performance.

name: Cross-sector partnership performance
authors_terms: ["performance of CSPs", "waste recycling performance", "environmental performance", "partnership performance"]
definition: The performance of a cross-sector partnership in creating social and environmental value, measured in this study by the percentage of household waste reused, recycled, or composted in each LSP, a key indicator of the environmental value created by LSPs.

name: Rate of entry into an organizational population
authors_terms: ["transition rate", "rate of entry into the population", "likelihood of entry", "likelihood of moving from pre-entry activity to becoming a fully established member"]
definition: The transition rate from representative office to branch office was formally defined as the probability that a foreign bank opens a branch office in Shanghai at (or shortly after) time t, given that it has maintained a representative office in the city up to time t. Successful entry into the population was defined as a successful application for branch bank status rather than the initial establishment of a representative office.

name: Waiting time
authors_terms: ["waiting time", "length of the organizing period", "duration of the organizing period", "gestation period"]
definition: A waiting time, defined as the length of the organizing period, also referred to as the gestation period, is used by the organizer to accumulate resources, to build up external ties with relevant actors, and to generate appeal for certain products or services. In this setting it is the time a bank spends between establishing a representative office and obtaining branch status.

name: Density of operational organizations
authors_terms: ["number of operational organizations", "number of organizations in a population", "branch office density", "size of the branch office population", "number of already-established organizations"]
definition: Density was a time-varying covariate specified for both representative offices and branch offices, and on the city level and the district level. It is a simple count of offices or branches, used to capture the competition and legitimation processes of density dependence.

name: Density of organizers
authors_terms: ["number of organizers", "number of other organizers", "representative office density", "number of aspirants"]
definition: Organizers are the representative offices that social actors use to seek entry into a broader population or community; with initial increases in the number of peers, being a candidate to enter a particular population would be legitimized, but when organizers become too numerous the effect is instead likely to be dominated by competition.

name: Size-localized density
authors_terms: ["nearness", "size localization", "number of similar-sized organizations already in operation", "the proportion of similar-sized organizations"]
definition: A measure of size effects was constructed based on the nearness between the size of an organizer and the sizes of the organizations already operating; this nearness variable showed a high value for a representative office if its parent bank was similar in size to the banks already maintaining a branch office anywhere in Shanghai. Organizations tend to interact most intensely with those organizations that are similar in size.

name: Home-region density
authors_terms: ["density of bank branches from the same home region", "number of operational organizations from the same home region", "density from the same home country"]
definition: Mimetic effects will be strongest within a community of foreign firms with similar regional identities in a host market, and organizations that originate from the same region may view each other as being part of the same cognitive category. Home region was defined in terms of Japan, Middle East, the rest of Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and Australia.

name: Economic adversity
authors_terms: ["recessionary economic periods", "recessionary periods", "economic recession", "the 2008 recession", "economic shocks", "expansionary periods", "period of economic munificence", "economic downturn"]
definition: A period in which the general economic environment is adverse, in this study the global recession of the years 2008-2011, contrasted with the preceding period of economic munificence (2005-2007). A global economic shock such as the 2008 recession can bring about seismic effects to the institutional environment and markedly change both the formal and informal rules of the game.

name: Firm effects
definition: The variability in firm profitability that is attributable to differences among firms within industries, estimated as the level-1 variance component of ROA. The three-level model partitions the variability in performance (ROA) into its components: among firms within industries, among industries and among countries.

name: Industry effects
definition: The variability in firm profitability that is attributable to differences among industries, estimated as the level-2 variance component of ROA divided by the total variance. Industry effects are the share of total variance in firm profitability explained by the industry to which a firm belongs.

name: Country effects
definition: The variability in firm profitability that is attributable to differences among countries, estimated as the level-3 variance component of ROA divided by the total variance. Country-specific factors such as the size of the country, the institutional framework, legal, government and political differences, and the utilization of production factors and technology can affect firm strategy and profitability.

name: Country-industry effects
authors_terms: ["country-industry interaction effects", "country-industry effects", "country × industry effects", "joint effects of country and industry"]
definition: The variability in firm profitability attributable to the joint or interaction effect of the country and the industry in which a firm operates. Because this interaction is another way of nesting one factor within another, the model is treated as a three-level model with crossed terms and an additional nesting level estimates the variance component for the interaction term Country × Industry.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Firm performance expressed in terms of economic attainment, measured principally as Return-on-Asset (ROA) ratios and averaged for each examined period. The grand mean ROA for all years across all countries is 1.35 percent.

name: Ethics program scope
authors_terms: ["scope of ethics programs", "scope of formal ethics activities", "scope of a corporation's ethics program"]
definition: The scope of a corporation's ethics program is defined as the number of different ethics program elements included in the formal ethics management effort. In some companies ethics programs are broad in scope, with multiple elements, including dedicated staff, supporting structures and policies, and extensive employee involvement; in others the scope of ethics management is limited.

name: Compliance orientation
definition: Some ethics programs embody a coercive orientation toward control that emphasizes adhering to rules, monitoring employee behavior, and disciplining misconduct; the authors refer to such programs as compliance-oriented.

name: Values orientation
definition: Formal ethics programs that emphasize support for employees' ethical aspirations and the development of shared values are referred to as values-oriented. Such programs aim to standardize behavior by creating commitment to shared values and encouraging ethical aspirations.

name: Top management commitment to ethics
authors_terms: ["top management's commitment to ethics", "executive commitment to ethics", "management commitment"]
definition: Executives who have a personal commitment to ethics regularly express concern about how companies' goals are achieved and communicate concern about their companies' nonfinancial obligations. Informants assessed how much top management was concerned with ethics by noting the amount of attention paid to ethics in high-level discussions, the attention paid to topics in high-level discussions being an indication of what top management thinks is important.

name: Awareness of US Sentencing Commission guidelines
authors_terms: ["top management's awareness of the USSC guidelines", "awareness of the United States Sentencing Commission's guidelines"]
definition: The more that a company's top management is aware of the United States Sentencing Commission's guidelines, which were released in 1991 and both increased penalties for convictions and allowed reductions for companies that had made formal, proactive efforts to control their own ethics and ensure legal compliance.

name: Media attention to ethical failings
authors_terms: ["media attention to a company's ethical failings", "media attention to a firm's ethical failures"]
definition: Media organizations in particular are in a position to exert pressure on organizations by publicizing companies' real or alleged ethical failings. Companies that have been the targets of critical media attention are more likely to develop visible policies and practices in an attempt to restore lost legitimacy.

name: Presence at Conference Board ethics meetings
authors_terms: ["company's presence at Conference Board ethics meetings", "presence at Conference Board meetings"]
