definition: The Conference Board is the leading business membership organization targeted toward high-level managers and holds a well-attended annual meeting on business ethics where corporate officers come to learn about ethics management; the meetings offer favorable descriptions of companies with broad-scope ethics programs and how-to-do-it sessions.

name: Inherited agglomeration effects
definition: Human capital that managers acquire while working in an industry hub that may be transferred to a spinoff; the economic benefits that accrue to managers while working at a parent firm in an industry hub that can be subsequently transferred to a spinoff, regardless of where the new venture is located.

name: Hedge fund performance
definition: Firms' information ratios, which measure performance net of systematic risk exposure per unit of idiosyncratic risk.

name: Relatedness of pre-founding experience
authors_terms: ["manager's pre-founding experience", "closely related experience", "manager's previous job in investment management"]
definition: A new venture will benefit more when a manager's previous job was more closely related to the new venture's operations because managers working in closely related functions will bring more relevant human capital to the new venture. In the empirical test, investment management is the type of job most closely related to hedge fund management.

name: CEO-employee pay disparity
authors_terms: ["CEO - employee pay disparity", "pay disparity", "internal pay disparity", "vertical pay disparity"]
definition: Pay disparity refers to pay differences among employees, among top executives, or between top managers (e.g., CEOs) and employees.

name: External stakeholder-employee treatment disparity
authors_terms: ["external stakeholder - employee treatment disparity", "external stakeholder treatment disparity", "treatment disparity"]
definition: The variable, External stakeholder - employee treatment disparity, was the ratio of External stakeholder treatment over Employee treatment.

name: Employee external whistleblowing
definition: Whistleblowing is 'the disclosure by organization members (former or current) of illegal, immoral, or illegitimate practices under the control of their employers, to persons or organizations that may be able to effect action'. Internal and external whistleblowing are defined as disclosing observed misconduct to an entity within the organization or an authority outside the organization, respectively.

name: Labor market mobility
definition: We utilized the decrease in NCA enforceability at the state level as shocks of enhanced Labor market mobility, which is determined by the jurisdiction of a specific state.

name: Employee loyalty to the organization
definition: Employee loyalty is defined as a bond an employee formed with the organization that involves feelings of attachment and dedication to the organization and one's readiness to support the organization. Loyalty refers to a bond to an organization and 'consists of feelings of attachment, of belongs, of strong wanting to be part of something, … and a willingness to follow faithfully the leadership or guidelines of the organization'.

name: Newspaper type
definition: Newspapers were typically categorized by the timing of their publication. Some newspapers were distributed in the morning, covering the previous day's events, while other newspapers were distributed in the evening, covering the events that occurred earlier on that same day.

name: TV station entry
definition: TV entry was staggered geographically and temporally, partly due to the Federal Communications Commission's decision to freeze new TV broadcast licenses during the Korean War. We create a dummy variable, TV in market, which equals one for all years, t, after a TV station enters newspaper i's local market.

name: Newspaper subscription price
definition: The subscription price charged by the newspaper firm to readers (denoted pn in the theoretical model).

name: Newspaper circulation
definition: Let Dn, Dt, and Dm be the single-homing demand for the newspaper, the single-homing demand for the TV station, and the multi-homing demand for both, respectively; the newspaper circulation is Dn + Dm.

name: Newspaper advertising rate
definition: Let the newspaper and the TV station charge a lump sum of alpha_n and alpha_t, respectively, to advertisers.

name: TV station advertising rate
definition: We focus on the rates that stations charged for 1 hr of advertising.

name: Share of single-homing consumers
definition: The market has one unit of consumers, among whom r of them, where 0 < r < 1, are multi-homing, meaning that they both read the newspaper and watch the TV station (and 1 - r are single-homing, meaning that they read either the newspaper or watch TV but not both).

name: Prior ties between alliance partners
authors_terms: ["prior ties", "prior alliance agreements", "number of prior alliance agreements with the same partner firm"]
definition: The previous alliance agreements, or prior ties, between the partnering firms; when firms engage in multiple alliances with the same partner over time they can observe the partner's patterns of behavior in a variety of circumstances.

name: Institutionalization-based trust
authors_terms: ["institutionalization-based trust", "trust based on institutionalization of norms of reciprocity and equity", "institutionalization"]
definition: Partners are confident that neither side will engage in behavior that is self-interested or opportunistic in nature, because such behavior would violate norms of conduct that partners have developed over time, and particularly norms of reciprocity and equity that they have internalized and institutionalized in their relationship.

name: Affect-based trust
definition: Partners trust each other that they will not behave in a self-interested manner, because such behavior would seriously degrade personal relationships based on friendship and emotional attachments that are important to them.

name: Partner knowledge
authors_terms: ["partner knowledge", "knowledge about a partner's anticipated patterns of behavior", "knowledge about a partner's behavior"]
definition: Knowledge about a partner's anticipated patterns of behavior, which helps to predict when the partner is likely to behave opportunistically and how to coordinate alliance tasks with the partner.

name: Market overlap
authors_terms: ["market overlap", "competition in end markets outside their alliances", "direct competitors"]
definition: The extent to which partners are direct competitors, assessed by the extent to which partners were operating in similar markets before the alliance, focusing on product markets, geographic markets and customer segments.

name: Cultural similarity
authors_terms: ["cultural similarity", "similarity in organizational cultures", "fit in partners' organizational cultures"]
definition: The fit in partners' organizational cultures, reflected in the extent to which the partners were similar in organizational cultures and management and operating styles at the outset of the collaboration and in their decision-making processes.

name: Firm capability
authors_terms: ["firm capability", "capability", "studio's capability", "level of advancement of a firm's capability"]
definition: Firm capability is defined as the set of organizational processes and routines that operate on a firm's resource base to create new value.

name: Firm growth
definition: Growth models typically focus on relative sizes of the variable of interest at two points in time; the authors use the relative size of studio revenue in the current and past time periods to arrive at their measure of revenue growth.

name: Number of large alliance partners
authors_terms: ["number of major partners", "number of large partners", "large partners", "alliances with large partners"]
definition: The contingency variable, i.e., the number of major partners, is calculated as the number of major studios by which the firm has a distribution or coproduction deal; large firm partnerships are the external dimension of a small firm's alliance portfolio.

name: Product market overlap
authors_terms: ["product market overlap", "market overlap", "overlap in product markets"]
definition: We study the heterogeneity of spillovers based on the overlap in product markets in which the accused peer and non-accused firms both operate.

name: Market classification granularity
authors_terms: ["granularity of the market classification", "fine-grained market classification", "coarse market classification", "product market classification"]
definition: The stigma effect becomes stronger than the competition effect when investors rely on a coarse market classification, whereas the competition effect becomes stronger relative to the stigma effect when they use a fine-grained market classification, because such a classification can discern which non-accused firms compete directly with the accused peer.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market valuation", "cumulative abnormal return", "CAR", "abnormal stock market returns", "stock market reactions"]
definition: To test Hypotheses 1 and 2, we employed the event study method, examining the abnormal stock market returns of non-accused firms around the date the information about the misconduct was first made public.

name: Investor sophistication
definition: Given their different levels of analytical skills and industry expertise, investors vary with respect to the granularity of the market classification they use for discerning firms; compared with less sophisticated investors, more sophisticated investors rely on a more fine-grained market classification to effectively map the competitive landscape and thus identify close competitors that may gain following the accusation against their industry peer.

name: Shareholding change in non-accused firm
authors_terms: ["shareholding change in non-accused firm", "change in shareholdings", "change in the investor's shareholding"]
definition: Per Hypothesis 3, our dependent variable is shareholding change in non-accused firm. It was calculated by subtracting the percentage of shares of an investor in the non-accused firm in the quarter prior to the accusation from the percentage of shares held in the quarter following the accusation event.

name: Pay inequality
definition: Inequality in pay among employees within the same organization, which can arise either from internal firm policies or from differences in external market benchmarks.

name: Divestiture
definition: Undertaken when the marginal cost of managing a particular business comes to exceed the marginal benefit of continuing to own and operate that business; managers divest one or more of their company's businesses.

name: Target acquisition likelihood
authors_terms: ["P(t)", "probability of acquiring a particular independent or component nursing home", "likelihood of acquiring target i"]
definition: The dependent variable in our study, P(t), is a chain's probability of acquiring a particular independent or component nursing home from among all possible targets, given that the chain made an acquisition during year t.

name: Proximity to chain's most recent acquisition
authors_terms: ["local in time", "geographically localized search", "Euclidean distance between target i and the Kth (last) of chain j's K prior acquisitions"]
definition: In particular, because choices and actions resulting from proximate prior searches are natural starting points for initiating new searches, chains should tend to acquire targets adjacent to their most recent acquisition (i.e., local in time).

name: Proximity to chain's nearest prior acquisition
authors_terms: ["local in space", "any of their own prior acquisitions", "Euclidean distance between target i and chain j's prior acquisition closest to target i"]
definition: In particular, because choices and actions resulting from proximate prior searches are natural starting points for initiating new searches, chains should tend to acquire targets adjacent to their most recent acquisition (i.e., local in time) and any of their own prior acquisitions (i.e., local in space).

name: Proximity to chain's current components
authors_terms: ["location momentum", "positional and contextual momentum", "distance from j's current components"]
definition: Consequently, while we conceptualize local search in terms of a chain's most recent and nearest prior acquisitions, we conceptualize location momentum in terms of its current components.

name: Similarity to chain's most recent acquisition
authors_terms: ["size, context, and compactness similarity", "organizational similarity", "similar in size (or operating context) to its most recent acquisition"]
definition: For example, as well as acquiring targets similar in size (or operating context) to its current components, a chain may also be more likely to acquire targets similar in size (or operating context) to its most recent acquisition or a prior acquisition located nearby.

name: Similarity to chain's nearest prior acquisition
authors_terms: ["organizational similarity", "similar in size (or operating context) to ... a prior acquisition located nearby"]
definition: For example, as well as acquiring targets similar in size (or operating context) to its current components, a chain may also be more likely to acquire targets similar in size (or operating context) to its most recent acquisition or a prior acquisition located nearby.

name: Similarity to chain's current components
authors_terms: ["spatial compactness", "similarity of the target's size and operating context with the chain"]
definition: Regardless of the impetus for its level of spatial compactness, we expect chains to be more likely to acquire targets that are a similar distance from its current components and thus compatible with capabilities associated with its level of spatial compactness.

name: Proximity to large chains' most recent acquisitions
authors_terms: ["trait imitation, time", "imitation of other large chains' most recent acquisitions"]
definition: For expanding chains, location choices of large chains may be a particularly important source of information to reduce uncertainty about locations that can support growth and about how large chains behave in general.

name: Proximity to large chains' nearest prior acquisitions
authors_terms: ["trait imitation, space", "large chains' acquisitions nearest to the target acquisitions"]
definition: Consequently, it is possible that large chains' most recent acquisitions and acquisitions nearest to the target acquisitions will be objects of imitation.

name: Proximity to large chains' current components
authors_terms: ["trait imitation, generalized", "large chains' locations, in general"]
definition: It is also possible that large chains' locations, in general, will be imitated.

name: Proximity to similar chains' most recent acquisitions
authors_terms: ["trait imitation of similar chains", "comparable organizations", "similar chains' most recent acquisitions"]
definition: As decision makers look for role models, they also monitor the behavior of a reference group of comparable organizations in similar situations, and their opinions and actions evolve toward those in their reference group.

name: Proximity to similar chains' nearest prior acquisitions
authors_terms: ["trait imitation of similar chains", "similar chains' acquisitions nearest to the target"]
definition: And, as for H3a-H3c, we considered similar chains' most recent acquisitions, acquisitions nearest to the target, and locations in general as possible foci of imitation.

name: Proximity to similar chains' current components
authors_terms: ["trait imitation of similar chains", "similar chains' locations in general"]
definition: And, as for H3a-H3c, we considered similar chains' most recent acquisitions, acquisitions nearest to the target, and locations in general as possible foci of imitation.

name: Standardization by the focal firm
authors_terms: ["Standards Own", "standard-owner firm", "standard-owner", "disclosure of SEPs by the focal firm"]
definition: Standardization refers to the convergence in technical specifications of a component or interface in the innovation ecosystem. The physical components embodying the standardized technical specifications or their IP are usually owned by a subset of firms; for the standard-owner firm, inclusion in the standard means that other parties now have to build their components based on the firm's standardized component.

name: Standardization by other firms
definition: The non-standard-owner firm is the firm who does not own any part of the standard and has to live with what is standardized; the firm experiences standardization through SEP disclosures made by other firms in the technological subcategories in which it is active.

name: Uncertainty over future financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm-level uncertainty", "uncertainty over its future financial performance", "firm level uncertainty over future performance", "Uncertainty"]
definition: A third form of firm-level uncertainty in future financial performance is whether the firm can appropriate value in the ecosystem, which is distinct from ecosystem-level uncertainty over coordination of development. It is measured with the firm's stock option implied volatility, which reflects the market's perception of the firm's future stock price performance at time t over the upcoming life of the option.

name: Presence of a strong rival in complementary technologies
definition: By 'strong rivals,' we refer to the presence of dominant firms, sometimes termed 'kingpins,' accounting for disproportionate importance in R&D for the complementary technologies; these strong rivals own a large portion of existing complementary technologies.

name: Firm complementary technologies
definition: Complementary technologies embody features that support and enhance the standardized component thereby increasing the overall value offering of the whole ecosystem. Because of their interdependent relationship with the standardized component, the value of each increases in the presence of the other.

name: Production assets
definition: We use the term 'production assets' broadly to capture the firm's physical production systems and commercialization capabilities.

name: Acquisition premium
definition: The acquisition premium captures the magnitude of the bid price being above the shares' market value and reflects management's overall perception (i.e., expectation) of a given deal's synergistic potential.

name: Political affinity
definition: Political affinity denotes the similarity of national interests in global affairs. Weak political affinity increases the likelihood of political and economic conflict and, in the context of cross-border acquisitions, increases the likelihood of government intervention in favor of the domestic target.

name: Target firm announcement returns
authors_terms: ["target firm's stock market return to an acquisition announcement", "target CAR", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: Our dependent variable is cumulated abnormal returns (CARs), which represent the portion of the return that is left unexplained by an economic model.

name: Acquirer firm announcement returns
authors_terms: ["acquiring firm's stock market return to an acquisition announcement", "acquirer CAR", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: Our dependent variable is cumulated abnormal returns (CARs), which represent the portion of the return that is left unexplained by an economic model.

name: Director stock option pay deviation
authors_terms: ["positive deviation from prior outside director stock option grant values", "relative outside director pay levels", "positive pay deviation", "director stock option grant value deviation", "relative pay values"]
definition: Relative outside director pay levels, i.e., whether the value of current pay is more or less than the value received in the prior year. The authors focus on positive deviation of director stock option grant compensation, when the value of current option pay exceeds the value received previously.

name: Firm strategic risk taking
authors_terms: ["firm strategic risk-taking intensity", "firm strategic risk", "strategic risk-taking behavior", "firm risk taking"]
definition: Strategic risk-taking is defined as significantly uncertain resource allocations with potential for an adverse impact on firm performance. The authors proxy firm-level strategic risk-taking intensity with three risk dimensions.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: The CEO's equity stake in the firm; behaviorally, as CEO ownership increases, wealth is even less diversified and entrenchment increases, creating stronger incentives for CEOs to mitigate performance monitoring and reject advice and recommendations for risky activities from outside directors.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality is well recognized as an indicator of CEO power and constitutes an important part of the board's structural arrangement affecting the control and involvement of the board's decision making. It refers to the situation in which the CEO also holds the board chair position.

name: Strategic leadership behaviors
definition: Strategic leadership is defined as the process of forming a vision for the future, communicating it to subordinates, stimulating and motivating followers, and engaging in strategy-supportive exchanges with peers and subordinates.

name: Executive influence on product-market innovations
authors_terms: ["executive influence on product-market innovations", "PM innovations", "executive innovation influence"]
definition: One of the two primary, but distinct ways that innovation occurs within organizations is the development of new product-markets; the measure captures the extent of executive influence on recent or shortly anticipated outcomes of that innovation process.

name: Executive influence on administrative innovations
authors_terms: ["executive influence on administrative innovations", "ADM innovations", "administrative innovation"]
definition: Another source of innovation occurs in the development of new and more efficient administrative mechanisms: new systems for strategic planning and control, new systems for training, development or promoting managers, and new departments or managerial positions for improving intraorganizational coordination.

name: TMT tenure heterogeneity
definition: A relatively diverse range of tenures within the top management team, computed as the standard deviation of executives' respective job tenures on the top management team divided by the mean of those tenures; the higher the resulting score, the greater the TMT tenure heterogeneity.

name: Social culture
definition: A social culture can be defined as a system of values, norms, attitudes, rituals, and elements of mental programming that are common for members of a social group; in this study the authors focus on socio-cultural clusters that transcend national boundaries.

name: Product adaptation
definition: Product adaptation is when the TMT 'adds, removes, or alters the products or service' (Dencker et al. 2009, p. 520). Such adaptations are major, observable changes to chemistry or architecture of the solar PV module.

name: Preentry experience breadth
definition: The diversity of industries in which TMT members have preentry experience; experience breadth refers to the variance in preentry experience across industries.

name: Industry preentry experience depth
definition: Experience depth refers to the concentration of preentry experience in the focal industry; it is the amount of a TMT's preentry experience in the focal industry.

name: Entrepreneurial preentry experience
definition: Preentry experience in entrepreneurial settings, which prior work suggests may build the ability to learn in uncertain settings and heuristics that facilitate product adaptation.

name: Business preentry experience
definition: Preentry experience in a business context, in contrast to preentry experience in a scientific context: TMTs from a predominantly business context tended to focus more on the commercial elements of the business.

name: Outcome control
definition: Outcome control refers to the prespecification by the controller of desired controllee outputs and the associated evaluation criteria. It uses a market-like system to encourage the controller to achieve desired outcomes.

name: Process control
definition: Process control refers to prescribing the methods and procedures that the controllee should follow; it attempts to coordinate controllee actions in a manner that the controller believes will increase the likelihood of achieving desired outcomes.

name: Technological modularity
definition: Technological modularity is defined as the degree of decoupling between the outsourced subsystem and the base system. A complex system exhibits modularity if its constituent subsystems can be designed independently but will work together to support the whole, achieved by codifying interface specifications and minimizing interdependencies.

name: Alliance performance
definition: Alliance performance is the performance of the outsourced software development project as assessed against the client's project needs, quality expectations, functional requirements, and objectives.

name: Differentiation strategy
authors_terms: ["differentiation dimension of product-market strategy", "differentiation-based product-market strategy", "differentiation strategy"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's product-market strategy is based on differentiation; managers have identified customer groups that desire distinctive benefits beyond those provided by non-differentiated products.

name: Cost-focus strategy
authors_terms: ["cost dimension of product-market strategy", "cost-focus", "cost-efficiency dimensions of product-market strategy", "cost-based strategies"]
definition: The degree to which the firm focuses on cost efficiencies in its product-market strategy.

name: Product-market scope
authors_terms: ["scope dimension of product-market strategy", "product-market scope", "market scope"]
definition: The degree to which the firm operates in many (versus few) markets or market segments.

name: Specialized marketing capabilities
definition: Specialized marketing capabilities are the functionally focused capabilities built around the integration of the specialized knowledge held by the firm's marketing employees. These reflect task-specific marketing activities such as marketing communications, personal selling, pricing, product development, and, in goods-based industries, distribution.

name: Architectural marketing capabilities
definition: Architectural marketing capabilities are the capabilities that direct the coordination of the specialized marketing capabilities, thus focusing resource deployments to achieve product-market goals.

name: Marketing capabilities integration
authors_terms: ["marketing capabilities integration", "capabilities integration", "integration of marketing capabilities"]
definition: Marketing capabilities integration reflects the combinative capabilities that derive from the integration of embedded marketing routines and practices that are used to generate a desired tangible or intangible output. The integration of the marketing knowledge embedded in specialized and architectural marketing capabilities provides the best opportunity for properly aligning marketing resources with the demands of the various product-market strategies.

name: Market effectiveness
definition: Market effectiveness deals with the degree to which the mid-range, concurrent, market-related performance goals of the organization is achieved.

name: Cash flow performance
authors_terms: ["cash flow", "subsequent one-year cash flow", "cash flow return on assets (CFROA)"]
definition: An objective measure of financial performance, cash flow, is used; cash flow has advantages as a measure of financial performance in that it is less influenced by accrual accounting methods and may be less sensitive to commonly used accounting manipulations.

name: Social CSR
authors_terms: ["social CSR", "social pillar", "social CSR investments", "social CSR engagement"]
definition: One of the three constituent dimensions of CSR in emerging market firms, captured by Eikon's social pillar, which includes 61 items across four areas: workforce quality, emphasis on human rights, organizational community involvement, and product responsibility.

name: Governance CSR
definition: One of the three constituent dimensions of CSR in emerging market firms, captured by Eikon's governance pillar based on 50 items across three areas: management quality (compensation, independence, diversity), shareholders' rights, and board composition and strategy.

name: Environmental CSR
definition: One of the three constituent dimensions of CSR in emerging market firms, captured by Eikon's environmental pillar based on 61 items across three areas: resource use, harmful gas emissions, and innovation in controlling environmental degradation.

name: Financial performance
definition: Performance was measured using percentage return on assets (ROA), which is computed by dividing earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation by total assets.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are defined as 'a set of firms which, though legally independent, are bound together by a constellation of formal and informal ties and are accustomed to taking coordinated action' (Khanna and Rivkin 2001, p. 47).

name: Policy nudge
definition: A policy nudge is 'any aspect of the choice architecture that alters people's behavior [...] without [...] significantly changing their economic incentives' (Thaler and Sunstein 2008, p. 6). In an organizational context, a nudge constitutes a subtle policy shift that encourages the beneficial alignment of organizational and societal goals without using financial incentives to accomplish such an alignment.

name: Enforcement of noncompete agreements
authors_terms: ["employee noncompete agreements (NCAs)", "NCA enforcement", "enforcement of noncompetes", "constraints on employee mobility"]
definition: Employee noncompete agreements are contractual provisions that expressly prohibit employees from joining a competitor, or forming a new firm as a competitor, within particular industries and geographic locations for a certain time period (Gilson, 1999).

name: Likelihood of becoming an acquisition target
authors_terms: ["acquisition likelihood", "likelihood of the firm becoming an acquisition target", "likelihood of being an acquisition target", "acquisition"]
definition: Our dependent variable, Acquisition, is a dichotomous variable that equals 1 if the focal firm is the target of an acquisition in a given year based on the acquisition announcements reported by SDC and 0 otherwise.

name: Knowledge workers
authors_terms: ["knowledge workers", "proportion of knowledge workers", "knowledge workers in its workforce"]
definition: We measured the level of knowledge workers employed in a focal firm's industry as a proportion of the total workforce employed in that industry. Using the OES occupational codebook, we defined knowledge workers to be those with an occupational code below 50,000, which includes occupations such as managers, sales workers, scientists, engineers, editors, computer programmers, IT professionals, and so forth.

name: In-state competition
definition: We measured the proportion of total U.S. sales generated by other firms located in the same state and same industry as the focal firm using data from the COMPUSTAT Segments file; the focal firm's own sales was excluded.

name: Intellectual property protection
authors_terms: ["IP regime", "IP protection", "intellectual property (IP) regime", "strength of the IP patenting regime", "stronger intellectual property regime"]
definition: We focus on the intellectual property (IP) regime as one mechanism for protecting knowledge and limiting the negative consequences of employee mobility. The strength of the IP patenting regime therefore affects the extent to which firms can use patents to retain knowledge for their exclusive use.

name: Network community membership
authors_terms: ["membership", "main component membership", "connection to the main component", "membership in the largest weakly connected component", "membership in a loosely linked, coherent community"]
definition: A firm's attachment, through at least one formal tie, to the largest weakly connected component of a network, which the authors treat as membership in a loosely linked but coherent community and as an entry ticket to a local technological community.

name: Network centrality
definition: The extent to which a firm sits astride network pathways between other organizations, based on Freeman's measure of betweeness, indicating a firm's ability to absorb (or interrupt) information flows through tightly sealed network pipes.

name: Innovation
definition: The firm-level innovative output that the authors study, operationalized as a count of patents assigned to the firm.

name: Institutional demography of network nodes
authors_terms: ["institutional demography", "node demography", "organizational form", "institutional diversity", "networks dominated by PROs", "reliance on firms"]
definition: The mix of organizational forms that populate a network, in particular whether the dominant nodes are public research organizations committed to open disclosure or commercial entities committed to proprietary claims; the authors argue that the characteristics of the dominant nodes can alter the flow of information throughout the entire structure.

name: Competitive threat
authors_terms: ["competitive threat", "competitive shock", "increase in competition", "tariff cut", "trade shock", "increase in international competition"]
definition: We exploit exogenous changes in product market competition as a main source of industry variation and study how diversifiers might improve (or not) their overall performance by redeploying non-scale free resources toward BUs that face increasing competitive pressure. Unlike environmental changes that lower demand, competitive shocks might increase or decrease the marginal value of resources applied to a particular sector.

name: Resource allocation
authors_terms: ["resource allocation", "resource redeployment", "resource reallocation", "within-firm transfers of resources", "cash transfers"]
definition: To capture within-firm transfers of resources, we use the difference between cash invested and cash generated. We follow Billett and Mauer (2003) to calculate the dependent variable, resource allocation, which we define as the difference between a BU capital expenditure and its own after-tax cash flow (ATCF).

name: Sunk costs
definition: To estimate sunk costs at the BU level, we use an asset redeployability measure developed by Kim and Kung (2017). The measure estimates the extent to which assets currently invested in one sector are specific to that sector or alternatively could be redeployed to other sectors.

name: Technological relatedness
definition: We consider cross-citations between a sector pair as a proxy for the extent to which the two sectors share a similar technological base. This measure thus captures the extent to which BU i shares a common technological base with the rest of the firm's BUs.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "operating cost efficiency ratio", "operating cost (expense) efficiency ratio", "top performance firms", "weak performance firms"]
definition: In this study, organizational performance is measured using the ratio of total operating expense to premium income, the operating cost efficiency ratio. This measure of expense efficiency captures a firm's cost advantage or disadvantage standing from current operations.

name: Operational dependency on information technology
authors_terms: ["IT expense ratio", "ratio of information technology expense to total operating expense", "operational dependency on information technology", "process integration and coordination through the technology"]
definition: McFarlan et al. (1983) characterize the ratio of information technology expense to total operating expense (IT expense ratio) as one measure of the degree of operating dependency on information technology. We believe the IT expense ratio reflects the extent to which the business processes of the firm are integrated and coordinated through the technology.

name: Information technology cost efficiency
authors_terms: ["IT cost efficiency ratio", "ratio of information technology expense to premium income", "cost economies of information technology"]
definition: The IT cost efficiency ratio is a single-factor expense measure of the cost economies of information technology. In this paper, three sources of information technology-based cost economies are relevant: scale economies, scope economies, and economies due to learning effects.

name: Firm size
definition: In this analysis, we use the premium income ranking as a proxy measure for firm size. Firm diversity as measured by firm size (e.g., sales, number of employees, etc.) is one factor that could influence organizational performance.

name: Executive age
definition: Executive experience, as represented by age, can be argued to influence the mental understandings executives use to process information during strategic decision making.

name: Technical education
definition: Education may be considered indicative of one's knowledge and skill base. An executive who has one type of formal education can be expected to have developed different problem-solving skills and mental models with which to evaluate situations than an executive with a different type of formal education.

name: Technical work experience
authors_terms: ["technical work experience", "primary technical work experience", "functional background"]
definition: Executives with backgrounds in R&D or engineering are arguably consistent with 'progress, invention, and improvement'; top executives with technical work experience can be expected to weight the information they consider when assessing potential technological alliances differently from executives without technical work experience.

name: Perceived technological emphasis
authors_terms: ["technological emphasis", "firm's emphasis on technology", "emphasis on technology"]
definition: The more executives perceive their firms to emphasize technology the more they can be expected to be concerned about their firms' dependency on specific core technologies, their capabilities to develop technology internally, and their potential for losing control over vital technological capital through strategic alliances.

name: Perceived firm risk orientation
authors_terms: ["risk orientation", "attitude toward risk taking", "firm's perceived risk propensity"]
definition: One of the organizational characteristics believed to influence an individual's risk perceptions is an organization's tendency to prefer certainty vs. uncertainty and risk avoidance vs. risk seeking.

name: Perceived successful collaborative experience
authors_terms: ["successful collaborative experience", "success with previous technological alliances", "experience and success"]
definition: A firm's overall successful collaborative experience is a function of both the number of these relationships that it had been involved in and the success of these relationships.

name: Opportunity-based alliance information
definition: Strategic intent creates an extreme misfit between resources and organizational ambitions, and challenges the organization to close the gap by systematically building new advantages aligned with tomorrow's opportunities. Thus, strategic intent implies a sizable 'stretch' for an organization seeking to attain clear ambitious goals.

name: Threat-based alliance information
definition: Some of the information processed by executives as they individually assess potential technological alliances can be categorized as information related to organizational opportunities and information related to organizational threats.

name: Relational risk
authors_terms: ["relational risk", "risk of partnering", "threats associated with relational risk"]
definition: Some of the risk perceived by executives assessing potential technological partners is associated with the risk of partnering or relational risk, due to the dual control nature of the relationship, the intrinsic incentive to cheat, and the uncertainty about the partner and its changing goals.

name: Performance risk
definition: A second type of risk is associated with the technology itself and its commercial success, resulting from the unpredictable nature of R&D activities, the high costs associated with development, questionable market acceptance, and the uncertain appropriability of the technology. This type of risk has been labeled performance risk because these risks exist even if alliance partners cooperate fully; performance risk embraces all kinds of hazards except those related to cooperation.

name: Assessment of potential technological alliances
authors_terms: ["assessment of the opportunity", "assessment of potential technological alliances", "attractiveness of alliances"]
definition: In order to 'come to conclusions' regarding the attractiveness of technological alliance opportunities, executives must evaluate the available information and draw conclusions about their potential.

name: External COO/president directors
authors_terms: ["external COO/presidents", "external COO/presidents on a firm's board", "external COO/president directors", "COO/presidents as outside directors"]
definition: Independent directors who hold a title of COO and/or president at their place of primary employment and do not also serve as CEO there; the authors argue such executives develop specific expertise in managing internal operations.

name: External non-COO/president directors
authors_terms: ["non-COO/president external executives", "external non-COO/president executives", "other external executives"]
definition: Independent directors who served as executive officers (e.g., holding titles such as CEO, CFO, or executive vice president) at their primary place of employment and did not also serve as either COO or president at their primary place of employment.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "industry-adjusted return on assets", "industry-adjusted ROA", "future firm performance"]
definition: Performance is measured as industry-adjusted return on assets (ROA), which the authors describe as closely linked to operational effectiveness and thus appropriate for the study; ROA is the firm's net income divided by the book value of its assets, minus the average ROA for the firm's industry.

name: Operational efficiency change
authors_terms: ["operational efficiency", "movement in a firm's operational efficiency", "declining operational efficiency", "declining cost efficiency", "declining overhead efficiency", "declining productivity"]
definition: The annual change in the firm's operational efficiency, which the authors measure in three ways as the extent to which growth in costs or expenses outpaces growth in revenue, employment, or employee productivity.

name: Customer-set connectedness
authors_terms: ["customer-set connectedness", "connectedness of a bank's customer set", "connectedness of a bank's customers", "mediator centrality"]
definition: The aggregate degree of connectedness of the individual affiliates of a mediator. In line with Bonacich's (1987) conceptualization of informational availability as a function of the information of those to whom an actor is connected, a bank that provides services to a customer set that other organizations seek is more informed than a bank that provides services to a customer set that is not particularly sought by other organizations.

name: Mediator investment-based specialization
authors_terms: ["mediator investment-based specialization", "bank's specialization in a customer's industry", "mediator specialization"]
definition: Mediator investment-based specialization is defined as the size of bank investments in each industry; it is the concentration of a mediator's activities in a specific industry, measured as the distribution of its affiliated organizations.

name: Organization survival
authors_terms: ["likelihood of survival", "organizational survival", "likelihood of any particular customer bankruptcy"]
definition: The continued operation of an affiliated organization, examined as the likelihood that a firm is still in business rather than the likelihood of its bankruptcy. Organizational failure is an ex post measure, which constitutes the ultimate measure of performance.

name: Organization age
definition: The time since an organization's founding. Young organizations are prone to higher failure rates due to the liability of newness, while older organizations may suffer from structural inertia that creates a gap between the organization and its competitive environment.

name: Bank loss
authors_terms: ["bank loss", "bank loss per failed customer", "bank's loss per bankrupt customer"]
definition: The loss incurred by a mediating organization on customers that fail. When bankruptcy is unavoidable the better-informed bank is in a position to withdraw financing early, get a hold of assets before bankruptcy is declared, and refuse to grant more loans, all of which lead to a reduction in asset loss.

name: Customer failure proportion
authors_terms: ["proportion of customer failures within a bank's portfolio of customers"]
definition: The share of firms that actually failed out of the total number of firms affiliated with each bank, reflecting the selection advantage of the mediator's customer set.

name: Business formation
definition: As defined in the USELM data file, business formation refers to the establishment of new operations in an industry. The formation may have been the result of an entrant that had not existed prior to its entry into the industry (an independent establishment) or from an already existing firm (a dependent establishment).

name: Formation size
authors_terms: ["formation size", "small business formations", "large business formations", "small and large business formations"]
definition: The size class of a business formation. Small business formation covers establishments with fewer than 20 employees and large business formation covers establishments with 100 or more employees.

name: Industry structure
definition: Standard models of entry suggest that the formation of new businesses is a function of entry barriers, entry inducements, and industry size. Industry structure, as it impacts the formation decision, is a multidimensional construct.

name: Sunk cost
definition: 'Sunk costs are fixed costs resulting from irreversible investments'. Higher sunk costs force a potential entrant to commit to the industry for a longer period of time because the investment cannot be transferred economically to some other use.

name: Industry concentration
definition: High industry concentration means large market shares held by a few incumbents; it is argued to facilitate collusion among firms, thereby erecting a barrier to new firm formation.

name: Vertical integration
definition: From the industrial organization economics perspective, vertical integration within an industry has been argued to deter entry because potential entrants may need to enter more than one stage in the production process to achieve competitive cost structures, thereby increasing the capital required for entry.

name: Excess capacity
definition: The existence of excess capacity in an industry is usually considered a barrier to entry because post-entry industry price levels will decline with the further addition of productive capacity, unless incumbent firms reduce output levels.

name: Industry profitability
definition: Past industry profitability has traditionally been viewed as an inducement to entry because the future is often viewed as an extension of the past.

name: Industry growth rate
definition: Industry growth has long been viewed as an inducement to entry: a growing demand creates a continual opportunity for new entrants to serve.

name: Niche dynamism
definition: Demand changes at a disaggregated (i.e., product) level, taken as a more appropriate indicator of the presence of new and growing niches within an industry. The presence of growing niches, even in the absence of overall industry demand growth, may signal opportunities for all formations.

name: Technological development
definition: Technological development within an industry, generally seen as an important factor in the formation of new firms because technological progress attracts entrants seeking to exploit new products and processes.

name: Product differentiation
definition: Entry theory has traditionally viewed product differentiation as an entry barrier because potential entrants must overcome incumbent advantages of customer loyalty, superior product design, control of distribution, and raised switching costs.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Joint involvement in multiple markets-joint location in physical or social space-creates a network of indirect ties between multimarket firms. Multimarket contact is not just another aspect of market structure, akin to concentration; it is experienced differently by firms with different product, client, or regional location profiles.

name: Market dominance
authors_terms: ["market dominance", "market structure", "spheres of influence", "dominated by a few large firms"]
definition: The proportion of a market controlled by the largest multimarket firms is a good indicator of the extent to which that market is dominated by one or a few incumbents. When a few multimarket firms control a large proportion of any market, other multimarket firms are motivated to forbear from aggressive expansion activity in that market.

name: Growth in current markets
authors_terms: ["growth in current markets", "growth within that market", "expansion in existing markets"]
definition: Growth within existing product, technology, or regional markets is a fundamental way in which organizations redefine their domains and therefore constitutes fundamental structural change for corporations. Growing in current markets is an aggressive act.

name: Entry into new markets
authors_terms: ["entry into new markets", "market entry", "entry into that market"]
definition: Entry into new markets is a fundamental way in which organizations redefine their domains and therefore constitutes fundamental structural change for corporations. Entry into new markets is an aggressive act.

name: International business advice network density
authors_terms: ["TMT international business advice network density", "IB advice network density", "advice network density", "density of the TMT's IB advice network"]
definition: The density of the TMT's international business advice network is the ratio of the actual number of IB advice-seeking relationships among pairs of TMT members to the total number of possible IB advice-seeking relationships among pairs of TMT members. The IB advice network is defined as the pattern of relations among members in which one member seeks IB advice from another member.

name: Internationalization extent
definition: The MNC's internationalization extent reflects the degree to which the firm is present in international markets. It is represented by the level of international sales and export sales as a percentage of total sales, the number of international employees as a percent of total employees, and the level of international assets as a percent of total assets.

name: Internal mode of international involvement
authors_terms: ["internal mode", "internal mode of international involvement", "international business modes of involvement", "IB modes of involvement"]
definition: An MNC can choose any combination of international business modes of involvement to carry out its activities in foreign markets, and these modes differ in the extent to which each may be considered internal, as opposed to external, to the corporation. In this study, an internal mode is defined to be one which clearly provides the MNC with control of subsidiaries via majority equity ownership.

name: Cross-national interdependence
definition: Interdependence is the extent to which a firm's entities which are dispersed across the nodes of its international network are linked in terms of knowledge flows and product flows. The nature of the MNC's interdependence reflects the type of international strategy being pursued by the firm to coordinate the various value-adding activities performed by its international subsidiaries.

name: Industry deregulation
definition: Deregulation amounts to an environmental change for the actors in an industry; for the airline industry in the United States, this change-as mandated in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978-was relatively abrupt.

name: Entrepreneurial attention
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial attention", "attentional orientation", "managerial attention", "attention toward an entrepreneurial orientation"]
definition: Attentional orientation is the degree of attention paid to some category of stimuli. We sought to measure the degree to which each letter contained words associated with the entrepreneurial problem, as opposed to the engineering problem, as conceptualized by Miles and Snow (1978).

name: Entrepreneurial strategy
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial strategy", "strategic change toward more of an entrepreneurial orientation"]
definition: Objective indicators of each airline's realized strategy that indicate its manifested commitment to the entrepreneurial problem as conceptualized by Miles and Snow (1978).

name: TMT industry tenure
authors_terms: ["average industry tenure", "average focal industry tenure", "industry tenure"]
definition: The mean number of years the executives had worked in the airline industry until the focal year.

name: TMT output-function experience
definition: The proportion of executives on the team whose primary experience had been in output-related functions such as marketing, sales, and customer relations.

name: TMT demographic heterogeneity
definition: The degree of diversity among executives' experience manifested in tenure, functional background, and so forth.

name: Performance-dependent pay
definition: The extent to which executive pay depended on company performance and other incentive factors, as opposed to a fixed level of salary.

name: TMT composition
definition: The annual compositional characteristics of each top management team, defined as all executives above the level of vice president; the relevant composition variables are industry tenure, output-orientation, industry-tenure heterogeneity, and functional heterogeneity.

name: TMT characteristics
definition: The personal givens-executive characteristics-that members of a TMT bring to an administrative situation, including psychological properties such as values and personality, as well as experiences such as tenure and functional backgrounds; in this paper, TMT composition and compensation.

name: Physical base of relatedness
definition: The physical base of relatedness concerns relations between the physical characteristics of products, such as raw materials used and plant and physical processes, and similarity or complementarity of the physical attributes of products is the overarching criterion for relatedness used by the Standard Industrial Classification Code. Diversification researchers have identified physical relatedness as the extent to which a firm's sales in different lines of business are concentrated within a more aggregated industry group rather than across industry groups.

name: Skill base of relatedness
definition: The skill base views each industry or line of business as a combination of occupational skills or bodies of knowledge required to produce a product, and it may consist of research and development teams, experienced salesmen, and managerial and other skills common to two or more products. The relatedness of different industries is determined by similarity in skill combinations, rather than by similarity in the physical attributes of products in the same industry group.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is assessed with four measures representing both accounting and market-based indicators: return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), market-to-book ratio (MBOOK), and Jensen's alpha (ALPHA).

name: Division innovation performance
authors_terms: ["a division's innovation performance", "innovation performance", "strong division (per patents)"]
definition: The innovation performance of a division, measured by its patents; the authors assume that a division's innovation performance relates more closely to early-stage knowledge sourcing, given the emphasis on research and creation of new ideas.

name: Division sales performance
authors_terms: ["a division's sales performance", "sales performance", "strong division (per sales)"]
definition: The sales performance of a division, which relates more closely to late-stage knowledge sourcing given the emphasis on commercialization of ideas. High sales performance reflects robust market conditions and strong internal capabilities to commercialize knowledge.

name: Early-stage knowledge sourcing
definition: Externally sourced knowledge that involves invention or experimentation with new ideas and has a longer gestation period; when a firm sources early-stage knowledge it may not know a priori whether the market will show promise when the technology is ready to be commercialized.

name: Late-stage knowledge sourcing
definition: Externally sourced knowledge for which market uncertainty is largely resolved, because the firm has a more precise estimate of the technology's market prospects.

name: Inequality in innovation performance
authors_terms: ["inequality in innovation performance across divisions", "Gini coefficient (per patents)"]
definition: The inequality of patent counts across a firm's divisions; inequality is an important dimension of heterogeneity, and greater inequality in patents implies a larger number of low-performing divisions that the firm needs to prop up in the early stage.

name: Inequality in sales performance
authors_terms: ["inequality in sales performance across divisions", "Gini coefficient (per sales)"]
definition: The inequality of sales across a firm's divisions; greater inequality in sales implies a smaller number of high-performing divisions that the firm can leverage in the late stage.

name: Centralized coordination function
authors_terms: ["centralized coordination function", "dedicated function for knowledge sourcing"]
definition: The presence of a centralized coordination function at the corporate level, which indicates a firm's ability to coordinate across divisions; the firm's choices regarding knowledge sourcing can differ from those of individual divisions because the former seeks to optimize opportunities across divisions.

name: Framing repertoire
definition: Audiences can evaluate framing cumulatively, basing their evaluations on a ''repertoire'' or portfolio of frames that an actor deploys over time rather than on an individual frame. In recurrent communications, audiences' evaluations are based on a repertoire or portfolio of contributions.

name: Framing repertoire resonance
definition: Frames that resonate with their intended audiences-showing alignment with the target's values, beliefs, and ideas-are effective in influencing others. Resonance pragmatically suggests the fulfillment of needs, expectations, and interests that arise from audience members' tasks and goals.

name: Framing repertoire consistency
definition: Consistency is a degree of predictability in framings over time (intraindividual), about maintaining focus in one's framing choices over time.

name: Framing repertoire novelty
definition: The novelty of an individual analyst's framing of a report refers to how different the evoked frames are from those predominant in recently published reports.

name: Audience appreciation
definition: By the term ''appreciation'' we refer to the conferral of value to an object or person that translates into prestige or esteem. Such appreciation can result, for example, in top placement in rankings, induction into a hall of fame, or bestowal of honors, awards, and prizes.

name: Individual status
definition: Status differences can be the result of processes of evaluations that occurred in the past-for example, the bestowal of an honor or an individual's top placement in a ranking (individual status).

name: Organizational status
definition: Status differences can result from affiliation with high-status others, such as a prestigious employer or university (organizational status). Association with high-status others can affect audiences' evaluations of one's quality or competence.

name: Presence of local competition
authors_terms: ["competition", "presence of competition", "a rival store competes in the same market", "COMP", "local competition"]
definition: Whether a competing store of the rival chain is present in the focal store's local geographic market, which the authors define as the 10-mile circle around the focal store. In a competitive market each store chooses product variety to maximize its own profit, whereas a monopoly market includes only one store.

name: Collocation
definition: Whether the nearest rival store is located within one mile of the focal store, that is, whether rivals are collocated in the same shopping plaza or across a street. Collocation strengthens competition and may also expand the market through agglomeration gains.

name: Product variety
authors_terms: ["product variety", "total product variety", "number of stock-keeping units", "SKUs"]
definition: The number of variants a store carries. The authors probe both the level and composition of product variety, that is, the number of variants and the proportion of overlapping products with competitors.

name: Product range overlap
definition: The extent to which the focal store's product assortment overlaps with that of the competing store, measured as the raw number of overlapping SKUs less the randomly drawn overlap. Differentiation is the reverse of product range overlap.

name: Store profit
authors_terms: ["profit", "equilibrium profit", "equilibrium profit increases with the level of differentiation"]
definition: The profit a store earns, which the authors model as depending on the store's demand and on the costs of carrying product variety. A store's equilibrium profit increases with the level of differentiation, and this positive impact is greater when there is more competition and an agglomeration effect.

name: Coordinated interaction
definition: The authors use the terms 'coordination' and 'coordinated interaction' from the Horizontal Merger Guidelines of the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission, avoiding the term 'implicit collusion'. Fully coordinated rival stores choose product variety levels to maximize joint profits instead of acting noncooperatively to maximize individual profit.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["organizational size", "large organizations", "small organizations", "large/small categorical measure of size"]
definition: Perhaps the single most important characteristic determining an organization's competitiveness is size, because various sources of competitive advantage are known to co-vary with size. The authors' main measure distinguishes between large and small firms, defined relatively for each year, and updated from year to year.

name: Prior exposure to competition
authors_terms: ["prior exposure to competition", "competitive experience", "exposure to competition", "experience-weighted overlap"]
definition: The cumulative prior exposure to competition of an organization or its current rivals, measured in organization-years. Red Queen evolution implies that organizations are both more viable, and more competitive, the more that they have faced competition in the past.

name: Organizational failure
definition: r(t) is the failure rate for organization j, modeled as a function of its baseline failure rate, its age, its current competitive context, and other observables. The authors measure t in terms of market tenure rather than organizational age because firms with operations in other markets may have been born before they entered the hard disk drive market.

name: Prior relationships
definition: In high-uncertainty situations such as new-venture investment, prior relationships serve as a social risk-reducing device, and therefore are likely to facilitate investment inflows, given that the universal criteria are met.

name: Third-party referrals
definition: As a type of triad ties, third-party referrals are expected to influence investment decisions of venture capitalists, assuming that the technical merits of a venture are perceived as strong.

name: Strong ties
definition: Strong ties was measured by a friendship item: 'The entrepreneur was a personal friend prior to seeing the business plan.'

name: Technology/products
definition: The technology employed or products offered by the venture would provide a significant competitive advantage, and the venture's technology had a strong proprietary position.

name: Entrepreneurial team quality
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial team", "team scale", "quality of the entrepreneurial team"]
definition: At least one member of the venture team had previous startup experience and at least one member had experience in the relevant industry.

name: Growth potential
definition: The venture is a potentially high growth firm and its competitive strategy is superior than its competitors.

name: Business plan quality
authors_terms: ["business plan", "business plan scale", "quality of the business plan"]
definition: The business plan was thorough in its coverage of key issues and did an excellent job of articulating the opportunity.

name: Investment selection
definition: Investment selection is a binary variable of one if the venture received an investment, and zero otherwise.

name: Contractual covenants
definition: The number of covenants in contracts, which protect interests of investors.

name: Investment delivery period
authors_terms: ["investment delivery", "speed of investment delivery", "investment delivery period"]
definition: Speed of investment delivery was measured as the number of months from the date of the positive investment decision to the date of the first injection of investment into the venture.

name: Venture valuation
authors_terms: ["venture valuation", "valuation of the entrepreneur's firm", "increase in valuation"]
definition: Venture valuation was measured as the difference in percentages of the initial valuation of the firm and the final valuation of the firm by the venture capitalist.

name: Performance variance
authors_terms: ["variance of product performance", "variance in performance", "performance deviation", "extreme (best or worst) outcomes", "deviation from mean performance"]
definition: Radical innovations are characterized by prior uncertainty and posterior variance in performance, so that activity that increases performance variance yields both extremely successful and extremely unsuccessful outputs. The paper measures it as the absolute deviation of a comic's within-year standardized collector value from the mean.

name: Mean performance
definition: Incremental improvements increase average performance by using existing knowledge, and extensive experience produces outputs with high average performance. The paper measures it as the within-year standardized collector market value of a comic.

name: Team size
authors_terms: ["number of creators", "team size", "high number of creators", "size of a team"]
definition: A high number of creators is an important source of diverse knowledge; as a result, the size of a team drives diversity in knowledge and ability to innovate.

name: Knowledge diversity
authors_terms: ["knowledge diversity", "diversity of backgrounds", "deep-level diversity", "cognitive diversity", "genre experience", "diverse knowledge"]
definition: Diversity of knowledge in teams has been termed 'deep-level diversity' (or 'cognitive diversity') to distinguish it from diversity in surface characteristics such as the demographic variables of age, gender, and race. The authors emphasize the less observable cognitive diversity that arises from varied work, task, and organizational experience.

name: Team experience
definition: An important characteristic of team composition is the experience that the members have in working together; teams with many prior collaborative projects have better communication and are thereby more likely to fulfill the goal of obtaining more creative outputs.

name: Creator workload
definition: Learning by doing is most effective when recent production is high, so it follows that a work unit with a full workload is likely to perform better than one that is underemployed.

name: Creator tenure
definition: Assuming that there is a set of learnable basic skills useful in creative tasks, if creative tasks are highly dependent on these basic skills, then total experience will matter most for performance.

name: Organizational resources
definition: Investing in work facilities can increase efficiency, and for creative work a technical and administrative support system that relieves creators of routine tasks has the same effect, as does organizational slack devoted to improving the knowledge of the innovators.

name: Single creator
definition: For individuals, combining diverse experiences does not have the coordination or access problems that arise in teams, so an individual can have more integrated, diverse knowledge without the interpersonal conflicts present in teams.

name: PE firm effect
authors_terms: ["PE firm effect", "PE firm level", "differences between PE firms"]
definition: The component of the variance in buyouts' performance that is explained by the private equity firm, reflecting differences between PE firms in their resources and value creation abilities. It is estimated as the random effect at the PE firm level (level 4) in the multilevel model.

name: Buyout performance
definition: The performance of each buyout, objectively measured as the internal rate of return earned by investors on the equity invested in the acquired company.

name: Time
definition: The passage of time, captured by the calendar year in which a buyout was acquired. The year effect is the component of variance in buyouts' performance associated with the acquisition year.

name: Buyout duration
authors_terms: ["Duration", "duration of the focal buyout", "duration of the investment"]
definition: The number of months between acquisition and exit of a buyout, used as a proxy for the degree to which investment performance is influenced by value addition rather than selection.

name: Economic development
authors_terms: ["developed vs. emerging economies", "developed economies", "emerging economies", "emerging markets"]
definition: The level of development of the economy in which a buyout is located, characterized by differences in formal and informal institutions and in the level of competition for acquisition targets.

name: Economic downturn severity
authors_terms: ["economic downturn", "severity of an economic downturn", "economic conditions", "GDP growth"]
definition: The severity of the economic downturn experienced during a buyout. The authors treat an economic downturn as a form of environmental jolt that makes value generation more complex and transformational.

name: PE fund effect
definition: The component of variance in buyouts' performance explained by the private equity fund, the organizational layer through which PE firms allocate their financial and nonfinancial resources among their investments; PE funds are nested within PE firms.

name: Buyout effect
definition: The component of variance in buyouts' performance explained by the individual buyout, which corresponds to the business-unit effect in previous variance decomposition studies.

name: Industry effect
definition: The component of variance in buyouts' performance explained by the industry in which the acquired company operates.

name: Mutual governance form
authors_terms: ["mutual form", "mutual S&Ls", "mutual associations", "mutual savings and loan associations", "mutual governance"]
definition: Mutual savings and loan associations combine roles that are separated within the stock form: their members are, at once, customers and owners. The structures and processes used to select, monitor, and evaluate managers differ substantially across the two forms, leading managers to have a much greater degree of autonomy and control within mutuals, and mutual S&Ls also tend to have different official purposes and missions than do stock form firms.

name: Asset reallocation
authors_terms: ["simple change in the percentage of nonmortgage assets", "change in the percentage of nonmortgage assets", "asset reallocation", "organizational change", "exploratory change", "move away from residential mortgage lending"]
definition: Moving assets away from residential lending and into other types of investments constitutes an important form of exploratory change for S&Ls. This is a particularly appropriate measure because it not only captures increases in nonmortgage assets, but it also decreases in mortgage assets (and the changing balance between the two).

name: Performance change
authors_terms: ["average annual change in ROA", "change in ROA", "ROA change", "return on assets", "performance"]
definition: Return on assets is a standard measure of performance in organizational research and a widely used metric in the S&L industry. The authors used a simple measure of annual change in ROA as the dependent measure in testing the performance predictions.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "economic performance of parent firms", "return on assets (ROA)"]
definition: The economic effect of alliances on parent firms. The authors chose an objective measure, return on assets, to capture the economic performance of parent firms in alliances rather than perceptual measures, which are more often subject to inconsistency and ambiguity.

name: Resource complementarity
definition: The degree to which alliance partners provide resources that differ from those of the focal firm. The measurement is based on a comparison between the focal firm's four-digit SIC code and that of its partners in alliance relations.

name: Own societal status
definition: Societal status refers to the social ranking of esteem that is ascribed by the society on the basis of a firm's conformity to social norms: social responsibility, financial soundness, innovativeness, long-term investment value, ability to attract and keep talented people, wise use of corporate assets, and so on.

name: Partner societal status
authors_terms: ["partner societal status", "partners with high societal status", "high-status partners"]
definition: The societal status of a focal firm's alliance partners. Partners' high societal status is identified in the same way as a focal firm's, using Fortune's 'Most Admired Corporations' rankings.

name: Own network status
definition: Network status refers to a firm's positional ranking in its interfirm networks; it concerns a firm's influence in interfirm relationships. A firm's eigenvector centrality captures its central position in a network in terms of the 'global' or 'overall' structure of the network.

name: Partner network status
authors_terms: ["partner network status", "partners of high network status"]
definition: The network status of a firm's alliance partners, calculated from the network status of a firm's alliance partners based on the five-year moving window.

name: Societal status asymmetry
definition: The construct is created for the societal status difference between a focal firm and its partners, thereby capturing their status interactions.

name: Network status asymmetry
definition: The construct is created for the network status difference between a focal firm and its partners.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The degree of turbulence or instability in the competitive environment, which shapes the complexity of decision making and accentuates firms' organizational efficiencies.

name: Firm age
definition: The age of the focal firm at the time of the alliance event, measured by subtracting the incorporated year from the alliance event year.

name: Affiliation-based hiring
definition: Hiring employees who share a prior employment or educational affiliation with the founder(s): the authors track the employment and education history of every founder and new hire for 10 years prior to joining the focal firm and define employees as (employment or educational) affiliation-based hires when they had an affiliation in common.

name: Employment affiliation-based hiring
authors_terms: ["employment affiliation-based hiring", "EMP-ABH", "hiring from founders' prior employment affiliations"]
definition: Hiring employees who share a prior employer affiliation with the founder(s); the authors verify whether the hire worked at the same physical unit and/or at overlapping time periods as the founder(s), and hires who did neither are distal employment ties.

name: Educational affiliation-based hiring
authors_terms: ["educational affiliation-based hiring", "EDU-ABH", "hiring from founders' prior educational affiliations"]
definition: Hiring employees who share a prior educational affiliation with the founder(s), measured by whether founders and hires attended the same education institution at overlapping time periods and/or specialized in the same subject.

name: Affiliation proximity
definition: We conceive proximal affiliations as common affiliation ties (employment or educations) with a high degree of overlap of individual experiences at those affiliations (e.g., in time and space), whereas distal affiliations are characterized by low or no overlap between individuals' former experiences at those organizations.

name: New venture performance
authors_terms: ["young firm performance", "venture performance", "firm profits", "firm sales", "firm exit"]
definition: We use three measures of firm performance: the firm's total sales, its yearly profitability, and its exit (hazard) rate, all measured in year t + 1.

name: Progression to lateral authority
authors_terms: ["progression to a lateral authority role", "progressing to lateral authority positions", "lateral authority roles", "progression"]
definition: We define it as authority over collective work that does not include vertical authority over individuals. When individuals gain lateral authority, they gain responsibility and decision rights over a greater proportion of collective work without supervising others.

name: Technical contributions
authors_terms: ["technical contributions", "technical contribution", "number of code commits", "number of resolved bugs"]
definition: By technical contributions, we refer to contributions to the 'technical' core of a project's work. For example, on a software project, a technical contribution would be working code.

name: Technical communication
