definition: When knowledge work is distributed, whether within an organization or outside it, engagement in conversational or discussion threads is the primary way in which individuals share knowledge and learn from each other on an ongoing basis. Individuals who are more active in technical discussions may be more likely to progress to positions of lateral authority.

name: Coordination work
definition: Coordination has been defined as managing interdependencies to achieve collective goals and is a central purpose of organizations. Coordination discussions focused on organizing projectwide affairs such as code releases, conferences, the project website, or the foundation's governance.

name: Boundary spanning
authors_terms: ["boundary spanning", "spanning subproject boundaries", "technical boundary spanning", "communication boundary spanning"]
definition: When coordinating work in progress, the coordination mechanism that may be most critical is the ability to share knowledge across subproject boundaries. Individuals who span subproject boundaries may help transfer knowledge, identify new ideas, enhance awareness of the broader project environment, and expose unattended or unidentified project interfaces.

name: Perceived firm status
authors_terms: ["firm status", "perceived status among potential employees", "firm prestige", "prestige score", "perceived employer status"]
definition: Status refers to a firm's position in a rank-ordering based on its affiliations with others, and potential employees infer a firm's status based on the willingness of others to hire the firm's current employees. The authors measure it as the aggregate perception in the associate labor market about a given firm's status, elicited by asking associates how prestigious it would be to work for the firm.

name: Career-advancing departures to high-status competitors
authors_terms: ["associate-to-partner departures to Vault 100 firms", "employee departures to higher-ranking positions with high-status competitors", "salient and positive employee departures", "departures that are both visible and consistent with career advancement"]
definition: Employee departures that are salient to outside observers because employees leave for jobs at high-status competitors and that are clearly positive in nature because departing employees experience a promotion in rank when moving to a competitor. Combining these two conditions, increased rates of employee departures involving rank promotions to high-status competitors are likely to result in firms being viewed more positively by potential future employees.

name: Employee departures to competitors
authors_terms: ["employee departures", "rate of employee departure", "departures to partner positions at other firms", "lateral moves", "employee mobility"]
definition: The main independent variable in the analysis is the number of employees in a firm that depart for partner positions at other law firms, normalized by the total number of lawyers at the focal firm in order to capture rate of departure.

name: Key success factors
definition: Key success factors are those tasks or attributes which are particularly mandated by the task environment.

name: Core technology
authors_terms: ["technology", "unit (small batch) technology", "mass (large batch) technology", "continuous process technology"]
definition: Technology is conceived of as unit (small batch), mass (large batch), or continuous process, and is represented by the three columns of Table 1.

name: Transaction complexity
definition: Transaction complexity is an index consisting of three highly correlated variables: infrequency of purchase, buyer-seller interaction (time, number of people involved in a specific purchase), and risk of product malfunction.

name: Firm strengths
authors_terms: ["strengths", "distinctive competences", "strengths that match the key success factors"]
definition: A key success factor resides in the environment, while a strength can be said to originate within the firm itself; the supposed ideal is to develop strengths that closely match the KSFs of the industry.

name: Profitability
definition: Organizational performance was operationalized as pre-tax return on assets, using data from annual reports and 10Ks.

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: Salter and Weinhold classified acquisitions into the broad groups of related and unrelated transactions, their overall criterion for relatedness lying in the key success factor of the acquiring and acquired firms. Acquisitions were classified as related if the bidding firm and the acquired firm shared at least one of the following characteristics: similar production technologies, similar science-based research, similar products and/or markets.

name: Total dollar gains from acquisition
authors_terms: ["abnormal dollar value changes", "dollar gains", "total dollar value changes", "standardized gain"]
definition: Value in this context should be reflected in the stock price of the firms (and specifically in the change in stock prices as the market adjusts its expectation of future earnings from the businesses). The abnormal dollar value change is the abnormal change in dollar value of the firm as the result of the acquisition announcement, and the gains of the acquired and the bidding firm are combined to measure the synergistic gains as a result of the transaction.

name: Acquired firm gains
authors_terms: ["gains to acquired firms", "cumulative abnormal returns of acquired firms", "returns to related target firms"]
definition: The wealth effect on the acquired firm, captured as the cumulative abnormal return on the target's stock around the acquisition announcement; the announcement of the acquisition by the bidder causes a revaluation of the earnings potential of the target.

name: Acquiring firm gains
authors_terms: ["gains to acquiring firms", "cumulative abnormal returns of acquiring firms"]
definition: The wealth effect on the bidding firm, captured as the cumulative abnormal return on the acquirer's stock around the acquisition announcement.

name: Feedback-seeking through monitoring
definition: Feedback-seeking through monitoring 'entails observing the situation and the behaviors of other actors for cues useful as feedback . . [and] . . . is thus a process of meaning construction, one that involves a fair degree of interpretation and inference' (Ashford and Cummings, 1983: 382-383).

name: Feedback-seeking through inquiry
definition: Feedback-seeking through inquiry 'is the individual's attempt to actually increase the amount of personally relevant data in his or her information environment by directly asking actors in that environment for their perception and/or evaluation of the behavior in question' (Ashford and Cummings, 1983: 385).

name: Culture distance
definition: The authors examine heterogeneity across countries 'by focusing on the culture distance between the 'host' country of the subsidiary and the 'home' country of its parent (Kogut and Singh, 1988)'; culture refers to the shared cognitive maps that guide inferences, decisions, and actions of a society of people.

name: Value chain scope
authors_terms: ["value chain scope", "breadth of value chain scope"]
definition: Breadth of value chain scope reflects the number of the following primary functions performed within the subsidiary's own boundaries: research and development, manufacturing, and marketing and sales.

name: Role conflict
definition: Role conflict refers to the degree of incompatibility between the different expectations associated with a work role.

name: Role ambiguity
definition: Many employees lack clear information about task objectives, role expectations, and scope of responsibility and authority, and thereby experience ambiguity in their job definitions; the authors predict asymmetric effects of role ambiguity on the two feedback-seeking modes.

name: HQ-subsidiary centralization
definition: MNC researchers have argued that centralization is 'one of the fundamental dimensions of organization design' (Egelhoff, 1988: 129); in this study it is indexed by the subsidiary president's influence over the outcome of nine strategically relevant decisions, where higher values indicate higher centralization.

name: HQ-subsidiary communication
authors_terms: ["HQ-subsidiary communication", "frequency of communication between a subsidiary president and corporate HQ executives"]
definition: We define HQ-subsidiary communication as the frequency of personal interactions between the subsidiary president and parent company executives.

name: Lateral integrative mechanisms
definition: The study focuses on those lateral integrative mechanisms which ensure coordination among peer subsidiaries in different countries (liaison positions, task forces and permanent committees).

name: Socialization mechanisms
definition: Organizational socialization is the process by which 'an individual is taught what behaviors and perspectives are customary and desirable within the work setting' (Van Maanen and Schein, 1979: 221); in the MNC context corporate socialization is a mechanism by which subsidiary managers' values and interests can become closely aligned with those of the parent corporation.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm growth was measured as growth in sales. Sales growth was measured as the proportionate increase in revenue over the year prior to which top management change or addition was measured.

name: Strategic diversification
authors_terms: ["strategic diversification", "diversification into new product areas", "strategic change"]
definition: Diversification, broadening the set of products and markets the firm competes in, also impacts the ability of current management to successfully manage the new venture. Strategic diversification was operationalized as diversification into new product areas.

name: Top management industry experience
authors_terms: ["top management industry experience", "top management experience", "industry experience"]
definition: Top management experience was an organization-level variable that measured the average amount of time that current top managers had worked in the semiconductor industry.

name: Top management functional diversity
authors_terms: ["top management functional diversity", "functional diversity of top management", "functional diversity"]
definition: Top managers were found to come from four types of primary functional experience. The entropy measure for top management functional diversity assesses whether top managers represent a wide variety of functions. Higher scores indicate a more diverse set of functional experiences for the top management team.

name: Inside ownership
authors_terms: ["inside ownership", "top management ownership", "management ownership", "ownership by insiders"]
definition: Top management ownership measured the proportion of total firm ownership held by individuals who were employees of the firm.

name: Chief executive ownership
authors_terms: ["chief executive ownership", "ownership by the chief executive", "CEO ownership"]
definition: Chief executive ownership measured the proportion of firm ownership held by the chief executive of the firm.

name: Venture capital ownership
authors_terms: ["venture capital ownership", "ownership by venture capitalists", "VC ownership"]
definition: Venture capital ownership measured the proportion of firm ownership held by venture capitalists who were funding the organization.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["outside directors", "proportion of outside directors", "outside board members"]
definition: Outside directors measured the proportion of board members who were not employed by the firm.

name: Venture capital director representation
authors_terms: ["venture capital directors", "venture capital representation on the board"]
definition: Venture capital directors measured the proportion of board members who were members of venture capital firms.

name: Top management team change
authors_terms: ["top management change", "change in top management", "changes in top management", "top management team change"]
definition: We define the top management team as the chief executive and all top managers reporting to the chief executive. We operationalize this as the sum of the number of additions to the top management team and the number of departures from the top management team.

name: Business embeddedness
authors_terms: ["business embeddedness", "relational business embeddedness", "external business embeddedness", "subsidiary business embeddedness"]
definition: The form of relational embeddedness with customers and suppliers in which relationships depart from arm's-length relations: the actors have known each other for a long time, have transacted over a long period, have adapted their business conduct to each other and are used to exchanging information about market conditions. It reflects to what extent the subsidiary's relationships with external suppliers and customers depart from arm's-length relations in its ordinary business operations.

name: Technical embeddedness
definition: The interdependencies between firms in terms of their product and production development processes; it reflects the fact that development activities in one firm can be more or less adapted to development activities in another firm. A high degree of technical embeddedness means that the two organizations are highly interdependent in terms of their technological activities.

name: Expected market performance
authors_terms: ["expected market performance", "expected subsidiary market performance", "expected performance"]
definition: The subsidiary's expected performance in its own market, measured by expected profitability, sales volume, and market shares as perceived by divisional HQ managers.

name: Subsidiary importance for competence development
authors_terms: ["subsidiary importance for MNC competence development", "importance for other MNC units' competence development", "importance for competence development"]
definition: The divisional HQ management's assessment of the subsidiary's importance for technical development in terms of product and production development for other sister units.

name: Perceived technological uncertainty
definition: Perceived technological uncertainty refers to an individual's perception that he or she is unable to accurately predict or completely understand some aspect of the technological environment. In NPD, project managers may have perceptions of technological uncertainty regarding the application of technology to the current development project or regarding impending changes in that technology.

name: Cross-functional integration
definition: Cross-functional integration in an NPD project team refers to the magnitude of interaction and communication, the level of information sharing, the degree of coordination, and the extent of joint involvement across functions in specific NPD tasks.

name: Skill and resource synergy
definition: Skill and resource synergy is the fit between a product concept and a firm's available resources and skills.

name: Development process proficiency
authors_terms: ["development process proficiency", "proficiency in the development process"]
definition: Proficiency in the development process is a team's ability to competently execute various marketing and technical activities.

name: Project outcomes
definition: Project outcomes comprise product competitive advantage and financial performance (for instance, the project-level return on investment). Product competitive advantage refers to a product's perceived superiority relative to competitive products; financial performance reflects the level of financial success achieved by the new product.

name: Marketing proficiency
definition: Marketing proficiency includes activities such as evaluating consumers and competitors, determining market characteristics and trends, carrying out marketing research, test marketing, and executing product launch.

name: Technical proficiency
definition: Technical proficiency encompasses such activities as conducting engineering and manufacturing evaluations, product testing, determining product specifications, prototyping, and building the final product.

name: Competitive and market intelligence
definition: Competitive and market intelligence entails early assessments of market size, consumer behavior, price sensitivities, and competitor activities.

name: Marketing synergy
definition: Marketing synergy refers to the project's fit with the available market research, sales force, distribution, and advertising and promotion skills and resources.

name: Technical synergy
definition: Technical synergy refers to a project's fit with available R&D, engineering, and production skills and resources.

name: Product competitive advantage
definition: Product competitive advantage refers to a product's perceived superiority relative to competitive products. It concerns the product's technical performance and quality, as well as the degree to which it meets customers' needs with unique features and capabilities.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance reflects the level of financial success achieved by the new product (for instance, the project-level return on investment).

name: Innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption", "adoption of an innovation", "placing an order for an innovative ship type", "early adopters"]
definition: The dependent variable is the event of placing an order for an innovative ship type. Shipping firms typically place orders for multiple ships at a time, and it is the order that corresponds to a decision to acquire one or more ships.

name: Prior innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["prior adoption", "having adopted an innovation", "firms that have ordered an innovative ship type"]
definition: Once the firm has adopted an innovation, it will accumulate experience that allows more precise judgment of the value, and it will gain competence in its use, increasing the expected value of the focal technology relative to others.

name: Geographic proximity to prior adopters
authors_terms: ["same cluster as early adopters", "geographical proximity", "a different nation than past adopters", "location in a different nation", "rapid diffusion within nations"]
definition: Geographical proximity is a mechanism that has been linked to competitive advantage in cluster theory. If a firm in the cluster adopts a valuable new production technology, then other firms in the cluster will be quicker to adopt it than firms outside the cluster.

name: Shared supplier ties
authors_terms: ["sharing a supplier", "same builder", "direct ties to builders", "connections to the same builders"]
definition: This argument points toward a revised cluster theory that directly examines the links between supplier firms that make production technologies and buyer firms that use it to gain competitive advantage. Firms that transact with the same set of suppliers have access to the same technologies.

name: Network cluster proximity
authors_terms: ["same network cluster", "different network cluster", "cohesive cluster", "structurally equivalent cluster"]
definition: Network ties can be analyzed directly to find which firms are closer to each other because they are connected to each other, and thus are a cohesive cluster, or are connected to the same third parties, and thus are a structurally equivalent cluster.

name: Network centrality
definition: Managers get access to more information when they are central in the network, causing central actors to be early adopters. In addition to this informational reason for central-actor adoption, centrality also has a competitive aspect, as central actors often occupy high positions on status hierarchies and are motivated to maintain these positions through means such as early adoption of innovations.

name: Startup acquisition
definition: The focus of this study is on high-tech startups that experience an acquisition. The analytic sample is restricted to firms that are acquired before the firm age of 10 (i.e., startups) and based in a high-tech industry.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["employee entrepreneurship", "rate of employee entrepreneurship", "same-industry employee entrepreneurship", "outside-industry entrepreneurship"]
definition: The main dependent variable is the target startup's rate of employee entrepreneurship, which is the rate at which the target firm's workers leave to become founders of new companies. Founders are identified as the set of individuals who (a) appear in the new firm at its first quarter of operations and (b) are among the top three earners at the new firm in the first year.

name: Target firm relocation
definition: As a part of their post-acquisition integration efforts, acquirers often move the target firm inside their existing establishments. Relocation is defined as a binary variable equalling 1 if the acquired establishment is moved to the location of, or absorbed by, the acquirer's headquarters within 3 years of the acquisition.

name: Founder status
definition: In the context of startups, extensive research shows that founders are central individuals who supply and embody the knowledge that undergirds the creation and growth of new firms. Acquirers typically place a heightened emphasis on retaining founders following an acquisition in order to facilitate the transfer of novel, tacit knowledge of the startup.

name: Foreign investor resources
authors_terms: ["a foreign firm's resources", "the U.S. investor's resources"]
definition: The resources that a foreign investor possesses and that host country executives appraise when evaluating inward FDI opportunities, encompassing both firm-specific resources and generic resources.

name: Firm-specific resources
definition: Host country executives are expected to prefer IJVs over divestitures when foreign investors possess unique resources, such as technological capabilities and unique competencies, because by establishing a joint venture managers can access directly and experience first-hand partners' firm-specific skills and knowledge, whereas the uniqueness of firm-specific resources makes it likely that the foreign owner appropriates their value in a divestiture.

name: Generic resources
authors_terms: ["generic resources", "resources of a more generic nature"]
definition: Resources of a more generic nature, such as financial capital and market knowledge, which host country executives can obtain efficiently through either an IJV or a divestiture, so executives are likely to be indifferent between the two modes when foreign investors possess them.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: The extent to which the U.S. firm possesses strong technological capabilities.

name: Unique competencies
definition: Unique competencies held by the U.S. firm.

name: Financial resources
definition: Financial resources that the U.S. firm is able to provide.

name: Market knowledge
definition: The extent to which the U.S. firm possesses market knowledge in China.

name: IJV attractiveness
authors_terms: ["IJV attractiveness", "attractiveness of the opportunity as a joint venture"]
definition: Executives' assessment of the attractiveness of an inward FDI opportunity when it is engaged as a joint venture.

name: Divestiture attractiveness
authors_terms: ["Divestiture attractiveness", "attractiveness of the opportunity as a divestiture"]
definition: Executives' assessment of the attractiveness of an inward FDI opportunity when it is engaged as a divestiture.

name: Preference for joint ventures over divestitures
authors_terms: ["Preference for IJV versus divestiture", "preferences for joint ventures over divestitures"]
definition: The variable Divestiture attractiveness was subtracted from the variable IJV attractiveness to create a third dependent variable, Preference for IJV versus divestiture, capturing executives' relative preference between the two governance modes for engaging inward FDI.

name: Hard-to-value intangible assets
definition: The degree to which the Chinese firm possesses intangible assets that are difficult for the U.S. firm to value.

name: Product market overlap
definition: The degree to which the two businesses' product markets overlap; the variable is inversely coded, such that the greater the variable's value, the less the amount of information asymmetry between the firms.

name: Foreign investor familiarity with the local business
authors_terms: ["Familiarity with Chinese business", "the U.S. firm's familiarity and knowledge of the Chinese business' resources and capabilities"]
definition: The U.S. firm's familiarity and knowledge of the Chinese business' resources and capabilities.

name: Reputable affiliations
definition: The extent to which the U.S. firm would consider the Chinese business' affiliated organizations reputable.

name: Asset specificity
definition: The level of unique asset investments required by the Chinese business.

name: Small numbers bargaining
authors_terms: ["small numbers bargaining", "Number of other investment opportunities"]
definition: The extent to which few exchange partners exist for a particular opportunity; the smaller the number of other U.S. firms interested in investment with the Chinese business, the greater the ex post exchange hazards.

name: Prior detailed contracts
definition: The level to which the U.S. firm has used detailed contracts with others in the past.

name: Favorable cooperative history
definition: Favorability of the U.S. firm's cooperative history with others.

name: Foreign institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign institutional ownership", "foreign institutional investors", "foreign investors", "foreign ownership"]
definition: The growth of foreign institutional ownership has put new pressure on Japanese firms to embrace global CSR standards; it is measured as the percentage of a company's shares held by foreign institutional investors.

name: Within-firm influence of CSR and IR managers
authors_terms: ["the within-firm influence of CSR and IR managers", "CSR/IR executives on the board", "CSR or IR board members"]
definition: The within-firm influence of CSR and IR managers, measured as the percentage of board members whose task areas described in the Handbook of Board Members include either CSR or IR. Board membership is seen as a better measure of their influence than the presence of a CSR or IR department, because in Japan the board of directors is the primary corporate decision-making body.

name: Gender diversity on boards
authors_terms: ["gender diversity on boards", "women's representation on boards of directors", "appointment of female directors"]
definition: Women's representation on boards of directors. Most Japanese companies still have no female directors, so the authors analyze the appointment of female directors rather than the proportion or the number of female directors.

name: Gender diversity in management
authors_terms: ["gender diversity in management", "representation of women in managerial positions", "log odds female managerial employees"]
definition: The representation of women in managerial positions, measured as the log odds that managers are women.

name: Gender diversity at lower ranks
authors_terms: ["gender diversity at these lower ranks", "gender diversity in non-managerial or entry-level positions"]
definition: Women's representation in non-managerial, white-collar positions and among new hires for non-managerial, white-collar jobs; both are measured as log odds, and the entry-level measure covers 2001-2008.

name: Merger participation
definition: MERGE is a dummy variable and is coded as 1 if the hospital was involved in a merger, or else 0. Hospitals that were involved in mergers or acquisitions were identified using past issues of the publication Modern Healthcare and the list was verified with Ohio State Health Department officials.

name: Change in high-profit service mix
authors_terms: ["high-profit services", "high-profit DRGs", "proportion of patients from high-profit DRGs", "presence in profitable, insured services"]
definition: High-profit DRGs are the top 15 DRGs that are consumed by commercially insured patients and where less than 5 percent of the patients are uninsured. A hospital's product-mix is defined as the proportion of services used by high-profit patients, and services used by low-profit patients.

name: Change in low-profit service mix
authors_terms: ["low-profit services", "low-profit DRGs", "shift away from low-profit services", "low-profit patients"]
definition: The top 15 services consumed by the uninsured were defined as the low-profit DRGs. Services used by uninsured patients tend to be less profitable than services used by the fully insured mainly because of high rates of default and higher collection costs and the high cost of emergency services used to a greater extent by the uninsured.

name: Change in high-profit market share
authors_terms: ["market share in high-profit services", "increase in post-merger market share in highprofit services", "Change in Market Share"]
definition: The Change in Market Share variable measures the percentage of the total patients in DRG i in hospital market k who were treated in hospital j in the post-merger year divided by the total patients in DRG i in hospital market k who were treated in hospital j in the pre-merger year.

name: Change in low-profit market share
authors_terms: ["market share in low-profit services", "decrease in post-merger market share in lowprofit services", "Change in Market Share"]
definition: The Change in Market Share variable measures the percentage of the total patients in DRG i in hospital market k who were treated in hospital j in the post-merger year divided by the total patients in DRG i in hospital market k who were treated in hospital j in the pre-merger year.

name: Market competition
authors_terms: ["competition", "degree of concentration in the market", "Herfindahl-Hirschman Index", "HHI"]
definition: In this paper, competition refers to the degree of concentration in the market, measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). The HHI is defined as the sum of the squared market shares of all the firms operating in the market. Thus, a highly competitive market is one which has low HHI.

name: Relative investment in physical capital
authors_terms: ["physical capital investment", "low investment relative to rivals in physical capital", "high investment relative to rivals in physical capital", "deviation from the norms of rivals"]
definition: Physical capital refers to assets such as buildings, equipment, and computer systems, and a bank's investment in physical capital is demonstrated by the cash flows directed toward these resources. Each bank's level of relative investment in physical capital was determined by comparing its investment level with the average investment level of its asset-class group.

name: Relative investment in human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital investment", "low investment relative to rivals in human capital", "high investment relative to rivals in human capital", "deviation from the norms of rivals"]
definition: Human capital refers to the skills, education, experience, and knowledge of the firm's employees, and a firm's investment in human capital is reflected by its cash flow directed to employees' salary and benefits. Each bank's level of relative investment in human capital was determined by comparing its investment level with the average investment level of its asset-class group.

name: Service sophistication of deployment
authors_terms: ["deployment decision: service sophistication", "resource deployment decisions", "service sophistication"]
definition: Resource deployment decisions involve the selection of the specific market segment(s) in which to engage the firm's resources. The requisite level of service sophistication can be represented on a continuum ranging from simple (i.e., retail or consumer banking) to complex (i.e., wholesale or commercial banking).

name: Firm performance
definition: Economic performance is the outcome of interest for this study; the authors employ a market-based measure of economic performance, Tobin's q, which compares the firm's market value to the replacement costs of its assets.

name: Regulatory uncertainty
definition: "the perception of significant regulatory instability"; in this setting organizations "could not know whether the policy would change or be repealed, or how the change would impact the organization."

name: Corporate structure
definition: The organizational division between headquarters and subsidiary units: "because corporate structure differentiates their problem-solving and learning activities, headquarters and subsidiaries differ in attention allocation on their strategic agendas." The exact regulations - including RPSs - faced by headquarters and subsidiaries differ.

name: Attention to renewable technologies
authors_terms: ["renewable agenda", "strategic agenda", "attention to renewable electricity technologies"]
definition: "organizational attention to renewable electricity technologies on the strategic agenda for each organization in each year"; the strategic agenda is the set of alternative courses of action headquarters and subsidiaries identify as important enough to take and disclose to stakeholders.

name: Complementary experience
definition: "a measure that identifies whether a single unit - either headquarters or subsidiary - possesses both operating experience and regulatory experience"; complementary renewable experience captures units that have regulatory and, in particular, renewable operating experience.

name: Shared experience
authors_terms: ["shared experience", "shared operating experience", "shared renewable operating experience", "shared regulatory experience"]
definition: The degree to which a unit - headquarters or subsidiary - gains knowledge from the unit it is directly connected to, because both units have experienced similar regulatory or operating experience; "if sender and receiver share the same experiences, then knowledge will not have to be transformed so as to conform to existing expectations."

name: Worker performance
definition: The measure of worker performance is the employer's answer to the question about the most recently hired worker's performance in the job into which he was hired. While the original tournament model is cast in terms of worker output, the empirical work uses the closely related concept of worker performance instead, substituting performance for effort.

name: Relative performance
authors_terms: ["relative performance", "relative worker performance", "performance relative to their peers", "P - P0"]
definition: A key idea in tournament theory is that workers are promoted not on the basis of their level of performance in an absolute sense but rather on the basis of their performance relative to their peers. Competitions based on relative performance arise when internal hiring policies are combined with fixed job hierarchies.

name: Wage spread
definition: The tournament prize is the difference in wages between the post-promotion and pre-promotion jobs, and this is chosen by the employer to induce the optimal level of worker effort. The spread, S, is the difference in wages between the post-promotion and pre-promotion jobs.

name: Promotion
definition: The basic idea of a tournament is that workers of a given rank in an organization compete for promotion to the next level of the job hierarchy, with the promotion (and its associated wage increase) awarded to the worker with the highest performance.

name: Expected promotion
definition: The survey asks whether the worker was promoted or was expected to be promoted within the next five years. PROMEXP equals one if a promotion was expected to occur within 5 years of the survey date and zero otherwise.

name: Luck
authors_terms: ["θ", "variance of the stochastic component of performance", "luck", "random 'luck' factors"]
definition: The stochastic components of performance over which the workers have no control are assumed to have mean zero, variance θ, and to be independent across workers. When random 'luck' factors become more important determinants of the promotion probability, the marginal return to effort declines and the worker's incentives to exert effort are depressed.

name: CEO need for achievement
definition: Need for achievement gauges a person's need to meet standards of excellence, to accomplish difficult tasks, and to attain success. It results in a way of life and basic attitudes and is not a simple, temporary drive.

name: Strategy-making rationality
definition: Analysis is the structured deliberation that goes into decisions—the systematic effort and thoroughness devoted to uncovering and assessing strategic problems and opportunities. Interaction describes managers' collaborating with and consulting one another to ensure enlightened and consistent decisions.

name: Structural formalization
definition: Formalization comprised codified rules and procedures, role specialization, and the use of formal controls.

name: Structural centralization
definition: Centralization is the distribution of power in an organization.

name: Structural integration
definition: Integration refers to the coordinative and collaborative devices a firm used.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty is defined as change and unpredictability in technology and in customer and competitor behavior.

name: Product innovation
definition: Product innovations are most prevalent and useful in uncertain environments in which competing products or customers' preferences alter significantly. Innovation is the strategy dimension associated with the strategic content of the business.

name: Firm size
definition: Size, here called LNSIZE, was measured as the natural logarithm of the number of full-time employees; the links of size to structure were included in the model to make it as complete as possible and to reduce specification error.

name: Institutional environment quality
authors_terms: ["institutional environment", "weak institutions", "adverse institutional environments", "opaque institutional environments", "Rule of Law (RL)", "Control of Corruption (CC)"]
definition: Differences across countries in the local institutional environment, such as the rule of law and the control of corruption; firms often adjust their strategies in response to local institutions, and weak institutions are environments lacking transparency, trust, and regulatory predictability.

name: New entry in the host country
definition: Whether the funding firm has newly established subsidiaries in the host country, captured by a dummy variable indicating that the firm set up new subsidiaries in the host country within the past 5 years.

name: External orientation of local activities
authors_terms: ["external orientation", "externally oriented managers", "externally oriented functions", "externally oriented activities"]
definition: The extent to which the funding firm's local activities are externally oriented, proxied by the titles of top managers at the local subsidiaries: externally oriented managers work in marketing, corporate outreach, or supply chain management, as opposed to internally oriented managers in R&D and production.

name: Corporate foundation giving
definition: The amount of money donated by a corporate foundation to non-U.S. beneficiaries in a host country in a year; the authors use corporate philanthropy to refer to giving through corporate foundations.

name: Direct local giving
definition: Donations that go directly to an agency in the beneficiary country, such as a donation to a charity in Indonesia for its post-tsunami recovery efforts.

name: Intermediated giving
definition: Donations that go indirectly by way of an intermediary outside of the beneficiary country, such as a donation to Doctors Without Borders in New York for malaria treatment in Mali.

name: Female founder
authors_terms: ["female founder", "female-led venture", "female entrepreneur", "gender of the entrepreneur"]
definition: Female gender stereotypes are incongruent with cultural images of entrepreneurship linked with stereotypically masculine characteristics, and female entrepreneurs are therefore viewed with skepticism.

name: Social impact framing
definition: A specific type of framing—social impact framing—that emphasizes a venture's attention to and care for the physical earth as well as the socioeconomic environment and consequent benefits to societal welfare.

name: Perceived warmth
definition: Warmth, an orientation toward the support of others, is associated with caring and a tendency toward helpful and conciliatory behavior.

name: Perceived competence
definition: Competence, a generalized interest in the pursuit and accomplishment of personal goals, is associated with ambition and agency.

name: Perceived business viability
definition: Judges' assessment of estimated business viability; in Study 1 judges were asked to respond to the question, 'Do you think this is a viable business in its current form?' In Study 2, following Kerr et al. (2014), measures of venture growth and venture financing were used to create an aggregate score for business viability.

name: Technological know-how
definition: A firm's technological know-how reflects its ability to generate new scientific discoveries and technological breakthroughs.

name: Market pioneering know-how
definition: A firm's market pioneering know-how indicates whether it can commercialize technological innovations before competitors do.

name: Spin-out generation
definition: Spin-outs are stand-alone entrepreneurial ventures founded by former employees of an incumbent firm that compete in the same industry as the parent but have no equity relationships with any incumbent; spin-out generation is the creation of such a venture by a firm's employees.

name: Entrant survival
definition: Survival, defined as whether a firm survived to the year following an observation, with acquisitions being treated as censored observations; the authors describe survival as a key dimension of performance for entrants.

name: Spin-out entrant
definition: A firm started by individuals who were employees of existing firms in the industry (incumbent firms) in the year prior to the spin-out's formation.

name: Incumbent-backed entrant
definition: Entrants affiliated with incumbent firms in the disk-drive industry, including subsidiaries, parent-sponsored ventures, and joint ventures.

name: Diversifying entrant
definition: Firms that existed in some other industry prior to entering the disk drive industry.

name: Parent technological know-how
authors_terms: ["parent technological know-how", "parent's technological know-how", "technological know-how of the parent"]
definition: The technological know-how of the parent incumbent, measured in the year preceding a spin-out's entry into the industry, which was an explanatory variable for Hypothesis 2.

name: Parent market pioneering know-how
authors_terms: ["parent market pioneering know-how", "market pioneering know-how of a parent"]
definition: The market pioneering know-how of the parent incumbent, measured in the year preceding a spin-out's entry into the industry, which was an explanatory variable for Hypothesis 2.

name: Physical differentiation strategy
authors_terms: ["physical differentiation strategy", "physical attribute-based differentiation", "differentiation strategy through superior physical product attributes", "physical product differentiation"]
definition: Publishers differentiate on the physical aspects of print guidebooks by using high quality paper, better bindings, and including color graphics. These approaches typically increase the book's density because they require high-density paper or other weight increasing measures.

name: Content-based differentiation
authors_terms: ["content", "book content", "content as a nonphysical differentiation attribute", "emphasis on nonphysical product attributes", "content volume"]
definition: Publishers who emphasized physical product attributes as part of their differentiation strategy in the pre-digital age respond to the product digitization threat by increasing their emphasis on nonphysical product attributes - namely, book content - as the differentiator.

name: Content development cost
authors_terms: ["content development cost", "high-cost content positioning", "high content cost", "internal supply cost of the nonphysical differentiator", "reliance on primary content"]
definition: Some content is more costly to develop than others; publishers that have chosen a high-cost content positioning face higher cost to add content, which could deter them from shifting toward emphasizing content as the differentiator. Primary content, like hotel and restaurant descriptions and reviews, needs to be up to date, so a book that relies heavily on it is more costly and time consuming to develop than one that relies on secondary content like history.

name: Demand diversity
authors_terms: ["demand diversity", "potential demand diversity", "external market demand for the nonphysical differentiator"]
definition: In book categories where customer content demands are diverse, a publisher is likely to find multiple niches in the content space that are profitable, whereas in categories where customer content demands are concentrated in a niche content space a publisher is less likely to find the content space outside of that niche profitable. The potential demand diversity of a product category is related to the number of attractions consumers can visit in the destination.

name: Product digitization
authors_terms: ["product digitization", "dematerialization of artifacts and material objects"]
definition: Product digitization is the "dematerialization of artifacts and material objects and their reduction to electronic information". As a result of dematerialization, digital products no longer have physical attributes that firms can leverage to distinguish them from the competition.

name: Offshoring to low-wage countries
authors_terms: ["production offshoring", "imports from low-wage countries", "LWC import share", "offshoring more production to low-wage countries"]
definition: Firms can redesign their supply chain to locate more-polluting production in LWCs to 'avoid' U.S. pollution standards, while assigning their domestic plants to produce in cleaner segments to 'comply' with the U.S. standards. The authors use manufacturing firms' imports from overseas to proxy for production offshoring.

name: Plant toxic emissions
authors_terms: ["toxic emissions", "domestic pollution", "pollution emissions", "emissions released on American soil"]
definition: Toxic emissions gauges the total plant-level toxic emissions, defined as a plant's all-media release of designated toxic chemicals, multiplied by the RSEI toxicity weight for each chemical; emissions to air are weighted using inhalation toxicity and emissions to other media are weighted using oral toxicity.

name: Local institutional pressure
authors_terms: ["local institutions", "local institutional pressure", "local institutional power", "institutional pressure for environmental performance"]
definition: Firms are subject to national regulations as well as local informal institutional pressures; American firms will engage in more pollution offshoring if their plants are located in counties where the local institutions can exert greater pressure on environmental performance, such as counties with a more informed (educated) population, a higher voter turnout in presidential elections, or a stronger presence of environmental nongovernment organizations (NGOs) like the Sierra Club.

name: Firm capability
authors_terms: ["firm capability", "plant capability", "productive capability", "technical capability", "environmental capability", "marketing capability", "productivity", "R&D and brand equity"]
definition: Firms' incentive to arbitrage institutional differences depends on the costs and benefits of arbitrage relative to those of strict compliance. These costs and benefits are partly driven by firm capabilities: less-capable firms often find it costly or challenging to meet environmental standards, whereas more-capable firms will find it relatively easy to remain profitable while achieving these standards.

name: Pollution content of imports
authors_terms: ["toxic imports", "pollution intensity of a firm's imports", "pollution content of a firm's imports"]
definition: The authors sum a firm's import value in each industry, weighted by the industry's pollution intensity, to derive the firm's toxic imports, which measures the toxic content of a firm's imports; scaling toxic imports by total imports measures the pollution intensity of a firm's imports.

name: Pollution content of plant output
authors_terms: ["toxic output", "toxicity-weighted output", "pollution content and intensity of a plant's output"]
definition: A plant's output in each industry is summed and weighted by the industry's pollution intensity to derive the overall pollution content and intensity of a plant's output, toxic output and (toxic output/plant shipment), respectively.

name: Pollution abatement costs
authors_terms: ["abatement costs", "pollution abatement expenditures", "total Pollution Abatement Operating Costs"]
definition: Abatement costs include pollution prevention, pollution treatment, waste recycling, and disposal.

name: Pollution prevention practices
definition: Plants can adopt pollution prevention practices such as operational and procedural as well as material and equipment changes; prior studies have shown that P2 practices reduce toxic emissions.

name: Production waste
definition: The total tonnage of production waste, i.e., the total amount of waste produced before treatment.

name: Energy efficiency
authors_terms: ["fuel consumption", "cost of fuel consumption per unit of output"]
definition: The cost of fuel consumption per unit of output is calculated as a measure of energy efficiency that could potentially explain the change in plant-level pollution emissions.

name: Business-domain capability
authors_terms: ["business-domain capability", "business-domain capabilities", "domain competence score", "domain experience", "client industry knowledge", "industry-domain knowledge", "know-why"]
definition: Business-domain capability is similar to know-why (Garud, 1997) and represents an understanding of the principles (cause-and-effect relationships) underlying a phenomenon (in this case, a customer's business in a specific industry sector). It was measured by the level of client industry knowledge of the project team.

name: Technological capability
authors_terms: ["technological capability", "technological capabilities", "technology competence score", "technology experience", "technological expertise", "know-how"]
definition: Technological capability is similar to know-how (Garud, 1997) and represents knowledge of the process by which a new technological product or service can be developed. It was measured by the level of technological expertise of the project team in the technology of the project in which the team had been deployed.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is an aggregation of project performance in this context since the focal firm delivers customized software to clients by executing multiple projects year after year. Since the firm delivers service to customers by executing multiple projects for different customers, it may be assumed that firm performance is an aggregation of project performance.

name: Firm social capital
authors_terms: ["firm social capital", "Firm Social Capital", "social capital of firms"]
definition: Social capital represents resources embedded in relationships. The authors represent firm social capital with degree centrality at the firm level, so that meaningful social capital in this context consists of being central in the sense of regular participation and interaction with other participants at committee meetings.

name: Firm influence in standards setting
authors_terms: ["firm influence in technical standards setting committees", "influence over standards", "firm influence"]
definition: Influence over which standards are developed and adopted, which the authors describe as an important aspect of performance for firms in high-technology industries: adopting a standard containing a firm's proprietary intellectual property rights can yield royalties, and standards that favour a firm's technological capabilities can yield competitive advantage.

name: Personnel inflows
definition: The hiring of individuals whose attributes are known by the group, considering only the job moves of meeting participants between the firms in the sample, and accounting for the amount of social capital (individual degree centrality) the incoming individuals carry.

name: Personnel outflows
definition: The loss of individuals whose attributes are known by the group, considering only the job moves of meeting participants between the firms in the sample, and accounting for the amount of social capital (individual degree centrality) the outgoing individuals carry.

name: Redundant participation
authors_terms: ["Redundancy", "redundant participation", "redundant ties", "exclusivity value of the connections"]
definition: The extent to which a firm has multiple boundary-spanners for the same interfirm tie, so that individual representatives with relationships to a given partner firm can substitute for each other. The authors argue that the net incremental value of a redundant tie should be lower than that of an exclusive tie, so redundancy in a new hire's interfirm relationships moderates the effect of hiring on the firm's social capital.

name: Strategic change
definition: Changes to a firm's business strategy; under conditions of strategic change firms may wish to dissolve interfirm ties that do not advance their new strategy, so the value of an exiting individual's relationships can depend on such change. The measure represents the count of subcommittees that a firm stopped participating in from one year to the next.

name: Top management team legitimacy
authors_terms: ["TMT legitimacy", "legitimacy of the top management team", "legitimacy", "legitimacy index"]
definition: TMT legitimacy in a pre-IPO firm may be viewed as the extent to which the composition, characteristics, or behaviors of the TMT contributes to the legitimacy of the firm.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: The difference between the IPO subscription (offering) price, fixed pre-IPO for insiders and investment banks, and the secondary market (opening) price; this difference is referred to as underpricing, or run-up.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "true market value of the firm", "economic potential"]
definition: The true market value of the firm, which underpricing separates from the value obtained by the owners at offering; differences between the two values suggest uncertainty in investors' initial evaluation of the firm.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "diversification of products", "product diversification", "range and relatedness of the products sold"]
definition: Diversification strategy is the range and relatedness of the products sold, one of the two fundamental elements of any MNE's resource deployment. Firms are classified using Rumelt's nine-category typology based on the specialization ratio and the related ratio.

name: Degree of internationalization
definition: Defining degree of internationalization as the extent to which total MNE sales are generated by foreign affiliates. It represents the firm's relative emphasis on foreign versus domestic operations, the second fundamental element of an MNE's resource deployment.

name: MNE performance
definition: The ratio of net annual profits-to-sales (return on sales), calculated as the mean after-tax profits-to-sales over the 5-year period 1977-1981 and chosen as the preferred measure of performance over an asset-based measure.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: The extent to which relationships with a given entity (here, political entity) by a focal firm are maintained over time.

name: Domain targeting
definition: A firm's targeting of CPA with a given governmental domain and the associated specialized knowledge and insights; targeting CPA to administrative domains involves trying to influence government after legislation is passed by swaying officials that are tasked with interpreting, implementing, and enforcing legislation.

name: Firm social reputation
definition: External evaluation of a firm's tendency 'to behave in a certain manner'.

name: Securing a desired governmental outcome
definition: Successfully achieving an outcome that is favorable to a firm, here winning a government contract dispute.

name: Industry competition
authors_terms: ["competition", "the nature of industry competition", "competitive interactions", "strategic complements", "strategic substitutes", "CSM", "Competitive Strategy Measure"]
definition: The concepts of strategic complements versus substitutes indicate whether a firm's marginal profits are increasing or decreasing in competitor output. Under strategic complements, an increase in competitor output will induce an individual firm to increase its own output, whereas under strategic substitutes the reverse holds.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The start-up's initial financing, i.e. the external debt raised relative to the total financing sources available at start-up. Highly leveraged start-ups may find it difficult to generate sufficient cash flows to meet their sizable debt obligations.

name: Post-entry exit probability
authors_terms: ["post-entry exit probability", "likelihood of exit", "exit risk", "post-entry exit", "start-up survival"]
definition: Exit is determined at the time the firm's employment falls to zero and does not become positive again in subsequent years. The hazard rate represents the probability that a start-up firm exits the industry within a particular time interval conditional upon survival until that period.

name: Adverse selection and moral hazard problems
authors_terms: ["adverse selection", "moral hazard", "adverse selection and moral hazard problems", "potential for adverse selection and moral hazard problems"]
definition: Adverse selection arises when financiers cannot accurately gauge the quality of the entrepreneurs and their products, which makes it more likely that poor-quality entrepreneurs are over-represented in the financial market. Moral hazard refers to the problem that entrepreneurs have an incentive to expropriate wealth from creditors by undertaking riskier projects than promised to the creditors.

name: Born global formation
authors_terms: ["born global formation rate", "born global formation rates", "born globals"]
definition: Born globals are 'young companies that derive a significant portion of their revenue from international sales' (Cavusgil and Knight 2015). The born global formation rate is the estimated percentage of societal members between the ages of 18 and 64 who have started a venture in the last three years where the venture has at least 25% of its customer base from foreign countries.

name: Crossborder economic freedom
definition: A composite index that assesses the degree to which a country's regulatory framework supports international business, including observations for the number of days for and costs of engaging in international trade activities. Economically open countries have a low regulatory burden on crossborder flows of goods and services.

name: Financial system global integration
definition: The degree to which a country's financial system is integrated into the global financial system; it is measured by the degree to which the inflow and outflow of equity, debt, money market instruments, and other financial transactions are permitted. Financial integration increases foreign venture capital investment and allows risk sharing as financial institutions cooperate and compete across borders.

name: Entrepreneurial norms
definition: The extent to which existing social and cultural norms encourage, or do not discourage, individual actions that may lead to new ways of conducting business or economic activities. Entrepreneurial norms provide cues of taken for granted behaviors that may include a fondness for risk, proactiveness, and optimism.

name: Entrepreneurial educational capital
definition: An institutional feature whereby a country's educational and training system generates a supply of individuals with an entrepreneurial mindset calibrated toward sensing and acting on market opportunities, by providing instruction in market principles, adequate attention to processes involved in new firm creation, and the ability to recognize opportunities.

name: Public governance quality
definition: Public governance quality refers to the degree to which government institutions are reliable, maintain public order, and promote the rule of law. Higher scores reflect more sound formal institutions governing economic activity.

name: Immigrant population
definition: First-generation immigrant population as a percentage of the general population; it is an indicator of the inflow of this unique form of human capital and its prevalence in society, and it reflects a set of underlying policies and institutions facilitating the inflow of immigrant populations.

name: Relative adjacent market size
definition: A causal condition capturing the ratio between the sum of the GDP of all bordering nations, using both land and maritime borders, and the domestic market size. The higher the ratio, the greater likelihood that an entrepreneur will look abroad rather than within his or her own domestic context for market opportunities.

name: Hygiene code compliance
authors_terms: ["hygiene code", "imperative code of hygiene", "regulatory compliance", "compliance with health regulations", "health grades", "hygiene"]
definition: The rational science-based imperative code of hygiene involving compliance with health regulations. It is an imperative code that relies on a scientific rationale to protect the public from possible sickness brought on by the consumption of food riddled with dangerous bacteria.

name: Authenticity
authors_terms: ["authenticity", "authenticity code", "context-activated code of authenticity", "attributions of authenticity", "interpretive code of authenticity"]
definition: Authenticity refers to the socially constructed attribution of whether or not an entity is 'real' in that it matches the cultural expectations of the particular type. It is the context-activated interpretive code of authenticity involving conformity to cultural norms.

name: Consumer value ratings
authors_terms: ["consumer value ratings", "consumer value rating", "star rating", "ratings", "value judgments"]
definition: Consumer perceived value is defined as the individual evaluator's 'overall assessment of the utility of a product [or brand, service, or experience] based on perceptions of what is received and what is given'; such perceptions of value shape consumer value ratings, which are frequently proclaimed in online forums such as review websites.

name: Ease of short-term travel between R&D centers
authors_terms: ["increased ease in short-term travel", "short-term visits", "short-term travel", "ease of short-term visits"]
definition: We distinguish between longer-term migration and short-term visits using the European Union (EU) definition of a short-term visitor as a person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for a period of up to 90 days.

name: Invention quantity
definition: Invention, defined as the upstream stage of innovation focused on idea creation (Garud et al. 2013), is the stage of innovation that is most dependent on intraorganizational knowledge flows.

name: Invention scope
definition: The scope of an invention serves as a prominent measurement for gauging the extent of a firm's knowledge recombination across different technology domains (Verhoeven et al. 2016).

name: Knowledge distance
definition: We define knowledge distance as the difference in the content of the knowledge utilized in each pertinent R&D center.

name: Cultural distance
authors_terms: ["cultural distance", "different spoken language", "absence of a common spoken language"]
definition: The cultural distance between R&D centers may also vary. Scientists in R&D centers located in countries with very different cultures may struggle to understand each other and to develop an understanding of the technical aspects of the problem (Keller and Loewenstein 2011). One driver of cultural distance is the absence of a common spoken language, such as English, shared by scientists in the two R&D centers; this is our primary empirical measure.

name: LBO status
definition: An LBO is a transaction in which a new private corporation buys out the equity of the public stockholders, usually with debt financing, resulting in the formation of a new privately held firm which typically has a very high debt/equity ratio and whose equity is closely held by a group of managers and large outside investors.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["firm growth", "rates of growth", "growth rates", "sales growth", "employment growth"]
definition: The rate of growth of the firm is an important determinant of its value. Firm growth was measured using changes in firm revenues and number of employees during the 3-year postbuyout period.

name: Total diversification
authors_terms: ["total diversification", "total firm diversification", "Jacquemin-Berry Entropy measure of diversification"]
definition: Total diversification is measured using the 4-digit SIC lines of business of the firm to estimate P_i, where P_i is the share of total firm sales of the ith line of business. Changes in total diversification are measured as absolute change during the 3-year postbuyout period.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: In contrast to related diversification, unrelated diversification is by definition not based on shared technologies, production processes or customers (Rumelt, 1974). Unrelated diversification is measured using the 2-digit SIC lines of business of the firm to estimate P_i.

name: Periphery business growth
definition: The periphery business portfolio is defined as those 4-digit SIC lines of business that are not in the same 2-digit SIC as the core business. Changes in sales and employment were measured for the 3-year postbuyout period.

name: Core business growth
definition: The firm's 'core business' was defined as the largest 4-digit SIC business in terms of sales, and the 'core business portfolio' as all 4-digit SIC activities that share the same 2-digit SIC as the core business. Changes in sales and employment were measured for the 3-year postbuyout period.

name: Periphery business portfolio
authors_terms: ["periphery business portfolio", "periphery portfolio", "number of periphery businesses", "peripheral lines of business"]
definition: Managers may reduce the total number of core or periphery businesses or reconfigure them by divesting and/or adding different lines of business. The periphery business portfolio is defined as those 4-digit SIC lines of business that are not in the same 2-digit SIC as the core business.

name: Core business portfolio
authors_terms: ["core business portfolio", "core portfolio", "number of core businesses"]
definition: The 'core business portfolio' was defined as all 4-digit SIC activities that share the same 2-digit SIC as the core business. Changes in the number of core businesses, and additions to and deletions from the core portfolio, represent changes in diversification strategy.

name: Network closure
definition: Redundancy in the information actors can access is a function of the degree of closure among a focal actor's direct ties: an actor connected to two alters who are directly connected to each other will likely access redundant information, whereas alters who are unconnected provide non-redundant information. In closed networks among groups of investors, most actor pairs have co-invested in the past and there is redundant information that facilitates shared beliefs.

name: Actors' knowledge similarity
authors_terms: ["actors' knowledge similarity", "knowledge similarity", "network specialization", "specialized networks", "diverse networks"]
definition: The extent to which network actors specialize in the same knowledge domains, or the extent to which network actors are specialized relative to one another. In specialized networks actors focus on similar knowledge domains; diverse networks have actors specialized in dissimilar knowledge domains.

name: Venture success
authors_terms: ["venture success", "success", "attracting a second round of funding"]
definition: The venture's ability to attract a second round of funding, which is a clear and positive signal either that the initial investors are happy with the venture's progress or that the venture has been able to attract new, possibly larger and more experienced investors.

name: Entry into a product category
definition: A developer's entry into a product category was measured as a dichotomous variable that equals 1 in the month that the developer first released app product(s) in the focal product category. For the same developer-month, the authors coded all of the other categories the developer could have entered but did not as 0.

name: User-side economies of scale
definition: User-side EOSL (Quadrant 1) arise when an acquirer and its target serve overlapping product categories such that the acquirer's value proposition can be amplified over the increased user base post-acquisition. EOSL arises when an acquisition occurs in the same market and the combined entity can leverage the increased scale to lower cost or increase willingness to pay.

name: User-side economies of scope
definition: User-side EOSP (Quadrant 2) occurs when a common user base can be potentially leveraged across an acquirer's and its target's nonoverlapping but related product categories. EOSP arises when an acquisition spans different markets, across which the acquirer gains advantage through sharing or reallocating resources.

name: Complementary-technology-side economies of scale
definition: Complementary-technology-side EOSL (Quadrant 3) occurs when an acquirer's set of complementary technologies can be applied in overlapping product categories with the target to reduce the cost and effort of developing, maintaining, or scaling its product or service.

name: Complementary-technology-side economies of scope
definition: Complementary-technology-side EOSP (Quadrant 4) occurs when a common set of complementary technologies can be applied across nonoverlapping product categories of an acquirer and its target so that the acquirer can more efficiently produce multiple products, services, or functionalities.

name: Opportunism
definition: In a joint venture setting, we define 'opportunism' as an act or behavior performed by a party to seek its own unilateral gains at the substantial expense of another party and/or the joint venture entity by breaching the contract or agreement, exercising private control, withholding or distorting information, withdrawing commitment, shirking obligation, or grafting joint earnings.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: Environmental volatility, often synonymous with uncertainty or dynamism, is the rate of change or the degree of instability of factors within an environment. This study proposes three interrelated yet distinct dimensions that constitute environmental volatility (higher-order concept) in a typical emerging economy: industry structural instability, information unverifiability, and law unenforceability.

name: Industry structural instability
definition: Structural instability, defined in this study as an objective construct measured by archival information, concerns the extent to which an industry's major structural attributes, such as sales growth, profit growth, and output growth, are unstable or fluctuate.

name: Information unverifiability
definition: Perceived information unverifiability thus refers to the degree to which the true information about macro- and micro-business environments facing an individual business is difficult to verify as perceived by executives.

name: Law unenforceability
definition: Legal protection of legitimate business activities and intellectual or industrial property rights is most often weak in emerging economies; this enforcement uncertainty, also treated as a perceived subjective variable, can be partly ascribed to long traditions of untrustworthy legal and governmental systems, lack of independent law enforcement, the deficiency of supervision mechanisms, and frequent unjustified law changes.

name: Industry growth
definition: Industry sales growth was measured by the compound growth rate (%) of the respective industry's sales from 2000 to 2002. The faster an industry grows, the smaller is the effect of environmental volatility on opportunism.

name: Local dependence
authors_terms: ["local dependence", "dependence on the host country environment"]
definition: A joint venture's local dependence associated with market orientation was defined as a dummy variable (1 if local market-focused, 0 otherwise-export-oriented). Economic exposure increases with dependence on the host country environment, and joint venture operations become more susceptible to impediment by environmental volatility.

name: Joint venture performance
definition: Joint venture performance, defined in this study as return on investment, sales growth, and overall satisfaction, which together reflect a joint venture's multidimensional (financial, market, and overall) achievement.

name: Overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence occurs when an individual's certainty that his or her predictions are correct exceeds the accuracy of those predictions. Overconfidence is excessive certainty about one's prediction.

name: Extreme certainty
definition: Extreme certainty occurs when an individual perceives virtually no possibility of failure. In this research, the authors identify the special case of extreme certainty as the most dramatic, and potentially damaging, case of overconfidence.

name: Extent of pioneering
definition: Product introductions that are more pioneering—that is, that create a distinct market category—are riskier than incremental product introductions, because pioneering introductions are unique and decision makers lack prior similar actions to help calibrate judgment.

name: Achievement of success factors
definition: The extent to which a new product introduction achieved the success factors that the manager associated with it had identified.

name: Research productivity
authors_terms: ["research productivity", "GHC performance", "performance on general human capital tasks", "professor performance"]
definition: Performance on general human capital tasks, proxied by a cumulative count of a professor's Financial Times 50 (FT50) publications; individuals with more FT50 publications will be viewed as high-research performers within their institutions.

name: Firm-specific administrative role
definition: A role that requires the person to engage in new tasks that involve an investment in firm-specific knowledge; the key proxy is whether the individual was an associate dean in any given year.

name: Total compensation
authors_terms: ["log of annual salary", "total compensation", "annual financial compensation", "compensation increases"]
definition: The professor's annual financial compensation, measured as the natural log of annual salary; most universities reported a nine-month base salary, but a few reported total annual compensation (including summer support).

name: Innovative differentiation
authors_terms: ["innovative differentiation", "differentiation via product innovation", "cost of innovation"]
definition: The type of differentiation strategy that strives to create the most up-to-date and attractive products by leading competitors in quality, efficiency, design innovations, or style. New-product development and implementation require the employment of experts who can identify the crucial parameters of an intricate, nonroutine design or marketing decision.

name: Marketing differentiation
authors_terms: ["marketing differentiation", "differentiation based on intensive marketing and image management"]
definition: The strategy of marketing differentiation attempts, through advertising, prestige pricing, and market segmentation, to create a unique image for a product. The pursuit of superiority in design does not necessarily accompany that attempt.

name: Cost leadership
definition: Porter's strategy of cost leadership requires firms to become the lowest cost producers in an industry, so that above-average returns can be obtained even with low prices. Much effort is devoted to cost control.

name: Strategic breadth
definition: Porter's focus dimension is the opposite of strategic breadth. A broad strategy will generally require a firm to confront and acknowledge great heterogeneity, that is, many differences in customer and competitor behavior in its target markets.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: The overarching construct of uncertainty is formed by unpredictability and dynamism, which are generally considered its key components. Environmental unpredictability is the difficulty of forecasting the behavior of competitors and customers.

name: Environmental unpredictability
definition: The difficulty of forecasting the behavior of competitors and customers. It is one of the two key components of the overarching construct of uncertainty.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism characterizes environments in which products and practices change quickly, such as the software industry. It is usually correlated with unpredictability and the two are generally considered the key components of uncertainty.

name: Market heterogeneity
definition: Heterogeneity refers to many differences in customer and competitor behavior in a firm's target markets. It is the third environmental dimension assessed alongside dynamism and unpredictability.

name: Use of liaison devices
authors_terms: ["liaison devices", "integrative liaison devices", "use of liaison (integration) devices"]
definition: Integrative liaison devices such as task forces and committees allow regular, personal, and intensive contact among experts and decision makers of different departments, and greatly facilitate collaboration among them.

name: Use of technocrats
definition: Specialized, highly trained professional technocrats such as scientists and engineers are indispensable for devising, assessing, implementing, and continually changing complex product designs.

name: Delegation of authority
definition: Complexity and changes in product designs create the need for the delegation of authority to the experts most capable of making critical decisions. The Aston measure used gauges the distribution of power to make very routine decisions.

name: Use of formal controls
definition: Formal controls are an aspect of formalization: there will be a strong emphasis on formal profit and budget controls in order to keep costs, and thus prices, at a minimum.

name: Firm performance
