definition: To ensure its unambiguous assessment, performance was measured with three distinct indices, and the sample was divided into clearly successful and clearly unsuccessful firms.

name: Organizational structure
definition: Four of the most commonly researched dimensions of structure are delegation, formalization, specialization, and integration. Because strategies were expected to influence actual tasks, the authors were mostly concerned with emergent structure—the procedures that were actually used—rather than with institutional structure, processes portrayed by policy manuals and organization charts.

name: Strategy-context complementarity
authors_terms: ["complementarities of strategy with structure and environment", "complementarities of strategy with both environment and structure", "complementarities"]
definition: A central contention of this research is that good performers will exhibit significant complementarities of strategy with structure and environment, so that the relationships predicted in the model will often be more significant among good than among poor performers. In short, complementarities of strategy with both environment and structure may be needed for good performance.

name: Organizational status
definition: We propose that the Fortune ranking confers a high-status distinction on companies ranked within the Fortune 500 category. Although nominally a ranking of the largest companies, the Fortune 500 has become an important status marker in the business community.

name: Employment-related corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["employment-based corporate social responsibility (CSR)", "employment-related CSR", "nonpecuniary employment-related CSR", "nonpecuniary employment CSR"]
definition: This type of CSR provides employees with a more hospitable workplace, and involves practices such as employee health and safety, union and employee relations, human capital development, supply chain labor standards, professional development, and work-life benefits. Such practices make the organization more attractive inasmuch as they signal to employees that the firm is a virtuous, more hospitable place to work.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Market uncertainty is related to the variability of the expected level of demand for a firm's products. It depends on exogenous factors, such as the economic cycle, the evolution of customer preferences, demographic changes, institutional factors.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty exists when it is not clear which technology will emerge to dominate in the industry. The established technology often competes with one or more alternative technologies.

name: Market valuation of R&D capital
authors_terms: ["market valuation of R&D capital", "market valuation of a firm's R&D capital", "V(R&D)", "value of R&D capital"]
definition: The coefficient gamma measures the market valuation of a firm's R&D capital. In practice, it expresses the market valuation of one currency unit invested in R&D by the firm as compared to one currency unit invested in tangible assets and it should reflect investors' expectations over the future economic benefits of R&D investments.

name: R&D capital
definition: K is the book value of the firm's technological knowledge, as measured by the R&D capital. The R&D capital (K) has been computed as a perpetual inventory of the past R&D expenditures.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: The set of growth opportunities (delta) existing in the industry; the authors state that the effect of the growth option on the value of R&D is bigger when growth opportunities within the industry are higher, because investing in R&D in fast-growing industries offers a wider set of opportunities to be potentially exploited.

name: Technology cumulativeness
definition: Technology cumulativeness (kappa), which according to Green and Scotchmer (1995) is intended as the degree to which future innovations build on previous ones.

name: Customer switching costs
definition: Market frictions that arise between suppliers and their buyers; customers who change firms in the second period must pay switching costs S, assumed to be lower than the utility provided by the products.

name: Multiproduct position
definition: Firm scope is the breadth of products offered by a company; a multiproduct firm provides both prepaid and postpaid services and enables potential transfers between the two, whereas single-product firms sell only one of the prepaid or postpaid services.

name: Firm performance
definition: The customer base and economic performance of a firm; in the stylized model, firm economic performance (revenue) is derived by multiplying market share and product price.

name: Multiproduct entry
authors_terms: ["multiproduct entry", "multiproduct entry strategy", "scope choice of entrants", "choice of scope"]
definition: The scope choice of a new entrant, which is less likely to pursue a multiproduct entry strategy - offering both prepaid and postpaid services - when switching costs are low than when they are high.

name: Innovation strategy
authors_terms: ["innovation strategy", "strategic intention to pursue innovation", "intention to pursue innovation", "emphasis on innovation"]
definition: A firm's strategic intention to pursue innovation, which the authors call 'innovation strategy'; intention to pursue innovation is different from innovation activities or innovative capability, which are more associated with innovation strategy implementation, whereas a firm's strategic intention is best measured by its resource allocation.

name: Employee group
authors_terms: ["employee group", "job family", "R&D employees", "R&D job", "strategic employee group"]
definition: Job family in the dataset provides three categories: R&D jobs, technical jobs and administrative jobs. R&D employees directly influence their firm's technological advantage and are treated as the strategic employee group in firms pursuing innovation.

name: Pay level
authors_terms: ["pay level", "relative pay level", "total pay", "short-term pay", "long-term pay"]
definition: Pay level is the amount of compensation an employee receives; for the measure of pay level the authors used total pay, short-term pay and long-term pay.

name: Compensation time horizon
authors_terms: ["compensation time horizon", "long-term to short-term ratio", "relative emphasis of long-term pay to short-term pay"]
definition: Compensation time horizon is an important dimension of compensation systems because some pay forms are based on short-term results (e.g., merit pay, annual bonus) while other pay forms direct attention to long-term outcomes (e.g., stock options, stock grants).

name: Stock option vesting period
authors_terms: ["stock option vesting period", "vesting period", "length of the vesting period"]
definition: Stock option vesting period refers to 'the amount of time it takes for an option to become exercisable'; recipients usually have to wait a specified number of years before exercising options to realize financial gains.

name: Value-added chain integration
definition: In this study, we considered the value-added integrating mechanisms to be changes in the structural hierarchy of a unit, enhanced integration of design (R&D) and manufacturing functions, and supplier integration.

name: Hierarchical integration
authors_terms: ["hierarchical integration", "structural hierarchy change", "changes in the structural hierarchy of a unit"]
definition: Hierarchical integration, or the degree of power sharing and vertical coordination in an organizational structure. In general, we propose that a hierarchy will operate more efficiently than formerly as a coordinating device for position relationships, with a high degree of power sharing between levels and coordinated decentralization.

name: Design-manufacturing integration
authors_terms: ["design-manufacturing integration", "design-manufacturing coordination", "integration of design and manufacturing", "design-manufacturing functional integration"]
definition: Design-manufacturing functional integration will be paramount to the capture of value via process innovation. In order to achieve both technical success and economic (cost) success, new processing systems depend greatly on these two functions working in concert with technology vendors.

name: Supplier integration
definition: The third and final mechanism chosen for the value-added chain as defined here is the suppliers of the components and raw materials that become inputs to a new processing technology. As Gerwin noted, the quality of inputs often determines the outcomes for computer-aided manufacturing as much as the success of a processing technology installation team.

name: Customer integration
authors_terms: ["customer alliance", "customer integration", "market-directed integration", "market- or customer-directed mechanisms"]
definition: The market integration construct focused on customers, and one viable scale emerged. We called such responses market- or customer-directed mechanisms; they are similar to Porter's channel and buyer value-added chains.

name: Manufacturing process capacity
authors_terms: ["contribution to manufacturing process capacity", "internal capacity", "productivity improvement", "throughput capacity"]
definition: First, contribution to manufacturing process capacity was assessed using system performance measures: scrap and rework rates, cycle time achieved, utilization, and throughput time reduction.

name: Manufacturing flexibility
definition: Second, we measured flexibility, in terms of changeover time, the number of part families scheduled on a system, and reduction in service calls to customers.

name: Strategic planning formality
authors_terms: ["strategic planning formality", "planning formality", "level of planning formality", "level of formality", "formality of planning"]
definition: The level of formality of a firm's strategic planning, compared across firms in terms of the completeness of, commitment to, and utilization of their strategic planning activities. The authors treat it as a multidimensional construct whose dimensions, such as the comprehensiveness of planning activity, can be scaled.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Firm performance was solicited in two ways: objective information on firm sales, return on assets (ROA) and return on sales (ROS) for the beginning and ending years of the 5-year period under study, and a subjective, numerical evaluation of the firm's performance on four dimensions in comparison to its overall industry.

name: Grand strategy
authors_terms: ["grand strategy", "overall grand strategy", "generic grand strategies", "grand strategy type"]
definition: A grand strategy is a comprehensive general plan of major actions through which a firm intends to achieve its long-term objectives. The four generic types used here are stability, internal growth, external acquisitive growth, and retrenchment.

name: Corporate investor investment experience breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of investment experience of corporate investors", "corporate investors' breadth of investment experience", "CORP_BREADTH"]
definition: We measured the breadth of investment experience of corporate investors and family investors as the unique number of sub-industries invested in by all major shareholders of the same investor type from the focal company.

name: Family investor investment experience breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of investment experience of family investors", "family investors' breadth of investment experience", "FAM_BREADTH"]
definition: We measured the breadth of investment experience of corporate investors and family investors as the unique number of sub-industries invested in by all major shareholders of the same investor type from the focal company.

name: External cooperation
definition: We define 'external cooperation' as the number of voluntary cooperation the focal firm has with other firms involving the exchange, sharing, or codevelopment of products, technologies, or services.

name: Innovation performance
definition: To measure innovation performance, we use the firm's patenting performance, differentiating between innovation quantity and innovation quality.

name: Product portfolio diversity
authors_terms: ["product portfolio diversity", "product portfolio breadth", "diversity of product-market categories", "diverse experience base"]
definition: We view product portfolio diversity as indicating the firm's experience of applying core competences in serving different product-market categories. It denotes the scope of the firm's experience base.

name: Design iteration
definition: Design iteration refers to the testing and tuning of product design through a sequence of problem-solving cycles, as opposed to developing the full design upfront.

name: New product performance
authors_terms: ["new product performance", "new product success", "continual attractiveness to users"]
definition: We examined new product performance by observing the extent to which a newly launched app continually appealed to the consumers.

name: Timing of ATM adoption
authors_terms: ["early adoption", "adoption timing", "investment timing", "early adopter", "first mover", "innovator", "early follower"]
definition: In this study, the term "early adopter" refers to banks that had installed ATMs by 1979 (20.2% of banks in our sample), while the terms "first mover" or "innovator" refer to the earliest adopters within this group, specifically, the 2.8% of sample banks that had adopted ATMs through 1973. The term "early follower" refers to early adopters that are not first movers.

name: Retail market share
authors_terms: ["market share", "retail market share", "personal loan market share", "retail loan market share"]
definition: ATMs affect the services that banks provide to their retail customers; they provide services to bank customers who invest personal and family funds and borrow funds for personal and family needs. As a result, ATM investments should have had an impact on bank market share in the retail banking segment.

name: Overall bank performance
authors_terms: ["overall bank performance", "overall business performance", "income", "IBITS", "change in operating income"]
definition: The authors used "income before income taxes and securities gains or losses" (IBITS) as a measure of bank performance; IBITS is described as a measure of overall bank performance that is most closely related to bank operations.

name: Bank size
definition: The size of banks in the U.S. and in the sample spans many orders of magnitude in terms of assets, so the authors used the base 10 logarithm of total assets as a measure of bank size. In the case of ATMs, "banks size was an asset that affected both operating costs and customer value."

name: Board gender diversity
authors_terms: ["board gender diversity", "board diversity", "gender diversity on the firm's board", "level of gender diversity on the firm's board", "female board representation"]
definition: Our primary independent variable is the level of gender diversity on the firm's board. We operationalized board-level gender diversity as the number of female board members at the time of the annual meeting in that calendar year.

name: Firm value
definition: Tobin's q is defined as the ratio of market value to book value of assets, and it is a broad-based reflection of the market's valuation of the firm as a whole, incorporating current performance as well as future growth opportunities.

name: Social performance rating for diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity strengths", "diversity strength score", "social performance ratings for diversity", "KLD STATS ratings"]
definition: The KLD STATS social performance ratings cover seven distinct dimensions of social and environmental performance: community, corporate governance, diversity, employee relations, environment, human rights, and product. For each dimension, the ratings identify specific items that constitute either a strength or a concern.

name: Perceived commitment to shareholder value
authors_terms: ["commitment to shareholder value", "weaker commitment to shareholder value", "caring about profit goals", "commitment to maximizing returns for its shareholders"]
definition: We argue that an increase in board diversity leads investors to update their beliefs about firm preferences. Specifically, we argue that a gender-diverse board is interpreted as revealing a preference for diversity and a weaker commitment to shareholder value.

name: Perceived concern for social performance
definition: A preference for diversity reflects a desire to attend to stakeholders other than financial market investors. In the experimental study, female-appointing firms were perceived as caring more about social performance than firms that appointed a male director.

name: Earnings pressure
authors_terms: ["earnings pressure", "pressure to meet or beat securities analysts' earnings forecasts", "intensity of earnings pressure"]
definition: The pressure to meet or beat securities analysts' earnings forecasts. The independent variables measure the intensity of earnings pressure that a firm experiences for a particular quarter.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["aggressiveness of competitive behavior", "competitive aggressiveness", "competitive behavior", "softening of competitive behavior"]
definition: The dependent construct is the aggressiveness of competitive behavior, which the authors measured by two variables, ticket price and flight frequency by an airline in a market. Lower levels of competitive aggressiveness than that which maximizes the firms' long-term performance take the form of higher prices and lower quality of service.

name: Institutional investor temporal orientation
authors_terms: ["dedicated institutional investors", "transient institutional investors", "temporal orientation of the institutional investors", "dedicated institutional investor ownership", "transient institutional investor ownership"]
definition: Companies have different types of institutional investors who differ significantly in terms of their investment time horizons. Dedicated institutional investors have large, long-term holdings concentrated in a few firms and are less sensitive to short-term earnings surprises, whereas transient institutional investors take small equity positions in many firms, trade frequently and are sensitive to companies' short-term earnings results.

name: Vesting of CEO stock-based incentives
authors_terms: ["unvested stock-based incentives", "vested incentives", "unexercisable stock options and restricted stocks", "exercisable stock options and common stocks", "temporal vesting of CEO stock-based incentives"]
definition: Companies usually impose a period of time before CEOs can exercise, or vest, their stock-based incentives. Unvested stock-based incentives cannot be exercised or cashed out in the near term, so they reduce the impact of short-term performance and resulting stock price variations on managers' decision making, whereas vested incentives are exercisable and common stock is owned.

name: Foreign subsidiary investment
definition: Foreign subsidiary investment proxies for the total equity investment in a host country, measured as the yearly number of subsidiaries that a focal firm has in any given foreign country. Subsidiary count captures substantial changes in a firm's resource commitment in a host country.

name: Volatility of political affinity
definition: The propensity for sudden and unpredictable shifts in the political relations between countries; volatility implies unpredictability and a sudden change occurring over a relatively short time.

name: Level of political affinity
definition: The similarity of two countries' national interests in global affairs; high political affinity is associated with cooperation and limited interference in the other country's affairs, while low political affinity reflects tensions between countries.

name: Political connections
definition: Political connections include equity-based connections (i.e., state ownership) and relationship-based connections, which are based on firms' ties with high-ranking government officials and allow firms to exert influence on policymaking. The authors focus only on relationship-based connections.

name: Internal hiring process
definition: Internal hiring processes are the different ways in which managers identify, evaluate, and select among potential internal candidates. Posting is a process in which a manager posts information about an open job to an internal job board and invites interested internal candidates to apply, whereas slotting is a process in which managers draw on their personal relationships in the organization to identify potential candidates for an open position and then select their preferred candidate for the job, without open competition.

name: Job performance
definition: I used multiple measures of job performance from HealthCo's annual performance evaluation as a first set of quality indicators. A worker's contribution score assesses his or her contribution to the success of the organization, department, or line of business, depending on the job, and a worker's competency score assesses his or her skills relative to the job requirements.

name: Turnover
definition: Turnover is a second indicator of match quality. I did not distinguish between voluntary and involuntary turnover, as both are indicators of poor matches, with both the worker and firm equally likely to terminate an ill-fitting employment relationship.

name: Subsequent promotion
definition: Because promotion typically indicates that an individual has excelled in his or her current role and/or is seen as having the potential to succeed in a job with more responsibility, I used subsequent promotion as a third indicator of quality.

name: Starting compensation
definition: The starting compensation is the natural logarithm of the total annual compensation the employee should expect to receive for the year, as reported in HealthCo's personnel records. The starting compensation recorded in the personnel record reflects the total compensation an individual should expect to earn during the year and is the figure he or she is most likely to negotiate.

name: Female board representation
authors_terms: ["female board representation", "female director representation", "proportion of female directors", "female directors"]
definition: Female board representation was operationalized as the number of female directors in a given firm-year divided by total board size.

name: Acquisitiveness
definition: A firm's acquisition intensity concerns the number of deals it engages in and the typical size of each deal (Hitt et al., 1996).

name: Acquisition size
definition: Acquisition size was operationalized as the total value of all transactions in a given firm-year, scaled by the annual sales of the acquirer.

name: Future-time framing
definition: A systematic cognitive tendency in an organization, due to the languages spoken there, that affects how the organization perceives the future; it is an organization-level cognitive tendency that affects corporate decisions through categorization and framing. The authors operationalize it with a language's future-time reference (FTR) criterion, which separates languages into two broad categories: those that require future events to be grammatically marked when making predictions and those that do not.

name: Corporate future orientation
authors_terms: ["corporate future orientation", "organizational future orientation", "future-oriented behavior", "future-oriented behaviors"]
definition: Firms' engagement in future-oriented behaviors, proxied by CSR and R&D, because to implement them firms must incur short-term costs to benefit from future benefits.

name: Home country linguistic diversity
definition: The linguistic diversity of an organization's home country, which refers to the extent to which people in the same country have different mother tongues; it is an important dimension of within-country heterogeneity.

name: Home country globalization
definition: A country's globalization, which facilitates the spread of ideas, information, images, and people across different cultures and language backgrounds; measured by the KOF index of the degrees of a country's global connectivity, integration, and interdependence in the economic, social, technological, cultural, political, and ecological spheres.

name: Foreign institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign institutional ownership", "foreign institutional investors", "foreign institutional holdings"]
definition: Ownership by institutional investors from foreign countries, who have increasingly become more salient to and active in companies, especially multinationals, and who can influence corporate decisions both through exposing the company to different languages and through their activism.

name: Target board meeting frequency
authors_terms: ["target board meeting frequency", "board meeting frequency", "group interaction frequency", "meeting frequency"]
definition: Board meetings are the focal point for directors to jointly collect, share, and analyze information, and the authors measure target board meeting frequency as the number of target board meetings that occurred during private negotiations. The authors treat target board meeting frequency as group interaction frequency.

name: Target value capture
authors_terms: ["target value capture", "value that the target captures at acquisition announcement", "value capture"]
definition: The value that the target captures at acquisition announcement, that is, the slice of the total value created through an acquisition that the target extracted during private negotiations.

name: Overboarded directors
definition: Target directors are overboarded if they serve on many boards; the authors classify a target director as overboarded if that director sat on three or more other boards in the year prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Directors experienced in acquisitions
authors_terms: ["directors experienced in acquisitions", "experienced target directors", "target director acquisition experience"]
definition: Target directors with prior experience in negotiating acquisitions, recognized when a director had served as a director for another firm that completed a public firm acquisition during the five years prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Female directors
definition: Female directors are minority directors who improve board information processing, as they encourage participation by soliciting input from all directors, stimulate information sharing and richer discussion of alternatives, and support diverse perspectives.

name: Acquisition initiation
definition: Acquisitions can be initiated by acquirers or targets; the authors expect higher acquisition complexity when the acquisition is initiated by the acquirer rather than the target.

name: Acquisition unrelatedness
definition: An acquisition is unrelated when the acquirer is in an unrelated industry, such that information asymmetry that stems from industry differences entails challenges in the form of processing information from unfamiliar domains for the target board.

name: Target diversification
definition: The extent to which the target operates in multiple industries; as the number of industries in which the target operates increases, the amount and diversity of information the target board needs to gather, share, and analyze in connection with acquisition negotiations also increases.

name: Political embeddedness
definition: Political embeddedness refers to an organization's ongoing structural relations to the state and its actors; these relations are simultaneously instrumental and affective as trust develops and favors are exchanged.

name: Organizational political embeddedness
authors_terms: ["organizational political embeddedness", "organizational embeddedness", "formal affiliation with the government"]
definition: Organizational embeddedness exists when the ties between an organization and the state involve a formal government affiliation. Examples of such ties include government contracts and partnerships between the state and non-profits, and the state can even be directly involved in non-profits in emerging markets.

name: Personal political embeddedness
definition: Personal embeddedness is created by individuals taking positions in both organizational and political spheres; thus, this form of political embeddedness is fundamentally personal in nature. Charitable organizations in emerging markets can be politically connected on a personal level by having current or retired politicians serving on their boards or management teams.

name: Corporate donations received
authors_terms: ["corporate donations", "total donations", "donations from domestic firms", "donations from foreign firms"]
definition: Total donations is the sum of corporate donations received annually by a charity, which the authors disaggregate into donations from domestic firms and donations from foreign firms.

name: Corporate donor identity
authors_terms: ["identity of corporate donors", "identity of donors", "domestic donors", "foreign donors"]
definition: Any single stakeholder group consists of actors with different motivations and priorities; the authors therefore distinguish different types of corporate donors, who differ in their perceptions of benefits and risks from engaging in philanthropy.

name: Distinctiveness
definition: The distance of a product's attributes from the categorical prototype; products are positioned farther from one another when their attributes are more different. The categorical prototype represents the typical or expected features and functionalities of products in a category.

name: App performance
definition: The economic performance of an app in terms of the quantity downloaded or sold. The number of downloads is used as a measure that directly reflects the app's legitimacy with customers and that can be applied consistently across both paid and free apps.

name: Revenue model
authors_terms: ["revenue model", "paid and free revenue models", "paid versus free models"]
definition: A revenue model describes the monetization approach used to generate sales from products; it addresses how firms capture value and is an essential aspect of their overall business model.

name: Privacy statement
definition: An explicit statement or policy describing the firm's privacy practices; a privacy statement is a relatively short, accessible summary that usually also directs customers' attention to the more detailed privacy policy.

name: Freemium revenue approach
definition: A free product with a premium option (i.e., freemium) allows customers to access basic features of a product or service for free and then charges for upgrades to this basic version.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is captured with a market-based performance measure, Tobin's Q, which the authors consider a forward-looking measure since it incorporates investors' expectations about firm performance.

name: Speed of pro-market reforms
authors_terms: ["speed of pro-market reforms", "speed of reforms", "rate of market liberalization achieved over time"]
definition: The speed of reforms is a country's rate of market liberalization achieved over time. Speed of reforms captures not only the change in the scope of reforms between periods (distance travelled), but also how quickly the economy achieves the new scope of reforms (time travelled).

name: Family influence
definition: Family influence is measured based on family involvement in ownership and management since together they make the pursuit of the family vision possible; family ownership allows the family to influence the vision of the firm and to sustain that vision across generations, and family management ensures that family managers' utility function includes family interests.

name: Institutional distance
definition: The differences in institutional environments that firms face across national borders; that is, the similarities/differences between countries in their institutional contexts (Kostova, 1996). Institutional distance disadvantages foreign firms vis-a-vis indigenous firms and gives rise to the liability of foreignness.

name: Foreign subsidiary performance
definition: Following prior industry studies, the authors adopt ROA (return on assets) as their Performance measure, calculated as the net income of the focal subsidiary divided by its total assets in each year.

name: Local isomorphism
definition: One option for foreign firms is to imitate local, domestic competitors-a strategy referred to as local isomorphism (Zaheer, 1995). Institutional theorists explain the widespread imitation of practices (i.e., isomorphism) as the outcome of a process by which firms attempt to acquire legitimacy.

name: Host country experience
definition: The authors measure host country experience as the cumulative number of bank-years of operation in the U.S. at the parent bank level at time t, reflecting experience with any U.S. banking operations established by the parent bank in the United States.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The measure of subsidiary performance (which the BEA terms 'profit-type return') is based on reported net income, but it is gross of foreign income taxes, excludes capital gains and losses and income from equity investments, and reflects certain other adjustments needed to convert profits from a financial accounting basis to an economic accounting basis.

name: Divestment
definition: The dependent variable is a binary variable that takes a value of 1 when a parent firm divests from a foreign affiliate; 'divestments' that result from parent firm death (as a result of a merger with another U.S. company, for example) are excluded, so parent firms need to be in existence in the year after the divestment to have divested operations.

name: Country growth
definition: To capture the growth opportunities in a country, the authors examine a country's gross domestic product (GDP) per-capita growth rate.

name: Policy stability
definition: Countries that have more checks and balances (such as the United States, Germany, and Switzerland) tend to have higher levels of policy stability because of the multiple veto points that make it difficult to change the status quo policies. When political institutions lack checks and balances, policy makers are relatively unconstrained in their choice of policies by other political actors.

name: Exchange rate volatility
authors_terms: ["exchange rate volatility", "real exchange rate volatility", "RER volatility"]
definition: Exchange rate volatility can be an important source of uncertainty for MNCs; because high levels of exchange rate volatility make it difficult to know what future benefits might be possible in a country, divesting would mean forgoing any potential future benefits when the environment ceases to be unfavorable.

name: Sunk-cost investment
definition: Sunk costs are expenditures that have been made that cannot be recovered (e.g., product development, the construction of a specialized production facility, or advertising expenditures); R&D investments create intangible, highly firm-specific knowledge assets that are tightly coupled to a firm, while PPE/Assets captures more tangible investments in plant property and equipment in the subsidiary.

name: Product market relatedness
authors_terms: ["related and unrelated subsidiaries", "related foreign subsidiaries", "unrelated business line operation", "product market relatedness"]
definition: Unrelated businesses are defined as those business activities that are not in the same three-digit SIC code as the firm's core business, where a firm's core industry is the largest three-digit SIC business in terms of total firm sales; subsidiaries that are in product lines related to a parent firm's core product lines benefit from firm knowledge and resources, from synergies that come from sharing resources, and from cooperation across subunits.

name: Rate of technology licensing
definition: The extent to which a firm licenses its proprietary technology to others; the careful comparison between the profit dissipation effect and the revenue effect explains whether a firm is licensing or not, and, if it does, how much it is licensing.

name: Number of potential technology suppliers
authors_terms: ["potential licensors", "number of potential licensors", "number of potential technology suppliers"]
definition: The presence of other sources of technological competencies, that is, how many other firms are capable of supplying the process for producing a given product. A technology holder's refusal to license will not block entry when the prospective licensee can obtain the technology from other potential licensors.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["licensor's market share", "market share in the product market", "market share in jk"]
definition: The licensor's share in the product market; firms that sell larger quantities, i.e., firms with larger market shares, suffer most from competition because the same reduction in the margin is multiplied by a higher volume of sales.

name: Technology-specific product differentiation
definition: Product differentiation implies that the price elasticities of demand for different varieties are not infinite at equal prices; the important factor is that product differentiation is technology-specific rather than firm-specific, so that two firms using different technologies would produce differentiated varieties.

name: Number of potential licensees
definition: The larger the number of potential licensees, the stronger the bargaining power of the licensor and, hence, the larger the revenue effect from licensing. The proxy for this variable is likely to underestimate the number of potential licensees, as it does not account for entry.

name: Bankruptcy filing
authors_terms: ["incidence of bankruptcy", "bankruptcy", "bankrupt firms", "control group of nonbankrupt firms", "bankruptcy status"]
definition: The dependent variable of interest is the incidence of bankruptcy, a dichotomous variable. Bankrupt and control firms were matched by firm size, industry, and the year in which the bankrupt firm filed.

name: CEO turnover
definition: In any one year for a given company, CEO change is a dichotomous variable. Either the CEO was replaced in that year or not.

name: Director turnover
authors_terms: ["director turnover", "board turnover", "board of directors turnover", "director changes"]
definition: Board turnover, for any given year, is a continuous variable: the number of board members who left the board over the 1-year period.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of outside directors", "outside directors", "independent directors"]
definition: Board composition, for example, focuses on the independence of directors, traditionally operationalized as inside vs. outside. Outside directors, by virtue of their independence from management, are believed to be more likely to fulfill directors' roles and protect the interests of shareholders.

name: CEO duality
definition: Over the duality is binary. Either the CEO concurrently serves as board chairperson or not. The prescriptive consensus is a preference for an independent structure where the positions of CEO and board chairperson are separate.

name: Firm exit
definition: Exit in this study is defined as firm closure. Therefore, our analysis refers to the timing in which an economic unit ceases to do business.

name: Current firm size
definition: Firm size is measured here by employment (number of workers); the authors note that the only reliable measure of the size of firms available is the firms' number of employees.

name: Founding firm size
authors_terms: ["initial size", "larger initial size", "size at founding", "departing point"]
definition: The firm's size at the time of founding, denoted x0. The authors argue that because firms adjust gradually toward their desired size it is relevant to know their departing point as well as their current position.

name: Current human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "skilled labor", "college graduates", "stock of human capital"]
definition: To proxy the firms' human capital, the authors computed the proportion of college graduates among each firm's labor force. Human capital, rather than physical capital, is argued to provide the basis for sustained competitive advantage.

name: Founding human capital
authors_terms: ["skilled labor at founding", "initial human capital", "human capital at founding"]
definition: The stock of human capital employed by the firm at the time of founding. What makes human capital difficult to imitate or trade is that the knowledge it embodies is, for the most part, tacit, and initial human resource decisions may outlast the decisions themselves.

name: Current macroeconomic conditions
authors_terms: ["current macroeconomic conditions", "macroeconomic conditions", "GDP growth", "the overall state of the economy"]
definition: The overall state of the economy is one condition that has long been indicated by economists as an important force driving firms out of business; it is characterized by gross domestic product (GDP) growth at each moment.

name: Founding macroeconomic conditions
authors_terms: ["macroeconomic conditions at the time of entry", "macroeconomic conditions at founding", "GDP growth at founding"]
definition: The macroeconomic conditions prevailing at the time of entry, denoted x0. The authors note that firms being created during downturns may end up with inferior resources that will have a long-lasting effect upon their chances of survival.

name: Current industry concentration
definition: Economists see firms' survival as being related to the structure of the specific markets in which entry takes place; the authors use industry concentration as a proxy for the degree of competition in the market.

name: Founding industry concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration at founding", "initial concentration", "industry concentration at founding"]
definition: The degree of competition in the market at the time of the firm's founding (x0); the authors note that density at the time of founding could have imprinting effects upon organizations.

name: Current entry rate
definition: Another element of the competitive structure of a market emphasized by economists is the extent of entry in that market; high entry rates increase competition, which makes survival more difficult.

name: Founding entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rates at founding", "entry rate at founding", "initial entry rate"]
definition: The extent of entry in the firm's market at the time of founding (x0); the authors argue that tight niche packing and resource scarcity are likely to be particularly relevant when entry rates are high.

name: Racial diversity
definition: Cultural diversity is taken to mean the representation, in one social system, of people with different group affiliations of cultural significance. In this article, the term 'cultural diversity' refers to racial diversity.

name: Business strategy
authors_terms: ["business strategy", "growth strategy", "downsizing strategy", "no growth or negative growth"]
definition: A growth strategy involves internal growth such as selling current products in additional geographic markets or acquiring additional business divisions, which typically involves diversification. A downsizing (no or negative growth) strategy, by contrast, promotes efficiency and focuses a company on staying lean and mean.

name: Firm performance
definition: The study used three measures to derive a more comprehensive picture of the impact of cultural diversity on financial performance: employee productivity as an intermediate output measure, and bottom-line measures of return on equity and perceptual market performance.

name: Selective disclosure
definition: A symbolic strategy whereby firms seek to gain or maintain legitimacy by disproportionately revealing beneficial or relatively benign performance indicators to obscure their less impressive overall performance. The measure represents the extent to which companies risk creating a misleading impression of transparency and accountability by disclosing relatively benign environmental metrics rather than those more representative of their overall environmental harm.

name: Environmental damage
definition: The environmental harm created by a company's operations, measured as the cost of the environmental damage created by the company, i.e., costs borne by society through the degradation of the environment but not borne by the firm that uses the resource or emits the pollutant. The authors argue that de facto environmental damage is also a kind of visibility, exposing organizations to attention from regulators and the public.

name: Environmental NGO density
authors_terms: ["environmental NGOs per million population", "density of environmental NGOs", "environmental NGO presence"]
definition: The presence of environmental nongovernmental organizations in a company's headquarters country, which the authors use to proxy local social movement processes; the local presence of NGOs is a key organizational mechanism of citizenry mobilization and activism that magnifies individual voices to intensify pressure on companies.

name: Civil liberties and political rights
authors_terms: ["civil liberties and political rights", "civil liberties", "political rights"]
definition: Assessments of civil liberties (such as freedom of expression and assembly) and political rights (such as free elections) in a country. Strong civil liberties and political rights secure the ability of civil society actors to criticize corporate behavior, to take social action, and to lobby for political support when companies violate global norms.

name: Exposure to global norms
authors_terms: ["globalization index", "KOF Index of Globalization", "connected to global society", "exposure to global norms"]
definition: The extent to which a population or civil society is exposed to new ideas and norms from other countries, a process that can result from international trade, employment of foreigners, interactions with foreign embassies and consulates, telephone and Internet information flows, and international tourism. Such exposure brings about a norm cascade whereby a norm diffuses across international borders, becomes taken for granted, and influences the activities of individuals and organizations.

name: Foreign stock exchange listing
authors_terms: ["listed on a foreign stock exchange", "foreign-listed", "list or cross-list their shares on foreign stock exchanges"]
definition: Whether a company lists or cross-lists its shares on a stock exchange outside its headquarters country, which tends to expose it to reporting requirements regarding governance and financial matters that are more stringent than those in its home country and to norms and practices valuing more comprehensive transparency.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["corporate strategy", "diversification strategy", "Rumelt's corporate strategy typology", "strategy categories", "the inferred goals of specific diversification strategy categories"]
definition: Rumelt's (1974) corporate strategy typology was selected as the proxy measure of top management's risk propensities and goals. For the purpose of this study, Rumelt's nine sub-categories were reduced to the four originally developed by Wrigley (1970): single, dominant, related and unrelated; these categories represent fundamentally different strategic approaches to diversification.

name: Debt levels
definition: The debt/equity mix at the level of the individual firm, that is how the business is financed long-term, without the fluctuations of short-term financing.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The firm's earnings rate, measured for this study as average return on assets over the period of the study; the measure uses earnings before debt charges and the tax-reducing effects of debt charges, so that return is not confounded with the firm's leverage.

name: Firm size
definition: The scale of the firm, measured in this study as average total sales over the study period.

name: Firm sales growth rate
definition: The rate at which the firm's sales grow; financial empiricists have historically agreed upon the positive relationship between firm growth and debt, and growth is measured by average growth rates calculated using a regression fit to a uniform growth model.

name: Capital intensity
authors_terms: ["firm capital intensity (CAPI)", "capital intensity", "employment of fixed assets"]
definition: Capital intensity, or the employment of fixed assets, which the authors note is generally synonymous with the concept of operating leverage and implies increased risk of future income variation.

name: Earnings risk
authors_terms: ["firm earnings risk (RISK)", "earnings risk", "earnings variability", "coefficient of variation of profit"]
definition: Total firm risk is generally thought of as the total ex-ante expected variation in the earnings of the firm, and conventional finance practice uses historic variability as the best available indicator of overall firm risk; higher earnings variability implies higher bankruptcy risk, especially to creditors.

name: Antitrust intervention
authors_terms: ["antitrust intervention", "competitive pressure against a dominant platform through antitrust", "unblocking competition", "the Microsoft antitrust intervention"]
definition: The intent of such antitrust intervention is to unblock competition and level the playing field, thus expanding opportunities for innovation. In contrast to traditional antitrust, work in this stream - particularly on platforms - emphasizes technology-based industries and 'innovation competition'.

name: Platform-complementor market share
authors_terms: ["platform-complementor's share in a market", "platform-complementor's market share", "Microsoft's market share", "the platform-complementor had high market share"]
definition: The share of a complementor market held by the platform's own in-house complementor; the authors exploit variation in Microsoft's market share across complementor markets to separate treated from control markets. The higher its market share, the higher the perceived contestability of the market after the antitrust intervention.

name: Complementor innovation
definition: We measured complementor innovation by yearly counts of patents each firm had applied for (and later received). Each patent thus identifies new problem-solving efforts that are added into the industry to capture market share.

name: Complementor profit
definition: We measured complementor profit as return on sales annually for each firm. ROS is more appropriate than alternatives such as return on assets because software firms rely primarily on intangible assets (e.g., human capital) and because software firms tend to reinvest their profits to continuously grow the business.

name: Complementor market share
authors_terms: ["low-market-share complementors", "high-market-share complementors", "their own pre-intervention market share"]
definition: There are likely differences across complementors that also depend on their own pre-intervention market share. High-market-share complementors have lower incentives because they likely have less room to grow, whereas low-market-share complementors have more room to grow and thus higher incentives.

name: Social underperformance
authors_terms: ["social performance below aspiration", "social performance shortfall", "social underperformance", "negative social performance feedback"]
definition: We argue that when a firm's social performance falls short of its aspiration, this underperformance prompts managers to undertake a moral cleansing process aimed at restoring their moral self-image.

name: Social overperformance
authors_terms: ["social performance above aspiration", "social overperformance", "positive social performance feedback"]
definition: We argue that when a firm's social performance exceeds its aspiration, this overperformance provides managers with a psychological license to implement ethically questionable practices.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR refers to activities that benefit society beyond the firm's economic, technical, and legal obligations (McWilliams and Siegel 2001).

name: Corporate social irresponsibility
definition: CSI refers to actions that adversely affect the firm's stakeholders' legitimate claims (Strike et al. 2006), and implies a violation of moral or legal norms that harms stakeholders.

name: Perceived firm sustainability image
authors_terms: ["perceived firm sustainability image", "perceptions of the firm's sustainability image", "perceived firm image", "firm's sustainability image", "organizational image"]
definition: Organizational image refers to 'relatively current, and temporary perceptions of an organization, held by internal or external audiences, regarding an organization's fit with particular distinctiveness categories' (Elsbach 2003, p. 300); the paper measures managers' perceptions of the firm's sustainability image, a cognitive appraisal reflecting awareness of the organization's ethical and social standing.

name: Moral self-image
definition: Individuals assess their moral self-image ('How moral am I?'; Monin and Jordan 2009) and detect discrepancies between their actual and aspirational levels of morality; prior good deeds boost one's moral self-image, whereas prior bad deeds diminish it.

name: Adverse events
definition: In our context, the adverse events are pipeline accidents, which are clearly documented by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA). PHMSA defines a serious accident as any pipeline accident that leads to any human fatality or injury or the evacuation of 25 or more persons and significant gas loss.

name: Capability reputation
definition: Capability reputation describes 'collective evaluations about the quality and performance characteristics of a particular firm.' It reflects the degree to which a firm is known for competence and quality, representing an overall capability related to performance enhancement (what it can do).

name: Character reputation
definition: Character reputation refers to 'collective judgments regarding a firm's incentive structures and behavioral tendencies based on observations of its prior actions.' It reflects the degree to which a firm is known for integrity and trustworthiness.

name: Event controllability
definition: Controllability refers to whether the adverse event could have been prevented or controlled; once exchange partners know that an adverse event could have been prevented or controlled, they are likely to question the firm's high reputation. Accidents induced by obvious force majeure, such as natural forces or outside forces, were considered uncontrollable, whereas causes such as corrosion that could have been prevented with regular maintenance were considered controllable.

name: Relationship formation
definition: Relationship formation is the process by which potential exchange partners decide whether to enter into a new exchange relationship with the focal firm; the key uncertainty at relationship formation is whether the firm will be able to provide quality services or goods.

name: Relationship dissolution
definition: Relationship dissolution is the process by which current exchange partners decide whether to withdraw from an existing exchange relationship; current partners are more concerned about uncertainty regarding an organization's future behavior, including blame shifting and stigma anxiety.

name: Fear of blame shifting
definition: The extent to which current exchange partners fear that the focal firm will shift blame for an adverse event; higher values indicate greater fear of blame shifting.

name: Corporate political lobbying
definition: Firms that engage in lobbying activities provide information that is relevant to political actors (such as regulators and legislators) to influence policymaking. Firms lobby for favorable public policies by generating position papers and technical reports, conducting research and surveys, and/or testifying as expert witnesses.

name: Influence over public policies
authors_terms: ["Influence", "influence on public policies", "political influence", "influence over public policies", "effectiveness of firms' lobbying efforts", "effectiveness of lobbying"]
definition: To measure the overall effectiveness of firms' lobbying, the authors construct the dependent variable Influence based on the firm's assessment of its recent, general (nonspecific to any government branch) influence on the laws and regulations that have a substantial impact on the firm's business.

name: Political competition
definition: The most commonly investigated type of political opposition originates from partisan competition among key policymakers who have veto power, which the authors label political (partisan) competition. When policymakers who occupy key policymaking positions that are independent from each other have diverse interests and policy stances, they perform checks and balances on one another, such as using the veto power associated with their independent position to stall or at least delay policymaking.

name: Electoral accountability
definition: Political scientists call the degree to which politicians risk losing office if they contravene voters' preferences 'political accountability' or 'electoral accountability.' Whereas partisan competition constrains a politician's actions through the veto power of political opponents at time t, electoral accountability constrains a politician's actions through concerns about his or her reelection or continued appointment in future elections.

name: Subnational government tiers
authors_terms: ["subnational government tiers", "number of government tiers", "GOVTIERS", "multiple subnational tiers of government", "multiple administrative levels"]
definition: In many countries there are executive, legislative, and judicial branches of governments at both the national and subnational levels, and the number of government tiers varies considerably across countries. The presence of multiple subnational tiers of government characterizes the basic structural configuration of the political system.

name: Political decentralization
authors_terms: ["decentralization", "centralization or decentralization", "decentralization of political power", "Federalism", "federalist system"]
definition: A critical indicator of political power distribution is the set of institutional rules regarding the centralization or decentralization in a country. When they institute clear rules that decentralize authority, as occurs in a federalist system as opposed to a centralized system, governments in lower administrative tiers have greater formal authority over policies affecting local economic activities.

name: Geographic diversification
definition: The geographic scope of a firm's business activities, reflected in the extent of a firm's foreign direct investment (FDI). The authors describe it as the extent of a firm's internationalization across stages of international expansion.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable was corporate performance, for which the authors constructed both accounting-based and market-based financial performance measures.

name: Intangible assets
definition: Intangible assets, such as technological know-how, patents, management skills, brands, and goodwill, are information intensive, and transactions with such assets are subject to market failure. Their development requires substantial investments in capital, time, and human resources, and their value is not likely to depreciate significantly when they are applied in different markets.

name: Technology assets
authors_terms: ["technology assets", "technological assets", "technological know-how and patents", "R&D-based assets"]
definition: Technology assets such as technological know-how and patents, measured with R&D intensity.

name: Advertising assets
definition: Advertising assets such as brand names and goodwill, measured with advertising intensity.

name: Technological partner expertise
authors_terms: ["technological knowledge", "technological knowledge of its technology partners", "technology expertise of technological alliance partners", "technological strength of a venture's technological alliance partners"]
definition: Technological knowledge is the idea set 'regarding scientific and technical advances on an applied, high-technology product'. Technological alliances involve the development of joint routines and capabilities, the sharing of intellectual and scientific skills, and perhaps joint research and development.

name: Foreign marketing knowledge
authors_terms: ["foreign marketing knowledge", "marketing knowledge of its foreign marketing partners", "number of foreign marketing partners"]
definition: Foreign marketing knowledge, or organized and structured information about marketing in countries beyond a firm's home base, incorporates information about host countries' financial, cultural, social, and political conditions as well as general facts about country differences and how international business operations are conducted.

name: Foreign marketing knowledge from domestic partners
authors_terms: ["foreign marketing knowledge from internationally experienced domestic partners", "marketing knowledge of its internationally experienced domestic partners", "number of internationally experienced domestic marketing partners"]
definition: Domestic partners with international experience may provide similar short-term benefits for internationalizing operations, but in the long term the value of knowledge from these domestic partners could dissipate as the ventures themselves gain more beneficial international marketing knowledge from, and assume similar marketing features as, their domestic partners because they are both from the same home culture.

name: Network cohesion
definition: The cohesion of a venture's network is gauged by the sum of the 'constraint' of each of a venture's relations. A high value of that sum indicates high cohesion in the venture's network, meaning there are fewer structural holes available in the network.

name: Initiation of foreign sales
authors_terms: ["initiation of foreign sales", "initial foreign market sales", "new venture internationalization", "likelihood of venture initiation of foreign sales"]
definition: The dependent variable was calculated as the hazard (the instantaneous rate) of a venture beginning international sales, coded 1 if the venture realizes an initial foreign sale, 0 otherwise. Foreign sales were defined as sales revenue derived from exports or other foreign operations.

name: Time
definition: The influence of differing lengths of time on the associations between two forms of alliances and the initiation of foreign sales is a distinctive aspect of the research, so a lagged model structure was necessary. All independent variables were lagged by one year to test for the short-term impact of alliance networks and by five years to test for long-term effects.

name: Stakeholder attention to firm CSR
authors_terms: ["stakeholder attention", "external stakeholder attention", "stakeholder attention to firm disaster relief CSR activities"]
definition: Just as managers have limited attention to spread among stakeholders, stakeholders also have limited attention that they may allocate to various firm social activities. Consequently, stakeholders must choose which firm CSR activities to pay attention to and only these firms will receive the rewards associated with stakeholder attention to firm CSR.

name: Disaster relief CSR
authors_terms: ["disaster relief CSR", "disaster relief CSR activities", "corporate disaster relief", "disaster relief CSR initiatives"]
definition: We focus on one form of CSR: disaster relief CSR wherein firms assist the victims of a natural disaster.

name: Disaster relief CSR value
authors_terms: ["Disaster CSR value", "monetary value", "size of the donation"]
definition: The first independent variable, Disaster CSR value, indicates the magnitude (monetary value) of a firm's disaster relief philanthropy (scaled by firm assets).

name: NGO partnership
authors_terms: ["NGO partner indicator", "partner NGO", "partnering with an established NGO"]
definition: Firms often seek to enhance the perceived legitimacy of their CSR efforts by partnering with an established NGO. Firms that partner with NGOs in delivering disaster relief CSR initiatives should receive greater stakeholder attention toward those activities than firms who engage in initiatives without an NGO partner.

name: CSR urgency
definition: The urgency or promptness with which a firm responds to a disaster with relief-oriented CSR (or at least concrete plans for relief-oriented CSR) may enhance the amount of stakeholder attention that the firm's disaster relief CSR receives.

name: In-kind contributions
definition: Firms may enact their relief efforts in different ways-with one of the primary distinctions being whether the firm donates cash or offers some form of in-kind assistance. Relief activities involving in-kind donations are more likely to be perceived by stakeholders to involve active participation by the firm because in-kind donations involve the giving of concrete goods or services.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: 'Expected' benefits are more visible in market measures of firm performance such as stock price than in period-delineated accounting measures of firm performance such as return on assets. Our study utilizes a market measure of CFP rather than an accounting measure in order to include these expected and longer-term potential benefits of CSR.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "relatively poor firm performance", "poor performance", "market-to-book value", "low performance"]
definition: We operationalized firm performance as market-to-book value of equity, measured at the end of the year prior to the survey date. We adjusted performance for the average market-to-book value among all firms in the industry over the prior three-year period.

name: Advice seeking from functionally similar executives
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers with similar backgrounds", "advice seeking from executives of other firms who have a similar functional background", "similar functional background"]
definition: We then created six count variables to indicate the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who (1) had a similar functional background to the CEO. Functional background was divided into three categories: throughput functions (i.e., operations, engineering, or research and development), output functions (i.e., marketing or sales), and peripheral functions such as finance and law.

name: Advice seeking from functionally dissimilar executives
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers with dissimilar backgrounds", "advice seeking from executives of other firms who do not have a similar functional background", "managers with a different functional background"]
definition: Six count variables indicated the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who had a different functional background to the CEO. Functional background categories were throughput functions, output functions, and peripheral functions such as finance and law.

name: Advice seeking from friends
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers who are friends", "advice seeking from executives of other firms with whom the CEO shares personal friendship ties", "friends of the CEO"]
definition: Respondents were asked to consider their personal relationship with each manager listed as an advice contact and to indicate whether they considered each person to be an acquaintance or a friend. Six count variables indicated the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who were friends of the CEO.

name: Advice seeking from acquaintances
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers who are not friends", "advice seeking from executives of other firms with whom the CEO does not share personal friendship ties", "acquaintances"]
definition: Respondents considered their personal relationship with each manager listed as an advice contact and indicated whether they considered each person to be an acquaintance or a friend. Six count variables indicated the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who were not friends of the CEO.

name: Advice seeking from same-industry executives
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers in the same industry", "advice seeking from executives of other firms in the same industry", "employment in the same industry"]
definition: We coded employment in the same industry as 1 if the CEO and the CEO's advice contact worked as full-time executives in an industry with the same primary, two-digit Standard Industrial Classification Code (SIC) code. Six count variables indicated the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who were in the same industry as the CEO.

name: Advice seeking from different-industry executives
authors_terms: ["advice seeking from managers in a different industry", "advice seeking from executives of other firms in different industries", "managers in a different industry"]
definition: Six count variables indicated the number of times (in the past year) that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who were not in the same industry as the CEO. Membership in the same industry was coded using primary, two-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes.

name: Corporate strategic change
authors_terms: ["change in corporate strategy", "strategic change", "change in product market diversification", "change in geographic diversification", "change in diversification"]
definition: We assessed two dimensions of corporate strategy: product market diversification and geographic diversification. We measured (absolute) change in product market diversification and geographic diversification over the two-year period following the survey date (change in product market/geographic diversification).

name: Product variety
authors_terms: ["product variety", "multiple product offerings", "number of products", "number of workstations", "multiple products", "product line breadth"]
definition: The number of distinct workstation products a firm offers; assuming that firms have fixed resources, the number of products also measures the average resources allocated to any particular product offering. Multiple offerings let boundedly rational managers hedge their guesses about both consumer preferences and the products rivals will offer.

name: Organizational viability
definition: Firm performance measured through exit from the workstation market; presence in the market is logically prior to making a profit in that market, exit can be observed for all companies, and firm exit should indicate poor performance.

name: Product market crowding
authors_terms: ["product market crowding", "product density", "number of products on the market", "total industry product offerings", "number of rival offerings"]
definition: The sum of the number of workstations offered by all rival firms in a given year; product market crowding increases both when new firms enter the market and when existing firms expand their product lines.

name: Product line culling
authors_terms: ["product line culling", "culling", "product line adaptation", "internal selection", "selection", "managerial selection"]
definition: The removal of poor performers from the product line, which the authors call the evolutionary model of product management: the firm sets up its own internal variation, selection and retention mechanisms to evolve its product mix, gaining information about consumer preferences and efficiencies while losing the ability to monitor the region of product space from which products were removed.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: The instability of consumer preferences over time; the authors note that ideally one would like information on the stability of consumer preferences over time, and operationalize volatility as the lack of autocorrelation in sales of the same product.

name: Multimarket contact between partners
definition: MMC occurs when firms encounter each other in multiple markets simultaneously.

name: Reciprocal multimarket contacts
authors_terms: ["reciprocal multimarket contacts", "reciprocal multimarket contacts between partners"]
definition: Reciprocal multimarket contacts are one of the two types of multimarket contacts distinguished by Gimeno (1999): dominance by one firm in some shared markets is reciprocated by the other firm's dominance in other shared markets.

name: Nonreciprocal multimarket contacts
definition: Nonreciprocal multimarket contacts are the other type of multimarket contacts: dominance by one firm is repeated, rather than reciprocated, across shared markets.

name: Strategic alliance survival
definition: Alliance survival is an indicator that an alliance remains functional and that partners have enough compatible ground to continue their relationship.

name: Technological overlap
definition: The degree of similarity between the technological knowledge stocks of firms (Jaffe, 1986) - henceforth their technological overlap - is a widely recognized indicator of alliance partners' ability to imitate each other's resources.

name: R&D alliance
authors_terms: ["R&D alliances", "R&D activities in an alliance", "alliances involving R&D activities"]
definition: Alliances involving R&D activities (henceforth R&D alliances) are '… the most knowledge-intensive type of alliance'.

name: Constellation aggregate passenger traffic
definition: The size of the aggregate customer base brought by group members, which influences the extent of inter-firm externalities generated by a constellation. A large aggregate customer base can attract more customers in a context of network externalities.

name: Diversity of international hubs
authors_terms: ["diversity of international hubs", "diversity of hubs", "hub diversity", "DiversHub"]
definition: The constellation exhibits high diversity in international hubs when members are positioned in distant cities/hubs, which expands the possibilities for connections; similar or proximate hubs tend to be substitutes rather than complements.

name: Relative seat capacity
definition: An obvious source of heterogeneity within an airline constellation is the size of individual members in terms of their traffic capacity; a carrier's relative size within its constellation is measured as the ratio of its available seat capacity to the total capacity of its constellation.

name: Control of critical hubs
authors_terms: ["control of critical hubs", "dominance of critical hubs", "DomHub"]
definition: Hubs that are natural points of traffic aggregation will be critical to the establishment of an international route network serviced by constellation members; the design of members' route networks will tend to emphasize use of those hubs.

name: Bilateral ties to key constellation members
authors_terms: ["bilateral ties to key constellation members", "InsideTie", "bilateral connectedness"]
definition: The extent to which firms establish bilateral codesharing and marketing agreements with key constellation members, which allows a carrier to benefit directly from passenger traffic that comes from those other firms.

name: Operational performance
definition: The load factor is a measure of aircraft capacity utilization. More precisely, it is the ratio of carrier i's total traffic, measured in revenue passenger kilometers (RPK), to its overall seat capacity, measured in available seat kilometers (ASK), at year t (%).

name: Membership in an explicit constellation
definition: An explicit constellation is a broad multiple-firm alliance: a group of firms pursuing joint action in a formal way through agreements that tend to have a multilateral fashion, supported by organizational mechanisms such as joint decision-making committees and common investment in brand names and technology platforms.

name: Negative media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage", "negative press coverage", "negative press", "negative coverage"]
definition: Negative media coverage is the negatively valenced press coverage a firm receives; the authors argue that the media act as social arbiters and that their negative evaluative judgments can adversely affect the perceptions of firms and firm leaders and ultimately lead to stigmatization.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "extent of strategic change", "magnitude of strategic change"]
definition: The authors conceptualize strategy as an observed pattern in an array of actions and decisions, particularly decisions regarding how to deploy key resources across different functional areas; strategic change refers to changes in the way firms deploy resources across time, and is defined as the extent to which a firm's strategy changes over time.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "proportion of outside directors", "percentage of outside directors", "outside ratio"]
definition: Independent boards are composed of outside directors without family or business ties to the firm, who are thought to be in a particularly strong position to impartially evaluate top management and are less likely to be beholden to the CEO.

name: Firm performance
definition: The financial performance of the firm is described as perhaps the most important indicator of overall firm success, and the performance of the firm sends a powerful signal to internal decision makers about the effectiveness of current strategies and the need for change.

name: Connection to focal government
authors_terms: ["connections to a focal government", "Acquiring firm's connection to focal provincial government", "connection to the focal provincial government"]
definition: A firm's pre-established connection to the focal government, defined as the public actor with the decision-making authority in a policy event; such a connection provides access through which the firm can engage in influence and helps develop mutual trust.

name: Connection to rival government
authors_terms: ["connections to a rival government", "Acquiring firm's connection to rival provincial government", "connection to a rival provincial government"]
definition: A firm's connection to a rival government, defined as another public actor competing with the focal government; the exchange relationship between a firm and a rival government may lead the focal government to perceive a coalition between the firm and the rival government.

name: Direct connection to constraining government
authors_terms: ["direct connections to a constraining government", "Acquiring firm's direct connection to central government"]
