definition: A firm's direct connection to the constraining government, defined as a public actor with power over focal and rival governments; in China the central government is the constraining government, and a firm may approach it through a direct connection (A-C) to mobilize its power resources over the focal government.

name: Indirect connection to constraining government
authors_terms: ["indirect connections to a constraining government", "Acquiring firm's indirect connection to central government"]
definition: A firm's indirect access to the constraining government obtained through the rival government (A-R-C) and the informal political network linking central and provincial officials, which is formed through birthplace, school, and workplace ties.

name: Similarity between focal and rival governments
authors_terms: ["similarity between the focal and rival governments", "Provincial official similarity", "Provincial GDP similarity", "Same greater administrative area"]
definition: The similarity between focal and rival governments, which the authors posit increases the intensity of rivalry because similarity influences both awareness and motivation and thus drives competitive tension and behavior.

name: Acquisition likelihood
definition: The likelihood that an acquiring firm's acquisition proposal is approved and realized; the authors argue that acquisition is a more relevant performance indicator than other measures, like survival or profitability, in the consolidating steel industry, since a successful acquisition indicates a performance gain that would help ensure survival and long-term profitability.

name: Qualified lead independent director
authors_terms: ["qualified LID", "quad qualified LID", "quad-qualified LID", "qualified lead independent director"]
definition: A qualified LID can be defined as an individual who possesses a combination of: independence (ability to be independent and objective), expertise (ability to lead and comprehend the issues at hand), bandwidth (ability to devote requisite time and attention to the focal company), and motivation (desire to engage in monitoring behaviors). All four of these attributes are needed for an LID to be a qualified monitor.

name: Corporate misconduct
definition: A qualified LID can help firms avoid 'missteps and misdeeds such as corporate fraud, embezzlement, and dubious transactions'; misconduct is measured through media reports of misconduct-related events in which the focal firm is identified as the accused defendant.

name: Shareholder proposals
definition: In recent decades, several large shareholders have raised their concerns through shareholder proposals which have become the most widespread and formal form of shareholder activism.

name: Board meeting attendance
definition: Past research has used attendance at board meetings as one of the key metrics to assess the level of board monitoring and engagement; board meetings are generally considered effective when all directors are present and engaged in boardroom discussions.

name: Director independence
definition: Independence is the ability to be independent and objective; in the measure it assesses if the LID predates the CEO's appointment, because only unaffiliated directors who predate the CEO's appointment can be considered truly independent.

name: Director expertise
definition: Expertise is the ability to lead and comprehend the issues at hand; in the measure it evaluates the LID's board experience for effective facilitation and oversight.

name: Director bandwidth
definition: Bandwidth is the ability to devote requisite time and attention to the focal company; in the measure it considers the LID's availability without a full-time job.

name: Director motivation
definition: Motivation is the desire to engage in monitoring behaviors; in the measure it examines adequate incentives for the role's demands.

name: PAE intermediation
authors_terms: ["PAE intermediation", "PAE intermediation in a technology class", "PAE brokerage"]
definition: Patent assertion entities acquire patents from inventors and pursue ex post licensing agreements by asserting these patents against firms allegedly using the patented intellectual property; they are purely intermediaries of intellectual property rights because they secure intellectual property from others rather than invent their own. PAE intermediation is the level of this intermediation activity within a given class of technologies.

name: Focused inventor
authors_terms: ["focused inventors", "focused inventor", "inventors with limited capacity to commercialize their inventions"]
definition: The first segment of inventors comprises those with limited capacity to commercialize their inventions (hereafter referred to as focused inventors), such as independent inventors, small firms, universities, and research labs. Because these inventors often lack the assets needed for commercialization, they customarily rely on bilateral licensing agreements to monetize their inventions.

name: Focused inventor entry
authors_terms: ["focused inventor new entrants", "entry of focused inventors", "begin producing patented inventions"]
definition: As PAE intermediation increases, technology classes attract the entry and participation of greater numbers of focused inventors relative to all inventor entrants. The measure is the count of focused inventors who applied for patents (and were subsequently granted) in a class for the first time in their history in a year.

name: Patented invention rate
authors_terms: ["patented invention rate", "rate of patented inventions", "rates of invention"]
definition: PAEs will not only entice proportionately greater numbers of focused inventors to enter the technology classes that they intermediate, but also will incentivize inventors who participate in these classes to produce patented inventions at higher rates. The measure is the number of patents applied for (and subsequently granted) by an inventor in a patent class in a year.

name: Incremental invention
definition: Incremental inventions are those that make minor improvements to existing technologies; they typically combine prior art from a narrow slice of the technological universe and are redundant with that prior art and other inventions that also build on the same narrow slice. The intellectual property boundary of an incremental invention and the claims within its affiliated patent overlap those of other complementary incremental inventions.

name: Past success in creative endeavors
definition: The literature on the effect of performance on organizational behavior defines success as performance above an aspiration level, and the authors assume that individuals determine whether they are performing well or poorly by comparing themselves to similar others, here peers in similar firms.

name: Creative output
authors_terms: ["creative output", "generating creative ideas", "likelihood of generating creative ideas", "generating a new creative idea"]
definition: The authors use the frequency of patenting to indicate creative output, and patent characteristics to examine the degree to which creative output is divergent (or incremental).

name: Divergence from previous solutions
definition: The extent to which a patented idea diverges from an inventor's previous patents, assessed on two indicators: the number of subclasses new to the inventor in which a patent is classified and the number of new citations a patent makes.

name: Working alone
authors_terms: ["working alone", "proportion of sole-inventor patents", "collaborate with others"]
definition: The extent to which an inventor works alone, measured as the inventor's proportion of patents in which he/she is the sole inventor.

name: Organizational norms for exploration
authors_terms: ["organizational norms for exploration", "norm for exploration", "organization's proportion of patents entering new subclasses", "organization's proportion of patents making new citations"]
definition: An organization's emphasis on the importance of exploratory behavior, reflected in the kinds of patents that the organization generates in aggregate.

name: Impact of creative ideas
definition: The impact of a patented idea is evidenced by the number of citations that a patent receives after it is granted; the more a patent is cited, the more it is used as a foundation for subsequent creative efforts.

name: Risk from partner-rival co-location
authors_terms: ["risk from partner - rival co-location", "risk of indirect knowledge leakage to rivals", "risk from partner - rival colocation"]
definition: This construct reflects the degree of harm a focal firm might incur if knowledge leaks from partners to rivals that are co-located with the partners. This risk of harm is made up of a number of components: it increases when (1) more rivals are co-located with the partner, (2) the rivals have stronger market positions in the particular product markets, and (3) the markets are more important to the focal firm.

name: Equity-based alliance governance
authors_terms: ["Equity Alliance", "equity-based alliance", "inclusion of equity", "equity arrangements", "equity participation"]
definition: Equity participation in R&D alliances between focal firms and partners may take several forms, including minority investment of the focal firm in the partner or the formation of a joint venture. Equity ownership helps align partners' incentives, delineates partners' rights, and provides hierarchical controls.

name: Alliance vertical scope
definition: Some R&D alliances involve a broader vertical scope as they entail other downstream activities, such as manufacturing and marketing. These R&D alliances (i.e., R&D plus manufacturing and/or marketing) are regarded as broader in vertical scope than pure R&D alliances.

name: Task interdependence
definition: A critical aspect of alliance design that is directly related to partners' tasks and interactions is their level of interdependence. The types of interdependence are pooled, sequential, and reciprocal, in order of increasing complexity.

name: Supervisory span of control
authors_terms: ["supervisory span of control", "span of control", "supervisory span", "spans of control", "broad spans of control", "narrow spans of control"]
definition: Supervisory span is measured as the number of full-time equivalent front-line employees per supervisor, across the five core station functions. Lead agents, who help supervisors direct the operation but are not responsible for discipline, coaching or feedback, are counted as front-line employees rather than supervisors.

name: Relational coordination
definition: Relational coordination is the management of task interdependencies carried out in the context of relationships with other group members. It includes a communication component, reflecting the frequency and timeliness of communication among group members, and a relational component, reflecting the strength of problem solving, helping, mutual respect, shared goals, and shared knowledge among group members involved in the same work process.

name: Group performance
definition: A flight departure is successful from the customer's point of view if no unnecessary hassles are involved and if the on-time arrival of both the customer and his or her baggage are achieved, and successful from the airline's point of view if these quality outcomes are achieved without excessive staffing or excessive gate time for the airplane. Performance measures therefore include quality as well as efficiency measures.

name: Premerger ties to both merging agencies
authors_terms: ["clients with premerger ties to both agencies", "having ties to both agencies", "client tied to both agencies premerger", "common clients"]
definition: Clients with ties to both agencies before the merger, that is, clients with preexisting relations with both parties of the merger. For these clients the merger reduces choice and thus represents a structural change to the exchange relation that adversely alters the power balance.

name: Exchange reduction
authors_terms: ["reduce exchange", "reduction of exchange", "withdrawal from exchange", "relation dissolution", "account dissolution"]
definition: Withdrawal from the exchange relation by a client, observed as dissolution of an account with the advertising firm. When a client dissolves an account, it puts the existing account under review and invites a set of advertising agencies to pitch, and dissolution occurs when the account is awarded to an agency other than the incumbent.

name: Client resource endowments
definition: Clients with higher tangible and intangible resource endowments are sought after by advertising agencies and tend to have ties to more advertising agencies; the revenue an advertising agency receives from each client account is usually a percentage of the client's advertising expenditure.

name: Agency status
definition: Clients use agency status as a proxy for the value of the creative resources agencies can provide; a high-status agency is valuable because status is a proxy for quality when there is uncertainty regarding the value of the outputs it produces.

name: Status inequality between merging agencies
authors_terms: ["unequal status", "difference in awards between the two agencies"]
definition: Many mergers involve agencies that have unequal status, which will represent a categorization problem: the client now finds that the postmerger agency has both low- and high-status components, and it is no longer clear that the high-status part will maintain the full attention of its best employees or that the low-status part will maintain its low price.

name: Relationship duration
authors_terms: ["relationship duration", "duration of the relationship", "average account duration"]
definition: The length of time the client has been in the exchange relation with the agencies. As the depth of interaction increases over time, exchange partners adopt a relational orientation leading them to be less instrumental or calculative, and relations become more deeply invested and normatively controlled.

name: Board chair human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "chair human capital", "Chair Human Capital", "firm-specific human capital", "generic human capital"]
definition: Human capital is defined as 'innate and learned abilities, expertise, and knowledge' (Castanias and Helfat, 2001: 662). For board chairs, specific human capital might consist of firm-specific human capital developed over time through experience working at, and most likely leading, the firm, while more generic forms are developed through experience at other firms in the same or related industries.

name: Board chair social capital
authors_terms: ["social capital", "chair social capital", "Chair Social Capital", "director social capital", "external connections"]
definition: Social capital is defined as 'the sum of the actual and potential resources embedded within, available through, and derived from the network of relationships possessed by an individual or social unit' (Nahapiet and Ghoshal, 1998: 243).

name: Board view of the chair as a resource
authors_terms: ["resource-based view of the board chair", "resource-based justification", "boards' view of their chair as a resource", "resource status", "resource-based view"]
definition: The resource-based view of the board chair role is based on the belief that the chair is a unique individual with specific strengths that are not easily replicated, often referring to the chair's experience in the industry or in general business and to the chair's talent, skills, etc. The authors postulate that some boards will view their chair as a unique firm resource.

name: Common institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["common institutional ownership", "common ownership", "common ownership between rivals", "shared ownership", "cross-ownership"]
definition: Common institutional ownership occurs when an institutional investor owns a sizeable number of shares of two publicly traded firms. Conceptually, the authors are concerned with common institutional ownership as overlap in the percentage of institutional ownership by common owners at the dyadic level.

name: Competitive repertoire dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["competitive dissimilarity", "dissimilarity of the firms' competitive action repertoires", "dissimilarity", "repertoire dissimilarity"]
definition: Competitive dissimilarity is the extent to which two rival firms deploy a common set of action types; a focal firm i's competitive dissimilarity with regard to rival firm j is the extent to which firms i and j deploy a common set of action types. The measure would equal zero if firm i's competitive portfolio were exactly identical to j's portfolio.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: Competitive aggressiveness is the volume of competitive actions, measured as the sum of competitive actions for both firms in an intraindustry dyad.

name: Joint performance
definition: 'Joint performance' refers to the collective performance of both firms in the rivalry; it is calculated by summing the ROAs of both firms.

name: Performance disparity
definition: 'Performance disparity' refers to the absolute value of the difference between rivals' performance.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "PROF", "return on assets", "return on equity", "return on sales", "sales growth"]
definition: Profitability can be defined as the differences between costs and returns when a firm provides certain products or services. The ability to earn higher profits requires the firm not only to create value, but also to capture the value it creates.

name: Innovator position
definition: SMTEs have to innovate continuously and exploit first-mover advantages as entry barriers to protect their innovations. Innovator position is measured by R&D expenditures, which are the average of the reporting business's annual expenditures on R&D expenses divided by revenues.

name: Market awareness
definition: Market awareness can be defined as a market's familiarity with a particular firm, brand, or product. It is measured by advertising expenditures, the average of the reporting business's annual expenditures on advertising expenses divided by revenues.

name: Niche operation
definition: SMTEs have to restrict their operation in certain market niches and concentrate their limited resources in these niches; such focus strategy relaxes size constraints and enables SMTEs to develop and maintain their technological leadership. Product scope is determined by an entropy measure based on SIC classification.

name: Internationalization
definition: Internationalization is determined as the extent to which a firm is involved in foreign activities. A firm's internationalization is measured by multinationality, that is, the proportion of total revenues earned overseas.

name: Political connection loss
authors_terms: ["loss of political connections", "unexpected loss of political connections", "connection loss", "tie disruption", "dissolution of political connections", "severance of political connections"]
definition: Political connections are boundary-spanning links between politicians and top executives; their loss is the involuntary severance of these ties when anti-corruption campaigns unexpectedly remove the connected officials, which disrupts both mechanisms and could enhance or inhibit innovation.

name: Firm innovation
definition: Innovation yields Schumpeterian rents, essentially supernormal profits obtained through product or process novelty; the authors study firms' innovation activities, evidenced by their patent applications.

name: External search breadth
authors_terms: ["external search breadth", "BREADTH", "breadth of external search", "search breadth"]
definition: External search breadth, which is defined as the number of external sources or search channels that firms rely upon in their innovative activities.

name: External search depth
definition: External search depth is defined in terms of the extent to which firms draw deeply from the different external sources or search channels; it is defined as the extent to which firms draw intensively from different search channels or sources of innovative ideas.

name: Innovative performance
definition: We use three proxies aimed at reflecting various types of innovative performance by firms, measured as the fraction of the firm's turnover relating to products new to the world market, to products new to the firm, and to significantly improved products.

name: Novelty of innovation
authors_terms: ["novelty of innovation", "degree of novelty of the innovation", "radical innovation", "incremental innovation"]
definition: The U.K. innovation survey provides estimates of the degree of novelty of innovation achieved by the firm. Taxonomies of novelty of innovation span from radical and truly revolutionary, such as the microchip, to the incremental, such as changing packaging on existing products.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity is measured as firm R&D expenditure divided by firm sales. Since absorptive capacity and R&D spending are closely linked according to Cohen and Levinthal, firms with high levels of R&D intensity are expected to be better able to exploit a host of search channels.

name: Legal protection of patents
authors_terms: ["legal protection of patents", "strength of the law", "stronger legal protection of patents", "pro-patentee shift in patent law", "change in the interpretation of patent law"]
definition: Courts would hold conventional and strategic patents to be valid and infringed with independent probabilities, νc(L) and νs(L), respectively, which increase in the legal protection of patents, L.

name: Strategic patenting
authors_terms: ["strategic patenting", "strategic patents", "strategic patent applications", "continuing patent applications"]
definition: Patenting for strategic purposes, including to gain bargaining advantage in negotiating licenses to patents for complementary technologies (exchange) or to defend against competitors or block potential competitors (blocking). We define strategic patents as those that are based on continuing patent applications.

name: Conventional patenting
definition: The conventional purpose in applying for a patent is to protect against imitation, and so, appropriate the returns to R&D. Conventional patents are those which are not subject to any continuations (referred to as 'stand-alone' patent applications).

name: Technological complexity
definition: Complex technology products are protected by larger numbers of patents than discrete technology products.

name: Patent ownership fragmentation
authors_terms: ["fragmentation of ownership of complementary technologies", "fragmented ownership of complementary patents", "ownership fragmentation"]
definition: Holdup costs are higher when the ownership of patents to complementary technologies is fragmented.

name: Manufacturing asset investments
authors_terms: ["investments in manufacturing facilities", "investments in manufacturing assets", "manufacturing assets"]
definition: Holdup costs increase in the incumbent firm's investments in manufacturing facilities, as these would be sunk if the incumbent cannot secure licenses to complementary technologies.

name: Local technological competition
definition: The degree of local, technological competition, represented by the geographical concentration of forward citations made by other businesses to patents assigned to any focal business for each circuit and year.

name: Business size
definition: In the context of strategic patenting for exchange, it is reasonable that the stakes increase with the incumbent's size, A = sH; similarly, in strategic patenting for blocking, A = s[P1 - P2].

name: Competitive entry
definition: A business entry occurs when a business in the same circuit first patented in a technological class (USPTO subcategory as of 2008) as the subject business.

name: Prior direct ties
authors_terms: ["prior ties", "prior strategic alliances", "direct ties", "previous direct contacts"]
definition: The number of prior ties provides an indication of the amount of information partners have about each other. The more information they have, the less serious will be information asymmetry problems in partner valuation, and prior collaboration also alleviates managerial indigestibility problems caused by differences in corporate cultures.

name: Network distance
authors_terms: ["network distance", "proximity in the alliance network", "shortest geodesic path", "indirect ties"]
definition: Network distance refers to the shortest geodesic path between two actors; the shorter the geodesic path, the closer two firms are in the alliance network. Indirect ties provide a rough idea about capabilities and trustworthiness but not the fine-grained information obtained in direct interaction.

name: Industry relatedness of dyad partners
authors_terms: ["intraindustry tie", "intrasegment tie", "interindustry tie", "ties within the same industry or industry segment"]
definition: A firm is argued to have the propensity to acquire the other company if it has similar technological competencies, i.e., when it is a member of the same industry or industry segment, whereas alliances are considered best when the partner has complementary or completely new technologies to offer.

name: International ties
definition: Strategic alliances and acquisitions can take place within a particular country or across national borders; the authors operationalize this by whether the two dyad partners are located in the same economic block (Europe, America, Asia) or not.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["network centrality", "betweenness centrality", "central position in the network of strategic alliances"]
definition: Network centrality refers to the importance of a specific organization for the overall structure of a network. In an information network, a company that has a high degree of centrality has the potential to control the flows of information between those other companies.

name: Alliance history
authors_terms: ["alliance history", "number of past strategic alliances entered by each firm"]
definition: The firm characteristic of interest is expressed in the number of alliances a firm has entered into previously (alliance history), an indicator of the capacity to gain timely access to new technological know-how.

name: Hierarchical governance
authors_terms: ["acquisition", "merger", "strategic alliance", "mode of external technology sourcing", "hierarchical governance under common ownership"]
definition: The crucial difference between strategic alliances and acquisitions is that the latter create organizational hierarchies in the classical sense, and the former do not; the paper focuses on the dividing line between hierarchical governance under common ownership and all setups in which hierarchical coordination is diluted.

name: Acquisition role
authors_terms: ["who acquires whom", "the acquirer and less likely to be acquired", "acquirer", "acquired firm"]
definition: Given that the form of the external link is that of an acquisition, the paper asks whether it can be predicted who acquires whom, focusing on the position of the acquired and acquiring firms in the prior overall network of interfirm relationships.

name: Organizational quality context
authors_terms: ["organizational quality context", "quality context", "organizational contextual variables", "quality environment", "organizational quality contexts"]
definition: Organizational quality context is the business unit manager's quality environment. It consists of such things as external quality demands, past quality performance, corporate direction and support in the area of quality, resources available for quality improvement, and the competitive forces that have a bearing on quality.

name: Actual quality management
authors_terms: ["actual quality management", "current practice of quality management", "quality management practice"]
definition: Actual quality management is defined as the manager's perceptions of the current practice of quality management in the unit.

name: Ideal quality management
authors_terms: ["ideal quality management", "ideal quality management practice", "beliefs concerning ideal quality management"]
definition: Ideal quality management is defined as a business unit manager's beliefs concerning what quality management should be in the business unit.

name: Resource redeployment potential
authors_terms: ["potential for resource redeployment", "potential for redeployment", "resource redeployment", "potential to internally redeploy resources"]
definition: The potential for redeployment is represented by r, and refers to the proportion of total investment, F, in the business that the firm is able to redeploy upon exit to other businesses inside the firm. More generally, it is a firm's capacity to efficiently transfer physical, human, intellectual, and organizational resources within the firm.

name: Speed of exit
definition: The speed of exit is measured as the percentage of exits that occurred within a certain number of 'years' after entry, contingent on eventual exit. With greater potential for redeployment, managers will require higher performance to persist in the business and will set a threshold that encourages earlier exit if profit falls below expectations.

name: Entry threshold
authors_terms: ["entry threshold", "expected profit needed to justify entry", "threshold of expected profit", "profit threshold for entry"]
definition: Managers, anticipating the effect of sunk costs on exit, should require a higher threshold of expected profit to justify entering a business when sunk costs are high. A decrease in sunk costs reduces the minimum threshold of expected performance that is required to justify entry.

name: Business relatedness
definition: Firms whose existing businesses are more closely related to the new business are likely to have a higher potential for resource redeployment. Relatedness is assessed with a similarity index, following the approach of Jaffe (1986), and two products are categorized as related if they appear together in the product portfolios of multiple firms in the CorpTech directory.

name: Likelihood of exit
authors_terms: ["likelihood of exit", "fraction of entries reversed via exit", "probability of exit"]
definition: Exit is identified when a product code stops being listed in the firm's product portfolio for two consecutive years.

name: Customer concentration
definition: Customer concentration captures a firm's degree of dependence on its most powerful customers. It is based on the percentage of a firm's sales to its major customers, that is, customers that account for over 10% of the sales.

name: Search depth
definition: Search depth concerns the 'accumulation of search experience with the same knowledge elements'; the more frequently a firm repeatedly uses prior knowledge, the deeper is its search attempt.

name: Search breadth
definition: Search breadth is how widely a firm searches for new knowledge; in the patent context, 'the proportion of previously unused citations' effectively proxies for this construct.

name: Existing-oriented attention
definition: The extent to which top executives pay attention to the existing assessment of the external environment, accumulated internal resources and capabilities, and management practices.

name: Future-oriented attention
definition: The extent to which top executives pay attention to the future evaluation of the environment, resources and capabilities, and management practices.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance feedback", "performance relative to aspirations", "positive performance feedback", "performance exceeding aspirations", "social performance feedback", "historical performance feedback"]
definition: Various forms of feedback, such as actual performance relative to aspirations, have major effects on firm search behavior. Positive feedback, such as performance above aspirational levels, typically ensures that lessons from earlier experiences are reinforced and the extant way of doing business continues largely unchanged.

name: Product market competition
definition: The degree of similarity between a focal firm's claimed or subjectively categorized products and services and those of other firms in the production space within and across industries.

name: Prior interorganizational mobility
authors_terms: ["prior interorganizational mobility", "prior mobility", "interorganizational mobility", "cross-firm mobility", "prior moves across organizations"]
definition: How much candidates have moved across organizations during their careers. The authors measure it as each candidate's rate of mobility relative to others with the same level of experience.

name: Functional diversity
definition: The breadth of the functions in which a candidate has worked, built up as interorganizational moves take people into different functional roles. Cross-firm mobility increases functional diversity because interorganizational moves are more likely to involve changes in function than are moves within organizations.

name: Industry diversity
definition: The diversity of the industries in which a candidate has worked, which prior mobility may increase because most managers must change organizations to gain experience in different industries.

name: Tenure with the current employer
authors_terms: ["tenure with the current employer", "tenure with most recent employer", "current tenure"]
definition: The length of time candidates have been with their current employer, which signals whether they have recently demonstrated the capacity to adapt and may indicate firm-specific skills.

name: Probability of receiving a job offer
authors_terms: ["offer received", "probability of being chosen by the hiring firm", "probability of receiving an offer", "likelihood of receiving an offer"]
definition: Whether a candidate is given an offer by the hiring firm at the final stage of the selection process, when the hiring firm conducts final interviews and decides which candidates to hire.

name: Profitability change
definition: Decline is defined as the process of decreasing performance over a prolonged period of time; performance is measured in terms of profitability. Profitability is measured by operating income to avoid noncomparabilities that arise because of differences in depreciation, pension pay and tax laws.

name: Sales volume adjustment
definition: The change in sales volume in response to changes in profitability. Sales volume time series are corrected for in-house supplies.

name: Cost efficiency
authors_terms: ["efficiency", "average cost", "total cost in US dollars per ton"]
definition: Efficiency is measured by average cost (c); in the ethylene data, efficiency is measured in terms of total cost in US dollars per ton.

name: Market exit
definition: Whether an organization leaves the market (exit) or continues to operate (stay). Outcomes include immediate exit and flight from losses; chronic failure is a form of staying in the market despite negative profits.

name: Fashion house creativity
authors_terms: ["FH creativity", "fashion house creativity", "creativity of fashion collections"]
definition: The creativity of these producers can be defined as their ability to produce novel and useful offerings. Novelty ... can be defined as how different new products are both from those of competitors and from the past products of the focal organization. In turn, usefulness can be construed as the commercial potential of the products under consideration.

name: Initial conglomerate creativity
authors_terms: ["Initial FC creativity -i", "initial fashion conglomerate creativity", "initial conglomerate creativity"]
definition: We computed Initial FC creativity -i as the average number of JdT points that the other houses inside the same fashion conglomerate had in the year when the house became affiliated (the subscript - i indicates the exclusion of the focal fashion house).

name: Concurrent conglomerate creativity
definition: We computed FC creativity-i as the average number of JdT points that the other houses inside the same conglomerate had in a specific year. Unlike Initial FC creativity -i, FC creativity -i is updated annually to capture concurrent effects.

name: Sectoral conglomerate affiliation
definition: We coded Affiliated equal to 1 if a fashion house becomes affiliated with a fashion conglomerate during our sample period, and zero otherwise. Sectoral conglomerates are entities that specialize in specific sectors and are firms 'composed of several unrelated businesses'.

name: Relational capital
definition: Relational capital, which is comprised of the relationship-specific assets that underpin relational governance, develops between partners over time through repeated exchange. The authors state that relational capital comprises three main elements: shared trust, routines, and norms.

name: Sales integration
definition: The firm boundary decision the authors study is the ongoing choice of medical device firms to integrate (or not) their sales function, that is, to move from an external sales force to an internal one. Integration is coded as an event that occurs when the firm division moves from external to internal sales.

name: New-to-the-world innovation
definition: The authors define innovation as the introduction of new-to-the-world products by the focal firm; innovative products are those launched by the firm in the year such products are first approved by the FDA for their product category. They signify devices that require new, product-specific, tacit information about their use to be transferred via the manufacturer-sales force and sales force-customer interfaces.

name: Change in focal downstream market
authors_terms: ["specialty change", "a change in a firm's focal downstream market", "change in focal medical specialty"]
definition: A change in a firm's focal downstream market is defined as a change in its focal medical specialty (e.g., from Cardiovascular to General Surgery). The focal downstream market of each firm division in each year is the medical specialty in which it has the largest number of products.

name: Innovation within the focal downstream market
authors_terms: ["innovative products within the focal specialty", "innovation within the focal downstream market"]
definition: The authors segment innovative products as either within or outside the existing focal downstream market (specialty) of the firm; innovations within the focal market are those in the firm's existing medical specialty, whose required knowledge is likely accessible within the existing sales channel.

name: Innovation outside the focal downstream market
authors_terms: ["innovative products outside the focal specialty", "innovation outside the focal downstream market"]
definition: The authors segment innovative products as either within or outside the existing focal downstream market (specialty) of the firm; innovations outside the focal market are those requiring knowledge that is not accessible within the existing sales channel.

name: Extent of collaboration
definition: We measured the extent of collaboration during a scientist-year by considering the mean number of coauthors (N in the formal model) for all the publications of that year.

name: Publication quality
definition: We measure quality (Q in our formal model) by observing the average number of citations received by a scientist for all the papers she or he published in a given year.

name: Publication productivity
definition: We measure NPubs, the productivity of a scientist's work (E in our formal model), by keeping the input constant (a scientist-year) and observing the number of papers published in a given year.

name: Fractional publication productivity
definition: Beyond simply capturing NPubs, our approach builds on Lee and Bozeman (2005) and also examines the 'fractional count' of paper published. As the simplest functional form of fractional counting of productivity, we compute Frac_Pubs the sum of 'papers shares' directly attributed to the scientist.

name: Scientific credit attribution
definition: As detailed in our formal model, we consider scientists' motivation to collaborate as dependent on (N), the share of their research output that is attributed to them (rather than to their collaborators). For a given (N), we compute the number of yearly citations attributed to a scientist's work by summing the citations attributed to the author for every paper of the year.

name: Family ownership
authors_terms: ["extent of family ownership", "extent of current control", "extent of the family's ownership control", "control"]
definition: The family's control of the firm through ownership, which is critical to creating and preserving socioemotional wealth because such control is what allows the family to pursue its interests through the firm. The extent of firm control indicates the family's existing involvement and captures its ability to influence firm decisions to provide socioemotional wealth to the family.

name: Duration of family ownership
authors_terms: ["duration of family ownership", "duration of control", "duration of ownership", "length of time or duration of control"]
definition: The length of time or duration of family control of the firm; duration of control is important because, over time, socioemotional wealth can increase through the heirloom effect and as the family firm becomes the depository of univocal reciprocity.

name: Intentions for transgenerational control
authors_terms: ["intentions for transgenerational control", "intention for transgenerational control", "transgenerational control intentions", "intentions for transgenerational family control"]
definition: Intention for transgenerational family control, proposed as the most important feature distinguishing family and nonfamily firms. It is tied to the family's vision for how the firm and the family will interact in the future and its expectations about the types of value exchanges that will flow from these future long-term interactions.

name: Perceived total value of the firm
authors_terms: ["total perceived value of the firm", "perceptions of the total value of the firm's equity", "acceptable sales price", "minimum acceptable sales price"]
definition: The controlling family's perceived total value of the firm, defined as the price at which the family would be willing to sell the entire business to nonfamily members; it is equal to the financial value based on cash flow and private benefits plus the additional value for which the family is willing to give up its socioemotional wealth endowment.

name: Corporate-level distinctive competence
authors_terms: ["corporate distinctive competence", "corporate level distinctive competencies", "corporate-wide distinctive competencies"]
definition: A distinctive competence represents those activities in which a firm, or one of its units, does better relative to its competition. Corporate-wide distinctive competencies, such as corporate R&D, outstanding executives and, as appropriate, centralized marketing, can result in relatedness across most or all of a firm's separate business units.

name: Production and operations competence
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence through the development of specific activities associated with the function; the production/operations activities include increased automation of production processes, improved plant layout, workflow and work environment and improved industrial engineering capabilities.

name: Marketing competence
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence; a competence in marketing, for example, can be formed through an emphasis on pricing strategies, advertising and promotion campaigns and market research strategies.

name: Finance competence
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence, formed through activities such as improving bond ratings and common stock market performance, developing a sound capital structure and effective capital expenditure evaluation procedures.

name: Engineering and research and development competence
authors_terms: ["engineering, research and development", "engineering, research and development activities"]
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence, formed through activities such as value analysis for improving present products, improvement in research and new product development capabilities and improved process engineering.

name: General administration competence
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence, formed through activities such as attracting and retaining competent top managers, developing an effective company-wide strategic planning system and achieving better overall control of general corporate performance.

name: Personnel competence
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence, formed through activities such as effective relations with trade unions, effective and efficient personnel policies and stimulating and rewarding creativity in employees.

name: Public and governmental relations competence
authors_terms: ["public and governmental relations", "public and governmental relations activities"]
definition: One of the functional areas in which a firm can develop a distinctive competence, formed through activities such as the ability to influence national policy in the industry, maintaining effective relationships with relevant regulatory bodies and improving the overall corporate image.

name: Firm performance
definition: The market price of a firm's stock reflects the organization's long-run performance potential on behalf of stockholders. In the light of the evidence, market returns were used to measure performance, defined as MR = (GMRi - RFRk)/B where B = beta measure of systematic risk, GMRi = geometric mean annual stock return for firm i and RFRk = geometric mean annual riskless rate.

name: Grand strategy type
definition: Grand strategy denotes an overall, primary and predominant strategy for achieving a firm's major plan in terms of overall sales and earnings goals. The focus is on the entire firm's goals rather than those of a single division or unit.

name: Principal industry type
definition: Executives noted their firm's principal industry, defined as the one in which the largest percentage of sales is earned. Industry type was measured on a nominal scale using four normative classifications: consumer durable, consumer non-durable, capital and producer goods.

name: Proportion of repeated partners
authors_terms: ["Percent Repeated Partners", "proportion of repeated partners", "percent of repeat partners", "percentage of repeat partners"]
definition: The configuration of the prime contractor's partnership system, captured as the proportion of repeated partners a prime contractor selects to complete the current project.

name: Depth of repeated partner relationships
authors_terms: ["Deep Partner Relationships", "Deep Repeated Relationships", "deep repeated partnerships", "depth of these relationships"]
definition: The depth of the specific, dyadic relationships a prime contractor has with its repeated partners, reflecting how often those partners have been used over the prime contractor's recent projects.

name: Revenue
definition: Revenue is a 'top-line,' market-based measure, based on customer satisfaction, and generally forward looking; one could say it represents the entire 'size of the pie.'

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability is a 'bottom-line,' accounting-based measure, founded on cost reductions and efficiency in implementation; among multiple partners, it can be thought of as how the pie is divided.

name: Position bias
definition: The extent to which organizational members direct their attention toward the immediate goals and priorities attached to their position. The authors state that when employees tend to identify with their role in the formal structure or position, they exhibit position bias.

name: Participation in strategic planning
authors_terms: ["participation", "participative planning", "employee participation in the strategic planning process", "participatory strategic planning"]
definition: Employees taking part in the strategic planning process, in which top management usually forms a number of temporary groups comprising employees from different units and hierarchical levels to analyze the performance of past strategies and the environment and to propose goals, strategies, plans, and budgets. The strategic planning process needs to include employee participation in order to become an integrative mechanism.

name: Communication of organizational priorities
authors_terms: ["communication of priorities", "goal communication", "communicating the organizational priorities", "communicating the resulting goals and priorities"]
definition: Top managers' effort to communicate and articulate to the entire organization the priorities that emerge from the planning process. The focus is on the one-way communication of the results of the strategic planning process once it has been brought to its conclusion.

name: Alliance portfolio competition
authors_terms: ["competition among alliance partners", "within-portfolio competition", "Competition (exogenous to F)", "technological competition"]
definition: Upstream technological competition among a focal firm's alliance partners, identified from the technology domains in which the partners are active; the competition score for each unique partner pair is the cosine similarity between the three-year patent technology subclass vectors of each firm in the pair.

name: Inventor network disconnectedness
definition: The extent to which inventors within a focal firm are unable to reach one another through the intrafirm inventor collaboration network. Knowledge safeguards restrict both the formation of new coinvention ties and the renewal of existing ones, so that the overall collaboration network of the firm demonstrates increased disconnectedness.

name: Technological bargaining power
definition: A firm's technological bargaining power over a focal partner stems from two key sources: its leadership relative to the partner across technological domains, and the presence of alternative partners within its portfolio who offer access to similar technologies as the focal partner.

name: Inventive output quality
authors_terms: ["quality of inventive output", "Quality of inventive output", "innovation quality"]
definition: The quality of the focal firm's inventive output, measured as the cumulative number of forward citations received by a firm's patents within 10 years of their application.

name: Generative appropriability
definition: The firm's capacity to capture a greater share of the future returns to its R&D activities by generating cumulative innovations that build on its existing stock of inventions, defined as the extent to which a focal firm builds upon its own prior inventions.

name: Action sequence simplicity
definition: The diversity and structure of the elements that form the stimulus affect the extent to which it is perceived as either simple (and clear) or complex (and confusing). Simple stimuli contain readily identifiable core patterns or tendencies.

name: Action sequence predictability
definition: The predictability or unpredictability of a stimulus depends on the extent to which the elements of a whole sequence exhibit across-time structural similarity.

name: Action sequence grouping
definition: Drawing from these ideas, we refer to the ordinal proximity among individual competitive actions in a sequence of actions as grouping.

name: Action sequence motif
definition: We refer to the underlying structural orderliness within a sequence of actions as motif.

name: Firm-specific ambiguity
definition: Ambiguity presents market participants with problems of interpretation and understanding, and not only of prediction. A high level of variation in analyst forecasts indicates a high level of ambiguity associated with a given firm, as even an expert audience exhibits multiplicity and divergence of interpretations about it; in contrast, low variance is indicative of low levels of firm-specific ambiguity.

name: Market value
authors_terms: ["investor valuations", "investor evaluations", "market value", "changes in firm market value"]
definition: The market value of the firm on the last day of the quarter captures all available information about the firm for the time period. It is the most forward-looking measure of the firm's value, as it captures investors' expectations about its future value-creating potential based on all actions undertaken in the time period.

name: Product price
definition: Our key independent variable was price, set at 5 Kw, 3 Kw, and 0 Kw (free). These three price points compare to a moderate discount, a deep discount, and a free pricing strategy, respectively.

name: Product usage
definition: The amount of the product a household actually used, measured from empty packets saved plus packets respondents reported using and discarding; usage and subsequent purchases are almost perfectly correlated.

name: Repeat usage
definition: None of the hypotheses yet addresses the issue of continued use after consumers obtain the product. Repeat consumers, who expend effort to obtain and use the product over time, form the foundation of a sustainable market-based or CSR engagement, particularly for nondurable goods.

name: Performance change relative to past performance
authors_terms: ["performance change", "performance development", "change in performance", "performance changes", "performance shortfalls", "current performance relative to past performance"]
definition: We measured the performance of the teams in each production trial by counting the number of sailboats made during the trial. This enabled us to study development in performance as the increase or decrease in total boats produced from one trial to the next.

name: Adoption of a new routine
authors_terms: ["adoption of new routine", "adoption of a new routine", "adoption of an innovative routine", "routine change", "decision to explore", "explore-exploit decisions"]
definition: Our primary dependent measure was whether the teams adopted the innovative production routine. The primary dependent measure was whether the team adopted the new routine in Trials 4 or 5.

name: Team emotional valence
definition: Our conception of emotion is based on Russell's circumplex model of affect (Russell, 1980) that distinguishes between pleasant and unpleasant (high/low valence) emotions, and active and passive (high/low arousal) emotions. Our distinction between positive and negative emotions relates to whether teams were induced to feel either high valence/high arousal (positive) or low valence/low arousal (negative) emotions.

name: Biotechnology firm size
definition: Larger size indicates greater access to financial and human capital as well as returns to scale in a firm's research spending due to the potential for leveraging common resource inputs, such as knowledge repositories and equipment, across multiple research programs.

name: Pharmaceutical firm size
definition: Larger size indicates greater access to financial and human capital as well as returns to scale in a firm's research spending due to the potential for leveraging common resource inputs, such as knowledge repositories and equipment, across multiple research programs.

name: Biotechnology firm research capability
authors_terms: ["biotech research capability", "upstream firm's research capabilities", "research capability"]
definition: Research capability refers to the extent of a firm's expertise in the scientific base of biopharmaceutical context.

name: Pharmaceutical firm research capability
authors_terms: ["pharma research capability", "downstream firms' research capabilities", "research capability"]
definition: Research capability refers to the extent of a firm's expertise in the scientific base of biopharmaceutical context.

name: Pharmaceutical firm drug development capability
authors_terms: ["pharma drug development capability", "downstream firms' drug development capabilities", "drug development capability"]
definition: Drug development capability refers to a firm's resources and capabilities in taking an investigational drug or a pharmaceutical compound through various stages of clinical trials, FDA approval, and product launch.

name: Joint value creation
definition: The model incorporates bilateral preferences as complementarities in the joint production (i.e., value creation) function. The identification of the joint production function is the focus of empirical estimation.

name: Patent war intensity
definition: For the purposes of our study, patent wars refer to battles among multiple firms to litigate regarding patent rights, or to secure patents for litigation, whether offensively or defensively, and other closely related events (e.g., patent portfolio acquisition). The authors use LexisNexis to construct a measure of patent war intensity in the smartphone industry based on media articles.

name: Share of business in a country
authors_terms: ["CountryShare", "the share of a firm's business in weak-IP markets", "the relative importance (share) of a focal firm's business in weak-IP markets"]
definition: Our dependent variable, CountryShare ijt, indicates the percentage of vendor i's total sales during quarter t that is attributable to country j. Compared with mere sales measures, this measure has the advantages of reflecting the strategic importance of a country to a vendor in a given period and is independent of the vendor's overall sales growth.

name: Country IP protection strength
authors_terms: ["IP_index", "strength of the IP system", "strong-IP systems", "weak-IP systems", "intellectual property (IP) protection"]
definition: This variable, which measures the strength of the IP system in a given country, is based on the Intellectual Property Rights Index (IPRI), which has been published annually since 2008 by the Property Rights Alliance. An increase in the IP_index jt reflects increased IP protection.

name: Patent stock
definition: This is a vendor-specific measure of patent counts. We count the number of patents for each vendor at the end of 2008 ... the number of patents granted before our sample period reflects the strength of a vendor's patent dispute-related bargaining position free of any right-censoring concerns.

name: Home country IP protection
authors_terms: ["WeakOrigin", "firms whose home countries have weak-IP systems", "firms from countries with weak-IP systems", "weak-IP origins"]
definition: In the context of patent enforcement, firms from countries with weak-IP systems may develop and carry over beliefs and strategic orientations toward patents that are poorly aligned with strong patent environments. The authors measure a vendor's country of origin as its headquarters' country.

name: Retrenchment
authors_terms: ["retrenchment", "retrenchment response", "degree of retrenchment", "cost and asset reductions"]
definition: A term that denotes a strong emphasis by the firm on cost and asset reductions as means to mitigate the conditions responsible for financial downturn; it is treated as an integral stage of the turnaround process.

name: Cost retrenchment
definition: One of the two target areas of the retrenchment response, defined as the net reduction in total costs between time-2 and time-3.

name: Asset retrenchment
definition: One of the two target areas of the retrenchment response, defined as the net reduction in long-term and short-term assets between time-2 and time-3.

name: Retrenchment focus
definition: The relative extent to which the retrenchment is pursued through asset versus cost reduction.

name: Turnaround performance
definition: The success of a firm in a turnaround situation in returning to predownturn performance; measured continuously as the net change in ROI between time-2 and time-4 and categorically as turnaround versus nonturnaround.

name: Turnaround situation severity
definition: An absolute measure of the severity of the turnaround situation in terms of firm financial health, i.e. the criticality of the downturn in terms of the threat of insolvency it posed to the firm.

name: Cause of the performance decline
authors_terms: ["cause of the turnaround situation", "cause of the decline", "causality"]
definition: The primary contextual factor of the turnaround situation concerning the sources of the performance problems, classified according to whether the sources originate external to the organization and beyond its control or internally.

name: External causality
definition: The degree to which a firm's performance problems are attributed to sources that originate external to the organization and beyond its control, such as economic problems, competitive change, technological change and social change.

name: Internal causality
definition: The degree to which a firm's performance problems are attributed to sources that originate internally, such as lack of operating controls, overexpansion, excessive leverage and top management factors.

name: Recovery response
definition: The second stage of the turnaround process, in which systematic investments are made to stimulate financial improvement; the intensity of the recovery response relates to the degree of strategy change present in the overall response.

name: Efficiency turnaround
definition: The recovery stage resembles an operating turnaround when new investments are primarily directed at achieving enhanced operational efficiency across a subset of previously served product-market combinations.

name: Entrepreneurial turnaround
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial turnaround", "strategic turnaround", "entrepreneurial recovery response", "selective product/market refocusing"]
definition: The recovery stage resembles a strategic turnaround when the investments are primarily directed at new products or serving new markets.

name: Order of entry
definition: A fund's position in the sequence in which funds entered a product category: an MMMF is defined as a first-mover if it was the first MMMF to enter one of the 33 product categories, and as an early-mover if it was either the second, third, fourth, or fifth MMMF to enter that product category.

name: Entry delay
authors_terms: ["entry delay", "delayed entry", "number of months of delay"]
definition: The length of time a follower waits before entering a product category after the first-mover's entry; the longer that a follower waits, the more time the first-mover has as a 'head start' to solidify its competitive advantage.

name: Market share
definition: The share of a product category commanded by an individual MMMF, defined with respect to its product category (i.e., ratio of fund TNA to product category aggregate TNA), rather than with respect to the entire MMMF industry.

name: Price
definition: The price the company managing the fund extracts for its service, known as the 'expense ratio,' which is expressed, like an interest rate, as a percentage of the invested assets per annum.

name: Number of competitors
authors_terms: ["number of competitors", "number of MMMFs in the product category", "number of funds in the product category"]
definition: The total number of MMMFs competing in a fund's product category, which is expected to influence fund families' pricing decisions and, in interaction with entry order, the erosion of entry-order advantages.

name: Social event sponsorship
authors_terms: ["Social events", "social event sponsorship", "corporate sponsorship of events that support social values", "sponsored social events"]
definition: We use 'social events' hereafter to refer to events for which the supported values pertain to social issues. Event sponsorship acts as value-bridging mechanisms, connecting the firm's strategy and its products to specific social issues.

name: Product entry price
definition: Entry price, is the price in dollars per ounce, at the time of a product's introduction. Price per ounce makes comparisons across products of different sizes (100 vs. 200 ml) meaningful.

name: Product longevity
definition: Products with symbolic meaning should invoke more demand at any time t and thus be culled later than equivalent products without any symbolic meaning. Each product enters the dataset when it appears on the webpage and exits when it disappears from the site.

name: Confluence of weak and inefficient formal institutions
authors_terms: ["confluence of weak and inefficient institutions", "strength-weakness composite institutional variable", "institutions", "institutional multiplicity"]
definition: Institutional multiplicity as a confluence of institutions is defined as dynamic interplay, mutual reinforcement, and cointegration of diverse rules and norms in which the effect of change in one rule and norm or a set of rules and norms is contingent upon other rules and norms in use. We used the strength-weakness composite institutional variable to capture the confluence of weak and inefficient political, regulatory, and economic institutions at the national level.

name: Network structural holes
definition: Structural holes are the absence of a link between two contacts who are both linked to an actor. Networks rich in structural holes are loose-knit and diverse networks that serve as bridging ties to distant clients.

name: Revenue growth
authors_terms: ["revenue growth", "revenue growth of new ventures", "venture growth"]
definition: Revenue growth is the difference between sales in two consecutive years divided by sales one year earlier. The variable revenue growth is the sum of revenue growth percentages divided by the number of revenue years.

name: Complementarity
definition: With reciprocal interdependence, teams may create complementarities that increase team output above the sum of its individual inputs; this incremental output is the returns to complementarity.

name: Player's share of firm surplus
authors_terms: ["player's share of firm surplus", "labor's share of firm surplus", "share of firm surplus", "share of surplus"]
definition: A player's share of firm surplus is the ratio of his wage to the firm surplus, i.e., the sum of team wages and operating profit.

name: Star status
definition: Stars are individuals who contribute disproportionately to a team's incremental surplus, making the team's interdependence asymmetric.

name: Team interaction
definition: Greater interaction among team members encourages the development of shared knowledge and communication, which in turn increases complementarity.

name: Player dominance
authors_terms: ["player dominance", "dominance of any single team member", "dominant player", "individual dominance"]
definition: An individual's disproportionate influence within a team has implications for complementarity.

name: Team orientation
definition: A team orientation involves developing shared cognition with fellow team members. It includes having the requisite task-specific knowledge (i.e., knowing who knows what) and team-member-specific knowledge (i.e., knowing and anticipating how a team member will behave in a range of circumstances).

name: Firm surplus
definition: Firm surplus is the sum of team wages and operating profit.

name: Gender
definition: Gender is the independent variable of central importance (1 = female); the analysis concerns gender gaps between men's and women's engagement in entrepreneurial activity.

name: Entrepreneurial activity
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial activity", "business start-up", "business ownership", "nascent entrepreneur", "established business owner"]
definition: I identified a respondent as being engaged in entrepreneurial activity if she or he reported being actively ''alone or with others, currently trying to start a new business'' (i.e., a ''nascent entrepreneur'') or ''alone or with others, currently the owner of a business'' that she or he helped manage (i.e., an established business owner).

name: Paid leave for mothers
authors_terms: ["paid leave", "government-paid leave for mothers", "parental leave", "maternity leave", "FTE paid leave"]
definition: Maternity and parental leave policies that provide mothers with job protection and income facilitate women's employment. Paid-leave provision was measured by the weeks of full-time equivalent (FTE) paid leave that the state makes available to mothers.

name: Public childcare provision
authors_terms: ["subsidized childcare", "government investment in childcare", "state childcare spending", "public provision of childcare"]
definition: The public provision of childcare also facilitates women's employment because it helps them meet the time demands of employment while minimizing the financial costs of purchasing childcare through the market.

name: Part-time employment
authors_terms: ["part-time work", "women's part-time employment", "availability of part-time work"]
definition: Some countries also explicitly encourage part-time employment as a strategy for women to combine employment with caregiving and household responsibilities.

name: Supportive work-family institutions
authors_terms: ["supportive work-family institutions", "institutions that mitigate work-family conflict", "institutions designed to reconcile work-family demands", "work-family policies"]
definition: Institutional arrangements such as paid leave, subsidized childcare, and part-time employment opportunities mitigate work-family conflict by providing workers with the financial and temporal resources needed to balance employment with family. Although countries differ in the extent to which they combine approaches or rely on any one approach, the three policies are similar to one another in that they mitigate work-family conflict.

name: Necessity-driven entrepreneurial motivation
authors_terms: ["motivated by limited employment options", "no better choices for work", "Plan B employment strategy", "fallback employment strategy", "necessity-driven"]
definition: Women entrepreneurs are more likely to opt for business ownership as a fallback employment strategy-that is, to be ''necessity-driven.'' The measure indicates whether an entrepreneur reports that she or he became an entrepreneur because she or he lacked a more desirable employment option.

name: Growth orientation
authors_terms: ["growth-oriented entrepreneurship", "growth orientation", "economic growth-oriented forms of entrepreneurship"]
definition: Because previous research suggests that multiple, qualitatively different criteria can be used to determine the degree to which a business is oriented toward economic growth, I relied on four separate indicators to gain leverage on the overall concept: current business size, growth aspirations, innovativeness, and the use of new technology.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: The dependent variable, IPO underpricing, is computed as the percentage of the difference between the offer price and the first-day closing price. The lower the difference, the more capital the firm is able to raise through the IPO, and reduced underpricing is viewed positively as a performance indicator and a metric of the IPO firm's success.

name: Director accumulated public board experience
authors_terms: ["directors' cumulative public company board experience", "accumulated (past) public company board experience of the directors"]
definition: Directors' cumulative public company board experience is measured as the average number of public company boards the directors served on in the past as reported in the prospectus. Directors include nonexecutive and executive directors and exclude the CEO.

name: CEO accumulated public board experience
authors_terms: ["CEO's cumulative public board experience", "accumulated (past) experience of the CEO in serving on public company boards"]
definition: CEO's cumulative public board experience is the number of public company boards the CEO served on in the past.

name: Director current public board appointments
authors_terms: ["directors' current public board experience", "board's current memberships on public company boards"]
definition: Directors' current public board experience is the average number of public company boards the directors currently serve on at the time of the IPO.

name: CEO current public board appointments
authors_terms: ["CEO's current public board experience", "CEO's current memberships on public company boards"]
definition: CEO's current public board experience is the number of public company boards the CEO serves on at the time of the IPO.

name: Director scientific educational background
authors_terms: ["directors' scientific educational background", "board's scientific educational background", "science education"]
definition: Directors' scientific educational background is measured as the proportion of directors (excluding the CEO) who have a bachelor's or above college degree in science. Scientific education provides a strong foundation to individuals' technology-based absorptive capacity.

name: CEO scientific educational background
definition: The CEO's scientific educational background is a dummy variable that takes the value of one if the CEO has a bachelor's or above college degree in science.

name: Director industry-specific experience
authors_terms: ["directors' years of biotech experience", "board's industry-specific experience", "board's industry experience"]
definition: Directors' years of biotech experience is measured as the average years of biotech experience of board members (excluding CEO). Past professional experiences within an industry context constitute strong indicators of industry-specific human capital.

name: CEO industry-specific experience
authors_terms: ["CEO's years of biotech experience", "CEO's industry-specific experience", "CEO's industry experience"]
definition: CEO's years of biotech experience is measured as the number of years of experience working in the biotech industry. Past professional experiences within an industry context constitute strong indicators of industry-specific human capital.

name: Patent pool formation
authors_terms: ["patent pool formation", "pool formation", "formation of a patent pool"]
definition: A patent pool is 'an agreement between two or more patent owners to license one or more of their patents to one another or third parties' and, at its most fundamental level, represents a formal knowledge sharing arrangement that aggregates IP rights among multiple entities for the purpose of developing and commercializing new technology-based products.

name: Licensor status
definition: Licensors are firms that own the essential patents, which are the core intellectual assets of the patent pool; they are firms that submitted patents for review by the independent examiner and had at least one patent deemed 'essential' and selected for inclusion in the pool.

name: Licensee status
definition: Licensees are firms that purchase the right to use these patents in the design of various products; they can only obtain the technology represented by the pool through the legal licensing and payment of fees associated with the use of the essential patents.

name: Quantity of innovation
authors_terms: ["quantity of innovation", "quantity of related patents", "patenting activity"]
definition: Quantity of innovation is the number of related patents generated by a given firm in a given year, where related patents are those patents that have a technology classification corresponding to one of the 10 classes representing optical disc technology.

name: Quality of innovation
definition: Quality of innovation is the citation count of related patents generated by a given firm from its grant date to the end of the study period in 2006, where related patents are those with a technology classification corresponding to one of the 10 classes representing optical disc technology.

name: High-performance work systems
authors_terms: ["high-performance work systems", "high-performance work system", "high-involvement human resource systems", "high-commitment HR systems"]
definition: A system of human resource practices designed to enhance employees' skills, commitment, and productivity in such a way that employees become a source of sustainable competitive advantage.

name: Labor productivity
definition: Labor productivity, defined as total output divided by labor inputs, indicates the extent to which a firm's labor force is efficiently creating output.

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: Industry capital intensity was the three-year (1997-99) average ratio of fixed assets to sales for firms in each industry defined at the three-digit SIC level.

name: Industry growth
definition: Industry growth was defined as the average five-year annual growth rate in value of shipments based on the data available in the U.S. Census of Manufacturers.

name: Industry product differentiation
definition: The three-year (1997-99) mean of the average ratios of R&D expenditures to total sales for all firms belonging to the sample firms' three-digit SIC industries was used as an indicator of industry product differentiation.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Following Keats and Hitt (1988), we assessed industry dynamism using a two-step procedure: first, the natural logarithm of sales for each three-digit industry for the years 1997-99 was regressed against time, and then the antilogarithms of the standard errors from these models were calculated. These antilogarithms represent an index of volatility or dynamism for each industry.

name: Chief executive officer position
definition: Although all members of the TMT would, rightly, be regarded to constitute the highest echelon of management, by position, the British CEO is held to be distinct; the role of the CEO is identified as the 'primus inter pares'—THE corporate leader. 'De facto' the CEO achieved the pinnacle, whereas members of the TMT either did not, or had yet to do so; 'de jure', the CEO is appointed in U.K. law by the Board of Directors.

name: Corporate experience
definition: Corporate influences, including tenure, mobility, functional experience and international exposure, grouped into the three areas of functional track, of the breadth of company experience, and of workload.

name: Self-concept
definition: The third group—that of self concept—is rooted in leadership research: the investigation of the self-perception of the managers themselves as to their personal beliefs and attitudes.

name: Domestic and educational influences
authors_terms: ["domestic influences", "domestic and educational influences", "domestic environmental and educational patterns"]
definition: Variables tested in this constituency emanate largely from research in organizational behaviour, and concentrate upon parental and childhood experiences and upon the extent of educational attainment.

name: Top management characteristics
definition: In order to evaluate the potential significance of different top management characteristics (TMCs), a research programme was therefore undertaken, based upon a common methodology. The study focused upon variations in experiences over three sets of variables: corporate influences; domestic influences; and their self-concept.

name: Specialized tribunal targeting
