authors_terms: ["institutional targeting", "venue targeting", "targeting the ITC venue", "choice between specialized and general-purpose tribunals"]
definition: Institutional targeting is the strategic act of choosing (and allocating resources) among alternative institutional venues to pursue organizational nonmarket goals. The focal institutional targeting strategy studied in this paper is a firm's choice between specialized and general-purpose tribunals.

name: Strategic stakes
definition: High strategic stakes are defined as valuable asset positions or concentrations of resources that are cospecialized with the focal disputed issue. High strategic stakes imply that there are broader repercussions from the dispute for firm rents, which can in turn create barriers for settlement.

name: Competitor institutional distance
authors_terms: ["competitor institutional distance", "institutional distance", "differences in the institutional backgrounds of the competing firms"]
definition: What is important for dispute settlement is the rival firm's 'institutional distance' from the focal firm; the greater this distance, the less likely settlement is. It is the distance between the firm's and its competitor's institutional backgrounds, measured with a cross-national index of patent strength.

name: Institution-specific capabilities
authors_terms: ["institution-specific capabilities", "tribunal-specific capabilities", "nonmarket capabilities with respect to a tribunal", "prior experience"]
definition: Firms may possess unique institution-specific capabilities or resources, which are often developed through prior experience at that venue; these capabilities may include firsthand knowledge about the institution, organizational routines for managing activities such as litigation or lobbying, and linkages with relevant players both within the institution and related to it. Tribunal-specific capabilities can give firms an advantage in pursuing adjudication more cost-effectively and in obtaining favorable outcomes at a particular venue.

name: Patent holder foreignness
authors_terms: ["foreign patent holder", "foreign asset holder", "domestic patent holder"]
definition: A lead patent holder is foreign if the headquarters or country of registration of the firm's ultimate parent was foreign, and is domestic if the ultimate parent is headquartered in the United States.

name: Challenger foreignness
definition: A lead challenger is foreign if the headquarters or country of registration of the firm's ultimate parent was foreign, and is domestic if the ultimate parent is headquartered in the United States.

name: Patent holder litigation success
authors_terms: ["Patent holder win", "patent holder winning a lawsuit", "success rates in patent litigation"]
definition: Our main dependent variable, Patent holder win, is a discrete variable equal to one if the patent holder won the focal dispute.

name: Nationalistic rhetoric
definition: If courts systematically rule against foreign firms because of nationalist concerns, particularly national well-being and economic independence, then their rulings will reflect such language. Judges rely on the language of court opinions to justify their decisions and legitimate their rulings.

name: Judicial ideology
definition: Judicial ideology reflects a judge's preferences or beliefs of an ideological character, including a tendency to favor certain types of public policies. It reflects policy preferences on a wide range of issues and not simply a preference for a specific political party.

name: Litigant nationality heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["mixed pairs", "disputes involving foreign and domestic firms", "domestic-foreign", "foreign-domestic"]
definition: Judgments in lawsuits involving foreign and domestic firms (as asset holders or challengers) are compared with those involving only domestic or only foreign firms; mixed pairs are disputes in which one party is foreign and the other domestic.

name: Threat from informal sector firms
authors_terms: ["competitive threat from informal sector firms", "perceived threat from informal sector competitors", "informal firm threat", "threat from informal sector firms"]
definition: The competitive threat a focal firm perceives from the informal sector competitor group. The informal sector consists of firms that are not formally registered with the state, and therefore do not pay taxes and other levies to the state, and that either use illegal means and/or pursue illegal ends.

name: Threat from foreign firms
authors_terms: ["competitive threat from foreign firms", "perceived threat from foreign competitors", "foreign firm threat"]
definition: The competitive threat a focal firm perceives from foreign multinational companies operating in the emerging market. Foreign firms typically enjoy superior technical resources, managerial capabilities, well-known brand names, and access to international networks, and a focal firm may perceive threats from this group when it faces a situation of resource similarity with it.

name: Engagement in corruption activities
definition: Corruption is a nonmarket competitive action when conceptualized in terms of giving bribes to government officials to further one's own interests, as it is essentially a financial incentive given to government officials to influence policy-making and policy-implementing in a way that favors the demander's interests.

name: Investment in HR training
authors_terms: ["investment in HR training", "HR training", "HR training investment"]
definition: HR training is a competitive action in a firm's resource market: it serves the traditional role of internal resource building by improving the quality of current employees, and it also serves as a resource preemption strategy used to retain human resources within the firm who might otherwise run out to or be poached by competitors.

name: Firm diversification
definition: The degree of firm diversification, that is, whether a focal firm has multiple product/service lines or relies on one product/service line. When a focal firm has multiple product/service lines, it has alternative markets to compete in and win even when it faces a high level of threat in a certain market.

name: Technological capability
definition: A firm's technological capability refers to a firm's ability to employ various technologies.

name: Corporate sexual equality
authors_terms: ["corporate sexual equality", "corporate equality index", "CEI", "sexual equality policies"]
definition: Corporate sexual equality measures how a firm treats its lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) employees, consumers, and investors. The authors describe it as a specific type of corporate social responsibility and an important form of a firm's diversity management.

name: Firm value
definition: Following the literature, the authors use stock returns (R) and Tobin's Q to measure firm value, defined as the monthly stock returns in percentage point and the ratio of the market value of assets to the book value of assets, respectively. A firm's market value should equal the present value of all its future cash flows.

name: Employee productivity
definition: The dependent variable of the model testing Hypothesis 2 is employee productivity; ideally, total output per employee is a precise measure of worker productivity, but due to data availability the authors use firm income per employee as an approximation.

name: CEO emphasis on strategic HRM
authors_terms: ["CEO emphasis on SHRM", "CEOs' emphasis on SHRM", "CEO emphasis on strategic HRM", "strategic emphasis"]
definition: Together, these items measure how much stress the firm's CEO places on achieving competitive advantage through leveraging human resources. The authors argue that CEOs' strategic emphasis is an important antecedent to firms' strategic resources and capabilities.

name: Commitment-based HR system
authors_terms: ["commitment-based HR systems", "commitment-based HRM", "commitment-based HR practices", "commitment-based HR system"]
definition: The commitment-based HRM systems that Korean firms adopted included selective staffing, relatively high levels of job security, and performance-based pay (i.e., individual incentive, merit pay, profit sharing), coupled with rigorous performance appraisal, employee participation, and team-based work. Such systems are argued to be strategic resources that increase employees' knowledge, skills, and abilities, increase their motivation, and organize work so that employees can further their firms' goals.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measured firm performance with three different variables: employee productivity, return on equity (ROE), and perceived performance, all outcomes that have been employed in extant SHRM research.

name: Employee productivity
authors_terms: ["employee productivity", "firm-level labor productivity", "labor productivity", "work productivity", "sales per employee"]
definition: Consistent with prior HRM research, our productivity measure is annual sales for 2006 (in Korean won) divided by the number of employees in the workforce. HRM scholars have described firm-level productivity as 'the crucial indicator of workforce performance'.

name: Return on equity
definition: Return on equity is one of the more distal measures of firm performance, based on financial accounting outcomes, that the authors contrast with intermediate indicators such as labor productivity.

name: Perceived firm performance
authors_terms: ["perceived performance", "perceived firm performance", "key respondents' perceptions of firm performance"]
definition: Previous HRM research has also employed key respondents' perceptions of firm performance, which tends to be positively correlated with financial performance but can sometimes differ from both productivity and financial performance.

name: Market share position
authors_terms: ["market share", "low share businesses", "high share businesses", "market share relative to combined share of three largest competitors"]
definition: Businesses were grouped by their market share relative to the combined share of the three largest competitors into a low share and a high share position; the paper contrasts businesses occupying a low share position with those occupying a high share position.

name: Business effectiveness
definition: Effectiveness distinguishes businesses by their return on investment: effective low share businesses are low share businesses achieving high ROI and ineffective low share businesses are low share businesses achieving low ROI. The strategies of effective low share businesses are expected to differ from those of ineffective low share businesses because of the difference in performance.

name: Product-market environment
definition: Product-market choice refers to the corporate level decision of participation in particular businesses, described by product and market characteristics together with variables pertaining to industry characteristics. The product-market choice serves to define the short term environment of a business.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Competitive strategy at the business level indicates how a business competes and allocates its resources, given the product-market choice. The chosen variables define the competitive position of a business relative to other sellers, include the emphasis given to various functional activities and reflect resource allocation priorities.

name: Administrative hierarchical distance
authors_terms: ["administrative hierarchical distance", "hierarchical distance to the central government", "distance to central"]
definition: The number of bureaucratic levels separating the central government and the governmental body that ultimately controls or monitors a firm. It reflects the number of governmental levels separating the central government from the level of government that holds the monitoring and/or control rights of a given firm, and thus is responsible for implementing environmental policy for that specific firm.

name: Corporate environmental actions
definition: Eligible actions include specific efforts to save energy and decrease pollution as well as activities aimed at propagating environmental protection concepts. Corporate environmentalism deals with the integration of environmental considerations into corporate actions.

name: Regulatory stringency
authors_terms: ["regulatory stringency", "stringency of sectorial regulation", "stringency of environmental regulation"]
definition: The stringency of environmental regulation faced by firms in a sector, which governments use to promote, facilitate, or enforce environmentally benign corporate behavior. The authors state that the environmental stakes are higher in environmentally disruptive sectors, but so are the economic interests, so that the opposing effects of mounting pressure and increased autonomy are both magnified in highly regulated sectors.

name: Environmental monitoring capacity
definition: A region that allocates more budget, staff, and equipment to assess the environmental compliance of local firms will induce these firms to engage in more environmental activities. It reflects the state's overall commitment to the environment and is independent of the administrative level of a firm's ultimately controlling government body.

name: User-industry spinout origin
definition: User-industry spinouts are new and independent ventures founded by entrepreneurs that cross industry boundaries from a downstream, user industry into a focal industry. What is critical is that they have pre-entry experience in a downstream firm in which the products of the focal industry are used or integrated into other final products.

name: Focal spinout origin
definition: New ventures created by the ex-employees of incumbent firms in the same industry are widely referred to as 'spinouts'. In this study these are firms founded by entrepreneurs whose last employment was in a semiconductor firm.

name: Other start-up origin
definition: A residual group of firms whose founders come from either universities or research institutes or who were previously employed in areas such as finance, venture capital, business software, business and/or engineering consultancy.

name: Firm survival
definition: Consistent with this literature, we use survival as our measure of success and treat firms that exit the industry as unsuccessful new ventures. Although we treat both exit by acquisition and exit by failure as cases of 'nonsurvival,' we capture these differences in our data.

name: Market-specific product entry
authors_terms: ["market-specific products", "market-specific semiconductors", "entry into market-specific product categories"]
definition: Market-specific semiconductors refers to chips that are targeted at specific application markets. The design of such devices requires some degree of knowledge and understanding of the applications or systems in which they are integrated.

name: Incremental reconfiguration
definition: By reconfiguration, we mean changes that affect particular structural units, e.g., mergers or splits, but that leave the overall organizational structure basically intact. Reconfigurations are thus incremental in the sense of being consistent with existing structural principles.

name: Discontinuous restructuring
definition: By organizational restructuring, we mean change in basic structural principles, e.g., change in the type of structural axes or the number of organizational layers. Restructurings are discontinuous in that the basic structure of reporting relationships is fundamentally changed organization-wide.

name: Organizational decline
authors_terms: ["organizational decline", "performance decline", "consecutive absolute performance declines", "prolonged performance declines"]
definition: With regard to organizational decline, we focus on consecutive absolute performance declines. Poor performance and the consequent squeeze on resources will increase the perceived need for discontinuous change whether or not it is shared by peers.

name: External CEO succession
authors_terms: ["top management change", "top management instability", "external CEO change", "new outsider CEO"]
definition: With regard to the disequilibriating impact of top management instability, particularly from outsiders, we focus on the appointment of an external CEO. External CEO Change is a dummy variable, coded 1 when the new CEO does not come from the company.

name: Strategic interconnectedness
definition: Organizational interconnectedness varies by strategy. Unrelated conglomerate strategies leave each business unit operating in distinct markets and managed independently: units are well insulated from shocks to any particular one. In undiversified or related-diversified firms, by contrast, resource sharing and market adjacencies are higher, creating more links across organizational units through which shocks can be transmitted organization-wide.

name: Resource accumulation lag
definition: We define a resource accumulation lag as the time a firm takes, on average, to accumulate the resources to produce one unit of output in a product-market of interest.

name: Likelihood of investment
definition: Our hypotheses concern the impact of resource accumulation lags and uncertainty on firms' likelihood of investment. We operationalized firms' investments in capacity expansion in the petrochemical industry as has been done in prior work on the topic.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: In this study, we focused on the most prominent driver of uncertainty in the petrochemical industry: demand. The corresponding measure was defined as the standard deviation of four years' worth of industrial production prior to the year under consideration.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: The study conceptualizes environment as a multidimensional construct. The questionnaire measures three dimensions, viz., complexity, dynamism, and hostility, for each of the eight environmental sectors: competitors, buyers, suppliers, technological, regulatory, economic, socialcultural, and international sectors.

name: Analyzer orientation
definition: As a unique combination of the Prospector and the Defender orientation, it represents a viable strategic alternative to the Prospector and the Defender, especially in China. It is effective both in stable and dynamic market domains and in seeking risk-adjusted efficiency and emerging market opportunities.

name: Prospector orientation
definition: The Prospector orientation tends to offer a frequently changing product line and competes primarily by stimulating new market opportunities and by experimenting with emerging trends and technologies.

name: Defender orientation
definition: The Defender orientation, which is rigid, shortsighted, nonadaptive, and risk-averse, is likely to be too conservative for MNCs that seek global competitive advantages. Its emphasis is on increasing efficiency of existing operations through continual improvements and developing a cost-efficient core technology while seldom adjusting internal configurations.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The study utilizes a subjective assessment of performance at the subsidiary level in return on assets, sales growth, and competitive position (e.g., market share) on a 5-point scale that ranges from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent in comparison with close competitors in the industry.

name: Perceived source trustworthiness
authors_terms: ["perceived trustworthiness", "trustworthiness", "perception of a source's trustworthiness", "source ability"]
definition: The scale was designed to assess the perceived trustworthiness of an organizational unit, focused on ability, i.e., the group of skills, competencies and characteristics that enable a party to have influence within a specific domain.

name: Causal ambiguity
definition: The existence of causal ambiguity means that the factors explaining the template's performance cannot be precisely determined (not even ex-post), and that it is therefore impossible to produce an unambiguous conception of how the template works, i.e., to produce a unique list of its key components and of how they interact.

name: Accuracy of reproduction
authors_terms: ["accuracy", "accuracy of the reproduction of the template", "effectiveness of the transfer"]
definition: The effectiveness of the transfer is operationalized by how accurately the recipient reproduces a replica of the template; a measure of accuracy must be sensitive to differences between the features of the replica and those of the original template, both to intended and unintended modifications introduced to the original template.

name: Innovation performance
definition: The authors define product innovation performance as new product sales: they operationalize innovation performance by measuring firms' turnover that pertains to new products.

name: Sequencing
authors_terms: ["sequencing", "resource allocation in a single step or across multiple steps", "sequentially allocating firms"]
definition: Instead of allocating all project resources in one go, as implied by a standard net present value investment model, resources are allocated over several steps.

name: Low initial commitment
definition: Real options logic holds that initial investments are exploratory and non-committal, meaning that projects compete for allocation of scarce later-stage resources. The measure captures the degree to which managers are committed to the continuous funding of their new product innovation projects.

name: Resource reallocation
definition: Resource reallocation is the reassignment over time of resources from deteriorating projects to more promising ones.

name: Fit between commitment and reallocation
authors_terms: ["fit between low initial commitment and reallocation", "fit", "match"]
definition: Fit between low initial commitment and reallocation is conceptualized as a match between two variables that individually do not have direct relationships with performance.

name: Tentativeness of bets
definition: The tentative variable distinguishes regimes making tentative bets from those making definitive bets, a qualitative difference captured by whether the firm displays either low commitment or reallocation.

name: Cost of entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["cost of entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurship costs", "entry cost reduction", "cost of entry", "costs of founding a new business", "entry deregulation"]
definition: The financial, bureaucratic, and time costs of founding a new venture. The authors exploit institutional reforms that reduced the costs of founding a new business: the On the Spot Firm ('Empresa na Hora') program, implemented at different moments across Portuguese municipalities, progressively decreased barriers to founding new ventures.

name: Employee wages
definition: The dependent variable wage is computed as the sum of the following monthly components: (a) base pay, or the gross amount of money paid in the reference month to employees on a regular monthly basis for their normal hours of work; (b) tenure-related payments; and (c) regular payments.

name: Employee wage position
definition: Employees in the top tercile of the municipality's wage distribution are classified as high earners, employees in the middle tercile as middle earners, and employees in the bottom tercile as low earners.

name: Ex ante propensity to become a founder
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurship probability", "ex ante probability of becoming a founder", "ex ante propensity to become a founder", "predicted probability of entrepreneurship"]
definition: An individual-level measure of ex ante propensity to become a founder, computed as the predicted probability of entrepreneurship. For individual-year observations after 2005, the predicted probability is computed in 2004, the last year available before the enactment of the shock, to mitigate endogeneity concerns.

name: Outside options in paid employment
authors_terms: ["outside options", "outside options as paid employees", "outside options within paid employment"]
definition: Outside options are more credible when they encompass readily available opportunities within the same occupation, industry, and region as the worker's current job. The measure is computed as the number of jobs in the same industry-occupation-region of the focal employee minus the number of similar jobs in the focal worker's firm.

name: Decentralized wage bargaining
authors_terms: ["decentralized bargaining", "decentralized salary negotiation process", "individual rather than collective wage setting", "firm-level bargaining"]
definition: The extent to which wage setting is decentralized and flexible rather than governed by centralized collective bargaining: employees are more adept at translating their bargaining power into remuneration when wages are determined on a more decentralized basis (e.g., at the firm level) compared with a more centralized approach (e.g., at the industry level).

name: Firm risk
authors_terms: ["risk", "accounting-based risk", "variance of ROE", "variance of returns", "total risk", "market-based risk", "beta", "systematic risk"]
definition: Bowman's measure of risk is accounting-based (i.e. variance of returns) and targeted at the firm level, whereas modern finance literature and the capital asset pricing model emphasize the variance in returns to investors and advocate the use of market-based risk measures.

name: Firm return
definition: The average ROE and variance of ROE were calculated from annual data for ROE derived for each firm in each two-digit industry.

name: Risk-return association
authors_terms: ["risk-return paradox", "negative association", "negative association ratio", "risk-return relationship", "risk-return performance", "risk-return profile"]
definition: Bowman noted the existence of a risk-return paradox for strategic management; namely, that business risk and return are negatively correlated across companies within most industries.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["environmental turbulence", "the more uncertain environment of the 1970s", "the more predictable and stable environment of the 1960s", "less predictable, ill-structured", "periods of economic stability", "environmental conditions"]
definition: The 1960s were a boom decade in which growth seemed eternal, where market structures were relatively stable and where inflation rates were low, whereas the 1970s saw the rise of the conglomerate, the energy crunch and the advent of added complexity in strategic decision-making; consequently the 1970s business environment was less predictable and ill-structured.

name: Industry performance level
authors_terms: ["High relative ROE (Birth/Growth)", "Medium ROE (Mature)", "Low ROE (Decline)", "growth industries", "high ROE industries", "declining industries", "low ROE industries"]
definition: Industries in each period were identified as being in one of three categories: High relative ROE (Birth/Growth), Medium ROE (Mature) and Low ROE (Decline), obtained by dividing the overall industry ROE distribution into tertiles.

name: Risk measure basis
authors_terms: ["accounting-based risk measure", "market-based risk measure", "variance of returns", "beta", "systematic risk", "total risk"]
definition: It is possible that risk-return performance may also depend upon the measure of risk chosen in the research: accounting-based measures (variance of returns) or market-based measures such as the beta from the capital asset pricing model.

name: Corporate interaction structure homogeneity
authors_terms: ["homogeneous units", "homogenous units", "homogeneous interaction structure", "proportion of homogeneous units", "hom/total units"]
definition: Business units that emphasize homogeneous interaction structures ('homogenous units') align incentives and goals among individuals of similar backgrounds, and a critical feature of homogeneous units is the strong similarity in how their employees view the world and perceive and prioritize problems. The proportion of homogeneous units is calculated by dividing the number of a structure's homogeneous units by the structure's total units (homogeneous + heterogeneous units).

name: Corporate interaction structure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneous units", "heterogeneous interaction structure", "proportion of heterogeneous units", "het/total units"]
definition: Business units that emphasize heterogeneous interactions ('heterogeneous units') facilitate cross-functional communication by grouping individuals with distinctive areas of expertise, and the benefits of such units mirror the limitations of a homogeneous grouping (and vice versa). The proportion of heterogeneous units is calculated by dividing the number of a structure's heterogeneous units by the structure's total units.

name: Shift toward homogeneous units
authors_terms: ["shift toward greater homogeneity", "Hom shift", "shifting toward a more homogeneous focus", "countering reorganization toward more homogeneous units"]
definition: A reorganization that increases the firm's number of homogeneous units and/or reduces its number of heterogeneous units is coded as a shift toward greater homogeneity.

name: Shift toward heterogeneous units
authors_terms: ["shift toward greater heterogeneity", "Het shift", "shifting toward a more heterogeneous focus", "countering reorganization toward more heterogeneous units"]
definition: A reorganization that increases the firm's number of heterogeneous units and/or reduces its number of homogeneous units is coded as a shift toward greater heterogeneity.

name: Time until the next reorganization
authors_terms: ["timing of the next reorganization", "days until the next reorganization", "number of days between reorganizations", "delay until the next reorganization occurs"]
definition: The posited mechanism is that different interaction structures systematically generate adjustment lags of different lengths, a dynamic that bears implications for the next reorganization's expected timing as a function of the firm's current interaction structure.

name: Blockholder ownership
authors_terms: ["blockholder ownership", "blockholder equity", "presence of nonboard blockholders", "nonboard blockholders"]
definition: Governance construct capturing the extent to which large blocks of equity are held by non-board members; blockholder equity positions were measured as the number of 5 percent owners who were not directors or employees and as the total percentage of equity owned by such owners. As continuous monitors, block shareholders may force managers to formulate justifiable strategies.

name: Proportion of board outsiders
authors_terms: ["proportion of board outsiders", "board outsider ratio", "ratio of directors who are independent outsiders to total board members", "board composition"]
definition: Governance construct for the representation of independent outsiders on the board, defined as the number of outsiders divided by total board size. Outsiders are directors with no past or present personal or professional relationship with the firm other than the position of director.

name: Board outsider equity
authors_terms: ["outside board member ownership", "board outsider equity", "outside director equity"]
definition: The equity held by outside board members, calculated as the sum of their equity holdings divided by the total equity of common shares outstanding. When outside directors have a substantial ownership position they may be more willing to exercise their authority to press for continuous strategic correction.

name: Board insider equity
authors_terms: ["inside board member ownership", "board insider equity", "inside (manager) board member equity"]
definition: The equity held by inside board members, who are executive officers that also serve the firm's board of directors. When insiders own substantial firm equity their bonding to firm outcomes is high, giving them an incentive to keep strategy in line with the preferences of other owners.

name: Relative product diversification
authors_terms: ["relative product diversification", "overdiversification", "firm diversification", "high relative product diversification"]
definition: Product diversification stated relative to the industry, calculated as firm diversification minus the average diversification of firms in the dominant industry because high relative product diversification is likely to be a better proxy for overdiversification than standard measures of diversification. Overdiversification is defined as product diversification beyond the level optimal for shareholders.

name: Relative debt
definition: Secondary strategy construct for firm leverage stated relative to the industry: long-term debt divided by total net sales and long-term debt divided by total assets, each adjusted by subtracting the dominant two-digit industry's average ratio. Relative diversification is expected to be directly related to relative debt, primarily through acquisition.

name: Relative R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["relative R&D intensity", "relative R&D investment", "relative R&D expenditures"]
definition: Secondary strategy construct for a firm's R&D investment stated at the firm-minus-industry level; high relative product diversification is argued to lead firms to emphasize financial controls, shifting risk to division managers who then reduce risky expenditures such as R&D.

name: Relative accounting performance
definition: Accounting-based performance assesses the past; it was measured with return on assets, return on equity, and return on sales, each adjusted by subtracting the dominant two-digit industry's average of the same indicator.

name: Relative market performance
definition: Market-based performance measures expected future value and was measured with three indicators: the Sharpe measure, the Treynor measure, and Jensen's alpha.

name: Divestment intensity
definition: The level of total divestiture activity a firm undertakes during restructuring, with divestiture defined broadly as including sales of assets, or sell-offs, management buyouts of divisions, equity carve-outs, and spinoffs.

name: Firm growth
definition: Growth is defined as the firm's change in revenue and assets, capturing the collective change in the firm's resource base.

name: Adaptive capability
definition: Adaptive capability is the firm's proficiency at altering its understanding of market expectations, and it increases as a result of increasing firm boundaries.

name: Entrepreneurial behaviors
definition: The entrepreneurial behaviors dimension, constructed by collapsing innovativeness and proactiveness, reflects the firm's commercialization of their innovations.

name: Managerial attitude toward risk
definition: Managerial attitude toward risk reflects senior managers' willingness to pursue opportunities with uncertain outcomes.

name: Acquired unit performance
authors_terms: ["acquired unit performance", "unit performance", "performance of the acquired unit"]
definition: The performance of the acquired unit was measured as the percentage of ROA (return on assets) of the acquired unit minus the mean ROA of the 2-digit SIC industry of the unit to control for potential industry effects.

name: Outside CEO succession
authors_terms: ["new outside CEO", "arrival of a new CEO from outside of the acquiring companies", "outside CEOs who were not involved with acquiring the poorly performing focal unit"]
definition: Faced with the prospect of divesting a poorly performing acquired unit, new CEOs can de-commit to the action by claiming that they did not make it; and that their actions are distinctive to those of their predecessors (Kelley and Michela, 1980).

name: Industry stability
definition: CEOs' ability to use attributional accounts to de-commit to a poorly performing acquisition is contingent on whether they operate under a relatively stable organizational context and industry environment.

name: Organizational slack
definition: In this study, the measure of absorbed slack is the debt to equity ratio that reflects the healthiness of the balance sheet and borrowing capacity (Bergh, 1995; Hambrick and D'Aveni, 1988).

name: Acquiring firm performance
authors_terms: ["acquiring firm performance", "overall firm performance", "better firm performance"]
definition: Performance of the acquiring firm was measured as the percentage of ROA of the firm relative to the industry average ROA, which was operationalized as a firm's ROA minus the 2-digit SIC industry average ROA (Bergh, 1997).

name: Divestiture
definition: We limit our study to disposals of acquired units rather than asset redeployment or partial disposal of assets within such units, as CEOs may acquire firms on the basis that they will subsequently divest some acquired assets (Capron, Dussauge, and Mitchell, 1998).

name: IEJV profitability
definition: IEJV performance was operationalized as IEJV financial profitability; in the TK data, IEJV profitability is based on managerial reports, that is, a perceptual assessment of venture performance rendered by the IEJV's general manager.

name: Equity ownership change
authors_terms: ["changes in IEJV ownership structure", "change in ownership control structure", "structural change", "ownership change event"]
definition: Changes in the relative ownership levels of existing partners served as both dependent and independent variables; the dependent variable was operationalized as an ordered and repeatable event variable, whose defining characteristic is that a subject can only experience one event at any given time.

name: Prior ownership change experience
authors_terms: ["state dependency", "stage of ownership changes (number of prior changes)", "sequential ownership changes", "prior ownership changes"]
definition: State dependency refers to situations where the probability of an IEJV experiencing a future ownership change event is influenced by the occurrence of previous ownership change events.

name: Shared equity ownership control
authors_terms: ["extent of shared equity ownership", "shared equity ownership control", "shared ownership control"]
definition: The extent of shared equity ownership between/among IEJV partners is measured on a continuum whose value originates at 0, a meaningful point indicating 100% ownership control by a single parent firm, with a maximum value of 1 indicating a completely even distribution of equity ownership between/among partners.

name: IEJV termination
definition: For the long-term outcomes of multiple ownership changes, IEJV termination was operationalized as the eventual demise of an IEJV relationship; it was used as an indicator of long-term organizational performance.

name: Firm status
definition: Status is traditionally defined as a relative position in a socially constructed hierarchy. Status serves to signal the unobservable qualities of firms, so that others can infer a firm's unobservable qualities from its status and decide how they should act toward it.

name: Acquirer-target status differential
definition: The authors emphasize the directional nature of status differentials by highlighting the accompanying behavioral order stemming from the alignment of the status-based roles with the role expectations embedded in the particular interfirm transactions. Status_Differential is the acquiring firm's status minus the target firm's status.

name: Market reaction to acquisition announcement
definition: Market responses are influenced by how likely the focal takeover will result in value creation for either or both parties; when the investors are optimistic about the prospect of the acquisition, they will react more positively upon the announcement of the deal.

name: Takeover deal completion
definition: When the acquirer-target status differential is prominent, the market will react positively and both the acquirer and the target will know the roles they are expected to play, reducing potential negotiation difficulties or transaction friction, so that the focal takeover transaction will more likely result in completion.

name: Post-acquisition performance
definition: Post_Performance is the acquirer performance after deal completion, measured with an accounting-based and a stock market-based method.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional ownership", "total institutional ownership", "total institutional holding", "institutional holding", "institutional investors"]
definition: Equity ownership of a firm by institutional investors, a term that includes a variety of organizations such as insurance companies, pension funds, and mutual funds, among others.

name: New product development
authors_terms: ["rate of new product development", "number of new products", "new product announcements", "firm innovation", "new products developed by the firm"]
definition: One of the actual outcomes of innovation: the number of new products developed by the firm, used instead of R&D intensity because R&D expenditures do not indicate whether there are truly differences in innovation across firms.

name: Pressure-resistant institutional ownership
definition: Ownership by institutions that have no business relationship with the firm; as they have only an investment relationship, a conflict of interest is unlikely and they are more able to exercise their voice over firm actions. Included in this category are public pension funds, mutual funds, and endowments and foundations.

name: Pressure-sensitive institutional ownership
definition: Ownership by institutions that have ongoing business relations with the firms in which they invest; the power gained from their ownership stake may be negated by their dependence on the firm for business activity. Pressure-sensitive institutions include banks, insurance companies, and nonbank trusts.

name: Adoptions by proximate others
authors_terms: ["adoptions by proximate others", "proximate adoption", "adoptions in nation", "adoptions of the same innovation"]
definition: Each adoption by others is modeled as influential if it is proximate to the potential adopter. The authors use same-nation headquarter of the airline as the proximity characteristic, so the variable counts prior adoptions of the focal aircraft by airlines headquartered in the focal airline's nation.

name: Competing innovation adoption by proximate others
authors_terms: ["adoptions of a competing innovative production asset by proximate others", "adoptions of the competing aircraft", "adoption of the competing type", "adoptions of the other airplane"]
definition: A proximate adoption of the other airplane is denoted O_no, where n is the focal observation and o the adopter of the other technology. If two innovative production assets are to be potentially adopted, the adoption of the first asset by a proximate other is expected to reduce the probability of adoption of the second asset by a focal firm.

name: Abandonments by proximate others
authors_terms: ["abandonments by proximate others", "proximate abandonment", "abandonments in nation", "complete abandonments"]
definition: Decision makers gain information when prior adopters abandon an innovation, and attention to an abandonment and the information necessary to judge that it was a result of disappointment with the innovation are both higher when the abandonment was proximate to the focal firm. Full abandonments occur when an airline sells all of its planes of the focal design.

name: Rate of adopting an innovative production asset
authors_terms: ["rate of adopting an innovative production asset", "event of placing an order for an innovative aircraft design", "adoption likelihood"]
definition: The dependent variable in the analysis is the event of placing an order for an innovative aircraft design. A firm remains at risk of adoption during the entire production period of the focal aircraft or for as long as the firm exists, whichever is smaller.

name: Knowledge retrieval
authors_terms: ["knowledge retrieval", "reabsorption of spilled knowledge", "re-absorption of previously spilled knowledge"]
definition: The reabsorption of one's own spilled knowledge that has been leveraged externally; more precisely, the extent to which an originating firm is able to build on knowledge that has spilled over and has been leveraged by external firms.

name: Knowledge retrieval frequency
definition: The number of times spilled knowledge is reabsorbed by the firm, captured as a count of the number of spilled patents that the originating firm cites.

name: Technological complexity
definition: A function of the level of interdependence between the components that form an invention.

name: Organizational coupling
definition: The extent to which units depend on one another for the completion of tasks; an organizational design characteristic measured as a function of interdependencies between units of an organization.

name: Joint task complexity
authors_terms: ["joint task complexity", "task complexity", "complexity of the joint endeavor"]
definition: Joint task complexity increases as either the scope or depth of interaction between two partners increases; scope refers to the area of the task interface between the partners and depth refers to the intensity of interaction between them.

name: Interpartner diversity
definition: Differences along social and cognitive dimensions-culture, managerial personalities, priorities, operating logics, and so forth-that reduce the organizational fit of two partners and make an alliance difficult or impossible to manage.

name: Mutual adaptation
authors_terms: ["mutual adaptation", "lack of mutual adaptation", "lack of willingness to adapt to each other's work styles"]
definition: Cases of mutual adaptation in work styles, which would be expected when two organizations collaborate closely, estimated by the degree to which the architects perceived both partners as having changed their ways of working to suit the needs of the other.

name: Cooperative problem solving
authors_terms: ["cooperative problem solving", "lack of cooperative problem solving"]
definition: Perception of equity in the problem-solving process; namely, when problems arose, to what extent the partners complied with the request of the other partner even at the expense of their own short-term interests.

name: Threat of opportunism
authors_terms: ["threat of opportunism", "threat of opportunistic behavior", "perception of the likelihood that a partner will act opportunistically"]
definition: A manager's perception of the likelihood that an alliance partner will act opportunistically, measured by the architect's opinion that the contractor would take advantage of opportunities to profit at the architect's expense.

name: Asset specificity
definition: A subjective measure of asset specificity in the context of a specific relationship: architects estimate the degree to which they feel they would lose non-recoverable investments (drawings, equipment, etc.) if the project were discontinued.

name: Interpersonal trust
definition: The degree to which an architect believes that their contact person in the contractor firm will look out for the architect's interests even when it is costly to do so; it corresponds to 'personal trust' in Williamson's (1993) typology.

name: Repeated relationship
definition: The number of prior projects on which the architect had worked with the contractor, which reduces the likelihood of adverse selection that may otherwise occur in situations of high information asymmetry.

name: Cooperation costs
definition: Costs incurred in order to undertake a collaborative activity with a partner, separate from those incurred in reducing the threat of opportunism from that same partner; they arise from task-related coordination needs and from social differences that require partners to interpret and in some cases adjust to resulting differences in behavior and preferences.

name: Managerial time and effort
authors_terms: ["time and effort to coordinate with a partner", "time and effort a manager must spend on an alliance"]
definition: The amount of manager time and effort expended on an alliance, operationalized by asking the architects to report to what degree they had to spend a significant amount of time and effort to coordinate with their alliance partner.

name: Costs of control
definition: Costs incurred in order to control or reduce the threat of opportunism from an alliance partner, conceptually separate from cooperation costs.

name: Reputation gap
authors_terms: ["reputation gap", "reputation gaps", "positive reputation gap", "negative reputation gap"]
definition: The reputation gap is defined as the difference between internal reputation—specifically how customer-facing employees perceive their company—and external reputation—specifically how customers perceive the company. The authors distinguish positive gaps, where employee views of the company's reputation are superior to those of customers, from negative gaps, where the reverse is the case.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["future sales growth", "year-on-year percentage sales growth", "year on year % sales trend", "future sales", "performance"]
definition: Year-on-year percentage sales growth was chosen as the performance measure because the hypotheses concern the prediction of whether customers would buy more or less into the future; it is the percentage change in annual sales revenue between the survey date and one year later.

name: Internal reputation
authors_terms: ["internal reputation", "employee views of reputation", "employee perceptions of reputation", "reputation as perceived by employees", "employee view"]
definition: Internal reputation is specifically how customer-facing employees perceive their company. The authors hold that this employee view of corporate reputation is variable and malleable rather than enduring, which distinguishes it from organizational identity.

name: External reputation
authors_terms: ["external reputation", "customer views of reputation", "customer perceptions of reputation", "customer view"]
definition: External reputation is specifically how customers perceive the company; the customers' view of reputation is the reference point that defines their expectations of the service business.

name: Partner-specific trust
definition: The focal firm's belief that the former partner intends to deliver on made promises and would not act in self-interest at the focal firm's expense.

name: Partner-specific routines
definition: Stable patterns of interaction between the focal firm and the partner/target firm; routines are patterned sequences of skilled actions that involve multiple, interdependent actors and store experiences of 'how things are done'.

name: Partner-specific value certainty
definition: Captures whether the prior alliance has led to a substantial accumulation of critical, private, partner-specific knowledge, encompassing knowledge as to the partner's strengths and weaknesses, compatibility of goals, strategy, structure, operations, technologies, quality standards and aspirations, as well as culture.

name: Future cooperation
authors_terms: ["either a subsequent alliance or acquisition", "no future cooperation", "future interfirm combinations"]
definition: The decision to access the partner firm's resources through a subsequent alliance or a subsequent acquisition rather than through no future cooperation.

name: Alliance choice relative to acquisition
authors_terms: ["comparative choice between alliances and acquisitions", "subsequent alliance versus an acquisition", "alliance over acquisition"]
definition: The comparative governance choice between entering a subsequent alliance with the former partner firm and acquiring that firm.

name: Perceptions of the merger announcement
authors_terms: ["perceptions of the merger announcement", "positive perceptions of the merger announcement", "executives' perceptions of the merger announcement"]
definition: Executives' perceptions of the merger announcement itself, which are heavily influenced by preacquisition events that send signals about the willingness of the acquiring firm to retain target company managers and create impressions about the executive's future role in the newly merged firm.

name: Interactions with acquiring firm top managers
authors_terms: ["interactions with acquiring company top managers following the merger", "positive interactions with acquiring company top managers", "TMT interactions"]
definition: Executives' perceptions of their interactions with top managers from the acquiring firm following the merger, which send strong signals to executives about their status as insiders or outsiders.

name: Perceived long-term effects of the merger
authors_terms: ["perceptions of the long-term effects of the merger", "positive perceptions of the long-term effects of the merger", "long-term effects"]
definition: Executives' perceptions of the long-term effects of the merger, which ultimately influence their decisions about staying or leaving and include the nature of the executive's postmerger job and subsequent treatment.

name: Executive retention
authors_terms: ["decision to stay rather than leave", "decision to stay or depart", "stayers and leavers", "executive departures"]
definition: Whether a target company top manager remained with the acquired firm following the acquisition. Managers still employed 6 years later were coded as 'stayers' and managers no longer employed were coded as 'leavers.'

name: Market entry proposal
authors_terms: ["Target proposal", "Target's tendency to propose to enter the same market", "proposal to enter a market", "Target's proposal behavior"]
definition: Our dependent variable is whether Target proposed to open a new store in a place in a year. It captures the second entrant's tendency to propose to enter a market in which a first entrant has been protested.

name: Protest sponsorship by local activists
authors_terms: ["nonunion-led anti-Walmart protest", "protests not spearheaded by protest-prone activists", "protests led by local residents, merchants, or politicians", "union-led anti-Walmart protest"]
definition: Protests led by individuals and small local groups belonging to a community are perceived by the second entrant to be indicative of the community's preferences, whereas protests spearheaded by protest-prone activists belonging to national social movement organizations are discounted because they reflect the position of the national leadership more than that of the local community.

name: Firm-targeted protest claims
authors_terms: ["protest with Walmart-specific claims", "protests with claims that are specifically targeted at the first entrant"]
definition: When activists specifically attack the firm that is the first entrant, the second entrant is likely to discount such protests because it has an identity that is differentiated from the first entrant. These Walmart-specific concerns include the lack of retail diversity due to too many Walmart stores nearby, problems with a particular location that Walmart chose, a poor proposal and planning process, neighbors' concerns over the design of a Walmart store, and public subsidy to a Walmart project.

name: Category-targeted protest claims
authors_terms: ["protest with general claims", "protest with store-size-cap tactics", "protests with claims that are targeted at the category of organizations"]
definition: When the protests assail the organizational form, the second entrant is likely to be deterred, because a stereotype of the category develops and all members of the category are de-individualized. General concerns include the disruption by the presence of a big retailing chain to the identity of a small town or historical district, the impact on local business, poor labor conditions, the antiunion attitude, reliance on imported goods, store size, or too many other big-box stores nearby; store-size-cap rules that limit the square footage of any new store are a severe measure to wipe out big-box stores.

name: First entrant's withdrawal rate due to protests
authors_terms: ["rate of withdrawal", "Walmart's rate of withdrawal due to protests", "rate of Walmart's withdrawal due to protests"]
definition: The first entrant's response to protests reveals its private assessment of the favorability of a market: the first entrant can be expected to persist in entering a market in the face of protest when the market opportunity is strongest, and is more likely to withdraw where the opportunities for profitability are meager or the resistance is strong.

name: Local knowledge
authors_terms: ["local knowledge", "Target lacking local knowledge", "Target without local knowledge"]
definition: Second entrants' local knowledge of a market conditions the effect of information spillovers from protests against the first entrant; the less familiar a second entrant is with a market, the more likely it is to rely on the signals of protests against a first-mover's bid to enter the market. Uncertainties about a market are greatly reduced once a market player has already entered a market or has had a previous experience in it.

name: Extra-industry professional network participation
authors_terms: ["practice network", "extra-industry professional network", "participation in an extra-industry network", "CSR practice network", "conference participation"]
definition: Professional networks associated with a practice serve as a 'vehicle for the definition and promulgation of normative rules about organizational and professional behavior,' and thus create normative pressures for organizational conformity. Interindustry networks of professions associated with a practice develop and disseminate norms, rules, and standards that organizations can adopt and use when accounting for and implementing a new practice.

name: Intra-industry prevalence of a practice
definition: The extent to which other industry members adopt a practice will likely increase the probability of another organization's adoption of that practice. The measure reflects the prevalence of a particular practice among organizations in the same industry and is an operationalization of the strength of mimetic isomorphic pressures for adoption.

name: Adoption of a corporate social responsibility practice
authors_terms: ["CSR practice adoption", "employee volunteering program", "EVP", "adoption of a CSR practice", "practice adoption"]
definition: The practice that we study is the employee volunteering program (EVP), a corporate social responsibility (CSR) activity designed to encourage organizational employees to offer their time and skills in service to the community. The EVP variable reflects the adoption of any type of EVP practice.

name: Adoption of a turnkey practice
authors_terms: ["turnkey practice", "day of service", "DOS", "less customized practice", "off the shelf"]
definition: The DOS practice has been implemented across a variety of organizations, in different industry contexts, and is readily available as an 'off the shelf' template that can be quickly and easily implemented by almost any kind of organization. Given their low degree of customization, DOS practices tend to be similar and relatively standardized; thus the authors treat DOS as a turnkey practice.

name: Adoption of a tailored practice
authors_terms: ["tailored practice", "skills-based volunteering", "SBV", "more customized practice", "built to order"]
definition: SBVs tend to be more complex, challenging to implement, and customized to fit both the organization's particular capabilities and the needs of the community served, such that they are 'built to order.' In spite of the greater efforts required to customize and implement SBVs, these practices can be advantageous in cultivating a favorable or distinctive organizational reputation; thus the authors treat SBV as a tailored practice.

name: Organizational infrastructure
authors_terms: ["organizational infrastructure", "infrastructure", "organizational preparedness to implement the practice"]
definition: The organization's infrastructure is important because it can indicate the organization's capability and readiness to implement a practice. The authors propose that the presence of organizational infrastructures that enable the implementation of a practice will increase the likelihood of adoption of that practice.

name: Governance and leadership involvement
definition: Organizations are more likely to adopt a practice when it is supported by individuals with higher status in the organizational hierarchy, and those in power are more likely to recognize, prioritize, and determine the organization's response to institutional complexity.

name: Organizational identity
definition: An organization's identity filters perceptions about the relevance and appropriateness of practices; practices that align with the organization's identity are perceived to be more appealing and legitimate and, in turn, are more likely to be adopted. An organization's identity is a claim to 'institutionally standardized social categories.'

name: Organizational elite standing in its field
authors_terms: ["elite standing in its field", "elite field position", "organizational eliteness", "size and status"]
definition: An organization's position in the field, particularly in terms of its size and status, can function as a filter in adoption. Large or higher status organizations are more vulnerable to institutional pressures because of their visibility and increased media attention.

name: Negative feedback in new domains
authors_terms: ["negative feedback in new domains", "poorly performing new funds in new domains", "Negative & New", "failures in new domains"]
definition: We categorize a domain as new if the firm has no prior experience in that category. Negative feedback in new domains where the firm has uncertain expectations will lead to a significant downward adjustment of expectations, meaning that managers effectively attribute the failure in that domain to the domain itself.

name: Negative feedback in experienced domains
authors_terms: ["negative feedback in experienced domains", "Negative & Experienced", "poorly performing funds in experienced domains"]
definition: We categorize a domain as experienced if the firm has operated at least one fund in that category previously. Negative feedback in experienced domains, on the other hand, will not lead to a significant adjustment of the expectation level due to a strong prior developed through previous experience.

name: Positive feedback in new domains
authors_terms: ["positive feedback in new domains", "Positive & New", "successful new funds in new domains"]
definition: New funds that generate cash inflows greater than the median cash inflow of all other funds in the same category during the same year are classified as positively performing products, while all others are classified as negatively performing products.

name: Positive feedback in experienced domains
authors_terms: ["positive feedback in experienced domains", "Positive & Experienced", "successful new funds in experienced categories"]
definition: New funds that generate cash inflows greater than the median cash inflow of all other funds in the same category during the same year are classified as positively performing products, while all others are classified as negatively performing products.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["FirmFlow", "net cash inflows into all funds offered by a provider", "firm-level net new cash inflow across funds"]
definition: Our measure of firm performance is commonly utilized in mutual fund industry research: the net cash inflows into all funds offered by a provider.

name: New product introductions in the focal domain
authors_terms: ["funds created in the same category as the focal fund", "new fund creation in the domain of poor performance"]
definition: The dependent variable is a count of new funds created, which we break into three categories: funds created in the same category as the focal fund (Model 5).

name: New product introductions in new domains
authors_terms: ["funds created in completely new categories for the firm", "more new products introduced in new domains"]
definition: The dependent variable is a count of new funds created, which we break into three categories: funds created in completely new categories for the firm (Model 6).

name: New product introductions in experienced domains
authors_terms: ["funds created in other categories in which the firm has prior experience", "increased new fund creation in experienced domains"]
definition: The dependent variable is a count of new funds created, which we break into three categories: funds created in other categories in which the firm has prior experience (Model 7).

name: Performance of the struggling new product
authors_terms: ["whether struggling funds recover differently based on the domain of the fund", "net new cash flow in its third year"]
definition: We investigate Hypothesis 5 by empirically evaluating the performance of funds in their third year, after they have been categorized as existing in new versus experienced domains (year one) and above versus below aspirations (year two). The dependent variable is the fund's net new cash flow in its third year.

name: Performance of existing products
authors_terms: ["future performance of the firm's existing funds", "net new cash inflow in each year (four plus) for existing funds"]
definition: To more directly test Hypothesis 4 about the cannibalization effects of negative feedback in new domains on existing funds, we evaluate the spillover effect on the future performance of the firm's existing funds.

name: Product customization
definition: Product customization is the costly modification of a product to cater to customer needs; termed adapting services, it significantly expands the functionality of a product by adapting it to novel conditions and helping customers develop new uses for it.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["firm survival", "market exit", "probability of exiting a product market"]
definition: The authors examine firm survival, which they model through the probability that a firm exits a product market: the dependent variable Market exit is a dummy variable set equal to 1 if firm i exits product market j in year t, and 0 otherwise.

name: Submarket potential
definition: Submarkets are likened to independent islands of activity within an industry and reflect unique production technologies on the supply side and user applications on the demand side; submarket potential is the extent to which an industry features such submarkets, which the authors argue is greater in the upstream laser industry because it features a general-purpose technology with wide-ranging applications.

name: Firm entry
definition: Entry is captured at the product market level by the number of entrants, i.e., firms entering a product market in a year.

name: Incumbent exit
definition: Incumbent exits are captured at the product market level by the number of exits, i.e., firms exiting a product market in a year.

name: Direct reporting relationship
authors_terms: ["direct reporting relationship", "formal reporting relationships", "environmental quality manager reports directly to the plant manager"]
definition: Formal reporting relationships determine how and where information flows within an organization and ultimately impact decision making; the direct form studied here is one in which a facility's environmental quality manager reports directly to the facility (plant) manager.

name: Plant manager incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["plant manager's salary is influenced by environmental performance", "whether or not a plant manager's compensation is tied to environmental performance"]
definition: A compensation component in which clear environmental criteria are used to adjust the plant manager's compensation, so that a portion of salary is tied to environmental performance.

name: Environmental quality manager incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["environmental quality manager's salary is influenced by environmental performance", "whether or not a tie between environmental quality manager's pay and environmental performance"]
definition: A compensation component in which clear environmental criteria are used to adjust the environmental quality manager's compensation, so that a portion of salary is tied to environmental performance.

name: Cross-functional coordination
authors_terms: ["cross-functional coordination", "inclusion of environmental quality managers in discussions concerning key strategic processes", "inclusiveness of strategic processes"]
definition: The degree to which environmental quality managers are included in discussions concerning key strategic processes, such as equipment choices, fundamental design issues, and potential process modifications. The authors describe this as congruence between the work of environmental management and the informal structure of an organization.

name: Toxic emissions
definition: A facility-level index of toxic releases in which emissions of each chemical are divided by the EPA reportable quantity for that chemical and aggregated across the chemicals released at a facility, then log-transformed. Emissions performance is used as one of the many possible measures of environmental performance.

name: Corporate blockholder performance
definition: Performance measures were abnormal returns earned by corporate blockholders. Because abnormal returns in this study were computed using the market-adjusted return model with size-based decile indices, an abnormal return equals the difference between a firm's total return and an index return computed by averaging the total return of a decile of similar-sized firms for a common time interval.

name: Supplier or customer relationship with the target
authors_terms: ["investments in customers or suppliers", "supplier or customer", "supplier or customer relationship"]
definition: The purchase of a minority-level equity blockholding in a trading partner reduces the risk of the target's opportunistic behavior by providing the corporate blockholder with influence over the target through its voice in the selection of the target's board and management. This is a partial form of integration chosen to optimize risk reduction and flexibility objectives.

name: Target cross-investment
definition: Cross-investment occurs when two firms invest in each other's stock. Cross-investments, which are common among the Japanese keiretsu, may serve as exchanged hostages to provide a measure of mutual control and defense from takeover.

name: Blockholding value relative to blockholder value
authors_terms: ["blockholding value ratio", "value ratio", "ratio of the value of the blockholding to the value of the blockholder"]
definition: Because the fraction of the target acquired times the value of the target equals the cost of the blockholding, it is posited that the extent of benefits associated with a blockholding is likely to vary by the ratio of the value of the blockholding to the value of the blockholder.

name: Internal agglomerations
definition: Geographically bounded, intrafirm linkages that positively impact performance and that prompt firms to collocate activities across the value chain. They are inferred from firms' location choices rather than measured directly.

name: Location choice
definition: The choice of an economic area in which a firm opens a new establishment in a focal bio activity at a given time.

name: External agglomerations
definition: Agglomeration economies arising across firms: collocated firms enjoy higher productivity because geographic concentrations attract larger pools of specialized labor and suppliers and facilitate knowledge flows, which exerts a multiplier effect on firm productivity.

name: Value chain activity
authors_terms: ["activity in the value chain", "bio activity", "value-chain activity"]
definition: The distinct activities of the biopharmaceutical value chain: R&D (associated with SIC code 8731), manufacturing (associated with SIC code 2830), and sales (associated with SIC code 5120).

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure is simply the number of years in which the CEO has served in his or her current position.

name: CEO international experience
definition: CEO international experience is a composite of two variables-the number of international assignments and total years in such assignments. International experience may serve as a proxy for the reduction of uncertainty and as a surrogate for accumulating cultural knowledge.

name: Degree of firm internationalization
authors_terms: ["degree of firm internationalization", "degree of internationalization", "firm internationalization"]
definition: The extent to which a given firm has international product-market exposure, captured through a multi-item construct rather than single indicators.

name: CEO succession origin
authors_terms: ["outside succession", "inside succession", "CEO succession", "nature of CEO succession"]
definition: CEO succession refers to whether the current CEO was employed by the focal firm immediately prior to his or her promotion to CEO (inside succession) or by another firm (outside succession).

name: Firm performance
definition: Past research has strongly urged the reliance on multiple measures, spanning both accounting and market return measures, to adequately capture firm performance. Whereas accounting-based measures reflect past and present firm performance, a market measure such as market-to-book ratio provides an indication of the firm's future performance potential.

name: Short-selling threat
authors_terms: ["short-selling threats", "short-sale constraints", "stock price decline risk", "stock price risk", "short-selling risk"]
definition: The lifting of short-selling constraints incentivized short sellers to trade on negative information, which made pilot firms more vulnerable to predatory trading and exposed them to heightened stock price decline risk.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "CSR score", "CSR activities", "CSR levels", "CSR investment"]
definition: Corporate social responsibility can generate insurance-like protection as it accrues moral capital among stakeholders and thus can lessen their negative reactions to adverse events (Godfrey, 2005).

name: Short interest
definition: In Figure 2, we plot scaled monthly short interests (monthly short interest divided by shares outstanding times 100) of these two types of pilot firms from pre- to post-Reg SHO period.

name: CSR strengths
definition: Mattingly and Berman (2006) find that CSR strength ratings differ from CSR concern ratings both conceptually and empirically, with the former representing firms' strategies, programs, and polices to promote 'community' and the latter being mostly related to actual social performance.

name: CSR concerns
definition: Mattingly and Berman (2006) find that CSR strength ratings differ from CSR concern ratings both conceptually and empirically, with the former representing firms' strategies, programs, and polices to promote 'community' and the latter being mostly related to actual social performance.

name: Direct CSR
definition: Following in the spirit of Mattingly and Berman (2006), we categorize actions toward stakeholders that directly transact with the firms as direct CSR (i.e., employee, product, human rights, and diversity dimensions).

name: Broad CSR
definition: We categorize actions toward other stakeholders as broad CSR (i.e., community and environment dimensions).

name: Firm size
definition: Small firms generally are more often targeted by short sellers due to their small market capitalization, low information transparency and weak financial resources.

name: Dominant function diversity
authors_terms: ["dominant function diversity", "dominant function diversity of a team"]
definition: The extent to which team members differ in the functional areas within which they have spent the greater part of their careers. The extent to which the dominant functions of a team's members are evenly distributed across all of the relevant functions is viewed as an indication of the team's breadth and balance of knowledge and expertise related to running all aspects of an organization.

name: Intrapersonal functional diversity
authors_terms: ["intrapersonal functional diversity", "functional breadth of individual team members"]
definition: This conceptualization of functional diversity focuses on the extent to which the individuals on a team are narrow functional specialists with experience in a limited range of functions, or broad generalists whose work experiences span a range of functional domains.

name: Information sharing
definition: Information sharing involves conscious and deliberate attempts on the part of team members to exchange work-related information, keep one another apprised of activities, and inform one another of key developments.

name: Unit performance
definition: Performance is measured as a management team's actual profitability relative to its targeted profitability for the survey year. These business unit management teams were held accountable for setting and achieving annual profitability targets, defined in terms of net operating profit before tax (NOPBT).

name: Information use
authors_terms: ["information use", "high levels of information use", "amount of information used", "information-rich scanning behaviors"]
definition: The amount of information in each case that was used to interpret strategic issues (information use). High scores on the scale indicated a more comprehensive use of available information for developing a strategic issue.

name: External scanning orientation
authors_terms: ["external scanning orientation", "information source", "external-internal information source", "scanning focus"]
definition: The focus of scanning on information generated from something external to the hospital rather than internal, measuring the extent to which CEOs used internal or external information for strategic interpretation purposes. Items were scaled so that high scores indicated high use of external information for interpretation.

name: Positive-gain interpretation
authors_terms: ["positive-gain interpretation", "positive-gain", "interpretation of strategic issues in positive-gain terms"]
definition: The extent to which a CEO labels a strategic issue as positive and as implying potential gain, drawn from Dutton and Jackson's (1987) strategic interpretation dimensions. The positive-negative and gain-loss dimensions were operationally indistinguishable and were collapsed into the composite variable 'positive-gain.'

name: Controllability interpretation
authors_terms: ["controllability", "interpretation of strategic issues as controllable", "controllable-uncontrollable dimension"]
definition: The extent to which a CEO uses the controllable label to describe a strategic issue, one of the three strategic interpretation dimensions (positive-negative, gain-loss, and controllable-uncontrollable). High ratings indicated that respondents labeled the case situation as controllable.

name: Product-service change
authors_terms: ["product-service change", "strategic changes in product-service offerings", "growth in product and service offerings", "organizational action"]
definition: We defined action as any significant change in ongoing organizational practices, such as a substantive alteration in product or service offerings.
