The measure assessed the extent to which hospitals added or deleted products and services over the three-year period following collection of the scanning and interpretation data.

name: Organizational performance
definition: How differences in the performance of similar organizations are related to differences in their ability to carry out the three sensemaking tasks; measures of performance outcomes for hospitals should reflect both efficiency indicators, such as productivity, and effectiveness indicators, such as financial viability.

name: Interlocking director political ideology
authors_terms: ["political ideology", "director political ideology", "interlocking director conservatism", "interlocking director liberalism", "director conservatism", "director liberalism", "conservatism-liberalism spectrum"]
definition: Directors' preferences are a function of their political ideologies, which comprise their 'set of beliefs about the proper order of society and how it can be achieved'. Political ideology is a continuous construct, and an individual can espouse an ideology at any position on the conservatism-liberalism spectrum.

name: Prior adoptions by interlock partners
authors_terms: ["prior adoptions by interlock partners", "baseline diffusion effect", "contagion effect", "the diffusion 'intercept'", "conservatism-weighted adoptions", "liberalism-weighted adoptions"]
definition: The baseline diffusion effect is captured by a variable equaling the count of all prior adoptions in the focal firm's network, entered in the contagiousness vector; all prior adoption events in the network are weighted by the ideology of interlocking directors who tie the focal firm to prior adopter firms.

name: Adoption of lone-insider board structure
authors_terms: ["lone-insider board structure", "CEO-only board", "adoption of a lone-insider board structure"]
definition: The lone-insider board structure refers to the arrangement where the CEO is the only inside (employee) director on the board.

name: Adoption of CEO-chair separation
authors_terms: ["CEO-chair separation", "split CEO-chair structure", "separation of the CEO and board chairperson roles"]
definition: CEO-chair separation (or split CEO-chair structure) refers to the practice of having someone other than the CEO serve as board chair.

name: Shareholder pressure for governance reform
authors_terms: ["shareholder pressure for governance reform", "governance pressures from shareholders", "governance proposals", "pressure from shareholders"]
definition: Boards should be more motivated to take actions that signal that the board is attempting to correct the problem when shareholders are publicly agitating for changes in the company's governance. It is measured as the number of governance-related proxy proposals submitted by the focal firm's shareholders in the prior year.

name: Institutional norms following the Sarbanes-Oxley Act
authors_terms: ["institutional norms", "institutional pressures", "passage of SOX", "SOX legislation", "post-SOX legitimization"]
definition: An interlocking director's latitude to act as a change agent depends upon the presence (or absence) of institutional pressures that constrain (or enhance) his or her ability to influence board decisions; the 2002 enactment of SOX imposed a stringent set of regulations aimed at improving governance quality and resulted in a much stronger set of norms regarding insiders' suitability for board service as well as CEOs' suitability for the board chair position.

name: Return on equity
definition: Return on Equity (ROE in percent) was calculated for each year as the measure of return.

name: Risk
authors_terms: ["risk", "variability in returns", "mean quadratic differences", "absolute differences in returns", "variance of returns"]
definition: Departures from the reference point in either direction are accompanied by a constant or increasing variability in returns, signifying equal or increasing risk, and the reference level is characterized as the level of minimal risk.

name: Reference point
authors_terms: ["reference point", "reference level", "individual reference level", "target level", "estimated reference point (REFw)"]
definition: Prospect theory assumes that choices are evaluated not in relation to an absolute utility but in relation to a subjective reference point, which determines whether an expected outcome is framed as a gain or a loss. The overall context of experience, consisting of past outcomes, expectations, social norms, and levels of aspiration, influences the formation of a reference point for evaluation of prospected outcomes.

name: Average return
definition: As the measure for the average return of individual companies, the median in the time series was chosen to minimize the influence of outliers in short time series.

name: Position relative to the reference point
authors_terms: ["relative position to the reference point", "returns above the reference point", "average relative position (c)"]
definition: An independent variable that controls for the average relative position of a firm to its estimated reference point within a time period, constructed by assigning the value 1 to a dummy variable if a firm had returns above the reference point at time t and zero otherwise and taking the average of this variable for the time period.

name: Return position relative to the industry median
authors_terms: ["above the industry median", "below the industry median", "industry median ROE"]
definition: Fiegenbaum and Thomas chose the industry's median return, within the time period under study, as a proxy for a firm's target level; each industry was divided at its median ROE into below and above median firms.

name: Asset sharing
authors_terms: ["asset sharing", "asset transfer", "relative size of the target to the bidder", "RELSIZE"]
definition: The relative size of the target to the bidder is often used as a proxy for gains from economies of scale and scope (see Seth, 1990b) and in the synergistic acquisitions regression acts as our measure of the potential to realize gains from asset sharing. In the case of asset sharing firms seek to reutilize their existing stock of valuable knowledge in new contexts.

name: Reverse internalization
definition: Gains may also be realized from 'reverse internalization': firms acquire skills and resources from cross-border acquisitions that are expected to be valuable in their home markets. The variable INTANG is a proxy for the reverse internalization hypothesis and is expected to capture the presence and magnitude of intangible assets in the target firm that are of value in combination with the assets of the bidding firm.

name: Market seeking
definition: Acquiring firms that undertake cross-border acquisitions for market-seeking motives are expected to consider targets in markets that are growing faster than their home markets, thereby representing higher growth potential. Firms will invest abroad when growth at home is limited or restricted and in the presence of trade barriers which restrict exports, i.e., for market development opportunities.

name: Financial diversification
definition: If national markets are segmented due to capital controls, information asymmetries and/or exchange controls, it may be possible for firms with multinational operations to realize diversification benefits which create shareholder value. These benefits arise from the reduced variability in the firm's earnings resulting from less than perfect correlation between earnings in different markets.

name: Empire building
authors_terms: ["empire building", "growth-seeking", "growth maximization", "managerial preferences for empire building", "RELSIZE"]
definition: Managerial models of the firm argue that managers pursue sales or growth maximization at the expense of shareholders' welfare. Since managerial compensation frequently is tied to the amount of assets under their control, managers are more likely to seek higher rates of growth in assets than profits.

name: Risk reduction
authors_terms: ["risk reduction", "risk reduction motive", "stabilize the firm's earnings stream", "REDVAR"]
definition: Managers may also have the incentive to engage in diversification activities in an effort to reduce the risk associated with their human capital. Managers may still seek to stabilize the firm's earnings stream by acquiring foreign (rather than domestic) firms, given low correlations between earnings in different countries.

name: Total gains to the combined firm
authors_terms: ["total gain", "TOTGAIN", "degree of value creation", "degree of value destruction", "value creation", "value destruction"]
definition: The total gain associated with the announcement to acquire the target is the difference between the value of the combined firm given the acquisition announcement and the sum of the value of the individual firms if the announcement had not been made. This increase in value is shared between the owners of the acquiring firm and the target.

name: Bidder announcement returns
authors_terms: ["bidder gains", "gains to bidders", "bidder losses", "losses to the acquirer", "CARBID", "abnormal returns to the acquirers"]
definition: We also consider how the different sources of gains are linked to wealth creation for bidding firm shareholders for synergistic acquisitions. We use the event study methodology to estimate abnormal returns to the acquirers and targets.

name: Project size
authors_terms: ["project size", "size of output of an individual project", "dollar amount raised"]
definition: One understudied aspect of the nature of experience is the size of output (e.g., square feet to be built, dollars to be raised) of an individual project. In settings such as underwriting the bulk of firms' activities occur as projects, and projects in these settings vary widely in size.

name: Capability development rate
authors_terms: ["capability development rate", "rate of improvement", "improvement rate", "learning rate", "adaptation rate", "λ"]
definition: The fraction of the gap between a firm's current and potential capability eliminated with each unit of activity; λ is the improvement rate, i.e., the fraction of the capability gap that is closed with each unit of experience.

name: Capability development potential
definition: The maximum capability level a firm could achieve through repeating a given set of activities over time; the maximum capability level a given firm would achieve through repeated activity.

name: Equity underwriting capability
definition: Our dependent variable, equity underwriting capability (capability), is measured using a survey of customer evaluations of banks' capabilities; GA's composite score serves as the measure of a bank's equity underwriting capabilities in a given year. Capability development more generally refers to changes in stocks of knowledge, individual skills, routines, systems, and procedures that enhance firms' performance along specific dimensions.

name: Experience
authors_terms: ["experience", "volume of a firm's experience", "cumulative activity", "deal volume"]
definition: qit is the volume of a firm's experience during that period. Learning occurs through repetition as firms accumulate knowledge, with each unit of activity closing a fraction of the capability gap.

name: Corporate PAC fundraising
authors_terms: ["PAC receipts", "PAC fundraising abilities", "PAC funds", "corporate PAC activity"]
definition: The amounts corporations raise through their political action committees and contribute to federal candidates. The paper explains variation among corporations in their abilities to raise such funds.

name: Federal government purchases
authors_terms: ["government purchases", "financial dependence on government", "dependence on revenues from the federal government"]
definition: The amount the federal government purchases from firms' product markets. Because a direct measure of firms' revenues from the federal government was unavailable, the authors used an index of the percentages of industries' goods and services purchased by the federal government.

name: Government regulation
authors_terms: ["federal government regulation", "governmental regulation", "exposure to governmental regulation"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's task environments are affected by federal government regulation. It was approximated by a five-category industrial classification variable designed to pick up the effects of varying degrees of economic regulation on firms' incentives and abilities to raise PAC funds.

name: Firm assets
definition: A continuous, firm-specific measure of corporate assets. Data on corporate assets came from Forbes (1980).

name: Market concentration
definition: The four-firm market concentration ratio of a firm's industry. A dummy variable equaled 1 if the ratio was greater than or equal to 50 percent and 0 otherwise.

name: Industry unionization
authors_terms: ["unionization", "rates of unionization", "percent of unionization in firms' industries"]
definition: The rate of unionization within a firm's industry, which the authors associate with union power and with political competition from union interest groups.

name: CEO celebrity status
authors_terms: ["CEO celebrity", "celebrity CEO status", "celebrity status", "celebrity CEOs", "star CEOs"]
definition: Celebrity is a unique form of social status that is conferred on CEOs by their peers. The authors build on research on celebrity CEOs, CEOs whom 'experts have anointed as a star performer'.

name: Celebrity recency
authors_terms: ["recent celebrity", "recently attained celebrity", "newly anointed celebrity CEOs", "longer-term celebrity", "recency effect"]
definition: The authors distinguish newly established celebrity CEOs (i.e., recent celebrity) from celebrity status that was granted to CEOs in the past (i.e., longer-term celebrity), arguing that the salience of external appraisals of others tends to diminish over time.

name: Acquisition premiums
definition: Acquisition price premiums are the price that a buyer pays in excess of the prevailing market value of a firm. Acquisition premiums are commonly defined as the acquirer's bid minus the target's preannouncement market value divided by the target's preannouncement market value.

name: Financial performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["financial performance relative to aspirations", "prior firm performance relative to aspirations", "financial performance relative to the industry average returns", "firm performance relative to aspirations"]
definition: Each individual firm's financial performance was measured by using buy-and-hold abnormal returns, and the firm's financial performance relative to aspirations is then calculated by subtracting the portfolio index returns from the individual firm's returns. The study focused on a firm's recent financial performance relative to social aspirations.

name: Sector technology intensity
authors_terms: ["technology intensity of sectors", "research intensity of industrial sectors", "research intensity of the sectors", "so-called high-tech sectors"]
definition: The research intensity of different sectors of industry, i.e., the role technological development plays in several fields. Sectors are distinguished as so-called high-tech sectors and other, medium and low-tech, sectors.

name: Research orientation of strategic technology partnering
authors_terms: ["research orientation of the strategic technology alliances", "research oriented character of strategic technology partnering", "T/M ratio", "technology-market ratio"]
definition: We define the technology-market ratio as the logio of the ratio between a firm's total number of prevailing research inclined strategic linkages and its total number of predominantly market-related strategic linkages. A positive value marks an inclination towards 'pure' technology cooperation; negative scores indicate a dominance.

name: Interorganizational mode of cooperation
authors_terms: ["interorganizational modes of cooperation", "organizational modes of cooperation", "modes of governance", "complex interorganizational modes of cooperation", "contractual arrangements"]
definition: We suggest a contrast between different organizational modes of cooperation with relatively strong modes of interorganizational governance such as joint ventures, research corporations and minority investment on the one hand, and contractual arrangements such as joint R&D agreements, technology exchange agreements, customer-supplier relationships and one-directional technology flows on the other.

name: Basic research motive
authors_terms: ["basic research", "performing basic research", "corporate basic research", "the motive of performing basic research"]
definition: Following Harrigan (1985) we assume corporate basic research to be of little relevance to interfirm technology cooperation. The argument is that either basic research is more or less a free good, for instance provided by a technological infrastructure, or if it is an essential corporate activity as in R&D intensive industries, it comes close to a company's corporate core and as such it is not a desirable subject for collaboration.

name: Specific learning capability
authors_terms: ["specific learning capability", "SLC", "partner-specific learning capability", "competitive learning capability", "competitive alliance learning"]
definition: SLC represents a firm's ability to learn from specific partners; it is developed through the deliberate allocation of resources toward the building of such a capability, including constant observation and information collection through close interactions in prior alliance relationships with the same partner. Unlike the concept of partner-specific absorptive capacity, SLC also incorporates the dimension of competitive learning, meaning that the firm intends to 'out-learn' the alliance partner by developing processes and routines that enable the acquisition of the partner's valuable know-how quicker than the partner.

name: Specific learning capability gap
authors_terms: ["specific learning capability gap", "SLCG", "SLC gap", "gap in their SLCs"]
definition: The authors take a dyadic approach and examine the gap between the two allying firms' SLCs; a higher SLC than its partner suggests that the focal firm has a better understanding of the partner firm's knowledge resources, and may have developed certain organizational mechanisms to acquire more technological knowledge from its partner than the other way around. A positive SLC gap signals to the market that the firm embodies a superior capability for learning know-how from its alliance partner and thus the potential to win a future learning race; a negative value suggests a heightened risk of being out-learned by the partner.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "CAR", "market returns", "stock performance"]
definition: CAR is an ex ante market-based measure of expected returns for a firm participating in a strategic alliance, used as a firm-level indicator of value creation upon the alliance announcement. The authors argue that when the focal firm has a higher SLC than its alliance partner, the market will anticipate superior performance and respond favorably by bidding up its stock price on alliance announcement.

name: Equity alliance governance
definition: Equity alliance governance specifies the rights and obligations of allying firms in terms of ownership shares in the alliance, while non-equity alliances or contractual alliances do not involve equity ownership. Although it facilitates knowledge sharing between partners through frequent interactions, the equity structure is also expected to reduce unintended knowledge leakage and promote long-term collaboration.

name: Market similarity between alliance partners
authors_terms: ["market similarity", "market similarity between partners", "overlap in their respective business markets", "market commonality"]
definition: Firms operating in the same product or technology groups are more likely to compete with each other; with increasing overlap in their respective business markets, firms in alliances are more likely to engage in learning races because they are then competing in both knowledge and customer bases. Market similarity is captured by the relatedness of the two firms' four-digit SIC codes.

name: Partner experience
authors_terms: ["partner experience", "prior exchange experiences", "prior experience with the focal partner"]
definition: Partner experience reflects the extent of experience between exchange partners developed during prior transactions.

name: Partner search
definition: Partner search is reflected by two related dimensions: supplier search time, the total time spent in persondays on supplier and product comparison and selection, and supplier evaluation, the time and effort spent on evaluating and comparing suppliers on four selection criteria.

name: Supplier search time
definition: Supplier search time indicates the actual effort exerted by the buyer to find a 'good' supplier, reflected by the total time spent in persondays on supplier and product comparison and selection.

name: Supplier evaluation
definition: Supplier evaluation reflects the buyer's focus in the search process on criteria considered important for supplier selection and transaction success, and thus measures the time and effort invested by the buyer in evaluating potential suppliers on the four selection criteria.

name: Supplier comparison information
definition: Supplier comparison information involves all potential exchange partners considered for a transaction and is collected before a specific supplier and product or service to be exchanged are chosen, typically during the partner search process.

name: Process and technology information
authors_terms: ["process and technology information", "processes and technology information"]
definition: Buyers may possess information about the processes and technology used by the chosen supplier, which we refer to as process and technology information.

name: Cooperation and dependence information
definition: Buyers may possess future-oriented information that involves expectations about the cooperation with the supplier, how to proceed under changing circumstances (e.g., scenarios), and mutual dependencies caused by cooperating with the supplier. We refer to this type of information as cooperation and dependence information.

name: Interfirm control mechanisms
authors_terms: ["control mechanisms", "use of control mechanisms", "interfirm control structures", "control design"]
definition: We follow Ouchi (1979) to conceptualize interfirm control structures as combinations of outcome and behavior control mechanisms. Jointly, these control mechanisms enable partners to align incentives, safeguard interests, and coordinate and align actions through planning, guiding, monitoring, evaluating, discussing, adjusting, and rewarding suppliers' outcomes and behaviors.

name: Outcome control
definition: Outcome controls specify and measure results to be achieved without interfering in the way that results are obtained.

name: Behavior control
definition: Behavior controls specify and measure desirable behaviors to achieve goals, without necessarily focusing on the extent of goal achievement.

name: Target industry knowledge intensity
authors_terms: ["target industry knowledge intensity", "industry knowledge intensity", "knowledge-intensive industries", "human capital", "general knowledge", "specific knowledge", "informal training"]
definition: This study focuses specifically on knowledge that resides in people—in other words, human capital—and treats knowledge as an input in the production process, where industries vary greatly in the amount and type of the resource used. The value of knowledge-based assets is less certain than that of tangible assets.

name: Bid premium
definition: Typically, a premium above the target's preannouncement stock price is ascribed to expected synergy or preemptive bidding.

name: Proportion of consideration paid in cash
authors_terms: ["percent cash", "noncash payment", "contingent payment", "contingent consideration", "medium of exchange"]
definition: A medium of exchange that is contingent upon the value created, so that noncash consideration is used when buyers are less certain about the actual value that will be created; whereas cash has a fixed value that does not depend on the outcome, stock, securities, or earnouts are more flexible.

name: Negotiation time
definition: The length of the negotiation process, which may be extended when publicly available information is less useful for targets in knowledge-intensive industries and lengthy integrative negotiations are needed to work out the details of an ongoing relationship.

name: Tender offer
definition: Tender offers also affect the amount of information available from the target. These arms-length transactions provide relatively limited opportunities for information exchange.

name: Related expertise
definition: Relatedness is the extent to which the buyer and target industries draw on similar forms of expertise.

name: Perceptions of the entrepreneur
authors_terms: ["perceptions of the founding entrepreneur", "perceptions of the entrepreneur", "assessments of the entrepreneur", "positive assessments of entrepreneurs", "EP"]
definition: Angel investors also relied on their personal observations of the founding entrepreneur. Angel investors considered their assessment of the entrepreneur to be the most important component of their decision to invest, and they reported relying heavily on their intuitive assessments of the entrepreneur.

name: Business viability data
definition: Business viability data comprised ''hard data,'' or information gathered from the business plan and financials or their own research. Investors attended to any numerically measurable information, such as potential market size, industry growth projections, or the entrepreneur's background, to assess the potential profitability of an investment.

name: Investment propensity
authors_terms: ["propensity to invest", "investment amount", "invest more", "likely to invest"]
definition: Investors' propensity to invest was measured using a 1-5 Agree-Disagree Likert scale on which investors assessed the extent to which they were presented an opportunity in which they would likely invest. In addition, we measured an assessment of probable investment amount based on the current state of the venture.

name: Extraordinarily profitable investment
definition: Generally, any venture that has undergone a successful exit, either from a successful acquisition or by going public through an IPO, or any venture that carries with it a large return to the investor, such as in the order of 10 times or greater return on investment, can be characterized as a homerun.

name: Venture performance
definition: Following Kerr, Lerner, and Schoar (2011), we used three categories of outcomes to measure entrepreneurial performance: venture survival, venture growth, and venture financing.

name: Funding decision
definition: The funding decision (by the competition judges) was based on real outcomes from the pitch competitions. We assigned a value of 1 to all entrepreneurs who received funding from the pitch competition and a value of 0 to all entrepreneurs who did not receive funding from the pitch competition.

name: Cultural attractiveness
definition: We define 'CA' as the desirability of a culture for members of another culture, based on the extent to which the former culture's practices reflect the latter culture's values.

name: Country reputation
definition: Reputation denotes a perception formed via public knowledge about an entity and its attributes. The reputation ascribed to a given entity is based on information of its past actions and decisions; for countries, these actions consist of the behaviors of a country's members and leaders.

name: Foreign direct investment inflows
definition: This variable captures the aggregate country-level FDI flow from a home into a host country in a given year. FDI is a momentous step of strategic importance and unusual uncertainty for MNEs resulting from the scale of capital committed to a less familiar foreign country.

name: Cross-border acquisition performance
definition: The performance of cross-border acquisitions, captured by whether the acquisition event had a positive or negative effect on acquirer shareholder wealth.

name: Stakeholder management
definition: Managing relationships with primary stakeholders - those stakeholders who bear some form of risk as a result of having invested some form of capital, human or financial, something of value, in a firm - including employees, customers, suppliers, community residents and the environment. Effective stakeholder management can constitute intangible, socially complex resources that may enhance firms' ability to outperform competitors in terms of long-term value creation.

name: Social issue participation
definition: Social issue participation refers to elements of corporate social performance that fall outside of the direct relationships to primary stakeholders, pertaining to a more 'broad' definition of social responsibility beyond the primary stakeholder exchange.

name: Shareholder value creation
authors_terms: ["shareholder value creation", "shareholder value", "shareholder wealth creation", "market value added", "MVA"]
definition: MVA is simply the difference between the cash that both debt and equity investors have contributed to a company and the value of the cash that they expect to get out of it. Essentially, MVA is the stock market's estimation of net present value.

name: Relative exploration
authors_terms: ["relative exploration", "proportion of exploratory alliances", "proportion of exploratory collaborations"]
definition: We capture the composition of two firms' collaborative portfolio using the concept of relative exploration, defined as the proportion of exploratory collaborations among all collaborations between a firm and its partner.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["competitive aggressiveness", "competition against its partner", "product-market competition with its partner"]
definition: Following prior studies, we measured the extent of competition in product markets that a firm undertakes against its partner using competitive aggressiveness, describing both the intensity and diversity of the firm's competitive actions.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: Relational embeddedness, reflected in repeated alliance ties between two firms, emphasizes cohesive and reliable relationships.

name: Positional embeddedness
definition: Positional embeddedness, reflected in network centrality, manifests a firm's status and power within the overall network.

name: Structural embeddedness
definition: The term structural embeddedness refers to the extent to which two firms are connected by common third parties: the more common ties the partners have, the more structurally embedded they are.

name: Equity stake misalignment
definition: The degree to which a parent's equity stake in a subsidiary departs from what would be theoretically expected given the uncertainty surrounding the subsidiary; it is measured as the residual, that is, the difference between the observed and predicted value, and its absolute value is used.

name: Equity stake adaptation
definition: Adaptation takes the form of adjusting the equity stake to be more consistent with what is optimal given the conditions in a given host country. Adaptability is conceptualized as encompassing the abilities to diagnose, orchestrate, and implement purposeful, alignment-enhancing adjustments.

name: Adaptation experience
authors_terms: ["Adaptation Experience", "direct experience", "experience with adapting equity stakes", "experiential learning"]
definition: The firm's own experience with the specific task of subsidiary ownership adaptation in the same national host environment, because the uncertainty conditions being adapted to are inherently local.

name: Vicarious adaptation learning
definition: Learning from the experience of other firms: exposure to other foreign firms adapting their equity stakes in their subsidiaries in a given host country, which helps the firm to recognize when its own equity stake is misaligned and how to make adaptations.

name: Cash holdings
definition: The parent firm's fungible slack resources, measured by its cash holdings, which are fully fungible and can be converted at any time for any purpose.

name: Ownership of value chain activities
authors_terms: ["ownership", "ownership patterns", "formal equity-based control of activities along the value chain", "vertical integration", "integration choice"]
definition: The authors contrast 'outsourcing' based on formal contracts with external parties, which they refer to as contracting, with formal equity-based control of activities along the value chain, which they term ownership. Ownership is supposed to provide the mechanism of fiat for adapting to disturbances, and the ownership mode is assumed to grant effective control rights over the associated activities in the value chain.

name: Variability of product attributes
definition: We term variability as any deviation in a production or service delivery process that yields products or services whose attributes differ from the firm's stated target specifications. Variability is expressed by lower variance in those attributes and higher reliability.

name: Organizational experience
definition: Cumulative experience is the cumulated number of patient encounters at the ED, accumulated over an organization's history and allowed to depreciate by a fixed parameter each year. In sum, the cumulative patient experience variable reflects the cumulative number of patients treated by the focal ED over time, on a logarithmic scale and accounting for depreciation in the effects of more distant patient encounters.

name: Performance problems
definition: The ED mortality rate variable tracks the percentage of patients seen by the ED who die within the department, used as an indicator of the quality and effectiveness of care received directly within the ED.

name: Constraint event volume
authors_terms: ["constraint event volume", "volume of constraint events", "cumulative diversion hours"]
definition: The volume of constraint events refers to the number of these instances within a fixed period of time; busier organizations are reflected through a higher overall volume of constraint events (e.g., a larger share of operating hours or production runs during the period that are affected by constrained capacity).

name: Constraint event balance
authors_terms: ["constraint event balance", "balance of constraint events", "cumulative diversion balance"]
definition: Their balance refers to the spread (rather than clustering) of these events across that time period. The cumulative diversion balance variable takes higher values when constraint events occur more smoothly across months during these years, and lower values when the events are more clustered or sporadically distributed over this timeframe.

name: Earnings pressure
definition: "We define earnings pressure as the tension felt by management about meeting or beating analysts' earnings forecasts." It results from the divergence between analysts' and management's earnings expectations and the market penalties for missing forecast consensus.

name: Capacity utilization
authors_terms: ["capacity utilization", "capacity utilization rate", "output relative to available capacity"]
definition: "Because earnings pressure takes place over a short period (a quarter or a year), we focus on its effect on determining output relative to available capacity, also known as capacity utilization."

name: Capacity share
definition: One of the four general dimensions of pricing power the authors focus on: "the capacity share dominance of a firm within a particular market." "When a firm with a dominant capacity share restricts output, it creates a price 'umbrella' that benefits its remaining output in the market."

name: Market concentration
definition: "A firm's ability to act as a price maker depends on the likely responses by other incumbents. If the firm faces a fragmented market structure with many competitors, this could reduce the short-term benefit of restraining output, since these competitors are likely to expand output accordingly."

name: Goal heterogeneity among competitors
authors_terms: ["goal heterogeneity among competitors", "for-profit rivals' capacity share", "market presence of for-profit competitors", "for-profit competitors"]
definition: "In some industries and markets, competitors have heterogeneous governance and strategic objectives... This heterogeneity of objectives is believed to complicate oligopolistic coordination and therefore increase competition." In the electricity industry investor ownership is complemented by government, municipal and cooperative ownership.

name: Competitors' capacity constraints
definition: "A firm's ability to exercise market power is limited if its competitors can easily and quickly expand capacity utilization to take advantage of the resulting residual demand."

name: Dominant rivals' earnings pressure
authors_terms: ["dominant rivals' earnings pressure", "earnings pressure by dominant competitors"]
definition: "To examine this cross-rival effect, we calculated dominant rivals' earnings pressure for each firm in each market, as the average of the earnings pressure measures of the publicly traded rivals in the focal market (excluding the focal firm), weighted by their respective capacity shares."

name: Consumer devaluation
definition: Evaluations that express consumer disappointment, in particular, can point to a negative disparity relative to expert evaluations of the same organization. We refer to this negative disparity as devaluation.

name: Likelihood of organizational public response
definition: The present study focuses on the decision of organizations to publicly respond to the market identity threat posed by consumer devaluations.

name: Justification in public responses
definition: To encompass the rationale and substance of responses, we refer to the concept of justification, focusing on its external connotation, which is described as an effort of organizations 'to make their actions logical and defensible' and 'to demonstrate evidences of rationality.' Justification entails 'rationalizing efforts' and 'deflection efforts.'

name: Organizational reputation
definition: We build on the existing literature and define reputation as the 'degree to which stakeholders evaluate an organization positively on a specific attribute, such as its ability to produce quality products.'

name: Market identity
definition: The concept of market identity differs from that of organizational identity because it involves the shared representations not only of internal members, but also of external experts certifying organizational claims. According to the sociological perspective, category membership defines the market identity of an organization and limits the range of its expected behaviors in the eyes of stakeholders.

name: Performance gap
definition: A performance gap is 'a discrepancy between an organization's current performance and potential performance' that triggers search activities. It is operationalized by accumulating the industry-adjusted profitability of the firm over 5 years, using industry-level profitability with the firm's sales breakdown into 3-digit SIC industries as a weighting factor.

name: Knowledge applicability
authors_terms: ["knowledge applicability", "applicability of the firm's knowledge base", "human resource profile dissimilarity"]
definition: The direction of search and selection is determined by the possibility of utilizing the firm's existing knowledge base after controlling for industry characteristics. The authors approximate the similarity of the knowledge base between firms and target industries with a human resource profile dissimilarity variable.

name: Similarity to prior entries
authors_terms: ["human resource profile dissimilarity measured from the previous entries", "sequential search"]
definition: Proposition 3 predicts that firms sequentially enter industries from more similar industries to less similar ones based upon experiences from previous entries; the measure is the human resource profile dissimilarity of a target industry evaluated from the closest industries that a firm previously entered at time t - 1.

name: Entry
definition: Entry and exit activities are understood as search and selection undertaken by the firm to improve its performance. Entry is defined by a number of establishments corresponding to each SIC industry from zero to a positive number.

name: Exit
definition: Exit and entry are two integral aspects of the decision on the scope of the firm, and exit is defined by change in the number of establishments from a positive number to zero, measured at 4-digit SIC.

name: Extensive search
definition: An extensive search takes place along a new knowledge dimension; the authors identify entry into a new 3-digit SIC industry (i.e., in which the firm did not previously operate) as extensive search.

name: Intensive search
definition: An intensive search does not need to acquire any additional knowledge; it only requires exploitation of an existing knowledge base. Subsequent entry into a 4-digit SIC industry within an existing 3-digit industry is characterized as intensive search.

name: Extensiveness of previous search
authors_terms: ["extensiveness of a firm's previous search activity", "extensive/intensive ratio"]
definition: The momentum of continuing the same type of search, measured as a ratio of extensive search to the total entry at the previous time period in terms of sales.

name: Accumulated extensive search
definition: The threshold effects that contribute to switching into another search mode, measured as a proportion of sales from businesses that a firm entered through extensive search from 1981 until time t - 1 to total sales of the firm.

name: Profitability change
authors_terms: ["change in ROA and OCF", "performance change", "improved profitability", "corporate performance"]
definition: The change in ROA and OCF that can be attributable to entry and exit activities during 1981-89; performance change is measured by subtracting the 3-year average of profitability in 1978-80 from the 3-year average of profitability in 1990-92, both in absolute terms and industry-adjusted.

name: Presence of a firm group
authors_terms: ["presence of a group of firms", "employment shares of various groups of firms", "foreign firms' presence"]
definition: Spillover effects are the positive influences caused by the presence of a group of firms on members of another group, which enhance the latter's chances of survival; competition effects are the negative influences caused by the presence of a group of firms on members of another group, which decrease the latter's chances of survival.

name: Non-HMT foreign firm presence
authors_terms: ["non-HMT foreign firms", "National non-HMT Foreign Firms' Employment", "Regional non-HMT Foreign Firms' Employment"]
definition: Non-HMT foreign firms come from outside Greater China and most possess transferable proprietary assets that local firms cannot access, but lack the locally embedded resource advantages enjoyed by indigenous firms and, to some extent, by the HMT firms.

name: HMT firm presence
authors_terms: ["HMT firms", "National HMT Firms' Employment", "Regional HMT Firms' Employment"]
definition: Because of the unique historical and social linkages between Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan and mainland China, HMT firms share many Chinese characteristics and differ substantially from the non-Chinese multinationals; because of their cultural origin, they enjoy some access to local knowledge and locally embedded resources.

name: Reformed local firm presence
authors_terms: ["reformed local firms", "National Reformed Local Firms' Employment", "Regional Reformed Local Firm's Employment"]
definition: 'Reformed local firms,' including private firms, shareholding firms, and limited liability firms, comprise the modernized and restructured Chinese companies; their number increased rapidly as conventional local firms declined.

name: Firm survival
definition: We treat Survival as a dichotomous variable that notes survival/exit. Exit occurs when a valid observation at time t does not show up in the database at time t + 1.

name: Market commonality
definition: Market commonality refers to the extent of market overlap among competitors, and the concept of market is broad enough to encompass geographic market, market segment, and brand.

name: Resource similarity
definition: Resource similarity indicates the extent to which competitors possess comparable types and levels of strategic endowments.

name: Lateral centralization
authors_terms: ["lateral centralization", "strategic role of lateral centralization", "subsidiary strategic role"]
definition: A foreign subsidiary with a strategic role of lateral centralization has worldwide responsibility for a complete set of value activities associated with a particular product or product line. Specialized knowledge about the product or product line resides in the subsidiary, with the subsidiary managing the research and development, production and marketing activities on a global basis.

name: Subsidiary autonomy
definition: Subsidiary autonomy is defined as the degree to which the foreign subsidiary of the MNC has strategic and operational decision-making authority.

name: Headquarters supervision
definition: Headquarters supervision refers to members of the subsidiary top management team who are from corporate headquarters; it is the presence at the foreign subsidiary of MNC headquarters personnel in positions that enable them to monitor subsidiary management behavior.

name: Bureaucratic monitoring
definition: Bureaucratic monitoring mechanisms are defined as information collected by headquarters concerning subsidiary management's actions and decisions.

name: Outcome measurability
definition: Outcome measurability is the degree to which the foreign subsidiary manager's outcomes are specifiable and quantifiable.

name: Industry volatility
definition: Industry volatility refers to the degree to which conditions fluctuate within the foreign subsidiary's industry.

name: Host country volatility
definition: Host country volatility refers to the stability of conditions in the host country in which the foreign subsidiary operates, particularly the stability of economic and political conditions.

name: Monetary incentive compensation
definition: Financial incentives are used to align MNC headquarters and subsidiary management goals, in which a portion of subsidiary management's compensation is outcome-based.

name: Headquarters-subsidiary interdependence
definition: International interdependence refers to the condition in which one subsidiary or subunit of the MNC relies on another subunit's activities or inputs in order to perform its role effectively; the headquarters-subsidiary version concerns interdependence between the foreign subsidiary and headquarters.

name: Inter-subsidiary interdependence
definition: International interdependence can be defined as the state in which the outcomes of a foreign subsidiary of a MNC influence or are influenced by the actions of another unit within the firm operating in a different country; the inter-subsidiary version concerns interdependence among foreign subsidiaries.

name: Vertical integrating mechanisms
definition: Vertical integrating mechanisms consist of various types of contact and communication between the managers of foreign subsidiaries and headquarters managers, with the goal of creating a shared understanding between subsidiary and headquarters management regarding the interests of the overall corporation and the role of the subsidiary.

name: Lateral integrating mechanisms
definition: Lateral integrating mechanisms refer to activities that facilitate contact among managers of different foreign subsidiaries, with the purpose of developing in subsidiary managers an understanding of the role of their particular subsidiary and of other subsidiaries in meeting overall corporate goals.

name: Non-monetary career-related rewards
authors_terms: ["non-monetary career-related rewards", "non-monetary career related rewards", "career-related rewards"]
definition: Non-monetary incentives related to the manager's career within the organization, such as expatriate assignments that provide managers with a more complete understanding of the firm's worldwide goals and activities.

name: Non-monetary subsidiary-related rewards
definition: Non-financial incentives in which the subsidiary manager receives additional resources from the MNC with which to better manage his or her subsidiary, such as additional managerial capabilities or the transfer of technology or know-how developed in other parts of the organization.

name: Replication
authors_terms: ["replication", "effort aimed at creating activities at one location that are identical to those at another location", "copying practices exactly"]
definition: I define replication as effort aimed at creating activities at one location that are identical to those at another location.

name: Adaptation
authors_terms: ["adaptation", "effort toward the goal of modifying or combining practices from a source unit"]
definition: I define adaptation as effort toward the goal of modifying or combining practices from a source unit.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: Replication and adaptation are modes, then, by which organizations accomplish knowledge transfer, which I define as the acquisition from another unit of useful information or practices.

name: Discrete knowledge
definition: A firm's knowledge is more discrete when it is more self-contained, with fewer connections to actors outside the firm, such as customers, suppliers, or local institutions and infrastructure.

name: Understanding of knowledge
definition: I define understanding of knowledge to represent two capabilities: the ability to predict how a change in one area of knowledge will affect other parts of the organization and the ability to identify the essential elements of a set of practices.

name: Performance of the receiving unit
authors_terms: ["performance at the receiving unit", "performance improvements at the receiving unit", "improvements in efficiency"]
definition: The performance of the receiving firm is measured as improvements in efficiency in the year after the knowledge transfer relationship was founded.

name: Market dominance
definition: Dominance can be defined as the observed pattern on the part of a firm to develop and maintain a strong and clear lead in market share over all other competitors for a prolonged period of time. Market share has generally been accepted as a measure of the dominance of a firm over its industry.

name: Purchase significance
authors_terms: ["significance of purchase", "purchase significance", "significance that consumers attach to the purchase"]
definition: A key aspect in which industries differ from each other is with regard to the significance that consumers attach to the purchase of their products, a distinction made between products that are purchased more frequently and those that are purchased less frequently. Consumers are likely to attach more significance to the purchase of shopping goods because of factors such as their higher purchase cost and the length of time that they are expected to last.

name: Convergence of consumer tastes
authors_terms: ["convergence of tastes", "convergence in tastes", "convergence of demand patterns", "demand convergence"]
definition: Another important aspect in which industries differ from each other lies in the extent of convergence or similarities in the tastes of their consumers that they have been able to develop. In industries that are characterized by a high degree of convergence in tastes, the bulk of sales come from a relatively narrow line of products that tend to satisfy the needs and tastes of almost all available consumers.

name: Information salience
definition: Industries differ significantly in the amount of product information that is available through several different types of channels to most existing or potential consumers. Greater levels of advertising can reduce reputational asymmetries by providing customers with easy access to information about competing products.

name: Coach's preferred strategy
definition: A coach's preferred strategy is the strategy the head coach used the most over the past 5 to 10 seasons; most coaches prefer one strategy over another as a guiding philosophy, or system, that stems from their own education, training, and experience.

name: Actual strategy
definition: The strategy a team actually implemented, defined as the one emphasized the most; coaches adopt a chosen strategy more congruent with the skills of the existing players when the team lacks the capabilities for the preferred strategy.

name: Strategy consistency
definition: Whether the team's actual strategy is consistent with the coach's preferred strategy, coded 1 for consistent and 0 for inconsistent.

name: Importance of recruit skills
definition: The importance a coach placed on each of the characteristics for which recruits were evaluated when recruiting players to implement his preferred strategy.

name: Human resource capabilities
authors_terms: ["team skills", "human resource capabilities", "human resource skills", "human capital pool"]
definition: The capabilities of the team's human capital pool, assessed as the level of skills the team as a group showed in the previous season.

name: Team performance
definition: How well the team performed, assessed both as a results or bottom-line measure (Sagarin's rankings) and as a behavioral measure (the coach's evaluation of day-to-day performance).

name: Task environment sector
authors_terms: ["sectors of the task environment", "task environmental sectors", "business environmental sector", "regulatory agencies"]
definition: Organizations interact with different sectors of the task environment, such as raw material suppliers, competitors, customers, suppliers of capital, labor, and regulatory agencies.

name: Sector importance
authors_terms: ["importance of each sector of the task environment", "importance of government actions", "perceptions of importance"]
definition: The importance respondents assigned to each sector of the task environment in the firm's planning and goal-setting activities.

name: Sector predictability
definition: The organization's ability to predict changes in the actions of a sector of the task environment.

name: Sector controllability
definition: The organization's ability to control for the effects of a sector of the task environment.

name: Organizational adjustments
definition: Miles (1975) classified organizational adjustments as changes in procedures, personnel, processes, structures, and strategies.

name: Adverse regulatory practices
authors_terms: ["adverse characteristics of regulatory agencies", "adverse practices of regulatory agencies", "specific characteristics of regulatory agencies"]
definition: Regulatory agencies differ in terms of the frequency of their contacts and of their inspections of firms, in their effects on managerial morale, in the magnitude of record-keeping costs imposed on firms, in the type of attitude and dispositions exhibited by inspectors in their routine inspections, and in the degree to which they are able to provide information on new requirements or interpretations of existing regulations.

name: Firm size
definition: Number of employees was used as the measure of firm size.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["firm age", "age of the organization", "age of firms"]
definition: Age, measured by the number of years of operation, was obtained from the questionnaire.

name: Industry
definition: Two industries with different public and regulatory exposure were deliberately selected, high technology/electronics and wood products; the two industries differ in one important dimension, stage of development.

name: Managerial assessments of regulatory relationships
authors_terms: ["managerial assessments of regulatory relationships", "managerial perceptions of agency relationships", "assessments of agency issues", "managerial perceptions of adverse regulatory practices"]
definition: The study relates firm size and age to managerial perceptions of agency relationships. These assessments comprise managers' ratings of the importance, predictability, and controllability of regulatory agencies, the characteristics of regulatory agencies they consider adverse, and the adjustments made in response to regulatory actions.

name: Differential benefits
authors_terms: ["differential benefits", "differences in partner benefits", "differences in partners' total benefits from an alliance"]
definition: Differential benefits refer to differences in partners' total benefits from an alliance, and they may arise in two ways. Differential benefits arise when an alliance partner gains more benefits than its counterpart which may stem from private benefit extraction and an unequal distribution of common benefits.

name: Common benefit potential of the alliance
authors_terms: ["common benefit potential of the alliance", "expected common benefit potential of the alliance", "CB"]
definition: The common benefit potential of a JV stems from the attractiveness of the JV's focal business and the complementary nature of the combination of partner resources. The right-hand side of the inequality comprises the expected common benefits of the alliance (CB), the partners' shares in common benefits, and the rate of reduction in the common benefit potential arising from opportunistic behavior.

name: Distribution of common benefits
authors_terms: ["distribution of common benefits", "unbalanced distribution of common benefits", "partners' respective shares (sx/y) in the common benefits of the alliance"]
definition: Sharing the expected common benefits of the alliance is an incentive alignment factor fostering mutual forbearance and deterring opportunistic behavior, and the way common benefits are shared also has vital implications for cooperative behavior. As one partner's share in the common benefits of the alliance increases, the other partner's share inevitably decreases.

name: Task interdependence
definition: Task interdependence refers to the extent to which partners' activities are linked by resource exchanges.

name: Dominant operational control
authors_terms: ["dominant operational control", "dominant operational control rights", "allocation of operational control"]
definition: The coordination requirements also make the allocation of operational control a central concern in alliance management, which involves assigning a hierarchy of managers with decision-making authority over mechanisms for behavior and output control. Operational control rights predominantly feature the appointment of top management in the alliance.

name: Entrepreneurial opportunity cost
authors_terms: ["opportunity cost", "opportunity costs", "entrepreneurial opportunity cost", "opportunity cost of entrepreneurship"]
definition: The value to the entrepreneur of the outside alternatives forgone by continuing the venture. The authors state that, all else equal, an entrepreneur with a high opportunity cost will value the option embodied in survival less than an entrepreneur with low opportunity cost, and that the entrepreneur has an opportunity cost for every period the firm survives.

name: Venture quality
definition: A summary measure of all factors that drive success, including the quality of the entrepreneur and of the idea itself, which determines the venture's overall probability of success and its hazard of cash-out and failure.

name: Start-up failure
definition: One of the two absorbing states for a start-up: the venture can fail (i.e., be dissolved), identified in the data as bankruptcy or acquisition on unfavorable terms.

name: Cash-out
definition: One of the two absorbing states for a start-up: a liquidity event consisting of an initial public offering or an acquisition on favorable terms, whichever was earlier.

name: Corporate culture strength
authors_terms: ["strength of corporate culture", "culture strength", "strong corporate cultures", "strength of corporate cultures"]
definition: A culture can be considered strong if those norms and values are widely shared and intensely held throughout the organization. This definition of culture strength entails no assumptions about which values and norms might enhance organizational performance.

name: Firm performance level
definition: The level (as opposed to the variability) of firm performance; corporate performance was measured by the yearly return on invested capital (ROI) and the yearly operating cash flow for the six years from 1979 to 1984.

name: Performance reliability
authors_terms: ["reliability of firm performance", "performance reliability", "performance variability", "reliable performance"]
definition: Performance reliability depends on two factors: the consistency with which a firm performs its organizational routines and the degree to which those routines are well adapted to changing environmental conditions. Reliability was operationalized in terms of the degree of variation about a predicted mean performance level; the greater the variation, the lower the reliability.

name: Industry volatility
definition: The industry volatility measure used below is the yearly mean of the betas for all of the sampled firms in an industry; industries undergoing fundamental change are likely to be characterized by greater uncertainty among investors and hence greater than average volatility in stock-market returns.

name: Market constraint
definition: Industries with higher market constraint scores are internally fragmented and face well-organized suppliers and buyers; Burt et al. (1994) showed that these markets are more competitive and have lower profit margins.

name: Low cost strategy
definition: Second, cost leadership strategies focus on being the lowest cost producers in an industry where cost per unit is minimized.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: Product or service offerings that are perceived industry-wide as being unique reflect differentiation strategies.

name: Asset parsimony strategy
definition: Asset parsimony strategies seek to reduce assets per unit of output. They are suitable for cost leaders operating in stable environments or for differentiators in flexible environments.

name: Firm performance
definition: Returns as used in our hypotheses are defined broadly to include both accounting and market value performance variables to reflect a full range of possible firm objectives.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: In the resource-dependence model, munificence is measured in terms of slack or scarcity of resources.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Complexity can be defined as the number and variety of organizations with which a firm must interact.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism is change that is hard to predict.

name: Environment type
authors_terms: ["environment types", "environment categories", "environment clusters", "Minimum Choice", "Differentiated Choice", "Maximum Choice", "Incremental Choice"]
definition: The distinguishing feature of the Hrebiniak and Joyce model (1985) is the interaction of choice and determinism. In Figure 1 these two are dimensions which define four environment types and the strategy types likely to be successful.

name: Institutional market orientation
authors_terms: ["current institutional environment", "degree of market orientation in the current environment", "degree of market orientation-business freedom-of institutions", "market orientation"]
definition: In the Northian view, institutions create the 'rules of the game' for a firm's activities. The current institutional environment measure captures the degree of market orientation-business freedom-of institutions.

name: Communist founding
authors_terms: ["founding institutional environment", "Communist-founded firms", "market-founded firms", "Communist institutional environment", "market institutional environment"]
definition: Founding in a Communist institutional environment was coded as 1 and founding in a market institutional environment (before or after the Communist influence) was coded as 0.

name: Strength of competitive aspirations
authors_terms: ["strength of competitive aspirations", "strength of aspirations", "strength of aspiration"]
definition: While aspirations are the desired level of future performance for a specific organizational goal (Greve, 1998, 2008), the strength of aspirations is defined as the magnitude of motivation to accomplish a goal (Cavusgil and Nevin, 1981). In other words, the strength of aspirations reflects the priority and/or importance assigned to specific goals of the firm.

name: Entrepreneur traits
definition: We included additional traits in our study that have been proposed as characteristics of successful leaders: tenacity, proactivity, and passion. Entrepreneurship theorists have proposed that tenacity and proactivity-initiative are important for the successful establishment and operation of new ventures.

name: General competency
definition: Competencies here refer to individual characteristics such as the knowledge, skills, and/or abilities required to perform a specific job. We focus on two general and two specific competencies that appear in common in entrepreneurship studies, the general ones being organizational skills and opportunity recognition skills.

name: Specific competency
definition: Boyatzis (1982) found significant performance relationships with 'general' people and organization competencies and 'specific' competencies (technical skill and industry skill). The greater the specific competency of a venture's CEO with respect to industry skill and technical skill, the greater the venture's growth.

name: Situationally specific motivation
definition: In this domain, we chose to study vision, growth goals, and self-efficacy as motivation concepts, because all three concepts have demonstrated significant empirical relationships with business performance and entrepreneurship theorists have pointed to the importance of vision, business goals, and self-efficacy for planning and venture performance. Entrepreneurs' self-efficacy is task-specific self-confidence in relation to their ability to start and 'grow' their ventures.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Following Porter (1980), we conceive of strategy in terms of three broad business-level choices: focus, low cost, and differentiation. Focus (a narrow scope) refers to competitive strategies that target a particular set of customers, segment of a product line, or geographic market; the low-cost strategy involves the construction of efficient-scale facilities and the aggressive pursuit of cost reduction; differentiation strategies are designed to create and market innovative, high-quality products and/or services industrywide.

name: Business environment
definition: This study focused on three dimensions of environment: dynamism, munificence, and complexity. Dynamism (negative stability) refers to the level of environmental predictability; munificence refers to an environment's support for organizational growth; complexity represents the concentration or dispersion of organizations in the environment.

name: Venture growth
authors_terms: ["venture growth", "average annual percent sales growth", "employment growth", "profit growth"]
definition: We chose venture growth as our performance measure, rather than other indicators of performance, because entrepreneurship researchers have pointed to growth as the crucial indicator of venture success.

name: Alliance portfolio
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio", "having an alliance portfolio", "presence of an alliance portfolio"]
definition: Alliance portfolios are defined as the sum of all alliances of a focal firm; firms with only one alliance do not have an alliance portfolio, but firms with two or more alliances do.

name: Alliance portfolio size
authors_terms: ["Number of alliances", "number of partner relationships", "count of the number of alliance partnerships", "number of alliances managed by a young firm"]
definition: The running sum of the total number of alliances in which a firm is active, that is, the number of partner relationships the young firm maintains within its portfolio.

name: Liquidity event likelihood
authors_terms: ["liquidity event", "liquidity event likelihood", "successful outcome", "successful firm outcome"]
definition: Both IPOs and acquisitions are considered liquidity events that allow investors, specifically venture capitalists, to liquidate their equity stakes and, thus, obtain returns on their investments. The authors examine young firms' likelihood of experiencing such an event.

name: Capital raised
authors_terms: ["Capital investment", "total amount of capital investments", "raised capital", "amount of capital raised"]
definition: Being able to raise outside capital is thought to serve as an important signal of a firm's quality to the marketplace, because venture capitalists apply rigorous screening processes and invest only in firms they believe are viable.

name: Functional variety
authors_terms: ["Functional variety (number of domains)", "functional variety experience", "experience with different functional domains", "functional diversity", "functional breadth"]
definition: Functional variety is a running sum of the number of functional domains (including marketing, manufacturing, and R&D) covered by the alliances in a firm's portfolio, so that a greater variety in functions within portfolios signals a broader reach of resources upon which young firms can draw.

name: Functional entropy
authors_terms: ["Functional entropy", "functional 'entropy'", "heterogeneity in distribution of functional alliances"]
definition: The authors refer to the heterogeneity in distribution of functional alliances within a portfolio as functional 'entropy'; the higher the number, the greater the heterogeneity in distribution of functional alliances in a firm's portfolio.

name: Multi-function alliance experience
authors_terms: ["Multi-function combo (number of years)", "Multi-function combo (count)", "multi-function combinations", "multi-function alliances", "combination alliances"]
definition: Each alliance within a portfolio need not belong to a single function, but could consist of multiple functions; multi-function combo experience is the running sum of the number of years in which the firm has had a multi-function alliance and, separately, the running sum of the actual number of multi-function alliances in each year.

name: Functional relationships
definition: The running sum of the number of total functional relationships, regardless of whether they are in single-function or multi-function alliances.

name: IPO likelihood
authors_terms: ["IPO likelihood", "IPO versus acquisition", "IPO outcome", "likelihood of the firm experiencing an IPO"]
definition: The hazard of undergoing an IPO (versus acquisition); the authors argue that an IPO outcome becomes more likely than an acquisition outcome as more of the external market perceives the young firm's viability to be increasing and as the young firm captures the interest of more investors.

name: Parent-progeny transfer
authors_terms: ["parent-progeny transfer", "volume of the parent-progeny transfer", "transfer of resources and routines", "parenting event"]
definition: Whenever personnel leave one organization to found a new organization in the same population, there is a transfer of resources and routines. The volume of resources and routines transferred to the new entity is likely to be a function of the founder's position in the parent organization.

name: Parent-progeny niche overlap
authors_terms: ["similarity of the parent's and offspring's scope", "niche overlap", "parent-progeny similarity", "parent-progeny overlap"]
definition: The parenting event is likely to create a niche overlap between the parent and offspring that arises from similarity in scope.

name: Time since parenting event
authors_terms: ["time since the parenting event", "parenting event clock", "number of years since the occurrence of the most recent parenting event"]
definition: To capture the temporal effect of the parenting event, the number of years since the occurrence of the most recent parenting event was recorded.

name: Founding team parent affiliation
authors_terms: ["proportion of founding members coming from parent organizations", "proportion of the firm's founding team with Silicon Valley parents", "proportion of the founding team with Silicon Valley parents"]
definition: The more a founding team is represented by members with a previous organizational affiliation within the focal population, the more easily the offspring should be able to leverage its resources and routines.

name: Firm age
definition: In measuring firm age, the year in which the law firm was first listed in the directory was considered to be the law firm's first year.

name: Parent firm size
definition: Firm size was operationalized in two ways: the total number of full-time partners and the total number of full-time associates.

name: Parent firm age
definition: In measuring firm age, the year in which the law firm was first listed in the directory was considered to be the law firm's first year.

name: Multiple parents
authors_terms: ["multiple parents", "more than one parent", "more than one Silicon Valley parent"]
definition: Taking a genealogical perspective on organizations also raises the compelling question of the effect on progeny of multiple parents. If routines are key to the transfer from parents to progeny, however, having multiple parents can be costly.

name: Parent firm failure
authors_terms: ["parent failure", "likelihood of parent failure", "firm failure", "organizational failure"]
definition: The year that a firm is no longer listed, or only has one attorney (i.e., is no longer a partnership) was considered the year of failure. A dichotomous variable for firm failure was coded one for the respective year.

name: Progeny firm failure
authors_terms: ["progeny failure", "offspring's likelihood of failure", "likelihood of progeny failure", "firm failure"]
definition: The year that a firm is no longer listed, or only has one attorney (i.e., is no longer a partnership) was considered the year of failure. A dichotomous variable for firm failure was coded one for the respective year.

name: Public tenure
authors_terms: ["public tenure", "the public tenure clock", "Very Low Public Tenure"]
definition: The public tenure clock marks the years a firm has been public, and as described next, we use this variable to assess the timing of initial SSP. Public Tenure equaled the count of years since a firm went public, which we marked by the year a firm's stock price was first quoted on a U.S. exchange.

name: Sustained superior performance
authors_terms: ["sustained superior performance (SSP)", "sustained superiority", "initial sustained superiority", "golden age of sustained superior performance"]
definition: We define sustained superiority to occur when a firm performs well enough across a forward-looking window of time to significantly rule out a random process as a sufficient explanation for the firm's results. Firms meeting these criteria are likely to have unusual capabilities to deal with external change.

name: Entrepreneurial creation
definition: The creation perspective holds that superior opportunities seldom exist ex ante, and managers must construct them step by step, so the metaphor is mountain building, not mountain climbing. A different route is entrepreneurial creation in which firms construct new opportunities step by step - a slower, more complex, and cumulative process.

name: Entrepreneurial discovery
definition: Drawing on Austrian economics, discovery theory holds that many opportunities are based on objective market imperfections, and entrepreneurs are tasked with spotting and quickly exploiting these prospects. In this view, opportunities are like mountains, and entrepreneurs with greater alertness can achieve superior results by being among the first to climb these peaks.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["return on assets (ROA)", "return on invested capital (ROIC)", "annual ROA", "ROA relative to industry-year medians"]
definition: We measured performance by return on assets (ROA) and return on invested capital (ROIC). In what follows, we report results for ROA relative to industry-year medians, which reveal relative advantage.

name: Timing of superior window onset relative to going public
definition: The Fast Superiority dummy, which was time invariant, equaled 1 if a superior window began in the same year a firm went public; it equaled 0 otherwise.

name: Elapsed time within superior window
definition: The Superior Window Clock started at 1 when a firm initially achieved ABSS and increased by 1 each year of a firm's tau-year window.

name: Short-selling-friendly environment
definition: The Reg SHO period is a proxy of a high short-selling risk or short-selling-friendly environment: removing the short-selling restriction for the randomly chosen pilot firms made it significantly easier for traders to short sell the stocks of these firms and substantially increased the risk of short selling for the pilot firms.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["number of outside directors", "outside director representation", "outside directors' presence on the board"]
definition: Outside directors are directors without any direct or indirect relationship with the firm (i.e., former employees, interlocks, and family members of a director or executive); the authors study the number of such directors on the board as the board composition outcome.

name: Outside director network size
authors_terms: ["outside director network", "size of outside directors' networks", "directors' networks"]
definition: Board connections through professional, educational, and personal relationships are a conduit of information exchange, and information is likely to travel outside the firm more effectively and quickly through directors with rich and broad connections.

name: Outside director busyness
definition: Serving on multiple corporate boards significantly increases directors' workload and thus reduces the time and attention they can devote to each board; the authors consider that outside directors are busy if they serve on three or more boards.

name: CEO duality
definition: A clear indicator of the CEO's power on the board is CEO duality; when CEOs serve as the chairperson of the board, they have greater power to direct board members' attention and the agenda of board meetings and to influence the director nominating process.

name: Nonindependent nomination committee
authors_terms: ["nonindependent nomination committee", "ratio of nonindependent directors on the nomination committee", "nonindependence of the nomination committee"]
