definition: Executives and directors under strong influence of the CEO (i.e., gray directors) sometimes sit on the nomination committee and exert direct and indirect influence on the director selection and hiring process; when nonindependent directors sit on the nomination committee it gives the CEO and other executives stronger influence over director nomination and selection.

name: CEO internal performance attributions
authors_terms: ["CEO Internal Attributions of Positive Firm Performance", "CEO Internal Attributions", "internal performance attributions", "internal attributions for a positive earnings surprise"]
definition: A CEO highlights the firm's strategic choices under their leadership as opposed to the external environment as the cause of positive firm performance, a self-serving narrative in which the CEO takes credit for the firm's positive performance outcome.

name: Analyst internal performance attributions
authors_terms: ["Analyst Internal Attributions of Negative Firm Performance", "Analyst Internal Attributions", "analysts' internal attributions of negative firm performance"]
definition: Financial analysts point to the strategies under the CEO's leadership as the cause of the performance downfall, rather than to external environmental factors, when firm performance turns negative.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Dismissal of chief executive officers, where a CEO involuntarily leaves the firm.

name: Expected spread
definition: The magnitude of the percentage spread, ROE - ke, expected to be earned, where ROE is the expected return per year on book equity investment and ke is the cost of equity capital. Value is created when a firm adopts strategies that produce a return which exceeds its cost of equity.

name: Earnings growth rate
authors_terms: ["earnings growth rate", "expected earnings growth rate", "rate of growth of earnings per year, g", "growth"]
definition: The expected annual rate of growth of earnings per year, assumed constant; it results in part from increases in net equity investments through time.

name: Firm value
definition: The warranted market equity value of the firm relative to the book value of equity, expressed as the market-to-book ratio V/B. A firm's management creates value for shareholders if V>B and destroys value if V<B.

name: Duration of exceptional spread
authors_terms: ["the number of years, n, during which future investment opportunities will be available", "the number of years over which the firm is expected to maintain its current ROE"]
definition: The number of years over which the firm is expected to maintain its current ROE and during which future investment opportunities will be available.

name: Noncompete enforceability
definition: The degree to which covenants not to compete are enforceable in a court of law, which varies considerably across states; for a given set of facts, workers in states with greater enforceability find it harder to win CNC-related litigation. Enforceability relates to whether the enforcement can withstand legal scrutiny, as opposed to the choice to enforce.

name: Within-industry spinout status
definition: Spinouts formed in the same industry as the parent firm are within-industry spinouts (WSOs); non-WSOs include spinouts formed in different industries from parent firms (out-of-industry spinouts or OSOs) and other types of new firms.

name: New firm entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rate", "rate of entry of WSOs", "entry rate of non-WSOs"]
definition: The number of new firms of each type (all new firms, WSOs, and non-WSOs) divided by the number of firms in the state-industry-year, with the data aggregated to the state-industry-year level.

name: Initial firm size
authors_terms: ["initial size", "average initial size", "minimum initial size", "maximum initial size"]
definition: The size of a new firm in its first year, as measured by employment in the first year; initial size is determined by the founders' human capital, so the minimum initial size of WSOs increases with enforceability.

name: Later-life firm size
authors_terms: ["later-life size", "log of employment at years 3, 5, and 7"]
definition: Firm size measured by employment three, five, and seven years after formation.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["survival probability", "probability of survival", "survive one, two, and three years"]
definition: Whether a new firm survives its initial years, measured by dummies for surviving one, two, and three years.

name: Founder human capital
authors_terms: ["founder human capital", "founders' human capital", "founders' earnings at the parent firm", "pre-founding earnings"]
definition: The human capital of a potential founder, which the authors assume is positively correlated with the new firm's profits and size, so that high human capital founders are better able to assemble more and higher-quality resources for their venture. Founders' earnings at the parent firm are assumed to be positively correlated with their level of human capital.

name: Parent firm size
authors_terms: ["parent firm size", "parent establishment size", "relative size of spinout"]
definition: The size of the predecessor establishment from which the founding cluster moved, which is defined as the parent; larger firms are more likely to win CNC litigation due to their resource advantage, so the litigation threshold is lower for larger parent firms.

name: Human capital of hired employees
authors_terms: ["average human capital of the employees hired", "higher-quality individuals", "employee characteristics", "average education of a new hire"]
definition: The quality of the employees a new firm hires; the framework predicts that if the hiring cost effect dominates, fewer firms will hire but the average human capital of the employees hired will be higher, and the authors interpret their results as showing that firms that grow hire higher-quality individuals.

name: Market orientation
definition: Market orientation is an ideology that places the highest priority on the creation and maintenance of superior customer value, and that urges employees to develop and exploit market information (Narver and Slater, 1990). Drawing from Narver and Slater (1990), market orientation is composed of three subcomponents: customer orientation (understanding customers' needs and wants), competitor orientation (understanding rivals' strengths and weaknesses and how they are satisfying customers' needs and wants), and interfunctional coordination (the firmwide use of the organization's resources in creating superior customer value).

name: Market information processing
definition: Thus, in our study, MIP encompasses generation of information pertaining to customer's needs, dissemination of that information organization-wide, and the process by which shared interpretation of the information arises. While devotees of Kohli and Jaworski (1990) refer to their conceptualization as market orientation, it is relabeled here as market information processing to avoid using 'market orientation' to refer to two different concepts.

name: Organizational responsiveness
definition: Responsiveness is a firm's propensity to act based on knowledge gained (Jaworski and Kohli, 1993).

name: Firm performance
definition: Three objective formative indicators (ROI, ROA, and ROE) obtained via Compustat and annual reports were used to assess performance in time t + 1. These measures were taken 1 year after the survey.

name: Within-firm communication
authors_terms: ["within-firm communication", "within-firm communication density", "communication within a firm"]
definition: Communication among workers who belong to the same firm. The authors partition the network data into two blocks, one for the acquiring firm's employees and one for the target firm's employees, and compare within-block with between-block communication.

name: Cross-firm communication
authors_terms: ["cross-firm communication", "between-firm communication", "communication across firms", "communication across firm boundaries"]
definition: Communication between workers from the acquiring firm and workers from the target firm. The authors argue that unless a relationship existed between the firms prior to the acquisition, little communication between workers across firms is likely to occur initially.

name: Time since acquisition announcement
definition: Time equals t0 + n, where t0 is the month in which the acquisition was announced and n equals the number of months after the acquisition. Data from the logs were extracted for analysis at intervals of four months between June 2002 and February 2005.

name: Brokerage positioning
definition: The extent to which a worker is a broker, boundary spanner, or gatekeeper. Betweenness represents the number of times that a worker is positioned along the shortest path (geodesic) between other pairs of workers, each geodesic weighted by the inverse of the number of geodesics connecting the pair.

name: Communication efficiency
definition: A worker who efficiently communicates is one who can communicate with all workers by using few intermediaries; efficiency is the amount of time until whatever is flowing (e.g., information, knowledge, gossip) arrives at its destination, so higher efficiency equates to earlier arrivals.

name: Common knowledge base
authors_terms: ["common knowledge base", "same job title", "shared language and knowledge"]
definition: The extent to which workers share common languages and practices, which makes knowledge assimilate more quickly because workers find it easier to communicate their ideas. Employees from a target firm are more likely to interact with employees from an acquiring firm whose knowledge base is closer to their own.

name: Task interdependence
definition: The extent to which work elements (e.g., workers, work units) are interrelated such that the elements affect each other. The authors focus on reciprocal interdependence, work in which there is extensive interaction and inputs and outputs move back and forth between workers, requiring continuous feedback and adjustment.

name: Cross-firm relationship
definition: A relationship between workers who belong to different firms — one employee from the acquiring firm and one from the target firm. The authors note that managers may seek to create relationships across firm boundaries to encourage knowledge transfer between the firms.

name: Predating insiders
authors_terms: ["proportion of insiders appointed before the CEO", "percentage of insiders who predate the CEO", "% insiders predating CEO"]
definition: Inside directors whose appointments predate that of the current CEO, who are argued to be more likely political contestants of the CEO than allies because a CEO is less likely to be committed to directors appointed by a predecessor and these directors are more likely to have been rival candidates for the CEO's position.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "power of the CEO in the board", "executive power"]
definition: The power a CEO exercises relative to other elite constituencies, which the authors argue should make it more likely that the CEO influences the firm's board structure and composition. Following Finkelstein (1992) they consider three aspects of the CEO's power: duality, stock ownership, and functional background.

name: CEO-only board structure adoption
definition: A board structure in which the CEO is the only insider on the board, which the authors describe as a variant of the supermajority outsider board that creates a structural hole between the organization and the board of directors that the CEO can then fill.

name: Sarbanes-Oxley period
definition: The new regime of corporate governance triggered by the adoption of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, under which board independence received increasing board attention and the power and perceived importance of CEOs with finance backgrounds was likely enhanced.

name: Change in firm performance
authors_terms: ["change in performance", "positive changes in firm performance"]
definition: A favorable change in firm performance, which the authors argue creates an elaboration opportunity because it is likely to draw attention to the CEO's success and increase the board's evaluation of the CEO's effectiveness, thereby increasing the CEO's influence on new board initiatives.

name: Takeover protection
authors_terms: ["takeover protection", "Delaware takeover protection", "protection from hostile takeovers", "threat of hostile takeovers"]
definition: Takeover protection indicates an array of devices, ranging from firm-specific antitakeover provisions in corporate charters to state antitakeover legislation, which aim to protect the firm from being taken over by a hostile acquirer. These devices reduce the influence of the takeover market, considered the major disciplinary mechanism to enforce managerial attention to the stock price.

name: Corporate attention to stakeholders
authors_terms: ["corporate attention to stakeholders", "attention to stakeholders", "attention to non-shareholding stakeholders"]
definition: Attending to stakeholders represents the efforts of the firm to proactively support the interests of primary non-shareholding stakeholders, such as employees, customers, communities, or the natural environment.

name: Attention to community
definition: KLD dimension that reflects how well companies cater to community; community is one of the five KLD dimensions consistently reported between 1991 and 2002 on which the study focuses.

name: Attention to minorities
definition: KLD dimension that reflects how well companies cater to diversity (used to proxy for minorities); minorities is one of the five KLD dimensions consistently reported between 1991 and 2002 on which the study focuses.

name: Attention to employees
definition: KLD dimension that reflects how well companies cater to employees; employees is one of the five KLD dimensions consistently reported between 1991 and 2002 on which the study focuses.

name: Attention to the natural environment
definition: KLD dimension that reflects how well companies cater to the natural environment; the natural environment is one of the five KLD dimensions consistently reported between 1991 and 2002 on which the study focuses.

name: Attention to customers
definition: KLD dimension that reflects how well companies cater to product quality (used to proxy for customers); customers is one of the five KLD dimensions consistently reported between 1991 and 2002 on which the study focuses.

name: Shareholder value
authors_terms: ["shareholder value", "long-term stock market value", "long-term shareholder value", "market-to-book ratio"]
definition: The market-to-book ratio (M/B) is used to calculate shareholder value in the short term (one year into the future) and in the long term (two and three years into the future). Intuitively, the measure equals the ratio of the firm's market value (equity plus debt) to the replacement cost of its physical assets (book value of assets).

name: CEO conscientiousness
authors_terms: ["CEO ' s observed level of conscientiousness", "CEO conscientiousness", "observed conscientiousness"]
definition: 'Conscientiousness' is defined as the tendency to be achievement oriented and self-disciplined as well as cautious, dependable, and deliberate.

name: CEO neuroticism
authors_terms: ["CEO ' s observed level of neuroticism", "CEO neuroticism", "observed neuroticism"]
definition: 'Neuroticism' is the tendency to exhibit emotional instability, which produces a number of cognitive, affective, and behavioral consequences such as higher stress, anxiety, depression, impulsiveness, and difficulty completing tasks.

name: CEO extraversion
authors_terms: ["CEO ' s observed level of extraversion", "CEO extraversion", "observed extraversion"]
definition: 'Extraversion' is the tendency to be sociable, gregarious, and outgoing, as well as ambitious, dominant, and excitement seeking.

name: Firm stock risk
authors_terms: ["firm stock risk", "stock risk", "systematic risk", "market perceptions of firm risk"]
definition: In this study, stock risk is viewed as the risk to shareholders of holding stock in a particular company and is measured as systematic risk, defined as βi estimated from the formula Rit = α + βiRmt + eit, where Rit is the rate of return for stock i during period t and Rmt is the market rate of return during the same period.

name: Shareholder returns
definition: The returns to shareholders of owning a firm's stock, assessed using total shareholder returns (TSR), calculated as the change in share price from the beginning to the end of the fiscal year plus dividends, divided by the beginning share price.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size", "firm's size relative to its competitors"]
definition: A firm's size relative to its competitors has been recognized as an important variable explaining firm strategic behavior and performance. It is measured by the firm's sales, averaged over the time period under analysis.

name: Output flexibility
authors_terms: ["output flexibility", "fluctuation in firm output", "flexibility in output volume", "volume flexibility"]
definition: The firm's flexibility in output volume: the small firm would vary its output over time in response to the changing market conditions, whereas the large firm is more likely to maintain a relatively constant level of output. Volume flexibility of the firm's cost function is represented by how flat the bottom is.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "firm performance", "risk-adjusted measures of return", "firm profit"]
definition: Two measures of returns are considered-namely, return on assets and return on sales. The two measures are divided by risk, measured as the variance of returns during the investigated time period, to create risk-adjusted measures of return.

name: Industry demand volatility
definition: The extent to which industry demand fluctuates over time; the ability to vary output over time is not of much value if the industry demand is very stable over time. Industry volatility is operationalized as the standard deviation of total industry annual sales during the time period under analysis.

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: The degree to which an industry requires capital: a major reason for the steepness of the cost curve is capital intensity. Capital intensity for an industry was calculated as the ratio of assets over sales.

name: Industry profitability
definition: Industries that are characterized by price competition tend to be less profitable than industries in which competition is based on differentiation. Industry average profit was calculated as the ratio of return over sales.

name: Breakthrough innovation
definition: Breakthrough innovations are a subset of innovations that enable firms to challenge the existing technological order and shape new trajectories. Empirically, the authors define them as the most highly cited patents, i.e., the top 2 percent of their sample.

name: Technologically distant national knowledge
definition: External knowledge that is outside the industry's technology classes and originates in the same national context; the authors describe it as technology spanning behavior within geographic boundaries, measured for each original patent as the number of cited patents assigned to a technology class outside the five classes comprising the biotechnology industry whose inventor location was the United States.

name: Technologically proximate international knowledge
definition: External knowledge from other countries but within the industry's technology boundaries, measured as the number of cited patents assigned to a technology class within the biotechnology industry whose inventor location was outside the United States.

name: Technologically distant international knowledge
definition: External knowledge that is both outside the industry's technology classes and originates outside the United States; the authors describe it as technology spanning behavior across geographic boundaries, measured as the number of cited patents outside the five biotechnology classes whose inventor location was outside the United States.

name: Abnormal stock returns
definition: Price reactions to the information reported in the Business Week cover stories, assessed with the market model event study method by examining the statistical significance of abnormal returns on a daily basis as well as cumulating them over a 3-day event period.

name: Board of director rating
authors_terms: ["favorable board of director ratings", "unfavorable board of director ratings", "ratings of boards of directors", "'best' boards of directors", "'worst' boards of directors"]
definition: In 1996 and 1997, Business Week published cover stories that identify the 25 'best' and 25 'worst' boards of directors of publicly traded U.S. corporations, based on a combination of data gleaned from publicly available sources and ratings collected through surveys of professional investors and other corporate governance experts.

name: Expert board ratings
authors_terms: ["expert ratings", "subjective expert ratings", "Board Performance Poll", "Survey Score", "expert survey"]
definition: Subjective expert ratings were derived from data collected in board performance surveys sent to managers of large money-management firms and pension funds, along with legal and academic governance experts; the scores were then aggregated into an overall Survey Score.

name: Board attribute data
authors_terms: ["board attribute data", "Governance Guideline Analysis", "objective ratings", "objective measures", "Governance Guideline Score"]
definition: The objective ratings were created from indicators of 'best practices' articulated by a group of governance experts; the investigators created three objective measures designed to correspond with three of the survey categories, and objective scores were combined into a summary Governance Guideline Score.

name: Geographic distribution of R&D activity
authors_terms: ["geographic distribution of R&D activity", "geographic distribution", "geographic scope", "geographic dispersion"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's new knowledge creation activity is spread over its R&D locations rather than concentrated in a few; the authors stress that when firms expand the geographic scope of their R&D activity, problem solving/new knowledge creation activity may not be equally distributed over all R&D centers.

name: Technological diversity of resources
authors_terms: ["technological diversity", "diversity of technological resources", "technological diversity of a firm"]
definition: The range of technological expertise and knowledge domains in which a firm is active; technologically diverse firms are more likely than technologically focused firms to limit different technological domains of expertise to individual R&D locations, so that as technological diversity increases across a firm, the diversity in any single unit is likely to decrease.

name: Intraorganizational linkages
definition: Ongoing relationships between researchers at different locations that imply the existence of ongoing relationships allowing the sharing and transfer of resources between units, and that enable knowledge sourced from one location to be utilized at a different location.

name: Innovation quality
authors_terms: ["quality of innovation", "quality of a firm's innovation output", "innovation quality"]
definition: The quality of a firm's innovation output defined as its impact, measured as the sum of the number of citations that each of the firm's patents had received; a patent cited by a larger number of future inventors has greater impact than a patent cited by fewer inventors.

name: Common venture capital backing
authors_terms: ["common VC", "common VC investor", "backing by a common VC", "sharing a common VC investor"]
definition: A dyadic measure that takes on a value of 1 if a VC firm invested in both firms within the three years prior to the date of the focal alliance, and 0 otherwise. The authors argue that a common VC can act as an information intermediary that privately and directly reduces information asymmetries between prospective alliance partners.

name: R&D alliance formation
authors_terms: ["R&D Alliance Formation", "likelihood two entrepreneurial ventures in the biopharmaceutical industry partner with each other to form an R&D alliance", "partner selection"]
definition: The likelihood that two entrepreneurial ventures in the biopharmaceutical industry partner with each other to form an R&D alliance; it takes on a value of 1 for realized alliances and zero for dyads of nonrealized transactions.

name: Product development stage
authors_terms: ["product development", "stage of product development", "Firm Product Development", "Partner Product Development"]
definition: A firm's stage of development is indicative of the maturity of its R&D resources and their commercial potential, and firms in early stages of product development present greater information asymmetries and risk of adverse selection to potential partners. It is measured as dummy variables that are equal to 1 if there is at least one drug application approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration agency for the firm at the time of the R&D collaboration, and 0 otherwise.

name: Partner-specific experience
definition: Previous collaborative agreements between firms are very useful in enabling firms to develop an understanding and specific knowledge about one another's technological resources. It is measured as the number of alliances between the firms during the five years prior to the focal alliance.

name: Patent cross-citations
authors_terms: ["cross-citations", "Cross-Citations", "patent cross-citations", "mutually draw on each other's knowledge bases"]
definition: One way in which firms become familiar with each other's technological resources is when they mutually draw on each other's knowledge bases in their prior technological activities such as patenting. It is measured as the number of patent cross-citations between a firm and its potential partner during the five years prior to the date of the focal alliance.

name: Technology relatedness
authors_terms: ["technology relatedness", "Technology Relatedness", "technological similarity", "commonality of firms' technological activities"]
definition: Partner firms can be able to directly assess each other's technological resources insofar as there is commonality among their activities and underlying technological resources. It is measured as the cosine of the angular separation in firms' patents across patent classes, which is often used as a measure of the degree of similarity in two firms' patent portfolios.

name: New field exploration
authors_terms: ["exploring new fields", "exploring a new field", "exploration of new fields", "exploration"]
definition: Exploring new fields is a binary indicator that equals one in the absence of any overlapping class between all prior patents and the focal patent. The authors argue that inventors who explore new fields are exposed to new knowledge, perspectives, and approaches.

name: Invention novelty
definition: The authors conceptualize novelty as a new combination of ideas or components. By their definition, an invention can be novel but not very valuable, valuable but not very novel, or varying degrees of both.

name: Invention value
definition: The authors conceptualize value as the future use or success of the invention. Forward citations are positively correlated with the private economic value of a patent.

name: Collaboration with experts in the new field
authors_terms: ["expert team", "collaborate with experts in the new field", "collaboration with field experts", "collaboration with experts"]
definition: Expert team is a binary indicator that equals one if at least one of the coinventors has a prior patent in the same class(es) as the focal patent. A collaborator with depth in the new field can guide the novice and winnow the novice's worst ideas while keeping the best.

name: Reliance on published science
definition: Science is a binary indicator that equals one if the focal patent cites nonpatent prior art, which are typically scientific publications. Scientific literature provides a map for inventive search and can be particularly helpful for novices who lack prior knowledge and expertise in a field.

name: Managerial stock ownership
authors_terms: ["managerial ownership", "managerial stock ownership", "managerial shareholdings", "TMT managerial ownership", "managerial equity ownership"]
definition: The percentage of equity owned by the top management team, which shifts risk to managers and represents endowed wealth whose value is incorporated into their personal wealth.

name: International diversification
definition: A firm's diversification across geographic markets, captured by both the number of geographic segments and the weight of each segment relative to the firm's sales.

name: Business diversification
definition: A firm's diversification across business segments, measured with an entropy measure over business segments.

name: Firm exploration tendency
authors_terms: ["firm exploration", "a firm's tendency to explore", "exploration tendency", "exploration level of the firm"]
definition: Exploration involves developing knowledge elements that are new to a firm, whereas exploitation entails leveraging and refining the firm's existing knowledge. Increase in the breadth of knowledge across various knowledge domains indicates the firm's tendency to explore.

name: Partner exploration
authors_terms: ["partner exploration", "exploration levels of its alliance partners", "exploration level of its partners"]
definition: The exploration level exhibited by the firm's alliance partners, which the firm observes through vicarious learning; the firm is expected to adjust its own exploration tendency in response to this level up to a threshold.

name: Competitor exploration
authors_terms: ["competitor exploration", "exploration levels of its primary competitors", "exploration level of its competitors"]
definition: The exploration level exhibited by the firm's five primary competitors, another reference group whose behavior the firm tracks and from which it learns vicariously.

name: Firm-specific uncertainty
definition: Firm-specific uncertainty refers to a 'lack of assurance about the probability and outcomes of corporate decisions.' It indicates the difficulty that managers face in predicting environmental trends in light of idiosyncratic internal factors, such as the firm's decisions, capabilities, and strategies.

name: Variation in partner exploration
authors_terms: ["variation in the exploration level of a firm's alliance partners", "variation in partner exploration", "variance in the exploration tendencies of alliance partners"]
definition: Incoherent behavior makes it difficult for the firm to identify the typical tendency in the reference group and to align its exploration tendency accordingly; variation in the exploration levels of partners inhibits monitoring, interpretation and synthesis.

name: Variation in competitor exploration
authors_terms: ["variation in the exploration level of a firm's primary competitors", "variation in competitor exploration", "variance in the exploration tendencies of the five primary competitors"]
definition: When alters in the reference group exhibit inconsistent patterns of exploration, it becomes more difficult to gain legitimacy by following their exploration tendencies, and convergence with the typical tendency is less likely to be deemed appropriate.

name: Technological proximity to partners
authors_terms: ["technological proximity", "technological proximity of a firm's alliance partners", "technological proximity to partners"]
definition: A key aspect of similarity is technological proximity, which refers to the extent of overlap in firms' technical knowledge domains, or 'the degree to which their technological problem-solving focuses on the same narrowly defined areas of knowledge.'

name: Technological proximity to competitors
authors_terms: ["technological proximity to competitors", "technological proximity of a firm's primary competitors"]
definition: Technological proximity refers to the extent of overlap in firms' technical knowledge domains, or 'the degree to which their technological problem-solving focuses on the same narrowly defined areas of knowledge'; applied here to the firm's primary competitors.

name: Institutional quality
authors_terms: ["Quality of Institutions", "quality of institutions", "institutional quality", "weak national institutions", "weak-institution countries"]
definition: Institutions are humanly devised constraints that structure human interactions (North 1990). They include formal rules, laws, and constitutions, as well as informal norms of behavior and conventions; this study focuses on formal institutions.

name: Cross-border supervision
authors_terms: ["differential supervision", "cross-border supervision", "foreign supervision", "local supervision", "allocation of supervisory responsibilities"]
definition: An important but understudied structural choice available to MNCs: differential supervision, or employing local or foreign supervision for their overseas subsidiaries. Local supervision of subsidiaries implies local autonomy for the local supervisory unit and subsidiaries as a group, whereas foreign supervision of frontline subsidiaries implies less local autonomy.

name: Task centrality
authors_terms: ["TaskCentrality", "task centrality", "tasks more central to their parent's global operations"]
definition: TaskCentrality reflects the centrality of the focal subsidiary's task in the MNC's task system. The authors argue that when a subsidiary's task is more tightly integrated into its MNC parent's global network, less local autonomy should be granted.

name: Alliance portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio concentration", "alliance portfolio concentration across geographic units", "concentration of the alliance portfolio across subsidiaries"]
definition: The extent to which the formation of a firm's strategic alliances is concentrated within a limited number of geographic units of the focal firm.

name: Alliance portfolio size
definition: The number of alliances in a firm's alliance portfolio; alliance portfolio size is measured as the sum of all operational alliances of the firm.

name: Firm performance
definition: We rely on Net profit margin to measure focal firms' performance. This measure is calculated by dividing the income before extraordinary items by the total sales.

name: Tacitness of know-how
authors_terms: ["tacitness of the know-how package", "tacitness of know-how", "tacitness"]
definition: The tacitness of the know-how package being transferred. As the need for tacit supporting skills such as marketing and management increases, so does the overall tacitness of the know-how package transferred.

name: Transaction-specific investment
definition: The size of investment that was made specifically to implement the know-how and, thus, could not be easily redeployed for other uses; higher values indicate greater levels of asset specificity.

name: Similarity of routines and culture
authors_terms: ["similarity of routines and culture", "similarity between transferor and recipient in their organizational routines and culture", "commonality in social fabric"]
definition: The extent of overlap in the transferor's and recipient's organizational routines and culture, capturing similarity in operational routines and in corporate culture.

name: Governance mode of know-how transfer
authors_terms: ["mode of know-how transfer", "internal transfer", "choice of equity joint venture", "market-hierarchy dichotomy"]
definition: The mode through which know-how is transferred, distinguishing within-firm transfer (equity joint venture) from transfer to an unaffiliated party on the market (licensing agreement).

name: Technology trajectory alignment
authors_terms: ["Alter Firm Alignment to Focal Firm Core Technology Trajectory", "alignment to the global trajectory"]
definition: The extent to which the external firm matches the global trajectory in its use of the focal firm's core technology.

name: Patent assertion
authors_terms: ["Alter Firm Patent Assertions in Focal Firm Core Technology Area", "patent assertions"]
definition: The number of court cases filed by the alter firm that reference a patent with its primary USPC code matching the core technology area of the focal firm.

name: Director interlock
definition: An interlock is formed when an individual initially affiliated with one firm (in the role of executive or director) is also added to another firm's board.

name: Patent litigation
definition: The likelihood of patent litigation between the two firms.

name: R&D alliance formation
definition: The formation of R&D alliances between the two firms.

name: Contractual governance
definition: Contractual governance involves the extent to which formal incentives/disincentives (typically financial) are used clearly to specify and control service activities between a buyer (i.e., customer firm) and supplier (i.e., service provider). The construct here represents the degree to which the service provider's near-term compensation and longer-term business opportunities are impacted by their performance against contractual service level agreements.

name: Relational governance
definition: Relational governance assesses the extent to which a business relationship involves commitment and cooperation from both parties, and performance targets that are less clearly specified. It represents the reliance upon committed and cooperative relations to govern the commercial exchange.

name: Provider opportunism
definition: Opportunism is defined as 'self-interest seeking with guile'. In this study, opportunism is reflected as a higher order construct comprised of shirking and poaching; two germane forms of opportunism in outsourcing relationships.

name: Shirking
definition: Shirking is the extent to which the provider deliberately underperforms or withholds resources when the customer is unable to detect the action.

name: Poaching
definition: Poaching, also referred to as diffusion risk, represents the degree to which the provider is inclined to utilize information obtained through the relationship for its own unauthorized benefit.

name: Individualism-collectivism
definition: The individualism-collectivism dimension reflects how tightly knit the social framework is in a society. In high individualism cultures there is a preference for a loosely knit social framework, whereas in more collectivist cultures individuals expect their relatives, clan, or other in-group to look after them.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: Uncertainty avoidance represents the extent to which a society feels 'uncomfortable with uncertainty and ambiguity' and a preference for 'beliefs promising certainty'.

name: Rationality
definition: 'Rationality is the reason for doing something and to judge a behaviour as reasonable is to be able to say that the behaviour is understandable within a given frame of reference' (Butler, 2002: 226). Procedural rationality is chosen to represent the synoptic perspective in the model.

name: Intuition
definition: Intuitive synthesis is taken, together with political behavior, to represent the incremental-political perspective on strategic decision making, in contrast to the rational-analytic perspective.

name: Political behavior
definition: The political perspective on strategic decision making assumes that decisions emerge from a process in which decision makers have different goals, forming alliances to achieve their goals in which the preferences of the most powerful prevail.

name: Strategic decision effectiveness
definition: Some authors investigate organizational performance, while others choose decision level as a focus instead of organizational level and examine strategic decision outcomes, such as effectiveness, success and quality.

name: Decision importance
definition: The perceived magnitude of impact of a strategic decision, which Papadakis, Lioukas, and Chambers (1998) find to be among the strongest explanations of decision-making behavior.

name: Decision uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty as used here refers to a specific decision, as opposed to environmental uncertainty in general (e.g., Papadakis et al., 1998). Decision making of the non-routine kind such as strategic decisions is liable to involve uncertainty.

name: Decision motive
definition: The way in which decision makers categorize and label a strategic decision as an opportunity or as a crisis, strongly affects the subsequent processes of decision making.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty attaching to the firm's environment in general, as opposed to uncertainty attaching to a specific decision.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental hostility vs. munificence is regarded as one of the most important factors for explaining strategic behavior (Castrogiovanni, 1991).

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance in this study was defined as how a firm performs in comparison to companies similar in size and industry, not only on financial indicators of performance, but on nonfinancial indicators as well.

name: Company size
definition: Many researchers have argued that company size can affect the strategic decision-making process (e.g., Fredrickson and Iaquinto, 1989; Snyman and Drew, 2003), such that larger firms will employ more formal and rational processes.

name: Historical legacy
authors_terms: ["historical legacy", "legacy of high status", "historical legacy of high or low status"]
definition: Once status differences form, they tend to be perpetuated. Status evolves in a privilege-perpetuating direction by means of historical legacy, which operates through the perpetuating effect of differing prior conditions.

name: Accumulation of positive associations
authors_terms: ["accumulation of positive association", "accumulation of positive associations", "associations with high-status organizations", "status contagion"]
definition: Given that status is fundamentally a relational concept, one mechanism for understanding changes in status differences among competing organizations over time is the accumulation of positive associations. More specifically, status contagion processes can provide privileges for organizations that interact with other organizations that have high status.

name: Accumulation of negative associations
authors_terms: ["accumulation of negative association", "accumulation of negative associations", "associations with low-status organizations"]
definition: Status can diminish over time, evolving in a privilege-reducing direction through the accumulation of negative association. A focal organization's status loss attributable to competing with low-status organizations is independent of that organization's competitive success vis-a-vis the lower-status organizations.

name: Performance against high-status teams
authors_terms: ["victory against high-status teams", "winning percentage against prior-year NCAA-invited teams", "win/lose record vis a vis these same schools"]
definition: It was also possible that victory against high-status teams would be another merit-based performance indicator (above and beyond overall win/lose records) that would predict a postseason tournament invitation.

name: Privilege
definition: Status generates social esteem and special, unearned (i.e., non-merit-based) benefits known as privileges, which are granted to and enjoyed by high-status actors in a social system. Both come from social beliefs that have little to do with assessments of quality and have much more to do with social or cultural categorization schemata or stereotypes.

name: Balance within the function domain
authors_terms: ["balance between exploration and exploitation within the function domain", "balance within the function domain", "function domain"]
definition: The function domain concerns the value chain function that alliances serve: 'a firm that collaborates with its partners in upstream activities of the value chain, such as R&D initiatives that may result in innovative technologies or products, engages in exploration in the function domain', whereas a firm that uses alliances for downstream activities such as commercialization 'pursues exploitation in that domain.' Balance within the function domain refers to simultaneously exploring and exploiting in that domain, which the authors argue imposes resource allocation trade-offs and conflicting organizational routines.

name: Balance within the structure domain
authors_terms: ["balance between exploration and exploitation within the structure domain", "structure domain", "structure exploration", "structure exploitation"]
definition: 'Exploration in the structure domain refers to a firm's tendency to seek opportunities by forming alliances with new partners that lack prior ties to the firm', whereas 'exploitation in the structure domain refers to a firm's efforts to consolidate its alliance portfolio by forming recurrent alliances with a select group of partners with whom the firm has established ties.' Balance within the structure domain means simultaneously forming ties with new partners and renewing ties with prior partners.

name: Balance across the function and structure domains
authors_terms: ["balance across domains", "balance between exploration and exploitation across the function and structure domains", "domain separation"]
definition: 'a firm can avoid these challenges and still enjoy the benefits of balance by exploring in one domain while exploiting in another.' Balance across domains 'enables the firm to simultaneously nurture organizational routines that regulate exploitation in one domain while supporting exploration in another.'

name: Firm performance
definition: To avoid possible bias in measuring the outcomes of exploration versus exploitation, 'we used two performance measures: net profit as a short-term performance measure ... and firm market value as a long-term performance measure.' 'Net profit is considered an accounting measure of financial performance', whereas 'market value represents investors' ex ante expectations about firms' future market performance.'

name: Firm size
definition: 'We measured firm size as the value of total assets reported in Compustat.' The authors argue that 'as the firm grows in size, it becomes more self-reliant and better able to carry out its internal operations', so that internal assets limit the resources available for collaborative engagements and its partnering routines become more rigid.

name: Product design change frequency
authors_terms: ["frequency of product design change", "frequency of strategic change"]
definition: We should expect both the frequency and magnitude of strategic change by the core firm to directly influence niche market performance and survival. One important dimension for this change is product design, where uncertainty about core product characteristics, popularity, obsolescence, or deterioration creates hazards for complementors.

name: Product redesign radicalness
authors_terms: ["major redesign", "major platform design", "more radical product design changes", "product design change"]
definition: While some redesigns are only cosmetic (e.g., reshaping the body paneling), other design changes include major structural overhauls, including new engines and new platforms. These major redesigns produce great uncertainty regarding the popularity of the new design as well as the devaluation of the old design.

name: Product durability
definition: Durable core products ensure a longer life with customers and generate a lengthy stream of payments to complementors. Low-durability core products instead generate more rapid replacement and uncertainty for complementors.

name: Core firm penetration
authors_terms: ["penetration by core firms", "captive lessor penetration", "captive penetration", "captive lessor involvement", "manufacturer leasing"]
definition: As core firms integrate into complementary markets, their involvement competes with existing firms. When a core firm identifies a complementary product or service as strategically important, its entry will crowd out existing niche market firms.

name: Core firm lease subsidization
authors_terms: ["subsidization", "lease subsidization", "subvention", "subsidized leases", "pricing a complementary good or service below cost"]
definition: The effect of captive lessor involvement is magnified when these manufacturer-owned subsidiaries subsidize residual values on specific vehicles. Subsidized leases tend to create large clusters of identical leases within a short period of time.

name: Residual value forecast error
authors_terms: ["residual value forecasting performance", "straight RV error", "absolute value RV error", "residual value losses", "residual value error"]
definition: I measure residual value forecasting performance by directly comparing the lessor's ex ante residual value forecast in the contract data with the actual blue book car value at lease-end. I compare these two values by calculating the percentage error from the original value of the car.

name: Exit hazard
authors_terms: ["hazard of exit", "firm exit", "market exit hazard", "time to exit", "exit"]
definition: In order to identify firm exit, a semi-parametric Cox proportional hazard model predicts the duration of a specific lessor in a model-specific market. The data identify the day of each market entry and exit.

name: Cultural spawning
authors_terms: ["cultural spawning", "cultural similarity", "cultural transmission from the parents to startups"]
definition: Cultural spawning measures to what extent each treated spawn startup's culture is more similar to its parent organization's culture than the matched twin's culture is to the same parent in a given year.

name: Founder tenure at parent organization
authors_terms: ["tenure at parent", "founder's tenure at the parent organization", "tenure"]
definition: Years worked at the parent organization were measured by counting from the first year that an individual founder appeared as working in the firm.

name: Parent cultural congruency
authors_terms: ["parent cultural congruency", "cultural congruency", "cultural congruency of a parent organization"]
definition: Cultural congruency is the degree to which the culture of an organization is composed of cultural elements that are consistent in their meanings and, hence, have internal compatibility (Craik and Lockhart 1972).

name: Parent cultural atypicality
authors_terms: ["parent cultural atypicality", "cultural atypicality", "cultural atypicality of parent organizations"]
definition: To measure the cultural atypicality of organizations, we take into account that an industry has groups of firms with similar products, and atypicality should be measured within such groups, rather than industry-wide.

name: Spawned startup status
definition: A startup was identified as spawned when its founder had previously worked at another technology company.

name: Organizational culture
definition: Organizational culture is a toolkit of meanings that employees utilize to solve problems within an organization, giving them resources in the form of 'diverse, often conflicting symbols, stories, and guides to actions' (Swidler 1986, p. 277).

name: Steering committee adoption
definition: We conceptualize steering committees as instruments that formalize joint administrative control by both partners through a well defined, dedicated interface to promote adaptation in a coordinated way during contract implementation. A steering committee can therefore be seen as an ' administrative apparatus ' that enables the parties to ' orchestrate coordinated adaptation to unanticipated disturbances '.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: It is uncertainty regarding cause - effect relationships and response options that is especially useful to conceptualize the technological uncertainty that affects alliance governance in the biopharmaceuticals sector. Technological uncertainty is native to innovation-intensive contexts because of the inherently uncertain nature of inventive activity.

name: Interdependence between partners
definition: Thompson (1967) originally conceived of different levels of interdependence between units of an organization based on their activities ' input - output relationships. These three types of interdependence, in increasing degree of interdependence, are pooled, sequential, and reciprocal.

name: Technology overlap
authors_terms: ["technology overlap", "overlap in partners ' technological resources", "overlapping domains of technological expertise"]
definition: Our final theoretical variable is the overlap of partners ' technological resources (i.e., Technology overlap ). These adaptation concerns become particularly severe when the partners possess overlapping domains of technological expertise.

name: Director gender
authors_terms: ["gender", "female executive directors", "male executive directors", "female indicator variable"]
definition: The gender of the executive director; the study compares female executive directors with male directors who performed the same role in an industry and size matched company.

name: Executive bonus
authors_terms: ["bonus", "bonuses", "the size of the bonuses paid to the executive directors", "bonus allocations"]
definition: The component of the compensation package that is explicitly designed to reward managerial (or firm) performance according to the Combined Code of Corporate Governance, namely the size of the bonuses paid to the executive directors, examined both in absolute and in relative terms.

name: Company performance
definition: Corporate performance measured by two categories of performance metrics that were distinguished following the theoretical literature: accounting-based performance measures and stock performance indicators.

name: Executive total compensation
definition: Total pay defined as the sum of base salary, bonus, other direct compensation, and incentive pay.

name: Exploratory learning
authors_terms: ["exploratory learning", "exploratory learning of absorptive capacity", "knowledge acquisition"]
definition: Exploratory learning refers to acquiring external knowledge, and it corresponds to the notion of potential absorptive capacity. In the context of absorptive capacity it comprises two essential process stages: recognizing external knowledge and assimilating this knowledge.

name: Transformative learning
authors_terms: ["transformative learning", "transformative learning of absorptive capacity", "knowledge retention"]
definition: Transformative learning links these two processes, and it refers to maintaining knowledge over time. It comprises two essential stages: maintaining assimilated knowledge and reactivating this knowledge.

name: Exploitative learning
authors_terms: ["exploitative learning", "exploitative learning of absorptive capacity", "realized absorptive capacity"]
definition: Exploitative learning relates to applying acquired knowledge, and it reflects the concept of realized absorptive capacity. Exploitative learning in the context of absorptive capacity comprises two process stages: transmuting the assimilated knowledge and applying this knowledge.

name: Absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["absorptive capacity", "overall absorptive capacity", "complementarity of the learning processes"]
definition: A recent process-based definition is that absorptive capacity is a firm's ability to utilize external knowledge through the sequential processes of exploratory, transformative, and exploitative learning.

name: Technological turbulence
definition: Technological turbulence refers to the rate of technological change.

name: Market turbulence
definition: Market turbulence relates to the degree of instability and uncertainty within a firm's markets.

name: Innovation
definition: Innovation is one of the two distinct dependent variables; it is measured with a three-item scale on the overall performance of the firm's new product development program.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is the second distinct dependent variable; it is captured with a scale for perceptual performance based on prior work, asking how the firm performs relative to its competitors.

name: Non-compete enforcement
definition: Postemployment covenants not to compete, whose enforcement varies significantly from state to state; Michigan inadvertently reversed its prohibition on enforcing them in 1985.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: The interorganizational movement of personnel among firms; here identified as an inventor changing employers, observed as a change in patent assignee.

name: Firm-specific skills
definition: Skills acquired through focus on firm-specific tasks or firm-specific training that may have become less relevant to other organizations, giving the inventor less external leverage.

name: Technical specialization
definition: The degree to which an inventor specializes in a narrow range of technologies rather than being a generalist, so that external opportunities are more likely to lie with competitors of the current employer.

name: IT assets
authors_terms: ["IT assets", "IT investments", "IT investment intensity", "investments in IT assets", "IT investment allocations"]
definition: Firms' investments in different types of IT, disaggregated by strategic purpose into infrastructure, transactional, informational and strategic assets. The authors distinguish assets, defined as investments in different types of IT, from capabilities, defined as practices and competencies that support the use of IT.

name: IT infrastructure
definition: IT infrastructure provides the foundation of shared IT services (both technical and human-e.g., servers, networks, laptops, shared customer databases, help desk, application development) used by multiple IT applications, and is typically funded to provide a flexible base for future business initiatives.

name: Transactional IT
definition: Transactional investments are made to automate processes, cut costs, or increase the volume of business a firm can conduct per unit cost.

name: Informational IT
definition: Informational investments provide information for managing, accounting, reporting, and communicating internally and with customers, suppliers, and regulators.

name: Strategic IT
definition: Strategic investments reposition firms in the marketplace by supporting entry into a new market or the development of new products, services, or business processes.

name: Total IT investment intensity
authors_terms: ["total IT intensity", "total IT investment", "aggregate IT investments", "IT intensity"]
definition: Firms' IT investment taken in the aggregate, as opposed to disaggregated by IT asset class; most empirical examinations of IT business value consider IT as an aggregate, uniform asset.

name: Organizational IT capabilities
definition: In the authors' model, IT resources are combinations of investment allocations and a mutually reinforcing system of competencies and practices that together represent organizational ITC. Systems of practices and competencies working in concert are expected to enable greater business value generation per IT dollar.

name: Human resource competency
definition: The human resource competency (HR) of firms is estimated by assessing (a) the technical and business skills of IT staff, (b) the IT skills of business users, and (c) the relative ability of firms to satisfy their demand for highly skilled IT labor.

name: Management competency
definition: The measure of management competency (MC) assesses both the degree of senior management commitment to IT projects and business unit involvement in IT decisions.

name: Internal IT use intensity
authors_terms: ["internal IT communication intensity", "IT use intensity for communication"]
definition: Internal IT communication intensity describes the degree to which internal communications and work practices are conducted electronically and measures the use of electronic communication media such as email, intranets, and wireless devices for internal communications.

name: Supplier-facing IT use intensity
authors_terms: ["supplier facing IT communication intensity", "supplier facing IT use intensity"]
definition: Supplier facing IT communication intensity describes the degree to which information exchanges with suppliers are conducted electronically via email, remote wireless connections, the Internet, and non-Internet electronic data interchange (EDI) connections.

name: Digital transaction intensity
definition: Digital transaction intensity (DT) measures the degree to which both internal and external transactions are conducted electronically, and is a linear combination of two ratios: electronic purchase orders to total purchase orders and electronic sales to total sales.

name: Internet architecture
definition: The degree to which firms employ Internet architectures in sales force management, employee performance measurement, training, and postsales customer support.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is treated as multidimensional, comprising profitability, market valuation, operational performance, and product innovation. These performance dimensions are distinct and trade off with each other.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability is one of the four categories of firm performance examined, measured by net margin and return on assets (ROA).

name: Market valuation
definition: Market valuation is one of the four categories of firm performance examined, reflecting the market's assessment of firms' future value and measured by Tobin's q.

name: Cost of goods sold
definition: Operational performance is one of the four categories of firm performance examined, measured by the cost of goods sold.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "innovation", "revenues from new and modified products"]
definition: Product innovation is one of the four categories of firm performance examined, measured by revenues from new and modified products.

name: Bank debt share
authors_terms: ["bank debt", "share of bank debt in a firm's debt portfolio", "involvement of banks as debt holders", "debt structure"]
definition: To account for the involvement of banks as debt holders in a firm, the authors use two proxies for the firm's debt portfolio composition. Banks can screen borrowers before a loan is provided and monitor during the loan issuance period, and due to their risk aversion have a strong incentive to reduce the risk of their loan portfolio.

name: Bank equity ownership
authors_terms: ["bank shareholdings", "bank ownership", "shareholdings of universal banks", "universal bank equity", "owner-creditor bank"]
definition: Ownership stakes of creditor banks could align interests between shareholders and creditors; compared to a pure creditor bank, an owner-creditor bank that monitors the investments should be more likely to finance projects that are expected to lead to higher returns despite a higher risk. The authors focus on the five largest owners of a firm and on universal banks, excluding investment banks.

name: Investment risk
authors_terms: ["investment risk", "FDI portfolio risk", "riskiness of a firm's investment policy", "risk of a firm's investment strategy", "risk of the portfolio of a firm's foreign direct investment activities"]
definition: Risk taking relates to 'the analysis and selection of projects that have varying uncertainties associated with their expected outcomes and corresponding cash flows.' To capture investment strategy risk, the authors use the risk of the portfolio of a firm's foreign direct investment activities.

name: Prior tie density
definition: We define 'tie density' as the number of repeated ties within a prospective group divided by the number of all possible dyadic ties among the group members. Tie density aggregates the extent of tie repetition among all dyads, and can range from complete novelty at one extreme (i.e., no tie repetition in any dyad) to complete closure at the other (i.e., tie repetition in every dyad).

name: Multiparty syndicate formation
definition: The dependent variable in our analysis was the formation of a specific syndicate, with '1' referring to a syndicate formed in reality and '0' referring to a hypothetical syndicate that could have been formed but was not. The focus is on syndicates of a size of three or more formed at the time of first-round investments in a venture.

name: Syndicate size
definition: We measured syndicate size using the total number of VC firms investing together to form a syndicate. Multiparty VC syndication deals exhibit considerable variance in syndicate size.

name: Network faultlines
authors_terms: ["network faultlines", "network fault line risks", "risk of network faultlines"]
definition: Network faultlines refer to a situation in which a division appears in group collaboration due to the presence of internal 'subgroups' with strong network connections (i.e., prior relationships) to one another but only weak or no connections to those outside of the subgroup.

name: Status heterogeneity
definition: The first, status heterogeneity, refers to differences in status among the VCs in a prospective syndicate. Status heterogeneity increases the risk that the VCs in the syndicate will bring different preferences and cognitive lenses when evaluating the venture's performance and deciding what to do next.

name: Status-based subgroups
definition: The second - status-based subgroups - refers to the potential emergence of subgroups whereby members of one subgroup are similar in status to one another but different from other subgroups. Analogous to network-based faultlines, status-based subgroups may also give rise to faultlines, but are rooted in status similarities rather than strength of network ties.

name: Industry popularity
definition: As targets for venture capital investment, industry sectors vary significantly in terms of how popular (or 'hot') they may be. These variations manifest themselves across industry sectors as well as time periods.

name: Mimicking local firms
authors_terms: ["mimicking local firms", "mimicking of local firms", "local isomorphism"]
definition: The frequency-based mimicking of local firms, measured as the number count of acquisitions conducted by local firms in the same host country and in the same industry in a three-year period prior to the transaction; the taken-for-granted characteristic of a governance mode is given if enough organizations adopt this practice.

name: Mimicking foreign firms
authors_terms: ["mimicking foreign firms", "mimicking of foreign firms", "foreign isomorphism"]
definition: The frequency-based mimicking of other foreign firms, measured as the number count of acquisitions conducted by other foreign firms in the same host country and in the same industry in a three-year period prior to the transaction; organizations facing ambiguous decision situations import clarity from the behavior of other organizations.

name: Cross-border entry mode
authors_terms: ["governance mode", "market entry governance mode", "ownership mode", "choice of acquisition as a market entry governance mode"]
definition: The adoption of governance mode is the dependent variable for the hypotheses testing and is categorized into either cross-border acquisitions or cross-border alliances. Ownership decisions may be a means of conformity to the foreign institutional environment.

name: Regulatory distance
definition: The difference in the regulatory institutional pillar between home and host countries; the regulatory pillar consists of laws, rules, and expectations of other organizations upon which a focal organization is dependent, and the ability of MNCs to understand and interpret local regulatory expectations is affected by the regulatory distance between home and host countries.

name: Normative distance
definition: The normative pillar refers to values, norms, and beliefs about human behavior that are socially accepted by individuals, which are manifested in the national culture of a given country; normative distance is the difference between home and host countries in these normative expectations.

name: Market pioneering capability
definition: The dynamic capability to create new markets through pioneering entry into emerging product generations. Firms that consistently engage in market pioneering across new product generations are likely to benefit from various demand- and supply-side isolating mechanisms that underlie first-mover advantage.

name: Market responding capability
authors_terms: ["market-responding capabilities", "sustained market-response capabilities", "responding to markets", "market responders"]
definition: The dynamic capability of entering new markets after they have been established by market pioneers; by entering new markets after they have been established by the market pioneers, market responders may offset the risks of being first, yet share the gains of a growing market segment.

name: Technological capabilities
authors_terms: ["technological capabilities", "technological know-how", "technology position", "technological leadership", "relative technological position"]
definition: A firm's proprietary technical/innovative capability, conceptualized in dynamic and relative terms such that it is measured in comparison to other competitors over time rather than in absolute, static terms; a critical technological performance parameter of disk drives is areal density.

name: Firm survival
definition: The likelihood that a firm continues to operate in the industry, computed as a dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a firm survived to the following year and 0 otherwise, with acquisitions being treated as censored observations.

name: Unrealized performance
definition: Unrealized performance 'refers to their valuation of equity stakes that are still to be exited (potentially many years ahead)' and is 'defined as the valuation of unrealized investments' reported as a percentage of called capital in a focal year of the first-time fund. It is expected to be a weaker signal than realized performance, as it remains a specific form of nonbinding communication by PE managers that is inevitably subjective.

name: Realized performance
definition: Realized performance - 'performance to which a definitive value has been assigned' - is 'defined as distributions to the LPs up to a focal year t as a percentage of called capital of the first-time fund', i.e., the income and capital realized from exiting investments. It is expected to represent a strong signal because it is factual data based upon hard outcomes rather than estimates.

name: Media attention
definition: Media attention is 'the number of citations in ProQuest of a specific PE firm in t - 1'. The authors treat media sources as information intermediaries whose coverage affects the observability of signals and the attention resource providers devote to firms.

name: Follow-on fund raising
definition: The dependent variable, raising a follow-on fund, 'captures the ability of PE managers to raise new financial resources from prospective capital providers and thereby remain in business'. It equals 1 when a new PE firm raises a follow-on fund in a focal year and 0 otherwise.

name: Eventual realized performance
definition: The realized performance at the end of the fund's economic lifetime, 'when all funds have been redistributed to the LPs', used as the correlate of the new PE firm's unobservable quality in the signal-strength analysis.

name: Certification
authors_terms: ["certification", "Airbnb Plus certification", "certification of offerings on a digital platform", "certification system"]
definition: Certification is used by organizations to 'formally acknowledge that [certain organizations or their offerings] meet a particular standard,' serving as a signal that an organization or its offerings are appropriate and reliable. By design, certification draws categorical boundaries between offerings, separating those that have been verified by the platform from those that have not.

name: Performance of noncertified offerings
authors_terms: ["performance of noncertified offerings", "absolute performance of noncertified actors", "revenue of non-Plus listings"]
definition: The performance of offerings that do not hold the platform's certification, assessed relative to their own prior trajectory, that is, compared with the counterfactual in which no certification program existed.

name: Platform-provided quality signal
definition: A quality indicator that the platform itself establishes and assigns to sellers who meet specific criteria, which helps buyers navigate offerings and reduces uncertainty about noncertified listings. The Superhost badge is an automatic recognition that hosts earn by meeting quantifiable criteria and is a quality indicator at the host level.

name: Buyer ratings
authors_terms: ["overall rating", "customer ratings", "highly rated by previous buyers"]
definition: Feedback and ratings that buyers provide for the offerings they have purchased or used; by aggregating ratings from past buyers, potential buyers gain valuable insights into the quality of the offerings before making a purchase.

name: Direct competition with certified listings
definition: The degree to which certified and noncertified offerings fall within the same consideration set and are directly juxtaposed, which is lower when buyers' idiosyncratic preferences such as specific price ranges, layouts, or location features exclude certified offerings from their preferred set.

name: Uniqueness of listing type
authors_terms: ["unique type", "uniqueness of the listings", "unique Airbnb listings"]
definition: The uniqueness of listings on Airbnb, measured by examining listing types that are less commonly available in traditional hotels. Because private and shared rooms offer lower privacy and greater opportunities for social interaction, they represent relatively unique types of accommodations compared with those typically found in traditional hotels, and so have fewer readily available substitutes outside the platform.

name: Catalyst of innovation
definition: Individuals who are able to stimulate and enhance the development of new ideas in their colleagues by providing them with relevant knowledge and who are recognized by their colleagues as key contributors to the process of generating innovations.

name: Diverse knowledge clique
definition: The configuration of internal social structure and external knowledge diversity in which an individual is embedded in a closed network (e.g., overlapping ties to common third parties) within an organization and has access to diverse external sources of knowledge.

name: Network redundancy
definition: Network redundancy refers to the situation in which ego's alters are also themselves connected.

name: External knowledge diversity
authors_terms: ["external knowledge diversity", "diversity of external knowledge", "knowledge diversity"]
definition: Heterogeneity in the type of knowledge sourced from outside the organization, captured based on the combination of scientific versus industrial sources of knowledge accessed by individuals in the sample.

name: Individual innovativeness
definition: The authors identify innovators based on the number of their patent applications, and capture the innovative outputs of individuals in the company from monthly reports that identified patent applications.

name: Star scientist presence
authors_terms: ["presence of a star", "star firm", "firms with stars", "presence of star scientists"]
definition: Stars are identified as individuals who have demonstrated disproportionately high levels of performance and have superior visibility in the external market. A scientist whose productivity score is at least two standard deviations above the average of all inventors in the sample is defined as a star.

name: Innovative productivity
definition: Innovative productivity reflects a firm's achievement of repeated innovative success and requires a firm to have the ability to access and effectively utilize the knowledge and tangible resources required for effective research in a defined domain.

name: Innovative leadership
authors_terms: ["innovative leadership", "innovative leadership among a firm's non-star scientists"]
definition: Innovative leadership is defined as the ability of a firm's members to initiate and lead innovation, and thus ultimately defines a firm's capacity to attain continuous innovative productivity. Innovative leadership reflects the ability of a firm's (non-star) scientists to initiate and lead research from innovation to patenting.

name: Breadth of a star's expertise
authors_terms: ["breadth of a star's expertise", "breadth of expertise", "breadth in a star's expertise"]
definition: The breadth of a star's expertise reflects the range of technological domains across which the star pursues research and can thus provide relevant, timely knowledge and access to opportunities for a firm. It reflects both the scope of a star's expert power, as well as the range of technological domains across which a star may require support in innovative initiatives.

name: Star's collaborative strength
authors_terms: ["star's collaborative strength", "collaborative strength", "extent of a star's collaborative strength"]
definition: A star's collaborative strength in a knowledge-based context is reflected in the frequency of collaboration between a star and his colleagues and is likely to foster greater balance in the exchange relationship. A star's collaborative strength, as reflected in the frequency and intensity of the star's collaboration with other scientists in the firm, is likely to influence the balance in the star's relationships with colleagues.

name: Performance relative to the aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to the aspiration level", "performance below the aspiration level", "performance above the aspiration level", "low performance"]
definition: The decision maker focuses attention on an aspiration level for performance and uses this aspiration level to code outcomes as failures when performance is below it and as successes when performance exceeds it. The aspiration level may be determined by the recent history of performance of the organization (historical aspiration levels) or by the performance of similar others (social aspiration levels).

name: Aspiration level
definition: The reference point against which performance is coded: historical aspiration levels are generated from the recent history of performance of the organization, while the social aspiration level is the average performance of other firms in the same year.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is a primary indicator of tangible resources and has been shown to reduce firm failure rates; a large stock of resources buffers a firm so that it can endure many periods of poor financial performance with little threat of failure.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risky decisions whose consequences are uncertain and may include losses; the specific risk behavior analyzed is factory expansion by Japanese shipbuilders.

name: Category innovation
