authors_terms: ["category innovation", "claiming a new category label", "introducing a new label"]
definition: A linguistic tactic where firms claim a new category label to describe the market they are in; a firm signals its position is not only differentiated but also categorically distinct from rivals and that a nascent market is emerging around its position. Firms engage in category innovation either with an entirely new label or by claiming a sparsely used label that is not yet socially defined.

name: Category combination
authors_terms: ["category combination", "combining market categories in products and technologies", "product offering combination", "technology combination"]
definition: Whether a firm combines categories in its offerings, captured by two measures: the market positions a firm takes and the extent to which the underlying technologies a firm develops combine elements of different categories. Together, they reflect complementary aspects of whether a firm is creating new combinations in its products.

name: Category leniency
definition: Market categories that remain lenient are fragmented, diverse, with ambiguous meaning and porous boundaries. Such categories emerge in contexts without strong intermediaries who influence sensemaking, where market participants frequently take claims of market affiliation at face value; leniency is measured on a continuum and can change over time.

name: Perceived passion
definition: Entrepreneurial passion is an entrepreneur's intense affective state accompanied by cognitive and behavioral manifestations of high personal value; to distinguish the affective from the cognitive dimension of the passion construct, the authors label the affective aspect 'passion' in this study. It is manifested through facial expressions, body movement, tone of voice, and other nonverbal cues.

name: Perceived preparedness
definition: Preparedness is the cognitive aspect of the passion construct: evidence for thorough preparation in refining a business idea, reflected in the quality of the business plan being presented and in the way the entrepreneur tackles and responds to questions from the VCs. It is manifested in the verbal content and substance of a presentation.

name: VC funding decision
authors_terms: ["VC's decision to invest", "investment decision", "funding decision", "whether or not the VCs intended to invest"]
definition: The venture capitalist's decision about whether a proposed venture is worth funding, expressed as an investment decision ('yes' or 'no') following the business plan presentation.

name: Business plan quality
authors_terms: ["quality of the business plan", "quality of business plan", "business plan quality"]
definition: The quality of the business plan being presented to VCs, which should reflect the entrepreneur's careful consideration of market needs, the product or service, market segments, competition, expected financial return, and the difficulties the venture may encounter.

name: Corruption pervasiveness
definition: Pervasiveness of corruption is "the average firm's likelihood of encountering corruption in its normal interactions with state officials"; it reflects the overall likelihood that a firm and its resources are required to be engaged with corrupt officials, and the degree to which corruption is dispersed broadly throughout the public sector in a country.

name: Corruption arbitrariness
definition: The level of uncertainty associated with corruption, or arbitrariness, reflects the degree of ambiguity associated with corrupt transactions in a given state.

name: Foreign entry mode
definition: Entry-mode decisions involve an MNE's choice among three alternatives: equity entry via a wholly owned subsidiary, equity entry via a joint venture, and nonequity entry.

name: Nonequity entry
definition: Nonequity entry includes all entry events in which the MNE is engaged for its technological and managerial competencies and does not assume any ownership (i.e., management contracts), and also cases that involve an initial equity contribution but for which the ownership stake is transferred to a local party as a stipulation of the initial contract (build-own-transfer projects).

name: Wholly owned subsidiary
definition: An equity mode of entry, part of the build-own-operate projects in which firms keep ownership and control, providing more control and profit potential than other modes.

name: Joint venture
authors_terms: ["joint venture with a local partner", "equity entry via a joint venture", "joint venture"]
definition: An equity mode of entry in which the MNE enters with a local partner; local partners reduce risks associated with equity entry and help overcome the liability of foreignness by providing access to location-specific knowledge and local networks, fostering external legitimacy, and lowering direct costs of entry.

name: Quality reputation
definition: We define and use the term reputation to mean the consumer's subjective evaluation of the perceived quality of the producer. Reputation is often discussed in terms of the perceptions of an organization's "goodness" or "badness" in the eyes of a particular audience.

name: Market share change
authors_terms: ["market share change", "rate of change in an automaker's market share", "market share growth", "market response to its product defect"]
definition: The dependent variable is therefore, the rate of change in an automaker's market share over the observation period. We use market share as the dependent variable in this analysis because market shares, unlike sales units, are not affected by temporal fluctuations in seasonal demand.

name: Product defect
definition: There has been very little exploration of the ways organizational reputation responds to the revelation of organizational errors in the form of product defects. We use official product recalls as our measure of product defects for these automakers.

name: Substitutability
definition: Product uniqueness or substitutability (the number of competing products with comparable levels of reputation). In our study, substitutability is proxied by the extent to which a reputation level is crowded by automakers.

name: Organizational generalism
definition: Identity focus in terms of whether the firm is a generalist or specialist. Specialists tend to produce a small number of vehicles with a narrow range of engine capacity, such as Kia. Generalists tend to produce vehicles over a large range of capacities, such as Ford.

name: Employment protection
definition: A class of employment protection laws, the implied contract (IC) exception, under which an employee can be dismissed only for 'good cause,' which increased the cost of dismissing employees; as restrictions placed on the ability of the employer to utilize labor, employment protection laws constrain making one specific adjustment to one specific resource: dismissing employees.

name: Firm performance relative to the industry benchmark
definition: Industry-adjusted ROA, calculated as the difference between firm performance and the industry benchmark, defined as the median ROA at the four-digit SIC level.

name: Positive performance relative to the industry benchmark
definition: Positive Performanceit takes the value of Performanceit if firm performance is above the benchmark and zero otherwise.

name: Negative performance relative to the industry benchmark
definition: Negative Performanceit takes the value of Performanceit if firm performance is below the benchmark and zero otherwise; it takes a negative value by construction, and the absolute value is used for the ease of interpretation.

name: Corporate adjustment activities
authors_terms: ["adjustment activities", "corporate activities used to adjust resources and execute change", "corporate strategic activities"]
definition: Corporate activities used to adjust resources and execute change; because each activity contributes only a partial result and depends on others to complete an intended change, constraining one can create a bottleneck that traps multiple other activities.

name: Employee hiring
definition: An adjustment activity that accesses new resources through 'make' by increasing the number of employees; the lower reversibility created by employment protection increases the risk of growth.

name: Employee dismissal
definition: The release of human resources by decreasing the number of employees, the specific adjustment to a specific resource that employment protection laws constrain.

name: Net capital investment
definition: Adjustment of the capital stock through capital investment above or below the amount necessary to simply maintain current assets in place.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: Accessing new human and other resources through 'buy', which also involves a significant degree of releasing redundant resources during post-merger integration.

name: Divestiture activity
definition: Business-unit level release of resources through the sale of business units.

name: CEO turnover
definition: Change in a firm's CEO; interdependencies should even extend to CEO turnover if firms try to compensate for the loss of flexibility in adjusting resources by seeking changes to how they are deployed.

name: Uncertainty in future firm performance
definition: Dispersion in analyst forecasts of firm earnings, a more general measure of the level of adjustment activities that increase the uncertainty of a firm's future performance.

name: Blind evaluation
definition: Blinding withholds information about the idea proposer from evaluators; in the blind condition the innovation manager received no information about the idea proposer ('Submitted by: N/A'), while in the non-blind condition the manager received the proposer's name, unit, and geographical location.

name: Idea evaluation score
authors_terms: ["Overall score", "evaluation score", "overall quality of the idea"]
definition: For each idea, evaluators were asked: 'On a scale of 1 to 7 (1 lowest to 7 highest), please assess the overall quality of the idea.' Overall score is the main dependent variable as specified in the pre-analysis plan.

name: Proposer gender
definition: Gender is a highly visible characteristic that can compensate for unobserved information and a common way to classify other people that occurs almost instantaneously; gender roles and stereotypes activated in this process result in cognitive bias influencing judgment and evaluation.

name: Shared organizational unit
definition: An idea proposer was part of the same division, function, or geographical market as the innovation manager evaluating the idea; at the industrial partner each employee belongs to one and only one division, function, or geographical market.

name: Shared geographic location
definition: An idea proposer was in the same country as the evaluator; being in the same unit does not always imply sharing a location, so location and unit are analytically separated.

name: CEO compensation monitoring
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation monitoring", "CEO monitoring", "monitoring of the CEO compensation process", "CEO monitoring scale"]
definition: Activities and policies directed toward the observation and control of CEO pay and the establishment of CEO incentive structures by boards, as representatives of shareholders; the scale describes aspects of a firm's CEO pay-setting process and the policies and practices governing it.

name: Firm performance
definition: The firm's financial outcomes; in study 1 measured by CCOs' subjective assessments of the firm's profitability, stock performance and overall performance trend relative to similar firms, and in study 2 by archival profitability and stock market indicators combined into an overall performance ranking.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Whether a firm is controlled by owners or by management, assessed by whether a single individual or institution outside the firm owns 5% or more of the company's stock; the level of CEO compensation monitoring is higher in owner-controlled firms than in management-controlled firms.

name: Number of application software producers
definition: The number of independent application software producers active on a platform; the explanatory variable of greatest interest in the analysis of variety and of producer scope.

name: Producers in the same software genre
authors_terms: ["NumProducersSameGenre", "adding producers in the same genre", "producers of similar applications"]
definition: The number of producers on a given platform working in a particular genre (e.g., databases, medical and health, games).

name: Producers in other software genres
authors_terms: ["NumProducersOtherGenres", "distinct and differentiated independent application producers", "producers of different kinds of software"]
definition: The number of producers working on the same platform in a genre other than the focal one, disregarded when a genre has not been specified for a title.

name: Software variety
definition: The total number of varieties in a system; Varieties is measured as the sum of varieties (or scope) offered by a given producer.

name: Producer product scope
definition: The number of application varieties developed by individual producers, measured as the count of the number of genres in which a producer has products.

name: Innovation investment incentives
authors_terms: ["individual producers' investment incentives", "innovation incentives", "investment incentives", "innovation efforts"]
definition: Individual producers' incentives to invest effort in developing new software; a shorter time taken to complete a new version, all else being equal, implies higher effort and input.

name: Structural power equality
authors_terms: ["structural power equality", "balance in structural power", "equality in structural power", "balance in the distribution of compensation, status, and representation"]
definition: Following Finkelstein (1992), we conceptualize structural power in terms of compensation, status, and representation. Theoretically, the greatest equality occurs when incentives and structural power among family and non-family TMT members are distributed evenly between family and non-family executives.

name: Firm performance
definition: 'Unsystematic return,' or idiosyncratic return, refers to returns driven by firm's resources and capabilities, and therefore indicates returns from idiosyncratic actions.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: 'Environmental dynamism' refers to the rate and unpredictability of change in the environment. It consists of instability and unpredictability: 'instability' is defined as the magnitude and frequency of change in the environment, whereas 'unpredictability' is defined as the irregularity in the pattern of environmental changes.

name: Governance performance
definition: We draw on governance ratings from GovernanceMetrics International (GMI) to measure governance performance. GMI ratings are based on indicators ranging from board accountability to financial disclosure and internal controls, and from shareholder rights to executive compensation and corporate behavior.

name: CEO founder status
authors_terms: ["non-founder CEO", "founder CEO", "whether the CEO is the founder"]
definition: Whether the CEO is the founder (versus a non-founder family member or non-founder non-family member) is a possible boundary condition for the benefits of structural power equality. Based on information in SEC Compact Disclosure filings and proxy statements, if the founder holds the title of the chief executive officer (CEO) we code it as '0,' or non-founder CEO (coded '1').

name: Competitors' product launches
authors_terms: ["Competitors' Product Launches", "competitors' product launches", "rivals' launches of new products", "competitive pressure from rivals' product launches"]
definition: We measured the extent of competitive pressure by the number of global new drugs launched by competitors in a given year in the therapeutic areas in which a sample firm was active. A higher number of launched drugs suggests stronger competitive pressures on the focal firm.

name: Technology licensing-in
definition: Like other knowledge-seeking actions, licensing enables firms to access knowledge and technologies developed outside their organizational boundaries. A license deal consists of a contract that affords a licensee the right to exploit a technology in exchange for the payment of upfront fees and/or royalties.

name: Innovation toward competition
authors_terms: ["Innovation Toward Competition", "innovation toward competitors", "innovation in areas where rivals launched new products"]
definition: We measured firm innovation using the count of successful patent applications from firm i in year t that were associated with therapeutic areas in which rivals exerted pressure on the firm through product launches. We are interested in examining innovation related to a firm's upstream R&D activities.

name: Cumulative R&D investments
authors_terms: ["Cumulative R&D Investment", "Cumulative R&D Investments", "accumulated R&D investments", "cumulative internal R&D investments"]
definition: These investments represent the time, capital, and skills expended to build up the resources and capabilities that position the firm with respect to its competitors. Such R&D investments lead firms to accrue a stock of path-dependent technological knowledge and expertise.

name: CSR contracting
authors_terms: ["CSR contracting", "integration of CSR criteria in executive compensation", "CSR-based incentives", "pay for social and environmental performance"]
definition: We follow corporate practice and define CSR contracting as the integration of CSR criteria in executive compensation, that is, the linking of executive compensation to social and environmental performance (e.g., CO2 emission reductions, employee satisfaction goals, compliance with ethical standards in developing countries).

name: Organizational time horizon
definition: We define 'organizational time horizon' as the executive team's attention to the long term. The authors argue that providing incentives based on social and environmental performance goals is likely to shift managers' attention toward longer-term efforts, leading them to adopt a longer time horizon.

name: Firm value
definition: Firm value captures the (expected) future profits of the firm. Formally, firm value V is the sum of the discounted expected future cash flows.

name: CSR initiatives
authors_terms: ["CSR initiatives", "corporate social responsibility", "social and environmental initiatives", "CSR performance"]
definition: CSR includes any corporate initiative pertaining to the firm's stakeholders - such as employees, customers, the environment, and the community at large - and hence is not limited to philanthropic initiatives.

name: Emissions
definition: Companies may take actions that reduce the detrimental impact (e.g., emissions) on the natural environment and the local communities in which they operate. The TRI database contains annual data on emissions of over 650 toxic chemicals from thousands of facilities in the United States.

name: Green innovation
definition: Companies can develop 'green' products and environmentally friendly production processes that benefit both the environment and local communities. More generally, innovative activities are characterized by long gestation periods, substantial resource commitments, and a high rate of failure.

name: Share of CSR-based compensation
authors_terms: ["share of CSR compensation", "share of CSR-based compensation", "extent of CSR compensation compared to total compensation"]
definition: We compute the share of CSR compensation, which is defined as the ratio of CSR-based compensation to total compensation. This measure allows the authors to study how the 'substantiveness' of CSR contracting affects firm-level outcomes.

name: Dependent stakeholder targeting
authors_terms: ["CSR contracting provisions targeted at the dependent stakeholders", "provisions specifically targeted at the natural environment and local communities", "specificity of the CSR criteria"]
definition: The analysis classifies CSR contracting provisions according to whether they are targeted at the dependent stakeholders (i.e., the natural environment and local communities), the key stakeholders (i.e., employees and consumers), or whether no specific stakeholder is mentioned. The authors argue that if executive compensation is linked directly to the natural environment and local communities, the incentives are likely to be more effective.

name: Stakeholder orientation
authors_terms: ["stakeholder orientation", "attention to nonfinancial stakeholders", "corporate attention to nonfinancial stakeholders", "firms' orientation toward stakeholders"]
definition: The attention to nonfinancial stakeholders, i.e., to any group or individual who can affect or is affected by the achievement of an organization's purpose. The authors obtain exogenous variation in stakeholder orientation from the enactment of state-level constituency statutes, which allow corporate directors to consider stakeholders' interests when making business decisions.

name: Innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation", "innovative output", "innovative activity", "increasing the quantity and quality of innovative output"]
definition: The firm's innovative output, which the authors expect stakeholder orientation to enhance by increasing the quantity and quality of innovative output; it is measured with patent-based metrics.

name: Originality
definition: Defined similarly to generality, but with respect to the citations given to other patents. Firm-level values are computed as the average across all patents for any given firm and year.

name: Generality
definition: One minus the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of the citations that the patent receives over patent classes: if citations to a patent are spread over a larger number of technology classes, the cited patent is regarded as more 'general'. Firm-level values are computed as the average across all patents for any given firm and year.

name: Tail innovation
authors_terms: ["hits and flops", "innovations in the tails of the distribution", "hits", "flops"]
definition: Innovations in the tails of the distribution of innovative outcomes, i.e., more hits but also more failures ('hits and flops') following the adoption of stakeholder-friendly policies.

name: Innovative productivity
definition: Employees' innovative productivity, measured by dividing the number of patents and citations, respectively, by the number of employees; the authors argue that stakeholder orientation raises it by improving employees' job satisfaction, commitment and retention.

name: Financial performance
definition: Corporate financial performance, for which ROA measures realized operating performance while Tobin's Q is a forward-looking measure that accounts for all future cash flows of the company; the authors distinguish its long-run from its short-run component.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: The percentage of shares owned by institutional investors, which the authors treat as reflecting shareholders' temporal orientation because institutional investors are less focused on short-term financial performance as they are better informed and hence better able to infer the company's long-term fundamental value.

name: Consumer-focused industry
definition: Industries in which goods and services are sold directly to individual customers.

name: High-polluting industry
definition: Industries engaged in less eco-friendly activities: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency identifies seven industry sectors that account for 92% of all disposal and other releases of TRI (toxic release inventory) chemicals, and companies in these sectors are referred to as operating in 'less eco-friendly industries'.

name: Experimentation
authors_terms: ["experimentation", "experimentation and trial and error", "employees' engagement in experimentation"]
definition: Employees' experimentation and trial and error, which the authors argue is encouraged by a work environment characterized by long-term commitment to employees and high tolerance for failure, leading to an increase in innovative output.

name: Director tenure
definition: The number of years that the director served on the board. The authors treat individual director tenure as a standalone characteristic that can influence governance effectiveness rather than only a group-level control variable and proxy for director experience.

name: Stock market reaction to director deaths
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns", "CARs", "investor reactions to director sudden deaths", "stock price reaction to director deaths"]
definition: The cumulative abnormal return around the first announcement of a director's death, which the authors use "reflecting investors' sentiment of the departure of a director"; if the director was valued, the authors expect the market to react negatively to the death.

name: Proportion of directors in prime tenure
authors_terms: ["percentage of directors in the prime tenure period", "%Outsiders in prime tenure period", "proportion of directors on the board in the prime tenure period"]
definition: A firm-year measure of directors in the prime tenure period, calculated by the authors as the ratio of outside directors in their prime to board size, with a range between 0 and 1.

name: CEO pay-performance sensitivity
authors_terms: ["pay-for-performance sensitivity", "sensitivity of CEO compensation to firm performance", "pay-performance sensitivity"]
definition: The effective alignment of CEO pay with shareholder interests; the authors note that the alignment of firm performance and CEO compensation is a key indicator of effective board performance and measure it in two ways.

name: Director involvement on key committees
definition: Following Faleye et al. (2011), the authors define an involved director as one who is a member of at least two of the three key committees (audit, nominating, and compensation).

name: CEO total compensation
authors_terms: ["change in total compensation", "total compensation", "CEO pay", "overall level of compensation"]
definition: The level of CEO compensation, which the authors argue should not change merely because a board contains more directors in the prime tenure period; compensation should change only if directors learn something about the CEO from performance.

name: Interorganizational learning
authors_terms: ["interorganizational learning", "interorganizational learning index", "learning alliances", "success at interorganizational learning within the alliance"]
definition: Learning of new external knowledge through interactive learning between a student and a teacher firm; the study measures the pharmaceutical firm's success at interorganizational learning within the alliance in terms of learning new skills or capabilities and technology or research developments.

name: Basic knowledge relevance
authors_terms: ["relevance of the student firm's basic knowledge", "basic knowledge", "biochemical knowledge", "relevance of biochemical knowledge"]
definition: 'Basic knowledge refers to a general understanding of the traditions and techniques upon which a discipline is based.' For pharmaceutical and biotechnological research, biochemistry is the basic knowledge, so the relevance of basic knowledge is the overlap between the student and teacher firms' biochemistry knowledge.

name: Specialized knowledge relevance
authors_terms: ["specialized knowledge", "nonbiochemical knowledge", "relevance of the student firm's specialized knowledge"]
definition: Specialized knowledge is defined as the overlap in the partners' knowledge of other, more specialized areas such as neurology and endocrinology; some fraction of the teacher's knowledge must be fairly diverse to permit effective, creative utilization of the new knowledge by the student.

name: Organizational structure similarity
authors_terms: ["organizational structure", "similarity of the student firm's and teacher firm's organizational structures", "formalization", "centralization"]
definition: Organizational structure is 'the degree of formalization and centralization used by the firm when allocating tasks, responsibilities, authority, and decisions.' A firm's valuable knowledge is embedded in its structure as well as its knowledge-processing systems, so students with very different structures from their teachers have difficulty assimilating knowledge.

name: Compensation practices similarity
authors_terms: ["compensation practices", "similarity of the student firm's and teacher firm's compensation practices", "compensation similarity"]
definition: Compensation practices vary from highly algorithmic and mechanistic to highly experiential and situation-specific, and the similarity of two firms' compensation policies serves as one proxy for the similarity of their knowledge-processing systems and norms.

name: Shared organizational problem set
authors_terms: ["number of shared research communities", "shared research communities", "overlap between the student's and teacher's dominant logics", "organizational problem set"]
definition: The overlap of the partners' dominant logics, i.e. the proportion of the teacher firm's organizational problem set that the student firm shares; the more familiar the student is with the types of problems and projects that the teacher prefers, the more readily it can commercially apply new knowledge from that teacher.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock price reactions", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal return", "stock market reaction"]
definition: Abnormal returns measured with standard event study methodology, on the premise that price changes reflect investor expectations of changes in a firm's future performance based on new information. Cumulative abnormal returns are calculated over a -2, +2 window around the layoff announcement.

name: Layoff announcement
definition: Firms employ layoffs as a means of and as a part of strategic responses to the competitive environment. Layoffs often accompany downsizing, downscoping, or restructuring strategies.

name: National institutional context
definition: The governance structures and employment policies of Japanese firms differ from their U.S. counterparts, and both agency theory and Aoki's theory suggest that U.S. and Japanese firms differ fundamentally in their use of layoffs. The differences include main bank ownership of debt and equity and equity cross-holdings in Japan that are absent in the United States.

name: Layoff permanence
definition: Permanent layoffs are due to long-term changes in the firm and its competitive environment, while temporary layoffs represent alternatives to inventory accumulation, simply a convenient way of dealing with seasonal demand shifts.

name: Multiple layoff announcements
authors_terms: ["multiple announcements", "single event", "a series of layoffs", "multiple vs. single announcements"]
definition: Layoffs may be announced as a single event or as part of a series of restructuring efforts (i.e., a series of different layoff announcements).

name: Layoff size
authors_terms: ["percentage of the work force laid off", "layoff size", "larger layoffs"]
definition: The percentage of the work force being laid off; intuitively, the magnitude of a layoff conveys a signal about the severity of the firm's problems.

name: Layoff proactivity
definition: Generally, proactive layoffs are defined as those that are part of an overall strategic objective, while reactive layoffs are responses to poor financial performance.

name: First layoff in industry
authors_terms: ["first layoff announcement in a given industry", "subsequent announcements", "sequencing of the layoff"]
definition: The sequencing of the layoffs within an industry may have an impact on the perception of investors, distinguishing the first layoff announcement in a given industry from subsequent announcements.

name: Family control
authors_terms: ["family firm", "family firms", "family control", "family ownership and control"]
definition: 'Family firms' are defined as those in which the founder or a member of his family by blood or marriage is an officer, director, or blockholder, either individually or as a group.

name: Family CEO
definition: 'Family-CEO firms' are those firms whose CEO is the founder or a member of the founding family. Within family firms, 'Non-Family-CEO firms' are those that are not managed by the founder or any member of the founding family.

name: Family CEO generation
authors_terms: ["founder-CEO", "descendant-CEO", "generation of the family firm", "generation of the family CEO"]
definition: Family-CEO firms are split into two categories: 'Founder-CEO firms' are those in which the CEO is the company's founder, regardless of whether other family members of the same or later generations serve as officers or directors in the firm. 'Descendant-CEO firms' are those in which the CEO is a descendant of the founder.

name: Corporate divestiture
definition: Divestitures are transactions that are believed to enable firms to reconfigure resources within their corporate portfolios and to remove obsolete or misaligned business units; the divestiture decision is the decision to undertake such a transaction.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "value created for a firm's shareholders", "firm performance", "stock market performance", "Tobin's q"]
definition: The dependent variable of interest in our study is the value created for a firm's shareholders by a given divestiture (not the value of the divested assets).

name: Hospital financial performance
authors_terms: ["hospital financial performance", "cash flow margin", "hospital cash flow"]
definition: The measure of hospital financial performance utilized was cash flow margin. Not-for-profit firms whose missions are service oriented and not profit maximization dominate the hospital industry, but all hospitals, whether for-profit or not, are necessarily concerned with an adequate cash flow to sustain operations.

name: Strategic competencies
authors_terms: ["strategic competencies", "the value of a hospital's strategic competencies"]
definition: Capabilities used to deliver services in service industries, like the general hospital industry, that result in superior rents will be called strategic competencies. Strategic competencies pertain to the services offered by an organization that are superior in the marketplace and result in competitive advantage.

name: Physician linkages
authors_terms: ["physician linkages", "strategic links with physician groups", "interorganizational linkages", "linkages with physicians"]
definition: The linkage of hospitals with various types of physicians groups may have a differential impact on the ability of a hospital to create a competitive advantage vis-a-vis rival hospitals and powerful MCS buyers. From the perspective of the hospital, linkages with physicians essentially provide access to patients.

name: Managed care buyer power
authors_terms: ["managed care buyer power", "managed care market power", "buyer power"]
definition: In essence, managed care is predicated on the concept of enhancing buyer power relative to health care service providers such as hospitals. The effectiveness of this buyer power may vary widely across the industry due to significant differences in the percentage enrollments in MCS and in the percentage of patients covered by Medicare and Medicaid payments in the various hospital markets.

name: Hospital rivalry
definition: Managed care has succeeded not only in enhancing the market power of health care buyers; it has also stimulated increased rivalry between hospitals that are vying for managed care patients. The variable used to measure the level of rivalry in each general hospital market is a modification of the Herfindahl index.

name: Inventor CEO hands-on involvement
authors_terms: ["inventor CEO hands-on involvement", "hands-on approach", "involvement", "hands-on inventor CEOs"]
definition: Whereas some inventor CEOs take a hands-off approach by simply allocating capital to innovation activities or setting broad, firm-level innovation policies, others might take a more hands-on approach by remaining directly engaged in the innovation process, meeting directly with R&D personnel, and directly contributing ideas and effort to specific innovations.

name: Exploitative innovation
definition: An exploitative approach takes advantage of firms' existing knowledge and capabilities to provide incremental innovations; exploitation involves 'the use and development of things already known.' Exploitative innovation involves a focus on the firm's existing knowledge base.

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: An exploratory approach involves broader search beyond firms' existing knowledge base and the pursuit of novel resource combinations that produce more profound innovations; exploration involves 'a pursuit of new knowledge.' Exploratory innovation reflects innovation that incorporates new knowledge.

name: CEO origin
definition: The strength of the relationship may vary depending on whether the inventor was internally promoted or externally hired into the CEO position; insiders are inventor CEOs appointed from within the firm or original founders, while outsiders are non-founder CEOs who had verified experience in an outside firm within 2 years of their appointment.

name: Founder status
definition: A specific type of insider that is particularly relevant in our case is being a founder. Founders have a strong sense of ownership and connection to their firms and the technologies upon which those firms were built.

name: Board industry diversity
authors_terms: ["board industry diversity", "diversity along the dimension of industry experience"]
definition: A characteristic of boards that is particularly relevant to how they might advise hands-on inventor CEOs is their degree of diversity along the dimension of industry experience; it is measured from the primary industry backgrounds of the board's directors.

name: Peer CEO dismissal
definition: CEO dismissal is forced resignation as opposed to routine retirement or voluntary exit; scholars classify CEO turnover as a dismissal if the CEO was fired, forced out from the position, or departed due to policy differences, or under the age and retirement criteria the authors describe.

name: Strategic risk taking
definition: The authors measure strategic risk taking with a summated measure designed to capture strategic risk taking on the whole, which they believe is consistent with their theory about overall strategic decision-making.

name: Constitutional constraints on shareholder power
authors_terms: ["constitutional constraints", "constitutional constraints on shareholder power", "constitutional limit provisions"]
definition: These provisions are mandates built into the firm's constitution (and thus hard to change) that make it difficult for shareholders to impose their will; they shield CEOs from shareholder influence, buffering them against one of the primary sources of job insecurity.

name: Product similarity
definition: A text-based analysis of firms' 10-K filings captures product similarity between firms; the relative number of words in common in product descriptions between firms reflects their product similarity, and a high product similarity score indicates competitive rivals.

name: Job insecurity
definition: Job insecurity refers to an individual's perceived threat to the continuity and stability of employment in his or her current job.

name: Vertical integration
definition: We define vertical integration as the combination of mortgage origination and securitization within a single parent firm. Mortgage origination, the 'upstream' function, is the process of creating and underwriting individual mortgages; securitization, the 'downstream' function, is the process of pooling together individual mortgages and issuing mortgage-backed securities.

name: Lending quality
definition: We construct a firm-year measure of lending quality as the incremental likelihood that a mortgage defaults if it is originated by that lender, controlling for the loan characteristics observable by external market participants. It is this set of actions that reduce underwriting quality that we predict is driven by weak governance in vertically integrated firms.

name: Corporate governance
authors_terms: ["corporate governance", "governance", "governance quality", "strong corporate governance", "weak corporate governance"]
definition: Governance represents an incentive and control system whereby ownership (shareholders) attempts to ensure high managerial effort on those activities that improve shareholder value. The control components of governance include both internal monitoring by boards of directors and external monitoring by shareholders (typically institutions).

name: Institutional ownership
definition: Research on external monitoring has studied the degree and composition of institutional investors since these shareholders are professional, informed owners who control more than 50 percent of all investment capital. The level and concentration of institutional investors have generally been associated with better firm performance.

name: Institutional investor composition
definition: Bank and Insurance refers to the percent of institutional owners that are depository banks or insurance companies, traditionally conservative, regulated owners, whereas Investment Companies refers to the percent of institutional owners that are hedge funds, family offices, or other investment vehicles that are traditionally more aggressive owners.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["firm failure", "firm in operation by end of 2010", "firm survival"]
definition: A 0/1 indicator that the lender was still operating at the end of 2010, used as one piece of evidence on whether higher default likelihood was a successful strategy as measured by ex post firm survival.

name: Firm-level economic performance
authors_terms: ["firm-level economic performance", "economic firm-level performance", "Tobin's q", "economic returns", "stock market-based measure of firm-level economic performance"]
definition: As a dynamic, forward-looking measure of firm-level economic performance, Tobin's q reflects the stock market's expectations about the future growth and profitability potential of the company. As a proxy for Tobin's q, we use the ratio of sum of (1) market value of equity and (2) book value of total debt to the book value of total assets.

name: History of R&D resource deployments
authors_terms: ["a history of increased resource deployments in R&D", "a history of increased R&D investments", "percentage increase in R&D deployments", "history of increased efforts in developing technological know-how"]
definition: To capture the historical dynamics in investment levels, we calculate the average percentage increase in R&D (and marketing) investments during the previous 3 years. This continuous measure captures relative magnitude of the changes in the level of dollar investments in R&D and marketing over 3 years.

name: History of marketing resource deployments
authors_terms: ["a history of increased resource deployments in marketing", "a history of increased marketing investments", "percentage increase in marketing deployments"]
definition: To capture the historical dynamics in investment levels, we calculate the average percentage increase in R&D (and marketing) investments during the previous 3 years. Development of an overall marketing capability and brand equity may require augmented investments in marketing for multiple years.

name: R&D deployment intensity
definition: Resource deployment intensity, which we use both to calculate the interaction variables and as control variables, is measured separately for R&D and marketing deployments. Investment intensity variables can be calculated as the level of investments divided by the firm's sales, assets, or number of employees.

name: Marketing deployment intensity
definition: Resource deployment intensity, which we use both to calculate the interaction variables and as control variables, is measured separately for R&D and marketing deployments. Investment intensity variables can be calculated as the level of investments divided by the firm's sales, assets, or number of employees.

name: Top management firm-specific experience
authors_terms: ["firm-specific experience of top managers", "executives' firm-specific experience", "top management firm-specific experience", "average firm tenure"]
definition: Resource-based theory maintains that managers' firm-specific experience involving tacit knowledge of a firm's resources and capabilities allows managers to make more informed resource allocation decisions that are unique to each firm. Compared to managers who are relatively new to the firm, managers with firm-specific experience are more likely to envision a superior 'subjective opportunity set for the firm'.

name: Institutional investor ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional investor ownership", "institutional ownership", "ownership by institutional investors", "institutional investor ownership %"]
definition: Institutional investors can provide effective monitoring and governance because their block ownership and large voting power make it easier and more economically rewarding to influence a firm's strategic decisions. Ownership by institutional investors constitutes one of the more visible forms of corporate governance in the context of technology firms that have completed an initial public offering.

name: Opportunity formation
definition: The entrepreneurial opportunity is defined as a potentially profitable but not yet exploited project. Opportunity formation denotes the process of forming a (likely loosely defined) idea into a workable project that can potentially be exploited.

name: Bottom-up initiative
authors_terms: ["bottom-up initiative", "bottom-up entrepreneurial initiative", "bottom-up processes", "bottom-up opportunity formation"]
definition: Bottom-up initiative is the firm approaching opportunity formation as a bottom-up process: opportunity formation starts deep within the organizational hierarchy and may only come to the attention of senior managers in a bottom-up way.

name: Employee diversity
authors_terms: ["employee diversity", "educational diversity", "employee educational diversity", "demographic diversity", "employee heterogeneity"]
definition: Employee diversity is a multidimensional and highly complex construct that captures how employees are heterogeneous in terms of their education, age, gender, tenure, and experience; the authors adopt employee educational diversity as the relevant proxy.

name: Senior management involvement
authors_terms: ["senior-level involvement in the entrepreneurial process", "senior management involvement", "direct involvement", "centralization"]
definition: Centralization refers to the distribution of entrepreneurial decision-making authority within the firm, and high values of the centralization measure are interpreted to reflect a high level of senior manager involvement in the entrepreneurial process.

name: Bankrupt firm delisting
authors_terms: ["bankrupt firm delisting", "hazard of delisting", "delisting from the stock market", "reorganization outcome"]
definition: 'Following existing studies ..., we focus on the delisting of public firms as a negative outcome of reorganization and as stock market survival or being acquired as a positive outcome to examine the extent to which stakeholder signals can predict the hazard of a bankrupt firm's delisting.'

name: De-diversification
definition: 'De-diversification, as a correction to a prior error ..., indicates that a bankrupt firm's turnaround strategy is underway.' It is measured as the change in the number of business segments between year t - 1 and year t - 2, namely a decrease in the number of segments.

name: Increase in alliance partners
authors_terms: ["increase in alliances", "increase in the number of alliance partners", "increase in alliance partners"]
definition: 'As a result, an increase in the number of alliances formed by a bankrupt firm can serve as an important signal to predict the firm's emergence because more partners are willing to endow the firm with exchange contracts.'

name: Increase in institutional investors
authors_terms: ["increase in institutional investors", "increase in the number of institutional investors", "institutional investments"]
definition: 'Taken together, an increase in the number of institutional investors a bankrupt firm attracted demonstrates that these investors have faith in the firm (D'Aveni, 1989), therefore signaling its perceived potential to emerge.'

name: Increase in securities analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["increase in securities analyst coverage", "increase in analyst coverage", "securities analysts' coverage"]
definition: 'We maintain that higher quality bankrupt firms are more likely to attract, sustain, and even increase analysts' attention. Lower quality bankrupt firms, on the contrary, may not be able to do so. Therefore, an increase in analyst coverage of a bankrupt firm signals that this firm has greater potential to emerge.'

name: Content newness
definition: The extent to which executive communication reveals new information, that is, the distinctiveness of the information provided. It is one attribute of the content of verbal communication, which refers to the message shared with an audience.

name: Composition simplicity
definition: ' Simplicity ' of language refers to the use of clear and concise expressions; simple communication avoids the use of obscure words, unduly complex words, and confusing jargon and uses shorter phrases rather than longer ones. It is an attribute of the composition of verbal communication, which refers to the type of language used to craft the message.

name: Delivery unscriptedness
definition: ' Delivery unscriptedness ' relates to the extent to which a speaker delivers a talk without a script. It is an attribute of the delivery of verbal communication, which refers to the actual presentation of the message.

name: Investor opinion convergence
authors_terms: ["investor opinion convergence", "convergence of investors' opinions", "convergence of investor opinions"]
definition: The convergence of investors ' opinions, defined as reduction of differences in investors ' valuations. The ' opinions ' of investors, referring specifically to their valuations of a firm, will converge (or diverge) when differences in their opinions decrease (or increase).

name: Earnings uncertainty
definition: ' Earnings uncertainty ' refers to ambiguity about future earnings that will accrue to the stockholders of a firm. It also can be thought of as uncertainty about the stockholders ' earnings tomorrow per dollars invested in the stock of a firm today.

name: Independent directors' CEO experience
authors_terms: ["board CEO experience", "CEO directors", "directors' experience of serving as CEOs at other companies"]
definition: One of the two types of board human capital, defined as directors' experience of serving as CEOs at other companies. Directors who have experience of working as CEOs at other companies ('CEO directors') have developed expertise specific to the CEO's job position.

name: Independent directors' industry experience
authors_terms: ["board industry experience", "industry experience", "experience of working in the focal firm's industry"]
definition: A type of board human capital defined as experience of working in the focal firm's industry. Independent directors with work experience in the focal firm's industry will have particularly relevant knowledge of that industry.

name: Board co-working experience
authors_terms: ["board co-working experience", "internal social capital", "directors' co-working experience on the focal board"]
definition: Internal social capital, defined as directors' co-working experience on the focal board. In work groups, internal social capital is developed through group members' experience of working together.

name: Board external directorship ties
authors_terms: ["external directorship ties", "external social capital", "the board's external directorship ties to other corporations"]
definition: External social capital, defined as the board's external directorship ties to other corporations. The board's network of external directorship ties is a major source of its external social capital.

name: Investor reactions to new CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["investor reactions to a new CEO appointment", "abnormal stock return", "cumulative abnormal return (CAR)", "stock market reaction"]
definition: Abnormal stock return refers to the difference between the observed return and the predicted or normal return for the firm's stock around the appointment of the new CEO. The authors examine board effectiveness by assessing investor reactions to the appointment of a new CEO, measured as the abnormal stock returns following the appointment announcement.

name: New CEO origin
authors_terms: ["new CEO origin", "internal vs. external succession", "insider and outsider"]
definition: New CEO origin was coded '1' if the new CEO was an insider and '0' if he or she was an outsider. The new CEO's origin is the succession type that is expected to condition the value of board social capital.

name: Design value
authors_terms: ["value of a design", "value of a design patent", "logValue"]
definition: The value the market places on a newly granted design. The authors follow Kogan et al. (2017) in holding that the stock market's reaction to the announcement of a granted patent captures how the market values the newly granted design.

name: Similarity to contemporary designs
authors_terms: ["SimContemporary", "similarity with respect to other contemporary designs", "similarity (with respect to contemporary designs)", "contemporaneous differentiation"]
definition: SimContemporary measures the focal design's sum similarity to other contemporary designs (in the same style) for which patents were granted within the last year (rolling 365-day window) of its grant date.

name: Similarity to near-past designs
authors_terms: ["SimNearPast", "similarity with respect to other near-past designs", "past anchoring"]
definition: SimNearPast is the focal design's sum similarity to other designs (in the same style) for which patents were granted within the two years preceding the last year (rolling window of 1,095 to 366 days).

name: Design similarity to reference designs
authors_terms: ["similarity", "reference design's similarity to the focal design", "similar versus dissimilar"]
definition: The degree to which a new design appears similar to designs it is compared with. In the paper's context the determination of similarity between designs is part of the patent examination process, which searches for prior patents similar in terms of overall 'visual impression'.

name: Expressive value
definition: Design reflects the users' esthetic and symbolic choices; dissimilar designs can help satisfy users' innate need for differentiation and hence generate greater expressive value.

name: Informational value
definition: Because many functional aspects of a product are not readily apparent, one fundamental purpose of product design is to inform consumers of the product's functionality. Because such understandings are established through experience and familiarity, designs that appear similar to other designs help deliver informational value.

name: Product visibility
definition: Product visibility is a necessary condition for expressive value because the purpose of using a design to express one's own uniqueness inherently requires a public display.

name: Technological lifespan
definition: The effective economic life of technology within an industry can be measured by the average lags in citations (i.e., the average time gap between a citing and a cited patent) of technological patents.

name: Temporal distance of the reference set
authors_terms: ["temporal distance", "temporal distance between a new design and its comparison", "reference designs' temporal distance"]
definition: A new design can be compared against contemporaries; alternatively, it can be compared with older designs that are introduced in the past. Because designs were introduced to the market at different points in time, the paper distinguishes a new design's similarity with respect to a contemporary reference group versus a past reference group.

name: Demand-based performance
definition: Revenue per available room, commonly called 'RevPAR,' is a demand-based, firm-level performance measure; it serves as the basis for long-term business planning and is used as a guide by investors and hotel owners and general managers.

name: Differentiation-based agglomeration
authors_terms: ["differentiation-based agglomeration", "proportion of lodging properties in a cluster that were pursuing a higher differentiation strategic orientation", "proportion of properties in cluster pursuing high differentiation"]
definition: For the test of Hypothesis 1a, agglomeration was measured as the proportion of lodging properties in a cluster that were pursuing a higher differentiation (i.e., product-quality) strategic orientation.

name: Low-cost-based agglomeration
authors_terms: ["low-cost-based agglomeration", "proportion of lodging properties in a cluster that are pursuing a lower-cost strategic orientation", "proportion of properties in cluster pursuing low cost"]
definition: Hypothesis 1b requires that agglomeration be measured as the proportion of lodging properties in a cluster that are pursuing a lower-cost strategic orientation.

name: Strategic distance
authors_terms: ["strategic distance", "distance between a firm's strategic orientation and the central tendency of the strategic orientations of other firms in the cluster", "distance between strategic orientation of hotel and central tendency in cluster"]
definition: Strategic distance is defined as the difference from the typical strategic orientation of firms in a cluster; the distance score is the absolute value of a firm's own value minus the cluster's central tendency.

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation", "product-quality strategic orientation", "product/service quality segment category"]
definition: Hotel properties are classified on the basis of the extent of their quality and service differentiation, and the classifications are an indication of the 'credible commitment' made by firms to a particular level of service quality. Widely used classifications in the industry include five levels: luxury, upscale, midscale with food and beverage services, midscale without food and beverage services, and economy.

name: Government normative pressure
definition: It follows, therefore, that by establishing the Council on Ethics and announcing the fund's exclusion decisions, the government exerts normative pressure for isomorphic actions by way of encouraging adoption of responsible investment principles in firms' decision making.

name: Imitation of a prominent actor's investments
authors_terms: ["imitation", "overlap with the sovereign wealth fund's investments", "mimetism", "mimetic mechanism"]
definition: The extent to which a focal firm imitates the sovereign wealth fund's cross-border investments serves as a mediator variable. Observations from the field point to several indicators suggesting direct imitation of the sovereign wealth fund's investments.

name: Responsible cross-border investments
authors_terms: ["responsible investments", "firms' responsible investments", "responsible cross-border investments", "responsible investment outcomes"]
definition: The key outcome of interest in this study is the likelihood that a focal Norwegian firm's cross-border investments in a given year comprise socially responsible targets.

name: Regulative pressure from government ownership
authors_terms: ["regulative pressure", "coercive pressure", "government ownership", "ownership ties with the government"]
definition: In lieu of such preferential treatment, when the government owns assets in a firm, it exercises greater regulative control on the firm's investments through both written rules and unwritten codes of conduct. Such firms are naturally subject to a greater degree of regulative pressure, and the logic for compliance emerges from the threat of legal, political, and financial sanctions rather than normative pressure alone.

name: Decentralization
definition: Decentralization refers to the delegation of authority to solve problems to lower levels of an organizational hierarchy. It reflects the autonomy of a project team to make decisions about operational goals and tasks and to solve problems.

name: Free flow of information
definition: Free flow of information refers to the extent to which large quantities of rich information can be transferred across individuals and organizational boundaries without encountering resistance. In the current study the authors focus on the access to and transfer of information among individuals in a project team.

name: Reach to customers
definition: Reach refers to the distance traversed to search for ideas and information. In this study the authors focused on reach to customers, defined as a project team's interacting with customers to comprehend their needs and market conditions that affect those needs.

name: Connectedness
definition: Connectedness refers to direct contact among individuals, such as project team members, members of other projects, and members of other organizations. In the current study it is defined more narrowly as the degree of interaction or direct contact between a project team and other organizational functions.

name: Temporal pacing
definition: Temporal pacing refers to the use of a formal procedure with clear guidelines, rules, and schedules for organizing, carrying out, and assessing the progress of a project team's activities.

name: Project leader expertise
definition: Project leader expertise refers to the degree to which a project's leader possesses skills, knowledge, and experience relevant to both technical and management aspects of the project.

name: Superordinate goal
definition: Superordinate goal refers to the degree to which project team members accept and identify with the overall goals of a project.

name: Solutions found
definition: Solutions found is the ease with which a project team identifies a large number of alternative problem solutions.

name: Problem-solving speed
definition: Problem-solving speed refers to the degree of speed associated with finding and implementing a solution.

name: Solution quality
definition: Solution quality refers to the degree to which a solution enhances new product quality and reflects the extent to which the solution generates fresh thinking in the project team, is creative, and is the right solution for the problem encountered by the team.

name: Development speed
definition: Development speed is the time elapsed between the conception and definition of a product and its readiness for market.

name: Product quality
definition: Product quality is the degree to which the product satisfies customer quality and performance requirements.

name: Defection to the out-group
authors_terms: ["defection", "defection to the out-group", "migration", "switching of a firm's listing"]
definition: The event of interest was the switching of a firm's listing from NASDAQ to NYSE; organizations voluntarily abandon listing in a stock exchange and join a new stock exchange. When faced with a threat to their social identity, organizations respond by migrating to the out-group.

name: Identity-discrepant cues
definition: An identity-discrepant cue was defined as the defection of a NASDAQ member to the NYSE. The number of identity-discrepant cues facing an organization was the cumulative number of defections on the ending date for each spell.

name: Ties to in-group members
authors_terms: ["strong ties to in-group members", "strong in-group (NASDAQ) ties", "strong in-group ties", "strong NASDAQ interlocks"]
definition: Strong ties consist of sent and received ties and arise when an executive of the focal firm sits on the board of another firm (sent) or when an executive of the other firm sits on the board of a focal firm (received). Strong ties to in-group members were defined for each focal organization as the sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that a firm's board had to boards in the NASDAQ stock market.

name: Ties to out-group members
authors_terms: ["strong ties to out-group members", "strong out-group ties", "strong NYSE interlocks"]
definition: Strong ties to out-group members were defined as the sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that a firm's board had to boards in the NYSE. Ties to out-group members are likely to undermine a focal organization's attachment to the in-group but also to diminish negative stereotyping of the out-group.

name: Defector's ties to in-group members
authors_terms: ["defector's strong ties to in-group members", "defectors' strong in-group ties", "defector's ties to in-group members"]
definition: A defector's strong ties to in-group members were defined as the sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that the defecting firm's board had to boards in the NASDAQ market. The more ties defectors have with in-group members, the less likely they are to be negatively stereotyped and the more influential a defection is as an identity-discrepant cue for remaining in-group members.

name: Ties to prior defectors
authors_terms: ["ties to prior defectors", "ties that a focal organization has with prior defectors", "proximity"]
definition: A focal organization's ties to prior defectors consisted of all nonduplicated ties to prior defectors in the sample. Direct ties with defectors enable the focal organization to learn about the value of mobility as an identity-enhancement strategy and promote vicarious learning.

name: Aggregate performance
definition: A firm's performance represents the aggregate performance of its multiple business units. The dependent variable, Mean, is measured by the mean ROS of the foreign affiliates within each parent firm, industry, and host country per year over the observation period.

name: Performance distribution skewness
definition: The shape of the performance distribution as defined by skewness; the authors argue that the performance distributions of successful firms tend to be characterized by a positive skew at the firm and segment levels over the long run, which they call the positive skew effect.

name: Performance distribution kurtosis
definition: High kurtosis is characterized by a high peak in the head or long tails with more outliers and thinner shoulders relative to the normal distribution.

name: Performance distribution variance
definition: High variance is characterized by a low peak in the head and heavy tails with many values deviating from the mean.

name: Perceived agreement
definition: Perceived agreement is the extent to which actors believe themselves to agree. It is largely an individual judgement about the similarity of one's position with that of another.

name: Actual agreement
definition: Actual agreement is the real concordance of the positions held by different parties. Actual agreement and accuracy combine an individual judgement with the real position of some group.

name: Accuracy of agreement judgements
definition: Comparing perceived and actual agreement implies a third dimension, accuracy, which indicates whether individuals perceive the level of agreement that actually exists.

name: Internal agreement
definition: Internal agreement concerns within group rather than between group agreement; it is the extent to which an individual agrees with his own organization. It is analogous to actual agreement, but the reference group is different.

name: Success expectations
definition: Managerial expectations of an acquisition's success potential are plausible intermediate performance measures. Overall expectations is an estimate of expectations of success, without reference to particular objectives.

name: Personal value of acquisition objectives
definition: Personal value measures the overall personal importance that respondents attached to acquisition objectives. It is the mean of the ratings of importance that were provided by each respondent for the 14 objectives.

name: Organizational affiliation
definition: Whether a respondent belongs to the acquiring or to the acquired hospital. The authors use it to test whether the dimensions of agreement differ between the two organizations.

name: Professional role
definition: The professional background of a respondent, distinguishing M.D.s from non-M.D.s. Doctors are said to have fewer reasons to agree with their own firms than hospital managers do.

name: Occupational task
definition: The task set of a respondent, classified as administrative, clinical, or joint. Joint tasks are those for which the incumbent may have both clinical and administrative duties.

name: Involvement in integration
definition: Involvement with integration was assessed for respondents by senior executives of each hospital. Involvement influences accuracy through access to information and also ties personal goals to outcomes.

name: Legitimacy shock
definition: Shocks to legitimacy can be triggered by sudden and exogenous events such as a surprising revelation of wrongdoing or by a social movement that quickly gains influence; they can deplete the social approval (legitimacy) on which organizations depend and produce far-reaching ripple effects on an entire category through a process of 'categorical delegitimation'.

name: Within-category typicality
authors_terms: ["typicality", "grades of membership", "grade of membership", "more typical", "less typical"]
definition: Typicality is defined as a high grade of membership within a given category and is achieved via compliance with prevailing norms and expected behaviors. Organizations within these categories that deviate from these categorical norms will be seen as less typical and will have low grades of membership.

name: Deposits
definition: The authors measure deposit holdings at the organization and at the market level: a commercial bank's deposit amount is calculated by summing up deposits across branches for a given bank in a given year, and deposit market share for a given market and year is the share of a category's deposits as a fraction of total deposits (credit-union deposits plus bank deposits).

name: Financial diversification
definition: Financial diversification refers to the extent to which a firm operates in different businesses with imperfectly correlated or even countercyclical revenue streams. It consists of diversifying a firm's business portfolio to allow revenue smoothing between the firm's business lines.

name: Free cash flow
definition: FCF is defined as operating cash flow minus cash dividends minus capital expenditures.

name: Interest alignment devices
definition: Agency theorists propose to (1) tie CEOs' salary to shareholders' objectives through variable compensation, (2) grant stock options to CEOs as part of their salary, and/or (3) make CEOs shareholders. Interest alignment through either device (variable compensation, stock options or shares) more strongly links CEOs' wealth to firms' performance.

name: Control devices
definition: Agency theorists have postulated that ownership concentration is likely to allow a better control of the corporation and its management in the interest of shareholders, and that blockholders are likely to exercise their influence through the board of directors. The board of directors is the apex of the internal control system and holds the ultimate responsibility for the firm's direction, including business diversification.

name: CEO variable compensation
definition: The ratio of variable compensation over total CEO compensation for a given year, indicating the extent to which the salary of the CEO is contingent upon some measure of firm performance.

name: CEO stock options
definition: One of the interest alignment devices: granting stock options to CEOs as part of their salary; the authors created a dichotomous measure for CEO stock options because of the apparent major importance for the board to offer stock options or not to the CEO.

name: CEO ownership
definition: Inside ownership refers to managers who are also owners (CEO ownership).

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Ownership concentration is expected to allow a better control of the corporation and its management in the interest of shareholders; it is measured as the share of stock owned by the largest owner in the given year.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "proportion of independent directors", "independent directors", "outside directors"]
definition: Outside directors are directors who are not employees of the firm; this is a commonly used measure of a board's monitoring propensity.

name: Chairman/CEO non-duality
authors_terms: ["chairman/CEO non-duality", "chairman/CEO duality", "separation of the chairman and CEO roles"]
definition: Chairman/CEO non-duality refers to a board leadership structure in which the positions of the chairperson of the board and of the CEO are split; agency theory advocates the split of the chairman and the CEO positions as an important condition for board independence.

name: Value creation
definition: To assess the effect of financial diversification on the shareholders' value, the authors used two measures: shareholder return and excess value. A negative excess value implies that the firm destroys value (i.e., trades at a discount) while a positive excess value implies that the firm creates value (i.e., trades at a premium).

name: Vertical integration
definition: The scope of the firm in the vertical dimension, i.e. the extent to which it carries out stages of production itself; the authors capture movement in it through the firm's change in the use of outsourcing, where increased outsourcing means a reduced level of vertical integration.

name: Market liberalization
definition: The opening of the economy through extensive trade, regulatory, monetary, and fiscal reform, which in Argentina began in 1989 and raised the potential market size for firms by reducing barriers to the international economy.

name: Labor reform flexibility
authors_terms: ["labor policy reforms", "labor reform", "flexibility of their labor policies"]
definition: The extent to which firms view changes in labor policy as increasing their flexibility by making restructuring and downsizing possible; before the reform process it had been essentially impossible to downsize.

name: Import cost reduction
authors_terms: ["cost of imported inputs", "import cost", "lower import costs"]
definition: The cost of importing inputs, which decreased as import barriers were lowered, making international sourcing of quality inputs much more viable.

name: Inflation reduction
definition: The lowering of inflation after the pegging of the peso to the U.S. dollar, which increased the ease of writing contracts since future prices could be specified more easily.

name: Sales to multinational enterprises
authors_terms: ["sell to multinational enterprises", "MNE sales", "selling to MNEs"]
definition: Selling to the multinational enterprises operating locally, one way of being exposed to heightened demand and competitive standards.

name: Technological application diversity
definition: Technological application diversity consists of the number of application domains in which the firm is involved or to which it applies its technological resources in each year; it provides a means for a firm to benefit from economies of scope by applying the same technology in different contexts.

name: Exploitation alliances
definition: Exploitation alliances that focus on the 'D' in the R&D process bridge the gap between rent generation and rent appropriation by uniting biotech firms with larger incumbent groups to manage the development, clinical trials, regulatory process, commercialization, and distribution phases.

name: Rent generation potential
authors_terms: ["rent generation potential", "rent generation", "publicized research outputs", "research outputs", "rent-accruing resources"]
definition: In science-based industries, research articles provide signals of scientific competency, the legitimacy of future products, and promises of profits, and thus indicate a firm's rent generation potential; the authors measure rent generation potential with two research outputs, articles and patents.

name: Rent appropriation
definition: Rent appropriation ensues only when rent potential can be realized and where the profits of this realization exceed the costs of deploying the necessary services.

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation", "strategic positioning", "service-oriented firms", "research-oriented firms", "service orientation", "research orientation"]
definition: Two broad strategic positionings exist in the biotech industry: research-oriented biotech firms seek to develop breakthroughs and appropriate the returns from them, while service-oriented firms are more deeply involved in providing day-to-day services for their clients or engineering new equipment.

name: MFO size
definition: Size acts as a proxy for a number of hard-to-observe risk factors. Size is also a visible indicator that is easy to compare across organizations and gives evidence of past success and future stability.

name: MFO financial performance
definition: Financial performance is a direct indicator of a firm's solvency and a strong proxy of its ability to repay loans.

name: Commercial funding
definition: Capital acquired by a focal MFO from commercial funders, which are primarily investment funds and private equities that raise money from private investors to lend to MFOs, as well as traditional banks that lend to MFOs.

name: Public funding
definition: Capital acquired by a focal MFO from public funders, which include government departments and aid agencies, as well as development finance institutions and offer subsidized loans to ventures deemed too risky for commercial investors.

name: Political uncertainty
definition: Political uncertainty reflects the possibility that political decisions or events in a country will affect the behavior or ownership of organizations in ways that negatively affect investment returns.

name: Financial uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty associated with a country's ability to finance its sovereign, commercial, and trade obligations; when a nation's ability to repay its debts declines it is more apt to face financial crises such as recession and/or interest rate spikes.

name: Superficial similarity
definition: Superficial similarity arises when two objects, concepts, or situations share basic information elements that resemble each other (e.g., they share similar features, such as their form, color, attributes, qualities). In the context of entrepreneurial opportunities for new technologies, superficial similarities arise when the basic elements of a technology resemble the basic elements of a market.

name: Structural similarity
