definition: Structural similarity arises when two objects, situations, or concepts share the same logical relationships between their respective components, parts, and other superficial elements. Structural similarity is high when the intrinsic capabilities of a new technology resemble the causes and mechanisms underlying latent demand in a market.

name: Opportunity beliefs
authors_terms: ["opportunity beliefs", "beliefs that a new technology-market combination represents an opportunity"]
definition: Participants' extent of certainty that a scenario does (or does not) constitute a potential business opportunity. In the early phase of entrepreneurial action, opportunity beliefs are primarily articulated along two dimensions: the fit between a new means of supply and a potential target market, and the feasibility of introducing the new means of supply in that market.

name: Entrepreneurial intent
definition: Entrepreneurial intent refers to individuals' stated desire to engage in start-up activities in the near future.

name: Prior knowledge of technologies
authors_terms: ["prior knowledge of technologies", "prior knowledge of technologies (Lichtenthaler, 2009)"]
definition: Individuals' prior knowledge of the technology presented and of the scientific and engineering principles underpinning the technology. Greater prior knowledge provides richer and deeper knowledge structures with which to interpret information, so that reasoning places more emphasis on structural similarities.

name: Prior knowledge of markets
definition: Individuals' prior knowledge of the market of interest and of the problems affecting this market and current solutions to this problem.

name: Innovation strategy
definition: One of the five independent constructs in the theoretical model; the literature reviewed generally agrees that organizations with formal strategies performed better than those without strategies, while SMEs typically have informal strategies largely driven by their CEOs.

name: Formal structure
definition: The main elements of formalization that past studies have found to be important for manufacturing SMEs are procedures and organizational standards. These elements are important because they enhance the clarity of the employees' roles and lead to employee commitment, involvement, and organizational effectiveness.

name: Customer and supplier relationships
authors_terms: ["customer and supplier relationships", "partnerships with customers and suppliers"]
definition: Developing partnerships with customers and suppliers allows manufacturing SMEs to maximize the use of their limited resources and can provide them with opportunities to acquire new skills and improve existing ones.

name: Innovation culture
definition: SMEs tend to have flexible innovation cultures, which are typically characterized by relatively low resistance to change, low risk aversion, and tolerance of ambiguity.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: Manufacturing SMEs are typically established around a single breakthrough technological capability and tend to direct most of their resources toward commercializing their technology.

name: SME performance
definition: An SME performance construct developed according to Venkatraman and Ramanujam's (1986) organizational performance framework; it consists of several dimensions of business and operational performance.

name: Interfirm human asset cospecialization
authors_terms: ["human asset specificity", "human asset cospecialization", "interfirm human asset cospecialization", "human cospecialization"]
definition: Human asset specificity refers to transaction-specific know-how accumulated by transactors through long-standing transactor relationships (e.g., dedicated supplier engineers who learn the systems, procedures, and individuals that are idiosyncratic to the buyer). Human cospecialization increases as transactors develop experience working together and accumulate specialized information, language, and know-how that allows them to communicate efficiently and effectively.

name: Interfirm physical asset specificity
definition: Physical asset specificity refers to transaction-specific capital investments (e.g., in customized machinery, tools, dies). Physical asset specialization allows for product differentiation and may improve quality by increasing product integrity (fit).

name: Interfirm site specificity
definition: Site specificity refers to the situation whereby successive production stages that are immobile in nature are located in close proximity to one another to improve coordination and economize on inventory and transportation costs.

name: Product quality
definition: 'The most pervasive definition of quality currently in use is the extent to which a product or service meets and/or exceeds a customer's expectations.' Products that meet customer quality expectations are characterized by design quality and conformance quality (produced parts conform to specifications).

name: Speed of new product development
authors_terms: ["new model cycle time", "speed of new product development", "speed to market", "speed of new product development"]
definition: The ability to develop new products rapidly; automakers who are able to develop new models more quickly than competitors have an advantage because their current models are more advanced and include the latest in technology.

name: Inventory holding costs
definition: The buffer stock between an upstream supplier and downstream assembler is the sum of the supplier's finished goods and the assembler's raw materials inventory. Transactors make site-specific investments in order to economize on inventory holding costs and transportation.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "return on assets", "ROA", "profits", "combined profitability of the transactors"]
definition: If relation-specific investments can increase quality, reduce new model cycle times, and minimize inventory costs, then these benefits should translate into higher profits; profitability is measured as pretax return on assets of the automaker and of its suppliers.

name: Interfirm asset specificity
definition: Williamson (1985) describes site, physical, and human asset-specific investments as durable investments in support of particular transactions. Firms may realize a competitive advantage when they develop a tightly integrated production network characterized by a high degree of interfirm specialization.

name: Market pioneering
definition: The first-entrant with the semi-submersible rig to a national market. The radical change involved in the semi-submersible's technology and the new geographical areas it opened up for exploration led to treating the first firm introducing it to a national market as a pioneer.

name: Prior pioneering experience
definition: Number of other markets in which entrant had been a pioneer prior to entry in this market. Interviews suggested that pioneers derive experience, customer contacts, reputation, or resources from a prior market start-up that gives them an edge in semi-submersible drilling start-ups elsewhere.

name: Market share
definition: Entrant's share of national market in 1984. Market share was measured by the number of semi-submersible rigs in a national market owned by an entrant divided by the total number of semi-submersible rigs in that market.

name: Quantum of change
authors_terms: ["quantum of change", "magnitude of the volatility in the firm's environment"]
definition: The quantum of change refers to the magnitude of the volatility in the firm's environment, where a higher magnitude of volatility implies a higher level of uncertainty; larger increases or decreases in resource levels entail more uncertainty than smaller increases or decreases.

name: Rate of change
authors_terms: ["rate of change", "pace of change in an industry"]
definition: The rate of change captures the pace of change in an industry; it differs from the quantum of change in that it reflects how often the growth path of the industry is altered.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: Heterogeneity refers to the extent to which industries require both dissimilar inputs and outputs.

name: Environmental concentration
definition: Concentration is the second component of complexity according to Dess and Beard (1984); it refers to the relative density of resources in the firm environment.

name: Share of time-bound alliances
authors_terms: ["share of time-bound alliances", "relative share of time-bound strategic alliances", "time-bound alliances"]
definition: Time-bound alliances are alliances the duration of which are prespecified for a specific time window; the paper studies the relative share of time-bound alliances within a firm's strategic alliance portfolio.

name: Share of open-ended alliances
definition: Open-ended alliances are those where no time limitation is present, i.e., alliances for which no ex ante termination date had been agreed upon at the time of alliance formation.

name: Dependence on a government jurisdiction
authors_terms: ["dependence", "magnitude of dependence", "resource dependence", "dependence on government", "dependence on a jurisdiction"]
definition: Firms depend on external actors to provide the resources they need, and this resource dependence grows as the need for the resources increases and as alternative sources of the resources decrease. The magnitude of dependence on a political jurisdiction reflects the importance of the jurisdiction to the firm.

name: Corporate political activity
definition: Corporate political activity, such as contributions to political campaigns, is used by firms to manage their dependence on government; political contributions give firms access to politicians and improve the election odds of politicians they prefer.

name: National media tenor
authors_terms: ["national media tenor", "negative national media coverage", "tenor of national media coverage"]
definition: The tenor of media coverage drives state uncertainty because negative coverage poses the threat of a political contagion. National media coverage poses the greatest threat of such a contagion, due to its scope, power, and legitimacy compared with more regional or local coverage.

name: Local media tenor
authors_terms: ["local media tenor", "negative local media coverage", "local media coverage"]
definition: Negative media coverage by publications in a jurisdiction might lead managers to fear that the coverage could trigger public policy changes in that jurisdiction; local media coverage specific to a jurisdiction could increase state uncertainty specific to that jurisdiction.

name: Oppositional social movement organization resources
authors_terms: ["SMO resources", "oppositional SMO resources", "resources of oppositional SMOs", "SMO income"]
definition: As SMOs gather more resources, they are more capable of distributing information to those capable of affecting institutional change, including politicians. Because financial resources signal public support and enable SMOs to fund public relations campaigns and lobbying, SMO income is a good indicator of influence.

name: TMT turnover
definition: TMT turnover creates response uncertainty by disrupting sensemaking and enactment related to response formulation, and it inhibits a firm's ability to respond to political dependencies with CPA expeditiously.

name: Politician turnover
definition: Politician turnover refers to changes in the executive and legislative branches in a jurisdiction, usually when politicians retire or lose re-election.

name: External social performance feedback
authors_terms: ["external social performance feedback", "performance relative to external social aspirations", "external social comparisons"]
definition: External social performance feedback is measured as the difference between a fund's achieved risk-adjusted performance and the external social performance aspiration, which is based on the risk-adjusted performance of other funds outside the firm and within the same fund category.

name: Internal social performance feedback
authors_terms: ["internal social performance feedback", "performance relative to internal social aspirations", "internal social performance comparisons"]
definition: Internal social performance feedback is the difference between the fund's achieved risk-adjusted performance and an internal social performance aspiration, which we constructed based on the risk-adjusted performance of other funds inside the firm and within the same fund category.

name: Organizational change
definition: Change is conceptualized as any adaptation in organizational routines and processes. In this seminal conceptualization, change is not associated with risk.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risk is variation in the distribution of possible outcomes and uncertainty associated with gains and losses. Variability in outcomes is one of the key elements of risk.

name: Risky change
definition: Risky change is defined as the types of decisions that involve change in stock composition and concurrent risk taking.

name: Knowledge specialization
definition: Knowledge specialization reflects a firm's specialization in certain technical domains. It helps a firm gain indepth understanding of its specific technological segments (Kogut and Zander, 1992).

name: Technical distance
definition: Technical distance refers to the degree of dissimilarity in the technology knowledge base between two firms.

name: Status distance
definition: Status distance reflects the dyadic differences in firms' centralitybased network status in their network relationships.

name: Network status
definition: In this study we investigate the role of network status, which refers to a firm's positional ranking in its interfirm networks as measured by its eigenvector centrality; it concerns a firm's influence in interfirm relationships (Podolny, 1993; Washington and Zajac, 2005).

name: Structural holes
definition: Firms can derive benefits from an 'open' network by arbitraging the resource and information flow between two otherwise disconnected actors in the network (Burt, 1992; Shipilov and Li, 2008). Such firms, which occupy structural holes or brokerage positions, can utilize their unique network positions to their maximum benefit.

name: Partnering for external resources
authors_terms: ["partnering vs. non-partnering", "non-partnering vs. partnering", "partnering over non-partnering"]
definition: By non-partnering, we refer to a firm's choice of relying on its own resource endowments without external resource combination with other firms, although the firm may (or may not) pursue resources independently. Under the first condition, firms decide whether to seek external resources through interfirm linkages (nonpartnering vs. partnering), given all the considerations of firm-level characteristics, dyadic difference, and network attributes.

name: Ownership control in external relations
authors_terms: ["acquiring over allying", "alliance vs. acquisition", "allying rather than acquiring", "governance modes"]
definition: The fundamental difference is that acquisitions afford complete ownership control of assets, while alliances only allow for partial control (Yin and Shanley, 2008). They entail different flexibilities and risks: acquisitions demand irreversible financial and managerial commitment from acquiring firms, while alliances allow piecemeal involvement and continuous reassessment of partners' contribution to the venture (Balakrishnan and Koza, 1993).

name: Rational decision-making
authors_terms: ["rational decision-making", "decision rationality", "process rationality", "rationality in strategic decision processes", "rationality"]
definition: The scale reflects a conceptualization of rationality that goes beyond formal systematic planning and views rationality as a strategy-making mode. Respondents reported the extent to which the company explicitly emphasizes a systematic search for opportunities and problems and a systematic consideration of costs and benefits when planning, participative decision-making, operations research techniques, explanation of proposed changes, participative consensus-seeking decision-making with feedback, and open channels of communication.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence refers to an environment's ability to support sustained growth of an organization. Castrogiovanni distinguishes among three different kinds of munificence: capacity, growth/decline, and opportunity/threat.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism was measured as the variability in the value of shipments and operationalized as the standard error of the regression slope coefficient of the value of shipments divided by the industry mean for the period 1975-84; this operationalization corresponds to Milliken's (1987) notion of state uncertainty.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured as return on assets (net income from continuing operations, excluding extraordinary items, divided by assets) and return on sales (net income from continuing operations, excluding extraordinary items, divided by sales).

name: Acquisition integration
definition: Integration of at least that part of the acquired company that houses a focal inventor, typically an R&D unit; the authors recognize that integration is not always company wide. Integrated acquisitions are required to adopt either the acquirer's procedures or a hybrid approach, and their members may even be physically relocated.

name: Loss of relative standing
authors_terms: ["inventor's loss of relative standing", "loss of relative standing", "loss of relative status", "relative standing"]
definition: Relative standing describes an individual's status relative to others in a proximate social setting; an inventor's loss of relative standing is the degree to which the inventor moved downward in the local status order once his company was acquired.

name: Divergence from acquirer's expertise
authors_terms: ["inventor's divergence from acquirer's expertise", "divergence from the acquirer's expertise", "expertise centrality", "divergent inventor"]
definition: The degree to which the individual acquired inventor worked in scientific domains that were peripheral to the main expertise of the acquiring firm. Some acquired inventors specialize in the same scientific domains as the acquiring firm's inventors, and others have expertise that is divergent and unfamiliar to the acquirer.

name: Preacquisition social embeddedness
definition: The degree to which the individual inventor depended on others in his preacquisition organization to carry out his knowledge-creation activities; some inventors more than others rely on collaborative relationships and are relatively socially embedded in their preacquisition company.

name: Postacquisition productivity
definition: The dependent construct, measured in two ways, both of them based on each inventor's successful patent applications after the acquisition: whether the inventor continued to patent at all with the newly combined company, and the patenting output of those known survivors.

name: Team status
definition: Status has been defined as the perceived quality of the products of a producer relative to either the products of similar others or its competitors, and it is generally considered as a signal used by relevant audiences to reduce the uncertainty surrounding the quality of the producer's products.

name: Status difference
definition: The amount of effort a firm obtains depends not only on a firm's status, but also on its status advantage over its partners; we measured the status difference between a race team and its engine supplier by subtracting the status of the engine supplier from the status of the race team.

name: Exchange partner effort
definition: We define effort as the determined attempt a firm makes to expend time and resources to address problems related to the products that an exchange partner has obtained from the firm.

name: Product quality
authors_terms: ["product quality", "quality of products", "quality of a firm's own products"]
definition: To the extent that effort from exchange partners has an effect on the quality of products, a firm that is able to secure greater effort from its exchange partners can produce better-quality products than a firm that is unable to secure the same level of effort from its partners.

name: Product quality problems
definition: Effort is especially crucial when a situation demands it—that is, when quality problems arise: once an exchange relationship is established, a firm may discover that the quality of its partner's products is less than satisfactory.

name: Component modularity
definition: A component is modular to the extent that it can be incorporated into a product without needing to be changed or requiring the rest of the product to be changed. Components with high modularity can be incorporated into multiple end products with little component or end-product refinement.

name: Relationship duration
authors_terms: ["relationship duration", "duration of relationships with buyers", "duration of buyer-supplier relationships", "maximum duration of customer relationship"]
definition: The duration of a supplier's relationship with a buyer, from which suppliers may gain value through mutual knowledge of partners' capabilities and routines, trust, and relationship-specific routines for coordination. We measured the duration of a supplier's relationship with an assembler as the cumulative years it supplied the given component for at least one model produced by that assembler.

name: Current autonomy
definition: Autonomy is the degree to which a supplier can act independently of its buyers. We refer to autonomy based on the balance between how dependent a supplier is on its current buyers and how dependent those buyers are on it as current autonomy.

name: Potential autonomy
definition: A supplier's potential autonomy measures its opportunities to form ties to new buyers-buyers with which it does not currently trade-relative to the buyers' opportunities to develop ties to new suppliers.

name: Customer vertical integration
authors_terms: ["proportion of vertically integrated customers", "vertically integrated customers"]
definition: An assembler can replace a supplier by vertically integrating production of the component the supplier provided. We therefore included the proportion of a focal supplier's customers that were vertically integrated as a complementary measure of autonomy; when this value is high, the supplier has less autonomy.

name: Customer status
definition: We measured status in terms of a supplier's highest status buyer, which would be the focus of other firms' search for information about the supplier's capabilities. The fact that a highly respected assembler chose a firm to supply components acts as a strong signal of that supplier's skills.

name: Supplier failure
definition: We defined supplier failure as a supplier shutting down its production in the automotive carburetor (clutch) market.

name: Strategy purity
authors_terms: ["strategy purity", "pure strategy", "pure business strategy", "mixed strategy", "strategy purity hypothesis"]
definition: A firm pursues a pure business strategy when it chooses either cost leadership or differentiation and pursues a mixed strategy when it simultaneously chooses both pure strategies. A pure strategy is characterized by a relatively high commitment to one strategic direction and a relatively low commitment to the other, while a mixed strategy is characterized by approximately equal commitments to the two strategies.

name: Market orientation of the institutional environment
definition: Country level differences in reforms and change processes created institutional environments with different degrees of market orientation. Institutional environments with a high degree of market orientation are characterized by market-based exchange, profit-driven incentives, and regulatory frameworks that support market behavior and reduce uncertainty; those with low market orientation are characterized by relationship-based exchange, government involvement in economic exchange, and political favoritism.

name: Success of change
authors_terms: ["performance", "success of change", "success of changes", "performance as strategic change"]
definition: Successful strategic change, adapting to the shifting environment, is critical in a transition economy and thus is an appropriate indicator of performance in the context of the study. Greater success of change indicates adherence to firm objectives and successful strategy execution and leads to subsequent improved performance.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: Under cost leadership, a firm emphasizes costs, efficiency, reliability, execution, or some combination thereof.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: Under a differentiation strategy, a firm emphasizes product leadership, innovation, flexibility, responsiveness, or some combination thereof.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["equity share of the largest shareholder", "equity ownership by the largest shareholder", "percentage of shares held by the largest owner", "concentrated ownership", "dominance of the largest owner"]
definition: If the largest shareholder has a high level of equity ownership and can thus extract more private benefits from the firm, he/she will have more to lose if control changes, giving the largest owner a greater incentive to resist any potential takeover. The controlling shareholder can be powerful because large share ownership allows direct involvement in the firm's operations.

name: Regional institutional development
authors_terms: ["regional institutional development", "level of institutional development", "institutional development"]
definition: In China, the level of institutional development varies substantially across regions. In regions with a higher level of institutional development, there are better contract enforcements and property rights protection, mitigating the power of the controlling shareholders to expropriate minority shareholders for private benefits.

name: CEO political connection
definition: Political connections exist between a firm and the government when the firm has a CEO who is currently serving as or was formerly a government bureaucrat (i.e., a current or former officer of the central or local governments).

name: Takeover risk
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of a firm experiencing a takeover", "risk of corporate takeovers", "probability of a corporate takeover", "corporate takeover"]
definition: A takeover (the event) was defined as a change in a firm's controlling shareholder where the new owner was not the state. Because of the potential for private benefits, controlling shareholders are more likely to resist corporate takeovers.

name: Client-specific capabilities
definition: Client-specific capabilities are a function of repeated interaction with a given client across multiple projects over time. They largely reflect tacit knowledge of the client's business domain and operating routines acquired through repeated interaction with the client.

name: Project management capabilities
authors_terms: ["project management capabilities", "software development and project management capability", "project capabilities"]
definition: Project management capabilities are acquired through deliberate and persistent investments in infrastructure (systems and processes) and training to improve the firm's software development processes. They reflect technical capabilities in software design, development, and execution.

name: Project performance
definition: Project-level financial performance, captured by project contribution, that is revenues minus costs. Firm profitability is essentially an aggregate of project-level contribution.

name: Acquisition announcement
definition: An acquisition announcement provides different signals to the market, depending on the underlying motives for acquisitions. According to the growth probability hypothesis, an acquisition in a growth market signals future growth potential for the remaining firms in that industry.

name: Rival firms' abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["rival firms' cumulative abnormal returns", "rival firms' CAR", "abnormal returns of the rival firms", "market reaction to the rival firms"]
definition: We followed a similar procedure to calculate the cumulative abnormal returns for each rival firm in the industry (CARr,i) and for each acquisition announcement, which produced 70,734 CAR observations. Each portfolio of CARs of the rival firms represents the average of the CAR of the individual rival firm in each industry after an acquisition announcement.

name: Acquiring firms' abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["focal firms' acquisition performance", "acquiring firms' CAR", "returns for the acquiring firm", "market reaction to the acquiring firms"]
definition: For each focal firm's acquisition, we measure acquisition performance with abnormal returns on stock prices (CAR [-2, +2]). A positive abnormal return suggests that the market perceives the acquisition favorably, which increases the wealth of the shareholders. A negative abnormal return signals a pessimistic view of the transaction and destroys the focal firm's shareholder wealth.

name: Industry concentration
authors_terms: ["degree of industry concentration", "industry concentration", "level of competition in an industry", "sales-based Herfindahl index"]
definition: Consistent with other studies (Chen et al., 2007), we use a sales-based Herfindahl index (Hp,t), which we normalize with the following equation. A high value of H*p,t indicates high concentration (low competition) in the industry.

name: Industry relatedness
authors_terms: ["industry relatedness", "horizontal acquisition", "non-horizontal acquisition", "related or unrelated industries"]
definition: We measure industry relatedness of the target and acquiring firms using the firms' four-digit SIC codes, which represents the most detailed industry information available through the SDC Platinum database. In line with extant literature, we develop a binary variable to classify acquirer and target firms as related if they have the same four-digit SIC code and unrelated otherwise.

name: Computerized dispatching adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of computerized dispatching", "computerized dispatching", "TECH", "productivity-enhancing information technology adoption", "information technology adoption"]
definition: Firms began adopting modern computerized dispatching systems, composed of a central computer that coordinates vehicles and communicates information to vehicle-level onboard computers. The authors treat the three types of computerized dispatching systems (partially automated, fully automated and GPS-based) identically.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["vertical integration", "asset ownership", "firm asset ownership", "fleet ownership", "fleet-owned taxicabs", "fleet ownership of taxicabs"]
definition: The firm's ownership of the assets used in production rather than contracting for them in the open market; in the empirical setting it is the proportion of taxicabs in a fleet that are owned by the firm rather than by drivers.

name: Workforce skill
authors_terms: ["worker ability", "worker skill", "skilled labor", "less skilled workforce", "deskilling within the firm", "reduction in skilled labor use", "unskilled labor"]
definition: High-ability taxicab drivers possess unique knowledge about the spatial and temporal variation in demand within a city, which allows them to be more productive than low-ability drivers. The authors treat each worker's skill as an exogenous endowment, akin to natural ability.

name: Intangible resources
authors_terms: ["intangible resources", "information-intensive assets", "rent-yielding information-intensive resources", "technology and marketing skills"]
definition: The dominant view in diversification research is that intangible resources, such as technology and marketing skills, encourage firms to diversify into new businesses in order to exploit the "public goods" nature of information-intensive assets.

name: Foreign direct investment
definition: I defined direct investment as setting up a foreign subsidiary by establishing a new plant, entering a joint venture, or acquiring a firm. An investment that expands an existing plant is also identified as a foreign investment.

name: Competitive advantage over local firms
authors_terms: ["competitive advantages over local firms", "international competitiveness", "R&D advantage", "advertising advantage"]
definition: Hymer (1960) made the point that foreign firms have intrinsic disadvantages and further conjectured that they need monopolistic advantages over local firms to compensate for those disadvantages.

name: Core business
definition: Firms will initiate foreign ventures from core businesses, where their resources are concentrated, moving to noncore businesses over time.

name: Accumulated foreign entry experience
definition: The accumulated total entry variable reflects accumulated experience in foreign entry; it is defined as the number of a firm's previous entries at the time of a new entry.

name: Business group membership
definition: Japanese firms are well known for their complex web of corporate networks, termed keiretsu. Members of the same business group often share research and investment and exchange personnel and information.

name: Operational performance
definition: The authors measure the operational performance of trial sites using two different dependent variables: Percent to Enrollment Goal, a measure of a site's production output, and Enrollment Per Study Coordinator FTE, a measure of productivity (output per unit input).

name: Organizational focus
authors_terms: ["focus", "operational focus", "any focus", "presence of either divisional or firm focus"]
definition: Following Skinner, we claim that an organization is more focused to the extent that it limits the set of conflicting or competing operational activities in which its workers and managers are engaged.

name: Divisional focus
definition: Focus at the level of an organizational subunit such as an individual plant or business unit; in this setting, community sites that conduct both patient care and clinical trials but have set up organizational partitions creating distinct business units for each function.

name: Firm focus
definition: Focus at the level of the entire firm; in this setting, dedicated research centers that only conduct clinical trials and are therefore focused at both the firm and, by definition, divisional level.

name: Scale
definition: Simple returns to scale permit firms to allocate the costs of fixed investments across more units of output; in this setting, an organization that can run more trials simultaneously may reduce per-patient costs such as patient recruitment or trial administration, and scale is defined as the number of FTE study coordinators at each site.

name: Learning
definition: The proposed benefits of learning (e.g., lower cost or improved quality) stem from the repetition of certain routines, and the most common proxy for learning is cumulative production volume.

name: CEO conservatism
authors_terms: ["CEO conservatism", "CEO ideology", "CEO political ideology", "the CEO's own ideology"]
definition: The political ideology of the CEO on the liberalism-conservatism continuum, captured from the CEO's long-term patterns of political donations. Higher values reflect higher degrees of conservatism.

name: Organizational liberalism
definition: Organizational ideology reflects the 'prevailing beliefs among organizational members about how the social world operates, including convictions about what outcomes are desirable and how they should be achieved'; the more liberal the organizational ideology, the more liberal the prevailing employee base.

name: CEO liberal activism
definition: CEO activism is defined as a business leader's public expression of a stance on some matter of current social or political debate; liberal activism is a CEO publicly backing the liberal stance on a contested issue, such as endorsing the letter urging repeal of North Carolina's HB2.

name: Bottleneck resources
definition: We define a bottleneck resource as a resource that is vital to the introduction of a new product but cannot be readily acquired or sold in the factor market.

name: Market relatedness
definition: We propose that market relatedness, or the extent to which the firm's existing market resources are similar and fungible across product market boundaries, is an independent and critical predictor of product market entry decisions.

name: Technological relatedness
definition: Technological relatedness - the ability to transfer and reuse existing technological resources - affects all facets of organizational growth, including the introduction of new products within existing markets, entry into new markets, the mode of product market entry, and postentry firm performance.

name: Product market entry
authors_terms: ["product market entry", "new product market entry", "new product entry"]
definition: We measure a new product entry based on the finest degree of characterization in the CorpTech data - 2,681 product categories - which is set to 1 if there is a listing in a new product category for the firm in a given year, and 0 otherwise.

name: Access to external technological resources
authors_terms: ["access to external technological resources", "ability to access and integrate new technological resources", "accessing technological resources externally"]
definition: The ability to assemble the rest of the bundle, in particular, by accessing new technological resources that are competitive or at least on par with competitors, serves as an important contingency to the applicability of Hypothesis 1; as accessing technological resources externally becomes easier, this should increase the salience of market resources in driving product market entry.

name: External technology acquisition
authors_terms: ["accessing technological resources through the external market", "external acquisitions", "external collaborative arrangements", "joint ventures and alliances"]
definition: We expect that new technological resources may be gained through external sources, consistent with our argument about the importance of markets for technology. Incumbents often use various collaborative arrangements to access new technologies, spanning acquisitions, alliances, licensing, and contract R&D.

name: Internal R&D
authors_terms: ["internal R&D activities relevant to the entering market", "internal research and development", "internal development of technological resources"]
definition: Firms will also engage in learning-by-doing and build up relevant technological resources internally over time.

name: Explorative innovation strategy
definition: Technological innovation activities aimed at entering new product-market domains; the exploration versus exploitation construct is extended to define this dimension of technological innovation strategy.

name: Exploitative innovation strategy
definition: Technological innovation activities aimed at improving existing product-market positions; the exploration versus exploitation construct is extended to define this dimension of technological innovation strategy.

name: Ambidextrous innovation strategy
definition: A firm can be regarded as ambidextrous if it scores high on both explorative and exploitative innovation strategies, in which case the product of the two scores would be a good proxy measure of ambidexterity.

name: Relative imbalance between explorative and exploitative innovation strategies
authors_terms: ["relative imbalance", "absolute difference between explorative and exploitative innovation strategies", "fit as matching"]
definition: The absolute difference between a firm's explorative and exploitative innovation strategy scores; the 'fit as matching' test is concerned with whether a match (a smaller absolute difference) between exploration and exploitation can enhance firm performance.

name: Sales growth rate
authors_terms: ["sales growth rate", "firm performance", "average sales growth rate"]
definition: The dependent variable is sales growth rate, measured as self-reported compounded average sales growth rate in the last three years (from 1996 to 1999 with 1996 as the base year).

name: Performance variation relative to mean
authors_terms: ["intragroup variation in performance, relative to their mean values of performance", "performance dispersion", "standard deviation/mean sales growth rate ratio"]
definition: An exploitative innovation strategy is more likely to result in less intertemporal performance variability than an explorative innovation strategy, and firms that emphasize explorative innovation should exhibit greater performance dispersion than those that emphasize exploitative innovation.

name: Product innovation intensity
definition: Product innovation intensity is measured as the percentage of total annual sales that consist of new/improved products introduced over the last three years.

name: Process innovation intensity
definition: Process innovation intensity is measured as the percentage of annual production volume using new/improved processes introduced over the last three years.

name: Relative compensation dispersion
authors_terms: ["compensation dispersion", "relative compensation dispersion", "pay dispersion", "relative Gini coefficient"]
definition: A firm's compensation dispersion, defined as the variation in employee pay within the firm, measured relative to competitors. To compute the measure, each firm's Gini coefficient is divided by the average Gini coefficient of other firms in the same state.

name: Relative individual performance
definition: Extreme high (low) performers are employees who are compensated significantly more (less) than coworkers in the same firm who have similar observable characteristics (e.g., education, seniority, age, gender, race).

name: Employee turnover
definition: Turnover is defined broadly as employee exit from an organization.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
definition: Entrepreneurship is the case in which the employee creates or joins a new venture, as opposed to mobility, when the employee joins an existing organization.

name: Network resources
definition: Network resources are the resources that are owned by its partners yet can be potentially accessed by the focal firm through its ties to these partners. Network resources encompass partners' tangible and intangible assets, including their human resources, financial assets, marketing efforts, R&D investments, and reputation.

name: Market performance
definition: The market performance measure captures the annual change in the market value of the firm's common shares. It is a financial measure based on investors' expectations about the future performance of the firm.

name: Relative partner profitability
definition: The relative profitability variable measures the mean difference between the return on assets (ROA) of partners in the alliance portfolio and the focal firm's ROA in a given year. It represents the relative bargaining power of partners based on the profitability of partners relative to the profitability of the focal firm.

name: Relative partner alternatives
authors_terms: ["relative alternatives", "relative partner alternatives", "relative availability of alternative alliances"]
definition: The relative alternatives variable captures the structural dependence of the focal firm on its alliance portfolio, under the assumption that partners with many alternative ties to other firms in the software industry hold strong bargaining positions. Higher values suggest that partners in the alliance portfolio have relatively more alternatives than the focal firm.

name: Bilateral competition
authors_terms: ["bilateral competition", "competition between the focal firm and its partners"]
definition: Bilateral competition is the level of competition between the focal firm and partners in its alliance portfolio, that is, the extent to which partners can be considered competitors of the focal firm.

name: Multilateral competition
definition: The extent to which partners in the alliance portfolio are considered direct competitors of each other can be referred to as multilateral competition. It evolves when the focal firm allies with multiple partners that operate in the same product markets or offer similar services.

name: Individual performance
definition: Our outcome of interest is the length of time it takes a radiologist to read a case (READTIME). Time to completion is a commonly used performance measure in the learning literature and an important measure for operational performance in this context.

name: Individual customer experience
definition: Individual customer experience (IndvlCustomer) is the cumulative number of prior cases read by a radiologist for the customer of the current case.

name: Customer-domain experience
definition: IndvlCustomerDomain represents the cumulative number of prior cases read by a radiologist in the domain, and for the customer, of the current case. The authors note that they refer to an individual's customer-domain experience and customer experience interchangeably.

name: Customer experience in other domains
authors_terms: ["IndvlCustomerOtherDomain", "experience gained from the same customer in different domains"]
definition: IndvlCustomerOtherDomain represents the cumulative number of prior cases (outside the domain of the current case) read by a radiologist for the customer, of the current case.

name: Other-customer experience in the same domain
definition: IndvlOtherCustomerDomain represents the total cumulative number of prior cases for a given radiologist that match the domain (e.g., body, chest, spine), but not the customer, of the current case.

name: Other-customer experience in other domains
definition: IndvlOtherCustomerOtherDomain represents the cumulative number of prior cases read by a given radiologist in all domains and for all customers other than those of the current case.

name: Individual variety in customer experience
authors_terms: ["individual variety in customer experience", "variety in customer experience", "varied experience", "IndvlCustomerFocus"]
definition: The authors ask whether greater variety in the customers with whom an individual works increases her rate of learning from customer-specific experience; they measure the degree to which a radiologist's cumulative volume prior to the current case is concentrated by customer.

name: Organizational customer experience
definition: OrgCustomer captures the depth of OutsourceCo's experience with a particular customer: the total number of prior cases a customer has sent to OutsourceCo, less the current reading radiologist's cumulative experience with that customer.

name: Firm centrality
definition: The network notion of centrality reflects the significance of a firm in its network. At the simplest level of conceptualization, a highly central firm is likely to be connected to many more partners than the less central firm, and centrality comes from being the object of relations from other contacts.

name: Network centralization
definition: Centrality is a firm-level construct, but the distribution of centrality among firms in a network gives rise to the construct of centralization, which indexes the tendency of a single firm to be more central than all others in the network. Thus, centralization provides an aggregate measure for the distribution of centrality among firms in a network.

name: Interblock relations
authors_terms: ["interblock relations", "relations between blocks", "pattern of relations between blocks"]
definition: In network terms, firms can be divided into blocks, with each block being composed of firms that are structurally similar, and relations among blocks can be analyzed. Our discussion characterizes structural change in terms of the relative centrality of participating firms and in patterns of relationships between blocks of firms.

name: Industry event type
definition: Our main thesis is that the structural impact of industry events may be either structure-reinforcing or structure-loosening. We view the structure of a network as being reinforced if, in general, hitherto powerful firms increase their network power while hitherto less powerful firms become even less powerful; the structure of a network is loosened if hitherto powerful firms decrease their network power while hitherto less powerful firms become more powerful than they were.

name: Technology block
definition: For purposes of analysis, firms may be divided into blocks, and we chose the criterion of contextual equivalence as it allowed us to capture change in patterns of relationship between strategically meaningful categories of firms. Each block in our analysis consists of firms that are similar on the attribute of technology.

name: Network restructuring
definition: The authors propose that key industry events provide occasions for network restructuring, where true structural change is evidenced by significant variation over time in the underlying pattern of relationships that bind a given set of actors. Structural change does not change merely because some actors leave a network position and others enter it, or merely because the rate of network activity increases or decreases.

name: Exposure to violent protests
authors_terms: ["exposure to violent protests", "proximity to violent protests", "proximity of an entrepreneur's business to events of violence"]
definition: Entrepreneurs' physical proximity to violent protests is converted into a measure of exposure using a quadratic distance decay function, with a cutoff point of 0.5 km after which the protest is assumed not to have an effect.

name: Business profits
authors_terms: ["profits last month (log)", "log profits last month", "business performance"]
definition: The outcome of interest in this study is entrepreneurs' business performance, operationalized as log profits last month, which is equal to profits during the month prior to the survey.

name: Local community ties
authors_terms: ["local community ties", "ties to local communities", "community ties"]
definition: Community ties represent a level of integration into the local community and familiarity with community members at large.

name: Non-colocated advice relationships
definition: Advice relations who are not located in the same neighborhood, that is, who are non-colocated, are less likely to have been exposed to the same disruption and are likely to remain sources of support.

name: Colocated advice relationships
definition: In local shocks colocated ties, which are located proximately to the focal entrepreneur, are likely to be exposed to the same shock.

name: Bridging ties
definition: Knowledge-sharing ties spanning internal boundaries in a formal organization, i.e., ties connecting individuals located in different parts of an organization that provide access to diverse sources of knowledge and information.

name: Tie strength
definition: A feature of the dyadic knowledge-sharing relationship; 'strength' refers to frequency of interaction between the two individuals.

name: Simmelian ties
definition: A tie is Simmelian when the parties involved are reciprocally and strongly tied to each other and they are both reciprocally and strongly tied to at least one common third party; equivalently, a Simmelian tie is a tie embedded in a clique.

name: Individual innovativeness
authors_terms: ["generation of innovation", "individual innovativeness", "individual innovative capabilities", "innovative performance", "patent generation"]
definition: Individuals' ability to generate innovations; the authors distinguish generating new ideas from implementing them into innovations, and note that having new ideas is not the same as translating them into innovative outputs.

name: Experience under a new incentive regime
authors_terms: ["experience under the new incentive regime", "cumulative sales", "cumulative experience"]
definition: Experience under the new incentive regime is measured by each outlet's cumulative sales of primary loans since its introduction. Cumulative sales reflect both experience and exposure over time as well as learning by doing.

name: Bank's share of value created
authors_terms: ["bank's share", "value appropriated by an organization as a percentage of the value created", "division of value"]
definition: The bank's share of value created is one minus the ratio of value appropriated by outlet employees to the value that the outlet created. It captures how the value created by an outlet is split between the firm and outlet employees.

name: Value created by employees
definition: The value created by employees is their contribution to the objective function of the firm. In this setting it is measured by the outlet's sales performance in primary loans, calculated as the difference between the outlet's total revenues from primary loans and the corresponding imputed costs of capital.

name: Value appropriated by employees
definition: The value appropriated by employees is the amount of the created value that is retained by them. In this setting it is measured by the sum of outlet employees' monthly bonus from the sale of primary loans.

name: Fraud
authors_terms: ["fraud", "fraudulent companies", "fraudulent firms", "misrepresentation of merit", "cooked its books", "misstatements of profit"]
definition: Fraudulent behavior is observed directly by comparing two sets of financial books filed by the same firms at the same time to two different state agencies; the presence or absence of discrepancies is used to classify firms as either ''fraudulent'' or ''honest.'' Almost every misstatement inflates the profit reported to MOST relative to the profit reported to SAIC.

name: Innovation grant award
authors_terms: ["Innofund grant", "state-funded innovation grants", "winning an innovation grant", "grant winners", "capital infusion from the Innofund"]
definition: The grant program studied is China's Innovation Fund for Technology-Based Firms, known as Innofund, under the Ministry of Science and Technology; all firms in the sample applied for a government-funded innovation grant, and winning a grant means the firm received an innovation subsidy from the Innofund.

name: Investment in organizational development
authors_terms: ["invest them in their intended, productive uses", "invest in organizational development and innovation", "human resource recruitment", "job postings", "recruitment ads", "invest grant awards in expanding the talent base of the company"]
definition: The authors examine firms' resource allocation through their human resource recruitment practices, measured by online recruitment ads, as a proxy for companies' intended investment levels; companies that fraudulently acquire resources for the intended purpose of investment are expected to be less likely to commit these resources to organizational development and innovation.

name: Significant technical advances
authors_terms: ["significant technical advances", "important (invention) patents", "invention patents", "fundamental innovation", "technically more meaningful innovations"]
definition: Some discoveries are challenging, and innovation of this type requires significant and persistent investment and effort; in the Chinese patent system, invention patents are much more significant than utility patents because they apply to novel products, processes, or their improvements.

name: Trivial innovation
authors_terms: ["trivial innovations", "superficial innovations", "more marginal (utility) patents", "utility patents", "window-dressing patents"]
definition: Innovations that are more superficial embody advancements that are smaller in nature and contribute much less to the progression of technology; they can play a dual role by providing legitimacy that shields an organization from external scrutiny and contributes to efforts to obtain additional external resources.

name: Executive beliefs
definition: Beliefs are defined here as the understandings about credible relationships between objects, properties, or ideas. We examine the normative beliefs of executives, which relate to the perceived importance of various business goals, and the cause-effect beliefs of executives relating to the efficacy of various business tactics in achieving organizational effectiveness.

name: Functional background
definition: Executives' functional background, i.e., the length of executives' exposure to various functional areas in their previous work histories, is likely to influence executive beliefs primarily through exposure over time to issues, such that the greater the length of time spent by executives in a given functional area, the more likely it is that their beliefs will be consistent with the functional goals of that area.

name: Current functional position
definition: Current functional position, i.e., the functional area of the current job, is more likely to affect executive beliefs by highlighting current organizational issues in that functional area.

name: Upper-echelon team member beliefs
authors_terms: ["beliefs of other upper-echelon team members", "beliefs of other members of the organization's upper-echelon team", "team member beliefs"]
definition: An important component of our theoretical model is a causal effect indicating that the beliefs held by an upper-echelon executive are determined in part by the beliefs of other members of the upper-echelon team.

name: Functional background similarity
definition: Functional background similarity was assessed by first calculating the absolute difference between the focal executive and each team member in the number of years spent in each functional area, then averaging these absolute differences across all functional areas and across all team members, and finally taking the multiplicative inverse to arrive at a similarity score.

name: Age similarity
definition: Age similarity was assessed by calculating the absolute difference in age between the focal executive and each team member, averaging across all team members, and taking the multiplicative inverse of this average.

name: Tenure similarity
definition: Tenure similarity and the interaction of tenure similarity and team member beliefs were calculated in a manner similar to that applied to age.

name: Consensus level
definition: The model represents committees as comprising N decision makers, of which C must approve a project for it to be approved by the committee (C stands for 'consensus level'). From the data set, organizational structure can reliably be coded into three nonoverlapping categories: mutual funds managed by one individual (1/1), managed by more than one individual operating independently (N/1, decentralized), and managed by more than one individual with unanimous decisions (N/N, centralized).

name: Number of projects accepted
authors_terms: ["number of approved projects", "number of projects pursued", "number of stocks bought"]
definition: One of the three outcomes predicted by the model: the number of approved projects, i.e., the number of projects (stocks) an organization decides to pursue. It is measured by the number of stocks a fund buys per quarter.

name: Omission errors
definition: Errors of omission (equivalent to Type I errors in statistics) correspond to missing good choices. In this setting, an omission error occurred whenever a fund failed to buy an asset that turned out to have a good performance.

name: Commission errors
definition: Errors of commission (equivalent to Type II errors in statistics) correspond to pursuing bad choices. In this setting, a commission error occurred whenever a fund bought an asset that turned out to have a poor performance.

name: Cognitive frame similarity
authors_terms: ["cognitive frame similarity", "similarity in cognitive frames", "organizational-level cognitive frames"]
definition: Cognitive frame similarity denotes the degree to which two organizations resemble each other in terms of their generalized organizational-level schemas of interpretation—that is, shared values, beliefs, and cognitive orientations.

name: Good faith provisions
definition: Good faith provisions are clauses rooted in, and explicitly referring to, the legally enforceable principle of 'honesty in fact and the observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing'.

name: Genuine good faith provisions
definition: Genuine good faith provisions are used without additional explicit stipulations to address cases in which partners fail to reach an agreement in good faith; contracting partners strongly depend on their ability to resolve a given issue in good faith.

name: Guarded good faith provisions
definition: In guarded good faith provisions, partners use good faith provisions in combination with explicit provisions; these good faith provisions include an explicit contractual remedy that takes effect when good faith efforts fail.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty arises from the unpredictability of future technological developments, which precludes a complete understanding of the available response options and their potential impacts on a strategic alliance.

name: General alliance experience
definition: The extent to which either partner has undertaken prior alliances; as general alliance experience increases, the partners' interpretive processes during contract negotiations become prestructured, reducing the influence of ad hoc, situated, and interactive sensemaking.

name: Organizational interdependence
authors_terms: ["organizational interdependence", "tightness of coupling", "level of coupling", "level of organizational interdependence", "partner interdependence"]
definition: Organizational interdependence refers to the tightness of coupling (Orton & Weick, 1990) and the level of mutual commitment between the partners (Leonard-Barton, 1995). It is also largely consistent with the extent to which a sourcing firm can exert hierarchical control as opposed to relying on market-contract control.

name: Technological uniqueness
authors_terms: ["technological uniqueness", "uniqueness of a technology", "unique know-how", "unique technology"]
definition: Technological uniqueness refers to the current prevalence of a technology within an industry. The more unique the underlying know-how, the greater the benefits gained by those firms that possess the know-how.

name: Imitability of technology
authors_terms: ["imitability", "difficulty of technical imitation", "difficult to imitate", "degree to which technological know-how is difficult to imitate"]
definition: Highly difficult imitation may be caused by various factors, including causal ambiguity, technological complexity, tacitness, and specificity. Much of the know-how supporting such products resides in individuals and is implicit rather than explicit.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technological uncertainty", "commercial uncertainty", "uncertainty associated with the technology"]
definition: Commercial uncertainty refers to the uncertainty associated with the commercial success of a technology. This uncertainty arises from the ambiguity as to whether the technology will work as it is designed to work and whether the marketplace will favor associated products and processes.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: The dynamism of a technology is not so much a question of design quality and initial market acceptance but of whether the underlying technology will be of ongoing value in a changing technological environment. Dynamic environments are characterized by short technological life cycles and the Schumpeterian process of creative destruction.

name: Sourcing performance
authors_terms: ["sourcing performance", "technology-sourcing performance", "sourcing outcomes", "composite sourcing performance", "technology-sourcing performance"]
definition: We define sourcing performance as the outcomes for a sourcing firm resulting from a sourcing partnership. It is a second-order latent construct with three dimensions: the sourcing firm's enhanced capabilities resulting from the sourced technology, the attainment of the firm's original objectives for sourcing the technology, and the estimated return on the sourcing firm's investment for the technology.

name: Acquisition premium
definition: The difference between the price paid to acquire a company and the estimated preacquisition value of the company, measured as the percentage difference between a purchase price and an IPO target's value four weeks prior to the announcement of the acquisition.

name: Investment bank reputation
authors_terms: ["investment bank reputation", "reputation of its investment bank", "reputation of an IPO firm's underwriter"]
definition: The reputation of the investment bank that took an IPO firm public, reflecting the matching process in which higher-quality firms are taken public by more reputable underwriters and lower-quality firms associate with less reputable investment banks.

name: Venture capitalist prominence
authors_terms: ["venture capitalist prominence", "VC prominence", "backing by prominent VCs"]
definition: Whether a firm was backed at the time of its IPO by a prominent venture capitalist, where prominence reflects the selectivity with which such VCs make investments and the costs borne by firms.

name: Alliances with prominent partners
authors_terms: ["number of alliances it has formed with prominent partners", "prominent alliance partners", "alliances with prominent partners"]
definition: The number of alliances an IPO firm has formed with prominent partners, where prominence is given by partners that are publicly listed and therefore act as well-known endorsers, counting alliances formed before and after the IPO but prior to the acquisition.

name: Knowledge distance
authors_terms: ["knowledge distance", "acquirers based in industries with different knowledge requirements", "dissimilar knowledge bases"]
definition: A continuous measure of the distance between the knowledge requirements of an acquirer's and a target's industries, used to capture the relatedness of acquirer and target as a determinant of the asymmetric information surrounding an individual M&A deal.

name: Cross-border acquisition
authors_terms: ["cross border", "cross-border acquisitions", "acquirers based in foreign countries"]
definition: Whether the acquirer of an IPO target was a foreign (non-U.S.) firm, a setting in which deals between foreign acquirers and domestic targets are argued to involve more information asymmetry problems.

name: Economic incentive alignment
authors_terms: ["ratio of common to private benefits", "common to private benefit ratio", "economic incentives", "incentive alignment", "common benefits", "private benefits"]
definition: Khanna et al. define 'private' benefits as those accruing to individual firms from activities not governed by the alliance, and 'common' benefits as those accruing to all participants in the alliance. Therefore, the probability of strategic alliance success depends on the extent to which the decision makers perceive common benefits to be greater than private benefits.

name: Incentive heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in strategic alliance partners' ratio of common to private benefits", "heterogeneous ratios of common to private benefits", "heterogeneity in the ratio of common to private benefits", "heterogeneity of decision makers", "asymmetric common benefits"]
definition: Given the need for coordination among strategic alliance partners, a key factor that can impact alliance success is whether decision makers are similar or different to each other in terms of perceived benefits of the strategic alliance. An increase in the heterogeneity of decision makers increases the difficulty of reaching the efficient economic outcome.

name: Communication
definition: The fundamental insight from classical organization theory is that effective coordination requires not only monetary incentives, but also nonmonetary rewards, and that both formal and informal managerial communication can increase the likelihood of cooperation and coordination. Communication can reduce coordination costs and address management issues related to bounded rationality and decision biases.

name: Alliance success
authors_terms: ["alliance success", "success in strategic alliances", "successful alliance outcomes", "realized value creation", "transfer of resources", "resources in alliance"]
definition: Successful strategic alliance outcomes rely on exchange partners choosing the payoff dominant strategy where they all cooperate toward the joint goal of economic value creation, rather than the risk dominant strategy of not investing in the joint alliance activity. The measures are highly correlated but they capture multiple aspects of the same question: to what extent did strategic alliance members create value?

name: Task interdependence
authors_terms: ["task interdependence", "task interdependence with nonprofit peers", "task interdependence with their nonprofit peers"]
definition: Reflecting the depth of such boundary-spanning, this study's primary independent variable is thus employees' task interdependence with nonprofit peers, or 'the extent to which group members rely on one another to complete their jobs'.

name: Partnership identity
authors_terms: ["partnership identity", "nonprofit partnership identity", "identification with the corporate-nonprofit partnership"]
definition: The partnership should become an important part of corporate volunteers' role identity or their cognitive model of their role as an employee of the firm. Employees embrace the partnership identity as they more strongly identify with and take pride in their role within the company's CSR programs.

name: Institutional learning
definition: Corporate volunteers to developing countries can engage in institutional learning: to learn from their nonprofit peers about overcoming the social, cultural, and economic issues that make it challenging for firms to operate in developing countries.

name: CSR recognition
definition: Returning volunteers need to perceive that their CSR activities are valued internally (henceforth, 'CSR recognition'). It reflects how employees felt they were treated during the year following their return compared to colleagues who had not completed an international assignment.

name: Identity strain
definition: A 'tension associated with one's employee identity being inconsistent with the current environment' that can increase attrition for returning international expatriates. The identity process describes how individuals strive to achieve congruence between inputs from the environment and their sense of what it means to be who they are.

name: Propensity for U.S. listing
authors_terms: ["capital market choice", "foreign IPO capital market choice", "choice of capital markets", "market choice", "exchange listing decisions"]
definition: The dependent variable in the study is binary: whether a foreign firm makes its IPO on the U.S. or U.K. exchanges between 2002 and 2006, with U.S. listed foreign IPOs coded 1 and U.K. listed foreign IPOs coded 0.

name: Founder-CEO leadership
definition: Founder-CEO was a dummy variable, coded as 1 if one of the original founders of a company was the CEO at the time the company went public. The authors treat the presence of founder-CEOs as the level of professionalization of the management team.

name: Executive stock options
authors_terms: ["executive stock options", "executive share options", "stock-based executive compensation"]
definition: Executive stock options was dummy coded as 1 if stock options were offered to the CEO prior to the firm's IPO.

name: Board independence
definition: Board independence is defined as the presence of directors who do not have any 'close personal or professional ties' with the firm, its subsidiaries or affiliates, or firm's management.

name: Board interlocks
definition: These links are directly related to board ties, measured in terms of the number of outside directorships ('interlocks') each individual board member holds in other organizations both within and outside the industry.

name: Underwriter prestige
definition: Highly prestigious underwriters may use their reputations to certify the quality of a foreign IPO and may be involved in active post-issue monitoring to protect their reputation assets.

name: Venture capital syndication
definition: Syndication is a means by which VCs can share risk through portfolio diversification, since for a given funds' size, syndication enables the spreading of capital across a greater number of investments. It is measured as the number of VC firms involved in an IPO.

name: Strategic planning process
authors_terms: ["strategic planning processes", "strategic planning system", "planning system", "planning process"]
definition: A firm's strategy requires specific information, and this information is provided in a large part by the strategic planning system. Planning as information gathering is concerned with environmental scanning, competitor analysis, and the retrieval of some internal information, while planning as programming represents the multitude of functions performed by planning to assist in the implementation of strategic decisions through information dissemination and integration.

name: Accounting control
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Integration and coordination
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Flexibility
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Goals and plans
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Scanning
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Breadth of analysis
authors_terms: ["Broad Analysis", "breadth of analysis", "breadth dimensions of planning"]
definition: One of the six planning dimensions produced by the rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the planning system items; exact factor scores were used in the regression analyses.

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["strategy content", "strategic orientation", "strategy type", "Miles and Snow strategy types"]
definition: Strategic content research focuses on the outcome of actual strategic decisions. The Miles and Snow (1978) typology is used to represent strategy content: Prospectors compete through new products, product innovation, and market development, while Defenders compete in relatively stable product markets and compete through cost leadership, quality, and service.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Archival measures of Return on Assets, Return on Equity and Loan Growth were gathered; an aggregate measure of performance was calculated by averaging the scores of the three years for each variable.

name: Technical capabilities
definition: Technical capabilities are scientific and technical expertise that contribute to creating new products. In agricultural biotechnology the technical capabilities behind trait development are plant biotechnology expertise along with plant physiology, molecular biology, biochemistry, and cell culture.

name: Specialized complementary assets
definition: Complementary assets are downstream resources that contribute to product delivery to customers and value capture. Specialized complementary assets are applicable in a limited set of industries, and are closely interdependent with particular products or technologies.

name: External sourcing mode
authors_terms: ["mode of external sourcing", "alliance versus acquisition", "the choice between alliances and acquisitions", "external sourcing modes"]
definition: The mode by which pre-entrants obtain needed resources from external sources, that is, an alliance or an acquisition. The dependent variable is a binary variable equal to one for alliances and zero for acquisitions.

name: Adoption of institutionally contested practices
authors_terms: ["adoption of institutionally contested practices", "stock option adoption", "stock-based incentive plan adoption"]
definition: Institutionally contested practices are new organizational practices that face stiff opposition from key constituents in potential adopters' primary institutional environment, though some actors in that environment may advocate them.

name: Affiliations with prestigious institutional environments
authors_terms: ["affiliations and exchange relationships", "ties to the United States", "association or exchange relationship with a prestigious institutional context"]
definition: Exchange relationships across national borders expose an organization to different practices, perspectives, values, and beliefs and provide learning conduits.

name: CEO graduate business education
authors_terms: ["CEO graduate business education", "graduate business education", "graduate degree in business"]
definition: CEOs with graduate business degrees should be more likely to acquire a deep knowledge about business practices outside their primary institutional environments than CEOs lacking such a specific educational background.

name: Prior adoption of institutionally contested practices
authors_terms: ["prior successful adoption of institutionally contested practices", "prior adoption of GAAP/IAS", "experience with contested practices"]
definition: Knowledge and experience gained from past situations give the firm adroitness when dealing with similar hotly contested situations in the present or the future.

name: Board interlocks with prior adopters
definition: Board interlocks represent strong network ties that enable participating organizations to engage in a continuous twoway communication that is based on mutual trust.

name: Prior adoptions within the industry
authors_terms: ["industry adoptions", "prior industry adoptions", "prior adopters within a firm's industry"]
definition: Structural equivalence explains innovation adoption as a consequence of imitating competitors who occupy a similar role in an environment.

name: Prior adoptions within the home country
authors_terms: ["German adoptions", "prior adopters within the DAX 100", "prior adopters within an organization's home country"]
definition: With respect to uncontested practices, it is well known that firms mimic other firms in their industry (Fligstein, 1991). When considering transnational diffusion of contested practices, other firms in a national economy may be logical referents.

name: Regulatory legitimization
authors_terms: ["regulatory legitimization", "regulatory legitimacy", "legal or regulatory changes", "change in German corporate law"]
