definition: Regulatory legitimacy, which is conveyed when a new practice is in line with existing rules and laws (North, 1990), is one of Scott's (2001) three pillars of legitimacy.

name: Adoption timing
definition: We defined pioneer adopters as firms that adopted stock option pay before it was formally legalized in 1998.

name: Repeat initiative taking
authors_terms: ["repeat initiative taking", "repeated generation of initiatives", "sustained initiative taking"]
definition: Our measure of repeat initiative taking was binary, taking a value of 1 if an idea initiator put forth an idea and submitted another idea during the next four years and 0 if he or she did not.

name: Initiative success
authors_terms: ["initiative success", "initiative outcome performance", "quality of an initiative"]
definition: We consider the rejection of an initiative by the management as a failure and the adoption or acceptance of an initiative as a success. We classified ideas as successful (i.e., we coded the variable with a value of 1 on a binary scale) if they passed the second screening when Enco reviewed the potential of the idea.

name: Initiator prior success experience
definition: For the analysis of repeat initiative taking, we separately tallied all successes that the initiator had experienced with both the focal initiative and any prior initiative. For the analysis of initiative success, we separately counted all successes that the focal initiator had experienced in initiating prior initiatives only.

name: Initiator prior failure experience
definition: For the analysis of repeat initiative taking, we separately tallied all failures that the initiator had experienced with both the focal initiative and any prior initiative. For the analysis of initiative success, we separately counted all failures that the focal initiator had experienced in initiating prior initiatives only.

name: Contributor prior success experience
definition: For the focal contributor of an initiative, we counted the prior success and failure experiences of initiating ideas and tallied them if there were more than one contributor to an initiative.

name: Contributor prior failure experience
definition: For the focal contributor of an initiative, we counted the prior success and failure experiences of initiating ideas and tallied them if there were more than one contributor to an initiative.

name: Commitment-based human resource practices
definition: This commitment-based approach emphasizes the implementation of a combination of HR practices that work together to motivate employees to contribute high levels of discretionary behaviors by aligning their interests with those of the organizations and creating a mutually reinforcing high-investment employer-employee relationship.

name: Climate for trust
definition: Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman defined trust as 'the willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party based on the expectation that the other will perform a particular action important to the trustor, irrespective of the ability to monitor or control that other party' (1995: 712). They suggested that trust is rooted in three interrelated components: ability (belief that the other is capable and skilled), benevolence (desire to do good for the other), and integrity (belief that the other is motivated by principles of fairness).

name: Climate for cooperation
definition: Following Wagner (1995), we defined a social climate for cooperation as the organizational norms that emphasize personal effort toward group outcomes or tasks as opposed to individual outcomes.

name: Shared codes and language
authors_terms: ["shared codes and language", "climate for shared codes and language"]
definition: Shared codes and language comprise a common set of terms, symbols, and understandings that allow individuals to communicate effectively with one another.

name: Knowledge exchange and combination
definition: Nahapiet and Ghoshal (1998) argued that new knowledge is created within organizations through the process of exchange and combination among employees. Implicit in this argument is the notion that exchange and combination create new knowledge by connecting previously unconnected ideas and knowledge or recombining previously connected ideas and knowledge in novel ways.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "revenue from new products and services", "one-year sales growth"]
definition: We measured firm performance as both revenue from new products and services and one-year sales growth, because these are good indicators of the extent to which high-technology firms have been able to innovate and create new knowledge.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Publics construct reputations from available information about firms' activities originating from the firms themselves, from the media, or from other monitors, and individual interpretations aggregate into collective judgments that crystallize into reputational orderings of firms in organizational fields. The eight attributes elicited from respondents were treated as components of an underlying and stable construct of reputation.

name: Market performance
definition: Market signals present information to constituents about firms' current activities, results, and prospects, and the market value of firms provides investors and their advisors, as well as competitors and other auditors, with both firm-specific and comparative information. It was gauged by the ratio of market to book value for September 27, 1985.

name: Market risk
definition: A market measure of risk was gauged by firms' beta coefficients on September 27, 1985; beta coefficients are commonly used measures of the systematic risk of a firm, the degree to which movement in a firm's stock is associated with general stock market movements.

name: Dividend yield
definition: The dividend yield, a ratio of dividend payout to stock price, is a useful indicator of whether publics take a short- or long-run view of firms.

name: Accounting profitability
definition: Since long-run effectiveness requires firms to be profitable, accounting data signal the merits of firms; prior-year accounting profitability was measured as return on invested capital at the end of fiscal year 1984, a measure independent of capital structure.

name: Accounting risk
definition: Constituents expect a high level of return from firms whose strategies demonstrate high levels of risk, and for two firms with similar levels of profitability greater risk should negatively influence publics' assessments. The level of accounting risk was estimated by the coefficient of variation of ROIC in the previous nine years.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional ownership", "concentration of a firm's equity among institutions", "institutional investors"]
definition: The composition of investors in firms' shares arguably sends a strong signal to their other constituents; the more institutional investors there are, the more likely some publics are to view firms favorably, taking it for granted that careful screening by well-informed portfolio analysts led to the institutional purchase decision.

name: Social responsiveness
definition: Perceptions of firms' concern for the wider society may influence judgments, with social responsiveness signaling that firms have achieved a mutualistic relationship with potentially powerful groups in their environments.

name: Media visibility
definition: The amount of information channeled through informal networks, the business press, and the mass media may bias publics' constructions of firms' reputations. Media visibility was estimated as the total number of articles written about a firm in 1985.

name: Media coverage favorability
definition: Firms frequently and nonnegatively touted by the media might develop better reputations than other firms. A favorability index captured the degree to which media reports were not negative, calculated as the proportion of positive and neutral ratings received.

name: Firm size
definition: As institutions in their own right, large firms tend to receive much public scrutiny, and the availability of information may benefit large firms disproportionately by inflating audiences' familiarity with their activities. Size was computed as a logarithmic transformation of total sales in 1984.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: Over time, advertising helps firms develop strategic positions that are differentiated from their competitors' and that provide them with a measure of goodwill from consumers and other stakeholders; differentiation may result from advertising allocations.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: At the corporate level, firms differ in their diversification postures, or the degree to which their activities span multiple related and unrelated businesses. Unrelated diversification may also make evaluation difficult and ambiguous by reducing the credibility and effectiveness of corporate information and advertising.

name: Perceived success in prior acquisitions
authors_terms: ["perceptions of success in prior decisions", "perceptions of past success", "perceived past success", "Past Success", "perception of prior success"]
definition: Managers' subjective perceptions of the degree of success achieved in the firm's prior strategic decisions, formed under outcome ambiguity, so that managers 'normally do not really know the overall performance of their previous experiences.' Respondents were asked to assess the degree to which past acquisitions conducted by the firm were successful.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "actual performance of the focal merger", "performance in the focal acquisition", "CARs"]
definition: The objectively quantifiable performance of the focal acquisition, assessed after completion of the integration process because the measure has to incorporate information about the degree of success of the postacquisition activities. It is measured as the acquiring firm's cumulative abnormal returns following the acquisition.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "stock of prior experience", "accumulation of experience", "stock of experience"]
definition: The stock of prior experience accumulated by the firm through decisions of the same type; the firm's Acquisition Experience was computed simply as the number of acquisitions completed by the acquirer prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Knowledge codification
authors_terms: ["knowledge codification", "codification", "deliberate learning processes", "investment in deliberate learning processes"]
definition: The level of codification of acquisition-specific knowledge that the acquiring firm has reached at the time of the focal acquisition, reflecting investment in deliberate learning processes through which knowledge is articulated and codified (documents, manuals, models and other tools of the acquisition process).

name: Experience heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["experience heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of the stock of prior experience", "heterogeneity in the stock of experience"]
definition: The degree of heterogeneity of the firm's stock of prior experience, i.e., the extent to which prior acquisitions differ from one another; in the case of acquisitions it takes the form of a wide variety of acquisitions completed before the focal one.

name: Abnormal market returns
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "CAR", "abnormal market returns", "gains from alliances"]
definition: We measured firm-level value creation effects of joint venture formation events by calculating the cumulative abnormal stock market return for each joint venture announcement. CAR is an ex ante market-based measure of expected return for a firm participating in a joint venture.

name: Partner-specific experience
definition: PSE refers to the specific experience that a firm has accumulated through recurrent alliances with the same partner. Such experience is dyadic rather than firm-specific.

name: General partnering experience
definition: GPE refers to the accumulated experience that a firm gains from any interfirm alliance that it has formed in the past.

name: Partner distinctiveness
definition: We thus define distinctive partners as those that reveal idiosyncratic attributes relative to the attributes of prior partners (how are you different?) rather than those that have unique identities (who are you?).

name: Technological firm resources
definition: This variable measured the resources that firms can use to engage in technology-intensive initiatives and in innovation activity, because high proportion of investment in R&D indicates commitment to technology development.

name: Financial firm resources
definition: This measure was an appropriate proxy for the firm's financial resources because it represents the munificence of funds available for investing in prospective projects and in ongoing operations.

name: Firm-specific uncertainty
definition: Firm-specific uncertainty refers to the lack of assurance about the probability and outcomes of corporate decisions (e.g., joint venture formation, mergers and acquisitions, entry to new markets, etc.), which derives from sources that are idiosyncratic and mostly internal to the firm.

name: Diversification
authors_terms: ["related diversification", "lateral diversification", "lateral entry", "taxicab to limousine diversifier", "firm scope", "horizontal integration", "diversified firm (sigma = 1)"]
definition: Lateral diversifiers from taxicab to limousine operations are defined as those firms that had SIC code 412100 and no limousines in their fleet in 1992, but had at least one limousine in their fleet by 1997. In the parameterization, sigma = {0,1} indexes whether the firm is a two-product firm or a focused firm.

name: Incumbency status
definition: theta = {0,1} indexes whether the firm is an incumbent or a start-up. Firms that existed in 1992, but were small or reported incomplete data, are properly treated as incumbents (rather than startups) in 1997 cross-sectional regressions.

name: Coordination costs
authors_terms: ["coordination costs", "costs of coordination", "costs of organizational interdependency"]
definition: This paper defines coordination costs as costs that arise from managing task interdependencies (Jones and Hill, 1988; Gulati and Singh, 1998). Thus, coordination costs are conceptually distinct from corporate-level agency costs in that they are costs of coordinating production across business units, even when the corporate center acts in good faith, effectively monitors its business units, provides appropriate incentives, and efficiently allocates capital.

name: Organizational rigidity
definition: The paper defines organizational rigidity costs as the costs of reformulating (or failing to reformulate) previously institutionalized routines and practices in legacy businesses (Leonard-Barton, 1992; Kaplan and Henderson, 2005). Conceptually, organizational rigidity includes both costs that arise directly from organizational adaptation and indirect costs of foregone productivity gains when adaption is too expensive to undertake.

name: Economies of scope
authors_terms: ["economies of scope", "synergies", "realized economies of scope", "potential economies of scope"]
definition: Synergies, or economies of scope, are, by definition, benefits that firms achieve through coordinating production across business units that cannot be achieved when production is optimized independently within business units (Teece, 1980, 1982). Accordingly, realized economies of scope associated with diversification are equal to potential economies of scope less the costs of implementing new coordination procedures.

name: Productivity
authors_terms: ["total factor productivity in quantities (TFPQ)", "total factor productivity", "business unit productivity", "physical asset utilization", "paid ride-miles per taxicab"]
definition: Empirical tests on taxicab performance, which is defined in terms of productivity as in Hill and Snell (1989), are facilitated by the relatively simple and homogenous production function in the taxicab industry. The key feature of the measure is that TFPQ can be interpreted as a measure of physical asset utilization relative to other fleets in the same market that is standardized to have mean zero within market (county).

name: Founding-era identity
authors_terms: ["Victorian Era firms", "Victorian Era firm", "firms founded before the commercialization of jazz"]
definition: Firms founded before the commercialization of jazz were fundamentally different than the firms founded to take advantage of the growing market in jazz. Firms founded in the Victorian Era were more rooted in the values of this period and actively sought alignment with the cultural elite.

name: Pseudonym use
definition: These types of reissues are referred to as pseudonyms (Sutton 1994). Pseudonyms are recordings that were reissued under fictitious names, and the authors restrict the concept to reissues made by the same record company that originally issued the recording.

name: White orchestra group
definition: White orchestras were the strongest signal of highbrow identity, but recordings from these groups had the poorest performance in the market for jazz. Highbrow jazz was music characterized by larger groups of classically trained white (Anglo) musicians who played more symphonic arrangements.

name: Black nonorchestra group
definition: In contrast, the work of black nonorchestras epitomized lowbrow and illegitimate music from the perspective of the cultural elite. Lowbrow jazz was typified by African-American and Creole musicians in smaller improvisational groups.

name: Highbrow output of Jazz Era firms
authors_terms: ["proportion of white orchestra recordings released by Jazz Era firms", "the market identity space for highbrow music became infiltrated by Jazz Era firms"]
definition: The authors reason that the more white orchestra recordings that Jazz Era firms released, the less distinct the identity of Victorian Era firms. The variable captures the annual proportion of white orchestra recordings released by Jazz Era firms.

name: Jazz Era firm market share
authors_terms: ["proportion of the firms in the market that are Jazz Era firms", "the degree to which the market was represented by Jazz Era firms"]
definition: The authors examine whether Victorian Era firms responded to periods in which a higher proportion of the jazz market was composed of new (Jazz Era) entrants. The variable is the annual proportion of the firms in the market that are Jazz Era firms.

name: Renaming to orchestra
authors_terms: ["renamed as 'orchestras'", "fictitious new name of the group contains the word 'orchestra'"]
definition: The authors test whether recordings using pseudonyms of lowbrow groups produced by Victorian Era firms were relabeled as highbrow products more consistent with elite values, by hypothesizing that if a black nonorchestra was selected as a source for a pseudonym, it was renamed as an 'orchestra' at a greater rate by Victorian Era firms.

name: Recording cost
definition: Multiple takes during the 1920s were very costly, resulting in musician and equipment fatigue. As with any cost, companies sought to minimize the number of takes.

name: Recording market success
definition: Rerecording by multiple labels indicates increases in that original song's popularity. The more popular a song, the more companies and labels reissued it.

name: CEO's use of metaphorical communication
authors_terms: ["metaphorical communication", "CEOs' use of metaphorical communication", "use of metaphorical communication"]
definition: Metaphorical communication denotes figurative linguistic expressions that convey thoughts and feelings by describing one domain, A, through another domain, B. It is a structural form of discursive framing that maps a familiar source domain onto a less familiar target domain.

name: Favorability of journalists' reporting
definition: The favorability of journalists' reporting captures how favorably journalists portray a firm in the statements they publish about it.

name: Favorability of analysts' evaluations
definition: The favorability of analysts' evaluations captures how favorably analysts assess a firm through their EPS forecasts and stock recommendations.

name: Negative earnings surprise
definition: Performance that negatively deviates from market expectations, that is, earnings below the mean of analysts' EPS forecasts.

name: Multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact", "multimarket contact ij", "MMC ij", "pairwise multimarket contacts"]
definition: multimarket contact is not an aggregate property of industries, markets, or firms; it is a property of the relationship between two firms. This relationship is defined by the intersection of their (multi)market activities, which is established through a dynamic interaction across markets and over time.

name: Market entry rate
authors_terms: ["a firm's rate of entry into a competitor's markets", "market entry", "entries into each other's markets"]
definition: Firms' entries into and exits from each other's markets are key competitive interactions. Defined at the dyadic level, firms' entries into and exits from each other's markets take on a role in competitive engagement.

name: Market exit rate
authors_terms: ["a firm's rate of exit from a competitor's markets", "market exit", "exits from each other's markets"]
definition: Although market entry is generally a strategic move, it is important to keep in mind that market exit is also often an outcome of interfirm rivalry. Multimarket contact creates important strategic exit barriers that lead firms to continue competing in markets where their presence provides beneficial deterrent effects.

name: Relative multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["relative multimarket contact", "MMC ij /Average MMC i with competitors other than j"]
definition: The level of multimarket contact with a given competitor relative to the firm's other competitors is a form of competitive asymmetry. Hypotheses 2a and 2b predict airlines will direct their competitive efforts towards low multimarket contact competitors as a consequence of forbearing from rivalrous actions with competitors with which they have higher multimarket contact.

name: Competitor relative size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "the competitor's relative size", "Size competitor j /Size airline i"]
definition: Hypotheses 3a and 3b predict that effects of multimarket contact on rates of entry and exit will be influenced by asymmetry in competitors' sizes. Firm size is a major determining factor in economic rivalry.

name: Target age
definition: An objective and observable differentiator of a target firm, namely its age at the time of acquisition, which begins an inherent conflict between risk and safety for the buyer. The age of the target at the time of acquisition is measured from company inception.

name: Value captured by the buyer
authors_terms: ["value captured by the buyer", "profit to the buyer", "buyer's profit", "acquirer profit", "abnormal returns for the buyer"]
definition: The profit to the buyer (winner in the auction) over and above the price paid for the target, which is affected by the opportunity for synergistic fit, the valuation uncertainty associated with the mature operations of the target, and the number of potential bidders.

name: Recent target patents
authors_terms: ["recent patents", "recent target patents", "recent R&D activity in the target"]
definition: Recent patents signal the presence of research and development activity in the target; these activities produce ongoing innovation, reduce concerns about aging and a lack of innovation, and indicate unexplored growth options that make an older target more akin to a young company.

name: Target ownership status
authors_terms: ["privately held status of the target", "target private status", "public/private status", "private target"]
definition: Whether the target is public or remains private at the time of acquisition; unlike public companies, a privately held target is not required to publicly disclose its financials and business conditions to its investors, does not benefit from analyst coverage, and has no public equity price available.

name: Signals of target quality
authors_terms: ["independent signals of higher quality", "signals of higher quality", "target technical quality"]
definition: Independent signals of higher quality such as those from patents, patent citations, and positive analyst coverage; the paper measures the technical quality of the target through a normalized citation-based patent stock measure.

name: Access to capital and resources
authors_terms: ["superior access to capital and resources", "alternative access to capital and resources", "venture capital funding"]
definition: When a target has alternative access to capital and resources such as through venture capital funding, there are fewer growth options that the target cannot exploit effectively on its own, less opportunity for private valuations by acquirers, and a lower probability of acquisition.

name: Probability of acquisition
authors_terms: ["probability of acquisition", "likelihood of acquisition", "risk of acquisition"]
definition: The probability that the target is acquired at age t, provided that the target has not been acquired until that time; it is equal to the probability that the bid discount is less than the highest bidder's private valuation of the target's unexplored growth options.

name: Firm capability
authors_terms: ["firm capability", "capability", "capability of the firm", "independent studio capability", "studio capability"]
definition: Generally defined as collections of organizational routines that operate on a firm's resource base to create new value, capabilities are believed to be essential elements of the competitive advantage of firms. In the applications of SFE in the strategy literature, capability is equated with efficiency and represents the intermediate transformation abilities of firms to turn inputs (i.e., resources) into outputs (i.e., desired performance outcomes).

name: Number of resource-rich alliance partners
authors_terms: ["No. of major partners", "number of resource-rich alliance partners", "number of major partners", "number of major studio partners"]
definition: No. of major partners is the number of major studios with which the focal independent studio has a partnership in a given year. Since there are six majors in the U.S. motion picture industry, this variable ranges from 0 to 6.

name: Alliance experience with resource-rich partners
authors_terms: ["alliance experience", "general alliance experience", "alliance experience with major partners", "alliance experience with resource-rich partners"]
definition: General alliance experience, as opposed to partner-specific alliance experience, is gained by allying with different partners during which alliance management learning accumulates and an experience curve develops. Alliance experience is measured as the total number of alliances the focal studio has had with majors in the past.

name: Partner turnover
authors_terms: ["partner turnover", "major partner turnover", "turnover of resource-rich partners"]
definition: High turnover of resource-rich partners-i.e., where the focal firm maintains a relationship with the average partner for a shorter period of time-weakens the impact of those partners on the firm's capability. Partner turnover is measured as the number of majors dropped from the focal studio's alliance portfolio since the last period plus the number of new partners added to the alliance portfolio.

name: Market niche specialization
authors_terms: ["level of specialization", "market-niche specialization", "specialization", "level of market-niche specialization"]
definition: According to this literature, an organization is labeled a specialist if it concentrates on performing one type of action efficiently and a generalist if it engages in different kinds of activities at lower depths than specialists active in the same niches. The level of specialization was then defined as 6 minus the number of distinct genres targeted by the studio's movies.

name: Social status
authors_terms: ["socially endowed high status", "high social status", "Bonacich measure of status", "status in the elite marriage network", "social endowment of high status"]
definition: High social status is defined here as being at the center of the elite marriage network between controlling owner-families. Status is 'a ranking in a hierarchy that is socially recognized and typically carries with it the expectation of entitlement to certain resources.'

name: Economic performance relative to peers
authors_terms: ["Mediocre ROA Performance", "mediocre economic performance relative to peers", "current-period mediocre economic performance", "middling ROA performance"]
definition: The measure captures current-period economic performance that is not keeping pace with industry peers. The authors define mediocre ROA performance as existing between the 25th and the 75th percentiles of industry-adjusted and industry-weighted ROA performance relative to peers.

name: Threat of falling high status
authors_terms: ["threat of falling high status", "Threat of FHS Definition 1", "Threat of FHS Definition 2", "Threat of Falling High Status"]
definition: The authors term 'threat of falling high status' the concept in which a firm has longstanding high social status (defined here as being at the center of the elite marriage network between controlling owner-families) but is threatened with an impending fall in status due to current-period mediocre economic performance relative to that of industry peers. The concept suggests that it is not the direct effect of high status or of temporary financial underperformance, but the interaction effect of the two, that leads firms threatened by a fall in high status to pay larger bribes than all other firms, ceteris paribus.

name: Large-scale corporate bribery
authors_terms: ["corporate bribery", "large-scale bribery", "Yearly Bribe Paid by Business Group", "annual bribe amount"]
definition: High-level corruption where companies pay bribes to senior politicians; here the bribes were paid not at the affiliate level but at the business-group level, through the group chairman's office, and were viewed and categorized as coming from the business group as a common entity controlled by the controlling owner-shareholder.

name: Innovation country-of-origin
authors_terms: ["innovation country-of-origin", "locally generated innovations", "nonlocally generated innovations", "home-country generated innovations", "third-country generated innovations", "patent local priority"]
definition: Innovations can either be generated in a firm's home country (the majority of firm innovations) and transferred to a foreign country, or they can be generated in a different foreign country (third-country innovations) and transferred into a foreign country. They can also be locally generated by MNC inventors within a foreign country.

name: Patent value
authors_terms: ["patent value", "value of firm innovations", "technological quality", "high value knowledge"]
definition: Knowledge value has long been linked to forward citations of subsequent patents to a focal innovation because these citations signal the technological importance and economic value of the innovation. Technological quality enhances the value of firm innovations, resulting in higher incentives to defend and protect the value of that resource from imitation by rivals.

name: Scope of usage across countries
authors_terms: ["scope of usage across countries", "geographic scope of protection", "patent family size", "widely used innovations"]
definition: The most frequently studied characteristics of firm innovations include how often a firm patent is cited by other patents and the geographic scope of protection of the patent; these characteristics capture the value of an innovation and how widely it is used across countries.

name: Multimarket overlap in knowledge activities
authors_terms: ["multimarket overlap in knowledge activities", "knowledge overlap", "multimarket contact", "multimarket knowledge overlap"]
definition: Multimarket contact refers to the extent of country overlap between two firms. We created our Knowledge Overlap measure by considering the multicountry overlap in knowledge activities with industry rivals.

name: Defending knowledge against infringement
authors_terms: ["defend innovations against infringement", "defends knowledge", "patent infringement litigation", "knowledge defense strategies"]
definition: This article's focus is on the strategic decisions to bring litigation cases against rivals' uses of their patented technologies. Firms themselves must enforce these exclusive rights through patent infringement litigation cases, and our dependent variable is a dummy variable for each patent family that is equal to 1 if an MNC files a case in a US Federal Court alleging infringement of their patented innovation.

name: Exploratory network cohesion
authors_terms: ["cohesion of a firm's exploratory network", "exploratory cohesion", "cohesion in the exploratory network", "cohesion of the exploratory alliance network"]
definition: Network cohesion captures the extent to which an actor's connections are redundant and can be substituted by other third-party ties, and depicts the extent to which an actor's ego network involves alters who are themselves closely linked. High cohesion in a firm's exploratory alliance network indicates strong embeddedness constraints.

name: Exploitative network cohesion
authors_terms: ["cohesion of a firm's exploitative network", "exploitative cohesion", "cohesion in the exploitative network", "cohesion of the exploitative alliance network"]
definition: Network cohesion captures the extent to which an actor's connections are redundant and can be substituted by other third-party ties, and depicts the extent to which an actor's ego network involves alters who are themselves closely linked. High cohesion in a firm's exploitative alliance network indicates strong embeddedness constraints.

name: Addition of new exploratory alliance partners
authors_terms: ["addition of new exploratory partners", "addition of new exploratory alliance partners", "adding new exploratory partners"]
definition: New partners refers to partners that have neither had a direct prior alliance with the focal firm nor a prior alliance with the focal firm's existing partners. The addition of new exploratory partners is the number of a firm's exploratory partners at Time t+1 that were in neither its exploratory alliance network nor its exploitative network at any time before.

name: Addition of new exploitative alliance partners
authors_terms: ["addition of new exploitative partners", "addition of new exploitative alliance partners", "adding new exploitative partners"]
definition: New partners refers to partners that have neither had a direct prior alliance with the focal firm nor a prior alliance with the focal firm's existing partners. The addition of new exploitative partners is the number of a firm's exploitative partners at Time t+1 that were in neither its exploratory alliance network nor its exploitative network at any time before.

name: Degree of relatedness
definition: The 'degree of relatedness' is a measure of current relatedness; it reflects the distance between the new market and the closest product currently in the firm's portfolio. We define the degree of relatedness as the distance between the market entered and the market in which the firm currently operates that is closest to the market entered.

name: Duration of relatedness
definition: The 'duration of relatedness' gives the period of time for which the degree of relatedness has been greater than zero. We measure the duration of Rnx(t) as the amount of time, in years, that elapsed since the initial observation of a greater-than-zero value of Rnx(t) until one year before firm n enters market x.

name: Trajectory of relatedness
definition: The 'trajectory of relatedness' gives the net change from the initial greater-than-zero value (i.e., the extent to which the firm has approached or moved away from the new market). When the difference in Rnx(t) is positive, the change shows firm n's movement toward market x; when the difference is negative, the change shows the firm's movement away from market x.

name: Acquisition as entry mode
authors_terms: ["entry mode", "acquisition as entry mode", "use of acquisition as entry mode"]
definition: Acquisition as entry mode is strictly defined as the purchase of an incumbent (or one of its business units) from the pool of producers operating in a target market. In contrast, internal development involves assembling the needed resources and capabilities from sources besides the incumbent pool.

name: Primary business domain location
authors_terms: ["inside vs. outside the firm's primary business domain", "where the new market resides", "primary business domain"]
definition: We propose that the connection between entry mode and relatedness is moderated by whether the new product market is inside or outside the firm's primary business domain. We consider an entry to be inside a firm's primary business domain if the product classification of the market in which the firm enters shares the same root of the hierarchy as the firm's primary business.

name: External financial resources
definition: Financial resources in the form of a high stock market valuation, measured by the ratio of market-to-book value, which the authors expect to be positively correlated with acquisition. Prior studies have offered contradicting arguments regarding the effect of external financial resources on entry mode.

name: Research intensity
definition: The firm's research and development intensity, measured as the ratio of R&D expenditures to sales in the year prior to entry. R&D-intensive firms are more likely to be able to develop in-house the technologies required for entry.

name: Incentive intensity
authors_terms: ["incentive intensity", "the incentive portion of pay", "pay mix", "the individual marginal gains in pay"]
definition: Incentive intensity is the marginal gains in pay individuals derive from group performance. Conceptually, it is the slope of the relationship between pay and measured performance.

name: Group size
definition: A group's size strongly influences its members' capacity to individually control their group's performance and subsequent individual pay. Clearly, a group member has more direct control over the performance of a small group than over that of a large group.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size defines the potential domain of negative comparisons and thereby defines the magnitude of these costs.

name: Organizational level of performance measurement
authors_terms: ["level of measurement", "organizational level at which performance is measured", "level of performance measurement"]
definition: The organizational level at which a plan measured group performance. Plans with lower-level measures, such as work team performance, are clearly more easily controlled by individual group members than plans that measure performance at higher organizational levels.

name: Management and professional participation
authors_terms: ["percent management", "percent professionals", "management participation", "percentage of plan participants who are managers", "percentage of plan participants who were nonmanagement professionals"]
definition: Employees in managerial positions have greater influence over individual performance than employees in lower-level positions. Managers and professionals have the authority to influence a broader set of performance-determining decisions than do lower-level employees.

name: Quality as a performance dimension
authors_terms: ["quality", "quality as a performance measure", "measuring quality", "measure and reward quality"]
definition: Typically quality is a performance dimension that is more difficult to accurately measure and control than other performance dimensions such as cost, output volume, or profitability. When quality is an important performance dimension, firms limit incentive intensity to increase attention to quality.

name: Number of performance measures
definition: Numerous performance measures in a group pay plan may further indicate complex and difficult performance measurement. Having numerous performance measures implies a broad range of important performance dimensions, some of which are potentially problematic to measure.

name: Plan age
authors_terms: ["age of plan", "length of time a group incentive plan has been in place", "longevity"]
definition: As cooperation is sustained over time and reputations for high effort and procedural fairness in rate adjustments emerge, the incentive intensity of group-based pay can increase.

name: Research experience
definition: The knowledge needed for revolutionary technological advances is gathered from deep, fundamental research, and is transferred through individuals; the authors focus on project members' research experience as the key empirical indicator.

name: Experimentation capacity
definition: The breadth of experimentation efforts is indicated by the experimentation capacity, defined as the number of different experiments that can be performed in a given unit of time. Running a number of experimental trials in parallel allows a broad set of possibilities to be examined rapidly and in a relatively unbiased fashion.

name: Minimum experimental iteration time
definition: The minimum time elapsed between the experimental design and its results; experimentation setups optimized for rapid, focused feedback rather than for broad, parallel examinations should be correlated with effectiveness in managing evolution.

name: Project experience
definition: Knowledge of the interaction between technology and environment is sticky or even tacit, so the retention of project-specific experiential knowledge is critical in improving the match between technology and environment.

name: Technological potential
authors_terms: ["technological potential", "technological potential TP", "revolutionary component of project performance"]
definition: Technological potential represents the maximum achievable performance given the product's base of fundamental technology. It is derived from a physical model of the product, based on fundamental principles, and provides a universal performance upper bound not related to the architecture of the product's design.

name: Technological yield
authors_terms: ["technological yield", "technological yield factor TY", "evolutionary component of project performance"]
definition: Technological yield is the ratio of actual realized performance divided by technological potential. Projects scoring high on yield have optimized the match between technology and its surrounding organizational environment; it measures how close a product actually comes to its maximum theoretical performance.

name: Project performance
definition: The performance of a semiconductor device, most critically its gate density, i.e., the number of transistors per unit of area on the integrated circuit, which drives both manufacturing cost and product performance.

name: Referrer-expert tie strength
authors_terms: ["Tie strength", "PCP-specialist tie strength", "R-E tie strength", "strong ties", "referral frequency"]
definition: Tie strength along the R-E edge, where the authors 'defined PCP-specialist tie strength as a count of the number of referrals from the former to the latter in the year preceding the first opinion consultation between patient and specialist, which we refer to as the ''index'' visit.' For ease of exposition they collapse tie strength to strong or weak.

name: Client trust in the expert
authors_terms: ["trust", "patient confidence in the specialist", "confidence that the patient places in the specialist", "trust in the expert's opinion", "confidence in the specialist's recommendations"]
definition: The confidence a client places in the expert consulted. The authors write that 'Patients who trust the advice they receive are less likely to request a second opinion and more likely to return to the specialist for follow-up care,' and hypothesize that as tie strength between referrer and expert increases, the client is more likely to develop trust in the expert's opinion.

name: Client-expert match quality
authors_terms: ["match quality", "quality of the match", "patient-specialist match quality", "expertise match", "diagnostic specialization"]
definition: The concordance between a client's needs and a provider's expertise: the authors refer to 'pairings with a lower degree of concordance between client needs and expert expertise' and state that 'specialist expertise in treating the patient's diagnosed condition-is an important dimension of patient-specialist match quality.'

name: Effectiveness of strategic responses
authors_terms: ["effectiveness of strategic responses", "EFFECTIVENESS", "perceived effectiveness of strategic responses"]
definition: The authors define 'strategic responses' as choices that require assessment of strategic interactions between competing firms, evaluation of partially or totally irreversible commitments, assessment of current circumstances and their unfolding dynamics, and integration of expertise across functions. The outcome measure is the perceived effectiveness of such responses in pricing, sourcing, plant siting and capacity utilization decisions.

name: Treasury functional orientation
definition: Treasury managers differed in their perceptions of the importance of their role as treasury specialists with the task of reducing foreign exchange risks to their firms' earnings, cash flows, or balance sheets (their 'functional' orientation).

name: Treasury service orientation
definition: Treasury managers differed in their perceptions of the importance of their role of providing service to operational divisions (their 'service' orientation), manifested as placing a great deal of emphasis on advice and assistance to the operating divisions.

name: Treasury decision time horizon
authors_terms: ["Treasury time horizon", "time horizon", "TIME FRAME", "decision time frame of the experts"]
definition: The time horizon within which Treasury operates, measured in months: some treasurers seemed to take a very short-term view of what they could and would do, while others took a long-term view that the authors felt was important for firms trying to build long-term strategic flexibility.

name: Incentives for interfunctional cooperation
authors_terms: ["incentives for interfunctional cooperation", "disincentives to cooperation", "economic disincentives", "DISINCENTIVES"]
definition: When knowledge has to be shared across different subunits for an effective strategic response, incentives promoting or hindering cooperation can be expected to have an impact on the strategic response; wherever cross-functional cooperation is desired, incentives may be required to overcome the costs to individuals of reaching out across intraorganizational boundaries.

name: Cross-functional integrating mechanisms
definition: Mechanisms such as cross-functional teams or integrated data bases that tend to bring together knowledge from different subunits within the firm, including task forces, entrepreneurial 'boundary-spanners' and information dissemination across functional boundaries.

name: Flexible and contingent planning
authors_terms: ["processes for flexibility", "contingent planning", "CONTINGENT PLANNING", "flexibility and contingency of the planning system"]
definition: The flexibility or rigidity of the firm's budgeting and planning processes, i.e. the extent to which alternative exchange-rate scenarios and assessment of foreign-exchange exposures were used in the medium and long-term planning processes of the firm.

name: Pilot CEO
authors_terms: ["Pilot CEO", "pilot CEOs", "CEO's hobby of piloting a private aircraft", "CEO's risky hobby", "risky hobby"]
definition: A chief executive officer who pilots a small aircraft as a hobby, captured by whether the CEO holds a private pilot license. Because of the high risk inherently involved in flying a small aircraft, pilot CEOs are likely to have a strong preference for risk taking.

name: Bank loan contract tightness
authors_terms: ["tighter terms", "unfavorable bank loan terms", "tighter bank loan terms", "bank loan contracting", "more scrupulously designed loan contracts"]
definition: The price term and nonprice terms of a bank loan contract that make it more scrupulous for the borrower: the drawn all-in spread (price term) and collateralization and the number of restrictive covenants (nonprice terms). A firm that is associated with a higher default risk will normally receive loan contracts that are more scrupulously designed.

name: Syndicate concentration
authors_terms: ["syndicate concentration", "lower syndicate concentration", "less concentrated lending arrangements"]
definition: The structure of a loan syndicate, reflecting the risk distribution among the lead bank and the other banks involved. The higher the syndicate concentration, the higher the proportion of the total loan that the lead bank would be responsible for.

name: CEO importance to the firm
authors_terms: ["how important the CEO is to his or her firm", "importance of a CEO to his or her firm", "key man insurance"]
definition: How important the CEO is to his or her firm. A CEO who is considered more important to his or her firm will be given more leeway and power in their decision making, so the firm's decisions are more likely to be influenced by the CEO's personal preferences; the authors capture this by whether the firm has purchased key man insurance for its CEO.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "lack of board independence", "independent outside director ratio"]
definition: The extent to which the board is composed of independent outside directors, measured by the independent outside director ratio. Independent outside directors provide more effective monitoring mainly because they have fewer conflicts of interests than inside or affiliated directors do.

name: Multiple-scenario evaluation
definition: The viewing of videos of all scenarios, viewing and discussing investment evaluations in individual scenarios, and discussing evaluations across all scenarios constitute the experimental treatment 'multiple-scenario evaluation.'

name: Single-scenario evaluation
definition: Reading of the assigned scenario, immersion, discussion of its implications, and evaluation of investments constitute the experimental treatment 'single-scenario evaluation.'

name: Confidence in judgment
authors_terms: ["confidence in judgment", "confidence in the recommendation", "confidence in their evaluations", "ex ante confidence", "prior confidence"]
definition: The subject's confidence in his/her recommendation about whether the planning agency should make a given investment, solicited with the investment recommendation in the pretest and the posttests.

name: Change in expert judgment
authors_terms: ["change in expert judgment", "change in judgment", "become more favorable", "become less favorable"]
definition: Any change in the expert judgment was denoted as to have become either more favorable or less favorable of the judged investment after the single-scenario evaluation.

name: Usefulness of the investment for the scenario
definition: If n investments were assessed in a workshop, an investment was denoted useful for Scenario X if it received a minimum of 1/n points in Scenario X (Condition 1) and its proportion of points was at least three times higher than its proportion of vetoes in that scenario (Condition 2).

name: Wastefulness of the investment for the scenario
definition: The criteria for wasteful investments is symmetric: they receive a minimum of 1/n vetoes (Condition 3) and the proportion of vetoes is at least three times that of points (Condition 4).

name: Preference for flexible investment strategy
authors_terms: ["preference for flexibility", "more flexible strategies", "flexible options", "higher flexibility"]
definition: Four generic strategies were specified for each segment: they ranged from the least flexible Option 1 (implementation of specific projects) to the most flexible Option 4 (allocation of funds to the segment).

name: Corporate effect
authors_terms: ["corporate effect", "corporate parenting advantage", "corporate parent influence", "corporate-level differences"]
definition: The corporate effect captures the portion of the variance in subsidiary performance attributed to differences among corporate parents. It includes all first-order corporate-level differences consequential to subsidiary performance, such as the quantity and quality of all resources and interactions that undergird parenting activities.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The performance of the legally separate subunits of multiunit firms; the authors use return on assets (net income divided by total assets) as their measure of subsidiary performance.

name: Subsidiary portfolio size
definition: A key distinction among corporate portfolios is their size, concerning the number of subsidiaries under the parents' purview.

name: Industrial relatedness
definition: The industrial similarity between a corporate parent and its subsidiary. When corporate parents and their subsidiaries share industrial similarities, parents can readily draw on their relevant resource base and mitigate the barriers associated with allocating resources in large portfolios.

name: Institutional distance
definition: The 'extent of similarity or dissimilarity between [...] institutions' of the parent's home country and the subsidiary's host country.

name: Acquired firm preacquisition performance
authors_terms: ["preacquisition performance", "return on common equity", "ROE", "acquired firm ROE"]
definition: The acquired firm's performance before its acquisition. The authors note that the performance of a company, particularly extreme performance, is commonly attributed to its top managers, so that good performance implies executive competence.

name: Relative preacquisition performance
authors_terms: ["relative ROE", "preacquisition performance of an acquired firm relative to that of an acquiring firm", "relative performance"]
definition: The preacquisition performance of an acquired firm relative to that of the acquiring firm. The combination of the high performance of an acquiring firm and the low performance of an acquired firm would particularly lead to perceptions of a wide gap in the relative standing of the two managerial groups.

name: Acquired executive departure
definition: The departure of the top executives of an acquired firm following an acquisition; the authors argue that voluntary and involuntary departures are propelled by the same forces and merge conceptually.

name: Relative size of the acquired firm
authors_terms: ["relative size", "the smaller an acquired firm relative to an acquiring firm"]
definition: The size of an acquired firm relative to that of its acquirer. A small acquisition presents Frank's classic case of a big frog in a small pond suddenly becoming a very small frog in a big pond, so that an executive of a small company suddenly lacks much significance when the acquiring company is very large.

name: Social climate of the acquisition
authors_terms: ["social climate", "amicability-hostility", "mutually negotiated unions", "uncontested tender offers", "contested tender offers", "friendly mergers", "hostile takeover"]
definition: The amicability or hostility of the acquisition process, categorised as mutually negotiated unions, uncontested tender offers, or contested tender offers, which shapes relations between acquired and acquiring executives.

name: Removal of autonomy
definition: The degree to which an acquired firm is closely integrated into the acquiring firm and required to adopt its policies and procedures rather than being permitted a high level of postacquisition autonomy.

name: Personal status bestowal
authors_terms: ["status bestowal", "personal status bestowal", "direct status bestowal", "top-level status"]
definition: Acquirers may mitigate status decline by bestowing status on acquired executives; for example, an acquired executive can be given a board seat or officership in a postacquisition firm.

name: Indirect status bestowal
definition: Status received indirectly when one or more acquired peers are granted top-level status: awarding top management team membership to even one acquired executive would seem to imply to other acquired officers that, as a group, they are seen as competent and as providing valuable services.

name: Relative standing
definition: Frank (1985) introduced relative standing to describe an individual's status relative to that of others in a proximate social setting, such as a neighborhood, a company, or a team. It derives from people's real or attributed abilities and performance and other status characteristics, all viewed in relation to those of others in a given social unit.

name: Hierarchy
definition: In line with the entrepreneurs' interpretation, the term 'hierarchy' in this study specifically refers to a formalized dimension of organizational structure represented by the number of hierarchical levels. It is distinguished from 'informal hierarchy' (i.e., an unofficial power/status ranking).

name: Creative success
definition: As noted earlier, creative success is defined as the novelty of the product, whereas commercial success is defined as its profitability. To realize creative success, a start-up must, by definition, set its product apart from existing ones by generating a variety of novel ideas.

name: Commercial success
definition: To survive and grow in their hostile environments, these nascent firms need to not only flexibly generate novel ideas to differentiate their products, but also efficiently execute those ideas to make profits. Commercial success was measured by the number of units sold globally (in millions).

name: Breadth of experience
definition: The breadth of experience is measured by the average diversity of functional domains which employees worked in. At the individual level, the breadth of experience (i.e., IndBreadth) was measured by the diversity across all functional domains in terms of 1 - HHI.

name: Social capital
authors_terms: ["social capital", "social capital developed through prior collaboration"]
definition: Social capital is computed by the average pair-wise social distance among employees in the prior five-year collaboration network, and is considered a measure of how closely the employees are connected through collaboration.

name: Formal control
definition: Formalization refers to the presence of written rules and procedures. The authors use Khandwalla's measure of formal control, a scale not reliant on the term formalization.

name: Decentralization
definition: Decentralization refers to the extent to which decision-making discretion is pushed down to lower levels of the organization.

name: Growth performance relative to the industry
definition: Managers rated performance over the past 3 years on 7-point scales with endpoints of 'well below industry average' and 'well above industry average.' Assessing performance over a multiyear period is the norm in self-reported measures of performance.

name: Customer product knowledge utilization
authors_terms: ["customer product knowledge utilization", "customer product knowledge use", "knowledge utilization"]
definition: Customer product knowledge utilization, a dimension of the firm's market orientation. On the survey, knowledge was defined as 'understanding some phenomenon.'

name: Foreign induced industry competitiveness
definition: Industry competitiveness induced by foreign direct investment; operationalized as the level of foreign induced industry competitiveness (or the market share of foreign funded enterprises).

name: Technological turbulence
definition: Environmental dynamism reflects the pace and regularity of change in the external environment; the authors study technological turbulence or uncertainty, indicating dynamism in products and processes.

name: Production technology routineness
definition: Production technology routineness is defined as the level of repetitiveness in transforming inputs into outputs.

name: Size
definition: Size, defined as operational scale.

name: Product-related coordination
definition: Such interdependence leads to the need for coordination and for structures to facilitate that coordination (e.g., Tushman and Nadler 1978, Sosa et al. 2004). We are concerned specifically with interdependencies across or within different product modules, and we term the associated coordination challenges 'interproduct coordination' and 'intraproduct coordination'.

name: Interproduct coordination
definition: On the left side of Figure 3, panel (a), we illustrate the case of interproduct coordination, in which multiple products are sold to a common customer. In such a situation, there are likely to be across-product interdependencies that are generated by the need for products to work together as a system to serve a single customer's needs (Teece 1982, Helfat and Eisenhardt 2004).

name: Intraproduct coordination
definition: On the right side of Figure 3, panel (a), we illustrate the case of intraproduct coordination, in which a single product is sold to multiple customers. In contrast to the previous example, there are no across-product interdependencies generated as a consequence of this pattern; rather, the interdependencies are within a given set of product activities.

name: Postshock adaptation performance
definition: We focus on the percentage change (as explained above, by using the semi-log model with the log of annual contract dollars as the dependent variable), not the absolute level of change, in contract dollars, to capture adaptation performance in the short run immediately after the shock. The dependent variable is the log transformation of a firm's yearly performance; thus, the interaction term captures the percentage change in performance for the same firm before and after the shock.

name: Product complementarity
definition: The idea underlying complementarity is that individual activities can be supermodular when working in conjunction with one another (Milgrom and Roberts 1990), and therefore that adaptation in the choices associated with one product area can influence the returns associated with another (Levinthal 2000).

name: Organizational grouping
definition: Stemming from Thompson's (1967) observation that reciprocal interdependencies are likely to be contained within modular units, this design feature enables interconnected sets of activities to exist within a distinct organizational structure, facilitating the flow of information across such activities.

name: Closure tie age
authors_terms: ["closure tie age", "age of closure ties", "closure tie longevity", "age of ties comprising closure positions"]
definition: The longevity of the ties constituting a firm's closure position, i.e., the number of years since the two banks first appeared as syndicate partners, for ties comprising closure triads in which the focal bank is a syndicate partner with two banks that are also partners. Closure ties tend to deepen and increase their efficacy over time as repeated interactions and third-party connections promote cooperative behavior and commitment.

name: Bridging tie age
authors_terms: ["bridging tie age", "age of bridging ties", "bridging tie longevity", "age of ties comprising bridging positions"]
definition: The longevity of the ties constituting a firm's bridging position, for ties comprising bridging triads in which the focal bank is a syndicate partner with two banks that are not tied to each other. Bridging ties are more likely to decay over time as the competitive nature of brokerage and absence of third-party connections inhibits development of embedded exchange relationships.

name: Firm performance
definition: An investment bank's annual market share, adopted as the performance metric given its salience in this industry, where underwriting fees and margins are relatively constant and earnings thus rise with increases in the volume of underwriting transactions.

name: Hybrid network position
definition: Network positions that contain elements of both bridging and closure; such positions enhance performance because the coexistence of clustered closure ties with distant bridging ties combines trust and close collaboration within groups with nonredundant information and ideas from other groups. Hybrid positions are precisely those described by Burt's concept of structural autonomy.

name: Parent's related operating experience
authors_terms: ["parent's related operating experience", "operating expertise from related experience", "related operating expertise", "cumulative related operating experience"]
definition: Related operating expertise enables value creation through scale and scope economies by combining the activities of different units.

name: Collocation
definition: Coordination from collocation refers to when parents and business units share a headquarters location, which results in improved coordination of activities.

name: Governance mode choice
definition: Governance modes are discrete, structural alternatives that are efficiently chosen to match attributes of the transaction and internal characteristics of the firm.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Our work is grounded in organizational economics and focuses on business unit performance, which in this context equates to chain performance.

name: Relationship satisfaction
authors_terms: ["relationship effectiveness", "satisfaction", "reseller satisfaction", "buyer satisfaction with a supplier relationship"]
definition: The effectiveness of the relationship between a buyer and a supplier, as indicated by the buyer's level of satisfaction with the focal supplier; reseller satisfaction was defined as a positive affective state resulting from the appraisal of the reseller's overall working relationship with the supplier.

name: Perceived economic payoffs
authors_terms: ["economic payoffs", "economic rewards", "perceptions of the level of economic payoffs", "payoffs"]
definition: The supplier's provision of economic rewards or payoffs, which reflect the buyer's ability to generate profits selling the supplier's product and are influenced by the supplier's selling price, her investments in the buyer, and promotional efforts in the buyer's market. Informants reported their perceptions of the economic payoffs (profits) from the supplier in question relative to alternative supplier relationships.

name: Inconsistency of economic payoffs across buyer relationships
definition: Buyers' judgments of the consistency of a supplier's practices across a set of connected interorganizational relationships; the consistency construct was operationalized as the standard deviation of the economic payoffs measure within a given territory, where a higher standard deviation reflects inconsistency across resellers in terms of their perceptions of economic payoffs.

name: Relationship age
authors_terms: ["length of the channel relationship", "log(Years of relationship)", "length of the relationship"]
definition: The length of the channel relationship, measured as the number of years that the focal reseller had been working with the supplier. Over time, as a buyer's ties with the supplier strengthen and take on embedded properties, the buyer is likely to evaluate the relationship based on internal standards established through actual experience with the focal supplier.

name: Relative economic payoff position
authors_terms: ["competitive standing", "dummy for whether economic payoffs below average in territory", "below-average levels of economic payoffs"]
definition: A dummy variable used to indicate whether the perceived level of economic payoffs for a reseller relationship was below or above the average level for the same variable across resellers in the same territory; the buyer's position within the comparison group is inferred from this comparison.

name: Authority–informal network consistency
authors_terms: ["consistency between the formal authority and informal networks", "consistency between the formal authority network and the informal social network", "overlap between authority and informal networks"]
definition: Consistency is the extent to which the formal and informal networks of a focal individual in the organizational context overlap by connecting to the same others and displaying the same patterns of relationships across the two networks. When the informal social structure overlaps with the formal authority structure, performance is enhanced.

name: Reciprocal workflow–informal network inconsistency
authors_terms: ["inconsistency between the reciprocally interdependent formal workflow and the informal networks", "inconsistency between the reciprocally interdependent workflow network and the informal social network", "inconsistency between the reciprocal workflow and informal networks"]
definition: Inconsistency is the lack of overlap between the formal and informal networks. For reciprocal workflow, when the informal social structure is inconsistent with the reciprocal workflow network, the focal organizational member benefits by combining resources accessed from the two independent networks.

name: Sequential workflow–informal network inconsistency
authors_terms: ["inconsistency between the sequentially interdependent formal workflow and the informal networks", "inconsistency between the sequential workflow network and the informal social network", "inconsistency between the sequential workflow and informal networks"]
definition: Inconsistency is the lack of overlap between the formal and informal networks. For sequential workflow, when the two networks are inconsistent and nonoverlapping, the information and advice that the organizational member receives from the informal network hurts organizational member performance.

name: Individual organizational actor performance
authors_terms: ["individual organizational actor performance", "individual performance", "organizational member performance"]
definition: Individual organizational member performance is measured using the company's formal evaluation system. Performance is broken down into three main components: knowledge growth, task performance, and contextual performance.

name: Technological distance between clusters
authors_terms: ["technological distance", "technological distance between clusters", "technological distance among clusters"]
definition: A team's technological distance is defined as the distance between the technological positions of the nanotechnology clusters in which the inventors on a team are located.

name: Breakthrough invention
definition: Following Ahuja and Lampert (2001: 523), the authors ''define breakthrough inventions as those foundational inventions that serve as the basis for many subsequent technological developments.''

name: Intra-cluster tie density
authors_terms: ["intra-cluster density", "density of intra-cluster ties", "density of intra-team ties among collocated team members"]
definition: The density of ties among collocated team members within a given location; the authors computed density of intra-cluster ties as the average number of prior collaborations among team members in the same geographic clusters.

name: Inter-cluster tie density
authors_terms: ["inter-cluster density", "density of inter-cluster ties", "density of ties with members located elsewhere"]
definition: The density of prior ties between team members located in different clusters; the authors operationalized density of inter-cluster ties as the average amount of prior collaborations occurring between members in different geographic clusters, including collaborations at other organizations.

name: Increase in partnership relatedness
definition: Partnership relatedness describes the similarity between partnership resources and the partner firm's internal resources. After partnership formation, relatedness may change as the partner firm adjusts its business portfolio, exiting existing markets or entering new markets.

name: Increase in partner firm marketing and R&D resources
authors_terms: ["increase in partner firm marketing and R&D resources", "increase in marketing resources", "increase in R&D resources"]
definition: During the lifetime of a partnership, the partner firm may experience increases or decreases in its amount of marketing and R&D resources. Given the same level of relatedness, an increase in firm marketing and R&D resources creates redundancy with partnership resources because it increases the likelihood of partnership resources becoming internally available.

name: M&A event
definition: During the lifetime of a partnership, the partner firm may become involved in M&A events such as acquiring other firms or being acquired by or merged with another firm. These events bring changes to the partner firm's resource portfolio.

name: Formation of competing partnerships
definition: A new partnership is termed competing if it is in the same industry as the focal partnership and carries out the same type of activities (manufacturing, marketing, or R&D) as the focal partnership.

name: Formation of multiple partnerships
authors_terms: ["formation of multiple partnerships", "formation of multiple partnerships with the same partner"]
definition: Formation of multiple partnerships is defined as the formation of other partnerships with the same partner after the focal partnership is formed. This creates multiple linkages between the current partner firms.

name: Decrease in the availability of alternative partners
authors_terms: ["decrease in the availability of alternative partners", "availability of alternative partners", "alternative partners"]
definition: Alternative partners are potential partners that are able to bring similar resources and serve similar purposes as the current partner. In this study, we define alternative partners for the focal partner firm as firms that are in the current partner's industry and have intentions to form partnerships in the focal partnership's industry to carry out the same type of activities (i.e., manufacturing, marketing, or R&D) as the focal partnership.

name: Competitor imitative activities
definition: We define competitor imitative activities as the partner firm's competitors forming partnerships in the same industry as the focal partnership.

name: Propensity of partnership termination
authors_terms: ["propensity of partnership termination", "propensity of termination", "partnership termination", "hazard rate of termination"]
definition: In this study, the event is partnership termination. A JV can be terminated through dissolution or acquisition.

name: Organization-level performance feedback
definition: At the organization level, firms may experience direct performance feedback during the execution of an innovative practice; performance feedback can be both a learning outcome and a learning input, and this study focuses on performance information as a learning input. Change in organizational performance is operationalized by the change in percentage of games won compared with the prior season.

name: Population-level vicarious information
authors_terms: ["vicarious information", "vicarious observations", "external network size comparison", "difference in population mean network size"]
definition: Organizations draw on vicarious learning by observing similar organizations to inform adjustments of their behavior, and may compare their network size to the predominant current network size of other similar organizations in the industry and adjust their network's size toward the industry average.

name: Change in network size
authors_terms: ["change in FT size next season", "incremental changes of network size", "incremental changes in traits of the innovation"]
definition: The study investigates incremental changes made after an innovation has been adopted, focusing on the adjustment of a single key innovation trait-the decision to maintain or change farm-team size. Change in FT size next season (Yj,t+1) is the dependent variable in all models.

name: Farm-team network size
definition: FT size is the number of minor league teams in a major league club's farm-team network. A larger network implied a larger player pool, with potentially positive effects on player development, but required a higher resource commitment.

name: Blockbuster successes
definition: Entrepreneurial endeavors that successfully cross their legitimacy threshold and gain support far exceeding it; such successes bring in a disproportionate number of new backers and encourage established backers to repeat the experience.

name: Unsung successes
definition: Entrepreneurial endeavors that gain enough support to meet their legitimacy threshold, but little more; they bring in a moderate number of new backers while discouraging established backers.

name: Path breaking failures
definition: Entrepreneurial endeavors that nearly reach their legitimacy threshold; they attract substantial support from new audiences and prime established backers to support related endeavors.

name: Broken path failures
definition: Entrepreneurial endeavors that fall well short of their legitimacy threshold; they garner little to no support and discourage established backers.

name: Resource acquisition
authors_terms: ["amount of funds pledged", "resource acquisition", "support from key audiences"]
definition: For conception-stage endeavors such as crowdfunding campaigns, resource acquisition 'represents a fundamental and measurable proxy for new venture legitimacy'; legitimacy hinges on support from key audiences, who often hold the purse strings.

name: Category-linking component experience
authors_terms: ["graphene experience", "experience with a category-linking component", "component experience", "component familiarity", "familiarity (experience level) with a category-linking component"]
definition: Experience with a component generates knowledge about the component, which can help the firm absorb distant knowledge whether it is new knowledge about characteristics of the component or knowledge of other components with which the familiar component is associated. Our knowledge of components within a category is enhanced by our experience with them.

name: Component prominence
definition: Component prominence is the extent to which the category-linking component is utilized within a knowledge category. In the case of patents, the more often a component is used in patents in that category, the more opportunities there are for comparing and contrasting that enable deductive and inductive thinking about the component and its relationships with other components within that category.

name: Knowledge distance overcome
authors_terms: ["maximum graphene-linked patent distance", "maximum category-linked patenting distance", "knowledge distance"]
definition: Distant knowledge categories are those for which there is little apparent similarity to the firm's existing knowledge base, making them difficult for organizations to comprehend.
