The distance between knowledge categories is determined by the similarity of the knowledge elements composing the categories.

name: Amount of distant knowledge absorbed
authors_terms: ["distant graphene-linked patenting", "the amount of knowledge they absorb from distant component-linked knowledge categories"]
definition: The amount of new knowledge a firm absorbs from distant component-linked knowledge categories, observed as the number of patents the firm files in distant graphene-linked patent classes.

name: Inward international activities
definition: Inward activities refer to the activities that domestic firms engage in with foreign firms in their home market, including technology imports, product imports, product agency business, original equipment manufacturing (OEM), inward franchising and licensing, and joint ventures.

name: Inward gain
authors_terms: ["inward gain", "a firm's gain from inward activities"]
definition: A firm's gain from inward activities (hereafter 'inward gain') refers to the benefits (e.g., capital, technologies, and knowledge) that the firm achieves from engaging in inward activities.

name: Resource fungibility
definition: Resource fungibility refers to the extent to which a firm's resources and capabilities can be deployed in multiple geographical and country settings. Resource fungibility represents a firm-level capability that enables the firm to deploy existing resources to new endeavors, thus reducing the cost of new investment.

name: Organizational resource fungibility
definition: Organizational resource fungibility refers to the extent to which a firm's organization-related resources and capabilities (e.g., organizational structure, culture, and management system) are adaptable across multiple geographical regions.

name: Technological resource fungibility
definition: Technological resource fungibility refers to the extent to which a firm's technological resources and capabilities (e.g., manufacturing technologies and new product development technologies) are adaptable across geographical regions.

name: Outward international activities
definition: Outward activities refer to the activities that domestic firms conduct in overseas markets, including franchising and licensing to foreign firms, overseas mergers and acquisitions, and establishing wholly owned subsidiaries in overseas markets.

name: Risk level of outward activities
authors_terms: ["high-risk outward activities", "low-risk outward activities", "risk levels of outward activities"]
definition: Different types of outward activities involve different levels of resource commitment and risk. For example, exporting, franchising, or establishing sales subsidiaries and R&D facilities in overseas markets tend to require less resource commitment than building joint ventures, acquiring firms, or establishing wholly owned production subsidiaries in overseas markets.

name: Firm risk propensity
definition: Firms differ in their risk propensity, which refers to a firm's proclivity to engage in risky projects and its managers' preferences for bold vs. cautious actions to achieve firm objectives.

name: Corporate spinout affiliation
definition: For the purposes of this study, and following Chesbrough (2003), we define corporate spinouts as the incorporation of a new independent organization, composed of former employees, a unit, or a division of the parent organization.

name: Extent of exploration
definition: Spinouts enhance explorative behaviors-i.e., the extent to which inventions are of higher technological distance from prior art in technological domains that are new for the inventor. The measure combines the number of claims and the novelty of technological classes to appraise whether the inventor's output is new with respect to his or her personal prior experience, as well as to the external world.

name: Reliance on parent company knowledge
authors_terms: ["rely on the parent company's knowledge", "share of citations to Xerox", "backward citations", "build on the parent organization's originating knowledge"]
definition: Our second dependent variable, share of citations to Xerox, relates to the extent to which inventors rely on parent organization knowledge for their inventive activities. Citations represent instances of the use of the cited firm's knowledge, so the proportion of the focal inventor's citations to Xerox's patents over total backward citations proxies the extent to which he or she builds on the originating parent's organizational knowledge.

name: Organizational socialization
definition: Socialization is the process by which members of an organization grow more alike and align with the prevailing organizational code, which hinders their learning. Socialization is a complex construct with different content areas; literature has mostly operationalized it using two proxies.

name: Information sharing
definition: Information sharing constitutes the exchange of information between buyer and supplier regarding end-user needs and preferences, market structures and acquisitions, technologies of products, strategies and finances of partners, and unexpected problems.

name: Joint sensemaking
definition: Joint sensemaking is defined as the development of insight, knowledge, and associations between past actions, the effectiveness of those actions, and future actions.

name: Knowledge integration
definition: Knowledge integration occurs when organizations develop relationship-specific memories whereby knowledge specific to that relationship is stored in organizations' collective cognitions, beliefs, and values, and idiosyncratic routines are developed in the form of encoded formal and informal procedures for how the parties interact.

name: Relationship performance
definition: A well-performing relationship exists if both dyad members are satisfied with the relationship's effectiveness (i.e., doing the right things) and efficiency (i.e., doing things the right way); the authors see relationship performance holistically in both efficiency and effectiveness dimensions and in absolute terms.

name: Cultural distance
definition: The authors hypothesize that the effects of relational learning on cross-national relationship performance of the dyad are negatively influenced by cultural distance between exchange partners, that is, distance between the countries representing the exchange partners.

name: Executive hierarchical level
authors_terms: ["hierarchical level", "executive level", "executive's level", "chief executives", "second-level executives", "third-level executives"]
definition: The level an executive occupies in the organization, distinguishing chief executives, second-level executives and third-level executives. Chief executives were asked to identify upper-level executives to participate.

name: Awareness of realized strategy
authors_terms: ["strategic awareness", "awareness of the organization's realized strategy", "agreement between an executive's perception of the organization's strategy and its realized strategy"]
definition: The degree of agreement between an executive's perception of the organization's strategy and its realized strategy, as externally measured.

name: Agreement with the chief executive's strategy
authors_terms: ["strategic awareness", "agreement between an executive's perception and the chief executive's perception of the organization's strategy"]
definition: The degree of agreement between an executive's perception and the chief executive's perception of the organization's strategy; the chief executive's view, rather than an external view, is the strategy benchmark.

name: Recent strategic change
authors_terms: ["recent strategic change", "recently changed their realized strategies", "longstanding strategies"]
definition: Whether an organization has recently changed, or is changing, its realized strategy, as opposed to having a relatively longstanding strategy.

name: Realized strategy
definition: Realized strategy is viewed as a reflection of 'actual' strategy, against which perceptions of strategy will be compared, and is operationalized through the Miles and Snow typology.

name: Executive perception of strategy
authors_terms: ["executive's perception of the organization's strategy", "perceptions of strategy"]
definition: An executive's own view of the organization's strategy, tapped by asking the executive to rate the organization's strategy on a 7-point scale representing the Miles and Snow typology.

name: Receptivity to public affairs information
authors_terms: ["receptivity to public affairs information", "receptivity", "breadth of contacts", "depth of involvement"]
definition: An organization's receptivity, defined in terms of both the breadth of outside contacts that company executives maintain in the public affairs environment and the depth, or length of time of company involvement with specific issues, affects both the richness of the organization's internal perceptions of the outside environment and its responsiveness to it.

name: Integration of public affairs information
definition: Organizations need integrating mechanisms to coordinate the specialized information collected by boundary-spanning units into a coherent picture of the public affairs domain; the authors defined integration in terms of the frequency of use of task forces and the degree of establishment of steering committees in public affairs.

name: Internal influence of public affairs
authors_terms: ["internal influence of public affairs", "influence of public affairs", "total influence"]
definition: The authors defined the internal influence of public affairs in terms of its importance (1) in matters that affect an organization's context, including how much time and attention the chief executive officer (CEO), board of directors, and annual planning process gave to public affairs, and (2) in the organization's executives' personal career progress, performance appraisals, career paths, and training programs.

name: Corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["social performance", "corporate social performance", "social responsiveness", "social performance ratings"]
definition: Companies with a strong internal public affairs structure were expected to achieve strong social performance ratings, as defined by stakeholders' perceptions of company responsiveness to public affairs.

name: Institutional influence
authors_terms: ["institutional influence", "institutional influences", "institutional pressures", "peer influence", "federal regulator influence", "PEER", "FEDERAL"]
definition: Institutional influences are external social pressures toward conformity. Institutional influences on bank operations and practices arise from peer banks (PEER) and federal examiners (FEDERAL).

name: Information systems outsourcing
definition: Outsourcing, the primary dependent variable, refers to the source of IS services a bank adopts. All but the first two sourcing alternatives (in-house operations and IS subsidiary at parent bank) were classified as IS outsourcing, while use of in-house IS services was considered insourcing.

name: External production cost advantage
definition: External production cost advantage (PRODCOST) is the degree to which an external service provider is perceived to have an advantage in production cost economies over internal bureaucratic management of IS services.

name: Slack resources
definition: Slack resources (SLACK) is the level of working capital, measured as the amount of financial resources available for IS relative to past years' resources and peer banks' resources allocated for IS. Organizations may not conform to institutional influences if they have the financial capacity or working capital to resist external pressures.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity (SPECIFIC) is the degree to which investments in IS yielded unique value to any single firm. Specific assets are physical and human assets that are specialized and unique to the extent that they generate less value outside the contractual relationship.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty (UNCERTAIN) is the rapid and unexpected change in IT developments.

name: Functional complexity
definition: Functional complexity (COMPLEX) is the degree of formal structural differentiation within an organization; in the context of the IS function the construct concerns the extent to which IS activities are diversified.

name: Supplier presence
definition: Supplier presence is the availability of reputable and trustworthy service providers (Walker and Weber 1984). In the market context studied, supplier presence (SUPPLIER) is the availability of reputable and trustworthy external IT service providers in the market.

name: Firm size
definition: Size (SIZE) is represented by a dichotomous variable, zero, for small banks and one for large banks. Small banks are those with assets less than $1 billion and large banks are those with assets of at least $1 billion.

name: Joint venture status
definition: Joint ventures are here defined as both greenfield joint ventures and partial acquisitions. JV is a dummy variable equal to one if a Japanese parent owned more than 5% but less than 95% of the subsidiary equity (i.e., if it had a joint venture stake); and equal to zero otherwise (a wholly-owned stake).

name: Parent stake termination
definition: Termination of a parent stake takes place when an affiliate is closed, liquidated, or goes bankrupt, or when a Japanese investor sells its full stake in an affiliate or its partial stake in a joint venture to an American firm, another Japanese firm, or a firm from a third country. Gross terminations are defined here as withdrawals from the United States due to liquidation/bankruptcy and selloffs.

name: Exit by liquidation
definition: Liquidation means that subsidiaries were closed, liquidated, or went bankrupt.

name: Exit by sale
definition: A stake that is sold to either the partnering firm or a third party is recorded as a sale.

name: Parent's US market experience
authors_terms: ["LOGEXP", "experience of the US market", "number of years elapsed between a Japanese parent's first entry into the United States and the year of establishment"]
definition: LOGEXP is a proxy for the extent to which Japanese investors know the U.S. market. It is the log of EXP, the number of years elapsed between a Japanese parent's first entry into the United States and the year of establishment of a particular subsidiary.

name: Affiliate product diversification
authors_terms: ["DIV", "affiliate manufactures a product different from that of the parent"]
definition: DIV is a dummy variable equal to one if the products manufactured by the subsidiary were different from those of the parent, and equal to zero otherwise.

name: Acquisition entry mode
definition: ACQ is a dummy variable equal to one if the affiliate was established through an acquisition, and equal to zero in the case of greenfield investment.

name: Industry growth
authors_terms: ["GROW", "growth rate of shipments of the U.S. 4 digit SIC industry entered"]
definition: GROW is the annual growth rate of shipments of the U.S. 4 digit SIC industry entered by Japanese affiliates from 1980 to the year of status change or the censoring year in the case of no change.

name: Parent size
authors_terms: ["SIZE", "employment of parent company at the time of entry"]
definition: SIZE is measured by the number of employees of the parent company at the time of its establishment of its U.S. affiliate.

name: Affiliate age
authors_terms: ["AGE80", "age of affiliate when it enters the risk set"]
definition: AGE80 is the age of the affiliate in 1980 when it became at risk.

name: Pre-entry experience
definition: Entrant heterogeneity at the time of entry: diversifying entrants possess a wide range of resources and capabilities that can be leveraged into a new industry, whereas entrepreneurial startups have no prior experience before their inclusion in the IDC database. Pre-entry experience is important because founding conditions that imprint on an organization can have long-lasting effects.

name: Firm survival
definition: Whether and when a firm leaves the personal computer industry; a firm is considered to have exited in year t if its unit sales for years t+1 to 1994 were zero, otherwise the exit date is right-censored.

name: Entry timing
definition: When a firm first entered the new industry, defined as the year in which the firm first sold a personal computer (less 1973); early entrants generally have higher survival rates than later entrants in new, technologically dynamic industries.

name: Technology standard adoption
authors_terms: ["product technology standard", "offering products incorporating the technology standard", "Intel x86", "migrating to the technology standard"]
definition: Whether or not a firm offers products incorporating the technology standard during its tenure in the personal computer industry; the firm must decide whether to enter with, or migrate to, the product architecture that becomes the industry standard.

name: Newest technology adoption
authors_terms: ["newest product technology", "products incorporating the latest technology", "newest technology", "latest technology"]
definition: Whether or not a firm offers products with the latest technology, i.e., products built on the newest (most advanced) microprocessor generation available at the time.

name: Exploration contract
definition: The exploration contract combines tolerance for early failure and reward for long-term success: subjects are paid 50% of the profits they make during the last 10 periods of the experiment, so they can fail at no cost in the first half while they explore new strategies and have a prospect of pay for performance later on.

name: Fixed-wage contract
definition: Subjects in the fixed-wage treatment group receive a fixed wage in each period of the experiment; in the lemonade stand experiment they are paid a fixed wage of 50 francs per period.

name: Pay-for-performance contract
definition: Subjects in the pay-for-performance treatment group are given a standard pay-for-performance (or profit sharing) contract, receiving a fixed percentage of the profits produced during the experiment; in the lemonade stand experiment this is 50% of the profits made during the 20 periods.

name: Termination threat
definition: Under the termination contract subjects receive the exploration contract, but the experiment ends after 10 periods if their profits in the first 10 periods are below a threshold; early termination can undermine the exploration behavior induced by the exploration contract by eliminating the tolerance for early failure.

name: Golden parachute
definition: The termination-with-golden-parachute treatment gives subjects a reparation payment of 250 francs if the experiment ends after 10 periods; such payments reintroduce the tolerance for early failure that is required to encourage exploration.

name: Risk aversion
definition: Risk aversion is the subject's attitude toward risk, which is elicited after the experiment and about which there is considerable heterogeneity across subjects; for the statistical analysis subjects are split into a less and a more risk-averse group based on the median observation of the measure in the sample.

name: Innovation success
authors_terms: ["innovation", "innovation success", "finding the optimal business strategy", "optimal business strategy"]
definition: Innovation is often defined as the production of knowledge through experimentation; in the experiment the authors measure how close subjects come to finding the optimal business strategy, both by whether they choose the highest-profit location and by the maximum, final-period and average profits they achieve.

name: Exploration behavior
definition: Subjects face the choice between fine-tuning the product choice decisions given to them by the previous manager (exploitation) or choosing a different location and radically altering the product mix to discover a more profitable strategy (exploration).

name: Effort
definition: Under a fixed-wage contract subjects do not have any explicit incentives for good performance, so they should minimize the costly contemplation effort necessary to find the best business strategy; effort is studied through time allocation and the recording of previous choices and outcomes.

name: Profit performance
definition: Subjects' overall performance in the experiment is measured by average profit; the authors also examine how close subjects come to the optimal strategy in terms of the maximum per-period profit and the final-period profit they achieve.

name: Product diversification
definition: 'Product diversification' means that firms have operations in more than one industry or product market. A firm's product diversification consists of 'related diversification' (i.e., products within the same industry group) and 'unrelated diversification' (i.e., products across different industry groups).

name: Secondary stakeholder diversity
authors_terms: ["secondary stakeholders", "diversity of secondary stakeholders", "scope of secondary stakeholders", "secondary stakeholder diversity"]
definition: 'Secondary stakeholders' refers to those that either indirectly influence or are influenced by the firm without legal obligations; they include institutions such as religious organizations, nonprofit organizations, and NGOs, but exclude governmental organizations. The variable of secondary stakeholders with which a firm maintains relationships is measured as the diversity of nonprofit organizations to which it donates.

name: Financial performance
definition: The authors chose return on assets (ROA) as the measurement of firm financial performance because this accounting-based performance indicator captures the efficiency of resource allocation via firm operation.

name: Threat interpretation
definition: A categorization of a strategic issue as a threat, influenced by whether the issue is seen in negative terms, as a potential loss, and as controllable/uncontrollable; the authors treat threat and opportunity as two separate diagnosis constructs and not merely ends of a continuum.

name: Opportunity interpretation
definition: A categorization of a strategic issue as an opportunity, influenced by whether the issue is seen in positive terms, as a potential gain, and as controllable/uncontrollable; it is measured separately from threat.

name: Feasibility
definition: Feasibility addresses the awareness and comprehension of causal relationships, alternatives, and the means to successfully carry out a response, and reflects managers' perceived level of understanding and capability to respond.

name: Urgency
definition: Urgency addresses the determination of how soon an issue response is required, depending heavily on rational consideration and executives' mental models, and involves the issue's importance, time pressure and visibility.

name: Favorability
definition: A construct identified in the commingled factor analysis, consisting of two opportunity items, positive and gain; it seems to reflect the extent to which a firm's response to a strategic issue will result in a positive gain.

name: Influence
definition: A construct identified in the commingled factor analysis, containing the three feasibility items and two items concerning controllability; it seems to reflect the perceived capacity of the organization to respond to a strategic issue.

name: Strategic issue response
authors_terms: ["strategic issue response", "intentions to respond", "actual responses", "response to strategic issues"]
definition: Responses to strategic issues, conceptualized along two dimensions: magnitude of response and domain of response (internal/external). The authors operationalize response both as intentions to respond and as actual responses undertaken.

name: Integrated EIV construct structure
authors_terms: ["FUI", "integrated model of SID", "three underlying constructs", "favorability, urgency, and influence"]
definition: The construct structure underlying a joint consideration of the threat-opportunity and feasibility-urgency frameworks, which the authors expect to reflect an integrative EIV model of three constructs corresponding to expectancy, instrumentality, and valence. The authors dub the resulting integrated model FUI (favorability, urgency, and influence).

name: Risk aversion
definition: Theories of risk aversion highlight heterogeneity with regards to individual comfort thresholds for risk and uncertainty.

name: Core self-evaluation
definition: Core self-evaluation (CSE) is a broad dispositional trait manifested by four elements of personality: self-esteem, generalized self-efficacy, locus of control, and emotional stability; it is theorized to reflect the fundamental appraisals individuals make about themselves, their capabilities, and their competence.

name: Hybrid entrepreneurship entry
definition: Hybrid entrepreneurship is the process of initiating a business while simultaneously remaining employed for wages.

name: Full-time self-employment entry
definition: Participants who started a self-employed business within a three-month window of exiting their paid job were treated as entering full-time self-employment, in contrast to those who entered through hybrid entrepreneurship.

name: Staged entry into full-time self-employment
authors_terms: ["staged entry", "staged entry process", "staged entry into full-time self-employment"]
definition: Entering full-time self-employment in a staged entry process (i.e., paid employment to hybrid entrepreneurship to full-time self-employment).

name: Self-employment survival
definition: Following extant research, the authors defined survival as the continuation of entrepreneurial effort.

name: Cognitive ability
definition: Cognitive ability is conceptualized as the general ability to think abstractly, learn from experiences, comprehend surroundings, and 'figure things out'.

name: Entrepreneurial experience
definition: Specific knowledge accumulated through prior (entrepreneurial) experience, which influences the ability to assess, assimilate, and make sense of new information.

name: Investment stage focus
authors_terms: ["stage of investment", "investment focus", "stage", "stage of companies they primarily targeted"]
definition: One of the most important strategic decisions faced by the founding partners of a VC firm is the stage of development of the companies in which they want to invest. Source data sets asked VC firms to indicate the stage of companies they primarily targeted in their investments, using five gradations.

name: Structural leverage
definition: The ratio of junior investment personnel to senior investment personnel. This variable indicates the degree to which senior members structure the firm to leverage the efforts of junior staff (Sherer 1995).

name: Fund performance
definition: Limited partners have begun to publish the returns of the VC firms in which they have invested, making it possible to study the performance implications of these VCs' strategy and structure choices. The performance models used the internal rate of return reported for each fund.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership concentration", "ownership share of the largest owner", "share of the largest owner"]
definition: The (voting) share of the largest owner. Ownership concentration measures the power of shareholders to influence managers.

name: Owner identity
authors_terms: ["owner identity", "identity of the largest owner", "owner category", "ownership category"]
definition: The identity of the largest owner - bank, institutional investor, (nonfinancial) company, family/single person/foundation or government. Whereas ownership concentration measures the power of shareholders to influence managers, the identity of the owners has implications for their objectives and the way they exercise their power.

name: Company economic performance
definition: Company performance is measured by three different variables: market-to-book value of equity, return on assets, and sales growth.

name: Shareholder value
definition: The market's valuation of company equity, measured by the market-to-book value of equity; stock prices are taken to give the stock market expectation of the long-term effects on profitability.

name: Profitability
definition: Return on assets, which measures current accounting profitability more than expected future earnings.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["sales growth", "growth of sales", "growth rates of turnover"]
definition: Growth of company sales (turnover), one of the three performance measures used in the study.

name: Complexity of existing business lines
definition: Corporate-level complexity in the firm's existing business lines, or the extent of their interdependence. It increases the prevailing coordination demand and exacerbates the coordination problem associated with input sharing.

name: Input similarity
authors_terms: ["input similarity", "INPUT SIMILARITY", "overlap in input requirements", "input sharing"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's primary industry, j, shares inputs with a target industry, k. A large correlation coefficient suggests a significant overlap in inputs required by the two industries.

name: Diversifying entry
definition: Whether firm i diversified from its primary industry j into industry k in year t. Any industry k in which firm i did not operate in the previous year (t-1) was treated as a potential target destination industry in the current year (t).

name: Cumulative task experience
authors_terms: ["Experience", "cumulative prior experience", "focal task experience", "experience in the focal task"]
definition: The knowledge that accrues from repeatedly doing something, where 'the taking of repeated action (i.e., doing) and the accrual of knowledge (i.e., experience) go hand in hand.' The authors operationalize it as an organization's cumulative prior experience performing PTCA.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The outcome of the focal task, measured as procedure failure: 'we focus our attention instead on a more prevalent outcome that also reflects procedure failure: the rate at which patients in a particular hospital require another procedure, or rework.' In the authors' words, 'in the context of the outcome variable under study, a lower value (i.e., fewer cases of rework) is better.'

name: Academic affiliation
authors_terms: ["academic affiliation", "Academic", "research orientation", "academic medical center (AMC)", "Council of Teaching Hospitals and Health Systems (COTH) membership"]
definition: The intensity of a hospital's connection with a medical school, from no affiliation to non-COTH medical school affiliation to membership in the Council of Teaching Hospitals and Health Systems. The authors argue that the strongest relationships (academic medical centers) bring research-oriented faculty appointments and additional performance targets that are not aligned with clinical care.

name: Teaching intensity
definition: The extent to which an organization is engaged in coaching and mentoring individuals receiving observational and hands-on training in regular work settings, captured by the number of interns and residents per hospital bed.

name: Insider ownership
definition: Greater stock ownership by managers has been proposed as a key means to align managers' interests with those of other stockholders, and subsequently to enhance firm performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is a multidimensional construct, so any single index may not be able to provide a comprehensive understanding of the performance implication related to the constructs of interest.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: A concept central to this perspective is environmental dynamism, that is, the rate of change, and the degree of instability, of factors within an environment.

name: Top management team size
definition: Team size refers to the number of corporate officers who were also board members, the authors' definition of a top management team. Team size and power distribution help determine the nature of a top team's information-processing capabilities.

name: CEO dominance
authors_terms: ["CEO dominance", "dominance", "distribution of power within top management teams"]
definition: CEO dominance is the extent to which a firm's chief executive officer dominates the distribution of power within its top management team; power is defined as the capacity of individual actors to exert their will. When power is unevenly concentrated in a firm's CEO, CEO dominance is high.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured with three indicators: return on assets, return on sales, and return on equity, which were standardized and averaged into a composite measure.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Turbulence refers to volatility or difficult-to-predict discontinuities in an environment. Turbulent environments increase both an organization's external linkages and the rate of change in those linkages.

name: Environmental discretion
definition: Managerial discretion refers to the latitude of action top management teams have in making strategic choices. Although discretion can be conceptualized at individual, organizational, and environmental levels, the authors focused only on environment-level discretion, called environmental discretion.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: The authors define CEO dismissal as an involuntary exit of the chief executive officer, in which the board forces the CEO out; CEO successions are coded as a dismissal when the announcement indicates a forced departure, news coverage shows the board contemplated removal over performance concerns, the CEO resigned immediately after a board meeting with no designated replacement, or the CEO left abruptly with a search firm hired to find a replacement.

name: Average analyst stock recommendation
definition: Average analyst recommendation refers to the average recommendation across investment analysts for a specific firm's stock, with a lower average referring to a less favorable (or more negative) stock recommendation. Analyst recommendations are visible signals that summarize analysts' evaluation of the future earnings prospects of the firm and convey their assessment about the abilities of the CEO.

name: Analyst recommendation change
authors_terms: ["change in average analyst recommendation", "analyst downgrade", "investment analyst downgrade"]
definition: A downgrade (e.g., from buy to hold) refers to a revision or change in the average analyst stock recommendation.

name: Percentage of sell recommendations
authors_terms: ["percentage of sell recommendations", "percentage of analysts that issue a sell recommendation"]
definition: The percentage of sell recommendations reflects the percentage of analysts that 'negatively' (underperform or sell) rate the firm's stock.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["prior firm financial performance", "firm's prior financial performance", "industry-adjusted ROA", "industry-adjusted stock return"]
definition: The firm's financial performance provides information regarding the past performance of the firm and its leadership, and is operationalized using both accounting and stock return measures of prior firm performance adjusted for industry differences.

name: Investment analyst credibility
authors_terms: ["credibility of investment analysts", "credibility ascribed to investment analysts", "pre- versus post-litigation"]
definition: Investment analysts are viewed to be credible to the degree that they are perceived as providing an independent, accurate assessment of the firm's future prospects. The litigation against investment analysts by Attorney General Spitzer, the SEC inquiry, and the penalties assessed against the 10 largest investment banks all served to undermine the credibility of analysts as external and independent experts.

name: New CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["new CEO dismissal", "dismissal of a newly appointed CEO"]
definition: New CEO dismissal refers to a situation in which a newly appointed CEO is dismissed within three years after taking office. A time-varying dichotomous outcome measure—new CEO dismissal—was coded 1 in a year in which a new CEO was dismissed and 0 otherwise.

name: New CEO origin
authors_terms: ["new CEO origins", "outside new CEO", "inside succession", "outside succession"]
definition: New CEO origins have typically been divided into two categories: inside CEOs who are hired from within the firm, and outside CEOs who are hired from the outside. Relative to an inside succession, an outside succession is characterized by a higher level of information asymmetry between the board and the new CEO.

name: Nominating committee independence
authors_terms: ["independent nominating committee", "nonindependent nominating committee", "independence of the committee"]
definition: This independence refers to the relative representation of outside directors on the committee. Firms with an independent nominating committee are those on which the number of outside directors was larger than that of inside directors.

name: External directorships
authors_terms: ["external directorships", "number of external boards", "nominating committee with more/fewer external directorships"]
definition: Directors' external directorships are positions on boards other than the focal firm's board and provide the firm with important sources of up-to-date information on other firms' practices and procedures. The number of external boards on which each of the outside directors on the nominating committee was serving was counted, excluding the focal firm's board.

name: Predecessor CEO disposition
authors_terms: ["disposition of the predecessor CEO", "predecessor dismissal", "dismissal of the predecessor CEO"]
definition: The disposition of the predecessor CEO—i.e., dismissal versus voluntary turnover—represents an important context of CEO succession.

name: Attention to framing mental activities
authors_terms: ["framing disposition", "framing disposition condition", "increasing attention to mental activities related to framing", "attentional engagement with the mental activities related to framing"]
definition: A framing disposition is the tendency to cycle more to and from the phases related to framing the problem, emphasizing the identification and connection of the problem's elements and the creation of coherence from fragmented elements; it leads to a continuous structuring and restructuring of the problem elements by identifying them, connecting them, and creating hierarchical structures of hypotheses and assumptions.

name: Attention to implementation mental activities
authors_terms: ["implementation disposition", "implementation disposition condition", "increasing attention to mental activities related to implementation", "attentional engagement with the mental activities related to implementation"]
definition: An implementation disposition is the tendency to cycle more to and from the phases related to implementing solutions to the problem, emphasizing anticipating possible contingencies and evaluating future outcomes; it leads to an elaborated deliberation about possible outcomes, such as thinking about potential contingencies and consequences, designing sequences of actions, simulating events, and evaluating possible outcomes.

name: Problem-focused problem-solving strategy
definition: One of the two emergent problem-solving strategies; it is an emergent pattern of attention, referred to as a problem-solving strategy, that relies on a framing disposition and cycles more to and from phases related to framing the problem.

name: Solution-focused solution strategy
definition: One of the two emergent problem-solving strategies; it is an emergent pattern of attention, referred to as a problem-solving strategy, that relies on an implementation disposition and cycles more to and from phases related to implementing solutions to the problem.

name: Deliberation effort
definition: Deliberation is the reflective, effortful thinking associated with type 2 processing, which the authors treat as consisting of two qualitatively distinct mental activities, framing and implementation; the amount of deliberation involved in each thought is measured as the time between moves.

name: Risk taking
authors_terms: ["risk taking", "going for it", "attempting a fourth-down conversion", "risky choice"]
definition: The 'riskiness' of a decision is associated with the likelihood of adverse outcomes and the magnitude of potential loss; a decision is considered risky to the extent that likelihoods are variable and that potential outcomes entail losses.

name: Performance below the aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below the aspiration level", "performance at or below the aspiration level", "performance shortfall"]
definition: Performance at or below the aspiration level, which is the 'smallest satisfactory level of performance' and the borderline between perceived success and failure; when performance is below this level, managers may find themselves concerned with either attaining aspirations or ensuring survival.

name: Performance above the aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance above the aspiration level", "performance above aspirations"]
definition: Performance above the aspiration level, where managers may find themselves concerned with either maintaining aspirations or experimenting with excess resources.

name: Deadline proximity
authors_terms: ["deadline proximity", "minutes remaining", "time remaining", "availability of time", "temporal proximity of deadlines"]
definition: The temporal proximity of the deadline that ends a performance period. The authors propose that the availability of time before the end of a given period represents a unique type of resource, and that its depletion can trigger shifts in the focus of organizational attention.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: This variable consisted of four items that measured the outcome of the acquisition and the integration process, using managerial evaluations of acquisition performance. This approach is in line with the essence of attribution research where perceptions rather than, for example, 'objective' assessments are the core of attributional analyses.

name: Attribution to managerial actions
authors_terms: ["attribution to managers' actions", "causal attributions to managerial agency", "attribution to manager's actions"]
definition: Respondents were asked to rate their perceptions based on the extent to which management's actions (1) had affected the outcome of the integration process, and (2) explained the overall success of the acquisition.

name: Attribution to cultural differences
authors_terms: ["attribution to cultural differences", "causal attributions to cultural differences"]
definition: Respondents were asked about the extent to which they perceived that cultural differences (1) had affected the outcome of the acquisition's integration process, and (2) explained the overall success of the acquisition.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: We measured personal acquisition experience by combining the number of acquisitions in which the respondent had been personally involved (1) on the acquiring firm side, and (2) on the acquired firm side. This sum index represented the person's combined prior experience of acquisitions.

name: Social affiliation
definition: Social affiliations are 'connections from common memberships in formal social institutions external to economic transactions,' such as religious groups, schools, alumni organizations, the military, clubs, and professional associations. The authors state that benefits are hypothesized to accrue from the presence of a social affiliation, and not from positions in a network or from prior interactions directly per se.

name: Human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "agent human capital", "agent experience", "total agent experience", "human capital applicability", "experience", "applicability", "% seller agent"]
definition: Human capital refers to an individual's knowledge, skills, and ability, and is acquired over time through professional experience as well as through formal training. Knowledge and skills can be specific to a transaction type, so human capital may not be broadly applicable across different types of transactions.

name: Transaction performance
authors_terms: ["transaction outcomes", "transaction performance", "agent performance", "professional performance", "improved transaction outcomes"]
definition: Final home sale price, time on market, and probability of sale are the primary metrics used to evaluate real estate transaction performance. Higher values of the first two metrics and a completed sale benefit sellers and agents.

name: Agent selection
authors_terms: ["selection process", "agent selection", "seller's choice of an agent", "agent choice"]
definition: The selection process underlying the consumer's decision to use a socially affiliated professional, i.e., the seller's choice of an agent from a risk set of alternative agents.

name: Cognitive processing type
definition: Dual-process theory describes human cognition as the interplay between type 1, intuitive, fast, unconscious, associative, heuristic processing and type 2, analytic, deliberative, time-consuming, effortful processing. The authors refer to the two processes as types 1 and 2 and advocate the parallel-competitive view, in which the two types of processing are initiated in parallel and compete for attention and cognitive control.

name: Organizational adaptation
authors_terms: ["organizational adaptation", "routine adaptation", "adaptation of organizational routines", "adaptation to discontinuous change"]
definition: Organizational-level adaptation is the modification of organizational forms to fit the new environment, that is, the adaptation or dropping of the existing set of organizational routines after a discontinuous change. It is measured by assessing the performance of coordinated behavior following a discontinuous change.

name: Environmental ambiguity
definition: Ambiguity refers to the degree to which decision makers lack information about the meaning and implications of particular events or situations. It is a critical dimension of environmental dynamism.

name: Deviation from optimality
definition: Routinized behavior might lead to an overreliance on previous patterns to the detriment of solutions closer to optimal, and such suboptimal patterns increase the number of moves beyond those required and reduce the efficient use of resources. The authors measure deviance from the optimal solution as the number of unnecessary moves used in each hand.

name: Speed of action
authors_terms: ["speed", "average move time per hand", "timely responses", "faster responses"]
definition: Differences in response speed between the two types of cognitive processes are examined as one of the behavioral dimensions along which the collective capacity to adapt is observed. Speed is measured through the average move time per hand and the time taken to complete the rounds.

name: Routinization
authors_terms: ["routinization", "routinized behavior", "reliance on specific patterns of behavior"]
definition: Routinization is the degree to which the groups relied on specific patterns of behavior. After routinization in the first round, adapting patterns is particularly difficult, so the authors examine whether groups recovered the reliance on a smaller set of patterns after the discontinuity.

name: Coordination efficiency
definition: The efficiency of coordination measures the increased ability of the groups to produce an acceptable result when communication is constrained. It is computed by regressing the number of moves on the hand number.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "dual governance structure", "dual leadership structure", "dual structure", "dual corporate governance structure"]
definition: CEO duality refers to a firm's CEO also serving as board chair. The dual governance structure is the governance choice whose selection the study models.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is the metric the authors take to be optimized in the firm's constrained optimization process; they note that there exists no single, unique measure of firm performance and therefore employ four alternatives.

name: Comparative advantage in performance
authors_terms: ["comparative advantage in performance", "comparative advantage", "self-select into the governance structure in accordance with comparative advantage"]
definition: If the self-selection process is based on comparative advantage in performance, then the estimated difference in the covariance terms must be greater than zero, that is, performance will be higher with self-selection than with random assignment.

name: Selection bias
definition: The selection bias that results from ordinary least squares estimation of the performance equations is, in effect, an omitted variables problem where the omitted variables are the inverse Mills terms; the endogeneity arises from a stochastic sorting process embedded in the covariances between the unobservables in the performance and governance structure selection equations.

name: Strategic variety
authors_terms: ["strategic variety", "strategic heterogeneity", "strategic homogeneity", "industry variety", "overall strategic variety", "strategic distance"]
definition: The degree to which the strategies pursued by firms in an industry differ from one another. The authors note that strategic distance has been defined as 'the degree to which strategies in different groups differ in terms of key strategic decision variables, such as advertising, cost structure, R&D, organization of production, etc.' (Porter, 1979: 218).

name: Industry profitability
authors_terms: ["average industry profitability", "industry performance", "average industry ROI", "industry profits"]
definition: The average profitability enjoyed by all the firms in an industry; the authors state that industry performance was measured as average ROI for all observations in each industry over the time period 1984-87.

name: Differentiation
definition: Differentiation is the 'state of segmentation of the organizational system into subsystems, each of which tends to develop particular attributes in relation to the requirements posed by its relevant external environment' (Lawrence and Lorsch, 1967b: 4). It refers to the degree to which organizational units have developed distinctive structural characteristics and their members have made behavioral accommodations to their environment.

name: Integration
definition: Integration refers to the achievement of collaboration between organizational subunits. It encompasses not only cooperation (alignment of interest) but also coordination (alignment of actions). Integration is the 'quality of the state of collaboration that exists among departments that are required to achieve unity of effort by the demands of the environment' (Lawrence and Lorsch, 1967a: 11).

name: Transaction instability
definition: We define 'transaction instability' as the extent and rate of change in demand and technology relevant to a particular transaction.

name: Reciprocal task interdependence
definition: In vertical relationships, reciprocal interdependence can arise when the design and production of the procured item require significant levels of joint activity by the buyer and supplier, requiring continuous adaptation in the vertical relationship as both parties engage in joint problem solving. The nature of interdependence implies a state of continuous adaptation between units as ongoing decision making about task allocation and continuous communication (mutual adjustment) is required.

name: Relationship performance
definition: Performance of the vertical relationship is the outcome on which the match between adaptive capacity and adaptation requirements impacts. Because objective data on exchange performance is considered confidential and is hard to collect, the authors use items capturing multiple facets of the satisfaction of the procurers with the supplier in comparison with alternative suppliers, which they expect to be strongly correlated with exchange performance.

name: Procurement mode
authors_terms: ["procurement mode", "mode of procurement", "make, buy, ally", "modes of organizing vertical relationships"]
definition: The procurement mode is the specific organizational arrangement used to procure a component. Different modes of procurement - make, buy, and ally - differ in terms of the extent of differentiation and integration between procuring and supplying units and therefore in their adaptive capacity for responding to changes in the exchange environment in a coordinated and cooperative manner.

name: Cultural omnivorousness
authors_terms: ["cultural omnivores", "cultural omnivorism", "cultural omnivorousness", "culturally omnivorous populations", "college graduate %"]
definition: Cultural omnivorousness refers to appreciation for a wide range of aesthetic experiences, consuming across lowbrow and highbrow varieties, which is characteristic of contemporary elites and grounded in higher education.

name: Ethnic diversity
definition: Diverse populations provide access to a variety of perspectives, encouraging the recognition of new opportunities; a community's ethnic diversity in particular should increase tolerance toward innovations that depart from type classifications.

name: Established craft organizations
authors_terms: ["incumbent craft organizations", "organizations with craft authenticity", "craft incumbents", "craft breweries", "farmers' markets"]
definition: Incumbent organizations that valorize craft as a route to authenticity attract the development of new craft organizations because they signal and inculcate demand for enterprises that focus on craft rather than type conformity.

name: Type-authentic organizations
authors_terms: ["organizations with a strong adherence to a traditional type authenticity", "established organizations with type authenticity", "steakhouse restaurants"]
definition: The presence of organizations with a strong adherence to a traditional type authenticity makes a community less hospitable to innovative craft entrants; these organizations signal and encourage demand for true-to-type offerings, which can constrain new producers from innovating.

name: Mass producers
authors_terms: ["mass producers", "organizations that engage in mass production", "mass production", "national chains", "chain restaurants"]
definition: Organizations that offer mass-produced and standardized products deter the development of entrepreneurs claiming any form of authenticity by disregarding the value of authenticity; they ignore local particularities and instead emphasize efficiency and reliability.

name: Craft organization foundings
authors_terms: ["craft organizations", "gourmet food trucks (GFTs)", "truck creation", "truck foundings", "truck births", "food trucks created"]
definition: The creation of new organizations that base their authenticity on craft rather than conformity to type expectations; in this study, the founding of gourmet food trucks, which stretched street food expectations by serving upscale cuisine in a mobile fashion.

name: Network resources
definition: Network resources inhere not so much within the firm but in the interfirm networks in which firms are located. They are a specific form of firm resources that can be considered to be 'strengths that firms can use to conceive of and implement their strategies'.

name: Alliance formation capabilities
authors_terms: ["alliance formation capabilities", "capabilities with alliance formation", "capabilities with alliances", "cooperative capabilities"]
definition: The authors' concern is not with technological or material resource-based capabilities but with organizational capabilities that enable firms to form alliances with greater ease. Firms build up concrete alliance formation capabilities with experience, which in turn enables them to form new alliances with greater ease and greater frequency.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "entry into alliances", "entering a new alliance", "alliance behavior"]
definition: A strategic alliance is commonly defined as any voluntarily initiated cooperative agreement between firms that involves exchange, sharing, or codevelopment. Alliance formation here is whether the firm entered any alliances in a given year, including ties with prior and with new partners.

name: Use of prescribed decision criteria
authors_terms: ["prescribed decision criteria", "prescribed decision practice", "decision rule", "formal decision criteria", "percentage of prescribed criteria", "reliance on prescribed criteria", "use of prescribed decision criteria"]
definition: We define the criteria included on the risk-rating guide as "prescribed decision criteria" because in its training materials, the bank identified these criteria as being the primary factors that loan officers should use to assess borrower risk. They are the organizationally prescribed information that decision makers are supposed to collect and use in making a judgment.

name: Use of ad hoc decision criteria
definition: In contrast to the formally prescribed decision criteria, we define these criteria as ad hoc because they were not included in reference materials, were not discussed during the formal training of commercial lenders, and were not included on the risk-rating guide in the lending procedure manual.

name: Decision size
authors_terms: ["size of the decision", "size of the loan", "decision importance"]
definition: Decisions with important consequences will prompt decision makers to be more or less inclined to adhere to prescribed practices, and such consequences could occur when the size of the decision is large (e.g., involves significant resources). Results suggest that decision makers are more likely to use intendedly rational processes as the size of the decision increases.

name: Relationship duration
authors_terms: ["duration of the relationship with the exchange partner", "duration of the exchange relationship", "duration of relationship", "relationship tenure"]
definition: Knowledge, experience, and trust accumulate as a relationship endures, and consequently, over time, exchange relationships evolve from information exchanges to institutionalized relationships. Thus, the duration of an exchange relationship reflects both learning and commitment.

name: Subunit size
authors_terms: ["subunit size", "branch size", "size of the bank branch"]
definition: A subunit's size may reflect the extent to which it emphasizes norms to comply with formal requirements. Organizational theory and research supports the idea that larger units are more likely to require decision makers to adhere to formal decision policies than smaller units.

name: Subunit customer base
authors_terms: ["customer base", "unit expertise in terms of customer base", "characteristics of the customer base"]
definition: One important aspect of a subunit's context is the type of customers the unit serves; subunits often specialize and target their services toward particular categories of customers. The idea is that the routines that develop around borrower evaluations are driven, in part, by the characteristics of the customer base that the branch serves.

name: Prior subunit performance
authors_terms: ["past performance", "prior unit performance", "prior performance", "each branch's prior performance"]
definition: Theories of success suggest that decision makers in highly performing units are more likely to be deemed competent and may be subject to less scrutiny than decision makers in poorly performing units, whereas decision makers in poorly performing units may feel added pressure to conform to the rules.

name: Organizational standardization pressures
authors_terms: ["strength of standardization", "degree of standardization", "pressures to standardize decision making", "standardization effort"]
definition: The strength of the institution's efforts to standardize decision practice across the organization's geographically separated subunits. Organization-wide rules signal the value and legitimacy of appropriate behaviors and thereby provide, through formal means, the principles of action, interaction, and interpretation that guide and constrain decision makers in accomplishing their tasks.

name: Change in decision assessment
authors_terms: ["stability in the risk-rating assessment", "change in the decision assessment", "change in the borrower's risk rating"]
definition: The outcome associated with the use of the prescribed criteria in which we were primarily interested was the stability in the risk-rating assessment. To assess whether or not there was evidence of stability, we measured the risk assessment of the borrower in both the prior (t-1) and the current year (T).

name: Respectability
definition: The type of symbolic capital consisting of the accumulated institutional recognition originating from outside the professional field of a cultural organization, associated with broad public recognition of an organization and constituted by institutional recognition and age.

name: Reputability
definition: The type of symbolic capital concerning an organization's recognition within a professional field; it resides in the professional merits of its members and superior professional performance and is constituted by celebrated artistic directors and cast members with recent professional award nominations.

name: Institutional recognition
definition: Symbolic capital originating predominantly from culturally entrusted, social reverence for tradition and heritage; theater federal status is the highest degree of accumulated recognition granted by the state.

name: Organizational age
definition: The age of a cultural organization, which signifies the preservation of tradition and thus proximity to the core values of audiences that revere organizations symbolizing tradition and professional continuity.

name: Artistic director celebrity
authors_terms: ["celebrity status of the artistic director", "celebrated artistic directors", "celebrity"]
definition: Professional acclaim and popularity espoused by a theater's artistic director, recognized as a popular culture figure who makes regular appearances in television shows, films, or TV series.

name: Professional award nominations
authors_terms: ["number of recent professional award nominations of the cast members", "cast member nominations", "total nominations"]
definition: The number of nominations received by a theater's cast members in the previous year for The Golden Mask, a national theater award and associated professional festival of theatrical arts, the most prestigious of all in the Russian Federation.

name: Corporate benefaction
definition: Whether a cultural organization obtains a corporate benefactor in a given year, operationalized as a binary variable indicating the presence or absence of corporate support in each theater each year.

name: Political orientation
definition: The public display of political sympathies by a cultural organization, differentiated into three levels: progovernment (strong support of the Russian government highlighted repeatedly in public interviews and actions), neutral (no explicit political orientation), and critical (consistent public criticism of the Russian government and current political system, and participation in opposition campaigns and social activism).

name: Openness to stakeholder involvement
authors_terms: ["openness to stakeholder involvement", "board of trustees", "presence of a board of trustees"]
definition: The degree of engagement of cultural organizations with stakeholders beyond potential donors, proxied by the presence of a board of trustees.

name: CEO-CFO language style matching
definition: LSM reflects the degree to which two people match each other's use of function words. 'Function words' (e.g., pronouns, propositions, articles) differ from content words in that function words reflect how people speak, whereas 'content words' (e.g., nouns, regular verbs, adjectives) capture what people say.

name: CFO compensation
definition: CFO compensation is typically determined by boards' compensation committees, but CEOs, who typically serve on their firms' boards and evaluate CFO performance, can also influence it.

name: CFO board membership
definition: A board seat at the CFO's focal firm. Board seats provide top managers with additional power and influence, and CFOs are less frequently granted board seats in their firms than are CEOs.

name: CEO power
definition: A CEO's ability to influence CFO-related personal outcomes hinges on the power that the CEO can exercise relative to board members, and powerful CEOs can impose strong influences not only on firm strategic decisions but also on board composition.

name: M&A intensity
definition: The firm's merger and acquisition activity, which the authors choose as their empirical context because M&As require active participation from both CEOs and CFOs, and which they measure with the number of M&As and the value of M&As.

name: Acquisition payment method
authors_terms: ["payment method", "percentage of cash payment", "percentage of cash (as opposed to stock)"]
definition: An acquiring firm typically has two ways to pay a target firm: cash and stock. Payment with stock implies that any risk involved in the deal is shared with the target firm's investors.

name: Investor reactions to M&A announcements
authors_terms: ["investor reactions to M&A announcements", "announcement returns", "stock market reactions"]
definition: Investors' reactions to a firm's M&A announcements, measured with cumulative abnormal returns - the returns over the event window minus the normal returns.

name: Foreign product market competition
authors_terms: ["foreign competition", "product market competition", "foreign product market competition", "competitive pressure from abroad", "competitive pressure that U.S. companies face from their foreign rivals"]
definition: The competitive pressure that domestic companies face from their foreign rivals, which the authors argue increases sharply when large import tariff reductions facilitate the entry of foreign competitors into local markets.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "social performance", "KLD index", "social and environmental practices", "social engagement"]
definition: An activity is considered to be socially responsible if it goes beyond the firm's maximization of its (single) bottom line and legal requirements and contributes to the social good.

name: Business-to-consumer sector
authors_terms: ["B2C sector", "business-to-consumer (B2C) sector", "companies selling to individual customers"]
definition: Companies selling to individual customers, as opposed to companies selling to industrial buyers; individual consumers are more responsive to companies' CSR engagement than industrial buyers, reflecting inherent differences in the purchasing decision-making process.

name: Inventor past performance
definition: Simple patent counts and citation-weighted patent counts were used as performance measures; insofar as a patent signifies novelty, the count measures the amount of novel knowledge created, and the citation-weighted count measures the quality-adjusted knowledge created. For measures of past performance, patent stock was constructed by cumulating the number of patents or citations up to period t-1.

name: Brokerage
definition: Actors are in a brokering position when they provide the only connection between two actors. Thus, any flow of information, knowledge, or products from one actor to another necessarily passes through the brokering actor.

name: Nonredundant collaboration tie formation
authors_terms: ["nonredundant tie", "new collaboration tie", "collaboration tie that increases brokerage"]
definition: Conditional on collaboration, three types of tie formation are possible: collaborating with an existing tie (a 'repeating tie'), collaborating with an inventor new to the focal inventor but linked to existing collaborators (a 'redundant tie'), and collaborating with an inventor new to everyone in the ego network (a 'nonredundant tie').

name: Inventor innovative performance
definition: Innovation is a knowledge-intensive activity, which builds upon identifying, acquiring, assimilating, and combining knowledge; patents are widely used to measure knowledge and technological innovation.

name: TMT agreement about decision-process comprehensiveness
authors_terms: ["TMT agreement", "agreement about the comprehensiveness of the strategic decision process", "TMT consensus", "agreement"]
definition: Agreement reflects a shared understanding of the decision-making process, which, in turn, reduces uncertainty and allows participants to focus on the substance of their decisions. In focusing on TMT agreement about a critical feature of the process, the authors investigate the extent to which executives agree in describing how their firm typically makes such decisions.

name: Strategic decision process comprehensiveness
authors_terms: ["comprehensiveness", "comprehensiveness of the strategic decision process", "comprehensiveness of the decision process"]
definition: Comprehensiveness is 'the extent to which an organization is exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions' (Fredrickson, 1984: 447), and it is regularly cited as a critical characteristic of strategic decision processes.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Return on assets (ROA), defined as net income before extraordinary items divided by total assets, was used as the measure of firm performance.

name: Past performance
definition: Past performance was calculated as a 5-year average ROA and includes the five consecutive years prior to and including the year the scenario-questionnaire instrument was administered.

name: Environmental stability
definition: A variety of measures (Dess and Beard, 1984) established that the environments of these industries were highly stable (paints and coatings) or highly unstable (forest products) during the study period.

name: Organizational size
definition: The log of the total number of employees was used as the measure of organizational size because most size measures (e.g., employees and assets) tend to be highly correlated.

name: TMT size
authors_terms: ["TMT size", "size of the top management team", "size of the team"]
definition: The size of the team was the total number of executives, including the CEO, that had been identified to participate during discussions with the CEO.

name: TMT organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["TMT tenure", "average organizational tenure", "average tenure", "mean number of years service"]
definition: Length of service, defined as the number of years an individual has worked for an organization, is the common definition of organizational tenure.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["poor firm performance", "performance", "total shareholder return (TSR)", "TSR change rate"]
definition: Firm performance in the main analysis is expressed as the average change rate of total shareholder return (TSR), operationalized as the firm's total return to shareholders (stock price changes and dividends) adjusted for industry effects.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: A dummy variable that is coded 1 in case of a CEO dismissal in a given year and 0 when there was either no CEO succession event or a routine succession event (voluntary turnover). Only those cases were classified as dismissals where clear signs of disagreement between the departing CEO and the supervisory board or controlling shareholders could be identified.

name: CEO relative status
authors_terms: ["CEO relative status", "social status", "relative social status of the CEO vis-a-vis the COB"]
definition: The number of outside directorships of the focal firm's CEO for each year under study relative to the number of outside board seats of the focal firm's COB. Outside directorships act as a source of status and intraboard power for the CEO.

name: Board network outsiders
authors_terms: ["board network outsiders", "board network outsiders who serve on the supervisory board"]
definition: The extent to which board members are board network outsiders reflects the proportion of the focal firm's supervisory board members who do not hold seats on other boards.

name: Turnover rate
definition: Turnover rates capture the departure of employees from an organization; higher turnover creates aggregate firm-specific in-role performance deficits and is part of a more generic problem of organizational control that lowers in-role performance.

name: In-role performance losses
authors_terms: ["in-role performance losses", "human capital losses", "in-role performance deficits"]
definition: The aggregate firm-specific in-role performance deficits that a workforce incurs through turnover; under the human capital view, higher levels of in-role performance are the outcome of human capital accumulations, so turnover lowers workforce in-role performance.

name: Social capital losses
authors_terms: ["social capital losses", "loss of structural hole bridges", "network disruptions"]
definition: Losses of organizational social capital through turnover, viewed at the collective level as the loss of structural hole bridges: if social capital at the collective level is created when relationships facilitate instrumental action among people, it is also lost when these relationships among people are dissolved, and the loss through turnover of employees who bridge many otherwise open communication links should be especially damaging.

name: Network density
definition: The number of relationships in a group relative to the number of possible relationships. At the sociological level, density provides an estimate of the number of redundant relationships in a network.

name: Store performance
authors_terms: ["store performance", "productivity", "sales per employee", "change in productivity", "change in sales"]
definition: Store-level performance of the restaurant units, focused on sales or revenue; sales is a critical performance outcome in service industries and high-customer-contact settings, as well as in highly competitive environments such as the restaurant industry.

name: Inside view forecasting
definition: A view that emphasizes a detailed comparison of the decision problem with a small number of source analogies (often one), in contrast to an outside view, which is a statistical and historical view of the problem that focuses on aspects generalizable to multiple cases.

name: Expected return
authors_terms: ["expected rate of return", "expected returns", "estimated mean return"]
definition: The rate of return participants expect for the investment project under review, stated after the inside view instructions and revisited as a revised estimate after the outside view.

name: Similarity-based forecasting
definition: SBF grafts the distribution-based reference class of reference class forecasting onto the similarity-based weighting of case-based decision theory; it rests on an unbiased reference class of similar cases and an endogenous method of assigning more weight to the most similar cases in the reference class.

name: Forecasting accuracy
definition: How closely a forecasting model's predictions match actual outcomes; in the paper forecasting accuracy was measured by the mean absolute relative error summed over all previous cases.

name: Multinational diversity
authors_terms: ["multinational diversity", "diversity of the countries to which it has expanded"]
definition: The extent to which a firm operates within diverse national markets, measured by the number of foreign countries the firm had entered at the time of the expansion.

name: Product diversity
authors_terms: ["product diversity", "diversity of the firm's product lines"]
definition: The extent to which a firm operates within diverse product markets, measured by the number of three-digit SIC codes in which the firm was active at the time of expansion.

name: Business relatedness of expansion
authors_terms: ["horizontal, related, and vertical expansions", "unrelated expansions", "expansion type"]
definition: How closely a foreign expansion is related to the firm's existing business: horizontal if within the same three-digit SIC category as the firm's core business activities, related if within the same two-digit SIC category but not the same three-digit category, vertical if within the firm's value-added chain, and unrelated if none of the above three categories applied.

name: Foreign entry mode
authors_terms: ["mode of foreign entry", "propensity of a firm to set up a new venture in a foreign country rather than to acquire an existing company", "propensity to expand through start-ups rather than acquisitions"]
definition: Whether a firm enters a foreign country by setting up a new venture (start-up) or by acquiring an existing company (acquisition).

name: Goal configuration
authors_terms: ["goal configuration", "goal concentration", "goal dispersion", "concentrated goal configuration", "dispersed goal configuration"]
definition: An organizational goal is defined as 'a desired state of affairs which the organization attempts to realize as espoused by top management.' The term goal configuration refers to the scope or breadth of the goals of the organization; goal configuration options range from concentrated, emphasizing a single goal or objective, to dispersed, where the firm emphasizes a comprehensive set of goals.

name: Firm nationality
definition: Firm nationality was operationalized as the firm's country-of-origin. National culture is often thought to influence the way that the environment is interpreted, resulting in different strategic responses by organizations in different country locations.

name: Industry position
definition: Within a global industry, the firm may strategically position itself in different industry segments: a global segment, in which industry forces span national boundaries thereby requiring the firm to 'integrate its activities on a worldwide basis'; a multidomestic segment which allows for differentiated strategic approaches across country locations; or a multifocal segment in which the firm simultaneously responds to local market conditions in each country while integrating activities worldwide.

name: Firm internationalization
definition: Firm internationalization was defined by the percentage of total sales that are earned abroad.

name: Breadth of rewards/compensation criteria
definition: The scope or breadth of the rewards/compensation criteria in relation to the goal configuration of the firm was the compensation dimension of interest in this study: if the firm is pursuing multiple goals, the reward structure should be based on multiple criteria, while a concentrated goal configuration would link compensation to a single performance outcome.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance was operationalized with three self-reported measures: after-tax return on assets, sales growth rate and a subjective measure of the firm's global performance over the last 3 years as compared to other firms in the industry in their country.
