Self-reported measures were necessary as secondary data were not consistently available or comparable for the three country locations.

name: Emerging strategy incorporation
definition: We use institutional support to underscore how these process mechanisms establish the conditions of change and the elements available for incorporation. We reintroduce the term incorporation in preference to the more common term 'adoption' because we focus on the external environment linkages of organizational elements and the distinctive processes that make emerging strategies available.

name: Dominant logic consistency
definition: Organizations typically operate according to a 'dominant logic' that summarizes the firm's strategic orientation to change and innovation opportunities and reflects its history of resolving prior crises. A dominant logic ('how we do this') guides resource allocation, sets the terms of organizational politics, and establishes routines and capabilities that create precedent for further innovation.

name: External rationalized charter
authors_terms: ["external rationalized charters", "rationalized external charters", "field-level external charter", "charters"]
definition: A field-level charter specified by authoritative experts establishes prototype strategies that come complete with theorized virtues and value and make possible elaboration and implementation of available emerging strategies. By charters, Meyer identified 'attributes of an organization's relation to its environmental context, not its internal structure'.

name: Fieldwide emulation
authors_terms: ["fieldwide emulation", "fieldwide counts", "total count of prior incorporations"]
definition: Standard diffusion research in organization studies initially focused on fieldwide counts as an indicator of the general legitimacy of a structure or strategy. These studies suggest prior incorporations confer legitimacy on emerging strategies and have a diffusely positive effect on the subsequent spread (or abandonment) of strategies.

name: Segment-specific emulation
definition: We contend that segment-specific processes affect incorporation. In the terrain of a field, 'location' matters, and this proximity can be spatial, social, and cognitive.

name: Identity-based emulation
definition: Common identity categorizations are another way that emulation processes can work. Key categories of identity for organizations are economic sector and governance mode, associated with different kinds of accountability mechanisms and resource streams; the authors argue that common governance mode provides an identity category that further facilitates emulation.

name: Interpartner trust
authors_terms: ["interpartner trust", "trust in ISAs", "ISA trust", "interpartner trust in an ISA"]
definition: Interpartner trust in an ISA concerns the willingness of a venturing firm's management to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations about the counterpart's intentions or behavior. The authors view beliefs and behaviors as separate facets or dimensions of a higher-order trust construct, proposing a third-order conceptualization of interpartner trust.

name: Alliance performance
definition: The authors conceptualize and validate ISA performance as a higher-order construct comprising effectiveness, the extent to which ISA goals and objectives are achieved; efficiency, the ratio of ISA performance outcomes to the inputs required to achieve them; and responsiveness, the ability of the ISA to adapt to environmental change.

name: Alliance size
definition: Alliance size distinguishes between small/intimate and large/bureaucratic alliances and is assessed by the number of full-time employees in the alliance. Size is associated with bureaucratic structuring and has a bearing on the nature and effects of organizational complexity in these businesses.

name: Distributive fairness
authors_terms: ["distributive fairness", "distributive fairness of the ISA arrangement"]
definition: Distributive fairness refers to a venturing firm's perceptions concerning the fairness of its earnings and other outcomes from alliance interactions. In ISAs it refers to the extent to which interparty sharing of monetary and nonmonetary rewards of collaboration is fair in view of each partner's contribution as well as its assumption of responsibility, risk, and burden.

name: Partner similarity
definition: Partner similarity describes the extent to which the partners overlap on strategic and organizational dimensions relevant to venturing success; it reflects the co-collaborators' organizational and strategic compatibility.

name: Employee access to paid family leave benefits
authors_terms: ["employee access to state PFL benefits", "employee PFL access", "access to state-provided PFL benefits", "state PFL programs"]
definition: State-sponsored paid family leave programs provide employees with a layer of financial security when they need time off to take care of a family member or a newborn. The New Jersey program makes eligible employees eligible for up to 6 weeks of PFL per year in the form of partial wage replacements to care for an ill relative or bond with a new child.

name: Venture profitability
definition: To measure venture performance, the author uses venture profitability. Profitability requires the firm not only to create value but also to capture the value it creates; it is directly related to the firm's competitive advantage.

name: Venture innovation type
authors_terms: ["venture innovation type", "venture innovativeness", "innovative versus noninnovative ventures", "high-tech"]
definition: The distinction between innovative and noninnovative ventures is crucial because they differ in startup processes, human capital strategies, and subsequent outcomes. Innovative ventures tend to demand and hire more knowledge workers with specialized industry experience and high levels of human capital.

name: Employment in key job functions
authors_terms: ["Number of Key Employees", "number of individuals responsible for key job functions", "employment for key job functions"]
definition: Number of Key Employees represents the total number of individuals responsible for key job functions and responsibilities and allows the author to examine whether employment growth or attrition in these areas occurs posttreatment.

name: Work time by owner-operators
definition: Work Time by Owner-Operators, the average number of weekly work hours for active owner-operators essential to business operations, is used as a proxy for how much people work in the absence of data on employee work time.

name: Average payroll expenses per employee
authors_terms: ["Average Payroll Expenses per Employee", "average payroll expenses"]
definition: Average Payroll Expenses per Employee represents the total payroll expenses on employee wages and benefits divided by the total number of employees.

name: Employee productivity
definition: Average Revenue per Employee equals total outputs (revenue from selling goods and services) divided by the total number of employees; this variable proxies for employee-level productivity.

name: Absorption of new venture technologies
authors_terms: ["absorption of new venture technologies", "absorbing new venture technologies", "absorb", "build on new venture technologies"]
definition: We considered a focal incumbent firm to have absorbed the focal new venture technology/patent when the focal incumbent firm used this technology in its own inventive pursuits.

name: Corporate venture capital investment
definition: A primary motivation for incumbents taking a minority stake in privately held entrepreneurial firms is to gain a window into the novel technologies of these ventures that they would not otherwise have. We used a continuous measure based on the cumulative investment that the focal incumbent firm had made in the focal new venture for each year.

name: Network clustering
definition: The structure of an inventor network can be characterized in part by its level of clustering. Clustering addresses the extent to which the collaborators of any given inventor are themselves directly tied to each other.

name: Network connectedness
definition: Connectedness is the extent to which inventors are tied directly or indirectly to every other inventor in the network.

name: Pre-buyout diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["pre-buyout diversification strategy", "pre-buyout diversification type", "initial diversification strategy"]
definition: Each firm's diversity type was classified for the pre-buyout period as single business; related business, where some common skills or resources are shared by the different businesses; unrelated business, where the firm engages in two distinct and unrelated lines of business; or conglomerate, where the firm engages in more than two unrelated lines of business. The classification scheme is derived from Rumelt's (1974) typology.

name: Post-buyout diversification strategy
definition: The diversification strategy type of the firm in the post-buyout period, classified with the same scheme as the pre-buyout classification. Firms that moved from a higher to a lower diversification type are described as having considerably focused their activities.

name: Buyout specialist participation
authors_terms: ["buyout specialist participation", "participation by a buyout specialist", "specialist-associated MBOs", "independent MBOs"]
definition: A buyout specialist derives the ability to be in the MBO business from the buyout fund it raises, and this fund is used to finance equity purchases in the buyout target; these specialists are important stakeholders in the post-buyout firm by virtue of their equity ownership and their control over the fund. Firms that underwent the MBO with the assistance of a buyout specialist are specialist-associated, while the remaining firms underwent the MBO without the participation of a buyout specialist (the 'independent' MBOs).

name: Buyout longevity
authors_terms: ["the time period under private ownership", "longevity of private ownership", "number of months under the MBO organizational form", "buyout longevity"]
definition: The period of time the buyout unit that makes the strategic decisions remains under private ownership, measured as the number of months under the MBO organizational form.

name: Debt service difficulty
authors_terms: ["payment difficulties", "difficulties servicing their debt", "financial distress", "status of debt obligations"]
definition: Difficulties in managing and fulfilling the debt obligations of the buyout, indicated by further financial restructuring (renegotiating or exchanging debt) and/or bankruptcy; the authors use the term 'failure' to refer to outcomes associated with further financial restructuring and/or bankruptcy.

name: Collaboration
definition: Our dependent variable, Collaboration, is a binary variable equal to one for each M&A lawyer dyad assigned to work on a focal M&A mandate and zero if the dyad was unassigned.

name: Prior collaboration
definition: Our baseline independent variable Prior Collaboration is computed as a binary variable equal to one if a lawyer dyad was assigned on another M&A mandate worked on by the law firm within the prior 24 months and zero otherwise.

name: Individual-level relationship with client
authors_terms: ["Individual-Level Relationship with Client", "individual-level external relational capital"]
definition: Individual-Level Relationship with Client captures the lawyer dyad's total prior experience working on M&A mandates for the focal client, which we measure as the sum of the number of prior M&A mandates each lawyer in the dyad has worked on for the focal client.

name: Firm-level relationship with client
authors_terms: ["Firm-Level Relationship with Client", "firm-level external relational capital"]
definition: Firm-Level Relationship with Client captures the firm's prior experience with the focal client, which we calculate as the number of prior M&A mandates the focal law firm has previously advised the client on, independent of the particular lawyers staffed on the deal.

name: Client status
definition: Client Status is a binary variable equal to one if the focal client is a FTSE 100 company listed on the London Stock Exchange and zero otherwise.

name: Switching proclivity
authors_terms: ["Switching Proclivity", "client proclivity to switch business between firms"]
definition: Switching Proclivity captures the degree to which clients distribute their M&A legal work among many different law firms as opposed to fewer.

name: Individual-level resource constraint
definition: Individual-Level Resource Constraint captures the capacity constraint of the lawyers in the dyad because of their workload at the time of the deal.

name: Firm-level resource constraint
definition: Firm-Level Resource Constraint is measured as the size of the focal firm's portfolio of clients. A larger portfolio of clients presents greater resource management complexity and resource constraint.

name: Private scope in public–private collaborations
authors_terms: ["private scope", "private scope in PPPs", "degree of private scope"]
definition: By the notion of private scope in PPPs, the authors refer to the structure and division of resource allocation and production activities along the various stages of the value chain and the interdependencies between these different activities. Private scope thereby covers a set of sequential value-creating activities in the partnership, such as asset design, building, leasing, and subsequent operations.

name: Public capabilities in public–private collaboration
authors_terms: ["public capabilities", "public capabilities in public–private collaboration", "public sector capabilities"]
definition: Public capabilities in PPPs pertain to the more specific set of abilities, skills, and routines of public agencies in crafting and implementing cross-sector collaboration, identified through experience-based attributes and governance-based attributes.

name: Private capabilities in public–private collaboration
authors_terms: ["private capabilities", "private capabilities in public–private collaboration", "private sector capabilities"]
definition: Private capabilities in public–private collaboration are the well-established abilities of private organizational actors to originate, develop, structure, govern, and execute public–private collaboration, based on prior partnering experience and on the establishment of specialized structures.

name: Quality of national institutions
authors_terms: ["quality of national institutions", "quality of institutions", "quality of the local institutional environment", "institutional quality"]
definition: The authors define the institutional environment as the set of stable rules that increase transparency, efficiency, and regulatory commitment in the public sector. A low-quality institutional environment is a weak institutional framework with unstable rules of law, lack of transparency, 'red tape,' and corruption.

name: Founder-CEO presence
definition: The presence of a company founder as CEO following a company's initial public offering, argued to be a sociopolitical transformational shield.

name: CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO ownership", "proportion of outstanding stock owned by a company's CEO", "CEO-retained ownership"]
definition: The proportion of outstanding stock owned by a company's CEO upon completion of its IPO, which provides the CEO with power and discretion within the firm.

name: Venture capitalist ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["venture capitalist ownership concentration", "concentrated ownership of stock by venture capitalists"]
definition: The degree to which a large proportion of an IPO firm's shares is concentrated in the hands of one or a few venture capitalists following the IPO.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["average management team tenure", "average tenure of a firm's top management team"]
definition: How much experience a top management team's members have working together at the time of an IPO, an indicator that they can function together effectively as a team and a source of internal social capital.

name: Deal network embeddedness
definition: The degree to which the relationships in an IPO deal network are embedded rather than arm's length, which depends on the frequency and the concentration of transactions between the actors involved and reflects the lead underwriter's prior transactions with the institutional investors placed in the deal.

name: IPO firm failure
definition: A firm's failure during the five years following its IPO, defined as delisting from the primary exchange on which a firm traded with a delisting code between 500 and 585.

name: Atypicality
definition: Organizations that differ in some way from the prototype of a category are then atypical; they are ill-fitting representatives of a category. Because borrowing elements from other distinct categories may result in a combination of features that would not normally be expected to go together, boundary spanning reduces similarity to a category prototype and thus increases atypicality.

name: Accountability
definition: We define accountability as whether an individual's decisions are monitored and they expect to have to justify their choices to others. People's felt accountability, their perception of accountability, rather than an objective accountability mechanism imposed upon them, drives behavior.

name: Appeal
definition: In line with prior research on categories, we define our dependent variable (DV) as appeal. One key difference between this measure and prior research that uses observational data is that this is an ex-ante evaluation rather than an ex post evaluation in which audience members experience or consume an organization's products.

name: Audience preferences
authors_terms: ["audience preferences", "preferences of the evaluator's audience", "others' preferences", "explicit audience preferences"]
definition: When the evaluator's audience's preferences are explicit, meaning that evaluators know what their audience prefers. The moderating effect of accountability is likely contingent upon the content of these preferences, whether an evaluator's audience prefers typical or atypical organizations.

name: Extramarket performance
authors_terms: ["extramarket performance", "X-Perf", "Change in Extramarket Performance", "extramarket returns", "product rent"]
definition: Extramarket performance (X-Perf) can be thought of as returns that exceed those normally achieved in the marketplace; the authors define 'extramarket performance' as the return to a horizontally merged product after controlling for industry- and population-level effects.

name: Horizontal merger
definition: Horizontal mergers are undeniably disruptive events that abruptly bring together firms and their respective sets of products and organizational attributes, and to strategy scholars the term 'horizontal' implies a high level of relatedness between firms.

name: Merger relatedness
definition: Cases are considered specialist related when the product of one firm (be it the buying or acquired firm) is in the same product 'family' or resource space as a product from the other firm; cases that involve branded food products from different product families are generalist.

name: Relative market share
definition: Since the PIMS studies of the early 1980s, strategists have argued that high share is associated with cost-based and revenue-enhancing synergies and market power; high-share products are more legitimate than low-share products and, consequently, should better capitalize on the changes in market structure that accompany a horizontal merger.

name: Merger-specific effects
definition: Each merger is unique, bringing together firms with different products, resources and capabilities, history, and core organizational features; Hypothesis 1c predicts that no two mergers are alike due to various administrative, resource, and cultural factors.

name: Premerger niche competitiveness
authors_terms: ["premerger structure", "marketpower effects", "premerger market conditions", "ex ante market forces"]
definition: IO's 'market power' hypothesis posits that the less competitive the structure of any given industry, the more horizontal mergers will improve a firm's market power (i.e., the firm's ability to set prices); imperfections in the extant structure of a given market allow merged firms to earn extramarket product returns.

name: Initial market concentration
definition: Concentration is the percentage of the market that is controlled by its largest inhabitants; the authors defined the level of market concentration before the merger, or Initial Market Concentration, as sales (in tons) of the top two products in each product category during 1983 divided by the total tonnage sold in that market niche in 1983 (including tons sold of private-label products).

name: Initial market density
definition: Most ecologists define intensity of competition in terms of density (the number of businesses competing in a product-market niche), and use density as a measure of the degree to which the carrying capacity of the niche is filled; Initial Market Density is a count of the number of different brands listed by SAMI in each product category during 1983.

name: Postmerger niche competitiveness
authors_terms: ["postmerger market forces", "merger-induced competitive changes", "ex post influences", "the less competitive the niche becomes after the merger"]
definition: The authors contrast the 'fixed' ex ante (premerger) conditions with the change in competitive conditions after the merger, noting that postmerger performance can be altered by unanticipated changes in the business climate and by rival firms that try to extract rents during the period of market adjustment.

name: Change in market concentration
definition: The Change in Concentration measure was computed by subtracting the Initial Market Concentration (1983) from that computed in 1985; the same was done for each subsequent postmerger year (1986-90).

name: Change in market density
definition: Six Change in Density measures were likewise computed, using Initial Market Density (1983) as the baseline.

name: Market growth
authors_terms: ["Market Growth", "growth in demand", "growth in a niche"]
definition: Ecologists and strategists note that change in the demand characteristics of a product-market niche influences competition; the authors computed six Market Growth measures by subtracting sales (in tons) observed for each product-market niche for each of the six postmerger years (1985-90) from the sales of that niche in 1983.

name: Protest scale
authors_terms: ["protest scale", "Feminist protest scale", "scale of street protests", "local protest scale", "protest size"]
definition: "We define [protest scale] as the total reported number of participants in community protests that occur during a given time period. Conceptually, this construct reflects both the number of participants in each event ... and the number of events that occur."

name: Business alignment with protest goals
authors_terms: ["business alignment", "align itself with the protest goals", "aligning their business with it", "appointment of new female directors"]
definition: The authors focus on whether firms appointed new female directors to their governing boards following the protests, because "this highly visible practice could help organizations better align themselves with the broad protest goal of increasing gender equity in society."

name: Community political ideology
authors_terms: ["Conservative state", "blue/red states", "community's dominant political ideology", "sociopolitical values of the community"]
definition: The community's prevailing sociopolitical values, preferences, and expectations, captured by state-level electoral results: "these labels signify general conservative or liberal identities that map onto polarized attitudes toward a range of social issues, lifestyles, and consumer products."

name: Organizational diversity climate
authors_terms: ["Diversity climate", "Gender diversity climate", "internal organizational alignment with protest goals"]
definition: An index of each firm's diversity climate built from employees' evaluations of their firm's working conditions, including diversity and inclusion, which the authors use as "a reflection of each firm's internal alignment with the Women's March protest goals."

name: CEO overcompensation
definition: The notion of overcompensation is relative: higher performers deserve higher compensation, and talent scarcity in some industries justifies more attractive packages. CEO overcompensation is a deviation from a norm that signals excessive remuneration levels.

name: Corporate philanthropy
definition: Corporate philanthropy is 'defined as voluntary and unconditional transfers of cash or other assets by private firms for public purposes' and 'involves the allocation of time, money, or goods aimed at addressing a social need'. It 'signals a willingness to act altruistically (other considering) as opposed to purely agonistically (self considering)'.

name: Media disapproval
authors_terms: ["media disapproval", "media disapproval of CEO overcompensation", "negative media evaluations", "negative evaluations"]
definition: Our dependent variable captures the media's negative evaluations of firms' CEO pay (hereafter, media disapproval). In the remainder of the paper, we write 'media disapproval' to refer to 'media disapproval of CEO overcompensation'.

name: Board size
authors_terms: ["board size", "larger boards of directors", "size of the board"]
definition: We used data on hospital board structure and composition to develop measures of board size and board diversity. We determined the total number of directors listed as active members on the board of directors.

name: Board diversity
authors_terms: ["board diversity", "more diverse boards of directors", "diversity of board membership", "occupationally diverse boards"]
definition: We developed a measure of board diversity that reflects differences in occupational or professional backgrounds (Kosnik, 1990).

name: Board outsider representation
authors_terms: ["board outside representation", "proportion of outsiders on the board", "percentage of outsiders on board"]
definition: We included a measure of the total proportion of outsiders on the board. We computed the proportion of total board membership held by outsiders. We distinguished between hospital management and physicians (insiders) and all other board members (outsiders).

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "strategic changes in medical services", "service additions", "service divestitures", "service reorganizations"]
definition: We examined three distinct types of strategic changes in medical services: service additions, service divestitures and service reorganizations. Changes in the scope and organization of services represent one of the most fundamental strategic responses to environmental contingencies.

name: External scientific knowledge
definition: External knowledge is knowledge generated outside of the organization. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on the external knowledge items revealed two distinct factors, one of which is external scientific knowledge.

name: External industrial knowledge
definition: External knowledge is knowledge generated outside of the organization. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on the external knowledge items revealed two distinct factors, one of which is external industrial knowledge.

name: Structural holes
authors_terms: ["structural holes", "network rich in structural holes", "brokering position", "brokerage"]
definition: For each individual in the sample structural holes are expressed as a decreasing function of the extent to which his/her relationships are embedded in a dense system of common third-party ties; 1 - constraint indicates network rich in structural holes.

name: Individual innovativeness
definition: The number of patents generated by respondents and granted by the USPTO represents the study's dependent variable, capturing individuals' ability to generate innovations.

name: Status inconsistency
authors_terms: ["status inconsistency", "status inconsistency of a business school", "BS status inconsistency"]
definition: Status inconsistency refers to the extent to which social actors occupy unequally ranked status positions accorded different amounts of prestige in different social systems. The status inconsistency of a business school refers to the extent to which the status of the accounting, finance, management, marketing, and operations departments differ.

name: Department status
authors_terms: ["department status", "status of department i", "academic department status"]
definition: Status is defined by the hierarchical position social actors occupy in a particular social system. Following prior status research, the status of an academic department depends on the status of the departments with which it exchanges PhD students, as captured by centrality in the PhD exchange network.

name: Business school status
definition: The status of a business school refers to its rank among other business schools. Focusing on research performance, the relevant ranking is based on the academic accomplishments of the faculty and doctoral students at the business schools, captured by centrality in the PhD exchange network.

name: Research performance
definition: We define business school performance in terms of research performance not because teaching performance is unimportant, but because research performance, as indicated by publications in top academic journals, is more directly comparable across business schools. We define research performance in terms of academic journal publications.

name: Founder-joiner gender match
authors_terms: ["same-gender founder", "gender homophily", "different gender combinations", "founder-joiner gender match"]
definition: Whether the joiner works with a founder of the same rather than a different gender; the authors conjecture that gender homophily between founders and joiners improves social identification and strengthens the founder's influence on employees' choice to follow a similar career path.

name: Joiner's transition to entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["propensity to start an entrepreneurial career", "transition to entrepreneurship", "decision to become an entrepreneur", "entrepreneurial career choice"]
definition: A joiner's decision to become a founder of a new firm after leaving the startup firm where he or she was employed.

name: Joiner gender
definition: Joiners are distinguished as female or male employees, and the authors argue that same-gender founders may play different roles and fulfill different needs for male and female joiners.

name: Female founder
definition: The founder of the new venture is a woman; female founders able to counteract gendered mental models can legitimize female entrepreneurship and be a more important source of mentoring for other women.

name: Founder performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the founder as an entrepreneur", "firm performance relative to the industry", "relatively high-performing firms"]
definition: The founder's performance as an entrepreneur, which may signal reputation and legitimacy; high-performing role models or mentors can be especially influential in the career development of more junior individuals.

name: Founder-joiner social identification
authors_terms: ["social identification", "similarity on other individual attributes", "social proximity"]
definition: Social identification between founder and joiner tends to increase if individuals have multiple attributes in common and their social category is made more salient by means of numerical cues; mentoring functions are often more effective with increased social identification between mentor and mentee.

name: Entrepreneurship-relevant experience gaps
authors_terms: ["joiner's entrepreneurship-relevant experience gaps", "lack of exposure to entrepreneurship", "previous exposure to entrepreneurship"]
definition: The lack of direct or indirect entrepreneurial career previews, such as not having worked in a young firm and not having an entrepreneurial parent, which could have changed an individual's beliefs about or preferences for entrepreneurship.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "strategic category", "Wrigley/Rumelt categories", "Wrigley and Rumelt classifications"]
definition: From a management perspective the significance of diversification is the need to extend the skills of the firm and to adjust organization to encompass a wider range of activities. The key features of diversification are the extent of the firm's involvement in activities which draw upon different skills and the way in which new activities are related to old activities.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "profit performance", "return on net assets", "return on equity", "return on sales"]
definition: The profit performance of the firms, reported as average profitability by strategic category and used as the dependent variable in the regression analysis.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured by firm revenue (£ millions); LSIZE is the logarithm of SIZE.

name: Capital intensity
authors_terms: ["capital intensity", "fixed capital per employee", "fixed assets per employee"]
definition: Capital intensity is the value of fixed assets per employee (£ thousand).

name: Leverage
definition: Leverage is the debt/equity ratio, measured as total borrowings as a proportion of shareholders' funds.

name: Industry membership
definition: The broad SIC industry group to which a firm belongs. The authors argue that a firm's choice of diversification strategy is influenced by its industry environment and that related diversifiers tend to be in industries with high levels of investment in transferable core skills such as R&D and marketing.

name: Sales growth
definition: Growth of firm sales over the period 1972-84, reported as average sales growth by strategic category.

name: Headquarters rating of subsidiary capabilities
authors_terms: ["rating of the focal subsidiary's capabilities by HQ", "corporate manager's rating of the focal subsidiary's market orientation", "market orientation capabilities (corporate rating)"]
definition: Subsidiary capabilities were operationalized as market orientation, defined as the continuous collection of information about customers' needs and competitors' capabilities and the use of this information to create superior customer value. The corporate manager's rating is the headquarters executive's assessment of a focal subsidiary's market orientation.

name: Peer rating of subsidiary capabilities
authors_terms: ["rating of the focal subsidiary's capabilities by its peer units", "peers' rating about the market orientation of the focal subsidiary", "market orientation capabilities (peer rating)"]
definition: The peers' rating of a focal subsidiary's market orientation, obtained by asking each respondent unit to vote for the most capable subsidiary in collecting, distributing, and analyzing and acting on market information.

name: Self-rated subsidiary capabilities
authors_terms: ["self-rating of its own capabilities by the focal unit", "focal subsidiary's self-rating of its market orientation", "market orientation capabilities (self-rating)"]
definition: The focal subsidiary's own assessment of its market orientation, measured using Jaworski and Kohli's (1993) established index.

name: Vertical knowledge outflows
definition: The aggregate volume of know-how about new products, new services, and marketing best practices transmitted from the focal subsidiary to the MNC headquarters.

name: Vertical knowledge inflows
authors_terms: ["vertical knowledge inflows", "inflows from the MNC headquarters", "VKI"]
definition: The aggregate volume of know-how about new products, new services, and marketing best practices received from the MNC headquarters by the focal subsidiary.

name: Horizontal knowledge outflows
definition: The aggregate volume of know-how about new products, new services, and marketing best practices transmitted from the focal subsidiary to other subsidiaries.

name: Horizontal knowledge inflows
definition: The aggregate volume of know-how about new products, new services, and marketing best practices received from other subsidiaries by the focal subsidiary.

name: Communication with headquarters
authors_terms: ["frequency of communication with HQ", "communication with headquarters", "communication with HQ"]
definition: The frequency with which subsidiary respondents indicated how often they communicated with HQ managers, face-to-face and through other means, to discuss operations.

name: Communication with peer subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["frequency of communication with other subsidiaries", "communication with peer subsidiaries", "communication with subsidiaries"]
definition: The frequency with which subsidiary respondents indicated how often they communicated with peer subsidiaries, face-to-face and through other means, to discuss operations.

name: Subsidiary isolation
definition: Subsidiaries isolated from the knowledge-transfer activities within the MNC; to be an isolated subsidiary, the focal unit should be isolated both in terms of outflows and inflows, both horizontally and vertically.

name: Subsidiary performance
authors_terms: ["subsidiary performance", "relative financial performance", "subsidiary's relative financial performance"]
definition: The focal subsidiary's relative financial performance on overall sales revenue, overall market share, and operating profit, as rated by corporate respondents.

name: CEO generalist human capital
authors_terms: ["Generalist CEO", "generalist CEOs", "general managerial knowledge and skills", "nature of the CEO's human capital", "CEO General Ability Index"]
definition: The extent to which a CEO has gained general managerial knowledge and skills that are not specific to a particular industry, firm, or domain, with studies distinguishing generalists (a broader set of managerial knowledge and skills not specific to a particular industry, firm, or domain) from specialists (a narrower but deeper set of knowledge and skills more closely tied to a specific industry, firm, or domain).

name: Acquisitiveness
definition: The number of acquisitions a firm engaged in during a given year.

name: Unrelated acquisitions
authors_terms: ["unrelated acquisitions", "diversifying acquisitions", "acquisitions outside a firm's main industry", "Num Diversify", "D(Diversify)"]
definition: An acquisition is typically considered an unrelated acquisition if the target operates in a different industry from the acquirer; in unrelated acquisitions the acquirer and target are usually different in terms of their products, markets, or technology and the level of post-acquisition integration is typically low.

name: CEO-acquisition fit
authors_terms: ["Fit", "fit between the nature of the CEO's human capital and the type of acquisitions the CEO engages in"]
definition: The fit between the nature of the CEO's human capital and the type of acquisitions the CEO engages in, that is, generalist CEOs engaging in unrelated acquisitions and specialist CEOs engaging in related acquisitions.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: CARs reflect the market's sentiment and assessment of an acquisition at the time of the acquisition announcement, and they are widely used as a measure of acquisition performance.

name: Generalist board
authors_terms: ["Generalist board", "generalist board", "nature of the human capital of the firm's board of directors"]
definition: Whether the board was a Generalist board, using the same methodology as the Generalist CEO measure, based on the average knowledge and skills of independent board members; Generalist board is a continuous measure.

name: Firm attributes complementary to generalist CEOs
authors_terms: ["firm size", "firm diversification", "firm acquisition experience", "firm-level attributes that may be complementary to the generalist CEO dimension"]
definition: Firm-side attributes that the authors argue may enhance the value of generalist CEOs, who in turn will prefer managing firms with such capabilities: larger firms and diversified firms typically involve more complex operations, coordination, and decisions, and the prior acquisition experience of the firm is more likely to be relevant to executives who aim to engage in acquisitions.

name: Corporate refocusing
definition: By this we mean the voluntary or involuntary reduction in the diversification of U.S. firms-usually, but not necessarily, achieved through major divestitures-what Bhagat, Shleifer, and Vishny (1990) call 'the return to corporate specialization'.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Profitability (DROS) = The firm's ROS minus its industry-weighted ROS. ROS is measured from Compustat as operating income before depreciation and interest as a percent of sales.

name: Over-diversification
definition: The authors argue that there is an optimal limit to how much firms can diversify, so that firms which diversify beyond their limit have 'excessive' diversification levels; the over-diversified firms are those we would expect to find diversified beyond their optimal level.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification", "diversification level", "entropy index of diversification (DT)", "Rumelt's strategic categories"]
definition: Each firm's diversification was measured by its entropy index of diversification (DT), calculated in the manner shown by Palepu (1985), and firms were also placed in their Rumelt (1974) strategic category in 1981 and 1987.

name: Disruptive know-how
definition: We define acquired disruptive know-how as the know-how of the acquired firm that has the potential to generate novel solutions and may threaten the acquirer's competitive position in one of its main lines of business. Acquired nondisruptive know-how is the know-how of an acquired firm that has the potential to incrementally improve-and thus be nonthreatening to-an acquirer's existing solutions and enable the acquirer to maintain its current technology and product portfolio.

name: Preserved integration
definition: Preserved integration refers to keeping the acqui-hired team together as a whole group by moving/recombining the group into a particular business unit following the acquisition, whereas dispersed integration refers to dismantling the team and allocating the team members to multiple business units.

name: Founder high status position
authors_terms: ["high status position", "High Status Position", "founder's position status"]
definition: In integrating the acqui-hired founder, the acquirer may allocate the founder to either a high status position such as Vice President or Senior Research Director, or to a lower status position such as Software Engineer or Lab Scientist. We label high status positions as those that include managerial/executive positions (e.g., Vice President) as well as nonmanagerial senior level positions (e.g., Senior Research Scientist).

name: Premature exit of acqui-hired founders
authors_terms: ["premature exit", "Premature Exit of Acqui-hired Founders", "early departure", "premature founder exit"]
definition: We define premature exit as the exit of the acqui-hired founder from the acquiring firm within a year after the acquisition. This is a conservative measure of premature exit as acqui-hired founders agree to time vested contracts that require them to stay with the acquiring firm for a predetermined period of time.

name: Acqui-hire team integration misfit
authors_terms: ["lack of acqui-hire team integration fit", "Disruptive know-how & Preserved Integration Misfit", "misfit", "lack of fit"]
definition: Building on H1, we define a lack of fit (i.e., ineffective integration) as the scenario in which there is disruptive know-how and dispersed integration. We use the absolute values of the residuals of the regression of disruptive know-how on preserved integration to indicate the lack of fit (i.e., misfit).

name: Acqui-hire founder integration misfit
authors_terms: ["lack of acqui-hire founder integration fit", "Disruptive know-how & High Status Position Misfit", "misfit", "lack of fit"]
definition: Building on H2, we define a lack of fit (i.e., ineffective integration) also as the scenario in which there is disruptive know-how and the founder is given a lower status position. We use the absolute values of the residuals of the regression of disruptive know-how on founder high status position to indicate the lack of fit (i.e., misfit).

name: Socially irresponsible employment practices
authors_terms: ["socially irresponsible employment practices", "socially irresponsible practices", "harmful employment practices", "irresponsible employment practices"]
definition: Wage theft is just one of many socially irresponsible employment practices that are widespread in the developing world. Others include excessive and involuntary overtime work, punitive workplace discipline measures, informalized employment, and off-contract work.

name: Manufacturing outcomes
definition: Classic indicators of manufacturing performance include product quality, on-time delivery, sales, costs, production speed, and flexibility. Our data measure two important manufacturing outcomes in thousands of factories in the developing world: product quality and on-time delivery.

name: Product quality
definition: Product quality is one of the classic indicators of manufacturing performance and can be profoundly shaped by the human capital of employees. It is captured here by an inspection pass rate indicating the percentage of 'passes' that each factory's products received in quality control inspections.

name: On-time delivery
definition: On-time delivery - defined as fulfilling manufacturing contracts on-schedule - depends on workers fulfilling daily production quotas to ensure that orders are completed in time for packing and shipping.

name: Order value
authors_terms: ["order value per employee", "ln order value per employee", "total annual value of orders"]
definition: We observe the total annual value of orders placed by the import-export agent at each factory. We natural-log-transform this measure to produce a more symmetrical distribution with fewer outliers.

name: Corporate giving
authors_terms: ["corporate giving", "legitimacy management cost", "ratio of corporate giving to sales"]
definition: We view corporate giving as an institutionalized practice that a firm employs to seek normative legitimacy of what an organization ought to be. Corporate giving is treated as a legitimacy management cost, that is, how much an organization spends in order to manage external legitimacy.

name: Positive media coverage of corporate giving
authors_terms: ["positive media coverage of a firm's corporate giving", "positive media attention to a firm's giving efforts", "positive media coverage"]
definition: The extent of positive media attention given to a firm's giving efforts, which can shape and elevate expectations of external audiences surrounding the focal firm. Increasing positive media coverage can act as a stimulus that reinforces a firm's current behavior and can impose pressures on decision-makers by focusing their attention on certain issues.

name: Negative media coverage of lawsuits against family owners
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage of lawsuits against a firm's family owners", "media attention to legal conflicts between family owners and external constituents", "media attention of lawsuits against family owners"]
definition: The degree of media attention on legal conflicts in which family owners are the target of legal actions brought by different stakeholders who are against their control and power structures. Typical types of such legal conflicts are inheritance tax evasion, deceptive accounting, intentional securities fraud, exploitation of minority shareholders, and illegal internal transactions between member firms within a business group.

name: Firm performance
definition: A firm's internal efficiency condition, captured by its profitability measured as the return on assets (ROA). The authors use it to construct interaction terms with the media coverage variables, and it is also controlled in the models.

name: Resource complementarity
definition: Gulati (1995b) suggests that complementarity between organizations within the same industry can be represented by non-overlap in the niches in which they operate. The investment banks that manage underwriting syndicates thus have an incentive to be alert to the complementarity of strengths between their organizations and their potential partners because cooperation will pay off when partners can complement each other's weaknesses.

name: Status similarity
definition: Firms considering alliances assess both the complementary capabilities and the status of their potential partners; firms of similar status are more likely to ally with each other.

name: Direct prior alliance experience
authors_terms: ["direct prior alliance experience", "direct ties", "direct prior alliance experience with a certain partner"]
definition: In forming strategic alliances, a natural solution for a firm is to first consider previous partners with which it has had direct prior alliance experiences.

name: Indirect prior alliance experience
authors_terms: ["indirect prior alliance experience", "indirect ties", "co-participation", "indirect alliance experience"]
definition: Two firms' indirect ties through a third party-a lead bank in the case of an investment banking syndicate-may enhance the chances that the two firms will form a strategic alliance because the indirect ties can function as an information conduit and because a common actor can play the role of a reference and become a mechanism for deterring opportunistic behaviors.

name: Reciprocity in opportunity exchange
authors_terms: ["reciprocity", "reciprocity in opportunity exchange", "reciprocal exchanges of alliance opportunities", "reciprocity in deal exchanges"]
definition: One of the key effects of the informational advantage that emerges from repetitive, long-term cooperative partnerships is the reciprocated exchange of economic opportunities. Reciprocity of economic exchange comes into play, making it attractive to exchange cooperative economic opportunities with only a few select long-term partners-given that each partner has a chance to give and take a certain number of cooperative opportunities.

name: Alliance formation
definition: We defined an investment banking firm's participation in an underwriting syndicate managed by a lead bank as an alliance. These syndications can be viewed as strategic alliances.

name: Synergistic gains
definition: Synergy exists in an acquisition when the value of the combined entity exceeds the sum of the values of the two combining firms (Bradley et al., 1988), i.e., when VC > VA + VT, where V refers to market value and the superscripts C, A and T refer to the combined, acquiring and target firm respectively. A valid analysis of the existence of synergistic gains should involve a comparison of the value of the combined firm after all gains are incorporated into stock prices with the (hypothetical) combined value of the two firms had there been no acquisition.

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: Merging firms may be considered related 'when a common skill, resource, market or purpose applies to each, i.e. if they employ similar production techniques, serve similar markets and use similar distribution systems, and employ science-based research' (Rumelt, 1974: 29).

name: Relative target size
authors_terms: ["relative size of the target to the bidder", "size of the target to the bidder"]
definition: Acquisitions which are characterized by a significant size of the target to the bidder have greater potential for creating synergy via increased market power, economies of scale or economies of scope. This relative size criterion is expected to be much less important for realizing gains from coinsurance or financial diversification.

name: Joint community affiliation
authors_terms: ["joint community affiliation", "community relations", "same community", "shared community affiliation", "buyer-seller community relations"]
definition: A joint community affiliation means that a buyer and a seller know one another from preexisting social communities and share a common history and identity about what it means to be a community member. Such affiliations transfer expectations of behavior from one context to the other and subject exchange partners to common normative expectations.

name: Deviation from local pricing norms
authors_terms: ["deviations from local pricing norms", "difference between prices", "deviations from the echelle price", "deviations from normative prices", "deviations from acceptable pricing behavior"]
definition: The extent to which the final transaction price deviates from established pricing norms in the community: starting from the actual price paid per kilogram of grapes, the author subtracts the normative price for these grapes according to the echelle des crus; the larger the difference, the greater the deviation.

name: Variance in final paid price
authors_terms: ["variance in price", "variance in final paid prices", "variance in the residuals"]
definition: The dispersion of the final price paid per kilogram of grapes across transactions. If grape sellers seek the appropriate, community-sanctioned pricing behavior when interacting with a buyer from their community, the variance in price is expected to be lower within a community.

name: Community cohesiveness
authors_terms: ["social cohesiveness", "community cohesiveness", "cohesiveness of the community", "social engagement"]
definition: The extent to which members take an active role in the everyday life of their community; social engagement is key to a community's cohesiveness and is fostered through collective participation in community organizations. The more cohesive a community is, the stronger the social pressure on its members.

name: Repeated exchange relations
authors_terms: ["repeated exchange", "repeated exchange relations", "long-term exchange relations", "relational capital", "relation duration"]
definition: Buyer-seller relations built through repeated exchange over time, which capture the relational capital developed between exchange partners. Such relations are measured by the duration of the exchange relation or by the concentration of a partner's exchanges with few partners.

name: Final paid price
authors_terms: ["final price", "final price paid per kilogram of grapes"]
definition: The final price paid per kilogram of grapes, net of transportation charges, which are always paid by the buyer.

name: Center of excellence
definition: A center of excellence is an organizational unit that embodies a set of capabilities that has been explicitly recognized by the firm as an important source of value creation, with the intention that these capabilities be leveraged by and/or disseminated to other parts of the firm.

name: Local industry diamond strength
authors_terms: ["strength and dynamism of the local industry 'diamond'", "Diamond Strength", "local business environment", "strength of the industry 'diamond'"]
definition: Fundamentally, this is an argument about locational advantage-the strength of the industry 'diamond' in a particular location, which provides a 'latent' opportunity for multinational firms to derive a learning benefit from that location.

name: External sources of competence
authors_terms: ["External Influence", "impact of external organizations on the development of a subsidiary's competence", "external sources of competence"]
definition: The connectivity of the unit to key actors and resources in the host country, measured as the impact of various organizations outside the boundaries of the firm on the development of the subsidiary's competencies. Competence development is facilitated by active participation of the subsidiary in the 'community of practice' that structures activity and relationships in a particular area.

name: Internal sources of competence
authors_terms: ["Internal Influence", "impact of other units within the multinational network on the development of a subsidiary's competence", "internal sources of competence"]
definition: Internal network linkages of the subsidiary to other parts of the multinational firm; the argument is that internal network linkages can work in a very similar way to relationships in the local market, i.e., by stimulating the emergence of new ideas and fostering the emergence of advanced capabilities in the subsidiary.

name: Parent firm investment
definition: A more fundamental role of the parent firm is typically as a provider of tangible resources, especially investment capital, needed by the subsidiary to develop the kind of advanced capabilities that may give rise to its eventual recognition as a center of excellence.

name: Subsidiary autonomy
definition: The process of subsidiary-driven charter extension requires the foreign subsidiary to have considerable autonomy in terms of the ability to identify and pursue interesting market opportunities without explicit permission from the parent company.

name: CEO activism
authors_terms: ["CEO activism", "CEO advocacy", "CEO support for police reform", "activist CEOs", "CEO message"]
definition: CEO activism is the phenomenon of CEOs taking public social and political stances that are unrelated to a firm's core business. CEOs may engage in activism to influence public discourse and policy, and the message may be interpreted through the lens of the policymaker's own ideology.

name: Support for police reform
authors_terms: ["support for police reform", "level of support", "support for a policy"]
definition: Policymakers' level of support for specific police reform policies: the creation of a national police misconduct registry and stricter standards for the use of no-knock warrants.

name: Willingness to privately meet with a CEO
authors_terms: ["willingness to privately meet with the CEO", "willingness to meet privately with the CEO", "privately meet with this CEO"]
definition: How likely a policymaker would be to privately meet with the CEO of a business that wants to open a facility in the policymaker's region. An official's willingness to take a meeting is commonly used as a measure of access to the policymaking process.

name: Willingness to publicly advocate for a company
authors_terms: ["willingness to publicly advocate", "publicly advocate that the company relocate", "advocate publicly for the CEO"]
definition: How likely a policymaker would be to publicly advocate that the company locate its new facility in the policymaker's community.

name: Bitcoin legalization
definition: Legalization is the regulative status in which a country classifies Bitcoin trading as legal. The authors state that legalization, often the result of a lengthy multistakeholder engagement and deliberation process, shows government support of a new industry and the associated organizational form, creates clear accountability, and makes compliance and taxation costs calculable.

name: Bitcoin illegalization
definition: Illegalization is the regulative status in which a country declares Bitcoin trading to be illegal. The authors argue that regulatory uncertainty permeating new organizational forms can be resolved if governments classify an activity as illegal, conclusively discouraging platform founding or even making it impossible.

name: Platform founding
authors_terms: ["platform founding", "founding of new Bitcoin trading platforms", "number of Bitcoin exchange platforms", "number of exchange platforms"]
definition: Platform founding is entrepreneurs establishing Bitcoin exchange platforms and providing the trading infrastructure in exchange for commissions on trades; it is in many ways a 'classical' entrepreneurial act that involves entrepreneurs and the formation of a legal entity. The authors measure it as the number of Bitcoin exchange platforms in a particular country and year, and consider founding a well-established measure of new market development.

name: Bitcoin trading volume
definition: Trading volume reflects the purchases and sales of Bitcoins on a particular exchange platform within a 24-hour timespan. Trading a fiat currency into Bitcoin is the most convenient way to participate in the DAO, so the authors consider trading volume on exchange platforms a key mechanism to assess the emergence and growth of the DAO.

name: Grand corruption
definition: Grand corruption is 'the abuse of power in the political domain and the related fraud in laws and policies'. This corruption form is related to the state and the extent to which politics and the ruling elite use their power and influence to design policies and activities that favor their interest.

name: Petty corruption
definition: Petty corruption refers to 'the everyday, street-level type of corruption that involves small payments, speed money and tips to people low in the hierarchy'. It involves individuals in lower-level offices, happens more frequently, and is smaller in scale than grand corruption.

name: Quality-adjusted innovation output
authors_terms: ["quality-adjusted innovation output", "quality adjusted innovation output", "firm-level innovation output", "weighted patent count"]
definition: we define firm-level innovation output as the sum of the technological innovations created by a firm over a given period. Quality adjusted innovation output is this construct corrected by its economic and technological value.

name: University research experience
authors_terms: ["university research experience", "academic research experience", "hires from universities", "hires from firms with university experience", "university scientific experience"]
definition: An important type of external experience that can be acquired by firms through recruitment is experience of academic research in a university context beyond the level of doctoral research.

name: Patenting-firm experience
authors_terms: ["experience of working in a firm with a strong technological record", "hires from patenting firms", "experience from employment in a technologically strong firm", "technological experience"]
definition: The authors treat (b) experience of working in a firm with a strong technological record as one of the two salient types of scientist experience, and argue that former employees of patent active compared to non-patenting firms are likely to have deeper and broader technological knowledge and to have the ability to utilize technological information.

name: Academic research-friendly organizational culture
authors_terms: ["research friendly organizational culture", "university research-friendly organizational culture", "academic research-friendly culture", "organizational research culture"]
definition: Organizational culture is defined generally as 'a system of shared values defining what is important, and norms, defining appropriate attitudes and behaviors, that guide members' attitudes and behaviors' (O'Reilly & Chatman, 1996, p. 166). A university research-friendly organizational culture emphasizes the importance of academic research and the associated norms and practices.

name: CEO political ideology
definition: CEOs' values conceptualized on the ideological dimension of conservatism - liberalism, also referred to as the right - left axis; ideologies are treated as values, with liberals placing higher value on equality and conservatives showing greater tolerance for unequal outcomes.

name: Organizational political ideology
authors_terms: ["organizational ideology", "organizational liberalism", "prevailing values among organizational members"]
definition: The prevailing beliefs among organizational members about what outcomes are desirable and how they should be achieved, expressed on the conservative - liberal axis; ideology is highly related to, but not synonymous with, organizational culture.

name: Evenhandedness in resource allocation
authors_terms: ["evenhandedness", "evenhandedness in resource allocation", "evenhandedness in capital allocation", "evenhanded resource allocations"]
definition: The degree to which every unit receives the same capital allocation (relative to its size), as opposed to disparity in allocations across units. It is a central construct in research on resource allocation in multibusiness firms.

name: CEO equity-based pay
definition: The degree to which CEO compensation is paid in stock and stock options rather than salary and cash bonuses, meant to motivate long-term, shareholder-aligned behaviors.

name: CEO shareholdings
definition: A CEO's equity ownership in the firm, which can range from minimal to substantial and which reflects both power and financial incentives.

name: Firm performance
definition: The firm's subsequent performance, measured with Tobin's q as the ratio of market value to the replacement cost of assets, which reflects both current realized performance and investors' assessments of the firm's prospects and health.

name: Firm performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["firm performance relative to aspirations", "performance attainment discrepancy", "performance feedback", "firm performance relative to the historic aspiration level"]
definition: Performance feedback is conceptualized as a simple construct where the historical aspiration level is subtracted from achieved performance; the resulting value is the performance attainment discrepancy, which is negative when achieved performance is below aspiration and positive when it is above.

name: Strategic resource divestment
authors_terms: ["resource divestment", "strategic resource divestment", "resource divestment capability", "total resource divestment", "developed resource divestment", "less developed resource divestment"]
definition: Resource divestment is defined as the disposition of an asset from the firm's resource portfolio, and the associated factor market transfer of that resource to another firm in the industry. The firm's resource divestment capability is an organizational change routine comprising two steps: the firm must first be motivated to engage in divestment and then decide which resources to divest.

name: Factor market bargaining power
authors_terms: ["monopsonistic factor market", "monopolistic factor market", "balance of bargaining power", "bargaining power"]
definition: At the extremes, a given factor market for strategic human resources can range from a monopoly to a monopsony. In a monopsonistic factor market there is only one firm that can buy a given strategic factor's productive output, resulting in contracts that grant bargaining power to the firm; in a monopolistic factor market the resource can sell its services to any firm in the industry, resulting in contracts that vest bargaining power with the strategic factor.

name: Strategic similarity
definition: Following Hatten and Hatten's (1987) definition, strategic similarity is defined as similarity in the general pattern of resource deployments and competitive orientations independent of the specific markets served by the firm.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: For any pair of competing firms in a market within the industry, multimarket contact reflects the number of other markets in the industry in which the same pair of firms meet as competitors. Thus, multimarket contact between two competing firms in a given market reflects the degree of market overlap between those firms in the other markets of the industry.

name: Intensity of rivalry
authors_terms: ["intensity of rivalry", "intensity of rivalry experienced by a firm in a market"]
definition: The intensity of rivalry experienced by a firm in a market can be captured by evaluating the impact of the pattern of competitive actions and reactions in the price-cost margin of a firm in a market. The rivalry experienced by a firm differs among markets, so the natural unit of analysis is the rivalry experienced by a firm within a particular market.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of outside directors", "percentage of outsiders", "percentage of insiders", "proportion of inside directors"]
definition: As an employee of the firm, an inside or management director usually holds a high-level executive position and devotes substantially full time and attention to the affairs of the corporation or one of its subsidiaries. An outside or non-management member, on the other hand, is not an employee of the company.

name: Shareholder suit incidence
authors_terms: ["incidence of suit", "incidence of shareholder suits", "boards sued", "stockholder suits", "shareholder suits"]
definition: If stockholders ever doubt that a board has properly performed its duties, they may file a lawsuit. The courts then determine whether or not a violation has occurred.

name: Suit outcome
authors_terms: ["outcome of suits", "outcomes of suits", "favorable outcomes", "unfavorable outcomes", "decisions favorable to the defendant"]
definition: By examining the outcomes of suits, therefore, we are better able to distinguish cases in which directors are proven to have violated their duties versus those which are simply frivolous or for which insufficient evidence is produced.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "the CEO also holds the position of chairman", "the CEO simultaneously serves as chairman", "positions of CEO and chairman held by a single individual"]
definition: Though it is common for the CEO to serve simultaneously as chairman, this arrangement has been severely criticized by many. Thus, there is an inherent conflict of interests in uniting both roles in one person.

name: Board political conservatism
authors_terms: ["board conservatism", "board ideology", "political ideology", "political conservatism", "political ideologies of board members"]
definition: Political ideology provides individuals a framework for understanding their social environment and their role within it. The authors measure the board's ideology as board conservatism, a weighted summation of individual directors' ideology values.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Companies that have committed misconduct sometimes seek to repair their image by disassociating themselves from leaders seen as responsible for financial malfeasance, hoping that the CEO's departure will signal to stakeholders that the firm takes the misconduct seriously and is earnest about reestablishing its reputation and legitimacy.

name: Group decision-making approach
definition: DI and DA build structured, constructive interpersonal conflict into the decision processes of top management groups facing complex, ill-defined (i.e. wicked) strategic problems. Consensus encourages open discussion among group members but does not formally structure or encourage conflict.

name: Group decision making
definition: A major premise underlying the use of groups in strategic decision-making is that groups can draw on the knowledge and perspectives of many people. The quality of a particular approach is a function of its ability to utilize the capabilities of individual group members.

name: Utilization of individual member capabilities
authors_terms: ["utilization of individual capabilities", "utilize the capabilities of individual group members", "utilization of members' capabilities", "synergy"]
definition: Two methods assess group utilization of individual capabilities: the difference between a group's performance and the average performance scores of its members, and whether a group's performance exceeds that of its best member. Synergy is said to exist when a group's performance surpasses that of the capabilities of its group members.

name: Decision performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "quality of recommendations", "validity of assumptions", "importance of assumptions", "number of assumptions"]
definition: Expert judges' ratings of each individual's and each group's recommendations and assumptions were used to assess performance. Two measures assessed the quality of the assumptions groups or individuals identified - validity and importance - and the judges also rated the global quality of each individual's or group's recommendations.

name: Firm–SMO collaboration
definition: We define a collaboration as organizations working together by committing resources to achieve mutually relevant outcomes. Collaborations are formal, interactional relationships like alliances that involve commitment of resources by parties to achieve a stated outcome.

name: Social movement contention
definition: Market contention, or stakeholders' use of confrontational tactics like boycotts, protests and lawsuits to directly challenge corporations. We define contentious interactions as those in which SMOs challenge firms with adversarial or confrontational actions that go beyond mere verbal criticism.

name: Partner SMO network embeddedness
authors_terms: ["partner SMO's ties to other SMOs", "indirectly tied SMOs", "board interlocks", "inter-SMO network"]
definition: The extent to which the collaborating SMO is centrally embedded within its social movement field, so that it can reach a broader population of SMOs in the field to share praise and advocacy for the firm. We test our ties hypotheses using board interlocks because they serve as conduits for the flow of information between organizations.

name: SMO contentious repertoire
authors_terms: ["tactical repertoire", "SMO contentious repertoire", "history of using contentious tactics"]
definition: One of the most salient and observable dimensions on which SMOs are typically categorized is their tactical repertoire, or the degree to which they employ contentious tactics like protests versus more collaborative tactics like cross-sector partnerships.

name: Grassroots contentious tactics
definition: Audiences look to organizational tactics and features grounded in ideals of grassroots mobilization, including those that draw on mass participation (e.g., protests, letter-writing campaigns), displays of spontaneity and emotion, participatory rather than professionally-driven organization, and grassroots membership.

name: Professional contentious tactics
definition: Tactics that rely on professionals (e.g., lawyers) and institutional arenas (e.g., regulatory hearings), such as lawsuits, regulatory interventions, or shareholder proxy proposals. Collaborations with SMOs using such tactics are less persuasive because their relative professionalization seeds doubt about the authenticity or sincerity of their motivations in making the tactical pivot to collaboration.

name: Collaboration form
definition: Bilateral collaborations involve only a focal firm and focal SMO, whereas multilateral collaborations involve consortiums of SMOs and firms.

name: Board experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["board experiential diversity", "experiential diversity", "experientially diverse board", "directors' experiential diversity"]
definition: Board experiential diversity coalesces from the directors' educational, industrial, and organizational experiences and can reflect the board's cognitive abilities to offer unique perspectives.

name: Radical innovation
definition: Radical innovation refers to inventions that deviate from their predecessors and set new paths for future technology; path-breaking patents are those that destabilize prior technological paths.

name: Industry competition
definition: Industry competition is the intensity of competition a firm faces in its industry; under high competition the board's advising role is prominent because firms often need strategic guidance, whereas low competition spawns agency problems and heightens the need for board monitoring.

name: Firm complexity
definition: Firm complexity indicates the degree of a board's advisory involvement; complex firms demonstrate greater advising needs from the board than simple firms do.

name: Board monitoring
definition: Boards are concurrently tasked with monitoring responsibilities, and research suggests independent directors raise monitoring strength.

name: Nonlocal director supply experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["nonlocal director supply experiential diversity", "nonlocal director supply"]
definition: The degree of diverse experiences of director candidates who reside at least 150 miles away but within one nonstop flight from a firm's HQ, weighted by the frequencies of nonstop flights connecting the firm HQ and director domicile locations.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration is theorized to be the most important industry structural element in the field of industrial organization (Bain, 1959; Caves, 1972; Koch, 1974; Mann, 1966). Prior industrial organization and strategic management theory suggests that industry concentration is an important structural characteristic of industries.

name: Product differentiation
definition: Product differentiation is theorized to be the second most important structural characteristic of industries (Bain, 1956, 1959; Caves, 1972). The most commonly utilized measure of the degree of product differentiation is advertising intensity.

name: Industry life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["stage of the life cycle", "stage of life cycle", "stage of the industry life cycle"]
definition: Stage of the life cycle is theorized to be one of the key structural characteristics of industries (Bain, 1959; Caves, 1972; Hofer, 1975). The stage of the life cycle categorization is based on both the market growth rate and additional information regarding customer acceptance of products.

name: Industry growth rate
authors_terms: ["industry growth rate", "market growth rate", "growth rate in the venture's industry"]
definition: Hambrick et al. (1982) delineate an important distinction between stage of the life cycle and industry growth rates: 'For most products, growth rates closely correspond with certain stages of the life cycle. The conceptual distinction is that each stage typically is attributed with characteristics in addition to growth rate, for example, customer adoption rates and the nature of competition.'

name: New venture performance
authors_terms: ["venture performance", "new venture performance", "firm performance", "measures of firm performance", "business performance"]
definition: Prior theory and research in the fields of industrial organization, strategic management, and entrepreneurship suggest that measures of business performance based on (1) return on assets (ROA), (2) return on equity (ROE), (3) return on sales (ROS), and (4) sales growth (SG) are the most important/appropriate goals of business enterprises. This research examined the influence of the three industry structural elements on these four measures of new venture performance.

name: Interorganizational trust
definition: The expectation held by one firm that another will not exploit its vulnerabilities when faced with the opportunity to do so; this expectation is based on three related components: reliability, fairness, and goodwill.

name: Alliance performance
