definition: Because financial profitability and survival are problematic indicators for alliances, alliance performance research has relied on managers' evaluations of alliance success; the authors rely on such managerial evaluations because their respondents were very well informed about the alliances.

name: Interdependence
definition: The degree of interdependence in an alliance increases with the importance and extent of the resources shared between partners and with the resulting overlap in division of labor between them, that is, the resulting shared responsibility for a number of tasks.

name: Interpartner competition
definition: Interpartner competition exists when a partner tries to maximize its private interests at the expense of the alliance or the other partner.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Instability is the degree of difference involved in an environmental change; environmental uncertainty results from changes in the economic conditions faced by an organization that are outside its control and hard to anticipate.

name: Environmental unpredictability
definition: Unpredictability is the degree of irregularity in an overall pattern of environmental change.

name: Shareholder value maximization practices
authors_terms: ["corporate practices to maximize shareholder value", "continued commitment to the dominant logic", "shareholder value-maximizing practices", "corporate harms"]
definition: The authors used a comprehensive set of indicators that have been identified in the literature as particularly salient manifestations of shareholder value maximization: mass layoffs, income inequality, and stock repurchases. They represent incumbents' continued performance of the dominant shareholder logic.

name: Corporate endorsement of social and environmental responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate attempts at endorsing environmental and social responsibility", "ostensible endorsement of the alternative logic", "strategic embrace of the stakeholder logic", "CSR"]
definition: Corporations' strategic embrace of the stakeholder logic, particularly manifested by CSR practices geared toward enhancing their external image as responsible actors, suggests that the traditional shareholder-centered governance is compatible with the emerging stakeholder-inclusive focus.

name: B Corp formation
authors_terms: ["newly certified B Corps", "formation of more B Corporations", "challenger mobilization", "emergence of mobilization for a market alternative"]
definition: The number of newly certified B Corps in each industry from 2007 to 2011, which reflects the emergence of mobilization for a market alternative.

name: Opposition frame
authors_terms: ["opposition frame", "opposition", "desire to oppose and transform the status quo"]
definition: A reason for certification that focuses on highlighting opposition to profit-maximizing businesses and challenging the status quo; challengers with the opposition frame emphasize continued marginalization of alternative values and beliefs and aim to transform the status quo.

name: Authenticity frame
definition: A reason for certification centered on authenticity concerns, in which the urgent problem is the hype of social responsibility and certification is seen as a way to prove authentic commitment to social and environmental values; challengers with the authenticity frame highlight a false settlement between what they see as conflicting logics and strive to reinforce their authentic distinction.

name: Inventor centrality
authors_terms: ["centrality", "Bonacich power", "centrality of an inventor in an intraorganization knowledge network"]
definition: The Bonacich power measure would suggest that an inventor is central to the extent that he or she copatents with other central inventors. The centrality of other inventors arises from the pattern of relations among all the inventors.

name: Structural holes spanned
authors_terms: ["structural holes", "spanning of structural holes", "structural holes constraint", "structural holes efficiency"]
definition: The structural hole approach focuses on the individual ego, and posits that individuals who span structural holes are better off; that is, inventors situated between other inventors who are not directly linked enjoy efficiency and control benefits (Burt 1992).

name: Intrafirm knowledge use
authors_terms: ["likelihood of his knowledge being selected by other inventors", "likelihood of their knowledge being selected by other inventors", "rate of intrafirm citation to a patent", "use of knowledge created by them"]
definition: We consider a patent citation as a choice made by the firm to build on knowledge contained in the patent. The dependent variable is the rate of intrafirm citation to a patent by inventors other than those who are involved in its creation.

name: R&D specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization", "specialization or concentration of the activities of the firm", "technological capabilities"]
definition: We define a capability as the specialization or concentration of the activities of the firm within certain areas (Selznick 1957, Smith 1799). Such specialization or concentration represents the firm's ability to perform activities in those areas as opposed to other areas.

name: Extra-institutional tactics
authors_terms: ["extra-institutional tactics", "extra-institutional tactical actions", "protests and boycotts", "confrontational tactics"]
definition: Protests and boycotts are often regarded as 'extra-institutional' tactics since they are used generally outside of legitimized, institutional means for corporate insiders seeking reform. Such tactics are seen as more disruptive, aggressive and radical.

name: Institutional tactics
authors_terms: ["institutional tactics", "civil lawsuits and proxy votes", "institutional means of conflict resolution"]
definition: Institutional tactics are those tactics that are enacted using an established, traditional mechanism for resolving conflict with corporations, such as the legal system or proxy vote procedures.

name: Event media attention
authors_terms: ["event media attention", "media attention received by the event", "negative media attention"]
definition: Tactics like boycotts, protests, rallies, and demonstrations are explicitly intended to generate negative media attention for the firm. The paper measures the media attention received by the event as the count of newspaper articles mentioning the event in the focal year, excluding the one used to code the event.

name: Investor environmental risk perceptions
authors_terms: ["investor environmental risk perceptions", "environmental risk perceptions", "assessments of environmental risk", "KLD negative"]
definition: Analysts' perceptions of environmental risk, a professional assessment of a firm's environmental vulnerabilities (i.e., a potential liability due to flawed environmental practices), and resultant potential economic consequences.

name: Activist group type
authors_terms: ["types of activist groups", "Activist religious", "Activist investors", "SMO", "activist individuals"]
definition: Each type of activist is coded consistent with prior research using a set of dummy variables: religious groups (Activist religious), activist investors such as pension fund managers and socially responsible investment groups (Activist investors), and nongovernmental organizations such as issue advocacy groups (SMO), with activist individuals serving as a referent group in the data.

name: Relationship value creation
authors_terms: ["relationship value creation", "value creation in the relationship", "value creation"]
definition: By relationship value creation, we mean the effect of the relationship on the joint economic performance of the partner firms. The authors define relationship value creation as the effect of the engagement in the relationship on the joint profitability of the partner firms.

name: Mutual dependence
authors_terms: ["mutual dependence", "relationship dependence", "mutual dependence between the exchange partners"]
definition: We view relationship dependence as the extent to which the outcome of one partner is contingent on the activities of the other. This corresponds to Pfeffer and Salancik's (1978) outcome dependence. In its turn, mutual dependence is defined as the strength of a balanced dependence relation between the partners.

name: Mutual commitment
authors_terms: ["mutual commitment", "mutual commitment to a business relationship"]
definition: We define mutual commitment as a willingness on the part of both partners to make short-term sacrifices to realize long-term benefits in the relationship (Anderson and Weitz, 1992; Dwyer et al., 1987).

name: Business network connection
definition: Business network connection is defined as the degree to which the focal relationship is directly connected to other relationships. Business networks are defined as two or more connected business relationships, and two exchange relations are connected if the exchange in one relation is contingent on exchange in the other.

name: First-mover status
definition: An indicator, 'FIRST,' was set to one for the 50 percent of sample companies categorized as first movers. Incorporation dates were used to determine market entry rank within competitive sets, except when a company diversified into its set from another line of business, in which case market entry order was based on website launch dates for all competitors in the set.

name: Winner-take-all market structural attributes
definition: In this research the phrase 'winner-take-all' is applied to markets with high concentration levels; to paraphrase Frank and Cook, references to 'winner-take-all' should be read to mean, 'winners-take-most.' A consistent approach was used to gauge the strength of three structural attributes that may engender or reinforce WTA competitive dynamics: network effects, fixed cost-based scale economies, and switching costs.

name: Investment in customer acquisition
authors_terms: ["accelerated growth strategies", "investment in growth", "heavy, preemptive investment in customer acquisition efforts", "IPO-year marketing spending", "commitment to accelerated growth", "marketing spending"]
definition: Accelerated growth strategies are defined here as efforts to acquire customers rapidly in new markets through heavy marketing spending, discounting aggressively, or absorbing rivals through mergers. Growth is 'accelerated' to the extent that a firm sacrifices current profits in order to maximize the present value of future profits.

name: Long-term return on invested capital
definition: Long-term returns are defined as the ratio of a company's equity and debt market value to the total amount of capital it had raised historically, with market values measured as of year-end 2001, 20 months after the Internet stock bubble burst.

name: Board industry expertise
authors_terms: ["board industry expertise", "industry expertise", "industry-specific board expertise", "role-specific industry experience"]
definition: Industry expertise is defined as role-specific industry experience; it enhances directors' ability to assess strategy-related topics in the industry and enables them to provide counsel and to monitor managers.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in a firm's financial resource allocation profile"]
definition: Strategic change is defined as a '[change in the] fundamental pattern of present and planned resource deployments'; the authors calculate it as the change in a firm's financial resource allocation profile.

name: Institutional information provision
definition: Environments with low institutional information provision are defined as countries with a weak disclosure standard, which impairs access to information about the firm's environment and situation.

name: Institutional control provision
definition: Institutional control provision is defined as the legal preconditions of a country's environment, such as the degree of creditor protection, prevention of director self-dealing activities, and laws on shareholder protection, that provide means for indirectly controlling executives' behavior.

name: Financial misrepresentation
definition: Financial manipulations that are implemented by clear, egregious, and material violations of appropriate accounting practices constitute misconduct, and the authors therefore focus on financial restatements triggered by accounting irregularities. These restatements represent major accounting rules violations that the GAO identified as intentionally improper.

name: Stock option share of CEO pay
authors_terms: ["proportion of CEO pay from stock options", "options/total compensation", "fraction of CEO compensation in options", "CEO stock option compensation"]
definition: Stock options offer strong encouragement to raise the stock price above the strike price; the stock price must rise above the strike price for executives to profit from their options. The importance of incentive compensation to a manager may depend on how much other compensation the manager receives, so incentives are measured by the option value relative to the CEO's total compensation.

name: Bonus share of CEO pay
authors_terms: ["proportion of CEO pay from bonuses", "bonus/total compensation"]
definition: Firms clearly represent bonuses as incentives, and while the bonuses paid in the past do not themselves offer incentive for future behavior, they serve as a proxy to indicate the size of potential future bonuses. Incentives are measured by the bonus value relative to the CEO's total compensation.

name: Social relative performance
authors_terms: ["social relative performance", "social-referent relative performance", "performance relative to industry", "social comparison"]
definition: A firm's aspirations rise or fall with respect to a social comparison to the performance of similar firms; for example, a firm's aspiration for sales growth may depend on how fast other firms in the industry have grown. A measure of relative performance is a firm's performance minus its aspiration level, so relative performance increases as firm performance improves.

name: Self-relative performance
authors_terms: ["self-relative performance", "self-referent relative performance", "performance relative to the firm's own prior performance"]
definition: The behavioral literature suggests that a firm's aspirations adapt to the firm's own historical performance: aspirations rise when a firm exceeds its past performance, and fall after the firm's performance declines. A measure of relative performance is a firm's performance minus its aspiration level, so relative performance increases as firm performance improves.

name: Performance above aspiration
authors_terms: ["positive relative performance", "positive instead of negative relative performance", "performance above the reference point", "performance above the firm's own prior performance"]
definition: A discontinuity should occur where performance equals aspirations; the aspiration point divides the range of potential performance into two broad categories. When performance is above aspirations, the probability of financial misrepresentation should generally be less than when it is below aspirations.

name: Diversification strategy type
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "strategy type", "strategy types", "patterns of strategy", "type of diversification"]
definition: Diversification strategy was classified according to Rumelt's (1974) typology. Three categories of strategy were used: related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated.

name: Entry mode
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "mode of diversification", "diversification mode", "mode", "internal development", "acquisition", "mixed mode"]
definition: Consistent with previous research, diversification mode was measured according to the relative frequency of acquisition used by the firm when entering new businesses. Firms may rely on internal development, on acquisition, or on a mixed mode of development.

name: Firm performance
definition: This study utilized four measures: (1) return on assets (ROA), (2) return on equity (ROE), (3) return on investment (ROI), and (4) sales growth (GRSALES). Averages were calculated over the time frame of each sample to provide an overall assessment of the performance effects of strategy and mode.

name: Strategy-mode fit
definition: Certain combinations of strategy and mode should outperform other combinations. Firms exhibiting the optimal matches between strategy and mode (related-constrained with internal development, related-linked with a mixed mode of development, and unrelated with acquisitive development) were compared to firms adopting the same strategy via different modes.

name: Pre-start-up experience
authors_terms: ["pre-start-up experience", "pre-startup experience", "prior firm experience", "firm experience prior to setting up a new venture"]
definition: Any experience that the firm has before the new plant venture starts operations is defined as pre-start-up experience. The level and type of this experience differ across incumbents, diversifying entrants, and de novo entrants.

name: New plant venture performance
definition: Total factor productivity (productivity) was chosen as the performance measure for testing the hypotheses. It provides a broader measure of overall manufacturing performance than other accounting-based measures such as profit-to-sales ratios.

name: Industry learning intensity
authors_terms: ["industry learning intensity", "importance of learning by doing in an industry", "learning environment"]
definition: A quantitative measure of the importance of learning by doing in an industry, computed as the coefficient on cumulative output in an augmented production function. The coefficient on cumulative experience in the decomposition of productivity is the industry learning intensity.

name: CEO succession with gender change
authors_terms: ["CEO succession with gender change", "gender change", "gender change effect"]
definition: CEO succession with gender change - a male CEO succeeded by a female or a female CEO succeeded by a male - is proposed to amplify the disruption of the CEO succession process.

name: Male-to-female CEO succession
definition: A succession in which a male CEO is succeeded by a female CEO; because men predominately occupy the CEO position, the authors describe male-to-female succession as a practice representing 'deviation from normal.'

name: Female-to-male CEO succession
definition: A succession in which a female CEO is succeeded by a male CEO; the authors note that female-to-male succession may be viewed as 'returning to normal.'

name: Post-succession firm performance
definition: Post-succession firm performance was measured by the average of a firm's return on assets (ROA) in the two half-year periods subsequent to the half-year during which a succession occurred.

name: Successor early departure
definition: A successor CEO was considered to have an early departure if s/he was no longer in the CEO position at the end of the second half-year subsequent to the half-year during which the succession occurred.

name: Proportion of female directors
authors_terms: ["proportion of female directors", "presence of other female directors"]
definition: Proportion of female directors was measured by the proportion of female directors (other than the female CEO successor if the successor was a female) on the firm's board in the year of succession.

name: Proportion of female top managers
authors_terms: ["proportion of female top managers", "proportion of females in a firm's top management team", "presence of other female top managers"]
definition: Proportion of female top managers was measured by the proportion of females (other than the female CEO successor if the successor was a female) in the top management team as reported in the firm's annual report in the year of succession.

name: Successor origin
definition: Inside successor was coded as a dummy variable, '1' if the successor CEO was promoted from within the firm and '0' if hired from outside.

name: Strategic investment announcement
authors_terms: ["strategic investment decisions", "corporate announcements of strategic investment decisions", "announcements of corporate investment decisions", "investment announcements"]
definition: Strategic investment decisions are major commitments of current resources made in anticipation of generating future payoffs. By definition, such decisions involve a current resource outflow and an uncertain payback.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction", "stock market's reaction", "stock price reaction", "abnormal return", "excess return"]
definition: In an informationally efficient market, stock price responses to corporate announcements represent the market's evaluation of corporate decisions. The actual return, minus the expected return, is called the 'abnormal' or 'excess' return.

name: Investment size
authors_terms: ["size of the investment", "investment size", "dollar amount of the investment", "dollar size of the investment"]
definition: To incorporate investment size into the analysis, the dollar amount of the investment was first divided by the total assets of the firm so that each investment was expressed as a relative percentage.

name: Investment duration
authors_terms: ["duration of the investment", "expected life span or duration of a corporate investment", "long-term investments", "short-term investments"]
definition: The expected life span or duration of a corporate investment was provided in 287 cases. This subsample was divided into two categories, short-term (less than 3 years) and long-term (more than 3 years).

name: Strategic investment type
authors_terms: ["type of investment decision", "joint venture formations", "research and development projects", "major capital expenditures", "product/market diversification"]
definition: The study examines the stock market's reaction to public announcements of corporate strategic investment decisions and includes a wide variety of strategic decisions: formation of joint ventures, research and development projects, major capital expenditures, and diversification into new products and/or markets.

name: Goal difficulty
authors_terms: ["goal difficulty", "personal goal difficulty", "personal goal", "assigned goal difficulty", "hard goal", "easy goal"]
definition: Two variables were used to measure goals. The first, assigned goal difficulty, represented the goal assigned in the letter from the chairman of the board and had two levels: hard (try to rank first or second in your group) and easy (make some profit). The second variable, personal goal difficulty, represented a student's personal, self-set goal.

name: Business strategy
authors_terms: ["task (business) strategy", "business strategy", "task strategy", "competitive business strategy", "strategy content"]
definition: Hambrick (1980) defined strategy as a pattern of important decisions that guide the organization in relationship with its environment and that affect the internal structure and process of the organization including its performance. Therefore, task strategy and competitive business strategy are one and the same in this study.

name: Volume strategy
definition: In the volume strategy, a firm achieves growth by keeping production levels high, increasing purchases of raw materials, hiring additional sales and production workers, and increasing sales through low prices; these activities are financed by increasing the amount of loans and stock issuance.

name: Quality strategy
definition: To use the quality strategy, a firm sells relatively few high-quality products at high prices; these sales are achieved by making continual and substantial improvements to the product, strongly promoting it locally and nationally, and constantly seeking environmental information about competitors' prices and sales.

name: Scan strategy
definition: In a scan strategy, a firm incurs substantial costs by seeking external environmental information about its competitors' sales, prices, production capacity, advertising budget, and number of salespersons and production workers.

name: Focus strategy
definition: A firm using a focus strategy serves a narrow target market by concentrating units for sale and salespeople in a specific area and supporting its sales effort through local advertising.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance feedback was provided to each participant in terms of their overall group rank after each decision period, based on equal weighting of seven financial performance measures: sales, income after tax, earnings per share, return on sales, return on assets, return on equity, and stock price.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign firms", "non-U.S. firms", "European firms", "foreign entrants", "entering subsidiaries of established foreign firms", "comparable domestic incumbents"]
definition: Over the last quarter of a century non-U.S. firms have entered the U.S. pharmaceutical market and have successfully positioned their subsidiaries among domestic firms. This research focuses specifically on the strategies and choices of European pharmaceutical firms in entering the U.S. market.

name: Parent firm resource base
authors_terms: ["resource base of the parent firm", "parental resources", "resource stocks", "existing pool of internal competencies, core skills, and core products", "strategic assets"]
definition: Hence, the process of establishing a competitive advantage in a new market has to draw on a firm's existing pool of internal competencies, core skills, and core products (Prahalad and Hamel, 1990; Bogner and Thomas, 1994; Tallman, 1991). Thus, when firms enter new geographic markets, this combination of market opportunity and resource constraint should lead their new subsidiary toward a competitive posture that reflects the underlying competence of the parent.

name: Strategic group position
authors_terms: ["strategic group positions", "strategic group membership", "competitive positions", "entry point", "entry position"]
definition: Caves and Porter (1977) suggest that strategic groups provide different opportunities for firms to enter and gain a position of competitive advantage in an industry. But they also note that, because of the variety of intraindustry barriers that entrants must consider, initial market entry is 'no longer a simple yes-no choice. Rather, entry must be targeted to a particular group'.

name: Expansion path
authors_terms: ["expansion path", "sequential entry strategy", "incremental process of change", "incremental market development"]
definition: This 'expansion path' (following Penrose, 1959) concerns the subsequent strategic decisions about growth after initial entry. McGee and Thomas (1986) suggest that after initial entry a firm can proceed to collect assets and build competencies as it moves sequentially into an industry's more desirable groups.

name: Strategic group mobility
authors_terms: ["movement in strategic group membership", "patterns of response to environmental change", "strategic responses", "movement patterns"]
definition: New entrants and established competitors change competitive positions over time. The final research hypotheses examine the movement patterns of the U.S. firms in comparison to the European firms over time.

name: Research activity
definition: For R&D, a measure of research activity (ARD) was developed that used a logged patent count.

name: Relative R&D pace
authors_terms: ["RRD", "relative acceleration or deceleration of a firm's R&D pace"]
definition: A second variable (RRD) measures the relative acceleration or deceleration of a firm's R&D pace. This allows for the R&D level to be assessed relative to the firm's historic allocations.

name: Research class relatedness
definition: Product mix variables were developed to measure how balanced a firm's product line was across both therapeutic and research classes. One scale was developed based on the relatedness across the research classes (HRD).

name: Therapeutic class relatedness
definition: For both measures Herfindahl-type indices were developed using the 7-year time frames. One scale was developed based on the relatedness across the research classes (HRD) and one on the therapeutic classes (HMK).

name: Clinical product mix
authors_terms: ["HOSP", "clinical/retail split", "product mix and research thrusts along this clinical/retail dichotomy"]
definition: A proxy measure that roughly identifies each firm's product mix and research thrusts along this clinical/retail dichotomy was developed by identifying the percentage of new drug approvals for delivery forms that are primarily used in a hospital or other clinical setting (HOSP).

name: Chronic care product mix
definition: Here the proxy attempts to measure the extent to which products approved by the FDA are targeted for long-term patient consumption (CHRN). Chronic care drugs hold high potential for profits because patients often refill the same prescription, perhaps for life.

name: Relative new product production
authors_terms: ["REPROD", "annual new product production relative to the industry as a whole"]
definition: Finally, a measure of each firm's annual new product production relative to the industry as a whole was taken (REPROD). Overall the variables used here correspond closely to many of the variables used by Cool (1985); the major difference here being the use of product and patent data, rather than sales data.

name: CEO age
definition: CEO Age is the age of firm owner-manager. The estimation sample includes firms for which the authors can identify the leading shareholder (at least 50% of the equity) and determine the CEO's age.

name: Firm investment
definition: Investment is the annual change in log total assets.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth is the annual change in log sales.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is measured by return on assets: net income over assets (net income over total assets for the focal year).

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["firm survival", "business survival", "probability of survival", "exit from business"]
definition: The likelihood of the exit from business, estimated with a Cox proportional hazards model in which the estimated hazard ratio compares the likelihood of exit for firms with young versus old CEOs; a hazard ratio lower than 1.0 suggests a lower likelihood of business failure.

name: Ownership change
definition: The likelihood that a firm changes ownership, examined as a function of measures of financial development, CEO's age, and other firm and geography controls.

name: Regional financial development
authors_terms: ["financial development", "regional financial development", "level of financial development of a region"]
definition: Financial development measures the ease of obtaining external financing in a region; it affects the ability of potential investors seeking to purchase a firm to obtain additional funding from either banks or private equity investors, and can facilitate ownership transfers.

name: Industry creativity
definition: Creative industries supply goods and services broadly associated with cultural, artistic, or entertainment value (e.g., advertising and fashion) and are characterized by a high level of uncertainty in demand, risk, and novelty, though not necessarily technological advancement.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: Intensity of R&D at the industry level characterizes an industry's technological dynamism.

name: Subjective stock option valuation
authors_terms: ["subjective stock option valuations", "stock option valuation", "holders' subjective valuations", "managers' subjective valuations"]
definition: Stock option valuation refers to the value holders place on stock options; subjective valuations are the values option holders perceive stock options to be worth, as opposed to the objective values assigned by normative models.

name: Objective stock option value
authors_terms: ["Black-Scholes values", "objective normative model valuations", "normative model valuations", "objective stock option valuations"]
definition: Black-Scholes valuations provide estimates of what outside investors would pay for stock options if they were traded on an open exchange; these valuations theoretically reflect the economic cost of options to a firm and thus represent their objective value.

name: Stock price volatility
authors_terms: ["volatility", "stock price volatility", "volatility of the stock underlying stock options"]
definition: Volatility reflects fluctuation in the value of an asset; the volatility of the stock underlying options symmetrically increases the range of potential positive and negative returns.

name: Stock price trend
authors_terms: ["stock price trend", "trend", "the direction of previous stock price movement"]
definition: Stock price trend is the direction of previous stock price movement, manipulated as flat (neutral), upward (positive) or downward (negative).

name: Stock option ownership
authors_terms: ["willingness to accept", "willingness to pay", "awarded stock options", "identical, not-yet-awarded stock options", "unexercisable stock options"]
definition: By virtue of possession, individuals perceive that the value of an owned asset exceeds the value of an identical, unowned asset; once stock options are awarded, holders count on receiving value from stock options and perceive this value as real wealth.

name: Alliance experience
definition: Experience measures count the number of alliances of a given contractual form entered into by the firm prior to and including the alliance in question, within the time window of the data; the experience measures thus have a lower bound of 1.

name: Value creation through alliances
definition: These excess returns reflect the expected value that the market believes the firm will capture by entering into the particular alliance.

name: Alliance capability
authors_terms: ["alliance capabilities", "firm fixed effects", "unobserved heterogeneity in capabilities"]
definition: Each firm fixed effect can be interpreted as a measure of that firm's alliance capability. It represents the market's perception of the amount of value that will be created, or destroyed (for those firms whose estimated capabilities are negative), on average, when that firm engages in an alliance.

name: Alliance contract form
authors_terms: ["joint ventures", "licensing contracts", "research joint ventures", "production joint ventures", "marketing joint ventures"]
definition: The term 'alliances' encompasses a medley of often vastly different organizational forms. Joint ventures are more likely to be observed in situations where alliance partners are faced with greater ambiguity, while licensing contracts are much more clearly articulated contracts.

name: Basic Internet adoption
authors_terms: ["basic Internet", "basic Internet adoption", "basic Internet technology", "Internet adoption", "adoption of basic Internet"]
definition: Our analysis focuses on basic Internet connectivity; prominent examples of basic Internet include Internet access or an internal intranet. An establishment is defined as a basic Internet adopter if it indicated that it had access to the Internet, had an internal intranet based on TCP/IP, or used the Internet for research purposes.

name: Cross-location research collaboration
authors_terms: ["collaborative patents", "cross-location collaborations", "collaboration between inventors in both MSAs", "geographically dispersed research teams"]
definition: CollaborativePatent is a dummy variable for whether there is a patent coinvented by researchers in both locations j and k of a particular firm i at time t, dated by application year. Based on coauthorship, the authors identify the incidence of collaborations that were performed between units in different MSAs in a given patent-application year.

name: Within-location research collaboration
authors_terms: ["collaborative patent among researchers within a single firm location", "within-location collaborations", "collocated research teams"]
definition: CollaborativePatent is a binary indicator for the incidence of a patent applied for in year t with at least two inventors in location j of a particular firm i. For these teams coordination costs will fall by less than for geographically dispersed teams.

name: Single-inventor patenting
definition: In our setting, lone inventors are those who work within large firms and that are listed as single inventors on a patent. To examine whether basic Internet adoption is associated with an increase in single-inventor patents, the authors reestimate the within-location equation using only single-authored patents.

name: R&D team experience diversity
authors_terms: ["experience diversity", "team experience diversity", "Team experience diversity", "diversity in task-related experience"]
definition: Team diversity is defined as an arrangement in which a team possesses different types of endowments—in this case, different types of task-related experience; diversity in task-related experience is a key dimension of diversity.

name: R&D team performance
definition: The speed of an F1 race car is key to race performance, which strongly depends on the R&D teams' work; the authors operationalize R&D teams' performance using the percentage deviation of their cars' qualifying time from that of the fastest car during the qualifying session.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "constructor size", "size of the firm", "size of an organization"]
definition: Firm size is considered to affect innovation positively because large firms have more resources available than small firms; the authors follow prior literature and proxy this measure by the annual budget (in constant USD) available to constructors.

name: Firm age
definition: This measure captures the age of the constructor, which is defined as the number of years elapsed from foundation. As firms become older they accumulate valuable experience, but firm age is also associated with greater structural inertia, local searches for solutions, and low adaptation to environmental changes.

name: Partner-to-junior ratio
authors_terms: ["partner-to-junior ratio", "leverage ratio", "partner-to-associate ratio", "promotion ratio", "ratio of junior lawyers to equity partners"]
definition: The ratio of equity partners to junior lawyers, where junior lawyers include associates and nonequity partners; the authors note that the industry calls its inverse the 'leverage ratio.' The model's promotion ratio (the proportion of juniors promoted to partner) is positively proportional to the partner-to-junior ratio.

name: Pro bono activity
authors_terms: ["pro bono", "pro bono activity", "pro bono work", "pro bono intensity", "pro bono services", "pro bono engagements"]
definition: Pro bono work is defined by The American Lawyer as legal services provided to those who could not otherwise afford them. The authors describe it as the most common type of socially responsible initiative in professional service industries.

name: Ranking stability
authors_terms: ["ranking stability", "temporal stability in rankings", "stability in rankings", "status stability in a given ranking"]
definition: The more rankings present temporal stability (so that the same candidates appear in the same positions year after year), the more the information they provide is already known and taken for granted. Our ranking stability measure is the average among ranked analysts of the number of years that they have each been ranked in the past.

name: Category change
authors_terms: ["category change", "changing a category", "structural change in rankings", "changes in the category structure"]
definition: The structural change we study is whether II changes a category in a given year - specifically, whether it drops the category, merges it with another, or splits it into two categories.

name: Selection threshold
definition: The selection threshold, Pg*, represents the economic and strategic dimensions of selection, and a firm is defined to be more selective if Pg* is higher. The firm will take the compound into clinical trials if it expects a net profit from its development, i.e., if PgV - D > 0 or Pg > D/V; Pg* = D/V is a threshold that is a function of the expected net additional revenue V and development costs D.

name: Innovation performance
definition: Pg, the probability that a compound will pass clinical trials and receive FDA approval, is a random variable drawn from a distribution with a firm-specific mean, SLmu (the innovative capability of the firm); once selected, approval takes place with probability Pg. The log of the odds ratio, ln(Pg/(1-Pg)), is assumed normally distributed with mean SLmu and unit variance, and SLmu depends linearly on a set of independent variables Z.

name: Program research scale
authors_terms: ["Scale_program", "scale at the program level", "research scale at the level of the program", "program scale", "program-level economies of scale"]
definition: The authors hypothesize that there are program-level economies of scale: a company with long-standing arrangements with academic hospitals for trials in an indication will find it easier to develop another compound within that indication than in others, implying a lower development cost. It is measured as the cumulative number of past projects for that indication.

name: Firm research scale
authors_terms: ["Scale_firm", "scale at the level of the firm", "firm scale", "overall research scale of the firm", "firm research scale"]
definition: Henderson and Cockburn (1996) identify three types of economies in research, one of which is economies of scale at the level of the firm; a larger firm with a diverse research portfolio may enjoy knowledge spillovers, may have a larger chemical library, and may have better models for interpreting results. Scale at the level of the firm is measured by the total number of ongoing projects in all indications.

name: Research scope
authors_terms: ["Scope", "span of the research across research areas", "economies of scope"]
definition: The span of the research across research areas (scope), which the authors treat as one of the three types of economies in research, namely economies of scope across research programs of the firm. Scope is measured by the Herfindahl index of diversification of projects across indications, for the firm.

name: Firm type
authors_terms: ["firm type", "Established Pharma", "Pioneer Biotech", "Other Biotech", "Other Pharma", "biotech firms", "established pharmaceutical firms"]
definition: The pharmaceutical industry has two fundamentally different types of firms, the established pharmaceutical producers and the biotechnology companies, separated by a large gap in time of entry and by differences in origin, time of entry and development. The authors distinguish four types of companies: Pioneer Biotech, Other Biotech, Established Pharma and Other Pharma.

name: Licensed compound status
definition: The database records the licensor and licensee(s), and the authors consider a project 'licensed' only if the agreement was signed in preclinicals. A lemons problem would exist if firms systematically licensed inferior drugs and kept superior ones in-house, so the relevant comparison is whether licensed compounds are drawn from a different distribution than those that firms develop in-house.

name: Competitive dominance
authors_terms: ["winning", "competitive dominance", "industry distributions of wins", "frequency distributions of wins", "performance disparities"]
definition: Firm performance is conceptualized as 'winning', i.e., as the distribution of long-term frequencies of industry leadership, measured by rank orderings of total profit, profit rates, and returns to shareholders. A significant Gini can be interpreted as prima facie evidence of competitive dominance by one or a few firms.

name: Perfect competitive parity
definition: The null distribution referred to as perfect competitive parity is defined as the condition that, over t years, each competitor finishes first t/n times, or if t/n is not an integer, rounded to its nearest equivalent.

name: Stochastic parity
authors_terms: ["stochastic parity", "randomly generated distributions of wins", "random performance variation"]
definition: The null model that compares actual Gini coefficients with expected Ginis under the assumption of random assignments of wins; stochastic parity can be defined as performance consistent with random processes.

name: Pareto parity
definition: Pareto's income distribution theory proposed that, when individual incomes are ranked, the rank-income relationship follows the form I = cr - a. The authors speculate that a power law, with a between 1 and 2, comprises a reasonable expectation for firm performance, and adopt Pareto's formulation with a = 1.5 as a null model.

name: Natural parity
definition: The null model that compares business performance distributions with those in other competitive domains, on the suggestion that there exists some level of 'natural parity' (or 'ordinary disparity') which researchers working from conventional stochastic models would not observe.

name: Market uncertainty
authors_terms: ["market uncertainty", "category uncertainty", "uncertainty over the value of a complementary product market", "uncertainty over market potential"]
definition: Uncertainty over how much unmet or latent demand exists in the particular complementary product market and what its nature is. It arises from ambiguity over how customer preferences are distributed and the rates at which customer needs are met or satiated, and fluctuates with macro-environmental factors.

name: Investment in enabling complements
authors_terms: ["platform owner's investment in enabling complements", "Apple API investments", "investments to enable complements", "invest in enabling third-party complements"]
definition: The platform owner's investment to draw and enable third-party complements onto its platform, done for example by improving the interfaces allowing complements' connection to the platform. In this setting APIs are the modular interfaces, developed and made accessible by Apple, allowing developers to connect and leverage the technological components and functionalities offered by the iOS platform.

name: Current revenue of complements in the market
authors_terms: ["revenue currently generated by existing complements in the complementary product market", "high-value category", "in-the-moneyness", "current value of the complementary market"]
definition: The extent to which the underlying complementary product market is currently of high value, which the authors borrow from the option concept of in-the-moneyness: the more that the underlying asset (complementary product market) is currently of high value, the lower the likelihood that at exercise time the underlying asset will be of low value. Categories currently generating high revenues are expected to generate high revenues in the future.

name: Complement multi-homing
definition: A complement multi-homes when it operates on more than one platform. Multi-homing is not cost-free; the complementor has to incur costs either to design its products to be flexible enough to operate on different platforms or to incur additional costs as and when it needs to modify its products to operate on a different platform.

name: Fine-grained revenue information
authors_terms: ["option fine-grained learning", "fine-grained information about revenue of existing complements", "fine-grained information"]
definition: The extent to which information about a complement's revenue is fine-grained, broken down by revenue generated across different features of the complement, rather than coarse, for example in the form of total revenue. This fine-grained information provides more nuanced details about user preferences and specificity on what features are in demand for the particular platform in question.

name: Complement complexity
authors_terms: ["option complexity", "complexity in the complement's construction", "complexity in the complement C's attributes"]
definition: Complexity refers to the number of attributes offered by complement C and the interdependence between them. A complement is less complex when it consists of fewer attributes, and can be more complex, for example an elaborate game with multiple features and levels.

name: Corporate refocusing
definition: A reduction in a firm's diversification through a return to its core business; the authors call it the appropriate remedial action for firms that have diversified beyond their optimal levels.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["market value", "shareholder wealth", "excess returns", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal return"]
definition: The authors state that in an efficient capital market the effects of refocusing announcements reflect the long-term consequences of refocusing and will be unbiased, neither too high nor too low on average.

name: Overdiversification
definition: A firm is overdiversified when its diversification exceeds its optimal limit, the point at which the marginal costs of additional diversification equal its marginal benefits; every firm has a different optimal point, dictated by its resources. If firms are overdiversified, their profitability and market value must suffer.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm diversifies away from its basic business; the authors argue that the marginal benefits of diversification decrease and its marginal costs increase as a firm diversifies further and further from its basic businesses.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitability, measured as return on sales adjusted for the firm's industry-weighted return on sales; poor profitability is expected to characterize overdiversified companies.

name: Production in the chemical industry
authors_terms: ["more production in the chemical industry", "market share", "firm size", "size"]
definition: Past research has measured this tendency toward a dominant strategy using market share or firm size. The extent of production in an industry is not, however, the sole determinant.

name: Focus on chemical production
authors_terms: ["focus", "production focused in chemicals", "the degree to which each firm focused on chemical production"]
definition: The extent to which a company is diversified will mitigate its risk and may also reduce the extent to which it is associated with a given industry.

name: Firm visibility
authors_terms: ["visibility", "better-known brand or corporate names", "brand identity", "visible corporate names"]
definition: Brand identity (for instance, Clorox) and visible corporate names also represent valuable assets that could be tarnished by the collective image of an industry.

name: Relative emissions
authors_terms: ["relative emissions", "higher levels of pollution relative to their industries", "relative environmental performance"]
definition: The relative environmental performance of a facility is given by the standardized residual, or deviation, between observed emissions and predicted emissions, given the facility's size and industry sector. Thus, if a facility emits more than predicted for its size and SIC code, it will have a positive residual and a positive score for environmental impact.

name: Sector emissions
authors_terms: ["sector emissions", "industry sectors with higher average levels of pollution", "the dirtiness of a sector"]
definition: We calculated the dirtiness of a sector as the total emissions for the sector divided by the total number of employees in it.

name: Responsible Care participation
authors_terms: ["Responsible Care participation", "CMA membership", "participate in its Responsible Care Program", "participate in the CMA's Responsible Care Program"]
definition: All members of the CMA are required to adopt Responsible Care as a condition of membership. CMA membership, and thus participation in Responsible Care, was coded as a binary variable.

name: Environmental improvement
definition: To test hypotheses concerning Responsible Care's influence on the environmental performance of chemical firms, we created two measures of annual improvement in environmental performance.

name: Post-inception period
authors_terms: ["inception of the CMA's Responsible Care Program", "the years 1990-96", "dummy variable for the years 1990-96"]
definition: We divided our panel into two periods (1987-89 and 1990-96) by creating a dummy variable for the years 1990-96. The dummy variable for 1990-96 indicates whether there has been a change in the industry's rate of improvement since the inception of the Responsible Care program.

name: Outward centrality in a mobility network
authors_terms: ["outward centrality", "Mobility out-degree", "out-degree", "outward mobility", "outward centrality in a mobility network"]
definition: Outward centrality is based on the mobility of employees who leave the focal firm: the higher the number of companies to which its former employees move to work, the higher the outward centrality of this organization in the mobility network.

name: Inward centrality in a mobility network
definition: Inward mobility is based on the mobility of employees who join the focal firm: the higher the number of companies from which it hires employees, the higher its inward centrality.

name: Organizational creative performance
definition: An organization's creative performance can be defined as its ability to produce ideas, products, or services that relevant observers perceive as novel and useful.

name: Creative director tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure of creative directors", "creative directors' tenure", "Tenure (director)", "organizational tenure"]
definition: One specific characteristic that may affect chief executives' information processing and decision making is their organizational tenure, which is associated with the strength of the chief executive's 'paradigm'-a model of how an organization's environment behaves, what options are feasible, and how the organization should be run.

name: Creative director accomplishments
authors_terms: ["accomplishments of creative directors", "creative directors' accomplishments", "Star (director)", "certification contests"]
definition: Accomplishments are made visible to the industry through 'certification contests' in which reputable third parties evaluate executives; creative directors are similarly evaluated through certification contests whereby their creative output receives awards.

name: Firm status
definition: The favorability of such perceptions, in turn, depends on a firm's status, which acts as a signal of its quality (Podolny 1993). Status positively affects a firm's performance as a result of the 'halo effect', where external stakeholders, such as distributors, critics, media, and end consumers, attribute expertise to high-status firms and view their behavior as more legitimate than that of other firms.

name: National system
definition: The complex milieu of interrelated social and economic factors, or institutions, that characterize the nation state within which a firm is principally located, or headquartered.

name: CEO effect
definition: In this stream of research, and in our paper, a CEO effect within a particular sample is the proportion of variance in a firm-level outcome variable that is statistically associated with, or can be attributed to, the presence of individual CEOs in the sample.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance indicators encompassing both accounting-based and market-based measures: return on assets, return on sales, sales growth, and market-to-book.

name: Perceived cultural compatibility
authors_terms: ["perceived cultural compatibility", "PCC", "perceived attractiveness of the buying firm's culture", "perceptions of cultural compatibility"]
definition: A construct that is intended to capture, at the top management team unit of analysis, the three social movement judgments (what was, what is, and what ought to be) into a single, continuously scaled measure, ranging from highly attractive to highly unattractive.

name: Removal of autonomy
authors_terms: ["removal of autonomy", "autonomy removal", "perceptions of autonomy removal"]
definition: The degree to which the strategy, systems, and procedures associated with the management of the acquired firms are removed from their discretion.

name: Relative size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "size of the acquired firm relative to the size of the buying firm"]
definition: The approximate size of the buying firm relative to the acquired firm at the time of the merger, as perceived by managers of the acquired firm; a small acquisition presents Frank's classic case of a big fish in a small pond.

name: Post-merger performance
definition: The acquired firm's performance since, and because of, the merger, as reported by the acquired firm's managers.

name: Relative standing
authors_terms: ["relative standing", "theory of relative standing", "diminished relative standing"]
definition: The theory asserts that the status individuals feel for themselves in a social setting is based on how they compare their status to others in a proximate social setting; the authors directly assess three perceptual indicators of relative standing among acquired executives.

name: National culture of the acquired firm
authors_terms: ["national culture", "home culture", "Nationality of the acquired firm"]
definition: The national culture in which the acquired managers' organizational culture is nested; the relationship between perceptions of relative standing and the acquired firm's performance may be contingent upon the acquired managers' home culture.

name: National cultural difference between merging firms
definition: A cross-national merger brings together two companies which themselves have different organizational cultures, but also two companies whose organizational cultures may be nested in different national cultures.

name: Corporate venture capital investment
authors_terms: ["corporate venture capital", "CVC", "Firm Sector CVC", "equity investment in new ventures", "investment in new ventures"]
definition: Corporate venture capital investments consist of minority equity stakes in relatively new, not publicly traded companies that are seeking capital to continue operation. The authors focus on firms' external innovative inputs and measure the amount a firm invests in ventures operating in a given sector.

name: Technological opportunity
definition: The marginal benefit of CVC should be greater from investments in ventures from industries with rich technological opportunities, that is, when 'technical advance, at prevailing input prices, is less costly' (Cohen, 1995). The level of technological opportunity is affected first and foremost by advancements in basic science and underlying technological fields.

name: Intellectual property protection
definition: A weak IP regime is one where ventures struggle to protect their inventions from imitation through legal mechanisms such as patents (Cohen et al., 2001). The IP Regime variable reflects the relative importance of patenting as a way to protect intellectual property, so that a higher value means patents are more effective in protecting inventors' profits.

name: Complementary assets
definition: Sectors differ in whether complementary capabilities (e.g., in manufacturing or distribution) are important to appropriate the returns to innovation; complementary assets are more tightly held by incumbents in sectors where large-scale manufacturing and distribution are important. CA Importance reflects the relative importance of complementary assets in bringing an innovation to market.

name: Cash flow
definition: Cash flow is a measure of the availability of funds; since insiders have superior knowledge of investment opportunities and outsiders recognize this information asymmetry, the cost of financing investment via external funds is higher than the cost of internal funding.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: Absorptive capacity is the ability of an investing firm to transfer or create knowledge through its interaction with a venture, which likely requires sufficient technical understanding to both grasp and capitalize on that knowledge. As originally conceived it is not a state variable but is domain-specific, so a firm may possess absorptive capacity in one domain of knowledge but lack it in another.

name: Presence of champions
definition: This study defines a championing role as one in which an individual strongly advocates a research and development (R&D) project and generates positive behavioral support for it or work on its behalf. The championing role exists even when others in the organization are neutral about or opposed to supporting the project.

name: Presence of antagonists
definition: The antagonist's role is one in which an individual strongly opposes a project and generates negative feelings about it, even when the project receives organizational support.

name: Project origination
definition: The source of suggestion for a project is part of the idea generation process, and projects may originate from a variety of sources, including R&D, marketing, or customer. For hypothesis testing the coding distinguishes between projects that R&D sources alone suggested and those that business sources outside R&D, including customers, suggested.

name: Project radicalness
definition: Radical projects are those with which the firm has little technical experience and that do not fit the business practices of the firm. Incremental projects are those with which the firm has technical and business experience.

name: Project type
definition: The study assessed the project's nature by requesting that participants choose one or more of four categories: establish new product, establish a new process, make recognizable changes to an existing product, and make recognizable changes to an existing process. By collapsing products together and processes together, the response was coded 1 for product, 2 for mixed, and 3 for process.

name: Resource allocation to a project
definition: Respondents indicated how frequently management assigned additional resources to a project, addressing assignment of additional personnel, increases in the budget, replacement of project members, and changes in the project team leader. A higher score indicated the addition of higher levels of resources for a project.

name: Project termination
definition: This measure detects whether a firm discontinued a project. One of the most difficult decisions in R&D management is the decision to terminate a project, and a political behavior interpretation suggests that champions and antagonists fight to advance a project regardless of its performance.

name: Project performance
definition: This study used seven items to assess the project's overall impact on representative business goals: profitability, sales volume, product cost, market position, employee benefits, stockholder benefits, and firm image. A higher score indicates a more positive performance impact.

name: Team performance
definition: A useful feature of esports as an empirical setting is that a team's performance in a match can be gauged objectively based on whether they won or lost.

name: Prior collaborative experience
authors_terms: ["prior collaborative experience", "prior collaboration", "collaborative experience", "team familiarity", "prior collaborative tie"]
definition: These teams often vary in their members' collaborative experience (sometimes referred to as team familiarity): when a new team is formed, some members might or might not have previously collaborated by virtue of belonging to the same pool of potential participants.

name: Tightly coupled prior collaboration
authors_terms: ["tightly coupled collaborative experience", "tightly coupled prior collaboration", "tightly coupled roles"]
definition: We make a binary distinction between tightly coupled pairs of roles that display high interdependence and loosely coupled ones that display low interdependence, although our arguments also apply to cases where interdependence varies continuously.

name: Loosely coupled prior collaboration
authors_terms: ["loosely coupled collaborative experience", "loosely coupled prior collaboration", "loosely coupled roles"]
definition: We make a binary distinction between tightly coupled pairs of roles that display high interdependence and loosely coupled ones that display low interdependence, although our arguments also apply to cases where interdependence varies continuously.

name: Task environment change
authors_terms: ["task environment change", "unfamiliar task environment", "game update", "patch", "post patch"]
definition: Game updates are modifications to the game code by Valve Corporation, its developer, that change the mapping from the players' actions to their outcomes in the game and hence affect the way players experience the game.

name: Family firm status
definition: We initially define family firms as those in which a firm's founder or a member of his/her family by blood or marriage is an officer, director, or blockholder.

name: Likelihood of hedge fund activism
authors_terms: ["Activist Targeted", "likelihood of activist hedge fund campaigns", "initiate campaigns"]
definition: Activist Targeted takes the value one if an activist hedge fund initiated a campaign against a firm in a given year, and zero otherwise.

name: Investor reaction to campaign announcements
definition: CAR is the cumulative sum of abnormal returns during an event window surrounding the announcement of a particular event (in our case, the announcement of an activist hedge fund campaign). Abnormal returns are the difference between a firm's expected and actual returns during the event window, where expected returns are predicted based on the firm's and the stock market's returns during an estimation window that occurred well prior to the event window.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["high growth firms", "low growth firms", "growth in sales revenues", "performance"]
definition: Secondary data from Inc, Standard & Poor, and Dun & Bradstreet were used to determine the compound rate of growth of sales revenues, our measure of 'performance'.

name: Relatedness to incubator organization
authors_terms: ["relatedness of product/market/technology choice", "closely related to the founder(s)' incubator organization", "incubator organizations"]
definition: Founders were asked to categorize the degree to which the product/market/technology of their start-up firm was related to that of the last firm the founder(s) worked for before starting their present firm.

name: Founding team size
authors_terms: ["size of founding team", "larger teams", "started by teams"]
definition: The number of individuals included on the initial team of founders was reported categorically.

name: Stability of initial product focus
authors_terms: ["stability of initial product focus", "stability of focus", "initial product/market focus"]
definition: Founders were asked to indicate the extent to which the initial product/market focus of their firm had changed since founding.

name: Early market entry
definition: The founders were asked to indicate the degree to which they attempted to gain first-mover advantages through an early entry strategy by describing the timing of their entry.

name: Geographic scope
definition: Founders were asked to indicate the percentage of their firm's sales revenues derived from foreign sales.

name: Acquisitiveness
definition: Founders were asked to indicate the extent to which acquisition had been a part of their firm's growth strategy by indicating categorically the number of acquisitions they had completed during the 5-year period.

name: Repeated partnerships
authors_terms: ["repeated partnerships", "repeated relationships", "repeated equity-based partnerships", "propensity to enter into repeated relations with prior partners", "repeated equity-based relationships"]
definition: The propensity of firms to enter into repeated equity-based relationships with prior partners, a key factor in the development of networks. It is accessed by counting the firm's repeated equity-based relationships with home-country and with host-country firms, and their total.

name: Economic performance
authors_terms: ["economic performance", "corporate economic performance", "firm economic performance", "firm performance"]
definition: Although it is widely recognized that firms pursue multidimensional goals, a mainstream view is that firms are fundamentally concerned with economic results; the authors therefore use several commonly used measures of performance.

name: Technical uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technical uncertainty", "technological uncertainty", "technological turbulence", "rate of technological change"]
definition: A key aspect of business environments; the percentage change in the number of patents in industry i between periods t and t-1 is a signal of the rate of technological change experienced by firms in that industry.

name: Interfirm modularity
definition: Following Sanchez and Mahoney (1996), we define interfirm modularity as the looseness of coupling between the outsourced project and outsourcing firm's technological portfolio with which it has functional, procedural, or informational interdependencies.

name: Outsourcee ignorance
authors_terms: ["outsourcee ignorance", "ignorance", "outsourcee ignorance of the outsourcing firm's private knowledge"]
definition: The outsourcee-while technically competent-might lack idiosyncratic knowledge of the project's business problem domain. We refer to the outsourcee firm's lack of such project-specific private knowledge as outsourcee ignorance.

name: Alliance performance
definition: Alliance performance assessed project outcomes in terms of system reliability, functionality, meeting planned objectives and requirements, and overall fit with outsourcer needs.

name: Seeking knowledge across subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["sought knowledge", "deciding whether to seek knowledge across subsidiaries", "decision to seek knowledge"]
definition: Whether a focal team in a focal subsidiary contacts other subsidiaries to inquire about potentially useful knowledge for a project; project managers indicated whether team members had sought knowledge in any of the other subsidiaries except the focal one.

name: Within-team network density
authors_terms: ["within-team network density", "density of a within-team network"]
definition: The number of ongoing established relations among team members, divided by the total possible number of such relations.

name: Within-team relation strength
authors_terms: ["average strength of relations in a within-team network", "average within-team relation strength"]
definition: The average strength of relations in the within-team network, that is, the frequency and intensity of interactions among team members.

name: Intersubsidiary network size
authors_terms: ["intersubsidiary network size", "the larger a focal team's intersubsidiary network"]
definition: The number of direct established relations a focal team has with other subsidiaries; the larger the network, the higher the number of direct intersubsidiary relations.

name: Intersubsidiary relation strength
authors_terms: ["average intersubsidiary relation strength", "average relation strength in a focal team's intersubsidiary network"]
definition: The average strength of the established relations in a focal team's intersubsidiary network; a set of relations with high average strength involves direct contacts that are themselves connected, whereas low average strength involves infrequent and nonintense interactions.

name: Perceived competition between subsidiaries
definition: A team and its subsidiary may compete with another subsidiary in the sense that both subsidiaries sell products to the same external markets and seek to develop the same types of products and technologies; perceptions of this competition are asymmetric across the two parties.

name: Dyadic transfer relation strength
authors_terms: ["dyadic transfer relation strength", "strength of dyadic transfer relations", "strength of the established relation between a team and the providing subsidiaries"]
definition: The strength of the established relation between a focal team and a subsidiary providing it with knowledge; when two parties to a transfer have developed a strong relation prior to the transfer effort, they have likely developed a shared communication frame.

name: Tacitness of transferred knowledge
definition: Tacit knowledge is knowledge that is difficult to articulate or that can only be acquired through experience.

name: Search costs
definition: Search costs are measured as the number of engineering-months that a product development team spends on search, an activity that involves looking for, identifying, and evaluating knowledge resident in other subsidiaries.

name: Transfer costs
definition: Transfer costs are measured as the number of engineering-months a team spends on the transfer process, which involves modifying, editing, and incorporating the knowledge into the team's product.

name: New firm entry
authors_terms: ["new firm entry", "entry", "gross entry", "rates of new firm entry"]
definition: New firm entry refers to the establishment of operations in an industry by a firm that did not exist prior to its entrance into that industry. It is a measure of gross entry since it includes all firms new to an industry rather than the number of new firms net of firms exiting the industry (net entry).

name: Pollution regulation compliance requirements
authors_terms: ["industry pollution regulation compliance requirements", "pollution abatement intensity", "pollution control requirements", "pollution regulation"]
definition: Pollution abatement intensity served as a proxy for pollution regulation compliance requirements. This operational definition represents the degree to which the studied industries were affected by, and reacted to, the pollution abatement compliance requirements established by environmental regulations.

name: Founder control
authors_terms: ["founder control", "control index", "degree of control retained by founders", "control of the CEO position", "control of the board of directors"]
definition: Control comes in both ex ante form and ex post form, with ex ante control driven by board representation and ex post control indicated by whether the founder has been replaced as CEO.

name: Startup value
authors_terms: ["company value", "value of the startup", "value creation", "company valuation", "total amount of capital raised"]
definition: Two different metrics are used to estimate the value of the company: most recent company valuation and total amount of capital raised.

name: Prior founding experience
authors_terms: ["prior founding experience", "the core founder has prior founding experience"]
definition: Core founders who have accumulated direct human capital in the form of prior founding experience should be able to keep more control.

name: Founder network hiring
authors_terms: ["tapped social networks to attract executive hires", "attracted executive hires", "tapping social networks to find executive hires"]
definition: The core founder's tapping of personal networks (social capital) to attract employees to the startup.

name: Founding team size
authors_terms: ["size of the founding team", "number of founders", "the larger the founding team"]
definition: The number of founders on the startup's founding team.

name: Cofounder work experience
authors_terms: ["cofounders' prior years of work experience", "more experienced the cofounders", "founding team's total years of prior work experience"]
definition: The prior work experience accumulated by the startup's cofounders, measured across the founding team.

name: Non-founding executive experience
authors_terms: ["non-founding executives", "exec hires' prior years of work experience", "more experienced the non-founding executives"]
definition: The prior work experience of the non-founding executives hired into the startup.

name: Venture capital financing
authors_terms: ["venture capitalists invested in last round of financing", "raise capital from venture capitalists", "VC backing", "VCs invested in last round"]
definition: Startups that raise capital from venture capitalists, who are known for providing value-added services to their portfolio companies and who demand less founder-friendly investment terms.

name: Angel investor financing
authors_terms: ["angels invested in last round of financing", "raise capital from angel investors", "angel capital"]
definition: Angel investors provide much less capital than do venture capitalists, take smaller equity stakes, and rely on more informal methods of control.

name: Industry segment capital intensity
authors_terms: ["segment's capital intensity", "capital-intensive industry segments", "high capital intensity"]
definition: The degree to which the startup's industry segment is capital intensive, which determines how critical it is to attract resources in order to grow value and thus how much control the company should have to give up.

name: Startup age
authors_terms: ["company age", "startup age", "as startups age", "younger and older startups"]
definition: How far the startup has evolved since founding; the need for, and potential impact of, attracting new skills should increase as the startup evolves.

name: Membership continuity
authors_terms: ["membership continuity", "continuity", "expected continued membership", "decision to stay in or leave"]
definition: The unit of analysis is the member organization, and the authors operationalize continuity as the expectation to remain a member of an R&D consortium.

name: Satisfaction with consortium performance
authors_terms: ["satisfaction with the performance of an R&D consortium", "satisfaction", "performance", "members' evaluations of a consortium's performance"]
definition: The authors investigate the influence of performance on consortium membership and contend that a positive relationship exists between satisfaction with the R&D consortium's performance and continuity in its membership; organizations more satisfied with an R&D consortium's performance are proposed to be more likely to continue their membership.

name: Importance of membership
authors_terms: ["importance of membership", "importance of the relationship or resources", "importance of the research"]
definition: A resource is important when it is a key part of the organization's operations and related to its primary focus or function; a resource is considered critical when it is a key part of the focal organization's operations or function or the extent to which the organization requires it for continued operation and survival.

name: Availability of alternatives
authors_terms: ["alternatives to an R&D consortium", "alternatives to the arrangement", "number of alternatives"]
definition: An organization's dependence on a specific relationship is also a function of the alternatives it has for obtaining the needed resources.

name: Knowledge-related involvement
