definition: In R&D collaboration, transaction-specific involvement generally consists of human or knowledge-related assets, and these assets may lead the contributing organization to remain in the relationship; the authors label control over or contribution of these assets 'knowledge-related involvement'.

name: Nonknowledge-related involvement
definition: Other assets are not likely to become transaction-specific, and discretion over less transaction-specific assets (e.g. financing, technical equipment) is likely to become a source of power that will decrease the likelihood of continuity; the authors consider providing nontransaction-specific assets to be nonknowledge-related involvement.

name: Learning from the consortium
definition: The authors' interest in member learning within a consortium relates to whether a member organization can develop or obtain information that will reduce its dependence on the consortium and lead to its departure; learning represents an outcome central to many members' participation in joint ventures.

name: Network ties
authors_terms: ["network relations", "network ties", "concurrent relationships", "additional relationship with another member"]
definition: In addition to the conditions identified by the power dependence perspective, transaction cost theory and network research identify a fourth condition: concurrent relations with other member organizations, i.e. the relationships a member organization has, in addition to the focal consortium, with another member.

name: Membership conditions
authors_terms: ["membership conditions", "conditions of membership", "conditions surrounding membership", "member conditions"]
definition: The decision to continue depends upon the nature of the membership in the venture and the context surrounding the membership: specifically, the degree of a member's dependence on the relationship and of commitments to the venture or to other partners. Because this decision encompasses not only the context surrounding the membership but also the nature of the relationship itself, the authors label this membership conditions.

name: Organizational ambidexterity
definition: The predominant view in this literature defines ambidexterity as firms' capability to balance, or simultaneously pursue, exploration and exploitation.

name: Change in exploration-exploitation allocation
authors_terms: ["exploration-exploitation change", "degree of change in the exploration-exploitation allocation"]
definition: The degree of change in the exploration-exploitation allocation in the subsequent period; exploration-exploitation change was operationalized as the difference between a firm's exploitation at t-1 and exploitation at t.

name: Unabsorbed slack
definition: Unabsorbed slack, which refers to uncommitted, ready-to-deploy assets, is suggested to be best applied to organizational ambidexterity.

name: Maintaining high levels of ambidexterity
definition: To measure maintaining high levels of ambidexterity, the authors calculated ambidexterity's arithmetic mean over three periods; maintaining ambidexterity is argued to result in returns from coalignment and learning in incremental change contexts.

name: Long-term firm performance
definition: Following most prior ambidexterity studies' approach to assess long-term firm performance, the authors rely on firms' accounting performance.

name: Exploration
definition: Exploration, which relates to 'things captured by terms such as search, variation, ... and experimentation', enables firms to adapt and embrace new knowledge.

name: Exploitation
definition: Exploitation, which refers to 'things [such] as refinement, ... selection, [and] implementation', allows firms to increase their operational efficiency.

name: Commitment to the status quo
authors_terms: ["commitment to the status quo", "CSQ", "adherence to existing strategy and leadership profiles", "belief in the enduring correctness of current organizational strategies and profiles"]
definition: Commitment to the status quo is 'belief in the enduring correctness of current organizational strategies and profiles'. Two organizational profiles shaped by executives are examined: organizational strategy and leadership.

name: Individualism
definition: A key dimension along which cultures differ concerns interpersonal relations: in cultures with strong individualist values, societal members perceive themselves largely as individual actors, and social norms typically affirm the positive qualities of individual achievement and personal discretion. By contrast, in societies emphasizing collectivist values, interpersonal relationships and group affiliation are highly touted.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: The value dimension of uncertainty avoidance concerns response to unstructured and ambiguous contexts. In high uncertainty avoidance cultures, societal members tend to feel uncomfortable dealing with uncertainty, so preferences lean toward greater structure, together with clear rules and standardized operating procedures.

name: Masculinity
definition: This value dimension addresses two issues: gender roles and qualities often ascribed to them. Hofstede's examination revealed significant differences in the extent to which cultures emphasize so-called 'masculine' qualities of assertiveness, ambition, and competition over more 'feminine' ones of modesty, caring, and solidarity.

name: Power distance
definition: The value dimension of power distance addresses the issue of social (in)equality. Cultures with low power distance values are typically more egalitarian in nature, while high power distance cultures are characterized by significant inequalities among their constituents.

name: Long-term orientation
authors_terms: ["long-term vs. short-term orientation", "long-term oriented values", "Confucian dynamism", "short-term orientation"]
definition: This fifth cultural dimension, also known as Confucian dynamism, refers to preferences between a forward-looking vs. more historical perspective. Cultures maintaining a long-term orientation are characterized by values emphasizing the future, including thrift and perseverance.

name: Exposure to comparative political information
authors_terms: ["exposure to comparative political information", "comparative political information", "presidential election"]
definition: Candidates campaign to influence voters during all elections, but particularly during presidential election years. Consequently, citizens are exposed to a substantial amount of information (largely media advertising, as well as nationally televised debates and seemingly incessant media commentary) that compares and contrasts candidates.

name: Managerial spending
authors_terms: ["managerial spending", "spending levels", "firm advertising spending level", "advertising spending", "training spending"]
definition: Once managers have made decisions on whether and which to purchase, they often need to decide how much to spend. For example, if a manager decides to advertise a product, they must then decide how much to spend on advertising.

name: Importance of negative information
authors_terms: ["importance of negative information", "reduced importance of negative information", "importance of negative attributes", "negative attribute importance"]
definition: In the whether-to-buy step, decision makers attach more weight to negative information than to positive information. However, when exposure to comparative political information predisposes decision makers to proceed directly to the which-to-buy step, the importance of negative information is likely to reduce.

name: Decision frame
authors_terms: ["decision frame", "rejection decision frame", "selection frame", "rejection versus selection"]
definition: If the individual's task is to reject undesirable or unacceptable options from a set of alternatives, then negative information might remain prominent. The literature has suggested that a rejection decision frame leads to greater focus on the negative attributes of the choice options.

name: Choice likelihood
definition: As a result, the whether-to-buy step is likely to be skipped altogether, which increases the likelihood of making a choice.

name: Firm headquarters location
authors_terms: ["U.S. headquarters", "headquartered in the United States", "headquartered outside the United States"]
definition: Our control group was a sample of non-U.S. firms operating during the same period as our U.S. firms, but whose headquarters were located outside the United States.

name: Temporal proximity to an election
definition: The intensity of campaign activities and voter attention to political information increases as Election Day approaches.

name: TQM implementation
authors_terms: ["degree of implementation of TQM practices", "degree of TQM practices implemented", "TQM practices", "degree to which TQM had been implemented"]
definition: The degree to which a comprehensive set of seven TQM practices has been implemented within an organization; the practices function as an interdependent system that supports the TQM philosophy.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational financial performance, adjusted for industry effects, used as a proxy for the supranormal rents associated with competitive advantage. The authors also use an industry-expert rating of hospital processes as an alternative proxy for competitive advantages gained through successful TQM programs.

name: Structural control
definition: The degree that the organizational structure emphasizes the control of procedures, systems, and job descriptions.

name: Structural exploration
definition: The exploration capability of the organizations with respect to allowing the flow of financial and operating information throughout the organization and the freedom to depart from past practices to adapt to a changing environment.

name: Heir apparent appointment
authors_terms: ["heir apparent appointment", "appointment of the heir apparent", "initiation of the process"]
definition: The appointment of the heir apparent signals the existence of a succession plan and the initiation of a relay succession process, and an heir apparent is an inside or outside executive who is the only person appointed as the president and/or COO of the firm and who is at least 5 years younger than the CEO.

name: Heir apparent promotion
authors_terms: ["heir apparent promotion", "promotion of the heir apparent", "promotion of the heir to the CEO position"]
definition: A well-managed relay succession is consummated with the promotion of the heir to the CEO position; this is the expected outcome of a relay succession process.

name: Heir apparent exit
authors_terms: ["heir apparent exit", "exit of the heir apparent", "heir apparent unexpectedly leaves the firm prior to promotion"]
definition: Many relay succession processes are interrupted by the unexpected exit of the heir apparent, that is, the heir apparent leaves the firm prior to being promoted to the CEO position.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is an important factor influencing the wealth effect of CEO succession, and it was measured as the return on assets (ROA) during the fiscal year prior to the year when the event of interest occurred.

name: Shareholder wealth
authors_terms: ["change in shareholder wealth", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "wealth effect"]
definition: Change in shareholder wealth was measured by abnormal returns, where a firm's daily abnormal return is the difference between the firm's actual daily return and the return predicted by the market model using the estimated parameters.

name: Nonrelay inside succession
authors_terms: ["nonrelay inside succession", "nonheir inside succession", "nonheir inside CEO promotion"]
definition: An inside CEO succession in which the new successor is not an heir apparent; the authors note that prior studies did not differentiate heir successors from nonheir inside successors.

name: Outside succession
definition: CEO succession in which the firm origin of the successor is outside the firm, i.e., the insider vs. outsider distinction in successor origin.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "proportion of outside board members", "board independence (narrow)"]
definition: Board independence is defined as the proportion of outside board members (directors who have never served as executive director, executive officer, employee of the company or any of its subsidiaries, as reported in the companies' annual report) over the total board size.

name: External audit fees
definition: Audit fees reflect the amount paid by the company for the professional examination and verification of the financial statements for the purpose of assessing their consistency, fairness, and conformation to accepted accounting principles. The dependent variable, total audit fees, is the natural log of audit fees.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Foreign ownership reflects the percentage of total outstanding shares held by non-Japanese investors. The measure captures institutional ownership from shareholder-oriented countries (United States and the U.K.).

name: Domestic ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["largest domestic shareholder", "domestic ownership concentration", "large domestic owners", "SH1 domestic"]
definition: Defined as the total stake of the largest domestic owner, which the authors treat as domestic ownership concentration and as a key potential deterrent of changes in board monitoring.

name: Firm risk
definition: Following Zajac and Westphal (1994) and Laeven and Levine (2009), the authors calculate firm risk as the annualized standard deviation of weekly equity returns.

name: Deviation from prior performance
definition: The authors focus on the deviation from prior performance, captured as the current performance compared with the average of the prior two years' performance, following Tuggle et al. (2010), where performance is measured with return on assets.

name: Supplier technical capabilities
authors_terms: ["technical capabilities", "technical capability", "a supplier's technical capabilities", "capabilities of suppliers"]
definition: Potential suppliers may differ in their technical capabilities and, thus, in their ability to produce a component according to the desired specifications and schedule. Firms develop capabilities by carrying out related activities repeatedly (Nelson and Winter, 1982; Nonaka and Takeuchi, 1995); differences in past activities thus lead to heterogeneous capabilities.

name: Prior transactions
authors_terms: ["prior transactions", "past transactions", "past interactions", "past experience", "extent of past transactions", "years of experience"]
definition: Thus, a buyer and supplier should be better able to address challenges of communication and governance the more they have transacted in the past. Past interactions improve communication between buyer and supplier in several ways and also reduce the cost of governance by building trust, by which I mean the expectation that one's exchange partner will not act opportunistically for one or more social, psychological, or economic reasons.

name: Internal supplier
authors_terms: ["internal supplier", "internal vs. external", "buyer and supplier belonging to the same firm", "common firm membership", "internal supply", "internalization"]
definition: Transaction cost economics argues that when the buyer and supplier belong to the same firm, challenges in governance are mitigated. Within the firm, governance costs are lowered by distinctive governance mechanisms including managerial fiat, a greater legal burden on employees as opposed to contractors to disclose information, and judicial forbearance; belonging to the same firm can also reduce communication costs.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technical uncertainty", "technological uncertainty", "uncertainty of the desired innovation", "perceived uncertainty"]
definition: The cost lines slope upwards because greater uncertainty increases the costs of governance and communication over the development cycle for an innovative component. In the context of technological innovation, uncertainty will be high when the desired innovation requires large advances beyond the current technological frontier.

name: Supplier selection
authors_terms: ["supplier choice", "supplier selection", "probability of the buyer choosing that supplier", "likelihood of a buyer choosing that supplier"]
definition: In the set of observations related to a manufacturer's introduction of a given innovation, this indicator variable was set to 0 for all suppliers except the one the manufacturer chose. Note that while a buyer may eventually use a number of suppliers for a given type of display, I focus on the single supplier used in a manufacturer's initial introduction of a notebook with a given display type.

name: Patenting activity
authors_terms: ["patent application stock", "patent filings", "patenting activities", "successful patent applications"]
definition: Patent application stock is defined as the number of applications filed by a focal start-up at time t that eventually result in the successful award of a U.S. patent. The authors measure a start-up's patenting activities based on its annual stock of successful patent applications, which allows private investors to respond to information revealed in patent applications prior to the several year delay typically required for the review process.

name: Founder prior IPO experience
authors_terms: ["prior IPO experience of founders", "founding team has no prior IPO experience", "founder entrepreneurial success", "initial reputation endowments"]
definition: Prior entrepreneurial success of the founding team, proxied by the prior IPO experience of founders and used by the authors to capture a start-up's 'high initial reputation endowment'. Founders with IPO experience are more likely to realize successful IPO exits and are advantaged when seeking capital from external sources, while start-ups lacking such experience face a wider information gap with investors.

name: Prominent VC backing
authors_terms: ["prominent VC investor", "prominent VC backing", "not backed by prominent VC", "VC prominence"]
definition: Backing by venture capital investors of high prominence; while the financial capital supplied by venture capitalists is relatively homogenous, VCs differ significantly in the quality of 'extra-financial' services they provide that aid in the growth and development of young companies. The authors code a lead investor as prominent if it falls in the upper half of the within-sample distribution of VC network centrality.

name: Reputation endowment
authors_terms: ["initial reputation endowments", "reputation endowments", "reputational advantages", "alternative quality signals"]
definition: Start-ups with superior reputation endowments, as conferred by founder backgrounds or third-party affiliations, are preferentially positioned to attract the resources required for growth and survival. In the IPO analysis the authors use low reputation endowments as inherited from founders or leased through prominent VC backing.

name: Start-up valuation
authors_terms: ["premoney valuation", "venture valuations", "investor estimates of start-up value"]
definition: Investor estimates of entrepreneurial-firm value, measured as the product of a start-up's share price before the funding round multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. A higher valuation in a focal funding round is good news for existing equity holders, as the wedge between the acquisition and current share price is larger.

name: Funding round stage
authors_terms: ["stage of financing", "early funding round", "earlier (versus later) funding rounds"]
definition: The stage of a start-up's financing; early stages of funding are characterized by greater technical and demand uncertainty in new venture product development, and as start-ups proceed through multiple funding rounds more information about their profit potential is revealed to investors. Early funding rounds denote first or second rounds.

name: IPO underpricing
authors_terms: ["underpricing", "discount placed on their equity offering", "percentage change in first-day stock price"]
definition: Such discounting or 'underpricing' occurs when the initial price at which shares are offered to public investors is significantly lower than the actual share price at the end of the first day of trading. The underpricing of initial share prices gauges the degree of asymmetric information between new listings and potential investors.

name: Regulatory restrictiveness
definition: Restrictiveness is the amount of regulation that prohibits specific activities and the technological components associated with them. In restrictive regulatory environments, firms are limited in what they are allowed to do and how they are allowed to do it.

name: Regulatory uncertainty
definition: Regulatory uncertainty is unpredictability about the set of activities that will remain permissible for firms in the forthcoming regulatory environment. It is also defined as unpredictability about the future caused by changes in industry policies.

name: Consolidating innovation
definition: Consolidating innovations are innovations that improve and refine existing technologies, often by using familiar technological components.

name: Destabilizing innovation
definition: Destabilizing innovations are innovations that challenge existing technologies, often by incorporating new technological components discovered from search.

name: Discontinuous risk
authors_terms: ["discontinuous risk", "disasters", "disaster severity", "terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and technological disasters"]
definition: We define discontinuous risk as the possibility that a disaster, which is episodic and often difficult to anticipate or predict, might occur and may have a substantial impact on a firm and its operating environment.

name: Disaster experience
authors_terms: ["experience in disasters", "disaster-specific experience", "firm experience with a specific type of disaster", "firm experience with discontinuous risks"]
definition: Firm experience with a specific type of discontinuous risk, gained by operating subsidiaries in countries affected by that type of disaster; such experience managing during sudden and devastating disasters is likely to generate important lessons that can only be attained from learning-by-doing.

name: High-impact disaster experience
authors_terms: ["experience in high-impact disasters", "experience with high-impact disasters"]
definition: Firms that experience severe high-impact events may have a transformative experience that translates into the development of experientially based capabilities for managing future disasters.

name: Low-impact disaster experience
authors_terms: ["experience in low-impact disasters", "experience with low-impact disasters"]
definition: Experience with low-impact disasters-disasters that result in little loss or damage-may cause minor disruptions to business but rarely induce major organizational or strategic changes, and is likely to have only a transitory affect on the firm.

name: Foreign entry and expansion
authors_terms: ["firm entry and expansion", "foreign entry and expansion", "entry and expansion decisions", "entry", "expansion"]
definition: Decisions related to which markets a firm should enter (foreign entry) and whether it should increase its level of investment (expansion).

name: Entrant type
definition: A technology was considered to have been introduced by a startup if the firm sold no products prior to its entry into the dominance battle, and to have been introduced by a diversifying entrant if the firm had sold at least one product before entering the dominance battle. A diversifying entrant is a firm that possesses pre-entry experience and that has commercial products before it enters the focal dominance battle, whereas a startup is an entrepreneurial firm that is created within the industry in which the dominance battle occurs.

name: Technology exit
definition: A firm's technology was considered to have exited from a dominance battle if the firm announced that it was discontinuing its technology, or if the technology was reported to have exited from the dominance battle or to have been removed from the product listing in the annual report, or if the firm had gone defunct.

name: Platform technology
authors_terms: ["platform technology", "platform technology-based dominance battle", "non-platform technology", "non-platform technologies"]
definition: A platform technology DD, such as Microsoft's Windows operating system, is a baseline technical architecture that allows other technologies to be developed on it; in contrast, a non-platform technology DD, such as Adobe's Postscript printer language, is an add-on feature that sits on a platform technology.

name: Emergence of a dominant design
authors_terms: ["emergence of a dominant design", "A DD has emerged", "dominant design", "DD"]
definition: A dominance battle may or may not lead to the emergence of a DD, but once a DD emerges, the industry will proceed to an 'era of retention' in which the DD becomes the entrenched industrial standard and alternative technology designs tend to be shaken out.

name: Impression offsetting
definition: Impression offsetting is a form of anticipatory impression management that is 'initiated to positively influence external perceptions of the organization by releasing positive, but unrelated information, in anticipation of an event becoming known that may negatively violate external stakeholder expectations.' With this impression management technique, firms 'offset' a potential negative reaction by intentionally releasing unrelated, positive information surrounding an announcement.

name: CEO stock option exercises
authors_terms: ["subsequent options exercises", "CEO option exercises", "exercising of stock options", "subsequent stock options exercised by the CEO"]
definition: Exercising options following an acquisition is an ex post behavioral outcome of CEO confidence in the long-term value-creation potential of a deal; if CEOs have low acquisition-related confidence, they are likely to exercise at least a portion of their at-risk stock options after acquisition announcements, to limit losses to accumulated equity value.

name: CEO age
definition: Research suggests that CEOs are increasingly sensitive to downside risks as they age; as CEOs age they tend to focus more on their financial security and retirement needs and have shorter career horizons.

name: Firm reputation
definition: CEOs have an elevated sense of downside risk when they lead high-reputation firms because their firms face greater scrutiny and suffer more negative market reactions for negatively perceived events than do firms without this asset. High-reputation firms are, by definition, well known and highly visible, thus their actions receive greater attention and scrutiny than similar actions taken by other firms.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: 'Dynamic industries' are characterized by instability and unpredictability, making it more difficult for external parties to assess the potential value of the acquisition, increasing CEO concerns about potential downside reactions.

name: Time to exit
authors_terms: ["exit time", "time to exit", "exit timing", "time to failure"]
definition: Time to failure is measured in quarters since founding or first observation; the dependent variable is implicitly the number of quarters the firm is under observation until exit.

name: Cumulative profits
definition: The running total of cumulative profits for each bank from the latter of entry or 1983Q1, which in the Ryan-Lippman model governs the firm's posterior that it is a high profit type.

name: Ex ante probability of success
authors_terms: ["p-zero", "probability of being profitable", "ex ante probability of success"]
definition: The probability of being profitable (p0 in the Ryan-Lippman model), a higher value of which means more information is required to convince the firm that it is unprofitable.

name: Profit volatility
definition: The volatility of the profit signal the firm receives about its type, measured as the standard deviation of quarterly firm profits while the firm is under observation.

name: Cost dispersion
definition: The dispersion of the ex ante distribution of firms' costs in the market, which determines the precision of the firm's priors about its costs; measured as the standard deviation of all banks' relative costs in the market during the period of observation.

name: Sunk cost of reentry
definition: The sunk cost k that a firm must re-incur if it leaves the market and later decides to re-enter, which makes it worthwhile to remain in the market when revenues are below production costs.

name: Demand growth
definition: The drift of the stochastic process followed by market demand (mu in Dixit), estimated from market-specific regressions of output growth.

name: Demand volatility
definition: The volatility of the stochastic process followed by market demand (sigma in Dixit), which the authors capture as the root mean squared error from the market-specific output growth regressions.

name: Separation of ownership and control
authors_terms: ["separation of ownership and control", "bank holding company", "BHC"]
definition: The extent to which ownership and control are separated, as in bank holding companies, which are separate legal entities that own 25 percent or more of a bank; theories emphasizing nonowner actors suggest that exit will occur later in organizations in which there is separation between ownership and control.

name: Profitability signal
definition: The profitability signal the firm observes about its present competitive environment and capabilities, proxied by current net income, i.e., net quarterly profit after tax, which managers weight asymmetrically when updating posterior expectations about future profitability.

name: Objective criteria
definition: A set of objective criteria are used to evaluate strategic alternatives, and alternative characteristics of acquisition candidates vary along an infinite number of objective dimensions; in this study the objective criteria on which to evaluate target firms were developed through a survey of the literature and recommendations from academic experts.

name: Evaluation of acquisition candidates
authors_terms: ["strategic evaluation of acquisition candidates", "evaluation of target firms", "attractiveness of the target firm as an acquisition candidate"]
definition: Executives' evaluation of target firms is modeled to examine the extent to which objective criteria are used; each executive rated the attractiveness of a target firm as an acquisition candidate and the probability that the firm would be acquired.

name: Industry
definition: Porter argues that the major aspect of the environment is the industry(ies) in which a firm competes, and industry structure is a strong influence on the competitive rules in the industry and therefore on firms' strategies.

name: Top executives' personal characteristics
definition: Schwenk suggested that individual characteristics affect the heuristics and cognitive maps used to make strategic decisions, and proposed three variable categories of individual differences: cognitive style, demographic factors, and personality traits. In this study several personal characteristics were examined.

name: Executive age
definition: Hambrick and Mason proposed that an executive's age affects strategic decisions; younger managers might not only evaluate riskier acquisition candidates more highly but also use and weight criteria differently than older managers.

name: Educational degree type
authors_terms: ["educational degree type", "type of education", "major area of study"]
definition: Hambrick and Mason suggested that executives' educational background provides an indication of their knowledge and skill base, and the type and amount of education one chooses serve as indicators of her or his values and cognitive preferences.

name: Level of formal education
authors_terms: ["level of education", "amount of education", "amount of formal education"]
definition: The amount of managers' formal education is proposed to relate to innovation, and those with less formal education may have greater variance in their cognitive models because these models are partially the product of more general educational training.

name: Amount of work experience
authors_terms: ["total amount of work experience", "amount of work experience", "years of work experience"]
definition: The amount of one's experience may affect the strategic choices made and the models/processes used in making those decisions; experience allows managers to test and fine-tune a cognitive model that produces more successful decisions.

name: Combination of functional experiences
authors_terms: ["type of work experience", "combination of different functional experiences", "functional experience"]
definition: The type of experience (e.g. function) may affect one's cognitive framework and strategic choices, and the type and weighting of those experiences may have helped shape a cognitive model used for making strategic decisions.

name: Executive level in the firm
authors_terms: ["level of the executive", "executive level", "level in the firm"]
definition: Criteria on which strategic choices are based may differ by the level of the executive (below the CEO), because of information availability and differences in incentive compensation; executive level serves as a proxy for differences in information availability and in incentive compensation.

name: Cognitive complexity
definition: Biere argued that cognitive complexity is an ability to differentiate the behavior of other individuals along a number of personal constructs; individuals with relatively complex cognitive systems have a greater number of personal constructs along which to differentiate behavior in others.

name: Risk propensity
definition: Strategic decisions may be partially affected by the managers' personal propensity toward risk, and an executive's risk orientation may affect the type of criteria used to evaluate strategic alternatives.

name: Entrant status
authors_terms: ["entrant", "incumbent", "entrants and incumbents", "whether the firm is an entrant or an incumbent"]
definition: Entrants are firms that enter an industry following a change in its institutional environment, whereas incumbents are the older firms already competing in the industry. 'New firms, or entrants to an industry, should thus be more diverse, and older firms, or incumbents, more similar.'

name: Institutional regime
definition: Whether a time period occurs under the regulated regime or the deregulated regime of prices and entry. 'Entry and price deregulation turn the traditional view of industry evolution on its head in that the industry is roughly mature under regulation and is subsequently rejuvenated when price and entry are removed from government control.'

name: Interfirm performance heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["interfirm heterogeneity", "heterogeneity among firms", "variance in performance", "performance variation"]
definition: The variation in performance across firms within an industry that is attributable to firm-specific factors. The authors argue that 'unique firm-level factors are thus likely to be a stronger contributor to performance differences among firms when firms are entrants than later when they converge on common practices.'

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["Return on Sales (ROS)", "Return on Assets (ROA)", "firm rates of return"]
definition: 'Performance is defined as either Return on Sales (ROS), which is Net Income over Sales, or Return on Assets, which is Net Income over Operating Assets.'

name: Disaster event
definition: We use the term 'disaster' to refer to 'exceptional events which suddenly kill or injure large numbers of people' (IFRC, 1995) and which 'overwhelm local capacity, necessitating a request to a national or international level for external assistance' (EM-DAT, 2007). Hurricane Katrina was a highly salient, vivid and negative event.

name: Social irresponsibility
authors_terms: ["social irresponsibility", "reputation for social irresponsibility", "bad deeds", "irresponsible behavior", "KLD concerns"]
definition: We approach social responsibility and social irresponsibility as conceptually distinct dimensions of CSR, and, thus, as conceptually distinct foundations of firms' reputations for CSR. Reputation is an assessment that allows stakeholders to estimate probabilities of future social behavior based on past behaviors.

name: Corporate philanthropic disaster response
definition: The likelihood of disaster donations, or 'corporate philanthropic disaster response' (Muller and Whiteman, 2009), in the days and weeks that followed Hurricane Katrina.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["Katrina-related abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "abnormal returns", "firm value"]
definition: Abnormal returns represent the differences between the ex post return of a security over the event window and the normal, expected return for the firm over the event window.

name: Associations with ousted corrupt officials
authors_terms: ["firms' associations with ousted corrupt officials", "treated firms' associations with corrupt officials", "TACO"]
definition: The total number of personal ties between a firm's executives/directors and all the corrupt officials indicted in the focal year, each political connection weighted by the collective degree centralities of the connected corrupt officials in the political network of all high-level officials.

name: Removal of existing political connections
authors_terms: ["removal of existing political connections with ousted corrupt officials", "removing existing connections with the ousted officials"]
definition: The number of outgoing upper echelons who had personal ties with any high-level officials who were removed due to corruption charges in the focal year, each removed political connection weighted by the sum of standardized degree centrality of all the connected corrupt officials in the experience-based political network across all high-level government officials.

name: Addition of new political connections
authors_terms: ["addition of new political connections with successors", "adding new connections with the successors"]
definition: The number of personal ties between newly listed upper echelons and the successors of all high-level corrupt officials who were dismissed in the focal year, each connection weighted by the standardized degree centrality of the successor in the experience-based political network of all high-level government officials.

name: Government dependence
definition: The extent to which the firm's operation relies on resources and support offered by the government.

name: Previous political power of corrupt officials
authors_terms: ["previous political power of ousted corrupt officials", "political power of corrupt officials"]
definition: The weighted sum of eigenvector centrality of all high-level officials who were removed from office because of corruption charges in the given year, where the sum is weighted by the percentage of ousted high-level corrupt officials who had prior employment experience in the firm's headquarter province.

name: Group membership
definition: The industry contains two technology-based groups, the integrated mills and the minimills, that differ in their use of technology and critical inputs; a strategic group comprises firms within an industry that have similar cost structures, degrees of product diversification, formal organization, or resource profiles.

name: Firm performance
definition: The financial performance measures employed in this study are return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA).

name: Defection from tradition
authors_terms: ["defection from 'tradition'", "hazard of defection", "rate of defection from that category"]
definition: We define a defection from 'tradition' as a producer's shifting from a history of exclusive use of botti to some use of barriques.

name: Insider defectors' grade of membership
authors_terms: ["average membership in 'traditionalist' style of partial defectors", "average GoM in 'tradition' of partial defectors", "grade of membership in the 'tradition' of partial defectors", "average GoM in the 'traditionalist' category among the partial defectors"]
definition: A producer's GoM in the old style in each vintage is the proportion of its Barolo/Barbaresco labels that received only botti aging. To test the first hypothesis, the authors measure the degree to which defectors fit the schema for the traditional style.

name: De novo spanners' grade of membership
authors_terms: ["average membership in 'traditionalist' style of de novo spanners", "grade of membership in the 'tradition' of the de novo producers who straddle 'tradition' and 'modernism'"]
definition: From the producer-level grades of membership the authors calculate the average GoM in the 'tradition' of the producers who entered as category straddlers, added to account for remaining effects of category spanning.

name: Tenure since partial defection
authors_terms: ["average tenure in category spanning of partial defectors", "average tenure of partial defectors since defection", "average time elapsed since partial defection"]
definition: The authors calculated the average number of years spent since producers who were 'traditionalist' started using barriques.

name: Political ideology incongruence
definition: A state in which a director and the incoming CEO possess opposing political views, arising as the two individuals start at political neutrality and move in different ideological directions.

name: Political ideology congruence
definition: A state in which a director and the incoming CEO share a political ideology, arising as the two individuals start at political neutrality and move in the same ideological direction.

name: Director departure
definition: Whether any given director left that position before or when their term was set to expire, meaning when they were available for re-appointment.

name: Familiarity with the incoming CEO
authors_terms: ["familiarity with the incoming CEO", "time shared with the CEO", "exposure", "contact"]
definition: The degree to which a director is familiar with, or has been exposed to, the incoming CEO, reflected in the number of years the focal director has spent at the same organization as the individual selected for the role of CEO.

name: Director political ideology
definition: An individual's position on the conservatism-liberalism spectrum, which research identifies as reflecting fundamental underlying values and beliefs.

name: Incoming CEO political ideology
definition: An individual's position on the conservatism-liberalism spectrum, which research identifies as reflecting fundamental underlying values and beliefs.

name: Fundamental organizational transformation
definition: Radical and discontinuous change of all or most organizational activities is necessary to break the grip of strong inertia. Fundamental organizational transformations were coded as occurring whenever substantial changes were observed in the strategy, structure, and power distribution domains of organizational activity.

name: Revolutionary transformation
definition: Revolutionary periods substantively disrupt established activity patterns and install the basis for new equilibrium periods. A revolutionary transformation was coded as occurring whenever changes in all three strategy, structure, and power distributions occurred within any two-year time period.

name: Small changes in activity domains
authors_terms: ["small changes in individual domains of organizational activity", "incremental change", "gradual, incremental transformation"]
definition: Nonrevolutionary views of organizational transformation emphasize the relative independence of organizational subunits as managers seek to adapt to changes in their local internal and external environments; over time, as subunits repeatedly alter their goals and relationships to local environments, the organization as a whole becomes transformed.

name: Performance crisis
authors_terms: ["performance crisis", "major declines in performance", "declines in the short-term performance", "market share decline"]
definition: Although declines in organizational performance may challenge the legitimacy of established courses of action, only large or long-sustained declines in performance are likely to trigger fundamental organizational transformations. A substantial decline in market share is considered to constitute an organizational crisis.

name: Environmental change
authors_terms: ["major environmental changes", "major changes in environmental conditions", "environmental jolts"]
definition: Environmental jolts are discontinuous changes that dramatically alter the competitive and operating conditions of an environment.

name: CEO succession
authors_terms: ["chief executive officer succession", "CEO succession", "installation of a new chief executive officer"]
definition: Chief executive officer succession, even in the absence of performance declines or major environmental change, should increase the likelihood of organizational transformation. New chief executive officers, especially those who come from outside organizations, stand uncommitted to the strategies and policies established by their predecessors.

name: Organizational status
definition: The social status of an organization is defined as the prestige granted to a firm because of its position in a social hierarchy. A firm achieves this position through market participants' ranking of the focal firm's visible traits, attributes, and actions.

name: Status distance
authors_terms: ["status distance", "status difference", "status distance between two firms"]
definition: Status distance is defined as the difference in status that exists between the firms traversed by the mobile employee. It is the difference in status that exists between two firms located in the same status hierarchy.

name: Hiring from a higher-status firm
authors_terms: ["hiring from a higher-status source firm", "hired above", "hiring from above", "inter-firm mobility (hires)"]
definition: Hired above is the entry of a partner from a firm that occupied a higher position in the status ranking than the focal firm.

name: Exit to a lower-status firm
authors_terms: ["exit to a lower-status destination", "exit below", "inter-firm mobility (exit)"]
definition: Exit below indicated that a partner had gone to a firm that occupied a lower position in the status ranking than the source firm.

name: Mobility event credibility
authors_terms: ["credibility of a mobility event", "credibility of the tie", "credible mobility event", "noncredible mobility event"]
definition: We contend that the credibility of a mobility event will influence when status transfers through it. A credible mobility event means that market participants view the change in employers as a signal of the hiring firm's quality, while a noncredible mobility event means the change in employers is seen as arising from a nonquality-related cause.

name: Postacquisition CEO departure
authors_terms: ["postacquisition CEO departure", "rate of postacquisition CEO departure", "CEO departure"]
definition: The departure of the CEO of an acquired, or target, firm following an acquisition. The authors treat it as a decision made by the CEO, for whom leaving 'represents a major strategic career decision,' and by the firm, for which 'a firm's decision to retain or dismiss a CEO will have important performance implications for that firm.'

name: CEO age
definition: The time a CEO spends in the position represents a significant investment in firm-specific human capital for both the individual and the firm, and so age is a major factor determining the level of firm-specific human capital investment. Age also influences the window of time in which future returns can be received.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Over time, the CEO of a firm develops expertise that only has value within that specific firm (Coffee, 1988). As a result, the longer a CEO has been with a firm, the higher that CEO's level of firm-specific human capital.

name: Acquisition relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "relatedness of an acquisition", "relatedness between an acquirer and a target firm"]
definition: The value an acquiring firm places upon a CEO's industry-specific skills is related to the relative abundance of those skills within the acquiring firm. When the acquiring firm's existing businesses are in areas unrelated to that of an acquisition, the acquirer will, by definition, lack the specific human capital needed to manage the acquisition.

name: Technological similarity
definition: The extent of technological overlap between a pair of firms, captured by a measure of technological distance between firm pairs during the 1980-1989 period. In the authors' analyses higher values of distance connote lower similarity.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: Whether the two firms' inventors were located in the same geographic region, where regions were defined as states within the United States and countries outside the United States (with California split and New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Pennsylvania combined).

name: Alliances
definition: Interfirm cooperative agreements that the authors treat as mechanisms for knowledge acquisition and learning. The recorded range includes joint ventures (for design or for fabrication), equity arrangements, marketing, design, fabrication, and extended licensing agreements.

name: Inventor mobility
authors_terms: ["mobility", "mobility of inventors", "mobility of engineers", "hiring inventors previously employed by the other firm"]
definition: The instances when an inventor moved to any of the focal firms from any other focal firm or incumbent in the overall set of firms, thus facilitating interfirm transmission of knowledge from their earlier employers to the focal firms.

name: Interfirm knowledge flows
authors_terms: ["knowledge flows", "interfirm knowledge flows", "knowledge building", "citations", "draw upon the knowledge stock"]
definition: The focal firm drawing upon the knowledge of another firm, observed through patent citations: each citation is treated as one instance of the focal firm drawing upon the knowledge of the cited firm.

name: Entry design choice
authors_terms: ["Entry Choice", "Entered with Intel MP", "entered with Other than Intel MP", "product design choice"]
definition: One of two variables constructed to test the proposed main effect, the choice of the dominant design; Entry Choice captures whether the firm selected the dominant design component when it entered. Firms chose the dominant design component when they shipped a personal computer with an Intel iAPX microprocessor.

name: Design strategy
authors_terms: ["Design Strategy", "design changes over time", "ending up with the dominant design", "chose the Intel microprocessor at entry and never changed", "never chose the Intel microprocessor"]
definition: The second of the two variables constructed to test the proposed main effect, the choice of the dominant design, which included design changes over time relative to the Intel microprocessor. Firms were classified into four design strategy alternatives that accounted for design changes after entry.

name: Firm success
definition: Success was operationalized using survival and market share in the PC market. Survival was measured as the number of years the firm shipped personal computers; market share was the percent of a firm's annual U.S. personal computer shipments to total U.S. personal computer unit shipments.

name: Investor growth orientation
authors_terms: ["Investor profile", "growth-oriented investors", "composition of investors", "investor composition", "investors' expectations and beliefs"]
definition: Our explanatory variable for Hypothesis 1 is a novel measure of the expectations and beliefs of the mutual fund investors holding a firm's stock, and specifically the extent to which they are growth- versus margin-oriented. The resulting Investor profile variable thus ranges from 1 to 5, with higher values indicating greater growth orientation of the investors that own the firm's stock.

name: Pre-change investor orientation
authors_terms: ["Initial investor profile", "initial investor profile", "pre-change investor profile", "pre-change categories"]
definition: Initial investor profile measures the investor orientation immediately prior to the onset of the industry change and is computed using the same weighted-average formula detailed above.

name: Analyst reaction favorableness
definition: 'Sell-side' securities analysts function as intermediaries in the stock market and issue periodic assessments of firms' current performance as well as their future prospects, issuing recommendations to 'buy,' 'hold,' or 'sell' firms' stocks. Our dependent variable is analysts' reactions using the Mean analyst recommendation value from the Institutional Brokers Estimate System (I/B/E/S) summary file, which averages recommendations across all analysts that track a firm, every quarter.

name: Strategic investments
definition: The strategic changes required to respond to technological change and compete in a converging industry often necessitate increased investments to develop new knowledge and capabilities in the new technology. Following prior research, we measure a firm's strategic investments using the logged value of Capital expenditure.

name: Elapsed convergence time
definition: Time period measures the number of periods elapsed following the start of the convergence between industries. Greater values for Time period correspond to the later years in our study.

name: Activist reputation for confrontation
authors_terms: ["activist reputation", "reputation for being confrontational", "an activist's reputation for being confrontational"]
definition: Reputation signals to others a specific behavioral attribute through the actor's past actions and leads to predictability and consistency in expectations of an organization's behavior. We measure an activist's reputation for being confrontational by examining its actions and behavior in early campaigns since these are likely to form the basis for its reputation.

name: Activist campaign success
definition: Our dependent variable is campaign success, which we measure by the extent of success by the activist in its campaign against a target company. We evaluate the success of the activist in achieving each of its stated goals.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Firm performance is measured as a firm's ROA minus the median firm ROA (excluding the focal firm) in a firm's core industry (2-digit SIC) in the year prior to the activist campaign.

name: Multiple activists
definition: A target firm may have multiple activist campaigns at the same time, each with its own demands of the board and management. We measure multiple activists as a dummy variable, which takes on a value of '1' if the campaign involves more than one activist, or a value of '0' if the campaign involves only one activist.

name: Managers' ambidexterity
authors_terms: ["managers' ambidexterity", "ambidexterity at the manager level", "a manager's ambidexterity"]
definition: We define ambidexterity at the manager level as a manager's behavioral orientation toward combining exploration and exploitation related activities within a certain period of time. Managers' ambidexterity is assessed by computing the multiplicative interaction between managers' exploration activities and managers' exploitation activities.

name: Decision-making authority
definition: A manager's decision-making authority is about the extent to which a manager has decision-making authority over how and which tasks the manager performs and his or her ability to solve problems and to set goals.

name: Formalization of tasks
definition: Formalization of a manager's tasks refers to the degree to which rules and codes describe a particular task; provide guides for decision making; and provide guides for conveying decisions, instructions, and information and the degree to which the manager has to conform to the task description.

name: Participation in cross-functional interfaces
authors_terms: ["participation in cross-functional interfaces by a manager", "cross-functional interfaces"]
definition: Cross-functional interfaces encompass lateral integration mechanisms such as liaison personnel, task forces, and teams; participation of managers in cross-functional interfaces increases their cooperation with other managers of different functions, units, and hierarchical levels.

name: Connectedness to other organization members
authors_terms: ["connectedness of a manager to other organization members", "connectedness"]
definition: Connectedness of a manager relates to the extent to which the manager is networked to other organization members across hierarchical levels and organizational units in terms of direct personal contacts. It refers to the size of the manager's network of direct contacts across hierarchical levels and organizational units and to the pattern of the manager's network in terms of density.

name: Exploration activities
definition: The exploration scale determines the extent to which a manager engaged in exploration activities last year. The seven exploration activity items were developed following the definition of ambidexterity at the manager level and based on the features by which March (1991) characterized the constructs of exploration and exploitation.

name: Exploitation activities
definition: The exploitation scale determines the extent to which the manager engaged in exploitation activities last year. The seven exploitation activity items were developed following the definition of ambidexterity at the manager level and based on the features by which March (1991) characterized the constructs of exploration and exploitation.

name: Short seller activism
authors_terms: ["short seller activism", "activist short seller", "targeting by an activist short seller", "activist short sellers"]
definition: A campaign where an activist short seller takes a short position in a company's stock and undertakes explicit actions to push its stock price downward. Activist short sellers profit by taking a short position in a firm and subsequently undertaking explicit actions aimed at pushing the firm's stock price downward.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The frequency with which firms engage in competitive actions in a given time period; equivalently, the number of competitive actions undertaken in a given time period. Competitive actions are moves firms use to improve their competitive positions and ultimately their performance and stock prices.

name: Implicit need for achievement
authors_terms: ["implicit need for achievement", "achievement motive", "need for achievement"]
definition: People with a strong implicit need for achievement seek to achieve a standard of excellence. High achievers keep a close eye on their performance, appreciate routine feedback, and derive satisfaction from performing well in achievement-related situations where their efforts are likely to gain recognition.

name: Implicit need for power
authors_terms: ["implicit need for power", "power motive", "need for power"]
definition: An implicit need for power causes a person to desire impact, control, or influence over another person or group and to work in ways that limit the extent to which others impact their decisions. Individuals with a high power motive favor an autocratic style of decision making that leaves little room for others' input.

name: Implicit need for affiliation
authors_terms: ["implicit need for affiliation", "affiliation motive", "need for affiliation"]
definition: Individuals with a strong implicit need for affiliation seek close relationships with others. Affiliation-driven individuals identify strongly with their organizations, perceiving their self-identities as intertwined with, or defining themselves in terms of, organizational attributes.

name: Industry overlap
authors_terms: ["INDUSTRY OVERLAP ij", "industry overlap", "same-industry", "overlap between the venture's industry and any of CVC's areas of operations"]
definition: The measure denotes whether the members of a venture-investor pair have their primary operations in the same industry. An entrepreneurial invention aimed at the industry in which a CVC's parent operates is highly relevant to the CVC's parent business and is likely to draw on technologies that the parent understands.

name: CVC investment relationship formation
authors_terms: ["CVC-entrepreneur investment relationship", "CVC-entrepreneurial investments", "investment dyad", "CVC-entrepreneur investment dyad", "investment relationship"]
definition: CVC investments are minority equity investments by established firms in entrepreneurial ventures. In the CVC setting, mutually profitable investment relationships might not be formed because a corporation will not invest unless entrepreneurs disclose details about their inventions.

name: Intellectual property protection regime
authors_terms: ["IPP regime", "intellectual property protection (IPP)", "IP regime", "intellectual property regime"]
definition: Teece defines IPP regime as 'the environmental factors, excluding firm and market structure, that govern an innovator's ability to capture the profits generated by an innovation'. There is significant interindustry variation in one's ability to protect and appropriate gains from an invention.

name: Organizational size
definition: Industry norms suggest that a farm winery is one that produces fewer than 50,000 cases of wine per year or has a storage capacity of less than 100,000 gallons. Growth beyond an optimal middle range may make it impossible for a farm winery to capitalize on its identity as being a local organization with a distinctive character.

name: Vineyard ownership
authors_terms: ["vineyard ownership", "ownership of vineyard land", "acres of vineyard owned", "own greater amounts of vineyard land"]
definition: Farm wineries that own vineyards can appeal to an even smaller niche by labeling their products as estate-bottled. Vineyard ownership allows farm wineries to exercise greater control over the quality of wine grapes and also to label their wines as estate-bottled and perhaps convey an image of higher product quality.

name: Farm winery founding rate
authors_terms: ["founding rate of farm wineries", "farm winery foundings", "founding rate"]
definition: The rate at which new farm wineries, the specialist organizational form in the wine industry, appear in the population; specialist organizations such as farm wineries are usually newly founded organizations.

name: Farm winery mortality rate
authors_terms: ["mortality rate of farm wineries", "farm winery mortality", "death rate"]
definition: The firm-specific instantaneous mortality rate of farm wineries, which is age-dependent; the authors estimate that farm winery mortality first increases and then declines with age, with the maximum mortality rate reached at an age of ten years.

name: Brand proliferation among mass producers
authors_terms: ["brand proliferation", "average number of brands per mass producer winery", "number of brands produced by mass producers"]
definition: One indicator of product differentiation is the number of brands produced by mass producers. The greater the average number of brands available in the market, the more difficult it is for a new brand to establish itself, so brand proliferation among mass producers will likely help them achieve a robust identity.

name: Advertising intensity among mass producers
definition: A generalist winery can achieve a robust identity by increasing advertising spending to create an image of quality. Economies of scale in promotion and advertising may allow major firms to charge higher prices for premium products.

name: Upgrading of subsidiary activities
authors_terms: ["upgrading of activities", "upgrading", "downgrading of activities", "sequential foreign investment decisions", "sequential investment decisions"]
definition: The sequential change in activities of existing subsidiaries in a host country is classified as upgrading, status quo, or downgrading as evaluated by the adjustment of product portfolios, number of plants, and local R&D activities. Upgrading is judged when technologically more advanced products, plants, or R&D labs are added, and downgrading when they are removed or the firm exits.

name: Local capability development
authors_terms: ["local capabilities", "firm-specific, location-bound capabilities", "local managerial capability", "local sourcing capability", "local manufacturing and engineering capabilities"]
definition: In this capability view, we argue that what determines the future upgrading of activities in a host country is active investments in firm-specific capabilities, not just the local experience gained from presence in a location. Knowledge accumulates through local manufacturing operations and is embedded in local managers, engineers, or production line workers.

name: Overall local experience
authors_terms: ["overall local experience", "duration of local operation", "local duration"]
definition: I first measure the overall local experience in terms of the duration of local operation. As long as a firm has limited its operations to simple assembly, a long history of local operations (measured in terms of the duration of local operations) does not necessarily guarantee that the location offers capabilities for more advanced activities.

name: Corporate-level capabilities
definition: Global capabilities of multinational corporations accumulate as these firms increase the share of production they do overseas and expand the scope of their overseas production networks. At the corporate level, I measured global capabilities in terms of overseas production ratio and the extent (number) of overseas manufacturing subsidiaries; I measure technological capabilities of a parent company in terms of R&D intensity.

name: Host country wage level
definition: Wages offer an important measure of comparative advantage. I use average annual wage per worker in the manufacturing sector as a measure for local wages.

name: Host country productivity
definition: When local wages go up, a host country can still pull in sequential foreign direct investment for more advanced activities, as long as the host country can offer a level of productivity that is high enough to offset the wage increase. I use manufacturing value-added per worker as a proxy variable of local productivity.

name: Host country investment incentives
authors_terms: ["government incentive policies on inward foreign investments", "host country environments", "country differences"]
definition: Country differences in government incentive policies on inward foreign investments critically influence sequential foreign investment decisions. Among the three countries that I am empirically investigating, Singapore has consistently offered the most favorable incentive policies to multinational corporations.

name: Team diversity
definition: We conceptualize the characteristics of team members in terms of two forms of diversity that are particularly relevant inside firms: their affiliations with formal organizational units and informal organizational communities.

name: Formal team diversity
definition: Team members may be officially affiliated with different formal organizational units, such as functional areas, product divisions, or departments, resulting in what is sometimes referred to as 'structural diversity'.

name: Informal team diversity
authors_terms: ["informal team diversity", "informal organizational communities", "communities of practice"]
definition: Team members may choose to be affiliated with different informal organizational communities that focus on particular topics in which they have an interest - that is, communities of practice.

name: Patent application scope
authors_terms: ["patent application scope", "patent scope", "number of claims", "total claims"]
definition: A patent application consists of a specification of the invention and a set of claims, each specifying possible improvements or variations that could be made to the invention to adapt it for different uses. The scope of a patent is typically measured by its number of claims.

name: Patent approval speed
definition: Firms can also benefit from greater patenting speed, in the form of faster approval of an application by a Patent Office, such as the U.S. Patent and Trade Office (USPTO). To measure patent approval speed, we identified the time taken (in years) for each patent that was ultimately granted to move from initial application to approval.

name: Team leader prior job experience
authors_terms: ["leader's prior job experience", "leader's first job", "general experience", "prior job experience"]
definition: The human capital literature highlights the potential value of general experience, which can be acquired in any job and is valuable across employers. Some will have limited general experience because they are in their first job, while others have held prior jobs.

name: Team leader prior patenting experience
authors_terms: ["leader's prior patenting experience", "leader's first patent", "specific experience", "prior patenting experience"]
definition: Specific experience is acquired in a particular firm and/or by performing a particular task. Some patent team leaders will have limited specific experience because they are filing their first patent for the firm, while others have filed prior patents.

name: Shareholder value change
authors_terms: ["financial gains/losses", "net present value", "change in the firm's market value", "changes in shareholder values", "abnormal returns"]
definition: The dependent measures of this study are the financial gains/losses or the net present value of the NPD announcement accruing to the partner firms.

name: Firm alliance experience
definition: A firm's alliance experience exposes it to rich combinations of processes, inputs, and outcomes and enables it to better adapt to contingencies as well as acquire new related knowledge.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["alliance scope", "broad scope alliance", "narrow scope alliance", "broad versus narrow"]
definition: Alliance scope refers to the breadth of functional activities (e.g., R&D, manufacturing, and marketing) that the partners agree to undertake during the tenure of the alliance.

name: Alliance type
definition: Scale alliances refer to partnerships in which resources are pooled for performing activities in the same stage(s) of the value chain, which in the case of an NPD alliance, is the R&D stage. Link alliances refer to partnerships in which resources are exchanged for performing activities relating to different stages of the value chain.

name: Partner alliance experience
authors_terms: ["partner alliance experience", "alliance experience of the partner firm"]
definition: In addition to own alliance experience, the alliance experience of the partner firm can play an important role in determining changes in the shareholder value of a firm.

name: Partner reputation
definition: Reputation refers to a global perception of the extent to which an organization is held in high esteem or regard by its key constituents on the basis of its past actions and future appeal.

name: Partner innovativeness
definition: Such informational advantages of smaller firms are captured by partner innovativeness (of the smaller firm).

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Corporate diversification can be viewed as a redeployment process of non-scale free capabilities that, while consistent with profit-maximizing decisions at the corporate level, may have a negative impact on performance at the market level.

name: Market relatedness
authors_terms: ["market relatedness", "relatedness between the firm's current market and the target market"]
definition: The baseline argument is that firms are more likely to diversify into the target market when the relatedness between the firm's current market and the target market is higher; markets within the same sector are more related to each other than those in different sectors.

name: Pre-entry capabilities
definition: Following Helfat and Lieberman (2002), a firm's pre-entry capabilities are defined as the stock of capabilities that a firm accumulates in the current market before the firm diversifies into a new market.

name: Relative demand maturity
authors_terms: ["relative demand maturity of its current market compared to the new market", "relative demand in the current market(s)", "relative maturity of the current market"]
definition: The relative maturity of the current market may result from the absolute decline of the current market, as in the defense industry after the Cold War or from the relatively faster growth of other markets, as in the hand-held device market vis-a-vis the desktop PC market.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["new product introduction", "innovation performance", "performance in its current market"]
definition: New product introduction is defined as the number of FDA approvals a given firm obtains in a given individual market in which it operates during a given year. This variable captures innovation performance.

name: Corporate-level performance
definition: To test the change in corporate-level profit in Hypothesis 4, the study uses an event study to examine the stock market's response to diversification moves, a forward-looking metric to assess the marginal return to a firm's investment decision.

name: Mover experience specialization
authors_terms: ["specialist movers", "generalist movers", "mover type", "new member experience", "specialist vs. generalist experience"]
definition: In our conceptualization of specialists and generalists, specialists are those who have worked in organizations with a high degree of division of work across individuals. Generalists are those who have worked in organizations with limited or no division of work across individuals.

name: Recipient group work division
authors_terms: ["recipient work division", "recipient group structure", "recipient group work division", "specialist/generalist work division"]
definition: The division of work within an organization shapes the extent of task specialization among its members. Participants in the specialist group work division condition were instructed to work in an assembly line in which each group member worked on only one part of the task, whereas participants in the generalist group work division condition completed all parts of the task.

name: Postmove group performance
authors_terms: ["postmove performance", "performance after the new member joins", "recipient group performance"]
definition: Performance was measured by the count of ships made by each group in the two postmove work periods; the experimenters assessed whether the products groups submitted met specifications based on objective criteria.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: Knowledge transfer is the process by which experience at one unit affects another (Argote and Ingram 2000). Knowledge transfer occurred when the groups adopted the mover's production routine in either of the postmove work periods.

name: Work division fit
authors_terms: ["work division fit", "mover work division fit", "mover experience of work division fit", "mover task fit"]
definition: 'Work division fit,' which indicates the extent to which the degree of work specialization with which a mover has gained experience in a donor organization matches the recipient organization's division of work.

name: Group learning
authors_terms: ["learning", "rate of increase in products", "improvement over time"]
definition: We measured knowledge transfer by the recipient group's adoption of the mover's routine and measured learning by the number by which the products increased from the first to the second postmove work period.

name: Structural knowledge
authors_terms: ["structural knowledge", "structural component of executives' knowledge", "experience with a unit's structural composition"]
definition: We call this structural component of executives' knowledge their 'structural knowledge.' Individual knowledge is built and applied within the context of structure.

name: Intrafirm executive mobility
authors_terms: ["executive mobility", "intrafirm mobility", "executive movement", "moves between business units"]
definition: We view executive mobility as firms leveraging executives' firm-specific expertise across business units and, potentially, as further development of the executive as a resource.

name: Acquired unit experience
authors_terms: ["executive came from an A unit", "executives from acquired units", "experience at acquired units", "acquisition experience"]
definition: We define acquired units as units that entered the firm as an acquisition. Compared to executives at core units, executives at acquired units are faced with many potential challenges, including balancing autonomy and integration, coordinating with the parent and adopting parent's standard operating procedures.

name: Internally developed unit experience
authors_terms: ["executive came from an I unit", "executives from internally developed units", "core executives", "experience at internally developed units"]
definition: We define internally developed units as those established within the firm that function as the firm's foundation due to the duration of time that is invested in establishing these units.

name: Recombined unit experience
authors_terms: ["executive came from a R unit", "executives with recombination experience", "executives from recombined units", "executive came from an A + A / I + I / A + I unit"]
definition: We define recombined units as those that were created as a combination of other units at the firm. Recombined units face challenges of integration and coordination with one another, just as newly acquired units face similar issues with the parent firm.

name: Mobility to acquired units
authors_terms: ["move to an A unit", "moved to an acquired unit", "executive was moved to an acquired unit"]
definition: Whether an executive was newly assigned to a particular destination unit at time t + 1, estimated separately for movement to an acquired unit.

name: Mobility to internally developed units
authors_terms: ["move to an I unit", "moved to an internally developed unit"]
definition: Whether an executive was newly assigned to a particular destination unit at time t + 1, estimated separately for movement to an internally developed unit.

name: Mobility to recombined units
authors_terms: ["move to an R unit", "moved to a recombined unit", "move to an A + A unit", "move to an I + I unit", "move to an A + I unit"]
definition: Whether an executive was newly assigned to a particular destination unit at time t + 1, estimated separately for movement to each form of recombined unit.

name: Intrafirm executive inflow
authors_terms: ["total number of executives from all other units", "number of executives moving into a unit", "sheer volume of executives"]
