definition: The total number of executives moved into a unit from all other units, used to capture sheer volume of executives moving into a unit.

name: Unit recombination
definition: In all recombination cases, either one unit loses its identity and moves into the other, or both units lose their identity and merge to form a newly identified unit. Reconfiguration includes whether the unit is retained versus divested or shut and, if it is retained, whether and how it is recombined with other units in the firm.

name: Unit structural stability
authors_terms: ["unit is unchanged", "structurally unchanged", "receiving unit remains unchanged", "no structural change"]
definition: A destination unit remains structurally unchanged when it is not recombined with another unit and is not divested or shut during the period.

name: Identification with strategic group
authors_terms: ["core firms", "secondary firms", "solitary firms", "group identification", "the degree to which they identify with their group", "positioning within the group structure"]
definition: Firms vary in the degree to which they identify with their strategic group, such that some firms follow the group strategy closely ('core firms') and others follow it less closely ('secondary firms'). Within an industry there are also solitary firms that are not members of any multifirm strategic group, so that some firms are strategically unique, some are loosely aligned with a multifirm group and others are tightly aligned with one.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "financial performance", "return on average assets", "ROA", "return on equity", "ROE", "operating profit margin", "OPM"]
definition: We used three measures of firm performance to test our hypotheses: return on average assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and operating profit margin (OPM).

name: Environmental performance
definition: The authors measure facilities' commitment and actions to reduce environmental release of toxic waste through onsite remediation efforts; their dependent variable directly measures the facilities' commitment to better environmental performance in an unambiguous manner.

name: Politically conservative community logic
definition: The politically conservative community logic refers to the constellation of beliefs, attitudes, and practices of actors that are antithetical to more centralized federal control and intervention-animated by a kind of libertarian ideology that underpins contemporary Republicanism.

name: Proenvironmental community logic
definition: The proenvironmental logic refers to a shared belief system in a community that attributes high intrinsic value to environmental goods and pollution reduction.

name: State logic
authors_terms: ["state logic", "state regulatory logic", "EPA enforcement actions", "EPA sanctions"]
definition: The central logic of the state has to do with the regulation of individual or organizational activities using a command-and-control framework based on law and bureaucratic hierarchy.

name: Market logic
authors_terms: ["market logic", "market logic pressure", "cost of off-site transfer"]
definition: Market logics are underpinned by the ideology of neoliberalism; the market logic that prioritizes profit, competitive advantage, and cost reduction is frequently perceived as having a negative effect on corporate environmentalism.

name: Cultural uncertainty avoidance
definition: UA refers to the degree to which a culture attempts to avoid anxieties associated with an unpredictable future. UA is, therefore, an indicator of the degree to which a culture values a sense of control.

name: Power distance
definition: Power distance is the cultural tendency to accept hierarchy or inequality across individuals.

name: Individualism
definition: Individualism is the cultural tendency to value the individual over the collective.

name: Masculinity
definition: Masculinity is the cultural tendency to value assertiveness and personal achievement over interpersonal relationships and nurturing behaviors.

name: Issue controllability
definition: Strategic issue attributes that reflect controllability in labeling threats are concerned with an indicated lack of control over the issue, response to the issue, or the issue's effect on the firm; issue attributes pointing toward the presence of control over the issue, response to the issue, or the issue's effect on the firm were identified as highly indicative of opportunity.

name: Threat discrimination
definition: Threat discrimination refers to those issue characteristics that fit well with the threat construct but not with the opportunity construct; threat was associated with issues characterized as negative, uncontrollable, and involving potential loss.

name: Opportunity discrimination
definition: Opportunity discrimination refers to those issue characteristics that fit well with the opportunity construct but not with the threat construct; opportunity issues were characterized as positive, controllable, and involving potential gain.

name: IPO firm dependence on transaction partner
authors_terms: ["dependence on a key customer or supplier", "dependence on a transaction partner", "dependence partners", "dependency"]
definition: The IPO firm often identifies in the S-1 document those transaction partners on which the IPO firm depends for either critical inputs or as a key source of revenue. If the IPO firm is dependent on a key customer or supplier, this will be noted as a separate risk factor.

name: Cumulative abnormal return
definition: The abnormal return of the ith stock at time t, ARit, can be calculated by subtracting the expected return in the absence of the event effects, E(Rit), from the actual return in the event period, Rit. The cumulative abnormal returns are the returns cumulated over the event period.

name: Long-term commitment
definition: A long-term relationship often requires firms in the dyad to develop dedicated linkages that enhance the benefits of complementarity. The long-term commitment allows the development of trust and facilitates the exchange of valuable and proprietary knowledge between transaction partners.

name: Business overlap
definition: A key question here is whether there is any overlap in business between the IPO firm and the transaction partner. In the case of a diversified partner, the partner may have business establishments in the industry of the IPO firm and offer generic products or services to the IPO firm.

name: Number of dependent transaction partners
authors_terms: ["number of dependent partners", "multiple transaction partners", "several partners on which it is dependent"]
definition: A unique dyadic relationship is less likely to exist when the IPO firm simultaneously identifies several partners on which it is dependent. This creates an opposite situation to market thinness, where highly specialized assets often result in a situation of small-numbers bargaining.

name: Turnover rate
authors_terms: ["turnover rate", "static turnover rates", "turnover rate level", "level of turnover"]
definition: Turnover rate represents the level of turnover per unit, that is, the absolute level of turnover as opposed to turnover rate change. Turnover rates emerge from individual turnover events and aggregate to collective levels over time.

name: Turnover rate change
authors_terms: ["turnover rate change", "changes in turnover rates", "turnover rate changes"]
definition: The turnover rate change over time, which the authors argue is conceptually and empirically distinct from the static turnover rate level. Turnover rate change evokes theoretical considerations not realized or observable in static turnover rates.

name: Unit performance
authors_terms: ["unit performance", "change in unit performance", "adjusted controllable unit profit"]
definition: To measure unit performance, the authors used adjusted controllable unit profit, an index of the unit's profitability under some management control, calculated on a quarterly basis.

name: Quality of turnover
authors_terms: ["quality of turnover", "turnover rate quality", "quality of those who leave"]
definition: Context-emergent turnover theory reconceptualizes the turnover rate definition to include both quantity and quality dimensions, with quality representing the unit competence or capacity lost. The quality of turnover is the aggregated service orientation of those who voluntarily left each unit.

name: Turnover dispersion
definition: Turnover dispersion is defined as the extent to which turnover events are spread across time, that is, the distribution of turnover events across time. High turnover dispersion is when events are more evenly distributed; low turnover dispersion means that turnover events are clustered.

name: Quality of replacement hires
authors_terms: ["quality of replacement hires", "replacement hire quality", "replacement quality"]
definition: The collective quality of the knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics of newly hired employees entering the unit, measured with the same service orientation assessment used for leavers. If replacement hires collectively have higher-quality KSAOs than those leaving, then the HCR erosion is minimized.

name: Quantity of replacement hires
authors_terms: ["quantity of replacement hires", "replacement quantity", "number of hires"]
definition: The quantity of replacement hires is the aggregate number of hires in each unit, per quarter, representing the inflow side of the human capital resource flow system.

name: Ownership type
definition: For this cross-ownership comparison of organizational culture, we selected three major ownership types that have been the focus of current enterprise management research in China: state-owned enterprises, domestic privately owned enterprises, and foreign-funded and controlled businesses.

name: Clan culture
definition: The Clan (consensual) culture is like an extended family where leaders act as mentors, facilitators, or parent figures. Clan cultures are friendly places to work where people share a lot about their personal values and goals.

name: Adhocracy culture
definition: The Adhocracy (entrepreneurial) culture can be characterized as a developing, dynamic, and creative workplace. Employees in this organizational culture are committed to experimentation and innovation.

name: Market culture
definition: The Market (competitive) culture is a hard-driving organization in which people are expected to be aggressive and goal-oriented producers. A key attribute of a Market culture is its focus on winning in a competitive external environment.

name: Hierarchy culture
definition: The Hierarchy (bureaucratic) culture has as its dominant attributes formalized rules, procedures, policies, and structures that govern what people do in the organization. The goals of a Hierarchy culture are stability, predictability, and efficiency in organizational operations.

name: Performance pay adoption
definition: Given that standard principal-agent analysis characterizes very general forms of state-contingent compensation contracts to solve the moral hazard problem, we measure the presence of performance pay with an indicator equal to 1 if any form of performance pay is present.

name: Principal control over tasks
authors_terms: ["PrincipalControl", "control by the principal", "centralization of decision authority", "decentralization of decision making from principals"]
definition: PrincipalControl counts the number of tasks that are carried out by the principal (business owners or headquarters) and corresponds to the theoretical variable of tasks allocated to the principal, and it is thus a measure of centralization of decision authority.

name: Managerial control over tasks
authors_terms: ["ManagerControl", "managerial authority", "concentration of decision making at the managerial level", "collected by managerial employees"]
definition: ManagerControl counts the number of tasks allocated to agents that are managerial employees and corresponds to the theoretical number of tasks decided by the managerial layer.

name: Nonmanagerial control over tasks
definition: NonManagerControl counts the number of tasks allocated to nonmanagerial employees and corresponds to the theoretical number of tasks decided by the nonmanagerial layer.

name: Task complexity
definition: To measure the complexity of tasks, we construct a variable at the individual task level based on the logic developed by Garicano (2000) that proposes a clear relationship between task complexity and the level of the organizational hierarchy to which a task is assigned, where the least complex tasks are assigned to the lowest level of the hierarchy, whereas increasingly more complex tasks are assigned to progressively higher levels.

name: Tax progressivity
authors_terms: ["tax progressivity", "income tax progressivity", "income tax progression", "residual income progression"]
definition: When tax progressivity is greater, marginal increases in income are more heavily taxed relative to low tax progressivity regimes, which reduces the likelihood of performance pay adoption. In this measure, ρ equals 1 corresponds to a flat tax system, whereas ρ < 1 implies that the tax system exhibits progressivity.

name: Misalignment between task allocation and performance pay
authors_terms: ["misalignment of task allocation and performance pay", "task allocation-performance pay misalignment", "relative misalignment", "task misalignment"]
definition: These variables measure the misalignment between task allocation predicted by performance pay and the actual task allocation at the firm as described by our theoretical analysis, with the lowest possible value being zero (no misalignment of task allocation and performance pay).

name: Firm mortality
definition: For our dependent variable, we use these data to construct a dummy variable equal to 1 if the organization experiences mortality by the time the WES is administered again, which captures the mortality event in the same year or following year after the survey is conducted.

name: Transaction characteristics
authors_terms: ["transaction characteristics", "transaction uncertainty and performance ambiguity", "these variables", "characteristics of transactions between organizations and clients"]
definition: Two transaction characteristics, transaction uncertainty and performance ambiguity, account for the levels of negotiating, monitoring, and enforcement costs in transactions between clients and organizations.

name: Transaction uncertainty
definition: Transaction uncertainty exists to the degree that organization-client transactions are unstandardized or unpredictable; the greater the level of such uncertainty, the greater the amount of information that an organization has to process to complete transactions efficiently, and thus the higher are its costs.

name: Performance ambiguity
definition: Performance ambiguity refers to clients' ability to monitor and evaluate the performance of the other parties and to determine the value of the objects of exchange.

name: Vertical differentiation
authors_terms: ["vertical differentiation", "number of supervisory levels", "span of control"]
definition: Levels of vertical differentiation are shown by the number of hierarchical levels and by span of control: the structure with the lowest level of vertical differentiation has the fewest hierarchical levels and the widest spans of control relative to size.

name: Horizontal differentiation
authors_terms: ["horizontal differentiation", "task-specialized units", "number of different departments or functions"]
definition: Horizontal differentiation is the number of task-specialized units, that is the fewest number of task-specialized units relative to size; it was measured as the number of different departments or functions inside an organization.

name: Task interdependence
definition: Organizations may adopt pooled, sequential, or reciprocal forms of task interdependence, depending on the level of transactional uncertainty.

name: Behavior control
definition: Control of the behavior of client-contact employees through supervision, assessed by the extent to which managers check what employees are doing on the job and get involved in helping employees perform their normal work activity.

name: Output control
definition: Output control is pay based at least in part on such outcomes as sales; any form of sales commission or performance-based compensation was considered evidence of output control.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization is the use of rules and procedures as a means of control; it was measured with Van de Ven and Ferry's (1980) 4-item scale.

name: Professional control
definition: Organizations can rely on professional control, in effect using extensive training or socialization to control behavior, and employ such professional control when uncertainty surrounding transactions with clients is high; the degree of employees' personal specialization was used as a proxy.

name: Alliance portfolio internationalization
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio internationalization", "API", "degree of foreignness of partners in a firm's alliance portfolio"]
definition: We introduce the concept of alliance portfolio internationalization (API) to describe the degree of foreignness of partners in a firm's alliance portfolio as defined by the cross-national differences between the firm's home country and its partners' countries of origin.

name: Financial performance
definition: Following prior research on the performance implications of international operations, we used profitability as our financial performance measure. We measured profitability by computing the firm's return on assets (ROA), which is a common measure used in financial performance studies.

name: Foreign partnering experience
authors_terms: ["foreign partnering experience", "experience with foreign partners", "accumulated experience with foreign partners"]
definition: In particular, the firm's accumulated experience with foreign partners can help the firm recognize national differences, bridge cultural, geographical, institutional, and economic differences, identify and assimilate valuable network resources, and leverage ties to nationally distant partners.

name: Subsidiary country overlap
authors_terms: ["subsidiary country overlap", "overlap in the locations of the firm's subsidiaries and its partners' countries of origin"]
definition: The notion of subsidiary country overlap refers to the case in which a firm maintains wholly owned subsidiaries in the home countries of its foreign partners.

name: Innovation shock
definition: We define an innovation shock as the introduction by a firm of a new product that stimulates a substantial surge and acceleration in demand for that product-a surge that was generally unexpected by market participants.

name: Hazard of industry exit
authors_terms: ["hazard rates of industry exit", "firm mortality", "exit rates", "industry exit"]
definition: Firms' hazard rates of industry exit are the rates at which firms leave the industry; the authors estimate a Gompertz hazard rate model of firm mortality and conduct the analysis at the level of the firm rather than at the level of the car model because their theory is about firms.

name: Repositioning away from the innovation shock segment
authors_terms: ["reposition away from the industry segment in which an innovation shock is introduced", "repositioning out of the low segment", "segment repositioning", "strategic repositioning"]
definition: If a rival's demand decreases and that rival does not imitate, then remaining viable in the industry requires repositioning to a more distant niche; in the analysis, repositioning is a low-segment firm's move to another segment while remaining in the industry.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age in years; firms that are older are thought (and have been found) to be at greater risk from structural inertia, and are also more likely to have rigid, bureaucratic organizational structures and incentive systems that raise their adjustment costs.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["LOG SIZE", "log of firm size", "larger incumbents", "firm size"]
definition: Firm size is another variable that is frequently used as a proxy for structural inertia; large firms typically have made larger fixed investments in complementary assets that are specific to a set of customers and are thought to suffer from more rigid bureaucracy and lower-powered incentives that inhibit repositioning.

name: Breadth of technological knowledge base
authors_terms: ["broader base of technological knowledge", "broader technological base", "NUMODEL", "number of car models"]
definition: The broader a firm's base of technological knowledge, the greater the likelihood of it being able to reposition away from the ISD, because a broader technological base reduces adjustment costs associated with acquiring or internally developing the kinds of extensions to the firm's technology base that are needed to successfully reposition.

name: Social imprinting
definition: The founding team's early emphasis on accomplishing the organization's social mission. Some founders emphasize the importance of the social mission at the time of founding while others instead emphasize the establishment of effective commercial operations.

name: Economic productivity
definition: A WISE's overall efficiency in turning inputs into economic outputs.

name: Social performance
definition: Building on Scott (1977), the degree to which an organization is effective at producing positive social outcomes; in this context, a WISE's effectiveness in enhancing the job market prospects of its beneficiaries.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The first environmental variable is dynamism (often called uncertainty) which is characterized by the rate of change and innovation in the industry as well as the uncertainty or unpredictability of the actions of competitors and customers.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: The second environmental dimension is hostility which represents the degree of threat to the firm posed by the multifacetedness, vigour and intensity of the competition and the downswings and upswings of the firm's principal industry.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: The final environmental dimension is heterogeneity or complexity which encompasses variations among the firm's markets that require diversity in production and marketing orientations.

name: Analysis in strategy making
definition: The first is analysis which is reflected by methodically and systematically taking more factors into account in decision making (analysis and multiplexity), ensuring the complementarity and synergy of different decisions (integration), planning for future contingencies (futurity), and developing levels of industry expertise at high levels of the organization.

name: Innovation in strategy making
definition: The second strategy-making dimension is innovation which includes introductions of new products and production-service technologies, the search for novel solutions to marketing and production problems, the attempt to lead rather than to follow competitors (proactiveness), and risk-taking.

name: Firm performance
definition: High performance samples contained only firms which performed well in both sales growth and profitability, whereas low performance samples performed poorly according to both criteria.

name: Client nationality match
definition: The match (or discrepancy) between the inspector's nationality and the client's nationality determines ingroup (vs. outgroup) in the authors' setting; since all inspectors were domestic individuals, domestic clients are ingroup members and foreign clients are outgroup members.

name: Inspection stringency
definition: Inspectors are tasked with examining a predetermined set of items for every vessel, but the extent of scrutiny applied to each item is left to the inspectors' discretion; all else being equal, longer inspection times can be interpreted as greater stringency on the part of the inspector, while shorter times suggest a more lenient approach.

name: Maritime accident
definition: A high-profile accident involving a domestic vessel that resulted in hundreds of casualties, over a hundred million US dollars in damages, and the bankruptcy of a major domestic corporation; it was revealed that the vessel failed to meet minimum safety standards that should have been rectified in the pre-departure inspection. The authors argue it acted as a scandal-like event that disrupted implicit trust toward ingroup clients.

name: Professionalism
definition: Professionalism involves an individual's sense of oneness with their profession and internalization of professional norms and standards; it is a dimension of human capital, with its degree shaping an agent's capacity to carry out regulatory duties impartially.

name: Violation of expectations
definition: Firms violate stakeholder expectations when their behaviors or outcomes do not match stakeholders' predictions, social norms, or both. In this study the authors focus on financial earnings misrepresentations, identified when firms are subsequently required to restate their financial position.

name: Violation severity
authors_terms: ["severity of the violation", "severity of the restatement", "downward restatement", "upward restatement"]
definition: The authors argue that the severity of the violation is likely to modify the nature of stakeholders' reactions, because the more severe the violation, the more uncertain stakeholders become about what the firm can or will do in the future. A downward restatement decreases stakeholders' wealth and represents a negative change, and thus entails a more severe violation than an upward restatement.

name: Rehabilitative efforts
authors_terms: ["rehabilitative efforts", "rehabilitative action", "replacement of an incumbent CEO"]
definition: Actions a firm takes after a violation of expectations that are geared toward shaping stakeholders' perceptions and restoring its credibility; the authors argue an ideal rehabilitative action should be observable internally and externally, symbolically important, and substantive rather than purely ceremonial.

name: Relative reliance on earnings
authors_terms: ["relative reliance on signals that are ordinarily stronger proxies but more susceptible to errors and manipulations", "reliance on earnings"]
definition: The degree to which shareholders use a particular signal in valuing a firm, reflected as the estimated coefficient of the signal covariate in the value relevance regression. Earnings per share is the signal the authors treat as ordinarily a stronger proxy but more susceptible to errors and manipulations.

name: Relative reliance on book value
authors_terms: ["relative reliance on signals that are ordinarily weaker proxies but less susceptible to errors and manipulations", "reliance on book value"]
definition: The degree to which shareholders use a particular signal in valuing a firm, reflected as the estimated coefficient of the signal covariate in the value relevance regression. Book value of equity per share is the signal the authors treat as ordinarily a weaker proxy but less susceptible to errors and manipulations.

name: Firm evaluation
definition: The judgments that stakeholders make about a particular firm regarding a specific dimension of interest; in the empirical context of this study the authors focus on how firm stock price reflects how shareholders evaluate a firm.

name: Number of parents
authors_terms: ["number of parents", "number of partners", "number of parties", "number of parent firms", "multiple partners", "multiple parties"]
definition: The number of parent firms who own and control the joint venture; a joint venture with three or more parent firms is referred to as a multi-party venture.

name: Contract completeness
definition: Contract completeness has to do with the extent to which relevant clauses or issues pertaining to building and managing a joint venture are clearly specified and codified in a venture's contract.

name: Partner cooperation
definition: The process of the exchange among parent firms, an evolving mechanism designed to ensure reciprocal dependence and strategic flexibility, largely manifested as multi-party cooperation and underlined by mutual attractiveness, attachment, and reciprocal exchange.

name: Joint venture performance
definition: Overall venture performance, defined as the venture CEO's satisfaction with various aspects of the venture's operational achievement (e.g., sales, profitability, management, reputation, and marketing).

name: Activity breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth", "increased breadth", "waste management breadth", "breadth of an ongoing activity", "changes in breadth"]
definition: The number of different processes making up an activity; greater breadth exposes organizations to diverse activities but also generates an additional need for coordination. Facilities can treat chemical waste using up to three active processes - recycling, energy recovery, and treatment - in addition to disposal, and the active processes can be pursued either on site or off site.

name: Cumulative experience
definition: Experience creates a growing stock of knowledge that improves performance, both through repetition of a routine and through realized modifications to the activity. The authors measure experience as the log of cumulative waste emitted for the focal chemical within the facility up until the year t-1.

name: Waste reduction performance
definition: The authors measure changes in waste at the facility-chemical-year level as the primary outcome; a decline in waste represents improved operational performance, whereas an increase in waste represents a performance decline.

name: Breadth in related activities
authors_terms: ["increase in breadth for a related activity", "changes in breadth in related waste management activities", "Facility change in breadth in any chemical", "breadth of related activities"]
definition: Because knowledge is likely to be shared in an organization, changes in the breadth of related (nonfocal) activities may influence the coordination costs and learning benefits of a focal activity. The authors measure how waste management actions for a nonfocal chemical affect waste reduction of the focal chemical.

name: Utility model patent application
authors_terms: ["utility model patent", "utility model patenting", "utility model patent applications"]
definition: A utility model patent is one of the two types of patents available from the State Intellectual Property Office of China; it lasts for 10 years and is generally perceived as a weaker or less clear form of IPR protection, and no substantive examination is required for it. The dependent variable indicates whether a patent is filed as a utility model patent, set to 1 if the firm applies for the utility model patent for a particular technology and 0 if the firm applies for an invention patent.

name: Strengthening of the formal IPR regime
authors_terms: ["IPR change in force", "IPR law change", "IPR regime strengthening", "2001 patent law amendment", "strengthening of IPR law"]
definition: The 2001 patent law reform provided new judicial protection and reduced the ambiguity specifically involving utility model patents, improving its application procedures and strengthening its enforcement and protection. The variable IPR change in force is an indicator that equals 1 for all years since the implementation of the major China IPR law change in 2001, and 0 for years prior to the change.

name: Firm nationality
authors_terms: ["Chinese firm", "Western firm", "Chinese firms", "Western firms", "local Chinese firms"]
definition: Chinese firm denotes whether the firm awarded the patent originates from or is home based in China; Western firm denotes whether the firm awarded the patent originates from or is home based in a Western country. The largest difference in embeddedness in China's informal institutions can be observed between local Chinese firms and Western firms operating in China.

name: De facto regional IPR quality
authors_terms: ["de facto IPR quality", "de facto legal protection", "de facto quality of the IPR and legal systems", "quality of regional IPR system"]
definition: Different regions in China are not equal in their degree of development in formal IPR and legal institutions, and the de facto quality of the IPR and legal systems across different regions of China varies significantly. De facto IPR quality is captured by the average of the number of patent applications and granted patents divided by the number of R&D or technical personnel in each provincial-level region in China.

name: Operational experience in China
authors_terms: ["operational experience in China", "local experiences and knowledge"]
definition: Operational experience in China is defined as the number of years the firm assigned to a particular technology patent has had formal operational facilities in China until the year of observation (i.e., patent application year).

name: IPO underpricing
definition: The market-ascribed value firm owners do not receive when their equity is sold, representing a financial loss for family owners, or 'money left on the table'.

name: Family firm status
definition: We categorized firms as family firms if 20% or more control rights were held by family members and if at least two family members were involved in the firm; the authors distinguish family, lone-founder, and nonfamily firms.

name: Founding generation family firm
authors_terms: ["founding generation family firms", "family firms with a founder family CEO", "founding generation family CEOs"]
definition: Family firms in the founding generation, that is, family firms with a founder family CEO. In these firms the founder typically holds the dominant share of ownership and the main SEW priority is ensuring that the business survives and grows before it is eventually passed on to later generations.

name: Later generation family firm
authors_terms: ["later generation family firms", "family firms with a later generation family CEO"]
definition: Family firms led by a later generation family CEO, in which repeated interactions between the family and business systems over time enhance family members' identification with the family firm.

name: Ownership retention
definition: The ratio of retained shares to the amount of post-IPO shares outstanding; the degree of ownership retention captures the extent to which family owners will enjoy continued control and influence after the IPO.

name: Market momentum
definition: The median change from the midpoint of the initial filing range to the final offer price for all IPOs issued in the prior month, which distinguishes the effect of hot versus cold IPO markets by capturing pre-issue excess demand.

name: Underwriter reputation
definition: Underwriter reputation is defined and reinforced over time by the members of the financial community; the authors measure it as the market share of the lead underwriter in terms of capital raised by the same underwriter in European IPOs during the sample period.

name: Relative R&D spending
authors_terms: ["relative R&D spending", "relative R&D intensity", "R&D spending as compared to industry competitors"]
definition: A firm's relative R&D spending is its R&D spending as compared to industry competitors, measured as the total R&D dollars spent per employee by each firm relative to its industry average.

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure was measured as the number of years since being appointed CEO. The authors argue that as tenure increases CEOs tend to make fewer changes in strategy and may have little interest in pursuing innovation through higher R&D spending.

name: CEO age
definition: CEO age was measured in years. Older executives tend to be more conservative, risk averse and less likely to spend money on long-term R&D given their shorter time horizons before retirement.

name: CEO stock ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO stock ownership", "value of stock holdings", "at-risk wealth"]
definition: The value of CEO stock ownership was measured as the number of shares owned by the CEO multiplied by the stock price per share on the last day of the stock market in the year sampled. Agency theory suggests that increased at-risk wealth encourages top managers to be more long-term oriented.

name: CEO career experience
definition: The authors argue that executives are acculturated into the norms of any business function where they have spent a considerable period of time, so each CEO's listed career experiences were coded into six categories: finance/accounting, legal, production/operations, administration, marketing/sales, and engineering/R&D.

name: R&D/engineering career experience
authors_terms: ["engineering/R&D career experience", "career experience in the R&D/engineering function"]
definition: Career experience in the engineering/R&D function, an output function that emphasizes growth through discovering new products and markets; CEOs with such experience are expected to favor higher R&D spending.

name: Marketing/sales career experience
authors_terms: ["marketing/sales career experience", "career experience in the marketing/sales function"]
definition: Career experience in the marketing/sales function, an output function that emphasizes growth through discovering new products and markets; CEOs with such experience are expected to favor higher R&D spending.

name: Finance/accounting career experience
authors_terms: ["finance/accounting career experience", "career experience in the finance/accounting function"]
definition: Career experience in the finance/accounting function, a throughput function that focuses on improving the efficiency of the organization, so R&D may be viewed as a discretionary expense subject to efficiency concerns.

name: Legal career experience
authors_terms: ["legal career experience", "career experience in the legal function"]
definition: Career experience in the legal function, a throughput function; CEOs with such experience may react to uncertainty with conservative moves that conserve cash and reduce R&D spending.

name: Production/operations career experience
authors_terms: ["production/operations career experience", "career experience in the production/operations function"]
definition: Career experience in the production/operations function, a throughput function focused on efficiency, so CEOs with such experience may look at R&D as a discretionary expense and reduce spending.

name: Administration career experience
authors_terms: ["administration career experience", "career experience in the administration function"]
definition: Career experience in the administration function, a throughput function focused on improving the efficiency of the organization, so R&D spending may be reduced.

name: CEO education level
definition: The amount of formal education attained by the CEO, measured on a four-point scale reflecting the highest level of education attained. More educated executives are generally assumed to have greater cognitive complexity and greater receptivity to innovation.

name: Type of higher education
authors_terms: ["type of higher education", "educational specialties", "educational fields of study"]
definition: The field of study of the higher education received by the CEO; the authors contrast business or legal academic training with training in science and engineering.

name: Business education
authors_terms: ["number of business degrees", "business or economics college degrees", "business academic training"]
definition: The number of business degrees represents the actual number of business or economics college degrees earned by the CEO at any level (undergraduate, master's, or Ph.D.). MBA programs are argued to attract conservative, risk-averse students, so CEOs with business training may be less inclined to pursue innovation through R&D spending.

name: Legal education
definition: Whether the CEO had obtained a legal degree, measured as a dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had obtained a JD degree, 0 otherwise. Legal education is argued to place little emphasis on innovation.

name: Science and engineering education
authors_terms: ["number of science/engineering degrees", "science and engineering training", "technical education"]
definition: The number of college degrees earned by the CEO in hard sciences or engineering. Schooling in science and engineering is argued to create managers with a more complete understanding of technology and innovation, who would favor high levels of R&D spending.

name: Democratic politician shareholders
authors_terms: ["Democratic politician shareholders", "Democratic political ownership", "number of Democratic politician shareholders"]
definition: Democratic members of Congress who hold ownership stakes in a firm's stock. The authors count them because politician-side reputational dynamics are likely to apply regardless of the size of an ownership stake and because activists become more aware of these shareholders as their number grows.

name: Financial activism
authors_terms: ["financial activism", "financially motivated shareholder activism", "targeted by financial activists"]
definition: Financially motivated shareholder activism, in which activists buy stakes in public corporations and then persuade or force boards and managers to make changes expected to immediately improve share prices. The authors measure whether a firm is targeted by such an activist.

name: Board Democratic partisanship
definition: The extent to which a firm's directors are ideologically liberal, measured from directors' political campaign contributions. Board members' political leanings can reveal much about their views on certain issues, including whether they prioritize stakeholders over shareholders.

name: Core/periphery bridge
definition: Brokers that span the core and periphery of networks - a core/periphery bridge - have access to unique knowledge in both the core and the periphery of the network and have been found to benefit from their position. For nonmigrant scientists working in peripheral institutions, the return home of scientists from more developed countries to their institution implies the formation of a core/periphery bridge connecting central and peripheral scientists at two distinct levels: directly at the individual level, and indirectly at the institutional level.

name: Publication output
definition: As a proxy for performance, I generate a number of publication count measures to identify changes in the publication rate of scientists.

name: Prior connection to the core
authors_terms: ["central connection", "connection to central scientists", "connection to the core", "connected to top global institution"]
definition: I define a central connection as a collaboration with either a scientist from one of the sample FIC AITRP U.S. training institutions, or with a scientist from one of the remaining institutions within the top 25 globally ranked institutions for health and medical training.

name: Knowledge flows
definition: Following a long line of research, I use publication to publication citations to measure knowledge flows among scientists.

name: Collaboration
definition: Collaboration patterns of nonmigrant African scientists are measured using coauthoring patterns in publication data.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "new product development", "drug innovation", "new drug development", "firm innovation"]
definition: In this study, the authors focus on product innovation in the pharmaceutical industry in the form of new chemical drugs. They measured firm innovation by calculating the total number of drug innovations invented by a firm in a given year.

name: Firm performance
definition: In both the finance and the strategy literatures, expected return has been conceptualized as the average return on sales, assets, or equity for firms undertaking a particular course of action.

name: Performance variance
authors_terms: ["variance in firm performance", "performance variance", "risk", "variability in returns", "risk in returns"]
definition: Risk has been conceptualized as the variability in returns, indicating uncertainty about the extent to which the expected return may be realized; riskier decisions imply a wider probability distribution around the mean.

name: Product development time
authors_terms: ["product development time", "drug development time", "length of the product development process", "development time"]
definition: A key attribute of the product development process is that it is usually lengthy and costly. When development time is longer, at a given rate of institutional change, the performance landscape is more likely to have shifted by the time the innovation is completed.

name: Rate of institutional change
authors_terms: ["rate of institutional change", "institutional change", "institutional transition", "provincial institutional change", "rate of institutional transition"]
definition: Following North (1990, 1993), institutions are defined as 'the rules of the game,' and moving from one structure to another during transition can create considerable uncertainty. The rate of institutional change is indicated by the yearly change in the percentage of state-owned firms within the pharmaceutical industry of each province, because economic transition keeps pace with the rate of privatization of state-owned enterprises.

name: Brokered access
definition: The supplier's network scope, defined as the degree to which the focal supplier enables the foreign subsidiary access to a broader, local network of suppliers.

name: Shared goals
definition: Shared goals refer to a bilateral understanding, approach, and vision for achieving tasks and outcomes, which ultimately promote the exchange relationship as a whole and help project the exchange into the future.

name: Trust
definition: At the interfirm level, trust refers to the extent to which a firm believes that its exchange partner is honest and/or benevolent.

name: Formal contracts
definition: Formal contracts spell out the obligations and roles of both parties in the relationship, arrange for enforcement by third parties, and specify objectives, rules, and procedures for resolving disputes.

name: Explicit knowledge acquisition
definition: Explicit knowledge is codifiable and can be transferred in formal language.

name: Tacit knowledge acquisition
definition: Tacit knowledge is complex, abstract, and difficult to codify.

name: Regulatory stringency
authors_terms: ["regulatory stringency", "regulatory environment", "stringent regulatory environment", "regulatory pressure", "coercive pressure"]
definition: Regulatory stringency, considered an important aspect of the institutional environment of hospitals, refers to the restrictiveness of regulation; a stringent environment is one that is highly restrictive or constraining.

name: System-model presence
definition: Our interest in mimetic pressures, or organizational modeling, can only be indirectly examined, by considering the extent to which multihospital systems operated in a region before the HAES Survey.

name: Multihospital system membership
authors_terms: ["system membership", "system member", "membership in a multihospital system", "boundary redefinition"]
definition: A multihospital system is defined as two or more hospitals that are owned, leased, sponsored, or managed by a single corporate entity; system membership indicates whether a hospital belongs to such a system.

name: System ownership type
authors_terms: ["type of system", "nonprofit system", "for-profit system", "public, government-controlled system", "religiously affiliated system"]
definition: Hospitals were classified by the type of multihospital system they belonged to: a public, government-controlled system; a secular, nonprofit system; a religiously affiliated system; or a for-profit system.

name: Buffering
definition: Buffering strategies were conceptualized and measured as strategies that protect the core technology of an organization by increasing the cushion or buffer between it and its environment.

name: Bridging
definition: Bridging strategies represent a completely different approach to boundary management because they involve creating linkages to other organizations rather than developing internal structural buffers; bridging is connecting an organization to other organizations.

name: Outside status
authors_terms: ["outside status", "product status earned in a leading foreign market", "status established within a leading foreign market", "product status in the United States"]
definition: We argue that status established within a leading foreign market, herein labeled outside status, signals implied recognition from out-group members, which encourages home country audiences to associate with the product in question. The independent variable in this study is product status earned in a leading foreign market (outside status).

name: Domestic market performance
authors_terms: ["domestic market performance", "domestic market sales", "product unit sales in a home country", "sales in home country", "sales of the product in a home country"]
definition: The paper argues that a positive product status accrued in a leading foreign country increases domestic market performance. The dependent variable, product unit sales in a home country, is the number of units of a focal model sold in the home country in a focal year.

name: Product price
definition: The authors argue that, compared with lower-priced goods, higher-priced goods are strongly related to self-concept, and that social approval plays a particularly important role in driving the purchase of high-priced goods. Price is measured as the suggested retail price of the product model in the United States (in thousands USD) for computational efficiency across the three different home countries in the study.

name: Luxury product category
definition: A luxury good is not just a premium-priced product, but 'an ephemeral status symbol'. Social and external motivations related to ostentation and status symbol accumulation drive the consumption of luxury goods, and the mere use or display of a particular luxury good brings prestige to the owner.

name: Economic distance
authors_terms: ["economic distance", "GDP distance", "economic distance between the home country and the United States", "similarity of economic conditions"]
definition: The impact of outside status on domestic market sales is argued to vary depending on the similarity of economic conditions between the foreign and the home country. To measure this variable, the authors calculated the Euclidean distance between the GDP per capita of the home country and of the United States for each year.

name: Buyer hiring from competing suppliers
authors_terms: ["buyer hiring from supplier's competitors", "hiring of employees (alumni) from a supplier's competitors", "competitor alumni", "hires from suppliers"]
definition: The paper highlights the importance of personnel changes at a buyer firm that involve the hiring of employees (alumni) from competitors of a supplier firm. When a buyer firm hires employees from a focal supplier's competitors, the strength of the relational assets shared between the competing suppliers and the buyer increases, diminishing the relative relational advantage enjoyed by the focal supplier.

name: Supplier alumni in the buyer firm
authors_terms: ["a supplier's alumni in a buyer firm", "buyer firm attorneys who are alumni of supplier", "focal supplier's alumni", "supplier alumni"]
definition: If a supplier already has its alumni working for a buyer, these (focal) supplier alumni may act as guardians and conservers of the supplier's relational advantage, in part because this valuable resource supports their own ability to perform and be rewarded for their organizational roles.

name: Buyer firm turnover
authors_terms: ["buyer firm turnover", "buyer attorney turnover", "turnover (departure) of buyer employees"]
definition: Turnover of buyer employees is the departure of employees from the buyer firm; research shows that turnover (departure) of buyer employees is associated with a higher incidence of disruption of existing business relationships with suppliers.

name: Geographic proximity of competitor hiring
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity in buyer firm hiring from competing suppliers", "local hiring", "proximal competitors"]
definition: We define a buyer firm's proximal (or local) geographic region as the Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) in which it is located, following prior research on employee mobility and geography. Buyer hiring from proximal competitors of supplier and buyer hiring from distant competitors of supplier are the variables for hiring occurring between the company and the competitors of the law firm.

name: Outsourcing
authors_terms: ["amount of outsourced business the buyer gives to the supplier", "count of patents outsourced to supplier", "patent prosecution work outsourced", "outsourcing relationships"]
definition: The amount of patent prosecution work outsourced by a Fortune 500 buyer firm to a given law firm in a given year. Patent prosecution is the work of drafting, filing, and getting patents granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office carried out by patent law firms (suppliers) for Fortune 500 firms (buyers).

name: Faculty pay
definition: The monetary reward that principals allocate to faculty members; it was operationalized as academic-year (nine-month) salary and as average annual percentage raises over the four years preceding the survey.

name: Top-tier journal publications
authors_terms: ["top-tier publications", "premier publications", "publications appearing in premier, refereed outlets"]
definition: All articles appearing in the 21 journals rated as top-tier in the authors' survey of management department chairpersons were considered premier publications; commentaries, book reviews, and rejoinders were not included.

name: Second-tier publications
definition: A second category of publications consisting of articles, book chapters, papers appearing in published proceedings, and the like that did not appear in one of the 21 top-tier journals.

name: Books published
definition: Books, excluding readers and edited volumes, were counted as a third category of publications.

name: Citation impact
definition: Citation counts are viewed as an indicator of how useful a person's research is to other investigators and of the influence a faculty member's research has had on the work of other scholars.

name: Teaching performance
definition: Teaching performance was assessed with respondents' typical student ratings, indicating students' perceptions of the individual's effectiveness as a teacher, and the administration's assessment of their classroom performance.

name: Job mobility
authors_terms: ["job moves", "number of previous institutional affiliations", "changes in institutional affiliation"]
definition: The number of permanent changes in school affiliations a respondent had made since obtaining a doctoral degree.

name: Doctoral-granting status
definition: A variable with a value of 1 if the school offered a doctoral degree in management and 0 if it did not.

name: Institutional funding source
authors_terms: ["institutional funding source", "privately funded universities", "publicly funded universities"]
definition: A dichotomous variable rated 0 if a school was privately funded and 1 if it was publicly funded.

name: Persistent superior economic performance
authors_terms: ["persistent superior economic performance", "PSEP", "superior economic performance", "SEP", "sustainability of abnormal returns"]
definition: Superior economic performance sustained over time; SEP was operationalized as statistically significant above average ROA (relative to other firms in the same industry) over a five-year period, and a firm was considered to have PSEP if it presented six consecutive windows (10 years) or more of superior performance.

name: Institutional weaknesses and volatility
definition: Companies in emerging economies face multiple institutional weaknesses and a more volatile macroeconomic environment, which increase the probability of exogenous shocks that jeopardize economic rent and compromise the sustainability of competitive advantages. These unexpected changes eventually erode the value of a successful strategy.

name: Competition inhibitors
authors_terms: ["institutional weaknesses that diminish imitative and competitive pressures", "collusion", "entrenchment", "barriers to protect strongholds", "group structure"]
definition: Several authors describe emerging economies as environments where institutional weaknesses diminish imitative and competitive pressures; when the institutional environment dampens competitive and imitative pressures, competition based on barriers to protect strongholds is easier and superior performance will persist longer. Entrenchment is one of the most salient practices local firms apply to deal with adverse institutional environments.

name: Time
definition: We examined changes in the rate at which firms exited the SEP stratum over time with the independent variable, period.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "development of the institutional context", "institutional context", "institutional environment"]
definition: Development of the institutional context, derived from 11 variables chosen to reflect different aspects of economic, political, and social institutional development; as institutions develop, contract enforcement improves, transaction costs and information asymmetries diminish, and rivalry increases.

name: Superior performance exit hazard
authors_terms: ["exit SEP", "exiting the superior performance stratum", "hazard of exiting SEP", "periods of SEP decrease in duration"]
definition: Following Wiggins and Ruefli (2005), exit SEP is defined as equal to 1 when a firm exited the superior stratum and 0 otherwise; the hazard function provides a convenient definition of duration dependence, so that periods of SEP decreasing in duration correspond to a higher hazard of exiting the stratum.

name: Multinational affiliation
authors_terms: ["type of company", "domestic companies", "multicountry firms", "MNC subsidiaries", "local companies"]
definition: The company's status as a domestic company, a company from the region with a presence in other emerging countries (multicountry firm), or a subsidiary of a multinational corporation. In general, MNCs have advantages in resource-based strategies, while local companies have advantages in institution-based strategies; multicountry firms fall somewhere in between.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "product diversification", "diversifying into different product areas", "unrelated diversification"]
definition: Because the data source only lists the major product categories of the parent company, the coding of subsidiary diversification only measures whether the foreign subsidiary is in the major areas of the parent firm. This can be seen as an indication of whether the subsidiary is in the core areas of the parent firm.

name: Entry mode
definition: The choice of entry strategy—whether through acquisition, joint venture, or greenfield investment—is related to the survival of foreign subsidiaries because these strategies differ both in expected riskiness and in the importance of various coordination costs. A greenfield investment is a start-up investment in new facilities, and a joint venture is the pooling of assets into a common but separate organization by two or more firms which share joint ownership and control.

name: Foreign investment experience
definition: Previous experience with foreign investment directly affects the parent's stock of experience in establishing and managing foreign subsidiaries. The authors examine whether the subsidiary is the first-time direct investment in the U.S.A. by a foreign parent or is a subsequent investment.

name: Parent commitment
definition: Additional investment is used to measure continued commitment from the parent company in the existing subsidiary. It is measured by the number of investments in addition to the initial investment by the foreign parent in the existing subsidiary over the sample period.

name: Foreign subsidiary survival
definition: For the purposes of this analysis, survival is defined as the continued presence of the foreign subsidiary in the U.S. host market, and failure as the subsidiary's exit.

name: Social vision communication
authors_terms: ["social vision communication", "social vision", "communicating a social vision"]
definition: Social vision communication refers to conveying an image of the future where environmental and societal issues are addressed by the venture's activities. Social vision communication emphasizes the well-being of other living creatures (physical, socio-economical, or psychological), both human and animal, as well as concern for nature and the environment.

name: Job applications
definition: The goal of recruitment is to attract a large pool of qualified applicants. The authors measure the outcome as the number of applications a venture receives and as the jobseeker's actual application decision.

name: Perceived career advancement opportunity
authors_terms: ["perceived opportunity for career advancement", "career advancement opportunities", "perceived career advancement opportunity"]
definition: Jobseeker perceptions of the venture as an opportunity for career advancement. The authors argue that social vision communication limits jobseekers' future outlooks on career advancement opportunities owing to limited returns on their employment investment and realization of personal ambitions on the one hand, and desired job characteristics on the other.

name: Minimum salary demands
definition: The minimum remuneration a jobseeker demands for seriously considering a vacancy. Jobseekers may set premiums or discounts to the minimum remuneration demanded, which quantify the perceived match between the applicant's needs and the vacancy's ability to meet them.

name: Remuneration offered
definition: The total remuneration package offered by the venture in its vacancy. Because vacancies often include equity next to salary and jobseekers tend to evaluate both in a total remuneration package, the authors combine salary and equity into one remuneration variable.

name: Perceived firm-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["employee perceptions of firm-specific human capital", "perceived FSHC", "perceived firm-specificity", "FSHCPerceived"]
definition: Employees reported the extent to which they believed their skills to be firm-specific. The measures capture the share rather than the stock of total knowledge and skills the employee perceives to be firm-specific.

name: Organizational tenure
definition: Tenure at a firm is often used as a proxy for firm-specificity; it is measured as the number of years a respondent was with a firm.

name: On-the-job training
definition: Internal training, particularly on-the-job training provided by the employer, is assumed to be relatively more firm-specific than training that takes place outside of the firm.

name: Organizational commitment
definition: Affective organizational commitment goes beyond intentions to stay at the firm - it reflects a positive attitude toward shared objectives.

name: Early-stage investment
authors_terms: ["early-stage investment", "tendency to invest in early-stage portfolio companies", "investments in early-stage portfolio companies"]
definition: The dependent variable is a VC firm's tendency to invest in early-stage portfolio companies based on all initial-round investments made by the VC firm each year, captured by the proportion of its initial-round investments in portfolio companies at the start-up stage.

name: Performance below aspiration
authors_terms: ["performance below aspiration", "performance < aspiration", "magnitude of underperformance relative to aspiration", "distance of performance below aspiration"]
definition: For a VC firm with performance below its aspiration, the performance outcome is categorized as a problem or failure that triggers problemistic search; the variable is calculated as the value of performance minus aspiration for those observations where performance is below aspiration and zero otherwise, and is then reverse-coded so that larger values represent increasing shortfalls of actual performance relative to aspiration.

name: Performance above aspiration
authors_terms: ["performance above aspiration", "performance ≥ aspiration", "magnitude of outperformance relative to aspiration", "distance of performance above aspiration"]
definition: When the VC firm achieves its aspiration, the performance outcome is categorized as a success and the firm is satisfied and not motivated to take risk; the variable equals performance minus aspiration when performance is above or equal to aspiration, and is set to zero otherwise, with higher values indicating better performance.

name: Network brokerage
definition: Brokerage is defined as the extent to which a firm is linked to other firms that are otherwise disconnected from one another; the higher the brokerage level, the more structural holes a VC firm has in its social network.

name: Network centrality
definition: Centrality refers to the extent to which a firm is connected to other firms through direct and indirect ties; a VC firm with a higher eigenvector centrality is connected to a group of VC firms that have more well-connected and powerful partners of their own.

name: Asset retrenchment
definition: Asset retrenchment refers to the net reduction of assets (Robbins and Pearce, 1992), such as closing plants, divesting equity (sell-offs, spin-offs, and equity carve-outs), and reducing stocks of property, equipment, and inventory (Morrow et al., 2004).

name: Cost retrenchment
definition: Cost retrenchment refers to the net reduction of total costs such as selling, general, and administrative expenses (SGA); interest expense; and miscellaneous costs (Robbins and Pearce, 1992).

name: Post-retrenchment performance
authors_terms: ["post-retrenchment performance", "long-term performance outcomes", "industry adjusted return on sales (ROS)"]
definition: We measured our dependent variable, firm performance, as industry adjusted return on sales (ROS) (i.e., firm ROS minus industry average ROS at the three-digit SIC code level). We measured performance three years after a retrenchment event to account for a potential recovery period.

name: Firm Ricardian rent creation focus
authors_terms: ["Ricardian rent creation focus", "Ricardian focus (Rf)", "firm-level Ricardian focus", "asset exploitation focus"]
definition: Ricardian rents are mainly achieved by owning valuable and rare resources (Mahoney and Pandian, 1992; Ricardo, 1963 [1817]). The key rent creation mechanism for firms with Ricardian focus is resource picking, that is, by purchasing resources from the strategic factor market (Barney, 1986) for less than their marginal productivity (Makadok, 2001).

name: Industry Ricardian rent creation focus
authors_terms: ["industry Ricardian focus (Ri)", "industry's Ricardian rent creation focus", "the extent to which the industry's business model is asset dependent and capital intensive"]
definition: It is likely that the dominant rent creation mechanism is relatively Ricardian in capital-intensive sectors, such as shipping, petrochemicals, steel, and hotels. Firms in these industries generate economic rents mainly through exploiting assets and resources previously purchased or internally developed.

name: Firm Schumpeterian rent creation focus
authors_terms: ["Schumpeterian rent creation focus", "Schumpeterian focus (Sf)", "firm-level Schumpeterian focus", "innovative posture"]
definition: Schumpeterian rents are mainly achieved by entrepreneurial risk taking based on unique capabilities (Mahoney and Pandian, 1992; Schumpeter, 1934). The main rent creation mechanism is building capabilities-the purpose of which is to improve the productivity of the other resources possessed by the firm, for example, R&D (Makadok, 2001).

name: Industry Schumpeterian rent creation focus
authors_terms: ["industry Schumpeterian focus (Si)", "industry's Schumpeterian rent creation focus", "knowledge-intensive industries"]
definition: The dominant rent creation mechanism tends to be Schumpeterian in knowledge-intensive industries, such as information technology and bio-technology. Economic rents in these industries largely depend upon a firm's explorative capabilities to innovate.

name: Stigma transfer concerns
authors_terms: ["concern about stigma transfer", "stigma transfer concerns", "concern with stigma", "fear of stigma transfer"]
definition: Audiences avoid stigmatized organizations in part because they fear that stigma will be transferred to them; they believe that stigma is contagious and could infect those associated with it.

name: Identity exposure through organizational names
authors_terms: ["exposure to dispensaries with identity names", "identity exposure through organizations' open actions", "organizational names", "dispensary name GoM"]
definition: Organizations can expose their identities to audiences by choosing names that reveal and broadcast what they do for business, which is one of the more overt and meaningful forms of valenced discourse an organization seeking to celebrate its identity can leverage. A name becomes an effective tool for identity exposure only if it reveals and broadcasts an organization's identity.

name: Identity exposure through customer open attitudes
authors_terms: ["exposure to reviews with open attitudes", "identity exposure through open consumer attitudes", "open attitude toward the cannabis market"]
definition: Customers gain more exposure to organizations' identities and the overall market when other customers openly discuss the market and its participants; a review is defined as having an open attitude toward the cannabis market if it includes words that have a non-zero association with marijuana.

name: Liberalism
definition: Political ideology is captured by a left-right divide in which the left serves as a proxy for liberalism, an orientation defined by tolerance of outgroups. The more liberal views an individual has, the more likely that person is to be tolerant toward a newly legalized market and the less likely to attach stigma to it.

name: Product name similarity
authors_terms: ["name similarity", "general name similarity", "similarity of a new product's name to the names of other products"]
definition: The similarity of a new product's name to names of other products on the market; a name conveys to audiences the product's similarity to products with similar names and its distinctiveness from products with dissimilar names.

name: Name similarity to popular products
authors_terms: ["name similarity to popular shows", "name similarity to popular products"]
definition: Name similarity to popular products, defined as products known and used by a great number of customers. Products are popular when they have high market share; in this setting shows are considered popular if they are ranked as Top 30 by Nielsen Ratings.

name: Name similarity to high status products
definition: Similarity of a new product's name to names of high status products, that is, products to which market critics confer high status because of their high quality. In this setting members of the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences play the role of critics and high status shows are those that won an Emmy award.

name: Product withdrawal rate
authors_terms: ["withdrawal rate", "rate of show withdrawal", "product market longevity"]
definition: The show-specific instantaneous rate of withdrawal from prime time plus during the show's first year (i.e., the first 12 months on the air). A TV show is considered to be withdrawn on the day it was cancelled by the network.

name: Genre popularity
authors_terms: ["genre popularity", "show's genre past popularity", "past popularity of the genre of a focal show"]
definition: The popularity of the genre in which a show is produced, i.e. the popularity of its content. It is captured by the number of Top 30 series within a focal show's genre in the prior year.

name: Product age
definition: The time that a show has been broadcast during prime time plus, measured in months during the show's first year on the air.

name: Broadcast season
definition: Industry research on seasonality of the TV series industry separates a year into fall, spring, and summer seasons, and the majority of new shows are introduced in the fall.

name: IOF service quality
authors_terms: ["quality of IOF provision", "% high quality IOF coverage", "IOF service provision", "service provided by IOF providers"]
definition: Our main measure of the quality of IOF provision is % high quality IOF coverage, measured as the proportion of blocks in a given census tract where IOF providers offer high quality service.

name: Cooperative presence
definition: We measure Co-op presence as a dummy variable indicating whether a cooperative ISP is present in a given census tract or not.

name: Cooperative coverage
definition: We measure % co-op coverage as the proportion of census blocks within a given tract that are served by any cooperative.

name: Cooperative provision
definition: The former measure thus captures whether a community is served by a cooperative at all, while the latter captures the extent of cooperative provision.

name: Community rurality
definition: We count as Rural any census tract that includes an area designated as rural by the US Census. Note that this measure is not time-varying within our sample period.

name: Community income
authors_terms: ["log(Median HH income)", "low-income communities", "high-income communities", "Persistent Poverty County (PPC)"]
definition: For Hypothesis 2b, which focuses on the differential effects for high- and low-income communities, we measure log(Median HH income) for a census tract.

name: Community social fragmentation
definition: Communities that are relatively socially fragmented, that is, that are made up of diverse ethnic or racial groups, are likely to have lower levels of generalized trust and weaker social norms, making it harder for members of such communities to cooperate.

name: Cooperative need diversity
authors_terms: ["Co-op variety", "diversity of needs a cooperative serves", "diversified cooperatives", "focused cooperatives"]
definition: We construct two measures of the diversity of needs a cooperative serves. Note that unlike our other moderators which are linked to heterogeneity between census tracts, these moderators are linked to heterogeneity among cooperatives.

name: Foreign entry location choice
authors_terms: ["region choice", "location choice", "probability Pi,j,t that firm i will choose region j at time t"]
definition: The focus of the analysis is the choice of the region or province in which a firm locates a foreign manufacturing entry. The dependent variable is the probability that firm i will choose region j at time t from the set of alternative regions.

name: Foreign investor agglomeration
authors_terms: ["assessment learning", "Japanese affiliate count", "all Japanese firms' affiliate count", "total number of previous entries in a region by model firms", "general model entries", "generic models"]
definition: In the assessment mechanism of social learning, firms make a general assessment of the feasibility of locating in a particular area based on existing economic activity. The larger the existing concentration of these models, the stronger the potential agglomeration benefits and the stronger the attraction of new firms to the region.

name: Specific model firm entries
authors_terms: ["bandwagon learning", "specific model firms", "bandwagon model", "specific (bandwagon) model entries", "bandwagon model counts"]
definition: With bandwagon learning, firms observe models (i.e., other firms) that provide an example of the focal behavioral act and thereby give specific information about the relative attractiveness or the legitimacy of a certain behavioral option; firms follow models with strong informational and/or legitimizing value, such as similar firms, members of the same institutional group, or high status firms.

name: Recentness of model entries
authors_terms: ["recentness of model behavior", "recentness", "age of affiliate count"]
definition: In bandwagon learning, recent examples of models locating in a certain area are more likely to influence a focal firm's decision than relatively 'old' examples, as the former provide the most accurate, up-to-date information on the current attractiveness of the location. Recentness of previous model behavior is an important theoretical separator between the operation of the assessment and the bandwagon learning mechanism.

name: Prior host-country experience
authors_terms: ["previous experience in the target country", "target country (i.e., China) experience", "China entry experience", "subsequent entries into additional provinces"]
definition: A firm's own previous entry experience in the target country, which decreases decision uncertainty. As decision experience is a prime way to decrease decision uncertainty, a firm's own previous entry experience in the target country is expected to be negatively associated with its tendency to imitate others.

name: Firm-SMO collaboration
definition: A collaboration is an interactional relationship in which organizations work together by committing resources to achieve mutually relevant outcomes; its key characteristics are that organizations interact in a purposeful way and that each party commits resources. It excludes purposeful but arm's-length transactions such as donations, logo licensing, or employee volunteering.

name: SMO cooperative repertoire
definition: The mix of tactics an SMO deploys in its interactions with firms, ranging from contentious tactics to arm's-length cooperation. The JF coefficient used to measure it assesses the relative proportion of contentious and arm's-length cooperative interactions SMOs have with firms, while accounting for the total volume of interactions.

name: Movement segmentation
definition: The degree to which moderate and radical SMOs in a movement lack cooperative ties relative to ties expected under random mixing. Negative values correspond to movements in which cooperative ties between moderate and radical SMOs are higher than expected under random tie formation, and positive values correspond to movements in which between-group ties are less than expected in a purely random network with the same group sizes and connectedness as the observed one.

name: SMO specialization in cooperative tactics
authors_terms: ["SMO specialization in cooperation", "specialization in cooperative tactics", "tactical specialization"]
definition: The degree to which the focal SMO's repertoire is more cooperative than that of the median SMO in its movement. It is calculated as the difference between the focal SMO's JF coefficient and the median JF coefficient of other SMOs in the movement, increasing in value the more cooperative the focal SMO's repertoire is relative to the movement median.

name: SMO ties to radicals
