authors_terms: ["SMO ties to radicals", "ties to radical peers", "preexisting ties with radicals"]
definition: The focal SMO's social position in the movement measured by its preexisting cooperative ties to radical SMOs. Preexisting ties enable the sharing of trustworthy and nuanced information about a potential collaboration or partner firm and facilitate the exploration of possible bases of compromise.

name: Firm contentious targeting
authors_terms: ["contentious targeting", "contentious challenges", "movement contention", "contentious challenges against the firm"]
definition: Movements engage in contentious targeting to problematize practices and targets; in naming and shaming firms, contentious targeting clearly delineates those firms as the adversaries of the movement. It is measured by summing all contentious challenges (e.g., protests, boycotts, lawsuits) a firm received on a given issue from SMOs in the movement in the preceding two years.

name: Geographic distance
definition: To compute a dyadic geographic distance between a new unit and each incumbent, we converted address information for each hotel in the STR census data into the longitude and latitude data through Texas A&M geocoding services. Then, we computed the shortest line between two units by using the STATA geodist command.

name: Incumbent type
authors_terms: ["incumbent type", "sister units", "rival units", "same-brand sister unit", "different-brand sister unit", "same-market-segment sister unit", "different-market-segment sister unit"]
definition: We consider both same and different brands of the same parent firm (e.g., Residence Inn and Fairfield Inn Suites belong to Marriott International) as sister units. We classified each incumbent as a rival unit, same-brand (same-market-segment) sister unit, or different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit, using information on parent company, chain affiliation, and hotel class (i.e., economy, midscale, upper-midscale, upscale, upper-upscale, and luxury) in the STR census data.

name: New unit size
authors_terms: ["new unit size", "size of a new unit", "size of a new hotel", "number of hotel rooms"]
definition: We measured the size of a new unit by the number of hotel rooms offered (Baum & Haveman, 1997), as reported in the STR census data. Because the number of rooms was highly skewed, we log-transformed this variable.

name: New unit quality
authors_terms: ["new unit quality", "quality of a new unit", "hotel class", "product segment (i.e., quality)"]
definition: We measured the quality of a new unit based on STR's taxonomy for hotel class. Prior research shows that when a hotel unit is classified as upscale or above, it is perceived as an externality contributor to incumbents, but when its quality is lower than upscale, it is an externality beneficiary.

name: New unit organizational form
definition: Prior studies suggest that size, quality, and organizational form (company-operation vs. franchise) are characteristics to determine whether firms are contributors or beneficiaries. We used the operation information in the STR census data to classify each hotel establishment as franchised or company operated.

name: Sister unit brand similarity
authors_terms: ["different-brand sister units", "same-brand sister units", "same-brand (same-market-segment) sister unit", "different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit", "brand-specific rivalry"]
definition: Multiunit firms often operate business units under different brands to service not only the same but also different market segments (Kalnins, 2017). Different brands allow multiunit firms to target distinct market segments in the same geographic area (Morgan & Rego, 2009).

name: Sister unit market segment similarity
authors_terms: ["same-market-segment sister unit", "different-market-segment sister unit", "market-segment-specific rivalry", "product segment", "hotel class"]
definition: Multiunit firms can provide products or services differentiated across distinct brands to appeal to different target customers or even to different needs of the same customer. We classified each incumbent as a rival unit, same-brand (same-market-segment) sister unit, or different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit, using information on parent company, chain affiliation, and hotel class (i.e., economy, midscale, upper-midscale, upscale, upper-upscale, and luxury) in the STR census data.

name: Operating synergy motive
authors_terms: ["operating synergies", "operating synergy acquisitions", "operating motives", "acquisition motives related to operating synergies"]
definition: Acquisition motives related to gains achieved through the combination of the acquirer's and target's resources, such as revenue growth through new product offerings or cost savings through economies of scale.

name: Financial synergy motive
authors_terms: ["financial synergies", "financial synergy acquisitions", "financial motives", "acquisition motives related to financial synergies"]
definition: Acquisition motives related to gains achieved through the combination of the acquirer's and target's financial structure, including tax savings, lower cost of capital, diversification of cash flow streams, and extraction of gains from well-managed but undervalued targets.

name: Long-term acquisition performance
definition: Buy-and-hold abnormal returns mimic a passive investment strategy in which an investor buys a stock and holds it over a certain period; the authors measure them over a 2-year interval after the acquisition announcement to capture the extent to which the acquisition is value enhancing or destroying over this period.

name: Relative product quality
authors_terms: ["relative product quality", "product quality", "superior product quality", "quality outputs"]
definition: For the purpose of our paper, quality may be described as the characteristics of a product or service that can contribute to the fulfillment of stated or implied customer needs and wants. The relative product quality variable represents an assessment of the SBU's output quality made by the management teams of the sample firms.

name: Relative market share
definition: The relative market share variable consists of the SBU's revenue share relative to its three largest competitors, again pooled for each firm.

name: Relative direct costs
definition: The direct costs variable reflects the SBU's cost structure relative to the three leading firms in its industry.

name: Returns
definition: The returns variable is proxied by using the average ratio of cashflow-to-total investment for the years of the study.

name: Systematic risk
definition: One component of a firm's risk - systematic risk - varies with macroeconomic forces. Thus, the variability of a firm's stock returns that covaries with economic cycles can be attributed to the systematic risk component. Because the focus of our study is on business units - which have nontradeable equity - we use the term systematic variance in returns as a proxy for systematic risk.

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: Another component of risk - unsystematic risk - varies with firm- and industry-specific factors, which are unrelated to macroeconomic forces. We use the term unexplained variance in returns as a proxy for unsystematic risk; it refers to that portion of variance in returns which is not explained by the individual accounting betas.

name: Cross-cutting ties
definition: Building on Simmel (1955) and Blau and Schwartz (1984), we define cross-cutting ties as those relations that provide access to geographically remote contacts beyond a focal firm's social boundary. In this study, cross-cutting ties are conceived of as relationships that link geographically dispersed groups whose face-to-face interactions are infrequent.

name: Organizational density
definition: Increases in organizational density-commonly defined as number of firms-augment the social recognition of this business and attract more entrepreneurs to it. Organizational density, a proxy for density-dependent legitimation and competition, was measured by the number of firms that operated in a given state.

name: New firm formation
authors_terms: ["number of new firms", "new firm formation", "number of de novo entries"]
definition: The number of new firms was measured by the number of de novo entries into the biotechnology industry in a given state. A de novo entry for year t is defined as an active business entity that hires at least one employee and that did not exist prior to year t.

name: Industry process complexity
definition: At a broad level one can conceive of the complexity of manufacturing plants as an increasing function of the number of process stages (N), and the degree of uncertainty and 'noise' arising at each stage. It is difficult to obtain good empirical measures of process complexity for such a large sample, and hence the authors rely on rather simple proxies that are easily available.

name: Industry learning intensity
authors_terms: ["industry learning intensity", "learning intensity", "rate of learning-by-doing", "learning rate", "learning coefficient"]
definition: In this study, we focus on the importance of accumulated experience in the production process as a measure of the importance of learning-by-doing in an industry ('industry learning intensity'). The coefficient on prior experience, lambda, denotes the industry learning intensity.

name: Firm performance heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of firm performance", "firm performance heterogeneity", "cross-sectional dispersion of firm performance", "dispersion of firm performance"]
definition: Unlike most studies in the literature, we use direct measures of performance heterogeneity, specifically the cross-sectional dispersion of firm performance.

name: Divestment of South African operations
authors_terms: ["divestment announcements of South African operations", "divestments of South African business units", "corporate divestments of South African operations", "divestment of South African business units"]
definition: 'We focus our study on a special case: corporate divestments of South African operations.' The authors examine firms' announcement that they are terminating their corporate business interests in South Africa.

name: Abnormal stock returns
definition: The excess return 'which is that portion of return attributable to firm-specific activity', obtained after adjusting the observed daily rates of return for the expected rates of return calculated according to the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

name: CSI coverage
authors_terms: ["CSI coverage", "CSI coverage in the media", "media coverage of CSI"]
definition: We define CSI coverage as the number of news articles per quarter that blame a firm for CSI. In terms of scope, CSI coverage pertains to ecological issues, community relations, labor relations, or corporate governance.

name: Financial risk
definition: We define financial risk as the expected downwards volatility of a firm's earnings (Bettis, 1983; Miller & Reuer, 1996; Ruefli, Collins, & Lacugna, 1999) and operationalize it as credit risk.

name: Reach of CSI coverage
authors_terms: ["the reach of CSI coverage", "reach of the media outlet", "reach of the source", "average reach", "high reach"]
definition: Thus, we define the reach of a media outlet as the extent to which its CSI coverage can reach a multinational firm's stakeholder network.

name: Severity of CSI coverage
authors_terms: ["the severity of CSI coverage", "severity of the criticism", "average severity", "high severity"]
definition: We define the severity of CSI coverage as the strength of this interpretive frame.

name: Competitive uncertainty
authors_terms: ["competitive uncertainty", "level of competitive uncertainty faced by a firm"]
definition: Competitive uncertainty is higher to the extent that top executives have difficulty reliably predicting or anticipating the actions of competitors or the consequences of these actions (i.e., in the absence of communication). It also arises from difficulties in inferring the intentions or plans of competitors from their actions alone.

name: Formation of board-friendship ties
authors_terms: ["board-friendship ties", "formation of board-friendship ties to CEOs of competitors", "board-friendship ties to rivals"]
definition: Board-friendship ties to competitors may help firms manage competitive uncertainty by facilitating interfirm cooperation that reduces the likelihood of destructive competition between firms, while also providing a source of competitive advantage relative to firms that lack such ties. An outside director who is a friend of a rival's CEO is able to inform the rival's CEO about the firm's future plans because of the director's role in overseeing these decisions.

name: Reconstitution of broken board-friendship ties
authors_terms: ["reconstitution of broken board-friendship ties", "reconstitution of broken ties", "maintenance", "rebuild the broken tie"]
definition: The maintenance of network ties includes the reconstitution of ties that are accidentally broken. A board-friendship tie to the CEO of a competitor was coded as broken if an outside director was friends with the CEO at time t−1, and there was turnover of the CEO and/or director during the subsequent 12 months.

name: Headhunter solicitation of director candidates
authors_terms: ["headhunter's solicitation of director candidates from a competitor's CEO", "headhunter solicitation of director candidates"]
definition: Whether a headhunter solicited director candidates from a competitor's CEO on behalf of the focal firm. Headhunters at leading search firms are perceived to have particular expertise and experience in the 'delicate social process' of eliciting sensitive information about external candidates for leadership positions.

name: Firm performance
definition: The focal firm's financial performance; effective coordination of major decisions with competitors through board-friendship ties to their CEOs can give the firm a higher degree of market power relative to consumers and suppliers, leading to better financial performance.

name: Rational-comprehensive decision making
definition: Rationality is the use of information for the purpose of selecting a sensible alternative in the pursuit of one's goals; at the decision level it is 'the extent to which the decision process involves the collection of information relevant to the decision and the reliance upon analysis of this information in making the choice.'

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The external environments of the LGI SBUs were designed using Duncan's (1972) conceptualization of dynamic vs. static environments; unpredictable markets, rapidly changing technology, and shifting competition characterize the dynamic environment, while the stable environment has predictable markets, stable technology, and well-established competitive relationships.

name: Decision quality
definition: Decision quality is the extent to which the alternatives selected in a decision are good rather than poor, as rated beforehand by a panel of industry and academic experts; for a decision where all good alternatives are selected quality equals 100, and when the number of poor points exceeds the number of good points quality is negative.

name: Nation-dyadic historical conflict
authors_terms: ["historical conflict", "nation-dyadic historical conflict", "nation-dyadic conflict", "cumulative number of conflicts", "historical conflicts"]
definition: We conceptualize nation-dyadic historical conflicts as both discrete events and significant contributors to the idiosyncratic, multifaceted, dynamic, historical, and sociological interaction of national identities that impact dyadic conflict.

name: Cross-border corporate deals
authors_terms: ["cross-border corporate deals", "cross-border corporate activity", "cross-border deals", "corporate deals", "nation-dyadic corporate deals"]
definition: Our main dependent variable is the occurrence of nation-dyadic corporate activity (acquisitions, JVs, and strategic alliances), that is, CORPDEALS, between nation i and j in year t.

name: Predictability of nation-dyadic conflict
authors_terms: ["predictability of nation-dyadic conflict", "predictability of a potential conflict", "unpredictability of dyadic conflicts", "conflict proneness"]
definition: We assume the position that all nation-dyads have the potential to experience conflict and that the likelihood of conflict is not entirely predictable. Thus, the occurrence of a nation-dyadic conflict harbors both risk (predictable) and uncertainty (unpredictable).

name: Generational distance from historical conflict
authors_terms: ["generational distance", "number of generations between historical conflicts", "generations passed since the last conflict", "GENDIST"]
definition: Generational distance from historical conflicts dampens the salience and impact of such sentiments on cross-border business decisions. To test Hypothesis 2, we constructed a count variable (GENDIST) representing the total number of generations between the first and final conflict between nations i and j in the previous year.

name: Professional education
authors_terms: ["professional identities", "professional education", "tertiary education in the social sciences, business and law", "combined percentage of graduates from tertiary education in the social sciences, business, and law"]
definition: The professional identities of individuals who belong to the same epistemic community are shaped by secondary socialization mechanisms, such as formal education, job training, and professional associations, and reflect the shared governing paradigm of their profession.

name: Frequency-based imitation
authors_terms: ["frequency-based imitation", "Number of Prior Acquisitions within the Venture's Subfield", "number of prior acquisitions targeting the venture's rivals"]
definition: Frequency-based imitation occurs when firms imitate the actions conducted by a large number of other firms (Haunschild & Miner, 1997). The authors define the model acquisitions as the previous acquisitions targeting the other ventures, that is, a focal venture's rivals, within the focal venture's subfield.

name: Trait-based imitation
authors_terms: ["trait-based imitation", "Prominence of Prior Acquirers within the Venture's Subfield", "acquirer prominence"]
definition: Trait-based imitation is a more selective imitation mechanism than frequency-based imitation (Haunschild & Miner, 1997), wherein certain characteristics of the model firms affect the extent of imitation. The prominence of the model firms as indicated by their size or profitability can be an important trait that can prompt imitation.

name: Likelihood of being acquired
authors_terms: ["likelihood of being acquired", "hazard of the focal venture being acquired", "M&A Event"]
definition: The dependent variable is the hazard of the focal venture being acquired in a given year. M&A Event is denoted as whether or not the venture became the target of an acquisition in each spell.

name: Exogenous technological uncertainty
definition: Exogenous technological uncertainty is defined as uncertainty related to the technological environment in a venture's industry subfield that is largely unaffected by the venture's own actions (Mitchell, 1988). It is highly related to the extent to which the technological landscape in a venture's subfield might change unexpectedly in the future.

name: Technological distance
definition: The technological distance between two firms reflects the extent to which the underlying technologies and the knowledge bases of the firms are different. When tech distance is low, firms tend to be more similar to each other in terms of the underlying technological resources and knowledge base they have been utilizing.

name: Cost efficiency advantage
definition: If firms are effectively pursuing a low-cost strategy, they will have a cost efficiency advantage if the difference in WTP and cost for a given product is greater than that of rivals. A large value suggests that a focal carrier possesses a cost efficiency advantage in market j and time t.

name: Horizontal differentiation
authors_terms: ["horizontal differentiation", "horizontal product differentiation", "rivalry restraint", "focus strategy", "Generic Strategy 3"]
definition: Horizontal differentiation acknowledges that two products may differ in their characteristics and that these differing features appeal to different groups of customers. By targeting a subset of customers, the focus strategist (practicing horizontal product differentiation) reduces rivalry by only competing with a subset of firms for the target customer segment.

name: Firm profitability
authors_terms: ["city pair direct profit", "firm profitability", "firm profit", "firm performance"]
definition: Whereas competitive advantage is achieving a greater difference between WTP and cost than one's rivals, a firm's profitability is the difference between its revenue (which is based on price) and its cost.

name: Knowledge observability
definition: Adopting Zander's definition, observability is "how easy it is to understand the activity by looking at and examining different aspects of the process or final product." It concerns active attempts to imitate a technology or process by competitors, and the authors treat it as close to the articulability–tacit dimension of knowledge.

name: System embeddedness
definition: System embeddedness refers to the extent to which the knowledge in question is a function of the system or context in which it is embedded. Embeddedness consists of many interacting components: the level of interdependence between individuals and teams working on related activities, the level of experience of those individuals, the inability to divide up or modularize a given activity, and the site specificity of an activity.

name: Interunit integration
definition: Interunit integration refers to the state of collaboration among units, and the techniques used to achieve this collaboration. It parallels Lawrence and Lorsch's (1967) measure of integration.

name: R&D unit autonomy
definition: Autonomy is the extent to which the R&D unit is able to make strategic decisions without the involvement of corporate headquarters.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: The authors focus on knowledge transfer between the R&D unit and other parts of the organization, treating it as a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for the attainment of competitive advantage.

name: Targeted shaming
authors_terms: ["targeted shaming", "listed as stingy", "stingy list", "international iron roosters"]
definition: Targeted shaming is a direct pressuring tactic in which the Web becomes a stage where targeted corporations are publicly displayed, sensitizing executives and spurring them to concede to prevent further damage to the corporation's public image.

name: Diffuse pressure from the online campaign
authors_terms: ["diffuse pressure", "diffuse pressure from the online campaign"]
definition: The online publicity and praise given to donors, the call to action for donations, and negative comments on low donations drew public attention to firms' giving, sensitized corporative executives to the changed host-country environment, and triggered social comparisons among corporations.

name: Self-presentation of CSR
authors_terms: ["self-presentation of CSR", "self-proclaimed CSR policy", "public displays of CSR"]
definition: A growing trend among firms worldwide to present their CSR activities in corporate reports, websites, and advertising; MNCs tend to adopt formal CSR reporting to enhance their legitimacy in the eyes of their home-country stakeholders, and their subsidiaries in China may have inherited this procedure.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: Corporate reputation is a general assessment of a firm's character and approval rating from the public. Because reputation is socially constructed and conferred by an external audience, a good reputation can be lost if that audience changes its perception as a result of a critical event.

name: Institutional logic of discretionary corporate philanthropy
authors_terms: ["institutional logic of discretionary corporate philanthropy", "home-country institutional logic", "institutional logic for corporate philanthropy in home countries"]
definition: Institutional logics shape organizational-level assumptions, values, and routines, and they guide decision makers' attention. Cross-national comparative research has found different national institutional logics for CSR: differences in national business systems give rise to explicit CSR in less regulated economies such as the United States, as opposed to implicit CSR in coordinated market economies such as Europe, Canada, and Japan.

name: Speed of corporate response
authors_terms: ["respond sooner", "respond more quickly", "how quickly MNC subsidiaries responded", "hazard rate of donation"]
definition: How quickly MNC subsidiaries responded to the online campaign with a donation. The dependent variable is the hazard rate of donation: at any given time, each firm in the risk set faces some underlying 'risk' that it will donate.

name: Magnitude of corporate response
authors_terms: ["magnitude of firm response", "magnitude of response", "total donation amount"]
definition: Because firms incur costs when responding to the demands of a social movement, they differ also in the magnitude of their responses.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age gauges not just the length of a firm's operational experience but also the duration of its exposure to environmental changes.

name: Rate of innovation
definition: We tested hypothesis 1, that older organizations will produce a greater number of innovations, by modeling the rate of patenting as a function of firm age and other covariates.

name: Technological self-citation
authors_terms: ["self-citing patents", "self-citation patenting", "build on their previous innovative activity", "greater tendency to build on their previous innovative activity"]
definition: We differentiated between two types of patents that can be issued to a firm: self-citing patents, which include one or more citations to the firm's prior patents and are thus related to prior endeavors, and non-self-citing patents, which do not build on the firm's earlier patented inventions and thus are a departure from a focal firm's previous innovative activity.

name: Age of cited prior art
authors_terms: ["age of the prior art cited", "average citation age", "citation lag", "age of the foundations of firms' current-period innovations"]
definition: We tested hypothesis 3, that old firms will be less likely than young firms to incorporate the most recent technological developments into their previous innovative activities, by measuring the age of the foundations of each firm's current-period innovations (i.e., the age of the prior art cited by a firm's current-period patents). We predict that the patents of older firms will include longer citation lags (the time elapsed between the application dates of the cited and citing patent).

name: Innovation impact
authors_terms: ["importance of firms' innovations", "influence of the organization's innovations on its technological community", "citation rate", "rate at which the patent is cited"]
definition: A final indication of the fit between a firm's innovative activities and the current technological environment is the influence of the organization's innovations on its technological community. Previous studies have shown that highly cited patents cover innovations that experts in a technological area perceive to have been the most important inventions in that area.

name: Competitive release
authors_terms: ["competitive release", "release of resources", "failure of near-center producers", "demise of regional utilities"]
definition: The release of resources that occurs through the failure of near-center producers, which disrupts the perceived unity of the market and makes the distinct identity of peripheral producers apparent to audience members. The authors argue that the beneficial effects accruing to peripheral organizations from competitive release are in addition to those elicited by market concentration.

name: Matching to local audience preferences
authors_terms: ["matching to local values and preferences", "matching", "localness", "greenness", "identity matching"]
definition: The correspondence between the identity claims of a peripheral producer and the values and preferences of its target audience; here, the extent to which localness and greenness, the features of the municipal utility identity, are endorsed by the inhabitants of the county in which the MU is located.

name: Engagement with claimed identity
definition: The active engagement of a peripheral producer with its claimed identity. In this setting, cooperation among MUs represented a credible commitment to their collective identity and augmented the salience of the MU identity in the eyes of audience members.

name: Organizational growth
authors_terms: ["growth rate", "organizational growth rates", "market success", "change in size"]
definition: The market success of the incumbent municipal utilities is framed with respect to organizational growth rates; the dependent variable of the study is the change in size of each MU, size being measured as retail sales of electricity to households.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: CEOs who have inflated views of themselves and who seek to have those positive self-views continuously reinforced; narcissistic CEOs have a high need for attention and praise as well as a strong desire to have their positive self-views reinforced.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Voluntary managerial 'actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law'.

name: Corporate philanthropy media profile
authors_terms: ["corporate philanthropy media profile", "CPMP", "high profile corporate philanthropy"]
definition: Media praise for CEOs following company philanthropic actions, assessed by a content analysis of key publications that cover general and business news.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Given the nature of our hypothesized effects and arguments, a widely accepted measure of operational performance captures the expected effects on the performance of firm operations caused by CSR decisions made by firms in the study.

name: Multipoint contact
authors_terms: ["multipoint contact", "MPC", "analyst's MPC on a focal firm", "analyst–firm MPC"]
definition: An actor's MPC in a focal domain describes the incidence of joint participation with competitors in other domains. MPC is specific to each analyst–firm pair and refers to the relatedness of the focal firm to other firms the analyst covered.

name: Forecasting accuracy
authors_terms: ["forecasting accuracy", "accuracy of earnings per share (EPS) forecasts", "accuracy"]
definition: A well-established metric reflecting analysts' firm-specific knowledge is the accuracy of earnings per share (EPS) forecasts. Accurately forecasting a firm's future EPS demonstrates the analyst understands major aspects of the firm's operations, as well as the market ecosystem affecting demand for the firm's products and services.

name: Information leadership
definition: Information leadership captures the extent to which a focal analyst's forecasts prompt rivals to update their own forecasts more than rivals' forecasts influence the focal analyst.

name: Forecast differentiation
definition: High quality forecasts are most beneficial for the analyst's reputation when the analyst can differentiate their forecasts from the consensus estimate. Differentiation is the difference between a focal analyst's annual forecast on a focal firm and the consensus estimate for all analysts covering that firm.

name: Forecast dispersion
definition: A measure for firm-level outcome uncertainty used in prior research is analysts' forecast dispersion. Dispersion reflects the inherent difficulty of deciphering a focal firm's prospects.

name: Attack visibility
definition: Most models of human motivation seem to assume that in order to respond to a threat, one must first notice it; thus in a corporate setting, the more obvious an attack, the greater the likelihood that it will be countered. Visibility is a tacit precondition of the expectancy model, since rivals will not be inclined to respond unless they are aware of an attack.

name: Response difficulty
authors_terms: ["response difficulty", "difficulty of response", "difficulty of responding", "perceived difficulty of retaliation", "response ease"]
definition: In a competitive situation, effort-performance expectancy will be reflected by the perceived ease of mounting appropriate retaliation; an action is more likely to evoke a response if it is easy to imitate. Response difficulty is the ease with which a competitor can respond in kind to an attack.

name: Attack centrality
definition: Centrality of attack reflects the degree to which the markets of a given competitor are threatened by an action. It captures the direct threat of an action to rivals in the markets under attack, and it is the extent to which the attack pertains to markets that are especially large, valued by, or vital to potential responders.

name: Competitive retaliation
definition: The proclivity of rivals to respond to a competitive attack. The consequences of a competitive action for an attacker depend at least in part on the number of responses that action provokes; for Hypotheses 1 to 4 the response variable is simply the number of responses evoked by an action, defined as the total number of competitors who actually respond to an action.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance was assessed using the three most widely accepted measures in the airline industry: total operating revenue per revenue passenger mile (RPM), operating profit per RPM and profit margin. To complement these measures the authors also used Standard and Poor's published stock ratings for each airline for each year.

name: Category spanning
authors_terms: ["style spanning", "category spanning", "spanning across winemaking styles", "producers' spanning across wine styles", "spanning of winemaking styles"]
definition: Style spanning is expressed by an index of concentration (1 minus the Simpson's index of diversity), calculated as the sum of the squared proportions of the wines in a winery's portfolio made in each style in a vintage. A winery can focus and not span by producing wines only in one style; the two categories correspond to styles associated with each method of production (aging), botti or barriques.

name: Critical ratings in blind tastings
authors_terms: ["Gambero Rosso ratings", "ratings assigned through blind tastings", "blind ratings", "ratings assigned blindly", "Gambero Rosso glasses"]
definition: In the Gambero Rosso guide, tasters do not know the price category of the wine or the identity of the winery whose wine is being rated. Ratings assigned through blind tastings are used as an assessment of the underlying characteristics of the wines and as a control for the underlying quality of the wine.

name: Critical ratings in nonblind tastings
authors_terms: ["Veronelli ratings", "star ratings", "ratings assigned through nonblind tastings", "nonblind ratings"]
definition: For the Veronelli guide the critic at least knows the producer's identity and other information that typically includes wine type, the area of production, and the vintage; the star ratings are supplied for individual wines after one or multiple tastings conducted during individual visits to the wineries. These ratings measure how favorably a wine was evaluated by a critic who is aware of the producer's identity.

name: CEO power over the board
authors_terms: ["CEO power over the board", "managerial power", "CEO power variables"]
definition: The manager with power over the board of directors is able to increase his or her own compensation; the manager can influence actions or inactions of board members, most notably via participation in director nomination and reappointment processes and via social ties with directors. The concept of managerial power is multidimensional and not easily observable, which is why the author uses a vector of variables to proxy for it.

name: SERP benefits
authors_terms: ["SERP benefits", "supplemental executive retirement plan benefits", "CEO SERP benefits", "pension increment"]
definition: SERP benefits increase executive postretirement income beyond the regular pension: under a SERP the firm makes ongoing payments to the retired executive on top of the regular pension until his or her death or even until the death of the surviving spouse. Executives accumulate ('earn') SERP benefits while working but receive SERP benefits only after retirement, and SERP benefits are paid to retired executives regardless of firm performance in the payout years.

name: Cash pay
definition: The author defines cash pay as the most transparent compensation component; it includes base salary and annual bonus.

name: Stock option grants
authors_terms: ["stock option grants", "value of annual stock option awards"]
definition: The author defines stock option grants as the middle ground in transparency: although most details on stock option grants are publicly available, stock option disclosures are not as transparent as straightforward cash pay disclosures.

name: Horizon problem
definition: When the anticipated tenure of the manager is shorter than the firm's optimal investment horizon, the manager would prefer projects with lower net present value but higher current earnings. The condition, commonly referred to as the horizon problem, should be especially pronounced prior to the manager's retirement.

name: SERP performance contingency
definition: CEOs with SERP arrangements in which pensionable earnings consist of base salary and performance bonus are directly contingent on firm earnings in SERP accumulation years via the bonus component, in contrast to SERPs in which pensionable earnings consist of base salary only and are therefore not directly contingent on firm earnings.

name: R&D expenditures
definition: Firm research and development expenditures; the author uses a relative measure of R&D expenditures to control for the variation in R&D across industries and firms of different sizes.

name: Investor gender
definition: The gender of the venture capital investor or investment partner involved in the venture's early financing round. The authors distinguish whether first round investors include female VC partners, male VC partners, or both, and identify a firm as being backed by a female (or male) VC based on the gender of the investment partner directly involved in the deal.

name: Founder gender
definition: The gender of the venture's founder or entrepreneur. Following prior work, the authors classify firms with at least one female founder as 'female-founded', and in the experiment they manipulate the gender of the entrepreneur presenting the pitch.

name: Second-round financing
authors_terms: ["second round of financing", "additional financing", "subsequent round of financing", "follow-on round"]
definition: Whether a venture raised a subsequent round of financing on a given day, conditional upon not having already received it. Raising a second round is treated as a strong, positive signal that investors evaluate the venture's future prospects favorably.

name: Pitch quality
authors_terms: ["pitch quality", "quality of the pitch", "evaluations of pitches", "quality of the business idea"]
definition: Observers' evaluation of the quality of an entrepreneur's pitch. After watching the video, participants were asked to evaluate the quality of the pitch, using composite measures adapted from prior research and pitch-competition scoring criteria.

name: Entrepreneur competence
authors_terms: ["entrepreneur competence", "perceptions of entrepreneur competence", "perceived competence", "discount in perceptions of competence"]
definition: Perceptions of the entrepreneur's competence, that is, the extent to which observers credit the founder's own skill and qualifications for her achievement. The authors theorize that future investors discount a female entrepreneur's competence as the key factor in an early-stage investment decision when the investment comes from a female investor.

name: Trust in local staff
authors_terms: ["trust in local mainland staff", "trust of Hong Kong managers in their local mainland staff", "trust in their staff in mainland China"]
definition: A psychological state comprising the intention to accept vulnerability based upon positive expectations of the intentions or behavior of another. Trust is measured as the Hong Kong managers' psychological state with respect to whether they have positive expectations of the intentions or behavior of local staff and are therefore willing to accept vulnerability towards them.

name: Perceived effectiveness of the legal system
authors_terms: ["effectiveness of China's legal system", "legal system effectiveness"]
definition: The Hong Kong managers' individual perceptions of the effectiveness of the Chinese legal system for their business, i.e. the extent to which the legal system in China is seen to provide an effective system of support for transactions.

name: Arbitrariness of officials
authors_terms: ["arbitrary behavior of officials", "arbitrariness of officials", "arbitrary behavior by government officials"]
definition: How arbitrary the respondents find the behavior of Chinese officials, reflecting high levels of inconsistency, arbitrariness, and corruption on the part of officials.

name: Availability of competent human resources
authors_terms: ["availability of competent human resources", "competent local HR"]
definition: Satisfaction with the availability in China of training, managers, and employees; the perceived availability of educational institutions and training that provide people with reliably certified competencies.

name: Development of personal rapport
definition: A strategy in active trust development of establishing personal rapport with the staff of operations in China, thereby establishing a system of personal relationships both within and outside the business venture.

name: Local recruitment of managers
authors_terms: ["managers recruited from China", "recruit managers for their operations locally", "localization"]
definition: A strategy of locally recruiting managers, through which investors demonstrate that they are willing to increase their vulnerability by relying on local managers rather than sending in expatriates.

name: Transfer of business practices
authors_terms: ["transfer of practices", "transferring practices to China", "transfer of business practices"]
definition: A strategy of active trust development in which a company attempts to substitute its own micro-institutionalization for the lack of institutional foundations, through importing its familiar practices, rules, and standards into its cross-border operations.

name: Performance of China operations
authors_terms: ["performance of their China operations", "performance of China-based operations", "growth of sales and profits"]
definition: Satisfaction with the performance of the firm's China operations and the growth of such operations in terms of sales and profit, measured as a second-order dependent variable hypothesized to correlate positively with the level of trust of Hong Kong managers in their local mainland staff.

name: CEO retirement
definition: CEOs approaching retirement are those in their last years in office, and their concern about labor market evaluation is likely to be strongest during the last couple of years before retirement.

name: Firm commitment to corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["firm commitment to CSR", "firm commitment to corporate social responsibility", "corporate social responsibility (CSR)"]
definition: The authors treat firm commitment to CSR as a long-term-oriented strategic investment: the financial return from commitment to CSR is not immediate and requires a time-consuming process of reputation build-up and firm-stakeholder relationship improvement, and CSR has a negative, or at best an unclear, short-term payoff.

name: CEO retirement age
authors_terms: ["CEO age", "age at retirement", "retires at an older age"]
definition: A good measure to gauge a retiree's intention to continue to participate in the workforce is his or her age at retirement; CEOs retiring at relatively older ages may be less interested in serving as corporate directors after retirement.

name: CEO retention on own board
authors_terms: ["CEO retention on the board", "retained on his or her own board", "retention on their own boards"]
definition: This dichotomous variable denotes whether the retired CEO served as a board member of the same firm after having stepped down from the CEO position.

name: Competitors' new technology adoption
authors_terms: ["competitors' new technology adoption", "the percentage of all TCM producers within that began introducing hybrid TCM in Western dosage form by the end of the previous year"]
definition: For every submarket in a given year, the percentage of all TCM producers within that submarket that had begun introducing hybrid TCM in Western dosage form by the end of the previous year. It indicates the amount of competitors in a market that had already adopted the discontinuous technology.

name: Firm performance
definition: To capture firm performance the author employed a firm's annual return on sales (ROS), measured as the ratio of firm profits to product sales in the same year.

name: Rural population
authors_terms: ["rural population", "yearly percentage of its rural population", "percentage of rural population"]
definition: The yearly percentage of a province's population that is rural, where a rural population is defined in the China Population Statistics Yearbook as all individuals whose livelihood depends on agriculture, hunting, fishing, or forestry. The measure was mean-centered before entry into the regressions.

name: Exclusive classic TCM formula ownership
definition: Exclusive formulae are often unique, secretive, or historic formulae newly uncovered by a firm, for which the Chinese SFDA typically grants 3 to 8 years of market exclusivity. The variable captures whether a firm owned any exclusive classic TCM formula in a given year.

name: Firm output scale
definition: Firm output scale, measured using the logarithm of a firm's annual sales.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Corporate reputations are conceptualized as subjective evaluations of firms' overall quality, reflecting a judgment of the firm's underlying capabilities and behavioral propensities that shape what it can do and what it is likely to do.

name: CEO media prominence
authors_terms: ["CEO Media Prominence", "CEO media coverage", "media attention", "CEO prominence"]
definition: The degree to which specific CEOs are salient to evaluators because information about them is available; the authors focus on leaders being prominent (i.e., well-known) as reflected in the volume of media coverage they receive.

name: Positive CEO media coverage
authors_terms: ["Positive CEO Media Tenor", "positive media attention", "positive coverage"]
definition: The favorable tenor of the media coverage that CEOs receive, which sends evaluative signals about leaders whose quality is difficult to assess and is thought to reduce uncertainty about leader quality.

name: Negative CEO media coverage
definition: The unfavorable tenor of the media coverage that CEOs receive, which sends evaluative signals about leaders whose quality is difficult to assess; when firms struggle, CEOs tend to receive substantial blame and criticism in the press.

name: CEO industry awards
definition: Industry and media awards constitute certification contests in which outside parties validate and enhance a leader's stature; they should increase CEOs' perceived quality and prominence.

name: CEO outsider standing
authors_terms: ["Outsider CEO", "outsider standing", "CEO insider or outsider standing"]
definition: Outsider CEOs are those brought in from a firm other than the focal firm, as compared to insider CEOs who have typically spent many years with the focal firm 'working up through the ranks' before taking office.

name: Threat of entry
definition: An entry plan signals credible entry intent but does not fully commit the firm to enter the market.

name: Incumbent capacity expansion
authors_terms: ["capacity expansion", "expansion of casino floor space", "capacity installations", "strategic investments"]
definition: In the casino industry, capacity is determined by casino floor space. From this perspective, floor space is the key strategic variable that casinos use to compete with other properties.

name: Entry plan failure
authors_terms: ["entry failure", "stalled entry", "likelihood of entry failure", "success of entry deterrence"]
definition: In the Gambling Business Directory, a failed entry attempt is registered as a property that is planned, but then the record becomes stale when it is not updated in the database thereafter.

name: Incumbent casino demand
definition: The cash withdrawal data allow me to observe incumbent casino demand at the zip code month level. As consumer demand takes less time to adjust than casino size, this analysis is conducted for a narrow window surrounding entry plans and new casino openings.

name: Attention to a document supplier
authors_terms: ["attention", "allocation of attention", "attention allocated to that supplier's documents"]
definition: The amount of time and energy that employees in an organization allocate to identifying, evaluating, and acquiring documents from electronic information sources in the organization.

name: Market segment crowdedness
authors_terms: ["crowdedness", "crowded segments", "crowded market segment", "crowded market niche", "degree of overlap"]
definition: A focal document supplier that offers the same knowledge content as a number of other suppliers in an organization has a high degree of overlap and operates in a crowded market niche or market segment. The higher this overlap, the more crowded the focal group's market segment, because other suppliers are offering much of the same knowledge content.

name: Topic concentration
definition: The first dimension is the extent of topic concentration based on the number of topic areas to be covered in the document supply. Choosing to offer documents on many topics is similar to pursuing a generalist strategy based on a broad product line.

name: Document selectivity
definition: The second dimension is the degree of document selectivity. Selective suppliers filter and edit documents to make sure that the documents they supply are of high quality and reduce the total number of documents they offer.

name: Function exploration-exploitation
definition: The value chain function that an alliance serves: firms that engage partners in R&D that may lead to innovative technologies and applications participate in exploration, whereas firms that rely on alliances for commercializing and using existing technologies or employing complementary partner capabilities undertake exploitation. Exploration alliances engage in upstream activities, enabling partners to share tacit knowledge and develop new knowledge, whereas exploitation alliances engage in downstream activities such as commercialization and marketing.

name: Structure exploration-exploitation
definition: The structure domain takes into account the network positions of a firm's partners: recurrent alliances between firms are considered a form of exploitation, and alliances formed with new partners are considered exploration. Forming alliances with partners with no prior ties to the firm is structure exploration, whereas forming recurrent alliances with prior partners is structure exploitation.

name: Attribute exploration-exploitation
definition: The attribute domain refers to intertemporal variance in the organizational attributes of a firm's partners. A deviation from a systematic pattern of alliance formation with partners that share certain organizational attributes is considered exploratory behavior, whereas persistently forming alliances with partners similar to prior partners in attributes such as size and industry focus is exploitation.

name: Function exploration experience
authors_terms: ["function exploration experience", "accumulated exploration experience within each domain"]
definition: A firm's accumulated exploration experience in the function domain: the same formula used for constructing its exploration measures is applied to all alliances the firm formed between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1) rather than to the alliances formed in year t.

name: Structure exploration experience
authors_terms: ["structure exploration experience", "accumulated exploration experience within each domain"]
definition: A firm's accumulated exploration experience in the structure domain: the same formula used for constructing its exploration measures is applied to all alliances the firm formed between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1) rather than to the alliances formed in year t.

name: Attribute exploration experience
authors_terms: ["attribute exploration experience", "accumulated exploration experience within each domain"]
definition: A firm's accumulated exploration experience in the attribute domain: the same formula used for constructing its exploration measures is applied to all alliances the firm formed between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1) rather than to the alliances formed in year t.

name: Time
definition: We measured time on the basis of the year in which alliances were formed; for each firm-year, our time clock ranged between 1 and 12, with 1 corresponding to 1990 and 12 corresponding to 2001.

name: CEO negative relative pay standing
authors_terms: ["CEO negative relative pay standing", "CEO relative pay standing", "CEO underpayment", "underpaid CEOs", "CEO negative relative standing status"]
definition: In this study, we use the terms CEO negative relative pay standing, CEO underpayment, and underpaid CEOs synonymously, to reflect the condition under which CEOs are paid less relative to their similar labor market peers.

name: Acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["acquisition activity", "acquisition behavior", "total acquisitions", "number of large acquisitions"]
definition: We measured total acquisitions as the number of acquisitions announced during a year and subsequently completed. We also captured a separate measure of acquisition activity that included only large acquisitions, calculated as the number of acquisitions whose total deal size was greater than $1 million.

name: Acquisition payment method
authors_terms: ["payment method", "use of stock as a payment method", "percentage of the stock used"]
definition: Specifically, acquirers generally finance acquisitions with cash, stock, or some combination. Payment in stock, as opposed to cash, allows the acquiring firm and its investors to share some of the acquisition-related risk with the acquired firm and its owners.

name: Subsequent CEO pay change
authors_terms: ["change in total compensation", "subsequent pay change", "subsequent CEO compensation increases"]
definition: The dependent variable in Hypotheses 3a and 3b is change in total compensation. To capture change in total compensation, we used the total CEO compensation each firm publicly reported during each year of our sample.

name: Long-term compensation change
definition: To test Hypothesis 4, we then separated total compensation into change in short-term compensation and change in long-term compensation.

name: Short-term compensation change
definition: To test Hypothesis 4, we then separated total compensation into change in short-term compensation and change in long-term compensation.

name: Ongoing knowledge brokering
authors_terms: ["ongoing knowledge brokering", "ongoing firm knowledge brokering", "ongoing firm knowledge-brokering stock", "knowledge brokering"]
definition: We use ongoing knowledge brokering to refer to the process of continuous exploratory search in which firms arbitrage and recombine knowledge across fields of technology for productive reuse. Ongoing knowledge brokering emphasizes the overlap between the technical domain a firm relies on and the technical area in which it produces new knowledge.

name: Initial knowledge brokering
authors_terms: ["initial knowledge brokering", "initial knowledge brokers", "initial nonbrokers", "venture ideation"]
definition: By initial knowledge brokering, we refer to situations in which founders originated venture ideas by transferring and recombining knowledge from one domain into another. Since the technology was widely available through a nonexclusive license from Stanford University, we define initial knowledge brokers as founders who recognized the Cohen-Boyer patent as a component of an entrepreneurial opportunity.

name: Innovation performance
definition: The dependent variable in Table 4 is the number of external forward citations within five years of patent issue, a well-established measure of innovative impact. We restrict the forward citation count to those made by external entities (by excluding self-citations) to explore the role of ongoing knowledge brokering across organizational boundaries.

name: External technical hiring
authors_terms: ["hired inventors with different technical knowledge stock", "hiring technical staff", "external mechanisms", "external boundary-spanning mechanisms"]
definition: Hiring inventors with prior experience in different technical areas allows a firm to introduce those areas into its existing repertoire of knowledge. The variable is a measure of the extent to which organizations hired technical staff with a different knowledge base relative to the firm's technical capability at that point in time.

name: Local component interdependence
definition: Local interdependence reflects the extent to which the elements around a focal node are loosely or tightly coupled. If all three nodes are interdependent, one can talk about high local interdependence; if they are not, one talks about low local interdependence.

name: Dispersion of components across clusters
authors_terms: ["dispersion across clusters", "component dispersion across clusters", "spread of components across multiple clusters"]
definition: Clusters are neighborhoods in which members are more tightly connected internally than to external nodes. One can conceptualize a firm's components as a set of elements that are primarily drawn from a single cluster or spread across multiple clusters in the innovation ecosystem.

name: Central component use
authors_terms: ["central component use", "use of central components", "central components"]
definition: Centrality means that a node is occupying an important network position. We theorize about eigenvector centrality, which considers not only the linkages of a focal node but also the connectedness of other nodes to which the focal node is linked.

name: Firm performance
definition: Web traffic is the main measure of performance of e-commerce firms, which is widely used by managers and investors. Traffic generates sales to customers and influences advertising revenues.

name: Negative shock to interdependencies
definition: External shocks to the ecosystem's alignment structure can be positive or negative. Yet, it is the negative shocks that are particularly important to understand as they have the potential to disrupt the ecosystem by undermining component interdependencies.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: The total number of prior acquisitions that an institution in our sample made between 1988, the year following the last major regulatory change (CEBA) that had significant impact upon bank acquisition strategies, and the year of a focal acquisition.

name: Focal acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["focal acquisition performance", "recent acquisition performance", "acquisition performance", "performance feedback"]
definition: The short-term importance of an event like an acquisition can be assessed by the price change in the acquirer's security during a period surrounding the event; this price change is calculated as the difference between the observed and the predicted, or normal, return for the same security.

name: Subsequent acquisition likelihood
authors_terms: ["likelihood of making a subsequent acquisition", "subsequent acquisition likelihood", "future acquisition likelihood", "acquisition behavior"]
definition: Our dependent variable, the likelihood of making a subsequent acquisition, was estimated as the hazard of a bank in the sample making a subsequent acquisition after a focal acquisition.

name: Platform owner entry
authors_terms: ["platform owner entry", "entry by the platform owner", "direct entry into complementors' domains"]
definition: Entry by the platform owner into complementors' domains with its own, first-party products. Such entry differs from a typical entry because the platform owner benefits from an advantageous position from the start, including outsized power to promote products of its choice and near-complete information about complementors' products.

name: Complementor positioning
definition: The choice to operate on either one or multiple platforms. Specialists are firms that operate only on the focal platform (singlehomers), while generalists are firms that operate both on the focal and on a competing platform (multihomers).

name: Effort allocation on the focal platform
authors_terms: ["effort allocation", "effort on the focal platform", "effort allocation on the focal platform"]
definition: Complementors' allocation of effort on the focal platform, which in this context is typically measured as product-related changes such as product innovation, product maintenance and new product release.

name: Effort allocation on the competing platform
authors_terms: ["effort on the competing platform", "effort allocation on the competing platform", "cross-platform allocation of effort"]
definition: Complementors' allocation of effort on the competing platform, measured as product-related changes such as updates to and maintenance of existing applications and the release of new applications on that platform.

name: Non-platform owner entry
authors_terms: ["entry by firms that are not the focal platform owners", "entry of another big player", "non-platform owner entries"]
definition: Entry by a large firm that is not the focal platform owner, examined through Microsoft's entry with the To Do application and SanDisk's Cloud application on the App Store as comparison cases to platform owner entry.

name: Normative employee management rhetorics
definition: According to normative rhetorics, employers can render employees more productive by shaping their thoughts and capitalizing on their emotions.

name: Rational employee management rhetorics
definition: According to rational rhetorics, work processes can be formalized and rationalized to optimize labor productivity, as can the reward systems that guarantee recalcitrant employees' adherence to these formal processes.

name: Scientific management rhetoric
definition: The scientific management rhetoric touted a variety of employee management techniques with the promise that they would increase labor productivity by streamlining and rationalizing work processes and by appealing to employees' economic self-interest. It advocates the achievement of these goals through the use of a combination of techniques that include time studies, motion studies, rate setting, job analyses, piece rates, and work measurements.

name: Systems rationalism rhetoric
definition: The systems rationalism rhetoric, which emerged during the 1950s and advocated the use of techniques for rationalizing production, such as statistical quality control, management by objectives, and cost benefit analysis.

name: Welfare work rhetoric
definition: The first normative employee management rhetoric in the United States was industrial betterment, or welfare work. Welfare work techniques were defined in 1919 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics as "anything for the comfort and improvement, intellectual or social, of the employees, over and above wages paid, which is not a necessity of the industry nor required by law."

name: Human relations and personnel management rhetoric
authors_terms: ["human relations/personnel management rhetoric", "human relations and personnel management"]
definition: The second normative rhetoric, which emerged during the 1920s and 1930s, has been called the human relations/personnel management rhetoric. Under this label fall not only the writings of academics in the fields of human relations and industrial relations, but also, more importantly, those of specialists in a profession first called employee management, then personnel management, and currently, human resource management.

name: Organization culture and quality rhetoric
authors_terms: ["culture-quality rhetoric", "organization culture and quality", "organizational culture and quality"]
definition: A third normative rhetoric emerged in the 1970s: organizational culture and quality. Under this label, coined by Barley and Kunda (1992), those authors placed writings of both academics and consultants stressing transformational leadership, strong employee values, and shared beliefs as the path to increased labor productivity.

name: Voluntary employee turnover
definition: A high rate of voluntary turnover among employees reveals widespread poor performance in retaining employees. Managers aspire to specific levels of voluntary employee exit (voluntary turnover).

name: Labor union activity
definition: Researchers have measured private sector labor union activity in varied ways: union foundings, the percentage of employees belonging to unions, and the frequency of strikes.

name: Long waves of macroeconomic activity
authors_terms: ["long waves", "Kondratieff long waves", "50-year cycles of macroeconomic activity"]
definition: Long waves are 50-year cycles of macroeconomic expansion and contraction.

name: Significant ownership with low expertise
authors_terms: ["SOLE Director", "significant ownership, low expertise", "outside director who has a large ownership stake but lacks top-level business experience", "directors who have large shareholdings but lack business expertise"]
definition: A SOLE Director (where SOLE is an acronym for 'significant ownership, low expertise') is defined as an outside or outside-related director who lacks top-level business experience (i.e., who is not the founder of a Fortune 500 company, not the current or retired CEO or chairman of a Fortune 500 company, and not a director of more than one Fortune 500 company) and who owns shareholdings of at least 0.1 percent.

name: Departure of significant owners with low expertise
authors_terms: ["departures of SOLE Directors", "SOLE Directors Decreases", "departures of such directors"]
definition: The dynamic implication of the first two hypotheses is that the departure from a company's board of one or more directors who have large ownership stakes but lack top-level business experience should be associated with higher firm value.

name: Firm value
definition: Our dependent variable is Tobin's q, approximated as a firm's current market-to-book ratio.

name: Cognitive ability
definition: Workers' productivity depends on unobservable traits, collectively called ability. Ability can be inferred from many traits and behaviors, but the signals of it available to employers are imperfect.

name: Observable signal of ability
definition: Although potential employers cannot observe workers' ability, they see a public, albeit noisy, signal of it. Employers base wage offers solely on this signal.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: The worker could reject all offers to become the residual claimant of his own productivity - an entrepreneur. Those who choose entrepreneurship are residual claimants of their talents, in contrast to employees who are paid according to their observable signals.

name: Earnings
definition: Annual Income is total net family income expressed in 2010$. Values are top-coded such that incomes of the top 2 percent of earners are coded as the average value of the top two percent.

name: Earnings variance
definition: All employees with a given signal earn the same wage, despite the fact that they have a range of abilities, whereas, since entrepreneurs earn according to their ability, their incomes are not only higher but exhibit greater spread.

name: Household net worth
definition: Net-worth is created by summing all asset values and subtracting all debts of respondent's family and expressed in 2010$. Net-worth of the top two percent are top-coded as the average of the top two percent.

name: Entrepreneurial advantage
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial advantage", "gap between ability and education", "ability-education gap", "ability-signal gap"]
definition: We derive a single measure of the extent of a worker's advantage in entrepreneurship relative to wage work, under either theory - we refer to it as entrepreneurial advantage. It is the difference between each individual's AFQT score and the median AFQT score for those sharing the individual's educational qualification.

name: Career stage
definition: Asymmetric information about worker ability is highest at the beginning of a worker's career, when he has no documentable experience or output. Over time employers get more information about a worker's ability than just education.

name: U.S.-based scientist status
definition: An indicator variable intended to capture whether a scientist was based at a U.S. institution immediately prior to the Bush policy change in 2001 and, hence, was directly affected by the shock. It is equal to one for all scientists whose primary affiliations were exclusively with U.S.-based institutions during the preshock period.

name: hESC research output
authors_terms: ["hESC citation-weighted publications", "hESC research output", "citation-weighted publications in the hESC subfield"]
definition: The authors measure scientists' research direction and output using their citation-weighted number of publications per year across different subfields of the stem cell domain. More specifically, they use the natural logarithm of one plus the number of forward citations to scientist i's publications in year t in hESC research.

name: Non-hESC stem cell research output
authors_terms: ["non-hESC stem cell research output", "non-hESC SC citation-weighted publications", "citation-weighted publications in non-hESC subfields"]
definition: The authors measure scientists' research direction and output using their citation-weighted number of publications per year across different subfields of the stem cell domain, whether in hESC or non-hESC research. The non-hESC measure is the natural logarithm of one plus the number of forward citations to scientist i's publications in a non-hESC subfield of stem cell research in year t.

name: Resource-acquisition effort for hESC research
authors_terms: ["efforts in securing alternative sources of funding for hESC research", "resource-acquisition effort", "affiliations", "collaborations"]
definition: The authors call the effort spent on securing resources for a project, such as funding, equipment, and material, 'resource-acquisition effort'. In the empirical setting they examine U.S. scientists' efforts to secure alternative sources of funding for hESC research through their institutional affiliations and their collaboration patterns.

name: Scientist ability or reputation
authors_terms: ["higher ability or reputations", "higher-ability scientists", "scientists' citations in the five years prior to the policy shock"]
definition: Ability or reputation of scientists, which the authors exploit as heterogeneity in scientists' pre-2001 publication records; in the analysis the sample is split according to scientists' citations in the five years prior to the policy shock relative to their cohort of scientists whose first publication is observed in the same year.

name: Stage fit
authors_terms: ["stage fit", "stage fit or misfit", "stage match", "stage mismatch"]
definition: The stage fit or misfit is between the VC owners' expertise and the strategic needs of the private firm at the stage of development the focal firm is in during each round of investment. The authors state that when VC owners possess the requisite expertise to address stage-specific strategic needs, there exists a stage match.

name: Industry fit
authors_terms: ["industry fit", "industry fit or misfit", "industry match", "industry mismatch"]
definition: When a VC owner has greater previous experience in a particular industry and is making new investments in firms in that same industry, the authors say there exists an industry match between VC expertise and the needs of the portfolio firm. Industry fit is calculated for a focal private firm as the aggregate number of prior investment experiences its VC owners have had in industries matching the focal firm's SIC1 industry.

name: Time-horizon fit
authors_terms: ["time-horizon fit", "time-horizon fit (misfit)", "time horizons fit or misfit", "loss of time-horizon fit"]
definition: Time-horizon fit reflects the count of prior experiences that a private firm's VC owners have had with firms whose time horizon (growth, profit, or blended orientation) matches that of the focal private firm at each financing round. A harmonious (matched) orientation in time horizons between a VC owner and the portfolio firm ensures congruence in strategic direction and activities.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the firm", "successful exit", "short-term post-IPO performance", "portfolio firm outcomes"]
definition: The performance of the firm is expressed in terms of its likelihood of successfully going public, and its short-term post-IPO performance. The authors state that these are the outcomes regarding the fit or misfit between VC owners' expertise and private firm strategic needs.

name: VC owner expertise
definition: In the study, VC owner expertise is defined in terms of the accumulated knowledge and skills that are formed as a result of prior investing activities in various firms. For a given VC owner at the time of a given investment, the experience-based expertise of the VC owner was measured by the count of prior investments made up to that point by that VC owner along each of the three dimensions of interest (stage of development, industry domain, and time horizons).

name: Parent financial crisis
definition: Crises in the external environment are transient perturbations whose occurrences are difficult to foresee and whose impacts on organizations are disruptive and potentially inimical. In this paper a parent financial crisis is a systemic banking crisis in the home country of a retail multinational.

name: Relative asset growth
definition: The paper theorizes about how changes in the supply of internal capital affect the growth of divisions relative to the growth of standalone firms, which the authors refer to as 'relative growth.'

name: Parent focus on essential products
authors_terms: ["parent focus on essential products", "emphasis on essential products or services"]
definition: The degree to which a parent focuses on essential products, like food; such parents are less exposed to financial crisis as demand for their products will be less constrained during the crisis, while retailers with a greater emphasis on nonessential products are more exposed.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: Geographic distance between a parent's home country and a division's host country, a central construct in understanding the relationship between parents and their various subsidiaries; proximity reduces the degree to which a parent transmits a shock to a division.

name: Organizational structure
definition: The degree to which the structure of the firm fosters coordination of its multidivisional activities versus allowing divisions to operate in a more autonomous manner.

name: Subsidiary age
definition: Older divisions are subsidiaries that have been operating for a longer time in a given host country; subsidiary age is one key determinant of subsidiary embeddedness.

name: Local capital availability
authors_terms: ["capital availability in a division's country", "local credit availability", "local capital availability"]
definition: The richness of the resource pool available from local stakeholders, that is, the availability of substitute sources of capital supply in the local market of the host country.

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence is defined as an exaggerated belief in one's own judgment and abilities. More precisely, overconfidence refers to the degree to which individuals overestimate the accuracy of their abilities, knowledge, and judgments.

name: Acquisition premium
definition: The acquisition premium is the percentage difference between the purchase price and the target firm's market value 4 weeks prior to the date of acquisition public announcement.

name: Predeal process pace
authors_terms: ["acquisition process pace", "predeal process pace", "pace of the predeal process", "decision process pace"]
definition: In the acquisition context, procedural rationality is reflected in the slow pace of the predeal processes during which the acquisition premium is contemplated. The pace of the predeal process is measured with the number of days between the date on which the acquirer and target signed the nondisclosure agreement and the date on which the deal was publicly announced.

name: Technological overlap between spinout and parent firm
authors_terms: ["technological overlap between spinouts and parent firms", "TOSP", "technological inheritance (or overlap)"]
definition: The extent to which the patent portfolio of a spinout is similar to that of its parent firm. The authors examine the competitive tension that arises because of technological overlap between spinouts and parent firms when corporate investors invest in spinouts.

name: Corporate venture capital investment
authors_terms: ["CVC investment", "investment by corporate investors", "likelihood of a corporate investor's investment in the spinout"]
definition: The dependent variable, CVC investment, is a binary variable that takes a value of 1 for a realized CVC investment dyad by a corporate investor i in a venture (or spinout) j in the year of t, and 0 otherwise.

name: Parent firm litigiousness
authors_terms: ["parent firm litigiousness", "parent firm's litigiousness for intellectual property rights", "parent firm's litigiousness"]
definition: We view a firm's litigiousness as a general indicator of its reputation for 'toughness' in enforcing the intellectual property rights associated with patents.

name: Technological overlap between corporate investor and parent firm
authors_terms: ["TOCP", "technological overlap between corporate investors and parent firms"]
definition: The level of technological overlap between corporate investors and parent firms, measured with Jaffe's (1986) measure during the five years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad.

name: Parent firm innovativeness
