definition: A parent firm's innovativeness is measured as the number of medical device products approved by the FDA during the 10 years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad; a parent firm's ability to launch new products is an important signal that can attract corporate investors' attention to spinouts' inherited knowledge.

name: Vertical resource dependence
authors_terms: ["vertical resource dependence", "dependence on exchange with a buyer or supplier firm", "resource dependence on a supplier or buyer organization"]
definition: The dependence of focal firm A on another firm B defined as dependence on exchange with a buyer or supplier firm; based on Emerson's conception of dependence power, it is given by the interaction of the availability of alternative providers of the resource and the perceived value of the resource to the focal firm's strategic position.

name: Capital dependence
authors_terms: ["dependence on financial institutions for capital", "financial dependence", "capital dependence"]
definition: The dependence of a focal firm (A) on financial institutions for capital; the availability of internal funds also determines a firm's dependence on financial institutions for capital.

name: Competitive uncertainty
authors_terms: ["competitive uncertainty", "competitive uncertainty (as determined by the level of industry concentration)"]
definition: Uncertainty from competitive interaction, which resource dependence theory suggests is highest when industry concentration is intermediate: as concentration increases, the effect of any one firm's actions on its competitors increases, yet at very high levels of concentration uncertainty is reduced.

name: Reconstitution of broken friendship ties
authors_terms: ["reconstitution of broken friendship ties", "reconstituted", "reconstitute the broken tie"]
definition: Among friendship ties at time t, a tie is classified as reconstituted if the person identified as a friend (X) at time t leaves their primary employer (A) during the three-year period between surveys or the focal CEO leaves his or her firm during that time, and the focal CEO at time t + 3 has a friendship tie to the CEO of A (or to an officer of A, in the case of a financial institution) that was initiated by the focal CEO since the tie to X was broken.

name: Family ownership
authors_terms: ["family ownership", "family % ownership", "percentage of the business held by family members", "percentage of shares owned collectively by all family members"]
definition: Family ownership is a matter of degree: the more shares a family owns of the business, the more there is at stake for them in its fate, and the more incentive and power they have to shape the firm's acquisitions strategy. It is computed as the percentage of shares owned collectively by all family members.

name: Acquisition volume
authors_terms: ["volume of acquisitions", "number of acquisitions", "value of acquisitions", "scale of acquisitions"]
definition: To assess overall acquisitions activity the authors counted the number of acquisitions made by a given firm in a given year; to determine the overall scale of the acquisitions they multiplied the average size of the acquisition in terms of purchase price by the total number of acquisitions.

name: Acquisition industry match
authors_terms: ["acquisitions industry match", "match between the firm's core industry and that of the acquisitions", "proportion of acquisitions made within the firm's core industry"]
definition: The match between the firm's core industry and that of the acquisitions, calculated as the ratio of the number of deals that were a standard industrial classification (SIC) code match for the firm to the total number of deals completed by the firm in each year.

name: Green investing
authors_terms: ["green investing", "proportion of green investment funds", "relative size of green investment in the economy", "green investment funds"]
definition: Green investing, i.e., investing with an explicit environmental mission, has been on the rise in the professional investment sector; the authors measure it as the proportion of green investment funds in a country's financial sector.

name: Corporate environmental performance
authors_terms: ["environmental performance", "environmental score", "corporate environmental performance", "firms' environmental performance"]
definition: The environmental score from ASSET4 is a z-score for each firm-year. It covers three major sectors, emission reduction, environmental product innovation, and resource deduction, and it represents an overall rating based on 136 public and objective data points compiled by trained analysts.

name: Social investment forum
definition: Social investment forums (SIFs) established by SRI professionals are organizations that coordinate financial, corporate, and environmental stakeholders and pool influence, resources, skills, information, and expertise to scale up the normative impact of green investors; the authors treat them as boundary organizations.

name: Shareholder protection policy
authors_terms: ["shareholder protection policy", "shareholder protection laws", "strong shareholder protection policies"]
definition: Strong shareholder protection policies, by which the state supports the financial logic, are laws and policies that protect shareholders' rights and enshrine shareholders' primacy in governing corporations. The measure captures the extent to which shareholders' rights are sufficiently implemented.

name: Environmental protection policy
authors_terms: ["environmental protection policy", "environmental protection laws", "stringency of national environmental regulation"]
definition: Strong environmental protection policies, by which the state supports environmental goals, are likely to have a positive effect on corporate environmental performance; states can impose taxes and penalties, set environmental standards, and enforce organizational compliance. The measure covers a broad range of environmental regulations, such as emission limits for a given substance, the tax rate for emission of NOx, and emission trading schemes for CO2 and SOx.

name: Corporate philanthropy
authors_terms: ["corporate philanthropy", "corporate charitable giving", "corporate giving", "charitable giving", "philanthropic contributions", "level of corporate philanthropy"]
definition: Corporate philanthropy is, by definition, gifts given by corporations to social and charitable causes, such as support for education, culture, or the arts; minorities or health care; or for relief funds for victims of natural disasters. Corporate philanthropy often extends beyond areas that are directly associated with a corporation's economic activities or legal requirements.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: Two measures of corporate financial performance were employed: return on assets (ROA) and Tobin's q. ROA is a common accounting-based measure, defined as net income over total assets.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism is the level of turbulence or instability in the competitive environment that increases the unpredictability of a firm's operational and financial outcomes.

name: Access to critical stakeholder resources
authors_terms: ["secure the acquisition of critical resources controlled by stakeholders", "reduce the risks associated with resource acquisition", "critical resources controlled by stakeholders", "reduce the firm's risk of losing critical resources"]
definition: Because the allocation and use of the resources necessary for a firm's continued survival are often not fully controlled by the firm, but rather by some key stakeholders, the firm faces uncertainty in securing those resources. Corporate philanthropy is regarded as a means by which a firm can reduce the risks associated with resource acquisition and reduce the risk of losing resources it already controls.

name: Rollout sequencing
definition: The global rollout of product-feature innovations can vary between a strictly sequential market-by-market launch pattern and a fully simultaneous all-markets-at-once pattern. Sequencing trades off the learning from debut markets against speed to market.

name: Innovation novelty
definition: The degree to which an innovation is newer to the market; with few other firms having launched a feature already, commercial viability cannot easily be inferred from competitive observation.

name: Commission-error experience
authors_terms: ["commission errors", "failure experience", "Type-I error history", "prior innovation failures"]
definition: The degree to which a firm has commercialized innovations that proved unsuccessful, i.e., a history of releasing unsuccessful innovations.

name: Omission-error experience
authors_terms: ["omission errors", "preemption experience", "Type-II error history", "missing hit features"]
definition: The degree to which a firm has not brought to market the innovations that proved successful for others, i.e., a record of missed hit features.

name: Competition in the focal innovation
authors_terms: ["competition in the focal innovation", "feature competitors", "innovation competition"]
definition: The challenging test environment of markets with rival offerings of the focal feature innovation, which minimizes the chance of generating false positives about wider commercial viability.

name: Consumer sophistication
definition: Consumer sophistication refers to the domain-specific readiness of consumers to adopt new products; markets with sophisticated consumers are those that show high levels of usage of the predecessor innovation most closely related to the focal one.

name: Debut market selection
authors_terms: ["debut market", "market of first entry", "initial launch country"]
definition: The choice of the initial launch country in sequential feature rollouts, that is, whether or not a given country was the market of first introduction.

name: Cost advantage
authors_terms: ["cost advantage", "cost advantage resulting from a firm's environmental strategy", "cost advantage it gains from environmental strategies"]
definition: The dependent variable is a subjective assessment of the cost advantage resulting from a firm's environmental strategy, assessed relative to the firm's major competitors. It captures how the implementation of best practices affects the competitiveness of a firm within its industry rather than absolute cost savings.

name: Pollution prevention technologies
authors_terms: ["use of pollution prevention technologies", "pollution prevention", "source reduction", "clean technologies"]
definition: Pollution prevention refers to efforts to reduce, change, or prevent emissions and effluent discharges through better housekeeping, materials substitution, recycling, or changes in the production process. Pollution prevention technologies, also referred to as source reduction or clean technologies, minimize the creation of pollution and wastes in production processes.

name: Innovation of pollution prevention technologies
authors_terms: ["innovation of proprietary pollution prevention technologies", "innovation of pollution prevention technologies", "technology innovation"]
definition: Innovation is the internal development of pollution prevention technologies, which is fundamentally different from technology diffusion, the adoption of technologies that are already developed. The proprietary nature of these internally developed technologies stems from protection through barriers to imitability, including secrecy and legal protection through patents.

name: Early timing of environmental strategies
authors_terms: ["early timing", "early timing of environmental strategies", "timing of environmental strategies"]
definition: Starting to address an environmental issue earlier than competitors or before the enactment of environmental regulations. Such anticipation is argued to lower compliance costs, allow learning curve effects, and let firms influence future regulation.

name: Process innovation and implementation capability
authors_terms: ["capabilities for process innovation and implementation", "capability for process innovation and implementation", "complementary assets"]
definition: Capabilities are capacities to deploy resources, usually in combination, to effect a desired end. The complementary assets of capabilities for process innovation and implementation concern the general innovativeness of a company relative to its major competitors and its propensity to update existing or implement new production technologies and equipment.

name: Task complexity
definition: An equilibrium's task complexity measures the degree of cognitive effort along the equilibrium path required to reach that equilibrium. The degree of cognitive effort required to reach an equilibrium may differ among equilibria.

name: Cardinality of choice space
authors_terms: ["cardinality of choice space", "cardinality of choice space (cx)"]
definition: The cardinality of choice space of equilibrium x is the maximum number of outcomes at any stage along the equilibrium path. A stage is equivalent to an information set facing the player along the path leading to equilibrium x.

name: Iterative knowledge of rationality
authors_terms: ["level of iterative knowledge of rationality", "iterative knowledge of rationality (rx)"]
definition: The level of iterative knowledge of rationality of equilibrium x is the number of mutual rationality levels needed to reach equilibrium x. In an extensive-form game this is equivalent to the number of backward induction steps.

name: Iterative knowledge of strategies
authors_terms: ["level of iterative knowledge of strategies", "iterative knowledge of strategies (sx)"]
definition: The level of iterative knowledge of strategies of equilibrium x is the number of levels of mutual knowledge of strategies needed to reach equilibrium x. It concerns knowledge about a player's action choice, not only the player's rationality.

name: Payoff disparity
definition: The payoff disparity of equilibrium x is the difference between the payoffs of the two players.

name: Equilibrium selection
definition: The selection of one equilibrium among multiple equilibria by subjects in a coordination game.

name: Strategies extending the existing technology
authors_terms: ["strategies that extend the existing technology and valuation model", "strategies that extend and preserve the existing technology", "strategies that extended or preserved the old technology", "film-extending strategies", "hybrid products", "wireline-extending strategies", "more exploitative strategies"]
definition: The incumbent firms simultaneously pursued strategies that extended or preserved the old technology: in photography, hybrid and film products that preserved a role for film technology in image capture, and in wireline telecommunications, long-distance services based on the existing wireline technology. The authors consider these more exploitative strategies relative to the firms' traditional skills, capabilities, and sources of profit.

name: Strategies responding to the new technology
authors_terms: ["strategies that depart from the existing technology and valuation model", "strategies that respond directly to the substitute technology", "products that incorporated the new technology", "digital strategies", "VoIP-based offerings", "more exploratory strategies"]
definition: Incumbents generally responded to the technological change directly by introducing products that incorporated the new technology: digital cameras in photography and phone services based on VoIP technology in wireline telecommunications. The authors consider these new products based directly on the new technology to be more exploratory strategies, as they depart from the existing technologies and firms' traditional valuation models.

name: Securities analysts' reactions
authors_terms: ["securities analysts' reactions", "analysts' reactions", "analysts' attention", "analysts' positive sentiments"]
definition: How securities analysts react as incumbent firms respond to radical technological change, assessed in three steps: counts of all mentions of the incumbents' products in analysts' reports, analysis of the texts associated with those mentions to judge whether reactions were generally positive or negative, and the turning points in analysts' ratings together with the justifications provided for the rating change.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The degree to which industries are subject to competition, which depends on various factors such as production and marketing costs, the degree of product heterogeneity, consumer demand growth rate, and the complexity of consumers' needs. Competitive intensity increases the higher the number of firms in the industry and the lower the concentration level.

name: Product line length
definition: 'Product line length' refers to the number of items/product variants in a product line.

name: External governance mode choice
authors_terms: ["use of external delivery model", "choice of external delivery model when sourcing business services globally", "external governance mode", "external sourcing"]
definition: The dependent variable takes a value of 1 when a company chooses to source a process from an external service provider, and a value of 0 when a firm sources the process internally through a captive services center. Only global (rather than domestic) sourcing projects are examined.

name: Process commoditization
definition: Commoditization refers to dynamics by which intermediate products, tasks, and processes become less firm-, product-, and industry-specific. One major property of commoditized processes is their redeployability, that is, their applicability across firm, product, and industry contexts.

name: Availability of external service capabilities
authors_terms: ["availability of external service capabilities", "availability of external services", "service capabilities"]
definition: By service capabilities we mean the productive capabilities that providers develop and market and that allow them to take on client tasks at increasingly lower costs and larger capacity. The more readily available these service capabilities are, the higher the likelihood that firms will outsource processes to suppliers.

name: Time of adoption
authors_terms: ["time of adoption", "early adopters", "late adopters", "early vs. late adoption"]
definition: Firm populations are composed of subpopulations of early and late adopters of certain sourcing practices whose rationale for making certain governance decisions may differ. A population of adopters of new practices, processes, or technologies is made of innovators, early adopters, majority of adopters, and laggards adopting an innovation over time.

name: Prior external governance choice
authors_terms: ["prior choice of external delivery model", "prior outsourcing decisions", "prior external governance choice"]
definition: Operationalized as a binary variable denoting whether or not a firm used an external governance mode for a particular process sourced abroad, at least once before making a particular new governance choice.

name: Prior internal governance choice
authors_terms: ["prior choice of internal delivery model", "prior captive decisions", "prior internal governance choice"]
definition: Operationalized as a binary variable denoting whether or not a firm used an internal governance mode for a particular process sourced abroad, at least once before making a particular new governance choice.

name: Accumulated recalls
definition: Accumulated Recalls of a firm for a specific year t is the cumulative count of recalls issued by the firm until the prior year (t - 1). Recall counts are accumulated over an equal number of years for each year in the main models.

name: Accumulated process-related recalls
authors_terms: ["Accumulated Process-related Recalls", "accumulated process-related recalls", "process-related recalls (Slip-up Failures)"]
definition: Accumulated Recalls are divided into Accumulated Process-related Recalls and Accumulated Design-related Recalls. Process-related recalls originate from defects that can be traced to shortfalls in process compliance, and they fit the description of slip-up failures.

name: Accumulated design-related recalls
authors_terms: ["Accumulated Design-related Recalls", "accumulated design-related recalls", "design-related recalls (Knowledge gap Failures)"]
definition: Accumulated Recalls are divided into Accumulated Process-related Recalls and Accumulated Design-related Recalls. Design-related recalls originate from causes related to the development or enhancement of products, overlooking failure modes and effects, underestimating the likelihood of failure-occurrences although in use, and unsuitable choices of design parameters, and they fit the description of knowledge gap failures.

name: Subsequent recalls
definition: Subsequent Recalls measures the total number of recalls in a firm-year. Following extant research, the authors use this variable to assess organizational learning from past recall experience.

name: Subsequent process-related recalls
definition: Subsequent Recalls are divided into Subsequent Process-related Recalls and Subsequent Design-related Recalls in a firm-year.

name: Subsequent design-related recalls
definition: Subsequent Recalls are divided into Subsequent Process-related Recalls and Subsequent Design-related Recalls in a firm-year.

name: Stocks of innovations
authors_terms: ["accumulated patents", "Accumulated Patents", "stocks of innovations", "stock of innovation (patents)"]
definition: Firms' stocks of innovations and their innovation efforts represent two integral aspects of the innovation capabilities of firms. Patents represent the generation of new processes and products; as such, accumulated patents represent experience in translating ideas into innovations by assimilating added information from external sources and internal developments.

name: Recent innovation efforts
authors_terms: ["lagged R&D intensity", "Lagged R&D Intensity", "recent innovation efforts", "R&D efforts"]
definition: Recent R&D efforts, represented by lagged R&D intensity, reflect the extent of firms' efforts to capture knowledge for innovations. Lagged R&D Intensity for year t is measured using R&D investment as a percentage of net revenue of the firm for the preceding year (t - 1).

name: Knowledge embeddedness
authors_terms: ["knowledge embeddedness", "knowledge embeddedness of the CASE platform"]
definition: Knowledge embeddedness refers to the extent to which relevant organizational knowledge has been codified and stored within the knowledge platform, i.e., the CASE repository. Therefore, knowledge embeddedness refers to the extent to which these types of systems analysis and design knowledge—planning, analysis, design, or construction—are codified and stored in the CASE repository.

name: Technology assimilation
authors_terms: ["assimilation of CASE knowledge platforms", "assimilation of CASE", "CASE assimilation", "assimilation of the CASE platform"]
definition: Assimilation is defined as the extent to which the use of the technology diffuses across the organizational projects or work processes and becomes routinized in the activities of those projects and processes. The assimilation of a CASE knowledge platform by an organization is defined as the proportion of the organization's systems development projects that substantively utilize the CASE platform.

name: Prior methodology use
definition: The extent to which the current systems development methodology was in use prior to the organizational adoption of the CASE technology. An entrenched prior methodology conditions the frames of reference of prospective users and could be likely to inhibit users from developing an appreciation of the value and role of the CASE platform.

name: Current methodology use
definition: The extent to which the methodology is currently in use within the organization; the concurrent introduction of a methodology and greater levels of its use are likely to influence greater assimilation of CASE platforms.

name: Methodology compatibility
definition: The compatibility between the methodology and the CASE platform as complementary innovations that are introduced into the organization; when the current methodology is compatible with the CASE platform, users are able to develop an integrative perspective about the manner in which the two reinforce each other.

name: Management championship
authors_terms: ["management championship", "senior management championship", "management championship of the CASE initiative"]
definition: Management championship refers to the extent to which an organization's senior management advocates the use of a technological innovation. High management championship would be said to exist where senior managers actively and openly champion the role of the CASE knowledge platform.

name: Intrafirm inventor network integration
authors_terms: ["network integration", "integration of a firm's internal inventor network", "integration of the intrafirm inventor network", "degree of structural integration within an intrafirm network of inventors"]
definition: Network integration has been defined as the degree to which formerly disconnected subgroups form new bridges to each other. At a whole-network level, a network is maximally integrated if there is a path between every pair of nodes, and becomes less integrated with each additional isolated 'component' in the network.

name: Generative appropriability
definition: Ahuja, Lampert & Novelli (2013) termed a firm's effectiveness in building on its own innovations before its rivals do 'generative appropriability,' and defined it as 'a firm's effectiveness in capturing the greatest share of future inventions spawned by its existing inventions'. It encompasses both the speed at which a firm develops follow-on innovations from its own innovations and its ability to prevent rivals from expropriating that knowledge.

name: Near decomposability
definition: Nearly decomposable structures consist of subunits within which interactions are frequent and intense, and between which interactions are less frequent and less intense. Simon (1962) emphasized that near-decomposable systems were those in which 'the interactions among the subsystems are weak, but not negligible'.

name: Invention age
definition: The number of months that have elapsed since the filing of the original priority application for a patent family.

name: Exploration alliances
definition: In exploration alliances, partner firms capitalize on their joint capabilities to discover new opportunities, build up new competencies, and adapt to environmental changes. Such alliances are coded as those that focused on the discovery and development of new technology.

name: Acquisitions of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["partner acquisition", "acquisitions of alliance partners", "acquisition of an alliance partner"]
definition: The dependent variable captures whether alliances evolve into acquisitions of alliance partners, coded as a dummy (1 = 'partner acquisition,' 0 = 'no partner acquisition').

name: Joint brokerage positions
definition: Joint brokerage positions refer to the collective network openness (opportunity for brokerage) enjoyed by two firms in an alliance as a whole; joint brokerage position captures the total amount of nonredundant information accessed by an alliance.

name: Relative centrality
authors_terms: ["relative centrality", "relative difference between two firms' degree centrality"]
definition: Relative centrality denotes the asymmetry in network positions between two alliance partner firms; since degree centrality is the extent to which a firm occupies a key position with direct ties to other network members, relative centrality is the relative difference between two firms' degree centrality.

name: Business unit headquarters relocation overseas
authors_terms: ["business unit HQ relocation overseas", "business unit headquarters moving overseas", "location of business unit HQ"]
definition: The extent to which a business unit's headquarters is located overseas rather than in the home country; the HQ's location can be conceptualized on a continuum from entirely based in the home country through to entirely relocated overseas.

name: Corporate headquarters relocation overseas
authors_terms: ["corporate HQ relocation overseas", "corporate headquarters moving overseas", "location of corporate HQ"]
definition: The extent to which the corporate headquarters, including its top management team, its HQ functions and its legal domicile, is located overseas rather than in the home country.

name: Business activities overseas
authors_terms: ["percent business unit activities overseas", "percentage of sales units outside Sweden", "percentage of manufacturing units outside Sweden"]
definition: The percentage of a business unit's sales units and manufacturing units that are located outside the home country, that is, the activities that have already moved overseas.

name: Attractiveness of host country business climate
authors_terms: ["perceived attractiveness of business climate", "attractiveness of the potential host country's business climate", "perceived attractiveness of local environment"]
definition: The perceived attractiveness of the potential host country's business climate in comparison with the home country location, encompassing agglomeration of related and supporting activities as well as economic stability, a supportive political environment and quality of life.

name: Foreign share ownership
authors_terms: ["influence of international shareholders", "percentage of foreign shareholders", "percentage of capital stock owned by non-Swedes"]
definition: The percentage of the MNC's capital stock owned by non-Swedish shareholders, one of two indicators of the influence of global capital markets on the MNC.

name: Primary stock exchange listing overseas
authors_terms: ["primary exchange overseas", "primary stock exchange listing outside Stockholm"]
definition: Whether the primary exchange on which the MNC's shares are traded lies outside Stockholm, one of two indicators of the influence of global capital markets on the MNC.

name: International customers and competitors
authors_terms: ["influence of international customers and competitors", "international influence from customers and competitors", "percent customers/competitors outside Sweden"]
definition: The extent to which the MNC's customers and competitors are located outside the home country, reflecting the internationalization of the stakeholders the corporate HQ relates to.

name: Interdependence between business unit and corporate headquarters
authors_terms: ["interdependence between business unit and corporate HQs", "level of interdependence"]
definition: The level of interdependence between the corporate and business unit levels; aligning the strategy of one business unit with the demands and constraints of other parts of the firm requires ongoing mutual adjustment between parties, which is best done face-to-face and through co-location of activities.

name: Concentration of share ownership
authors_terms: ["concentration of share ownership", "dispersed ownership of MNC", "percent shareholding of the largest shareholder"]
definition: The percentage of voting rights held by the largest single investor in the company; ownership structure is viewed as a continuum from dispersed ownership, in which the stock is widely held, to ownership concentrated in one family or the national government.

name: Pay premium
definition: Executive compensation above (or below) the amount predicted by firm and job characteristics; if an executive earned more or less than what was predicted on the basis of objective characteristics of his or her firm and job, the authors interpreted the difference as the pay premium.

name: Executive power
definition: Executive power is defined as the ability to influence stakeholders; it emerges from multiple sources, such as position, charisma, and knowledge.

name: Governance strength
definition: A firm's governance strength is a function of its governance structure, which is defined by the policies and practices that are in place to monitor the performance of key executives.

name: Abnormal stock performance
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock performance", "abnormal stock returns", "stock performance", "two-day cumulative abnormal stock price reaction"]
definition: Stock performance was calculated as the two-day cumulative abnormal stock price reaction to key executives' sudden death. Prediction errors come from subtracting predicted returns from actual returns for each day of the event window, and cumulative prediction errors are the sum of the prediction errors during the event window.

name: Industry velocity
definition: Industry velocity reflects the speed (frequency of changes and the time span of intervals between these changes) and unpredictability of changes in industry variables. It comprises both rate (speed) and volatility (unpredictability) of changes in industry variables.

name: Attention focus on the task sector
authors_terms: ["attention focus", "attention focus on the task sector", "attention focus toward external environment"]
definition: Attention focus refers to the degree to which top managers' subjective representations of their external environment are dominated by concepts related to one (or more) domain over others. The task sector includes those aspects of the environment that have direct transactions with the firm such as competitors, suppliers, and customers.

name: Attention focus on the general sector
authors_terms: ["attention focus", "attention focus on the general sector", "attention focus toward external environment"]
definition: Attention focus refers to the degree to which top managers' subjective representations of their external environment are dominated by concepts related to one (or more) domain over others. The general sector includes more macrolevel dimensions such as social, demographic, economic, and political.

name: Proactive environment-strategy causal logic
definition: Top managers attempt to construct their environments through their strategies rather than developing strategies in response to environments, resulting in strategy → environment beliefs, or proactive logics. Proactive logics are defined as strategy → environment links in the causal maps.

name: Deterministic environment-strategy causal logic
definition: Top managers thus assume the environment to determine strategy; such environment → strategy beliefs represent deterministic logics. Deterministic logics are defined as environment → strategy links in the causal maps.

name: Speed of strategic response to general sector changes
authors_terms: ["speed of response to changes in the general sector", "speed of strategic responses"]
definition: Speed of strategic response was measured as the number of days between the occurrence of an event and the initiation of the first strategic response. The fewer the number of days between the occurrence of the environmental event and the initiation of the strategic response, the faster the speed of response.

name: Speed of strategic response to task sector changes
authors_terms: ["speed of response to changes in the task sector", "speed of strategic responses"]
definition: Speed of strategic response was measured as the number of days between the occurrence of an event and the initiation of the first strategic response. The fewer the number of days between the occurrence of the environmental event and the initiation of the strategic response, the faster the speed of response.

name: Functional specialization
authors_terms: ["functional specialization", "cross-functional involvement", "functional specialization in the IP value chain"]
definition: The extent to which professionals in each of the constituent functional units of the IP organization (R&D, legal, and business development) are involved in activities within and outside their home units; cross-functional involvement is its inverse.

name: Patent grant success
authors_terms: ["patent grant success", "fastgrant achievement", "rapid patent protection", "hazard of patent grant"]
definition: The ability of a firm to obtain patent protection quickly, conditional on filing: the primary indicator of success at achieving patent protection is simply whether or not a patent was granted on an application, and the authors focus on obtaining speedy patent grants.

name: Supply-side search
authors_terms: ["supply-side search", "nonlocal supply-side search", "boundary-spanning supply-side search", "supply-side exploration"]
definition: Supply-side search encompasses all search for new knowledge relating to technological as well as organizational aspects having a bearing on input-output conversion.

name: Demand-side search
authors_terms: ["demand-side search", "nonlocal demand-side search", "demand-side exploration-exploitation", "boundary-spanning demand-side search"]
definition: Demand-side exploration-exploitation has to do with the effort devoted to the discovery of new insights in own and allied markets regarding market structures and segments, product use and substitution patterns, and customer preferences and needs.

name: Geographic search
authors_terms: ["geographic search", "spatial search", "boundary-spanning geographic search", "nonlocal spatial search"]
definition: A spatial exploration-exploitation dimension that relates to the quest for opportunities, localized know-how, and operational experience in different geographic regions.

name: Innovativeness
definition: Innovativeness is the ability to introduce successful new products and services.

name: Environment dynamism
definition: Dynamism is viewed in this study as the rate and unpredictability of technical change in the environment.

name: Exploration-exploitation orientation
definition: Exploration and exploitation are conceptualized as greater or lesser amounts of supply-side, demand-side, and geographic search in domains external to the organization to gather new knowledge elements and discover fresh opportunities; while a greater amount of search in nonlocal domains denotes a higher exploration orientation, a lesser amount of such nonlocal search is indicative of a higher exploitation orientation.

name: Interorganizational learning
definition: Firms can access new knowledge in the technological arena and transfer this knowledge back to their R&D units, resulting in innovations that embody interorganizational learning. The dependent variable is interorganizational learning between pairs of mobile handset manufacturing firms participating in SSOs.

name: Dyadic corporatism
authors_terms: ["dyadic corporatism", "dyadic institutional logic", "corporatist logics of firms in a dyad"]
definition: Corporatism is construed as located in the realm of institutional behavior, an exploration of how society is organized to achieve its economic goals, in which more corporatist societies adhere to a logic of cooperation. The dyadic institutional logic is operationalized as the weighted average of the Hicks-Kenworthy corporatism values for the two firms in a dyad.

name: Dominant institutional logic in the arena
definition: A dominant institutional logic, representing a larger proportion of the participants, becomes manifest in an SSO's material structures and symbolic practices and focuses the SSO's attention on specific values and ideals, such that a distinctive corporatist or pluralist logic permeates the arena. The dominant logic within an SSO is operationalized based on the extent to which firms in SSOs and the SSO sponsors originate from more corporatist versus less corporatist (or pluralist) countries.

name: Technological distance
definition: The measure captures the dissimilarity of two firms' technological profiles. Learning across technological boundaries calls for experimentation with new alternatives whose returns are uncertain, distant, and often negative, and technologically distant knowledge tends to be more complex, systemic, and difficult to transfer between organizations.

name: Governance mode
authors_terms: ["governance mode", "firm boundaries", "acquisition rather than licensing", "external sourcing modes"]
definition: We focus on the two polar extremes: market contracting through licensing versus the use of firm hierarchy through acquisition. Licensing represents a market contracting option for technology sourcing, whereas an acquisition is defined as one firm buying another with the intent of gaining access to the acquired firm's technology.

name: Threat of opportunism
definition: This potential for opportunism represents an important threat in the governance mode decision: a threat centered on the relationship aspects of interfirm arrangements. The potential for opportunism and self-interest exists for both parties to a licensing agreement, owing to the low level of mutual commitment.

name: Threat of commercial failure
authors_terms: ["perceived threat of commercial failure", "threat of commercial failure"]
definition: An options perspective on firm boundaries focuses on the threat of commercial failure. In an external technology-sourcing agreement, this threat arises from uncertainty about the technology itself, about its design efficacy and market acceptance.

name: Opportunity for sustainable advantage
authors_terms: ["perceived opportunity for sustainable advantage", "opportunity for sustainable advantage", "opportunity for gain"]
definition: A resource-based view of the firm focuses on the opportunity for gain from transactions. A firm has a competitive advantage if it is able to create value in a way that its competitors cannot, and such an advantage is sustainable if it continues to exist despite competitors' efforts to duplicate the advantage.

name: Management stockholdings
definition: One means by which to align the divergent interests of professional managers and shareholders is to compensate managers through stock ownership. The magnitude of stock owned by top management increases the congruence of management and shareholder risk preferences.

name: Firm risk orientation
authors_terms: ["firm risk orientation", "firm risk preference", "risk orientation", "propensity for risk taking"]
definition: An important component of a firm's overall strategic orientation is its risk orientation, as reflected by previous resource allocation decisions. These values regarding risk taking develop over time and are a result of each firm's business environment, its founder's values, and systematized routines.

name: Organizational slack
definition: An organization's excess resources are referred to as slack. Past research has divided slack into three categories - available, recoverable, and potential - and offered several accounting-based measures for each.

name: Market adoption
definition: In order for firms to survive within an emerging market, their products and/or services must achieve legitimacy and widespread market adoption among consumers.

name: Localized competition
definition: Competitive intensity that is a function of similarity between organizational resource requirements and target markets, and that intensifies when geographic markets are meaningful for resource distribution and firm outputs.

name: Regional market logic
authors_terms: ["market logic", "regional market logic", "a regional market logic"]
definition: A market logic valorizes economic efficiency and profits with rewards going to the best performers; the authors propose that a strong regional market logic prioritizes economic profits, competitive advantage, and cost efficiency.

name: Regional proenvironmental logic
definition: A regional proenvironmental logic is defined as attributing high value to protection of the natural environment; the authors treat it as a specific type of social welfare logic capturing an environmentalist focus on reducing the environmental and health impacts of commercial construction.

name: Institutional complexity
definition: Institutional complexity exists in a regional community when the realization of one logic's goals undermines the realization of another's; in this study the measure refers to situations in which the market and proenvironmental logics in a region are both at high levels.

name: Organizational form
authors_terms: ["de novo firm", "de alio firm", "organizational form", "de novo entrants", "de alio incumbents"]
definition: The organizational form of entrants distinguishes de novo (i.e., entrepreneurial start-ups) from de alio (i.e., diversifying incumbents) firms entering the emerging market.

name: Firm survival
definition: For the sake of theory development, 'survival' simply denotes that a firm leaves a market because of a lack of success (e.g., not because of a successful acquisition, exit through merger, rebranding, etc.) and no longer offers its products to the market.

name: Number of female directors
authors_terms: ["number of female directors", "female board membership", "female representation on the board", "female directors"]
definition: We measured the number of female directors on the board as the total number of women serving on the board.

name: CEO strategic attention breadth
authors_terms: ["CEO strategic attention breadth", "breadth of CEO strategic attention", "executive attention breadth"]
definition: Executives' strategic attention breadth varies, with some executives attending to narrower issue sets and others attending to broader issue sets. The authors state that larger values indicate a greater breadth of strategic attention.

name: CEO gender
definition: The gender of the firm's chief executive officer; among the 2,611 CEOs in the final sample, 5.29% of the CEOs were female. The authors argue that female CEOs, as generally more comprehensive information processors, may approach their roles with wider strategic attention breadth than male CEOs.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The length of a CEO's time in office; the authors calculated the CEO's tenure by subtracting the year of appointment from the year of the conference call. CEO tenure has long been argued to lead to cognitive restriction, where longer tenured CEOs tend to follow a familiar cognitive paradigm and, consequently, have narrower attention.

name: CEO overpayment
definition: CEO overpayment occurs when CEOs are paid more than their peers who have similar human capital and lead firms of similar size and performance.

name: Firm market performance
authors_terms: ["long-term market performance", "buy and hold abnormal returns", "BHAR", "firm market performance"]
definition: We focused on buy and hold abnormal returns (BHAR), which is a long-term financial market return measure. The authors argue this market performance metric can capture both shorter and longer-term implications of firm actions.

name: Family ownership
definition: The authors refer to firms whose owners are family members as family-owned firms and include only those that have two or more family-related shareholders. Family owners are defined as two or more family-related individuals who hold significant stakes in the same firm.

name: Married family ownership
authors_terms: ["married owners", "married-owner family firms", "married family owners", "marital ties"]
definition: The bond between husband and wife is described as one of the strongest family ties, and married owners are those for whom the firm is perceived as a legacy or bequest to their children. A family-owned firm is said to have married owners if the two leading shareholders have the same last name and are of different gender.

name: Strategic conservatism
definition: Our measures of conservatism are firm-level sales growth, cash reserves (liquidity), use of debt (leverage), and investment. More conservative behavior is associated with lower sales growth, greater liquidity, lower leverage, and lower investment.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance as measured by returns on assets and profit margins.

name: Employment costs
definition: The authors suggest that, because family-owned firms provide greater employment security to their workers, they tend to have lower employment costs; they examine wage costs as a potential mechanism driving the higher profit margins and ROA of family-owned firms.

name: Subpopulation entry rate
authors_terms: ["subpopulation entry rate", "rate of entry into a subpopulation", "annual count of bank entries"]
definition: The annual count of bank entries, sorted into home country subpopulations; the analysis of entries into subpopulations was based on the founding of the first organization of that subpopulation.

name: Fuzzy density
definition: Fuzzy density is the sum of the grades of membership in a population. Hannan and his colleagues proposed redefining the density of a population as equal to the sum of the grades of membership of all the participants, and called this new density measure 'fuzzy population density.'

name: Contrast
definition: Contrast is the population's average grade of membership. A population with a high degree of contrast contains a high proportion of organizations with a high grade of membership, so it stands out with greater contrast from its background.

name: Audience acceptance
authors_terms: ["audience acceptance", "public acceptance", "acceptance by external audiences", "media acceptance"]
definition: The audience acceptance of an organizational population is defined here as the extent to which that population resonates with the general public; the greater this acceptance, the more it provides guidance to entrepreneurs and business owners seeking entry.

name: Grade of membership
authors_terms: ["grade of membership", "subpopulation grade of membership", "low-grade-of-membership firms", "high-grade-of-membership firms"]
definition: A member's grade of membership is a measure of the member's degree of fit with a population and its typicality. Grades of membership reflect both the extent to which organizations fit into a population as well as their degree of typicality.

name: New market niche volume
authors_terms: ["volume of a new market niche", "niche formation", "volume of beer imports", "new market segment", "new market niche"]
definition: New market niches emerge as a result of discontinuities in an industry's environment; these discontinuities may reflect changes in technology or consumer behavior. Given an underlying change in consumer preferences, the influx of firms into a new market segment or niche in a mature industry is likely to be greater as the new market niche expands in volume.

name: Resource-partitioning
definition: According to the resource-partitioning model, as industries mature they come to be dominated by a few generalist firms that attempt to draw on the largest possible resource space, the center of the market, opening up pockets of resources on the periphery that specialists then exploit. The level of industrial concentration has implications for the dispersion of resources within a market.

name: Founding rate of specialist firms
authors_terms: ["founding rate of microbreweries and brewpubs", "founding rate of firms in that niche", "founding rate of specialists", "state-level microbrewery foundings", "brewpub founding rates", "entry of firms into new market segments"]
definition: The founding process is modeled by defining the population as the unit of analysis and treating foundings as events in a point process; organizational ecologists typically assume a constant rate of founding with log-linear dependence on covariates. The outcome examined is the entry of firms into new market segments of a mature industry, measured as state-level foundings of microbreweries and brewpubs.

name: Organization acquisition experience
definition: The number of acquisitions a firm has made prior to the focal acquisition; the authors operationalize acquisition experience as the total number of acquisitions greater than $10 million in asset value made by a firm from 1948 up to the acquisition of interest.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The importance of an event like an acquisition may be assessed by the security's price change during a period surrounding the event. This price change is sometimes called an abnormal return and is calculated as the difference between the observed return for a security and the predicted or normal return for the same security.

name: Target-to-target similarity
definition: Target-to-target similarity compares an acquisition with previous acquisitions made by the same firm. We measured it as the proportion of previous acquisitions made by a firm that shared the same 4-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code as the current acquisition.

name: High-status moral advisor endorsement
authors_terms: ["affiliations with high-status moral advisors", "endorsements from high-status moral advisors", "high-status endorsements", "Count of sheikhs"]
definition: Affiliations with high-status moral advisors, that is, individuals who possess the authority and influence to 'provide clarity and guidance to others regarding what is right in terms of values and actions.' In this setting the advisors are Shariah scholars, and status is proxied by the honorific title of 'sheikh,' which denotes scholars who are more esteemed than other Shariah scholars.

name: Consumer willingness to accept lower financial returns
authors_terms: ["consumers' willingness to accept lower financial returns", "acceptance of lower financial returns", "willingness to forgo higher returns"]
definition: The value that consumers place on high-status moral advisors' affiliations can be seen in consumers' willingness to accept lower financial returns in exchange for the reassurance these endorsements provide; coupon rates are used to infer the value consumers place on these endorsements, that is, their willingness to forgo higher returns.

name: Shariah compliance
authors_terms: ["Shariah compliance score", "compliance with more strict interpretations of morality", "compliance with more stringent interpretations of morality"]
definition: A product's compliance with more strict interpretations of morality in the sukuk market. It is rated by IdealRatings on the basis of 21 general and 23 product-specific criteria that comprehensively cover all sukuk standards across different Shariah schools of thought, with each criterion weighted by its importance in Shariah law.

name: Decreased internationalization
definition: A reduction in a firm's international presence between record years; the authors describe its components as retrenchment, whether by ceasing to operate overseas manufacturing facilities or by becoming a U.S.-only participant.

name: Increased internationalization
definition: An increase in a firm's international operations between record years; the authors discuss changes such as becoming international and initiating overseas manufacturing.

name: Importing
definition: A firm's strategy of importing medical goods for sale in the United States; the importer category applies to firms that import a nontrivial and verifiable portion of the medical goods that they sell in the U.S. Selling medical goods in the U.S.A. that were manufactured overseas in a company-owned plant is not treated as importing.

name: Market share change
authors_terms: ["market share change", "change in market share", "market share increase", "current market share"]
definition: The change in imaging equipment industry market share held by a manufacturer from one period to the next.

name: Survival
definition: The length of continued participation of a corporation in the American market after a given year, which the authors also refer to as survival. An exit was recorded if an imaging business unit was dissolved or if a corporation sold its imaging equipment subunit to another firm.

name: International presence
definition: The extent of a firm's medical sector operations outside the United States, classified for each record year into categories of international strategy. Multinational status was assigned to firms that the editors of the guides judged to possess 'a combination of domestic and foreign manufacturing, as well as importing and exporting', such that the firms have achieved 'truly international scope and influence' in their medical sector activities.

name: Strength of the base in a key market
authors_terms: ["a strong base in a key market", "preparedness", "a base from which to support international expansion", "ready to expand"]
definition: The authors argue that to gain from increased international presence in technically sophisticated industries a firm must have a strong base in a key market, and they describe the winner firm's strength in the key American market as the base for successful expansion.

name: Focused management of the expanding business
authors_terms: ["focused management", "expand in product areas in which it is a serious competitor", "focus"]
definition: The authors argue that a firm must expand in product areas in which it is a serious competitor, and they observe that the more successful firms had both the incentive to attend to their imaging equipment business and the focus to do so successfully while undertaking international expansion.

name: Learning from international experience
authors_terms: ["learning from international experience", "learn from your international operations", "use the foreign operation to learn about technical advances"]
definition: The authors argue that a firm must use the foreign operation to learn about technical advances, as well as to gain foreign sales; the more successful firms improved the products sold in the United States by incorporating some of what they learned from their manufacturing and sales operations in other national markets.

name: Specialization in generality
definition: The strategy this paper focuses on, specialization in generality, emerges when firms simultaneously choose to invest in upstream resource generality and to trade in intermediate markets because there is complementarity between the two activities.

name: Investment in general upstream resources
authors_terms: ["investment in general upstream resources", "investment in generality", "investing in general upstream resources"]
definition: One of the two decisions the firm makes is whether to invest (versus not invest) to increase the generality of its upstream resource stock.

name: Trading in intermediate markets
authors_terms: ["trading in intermediate markets", "trading as an upstream supplier", "vertical specialization via trading in intermediate markets"]
definition: The second decision is whether to sell the intermediate products or services deriving from these upstream resources to downstream firms (versus using such resources to enter into downstream markets themselves).

name: Downstream production cost
authors_terms: ["downstream production cost", "increase in downstream production costs", "compliance shock", "regulatory shock"]
definition: Some U.S. states enacted laser safety regulations that increased the costs of downstream operations by establishing new rules that laser system manufacturers (firms operating downstream) must follow to reduce the risk of accidents.

name: Lack of downstream assets
authors_terms: ["lack of downstream assets", "no prior downstream assets", "no downstream assets and capabilities"]
definition: One factor affecting the complementarity condition is whether firms already possess or not downstream assets and capabilities that can be reused when entering new downstream markets; firms with no prior downstream assets have no incentive to invest in generality for entering multiple downstream markets.

name: Breadth of demand
authors_terms: ["breadth of demand", "broad demand", "breadth versus depth of intermediate demand"]
definition: We refer to 'broad' demand for intermediate products and services to describe the case of several equally relevant downstream markets, each populated by a similar number of downstream firms; 'deep' demand describes a situation of few large markets populated by most firms.

name: Innovation radicality
definition: R&D projects can be of different types, ranging from incremental modifications of existing technology to ambitious projects intended to make radical changes in technology to develop 'next generation' products. In general, radical innovations are based on new design concepts that break existing paradigms, whereas incremental innovations are based on minor changes or improvements in a current technology.

name: Intellectual property rights protection
authors_terms: ["intellectual property protection", "intellectual property rights protection", "protection", "intellectual property protection in the market"]
definition: Partner firms in an R&D alliance also rely on formal protection of proprietary assets such as patents and copyrights; intellectual property protection levels vary significantly among countries. External protection through intellectual property laws is the typical mechanism offered by the market.

name: Prior ties with alliance partner
authors_terms: ["friends, acquaintances, and strangers", "partner selection", "prior partners", "prior partnerships", "prior interactions"]
definition: We define friends as potential alliance partners with whom a firm has developed 'strong-form' trust through multiple previous interactions. We define acquaintances as potential partner firms that know each other through a few prior interactions, whose trust is semistrong or weak, and strangers as potential alliance partners that are unknown to each other, between whom the form of trust is weak.

name: Equity-based governance
authors_terms: ["governance structure", "equity-based governance structure", "equity joint venture", "equity-based joint venture", "equity"]
definition: Firms forming an R&D alliance decide how to allocate responsibilities and authority between partners, that is, the governance structure. Equity-based governance structures more effectively promote knowledge sharing and protect core technologies from appropriation by opportunistic partners than non-equity-based structures.

name: Alliance scope
definition: An R&D alliance can focus exclusively on R&D activities. An increase in the vertical scope of the alliance integrates R&D with other activities, such as manufacturing and/or marketing; in such cases, the extent of knowledge sharing and coordination inevitably increases.

name: Product niche
definition: The concept of product niche describes a firm's competitive position based on an analysis of the competitive intensity surrounding what products the firm offers. A product niche describes the extent to which a firm's product lines differ from those of its competitors.

name: Process niche
definition: The concept of process niche describes a firm's competitive position based on an analysis of how the firm operates its business. A process niche captures the extent to which a firm differentiates itself by operating its business using a distinctive process or processes.

name: Network embeddedness
definition: Network embeddedness describes the structure of a firm's relationship with other firms—specifically, the extent to which a firm is connected to other firms and how interconnected those firms are, in turn, to each other. High network embeddedness means that a firm belongs to a dense network among other firms, many of which are tightly connected with each other.

name: Firm performance
definition: The definition of firm performance includes two domains of interest: financial returns and market success. The authors' performance measure, the number of successful IPOs, appears to emphasize market success.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: Underpricing occurs when the initial offer price of an IPO is lower than the closing price at the end of the first day of trading, meaning that the value at which the firm sells shares to the investment community is lower than their actual market value. When an offering is underpriced, management has 'left money on the table.'

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D expenditures are an input to the innovation process. They represent the amount of research and development effort a firm is undertaking and are an indicator of the level of firm innovation activities.

name: Patent stock
definition: Patents are an output (albeit an intermediate one) of research and an additional indicator of firm innovation activity. The information contained in a patent by itself provides little, if any, information about the ability of the innovating firm to extract value from the invention.

name: Transparency of the link between patents and value appropriation
authors_terms: ["transparency of the link between patents and value appropriation", "high transparency", "low transparency", "discrete product technology", "complex product technology"]
definition: In some contexts, the link between patents and value appropriation is transparent, but in others it is not. We propose that the transparency of the link between a patent and value appropriation influences information asymmetries and associated underpricing.

name: Emerging market entry
definition: Our dependent variable, entry jit, is an indicator coded as 1 if firm j entered host country i in year t. Following the definition of direct investment of the OECD and the IMF, we ascertained market entry if a firm established a wholly owned facility or acquired at least 10 percent of the ordinary shares of a host country firm.

name: Board interlocks to experienced partners
definition: Board interlocks are established when an individual affiliated with one firm serves on the board of another firm, and function as one of the most important sources of learning regarding strategic issues. We measure interlocks by counting ties to other firms that have previously entered former Warsaw Pact countries.

name: Incoming board interlock
definition: Incoming ties are established by managers of firms with market entry experience who serve on the focal firm's board.

name: Outgoing board interlock
definition: Outgoing ties are created by managers of the focal firm who serve on the board of other companies that have already entered particular emerging markets.

name: Indirect board interlock
definition: Indirect ties are formed by individuals who serve on the board of the focal firm as well as on the board of another experienced firm but are managers neither of the experienced firm nor of the focal firm.

name: Formal authority
definition: While multiple forces affect executive discretion, we focus on the formal authority vested in CEOs relative to non-CEO executives. CEOs are more likely to be persuasive when bringing their knowledge to bear on the firm's existing strategy and to affect the course of the firm in ways that other executives cannot.

name: Focal firm related experience
definition: To capture a firm's related experience, we measured each firm's general regional experience with running operations in former Warsaw Pact countries as the number of years since a firm's first market entry in any of the 21 countries.

name: Specific expertise cues
definition: By specific expertise cue, we mean distinctive skills germane to the task at hand, such as directly relevant prior work experience. Personal characteristics that are believed to be informative about an individual's expertise in a clearly defined and specifiable task are referred to as specific expertise cues.

name: Diffuse status cues
definition: By diffuse status cues, we mean observable attributes such as personality traits, ethnicity, age, gender, or educational achievement that actors situated in a particular cultural and societal context treat as status markers that signify general ability and competence. Personal characteristics that indicate general ability that is applicable to more than one task are referred to as diffuse status cues.

name: Task position occupancy
authors_terms: ["task position", "formal task position", "task position allocation", "position occupant"]
definition: Within a given organization, we observe only a specific manifestation of the abstract role in the form of a given task position. Following prior work we assume that formal task positions are exogenous to the co-founders.

name: Task position rank
authors_terms: ["higher-ranked task position", "hierarchically ordered task positions", "rank ordering of positions"]
definition: We assume task positions can be arranged in a hierarchy such that some positions are seen as more important and powerful than others.

name: Team functional background homogeneity
authors_terms: ["homogeneity of prior functional backgrounds", "team functional diversity", "dominant functional diversity"]
definition: Dominant functional diversity refers to the extent to which team members differ in the functional areas within which they have spent the greater part of their careers. When founding team members have a high degree of homogeneity in their dominant functional work experience prior to joining the start-up, the founding team has little variance in terms of specific expertise cues.

name: Position-occupant status fit
authors_terms: ["fit between the task position and the diffuse status cue of the position occupant", "team fit on diffuse status cue", "typicality of position occupants"]
definition: Position-occupant fit can be conceptualized in terms of the horizontal dimension of occupants' specific expertise cues as well as the vertical dimension of occupants' diffuse status cues. We measured the fit between the task position and the diffuse status cue of the position occupant, aggregated across all positions in the focal founding team.

name: Venture financial performance
authors_terms: ["venture performance", "venture valuation", "value of equity", "financially valuable ventures"]
definition: At the end of the simulation, we measured venture performance as the equity value of the venture using discounted free cash flow techniques.

name: Individual performance evaluation
authors_terms: ["individual performance", "option pool", "percentage share of the total founder's equity pool", "performance evaluation"]
definition: We measured individual performance as the focal founding team member's percentage share of the total founder's equity pool. A larger percentage share of equity received by a particular founding member indicates the superior contribution by that member toward the team's collective task of creating a financially valuable venture.

name: Pay level
definition: Pay level represents a firm's average compensation relative to that of other, competing organizations, and is often labeled as leading, matching, or 'lagging' the market. An organization with a policy of leading the market offers higher than the average wage of the relevant labor market; a policy of lagging the market signifies lower-than-market-average wages.

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay structure", "pay structures", "pay dispersion", "degree of hierarchy in a pay structure", "hierarchical pay system", "egalitarian pay structure"]
definition: An organizational pay plan is also characterized by its pay structures, a term for the array of pay rates within the organization and representing the degree of slope in its pay policies. Pay structures can be broadly characterized as egalitarian, a term that indicates a compressed pay distribution, or as hierarchical, which indicates more widely dispersed pay.

name: Resource efficiency
definition: To represent the efficiency with which each organization used its resources, the authors applied a metric of hospital efficiency common in research on health care management: average length of stay. Typically, hospitals with shorter lengths of stay are considered to be more efficient in their use of resources.

name: Patient care outcomes
authors_terms: ["patient care outcomes", "patient care", "adjusted coronary survival", "adjusted survival"]
definition: One important consideration when examining hospital performance is the effectiveness of patient treatment. The authors examined each hospital's adjusted coronary survival rate for heart attack patients as a dependent variable.

name: Financial performance
definition: Return on assets (ROA) is used to measure organizational financial performance; it is the most ubiquitous measure of organizational financial performance for strategy studies evaluating this outcome. This measure captures a hospital's ability to both control its expenses and use its assets to generate income.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The authors investigated the relationship between organization-level compensation decisions and organizational performance, examining how companies' pay structures and pay levels relate to resource efficiency, patient care outcomes, and financial performance. The dependent variables are described as capturing different dimensions of performance.

name: Extent of IT penetration
authors_terms: ["extent of IT penetration", "extent of automation", "IT penetration"]
definition: Information technology can be conceptualized in terms of the technology itself, the extent of penetration of the technology within the organization, and the actual use of the technology by individuals. The extent of IT penetration measures the degree to which automation has been applied in the organization broadly, across functions horizontally, and across roles or levels of the organization hierarchy vertically.

name: Middle management workforce size
authors_terms: ["number of middle managers", "ratio of middle managers", "middle management", "size of the middle management workforce"]
definition: Middle managers operationalize, detail, further define, and disseminate information about objectives, policies, and structural changes formulated at the top of the hierarchy, and they mediate between top and operations level managers. In this study the lower boundary of middle management was set above first level supervisors and the upper boundary below the department head.

name: Centralization of organizational decision authority
authors_terms: ["degree of centralization of organizational decision authority", "organizational decision authority"]
definition: Organizational decision authority refers to the distribution of the authority to make decisions affecting the organization. The distribution element refers to the degree of concentration of authority, or the minimum level of the hierarchy at which organization decisions can be made.

name: Centralization of computing decision authority
authors_terms: ["degree of centralization of computing decisions", "computing decision authority"]
definition: The degree of centralization of computing decisions refers to whether control over computing resources is centralized in top management or decentralized to middle managers. Computing decision authority refers to the distribution of authority regarding significant computing decisions.

name: Middle manager influence
definition: When decisional control is centralized, top managers will have greater influence and their interests will be better served; conversely, when control is decentralized, middle managers will have greater influence and their interests will be better served. The interests of the dominant coalition will be enhanced to the extent that control over IT coincides with the general structure of control in organizations.

name: Variance in relative technological proximity
authors_terms: ["variance in relative technological proximity", "variance in relative technological proximity (distance)", "variance of technological proximity"]
definition: The variance in relative technological proximity is the variance of the technological proximity between the focal firm and its partners, where technological proximity between two firms is computed as the uncentered correlation between their respective vectors of technological capital. Higher values indicate a higher level of variance.

name: Innovative performance
definition: The dependent variable of this study, innovative performance, measures the innovation output of the focal firms using weighted patent counts.

name: Sourcing mode diversity
definition: The extent to which a firm balances the different external sourcing modes used in its technology-sourcing portfolio, calculated with the Herfindahl index as 1-H. The external sourcing partnerships under study include CVC investments, strategic alliances, joint ventures, minority holdings, and M&As.

name: Industry clockspeed
definition: Fines (1998) introduced the concept of industry clockspeed to capture the rate of industry change driven by endogenous factors (technological and competitive). He identified three facets of industry clockspeed: product, process, and organizational.

name: Complexity of strategic schemas
definition: Complexity reflects the differentiation and integration in a strategic schema. Differentiation reflects the breadth or variety of environmental, strategy, and organizational concepts embedded in the schema, whereas integration reflects the degree of connectedness among these concepts.

name: Focus of strategic schemas
definition: Focus reflects the degree to which a strategic schema is centralized around a few 'core' concepts. In a focused schema, there is a clear distinction between the core and peripheral sets of knowledge structures.

name: Strategic flexibility
definition: Strategic flexibility refers to the ability to precipitate intentional changes and adapt to environmental changes through continuous changes in current strategic actions, asset deployment, and investment strategies. Firms realize strategic flexibility through their strategic actions, and flexible firms exhibit both diversity in strategic responses and rapid shifts from one strategy to another.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is the outcome of the theoretical model; the contingency view in strategy proposes that the fit between strategic actions and the industry context predicts firm performance. The authors measure it with sales growth, return on investment and net income growth.

name: Labor-management conflict
authors_terms: ["conflict management", "conflict in negotiations and contract administration", "level of conflict", "conflict intensity", "conflict between labor and management at the shop floor level"]
definition: The first of two key dimensions of an industrial relations system identified in the model - conflict management - which captures the most important process aspects of U.S. collective bargaining, negotiations and contract administration. The authors hypothesize that indicators of a relatively high degree of conflict between labor and management at the shop floor level will be associated with lower efficiency, poorer quality, and generally poorer organizational performance.

name: Individual attitudes and behavior
authors_terms: ["individual attitudes and behavior", "worker attitudes and work behavior", "individual worker attitudes and work behavior", "attitudinal climate"]
definition: The second key dimension of an industrial relations system identified in the model, reflecting the motivation, attitudes, and behavior of individuals and informal work groups.
