The authors hypothesize that measures of employee participation in suggestion programs, employee attitudes, and absenteeism rates are all part of an underlying construct that they call the individual attitudes and behavior dimension of the performance of industrial relations systems.

name: Involvement in quality-of-working-life programs
authors_terms: ["quality-of-working-life efforts", "QWL programs", "involvement in QWL programs", "participation in programs addressing the quality of working life"]
definition: Efforts to improve the quality of working life that attempt to intervene in and modify the performance of industrial relations systems and to enhance organizational performance. The company's QWL activities included quality circles, informal meetings between plant managers, workers, and union officials, and other forms of enhanced communication between labor and management.

name: Organizational effectiveness
definition: This study treats economic performance as one - if not the - key dimension of organizational effectiveness; the broader construct is not necessarily synonymous with economic performance.

name: Economic performance
definition: The economic performance of each plant, described by the authors as most likely the most important dimension of organization effectiveness. Direct labor efficiency and product quality in each plant were the measures of economic performance.

name: Differentiated replication strategy
definition: With replication, firms build upon their capabilities in project categories in which they are already successful; a differentiated replication strategy concentrates this effort on genres in which the studio has recently been successful but none of its rivals has.

name: Differentiated renewal strategy
definition: With renewal strategies, firms ramp up their capabilities in categories where they have not had much recent success; a differentiated renewal strategy pushes for capabilities in genres where neither the studio nor any of its rivals has had recent success.

name: Undifferentiated replication strategy
definition: Undifferentiated replication is based on the share of the studio's output devoted to genres that had appeared on its own top list as well as on the list for at least one of its competitors.

name: Financial performance
definition: Return on sales (ROS) was used as the primary indicator of financial performance, as it best reflects how much profit a film studio has made on its revenue base; return on assets was used as an alternate performance measure.

name: Access to markets and customers
authors_terms: ["access to markets and customers", "control of theaters", "theaters owned"]
definition: The control of theaters represented a significant resource that provided access to major markets and audiences; the theaters a studio owned or leased could enable it to use replication strategies to keep serving the same audiences in the same markets.

name: Knowledge and skill resources
authors_terms: ["pool of knowledge and skills", "knowledge and skill-based resources", "stars under contract"]
definition: The most prominent resource providing the studios with a pool of skills and knowledge were the top stars each had under long-term contract; a larger base of outstanding employees with diverse skills provides the firm with more possibilities for resource combinations.

name: Industry demand
authors_terms: ["industry demand", "level of industry demand", "spending on movies (by consumers)"]
definition: The level of industry demand was measured by the percentage of household recreational spending devoted to movie attendance, a measure that could be used across the entire period because it represented the demand for movies relative to all other forms of entertainment and recreation.

name: Shifts in demand
authors_terms: ["shifts in the level of demand", "stability of consumer tastes", "new genres in top 10 films", "turnover among the top genres"]
definition: In order to assess the stability of consumer tastes, the authors obtained an annual measure of the number of new genres among the top 10 films for the industry, that is, genres that had not appeared on that list for at least the previous two years.

name: Cross-community brokerage
authors_terms: ["cross-community brokerage", "hub's brokerage across communities", "brokerage across communities", "hubs"]
definition: Hubs are community members who broker across communities disproportionately more than their fellow community members. An actor's brokerage opportunities across communities are the number of open triads in which at least one of the three actors belongs to a different community, so that two unconnected others need to go through the focal actor to reach each other across communities.

name: Creative project performance
authors_terms: ["show performance", "a show's performance", "success of projects", "performance of projects"]
definition: The success of a collective creative project, which in this setting is the show's viewership ratings: production companies and TV channels are focused on viewership ratings, and advertisers use them to assess a show's performance and set revenues.

name: Network community
definition: Groups of individuals who have more ties to each other than to outside actors; most interactions happen within communities, whose members consider each other network neighbors and share a sense of identity and positive mutual sentiments.

name: Social activist boycott
definition: Boycotts are a contentious tactic through which activists use the media to disseminate vilifying claims about a targeted firm. They are a type of contentious crisis, in which a firm is publicly implicated in controversies within a socially or politically divisive context.

name: Boycott ideological orientation
definition: Boycotts are often ideologically valenced and can be categorized as conservative or liberal. The boycott ideology variable captures the ideological orientation of the activist campaign, coded as liberal, conservative, or unclassifiable on a political spectrum.

name: Director political ideology
definition: Political ideologies proxied by campaign contributions reflect packages of stable, deeply held core values. Ideology refers to a bundle of core values that capture 'a set of beliefs about the proper order of society', corresponding in the U.S. context to a conservative–liberal continuum.

name: Ideological alignment
definition: The alignment between a director's personal ideology and that of the activist challengers. For ideologically aligned directors, the activists' vilifying claims highlight inconsistencies between the firm's perceived values and the director's personal values, whereas for ideologically opposed directors the claims highlight congruence.

name: Board turnover
definition: The departure of directors from a corporate board, which may be involuntary or voluntary. It is exceedingly rare for directors to be fired, so regardless of whether turnover is voluntary or involuntary, exit typically occurs at the natural expiration of a director's term, at which point an exiting director will simply not be re-nominated for a new term.

name: Stock market reaction to the boycott
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns", "CARs", "stock market reaction", "the market's response to the boycott", "adverse market responses"]
definition: Directors are expected to allocate their attention toward social issues that produce a more adverse stock market response. Adverse market responses to boycotts represent a rough proxy for issue salience by capturing the extent to which the market perceives the issue as one that is important enough to pose a threat to the firm's ongoing performance.

name: Enhanced identification
definition: The strengthening of a director's identification with the firm or its values in response to an ideologically opposed boycott; the statement proposes that this enhanced identification decreases the director's propensity to exit the board.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact exists when two firms simultaneously operate in two or more markets. For firm i in a focal market n, the authors measure it as the average number of contacts that firm i has with the incumbents in market n in markets different from focal market n.

name: Entry into new geographic markets
authors_terms: ["entry rates", "entry into new markets", "entry into new geographical markets"]
definition: Firms' entries into new markets are key strategic movements; the speed and intensity of entry into new markets are signs of aggressive behavior or connivance with multimarket rivals. The dependent variable is the hazard that a savings bank enters a certain geographical market, given that it does not have current activities in the market.

name: Strategic dissimilarity
definition: The average strategic dissimilarity between a potential entrant and the incumbents in the focal market, built from firms' scope and resource commitments. The measure takes a value of '0' when there is maximum strategic similarity and '1' in the case of maximum dissimilarity.

name: Reciprocity of multimarket contacts
definition: Reciprocal multimarket contact arises when two firms share two (or more) markets but their relative strategic position in those markets is different: when firm A dominates in market m and firm B dominates in market n, the asymmetric relationship is reciprocal.

name: Seller concentration
definition: The number and size distribution of firms competing in a market; the authors measure it through a province Herfindahl using the number of branches as a proxy for market share.

name: CFO gender
authors_terms: ["Female CFO", "CFO gender", "executive gender", "gender of the chief financial officer"]
definition: The gender of the firm's chief financial officer, which the authors argue may affect financial reporting because of gender differences in ethics and risk taking. Executives are classified as CFO from their title and their gender is identified from Execucomp.

name: Financial misreporting
authors_terms: ["financial misreporting", "financial statement irregularities", "financial reporting quality", "financial misstatements", "FSD Score"]
definition: A specific form of corporate misconduct that involves issuing inaccurate financial statements. The authors measure the likelihood of financial misreporting with the Financial Statement Deviation (FSD) Score, which captures the extent to which leading-digit distributions in a firm's financial statements deviate from Benford's Law.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: Institutional ownership is the number of shares held by institutions scaled by total shares outstanding. Institutional owners hold large stakes, centralize the voting power of their clients and are required by fiduciary obligations to monitor managers, thus constraining the discretion available to management.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: Analyst coverage is the total number of analyst estimates of earnings per share (EPS) provided for the fiscal year-end. Managers at firms with greater analyst coverage expect and receive more scrutiny, which limits the discretion managers have to act as they desire.

name: Journal hierarchy tier
authors_terms: ["journal hierarchy", "top-tier journals", "first tier", "second tier", "third tier", "lower-tier journals"]
definition: The three-level hierarchy of strategic management journals used in the study: the first tier consists of the number one, two and three journals in the Franke et al. (1990) study, the second tier their number seven, eight and nine listings, and the third tier their number 13, 16 and 17 entries.

name: Publication of replication research
authors_terms: ["replication research", "replications with extensions", "publication frequency of replication research", "publication incidence"]
definition: The publication incidence of replications and replications with extensions: a replication is a substantial duplication of a previously published empirical research project that is chiefly concerned with increasing the internal validity of the research design, while a replication with extension is a duplication of a previously published empirical research project that is primarily concerned with increasing the external validity, or generalizability, of previous research findings.

name: Publication period
authors_terms: ["1976-85", "1986-95", "more recent years than for earlier ones"]
definition: The two ten-year periods, 1976-85 and 1986-95, into which the study's 20-year window is divided when comparing the publication frequency of replication research.

name: Replication outcome
authors_terms: ["outcomes of replications", "support, partial support, or conflict"]
definition: The outcome of a replication study relative to the original findings; the outcomes from a replication study either support, partially support, or conflict with the original findings, and classification is based on the conclusions reached by the replicating author(s).

name: Timeliness of replication research
authors_terms: ["timeliness of replication research", "time lags between the original and replication studies"]
definition: The time lag between an original study and a replication of it; rapid attempts to replicate the findings of original studies are preferable to those conducted at later dates, and replications that either confirm or contradict the findings of the original work in a timely manner are especially important.

name: Publication of comments and rejoinders
definition: The publication frequency of research comments and rejoinders, which provide a forum for publicly debating the integrity of a discipline's literature.

name: Strength of community property rights
authors_terms: ["strength of property rights", "property rights", "Aboriginal title", "treaty rights", "modern treaties"]
definition: Property rights delimit the range of privileges granted to individuals over specific resources; they are defined as the right, or 'bundle of rights' (Coase, 1960), to exploit and alienate a resource, and thus, the right to exclude others from that resource. The strength of property rights can vary within countries as a function of the extent to which an individual's or a community's claim to land has been recognized.

name: Extra-institutional mobilization
definition: Extra-institutional mobilization refers to a community's actions outside existing institutional channels (regulatory procedures and the court system) intended to suspend a firm's operations or to alter its practices.

name: Institutional action
authors_terms: ["institutional action", "history of institutional action", "legal and regulatory action"]
definition: Institutional action is action taken via regulatory or legal channels; local communities can take action through existing institutional channels-through the judicial system or the regulatory process.

name: Value of a community benefits agreement to the firm
authors_terms: ["value to the firm", "the value of CBAs", "market's reaction to a CBA announcement", "investors' reactions", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: We argue that the mechanism through which CBAs create shareholder value is by increasing the firm's access to a specific site, and we propose that investors assign more value to a CBA signed with local communities that have strong property rights and histories of collective extra-institutional mobilization or institutional action.

name: CEO Machiavellianism
definition: The concept of Machiavellianism, as introduced by Christie and Geis (1970a), refers to a personality trait that exhibits the main behavioral patterns espoused by Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince: mistrust in others, opportunism, emotional detachment in interpersonal relationships, lack of conventional morality, and a strong motivation to 'win' in interpersonal transactions or situations.

name: Acquisition premiums
definition: Acquisition premiums reflects the amount a firm overpays for another firm in the acquisition process.

name: Production costs
definition: Production costs reflects the costs associated with the general operations and production of the firm's products.

name: Debt financing costs
definition: Financing costs reflects firms' costs for securing and servicing debt.

name: School-to-work participation
definition: The intensity or degree to which firms offer work-based learning activities or establish linkages with schools; the 1997 NES included 20 such activities that represent these linkages.

name: Market efficiency
definition: The extent to which schools provide applicants who are well prepared for work; if schools fail to do so, the cost to the firm of recruitment, selection, and training will increase, which is a signal to the firm of the market's inefficiency.

name: Human capital factor market quality
authors_terms: ["quality of a firm's factor market for human capital", "quality of the factor market for human resources", "factor market for human resources"]
definition: Local and regional schools represent a factor market for human capital; if companies perceive surrounding educational institutions as producing qualified individuals with a capacity for learning, they would be inclined to participate in that factor market and acquire this resource for future use.

name: Transaction frequency
authors_terms: ["transaction frequency", "frequency of transactions", "hiring frequency", "percentage of new hires at lower levels"]
definition: The greater the frequency of the transaction, the more likely it is that the firm will internalize the process.

name: Transaction uncertainty
definition: Increasing levels of transaction uncertainty also serve to increase the cost of transactions; in this event, it becomes more efficient for the firm to take over the market mechanism by regulating the exchange internally.

name: Asset specificity
definition: The more specific the asset is to the firm, the more likely it becomes that the firm is able to produce that asset more efficiently (at lower costs) than the market, thus providing an incentive to internalize the process.

name: Employee opportunism
definition: Individuals are assumed to act in their own self-interest or with opportunism; this assumption accounts for the need for monitoring systems and/or hierarchical structures within organizations.

name: Building firm-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["building firm-specific human capital", "firm-specific human capital", "firm-specific training"]
definition: Organizational mechanisms for employee learning, such as training, job rotation, empowerment and the like, may be viewed as a method for building firm-specific human capital.

name: Inimitable asset stock
authors_terms: ["inimitable asset stock", "asset stocks", "investment in new physical assets"]
definition: Physical resources such as plant, equipment, and technical systems can determine a firm's competitive advantage, and the accumulation of critical physical resources builds asset stocks; to the extent that new physical systems indicate building an inimitable asset stock, school-to-work programs may be viewed as one type of complementary asset.

name: Asset reconfiguration
definition: Companies must be prepared and able to reconfigure their asset structure to adapt to changing environmental demands; one of the most effective ways of doing this is through benchmarking, an organizational process that maintains parity with competitors and cultivates continuous improvement.

name: Skill reconfiguration
authors_terms: ["skill reconfiguration", "increase in skill requirements", "changing employee skill sets"]
definition: As skill requirements transform, the firm's knowledge base must be updated as well; school-to-work programs may be considered avenues for skill reconfiguration.

name: Process entropy
authors_terms: ["process entropy", "state of high entropy", "unintended instability in routines", "adherence to 'routines as targets'"]
definition: Applied to organizational systems, movement toward a state of high entropy describes a natural tendency of organizational systems to lose their orderliness and approach a state of disorganization in the absence of disciplining forces to halt such a decay. The authors use the term 'process entropy' to describe the level of unintended instability in routines, caused by failures to adhere to operational routines.

name: Elapsed time since renewal
authors_terms: ["absence of a renewal", "time since the last inspection", "Time since last"]
definition: The time that has passed since the last renewal, where renewals are events that refocus or 'add energy' to the system to maintain or reduce the state of process entropy; all inspections serve as externally driven renewals. The independent variable to test H1 is the number of days since the last inspection occurred.

name: Organizational shock
definition: Substantive organizational shocks, such as mergers, acquisitions, corporate restructuring, or process reengineering initiatives, will distract managerial attention, create new objectives, and potentially induce ambiguity with respect to the precise nature of a routine to be followed. In Hypothesis 2 the authors assert that organizational shocks can affect existing adherence to prescribed operational routines and influence the level of process entropy in facilities.

name: Foreignness
definition: For the purposes of this paper, we define a foreign firm simply as one in which the controlling shareholder (typically the largest single shareholder) is a national or firm from a country other than the country of location. Irrespective of the origin, the liability of foreignness implies that foreign firms operating in a particular market will be subjected to higher costs compared to local firms, all else being equal.

name: Survival
definition: Our measure of the survival of trading rooms is the continued existence of the trading room in the market-making segment, with exit represented by delisting from this directory of market makers. In examining factors that affect the survival of firms, we present several analyses of the survival phenomenon.

name: Tenure in location
authors_terms: ["tenure of a foreign trading room in a particular location", "tenure", "duration time", "tenure in industry"]
definition: As the tenure of foreign firms lengthens in their country of location, they are likely to learn about their new environments and gradually get integrated into those environments, so that some of the difficulties they face due to their initial lack of experience of that country will diminish over time. Time represents the duration that a room survives since the time we begin studying it.

name: Deregulation and global market integration
authors_terms: ["deregulation", "global market integration", "period of higher global market integration"]
definition: Even within the 20-year time period of this study, the financial services industry has been subject to a major wave of deregulation in the early 1980s resulting in increasing levels of global market integration. The deregulation of these markets did make it easier for foreign firms to establish a presence in several countries.

name: Proportion of foreign competitors in location
authors_terms: ["percentage of foreign firms in an environment", "proportion of foreign competitors in location", "number of foreign competitors in each location"]
definition: We also expect that the mix of foreign vs. local competitors will affect the survival rates of firms in a particular location. If foreign firms are at a competitive disadvantage as we suggest in Hypothesis 1 above, a location with a larger proportion of foreign firms will present weaker levels of competition than would a location with more local firms, controlling for the number of firms.

name: Trading room scale
definition: At the level of the trading room, we expect larger trading rooms to have a better chance of survival in foreign currency trading. For one, the more traders they have, the greater the information inflow and the volume of trades they can handle.

name: Parent bank financial strength
authors_terms: ["parent size", "financial strength of the parent bank", "financial strength", "size and financial strength of the parent bank"]
definition: Another source of scale-related competitive advantage that the trading room can draw on is the parent bank's size and financial strength. The greater the assets of the parent corporation, the more the capital likely to be available to an affiliated trading room to help tide it over periods of poor performance.

name: Multinational FX operations
authors_terms: ["multinational FX operations", "multinational network", "affiliation with a multinational network"]
definition: Being affiliated with a parent bank that has FX operations in more than one country could also provide a trading room with greater resources in the form of information or access to multinational clients that a trading room whose parent only operates in one country may not have access to. Further, a trading room which is affiliated to a parent with multinational FX operations may be in a better position to be cross-subsidized by its parent bank's earnings on this line of business elsewhere.

name: Hierarchical mode of control
authors_terms: ["mode of control", "hierarchical mode of control", "layers of hierarchy", "bureaucratic layers of management", "hierarchical control"]
definition: In such a situation, attempts to control traders through authority limits and layers of hierarchy are likely to constrain traders' abilities to take full advantage of profit opportunities as they arise, and are therefore likely to have a negative impact on profitability. In such a context, a trading room with few layers of authority and few bureaucratic controls is likely to do better than one with a very hierarchical mode of control.

name: Adoption of electronic dealing technology
authors_terms: ["adoption of technology", "electronic dealing system", "Reuters dealing system", "technology adoption"]
definition: Since around 1981, currency trading rooms have had the choice of adopting an interorganizational electronic network on which information can be exchanged and deals done with banks worldwide at close to zero marginal cost, thanks to an electronic dealing system introduced by Reuters. We propose, because of the ease and lower cost of cross-border communication and dealing provided by this technology, which can contribute to improving the private information flows into a trading room and thus provide a source of competitive advantage.

name: Congressional testimony
authors_terms: ["Congressional testimony", "testifying before Congress", "a firm representative testifying before Congress"]
definition: Congressional testimony is one of the most highly sought after, influential, and publicly viewed points of governmental access for firms. To provide oral testimony, a witness must be selected by the committee, and this selection is typically granted only to key players in the political arena.

name: Investor reactions
definition: Our dependent variable of cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) was calculated using the three-day event window of (-1, +1) to account for possible early information regarding the testimony, as well as for reactions following the testimony. This is calculated with the Fama-French four-factor model.

name: Witness status
authors_terms: ["witness status", "status of the witness", "status of the individual testifying"]
definition: There is a large degree of variation between the titles and status of the individual testifying, ranging from rank-and-file employees to the CEO of the organization. Individuals whom have ascended to higher ranks in an organization are typically perceived of as having higher status.

name: Testimony length
definition: A firm representative testimony length is likely to be interpreted as indication of firm political influence; a longer testimony indicates that Congressional members will consider and apply the information presented by the firm representative. Our measure of testimony length is the total number of words that the witness spoke in the testimony.

name: Committee jurisdiction
authors_terms: ["committee jurisdiction", "committee industry jurisdiction", "jurisdiction of the Congressional committee"]
definition: Within the Congressional committee system, certain committees have direct jurisdiction over different industries. Specific jurisdiction of committees encourages members of each committee to develop a specialized knowledge of the committee's subject matter pertinent and then use that knowledge to draft public policy regarding the industry over which their jurisdiction presides.

name: Regulatory risk
definition: Regulatory risk (i.e., the uncertainty created for firm outcomes stemming from potential policy changes and government actions).

name: Negative Congressional tone
definition: Testimonies in which Congressional members are more negative in tone provide uncertainty for investors because this tone may indicate a greater likelihood of future governmental targeting in the form of regulation, legislation, or other public policy. Our measure of negative Congressional tone was created using computer-aided content analysis (CATA), assessing the number of negative words spoken by committee members.

name: Media attention
definition: Our primary measure of media attention is the number of articles focusing on the congressional hearing within our event window (-1,1). Greater media attention (a) provides a context for investors to judge the importance of the indicator being sent, (b) amplifies the strength of the indicator, (c) increases the consideration of the indicator by more receivers.

name: Organizational dissolution
definition: Dissolution was coded when the name of a firm permanently disappeared from the directories without the incidence of an acquisition or name change. The study attempts to deepen understanding of the determinants of organizational dissolution.

name: Industry-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["industry-specific human capital", "industry-specific human capital developed through professional education", "industry-specific human capital developed through industry experience"]
definition: Industry-specific human capital in this study is knowledge about complicated auditing routines (e.g., statistical sampling, risk analysis, and analytical review) and financial accounting (e.g., measurement methods, regulations, and standards) that cannot be completely transferred to other industries and can be developed through professional education and industry experience.

name: Firm-specific human capital
definition: Firm-specific human capital is knowledge about unique routines and procedures that have limited value outside the firm in which the capital base has been developed. As professionals' time with a given firm grows, they develop more firm-specific human capital through within-firm training programs and on-the-job experience.

name: Firm-level social capital
authors_terms: ["social capital", "firm-level social capital", "connectedness with potential clients"]
definition: Social capital is defined in terms of supporting relationships with other economic actors, most notably, potential clients. An organization's social capital is defined as the aggregate of firm members' connectedness with potential clients.

name: Founding type
authors_terms: ["founding type", "firms founded by a split", "newly created firms emerging out of splits", "de novo foundings", "foundings"]
definition: A founding was coded when a new name appeared in the directories for the first time and neither an acquisition nor a name change accounted for the new entry. For the test of Hypothesis 5a, the authors created a dummy variable, founding type, set to 1 if a particular firm was founded by a split and to 0 otherwise; a split was coded when at least two partners left and formed a new firm.

name: Acquisition name change
authors_terms: ["acquisition with name change", "acquisitions involving name changes", "acquisition without name change", "name change"]
definition: When two or more firms joined and adopted a new name, the event was coded as an acquisition with name change; when a resulting firm adopted one of the pre-existing names, the event was coded as an acquisition without name change. Name changes were coded when the name of a firm differed from its previous name but at least two-thirds of its partners had continued their affiliation with the firm.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["business group affiliation", "BG affiliation", "group affiliation", "affiliation to business groups"]
definition: Business groups are legally independent firms 'bound together by a constellation of formal and informal ties' that are coordinated by a central or core entity; affiliation indicates that a focal firm is a member of such a group.

name: International search propensity
definition: The first step of a firm's international search behavior modeled as a two-step decision process, namely deciding whether to export.

name: International search intensity
authors_terms: ["international search intensity", "search intensity", "extent of export sales"]
definition: The second step of a firm's international search behavior, namely the extent of export sales conditional on having chosen to export.

name: Scope of institutional change
authors_terms: ["scope of institutional changes", "narrow-scope institutional change", "broad-scope institutional change", "industry-specific change"]
definition: Institutional transitions can vary along a continuum from being broad in scope (i.e., influencing a number of industries) to being narrow in scope (i.e., industry specific); broad-scope changes affect the business group as a whole whereas narrow-scope changes have a greater impact on particular affiliates.

name: Business group age
definition: The age of the business group, computed from the year of incorporation of the group's oldest affiliate; older business groups are more embedded in the preliberalization environment and rely on prior templates for success, which amplifies inertial forces.

name: Business group-affiliate age gap
definition: The distance between the focal affiliate's age and the age of the business group; affiliates that are younger relative to the group's founding are perceived as peripheral to the core functioning of the group and receive the least support for an external search.

name: Industry distance from founding affiliate
authors_terms: ["focal-founding affiliate industry distance", "industry distance", "affiliates in industries that are more distant from the founding affiliate's industry"]
definition: The distance between the industry in which the business group was founded (its oldest affiliate) and the industry of the focal affiliate; affiliates distant from the founding industry are perceived as peripheral to the core functioning of the group.

name: Affiliate resources
authors_terms: ["affiliate's resources", "stock of resources", "firm financial resources", "firm nonfinancial resources"]
definition: The stock of financial and nonfinancial resources possessed by an affiliate, which reduces its dependence on the business group core and affords it greater autonomy in decision making, risk taking and exploration.

name: Intragroup position
authors_terms: ["intragroup position", "affiliate's position within the business group", "position within the group"]
definition: The strength of an affiliate's position within the business group, reflected in its contribution to the group in terms of revenue, reputation, leverage, and legitimacy, which confers prominence, visibility and bargaining power within the group network.

name: Industry market position
authors_terms: ["market position", "position within the industry", "standing in the industry", "dominant market position"]
definition: A firm's standing in its industry, a consequence of consistent firm performance or realized effective managerial action leading to enhanced credibility, market power, brand image, and reputation.

name: Brokerage
definition: The authors refer to 'brokerage position' as the location of an actor in a triad (or higher-order social structure) in which the actor's partners are disconnected. Actors with unconnected partners are commonly referred to as brokers, and the degree of brokerage is conceptualized as access to structural holes.

name: Status dissimilarity between partners
authors_terms: ["status difference", "status dissimilarity", "status-heterophilous ties", "status-homophilous ties", "downward ties", "upward ties"]
definition: The status difference of the lead and a colead bank is a continuous variable that ranges from 0 to 1, where high values indicate higher status dissimilarity between the two banks, low values indicate similarity between the banks, and zero indicates that lead and colead have exactly the same status. A status-heterophilous tie spans different status positions; a downward tie is one in which a higher-status actor initiates a tie to a lower-status actor and an upward tie one in which a lower-status actor initiates a tie to a higher-status actor.

name: Social aspiration level
definition: A bank's social aspiration level is based on the market shares of other banks in the network, weighted by market share similarity: the greater the difference between the market shares of banks i and j, the less weight bank i would give to j's market share when setting i's aspiration levels.

name: Historical aspiration level
definition: Historical aspiration levels adapt to experience by an 'anchoring and adjustment' heuristic in which the aspiration level is adjusted by the most recent performance; the weight given to the immediate prior performance compared with more distant performances is a number between 0 and 1, so an aspiration heavily weighted toward recent performance adjusts quickly to short-term performance variations.

name: Aspiration-performance gap
authors_terms: ["aspiration-performance gaps", "performance relative to aspirations", "relative performance", "Social aspiration performance", "Historical aspiration performance", "underperformance", "overperformance"]
definition: A relative performance measure defined as the value of the performance metric minus its social (or historical) aspiration, both measured at time t. Consistent with prior research in performance feedback, a spline function is implemented to enable comparison of the slopes above and below the aspiration-level point, splitting each relative performance variable into a part above zero and a part below zero.

name: Firm newness
definition: We used time of organizational founding to define newness. Specifically, we defined new firms as newly founded organizations and established firms, as organizations already in existence.

name: Innovation
definition: Following prior research, we define innovation as 'a process that begins with an invention, proceeds with the development of the invention, and results in the introduction of a new product, process or service to the marketplace' (Edwards & Gordon, 1984: 1).

name: Competition
authors_terms: ["competition", "degree of competition", "number of competing firms", "competitive markets"]
definition: The degree of competition in an environment, one of four environmental dimensions relevant to innovation. Markets differ significantly in the number of competing firms they contain.

name: Financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources", "availability of financial resources", "venture capital", "venture capital funding"]
definition: The availability of financial resources influences innovation because access to capital allows an innovator to follow the normal path of developing the new product before selling it to others. Access to venture capital, which varies across environments and over time, makes new firms more innovative.

name: Manufacturing intensity
definition: If innovation in a given market is manufacturing intensive—that is, if it depends on the joint exploitation of manufacturing assets and new technology—new firms will have lower rates of innovation than they will have in less manufacturing intensive markets.

name: Market size
authors_terms: ["market size", "size of the market", "small markets", "large markets"]
definition: The size of the market influences innovation because the innovator needs to believe that the market size is sufficient to justify the investment of time and money in the uncertain activity of developing new products in place of investing in other activities.

name: Leverage
definition: Leverage is measured as the ratio of the book value of total debt (long-term and short-term debt) to market value of equity and book value of debt. The authors treat leverage as the observed expression of the firm's capital structure and of its ability to borrow.

name: Asset redeployability
definition: For our purposes, firm specificity implies that the value of the asset is greater in its use within a particular firm rather than in its next best use in some other firm. In the event of bankruptcy and liquidation, the firm's more specialized assets face a greater loss in value.

name: Investment in tangible assets
definition: Depreciation is usually proportional to the value of physical assets such as buildings, plant and equipment, that act as collateral and provide security for lenders. The ratio of depreciation to total assets is therefore an index of the extent to which the assets of the firm are redeployable.

name: Investment in intangible firm-specific assets
definition: Many firm specific assets are intangible - for example R&D and advertising - and difficult to measure and evaluate. Such firm specific assets, especially intangible assets like R&D, may be difficult for outsiders to monitor, understand, and evaluate.

name: Investment in reputational assets
definition: After some period of time, these reputational assets, even though they are firm specific and intangible, form a basis of security for lenders. The firm's reputation can be seriously damaged if it defaulted on a loan.

name: Earnings volatility
definition: Various measures have been used in the literature to measure the earnings volatility or business risk which is predicted to be negatively related to leverage.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: The firm's growth opportunities are difficult to measure and guidance from previous studies is scant.

name: Firm-specific effects
definition: The firm effects will take into account unspecified resources, growth opportunities, contractual relationships (formal or implicit) and skills.

name: Industry effects
definition: The industry effect is meant to capture various unspecified structural characteristics that may affect leverage. These will include entry barriers, capacity conditions, industry growth rate, factor market conditions, and industry-wide business risk and industry-specific capital market imperfections.

name: Year effects
definition: The year effect is expected to pick up any year to year changes in policies and regulations - for example, tax reforms - that might affect capital structure decisions.

name: Product diversity
authors_terms: ["product diversity", "degree of product diversity", "Product Diversity", "product diversification", "product mode of diversification"]
definition: The primary measure of Product Diversity is a Herfindahl-type measure of product diversity. Such a measure takes into account both the number of segments in which the firm operates and the relative importance of each segment to the firm's sales.

name: Multinationality
authors_terms: ["multinationality", "degree of multinationality", "multinational diversity", "Foreign Sales Ratio (FSR)", "international diversity"]
definition: Measures of multinationalization should reflect the relative size and strategic importance of foreign and domestic operations. The degree of multinationality is the relative intensity of internalized international operations (foreign direct investment) compared to international market activities (exports or licensing).

name: Export intensity
authors_terms: ["Export Sales Ratio (ESR)", "export intensity", "level of export sales", "exports"]
definition: The ratio of export sales to total firm sales; the authors suggest that exporting should be tested also as a means of international market diversification, and note that the economics literature suggests economies of scale in production and access to more diverse markets will result in positive performance effects from increasing exports from the home market.

name: Internalization
definition: A measure of internalization, or the relative use of internal international operations versus exports to service foreign markets. The firm with greater relative levels of internal control of international operations relative to market control will be higher on this ratio, regardless of total levels of participation in international markets.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use multiple indices, as any single measure may generate criticism. To facilitate comparison with prior research, the initial measures were after-tax figures for return on assets (ROA), return on total sales (ROS) and sales growth.

name: Keiretsu affiliation
definition: One aspect of large Japanese multinationals is that many of them are members of keiretsu, families of firms in related and unrelated industries with interlocking ownership and unique inter-firm relationships. Positive keiretsu membership in this study represents only the closest level of affiliation, those companies which are part of the 'president's council' or equivalent.

name: Strategic time periods
definition: A better approach would be to find periods of years during which strategies are stable. If no changes appear within a block of years, that block is taken to be a single group for analytical purposes.

name: Response delay
definition: Response delay is the amount of time it took a firm to respond. It is calculated in working days as the difference between the date of the action and the date of the response.

name: Responder performance
definition: This study uses a short-term marketbased performance measure because it provides for a direct link between individual firm actions and performance effects. For the responder, the relevant performance effect is the wealth created by his/her response.

name: First mover performance
authors_terms: ["first mover performance", "actor performance", "wealth effect of the response for the original actor"]
definition: In competitive environments, the first mover's ability to reap the benefits of a move is time dependent: the later the first moving firm faces competitive responses, the more time it has to absorb first mover benefits. The wealth effect of the response for the original actor is determined by calculating a stock effect for the first mover on the day of the response.

name: Knowledge sharing
definition: Knowledge sharing between one subsidiary and another consists of organizational processes, systems, tools, practices, and the related know-how that is given to and received from a subsidiary; the measure focuses on the outflow of knowledge from the focal subsidiary to other parts of the MNC.

name: General manager MNC performance pay
authors_terms: ["GM compensation based on MNC performance", "the percentage of compensation for subsidiary general managers that is based on the performance of the entire MNC"]
definition: GM compensation based on MNC performance is the percentage of total compensation for the general manager that is based on overall MNC performance.

name: Top management MNC performance pay
authors_terms: ["other top management compensation based on MNC performance", "the percentage of compensation for other subsidiary top management (excluding the general manager) that is based on the performance of the entire MNC"]
definition: Other top management compensation based on MNC performance is the percentage of total compensation for the other top management (excluding the GM) based on overall MNC performance, where other top management includes all who report directly to the general manager.

name: Shared vision
definition: Shared vision is a scale measuring the alignment of objectives among different subsidiaries; informal control mechanisms in knowledge-focused organizations aim at creating a shared vision and value system that supports the creation of social networks that engage in knowledge sharing.

name: Subsidiary host country
definition: Subsidiary host country takes on the value of 0 when the subsidiary is located in Finland and 1 when it is located in China; China is in the process of transforming from a planned to a market economy while Finland is a small Western industrial country.

name: Patent invalidation
definition: The invalidation of a patent through a validity challenge, after which all firms gain freedom to operate with respect to the original innovation.

name: Follow-on innovation
definition: Firms develop new products and processes building on prior ('original') innovations.

name: Original innovation value
definition: The value of the original innovation, which increases product market revenues of the patentee and all licensees.

name: Follow-on innovation value
definition: The value of the follow-on innovation, which further increases revenues for the firm that innovates and can affect licensing and rent dissipation.

name: Product market competition
definition: The extent to which the patentee and potential licensees compete in the same product market, which affects rent dissipation and transaction costs of licensing.

name: Patent thicket density
definition: Particularly in complex technology fields, multiple patents may protect different aspects of the original innovation, creating a patent thicket. The patent thicket density is measured by counting citation constellations in which three patentees can mutually block each other.

name: Examiner participation
authors_terms: ["examiner participation", "participation of the granting examiner in the opposition division", "granting examiner's participation"]
definition: The participation of the patent's granting examiner in the opposition division, which decides on invalidation; the granting examiner is one of the three division members and has an equal vote on the opposition outcome.

name: Potential director's market-specific experience
authors_terms: ["potential director's experience", "experience of a director in the markets the focal firm is considering entering", "a director's market-relevant experience"]
definition: Each potential director's experience in the markets the focal firm is considering entering, captured by examining the activities of the firms where these potential directors had served. The authors rely on the assumption that experience is developed from accumulated learning with similar activities, so greater exposure to new-drug introductions in a given therapeutic market provides directors with greater market-specific understanding.

name: Interlocking directors' market-specific experience
authors_terms: ["interlocking directors' experience", "directors' market experience", "directors' market-specific experience"]
definition: Current interlocking directors' experience in a given market, captured by examining the new-drug-introduction activities of the firms on whose boards these directors served. Directors gain market-specific knowledge from participating in board-level discussions of strategic activities at incumbent firms.

name: New-director appointment
definition: Whether a focal firm (that was considering entering a new market) appointed a new director who currently served on another pharmaceutical firm's board.

name: New-market entry
definition: Whether the focal firm had entered into a new therapeutic market or not.

name: Financial restatements
definition: Directors are often stigmatized for their firms' accounting irregularities, and this bad reputation has strong negative consequences for directors; the authors therefore expect directors to show a lower willingness to join firms whose reputation has been damaged by recent financial irregularities.

name: Relative status
authors_terms: ["relative status", "status differential between the focal and the incumbent firm"]
definition: The difference between the focal firm's status and the status of the firm(s) where the potential director currently serves, where status is assumed to be captured by partnerships with other firms in the same industry; higher values imply the focal firm had a higher status than the firm(s) where the potential director currently served.

name: New-product development experience
definition: The number of new drugs the focal firm had developed in the recent three-year window. Firms that have introduced many new products have developed routines that enable them to identify the information critical to introduce a new product into a specific market and to decode and process that information.

name: Market overlap
authors_terms: ["market overlap", "ex ante market overlap between interlocked firms"]
definition: The ex ante degree of market overlap between the focal firm and the incumbent interlocked firm(s). A higher degree of market overlap with interlocked firms implies a greater risk of anti-trust investigation after entering a market in which an interlocked firm is already active.

name: Strong-ties network effects
definition: Borrowing from social network theory, the author divides a technology's total network into 'a part that has strong ties with a given user or potential user, and the rest of the network,' so that strong-ties network effects capture the relative network size of a technology in the specific part of the network where the user has strong ties.

name: Classical network effects
authors_terms: ["classical network effects", "world network", "total network size", "installed base"]
definition: Network externalities describe a situation in which 'the utility that a user derives from consumption of the good increases with the number of other agents consuming the good'; total network size, 'the total number of consumers owning units of hardware that are compatible with the individual's unit,' is taken as the measure of the strength of network effects.

name: Technology choice
definition: The dependent variable registers each operator's choice of technology among the incompatible alternatives available to it at entry.

name: Internal knowledge variety
definition: A firm's internal knowledge variety (IKV), which reflects the dispersion of inventive activity across technological domains. We measure IKV as the distribution of patents across all 64 pharmaceutical patent classes, using the inverse of the nonbiased Herfindahl Index proposed by Hall (2002).

name: External knowledge distance
definition: The average knowledge distance between the firm and its partners, external knowledge distance (EKD), to indicate the degree that members of the firm will be exposed to knowledge from novel or familiar domains. We measure EKD by estimating the angular separation between a firm and all of its partners' patent portfolios.

name: Inventive performance
definition: To assess the usefulness of a firm's solutions to complex problems, we examine patenting outcomes. We define our dependent variable, a firm's Inventive performance, as the number of citations that a firm's patents receive.

name: Tie strength
definition: Granovetter (1973) defined tie strength in terms of a combination of the amount of time, emotional intensity, intimacy, and reciprocity associated with a relationship, or tie. The relational dimension of networks describes the quality of relationships, including their frequency, degree of closeness, and level of trust.

name: Centrality
definition: Centrality represents the position of an actor in a network and is defined most broadly by number of direct ties.

name: Structural holes
definition: When a focal actor in a network is connected to partners that are unconnected to each other, there is a gap, or structural hole, in the network.

name: Shared vision
definition: Shared vision refers to the degree to which members of an initiative group share goals and aspirations with other organizational units and with their organization as a whole. The cognitive dimension of networks reflects the similarity between the interpretations, mental models, and worldviews of the focal actor and others in a network.

name: Degree of exploration
definition: The degree of exploration is conceptualized as a continuum, representing the extent that strategic initiatives draw on existing knowledge within a firm (more exploitive initiatives) or on knowledge that is new to the firm (more exploratory initiatives).

name: Initiative performance
authors_terms: ["initiative performance", "performance of a strategic initiative unit", "group performance"]
definition: Items focused on the extent to which several goals and objectives were achieved, assessed for an initiative over the last three months on dimensions such as staffing, time, quality, reliability, cost, efficiency, user/client satisfaction, service, and objective expectations.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: When firms have a larger absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990), they can afford to outsource activities to more cognitively distant offshore suppliers. The key indicator of absorptive capacity is the firm's internal R&D intensity (Cassiman and Veugelers, 2006; Cohen and Levinthal, 1990), which is needed to understand and use the complementary capabilities accessed through offshore R&D outsourcing.

name: R&D outsourcing
definition: We view outsourcing as the procurement of activities from independent suppliers, in contrast to internal sourcing (within a business) and affiliate sourcing (elsewhere in a corporation).

name: Offshore R&D outsourcing
definition: Offshore outsourcing refers to activities procured from independent suppliers located abroad. The country-level drivers of cognitive distance are differences in institutions and cultures.

name: Domestic R&D outsourcing
definition: Outsourcing is the procurement of activities from independent suppliers. Domestic R&D outsourcing represents all spending on transactions with independent R&D suppliers within France.

name: Innovation
definition: When investigating the effects of outsourcing we look at both product and process innovation: both matter for the long-term competitive advantage of firms in the marketplace.

name: Family ties
definition: Family ties exist when the agent is a member of the extended family that owns the firm; in a family contracting situation the relational contract between the family-owned firm and the agent involves a common bond and a set of mutual expectations that are more likely to be based on emotions and sentiments than a nonfamily relational contract.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is judged against criteria specified for the agent; for the newspapers studied, the volume of circulation is an excellent performance measure, a number that is not subject to accounting manipulation and that can be meaningfully and unambiguously tracked both longitudinally and cross-sectionally.

name: Business risk
definition: Business risk is performance variance relative to performance level, one of the most widely used measures of business risk in the strategic management literature; during the tenure of each executive it is captured by the ratio of the variance in circulation to a term consisting of average circulation minus minimum circulation squared, logged because the distribution that best fitted the data was lognormal.

name: Executive tenure
definition: Executive tenure is the length of time the executive holds the job, recorded for each CEO and editor as the time between the date of hiring and the date of termination, or 1993 if the individual was still on the job; an agent-principal family contract is argued to reduce an executive's employment risk.

name: Relational contract strength
authors_terms: ["relational contract", "strongly relational contract", "weakly relational contract", "relational agency contract", "executive level"]
definition: A relational contract is one that broadly states the terms and objectives of an agency relationship; such contracts are ambiguous rather than explicit, and the parties do not agree on detailed plans of action but on goals and objectives. A contract with a CEO is by necessity more strongly relational than a contract with an editor.

name: CEO succession
definition: Senior managers are dismissed when the board responsible for monitoring their behavior has decided that they are incompetent or lagging behind their counterparts in competing firms in skills and abilities, and dismissal is the ultimate sanction conditioning their behavior; the study examines succession events in which a firm replaced its CEO.

name: Organizational survival
definition: Organizational survival is how long the newspaper remained in circulation following each CEO succession event up to the next succession event, if any; if the newspaper went out of business after a particular CEO's departure, the period from the date of succession to the date the paper ceased to be published is the measure of survival length.

name: Managerial level
authors_terms: ["management level", "managerial level", "top, middle and lower level", "institutional, managerial, and technical levels"]
definition: Managerial tasks are typically grouped within three distinct (i.e. qualitatively different) yet interrelated levels, and, as proposed by Parsons (1960), the managerial 'task' differs among the institutional, managerial, and technical levels. Top managers were defined as the chief executive officer and his immediate subordinates of at least vice-presidential rank; middle managers were defined as those who had at least two levels of supervisors under their responsibility and no more than two reporting levels below top executives; lower-level managers were defined as those reporting to middle-level managers or below.

name: Importance of strength and weakness indicators
authors_terms: ["strength and weakness indicators", "indicators of strengths and weaknesses", "importance of strength and weakness indicators", "decision factors"]
definition: A critical component of the formulation process is identification of a firm's internal strengths and weaknesses and its external opportunities and threats. The decision-influencing cues (strength and weakness indicators) and their weights are depicted in a quantitative representation of the person's cognitive model (schema) regarding the organization's strength and weakness indicators.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: The instrument contained six scales, composed of 25 items, that measured perceived uncertainty in six major dimensions of a firm's external environment: (1) suppliers of raw materials and parts; (2) competitors' behavior; (3) clients; (4) financial/capital markets; (5) government regulatory agency actions; and (6) behavior of labor unions.

name: Firm context
definition: Managers within firms have unique histories thereby affecting their schemas. In addition, firms in different industries face different competitive conditions (Porter, 1980).

name: Formal governance mechanisms
definition: Formal governance mechanisms are generally understood to include 'depersonalized exchanges, a reliance on financial parameters, and the drafting and implementation of formal contracts.'

name: Relational governance mechanisms
definition: Relational governance mechanisms are generally understood to include people- or social-based mechanisms that enhance open communication and the sharing of information, trust, dependence, and cooperation. They refer broadly to mechanisms that enhance the building of trust and social identification.

name: Knowledge-based assets
definition: Knowledge-based assets are a firm's intangible know-how and skills. Examples include marketing knowledge and customer service expertise.

name: Property-based assets
definition: Property-based assets are legal properties owned by firms including physical resources (e.g., buildings, infrastructure), financial capital, and the like.

name: Alliance performance
authors_terms: ["alliance performance", "overall alliance performance", "overall success of the alliance"]
definition: Our measure of overall alliance performance is based on the degree to which the alliance achieved 13 goals, weighted according to the extent to which each goal was rated as 'relevant to the alliance.'

name: Short-selling pressure
definition: Short sellers borrow and sell shares in the market in the hope of repurchasing them at a lower price; because they profit from downward stock price movements, they place firms under scrutiny for any sign that current valuations are too high. An increase in short-selling pressure is a disruptive event that may alter organizational rhythms and create a sense of urgency.

name: Workplace injuries
definition: Work-related injuries that 'result in days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, [and/or] loss of consciousness or medical treatment beyond first aid.'

name: Analyst horizon
authors_terms: ["analyst horizon", "analysts' horizons", "long-term-oriented analysts", "analysts with longer time horizons"]
definition: The time horizons of the earnings per share forecasts issued by the analysts covering a firm; analysts vary in the attention they allocate between firms' short- and long-run performance prospects, and analysts with longer time orientations issue long-term EPS forecasts.

name: Investor horizon
definition: The investment horizons of a firm's shareholders: dedicated institutional investors acquire concentrated equity in a few firms and have extended investment horizons, whereas transient institutional investors hold a dispersed portfolio of firms and have shorter investment horizons.

name: Employee bargaining power
authors_terms: ["labor union", "labor unions", "employees' bargaining power", "employee salience", "union strength"]
definition: Employees' power to achieve salience and demand managerial responses, which is higher if they belong to strong labor unions because unions can monopolize the labor supply and extract rent, and because union pressure raises the immediate costs and urgency to firms from employee injuries.

name: TMT horizon
authors_terms: ["TMT horizon", "top management team horizons", "TMT long-term orientation", "time orientation of the TMT"]
definition: The degree to which the top management team prioritizes short- versus long-term outcomes; firms with long-term-oriented management teams are less concerned with meeting quarterly earnings targets and more concerned with ensuring long-term value creation.

name: Safety expenditures
definition: Discretionary selling, general, and administrative expenditures estimated following Caskey and Ozel (2017), which are likely to capture changes in discretionary safety expenditure.

name: Workload
definition: The intensity of work firms impose on employees; firms may boost short-term performance by imposing heavier workloads, and high workloads deplete mental and physical strength, increasing injuries.

name: Supplier IT capabilities
definition: A supplier's competence in designing IT applications and technical systems and in delivering them to clients through consulting, user training, and project and relationship management skills.

name: Client operational capabilities
authors_terms: ["client operational capabilities", "client firm operational capabilities", "operational capabilities"]
definition: Operational skills that reflect a client's knowledge and ability to efficiently execute a respective business process; client operational capabilities relate to business knowledge in day-to-day problem solving activities within a business process.

name: Client firm performance
authors_terms: ["client firm performance", "focal client firm performance", "return on average assets (ROA)"]
definition: A client's return on average assets (ROA), which captures a firm's ability to generate profits from its business operations or losses, if costs exceed revenues.

name: Locus of supplier capability deployment
authors_terms: ["locus of supplier capability deployment", "locus of capability deployment", "in-sourcing", "outsourcing"]
definition: Whether supplier IT capabilities are deployed in colocation with client operational capabilities by in-sourcing the supplier's capabilities or decoupled from client operational capabilities by outsourcing the respective activity; the locus is either at the client (in-sourcing) or at the supplier (outsourcing).

name: Application endorsement
definition: Endorsements generally involve conveying support for certain job candidates, especially when screening applicants. Frequently, the endorser directly targets the ultimate organizational decision makers with authority over the final selection decision, with the goal of encouraging them to pay attention to a specific candidate.

name: Assessed applicant qualifications
authors_terms: ["applicants' qualifications and competencies", "competency scores", "reader competency scores", "interviewer competency scores", "competency assessments", "better qualified"]
definition: The school uses a competency assessment tool to systematically evaluate applicants' qualifications, scoring them on nine competencies specific to their individual qualifications; all nine are scored on a 5-point scale ranging from deficient to exceptional.

name: Interview invitation
definition: Based on the readers' competency assessments, the senior directors of admissions choose applicants with strong competency scores and extend interview invitations.

name: Offer of admission
definition: Offers of admission are determined by senior directors of admissions, who are aware of each application's endorsement status, based primarily on the review of interviewers' competency scores.

name: Post-admission performance
authors_terms: ["better performer", "better performers", "performance after joining the school", "job market performance", "academic performance"]
definition: The authors ask whether endorsed applicants tend to outperform their non-endorsed peers after joining the organization; in this setting they test higher performance after joining the school, as measured by final GPA, academic awards, and job salary.

name: Organizational citizenship behavior
authors_terms: ["better citizens", "better citizen", "pro-organizational behaviors", "student club leadership", "student leadership activities"]
definition: Candidates who, upon joining the organization, are more willing to support the organization and its members, engaging in pro-organizational behaviors like volunteering to participate in important organizational activities, advising organizational members, or contributing valuable resources to the organization.

name: Alumni giving
authors_terms: ["better alumni", "alumni giving activities", "monetary donations to the school", "school gift amount"]
definition: Endorsed applicants may be favored because they are expected to be better alumni than non-endorsed applicants, as shown, for example, by donating more resources to the school.

name: Internal human resource manufacturing sources
authors_terms: ["internal HR-based manufacturing sources", "internal HR manufacturing sources", "internal manufacturing-related HR skills", "internal human resources"]
definition: The HR component of internal manufacturing capabilities usually includes the knowledge, expertise, talents, creativity, and skills of a firm's manufacturing personnel, and reflects strong internal manufacturing-related HR skills among a firm's management and employees.

name: External human resource manufacturing sources
authors_terms: ["external HR-based manufacturing sources", "external HR manufacturing sources", "external human resources"]
definition: HR-based manufacturing capabilities that are assembled from external sources by joining strategic alliances, employing consultants and outside experts, or maintaining close ties with universities and other research centers; the factor also showed the use of external consultants and temporary employees.

name: Internal technological manufacturing sources
authors_terms: ["internal technical manufacturing sources", "internal manufacturing technology sources", "internal proprietary manufacturing technologies"]
definition: A key source of manufacturing capabilities is the firm's technological core, systems, assets, and resources; the factor showed the existence of strong internal manufacturing technological resources and facilities.

name: External technological manufacturing sources
authors_terms: ["external technical manufacturing sources", "external manufacturing technology sources"]
definition: A firm can also use external sources to obtain modern manufacturing technologies; the factors captured the use of joint ventures and alliances in manufacturing and a firm's use of outsourcing and licensing.

name: Manufacturing integration in technology commercialization
definition: Integration is the process by which the firm coordinates and deploys its different manufacturing sources in order to achieve successful TC. It includes the approaches, systems, and processes management uses to involve the firm's manufacturing staff in the TC process.

name: Technology commercialization success
definition: Successful TC is multifaceted. It refers to a firm's ability to: (1) develop and introduce a large number of product and process technologies; (2) create radically new products; (3) expedite the introduction of these new products to the market; and (4) create new knowledge.

name: Prior relative pay
authors_terms: ["Prior Relative Pay", "relative pay in their prior TMT", "prior firm relative pay", "executive relative pay in a prior TMT"]
definition: The ratio of the mean of TMT pay to the focal executive's pay, so smaller values indicate an executive earns relatively more. Executives who experienced larger relative pay disparity in a prior TMT are those with lower relative pay in that TMT.

name: TMT pay dispersion change
authors_terms: ["difference in pay dispersion between executives' new TMT and their prior TMT", "pay dispersion difference", "change in TMT pay dispersion", "New Pay Dispersion"]
definition: The difference (change score) in pay dispersion between the executives' new TMT and their prior TMT, where pay dispersion is calculated in both the new and prior firm TMT as the coefficient of variation in pay.

name: Relative pay improvement
authors_terms: ["difference in relative pay between executives' new TMT and their prior TMT", "improvement in relative pay", "relative pay advance", "New Pay Disparity"]
definition: The difference in relative pay between the executives' new TMT and their prior TMT, capturing whether executives move to TMTs in which their relative position is better than it was in the prior TMT.

name: Advertising expenditure
definition: Firms invest in advertising for a variety of reasons that include information dissemination, product differentiation, and brand building. These efforts are intended to increase firm sales by stimulating demand (i.e., increasing volume), allowing firms to charge more per unit, or both.

name: R&D expenditure
definition: R&D expenditure has generally been used to measure firm investment in innovative effort that is expected to foster technological innovation (either product or process) and hence future sales. Thus, R&D is intended to benefit the firm either through increased revenue or decreased cost.

name: Domestic sales
definition: The survey collects data on total sales and export sales; we therefore calculate domestic sales by subtracting export sales from total sales.

name: Export sales
definition: The convention in this literature is to use the term 'export performance' when referring to 'export sales,' but we prefer to use the term 'export sales' rather than 'export performance' because it better describes the phenomenon. Previous work defines export performance as the level of export sales or the level of export intensity (i.e., export sales divided by total sales).

name: Domestic market growth
authors_terms: ["growth in domestic GDP", "domestic GDP", "growth in the domestic market", "economywide growth"]
definition: We expect growth in the domestic market to increase sales for firms in the domestic market. All things equal, growth stimulates demand and provides opportunities for all firms to amplify their sales volume.

name: Foreign market growth
authors_terms: ["growth in foreign GDP", "foreign GDP", "growth in foreign economies", "growth in distant markets"]
definition: The international trade literature has long stressed the connection between foreign GDP and export sales. As foreign markets grow, countries are more likely to engage in trade.

name: Real exchange rate
authors_terms: ["real exchange rate", "firm-specific real exchange rates", "firm-specific exchange rate index", "home-country currency depreciation", "exchange rate changes"]
definition: Firm-specific exchange rates reflect exchange rate changes most applicable to a firm's export portfolio. Because the measure is expressed as pesetas divided by the foreign currencies, increasing values indicate depreciation of the peseta and decreasing values indicate appreciation of the peseta.

name: Applicant gender
authors_terms: ["gender of the applicant", "gender of the inventor", "female inventor", "Female Inventor (FI)", "female-sounding names", "female name"]
definition: The gender of the inventor, deduced from the given name stated in the application; without any prior contact, the name on the application is the only way for the examiner to deduce the gender of the inventor.

name: Patent grant
authors_terms: ["granted patent application", "grant rate", "outcome of the application process", "granting of a patent"]
definition: The outcome of the review process: a dummy variable that takes value one if the applicant's application in an art unit and filing year is granted by the examiner.

name: First action allowance
authors_terms: ["first action allowance", "first-action approval", "first action on the merits"]
definition: The decision at the first decision point of the examiner after the first evaluation; the dependent variable is coded as one if the patent application is granted in this first round, so a rejection at this stage is consistent with deferring a decision for later.

name: Examiner gender
authors_terms: ["gender of the examiner", "gender of the reviewer", "female examiner", "Examiner Female"]
definition: The gender of the reviewer (examiner) who decides on the application, identified from the reviewer's name.

name: Examiner experience
authors_terms: ["examiner experience", "experience of the reviewer", "years of experience", "examiner's experience"]
definition: Experience as an indicator for specialization in resolving complex applications into a simple pass/fail decision and, thus, dealing with ambiguous situations.

name: Examiner workload
authors_terms: ["examiner workload", "workload of the examiner", "workload pressure", "Examiner Workload"]
