definition: A source of cognitive pressure related to hitting targets for performance reviews or performing according to expectations: patent reviewers usually multitask, reviewing several applications at a time, while managing their workload to hit their production requirements.

name: Multipoint contact
definition: A hospital's degree of intermarket contact with its competitors in a particular service market. Multipoint competition was operationalized for each of a hospital's services as the extent to which that hospital's other services were also offered by its competitors in that particular service market within its county.

name: Market exit
definition: Withdrawal from a market; an observation was included in the dataset if, for a given service, a hospital offered the service in the prior year and thus was capable of exiting that market in the current year.

name: Contracting for service provision
definition: The way in which a service is provided: organizations can operate in markets either by providing products and services developed with their own assets or through market-based transactions such as contractual agreements with other organizations.

name: Chief executive change
definition: A change in the organization's chief executive. Executive change, in particular a chief executive change, is an important mechanism for overcoming inertia and political resistance, and a new chief executive with new skills and perspectives is likely to make decisions and take actions that produce strategic changes.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Hospital performance is a multidimensional construct for which the authors developed two measures. Poor performance seems likely to exacerbate pressures for market exit, because firms may respond to a performance downturn by reducing services and downsizing the organization.

name: High reputation
definition: Reputation is defined as the 'broad public recognition of the quality of a firm's activities and outputs' (Pollock et al., 2015, p. 484). It builds on stakeholders' rational assessment and appreciation of a firm's past behaviors and performance, which then influences future expectations about the firm.

name: Celebrity
definition: Celebrity is defined as the 'high level of attention and ... positive emotional responses from stakeholder audiences' (Rindova et al., 2006, p. 51). It is primarily driven by the emotional aspect, as stakeholders' positive emotional reactions and attachments to media portrayals of firms' surprising and nonconforming behaviors are how celebrity creates value.

name: Misconduct scandalization
definition: Scandals are 'publicized transgressions that run counter to established norms' (Piazza & Jourdan, 2018, p. 165), and just becoming public knowledge is insufficient to scandalize misconduct, which 'requires ongoing media coverage after the misconduct's disclosure' (Adut, 2005). The authors 'focus on whether and how different social approval assets stimulate media coverage of firms' misconduct in the days immediately following its disclosure'.

name: Objective misconduct severity
definition: Objective severity reflects 'the measured harm' or 'extent' of the violation (Busenbark et al., 2019, p. 2083). It is reflected in the misconduct's magnitude and creates a negative expectancy violation based on general societal expectations of appropriate behavior.

name: Perceived misconduct severity
definition: Perceived severity less clearly depicts direct harm but instead reflects 'shared perceptions of issue salience' (Wang et al., 2021, p. 285) induced by 'external observers who are not formally tasked with imposing penalties' (Busenbark et al., 2019, p. 2083) - typically operationalized as media attention to the violation.

name: Country risk
definition: 'Country risk' is a multidimensional construct encompassing many types of country-specific political and economic hazards. In this study, we use the terms 'country risk' and 'institutional hazards' interchangeably.

name: Operational integration
authors_terms: ["operational integration", "subsidiary intrafirm trade integration", "internalization of a subsidiary's revenue stream"]
definition: The extent to which a focal subsidiary is integrated into an MNC's global production and trading network—that is, the extent to which the subsidiary sells its goods and services within the MNC instead of relying on external markets. The extent to which the subsidiary's output is traded within the MNC's internal market rather than externally reflects this operational integration.

name: Political strategy capabilities
authors_terms: ["capabilities in deploying political strategies", "political strategy experience", "ability to manage institutional idiosyncrasies"]
definition: Capabilities for deploying political strategies, which are intended to reduce the actual level of external political hazards to which a subsidiary is subject. MNCs with greater experience operating in high-risk countries are more likely to have stronger capabilities for political strategies.

name: Operational integration capability
authors_terms: ["capabilities for operational integration", "prior experience with intrafirm trade"]
definition: An MNC's capabilities for operational integration, the complex task of organizing an MNC network to conduct intrafirm trade. An MNC with greater prior experience in intrafirm trade across subsidiaries is likely to become more competent at deploying operational integration in an additional subsidiary.

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: The authors focus on CEOs' overestimation of their own managerial skills; they conceptualize overconfidence simply as the overestimation of one's actual ability. Because of this overestimation, an overconfident CEO will have an inflated perception of the firm's future financial prospects.

name: Firm risk taking
definition: The authors measure firm risk taking as a multidimensional construct, because each spending category just provides a partial picture of a firm's overall risk taking; by summing up measures of different categories they generate a more complete picture.

name: Negative performance feedback
authors_terms: ["negative performance feedback", "distance aspirations (negative)", "negative distance from aspiration levels"]
definition: The CEO receives performance feedback in the form of the firm's realized financial performance relative to the aspiration level, and uses this information to update her belief. Performance feedback is derived as the difference between the firm's actual performance and its aspiration level, and the negative distance captures the case in which performance falls short of the aspiration level.

name: Positive performance feedback
authors_terms: ["positive performance feedback", "distance aspirations (positive)", "positive distance from aspiration levels"]
definition: The CEO receives performance feedback in the form of the firm's realized financial performance relative to the aspiration level, and uses this information to update her belief. Performance feedback is derived as the difference between the firm's actual performance and its aspiration level, and the positive distance captures the case in which performance exceeds the aspiration level.

name: Distance from the survival level
definition: At times firms try to ensure that performance exceeds a minimal survival level, the performance level at which the firm's existence is threatened. The authors use Altman's (1968) Z-score as an indicator of how close a firm is operating to its survival level.

name: Vertical ties
authors_terms: ["vertical ties", "vertical relationships", "past (issuer-bank) vertical ties", "vertical ties with issuer (jz)", "vertical buyer-supplier ties"]
definition: An organization can act as a producer and, in so doing, be embedded in a network of 'horizontal' collaborative relationships with the other producers. At the same time, the same organization can also be a supplier to customers leading to the emergence of 'vertical' relationships with them.

name: Prior horizontal ties
authors_terms: ["prior horizontal ties (ij)", "past (bank-bank) horizontal ties", "horizontal relationships", "horizontal producer-producer ties"]
definition: An organization can act as a producer and, in so doing, be embedded in a network of 'horizontal' collaborative relationships with the other producers. In a multiplex triad two producers are linked by horizontal producer-producer ties and at the same time are connected to a common customer via vertical buyer-supplier ties.

name: Horizontal tie formation
authors_terms: ["formation of a future (bank-bank) horizontal tie", "PO tie (ijz)", "horizontal syndicate tie", "an investment bank's choice of members in its PO syndicate"]
definition: Our dependent variable was an investment bank's choice of members in its PO syndicate. This was a dichotomous variable (PO tie (ijz)) coded 1 if bank i formed a tie with another investment bank j to place an offering for issuer z, and 0 otherwise.

name: Underpricing
authors_terms: ["underpricing", "underpricing in vertical ties (jz)", "underpricing of the offering"]
definition: The issuer tends to receive a lower price for its offering compared to the price at which this offering is being resold by investors, resulting in the phenomenon called 'underpricing'. The higher the underpricing, the more money the issuer has left on the table for the investors.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: KLD is an independent social choice investment advisory firm that compiles ratings of how companies address the needs of their stakeholders. For each stakeholder group, strengths and concerns are measured to evaluate positive and negative aspects of corporate actions toward stakeholders.

name: Government procurement contracts
authors_terms: ["government procurement contracts", "procurement contracts", "allocation of procurement contracts"]
definition: Procurements is the dollar amount of procurement contracts allocated to the company by the U.S. government in a given year.

name: Length of the government-supplier relationship
authors_terms: ["relationship length", "length of the relationship", "past interactions between the government and the company"]
definition: Relationship length is the number of years since the company has been receiving procurement contracts. Government agencies face lower information asymmetries with companies they have been interacting with for a long time, as such companies build up reputation through past interactions.

name: Product market competition
definition: To measure the degree of product market competition, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of industry concentration is computed as the sum of squared market shares of all companies in a given 2-digit SIC industry and year. Higher values of the index represent lower competition.

name: Contract duration
definition: Multi-year projects are procurement projects that span multiple years and are prone to a classic hold-up problem, as contractors have more bargaining power once the project has started and can hold up the government by renegotiating the contract terms to their advantage.

name: Contract scale
definition: Due to their scale, it is harder to contract upon all potential contingencies and determine the costs ex ante; large-scale contracts are more likely to entail adaptations and renegotiation. A contract is coded as large if the dollar amount is greater than the average across all contracts awarded in the same year.

name: Contract pricing type
definition: In cost-plus contracts (as opposed to fixed-price contracts), no price is pre-specified, but the supplier is reimbursed for the costs of executing the contract plus a fee.

name: Defense contract
definition: The government agency's purchasing decision - particularly related to defense spending - may be fully determined by distributive politics or influenced by political connections and political contributions. CSR may be less of a credible signal in the defense industry, and companies in the defense industry may not face a need to differentiate themselves given the limited number of military contractors.

name: Predecessor retention as board chair
authors_terms: ["predecessor retention", "retention of the predecessor CEO as board chair", "predecessor retained", "retention as chair"]
definition: In many cases, outgoing CEOs do not fully depart the scene, but instead remain for some period as chair of the board. The authors posit that the retention of the former CEO as board chair restricts a successor's discretion, dampening both the new person's ability to make changes as well as his or her potential to greatly alter the firm's performance.

name: Predecessor departure from board chair
authors_terms: ["departure of the predecessor CEO as board chair", "first free year", "predecessor's ultimate departure as chair"]
definition: Once the predecessor completely departs, the successor CEO will finally have the latitude to enact strategic change. Without the predecessor present to explicitly or implicitly influence decisions, and without any discomfort in the proposal of such changes, much of the constraint described above is now absent.

name: Post-succession strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "post-succession strategic change", "resource reallocation", "acquisitions", "divestitures", "TMT additions", "TMT departures"]
definition: Strategic change was conceptualized broadly, to encompass an array of important domains of choice that have implications for the form and fate of firms. The domains examined were resource reallocations, acquisitions and divestitures, and top management team (TMT) staffing.

name: Post-succession performance change
definition: When a predecessor is retained as chair, change is dampened, which, in turn, reduces the likelihood of large shifts in performance from the baseline level left by the prior CEO. Performance change was calculated as the absolute difference, without regard to sign, in each measure between presuccession levels and the focal year, net of median performance change in the three-digit industry.

name: Economies of scale
definition: One structural driver involves economies of scale that can be gained from integrating operations across countries. Scale economies are associated with such activities as research and development, raw material procurement, manufacturing operations, marketing, and sales.

name: Differential comparative advantage between countries
authors_terms: ["differential comparative advantage", "differences in comparative advantage across countries", "comparative advantage between countries"]
definition: A second structural driver is the differential comparative advantage that may exist between countries. The decision to locate certain value-added activities in a single global location is a function of both the availability of scale economies and also the existence of differential comparative advantage between countries.

name: Standardization of market demand
authors_terms: ["standardization of market demand", "standardized market demands", "standardization of demand"]
definition: The third structural driver is the permeability of borders to the flow of information and technology. This has led to a gradual homogenization in demand patterns among consumers worldwide, and a corresponding increase in standardization for product offerings and distribution systems.

name: Global competitive actions in the industry
authors_terms: ["global competitive actions", "competitive action", "competitive actions within the industry", "level of collective global competition in the industry", "competitive determinants"]
definition: The competitive determinants are the level of collective global competition in the industry; the common or shared strategy of group members overwhelms the individual strategy of an individual business.

name: Global integration of business activities
authors_terms: ["global integration of business activities", "global integration strategy", "business unit integration", "level of global integration"]
definition: The appropriate dimension of strategy here is the business unit's global integration strategy, which can be defined as 'rationalization that may entail standardization of product, centralization of technological development, or the vertical or horizontal integration of manufacturing'.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Conceptually, it is the ability of the business to generate a superior performance relative to its industry that was viewed as most relevant, rather than absolute measures of performance.

name: Collective organizational engagement
definition: The shared perceptions of organizational members that members of the organization are, as a whole, physically, cognitively, and emotionally invested in their work. It is a firm-level construct and an indicator of the overall motivational environment within the firm.

name: Motivating work design
authors_terms: ["motivating work design", "motivating work designs", "motivational work designs", "enriching entry-level motivating work design"]
definition: The firm-wide use of motivational work designs; drawing upon Hackman and Oldham's (1976) job characteristics model, these are autonomy, skill variety, task significance, task identity, and feedback.

name: HRM investments and expectation-enhancing practices
authors_terms: ["HRM practices", "HRM investments and expectation-enhancing practices", "HRM expectation-enhancing practices", "HRM inducements and investments"]
definition: HRM practices categorized along two dimensions: those practices that focus on the firm's expectations of employees (HRM expectation-enhancing practices) and those that enhance the employees' expected rewards and outcomes (HRM inducements and investments). When both are high, the employee-firm relationship shifts toward a long-term, open-ended relationship in which both employees and the firm commit to and invest in one another's future growth and development.

name: CEO transformational leadership
definition: Transformational leadership behaviors exhibited by the CEO, such as sharing compelling visions, intellectually stimulating followers, and setting challenging goals and expectations, which uniformly influence the organization as a whole.

name: Strategic implementation
definition: The top management team members' willingness to specify and pursue strategic objectives, and to adopt clearly defined metrics to dynamically monitor progress.

name: Firm performance
definition: The value created by the firm as indicated by increased firm performance; it is assessed with a broad accounting-based measure of business performance, with return on assets viewed as the best indicator of firm performance in the industry.

name: Main rival exit
authors_terms: ["exit of a main rival", "rival exit", "the exit of Circuit City", "exit of the rival store"]
definition: A main rival's exit disrupts the equilibrium the rival firms developed with each other; without the rival, the surviving firm enjoys a temporary monopoly that is fraught with uncertainty and threat because it attracts potential new entrants.

name: Product variety change
authors_terms: ["product variety", "product variety expansion", "store-level product variety", "change in the logged number of a surviving store's total product variety (SKUs)", "Δ PV"]
definition: The change in the logged number of a surviving store's total product variety (stockkeeping units, SKUs) after the rival chain exits; Equation (7) produces a logged ratio directly, which removes any variety change related to magnitude.

name: Colocation
definition: We categorize a preexisting local market as either a colocated market or a non-colocated market, according to whether the nearest rival is colocated (i.e., within walking distance) or not. These two variables describe the two mutually exclusive competitive market structures prior to the exit of Circuit City.

name: Market expansion
authors_terms: ["market expansion", "opening new stores", "new store opening", "ENTRY", "store-opening decision"]
definition: Expansion of market coverage through the opening of new stores, which incurs higher fixed costs and may cannibalize the sales of existing stores but allows the retailer to occupy the vacant side of the market and deter potential competitors from entry.

name: Customer demand
definition: The total amount of energy sold to a utility's customers each year in megawatt hours. Customer demand is driven by the population in a company's assigned service territory and by per-capita energy use.

name: Internal generation
definition: The megawatt hours of energy sourced internally (via generation), which captures how a utility's make-or-buy decision responds to increases in customer demand.

name: ISO membership
authors_terms: ["ISO membership", "membership in an independent system operator", "ISO"]
definition: Membership of a utility in an independent system operator, a regional organization that manages transmission assets on a nondiscriminatory basis and facilitates a wholesale electricity market. ISO membership does not change the characteristics of power purchase transactions, but it reduces the bilateral dependency between independent electricity suppliers and the utilities that purchase their power, lowering transaction costs.

name: Interconnection standards policy
definition: State-level policies passed in 40 states whose common purpose was to clarify the rules under which power producers contracted for access to utility-owned transmission grids, guaranteeing access at reasonable rates and providing standard rates and responsibilities.

name: Prior contracting experience
definition: We constructed a proxy for contracting experience based on a firm's prior reliance on purchased power to serve demand. The firm acquires this design capability through experience writing and operating under contracts formed in uncertain environments.

name: Production capabilities
definition: This provides an aggregate measure of a multitude of capabilities and resources underlying the capacity for low-cost production, including access to low-cost inputs, production efficiency, and optimal management of the dispatch of generating plants.

name: Market competition
definition: Reduced output import tariffs mean lower entry barriers of foreign products into the Chinese market, and hence, indicate stronger competitive pressure on Chinese firms.

name: Environmental performance
authors_terms: ["environmental performance", "firms' environmental performance", "firms' curtailment of public 'bads'"]
definition: In this research, we define environmental performance as the firms' curtailment of public 'bads' in the form of environmental pollution beyond the level required by the law. This definition implies that to be environmentally responsible firms will incur additional costs in their provision of private goods.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: A cost leadership strategy typically requires large-scale production, rigorous process improvements, learning by doing, cost control, and cost minimization in R&D, advertising, sales, and services.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: Differentiation is the process of distinguishing a product or service from others and making it more attractive to a particular target audience or market. The objective of differentiation is to develop a position that potential customers see as unique, thereby softening price-based competition.

name: Industry variety
authors_terms: ["industry variety", "variety", "strategic variety", "variety of firm strategies", "diversity in competitive strategy"]
definition: In theoretical terms, such a phenomenon can be called 'industry variety'. It is our belief that useful industry-level theory can be developed by defining variety as the number and diversity of competitors in an industry and then examining its relationship with industry performance as well as key contingency variables. In this study, industry variety was defined as strategic diversity among competitors and was measured by production, marketing, and research and development characteristics.

name: Industry performance
definition: To be consistent with past research, both accounting and market-based measures of performance were used (Chakravarthy, 1986; Keats, 1988; Venkatraman and Ramanujam, 1986). To calculate industry performance, the values of these two variables for the individual firms in each industry were aggregated.

name: Industry life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["stage of industry life cycle", "stage in the industry life cycle", "life cycle stage", "evolution of an industry"]
definition: The familiar product life cycle concept (Rink and Swan, 1979)—which divides the process of development into phases such as introductory, growth, mature, and decline—remains the best overall means of characterizing the evolution of an industry. Growth industries were defined as those with average annual sales increases (in constant 1982 dollars) above 10 percent over the 6-year period, mature industries as those with sales increases of 1-10 percent, and declining industries as those with negative sales increases.

name: Foreign competition
authors_terms: ["level of foreign competition", "amount of foreign competition", "foreign competition"]
definition: The amount of foreign competition in an industry was defined by the ratio of imports to total new shipments (domestic and foreign), and was considered to be substantial if greater than 10 percent. Industries with import ratios below 10 percent were considered to be low in foreign competition.

name: Firm visibility
authors_terms: ["visibility", "media exposure", "firm visibility in the news media"]
definition: The extent of a firm's exposure to diverse stakeholder groups, indicated by the number of times the firm is mentioned in mainstream media such as newspapers.

name: Balancing framing
definition: A framing approach in which a firm states that it adheres to shareholder value management but qualifies this statement by simultaneously affirming the legitimacy of the claims of other stakeholder groups, seeking to accommodate the diverging interests of different constituents.

name: Acquiescence framing
definition: A framing approach that implies an organization is consciously obedient to norms and institutional processes; regarding a shareholder value orientation, the firm publicly expresses its explicit espousal of a shareholder value orientation without qualification or alteration.

name: Government ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership by German federal or state government", "government ownership", "government entities"]
definition: The extent of a firm's ownership by German federal or state governmental entities, which have to attend to the interests of several corporate stakeholders and are less likely to support a strategic shift that privileges the interests of one stakeholder group over those of others.

name: Family ownership
definition: The extent of a firm's ownership by families, which tend to have long associations with the firms they founded and to subscribe to the traditional view of firm governance, stressing long-term capital investment, survival of the firm, and the intention of passing the firm on to descendants.

name: Domestic bank ownership with balancing framing
authors_terms: ["ownership by German banks that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation using a balancing framing", "bank ownership, balancing frame"]
definition: The extent of a firm's ownership by domestic banks that have themselves announced a move toward a shareholder value orientation and relied on a balancing framing, so that the interests of these owners figure prominently in the framing of strategic change.

name: Structural change
authors_terms: ["structural change", "practices commensurate with a shareholder value orientation", "implementation of structural changes"]
definition: Governance practices that demonstrate a credible commitment to a shareholder value orientation: value-based management control systems, stock option plans for company management, and internationally accepted accounting standards.

name: Stock evaluation
authors_terms: ["stock evaluations", "total stock market returns", "total investment return"]
definition: The evaluation of a firm by financial markets, examined as the effect of frame choice on the evaluation of a firm by financial markets and measured as total stock market returns.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups can be defined as a set of legally independent firms, operating in multiple sectors, that are linked to each other through persistent formal (e.g., equity) and informal (e.g., family) ties. These features distinguish business groups from other organizational forms such as holding companies, strategic alliances, and conglomerates and have pivotal implications for individual firm innovation.

name: Firm innovation
definition: We measured innovation in terms of the number of successful U.S. patent applications submitted by our sample firms.

name: Institutional infrastructure for innovation
definition: We use institutional infrastructure for innovation to denote the set of systems that allocates financial and technological resources and facilitates the flow of ideas that are directly related to firms' innovativeness.

name: Affiliate profitability
authors_terms: ["affiliate profitability", "profitability of other affiliates in the same group"]
definition: First, we argue that business groups' internal capital markets can substitute for poor external capital markets. The larger and richer the internal capital markets, the greater the positive impact of group affiliation; affiliates are thus more innovative.

name: Technological knowledge of other affiliates
authors_terms: ["affiliate patent stock", "technological knowledge held by other affiliates", "groupwide technological knowledge"]
definition: We believe access to groupwide technological knowledge is an intangible resource that benefits affiliates' innovation. When a firm's other affiliates are actively innovating, the focal firm can benefit from their technological knowledge.

name: Group unrelated diversification
definition: Evidence from U.S. conglomerates shows that unrelated diversification is likely to hurt affiliates' innovativeness, as it discourages risk taking and promotes free riding (Teece 1996). Unrelated diversification leads corporate executives to shift their attention away from strategic objectives such as R&D and toward financial objectives such as profitability (Hoskisson and Hitt 1988).

name: Robust interpretation of tradition
authors_terms: ["robust interpretation", "robust interpretation strategy", "robust interpretations of tradition"]
definition: In the opera industry, a robust design strategy is deployed through interpretations that preserve the core aspects of a particular opera (i.e., its music and dramatic content) while departing from it on features that are more peripheral (i.e., its visual staging).

name: Radical interpretation of tradition
authors_terms: ["radical interpretation", "radical interpretation strategy", "radical interpretations of tradition"]
definition: Radical interpretations modify the very essence of traditional operas by manipulating their core features. Generally, they involve dramaturgic alterations (i.e., changes to the libretto) which almost invariably are also accompanied by innovative visual elements, thus challenging more profoundly the artistic vision of the authors of the original opera.

name: Audience appeal
definition: We followed the lead of previous studies and relied on attendance - that is, the total number of people present at the opera's opening and any subsequent re-runs - as an indicator of audience appeal.

name: Audience composition
definition: Our interviews and archival sources suggest that opera goers too exhibit significant variability in their orientations, and that this variability maps onto two distinct opera goers' segments: season-ticket holders and single-ticket holders. There is indeed evidence that season- and single-ticket holders differ along several important dimensions.

name: Buyer-supplier network centrality
authors_terms: ["buyer-supplier centrality", "the centrality of a group affiliate's position in the intragroup buyer-supplier network", "buyer-supplier ties"]
definition: The extent to which a group affiliate occupies a central position in the intragroup buyer-supplier network, i.e., having more direct buyer-supplier ties with other affiliates (buyer-supplier ties exist when affiliates within a group engage in buyer-supplier relations).

name: Equity network centrality
authors_terms: ["equity centrality", "the centrality of a group affiliate's position in the intragroup equity network", "equity ties"]
definition: The extent to which a group affiliate occupies a central position in the intragroup equity network, where equity ties exist when affiliates own equity stakes in each other through cross holdings.

name: Director network centrality
authors_terms: ["director centrality", "the centrality of a group affiliate's position in the intragroup director network", "director ties"]
definition: The extent to which a group affiliate occupies a central position in the intragroup director network, where director ties exist when an individual sits on the board of multiple affiliates.

name: R&D capability
definition: The set of organizing processes and principles that a firm uses to deploy its resources to develop new products and improve manufacturing processes in response to the change in external environment. It is measured as the efficiency with which a firm employs a given set of resources (inputs) at its disposal to achieve certain objectives (outputs).

name: Director network density
authors_terms: ["director density", "density of the director network", "dense director network"]
definition: Network density captures the degree of connectivity between network partners; it is maximized (minimized) when all (no) network partners are connected to each other. Director density is the ratio of actual director ties among affiliates within a business group to the total number of potential director ties in that group.

name: Equity network density
authors_terms: ["equity density", "density of the equity network", "dense equity network"]
definition: Network density captures the degree of connectivity between network partners; it is maximized (minimized) when all (no) network partners are connected to each other. Equity density is the ratio of actual equity ties among affiliates within a business group to the total number of potential equity ties in that group.

name: Total diversification
authors_terms: ["total diversification", "DT", "index of total diversification", "entropy measure of diversification"]
definition: The entropy measure of total diversification is a weighted average of the shares of the firm's industry segments, the weight for each segment being the logarithm of the inverse of its share; it thus takes into consideration the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each of the segments in total sales.

name: Related diversification
definition: The related component of the entropy measure measures the distribution of the firm's output among related products within industry groups; the related diversification arising out of operations within an industry is the weighted sum of the shares of each of the product segments in the firm's sales in that industry.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: The unrelated component of the entropy measure measures the extent to which a firm's output is distributed in products across unrelated industry groups, computed as the weighted sum of the shares of each of the industries in the firm's total sales.

name: Profitability
definition: The performance measure employed in this study is profitability, and return on sales (ROS) is used as a measure of firm profitability, computed as the net profit after taxes (excluding extraordinary items) as a percentage of net sales.

name: Profitability growth rate
authors_terms: ["profitability growth rate", "growth rate of return on sales", "ROSG"]
definition: Profitability growth rate between two years has been computed as a percentage change in ROS from the base year to the final year.

name: Outside directorship
definition: Directors are typically grouped into two categories: inside directors are current or former employees of a company, who hold or have held high-level executive positions, whereas outside members are valued because of their breadth of experience and knowledge, their contacts outside a firm, and their independence from the CEO and other top executives.

name: Business executive occupation
definition: Occupation is a directorial characteristic in which directors are distinguished by whether they come from business occupations (business executives) or from nonbusiness occupations such as attorneys, teachers or educational administrators, and consultants.

name: Board tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure", "length of time a member has served on a board"]
definition: Tenure is the length of time a member has served on a board.

name: Female directorship
definition: Gender is a directorial characteristic of interest; the authors examine whether women who are directors are given responsibilities and duties equal to those of their counterparts who are men, and whether their presence on boards reflects tokenism.

name: Major committee membership
authors_terms: ["committee membership", "membership on the major board committees", "major committees", "key committees", "important committees"]
definition: Membership on the four board committees that are commonly found in organizations and are frequently cited as having the greatest influence on corporate activities: the audit, nominating, compensation, and executive committees.

name: Underpricing
definition: Underpricing refers to the percentage change in stock price on the first day a stock trades on a public exchange. The level of underpricing is considered important information about a newly public firm because it is the first opportunity for the market to 'price' the firm, and it reflects the difference between where a highly informed agent - the underwriter - and the market set the price for the firm's stock.

name: Status
definition: 'Status, for organizations as well as individuals, is broadly understood as the position in a social hierarchy that results from accumulated acts of deference.' The sociocognitive content of status is grounded in observers' perceptions that a firm is favored by other high-status actors based on its observable patterns of affiliation.

name: Celebrity
definition: Rindova and colleagues (2006) defined celebrity as commanding high levels of public attention and positive emotional responses from stakeholder audiences. Prior empirical research on firm celebrity has operationalized the construct as a combination of high levels of public attention and positive emotional responses from stakeholders.

name: Strategic alliance formations
definition: A strategic alliance is 'any voluntarily initiated cooperative agreement between firms that involves exchange, sharing or co-development, and can include contributions by partners of capital, technology, or firm-specific assets'. Strategic alliances provide key resources that newly public firms need to continue growing.

name: Not-sold-here tendencies
authors_terms: ["not-sold-here (NSH) tendencies", "NSH attitudes", "protective attitudes toward external knowledge exploitation"]
definition: Analogous to NIH (Katz and Allen 1982), we define NSH tendencies as protective attitudes toward external knowledge exploitation. In contrast to NIH, NSH involves a positive attitude toward the knowledge that could be transferred; the firm's knowledge is considered valuable, and this leads to protective attitudes regarding outward knowledge transfer.

name: Prior experience in external knowledge commercialization
authors_terms: ["prior experience", "experience in external knowledge exploitation", "time of actively commercializing knowledge externally"]
definition: A firm's prior experience in externally leveraging knowledge, measured as the time (in years) that the companies have actively commercialized knowledge assets; the focus is on active commercialization because some firms had to externally leverage knowledge in the past without actively addressing this issue.

name: Product diversification
definition: The degree of product diversification, which reflects a firm's complementary assets in different application areas; it reflects a firm's possibilities of internally applying knowledge in its product business by leveraging its complementary assets.

name: Transaction frequency in knowledge markets
definition: Transaction frequency captures to what degree knowledge transactions are common in a firm's knowledge areas and whether knowledge markets have already existed for a long time; the four-item construct also describes to what degree the pricing mechanisms for knowledge resemble ideal market conditions.

name: Competitive activity in knowledge markets
definition: Competitive activity in knowledge markets refers to the number of potential knowledge suppliers, and it may affect the ease of accessing the knowledge markets. The items capture the external knowledge exploitation activities of a firm's competitors and the need for convincing potential knowledge recipients of the superiority of the firm's knowledge.

name: Extent of external knowledge exploitation
authors_terms: ["external knowledge exploitation", "extent of external knowledge commercialization", "outward knowledge transfer"]
definition: External knowledge exploitation refers to the commercialization of knowledge assets, for example, by means of technology licensing. To capture the extent of external knowledge exploitation, the authors used a firm's revenues in this area and its activity relative to competitors as dependent variables.

name: Inbound mobility
authors_terms: ["inbound mobility", "scientists' inbound mobility", "inbound scientists' mobility", "external recruiting", "scientific recruitment"]
definition: We view inbound mobility as a social phenomenon that likely shapes the local social dynamics in the hiring organization and affects the research performance of incumbent scientists. The main independent variable is inbound mobility, measured as the sum (for all new hires) of the average impact factor of the journals in which new hires have published within five years prior to joining the focal department.

name: Incumbent scientists' research performance
authors_terms: ["incumbents' research performance", "research performance of incumbent scientists", "incumbents' research output"]
definition: The dependent variable is incumbents' research performance; we are interested in variations in a department's research output in response to inbound mobility, after excluding the direct contributions of the new hires.

name: Organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure", "shorter (cf. longer) organizational tenure", "longer organizational tenure"]
definition: Organizational tenure-that is, how long the faculty members have been employed by the focal department-is a central factor to consider when explaining the response of incumbent scientists to the arrival of new colleagues.

name: Research expertise diversity
authors_terms: ["department's research expertise diversity", "research expertise diversity", "diversity of a department's research expertise"]
definition: We contend that when academic departments pursue research endeavors in diverse knowledge domains, the susceptibility of incumbent scientists to peer effects induced by the new hires is likely to be lower, at least at the margin. To measure a department's research expertise diversity, we used one minus the Herfindahl index, a standard approach that gives a sense of how focused or diversified the focal department is.

name: Internal collaborative environment
authors_terms: ["internal collaborative environment", "internal collaborations", "internal cooperation", "inclined to collaborate internally"]
definition: With our internal collaborative environment variable, we seek to gauge the ties among department members that facilitate internal knowledge flows. We expect academic departments, in which faculty members tend to collaborate internally, to assimilate and capitalize better on new recruits' knowledge and benefit more from learning by hiring.

name: Managerial entrenchment
authors_terms: ["managerial entrenchment", "entrenchment", "antitakeover provisions (ATPs)", "takeover protection", "takeover defenses", "preponderance of ATPs"]
definition: Entrenchment exists when managers are insulated from the disciplinary market for corporate control, here through a preponderance of antitakeover provisions; takeover protection removes the risk that opportunistic takeovers deter managers from making long-term investments.

name: Hard-to-value firm
definition: Hard-to-value firms have investments that are difficult to value and strategies that can be difficult to quantify, because their investments can be long term, rely on intellectual capital, and/or depend on key personnel.

name: Market reaction to acquisitions
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "short-run market returns", "the market reacts more positively", "shareholder wealth"]
definition: The market's reaction to the acquisition announcement, measured as the cumulative abnormal returns accruing to the bidder around the announcement.

name: Long-term firm value
authors_terms: ["long-term acquirer valuations", "long-run firm value", "post-takeover valuations", "industry-adjusted Tobin's Q"]
definition: The acquirer's value after the takeover, measured as the industry-adjusted Tobin's Q estimated j years after the announcement; the industry-adjusted Tobin's Q is the firm's Tobin's Q less the average Tobin's Q for all firms in its SIC 4-digit industry and year.

name: Value-creating innovation
authors_terms: ["value-creating innovation", "innovation that creates value", "value-creating innovation in acquisitions"]
definition: A takeover that both creates value (the CAR is positive) and is innovative, that is, an increase in the acquirer's R&D and/or the acquisition of a high-tech target.

name: Takeover premium
definition: The premium paid to acquire the target, the transaction value divided by the target's share price before the acquisition; because premiums are unobserved in acquisitions of unlisted targets and can be endogenous with CARs, the models use a Proxy Premium defined as the average takeover premium paid for companies in the target's industry in the year of the acquisition.

name: Emerging technology capabilities
authors_terms: ["Capabilities in the emerging technology", "capabilities in the new technology", "technological capabilities in the emerging technology"]
definition: Core capabilities are the set of routines involving physical assets, knowledge, and competencies that are intrinsic to the engineering and manufacturing of a product—for example, technological skills. In a biotechnological search, therapeutic proteins are synthesized through the manipulation of the genetic structure of cells, building on a distinct set of capabilities in molecular biology and biochemistry.

name: Traditional technology capabilities
authors_terms: ["Capabilities in the traditional technology", "core capabilities in the traditional technology", "technological capabilities in the traditional technology"]
definition: Core capabilities are the set of routines involving physical assets, knowledge, and competencies that are intrinsic to the engineering and manufacturing of a product—for example, technological skills. The traditional process required the synthesis and the test of several hundred organic compounds, which involved strong capabilities in organic chemistry.

name: Complementary capabilities
definition: Complementary resources and capabilities are those required to profit from core knowledge, and thus comprise the set of routines involving physical assets, knowledge, and competencies that contribute to the production of or enhance the commercial utility of a product. In this paper, we focus on those complementary capabilities that allow the firm to combine and integrate its core capabilities to develop new potentially viable products.

name: Entry into emerging technological fields
authors_terms: ["likelihood of entry", "entry into new fields of the emerging technology", "entry into emerging technological fields"]
definition: The analysis involves the likelihood of entry: the firm's decision to enter into an emerging technological field, which are related to firms' existing capabilities. A firm is recognized as entering the emerging technological field through either alliance or internal development.

name: Entry mode
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "entry mode", "choice of entry mode"]
definition: Firms can enter an emerging technological field through internal development or by forming relationships with other organizations. External relationships included equity-based associations, such as joint ventures and direct investment, and nonequity associations, such as technology licensing, technology exchanges, testing agreements, and research contracts.

name: Educational diversity in top management teams
authors_terms: ["Diversity_TMT_Education", "educational diversity in TMTs", "TMT diversity", "TMTs' educational diversity"]
definition: The diversity of educational backgrounds measured by subject among the members of the top management team, i.e., the variety of educational fields represented on the team. Diversity of educational backgrounds is strongly associated with the variety of the knowledge pool, as well as creative thinking and innovation.

name: Educational diversity in middle management teams
authors_terms: ["Diversity_MMT_Education", "educational diversity in MMTs", "MMT diversity", "MMTs' educational diversity"]
definition: The diversity of educational backgrounds measured by subject among the members of the middle management team, constructed analogously to the TMT measure. Diversity in educational backgrounds ensures that MMTs have access to a broader set of skills.

name: Innovation engagement
authors_terms: ["Innovation engagement", "the decision to innovate", "the decision to engage in innovation activities"]
definition: The strategic choice of a firm to engage in innovation activities at all, captured through a wide range of investment inputs into the innovation process rather than R&D only. This variable reflects the strategic choice to engage in innovation.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["Product innovation", "the firm's likelihood of introducing new products", "innovation outcome"]
definition: A product innovation, in line with the Oslo Manual guidelines, is defined as the successful market introduction of a new or significantly improved service or good with respect to its capabilities, user friendliness, components, or subsystems. It is a direct measure of innovation output.

name: Market novelty of product innovation
definition: The degree of novelty of introduced product innovations. A new-to-firm innovation refers to a purely imitational product innovation, while a new-to-market innovation is an innovation for which there was no comparable previous solution available on the market; the latter therefore has a higher degree of novelty.

name: Vision content
authors_terms: ["vision content", "content of strategic visions", "vision self-evaluations", "elements of the visions executives articulate"]
definition: The elements of the visions executives articulate. The present study focused on vision content, or the elements of the visions executives articulate, and the relationships between a vision's content and its organizational and individual context.

name: Vision horizon
definition: How far into the future an executive's vision for his or her firm extends; executives were asked how far into the future their visions for their firms extended.

name: Perceived change in the firm
authors_terms: ["perceived change in a firm", "speed of change within their firms", "rapidity of change in the firm"]
definition: The executive's perception of how rapidly changes are occurring in his or her firm, obtained with the question "How rapidly are changes occurring in your firm?"

name: Perceived change in the industry
authors_terms: ["perceived change in an industry", "speed of change within their industries", "external change"]
definition: The executive's perception of how rapidly changes are occurring in the industry, obtained with the question "How rapidly are changes occurring in the industry?"

name: Executive tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure in a present position and firm", "tenure in their position", "tenure in the firm"]
definition: How long an executive has been in his or her present position and how long he or she has been in the firm; long tenure is associated with resistance to change and a narrowing of perspective.

name: Perceived control
authors_terms: ["amount of control", "perceptions of their control", "how much control they exercised in their organizations"]
definition: How much control the executive exercises in his or her organization, as reported by the executive.

name: Desire for control
authors_terms: ["need for control", "desire for increased control", "how much control they would like to exercise"]
definition: How much control the executive would like to exercise in his or her organization.

name: Firm partisan positioning
authors_terms: ["partisan positioning", "firm-level partisanship index", "partisanship index", "firm partisanship", "partisan position"]
definition: A signal of the degree (from 100% Democratic to 100% Republican) to which a firm is aligned with a specific political party in the social and political spaces in which it operates, established by the partisan balance of the firm's corporate PAC contributions.

name: COVID-19 risk disclosure
authors_terms: ["disclosed COVID-19-related risk", "COVID-19 risk disclosure", "disclosed COVID-19 risk", "voluntary disclosure of COVID-19-related risks"]
definition: The firm's voluntary disclosure of COVID-19-related risks in its earnings call, measured as the count of COVID-19 synonyms occurring in conjunction with a risk synonym (within 10 words), multiplied by 1,000 and divided by the total document length.

name: Executive pay disparity
definition: The size of the observed differences between chief executive officer (CEO) incomes and those of other executives in the top management team (TMT).

name: Firm performance
definition: Return on assets is a common measure of organizational profitability that reflects operational performance, capturing whether management has effectively deployed firm assets and being independent of market preferences or equity-based efficiency considerations.

name: Heir apparent
definition: The selection of an heir apparent is the most common form of succession planning in corporate America, generally referred to as a 'relay succession' in which the heir apparent is selected by the organization well in advance of a succession event and the subsequent time period is utilized to 'groom' the heir apparent for the top job.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "power differential between the CEO and the CEO's top team"]
definition: The power differential between the CEO and the CEO's top team, visible to TMT members in the form of different ownership positions, titles within the organization, or pay differentials between the CEO and the members of the CEO's top team.

name: TMT member eligibility
definition: The similarity in relevant characteristics between the CEO and the CEO's top team; TMT eligibility reflects the comparison between the aggregated individual level characteristics at the team level and the same characteristics of the CEO.

name: Product reliability
definition: The definition of quality used in this study is a product's reliability, measured by frequency-of-repair rates. In two separate sets of analyses the repair record of a car model is measured at two different milestones: during the third year of ownership and during the sixth year of ownership.

name: Cumulative production experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative production output", "cumulative production experience", "cumulative output", "production experience"]
definition: x is that car model's cumulative output up through the previous year, i.e., the experience accumulated as more cars of a given model go down the assembly line. Cumulative experience (based on production volume) is the traditional driver of learning curves.

name: Time in production
authors_terms: ["year of production", "passage of time", "number of years since a car model began its production life", "years in production"]
definition: The passage of time is captured by year of production: dummy variables are used for each year that a car model has been in production, up through the 13th year, i.e., the number of years since a car model began its production life.

name: Platform production experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative production output of its platform", "vehicle platform", "sibling output", "cousin output"]
definition: In the automobile industry, the opportunity to share similar information and technology could potentially occur among car models within the same product 'family,' called a vehicle platform; each car model has been designated as belonging to a narrowly defined car platform, containing several 'sibling' models, and to a broadly defined platform, containing several sets of siblings ('cousins').

name: Division production experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative production output of its division", "division output"]
definition: It is easier to transfer knowledge across groups or organizations if they have a shared culture, so among car models in the same division or company we might expect to see some knowledge transfer.

name: Company production experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative production output of its company", "firm output"]
definition: Among car models in the same division or company, we might expect to see some knowledge transfer, since it is easier to transfer knowledge across groups or organizations if they have a shared culture; among U.S. automakers too there is a shared 'Detroit' culture of sorts.

name: Industry production experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative production output of its industry", "Big Three output", "industrywide production"]
definition: Industrywide production is defined in this study as all United States and Canadian output produced by the Big Three.

name: Timing of new product introduction
authors_terms: ["debut year", "a car model debuts", "all-new car model introduction", "major overhaul"]
definition: The debut of a new model provides a window of opportunity for manufacturers to incorporate the very latest knowledge on design, materials, assembly, etc., because the usual constraints (e.g., the large costs in changing any production line technologies) are temporarily lifted when a new product line debuts. The unit of analysis is the car model produced over the four- to thirteen-year period following a major overhaul, and the determination of a major redesign or introduction was done by coding the descriptions in Ward's Automotive Yearbook.

name: Intra-regional diversification
definition: INTRA captures geographic diversification across countries within a region, based on the foreign firm's presence within a region measured with both sales and subsidiary diversification. The regional classification draws boundaries according to four regions: Africa; Asia and Pacific; Europe; and the Americas.

name: Inter-regional diversification
definition: INTER captures diversification across different regions, where the measure is based on the foreign firm's presence within a region captured with both sales and subsidiary diversification measures. Here, m is the number of regions in which a firm derives sales or has subsidiaries, and P i is the proportion of the i th region to a firm's total sales or total number of subsidiaries in all regions.

name: Total geographic diversification
definition: Total geographic diversification (TOTAL) consists of intra-regional (INTRA) and inter-regional (INTER) dimensions, that is, TOTAL = INTRA + INTER, and refers to the combined intra- and inter-regional geographic diversification of the firm.

name: MNE performance
definition: The multinational enterprise's corporate-level performance, measured by return on assets (ROA), following previous literature on geographic diversification (Hitt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 1988).

name: IPO underpricing
definition: The discount at which IPO shares are sold relative to their subsequent market price; the authors observe that IPOs are 'routinely underpriced (sold at a discount) at their initial offering' and describe a successful offering as one with 'minimal or nonexistent underpricing'.

name: Board knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["board knowledge breadth", "knowledge breadth", "breadth of general knowledge", "general knowledge", "board experience"]
definition: "the board's breadth of knowledge refers to the extent to which its collective set of experiences and expertise spans multiple domains (i.e., general business knowledge)".

name: Board knowledge depth
authors_terms: ["board knowledge depth", "knowledge depth", "depth of technical knowledge", "board technical expertise"]
definition: "the depth of knowledge refers to the extent to which the board possesses highly sophisticated and specialized expertise regarding the technical aspects of the IPO process".

name: External knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["external knowledge breadth", "external knowledge", "general knowledge available in the environment", "educational attainment"]
definition: The extent of general knowledge available in the environment in which the IPO firm operates, which the authors describe as relatively extensive available information on the overall economy that boards can draw on.

name: External knowledge depth
authors_terms: ["external knowledge depth", "external knowledge", "IPO-specific knowledge available in the environment", "IPO activity"]
definition: The extent of specialized, IPO-related knowledge available in the environment in which the firm operates, such as information on the legal, accounting, and financial aspects associated with IPOs.

name: Shareholderism
authors_terms: ["shareholderism", "shareholderism index", "support for shareholder wealth maximization", "shareholderist stance", "shareholder orientation"]
definition: The authors propose that directors may harbor a general stance on the primacy of shareholders and term this stance 'shareholderism' to denote its ideology-like nature; shareholderism is a motivated, principled approach that generally considers it a desirable strategy to enhance shareholder value.

name: Personal values
definition: Personal values are abstract desirable goals that serve as guiding principles in peoples' lives; unlike specific goals or attitudes they transcend specific situations and they are ordered by their subjective importance, forming a hierarchy of value priorities.

name: Power values
definition: Power values reflect appreciation for wealth attainment and control; power, in the sense of control over people and resources, is also reflected in the view of stakeholder value as subordinate to and instrumental for the enhancement of shareholder value.

name: Achievement values
definition: Achievement values reflect appreciation for success in competitive settings through hard work, self-challenge, and persistence.

name: Universalism values
definition: A broad other-regarding concern for multiple stakeholders is especially reflected in universalism as the motivation to understand, accept, and care for other people (whether familiar or not), humanity, and the environment.

name: Benevolence values
definition: Benevolence reflects the motivation to help others in one's ingroup; in the corporation, these could be the employees.

name: Self-direction values
definition: Self-direction is one of the openness-to-change values in Schwartz's model; the authors argue that shareholder-oriented strategies will be associated with openness-to-change values, that is, self-direction and stimulation.

name: Stimulation values
definition: Stimulation is the second openness-to-change value in Schwartz's model; the theory implies that an emphasis on self-direction and stimulation on the openness-to-change pole will be associated with shareholders' interest.

name: Employee representative role
authors_terms: ["employee representative", "employee representative directors", "employee representatives", "board position", "role on the board"]
definition: Employees, through their trade unions, have the right to appoint directors under Swedish law; employee representatives are not responsible for handling the affairs of the firm's employees and owe the same legal duties, as do regular directors, to the company as a whole.

name: Exploration alliances
definition: Alliances entered into with the motivation to discover something new, focusing on the 'R' in the research and development process and on the upstream activities of the value chain (basic research, drug discovery and development).

name: Products in development
definition: A count of each firm's biotechnology products in development that have successfully entered clinical trials but have not yet reached the market for pharmaceuticals.

name: Exploitation alliances
definition: Alliances that focus on the 'D' in the research and development process and are entered into with the goal to join existing competencies across organizational boundaries in order to generate synergies, which are then shared across the partners.

name: Products on the market
definition: A count of each firm's biotechnology products that successfully completed all stages of the product development process and are now commercialized.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size measured by the number of employees as a proxy, since most biotechnology firms do not have a positive revenue stream at this point.

name: CEO star status
authors_terms: ["CEO star status", "star status of a CEO", "CEO status", "CEO celebrity", "medal-winning CEO", "star CEO"]
definition: Status can be considered 'an actor's position in a hierarchical order' (Podolny 2005, p. 13). We use the results from Financial World's widely publicized CEO of the Year contest to measure the status of CEOs in our sample.

name: CEO-top management pay gap
authors_terms: ["CEO-top management pay gap", "difference in compensation between the CEO and other members of the top management team", "pay gap"]
definition: We computed the gap between CEO and non-CEO pay in a firm by logging the difference between the CEO's TDC1 compensation and the average TDC1 of the four other executives listed for the same firm in EXECUCOMP.

name: Top management team member compensation
authors_terms: ["average compensation of other members of the top management team", "average top management team member pay", "average top manager TDC1"]
definition: For our primary measure of top management team compensation, we logged the average TDC1 amounts of the four other executives listed for a focal firm.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["subsequent firm performance", "firm performance", "firm accounting and stock performance"]
definition: We used both an accounting and a market return measure to assess firm performance for each year from 1992 through 1996. Both variables represent important metrics that are commonly used to assess the quality of the contribution of the CEO and the top management team.

name: Promotion to CEO
authors_terms: ["promoted to CEO", "executive promotion to CEO", "likelihood of being promoted to CEO themselves"]
definition: We constructed a dummy variable that took the value of '1' when a non-CEO member of a top management team was promoted to CEO of either his or her current firm or another firm within five years after his or her last appearance as a top management team member in our sample.

name: State certainty
authors_terms: ["state certainty", "state uncertainty", "certainty about the occurrence of a change"]
definition: State uncertainty occurs when managers do not feel confident that they understand what the major events or trends in an environment are or feel unable to accurately assign probabilities to the likelihood that particular events or changes will occur.

name: Effect certainty
authors_terms: ["effect certainty", "effect uncertainty", "seeing a change as a threat", "significant strategic issue"]
definition: Effect uncertainty exists when managers are unsure about what effect an environmental event or change will have on their organization and thus are uncertain about whether a change poses a significant threat or opportunity for the organization. In this research, effect certainty was high for a change to be classified as a threat or opportunity, and the effect certainty score was treated as a surrogate for the degree to which administrators saw the trend as a potential strategic issue for their institution.

name: Response certainty
authors_terms: ["response certainty", "response uncertainty", "confidence in the ability to respond effectively"]
definition: A high degree of response uncertainty indicates that a decision maker is not confident about how to respond to some environmental change, because he or she is either not sure what the response options are or is unsure about the likely effectiveness of each possible strategy for achieving desired organizational outcomes.

name: Resource dependence
authors_terms: ["resource dependence characteristics", "resource dependence", "dependence on undergraduate programs", "selectivity"]
definition: I defined resource dependence characteristics as factors that made a college or university more or less dependent than its competitors on the pool of 18-22-year-old recent high school graduates or that made it more or less powerful than its competitors in securing resources from this pool.

name: Perceived organizational effectiveness
definition: Managers' perceptions of an organization's past or current effectiveness, assessed with items asking respondents to estimate attributes of their college's academic effectiveness.

name: Perceived sense of organizational identity
authors_terms: ["sense of organizational identity", "sense of institutional identity", "perceived institutional uniqueness", "sense of uniqueness"]
definition: Martin, Feldman, Hatch, and Sitkin (1983) suggested that an important component of organizational culture may be the strength of an organization's identity, or the degree to which its members perceive it to be unique or special. These perceptions may or may not reflect reality, but they will influence organizational members' attitudes and behavior in either case.

name: Perceived decentralization
authors_terms: ["perceived extent of decentralization", "decentralization", "participation in strategic decision making", "participatory strategic planning process"]
definition: Decentralization of strategic decision-making responsibilities allows managers to be exposed to the opinions of others who may be more active boundary spanners than themselves, and was measured as the degree to which an institution's structure supported administrative participation in key decisions.

name: Regional demographic decline
authors_terms: ["region", "regions of low decline", "regional differences in birthrates"]
definition: Because the national estimate of the decline in the number of 18-22-year-olds is based on averaging data on birthrates across states and there are large regional differences in birthrates, the location of a college should affect administrators' interpretations of the national estimate; some regions were expected to be hit hard while others, such as the Southwest, would benefit from migration.

name: Legal liability threat from employee exposure to hazardous materials
authors_terms: ["threat of legal liability", "potential liability", "legal liability stemming from employee on-the-job exposure to hazardous materials"]
definition: The threat that a firm will be held financially liable because employees were exposed to hazardous materials on the job and that exposure is traced to disease, disability, or death. We assumed that the greater the percentage of employees in an industry exposed to hazardous materials while on the job, the greater the threat of legal liability to firms in that industry.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["vertical integration", "level of vertical integration", "vertically integrated production"]
definition: The portion of a firm's business revenues generated by activities conducted within the boundaries of the firm; a firm with a high value-added-to-sales ratio has brought many value-creating activities inside its boundaries, consistent with a high level of vertical integration.

name: Past vertical integration
definition: The past level of a firm's vertical integration, which reflects management's views on what level is appropriate on the basis of transaction costs, resource dependence, and strategic considerations.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: The level of technological uncertainty facing a firm, which Walker and Weber (1984) argued is positively associated with vertical integration because administrative costs of managing interfaces with outside suppliers may become higher than the costs of coordinating internal engineering and production.

name: Industry concentration
authors_terms: ["market concentration", "industry concentration", "level of concentration of a firm's industry"]
definition: The concentration of a firm's market, which Harrigan (1984, 1985) argued will be positively associated with vertical integration because competition is less volatile in highly concentrated markets.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: The level of uncertainty in the demand for a firm's products; high uncertainty gives firms an incentive to maintain flexibility and thus to avoid vertical integration, though Walker and Weber (1984) argued the opposite.

name: Small firm production
authors_terms: ["small firm production", "percentage change in the number of small firms"]
definition: Change in the number of small firms producing in an industry, where small firms are those with assets of less than $100,000; small firms have incentives to enter hazardous production because limited liability rules protect their owners' personal wealth.

name: Industry growth
definition: Growth of an industry; it is often less costly for firms to acquire customers in fast-growing industries, and small firms may be attracted because growth creates new product or geographic niches.

name: Relative energy costs of small and large firms
definition: Energy costs as a significant portion of the cost of doing business; if large firms employ more energy-intensive technology than small firms, small firms enjoy an energy cost advantage.

name: Syndication
definition: Syndication is the joint investment of two or more VC firms in a portfolio company that involves significant financial contributions and managerial oversight and guidance. In the analysis the outcome is an indicator equal to 1 if the two firms in the dyad jointly invested in their first round via a syndicate during the focal year.

name: Direct withdrawal from shared syndicates
authors_terms: ["direct withdrawal", "Direct Withdrawal Rate", "withdrawal from syndicates with the focal VC"]
definition: A withdrawal is the permanent disappearance of a VC firm from the ranks of coinvestors in a syndicate. The direct withdrawal rate captures how often a firm withdrew from syndicates in which the other firm in the dyad continued participating.

name: Overall withdrawal rate
authors_terms: ["overall withdrawal rate", "overall history of withdrawals", "track record of withdrawals", "proportion of past withdrawals"]
definition: The alter's overall history of withdrawals, computed as the firm's total number of withdrawals over the preceding five years divided by the total number of unique syndicates in which it had participated. A history of repeated withdrawals can create a global signal of unreliability that can affect all prospective syndication partners.

name: Social overlap with abandoned coinvestors
authors_terms: ["social overlap to abandoned", "connections to abandoned syndication partners of the alter", "ties to the abandoned coinvestors of the alter"]
definition: The firm's social overlap with the coinvestors that the alter has previously abandoned, that is, its connections to the syndication partners that the prospective alter withdrew from. Such connections are the conduit through which negative private information about the alter is presumed to spread.

name: Social overlap with non-abandoned coinvestors
authors_terms: ["social overlap to non-abandoned", "connections to non-abandoned coinvestors of the alter"]
definition: The firm's social overlap with the alter's prior coinvestors that the alter has not abandoned, which previous research expects to be a conduit for positive private information.

name: Product proliferation
definition: Product proliferation is the strategy whereby a firm extends its product offer in a market or submarket so as to saturate the product space and minimize unmet demand.

name: Product space complexity
definition: We define the complexity of a product (sub)space as a function of heterogeneity and interdependence in the attributes of products offered in this (sub)space. We adopt the authors' approach to measuring complexity by way of heterogeneity, while interdependence is held constant throughout the study period.

name: Imitative product introduction
definition: Our dependent variable is the number of singles released by a major in a given style-year (OwnSingles). The authors interpret a major's releases in a subspace where a rival has proliferated as imitation of the rival's products, describing product proliferation as triggering a reaction whose direction depends on subspace complexity.

name: Buy-out size
authors_terms: ["larger buy-outs", "smaller buy-outs", "transaction value", "size of the buy-out"]
definition: Buy-outs are differentiated by the value of the transaction, a large-small split being made at transaction values above and below the median value for each year; the authors also note that size exerts a considerable effect on the financial and governance structures of buy-outs.

name: Management equity ownership
authors_terms: ["managerial equity stake", "management equity stakes", "management have majority equity ownership", "managerial equity holding"]
definition: Buy-outs involve significant direct equity ownership by managers, stock options and, in the U.K. at least, 'equity ratchets' by which the management team's proportion of voting equity may be increased conditional upon medium term performance targets. Especially in smaller buy-outs, management have majority or even supermajority equity stakes.

name: Buy-out longevity
authors_terms: ["longevity of the buy-out", "exit", "early exit", "exit timing", "how long buy-outs last"]
definition: How long the buy-out form lasts; the authors count as an exit flotation, sale to a third party or secondary buy-out/buy-in.
