There is no reason why the buy-out arrangement should be permanent, and buy-outs may come up against new constraints and require to exit to continue to survive or develop.

name: Employee share ownership
definition: Employees owning shares in the company where they work are likely to have an undiversified portfolio of assets, producing a medium to long-term desire on the part of management and employees to sell some or all of their shares and reinvest the proceeds in a more diversified portfolio.

name: Internal share market liquidity
definition: With a workforce which is relatively stable in size and with little staff turnover, the internal share market of an employee buy-out may soon run out of sufficient liquidity to operate effectively.

name: Capital expenditure needs
authors_terms: ["significant sums for capital expenditure", "capital commitment", "investment needs", "need for extra finance"]
definition: Whether buy-outs require significant sums for capital expenditure programs beyond the levels initially envisaged in the buy-out, and the extent to which finance servicing costs and investment needs can be met from internal generation of funds.

name: Environmental dynamism
authors_terms: ["significant structural changes in the market", "rapidly changing markets", "rapid restructuring and merger activity", "environmental dynamism"]
definition: Life-cycle theories suggest that the most important company-related characteristics likely to influence the longevity of a given organizational form concern rapidly changing markets, a fast growing company, concentrating markets where it is necessary to have sufficiently large critical mass to survive, and relatively high levels of merger activity.

name: Pre-buy-out constraints
authors_terms: ["pre-buy-out constraints on development", "constraints imposed by the former parent", "access to investment funds and ability to exploit new markets"]
definition: Divestment buy-outs or those arising on privatization from the public sector may have experienced severe pre-buy-out constraints on investment policies, new product development, internal control mechanisms, etc. frequently imposed by private sector parents.

name: Catching-up difficulties
authors_terms: ["catching-up", "problems in catching-up in rapidly changing markets", "difficulties in catching-up"]
definition: Where a division has been constrained and has lost ground in a rapidly growing market it may be difficult to catch-up, indicating that exit to become part of a larger group is warranted.

name: EMNE acquirer
definition: We classify target and acquirer companies as DMNEs if they come from developed countries, and EMNEs if they come from 'Emerging Market and Developing Economies' according to the IMF's classification. The country effect is the baseline constraint that all EMNE acquirers face because of where they are from.

name: Target TMT retention
authors_terms: ["TMT Retention Rate", "target TMT retention rate", "retention of the target's top management team (TMT)"]
definition: High target TMT retention rate has been identified as a key characteristic of light-touch integration. Our dependent variable is the TMT Retention Rate in the target firm, measured as the ratio of the retained target TMT 2 years after the transaction to the pretransaction TMT.

name: Cohort cross-border acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["cohort experience", "cohort or peer group", "vicarious learning", "Cohort L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience"]
definition: We define a firm's cohort or peer group as other MNEs from the same home region expanding abroad around the same time. We classify acquiring firms as part of the ultimate acquirer's cohort if they are located within 150 km of its headquarters city.

name: Firm cross-border acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["firm experience", "experiential learning", "Firm L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience"]
definition: As EMNE acquirers continue to do cross-border acquisitions, they can gain new knowledge about the local market and knowledge about managing cross-border acquisitions and integrations in general.

name: Ethnic community size
definition: The size of the Korean ethnic community in a location, captured by the count of Chaoxian - those that moved to China pre-1949 and their descendants - by province and year. Ceteris paribus, the larger the size of an ethnic community in a location, the greater the likelihood that a bank from a country of the same ethnic origin will invest in that location.

name: Foreign location choice
definition: A bank's choice of a foreign province in which to invest, estimated as the conditional probability that a province is chosen from among a set of alternative locations. The dependent variable is coded as 1 if a Korean bank made an investment in a province in a year, and 0 otherwise.

name: Property rights law strength
definition: The quality of property rights laws, one of the most common indicators of institutional strength, which captures the quality of rules as well as the ability of the government to enforce them. In emerging markets such as China, the strength of such laws differs considerably across provinces.

name: Macroeconomic uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty about economic prospects, which makes forecasting opportunities and risks difficult and calls into question the effectiveness of existing formal institutions. The authors propose two sources of uncertainty relevant to foreign banks in China: macroeconomic instability and lending uncertainty.

name: Lending uncertainty
definition: An industry-specific source of institutional instability: uncertainty about the hazards involved in the basic steps of the lending process - customer screening, loan collections, and dispute resolution - reflected in the variability of interest rates on loans in a location.

name: Challenger imitation
definition: The second strategy takes the leader's challenger, that is, the second-placed rival, as the target for imitation. In this case, the leader takes the challenger's prior period configuration as a reference point in a distant search process.

name: Neighbor imitation
authors_terms: ["neighbor imitation", "neighbor imitation strategy", "imitating the rival that is closest to her on the landscape"]
definition: The leader imitates the rival that is closest to her on the landscape (i.e., her neighbor), the rival that is most similar to the leader in terms of their configuration. The prior period configuration of this rival is then taken as the leader's reference point for a distant search process.

name: Change in performance gap
authors_terms: ["change in performance gap", "performance gap erosion", "strategic risk"]
definition: Our dependent variable captures the change in performance gap of the leader over her rivals over the upwind leg, which is the minimum difference between the performance gap of the leader at the start of the upwind leg and her performance gap at the leg's end, relative to competitors who were second, third, and fourth at the start of the upwind.

name: Magnitude of environmental change
authors_terms: ["magnitude of environmental changes", "magnitude of wind shifts", "magnitude"]
definition: To measure the magnitude of environmental changes we take the average extent (in degrees) of wind shifts over the course of the upwind. The weight w used in the simulation reflects the magnitude of environmental changes.

name: Frequency of environmental change
authors_terms: ["frequency of environmental changes", "frequency of wind shifts", "frequency"]
definition: We use detailed data on wind direction during the upwind to calculate the frequency of environmental changes as the number of wind shifts over the upwind normalized by the upwind's duration. The frequency f of changes corresponds to the length of intervals between periods in which the landscape is altered.

name: Extent of imitation
definition: To capture the extent to which the leader imitates lower-ranked rivals, we include an extent of imitation variable that takes on the maximum value of the leader's imitation of her rivals, corresponding to the extent to which the leader imitated the rival who was the focus of her imitation efforts during the upwind.

name: Electronic integration
definition: A specific form of vertical quasi-integration achieved through the deployment of dedicated information systems between relevant actors in adjacent stages of the value-chain; the authors conceptualize the degree of electronic integration as the level of an independent agency's dedication to an insurance carrier whose proprietary IOS serves as the primary infrastructure for the conduct of the business.

name: Business process asset specificity
definition: The extent of customization of the agency's business processes relative to the interfaced insurance carrier; business process asset specificity incorporates notions of human and procedural asset specificities, covering the skills, knowledge and experience of the agency's personnel that are specific to the IOS-mediated business process and the degree to which the agency's workflows and processes are customized to exploit IOS capabilities in accordance with the principal's requirements.

name: Trust
definition: Trust is defined as "the extent to which negotiations are fair and commitments are upheld" between the parties in a relationship; it can be viewed as the obverse of opportunism, since it reflects one party's belief that its requirements will be fulfilled through future actions undertaken by the other party.

name: Reciprocal investment
definition: The extent to which the principal invests resources in the relationship with the agency; within electronically-interfaced relationships these refer to investments in systems as well as in providing customized training and the underlying hardware, software and communication support to use the interfacing system.

name: CEO origin
authors_terms: ["CEO origin", "CEO origin as an outsider", "outsider CEO"]
definition: CEO origin refers to whether an incumbent CEO was an employee of the firm he or she leads at the time of appointment as CEO.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "early years of tenure", "early CEO tenure"]
definition: The early years of a CEO's tenure, the period in which new CEOs must establish their authority in the top position and are at a higher risk of power contests with senior executives.

name: Non-CEO inside directors
authors_terms: ["non-CEO inside directors", "proportion of non-CEO inside directors"]
definition: Inside directors are directors who are also executives of the firm on whose board they serve; non-CEO inside directors are those inside directors other than the CEO.

name: Non-CEO executive ownership
authors_terms: ["non-CEO executive ownership", "stock ownership by senior executives"]
definition: Stock ownership by senior executives is an important source of power that increases the incentives senior executives have to challenge their CEO and the credibility of their concerns about the CEO's leadership.

name: CEO dismissal followed by inside succession
authors_terms: ["CEO dismissal followed by inside succession", "dismissal, insider"]
definition: A subset of inside CEO successions resulting from power contests within top management groups in which the CEOs are dismissed and have no influence over successor selection; it is coded 1 when a current executive of a firm became CEO after the predecessor's dismissal and 0 otherwise.

name: R&D unit role
authors_terms: ["R&D unit role", "R&D unit type", "typology of R&D units", "local adaptor", "international adaptor", "international creator"]
definition: Prior research types foreign R&D units primarily according to the nature of their activity, i.e. whether they are responsible for adapting technology, developing new products, undertaking pure research, etc. Three types are distinguished here: the local adaptor, the international adaptor and the international creator.

name: Centralization
definition: Centralization, in which decision-making power is retained at the headquarters. It is probably the most important aspect of control, in that it indicates the extent to which head office managers actively influence decisions made in the R&D unit.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization, in which decision-making is routinized through rules and procedures.

name: Socialization
definition: Socialization, whereby organization members develop common expectations and shared values that promote likeminded decision-making.

name: Vertical communication with head office
authors_terms: ["vertical communication", "vertical lines of communication with entities in the head office"]
definition: Vertical lines of communication with entities in the head office. These are overlain on, and often part of, the MNC's control mechanisms, but they are conceptually separate in that it is possible to have vertical communication without control and, indeed, control without communication.

name: Lateral communication with other R&D units
authors_terms: ["lateral communication", "lateral lines of communication with other international R&D units"]
definition: Lateral lines of communication with other international R&D units. These are particularly important when there are task interdependencies, for example in international innovation projects, but they are also useful for promoting the flow of new ideas between units.

name: Lateral communication with other functions
authors_terms: ["lateral lines of communication to other functions"]
definition: Lateral lines of communication to other functions, notably manufacturing and marketing, within the same subsidiary. These are most necessary where there are interdependencies, but there is potential for synergistic interaction as well.

name: External communication
authors_terms: ["external communication", "lines of communication to external entities"]
definition: Lines of communication to external entities such as customers, suppliers, and local universities, that comprise the environment in which the MNC is embedded. These lines of communication facilitate the adoption of new ideas by the MNC and responsiveness to local contingencies.

name: Task-specific skills
authors_terms: ["task-specific skills", "task specific skills", "transferable skills", "Characteristic Selectivity", "manager specific (task specific)"]
definition: The skill component captured by Characteristic Selectivity is labeled manager specific (task specific) and transferable across firm boundaries. Task-specific skills are the skills needed to perform well within a task, which are relatively well defined but vary substantially across tasks in the industry and occupation.

name: Firm-specific skills
authors_terms: ["firm-specific skills", "firm specific skills", "nontransferable skills", "Average Style", "Characteristic Timing"]
definition: Performance on Average Style is expected to depend on detailed knowledge of the firm's policies and aims and to largely reflect firm-specific skills, and timing skill is expected to depend on the manager's experience in the firm and thus reflect more firm-specific skills. Firm-specific skills are similar to the notion of cospecialized assets and create a wedge between productivity in the firm and the outside market.

name: Mentoring
definition: Firms frequently rely on peer mentoring as a means of transferring task-specific skills across cohorts in the firm, and experienced employees with task-specific skills are in the best position to provide such mentoring. Mentorship cannot be mandated but must arise as a by-product of regular activity, and its value goes beyond the mentor-mentee relationship, creating a positive externality that accrues mostly to the firm.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risk taking is identified as an act by an existing manager of starting a new solo-managed fund, which is a common but risky activity both for the manager and the firm. Workers with transferable skills may be more willing to take on risky tasks, that is, tasks with a high probability of failure, even when failure can lead to losing one's current employment.

name: Positive spillovers at the firm level
authors_terms: ["spillovers", "demand-side spillovers", "positive spillovers at the firm level"]
definition: The measure of spillovers captures the effects of a manager's skill in managing a focal fund on her ability to draw in new investments to the firm. The authors define spillovers as the cash inflows accruing to all the funds offered by the management company, excluding those managed by the focal manager.

name: State ownership
authors_terms: ["state ownership", "state share", "state capital", "SOE dummy", "minority state ownership"]
definition: State ownership refers to the percentage of ownership stake that the government holds in a firm; SOEs are firms with majority government ownership. Firms may be majority state-owned (an SOE), minority state-owned (a mixed firm), or privately owned without state capital.

name: R&D input
definition: The resources a firm devotes to research and development; state ownership could enable a firm to obtain more resources for innovation (i.e., more R&D input). The authors measure R&D input as R&D expenses divided by a firm's total sales in Study 1 and as firms' cumulative R&D investment in Study 2.

name: Innovation output
definition: The innovation a firm generates: the new product value that a firm can generate in the market indicates the commercial significance of the firm's product innovation, and in Study 2 innovation output is measured with invention patents.

name: Institutional development
definition: Institutional development is the degree to which market fundamentals support economic activities, including the proportion of resources allocated through the market, the percentage of products with market-based prices, and the development of market intermediaries and legal systems.

name: Industrial competition
definition: Industrial competition refers to the extent of competition a firm confronts in its industry; in highly competitive markets, competitive rivalry is intensive and product choices are abundant.

name: Start-up status
definition: Whether an enterprise was established as a new venture within the previous five years; start-ups in general are more innovative, because after routines are formed in established firms, the likelihood of adopting new alternatives decreases.

name: Strategic group membership
definition: The procedure to identify strategic groups is based on the proposition that firms having a similar strategic posture (in terms of the eight key strategic variables), will be clustered in the same strategic group.

name: Firm performance
definition: Three different sets of performance measures were constructed; namely, (a) the combined ratio (COM), a common measure used in the industry to indicate the overall performance level of an insurance company; (b) the firm's share (MS) of industry volume; and (c) weighted market share (WMS) which indicates the firm's dominance of particular lines of insurance.

name: Economic performance
definition: The economic dimension includes measures such as the combined ratio (COM), market share (MS), and weighted market share (WMS).

name: Performance risk
definition: The risk dimension used the standard deviation of each one of the three measures.

name: Risk-adjusted performance
definition: The risk-adjusted measures used the ratio of the economic measures over their relevant risk measures.

name: Personal lines scope
definition: Personal lines of insurance include policies that are sold to individuals while those sold to businesses are called commercial lines. The firm's decision about how to deploy their underwriting efforts between these two insurance types can have an important impact on the firm's strategy.

name: Property-liability product mix
definition: A variable PPROP which measures the extent of activity in the P/L segment relative to P/L and life insurance combined was constructed to describe the product mix aspect of firm strategy.

name: Line-of-business diversification
definition: The diversification variable (DIVER) more particularly examines the broad extent of an insurance firm's diversification across lines of businesses. The aims of greater line of business diversification typically include income improvement, risk reduction and the exploitation of economies of scope.

name: Firm size
definition: While there is debate about whether economies of scale exist in the insurance industry (Joskow, 1973; Greehan, 1977; Johnson et al., 1981), size (in terms of premium volume) is regarded as a key strategic decision for insurance companies.

name: Operational efficiency
definition: Control of expenses reflects operational efficiency. The expense ratio is the ratio of underwriting expenses to net premiums written, and it enables a broad comparison of the efficiency of different insurance organizations.

name: Reinsurance
definition: Reinsurance is 'a contractual arrangement under which one insurer, known as the ceding company, buys insurance from another insurer, called the reinsurer' (Webb et al., 1974).

name: Financial leverage
definition: Leverage, the ratio of net premiums earned to policyholders' surplus, is considered as an important strategic variable for the study.

name: Investment strategy
definition: A measure PSTOCK, defined as the proportion of stocks in the investment portfolio, will be used to describe insurance investment strategies. A higher value of PSTOCK is considered to be associated with a higher level of risk taking.

name: Planning system sophistication
definition: Corporate-level planning systems were assumed to exist on a continuum of increasing sophistication, with planning sophistication defined as a combination of the level of planning openness and the planning horizon. Five key points on that continuum were defined: short-term forecasting, budgeting, annual planning, long-range planning and strategic planning.

name: Importance of external and environmental information
authors_terms: ["external and environmental types of information", "external information", "environmental information"]
definition: Environmental information is factors outside the enterprise with which the enterprise did not directly interact, but which might affect operations, including both the broader social/economic climate and areas into which the firm might expand in the future. External information is factors outside the enterprise with which the enterprise interacted directly on a regular basis.

name: Informal sources of information
authors_terms: ["informal sources of information", "personal sources of information", "sources of information"]
definition: The external search or environmental scan required by strategic planning leads the organization to seek information that is often communicated through informal channels. The questionnaire measured the importance to the planning process of eight sources of information, including personal contact with superiors, subordinates and outsiders.

name: Perceived environmental complexity
definition: Environmental turbulence has most frequently been discussed as consisting of two dimensions: complexity—the number of factors that must be addressed. Complexity was defined as the number of factors taken into account in the planning process.

name: Perceived environmental volatility
definition: Environmental turbulence consists of complexity and volatility—the rate of change of those factors. Respondents indicated the relative volatility of the information types over the last 3 years, taking into consideration both the frequency and the magnitude of fluctuations.

name: Senior management involvement
authors_terms: ["senior management involvement", "chief executive officer's active involvement in the planning process"]
definition: The importance of the chief executive officer's active involvement in the planning process has been emphasized by a number of authors. Senior management involvement in the planning process was evaluated as the importance of four possible levels of activity.

name: Division of labor
definition: Two agents must match one seller activity to one buyer activity, either internally via dual agency or externally by dividing labor. The division of labor allows individuals to focus their time on a narrower band of activities and increase productivity through specialization, but this comes at a cost because they divide the value they help create.

name: Transaction value
authors_terms: ["property type", "property prices", "transaction types", "underlying value of the property being transacted", "opportunities"]
definition: θ represents the underlying value of the property being transacted, with bigger, more luxurious, properties having a higher θ. In the empirics, property type is identified by dummies corresponding to quintiles of the distribution of property prices in a given month and market, from low-end (Q1) to top-end (Q5) properties.

name: Market size
authors_terms: ["market size", "extent of the market", "number of listed properties for sale"]
definition: M measures market size, that is, the mass of properties for sale in the market; in the empirical analysis market size measures the number of listed properties for sale in a given month in a given market.

name: Market heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["market heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of the market", "disparity between good transactions and other transactions"]
definition: The upper and lower bounds of the distribution of transaction types determine the heterogeneity of the market: as the difference between them increases, heterogeneity increases, and market heterogeneity is proportional to the standard deviation of the distribution of types. In the empirics it corresponds to the standard deviation of the price of listed properties for sale in a given month in a given market.

name: Pre-entry capabilities
definition: The literature has considered pre-entry capabilities to comprise both corporate-level integrative capabilities and function-level complementary assets, such as those in manufacturing, marketing, or distribution.

name: Technology choice at entry
authors_terms: ["technology choice", "technology choices at entry", "cSi technology", "crystalline silicon", "thin film technologies"]
definition: Firms entered and commercialized modules drawing on four different technologies (crystalline silicon [cSi], cadmium telluride [CdTe], copper-indium-gallium-diselenide [CIGS], and amorphous silicon [aSi]), and a firm's choice to pursue a given technology during industry emergence reflects a boundedly rational decision ex ante based on the nature of the technology and the nature of the firm's pre-entry capabilities.

name: Firm exit
definition: The dependent variable, exit, is a binary variable equal to 1 if the firm exits the solar PV module manufacturing industry during the shakeout period and zero otherwise.

name: Exit via acquisition
authors_terms: ["exit via acquisition", "acquisition (as opposed to dissolution)", "exit pathways", "mode of exit"]
definition: Although firms may exit via dissolution, which results in the dissolution of both the firm and its capabilities, firms may also exit via acquisition, which results in the dissolution of the firm but the retention of its capabilities within the industry.

name: Prior movers' domestic market share
authors_terms: ["prior movers' market shares", "prior movers' domestic market share"]
definition: The market shares that prior movers hold in the domestic market segments of a focal firm. The authors argue that the domestic market shares of prior movers determine the visibility of their strategic actions and whether those actions are perceived as threatening or as appropriate reference points.

name: Focal firm's domestic market share
authors_terms: ["focal firm's domestic market share", "firm's market share in the domestic market segments of prior movers"]
definition: A firm's share in the domestic market segments of prior movers, which the authors link to the firm's ability and motivation to respond to prior movers' international entry moves, since large-share firms are more motivated and better resourced to respond.

name: Interorganizational mimicry
definition: Clustering may be the result of interdependent or mutually referential decision making in which actions by some firms increase the likelihood of other firms taking the same action; the authors call this actor-level behavior interorganizational mimicry.

name: Long-distance company status
authors_terms: ["long-distance companies", "Bell Regional Holding Companies (Baby Bells)", "regional holding companies (RHCs)"]
definition: The distinction between the long-distance telephone companies, which competed head-to-head in the national market with little geographic or product differentiation, and the Bell Regional Holding Companies (Baby Bells), which operated local exchange services as regulated regional monopolists in separate, nonoverlapping regions.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: The complexity of the environment faced by a national subsidiary, assessed relative to the other subsidiaries of the same MNC; increased environmental complexity results in increased interdependency because both headquarters and the subsidiary are posed with mutual vulnerability.

name: Local resources
definition: The level of resources available to the subsidiary locally; as the resource levels of the subsidiary increase, the independent interests of the subsidiary and the headquarters may diverge.

name: Centralization
definition: The lack of subsidiary autonomy in decision-making: a governance mechanism in which the decision-making process is hierarchically organized with the headquarters often making most of the crucial strategic and policy decisions.

name: Formalization
definition: The use of systematic rules and procedures in decision-making; formalization may be interpreted as the routinization of decision-making and resource allocation.

name: Normative integration
definition: Consensus and shared values as a basis for decision-making; normative integration leads to domain consensus and shared values and facilitates cooperation and participative decision-making.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The overall performance of the subsidiary as assessed by a senior corporate respondent, used as the dependent variable in the tests of fit.

name: Context-structure fit
definition: The conditions of 'fit' between the particular contextual conditions that characterize a subsidiary and the structure of the headquarters-subsidiary relation; there is a fit structure of the headquarters-subsidiary relation that is expected to lead to improved subsidiary performance.

name: Subsidiary context
authors_terms: ["subsidiary context", "contextual conditions", "conditions that characterize a subsidiary"]
definition: The contextual conditions faced by a national subsidiary, differentiated into four categories based on the joint conditions of its local resource levels and environmental complexity relative to the other subsidiaries in the MNC.

name: Headquarters-subsidiary structure
definition: The structure of the headquarters-subsidiary exchange relation, characterized by the combination of centralization, formalization and normative integration that governs it.

name: CEO narcissistic admiration
definition: Narcissistic admiration reflects an intensified self-enhancement strategy aimed at achieving social admiration and elevating one's status through assertive behavior, such as charming others, striving for uniqueness, and engaging in grandiose fantasies, reflecting the mindset 'Let others admire you'.

name: CEO narcissistic rivalry
definition: Narcissistic rivalry involves a self-defensive strategy focused on countering perceived threats to one's dominance through antagonistic behavior, such as devaluing others, being aggressive, and maintaining a relentless drive for supremacy, encapsulated by the belief 'Don't let others tear you down'.

name: Investor sentiment
definition: Investor sentiment is a reflection of the holistic positive or negative evaluation of a venture. It is reflective of an integrated appraisal, resulting in a positive or negative inclination toward a particular investment.

name: New venture funding
definition: New venture funding is operationalized as the natural logarithm of the total dollar value of funding received by each CEO who pitched on Shark Tank.

name: Adoption of governance practices
authors_terms: ["adoption of governance practices", "adoption of practices", "board reform", "Adopt"]
definition: Our dependent variable is firm adoption of governance practices in line with the logic of board reform; these are the same practices used by the Clarkson Centre to construct the BSCI.

name: Governance rating performance
authors_terms: ["BSCI", "BSCI score", "performance on a rating", "performance on the governance rating", "performance on external ratings"]
definition: Our profitability and rating performance measures were firms' ROA and BSCI, respectively; the former measure was obtained from COMPUSTAT and the latter from the Clarkson Centre. The BSCI score ranged between 0 and 100 points, with higher scores indicating better governance.

name: Profitability
definition: Our profitability and rating performance measures were firms' ROA and BSCI, respectively. If the firm does not generate satisfactory financial results, it will simply not be viable for very long, so profitability is critical.

name: Social aspirations
definition: Reliance on social aspirations means that the firm uses the performance of the peer group as a reference.

name: Historical aspirations
definition: Reliance on historical aspirations means that the firm uses its own past performance as a reference.

name: Prior bank usage
authors_terms: ["bank on prior acquisition", "banks on prior acquisitions", "banks that work on their clients' prior acquisitions"]
definition: The extent to which a firm hired banks on its prior acquisitions; hiring any bank exposes a firm to bank influence processes, and banks that advise on a greater number of a firm's acquisitions have greater access to that firm.

name: Prior use of the focal bank
authors_terms: ["focal bank on prior acquisition", "a bank that works on a client's acquisition"]
definition: Whether a firm used the same bank on its prior acquisition that it did on its focal acquisition, which the authors describe as a stronger test of bank influence.

name: Prior acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["performance of prior acquisition with bank", "performance of that acquisition"]
definition: The wealth that investors expect an acquisition to generate, which translates into the extent to which investors bid the acquiror's share price up or down when the deal is announced; here it is the performance of the prior acquisition on which a bank was hired.

name: Stock financing experience without banks
authors_terms: ["stock financing without banks", "experience at making stock-financed acquisitions without banks"]
definition: The extent to which clients have previously undertaken stock-financed acquisitions without banks, from which they learn about stock-financed acquisitions and about banks' contributions to them.

name: Bank use on stock-financed acquisitions
authors_terms: ["bank and stock financing", "focal bank and stock financing", "hiring a bank on a focal stock-financed acquisition"]
definition: The joint choice of hiring a bank and using stock to finance an acquisition, an outcome that most extensively applies banks' expertise because it allows banks to utilize and demonstrate their knowledge of equity securities.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The abnormal or excess returns of the acquiring firm around the announcement of the acquisition, estimated with a market model against equally weighted market returns.

name: Insider purchases
definition: Shares purchased on the open market by all insiders, measured as the number of shares purchased multiplied by the average purchase price for all insider purchases in a given year. Open market purchases are treated as strong positive signals about the firm, and other transactions such as option exercises are set aside.

name: Patent count
definition: The number of patents applied for in a given year, which is not a measure of breakthrough innovation but may be an important indicator of potential success, particularly in uncertain or fast-paced environments.

name: Patent citations received
authors_terms: ["Cites received", "patent citations received", "citations a patent receives"]
definition: The number of times a patent is cited in subsequent patents, which measures the extent to which a given innovation serves as a platform for subsequent innovation. The more citations a patent receives, the greater the economic value.

name: Breakthrough patent count
definition: The number of patents a firm applied for that were ultimately in the top 10 percent most heavily cited in their technology subfield. Such breakthrough patents are tremendously valuable as foundations for firms to build upon.

name: Number of patent claims
definition: The number of claims made about what the innovation will do, reflecting the number of distinct uses specified for the innovation in the patent. A patent on a technology that may be used in a number of ways may be more valuable than a patent that specifies a single application or use.

name: Citation lag
authors_terms: ["Cite lag", "citation lag", "lag before a patent is cited", "length of time before the firm's top patent is cited"]
definition: The citation lag in years for the firm's strongest patent, capturing the speed with which follow-on work building on the patent is under way. Some patents have a more immediate impact while for others importance becomes visible only after a significant lag.

name: Patent activity
authors_terms: ["patent activity", "portfolio of patent activities", "profile of activities"]
definition: The progress of the overall profile of a firm's innovation activities in a given year as well as specific breakthroughs that may occur in that time frame. The hypotheses focus on different aspects of patent activity.

name: Mergers and acquisitions
definition: The paper studies M&A deals; the treatment consists in engaging in an M&A, whereas the control firms do not. The unit of analysis is the M&A combined unit, considering the acquiring and the target firm together as a single entity.

name: Patenting output
definition: Firms' patenting output is measured through the number of patent applications per year. The paper considers the outcome of the innovation process as assessed by both patenting quantity and quality.

name: Patent quality
authors_terms: ["patenting quality", "quality of the patenting output", "quality of inventions", "patent quality"]
definition: The authors consider three different and complementary dimensions of patent quality: impact, originality, and generality. The impact of a patent denotes its influence on future inventions, generality refers to its degree of applicability across scientific and technological fields, and originality indicates the extent to which an invention synthesizes different inputs departing from the current state of knowledge.

name: Strategic complementarity
definition: Complementarity is defined as different characteristics that are independent and mutually supportive (Tanriverdi and Venkatraman, 2005; Wang and Zajac, 2007).

name: Cultural fit
definition: In this paper, therefore, we focus on the organizational dimension of culture, defined as beliefs, values, and assumptions shared by the members of an organization (Schein, 1985). We rely on cultural fit—which allows similarities as well as differences that mutually support each other—rather than on cultural similarity.

name: Degree of integration
definition: As the degree of integration goes in one line with the scope of interaction and coordination between the two merging firms (Shrivastava, 1986). The degree of integration is assessed on different organizational levels.

name: Speed of integration
definition: The speed of integration describes the time period from the closing of the deal to the desired degree of integration (Homburg and Bucerius, 2006).

name: M&A success
definition: M&A success is the dependent variable of the study. The authors state that it should consist of multiple measures, and with self-reported data they suggest at least two success dimensions, one objective and one subjective.

name: Customer-to-supplier knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfers", "knowledge sharing", "knowledge-sharing activities", "time spent on knowledge transfers", "quality assistance", "inventory assistance", "knowledge acquired"]
definition: Knowledge-sharing activities in which personnel from the automaker and the supplier meet on a face-to-face basis to exchange technical information at the supplier's plant, and the extent to which the supplier reports having actually acquired valuable knowledge from each customer to help it improve quality or costs.

name: Product quality
definition: The quality of the supplier's product for a particular customer, measured as the plant's number of defective parts per million produced for that customer.

name: Supplier operational productivity
definition: The productivity of the supplier's operations for a particular customer; previous research has found a strong correlation between inventory reductions and productivity growth, so inventories (raw materials, WIP, and finished goods) directly attributable to each customer as a percent of sales to that customer are used as a measure for inventory costs.

name: Network constraints
authors_terms: ["network constraints", "customer policies", "constraints imposed by the customer"]
definition: Barriers to transferring knowledge employed in one manufacturing cell to another that arise from the customer's network: customer policies and behavior that do not allow the supplier to easily change the process, so that the supplier's operations represent one node whose change is constrained by that node's connections to other parts of the network.

name: Internal process rigidities
definition: Rigidities in the layout of the manufacturing cells for the U.S. customer—high levels of automation or large capital investment in heavy equipment, machines bolted or cemented into the floor, trenching in the floor, or hardwired utilities—that increase the costs of change and create a significant time lag before a new process is implemented.

name: Corporate interdependence
definition: Corporate interdependence is the degree to which the performance of a corporation as a whole depends on resource sharing and coordination among its constituent units. The four diversification postures can be arrayed from low to high interdependence in the following order: unrelated, related-linked, related-constrained, and vertically integrated.

name: Top management team social cohesion
definition: Cohesion aids communication and collaboration within a top management team; although excessive cohesion may create a harmful insularity from external forces, evidence strongly indicates that cohesion facilitates the internal communication needed in situations of high interdependence, because abundant interunit negotiation, compromise and collaboration are greatly aided if corporate managers have a well-developed rapport and a common outlook and language.

name: Corporate-wide operating knowledge base
authors_terms: ["corporatewide operating knowledge base", "companywide operating knowledge base", "corporate-wide operating knowledge base", "firm-wide operating knowledge base", "knowledge base"]
definition: Top management must possess knowledge of corporate-wide operating activities in order to exploit potential cooperation opportunities and coordinate interunit flows between business units; in low-interdependence firms such knowledge is less relevant. Firm-wide experience among top executives, acquired partly through interunit transfers, imbues them with a firm-wide perspective and provides the knowledge base for negotiating, arbitrating, and coordinating interunit relations.

name: Corporate performance
definition: Profitability was measured as return on assets (ROA), defined as net income after taxes divided by total assets; highly correlated with return on equity, ROA is less sensitive to firm capital structure and allows comparisons with numerous other studies on diversification.

name: Stretch goals
authors_terms: ["stretch goals", "stretch profit goal", "stretch compared with moderate organizational goals", "exogenous goal for performance"]
definition: By definition, stretch goals are difficult to achieve and are therefore likely to be achieved by only a few organizations. A stretch target is one that the organization cannot achieve simply by working a little harder or a little smarter; the exogenous goal for performance is set for decision makers by others, for example a stretch goal set for managers by the CEO or board.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Cumulative net income is adopted as the organizational performance measure for each simulated firm. Performance is measured by cumulative net income at the end of the third simulation round.

name: Performance variance
authors_terms: ["performance variance", "variance in performance", "higher variance in performance"]
definition: The focus here is on performance variance across a large sample of organizations at a particular time rather than performance variance over time for particular organizations. Stretch goals compared with moderate goals should generate higher performance variance across organizations.

name: Performance skewness
definition: The feedback processes amplify the success of those with the skill or luck to do well, stretching the performance distribution to the right, high-performance tail, while the erosion of goal commitment and adoption of survival strategies truncates the left, low-performance tail. These effects combine to generate right-skewed organizational performance distributions.

name: Risk-adjusted performance
definition: Risk-adjusted performance is frequently operationalized by the Sharpe ratio, the ratio of mean performance to its standard deviation.

name: Willingness to take risk
authors_terms: ["willingness to take risk", "risk taking", "managerial intentions to take risk"]
definition: A large attainment discrepancy motivates greater willingness to take the risk of engaging in distant search. Larger attainment discrepancies increase the willingness to take risk that comes with greater distant search for new strategies and increase risk taking more generally.

name: Goal commitment
definition: Decision-makers' willingness to erode their goals is a negative function of goal commitment, defined as the determination to reach a specific goal. Large and persistent attainment discrepancies undermine goal commitment because decision makers come to believe that the goal is not attainable.

name: Performance relative to the exogenous goal
authors_terms: ["deviation from the exogenous goal", "low performance relative to exogenous goals", "performance shortfall"]
definition: The deviation from the exogenous goal, computed as the exogenous goal for cumulative profit at the end of the round less actual cumulative net income achieved. Participants who perform poorly relative to the exogenously assigned goal decrease their commitment to that goal.

name: Structural integration
definition: In acquisitions, the choice between structural integration and its converse, structural separation, is a fundamental choice about the form of the combined organization. These correspond to situations in which the acquired firm is completely integrated into the acquirer and loses its distinctive identity as an organizational unit, or it is preserved as a distinct organizational entity within the merged firm.

name: Knowledge leverage
authors_terms: ["knowledge leverage", "leveraging what the acquired firm 'knows'", "leveraging the existing knowledge of acquired firms", "leverage of the existing knowledge base"]
definition: When acquirers use the acquired firm's existing knowledge as an input to their own innovation processes, they are primarily leveraging what the acquired firm 'knows.' The stock of technological knowledge in an acquired firm at the time of acquisition includes knowledge embodied in artifacts as well as embedded in the minds of individuals that pertains to existing technologies.

name: Capability leverage
authors_terms: ["capability leverage", "leveraging what the acquired firm 'does'", "leveraging the innovative capabilities of acquired firms", "leverage of innovation capabilities"]
definition: When acquirers rely on the acquired firm as an independent source of ongoing innovation, they are primarily leveraging what the acquired firm 'does.' The capability to generate further innovations is primarily resident in individual and group processes that allow for the recombination of existing knowledge into new knowledge.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: Experiential learning is a fundamental mechanism through which limitedly rational individuals come to grips with complexity; we expect that, through experience, acquirers learn how to better manage the consequences of structural integration.

name: Corporate scandal exposure
authors_terms: ["corporate scandal", "FB-CA scandal", "scandal involving the project-holding firm", "scandal-tainted firm", "scandal-tainted projects"]
definition: Based on cognitive dissonance theory, the authors posit that a corporate scandal is likely to trigger cognitive dissonance among the ecosystem stakeholders of the implicated firm, because their positive views of its projects conflict with their negative perceptions of the firm.

name: Stakeholder engagement
definition: The engagement activities of OSS developers in a focal project, which the authors measure with monthly counts of code commits, pull requests, issue reports and comments, and with the total of those activities.

name: Choice space
definition: When making decisions, people consider the scope of comparable choices that are cognitively relevant to the decisions, which we refer to as their choice space.

name: Social embeddedness
definition: Social embeddedness refers to the extent to which an individual is involved in social relationships in a specific field.

name: Team knowledge distance
authors_terms: ["knowledge distance", "team member knowledge distance", "team knowledge distance"]
definition: Knowledge distance reflects the differences in knowledge among inventors or how distinct each member's knowledge is from the other inventors.

name: Technological impact
definition: Technological impact is defined as the number of forward citations to a focal patent.

name: Density of prior collaborations
definition: Density is the degree of interconnectedness of team members, or the extent to which inventors on the team have worked together in the past.

name: Centralization of prior collaborations
definition: Centralization of the ties among team members refers to a central member's unmediated relationships to other members who themselves are unconnected; in this context, it indicates that one or a few members have collaborated with many other members who themselves have not collaborated with each other.

name: Subgrouping of prior collaborations
definition: Teams with a high degree of subgrouping are characterized by dense prior collaboration ties among subsets of team members who otherwise have few or no connections to others on the team; subgrouping refers to a pattern of prior collaborations in which a set of team members has collaborated extensively with each other but not with members outside their set.

name: Inbound tie arrival
authors_terms: ["inbound tie arrival", "arrival rate of new citation ties", "tie formation", "rule tie formation", "citation tie"]
definition: CPGs often become connected through citation ties, that is, healthcare organizations add text to CPGs that references other CPGs specialized on related methods, conditions, and practices. The dependent variable is the probability of receiving an inbound tie during a subepisode.

name: Rule density
definition: The intensity of discovery of the relevance of a focal rule to other rules is a positive function of the rules available to connect with in the rule system, and this increases with rule density (i.e., the count of rules in the rule system).

name: Rule change activity
authors_terms: ["rule change activity", "rule change activities", "rule making and revising activities", "rule birth", "rule revision"]
definition: Making and revising of rules in the system present opportunities/occasions for discovering relevance; the authors expect a positive effect of the rule change activity (birth rate and the revision rate) in the system on the arrival rate of citation ties at the focal rule.

name: Encoded knowledge volume
authors_terms: ["encoded knowledge volume", "volume of knowledge encoded in the focal rule"]
definition: A rule that encodes a large volume of knowledge provides more opportunities to discover relevance. A rule rich in encoded knowledge presents a more salient and attractive target for citing.

name: Inbound network size
authors_terms: ["inbound network size", "size of the inbound network of the focal rule", "ego network"]
definition: Individual rules become embedded in a rule network, that is, each rule develops an ego network of other rules connected by direct ties to the focal rule; the rate of tie arrival of the focal rule should decrease with the number of ties already present in its ego network.

name: Rule version age
authors_terms: ["version age", "the age of the focal rule version"]
definition: A new version of a rule incorporates new knowledge, which (re)starts a sorting process of its own related to that new knowledge; version age is the number of years between the effective date of a guideline version and the beginning of the current subepisode.

name: Stock repurchase program announcement
authors_terms: ["stock repurchase programs", "stock repurchase announcements", "stock repurchase activity", "open market announcements"]
definition: At a fundamental level, stock repurchase exchanges corporate cash for outstanding company stock (firms sometimes finance repurchases with new debt). Repurchase plan announcements typically lead to significantly positive market reactions, demonstrating that stock repurchase programs appeal to shareholders.

name: Research and development intensity
definition: We examine the role played by one major determinant of such complexity—research and development intensity—in the motive to announce stock repurchase programs. Research intensity exacerbates information asymmetry because of the complex, time- and path-dependent nature of the inputs of such resources.

name: CEO stock option pay
authors_terms: ["CEO stock option pay", "stock option pay", "risky stock-based incentives", "outcome-based incentive"]
definition: The value of stock option pay, however, typically depends entirely on increases in the firm's share price. We measured CEO stock option pay as the proportion of total annual pay given in stock options.

name: Performance expectations
definition: Investors, analysts, and other corporate constituents all develop expectations about a firm's future performance, and failure to meet these can increase the personal risk to executives. When performance expectations are high, executives will likely engage in satisficing strategies.

name: Unmet performance expectations
authors_terms: ["unmet performance expectations", "performance expectations not met", "failure to meet expectations", "missed performance expectations"]
definition: Regardless of its absolute levels, how performance stacks up with expectations can have a strong bearing on executives' perceived need to take action. By generating immediate positive returns for shareholders, stock repurchase programs close the gap between expectations and achieved results, thereby reducing executives' employment risk.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: A foreign subsidiary is any host country operation (e.g., sales offices, branch offices, plants, or local headquarters) controlled by a foreign parent. The domestic comparison group consists of U.S. firms operating in the same 4-digit SIC code and in the same location as the foreign subsidiaries.

name: Labor lawsuit judgments
definition: Labor lawsuit judgments are judgments in labor lawsuits brought against a firm in courts with jurisdiction in the focal firm's specific location. They directly measure only labor-related disadvantage and cannot be manipulated through transfer pricing or income shifting between parent and subsidiary.

name: HR officer nationality
authors_terms: ["American in charge of HR issues", "USHR", "nationality of the officer handling HR issues"]
definition: Whether the officer in charge of HR issues at the focal subsidiary is an American rather than an expatriate. Americans likely have a better understanding of U.S. legal and cultural norms and more experience working with U.S. employees.

name: HR professional staffing
definition: Whether the focal subsidiary's officer in charge of HR issues is an HR professional; if HR or Personnel is part of this officer's title, the officer is an HR professional. HR professionals may benefit from their previous experience and network connections in identifying and implementing accepted HR practices.

name: Top officer nationality
definition: Whether the focal subsidiary has had an American top officer (titles vary from CEO, President, to Chairman). American top officers are more familiar with U.S. cultural and legal norms than expatriate top officers are.

name: Subsidiary autonomy
definition: The level of adaptation to host country practices likely depends on the level of autonomy given foreign subsidiaries, and a key issue in autonomy is the chain of reporting among operations in an MNE. Greater autonomy from parent firms may facilitate foreign subsidiary adaptation to local conditions.

name: Affiliated U.S. operations
authors_terms: ["USOffices", "number of affiliated U.S. operations", "affiliated U.S. operations", "host country affiliations"]
definition: The total number of affiliated U.S. operations of the focal subsidiary's parent. An affiliated network may be a foreign subsidiary's best opportunity for vicarious learning, learning from the experience of others.

name: Subsidiary age
definition: Age represents the number of years the focal firm has operated in the particular metropolitan location, rounded to the nearest year. Older foreign subsidiaries may have learned to minimize their exposure to labor lawsuit judgments.

name: Knowledge cluster characteristics
authors_terms: ["knowledge cluster characteristics", "higher-knowledge cluster characteristics", "knowledge cluster dimension", "knowledge clusters"]
definition: The salient feature of the knowledge cluster is the presence of localized interfirm knowledge spillovers. Thus, the knowledge cluster dimension stems from the level of interfirm knowledge spillover, firm spatial proximity, common pool of knowledge, rate of imitation, and overlap in the final markets.

name: Managerial corporate characteristics
definition: According to the classical Chandlerian-Penrosian view, the managerial corporation is characterized by a division of the organization into subunits focused on specific activities or operations, by a coordination of these subunits and their activities, by hierarchical decision making, and by an ex ante assessment and selection of activities and projects.

name: Mean of regional rewards
authors_terms: ["mean of the reward distribution", "expected rewards", "average level of rewards", "Salary"]
definition: As a proxy of the rewards of a city we use the salary of resident managers in the city. Managerial salaries reflect the productivity of the managerial function; they are linked to the performance of the organization.

name: Dispersion of regional rewards
authors_terms: ["dispersion in the reward distribution", "variability of rewards", "Salaryspread"]
definition: The standard perspective about the dispersion of the returns of a set of activities is that the total dispersion is a function of the variances of the individual activities and their combined covariances.

name: Executive long-term incentives
definition: The objective of long-term executive compensation is to focus executives' effort on creating long-term value, thus fostering organizational long-term orientation. Companies can foster a long-term orientation by providing long-term incentives to their management team (e.g., by linking their compensation to long-term performance).

name: Firm value
definition: Firm value V is the sum of the discounted expected future cash flows. Such short-termist behavior translates in lower firm value, as managers turn down valuable investment opportunities.

name: Operating performance
definition: The paper examines the effect of passing long-term incentive proposals on operating performance and considers three measures of operating performance (return on assets, net profit margin, and sales growth).

name: Innovation investment
definition: Innovative activities are characterized by long gestation periods and a high rate of failure. Given these inherent features of innovation, prior research argues that a long-term orientation is important for innovation.

name: Stakeholder relations engagement
definition: Long-term horizons are important to establish and strengthen relationships with the company's stakeholders (e.g., employees, customers, community, etc.). Repeated interactions help develop relationships, empathy, and trust.

name: Organizational long-term orientation
definition: An organization's time orientation is reflected by its discourse; the authors construct an index of long-term orientation based on the organization's discourse, where companies that use long-term keywords more frequently are more likely to have a longer-term orientation.

name: Funding performance
definition: We measured a project's funding performance using two variables: (1) the number of backers who pledge money to the project and (2) the total amount of funding in U.S. dollars pledged by backers (i.e., funding amount).

name: Peak displayed joy
authors_terms: ["peak displayed joy", "peak joy", "level of peak displayed joy", "peak displayed joy level"]
definition: We focus on entrepreneurs' peak displayed joy (i.e., the highest level of joy displayed by entrepreneurs) in this study. For each video, we identified the highest displayed joy score within all frames of the video as the peak displayed joy.

name: Peak displayed joy duration
authors_terms: ["peak duration", "peak displayed joy duration", "total length of time for peak displayed joy", "total time length of peak displayed joy"]
definition: Peak duration refers to the total length of time (in seconds) during which the entrepreneurs' displayed joy reaches the peak level during the pitch.

name: Beginning-phase peak displayed joy
authors_terms: ["beginning phase's peak displayed joy", "peak displayed joy at the beginning phase"]
definition: To compute peak displayed joy in the beginning phase of the pitch, we partitioned each pitch video into three parts and identified the intensity of peak displayed joy in the first third partition.

name: Ending-phase peak displayed joy
authors_terms: ["ending phase's peak displayed joy", "peak displayed joy at the ending phase"]
definition: To compute peak displayed joy in the ending phase of the pitch, we partitioned each pitch video into three parts and identified the intensity of peak displayed joy in the last third partition.

name: Middle-phase peak displayed joy
definition: To compute peak displayed joy in the middle phase of the pitch, we partitioned each pitch video into three parts and identified the intensity of peak displayed joy in the remaining middle partition.

name: Beginning-phase peak displayed joy duration
authors_terms: ["beginning phase's peak duration", "beginning phase's peak duration squared"]
definition: We identified the duration of peak displayed joy in each of the three partitions of the pitch video, including the beginning phase as the first third partition.

name: Ending-phase peak displayed joy duration
authors_terms: ["ending phase's peak duration", "ending phase's peak duration squared"]
definition: We identified the duration of peak displayed joy in each of the three partitions of the pitch video, including the ending phase as the last third partition.

name: Middle-phase peak displayed joy duration
definition: We identified the duration of peak displayed joy in each of the three partitions of the pitch video, including the middle phase as the remaining partition.

name: Novelty of geographic location of investments
authors_terms: ["novelty of the geographic location of investments", "novelty of FDI location decisions", "strategic novelty"]
definition: The novelty of the geographic location of a new investment, ranked from an investment in the home country to an investment in a new country in a new cultural block. A first-time investment in a new cultural block means investing in a cultural and institutional setting that differs considerably from that in which the firm has previously invested, making the investment particularly innovative.

name: TMT tenure diversity
definition: TMT tenure refers to the number of years of membership of an individual in the TMT; TMT tenure diversity implies heterogeneity in experience, skills, networks, and viewpoints concerning the focal task of evaluating foreign investments.

name: TMT educational diversity
authors_terms: ["TMT educational diversity", "educational diversity", "diversity in type of education"]
definition: Diversity in type of education, being an engineer, a lawyer, or having an MBA, which may imply different skills, views, and ways of understanding and evaluating investments.

name: Strong faultline settings
definition: Faultlines are the process by which TMTs divide themselves into subgroups based on demographic attributes; the formation of subgroups is particularly likely in strong faultline settings, when several demographic attributes become aligned in the same way, dividing teams into hardened subgroups.

name: Overlapping team tenure
authors_terms: ["overlapping team tenure", "tenure overlap", "TLAP", "common historical experience", "overlapping tenure"]
definition: The overlap in tenure of team members, used as a proxy for their social interaction over time.

name: TMT demographic diversity
definition: Much of upper-echelon research explored how TMT demographic diversity or 'heterogeneity' influences strategic innovation; the authors use the two terms interchangeably.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: CSP is a multidimensional construct, with behaviors ranging across a wide variety of inputs (e.g., investments in pollution control equipment or other environmental strategies), internal behaviors or processes (e.g., treatment of women and minorities, nature of products produced, relationships with customers), and outputs (e.g., community relations and philanthropic programs).

name: Financial performance
definition: Firm financial performance (profitability) was measured using three accounting variables: return on assets, return on equity, and return on sales, providing a range of measures used to assess corporate financial performance by the investment community.

name: VDO affiliation
definition: Venture development organizations (VDOs) are typically entities that offer new firms a combination of concept evaluation, mentorship, networking assistance, and funding access in exchange for a client company fee. A relationship with a VDO serves as a meaningful signaling mechanism to outsiders.

name: Founder managerial experience
authors_terms: ["managerial experience", "prior managerial experience", "managerial experience of the founder"]
definition: The prior managerial experience of the founding team; outside investors look to the managerial experience of the founding team as a signaler characteristic that identifies high-quality new ventures.

name: Product introduction
authors_terms: ["product introduction", "having at least one product introduced to the market", "products on the market"]
definition: A signaling action that is both costly and difficult to imitate is to introduce a product onto the market; introducing a new product to the market signals to investors about the young firm's prospects and ability.

name: Operating from commercial property
authors_terms: ["commercial property", "operating from commercial property", "located in commercial/non-residential areas"]
definition: Whether or not the entrepreneur has gone beyond working from home and taken the added step of moving into commercial property, a blunt indicator of managerial commitment whose consequences are greater if the venture fails.

name: Receipt of initial external capital
authors_terms: ["capital received", "receiving external capital", "initial external capital", "external capital investment"]
definition: The capital required for sustained growth often outstrips the abilities of founders, friends, and family; obtaining external financing is critical to startup performance and acquiring initial external capital represents a major accomplishment.

name: Closeness centrality
authors_terms: ["closeness centrality", "centrality", "central position in an industry alliance network"]
definition: A firm's centrality refers to the extent to which it occupies a central position with ties to other network members, describing the firm's ability to access information and resources. Of the various measures of centrality, the authors argue that closeness centrality is the most appropriate because it captures both direct and indirect relationships and enables a firm's independent access to all other network members in the shortest number of steps.

name: Structural hole positions
definition: A firm's structural hole positions refer to its brokerage locations between two otherwise disconnected firms in the network, representing the broker firms' ability to monitor and manipulate the flow of information and resources. Structural holes emphasize the strategic controls of such accesses and are more dynamic and transitory in nature than closeness centrality.

name: Exploitation learning tendency
authors_terms: ["exploitation learning tendency", "exploitation alliance ratio", "exploitation (as opposed to exploration) learning tendency"]
definition: Firms' exploration and exploitation learning tendencies are reflected through their prior alliance formation, with exploitation alliances focused on short-term economic benefits and exploration alliances on experimentation, variation, search and innovation. A value closer to one means that the focal firm has a larger composition of exploitation alliances or a stronger learning tendency toward exploitation; a value closer to zero means a stronger learning tendency toward exploration.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["level of institutional development", "institutional development", "institutional environment", "market-based institutions"]
definition: The degree to which the formal institutional environment supports complex market-based transactions such as M&As; compared with the United States, China's formal institutional framework is relatively underdeveloped, often manifested in strong government intervention, insufficient legal protection, regional controls with fragmented bureaucracy, and weak market monitoring mechanisms.

name: M&A activities
definition: The overall M&A activities of a focal firm as a result of its alliance network embeddedness and exploration/exploitation learning under different institutional environments, captured by the number of M&As initiated by a focal firm in each year and targeting both prior alliance partners and non-alliance partners in each electronics industry alliance network.

name: Board undervaluation
definition: Board undervaluation refers to the average director undervaluation on the board, and it represents the extent to which the overall board leadership structure cannot be explained by normatively accepted criteria. Director undervaluation occurs when a director's chair appointments are not explained by normatively accepted or legitimate factors for determining such positions.

name: Turnover of undervalued directors
authors_terms: ["turnover levels of undervalued directors", "turnover levels", "aggregate turnover levels", "collective turnover of directors"]
definition: Turnover levels of undervalued directors are the count of undervalued directors who were on the board at IPO and exited the focal firm within 3 years post-IPO.

name: Frequency of board meetings
authors_terms: ["frequency of board meetings", "frequency of board interactions", "board meetings"]
definition: Board meetings are the primary forum in which all board members interact to work on significant strategic issues and operational matters; the frequency of board meetings is measured as the average number of board meetings from the IPO year to the third year post-IPO.

name: Founder-CEO
definition: Founder-CEO is coded as 1 if the CEO is also the founder of the firm; if not, it is coded as 0. Founder-CEOs are usually the primary source of the initial and now (with an IPO) successful vision of the organizations and often are perceived to have and do have significant control over their organizations.

name: Industry experience breadth
authors_terms: ["industry generalist", "industry specialist", "breadth of industry experience", "industry category spanning", "industry specialization"]
definition: The extent to which a lead founder's work experience spans multiple industries. Audiences categorize lead founders' industry experience into standardized industrial classifications, and founders whose experience spans industries are industry generalists rather than industry specialists.

name: Functional experience breadth
authors_terms: ["functional generalist", "functional specialist", "breadth of functional experience", "functional category spanning"]
definition: The extent to which a lead founder's work experience spans multiple functional areas. Audiences categorize lead founders' functional experience using standardized occupational classifications, and founders who have worked across functions are functional generalists rather than functional specialists.

name: Category spanning
authors_terms: ["category spanning", "founder's breadth of experience", "generalist", "full generalist", "partial specialist", "full specialist"]
definition: A founder's experience spanning multiple categories. Entities that span multiple categories, generalists, create ambiguity and audience members tend to evaluate these category spanners less favorably; in this paper full specialists have worked in the same industry and the same function, partial specialists have worked in the same function across industries or in different functions in the same industry, and full generalists have worked across functions in various industries.

name: Funds raised at IPO
authors_terms: ["funds raised at IPO", "IPO proceeds", "resource acquisition", "investment proportion"]
definition: The resources an entrepreneurial venture acquires at its initial public offering, which reflect public investors' interest in the venture and indicate the value of the focal firm.

name: Trust in the lead founder
authors_terms: ["investors' trust in the lead founder", "trust", "trust in a founder"]
definition: Investors' trust in a lead founder is defined as the willingness to 'accept vulnerability based upon positive expectations of the intentions or behavior of another'; it comprises a willingness to accept vulnerability to the actions of another party and positive expectations regarding that party's intentions, motivations, and behavior despite uncertainty.

name: VC-retained equity
authors_terms: ["VC-retained equity", "proportion of VC-retained equity", "venture capitalists' involvement", "VC affiliations"]
definition: The proportion of a venture's equity held by venture capitalists at IPO; venture capitalists' engagement is represented by the proportion of equity they retain at IPO, and their involvement signals that the focal lead founder has passed the trustworthiness due diligence of the VC firm.

name: Perceived consistency of the lead founder
definition: Investors' perception that a lead founder behaves consistently and predictably to deliver the business plan pitched at IPO instead of pivoting the focal firm in new directions not anticipated or desired by investors.

name: Competence concerns
authors_terms: ["concerns about competence", "perceived competence", "concerns about the lead founder's competence"]
definition: Audience concerns that a producer lacks the domain expertise, in-depth knowledge, or ability to manage the growth of the focal business, a known alternative mechanism of the generalist penalty.

name: CEO succession
definition: The chief executive officer was considered as either the Chair of the Board of Directors (unless the Chair was listed as an outsider with other full-time responsibilities), the CEO, or the President of the firm in cases where no other individual was listed as Chair or CEO. CEO succession was coded as 1 for any year in which a new individual was installed in office.

name: Executive-team change
definition: For each year of a firm's existence other than the first year, the membership of the executive team (not including the CEO) was compared with membership of the preceding year. All executives down through the vice-president level were included as members of the executive team.

name: Strategic reorientation
definition: Reorientations are defined as discontinuous and simultaneous changes in organization strategy, structure, power distributions, and control practices (Tushman and Romanelli 1985). Reorientations were defined as having occurred only when strategy, structure and formal control all changed [i.e., all were coded 1] within a two-year period.

name: CEO origin
definition: Successors were also coded as internal promotions or external recruitment. A successor was coded as externally recruited if he or she held a position outside the organization less than one year prior to being appointed CEO; otherwise the new CEO was coded as an insider.

name: Organization performance
definition: Organization performance was measured by return on assets (ROA). These data were measured yearly for each firm. To test Hypothesis 5, organizations were classified into three historical performance categories by comparing firm ROA to industry-average ROA for each year of a company's life.

name: Complexity of technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["complexity", "the complexity of a firm's technological knowledge"]
definition: Complexity is defined according to dimensions that increase the difficulty of comprehending how a system functions or produces some outcome; a complex system consists of many unique and interacting elements which have equally important effects on the outcomes produced by the system.

name: Tacitness of technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["tacitness", "the tacitness of a firm's technological knowledge", "tacit knowledge"]
