definition: The knowledge employed in design problem solving is tacit when an engineer cannot fully explain which parameters are responsible for changes in performance; tacitness covers both the inability to articulate what one knows about achieving an observed performance outcome and the personal nature of knowledge.

name: Specificity of technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["specificity", "the specificity of a firm's technological knowledge", "resource specificity", "design specificity"]
definition: Resources are described as being specific when they are maximally effective in a particular use or when utilized by a particular firm. Two facets are distinguished: resource specificity, the extent to which what a firm knows about product components is specific to a customer, application, or component varieties, and design specificity, the extent to which a firm acquires specialized architectural knowledge by tailoring its formulas for individual customers and applications.

name: Persistence of major performance advantages
authors_terms: ["persistence of its major performance advantages", "Months to Imitate", "Persistence-Major", "persistence of major improvements"]
definition: The advantage that a firm derives from its distinct technological knowledge will persist until competitors are able to achieve equivalent product performance; a major improvement offers customers substantially higher performance than existing versions of a product or embodies a new combination of performance characteristics.

name: Persistence of minor performance advantages
authors_terms: ["persistence of its minor performance advantages", "Persistence-Minor", "persistence of minor advantages", "duration of minor advantages"]
definition: The persistence of minor advantages is the extent to which competitors tend to replicate a firm's incremental product improvements in more or less time than the firm took to develop them.

name: Technological experience
definition: Technological skills were operationalized by two variables, information technology experiences and investment in systems and equipment. The first variable consisted of the cumulative number of times a bank had been involved in information technology projects.

name: Technological investment
authors_terms: ["investment expenditure, systems and equipment", "investment in systems and equipment", "learning by using", "learning by doing"]
definition: The second information technology variable was obtained from a time series of annual reports and is also presumed to signal cumulative skills. Increased investment in systems and equipment reflects "learning by using" (Rosenberg 1982) and permits a firm to produce its output more efficiently.

name: Interfirm networking
definition: Networking increases variety and serendipity. Networks give better access to new developments that reside in significant other organizations, particularly carriers of exogenous technologies.

name: Technological intensity of interfirm linkages
authors_terms: ["proportion of technological exchange relationships", "technological intensity of interorganizational conduct", "proportion of technological linkages"]
definition: A separate networking measure, signalling the saliency of technology in interfirm networking was constructed: "proportion of technological exchange relationships". It conveys the technological intensity of interorganizational conduct, and might furnish additional insight on the innovation likelihood.

name: Technological innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["innovation", "adoption of a new technology", "probability of innovation", "home banking"]
definition: The dependent variable takes, therefore, two forms: adoption of a new technology, and choice of structural arrangement (internal versus external) to implement the adoption.

name: Organizational form of innovation implementation
authors_terms: ["form of implementation", "internal versus external", "structural arrangement", "organizational form", "mode of entry"]
definition: Organizations often face the vexing choice of implementing innovation internally or through some external form.

name: Diversifying acquisition likelihood
authors_terms: ["diversifying acquisitions", "acquisition likelihood", "propensity to engage in diversifying acquisitions"]
definition: Corporate acquisitions entail the absorption of one firm by another; the diversifying acquisitions of the 1960s brought together firms producing in different industries that were not linked by buyer-supplier relations. The paper models the likelihood that large corporations completed such acquisitions.

name: Upper-class social origins
authors_terms: ["social status at birth", "upper-class social origins", "upper-class background", "social register/elite secondary school CEO"]
definition: Social status at birth is one dimension of the class system and thus an axis along which corporate elite members can be distinguished from one another. Only descendents of families of longstanding wealth and social prominence gain admission to exclusive secondary schools and listing in restricted social registers.

name: Jewish religious affiliation
authors_terms: ["Jewish CEO", "Jewish", "marginal with respect to religious affiliation"]
definition: Baltzell maintained that social status in the U.S. has been segregated along religious lines; Hirsch (1986) and Espeland and Hirsch (1990) described the corporate elite members who pursued diversifying acquisitions in the 1960s as being disproportionately Jewish.

name: South or West corporate headquarters
authors_terms: ["South/West corporate H.Q.", "situated in the South or West", "marginal with respect to ... regional location"]
definition: Baltzell maintained that social status in the U.S. has been segregated along regional lines, characterizing the upper class as a Protestant and northeastern phenomenon; Hirsch (1986) and Espeland and Hirsch (1990) described the acquisitive elite members as disproportionately from the South or West.

name: Exclusive social club membership
authors_terms: ["exclusive social club CEO", "belonged to exclusive social clubs", "membership in exclusive social clubs"]
definition: Corporate elite members come to know and develop relationships with one another through common memberships in exclusive social clubs and corporate boards of directors. Membership in exclusive clubs and possession of corporate board seats go hand in hand.

name: Sent industrial interlocks
definition: When a corporation's managers sit on another firm's board of directors, they create "sent" interlocks between their corporation and the other firm, obtaining access to information about that firm and formal authority over it.

name: Received industrial interlocks
definition: Outside directors who are principally affiliated with other industrial firms create "received" industrial interlocks between the focal corporation and these other firms; such directors had a self-interest in dissuading the corporations on whose boards they sat from pursuing acquisitions.

name: Neutral industrial interlocks
definition: Outside directors can also sit on the boards of other firms with which they are not principally affiliated, creating "neutral" industrial interlocks between the focal corporation and these other firms; directors who create many neutral interlocks are considered the most central members of the business elite.

name: Elite undergraduate education
authors_terms: ["elite undergrad. degree CEO", "undergraduate degree from an elite college or university"]
definition: Degrees from elite universities or professional schools are sometimes considered indicative of upper-class standing, because admission to such schools is more open to persons of high social status and because attendance at such schools socializes students into upper-class norms and plugs them into elite social networks.

name: Elite MBA education
authors_terms: ["elite MBA degree CEO", "M.B.A. degree from an elite graduate school of business"]
definition: Higher educational attainment is another dimension of the class system. Elite graduate schools of business disseminated a conception of managerial control—the "firm-as-portfolio" model—that fostered acquisition behavior in this period.

name: Concentrated family ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership concentrated in the hands of a few related individuals", "ownership assoc. with CEO", "ownership assoc. with other top mgrs.", "ownership assoc. with outsiders"]
definition: The classical Marxian dimension of the class structure pertains to the extent to which corporate elite members own the means of production. The paper records the percentage of outstanding common stock greater than 3 percent held by a group of individuals related by kinship or partnership.

name: Ownership representation in top management
authors_terms: ["ownership in the hands of individuals represented in top management", "ownership assoc. with CEO", "ownership assoc. with other top mgrs."]
definition: Ownership groups are distinguished according to whether they were represented in the CEO position, represented in other top management positions, or were outsiders (who were typically represented on the board of directors). Owners involved in top management are likely to improve their social standing as their firms grow.

name: Upstream employment affiliations
authors_terms: ["prominent upstream employment affiliations", "TMT upstream employment affiliations"]
definition: Prominent upstream employment affiliations derive from top managers' employment at research and development institutions such as prestigious universities or government-based institutions such as the National Science Foundation.

name: Horizontal employment affiliations
authors_terms: ["prominent horizontal employment affiliations", "TMT horizontal employment affiliations"]
definition: Prominent horizontal employment affiliations derive from top managers' employment at companies in the same industry or sector.

name: Downstream employment affiliations
authors_terms: ["prominent downstream employment affiliations", "TMT downstream employment affiliations"]
definition: Prominent downstream employment affiliations derive from top manager's employment at downstream organizations-that is, with companies that are one step closer in the business cycle to bringing a young firm's products to market.

name: Employment affiliation diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of TMT employment affiliations", "TMT diversity of employment affiliations"]
definition: We also assessed resource legitimacy signals that may be indicated by the diversity of TMT employment affiliations. We measured diversity of TMT employment affiliations two ways.

name: Role legitimacy
authors_terms: ["role legitimacy", "the match between top management backgrounds and the roles served by core members of the top management team"]
definition: We call this matching of previous experiences to current roles, 'role legitimacy.' Role legitimacy stems from the backgrounds of key top managers, and thus differs from the majority of TMT studies that have focused on the composition of a TMT or upper echelon as a whole.

name: Underwriter prestige
authors_terms: ["underwriter prestige", "prestige of the lead underwriter", "prestige of a firm's lead underwriter"]
definition: We focused on the prestige of the lead underwriter as one important endorsement legitimacy signal for young firms undertaking an IPO.

name: Top management team composition
authors_terms: ["composition of a firm's top management team", "composition of the TMT"]
definition: We propose that the composition of the TMT has a symbolic role at the time of IPO in addition to the more concrete operational activities of the team, and that this in turn can affect the decisions of important resource-holders, such as investors.

name: Investor decisions
authors_terms: ["investor decisions", "number and quality of institutional investors", "number of dedicated institutional investors"]
definition: In the present study, we focus on an important outcome for firms undertaking an IPO-the quantity and quality of investors who decide to invest in an issuing firm.

name: Inventive performance
definition: Inventive performance in any period is the inventive output or number of inventions.

name: Search in novel technological areas
authors_terms: ["search in novel areas", "novel technology areas", "new technological areas", "novel areas"]
definition: Search in areas that are new to the firm increases the firm's inventive performance by improving its understanding of emerging fields.

name: Partner diversity in technological distance
authors_terms: ["diversity of its learning alliance partners in terms of technological distance", "variance of technological distance", "diverse partners"]
definition: The diversity construct in this hypothesis has two aspects: 1) having more distant partners (which we argued increases a focal firm's inventive performance); and 2) avoiding having excessive distal partners (which we argued would be counterproductive) and balance the portfolio by having more proximal partners.

name: Exploration of scientific knowledge
authors_terms: ["exploring scientific knowledge", "scientific knowledge in the public domain", "public science", "scientific search", "search in public science"]
definition: Hypothesis 3 predicts a nonlinear effect of exploring scientific knowledge gained either by working with university scientists or reading scientific publications.

name: Strategic orientation
definition: A dimensionality approach to strategic orientation was used in this study (Miller and Friesen, 1982; Venkatraman, 1989). Specifically, the five dimensions used to operationalize strategic orientation were conceptualized and their measures validated by Venkatraman (1989).

name: Proactive strategic orientation
definition: The third strategic orientation is composed of three closely related dimensions, namely Proactiveness, Futurity and Riskiness. This close relationship would seem intuitively reasonable since a proactive stance would seem to require the assumption of some risk and a future orientation.

name: Analysis strategic orientation
definition: Two are composed of a single dimension each, namely, Analysis and Defensiveness. Indeed for practical purposes, the analysis strategic orientation appears to be a 'hybrid' of proactive and defensive strategies (Miles and Snow, 1978; Shortell and Zajac, 1990).

name: Defensive strategic orientation
definition: Two are composed of a single dimension each, namely, Analysis and Defensiveness. Managers of electronics firms in the China sample are likely to adopt defensive strategies and are reluctant to engage in more expensive and risky strategic moves, when facing increasingly hostile, complex and dynamic environments.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Finally the Complexity dimension was measured by heterogeneity and diversity of these elements in the environment.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The Dynamism dimension was measured by variability and predictability of these elements.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: The Hostility dimension was measured by the importance and availability of resources controlled by different environmental elements.

name: Overall firm performance
definition: Five questions were devised to capture a firm's relative performance (Khandwalla, 1976). These questions asked managers to identify their performance relative to close competitors based on after-tax return on total assets, after-tax return on total sales, total sales growth, overall performance and success, and competitive positions.

name: Profitability
definition: In the PRC, firms are usually appraised and evaluated by the government based on profitability related performance criteria, thus profitability is usually perceived by managers as a 'hard standard' while other performance measures such as market share may be viewed as a 'soft standard.'

name: Market share
definition: As market oriented practices and western management concepts are adopted by Chinese managers, market share has become a legitimate strategic goal.

name: Narrative distinctiveness
definition: Narrative distinctiveness captures the degree to which the content of a listing's narrative deviates from the content of the prototypical narrative in the listing's category. An optimal level of narrative distinctiveness - defined as the degree to which a narrative's content is distinctive from the content of a prototypical narrative in its category - is needed to reconcile the opposing demands for legitimacy and differentiation.

name: Category distinctiveness
definition: Category distinctiveness is defined as a category's relative position vis-a-vis other categories at the same horizontal level in its classification system and reflected in the uniqueness of a given category's prototype relative to the prototypes of other categories in the same classification system. Following Lo et al. (2020), the authors define it as a category's 'relative position in the broader classification and meaning system', so that a category becomes more distinctive if its prototype exhibits a higher distance to the prototypes of all other categories at the same horizontal level.

name: Price premium
definition: The authors focus on the price premium that Airbnb hosts can command for their listings - an important indicator of the relative demand for a listing in a context in which the supply of a given accommodation is fixed. Price premium represents the degree to which a listing's price exceeds the average price in that geographic area.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technological uncertainty", "uncertainty embodied by an invention", "uncertainty regarding the commercial potential of the patent", "technological maturity"]
definition: Uncertainty regarding the commercial potential of the patent, which is likely to be higher for technologies that are more 'basic' or more 'distant' from commercialization; for many university inventions technical, manufacturing, and commercial feasibility are all subject to varying degrees of uncertainty.

name: Evaluation capability
authors_terms: ["ability to evaluate external information", "ability to evaluate an invention", "the firm's capability in evaluating scientific developments", "expertise"]
definition: The dimension of a firm's technological knowledge that enables it to assess the range of potential payoffs of the patent under consideration; it reflects the ability to monitor, assimilate and evaluate external technologies rather than to commercialize them.

name: Related technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["technological knowledge related to an invention", "related technological knowledge", "related technological assets", "the firm's stock of technological knowledge"]
definition: The share of the firm's knowledge base that bears on the invention under consideration; a high share of patenting in the primary patent class of the licensed patent indicates that a substantial proportion of the firm's innovative activity has occurred in the area represented by that patent class.

name: Option contract purchase
authors_terms: ["purchase an option contract", "the option choice", "take an option", "purchase an option"]
definition: The firm's purchase, prior to making a licensing decision, of an option agreement under which it obtains the right, but not the obligation, to license the technology at a future date at some cost.

name: Licensing
authors_terms: ["license the invention", "licensing decision", "probability of licensing", "commit to a license"]
definition: The firm's decision to enter an exclusive license committing it to undertake efforts to commercialize the university technology, as opposed to rejecting the technology.

name: Election years
definition: Election years are the years in which the relevant election took place; the theory treats the state (gubernatorial) election as the relevant election because state elections determine the government leaders who oversee the SOEs in question. Elections are held in October, relatively late in the year.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is captured with return on sales, i.e., operating profit margin, calculated as net income before interest and taxes over sales. This is a commonly used measure that reflects contemporaneous performance over the short run.

name: Employment level
authors_terms: ["employment", "workforce at the utility level", "log employment", "level of employment"]
definition: The workforce at the utility level, defined as the total employment at the utility, measured in logarithmic scale. Excess-and largely unproductive-employment is common in many SOEs.

name: Community poverty
authors_terms: ["community poverty", "economically disadvantaged communities", "poorer communities", "socio-economic conditions of communities"]
definition: Community poverty reflects the level of poverty in the municipality, constructed from the average income per capita in logarithmic scale, reverse coded. Communities with economically disadvantaged constituents both attract the interest of vote-seeking politicians and allow them to more effectively push SOEs to boost employment before elections.

name: Private investors in state-owned enterprises
authors_terms: ["SOEs with private investors", "presence of private investors", "private investors in SOEs"]
definition: SOEs with private investors are state-owned enterprises that have admitted private investors as minority shareholders; private investment has typically occurred through public listing and, in most cases, conceded the appointment of independent external members to the board of directors. These hybrid SOEs need to balance the interests of state and private actors.

name: Organization form
definition: Organization form distinguishes how water service is provided: state-owned enterprises are incorporated under corporate law, have their own legal status, and their organizational structure resembles that of private companies, whereas departments are conventional municipal waterworks departments controlled by local governments. The comparison group for the analyses includes private firms and local waterworks departments.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: By engaging in repeated exchange with the same partners, i.e., increasing relational embeddedness, firms reduce uncertainty. Relationships become embedded over repeated interactions, which facilitate information sharing and trust development, further increasing the embeddedness of the relationship.

name: Competitive overlap
authors_terms: ["competitive overlap", "competitive overlap increase", "increase in competitive overlap", "difference in competitive overlap"]
definition: Competitive overlap exists between two or more firms when they occupy the same space within an industry or a network, and the intensity of competition among these overlapped firms is a function of the number of similar firms (i.e., crowding) in the same space.

name: Client relationship dissolution
definition: The dependent variable, client relationship dissolution, is a dichotomous variable set to 1 if the client relationship dissolved in that year. A relationship is coded as dissolved the first year the advertising firm no longer lists the client account in its Red Books record.

name: Corporate philanthropic contributions
definition: For each firm-year, the authors recorded their dependent variable, corporate philanthropic contributions (CPC), as the total amount of grants given to charity either through a foundation or directly by the corporation.

name: Institutional equivalence
authors_terms: ["institutional equivalence", "institutional equivalents", "presence of institutional equivalents", "absence of institutional equivalents"]
definition: Institutional equivalents are organizations that are embedded in the same set of fields. In this context, two firms are institutional equivalents if they operate in the same industry and are headquartered in the same geographic community, which gives the focal firm a clear and well-defined reference category of peers to imitate.

name: Philanthropic contributions of institutional equivalents
authors_terms: ["CPC of institutional equivalents", "institutional equivalents' average giving", "philanthropic giving of institutional equivalents", "contributions of institutional equivalents"]
definition: The average level of philanthropic giving among a firm's institutional equivalents, which the authors conceptualize as its community peers that are also simultaneously its industry peers. Institutional equivalents are the primary reference group for a firm when making decisions about philanthropic giving.

name: Philanthropic contributions of industry peers
authors_terms: ["CPC of industry peers", "industry peers' giving", "philanthropic contributions of industry peers"]
definition: The average level of corporate philanthropic contributions among a firm's industry peers, defined as Fortune 1000 firms in the same two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code as the focal firm.

name: Philanthropic contributions of community peers
authors_terms: ["CPC of community peers", "CPC of local peers", "community peers' giving", "local peers"]
definition: The average level of corporate philanthropic contributions among a firm's community peers, defined as Fortune 1000 firms headquartered in the same core-based statistical area (CBSA) as the focal firm.

name: Industry-community difference
authors_terms: ["industry-community difference", "difference between the philanthropic contribution levels of industry peers and community peers", "industrycommunity difference"]
definition: The absolute value of the difference between industry peers' giving and community peers' giving; conceptually, this variable captures the degree of dissimilarity between industry and community peers' levels of philanthropy.

name: Firm size
definition: Following prior research, the authors measured firm size as sales revenue. Their argument is that large firms are more visible, receive more scrutiny, and are thus especially susceptible to institutional influences.

name: Financial performance
definition: The focal organization's financial performance, measured as return on assets (ROA). Prior literature holds that organizations with lower performance are more likely to imitate other firms because they have greater motivation to learn from others and a greater need to justify their behaviors.

name: Sense of responsibility to the community
authors_terms: ["sense of responsibility", "sense of responsibility to the community", "members' sense of responsibility"]
definition: The sense of obligation or responsibility that customers perceive as a result of their relationships with peer customers in the community, which drives collective action and helpful behavior toward others in the group.

name: Expectations of self-image enhancement
authors_terms: ["expectations of self-image enhancement", "expectations of private rewards related to reputational gains", "reputational gains"]
definition: Expectations of private rewards related to reputational gains; members who help others by sharing their expertise have the potential to enhance their prestige or status in the community, and such rewards accrue primarily to contributors.

name: Expectations of expertise enhancement
authors_terms: ["expectations of expertise enhancement", "opportunity to learn or enhance one's expertise", "learning"]
definition: Expectations of the second private reward, the opportunity to learn or enhance one's expertise in a subject area, which accrues largely to those who participate in the interactions as active involvement in problem-solving is fundamental to learning.

name: Sense of partnership with the company
authors_terms: ["sense of partnership", "sense of innovation partnership", "sense of partnership with the company"]
definition: Customers' perceptions regarding their role as the company's innovation partner, based on the extent to which information regarding the goals, processes, and outcomes of innovation has been shared with them and on quick feedback on their inputs.

name: Customer-community identification
definition: Customer-community identification, defined as the extent to which a customer relates to or perceives 'kinship' with the other members of the customer forum.

name: Customer-company identification
definition: Customer-company identification indicates the extent to which the customer relates to the overall image projected by the company, reflecting customers' perceptions of the overlap of their own values with the core or defining characteristics of the company.

name: Contribution to community
authors_terms: ["contribution to community", "contributions to the community", "contribution to the community in product support"]
definition: Customer participation in the online customer forum that involves answering peer customers' product-related queries and sharing product expertise with them, i.e. product support to peer customers.

name: Contribution to company
authors_terms: ["contribution to company", "contributions to the company", "contribution to the company in product development"]
definition: Contributions to the company by way of product improvement ideas and suggestions, i.e. product ideation directed at the host company.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: An inflated sense of self, feelings of entitlement, and a tendency to be arrogant, exploitative, and manipulative.

name: Positive tone in board risk-taking discussion
authors_terms: ["positive tone in board discussions about risk-taking", "positive risk-taking discussion", "positive affect of risk-taking discussion", "proportion of positive risk-taking discussion", "positive group affective tone"]
definition: The relative amount of positive tone versus overall tone expressed by directors in discussing risk-taking, that is, the proportion of positive affect words among all positive and negative affect words used in the board's risk-taking discussion.

name: Firm risk-taking
definition: Risk-taking expressed as a form of spending that yields uncertain returns, calculated from three forms of spending typically identified as having uncertain returns: R&D, capital expenditures, and acquisitions.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality occurs when a CEO is also the board chair and represents structural power to be the unequivocal leader of an organization.

name: Modern patent pool formation
authors_terms: ["modern patent pools", "formation of modern pools", "addition to a pool", "pooled standards"]
definition: A patent pool is an agreement between two or more parties to license their patents on a particular technology to one another and to third parties based on some fixed terms. Traditional patent pools in the United States date back to the 1850s; the first modern pool, the MPEG-2 pool, was formed in 1997 under new DOJ and FTC guidelines.

name: Follow-on innovation based on pooled standards
authors_terms: ["follow-on innovations based on the pooled technology standards", "follow-on innovation", "technological development based on the pooled standards", "subsequent innovation"]
definition: I use the number of subsequent patent citations to a patent as a proxy for the total amount of follow-on innovation built on that patent. I use the total amount of patenting in a technology subclass as a proxy for the total amount of innovative activity in that technology subclass.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Firms with downstream products are marked as vertically integrated. Nonintegrated entities include firms that do not manufacture any downstream products, universities, nonprivate research labs, and independent inventors not associated with any institution.

name: Pre-entry experience
definition: I define new entrants in a particular upstream technology market as all the firms that are granted a patent for the first time in any given technology subclass. Subsequently, I define startups as new entrants that have never patented before, and diversifying entrants as those that have previously patented in other technology subclasses.

name: Technological innovation rate
definition: I estimate the change in the patenting rate of vertically integrated firms relative to that of technology-focused upstream firms after the formation of the MPEG-2 pool. The use of publicly listed firms enables me to identify changes in the patenting rate of these firms above and beyond what would be expected from changes in their sales and R&D investments.

name: Public reputation concern
authors_terms: ["public reputation concern", "reputation concerns", "concern over public reputation", "concern with public reputation"]
definition: A director's concern over his or her public reputation as a dutiful fiduciary of shareholders' interests, an incentive to monitor insider activities in order to prevent the observable negative firm outcomes that can result from lax monitoring.

name: Director labor market concern
authors_terms: ["director labor market concern", "job prospects concern", "concern with the director labor market", "labor market concerns"]
definition: A director's concern over his or her prospects for future board positions, nomination for which is heavily influenced by powerful insiders who prefer passive and compliant independent directors.

name: Boardroom transparency
definition: The extent to which individual directors' boardroom actions are made public to external observers; the authors describe it as a reduction in the information asymmetry that exists between boards and external observers.

name: Independent director monitoring behavior
definition: The vigilance with which independent directors monitor corporate insiders; in this study it is operationalized as the director's voting choice on proposals through which insiders would extract private benefits.

name: Ties to immigrant entrepreneurs
authors_terms: ["ties to immigrant entrepreneurs", "ties to Indian immigrants", "ties to immigrants", "ties to immigrant founders"]
definition: We focus on individual immigrants and define a tie as formed when VCs invest in startups led by individual immigrants, instead of inferring potential ties based on exposure to an immigrant population. These immigrants enter the network of trusted entrepreneurs in which the VC previously invested, potentially providing information and connections that facilitate new investments for the VC.

name: Investments in the immigrants' home country
authors_terms: ["investments in India", "number of Indian startups", "foreign investments", "investments made by the VC firm in the immigrants' home country"]
definition: The first outcome of interest is the number of Indian startups in which each U.S.-based VC firm invests. We count those investments during the 5 years following the focal year.

name: Foreign investment performance
authors_terms: ["exit", "successful exit", "liquidity event", "performance of the VC firms' investments in India"]
definition: Ties to immigrant entrepreneurs should also enhance the success of VC's investments abroad. We focus here on achieving a successful exit - the third crucial activity influencing VC performance.

name: Domestic competition
authors_terms: ["total U.S. VC in preferred sector", "competition for deals in a VC firm's primary domestic market", "domestic competition", "push factor"]
definition: The push factor reflects the level of competition the firm faces domestically, which creates pressure to consider alternative investment locations. When a VC firm faces little domestic competition for startups in its desired investment segment, the imperative to consider geographic diversification is weak because the firm can source unique deals in that market.

name: Comobility
authors_terms: ["comobility", "co-mobility", "joint mobility", "joint transfers of workers", "co-movers", "move jointly with colleagues"]
definition: Joint transfers of workers, i.e., workers moving together with colleagues to a new employer. Comobility is not defined as two workers moving from one firm to another firm but from the same establishment within the sending firm to the same establishment at the receiving firm.

name: Wage gain from job mobility
authors_terms: ["wage premium", "initial wage premium", "wage gain", "change in wage"]
definition: The wage change computed as the difference of the initial (log) hourly wage at the receiving firm and the last (log) hourly wage at the sending firm. We examine the initial wage rather than subsequent wages.

name: Occupational skill level
authors_terms: ["skill level", "occupational skill level", "individual contributor, occupational skill level"]
definition: The skill level indicated by the International Standard Classification of Occupation (ISCO), which indicates occupation and skill level: 4 = Professionals; 3 = Technicians and Associate Professionals; 2 = Clerical, Service, and Sales Support, Agricultural/Forestry, Plant/Machine Operators/Assemblers; 1 = Elementary Occupations.

name: Managerial occupation
definition: Whether the worker occupies a managerial role, which the authors argue may be especially valuable in the context of comobility. Our data also identifies those in a managerial role.

name: Skill relatedness among co-movers
authors_terms: ["related skills", "related but not identical occupations", "co-movers have related occupation", "identical skills"]
definition: The interrelationship of skills among co-movers, which may be unrelated, identical, or related but not identical. Two co-movers have related skills if they share the same initial digit of the four-digit ISCO occupational code but the remaining three digits do not match.

name: Social proximity
definition: The closeness of the social association between business partners: individuals may have better access to, and superior information about, opportunities within their social networks, and after forming a partnership shared norms and discourse may improve coordination and monitoring among socially close individuals. In this study social proximity is induced by shared ethnicity between VC partners and start-up executives.

name: Investment selection
definition: The probability that a given VC invests in a given company, i.e., a VC–company match. Because the set of companies that VCs evaluated is unobserved, the authors compare actual matches with feasible but unrealized counterfactual VC–company pairs.

name: Investment acceptance threshold
definition: The quality signal at which a VC accepts a company for investment; the cutoff signal above which the VC accepts the company always signifies the same optimal posterior success probability.

name: Investment performance
definition: Investment success, measured primarily by companies' successful exits via IPOs and acquisitions. The authors also use companies' financial performance after IPOs, including net income, to measure performance for a subset of the companies for which such data are available.

name: Executive gender
definition: The gender of the newly appointed top executive; the authors state that 'Gender is coded as 1 for female and 0 for male.'

name: Stock market reaction to executive appointment announcements
authors_terms: ["stock market reactions", "investor reactions", "cumulative abnormal returns", "CARs", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Investor reaction to the announcement of a top executive appointment, measured as cumulative abnormal returns; the authors assume that investors' reactions following an announcement of an executive appointment signal their beliefs about a leader's potential and subsequent firm performance.

name: Popular press attention to a new CEO
authors_terms: ["attention in the popular press", "number of articles", "more articles written in the popular press"]
definition: The amount of popular press coverage received by a newly appointed CEO, measured as the number of articles written about the CEO during the initial year in office.

name: Media framing of CEO appointments
authors_terms: ["information that highlights gender, gender-related, job and organizational considerations", "influential words", "manifest text analysis"]
definition: The content of news reports following the announcement of a newly appointed CEO, specifically whether reports depict information that highlights gender and gender-related considerations or information that is job and organization focused.

name: Executive position level
definition: Whether the appointment is to the CEO position or to another top management team position (Chief Financial Officer, Chief Operating Officer, President, and Executive Vice President).

name: Firm insider status
authors_terms: ["firm insider", "insider/outsider status", "promoted from within the firm"]
definition: Whether the executive is promoted from within the firm rather than coming from another firm; the authors argue that insiders have more firm-specific knowledge and that compared to outsiders they are more likely to face a supportive executive team.

name: Innovative output
definition: The dependent variable for this study is the innovative output of pharmaceutical firms within biotechnology. To specifically assess the pharmaceutical firm's innovative performance in biotechnology, we proxied their innovative output by the number of biotechnology patent applications granted in each year during the 1980-2001 study period.

name: Intellectual human capital
definition: We consider intellectual human capital to be highly skilled and talented employees like research scientists, who hold advanced graduate degrees and doctorates. Thus, the total number of a firm's scientists who published in academic journals was our proxy for a firm's intellectual human capital.

name: Star scientists
definition: We understand a star scientist to be someone who is, by an order of magnitude, both more productive in and more influential on a specific research field than the average (nonstar) scientist active in this field.

name: Nonstar scientists
definition: This process also implies that the difference between total scientists and star scientists is our proxy for nonstar scientists, which we insert in the regression analysis to isolate the effect of star scientists on innovative output more fully.

name: R&D capability
definition: Following prior research (Rothaermel and Hill 2005), we proxied a pharmaceutical firm's R&D capability by its R&D expenditures, while explicitly controlling for firm revenues.

name: Biotechnology alliances
authors_terms: ["strategic alliances", "biotech alliances", "alliances with new technology providers"]
definition: Strategic alliances are voluntary arrangements between firms to exchange and share knowledge and resources with the intent of developing processes, products, or services (Gulati 1998). To document the alliances that the pharmaceutical firms entered with providers of biotechnology research, we tracked each firm's alliances with universities, research institutions, and biotechnology firms.

name: Biotechnology acquisitions
definition: Acquisitions are an increasingly important strategic tool for attaining the external technological know-how to supplement internal R&D efforts in a timely manner. Following Higgins and Rodriguez (2006), among others, we used the SDC Platinum database, published by Thomson Financial, to identify the number of biotechnology acquisitions a pharmaceutical firm had consummated during the study period.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["organizational size", "scale of operations", "annual production of automobiles"]
definition: Organizational size is conceptualized and measured as scale of operations, specifically the firm's annual production of automobiles; the authors argue that in analyses of competition, conceptualizing size as scale is more revealing than capacity of the pressures to which a firm is subjected or which it exerts on its peers.

name: Relative size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "relative position in the size distribution", "position in the size distribution"]
definition: Relative size is the ratio of each firm's size to the size of the largest firm in the national population of automobile producers at the time.

name: Aggregate distance from larger competitors
authors_terms: ["scale-based competition", "scale-based selection", "aggregate distance from larger competitors", "aggregate distance of a firm from its larger competitors"]
definition: The scale-based competitive selection pressure faced by a firm depends on the number of larger competitors it faces, who each hold a scale advantage over the smaller focal firm, as well as the distance of each larger competitor from the focal firm on the scale dimension, with distance reflecting the extent of the advantage; combining these considerations into a single organization-specific environmental measure yields the aggregate distance from larger competitors.

name: Mortality rate
authors_terms: ["mortality", "ending events", "disbanding/exit to another industry", "rate of mortality"]
definition: For automobile firm mortality or ending events, the most important distinctions concern disbanding of the firm, exit to another industry, or merger or acquisition by another firm; because of the ambiguous meaning of mergers and acquisitions, the analysis is based on disbanding and exit to another industry.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Market risk accounts for 20-30 per cent of the total risk of a stock and relates to general market trends. As shareholders can average out non-market-related risk by combining securities in portfolios, it is the risk portion of the return which remains (beta) which is of concern at the portfolio level, and beta is thus the risk measure of concern to a manager aiming to maximize the value of the firm.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Diversification in which a firm's businesses are not related from a strategic point of view, so that firms rely largely on highly general financial or managerial/control competences which are not directed specifically to the critical success factors of a given market.

name: Market power
definition: The presence of market power in a firm's respective markets; firms pursuing unrelated diversification, relying on general financial or managerial competences rather than skills directed to the critical success factors of a market, are expected to have low market power. A weighted market share index was selected as an indicator of the presence of market power.

name: Capital intensity
definition: The extent to which a firm's resources are committed to capital investments such as vertical integration or scale-intensive plants; low capital intensity means fewer heavy capital investments, and the depreciation/sales ratio was used as a measure of capital intensity.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The amount of debt in a firm's capital structure, defined as (book value of debt)/(book value of equity); diversified cash flows and increased firm size are argued to lead to increased debt positions in highly diversified firms.

name: Knowledge transfer between partners
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfers", "knowledge build-up", "the degree to which partners build upon each other's knowledge", "cross-citations", "knowledge flows"]
definition: We are mainly interested in the extent to which partners build on each other's knowledge post-formation, and measure this as the number of times partners cite each other ex post while excluding citations that originated during patent examination. The degree to which partners build on each other's knowledge derives from both firm- and dyad-specific characteristics.

name: Technology overlap
authors_terms: ["technology overlap", "similarity of the knowledge bases of the partners", "overlap in knowledge bases of the partners"]
definition: Our first explanatory variable is a measure of the firms' technology overlap and quantifies how close the partners are in technology space. Greater similarity between the focal firm and the partner's knowledge bases indicates that the partner possesses prior experience working in technology areas closely related to those of the focal firm.

name: Value of partners' knowledge
authors_terms: ["value of the partners' knowledge", "value of a firm's knowledge", "value of technological resources", "value of R&D firm knowledge", "value of client firm knowledge"]
definition: Our second explanatory variable is a partner-specific measure of the value of technological resources, which we build for the partner's patent portfolio. As the intrinsic value of a firm's knowledge increases, the opportunities created for a partner upon absorbing any spillovers, and thus the private benefits of collaboration, become more valuable for the partner.

name: Steering committee
definition: Partners can establish jointly staffed steering committee that control the activities of the alliance and contractually stipulate the design, functions and performance of these board-like structures. Such committees are authorized to form and dismiss subcommittees or project teams, to alter the conduct of activities within the scope of the alliance, and to address conflicts between the participants.

name: Board undervaluation
authors_terms: ["board undervaluation", "underutilization of directors in the board leadership roles"]
definition: Board undervaluation is the average degree to which directors' qualifications based on normatively accepted criteria for board leadership are not duly reflected in their appointments to the board chair and committee chair positions. In simpler terms, board undervaluation refers to the underutilization of directors in the board leadership roles.

name: Director undervaluation
definition: An outside director is undervalued when the director's experience, qualifications, and overall fitness according to normatively accepted criteria for chair appointments are high vis-à-vis fellow outside directors on the board but not recognized by appointments to the chair positions.

name: Director turnover
definition: Director turnover captures whether outside directors exit the firm; it is measured with a binary variable coded as 1 if any outside director exits the firm in a certain year and 0 otherwise.

name: New director qualifications
definition: The qualification index is a weighted average of the right-hand-side variables in Equation (1) where coefficients are used as weights. It is constructed for each director who was on the board in a given year-end and then averaged across all the new directors in that year.

name: Firm performance
definition: Return on assets (ROA) is an appropriate measure of firm performance in this study because it captures the efficiency with which firms generate profits using certain level of assets.

name: Forward patent citations
authors_terms: ["forward citations", "cites to patent", "patent citation rate", "highly cited patents"]
definition: Forward citations count the number of times a patent (the 'cited patent') is included in the prior art of subsequent patents. The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that patent citations contain information about a patent's technological importance, and that they can also be used as a proxy for economic value to the innovator.

name: Scientific publication quality
authors_terms: ["firm average cites to publications", "citations to a firm's publications", "quality of the firm's stock of scientific knowledge", "scientific research capabilities", "highly cited papers", "important science"]
definition: This variable captures citations to a firm's publications and is our primary measure of firm-level scientific research capabilities. The measure, therefore, represents the relative quality of the firm's stock of scientific knowledge, cumulated from the start of the publication period up to the time of the observed innovation.

name: Publication volume
authors_terms: ["publication volume", "number of firm publications", "volume of publishing"]
definition: The total number of firm publications, cumulated up to the year in which the observed patent was filed. This gives an indication of the volume of publishing.

name: Research collaboration
definition: We measure research collaboration as represented by articles in which both the firm and an outside organization are listed as institutional affiliations of one or more of the authors.

name: Science intensity
authors_terms: ["science intensity", "firm science intensity", "patent science intensity", "science intensity of firm's patents"]
definition: We measure the closeness of the firm's technologies to knowledge produced in open science. Science intensity is a 'backwards' citation count, measured as the number of times a patent references nonpatented literature in its prior art.

name: Bridging scientists
authors_terms: ["joint patent-publishers", "percent of joint patent-publishers", "bridge scientists", "technological gatekeepers"]
definition: We identify these individuals as forming a group of joint patent-publishers. We expect that this measure of overlap between scientists who publish and patent at the firm level is an important indicator of the degree to which a firm is able to successfully translate research into invention.

name: Status in the scientific community
definition: Citations to papers are an important way that scientists evaluate their relative standing, by which they exchange gifts, acknowledge prestige, and seek to prevail in their arguments.

name: Wealth creation
definition: An attempt is made to estimate the difference between actual shareholder returns post bid and the returns that would have been received in the absence of a bid. This difference, generally referred to as the abnormal return or prediction error, is taken as a measure of wealth creation, i.e., the value-enhancing effect of the bid.

name: Bid resistance
authors_terms: ["mood of the bid", "bid resistance", "MOOD", "hostile bids", "bid hostility"]
definition: The mood of a bid measures the response of target management to an offer by a raider firm and summarizes the decision-making variable under scrutiny. A bid is considered hostile if the target company publicly rejects the bid and also engages in a clear defense strategy.

name: Industrial relatedness
authors_terms: ["industrial relatedness", "INDFIT", "relatedness between bidder and target", "related bids", "unrelated bids"]
definition: INDFIT is a measure of relatedness between bidder and target. Industrial relatedness, a priori, is an important determinant of wealth creation in takeovers.

name: Target market valuation
authors_terms: ["VALR", "valuation ratio of the target firm", "market valuation of the target", "proxy for Tobin's q ratio"]
definition: VALR is the valuation ratio of the target firm and is introduced as a measure of financial performance before the bid. It is a proxy for Tobin's q ratio and is defined as the market value of the company at the end of the fourth month before the bid divided by the book value of equity.

name: Bidder-target valuation difference
authors_terms: ["VALRDIF", "difference between VALR of bidding and target companies", "difference in market valuation of bidder and target"]
definition: The second valuation variable is VALRDIF, which measures the difference between VALR of bidding and target companies.

name: Managerial share ownership
authors_terms: ["managerial share ownership", "TDIRSHR", "managerial equity in target firms", "director shareholdings"]
definition: TDIRSHR is defined as the proportion of shares of the target firm held by its directors. The ownership of vote-carrying shares by management is motivated by the desire for direct monetary gain as well as the possibility of exercising control over the company.

name: Large shareholdings
definition: LRGSHR is defined as large shareholdings held by individuals or institutions, i.e., ownership that collectively amounts to at least 5 percent of the total equity.

name: Bidder toehold
authors_terms: ["BTOEHOLD", "bidder toehold", "bidder holdings in the target firm", "shareholdings by the bidder firm"]
definition: BTOEHOLD is defined as the percentage of shares of the target company owned by the bidding company management before the bid.

name: Bidder gearing
authors_terms: ["BIDGEAR", "gearing in the bidding company", "debt in the bidder firm"]
definition: BIDGEAR measures gearing in the bidding company. Gearing is expressed in each case as total debt over the book value of total assets.

name: Gearing difference between bidder and target
authors_terms: ["GEARDIF", "difference in gearing between bidding and target company"]
definition: GEARDIF measures the difference in gearing between bidding and target company, where gearing is expressed in each case as total debt over the book value of total assets.

name: Knowledge transfer capability
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfer capability", "supplier's knowledge transfer capability", "ability to transfer knowledge", "codevelopment experience"]
definition: We define a supplier's knowledge transfer capability as its ability to identify and communicate the value of its technology and to transfer the necessary know-how to potential buyers.

name: Out-licensing
definition: The firm may exploit opportunities in this industry through licensing, which means selling the inventions to the incumbent firms of this industry ('buyers,' 'incumbents,' or 'licensees').

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: The absorptive capacity is a firm's ability to acquire, assimilate, and exploit knowledge created outside its organization (Cohen and Levinthal, 1989). High absorptive capacity is often the result of continuous R&D targeted toward monitoring and learning about new developments created by other organizations.

name: Asset cospecialization
authors_terms: ["cospecialization", "industry asset cospecialization", "cospecialized complementary assets", "cospecialization between R&D and downstream activities"]
definition: The costs (A) are a function of asset cospecialization (k), which is the extent to which commercialization requires cospecialized complementary assets, such as specialized knowledge generated during development, manufacturing, and marketing that entails a mutual dependence between development and commercialization activities.

name: Primary-line diversification
authors_terms: ["primary-line diversification", "primary product line diversity", "diversification in its primary product line", "within-business diversity", "related diversification"]
definition: Firms vary widely in the diversity of products they offer within a single industry, and a firm's primary line is the one with the highest level of sales in the prior year. This measure accounts for two elements of diversification: the number of products and the relative importance of each.

name: Primary-line product introductions
authors_terms: ["primary-line introductions", "new product introductions in its primary product line", "introducing a new product inside its primary line", "related diversification"]
definition: Additions to a firm's primary product line represent developments that are highly related to established activities. Primary-line introductions count the number of new products that a firm introduced within its primary line during the current year.

name: Outside primary-line product introductions
authors_terms: ["outside primary-line introductions", "introducing a new product outside its primary line", "less related diversification", "exploratory launches in nonprimary lines"]
definition: Introductions outside the primary line tend to be carried out by more peripheral and less dominant subgroups who are more likely to experiment with novel approaches. Outside primary-line introductions count the number of new products introduced this year that were not members of a firm's primary line.

name: Competitive and technological change
authors_terms: ["competitor introductions", "aggregate number of new product introductions by competitors", "level of competitive and technological change", "level of environmental change", "environmental flux"]
definition: In technology-intensive settings, where new product introductions are the primary vehicle of innovation, technological change, and competitive thrusts, the aggregate number of new product introductions by the other organizations in a focal firm's industry serves as a strong proxy for the level of competitive and technological change in its environment.

name: Organizational failure
definition: A firm was coded as failing in year t if it sold no personal computers in year t + 1. Failures included the deaths of entire firms and industry exits by multibusiness corporations.

name: Intangible assets
authors_terms: ["intangible assets", "intangible technological assets", "technology and product differentiation", "R&D intensity", "product differentiation"]
definition: Firm-specific intangible assets such as technology and product differentiation through branding and advertising, which tend to have the characteristics of a public good.

name: Product variability
authors_terms: ["product variability", "standardized products in large batches", "mass production technologies", "product adaptation"]
definition: The need to adapt the product to customer or, in general, national market characteristics; the authors distinguish firms manufacturing standardized products in large batches from firms making products to variable specifications.

name: Resource availability
authors_terms: ["resource availability", "the level of resources available", "size of the firm", "resources available to implement forward internalization"]
definition: The resources available to the firm to implement forward internalization, obtained internally through the use of its own cash flows or externally from the financial markets.

name: Commitment to exports
authors_terms: ["commitment to exports", "commitment to export activities", "commitment to export sales", "export intensity"]
definition: The extent to which the firm is committed to export markets for sales.

name: Competitor country development
authors_terms: ["level of development of the country where the firm's international competitors are located", "relative level of economic development of the countries where the firm's competitors are located", "competitor location development"]
definition: The relative level of economic development of the countries where the firm's competitors are located, compared with the firm's home base.

name: Export market potential
authors_terms: ["export potential of foreign markets", "growth potential of the market abroad", "potential and attractiveness of the export market", "export market potential"]
definition: The potential and attractiveness of the export market relative to the home market, as perceived or actually experienced by the firm.

name: Institutional and cognitive constraints
authors_terms: ["institutional and cognitive constraints", "perceived market access disadvantages", "perceived lack of knowledge about foreign markets", "institutional access barriers to entry", "liability of foreignness"]
definition: Obstacles in the export market classified either as institutional access barriers to entry or as perceived lack of knowledge about the foreign market.

name: Export internalization
authors_terms: ["internalization of exports", "internalization of export activities", "downstream vertical integration into the foreign market", "forward integration into foreign markets"]
definition: The firm's downstream vertical integration into the foreign market, i.e., the extent to which it locates distribution, sale, and service activities in the foreign countries in which its products are sold.

name: Internalization mode
authors_terms: ["mode of internalization", "specific institutional arrangement", "commercial alliances", "proprietary distribution"]
definition: The specific institutional arrangement chosen by the firm to internalize its export activities, distinguishing commercial alliances with a foreign partner from wholly owned proprietary distribution abroad.

name: Initial NPE litigation
definition: The first patent lawsuit filed by a non-practicing entity against a target firm, which the authors treat as a plausibly exogenous, sudden and unanticipated event; the reaction of target firms to subsequent NPE litigations might be affected by the reaction to the first one.

name: Inward innovation strategy
authors_terms: ["inward innovation strategy", "in-house patented innovations", "backward self-citations", "draw more upon their in-house technologies"]
definition: Target firms shift to a more 'inward' innovation strategy, drawing more upon their in-house technologies to reduce the potential legal ground for further NPE lawsuits; a higher number of self-citations indicates that a firm internalizes more knowledge created by its own R&D efforts.

name: External use of patented innovations
authors_terms: ["forward non-self-citations", "used less by nontarget peer firms", "forward non-self-citation"]
definition: A patent's forward non-self-citation refers to the citations made by applicants who are not the patent holders themselves; forward non-self-citations capture other (nontarget) firms' tendency to undertake follow-on R&D on the patented technologies held by the target firm.

name: Innovation costs
authors_terms: ["innovation costs", "number of inventors per patent", "more (less) inventors per patent"]
definition: The costs associated with being 'held up' by NPEs, which are higher when target firms have invested more in technologies later claimed in the NPE's patents; the authors use the number of inventors per patent as a proxy for the innovation development cost of a given patent.

name: Product market competition
definition: The risk and cost of being held up would be higher in a competitive product market in which the target firms operate, where multiple firms compete in similar technological areas; firms in such markets must respond quickly to emerging threats to survive.

name: Dynamic liability of foreignness
authors_terms: ["dynamic liability of foreignness", "time-weighted average distance", "distance with the home base", "dynamic distance between the home base and the host country"]
definition: We show that the characteristics of the home base, more so than those of home country, define the liability of foreignness that MNEs face, thus influencing the decision to enter additional foreign countries. We formulate and measure the liability of foreignness specifically for each firm as the distance between the home base and the host country.

name: Static liability of foreignness
authors_terms: ["static liability of foreignness", "static distance between the home country and the host country", "distance with the home country", "static Mahalanobis distance"]
definition: The most direct way in which scholars have conceptualized and measured the home-country effect and the liability of foreignness when considering its impact on foreign entry decisions is in terms of the distance between the home country and the host country. The liability of foreignness is higher if the host country is more distant, i.e. more different from the home country along a number of relevant dimensions.

name: Diversity of foreign experience
authors_terms: ["diversity of foreign experience", "diversity of experience", "diversity of the home base", "weighted standard deviation of distance"]
definition: Diversity of experience refers to not only the number of foreign countries a multinational has invested in, but also the diversity in institutional contexts in which it has learned to operate. When firms face idiosyncratic challenges and opportunities in different countries, they develop unique search paths and thus create routines to solve problems.

name: Foreign market entry
authors_terms: ["foreign market entry", "foreign entry", "foreign entries", "foreign direct investments"]
definition: We show that the characteristics of the home base, more so than those of home country, define the liability of foreignness that MNEs face, thus influencing the decision to enter additional foreign countries.

name: Innovative intensity
authors_terms: ["innovative intensity", "intensity of its innovative activity", "history of innovative activity", "overall level of innovative activity"]
definition: The innovative intensity variable is the total count of innovative acts during the previous five years divided by total bank assets. A firm's innovative activity comprises all of the new-to-the-firm strategic attributes, and all modifications to its existing attributes.

name: Competitor innovative intensity
authors_terms: ["other banks' innovative intensity", "competitor innovative intensity", "innovative intensity of competing banks"]
definition: The other banks' innovative intensity variable is the same five-year count of innovations by all other banks in the sample divided by the sum of their bank assets.

name: First-mover propensity
authors_terms: ["propensity to move first", "industry firsts", "firsts", "moving first", "true innovations"]
definition: A bank's propensity to move first is reflected by a count of the number of reported Australian firsts during the previous five years. The subset of adoptions or modifications that represent industry firsts are 'true innovations.'

name: Innovation focus
authors_terms: ["focus", "focused innovative activity", "degree of focus", "concentrates on one of the three innovation categories"]
definition: The focus variable is a measure of the degree to which a bank concentrates on one of the three innovation categories. It is calculated by first summing the five-year counts of product-related, process-related, and distribution-related innovative acts and then dividing each by the five-year count of total innovative acts.

name: Innovation consistency
authors_terms: ["commitment", "consistency", "year-to-year consistency in the composition of their innovative activity", "consistency of innovative activity over time"]
definition: The commitment variable reflects the year-to-year changes in each category's proportion of innovative activity. Firms that are sensitive to changes in the flow of profitable new ideas will adjust the composition of their own innovative activity from year to year as different areas become more prominent innovation sources.

name: Divergence from the industry norm
authors_terms: ["divergence", "degree of divergence", "diverges from the corresponding industry norm", "pattern mapping"]
definition: The divergence variable reflects the extent to which a firm's own innovative activity follows the corresponding industry norm. It is calculated based on the differences between the proportion of a firm's own innovative activity devoted to each category and the corresponding industry averages.

name: Financial performance
definition: The financial performance measure used to test these hypotheses is bank return on total assets (ROA). Accounting rates of return are used extensively by scholars examining the dynamics of firm profitability.

name: Executive social capital
authors_terms: ["executive social capital", "executives' social capital", "executive social capital endowments"]
definition: The web of an executive's personal ties with external stakeholders. The authors limit executive social capital to outward networks, that is, connections with outside stakeholders beyond their firms, and capture the effects of inward connections separately as peer social capital.

name: Peer social capital
definition: The social capital of other executives and directors in the declining firm.

name: Alliance network
authors_terms: ["alliance network", "firm's alliance network", "firm alliance network", "firms' alliance networks"]
definition: The web of collaborative relationships between the declining firm and its inter-firm partners.

name: Ship jumping
definition: Voluntary exit from the declining firm and accepting employment elsewhere. The authors capture it as the proactive departure from the company in the 2 years prior to its *ST announcement.

name: Prior board experience at the focal firm
authors_terms: ["prior board experience at the focal firm", "prior focal board experience"]
definition: Prior board experience at the focal firm refers to a new CEO's experience of serving on the board of the focal firm before becoming the CEO.

name: Prior board experience at other firms
authors_terms: ["prior board experience at other firms", "prior other board experience"]
definition: Prior board experience at other firms refers to a new CEO's experience of serving on the board of other firms before becoming the CEO.

name: Strategic change
definition: We conceptualized strategic change as reallocations of resources across a set of important strategic domains in the firm and used changes in the following six key strategic dimensions to measure strategic change.

name: Social status
definition: Social status is the standing, worth, esteem, or prestige of an actor arising from its position in a given setting-that is, its relationships to others. A firm's social status depends on the social status of the other firms or actors to which it relates.

name: Brokerage advantage
definition: Brokerage advantage refers to the benefits obtained from regulating information flows. A broker benefits from its ability to bring together separate groups from opposite sides of the 'structural holes' in a network.

name: Foreign market entry
authors_terms: ["foreign market entry", "rate of foreign market entry", "entry"]
definition: The dependent variable (an event) equaled 1 if firm i entered country j during year t. Each venture capital firm was at risk of entering a country during a given year.

name: Presence of home country partners
authors_terms: ["presence of a home country partner", "presence of syndicate partners in each country"]
definition: We measured the presence of firm i's syndicate partners in country j with a dummy variable coded 1 if any of firm i's syndicate partners in its home country network had made at least one investment in country j up until year t - 1.

name: Long-tenured independent director presence
definition: We define a long-tenured independent director (LTID) as one with tenure of 15 years or more, coinciding closely with both the mean and median tenure of the longest-serving independent board member of the firms in our data. LTID is an indicator variable taking the value 1 if, in a given year, a firm has an independent director with tenure of 15 years or more.

name: Firm performance
definition: Tobin's q, that is, the ratio of the market value of a firm's assets to their replacement value, is a standard forward-looking measure of firm performance across the social sciences and is particularly appropriate to test our theory because it reflects the market's collective perspective of the value the LTID's presence will add by, in part, protecting against strategic and leadership errors.

name: Firm complexity
definition: Advice, such as that provided by an LTID, is intuitively more valuable to the CEO and other top managers if the firm's operations and strategic situation are inherently complex. We calculate the indicator Complex based on firm complexity from Coles et al. (2008), which is derived from a factor analysis of three observable firm attributes that make firm governance more complicated and thus boards more useful: diversification, size, and leverage.

name: Firm maturity
definition: An LTID will be most useful for firm performance if the firm is mature, that is, if it is in the stable stage of its lifecycle. We define the indicator Mature to correspond to the so-named stage in the eight-stage firm lifecycle classification system developed by Dickinson (2011).

name: Number of CEOs during the longest-serving director's tenure
definition: Number CEOs is a count of how many CEOs the firm's longest-tenured director (who may or may not be an LTID) has served with at the firm. The more CEOs with whom an LTID has worked during her tenure, the greater the number of leadership styles and strategies she will have seen implemented at her firm and thus the more valuable her experience.

name: Managerial entrenchment
definition: Entrenchment of top management is a primary concern of those who study boards with an agency lens. We measure Entrenchment using the index created for this purpose by Bebchuk et al. (2009) ... This index is a count of how many of the following provisions a firm has, where a higher number indicates that the firm's management is more entrenched, because the provision makes it harder to replace them.

name: Supply of first-generation ethnic migrant inventors
authors_terms: ["supply of first-generation ethnic migrant inventors", "first-generation ethnic migrant inventors", "New Ethnic Inventors", "Chinese/Indian inventors"]
definition: First-generation ethnic migrant inventors are residents of the home regions of the knowledge in question who migrate themselves to the host firm. The authors argue they have both the absorptive capacity and the career incentives to transfer to their host firms knowledge previously locked within the cultural contexts of their home regions.

name: Codification of home-region knowledge
authors_terms: ["rate of codification", "codification of herbal knowledge", "herbal patenting", "Log Patent Count"]
definition: The rate at which knowledge previously locked within the cultural context of ethnic migrant inventors' home region is codified at their host firms, observed for this setting as herbal patenting by U.S. assignees.

name: Inventor team ethnic composition
authors_terms: ["Fully Ethnic", "Nonethnic", "Mixed Team", "teams composed solely of ethnic migrants", "teams that include nonethnic inventors"]
definition: Indicator variables specifying whether the set of inventors on a patent is uniformly Chinese/Indian (Fully Ethnic), uniformly non-Chinese/Indian (Nonethnic), or of mixed ethnicity (Mixed Team).

name: Knowledge reuse
definition: In this setting, the authors frame knowledge reuse as the ethnic migrant inventor's appropriation of knowledge from the home country and codification of that knowledge in the new context of a western firm. They build on prior work designating 'recombinant reuse' as reconfiguring combinations already known to the firm.

name: Knowledge recombination
definition: In this context recombination is more likely to consist of recombinant creation, or recombining knowledge components from the western context with knowledge components previously embedded in the ethnic migrant inventor's home region.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "performance above aspirations", "peer social performance comparison", "internal social performance comparison", "historical performance comparison", "social aspirations", "historical aspirations", "performance shortfalls"]
definition: Performance aspirations are reference levels for business unit performance: historical comparisons use the prior performance of a focal unit to determine aspirations, while social comparisons use the performance of similar peers to determine aspirations. Each comparison is measured as current business unit return on assets minus the relevant reference level of return on assets.

name: Overinvestment
authors_terms: ["overinvestment", "overinvestment in response to performance below aspirations"]
