definition: Overinvestment is defined as the allocation of relatively more capital to business units with relatively worse risk-adjusted prospects for future growth.

name: Underinvestment
authors_terms: ["underinvestment", "underinvestment in response to performance above aspirations"]
definition: Underinvestment is the allocation of relatively less capital to business units with relatively better risk-adjusted growth prospects.

name: Variance in business unit performance
authors_terms: ["variance in business unit performance comparisons", "variance in performance discrepancies", "performance dispersion", "VPC"]
definition: The variance in business unit performance comparisons, measured separately for each performance comparison and only for firms with two or more business units.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack, or resource abundance, refers to resources that have not been committed or deployed in the system and are available for the discretionary use of management. In the context of capital allocation it is best represented by cash flow, resources available for investment.

name: Ownership transfers
authors_terms: ["ownership transfers", "ownership transfers in these other zips", "transfers"]
definition: Ownership transfers are cases in which new owners undertake operation of existing business outlets. We argue that ownership transfers generate and release vicarious information.

name: Exit-entry pairs
authors_terms: ["exit-entry pairs", "contemporaneous exit-entry pairs", "exit-entry pairs in these other zips"]
definition: Exit-entry pairs are cases in which an entry is matched by an exit during the same time period in the same market. More so than cases of exit or entry alone, exit-entry pairs give others the opportunity to learn vicariously.

name: Outlet exit
definition: We define an event as an outlet exit only if the outlet shuts down or the location converts to an entirely different type of business. We do not consider outlets to have exited merely due to changes of ownership or business name, as long as someone is operating the same type of business at that location.

name: Participation in regulatory design
authors_terms: ["participation", "participation in the regulatory design process", "providing comments on a draft regulation", "submission of comments by firms on draft versions of government regulations"]
definition: The particular form of participation we examine in this paper is submission of comments by firms on draft versions of government regulations that aim to limit the negative effects of business operations on workers, communities, and the natural environment.

name: Government responsiveness
authors_terms: ["government responsiveness", "responsiveness to participation", "Participation with Government Response", "Effective Participation"]
definition: We propose an important contingency to help explain these mixed results on how firm participation in the regulatory design process affects regulatory compliance: whether or not the participating firm sees government as responsive to its input. The legitimacy mechanism underlying Hypothesis 1 (H1) rests upon a simple but important assumption: participating firms must feel that the input they provide matters to government.

name: Regulatory compliance
definition: We operationalize our key outcome of interest, a firm's regulatory compliance, in four ways. All four of these variables capture compliance with Vietnam's Labor Code, which was passed on June 18, 2012 and went into effect on May 1, 2013, just two months before implementation of our survey.

name: Government legitimacy
definition: We construct a latent measure representing firm perceptions of government legitimacy using the following indicators from the PCI survey. In sum, we separate perceptions of legitimacy into three components: (1) overall attitude of the authorities; (2) whether authorities abuse their positions; and (3) fairness in application of government rules.

name: Decision centralization
authors_terms: ["decision centralization", "decision (de)centralization", "centralization of decision rights", "centralized decision making (CDM)", "decentralized decision making (DDM)"]
definition: Whether rights to make group decisions are centralized in a specific member rather than shared through majority voting; the authors state that 'We hypothesize that centralization of decision rights: whether rights to make group decisions are centralized in a specific member ... will weaken the aggregation effects.' In the DDM condition a group of participants makes a decision based on a majority rule, whereas in the CDM condition a group decision is made by its leader, who is randomly assigned and fixed for the entire game.

name: Update rate
authors_terms: ["update rate", "degree of recency", "rate of adjusting beliefs toward feedback", "φ"]
definition: The extent to which a learner adjusts beliefs toward feedback, i.e., the weight on performance feedback in an exponentially weighted average of existing belief and recent feedback; as it increases, recent feedback is given greater weight, beliefs are adjusted to new information more quickly and the influence of old experiences fades away more rapidly (shorter memory span).

name: Exploration rate
definition: A tendency to deviate from maximizing choices in current beliefs, i.e., the degree to which action selection depends less on the subjective valuation of the options; when it is high, choice depends less on subjective valuations and the learner explores more.

name: Learning performance
definition: The proportion of good investment decisions, i.e., choosing the option with the higher success probability, grouped into time blocks.

name: Political ties
authors_terms: ["political ties", "organizational ties to political stakeholders", "relationships with political stakeholders"]
definition: We coded a firm as having political ties if one of its large shareholders, board members, or top firm officers was a member of the legislature or the national or provincial executive; a cabinet member or agency chief; or a close relative (such as a sibling or spouse) of a top politician.

name: Military ties
authors_terms: ["military ties", "organizational ties to military stakeholders", "firm-military relationships"]
definition: In contrast to political ties that provide ventures access to financial and policy resources, we propose that because of the military's coercive power, the key resource that can derive from firm-military relationships is security, in the form of either physical or symbolic protection.

name: Venture survival
definition: We examine the impact of these relationships on survival because most ventures fail within the first few years, and because organizational survival is a precondition for profitability and growth.

name: Declining economic environment
definition: We measured declining economic environment using the average change in imports and exports over a four-year running average.

name: Political effectiveness
definition: Another factor that may differentially moderate the benefits of government stakeholder relationships is their political effectiveness, or stakeholders' ability to credibly enact or alter policy.

name: Armed conflict
definition: We measured armed conflict using the yearly sum of incidents of armed activity and violence that resulted in at least 500 directly related deaths over the course of a year.

name: Political revolutions
definition: At the extreme end are political revolutions, defined as forceful extraconstitutional changes to the power structure of a regime where one polity replaces another.

name: Monitoring effectiveness
definition: In this article, we expand firm-level notions of monitoring to include large institutional owners' investment portfolios and suggest that portfolio characteristics affect owners' motivation and capacity to monitor, which compromises the positive effects of monitoring at the firm level. Our framework differentiates the monitoring effectiveness of large investors on the basis of their ability to monitor a focal firm and their incentives to monitor, as reflected by their portfolio structure.

name: Largest institutional owner stake
authors_terms: ["largest institutional owner stake", "large institutional ownership at the firm level", "percentage ownership of the largest owner", "ownership of the largest institutional owner"]
definition: Following Thomsen and Pedersen (2000), we measure this variable as the percentage of shares owned by the largest institutional owner (top institutional owner's shares divided by firm's total number of outstanding shares) in the focal firm. As the percentage of shares owned increases, owners can exercise more influence over the firm and monitor more effectively.

name: Portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["portfolio concentration", "average portfolio holdings", "average holdings", "size of portfolio holdings"]
definition: Following Bushee (1998) we measure this variable as the average value of the investments in the institutional owner's portfolio. Thus, it measures the tendency of the top institutional investor to hold large stakes in its portfolio.

name: Portfolio blockholding
authors_terms: ["portfolio blockholding", "portfolio blockholdings", "proportion of blockholdings in the portfolio"]
definition: This variable measures the tendency of the top institutional blockholder to invest in large blocks. Therefore, this variable provides a more conservative measure of the propensity of the largest institutional investor to monitor firms in its portfolio other than the focal firm.

name: Portfolio turnover
authors_terms: ["portfolio turnover", "institutional ownership turnover at the portfolio level"]
definition: This variable measures the trading behavior of the largest institutional investor. Investors with high portfolio turnover could be less prone to hold stocks over longer time periods and thus less likely to engage in costly monitoring efforts.

name: Firm significance in portfolio
authors_terms: ["firm significance in the portfolio", "portfolio firm significance", "significance of the target firm within the portfolio", "significance of the firm in the portfolio"]
definition: This variable reflects the percentile ranking of the focal firm in the portfolio of its largest owner, based on the dollar value of the investments. The measure is inversed, so a higher number indicates that the focal firm is of greater importance to the institutional owner.

name: Gatekeeper consideration of contestation
authors_terms: ["Vogue consideration of contestation over fur", "Vogue consideration of contestation over fur use", "gatekeeper consideration of external contestation over fur use", "gatekeeper discourse on ethics", "Vogue's consideration of contestation over fur use", "consideration of external contestation over the practice from prominent gatekeepers"]
definition: To measure gatekeeper discourse regarding societal contestation over the ethics of fur use and related production concerns, we analyzed the text of Vogue runway collection reports over time. Editors provide contextual notes and commentary on the designer's conceptual approach and inspiration.

name: Use of a contested cultural practice
authors_terms: ["use of a cultural practice", "fur use", "use of fur in runway collections", "use of fur"]
definition: Our outcome variable was a dichotomous indicator equal to one if a fashion house used fur in a given year and zero otherwise. We determined whether a fashion house used fur in each year's Fall or Spring collections using Vogue's runway reports.

name: Antifur social movement activism
authors_terms: ["antifur social movement action", "antifur social movement activism", "antifur events", "antifur collective action"]
definition: Our measure antifur social movement action counts events targeting the fashion houses in all four countries in the prior year. Events covered in multiple newspapers or articles were counted once in the analysis.

name: Fashion house status
definition: Our measure of fashion house status reflects industry insiders' assessments of fashion houses' relative social position and is based on the hiring of fashion models by fashion houses each season. Higher-status houses have higher centrality; they overlap in their hiring of higher-status models.

name: Tacitness of overseas information
authors_terms: ["extent of tacitness in overseas information acquired", "degree of tacitness in overseas information", "tacit overseas knowledge"]
definition: Tacit overseas knowledge is 'the knowledge of the differences among overseas markets that is difficult to codify and transfer in a systematic way.' When information about the differences among countries was more complex, less codifiable, and more difficult to observe, that information was considered more tacit and less explicit.

name: Cross-national teams
definition: Cross-national teams co-locate the managers who possess the requisite tacit overseas information with other managers who can assist in interpreting that information and applying it in product design.

name: Prior overseas experience of team members
authors_terms: ["teams with domestic members who have prior overseas experience", "prior overseas experience"]
definition: Such experience provides the team with a greater ability to make sense of new country-specific information, to absorb it effectively, and to apply it to the creation of new knowledge.

name: Frequency of communication with overseas managers
authors_terms: ["frequency of communication between team members and overseas managers", "communication intensity"]
definition: Communication intensity is measured as the frequency of interactions between project members and overseas managers via telephone, fax, and e-mail.

name: Transnational new product development capability
definition: 'The ability to consistently and successfully introduce new products simultaneously in multiple country markets.' The authors focus on consistency, success, and simultaneity of new product introductions.

name: Business performance
definition: Following Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1987), this measure captured multiple dimensions of business performance-namely, how satisfied managers were, vis-à-vis their competitors, with their division's growth in sales, growth in market share, return on investment and return on sales.

name: Prior communication experience
definition: Communication between the acquiring and acquired firms in the pre-acquisition stage, which can provide information that alleviates both operational and behavioral challenges to value creation. When acquired and acquiring firms have engaged in prior communication, the increased flow of information and creation of social norms enable a smoother transition to activities performed within the integrated organizational design.

name: Prior resource allocation experience
definition: Joint resource allocation decisions made by the managers of the two firms in the pre-acquisition stage, which provide hands-on knowledge of the task and partner-specific absorptive capacity. The task-based incentives drive resource allocation choices by the partners.

name: Pre-acquisition organizational architecture
definition: The type of prior relationship between target and acquiring firm, which flows from the potential combinations of organizational architectural elements: an organizational structure associated with the ability to communicate and an organizational structure associated with resource allocation. The four types are complete alliance, allocation only, communication only, and outright acquisition.

name: Post-acquisition performance
definition: Post-acquisition performance is determined by many factors; in this study the authors focus on post-acquisition coordination, i.e., the coordination of value-creating combined activities among the acquired and existing divisions after the dissolution of firm boundaries.

name: Equality of value appropriation
authors_terms: ["value appropriation", "equitable sharing of the value created", "relative contributions"]
definition: The relative contributions and hence benefits appropriated by the alliance partners when a payoff-dominant equilibrium is reached; for acquisitions that achieve payoff-dominant outcomes, examination of the relative contributions of the various parties determines whether the value is being appropriated equally or unequally.

name: Pre-acquisition alliance performance
authors_terms: ["pre-acquisition alliance performance", "prior success", "success in the alliance stage", "pre-acquisition value-creation success"]
definition: Value-creation success in the pre-acquisition alliance stage, that is, whether the threshold value of resources allocated to the combined activities was met during the pre-acquisition stage.

name: Pre-acquisition contribution routines
authors_terms: ["pre-acquisition contribution ratio", "resource allocation routines (value allocation) established in a pre-acquisition alliance", "contribution ratio in alliance stage"]
definition: The resource allocation (contribution) routines established between the alliance partners in the pre-acquisition stage, captured by the relative contributions of the managers in successful alliance-stage rounds.

name: Post-acquisition contribution routines
authors_terms: ["post-acquisition contribution ratio", "resource allocation routines adopted in the new, integrated organizational context"]
definition: The relative contributions of the managers to the combined activities after the acquisition, reflecting whether the resource allocation routines formed in the alliance stage are retained in the integrated organizational context.

name: Signal credibility
definition: The construct captures the extent to which an observer can correctly interpret a signal as a reliable indicator of quality in a population of firms; the authors formally define signal credibility as the correlation between a signal and quality for an entire population of firms at a given point in time.

name: Signal accuracy
definition: The term denotes the extent to which a specific organization emits a signal consistent with its underlying quality.

name: Signal variance
authors_terms: ["variance of signals", "signal variance", "variance in warranty coverage", "variance in signaling choices", "high variance", "low variance"]
definition: The dispersion of the signals generated by the members of a population; whereas separation yields variance in signals within a population, pooling implies no variance, and low variance can accompany highly similar but uninformative signals.

name: Warranty coverage
definition: When providing a warranty, the seller in effect enters into a contract with the buyer that the product or service sold will satisfactorily perform its intended function when properly used; the authors focus on the mileage and duration of the coverage offered.

name: Product quality
definition: The underlying quality of the vehicles produced, which the authors operationalize through reliability as reported by Consumer Reports, whose automobile reviews 'focus strictly and solely on reliability as an indicator of quality'.

name: Institutional prevalence
authors_terms: ["institutional prevalence", "prevalence of a particular name attribute"]
definition: Institutional prevalence was measured as the pervasiveness of a particular name attribute within institutional fields, a measure the authors describe as consistent with prior institutional research and as one principal indicator of the strength of mimetic processes.

name: Prior name attributes
authors_terms: ["old name's length", "old name's ambiguity", "old name's domain specificity", "attributes of an old organizational name"]
definition: Three attributes of old organizational names, length, ambiguity, and domain specificity, were measured in the same manner as for new names.

name: New name attributes
authors_terms: ["new name's length", "new name's ambiguity", "new name's domain specificity", "attributes of a new organizational name"]
definition: The attributes encoded in the new organizational name: name length, name ambiguity (use of fictitious or unfamiliar words), and domain specificity (use of specific identity descriptors).

name: Symbolic isomorphism
definition: The resemblance of an organization's symbolic attributes to those of other organizations within its institutional field; in study 2 it is measured as organizational conformity to institutionalized naming practices.

name: Understandability
definition: Following Suchman's conceptualization that organizations are legitimate when they are understandable, the authors used understandability as a measure of legitimacy, as it reflects a cognitive orientation to constitutive or binding rules such as those characterizing naming practices.

name: Audience orientation
definition: Whether audience members have experience in, or educational or professional affiliation with, utilitarian organizations, which emphasize economic rationality and efficiency, as opposed to ideological organizations, which emphasize cultural, aesthetic, or expressive functions.

name: Stakeholder regulatory sanctions
authors_terms: ["stakeholder regulatory sanctions", "stakeholder-related regulatory sanctions", "involvement in stakeholder regulatory sanctions", "violations of stakeholder rights"]
definition: Violation Tracker gathers information on regulatory violations of stakeholder rights, such as those concerning consumer protection, employee wages, discrimination, environmental protection, trade violations, and other issues.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Our dependent variable, CEO dismissal, is coded 1 if a CEO is dismissed in a year, 0 otherwise; the underlying data documents the reasons for CEO departure (e.g., voluntary, involuntary).

name: CEO communion
definition: Communion reflects the focus on integrating oneself into the larger social unit by caring for others and the motive 'to be part of a community, to establish close relationships with others, and to subordinate individual needs to the common good'.

name: CEO agency
definition: Agency reflects the focus on individuation, personal goals, and the motive 'to be independent, to control one's environment, and to assert, protect, and expand one's self'.

name: CSR efforts
definition: The growing emphasis on CSR reflects a broader focus on stakeholders over CEOs' personal interests, serving as a key indicator of CEOs' commitment to stakeholder concerns; the database collects ratings of CSR 'strengths' (positive qualities) and 'concerns' (negative issues) across areas such as product quality, employee relations, community relations, diversity, and environment.

name: Media sentiment
authors_terms: ["media sentiment", "favorable media sentiment", "media coverage", "composite sentiment score"]
definition: The media plays a pivotal role as an information intermediary for stakeholders; media coverage functions as a broader contextual factor, offering external validation or social approval for boards when evaluating CEOs, and media sentiment serves the role of reinforcing or weakening these expectations.

name: Political ties to the ruling party
authors_terms: ["ties to the ruling party", "political ties to the ruling party", "political ties with KMT", "political ties with the DPP"]
definition: Ties a business group maintains with the political party that controls government power. The ruling party of a united government is a high-power and prominent partner for firms because it allocates resources and shapes the regulatory environment; under divided government the ruling party controls only the executive branch.

name: Political ties to opposition parties
authors_terms: ["ties to opposition parties", "political ties with opposition parties", "opposition party with legislative authority"]
definition: Ties a business group maintains with political parties that do not control the executive. Opposition parties under a united government are low-power partners because of the lack of mandatory influence, whereas in a divided government the opposition party with legislative authority is comparably powerful because it affects laws and rules via legislative power.

name: Portfolio diversity of political ties
authors_terms: ["diversity of a portfolio of political ties", "portfolio diversity", "diverse portfolio of political ties"]
definition: The diversity of a firm's portfolio of political ties, computed with the Blau Index of Variability as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of a focal business group's ties with each of the political parties. A diverse portfolio of ties with different political parties suggests that the focal firm's target is multiple political parties, whereas a focused portfolio implies more concentrated political tactics.

name: Entry into unrelated industries
authors_terms: ["entry into new industries", "entry into unrelated industries", "unrelated diversification", "number of entries"]
definition: Entry into industries that are new to the group's industrial profile: groups entered unrelated industries if those 2-digit industries that were not present at time t appeared at time t + 2 in their industrial profiles.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The debt ratio of a firm indicates its dependence on external financial resources; highly leveraged firms have greater dependence on such resources relative to counterparts with low debt ratios.

name: Market entry experience
authors_terms: ["experience in market entry", "experience in market entry"]
definition: Experience in market entry represents a firm's internal capability of market entry: market entry is a learning-by-doing process that allows firms to develop the internal capability to execute projects and to accumulate and deploy tacit knowledge for setting up new operations across different industries, reducing their dependence on political ties.

name: Indications of rivals' strategic stakes
authors_terms: ["indications of rivals' strategic stakes", "reexamination certificates", "patent reexamination certificates", "'keep out' signs"]
definition: Indications, in the form of patent reexamination certificates issued to rivals, of the strategic stakes rivals hold within a technological space. They indicate where rivals' strategic stakes lie rather than what they are, without materially increasing the details of the patented technology revealed to the public.

name: Inventive effort
definition: A firm's allocation of research and development effort across technological spaces, where technological space is 'an area of potential research and development (R&D) investments where the resultant inventions have similar nature and usage'.

name: Downstream capabilities
authors_terms: ["downstream capabilities", "production capabilities", "product market and distribution abilities"]
definition: Rivals' production systems, product market and distribution abilities that allow them to quickly test and implement technologies and to capture subsequent innovative opportunities. 'Rivals' existing production systems allow them to quickly test and implement technologies and generate a high volume of resultant products to spread fixed cost rapidly and capture market share within a short period of time.'

name: Relative downstream capabilities
authors_terms: ["rivals' downstream capabilities relative to the focal firm's downstream capabilities", "how these downstream capabilities compare to the focal firm's own downstream capabilities"]
definition: Rivals' downstream capabilities considered relative to the focal firm's own downstream capabilities, which shapes the focal firm's assessment of whether it is too late to subsequently allocate inventive effort in a technological space populated by these rivals.

name: Litigation experiences
definition: Rivals' accumulated experience with patent litigation, which enhances their abilities to detect infringements, navigate the different courts and corresponding processes, manage settlements, and so forth.

name: Type-based related alliance experience
definition: Type-based related experience, defined by the amount of experience derived from past alliances that resemble the current alliance with respect to the functional type. Functionally related experience increases the firm's ability to form and manage alliances in a specific domain such as in marketing or R&D.

name: Partner industry-based related alliance experience
definition: We attempt to measure related experience based on partners' industry focus. Previous relationships with partners in a particular industry can be more instrumental if the new partner is also from the same industry than if it is from a different one.

name: Type-based experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["type-based experiential diversity", "type-based diversity in alliance experience"]
definition: Experiential diversity may be viewed as the breadth of alliance experience, measured here based on the functional type of the alliance. Diverse experience based on a variety of functional types can add value to future alliances.

name: Partner industry-based experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["partner industry-based experiential diversity", "partner industry-based diversity in alliance experience"]
definition: Experiential diversity measured based on the industry of the alliance partners. Experience based on a diverse array of industries can assist the firm in reducing uncertainties in forming and managing alliances with partners from a particular industry.

name: IT-enabled knowledge integration capability
authors_terms: ["IT-enabled knowledge integration capability", "IT enablement", "IT-enabled knowledge integration"]
definition: We measured IT-enabled knowledge integration capability (IT enablement) by the extent to which a firm uses IT-based tools to capture and codify knowledge. IT-enabled capabilities in knowledge integration can help the firm better institutionalize alliance know-how accumulated from previous alliances.

name: Ex ante value gains from an alliance
authors_terms: ["ex ante value gains", "abnormal stock market returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "incremental value expected from an alliance"]
definition: Abnormal returns have been widely used as a measure for the incremental value expected from an alliance, i.e., ex ante value gains. Given the data challenge in finding a direct measure for alliance performance, abnormal returns represent a sufficient measure at the alliance level to capture the incremental value expected from an alliance.

name: Strategic human capital departure
definition: Employees with valuable, rare, inimitable, and nonsubstitutable knowledge, skills, and abilities are referred to as strategic human capital (SHC). The paper examines the departure of these employees, emphasizing that it is important to distinguish between the departure of strategic and non-SHC.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measure firm performance as return on assets (ROA), that is, net income divided by total assets.

name: Employee-firm relationship strength
authors_terms: ["EF relationship strength", "employee-firm (EF) relationship", "employee relations", "relationship-based employee governance mechanisms"]
definition: Relationship-based employee governance mechanisms foster trust and commitment between the firm and its employees, and provide benefits in terms of increased efficiency, productivity, cooperation, and innovation. The strength of this relationship reflects how much a firm invests in building and maintaining relationships with its employees.

name: Proximity to a nuclear facility
authors_terms: ["Nuclear proximity", "close proximity to a nuclear facility", "firms located within 50 miles of any operating nuclear plant"]
definition: Whether a firm is located in close geographical proximity to an operating nuclear plant in the United States rather than farther away. Firms located within 50 miles of any operating nuclear plant are considered as the treatment group companies.

name: Novel partner selection
authors_terms: ["novel supplier selection", "novel partner adoption", "novel external partner selection", "interorganizational tie novelty"]
definition: The selection of an external partner with whom the firm has not previously partnered, a tie that can provide new sources of knowledge but that entails risk because of altercentric uncertainty and the absence of established routines. The authors identify novel partners by capturing when a supplier is used for the first time within the focal technology category in the company's records.

name: Initiator formal power
authors_terms: ["initiator formal power", "formal power of the initiator"]
definition: The formal power held by the person who initiates a supplier proposal, rooted in the formal structure, defined as the set of codified rules, processes, and procedures that control and coordinate resources and activities. Formal power is backed by legitimate authority, is bestowed through explicit processes, and is therefore relatively uncontested.

name: Initiator informal power
authors_terms: ["initiator informal power", "informal power of the initiator"]
definition: The informal power held by the person who initiates a supplier proposal, derived from informal organization, defined as the emergent patterns of individual behavior and interaction among individuals, as well as the norms, values, and beliefs that underlie such behaviors and interactions. Informal power is measured as a function of one's prior interactions in time-varying collaboration networks and is subjective, transient, and more likely to be perceived as contestable.

name: Teammate formal power
definition: The formal power held by the initiator's teammates, the team members who react to the initiator's proposal by supporting or challenging it. Teammates in positions of formal power are more likely to demand (or preemptively receive) justifications for risky proposals and are more likely to challenge risky proposals than teammates who lack formal power.

name: Teammate informal power
definition: The informal power held by the initiator's teammates. Teammates in positions of informal power are more likely to challenge risky proposals given their own concerns about losing power, and they may be more assertive in demanding justification for risky projects, in comparison with teammates who lack informal power.

name: Geographic distance between exchange partners
definition: Geographic distance between parties greatly increases exchange challenges. Information transfer between parties is more difficult with greater geographic distance and leads to increased exchange uncertainty.

name: Measurement difficulty
authors_terms: ["measurement difficulty", "quality of project output is difficult to measure", "cost of measuring quality after project completion"]
definition: For certain deliverables, quality is not readily apparent ex post. Measurement difficulty means the cost of measuring the quality of project output after project completion is high.

name: Prior relationship breadth in other lines of business
authors_terms: ["prior relationships in other lines of business", "relationship breadth", "breadth"]
definition: If prior relationships exist in other lines of business (i.e., the buyer procures goods or services from other supplier business units), the buyer is especially important to the supplier, given the project portfolio. Relationship breadth captures the extent of non-IT services provided by Compustar for each customer.

name: Reusable technology
definition: Buyers are also particularly important to suppliers when the technology in a focal exchange can be reused (with minor modifications) for other potential projects. Reuse means a project has the potential to produce knowledge that Compustar could reuse for projects with other customers.

name: Duration safeguard framing
authors_terms: ["duration safeguard framing", "contract framing", "extendibility provision", "early termination provision"]
definition: When a buyer and supplier include a duration safeguard in their contract, they must decide on whether to frame it as an extendibility provision (i.e., a shorter contract with an option to extend) or an early termination provision (i.e., a longer contract with the option to terminate early). Only the decision at the project milestone (i.e., whether to terminate or extend) differs between the two provisions.

name: Downstream complementary assets
authors_terms: ["downstream complementary assets", "DCAs", "stock of downstream complementary assets", "stock of complementary assets"]
definition: We define downstream complementary assets (DCAs) as those assets that are used in 'sales and distribution' of a product (Teece, 1988: 266) and in providing 'training, support, and servicing' to customers (Teece, 1986: 298).

name: Matching novel performance features
authors_terms: ["matching the novel performance features of the disruptive product", "matching the flexibility of the disruptive product", "Matching Disruptive Products"]
definition: The extent to which the values of the four performance features in a U.S. product matched the combination of the performance features in the most flexible disruptive product in a product class.

name: Technological diversity
authors_terms: ["technological diversity", "partner technological diversity", "diversity of partner technological capabilities", "capability diversity"]
definition: Technological diversity is measured by the extent to which alliance partners patent in the same technology classes, and effectively captures the technological position of one partner firm relative to another. It is akin to measuring the angle between the individual vectors that represent the patent portfolios of allying firms.

name: Firm innovative performance
definition: Using the compiled patent data, the authors measure each firm's innovative output after alliance commencement via a count of citation-weighted firm patents in a four-year postalliance window, labeled postalliance patents. Patents are treated as reasonably reliable indicators of innovative performance.

name: Alliance organizational form
definition: In organizing their alliance activities, firms choose among alternative forms; the authors focus on two: bilateral contract and equity joint venture. A bilateral contract pools capabilities without a separate legal identity, whereas an equity joint venture creates a new entity jointly owned and operated by the collaborating firms.

name: Communal threats
authors_terms: ["communal threats", "perceived communal threats", "category-directed protests and lawsuits"]
definition: Communal threats target the entire market category. They pose an equal risk of negative consequences for all members in the new market category.

name: Individual threats
definition: Individual threats target individual entrepreneurs. They have unequal impacts on a focal venture and its competitors.

name: Collective identity promulgation
authors_terms: ["promulgation of the promoted collective identity", "entrepreneurial promotion of the collective identity", "renewable-energy identity frames", "renewable-energy identity framing"]
definition: The efforts of ventures to promote frames aligned with the promoted identity narrative of the market category; in this setting the renewable-energy frame projected an identity related to environmental sustainability and renewable-biomass energy. An entrepreneurial collective identity is an intersubjective shared attribute that defines a collection of ventures operating in a particular market category.

name: Peer framing
definition: Peer framing is the extent to which the focal entrepreneur's peer group engages in promulgating the same collective identity.

name: Industry churn
definition: Studies of industry churn highlight a dynamic environment with a high rate of entries and exits as a key process with which to explain industry evolution and firm-level competitive dynamics. Frequent entries of new members and exits of old ones can make it difficult for firms to maintain extended, stable relationships with each other.

name: Collective identity recognition
authors_terms: ["collective identity recognition", "audience recognition of a collective identity", "RPS inclusion"]
definition: Formal recognition of a collective identity in state law and policy represents evidence of cognitive legitimacy, as legislation rarely passes unless at least a plurality of constituents endorses it.

name: Contribution to crowdsourced public goods
authors_terms: ["contribution to OSS", "contributing to the creation of a public good", "firms that pay their employees to contribute"]
definition: Contribution by a firm's employees to the creation of a crowdsourced public good, where the firm pays the employees to contribute rather than their contributing on their own time.

name: Content contribution
definition: A contribution in which an individual writes the computer code for a change, usually a small one- or two-line change to the existing code to address a bug, improve efficiency, or add a new feature, and then receives feedback from others that have more experience with the good.

name: Editorial contribution
definition: A contribution in which an experienced individual provides feedback to and signs off on another contributor's code, so that it is added to the beta version of the source code; the authors note that knowledge does not spill up from the less experienced content contributor to the editor.

name: Open source software usage
authors_terms: ["OSS usage", "utilization of open source software", "intensity of OSS usage"]
definition: The firm's use of open source software as an input; the authors measure the intensity of OSS usage at the firm through the number and type of operating systems used, with open source operating systems frequently indicating wider OSS usage.

name: Management of the public good
authors_terms: ["versions of the good the firm manages", "managed by a third party", "noncommercialized OSS", "commercialized OSS"]
definition: Whether the firm directly uses the crowdsourced public information good or buys a commercialized and packaged version of the good from a third party; when a firm relies on a third party to package the good, it relies on that third party to make any updates or changes to the good.

name: Returns to open source software use
authors_terms: ["productivity returns from the use of the good", "productive value from usage of OSS", "increased benefit contributors obtain from using OSS"]
definition: The value a firm captures from its use of a crowdsourced public good; the authors compare the increased productivity benefit from using OSS that a contributor obtains after it starts contributing with that obtained by a noncontributing, free-riding peer.

name: Value-added productivity
definition: Value-added productivity, obtained by subtracting operating costs (not including labor) from sales, is used as a measure of output rather than raw output to remove concerns about trends in the economy or demand shocks.

name: Frequency-based imitation
authors_terms: ["frequency-based imitation", "prior plant locations by other firms", "prior plant locations by all other firms"]
definition: Frequency-based imitation occurs when decisions are based purely on the number of other firms that have adopted a given strategy.

name: Industry-based imitation
authors_terms: ["trait-based imitation", "prior plant locations by firms in the same industry"]
definition: A more selective process than frequency-based imitation is trait-based imitation, in which the practices of subsets of the population enjoying high status or high similarity to a focal firm receive additional weight in the design of imitative strategies. Studies of diversification have found that the size and success of a firm enhance the sensitivity of its peers to its actions, as does its industrial context.

name: Business group imitation
authors_terms: ["prior plant locations by firms in the same business group", "horizontal keiretsu", "business group membership"]
definition: Horizontal keiretsu are business alliances in which member firms are integrated by such mechanisms as cross-appointments of directors and executives, cross-shareholdings, and joint projects. The mechanisms linking horizontal keiretsu members foster good information flows between companies.

name: Political hazards
definition: In the presence of political hazards, defined as the presence of political institutions that induce policy uncertainty, evaluation of likely future investment conditions is prone to substantial error. We refer to countries that lack strong constraints on policy changes as politically hazardous.

name: Host-country experience
authors_terms: ["firm-specific uncertainty", "host-country experience", "prior investment experience in that specific country"]
definition: An important source of heterogeneity in a firm's propensity to locate a plant in a country is its prior investment experience in that specific country. Firms new to a market are unlikely to have developed a heuristic for making an investment or to have a system in place for determining and analyzing the relevant information; inexperience thus heightens uncertainty about the market.

name: International experience
authors_terms: ["prior international experience", "international experience of investing firm", "a firm's stock of international experience"]
definition: A firm could have made previous international expansions in countries other than the one under consideration. In addition to using interorganizational mimetic strategies, firms can draw on their own previous international expansions for informational cues and rules of thumb on how to respond to conditions in another country.

name: International plant location
definition: The international plant location decision we examine represents organizational growth in the form of the foundation of a new subsidiary company for the purpose of manufacturing in a country different from an organization's home country.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["change in product-market strategy", "diversifying change in strategy", "strategic change"]
definition: Strategy is the firm's product-market diversification, categorized into nine levels with Rumelt's classification system using specialization and relatedness ratios. A strategic change is a move between these categories; because there were too few instances of decreased diversification, only diversifying strategic changes were considered.

name: Structural change
authors_terms: ["change in administrative structure", "decentralizing change in structure", "structural change"]
definition: Administrative structure was measured with a collapsed version of Rumelt's categories, ranging from functional firms to holding companies. A structural change is a move between these categories; because there were too few instances of increased centralization, only decentralizing structural changes were considered.

name: Magnitude of strategic change
authors_terms: ["magnitude of a change in strategy", "magnitude of the most recent diversifying change"]
definition: The authors argue that some changes in product-market strategy involve radical transformations of domain or position and others only incremental changes, and that the magnitude of a change in one attribute affects the likelihood that the other attribute will be changed in response.

name: Magnitude of structural change
authors_terms: ["magnitude of a change in structure", "magnitude of the most recent decentralizing change"]
definition: Structural changes differ in how fundamental an alteration of the formal and informal systems of the organization they represent, and the authors argue that a large change in structure produces a greater alteration of the cognitive maps and skills of managers than a small change.

name: Time elapsed since strategic change
authors_terms: ["time elapsed since a change in product-market strategy", "time since last diversifying change"]
definition: The literature on the timing of changes suggests that both links decay over time and that changes will tend to cluster together; the authors expect the probability of a subsequent structural change to be initially high after a strategic change and then to decline over time.

name: Time elapsed since structural change
authors_terms: ["time elapsed since a change in administrative structure", "time since last decentralizing change"]
definition: The authors expect the general temporal form of the structure-to-strategy link to be similar to that of the strategy-to-structure link, with changes in strategy produced by changes in structure occurring sooner rather than later.

name: Acquiring stage market power
authors_terms: ["market power", "the acquiring firm's industry seller concentration", "seller concentration ratio"]
definition: The market power of the acquiring firm's production stage, represented by the seller concentration ratio of its industry, the proportion of industry sales accounted for by the four largest sellers.

name: Target stage market power
authors_terms: ["market power", "the target firm's industry seller concentration", "seller concentration ratio"]
definition: The market power of the target firm's production stage, represented by the seller concentration ratio of its industry, the proportion of industry sales accounted for by the four largest sellers.

name: Relative market power
authors_terms: ["relative market power", "asymmetric market power", "asymmetric distribution of market power"]
definition: A measure of the relative market power of the acquiring and acquired firms: it has a high value when the target firm's stage has the market power, equals unity when both stages have equal market power, and has a low value when the acquiring firm's stage has the market power.

name: Acquiring firm revaluation
authors_terms: ["revaluation of the acquiring firm", "gains to the acquiring firm", "acquiring firm's standardized cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: The change in the market value of the acquiring firm associated with a vertical merger announcement, measured by cumulative abnormal returns.

name: Target firm revaluation
authors_terms: ["revaluation of the target firm", "gains to the target firm", "target's standardized cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: The change in the market value of the target firm associated with a vertical merger announcement, measured by cumulative abnormal returns.

name: Rival firm revaluation
authors_terms: ["gains to the rivals", "the change in the value of the rivals of the acquiring firm", "the other incumbents in its stage"]
definition: The change in value of the rivals of the acquiring firm, that is, the other incumbents in the acquiring firm's stage.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth is the percentage change in a company's car sales revenues from the beginning of one 3-year period to the end of the same period.

name: New product introduction rate
authors_terms: ["new product introduction rate", "frequency of new products"]
definition: The new product introduction rate measures the frequency of new products within each firm. We calculated the new product introduction rate for each manufacturer during each of the 3-year periods by taking the number of new product introductions and dividing this by the number of product offerings in the base year.

name: Rapid design transfer
authors_terms: ["rapid design transfer", "rapid (or concurrent) design transfer", "concurrent design transfer"]
definition: In the second type, rapid design transfer, a new project begins to transfer a core design from a base project before the base project has completed its design engineering. We defined rapid design transfers as projects where the transfer from a base project occurred within 2.0 years of the introduction of the base design.

name: Sequential design transfer
definition: The third type, sequential design transfer, transfers a design from a base model to a new product after a previous project has finished developing the base model.

name: New design strategy
definition: We categorize new projects that develop platforms primarily from scratch without a preexisting base design as the first type, new design strategy.

name: Design modification strategy
definition: The last type, design modification, refers to a project that replaces an existing product and contains a core design inherited from the predecessor product.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Our primary independent variable, CEO tenure, was measured as the number of quarters that the CEO had been in office (as of quarter t). The authors use CEO tenure to proxy for the accumulation of expertise in the CEO role.

name: CEO cognitive complexity
definition: We define cognitive complexity as the degree to which one engages in differentiated (as opposed to unitary) and nuanced (as opposed to black-and-white) thinking. It deals strictly with cognitive complexity of CEOs in their CEO roles.

name: Systemic industry dynamism
definition: Industries vary widely in their inherent, or systemic, degrees of dynamism. The measure is based on the long-term, or inherent, degree of volatility of stock returns in each industry.

name: Industry jolts
definition: The industry might also occasionally encounter extraordinary and abrupt increases in dynamism or industry jolts, that greatly exceed the industry's prevailing degree of dynamism.

name: CEO positional power
definition: The term positional power designates the degree to which nonpersonal factors confer relative autonomy on the CEO (in contrast to personal sources of power, such as charisma or valued credentials).

name: Competitor acumen
definition: We define competitor acumen as the extent to which a focal firm's assessment of a given rival's prioritization of competitors-that is, the relative degrees of importance the rival places on its competitors-reflects the rival's own view.

name: Relational competitive embeddedness
definition: Focusing on dyadic market-engagement relationships between firms, relational competitive embeddedness captures the intensity of a focal firm's market engagement with a rival, encompassing the strategic significance of markets from the focal firm's as well the target rival's perspective.

name: Structural competitive embeddedness
definition: Structural competitive embeddedness takes into account the patterns of interactions with players beyond the dyad. That is, it embraces the overall network structure of competitive relationships surrounding a focal firm and a given rival.

name: Resource deployment capability
definition: Resource deployment capability reflects how quickly a focal firm can mobilize its existing resources to the market(s) in which it engages with a given rival. It indicates the firm's readiness to contest a rival with its existing available resources in a specific market.

name: Relative market share gain
authors_terms: ["relative market share gain", "relative market share change", "change in the market share gap"]
definition: Because our research focuses on the firm-dyad level of analysis, we were particularly interested in the competitive outcome between a pair of firms, as manifested in the change in the relative market shares (relative market share change) of a focal firm and a rival in a given market.

name: CEO-HPE pay disparity
authors_terms: ["CEO - HPE pay disparity", "pay disparity", "executive pay disparity", "CEO-executive pay disparity", "pay dispersion", "pay gap"]
definition: CEO - HPE pay disparity contains two components: incumbent CEO pay (CEO pay) and the pay of the HPE (HPE pay). The authors describe it as the pay disparity between the CEO and the firm's next highest paid executive (HPE).

name: Outside CEO succession
authors_terms: ["outside CEO succession", "outside successor", "outside CEO successor", "choice of an outside CEO"]
definition: The board's choice of an outside CEO, an indicator of ineffective succession planning. Outside CEO succession was a dichotomous variable: 1 = outside succession; 0 = inside succession.

name: Linking pin directors
definition: Boards can use linking pin directors - directors who simultaneously serve on multiple committees - to reduce information asymmetries and improve decision making. The authors focus on linking pin directors who serve on the committees with CEO succession and executive compensation duties (CS linking pin directors).

name: Competitive familiarity
definition: Repeated competition followed by collaboration, or 'competitive familiarity,' emerges from a wide range of organizational interactions; the authors propose that when competitive behavior is observable, competitive familiarity will tend to improve organizational performance by facilitating learning among teammates.

name: Cooperative familiarity
definition: Repeated collaboration among teammates engenders cooperative familiarity, characterized by the development of cognitive, social, and organizational systems, based on trust and transactive memory systems - knowledge of who knows what (and who does not know what) in a group.

name: Team performance
definition: Team performance is the outcome of team efforts in a match; a player's ranking (MMR), and hence their status and eligibility for high-profile tournaments, is completely determined by team outcomes.

name: Implicit coordination
definition: Implicit coordination 'takes place when team members anticipate the actions and needs of their colleagues and task demands and dynamically adjust their own behavior accordingly, without having to communicate directly with each other or plan the activity'.

name: Explicit coordination friction
definition: Playing on a nonhome server increases latency and the probability that teammates do not share a common language, so that in matches where one or more players are not playing on their home server, explicit coordination frictions should increase.

name: CEO agentic value display relative to industry peers
authors_terms: ["agentic values", "agentic value display", "CEO relative agentic value display", "displays of agentic values", "agentic language"]
definition: Agentic values refer to 'a person's striving to be independent, to control one's environment, and to assert, protect and expand one's self'. Agentic values emphasize one's independence and control, and the paper focuses on CEOs' displays of agentic values relative to their industry peers, rather than their actual agentic values.

name: Shareholder activism
authors_terms: ["shareholder activism", "ownership activism", "ownership-based activist campaigns", "targeted by activist shareholders"]
definition: Ownership activism occurs when an investor acquires a significant equity stake in a company with the intent to influence or control management. The dependent variable is equal to one in the year a firm is targeted by an activist shareholder and zero otherwise.

name: Control activism
definition: Activist shareholders most often seek control by demanding the termination and replacement of the incumbent CEO and directors; the authors refer to such cases as 'control' activism.

name: Noncontrol activism
definition: Activism motivated by noncontrol reasons, that is, filings whose stated purpose pertained to disputes, concerns, or discussion rather than control.

name: Corporate-level investment
definition: Corporate investment requires an ongoing and significant commitment of resources, making it difficult for the firm to overturn, and usually has a long investment horizon. Following prior research the authors focus on R&D, acquisitions, and capital expenditures as one category of corporate investment.

name: Stakeholder investment
definition: CSR refers to a set of practices and policies that voluntarily internalize stakeholder concerns into a company's operations, which goes beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law and can be viewed as a form of investment. It is measured across the environment, community, product, employee, and diversity dimensions.

name: Financial incentives
authors_terms: ["task fee", "task-level financial incentives", "changes in financial incentives", "compensation for a particular professional task"]
definition: The main independent variable is the task's fee, which is the dollar amount paid to a physician, by the MOHLTC, when the physician performs a particular task.

name: Task volume
authors_terms: ["task volume", "provision of a task", "amount it is provided"]
definition: The main dependent variable, task volume, is the total number of times task i is performed by physicians belonging to a given specialty s, in quarter t.

name: Jurisdictional dominance
definition: Jurisdictional dominance captures the extent to which a profession controls the provision of a particular task. This concept loosens the assumption that professions maintain exclusive control over tasks, replacing it with a more flexible depiction where a profession may have complete control over some tasks (i.e., they are its sole provider), while other tasks may be shared across multiple professions.

name: Jurisdictional prominence
definition: This characteristic of professions' work tasks - what I refer to as a task's jurisdictional prominence - differs from the usual conceptions of jurisdictional control. Jurisdictional prominence captures how common a task is performed in a profession relative to other tasks; rather than focusing on between-profession jurisdictional dynamics, this focuses attention on within-profession heterogeneity across tasks.

name: Firm wage arrears
authors_terms: ["wage arrears", "firm-level arrears", "arrears (months)", "arrears (dummy)", "the delayed payment of wages"]
definition: Wage arrears—the late payment and nonpayment of contractual wages to employees—first became substantial in Russia in 1993. The Russian Labor Code explicitly outlawed them.

name: Community prevalence of wage arrears
authors_terms: ["local arrears", "community wage arrears norm", "the local norm", "prevalence of a deviant practice in a community", "the level of arrears in the community"]
definition: Like a practice measured at the organizational level, a community norm can be defined in terms of either the frequency or intensity of its use. Theory provides little guidance on which measure is preferable, so we examine both.

name: Employee turnover
definition: Hirschman (1970) identified two primary mechanisms by which workers are able to challenge organizational activity: exit and voice.

name: Employee strikes
definition: Hirschman (1970) identified two primary mechanisms by which workers are able to challenge organizational activity: exit and voice.

name: Strategic planning
definition: a formal, administrative process that calls for an explicit procedure to determine specific, long-range objectives and generate alternative strategies, requiring both strict implementation and an explicit system to monitor results (Armstrong, 1982). As a bureaucratic process, strategic planning can be either coercive or enabling in nature (Adler and Borys, 1996).

name: New product development projects
authors_terms: ["NPD projects", "new product projects", "NPD project proliferation", "innovative activity"]
definition: the number of NPD ideas and subsequently the number of funded ideas-what we define as NPD projects. The variable New product projects indicates the number of NPD projects initiated during the previous 12 months at the SBU level; it captures the firm's innovative activity.

name: Financial performance
definition: The variable ROI indicates the SBU's ROI as a percentage one year following the first survey; it measures the firm's financial performance.

name: Firm age
definition: The variable Firm age indicates the number of years from the SBU's establishment to the year of the survey.

name: Risk taking
definition: the degree to which a firm makes decisions with uncertain expected outcomes, with hard-to-achieve decision goals, and with potential outcomes that include some extreme consequences (Sitkin and Pablo, 1992).

name: Knowledge-based reward systems
definition: the extent to which evaluations and rewards of employees are based on the accumulation of new knowledge and its use in idea generation.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: Corporate strategy broken down into four categories: single business (the core business contributes 95 percent or more of total turnover), dominant business (one business contributes at least 70 percent but less than 95 percent of turnover), related diversification (the core business does not contribute as much as 70 percent of total turnover and diversification has involved areas related to its core skills) and unrelated diversification (the core business does not contribute as much as 70 percent of total turnover and there are no links between the businesses).

name: Divisionalization
definition: A firm's structure measured following the Rumelt (1974) approach: functional (units deal with business functions such as sales, marketing or manufacturing), functional-with-subsidiaries (basically functional but also with one or more separate product divisions reporting to top management or to a functional manager), holding (an association of firms or divisions commonly owned by a parent, with an almost complete lack of management at the top) and multidivisional (organizations split into a number of quasiautonomous divisions, with the head office solely responsible for strategic decisions).

name: Top executive humility
authors_terms: ["executive humility", "leader humility", "top executive's humility", "humble top executives", "humble leaders"]
definition: Leader humility, a leader's orientation grounded in a transcendent self-concept, desiring accurate self-knowledge, appreciating others, and keeping an open mind.

name: Middle manager job satisfaction
authors_terms: ["MM job satisfaction", "job satisfaction", "middle manager's job satisfaction"]
definition: Job satisfaction is envisioned as a fundamental mechanism linking distal work environmental factors, such as leadership, to turnover: when workplace conditions are satisfying, employees feel lower movement desirability and less often seek jobs or eventually leave.

name: Middle manager voluntary turnover
definition: Voluntary turnover comprises quits due to dissatisfaction with the company, pay, or supervisors; better career opportunities elsewhere; further education; health issues or pregnancy; or family migration.

name: Top management team faultlines
definition: TMT faultlines, representing hypothetical dividing lines that split a TMT into homogeneous subgroups based on members' alignment along one or more attributes.

name: Franchise system size
authors_terms: ["franchise system size", "system size", "size of the franchise system", "number of outlets in the franchise system"]
definition: We measure the dependent variable, size of the franchise system, as the natural logarithm of the number of outlets in the franchise system in the year of observation. The authors state that the number of outlets in the system is a good measure of size, and changes in this variable represent system size.

name: Royalty rate
authors_terms: ["royalty rate", "royalties", "royalties paid as a percentage of the franchisee's sales to end customers"]
definition: Franchisees pay franchisors primarily through royalties paid as a percentage of the franchisee's sales to end customers and up-front fixed franchise fees. Because royalties depend on the value of the system's business concept, the royalty rate can provide a credible signal of system quality and affect system size by impacting the ease of attracting franchisees.

name: Up-front franchise fee
authors_terms: ["up-front fixed franchise fees", "fixed franchise fee", "franchise fee", "up-front fixed fee"]
definition: The fixed franchise fee is the other pricing variable that franchisors use to attract new franchisees and add outlets to the system; it is the dollar amount paid by the franchisee to the franchisor as an up-front fee to open an outlet.

name: Franchisee initial investment
definition: A franchisee's initial investment includes capital expenditures on items such as real estate, training, equipment, and consulting fees.

name: Proportion of company-owned outlets
authors_terms: ["proportion of company-owned outlets", "ownership of outlets", "company ownership of outlets"]
definition: Under strategic control, the strategic franchisor decisions include proportion of ownership of the outlets and the decision to finance the franchisees. Ownership of outlets is measured as the ratio of company-owned outlets to the total number of outlets in the system.

name: Franchisee financing
definition: Franchisors can also finance new franchisees to get them started and thereby reduce the franchisees' risk levels. Financing of franchisees also signals the franchisor's commitment to and control over the system size and its seriousness about the success of the franchisees.

name: System age
authors_terms: ["time franchising", "as the system ages", "number of years since the franchise system was established"]
definition: For each year of observation, the authors measure time franchising as the number of years since the franchise system was established.

name: Growth option value
definition: The portion of a firm's value attributable to growth options. Kester defined growth option value as the proportion of a firm's market value that is attributable to growth options.

name: International joint ventures
definition: Cross-border equity joint ventures, which the authors argue involve high levels of uncertainty. IJVs also experience some unique sources of uncertainty owing to heterogeneous external environments across national borders.

name: Minority IJVs
definition: Minority IJVs are ventures in which a firm holds an equity stake of less than 50 percent. By holding less equity, the firm is able to put less capital at risk up front, as well as capture greater value if conditions prove to be favorable ex post.

name: Nonminority IJVs
definition: Nonminority IJVs are ventures in which a firm's equity stake is 50 percent and above. Higher initial ownership stakes in IJVs involve greater initial commitments.

name: Core IJVs
definition: Core IJVs are IJVs operating in the firm's primary business at the four-digit SIC level.

name: Noncore IJVs
definition: Noncore IJVs are IJVs outside of the firm's primary business, i.e., ventures that do not operate in the firm's primary business at the four-digit SIC level.

name: IJVs in emerging economies
authors_terms: ["IJVs in emerging economies", "IJVs located in emerging economies", "IJVs in emerging/developing economies"]
definition: IJVs located in emerging/developing economies, defined by the United Nations on the basis of the World Bank's World Development Indicators: all countries other than the 24 high-income OECD members were considered emerging/developing economies. The underdevelopment of market-supporting institutions in an emerging economy presents many sources of uncertainty to firms operating there.

name: IJVs in developed economies
authors_terms: ["IJVs in developed economies", "IJVs located in developed economies"]
definition: IJVs located in developed economies, which were the 24 high-income Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development members, all of which were represented in the sample. In developed economies, market-supporting institutions are well developed.

name: Relational debt
authors_terms: ["relational debt", "ratio of relational debt to total debt", "bank loans", "reliance on relational debt"]
definition: Following the terminology used in the theory of contracts, the authors classify debt contracts into two types: transactional debt has simple performance attributes and a fixed time period; relational debt has extended duration and complex performance attributes. Loans are private transactions between a firm and financial intermediaries such as banks and insurance companies, and are therefore considered relational debt.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Investments in R&D create knowledge-based intangible assets that have the greatest value when utilized in conjunction with a firm's complementary assets. They are subject to hazards of asset specificity, uncertainty, and weak appropriability.

name: Firm performance
definition: Misalignment between debt structure and R&D can impose unnecessary costs, distort incentives, and impair firm performance. Performance was proxied by the market-to-book ratio, which incorporates not just current performance but also expected future performance.

name: Perceived competitive tension
authors_terms: ["perceived competitive tension", "perceived tension", "competitive tension", "perceived competitive tension, insiders", "perceived competitive tension, outsiders"]
definition: Perceived competitive tension denotes the extent to which a firm's managers and industry stakeholders consider a given rival to be the focal firm's primary competitor. More generally, competitive tension is the strain between a focal firm and a given rival that is likely to result in the firm taking action against the rival.

name: Relative scale
definition: Awareness is indicated by relative scale, defined, per Baum and Korn (1999), as a competitor's operating capacity compared with that of a focal firm's, which captures visible size or scale disparities.

name: Rival's attack volume
authors_terms: ["rival's attack volume", "volume of a rival's attack", "attack volume"]
definition: Motivation is reflected by a rival's attack volume, defined, per Ferrier (2001), as the extent to which a focal firm's markets are under attack by a given rival's actions.

name: Rival's capability to contest
definition: Capability is signaled by a rival's capability to contest, defined as the operational ability of a given rival to challenge a focal firm in the marketplace, and describes the rival's relative resource-deployment ability compared with the focal firm's. It derives from a similarity consideration, when the rival and the focal firm have highly similar resource profiles, and a salience consideration, when the rival is a significant player in the resources the focal firm values most.

name: Focal firm's attack volume
authors_terms: ["volume of a focal firm's attack", "volume of attack on rival", "volume of a focal firm's attacks on a rival's markets"]
definition: The volume of a focal firm's attack on a given rival's markets, that is, the firm's consequent competitive action against the rival. Strong perceived tension increases the volume of a firm's attacks on a rival's markets.

name: Firm-level multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact", "firm-level multimarket contact", "firm-level contact", "count of multimarket competitors"]
definition: The firm-in-market level of multimarket contact is the multimarket contact that a given firm has with all its competitors in a given market, which is suitable for testing its commitment to mutually forbear against competing. At the firm level, it is the count of firms that have multimarket contact with the focal firm.

name: Market-level multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["market-level multimarket contact", "market level of multimarket contact", "overall level of multimarket contact"]
definition: The market level of multimarket contact is the multimarket contact of all firms present in the market, which is suitable for testing the effect of the overall level of mutual forbearance in a market. At the market level, the measure is the count of firms that have one or more multimarket competitors present in the market.

name: Sales growth deviation
authors_terms: ["sales growth", "sales growth deviation", "positive deviation", "deviation from median sales growth"]
definition: The difference between the focal firm growth rate in the market and the median growth rate of all firms in the market, which is positive for a firm that defects and zero for a firm that does not. The sales growth of the firm that defects is also a good candidate for a signal that can help competitors discover that it has defected.

name: Principal champion hierarchical level
authors_terms: ["principal champion's hierarchical level", "hierarchical level of the principal champion", "level of the principal champion"]
definition: The hierarchical level in the organization of the venture's principal champion, the champion whose involvement is viewed as the most crucial in the transformation from concept or prototype into new commercial business.

name: Principal champion organizational location
authors_terms: ["organizational location within the firm", "corporate principal champion", "corporate headquarters"]
definition: The principal champion's location within the firm, distinguishing champions from corporate headquarters, many of whom occupy staff or support positions, from champions in other locations such as operating units.

name: Dual-role champion
authors_terms: ["dual-role champion", "dual-role champions", "one champion playing both roles"]
definition: A principal champion who plays both the role of product champion and organizational sponsor, taking on most or all of the key functions of both, including direct involvement in product definition and coaching and mentoring the venture on key decisions.

name: Venture innovativeness
definition: The degree to which a venture is first to create a new market relative to other firms through the commercialization of a product based on new technology.

name: Science park membership
definition: The science parks provide a variety of services and individualized mentoring—all within a shared physical infrastructure. These science parks require neither an equity stake nor a specific residence time, and can be considered business incubators with a technology focus.

name: Returnee
definition: Returnees are individuals who have studied or worked abroad and then come back to their home countries (Li et al., 2012). In China, returnees have started many of the country's most successful Internet firms such as Baidu, Sina, and Dangdang.

name: Local elite
definition: Local elites are often well educated in top domestic universities, particularly in science and engineering (Hoskisson et al., 2000) as governments often cultivate such talent through major infrastructure investments. They typically understand the local context and possess local business ties (Oi, 1995), but often lack managerial skills (Hoskisson et al., 2000).

name: Public policy resource access
definition: Our dependent variable is Public policy resource access. This variable is measured by whether the focal firm participated in the two major government programs that provide public resources to technology-based ventures.

name: Regional network centrality of MNCs
authors_terms: ["MNC centrality", "centrality of the MNCs in the regional network", "MNC regional network activity", "Regional network centrality"]
definition: We constructed a network using all the alliances in a region over a five-year window prior to year t. We then calculated the MNC's average network centrality as the ratio of the cumulative degree centrality of all the MNCs in the region divided by the number of MNCs active within this region in that period.

name: Alliance experience with MNCs in the region
authors_terms: ["direct alliances a start-up has with MNCs in the region", "alliance experience with MNCs", "Alliances with MNCs in region"]
