definition: To measure this variable, we created a count variable: the number of alliances with MNCs in the region prior to the time of the international alliance event. As with the network variables, we used a five-year window prior to the year of the event for the count.

name: International alliance formation rate
authors_terms: ["international alliance formation rate", "international alliance-formation rate", "international alliance formation activity", "international alliances"]
definition: International alliance formation activity is defined as alliances with partner organizations located outside Germany. The dependent variable is a start-up's international alliance-formation rate, which provides information on the time span between successive events; higher values of the rate correspond to shorter times between events.

name: Change in CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["changes in CEO rewards", "changes in CEO compensation", "changes in senior manager rewards", "changes in compensation", "managerial rewards"]
definition: Changes in senior manager rewards are defined as the before versus after percentage changes in acquiring firms' CEOs' salaries, bonuses, and value of stock options.

name: Acquisition returns
authors_terms: ["returns accruing to their shareholders as a result of acquisitions", "returns", "acquisition-related returns", "corporate returns"]
definition: We related CEO rewards to two measures of returns: cumulative abnormal returns estimated with event study methodology for two event windows, and the year-over-year percentage change in an acquiring firm's return on equity.

name: Change in firm size
authors_terms: ["increase in firm size owing to an acquisition", "increases in the size of a firm", "changes in sales", "firm growth"]
definition: Pre- and postacquisition changes in firm size were measured as percentage changes in sales, indicating the percentage changes in the acquiring firms' sales in the year following the merger versus the year of the merger announcement.

name: External monitoring
authors_terms: ["external monitoring activities", "external monitors", "vigilant monitoring", "lax monitoring", "intensity of monitoring"]
definition: External monitors are actors who are not executives of the enterprise; these actors directly or indirectly monitor managerial decisions and perform the function of decision control so that costly executive decisions may be confronted. Monitoring may be more vigilant with a higher number of security analysts following a firm, with increases in the firm's proportion of independent outside directors, and with higher levels of investments by activist institutions, and may be weak when few analysts follow an enterprise, when the proportion of independent outside board members is low, and when the level of investment by institutions is low.

name: Director capital
definition: The construct of interest in our study is director capital. Following prior research, we disaggregate director capital into two components-relational capital and human capital.

name: Relational capital
definition: Relational capital refers to the resources embedded in their networks of personal and professional connections. Relational capital stems from directors' professional networks.

name: Business expert human capital
definition: Business experts are active or former top executives at other firms who are familiar with running complex organizations, giving them the expertise to understand competitive issues and evaluate managerial decisions.

name: Professional specialist human capital
definition: Professional specialists have backgrounds in law, capital markets, or other industry-specific areas (e.g., environmental impact mitigation) that facilitate a board's ability to understand more technical aspects of firm operations.

name: Director exit
definition: Our dependent variable, director exit, takes a value of one if a director departs the board by the time he or she would next come up for reelection following the fraud announcement. This variable is equal to zero if the director remains on the board beyond this point in time.

name: Density of the established population
definition: The annual number of commercial banks, an established population from which an emergent population can source legitimacy and with which it competes for resources.

name: Density of the emergent population
definition: The annual number of financial cooperatives; its low-level increases trigger the violation-by-comparison effect and its high-level increases drive constitutive legitimation.

name: Categorical name change
authors_terms: ["categorical name change", "cumulative number of categorical name changes in the population", "C_c"]
definition: Name changes that instantiate departures from the common name by which the audience refers to the entire class of similar organizations, thereby disrupting external perceptions of a category.

name: Organizational failure
definition: The hazard that a financial cooperative disbands, modeled as a function of organizational age, population age and covariates.

name: Identity overlap
authors_terms: ["overlap in identity space", "identity overlap", "overlap of its less-restrictive identity", "less-restrictive identities of the two overlap"]
definition: The sharing of general, less-restrictive identities by two organizational populations, which places organizations with different forms closer to or farther from each other in identity space. The mutualistic benefits pertain to the emergent population that can source legitimacy from an established one, but only to the extent that the less-restrictive identities of the two overlap.

name: Resource overlap
authors_terms: ["resource overlap", "overlap in resource space", "shared dependence on resources"]
definition: Overlap in the resource space of two interdependent populations: while identity overlap makes legitimacy transfer possible, shared dependence on resources incites diffuse rivalry between members of different populations.

name: Diversity of FDI country origins
authors_terms: ["the diversity of FDI country origins", "diversity of FDI country origins"]
definition: We define the diversity of FDI country origins as the extent to which foreign firms in an industry are from different country origins.

name: Domestic firm productivity
authors_terms: ["the productivity of domestic firms", "domestic firm productivity", "domestic firms' productivity"]
definition: In the FDI spillover literature, domestic firm productivity is estimated by using a log-linear Cobb-Douglas production function.

name: Domestic firm size
authors_terms: ["the size of the domestic firms", "domestic firm size", "large domestic firms", "small domestic firms"]
definition: The authors treat domestic firm size as a characteristic of domestic firms that proxies for absorptive capacity, arguing that 'large domestic firms tend to have stronger capacity than small ones to learn technologies and management practices brought by foreign firms from different country origins.'

name: Technology gap
authors_terms: ["technology gap", "the technology gap between FDI and the domestic firms"]
definition: In this study, technology gap refers to the extent to which FDI in an industry is technologically advanced relative to a domestic firm in the industry.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissism is the degree to which an individual has an inflated self-view and craves affirmation of that self-view; it is conceptualized as a personality dimension along which all individuals can be arrayed, and there is considerable variance in narcissistic tendencies across CEOs.

name: CEO prior board experience
authors_terms: ["CEO's prior experience", "the corporate strategies that the CEO witnessed at other firms"]
definition: A given type of corporate strategy that the CEO has witnessed as a member of other boards; it is measured by the degree of acquisition emphasis and international diversification for each firm where the CEO held a board position in the previous three years.

name: Other directors' prior board experience
definition: A given type of corporate strategy that other directors of the focal board have witnessed at other firms, calculated similarly to the CEO's prior experience.

name: Corporate strategy
authors_terms: ["corporate strategies", "a given type of corporate strategy", "acquisition emphasis", "international diversification"]
definition: The acquisition emphasis of a firm's growth strategy, defined as the firm's total acquisition expenditure relative to its size, and the firm's level of international diversification, defined as the degree to which a firm expands beyond its domestic market into other countries.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "the CEO's power relative to other directors"]
definition: The degree to which the CEO is powerful relative to other directors, measured by seven indicators widely used in existing research.

name: Status of firms tied to the CEO
authors_terms: ["status of firms tied to the CEO", "status of other firms with which the CEO was previously associated"]
definition: The status of the other firms with which the CEO was previously associated, where firm status is measured by firm size, performance relative to the industry, and whether the firm was ranked among the top 50 America's Most Admired Companies by Fortune magazine.

name: Autonomy
definition: Autonomy captures the degree to which the inventor is given 'substantial freedom, independence, and discretion [...] in scheduling the work and in determining the procedures to be used in carrying it out'; the authors' focus is autonomy within the assigned project boundaries, that is, the freedom, once a problem has been set, to attack it by means determined by oneself, within given organizational resource constraints.

name: Project-relevant capital
definition: Project-relevant capital (PRC) denotes the resources that are relevant for the specific project, as opposed to the ones that are owned by the firm as a whole; it is associated with greater productivity of a researcher's contribution to a given project, improving both the scientific and the commercial value of the project.

name: Scientific value
definition: A research project in the industrial setting produces scientific and commercial value according to a classical joint production process: while the manager targets the commercial value, the researcher's decisions target the scientific value, for example by clarifying the underlying scientific mechanism.

name: Commercial value
definition: Commercial value refers to the extent to which the project output is aligned with the commercial scope of the firm, that is, whether the firm uses the patented invention commercially in a product, service, or manufacturing process.

name: Market repositioning
definition: Repositioning here refers to the extent to which actors change their market positions. Actors' repositioning will imply that their identities are in flux, as their adherence to market prototypes and their categorical memberships are modified.

name: Audience churn
definition: Repositioning may lead to a greater degree of audience churn (i.e., the turnover of audiences). Analyst churn measures the turnover of a firm's coverage analysts.

name: Analyst forecast accuracy
authors_terms: ["forecast accuracy", "accuracy of audience evaluation", "relative accuracy", "accuracy ranking"]
definition: The accuracy of audience evaluation, examined via the accuracy of financial analysts' forecasts. A forecast is more accurate if it is closer toward the firm's actual earnings.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: An aggregate measure of CSP was designed to incorporate the community relations, diversity, employee relations, environment, and product dimensions of the KLD data; KLD evaluates each dimension in terms of strengths and concerns. CSP is a multidimensional construct that encompasses a large and varied range of corporate behaviors.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "equity value", "price of the firm's equity", "share price"]
definition: The dependent variable, firm value, was measured as price of the firm's equity; in the valuation model P is the equity value (per share) of firm i at the end of fiscal year t.

name: Industry litigation risk
definition: Industries vary widely in terms of the level of litigation risk their firms face, and the clustering of litigation among certain industries has been widely documented. Firms in industries with high litigation risks should be more likely to benefit from CSP as an ex ante defense strategy.

name: Financial distress risk
authors_terms: ["financial distress", "distress risk", "risk of financial distress", "high distress risk"]
definition: Here, 'financial distress' refers to a low cash flow state in which a firm incurs losses without being insolvent. Altman's Z-score was used to measure the likelihood of a firm experiencing financial distress or bankruptcy.

name: Industry social contestability
authors_terms: ["socially contested industry", "socially contested industries", "industry social contestability"]
definition: Stakeholders may discount the CSP of a firm operating in industries such as alcoholic beverages, tobacco, firearms, and gambling, hereafter termed 'socially contested' industries; for such firms, CSP activities are more likely to be perceived by stakeholders as lacking a moral basis.

name: Human capital investment
authors_terms: ["effective investments in human capital", "human capital investments", "investments in training and human capital", "investments in the training and education of employees", "general training"]
definition: Investments in the training and education of employees that develop and nurture the knowledge and skills of these employees, thereby improving their productivity. General training is defined as building human capital in the employee that has value both to the training firm and to other firms.

name: Stock price reaction
authors_terms: ["stock price reaction", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "financial performance"]
definition: The stock market reaction to the signal of a firm's effective investments in human capital; these financial performance measures represent unexpected returns on a risk-adjusted basis.

name: R&D intensity
definition: High R&D intensity is often taken as an indication of the importance of knowledge and technology in a firm or industry; it is measured as R&D investment divided by sales.

name: Physical capital intensity
definition: High physical capital intensity could indicate that a firm has simply substituted away from labor and is now employing more automated equipment and procedures that require fewer and less-skilled employees; it is measured as physical capital investment divided by sales.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: Advertising is an (imperfect) measure of product differentiation, that is, of the firm's sunk cost expenditures to communicate its products' attributes and develop a brand.

name: R&D intensity × physical capital intensity interaction
definition: The interaction (product/combination) of a firm's R&D intensity and physical capital intensity; higher values indicate firms that are high on both R&D intensity and physical capital intensity.

name: Alliance experience
authors_terms: ["alliance experience", "prior alliance experience", "stock of prior alliance experiences"]
definition: The firm's stock of prior alliance experiences accumulated at the time of the focal acquisition, measured as the number of alliances completed by the acquiring firm with other banks prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Post-acquisition performance
definition: The acquiring bank's (3-4 year) performance surrounding an acquisition event, measured with one accounting-based and one financial-based indicator.

name: Level of integration
definition: This dimension captures the extent to which the two organizations integrate their structures, align their activities, and merge their cultures.

name: Relational quality
definition: The degree to which the two organizations invest resources, time, and managerial attention in the development and continuation of the quality of their relationship.

name: Patent portfolio
authors_terms: ["patent stock", "patent portfolio", "intellectual property portfolio", "stock of patents"]
definition: A firm's patent portfolio can enable the firm to mitigate appropriation concerns that arise across multiple deals. This occurs when patents are not specific to an individual deal, but rather apply across multiple technology commercialization projects, acting as a 'patent thicket' that makes it more difficult for collaborative partners to expropriate the innovating firm's technology.

name: Prior partner experience
authors_terms: ["prior partner experience", "aggregate partner-specific experience", "repeated collaborative experience with existing partners"]
definition: A firm's prior experience with collaborative partners, which can act to foster trust between the parties and/or build interorganizational reputation, thereby mitigating appropriation concerns for both current and new partners.

name: Governance capability
authors_terms: ["governance capability", "governance mode capabilities", "equity-use deal stock", "license-only deal stock"]
definition: A governance capability is therefore a firm's aggregate collection of knowledge, routines, and organizational structures associated with a particular collaborative mode. In conceptualizing governance capabilities, the authors focus on firms' prior governance structuring experience.

name: Equity use
definition: The first, equity use, is an indicator of organizational hierarchy (among other things). In general, equity is tied to greater formal control in interorganizational governance, which may be particularly important in mitigating the threat of transactional hazards.

name: Arm's-length licensing
definition: Licensing enables firms to utilize markets for technological assets while avoiding more integrated and hierarchical contractual forms. In this study the authors focus on 'pure' technology licensing in order to capture arm's-length innovation transfer effects.

name: Governance capability deviation
authors_terms: ["equity-use negative deviation", "license-only negative deviation", "governance capability deviations", "deviations from existing governance capabilities"]
definition: For a particular mode, the deviation variable is constructed by taking the difference between the percentage of all prior cooperation events utilizing a particular mode (based on the stock of such experience) and the percentage of all current year cooperation events utilizing that mode. Positive values of these deviation variables suggest that historic use of a given governance mode exceeds current usage.

name: Firm valuation
definition: For firms' private years, we use the valuation at the most recent round of venture funding, while for public years we use market capitalization. The variable is meant to capture the overall value of the firm as assessed by its shareholders.

name: External financial conditions
authors_terms: ["external financial conditions", "'hot' capital markets", "Lerner index level", "munificence of external funding"]
definition: An index tracking the munificence of external funding from VCs, corporations, and the public markets available to biotechnology firms. In 'hot' markets, markets are generally less risk averse and more forgiving of managerial decisions in new capability investments.

name: Terrain unfamiliarity
authors_terms: ["terrain unfamiliarity", "unfamiliar TMT search selection", "unfamiliar search selection"]
definition: Terrain unfamiliarity refers to the extent to which search by members of a TMT focus on unfamiliar information. Unfamiliar terrains are more likely to contain novel, salient, and vivid information and are thus more likely to capture searchers' attention.

name: Terrain distance
authors_terms: ["terrain distance", "distant TMT search selection", "distant search selection"]
definition: Terrain distance refers to the extent to which search by TMT members focus on information outside their organization when searching.

name: Terrain source diversity
authors_terms: ["terrain source diversity", "diverse TMT search selection", "diverse search selection"]
definition: Terrain source diversity refers to the range of sources utilized by a TMT to acquire information.

name: Search effort
definition: We define search effort as extent of investment in search activities relative to other tasks. Search effort is the extent to which the members of a TMT devote time and energy to search rather than to other activities.

name: Search persistence
definition: We define search persistence as the intensity of search with respect to the duration of search. Search persistence is defined as the extent to which, on average, members of a TMT continue to gather information despite the number of alternatives that have been found, in order to be exhaustive in determining optimal outcome.

name: New product introductions
definition: As have prior researchers (Katila, 2002; Smith et al., 2005), we adopted new product introductions as our dependent variable. Specifically, we measured new product introductions in two different time frames: the total number of new product introductions for each firm in 2006, the year following our collection of the independent variables, and the average number of new product introductions for each firm in 2006-08.

name: Relative shareholder rights protection
authors_terms: ["difference in acquirer-target shareholder rights", "shareholder rights differences", "legal protection of shareholder rights in the acquirer country when compared to the target country"]
definition: Comparative legal scholarship and more recent economic analyses show that shareholders' interests receive different degrees of legal protection across countries. We measured changes in shareholder rights after the merger by calculating the difference between acquirer country shareholder rights and target country shareholder rights.

name: Employment protection
authors_terms: ["target country labor rights", "legal protection of the target firm's employee rights in the target country", "labor rights protection"]
definition: Stricter employment protection laws are associated with lower turnover in the labor market and with extended periods of work and unemployment. The more a country's corporate governance institutions protect workers' rights, the lower the employer autonomy and the lower the geographical and professional mobility of its labor force.

name: Target asset restructuring
authors_terms: ["asset restructuring", "post-acquisition target asset restructuring", "restructuring the target's assets", "target firm restructuring"]
definition: Asset restructuring refers to actions such as the disposal of some of the acquired assets (which may entail layoffs), the recombination of those kept by the acquirer under a different organizational or managerial structure, and the elimination of redundant activities and inefficient management practices, most likely in the target firm.

name: Resource redeployment
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment", "leveraging the target's resources", "redeploying resources across the merging firms"]
definition: Resource redeployment refers to an actual shift of technological, marketing, or operational knowledge from the acquirer to the target or vice versa, which may affect employees in various ways.

name: Acquisition experience
definition: Acquisition experience is a self-reported measure of the number of acquisitions made by the acquirer within the five years preceding the acquisition of the specific target.

name: Certifications
definition: A certification contest is a competition in which actors in a given domain are ranked based on performance criteria that are accepted by key stakeholders as being credible and legitimate. For MLB players, certifications exist in the form of awards players win during the course of their careers as a result of assessments by observers.

name: Technical performance
authors_terms: ["technical performance", "level of technical performance", "career standards statistic", "Bill James statistic"]
definition: The authors calculated the career standards statistic (James 1994) to assess the overall level of a player's technical performance. Players who score 35-59 are thought to have a level of technical performance that is near the uncertain standard for induction into the Hall.

name: Reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "long-term reputation", "assessment of actors", "induction into the Hall", "voting for the Hall"]
definition: Reputation is the collective judgment of observers regarding the quality or capabilities of a focal actor within a specific domain that is earned over time. Induction into the Hall is an omnibus assessment of the quality of a player's career and as such is consistent with this definition of reputation.

name: Scanning emphasis on the external task environment
authors_terms: ["scanning emphasis on the task environment", "scanning emphasis on external task sectors", "external task environment", "scanning the external task environment"]
definition: The relative importance the CEO places on information from the task sectors of the external environment, made up of the market, technological, and competitive sectors. Scanning emphasis on external task sectors is advantageous in dynamic environments because it helps executives keep track of and react to competitors' initiatives, sensitizes them to available technological solutions, and helps identify changes in customer tastes.

name: Scanning emphasis on the external general environment
authors_terms: ["scanning emphasis on the general environment", "scanning the general environment", "external general environment", "general sectors of the external environment"]
definition: The relative importance the CEO places on information from the general sectors of the external environment, made up of the sociocultural, economic, and political/legal sectors. Scanning these more remote domains under stable conditions can open up possibilities for developing long-term, resource-enhancing opportunities and for identifying major threatening events.

name: Scanning emphasis on internal innovation functions
authors_terms: ["scanning emphasis on innovation", "scanning emphasis on internal innovation", "innovation-related internal functions", "innovation functions in the internal environment"]
definition: The relative importance the CEO places on information from the internal functions associated with innovation, that is, product R&D, market research, and basic engineering. Sensitivity to trends and developments related to basic engineering, technology and markets through these functions permits firms to pursue innovation.

name: Scanning emphasis on internal efficiency functions
authors_terms: ["scanning emphasis on efficiency", "scanning emphasis on internal efficiency", "efficiency-related internal capabilities", "efficiency functions"]
definition: The relative importance the CEO places on information from the internal functions associated with efficiency, that is, cost controls and operating efficiency. Firms that pay more attention to functions such as cost control and operating efficiency typically tend to emphasize efficiency.

name: Perceived environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism describes the rate and the unpredictability of change in a firm's external environment (Dess and Beard, 1984). The authors measure the CEOs' perceptions of the level of dynamism because executives act on their perceptions.

name: Firm performance
definition: CEOs' subjective estimates of performance compared to similar firms in their industry, elicited as five-year averages because short-term performance variations were to be minimized. The authors treat performance as multidimensional, using accounting return, sales growth, and overall performance/success.

name: R&D budget centralization
authors_terms: ["centralization of R&D budget authority", "budget centralization", "centralization (decentralization) of R&D", "formal R&D structure"]
definition: Prior literature conceptualizes a firm's R&D activities as centralized if lab directors report to corporate management, and decentralized if they report to divisional management. The authors observe this through the share of a firm's R&D budget that is provided by corporate headquarters rather than by business units, and capture changes in that share over time.

name: Intrafirm inventor network connectedness
authors_terms: ["connectedness of its intrafirm inventor network", "network connectedness", "relative giant component size", "normalized entropy"]
definition: Network connectedness measures the fraction of nodes in a network that are connected to each other; a network is maximally connected if there is a path, however long, between every pair of nodes. In the case of a firm's internal inventor network, nodes correspond to inventors, and the network becomes less connected with each additional isolated component.

name: Breadth of innovative search
definition: The breadth of technological search is measured as a function of the technology classes of the patents cited by a patent, calculated as one minus the Herfindahl index of the primary U.S. patent classes of the cited patents. The authors argue that centralized R&D makes researchers likely to search more broadly for inputs into innovation than if they are responsible for one division's domain only.

name: Breadth of innovative impact
definition: The breadth of innovation impact is measured by one minus the Herfindahl index of the primary U.S. patent classes of the patents that cite a focal patent. Centralized R&D is believed to incentivize researchers to produce innovations that are applicable to the firm broadly rather than to a single division.

name: Unit ambidexterity
definition: Unit ambidexterity refers to an organizational unit's ability to exploit value from existing markets, competencies, and resources, while it simultaneously explores new markets, products, and opportunities. The authors conceptualize it as a multidimensional construct comprising the non-substitutable combination of exploratory and exploitative innovation.

name: Unit financial performance
definition: The financial performance of each unit was measured by the unit's average profitability for two consecutive years, using a unit's profitability-achieved rate, namely a unit's actual profitability divided by its target profitability.

name: Structural differentiation
definition: Structural differentiation captures the subdivision of organizational tasks and domains across units, possibly to enable each unit to develop a more focused set of competencies and expertise.

name: Centralization of decision making
definition: Centralization reflects the extent to which decision making is concentrated at higher levels of an organization, and thus concerns the role of formal authority and hierarchical mechanisms in the company's decision-making process.

name: Resource munificence
definition: Resource munificence captures the availability of nonabsorbed, financial resources within each branch that are available for immediate deployment.

name: Resource interdependency
definition: Resource interdependency refers to the extent to which units are dependent on other units' resources for their own functioning, that is, the extent to which units must exchange information and resources or work together to complete their tasks and activities.

name: Corporate acquisitions
definition: For most firms, an individual acquisition is a part of an overall acquisition strategy resulting in a sequence of acquisitions. Acquisitions have been widely regarded as an important corporate strategy.

name: Firm performance
definition: Scherer (1988) argues that changes in share price may not reflect efficiency gain or loss, and that it is useful to look at firm profitability. Hence, we use accounting returns as our measures of firm performance.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Organizational slack is defined as a cushion of resources that allows an organization to adapt to internal or external pressures as well as to initiate changes in strategy in regard to the external environment (Bourgeois, 1981).

name: Current R&D effort
definition: The empirical analysis undertaken here utilizes R&D expenditures as a proxy for R&D effort. The expenditure levels for the various R&D activities provide a measure of the resources devoted to the R&D efforts, and also reflect company policies for allocation of R&D funds.

name: Past R&D effort
authors_terms: ["past efforts in each R&D activity", "lagged R&D intensity", "lagged dependent variable"]
definition: The influence of the lagged dependent variable provides a measure of path dependence. The higher the estimated coefficient on the lagged dependent variable, the greater the path dependence.

name: Firm
definition: If firms come into existence with different initial knowledge bases, if organizational learning is path-dependent, and if the transfer across firms of organizational knowledge obtained via path-dependent R&D is difficult (or even just imperfect), then firms may not have the same R&D-related knowledge bases.

name: R&D activity
definition: For purposes of this analysis, an R&D activity is defined as that directed toward a particular type of business application (e.g., oil and gas recovery R&D or oil refining R&D).

name: Within-firm R&D effort allocation
authors_terms: ["pattern of within firm differences in R&D effort", "R&D share"]
definition: By construction, the firm-level average share variables make it possible to investigate differences between firms in the pattern of within firm differences in the allocation of R&D effort across activities.

name: Performance shortfall
authors_terms: ["performance shortfall", "performance below aspiration", "magnitude of performance shortfall", "performance declines"]
definition: A firm's performance relative to its aspiration level, that is, the extent to which performance falls below the aspiration level. The more negative the value of performance below aspiration, the larger the performance shortfall.

name: Risk-taking motivation
definition: Firms' motivation to take risks, which is distinct from their ability to do so. The authors state that firms' motivation to take risks hinges on their chosen reference points and the shifts between these reference points.

name: Concern for firm survival
authors_terms: ["concern for firm survival", "concern for survival", "perception of threat to survival"]
definition: Managers' concern that their firm's survival is threatened. The perception of threat to survival is not solely determined by an 'objective' measure of performance, but also influenced by the application of mental models that define which levels of poor performance or external events constitute a threat to the organization.

name: Managerial confidence
definition: Managers' belief in their own abilities and/or in their firms' abilities to achieve desired targets.

name: Performance momentum
definition: A sustained and systematic trajectory of success or failure relative to aspirations over multiple time periods. It can manifest as outperformance momentum or underperformance momentum, referring to persistent outperformance or underperformance relative to the firm's aspiration over multiple time periods without counteracting outcomes.

name: Risk taking
definition: Firms' risky activities, which the authors assume are jointly determined by their risk-taking motivation and their risk-taking ability. Risk taking can be affected by both the motivation and the ability to take risks.

name: Relative performance
authors_terms: ["relative performance", "relative comparison", "relative judgment", "performance relative to others"]
definition: Individuals compare the object to be evaluated to other objects already rated, and the object's performance relative to these other objects critically affects the evaluation outcome: the poorer the object appears in comparison to others, the worse the evaluation.

name: Categorical coherence
authors_terms: ["categorical coherence", "coherence", "fit within category", "fit within category boundaries", "fit within industry boundaries"]
definition: Stocks vary in their categorical coherence, or the ease by which they fit into the generalized industry categories. A stock with high coherence is followed by analysts who all follow the same stocks, suggesting a firm with a typical market identity and generalized agreement on the standards for evaluation; a stock with low or no coherence is covered by analysts with few (or no) stocks in common.

name: Analyst rating
definition: The recommendation in analyst reports takes the form of a rating from the brokerage's rating system, a hierarchical set of categories used to rate stocks as above average, average, or below average.

name: Pursuit of radical invention
authors_terms: ["pursuit of radical invention", "pursuit of potentially radical opportunities", "pursuit of potentially radical inventions", "potentially radical inventions"]
definition: The choice to pursue radical technologies is the decision to undertake organizationally radical invention (Henderson, 1993), i.e., to draw on knowledge sources that are fundamentally different from those used before, in the hope that these inventions will prove economically radical. The authors identify potentially radical inventions as those that draw on knowledge that has never or rarely been used before by inventors in the same field, and that therefore represent 'unprecedented combinations'.

name: Success of radical invention
authors_terms: ["success of potentially radical inventions", "success of this pursuit", "innovative success", "citations", "breakthrough"]
definition: We use a firm's patents to measure the extent and direction of its inventive efforts (Eggers, 2012; Ghosh et al., 2014) and measure the success of those efforts by the citations its patents receive (Ahuja & Lampert, 2001; Fleming, 2001). The authors' empirical approach distinguishes the potential radicalness of an invention from its eventual success.

name: Technological performance above aspirations
definition: Aspirations emerge from comparisons with other similar firms and with the firm's own past performance (Baum & Dahlin, 2007; Greve, 1998), so that a firm performing above aspirations is outperforming its competitors and its own ex ante expectations. While performance above aspirations leads to a focus on the prospect of loss, performance below aspirations is likely to drive managers to focus on the prospect of gain.

name: Technological performance below aspirations
definition: A firm performing 'below aspirations' is being outcompeted by its competitors and performing below its own ex ante expectations, and its performance below aspirations is likely to drive managers to focus on the prospect of gain, increasing their willingness to take risks. Aspirations emerge from comparisons with other similar firms and with the firm's own past performance.

name: Technological performance in a technology area
authors_terms: ["prior performance in a technology area", "local productivity", "the firm's productivity in a patent class"]
definition: A firm's chances of successfully developing an invention that has substantial impact are likely to be higher in areas of existing strength, i.e., technology areas where it has outperformed its peers in the past and where the firm's existing capabilities are likely to be strong. The measure is the firm's productivity in a patent class: the average number of citations received by the firm's patents that were filed in the previous year in the focal technological category.

name: Technological diversification
definition: A substantial number of firms operate across multiple technologies (Breschi, Lissoni, & Malerba, 2003; Gambardella & Torrisi, 1998; Patel & Pavitt, 1997), and this may impact a firm's propensity to pursue radical invention. The authors capture a firm's technological diversity with a patent-based measure of concentration, a Herfindahl measure based on the patent classes in which the firm patented, with higher levels representing firms that are concentrated in fewer classes.

name: Firm-level technological performance
authors_terms: ["firm productivity", "firm's overall technological performance", "general technological performance", "firm-level technological performance"]
definition: For firm-level technological performance (Hypothesis 4), the authors use a measure of the firm's general technological performance, calculated analogously to local productivity, aggregated to the firm-year level, using the share of the firm's patents in each category as weights.

name: CEO equity ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO equity ownership", "management equity ownership", "owner-managed firms", "companies led by agent CEOs", "agent-led companies"]
definition: In companies with a single class of equity, CEOs owning more than 20 percent of their company's equity were defined to be owner-managers. Two other groups were categorized as owner-managed because their governance arrangements served to align CEOs' personal financial interests with those of shareholders, and to limit CEOs' human capital risk.

name: Firm diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification", "diversified companies", "focused firms", "segments outside of the cable industry"]
definition: The measure of diversification used instead was a continuous variable ('SEGMENTS') reflecting the company's number of business segments outside of the cable industry. Vertical integration into cable programming services was not measured by SEGMENTS; the effects of vertical integration were reflected through an indicator variable (VERT).

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Turbulence is defined here as rapid, discontinuous, and unpredictable change in multiple factors significant to a firm's long-term performance, such as technology, regulation, or customer demand.

name: Horizontal expansion through acquisitions
definition: When they confront conditions of increasing environmental turbulence in a given line of business, companies necessarily will respond by expanding that line of business horizontally, idling, or divesting some or all of its assets. Committing additional resources to the business in an effort to expand horizontally could be described as risk-taking behavior, at least from the managers' perspective.

name: Divestiture of cable assets
authors_terms: ["divestiture of assets", "risk avoidance", "exit that business", "divest divisions", "CONTRACT"]
definition: By extension, divesting assets could be described as risk avoidance, since selling assets should yield fairly predictable proceeds in a liquid market. Risk taking and avoidance are measured as horizontal expansion through acquisitions and as the divestiture of assets, respectively.

name: Strategic orientation
definition: The strategic types of firms within the Miles and Snow (1978) typology, which not only describes firms' strategic orientations but also the structures, processes, and human resource practices likely to be most suited for a given strategy. The paper focuses on Prospectors and Defenders, which offer the clearest implications for variations in incentive mechanisms, with Reactors treated as the base case.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "accounting performance", "market-based performance", "return on capital employed", "market return"]
definition: Firm performance is the dependent variable and was operationalized with two different measures—one accounting and the other market-based. Accounting performance was defined as the annual return on capital employed, while market-based performance was defined as total market return to shareholders.

name: Annual bonus plan
authors_terms: ["annual bonus plan", "annual bonus plans", "short-term bonus plans"]
definition: Annual bonus plans tend to emphasize short-term performance because, in general, they use annual accounting indicators of financial performance to evaluate managers. Annual bonus plan = 1 if the firm had an annual bonus plan for executives/managers based on the financial performance of the past year and 0 otherwise.

name: Long-term cash-accounting incentive plan
authors_terms: ["long-term performance plan-accounting measures", "long-term performance plan-cash incentive", "long-term plan (cash/accounting)"]
definition: Long-term performance plans use a longer time period (typically 3-5 years) to evaluate managerial performance and hence are likely to foster a longer decision horizon among managers. The cash/accounting variant refers to long-term incentive plans that offer cash incentives and/or use accounting measures such as return on equity, return on capital employed and earnings per share as performance criteria.

name: Long-term stock-market incentive plan
authors_terms: ["long-term performance plan-market measures", "long-term performance plan-stock incentive", "long-term plan (stock/market)"]
definition: Long-term performance plans use a longer time period (typically 3-5 years) to evaluate managerial performance. The stock/market variant refers to long-term incentive plans that offer stock incentives (e.g., performance shares, performance units and restricted stock awards) and/or use market measures such as share price growth/appreciation and market return as performance criteria.

name: Stock option plan
definition: Stock option plans are similar to stock-based long-term performance plans with one major difference: often they do not specify the time period for evaluation and/or the specific performance criteria, and hence offer greater scope for the inclusion of subjective, qualitative factors in the evaluation process. Stock option plan = 1 if the firm had a stock option plan for executives/managers and 0 otherwise.

name: Innovative knowledge assets
authors_terms: ["innovative knowledge assets", "innovative knowledge", "firm innovative knowledge assets", "innovative knowledge input", "innovative knowledge output", "firm-specific innovative knowledge assets"]
definition: Among various types of firm knowledge, innovative knowledge assets, which may include information, know-how, and technologies that help a firm improve its product effectiveness and process efficiency, have the very characteristics of resources that are able to bring superior performance to a firm.

name: Firm economic performance
definition: We used market value to represent each firm's economic performance. Unlike return on assets, the market value of a firm is forward looking, as it incorporates stock market expectations about future returns.

name: Monitoring governance mechanisms
authors_terms: ["monitoring", "monitoring governance mechanisms", "monitoring mechanisms", "monitoring-based governance", "monitoring-based governance mechanisms"]
definition: Monitoring refers to 'observation of an agent's effort or outcomes that is accomplished through supervision, accounting controls, and other devices'; monitors oversee the activities of top managers to ensure they behave in a way that is consistent with the interest of the owners. It is one of the two fundamental mechanisms of corporate governance, alongside incentives.

name: Incentive-based governance mechanisms
authors_terms: ["incentive-based corporate governance mechanisms", "incentive-based governance", "incentives", "incentive alignment", "incentive-based mechanisms"]
definition: According to agency theory, incentive-based governance motivates managers to serve owners' interests by directly linking the managers' personal gains with a firm's performance. Managerial equity ownership and managerial compensation contingent on firm performance are the two most prevalent examples of incentive-based corporate governance mechanisms.

name: Central government linkage
authors_terms: ["institutional linkage to the central government", "central government linkage", "central government ownership", "national political appointment"]
definition: Institutional linkage to central government can channel normative influence and expose firms to direct and heightened attention from the central government.

name: Firm size
definition: Large organizations typically bear the brunt because institutional pressures are rarely applied uniformly and large organizations attract more attention and scrutiny. Large firms can be more vulnerable to loss of legitimacy and image (than smaller firms), and hence are less willing to risk losing the approval from the central government and the general public by producing lower quality CSR reports.

name: Speed of CSR report issuance
authors_terms: ["speed of adoption", "issuance speed", "how quickly a firm issued a CSR report", "issue CSR reports more swiftly"]
definition: Given our theoretical interest in the two important dimensions of organizational response to institutional complexity, the speed of adoption and substantive implementation, i.e., report quality, we examined two dependent variables; to predict how quickly a firm issued a CSR report after the announcement of the guidelines, we used discrete-time event history analysis, and hence the dependent variable is the hazard rate of issuing a report.

name: CSR report quality
authors_terms: ["report quality", "quality of CSR reports", "substantive implementation", "substantiveness in implementation"]
definition: Practice implementation is the substantive dimension of a firm's response. This measure thus indicates the attention and resources devoted to CSR activities.

name: Provincial government GDP growth priority
authors_terms: ["priority given by the provincial governments to GDP growth", "provincial government GDP priority", "priority given to GDP growth by some provincial governments", "local government's commitment to GDP growth"]
definition: This obsession with GDP growth in China represented a specific way of pursuing economic development, leading to maximization of short-term economic growth at the expense of social and environmental sustainability. With high priority given to GDP growth, local governments may simply have regarded CSR as a cost or distraction.

name: Decoupling response in CSR reporting
authors_terms: ["decoupling response", "a specific form of decoupling", "decoupling", "symbolic adoption", "early issuance and low-quality reports"]
definition: We highlight the speed of adoption and identify a specific form of decoupling that combines early issuance and low report quality to capture the strategic response of highly scrutinized firms to conflicting institutions.

name: Strategic decision speed
authors_terms: ["strategic decision speed", "decision speed", "strategic decision-making speed", "fast strategic decision-making"]
definition: Three decision scenarios were used to measure decision speed: (1) an acquisition decision, (2) a new product introduction decision, and (3) a technology adoption decision. Decision speed was measured as the average of three items (one for each of three scenarios).

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "growth and profitability", "firm growth", "profit % of assets"]
definition: Initially, we intended to study firm performance as an amalgamation of three important firm outcomes: sales growth, employment growth, and pretax net profit percentage of total assets. Factor analysis indicated that the two measures of growth and the measure of profit were distinct, and we decided to analyze the data with two types of firm performance: growth and profit.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism (instability or turbulence) refers to the level of environmental predictability; it is manifested in the variance in the rate of market and industry change and the level of uncertainty about forces that are beyond the control of individual businesses.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence (capacity) refers to the environment's support for organizational growth, and it is manifested in high industry sales growth.

name: Centralization of strategic management
authors_terms: ["centralization of strategic management", "centralization of strategy", "strategic centralization"]
definition: Centralization refers to the concentration of authority and power in a firm. The more centralized, the less widespread is decision-making power with regard to policy and task performance.

name: Decentralization of operations management
authors_terms: ["decentralization of operations management", "decentralization of operations", "operational centralization"]
definition: Low operational centralization (decentralization) involves behaviors usually associated with self-managed teams.

name: Formalization of organizational routines
definition: Formalized organization structures are characterized by explicitly articulated and written firm policies, job descriptions, organization charts, strategic and operational plans, and objective-setting systems.

name: Informalization of non-routines
authors_terms: ["informalization of non-routines", "informality", "informal non-routine policies, processes, and networks"]
definition: We believe that formalization of routines speeds strategic decision-making and that maintaining informal non-routine policies, processes, and networks enhances the use of fast a-rational processes.

name: Firm age
definition: A firm's age from founding, used as the indicator of structural inertia: the older the firm, the less likely it is to engage in change or adaptation because the proliferation of rules, routines, and internal organizational arrangements over time reinforces its adopted course of action.

name: Prior entry by group affiliates
authors_terms: ["previous group entry", "entry by other firms in the same cluster or group", "business group effects"]
definition: The establishment of plants in the foreign country by other firms belonging to the same business group, which provides member firms with information and legitimacy about foreign opportunities and how to pursue them.

name: Industry imitation
authors_terms: ["industry imitation", "percent same-industry entry", "proportion of same-industry entry", "organizational field effects"]
definition: Imitation in the organizational field: as an increasing proportion of firms in the same home country industry go abroad, the uncertainty of foreign market entry is reduced and the legitimacy of such a move is enhanced, leading more firms to follow.

name: Own prior foreign entry
definition: Whether the focal firm has itself already set up a plant in the foreign country, which distinguishes first entries from subsequent entries and gives the firm first-hand knowledge and experience of the foreign environment.

name: Foreign expansion rate
authors_terms: ["rate of foreign expansion", "rate of entry in a foreign country", "rate of establishment of new plants"]
definition: The rate at which a firm sets up manufacturing plants in a foreign country, treated as an instance of organizational and strategic change shaped by structural inertia and imitation.

name: Corporate social responsibility strengths
definition: CSR has typically been described as either an instrumental activity aligned with a firm's business model and designed to create shareholder value or as a normative, values-driven activity designed to benefit society with limited expectations for economic returns to the specific firm. The authors measure the focus of a firm's CSR efforts using the index of KLD strengths.

name: CEO foundation board joining
authors_terms: ["joining a foundation's board", "foundation board addition", "CEO choice (Corp.-Found. Link)", "CEO's tie to a nonprofit foundation board"]
definition: A CEO's tie to a nonprofit foundation board. CEOs' engagement in foundations has often been portrayed as a discretionary activity par excellence, neither required nor standardized.

name: Similarity in social cause priorities across corporation and foundation
authors_terms: ["similarity in social cause priorities", "similarity between foundation and corporate causes", "dissimilarity", "similarity in future social cause priorities after foundation selection"]
definition: A measure of similarity in social cause priorities, based on corporation KLD scores and foundation grant making across the four social domains of Environmental, Human Rights, Community, and Employees & Diversity.

name: CEO time on foundation board
authors_terms: ["time since CEO joined", "CEO time on foundation board"]
definition: The time elapsed since the CEO joined the foundation's board, used as the independent time variable in the growth curve model of similarity.

name: Change in corporate CSR cause priorities
definition: Whether the corporation deviates away from or gets closer to the middle point between the firm's CSR emphases and the foundation's cause priorities, with a negative value reflecting divergence.

name: Change in foundation grantmaking cause priorities
definition: Whether the foundation deviates away from or gets closer to the middle point between the firm's CSR emphases and the foundation's cause priorities, with a negative value reflecting divergence.

name: Employee-related CSR
authors_terms: ["employee-related CSR", "employee-related KLD index", "employee-related KLD strengths", "employee-related CSR policies"]
definition: Employee-related CSR programs are those directed at a company's employees; examples include investments in work-life balance (e.g., childcare, flextime), health and safety, and employee involvement. In the data, the employee-related KLD index is constructed by summing up all KLD strengths pertaining to employee relations and diversity.

name: Unemployment insurance benefit generosity
definition: The UI system in the United States provides temporary income to eligible workers who become unemployed through no fault of their own (i.e., involuntarily) and meet the eligibility requirements under the relevant state law. To measure the generosity of UI benefits, the authors compute a state's UI benefit as the product of the maximum benefit amount and the maximum duration allowed.

name: Industry labor intensity
definition: Labor-intensive industries are industries in which companies' operations rely more substantially on human capital; labor intensity is defined as the ratio of labor and pension expenses to sales, averaged across all companies in the same 2-digit SIC industry.

name: Product market competition
definition: The intensity of rivalry in a company's product market; the authors measure it by using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of industry concentration at the 2-digit SIC level, which is a measure of concentration and hence an inverse measure of competition.

name: Stakeholder dissatisfaction
definition: The authors argue that employees' incentives to be productive can be provided by decreasing their dissatisfaction, which is particularly relevant in stigmatized industries that are more likely to be associated with stakeholder dissatisfaction, such as 'dirty' industries. High-polluting industries are used to identify such industries.

name: Technology sourcing mix
authors_terms: ["technology sourcing mix", "(external/total) tech sourcing", "internal-external technology sourcing mix"]
definition: A firm's technology sourcing mix is measured by the ratio of its external technology sourcing over its total technology sourcing, which is the sum of its internal and external technology sourcing, bound between 0 and 1.

name: Technology sourcing mix of known technology
authors_terms: ["technology sourcing mix of known technology", "(external/total) tech exploitation", "external technology exploitation"]
definition: Known technologies are 'technologies that are being used by the firm for some time. They are not new to the firm or the industry'; when a firm sources these known technologies it engages in exploitation.

name: Technology sourcing mix of new technology
authors_terms: ["technology sourcing mix of new technology", "(external/total) tech exploration", "external technology exploration"]
definition: New technologies are defined as the inverse of known technologies, because what is not known must be new; when a firm searches for new technologies, it engages in exploration.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: The ability of a firm to recognize the value of new, external information, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends; it is generally developed through continuous funding of and engaging in R&D over time.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Firm performance is a multidimensional construct, assessed here along two dimensions: firm innovativeness and firm financial performance; financial performance is proxied by a firm's return on equity.

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: Firm innovativeness is proxied by the total number of patents assigned to the firm by the U.S. PTO during the four-year time period between 2000 and 2003.

name: Social structure disintegration
authors_terms: ["social structure disintegration", "social structure loss", "loss of social structure", "disintegration of social structure"]
definition: Social structure is defined as family and community relationships. As a household's social structure disintegrates, its working and adult members are lost through events such as illness, death, break-up, incarceration, HIV/AIDS, or conflict with neighbors.

name: Initiating action to start a business
authors_terms: ["initiating action to start a new business", "initiating action", "initiating action to start a business", "initiates action to start a business"]
definition: This category consists of individuals who expressed interest in starting a business in the next three years and had already started work on a new business. It is distinguished from merely intending to start a business.

name: Income lost
definition: Total income lost by a household due to all types of shocks over the three years before the focal year, read against the focal year's income as a reference point: households in the domain of loss have lost more notional income than they earned in the focal year.

name: Household head gender
definition: Whether the household head is male or female; in this patriarchal context a woman only becomes the household head when the male head dies or becomes incapacitated.

name: Community institution membership
authors_terms: ["community institution membership", "community credit", "access to community resources", "membership in a local credit community institution"]
definition: Membership in community institutions that offer access to group credit, providing household heads with capital resources and shared risk. It is measured as whether household members belonged to a community group used for raising loans.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "duality", "CEO-chair", "consolidation of CEO and Chairman positions"]
definition: CEO duality exists when a firm's chief executive also serves as Chairman of the board of directors. Otherwise, the board is described as having an independent structure.

name: Firm performance
definition: Policy decisions made by the CEO and board are not likely to be reflected in the balance sheet for several years. Consequently, performance was operationalized as average return on investment (ROI) over the 5-year period 1980-84.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence measures the abundance of resources in the environment. Scarcity implies greater uncertainty regarding access to resources; consequently, munificence is negatively related to uncertainty.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism measures environmental volatility, and is positively associated with uncertainty.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Complexity measures inequalities among competitors, and is positively associated with uncertainty (Dess and Beard, 1984).

name: Ethnic community knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["ethnic community knowledge sourced", "knowledge sourced from the ethnic community", "ethnic knowledge sourcing"]
definition: The ethnic knowledge sourcing variable reflects the proportion of knowledge sourcing by the Indian inventor that is attributable to the ethnic community. Cited patents (and their inventors) were classified as belonging to the ethnic community if the cited inventor had an Indian name.

name: Ethnic community collaboration
authors_terms: ["ethnic community collaborators", "ethnic collaborators", "collaboration with other inventors in the ethnic community"]
definition: To evaluate the extent of collaboration with other inventors in the ethnic community, we considered copatenting by individuals on patents. We measured ethnic community collaborators as a count of the distinct Indian copatenters indicated on the patent portfolio of the inventor in year t.

name: Quality of inventor innovation
definition: Our measure of innovativeness is a forward citation-weighted measure of the number of patents produced by the Indian inventor in a particular year. It therefore provides a snapshot of inventor innovation quality as well as productivity.

name: Switching between external and internal engagement
authors_terms: ["switching", "degree of switching", "switching between external and internal engagement", "engagement dynamics"]
definition: Switching is focusing more on one type of engagement over the other at different points in time. The authors focus on the degree of the switch at each switching occasion, that is, how much individuals switch from focusing relatively more on one engagement type during a time period (t) to focusing relatively more on the other engagement type during the next time period (t + 1).

name: Knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfer", "external knowledge transfer", "inflow of external knowledge"]
definition: Knowledge transfer is the amount of technological, market, and business-model knowledge that boundary spanners transferred from external knowledge sources that were part of the program to the home organization at each measurement occasion.

name: Transspecialist knowledge
authors_terms: ["transspecialist knowledge", "knowledge that is transspecialist in nature"]
definition: Whereas within-expertise knowledge draws from a single area of expertise, transspecialist knowledge draws from multiple expertise areas with inherent interdependencies. It is a salient component of knowledge complexity.

name: Organizational distance
authors_terms: ["organizational distance between source and recipient units"]
definition: Organizational distance can be described in terms of the degree to which organizations fundamentally differ in their institutional heritage, routines of behavior, practices, values, and professional language.

name: Progression in the boundary-spanning process
authors_terms: ["progression in the boundary-spanning process", "boundary-spanning phases", "phase of the boundary-spanning process"]
definition: Early phases of the boundary-spanning process are characterized primarily by knowledge scouting, evaluating the fit of external knowledge, and making connections, whereas later phases shift toward problem redefinition, technical integration, rearchitecting knowledge, and conflict resolution. The authors assume a gradual and continuous shift in the relevance of boundary-spanning activities across these phases.

name: Research output
authors_terms: ["research output", "publication output", "quality-adjusted publication rate", "publications in 2 years prior to survey", "citation-weighted publications", "research productivity"]
definition: Research output is defined in terms of an effort-adjusted unit of publication, for example an article in a leading journal; other types of output, such as books, could be expressed in terms of this unit based on the research time they require.

name: Time spent with research staff
authors_terms: ["time spent with research staff", "time spent on advising research staff", "advising time", "hours per week advising and/or counseling students"]
definition: Advising includes all interactions intended to train students, postdocs, and research staff or to manage the research projects and teams of researchers in the research group the scientist leads.

name: Research funding
authors_terms: ["having funding", "received funding", "external or internal funding", "whether she received any funding for her research"]
definition: The authors do not observe the amount of funding a faculty member has received; they rely on whether the faculty member received any research funding (external or internal) in the 2 years prior to each survey wave, and expect this measure to capture the basic variance in funding per faculty member across departments.

name: Research model
authors_terms: ["funded research model", "hands-on research model", "research model", "mode of operation"]
definition: Two distinct organizational patterns for scientific research: in the funded research model the scientist acts as team manager and entrepreneur, obtaining funding to sustain a sizable research team and often not executing the actual research, whereas in the hands-on research model the scientist is highly engaged in executing research projects, trains fewer graduate students and postdocs, works in smaller teams, and demands less funding.

name: Funded model dominance in a field
authors_terms: ["field effect", "domains in which the funded model dominates", "domains in which the hands-on model is more common"]
definition: Given the potential importance of field effects, the model predicts that scientists in the same field would on average follow the same research model (i.e., funded versus hands-on); fields therefore differ in whether the funded or the hands-on model dominates.

name: Unexpected absence of research staff
authors_terms: ["unexpected absence of research staff", "negative (positive) exogenous shock to research staff", "gone unexpectedly absent"]
definition: A graduate student, postdoc, or research staff member who has gone unexpectedly absent - for example, because of visa or health issues - as reported by the faculty member who advised that person.

name: Operating experience
authors_terms: ["operating experience", "experience", "cumulative production volume", "cumulative number of flights"]
definition: By accumulating operating experience, organizations should become more efficient; cumulative volume is a proxy variable for knowledge acquired through repeated production. To measure operating experience, learning-curve scholars typically use cumulative production volume.

name: Customer dissatisfaction
definition: Customer dissatisfaction occurs when ex ante expectations about a product or service exceed ex post perceptions of the product or service. The more perceptions fall short of expectations, the higher customer dissatisfaction will be.

name: Airline focus
definition: Focused airlines achieve market focus by cherry picking routes in North America only. Focused airlines achieve operating focus by flying only a few plane types, whereas full-service airlines offer both continental and intercontinental services and operate several hubs.

name: Airline identity
definition: The specific airline unit in the authors' time-series cross-section data: units are fixed, there is no sampling, and the authors are interested in specific units ('how does Southwest compare with American?').

name: GBEL certification adoption
definition: GBEL is a government led voluntary program developed by the Chinese Ministry of Urban and Rural Development (MOHURD). The primary outcome variables measure annual adoption of the two voluntary certification programs: GBEL and LEED.

name: LEED certification adoption
authors_terms: ["LEED", "LEED certification", "LEED adoption", "Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design"]
definition: LEED is an international standard with multi-stakeholder engagement created and managed by the US Green Building Council (USGBC). For each city, the authors collect data on new LEED certifications at the city-year level.

name: LEED accredited professional supply
authors_terms: ["LEED AP", "LEED Accredited Professionals (APs)", "LEED related human capital investment", "supplier entry", "supplier adoption"]
definition: In addition to managing the LEED standard, USGBC offers professional accreditation under the 'LEED AP' brand for various types of building-industry professionals (e.g., architects, designers, and contractors) to certify their advanced knowledge of green building practices.

name: Multi-labeling
authors_terms: ["multi-labeling", "multi-labelling", "joint adoption of two or more labels"]
definition: We use the term 'multi-labeling' to describe products that simultaneously adopt multiple certifications.

name: Project-level economies of scope in certification
authors_terms: ["project-level economies of scope", "building level scope economies", "economies of scope", "firm or project level economies of scope"]
definition: If different certification programs have some shared requirements, then the marginal cost of adopting a second label will decline once a firm makes the investments required to achieve its first label. As long as the marginal costs of a second certification decline by more than the marginal benefit (i.e., scope economies are large relative to any reduction in signaling benefits) then project-level economies of scope can be a source of positive spillovers between labels.

name: Latent demand for green building
authors_terms: ["latent demand", "local demand for environmental amenities", "local taste for green products", "environmentalism", "green index"]
definition: Our conception of user spillovers assumes that there is a latent demand (i.e., unrealized willingness-to-pay) for products that address a particular class of problems. The authors use the 'China Green Low-Carbon City Index' as a variable that captures local taste for green products.

name: Government financial subsidies for GBEL
definition: The Chinese government provides builders with a number of incentives to adopt GBEL, including financial subsidies to GBEL buildings, prizes, and better conditions on loans. A key explanatory variable measures provincial or city level financial subsidies to adopt GBEL, hand collected from MOHURD and local government websites.

name: Strategic scope group
definition: An SSG includes firms within an industry that define their scope, using a four-dimensional 'strategic space' (buyer types, product types, geographical reach and level of vertical integration), in a similar way.

name: Strategic group
definition: An SG includes firms within an SSG that deploy their resources in a similar way and that compete in the same way.

name: Performance
definition: A risk-adjusted profitability measure was operationalized for testing the formal research hypotheses; a risk-adjusted ROA is calculated before taxes and debt charges.

name: Firm size
definition: Volume is a measure of firm size and used as a proxy for the geographical reach of the firm, which is essentially a size dimension as well.

name: Product range
definition: The number of product types is in the first place used as a measure of competitive scope, but as with the variable volume it also has implications for the potentiality of arriving at competitive advantages.

name: Product type orientation
authors_terms: ["type of firm", "percentage of pils production in total output"]
definition: Rather than using a categorization into 'mainly pils brewers' and 'mainly non-pils brewers,' the type of firm is operationalized as the percentage of pils brewed relative to the total volume of beer produced of whatever type.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Channel control is a measure of the resources committed to gain control over the distribution channels; it is a measure of forward vertical integration, but a measure (of one source) of seller power as well.

name: Corporate identity
definition: The second factor, corporate identity, is considered as a differentiation dimension. The higher the importance of self-made output, the more important is the capital intensity and the investment intensity.

name: Marketing differentiation
definition: The third factor is labeled as 'marketing differentiation' in light of the high loading of the advertising intensity. Advertising intensity is supposed to be the single best indicator of a differentiation strategy.

name: Innovative differentiation
definition: The fourth factor, innovative differentiation, is aimed at creating new product-market combinations. It resembles the prospector strategy of Miles and Snow (1978).

name: Brokerage
definition: Structural holes are a feature of network position and brokerage is an action taken by virtue of occupying a position marked by structural holes; in this study the authors use these two terms interchangeably.

name: Exclusive brokerage
definition: Structural holes uniquely bridged by just one firm, illustrated by the gap bridged only by J, who is a sole mediator. Betweenness centrality 'is a count of the structural holes to which a person has monopoly access' and thus captures the absence of competition in access to structural holes.

name: Market crisis
definition: Crises are 'sudden, unexpected, and massively disruptive' events in which society and normal operations are interrupted. The two main disruptions caused by crises which are most relevant to brokerage are scarcity and uncertainty.

name: Crisis onset speed
authors_terms: ["speed at which crisis encroaches", "fast-burning", "creeping crisis", "long incubation"]
definition: Not all crises are fast-burning; some crises emerge slowly, over a 'long incubation' period, and are thus neither sudden nor unexpected, giving firms time to prepare.

name: Crisis severity
authors_terms: ["magnitude of the crisis", "first-order change", "second-order change", "unimaginable crises"]
definition: The magnitude of the disruption caused by a crisis, ranging from first-order change, which occurs around an organization when there are continuous, incremental variations in its environment but the system stays unchanged, to second-order change that 'transforms fundamental properties or the states in the system', and on to existential shocks.

name: Cost of maintaining exclusive brokerage
authors_terms: ["costs of maintaining exclusive brokerage positions", "strenuous efforts to monopolize structural holes"]
definition: The egocentric and altercentric costs of maintaining exclusive structural holes, which may extract extraordinary attention and time from the focal ego and require much monitoring and the careful cultivation of loyalties at both ends of the structural hole.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors operationalize bank performance at time t by the revenue of a bank during that period, that is, the total dollar value it receives from all of its deals.

name: New partners
definition: The number of new partners of the focal bank in the period {t+1, t+2} compared with the period {t-1, t}.

name: New clients
definition: The number of new clients of the focal bank in the period {t+1, t+2} compared with the period {t-1, t}.

name: Sectoral stability
