definition: The extent to which investment banks sustain their industry presence after the crisis hit the market, measured by the similarity between the sectors in which the bank did business pre-crisis and the sectors in which it does business after the crisis.

name: Ambidextrous strategic response
definition: A combination of innovating, that is, conducting strategic renewal in response to crisis, and persevering, preserving the status quo of a firm's business activities in times of crisis, so that crisis-exposed banks simultaneously stabilize and renew their strategies.

name: Partner's service quality
authors_terms: ["partner's service quality", "PARTSQ", "perceived service quality of a service partner"]
definition: Overall service quality is conceptualized as the degree to which a company offers excellent service; PARTSQ captures customer perceptions of the excellence of the service provided by the partner (MARTA) on its rail service to the airport, including key processes in the experience such as timeliness, ease of (de)boarding, and quality of the transportation experience.

name: Primary provider's service quality
definition: Customer perceptions of the service quality offered by the primary provider (Delta), assessed as the overall quality of the check-in experience, the quality of interactions with the Delta service agents, and the excellence of service with respect to waiting time.

name: Waiting time
authors_terms: ["waiting time", "WAIT", "in-queue waiting time", "length of time in line"]
definition: In a two-phase partnered service, the seamlessness of the service can be gauged by the waiting time from the point when service is completed by the partner provider until service is commenced by the primary provider; here it is the length of time each respondent spent in the Delta check-in queue, timed and recorded by the interviewer.

name: Perceived value of the partnered service
authors_terms: ["perceived value", "value", "added-value", "perceived value of the partnered service"]
definition: Service value is the difference between the benefits received from using a service and the cost (monetary or nonmonetary) of receiving the service; in the context of the service partnerships examined here, the value received is based on customers' assessment of the added benefits of the partnership above and beyond those of the standard service.

name: Reuse intentions
authors_terms: ["reuse intentions", "INTENT", "intentions to reuse the partnered service", "intention to reuse a partnered service"]
definition: Consumers' intentions to reuse the partnered service in the future, assessed as how likely they would be to use the remote Delta check-in counter on future trips to and from Hartsfield International Airport.

name: Implementation of popular management techniques
authors_terms: ["popular management techniques", "the adoption of popular management techniques", "TQM implementation", "the implementation of total quality management"]
definition: A measure that assesses the extent to which corporations in the sample implemented a currently popular management technique, total quality management. The authors note that such a dummy coding can only be considered an approximate and fairly conservative measure of implementation.

name: Informational linkage with popular management techniques
authors_terms: ["informational measures", "informationally linked with popular management techniques", "PMT exposure", "PMT focus", "informational linkage"]
definition: Because reputations are a function of what external parties see the organization doing, the authors created two informational measures linking sampled corporations with popular management techniques. These citation data measure the informational linkage of a particular firm with popular management techniques.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Each company's economic performance, recorded as return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS); an overall performance measure was created by normalizing each indicator and aggregating the scores.

name: External reputation
definition: Fortune magazine's "Most Admired" ratings of companies in their own industries, comprising ratings on eight dimensions of corporate reputation and an overall measure of admiration; significant changes in reputation may often be what drives the institutional basis of behavior.

name: Perceived innovativeness
definition: The rated innovativeness of the firm, one of the individual aspects of corporate reputation recorded from the Fortune survey; information linking the firm with popular management techniques may influence the perception of innovation.

name: Perceived quality of management
authors_terms: ["quality of management", "perceived management quality", "outsiders' opinions of the management of the firm"]
definition: The rated quality of management of the firm, one of the individual aspects of corporate reputation recorded from the Fortune survey; observers may perceive that managers are well qualified and of high ability when they are using the latest techniques.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "CEO salary and bonus", "long-term compensation"]
definition: Financial compensation provided to the chief executive officer; boards of directors have been found to use psychological as well as economic referents in determining compensation for the chief executive officer. Short-term compensation is salary and bonus; long-term compensation includes restricted stock grants, long-term incentive payouts, the Black-Scholes value of stock options granted, and all other long-term compensation.

name: Cognitive flexibility
definition: The ability to match the type of cognitive processing with the type of problem at hand. This matching depends on two conditions being met: decision makers need to be able to describe the type of problem they face, and they need to consider different possibilities.

name: Decision-making performance
authors_terms: ["decision-making performance", "performance", "cumulative performance", "performance in Task 1", "performance in Task 2"]
definition: How well a participant performed in solving each problem, evaluated independently for the two problem types and taking into account the different problems' objectives; the two scores were standardized and added to create a unique performance measure summarizing how well a participant performed in solving both problems.

name: Task structure
authors_terms: ["well-structured problems", "ill-structured problems", "type of problem", "task structure", "type of task"]
definition: Well-structured problems are those in which a strategic decision maker faces uncertainty about outcomes in a context in which the current and end states are clearly identified, and the options and methods to identify a solution are known (through experience) or knowable (through computation). Conversely, ill-structured problems are those where there is great uncertainty about both current and end states, no repertoire of solutions is available, and they need to be learned or discovered.

name: Type of cognitive processing
authors_terms: ["Type 1 processing", "Type 2 processing", "type of cognitive processing", "processing type", "response time", "processing time"]
definition: Type 1 processing corresponds closely to automatic processing; it is faster, has higher capacity, and proposes intuitive answers to problems as they arise. Type 2 processing corresponds to controlled processes; it is slower, has a limited capacity, and provides reflective answers.

name: Local corporate density
authors_terms: ["corporate density", "local corporate density", "density of corporations", "dense population of local corporations"]
definition: The population of locally headquartered corporations in a community. The authors argue that a dense population of local corporations in a community leads to growth in nonprofits through direct effects such as philanthropic giving, executive leadership, aggregation of donations, and employee volunteering.

name: Elite-oriented nonprofit growth
authors_terms: ["elite-oriented nonprofits", "growth of elite-oriented nonprofits", "elite-oriented cultural and educational institutions"]
definition: Elite-oriented nonprofits are those organizations that focus on the enrichment of the local cultural environment or the preservation of elite-oriented values and traditions, whose primary, direct beneficiaries are white-collar, college-educated community residents.

name: Social welfare-oriented nonprofit growth
authors_terms: ["social welfare-oriented nonprofits", "social welfare nonprofits", "growth of local social welfare nonprofits"]
definition: Social welfare nonprofits are those organizations that address the amelioration of local social problems or human needs in the community, such as health care, crime, housing, and other important local social concerns associated with community well-being.

name: Local network cohesion
authors_terms: ["local network cohesion", "network cohesion among local corporations", "mean local degree", "relational network linking corporate decision makers"]
definition: The relational network linking corporate decision makers, described as encouraging high levels of corporate involvement in nonprofits; measured as the average number of network ties each firm in a CBSA maintains with other firms in its CBSA.

name: Upper-class social club presence
definition: An important local institution for elite cohesion; these clubs are foci for elite interaction that provide institutionalized informal settings in which elites are socialized and socially controlled to adhere to normative business attitudes and behaviors.

name: Northeast regional location
authors_terms: ["Northeast", "regional culture", "location in the Northeast", "cultures of trusteeship"]
definition: A community's embeddedness in an established regional culture; the authors center their attention on the northeastern United States, where a civil privatism model of trusteeship developed based on the early example of Boston.

name: Early establishment of the business community
authors_terms: ["early establishment of the business community", "long-established corporate sectors", "community tradition"]
definition: Patterns established early in a community's history tend to be enduring and to exert a contemporary influence; cities that established early local cultures encouraging nonprofit support are likely to have greater growth in nonprofits.

name: Monitoring potential of the board of directors
authors_terms: ["monitoring potential of the board of directors", "monitoring by the board of directors", "PNOD"]
definition: The ability of the board to perform the decision control function is here called its monitoring potential, the level of which is determined by the need for board monitoring.

name: Monitoring by large outside shareholders
authors_terms: ["monitoring by large outside shareholders", "monitoring potential of large outside shareholders", "monitoring potential of concentrated share ownership"]
definition: In a corporation characterized by diffused share ownership across a large number of shareholders with small equity stakes, no individual shareholder has the incentive to monitor the actions of managers. However, to the extent that any shareholders have a comparatively large equity stake, they have increased incentive to monitor both the decision plans and decision outcomes of managers since they will bear greater proportions of the costs associated with the value-destroying decisions of the firms' managers.

name: Managerial share ownership
authors_terms: ["incentive effects of managerial share ownership", "managerial shareholdings", "managerial holdings of stock", "PSTM"]
definition: When managerial holdings of stock are large, the manager-shareholder agency conflict is mitigated. Furthermore, in firms where managerial incentives such as share ownership have acted to align the interests of managers and shareholders, the monitoring role of the board of directors is expected to be relatively less important.

name: Mutual monitoring by the top management team
authors_terms: ["mutual monitoring by managers", "mutual monitoring by inside directors", "potential for mutual monitoring", "dispersion of the top management team's voting power"]
definition: Mutual monitoring systems within the firm act to curb individual managers' freedom to take actions in their own interests but contrary to those of shareholders. When top managers are in competition for control of the firm, they have the incentive to monitor the decisions of other members of the top management team.

name: Top executive dominance
authors_terms: ["dominant top executive", "position power of the top executive", "BOSS"]
definition: Top executive dominance is considered to be high when the top executive holds all of the positions of Chairman, CEO or President that exist in the firm (BOSS = 1), and low when these positions are shared between two or three individuals (BOSS = 0). Dominance is examined through the number of titles held by the top executive.

name: Downside risk
authors_terms: ["downside risk", "performance that falls below certain target"]
definition: Downside risk is a function of the deviation of the firm's return on assets from the industry mean in the preceding year, which is considered the target level; it is performance that falls below certain target. The measure focuses on performance outcomes that only fall below some target level, unlike conventional variance-based measures of risk that incorporate the entire distribution of firm performance.

name: Multinationality
authors_terms: ["multinationality", "number of countries in which the firm operates manufacturing affiliates"]
definition: Multinationality is measured as the number of countries in which the Japanese firm operates manufacturing affiliates. Its use as a measure of the switching options embedded in multinational investment reflects the idea that operating subsidiaries located in separate countries can provide the multinational firm with the valuable option to shift production because of fluctuations in variable labor cost, exchange rate, as well as other economic parameters.

name: Cost subadditivity
authors_terms: ["cost subadditivity", "subadditivity", "labor cost correlations", "correlations in labor costs"]
definition: Subadditivity between two real options, A and B, in an option portfolio means that the value of a portfolio of options may be less than the summation of the values of these options if they were independent. In multinational operations it arises from correlations in the economic conditions, such as labor cost developments, of the host countries in which the firm operates; a high correlation indicates high-cost subadditivity, meaning that labor cost levels develop in a similar manner across host countries and there are limited opportunities to exploit country differences in labor costs.

name: Equity share
definition: The equity ownership of foreign affiliates affects the distribution of incentives and control rights throughout the firm's international operations; greater control rights are put in the hands of host-country partners when the firm has a smaller equity share, and their objectives are more likely to be country-specific. Greater equity share gives the firm control over its affiliates and facilitates the coordination of cross-border activities among its portfolio of affiliates.

name: Expatriate assignment
definition: The assignment of expatriates to an affiliate helps to ensure that the way the affiliate is managed is in line with the global interest of the parent company to enhance system-wide coordination. The use of expatriates is an important means through which a firm's human resource management system coordinates activities among dispersed affiliates in order to benefit from operating flexibility.

name: Category spanning
authors_terms: ["category spanning", "categorical spanning", "industry spanning", "spanning across activities", "spanning width", "breadth"]
definition: Spanning is a firm having activities across more than one industry category; the authors state that "the penalty for spanning industries can hold in general, but firms can also use self-descriptions to reduce it" and that existing research "has defined broad self-descriptions as boundary spanning." Spanning is measured both as assigned externally, through coverage mismatch, and as driven internally, through the number of unique words in the firm's 10-K narrative.

name: Linguistic alignment
definition: "We develop the new concept of linguistic alignment, defined as the match of the linguistic organizational self-description and the environmentally imposed expectations." It is partly self-defined and partly environmentally imposed, and it can change over time.

name: Stock market performance
authors_terms: ["stock market performance", "excess value", "firm value", "firm performance", "market evaluation"]
definition: "Our dependent variable is a firm's excess value from diversification"; the valuation of a firm divided by its expected value differs across firms and this is called the 'excess value.' "A positive excess value indicates that diversification enhances the value of segments beyond that of their stand-alone counterparts, and negative implies that diversification reduces value."

name: Linguistic alignment change
authors_terms: ["linguistic alignment change", "change by firm", "alignment change by analyst"]
definition: The analysis of change in linguistic alignment distinguishes "which side of the linguistic alignment led to the effects because the changes in linguistic alignment can result from changes in self-description, audience expectation, or both." The authors report that the change of linguistic alignment and its performance impact are mainly derived from the audience's changed expectations rather than from the firm's own change in self-description.

name: Organizational membership
authors_terms: ["membership on a particular organization's TMT", "organizational/TMT membership", "membership in a particular firm's TMT", "affiliation with a particular firm's TMT"]
definition: The variable used to predict the similarity/dissimilarity of the views of TMT members in the same organization was membership on a particular organization's TMT.

name: Industry membership
authors_terms: ["participation in a particular industry", "the industry in which the informant's organization was nested", "industry membership"]
definition: Because organizations are nested within industries, and because top managers' participation in a particular industry could affect their views concerning their organization's environment, the authors determined the particular industry in which the TMT member participated.

name: Perceptual homogeneity
authors_terms: ["homogeneity of perceptions within top management teams", "commonality of views about a firm's environment", "homogeneity in executives' perceptions", "similarity of perceptions"]
definition: The degree of homogeneity in executives' perceptions within firms and within industries, i.e. the relative proportion of agreement about organizational environments.

name: Perceived environmental instability
definition: Perceived instability reflects the degree to which managers reported the environment as unstable.

name: Perceived environmental munificence
definition: Perceived munificence reflects the degree to which top managers reported the availability of resources in the environment as growing (or declining) which is indicative of the extent to which the environment is supportive of sustained stability or growth for the organization and its competitors in the same industry.

name: Perceived environmental complexity
definition: Perceived complexity reflects the degree to which top managers view the environment as complex.

name: Perceived environmental hostility
definition: Perceived hostility was defined as the extent to which top managers characterize their environment as hostile.

name: Perceived environmental controllability
definition: Perceived controllability reflects the extent to which managers characterize their environment as controllable or uncontrollable.

name: Community consensus around a resource conservation logic
authors_terms: ["resource conservation logic", "community consensus around a resource conservation logic", "strength of community consensus around a resource conservation logic"]
definition: A competing institutional logic that emphasized the reduction of demand and the meeting of remaining demand from environmentally sustainable sources. Its guiding principle is that it can be better both economically and environmentally to reduce and spread out demand than to build power plants to meet it.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Emerging technologies face extreme uncertainty that may modify the influence of local institutional logics. These dimensions of uncertainty include whether they will 'work,' whether they will be manufacturable at scale and at a reasonable cost if they do work, whether they will be reliable, and what standards may emerge that may shape interoperability and economies of scale.

name: Knowledge spillovers
definition: Where a particular institutional logic dominates, individuals typically share a depth of knowledge in specific areas related to that logic and they are motivated to share this related knowledge with one another. Such regions also share a common vocabulary and 'cultural codes' that can aid such sharing.

name: Wind and solar energy equipment manufacturing
authors_terms: ["wind and solar energy equipment manufacturers", "number of wind and solar energy equipment manufacturers", "wind energy equipment manufacturers", "solar energy equipment manufacturers"]
definition: Firms manufacturing components and systems for wind and solar energy generation equipment located in a region. Because different components and systems are needed for the two technologies, for each year an MSA has a different number of manufacturers for solar and for wind.

name: State financial incentives for renewable energy
authors_terms: ["state wind and solar incentives", "financial incentives", "renewable energy incentives", "number of statewide wind incentives", "number of statewide solar incentives"]
definition: States can and do target financial incentives such as tax credits, rapid depreciation, and other stimuli specifically toward solar and/or wind. Hypothesis 4 tests the relationship between a supportive institutional logic and financial incentives for renewable energy at the state level, with separate variables for wind and solar because states adopted different policies toward the two technologies.

name: Time
definition: The passage of years, which the authors argue will cause the influence of a local institutional logic to wane as companies stabilize their economic fundamentals and begin to create dependable resource flows.

name: Personal imprint publishing
authors_terms: ["personal imprint publishing", "personal imprints", "imprints", "product development via personal imprint publishing"]
definition: Personal imprint publishing is an organization structure in conformity with an editorial logic, in which attention is focused on developing author-editor networks by organic growth and building personal imprints; the number of personal imprints is a measure of the editorial control of the firm and the market.

name: Contractual product distribution
authors_terms: ["distribution contract", "product distribution via contractual relationships", "contracting marketing"]
definition: Publishers can contract with other publishers and distributors that have established marketing and distribution resources instead of vertically integrating marketing and distribution; contracting marketing, although ensuring broad distribution of current products, can inhibit the development of future products.

name: Acquisition growth
definition: Acquisition growth is growth through acquiring other firms, in which a corporation either acquires other firms and designates them as divisions or is itself acquired and turned into a division of an existing M-form organization.

name: Resource competition
definition: Resource competition is a ratio measure of the annual count of potential competitors (all publishing organizations) relative to available resources (the number of students enrolled in colleges and universities).

name: Divisionalization
authors_terms: ["divisionalization", "rate at which a firm becomes a division of an M-form organization", "transition to a divisionalized structure"]
definition: Divisionalization is the change in organization structure in which the organization switches its structure to become a division of an M-form organization.

name: Institutional logic
definition: Institutional logics define the norms, values, and beliefs that structure the cognition of actors in organizations and provide a collective understanding of how strategic interests and decisions are formulated; the two ideal types examined here are an editorial logic, prevailing during the 1960s and early 1970s, and a market logic, prevailing since the mid 1970s.

name: Reputation information
definition: Information summarizing a partner's past play in alliances, comprising the partner's cooperation history, defection history, exit history and historic alliance stage completion ratio, made available to a firm before it decides whether and how to ally.

name: Cooperation
authors_terms: ["cooperation", "cooperative play", "overall cooperation level", "cooperation in the initial stage"]
definition: A firm's cooperative play within an alliance, captured as the proportion of cooperative choices in the stages of alliances played before an exit.

name: Alliance length
authors_terms: ["alliance length", "average alliance length", "stages completed before a partner exits"]
definition: The number of alliance stages completed before a partner exits, expressed as the proportion of alliance stages played pre-exit relative to the possible alliance stages.

name: Alliance payoffs
definition: The overall welfare partners obtain from the alliance, measured as the average alliance stage payoff of players.

name: Belief in partner cooperation
authors_terms: ["beliefs about a partner's future cooperation", "beliefs of partner cooperation", "belief in partner cooperating"]
definition: A player's estimate of the probability that the partner it is paired with will cooperate in the coming trial.

name: Business risk
authors_terms: ["business risk", "risk", "systematic risk", "unsystematic risk", "stock market risk", "income stream risk"]
definition: Risk is uncertainty about outcomes or events, especially with respect to the future. Typically defined as greater variability in organizational returns and increased chances for corporate ruin, business risk was measured as the volatility in an organization's performance: as variation in a firm's income stream and as variability in the firm's stock market returns.

name: Incentive pay
authors_terms: ["incentive pay", "performance-contingent pay", "outcome-based pay", "bonus-to-base ratio", "use of incentive pay"]
definition: Incentive or performance-contingent pay refers to that portion of pay that is dependent upon firm performance and is not added to base pay.

name: Base pay
definition: The principal's primary choice centers on creating the balance between base (behavior-based) pay and incentive (outcome-based) pay. In classic definitions of agency theory, insurance is operationally defined as higher base pay, and internal labor markets theory holds that people require higher pay levels in exchange for reduced stability in their employment and future income streams.

name: Firm performance
definition: Agency theory focuses on maximizing organizational performance, and the principals of the sampled firms were the owners of their common stock, so performance was measured as total shareholder return, the one-year total gain (loss) a shareholder received for holding the firm's common shares.

name: Managerial control
authors_terms: ["managerial control", "manager-controlled firms", "owner-controlled firm", "owner control", "outside ownership", "managerial capitalism"]
definition: Firms vary in the control their principals have over the structure of agents' pay. An owner-controlled firm has at least one large external shareholder (a strong principal) who controls a significant proportion of the firm's outstanding stock; in the absence of such a large shareholder, managers are subject to weaker principal control.

name: Negative earnings surprise
authors_terms: ["negative earnings surprise", "low earnings relative to consensus forecasts", "(low) reported corporate earnings vs. forecasts"]
definition: Earnings below consensus forecasts of security analysts, described as unexpectedly low earnings or a ''negative earnings surprise''; such disclosures raise the risk of negative media coverage about firms' leadership and create uncertainty about whether performance is due to internal or external causes.

name: Impression management support provision
definition: Communications in which corporate leaders make positive statements about the leadership of particular other firms, or make attributions about the performance of those firms that reflect well on their leaders; such communications typically include positive statements about a CEO's leadership and strategy and/or external attributions for low performance at the CEO's firm.

name: Prior receipt of impression management support
authors_terms: ["received IM support", "prior IM support by alter", "prior IM support by other CEOs"]
definition: IM support consists of communications that typically include positive statements about a CEO's leadership and strategy and/or external attributions for low performance at the CEO's firm. In the reciprocity arguments this is the support a focal CEO has received from another CEO following a negative earnings surprise at his or her own firm.

name: Awareness of a peer CEO's impression management support to others
authors_terms: ["awareness of prior IM support by alter for other CEOs", "CEO's awareness of IM support by alter"]
definition: The focal CEO's awareness of instances in which another CEO (alter) has previously provided IM support to other CEOs; CEOs were asked to indicate the number of instances of such support by alter that they were aware of, for each CEO.

name: Negativity of journalists' reporting about the firm's leadership
authors_terms: ["negativity of journalists' reporting", "negative statements about the firm's leadership", "external attributions for low performance"]
definition: Less negative reporting is indicated by fewer negative statements made by the journalist about the firm's leadership and more external attributions for low firm performance; each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample was coded as positive, negative, or neutral.

name: Impression management about one's own firm
authors_terms: ["impression management by the focal CEO", "impression management by top executives and other staff about their own firms", "impression management by leaders and staff about their own firms"]
definition: Impression management by corporate leaders on behalf of themselves and their firms, which likewise includes external attributions for relatively low firm performance and positive claims about leadership and strategy.

name: Decision speed
definition: Decision speed refers to how quickly organizations execute all aspects of the decision-making process, spanning from the initial consideration of alternative courses of action to the time at which a commitment to act is made.

name: Entrepreneur age
definition: Individual age is a commonly used reference point in the study of life course dynamics. Entrepreneurs were asked to report their age.

name: Prior new venture experience
authors_terms: ["prior new venture experience", "prior entrepreneurial experience", "prior venture", "prior experience as an entrepreneur"]
definition: Prior experience as an entrepreneur is an important form of domain-specific experience, because the strategic challenges faced by new ventures often differ significantly from those faced by larger, more established firms. Entrepreneurs reported the number of times they had previously been involved in founding or managing a new venture.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "strategic variation", "level of strategic change in the pattern of resource allocation"]
definition: The variation over time in a firm's pattern of resource allocation in key strategic dimensions that goes beyond industry-wide changes in these dimensions.

name: Firm performance
definition: Industry-adjusted annual return on assets, obtained by subtracting the industry median ROA (excluding the focal firm) from the focal firm's annual ROA.

name: CEO origin
definition: Whether the CEO was hired from outside the firm (an outside CEO) or promoted from within the firm (an inside CEO).

name: Foreign investment announcement
authors_terms: ["Foreign Announcement", "MNE investment", "MNE investment announcements", "FDI announcement", "MNE's announcement of investment"]
definition: A dummy variable capturing whether or not there was one or more foreign investment projects announced in a given industry and year. The announcement date of the project reflects the initial stage of investment, when the promoters of the project announce their intention to invest in a project.

name: Local firm expansion announcement
authors_terms: ["Local Firm Expansion", "local expansion announcements", "local firm's announcement of expansion", "announcement of expansion"]
definition: Our dependent variable measured whether or not a firm announced an expansion of its operations. We used a binary indicator Local Firm Expansion to capture whether or not the firm announced one or more projects in a given industry and year.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["Group Affiliation", "membership in a business group", "business group membership", "group membership"]
definition: We adopted CMIE's classification of firms into business groups and created a dummy indicator Group Affiliation that takes the value of 1 when the firm belongs to a group and 0 when the firm does not belong to a group.

name: Business group professionalization
authors_terms: ["Group Professionalization", "level of professionalization of the business group", "professionalization of the group's management", "professionally managed groups"]
definition: We measured the extent of professionalization of the business group as the percentage of firms in the group in which family members occupy no executive positions in the firm (i.e., the member firm uses only professional managers).

name: Business group directorship network density
authors_terms: ["Group Density", "density of the business group's directorship network", "density of interlocking directorates", "density of interfirm communication"]
definition: To measure the extent of interlocking directorates within the group, we used the variable Group Density, which we operationalized as the total number of instances in which two member firms employed the same director on their board, divided by the total number of potential overlaps in the group.

name: Promoter family ownership
authors_terms: ["Promoter Ownership", "level of ownership of the firm by the promoter and promoter's family", "ownership in the member firm by the promoter and his family"]
definition: Promoter Ownership reflects the percentage of the firm's equity that was held by the promoter or family members. A 'promoter' refers to the founder, who maintains effective control of the business; the term generally encompasses those who have a controlling interest in the firm with a 20% or more equity holding.

name: Control-cash flow rights wedge
authors_terms: ["Control - Cash Flow Rights Wedge", "wedge between control rights and cash flow rights", "wedge"]
definition: The difference between control rights and cash flow rights of promoters. This 'wedge' between control rights and cash flow rights is the mechanism by which resources can be tunneled from firms owned by outsiders to firms associated with the promoter family.

name: Centrality in the group directorship network
authors_terms: ["Group Affiliate Binary Centrality", "firm's centrality in the directorship network", "centrality in its business group's board of directors network", "Group Affiliate Centrality"]
definition: To measure a firm's centrality within its business group's directorship network, we used the variable Group Affiliate Binary Centrality, which reflects the number of other firms in the network with which a given member firm shares directors.

name: Second-order knowledge intermediaries
definition: Organizations that engage with FOKIs to acquire industry knowledge and develop industry-building capabilities and can diffuse that knowledge to support entrepreneurial entry in secondary countries.

name: Entrepreneurial entry
definition: The dependent variable, entrepreneurial entries, was measured as the number of domestic clean cookstove companies entering country i in year t.

name: SOKI-type imbalance
authors_terms: ["SOKI-type imbalance", "imbalance between the number of company and nonprofit second-order knowledge intermediaries"]
definition: The absolute value of the difference between the number of company SOKIs and nonprofit SOKIs operating in country i in year t−1.

name: SOKI geographic dispersion
authors_terms: ["SOKI geographic dispersion", "SOKIs' geographic dispersion", "geographic dispersion of second-order knowledge intermediaries"]
definition: The average number of countries in which SOKIs operating in country i were active in year t−1.

name: Domestic overlapping industry knowledge
authors_terms: ["domestic industry actors with categorically overlapping industry knowledge", "percentage of domestic industry actors with clean cookstove knowledge"]
definition: Domestic industry actors operate solely within a single country and also accumulate local industry knowledge; the paper focuses on those whose knowledge categorically overlaps with SOKIs' knowledge.

name: Exposure to a returning rotator
definition: Having a colleague in one's academic unit who has returned from a secondment as an NSF rotator; the authors argue that such seconded employees are 'double embedded' in both the home and the host organization, which lets them pass new, nonoverlapping knowledge to colleagues who never moved.

name: NSF grant acquisition
authors_terms: ["NSF grant acquisition record", "research funding", "sum of funds raised from the NSF", "NSF funding"]
definition: The research funding a scientist raises from the NSF, measured as the inflation-adjusted sum of funds raised by each scientist; the sums reflect new grants raised ex post and not continuations or extensions of existing grants.

name: Tenure in the academic unit
definition: The length of time the seconded employee has spent in her academic unit before rotation; individuals with longer tenure at an organization are more deeply embedded and tend to develop better communication channels with colleagues, and the tenure of the seconded employee also captures tenure overlap with her colleagues.

name: Knowledge similarity
authors_terms: ["Knowledge Similarity", "similarity in knowledge", "similarity in the specific knowledge base"]
definition: The extent to which the rotator and her colleague work on similar research topics; a common knowledge base makes knowledge transfer easier so the effectiveness of knowledge transfer is expected to be greater among those working on similar research topics.

name: Productivity similarity
definition: Similarity between the rotator and her colleague in scientific productivity, influence, and reputation; such similarity can lower the cost of knowledge transfer, and returning rotators are expected to spend more time with their more similar colleagues.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["integration", "degree of integration", "integration in retail loan production", "retail integration"]
definition: The dependent variable is integration in retail loan production; more specifically, the percentage of total loans produced through a bank's own retail branches (as opposed to those purchased from brokers or correspondents) in terms of dollar value. Mortgage banks can be fully integrated, fully specialized, or use a mixed mode.

name: Information asymmetry
authors_terms: ["information asymmetry", "transaction costs", "problems of assessing the quality of what is traded", "measurement costs", "transaction risks"]
definition: Ex ante information asymmetry can create situations in which market transactions can be costly or impossible due to the fear of strategic misrepresentation described by Akerlof (1970) as the 'lemons problem.' This information asymmetry can arise from the limited ability to measure or assess intermediate goods.

name: Productive capability in loan origination
authors_terms: ["productive capabilities", "productive capability", "efficiency in origination", "labor productivity", "operating margin"]
definition: Productive capabilities are the operational efficiency of a portion of a production process. Productive capabilities in loan origination determine the efficiency with which a mortgage bank or a mortgage broker undertakes pre-qualification, document generation, application processing, credit analysis and underwriting, and approval.

name: Productive capability in loan warehousing
definition: Productive capabilities in warehousing affect the performance of engaging in pipeline/warehousing analysis and the transfer to the secondary market (ability to manage interest rate risk, prepare the loan bundles for sale to secondary market investors, etc.).

name: Categorical status
authors_terms: ["categorical status", "higher categorical status", "marginal inclusion in an organizational prestige ranking", "inclusion in the Vault Law 100", "marginal inclusion"]
definition: Categorical status is defined as 'shared beliefs about the relative esteem of different types of organizations' (Sharkey, 2014, p. 1381). The authors use status as the extent to which an organization is esteemed or respected relative to its peers, and treat the Vault Law 100 boundary between ranked and unranked firms as marking a salient distinction in categorical status.

name: CSR support policies
authors_terms: ["CSR support policies", "formal policies supporting CSR", "pro bono support policies", "policies that support CSR", "pro bono policies"]
definition: Typically, a first step that firms take when they begin engaging in CSR is to implement formal policies or reports, which can support CSR activity and also serve as a visible symbol of the firm's commitment to social responsibility. To demonstrate their commitment to pro bono work, firms typically institute formal policies that reward lawyers for participation.

name: Typicality of CSR portfolio
authors_terms: ["typicality of their CSR portfolios", "typicality of a firm's CSR portfolio", "typicality of pro bono support portfolio", "typicality of policies"]
definition: Past studies suggest that a portfolio of practices or policies will be interpreted as more typical as its composition becomes more similar to the average of its peers; in contrast, the combination will appear more atypical as its composition deviates more from the average configuration.

name: Rank volatility
authors_terms: ["rank volatility", "rank instability", "historical rank volatility", "volatility in rank position"]
definition: Given the recurrent nature of rankings, firms likely become attuned not only to the absolute level of their rank in a given year but also to their historical trajectory. Firms whose positions have historically been more volatile are likely to view their standing as tenuous.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "firm specificity", "firm-specific assets", "specificity of an activity"]
definition: Firm-specific assets were defined by human assets, physical assets, and company-specific routines and knowledge that were not redeployable to alternative uses. Both transaction cost and knowledge-based explanations begin with the assumption that efficient production necessitates specialized investments in physical and human assets.

name: Measurement difficulty
authors_terms: ["measurement difficulty", "difficulty in measuring the performance of an activity", "measurement accuracy", "measurability of outputs"]
definition: Consistent with previous work, our measurement focused on the level of difficulty in measuring worker performance. Markets succeed when they meter effectively; when contributions from an outside supplier cannot be accurately assessed, adequate contracts will be costly to craft.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: A high level of technological change characterizes the provision of information services. We measured the degree of change in both skills and technology using two items.

name: Scale economies
authors_terms: ["economies of scale", "scale economies", "scale of demand", "internal scale", "scale of internal demand"]
definition: The degree to which a firm had scale sufficient to support the efficient production of a service. Larger internal scale increases the probability of efficient internal production and thereby encourages vertical integration.

name: Skill set magnitude
authors_terms: ["skill set", "magnitude of the skill set", "skill set size", "size of the required skill set"]
definition: The skill set required for an IS activity varied depending on the scope of knowledge required to perform a particular task. A job that required extensive knowledge and skills required personnel with significant training and education.

name: Market governance performance
authors_terms: ["performance of markets", "market performance", "performance of outsourced exchanges", "performance of governance through the market", "performance of externally sourced activities"]
definition: The performance of a service purchased in the market (P m), reflecting both transaction cost and production cost efficiency. Our interest was in a broader measure of institutional performance, one that could encompass a broad range of performance features across both market and hierarchical exchanges.

name: Firm governance performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "internal performance", "performance of internally governed exchanges", "performance of governance through firm organization", "hierarchy performance"]
definition: The performance of the same service governed through a firm (P f), reflecting both transaction cost and production cost efficiency. Our interest was in a broader measure of institutional performance, one that could encompass a broad range of performance features across both market and hierarchical exchanges.

name: Outsourcing
authors_terms: ["boundary choice", "governance choice", "make-or-buy decisions", "vertical integration", "internalization", "percentage of outsourcing"]
definition: Most empirical work in TCE measures the governance choice as a discrete event: companies choose either to make or buy. A functionally similar set of activities, however, can be wholly or partially outsourced, and boundary decisions in information services appear to be in a state of evolution toward greater outsourcing.

name: Negative external evaluations
definition: Analysts' negative forward-looking evaluations of a firm, which occur if the firm is expected to underperform and are represented by downgrades in analyst recommendations (a 'sell' recommendation).

name: Positive external evaluations
definition: Analysts' positive forward-looking evaluations of a firm, which occur if the firm is expected to outperform and are represented by upgrades in analyst recommendations (a 'buy' recommendation).

name: Organizational time horizon
definition: An organization's time horizon is 'the temporal distance into the past and future that individuals and collectivities typically consider when contemplating events that have happened, may have happened, or may happen' (Bluedorn 2002, p. 114). Organizations with longer horizons focus on the more distant past or remote future, and those with shorter horizons focus on the more recent past or near future.

name: Investment horizon
definition: Investment horizon refers to the 'ex ante managerial expectation about the duration of time over which potential firm investments will generate productive returns' (Reilly et al. 2016, p. 1173); it is synonymous with payback period and payoff horizon. Whereas time horizon is a cognitive construct, investment horizon pertains to decision-making actions or behaviors regarding a firm's portfolio of investments.

name: Short-term investor ownership
definition: The composition of a firm's investors by their investment horizons; transient investors tend to focus on quick, incremental returns by hastily trading many small positions in many firms, whereas dedicated investors tend to have large, long-term holdings concentrated in a small number of firms.

name: Analyst recommendations
authors_terms: ["analyst recommendations", "analysts' recommendations", "buy, hold, and sell recommendations"]
definition: Analysts recommend that investors buy, sell, or hold the shares of a firm depending on whether the firm is expected to outperform, underperform, or perform equally to its benchmarks or the market.

name: Sequencing of prior evaluations
definition: Negative evaluations that follow positive evaluations are seen as more problematic and, therefore, more urgent to address than negative evaluations that follow negative evaluations.

name: Timing of evaluation in the fiscal year
definition: Compared with events earlier in the cycle, events near the end of an information cycle are often more material; actors can reflect on the whole cycle, synthesize and analyze the entire extent of information, and place recent events into greater perspective.

name: Success experience
definition: We define success experience as a firm's cumulative history of periods of exceptionally strong performance. We define a success experience as occurring when a bank in the sample experienced unusually strong performance.

name: Recovery experience
authors_terms: ["recovery experience", "recovery experiences", "recovery experience of a firm"]
definition: Recovery experience is a type of failure experience defined as occurring when a firm experiences extremely poor performance but later overcomes it. We define a recovery experience as occurring when a bank that experiences a critical financial distress that puts it at high risk of failure overcomes the crisis and returns a normal level of performance.

name: Bank failure rate
authors_terms: ["failure rate of the bank", "hazard rate of failure", "bank failure", "failure rates"]
definition: The dependent variable is the unobserved hazard rate of failure of banks in the sample. Banks were considered to have failed if they were (1) liquidated or (2) merged with another bank with FDIC financial assistance.

name: Intra-industry product diversity
authors_terms: ["intra-industry product diversity", "product diversity", "intra-industry diversity", "intra-industry product diversity"]
definition: Intra-industry product diversity is defined as the degree of variation in a firm's portfolio of related products in a particular industry. Intra-industry diversification entails a firm's presence in more than one market niche or product line within a single industry.

name: Firm performance
definition: Following prior research on intra-industry diversification in the software industry, the authors adopt sales growth as a measure of firm performance, a measure especially relevant to software firms, which reach profitability only at a relatively late stage of their lifecycle.

name: Technology intensity
definition: A firm that invests extensively in research and development is more technology-oriented, is likely to rely on idiosyncratic and specialized resources, and can better leverage its technology. Technology intensity was measured as the firm's R&D investment divided by its sales during the year in question.

name: Intra-industry diversification experience
authors_terms: ["intra-industry product diversification experience", "diversification experience", "prior diversification experience"]
definition: Intra-industry product diversification experience was measured by calculating a weighted average of product diversity during the period from 1985 to t-1. The experience decay function assigns higher weight to more recent years while avoiding left censoring bias.

name: Hybrid coproduction
definition: A Hybrid coproduction is a film coproduced by a mixture of at least one generalist and at least one specialist production company. Films are defined as coproductions when they are made by two or more distinct production companies.

name: Central coproduction
definition: A Central coproduction is coproduced by at least two generalists and no specialists.

name: Peripheral coproduction
definition: A Peripheral coproduction is coproduced by at least two specialists and no generalists.

name: Hybrid coproduction experience
authors_terms: ["hybrid coproductions", "experience in hybrid coproductions", "cumulative experience in hybrid collaborations"]
definition: Like the variable for hybrid coproductions at the film level, we construct a variable for hybrid coproductions at the production company level that measures a company's cumulative experience in hybrid collaborations up to the previous year. The variable Hybrid coproductions counts a production company's cumulative hybrid coproduction films in its production history.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "innovation", "new creative features", "new combinations of creative features"]
definition: Creative features represent what King (2009, p. 35) calls the 'textual qualities' of characters, story line, and esthetics within a film. We analyze innovation in terms of new creative features and new combinations of existing creative features used by production companies in their films through the keywords used to describe each film.

name: Competitive differentiation
definition: We examine differentiation in two ways. In the first, we measure a company's differentiation in terms of the keywords of its films from the keywords of the other companies within the same market segment; second, we measure a company's differentiation from its own prior products.

name: Organizational exit
definition: A production company exits the population if it does not release another film within the 95th percentile of interarrival times - five years - and does not release a subsequent film during the sample period.

name: Organizational generalism
definition: Generalists are both larger and operate across a wider niche. A production company is defined as a generalist if it is in the top quartile of niche width in terms of the genres it releases films in a given year of production.

name: Out-of-the-money stock options
definition: Out-of-the-money options (sometimes referred to as 'underwater' options) are worth zero because the current market value is lower than the strike price.

name: In-the-money stock options
definition: In-the-money options are positively valued stock options-that is, the grant price is below the current market price.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: Compared to stock options, stock ownership has a more direct effect on executives' current wealth, because executives actually own the stocks in the most real sense.

name: Earnings manipulation
definition: Earnings manipulation is intentional misapplication of accounting rules and misreporting of financial results that causes reported income to be larger or smaller than it would otherwise be.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance has been shown to be an important predictor of executive decision-making behaviors and also constitutes an indicator of personal performance because shareholders, and even CEOs themselves, usually attribute a firm's poor performance to its top executives.

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure was the number of years that an individual had served as CEO of his or her present company.

name: Environmental capabilities
definition: Specialized capabilities whose differences produce varying levels of environmental performance; Hart (1995: 991) argues that 'waste minimization' is a 'specialized capability' that simultaneously facilitates pollution reduction and cost savings. The authors note that a corporation's environmental capabilities partly drive the environmental performance that its facilities demonstrate.

name: Relative environmental capabilities
authors_terms: ["relative endowments of the selling and acquiring owners", "relative corporate environmental performance", "less/more wasteful acquirer"]
definition: The relative endowments of environmental capabilities of the selling and acquiring firms, which the authors argue determine the direction of capability transfer. When a firm with relatively lower performance acquires a facility from a seller that has higher performance, the buyer's incumbent units will have access to superior capabilities.

name: Change in environmental capabilities
authors_terms: ["changes in environmental capabilities", "change in waste generation"]
definition: The authors operationalize their dependent variable, changes in environmental capabilities, as the change in waste generated for a given chemical. Positive values for Change in Waste Generation correspond to an increase in waste generation in year t+1 relative to the previous year for a given chemical, so the facility would experience a worsening of its environmental capabilities.

name: Middle management involvement in strategy
definition: The strategic involvement of middle-level managers in the strategic process; the purpose of the study was to investigate the relationship between middle management involvement in strategy and organizational performance.

name: Strategic consensus
definition: Consensus is defined as shared strategic understanding and commitment; this construct was defined as the product of middle management commitment to, and understanding of, strategy.

name: Strategic understanding
definition: Middle-level managers' shared understanding of the organization's strategic priorities; since priorities do not depend on an explicit articulation of ends and means, they are suited for measuring shared understanding in both synoptic and incremental contexts.

name: Strategic commitment
definition: Middle management's commitment to strategy, one of the two components whose product defines strategic consensus.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["organizational performance", "subjective measures of organizational performance", "measures of organizational performance"]
definition: The organization's recent performance; because comparable objective performance data were not available for all firms, subjective measures of organizational performance were obtained from company CEOs.

name: Director death
authors_terms: ["death of a company director", "director death", "director deaths", "death of a director", "death of a role-relational peer"]
definition: Chief executive officers (CEOs) experiencing the death of a role-relational peer, in this case a director at the same firm, which the authors argue triggers mortality salience.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "organizational prosocial behavior", "corporate prosocial behavior"]
definition: CSR can be defined as "context-specific organizational actions and policies that take into account stakeholders' expectations and the triple bottom line of economic, social, and environmental performance" (Aguinis 2011, p. 855).

name: Director appointment during CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEOAppointee", "director appointment within the CEO's tenure", "relational connection"]
definition: A widely studied example of professional closeness in the upper echelons of organizations is whether a director was initially appointed during the tenure of the CEO.

name: Death suddenness
definition: Following Nguyen and Nielsen (2010, p. 553), a death was characterized as being sudden if it was unexpected and occurred "instantaneously or within a few hours of an abrupt change in the person's previous clinical state."

name: Academic origin
authors_terms: ["institution of origin", "institutional origin", "institutional environment of origin", "academic origin", "industrial origin"]
definition: The publication's institution of origin, that is, whether it stems from an academic or an industrial organization. Inventors are posited to use this attribute as an informational cue when deciding how much attention to pay a scientific publication.

name: Attention to science
authors_terms: ["inventors' attention", "attention", "selective attention", "attention to the scientific literature"]
definition: The amount of attention inventors allocate to a scientific publication; inventors select how much attention each scientific publication will receive, and attention is a necessary though not sufficient driver of knowledge transfer.

name: Emerging competence
definition: Competence is defined in operational terms as the degree to which the firm or its subunits can reliably meet or exceed objectives. The level of competence of an organizational subunit can be assessed by the extent to which ex post results are in the neighborhood of or above ex ante expectations.

name: Comprehension
definition: Comprehension is the outcome of a process by which elements of individual know-how and skill become linked, so that a group can respond as if the complexity of the system were understood by the group. It represents the extent to which the project team is confident that it understands cause/effect relations for the most critical factors relating to success of the initiative.

name: Deftness
definition: Deftness is a quality in a group which permits heedful interactions to be conducted at minimal cost, allowing those in a new initiative to minimize opportunity, transactions and agency costs. It represents the extent to which the processes by which a team solves problems are effortless, effective and well-honed.

name: Rival hiring of a key employee
authors_terms: ["key hire", "hiring a key employee", "key employee mobility"]
definition: The head coach of the opposing team has experience with the advantageous set of routines that make up the West Coast Offense. An organization that hires a key employee from another organization with an advantageous set of routines will increase its ability to imitate those routines or to design an improved head-to-head competitive response.

name: Rival past exposure to the routines
authors_terms: ["past competition", "experience competing against organizations that hired a key employee"]
definition: The number of times that the opposing team's head coach has competed against a first- or second-generation Walsh assistant. The diffusion of the advantageous set of routines through key employees' interorganizational mobility exposes a focal organization to more frequent encounters with aspects of the advantageous set of routines.

name: Rival expected exposure to the routines
definition: The number of games in the current season scheduled against first- or second-generation Walsh assistants. The expectation of future competition against organizations with an advantageous set of routines promotes search and learning effort and focuses attention on developing counterstrategies.

name: Competitive performance in head-to-head competition
definition: A team's competitive and strategic abilities in a head-to-head competition, measured by point margin: the number of points scored in a game by the 49ers minus the points scored by their opponents. The margin of victory is the best measure of the relative strength of the two teams.

name: Firm exit rate
definition: The conditional probability of a biotechnology firm's exiting at time t. Exit was defined as the failure of a firm or closure of a subsidiary; name changes and acquisitions were not considered failures because the firms continued to operate.

name: Rivals' alliances
definition: The aggregate number of alliances a focal biotechnology firm's rivals had at the start of each year with each type of partner organization. Rivals were defined as those companies that operated in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the focal firm and were not its partners.

name: Rivals' horizontal alliances
authors_terms: ["horizontal alliances", "rivals' alliances with other biotechnology firms"]
definition: Rivals' links to other firms in the same industry, which, in contrast to vertical alliances, do not tap resources outside of the focal industry.

name: Rivals' upstream alliances
definition: Rivals' alliances that link technology-based firms to sources of research knowledge, such as universities, research institutes, government labs, hospitals, and industry associations.

name: Rivals' downstream alliances
definition: Rivals' alliances that link firms in a technology-based industry to sources of complementary assets, commercialization knowledge, and capital outside of the existing industry boundaries, such as pharmaceutical, chemical, and marketing firms.

name: Rival partners' alliances
definition: The aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rival partners, that is, firms that are simultaneously its rivals and its partners, had at the start of each year with each type of partner organization.

name: Current option wealth
definition: Martin and colleagues (2013: 454) defined current option wealth as 'only the value that has already accumulated in options from increases in a stock price above the options' exercise price.' This value is the amount of wealth CEOs perceive they have gained (i.e., endowed), because they can exercise their options at any time to secure that value.

name: Prospective option wealth
definition: Prospective option wealth is 'the potential future gains to wealth that might be realized over and above the current accumulated value in their stock options'. Prospective wealth offers unlimited upside potential, to whatever level the stock price rises to prior to the option's expiry, and limited downside potential, to the value of the option contract itself.

name: Present temporal focus
definition: Individuals who have a strong present temporal focus possess a 'here-and-now' orientation whereby most of their attention focuses on their immediate surroundings. Present-focused individuals emphasize the current timeframe in their decision making and give little consideration to the future consequences of their actions.

name: Future temporal focus
definition: Future-focused CEOs tend to contemplate what the future holds while envisaging and reenvisaging future events and scenarios. As such, much of their attention is on future matters and outcomes.

name: M&A investment
definition: Gamache and McNamara (2019) noted that acquisition spending reflects not only the number of acquisitions a CEO can undertake but also a CEO's propensity to pursue further acquisitions, the size of deals the CEO is willing to pursue, and the CEO's aggressiveness in finalizing deals.

name: Explorative new products
authors_terms: ["explorative new products", "explorative products", "new product exploration", "exploration in new products"]
definition: New products that are meaningfully distinct from-rather than similar to-competing products, reflecting that the firm seeks variance from the norm in its competitive domain. Explorative new products set the firm apart from its competitors.

name: Willingness to cannibalize
definition: The extent to which a firm is prepared to reduce the actual or potential value of its investments in organizational resources and competencies.

name: Future-oriented market scanning
definition: The extent to which organization members devote efforts to learn about future customer needs and potential competitors in their organization's future market environment.

name: Customer turbulence
definition: Turbulence in the customer sector of the firm's task environment, a sector that the authors distinguish from the environment as a single entity; environmental turbulence refers to the rate and uncertainty of changes in the organization's environment.

name: Competitive turbulence
authors_terms: ["competitive turbulence", "turbulence in the competitive environment", "competitor turbulence"]
definition: Turbulence in the competitive sector of the firm's task environment, where competitors move in and out of markets and shift their strategies.

name: Technological turbulence
definition: Turbulence in the technological sector of the firm's task environment, which renders the existing technologies of the firm less useful as the basis for products that will stand out in the marketplace.

name: Firm foreignness
definition: Foreignness is measured as whether the firm being evaluated is headquartered in a different country than the stakeholder; because foreignness can vary by degree, the authors also capture cultural and regulatory distance between the MNC's home country and the host country.

name: Stakeholder evaluation of social performance
authors_terms: ["stakeholder rating of firm's social performance", "stakeholder evaluation", "evaluations of their social performance", "firm's social performance"]
definition: Social performance is firms' value creation for actors in their social, political, and natural environments, and is inherently perceptual; the authors solicit stakeholders' own evaluations of how well a firm honors its responsibilities toward society.

name: CSR valence
authors_terms: ["CSR valence", "do-good CSR", "do-no-harm CSR", "CSR type", "do good versus do no harm"]
definition: A distinction exists between do-no-harm CSR (attenuating negative externalities such as pollution) and do-good CSR (increasing positive externalities such as when firms up-skill their workforce and promote the diffusion of environmentally friendly technologies).

name: Internal attribution
definition: Causes of behavior categorized as internal to the actor (e.g., ability, intrinsic motivation); in the experiment it is the influence attributed to managers and shareholders, who have an ownership stake or direct influence on resource allocation.

name: External attribution
definition: Causes of behavior categorized as external to the actor (e.g., social influence, situational constraints); in the experiment it is the influence attributed to employees, consumers, government and the local community.

name: Company impression
definition: Participants' overall impression of the company, measured on three nine-point scales anchored between bad/unfavorable/negative and good/favorable/positive.

name: Geographic distance
definition: Geographic distance is the distance between actors in relevant units of space such as miles.

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: Related or complementary acquisitions, where acquirers and targets commonly redeploy and integrate resources, produce greater synergy benefits than are available in unrelated acquisitions, where firms have no interdependent relationship and remain autonomous for extended periods.

name: Acquisition completion
definition: Never explicitly defined in a sentence of its own, but the authors state that if both firms agree to all terms, the acquisition is completed by the act of submitting appropriate documents to the relevant authorities, following which one firm survives and integrates all assets and liabilities and the other ceases to exist as a legally independent entity.

name: Prior related acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["direct experience in related acquisitions", "prior related experience", "related experience"]
definition: Related experience counted the number of related acquisitions implemented prior to the focal acquisitions.

name: Prior distant acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["direct experience in distant acquisitions", "prior distant acquisition", "distance experience"]
definition: Distance experience was calculated as the average distance, in miles, for all acquisitions announced prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Contextual experience in the target region
authors_terms: ["contextual experience", "contextual knowledge", "prior acquisition in target state"]
definition: As well as direct experience with related and distant acquisitions, acquirers can accumulate contextual knowledge about distant markets that reduces the extent of information they require while searching for targets within those regions.

name: Vicarious experience
authors_terms: ["vicarious experience", "secondary sources of information", "intermediaries", "multiple organizational units"]
definition: A process of vicarious learning from secondary sources could contribute to information gathering in unfamiliar contexts, increasing the likelihood of acquisition completion.

name: Proportion of experienced investors in a location
authors_terms: ["percentage of sequential investments by other firms in a location", "percentage of sequential FDI entries in the same industry in the same province", "proportion of experienced investors", "distribution of experience among the reference group"]
definition: The percentage of sequential FDI entries in the same industry in the same province was computed by dividing the number of sequential investments by the total number of investments by all other U.S. firms in the same industry in the province or municipality. It captures the proportion of experienced investors among the prior entrants in a location as a measure of the distribution of experience in the reference group.

name: Foreign direct investment location choice
authors_terms: ["FDI location choice", "location choice", "probability that a subsequent entrant will choose that location"]
definition: The dependent variable, FDI location choice, was a dummy variable coded as '1' if a foreign investment was located in a particular province and as '0' otherwise.

name: Host country experience
authors_terms: ["firm's experience in China", "FDI experience in China", "experience in the host country", "firm's prior investments in China"]
definition: An investing firm's experience in China was represented by a count of the number of previous investments by the parent firm in China. A learning firm's own FDI experience in the host country is an important factor moderating the influence of model organizations in determining its FDI location choice.

name: Location-specific experience
authors_terms: ["firm's prior investments in the province", "experience in the specific location", "FDI experience in the same province"]
definition: Experience is most likely to be considered relevant and transferable when it was gained in the specific location where an investment is being contemplated. More experience in a location implies more knowledge about it, which should make a firm less sensitive to others' actions.

name: Experience in other host country locations
authors_terms: ["firm's prior investments in other provinces", "experience in other provinces", "experience elsewhere in the country"]
definition: If a firm's prior experience was acquired in other locations, it may not be entirely relevant and/or easily transferable. Prior experience in other locations may provide little location-specific knowledge or local connections.

name: Phase III clinical trial failure
authors_terms: ["failure of a compound in phase III clinical trials", "phase III failure", "failure of a late-stage development project"]
definition: The study is designed around the failure of development projects currently undergoing phase III clinical trials, which is the final stage in the development process, where the efficacy and safety of the drug is investigated in a large sample of patients. Common causes for failures at this stage include adverse side effects of the drug and harmful interactions with other drugs.

name: Firm value change
authors_terms: ["change in the value of a pharmaceutical firm", "cumulative abnormal return", "CAR", "impact of the failure", "value of a project to a firm"]
definition: This change in the value of the firm (as measured by the stock markets) due to the failure of a development project, with all other factors affecting the firm's value being held constant, is an empirical measure of the value of the failed project to the firm. Failure of a late-stage development project represents the loss of potential future sales for a firm, which should lead to a decrease in the value of the firm.

name: Change in time-adjusted probability of indication success
authors_terms: ["UPDelta TAPIS", "change in the time-adjusted probability of success for an indication", "TAPIS"]
definition: The time-adjusted probability of indication success (TAPIS) is proportional to the expected financial returns from the development projects. The marginal value of a phase III compound, or the impact of losing a phase III compound in the portfolio, is proportional to the consequent change in TAPIS when the number of phase III compounds falls by one.

name: Phase II buffer
authors_terms: ["phase II buffer", "unanticipated demand for phase III resources", "realized phase II success rate"]
definition: The unanticipated demand for phase III resources at the time of the failure is captured by the difference between the recent and the expected phase II success rate for the firm in question (phase II buffer). The higher the utilization, the higher the benefit of a failure, because the extent of the acceleration and the number of projects that benefit from this acceleration are both higher at higher levels of utilization.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "stock market reactions", "market value", "stock market reaction"]
definition: The abnormal return associated with a joint venture announcement, that is, the return in excess of the expected return estimated from a market model; this market-based referent is used to assess the impact of joint venture formation on parent firms.

name: Joint venture product-market scope role
authors_terms: ["roles of joint ventures", "how joint ventures influence product-market scope", "role classification"]
definition: The role a joint venture plays in the product-market activity of its parents, conceptualized along two dimensions, product expansion (adding new products) and market expansion (serving new customers), yielding the identical, related-supplementary, related-complementary, and unrelated categories.

name: Relatedness of joint venture to focal parent portfolio
authors_terms: ["degree of relatedness with a focal parent's portfolio", "parent with opportunity", "parent without opportunity"]
definition: The extent to which a joint venture's business corresponds to the businesses of a focal parent, captured by the parent's sales portion in businesses related to the joint venture, and argued to determine how the benefits from the venture are divided between the parents.

name: Relatedness of joint venture partners
authors_terms: ["related partner", "unrelated partner", "degree to which partners operate in related businesses"]
