definition: The degree to which the partners of a joint venture operate in related businesses; parents whose partners have operations in related businesses form the related-partner subgroup and those whose partners operate in unrelated businesses the unrelated-partner subgroup.

name: Relative size of joint venture partners
authors_terms: ["relative sizes of the partners", "larger partner", "smaller partner"]
definition: The size of a parent relative to its joint venture partners, indicated by the market value of the partner's common stock; the parent with the larger common stock market value is the larger partner and the other the smaller partner.

name: Managerial assessment of joint venture contribution
authors_terms: ["managerial assessments of the effects of joint venture formations", "managerial assessments of joint venture performance"]
definition: Managers' assessments of a joint venture's outcomes in relation to five key objectives, measured against their expectations; the authors treat these assessments as the realized strategies of joint venture formation.

name: Joint venture relatedness
definition: The extent to which a joint venture combines resources in a related rather than an unrelated manner, as argued by the relatedness hypothesis from diversification and mergers research, which the authors extend to joint venture formation to hypothesize that related joint ventures will outperform unrelated ones.

name: Dollar value of joint venture gains
definition: The dollar value of a parent's gain from joint venture formation, as used when predicting that the dollar values of smaller and larger partners' gains will be approximately equal.

name: Preentry technological experience
definition: We consider preentry technological experience as experience in a focal technological paradigm (Teece 1986, Helfat and Lieberman 2002). To be 'preentry' experience, it must be accumulated in a different domain - using the technology for a different product or offering the product to a different set of customers.

name: Preentry market experience
authors_terms: ["preentry market experience", "market experience", "prior domestic fixed-line telecommunications experience", "MarketExp"]
definition: We define preentry market experience as experience with the same users but a different technology. In this context, in-country experience with previous telecommunications technologies, most relevantly fixed-line service, provides preentry market experience.

name: Usage intensity
authors_terms: ["average usage intensity", "usage intensity", "Usage", "average monthly minutes of use"]
definition: Average usage intensity on each operator's 2G network (minutes of use, Usage). The average usage intensity of a firm's user base is used to infer the relative presence of high-intensity users.

name: Market penetration
authors_terms: ["market penetration", "number of users", "Subscribers", "number of 2G subscribers on the network as a share of the country's population"]
definition: The number of 2G subscribers on the network as a share of the country's population (Subscribers). Firms better positioned to attract mass market users will experience a high level of market penetration independent of entry timing.

name: Entry timing
definition: If a firm entered a country in the first quarter in which 2G was originally offered (including firms that entered before the first quarter of our data), we tag them as an early entrant.

name: Number of strategies identified
authors_terms: ["number of strategies identified", "number of strategies listed", "number of taxonomic categories", "differentiation"]
definition: Our first dimension of the complexity of a TMT's mental model of cognitive strategic groups is the number of strategies being pursued within the industry. The number of taxonomic categories reflects the number of 'general strategies' listed by each manager.

name: Number of competitors categorized
authors_terms: ["number of competitors categorized", "number of firms coded", "number of firms categorized", "number of competitors that top management teams categorize into their strategic group knowledge structures"]
definition: Management teams are anticipated to vary in the number of competitors of which they are strategically aware. The number of firms categorized reflects the number of firms contained in the questionnaire for which a respondent felt comfortable identifying a generic strategy.

name: Average strategic group size
authors_terms: ["average group size", "average size of strategic groups", "average cognitive strategic group size"]
definition: By dividing the number of competing firms for which the TMT can identify a predominant strategy by the number of strategies identified, we can measure the average size of the strategic groups identified by the TMT. This aspect of complexity combines the two differentiation dimensions of number of strategies and number of firms with identified strategies to obtain an integrative or structural dimension of strategic group knowledge structure complexity.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "subsequent firm performance", "return on average assets", "ROA"]
definition: The measure of subsequent performance used in this study was average Return on Average Assets (ROA) for the years 1995 and 1996. Sheshunoff Information Services describes ROA as the best indicator of earnings efficiency.

name: Complexity of strategic group knowledge structures
authors_terms: ["complexity of the cognitive strategic groups", "complexity in knowledge structures", "degree of complexity of the cognitive strategic groups", "complexity of strategic group knowledge structures"]
definition: The level of complexity found in the cognitive strategic group knowledge structures held by top management teams, a primary dimension on which their models of competition may differ. Complexity in knowledge structures is a multidimensional construct, best assessed with multiple measures, seen in both the number of categories identified by a respondent and the amount of data points coded into each category.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspiration level", "performance adjusted by the aspiration level", "ROA minus aspiration level", "performance above aspiration level", "performance below aspiration level"]
definition: Managers evaluate organizational performance relative to their 'aspiration level' and initiate problemistic search when performance is low. Following Cyert and March (1963: 123), I computed aspiration level (A) as a mixture of social and historical aspiration levels.

name: Aspiration level
definition: An aspiration level, 'the smallest outcome that would be deemed satisfactory by the decision maker' (Schneider, 1992: 1053), is used by 'boundedly rational' decision makers to determine the boundary between success and failure in continuous measures of performance (March & Simon, 1958).

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack exists as use of administrative resources beyond what is necessary for the short-term operation and maintenance of an organization. Slack refers to the stock of resources available to an organization, such as employees' time, underused capital, and underused facilities.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Search through R&D, which is the organizational process most directly involved with innovations, is one component of organizational search.

name: Innovation launch rate
authors_terms: ["innovation launches", "rate of launching innovations", "annual innovation launches"]
definition: The probability that a firm will launch an innovation equals the probability that an innovation is in the solution pool multiplied by the probability that an innovation in the pool will be launched.

name: Stock concentration
definition: The accountability of managers to stockholders is a function of the concentration of stockholdings, concentration being measured by the percentage of common stock held in blocks of 0.2 percent or more. The greater the stock concentration the greater stockholder power, and the more likely it is that the firm will pursue strategies consistent with maximizing stockholder welfare.

name: Management stockholdings
definition: The extent to which managers receive a substantial proportion of their income through stock holdings in the firm. Agency theory argues that stock-based compensation schemes are a device for aligning the interests of management and stockholders, so the greater the extent of management stockholding the more likely the firm is to adopt strategies consistent with maximizing stockholder wealth.

name: Outsider representation on the board
authors_terms: ["board composition", "the ratio of inside to outside directors", "influence of outsiders on the board", "IN/OUT"]
definition: The ability of the board to act as a guardian of stockholder welfare is claimed to be a function of board composition, with the ratio of inside to outside directors argued to be of critical importance. The interests of insiders are theorized to be aligned with those of management, while those of outsiders are aligned with stockholders.

name: Innovation strategy
definition: An emphasis upon competing through research-based innovations, regarded as a high-risk/high-return strategy: the high return comes from the quasi-monopoly rents created by a successful innovation, the high risk from the high failure rate of most innovations.

name: Diversification
definition: The extent to which the firm's activities are diversified. Extensive and unrelated diversification is argued to be favored by managers because it is often the best way to maximize the size of the firm and allows them to diversify their own employment risk, whereas stockholders are argued to prefer limited and related diversification only.

name: Profitability
definition: Firm performance, measured by return on assets; implicit in the arguments is the idea that stockholder and management preferences for different strategies have tangible performance consequences.

name: State capacity
authors_terms: ["state capacity", "administrative ability of the state", "administrative infrastructure", "capacity of the state"]
definition: State capacity can be broadly defined as the administrative and organizational ability of the state to identify, evaluate, formulate, and implement policies. It is the administrative infrastructure that enables states to pursue certain goals or priorities, to implement policy, and to get things done.

name: Economics profession influence
authors_terms: ["normative influence of the professions", "economics profession", "normative mechanism of adoption", "economics articles"]
definition: The normative mechanism of adoption relates to the professions, which identify, frame, and solve problems in specific ways inspired by their own history, tradition, culture, and technical knowledge. In the case of the adoption of minority shareholder protections, we would expect the presence of a strong and vibrant economics profession in a given country to promote the adoption of legal protections for minority shareholders.

name: Imitation among countries
authors_terms: ["mimetic behavior", "frequency-based imitation", "trait-based imitation", "imitation of other countries"]
definition: Mimetic behavior refers to the imitation of practices deemed to be the most legitimate or effective within a certain field in which actors mutually recognize each other's presence and actions. In addition to peer-to-peer, frequency-based imitation, research has documented the importance of trait-based imitation of actors perceived as being leaders, high performers, more prestigious, or more legitimate.

name: Coercive pressure by multilateral agencies
authors_terms: ["coercive effect of multilateral agencies", "coercive pressures", "IMF credit", "IMF loan program"]
definition: The coercive effect of multilateral agencies such as the IMF on the policymaking process; loans from the IMF harbor a potential for coercive adoption because they make countries dependent upon a single (or several similar) sources of support for vital resources.

name: Minority shareholder rights protection
authors_terms: ["minority shareholder rights", "legal protection of minority shareholder rights", "shareholder rights protections", "minority shareholders' legal protections"]
definition: Legal provisions aimed at protecting minority shareholders' rights against the actions of large shareholders and managers. The ten key legal provisions identified by legal scholars as most relevant to the protection of minority shareholder rights cover powers of the general meeting, agenda-setting power, anticipation of shareholder decision, prohibition of multiple voting rights, independent board members, feasibility of directors' dismissal, private enforcement of directors' duties, shareholder action against resolutions of the general meeting, mandatory bid, and disclosure of major share ownership.

name: Stock market development
authors_terms: ["stock market development", "development of the stock market", "market development"]
definition: The development of the stock market in terms of capitalization, traded stocks, and turnover; the three variables obtained from the World Bank loaded onto a single factor of stock market development.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: Societies high in uncertainty avoidance tend to prefer rules, and to operate in predictable situations, as opposed to situations where the appropriate behaviors are not specified in advance. In these societies, people are uncomfortable with high risk and ambiguity.

name: Power distance
definition: Power distance is the degree to which differences in power and status are accepted in a culture. Some nations accept high differences in power and authority between members of different social classes or occupational levels; other nations do not.

name: Individualism-collectivism
definition: Individualism-collectivism refers to whether individual or collective action is the preferred way to deal with issues. In cultures oriented toward individualism people tend to emphasize their individual needs, concerns, and interests over those of their group or organization.

name: Masculinity-femininity
definition: The masculinity-femininity dimension of a culture refers to the degree to which values associated with stereotypes of masculinity (such as aggressiveness and dominance) and femininity (such as compassion, empathy, and emotional openness) are emphasized.

name: Total CEO pay
definition: CEO total pay is measured by the total compensation estimates reported by Towers Perrin. It is indicative of the average total wealth that the CEO obtains from a firm in each culture.

name: Proportion of variable CEO pay
authors_terms: ["the proportion of variable compensation to total CEO compensation (VC/TC)", "proportion of variable pay to total compensation"]
definition: The proportion of variable compensation to total CEO compensation (VC/TC) is the ratio of the sum of annual bonus plus long-term incentives to total compensation. This has been argued to be a measure of the extent to which performance risk is transferred to the CEO.

name: CEO-to-worker pay ratio
authors_terms: ["the ratio of CEO pay to the lowest level employees (CEO/Worker)", "pay ratio CEO/man. employee (CEO/ME)"]
definition: The ratio of CEO pay to the lowest level employees (CEO/Worker) is measured by the ratio of CEO total compensation to total compensation of manufacturing workers in the respective country. This measure is an indicator of the pay inequality.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm financial performance", "accounting performance", "ROA", "return on assets", "firm performance"]
definition: We rely on the traditional measure of accounting profitability in the literature, ROA, computed as net income before extraordinary items divided by total assets, obtained from Compustat.

name: Performance relative to industry median
definition: For each firm within its four-digit SIC primary industry, a dummy variable indicates whether the firm has its ROA below the industry median for the given year.

name: Performance volatility
definition: We measure ex post income stream risk by calculating the standard deviation of the firm’s ROA for the subsequent five years.

name: Performance unpredictability
definition: We also measure ex ante income stream risk by estimating the dispersion among analyst forecasts, AnalystDisp, as the standard deviation of analysts’ earnings per share forecasts made one year in advance.

name: Negative external shocks
definition: We create a dummy, Recession, for when the GDP growth is negative for the year.

name: Positive external shocks
definition: We also create a dummy, Boom, for when the annual GDP growth exceeds 4%.

name: Headquarters' attention
definition: Headquarters' attention is defined as 'the extent to which a parent company recognizes and gives credit to a subsidiary for its contribution to the MNE as a whole'.

name: Expatriates in the subsidiary
authors_terms: ["expatriates", "number of expatriates", "employees coming from headquarters to work in foreign subsidiaries"]
definition: Expatriates are employees coming from headquarters to work in foreign subsidiaries; the variable captures the number of expatriates in a subsidiary.

name: Subsidiary size growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the subsidiary in terms of size", "size growth", "growth in size"]
definition: Growth in size represents an increase in the subsidiary's pool of resources, measured as growth in the subsidiary's total number of employees.

name: Subsidiary sales growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the subsidiary in terms of sales", "sales growth", "growth in sales"]
definition: Growth in sales corresponds to a measure of performance of the subsidiary.

name: Market growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the subsidiary's market", "market growth", "growth in the size of the market"]
definition: Growth in the size of the market in which the subsidiary operates, measured through the number of cars sold in the host country.

name: Multiple R&D locations
authors_terms: ["multiple R&D locations", "multilocation of R&D", "number of R&D locations", "R&D locations"]
definition: This location choice requires firms to make a simultaneous choice about the organizational structure of innovation activity: almost by definition, multiple locations per firm imply some degree of decentralization. The key explanatory variables relate to the number of locations where firms carried out R&D activities within Finland.

name: External knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["external knowledge sourcing", "extent of external knowledge sourcing", "external sources of knowledge", "external knowledge sources"]
definition: Multiple locations enable the firm to access a larger number of different knowledge sources outside of the organization. The authors constructed a summary variable that reflects the extent of external knowledge sourcing per firm.

name: Innovation output
definition: The dependent variables measure innovation output per firm. To measure innovation output, the authors utilized binary variables as well as sales revenue data, and the sales variables measure the extent of commercial success.

name: New-to-the-market innovation output
definition: R&D directed toward product- and market-specific innovation is likely to include a greater emphasis on incremental and imitative innovations, in order to satisfy customer demand for new products and product enhancements that competitors may already have successfully introduced. For purposes of our analysis, new-to-the-market innovations include all types of novel innovations.

name: Breadth of innovation output
authors_terms: ["range of innovation output", "range of applicability of each firm's innovations", "range of important innovation effects", "breadth of innovation output", "wider range of applications"]
definition: In addition to the binary and sales variables that measure the amount of innovation output, we created two dependent variables reflecting the range of applicability of each firm's innovations, in order to test Hypotheses 3A and 3B.

name: Antibiotic innovation
definition: We define firm j as an 'antibiotic innovator' if it generated at least one new antibiotic by 1960. Otherwise, firm j is classified as an 'imitator.'

name: R&D investment
authors_terms: ["R&D inputs", "R&D investments", "commitment to innovation", "number of biologists and other scientists"]
definition: SCIENTISTS represents the total number of scientists and engineers hired to do pharmaceutical R&D at a particular point in time. It measures a firm's general commitment to R&D; BIOLOGISTS represents the number of biologists hired to do a firm's pharmaceutical R&D at a particular point in time.

name: New chemical entity output
definition: Our source for R&D outputs is Review of Drugs, 1941-1961: Single Chemical Entities Introduced in the United States and Patent Status (De Haen 1962). Our measure of significant innovative outputs comprises these chemical entities; n_it is the number of new chemical entities (NCEs) for firm i in time interval t, which measures innovative performance.

name: Shared prior-industry beliefs
authors_terms: ["shared beliefs", "industry-level frames", "industry recipes", "shared or interlocking metaphors or worldviews", "industry model"]
definition: Similar prior experiences and ongoing interactions give rise to a shared set of beliefs for members of the same industry. Firms from the same prior industry are likely to make similar assessments of which product features customers will value and are therefore likely to first introduce a given feature at a similar time.

name: Imitation of same-industry peers
definition: Firms are more likely to imitate the practices and behaviors of similar, comparable firms than to imitate firms they categorize as distant, and this tendency for mimetic isomorphism is heightened under conditions of high uncertainty such as entry into new markets.

name: Peer entry by firms from different prior industries
authors_terms: ["concurrent entry by firms from a different prior industry", "cumulative previous entry by firms from a different prior industry"]
definition: Counts of the number of other firms with a different prior industry affiliation that introduced a particular feature in year t, and the cumulative number of such firms that had introduced the feature as of year t-1. These terms are the comparison to the influence of firms from the same prior industry.

name: Presence of same-prior-industry firms in a feature
authors_terms: ["firms from the same prior industry present in feature", "market presence of firms from the same prior industry in the feature", "influence of other firms from the same prior industry"]
definition: A count of the number of firms from the same prior industry that are currently in the market with a camera that has the feature, representing the ongoing influence of other firms from the same prior industry on a firm's commitment to that feature.

name: Firm experience with a product feature
authors_terms: ["firm experience in feature", "firm's own experience with features", "firm feature experience"]
definition: The cumulative number of models with the feature that the firm has introduced as of year t-1. As a firm gains its own experience with a feature it gains knowledge about the level of demand and access to information from customers, so prior industry beliefs and peers play a smaller role.

name: Initial introduction of a product feature
authors_terms: ["initial introduction of a feature", "initial product feature introduction", "timing of initial product feature introduction"]
definition: The timing of a firm's first introduction of a model with a particular product feature, which reflects the firm's framing of the opportunity in the context of high uncertainty.

name: Ongoing commitment to a product feature
authors_terms: ["ongoing commitment to a feature", "commitment to that product feature", "continued introduction of models with specific digital camera features"]
definition: A firm's continued incorporation of a particular product feature in the models it introduces, measured as the number of digital cameras introduced by the firm in a year that had the feature; for resolution it is indicated by continuing to introduce increasingly higher resolution cameras.

name: Competitive behavior
definition: Based on theories of identity and identification and on social identity theory, we define competitive behavior as the actions individuals target toward a competitor to maintain or enhance their self-esteem. The authors consider an increase in the number of actions a player targets toward a competitor as more competitive behavior.

name: Former employer
definition: The opposing organization for which the focal individual has previously played; in the study, the opposing player's current team whenever the focal player has ever played for it.

name: Former colleague
definition: A person with whom the individual previously worked in the same organization; in the study, a pair of players who have ever played together in a team, whose coworker-coworker role-relationship evolves into an ex-coworker-ex-coworker or friend-friend role-relationship.

name: Transfer mode
definition: Two knowledge transfer modes—front-loading and back-loading—based on whether the affordance for tacit knowledge exchange provided by the transfer methods used is higher during the initiation or during the implementation phase of a transfer.

name: Experienced difficulty of knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["transfer difficulty", "stickiness", "experienced difficulty of knowledge transfer", "difficulty of knowledge transfer"]
definition: The degree of difficulty experienced in a transfer, reflected in the number and intensity of distinct moments of difficulty or its eventfulness; a transfer is stickier when efforts to resolve transfer problems become noteworthy.

name: Causal ambiguity
definition: The extent to which organizational members understand the relationships between the practice's inputs and its outcomes, or irreducible uncertainty about what the factors of production are, how they interact, and their link to performance outcomes.

name: Arduous relationship
authors_terms: ["arduous relationship", "arduousness of the relationship", "relationship between the source and recipient of knowledge"]
definition: The nature of the preexisting relationship between the source and recipient of knowledge; an arduous relationship is one where differences strain communication and collaboration and distance the parties involved, and is a significant barrier to knowledge transfer.

name: Affordance for tacit knowledge exchange
definition: The extent to which a method affords interaction between source and recipient, personalized communication, recipient observation of the knowledge in use, and recipient practice; the action potential that can be taken given a specific tool, method, or technology.

name: Joint problem solving with lead suppliers
authors_terms: ["joint problem solving with lead suppliers", "joint problem solving with suppliers", "joint problem-solving arrangements"]
definition: Joint problem solving is defined as the degree to which the parties to an exchange 'share the responsibility for maintaining the relationship itself and for problems that arise as time goes on'.

name: Joint problem solving with lead customers
authors_terms: ["joint problem solving with lead customers", "joint problem solving with customers", "joint problem-solving arrangements"]
definition: Joint problem solving is defined as the degree to which the parties to an exchange 'share the responsibility for maintaining the relationship itself and for problems that arise as time goes on'; parallel instruments were developed to measure the extent to which a firm has embedded ties with its lead customer and lead supplier.

name: Information sharing with lead suppliers
authors_terms: ["information sharing", "information sharing with lead suppliers", "information sharing with suppliers"]
definition: Information sharing captures 'the degree to which each party discloses information that may facilitate the other party's activities'.

name: Information sharing with lead customers
authors_terms: ["information sharing", "information sharing with lead customers", "information sharing with customers"]
definition: Information sharing captures 'the degree to which each party discloses information that may facilitate the other party's activities'; parallel instruments were developed for the lead customer and lead supplier relationships.

name: Trust in lead suppliers
authors_terms: ["interorganizational trust", "trust in lead suppliers", "trust in suppliers"]
definition: Interorganizational trust refers to a common expectation among the members of an organization that another organization '(i) makes good faith efforts to behave in accordance with any commitments both explicitly or implicit, (ii) is honest in whatever negotiations preceded such commitments, and (iii) does not take excessive advantage of another even when the opportunity is available'.

name: Trust in lead customers
authors_terms: ["interorganizational trust", "trust in lead customers", "trust in customers"]
definition: Interorganizational trust describes the extent to which the members of a focal firm have a collectively held trust orientation toward a customer or supplier firm; it reflects the degree to which the exchange partner is fair in its dealing and does not try to take advantage of the focal firm.

name: Acquisition of competitive capabilities
authors_terms: ["acquisition of competitive capabilities", "acquisition of capabilities", "competitive capabilities"]
definition: Competitive capabilities are the set of organizing processes and principles a firm uses to deploy its resources to achieve strategic objectives. Consistent with Meyer and Goes (1988) capabilities are viewed as being acquired through a multistage, organizational process.

name: Board tie
definition: Throughout the paper, we use the terms board tie, shared director, and common director interchangeably to refer to the phenomenon of a common director serving on both the supplier's and the buyer's boards. Board Tie is an indicator that equals one if supplier i and buyer j share at least one common director in year t and zero otherwise.

name: Buyer-specific innovation
definition: We develop a text-based measure of suppliers' buyer-specific innovation by analyzing the technical language of patent claims. By identifying buyer-specific terms in supplier patents - technical words or phrases that appear in both a supplier's and a buyer's patents but not in the patents of the supplier's other buyers - we quantify buyer-specific innovation within supply chain relationships.

name: Number of alternative suppliers
authors_terms: ["number of alternative suppliers", "peer suppliers", "High Peer Suppliers"]
definition: A larger set of potential alternative suppliers increases the buyer's ability to switch suppliers, which makes the supplier more vulnerable to buyer opportunism in the presence of buyer-specific investments.

name: Buyer growth opportunities
definition: Hayashi (1982) shows that the average Q - the ratio of the market value of the firm's existing capital stock to its replacement cost - summarizes all the relevant information about the firm's investment opportunities. Consistent with prior literature, we measure Tobin's Q as the market value of equity plus the book value of assets minus the book value of equity divided by the book value of assets.

name: Supplier R&D investment
definition: Supplier R&D is the supplier's total research and development expenditures in year t. We use total R&D investments as the dependent variable rather than total capital expenditures because R&D tends to be driven more by relationship-specific investments than other types of investments.

name: Supply chain relationship longevity
authors_terms: ["relationship longevity", "longevity of supply chain relationships", "relationship duration"]
definition: Ln(Relationship longevity) is the natural logarithm of the number of years from the year in which a supply chain relationship was first established between firms i and j until the end of our sample period or the last year of the relationship, whichever is earlier.

name: Economic shock
definition: An economic shock is a type of a severe environmental shock that significantly increases the risk of firm failure across a range of industries, economy wide. An environmental shock is an unanticipated and disruptive change in a firm's external environment.

name: Growth reconfiguration
definition: The term reconfiguration refers to the restructuring and integration activities that occur in the process of growth or retrenchment, recognizing that the gains from an increase or decrease in size are also influenced by the costs incurred in the process of change (Penrose, 1959).

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured as the next period return on assets (ROA), which records the extent to which a firm is able to profit on its invested resources.

name: Risk of firm failure
authors_terms: ["firm failure", "risk of firm failure", "risk of failure"]
definition: The ending event of firm failure was recorded when a firm exited by means of acquisition, bankruptcy, or dissolution.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack is the availability of uncommitted or unabsorbed financial resources that can shield firms from the disruptive effect of an external shock (Bourgeois, 1981; Cyert and March, 1963; Thompson, 1967).

name: Product diversification
definition: Product diversification influences whether firms are able to access growth opportunities during an economic shock. These arguments suggest that product diversification increases discretion in growth and divestiture, but also limits the ability of firms to respond to an economic shock.

name: Institutional development
definition: Institutional development supports business reconfiguration by facilitating access to capital, labor, and information resources (Tybout, 2000).

name: Knowledge sourced
authors_terms: ["knowledge sourced", "interfirm knowledge transfer", "level of knowledge sourced from a hired engineer's previous firm", "learning-by-hiring"]
definition: The extent of knowledge sourced from the hired engineer's previous firm, operationalized as the number of citations each hiring firm patent makes to any patent from the mobile engineer's previous firm. An increase in this measure indicates an increase in the degree to which a patent builds upon knowledge from the mobile engineer's previous firm.

name: Firm path dependence
definition: Evolutionary economics proposes that the search for new knowledge is often localized or path dependent; i.e., it is influenced by a firm's past experiences. Hence, this path dependence impedes a firm's receptivity to external knowledge by reducing the motivation and ability to seek, recognize, and assimilate knowledge that may be distant from its current practice.

name: Expertise fit with hiring firm
authors_terms: ["Expertise Fit", "fit between a hiring firm's core technology and the mobile engineer's expertise", "engineer's area of technological expertise matches the hiring firm's area of technological expertise"]
definition: The fit between a hiring firm's core technology and the mobile engineer's expertise, operationalized as a dummy variable that takes on a value of one if the mobile engineer's prior area of expertise and the hiring firm's core technology are identical, and a value of zero otherwise.

name: Innovation area
authors_terms: ["Innovation Area", "innovation area fit", "engineer pursues innovative activities in the hiring firm's core area of technological expertise"]
definition: This variable indicates whether the hired engineer innovates in the new firm's core technology area or in a peripheral technology area.

name: Geographic scope of mobility
definition: Whether the hired engineer's move is domestic or international: mobility from a U.S. firm to a U.S.-based R&D lab of a non-U.S. firm is coded as one and mobility to a non-U.S.-based operation of a non-U.S. firm is coded as zero.

name: Pro forma forecasts about parent companies
authors_terms: ["pro forma forecasts", "# annual EPS forecasts", "EPS growth forecast", "financial statement index"]
definition: The pro forma forecasts analysts produce about diversified parent companies: information on a firm's expected future financial condition, such as growth forecasts and pro forma financial statements, which is a key input into the production of accurate forecasts.

name: Pro forma forecasts about spun-off subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["pro forma forecasts", "pro forma forecasts about spun-off subsidiaries"]
definition: The pro forma forecasts analysts produce about spun-off subsidiaries, measured as the number of years for which annual EPS is forecast, whether EPS growth is forecast, and the number of pro forma financial statements produced for these units.

name: Analysis of spin-off rationale
definition: Whether an analyst describes the rationale for an upcoming spin-off in his/her report; such research reflects situations in which analysts put more effort into understanding diversified companies.

name: Analysis of conglomerate discount
definition: Whether an analyst discusses the conglomerate discount in his/her report; such research reflects situations in which analysts put more effort into understanding diversified companies.

name: Analysis of business segments
definition: Whether an analyst includes segment-level financial information in his/her reports, that is, whether the analyst studies the business segments operating within the diversified parent company.

name: Analysts' research about parent companies
authors_terms: ["analysts' research", "research that analysts produce about the diversified parent companies"]
definition: The research that analysts produce about diversified parent companies, comprising pro forma forecasts and analyses of the spin-off rationale, the conglomerate discount, and the parent companies' segments.

name: Analysts' research about spun-off subsidiaries
definition: The research that analysts produce about spun-off subsidiaries, comprising pro forma forecasts about these units and analysis of the segments operating within their parent companies.

name: Parent earnings forecast accuracy
definition: The accuracy of the earnings forecasts analysts make about the divesting parent companies; higher values mean more accurate forecasts, since higher values of EPS forecast error indicate that a forecast is less accurate and vice versa.

name: Subsidiary earnings forecast accuracy
definition: The accuracy of the earnings forecasts analysts make about the spun-off subsidiaries; higher values mean more accurate forecasts, since higher values of EPS forecast error indicate that a forecast is less accurate and vice versa.

name: Firm diversification
definition: The level of diversification within the parent firms, represented by the Herfindahl Index, calculated as the sum of the squared shares of a firm's total sales provided by each of its segments.

name: Spin-off size relative to parent
definition: The size of the spun-off subsidiary relative to its parent company, measured as the total assets of the spun-off subsidiary over the total assets of its parent company.

name: Multiple divestitures
authors_terms: ["multiple divestiture", "multiple spin-offs at the same time"]
definition: Whether a firm undertakes several spin-offs at the same time; two or more spin-offs by the same parent are defined as a multiple divestiture when either the announcement or the effective dates of the transactions occur within a week of each other.

name: Prior stock price history
authors_terms: ["stock price history", "no stock price history", "tracking stock"]
definition: Whether the spun-off subsidiary had a stock price history as an independent company before the spin-off; the sole occasion in which a spun-off subsidiary might have such a history is when the divesting parent company created a tracking stock for it before spinning it off.

name: Industry relatedness of subsidiary to parent
authors_terms: ["unrelated", "not in the same industry as their parent firms", "share a four-digit SIC code"]
definition: Whether the spun-off subsidiary operates in the same industry as its parent company, as indicated by whether the parent and the spun-off subsidiary share a four-digit SIC code.

name: Shared procedural justice
authors_terms: ["shared procedural justice", "shared justice perceptions", "shared perceptions of procedural justice", "level of shared procedural justice"]
definition: The level of perceived procedural justice commonly agreed upon by both parties to an alliance, as reported through their boundary spanners; the level of shared procedural justice is defined as an interaction term, the mean of the two parties' perceived procedural justice scores multiplied by the interparty agreement estimate.

name: Unilateral procedural justice
authors_terms: ["unilateral procedural justice", "unilaterally perceived procedural justice", "one-sided perspective", "unilateral judgments"]
definition: The level of procedural justice unilaterally perceived by each individual party to an alliance, as opposed to the perceptions commonly agreed upon by both parties.

name: Alliance profitability
definition: The financial returns of an alliance, measured by averaging return on investment (ROI; net profit/total investment) for the alliance.

name: Cultural distance
definition: The cultural difference between an alliance's two partner firms, measured via Kogut and Singh's composite index and Hofstede's latest data set, which contains five cultural dimensions (power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individuality, masculinity, and long-term orientation).

name: Structural uncertainty
definition: Structural uncertainty was defined as the geometric average of standard deviations in the output, sales, and profits of the industry in which an alliance participated.

name: Directors' prior CEO compensation experience
authors_terms: ["average prior CEO compensation (relative to market) experienced by directors", "average prior CEO compensation level (relative to market) experienced by directors", "directors' premeeting average position on CEO compensation"]
definition: The compensation level (relative to market) that directors on average tend to support prior to discussions about the focal CEO's compensation should reflect the average prior compensation level (relative to market) they experienced across different boards. It is measured as the mean, across all outside directors, of the median CEO compensation level (relative to market) witnessed by each director in the previous three years across all public boards, including the focal board.

name: CEO compensation relative to market
authors_terms: ["focal CEO's compensation relative to market", "focal CEO's annual total compensation level relative to the market"]
definition: During board discussions of CEO compensation, directors typically need to decide the focal CEO's annual total compensation level relative to the market. The dependent variable captures the extent to which the focal CEO's compensation is above or below the market (i.e., peer CEOs' median compensation).

name: Relative similarity in firm size
authors_terms: ["relative similarity in firm size", "relative similarity of the minority's prior decision context in terms of firm size"]
definition: Measured as the total asset difference between the focal firm and the average firm previously served by the majorities (measured as the number of standard deviations in total assets) divided by the size difference between the focal firm and the average firm previously served by the minorities.

name: Relative similarity in industry
authors_terms: ["relative similarity in industry", "industry similarity", "relative similarity of the minority's prior decision context in terms of industry of affiliation"]
definition: The industry similarity between the focal firm and another firm was measured as k if they share the same k-digit SIC code and 0 if they are in totally different industries. Relative similarity in industry (minority versus majority) was then calculated as the average industry similarity between the focal firm and firms previously served by the minorities divided by the average industry similarity between the focal firm and firms previously served by the majorities.

name: Demographic homogeneity among outside directors
authors_terms: ["demographic homogeneity among directors", "demographic homogeneity among outside directors"]
definition: Demographic homogeneity among outside directors was measured according to functional background, industry of employment, highest degree obtained (i.e., Ph.D., master's, bachelor's, or associate's degree), and gender. The authors argue that, holding the diversity of directors' views on CEO compensation constant, demographic homogeneity can promote open communications and mutual trust among directors.

name: Outsiders' power relative to insiders
authors_terms: ["outsiders' power relative to insiders", "outside directors' power relative to inside directors"]
definition: Behavioral research on boards suggests that outside directors' power relative to inside directors is a key factor that determines the degree to which they are able to influence compensation decisions based on their opinions. It is measured by an index based on four measures of outsiders' power widely used in prior research.

name: Multinationality
definition: We use the term multinationality to refer to the extent of a firm's operations outside its home country. Alternate terms used in prior studies for the same construct include 'geographic diversification' and 'internationalization'.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance consequences of a firm's multinationality; L&B measured firm performance using both accounting and market-based measures, while this replication uses an accounting-based measure, return on assets, as the primary dependent variable.

name: Intangible assets
definition: The level of a firm's intangible assets, in this study captured by the firm's R&D intensity, i.e. the parent firm's R&D spending as a percentage of its sales.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "total diversification", "entropy measure of diversification", "corporate diversification strategy"]
definition: Diversified firms may also be distinguished by the varying degrees of emphasis managers place on the dominant (usually the original) business and by the nature of relations among divisions, which may be related or unrelated. Dominant-business, related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated diversification are the four major categories of diversified firms typically studied.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity, the dependent variable used in the study, was measured as a firm's reported spending on research and development per $1,000 of sales. This variable is the most commonly used measure in studies of R&D intensity.

name: Related diversification
definition: DR was defined as the related diversification arising out of operating in several segments within an industry group.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: DU was defined as unrelated diversification between industry groups.

name: Reservations about stock repurchase plans
authors_terms: ["analysts' reservations about stock repurchase plans", "reservations about repurchase plans", "own reservations"]
definition: An analyst's own reservations about whether the adoption of stock repurchase plans reflects well on firms' future profitability, that is, reservations about the performance benefits of repurchase plans and whether such plans bode well for future firm profitability.

name: Perceived reservations of other analysts
authors_terms: ["perceived reservations of others", "perception of others' reservations", "perception that other analysts have reservations"]
definition: An analyst's perception of the extent to which other analysts share his or her reservations about whether the adoption of repurchase plans reflects well on an adopting firm's future profitability.

name: Communication ties to other analysts
authors_terms: ["communication ties", "informal dyadic communication", "frequency of communication ties to other analysts"]
definition: The frequency of an analyst's communication with other analysts; the authors use the term 'communication ties' to refer to informal dyadic conversations between analysts, and measure it as the total amount of time spent communicating with other analysts during the prior year.

name: Earnings forecast
definition: The focal analyst's subsequent earnings forecast following the focal repurchase plan adoption, expressed in dollars per share of common equity.

name: Change in stock recommendation
authors_terms: ["upgrade", "more positive stock recommendation", "change in stock recommendations"]
definition: A dichotomous measure that indicates whether the focal analyst's subsequent report following the focal adoption included an upgrade (i.e., a more positive stock recommendation) for the adopting firm.

name: Pluralistic ignorance
definition: Pluralistic ignorance is a systematic tendency for members of a group or community to underestimate the extent to which others share their concerns about practices, policies, or events under the group's purview.

name: Marketing-related capabilities
definition: Marketing-related capabilities are those that provide links with customers; they enable JVs to compete by predicting changes in customer preferences as well as creating and managing durable relationships with customers and channel members. The marketing-related capabilities, focusing on market sensing and external linking capabilities, were developed from Day (1994).

name: Technology-related capabilities
definition: Technology-related capabilities are those that develop and produce technology; these enable response to the rapidly changing technological environment. The technology-related capabilities, focusing on technology development, new product development, and manufacturing processes, were drawn from Day (1994).

name: Performance relative to objectives
definition: The dependent construct performance relative to profit, sales, and ROI objectives was measured on 11-point scales anchored 'low'/'high'. The authors tap performance by considering profit, sales, and ROI relative to objectives.

name: Technological turbulence
definition: Perceived technological turbulence refers to the state of technology in the industry, the rate of change in technology, and the JV's inability to accurately forecast the changes in the technology.

name: CEO time urgency
definition: Time urgency, a subcomponent of the type A behavior pattern, is a relatively stable trait. Time-urgent people are acutely aware of the passage of time and feel chronically hurried.

name: CEO pacing style
definition: Pacing style refers to how individuals distribute their effort over time in working toward deadlines. As a relatively stable behavioral tendency, pacing style is represented as a continuum of how closely the intensity of work is paced to the deadline.

name: CEO temporal leadership
definition: Temporal leadership, defined as the set of a leader's behaviors pertaining to the management of the temporal aspects of a team's task, includes three interrelated activities: scheduling, temporal synchronization, and the allocation of temporal resources.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
definition: Corporate entrepreneurship, also referred to as intrapreneurship, is a broad, multi-dimensional concept that lies at the intersection of entrepreneurship and strategic management, defined as a set of firm activities encompassing innovation, corporate venturing, and strategic renewal.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "market share performance (MSP)", "change in market share"]
definition: Firm performance was assessed on the basis of market share performance (change in market share).

name: Number of alliance agreements
authors_terms: ["number of long-term horizontal alliance agreements", "number of alliance agreements (NoA)", "intensity of cooperation"]
definition: To measure intensity of cooperation we counted the number of alliance agreements that a firm had with its competitors.

name: Number of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["number of competitors linked to the firm through alliances", "number of partners (NoP)"]
definition: Hypothesis 2 is framed in terms of the number of competitors linked to the firm through alliances, rather than the number of alliances. NoP is the number of competitors with whom the firm entered into one or more alliance agreements during the 1978-87 period.

name: Deviation from intermediate firm size
authors_terms: ["deviation of firm size from the intermediate value of firm size in the industry", "SIZEDEV"]
definition: Mean firm size served as the benchmark for intermediate firm size. Firm size deviation was calculated as the absolute deviation of actual firm size from mean firm size.

name: Firm size
definition: Production data for each firm were obtained from World Motor Vehicle Data. Average annual unit production by the firm (AAPf) was used to assess firm size.

name: Alliance concentration within a subnetwork
authors_terms: ["proportion of partners found within the boundaries of a subnetwork", "highest proportion of linkages within a single subnetwork (HPLWSS-N)"]
definition: Each firm's highest proportion of linkages within a single subnetwork (HPLWSS-N) was then calculated by dividing each firm's NoPm by its total number of partners (NoP).

name: Alliance partner size
authors_terms: ["size of its partners", "average size of its actual partners", "difference between average actual and average potential partner size (DPAPS)"]
definition: The difference between average actual and average potential partner size (DPAPS) indicates a firm's preference for larger or smaller partners relative to what would be expected if choices were made at random among potential partners.

name: Information withholding
definition: Organizational scholars have established that information withholding-the intentional failure to share potentially useful information with others-can impede intra-organizational learning processes that are critical for successful firm performance.

name: Reference group information withholding
authors_terms: ["RG w/h level", "information withholding by reference group members", "withholding behaviors of reference group members", "levels of information withholding in reference groups"]
definition: RG w/h level is the average number of times that the members of each group reported withholding information from another scientist who requested it.

name: Variance in reference group information withholding
authors_terms: ["RG w/h variance", "variance in information withholding", "crystallization", "variance in withholding among reference group members"]
definition: Crystallization refers to the extent of agreement among group members about the level of the behavior in which an individual can appropriately engage. RG w/h variance is the standard deviation in the number of times that the members of each group reported withholding information.

name: Reference group attitudes to information withholding
definition: RG w/h attitudes is the average of the reference group members' responses to the following statement: 'Academic scientists should freely share information, data, or materials with all academic scientists', where a higher score indicates more favorable attitudes to withholding in the group.

name: Professional similarity of reference group members
authors_terms: ["professionally similar", "professional similarity", "more professionally similar to the scientist"]
definition: We examined three levels of professional reference groups for the life scientists in our sample based on professional field, specialty, and status. The three levels of reference groups enabled us to test the influence of groups of increasing professional similarity to the focal scientist.

name: Managerial activities
authors_terms: ["managerial activities", "managerial and structural characteristics", "planning, organizing, and controlling activities"]
definition: This construct is broadly defined to encompass planning, organizing, and controlling activities of executives in small firms. Planning is characterized by information gathering and information processing.

name: Information gathering
definition: Planning is characterized by information gathering and information processing. The information gathering (defined in terms of scanning and futurity) were operationalized using definitions in Miller (1987a, 1987b).

name: Information processing
definition: Planning is characterized by information gathering and information processing. The information processing (defined in terms of analysis and interaction with others) were operationalized using definitions in Miller (1987a, 1987b).

name: Organizing
definition: Organizing is described in terms of decentralization and specialization. As small firms grow, their CEOs face the challenges of large-scale operations and administrative complexity.

name: Control
definition: Finally, the concept of control is represented by two variables: formality and cost control.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: In the current study, entrepreneurial orientation is defined as the firm's degree of proactiveness (aggressiveness) in its chosen product-market unit (PMU) and its willingness to innovate and create new offerings.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: The environmental turbulence construct is defined in terms of dynamism: unpredictable environmental changes; hostility: environmental threats to the firm's vitality; and heterogeneity: diversity of the firm's environments.

name: Firm growth
definition: The role of a firm's past growth performance as an important contextual construct has been studied and reported in small business literature. Growth was measured by using the actual change in (1) the number of employees over a 5-year period and (2) the dollar sales volume over a 4-year span.

name: Quantitative analysis
definition: Analyses that produce large-N numerical information intended to be representative and statistically consistent (e.g., data analytics, fixed-response surveys, or A/B testing); the authors treat these as one end of a methodological spectrum.

name: Qualitative analysis
definition: Analyses that produce small-N non-numerical information that is richly descriptive and contextual (e.g., focus groups or interviews); the authors treat these as the other end of the methodological spectrum.

name: New-product sales
authors_terms: ["new-product sales", "commercial success of new products", "new-product innovation success"]
definition: The commercial success of new-product innovations, operationalized as the sum of dollar sales of product i in the two quarters that conclude the two-year post-launch period.

name: Methodological pluralism
authors_terms: ["methodological pluralism", "complementarity of quantitative and qualitative analysis"]
definition: The authors conceptualize methodological pluralism in organizations as comparatively high reliance on both quantitative and qualitative analysis, relative either to low reliance on both or to high reliance on only one method.

name: Hits
definition: Products that reached the top 5 percent of new-product sales in each product group, which accounted for about 50 percent of total new-product sales in the authors' sample.

name: Flops
definition: Products in the bottom 50 percent of new-product sales in each product group, which accounted for about 5 percent of total new-product sales in the authors' sample.

name: Organization size
authors_terms: ["organization size", "size", "natural log of the number of year-round employees"]
definition: Organization size was measured by the natural log of the number of year-round employees.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: Perceived environmental uncertainty was measured with a modified version of the Downey, Hellriegel, and Slocum (1975) adaptation of the Duncan (1972) instrument, which asks for only 3 external environmental factors from a list of 14.

name: Technology policy
definition: An aggressive technology policy is a long range strategy for the adoption and production of process, product, and service innovations. This policy is one type of long range environmental coping mechanisms.

name: Performance gap
definition: The existence of a performance gap, or performance below standards and expectations, has long been implicated in the literature as a stimulus of innovative activity.

name: Direct market policy
definition: Direct marketing to customers with top management involvement was hypothesized as an important feature of the innovation process for suppliers. This variable is distinct from the concept of market strategy, which usually is considered to be the choice of market and product mix.

name: Top management involvement with customers
authors_terms: ["top management customer relations", "top management-customer interface", "top management customer policy"]
definition: Firms were coded according to the extent to which a special priority system was used by top managers for becoming involved with customers. In other words, high scores were assigned for specific priority systems, lower scores were assigned for vague priority systems, and lowest scores for no priority system.

name: Innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation", "innovation outcomes", "rate of product and process innovation"]
definition: The dependent, innovation variables are rate of product and process innovation.

name: Product innovation rate
authors_terms: ["rate of product innovation", "rate of new product introduction"]
definition: The rate of product innovation, the number of new products introduced during the last three years.

name: Radical product innovation
authors_terms: ["introduction of one particular radical product", "radical product introduction", "retortable packaging"]
definition: The introduction of one particular radical product, retortable packaging or equipment to form, fill, seal, and process retortable packaging. This technology is a flexible or semirigid package that is thermostabilized like a metal can and is shelf-stable.

name: Radical process innovation
authors_terms: ["rate of radical process adoption", "major or radical process innovations"]
definition: The number of major or radical process innovations (incorporating technology new to the industry).

name: Incremental process innovation
authors_terms: ["rate of incremental process adoption", "minor or incremental process innovations"]
definition: The number of minor or incremental process innovations.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: The extent to which shares are held by a dominant or majority shareholder; such a shareholder has both the incentive and the ability to monitor management, so that concentrated ownership is a powerful constraint on managerial discretion.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Firm performance, measured by return on assets; ROA is measured as the ratio of net income to total assets and is the dependent variable in all equations.

name: Diversification
definition: The extent to which the firm operates across multiple product market segments. The authors assume that unmonitored managers in firms with low ownership concentration will diversify in ways inconsistent with profit maximization, so that excessive diversification reduces profits.

name: National system of corporate governance
authors_terms: ["national system of corporate governance", "Anglo-American model", "Continental European model", "internal constraints", "external constraints"]
definition: The country-specific nexus of constraints on managerial behavior. In France and Germany the main constraints appear to be internal, emanating from owners and boards; external constraints, particularly markets for corporate control, are relatively more powerful in the United States and the United Kingdom; Canada relies on both.

name: Brand name reputation
definition: Brand name reputation is a key determinant of whether or not potential customers patronize an establishment, and restaurant chains build reputations by establishing multiple outlets within a region, thereby creating visibility as well as economies of scale in both advertising and purchasing.

name: Top management team experience
authors_terms: ["top management team experience", "TMT experience", "top management experience"]
definition: An experienced and knowledgeable top management team (TMT) can also be a strategic resource. Because the restaurant industry is relatively stable, executives with knowledge of operational practices and the idiosyncratic characteristics of a specific restaurant concept are best suited to build and maintain the consistent service standards and cost controls that offer a foundation for long-term success.

name: Slack capital
definition: A third variable, slack capital, is generally not considered to be a strategic resource (cf. Barney, 1991). In certain circumstances, however, slack capital can be rare (e.g., Martin and Justis, 1993), which is one important quality of a strategic resource (Barney, 1991).

name: Outlet-level asset specificity
definition: Specific assets, in contrast to general purpose assets, are costly to redeploy to alternative uses (Williamson, 1991). If assets required to operate these new outlets (e.g., physical plant, kitchen equipment) cannot be easily transformed for use in another type of restaurant or another business (i.e., the assets are highly specific), then cooperative partners must continue to cooperate with the firm in order to recover their investment.

name: Specific knowledge
authors_terms: ["specific knowledge", "specific knowledge that is costly to transfer"]
definition: Knowledge can be categorized as general knowledge that is easy to transfer to agents or specific knowledge that is costly to transfer (Jensen and Meckling, 1995). Specific knowledge is often tacit (Polanyi, 1962) or complex (Shane, 1998) and therefore costly to transfer to agents (Jensen and Meckling, 1995).

name: Geographic dispersion
definition: The geographic dispersion of operations affects the costs of organizing in many service industries where operations must be located in close proximity to consumers (Carman and Langeard, 1980). As geographic dispersion increases, the firm must hire additional district and regional managers to visit and monitor outlet-level managers.

name: Interfirm cooperation
definition: Interfirm cooperation exists when two or more otherwise sovereign organizations act in concert to pursue mutual gain (Borys and Jemison, 1989).

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is a multidimensional construct; thus multiple, disparate measures should be examined (Venkatraman and Ramanujam, 1986).

name: Resources
definition: Resources can be defined as 'those assets that are tied semi-permanently to the firm' (Wernerfelt, 1984: 173). Following Barney (1991) and Peteraf (1993), we use the term resources broadly to refer to both resources and capabilities.

name: Exchange conditions
definition: The important conditions that affect an exchange are perhaps best described by the two theories most central to the OE paradigm: transaction costs and agency theory. The former focuses on the characteristics of an exchange that encourage managers to increase firm boundaries (i.e., full ownership), share with others (i.e., interfirm cooperation), or exchange in markets.

name: Contingency fit
definition: A congruence notion of fit in which high performance occurs when the organizational response variables (technology, structure, and culture) match the environmental contingency variable (environmental turbulence); deviation from the optimal fit line is contingency misfit.

name: Institutional fit
definition: Institutional fit is defined as 'the degree of compliance by an organization with the organizational form of structures, routines, and systems prescribed by institutional norms' (Kondra and Hinings 1998, p. 750). The impact of a firm's organizational design variables on firm performance depends on their similarity to the organizational design variables of high performers in an organizational field.

name: Metafit
definition: A combined contingency and institutional fit approach; the notion of metafit proposed by Donaldson (2008a) suggests that a sound and fully comprehensive organizational design analysis should supplement contingency analysis with institutional analysis. Contingency and institutional fit are complementary and interact in what might be called metafit.

name: Firm performance
definition: The outcome of fit between the organization and its environment, studied as short-term organizational performance and measured with three survey items that correlate highly with return on assets.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Environmental turbulence is operationalized as the product of the level of dynamism within the market environment and the degree to which changes are unpredictable.

name: Organizational technology
definition: The hardware (such as machines and equipment) and software (knowledge) used in transforming inputs into outputs (Volberda 1996).

name: Organizational structure
definition: The actual distribution of responsibilities and authority among the organization's personnel and the process regulations of decision making, coordination, and execution.

name: Organizational culture
definition: The set of beliefs and assumptions held relatively commonly throughout the organization and taken for granted by its members (Bate 1984).

name: Industry concentration
definition: Concentration is measured by the 10-firm concentration ratio (CR10), and the paper assumes that collusion is easier with higher industry concentration.

name: Innovation implementation
definition: A measure of how much of the possible innovations were implemented in the industry in a given year, constructed from hedonic prices of personal computers and from the number of related patents.

name: Incumbent exit
definition: The yearly number of firms exiting from incumbency as a top-10 net profit-maker.

name: Lock-in technology strategy
definition: Static efficiency entails producing at a lower cost than dynamically efficient competitors in the short run but at a higher cost in the long run. Any strategy that does not allow a firm to switch to the new technology without cost or delay is considered statically efficient, and the best practice of these strategies is called the 'lock-in' strategy.

name: Entry of new firms
authors_terms: ["entry", "new entry", "entry by new firms", "entrepreneurial entry", "entrepreneurial emergence"]
definition: The entrepreneur is defined in this paper as a new firm with new technology. Entry by new firms occurs in the final period whenever an incumbent locks-in in the first period, because the reduction in variable costs embodied in the new technology allows at least two low-cost firms to produce.

name: Total company profits
authors_terms: ["Total Company Profits", "profits summed over all producing companies"]
definition: The profits summed over all producing companies.

name: Consumer surplus
definition: The surplus accruing to consumers; under Cournot competition, when firms are statically efficient it is a certainty that the price and the supply available to the consumer will be improved.

name: Total welfare
definition: Total welfare is the sum of the change in total company profits and the change in consumer surplus; this welfare measure does not take into account the extra costs involved due to the emergence of entrepreneurship, namely the cost of bankrupt incumbents plus the cost of setting up replacing entrants.

name: Status of affiliates
authors_terms: ["status of an actor's affiliates", "winery status", "average appellation status over prior 3 years", "vineyard status", "organizational status"]
definition: Wineries acquire their status by affiliating with appellations of a given position in the overarching status hierarchy. The status hierarchy itself arises from the pattern of cross-regional affiliations that wineries engage in through the appellation designations they place on their labels.

name: Status of bottle affiliation
authors_terms: ["bottle status", "status of the appellation listed on the bottle", "the status of a given bottle's affiliation", "high-status affiliation"]
definition: A bottle's status in year t simply derives from the most recently measured status score of the appellation with which the bottle is affiliated.

name: Past quality
authors_terms: ["past demonstrations of quality", "past quality", "average quality of wine over prior 3 years", "reputation"]
definition: The quality of past offerings certainly provides one source of expectations. A vineyard's past quality was operationalized as the average quality of all bottles of wine reported for the winery over the three prior years, a moving three-year window.

name: Market rewards
authors_terms: ["rewards in the market", "wine price", "price", "the price that a winery commands for a particular bottle of wine"]
definition: The price that a winery commands for a particular bottle of wine, which the authors model as a function of factors at the level of the bottle, the winery, and the market environment.

name: Quality of production
authors_terms: ["quality level at which that actor chooses to produce", "investment in quality", "quality of the primary grape used in production", "quality of a particular bottle of wine", "bottle quality"]
definition: The status of an actor's affiliations may also influence the quality level at which that actor chooses to produce, assessed in two stages: the quality of the raw material (the primary grape used) and the perceived quality of the final bottle of wine.

name: Alliance performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["Alliance Performance", "past alliance performance", "prior alliance performance", "alliance performance relative to the firm's aspiration levels"]
definition: The performance of previous products a firm has launched through alliances, relative to the firm's aspiration levels. It blends social and historical comparisons: the product's performance is compared with the industry average and alliance NPIs' performance is compared with the firm's independent NPIs' performance.

name: Subsequent make-or-ally choice
authors_terms: ["Subsequent Independent NPI", "Subsequent NPI independence", "make-or-ally choice", "Alliance to Independence", "switch to independent operations"]
definition: A firm's subsequent choice between continuing to ally with other firms and switching to independent operations for a new product introduction. An aircraft project undertaken by a single prime contractor is classified as an independent NPI, whereas alliance NPIs include those in which at least two firms carried out the tasks related to market research, product design, manufacturing, and sales.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: The intensity of competition in a firm's area of business at the time of product introduction; competition becomes more intense when the number of firms in a business area rises.

name: Breakthrough performance
definition: Significantly better performance than the industry average; not merely satisfactory performance and incremental improvement, but extraordinary performance vis-à-vis peers.

name: Google blockade
authors_terms: ["China's unexpected blockade of Google", "the blockade of Google", "blockade of Google", "China X blockade of Google"]
definition: On June 1, 2014 all direct visits from China to Google services worldwide were suddenly blocked, with no prior notice and no explanation given; the blockade lasted more than 5 years and remained in force.

name: Technological search distance
definition: Technological distance refers to the extent of search among distant disciplines and technological fields; it captures how widely one explores distant knowledge fields for an invention.

name: Cognitive search distance
definition: Cognitive distance is the extent of search among knowledge that is not noticeable to inventors; it refers to the extent to which inventors searched for knowledge with low visibility.

name: Inventor network
authors_terms: ["inventor network", "inventor collaboration networks", "social collaboration networks", "social collaboration network accessible to the inventor team"]
definition: The size of the social collaboration network accessible to the inventor team, an offline knowledge channel through which inventors can access distant knowledge and which functions as a transactive memory of 'who knows what'.

name: Proximity to science
authors_terms: ["proximity to science", "technological fields that are proximate to science", "distance to science"]
definition: The proximity of a technological field to science, capturing a technological field's reliance on science as knowledge inputs; a higher value represents a closer link to science.

name: Complementarity of top management team functional backgrounds
authors_terms: ["complementarity", "complementary top management teams", "complementary backgrounds", "differences in functional backgrounds", "complementary (i.e., dissimilar) competencies"]
definition: In this paper complementarity has been interpreted in terms of differences in functional backgrounds. Having different sets of functional backgrounds that supplement one another can create synergy because deficiencies in one firm can be offset by strengths in the other firm.

name: Postacquisition performance
definition: The postacquisition performance of the consolidated organization was chosen as the dependent variable; the analyses were conducted using accounting measures of performance, measured as the ROA averaged for a period of 3 years immediately following the acquisition.

name: Top management team turnover in the acquired firm
authors_terms: ["TMT turnover", "top management team turnover", "turnover among the acquired firm top management team"]
definition: The mediating variable is the TMT turnover in the acquired firm, measured as the proportion of change in the TMT between the time of the acquisition and 3 years after the acquisition. High turnover in the acquired firm's management will adversely affect the postacquisition performance of the organization.

name: Acquisition type
definition: Related acquisitions entail acquiring businesses that build on, draw strength from, and enlarge some central strength or competence; both financial and operational synergy can be realized in related acquisitions, whereas the likelihood of realizing operational synergy is limited in unrelated acquisitions. Firms were classified as related if the two firms belonged to the same dominant 2-digit SIC group at the time of the acquisition, and unrelated otherwise.

name: Benefits from information asymmetry
authors_terms: ["information asymmetry", "benefits from information asymmetry", "source of benefits", "client-relatedness"]
