definition: Generally, service sellers have more information than buyers do about the quality of their services, and this asymmetry complicates the buyers' choice. Diversified service firms can gain a competitive advantage by meeting multiple needs of existing satisfied buyers, so these benefits arise from sources outside the firm, i.e., the buyers.

name: Economies of scope
definition: Economies of scope arise when the joint cost of producing two or more outputs is less than the sum of the costs of producing each output by itself. Such cost benefits may arise when businesses share some unique factor of production, whether a management or distribution system, a product or process technology, or a plant and equipment.

name: Service characteristics
authors_terms: ["service characteristics", "search services", "experience services", "search, experience, and credence qualities"]
definition: The extent of information asymmetry varies with service characteristics, which can be examined by differentiating services in terms of three attributes: search, experience, and credence qualities. Although each service is composed of a mix of these qualities, for most services one attribute dominates, and it is sufficient here to distinguish search services from experience and credence services.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance effects of diversification moves are assessed by 'the impact of an event on a firm's common stock value by measuring the difference between actual and expected stock returns during a specific time period surrounding an event'.

name: Female founder
definition: Gender is a multilevel system of broadly held cultural beliefs regarding appropriate behavior for women and men that is enacted by individuals and is manifested in everyday interactions as well as in societal-level processes. All applicants were asked to state their gender, and female gender was coded as 1 for applicants self-identifying as female and 0 for male.

name: Commercial activity
definition: An increasing number of social ventures engage in commercial activity to financially sustain their operations, thereby diverging from the traditional charity model. Our dependent variable, commercial activity, is a five-point scale that measures the degree to which a venture uses commercial activity.

name: Community female business ownership
authors_terms: ["community female business ownership", "female business owners", "proportion of female business owners", "presence of female business owners"]
definition: The presence of female business owners within a local community; female business owners are uniquely situated at the intersection of local communities and the business sector and may influence cultural beliefs about gender within these communities.

name: Serial sales process
authors_terms: ["serial sales process", "serial sales system", "liner/closer system", "turnover system", "serial process"]
definition: Other dealerships have what the industry calls a 'liner/closer' or 'turnover' system, which is what I am calling a serial sales process. Each customer first meets a 'liner'-typically a less experienced salesperson-who discusses the car with the customer, takes her on test drives, and finally begins the negotiation; if the liner is having trouble with the sale, he can call over a 'closer' to finish the negotiation.

name: Negotiated price
definition: One factor determining whether a vendor or customer captures the value from a transaction is the price. If the price is very close to the maximum the customer is willing to pay, he or she gets very little value from the transaction, leaving the lion's share to the seller.

name: Customer transaction cost
definition: She can choose to leave f1 to buy at the other dealer, f2, and incur the pseudo-switching cost t_j, where c > t_j > 0 of having to leave and travel to the other dealership. Dealers believe the serial sales system makes it more difficult for customers to leave the dealership, which could be thought of as inducing a psychic pseudo-switching cost.

name: Dealership outside option
definition: Each dealership's outside option of represents its expected profit if it did not sell the car to the current customer. The lower bound is her outside option because she would not participate in the group if she could do better outside of it.

name: Appropriation factor
definition: In cooperative games, bargaining ability is represented through the appropriation factor of the firm, which represents the firm's preferences over cores. Typically, they are thought of as the point within the core at which the firm believes the final price will fall after the unmodeled bargaining.

name: Customer bargaining ability
definition: Zettelmeyer et al. (2006) showed that customers who do not use the Internet in their vehicle search are worse bargainers. This suggests that use of the Internet for price research seems to result in greater bargaining ability in a value-based strategy sense.

name: Idling cost of closers
authors_terms: ["idling cost", "extra staffing cost", "slack labor requirement", "cost in unallocated labor"]
definition: The disadvantage of the serial sales system is that it requires these skilled salespeople to be available when a liner needs them. This slack labor requirement results in extra cost, which is why the serial sales system is not always the better choice; the cost in unallocated labor that dealers described as the drawback of the serial sales system is represented by k.

name: Contracting
definition: Organizational boundaries describe which activities are conducted within a firm's hierarchy and which activities are conducted outside the hierarchy with market or other types of relationships; the study highlights contracts and internalization as alternative organizational boundaries. Contracting is represented by dichotomous variables that indicate whether contracting for a function was an important organizational arrangement employed by a firm.

name: Economic performance
definition: We used two accounting-based measures of performance: Sales and Net Income. Sales represents the revenues generated from the sales of a firm's products and services. Net Income is the firm's revenues minus its costs, including taxes as costs.

name: Technological intensity
definition: Technological innovativeness is likely to affect the desirability of internalization over contracts because when more valuable holdings of R&D know-how exist the transaction costs of contracts, especially R&D contracts, will be exacerbated. R&D intensity was measured with a firm's annual spending on R&D.

name: Vertical market focus
authors_terms: ["vertical market focus", "vertical markets strategy", "focus strategy", "vertical markets"]
definition: This strategy is commonly exhibited in the computer industry in the form of a vertical market focus. 'Vertical markets' refers to specific industrial niches for computer products, and the breadth of these niches varies considerably.

name: Customized service
authors_terms: ["customized service", "customized service strategy", "customizing of a firm's products"]
definition: One type of service that may influence contract performance is the customizing of a firm's products. This is because customizing products may result in the development of know-how and other assets that are highly specialized to a firm-customer relationship.

name: Administrative reorganization
definition: Administrative reorganization, the dependent variable, was viewed as the adjusting of administrative duties in response to various contextual configurations. The study focused on more radical changes, such as task reassignments requiring title changes and the addition or deletion of positions.

name: Organizational age
definition: Older organizations have established formal and informal relationships both internally and externally, a condition that fosters behaviors guided by institutionalized norms and habit. The traditionalism and established relationships associated with old age can inhibit reactions to changing size, resulting in a decreased propensity for structural change.

name: Organizational size
definition: Size was operationally defined as the number of students each school had in 1969. Enrollment is a major resource base for colleges and universities.

name: Change in size
authors_terms: ["change in size", "growth or decline", "proportional change in size"]
definition: Change in size (growth or decline) was operationally defined as the proportional change in the number of full-time equivalent students between 1969 and 1974.

name: Life cycle configuration
authors_terms: ["life cycle stages", "life cycle configurations", "contextual configurations", "configurations of context"]
definition: Typically, organizational age, size, and growth or decline (change in size) are among the characteristics that define life cycle stages. Studies of such configurations of context can resolve some of the extant theoretical and research contradictions, because configurations of context influence managerial decision making and organizational structure.

name: Frequency of VC-CEO interaction
authors_terms: ["frequency of VC-CEO interaction", "frequency of interaction", "intensity of VC-CEO interaction"]
definition: The frequency of interaction between a venture capitalist and a venture's CEO, measured across face-to-face, telephone, and written modes of contact.

name: Management ownership
authors_terms: ["management ownership", "management's ownership of a venture", "management ownership level"]
definition: The share of a venture's equity held by its managers. Agency theory suggests venture capitalists will see managers who own small shares of their firms as posing greater agency risks than those holding larger shares.

name: Goal congruence
authors_terms: ["goal congruence", "VC-CEO goal congruence", "congruence between the goals of a lead investor and a venture's CEO"]
definition: The congruence between the goals of a lead investor and a venture's CEO, captured by how similarly the two parties weight financial and nonfinancial objectives.

name: CEO new venture experience
authors_terms: ["CEO's new venture experience", "CEO venture experience", "start-up experience"]
definition: A CEO's prior experience launching and building new ventures, ranging from no prior new venture experience to having previously founded or co-founded a venture.

name: Venture stage of development
authors_terms: ["stage of a venture's development", "financing stage", "stage of venture development"]
definition: The stage of a venture's development, identified with the vocabulary used in Pratt's Guide to Venture Capital Sources, ranging from seed financing to bridge-acquisition.

name: Technical innovation
authors_terms: ["technical innovation", "level of innovation being pursued", "degree of innovation"]
definition: The extent to which a venture is pursuing technical innovation relative to competitors in terms of product design, process technology, and R&D spending.

name: Venture-level uncertainty
definition: In the context of the VC industry, uncertainty at the venture level is manifested as VC firms' challenges in accurately estimating the investment returns from investing in the ventures; the key venture-level uncertainty concerns the target venture's prospects, and it is greater the earlier the venture's investment stage is.

name: Country-level uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty at the country level relates to the institutional environments with which organizations interact and by which they are affected, and it is high when the rule of law, contractual enforcement, and investor protection are weak.

name: International experience in managing venture-level uncertainty
authors_terms: ["international experience in managing venture-level uncertainty", "experiential venture-level learning", "early-stage experience"]
definition: This dimension of a VC firm's international experience reflects the knowledge stock that the firm has accumulated by investing in early-stage ventures in non-domestic countries.

name: International experience in managing country-level uncertainty
authors_terms: ["international experience in managing country-level uncertainty", "country-level international experience"]
definition: This dimension of a VC firm's international experience reflects the knowledge stock that it has accumulated by investing in foreign countries with high country-level uncertainty.

name: International experience in the host country
authors_terms: ["international experience in the host country", "host country-specific experience", "host-country experience"]
definition: This variable reflects firms' knowledge of and experience with prior ventures in the focal host country.

name: Partnering with local VC firms
authors_terms: ["partnering with local VC firm(s)", "partnering with local firms", "syndication with local VC firms"]
definition: A multilayered decision in which, having decided to enter a foreign market and to partner, the firm must choose with whom to partner: partnering with at least one local VC firm in the foreign venture, rather than investing alone or only with other foreign VC firms.

name: International diversification
authors_terms: ["international diversification", "level of international diversification", "international dispersion and embeddedness"]
definition: International diversification reflects the extent to which an MNC depends on, interacts with, and is embedded in the current GBE. The authors adopted the entropy measure of international diversification to measure an MNC's level of international dispersion and embeddedness.

name: Short-term performance
definition: We measured MNCs' immediate performance after the September 11 attacks using their cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) on shares. We consider MNCs' performance in two stages-inmediately after and one year after an exogenous shock.

name: Long-term performance
definition: We measured long-term MNC performance after the September 11 attacks using the firm's q-ratio for 2002. Tobin's q is a future-oriented and riskadjusted capital-market measure of performance that reflects both current and anticipated profitability.

name: Absorption speed
authors_terms: ["absorption speed", "speed of absorption", "speed of external knowledge absorption", "speed of knowledge absorption"]
definition: We define absorption speed as the time it takes for the organization to assimilate and apply external knowledge in its own knowledge production. It is the inward-looking, pace dimension of absorptive capacity.

name: Technological distance
authors_terms: ["Technological distance", "technological distance", "distance between the externally acquired knowledge and the firm's knowledge base"]
definition: The technological distance between the firm's knowledge base and the acquired external knowledge: firms that acquire technologically distant knowledge have limited prior related in-house knowledge, which makes learning difficult. It is measured by the patent class connected to the licensed technology and the technology classes in which the licensee was active prior to the licensing event.

name: Intrafirm inventor task network diversity
authors_terms: ["Intrafirm inventor task network diversity", "task network diversity", "network diversity"]
definition: Task network diversity refers to the diversity of technical expertise available in the task relationship network among inventors. In our context, it refers to the variety of relevant areas of technological expertise of the inventors collaborating on the inventive task within the firm.

name: Intrafirm inventor task network density
authors_terms: ["Intrafirm inventor task network density", "inventor task network density", "network density"]
definition: Density captures the extent to which potential linkages within a network are realized, and is a commonly used measure of network structure. Dense (or cohesive or closed) networks are comprised of closely interconnected members, and therefore, allow for better tacit coordination.

name: Paradigm-changing innovation
authors_terms: ["paradigm-changing innovations", "paradigm-changing technologies", "paradigm-changing technology patents", "factor-substituting innovations", "factor-substituting innovations"]
definition: Innovative efforts that focus on replacing the input with another (e.g., inventing a process or product that runs on solar energy rather than oil). Given the magnitude, range, and type of efforts involved in factor substitution of a key input, the authors describe such efforts as paradigm-changing innovations, which are akin to developing a new technological paradigm.

name: Paradigm-deepening innovation
definition: Innovative efforts that focus on using the input more efficiently (e.g., inventing processes or products that use less oil), which help perpetuate the existing paradigm. Factor-saving innovations may be described as paradigm-deepening innovations.

name: Input-relatedness
authors_terms: ["input-relatedness", "related diversification", "relatedness of a firm's businesses", "factor-market diversification"]
definition: The similarity of resources used by a firm's different businesses; this resource similarity, or input-relatedness, forms a key basis for realizing economies of scope. The authors conceptualize businesses to be related when they share similar inputs and production processes.

name: Oil dependence
authors_terms: ["Total oil dependence", "overall dependence on oil", "oil dependence"]
definition: A firm's overall dependence on oil as an input, built from the IO table and TRINET data as the sales-weighted sum of the industry-specific oil dependence of the four-digit industries in which the firm operates.

name: ISO 9000 adoption
definition: ISO 9000 is a set of international standards for the development of quality management systems. ISO 9000 certification means that an organization has established appropriate process procedures and management control mechanisms in various organizational functions.

name: CEO total cash compensation
definition: Total cash compensation is an ex post measure that rewards a CEO for his current performance and reinforces the appropriate results he has achieved. Large U.S. corporations usually pay their CEOs short-term cash compensation, which comprises salaries and bonuses.

name: CEO stock options
definition: Stock options are an ex ante measure that aims to align executives' future interest with increases in shareholders' wealth in the long term.

name: Firm performance
definition: Return on assets (ROA), measured as operating income (before depreciation, interest, and taxes) divided by total assets, is the most widely used firm performance variable in organization research, particularly for the manufacturing industry.

name: Bribery activity
definition: Supply-side bribery, whereby firms attempt to gain advantages by inducing public officials to misuse their position or authority; active bribery originates on the supply side as a strategic influence mechanism and involves firms engaging public officials using the temptation of payments as a method of influence and coercion. The measure is based on managerial self-reports regarding firm bribery activity and its frequency, focused on bribery occurring within a firm's home country.

name: Achievement orientation
definition: An achievement orientation has been considered a fundamental determinant of self-worth that is based on reaching certain goals, and the GLOBE performance orientation items measure the extent to which a society 'encourages and rewards group members for performance improvement and excellence.'

name: In-group collectivism
definition: As cultures emphasize values rooted in belongingness within larger groups, tribes, and even nations, a society becomes increasingly collectivist; the GLOBE measure focuses on collective beliefs that a group's members should take pride in one another's work and accomplishments, tapping group cohesiveness and loyalty.

name: Humane orientation
definition: A humane orientation concerns relationships and the ways people treat one another, defined as 'the degree to which an organization or society encourages and rewards individuals for being fair, altruistic, friendly, generous, caring, and kind to others.'

name: Welfare socialism
authors_terms: ["welfare socialism", "extent of welfare socialism", "social welfare policies"]
definition: Polities with more social welfare structures isolate individuals and firms from the 'vicissitudes of the market' and help prevent a 'self-serving economic system where everyone looks out for his/her own interests'; in countries dominated by welfare socialism, firms strive to meet societal goals rather than the more individualistic, self-interested goals that predominate in the absence of welfare socialist policies.

name: Political constraints
definition: Governmental 'checks and balances' in the form of regulations that are imposed to limit and constrain the powers of politicians and lawmakers; the index assesses the existence and strength of veto power in a nation's political system and the distribution of office holders with various political preferences over and within government branches.

name: Financial constraints
authors_terms: ["perceived financial constraints", "managerial assessment of financial constraints", "firm financial constraints"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's decision makers perceive that financial constraints are blocking goal achievement; measured as managerial assessment of the extent to which respondents believed financial issues obstructed firm growth and development.

name: Competitive intensity
authors_terms: ["perceived competitive intensity", "managerial assessment of competitive intensity", "competitive intensity"]
definition: The rivalry a firm encounters, assessed as the perceived number of significant competitors in the firm's primary strategic group; the WBES instrument asked managers to evaluate the number of significant rivals their firms regarded as viable competitive threats in their major product categories.

name: CEO prevention focus
definition: Someone high in prevention focus will pursue goals based on a striving toward their 'ought self' or who they 'should' be based on a sense of duty and responsibility. A prevention focus is associated with the desire to ensure correct rejections, avoid committing errors, and the tendency to view situations in a loss/non-loss frame.

name: CEO promotion focus
definition: Someone high in promotion focus will pursue goals based on a striving toward ' ideals ' or what ' could ' be. A promotion focus is associated with a desire to ensure hits, insure against errors of omission, and the tendency to view situations in a gain/non-gain frame.

name: Engagement in governance-oriented initiatives
authors_terms: ["engagement in governance-oriented initiatives", "governance-oriented stakeholder strategies", "governance-oriented initiatives"]
definition: Governance-oriented stakeholder strategies reflect an agency logic, emphasizing accountability to shareholders and the avoidance of costs associated with the separation of ownership and control; they focus on adopting an array of agency-derived governance prescriptions, including limiting top management compensation, increasing decision-making transparency, and managing risks through strong governance structures.

name: Engagement in socially-oriented initiatives
authors_terms: ["engagement in socially-oriented initiatives", "socially-oriented stakeholder strategies", "socially-oriented initiatives"]
definition: Socially-oriented stakeholder strategies reflect a broader stakeholder logic to promote positive social and environmental wellness initiatives usually tied to a wider breadth of stakeholders, such as engaging in corporate philanthropy, showing concern for employee and consumer welfare beyond what is required by law, and prioritizing environmental sustainability.

name: Receptivity to governance-oriented activism
authors_terms: ["receptivity to governance-oriented activism", "receptivity to governance-oriented stakeholder activism"]
definition: Governance-oriented activism encompasses issues raised by stakeholders that are geared toward encouraging management to adopt certain governance policies and practices; the overall intention usually being to improve firm governance for the benefit of its shareholders. Prior research has used accommodation, voting, and challenge to represent decreasing levels of receptivity to a proposal.

name: Receptivity to socially-oriented activism
authors_terms: ["receptivity to socially-oriented activism", "receptivity to socially-oriented stakeholder activism"]
definition: Socially-oriented activism encompasses issues brought forth by stakeholders that are geared toward encouraging management to adopt certain policies and practices related to environmental, community, consumer, or employee well-being. Prior research has used accommodation, voting, and challenge to represent decreasing levels of receptivity to a proposal.

name: Macroeconomic uncertainty
definition: Unexpected variations in gross domestic product (GDP) growth rates and other macroeconomic magnitudes in the host country. Firms prefer to enter markets with low levels of macroeconomic uncertainty because such variation makes it difficult to plan and manage foreign market entries.

name: Policy instability
authors_terms: ["policy instability", "policymaking discretion", "policy risk", "lack of institutional constraints on the executive branch of government", "governmental policymaking discretion free from institutional constraints"]
definition: The concept of 'policy instability' refers to the likelihood that the government might change the rules of the game in a way that adversely affects the interests of the foreign entrant. Governments differ in the discretion they enjoy in decision making, so that a lack of institutional constraints on the executive branch reduces the credibility of commitments and increases policy instability.

name: Foreign market entry
authors_terms: ["foreign entries", "entries into Latin American countries", "foreign market entries", "number of entries"]
definition: The occurrence of firm entries into specific foreign countries, counted in each firm-country-year; entries are foreign direct investments that entail effective involvement of the firm in the management of a regulated service in a Latin American country.

name: Partial state ownership
authors_terms: ["partial state ownership", "partially owned by the state", "partially privatized SOEs", "partial privatization", "firms partially owned by the state"]
definition: Ownership in which the state holds a stake in the equity of the company, that is, firms that have been partially privatized. The authors contrast these firms with firms wholly owned by the state and with fully privatized, publicly listed firms.

name: Foreign experience
authors_terms: ["experience in foreign countries", "previous firm entries in Latin America", "foreign experience", "previous foreign experience"]
definition: The firm's accumulated experience of foreign expansion, measured through the number of previous entries into Latin American countries made by the company as of the end of the previous year.

name: Self-asserted comparison
definition: Self-asserted comparison refers to the situation where a focal firm compares itself with a target firm in a given product market, but consumers do not consider these firms as comparable in that market.

name: Self-dismissed comparison
definition: Self-dismissed comparison is where a focal firm does not compare itself with a target firm in a given product market, but consumers consider the two firms as comparable.

name: Relative reputation
authors_terms: ["relative reputation", "reputation of the target firm", "third-party evaluations of an automaker's product quality"]
definition: We focus on the relative reputation between a focal firm and a target firm; the variable relative reputation is created by subtracting a focal firm's reputation from a target firm's reputation, so a positive score indicates that the target firm is more reputable than the focal firm.

name: Competitive action volume
authors_terms: ["relative volume of competitive actions", "competitive actions", "competitive action"]
definition: Common competitive actions include aggressive advertising campaigns or marketing activities, and introducing new products against specific rivals. The relative volume of competitive actions is operationalized by subtracting the target firm's volume of competitive actions from the focal firm's volume of competitive actions.

name: Relative sales growth
authors_terms: ["focal firm's sales growth relative to a target firm's", "relative sales growth", "sales growth relative to the target firm"]
definition: When comparing two firms, we consider relative sales growth an important market outcome for competitive comparison. After we acquired each firm's sales growth, we subtracted the target firm's sales growth from the focal firm's to see relative sales growth.

name: Civic activism
definition: The authors distinguish within-the-system civic activism, private and individual actions channeled through formalized state complaint processes, from outside-the-system civic activism, protests that are contentious collective actions occurring in public; they refer to both together as environmental activism, which directs government attention to environmental issues.

name: Environmental complaints
definition: Within-the-system civic activism: private, individual complaints that citizens send through the formalized complaint processes set up by the state, which convey citizens' grievances to officials and provide feedback to the state.

name: Environmental protests
definition: Outside-the-system civic activism: contentious, collective actions involving more than one participant and occurring in public or in meetings open to the public, which deviate from the institutional arrangements set up by the state, draw public attention, and exert public pressure on the government.

name: Government bureaucratic capacity
authors_terms: ["government's bureaucratic capacity", "governmental bureaucratic capacity", "bureaucratic (or administrative) capacity"]
definition: The ability of a government to implement its functions; the authors' measure assesses the protection of property rights, the effectiveness of judicial systems, and the efficiency of public administration.

name: Media development
definition: The development of traditional and new media resulting from governmental deregulation, increased privatization of media firms and platforms, commercialization, and market competition; it describes a process in which the government is still involved in the media and is not the same as media independence.

name: Environmental penalty severity
definition: The level of severity of the administrative punishments that local environmental protection bureaus give to firms that violate environmental law, ranging from a warning requiring mandatory treatment and a fine to an operation suspension for rectification.

name: Interpersonal cultural heterogeneity
definition: By interpersonal heterogeneity we refer to misalignment in cultural perceptions among the individuals who make up the organization. Organizations exhibit greater interpersonal heterogeneity when their members diverge from one another in describing the culture.

name: Intrapersonal cultural heterogeneity
definition: By intrapersonal heterogeneity we mean the breadth of cultural beliefs to which those individuals subscribe. Organizations exhibit greater intrapersonal heterogeneity when their members have access to and draw from a more diverse cultural toolkit.

name: Capacity for efficient execution
authors_terms: ["capacity for efficient execution", "capacity for effective execution", "profitability"]
definition: We propose that interpersonal heterogeneity will weaken an organization's coordination and cohesion and will therefore undermine its capacity for effective execution. We link the capacity for efficient execution to firms' profitability, as measured by return on assets (ROA).

name: Capacity for creativity and innovation
authors_terms: ["capacity for creativity and innovation", "capacity for creativity", "creativity and innovation"]
definition: Because creativity and innovation stem from the recombination of previously unrelated ideas, a wide cultural toolkit should-all else equal-be conducive to individual creativity. Organizations whose members draw on broader cultural toolkits tend to exhibit a greater capacity for creativity and innovation.

name: Invention importance
definition: Importance measures the magnitude of the economic value of an invention.

name: Invention radicalness
definition: Radicalness measures the degree to which an invention, however large or small in economic value, differs from previous inventions in the field.

name: Patent scope
authors_terms: ["patent scope", "scope of the patent", "breadth of the protection of the technology"]
definition: Patent scope measures the breadth of intellectual property protection for the invention, however large or small its economic value, and however similar or different the invention is to previous inventions in the field.

name: New firm formation
authors_terms: ["firm formation", "commercialized through the establishment of a new firm", "the formation of a new firm"]
definition: The commercialization of an invention through the establishment of a new firm. The dependent variable was coded 1 in the year that the patent was first licensed if the patent was licensed to an (unincorporated) individual or was licensed to a firm that was incorporated after the patent application was submitted.

name: CSR engagement
definition: CSR refers to corporate actions, not required by law, that attempt to further some social good and extend beyond the explicit transactional interests of the firm. The authors treat CSR as an important element of strategic investment and as a form of reputation building or maintenance.

name: Short-term CSR engagement
definition: Short-term CSR engagement is proxied by the adjusted KLD score of the firm in the year in question.

name: Long-term CSR engagement
definition: Long-term CSR engagement is the average long-term CSR engagement of firm i in year t, where the specification assumes that the effects of long-term CSR engagement are progressively reduced over a three-year period, with greater weight placed on more recent observations to balance responsiveness versus stability.

name: Insurance-like effect
definition: The term insurance-like effects refers to the ways in which, on the occurrence of a negative event relating to the corporate operations of a firm, CSR engagement can reduce any potential impact on its stock price. Engagement in CSR can be regarded as an insurance premium that the firm pays to avoid, or reduce, any loss of market value as a result of such negative events.

name: Repetition of negative events
definition: The authors argue that repeated negative events will deplete a firm's moral capital; thus, when negative events occur repeatedly, the firm's moral capital is reduced, as is the CSR protection arising from such moral capital.

name: Goodness of ideas
authors_terms: ["goodness of ideas", "good ideas", "ability to generate good ideas", "idea score"]
definition: Following Amabile's consensual approach, ideas are considered 'good' when multiple expert observers within the organization agree that they are; good ideas should be ones that are consistently evaluated as 'good' by expert observers.

name: Network constraint
definition: Constraint on an individual is high if his or her communication partners normally talk directly to each other or if they transfer information indirectly via a shared contact. Network constraint is a summary measure that captures the extent to which a focal actor bridges connections who do not talk to each other.

name: Attention allocation
authors_terms: ["attention allocation", "divided attention", "focused attention", "attention to ties' information"]
definition: Attention allocation indicates the extent to which a focal actor divides his or her attention to information coming from across all communication partners. A high Herfindahl score indicates divided attention while a low score indicates focused attention.

name: Tie strength
definition: Tie strength refers to the extent to which a focal actor communicates with his or her colleagues frequently and feels emotionally close with them.

name: Returning family succession
authors_terms: ["Type-R succession", "returning family successions", "return to a family CEO"]
definition: We designate these as ' Type-R ' successions to denote the return to a family CEO after a period of professional leadership.

name: Firm performance
definition: To measure financial performance, that is, the dependent variable in our regression analysis, we employ the ratio of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization scaled by total assets (ROA), trimming 1% of observations in the extreme right and left tail of the distribution to reduce the risk of outliers.

name: Industry volatility
authors_terms: ["industry volatility", "industry turbulence", "turbulence in the firm's industry", "volatility of industry revenues"]
definition: Our arguments suggest that the performance effect of Type-R successions is negatively moderated by industry volatility; turbulent industry conditions have been shown to put a premium on novel and very different kinds of products, and may make longer-term orientations and relationships less feasible.

name: Reliance on innovative inputs
definition: In some companies, the reliance on state-of-the-art, cutting-edge technical inputs and related administrative talents may become more important than family values, reputation and legacy, again making Type-R successions less valuable. This is likely to be the case for firms where, prior to his/her departure, the professional CEO has significantly invested in advanced, knowledge-intensive projects, that is, those demanding ample research and development (R&D) expenditures.

name: Employee satisfaction
definition: Employee satisfaction captures the degree to which an employee is content with their job at the firm. The authors use the publicly available, employee-supplied overall job satisfaction rating of the firm on Glassdoor as a new and specific form of public stakeholder assessment.

name: CEO compensation
definition: The authors examine CEO compensation through the bonuses paid to CEOs, because research suggests that relative to equity-based compensation, nonfinancial performance metrics such as employee satisfaction ratings are most likely to be weighted in the CEO's contract through bonus payments.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: The ultimate test of whether a board concludes a CEO is performing acceptably is the CEO's retention or dismissal; dismissal equals one if the CEO was fired and zero otherwise.

name: Human capital intensity
authors_terms: ["Human Capital Intensity", "human capital intensity", "reliance on human capital"]
definition: Human capital should be more important to the firm, and thus more influential in informing a CEO's evaluation, when the firm's strategy relies more on generating intangible assets. The authors argue that firms that rely on highly skilled labor will likely need to furnish employees with higher compensation, leading to higher costs per employee hired relative to firms employing low-skilled labor.

name: Board-level CSR committee
definition: Establishing a board-level CSR committee provides a visible signal of a firm's integration of stakeholder considerations and a public means by which the board can let investors know the firm and its board are considering stakeholder concerns.

name: Firm reputation
definition: The authors gauge firm reputation using Fortune Magazine's 'Most Admired Companies' list, an independent and publicly available measure that appears to capture the construct 'corporate reputation'. High-reputation firms are held to higher standards and more is expected of them.

name: Organizational size
definition: We construe organizational size as an important source of structural complexity and variability that reorders otherwise similar organizations on the core-periphery dimension. We measured organizational size as scale of operations, specifically the firm's annual production of automobiles.

name: Organizational niche width
authors_terms: ["organizational niche width", "niche width", "technological niche width", "NW", "broad niche width"]
definition: Technological niche width (NW) is defined as the range of engine capacity in horsepower across all models produced by each firm in any given year. Organizations with broad niche width are generalists in ecological theory, operating across multiple environmental states.

name: Market center stability
definition: We conceive of the organizational environment in terms of the structure of the market center, defined by the technological niches of the four largest firms in the industry. Market-center stability is a dummy variable that equals unity if the midpoint of the technological niches of the four largest firms in the market does not shift between two consecutive years.

name: Niche center change
authors_terms: ["niche-center change", "change in market position", "absolute position change", "position change"]
definition: We define change in market position as shifts in the center of a technological niche (initiated by the organization). Absolute position change (niche-center change) refers to the difference in each firm's niche midpoint between two consecutive years.

name: Rate of niche position change
authors_terms: ["rate of position change", "propensity to shift niches", "niche change rate"]
definition: We attempt to explain, first, auto firms' propensity to shift niches and, secondly, their likelihood of surviving such shifts. Absolute position change (niche-center change) refers to the difference in each firm's niche midpoint between two consecutive years.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: Organizational life histories end in a variety of ways: disbanding of the firm, exit to another industry, or merger or acquisition by another firm. The outcome event of interest in this analysis is disbanding/exit to another industry, defined to include events of unknown type.

name: Relative momentum of change
authors_terms: ["relative momentum of change", "cumulative niche-center change", "cumulative change", "prior change experience"]
definition: Because our argument refers to the relative difference in propensity to change between firms with and without prior change experience, we use the term "relative momentum of change" to describe this difference in the likelihood of undergoing internal transformation between the two sets of organizations.

name: Task complexity
authors_terms: ["task complexity", "complexity", "degree of task complexity", "number of interdependencies"]
definition: Complex task systems contain a large number of interdependent tasks. Task complexity is the number of segment pairs in the firm's portfolio that are interdependent with each other, or the number of xs in the task matrix.

name: Task decomposability
definition: A task system is highly decomposable when its tasks can be divided into discrete subsystems, with dense interdependencies within subsystems and sparse interdependencies between them. Decomposability describes the distribution pattern of interdependencies.

name: Divisionalization
definition: The degree of divisionalization measures the extent of horizontal segmentation at the lowest level of organization structure. The author defines divisionalization as the number of divisions and majority-owned subsidiaries that have no subordinate divisions or subsidiaries.

name: Organizational hierarchy
definition: The degree of hierarchy measures the extent of vertical coordination above the lowest level; the more organization units there are between the top management team and the divisions, the more hierarchical is the structure.

name: Firm equity
authors_terms: ["firm capital structure", "firm equity", "equity/sales", "equity to sales", "equity financing"]
definition: Firm capital structure can be measured in a variety of ways, normally involving some measure of equity or liabilities adjusted by some measure of size, usually by arithmetic division. Ceteris paribus, low equity to sales indicates a relatively leveraged firm, meaning that, in general, debt will be higher as equity to sales drops.

name: Sector dynamism
definition: Dynamism is defined as the rate and instability of environmental change at the sector level that results in a deficit of information needed to fully understand cause and effect relationships.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variables that we use enable us to examine two distinct measures of firm performance (profitability and productivity) that were provided or could be calculated.

name: Leverage
definition: Leverage is the proportion of debt financing in a firm's capital structure, computed as total debt (long-term debt and debt in current liabilities) divided by book value of total assets.

name: Exploitation of own prior knowledge
definition: The degree to which a firm builds on and utilizes its own prior knowledge in its innovation trajectory, captured through self-citations; self-citations represent the extent to which a firm is able to internalize the spillovers created by its own developments.

name: Suboptimal exploration
definition: Firms with a lower than median ratio of self to total citations compared to industry peers, but a higher than median stock of patents compared to industry peers (adjusted for firm size). The measure captures firms possessing strong technological capabilities that are also underutilizing these capabilities.

name: Leverage increase
definition: An increase in the firm's leverage, coded as one when the difference in debt levels as a percentage of assets was greater than 5%.

name: Firm value
definition: Firm value measured by Tobin's q, calculated as the market value of the firm divided by the book value of total assets.

name: Claim origin
definition: Claims stemmed from stakeholders who had roles that put them internal, external, or both internal and external to the organization.

name: Claim type
authors_terms: ["type of claim", "claim type", "the nature of a claim"]
definition: Analysis of the cases uncovered four types of claims, called conflict, adaptation, innovation, and performance; the type of claim which initiates decision making may influence decision making success.

name: Direction type
authors_terms: ["direction", "types of direction", "type of direction", "decision maker directions"]
definition: After stakeholders identified concerns and needs, strategic decision makers examined their claims and set directions that suggested how to respond; strategic decision makers used four types of direction to guide strategy development, called vision, problem, goal, and justification.

name: Decision making success
authors_terms: ["decision making success", "decision success", "success of a strategic decision making effort", "success indicators"]
definition: The consequences of a strategic decision making effort, measured by decision adoption, value, and development time; success can be connected to use, value, and time to complete.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack represents excess uncommitted financial resources, including cash and receivables; these financial resources are highly flexible and can be applied to a wide range of activities, thereby constituting high-discretion slack.

name: R&D investments
definition: R&D investments are investments that often entail search into unknown territories, and their outcomes are neither immediate nor certain. They are measured as R&D intensity, the ratio of R&D expenditures to total sales.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family ownership is the sum of equity ownership by family members, including founders and descendants. Founders and their family members possess a large proportion of equity ownership and serve as CEOs, chairpersons, or other members of the top management team.

name: Affiliated ownership
definition: Affiliated ownership is the sum of equity ownership by firms and financial institutions that belong to the same business group. Group-affiliated firms feature interlocking ownership structures and are able to gain access to inside information and share resources within the business group.

name: Domestic institutional ownership
definition: Domestic institutional ownership is the total percentage of equity ownership held by domestic institutional investors composed of insurance companies, securities firms, and merchant banks, which do not belong to the same group as the firm being examined.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Foreign ownership is measured as the percentage of equity ownership held by both foreign firms and foreign financial institutions. Foreign investors in emerging economies tend to be predominantly institutional investors from U.S. and European financial institutions.

name: Firm exit from an alliance
authors_terms: ["firm exit", "exit of a firm from an alliance", "member firm departing"]
definition: Firm exit refers to the decision of an individual firm to withdraw from an interfirm alliance. Similar to Greve et al. (2010), I distinguish between a member firm ceasing to be in an alliance, and project termination in which case an entire project, and thus the alliance as a whole, is brought to an end.

name: Firm entry into an alliance
authors_terms: ["firm entry", "entry into an alliance", "new firm entering an existing alliance"]
definition: Firm entry refers to a new firm entering an existing alliance to take up an ownership stake in the project.

name: Resource base of the reconfiguring firm relative to the alliance
authors_terms: ["resource base", "munificent firm", "munificent resource base", "nonmunificent resource base"]
definition: I focused on the financial resource base that each firm can bring to the table, relative to that of the other collaborating firms. Rather than relying on an absolute measure of size, which can vary widely between mining firms, I computed a relative measure specific to each alliance: I consider a firm to be 'munificent' when it holds more financial assets than the mean of the financial assets of the other collaborating firms combined.

name: Environmental dynamism
authors_terms: ["environmental dynamism", "dynamism", "dynamism in the external environment of the alliance"]
definition: The functionality or dysfunctionality of alliance partner reconfiguration is likely to be contingent on the degree of dynamic change in the task environment in which a project operates. Environmental dynamism is a time-varying covariate that captures price trend variability over the preceding 12 months for each mineral explored by the focal project.

name: Unplanned project termination
definition: I only coded as an unplanned project termination event, a mineral exploration project that was terminated during the exploration phase; i.e. a venture that was terminated before reaching the planned goal of becoming operational and turning a profit.

name: Female CEO appointment
definition: The gender of the newly appointed chief executive officer; the authors examine gender because it is one of the most salient and commonly used attributes in initial impression formation, and board chair orientations are typically adopted at the beginning of a CEO's tenure.

name: Collaboration board chair orientation
definition: The 'collaboration' board chair orientation, which consists of advising and guiding the CEO and reducing the CEO's job demands; as part of it the chair provides advice and guidance to bolster rather than control the CEO, and supports the CEO by relieving the CEO of the burdens of board leadership.

name: Control board chair orientation
definition: The 'control' board chair orientation, which consists of monitoring and overseeing the CEO; agency theorists argue the board chair must be separate from the CEO so as to monitor and control the CEO's behavior and keep it in line with shareholders' interests.

name: Female board representation
authors_terms: ["Female directors", "female board representation", "female representation on the board"]
definition: The percentage of non-CEO directors on the board who are female.

name: CEO subgroup power
authors_terms: ["CEO subgroup power", "power of the CEO subgroup", "subgroup power"]
definition: The capacity to exert the CEO subgroup's will to alter the other subgroups' attitudes and behaviors despite resistance, which stems from access to and control over valued resources.

name: CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["CEO dismissal", "CEO firing", "the board's decision to fire the CEO"]
definition: The board's decision to dismiss the CEO, which is decided at the board level and has poor firm performance as a primary predictor.

name: Firm performance decline
authors_terms: ["performance decline", "firm performance decline", "a significant drop in firm performance"]
definition: A significant drop in firm performance that can threaten corporate legitimacy and elicit negative reactions among shareholders and market observers such as stock analysts.

name: Contentious private politics
definition: Contentious private politics deploys contentious tactics against firms, such as boycotts, protests, or lawsuits, and includes all instances of an SMO contentiously targeting a firm.

name: Cooperative private politics
definition: Cooperative private politics relies on collaborations between SMOs and firms, defined as organizations working together by committing resources to achieve mutually relevant outcomes. The theoretical arguments pertain to intensive collaborations, which are focused on internal corporate processes and product development.

name: Issue materiality
definition: Material issues are movement-advocated issues interpreted by managers as related to a firm's strategic goals and performance, described as 'materially supporting' or 'materially challenging' strategic goals. SASB classifies an issue as material to a given industry if the issue can affect either the operational or financial performance of firms within that industry.

name: Green innovation
definition: Innovation is defined as a process of discovering, recombining, and integrating existing pieces of knowledge to generate new ones, and the paper measures firms' innovation on the movement-advocated climate issue with patent counts. Green patents is the number of patents applied for by a firm on a given climate issue in a year.

name: Innovation from distant recombination
authors_terms: ["green patents from distant recombination", "distant recombination", "novel innovations"]
definition: Innovations from distant recombination are patents whose combination of subclasses is new compared with all previous patents that have ever been granted until then. Novel innovations recombine disparate knowledge components and often result from firms accessing new and diverse knowledge outside the firm.

name: Local density
definition: Population density is the number of organizations in a defined population. The density that a respondent faces during his or her self-employment spell is localized in terms of both industry type and geographic location.

name: Exit hazard
definition: Exit occurs the first time that profit falls below w, the return from wage employment. This is a classic first-passage problem, in which the authors seek the distribution across firms of the time that elapses between entry and profit falling below the exit threshold, w.

name: Profit level
definition: Agents creating a business begin with profit that then evolves stochastically. The earnings of the self-employed are measured as the sum of military income, wage and salary income, and business or farm income in the previous calendar year.

name: Initial profit
definition: Prediction 4 concerns initial profits, which the authors take to be earnings in the first year of the self-employment spell. The predicted relationship between density and initial earnings is an immediate consequence of the model's assumptions.

name: Profit growth
authors_terms: ["growth rates of surviving firms", "earnings growth rate", "growth in self-employment earnings", "profit growth"]
definition: The growth rates of surviving firms over the interval (t, t+τ) conditional on profit at time t.

name: Opportunity cost of entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["opportunity cost of entrepreneurship", "opportunity cost of entrepreneurs' time", "return from wage employment", "postdissolution earnings", "outside opportunities"]
definition: w, the return from wage employment, is the opportunity cost of running the business. Greater density increases the opportunity cost of entrepreneurship because the thicker labor market provides improved outside opportunities.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership concentration", "ownership by five largest blockholders", "ownership stakes of shareholders", "ownership concentration among blockholders without regard to identity"]
definition: A measure of ownership concentration that does not distinguish shareholders' identities, equal to the percentage of a company's outstanding shares held by its five largest blockholders; it is identical to the primary measure used by Prowse (1992).

name: Financial institution ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership by financial institutions", "shareholdings of Japanese financial institutions", "ownership shares of Japanese financial institutions"]
definition: The percentage of a company's outstanding shares held by Japanese financial institutions; such shareholders are commonly also a corporation's creditors, buyers, suppliers and business partners.

name: Nonfinancial corporate ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership by nonfinancial companies", "ownership by nonfinancial corporations", "shareholdings of Japanese nonfinancial corporations"]
definition: The percentage of a company's outstanding shares held by Japanese nonfinancial companies; such shareholders are commonly also a corporation's creditors, buyers, suppliers and business partners.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The dependent variable in all equations, measured as return on assets (ROA), the ratio of net income to total assets; accounting-based measures such as ROA are preferable in studies relating ownership structure to financial performance because stock market returns are expected to adjust for divergences between shareholders and managers.

name: Prior profitability
definition: A firm's profitability in the previous period, entered in the redistribution model as the lagged dependent variable; the authors assumed a one-period lag, and the lower the coefficient on this term, the greater the redistribution effect.

name: Credibility as a defender
authors_terms: ["credible defender", "credibility", "reputation as a credible defender", "credibility as a defender", "reputation for being a credible defender"]
definition: Deterrence occurs if two conditions are met. First, the attacker must believe that the defender is willing and able to fight-what we define as a credible defender. The authors use the phrases "reputation as a credible defender" and "credibility" interchangeably.

name: Competitive attack
definition: The dependent variable, in keeping with the defender-attacker logic, is whether a given team, which we will call the attacker, reports attacking a given rival, which we will call the defender, in the current period.

name: Relative level of activity
authors_terms: ["relative magnitude of a firm's activity", "level of activity", "relative activity", "relative expense", "relative number of product introductions and modifications"]
definition: When we discuss activity, we mean any activity that could affect a competitor (cf. Porter's 1980 definition of market signals above). This could range from changing prices to filing lawsuits. Judgments of magnitudes will almost certainly be relative ones, so magnitude of activity relative to industry practice should be a strong determinant of a firm's reputation as a credible defender.

name: Consistency of activity
authors_terms: ["consistency of activity", "consistency in expense", "consistency in product introductions and modifications", "consistency of activity over time"]
definition: It also seems reasonable that not only general relative activity levels but a consistent pattern of activity over time should matter in a credibility inference. A firm that always reacts at a fairly high level should be seen as more likely to react in a given situation than a firm that often reacts at a high level, but exhibits a great deal of variability.

name: Marketplace success
definition: Successful firms will be seen as credible defenders for two reasons. First, successful firms are likely to be seen as intelligent. The second reason successful firms will be seen as credible is that successful firms typically have greater resources to expend in the future, making it more likely that they can retaliate effectively against an attacking firm.

name: Unrelated diversification
authors_terms: ["unrelated diversification", "degree of unrelated diversification", "level of unrelated diversification"]
definition: Diversification is unrelated if a firm engages in dissimilar businesses. The challenges of information complexity and HQ detachment are particularly severe in the case of unrelated diversification, where firms operate in multiple dissimilar businesses whose SBUs operate in industries with very different underlying characteristics, such as resource requirements, competencies, and market dynamics.

name: Resource allocation adjustment
authors_terms: ["degree of adjustment in resource allocation", "adjustments in resource allocation", "resource allocation adjustments", "degree of adjustments in resource allocation"]
definition: The dependent variable is a firm's degree of adjustment in resource allocation, the degree to which firms change their resource allocation to business units from year to year. Our measure captures a firm's change in its resource allocation across its four-digit SIC businesses.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism reflects the volatility and unpredictability of change in a firm's external environment. Dynamic environments are characterized by rapid, frequent, amplified, and nonlinear changes, reflecting the volatility and unpredictability of external conditions.

name: Industry competitiveness
definition: Competitive industries are characterized by a high number of firms with comparable resources and capabilities, reducing the ability to coordinate strategies.

name: Market entry experience
authors_terms: ["market entry experience", "recent experience in entering new markets", "recent market entry experience"]
definition: We focus on a particularly relevant strategic change experience for highly diversified firms, recent experience in entering new markets. Firms that enter a new industry will gain experience in creating and operating in a new business, developing the required capabilities, and allocating resources to the new business.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack refers to excess resources, both financial and human, that exceed the immediate operational needs of a firm.

name: Chief sustainability officer presence
definition: We define CSOs as those executives who take primary responsibility for corporate sustainability or issues related to corporate social performance. The authors argue that the CSO as a specialized top executive can serve as an attention carrier for all issues related to corporate social performance.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate socially responsible activities", "CSR", "CSR performance", "socially responsible activities"]
definition: The former refers to voluntary corporate actions designed to improve social conditions. Engagement in CSR activities indicates the willingness of the firm to satisfy its stakeholders' request and generates positive externality to the society.

name: Corporate social irresponsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate socially irresponsible activities", "CSiR", "CSiR performance", "socially irresponsible activities"]
definition: CSiR activities, such as labor law violation, product defects and large-scale recalls, undermine the legitimate interests of its stakeholders and violate widely accepted social norms. It pertains to 'the set of corporate actions that negatively affects an identifiable social stakeholder's legitimate claims in the long run.'

name: Sustainability committee
authors_terms: ["sustainability committee", "specialized board committee on sustainability issues"]
definition: A firm that has set up a committee specifically for sustainability issues exposes its senior executives to more frequent discussion about the importance and urgency of improving the firm's social performance. Firms may set up a board committee to focus on sustainability issues.

name: Industry culpability
definition: Certain industries, such as tobacco, gambling, and munitions, often face serious questioning about their social responsibility. Firms in these industries are under more intense scrutiny and face more social pressure.

name: Relational shocks
definition: We define relational shocks as disruptive events that change the relationships between an executive and those with whom he/she works closely. The authors consider two relational shocks that influence executive turnover: (a) outside CEO succession, and (b) when other members of the TMT exit the firm.

name: Reputational shocks
definition: Reputational shocks are specific events at the firm level that pose a threat or risk to the executives' and firm's reputations as viewed by stakeholders outside the firm.

name: Executive pay disparity
authors_terms: ["executive pay disparity", "pay disparity", "relative pay", "higher relative pay", "total pay disparity"]
definition: We focus specifically on pay disparity because within the shock perspective of turnover, it is theorized that in the face of shocks, individuals stay or leave a firm depending on whether there are significant sacrifices that individuals would have to make if they were to leave the firm. In terms of what might help an executive feel embedded, higher pay is a valuable resource that executives seek to maximize as it is an important indicator of the amount of status and social influence an executive has in the organization relative to other executives.

name: Top executive turnover
definition: Top executive turnover captures whether an individual top executive departs from his or her current firm.

name: Late mover performance
authors_terms: ["early market success", "early performance", "early market performance", "market performance of late movers", "market penetration"]
definition: The early success of a late mover in the market is reflected in its ability to penetrate the new product category, assessed first by its survival beyond the first four years and then by the market share it is able to develop shortly after entry.

name: Market opportunity
authors_terms: ["market opportunity", "market conditions at the time of entry", "entry conditions"]
definition: The performance of a late mover is likely to depend upon the conditions that it faces on entry, which reflect the extent of opportunity that may still be available in the market at the time that the late mover chooses to enter. The degree of market opportunity will depend on the number of competitors that have already entered and the extent to which they have managed to penetrate the newly created market.

name: Firm resources
definition: The prospects of early success for the late mover in the new product category depend on the availability and relevance of its resources; in particular, a firm is likely to develop a significant share of the new market if its large size and its prior experience can allow it to draw upon its considerable resources.

name: Strategic positioning
definition: The early success of a late mover in the new product category will depend on the strategic positioning that it is able to develop, and its performance will therefore be tied to the positioning of its product relative to all other firms that are already in the market.

name: Partner R&D centralization
definition: Centralization reflects where decisions are made within an organization; more centralized organizations are ones where formal decision-rights are retained closer to the 'center' of the organization. Managers leading a centralized R&D unit have decision rights across the complete portfolio of the firm's inventions and hierarchical authority over the parts of the organization working on these inventions, whereas in decentralized R&D units managers only have decision rights for the relevant sub-portfolio.

name: Startup realized inventions
definition: The outcome is characterized as the development of realized inventions, i.e., prototype applications that can potentially be commercialized. It is measured as the number of new drugs belonging to the entrepreneurial firm that enter phase 1 of clinical trials.

name: Incumbent knowledge diversity
authors_terms: ["Therapeutic Diversity Incumbent", "diversity of the corporate investor's technological expertise", "diversity of knowledge available"]
definition: The diversity of knowledge in the incumbent firm, captured as the diversification of its drug development portfolio across therapeutic classes. A more diverse knowledge base spans a broader array of domains, so the additional pathways through which knowledge can reach the startup become more valuable.

name: Startup knowledge need diversity
authors_terms: ["Therapeutic Diversity Startup", "diversity of the startup's knowledge needs"]
definition: The breadth of the application areas to which startups are attempting to direct their technologies, with a higher value indicating that a startup's pre-clinical portfolio is spread over a wider range of therapeutic areas. Startups with technologies focusing on a wider range of application areas are likely to benefit more from access to a wider array of expertise.

name: Insider CVC managers
authors_terms: ["Insider CVC Managers", "CVC managers with prior experience working in the firm in operational roles", "insiders"]
definition: CVC managers with prior experience working in the incumbent firm in operational roles (i.e., insiders) will have developed stronger informal relationships and a better understanding of the decision processes within their firms that they can employ to accelerate resource flows towards the startup.

name: Colocation with partner headquarters
authors_terms: ["HQ Colocation", "geographically collocated with the corporate investor's headquarters"]
definition: Whether the startup's and the incumbent firm's headquarters are located in the same 2 digit zip code, which roughly encompasses metropolitan areas in the US. The mechanism concerns startups leveraging the formal authority of senior executives based at the partner's corporate headquarters.

name: Top management team turnover
authors_terms: ["TMT turnover", "TMT-level turnover", "top management team turnover", "TMT churn", "collective-level turnover"]
definition: Team-level TMT turnover was measured by analyzing the rate of executive departure across a three-year time period. The number of executives who left the TMT within a three-year period were then summed and divided by the total number of executives employed by the firm during the same three-year time span.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was assessed using a rolling three-year average of return on assets (ROA). An average was utilized because it allows for the smoothing of yearly fluctuations in performance.

name: Average TMT organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["average TMT organizational tenure", "average TMT tenure", "average organizational tenure of the TMT", "average firm tenure of the TMT"]
definition: This measure was operationalized as the average organizational tenure of executives within the TMT for a given year. Organizational tenure increases firm-specific human capital in the form of greater depth and breadth of explicit and tacit knowledge.

name: Industry instability
definition: Industry instability refers to the predictability of relationships among customers, suppliers, regulatory agencies, and competitors in the environment as well as the general trends within the industry.

name: Industry munificence
definition: Industry munificence, or market growth, is a construct that refers to the level of resource abundance that exists within a firm's external environment. Munificent environments tend to be those characterized by abundant growth opportunities and fewer external threats.

name: Industry complexity
definition: Industry complexity refers to the various dimensions a firm faces in its industry with regard to the number and size of its competitors. Organizations in concentrated industries, or more monopolistic environments, are generally thought to face less complexity.

name: Firm financial strength
authors_terms: ["firm financial strength", "financial strength of the firm", "financial positions of divesting firms", "firm's financial position"]
definition: The financial position and performance of the divesting parent firm, read both against the firm's competitive group and against the firm's own prior record. The research used statistics from Standard & Poor's Industry Surveys to test hypotheses about firm financial strength.

name: Unit strength
authors_terms: ["unit strength", "unit financial strength", "unit competitive strength", "lack of strength", "low strength unit"]
definition: The strength of the business unit that is a divestment candidate, which has two facets of interest in this research: financial strength and competitive strength. Firms' managers' assessments of units' competitive positions and of their performance compared with that of other units, to that planned and to that of alternative resource uses were used as measures of unit strength.

name: Unit interdependency
authors_terms: ["unit interdependency", "interdependencies between divestment candidate units and firms' other business units", "barriers to exit"]
definition: The degree to which a business unit is tied to its firm's other business units through sharing of technology, facilities and customers and through interfirm sales and purchases. Certain characteristics of firms and their units have been suggested in the literature as creating barriers to exit through highly interdependent relationships among units.

name: General economic environment growth
authors_terms: ["general economic environment growth", "general economic conditions", "general economic cycle"]
definition: The general external economic conditions within which the firm and its units were operating at the time of the divestment decision. General economic conditions affect firms' decision-making through differences in availability and cost of credit, demand for goods and services and resulting price levels.

name: Managerial attachment
authors_terms: ["managerial attachment", "attachment between the unit and the divestment decision-maker"]
definition: The degree and nature of relationships between divestment decision-makers and business units which are divestment candidates. The greater the involvement with a unit and attachment to a unit which senior managers have, the less likely it is that those managers will be able objectively to consider that unit's divestment.

name: Divestment decision
definition: Corporate divestment can be defined as a firm's decision to dispose of a significant portion of its assets; for these purposes divestments consisted of whole business units or divisions of large diversified firms.

name: External innovation linkage breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of innovation linkages", "breadth of linkages", "linkage breadth", "openness", "breadth of plants' collaborative activity", "number of linkages"]
definition: The count of the different types of external innovation partners with which each plant was working, used as the measure of openness in external innovation linkages. Breadth raises the chance of obtaining useful external knowledge but is subject to limits arising from search costs and managers' limited attention.

name: Prior linkage breadth
authors_terms: ["prior linkages", "previous openness", "prior openness", "previous innovation linkages", "prior breadth of openness", "experience of external collaborations"]
definition: Whether, and how extensively, the plant used external innovation linkages in previous survey periods. It is used to partition current breadth between plants that had and had not undertaken external innovation linkages in a previous period.

name: Innovation output
authors_terms: ["innovation output", "innovation performance", "innovative sales", "new or improved products"]
definition: The innovation output of the plant, captured both by the importance of innovative products in the unit's sales portfolio and by the value of sales of innovative products.

name: Discontinuous increase in relational capital
authors_terms: ["discontinuous increase in the value of relational capital", "discontinuous increases", "relational capital discontinuities", "discontinuous increase"]
definition: Because the value of relational capital is tied to the resources the contact controls, sudden changes in the contact's ability to deliver these resources can provide a sudden shock to the value associated with the relationship and thereby the employee's ability to create value through it. The authors measure this by tracking changes in the power of politicians connected to lobbyists in the sample.

name: Employee exit
definition: The binary dependent variable is employee exit, coded '1' if a lobbyist's primary employer had changed since the previous period and '0' otherwise; it comprises both mobility to established firms and employee entrepreneurship.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
definition: Following the conventional definition of employee entrepreneurship, the paper codes this as '1' if a lobbyist either creates or joins a start-up after leaving a firm in the lobbying data in the previous period; employee entrepreneurship is a subset of employee exit.

name: Mobility to established firms
authors_terms: ["mobility to established firms", "employee mobility", "movements to established firms"]
definition: Employee mobility is defined as movements to established firms, i.e., exit to an existing employer as opposed to the creation of a new firm; together with employee entrepreneurship it constitutes employee exit.

name: Firm-employee knowledge distance
authors_terms: ["firm-employee distance", "firm-employee knowledge distance", "employee's distance from the firm's core knowledge", "firm-employee knowledge distance"]
definition: The measure of employee-firm distance captures an employee's location vis-a-vis the firm's location in the knowledge space. Conceptually, firm-employee knowledge distance captures whether an employee is peripheral to the firm's core value creation.

name: Stigmatizing labels
definition: Instances of labeling-based condemnation from specific social actors.
