Stigmatizing labels are a signal to a firm's economic supporters and potential investors that its legitimacy is in jeopardy - that is, that the organization's actions have deviated from the social norms, values, and expectations of relevant audiences.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: Event studies measure the effect of an unanticipated event on stock prices, where abnormal returns reflect shareholders' reactions to the availability of new information and are calculated by subtracting the expected return for the stock from its actual return.

name: Illegality-based stigmatizing content
definition: Accounts that accused arms producers of rule violations, fraud, bribery, and the leaking of secrets; labels that paint the behavior of a firm as at odds with established rules and laws and problematize its ability to conform to the regulatory demands of its environment.

name: Harm-based stigmatizing content
definition: Labels that highlight how the conduct of arms producers caused physical and social harm to stakeholders and, by extension, to society at large, emphasizing aspects such as death, killing, damage, torture, and the promotion of conflict, as well as global insecurity and instability.

name: Associative stigmatization
authors_terms: ["associative stigmatizing labels", "stigma by association", "associative stigmatization", "stigmatizing labeling by association", "unethicality (affiliates) stigma"]
definition: Condemnation directed at the economic exchange relationship between arms producers and third parties, problematizing affiliations and transactions (e.g., investing in, working for, or being sponsored by arms producers) as inappropriate and unethical.

name: Political actors
definition: Stigmatizers occupying a political subject position, comprising politicians and elected officials, who are best positioned to evaluate compliance with legal requirements and are able to conduct investigations and impose burdensome sanctions.

name: Civil society actors
definition: Stigmatizers in civil society, such as journalists, activists, and religious organizations, whose role is to editorialize and evaluate the activities of firms with respect to the overall well-being of society.

name: Financial actors
authors_terms: ["financial actors", "investors", "financial analysts", "current investors", "potential investors or customers"]
definition: Stigmatizers who are market actors, such as investors and financial analysts, who have the knowledge base and expertise required to calculate the costs and benefits of transacting with the firm.

name: Chief strategy officer presence
definition: The variable CSO presence refers to a firm's decision to have a CSO in its TMT or not. CSOs are those senior executives in the TMT who are explicitly responsible for a firm's strategy.

name: Diversification
definition: The extent of a firm's business portfolio diversification increases the complexity of strategy tasks. It concerns the degrees of related, unrelated, and total diversification of a firm's business portfolio.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: A firm's acquisition activity creates additional task demands and complexity for a firm's senior management. In firms that frequently engage in acquisitions, the TMT has a greater need to delegate these additional tasks to a specialist executive.

name: Alliance activity
definition: A firm's alliance activity requires a high level of management attention, particularly when firms maintain an alliance portfolio. Alliances, joint ventures, and other strategic partnerships between two or multiple firms are formed to develop new businesses, enter new markets, or acquire knowledge.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is among the most common determinants of organizational task demands and of strategic complexity; there is a positive relationship between a firm's size and its complexity, which may require task division and specialization from the TMT.

name: TMT role interdependence
definition: A firm's TMT role interdependence refers to the extent of information and resource sharing between TMT members as well as to the coordination within the TMT. It affects the strategic complexity of the firm.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is analyzed with two measures: an accounting-based performance measure extensively used in prior TMT research and a market-based measure reflecting the stockholders' premium placed on the firm's equity.

name: Presence of a distinct team leader
authors_terms: ["presence of a distinct leader", "distinct leader", "clear leader", "single leader"]
definition: A nascent venture needs a clear leader to moderate team discussions, decide on collective goals, and to move the venture forward; teams with a distinct leader are better at focusing their actions in a unified direction. Teams without a clear leader run the risk of straying from their entrepreneurial intents, while those with multiple leaders can be torn between the leaders who can lead the teams in different directions.

name: Educational background diversity
definition: Educational diversity leads to different cognitive styles and perspectives in the team. Having different views is beneficial as members analyze problems from multiple approaches, consider the pros and cons, and use different criteria to choose a course of action.

name: Open communication
definition: This study focuses on the degree to which members communicate openly to one another. With open communication, team members will tolerate, encourage, and engage in frank expression of views.

name: Social integration
definition: Social integration is a multifaceted phenomenon that includes social interaction, group pride, and spirit.

name: Team viability
authors_terms: ["perceptions of team viability", "perceived team viability", "team viability"]
definition: What is important for a nascent venture is that the members stay together and remain excited about the team's ideas. The two measures of effectiveness that we focus on are member perceptions of team viability and member satisfaction with the venture.

name: Member satisfaction
definition: Member satisfaction with the venture is one of the two measures of effectiveness that the authors focus on. To be consistent with past work on teams, the authors used team viability and satisfaction to represent perseverance.

name: Intrafirm collaboration network centrality
authors_terms: ["collaboration centrality", "collaboration betweenness centrality", "intrafirm collaboration betweenness centrality", "collaboration (betweenness) centrality"]
definition: The extent to which the inventor is on the shortest path connecting other colleagues who themselves are not directly connected in the intrafirm collaboration network. It reflects the relational skills and capabilities inventors need to collaborate with others and achieve a central position.

name: Intrafirm technological recombination network centrality
authors_terms: ["technological centrality", "technological betweenness centrality", "intrafirm technological betweenness centrality"]
definition: The extent to which the technological components invented by the inventor or the inventor's technological experience are on the shortest path in the recombination of other technological components in the firm's technology recombination network. Technological centrality is associated with highly specialized tacit knowledge and with expertise about the firm's combinatorial 'know-how' and 'know-why.'

name: Outward mobility to any type of new employment
authors_terms: ["mobility (any type)", "outward mobility", "move to any type of new employment"]
definition: Leaving the firm to join another employment context, that is, either joining another firm or starting a new venture.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
definition: Leaving the firm to either start or join the founding team of a new venture.

name: Mobility to another employer
authors_terms: ["mobility to another employer", "moving to another employer", "move to an existing employer"]
definition: Being recruited by another firm, i.e., leaving the focal firm to join another existing employer.

name: Voluntary turnover rates
authors_terms: ["voluntary turnover rates", "unit-level voluntary turnover", "turnover rates", "collective turnover"]
definition: Turnover rates are defined as 'aggregate levels of employee departures that occur within groups, work units, or organizations.' The authors focus on voluntary departures at the unit level and on the quantity dimension of collective turnover.

name: Transfer-out rates
definition: A within-system human capital flow through which employees transfer from a focal unit to other units of the same organization, depleting the unit's human capital resource.

name: Hiring rates
definition: A boundary-spanning process through which the unit hires new employees from outside the organization, replenishing the human capital resource.

name: Transfer-in rates
definition: A within-system process through which employees transfer into a focal unit from other units of the same organization, replenishing the unit's human capital resource.

name: Job demands
definition: Job demands capture the amount of work faced by employees; at the unit level it is a description of the required work for an average employee, quantifying the ratio of required output to human resources available in a unit.

name: Patient satisfaction
definition: Patient satisfaction is the measure of unit performance in the study, assessed through a questionnaire administered to patients immediately following their hospital stay.

name: Performance shortfall
authors_terms: ["performance shortfall", "performance below aspirations", "performance relative to aspirations", "distance from aspiration levels"]
definition: Historical comparison-based performance shortfall is thus the absolute value of the difference between current performance and current aspiration. The social comparison-based shortfall is the absolute value of the difference between the focal firm's performance and the average performance of its peer group.

name: Acquisitions
definition: Clearly, acquisitions are resource-consuming organizational changes. In an acquisition, the firm commits substantial additional financial and managerial resources to acquire a majority interest in another firm with the goal of achieving a positive performance impact.

name: Divestments
definition: Management can also opt for the opposite strategy and choose to free resources by divesting underperforming units to improve profitability. Divestment may improve short-term profitability by converting tied-up resources into liquid assets that can be reinvested into the firm's core business.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack can be understood as a resource that the organization can draw upon to implement strategic actions that it may seek to undertake and as a buffer that protects the firm from the immediate consequences of performance below aspiration levels.

name: CEO family membership
authors_terms: ["CEO family status", "family-member CEO", "family CEO", "CEO family ties", "family ties between principal and agent"]
definition: A dummy variable that took a value of 1 when the CEO belonged to the family that controlled the firm as per the authors' definition of family ties, and 0 when the CEO was not a member of the family.

name: CEO total compensation
authors_terms: ["total compensation", "total CEO pay", "CEO pay level", "CEO compensation level"]
definition: The total compensation received by the CEO, the sum of salary, bonuses, and long-term income (LTI).

name: Long-term income
definition: Long-term income, one component of CEO compensation; to control for collinearity between the amount of long-term income and total compensation level, the authors calculated a residual score for LTI, 'partialing out' the common scale effect it shared with total compensation.

name: Long-term income proportion of pay
authors_terms: ["LTI mix", "LTI as a proportion of total compensation", "percentage of long-term income in the total compensation packages"]
definition: Long-term income (LTI) as a proportion of total compensation (LTI mix).

name: Family ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of ownership in the hands of family members", "percentage of stock owned by family members (excluding the CEO)", "family ownership concentration", "percent family ownership"]
definition: The percentage of stock owned by family members, excluding the CEO.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of stock in the hands of institutional investors", "percent institutional ownership", "institutional investors", "institutional blockholders"]
definition: The percentage of stock owned by institutional investors, which included public pension funds, mutual funds, insurance companies, banks, nonbank trusts, and corporate pension funds; family trusts and/or foundations were not considered as institutional investors.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity, measured as the ratio of R&D expenditures during the 1995-98 period divided by the natural logarithm of sales.

name: Business risk
definition: Business risk is defined as variability in firms' stock market returns and is measured in two ways: as systematic and as unsystematic risk; the authors use the term business risk as a generic label that encompasses both forms of risk.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Systematic risk is the part of the variance in a firm's returns that can be explained by changes in the market, reflecting macroeconomic or industry-wide forces.

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: Unsystematic risk captures the variations in firm returns that are the result of factors specific to an organization itself, reflecting conditions unique to a firm.

name: Audience composition premium
definition: Essentially, the concept of audience composition premium captures the increase in positive evaluations due to the composition of audiences evaluating a firm. We conceptualize the 0.5 points above the total average rating in Position 1 a premium gained through an optimal composition of audiences evaluating the firm.

name: Aggregate evaluation
definition: Any aggregate evaluation that a firm receives depends on the specific group of audiences that decide to evaluate it. In the empirical context, the authors test the effect of audience composition premium on the aggregate investment recommendation a firm receives from the analysts who follow it.

name: Dispersion in audience predispositions
authors_terms: ["dispersion in audience predispositions", "the degree of dispersion in audience predispositions toward a firm"]
definition: Our proposed approach of aiming to gain a higher audience composition premium is most beneficial when there is a high degree of dispersion in audience predispositions toward a firm. Our conceptualization of dispersion in audience predispositions aims to capture a characteristic of the firm rather than a specific group of audiences.

name: Heterogeneity in engaged audiences' evaluative schemas
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in the evaluative schemas of the audiences a firm engages with", "the degree of heterogeneity in the evaluative schemas of the audiences a firm engages with"]
definition: We suggest that engaging with a group of audiences holding a moderate degree of heterogeneous evaluative schemas maximizes a firm's ability to gain an audience composition premium. Empirically, the authors measured the heterogeneity in the evaluative schemas of the audiences a firm engages with during its earnings calls by investigating the heterogeneity in broad conceptual concerns raised in the questions the firm decided to engage with during its calls.

name: Knowledge of audience evaluative schemas
authors_terms: ["the firm's knowledge and learning about its audiences and their evaluative schemas", "learning about audiences"]
definition: We propose there is a positive relationship between the heterogeneity in the evaluative schemas of the audiences that a firm engages with and the firm's knowledge and learning about its audiences and their evaluative schemas. Firms are successful in optimizing their positioning relative to their heterogeneous audiences to the extent that they learn and become cognizant of audiences' distinctive evaluative schemas.

name: Work experience
definition: Our measure of experience is the difference between the date that the focal job began and the date that the worker's first regular postcollege job began, minus any time that the worker spent out of the labor market.

name: Workplace size
definition: We measure workplace size using the question, 'How many employees worked/work for your employer at your primary job site?' Note that this question refers to establishment size rather than firm size (we did not collect data on firm size).

name: Industry occupational intensity
authors_terms: ["occupational intensity", "occupationally intensive industries", "organizations in occupationally intensive industries"]
definition: We focus on a particular characteristic of industries that affects how they use the skills of a given occupation: their occupational intensity, defined as the extent to which the industry employs workers who are members of the focal occupation. Where organizations within an industry are more dependent on the skills of a particular occupational group, they are likely to have higher demands for that group's skills.

name: Regional occupational intensity
authors_terms: ["regional occupational intensity", "regional proportion of jobs in occupationally intensive industries", "local labor markets that have a higher proportion of jobs in occupationally intensive industries"]
definition: At the labor market level, regions with a higher density of organizations within occupationally intensive industries will have higher demands, and offer greater rewards, for skills. We calculated the proportion of jobs in each MSA that were in occupationally intensive industries using secondary data, rather than our survey.

name: Turnover
definition: We analyze the determinants of turnover based on the reported end dates of jobs. Job spells that were still ongoing at the time of the survey were treated as censored spells in our event history analyses (i.e., not involving turnover).

name: Small related acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["prior experience in small, related acquisitions", "prior small related acquisition experience", "experience in small related acquisitions"]
definition: Prior experience in small, related acquisitions was calculated similarly, with prior acquisitions that were less than $100 million.

name: Large related acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["prior experience in large related acquisitions", "prior large related acquisition experience"]
definition: Prior experience in large related acquisitions was measured as the natural log of the total number of prior deals that were at least US$100 million and in the same two-digit primary SIC code as the focal target.

name: Postdeal performance
authors_terms: ["postdeal performance", "change in return on assets", "change in ROA"]
definition: We assessed each combined firm's postdeal performance as return on assets (ROA), because it is less sensitive to estimation bias due to changes in leverage or bargaining power following M&As and is used frequently to evaluate strategic actions.

name: Product dissimilarity
definition: Product dissimilarity refers to differences between an acquirer and its target in features of the products or services provided in the marketplace, customer groups served, and distribution channels utilized.

name: Geographic reach dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["geographic reach dissimilarity", "dissimilarity in geographic reach", "geographic markets served"]
definition: Domestic firms can vary considerably in geographic reach-that is, the geographic areas in which they operate; the geographic reach dissimilarity factor represented a single item that gauged the extent to which the two firms operated in dissimilar geographic markets prior to their deal.

name: Cultural dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["cultural dissimilarity", "initial perceptions of dissimilarities in organizational cultures", "perceived cultural similarities", "cultural similarity"]
definition: Initial perceptions of dissimilarities in organizational cultures are differences between a target's and acquirer's organizational values and practices used to reinforce those values that decision makers notice early in an acquisition.

name: Target management retention
authors_terms: ["target management retention", "retention of target top managers"]
definition: Target management retention was calculated as the number of target top managers retained as executive officers divided by the number of target top managers before the deal.

name: Level of integration
definition: For large acquisitions, lower integration levels entail more cautious, selective consolidation, and preservation of autonomy of units; level of integration was assessed by a survey item asking respondents to indicate how operations of the two firms changed following the deal.

name: Upper-management racial diversity
authors_terms: ["upper-management racial diversity", "racial diversity in the upper echelons", "racial diversity as variety"]
definition: Racial diversity is defined in this study as the presence of employees within management who differ in racial background instead of all belonging to one race. Upper management is the corps of people who formulate strategies for the firm, including the CEO and those who frequently interact with the CEO.

name: Lower-management racial diversity
authors_terms: ["lower-management racial diversity", "racial diversity in the lower echelons", "racial diversity as variety"]
definition: Racial diversity is defined in this study as the presence of employees within management who differ in racial background instead of all belonging to one race. Lower management implements policies, programs, and directives of upper management.

name: Racial diversity congruence between upper and lower management
definition: Racial diversity congruence is defined as having very similar racial diversity scores within 0.5 standard deviation of each other between the two management tiers. Racial diversity incongruence refers to a mismatch or asymmetry between the racial diversity of upper management and that of lower management.

name: Firm productivity
definition: Productivity at time t+1, an intermediate measure of organizational effectiveness, was measured as revenue divided by number of employees (thousands of dollars per employee).

name: Expertise distance
definition: The degree to which a highly novel technological idea is intellectually removed from a decision-maker's personal domain of expertise; the authors state that 'the further removed they are intellectually from the idea' the more distant the decision-maker. Domain expertise is considered a primary indicator of distance.

name: Investment propensity in novel ideas
authors_terms: ["investment propensity", "propensity to invest in highly novel technological ideas"]
definition: Decision-makers' willingness to commit financial resources to a novel technological idea, used by the authors and prior studies as a proxy for actual investment decisions.

name: High-level construal
definition: High-level construals are abstract and decontextualized, and 'work to expand people's mental horizons, helping them connect to their broader, more distant goals and desirable end-states'.

name: Low-level construal
definition: Low-level construals are concrete and contextualized, and 'tend to contract people's mental horizons, focusing their attention on the unique and idiosyncratic demands of present circumstances'.

name: Perceived novelty
definition: Decision-makers' perception of the extent to which an idea is novel; novelty is associated with a proclivity toward uncertainty, and the more novel an idea is perceived to be the more uncertainty exists about whether it is useful and feasible to pursue.

name: Perceived usefulness
definition: Decision-makers' perception of the extent to which an idea is useful and feasible; usefulness is associated with feasibility and the reduction of uncertainty.

name: Product-market diversification
authors_terms: ["product-market diversification", "degree of diversification", "diversification in four-digit markets", "diversification"]
definition: This research measured diversification as a continuous variable, using four-digit SIC revenues; highly diversified firms had high index values and firms with low levels of diversification had low values.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["market share", "weighted market share", "firm's share in four-digit market"]
definition: The specific power a firm has in a market, described by the authors as its market share and the specific skills required to gain dominance in a particular market.

name: Market profitability
authors_terms: ["market profitability", "industry profitability", "average levels of profitability", "weighted industry return on assets"]
definition: The average profitability of the markets in which a firm competes, measured at the three-digit industry level as industry return on assets.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration", "concentration levels", "four-firm concentration", "twenty-firm and fifty-firm concentration levels"]
definition: The level of seller concentration in the markets in which a firm competes, compared across diversifier groups at the four-, eight-, twenty-, and fifty-firm levels.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "firm profitability", "return on invested capital", "overall performance levels of firms"]
definition: Return on invested capital (ROIC) measured overall performance levels of firms; this performance measure controls for differences in financial structures across firms.

name: Executive turnover
authors_terms: ["executive turnover", "executive turnover due to backdating", "executive turnover associated with backdating"]
definition: Executive turnover is coded as a dummy variable equal to '1' for a firm where at least one executive or director was fired or resigned in connection with the firm's backdating investigation and '0' otherwise.

name: Firm position in the backdating wave
authors_terms: ["firm position in the backdating wave", "pervasiveness of the misconduct", "pervasiveness of backdating", "position of the firm's first news on backdating scrutiny in the backdating wave"]
definition: We created a cumulative count measure of a firm's position in the backdating wave by counting the number of firms that had news of scrutiny for backdating prior to the focal firm's backdating news. The pervasiveness of the misconduct makes it easier for the board to justify or rationalize the firm's transgression, since it appears 'less inappropriate.'

name: Media attention to misconduct
authors_terms: ["media attention to backdating", "amount of media attention", "media attention"]
definition: The media plays a prominent role in corporate scandals by drawing public attention to corporate misconduct as well as by defining the public's perception of the wrongdoing. To measure media attention on backdating, we counted the number of articles over a 31 day period surrounding the date when each firm was first identified in the news as being under scrutiny.

name: Financial ramification of misconduct
definition: Backdating is a more serious transgression when it results in materially significant additional compensation expense and/or a restatement of the firm's earnings. The financial ramification of the firm's backdating makes it critical for the board to hold executives responsible even if other firms have also been implicated in backdating.

name: Legal ramification of misconduct
definition: There are also legal ramifications associated with backdating when the SEC or DOJ singles out the firm as a target of investigation. Thus, a SEC/DOJ investigation can be a credible and visible signal of the severity of the firm's backdating.

name: Social product features
definition: Social product features enable user interactions, which, when present, generate value in use. If a product manages to attract a large user base, social features add network value to a product's standalone value.

name: Platform installed base size
authors_terms: ["platform installed base", "installed base size", "genre installed base", "demand potential"]
definition: A game's demand potential is defined by the number of registered users on Steam - the platform's installed base - at the time of release. Products on digital platforms can only be adopted by those users who have first adopted the platform itself.

name: Superstar product
definition: Superstars are the top-performing products in a market, which enjoy exponentially superior performance - often expressed in terms of downloads or revenues - compared to the products they compete with.

name: Freemium business model
definition: The freemium business model - where a firm offers a base product for free and users can pay for premium content and features after they have adopted the base product. Free-to-play games generate revenues exclusively from in-app purchases.

name: Proximity to environmentally sensitive water source
authors_terms: ["water risk-adjusted proximity", "proximity to an environmentally sensitive water source", "mine location"]
definition: We argue that mine proximity to an environmentally sensitive water source is a proxy measure for the potential nonmarket risks associated with stakeholder collective action and is identified as such by stock markets. It is water risk-adjusted proximity, that is, the degree of both quantity and quality water risk weighted by distance, which we note is an inverse measure of distance.

name: Stock market reaction to mine announcements
definition: The event study approach examines the degree to which the stock market responds negatively (positively) to negative (positive) announcements regarding events associated with the firm, and thus in principle avoids interpretation problems associated with confounding events. CAR reflects the total impact of an event on a company's stock price.

name: Mineral type
authors_terms: ["type of mineral", "nature of the ore being mined", "gold mine"]
definition: In general, the environmental impacts of mining operations differ significantly by ore type and grade, mineral composition, mining methods (e.g., open pit vs. underground), and technology. In the same vein, the impact on water, the most important resource in mining operations, also differs based on these factors, which are largely determined by the type of mineral being mined.

name: Type of water source
definition: The nearest significant water source to a mine could be a river or a lake. We argue that the negative impacts of mining operations on rivers and lakes are not the same, nor are the potential responses of affected communities. These differences arise from a fundamental distinction between rivers and lakes: mobility.

name: Institutions supporting collective action
authors_terms: ["institutions supporting collective actions", "host country institutions", "institutional context"]
definition: We argue that the ability of local stakeholders to engage in effective collective action is stronger in countries with institutions that support movement mobilization (mobilizing structures), access to political channels (political opportunity), and freedom of information including a free press (framing structures). These correspond to the critical success factors identified in the social movements literature.

name: Environmental performance improvement
authors_terms: ["environmental performance improvement", "performance improvement", "environmental performance trend", "improvement in environmental performance"]
definition: The performance trend on the disclosed environmental metric following mandatory information disclosure; the authors measure it as the trend in toxic chemical releases, so lower releases over time represent greater improvement.

name: Headquarters proximity
definition: Whether an establishment is located in the same city as its corporate headquarters. The authors argue that proximity to headquarters magnifies external and internal pressure and facilitates monitoring and assistance.

name: Sibling proximity
authors_terms: ["proximate sibling", "proximity to sibling", "proximate to corporate siblings"]
definition: Whether an establishment has at least one corporate sibling establishment reporting to TRI in the same city, which the authors argue increases embeddedness, reputational spillovers, and opportunities for capability transfer.

name: Same-industry sibling proximity
authors_terms: ["proximate same-industry sibling", "proximate siblings in the same industry", "same-industry corporate siblings"]
definition: Whether an establishment's proximate corporate sibling operates in the same industry. The authors argue that same-industry proximate siblings are more likely to have similar production processes and transfer capabilities.

name: Establishment size
definition: The size of an establishment, measured by employment and used by the authors to represent its potential power to influence state regulatory agencies and resist local pressure.

name: Regional density
definition: The number of other TRI-reporting establishments in the establishment's region. The authors distinguish dense regions with many establishments from sparse regions with few establishments.

name: Parent firm ownership
authors_terms: ["public ownership", "publicly traded firms", "privately held firms", "ownership structure"]
definition: Whether an establishment's parent firm is publicly traded or privately held. The authors code public ownership as 1 for establishments owned by publicly traded firms and 0 for those owned by privately held firms.

name: Strategic negativity
authors_terms: ["strategic negativity", "negative tone", "negativity in prepared remarks", "negative speech"]
definition: We define strategic negativity as an OIM strategy the CEO employs to reduce a perceived high-expectation hazard. Not all negative speech is strategic negativity; it is the CEO's intent of preventing a rise in expectations that makes negativity 'strategic.'

name: Material positive news
authors_terms: ["material positive news", "positive material surprise", "positive earnings surprise", "PS"]
definition: The impetus of 'material positive news' - that is, exceptionally favorable news about the firm - which the authors view as a necessary but not sufficient condition to provoke strategic negativity. They operationalize it in this context as a material positive earnings surprise, a surprise in the extreme industry quartile.

name: Expectation-updating opportunity
authors_terms: ["expectation-updating opportunity", "expectation-updating stimulus", "fiscal quarter", "turn of a fiscal year"]
definition: An opportunity in which stakeholders are willing and able to update their expectations, that is, an event that prompts stakeholders to reconsider their prior beliefs. The authors focus on the turn of the firm's fiscal year (Q4 and Q1) as a natural expectation-updating juncture.

name: Environmental performance
definition: As have previous studies, we measured environmental performance using toxic emission levels. Our measure of environmental performance (the dependent variable in our model) was the total on- and off-site TRI releases reported for a plant by EPA.

name: Community income
authors_terms: ["community income", "per capita income", "county-level per capita income"]
definition: Community income was approximated by per capita income in the county where a plant was located. This proxy captured the heterogeneous capacity of this stakeholder group to influence organizational outcomes.

name: Community population density
definition: We suggest that population density in the area where industrial operations are located captures the intensity of the area's residents' reaction to their exposure to pollution sources-given the proximity of their place of residence to those pollution sources.

name: Community environmental preferences
authors_terms: ["community environmental preferences", "environmental preferences", "membership in environmental organizations"]
definition: Community environmental preferences also capture a dimension of stakeholder pressures that potentially drives managerial decision making. Membership in environmental organizations was considered as an indicator of the revealed environmental preferences of a geographic community.

name: Legislative environmental voting record
authors_terms: ["district voting records", "environmental voting record", "proenvironment voting record", "voting record of a member of Congress"]
definition: We first hypothesized that the level of manufacturing activities' toxic releases is negatively related to a proenvironment position held by a state's elected delegation to Congress. A delegation's voting record on major environmental issues is indicative of its pro- or antienvironment position.

name: State environmental budget allocation
authors_terms: ["state environmental budget", "environment-related budget allocations", "environmental budget/state budget"]
definition: We used information on a state's environmental budgets and environmental agency employment to capture the state's regulatory stringency, its fiscal capacity (to pay for policies), and its institutional capacity (to develop, among other things, science-intensive policies).

name: State environmental agency employment
authors_terms: ["state environmental agency employees", "environmental employees/state employees", "environmental agency employment"]
definition: We measured a state's environmental investment in people as the ratio of state environmental agency employment to the total number of state employees. The latter was intended to capture a state's long-term commitment to environmental protection and to building institutional capacity to support that commitment.

name: Key executive plurality
authors_terms: ["key executive plurality", "multiple hats", "plurality", "consolidation of authority", "power accumulation"]
definition: This power accumulation through the wearing of multiple hats can be viewed as creating agency costs and, therefore, as detrimental to shareholder wealth. For this study, we are interested in an individual with the title President, CEO and/or Chair of the Board of Directors.

name: Shareholder wealth
authors_terms: ["shareholder wealth", "stock market reaction", "abnormal stock returns", "mean cumulative prediction error (MCPE)"]
definition: A MCPE can be interpreted as an abnormal stock return that has been adjusted for overall stock market movement and the firm's risk level. Positive MCPEs are normally associated with announcements that increase shareholder wealth, while negative MCPEs are associated with announcements that decrease shareholder wealth.

name: Knowledge acquisition
authors_terms: ["knowledge acquisition", "successful knowledge acquisition", "level of knowledge acquired"]
definition: Knowledge acquisition is often defined in terms of the successful transfer of knowledge from a source to a recipient. The acquisition process ends once a recipient (sufficiently) understands whatever knowledge the source has shared.

name: Cross-unit transfer
definition: The authors assumed that each team, laboratory, and technological road map represented a distinct stock of knowledge and expertise, and defined a cross-unit transfer in terms of the number of organizational units it spanned.

name: Tie strength
definition: The strength of the interpersonal relationship between two individuals influences their willingness to engage in knowledge transfer and the amount of effort they dedicate to the activity. Strong interpersonal connections are characterized by a greater degree of trust and cooperation.

name: Network cohesion
definition: When individuals are embedded in a dense web of strong third-party ties, network cohesion is high; trust, cooperation, and the desire or motivation to assist one another are more likely to develop in a cohesive or closed group. When the indirect constraint term c_ij was high, the network surrounding i and j's relationship was characterized by closure, or a high level of network cohesion.

name: Network range
definition: Individuals with more range across their personal networks maintain relationships that cut across nonredundant network clusters. Clusters in a network often represent distinct stocks of knowledge, information, and frames of reference.

name: Business unit reorganization
authors_terms: ["reorganization", "business unit reorganization", "degree of reorganization", "degree of unit reorganization", "unit reorganization"]
definition: Business unit reorganization is the creation of units, deletion of units, or recombination of units within the firm; the resources and activities of these units still remain within the organization, but the structural location where these resources and activities reside have been altered somehow. Unit acquisitions and divestitures, which are choices made by firms to obtain new or discard existing resources and activities, are not considered reorganization events in this study.

name: Radical innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation", "radical innovation", "degree of innovation", "internal entry into new product markets"]
definition: Innovation is generally considered to be the creation of new resources by the firm. In this paper, innovation is observed at the product level and is radical, representing internal entry (i.e., not via acquisition) into new product markets; incremental innovations, namely changes within existing product lines, are not addressed here.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: Firms following a strategy of cost leadership aim at efficient-scale production and focus on variables that contribute to relative low-cost positions.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: Firms pursuing a differentiation strategy aim to create a distinct value or image for a product or service.

name: Focus strategy
definition: Firms following a focus strategy attempt to serve a specific market segment more efficiently or effectively than competitors that compete more broadly.

name: Behavior-based control orientation
definition: Behavior orientation referred to the extent to which a manufacturer attempted to approximate a behavior-based contract with distributors.

name: Contractual restrictions
definition: Contractual restrictions reflect the degree to which the manufacturer attempts to constrain the distributor's autonomy with regard to product marketing decisions. Contractual restrictions [are] the degree to which formal agreements restricted the distributor's freedom of choice.

name: Channel coordination
definition: The manufacturer's coordination of distributor activities; manufacturers were asked to indicate the extent to which they attempted to coordinate distributor activities, for example implementation of sales promotions and dealer service standards.

name: Distributor support
definition: Manufacturer support refers to the assistance a manufacturer makes available to distributors in its channel system (e.g., promotional material, consumer hot-lines).

name: Distribution intensity
definition: Distribution intensity refers to the number of distributors used by a manufacturer within a market area. Less intensive distribution indicated greater manufacturer selectivity in signing up retail dealers.

name: Target focus
definition: Target focus reflected the intended scope of the market for a product, from broad to narrow.

name: Product range
definition: Product range represented the range of customer needs served by the product.

name: Product technology
definition: Product technology referred to the technological superiority of the product relative to its competition.

name: Product price
definition: Product pricing, i.e., the brand's pricing strategy relative to its competitors.

name: Networking actions
definition: Behavioral repertoires in the formation and management of interpersonal ties. The authors argue that entrepreneurs' networking behaviors can be succinctly described through two formative constructs: network-broadening actions and network-deepening actions.

name: Network-broadening actions
definition: Network broadening encompasses entrepreneurs' behavioral repertoires in forming new interpersonal ties. It refers to the extent to which an entrepreneur reaches out to new people and establishes interpersonal knowledge about them.

name: Network-deepening actions
definition: Network deepening consists of entrepreneurs' behavioral repertoires in managing their existing interpersonal ties. It refers to the extent to which an entrepreneur strengthens ties to existing personal network contacts by time pacing interactions with them, overlaying friendships over purely business relations, and preserving existing ties.

name: Reliance on referrals
authors_terms: ["reliance on referrals", "reliance on referral-based search", "referral-based search", "mode of search"]
definition: The first dependent variable in this study is the entrepreneur's reliance on referral when searching for new exchange partners for her venture. It is calculated as the ratio of potential exchange partner organizations that were accessed through a referral to the total number of potential exchange partner organizations accessed during the two-month period.

name: Addition of new exchange partners
authors_terms: ["addition of new exchange partners", "new economic exchanges", "initiation of an economic exchange relationship"]
definition: The second dependent variable in this study is the initiation (or not) of an economic exchange relationship between the focal entrepreneur's venture and the organizations targeted in Phase I. Addition of new exchange partners was then coded as the count of new interfirm exchange ties initiated between the focal venture and the target organizations (potential customers, alliance partners, and/or suppliers).

name: Goal-based categorization
definition: A categorization process in which audiences evaluate entities in terms of how they can meet one's needs, assessing whether offered attributes can serve the goal at hand rather than checking similarity with a stored prototype.

name: Prototype-based categorization
definition: A categorization process in which evaluators assess offerings based on a prototype stored in their memory and search for instances that possess the attributes that best represent the category.

name: Product ambiguity
definition: The presence of one or several unclear attributes that are subject to multiple interpretations with respect to an existing product category, such that audiences cannot associate the attribute with a corresponding product category.

name: Offering evaluation
authors_terms: ["evaluation", "likability", "evaluation of an ambiguous product", "perceived market success"]
definition: Audience members' evaluation of a product offering, captured by the likability of the offering and, in Study 2, by a combination of likability and perceived market success.

name: Perceived utility of unclear attributes
authors_terms: ["perceived utility of the unclear attribute", "perceived utility of unclear product attributes", "perceived utility of the (un)clear attribute"]
definition: The value an evaluator ascribes to an unclear product attribute as useful for achieving the goal at hand; under goal-based categorization evaluators examine whether attributes can serve a pursued goal and reward them more.

name: Ordinary capabilities
definition: we define ordinary capabilities as those capabilities through which a firm 'makes its living' in the short term. Ordinary capabilities are distinct from generic capabilities in that the latter refers to a view of capabilities by their functional area classification.

name: Dynamic capabilities
definition: we define dynamic capabilities as those capabilities used to extend, modify, change, and/or create ordinary capabilities.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: We define environmental dynamism as a change in the competitive environment that affects how firms compete with each other and how they respond to customer needs and developments in the industry. Environmental dynamism reflects the 'amount and unpredictability of change in customer tastes, production or service technologies, and the modes of competition in the firm's principal industries'.

name: Capability heterogeneity
definition: The heterogeneity of a capability is a characteristic that indicates how different a capability is from capabilities in other firms. In our view, a capability can vary from being homogeneous to heterogeneous along a continuum.

name: Relative firm performance
authors_terms: ["relative firm performance", "process-level relative performance", "firm-level relative performance", "RFPP", "RFPF"]
definition: we consider process-level and firm-level performance as 'relative' to the firm's industry (Ordanini and Rubera, 2008) and therefore use the term relative firm performance in this study. The process-level measure focuses on the benefits to the firm without any explicit measure of costs, whereas the firm-level measure captures both the benefits and costs of using capabilities.

name: Organizational form
authors_terms: ["organizational form", "strategic form", "Miles and Snow's strategic types", "organizational configurations"]
definition: Miles and Snow's (1978) strategic types (Prospectors, Defenders, Analyzers, and Reactors) are used as composite measures of the organizational configurations of strategies, structures, and systems. Reactors are defined as those organizations that fail to achieve a coherent configuration among strategic variables.

name: Organizational performance
definition: A composite performance measure was generated with five indicators: total margin (TM), operating margin (OM), total revenue relative to adjusted patient days (TR), the ratio of net operating revenue to the total number of beds for each hospital (NOR), and percent occupancy (OCC).

name: Between-form change
definition: By comparing each hospital's strategic form before the environmental shift to its strategic form after the environmental shift, the authors were able to identify which hospitals changed form and the alternative form to which they changed.

name: Within-form response
definition: Within-form organizational responses were examined in terms of the changes within the same three variables that were used to classify organizational form (i.e., costs: CHGCOSTS; services: CHGSO; and operating slack: CHGOS).

name: Plant efficiency
definition: Direct measures of efficiency are not available, but the most obvious indicator of a plant's efficiency is its capacity: larger plants have significant cost advantages over smaller plants, and size is also an indicator of age, with large plants tending to be relatively young and therefore incorporating modern facilities.

name: Product quality
definition: Individual plants vary according to the differing durability and aesthetic qualities of the bricks they produce, with the clay the main determinant of quality. To test the role of quality in determining closure programs the authors define dummies indicating whether the aesthetic appearance of the brick is of low or high quality.

name: Competitive intensity
authors_terms: ["level of competition", "rivalry", "regional Herfindahl index", "intense competition", "reduction in capacity by local rivals"]
definition: The level of competition in the region in which a plant competes is captured by three variables used to control for interaction effects and the level of competition: the log absolute value of any decrease in capacity undertaken by rival firms in the same region during the previous year, the corresponding measure of rival increases in capacity, and the regional Herfindahl index.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["capacity share", "share", "market share", "size-exit relationship", "firms with the largest market shares"]
definition: The size-exit literature predicts that firms with the largest market shares are the first to close capacity. SHARE measures the firm's regional operational capacity at the beginning of the period as a proportion of the total capacity of plants within range of that region.

name: Mergers and acquisitions
definition: The concentration phase of Bower's restructuring sees a concentration within the industry resulting from mergers, acquisitions and takeovers, which Bower identifies as the key for achieving rationalization as the reduction in the number of rival firms effectively removes the competitive barriers that prevent capacity exit.

name: Acquiring firm ownership
authors_terms: ["ACQUIRER", "plants owned by an acquiring firm prior to the acquisition"]
definition: During the year of acquisition, ACQUIRER takes the value one for plants owned by an acquiring firm prior to the acquisition; when discussing the barrier to exit literature, such plants are the ones to which managers have a personal commitment.

name: Newly acquired plant ownership
definition: During the year of acquisition, ACQUIRED takes the value one for newly acquired plants. Following an M&A the acquiring firm is in possession of newly acquired plants for which there is no great emotional attachment, so such plants are more likely to be closed than those previously owned by the acquiring firm.

name: Plant geographic isolation
authors_terms: ["rural or village setting", "geographically isolated plants", "isolated or rural plants"]
definition: Employment concerns are likely to be exacerbated for plants that are geographically isolated, since there are likely to be limited relocation opportunities and poor alternative employment prospects for staff made redundant. Employee loyalty is less of an obstacle to plant closures if the firm has other plants in the vicinity.

name: Firm diversification
definition: Plants owned by a diversified firm that does not manufacture bricks as its core business; large diversified firms are argued to be more dispassionate and more experienced at making tough decisions regarding uneconomic production facilities.

name: Plant closure
definition: Because continuous kilns consume large amounts of fuel irrespective of output, firms facing declining demand must cut production by switching kilns off, which amounts to effective closure of capacity since once kilns are allowed to cool the plant deteriorates and restarting production involves potentially large and unpredictable investments.

name: Supplier employee losses
authors_terms: ["supplier employee losses", "supplier employee mobility", "employee losses", "employee departures"]
definition: When employees depart from suppliers, the relational capital shared between buyers and their portfolio of suppliers declines. This results in buyers facing higher costs of contracting.

name: Insourcing
definition: We use Insourcing ratio as the dependent variable. This is the percentage of patent applications filed using an in-house attorney by buyer i in year t.

name: Buyer insourcing capacity
definition: Buyers with a relatively large insourcing capacity will face lower costs of bringing additional work in-house, as they enjoy scale economies and have set procedures and channels for recruiting new talent.

name: Buyer-supplier input similarity
authors_terms: ["Buyer-supplier input similarity", "similarity between the inputs produced by the suppliers experiencing employee losses and the inputs produced by the focal plural-sourcing buyer firm"]
definition: The buyer firm's costs of bringing work in-house following supplier employee mobility will depend on the degree of similarity between the activities performed by the in-house department and the suppliers experiencing employee losses.

name: Within-portfolio supplier employee losses
authors_terms: ["Within-portfolio supplier employee losses ratio", "within portfolio losses"]
definition: We isolate supplier employee losses inside the buyer's portfolio - that is, patent attorneys that left the law firms used by buyer firm i to join other competing law firms that were also used by buyer firm i in year t - 1.

name: Supplier input similarity
authors_terms: ["Supplier input similarity", "similarity between the activities performed by suppliers"]
definition: This measure is high when other law firms in the buyer's portfolio file patents in technology areas similar to those of law firms with employee losses.

name: Idea framing abstractness
authors_terms: ["construal framing", "abstract why framing", "concrete how framing", "why frame", "how frame", "strategic framing"]
definition: In the low-level construal, the description of the idea focuses on how the idea operates; in the high-level construal, it focuses on why the idea is beneficial. Thus, the concrete framing emphasizes the ways in which the idea can be used, while the abstract framing the reasons to consider it.

name: Audience expertise in idea evaluation
authors_terms: ["expertise", "domain-relevant expertise", "level of expertise in idea evaluation", "novices", "experts"]
definition: Expertise is defined as 'a high level of domain-specific knowledge acquired through experience', and this research suggests that knowledge is organized around schemas that differ between novices and experts. While experts are individuals who have acquired domain-relevant knowledge about novel idea evaluation over long periods of time, novices are not used to approach the idea evaluative task.

name: Appreciation of novel ideas
authors_terms: ["idea attractiveness", "investment propensity", "investment amount", "appreciation of novel ideas", "evaluative responses", "willingness to support"]
definition: The authors analyze three types of evaluative outcomes: attractiveness of the idea (the extent to which audiences like and are willing to collect additional information on the business idea); propensity to invest in the idea (the actual amount of an earned bonus audiences are willing to give in support of the idea); and investment amount (the imaginary amount audiences are willing to invest in the idea).

name: Perceived usefulness
definition: Research has shown how external stimuli are perceived to be more useful when they are congruent with evaluating audiences' mental representations; the authors explored whether the perceived usefulness of novel ideas mediates the effect of construal framing on the evaluation of novices and experts.

name: Limited cross-industry skill transferability
authors_terms: ["limited transferability of skills across industries", "cross-industry skill transferability", "cross-industry mobility frictions", "P(Stay in industry in 4 months)", "industry specificity"]
definition: The measures we develop build on the logic from prior literature that the skills associated with a job will be differentially transferable across industries. More specifically, we measure cross-industry transferability of skills based on the extent to which an individual in a given job is likely to move across industries, where we conceptualize a job as a combination of an occupation and an industry.

name: Noncompete enforceability
authors_terms: ["noncompete enforceability", "enforceability of covenants not to compete", "noncompetes", "within-industry mobility friction"]
definition: One prominent within-industry friction is noncompete enforceability, which does not change the value of a given worker within the industry, but imposes costs to moving between competitors through the threat of litigation.

name: Employee tenure
definition: To examine our tenure hypothesis, we utilize the employee's reported Tenure (in months) with the employer.

name: Experience at hire
authors_terms: ["postgraduation experience at hire", "initial experience", "experience when hired", "less experienced employees"]
definition: To measure the Postgraduation experience at hire of the employee, we calculate the number of months between when the individual reports finishing his or her highest degree of education and when being hired into a job.

name: Firm-sponsored training
definition: The SIPP contains training data reflecting answers to the question: 'During the past year, has [the respondent] received any kind of training intended to improve skill in one's current or most recent job?' For our training dependent variable, we utilize a dummy for whether the respondent reports the firm paying for the most recent training event.

name: Training in new and upgrading skills
authors_terms: ["new skills training", "upgrading skills training", "new or upgrade skills training"]
definition: Training of new skills includes teaching an employee how to use new equipment, software, and machinery, or teaching other new procedures. Upgrading skills training expands on the skills that the employee already has.

name: Training in basic skills and organizational policies
definition: Basic skills are those that are required for the job and include training in office software, work routines and management practices. Organizational policies are a closely related category and include training of internal firm guidelines and required procedures.

name: Employee wages
definition: With regards to wages, the SIPP asks respondents about their monthly earnings, which we convert to hourly wages by dividing reported monthly earnings by the product of reported hours worked per week and 4.33 (since there are 4.33 weeks in a month).

name: Knowledge scope
definition: Knowledge scope is the variety of knowledge used by an organization's members. This variety is a form of diversity and can be measured as a categorical difference across an organization's members.

name: Hierarchy expansion
authors_terms: ["hierarchy expansion", "expansion of hierarchy", "expansion of hierarchy in organizations"]
definition: Our main dependent variable, Hierarchy expansion, is a binary variable capturing the addition of a management layer, defined as hiring at least one employee from the manager level.

name: Task similarity
definition: We calculate Task similarity - the extent to which two occupations require similar tasks - as the cosine similarity of their tasks. Task similarity equals 1 when the two occupations have identical tasks and 0 when they have no common tasks.

name: Shared prior experience
authors_terms: ["shared prior experience", "shared experience", "shared experience at previous employers"]
definition: Shared prior experience is the size of the largest, multi-employee connected component of employees in the shared experience network divided by team size. In our context, this connected component is the largest set of employees who can be linked by shared work experience at one or more firms.

name: External knowledge pool
authors_terms: ["external knowledge", "pool of external knowledge", "knowledge of rivals", "external knowledge pool", "external knowledge environment"]
definition: The stock of knowledge available to a firm outside its own boundaries, measured as the knowledge embodied in rival firms in the same market. The extent of vicarious learning is a function of the size of the external knowledge pool, firms' ability to absorb external knowledge, and firms' impetus to acquire that knowledge.

name: Rate of experiential learning
authors_terms: ["rate of experiential learning", "experiential learning", "learning from experience", "rate a firm learns from experience"]
definition: The rate at which a firm's cost declines with cumulative experience, i.e., the firm-specific coefficient of learning from experience in the learning curve model; x < 0 implies cost reduction and, hence, learning.

name: Problems in experiential learning
definition: A problem emerges when performance falls below expectations; the locus of attention in experiential learning is a problem that emerges in the process of engaging in productive activity and the subsequent search for solutions.

name: Entrant status
definition: An entrant is a new commercial banking institution; entrants are firms that entered within the years 1984-1997 in the sample, while incumbents are defined as those firms founded prior to 1975.

name: Vicarious learning
definition: Learning from the knowledge and experience of rivals, occurring through knowledge conduits such as observing artifacts of rivals' internal activities or acquiring knowledge directly from rivals' employees.

name: Cost efficiency
definition: The log of firm i's costs relative to a firm on the cost frontier, so that lower values correspond to increased efficiency, i.e., lower cost.

name: Negative media coverage of mutual fund fees
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage of mutual fund fees", "negative fee articles", "negative coverage of fees", "negative articles on fees", "negative media coverage"]
definition: We will use the term media coverage to refer to the volume and the tone of the material published by the business press. The media coverage was considered negative if the articles reported that mutual fund fees are too high or if the article explicitly told the reader to consider mutual funds with lower fees.

name: Mutual fund fee level
definition: The total expenses of a mutual fund comprise both fees and other costs, while the business press focused on the fees because this was in most cases the only expense information available from the funds.

name: Net flows into mutual funds
authors_terms: ["financial net flows", "net flow of money", "Ln Net flow", "investment flows into mutual funds"]
definition: Our dependent variable is defined as the logarithm of the net flow of money to a fund at time t.

name: Dominant field position
authors_terms: ["dominant field positions", "position in the field", "field position", "bank-sponsored mutual funds", "bank-owned funds", "banks"]
definition: The structural position of an organization is, for several reasons, closely linked to an organization's ability to resist temporary whims of market processes—including challenges from the business press. Apart from their greater capacity to respond to criticism, organizations that occupy a dominant structural position are also viewed as more creditable in their counterarguments.

name: Firm performance severity
authors_terms: ["firm performance severity", "performance severity", "severity of losses", "situation severity"]
definition: Firms in turnaround situations vary in the severity of their situations, specifically the magnitudes of their losses. The variable firm performance severity was measured by reverse coding firm performance at Year 0, i.e., the year when the firm entered its turnaround situation.

name: Industry performance severity
definition: Turnaround researchers distinguish troubled firms in relatively healthy industries from those in struggling, low-profit industries; the worse the industry's health, the greater the call for strategic deviance from industry norms. We first identified an industry as struggling if its median ROE-COE spread was negative during all the Years -2, -1, and 0, and then reverse coded industry median performance at Year 0 to measure industry performance severity.

name: CEO replacement
definition: Whether the firm replaced its CEO, and when; we used the Execucomp and Factiva databases to identify whether and when firms replaced their CEOs and analyzed replacements occurring in Years 0 and +1, where Year 0 is the year of initial losses.

name: Incumbent CEO tenure
definition: The variable incumbent CEO's tenure was measured by the number of years the incumbent had been CEO in the focal firm. Long-tenured executives are often cognitively constrained, possessing limited perspectives on alternatives.

name: Incumbent industry tenure
definition: The variable incumbent's industry tenure was the number of years the incumbent CEO had worked in the focal firm's primary industry (three-digit SIC). Just as a CEO's tenure on the job tends to bring about a commitment to the company's status quo, so too does tenure in the industry bring about an adherence to the industry's norms and mind-sets.

name: Incumbent functional background
definition: A CEO's primary functional background was that in which he or she had the longest employment history, categorized as output (marketing, sales, and product development), throughput (operations, engineering, and accounting), or other (law, consulting, finance, general management). Executives who have been immersed in a particular function attend to certain information and interpret it in ways that suit their functional expertise.

name: Successor company outsiderness
definition: A successor hired from outside the company, without historical embeddedness with the focal firm or its strategy, and thus with few social or cognitive constraints.

name: Successor functional background
authors_terms: ["throughput-oriented successor", "successor with experience primarily in throughput functions", "functional experience"]
definition: Successor CEOs who have significant throughput-oriented experience tend to fit with the requirements imposed by severe performance; such executives will have the efficiency-oriented expertise needed to enhance the chance of successful turnaround.

name: Successor industry outsiderness
definition: A new CEO who has minimal commitments to the focal industry's norms and practices-an industry outsider. Such an executive provides fresh perspectives, new knowledge, and new expertise to facilitate the requisite departure from industry recipes.

name: Subsequent firm performance
definition: We assessed a firm's subsequent performance, or its degree of turnaround success, by examining two measures: ROE and market-to-book value of common equity (MTB), investigated at Years +2, +3, and +4 where Year 0 was the year of initial losses.

name: Host-country policy risk
definition: Policy risk is the risk that a government will opportunistically alter policies to directly or indirectly expropriate a firm's profits or assets. The specific source of policy risk on which the authors focus is the extent to which the formal policy-making process lacks checks and balances or 'institutional constraints' that would otherwise constrain the behavior of policy makers.

name: Foreign entry
definition: The dependent variable is a binary measure that takes a value of 1 if a firm invested in a new generation facility (i.e., a facility in which it had not previously invested) in a country in a given year, and 0 otherwise; it captures a firm's choice among potential host countries.

name: Home-country institutional constraints
definition: The extent of institutional constraints on policy makers-checks and balances-in a firm's home-country policy-making environment. Policy-making systems requiring agreement among more numerous and diverse institutional actors to change policy are characterized by relatively high stability and thus a relatively low level of policy risk; systems in which policy-making authority is more concentrated or shared among actors with similar preferences pose a higher level of policy risk.

name: Home-country income inequality
definition: A firm's home-country level of income inequality, one of the two main types of home-country socioeconomic cleavages linked to the intensity of political rent seeking. Higher income inequality is associated with greater redistributive pressures-and thus a more contentious policy-making process-because governments may be able to increase their political support by expropriating industries or businesses that serve substantial parts of the population.

name: Home-country ethnic fractionalization
definition: The degree of fragmentation among a firm's home-country resident ethnic groups, the second main type of home-country socioeconomic cleavage linked to political rent seeking; ethnically polarized societies are argued to be prone to competitive rent seeking by the different groups. The ELF index measures the probability that two randomly selected people from a given country do not belong to the same ethnolinguistic group.

name: Focal firm imitation scope
authors_terms: ["imitation scope", "scope of imitation", "focal firm's scope of imitation of new product technologies", "how much to copy"]
definition: The extent to which a firm (in a given period) imitates a wide number (as opposed to a narrow number) of new product technologies introduced by competitors.

name: Focal firm average speed of imitation
authors_terms: ["average speed of imitation", "imitation speed", "how fast to copy"]
definition: The average time it takes for the focal firm to adopt the set of new product technologies introduced by rivals.

name: Rivals' imitation scope
authors_terms: ["rivals' imitation scope", "scope of rivals' imitation of new product technologies"]
definition: The number of imitative actions taken by all competitors of the focal firm (in a focal technological system), after subtracting the total number of imitations realized by the focal firm itself in the same period.

name: Rivals' average speed of imitation
authors_terms: ["rivals' average speed of imitation", "rivals' imitation speed"]
definition: The average length of time it took rivals to act after a new product technology was introduced.

name: Sales performance
authors_terms: ["focal firm performance", "sales performance", "number of handsets sold"]
definition: Focal firm performance was operationalized using the number of handsets sold on a yearly basis (i.e., sales performance) in the U.K.

name: Product technology heterogeneity
definition: The level of product technology heterogeneity expresses the extent to which products launched by all competitors are equipped with similar or different technologies. A low level of product technology heterogeneity is the result of a 'high degree of design dominance,' while a high level of product technology heterogeneity is the product of a 'low degree of design dominance.'

name: Executive political orientation
definition: We extend upper-echelon theory and research by focusing on a managerial characteristic that may reflect executives' underlying attitudes toward risk and uncertainty: personal political orientation. Political orientation may be an indicator of underlying differences in executive conservatism.

name: Tax avoidance
definition: We define tax avoidance as anything that reduces the firm's taxes relative to its pretax accounting income. Since engaging in tax avoidance has the potential to boost the bottom line directly and can also increase the firm's risk exposure, a firm's tax avoidance can be used as a proxy for the level of risk a firm's leadership is willing to take.

name: Managerial entrenchment
definition: CEO entrenchment is thought to limit the board's ability to monitor effectively CEOs. Firms with entrenchment scores at or above the median score in the sample were considered entrenched.

name: New TMT member political orientation
authors_terms: ["personal political orientation of new TMT members", "new executive's political orientation"]
definition: The personal political orientation of newly hired or promoted top management team members, whose attitudes toward uncertainty and risk are expected to resemble those of the current executives.

name: Incoming CEO political orientation
authors_terms: ["personal political orientation of the incoming CEO", "new CEO's political orientation"]
definition: The personal political orientation of the CEO who takes office after a succession, which a departing CEO is likely to try to align with his or her own by promoting a like-minded individual.

name: Value creation in acquisitions
authors_terms: ["value created", "total value created in the merger", "normalized total value created", "NTVL"]
definition: Value is created when these assets are used more effectively by the combined firm than by target and bidder separately. The dependent variable NTVL represents the dollar gain created in an acquisition per dollar of equity involved in the transaction.

name: Identical strategic fit
authors_terms: ["identical fit", "identical strategic fits", "percentage of identical strategic fits"]
definition: In the identical fit category the bidder and target are in the same business.

name: Related-supplementary strategic fit
definition: A related-supplementary target business provides the bidder primarily with access to new customers and markets rather than with new assets or products. If the target business permits entry into a new but related industry, then the fit is related-supplementary.

name: Related-complementary strategic fit
definition: Related-complementary target businesses provide the bidder with new products, assets or skills for product markets currently served by the bidder rather than with access to new markets. If the target unit permits the bidder firm to expand its product line or strengthen its competitive position in a given market, or to integrate forward or backwards, then the fit is related-complementary.

name: Unrelated strategic fit
definition: Affirmative answers to fewer than three questions indicate that the businesses are unrelated. If the assets of the two businesses are unrelated, then little possibility exists for developing economies of scope.

name: CEO appointment following an interim period
authors_terms: ["CEO appointment following interim period", "interim CEO succession", "permanent CEO appointed following an interim period"]
definition: An interim CEO succession is one in which a CEO is appointed following an interim period, that is, the permanent CEO directly succeeded an interim CEO. This contrasts with direct successions in which one permanent CEO directly replaces another.

name: Postsuccession firm performance
authors_terms: ["postsuccession firm performance", "one-, two-, and three-year postsuccession firm performance"]
definition: We measure firm performance with an operational measure, return on assets (ROA), calculated as a firm's annual net income divided by its total book value of assets. We focus our main analyses on a firm's one-, two-, and three-year ROA following the CEO succession.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity was measured as a composite index that considered environmental dynamism, strategic differentiation of peer firms, and industry R&D intensity. More complex external environments-characterized by greater dynamism, more diverse firm strategies, and more intensive research and development (R&D) activities-are more difficult to evaluate.

name: CEO managerial demands
authors_terms: ["CEO managerial demands", "managerial demands of the CEO role", "executive job demands"]
definition: Following research on executive demands (Hambrick et al. 2005), the managerial demands of the CEO role were measured as a composite index that considered the firm's size, its degree of diversification, and its acquisition activity. More complex organizational characteristics, such as increases in size, diversification, or acquisition activity, make the role more demanding and more complex.

name: Potential external CEO candidates
authors_terms: ["potential external candidates", "number of potential external CEO candidates"]
