definition: The measure of the number of potential external CEO candidates was developed following Zhang and Rajagopalan (2003, 2004), who consider a possible candidate for the CEO position to be an executive holding a position of executive vice president (EVP) or higher. Likely sources of external candidates are firms within the focal firm's industry (four-digit SIC) that are equal to or larger than half the size of the focal firm.

name: Knowledge breadth
authors_terms: ["knowledge breadth", "knowledge breadth (clustered)", "number of knowledge sources", "breadth of knowledge search"]
definition: A key choice concerning the search for solutions is knowledge breadth, i.e., the number of information sources that firms utilize, such as knowledge from customers, suppliers, or employees. Greater knowledge breadth means a larger number of knowledge sources used in searching for solutions.

name: Cumulative knowledge breadth
definition: The cumulative knowledge breadth measure counts the total number of different knowledge sources used in the periods prior to the current year t. The cumulative knowledge breadth (clustered) measure takes into account only the cumulative number of unique clusters over time.

name: Operational performance
definition: Operational performance can include operational efficiency in terms of cost per unit produced, and/or operational effectiveness in terms of quality per unit, such as the level of waste produced for a given volume. Because facilities are engaged in waste reduction, increases in waste indicate lower operational performance while decreases in waste indicate higher operational performance.

name: Diversity of businesses
authors_terms: ["diversity of businesses", "diversity of the business portfolio", "diversity of the portfolio of businesses", "diversity of products-markets"]
definition: The diversity of the business portfolio of a firm in the industry, evaluated by the number of products x markets. The authors stress that as businesses are different the CEO's cognitive map may be chunked into separated clusters of constructs corresponding to the different businesses.

name: Geographic scope
authors_terms: ["geographic scope", "international geographic scope", "geographical limits of its targeted markets"]
definition: The geographic scope of the company determines the number of competitive systems in which the firm is involved; it was evaluated by the geographical limits of the firm's targeted markets in the industry.

name: Links with foreign parent companies
authors_terms: ["links with foreign parent companies", "links with (foreign) 'parent' companies", "interactions with a parent company"]
definition: The interactions of the firm with a parent company; a multinational or transnational firm has operations worldwide and top managers face both the diversity of markets and the diversity of management practices in their interactions with parent companies.

name: Comprehensiveness of cognitive maps
definition: The ability to perceive several dimensions in a stimulus array is referred to as differentiation or comprehensiveness. A manager's comprehensiveness was measured by the number of elements (concepts) in the cognitive map.

name: Connectedness of cognitive maps
definition: The development of connections among the differentiated characteristics is referred to as integration or connectedness. Connectedness of a manager's map of the structure of the industry was measured by the number of links between concepts divided by the total number of concepts in the map.

name: Cognitive complexity
authors_terms: ["cognitive complexity", "complexity of a manager's cognitive map", "combined measure of comprehensiveness and connectedness"]
definition: According to complexity theory, the complexity of an individual conceptual system is determined by two interdependent aspects: the number of parts or dimensions of the system and the nature and extent of rules for integrating them. The combined measure of complexity of a cognitive map is the number of links between concepts in the map, i.e. the score of comprehensiveness multiplied by the score of connectedness.

name: Stretch goal for idea generation
authors_terms: ["unit's stretch goal", "stretch goal", "stretchiness of the goals", "unit-level stretch goal"]
definition: Although any challenging goal may heighten expectations, stretch goals have 'an objective probability of attainment that may be unknown but are seemingly impossible given current capabilities' (Sitkin et al. 2011, p. 547). In this setting, the firm set unit-specific targets for the total revenue (in Euros) to be generated by the new business opportunities identified, and employees reported how stretched they perceived the idea generation goal in their unit to be.

name: Participation in idea generation behavior
authors_terms: ["participation in idea generation behavior", "participation", "participates in idea generation behaviors"]
definition: First, by stretching a target regarding the generation of new ideas, a unit may foster participation by inviting those who have not previously been suggesting ideas. Participation captures whether an employee engages at all, that is, submitting at least one idea.

name: Engagement in idea generation behavior
authors_terms: ["engagement in idea generation behavior", "engagement", "engages in idea generation behaviors"]
definition: Second, setting a seemingly unattainable target regarding idea generation may also encourage employees to expand additional efforts and to engage more intensely in such behavior. Engagement captures how much an employee engages, that is, submitting multiple ideas.

name: Fruitful ideas
authors_terms: ["fruitful ideas", "fruitful (useful, beneficial) ideas", "number of fruitful ideas submitted"]
definition: We measured the number of fruitful ideas submitted based on the number of ideas that were subsequently accepted and sold to customers. Fruitful ideas are the useful, beneficial ideas among those generated by employees.

name: Futile ideas
authors_terms: ["futile ideas", "futile (rejected, worthless) ideas", "number of futile ideas submitted"]
definition: Fourth, we measured the number of futile ideas submitted based on the number of ideas that were ultimately rejected by the organization. Rejections were typically based on technical feasibility, (technical) misalignment with the firm's strategy, issues with implementation in the market (i.e., regulatory issues), or lack of demand.

name: Prior success in generating fruitful ideas
definition: Whereas prior success indicates whether an employee has been successful in generating one or more fruitful ideas in the past, organizational tenure refers to the length of his or her employment in the firm.

name: Organizational tenure
definition: Organizational tenure refers to the length of his or her employment in the firm.

name: Hierarchical position
definition: Hierarchical position indicates the position an employee occupies within the hierarchy of the organization.

name: Relationship duration
authors_terms: ["duration of the relationship", "duration of a customer relationship", "length of the bank's association with a customer", "length of the relationship", "duration of relationship"]
definition: How long a customer has been with a bank should influence risk assessment. The number of years the bank had loaned to a given customer measured the duration of the relationship.

name: Loan size
authors_terms: ["loan size", "loan amount", "outstanding amount of a loan"]
definition: The outstanding amount of a loan in millions of dollars measured its size; the value of a loan to a bank depends on its size.

name: Industry excitement
authors_terms: ["excitement value of a borrower's industry", "industry excitement", "excitement value", "degree of excitement an industry conveys"]
definition: In general, the excitement an industry conveys should increase the difficulty of assessing the risk a borrower from that industry presents, whether that risk is high or low.

name: Branch performance
authors_terms: ["branch performance", "prior performance levels", "performance of a branch", "relative profitability of each branch"]
definition: We measured the performance of a branch as its profitability in the prior year. Since the bank changed its profitability measures during the span of the study, an ordinal variable reflected the relative profitability of each branch in each year.

name: Standardization
authors_terms: ["standardization", "organizational standardization", "degree of standardization in the loan review process", "standardization of the loan review process"]
definition: We refer to increased specification of decision processes as standardization. Over the study period, the degree of standardization found in the bank's loan review process substantially increased.

name: Direction of risk rating error
authors_terms: ["risk-rating errors", "direction of risk-rating errors", "risk assessment error", "over- or underestimate the risk"]
definition: Observations were classified as overrated: a banker assessed the risk as higher than the model did, and the banker moved toward the model's assessment within two years; underrated: the banker assessed the risk as lower than the model did and moved toward the model's assessment within two years; and other: the model and the banker agreed, or they disagreed but the banker did not move toward the model.

name: Risk rating accuracy
authors_terms: ["accurate risk rating", "prevalence of risk-rating errors", "number of misrated loans", "overall error rates", "reliability"]
definition: Management may change risk assessment processes to achieve two different objectives: to reduce bias (consistent tendencies to over- or underrate loans) and to increase reliability (as manifested by lower overall error rates).

name: Crowdsourcing governance mode
authors_terms: ["governance interventions", "governance instruction sets", "governance modes", "governance of the crowd"]
definition: The independent variable is one of three modes of governance intervention assigned to the specific event: governance for offering solutions only, governance for offering problem frames, and governance for offering and integrating others' problem frames.

name: Problem constraint
authors_terms: ["problem type", "unconstrained problem", "constrained problem", "level of constraint", "degrees of freedom"]
definition: The problem type posed to the crowd by the firm: problem statements expecting solutions that simultaneously embody new products and new markets are unconstrained because they neither restrict the solver to a market nor products, whereas constrained problems can be specified well a priori.

name: Solution idea implementability
definition: As dependent variables, based on Amabile's (1983) notion of innovation as useful novelty, the authors used both the solution idea's implementability and its novelty, as evaluated by the executives and then standardized.

name: Solution idea novelty
definition: As dependent variables, based on Amabile's (1983) notion of innovation as useful novelty, the authors used both the solution idea's implementability and its novelty, as evaluated by the executives and then standardized.

name: Problem frame offering
authors_terms: ["problem frames", "problem framing elements", "number of problem framing elements in trace", "expressed number of problem frame elements in trace"]
definition: Here, a problem frame refers to an interpretation of the problem and the associated innovation landscape based on prior experience and context. To identify framing elements, we had coders manually code all 2428 postings for the presence of any of three problem framing elements (facts, tradeoffs, and examples).

name: Integrativeness of solution
authors_terms: ["integrativeness of solution", "integrativeness of solution idea", "integrate prior frames", "integrate others' problem frames"]
definition: Such integration is a cognitive process of considering frames offered by others and reusing and recombining elements of those frames into their own experiences and contexts. We constructed a dependent variable called integrativeness of solution using a text analytics approach measuring the similarity between the solution and the problem frame elements across the solution's trace (i.e., the five posts that precede the solution).

name: Strategic alliances
authors_terms: ["strategic alliances", "alliance intensity", "the number of strategic alliances among incumbents of a market", "direct linkages"]
definition: Strategic alliances are voluntary arrangements between competing firms involving exchange, sharing, or the codevelopment of products, technologies, and services. They are a typical type of direct interorganizational linkage that comes into existence when organizations actively seek one another out and make a deliberate choice to collaborate.

name: Common ownership ties
definition: Indirect linkages that are created when competing firms are connected to the same third-party, here common ownership ties through shared institutional investors. Institutional investors with equity stakes in multiple competing firms are motivated and able to mediate and sanction conflicts between the firms they own.

name: Common analyst ties
authors_terms: ["common analyst ties", "common analyst coverage", "common financial analysts"]
definition: Indirect linkages created through shared financial analysts. Analysts hold impartial positions and, because their forecasting accuracy and compensation suffer when the firms they cover are at war, they can mediate conflicts between firms they cover and use their opinion leader status to sanction undesirable competitive behavior.

name: War spillover from other markets
authors_terms: ["incumbents at war in other markets", "the proportion of incumbents at war in other markets", "spillover of competitive wars"]
definition: Once competitors enter into wars in other markets, these wars may spill over to the focal market, where the competitors are also present. The construct captures the proportion of incumbents in a focal market that were at war in other markets during the previous period.

name: Competitive war occurrence
authors_terms: ["competitive war", "war occurrence", "price war", "the likelihood of a competitive war occurring in that market"]
definition: Competitive wars are often waged to redefine the status quo or renegotiate the rent distribution in a market, and through extreme aggression and destruction war participants hope to shape the future behavior of their rivals. In this study the occurrence of wars is captured with price wars, a period in which the firms in a market set prices that are significantly below the usually prevailing prices.

name: Public governance
authors_terms: ["public (as opposed to private) governance", "public governance", "public ownership", "governance mode"]
definition: Governance is a 'syndrome of attributes' influencing how managers both operate and affect organizational performance; public (state-owned) organizations are characterized by lower-powered incentives, bureaucratic rules, and restrained managerial autonomy, in contrast to the greater autonomy and higher-powered incentives of private organizations.

name: Human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "human capital resources", "enhanced human capital", "stock of human capital"]
definition: The stock of human capital in an organization, that is, the set of knowledge and skills embedded in workers and that can be used for productive purposes; in this context, the authors consider human capital to be the presence of well-trained (i.e., highly educated) teachers/school managers.

name: Technological resources
authors_terms: ["technological resources", "administrative technological resources", "technological support resources", "technological infrastructure"]
definition: Technological resources support a myriad of activities within schools and are recognized as enablers of superior performance; access to adequate support resources, such as administrative infrastructure and information technology (IT) systems, facilitates school planning, monitoring of student performance, and the identification of areas requiring substantial improvement.

name: Superior management practices
authors_terms: ["superior practices", "superior internal operational practices", "external engagement practices", "management index"]
definition: A practice is 'a defined activity or set of activities that a variety of firms might execute' that managers adopt to execute their required tasks; not all practices lead to superior performance, and organizations may differ in their ability to select a subset of practices that are performance enhancing, which the authors henceforth refer to as 'superior' practices. The authors distinguish two general sets of practices that schools can implement: internal operational practices and external engagement practices.

name: Social and environmental practices
authors_terms: ["social and environmental practices (SEPs)", "sustainable business practices", "high SEPs", "social and environmental practices"]
definition: We define SEPs as organizational practices that have a positive effect on society by improving the firm's impact on the social and natural environments. SEPs can include community relations, diversity, employee relations, human rights, product quality and safety, and environment and corporate governance practices.

name: Financial volatility
authors_terms: ["financial volatility", "volatility in financial performance", "stock return volatility", "volatility of treated firms"]
definition: Previous literature on resiliency argues that high volatility in returns and markets tends to signal low resilience. Examples of high financial volatility include the erratic changes in IBM's earnings, which plummeted from a profit of $6 billion in 1990 to a loss of nearly $8 billion in 1993.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth over the long term", "higher growth", "net sales growth", "growth"]
definition: Growth over the long term was measured as the accumulation of net sales growth from 1994 to 2008. Accumulated growth is a better measure for capturing the differences between treated firms and control firms than year-over-year growth because growth occurs continuously and incrementally over time.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["survival rates", "rates of survival", "firm survival", "probability of survival"]
definition: SEPs help buffer firms from disruptions and reduce firms' vulnerability to crashes, increasing firms' probability of survival. Failure is coded when a firm fails during the 15-year period; there are several reasons for failure, including acquisition or merger, liquidation, and bankruptcy.

name: Short-term profitability
definition: Finally, short-term profitability is measured by the change in ROA between two consecutive years. ROA is one of the most commonly used financial measures to assess the financial performance of a firm's operations.

name: Corporate sustainable development
definition: Organizations must apply the principles of sustainable development to their products, policies, and practices in order to express sustainable development, and corporate sustainable development is achieved only at the intersection of environmental integrity, economic prosperity, and social equity, all three of which are necessary conditions.

name: International experience
definition: International experience is developed by operating in, and depending upon, foreign markets; through this experience firms acquire knowledge from multiple jurisdictions and develop capabilities in coordinating distant parts of the organization and in developing organizational structures and systems that allow coordination across different regulatory structures.

name: Capital management capabilities
definition: Capital management capabilities are developed by managing physical assets and technologies; firms with these capabilities are more likely to be aware of sustainable development issues and will attempt to adopt best practices and superior technologies in order to avoid expensive capital refits associated with changing environmental and social regulations.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Organizational slack is 'that cushion of actual or potential resources which allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for adjustment or to external pressures for change' (Bourgeois, 1981: 30); it allows firms to make investments in resources and capabilities that may not have an immediate pay-off.

name: Fines and penalties
definition: Fines and penalties reflect coercive pressures imposed by institutions that directly influence firms; firms that have previously incurred fines are scrutinized closely by the government and special interest groups because of their loss of legitimacy and will subscribe to a higher standard of corporate sustainable development.

name: Mimicry
definition: Firms actively attempt to reduce the level of uncertainty in their organizational environment by imitating the structures and activities of similar firms, capitalizing on the successes of their peers.

name: Media attention
definition: The media assigns importance to some issues and exposes gaps in others, becoming part of the institution-building process that shapes the norms of acceptable and legitimate sustainable development practices; the total amount of media coverage raises the firm's visibility, inviting further public attention and scrutiny.

name: Time period
definition: Time is represented by a linear trend variable with values from one to four to represent each contiguous panel, used to test whether the influence of the independent variables on corporate sustainable development changes over time.

name: Context of the transfer
authors_terms: ["context of the transfer", "characteristics of the context of the transfer"]
definition: The authors connect characteristics of the context in which knowledge is transferred, expectations of conformance to norms of knowledge use, and the intention to transfer knowledge, and they refer to the set of contextual characteristics as the 'context of the transfer'.

name: Reputation of the knowledge recipient
authors_terms: ["reputation of the knowledge recipient", "reputation of the knowledge receiver", "reputation of the recipient"]
definition: Reputation is defined as an actor's ability to deliver valued outcomes; with respect to firms, it 'refers to the perceptions by [an actor]'s audience about the [actor]'s ability to provide value'.

name: Degree of competition
authors_terms: ["degree of competition", "competition between the knowledge holder and the knowledge recipient"]
definition: The paper manipulates the degree of competition between the knowledge holder and knowledge recipient through two variables; all interviewees suggested that competition is best assessed by two measures: geographical proximity and product positioning.

name: Visibility of the recipient's behavior
authors_terms: ["visibility of the behavior of the knowledge recipient in the social group", "visibility of the recipient's behavior", "visibility to third parties"]
definition: According to the authors' informants, such visibility varies with the degree to which the actions of a particular recipient could be observed by intermediaries like customers and critics.

name: Conformance assessment
authors_terms: ["conformance assessment", "expectation that a knowledge recipient will conform to norms of knowledge use", "expectations of norm conformance"]
definition: 'Conformance assessment,' defined here as one party's inference about another's propensity to abide by a social norm; in the study it is the reported likelihood that a respondent would expect the chef described in the scenario to conform to the social norms operating in the industry.

name: Intention to transfer knowledge
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfer intention", "intention to transfer knowledge", "propensity of the knowledge holder to transfer knowledge"]
definition: The reported likelihood that a respondent, if asked, would transfer culinary knowledge to the chef described in the scenario, measured separately for recipes, signature dishes, and cooking techniques.

name: Tie formation intention
authors_terms: ["tie formation intention", "intention to form an interpersonal tie", "interpersonal tie formation intentions", "entrepreneurs' tie formation intentions"]
definition: An entrepreneur's intention to form a tie to a new person with whom the entrepreneur interacts; after at least one interaction, the entrepreneur evaluates whether he/she intends to follow up with subsequent interactions and thereby attempt to build a relationship.

name: Caste homophily
definition: The similarity in caste between an entrepreneur and a new person, calculated as the joint probability of the entrepreneur and new person belonging to the same caste.

name: Language homophily
definition: The similarity in language between an entrepreneur and a new person, calculated as the joint probability of the entrepreneur and new person being proficient in the same Indian language.

name: Occupational similarity
definition: Similarity of occupation; in this context, a focal entrepreneur and a newly encountered person are occupationally similar when the new person is also an entrepreneur/business founder.

name: Task complementarity
definition: The extent of overlap between entrepreneurs' current task priorities and the resources potentially available from a new person.

name: Social similarity
definition: Similarity between individuals on sociodemographic attributes; research on homophily distinguishes ascribed attributes (largely inherited) such as race, ethnicity, and gender from achieved attributes such as occupation or education.

name: Match quality
definition: Fit between an entrepreneur and a new person on the match criteria (social similarity and task complementarity) identified in the hypotheses.

name: Interfirm exchange relationship formation
authors_terms: ["initiation of economic exchange", "formation of interfirm exchange ties", "exchange relationship formation", "interfirm tie formation", "formation of economic exchange relationships"]
definition: The formation (or not) of an interfirm exchange relationship between a focal entrepreneur's venture and the organization represented by a new person.

name: Firm market value
definition: A firm's Tobin's q value is used to measure firm performance. Tobin's q is defined as the ratio of the market value of the firm to the replacement cost of its tangible assets.

name: Developing country foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["NewDevelopingFDI", "developing country investment", "FDI in developing countries", "developing country location investment"]
definition: A firm's foreign investment is defined as a firm's number of advanced country foreign subsidiaries (NewAdvancedFDI) and a firm's number of developing country foreign subsidiaries (NewDevelopingFDI) for each year from 1981 to 2000. All other countries are classified as developing countries (including Mexico and most Asian countries (not Japan), Central and South American countries, Eastern European countries, ex-Soviet bloc countries, Russia and African countries).

name: Advanced country foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["NewAdvancedFDI", "advanced country investment", "FDI in advanced countries", "advanced country location investment"]
definition: A firm's foreign investment is defined as a firm's number of advanced country foreign subsidiaries (NewAdvancedFDI) and a firm's number of developing country foreign subsidiaries (NewDevelopingFDI) for each year from 1981 to 2000. Advanced countries include the United States, Canada, Western European countries, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.

name: Level of multinational operations
authors_terms: ["multinationality levels", "levels of multinational operations", "levels of multinationality"]
definition: Firms can be categorized as having different levels of multinationality, based on how extensive their operations are in foreign countries. Firms with low levels of multinational operations have few foreign subsidiaries (and have less ability to manage or hedge risk, and fewer learning experiences from previous foreign investments), while firms with high levels of multinational operations have much more extensive operations abroad.

name: Industry knowledge intensity
authors_terms: ["knowledge intensity of the firm's industry", "high knowledge-intensive industries", "low knowledge-intensive industries", "high R&D-intensive industries"]
definition: High knowledge-intensive industries are characterized by relatively large outlays on R&D with the knowledge coming from this R&D transferable across many different locations. Low knowledge-intensive industries are characterized by competitive advantage that rests more on country-specific factors, with foreign investment in these industries often associated with the exploitation of raw materials and cheap labor.

name: Temporal frame of reference
authors_terms: ["temporal frames of reference", "ego-moving frame", "time-moving frame", "ego-moving language", "time-moving language", "spatiotemporal language"]
definition: The analogies that map time to space are known as temporal frames of reference. The time-moving frame is one in which the future 'happens' and moves toward the speaker (e.g., 'the deadline is approaching'), whereas the ego-moving frame is one in which an agentic speaker moves toward the future (e.g., 'we are approaching the deadline').

name: Control beliefs
authors_terms: ["control beliefs", "locus of control", "internal locus of control", "strategic locus of control"]
definition: Locus of control is 'the degree to which persons expect that a reinforcement or an outcome of their behavior is contingent on their own behavior or personal characteristics (internal) versus the degree to which persons expect that the reinforcement or outcome is a function of chance, luck, or fate, is under the control of powerful others, or is simply unpredictable (external)'. Managerial agency is important to future-oriented action.

name: Discounting of future returns
authors_terms: ["discount rates", "discounting of future returns", "intertemporal choice", "present time perspective", "how people value future returns"]
definition: The matching task is 'an established way of measuring intertemporal choice that predicts behavior in the face of trade-offs between short- and long-term returns'. In the task, subjects indicate how much money they would need to receive after 1, 5, 10, and 20 years instead of receiving $1,000 tomorrow, and the points of indifference can be converted into discount rates over the various time intervals.

name: Support for long-term strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["support for the acquisition", "support for the long-term decision", "long-term focus in strategic decisions", "long-term decision", "long-term strategies"]
definition: Subjects are asked whether a likely NPV-positive acquisition is sensible when 'if you advise in favor of the acquisition, the firm will probably miss its short-term earnings forecast even if the acquisition leads to earnings increasing in subsequent years'. Support of this kind underpins decisions that privilege long-term returns over short-term returns.

name: Alliance formation for new resources
authors_terms: ["alliances for new resources", "new-resource alliances", "formation of alliances for new resources"]
definition: New resources: the discontinuity required firms to develop new resources in the form of information technology (IT) and other combinatorial platforms and screening tools to facilitate rapid evaluation and management of large volumes of complex data.

name: Alliance formation for reinforced resources
definition: Reinforced resources: to gain from the new resources, firms also invested in complementary areas such as artificial intelligence and mathematical modelling, which could be applied to instrumentation and robotic testing for rapid screening of compounds. The discontinuity reinforced the value of such resources.

name: Alliance formation for challenged resources
definition: Challenged resources: the value of other complementary resources was challenged by the technological discontinuity. These resources needed to be transformed through changes to their technical or functional bases to co-specialized assets that support new resources.

name: Alliance termination for reinforced resources
authors_terms: ["alliances for reinforced resources terminated", "termination of alliances for reinforced resources"]
definition: The second means of portfolio reconfiguration is termination, which takes place through two mechanisms. First, firms can terminate alliances to reflect reduction in the value of particular resources, which we term a resource-value mechanism; second, firms can drop alliances from their portfolios in order to reduce the cost of managing multiple alliances, which is a carrying-capacity mechanism.

name: Alliance termination for challenged resources
authors_terms: ["alliances for challenged resources terminated", "termination of alliances for challenged resources"]
definition: The second means of portfolio reconfiguration is termination, which takes place through two mechanisms. Firms may terminate alliances for challenged resources either because they decide not to invest in transforming them or to free carrying capacity within the alliance portfolio.

name: Alliance termination for unaffected resources
authors_terms: ["alliances for unaffected resources terminated", "termination of alliances for unaffected resources"]
definition: Because the value of unaffected resources is unchanged, firms may continue to use these resources; however, carrying capacity limits may lead firms to terminate alliances for unaffected resources in order to focus on the alliances for new resources.

name: Perceived negative inequity
definition: The firm perceives negative inequity if its own outcome-to-input ratio is less than its partner's. A firm experiences equity when it perceives that the outcomes it and its partner receive are proportional to their respective inputs to their relationship.

name: Perceived positive inequity
definition: The firm perceives positive inequity if its own outcome-to-input ratio exceeds that of its partner. Positive inequity leads to guilt for not pulling one's own weight or for receiving disproportionately great outcomes.

name: Hostility toward partner
definition: Negative inequity incites hostility in an undercompensated firm, which resents its perceived outcomes being below what they should be. Hostility is measured by items assessing hostility, anger, frustration, and resentment toward the principal supplier.

name: Trust in partner
definition: Trust was measured with ten items, five assessing the supplier's honesty and five measuring the supplier's benevolence. Negative inequity undermines prediction-based trust, and a firm facing undercompensation may conclude that the partner does not have the firm's best interests at heart.

name: Relationship continuity
definition: Relationship continuity was measured with a three-item scale addressing the dealer's confidence that the relationship would continue. It is a key indicator of the health of an interorganizational relationship.

name: Guilt
definition: Positive inequity leads to guilt for not pulling one's own weight or for receiving disproportionately great outcomes; guilt plays a central role in positive inequity. A single item assessed the dealer's guilt when reflecting on the relationship with the supplier.

name: Behavior control
definition: Behavior control, or control over activities that transform inputs into outputs, can be achieved by explicitly setting operating procedures and rules and by managers closely monitoring and evaluating employees' compliance with these rules and procedures.

name: Outcome control
definition: Outcome control, or control over product and service outcomes, can be achieved by setting targets, such as financial results, for employees to pursue and by providing rewards and punishment for, respectively, success and failure in the achievement of these targets, for example, with the help of performance-related contracts, bonuses, or profit-sharing plans.

name: Managerial politics
definition: Managerial politics represent ways managers can contribute to the political environment, for example, by suppressing employees' views if they are critical of well-established ideas or if they challenge the strategic views of management. The measure captures the extent to which employees were encouraged to speak out frankly and the extent to which they were encouraged to challenge or to refute managers' strategic views and ideas.

name: Group politics
authors_terms: ["group politics", "group (i.e., horizontal politics)", "coworker and clique political behavior"]
definition: Group politics represent cliques, informal networks, and favoritism replacing merit in determining who gets ahead in an organization.

name: Strategic initiative performance
authors_terms: ["strategic initiative performance", "initiative performance", "performance of strategic initiatives"]
definition: The performance of strategic initiatives, or the extent to which goals and objectives of initiatives are being achieved.

name: Attention to brokers
authors_terms: ["attention to brokers (ATB)", "attention to brokers' information", "attention to information coming from broker alters"]
definition: 'Our independent variable measures the extent to which a focal engineer paid more attention to information coming from alters with low constraint (i.e., brokers) than he or she did to information coming from alters with high constraint (i.e., non-brokers).'

name: Innovative performance
definition: 'The dependent variable was an engineer's innovative performance score, which captured the degree to which the engineer was involved in and contributed to the process of innovation - from idea generation to implementation - in the firm's products or processes during a calendar year.'

name: Network constraint
definition: 'Network constraint measures the degree to which an individual spans social connections across structural holes (Burt, 1992). People with less constrained networks bridge structural holes and are more likely to access non-redundant information. That is, brokers have a low score in network constraint whereas non-brokers have a high constraint score.'

name: Innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["adopt a disappointing innovation", "first-time order for a fast ferry", "first adoption"]
definition: The dependent variable in the main analysis is the event of placing a first-time order for a fast ferry. A firm remains at risk of adoption until it orders a fast ferry or no longer owns other passenger ships.

name: Use of the innovation by proximate firms
authors_terms: ["use of the innovation by proximate firms", "started using it", "same-nation deliveries", "second-hand receipts"]
definition: Post-adoption use of the innovation by other firms, which reveals value information that can leak to potential adopters; the prediction is that use of the innovation by proximate firms reduces the likelihood that a focal firm will adopt the innovation. Delivery allows the firm to operate the ship and learn its true value, and potentially this information leaks to other firms as well.

name: Adoption by proximate firms
definition: The information that a firm has ordered a fast ferry reveals its decision, and hence can influence the diffusion process; observation of adoptions by other firms in the focal firm's nation is the standard diffusion signal.

name: Sale or abandonment by proximate firms
definition: Post-adoption actions of firms that have used the innovation, from which a potential adopter may infer that the innovation had negative value. When a firm sells its last fast ferry, the author terms that an abandonment.

name: Common prior company affiliations
authors_terms: ["common prior company affiliations", "common prior company affiliation", "common company affiliations", "shared affiliations"]
definition: Commonalities among the members of a new firm's founding team who have worked at the same company, based on a shared understanding of how organizational work should be managed and coordinated. Founding team members with common prior company affiliations have a shared language, culture, and narratives.

name: Diverse prior company affiliations
authors_terms: ["diverse prior company affiliations", "diverse company affiliations", "diverse affiliations"]
definition: Founding teams whose members come from a wide array of past companies bring diverse knowledge and contacts to their firms, and a variety of perspectives that stimulates innovation and the discovery of new alternatives. This diversity provides access to external social capital, new insights and knowledge.

name: Exploitative behavior
definition: Exploitative behaviors are those that build upon existing products and technologies and are efforts to seek competitive advantage through technical enhancements or cost advantages. Exploitative behaviors are variance-decreasing and efficiency-oriented and involve incremental innovation, implementation, refinement, routinization, local search, and efficiency.

name: Explorative behavior
definition: Exploratory behaviors are those that increase variance and generate internal variety; exploration involves radical innovation, creating new markets and products, experimentation, broad search, frequent change, and discovery. Here the focus is on exploration through technical innovation.

name: Combined prior company affiliations
authors_terms: ["both common and diverse prior company affiliations", "high common and high diverse prior company affiliations"]
definition: Teams with both common and diverse prior company affiliations will have the shared understandings to efficiently transmit knowledge and the unique perspectives to support innovation and change. Having a mix of both diverse and common team affiliations should be a precursor to organizational ambidexterity.

name: Firm growth
definition: In new ventures, firm growth is an important marker of success; particularly in this time period and region, firms desired growth. Firm growth was measured as growth in employees.

name: Environmental performance
definition: We measure environmental performance using corporate-wide toxic pollution, an outcome metric employed by many other scholars. Specifically, we use the total pounds of toxic chemical emissions each firm reported to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) as production waste, transfers, and releases.

name: Initial environmental rating
authors_terms: ["initial rating poor", "initial rating mixed or good", "initial KLD environmental ratings"]
definition: We created a dummy variable, initial rating poor, to indicate firms that had initial KLD environmental ratings consisting only of concerns (no strengths). Such a rating suggests corporate behavior that violates taken-for-granted norms.

name: Environmental regulatory stringency
definition: Firms in industries subject to significant environmental regulations 'face greater exposure to the public policy process', and face a higher risk that a poor rating might provoke negative media coverage and concern within the communities surrounding their plants. Firms that face greater regulatory threats are thus more likely to invest in environmental improvements.

name: Environmental efficiency
definition: Environmental efficiency (or 'eco-efficiency') refers to the extent to which a firm's environmental impacts or resource intensity are minimized, normalized by its production level.

name: Inexperience with regulations
authors_terms: ["firms' inexperience with regulations", "inadequate experience in dealing with the CP program", "less-experienced firms", "first certification", "less-knowledgeable firms"]
definition: Firms' inadequate experience in dealing with the CP program. A plant that was the first to become certified in the program within the company would be less experienced with program details.

name: Noncompliance record
authors_terms: ["noncompliance record", "records of noncompliance", "environmental violations", "historically poor compliers"]
definition: Records of firms' environmental violations detected through online monitoring and regular on-site inspections before joining the Cleaner Production program; historically poor compliers are likely to be under the spotlight of inspection.

name: Novel technology adoption
authors_terms: ["novel technology", "novel technologies", "adoption of novel technology that is consistent with social goals"]
definition: Plants using novel technologies, i.e., those that use relatively clean fuel sources such as natural gas, biomass, and biogas; established technologies are coal-fired plants burning 'brown' coal.

name: Institutional linkage to government
authors_terms: ["institutional linkage to the government", "inadequate institutional linkage to the government", "less-connected firms", "political connections", "linkage to the government"]
definition: Firms' structural linkage to the government. Less-connected firms lack political channels to the state and are often in an inferior position relative to those with such channels; the measure is based on the proportion of majority shareholders that are SOEs or directly owned by the government.

name: Intermediary choice
authors_terms: ["intermediary choice", "selection of public intermediaries", "selection of private intermediaries", "choice of public intermediaries", "reliance on private intermediaries", "selection decisions"]
definition: The dependent variable intermediary choice was a dummy: a power plant was coded as 1 if it hired a public intermediary (e.g., local EPB-affiliated service center and government-sponsored environmental associations) to audit its CP program implementation and 0 if it hired a private intermediary (e.g., university lab, industrial association, or private consulting firm).

name: Regulatory change
definition: Regulatory change was coded as 1 if a power plant filed a CP application within these three years and 0 otherwise. The author focuses on regulatory changes that always happen to tighten, since the general trend is more tightening as opposed to lax regulatory requirements.

name: Political commitment to environmental protection
definition: Political commitment to environmental protection was deemed equal to 1 if a sampled plant was located in a so-called National Environmental Model City (NEMC) or an NEMC-to-be within two years of joining the CP program, and 0 otherwise. The NEMC policy was initiated in 1996 to encourage local political leaders to address pollution and aim for sustainable urban development.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "marketization", "government and market relations", "government intervention in the market", "institutional efficiency"]
definition: The National Economic Research Institute (NERI) index captures local institutional efficiency in China; the first dimension, government and market relations, captures the business costs of dealing with governmental control, the proportion of resource allocation by the market, and reduction in government interference in the business sector. The higher the index, the more noninterventionist the government is.

name: Organizational structure
definition: The four elementary types of structure commonly used by MNCs are worldwide functional divisions, international divisions, geographical regions, and worldwide product divisions. These basic structures also become the building blocks for more complex structures (matrix and mixed structures).

name: Product division dimension
authors_terms: ["product division dimension", "worldwide product division dimension", "PD dimension"]
definition: The structure providing the most product-related information-processing capacity between the centers of product knowledge in the parent and the foreign subsidiaries is the worldwide product division structure. It utilizes several separate information-processing channels between a subsidiary and the parent, one for each product division in the subsidiary.

name: International division dimension
definition: An international division structure concentrates the limited international expertise of a firm in one division so that it can attain a critical mass and level of specialization that can then be efficiently focused on a relatively small set of foreign operations. Since it hinders information processing and synergy between international and domestic operations, this loss is most acceptable when foreign operations are small.

name: Geographical region dimension
definition: Geographical region structures largely provide good coordination within a region (and poor coordination between regions), and such coordination is primarily required to optimize regional sourcing strategies.

name: Worldwide functional or product division dimension
authors_terms: ["worldwide functional division dimension", "worldwide product division dimension", "FD dimension", "PD dimension"]
definition: The information-processing capacities of the worldwide functional and product division structures clearly facilitate implementing a global sourcing strategy, with high levels of intracompany transfers. The first provides global coordination across all manufacturing operations within a company. The second provides global coordination across all manufacturing operations within a product or business area.

name: Foreign product diversity
definition: As product diversity increases, there is an increase in both market diversity (environmental complexity) and manufacturing and technical diversity (technological complexity).

name: Size of foreign operations
definition: Size of foreign operations (as a percentage of total company operations) was one of the two key contingency variables of the Stopford and Wells (1972) Model.

name: Size of foreign manufacturing
definition: Size of foreign manufacturing was established by Egelhoff (1988a) as an important discriminator between firms with geographical region structures and firms with worldwide product division structures. Regional product development and sourcing can only develop after there is sufficient foreign manufacturing to largely supply foreign sales from foreign manufacturing.

name: Intracompany transfers
definition: Intracompany transfers between the German parent and its foreign subsidiaries as a percentage of total sales capture one of the more important new trends in international strategy: more global sourcing patterns.

name: Size of foreign R&D
definition: Foreign R&D as a percentage of total R&D captures the international dispersion of technology development, one of the more important new trends in international strategy.

name: R&D centralization
authors_terms: ["R&D Centralization", "centralization of R&D", "centralized R&D decision making", "internal R&D structure", "R&D organizational structure"]
definition: R&D Centralization captures whether decisions related to R&D are being made centrally within the client firm. In centralized R&D organizations, authority over R&D decisions rests with a single R&D head who is responsible for all consequential innovation-related decisions of the firm rather than multiple unit heads or therapeutic area leads.

name: Client intellectual property rights
authors_terms: ["client's intellectual property rights", "client's IP rights", "control rights over intellectual property", "upstream rights"]
definition: Upstream rights, or rights related to intellectual property, generate long-term value and can provide the firm with competitive advantages in the longer run. As the alliance's outcome is uncertain and contracts are incomplete by nature, the control of property rights plays a critical role in a firm capturing the value from the alliance.

name: Vertical alliance scope
authors_terms: ["vertical scope of the alliance", "Vertical Alliance Scope", "vertical, or functional, scope"]
definition: Vertical scope pertains to the range of functional activities partners engage in, from narrowly focused endeavors such as R&D to more comprehensive collaborations that also span manufacturing, marketing, and distribution.

name: Horizontal alliance scope
definition: Horizontal scope involves the diversity of therapeutic areas covered in an alliance. In the biopharmaceutical industry, each therapeutic area is considered a different product market, and firms ally with each other in one or more product markets.

name: Technology interdependence
definition: In R&D alliances, partners can depend on each other to perform upstream activities, such as joint research and technology development; this has been referred to as reciprocal interdependence, where both partners mutually depend on each other to develop products or perform certain activities.

name: Internal R&D scope
authors_terms: ["Scope of R&D (Client Firm)", "scope of R&D conducted within the client firm", "internal R&D scope", "breadth of R&D within the client firm"]
definition: The breadth of R&D within the client firm reflects its potential ability to work with diverse pieces of knowledge, and a broad R&D scope enables a firm to benefit from a wider breadth of knowledge search. Conversely, a narrow internal R&D scope may limit the potential benefits of centralization.

name: Underperformance duration
authors_terms: ["underperformance duration", "duration of underperformance", "duration", "length of time that a firm has been performing below its aspiration level"]
definition: We define underperformance duration as the length of time that a firm has been performing below its aspiration level.

name: Innovative search magnitude
authors_terms: ["innovative search magnitude", "search magnitude", "magnitude", "magnitude of innovative search"]
definition: Innovative search magnitude represents the total amount of effort firms put into innovation activities, which in high-tech companies is typically governed by R&D outlays. It is the total amount of effort devoted to innovation activities.

name: Innovative search scope
definition: Innovative search also varies in terms of its scope, which is the degree to which new knowledge is pursued. A narrow search scope indicates that a firm uses knowledge elements that are closely related to its existing knowledge base.

name: Innovative search depth
definition: While search scope refers to the breadth of knowledge exploration, search depth is defined as the degree to which a firm's search revisits prior knowledge. That is, the degree to which existing knowledge is reused and exploited.

name: Firm performance
definition: Following Bromiley and Washburn (2011) and Chen and Miller (2007), we use return on assets (ROA) as a measure of performance, capturing efficiency. This variable is lagged 1 year relative to the dependent variable.

name: Social aspiration level
definition: Generally, aspirations are formed by benchmarking performance relative to firms' own historical performance and/or the performance of industry peers (social aspiration). Industry aspiration at t-1 is measured as the median performance of firms in the same industry as the focal firm at t-2.

name: CEO risk taking
authors_terms: ["risk taking", "strategic risk", "CEO risk taking", "risk-taking composite", "strategic risk profile"]
definition: Risk taking reflects the CEO's choice of investment risk from among the firms' investment opportunity set. The authors are concerned with measuring the degree of overall strategic risk a CEO knowingly accepts when deciding to increase or decrease investment in various strategic alternatives.

name: Variability of essential compensation
authors_terms: ["variability of essential compensation", "variability of essential pay", "variability of pay", "pay variability"]
definition: Conceptually, variability combines both the potential losses to compensation as well as potential gains. A high score on the measure corresponds to high variability in those elements of compensation that are largely devoted to essential expenses.

name: Downside risk of essential compensation
authors_terms: ["downside risk of essential compensation", "downside pay risk", "downside risk to essential pay", "downside compensation risk"]
definition: Downside risk is distinguished from variability in that it captures the potential for losing something of value, while variability captures fluctuations in the future size of that value. Downside risk exposure to essential pay corresponds to the potential of losing a portion of pay critical to maintaining the executive's standard of living.

name: Employment risk
definition: The threat of dismissal seriously jeopardizes the CEO's future income. Employment risk represents an even more severe threat to wealth than either form of compensation risk.

name: Value of unexercised stock options
authors_terms: ["value of stock options", "value of unexercised stock options", "intrinsic value of stock options", "options value"]
definition: BAM stresses the important role that the 'intrinsic value' of unexercised stock options may play in determining the risk-taking posture of the CEO, and argues that a portion of the current value of positively valued stock options, like that of owned stock, becomes part of perceived current wealth.

name: Current capability relevance
authors_terms: ["capability relevance", "current capability relevance", "composite degree of relevance", "CDR"]
definition: Capability relevance is defined as the aggregate of the part of each individual capability that can contribute to the development and commercialization of a focal product. A firm's current capability relevance is measured annually during the course of market development; it captures the part of a firm's overall capabilities that matches what is required to enter and succeed in a product market.

name: Initial capability relevance
definition: A firm's initial capability relevance is its capability relevance with respect to a product market set at the time of market emergence. It distinguishes the initial condition of a firm from its current capability relevance, which is measured annually during the course of market development.

name: Entry timing
definition: The timing of a firm's entry into a product market, estimated through a hazard-rate framework in which earlier entry corresponds to higher entry rate; higher entry rate implies higher entry probability by any given fixed time.

name: Time since market emergence
definition: Time since market emergence is the number of years elapsed since the emergence of the focal product market, entered as t in the models. It is used to trace how capability relevance evolves over the course of market development.

name: Product development failure
definition: Product development failure results when concerns regarding the safety and/or efficacy of the drug, based on the previous phase of testing, prevent its progress to the next phase of development. A drug is recognized as a failure if its final recorded status in the Pharmaprojects database indicated that the firm permanently discontinued the drug development.

name: Novel drug innovation
authors_terms: ["novel drug innovation (NDI)", "novel product development", "new chemical entities (NCEs)", "novel knowledge creation"]
definition: We conceptualize NDI as the creation of knowledge that is new to the world (i.e., knowledge that was previously undiscovered), as reflected in new chemical entities (NCEs).

name: Prolific inventors
definition: Prolific inventors, identified as 'individuals who have demonstrated disproportionately high levels of performance and superior visibility in the external market'. After calculating the productivity of all of the inventors in our sample, we categorized certain inventors as prolific inventors if their individual productivity was greater than two SDs above the mean.

name: Prolific inventors' collaborative strength
definition: Prolific inventors with a great deal of collaborative strength, reflected in extensive and repeated intrafirm research collaborations, gain broader recognition as innovative leaders in the firm. We operationalized a prolific inventor's collaborative strength as the level of co-invention frequency between a prolific inventor and his or her colleagues in the firm in a prior 5-year window.

name: Prolific inventors' tenure
definition: We operationalized a prolific inventor's tenure as inventor i's organizational tenure in the firm, as defined by the total number of years since inventor i's first patent application in the firm.

name: Intangible asset stock
authors_terms: ["intangible asset stock", "asset stock", "knowledge stock", "R&D assets", "R&D stock"]
definition: Dierickx and Cool (1989) develop a descriptive model of asset stocks which they define as "flows in" minus the "flows out," where inflows are instantaneous investments in an asset stock, and the outflows are the erosion of existing asset stocks. Intangible asset stocks at the beginning of a period combine with current period investments to create additional intangible assets.

name: R&D investment
authors_terms: ["asset flows", "current period investments", "investment (I)", "current year spending on R&D"]
definition: Investment in intangible asset stock in period t; in the empirical model it is measured as current year spending on R&D. The first hypothesis contrasts these asset flows with asset stocks as the source of rents.

name: Firm output
definition: Output of firm i in year t, modeled with the knowledge stock, physical capital, labor and industry knowledge spillovers; in the empirical model output is measured as total firm sales in the observation year.

name: Intangible asset accumulation process
authors_terms: ["asset accumulation process", "characteristics of the asset accumulation process", "intermediate good-production function"]
definition: The intangible asset accumulation process described in the literature resembles an internal intermediate good-production function-firms produce their intangible asset stocks from existing asset stocks and current period investments. Time compression diseconomy, asset mass efficiency and asset erosion are modeled as features of that process.

name: Asset erosion
definition: Asset erosion is the intangible asset equivalent of physical capital depreciation. Intangible assets are not consumed in use, but their value may nevertheless erode, either because the firm is unable to maintain proprietary rights, or because new assets or technological advances render them obsolete.

name: Time compression diseconomy
definition: Time compression diseconomies are described in Dierickx and Cool (1989) as diminishing returns to current period investments. The phenomenon is referred to as convex adjustment costs, wherein the cost of expansion increases if the rate of expansion is accelerated.

name: Asset mass efficiency
definition: Asset mass efficiencies are economies of scale in the production of intangible asset stock from existing asset stock, such that the productivity of investments in the current period increases with larger asset stocks.

name: Rival mobility
definition: The mobility deterrence literature examines the ability of capital accumulation to deter rival mobility. If the accumulation process inhibits rival mobility, consistent investment should yield asset stocks whose value increases in perpetuity-preventing firms from catching up.

name: Commitment
authors_terms: ["commitment", "willingness to exert effort on behalf of the relationship"]
definition: Commitment refers to the willingness of trading partners to exert effort on behalf of the relationship. It suggests a future orientation in which partners attempt to build a relationship that can weather unanticipated problems.

name: Coordination
definition: Coordination is related to boundary definition and reflects the set of tasks each party expects the other to perform.

name: Interdependence
definition: Interdependence results from a relationship in which both firms perceive mutual benefits from interacting and in which any loss of autonomy will be equitably compensated through the expected gains.

name: Trust
definition: Trust is the belief that a party's word is reliable and that a party will fulfill its obligation in an exchange.

name: Communication quality
definition: Communication quality is a key aspect of information transmission; quality includes such aspects as the accuracy, timeliness, adequacy, and credibility of information exchanged.

name: Participation in planning
definition: Participation refers to the extent to which partners engage jointly in planning and goal setting.

name: Information sharing
authors_terms: ["information sharing", "extent of information sharing between partners"]
definition: Information sharing refers to the extent to which critical, often proprietary, information is communicated to one's partner.

name: Joint problem solving
definition: Firms in a strategic partnership are motivated to engage in joint problem solving since they are, by definition, linked in order to manage an environment that is more uncertain and/or turbulent than each alone can control. When parties engage in joint problem solving, a mutually satisfactory solution may be reached, thereby enhancing partnership success.

name: Persuasion
definition: Partners often attempt to persuade each other to participate in adopting particular solutions to the conflict situation; these persuasive attempts will generally be more constructive than the use of coercion or domination.

name: Destructive conflict resolution
authors_terms: ["destructive conflict resolution techniques", "severe resolution", "domination and harsh words"]
definition: The use of destructive conflict resolution techniques (e.g., domination, confrontation) are seen as counter-productive and are very likely to strain the fabric of the partnership. These include domination and harsh words.

name: Outside arbitration
definition: In some partnerships, the method of conflict resolution is institutionalized, and third party arbitration is sought; 'internal resolution' (i.e., not relying on outside parties) shows a greater promise of long-term success.

name: Smoothing over problems
definition: Conflict resolution techniques such as smoothing over or ignoring/avoiding the issue are at odds with the norms and values espoused in more successful strategic partnerships; smoothing or avoiding fails to go to the root cause of the conflict and tends to undermine the partnership's goal of mutual gain.

name: Partnership success
definition: The authors use two indicators of partnership success: an objective indicator (sales volume flowing between dyadic partners) and an affective measure (satisfaction of one party with the other). A partnership which generates satisfaction exists when performance expectations have been achieved.

name: Private paying patient proportion
authors_terms: ["proportion of private paying patients", "proportion of non-Medicare/Medicaid inpatient days", "private paying patients"]
definition: The share of the patients a hospital treats who pay privately rather than through Medicare or Medicaid. Hospitals with low proportions of private paying patients have reduced opportunities to ameliorate the effect of the prospective payment system, since cost shifting occurs when private insurance patients are charged more than Medicare patients to make up for revenue losses on Medicare reimbursements.

name: Occupancy rate
definition: Occupancy captures the extent to which hospitals are covering their costs of medical and nonmedical personnel (e.g., nurses) effectively. In the presence of economies of scale, hospitals with lower levels of output and, consequently, occupancy will have higher costs.

name: Range of services offered
authors_terms: ["full range of services", "range of services", "service offerings", "assortment of medical services"]
definition: Hospitals produce a varied assortment of medical services and other outputs such as education, training and research. If economies of scope are present among hospital services, then a firm that does not offer the full range of services will have higher costs.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Failure to adapt to the changed (post-PPS) environment results in the demise of the organization through closure or bankruptcy; organizations that are misaligned will fail, they will be selected out of the population.

name: Economies of scale
authors_terms: ["economies of scale", "scale economies", "increasing short-run returns to scale"]
definition: Scale economies are cost advantages based on the amount of output in a given period. If an increase in output is more than proportional to the increase in inputs, economies of scale are said to exist.

name: Economies of scope
authors_terms: ["economies of scope", "scope economies", "local economies of scope", "cost complementarities"]
definition: Economies of scope are advantages based on the composition of the output, as opposed to advantages due to output volume. Economies of scope exist if the cost of jointly producing some set of outputs is less than the cost of producing the same outputs separately.

name: Relative competitive position
authors_terms: ["relative competitive position", "relative effort level", "competitive advantage (CA)", "competitive parity (CP)", "competitive disadvantage (CD)", "strategic effort dimension"]
definition: If the quality of effort is assumed to be the same for all competitors, then the relative effort levels more, about the same and less, roughly correspond to competitive advantage (CA), competitive parity (CP) and competitive disadvantage (CD), respectively. The competitive profile of a business along each strategy effort dimension during a period is described by its relative position relative to its competitors.

name: Market share
definition: Since the PIMS database pools cross-sectional data from a sample of businesses across different industries, it seems more appropriate to use relative market share, which captures the competitive essence of the business's position. The PIMS study defines relative market share for business 'i' in terms of the market share of business 'i' and the market shares of its three largest competitors.

name: Change in relative competitive position
authors_terms: ["change in relative competitive position", "change in competitive profile"]
definition: The change in relative competitive position of business 'i' along the jth strategic dimension over the period 't' to 't + 1', ranging from positive changes (competitive disadvantage to competitive advantage, disadvantage to parity, parity to advantage) to negative changes (advantage to parity, parity to disadvantage, advantage to disadvantage).

name: Change in market share
authors_terms: ["percentage change in market share", "point change in market share", "change in market share"]
definition: The change in market share of business 'i' over the period 't' to 't + 1', expressed either as the percentage change in market share or as the point change in market share of the business over that period.

name: Acolyte status
authors_terms: ["acolyte", "acolytes", "acolyte status", "high-reputation ties", "ties to high-reputation industry leaders"]
definition: An acolyte is an individual who has experience working on the same management team as a high-reputation leader. Acolytes are subordinates with work connections to industry leaders who possess high reputations derived from prior performance.

name: Evaluative certainty
definition: We define evaluative certainty as the extent to which attributions concerning a social actor's characteristics and capabilities are shared by others within a social field. This is the extent to which information is available concerning an individual's relevant work performance.

name: Knowledge match with high-reputation leader
definition: Those tasked with evaluating candidates are likely to perceive greater coherence and to assume greater expertise when there is an affinity of specialization between the leader and the acolyte. The authors determined whether a particular acolyte's experience matched that of their associated high-reputation leader.

name: Promotion
definition: Coaching positions were coded according to a five-level hierarchical scale reflective of coaching tiers; the overall binary coach-year promotion variable was coded as 1 in a particular year if an individual worked at a level higher than that of the previous year, and 0 otherwise.

name: Post-promotion outcome
definition: Hypotheses 3a and 3b are competing hypotheses concerning the relative likelihood of acolytes and non-acolytes achieving superior outcomes after being promoted. A positive outcome was coded as being a further promotion or lateral move, and a negative outcome as being a demotion.

name: First partners' reputation
authors_terms: ["first partners' reputation", "reputation of a newcomer's initial partners", "initial partners' reputation", "partners' reputation"]
definition: Reputation is a 'perceptual representation of a company's past actions and future prospects that describes the firm's overall appeal to all its key constituents when compared to other leading rivals' (Fombrun, 1996: 72); it represents an economic signal of quality rooted in organizations' past achievements and performance. The construct is applied to the coinvestor(s) in the newcomer's first recorded syndicated investment, capturing the quality of the partners with whom the newcomer first affiliated.

name: First partners' past cohesion
authors_terms: ["first partners' past cohesion", "past cohesion of its initial partners' network", "cohesion of the network that a newcomer entered"]
definition: The extent and intensity of past collaborations between the newcomer's first partners prior to entering the syndicate with the newcomer; it is calculated as the valued density of relations among the first partners, excluding the newcomer, in the five-year window preceding the formation of the syndicate. Cohesive dense networks are known to promote trust, curb opportunism, and facilitate the transfer of norms in networks.

name: Network status
definition: Network status represents how centrally positioned an organization is relative to others in the industry, and status is a sociological concept based on current affiliations with central others. Achieving status is considered an important organizational outcome in itself.

name: Industry learning-by-doing rate
authors_terms: ["LBD rate", "learning-by-doing rate", "industry-level LBD rate", "learning intensity rate"]
definition: LBD rates refer to the degree to which production performance in an industry is dependent on accumulated experience in direct production. Industries with higher LBD rates are those where performance improvement is very sensitive to own experiences in real production environments (not in laboratory settings).

name: Learning-by-doing rate distance
authors_terms: ["Difference of LBD Rate", "LBD distance", "distance between the LBD rates in a diversifying firm's home and target industries"]
definition: The greater the distance between the LBD rates in a diversifying firm's home and target industries, the less likely the firm is to have second-order knowledge relevant to the target industry. It is measured by the absolute difference between LBD Ratei and the LBD rate in target industry j.

name: Diversifying entry
definition: Diversifying Entryit is coded as one if firm i is reported as being involved in at least one new industry in year t where it was not in year t-1 and zero otherwise; Diversifying Entryijt is coded as one if firm i is reported as being involved in target industry j in year t while it was not in year t-1 and zero otherwise.

name: Perceived quality
definition: A dimension of organizational reputation that captures the degree to which stakeholders evaluate an organization positively on a specific attribute, such as ability to produce quality products.

name: Prominence
authors_terms: ["prominence", "prominence in the minds of stakeholders", "collective recognition", "recognition"]
definition: A dimension of organizational reputation that captures the degree to which an organization receives large-scale collective recognition in its organizational field.

name: Price premium
definition: The higher prices that buyers are willing to pay for the products of an organization with a favorable reputation, because reputation reduces stakeholder uncertainty about the value of future exchanges.

name: Quality of inputs
definition: The quality of the resources an organization uses as inputs in its production or service delivery processes; in the educational process of an MBA program, incoming students constitute the major resource input.

name: Quality of productive assets
authors_terms: ["quality of productive assets", "quality of the productive assets", "quality of its knowledge assets"]
definition: The quality of the productive assets of a firm, and especially the quality of its knowledge assets, which can be used as a signal of quality because they affect the quality of products.

name: Position in media rankings
authors_terms: ["media rankings", "position in media rankings", "rankings and ratings"]
definition: Direct evaluations of organizations offered by media organizations in the form of rankings and ratings, which reduce stakeholders' need to evaluate the attributes and quality of an organization directly.

name: Expert intermediary certifications
authors_terms: ["expert intermediary certifications", "certifications of achievement", "certifications from expert intermediaries", "publications in premier journals"]
definition: Certifications by expert intermediaries that an organization's level of achievement meets explicit or implicit standards of excellence in a given field, granted after rigorous scrutiny using specialized knowledge.

name: Affiliation with high-status actors
authors_terms: ["affiliation with high-status actors", "ties to high-status actors"]
definition: An organization's affiliations with high-status actors, which increase prominence because such affiliation enables stakeholders to assume that the high-status actors, who are believed to be well informed, have evaluated the organization positively.

name: Risk planning
authors_terms: ["planning", "risk planning", "planning and risk management", "classic planning and risk management methods"]
definition: This incremental search based on an initial solution corresponds to risk planning: the team chooses estimated best values at the outset (a 'plan') and makes small adjustments in execution to respond to uncertainty in the precise parameter values (risk management).

name: Trial-and-error learning
definition: Trial-and-error learning refers to actively searching for new information and flexibly adjusting activities and targets to this new information, applying new and original problem solving (not only triggering preset contingency plans) as new information becomes available.

name: Selectionism
definition: Selectionism refers to trying several candidate solutions and selecting the one that works best ex post, or in other words, generating enough variety that at least some variants will yield desirable results.

name: Unforeseeable uncertainty
