definition: Unforeseeable uncertainty refers to the presence of influence variables that are relevant to the venture's success, but cannot be recognized by the management team at the outset, and cannot, therefore, be included in initial planning and risk analysis.

name: Complexity
definition: Complexity refers to the number of decision variables a venture has to consider and the number of interactions among these decision variables. An interaction means that the best value of decision variable a1 depends on the value of decision variable a2.

name: Venture performance
definition: The authors conceptualize a venture as an outcome represented by a payoff function and ask which management approach offers effective decisions that lead to high performance (value of solutions produced). In the survey this is the respondent's qualitative evaluation of the success of the startup considering all aspects of performance.

name: Market tests
definition: The product can be 'perfectly' tested, that means, tested under fully realistic circumstances, for example, fully functional in the true market, so that the truly best of the trials that have been developed can be chosen.

name: Similarity in domain knowledge
definition: A firm's domain knowledge refers to the knowledge it possesses in distinct technological areas. Similarity in domain knowledge exists between two firms when they possess knowledge in common domains.

name: Dissimilarity in architectural knowledge
authors_terms: ["dissimilarity in architectural knowledge", "dissimilarity in architectural knowledge (common domain pairs)", "architectural knowledge", "coupling"]
definition: Architectural knowledge refers to the knowledge that a firm possesses about how to combine knowledge from different domains. Dissimilarities in architectural knowledge exist between two firms when they have different levels of coupling between domains, and the authors focus on dissimilarity in architectural knowledge for domain pairs common to both firms.

name: Alliance formation
definition: The dependent variable is alliance formation between the focal firm and its partner. A technological alliance is one that involved R&D, cross-licensing, or manufacturing as per the SDC's classification.

name: Knowledge base decomposability
authors_terms: ["degree of knowledge base decomposability", "decomposability of a firm's knowledge base", "modularity"]
definition: The degree of decomposability indicates the extent to which the knowledge base of a firm can be divided into clusters of domains. A cluster is a group of domains that are tightly coupled with each other.

name: Foreign equity ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign equity ownership", "foreign equity", "equity ownership", "equity levels", "equity position"]
definition: Equity signals the extent of potential for opportunism and the subsequent commitment to the governance process, and thus provides a fine-grained operationalization of the organizational arrangement for mitigating opportunism. Equity also signifies the level of influence a partner can exercise in the IJV, so ceteris paribus a higher level of foreign equity corresponds to greater influence by, and commitment of, the foreign partner.

name: Subsidiary mortality
definition: We treat subsidiary mortality from the foreign partner's perspective. Subsidiary mortality is triggered when the foreign partner ceases its ownership of the subsidiary either by dissolution or by divestment to the local partner.

name: Knowledge creation
definition: Knowledge creation involves searching for, discovering, and integrating knowledge; developing innovative ideas and new practices; and learning from newcomers and parties that furnish external knowledge. Newly created knowledge can be then codified and disseminated for subsequent application.

name: Knowledge application
definition: Knowledge application concerns the exploitation and transformation of knowledge into commercial technologies and products.

name: Academic collaboration
authors_terms: ["academic collaboration", "collaboration between teams of scientists", "collaboration with fellow scientists", "collaboration with academic collaborators"]
definition: Academic collaboration takes place when teams of scientists work together to produce scientific knowledge. Academic collaborators promote research at several stages, including research design, provision of equipment, experiments, analysis, and the write-up of scientific reports.

name: Industry collaboration
definition: University-industry collaboration takes various forms, including corporate visits, consultation, licensing of technology, commercialization, agreements with prospective customers and suppliers, and involvement in research consortia.

name: Internal resources
definition: We focused on the research program's funding as a primary resource that serves for garnering all types of internal resources employed by the research program, including personnel, laboratory equipment, and materials. Internal resources serves for obtaining dedicated personnel, equipment, and materials needed for carrying out scientific research.

name: R&D decentralization
authors_terms: ["R&D Decentralization", "decentralized R&D designs", "decentralized R&D units", "centralized R&D units", "centralization or decentralization of R&D"]
definition: Firms can centralize R&D to obtain scale and scope benefits as well as undertake nonbusiness unit-specific R&D, or they can decentralize R&D to enable the R&D units to focus on business-specific problems and be closer to end markets and customers. The variable R&D Decentralization is set to one if there are multiple R&D groups reporting to separate members within the top management team and zero if the firm has a single centralized R&D group reporting to a TMT member.

name: External sourcing of inventions
authors_terms: ["External Sourcing", "externally sourced inventions", "external sourcing of inventions", "proportion of externally sourced inventions"]
definition: External sourcing of inventions can enable firms to access inventions by drawing on external sources of knowledge and supplement their internal invention efforts. The key dependent variable pertains to the proportion of inventions entering a firm's innovation pipeline that are sourced externally in a focal year, because the theory pertains to the extent to which firms replenish their innovation pipelines with externally sourced inventions.

name: Invention novelty
authors_terms: ["novelty", "degree of novelty", "novelty to the focal firm", "Low Novelty", "Moderate Novelty", "High Novelty"]
definition: We focus on novelty to the focal firm, specifically the extent to which the focal invention draws on a firm's existing, internal knowledge base (Grant 1996, Galunic and Rodan 1998, Macher 2006). Thus, such inventions are novel to the focal firm but not necessarily to the world.

name: Mode of external sourcing
authors_terms: ["modes of external sourcing", "licensing mode", "acquisition or alliance modes", "alliances, acquisitions, and licensing"]
definition: Firms can access external inventions through a variety of modes, such as alliances, acquisitions, and licensing (Van de Vrande et al. 2006, Klueter et al. 2017). These modes represent different levels of resource commitments by firms.

name: Lobbying of a regulatory agency
definition: Lobbying enters this stopping problem not as a source of persuasion tied to a particular submission, but as an ongoing interaction that affects regulators' confidence in a firm's overall vigilance and reliability.

name: Regulatory approval time
authors_terms: ["time to approval", "approval time", "time to approval", "decision speed"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the number of calendar days from the date FDA acknowledges receipt of a 510(k) application to the date of FDA's approval decision. This measure captures the full duration over which discretionary review decisions accumulate, including any AI request periods.

name: Recent product recall
definition: According to the U.S. FDA (2021), a product recall is defined as 'a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that the FDA considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action.' Recalls typically occur due to manufacturing defects, packaging errors, or software glitches.

name: Innovation leadership
definition: This variable captures a firm's innovation reputation as perceived by external audiences, measured as the number of breakthrough patents by each firm in the previous year.

name: Capability value
definition: Value refers to the value creation potential and the strategic importance of an IS process.

name: Capability rarity
definition: Rarity refers to the uniqueness of a capability relative to other (supplier) firms in the factor market. If, for a given IS process, suppliers in factor markets (relative to the focal firm) do not possess knowledge and skills, equipment and machinery or do not have sufficient productive capacity, then the capabilities related to the IS process are rare.

name: Capability inimitability
definition: Inimitability provides an indication of the durability of value-creating and rent-seeking advantage. IS processes are more inimitable when they draw upon several different technologies, are not easily reverse engineered, are associated with tacit knowledge, and are complex.

name: Outsourcing
definition: Respondents provided information on the extent to which a given firm IS process had been outsourced, and this ranges from 0 to 100. The authors equate a lower likelihood of outsourcing with a lower likelihood of a firm using market governance.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: We measure executive ownership as the percentage of shares outstanding owned by the CEO. Ownership is framed as an incentive alignment mechanism that ties managerial wealth to shareholder interests.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: We focus on diversification based on the various business segments of a firm. We measure diversification with both the Berry-Herfindahl (Jacquemin and Berry, 1979) and entropy (Palepu, 1985) diversification indices, calculated using the reported company's sales in the Compustat Business Segment database.

name: Related diversification
definition: Because managers may believe that related and unrelated diversification have different risk profiles, we separate total diversification (entropy) into its components: related (DR) and unrelated (DU) diversification.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Because managers may believe that related and unrelated diversification have different risk profiles, we separate total diversification (entropy) into its components: related (DR) and unrelated (DU) diversification.

name: Competition among syndicate members
authors_terms: ["competition among syndicate members", "competition among VC syndicate members", "multilateral competition"]
definition: Competition among syndicate members arises when they have other investments in the same market niche as a focal syndicate start-up. The degree of competition among VC firms in a given industry segment increases with the number of start-ups in that same industry segment in syndicate members' portfolio.

name: Start-up IPO probability
authors_terms: ["probability of an IPO", "probability of a start-up IPO", "syndicate performance", "success of a VC syndicate"]
definition: The dependent variable in this analysis is the probability that a start-up supported by a focal syndicate will undergo an initial public offering (IPO). The authors focus on the probability of an IPO as an unambiguous indicator of success of a VC syndicate supporting a start-up.

name: Performance relative to historical aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to historical aspirations", "relative historical performance", "relative performance"]
definition: Firms compare realized performance on a specific goal with their aspired performance for that goal and adjust their behavior depending on whether they are below or above their aspiration levels; historical aspirations are constructed from firms' own experience.

name: Performance relative to social aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to social aspirations", "relative social performance", "relative performance"]
definition: Firms compare realized performance on a specific goal with their aspired performance for that goal and adjust their behavior depending on whether they are below or above their aspiration levels; social aspirations are constructed from observation of other similar firms that they include in their reference groups.

name: Historical performance variance
authors_terms: ["historical performance variance", "goal asymmetry", "variance in relative historical performance"]
definition: To capture partners' goal asymmetry, the authors use the within-syndicate variance in the performance relative to historical aspirations variable. The greater the variance in relative performance in a syndicate, the greater the differences among syndicate members with respect to prioritization of the goal of joint investment returns vs. preservation of competitive advantage.

name: Social performance variance
authors_terms: ["social performance variance", "goal asymmetry", "variance in relative social performance"]
definition: To capture partners' goal asymmetry, the authors use the within-syndicate variance in the performance relative to social aspirations variable. The greater the variance in relative performance in a syndicate, the greater the differences among syndicate members with respect to prioritization of the goal of joint investment returns vs. preservation of competitive advantage.

name: Global mimetism
authors_terms: ["global mimetism", "industry-wide mimetism", "total density", "aggregate number of prior alliances"]
definition: We label this aggregate pattern of diffusion global mimetism to highlight that it focuses on the prior alliances in the industry as a whole. The likelihood that two firms will form an alliance in any period depends on the aggregate number of alliances formed in the industry in prior years.

name: Local mimetism
authors_terms: ["local mimetism", "group density", "density of ties across strategic groups"]
definition: We label the idea that firms are more likely to imitate the behavior of those most like them local mimetism. The major driver of network formation in an industry is local mimetism - firms mimic the behavior of those they view as strategically similar or as belonging to the same strategic group.

name: Strategic group membership
definition: Strategic groups can be defined as groups of firms in an industry that share the following characteristics: (a) they follow similar strategies; (b) they resemble each other more closely than any other firms outside the group; and (c) they respond relatively similarly to market opportunities and threats.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "likelihood of an alliance being formed", "probability of an alliance being formed"]
definition: The central concern of this paper is to understand the factors that affect the likelihood that any given pair of firms will form an alliance during any period T.

name: Stock concentration
authors_terms: ["stock concentration", "ownership structure", "concentration of stockholdings", "Herfindahl measure of stock concentration"]
definition: The concentration of stockholdings is the authors' measure of ownership structure; it captures the size distribution of stockholdings, that is, the percentage of common voting stock held in blocks of 0.2 percent and more and the inequality in the size of holdings.

name: Management stockholdings
definition: The extent to which managers are themselves significant stockholders; when managers are themselves significant stockholders, they are more likely to make decisions consistent with maximizing stockholder wealth, since that will maximize their own income and wealth.

name: Unrelated diversification
authors_terms: ["unrelated diversification", "extent of unrelated diversification", "diversification outside the primary two-digit industry"]
definition: The extent to which a firm is active in two-digit SIC industries outside its primary two-digit industry; the greater a firm's involvement in activities outside its primary two-digit industry, the more likely it is that some are unrelated to the firm's core skills.

name: Related diversification
definition: Diversification within a firm's primary two-digit industry, which tends to have the most potential to allow a firm to realize economic benefits from resource sharing or skill transfers and is thus most likely to be associated with superior productivity.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D expenditure per employee", "investment in R&D", "R&D expenditure"]
definition: A firm's long-run commitment to R&D and innovation, proxied by R&D expenditure per employee; investment in R&D is a high risk-high return strategy that may be in the best interests of stockholders but is less attractive to risk-averse managers.

name: Capital intensity
authors_terms: ["capital intensity", "capital-to-labor ratio", "ratio of capital to labor"]
definition: Capital intensity refers to a firm's ratio of capital to labor.

name: Firm productivity
definition: Value added per employee, where value added = (pretax income + capital costs + employment costs)/number of employees; the authors use it rather than profitability because they believe it to be a less ambiguous measure of efficiency.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity refers to the degree of idiosyncrasy of an investment required to produce the good for the sourcing firm; the more idiosyncratic the investments required, the more likely the firm will prefer to produce the good itself since the costs of protecting against potentially opportunistic suppliers is greater than the cost of producing internally.

name: Volume uncertainty
definition: This uncertainty refers to unpredictability of demand and an accompanying inability to accurately forecast and schedule production.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: This variable measures the likelihood that technological change will occur; it can refer to the innovation potential for either the good or the processes used in its production.

name: Performance uncertainty
definition: This uncertainty refers to the difficulty in predicting how a good will perform in the firm's subsequent production processes. In this context it is operationalized as information asymmetry, such as when simple inspection techniques are not adequate to evaluate quality, when production problems occur that cannot be traced to a specific cause, and when it is difficult to compare goods from different suppliers.

name: Firm scope economies
definition: Scope economies involve a reduction in overall production costs from producing two goods simultaneously, leading to a fuller utilization of sharable upstream inputs; the measures reflect the extent to which the firm's overall costs were reduced by producing the good along with its other products.

name: Supplier scope economies
definition: Scope economies for the firm are independent from those of its suppliers since each has its own established product mix and resource base; supplier scope economies reflect the extent to which suppliers can reduce their overall production costs by making the good along with their other products.

name: Firm expertise
definition: The extent to which the firm has considerable skills and capabilities for producing the good and an understanding of the underlying technology, incorporating its understanding of the base technology and its related skills.

name: Supplier expertise
definition: The extent to which suppliers have considerable skills and capabilities for producing the good and an understanding of the underlying technology; suppliers' costs depend upon their relative expertise, resources, and capabilities.

name: Percentage of requirements produced internally
authors_terms: ["percentage produced internally", "percentage of internal production", "percentage of its requirements the firm will produce internally", "degree of internalization"]
definition: The key variable of the continuum view is the percentage of the firm's requirements for a good that it produces internally, read from the survey answer ordered from 0 to 100 percent produced internally.

name: Concurrent sourcing
definition: Firms can and do simultaneously make and buy the same good, a phenomenon this paper terms concurrent sourcing. The term is used to refer to only backward, partial vertical integration of a homogeneous good (or service) by a single firm.

name: Implementation speed
definition: The authors define implementation speed as "the number of years that had elapsed between the initiation and completion of M-form adoption"; at the extremes, transformations can be implemented gradually, involving minor, sequential changes over five to seven years or longer, or in a frame-breaking manner involving simultaneous, rapid, and sharp shifts in organizational features over one or two years.

name: Transition performance
authors_terms: ["transition performance", "performance change during the M-form transition period", "performance deterioration during transition"]
definition: Transition performance change is "the difference between the average annual industry-adjusted ROA during the transition period and prior performance, calculated as the average industry-adjusted ROA for the five years prior to reorganization." The transition period itself may be "marked by substandard and deteriorating performance."

name: Performance recovery time
authors_terms: ["recovery time", "performance recovery time", "rate of performance recovery"]
definition: "Recovery time was measured as the number of years, after the reorganization was completed, it took each firm's industry-adjusted ROA to reach or exceed its prior performance." Recovery is described as a necessary precondition for obtaining the economic benefits of M-form adoption.

name: Prior diversification strategy
definition: "Strategies differ in the level of interdependence they create between a company's business units." The firms studied pursued vertical, related, and unrelated diversification strategies, "primarily corresponded to the dominant-vertical, related-constrained, and acquisitive conglomerate strategies in the familiar Rumelt (1974) typology."

name: Oppositional product name
authors_terms: ["oppositional names", "oppositional beer name", "oppositional product names", "anti-mass-production reference"]
definition: Names of products that, by embodying linguistically the narrative of an oppositional discourse, convey the ideology of an oppositional market; in the craft beer market, a name contains an anti-mass-production reference, defined as any word that conveys small-scale production, artisanality, exclusivity, authenticity, and quality.

name: Product appeal
definition: The actual appeal of a product is driven by (1) its intrinsic appeal defined as the perceived fit between product attributes and a consumer's taste and (2) a producer's engagement of consumers with the intent to convert the product's intrinsic appeal into actual appeal.

name: Similarity to incumbent prototype product
authors_terms: ["similarity to a prototypical incumbent product", "products associated with prototype products in the incumbent market", "American lager"]
definition: The authors consider one key product feature—similarity to a prototypical incumbent product—that may drive incongruence between an oppositional name and the product it is attached to. A prototypical product includes the most salient features associated with its category.

name: External organizational identity
authors_terms: ["external organizational identity", "organizational identity congruent with the collective identity of the market", "brewery cumulative beer style count"]
definition: The extent to which a brewery has developed an external identity congruent with the collective oppositional codes of the craft beer market. Firms have to present their internal identity to the outside world in such a way that it compels audiences to notice and assign it to these firms as external identity.

name: R&D resource congestion
authors_terms: ["R&D resource congestion", "capacity-constrained resource congestion", "resource congestion", "R&D capacity-constrained resource congestion"]
definition: The capacity-constrained resources of a focal firm's partners diminish in effectiveness for the focal firm when faced with multiple claims on their use from the partners' other partners. These constraints arise when there are spillovers in capacity-constrained resource demands from the firm's partners' other R&D relationships, that is, when the same capacity-constrained R&D resources are shared across multiple partners.

name: Innovation output
definition: Innovation output is measured using patent data. Patents are a key metric for innovation in the biopharmaceutical industry, with their economic value best captured through forward citations.

name: Early-stage R&D productivity signals
authors_terms: ["early-stage R&D-related productivity signals", "early-stage product pipeline", "signals of early-stage productivity"]
definition: A focal firm may garner greater attention and higher levels of capacity-constrained knowledge resources from its R&D alliance partners when it displays visible signs of progress in early-stage product development. In the biopharmaceutical context, products entering a preclinical trial stage (i.e., before human trials begin) are a key indicator of R&D success.

name: Industry overlap with partners' partners
authors_terms: ["focal-partners' partners industry overlap", "industry overlap between the focal firm and its partners' partners"]
definition: A second factor shaping partner attention allocation in alliance settings is the distinctiveness of the focal firm vis-a-vis its partners' other partners. Such industry-related overlap causes the focal firm to be more substitutable and less distinctive from the perspective of its partners.

name: Promotion contract framing
definition: Promotion contract framing (e.g., bonus payment only if >90% of a supply chain's cost-saving target is achieved) is designed to achieve a maximal goal by directing a firm's attention to focus on gains, promoting flexibility, and engendering greater risk tolerance. It is the way contract clauses are contextually presented to influence a firm's interpretation of obligations and the nature of the buyer-supplier relationship.

name: Prevention contract framing
definition: Prevention contract framing (e.g., penalties for 'nonperformance' in relation to delivery delays, product damages, and any direct losses) is designed to fulfill a minimal goal by directing firms' attention to focusing on loss avoidance, encouraging vigilant behaviors, and provoking greater risk aversion. It is a way of contextually presenting contract clauses that shapes how each party perceives and reacts to the contract.

name: Supplier exploration
definition: Exploration refers to a supplier's activities of acquiring new knowledge, skills, and market opportunities to develop innovative products or services. It enhances variety in experience through experimentation, trialing, and free association.

name: Supplier exploitation
definition: Exploitation refers to a supplier's activities of adjusting procedures, rules, and policies that facilitate gaining insight into improving efficiency or decreasing costs. It creates reliability in experience through refinement, production, and focused attention.

name: Relative technological intensity
authors_terms: ["relative technological intensity", "relative technological advantage", "R&D difference", "relative position of the two countries"]
definition: To capture the effect of technology in the home and host countries, we used the sum and difference of R&D intensities (R&D expenditures divided by industry size) within industries in the home and host countries. The former captures the overall technological intensity of a sector, whereas the latter captures the relative position of the two countries.

name: Propensity to enter by acquisition
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "proportion of entries by acquisition", "build vs. buy choice", "acquisition or greenfield"]
definition: Our variable of interest is a binary response-acquisition or greenfield-for each individual entry. However, our independent variables are at the industry level, so we used a grouped data approach, and analyzed the proportions of acquisitions within a group.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: We utilized advertising expenses and sales expenses, respectively, as measures of brand equity and the intensity of distribution in the entered industries.

name: Salesforce intensity
definition: Existing marketing relationships are a valuable firm-specific resource, and are perceived to be essential to gaining firm-specific competitive advantage. We used salesforce information as the second measure of the intensity of distribution.

name: Frequency of environmental variation
definition: Frequency is how often change occurs, measured as the number of slope reversals in a time series divided by the total number of observations. This gives the probability of a reversal in any period.

name: Amplitude of environmental variation
definition: Amplitude of variation is a measure of magnitude, the degree of difference involved in each change. It is distinguished from frequency, how often change occurs, and from predictability, the foreseeable portion of change.

name: Predictability of environmental variation
definition: Predictability is the degree to which the future can be anticipated solely on the basis of knowledge of the past. It is the foreseeable portion of change.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Researchers have generally captured environmental variation with a measure of instability, which has also been labeled dynamism or volatility. Instability has typically been measured as a coefficient of variation or as a variant of such a statistic.

name: Managerial perceptions of seasonality
authors_terms: ["managerial perceptions of seasonality", "reports of a seasonal environment", "off-season"]
definition: The authors expect that managers will consistently report similar perceptions of systematic environmental variation, and one type of systematic variation is seasonal variation. Sales are perceived as demonstrating systematic, seasonal variation only if they vary substantially with wavelike regularity.

name: Acquisition status
definition: Combining independent firms into a larger postacquisition entity; the paper contrasts the target's operations after the acquisition with the period when the firms were independent, because firms are either independent or combined at any point in time.

name: Diseconomies of managing
definition: Coordinating and managing becomes disproportionately difficult as firm size increases, so that the effort required to manage the combined entity exceeds the effort to manage the firms separately. Diseconomies of managing stem from control loss resulting from many forces including 'malcoordination' and 'data transmission losses.'

name: Civil lawsuit judgments
definition: Civil lawsuits reflect that a party has not fulfilled a legal obligation or has not taken actions that a prudent firm should exercise; they typically capture substantial disputes related to imprudent action, negligence, or mismanagement of relationships.

name: Target firm size
authors_terms: ["target firm size", "size of the acquired firm", "target revenues"]
definition: The size of the acquired operations, which determines how much the management task of the acquiring firm grows because the acquirer grows by the size of the target firm's operations. The authors measure it by firm revenues because that is the most comprehensive measure of size they can access from a source where the data are comparable.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Whether the acquiring firm is foreign owned rather than U.S. owned; because all targets are U.S.-owned firms, foreign acquirers change the nationality of control of the target.

name: Firm capabilities
definition: Strategy research hypothesizes that managers obtain competitive advantages via the use of different capabilities that give them an advantage in bringing certain types of products or new technologies to market. Managers should introduce new products and technologies that best complement their existing set of capabilities.

name: Product substitutability
definition: Many industry analysts divide the automobile industry into market segments. Models in each segment have similar characteristics and thus are substitutes.

name: Distance to nearest own model
authors_terms: ["distance between product i and firm f's nearest existing model", "distance to the nearest existing model of the introducing firm", "Sijt"]
definition: The distance between product i and firm f's nearest existing model, j, in the product attribute space.

name: Distance to nearest rival model
authors_terms: ["distance between product i and the closest product of any rival", "distance to an existing rival model", "Sirt"]
definition: The distance between product i and the closest product of any rival, r, of firm f, in the product attribute space.

name: Firm market share
definition: Shareft is the market share of firm f during period t.

name: Entrant status
definition: Entrantft is set equal to one if firm f or a division of f did not manufacture a model in the United States prior to 1980.

name: Foreign manufacturer
definition: Importft is set equal to one if firm f is a foreign manufacturer during period t and zero otherwise.

name: New model introduction
definition: Let yfit = 1 if firm f introduces new model i and zero otherwise.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The performance of an acquisition can be assessed by the security's price change in response to the acquisition, and it is calculated as the difference between the observed return for a security and the normal return for the same security during the period around the acquisition. The magnitude of the CAR at the time of an acquisition announcement provides a measure of the impact of the acquisition on the value of the acquiring firm.

name: Strategic complementarity
authors_terms: ["strategic complementarity", "complementarity in product strategy", "complementarity in product strategy"]
definition: Strategic complementarity, defined as the extent to which the product strategies of an acquirer and a target are different, will create value that was absent before the acquisition by allowing the merged firm to combine or reconfigure different resources and capabilities.

name: Market complementarity
definition: This second type of complementarity measures the degree to which the characteristics of the target's markets complement those of the acquirer's existing markets. This market complementarity can offer opportunities for value creation by allowing merging firms to exploit differences in their relative markets.

name: Acquirer strategic focus
definition: Strategic focus, defined as the degree to which a firm's business portfolio is concentrated on one or a few business areas, has long been recognized as one of the key indicators of a firm's strategic and organizational profile. This variable measured the degree of concentration in the core business portfolio of an acquirer.

name: Out-of-market acquisition experience
definition: Our theory holds that banks with out-of-market acquisition experience are more capable of realizing the potential benefits of market complementarity. We operationalized out-of-market acquisition experience as the sum of the total number of acquisitions from 1988 to the year of the focal acquisition that a bank made outside the state in which its primary operations were located.

name: Relative attention allocation in adaptive aspirations
authors_terms: ["relative attention", "attention allocation in adaptive aspirations", "relative allocation of attention to the respective reference points"]
definition: The relative attention that organizations allocate to the different reference points (prior aspiration, prior performance, and prior performance of reference groups) in adaptive aspirations; the more relative attention a reference point receives the more sensitive the organization is to that reference point in the aspiration adaptation equation.

name: Attention to prior aspiration
authors_terms: ["attention to prior aspiration", "weight on prior aspiration (a1)", "relative attention to prior aspiration"]
definition: Relative attention allocated to the focal organization's prior aspiration (a1), which together with attention to prior performance (a2) represents learning from own experience in the aspiration adaptation equation.

name: Attention to prior performance
authors_terms: ["attention to prior performance", "weight on prior performance (a2)"]
definition: Relative attention allocated to the focal organization's prior performance (a2), which together with attention to prior aspiration (a1) represents learning from own experience in the aspiration adaptation equation.

name: Attention to external reference group performance
authors_terms: ["attention to competitors' prior experience", "weight on competitors within the same content category (a3)", "relative attention to the performance of external reference group"]
definition: Relative attention allocated to the performance of the external reference group (a3); if an organization allocates high relative attention to its competitors' prior experience it prefers nonlocal search and exploration to local search and exploitation.

name: Attention to internal reference group performance
authors_terms: ["weight on sister magazines within the same publisher (a4)", "attention to the internal reference group"]
definition: Relative attention allocated to the performance of the internal reference group (a4), consisting of sister organizations under the same parent organization.

name: Early organizational life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["early stage of the organizational life cycle", "early in their life cycles"]
definition: A dummy variable specifying whether a given magazine was within six years of its founding and therefore in the early stage of the organizational life cycle; the six-year period follows the entrepreneurship literature, where new ventures are defined as companies six years old or younger.

name: End of organizational life cycle
authors_terms: ["end of the organizational life cycle", "end of life cycle"]
definition: A dummy variable marking whether a given year was the last full year a magazine was in business, thus signaling the approaching end of the organizational life cycle.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational age was measured as years since a magazine started its first issue; for magazines of foreign origin, organizational age is measured as years since the foreign origin magazine started its first issue in Germany.

name: Parent organization age
definition: Parent (publisher) age was measured as years since a publisher was founded; the more experience the corporate parent has, the more experience the focal organization can draw on.

name: Aspiration level
definition: The aspiration level at any time is a function of the relative attention the organization currently allocates to the different reference points in adaptive aspirations; it was measured as the number of magazine copies printed.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational performance was measured as the number of magazine copies sold.

name: External reference group performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the external reference group", "competitors' prior performance"]
definition: The performance of the external reference group, calculated as the average performance of magazines in the same content category, i.e. competing organizations in the same product market.

name: Internal reference group performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the internal reference group", "performance of sister magazines"]
definition: The performance of the internal reference group, calculated as the average performance of magazines that are published by the same publisher, i.e. sister organizations under the same parent organization.

name: Diversifying entry
definition: The dependent variable, Div_ij, is derived from the Trinet database and is coded as a categorical variable: Div_ij = 1 if firm i enters industry j between 1981 and 1985, and 0 otherwise.

name: Absolute technological resource applicability
authors_terms: ["AbsTech", "absolute level of firm i's patent portfolio that is likely to be applicable to industry j", "applicability of a firm's existing technological resources"]
definition: AbsTech_ij is defined as the absolute level of firm i's patent portfolio that is likely to be applicable to industry j.

name: Relative technological resource applicability
authors_terms: ["RelTech", "relative applicability of firm i's patent portfolio to industry j"]
definition: RelTech_ij is defined as the applicability of firm i's patent portfolio to industry j, relative to the applicability of firm i's patent portfolio to other industries.

name: Feasibility of licensing technology
definition: Royalty_j is defined as the feasibility of licensing innovations in industry j. I assume that the more important license royalties are as a method of appropriating returns to innovation in industry j, the lower the hazards and, hence, transaction costs associated with contracting for technology in industry j.

name: Importance of secrecy
definition: Secrecy_j is defined as the importance of secrecy to appropriating returns to innovation in industry j.

name: Tacit knowledge
definition: Learning_j is defined as the importance of learning curve advantages to appropriating returns to innovation in industry j. I assume that in industries where learning curve advantages are efficacious, knowledge is sufficiently tacit that it does not leak out of the learning firm.

name: External exploitation experience
authors_terms: ["external exploitation experience", "external exploitation", "alliance exploitation experience", "exploitation alliances"]
definition: We measured external exploitation experience by the percentage of licensing and manufacturing agreements within the biotechnology field. These proxies can also be viewed as the firms' strategic orientation toward exploration and exploitation.

name: External exploration experience
authors_terms: ["external exploration experience", "external exploration", "alliance exploration experience", "exploration alliances"]
definition: We proxied external exploration experience by the percentage of R&D alliances entered into by the pharmaceutical firm in the biotechnology field up to, but not including, the year of the focal project.

name: Internal exploration experience
definition: A firm's internal exploration experience is captured by the lagged, cumulative number of R&D projects that a firm had initiated in a particular therapeutic domain. Projects contribute to a firm's internal exploration experience if the focal firm is listed as the lead firm for the project.

name: Internal exploitation experience
definition: To capture internal exploitation experience, we collected historical pharmaceutical sales data for the firms in the sample. We used the cumulative percentage of sales derived from that therapeutic class as a proxy for internal exploitation experience.

name: R&D project performance
definition: We use time to drug approval of biotechnology-based R&D projects undertaken by established pharmaceutical firms to assess the performance impact of external exploratory and exploitative activity. Project termination is a more common occurrence in this context and provides important complementary insights into project outcomes.

name: Worker tenure
definition: I examine the reasons for changes in worker tenure, defined as the length of time that workers have spent with their current employer.

name: Industry unionization
definition: Historically, industries have varied substantially in their levels of unionization, reflecting idiosyncratic factors such as the nature of the work and the era in which the industry developed. These unionization rates have also shown substantial effects on the behavior of all organizations in the industry by raising the threat that nonunion firms might become organized and establishing industry-wide norms.

name: Import competition
authors_terms: ["import competition", "import penetration", "industry levels of import competition", "foreign competition"]
definition: I calculated import penetration using industry-level data on the gross value of imports from 1979 to 2006. I then calculated import penetration rates by dividing total industry imports by gross industry output, taken from the National Income and Product Accounts.

name: Technology intensity
authors_terms: ["technology use", "technology intensity", "IT intensity", "investments in new technology", "technological change"]
definition: I calculated industry-level spending on information technology using data from the input-output tables of the National Income and Product Accounts. I then calculated IT intensity by dividing each industry's total purchases of IT-specific goods and services by the total purchases of those industries in that year.

name: Organizational size
definition: The March supplement asked workers, 'Counting all locations where this employer operates, what is the total number of persons who work for 0 0 0 's employer?' I consolidated the different response categories into three: under 25 workers, 25-999 workers, and 1,000 workers or over.

name: Calendar year
definition: I assess changes in tenure over time using a linear year variable. A significant negative effect of year on tenure indicates that tenure declined over time, holding worker demographics, occupation, and local unemployment constant.

name: Serious errors
authors_terms: ["serious errors", "serious drug error", "serious drug errors", "drug errors", "safety-related drug error"]
definition: Serious errors are 'organizational processes that result in a failure with significantly adverse outcomes.' In the pharmaceutical context they are drug errors: cases in which evidence about a new or existing drug raises safety-related concerns about adverse effects that outweigh its potential merits, thus resulting in its withdrawal from the market or significantly limiting the scope of potential users.

name: Safety focus
definition: A focus associated with avoiding Type I errors (i.e., avoiding doing something that might result in a serious error). In this study a firm's safety focus is captured by the clinical trials it conducts, which constitute the firm's main efforts to determine drug safety and require a significant investment of resources.

name: Innovation focus
definition: In the pharmaceutical industry the predominant focus competing with safety is new product innovation, an activity requiring massive, long-term investments; patent counts are used as an indicator of innovation output.

name: Time elapsed since serious error
authors_terms: ["time elapsed since last serious drug error", "time elapsed since the error", "times elapsed since last serious drug error", "time elapsed"]
definition: The time that has passed since the occurrence of the last serious drug error. The authors argue that as time passes, regulatory and public attention to the error are likely to decline, so the effect of the error on the firm's foci fades. They entered time elapsed as a control and test its moderating role through graphical analysis and formal econometric tests of differences in marginal effects across levels of time elapsed.

name: Founding team diversity
authors_terms: ["diverse founding teams", "diverse team", "diversity of functional roles", "functional diversity"]
definition: A diverse team is the number of functional roles present on the founding team, spanning technology, finance, sales and marketing, and other roles. Diversity is thought to improve firm performance because it ensures that the top management team has a broader spectrum of experience and capabilities.

name: Founding team technical focus
authors_terms: ["technically focused team", "technically focused founding team", "technology-focused founding teams", "technical focus"]
definition: A team composed solely of engineers or scientists with chief technology officer or vice president of engineering roles would be highly technically focused. The variable is coded 1 if the founding team was entirely composed of individuals who indicated that their role at founding was focused on the development of the technology.

name: Innovation strategy
definition: A firm's strategy to be an innovator: innovators introduce new products and services and primarily compete based on their technical edge, whereas a noninnovation-based firm tends to compete on dimensions other than technological innovation since it is not developing new-to-the-world products.

name: Commercialization environment
authors_terms: ["commercialization environment", "competitive commercialization environment", "cooperative commercialization environment", "competitive versus cooperative with incumbents", "business environment"]
definition: A competitive commercialization environment is one in which the patent channel of appropriability is relatively weak while incumbents' extant complementary assets for commercialization are largely disrupted. A cooperative commercialization environment is defined in the opposite way, where patent protection is effective and the importance of incumbents' existing complementary assets is sustained.

name: Venture performance
definition: Following many studies in the literature, entrepreneurial success is measured through observed IPO or acquisition liquidity events, that is whether the enterprise and its equity holders achieve liquidity via an 'exit' event such as an acquisition or IPO.

name: Platform usage
definition: TVisits is the number of monthly platform visits; for target firms with multiple platforms, TVisits includes the monthly visits for all platforms. Many platform strategies initially focus on generating user engagement with the expectation of high revenues and profits later.

name: Firm value
definition: Acquisitions of firms that generate revenue from advertising, subscription, or referral fees provide a concrete measure of firm value; TValue is the price paid for the target. A key question is how platform business models can translate network effects for the individual user into firm value.

name: Platform content type
authors_terms: ["platform categories", "firm-generated content platforms", "user-contributed content platforms", "interaction platforms", "FGC", "UCC", "IGC"]
definition: Through an iterative grounded process we developed 15 subcategories of platforms and then conceptualized these subcategories into three categories based on how the content on the platform is generated: user-contributed content platforms, firm-generated content platforms, and interaction platforms.

name: Availability of an alternative platform
definition: We also measure switching cost through the availability of an alternative platform with similar functionality that should reduce switching cost for the user. A close alternative reduces the inconvenience of switching, and the competing platform is likely to provide tools to make the switch easier.

name: Interaction tools
definition: Platforms that provide complex interaction tools create higher switching costs because of the cognitive costs associated with learning the tool. Complex interactions on the platform require familiarity with the interface, and users are less willing to learn a new interface.

name: User data
definition: Significant user data on a platform can arguably also create switching costs because it may be difficult to transfer data to another platform or find the same content elsewhere; however, value propositions based solely on user data (without interactions) engender low switching costs.

name: Community features
definition: Platforms that foster a sense of community create switching costs for the user who is less willing to leave a familiar community of other users. Repeated interactions within a community facilitate discernment about the intentions and credentials of other members, and platform usage is likely to be more engaging.

name: CEO core self-evaluation
authors_terms: ["core self-evaluation", "core self-evaluations", "CEO core self-evaluation", "sense of self-potency"]
definition: A broad personality trait that captures the common elements embedded in self-esteem, generalized self-efficacy, emotional adjustment, and locus of control, and an enduring assessment of worth and competence or self-potency.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: Defined as capturing the strength of a firm's 'impetus to innovate, take risks, and aggressively pursue new venture opportunities'.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: An environment in which 'there is rapid and discontinuous change in demand, competitors, technology, or regulation so that information is often inaccurate, unavailable, or obsolete'.

name: Foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["foreign direct investment", "FDI", "manufacture in the United States", "manufacturing investment", "INV"]
definition: The paper focuses on the determinants of the decision of Japanese firms to manufacture a given product in the United States, so that a firm's decision to manufacture abroad depends on location, governance, and strategic factors.

name: Plant minimum efficient scale
definition: When the product produced by a firm has a relatively large plant minimum efficient scale (MES), it makes sense to centralize production in a few plants in order to exploit economies of scale and to serve foreign markets through exports from that plant.

name: Transportation costs
definition: High transportation cost results in an increase in delivered cost, and, everything else constant, encourages foreign production over exports; the relationship holds if the firm's production is sold to customers in the target market.

name: Trade barriers
authors_terms: ["tariff and nontariff barriers", "trade barriers", "U.S. trade barriers", "TB"]
definition: A firm can bypass tariff and nontariff barriers on its exports by establishing manufacturing facilities abroad.

name: Natural resource intensity
definition: International differences in production costs are higher for inputs which incur high transportation costs, for example natural resources and unskilled production workers; Japan is poor in natural resources while the U.S. is relatively resource-abundant, so Japanese firms in natural resource-intensive industries are more likely to serve the U.S. market through U.S.-based plants.

name: Follow-the-customer pressure
definition: Firms may find it desirable to follow their longstanding customers into foreign markets; it has been argued that many Japanese second-tier subcontractors have invested in the U.S. at the request of their first-tier customer.

name: Technological know-how
authors_terms: ["technological know-how", "research and development intensive", "R&D intensity", "proprietary knowledge", "RND"]
definition: The basic problem with the transfer of knowledge is one of information asymmetry; knowledge is often difficult to codify into patents and patent rights offer uneven protection, so firms which invest in the generation of knowledge will often find it necessary to exploit it abroad through internalization, i.e., through foreign manufacture.

name: Reputation
definition: Another type of firm-specific advantages is reputation (goodwill); trademarks are property rights on reputation, and the ability of a firm to exploit its reputation depends on the extent to which trademarks are protected from unauthorized imitation. When the cost of preventing the renter from debasing quality is high, the firm which has invested in reputation will internalize its transfer.

name: Experience and scope economies
definition: A foreign firm which is already manufacturing product j in the U.S. market should have a higher propensity to manufacture other products k ... n in the United States, because the knowledge gained in producing one product in the U.S. can be transferred to another product and because the manufacture of additional products may benefit from scope economies in production or distribution.

name: Host industry concentration
authors_terms: ["U.S. industry concentration ratio", "concentration ratio of the target U.S. industry", "USCON"]
definition: While highly concentrated U.S. industries may deter entry by weaker domestic firms, the authors expect that they will attract multinational firms; Japanese entry is more likely the more highly concentrated the U.S. target industry.

name: Exchange-of-threat
definition: A good strategy for firms who see foreign firms enter their own domestic market is to retaliate by invading the invader's home market, a strategy called 'exchange-of-threat'.

name: Prior entry by domestic rivals
authors_terms: ["other Japanese members of that industry have already invested in the United States", "its domestic rivals have already made previous investments in the U.S.", "follow-the-leader", "FOLLOW"]
definition: In the maturing stage of the product cycle, the foreign investment of one industry member threatens the established market position of all others and triggers their subsequent investment, a type of behavior which has been called 'follow-the-leader'.

name: Domestic industry concentration
authors_terms: ["loose oligopolistic industry", "tight oligopolistic industry", "industry concentration ratio"]
definition: Follow-the-leader behavior is prevalent only in a loose oligopolistic industry because firms in a tight oligopolistic industry will collude instead; the range of a loose oligopoly is between 1000 and 1800 in terms of the Herfindhal-Hirschman Index.

name: Domestic market share
authors_terms: ["market share in Japan", "domestic market share", "SHARE", "SHARE squared"]
definition: It may be useful to distinguish between dominant firms, which have a solid domestic foothold and strong competitive advantages and the largest domestic market shares, and dominated firms; dominated firms with medium market shares are expected to have a greater tendency to manufacture abroad than dominant firms or dominated firms with smaller market shares.

name: Host industry growth
authors_terms: ["growth rate of the target U.S. industry", "GROWTH"]
definition: Japanese investors should have greater incentives to manufacture products in the U.S. when the demand for these products is growing rapidly.

name: CVC ownership
authors_terms: ["CVC ownership", "proportion of shares held by CVC firms"]
definition: The share of an entrepreneurial venture held by corporate venture capital (CVC) firms; when CVC investors hold greater ownership they are more likely to maintain a board seat and influence the venture's strategic direction. The authors measure it as "the proportion of shares held by CVC firms, which is calculated as the percentage of the total number of the venture's shares."

name: Founder incumbency
authors_terms: ["founder incumbency", "founder as an incumbent top manager", "founder managers"]
definition: Whether the founder is still an incumbent top manager of the venture; founders can exert influence on firm strategy as long as they have legitimacy and structural power based on hierarchical authority. It takes a value of 1 if the founder is a CEO or a technology-related executive, such as a CTO or chief scientist, and 0 otherwise.

name: R&D intensity
definition: The venture's R&D investment normalized by firm size, which serves as both an input measure for technological innovation and a long-term strategic resource allocation decision. It is measured as the ratio of R&D expenditures to total assets.

name: Within-industry diversification
authors_terms: ["within-industry diversification", "product scope", "within-industry product scope", "number of product categories"]
definition: For within-industry diversification, I developed a count measure for a firm's number of product categories in each year (within each firm's core six-digit NAICS industry). The term 'product category' refers to products that differ in their technological specifications and design.

name: Within-industry diversification change rate
authors_terms: ["within-industry diversification change rate", "rate of change of within-industry diversification", "rate of within-industry diversification", "rate of change"]
definition: My measure of the within-industry diversification change rate was the annual increase in the number of new product categories of a given firm divided by the total number of product categories in the preceding year.

name: Firm performance
definition: I have used Returns on Sales (ROS) as my measure for firm performance. ROS is a highly acceptable measure for firm short-term economic performance.

name: Technological diversity
definition: The IV used for within-industry diversification is the number of technology domains to which the firm's patents are classified in each year. The number of technology domains therefore reflects the technological diversity of the firm.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "abnormal stock market returns", "abnormal stock market return", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: A risk-adjusted return in excess of the average stock market return around the alliance announcement date. Our measure of abnormal stock returns is based on the familiar market model residual.

name: Alliance type
definition: Technological alliances involve cooperation in upstream value chain activities such as R&D, engineering, and manufacturing, whereas marketing alliances involve cooperation in downstream value chain activities such as sales, distribution, and customer service.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Profitability was measured as the accounting rate of return, or the ratio of net income to book value.

name: Relative size of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["relative size of alliance partners", "smaller partner", "larger partner", "firm size"]
definition: Firms entering strategic alliances may experience asymmetric resource dependence: larger firms usually seek out smaller, innovative firms for their technological know-how. For each alliance in the sample, total assets, total sales, and number of employees were used to classify each firm as the small partner or the large partner.

name: Investor uncertainty
definition: Variability in stock returns has been traditionally used in the accounting and finance literature as an empirical proxy for uncertainty.

name: Scientific certifications
authors_terms: ["premier scientific publications", "scientific certifications", "publications in premier scientific journals"]
definition: The acceptance of articles for publication in premier scientific journals constitutes a form of certification of the knowledge that those articles portray. Firms that succeed in having articles placed in premier journals develop a reputation for conducting high-quality research.

name: Regulatory certifications
authors_terms: ["regulatory approvals", "regulatory certifications", "FDA approval of new drugs"]
definition: Regulatory agencies are established by legal mandate precisely to mitigate uncertainty that could otherwise result in market failure. Regulatory certifications, besides establishing the validity of a particular product whose market introduction is approved, invest the firm introducing the product with enhanced reputation.

name: Scientific certification advantage
authors_terms: ["pioneer's advantage in premier scientific publications", "scientific certification advantage", "relative certifications"]
definition: A pioneer's advantage in scientific certifications relative to a particular rival may suggest the extent to which it has an advantage over that rival in moving fast enough to market and creating deterrent effects that diminish that rival's value capture prospects.

name: Regulatory certification advantage
authors_terms: ["pioneer's advantage in regulatory approvals", "regulatory certification advantage"]
definition: The greater a pioneer's regulatory certification advantage, the greater its lead in establishing the confidence of stakeholders that its efforts to draw on the new knowledge underlying the new field will result in a product that is appropriate for commercialization.

name: Scientific certifications of a pioneering innovation
authors_terms: ["premier scientific publications about a pioneering innovation", "scientific certifications of a pioneering innovation", "premier scientific publications on a pioneering drug"]
definition: Because scientific certifications attest to the validity of knowledge, publications about a pioneering innovation in premier scientific journals represent an important milestone in the development of a new technical field.

name: Regulatory certification of a pioneering innovation
authors_terms: ["regulatory approval of a pioneering innovation", "FDA approval of a pioneering drug"]
definition: Because regulatory certifications certify that new products are appropriate for market introduction, the regulatory approval of a pioneering innovation constitutes a landmark in the evolution of a new technical field.

name: Entry into a new technical field
authors_terms: ["rivals' entries into a new technical field", "rivals' entries into a new mechanism of action"]
definition: A new technical field arises when new knowledge is applied to address the technical problems of a product class; upon observing that a firm has pioneered a new technical field, rivals have incentives to enter that field. For each rival-mechanism-year observation, entry is observed when the focal rival created a drug drawing on the new mechanism.

name: Category spanning
definition: 'Category spanning' refers to organizations' involvement in several activities that comprise distinct cognitive sets.

name: Evaluation
definition: 'Evaluation,' as a set of processes that contributes to making judgments and assessing entities, requires categorization. Where quality is difficult to observe and judge, evaluation is taken as an indirect indicator of capability and commitment.

name: Performance
definition: Producers who are better evaluated are more likely to benefit from superior revenues; the variable performance is based on the revenue per lawyer (RPL) at the law firms' branch office, a commonly used measure of performance in law firm and professional service firm studies.

name: Inclusive category combination
definition: Inclusiveness is the cumulative frequency of conjoint categories at different levels of combination (duos, trios, and so on); it is the degree of insertion of category combinations in the entire population of producers for each location each year.

name: Independent director appointment
authors_terms: ["independent director appointment", "likelihood of the parent firms appointing independent directors to the JV board", "presence of independent directors on JV boards"]
definition: Independent directors in joint ventures are nonaffiliated directors who are jointly appointed by the partners. Because of this joint appointment, their primary loyalty is to the joint venture.

name: Market overlap
definition: Market overlap, or the extent to which JV partners compete in common end markets, is an exchange risk that is unique to JVs because the parent firms remain independent organizations.

name: Joint venture functional scope
definition: Functional scope refers to the number of different functional activities (e.g., R&D, manufacturing, and marketing) that partners undertake during the collaboration.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty refers to the rate of change, unverifiability or variability of the external environment (Luo 2007).

name: Contractual complexity
definition: The more complex a contract, the more likely the partners have defined roles and responsibilities at the outset of the collaboration, as well as procedures for monitoring, penalties for noncompliance, and specific processes for dispute resolution.

name: Prior ties
definition: Prior ties, or a history of collaboration between partner firms, reduce behavioral uncertainty and goal conflicts between partners. Prior relationships also help firms to develop routines that facilitate communication between JV shareholders and promote the development of problem-solving procedures.

name: Firm age
definition: Age was measured by the number of years that a firm had participated in the personal computer industry.

name: Technology strategy
definition: Proprietary strategists offer products whose key technologies are internally developed and firm-specific; standards-based strategists offer products whose key technologies conform with open and publicly available specifications. Such technologies are externally developed, non-unique, and shared with a number of other firms.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth, used in the strategy literature to assess firm performance, is a particularly strong indicator, in this industry, of a firm's technological viability.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: The dependent variables examined here are failure rates and rates of sales growth; failures included the deaths of entire firms and industry exits by multibusiness companies.

name: Demographic similarity to incumbents
authors_terms: ["similarity along shared dimensions", "similarity to incumbents along shared demographic dimensions", "demographic similarity", "similar dimensions"]
definition: The degree to which a new director is similar to incumbents of the focal board along the demographic dimensions on which the director is similar to half or more of the incumbents (shared dimensions).

name: Demographic difference from incumbents
authors_terms: ["difference along dissimilar dimensions", "demographic difference", "dissimilarity along each dissimilar dimension", "dissimilar dimensions"]
definition: The degree to which a new director differs from the majority of incumbent directors along the demographic dimensions on which the director is different from more than 50 percent of incumbents (dissimilar dimensions).

name: Prior common board appointments
authors_terms: ["prior common board appointments", "prior common board ties", "prior social ties"]
definition: Incumbents' prior common board ties to a new director, measured as the total number of incumbents who had prior common board appointments with the new director.

name: Director tenure
definition: The number of years that a demographically different director served on the focal board.

name: Major board committee membership
authors_terms: ["committee appointment", "member of a major board committee", "served on the focal board's major committees"]
definition: A demographically different director's service on one of the focal board's major committees, namely the compensation, audit, nomination, and corporate governance committees, which allow directors to exert great influence over major board decisions.

name: Major board committee chair appointment
authors_terms: ["committee chair appointment", "chair of a major board committee"]
definition: A demographically different director's service as chair of one of the focal board's major committees, namely the compensation, audit, nomination, or corporate governance committee.

name: CEO media appearances
authors_terms: ["CEO media appearances", "CEO appearances in the media", "CNBC interview", "CEO news articles", "media appearance"]
definition: We propose that CEOs' media appearances will increase their visibility in the managerial labor market. CEO appearances in the media were measured using two different media appearance measures: appearance in CNBC interviews and major U.S. news articles.

name: CEO compensation
definition: Our dependent variable is the CEO's total compensation (TDC1) in the Execucomp database, which is the sum of the CEO's salary, bonuses, other annual compensation, total value of restricted stocks granted, total value of stock options granted (using the Black-Scholes formula), long-term incentive payouts, and all other total compensation.

name: Firm size
definition: Large firms and their CEOs are generally well recognized and highly visible in the managerial labor market because of these firms' significance and influence on the economy. This variable was measured as the natural log of the total assets of the firm.

name: Stock market performance
authors_terms: ["stock market performance", "strong stock market performance", "market performance"]
definition: Strong stock market performance of the CEO's current company can serve as supportive evidence for the CEO's ability. This variable was measured by the holding period return over the 12 months until the end of the fiscal year.

name: CEO founder status
definition: Founder CEOs have a strong attachment and commitment to their companies because they identify themselves strongly with the companies they created. This dummy variable indicates whether the CEO is a founder of the company.

name: CEO equity ownership
definition: If a CEO has substantially large equity ownership, it creates a monetary ownership effect, making his or her decisions and behaviors more in line with the company's well-being. When CEOs own a substantial amount of the company equity, their identities are tied to their organizations.

name: Alliance performance
authors_terms: ["alliance performance", "performance of a strategic alliance", "fulfillment of major strategic needs", "indirect performance indicators"]
definition: Alliance performance is assessed through the fulfillment of major strategic needs, on the logic that when very important strategic needs are being met very well, an alliance can be said to be performing well, and through indirect performance indicators, which capture other critical dimensions of alliance performance including net spillover effects for the parent firms, relative profitability, and overall performance assessment.

name: Pattern of payoffs
definition: The stability of a cooperative relationship is a function of the overall payoff structure, or of the relationships among values placed upon outcomes that reflect the two-by-two matrix of behavioral combinations (cooperation or defection by firm A and firm B); it is captured by the payoff residuals UD - MC, MC - MD, and UD - UC.

name: Payoffs from unilateral cooperation
authors_terms: ["payoffs from unilateral cooperation", "the payoff of unilateral cooperation", "unilateral cooperation (UC)"]
definition: The payoff a firm receives when it cooperates (abides by the letter and spirit of the partnership agreement) while its partner defects; in the prisoner's dilemma the "sucker" draws a very heavy sentence, so unilateral cooperation is the least preferred outcome in the preference ordering UD > MC > MD > UC, and the larger the potential losses from being exploited by a partner, the smaller the payoff of unilateral cooperation.

name: Shadow of the future
definition: The bond between the future benefits a firm anticipates and its present actions is called the "shadow of the future." Cooperative performance is better promoted the longer the shadow of the future, or the thicker the nexus between current moves and future consequences, since forward-looking expectations of gains hold in check proclivity toward agreement violations.

name: Behavioral transparency
definition: Behavioral transparency refers to the speed and reliability with which alliance partners learn about each other's actions, and it is a function of the speed and reliability with which they learn about each other's actions.

name: Frequency of interaction
definition: Frequency of interaction is the regularity with which the partners interact; making interactions frequent means little time elapses between assessments of the outcomes of an alliance, so the next move looms larger than it otherwise would.

name: Time horizon
authors_terms: ["time horizon", "length of time horizons", "long time horizons"]
definition: Conceptually, most interfirm alliances parallel iteration of unknown length, since they are created with no terminal date; the level of cooperation between partners may be expected to be positively related to the length of time horizons, which in turn is a positive function of the intended duration of a cooperative relationship and the perceived likelihood of the alliance lasting through the intended duration.

name: Perception of opportunistic behavior
authors_terms: ["perception of opportunistic behavior", "perceived opportunism", "perception of opportunism", "perceived probability of opportunism"]
definition: Opportunism is self-interest-seeking with guile: a firm does not abide by the terms of the agreement in order to exploit the other for short-term gain, and the design of appropriate governance structures is partly a function of the perceived probability of opportunism, which is rendered difficult to assess by the opacity of opportunistic inclinations.

name: Contractual safeguards
definition: Ex post deterrents consist of contractual safeguards, or stipulations in a formal partnership agreement, that inflict penalties for the omission of cooperative behaviors or commission of violative behaviors; such safeguards are structurally embedded deterrents to opportunism and can theoretically be expected to vary proportionally with the perception of opportunistic behavior.

name: Nonrecoverable investments
authors_terms: ["nonrecoverable investments", "ex ante deterrents", "nonsalvageable costs", "nonrecoverable investments in cash and kind"]
definition: Nonrecoverable investments include specific physical assets like plant and equipment and also site specificity, human asset specificity, and dedicated assets; in each case these involve alliance-specific costs that are incurred in advance of alliance commencement and whose value for alternative uses is greatly reduced, sometimes to the level of scrap value only, so that these costs are largely sunk.

name: Cooperative history
definition: With an evolving history, each partner has the opportunity to assess the willingness and ability of the other to abide by the letter and spirit of the partnership agreement; the variable is set to zero if there were no prior alliances between two partners.

name: Exchange history
authors_terms: ["exchange history", "repeat exchanges", "duration of prior exchanges", "frequency of prior exchanges", "shadow of the past"]
definition: The history accumulated between exchange partners through repeated prior transactions; here, the frequency of prior relationships in all financial transactions including M&As is used as a proxy for the exchange history between the acquirer and the advisor.

name: Advisor opportunism
definition: The realization of gains by reneging, which in this setting is the financial advisor's opportunistic behavior toward the acquirer; the degree of advisor opportunism manifests itself as the amount of overpayment for the acquisition target.

name: Trade uncertainty
