definition: The uncertainty about the quality of the exchanged good, which impacts the probability that deviant behavior is detected; in an M&A transaction the degree of uncertainty is higher if less information about the target is available to the acquirer and if the target's value is more difficult to estimate.

name: Shadow of the future
authors_terms: ["shadow of the future", "expectation of future exchanges", "prospects of future exchanges", "future exchange prospects", "propensity of repeats"]
definition: The expectation that the other party will reciprocate in kind, i.e., the perceived time horizon of future exchanges; the longer the relationship is expected to continue, the less likely the actor is to behave opportunistically in pursuing immediate gains.

name: Local CSR density
definition: Local CSR density is the spatial distribution of CSR engagement by firms around the focal firm as determined by the location of its headquarters. As the number of firms active in CSR engagement in the local area surrounding the focal firm increases, or as the level of their engagement increases, local CSR density increases.

name: Proximity to major cities and financial centers
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity", "proximity to major cities and financial centers", "distance", "proximity to large cities"]
definition: By geographic proximity the authors mean simply 'the spatial or physical distance between economic actors'. The main mechanism behind proximity that generates influence is face-to-face contact.

name: CSR engagement
definition: Following McWilliams and Siegel, corporate social responsibility is defined as 'actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law.' The authors follow the usage of Godfrey, Merrill, and Hansen by referring to these actions as CSR engagement, whose level varies along a continuum from low to high engagement.

name: Cost of equity capital
authors_terms: ["cost of equity capital", "cost of equity", "equity financing costs", "equity pricing"]
definition: The cost of equity is the rate of return required by equity investors given their perception of a firm's riskiness. It measures external equity financing costs, and as such, influences both investment and financing decisions.

name: Preferential linkage
authors_terms: ["preferential linkage", "network linkage", "linkage", "attachment", "developer's choice to release a game title for a given console"]
definition: Game developers reveal their relationship intent with every game launch, and these decisions collectively drive the evolution of the network. The dependent variable is a developer's choice to release a game title for a given console, defined as categorical and time-varying.

name: Platform overlap density
authors_terms: ["density overlap", "overlap density", "platform overlap density", "domain similarity", "niche crowding"]
definition: Density overlap-or domain similarity-refers to overlap in the resource positions of sets of organizations and recognizes that competition exists within networks; when organizations occupy the same niche or overlapping niches, there is a high potential for competition for the underlying resources. A platform's niche consists of the set of developers and the titles that they have released for the platform.

name: Platform embeddedness
definition: In this setting, embeddedness is manifested through the pattern of distribution of titles offered by the different developers for the different platforms; in the terminology of Uzzi (1996), a platform is tightly coupled when its set of video games is offered by a small number of developers.

name: Platform dominance
definition: Our third explanation is based on the relative market positions of platforms within the network of video game developers and game console producers, and the expectation is that developers will be attracted to the platform that is dominant at a given point in time.

name: Platform age
definition: One way in which dominant platforms with extensive network connections lose their attractiveness is that their functionality declines relative to that of newer platforms, and the introduction of a new platform poses a new challenge for all developers. Platform age is defined in months on the release date of a game title as the difference between that date and the console's launch date.

name: Organizational boundary-spanning exploration
authors_terms: ["organizational boundary-spanning", "exploration that spans organizational boundaries", "exploration beyond organizational boundaries", "exploration within organizational boundaries", "self-citations"]
definition: Exploration that spans the organizational boundary draws on knowledge generated beyond the firm's boundary, rather than relying inward on internally generated developments; the firm must import knowledge from other organizations.

name: Technological boundary-spanning exploration
authors_terms: ["technological boundary-spanning", "exploration within technological boundaries", "exploration that spans technological boundaries", "exploration beyond technological boundaries", "disk citation"]
definition: Exploration is classified by whether the built-upon knowledge is from similar or distant technology, so technological boundary-spanning exploration builds upon knowledge from technological domains distant from the firm's focal technology.

name: Local exploration
definition: 'Local' exploration builds upon similar technology residing within the firm. Thus, neither the organizational nor the technological boundary is spanned during this type of exploration—all activity is contained within the technological subunit.

name: External boundary-spanning exploration
definition: 'External boundary-spanning' exploration integrates knowledge from other organizations that is close to the technology of interest. The technological subunit utilizes knowledge from its own technological domain, but obtains the knowledge from external sources.

name: Internal boundary-spanning exploration
definition: 'Internal boundary-spanning' exploration integrates technologically distant knowledge residing within the firm. The technological subunit utilizes knowledge from a different technological domain, but is able to obtain that knowledge from another subunit within the firm.

name: Radical exploration
definition: 'Radical' exploration builds upon distant technology that resides outside of the firm. The technological subunit utilizes knowledge from a different technological domain and does not obtain that knowledge from other subunits within the firm.

name: Domain impact
authors_terms: ["domain impact", "impact on subsequent technological evolution within the domain"]
definition: We use the term 'impact' to denote that knowledge has been retained and built upon as technology continues to evolve; domain impact represents the firm's ability to maintain continued technological leadership within the particular product class arena and its associated technological community.

name: Overall impact
authors_terms: ["overall impact", "impact on subsequent technological evolution beyond the domain"]
definition: In contrast to influencing a specific technological domain, some new knowledge may be influential beyond its focal technological domain; overall impact represents the firm's ability to create broadly useful technological developments.

name: Prior investor reaction to same-type deals
authors_terms: ["prior investor reaction", "strong prior responses to deals of the same type", "prior CARs to deals of the same type", "CAREXPACQ", "CAREXPALL"]
definition: The stock market response to the firm's earlier deals of the same type, taken in absolute value. A large prior response indicates that more information about the firm's capabilities has been disseminated into the investor community.

name: Same-type deal experience
authors_terms: ["deal experience", "concentrated deal experience", "portion of all prior deals as acquisitions", "portion of all prior deals as alliances", "ACQEXP", "ALLEXP"]
definition: The firm's accumulated experience with a particular deal type, expressed as the portion of all of the firm's prior deals that are acquisitions (or, for alliance experience, that are alliances). Firms that concentrate on one type of deal are described as having a track record in that type.

name: Change in investor reaction between successive deals
authors_terms: ["change in market reaction for successive acquisition (alliance) deals", "incremental change in CARs", "CHGCAR ACQ", "CHGCAR ALL"]
definition: The change in the stock market response between the focal deal and the firm's prior deals of the same type, computed as the difference between the absolute value of the cumulative abnormal return for the focal deal and the average absolute value of the cumulative abnormal returns for the firm's prior same-type deals.

name: Deal type
authors_terms: ["whether a deal was either an acquisition (ACQ) or an alliance (ALLIANCE)", "deal type", "type of deal"]
definition: The form of the focal boundary-spanning transaction, distinguishing acquisitions from alliances among the deals announced by the firm.

name: TQM job design
authors_terms: ["TQM role", "TQM job", "dual work", "dual TQM job", "dual work design"]
definition: Work under TQM in this sense is 'dual.' TQM combines two distinct types of tasks—standardized production and continuous improvement, execution and conceptualization—into one job role.

name: Standardized production work
definition: The TQM role includes standardized production tasks: prespecified production routine/s executed either individually or in work teams. This work is programmed—consistent with March and Simon (1958), programmed work is labeled 'standardized production.'

name: Continuous improvement work
definition: The TQM role also includes continuous improvement tasks: problem-solving activities associated with improving the prespecified production routines. This work has nonprogrammed means and programmed ends.

name: Innovation work
definition: Nonprogrammed work, for which neither the means nor ends of the work are well defined; the authors label nonprogrammed work 'innovation work.'

name: Avoidance
definition: Avoidance is operationalized here as a 'line employee response of electing not to perform the continuous improvement work.' Borrowing from Latack's (1986) empirical research, avoidance is identified as one mechanism for coping with role challenges.

name: Switching
definition: Integration takes the form of switching between the two roles, as the work requires. Such switching is an unscheduled response to critical cues in the environment indicating opportunities to improve procedures or quality problems in production, and reflects a change of attention while on the job.

name: Role conflict
definition: Avoiding the TQM job leads to role conflict from the continuing and heightened role disagreement. In this study role conflict was measured with five items selected from Rizzo et al.'s (1970) scale and reworded to reflect the language of the participants.

name: Role overload
definition: Avoiding the integration of the TQM job leads to role overload: the two distinct types of work—standardized production and continuous improvement—may be perceived as a nonexecutable set of role expectations.

name: Job satisfaction
definition: Satisfaction was measured with three measures, satisfaction with the job, the work, and the coworkers. The authors expect switching to be associated with higher levels of job satisfaction, arising from performing the enriched work of continuous improvement.

name: Plant performance
definition: Plant performance was measured via classifications of TQM performance (high, medium, and low) for each plant, as judged by eight senior managers (two from each division) and by two to six relevant peer managers from other plants.

name: Degree of TQM implementation
authors_terms: ["stage of TQM implementation", "degree of TQM implementation", "stage of implementation"]
definition: Observations of degree of implementation of TQM were coded in a variable, which ranged from 1 to 3 (3 reflected full implementation). The variable differed from measures of performance in that it was based on observed levels of TQM activities.

name: Information acquisition rigidity
authors_terms: ["rigidity in decision behaviors", "information acquisition rigidity", "decision rigidity", "rigidity measure"]
definition: Rigidity is consistency of information processing across all problem situations. The rigidity measure used contrasts the information acquired by experts in ill-structured settings with the information the same experts acquired in structured settings.

name: Problem setting
authors_terms: ["problem setting", "structured problem setting", "ill-structured problem setting", "structured decision situation"]
definition: A structured setting matches an expert's experience base, and an ill-structured setting is one in which the expert lacks professional experience. Ill-structured settings are those that have not been encountered in quite the same form and for which no predetermined and explicit set of ordered responses exists in the organization.

name: Financial information acquisition
authors_terms: ["financial information", "semantic information", "amount of financial information acquired", "information utilization"]
definition: The total amount of financial (semantic) information acquired, regardless of the category the information originated in. Semantic information is the most concrete type of information, represented by facts without contextual referents as to how the facts are interpreted or learned; in research on cognitive accounting, financial ratios have been viewed as semantic information.

name: Strategic information acquisition
authors_terms: ["strategic information", "episodic information", "amount of strategic information acquired"]
definition: The total amount of strategic (episodic) information acquired, regardless of the category the information originated in. Most strategic information can be considered episodic because it represents the qualitative context in which business analysts interpret information.

name: Lender type
authors_terms: ["lender type", "type of professional experience", "professional background", "venture capitalists", "commercial lenders"]
definition: Venture capitalists and commercial lenders perform the same general lending task, judging the likelihood of timely repayment, but the two groups perform the task in different problem settings. A person's type of professional experience has been shown to be related to the content of his or her belief structure.

name: Firm financial condition
definition: The financial condition of the case firm, ranging from a prosperous firm to a near-bankrupt firm, which will likely cue a very different set of stimuli for a business analyst.

name: Knowledge relatedness
definition: We define knowledge relatedness as 'the extent to which a multibusiness firm uses common knowledge resources across its business units.'

name: Product knowledge relatedness
definition: Relatedness of the knowledge embedded in products, which is an important source of cross-business synergy; synergies can arise from product knowledge created inside the firm as well as product knowledge acquired from outside through alliances of the firm. Internal product knowledge resides in product and manufacturing platforms.

name: Customer knowledge relatedness
definition: Customer knowledge refers to the needs, preferences, and buying behaviors of customers—why they purchase specific products and services, which product/service attributes they value, what value they hope to get by using them, and what their businesses are about. Customer knowledge is also a source of cross-business synergy in multibusiness firms.

name: Managerial knowledge relatedness
definition: Managerial knowledge consists of managerial insights, experiences, and best practices of a firm. We focus on three facets of managerial knowledge that are critical for a multibusiness firm: investment management, risk management, and alliance management.

name: Knowledge complementarity
authors_terms: ["knowledge complementarity", "complementarity of product knowledge relatedness, customer knowledge relatedness, and managerial knowledge relatedness", "cross-business knowledge synergy"]
definition: We define knowledge complementarity as the 'the extent to which a multibusiness firm uses a complementary set of common knowledge resources across its business units.' This construct is derived from the economic theory of complementarities: complementary resources create super-additive value synergies.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: The corporate financial performance of multibusiness firms, assessed with objective market-based and accounting-based performance measures. Three widely used objective measures of firm performance in the diversification literature were adopted as dependent variables: return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and Tobin's Q.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["top management team heterogeneity", "TMT heterogeneity", "TMT demographic heterogeneity"]
definition: Top management team (TMT) demographic heterogeneity is widely viewed as a proxy for cognitive and experiential heterogeneity. The composition of a TMT shapes the lenslike cognitive structure that defines its members' collective field of vision.

name: Past performance
definition: The important issue for organizations is how past performance impacts preparedness and motivation for future action; attributions of the discrepancies between organizational goals and actual performance influence the likelihood of predictable behavior or strategic change.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Organizational slack is defined as a buffer or cushion of actual or potential resources that may or may not be currently in use.

name: Competition-buffered industry environment
definition: Firms competing in a competition-buffered industry environment—high levels of growth, concentration, and/or barriers to entry—will compete less aggressively; high levels of industry growth, barriers to entry, and industry concentration all buffer industry participants from intense competition.

name: Attack volume
definition: Volume, defined as the number of action events that comprise the attack; the simplest dimension of a sequence of events is the total number of competitive action events that comprise each attack.

name: Attack duration
definition: This dimension is defined as the time elapsed from the beginning to the end of a sequence of action events.

name: Attack complexity
definition: Complexity, or the extent to which all possible types of action events are represented in the attack; defined as the extent to which a sequence of actions is composed of actions of many different types (as opposed to a simple attack consisting of a few types).

name: Attack unpredictability
definition: Unpredictability, or within-firm variability in the sequence of action events occurring from one attack to the next; defined as the extent to which a firm's sequential order of competitive actions is dissimilar from one attack period to the next.

name: Relative performance
definition: Market share gain is both a key organizational objective and a measure of standing vis-à-vis competitors that managers often believe to be associated with higher profits.

name: Individual utilization
authors_terms: ["utilization", "individual constraint", "current workload", "staffings in last six months", "level of utilization in the past 180 days"]
definition: An individual's workload can be measured by the number of projects the worker is involved with; as an individual's workload increases, his or her ability to take on more work decreases.

name: Staffing on a new project
definition: At its most abstract, human resource allocation takes as input the opportunities that need to be addressed and the existing current set of resources as well as their availability, and returns as output a matching of resources to opportunities. The dependent variable is an indicator variable that takes a value of 1 if the partner has been staffed on the project and 0 otherwise.

name: Firm-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["firm-specific human capital", "firm-specific capital", "firm-specific knowledge and skills", "relative seniority"]
definition: Firm-specific knowledge and skills include knowing how to get things done in a particular firm, maintaining a personal network and exchanging favors with colleagues, and being able to mobilize resources within a firm such as having access to the most appropriate associates. This makes human assets with high firm-specific human capital better able to execute smoothly a project and better able to successfully coordinate multiple projects simultaneously in these types of firms.

name: Rent-sharing system
authors_terms: ["rent-sharing system", "compensation system", "lockstep system", "firm-performance-based rent-sharing system", "individual-performance-based rent-sharing system", "merit-based compensation system"]
definition: The two most common rent-sharing systems among professional service firms are firm-performance-based and individual-performance-based rent-sharing systems. In the former, rents are shared among individuals according to a predetermined formula as in a group-performance-based compensation system, where the reference group encompasses the whole firm.

name: Top management team linkage ambiguity
authors_terms: ["linkage ambiguity among the TMT", "linkage ambiguity", "linkage ambiguity among top managers"]
definition: Linkage ambiguity is ambiguity among decision-makers about the link between competency and competitive advantage. Linkage ambiguity is high when managers differ in their beliefs about the contribution of a competency to their firm's competitive advantage.

name: Middle manager linkage ambiguity
definition: Linkage ambiguity is ambiguity among decision-makers about the link between competency and competitive advantage. Linkage ambiguity is high when managers differ in their beliefs about the contribution of a competency to their firm's competitive advantage.

name: Characteristic ambiguity
definition: Characteristic ambiguity focuses on the 'characteristics of competencies ... that can be simultaneous sources of advantage and ambiguity'. Characteristic ambiguity is ambiguity inherent to the resource itself.

name: Tacitness
definition: Tacitness reflects the extent that a competency is 'intuitive, non-verbalized and yet unarticulated'. Tacit knowledge is inherently more ambiguous than articulated knowledge.

name: Competency culture location
definition: Competencies are also characterized as causally ambiguous when they reside in organizational culture and values because they may be more uncertain and less mobile than knowledge that resides in an individual or small group of individuals.

name: Competitive advantage of competencies
definition: The competencies that managers believe provide a firm with a clear competitive advantage relative to members of a strategic group. High scores indicate that managers believe a competency provides their firm superior competitive advantage; low scores indicate that managers believe that the firm's competency is competitively inferior.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable in the model is firm performance, operationalized based on financial data from secondary sources, such as return on assets (ROA).

name: TMT average incentive-based pay proportion
authors_terms: ["average proportion of TMT incentive-based pay", "average proportion of TMT incentives", "average TMT incentive levels", "average proportion of a TMT's incentives"]
definition: The average proportion of TMT incentive-based pay reflects the sum of TMT members' granted and held incentive-based compensation forms divided by their total compensation.

name: Within-TMT incentive heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["within-TMT incentive heterogeneity", "within-team incentive heterogeneity", "within-TMT incentive portfolio heterogeneity", "the variance among TMT members' incentive portfolio levels"]
definition: within-TMT incentive heterogeneity, or the variance among TMT members' incentive portfolio levels. We operationalized within-TMT incentive heterogeneity with the gini coefficient of the proportion of TMT incentive-based pay in their portfolios for each TMT member (the top five managers). The gini coefficient ranges from zero, indicating 'complete agreement,' to one, indicating 'complete disparity'.

name: Announced acquisition investment
authors_terms: ["acquisition investment", "announced acquisition investment", "level of announced acquisition investment", "large acquisition investments", "large acquisition investments TMTs make"]
definition: For each year in our dataset, acquisition investment reflects the annual investment in majority public and private (51% or greater) acquisition transactions each firm announced and subsequently completed, and in which the individual acquisition value was greater than $10 million as reported in the SDC database.

name: Investor reaction to acquisition announcements
authors_terms: ["investor responses to acquisition announcements", "investor reactions", "announcement cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "investor responses"]
definition: investor reactions to acquisition announcements (announcement cumulative abnormal returns, or CARs) serve 'as salient signals of investors' expectations of the potential long-term firm value creation inherent in those impending acquisitions'.

name: Mental models
authors_terms: ["mental models", "shared mental models", "collective mental models", "cognitive mental models", "company-level mental models"]
definition: These letters are official documents that discuss themes important to the firm. These themes partially outline company-level mental models by publically addressing major priorities.

name: Cognitive strategic groups
definition: In our study, we call strategic groups clustered on such cognitive dimensions 'cognitive strategic groups,' and we use themes from annual reports to measure changes in the collective mental models (Peteraf and Shanley, 1997) which guide performance.

name: Performance-based strategic groups
authors_terms: ["performance strategic groups", "performance-based strategic groups", "strategic groups clustered by performance"]
definition: Cool and Schendel (1987) used a combination of performance measures to identify strategic groups in a careful examination of the American pharmaceutical industry. Building on prior lines of inquiry, they employed two concepts, strategic scope and strategic resources, to define strategic group membership.

name: Strategic intent
authors_terms: ["strategic intent", "strategic intentions", "future-oriented strategic intentions", "cognitive strategic group goals", "future-oriented strategic themes"]
definition: Such sensitivity to changing factors makes themes particularly useful measures when studying the strategic intent of a company (Hamel and Prahalad, 1989). In turn, strategic intentions measured by themes provide skeletal structures for 'cognitive oligopolies' (Porac et al., 1989).

name: Strategic performance
definition: Reports about performance are written in the present or past tenses (we sold more than ...). Present and past tense sentences were used for a similar identification of performance strategic groups based on reports of achievement in the present and near past.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreigniness", "foreignness", "foreign-owned defense contractors", "U.S. subsidiaries of foreign defense contractors"]
definition: I define a firm as foreign-owned - that is, as a U.S. subsidiary of a foreign defense contractor - if its GUO, the firm at the top of the corporate family tree that influences the decisions and operations of the U.S. subsidiary, is foreign. Thus the only difference between U.S. and foreign-owned defense contractors is the ownership of the company.

name: Outside lobbying spending
authors_terms: ["average outside lobbying expense", "outside lobbying expense", "spending to hire outside lobbyists", "hiring outside lobbyists"]
definition: To create a variable that captures how much each firm spent to hire outside lobbyists to address defense-related issues, I use lobbying transaction reports; I construct annual outside-lobbying spending on defense-related issues by each defense contractor.

name: Defense contract awards
authors_terms: ["U.S. defense contract awards", "defense-contract amounts", "U.S. government defense-contract awards", "amount of a defense contract award"]
definition: The dependent variable is the logged dollar amount of U.S. defense weapons-system contracts awarded to a given firm in a given year. The amount of the contracts is aggregated by each defense contractor annually.

name: Duration of lobbying contract
authors_terms: ["duration of lobbying contract", "duration of the lobbying contract", "longer relationships", "long-term relationships"]
definition: To measure the duration of a lobbying contract, I calculate the average number of years that an outside lobbyist is employed by a lobbying firm-lobbying client.

name: Immigrant entrepreneur group membership
authors_terms: ["immigrant entrepreneur group member", "group member", "Gujarati hotel ownership", "immigrant entrepreneur group"]
definition: Owners belonging to an immigrant entrepreneur group, where the social structures underlying such groups are family relations and common ethnic (or regional) backgrounds. Membership is identified in the data from owner surnames designated as Gujarati and from incorporated hotels having a partner with a Gujarati surname.

name: Proximity to high-resource group member establishments
authors_terms: ["proximate high-resource group member establishments", "proximate branded hotels owned by Gujaratis", "proximate Gujarati hotels"]
definition: Branded-chain hotels in the vicinity of the establishment under observation that are owned by members of the immigrant entrepreneur group. Branded chain affiliation is an easily observable indicator that a firm possesses resources and has the ability to contribute to social capital.

name: Proximity to high-resource nonmember establishments
authors_terms: ["proximate high-resource nonmember establishments", "proximate branded hotels owned by non-Gujaratis"]
definition: Branded-chain hotels in the vicinity of the establishment under observation owned by individuals who are not members of the immigrant entrepreneur group, mostly from the native population of the same industry.

name: Proximity to low-resource group member establishments
authors_terms: ["proximate unbranded motels owned by Gujaratis", "other low-resource member establishments"]
definition: Unbranded motels in the vicinity of the establishment under observation that are owned by members of the immigrant entrepreneur group. Unbranded motels unaffiliated with national chains are owned by individuals who possess few resources.

name: Proximity to low-resource nonmember establishments
definition: Unbranded motels in the vicinity of the establishment under observation that are owned by individuals who are not members of the immigrant entrepreneur group.

name: Establishment survival
definition: Motels are considered survivors as long as they remain open for business. They are 'at risk of failure' until they have permanently closed down; changes of ownership or 'doing business as' name do not count as failure.

name: Location choice
definition: In our setting, a new hotel owner chooses from among geographic locations based upon attributes of the locations; the alternatives are the zip codes in Texas with at least one hotel present.

name: Production experience
definition: Firms get better at making things as they gain experience producing them; cumulative production measures this because it more closely relates to the number of trial-and-error experiments that have occurred, x measuring the cumulative number of units produced.

name: Vertical integration
definition: The degree to which a firm produces its own components rather than purchasing them; an observable feature that closely reflects the degree of interdependence in production. Interdependence refers to the degree to which two or more activities interact to determine an outcome jointly.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: Environmental stability is consistency over time in the mapping of activities onto performance; the authors operationalize volatility as its absence, where the factors of success in one period bear no relation to those in the next.

name: Firm performance
definition: Organizational performance is evaluated both by examining firm growth rates and by modelling exit rates, market exit occurring when a company no longer markets a workstation product or is acquired.

name: Political competition
authors_terms: ["political competition", "political competition between two factions: the ruling party and the opposition"]
definition: The voters have a realistic ability to throw out those currently in power and replace them with an alternative opposition party or opposition coalition, and social actors recognize this fact, and therefore those currently in power act taking their fear of being replaced into account.

name: Corporate bribery
authors_terms: ["corporate bribery", "corporate bribery of high-level government officials", "bribery amount"]
definition: Corporate bribery of high-level government officials is one of the two nonmarket strategy activities the authors focus on; it is covert and illicit. The former tends to be illegal and is deliberately kept secret.

name: Contributions to politically connected charities
authors_terms: ["corporate contributions to politically connected charities", "politically connected charity contributions", "politically connected charity donations"]
definition: Corporate contributions to politically connected charities are concealed yet licit nonmarket activity; these contributions often commingle legitimate charity activities together with elements that may be perceived as quasi-bribery.

name: Change in ranking position
authors_terms: ["changes in rankings", "falls and rises in rankings", "Fall", "Rise", "change in rank", "ranking position"]
definition: The key independent variables are changes in rankings, measured as a firm's fall or rise in rank between two consecutive years. The direction of change, whether it is a rise or fall in rank, is treated as one important contingency that shapes how much a change in ranking affects audience assessments.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: The dependent variable is Cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), a measure that scholars frequently use to examine how investors react to new market information. A negative CAR indicates negative stock market reactions to an event, while a positive CAR suggests positive reactions.

name: Media coverage
definition: Media coverage is the total number of media articles mentioning a firm during the full calendar year prior to the announcement of the rankings. Media outlets shape investor perceptions with information about firms' behaviors, financial performance, and market trends.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: Security analyst coverage is the sum of unique earnings estimates by financial analysts during the calendar year prior to the publication of rankings. Security analysts generate research reports that encapsulate earnings forecasts, investment recommendations, and industry assessments, helping investors to assess firms' financial performance.

name: Audience sophistication
definition: Audiences consist of individuals with diverse levels of knowledge, specialization, and preferences. One key dimension in which audiences differ is their sophistication: the ability to gather and process different pieces of information to assess an organization.

name: Previous ranking position
authors_terms: ["Previous rank", "prior ranking position", "previous ranking position", "Ranking position"]
definition: Organizations hold various ranking positions before experiencing rises and falls with the announcement of new rankings. The authors assess a firm's previous rank both with three tiers based on the previous ranking and with a continuous measure of the actual prior-year rank.

name: Independent director dissent
definition: Dissent is an independent director's non-confirming opinion (a dissent or abstention) on a board matter, recorded in the joint opinion report the independent directors issue after a board meeting that has discussed a material matter.

name: Appointer-appointee tie
authors_terms: ["appointer-appointee tie", "social exchange tie with the board chair", "appointed by the board chair"]
definition: The dyadic social exchange relationship between an independent director and the board chair; independent directors are defined as appointed by a board chair if they joined the board after the chair assumed office.

name: Breakdown of the appointer-appointee tie
authors_terms: ["breakdown of the social exchange relationship", "departure of the appointing chair", "chairperson departure", "post-chairperson departure"]
definition: A breakdown of the social exchange relationship between the independent director and the board chair who appointed the director, which occurs when that appointing chair leaves the board.

name: Endgame of the board game
authors_terms: ["endgame", "end of the board 'game'", "the board 'game' is reaching its last round"]
definition: The end of the board 'game' is the situation in which an independent director foresees a breakdown of the social exchange relationship in the near future, either because the director him- or herself is about to leave the board or because the current board chair is about to leave the board.

name: Employee inflow from clients
authors_terms: ["gain from client", "gaining an employee from a potential client", "hiring an employee from a potential client", "mobility between cooperators"]
definition: Personnel flows in which a firm hires from a potential cooperator, such as a client. These types of personnel flows have the potential to create or strengthen network ties between the focal firm and client company.

name: Employee outflow to clients
authors_terms: ["loss to client", "losing an employee to a potential client", "mobility between cooperators"]
definition: Personnel flows in which a firm loses employees to a potential cooperator, such as a client. An employee that leaves a firm to join a potential client can be an ambassador for the services of his former employer, generating external social capital.

name: Employee inflow from competitors
authors_terms: ["gain competitor-client tie", "gaining an employee from a competitor", "employee mobility between competitors"]
definition: When individuals move between competing firms, they may transfer their external social capital to their new employers, who may now have greater access to business opportunities involving the clients of the employees' former employer.

name: Employee outflow to competitors
authors_terms: ["loss to competitors", "employees that move to competitors", "employee mobility between competitors"]
definition: The loss of human capital through employee exit can be made up by hiring, but when employees go to work for competitors, they enable these rival firms to compete much more closely with their former employers; the loss of client-related social capital to competitors can be particularly damaging.

name: Patent business from client
authors_terms: ["patent work", "volume of patent business", "amount of patent business", "patent filings"]
definition: The volume of patent business outsourced by a particular company to a focal law firm in a given year.

name: Completion of product development
authors_terms: ["completion of product development", "finishing development of the initial product", "shipping the first product"]
definition: One of the critical milestones in the growth of a technology-based company is finishing development of the initial product, which helps resolve much of the technical uncertainty regarding the feasibility of developing the product. In almost all of the companies studied, the completion of product development was closely linked to the shipping of the first product to customers.

name: Outside financing rounds
authors_terms: ["raising a new round of financing", "round of outside financing", "rounds of financing", "financing round"]
definition: Investors try to reduce uncertainty over time by 'staging' their capital investments across multiple, smaller 'rounds' of investment that are months or years apart. Start-ups therefore typically have to go through multiple rounds of negotiating with their investors.

name: Amount raised in the latest financing round
authors_terms: ["amount raised in the last round", "money raised by a company in its latest round of financing", "doing a big round"]
definition: When they are raising new rounds of financing, companies can choose to raise a lot of capital during the round, or a little bit of capital. The more capital raised in each round, the higher the percentage of the company that the inside executives have to give up to outside investors.

name: New investor participation
authors_terms: ["adding new investors", "new investors", "mix of existing versus new investors"]
definition: Each funding round, a company can either raise money from its existing investors or it can seek to add new investors. It is often easier to raise money from existing investors, for they are already familiar with the company, have relationships with the existing executives, have a strong interest in seeing the company succeed, and may not wish to have their equity positions diluted.

name: Insider equity control
definition: For critical decisions, such as whether to replace a Founder-CEO, the key turning point is whether outside investors own more than 50% of the company and therefore have 'equity control'. The higher the percentage owned by outside investors, the more decision-making control the outside investors should have about important issues.

name: Founder-CEO succession
definition: The destination state of interest is the exit of the Founder-CEO from the role of CEO, with the subsequent entry into the firm of the second CEO. To measure Founder-CEO succession, the likelihood that the founding CEO would be replaced was modeled.

name: CEO political orientation
authors_terms: ["CEO political orientation", "personal political orientation", "political orientation", "risk tolerance", "risk propensity"]
definition: As a reflection of a CEO's underlying tendencies, political orientation serves as a measure of risk propensity because it captures a CEO's conservatism, which refers to an individual's psychological need to reduce uncertainty and ambiguity. It is a continuous measure based on the relative political donations to each party, capturing whether a CEO is Democratic-leaning or Republican-leaning.

name: Initial performance-based pay
definition: By performance-based pay, we refer to the portion of pay that is not fixed but is linked to some level of firm performance (e.g., stock options or bonuses). We operationalized CEO initial Performance-Based Pay as the ratio of performance pay to initial total pay in the year of the succession.

name: VC prominence in syndicate networks
authors_terms: ["VC prominence", "VC prominence in syndicate networks", "prominence of the VCs investing in a given new venture", "affiliations with prominent VCs"]
definition: VCs that are well connected to other VCs through extensive direct and indirect co-investment ties achieve prominent positions in VC syndicate networks and are perceived to be of higher quality. This measure represents the prominence of the VCs investing in a given new venture in VC syndicate networks.

name: Prominence in alliance networks
authors_terms: ["alliance prominence", "new venture's prominence in alliance networks", "prominence in networks of previous alliances"]
definition: Organizations themselves can achieve prominence in networks of prior alliances (i.e., alliance prominence), by forming extensive direct and indirect alliance ties to other organizations in alliance networks.

name: Future alliance formation
authors_terms: ["likelihood of future alliance formation", "future alliance formation"]
definition: Our level of analysis is the dyad-year, and the dependent variable is whether or not a particular new venture (i) and established company (j) form an R&D alliance in a given year (t).

name: Knowledge complexity
definition: I define complex knowledge as a recipe that has many interdependencies between its ingredients. Two ingredients are considered interdependent if a change in one ingredient affects performance of another ingredient.

name: Employee mobility
authors_terms: ["employee mobility", "mobility", "intra-industry employee mobility", "employee moves to rival firms"]
definition: Intra-industry employee mobility (i.e., individual moves to another firm in the same industry) is a powerful engine of knowledge diffusion between firms, established and start-ups alike.

name: Team mobility
authors_terms: ["team mobility", "moving to rival firms together with co-inventors", "team movement"]
definition: Team movement allows groups of collaborators to remain intact, maintaining communication routines and social interaction developed while working at the parent firm and retaining the coordination that is critical for implementing and improving complex recipes.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
definition: Employee entrepreneurship-the intra-industry founding of a new venture by an individual who previously worked for an incumbent firm-has been heralded as a hallmark of innovation.

name: Team entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["team entrepreneurship", "team founding", "team employee entrepreneurship", "founded the firm together with individuals"]
definition: The solution, again, may be to found the firm together with individuals who helped to co-develop the complex recipe within the incumbent firm. The founding team members not only serve as important complementary assets for determining the survival of the new venture, but they also allow the coordination developed while collaborating within the parent organization to continue.

name: CEO name uncommonness
authors_terms: ["CEO name uncommonness", "name uncommonness", "CEOs' uncommon names", "uncommon names"]
definition: The uncommonness of a CEO's given name. Following prior research on uncommon names, the authors calculated the commonness of a CEO's given name as the frequency of its appearance (by gender) in the SSA data set, and their measure of name uncommonness is simply the negative value of the measure of name commonness.

name: Strategic distinctiveness
definition: The degree to which a firm's strategy differs from the strategies of other firms in the same industry.

name: CEO confidence
definition: Psychological research suggests that self-confidence is the belief that one can achieve desirable outcomes despite uncertainty. The authors argue that more confident CEOs are more likely to believe that they can achieve desirable outcomes despite uncertainty.

name: CEO power
definition: Corporate governance research suggests that CEOs' influence over strategic decisions is often contingent on their power relative to boards of directors.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence refers to the capacity of the environment to support business growth.

name: Market commonality
authors_terms: ["market commonality", "market commonalty", "the degree of presence that a competitor manifests in the markets in which it overlaps with the focal firm"]
definition: Market commonality is 'the degree of presence that a competitor manifests in the markets in which it overlaps with the focal firm' (Chen, 1996: 106). It is used as a means of empirically assessing a firm's motivation to engage, or not engage, in competitive activity.

name: Resource similarity
authors_terms: ["resource similarity", "resource similarity is the extent to which competitors possess comparable strategic endowments"]
definition: Resource similarity is 'the extent to which a given competitor possesses strategic endowments comparable, in terms of both type and amount, to those of the focal firm' (Chen, 1996: 107). It represents the capability of competitors to respond.

name: Foothold attack
definition: A foothold attack occurs when a competitive action such as making an acquisition or beginning a promotional campaign is made via a foothold. At a given point in time, a firm that owns a foothold can launch a foothold attack, withdraw the foothold, or simply maintain the foothold.

name: Foothold withdrawal
definition: A foothold withdrawal occurs when a firm ceases selling products or services in the foothold's market.

name: Foothold
authors_terms: ["foothold", "footholds", "small position that a firm intentionally establishes within a market in which it does not yet compete"]
definition: A foothold is a small position that a firm intentionally establishes within a market in which it does not yet compete. By small position the authors mean owning a very modest amount of market share, and intentionally establishes denotes that small positions resulting from the decline of an underperforming unit are excluded.

name: CEO career horizon
authors_terms: ["CEO career horizon", "CEO's expected tenure with the firm", "career horizon"]
definition: The governance mechanism the authors consider is the CEO career horizon, defined as the expected amount of time left before a CEO is dismissed or retires. It is also described as the expected amount of time before a CEO is dismissed or retires.

name: Real option intensity
authors_terms: ["real option intensity", "real options investments", "real options portfolio"]
definition: Real option intensity is the sensitivity of firm value to changes in firm-level uncertainty (i.e., changes in firm-level stock return volatility). It is a firm-level measure of a real options portfolio rather than the typical transaction-level measure focusing on a single type of real options.

name: CEO long-term incentives
definition: Long-term incentives are incentives aligning the interests of CEOs (especially CEOs who are likely to prioritize short-term benefits) with those of shareholders. They are approximated with unexercised options (exercisable + unexercisable) and restricted stock holdings scaled by total compensation.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: Institutional ownership helps to effectively monitor CEOs and lead them to focus on long-term investments. It is calculated as the ratio of stock owned by institutions.

name: Capability exploitation
definition: Capability exploitation concerns the extent to which a firm exploits rent-generating resources that are firm specific, difficult to imitate, and able to generate abnormal returns. It is the extent to which an MNE parent has exploited distinctive resources that are rare and firm-specific, inimitable, and rent-generating for operations in China.

name: Capability building
definition: Capability building involves the extent to which a firm commits to building new capabilities through learning from other organizations, creating new skills, or revitalizing existing skills in new situations. In this study it focuses on how to develop and build new competencies needed for local operations.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity as perceived by foreign managers concerns the extent to which environmental factors in a host country are diverse and heterogeneous. It is a multidimensional construct consisting of diversity and heterogeneity, each containing macroeconomic, political/legal, and sociocultural segments.

name: Structural uncertainty
definition: Structural uncertainty involves the volatility and variability of the industrial environment or related market structure.

name: Business cultural specificity
definition: Business cultural specificity as perceived by foreign managers refers to the unique characteristics of a host country's business culture and how much they vary from international standards.

name: Entry mode
authors_terms: ["entry mode", "wholly owned entry mode", "fully owned entry mode", "joint venture mode"]
definition: Choosing an entry mode strategy is important during international expansion because it is tied to an MNE's core competency contributions, control over subsidiaries, parent-subsidiary relations, and vulnerability to external changes in a host country. The most prevalent and predominant entry modes used by MNEs investing in emerging markets such as China are joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries, and entry mode is defined as one if wholly owned and zero otherwise (joint venture).

name: Market orientation
definition: This study defines market orientation as whether an MNE subunit targets the host country market as opposed to export markets.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: Subsidiary performance was measured by ROI (net return/total investment) in 1997, and the sample firms were separated into a high-performance and a low-performance group based on the mean score of subsidiary performance.

name: Association with failure
authors_terms: ["association with failure", "association with a failed employer", "strength of association with failure"]
definition: Association with failed organizations is a negative status characteristic because such associations often cause others to doubt an individual's character and competence. We consider association with failure to be a specific status characteristic that informs evaluators about an individual's competencies.

name: Educational prestige
authors_terms: ["educational prestige", "prestige of the law school attended", "elite law school graduate"]
definition: Educational prestige represents a status characteristic based on group affiliation that informs evaluators' expectations of one's ability and performance at a wide variety of tasks.

name: Intraprofessional status loss
authors_terms: ["intraprofessional status loss", "regaining employment at a lower-status employer"]
definition: We therefore expect that individuals displaced by organizational failure will typically regain employment at organizations of lesser status than the failed employer, what we term intraprofessional status loss.

name: Unethical acts
definition: We define unethical acts as acts that are illegal under state or federal laws or acts that are 'morally unacceptable to the larger community' (Jones 1991, p. 367). These may range from the clearly illegal acts of violating environmental laws or obstruction of justice to legal, but generally disfavored acts, such as paying greenmail to a corporate raider.

name: Illegitimacy of unethical acts
authors_terms: ["degree of illegitimacy", "perceived illegitimacy", "illegitimacy of the acts", "average illegitimacy of acts"]
definition: We constructed a measure designed to capture the perceived illegitimacy of the unethical acts in our sample. To obtain data on the perceived illegitimacy of each of these acts, we asked 34 individuals to complete a survey asking them to indicate the degree of illegitimacy (i.e., how appropriate is it for a firm to be engaging in this type of act) on a five-point scale.

name: Network partner quality
authors_terms: ["network partner quality", "quality of network partners", "quality of the firms in the network", "quality network"]
definition: We have identified three characteristics of network participants that seem to be key dimensions of quality: firm reputation, profitability, and size. It is, therefore, likely that having partners of good reputation, large size, and good profitability will indicate that a firm has a quality network.

name: Positional prominence
definition: A firm is prominent if its network partners are well connected in their own networks. As Nohria (1992, p. 6) explains, 'An actor's prominence increases as the actor is the object of relations from many others who are in turn the object of many relations.'

name: Network cohesion
definition: Structural cohesion reflects the connectivity among a focal firm and its network partners (Friedkin 1998, Burt 1992) and is 'the extent to which a relationship is surrounded by strong third-party connections' (Reagans and McEvily 2003, p. 245). We define structural cohesion as the presence of a strong third party for a potential relationship.

name: Network partner exit
authors_terms: ["exit of higher quality partners", "higher quality firms leaving the network", "higher reputation firms dropping out", "more legitimate firms sever relationships with their less legitimate partners"]
definition: We further hypothesize that large, successful, good reputation firms will sever relationships with firms whose legitimacy is declining as a result of an unethical act.

name: Network partner replacement
authors_terms: ["their replacement with lower quality partners", "lower quality firms taking their place", "lower reputation firms joining the firm's network"]
definition: We further hypothesize that focal firms will be forced to replace these high-quality partners with smaller, less successful, poorer reputation firms.

name: Impression offsetting
authors_terms: ["impression offsetting", "offsetting", "positive, but unrelated, information", "positive unrelated information"]
definition: We define impression offsetting as: organizational actions initiated to positively influence external perceptions of the organization by releasing positive, but unrelated, information, in anticipation of an event becoming known that may negatively violate external stakeholders' expectations.

name: Prior acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["prior acquisition activity", "recent acquisition activity", "acquirer prior acquisition activity", "serial acquirers"]
definition: As a firm's prior actions inform its predictive expectancies, one particularly salient source of such expectancies is the firm's acquisition history: as norm deviating behavior accumulates through behavioral repetition, a larger negative expectancy violation reaction is generated as compared to a single behavior.

name: Acquirer reputation
definition: Because firm reputation is based upon the ability to consistently deliver quality, shareholders will likely hold the predictive expectancy that high-reputation firms will continue to perform at a high level.

name: Target relatedness
definition: Although all acquisitions carry significant risk, unrelated acquisitions are generally considered riskier and are thus more likely to lead to a negative expectancy violation; acquirers that have knowledge of their own industry may be less able to assimilate and use knowledge from a target organization in a different, unrelated industry.

name: Target profitability
definition: If a target organization is currently profitable, an acquirer may be effectively acquiring a revenue stream and some opportunity to increase efficiency by consolidating support functions such as marketing and accounting; acquiring an unprofitable target combines the challenge of integrating the two companies as well as transforming an acquired unprofitable organization into a profitable component of the acquiring firm.

name: Cumulative abnormal returns
definition: Cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) are the sum of daily abnormal returns for a security over a period that captures the influence of the event during that period.

name: Organizational decline
definition: Decline refers to decreasing internal resource munificence over time. Declining organizations are declining with respect to two critical resources: financial and human (managerial) resources.

name: Domain initiative
authors_terms: ["domain initiative", "entering new lines of business", "mergers and acquisitions"]
definition: Postdecline firms fail to make strategic changes and ignore the need for significant domain initiatives, such as entering new lines of business or acquiring new subunits. Strategic variables were assessed through measures of domain initiative.

name: Downsizing
definition: Downsizing involves changes in organizational size and scope, such as limiting sales, selling off fixed assets or subsidiaries, and pruning product-market domains.

name: Centralization
authors_terms: ["centralization", "centralization of the decision-making process", "CEO span of control", "span of CEO control"]
definition: A typical centralization action is increased supervision of the decision-making process by a central authority like the chief executive officer (CEO). An increasing span of CEO control, or increase in the percentage of top managers reporting directly to the CEO, would evidence centralization.

name: Top team legal and financial background
authors_terms: ["financial people", "legal people", "people with legal, financial, or accounting backgrounds"]
definition: Cash-starved postdecline firms may create top-management teams that are unbalanced, with an overemphasis on serving their creditors' demands. Postdecline firms seek the managers best trained to deal with creditors and short-term cash goals and are likely to hire people with finance, accounting, and legal backgrounds.

name: Top team marketing, R&D, and operations background
definition: An efficiency orientation may lead firms to cut back discretionary expenditures and managers in critical functions such as marketing, R&D, and throughput. Throughput refers to production activities, or to operations in nonmanufacturing firms.

name: Consequences of decline
authors_terms: ["consequences of decline", "strategic and managerial consequences of organizational decline", "postdecline characteristics"]
definition: Postdecline firms are distinguishable from firms that have not declined because the former are paralyzed strategically. Postdecline firms also engage in downsizing and centralization, and they have inadequately staffed top management teams that contribute to their paralysis.

name: Postdecline lingering
definition: Lingering is exemplified by firms that decline, either rapidly or gradually, but then delay bankruptcy for several years. They exist in a postdecline state of inadequate financial and managerial resources.

name: Industry demand growth
authors_terms: ["industry demand growth", "industry growth", "growth in the rate of demand", "growing demand"]
definition: An improving environment, one in which demand is growing, may delay the failure of some weak firms in post-organizational decline because, as demand grows, competitive pressures are lessened and industry shakeouts are avoided (Porter, 1980).

name: Industry demand uncertainty
authors_terms: ["industry demand uncertainty", "demand uncertainty", "uncertainty with respect to the rate of demand growth"]
definition: Uncertainty with respect to the rate of demand growth may encourage creditors to allow a troubled debtor firm to linger. If next year's demand growth is unpredictable, it is impossible to be sure about the firm's fate, perhaps encouraging creditors to hold a false hope of recovery.

name: Asset downsizing ability
authors_terms: ["asset downsizing ability", "ability to liquidate fixed assets", "fixed assets that can be liquidated", "net fixed assets"]
definition: Some large postdecline firms may be able to forestall bankruptcy because they are capable of staving off their creditors' demands for cash with their great ability to downsize their operations. Postdecline firms with large amounts of fixed assets can generate cash through prebankruptcy liquidation.

name: Creditor commitment
definition: The literature on commitment suggests that firms owing significant sums of money ensnare creditors because lenders delay the recognition of significant losses. Postdecline firms may be able to delay bankruptcy for size-related reasons.

name: Interpersonal social ties
definition: Social ties are interpersonal relations defined by noneconomic content, such as acquaintance and friendship. Social ties have noneconomic content that is sufficient for their full-fledged existence when economic use is absent.

name: Collegial signal
authors_terms: ["collegial signal", "signal of collegiality", "affirmation of collegiality", "collegial aspect of competition"]
definition: A signal of collegiality affirms the signal origin company's and the competitor's shared professional affiliation. Collegial signals are affirmations of the collegial relation that, together with goal conflict, constitutes the competition relation.

name: Goal conflict signal
authors_terms: ["signal of goal conflict", "goal conflict signal", "goal conflict aspect of competition"]
definition: A signal of goal conflict affirms to a competitor the incompatibility of the signal origin company's and the competitor's goals. Signals are affirmations of either of the two aspects of the competition relation, and they may travel without being intentionally communicated.

name: Status competition
authors_terms: ["status competition", "status rivalry", "competition for status", "competition for recognition"]
definition: Company leaders' perception that an indication competitor regards competition with their company as a means of claiming peer recognition, or status, within the industry. Status rivalry is one of the two signals of goal conflict that featured in the drug developers' accounts.

name: Stakeholder trust in the organization
definition: Following Rousseau et al. (1998), we define trust as the psychological willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party (individual or organization) based on positive expectations regarding the other party's motivation and/or behavior. Stakeholder trust in organizations entails the willingness of individuals (customers, employees, etc.) to accept vulnerability to the actions of an organization based on positive expectations.

name: Integrity
definition: Attributions of integrity gauge whether a trustee is perceived as forthcoming, honest, and of requisite moral character. Integrity refers to an organization's general tendency (or propensity) to act fairly and ethically.

name: Benevolence
definition: Attributions regarding benevolence gauge whether the trustee exhibits goodwill toward the trustor and has concern for the trustor's wellbeing. Benevolence refers to the organization's concern for their stakeholders' well-being.

name: Transparency
definition: Transparency, or the perceived willingness to share trust-relevant information with vulnerable stakeholders, is a distinct critical dimension of trustworthiness, which the authors include as a separate dimension rather than subsuming it under integrity.

name: Identification
definition: According to Lewicki and Bunker (1996), identification-based trust stems from the understanding and internalization of the interests and intentions of the other party, based on shared values and commitment.

name: Managerial competence
definition: Managerial competence is implicated in the organization's ability to make strategic decisions and manage stakeholder relationships, such as decision-making ability and strategic vision, which are essential for long-term survival and competitiveness.

name: Technical competence
definition: Technical competence is implicated in the organization's ability to deliver high-quality products and services.

name: Relationship depth
definition: Depth is a measure of the extent and intensity of a stakeholder's interaction with an organization. Relationship depth refers to the intensity and intimacy of a relationship; although it is often difficult to assess the precise depth of a relationship, it can be approximated, at least in part, by interaction frequency and relationship duration.

name: Stakeholder locus
definition: The locus dimension captures the stakeholder's position (internal versus external) vis-à-vis the organization, based on extant stakeholder research that distinguishes between internal and external stakeholders. Employees and investors are viewed as internal stakeholders because they represent the organization; customers and suppliers are external stakeholders.

name: Severity of bank runs
authors_terms: ["severity of bank runs", "bank runs in 1893", "number of banks that suffered depositors' runs", "severe bank runs"]
definition: The severity of bank runs in a city during the Panic of 1893, measured as the number of banks that suffered depositors' runs. A bank run is a display of distrust against banks by community members and a breach of trust among community members.

name: Community collective action
authors_terms: ["community collective action", "currency substitutes", "issuing currency substitutes", "issuing small denomination currency substitutes"]
definition: The community collective action of issuing small denomination currency substitutes, which were issued by banks for public circulation. Issuing currency substitutes required trust and cooperation among nonbank businesses and individuals in the community.

name: Organizational collective action
definition: The organizational collective action of mutual lending, typically coordinated by a local banking clearing house, which pooled the resources of member banks and served as the lender of last resort by issuing clearinghouse loan certificates.

name: Bank run hazard
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of a bank run", "mean hazard of bank runs", "risk of a bank run", "maximum hazard of bank runs"]
definition: The hazard that banks in a community were at risk of a bank run, obtained as hazard rates of a bank run for each city during the time period of the 1893 bank run; banks are more at risk of a run when there are bank runs in nearby communities, in banks of the same form, and in communities with similar demographic characteristics.

name: Direct experience of the prior crisis
authors_terms: ["percentage of banks in 1907 that were founded before 1893", "percentage of banks that survived the Panic of 1893", "percentage of survived banks", "banks that existed during the bank runs"]
definition: Banks' experience of the Panic of 1893, measured as the percentage of banks in 1907 that were founded before 1893.

name: Local clearinghouse founding
authors_terms: ["building a clearinghouse after the Panic of 1893", "built a local clearinghouse", "founding of a clearing house", "building clearinghouse"]
definition: The establishment of a formal institution that encoded inferences from history into routines for collective action: a clearinghouse built by local banks after the Panic of 1893 indicates that banks had reflected on past experience, recognized their common fate, and attempted to address the problem jointly.

name: Forward channel integration
authors_terms: ["forward channel integration", "level of forward channel integration", "channel integration", "level of channel integration"]
definition: Channels of distribution are the means by which manufacturers make their finished products available for purchase by end customers. They can be completely integrated (direct), where the firm uses its own human and physical assets to gain and fulfill customer orders, completely nonintegrated (indirect), where the firm uses independent firms named intermediaries to gain and fulfill customer orders, or somewhere in between, which is most common.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity is the extent to which specialized investments are needed to support an exchange. Specific assets, whether physical or intangible, cannot be redeployed to another application or relationship without a significant loss in value.

name: Internal uncertainty
definition: Internal uncertainty is the extent to which it is difficult to assess performance. It is measured as the extent to which it is difficult to assess performance in the channel of distribution, where the ability of the firm to discern what is contributing to sales with end customers (e.g., salesperson effort) is the key performance issue.

name: External uncertainty
definition: External uncertainty is the extent to which it is difficult to accurately predict future states of the world. The construct is driven by an industry environment that is very dynamic (fast changing) and/or very complex and difficult to grasp.

name: Firm market power
definition: We define 'market power' as a firm's ability to influence the actions of others in a product-market. Given our focus, the ability of the firm to influence independent channel intermediaries is of main concern.

name: Stock exchange listing
definition: The exchange on which a firm is listed determines whether it faces a mandate for a lead director: the NYSE required that a nonmanagement director must preside at executive sessions and the company must disclose the name of that lead director on its website or in its proxy statement, whereas the NASDAQ did not enact any specific rule about appointing a lead director or making that person known to the public.

name: CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["CEO dismissal", "dismiss the CEO", "firing the CEO", "forced turnovers"]
definition: Termination of employment is the last resort that boards use to discipline CEOs for poor performance; the authors classify dismissals based on firm press releases and news reports to identify forced turnovers from the larger set of all CEO turnovers.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "separate the CEO and board chair", "separation of these roles"]
definition: CEO duality receives a value of '1' if a CEO is also Chair of the Board and '0' otherwise in a year; shareholders generally desire separation of the board chair role from the CEO because it diffuses power and signals the CEO's willingness to succumb to external governance in the face of poor performance.

name: Excess CEO compensation
definition: Excess CEO compensation reflects whether a CEO is paid more than warranted for a given level of performance (accounting for important organizational and CEO factors), and is about deviations in CEO pay that result in overpayment, where the CEO is unnecessarily appropriating rent.

name: Operating performance
definition: The authors use operating performance, measured as ROA, instead of market performance because the latter can be influenced by managers' impression management, and they theorize that lead directors will actually make firms more efficient.

name: Dedicated institutional investor ownership
definition: DIIs concentrate their shareholdings into a small number of firms that they hold for an extended period of time; they are impervious to short-term earnings reports and instead are concerned with a firm's ability to compete over time.

name: Lead director adoption timing
definition: Tolbert and Zucker describe a two-stage model of adoption motivations, where early adopters are substantive and late adopters are symbolic; the authors define early adopters as firms that adopted in 2003 and 2004.

name: CEO-lead director relative standing
authors_terms: ["CEO-lead director relative standing", "lead director's status", "high-status lead directors"]
definition: The lead director's status, or relative standing, compared to the CEO; when lead directors have a lower relative standing than the CEO they are beholden to the CEO, whereas lead directors with higher relative standing have more power to implement the kind of changes they desire.

name: Synergy realization
definition: The actual net benefits (reduced cost per unit, increased income, etc.) created by the interaction of two firms involved in a merger or acquisition.

name: Combination potential
definition: The various sources of synergy define a combination's potential, which in turn is expected to affect the extent to which synergies will be realized in an acquisition. The authors conceptualize the combination potential of M&As in terms of both the strategic similarity and the strategic complementarity of operations of the joining firms.

name: Organizational integration
definition: The degree of interaction and coordination between the two firms involved in a merger or acquisition.

name: Employee resistance
definition: The individual and collective opposition of employees to the combination and subsequent integration of the joining firms.

name: Management style similarity
definition: The degree to which managers in combining organizations emphasize risk-taking, authority, and structure.

name: Cross-border combination
definition: Synergy realization may be affected by whether the joining firms are located in the same country, that is, whether the bidder and target were headquartered in different countries.

name: Relative size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "relative company size", "relative size of target to bidder"]
definition: The relative size of a target firm and a bidder (or a junior partner and a senior partner in a merger), which may be an important consideration in explaining synergy realization.

name: Local corporate ethanol production capacity
authors_terms: ["local corporate ethanol production capacity", "local corporate ethanol plant capacity", "corporate prevalence", "local diffusion of corporations"]
definition: The production capacity of corporate ethanol plants in a county and the counties adjacent to it. The authors argue that the presence of corporate plants means demand for local corn will be high, so there is no economic need for farmers to establish a cooperative.

name: Cooperative founding
authors_terms: ["cooperative founding", "the rate of cooperative plant founding", "cooperative plant founding"]
definition: The rate of cooperative plant founding in a given U.S. county. Founding is understood as an arrival process and therefore modeled as a semi-Markov process.

name: Threat of vertical integration
authors_terms: ["threat of vertical integration", "vertical integration threat (VIT)", "corporate farming", "potential to enter into farming"]
definition: The potential of corporate ethanol producers to vertically integrate backward into farming, which exists in communities that have no anti-corporate farming laws. Corporate involvement in agriculture violates the ideological beliefs of independent farmers and challenges their identity, triggering ideological opposition to the proliferation of corporate ethanol plants.

name: Anti-corporate climate
definition: Anti-corporate sentiments embedded in deep-seated distrust of the corporate logic of governance, stressing instead community autonomy and commonwealth. Such sentiments have spurred social movements to target corporations, and they vary greatly among communities.

name: Supportive organizational infrastructure
authors_terms: ["organizational infrastructure in support of cooperative ideology", "supportive organizational structure (SOS)", "a well-developed, activist organizational infrastructure"]
definition: Anti-corporate social movements acting as 'organization-generating organizations' that provide the supportive social structures facilitating collective action and resource mobilization for the cooperative form. In this study the infrastructure is captured by the tenure of the Farm Bureau, the largest agrarian social movement organization in the United States.

name: Big business corporate ownership
authors_terms: ["big business corporations", "corporate ethanol production controlled by oil and agribusiness companies", "the common foe"]
