definition: Ethanol plants owned by oil companies and agribusiness companies, which are more likely than other corporations to be perceived as a salient threat and the common foe and therefore to fuel anti-corporate sentiments.

name: Incentive compensation
definition: Under incentive compensation, participants were told that the company's executive compensation was performance based, consisting of a base salary plus performance bonuses of up to 100% of the base salary.

name: Executive core self-evaluation
definition: CSE is an individual's fundamental and enduring self-assessment of personal worth and competence, recognized as a higher-order dispositional trait that concisely explains the common variance of four highly correlated traits: self-esteem, generalized self-efficacy, emotional stability, and locus of control.

name: Organizational performance context
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "organizational growth and decline", "firm performance contexts", "performance context"]
definition: Firm performance is an important situational contingency that influences the effects of incentive compensation; the two versions of the simulation represent organizational growth, in which the company was growing and enjoying good performance, and organizational decline, in which the company was declining and suffering poor performance.

name: Perseverance
definition: Perseverance is a person's tendency to persist and endure when facing challenges in the pursuit of a goal. The manifestation of perseverance includes greater effort and endurance when pursuing goals in the face of setbacks.

name: Competitive strategy focus
definition: The extent to which participants devoted their budgetary resources to competitive strategies that sought to improve the company's competitive position as opposed to public relations strategies that sought to favorably present the company and its executives to key stakeholders.

name: Ethical behavior
definition: After being informed that fraudulent reporting of revenues and expenses by the company's chief financial officer had been uncovered, participants could choose to restate as many of the previous fraudulent reports as they desired, or none at all; participants were assessed to be more ethical if they restated more reports.

name: Strategic risk taking
definition: A greater risk-taking approach involved concentrated allocations to only a few strategies, while a lower risk-taking approach involved dispersed allocations to many different strategies, because each competitive strategy is implicitly assumed to have the same level of risk so that any portfolio of strategies must be less risky than any single strategy.

name: SMO prominence
authors_terms: ["SMO prominence", "Greenpeace prominence", "prominence of an SMO within an industry"]
definition: In this paper, we define SMO prominence as the attention given by the industry to an SMO. It reflects industry-level attention, or the selective focus of attention that industry participants pay to a particular actor, situation, or event.

name: Firm commitment to an industry
authors_terms: ["commitment", "increased firm commitment", "production expansion", "commitment to the industry"]
definition: By commitment, we refer to concrete investments in production, not symbolic claims or mere presence in an industry. To proxy for increased firm commitment, we first coded firms' annual production of solar PV cells in megawatts (MW) in each country.

name: Local support for the focal SMO
authors_terms: ["Greenpeace local support", "local SMO support", "strength of environmental movement support", "support for the focal social movement organization"]
definition: Our second hypothesis requires a proxy for the strength of environmental movement support in a given country; the variable Greenpeace local support is proxied by the number of paying Greenpeace members in a country per year.

name: Past commitment to the industry
authors_terms: ["past commitment", "prior commitments", "prior engagements in favor of the industry", "prior investment behavior"]
definition: A firm's sensitivity to cues about an alternative industry's economic potential propagated by SMOs is reflected by the firm's prior engagements in favor of the industry. We captured a firm's past commitment relative to competitors by taking its share of production over total European PV production for that year.

name: Adversarial relationship with activists
authors_terms: ["Adversarial relationship", "adversarial relationship with activists", "history of associations with activists", "prior relationship with SMOs"]
definition: A firm's prior relationship with SMOs influences the outcome of its investments, because this relationship can alter the SMOs' reactions to the firm's decisions. We coded the number of instances in which firms appear to be targeted by environmental activists or groups through protests, boycotts, demonstrations, or lawsuits.

name: Firm size
definition: The total number of persons who worked for the respondent's employer during the preceding calendar year, counting all locations where the employer operated.

name: Wages
definition: The logged hourly wage, calculated as the inflation-adjusted annual wage and salary earnings divided by annual work hours.

name: Firm-size wage premium
definition: The wage premium that otherwise identical workers earn by working for large firms, relative to smaller firms.

name: Wage position
authors_terms: ["wage percentiles", "wage distribution", "low- and middle-wage workers", "high-wage workers"]
definition: Workers' location in the wage distribution, indicated by the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of logged wages.

name: Wage inequality
definition: The dispersion of wages in the labor market, reflected in a widening wage distribution and gaps between wage percentiles.

name: Time period
definition: The period of observation from 1989 through 2014 over which changes in the firm-size wage premium are examined.

name: Trust
definition: Consistent with Ganesan (1994), we operationally define trust as consisting of two dimensions: (1) benevolence; and (2) competence (see also Moorman, Zaltman, and Deshpande, 1992).

name: Complementarity
definition: Complementarity is a critical element in partner selection and attractiveness assessment as it affects the extent to which the image orientations, abilities, and activities of organizations can be integrated successfully. Our definition of complementarity focuses specifically on the fit between partners as viewed by one important stakeholder group, e.g., customers.

name: Commitment
definition: Commitment is described as a pledge by alliance members to undertake specific actions that will facilitate the attainment of the alliance's goals and objectives and is an essential part of successful long-term relationships. Commitment is conceptualized as tangible contributions made by partners to an alliance project.

name: Financial payoff
definition: To the extent that the inherent financial payoffs associated with allying with some partners is greater than that of others, the attractiveness of these partners and their likelihood of selection should also be greater. Financial payoff is operationalized in this study as the worth of the alliance based on the monetary output associated with it.

name: Partner attractiveness
definition: Partner attractiveness is defined as the degree to which the initiating firm in a particular alliance project sees a partner as desirable, favorable, appealing, and valuable.

name: Process manageability
definition: Conceptually, process manageability is defined as the degree of interaction, including communication and coordination, perceived to be required by the initiating partner in the process of implementing and sustaining the alliance tasks of the particular alliance project.

name: Outcome interpretability
definition: Outcome interpretability refers to the degree of difficulty associated with being able to interpret or understand with certainty the exact outcomes of a particular project-in this case, an alliance project.

name: Bootlegging
authors_terms: ["bootlegging", "bootlegging activities", "bootlegging time", "underground R&D efforts", "bootleg efforts", "unofficial side projects"]
definition: We define bootlegging as the process by which individuals take the initiative to work on ideas that have no formal organizational support and are often hidden from the sight of senior management, but are undertaken with the aim of producing innovations that will benefit the company. It is an R&D activity in which motivated individuals secretly engage in bottom-up, nonprogrammed innovation efforts not officially authorized by management but which are for the benefit of the company.

name: Change in bootlegging
authors_terms: ["growth in bootlegging time", "increases in individual bootlegging", "changes in levels of bootlegging efforts"]
definition: The authors focus on increases in the level of individuals' bootlegging efforts during a period of organizational change toward greater formalization of the R&D process, as distinct from the level of bootlegging activity.

name: Individual innovative performance
authors_terms: ["innovative performance", "individual innovation performance", "innovation rating", "individual innovative performance"]
definition: The ability of the individual R&D scientist or engineer to contribute to the development of novel and useful ideas that will create value for the organization, assessed on the basis of their individual contributions to successful outcomes.

name: Unit innovative performance
authors_terms: ["unit-level innovative performance", "unit innovative performance", "innovative performance of the R&D unit", "unit-level performance"]
definition: Within large R&D organizations, there is considerable variation in the productivity of different R&D units; some have better track records of generating innovations than others.

name: Unit bootlegging
authors_terms: ["unit-level bootlegging", "unit bootlegging time", "average unit bootlegging", "average bootlegging time of colleagues"]
definition: R&D units in large organizations can differ substantially in the extent to which members of the unit work beneath the surface of the formal organizational structure, deviating from organizational norms over the allocation of time exclusively to formal projects.

name: Strategic autonomy
definition: Some organizations formally grant staff a degree of strategic autonomy that gives researchers the opportunity to define their own research agendas and goals and set the overall direction of their R&D undertakings (Amabile and Gryskiewicz 1987, Bailyn 1985). The authors propose that bootlegging is a vehicle that enables individuals to obtain greater strategic autonomy in their R&D efforts.

name: Depth of embeddedness
definition: The strength of a prospective newcomer's past relationships with any incumbent member of the collaboration; it indicates the level of alignment between the prospective newcomer and a single incumbent member.

name: Breadth of embeddedness
definition: The proportion of incumbent members with which the newcomer has had prior ties; it denotes the prospective newcomer's familiarity with a dispersed set of incumbent members in a collaboration.

name: Network faultlines
definition: Faultlines are hypothetical dividing lines that divide a group into subgroups based on individual attributes; applied to interorganizational collaborations, the dispersion in the strength of relationships among members may lead to faultlines based on patterns of past ties.

name: Status of the strongest tie
authors_terms: ["status of the strongest tie in the syndicate", "strongest tie status"]
definition: Status is a source of power in a collaboration: status position is a well-understood source of power in groups, as high-status firms control more resources and have more leverage than other firms. The construct concerns the status of the member to which the newcomer is most strongly tied.

name: Newcomer experience
definition: The prior experience of the prospective newcomer, which improves its capabilities to conduct effective negotiations, understand and reconcile potentially conflicting goals, and find compromise solutions.

name: Newcomer participation
authors_terms: ["VC firm participation", "firm participation", "participation in the syndicate"]
definition: Whether a focal VC firm participates in a syndicate in a given round; a focal VC firm refers to a prospective newcomer VC firm at risk of joining a syndicate.

name: Strategic purity
authors_terms: ["strategic purity", "purity", "pure strategy", "pure strategies", "hybrid strategy", "in-the-middle strategy", "stuck in the middle"]
definition: Purity is defined by emphasizing one dimension of strategy relative to the other, not as absolute adherence to one strategic type over the other. A business's strategic purity can be defined as the ratio of the subset of activities (or intentions) consistent with one strategy relative to the subset of actions consistent with another strategy.

name: Firm performance
definition: Operating margin was calculated as gross revenues minus gross expenses, expressed as a percentage of revenues. Operating margin was selected over alternative measures, such as revenue growth or growth in size, because it measures value creation and capture, the essence of an effective strategy.

name: Operating excellence
definition: The factor the authors labeled operating excellence (O) is the summed score (maximum 20) for reducing operating costs, improving coordination with customers and suppliers, reorganizing the work process, and improving measures of performance. The central elements of an operational excellence, exploitation, defender or cost strategy are cost, efficiency, reliability, refinement, and execution.

name: Product leadership
definition: Product leadership (P) is the summed score (maximum 20) for developing new products and services, undertaking R&D, total quality management, and developing new operating techniques. This dimension in strategic space is most consistent with Treacy and Wiersema's product leadership strategy and also has much in common with exploration, prospecting and, to a lesser extent, differentiation.

name: Pure-financial diversification
definition: Diversification into unrelated businesses, in which the firm attempts to gain financial benefits from an increased ability to carry leverage due to a greater stability of cash flows. The study focuses on the reduction in total variability of operating cash flows as a manifestation of pure-financial diversification.

name: Related diversification
definition: A diversification strategy that attempts to exploit operating synergies, in which individual units are operated as a single organization (e.g. scale economies, economies of scope, complementary operations). The measure DR captures diversification of related businesses within the same broad two-digit SIC industry.

name: Total diversification
definition: Traditional Berry-Herfindahl type measures of diversification rely on the Standard Industrial Classification system for examining the extent of the firm's operations in different industries. In this study the operating income of each segment is used to compute diversification.

name: Profitability
definition: Two measures of profitability are considered; the first measure is a cash-flow surrogate and an additional profitability measure is used to facilitate comparisons with previous studies. FFOTA is the funds from operations divided by total assets and NITA is the return on assets.

name: Profitability variability
authors_terms: ["variability of profits", "variability of cash flows", "operating risk", "earning variability", "variability measures"]
definition: Measures of variability are computed by estimating the standard deviation of the profitability measures over the 10-year period 1974-83. Lower variability indicates more stable cash flows, i.e. lower operating risk.

name: Financial leverage
definition: Financial leverage is estimated as the ratio of total debt to total assets. Firms that engage in pure-financial diversification are expected to issue more debt to benefit from additional tax deductions of interest.

name: Media coverage of #MeToo
authors_terms: ["media coverage of #MeToo", "cumulative media coverage of #MeToo", "media coverage of #MeToo in prior week", "recent level of coverage"]
definition: Media coverage of #MeToo is the total count of articles in major news outlets that referred to #MeToo in a particular week. The recent level of coverage is the count of articles that referred to #MeToo in the previous week, and cumulative coverage is the number of articles that referenced #MeToo from the onset of coverage to the present.

name: Gender dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["gender difference between incumbent and candidate", "gender differences between an incumbent director and a potential board candidate", "gender similarity"]
definition: Gender difference between an incumbent director and a potential board candidate indicates whether or not the incumbent director and the candidate possess the same gender category. Gender itself is a salient basis for ingroup/outgroup categorization among directors.

name: Demographic similarity beyond gender
authors_terms: ["demographic similarity of an incumbent director and a potential board candidate on characteristics beyond gender", "demographic similarity beyond gender"]
definition: Similarity between an incumbent director and a potential board candidate on salient demographic characteristics other than gender, including functional background, race, age, and educational background. Such similarity provides a basis for presumptive, category-based trust that may alleviate anxieties about a board candidate's behavior.

name: Board ties
authors_terms: ["direct and indirect board ties", "direct board ties", "indirect board ties", "common board ties"]
definition: Direct board ties are the number of other boards on which the incumbent director and the board candidate both held an appointment. An indirect board tie exists between an incumbent director A and a potential board candidate B when A sits on another board with a third director C, who also sits on a different board with B.

name: Organizational identification
authors_terms: ["organizational identification", "identifies with the organization", "identifies with the focal organization"]
definition: Organizational identification is the extent to which individuals intertwine their view of themselves with salient characteristics of the organizations to which they belong. When individuals strongly identify with an organization, they tend to be especially concerned about the image that the organization portrays to the public and derive self-worth from helping the organization to maintain a positive external image.

name: Attractiveness as a board candidate
authors_terms: ["attractiveness of individuals as potential board candidates", "perceived attractiveness of individuals as potential board candidates", "assessment of the individual's attractiveness as a board candidate"]
definition: The perceived attractiveness of an individual as a potential board candidate, assessed by an incumbent director as if the director served on the nominating committee and the individual were an actual board candidate.

name: Categorical distance
definition: The perceived relatedness of two categories. The distance between these categories is a subjective measure reflecting how similar the members of a given class perceive another class as being; distant categories are perceived as sharing few elements, speaking to unrelated audiences, or emphasizing different characteristics.

name: Superordinate classification
authors_terms: ["superordinate category", "superordinate class", "inclusive superordinate categories", "higher-order category", "level of classification"]
definition: People can shift not just horizontally between classes, but also vertically between levels of abstraction, and can resolve contentious categorizations through the use of 'inclusive superordinate categories.' The inclusion of more unfamiliar or perceptually distant elements could effectively stop the classification process at a more abstract level.

name: New entrant performance
authors_terms: ["performance of new entrants", "consumer response", "consumer receptivity", "song sales", "sales", "song quality", "consumer interest"]
definition: The paper examines both the individual-level reception to spanning different distances and the commercial consequences of spanning for a given artist, and predicts that consumers become less and then more receptive as the categorical distance increases.

name: Organizational reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "Number of Positive Media Reports", "favorable media coverage", "social proofs of competence"]
definition: Consumers who cannot judge a firm's competence are obliged to use 'social proofs' of competence, such as reputation or status. Reputation is especially significant in PSFs because of the intangibility of the service and the importance of the professional.

name: Balanced diversification
definition: The degree of balance in the diversification of an accounting firm's portfolio is the extent to which the firm generates income from each of the four lines of service: audit and accounting, tax advice, management advisory services, and outsourcing and other services.

name: Leverage ratio
definition: In professional service firms, leverage refers to the ratio of total number of professionals to partners and is the 'mechanism that drives promotion rates.' Leverage rates thus signal to professionals their chances of becoming partners.

name: Firm performance
definition: Accounting firms are neither publicly traded nor under any requirement to report profits, and rarely do so. Therefore, we measured performance by revenues per professional (R/P), a commonly computed index of relative performance in studies of professional services generally.

name: Internal patent law expertise
authors_terms: ["in-house patent law expertise", "internal patent law expertise", "patent law expertise", "in-house legal resource", "internal patent attorneys"]
definition: To file patents, firms need to access specialized legal resources for conducting prior art searches, drafting patent applications, and prosecuting these applications at the patent office; an important additional resource is patent law expertise, which essentially resides in the knowledge and capability of patent attorneys.

name: Firm R&D
definition: R&D is seen as an input into the production of firm-specific knowledge resources, which in turn facilitate the identification, assimilation, and exploitation of information generated both within and outside the firm.

name: Firm-patenting performance
definition: Patents are tangible manifestations of a firm's ideas, techniques, and products, and are therefore an important indicator of innovation; firm-patenting performance is measured as the count of all (granted) U.S. patents filed by the firm in a given year.

name: TMT patent law background
authors_terms: ["TMT patent law background", "TMT patent background", "TMT background"]
definition: The TMT of a firm is the group of decision makers primarily responsible for making key decisions about the allocations of firm resources and for coordinating the deployment of these resources; the patent law background of a firm's TMT is coded by whether or not at least one member of the TMT was a patent attorney.

name: Industry patenting pressures
authors_terms: ["industry patenting pressures", "pressures for patenting performance", "patenting pressures", "systems-based industries"]
definition: Industry conditions can make certain organizational outcomes such as increasing patenting performance more, or less, valuable to firms, and in turn influence the amount of attention firms give to achieving these outcomes versus other competing goals; the value of deploying legal resources for increasing patent production may be greater for firms in systems-based, compared to materials-based, industries in the time frame of the study.

name: Centralization of strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["centralization of strategic decisions", "vertical allocation of decision rights"]
definition: Decisions made close to the owner of the property right are conventionally considered more centralized than those made at lower hierarchical levels; strategic decisions contain fundamental issues related to the firm's mission and to its objectives, policies, and strategies in the long run.

name: Centralization of operating decisions
authors_terms: ["centralization of operating decisions", "vertical allocation of decision rights"]
definition: Operating decisions appear to be short-term oriented; on the shop floor they include the daily and weekly production plan, the definition of employees' tasks, the control of results, and the modification of the production plan and processes in the face of unexpected shocks.

name: Worker opportunism
definition: One of the two kinds of behavioral uncertainty the authors acknowledge, referring to workers' opportunistic conduct in the employment relationship, i.e. the propensity of operators to act on their own behalf and to reduce the quantity and quality of output.

name: Managerial opportunism
definition: Employer opportunism can be developed from the capacity of a central unit to impose orders that, despite exceeding the previously agreed limits, do not need to be confirmed; it is the second kind of behavioral uncertainty, alongside employee opportunism.

name: Human specificity
definition: Human specificity is directly related to the effects of 'learning by doing'; what makes human specificity different from human skills is that it cannot be easily reproduced outside of a particular organization, which creates a situation of bilateral monopoly.

name: Temporal specificity
definition: Temporal specificity relates to work units that are closely linked to each other, so that a dysfunction in one of them causes serious damage to the others; the investment in a specific design of the production process would cause lock-in effects among different work stations.

name: Parametric uncertainty
definition: Parametric uncertainty arises from the changing conditions of the economic and technological environment, which may put the transaction's expected outcome in danger; in a labor transaction it is the possibility that different eventualities influence the transaction's execution and outcome.

name: Frequency of transactions
definition: The frequency of transactions concerns the degree to which a particular exchange between two agents is repeated; in the case of a labor transaction it refers to the degree to which a particular employee repeats his or her tasks.

name: Specialization
definition: The extent to which operators concentrate on the same tasks rather than rotating among different tasks; the authors treat specialization as the main organizational topic regarding the horizontal assignation of decision rights.

name: Teamwork
definition: Workers at the same hierarchical level sharing specific tasks with other workers to solve particular problems through permanent or temporary groups.

name: Leader position
authors_terms: ["leader", "leaders", "leadership position", "holding the lead", "being in the lead"]
definition: The structural position at the top of a competitive ranking. The authors posit that holding the lead in a competition narrowly channels leaders' attention to maintaining their lead.

name: Follower position
definition: The position of competitors below the leader in a competitive ranking. In line with the variable risk preferences model, the authors conjecture that followers may shift their focus of attention between their aspiration and survival points.

name: Aspiration point focus
authors_terms: ["aspiration point focus", "aspiration level", "aspiration point", "social aspiration level"]
definition: The social aspiration level for all competitors is set by the leaders' performance, and leaders focus on their aspiration level, which is maintaining the lead. As the gap between the leaders' resources and the nearest followers' resources increases, the level of risk needed to maintain the lead decreases.

name: Survival point focus
definition: Survival is the ability to compete in subsequent rounds of a tournament; in other words, survival is 'living to fight another day.' In the Jeopardy! TOC survival means advancing to the second round of the tournament as a wild card.

name: Risk taking
authors_terms: ["risk taking", "bet size", "amount of points risked", "bet amount"]
definition: The amount of points a competitor places at risk on the last clue of his or her first-round game, which is the dependent variable in the study. Risk taking is sensitive to the risk taker's resources relative to the survival and aspiration levels and to which of the two reference points the risk taker focuses on.

name: Excessive risk taking
authors_terms: ["unnecessary risks", "excessive risk taking", "riskier strategy", "shutout bet", "liability of leading"]
definition: The propensity among leaders to take unnecessary risks to stay in the lead, which the authors call the liability of leading. Choosing the riskier of two available strategies when it reduces the probability of advancing supports this proneness to excessive risk taking to maintain the lead.

name: Contractual governance structure
authors_terms: ["contractual governance", "contractual detail", "level of contract detail", "degree of contractual governance", "contractual complexity"]
definition: The degree to which parties rely on contractual governance structures, measured as the number of provisions in the formal contract; higher scores represent a greater reliance on contractual governance. Contracts vary widely in their intent and complexity, and what varies across relationships is the degree to which contractual mechanisms are leveraged.

name: Coordination focus
definition: The degree to which the contracting process is focused on coordinating the parties' expectations and behaviors, as proxied by the share of coordination provisions in the contract. Contracts serve at least two distinct purposes, control and coordination.

name: Rights-based approach
definition: A primarily distributive, adversarial, and competitive approach that relies 'on some independent standard with perceived legitimacy or fairness to determine who is right.' Parties adopting it focus on arguments portraying their own position as legitimate and the other's claims as invalid.

name: Interest-based approach
definition: An integrative, consensual, and problem-solving approach in which parties share information about their perspectives and underlying interests and emphasize mutually acceptable alternatives to escalating the conflict.

name: Power asymmetry
authors_terms: ["power asymmetry", "asymmetry", "imbalance of power", "asymmetry of revenues", "asymmetry of alternatives"]
definition: The degree to which the two parties differ in firm strength, considered both through alternatives to reaching agreement and through the resources a party can mobilize when attempting to coerce the other side. Power is the inverse of dependence.

name: Dispute resolution costs
authors_terms: ["cost of dispute resolution", "dispute resolution costs", "external resolution costs", "legal fees"]
definition: The costs incurred to resolve the dispute, estimated using the legal fees paid by the client to the law firm. These figures underestimate the total costs of the dispute because they capture fees paid by one disputant only and exclude non-legal costs.

name: International interdependence
definition: International interdependence is the condition in which subsidiaries or units of the MNC rely on other units' activities or inputs in order to perform their role effectively. With increased international interdependencies, the actions and decisions taken at a particular R&D unit have a greater impact on activities throughout the organization.

name: R&D unit strategic mandate
authors_terms: ["R&D mandate", "strategic mandate", "strategic mission", "mandates of R&D units", "R&D units' mission"]
definition: R&D units are distinguished into (1) adaptors of products to local market needs, (2) units that exploit the firms' technology competences on a global basis, and (3) R&D units established to augment or create new technological competences abroad, referred to as local adaptors, international adaptors and international creators respectively.

name: Centralization
definition: Centralization is a type of control where decision-making power is retained at the headquarters. The literature on organizational power refers to headquarters' ability to exercise control via hierarchical authority, a concept close to the authors' notion of direct control.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization is a type of control where decision-making power is routinized through rules and procedures.

name: Socialization
definition: Socialization is a type of control whereby organizational members develop common expectations and shared values that promote like-minded decision making.

name: Technological overlap
definition: The degree of similarity in the technological knowledge domains of a pair of firms.

name: Geographical overlap
definition: The degree of physical proximity between the headquarters of a pair of firms.

name: Product market overlap
definition: The degree of similarity between the product markets of a pair of firms.

name: Invention performance
definition: The extent to which the firm generates novel technological knowledge in terms of the number and technological value of its patented inventions.

name: Spanning structural holes
definition: The focal firm's spanning of structural holes in the competition network - that is, paying attention to competitors who ignore each other.

name: Attention to peripheral competitors
definition: The focal firm's relations with competitors in the periphery of the network - in other words, firms that are perceived as competitors by the focal firm, but not by other firms in the focal firm's markets.

name: Competitor churn
definition: Year-to-year turnover in perceived competitors, including both additions of new competitors and pruning of existing ones.

name: Product introductions
definition: New infrastructure software products introduced and subsequently shipped by each firm yearly; introduction of a brand-new product is a major innovation and product-development effort.

name: CEO social status in the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["CEO's social status in the corporate elite", "social status in the corporate elite", "status in the corporate elite"]
definition: Status in the corporate elite is derived from prestigious social affiliations such as board appointments at large firms and nonprofit organizations, as well as elite educational credentials such as degrees from Ivy League schools or other prestigious universities. High-status leaders exert a disproportionate influence over decision making on a range of policy issues that affect the personal and career interests of other managers.

name: Alters' social status in the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["status of potential ingratiators", "social status of alters", "status of alters"]
definition: The social status in the corporate elite of the other top managers and directors with whom a CEO interacts, measured with the same indicators of corporate and nonprofit board appointments, elite education, board-prestige and club memberships used for CEOs.

name: Received flattery and opinion conformity
authors_terms: ["flattery and opinion conformity directed at the CEO", "received flattery and opinion conformity", "ingratiation", "ingratiatory behavior"]
definition: Common forms of ingratiatory behavior include flattery and 'opinion conformity,' or verbal statements that validate the opinion held by another person. The present study focuses on forms of flattery in which managers and directors subtly exaggerate or overstate their opinion of the CEO's strategic judgment or leadership capability.

name: CEO self-enhancement
authors_terms: ["self-enhancement", "self-enhancement in regard to strategic judgment and leadership capability", "overconfidence", "self-enhancing cognitions"]
definition: Self-enhancement is commonly defined by social psychologists as the overestimation of one's abilities and is routinely measured as a positive difference between self-assessed abilities and the assessment of one's abilities by others. In the present context, CEOs exhibit self-enhancement to the extent that they assess their strategic judgment or leadership capabilities more positively than their peers do.

name: Change in firm strategy
authors_terms: ["change in firm strategy", "strategic change", "change in business strategy", "change in corporate strategy"]
definition: Our measure of strategic change reflects changes in key dimensions of both business strategy and corporate strategy. Business strategy is operationalized according to resource allocations across the primary functional areas of the firm, together with change in product market diversification as a key dimension of corporate strategy.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "low firm performance", "performance relative to competitors"]
definition: We used three measures of firm performance: market-to-book value of equity and total stock returns (as market-based measures) and return on assets (as an accounting-based measure). We defined low firm performance as performance that is low in comparison to competitors.

name: Emerging economy
definition: Firms in emerging economies (hereafter EE) are embedded in institutional environments that do not favor competition. The authors contrast an emerging economy (India) with a developed economy (the United States), two large countries that fell on opposite extremes in terms of the development of their institutional environment.

name: Persistence of superior performance
authors_terms: ["persistence of superior performance", "persistence of superior firm performance"]
definition: Performance persistence is defined as the percentage of a firm's performance from previous periods that still remains in the current period. Superior performers are firms whose performance in the first 2 years after their entry into their country sample was greater than the average performance in their country.

name: Persistence of poor performance
authors_terms: ["persistence of poor performance", "persistence of poor firm performance", "recovery from poor performance"]
definition: Poor performance will persist when the institutional environment dampens competitive pressures in factor markets and prevents resource redeployments from poorly performing firms. Persistence is the percentage of a firm's performance from previous periods that still remains in the current period.

name: Business group or MNC affiliation
authors_terms: ["affiliated firms", "intermediate governance structures", "firms that are subsidiaries of foreign multinational corporations", "firms affiliated with a business group"]
definition: Affiliated emerging economy firms are firms that are subsidiaries of foreign multinational corporations or firms affiliated with a business group. Such intermediate governance structures are argued to substitute for the market for corporate control and to give their affiliates preferential access to valuable resources.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is defined as the relative profitability advantage enjoyed by a firm in period t and is measured by normalized returns (NROA) and firm-specific rent (FSR).

name: Target technological overlap
definition: The proportion of the target's knowledge base that the acquirer already possesses; the portion of the target's knowledge already known by the acquirer.

name: Acquirer technological overlap
definition: The proportion of the acquirer's knowledge base duplicated by the target; the degree to which the acquirer's existing knowledge is duplicated by the target's knowledge.

name: Target technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities refer to the ability of a firm to actually create impactful innovations; the target's capabilities are its citation-weighted patents.

name: Acquirer technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities refer to the ability of a firm to actually create impactful innovations; the acquirer's capabilities are its citation-weighted patents.

name: Acquisition value creation
authors_terms: ["value creation", "cumulative abnormal return", "abnormal returns", "CAR", "shareholder value creation"]
definition: Our measure of value creation is cumulative abnormal return of the acquirer's stock. It captures investors' perceptions of the acquirer's ability to create future cash flows from unique and potentially inimitable synergies generated by recombining its technological capabilities with those of the target.

name: Product valuation
definition: The valuation of a product in the marketplace, measured in this setting by wine price; wine price is carefully set by wineries based on a process of interactive evaluation among winemakers and consumers, mediated by wine critics and government agencies.

name: Evaluated status
definition: Market status generated by a critical rating or ranking of one's quality performance; in contrast to categorical status based on a general institutional classification of group membership, evaluated status is based on a critical assessment of an individual's quality performance, which often requires individual effort in open competition.

name: Appellation status
definition: Categorical status based on the government classification of a wine's geographic origin, which divides the origin of grapes into a state, a county and an American viticultural area; because the official approval and a higher institutional standard of an AVA embody the core value in the wine world, the governmental classification imposes a higher categorical status on an AVA appellation than on a California or county appellation.

name: Extra designation status
definition: Categorical status marked by a special designation of a vineyard or of a wine characteristic inscribed on the wine label; a wine is entitled a vineyard designation by meeting a high standard of wine regulation, sometimes winemakers label a wine's particular characteristic with a descriptive term such as 'estate bottled', 'late harvest', or 'reserve'.

name: Organizational status
authors_terms: ["organizational status", "winery's organizational status", "winery's average wine score", "winery's recent average product rating"]
definition: A firm's organizational status, based on its standing of perceived quality performance relative to other competitors, plays an important role in product valuation; a winery's organizational status is derived from a critical assessment of its overall performance in the past.

name: Status consistency
definition: Status consistency is the positive congruence among a set of status indicators, which tends to reinforce one another, yielding additional returns beyond the contribution of each individual one; conversely, when status indicators are inconsistent, the status claim of the positive indicator is undermined and its returns decrease accordingly.

name: Decentralization of decision rights
authors_terms: ["home rule", "decentralization of decision rights", "delegation of decision rights", "decentralization of the capital allocation process", "centralization of decision rights"]
definition: A structural choice between centralization of decision rights (assigning the power for decision-making to one or several individuals at a higher level in the organization) and decentralization of decision rights (delegating decision-making to lower organizational levels). In this setting, home rule authority provides municipalities with decision rights to make spending choices according to the needs of the local population.

name: Capital reallocation
definition: The dependent variable, Capital reallocation, is measured by a change in capital expenditures in any given year as compared to the allocation in the previous year. Capital expenditures represent expenditures for purchase or construction of buildings and other improvements, purchase of land, equipment and existing structures, and payments on capital leases.

name: Special district prevalence
authors_terms: ["special purpose districts", "special districts", "number of special districts", "prevalence of special districts"]
definition: Special districts are governmental units that have substantial administrative and fiscal autonomy; they have a separate budget, and the functions they undertake include, inter alia, fire protection, provision of water supply, provision of housing, and the construction and maintenance of highways. The United States Census Bureau defines special districts as 'Independent, special-purpose governmental units that exist as separate entities with substantial administrative and fiscal independence from general-purpose local governments.'

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["outside directors", "representation on the board by outside directors", "proportion of outsiders on the board", "outsider directors"]
definition: Since inside directors tend to be defined as directors currently serving as firm officers, outside directors are often defined as 'all non-management members of the board'. In this article, 'outsider directors' specifically refer to non-management, non-government directors.

name: Affiliated outside directors
authors_terms: ["affiliated outside directors", "affiliated directors", "institutional directors", "institutional (legal person) investors"]
definition: Affiliated outside directors are defined as non-management directors who have family and/or professional relationships with the firm or firm management. The authors report that institutional directors represent entities which have some identifiable professional relationships with the firm, thus becoming affiliated directors.

name: Non-affiliated outside directors
definition: Non-affiliated outside directors are defined as non-management directors with no family and/or professional relationships with the firm or firm management. The authors suggest that in general, individual directors are non-affiliated outside directors.

name: Firm performance
definition: Since a single measure such as ROE may be inadequate, we use a second measure, sales growth (annual growth of total revenue), to triangulate the important construct of firm performance. Theoretically, ROE is a financial measure that agency theory is more concerned with, and sales growth represents resource inflows closer to the spirit of resource dependence theory.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: Poor prior performance of the firm may prompt more appointment of outsiders on the board who may help the turnaround process; in this manner, poor performance acts as a catalyst to trigger organizational changes. Prior performance is measured by all previous years' ROE and sales growth.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured by the logarithm of total assets. Resource dependency theory posits that because larger firms have more uncertainty and interdependence with environmental contingencies, their boards would be larger with more outsiders.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["firm age", "young firm age", "younger firms", "older, more established firms"]
definition: Firm age is based on the founding year of the listed firm. Older, more established firms usually have well-entrenched structures supported by vested interests, and initially may not be interested in introducing new governance practices, whereas younger firms may be more likely to appoint outsider directors.

name: Appointment of outside directors
authors_terms: ["appointment of outside directors", "appointment of new outside directors", "appointing outside directors to the board"]
definition: To test Hypotheses 2-5, we record the appointment of new outside directors for each year. In the hazard model, h(t) is the hazard function, in this case the rate of moving from having no outside directors (0) to having some outsiders on the board (1).

name: Expertise overlap
definition: The first dimension, expertise overlap, relates to the degree of commonality among the human capital in the cluster. When a cluster hire involves a considerable amount of overlap in areas of expertise, the hired individuals share a common body of knowledge related to their task-oriented functions.

name: Co-mobility
definition: The second dimension, co-mobility, refers to the degree to which individuals in the cluster hire move from the same prior employer. When a cluster hire involves a considerable amount of co-mobility, it brings to the hiring firm highly skilled individuals who share experiences from working at their prior employer.

name: Existing strategic human capital depth
authors_terms: ["existing strategic human capital depth at the hiring firm", "existing depth of strategic human capital", "depth of strategic human capital at the hiring firm"]
definition: In situations where the firm has considerable depth in the knowledge domain the cluster brings, there is a higher probability that the specific knowledge and skills brought by the individuals in the cluster hire is redundant with the strategic human capital already present at the firm. The existing strategic human capital depth at the hiring firm was measured as the average number of partners at the hiring firm with expertise in areas represented in the cluster hire.

name: Change in firm profitability
authors_terms: ["change in firm profitability", "change in profits per partner"]
definition: We measured change in firm profitability by calculating the difference in profit per partner between 2010 and 2011. Profit per partner in the professional service firm context is analogous with return on equity, and has been used as a measure of firm profitability in prior law firm studies.

name: Contractual complexity
definition: One dimension of neoclassical contracts is complexity, which takes 'account of many future contingencies that would change the value of performance.' The measure captures the degree to which clauses contain contingencies for different situations, in line with prior research that examines complexity as the scope of clauses found in exchange agreements.

name: Contractual recurrence
definition: Recurrence, a second dimension of contracts, refers to whether parties rely on the expectation of continued exchanges to coordinate and safeguard transactions. The measure assesses one party's expected continuity in its future exchanges with its partners.

name: Procedural fairness
definition: Procedural fairness addresses the process of how an allocation decision is made. It is based on perceptions of the use of accurate and consistent procedures in decision making and granting voice to those that are subject to the procedures.

name: Distributive fairness
definition: Distributive fairness refers to the evaluation of an outcome related to an allocation decision, such as compensation that a party receives. Perceptions of equity are intrinsic to the concept.

name: Socializing
definition: Socializing is the process by which parties interact through social activities in an attempt to learn and share values, norms, and goals; it reflects the deliberate attempts of organizational members to interact with others through social activities and personal relationships.

name: Monitoring
definition: Monitoring refers to one party's efforts to measure explicitly the other party's operations and actions; it allows one party to observe and measure another party's behavior or processes.

name: Exchange performance
definition: Exchange performance has two aspects: an assessment of the partner's task performance, and satisfaction with the focal relationship; the authors define it as one partner's assessment of the other party's task performance and its satisfaction with the relationship.

name: Earnings management
authors_terms: ["earnings management", "income-increasing earnings management", "impression (earnings) management", "discretionary current accruals"]
definition: We define earnings management as the use of flexible accounting principles that allow managers to influence reported earnings, thereby causing reported income to be larger or smaller than it would otherwise be.

name: CEO/chair duality
authors_terms: ["CEO/chair duality", "dual leadership structure", "duality-creating succession", "dual position of CEO and chair"]
definition: If the company's CEO is the board chair, the primary monitor of management is management itself. An executive put into the dual position of CEO and chair has both greater expectations for improved performance and greater power to control the impressions a firm makes as it releases accounting information.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: To determine prior firm performance, we computed cumulative abnormal returns (the summed daily abnormal returns) over a 200-trading-day period extending from 350 days prior to an announcement date to 150 days prior to the announcement date as measures of prior firm performance. If this variable is positive (negative) it means that the firm's stock has performed well (poorly) relative to the stock market.

name: Domestic brokerage triads
definition: A domestic configuration is the opposite: a broker whose partners are both from the same, or 'domestic,' institutional setting as the broker.

name: Mixed brokerage triads
definition: A mixed configuration consists of a broker with one partner from a different institutional setting (foreign) and one from the same as the broker (domestic).

name: Foreign brokerage triads
definition: A foreign configuration consists of a broker whose partners are both embedded in an institutional setting different, or 'foreign,' from that of the broker.

name: Innovation volume
definition: The amount or productivity of the firm's innovation. The authors distinguish it from radicalness as one of two aspects of a firm's innovative output.

name: Innovation radicalness
definition: The radicalness of the knowledge produced by a firm, or the extent to which it departs from and undermines the status quo; later stated as the extent to which the firm's innovations alter technological domains.

name: Bank performance
definition: Two measures capture bank performance: (1) return on assets, which is the ratio of net earnings available to common stockholders divided by average annual assets; (2) stock market return, which is the change in year-end stock prices, plus annual dividends, divided by the prior year-end stock price. Both measures are deemed relevant for the evaluation and reward of bank executives.

name: Executive compensation
definition: Compensation received by chief executive officers (CEOs) is studied, since CEOs are clearly responsible for overall bank performance. This study focuses on total compensation—annual salary, short- and long-term bonuses, stock and stock option grants—as the measure that is most reliable and comparable across firms.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: Managerial discretion, i.e., the decision-making latitude held by executives, may provide some insights into the determination of their compensation. Managerial discretion is proxied by a single composite measure inferred from five distinct dimensions.

name: Boycott targeting
definition: Social movement activists use boycotts in an effort to compel a targeted organization to change a specific practice or policy, and boycotts present a promising context for an inquiry into targets' responses to defend and protect their public image.

name: Reputational threat
authors_terms: ["reputational threat", "boycott's level of reputational threat", "level of threat", "media attention"]
definition: Reputational threats cast doubt on the carefully cultivated image that an organization projects to its audiences, challenge the firm's claimed conformity to socially acceptable norms, and potentially erode its reputation and field position. As the strength of a reputational threat increases, so should the likelihood that the threatened organization will be compelled to respond defensively.

name: Reputational field position
authors_terms: ["field position", "reputational standing", "pre-boycott reputational field position", "reputational ranking", "current field position"]
definition: Given that the efficacy of activists' challenges is based on reputational threat, a firm's field position can be seen as its relative standing in the field's reputational hierarchy.

name: Pre-threat impression management
authors_terms: ["pre-boycott prosocial claims", "pre-threat prosocial claims", "impression management repertoire", "performance repertoire"]
definition: Corporate actors have a repertoire that they activate when responding to activists' challenges and other external threats, and organizations construct these performance repertoires over time. Firms that routinely disseminate prosocial claims will be more likely to draw on this tactic when responding to a threat because they have learned and routinized the necessary procedures for using the tactic.

name: Post-threat impression management
authors_terms: ["prosocial claims", "post-boycott prosocial claims", "post-threat prosocial claims", "post-threat impression management", "corporate social responsibility advertising"]
definition: Prosocial claims are public claims of corporate social actions: voluntary actions that extend beyond the mere transactional interests of the firm to provide social benefits to a firm's constituents or to address general social problems. Unlike the concept of corporate social activity, prosocial claims are a communicative strategy, a tool of impression management that protects a firm's image by diluting, rather than refuting, the negative claims made by activists.

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence may be defined as 'the tendency of individuals to overestimate their abilities' and refers to the extent to which individuals tend to overestimate the accuracy of their knowledge and judgments. It includes a 'better-than-average' effect and a 'miscalibration' effect, the latter being the focus of this paper.

name: Management forecast accuracy improvement
authors_terms: ["improvement of management forecasting accuracy", "improvement of management forecast accuracy", "forecast accuracy improvement"]
definition: The improvement of management forecast accuracy from time t - 1 to time t (with t >= 2), i.e., how much more accurate a CEO's subsequent management earnings forecast becomes relative to the prior one.

name: Prior forecast error valence
authors_terms: ["prior forecast optimism", "forecast error valence", "prior optimism", "optimistic forecast", "pessimistic forecast"]
definition: Whether a prior forecast error was optimistic or pessimistic; errors are likely to have a differential impact depending on their valence, or whether prior forecast errors were optimistic or pessimistic.

name: Forecast time horizon
authors_terms: ["time horizon", "time horizon of the prior management forecast"]
definition: Time horizon of the prior management forecast (at time t - 1), calculated as the log of the number of days between the management forecast date and the fiscal year-end date; the earlier a forecast was issued, the greater the time horizon.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: Managerial discretion, or latitude of executive action, refers to the extent to which CEOs have a broad or narrow range of strategic actions from which to choose.

name: Board expertise-risk misalignment
authors_terms: ["misalignment", "board misalignment", "misalignment between board expertise and firm risks"]
definition: We term it 'misalignment' if the collective expertise of the directors does not adequately address the firm's risks. The greater the score, the more poorly aligned are the boards' expertise relative to the firms' risks.

name: Strategic board reconfiguration
definition: Boards would 'strategically reconfigure' themselves to improve their composition and consequently, improve firm performance. In this process, boards assess firms' future risks and challenges, compare the domains of the future risks with the domains of expertise currently on the board, and then make changes in the composition of the board accordingly.

name: Firm performance
definition: We used the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) over the subsequent fiscal year to measure firm performance. This market-based measure is an established proxy of firm performance.

name: Board collective expertise
definition: Expertise or the 'ability to comprehend the issues at hand' is a domain-specific human capital dimension, acquired from directors' prior experiences, and varies by director. When aggregated together at the board level, the sum of director expertise comprises the boards' expertise bundle.

name: Firm forward-looking risks
definition: Firm risks are the basis of the challenges which boards should be positioned to address in the course of their duties. Since 2005, publicly traded firms in the US have been required by the SEC to disclose in their 10-K form the most significant factors that make the company speculative or risky in Section 'ITEM 1A-Risk Factors'.

name: Bilateral investment treaty
authors_terms: ["bilateral investment treaty", "BIT", "supranational institutional safeguards", "supranational institutional agreements"]
definition: BITs are contracts signed by two countries with the objective of promoting and protecting investments by investors from one country in the other country. Most BITs give access to international arbitration institutions, which provides a mechanism for countries to credibly commit to treat foreign investors fairly.

name: Political competence
definition: Firm political competence is a firm's expertise in dealing with and influencing political authorities, and is considered an outcome of firms' prior exposure and experience with politically challenging environments in which rule of law is limited.

name: Political connections
definition: Firm political connections are close ties with individuals holding or having held high-ranking positions in the government.

name: International investment location choice
authors_terms: ["international investment location choice", "likelihood of investment", "likelihood of choosing a given host country"]
definition: The dependent variable captures the likelihood of a firm choosing a given host country as the location of an international investment, where each investment made by a firm is compared to all host country options that the firm could have chosen.

name: Escalation of commitment
authors_terms: ["escalation of commitment", "escalating commitment", "escalation behavior", "escalating tendency", "further resource commitment"]
definition: Firms display escalation behavior when they have performed poorly in a target location but still are inclined to make-rather than withhold-further resource commitment.

name: Larger competitors' action volume
authors_terms: ["larger competitors' action volume", "action volume", "larger rivals' high action volume"]
definition: Action volume is a basic and frequently examined characteristic of a rival's action repertoire, defined as the total number of actions taken by a certain rival over a given time period.

name: Smaller competitors' positive performance
authors_terms: ["smaller competitors' positive performance", "smaller competitors' successful experience", "competitors' positive performance"]
definition: The authors distinguish between competitors' positive performance (operating profitably in a target location) and their negative performance (operating at a loss in the target location).

name: Larger competitors' negative performance
authors_terms: ["larger competitors' negative performance", "larger competitors' unsuccessful experience", "competitors' negative performance"]
definition: The authors distinguish between competitors' positive performance (operating profitably in a target location) and their negative performance (operating at a loss in the target location).

name: Platform relatedness
authors_terms: ["platform relatedness", "OS platform relatedness", "platform relatedness strategy", "related platform diversification strategy"]
definition: We define the OS platform relatedness of a software firm as the extent to which the firm develops its products (applications) for similar OS platforms that share common development resources.

name: Product-market relatedness
definition: We define product-market relatedness as the extent to which a firm's product (application) offerings serve multiple software product (application) needs of the same customer base.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["sales growth", "firm sales growth", "firm i's sales growth"]
definition: Sales growth, a financial performance measure, is commonly used in measuring the performance of diversification strategies. Firm i's sales growth was computed as the logarithm of a firm's total revenues in year t + 1 divided by total revenues in year t.

name: Market share
definition: Market share, an operational performance measure, is an important measure of firm performance, especially in sectors characterized by network externalities, customer switching costs, and lock-in. Firm i's market share in year t + 1 is computed as the sum, over all product-markets, of the sales-weighted shares of each product-market.

name: Market development
definition: The concept of market development encompasses many aspects of commercial institutions; the authors focus on three dimensions that reflect crucial aspects of market-oriented development: labor markets, capital markets, and legal transparency. High values of Market Development indicate less severe voids in commercial institutions in a country.

name: Private sponsorship
authors_terms: ["private sponsors", "privately owned incubators", "privately sponsored incubators", "for-profit private organizations"]
definition: Privately owned incubators are motivated to improve the business environment in ways that will accrue the greatest returns on investments for sponsors, and have more skill than nonprivate sponsors in raising and investing financial capital.

name: Academic sponsorship
definition: With a strong motivation to support start-ups as part of their entrepreneurial mission and with faculty and facilities as their key resources, academic-sponsored incubators are expected to provide physical space, training, and consulting among their services, while lacking expertise in investing and access to capital.

name: Government sponsorship
definition: Governments tend to encourage entrepreneurship under 'corporatist and associational institutional structures,' particularly as their countries become more market oriented, and commonly have substantial physical space available for their use.

name: NGO sponsorship
definition: The structure of NGO interests suggests that most non-profits are primarily motivated to maintain continuous operations and establish identity within a specific domain of expertise, sharing their knowledge with incubatees pursuing aligned goals.

name: Market infrastructure finance services
authors_terms: ["MID-Finance", "MID services involved in providing financial capital", "financial capital services"]
definition: MID-Finance covers services aimed at filling voids in financial markets, comprising three items: seed capital, equity financing, and venture capital.

name: Market infrastructure space services
authors_terms: ["MID-Space", "MID services involved in providing space", "physical space"]
definition: MID-Space covers services aimed at filling voids of facilities, comprising three items: shared workshops, shared laboratories, and office space.

name: Business capability training services
definition: BCD-Training covers services aimed at training incubatees, comprising three items: mentoring/coaching, financial management training, and training in business management.

name: Business capability consulting services
definition: BCD-Consulting covers services associated with consulting and support services, comprising three items: pre-incubation services, incubation program for resident clients, and incubation program for non-resident clients.

name: Relative emphasis on business capability development
authors_terms: ["BCD-Ratio", "ratio of BCD to MID services", "relative emphasis on MID and BCD"]
definition: The proportion of the 12 services in the BCD and MID categories for each incubator that fell into either of the two BCD categories; larger values mean that an incubator placed greater emphasis on BCD relative to MID.

name: Institutional exclusion
definition: Institutional exclusion occurs when incumbents attempt to maximize rewards by restricting access to resources and opportunities to a limited circle of the eligible. It is measured as the extent to which the market was beyond the control of the NYCHA.

name: NYCHA membership
definition: Affiliation with the New York Clearing House Association, coded 1 for banking organizations that were affiliated with the NYCHA in a given year. To be admitted, a bank had to possess a minimum amount of capital and surplus and be approved by a large majority of existing members and by the Clearing House Committee.

name: Organizational failure
authors_terms: ["bank failure", "hazard of failure", "likelihood of failure", "failure rate"]
definition: The dependent variable is a banking organization's hazard of failure in a year. Failure includes liquidation and absorption by another banking organization; voluntary mergers are treated as right censored.

name: Non-member failure rate
authors_terms: ["non-CH member banks' failure rate", "non-NYCHA members' failure rate", "the failure rate for the rest of the market"]
definition: The number of non-NYCHA member banks that failed in the previous year.

name: Interlock network density
authors_terms: ["interlock network density", "CH interlock density", "NYCHA interlock density"]
definition: The density of the interlock network among NYCHA member banking organizations, measured as the ratio of the number of existent interlock ties between any pair of banking organizations to the total number of all possible ties between them.

name: Social club network density
definition: The social-club network density among NYCHA bankers, calculated from the NYCHA banking organization presidents' affiliations with social clubs in New York City.

name: Network centrality
definition: Network centrality is measured for each individual banking organization as the eigenvector centrality of a banking organization in the interlock or social club networks.

name: Country economic importance
authors_terms: ["economic importance", "economic importance of a country to the MNE", "economically connected MNEs"]
definition: The extent to which the firm sells, buys, or rents inputs, final products, or services or hires human capital in the country. The larger the economic importance of a country for the MNE, the greater the shock to firm performance and the incentive to allocate resources toward the country's market recovery.

name: Company philanthropy
definition: The firm's philanthropic response to an institutional disruption; the dependent variable Donation is a continuous variable of the total U.S. dollar amount donated, logged for the analyses.

name: Country market concentration
authors_terms: ["Dominant MNE Index", "index of dominant MNEs", "concentration of large firms in the country"]
definition: A country's index of dominant MNEs reflects the concentration of large firms in the country. It is a Herfindahl-Hirschman index calculated at the country level as the sum of squares of the proportion of revenues of the largest five firms in the focal country in the year of the institutional disruption, ranging from zero to one.

name: Host-country public aid
authors_terms: ["Host-country public aid", "host country public aid", "public aid"]
definition: Public relief and recovery coming from the host country government. A recent history of substantial host country public aid to restore human welfare, damaged infrastructure, and other factors necessary for market-oriented institutions fosters an expectation by firms that public aid will fund the country's recovery.

name: Foreign public aid
authors_terms: ["Foreign public aid", "foreign public aid", "foreign aid", "public aid"]
definition: Public relief and recovery coming from foreign governments and multilateral agencies, such as the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. Host country public aid and foreign public aid are two distinct sources of aid that MNEs consider in donating.

name: Regulatory quality
definition: Government commitment and ability to formulate and implement policies to permit and promote private sector development; the variable 'captures perceptions of the ability of the government to formulate and implement sound policies and regulations that permit and promote private sector development'.

name: Institutional disruptions
definition: The severe and systemic, yet sudden, unpredictable, and temporary breakdown of market-oriented institutions, which are the intangible and physical factors necessary for business activities. They are characterized by short-lived temporality, suddenness and unexpectedness, high severity, and pervasiveness.

name: Informational faultline strength
definition: Informational faultlines, the alignment of team member task-related attributes to form subgroups, are distinguished from alignments based on less task-relevant demographic characteristics; faultline strength increases as the strength of alignment of team member attributes increases.

name: Firm performance
definition: As a more comprehensive measure of current and future growth opportunities for the firm, the authors use Tobin's Q, a ratio of current market value to the replacement value of assets, together with ROA as an indicator of resource utilization efficiency.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism explains the level of instability and unpredictability in the environment. Dynamism consists of both instability (or the magnitude and frequency of change in the environment) and unpredictability (or the lack of regularity in patterns of change in environment).

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity is the number, diversity, and distribution of external factors and parties with which a unit must interact.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence is the degree to which environmental resources support the growth and performance of units, describing the relative abundance or scarcity of necessary resources in the industry environment.

name: Country-specific advantage
authors_terms: ["country-specific advantage", "country-specific advantages", "comparative advantage of nations", "comparative advantages of nations"]
definition: For one reason or another, firms of a particular nationality may have a certain advantage or competitive edge over firms of other nationalities. These comparative advantages define the pattern of international production and competitive advantages of nations.

name: International cooperation
authors_terms: ["international cooperative relationships", "international interfirm cooperation", "cooperative relationships with foreign firms", "international cooperative agreements"]
definition: The dependent variable in our model is the nationality of the partnering firm in a cooperative relationship formed by a Japanese company. These partners are categorized into three groups: Japanese, American and other.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of the firm", "employment level", "smaller firms", "larger firms"]
definition: The size of the firm can be approximated by the average sales of the firm during the period when the cooperative relationship was established, or by the level of employment (number of employees) of the firm.

name: Diversification
definition: The degree of diversification of the sampled firm is measured at two levels: SIC2 counts the number of industries, by the two-digit SIC code, in which the sampled firm operates, and SIC4 counts the number of four-digit level industries in which the firm conducts business. The two-digit level really measures unrelated diversification, while SIC4 captures related diversification.

name: Incumbency
definition: A discontinuous technological change opens up opportunities for entrepreneurial firms to enter the market to develop and exploit the new technology. The new entrants in the biotech-pharmaceutical industry in Japan are mostly firms which are well established in other industries.

name: Pharmaceutical product commercialization
definition: DRUG indicates whether or not the sample cooperative relationship involves the commercialization of a pharmaceutical product.

name: Technology transfer and licensing
authors_terms: ["TECHNOLOGY", "technology transfer and licensing", "technology transfer or licensing"]
definition: TECHNOLOGY measures if the relationship entails technology transfer and licensing.

name: Research function
definition: The cooperative relationships considered in this study may involve different functional areas of the commercialization process: research, development, manufacturing, marketing or combinations of these functions. These functions are represented by four dummy variables indicating if the particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship.

name: Development function
definition: The cooperative relationships considered in this study may involve different functional areas of the commercialization process: research, development, manufacturing, marketing or combinations of these functions. These functions are represented by four dummy variables indicating if the particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship.

name: Manufacturing function
definition: The cooperative relationships considered in this study may involve different functional areas of the commercialization process: research, development, manufacturing, marketing or combinations of these functions. These functions are represented by four dummy variables indicating if the particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship.

name: Marketing function
definition: The cooperative relationships considered in this study may involve different functional areas of the commercialization process: research, development, manufacturing, marketing or combinations of these functions. These functions are represented by four dummy variables indicating if the particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship.

name: Timing of relationship formation
authors_terms: ["TIME", "year of formation of the cooperative relationship", "timing of relationship formation"]
definition: TIME is the year of formation of the cooperative relationship.

name: Degree of technology outsourcing
authors_terms: ["degree of outsourcing", "degree of technology outsourcing", "degree of new technology outsourcing", "technology outsourcing"]
