definition: A firm's degree of outsourcing is the extent to which it relies on a third party's expertise versus efforts of its own staff to adopt a new technology.

name: Integrative capabilities
authors_terms: ["integrative capabilities", "integrative capabilities related to the technology", "capability"]
definition: Integrative capabilities reflect a firm's capacity to use and assimilate a new technology into its business processes and build upon it. They reflect a client firm's skills in tailoring a technology to firm-specific needs to enhance its application.

name: Performance in the market
authors_terms: ["performance in the market", "customer adoption", "online customer adoption"]
definition: A firm's performance in the market is assessed as customer adoption, that is, the extent to which a firm's customers use a new technology.

name: Experience in prior related technology
authors_terms: ["experience in prior related technology", "prior related experience", "prior experience"]
definition: Experience in prior related technology is defined as previous PC banking offerings that are a predecessor technology to Internet banking; PC banking familiarized banks with remote customer self-servicing technology and offered services similar to the basic services offered by Internet banking.

name: Founding team financial logic representation
authors_terms: ["internal representation of a financial logic", "representation of a financial logic", "financial logic", "financial experience of the founding team"]
definition: Founding teams may become carriers of financial and community logics into hybrid organizations if individuals in those teams have internalized the assumptions, values, and preferences associated with those logics. Founders with financial careers are likely to have assimilated a financial logic, carrying cognitive and motivational factors associated with a financial orientation that could lead them to be predisposed to tolerate certain risks.

name: Founding team community logic representation
authors_terms: ["internal representation of a community logic", "representation of a community logic", "community logic", "community involvement of the founding team"]
definition: Founders actively involved in community associations are likely to have internalized certain cognitive and motivational factors associated with a community logic, an institutional order based on the significance of local proximity, community identity and culture, interrelationships and networks, and local needs.

name: Organizational risk taking
authors_terms: ["organizational risk", "risk taking", "risky practices", "risk exposure", "use of risky deposit instruments"]
definition: The degree of risk taking in the organizations founders create, associated with aggressive growth intentions and reflected in practices such as the use of brokered deposits that expose a bank to cash flow liquidity risk.

name: Founding team size
authors_terms: ["size of the founding team", "size of the board", "team size", "founding team size", "larger founding teams"]
definition: The number of members of the founding team, measured through the founding board of directors, which is the proxy used for founding teams and which always includes the CEO and, with 30 percent of the teams, other members of the management team.

name: Influence of a resisting professional group
authors_terms: ["analyst intensity", "internal resistance", "professional influence", "relative analyst intensity", "strength of the financial professional collective"]
definition: The strength of the financial professional collective of the focal firm, relative to other firms in the industry, as resistance to adoption is exerted by finance professionals.

name: Propensity to adopt a practice
authors_terms: ["propensity of the organization to adopt", "rate of adoption not from contagion", "propensity (rate of adoption not from contagion)"]
definition: The rate at which a focal organization adopts a practice not from contagion, i.e., its own baseline inclination to introduce the practice.

name: Observed adoption performance of earlier adoptions
authors_terms: ["average fund size", "observed adoption performance", "observable adoption performance", "prior adoption performance"]
definition: Information about how well a practice performed for earlier adopters, proxied by the absolute size of a fund introduced by an earlier adopter, since it gives positive or negative adoption performance information to a prospective adopter.

name: Susceptibility to earlier adoptions
authors_terms: ["susceptibility to contagion influence", "susceptibility of a focal organization to earlier adoptions", "susceptibility to influence from earlier adopters"]
definition: The extent to which a focal organization is influenced by the adoption behavior of earlier adopters; a deviance discount lessens susceptibility to earlier adoptions.

name: Deviance discount
authors_terms: ["deviance discount", "deviance discounting", "deviance discount placed on earlier observed adoption performance"]
definition: A systematic downgrading of the observed adoption performance of controversial practices, which limits the contagion of such practices.

name: Adoption of a deviant practice
definition: A firm's introduction of a given mutual fund product category, modeled as the hazard of adoption given that the firm has not yet adopted.

name: High-status affiliations
authors_terms: ["appearances with high-status alters", "high-status alters", "high-status affiliations", "affiliations with prominent alters"]
definition: Affiliations are conceptualized as unfolding at the interface between actors and audiences, so that audiences infer the existence of an affiliation from joint participation in common events or activities. Status is conceptualized as rooted in acts of deference, where measures based on prizes or awards reflect the extent of respect accorded to an actor.

name: Survival
authors_terms: ["band survival", "survival", "artistic survival", "odds of survival", "hazard of failure"]
definition: Artistic survival, that is, whether entrants continue to appear in live concerts.

name: Concert revenues
definition: Commercial performance, that is, concert revenues: the dollar amount of revenues attributable to each individual artist or group.

name: Band age
definition: Band age is measured through a simple count of the years elapsed since the first appearance of the entrant in our data.

name: Dominant firm product-space movement
authors_terms: ["CCTV1 approach", "CCTV1 recede", "approach", "recede", "dominant firm shifts its position", "movements by the dominant firm"]
definition: To capture the directionality of CCTV1 movements, we created two variables, approachis (CCTV1 moved closer to the satellite channel), and recedeis (CCTV1 moved away from the satellite channel).

name: Repositioning
definition: We study competition as an impetus for firms to reposition-to abandon their current positioning strategy and adopt a new one. The dependent variable repositionis is defined as the change in product spatial distance between a satellite channel i and CCTV1 in a time slot s, subsequent to the CCTV1 programming shift.

name: Competitive strength
definition: Prior research suggests that firms' competitive strength may reside in specific product markets and at the broader firm level. At the firm-market level, we measure competitive strength of each satellite channel by their audience rating shares; at the firm level, we measure the competitive strength by each satellite channel's capability in offering particular types of programming content.

name: Customer preference concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of customer preferences", "customer concentration", "customer preference concentration"]
definition: The concentration of customer preferences influences a firm's benefit calculation in a number of ways. First, a concentrated distribution implies fewer viable locations. When customers are concentrated around a small number of locations in a product space, a firm is less likely to find the product space outside of these locations profitable, which limits destination options.

name: Product-location commitment
definition: A firm's incentive to reposition may be lower when the opportunity cost associated with leaving the current location is high. If the investments are specific to a location, however, their potential to generate future income will vastly diminish when the firm leaves the location.

name: Corporate aggressiveness
definition: Aggressiveness involves: (1) the depth of the resource commitment, and (2) the riskiness associated with resource allocations designed to achieve innovation and improve market share. High values indicate a more aggressive, opportunistic posture, and low values indicate a more conservative posture.

name: Change in corporate aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["change in corporate aggressiveness", "propensity to change corporate posture", "propensity for firms to change their corporate aggressiveness"]
definition: Change occurs in this analysis when firms alter their resource allocations in ways that shift the value of the corporate aggressiveness index.

name: Organizational inertia
definition: Inertia originates both in prior resource commitments that carry the organization forward and in contextual forces that inhibit change. These organizational-level forces act as inhibitors-they reduce a firm's flexibility in redeploying its resources.

name: Prior performance
definition: Prior performance affects change in two ways: on the one hand, performance outcomes present managers with feedback regarding the appropriateness of their actions; on the other hand, performance outcomes present managers with different degrees of slack.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: Sector volatility gauges the uncertainty faced by the corporate enterprise as a whole. A measure of sector volatility was calculated by aggregating the sale volatility coefficients of individual firms within a sector.

name: Size of loss
authors_terms: ["size of loss", "size of ego's potential loss", "size of possible loss", "size of the loss"]
definition: The size of the loss ego incurs if the partner behaves opportunistically; it is the maximum for which X can be held up and is equal to the total value of Y relative to that of the next-best option, plus the switching costs that X would incur in switching to the next-best alternative.

name: Probability of loss
authors_terms: ["probability of loss", "perceived probability of loss", "perceived probability of loss rather than its size"]
definition: The probability that alter will behave opportunistically. It is one of the two dimensions of the risk of opportunism, the other being the loss ego incurs if alter does defect.

name: Partner's relative value
authors_terms: ["value of alter", "the value that a partner offers relative to the next-best alternative", "alter's relative value", "value of the partner"]
definition: Value is specified in relative terms, as excess over the next best alternative partner. Value is higher to the extent that the partner has a unique, valuable offering, and it is at its highest when the partner has a monopoly.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "switching costs", "switching costs of ego", "dedicated and transaction-specific investments"]
definition: Switching costs for X are constituted by assets that are owned or guaranteed by X and are specific to the relationship, that is, they would need to be incurred again in a similar relation with another partner. Dependencies are the result of such specific investments, which are worth less or nothing outside a given alliance.

name: Legal ordering
definition: Means of constraining opportunism that include contracts and monitoring, which Williamson (1975) called legal ordering. In legal ordering compliance with the terms of an agreement is imposed by means of contracts that can be enforced in a court of law.

name: Private ordering
definition: Restraint of opportunism through a reputation mechanism, or posting of hostages, which Williamson (1985) called private ordering. In private ordering it can take the form of posting hostages, reputation mechanisms, and other restraints.

name: Restriction of room for opportunism
authors_terms: ["restriction of room for alter's opportunism", "restriction of room", "restriction of opportunism"]
definition: Governance that restricts the opportunities for a partner's opportunism: ego can limit room for alter's opportunism through contracts and monitoring. Restriction of room for alter's opportunism was the aggregate of a legal ordering scale and a private ordering scale.

name: Trust
definition: X trusts Y to the extent that X chooses to cooperate with Y on the basis of a subjective probability that Y will choose not to employ opportunities for defection that X considers damaging, even if it is in the interest of Y to do so. An individual trusts someone if he or she believes the other is likely to cooperate even if the latter is not coerced to do so and has no direct material interest in doing so.

name: Institutionalization
definition: One dimension of trust is the institutionalization of values and norms that constitute an ethics of transactional relationships.

name: Habitualization
authors_terms: ["habitualization", "partners' having established habits, bonds, good communication, and empathy"]
definition: A second dimension of trust is habitualization, defined as familiarization, habit formation, and bonding generated or confirmed by positive experiences.

name: Value of ego for alter
authors_terms: ["value of ego", "value of ego for alter", "the value one partner offers another", "the relative value offered by ego to alter"]
definition: The value that ego offers to alter relative to the partner's next best alternative. Ego can reduce alter's incentives for opportunism by increasing the uniqueness of ego's value for alter.

name: Relationship continuity
authors_terms: ["continuity", "past growth of a relationship", "long-term perspective", "future perspective"]
definition: In long-term relationships there is more at stake, yielding a positive effect on size of loss, but long-term relations also offer more possibilities of establishing personal ties and of growing trust as an invisible asset. Continuity of the relationship was an aggregate of two scales, past growth of the relationship and future perspective.

name: Restraint of alter
authors_terms: ["restraint of alter", "limitation of alter's inclination toward opportunism", "restraint of alter's opportunism"]
definition: Other factors that promote a partner's dependence, and thereby reduce his or her incentives for opportunistic behavior, have a negative effect on the perceived probability of loss. Limitation of alter's inclination toward opportunism, or restraint of alter, was composed of five items.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: Some people (and some firms) are more sensitive to risks (exhibit higher uncertainty avoidance) than others. Uncertainty avoidance, originally conceptualized as a dimension of national culture by Hofstede (1980), was later shown to also be associated with organization-level variables.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of the firm of a focal agent", "size"]
definition: The size of the firm of a focal agent. A large firm is likely to be subject to lower transaction costs and relational risk than a small firm, as a result of its high capacities for search, contract design, monitoring, and litigation.

name: Cooperation
definition: The extent to which partners cooperate, where trust is a source of cooperation that coexists with sources of cooperation based on self-interest and coercion.

name: General collaborative experience
definition: The stock of collective experience a firm accumulates on how to handle the complexities of the alliance process, measured as the number of prior agreements with any partner on any subject.

name: Technology-specific experience
definition: Experience from previous alliances completed in similar technical domains, i.e., the number of prior agreements with any partner in product areas similar to the one of the focal agreement.

name: Partner-specific experience
definition: Knowledge accumulated about the partnering firms themselves: as partners work through the operational details of the collaborative agreement, both develop a more refined understanding of each other's cultures, management systems, capabilities and weaknesses.

name: Equity governance
definition: A governance structure in which equity ownership is employed, either one partner owning a minority stake in the other partnering firm or the two firms creating a new entity whose ownership is shared among them; nonequity arrangements are governed solely through a contract.

name: Alliance performance
definition: A firm's overall achievement of its objectives in the alliance as well as the degree to which the collaboration contributes to the firm's accumulation of knowledge and to the creation of new opportunities for the firm.

name: Technological discontinuity
definition: A technological discontinuity is 'technical advance so significant that no increase in scale, efficiency, or design can make older technologies competitive with the new technology.' The study focuses on competence-destroying discontinuities, which require new skills, abilities, and knowledge in both the development and production of the product.

name: Complementary assets
authors_terms: ["complementary assets", "type of complementary assets", "generic complementary assets", "specialized complementary assets"]
definition: Commercialization of an innovation requires that the know-how be utilized in conjunction with other capabilities or assets, which are obtained from complementary assets. Complementary assets that are generic need not be adjusted to the innovation, because they can frequently be contracted for in the market on competitive terms, whereas specialized complementary assets exhibit unilateral dependence between the innovation and the complementary assets and are frequently built over long periods of time.

name: Incumbent industry performance
definition: Incumbent industry performance, proxied by industry return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA), is the dependent variable used to test the industry-level hypotheses and is examined as time series of overall industry performance in each of the four industries.

name: Incumbent firm performance
definition: Incumbent firm performance, measured as incumbent firm ROE and ROA, is the dependent variable used to test the firm-level hypotheses in the postdiscontinuity time period.

name: Financial strength
definition: Financial strength allows incumbent firms to change strategies quickly through pursuing capital-intensive options such as acquisitions. An incumbent firm's financial strength is measured by the sum of its cash and all securities readily convertible to cash as listed in the current assets section of the balance sheet, which the authors interpret as free cash flow.

name: R&D capability
definition: R&D capability reflects a firm's strength in discovery and innovation; ongoing investments in R&D create a firm-specific capability that may enable a firm to value, assimilate, and exploit new knowledge. The authors proxy an incumbent firm's R&D capability by its R&D expenditures.

name: Technology policy
authors_terms: ["technology policy", "degree of aggressiveness of technology policy"]
definition: Technology policy is defined as "the long-range strategy of the organization concerning the adoption of new process and material innovations and the orientation of new product or service innovations." It refers to the degree to which a firm aggressively pursues technological changes in terms of process innovation, product innovation, technological forecasting activities, and recruitment of qualified human resources.

name: Determinants of technology policy
definition: The determinants of technology policy that act as predictor variables comprise the structural characteristics of the firm, scanning, and strategic orientation (STROBE).

name: Technocratization
definition: A concentration of technical and scientific knowledge, also termed technocratization, which has been shown to be a crucial determinant of innovativeness and a significant predictor of organizational technology policy; it is measured as the number of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technicians divided by the total number of employees.

name: Formalization
definition: A structural characteristic reflecting the degree to which the firm relies on formal rules and defined responsibilities: complete job descriptions for all jobs, strict adherence to company rules, and no arguments about job overlap among managers.

name: Centralization
definition: A structural characteristic reflecting the concentration of decision-making authority, captured by the level of management responsible for making decisions such as capital budgeting, introduction of new products, acquisitions, pricing of major product lines, entry into major new markets, and hiring and firing of senior personnel.

name: Scanning mechanisms
definition: Strategic awareness of the competitive actions undertaken by direct competitors and of prevailing market conditions appears to be a crucial organizational function that promotes within the firm activities aimed at defining clients' opinions, conducting market studies, following competitors' strategies, and predicting sales behavior and customer needs; the systematic use of scanning mechanisms directed at the identification of opportunities and threats from competitors or from emergent technologies is viewed as a powerful determinant of technology policy.

name: Strategic orientation of business enterprise
authors_terms: ["STROBE", "strategic orientation", "strategic orientation of the business enterprise"]
definition: Strategic orientation of the business enterprise or STROBE reflects the actual strategies pursued by a firm with respect to its competitors and involves a host of organizational activities, whether product-related, price-related, process-related, or financially related. The STROBE measure characterizes a firm along six dimensions that correspond to traditional strategic orientations: aggressiveness, analysis, defensiveness, futurity, proactiveness, and riskiness.

name: Aggressiveness
definition: The aggressiveness dimension reflects a firm's market share seeking behavior.

name: Analysis
definition: Analysis captures the presence of formal planning and evaluation activities with respect to strategic alternatives.

name: Defensiveness
definition: Defensiveness relates to the emphasis a firm places on performance monitoring and enhancement of core manufacturing competencies.

name: Futurity
definition: The futurity dimension denotes the presence of a long-term view, supported by ongoing evaluation of significant trends, and of activities such as R&D, that are designed to provide longer-term benefits for the firm.

name: Proactiveness
definition: Proactiveness emphasizes an opportunity seeking behavior, "first-to-market" innovativeness, and strategic acquisitions that support the preceding elements.

name: Riskiness
definition: The riskiness dimension relates to risk management in terms of resource allocation decisions, operations, and choice of projects.

name: Realized innovative efforts
definition: Realized innovative efforts (or predicted variables) in SMEs are usually of three types: traditional R&D investments mainly aimed at improving or modifying existing products; the adoption of computer-based information and manufacturing technologies; and the extent of external technological experience and know-how with respect to new technological developments.

name: R&D investment
definition: The first type of realized innovative efforts, associated with traditional R&D investments mainly aimed at improving or modifying existing products, and, more rarely, developing new ones.

name: Process innovativeness
authors_terms: ["degree of process innovativeness", "innovativeness score for computer-based applications"]
definition: The second type of innovative effort concentrates on improving existing practices through the adoption of computer-based information and manufacturing technologies; the degree of process innovativeness is a composite measure of the level of process innovativeness using data on computer-based administrative and manufacturing applications.

name: External technological experience
definition: The third type of realized innovative efforts represents the extent of external technological experience and know-how with respect to new technological developments, the commercial availability of new technologies and the comparative advantages that may be derived from the new technologies.

name: Perceived environmental hostility
definition: Environmental hostility captures the perceived threats to the very survival of the firm, namely increasingly harsh competition on product prices, depleting markets, scarcity of qualified and specialized labor, difficulty of access to raw materials, components or parts from suppliers, and government intervention.

name: Perceived environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism, also referred to as uncertainty, reflects the perceived degree of unpredictability and rate of change of the external environment.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance is one of the two types of performance of critical importance for SMEs, given the lack of financial resources in these firms; it is assessed by perceptual measures that have been used extensively by other researchers and have been shown to correlate highly with objective measures such as return on assets.

name: Export performance
definition: Export performance is the second type of performance of critical importance for SMEs: with the opening up of new markets, SMEs are subjected to increased competition from new rivals and therefore must themselves broaden their reach by developing new markets. Factual measures were used for export performance.

name: Lead entrepreneurs' initial resource contributions
authors_terms: ["initial contributions of resources by lead entrepreneurs", "lead entrepreneurs' initial contributions", "resource contributions from the lead entrepreneur", "founding entrepreneurs' initial contributions"]
definition: The resources lead entrepreneurs contribute to the new venture early in the start-up process: (1) the amount of initial financial resources contributed by the lead entrepreneur in the first year and (2) whether the lead entrepreneur worked more than 35 hours per week for the start-up.

name: Team members' resource contributions
authors_terms: ["resource contributions", "team members' contributions", "cofounders' resource contributions", "resources contributed to the business by a cofounder"]
definition: Resources contributed to the business by a cofounder, measured for two venture-specific resources: (1) the financial contributions by a co-owner-founder to the venture (in individual-year units) and (2) whether a co-owner-founder works full time (in individual-month units).

name: Formal contracts
authors_terms: ["formal contracts", "formal agreements", "signed a formal agreement", "written documents that signal teams' commitment to prescribing individual members' contributions"]
definition: Adopting written documents that signal teams' commitment to prescribing individual members' contributions is measured by whether owners had signed formal agreements regarding their ownership.

name: Interdependency among activities
definition: Interdependencies exist whenever the value of conducting one or more activities in a particular manner depends on how a firm conducts other activities. An industry's potential for interdependency among activities is the latent possibility of interdependency between activities in the industry's production function, an industry attribute exogenous to the actions of firms.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Tobin's q is calculated from the assumption that the market value of a firm in a time period is a function of the scale of its tangible and intangible assets and of additional factors, such as interdependency among activities, that magnify or reduce the return that firms can generate with assets invested in those industries. Qit is the ratio of the market valuation of the firm to the value of tangible assets, commonly referred to as Tobin's q.

name: Within-industry variance in firm profitability
authors_terms: ["variance in profits", "variance in Tobin's q", "VarQ", "second moment"]
definition: VarQ represents the second (variance) moment of q for all firms within the same four-digit SIC industry for each year in the panel, and is calculated as the standard deviation of FirmQ.

name: Within-industry skew in firm profitability
authors_terms: ["skew of firm performance distributions", "skew in Tobin's q", "SkewQ", "third moment"]
definition: SkewQ represents the third (skew) moment of q for all firms within the same four-digit SIC industry for each year in the panel.

name: Supplier trust in the buyer
authors_terms: ["trust", "supplier trust in the buyer", "buyer trustworthiness", "interorganizational trust", "perceived trustworthiness"]
definition: Trust is defined as one party's confidence that the other party in the exchange relationship will not exploit its vulnerabilities, and the authors characterize interfirm trust as a construct based on three related components: reliability, fairness, and goodwill/benevolence. In this study they consider trust by an automotive supplier in its automaker customer, i.e., the perceived trustworthiness of the automaker.

name: Ex ante transaction costs
authors_terms: ["ex ante transaction costs", "ex ante contracting costs", "contracting costs", "negotiating"]
definition: Ex ante transaction costs, or search and contracting costs, include the costs of locating a desirable trading partner and then negotiating and writing a mutually acceptable agreement.

name: Ex post transaction costs
authors_terms: ["ex post transaction costs", "ex post contracting costs", "monitoring and enforcement costs", "ex post haggling"]
definition: Ex post contracting costs, or monitoring and enforcement costs, refer to the costs associated with monitoring the agreement and then taking the actions necessary to ensure that each party fulfills the predetermined set of obligations.

name: Buyer transaction costs
definition: The authors state that the greater the supplier trust in the buyer, the lower the total transaction costs incurred by the exchange partners, a conclusion that follows directly from the ex ante and ex post hypotheses. For the automaker-level hypothesis the proxy is procurement costs, i.e., the average procurement dollars per person in the purchasing department of the automaker.

name: Supplier information sharing
authors_terms: ["supplier information sharing", "information sharing", "sharing of confidential/proprietary information"]
definition: Information sharing was operationalized as the extent to which the supplier shares confidential/proprietary information with automaker buyers and engineers. The sharing of sensitive information such as costs and proprietary technology is described as a critical factor for joint efforts to minimize costs.

name: Profit performance
definition: A buyer with a trustworthy reputation in exchange relationships should have lower transaction costs, which in turn should translate into better profit performance; profitability is measured as ROA, or pretax profits divided by assets.

name: HTF product introductions
authors_terms: ["HTF product introductions", "new HTF product introductions", "HTF products"]
definition: Products at the high-technology frontier represent 'technology push' efforts driven by the technical possibilities of industry research and development (R&D); HTF products represent leading-edge technology developments, are risky, require substantial 'lumpy' R&D investments, and tend to be aimed at small, niche markets with low growth rates. New product introductions, the dependent variable, is the number of HTF product introductions by a firm in a given year.

name: LTF product introductions
authors_terms: ["LTF product introductions", "new LTF product introductions", "LTF products"]
definition: Products at the low-technology frontier represent 'market pull' efforts and are driven by the fusion of user needs and technical possibilities; LTF products typically require lower R&D investments relative to HTF products, are aimed at the large mass market, and have strong anticipated growth rates. New product introductions, the dependent variable, is the number of LTF product introductions by a firm in a given year.

name: HTF introductions of similarly sized firms
authors_terms: ["HTF product introductions of similarly sized firms", "HTF product introductions of their size peers"]
definition: The HTF product introductions of other firms of similar size to the focal firm. Organizations of similar size generally rely on the same resources and face similar constraints, and this match of size and strategy profiles suggests the appropriateness of size peers as good learning targets; their HTF introductions contain diagnostic information on the technical feasibility of HTF products.

name: HTF introductions of successful firms
authors_terms: ["HTF product introductions of successful firms", "HTF products introduced by successful firms"]
definition: The HTF product introductions of other firms perceived to be successful. Highly profitable organizations are naturally viewed as more successful than less profitable organizations, and the firm's profitability, measured as return on assets, is the indicator of its success.

name: HTF introductions of firms from the same origin industry
authors_terms: ["HTF product introductions of firms from the same origin industry", "HTF products of firms within the same origin industry"]
definition: The HTF product introductions of firms that entered the converging market from the same origin industry as the focal firm. The shared knowledge base of firms from within a given origin industry is likely to create greater absorptive capacity for vicarious learning, and similar industry networks may facilitate the transfer of HTF technical knowledge.

name: HTF introductions of firms outside the origin industry
authors_terms: ["HTF product introductions of firms outside the origin industry", "HTF product introductions of firms from outside their origin industry"]
definition: The HTF product introductions of firms from outside the focal firm's origin industry, which generate information about technology developments outside their origin industry's knowledge domains and are different but still complementary knowledge.

name: LTF introductions of firms from the same origin industry
authors_terms: ["LTF product introductions of firms from the same origin industry", "LTF products of firms from their origin industry"]
definition: The LTF product introductions of firms from the same origin industry as the focal firm. These firms directly compete for resources in the converging market, and the threatening, competitive aspects of their new LTF product introductions are likely to be more salient than their informational value.

name: LTF introductions of firms outside the origin industry
authors_terms: ["LTF product introductions of firms outside the origin industry", "LTF products of firms from outside their origin industry"]
definition: The LTF product introductions of target firms from outside the focal firm's origin industry, which increase the perceived competition for LTF products and may lead the focal firm to infer that the resources and competencies of firms from its origin industry are not adequate to compete effectively.

name: LTF product introductions of other firms
authors_terms: ["LTF products of other firms", "LTF product introductions of similarly sized and successful firms"]
definition: The LTF product introductions of other firms in the market. Because HTF products are driven by technology push and not by market pull, the authors do not anticipate vicarious learning for new HTF products from the LTF products of other firms.

name: Pathos appeals
definition: Pathos appeals are signals that stimulate the receiver's emotions (e.g., alarming statements to trigger anxiety) and thereby attract the receiver's attention.

name: Logos appeals
definition: Logos appeals are signals that convey information about a focal economic activity (e.g., characteristics of a new product to be developed) used to reduce activity-related information asymmetry.

name: Ethos appeals
definition: Ethos appeals are signals that convey information about the firm seeking resources (e.g., claims related to the capabilities of a firm), aiming to reduce firm-related information asymmetry.

name: Activity-related substantive signals
authors_terms: ["substantive signal: product", "substantive signals: product", "product-related substantive signals", "activity-related substantive signals"]
definition: Substantive signals provide relevant information that is more costly for low-quality than it is for high-quality senders; product-related substantive signals must convey information about the final product.

name: Firm-related substantive signals
authors_terms: ["substantive signal: firm", "substantive signals: firm", "firm-related substantive signals"]
definition: Substantive signals provide relevant information that is more costly for low-quality than it is for high-quality senders; firm-related substantive signals must refer to the developer's capabilities.

name: Resource contributions
definition: Resource contributions is the amount of money a campaign received as a percentage of the amount requested.

name: Venture incubation
definition: Through a combination of funding, peer support, and feedback from mentors, incubators catalyze entrepreneurial resource mobilization and serve as windows into early-stage venture development. Participants in this incubator receive one-on-one mentoring, in-class training covering business topics, and a small sum of kickstarter funding.

name: Sales revenue
authors_terms: ["sales revenue", "change in sales revenue", "business revenue", "sales growth", "revenue growth"]
definition: The change in sales revenue for the businesses, in Rand, between the time of applying to the incubator (T0) and six months after applying (T1). In the second study, monthly business revenue (in Rand, logged) is one of the variables that measure business performance after incubation.

name: Employment growth
definition: The change in employee headcount, including both paid full-time and part-time employees, between the time of applying to the incubator and six months after applying.

name: Mentor ability
authors_terms: ["mentors' ability", "high-ability mentors", "mentor ability", "mentors' expertise", "mentors' track records"]
definition: This study operationalized mentors' ability as the lagged average score improvement of participants paired with each mentor in prior cohorts. Thus, mentors' ability measured mentors' demonstrated track records from work with participants from past cohorts.

name: Entrepreneurial learning
definition: Each participant's final exam score measured their knowledge of the material covered in the incubator after completing the 24-week incubation program. This measure captured participants' learning by differencing their final scores from their baseline scores.

name: Pre-entry knowledge
authors_terms: ["pre-entry knowledge", "baseline exam performance", "baseline exam score", "baseline knowledge"]
definition: Each participant's baseline exam performance, on a scale of 0-100, measured their baseline knowledge coming into the incubator, including their understanding of basic business operations and management concepts such as bookkeeping, operations, strategic planning, and sales and marketing; this score proxies for a participant's human capital, based on prior education and work experience.

name: Prior work experience
authors_terms: ["pre-entry experience", "prior work experience", "experience", "age at the time of participating"]
definition: The authors treat entrepreneurs' age at the time of participating in the incubator as experience: the benefits of mentoring are argued to be larger for entrepreneurs with less pre-entry knowledge and experience coming into the incubator. Older participants are described as having more prior work experience and higher baseline scores than younger participants.

name: Business profitability
definition: Monthly business profits, in Rand and logged, collected over 12 consecutive months after participants graduated from the incubator; one of the variables that measure business performance.

name: Social capital from peer managers
authors_terms: ["social capital developed from the networking relationships and ties with top managers at other firms", "social capital from top managers at other firms", "social capital from managers at other firms"]
definition: The managerial social capital that is developed by an organization's top management through personal and social networking relationships and ties with top managers at other firms (suppliers, buyers, and competitors).

name: Social capital from government officials
authors_terms: ["social capital developed from the networking relationships and ties with government officials (political leaders and bureaucratic officials)", "social capital from government officials"]
definition: The managerial social capital developed from networking relationships with government officials such as politicians at different levels of government and with bureaucratic officials in regulatory, supporting, investment, and industrial institutions.

name: Social capital from community leaders
authors_terms: ["social capital developed from the networking relationships and ties with community leaders", "social capital from community leaders"]
definition: The managerial social capital developed from networking relationships with community leaders such as local chiefs and kings and religious leaders, who serve as local bridges between an organization and the community.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Firm performance assessed as the respondents' rating of their firms on five growth and profitability measures relative to the major competitors in their industry.

name: Low-cost strategy
definition: An organization implementing the low-cost strategy emphasizes operational efficiency and achieving a low-cost position relative to competitors through tight cost and overhead control and cost minimization.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: An organization implementing the differentiation strategy focuses on creating and providing products or services that customers perceive as unique and valuable as compared to those of its competitors.

name: Integrated strategy
authors_terms: ["integrated strategy", "integrated low-cost and differentiation strategy", "combination strategy of low cost and differentiation"]
definition: The pursuit of the low-cost and differentiation strategies simultaneously, focusing on achieving both low cost and differentiation.

name: Firm-university co-authorship linkages
definition: For each firm unit-university-year observation, this variable contains the number of scientific articles published in that year that listed at least one co-author affiliated with that firm and at least one co-author affiliated with that university.

name: Intrafirm collaboration linkages
authors_terms: ["intrafirm collaboration linkages", "intrafirm linkages", "intrafirm collaborations", "internal collaboration linkages"]
definition: Instances in which a patent lists one co-inventor in one location and another co-inventor in another location capture intrafirm collaboration linkages; the measure captures the extent to which inventors within a particular R&D unit of a firm are involved in collaborative inventions with inventors in other units.

name: University-rival co-authorship linkages
authors_terms: ["university-rival co-authorship linkages", "co-authorship linkages with rivals", "collaboration linkages with rivals"]
definition: To measure the extent to which a university exhibits collaboration linkages with rivals of the focal firm, this variable has the number of scientific articles published in that year that listed at least one co-author affiliated with any of the nonfocal sample firms and at least one co-author affiliated with that university.

name: Formal contracting with communities
definition: A contract is defined as 'an agreement between two or more parties that is binding on those parties, to the degree that to renege on the agreement will be costly' (Argyres and Liebeskind 1999, p. 51). Firms can use contracts to govern transactions for access to valuable sites, and CBAs are the form these contracts take in firm-community relations.

name: Use rights
definition: Use rights (usus) are the rights to use or enjoy a thing possessed, directly and without altering it. They are relevant because they can be a source of conflict while simultaneously affording a community the right to seek sanctions against those that interfere with their rights.

name: Negative externalities
definition: Externalities are 'harmful effects on others', illustrated by 'a factory the smoke from which has harmful effects on those occupying neighboring properties' (Coase 1960, p. 1). They are social costs incurred where property rights cannot be effectively defined.

name: Community capacity for collective mobilization
authors_terms: ["capacity for collective mobilization", "capacity for collective action", "community mobilization", "mobilization capacity"]
definition: Local communities vary in their ability to overcome the pervasive collective action problem, to organize collectively to articulate their interests, and to take action to assert them. Communities that mobilized in the past are more likely to do so again because they develop a shared understanding of their goals and interests, relationships, and norms for monitoring and coordinating mechanisms for subsequent action.

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation", "overall strategic orientation", "prospector, analyzer or defender"]
definition: The overall strategic orientation of the corporations, namely prospector, analyzer or defender. Based on the changes that took place in each company, Miles labeled Philip Morris as a prospector, R. J. Reynolds as an analyzer, and American Brands as a defender.

name: Outsider orientation
definition: An upper echelon executive whose tenure in a company was shorter than 5 years was categorized as an outsider to that company, even though the individual might have worked for another firm in the same industry or a firm in another industry. The individual was classified as an insider after his fifth year in office in the company.

name: Functional orientation
definition: Functional responsibility of upper echelon executive, as indicated by the title of his vice-presidential office, was defined as the functional orientation of the executive. However, where the executive worked in more than one functional track the track in which he spent most number of years was defined as his functional orientation.

name: Proportion of marketing and R&D executives
definition: The proportion of a firm's upper echelon executives whose functional orientation is marketing or research and development, as indicated by the titles of their vice-presidential offices.

name: Proportion of production and finance executives
definition: The proportion of a firm's upper echelon executives whose functional orientation is production or finance, as indicated by the titles of their vice-presidential offices.

name: Product-market aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["Miles and Snow typology", "business-level strategies", "Prospectors", "Defenders", "rate of product, market change", "product market aggressiveness"]
definition: The study hinges on the descriptive conceptualization of strategy as a pattern in a stream of important decisions, focusing on business-level strategies ('How does the firm compete in a given business?') rather than on corporate-level strategies. The key dimension underlying the Miles and Snow typology is the organization's rate of product, market change: Defenders offer a stable set of products or services and compete on price, quality, service and delivery; Prospectors attempt to pioneer in product or service developments; Analysers are an intermediate type.

name: Environmental scanning
definition: The concept of scanning, as used here, includes both formal and informal search, and both directed and undirected viewing. Organizations differ in what environmental sectors they scan and how much they scan.

name: Entrepreneurial scanning
definition: Scanning of the entrepreneurial sector, which covers product market trends or events, for example demographic shifts affecting demand for the organization's products.

name: Engineering scanning
definition: Scanning of the engineering sector, which covers events or trends bearing on rationalizing the manufacture or delivery of products or services, for example new developments in process technology.

name: Administrative scanning
definition: Scanning of the administrative sector, which covers events or trends bearing on determination of roles and relationships in the organization, for example new approaches to developing managers.

name: Regulatory scanning
definition: Scanning of the regulatory sector, which covers government regulations, taxes, sanctions, accreditations, litigations and similar mandated constraints, for example court cases involving the industry.

name: Agent monitoring
definition: Monitoring is the extent to which principals observe the behavior of agents; the authors identified three direct agent monitoring measures (computer tracking, communication systems, and narrow supervisory span) and indirect monitoring measures (relays and scheduling stability, and job programmability).

name: Agent tenure
definition: Agent tenure is studied less often, but many agency and collaborative arguments implicitly derive from agent tenure since long-term relationships allow principals to accumulate richer information on agent behaviors.

name: Performance-contingent compensation
authors_terms: ["performance-contingent compensation", "performance-contingent compensation systems", "outcome-based pay", "performance-based pay", "performance-contingent pay"]
definition: We use performance-contingent compensation for such a test since it represents risk transfer, a central aspect of both perspectives. Reliance on performance-contingent compensation reflects different assumptions about the interests and motivations of principals and agents, since performance-contingent compensation embodies more risk for the agent (than, say, seniority-based pay).

name: Relatedness
definition: Diversifying entrants differ in the degree of relatedness, r, or potential for resource sharing, between their old and new segments. The potential for resource sharing is greater between more related segments than between less related segments.

name: Firm capability
definition: Capabilities are defined as the ability to deploy resources, through organizational routines and processes, to produce a given amount of output, perform a set of coordinated tasks or effect a desired end. Capabilities are independent of resources and differ between firms within the same industry.

name: Diversifying entry
definition: Firms will compare profits from different combinations of output choices (i.e., always one unit in the old segment and zero vs. one unit in the new segment) to make their entry and exit decision.

name: Post-entry exit
definition: When the market condition in the new segment unfavorably deviates from expectation, it tightens the criteria for survival and drives out some low capability firms from the new segment. Firms whose capability is below the exit threshold exit the new segment.

name: Post-entry cost shock
definition: Post entry, firms experience an unexpected cost shock, d, which raises the post-shock unit cost in the new segment.

name: Peripheral knowledge
definition: Peripheral knowledge is defined as the outsourcing firm's knowledge in the domain of the activity that is outsourced to another outside firm. In software services alliances it refers to the outsourcer's technical knowledge specific to the outsourced project.

name: Outcome control
definition: Outcome controls refer to the prespecification of the desired interim and final outputs without regard to the process by which the outputs are achieved; they prespecify what the outsourcee should accomplish.

name: Process control
definition: Process (or behavior) controls refer to explicitly prescribing the methods and procedures to be adopted by the outsourcee in undertaking project activities; they prescribe how the outsourcee should achieve the outcome.

name: Alliance performance
definition: The outsourcing firm's assessment of the outsourcee's work on the outsourced project relative to other IT projects, covering items such as adherence to budgets and schedules, work quality, meeting alliance goals and objectives, and overall efficiency and effectiveness of the delivered software application.

name: CEO personality
authors_terms: ["CEO personality", "psychological attributes of CEOs", "personality attributes of CEOs", "five-factor model of personality"]
definition: CEO psychology research describes how CEOs broadly evaluate themselves and their relationships to their environments across situations; the personality traits of the five-factor model are treated as broad personality constructs, each capturing a unique set of psychological traits.

name: CEO conscientiousness
definition: Conscientiousness reflects the degree to which someone shows dependability and an achievement orientation. Dependability is a concern for legalism or commitment to established rules, and an achievement orientation represents a need for control and a need to receive concrete feedback on actions.

name: CEO emotional stability
definition: Emotional stability is the ability to adapt to diverse situations and to cope with stress; it reflects a capacity for emotional adjustment and self-confidence.

name: CEO agreeableness
definition: Agreeableness represents the tendency to be altruistic (empathetic, kind, cooperative, trusting, and gentle) and compliant (modest, having a values affiliation, and conflict avoiding).

name: CEO extraversion
definition: Extraversion represents sociability and expressiveness; extraverted leaders tend to take the initiative in social settings and are expressive and articulate individuals who persuade, influence, and organize others.

name: CEO openness to experience
authors_terms: ["openness to experience", "openness to new experience", "CEO openness to experience"]
definition: Openness to experience represents the tendency to be creative, imaginative, perceptive, and thoughtful; people who are open to new experiences are intellectually curious, open to a wide range of stimuli, value unusual thought processes, and have a strong need for change.

name: Strategic flexibility
definition: Strategy scholars have defined strategic flexibility as a firm's ability to precipitate strategic changes; Aaker and Mascarenhas (1984) defined it as the ability to adapt to substantial, uncertain, and rapidly occurring environmental changes that meaningfully impact firm performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is assessed with three established accounting-based measures taken from the financial records provided by the sampled firms: return on assets, return on sales, and return on investment; market-based measures could not be included because the sampled firms were proprietary or partnership firms.

name: Degree of internationalization into a country
authors_terms: ["degree of internationalization into a country", "propensity of MNEs to internationalize into a country", "MNE's degree of internationalization into a host country"]
definition: This multidimensional measure better captures the MNE's internationalization as it reflects the breadth of internationalization into a country (i.e., the number of foreign subsidiaries) and its depth (i.e., the degree of commitment to each country based on the relative number of employees) simultaneously.

name: Prior internationalization into a region
authors_terms: ["prior internationalization into a region", "prior level of internationalization into this country's region"]
definition: Prior internationalization into a region also helps MNEs in this learning process because geographic agglomeration can facilitate flows of knowledge within a firm.

name: Regional regulatory control
authors_terms: ["regulatory control of its region", "regional regulatory control", "Regulatory control-region"]
definition: The regulatory control factor measures the degree of government involvement in business through laws, regulations, and government policies, which constrain behavior through rule-setting, monitoring, and sanctions. Each geographic region can be described by the general (i.e., average) characteristics of the institutional environments of the countries within it.

name: Region-relative regulatory control
definition: This variable reflects the variations and indicates the position of a country relative to the general tendency in its region. It is calculated as the country's original institutional score minus its respective region-level institutional score.

name: Regional political democracy
definition: The political democracy factor refers to the level of discretion and power a government maintains over its citizenry, measured through the country's civil liberties, political rights, executive political restrictions, and political constraints.

name: Region-relative political democracy
definition: The country-level region-relative variable captures a country's score on an institutional variable relative to the countries in the same region, not relative to all other countries.

name: Regional capital investment
authors_terms: ["capital investment in its region", "capital investments of the region", "Capital availability-region", "Market liquidity-region"]
definition: A country's capital investments, or the commitment of capital or money to purchase assets, promote an economy's strength and liquidity, thereby increasing a location's attractiveness for MNE investment and serving as a proxy for the strength of economic institutions.

name: Region-relative capital investment
definition: The country-level region-relative variable captures a country's score on an institutional variable relative to the countries in the same region, not relative to all other countries, and is calculated as the country's original institutional score minus its respective region-level institutional score.

name: General human capital investment
authors_terms: ["firm-sponsored investments in the general human capital", "general skills training", "investments in the general skills of contract workers", "training program"]
definition: Human capital is knowledge and skills with the potential to create economic value, and general human capital refers to skills that are transferrable across organizations and contexts. Firm-sponsored investments in the general human capital of contract workers take the form of general skills training programs offered to these workers.

name: Worker performance
definition: The performance effects of investments in general human capital, that is, the productivity of the contract worker in tasks conducted within the work arrangement. It is measured as the sales of a contract worker (the total value of sales orders across all direct representatives managed by the worker) and as the worker's individual gains (compensation).

name: Work arrangement duration
authors_terms: ["expected duration of work arrangements", "duration of the relationship between the firm and contract workers", "continuing in the work arrangement", "prolonging the work arrangement"]
definition: The expected duration of the work arrangement between contract workers and the firm, that is, whether the contract worker remains in the flexible work arrangement after concluding the firm-sponsored training.

name: Relational benefits framing
definition: A framing of a training program that emphasizes how the program can enhance the connection between the firm and the contract worker. Instead of emphasizing benefits that accrue to the firm or to the contract worker uniquely, the relational benefit framing underscores a potential strengthening of the ongoing flexible work arrangement in a way that generates mutual gains.

name: Manager promotion of training
authors_terms: ["promote the training program", "promotion of training opportunities", "firm manager promoted the training"]
definition: The decision of the immediate manager of contract workers to promote the firm-sponsored training opportunity to contract workers; promotion of training opportunities is one of the tasks under the responsibility of these managers.

name: Contract worker engagement with training
authors_terms: ["engage with the training program", "enroll in it", "contract worker started the training", "contract worker concluded the training"]
definition: The voluntary enrollment of contract workers in the firm-sponsored training program, measured from the workers' perspective as whether the contract worker started the training and whether the contract worker concluded the training.

name: Call option buyer position
authors_terms: ["purchasers", "call option buyer", "buying a call option", "buyers' prices"]
definition: A call option purchaser holds the right to wait until the lottery outcome is known before deciding whether to accept or decline its outcome. The call option buyer seeks exposure to a potential upside outcome.

name: Call option seller position
definition: The call option seller is already exposed to the probabilistic outcome associated with holding the lottery and seeks to exchange a possible gain for a sure current call option sale price.

name: Put option buyer position
authors_terms: ["put option buyer", "buying a put option", "buyer of the put"]
definition: Consider an individual who is exposed to a potential loss, who seeks to hedge the downside portion of this exposure by purchasing a put option. The value of the put option comes from the possibility of avoiding the loss x2.

name: Put option seller position
definition: Put option sellers have no preexisting exposures. Rather, they make discretionary choices to take on avoidable potential losses.

name: Call option price
authors_terms: ["call option price", "option price", "the maximum price they would be willing to pay to buy the option", "the minimum they would be willing to receive to sell the option"]
definition: The option price is the value of the option at the time of exchange between buyer and seller. For each item, respondents were asked to indicate the maximum price they would be willing to pay to buy the option or the minimum they would be willing to receive to sell the option.

name: Put option price
definition: The option price is the value of the option at the time of exchange between buyer and seller. For each item, respondents were asked to indicate the maximum price they would be willing to pay to buy the option or the minimum they would be willing to receive to sell the option.

name: Exercise price
definition: A call option provides its holder the possibility (but not the obligation) to purchase a particular asset at a given price (known as the exercise or strike price); a put option confers the prerogative to sell an asset at a specified exercise price.

name: Option duration
definition: The time up to an option's expiration. Options with a fixed exercise date on which the option can be exercised are known as European options, in contrast with American options, which can be exercised anytime during their duration.

name: Implicit discount rate
definition: The implicit rate at which an option payoff realized in a later period is discounted relative to a payoff realized in the current period, computed from respondents' reported values for options with different durations.

name: CEO extraversion
definition: Extraversion reflects a tendency for positive affect, assertive behavior, decisive thinking, and a desire for social engagement. It is one of the Big Five personality traits, the others being openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability.

name: M&A likelihood
definition: A firm's likelihood to acquire, captured as M&A propensity, a binary variable that equals 1 if the firm completed at least one deal in a particular year and 0 otherwise, and as M&A frequency, the total number of M&As made by each firm in a given year.

name: M&A deal size
authors_terms: ["M&A deal size", "M&A size", "deal size", "average transaction value"]
definition: The transaction values of all completed M&As made by firm i in year t, summed and then standardized by dividing by firm i's total assets in year t, and additionally divided by the number of M&As in the year to estimate the average transaction value of the deals.

name: Board network size
authors_terms: ["CEO's board network size", "CEO board network", "CEO outside board network", "board networks"]
definition: For CEOs, board networks often are the most influential sets of connections among their instrumental networks. We collected information on CEOs' outside board memberships and, in each fiscal year, counted the number of boards on which a CEO served, excluding the focal firm's board.

name: Industry competitiveness
definition: Industry competitiveness refers to the number of firms competing for the same product market. It indicates whether CEOs and others have clear and consistent information that pursuing M&As is an adequate response to competitive dynamics.

name: Managerial entrenchment
definition: Corporate governance is intended to put controlling and monitoring provisions in place to assure the suitable alignment of a CEO's behavior with the interests of a firm's owners and other stakeholders; managerial entrenchment reflects a lack of such provisions. Managerial entrenchment reflects the extent to which CEOs have the freedom to behave in accordance with their own personalities and thus reflects a form of situational strength.

name: Shareholder reaction to M&A announcements
definition: We used standard market-adjusted models to calculate daily abnormal stock returns around the M&A announcement date for each acquirer and added daily abnormal returns to measure the cumulative abnormal return. A positive CAR suggests that investors believe that the deal will create shareholder value, while a negative CAR suggests the deal will destroy shareholder value.

name: Limit pricing
definition: A limit pricing strategy is one in which the incumbent firm uses low prices to signal its low costs to a potential entrant. If the signal is effective, the potential entrant realizes that the incumbent will be able to price the entrant out of the market if it were to enter.

name: Potential entrant industry origin
authors_terms: ["type of potential entrant", "entrant type", "potential telecom entrants", "potential cable entrants", "firms outside the industry"]
definition: Potential entrants are divided into two mutually exclusive categories: cable entrants, which come from within the cable industry, and telecom entrants, which come from outside the cable industry. The differences in technology suggest that to the extent asymmetric information exists at all it is likely higher between incumbents and telecom entrants than between incumbents and cable entrants.

name: R&D consortium membership
authors_terms: ["membership in R&D consortia", "members of R&D consortia", "CableLabs membership", "nonmembership in CableLabs"]
definition: In 1988, incumbent cable system operators established an R&D consortium called CableLabs to develop new technologies for cable systems; the standards are disseminated to members through documents and technical demonstrations at annual members-only conferences. Cable entrants are not members of CableLabs and non-cable operators, including telecom entrants, are explicitly denied membership.

name: Threat of entry
definition: The probability of entry into the incumbent's market increases with the geographic proximity to a potential entrant. Entrants typically focus on a specific geographic area and base entry decisions on the proximity to their existing systems.

name: Connectedness to learning-oriented intergovernmental organizations
authors_terms: ["IGO connectedness", "connectedness to the learning-oriented IGO network", "learning-oriented IGO connectedness", "connectedness with learning-oriented IGOs"]
definition: Our main independent variable is the extent of a country's connectedness with learning-oriented IGOs. We measured IGO connectedness as the natural log of the total number of active learning-oriented IGOs worldwide that a country is a member of in a given year.

name: National innovation
definition: Our analysis requires a country-specific indicator of innovation in a given year. We followed prior researchers and used the number of patent applications with first-inventor location in that country under the USPTO system, which includes innovations by domestic firms as well as local subsidiaries of multinational corporations.

name: Complementary opportunities
definition: Domestic complementary opportunities are product sectors in which the country does not have an advantage (hence represent opportunities for expansion), and that are complementary to product sectors in which a country currently has advantages. Thus externally acquired knowledge, assets, and capabilities can be leveraged in new but closely related product sectors.

name: Domestic coordinating mechanisms
authors_terms: ["domestic coordinating mechanisms", "market-based domestic coordination", "market modes of coordination", "domestic coordination (market)"]
definition: Scholars have proposed that coordination mechanisms among firms and other entities are an important parameter of the national institutional context that can account for differences in innovative efforts and economic outcomes across countries. We measured the extent to which the relations between firms and other actors rely on competitive markets.

name: Interest group rivalry
authors_terms: ["rivalry from competing interest groups", "interest group rivalry", "demand-side rivalry", "competition from organized interest groups"]
definition: Opposition a firm faces from competing demanders of public policy, including rival firms, consumers, and activist interest groups, who mobilize against the firm's preferred policy. As opposed interest groups compete more vigorously against a firm for their preferred policies, policy makers' bargaining positions improve, enabling them to demand more in return for policy favors.

name: Rivalry between elected politicians
authors_terms: ["rivalry between politicians", "political rivalry", "electoral competition or rivalry", "rivalry among elected politicians"]
definition: The intensity of competition for office among electoral candidates and party coalitions. Recent research suggests that elected politicians are more receptive to interest group demands for regulatory favors when electoral competition or rivalry is strong.

name: Regulatory agency resource base
authors_terms: ["resource base of a relevant regulatory agency", "PUC resources", "resources of the regulatory agency", "regulatory agency resources"]
definition: The financial and experiential resources an administrative agency can draw on to obtain its own information, assess firms' arguments, and counter firms' policy proposals. Less well endowed agencies will be more dependent on the information provided by firms in formulating their decisions, lending a natural bias toward the firms.

name: Firm experience with government policy makers
authors_terms: ["experience in dealing with government policy makers", "firm experience", "repeated interactions", "prior rate reviews"]
definition: The extent to which a firm has repeatedly interacted with government policy makers. Firms that frequently engage with the government have a chance to build trustworthy reputations and to learn from experience the patterns of behavior and preferences of policy makers.

name: Learning from other firms' interactions with government policy makers
authors_terms: ["opportunity to learn from other firms' interactions with government policy makers", "learning from other firms' experience", "observing others' past nonmarket interactions"]
definition: The opportunity for a firm to learn from other firms' experience in similar nonmarket settings. Some of the heterogeneity among firms' nonmarket performance is therefore likely to stem from whether they have been able to learn from others' experiences.

name: Nonmarket strategy performance
authors_terms: ["nonmarket strategy performance", "performance of a firm's nonmarket strategy", "ability of firms to effect favorable public policy decisions"]
definition: The ability of firms to effect favorable public policy decisions. Relative to a given status quo policy, performance measures the ability of a firm to either achieve policy closer to its preferred position or block proposals that move policy further from that position.

name: Nonmarket strategy implementation
authors_terms: ["implementation of a nonmarket strategy", "rate review initiation", "decision to initiate a rate review"]
definition: A firm's decision to implement a nonmarket strategy aimed at changing an existing regulation. A utility's initiation of a rate review is a clear indication of the implementation of such a strategy.

name: Divestment intensity
definition: The amount of change involved in corporate refocusing, operationalized as the intensity of a firm's program of divestitures.

name: Post-refocusing CEO total compensation
authors_terms: ["post-refocusing level of its CEO's total compensation", "total CEO compensation", "post-refocusing CEO compensation"]
definition: The total compensation paid by a company to its executive after the refocusing program is completed.

name: Pre-refocusing firm performance
definition: Accounting performance of the firm prior to the refocusing program, measured as return on assets.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "proportion of independent outside directors on the board"]
definition: The proportion of independent outside directors on the board, that is, outside directors with no other affiliation with the firm except as directors.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: A characteristic of dynamic industries involving high uncertainty and rapid change.

name: Generational product innovation
definition: A GPI represents a substantial advance in the technical performance of an existing product within a technological regime, where a technological regime is a common set of scientific and technical principles that generate patterns of solutions for particular technological problems and support periods of cumulative advance along accepted technological trajectories.

name: Time since previous innovation
authors_terms: ["time since previous innovation", "time since prior innovation", "elapsed calendar time since the prior innovation release"]
definition: In this stream of research, the time since the previous innovation is a central factor that shapes innovation releases. Our measure is the elapsed calendar time since the prior innovation release for the product line.

name: Market concentration
definition: Market concentration is a function of the number of products in a market and their respective shares of total sales.

name: Competitor innovation
authors_terms: ["competitor innovation", "competition innovation", "release of a generational product innovation by a competitor"]
definition: Competitor innovation events center on interdependence in the form of innovation rivalry among competing products.

name: Complementary innovation
authors_terms: ["complementary innovation", "complementary innovations", "technological opportunity event", "technological opportunity events"]
definition: By contrast, complementary innovations focus on the interdependence among technologies within larger systems. The value of many products is influenced by their interdependence with complementary technologies.

name: Diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm expands the scope of its operation, products, or services beyond its core business, market, or industry.

name: Asymmetric pressure
authors_terms: ["asymmetric pressure", "asymmetric competitive pressure", "differential exposure to competitive pressure"]
definition: The differential exposure to the cumulative competitive pressure from all competitors.

name: Network convergence
definition: Convergence occurs when technologies, capabilities, firms, industries, or landscapes coalesce. The network statistic of convergence captures the endogenous dependence of the competition network on the frequency of transitive competitive encounters.

name: Degree of separation
definition: In network space a degree of separation refers to the spatial gaps between firms, such as number and lengths of connections or paths. The degree of separation between firms i and j is the fewest number of steps (i.e., shortest path length) between them.

name: Competitive encounters
definition: The dependent variable measures whether a competitive encounter occurred between two firms in a period; competitor identification studies follow focal firms over an extended period because firms rarely compete with all other firms at any given moment.

name: Product development
authors_terms: ["product development", "product development processes", "internal technology exploitation", "internal identification", "internal commercialization"]
definition: The internal technology exploitation process of a firm, which refers to the identification of innovation opportunities and to the commercialization of new products; it indicates innovative capacity. The measures capture to what degree a firm has set up high quality processes for these major tasks, that is, its competence level in the different process stages.

name: Technology licensing
authors_terms: ["technology licensing", "technology licensing processes", "external technology exploitation", "external identification", "external commercialization", "desorptive capacity"]
definition: The external technology exploitation process, which includes the identification of licensing opportunities and the subsequent commercialization by transferring knowledge across a firm's boundaries. The measures capture to what degree a firm has set up high quality processes for these major tasks.

name: New product revenues
authors_terms: ["new product revenues", "percentage of revenues from new products", "percentage new product revenues"]
definition: A firm's new product revenues capture the success in internally exploiting technology, measured as the share of revenues from new products.

name: Licensing performance
definition: Licensing performance captures a firm's success in externally exploiting technology.

name: Firm performance
