definition: Firm performance, captured with return on sales data for the year of the survey and for the subsequent year.

name: Corporate profitability
definition: Corporate ROA is operating return on assets (profits before interest, taxes, and depreciation) divided by total assets for corporation J in year T.

name: Business segment performance
authors_terms: ["Segment ROA", "Business Segment ROA", "business segment profitability", "segment effect"]
definition: Segment ROA is operating return on assets for business segment I of corporation J in industry K in year T. The authors adopt the term 'segment' in parallel to Rumelt's usage of 'business unit' because their data are at the business segment level.

name: Industry profitability
definition: Industry ROA is the average operating return on assets for the business segment's industry K in year T. The authors use the industry's profitability as a proxy for differences in industry structures that enable firms to avoid competition.

name: Financial leverage
authors_terms: ["Corporate Debt to Total Assets", "debt to total assets", "corporate financial leverage", "leverage"]
definition: Debt/Total Assets is total corporate debt divided by the sum of debt plus equity for corporation J in year T. It is included as a measure of the absence of slack at the corporate level, following Hoskisson et al. (1993b) and Lubatkin and Chatterjee (1991) as a proxy for financial leverage.

name: High-performance work systems
authors_terms: ["high-performance work systems", "HPWS", "HPWS utilization", "high-performance HR practices", "high-performance work practices"]
definition: Although the concept of an HPWS has not been consistently and precisely defined in the literature, it has generally been utilized to describe a system of horizontally and vertically aligned employment practices designed to affect both the ability and the motivation of employees.

name: Organizational ambidexterity
definition: Organizational ambidexterity (OA) refers to the ability of an organization to efficiently take advantage of existing market opportunities while creating and innovating to meet the challenges of future markets.

name: Firm growth
definition: We use the average of sales and employee growth for the years 2008, 2009, and 2010; sales growth and employee growth are each measured as a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR).

name: Exploration
definition: Organizational ambidexterity focuses on the ability of the organization to both efficiently exploit its existing competencies (via 'exploitation') and foster the innovativeness (via 'exploration') to bring forth the products and services that will enhance future firm competitiveness.

name: Exploitation
definition: Organizational ambidexterity focuses on the ability of the organization to both efficiently exploit its existing competencies (via 'exploitation') and foster the innovativeness (via 'exploration') to bring forth the products and services that will enhance future firm competitiveness.

name: Business similarity
authors_terms: ["business similarity", "similarity between the businesses of the firm and the target", "firm-target similarity"]
definition: Business similarity between the firm and the partner's acquisition target means that the firm and the target are likely to possess similar resources and compete in the same product markets. Business similarity and complementarity are assumed to be associated with resource similarity and complementarity.

name: Business complementarity
authors_terms: ["business complementarity", "complementarity between the businesses of the firm and its partner's target", "firm-target complementarity"]
definition: Complementarity is a condition whereby combining one resource with another increases the marginal returns from that resource. Business complementarity implies differences between firms' resources as well as interdependencies between them in a way that is mutually beneficial.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: Relational embeddedness refers to a cohesive relationship built on social attachment and interpersonal ties. It evolves with frequent and repeated interactions with a partner and supports coordination and learning of specialized knowledge.

name: Change in alliance value
authors_terms: ["change in alliance value", "expected value of the alliance to the firm", "value of the alliance to the firm", "firm CAR"]
definition: The value that the firm can create and capture from its alliance with the partner following the partner's acquisition of the target. The dependent variable is measured by the firm's cumulative abnormal return (CAR) around the announcement of the partner's acquisition, which reflects investors' expectations about the added value that the alliance will potentially create for the firm following the acquisition.

name: Contingency planning
definition: Contingency planning clauses can thus be defined as the parts of a contract that are designed to support within-agreement adjustments by proscribing the ways in which the contractual partners will deal with problematic contingencies that might arise during the execution of the contract.

name: Task description
definition: A second way in which parties may choose to write more complete contracts is by including more detailed specification of the task to be completed. Task description terms are often important because agreeing on a description of the task to be completed is necessary for the parties to come to a meeting of the minds, which is in turn a requirement for a contract to be legally valid.

name: Relationship history
definition: Relationship history measures the amount of time in weeks that Compustar had worked with a particular business unit of a partner company prior to signing the contract in question. This variable is aimed at capturing effects of partner-specific learning (or trust) over time.

name: Turnaround situation
authors_terms: ["companies in turnaround situations", "new CEOs hired in turnaround situations", "firms in turnaround situations"]
definition: Companies in turnaround situations are those that had operating returns on equity before extraordinary items greater than their cost of equity for at least two consecutive years, immediately followed by a year of operating loss (again, before extraordinary items); these companies had abruptly swung from satisfactory performance to very poor performance.

name: Initial total pay
authors_terms: ["new CEO's initial total pay", "initial total pay", "total pay"]
definition: The new CEO's initial total pay is defined as the first year's total remuneration, including all forms of compensation received in the succession year, which is defined as Year 0; initial total pay includes fixed salary, performance bonus, life insurance, options, and restricted stocks.

name: Proportion of performance-based pay
authors_terms: ["performance-based pay", "proportion of performance-based pay", "initial performance-based pay"]
definition: The performance-based pay is the value of options, restricted stocks, and bonuses; the proportion of performance-based pay is the ratio of its value to the total pay.

name: CEO origin
definition: Depending on whether a CEO is appointed from within or from outside the firm, prior studies distinguish between 'insiders' and 'outsiders' in terms of origin; compared to inside successors, outsiders have much more to learn to become familiar with the new company, thus increasing the quantitative workload.

name: Pay premium
authors_terms: ["pay premium", "PP-residuals of total pay", "PP-residuals of performance-based pay"]
definition: Pay premium is the amount paid over and above what a CEO would expect in normal market conditions (i.e., taking into account firm, industry, and individual characteristics); it is measured as the difference between the new CEO's actual pay and the estimated pay.

name: Retrenchment and restructuring turnaround initiatives
authors_terms: ["retrenchment and restructuring turnaround initiatives", "turnaround initiatives", "retrenchment and restructuring"]
definition: Retrenchment and restructuring strategies include downsizing (i.e., disposal of fixed assets or reducing head count), cost cutting (e.g., cutbacks in administrative, R&D, and other discretionary expenses), and product/market refocusing (e.g., reducing the scope of business lines and geographical markets, and shifting the emphasis to more defensible and lucrative segments).

name: CEO credentials
definition: CEO credentials influence the pay level an executive will receive and include CEO prestige and industry experience. A new CEO was regarded as possessing prestigious working credentials if he or she had been employed by a prominent firm at the level of vice president or higher, or had sat or was currently sitting on the most prominent firm's board, and as possessing prestigious educational credentials if he or she had received a degree from an elite institution; industry experience was measured by the sum of company tenure and industry tenure beyond the focal firm.

name: Intended termination
definition: The intended termination perspective suggests that IJVs are formed for specific purposes, and that IJV termination occurs when the initial purposes of formation have either been achieved or have disappeared; intended termination includes IJVs that were terminated because the initial purposes were fulfilled.

name: Unintended termination
definition: The unintended termination perspective suggests that IJV termination occurs due to unanticipated contingencies that emerge after the formation of the IJV; unintended termination includes IJVs that were terminated because of unanticipated contingencies.

name: Longevity
definition: We use longevity in the analyses as a proxy for the likelihood of survival, and measure the longevity of an IJV by the year count between the year of establishment and the year of termination.

name: Strategic asset seeking
authors_terms: ["strategic asset seeking", "access to know-how and technology"]
definition: One of four broad purposes of IJV formation, namely access to know-how and technology (strategic asset seeking) in the host country. Strategic assets are firm specific in nature, and are possessed only by particular firms in a host country.

name: Changes in parent firm conditions
authors_terms: ["changes in the parent firm conditions", "changes in the parent firm"]
definition: One of the three types of unanticipated contingencies: changes in the conditions of the parent firms, which are internal matters that are the responsibility of the parent firms and are more controllable than changes in external conditions.

name: Changes in external conditions
authors_terms: ["changes in external conditions", "changes in the external conditions"]
definition: One of the three types of unanticipated contingencies: changes in external conditions, which are beyond the reach of the influence of the parent firms and are less controllable.

name: Changes in the inter-partner relationship
authors_terms: ["changes in the inter-partner relationship", "changes in the relationship between partners"]
definition: One of the three types of unanticipated contingencies: changes in the inter-partner relationship, which are a result of changes in the interests and goals of the IJV partners and are more difficult to handle than changes in the parent firm conditions.

name: Foreign subsidiary ownership mode
authors_terms: ["IJV", "WOS", "wholly owned subsidiary", "ownership structure of foreign subsidiaries"]
definition: We define an IJV as a Japanese foreign affiliate that shares 20 percent or more and less than 95 percent of its equity ownership with a foreign firm or firms, and a WOS as an affiliate that shares 95 percent or more of its equity ownership with a foreign firm or firms.

name: Cultural distance between partners
definition: The cultural distance between IJV partners can be a source of misunderstanding and miscommunication, and can have a negative impact on an IJV's likelihood of survival; it represents the institutional conditions that are present at the birth of the IJV.

name: Ownership structure of the parent firms
authors_terms: ["ownership structure of the parent firms", "percentage of equity of an IJV owned by the largest Japanese parent firm"]
definition: The ownership structure of the parent firms determines the division of control between the partners; IJVs are suggested to be more likely to survive when one partner holds either a majority or minority share than when both partners hold an equal share.

name: IJV size
definition: Organizational ecology suggests that size and age are major determinants of the disbanding of organizations, in that smaller organizations face greater liabilities as a result of their size; only organizational size is present at the formation of an IJV.

name: International experience of the parent firms
authors_terms: ["international experience", "international experience of the parent firms"]
definition: Firms with less foreign experience are more likely to face the liability of foreignness in their overseas operations, and hence face a higher risk of termination.

name: Founder status
definition: Founders can be viewed as stewards who, because they identify closely with and gain nonmaterial rewards from their ventures, are likely to accept less cash compensation than nonfounders, who are more properly viewed as the agents of agency theory.

name: Cash compensation
definition: The main dependent variable was each executive's cash compensation, which comprises both salary and bonus.

name: Executive equity holdings
authors_terms: ["executive equity holdings", "equity holdings", "percentage of equity held by the executive"]
definition: Executives' 'psychological ownership' of an organization, whether founded by them or not, can be strongly influenced by their equity ownership. The more equity they own, the more executives' identities are tied to their organizations and the more stewardlike their behavior.

name: Firm size
definition: As a new organization grows and the division of labor deepens, its structure becomes more formalized and professionalized. Roles become more defined, coordination becomes more formal, and controls are instituted to facilitate organizational activities.

name: Rounds of financing
authors_terms: ["rounds of financing", "rounds of outside financing", "rounds raised"]
definition: Capital constraints drive new ventures to outside investors who reduce their own investing uncertainty by staging their capital investments across multiple rounds of investment months or years apart. Each round of investment can bring new contractual requirements that decrease performance ambiguity.

name: Platform quality
definition: The overall quality of a platform on the consumer side, assumed constant over the platform's life cycle, which captures technical capability as well as other factors affecting consumers' perception of quality such as brand image and distribution channel management. The authors use the ratio Q = QE/QI, which measures the entrant's quality advantage over the incumbent.

name: Strength of indirect network effects
authors_terms: ["strength of indirect network effects", "indirect network effects", "e"]
definition: Indirect network effects arise because consumer demand for a platform depends on application availability while the supply of applications depends on the platform's installed base of consumers. The parameter e measures the extent to which consumers care about application variety.

name: Consumers' discount factor
authors_terms: ["discount factor", "consumers' discount factor of future applications", "φ"]
definition: The discount factor of consumers' future utility from applications. When φ = 0 consumers place no value on future applications and are essentially myopic; as φ approaches 1, consumers are patient and value future applications as much as those currently available.

name: Installed base of consumers
definition: The installed base of consumers associated with a platform at the beginning of a period. The authors use the term 'installed-base advantage' to refer to advantages in both the installed base of consumers and the application supply.

name: Application variety
authors_terms: ["application variety", "game variety", "number of applications", "discounted total number of applications", "Njt"]
definition: The applications associated with a platform, comprising applications available today and those to be released in the future, with future applications discounted by the consumers' discount factor. Njt is the discounted total number of applications associated with platform j in period t.

name: Developer entry
authors_terms: ["number of new developers", "number of new games released", "new applications", "Δnjt"]
definition: The number of new application developers supporting a platform in a period; each developer supplies one application. Developers choose platforms to maximize their profits from the sale of applications, and entry follows a free-entry condition.

name: Developer fixed costs
authors_terms: ["fixed cost of supporting platform j", "Fjt", "ratio of the two fixed costs", "F"]
definition: The fixed cost a developer incurs in supporting a platform in a period. The authors assume the fixed cost drops at the same rate for both platforms and let F = FIt/FEt be the ratio of the two fixed costs, which measures the cost advantage of the entrant over the incumbent on the developer side.

name: Entrant market share
authors_terms: ["market share", "market share on the consumer side", "percentage of new consumers choosing platform j", "sjt"]
definition: The percentage of new consumers who choose a platform in a period. The authors use market share as their measure for platform success and focus on the entrant's market share relative to the incumbent's.

name: Degree of diversification
definition: The extent to which the established firm is diversified across industries. Drawing on Hofer and Chrisman's theoretical work, the authors suggest that firms that are more diversified may do better in the dynamic environment of young industries.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size and financial strength are indicative of the level of financial resources possessed by the parent, which affects the resources available to a new business.

name: Financial strength
definition: Together with firm size, financial strength indicates the level of financial resources possessed by the parent firm, which affects the resources available to the new business.

name: Strategic importance
definition: The 'strategic importance' of a business to its parent, which is an important factor in the resource allocation decisions of top management; a business of high strategic importance may receive a disproportionate share of the firm's resources.

name: Earliness of entry
authors_terms: ["time of entry", "early entry", "order of entry", "enter earlier"]
definition: How early the established firm enters a new industry; early entry may lead to rapid movement down the experience curve and subsequent cost advantages and may make it easier to establish channels of distribution and gain consumer acceptance.

name: Vulnerability
definition: Vulnerability refers to the extent to which a firm's existing business is threatened by the emergence of a young industry.

name: Product-market maturity
authors_terms: ["product-market maturity", "maturity of the firm's markets", "more mature markets", "less mature markets"]
definition: The maturity of the product-markets that a firm serves. While the product life cycle has traditionally been considered a business level concept, its extension to the corporate level suggests that firms whose markets are less mature may possess skills and organizational characteristics which differ from those of firms whose markets are more mature.

name: Parent-business relatedness
definition: The relatedness between the performance of an individual business and its relatedness to the parent, considered in terms of patterns of linkage among all a firm's businesses.

name: R&D emphasis
authors_terms: ["corporatewide emphasis on research and development", "R&D emphasis", "corporate-wide orientation toward R&D"]
definition: A corporate-wide emphasis on research and development; firms with such an emphasis may be better equipped to undertake the tasks associated with innovation, both to introduce technical advances to the market and to retaliate against the innovations of competitors.

name: Business unit autonomy
definition: The amount of influence a business has over decisions that are important to its success.

name: Functional authority
definition: The degree to which a business has complete authority over key functional areas, versus sharing authority with other units.

name: Performance in the young industry
authors_terms: ["performance", "higher levels of performance", "lower levels of performance"]
definition: The authors focus on performance in the given young industry, not on total corporate performance.

name: Degree of internationalization
definition: The firm's degree of internationalization was measured using a variation of Sullivan's (1994) composite measure, combining four dimensions of internationalization.

name: CEO compensation
definition: The total of all forms of compensation (including salary, perquisites, bonus, provident fund, and commission) granted to the CEO during the year, used as the logarithm of that total.

name: Board structure
definition: Board structure was the proportion of outside directors, where outsiders were board members who were not otherwise employed by the firm.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality, implying that the positions of CEO and the board chair are vested in the same person, is an indication of high CEO power.

name: Family control with family management
authors_terms: ["family controlled and family managed (FCFM) firms", "FCFM firms", "FCFM dummy"]
definition: Firms in which the family has both ownership control as well as management control; a firm is family controlled if any two of three ownership/board criteria are met and family managed if any two of three management criteria are met.

name: Family control with nonfamily management
authors_terms: ["family controlled and nonfamily managed (FCNFM) firms", "FCNFM firms", "FCNFM dummy"]
definition: Firms in which the family has ownership control but the CEO is an unaffiliated, nonfamily appointee, so family owners do not invest a similar degree of effort and time in managing the firms.

name: Innovations by other organizations
definition: Activities are deemed innovative if they differ significantly from current or recent activities. In this setting innovations are adoptions of new radio formats by other stations.

name: Rate of organizational change
definition: The rate at which organizations in a population change their activities; the most inclusive event consists of all changes in format or production, effectively counting all entries in the M Street Journal.

name: Mimetic change
definition: Entry into one of the innovative formats, Soft Adult Contemporary, New Age, Urban Contemporary, and Soft Urban Contemporary; this event represents mimetic behavior.

name: Nonmimetic change
definition: Format change consists of all format changes except entry into innovative or satellite formats, and is thus a nonmimetic change of format. Innovative change represents imitation and the other changes (format, satellite entry, and production changes) represent non-imitative change.

name: Size of the innovating organization
authors_terms: ["size of corporation", "corporate size", "size of the innovating organization"]
definition: Innovations by large organizations are likely to be viewed as threats and to elicit a commitment response. The corporate size of the innovator is measured as the number of stations the corporation owns.

name: Market share of the innovating organization
authors_terms: ["market share of the local innovating organization", "market share"]
definition: if the innovator obtains a large market share, the innovation is more threatening and thus more likely to lead to a commitment response.

name: Relational embeddedness
authors_terms: ["relational embeddedness", "supplier's relational embeddedness with its existing buyers", "relational ties"]
definition: The extent to which the supplier participates in longer-term committed exchange relationships with its portfolio of buyers. Relational embeddedness refers to the quality of interfirm ties, as contrasted with structural embeddedness, which refers to the configuration of those ties.

name: Business growth
definition: The ability of supplier firms to increase the volume of outsourced business they capture from buyers, which the authors label business growth; in the empirical setting it is defined as the annual change in the volume of patent legal work undertaken by a focal patent law firm.

name: Cross-servicing ability
definition: The extent to which suppliers simultaneously offer and fulfill a broad range of their buyers' needs across multiple domains.

name: Buyers' relational commitment
definition: Buyers' broad commitments to work with the same supplier(s) in the future; buyers may signal their relational commitment to a supplier by giving the supplier a higher share of their outsourced work.

name: Inhouse concurrent sourcing
definition: The extent of insourcing by a supplier's existing buyers, i.e. the weighted average share of patents prosecuted internally (instead of being outsourced) by the focal supplier's portfolio of buyers.

name: Buyer-specific knowledge
definition: A supplier's detailed knowledge of a buyer's business, such as its idiosyncratic technologies, operational interdependencies, and strategic priorities; it is idiosyncratic in nature and its relevance is limited for serving other buyers beyond the focal dyad.

name: Number of small failures
authors_terms: ["small failure experience", "number of failures", "quantity of a firm's small failures", "failures (total)", "total number of expired patents"]
definition: Small failures in experimentation are observed as a firm's voluntary discontinuation of patents before the end of their legal life; the quantity of these failures is the number of patents discontinued due to non-payment of maintenance fees by the firm each year.

name: Importance of small failures
authors_terms: ["importance of failures", "small failures of higher importance", "importance of a discontinued patent"]
definition: The authors define the importance of a small failure in terms of the project's expected performance before it eventually failed, that is, decision makers in the firm had more expectations from a more important project before failure. In pharmaceutical R&D a project's importance is highly related with its scientific value, or its impact on subsequent research.

name: Earliness of small failures
authors_terms: ["timing of failures", "early failures", "small failures earlier in the R&D process", "failures after 4 years", "failures after 8 years", "failures after 12 years"]
definition: In the context of innovation, the timing of a failure refers to the point in the R&D process at which a firm faces and acknowledges the failure; a patent discontinued at 4 years is expected to have elicited feedback earlier than a patent discontinued at 12 years.

name: R&D output
authors_terms: ["R&D output", "R&D output amount", "patent count", "number of patents filed"]
definition: R&D output has been used as a measure of innovation performance and represents a higher rate of innovation output; it is measured as the number of successful patent applications by a firm in a given year.

name: R&D output quality
authors_terms: ["R&D output quality", "quality of R&D output", "quality of innovations", "forward citations to patents"]
definition: Unlike output in manufacturing, in which units without defect are identical, R&D output varies greatly in terms of quality; the quality of R&D output is the total number of citations to all successful patents.

name: Family presence in the inner circle
authors_terms: ["family presence in the inner circle", "family presence in the top leadership", "percentage of family ties", "family leadership"]
definition: The inner circle is the set of leaders possessing the greatest decision-making power in the business group, and the majority of inner-circle members are family members of the key leader. Family presence is captured by the percentage of family ties, counting only the dyadic ties between the key leader and other top executives and including members from both immediate and extended family.

name: Key leader generation
definition: The key leader is the founder of the group or the son of the founder; second-generation key leaders are successors of the founding generation, and most groups are still in the hands of either the founders or the second-generation successors.

name: U.S. management education
authors_terms: ["management education from the United States", "U.S. management education", "U.S.-educated key leaders", "business education from U.S."]
definition: Key leaders of business groups can be freed from the dominant cognitive model of family leadership by acquiring a management education in the United States, through which they can transport business models learned in the United States across contexts to Taiwan. In most cases such education was at the graduate level (e.g., MBA).

name: Market transition
definition: The market-oriented transition in emerging economies, in which privatization and deregulation intensify competitive pressures while Western ideologies and business models flow in through global investors, consultants, and international organizations. In Taiwan 1987 marked the beginning of large-scale economic liberalization and political democratization.

name: Industry diversification
authors_terms: ["industry diversification", "group diversification", "highly diversified business groups", "high diversification"]
definition: Industry diversification is a widely adopted response by business groups to cope with market competition, involving operation in a diverse range of competitive industries. When business groups are involved in a diverse range of competitive industries, family leaders can appear to be less suitable due to the relative homogeneity in their experience, information, and background.

name: Presence of a board finance committee
definition: A finance committee is a voluntary committee charged with approving and reviewing a broad range of finance-related policies and strategies for which the CFO is typically responsible.

name: CEO financial background
authors_terms: ["a CEO with a financial background", "CEOBkg", "CEO with financial expertise"]
definition: We code the CEO as having a financial background if we find evidence of any of the following: a) Certified Public Accountant designation, b) experience working for a financial services firm, c) experience serving as a CFO, controller, treasurer, or vice president of finance, d) a degree in finance or accounting (including a finance MBA), or e) other financial experience.

name: Extent of CFO incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["CFO incentives", "the extent of CFO incentives", "CFO contractual incentives", "CFO incentive compensation"]
definition: The extent to which the firm relies on contractual incentives, rather than monitoring, to address the agency problem for the CFO position. It is measured alternatively as the ex ante incentives of the CFO's equity portfolio, the incentives from annual equity grants, the value of equity compensation as a proportion of total compensation, and the ex post pay-for-performance sensitivity.

name: Acquired unit performance
authors_terms: ["acquired unit performance", "unit performance", "unit's performance", "negative unit performance", "unit's loss", "unit losses"]
definition: The performance of a formerly acquired unit, measured so as to incorporate the effects of a reference point: the percentage of ROA of an acquired unit minus the mean ROA of the unit's industry.

name: Divestiture of formerly acquired units
authors_terms: ["divestiture", "probability of divestiture", "divestiture likelihood", "organizational choice (i.e., divestiture)", "decision to divest"]
definition: An acquirer's choosing to divest a formerly acquired unit because of its poor performance, a major strategic choice made in the domain of losses, as opposed to maintaining a loss-generating acquired firm in the hope of future recovery.

name: Ambiguity
authors_terms: ["ambiguity", "ambiguity in a focal unit's industry", "high ambiguity"]
definition: Equivocalness and confusion resulting from multiple possibilities; the breakeven reference point as well as the threat point are determined subjectively and are influenced by contextual factors such as ambiguity and vagueness.

name: Failure to improve unit performance
authors_terms: ["failure to improve unit performance", "failure to improve the performance", "failure"]
definition: The situation in which an acquired unit performs poorly and the performance is not improved and continues to decline, so that simple alternatives fail and more drastic alternatives must be sought.

name: Resource availability
authors_terms: ["resource availability", "uncommitted resource availability", "potentially available level of resources", "slack", "slack resources"]
definition: The resources available in the parent firm of a focal acquired unit, examined as uncommitted resource availability (the quick ratio) and as potentially available resources, or borrowing capacity (the debt-to-equity ratio).

name: Divestiture experience
definition: The degree of a firm's former experience with divestitures, measured as the number of divestitures in the three years before a focal year, counted and accumulated as a running average for each year.

name: Relative unit size
authors_terms: ["relative size", "unit relative size", "unit's size relative to its acquirer's size"]
definition: The size of an acquired unit relative to the acquiring firm, measured as the ratio between the unit's annual sales and its parent firm's sales.

name: Strategic repertoire variety
definition: Strategic repertoire is the aggregate number of a firm's competitive actions at a given point in time; a firm with a larger number of different competitive actions displays higher strategic variety, and vice versa. The index counts the number of the 34 competitive actions that a venture rates as a key part of its strategy, so a higher score indicates higher strategic variety.

name: New venture growth
definition: Growth of new ventures, which the authors measure as sales growth figures averaged over the two-year (2006 and 2007) period following the survey data collection, thus avoiding the reverse causality problem.

name: Venture origin
definition: The origin of a new venture, that is, whether it was created by independent entrepreneurs or by established corporations. Independent and corporate ventures often have different knowledge bases, resources, and capabilities and differ in their goals.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Dynamism refers to the magnitude of change in a firm's industry and market conditions; the authors' broader definition captures market and industry changes that are hard to predict and difficult to plan for and, as a result, increase managers' uncertainty.

name: Subnational region
authors_terms: ["subnational region", "region", "states in the United States", "provinces and cities in China"]
definition: We regard these regions as territorial entities (i.e., states or provinces) whose political boundaries coincide with their institutional boundaries. Foreign affiliate performance is also influenced by subnational institutions (the economic, political, and social institutions in different regions within the host country).

name: Foreign affiliate performance
authors_terms: ["foreign affiliate performance", "return on sales (ROS)", "ROS deviation", "performance of foreign affiliates"]
definition: Analysis of the average ROS across subnational regions shows the extent to which the average foreign affiliate performance in one such region varies from that in others, whereas analysis of ROS deviation examines the extent to which the variation in foreign affiliate performance differs across these regions.

name: Host country economy type
definition: Whether the host country is an emerging economy or an advanced economy; the statement compares China (emerging) and the United States (advanced).

name: Game-theoretic alliance structure
definition: In this paper structure refers to three specific attributes of the alliance: pattern of payoffs, shadow of the future, and the number of players. These dimensions serve both as proximate explanations of cooperation and as targets of higher-order strategies to promote cooperation.

name: Shadow of the future
authors_terms: ["shadow of the future", "length of time horizon (HORIZON)", "frequency of interaction (FROINT)", "behavior transparency (TRANS)"]
definition: The prospect of continuing interaction, signaled by expectations of a durable and strategically desirable relationship, affects the likelihood of cooperation by encouraging strategies of reciprocity. The specific factors that make the shadow of the future an effective promoter of cooperation are behavior transparency (TRANS), frequency of interaction (FROINT), and long time horizons (HORIZON).

name: Joint product lost to unilateral defection
definition: One of three residuals reflecting the pattern of payoffs, (UD-MC) captures the joint product lost to unilateral defection.

name: Loss from alliance breakup
definition: One of three residuals reflecting the pattern of payoffs, (MC-MD) captures the loss to complete breakup of the SA.

name: Cost of unrequited cooperation
definition: One of three residuals reflecting the pattern of payoffs, (UD-UC) captures the cost of unrequited cooperation.

name: Alliance performance
definition: Performance is conceptualized to be a composite variable consisting of three components: (a) (importance X fulfillment of strategic needs), or PERF1; (b) net spillover effects, or SPILLNET; and (c) overall performance assessment, or OVRALPER.

name: Partner nationality
authors_terms: ["partner nationality", "nationality of the partner firm", "intercountry differences"]
definition: The present study stratified the total sample into subgroups by partner nationality and retested the structure-performance relationship, since international SA partners may be characterized by major differences along multiple levels of analysis and culturally-, nationally-, and organizationally-inculcated norms.

name: Likelihood of cooperation
definition: The likelihood or tendency that alliance partners will cooperate rather than defect, as referenced in the authors' statement about gains from unilateral defection relative to unilateral cooperation.

name: Breadth of innovation objectives
authors_terms: ["breadth of innovation objectives", "breadth of objectives", "innovation objectives", "objectives"]
definition: Within their general innovation activities, firms are likely to have specific product and process objectives, such as the development of a completely new product, the improvement of an existing product, reduction of labor costs, or improved manufacturing flexibility; these are the 'technical goals' that are the focus of the study. The key explanatory variable represents breadth of innovation objectives that firms pursued in their innovation activities.

name: Breadth of knowledge sources
authors_terms: ["breadth of knowledge sources", "breadth of sources", "knowledge sources", "sources of information"]
definition: In their innovation activities, firms may seek information from a variety of sources, including the firm's own industrial R&D, other firms in the same industry, customers, suppliers, university research, government research laboratories and agencies, and professional and technical societies; the analysis focuses on types of knowledge sources connected to different parts of the value chain or activity system. The key explanatory variable represents breadth of knowledge sources that firms utilized in their innovation activities.

name: Innovation success
definition: The R&D survey provides information on innovation success, including whether or not the firm introduced technological innovations and the percent of firm sales derived from the introduction of technologically new products. By using both the binary innovation and product sales variables, the authors obtain a fuller picture of innovation success.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty in a business unit's environment", "uncertainty in the business unit's environment", "uncertainty"]
definition: Uncertainty in the environment within which a business unit operates; the authors argue that greater stock price volatility indicates the presence of widespread uncertainty about the future, and measure it from the time-varying conditional variance of industry portfolio returns.

name: Divestment mode
authors_terms: ["divestment mode choices", "divestment alternatives", "modes of divestment", "divestment mode choice"]
definition: The mode through which a business unit is divested; the authors investigate the relationship between uncertainty in a business unit's environment and divestment mode choices (i.e., non-divestment, staged divestment, and complete divestment), where spin-offs and equity carve-outs are staged divestments and sell-offs are complete divestments.

name: Dominant initial strategy
authors_terms: ["dominant initial strategy", "dominant strategy at founding", "single or dominant strategy"]
definition: The adoption at founding of a single or dominant strategy, an aspect of the initial strategy that may restrict the range of future strategies the organization might consider. The extent to which the initial strategy is dominant is one factor that can influence the imprinting of an organization's strategy.

name: Distribution of functional influence
authors_terms: ["distribution of functional influence", "distribution of influence", "functional influence"]
definition: The distribution of power and influence among functions within an organization at founding, which can act as a source of potential support for its initial strategy. Over time a strategy can become further reinforced and institutionalized through the influence of powerful functional groups that are themselves supported by that strategy.

name: Management ownership
definition: The extent to which an organization's managers control ownership at founding; if managers control ownership at founding, the extent of subsequent deviation from an initial strategy may be less than if owners are not managers. Owner-managers are likely to be closely involved in formulating the founding strategy, which may make them unwilling to attempt significant changes in it.

name: Organizational performance since founding
definition: A firm's level of performance since founding. Firms will retain their founding strategies to a greater extent when their performance since founding has been satisfactory, leading to few internal and external pressures for change.

name: Organizational age
definition: The age of a firm, which offers some indication of the amount of environmental variation it may have experienced since founding. Older organizations will have had more time and thus will have faced more pressure to deviate from a strategy adopted early.

name: Founding entrepreneur's tenure
definition: The length of time that the founding entrepreneur remains with a firm after its founding; entrepreneurs who stay with a firm after founding for a lengthy period are able to institutionalize initial strategic and structural decisions.

name: Strategic change from founding
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in strategy", "degree of change in strategy", "difference scores"]
definition: The extent to which an organization's strategy has changed from the strategy adopted at founding. Because strategy is relatively inertial, the strategy an organization first adopts will circumscribe later strategic change.

name: Negative affect
definition: One of the two dominant dimensions of affect structure identified from the seven basic emotions; anger, fear, sadness, and surprise have strong primary loadings on this first component.

name: Positive affect
definition: One of the two dominant dimensions of affect structure identified from the seven basic emotions; happiness loads strongly on this second component.

name: Underpricing conformity
definition: Underpricing conformity is defined as the deviations in absolute value from the market's average underpricing level. This figure is multiplied by negative one to be consistent with the definition of conformity in Delgado-Garcia and de la Fuente-Sabaté (2010).

name: Underpricing level
definition: Underpricing level is defined as the difference between the closing and opening price divided by the opening price on the first day of trading.

name: Asymmetric information
definition: The word count for each ICO whitepaper is used as a proxy for the level of asymmetric information; the rationale is that longer whitepapers contain more information.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact counts the number of markets in which a firm meets its competitor outside the focal market.

name: Service quality
definition: On-time performance as a product quality variable is measured as the average number of minutes delay relative to the scheduled arrival time. For transfer passengers, service quality depends on the quality of each segment and the quality of the connection between them.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["size of the firm", "size of airlines", "number of routes they operate", "number of markets in which the airline is active"]
definition: The impact of multimarket contact on product quality is firm related and depends on firm size or its dominance in the market. The authors measure the size of airlines in terms of the number of routes they operate.

name: Interlining between airlines
authors_terms: ["interlining", "share of interlining transfer passengers", "passengers with inter-airline transfer"]
definition: The share of passengers that make a transfer between airlines, which the authors use as a proxy for cooperation between airlines in improving the compatibility between flights.

name: Acquirer asset divestiture
authors_terms: ["asset divestiture", "divestiture of the acquirer's assets", "acquirer asset divestiture", "divestiture of the acquirer's assets (H1a)"]
definition: Asset divestiture is the extent to which merging firms dispose of their physical assets and cut back their personnel in different areas; here it refers to the extent to which the acquiring firm divests its own assets.

name: Target asset divestiture
authors_terms: ["asset divestiture", "divestiture of the target's assets", "target asset divestiture", "divestiture of the target's assets (H1b)"]
definition: Asset divestiture is the extent to which merging firms dispose of their physical assets and cut back their personnel in different areas; here it refers to the extent to which the acquired (target) firm's assets are divested.

name: Cost savings
definition: Cost-based synergies arise when the divestiture of the assets of the merging firms leads to cost savings. Cost reduction is operationalized as the acquisition's positive impact on product costs and input prices.

name: Market coverage
definition: Horizontal acquisitions can increase market coverage through the geographic extension of the market and through product line extension; greater market coverage allows the merged firm to sell existing products to a wider body of consumers, thus enhancing revenues.

name: Innovation capability
authors_terms: ["innovation capability", "improvement of product innovation capabilities", "innovation capability enhancement"]
definition: Horizontal acquisitions can enhance innovation capability by using the superior innovation capability (proprietary technology, patents, know-how) of one of the merged firms to enhance product features (product innovation capability) or to improve organizational and marketing effectiveness (e.g., time to market, customer satisfaction).

name: Long-term acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "long-term performance of the merging firms", "long-term acquisition performance"]
definition: The long-term performance of an acquisition is measured by self-reported measures of changes in market shares, sales, intrinsic profitability, and relative profitability compared to industry average since the acquisition.

name: Resource redeployment to the target
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment", "redeployment of the acquirer's resources to the target", "resource redeployment to target", "resource redeployment to targets"]
definition: Resource redeployment is the extent to which a target or acquiring firm uses the other firm's resources (R&D capabilities, manufacturing know-how, marketing resources, supplier relationships, and distribution expertise), which may involve physical transfer of resources to new locations or sharing resources without physical transfer; here the resources flow from the acquirer to the target.

name: Resource redeployment to the acquirer
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment", "redeployment of the target's resources to the acquirer", "resource redeployment to acquirer", "resource redeployment to acquirers"]
definition: Resource redeployment is the extent to which a target or acquiring firm uses the other firm's resources (R&D capabilities, manufacturing know-how, marketing resources, supplier relationships, and distribution expertise), which may involve physical transfer of resources to new locations or sharing resources without physical transfer; here the resources flow from the target to the acquirer.

name: Price format flexibility
authors_terms: ["price format", "flexibility in price determination mechanism", "price determination mechanism", "flexibility or incompleteness of price provisions"]
definition: Price provisions are organized along a continuum of flexibility or incompleteness, defined as the degree to which prices are known with certainty at the onset of the contract execution stage. The focus is on the contractual process agreed upon ex ante to determine the final price, rather than on the level of price chosen in a particular BCC.

name: Interface complexity
definition: We define this as the extent to which the technical interdependency between the focal component and the end product is intricate and complicated.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty is defined as the inability to accurately predict the technological evolution and development of the focal component.

name: Preexisting differentiation capability of the vendor brand
authors_terms: ["preexisting differentiation capability of the vendor brand", "preexisting differentiation", "preexisting capability of the vendor brand"]
definition: We define the preexisting differentiation capability of the vendor as the level of 'value-add' by the vendor at the contract initiation or writing stage. This differentiation gain is a result of the unique, nonimitable, and preexisting resources/capabilities of the vendor (e.g., superior product design and development skills) that enable it to create valuable products/services independent of the relationship with the focal OEM.

name: OEM brand strength in customer markets
authors_terms: ["preexisting brand strength of the OEM in its customer markets", "brand strength of the OEM", "OEM's brand strength"]
definition: A parallel safeguarding argument can be made for the preexisting brand strength of the OEM in its end-customer market, i.e., the value generated by these firm-specific assets/resources that is at stake in relational exchanges. OEM's brand strength is a four-item, semantic differential scale that captures the OEM's strength in its own customer market for its most important product line in which the branded component is incorporated.

name: Realized differentiation
definition: Realized differentiation is a four-item scale that captures the extent to which this branded component improves the customer's perceptions of the OEM's product. This measure captures both the preexisting differentiation of the vendor brand and the differentiation provided by the within-contract customization activities.

name: Divergent organizational change
definition: Divergent organizational change occurs, by definition, when an organization abandons an institutionalized template. In this study it is rural hospital conversion: a rural community hospital leaves the defining business of hospitals—acute inpatient care—and converts all of its capacity to become a provider of other kinds of health care.

name: Local market demand
authors_terms: ["demand", "level of demand in an organization's local market", "consumer demand"]
definition: Insufficient consumer demand for organizations' products and services is an important cause of divergent organizational change. Markets with low levels of local consumer demand are likely to promote divergent change because these markets cannot support all of the organizations that are operating with the same or similar resource needs.

name: Geographic proximity to competitors
authors_terms: ["geographic distance between competitors", "geographic proximity", "distance to nearest hospital"]
definition: Results from several empirical studies show that the addition of an organization to a population has stronger competitive effects on neighboring organizations than on those that are more distant. Organizations that have similar products and services and are located in close proximity in local markets will face relatively strong competition, because they are trying to attract the same limited pool of consumers.

name: Size relative to competitors
authors_terms: ["size relative to competitors", "relative bed size", "size disadvantages"]
definition: The size of organizations relative to competitors in their local market is likely to influence which of them will be unsuccessful and thus be forced to search for an alternative template; there is likely to be a competitive disadvantage for organizations that are relatively smaller than their local counterparts.

name: Service and product mix relative to competitors
authors_terms: ["service and product mix relative to competitors", "relative competitive advantage due to service mix", "disadvantages in services and products relative to local market competitors"]
definition: Organizations that produce goods and services that are more attractive than those produced by their otherwise similar competitors are likely to be winners in head-to-head competition for customers in local markets. Organizations with a relative edge in product and service offerings will be able to maintain their status quo, while losers must differentiate themselves and seek alternatives.

name: Conformity to regulatory requirements
definition: Such organizational fields have regulations that create and reinforce routines and structures that are intended to make organizations reliable and accountable for their performance. Organizations that fail to conform to such regulations risk losing their legitimacy and external support.

name: Pro-competition regulation
authors_terms: ["pro-competition regulation", "legislation that promotes and limits competition", "diversification law"]
definition: Government regulation and policy also affect divergent change by increasing or decreasing the level of competition that organizations face in local markets. Government policy promotes competition through antitrust laws that aim to prevent or break up monopolies among existing firms.

name: Anti-competitive regulation
definition: Policies can weaken competition by regulating several aspects of markets, including the production of goods and services, prices, and labor wages. The effect of such anticompetition policies is to reduce organizations' uncertainty about resources and provide them with a stable market environment, thus reinforcing the viability of current templates.

name: Legislation supporting current templates
authors_terms: ["legislation that provides resources to support current organizational templates", "capital funds for rural hospitals", "reduction in regulation to reduce operating expenses"]
definition: Policies inhibit divergent change to the extent that they increase resources that flow directly to organizations to support their current templates.

name: Legislation supporting alternative templates
authors_terms: ["legislation that provides resources to support organizations' use of alternative templates", "capital for rural hospital conversion"]
definition: Government policies can promote divergent change by providing resources and financial incentives intended to stimulate and support organizations' searches for and implementation of alternative templates.

name: For-profit ownership
authors_terms: ["hospital ownership", "public and private non-profit ownership", "for-profit organizations", "property rights norms"]
definition: Norms about property rights define who owns or has claims on firms' assets and profits. The more that property rights in an organizational field consist of public rather than private ownership of firm assets, the less likely it is that divergent organizational change will occur.

name: Centralized governance norms
authors_terms: ["governance norms", "membership in a multihospital system", "multihospital system member", "members of multidivisional firms"]
definition: Governance norms that specify central control of complex organizations will promote divergent change among the various units or divisions that belong to such organizations. This is because central control weakens the importance, meaning, and identity of subunits.

name: Nonlocal models of divergent change
authors_terms: ["cognitive models of divergent change", "nonlocal models of such change", "conversion available as a model", "conversion rate in state"]
definition: Cognitive elements promote divergent change by providing models of such change for organizational decision makers to imitate. Organizations will imitate other organizations that face a similar or equivalent pattern of market and institutional forces.

name: Generalized favorability
authors_terms: ["generalized favorability", "being liked", "well-liked", "the evaluative generalized-favorability dimension of reputation"]
definition: The generalized-favorability view of organizational reputation reflects the overall, evaluative assessment of an organization by multiple audiences; it is frequently characterized as 'a global impression of the organization' with judgment. Generalized favorability reflects multiple constituents' approach-avoidance judgment about a firm.

name: Being known
definition: The being-known dimension has been developed to capture stakeholders' 'awareness of the firm without judgment,' emphasizing the visibility of, and public attention to, information about the firm. Being known reflects the extent to which stakeholders possess information about a firm and their consequent nonevaluative recognition of the firm.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "firm's financial performance", "crisis-related abnormal returns", "shareholder value", "stock market reactions"]
definition: Corporate reputation is critical in shaping evaluators' initial perceptions and responses at the onset of a crisis, and ultimately, influences a firm's financial performance. To capture the potential impact of a crisis on firm value, the authors analyze a corporation's cumulative abnormal adjusted return (CAR) associated with a crisis over a 3-day (-1, 1) time window.

name: Attribution of crisis responsibility
authors_terms: ["attribution of crisis responsibility", "responsibility attribution", "attribution of crisis responsibility to the focal firm"]
definition: At the onset of a crisis, stakeholders rely on the characteristics of a crisis-including its perceived intentionality, controllability, and severity-to formulate initial attribution of responsibility when causes and effects of the crisis are unknown. Recent research has identified three crisis clusters, that is, victim, accidental, and intentional.

name: CEO/COO duo
authors_terms: ["CEO/COO duo", "presence of a COO", "presence of an executive in a COO position", "presence of a CEO/COO duo"]
definition: The study focuses on instances where a CEO formally delegates leadership functions to a COO, rather than on whether or not an executive with a COO title is present. A firm employs a CEO/COO duo when an executive other than the CEO holds the COO/president title and serves primarily as a COO rather than an heir apparent.

name: Firm performance
definition: The study uses two measures of firm performance: average return on assets (ROA) and average market-to-book ratio (MTB).

name: TMT functional heterogeneity
definition: Functional heterogeneity captures the extent to which there is a heterogeneous mix of functional experience within the TMT, and by extension whether team members use a limited or varied set of functionally based schema for decisions. It is the extent to which TMT members possess a variety of functional backgrounds.

name: TMT tenure heterogeneity
definition: Tenure heterogeneity captures whether TMT members possess schema that have been shaped by a set of common versus unique managerial experiences. It relates specifically to whether members of the TMT share common managerial experiences, in terms of both team tenure and organizational tenure.

name: TMT age
authors_terms: ["TMT age", "TMT average age", "average age of TMT members"]
definition: Theory suggests that TMTs with older members are less likely to engage in exhaustive information-processing, because older executives are more likely to develop rigid cognitive models that limit the flexibility of information search and interpretation. TMT average age was measured as the average age of TMT members.

name: Newborn gender
authors_terms: ["newborn gender", "gender of a newborn", "newborn son", "newborn daughter", "heirs' gender composition"]
definition: For each household, we constructed a variable to capture the occurrence of a new son/daughter within the time frame between two consecutive survey waves.

name: Technology adoption
authors_terms: ["technology adoption", "technology adoption decisions", "adoption of new technologies"]
definition: Among these adjustments, we qualified as technology adoption decisions those involving the introduction of new inputs, processes, or tools—such as those required when changing crop types, adopting new seed varieties, implementing soil and water conservation practices (e.g., contour plowing, mulching, and terracing), or constructing water-harvesting systems.

name: Within-organization distinctiveness of product design
definition: Within-organization distinctiveness of product design refers to the extent to which a focal product's design is distinct from the prototypical design of all products produced by the same organization. It captures the product-level distinctiveness of design in an intraorganizational context.

name: Between-organization distinctiveness of product design
definition: Between-organization distinctiveness of product design refers to the extent to which a focal organization's prototypical product design is distinct from the prototypical design of the industry. It reflects the organizational level distinctiveness of product design in an interorganizational context.

name: Market performance
definition: We focused on the market performance of the car models as the dependent variable. Specifically, we measured unit sales as the number of units (in thousands of units) of each car model sold in the U.S. market in each year of the sample period.

name: Evaluator group-venture similarity
definition: A dummy variable with 1 indicating that one or more evaluators in the focal evaluator's group were working at the two top universities and that one or more members of the focal venture founding team graduated from the two top universities.

name: Venture evaluation
definition: This is a continuous variable measured by the total score that a venture received from each evaluator as an overall assessment that varies from 0 to 100.

name: Challenging questions
definition: Conceptually, challenging questions refer to instances in which evaluators ask questions in an aggressive manner to expose problems and weaknesses.

name: Focal firm actions
authors_terms: ["firm actions", "focal firm actions", "firm total actions", "firm activity"]
definition: We define firm actions as 'externally directed, specific and observable competitive moves initiated by a firm to enhance its relative competitive position.' Five types of focal firm actions were measured: pricing, capacity, geographic, marketing, and product introductions.

name: Rival firm actions
authors_terms: ["rival actions", "rival firm actions", "rival total actions", "rival activity"]
definition: Rival actions are defined as the externally directed competitive moves of all rivals in the industry in which the focal firm's participation is being studied.

name: Rival action speed
definition: Rival firm action speed quantified the average length of time it took rivals to act after a focal firm acted.

name: Focal firm performance
definition: We focus on short-run performance, or the effects of focal firm action and rival action on focal firm performance in a given year. Focal firm performance was operationalized with accounting measures of return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA) in the same year as the action measure.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration, commonly measured by the percentage of the market share held by the largest firms in an industry (the Herfindahl index), is an important industry characteristic.

name: Industry demand
authors_terms: ["industry demand", "industry growth", "industry growth rate", "growth rate of industry demand"]
definition: The growth rate of industry demand should also have an impact on Red Queen competition. Industry demand was measured as industry growth, defined as the percent change in sales from the previous year to a focal year.

name: Market position
authors_terms: ["market position", "relative market position", "market share rank", "market leadership"]
definition: Relative market position was measured as rank order based on market share for each firm in each industry for each year. Research on the Red Queen effect has suggested that market leaders are less affected by Red Queen competition than are other firms.

name: Risk-adjusted financial performance
definition: 'our dependent variable is the risk-adjusted financial performance of a given SRI fund in a given month. Risk-adjusted performance (RAP) is defined as the average monthly return, measured as the percentage change in a fund's market value from the beginning to the end of a given month, adjusted by the fund's specific beta'. RAP 'captures the fund's return over and above what is expected based upon its beta'.

name: Screening intensity
authors_terms: ["screening intensity", "intensity of social screening", "number of social screens"]
definition: 'We refer to an SRI fund's choice of number of screens to apply to its investment portfolio as its screening intensity. Screening intensity varies from 1 to 12.'

name: Labor relations screening
definition: Screening on labor relations criteria: a fund selects firms for its portfolio according to their labor relations. The authors created a dichotomous workforce-related variable in order to test Hypothesis 2.

name: Equal employment screening
definition: One of the two workforce-related screening variables defined in order to test Hypothesis 2, coding whether a fund screens on equal employment criteria.

name: Community relations screening
definition: Screening on community relations criteria: a fund selects firms for its portfolio according to their record with the local community, the screen tested in Hypothesis 3.

name: Community investment screening
definition: One of the two community-related screening variables the authors use as a test of Hypothesis 3, coding whether a fund screens firms on what it deems as a poor community record.

name: Environmental screening
definition: Screening on environmental performance criteria: a fund selects firms for its portfolio based on their environmental performance, the screen tested in Hypothesis 4.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: The success of an IJV's local operations and expansion in these economies will largely depend upon its local partner's absorptive capability, or its ability to acquire, assimilate, integrate, and exploit knowledge and skills.

name: Market power
definition: A local partner's market power often represents its industrial and business background, market position, and established marketing and distribution networks.

name: Product relatedness
definition: The product diversification relationship between a local partner and the IJV in which it participates can influence the venture's economies of scale and scope, and efficiency of transaction costs.

name: Market experience
authors_terms: ["market experience", "industrial experience", "industry experience", "length of a local partner's market experience"]
definition: A local partner's established history and strong background in the market often result in a good reputation or high credibility in the industry.

name: Organizational form
authors_terms: ["organizational form", "organization form", "state-owned local partners", "privately or collectively-owned local partners"]
definition: A local partner's organizational form influences not only its motivation for forming an IJV, but also its commitment and contribution to the operation of the IJV.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size with respect to the number of employees makes an important contribution to economies of scale, market power, process innovation, and organizational image.

name: International experience
definition: A local firm's international experience, through import and export business or cooperative projects with other foreign investors, proves to be a very desirable attribute because this experience represents superior knowledge, skills, and values regarding modern management methods.

name: Organizational collaboration
definition: As the length of the interaction between partners increases, the economic transactions become increasingly embedded within the social relations of the two partners, which in turn deters opportunism.

name: Return on investment
definition: Based on the above criteria, four measures have been retained finally and will be used in this study. These are return on investment, local sales revenue/investment, export revenue/investment, and operational risk.

name: Local market expansion
definition: Based on the above criteria, four measures have been retained finally and will be used in this study. These are return on investment, local sales revenue/investment, export revenue/investment, and operational risk.

name: Export performance
definition: Based on the above criteria, four measures have been retained finally and will be used in this study. These are return on investment, local sales revenue/investment, export revenue/investment, and operational risk.

name: Operational risk
definition: This study measures the operational risk facing IJVs by computing the geometric average of the standard deviations of venture performance measures (see Appendix 1). In essence, this index is equivalent to the accountingbased risk calculation used in the strategic management literature.

name: Public sponsorship
authors_terms: ["public sponsorship", "organizational sponsorship", "cumulative amount of public sponsorship received", "sponsorship"]
definition: A common form of organizational sponsorship, defined as a provision of external resources to a focal organization by a public actor (e.g., state, political, or governmental agency), whereby such provision takes place outside market exchange mechanisms with an aim to selectively alter the focal organization's emergence, survival, or performance.

name: Market performance
definition: Market performance captures a firm's annual return on investment as a ratio of theatrical revenues (box office) over production costs.

name: Horizontal scope
definition: The breadth of the firm's resource accumulation and allocation patterns in the chosen market position: generalist firms operate in several product segments, relying on a broad resource base to appeal to a wide range of customer tastes, while specialists operate in a single product segment, with focused and more narrow resource accumulation patterns related to a more limited horizontal product strategy.

name: Market orientation
definition: The extent to which a firm engages in the generation, dissemination, and response to market intelligence, pertaining to current and future customer needs, competitor strategies and actions, channel requirements and abilities, and the broader business environment.

name: Resource profile
authors_terms: ["resource profile", "reliance on external idiosyncratic resources", "depth", "external idiosyncratic resources"]
definition: The set and type (i.e., the degree of idiosyncrasy) of resources and capabilities employed in the firm's vertical chain of activities used to produce a good; organizations relying on external idiosyncratic resources are those that rely comparatively more on externally sourced rare, valuable and inimitable assets than on internally developed and fully integrated ones.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the petitioning firms", "firm performance", "market measures of performance", "shareholder value", "market value"]
definition: The value of the firm as reflected in security prices. The authors argue that market measures of performance offer a direct measure of shareholder value, one which may more readily represent the value of the firm than traditional accounting measures of performance.

name: ITC anti-dumping determination
authors_terms: ["anti-dumping decisions", "ITC decisions", "preliminary determination", "final determination", "affirmative ruling", "negative determination"]
definition: The International Trade Commission's decision on an anti-dumping petition at each of two stages: the preliminary determination, which evaluates whether there is a 'reasonable likelihood' of injury to the industry, and the final determination, which results from a more extensive review of the petitioners' evidence of sales at less than fair value. An affirmative ruling at the final stage results in a long-term anti-dumping duty, while a negative ruling eliminates the duty imposed after the preliminary ruling and terminates the process.

name: Anti-dumping petition filing
authors_terms: ["filing an anti-dumping petition", "initial filing of the petition", "anti-dumping actions", "anti-dumping petitions"]
definition: The initiation of an anti-dumping petition, which is filed by a company or group of companies on behalf of the domestic industry. The authors argue that simply filing an anti-dumping petition may represent a credible threat to foreign competitors that seek increased market share in the United States.

name: Dispositional optimism
definition: Unlike overconfidence, which is related to the evaluation of one's skills, dispositional optimism is the tendency to believe that one is more likely to experience favorable than unfavorable events (Scheier and Carver 1985). The theory of optimism is about generalized expectancies, viewing optimism and pessimism as confidence and doubt pertaining to life in general.

name: Negative feedback
definition: Negative feedback (i.e., failure) provides significant learning opportunities because it highlights the discrepancy between a desired outcome and the outcome actually accomplished and may, thus, prompt consideration of how to adapt and succeed in the future.

name: Downward revision of expectations
authors_terms: ["downward revision", "downward revision of expectations", "belief updating", "revise downward their expectations"]
definition: The paper's dependent variable is a continuous measure of the difference between the expected number of correct answers in the next round and the expected number of correct answers in the previous round, coded such that greater values correspond to larger downward adjustments in expected task performance.

name: R&D expenditures
definition: R&D activity is often perceived as a risky undertaking that yields uncertain returns; optimism impairs the entrepreneur's ability to generate innovation output from a given amount of innovation input, that is, R&D investment.

name: Innovation output
definition: The paper links R&D inputs to patents, an innovation output that is widely used as an indicator of technological change. Innovation effectiveness is defined as the ability to transform R&D into patents (Hirshleifer et al. 2013).

name: Social proximity
definition: Following prior research, we measure social proximity using shortest path length, defined as the minimum number of edges required for knowledge to flow between two individuals. This measure captures whether two individuals are socially connected and, if so, how many steps separate them.

name: Science-to-technology knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfer from academia to industry", "incorporation of academic science into corporate technology", "building on academic science", "science-to-technology knowledge transfer", "knowledge integration"]
definition: We use corporate patent citations to academic papers as an indicator of knowledge integration. The authors describe this as science-to-technology knowledge transfer, their focal context.

name: Active engagement in scientific research
authors_terms: ["active engagement in scientific research", "actively engaged in scientific research", "active inventor-authors"]
definition: Active engagement in scientific research enables corporate inventors to develop and maintain personal absorptive capacity—that is, the ability to recognize the value of new external scientific knowledge, assimilate it, and apply it in the development of commercial technology.

name: Scientific expertise alignment
authors_terms: ["closely related scientific expertise", "alignment between an inventor's scientific expertise and the focal academic research", "scientific expertise closely related to the focal academic science"]
definition: Corporate inventors' ability to leverage social networks may also depend on how closely their scientific expertise aligns with the academic knowledge they seek to integrate. When corporate inventors possess scientific expertise closely related to the focal academic domain, their interpersonal ties to academic scientists are more likely to support meaningful knowledge exchange.

name: CVC intensity
authors_terms: ["CVC intensity", "CVC spending relative to total R&D investments", "external corporate venture investing"]
definition: For the sake of brevity, we refer to the magnitude of a firm's CVC spending relative to its total R&D investments as its 'CVC intensity.'
