CVC Intensity captures the ratio of external corporate venture investing to total (both internal R&D and external CVC) investing in the year the technology startup is acquired.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "acquirer performance", "abnormal return", "future profits (net of purchase price) anticipated from each deal"]
definition: Acquirer performance is estimated using an event study of the market reaction to acquisition announcements, which indicates future profits (net of purchase price) anticipated from each deal. We use an event study of the stock market's reaction to the acquisition announcement to estimate the discounted future value anticipated from a focal acquisition (net of purchase price).

name: CVC program stability
authors_terms: ["stability", "Stability Index", "stable CVC programs", "continuity of a firm's CVC-related activities"]
definition: We use an indirect measure based on the extent to which a given corporate investor has maintained continuous commitment to CVC investing as of a focal acquisition year. The Stability Index measures the number of years that a firm invests in startups (beginning with the first year of CVC investments through the year of the acquisition) divided by the total number of years since the firm's initial CVC investment.

name: Unethical behavior beneficiary
authors_terms: ["pro-organizational unethical behavior", "proself unethical behavior", "beneficiary of the unethical act", "pro-organizational (versus proself) unethical behavior"]
definition: Unethical acts are distinguished by whether they benefit the firm (pro-organizational unethical behavior, such as overcharging customers to benefit the firm) or an isolated individual (or group) who committed the act (proself unethical behavior, such as stealing from the organization to benefit the actor). This distinction is crucial to both stages of the model.

name: Moral judgments of unethical behavior
authors_terms: ["moral judgments", "moral judgment of the unethical act", "moral judgments of the actor(s)", "judgments of the unethical act"]
definition: Moral judgments of the act were operationalized by asking coders how strongly they agreed or disagreed that the act was (1) wrong, (2) immoral, and (3) unethical, with higher values indicating an act being evaluated as more immoral. Our model is consistent with dominant ethical decision-making frameworks suggesting people first have to notice a moral issue, then formulate judgments about it, and these judgments in turn guide their reactions.

name: Morality of the organization's goals
authors_terms: ["morality of the organization's goals", "perceived morality of the organization's goals", "morality of organizational goals", "morality of the organization's goal"]
definition: Whereas some firms are focused exclusively on generating profit, and might not be perceived as pursuing a socially valued mission, others pursue a profit-maximizing and a prosocial mission simultaneously. Our conceptualization of the morality of an organization's goals resembles the notion of CSR but represents a more general construct in that even when firms are pursuing their direct economic goals, these goals can still vary in the extent to which they generate social utility.

name: Stock performance
authors_terms: ["stock market responses", "stock performance", "event-related stock market reactions", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "estimated stock performance", "anticipated stock performance"]
definition: Negative public responses to organizational unethical acts, such as legal sanctions, consumer boycotts, and lower willingness to invest in the firm, should be reflected in a stock price decrease. In study 1 the dependent variable was event-level cumulative abnormal returns of stocks within firms in which unethical behaviors occurred; in study 2 participants estimated the percentage gain or loss in the focal firm's stock relative to its expected value.

name: Scope of business advisory services
authors_terms: ["scope of business advisory services", "number of services", "scope of services", "scope of related diversification"]
definition: The scope of the business advisory services small firm accountancy practices supply, that is, services over and above standard accountancy services.

name: Heterogeneity of human capital
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of human capital", "heterogeneous human resources", "heterogeneity of its human capital"]
definition: The degree to which the practice's front-line staff differ in professional training and formal education; at one extreme are practices entirely composed of authorized accountants, at the other practices that contain individuals with bachelor's level degrees. Such heterogeneity is argued to augment the capability for developing the practice's service portfolio.

name: Internal development routines and systems
authors_terms: ["specific, identifiable routines and systems aimed at reconfiguring the competency base of the practice", "internal development routines and systems", "skills development plan"]
definition: Specific systems that enable the practice to develop and thereby regularly reconfigure its competency base in a firm-specific and therefore inimitable manner, at the very least involving clearly defined policies and plans for the development of its human resources.

name: Range of external alliances
authors_terms: ["range of its alliances with external complementary service providers", "range of strategic alliances", "external alliances"]
definition: The facility to nurture alliances for joint problem solving and service development with different but complementary business service providers; the diversity or range of a firm's interorganizational ties can function as a proxy for a dynamic capability.

name: Client firm size
authors_terms: ["proportion of relatively large client firms served by the practice", "large clients", "client portfolio"]
definition: Client size is one crucial parameter for the positioning of an accountancy practice; larger client firms tend to be more organizationally complex and have a greater capacity to demand, purchase, and utilize specialized business services.

name: Strategic intent
authors_terms: ["strategic intent", "intention of seeking out new markets or launching new services"]
definition: A consistent ambition to set targets that imply a sizable stretch for an organization; in this context, a well articulated aspiration to search for new opportunities and new markets through the broadening of the scope of related services.

name: International diversification
authors_terms: ["international diversification", "firm international diversification", "degree and scope of international diversification", "geographic diversification"]
definition: International diversification refers to a firm's expansion beyond its domestic market into other regions or countries or the extent of a firm's international operations. It is defined as the decision to expand the scope of a firm's business beyond its domestic market.

name: Foreign competition in the domestic market
definition: Foreign competition in a market consists of imported goods and goods produced and sold domestically by the affiliates of foreign-owned companies (i.e., foreign domestic production). The extent of foreign competition in a firm's core business in its domestic market is likely to influence a firm's international diversification strategy.

name: Industry globalization
authors_terms: ["industry globalization", "globalization of markets and industries", "world industry trade volume", "intra-industry trade"]
definition: Industry globalization is a process characterized by growing linkages among national markets in terms of consumers, production activities of firms, and the extent of the relevant market in which firms compete. A global industry is one in which domestic markets are integrated across national boundaries, where competition among firms takes place on a worldwide basis, and where a firm's competitive position in one country is affected by its position in other countries.

name: Product diversification
definition: Product diversification concerns the extent of diversity in a firm's lines of business, and past decisions to expand a firm's business portfolio by product diversification are argued to constrain its ability to subsequently undertake geographic expansion.

name: Premium market position
definition: A market position aggregates a distinct set of interdependent strategic choices including choices about resources, prices, quality, and submarkets. In the airline industry, FSCs provide a premium service and attract consumers who value quality more than price while incurring higher operating costs, whereas LCCs save operating costs by providing a standardized, low-cost service targeted at more price sensitive consumers.

name: Entry threat
authors_terms: ["threat of entry", "entry threat", "threatened route", "threat of entry from an LCC"]
definition: Routes are treated as threatened by Southwest's entry when Southwest already operated at the second endpoint, so that it would likely start to fly the threatened route; the sample period is the 25-quarter window surrounding the quarter during which Southwest started operating in the second endpoint of the route.

name: Seat capacity
definition: SeatCapacity_rit is the total number of installed seats on flights flown by carrier i on route r (a directional origin–destination pair) at time t.

name: Within-submarket demand substitutability
authors_terms: ["demand substitutability between customer segments", "within-submarket demand substitutability", "substitutability between customer segments"]
definition: Demand substitutability between customer segments within a single threatened submarket, or the degree to which a product targeted for one segment could be substitutable for a product targeted for another segment.

name: Between-submarket demand complementarity
authors_terms: ["complementarity in demand across the incumbent's submarkets", "demand complementarity between its threatened and unthreatened submarkets", "complementarity"]
definition: The premium incumbent operates and maximizes the joint profits in two submarkets with complementary demand, and m represents the degree of complementarity between the two submarkets; entry increases total demand in the contested submarket, thereby benefiting the incumbent's complementary and unthreatened submarkets.

name: Subunit extent of practice implementation
authors_terms: ["subunit extent of practice implementation", "practice implementation", "extent of practice implementation"]
definition: The extent to which a subunit implements a practice adopted by the firm into concrete actions, as opposed to formal adoption, and which may vary across subunits and practices (decoupling).

name: Pressures from headquarters
authors_terms: ["pressures from headquarters", "headquarter pressures", "headquarters' pressures", "coercive pressures from headquarters", "corporate mandate"]
definition: Top-down influences from headquarters, which can exert coercive power on the subunits; headquarters attempt to increase their subunits' conformity by using communication, monitoring, control, allocation of resources, and incentives, and subunits under more scrutiny tend to respond more extensively.

name: Practice implementation by peer subunits
authors_terms: ["implementation by peers", "implementation by peer subunits", "practice implementation by peers"]
definition: The extent to which a subunit's peer subunits (sister units in the same operating branch) implement the practice; peers' behavior constitutes a social proof that allows a subunit to infer the value of a practice and limits its search cost.

name: Value consistency
authors_terms: ["value consistency", "consistency of a practice with a subunit's values", "consistency with organizational values"]
definition: The consistency of a practice with a subunit's values, which informs the unit's propriety judgment and affects its ability and willingness to implement the practice more or less extensively.

name: Organizational distance
definition: The number of intermediate subsidiaries separating a focal subsidiary from headquarters. Organizational distance is ownership level minus one, where all apex firms are located at level 1 and each step down the control chain adds one level.

name: Subsidiary autonomy from headquarters
authors_terms: ["subsidiary autonomy", "autonomy from headquarters", "perceived level of autonomy", "investment autonomy"]
definition: The more headquarters are involved in allocating budgets and resources to a focal subsidiary, the less autonomy the managers of the subsidiary enjoy. Autonomy, especially investment autonomy, is constrained because headquarters can transfer funds from one unit to another.

name: Managerial practices supporting decentralization
authors_terms: ["managerial practices that support decentralized decision-making", "goal clarity", "effective internal control mechanisms", "goal setting", "performance review"]
definition: Before decision-making authority can be decentralized, headquarters must make sure that subsidiaries can operate autonomously in an effective manner: clear goals must be provided and rigorous internal controls must be established.

name: Group membership
definition: A corporate group is a confederation of two or more legally independent firms that are controlled by the same ultimate owner. The effect of group membership, originating from headquarters' resource allocation role, should diminish as we move down the group pyramid.

name: Responsiveness to industry conditions
authors_terms: ["responsiveness to industry growth", "response to changing industry conditions", "insulation from external economic conditions", "differential responsiveness"]
definition: The relationship between the realized growth rate of a subsidiary and the aggregate industry growth rate. If subsidiaries lower down the pyramid are more autonomous, their response to changing industry conditions should be more similar to that of matched standalone firms.

name: Headquarters-subsidiary closeness
authors_terms: ["closeness between headquarters and a focal subsidiary", "closeness measures", "industrial or geographical proximity", "social ties"]
definition: Subsidiary characteristics associated with greater 'closeness' between headquarters and a focal subsidiary, which tend to reduce the effects of organizational distance on subsidiary performance. Characteristics associated with greater closeness may include social ties among managers (for instance due to family relationships or same ethnicity), board overlaps, and industrial or geographical proximity.

name: Magnitude of R&D spending increases
authors_terms: ["compact, significant increases in R&D spending", "compact, significant increases in R&D expenditure", "R&D spending increases"]
definition: The firm's largest one-year change in R&D spending over the study period, measured as the maximum of the absolute value of the firm's normalized residuals from a GARCH time trend of R&D spending. The larger the single-year change in R&D expenditure, the more risk incurred by the firm from significant organizational change.

name: Magnitude of R&D spending decreases
authors_terms: ["compact, significant decreases in R&D spending", "compact, significant decreases in R&D expenditure", "R&D spending decreases"]
definition: The firm's largest one-year change in R&D spending over the study period when that change is negative, measured as the absolute value of the largest normalized residual from a GARCH time trend of R&D spending. Such changes occur as firms return to exploitation once R&D-based exploration has yielded new forms of competitive advantage.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: The firm's ability to recognize commercially valuable new knowledge and to assimilate it into its innovation processes, beyond merely being exposed to new sources of knowledge. Firms develop absorptive capacity in a path-dependent way by engaging in R&D over time.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Firm failure is de-listing due to bankruptcy or liquidation. The dependent variable is the logit that the firm will fail within three years after its largest annual change in R&D spending.

name: Earnings underperformance relative to industry peers
authors_terms: ["firm earnings underperformance relative to industry peers", "earnings underperformance relative to target", "underperformance relative to peers"]
definition: A lower partial moment of the firm's earnings underperformance relative to target, where the firm's earnings benchmark is the average return on assets of the industry within which the firm competes from the previous year.

name: Sensemaking perspective
definition: Individuals in the role of observers interpreting others' actions produce causal explanations that differ markedly from those they produce as actors making sense of their own behaviors; attributional tendencies are thus pulled in different directions depending on the perspective taken.

name: Organizational outcome valence
definition: Outcomes experienced by the focal organization, described with statements that were intentionally equivocal in their internal or external origin but well defined in their positive or negative implications; the same statements were worded to indicate either success (positive outcomes) or failure (negative outcomes).

name: Internal attribution
definition: Attribution of outcomes to internal, organizational factors. Among managers, self-serving bias manifests itself as a tendency to attribute the successful performance of one's own organization to internal, organizational factors such as plentiful financial reserves, proprietary cutting-edge technology and proven management ('strengths'), whereas actor-observer effects lead them to attribute the failures of other managers' organizations to internal, organizational 'weaknesses'.

name: External attribution
definition: Attribution of outcomes to external, environmental factors: 'threats' defined as negative environmental conditions likely to stimulate loss and over which organizational management has relatively little control, and 'opportunities' defined as positive environmental situations in which gain is likely and over which organizational management has at least a fair amount of control.

name: CEO minority status
authors_terms: ["minority status", "Minority CEO", "female and ethnic minority CEOs"]
definition: Persons of minority status are defined here as female or ethnically diverse individuals. Our primary independent variable was whether a firm had a CEO of minority status, which we defined as being either a female or an ethnic minority.

name: CEO compensation
definition: Our dependent variables were the total annual compensation paid by a firm to its CEO. For CEO compensation, we combined both short-term and long-term compensation components since the exclusion of either form would have underestimated the CEO's total remuneration.

name: CEO job exit
authors_terms: ["CEO job exit", "job exit", "likelihood of job exit"]
definition: We measured CEO job exit with a binary indicator that took a value of 1 if a firm reported a change in its CEO position in a given year and 0 otherwise.

name: Geographic proximity between an existing unit and acquired units
definition: Proximity is an independent variable that measures the overall geographic proximity between an existing unit and all the units acquired by the company during a time period. An existing unit that is geographically close to a recently acquired unit is expected to bear most of the 'costs' associated with managerial distraction and resource transfer during the integration process.

name: Operational similarity between an existing unit and acquired units
definition: Similarity is an independent variable that measures the overall operational similarity between an existing unit and all the units acquired by the company during a time period. Operational similarity is the extent to which a unit has operational attributes and characteristics that are comparable to the ones of another facility.

name: Operational performance of an existing unit
definition: Production yield is the operational performance variable and is measured in kilograms of sucrose produced per ton of sugarcane harvested. Lower values of Production yield mean that the unit is producing less output per ton of sugarcane harvested.

name: Time since a geographically close acquisition
authors_terms: ["number of harvests since the last geographically close acquisition"]
definition: Five binary variables are used to indicate the number of harvests that have taken place since the last geographically close acquisition. A geographically close acquisition takes place when the proximity between the acquiree and the focal unit is in the 85th percentile of all the proximities between the units of the company.

name: Time since a similar acquisition
authors_terms: ["number of harvests since the last similar acquisition"]
definition: Five binary variables are used to indicate the number of harvests that have taken place since the last similar acquisition. A similar acquisition takes place when the similarity between the acquiree and the focal unit is in the 85th percentile of all the similarities between the units of the company.

name: Strategic relatedness of board appointments
authors_terms: ["strategically related board ties", "strategically related board appointments", "related board ties", "relatedness of board ties"]
definition: Strategically related board ties refer to a director's appointments to the boards of other companies that follow similar corporate strategies and operate in similar product-market and international market contexts.

name: Strategic heterogeneity of board appointments
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in strategic relatedness", "complementarity in strategic relatedness", "heterogeneous board ties", "strategic heterogeneity"]
definition: The extent to which a director's board appointments to other firms differ from the appointments of other directors, or to which a board's portfolio of director appointments is heterogeneous, in their strategic relatedness to the focal firm; an optimal portfolio in unstable environments may mix ties to strategically similar and dissimilar firms.

name: Perceived ability to contribute to board discussions
authors_terms: ["director's perceived ability to contribute to board discussions", "perceived ability to contribute"]
definition: The degree to which directors perceive that they have sufficient knowledge on relevant strategic issues to contribute to board discussions and the degree to which they feel adequately prepared to contribute.

name: Board monitoring of strategic decision making
definition: The extent to which the board monitors strategic decision making or evaluates CEO performance, assessed at the board level.

name: Board advice interactions on strategic issues
authors_terms: ["board advice interactions", "advice and counsel discussions with board members"]
definition: The extent to which the CEO solicits board input on corporate strategy and the frequency of advice and counsel discussions with board members, assessed at the board level.

name: Environmental stability
definition: Environmental stability refers to the extent to which a firm's competitive environment is complex, uncertain, and prone to strategic change; unstable environments are characterized by a relatively high level of unpredictable change or volatility.

name: Board involvement in strategic decision making
authors_terms: ["board involvement in strategic decision making", "involvement in monitoring and advice interactions", "board monitoring and advice interactions"]
definition: Boards may contribute to strategic decision making by regularly monitoring the decision-making process, as suggested by agency theorists, or by providing advice to top managers on strategic issues. The provision of advice and counsel and the exercise of control are two primary components of a board's internal administrative function.

name: Time period
authors_terms: ["since the early 1980s", "the early 1980s", "the post-1990 period", "panel years"]
definition: The four panel years in which the network was observed, 1982, 1986, 1990, and 1994: "These years were chosen to capture both the beginning and the end of our hypothesized transition period." The two intermediate years allow the authors to examine whether the changes observed represent a trend.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["centrality of bank boards", "centrality of banks", "centrality in the network of interlocking directorates", "number of interlocks", "Bonacich centrality"]
definition: A firm's position in the network of interlocking directorates: "Virtually all research has found banks to be the most central firms in the network, arguably reflecting the importance of their influence in directing capital flows." Centrality is measured by the number of interlocks (degree), the Bonacich measure, and Freeman betweenness.

name: Bank received ties
authors_terms: ["bank received ties", "number of executives of nonfinancial corporations sitting on bank boards", "number of Fortune-firm executives who sat on its board", "bank-received ties"]
definition: The number of executives of nonfinancial corporations sitting on a bank's board: for each bank the authors determined "the number of Fortune-firm executives who sat on its board (bank received ties)".

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "z-score of return on assets relative to Fortune firms in the corporation's primary 2-digit SIC category", "return on assets", "market/book ratio"]
definition: A firm's profitability relative to comparable firms, measured as the z-score of return on assets relative to Fortune firms in the corporation's primary 2-digit SIC category averaged over three years. Resource dependence arguments hold that poorly performing firms are more likely to appoint bankers, while the officers of strong performers are attractive as bank directors.

name: Firm indebtedness
definition: The extent to which a firm relies on debt, which the authors measure with capital structure (the debt/equity ratio) and solvency (the quick ratio). Resource dependence arguments hold that "firms that are performing poorly or that have high levels of debt will be more likely to appoint bankers to their boards".

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm, which the authors treat as an indicator of visibility and prestige: "Not only are large firms highly visible, but size is an indicator of prestige."

name: Banker appointment to board
authors_terms: ["appointment of a banker to its board", "appointing bankers to their boards", "added a bank executive to the board"]
definition: The formation of a bank-nonfinancial interlock through the appointment of a bank executive to a nonfinancial firm's board: "bankers are invited onto the boards of highly indebted nonfinancial firms to ensure continuing flows of capital as well as to allow banks to influence the firm's decision-making structure".

name: CEO appointment to bank board
authors_terms: ["appointment to a bank board", "its CEO will be appointed to a bank board", "CEOs joined major bank boards"]
definition: The formation of a bank-nonfinancial interlock through the appointment of a nonfinancial firm's chief executive to a bank board: bankers "will want on their boards representatives of a range of leading nonfinancial corporations, who can provide valuable information about the status of their industries".

name: Board size
authors_terms: ["board size", "size of its board", "median bank board size"]
definition: The number of directors on a firm's board, determined for each bank from the board data; the authors report that bank boards became substantially smaller over the sample period.

name: Change in domestic corporate lending
authors_terms: ["change in the bank's level of domestic commercial and industrial lending", "change in C&I loans", "domestic C&I lending"]
definition: The change in a bank's volume of domestic commercial and industrial lending, the principal independent variable in the authors' analysis of changes in bank board size, bank-received ties, and centrality: "a decline in domestic lending was associated with declines in board size, number of corporate executive outside directors, and number of interlocks".

name: Interlock adoptions of the same practice
authors_terms: ["interlocked same second-wave practices", "interlock adoptions", "adoptions of the same practice by interlocked organizations"]
definition: The cumulative adoption of the same practice among the interlock ties of a focal organization; the value increases when the organization has a larger number of interlock ties that have adopted the same second-wave governance practice.

name: First-wave practice adoption
authors_terms: ["own first-wave practices", "prior adoption of the first-wave practices", "adoption of the first wave of practices"]
definition: An organization's own adoption of the logic-defining first-wave practices (director independence, CEO-board chair split, and audit and compensation committee independence), which signifies its commitment to the underlying institutional logic.

name: Retention of contesting-logic practices
authors_terms: ["own director loans/pensions", "retention of practices from a contesting institutional logic", "retention of practices justified by the management-controlled-board logic"]
definition: An organization's retention of practices that are inconsistent with the logic underlying the second-wave practices, such as interest-free director loans and director pensions.

name: Adoption of other practices from the same wave
authors_terms: ["own other second-wave practice", "adoption of other practices from the same wave"]
definition: An organization's prior adoption of the other of the two focal practices from the same second wave sharing the same institutional logic (board evaluation or director evaluation).

name: Second-wave practice adoption
authors_terms: ["own second-wave adoption", "adoption of a second-wave practice", "second-wave practices"]
definition: Adoption of the second wave of board reform practices aimed at altering processes in the boardroom, notably formal processes for evaluating the performance of individual directors and of a board as a whole.

name: Interlock partners' first-wave practice adoptions
authors_terms: ["interlocked first-wave practices", "interlocks' adoption of the first-wave practices"]
definition: The summed adoption of first-wave board reform practices by an organization's interlock partners, obtained by counting how many of the possible set of four first-wave practices each interlock had adopted and adding these adoptions up for all of the organization's interlocks.

name: Ecosystem complexity
definition: We first consider the structure of complementor's interdependence in the ecosystem based on the number of unique components that interact with a complementor's product. We refer to this structural feature as ecosystem complexity.

name: Ecosystem experience
definition: Ecosystem experience, which spans the entire period of participation in an ecosystem and not just the period of superior performance, will help confer several types of learning-based advantages on leader firms.

name: Platform transition
authors_terms: ["platform transition", "generational transition initiated by the platform firm", "technology transition initiated by platform firms"]
definition: We then consider the impact of generational transitions initiated by platform firms (e.g., new generations of gaming consoles introduced by Sony, Nintendo, or Microsoft). These transitions represent a common means by which platform firms compete and create value over time.

name: Sustainability of superior performance
authors_terms: ["sustainability of superior performance", "sustaining superior performance", "sustain its superior performance"]
definition: We focus on the performance of complementors within a platform-based ecosystem. In particular, we take into account that there are performance differences among complementors within an ecosystem, and we explore the extent to which a high performing complementor can sustain its performance advantage within an ecosystem.

name: Racial salience
authors_terms: ["racial salience", "salience of race", "high-salience events", "racially salient events", "racial prime", "article prime", "priming"]
definition: Salience refers to the phenomenon that when one's attention is differentially directed to one portion of the environment rather than to others, the information contained in that portion will receive disproportionate weighting in subsequent judgements. The authors argue that an event that alters the salience of race will also alter the prevalence of discrimination, because people who are more attentive to race are more prone to discriminate.

name: Founder race
authors_terms: ["signaled race of a founder", "race of the founder", "Black founder", "solo Black founder", "out-group founders", "in-group founders"]
definition: The treatment in the experiment was variation in the signaled race of a founder, with the project held constant. In the field data the authors identified projects initiated by individual (solo) founders of different races and constructed the variable solo Black founder.

name: Founder evaluation
authors_terms: ["evaluation of the founder", "assessment of out-group individuals", "perceived quality", "likelihood you would support the project", "likelihood others would support the project", "perception of the project's odds of success", "likelihood of recommending"]
definition: Early-stage firms and their founders are often intertwined to the point where evaluation of the idea or the project is largely a referendum on the founder. The authors considered three specific measures of quality: (1) perceived quality, (2) likelihood you would support the project, and (3) likelihood others would support the project.

name: Perceived founder ability
authors_terms: ["assessment of founder skill", "founder aptitudes", "deliver on time", "match their advertised quality", "fail to deliver", "receive complaints"]
definition: The authors asked respondents to rate the skill of the founder along four plausible dimensions: (1) likelihood they will deliver on time, (2) likelihood they will match their advertised quality, (3) likelihood they will fail to deliver entirely, and (4) likelihood they will receive complaints from future supporters.

name: Crowdfunding campaign success
authors_terms: ["likelihood of success", "fundraising outcomes", "succeeded in reaching its fundraising goal"]
definition: Given the authors' core interest in backers' behaviors, the outcome of interest is a binary indicator of whether the project succeeded in reaching its fundraising goal.

name: Event narrative framing
authors_terms: ["placement of responsibility", "procustumer condition", "propolice condition", "the manner in which an event is depicted", "changes in the emotional valence of the story"]
definition: The authors test how changes in the placement of responsibility (e.g., the victim was innocent versus the victim shares responsibility) and the degree of arousal elicited by the news media (e.g., anger) influence the propensity to demonstrate out-group support. Accounts were selected after testing seven versions of the story to identify two that did not vary in awe, utility, interest, complexity, or length but that gave readers different impressions of whether the customers or the police were responsible.

name: Lost leadership
definition: In this paper, we call a leader any participant that temporarily holds a prize-eligible position. We refer as a former leader to a participant who is not currently a leader but has been among the leaders and later lost leadership position before the end of the contest.

name: Effort provision
definition: Using controlled-environment data allows us to observe and measure each team's effort directly by focusing on input rather than output-based proxies. In the bank setting, we operationalize the dependent variable, effort, using daily productivity.

name: Effort toward alternative goals
authors_terms: ["substitution of effort away from other goals", "alternative goals", "secondary loans", "effort substitution"]
definition: Among a multitude of goals that outlets faced, three were particularly important: being eligible for a prize in the tournament, achieving the monthly bonus, and selling other products. Secondary loans were incentivized with a separate piece-rate plan, but their sales did not contribute to the tournament goal.

name: Category member reputation
definition: The reputation of category members other than the firm in crisis, understood as stakeholders' perceptions of a restaurant that need to be continually reinforced. The authors state that because Yelp is 'a direct reflection of stakeholders' perceptions, we chose Yelp reviews as our indicator of other firms' reputations.'

name: Salience of the capability failure
authors_terms: ["salience", "Salience of capability failure", "Saliency of capability failure", "cognitively available"]
definition: The extent to which the negative event precipitating the spillover is cognitively available to the stakeholders making assessments: 'reputation spillover effects will only persist as long as the event precipitating the spillover continues to be salient, or cognitively available to the stakeholders making the assessments.'

name: Associability
authors_terms: ["associability", "highly associable category members", "same industry sub-type", "geographic proximity"]
definition: The degree to which other firms are seen as similar enough to the focal actor to be affected by a spillover: 'different, more specific combinations of characteristics may be used to determine the associability ... of different firms with the focal actor, which can influence whether or not others are affected by the reputation spillover.' In this context, Mexican restaurants that are geographically proximal to a Chipotle have the greatest associability.

name: Internal corporate governance code adoption
definition: The specific kind of substitution response that we study is the development of internal standards in response to nonmandatory external standards. These standards often take the form of ICGCs approved by the boards of directors and publicized as the official guidelines regulating corporate governance practices within the firm.

name: Code ceremoniality
definition: Internal standards such as corporate codes can be considered ceremonial if they are not likely to have practical consequences for organizational operations; such codes have superficial content and do not describe specific requirements needed to monitor and enforce compliance. ICGCs lie on a continuum that ranges from ceremonial to substantive.

name: Stock exchange trading
authors_terms: ["RTS/MICEX trading", "shares traded at stock exchanges", "publicly traded firms"]
definition: Firms whose shares are traded at major Russian stock exchanges; publicly traded firms are likely to receive greater scrutiny of their corporate governance practices than privately held firms.

name: Stock exchange quotation listing
definition: Being included in the quotation lists of the RTS and MICEX, which refers to being included in quotation lists rather than merely being admitted for trading and imposes special requirements on share issuers over and above the requirements needed to have shares traded.

name: Depositary receipt issuance
definition: To initiate trading outside of Russia, Russian corporations deposit their shares in banks, which issue depositary receipts that can be traded at foreign stock exchanges; American depository receipts (ADRs) are issued for trading in the United States, and global depository receipts (GDRs) are issued for trading in other countries, primarily in Europe.

name: Regional prevalence of prior adopters
authors_terms: ["prior region adopters", "prior adopters in the same region", "regional proximity"]
definition: Firms are more likely to observe and imitate prior adopters located in the same region than adopters located in other regions; regional proximity is operationalized as a location in the same region.

name: Industry prevalence of prior adopters
authors_terms: ["prior industry adopters", "prior adopters in the same industry"]
definition: Firms tend to watch especially closely their competitors and are more sensitive to information about adoption of new practices by firms in the same industry.

name: Board interlocks with prior adopters
authors_terms: ["interlocks to adopters", "board interlocks with prior adopters"]
definition: Board interlocks with prior adopters increase the chances of adoption by the focal firm; these interlocks serve as communication channels and induce adoption by providing direct access to information about a practice and about the experience of those who have already adopted this practice.

name: Ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership concentration", "shareholders with large blocks of shares", "concentration of ownership"]
definition: One factor that makes a firm less dependent on minority shareholders is the presence of shareholders with large blocks of shares; in Russia even some of the largest firms have high ownership concentration, with a large proportion of shares owned by one shareholder.

name: Relative profitability
definition: Profitable firms will experience less pressure from shareholders and will have more latitude in choosing their corporate governance practices; profitability is also related to capital needs, as profitable firms are less likely to depend on investors for new funds.

name: High-involvement work practices
definition: HR practices that create firm-specific employee capabilities difficult for other firms to imitate or transfer, covering a wide range of systems and routines including training, teams, incentives, flexible job design, and information sharing.

name: Layoffs
definition: Layoffs are permanent separations initiated by an organization and implemented either all at once or phased in over time.

name: Workplace productivity
definition: Workplace productivity is measured as the logarithm of revenues minus expenditures per employee, capturing both revenue generated by employees and the costs of maintaining a highly skilled workforce.

name: Continued investments in high-involvement work practices
authors_terms: ["continued investments in high-involvement work practices", "discontinued investments in high-involvement work practices"]
definition: Continued investments in high-involvement work practices are investments in these practices that are maintained throughout a layoff period; discontinued investments are a workplace's reduction of investments in such practices throughout a layoff period.

name: Learning rate
definition: Organizational learning scholars typically model the learning curve as a function of cumulative output: performance increases or cost decreases, with the number of units of production, usually at a decreasing rate. In the standard formulation, b is the learning rate, and rather than modeling the outcome as a decrease in labor hours, we model the outcome as an increase in scores, resulting in a negatively accelerated increasing curve.

name: Task specialization
definition: Specialization is the degree to which an individual, group, or organization performs a narrow range of activities. Within the firm, specialization refers to the extent that individuals or groups are assigned to a narrow or wide range of tasks, and is often referred to as the division of labor.

name: Relatedness of task variation
definition: Related task variation (varying the content or context of the task) may enhance the learning process through facilitating the development of more abstract principles (or "schema") related to a general class of tasks. Both variation and relatedness are multidimensional and continuous constructs, and relatedness is a matter of both degree and kind.

name: Affiliate R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["affiliate R&D intensity", "R&D intensity of foreign affiliates", "R&D intensity"]
definition: The R&D expenditures of a foreign affiliate relative to its sales. R&D expenditure in the MITI survey is defined as personnel and nonpersonnel expenses for testing and research, including the depreciation amount of R&D-related tangible fixed investments and shared joint research expenses and research consignment fees; it encompasses expenses to create new knowledge about products or to develop new applications of existing knowledge, and includes development and technological innovation to improve products and production processes.

name: Parent international experience
definition: Experience accumulated by the parent firm in operating a network of international manufacturing and marketing operations, which is treated as the prime source of organizational learning relevant for international R&D operations. Firms that have been relatively early in setting up manufacturing operations abroad are more likely to have built up critical organizational know-how on international transfers of technology and tacit knowledge.

name: Affiliate experience
definition: The operating experience of the individual affiliate in the host country. Affiliates that have been operating longer in a host country are more likely to have developed know-how on product and process adaptation, to have gained access to local know-how-sharing networks, and to have established themselves as a reliable factor in the firm's manufacturing and R&D network.

name: Parent R&D capabilities
authors_terms: ["parent R&D intensity", "parent firm R&D intensity", "R&D capabilities"]
definition: The technological capabilities of the investing parent firm, for which the parent firm's R&D intensity is used as a measure. If a firm possesses important R&D capabilities it is likely to establish foreign affiliates to exploit its technologies abroad, and it is more likely to choose wholly owned affiliates.

name: Minority joint venture ownership
authors_terms: ["minority joint venture", "minority owned or balanced stake joint venture", "minority owned venture"]
definition: Foreign ventures set up with a local partner in which a local partner had an equity stake of 50 percent or more, so that the Japanese firm cannot exercise full managerial control; balanced stake joint ventures are included in this category. Joint ventures are preferred if collaboration with the local partner provides complementary resources, which may consist of specific technologies or local market knowledge.

name: Entry through acquisition
definition: Foreign entry by purchasing a stake in an existing foreign firm rather than expanding through internal growth. Acquisitions are often chosen to move away from existing bounds of organizational learning and to access complementary foreign R&D capabilities, R&D management practices and organizational know-how, and the acquired affiliate by definition does not have to go through the time-consuming process of incrementally building up its knowledge base.

name: National conflict
authors_terms: ["national conflict", "national conflict between their country of origin and host country", "U.S.-China conflict", "After Conflict"]
definition: Large-scale national tensions, such as those between the United States and China, can create an atmosphere of unease for immigrant workers who identify with the nations involved in disputes with their host country.

name: Workplace effort
authors_terms: ["workplace effort", "workplace efforts", "number of patent applications", "working hours"]
definition: High-skilled immigrants strive to increase their workplace efforts to enhance their professional value in the host country, and the number of applications more directly reflects inventors' attempts to demonstrate their productivity and engagement in research and development.

name: Career debut location
authors_terms: ["Career Debut in the US", "career debut location", "immigrated to the United States midcareer"]
definition: Inventors who relocate to the host country midcareer may experience heightened identity-based concerns during national conflicts between their home and host countries, whereas those educated in the host country often assimilate more readily.

name: Westernized legal first name
authors_terms: ["Western First Name", "Westernized Legal First Name", "ethnically distinctive legal first names"]
definition: Inventors with culturally distinct or nonassimilated first names may maintain stronger ties to their country of origin, which could heighten identity-related concerns during a national conflict.

name: Immigration sponsorship dependency
definition: Corporate inventors with ties to the conflicting country face heightened career concerns because of their reliance on employer sponsorship, whereas academic inventors typically benefit from higher career stability and have access to self-sponsored green card options.

name: Regional anti-immigrant sentiment
definition: Immigrant inventors residing in regions with heightened anti-immigrant sentiment may experience greater pressure to enhance their workplace performance during national conflicts between their home and host countries.

name: Identity-based career concerns
definition: Identity concerns refer to challenges individuals face regarding their personal, social, or cultural identity. When there is a conflict between the home and host countries, identity concerns of immigrants working in the host country can be magnified because of their identification with their home country, contributing to heightened workplace concerns.

name: Internationalization experience
definition: Internationalization experience is a function of the extent to which a firm has operated in international markets previously. Firms that have accumulated extensive international experience have general knowledge about operating in international environments.

name: Host country experience
authors_terms: ["host country experience", "local host country experience", "local country experience", "parent firm host country experience"]
definition: Local host country experience is the extent to which the firm has operated in the local country environment. Multinational firms resolve local knowledge disadvantages by accumulating local host country experience.

name: Technological knowledge
definition: Technological knowledge is a function of the proprietary technological knowledge-generating activities within a firm. It provides a firm with advantages in its international expansion activities, particularly compared with firms that do not possess equivalent levels of technological knowledge.

name: Marketing knowledge
definition: Marketing knowledge is the capability to analyze markets, build and maintain brands, and develop plans to sell products and/or services. Marketing knowledge may be rare, but its value depends on the context; that is, it may be location specific.

name: Subsidiary short-term performance
definition: The financial performance of a subsidiary in the short term after its establishment, measured as subsidiary profitability in 1994, given that subsidiary performance is unstable for the first 2 years following inception.

name: Subsidiary long-term performance
definition: The financial performance of a subsidiary over the longer term, measured using subsidiary profitability in 1999, 2001, and 2003.

name: Medical orientation of identity claims
authors_terms: ["identity-statement medical orientation", "medical-use focus in identity statements", "medical orientation", "medical-use identity orientation"]
definition: The extent to which each dispensary's self-description shows a clear medical orientation, as reflected in explicit references to the therapeutic functions of cannabis, diseases, symptoms, and medical conditions, as well as general references to medicine and patient care.

name: Recreational dispensary competitive density
authors_terms: ["recreational dispensary competitive density", "localized density of recreational dispensaries", "lagged recreational dispensary county count"]
definition: The one-month lagged localized density of recreational dispensaries each medical dispensary faces, measured as the count of recreational dispensaries listed on Weedmaps as operating in the same county as the focal medical dispensary.

name: Local voter support for recreational cannabis legalization
authors_terms: ["Local Support for Recreational Cannabis", "county recreational voter support", "voter support for recreational cannabis legalization", "voter support for recreational dispensaries"]
definition: Local voter support for recreational dispensaries, measured through the percentage of voters in the county who voted in support of the state ballots legalizing recreational cannabis use and sales.

name: Customers' recreational orientation
authors_terms: ["customers' recreational orientation", "reviewers' product orientation", "reviewer product focus", "clientele recreational orientation"]
definition: The recreational orientation of a dispensary's customer base is the proportion of its total reviews that demonstrate a recreational orientation; a review is treated as demonstrating a recreational orientation if it includes references to cannabis products.

name: Knowledge ambiguity
definition: Knowledge ambiguity refers to the same underlying notion of transferability (its ease or the lack thereof) of knowledge and encapsulates a lack of understanding of the logical linkages between actions and outcomes, inputs and outputs, and causes and effects that are related to technological or process know-how.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: Knowledge transfer depends on how easily that knowledge can be transported, interpreted, and absorbed; the study examines the transfer of a partner's technological or process know-how back to the firm.

name: Tacitness
definition: Tacitness is the implicit and noncodifiable accumulation of skills that results from learning by doing; tacit knowledge cannot be easily communicated and shared and is deeply rooted in action and in an individual's involvement within a specific context.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Durable investments that are undertaken in support of particular transactions; transaction-specific skills and assets that are utilized in production processes and provision of services for particular customers.

name: Complexity
definition: Complexity refers to the number of interdependent technologies, routines, individuals, and resources linked to a particular knowledge or asset.

name: Prior experience
definition: For a knowledge seeker, prior experience with a given asset or knowledge base predetermines the level of familiarity and comfort with both information content and context, and thus favors the transferability of knowledge; learning is limited by the degree of experience of the knowledge seeker.

name: Partner protectiveness
definition: The attributes of the information provider that are explicit indicators of the degree of protectiveness desired by the information transmitter vis-a-vis its knowledge base; some partners manage to be less transparent or open than others.

name: Cultural distance
definition: In international strategic alliances, cultural differences produce additional difficulties and challenges for managers, who must allocate more time on communication, design of compatible work routines, and development of common managerial approaches.

name: Organizational distance
definition: The degree of dissimilarity between the partners' business practices, institutional heritage, and organizational culture.

name: Collaborative know-how
definition: Past experience with collaboration leads to the emergence of a distinct form of collaborative know-how that affects the ability of firms to understand and adopt proper procedures for information gathering, interpretation, and diffusion; experience and expertise in interfirm cooperation.

name: Learning capacity
definition: Strategic alliances are formed for different reasons and the extent of knowledge transfer is linked to the goals of each partner; the dedicated resources deployed shape the firm's overall learning capacity, and the appropriateness of resource deployment, both human and support assets, shapes the learning outcomes.

name: Alliance duration
definition: The length of time an alliance has sustained itself, computed from the date of inception of the alliance as reported in the questionnaire; alliance age distinguishes 'younger' (more recent) from 'older' (more established) alliances.

name: Influence sector
authors_terms: ["influence sector", "industry and business groups", "societal interest groups", "nonlegislative governmental bodies"]
definition: The political influence process can be reduced to three distinct sectors: industry and business groups, societal interest groups, and nonlegislative governmental bodies. These three major sectors frequently oppose each other on specific pieces of legislation.

name: Influence strategy
authors_terms: ["influence strategies", "influence techniques", "information-based strategy", "public exposure and appeals", "direct pressure", "political strategies"]
definition: Four influence strategies emerged from the interviews: strategies based on information; strategies relying on public exposure and appeals; strategies employing direct power; and strategies depending on political pressure, each associated with specific techniques.

name: Perceived impact on the legislative process
authors_terms: ["perceived impact", "impact on the legislative process", "impacts on the legislative process"]
definition: The perceived effect of an influence technique on key legislative policymakers; influence strategies should be perceived as having varying impacts on the legislative process.

name: Influence mode
definition: Modes of action taken by the influencing agent may be positive, tending to increase focal person satisfaction, or negative, which may produce the desired effect but may reduce the satisfaction of the focal person. Organizations operating in the intentional channel characteristically employ persuasion (positive) and obligation (negative).

name: Scientist specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization", "scientist specialization", "specialized experience", "scientist's specialization", "knowledge concentration in a technology"]
definition: Specialization pertains to the process of concentrating on and becoming proficient in a particular subject, task, or technology, such as the extent to which a scientist is focused on a technological area.

name: R&D productivity
definition: R&D productivity is defined as total innovative output for a given effort, such as number of patents that a scientist receives for their work in a period.

name: Innovation impact
authors_terms: ["innovation impact", "impact of innovations", "citation count", "impact of a scientist's innovations"]
definition: Innovation impact means the recognition that an innovation receives from the technological community, such as the number of forward citations to a patent.

name: Collaborator change
definition: Collaborator change is a change in the people who work with one another in a team, whether by entry or exit.

name: Technologically related diversification
authors_terms: ["technologically related diversification", "technologically related firm diversification strategies", "degree of such diversification", "related diversification", "technological relatedness"]
definition: Technologically related firm diversification strategies in manufacturing firms are broadly defined to include technological and exploration spillover, vertical integration, and product complementarity (Pearce, 1983). Technological and exploration spillover, vertical integration, and product complementarity categories are taken to reflect technological relatedness in contrast to technologically unrelated conglomerate diversification.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "firm profitability", "market perception of firm value", "market perceptions of firm value", "future risk-return trade-off"]
definition: The concept of firm performance considered here is multidimensional, including accounting measures of firm profitability and market perceptions of firm value. It may be more interesting to define firm performance as the firm's future opportunities and profitability, and the market-to-book value and the relative excess valuation of the firm are measures that assess the firm's future risk-return trade-off as perceived by the market.

name: Hierarchical distance from the parent company
authors_terms: ["level of subsidiary layers", "hierarchical distance from the parent company", "lower level of subsidiary layers", "lower in the corporate hierarchy"]
definition: The number of subsidiary layers that exist between a business establishment and its parent headquarters: '0' for the parent headquarters and parent establishments that operate under the direct authority of the parent headquarters, '1' for the first-level subsidiary headquarters and their establishments, '2' for the second-level subsidiary headquarters and establishments, and so on. A higher value means that a given establishment occupies a lower level in the corporate hierarchy with a greater organizational distance from the parent company.

name: Pollution-intensive activities
definition: Business activities that generate toxic pollution, identified by whether a business establishment is listed in the EPA's Toxic Release Inventory program; a dichotomous indicator of whether the business establishments perform pollution-intensive activities.

name: Home state environmental stringency
authors_terms: ["environmental stringency of the home states", "home state environmental stringency"]
definition: The stringency of environmental policies and regulations in the home states where parent headquarters are located, assessed by calculating the average z-score of government environmental expenditures and inspection activities of those states.

name: Host state environmental stringency
authors_terms: ["environmental stringency of the host states", "host state environmental stringency"]
definition: The stringency of environmental policies and regulations in the host states where the business establishments are operated, assessed by calculating the average z-score of government environmental expenditures and inspection activities of those states.

name: Toxic emissions
authors_terms: ["toxic emissions", "degree of toxic emissions", "logged toxicity-weighted amount of toxic emissions"]
definition: The logged toxicity-weighted amount of toxic emissions released into the environment by an industrial facility.

name: Cross-organization collaborations
authors_terms: ["cross-organization collaborations", "crossorganization collaborations", "external collaborations", "coauthorship across organizational boundaries"]
definition: We define cross-organization collaborations as team production events where contribution and output are shared and the relationships exist across an organization boundary. Cross-organization collaborations are thus an antecedent to relational capital.

name: Mobility to a previous collaborator's organization
authors_terms: ["Mobility to Coauthors", "moving to a coauthor's organization", "mobility to a previous collaborator's organization", "moves to a university where one of their previous coauthors is affiliated"]
definition: Researchers moving to a university with which at least one of their coauthors has been affiliated (in a five-year rolling time window), as opposed to moving to an institution where no coauthors are employed or not moving at all.

name: Postmobility productivity
definition: The cumulative count of journal articles published by each individual up to each point of time adjusted by academic tenure, within a five-year rolling window.

name: New coauthors among current colleagues
authors_terms: ["Current Colleague-New Coauthors", "Current Colleagues - New Coauthors", "number of new collaborators in the new organization", "new coauthors that are also colleagues"]
definition: The number of unique new coauthors that are also colleagues of the focal individual in the current employer in every period. A coauthor is classified as new depending on whether the coauthor appeared in the five-year rolling window for the first time.

name: Identity construction
authors_terms: ["identity constructions", "the identity constructed for a firm in an entrepreneurial narrative", "type of identity constructed for an entrepreneurial firm"]
definition: Entrepreneurial narratives 'are primarily designed to create as comprehensible an identity as possible for an entrepreneurial firm'; narratives shape not only how individuals view themselves, but also how others view them.

name: Story elaboration
authors_terms: ["story elaboration", "elaboration", "degree of elaboration evident in the rationales for intended initiatives", "elaborating the rationale behind a firm's intended actions"]
definition: The degree to which an entrepreneurial narrative 'elaborated how the proposed initiatives would attenuate the risks the firms were facing', as captured by the density of a firm's risk-strategy links.

name: Contextual familiarity
definition: The degree to which familiar contextual symbols were invoked in an entrepreneurial narrative, that is, intended strategic actions that other IPO firms in the same industry commonly mentioned (listed by more than 50 percent of the prior year's IPO firms in the industry).

name: Contextual unfamiliarity
definition: The degree to which unfamiliar contextual symbols were invoked in an entrepreneurial narrative, that is, intended strategic actions that other IPO firms in the same industry infrequently mentioned (listed by 50 percent or less of the prior year's IPO firms in that industry).

name: Resource acquisition
authors_terms: ["resource acquisition", "resource acquisition ability", "firms' ability to acquire externally provided capital", "external resource acquisition"]
definition: The process of acquiring resources such as financial, physical, human, and intangible capital from others; measured by 'three dependent variables to capture a firm's ability to acquire externally provided capital at different stages of the IPO process and its overall effectiveness in doing so.'

name: Board capital breadth
definition: Board capital breadth is defined as the portfolio of directors' functional, occupational, social, professional experiences and extra-industry ties and captures the heterogeneity of the directors' human and social capital. It builds on the research literature on group heterogeneity and captures multiple aspects of heterogeneity of human and social capital.

name: Board capital depth
definition: Board capital depth refers to the embeddedness of directors in the firm's primary industry through interlocking directorships, managerial positions, or occupational experience in the primary industry of the firm, and is the sum of the directors' intra-industry human and social capital. It captures the industry-based shared mental models of the directors at the board level.

name: CEO power
definition: We adopt Finkelstein's definition of CEO power, as 'the capacity of individual actors to exert their will' (Finkelstein, 1992: 506). Executive power may have multiple sources such as structural power based on organizational structure and hierarchy, ownership power based on the shareholdings of the manager, and expert power originating in the manager's relevant expertise.

name: Strategic change
definition: Strategic change, the difference in the 'fundamental pattern of present and planned resource deployments' (Hofer and Schendel, 1978: 25; Rajagopalan and Spreitzer, 1997), has been operationalized as having two components: strategic variation, or departures from the firm's historic resource allocation pattern, and strategic deviation, or departures from industry norms of resource allocation. Carpenter's development of strategic change includes strategic variation, a change in the 'pattern of a firm's resource commitments over time, relative to its past pattern,' and strategic deviation, a shift away from the 'firm's resource commitments from industry norms of competition'.

name: Interpretive ambivalence
definition: Ambivalence refers to holding competing evaluations of an issue (Kaplan, 1972). The simultaneous presence of positive and negative evaluations associated with the same issue is referred to as attitudinal ambivalence (Kaplan, 1972; Thompson, Zanna, and Griffin, 1995).

name: Strategic orientation
definition: A firm's strategic orientation - the belief of how the firm should generally position itself and respond to developments in its environment - is an important filter of information that is embedded in the firm's culture, structure, and routines (Daft and Weick, 1984; Thomas and McDaniel, 1990). Domain-offensive strategies are associated with exploring and capitalizing on new opportunities, while domain-defensive strategies lead to a bias toward exploiting existing capabilities (Gioia and Thomas, 1996).

name: International experience
definition: Experience in a related domain generally guides issue interpretation (Denison et al., 1996; Weick, 1995) and influences a person's ability to elaborate on an issue (Eagly and Chaiken, 1998). The relevant experience domain in our study is a firm's past activities in foreign markets.

name: Top management team functional diversity
authors_terms: ["functional diversity", "functional heterogeneity", "diversity of the top management team"]
definition: Strategy scholars have argued that top managers with different functional specializations have different schemas or frames of reference (e.g., Michel and Hambrick, 1992). Different functional responsibilities lead managers to look at the EU enlargement from different angles and a heterogeneous team is expected to attend to a wider spectrum of attributes.

name: Top management team size
authors_terms: ["top management team size", "TMT size", "size of the team"]
definition: The size of the team is an important covariate of TMT heterogeneity not tied to functional responsibilities (Carpenter and Fredrickson, 2001). Larger teams tend to be more diverse (Amason and Sapienza, 1997).

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Executives of more diversified companies hold more complex mental models, seek information about diverse aspects, and are exposed to business-unit managers who frame the issue from their industry's standpoint (Gilbert, 2006). Our measure of diversification is based on the number of different industries in which a company operates.

name: Sense of organizational controllability
authors_terms: ["sense of organizational controllability", "sense of organizational control", "sense of control", "perceived controllability"]
definition: Sense of organizational controllability refers to the perception of how much control the organization has over the environment (Wood and Bandura, 1989). Control, in this context, refers to the perceived ability of the firm to control an issue, not to the CEO being personally in control.

name: Knowledge reuse potential
authors_terms: ["reuse", "positive knowledge spillovers", "potentially reusable knowledge", "newly created knowledge"]
definition: Spillovers can provide future benefits, including the creation of knowledge that can be reused to lower the cost of completing future transactions. The potential for positive knowledge spillovers, such as a supplier's potential reuse of knowledge from a project, creates uncertainty and an incentive problem.

name: Proprietary technology exposure
definition: The need to protect the supplier's existing proprietary technology is expected to decrease the likelihood of subcontracting because allowing existing knowledge to leak to other firms is a negative knowledge spillover. Subcontractors require detailed access to the technology involved in their portion of a project.

name: Reputation spillover potential
authors_terms: ["disrupt", "reputational spillovers", "reputation-impairing spillovers", "potential to influence a supplier's reputation"]
definition: Transactions differ in their potential to affect a supplier's reputation: some transactions have limited visibility and contribute little to a firm's reputation, either positively or negatively, while other projects are much more critical to customers, so that mistakes can diminish a supplier's reputation.

name: Task description detail
definition: Contracts with more detailed task descriptions can help the parties align their expectations, and a more detailed description of a task decreases the risk of opportunism and misunderstandings. The description variable captures the amount of detail in the contract that went into describing the task.

name: Subcontracting
definition: The second governance choice, the supplier's decision about how to complete the project, involves choosing to use employees or a subcontractor. Subcontracting can be desirable owing to gaps in the supplier's internal skill base, a lack of available internal resources, and advantageous governance properties.

name: Constituency-based status
authors_terms: ["status hierarchies", "multiple status hierarchies", "favorable ranking by a constituency", "status in the opinion of different stakeholders"]
definition: Status may be a multidimensional construct and is in the eye of the beholder: each constituency ranks an organization according to its own preferences, so an organization may be ranked high by one constituency and low by another.

name: Status in the national business community
authors_terms: ["national business community rankings", "favorable ranking by the national business community", "reputation among recruiters, top executives and business school deans"]
definition: The social evaluations by the national business community, based on its satisfaction with and admiration for each school as measured by rankings from recruiters for large companies, top executives and business school deans.

name: Status in the academic community
authors_terms: ["academia's rankings", "favorable ranking by the academic community", "reputation among academics"]
definition: The social evaluations by the academic community, based on its admiration for the quality of faculty, measured by aggregating the reputations of each school's faculty members.

name: Status in the opinion of MBA students
authors_terms: ["student rankings", "favorable ranking by MBA students", "students' satisfaction with and admiration for their own school"]
definition: The evaluations by students, based on students' satisfaction with and admiration for their own school as measured by the average response of recent MBA graduates to a questionnaire item.

name: Input creaming
authors_terms: ["input creaming", "creaming", "attractiveness to students and selectivity by the school"]
definition: Schools with high status rankings may engage in creaming, skimming off the most desirable students, being selective about student inputs and attracting quality MBA students, Ph.D. students and executive education participants.

name: Foreign MBA student share
authors_terms: ["scrambling for inputs", "percent foreign students in MBA program", "high percentage of foreign MBA students"]
definition: Schools that have low status in the business community but high status in the academic community find other sources of high quality students, accepting a high percentage of international students into their MBA programs.

name: MBA program size
definition: Schools that favorably impress students may be associated with smaller applicant pools and must achieve selectivity by restricting class size, that is, by having small MBA programs and low input needs.

name: Undergraduate business major share
authors_terms: ["input avoidance", "percentage of MBA students whose undergraduate major was business"]
definition: Schools with a favorable ranking by any of the three constituencies are able to avoid MBA applicants whose undergraduate major was business, because undergraduate business programs are offered by lower-tier universities and the educational value added by an MBA is lower for such students.

name: Student academic quality
authors_terms: ["input targeting", "high average GMAT scores", "quality of students attending the school"]
definition: Schools with favorable rankings by the academic community are expected to attract and recruit academically oriented students to keep their standards up, so the academic quality of their students, as evidenced by average GMAT scores, is expected to be high.

name: MBA output streaming
definition: Schools with high status rankings may engage in selective outplacement, directing graduates into the most desirable and visible jobs such as high paying jobs, consulting positions and positions as CEOs of large firms.

name: Ph.D. graduate placement
authors_terms: ["Ph.D. output streaming", "number of Ph.D. graduates on the faculties of top business schools"]
definition: Schools with favorable reputations in the academic and national business communities should have an enhanced ability to place Ph.D. graduates at other top schools of any type or level of status.

name: Senior faculty trained at high-academic-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools ranked high by academia"]
definition: The percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by the academic community.

name: Senior faculty trained at high-business-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools ranked high by the national business community"]
definition: The percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by the national business community.

name: Senior faculty trained at high-student-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of senior faculty trained at schools ranked high by students"]
definition: The percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by MBA students.

name: Senior faculty trained at low-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools ranked unfavorably by all three constituencies"]
definition: The percentage of a school's senior faculty trained at schools that are ranked unfavorably by all three of the constituencies studied.

name: Junior faculty trained at high-academic-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of its junior faculty trained at schools ranked high by academia"]
definition: The percentage of a school's junior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by the academic community.

name: Junior faculty trained at high-business-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of its junior faculty trained at schools ranked high by that community"]
definition: The percentage of a school's junior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by the national business community.

name: Junior faculty trained at high-student-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of its junior faculty trained at schools ranked high by students"]
definition: The percentage of a school's junior faculty trained at schools with a favorable ranking by MBA students.
