name: Junior faculty trained at low-status schools
authors_terms: ["percentage of its junior faculty trained at schools with similar unfavorable rankings"]
definition: The percentage of a school's junior faculty trained at schools that are ranked unfavorably by all three of the constituencies studied.

name: Practice utilization
definition: Utilization is the extent to which a firm repeatedly exercises a practice; repeated exercise lets firms gain experience and expertise with the practice and signifies commitment through repeated investment.

name: Internal hires
definition: Staffing a practice with managers whose career background is in the adopting firm; internal hires bring firm-specific expertise and pre-existing social ties to other parts of the firm.

name: Practice hires
definition: Staffing a practice with managers who have practice-specific career backgrounds, which provides practice-specific expertise and social ties to other practitioners.

name: Practice abandonment
definition: A firm's decision to cease a practice it had previously adopted; unlike adoption, abandonment decisions must also account for the firm's own direct experience with the practice.

name: Industry referent abandonment
definition: Abandonment pressure arising from the exit decisions of industry peers, which form a natural reference group for the focal firm.

name: Practice referent abandonment
definition: Abandonment pressure arising from the closures of independent venture capital firms, the practice experts from which CVC practices originated.

name: Competitive simplicity
definition: This research focuses only on the concept of competitive simplicity—the tendency of firms to concentrate on fewer competitive activities than do their direct rivals. Simplicity may be manifested in at least three related aspects of competitive repertoires: range, concentration and dominance.

name: Market performance
authors_terms: ["market performance", "R/ASM", "passenger operating revenues per available seat mile flown"]
definition: We gauged market performance by computing passenger operating revenues per available seat mile flown: R/ASM. This indicator has the advantage of reflecting not only the load factor of the airline, that is, the percentage of seats it fills, but also the revenue produced thereby given an airline's capacity.

name: Breadth of competitive experience
authors_terms: ["breadth of experiences", "breadth of competitive experiences", "a recent history of broad competitive experience"]
definition: Firms that have competed using a broad arsenal of weapons will have learned much about a variety of competitive methods. Breadth of experiences was measured by the number of types of decisions reported in the preceding year.

name: Organizational age
definition: Older organizations will have had the time to build confidence in favorite tactics, to develop the specialized skills and programs necessary to implement these tactics, and to establish a supportive infrastructure. Firm age was measured in years since founding.

name: Organizational size
definition: Managers of large firms may feel that they are rich and powerful enough to ignore their weaker rivals, which may prevent them from broadening their cognitive models and strategies in response to market developments. The size of the organization was measured as the number of employees.

name: Market diversity
definition: Market diversity was assessed by the number of segments and actors in an airline's market environment. These were measured by a composite index gauging (a) the number of different airports served by each airline, and (b) the number of competitors faced by each airline.

name: Market growth
definition: Market growth is an important indicator of environmental munificence. It was measured by the level of growth in total industry volume as reflected by annual change in total revenue passenger miles for the entire domestic airline passenger business.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Our measure of market uncertainty was intended to assess the dynamic nature of industry competition, which is in part reflected by changes in the actors comprising an industry or market. Our uncertainty index comprised three components: the annual number of route entries by new carriers, route exits, and bankruptcies.

name: Nonsettlement of patent litigation
authors_terms: ["nonsettlement", "settlement", "decisions not to settle", "decision to continue litigation"]
definition: The decision to continue litigation rather than settle the suit. Nonsettlement arises when other considerations overwhelm the basic incentives to settle that are created by the 'bargaining surplus' from the large costs entailed in patent litigation.

name: Patentee strategic stake
authors_terms: ["patentee's strategic stake", "strategic stakes", "strategic stake in the litigated patent", "self-citations to the litigated patent"]
definition: Strategic stakes are asymmetric stakes that arise because the greater the assets associated with a litigated patent, the more difficult it becomes to craft suit settlement contracts that capture the benefits conferred by the patent. When such stakes are high, the patentee is generally unwilling to accept a competitor within the commercial space of the patent.

name: Nonpatentee strategic stake
authors_terms: ["strategic stakes of the nonpatentee", "nonpatentee's citations to the patent"]
definition: The nonpatentee's strategic stakes in the domain of the litigated patent give it greater expected returns from fighting the suit by virtue of its continued rent stream from that domain, so it is unwilling to merely stop infringement and forego its own commercial opportunities.

name: Patent age at suit filing
authors_terms: ["the earlier a patent is sued in its lifetime", "suits filed late in the life of a patent", "time lag between patent issue and suit filing"]
definition: If the patent is due to expire shortly after the suit, patentees are less likely to gain strategically from exclusivity in the patent's domain, and suits filed late in the life of a patent are more likely to center on damages for past infringement than on building the patentee's competitive advantage for the future.

name: Mutual hold-up
definition: When faced with a patent suit, a systems product firm may be able to threaten its rival with a patent 'counter-suit' using one or more of its own patents, which would in effect prevent either firm from commercializing the end product. This mutual hold-up imposes additional costs of pursuing suit on both parties, increasing the bargaining surplus available and encouraging settlement.

name: Counter-suit filing
definition: The actual filing of a counter-suit acts as a credible signal of the defendant's willingness and ability to enforce its own patents, making the mutual hold-up threat that much more imminent.

name: Systems product industry
definition: Systems product industries, such as the computer industry, make products that include numerous patented inventions which may be owned by many different firms, so firms must devise mechanisms to obtain access to each other's patents to commercialize products. The empirical analysis compares computers, which exhibits strong systems products features, with research medicines.

name: Product exploration
definition: We define product exploration as an organizational emphasis on introducing radical innovations that extend existing product competencies.

name: Product exploitation
definition: Product exploitation is defined as an organizational emphasis on marketing existing or incrementally modified products that capitalize on existing product competencies.

name: Financial slack
definition: Financial slack refers to the level of liquid assets, such as cash on hand, that is available to an organization. Though valuable, financial slack is a generic and therefore less rare resource, and it is the least absorbed form of slack and the easiest to redeploy.

name: Customer relational slack
definition: We define customer relational slack as the slack attributable to relational, or committed, customers, who are valued resources providing tangible benefits to an organization. Customer relational slack is built through painstakingly garnered reputation and trust and is a relatively rare and unabsorbed resource.

name: Operational slack
definition: Operational slack derives from unused or underutilized operational resources, such as excess production capacity. Because operational slack is absorbed and generally tied to a specific purpose within an organization, it is relatively difficult to reallocate to alternative uses in the near term.

name: Human resource slack
definition: Human resource slack refers to specialized and skilled human resources that are rare and absorbed. Human resource slack also is absorbed because the resources are tied up in the organization's current operations.

name: Environmental threat
authors_terms: ["environmental threat", "environmental threat perceptions", "threat perceptions", "opportunity and threat perceptions"]
definition: Opportunity and threat perceptions refer to managerial appraisals of the extent to which an organization's operating environment promises losses versus gains.

name: Strategic conformity
definition: Conformity has been defined as doing what the majority are doing; strategic conformity for these authors is defined as adherence to industry norms, i.e., proximity to industry medians, in investments in innovation and promotion, capital intensity, dividend policy, financial structure, and risk-taking behavior.

name: Family ownership and management
authors_terms: ["family dummy", "family involvement", "family ownership or management", "family firms"]
definition: The governance arrangements of the organization, its ownership and its management, define whether institutional or strategic rationales prevail; major publicly traded family businesses are those in which a family has an influential ownership stake and/or managerial role.

name: Family vote control
authors_terms: ["family control", "percentage of family votes", "percentage of votes controlled by the dominant owning family"]
definition: Family owners can only influence strategies when they have enough votes to shape policy at the board level, so family control is the percentage of votes controlled by the dominant owning family.

name: Family CEO
authors_terms: ["family management", "family CEO", "a family member serves as CEO"]
definition: Family management is an important socioemotional wealth priority in some family businesses and exists where family firms are run by family members.

name: Later-generation family executive
authors_terms: ["later-generation family executives", "family later CEO", "family later chairman", "later-generation family member serves as a top executive"]
definition: In public businesses it is later-generation executives who are most likely to owe their positions to family membership, and they are the family members beyond the first generation who serve as top executives such as CEO or chairman.

name: Founder executive
authors_terms: ["family founder CEO", "family founder chairman", "founders", "founder-generation family CEOs or chairmen"]
definition: Founders of large public firms have proven their competency by making pivotal contributions in creating a substantial enterprise, and are typically more entrepreneurial than their successors.

name: Breadth of family involvement
authors_terms: ["family involvement", "number of family officers", "number of family directors", "family generations"]
definition: The chances that socioemotional wealth becomes an important objective increase as more family directors, officers, and generations assume key positions in the firm.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was assessed as return on assets and Tobin's q.

name: Innovative performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["poor innovative performance", "innovative performance below aspirations", "performance below the aspiration level", "innovative performance relative to aspiration level"]
definition: Organizational decision makers compare the organization's performance against its aspiration levels, which are formed from its own past performance (historical aspirations) and from the performance of similar firms in the industry (social aspirations). For both types of aspirations, performance below the aspiration level equals 0 when performance is above the aspiration level, and equals performance minus aspiration level when performance is below the aspiration level.

name: Financial slack
definition: The stock of excess financial resources, which by buffering organizations from the threat of failure permits managers to respond to low performance by increasing investments in innovative competencies. For financial slack the authors use the category of potential slack, which reflects the ability of the firm to take on further debt.

name: Technology-sourcing vehicle diversification
authors_terms: ["vehicle diversification", "diversification of the portfolio of technology-sourcing vehicles", "diversification"]
definition: Change in diversification reflects changes in the way a firm distributes its R&D resources across different technology-sourcing vehicles. The more vehicles a firm employs and the more equally it distributes its R&D budget across them, the more diversified its portfolio.

name: Technology-sourcing vehicle dissimilarity
definition: Dissimilarity indicates whether a firm responds to poor innovative performance by investing in new vehicles or by reverting to tried and tested vehicles; it is the difference in the particular types of vehicles that comprise the portfolio across consecutive years.

name: Innovative performance
definition: Innovative performance is measured as the number of patents granted to a firm or its subsidiaries in a given year; patents are an externally validated measure of technological novelty, and firms that patent more than their peers are considered to be on the technological and innovation frontier of their field.

name: Direct performance feedback
authors_terms: ["direct performance feedback", "performance below aspirations", "performance-aspiration gap", "own performance"]
definition: The focal constructor's performance relative to its aspiration level, where the aspiration level is a weighted average of the social aspiration level and the historic aspiration level. The performance-aspiration gap in the focal year is calculated by subtracting the weighted average aspiration level from performance.

name: Vicarious performance feedback
authors_terms: ["vicarious performance feedback", "vicarious performance-aspiration gap", "other users' performance falls below their historic levels"]
definition: A vicarious analogue to performance feedback in which a focal firm's behavior responds to the track-record deviations of firms that are also exchange partners of its own partners. The variable captures the deviation of the focal constructor's joint component users from their historic levels of performance, as perceived by the focal constructor.

name: Supplier tie dissolution
authors_terms: ["tie dissolution", "end an exchange relationship", "terminate its supplier relationship"]
definition: Whether the exchange tie is dissolved, measured at the constructor-supplier-year level of analysis as the termination of a supplier relationship.

name: Number of joint component users
authors_terms: ["number of joint component users", "number of other firms using the same component", "number of engine users"]
definition: A count of the number of structurally equivalent constructors who use engines from the same supplier as the focal firm.

name: Geographic distance to supplier
definition: The geographic distance between the focal firm and its engine supplier, which the authors argue provides alternate, forward-looking information about the supplier and may imply social and emotional attachment.

name: Negotiator problem-solving approach
definition: The problem-solving approach to business negotiations is defined as a set of negotiation behaviors that are cooperative, integrative, and information exchange-oriented. PSA involves an emphasis on questions and getting information from clients about their needs and preferences.

name: Partner problem-solving approach
definition: The bargaining partner's problem-solving approach, i.e. the same set of cooperative, integrative, and information-exchange-oriented negotiation behaviors assessed for the other party in the dyad.

name: Negotiator profits
definition: A commonly used measure of negotiation outcomes is profits (both individual and joint) attained by bargainers in negotiation simulations; individuals should (and usually will) try to maximize their own economic rewards while attempting to keep partners satisfied.

name: Partner satisfaction
definition: The partner's satisfaction with the outcome of the negotiation, one of the two negotiation outcome variables included in the study.

name: Interpersonal attraction
definition: Another important construct is attractiveness of the negotiator, understood in the sense of attraction to a source (like-dislike, friendly feelings, etc.), which the authors link to the partner's satisfaction with the negotiation.

name: Negotiator role
authors_terms: ["role of the negotiator", "buyer or seller", "role constraints"]
definition: The negotiator's role in the negotiation, either buyer or seller; Graham et al. (1988) found the negotiator's role to be the most important causal factor in negotiations between Japanese.

name: Period preceding CEO stock option grants
authors_terms: ["period preceding CEO stock option grants", "period leading up to an option grant", "pregrant period", "option grant period", "period before an option grant"]
definition: The window of time leading up to the date on which a CEO is granted stock options. The authors argue that this period is unique because it is the one instance when CEOs are incentivized by options to reduce the stock price of their company.

name: Cumulative abnormal return
definition: Event studies capture the abnormal stock market return around an event - in this case, the period leading up to a CEO's stock option grant. The average CAR across all option grants was used to test Hypothesis 1, and the individual CARs associated with each grant were used as the dependent variable in the tests of Hypotheses 3, 4, and 5.

name: Negative press releases
authors_terms: ["negatively valanced press releases", "negative press releases", "negative news", "overall affective tone", "negative releases"]
definition: The authors propose that firms will release a higher quantity of relatively negative, or less positive, press releases; they do not imply that firms release extremely or strictly negative press releases. Press releases are generally positive, and what is examined are relatively negatively valanced press releases compared to other press releases.

name: CEO underpayment
definition: CEO underpayment represents the difference between a CEO's actual pay and how much that particular CEO should receive, relative to other CEOs, as indicated by industry, firm size, performance, and other factors.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: The extent to which managers can pursue varied courses of action (Hambrick & Finkelstein, 1987); the authors also describe it as the latitude CEOs have to consider multiple courses of action.

name: Organizational change
definition: We are theoretically interested in organizational adaptation and change. Empirically, we operationalized change in two ways: lineup change and coach change.

name: Distance from reference group threshold
authors_terms: ["distance from reference group threshold", "distance of organizational performance from the reference group threshold"]
definition: We calculated the difference in points between the focal team and the team that occupied the threshold rank after each round. The reference group threshold is the 15th rank in the overall standings, the last rank that allows a team to remain in the Bundesliga.

name: Distance from top performance threshold
authors_terms: ["distance from top performance threshold", "distance of organizational performance from the top performance threshold"]
definition: The rank needed to participate in the UEFA Cup is the contextually relevant operationalization of the top performance threshold. A team's performance above the top performance threshold will be an increasingly positive number, whereas the distance below that threshold will be increasingly negative.

name: Historically based social aspiration threshold
definition: We argue that decision makers benchmark performance on the social performance threshold most proximal to the organization's historical performance. We refer to this as the historically based social aspiration threshold (HiBSAT).

name: Performance below the HiBSAT
definition: We then constructed a spline function of this variable for performance below and above the HiBSAT. In this way we calculated the variables performance below and above HiBSAT, which measure the distance in points to the HiBSAT for all Bundesliga teams at each round during a given season.

name: Performance above the HiBSAT
definition: We then constructed a spline function of this variable for performance below and above the HiBSAT. In this way we calculated the variables performance below and above HiBSAT, which measure the distance in points to the HiBSAT for all Bundesliga teams at each round during a given season.

name: Female CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["appointment of a female CEO", "female CEO succession event", "appointment of a new female CEO"]
definition: A succession event at one firm resulting in the appointment of a female CEO; the authors argue that such an appointment may implicitly serve as an endorsement of female CEOs in general.

name: Female CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["female CEO dismissal", "dismissal of a female executive", "CEO departures at female-led firms"]
definition: A succession event resulting in the dismissal of a female CEO, which the authors argue receives a greater degree of publicity and scrutiny than male CEO departures.

name: Peer firm stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reactions", "intragroup stock market effects", "abnormal returns"]
definition: The stock market reaction of other firms with existing female CEOs around a CEO succession event at another firm, where abnormal returns for peer firms are the difference between the actual return and the expected return generated by the market model.

name: CEO gender
definition: The gender of the appointed CEO, which the authors contrast by comparing appointment announcements of female CEOs with announcements of male CEO counterparts.

name: Media linkage of CEOs as a group
authors_terms: ["link female CEOs together", "reference to other female executives", "entitative group"]
definition: Links drawn in appointment announcement articles between the appointed executive and other executives of the same gender, which the authors interpret as the media reporting on female CEOs as a coherent group rather than as individuals.

name: Entrepreneurial culture
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial culture", "country of ancestry entrepreneurial culture", "revealed preferences for entrepreneurship", "national culture"]
definition: We define entrepreneurial culture as patterned variation of values, preferences, cognitions, and norms across societies that consciously and unconsciously affect entrepreneurial behavior, and we conceptualize entrepreneurial culture as cross-country variation in entrepreneurial behavior.

name: Self-employment
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurship", "self-employment", "entrepreneurship status", "individuals' occupational choice to work for their own account"]
definition: We define entrepreneurship as individuals' occupational choice to work for their own account and assume the corresponding risks and uncertainty. We operationalize entrepreneurship as individuals' occupational choice to work for their own account.

name: Non-core divestment
authors_terms: ["noncore businesses", "NonCore", "divested businesses outside the parent's core business", "noncore divestments"]
definition: Noncore businesses are businesses that are unrelated to the firm's primary business activities and share few, if any, resources with them. The measure takes the value of 1 if the SIC code of the divested business differs from the parent's primary industry at the two-digit SIC code level.

name: Rival R&D intensity relative to parent
authors_terms: ["rivals' R&D intensity", "Rival R&D Intensity Higher than Parent", "rivals spend more on R&D than their parents"]
definition: Lines of business where the level of investments in long-term strategic assets by the business's rivals is greater than the level of investments in such assets by the corporate parent, where R&D intensity is the ratio of R&D spending to sales.

name: Rival new asset durability relative to parent
authors_terms: ["rivals' long-term capital investments", "Rival New Asset Durability Higher than Parent"]
definition: New asset durability is calculated as the average expected life of new capital assets by dividing capital expenditure in a year by the portion of the depreciation expense attributable to this capital expenditure; the construct compares the new asset durability of the divested business's rivals to that of its parent.

name: Parent executive long-term incentives
authors_terms: ["long-term incentives of a parent's top executives", "Parent Executive Long-term Compensation", "executive long-term compensation"]
definition: Long-term incentives, such as stock options or stock ownership, may better align managerial interests with those of shareholders, increasing managerial willingness to invest in long-term assets; they are measured as the long-term elements of executive compensation relative to total executive compensation.

name: Divisional executive long-term incentive gap
authors_terms: ["long-term incentives of divisional executives of a parent relative to its corporate executives", "Parent Corporate vs. Divisional Executive Long-term Compensation Difference"]
definition: Strong incentives at the top may not translate into strong incentives at lower levels, so that 'high powered incentives in firms are subject to degradation'; the construct is the gap between the long-term compensation of corporate-level ('C-level') executives and that of executives without corporate-level titles, scaled by the level of corporate long-term compensation.

name: Private equity acquisition
authors_terms: ["PE buyout", "private equity buyout", "acquired by a private equity firm"]
definition: Conditional on a public firm having chosen to divest an asset, the chance that it is acquired by a PE firm rather than a corporate acquirer.

name: Path length in the knowledge network
authors_terms: ["path lengths in the knowledge network", "path length", "closeness centrality", "close related"]
definition: A geodesic is the shortest path length (i.e., the one with fewest intermediaries) between a focal division and another division in a knowledge network. A focal team is likely to benefit from short path lengths in the knowledge network (i.e., few intermediaries required to connect a team in a focal unit with other units), because long paths distort information about opportunities for knowledge use.

name: Knowledge acquired from other units
authors_terms: ["amount acquired knowledge", "amount of acquired knowledge", "knowledge obtained from other business units", "software and hardware from other divisions"]
definition: The most common knowledge that project teams received from other divisions took the form of technical solutions embodied in already developed software code and hardware components. The authors focus on software and hardware that the focal team obtained from other divisions to solve emerging, ad hoc problems.

name: Project completion time
authors_terms: ["project completion time", "completion time", "project task performance", "project completion rate"]
definition: Project completion time is the number of months from the start of concept development to the time of market introduction for a given project (or time to the end of the study period or cancellation for ongoing and canceled projects, respectively). The authors use it to assess project task performance.

name: Direct interunit relations
authors_terms: ["number of direct relations in the knowledge network", "direct relations", "advice-seeking relations", "outdegree related"]
definition: Established interunit relations are regularly occurring informal contacts between groups of people from different business units in a firm. Direct relations are the preexisting divisional ties in which people in the focal unit go to other divisions for advice, and they need to be maintained by people in the focal business unit.

name: Noncodified knowledge
definition: Noncodified knowledge is knowledge that is difficult to adequately articulate in writing. When it must be transferred, a team spends significant time extracting, moving, and incorporating knowledge from other subunits.

name: Related knowledge among business units
authors_terms: ["relatedness in knowledge content", "related knowledge", "extent of related knowledge", "relatedness in skill base"]
definition: Related knowledge is expertise in the firm's business units that can be useful for tasks performed in a focal business unit. For a given project, divisions had related knowledge when they possessed a technical competence that matched the requirements listed by the project manager.

name: Fieldwide critical events
authors_terms: ["fieldwide critical events", "fieldwide events", "fieldwide critical ethics events", "broad, fieldwide critical events"]
definition: Events that influence populations of firms across industries and fields; fieldwide events, such as a new federal law or wideranging court ruling, affect broad swaths of industries and firms and become emblematic of moments in time.

name: Ethics and Compliance Officer adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of the ECO position", "ECO adoption", "timing of adoption", "year of ECO adoption"]
definition: Adoption is primarily a response to external pressures for change that signals compliance but may not alter operations; the decision to adopt is likely driven by broad, fieldwide critical events.

name: Firm-specific critical events
authors_terms: ["firm-specific critical events", "firm-specific critical ethics events", "firm-specific events", "media reports of ethics transgressions"]
definition: Firm-specific critical events are events that focus attention on individual firms; they arise in response to specific behaviors that invite increased monitoring of internal operations.

name: Extent of implementation
authors_terms: ["extent of implementation", "implementation of the ECO position", "resource commitments in implementation"]
definition: The possession, allocation, and use of resources as evidence of commitment to a position; the greater the ECO's access to valuable resources, the greater the firm's commitment to the position.

name: Offshoring of primary functions
authors_terms: ["offshoring", "offshoring primary functions", "extent of offshoring primary functions"]
definition: Offshoring refers to the assignment of business functions to locations outside of the firm's national borders in support of domestic rather than foreign business operations. Primary functions are the primary providers of knowledge for generating new products and services: production, R&D, and engineering.

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: Innovativeness refers to the introduction of products or services that are new to the firm.

name: TMT informational diversity
definition: TMT informational diversity captures the degree of heterogeneity in knowledge bases and perspectives that TMT members bring to the team. Informational diversity arises from differences in individual characteristics such as educational background or previous functional roles.

name: TMT shared vision
definition: TMT shared vision represents the collective goals among TMT members regarding a common and desired strategic direction of the firm.

name: CEO tenure
definition: We measured CEO tenure as the number of years of CEO experience in the position. CEO tenure acts as a proxy for a CEO's knowledge and influences within the firm and outside the firm.

name: Firm-employee relationship strength
definition: Literature defines firm-employee relationships as the exchange of trust and commitment between the firm and the employee.

name: Firm-customer relationship strength
definition: The measure gauges the strength and quality of corporate actions in building long-term relationships with external stakeholders-customers, i.e., how well firms take care of and build long-term relationships with their customers.

name: Industry uncertainty
definition: Formally, industry uncertainty refers to the degree to which a firm operates in industries that are unstable and unpredictable and have short product cycles, fierce competition, and volatile sales responses.

name: Firm performance magnitude
definition: Performance magnitude is measured as the abnormal return beyond what is normally expected from the broad financial markets.

name: Firm performance volatility
definition: Performance volatility refers to the firm idiosyncratic vulnerability or risk of financial performance after accounting for the broad market fluctuations.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
definition: CE is defined as the sum of a firm's innovation, venturing, and strategic renewal activities. CE was modeled as a meta-construct consisting of the sum of a firm's innovation, venturing, and strategic renewal activities.

name: Structural differentiation
definition: Structural differentiation is the degree of 'separation of exploitative and explorative activities into distinct organizational units'. The items captured the extent to which organizations separate entrepreneurial and efficiency activities in separate organizational units.

name: Shared vision
definition: A shared vision embodies the extent to which members of an organization share collective goals and aspirations; it taps into the extent to which there is a common purpose and organizational members' agreement and commitment to it.

name: Senior team social integration
definition: Senior team social integration represents 'the attraction to the group, satisfaction with other members of the group, and social interaction among the group members'.

name: Cross-functional interfaces
definition: Cross-functional interfaces provide direct, lateral relations between units through, for example, liaison roles, cross-unit teams and task forces; they gauge the extent to which firms use formal boundary-spanning integration mechanisms such as task forces, cross-departmental teams, and coordination of knowledge flows.

name: Organizational size
definition: Organizational size as reflected in number of employees is a key organizational design contingency.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism refers to the degree of change and instability of the environment; it pertains to the rate of change of the competitive environment.

name: Scope of opportunity
authors_terms: ["scope of the opportunity", "scope of the opportunity area", "scope of a patent", "overall potential", "number of claims"]
definition: The scope of an opportunity is potential access to other avenues of growth or, in other words, the variance underlying such investments. The greater the scope of an opportunity area, the greater is the potential upside of an uncertain investment.

name: Extensiveness of previous commitments
authors_terms: ["extensiveness of prior experience", "extensiveness of previous commitments", "cumulative number of new areas entered"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's resources are already engaged in the pursuit of other attractive opportunities, so that regardless of the inherent attractiveness of a new opportunity it is likely to value new ones less. Extensive prior commitment is likely to dampen enthusiasm for subsequent investment.

name: Cumulative investment experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative investment experience", "prior experience", "experience or previous track record of investing in new areas"]
definition: A portfolio-related characteristic consisting of the firm's experience or previous track record of investing in new areas, reflected in the cumulative number of patents it has been granted.

name: Competition in the technological area
authors_terms: ["effects of competition", "competition in those areas", "competitive effects"]
definition: The behavior of competing organizations taking out options in a new technological area, which both signals the attractiveness of the area and, because knowledge development is cumulative, makes the arena more valuable by increasing the total investment in knowledge creation across all actors in the area.

name: Propensity to take out growth options
authors_terms: ["propensity to take out growth options in a new technological area", "propensity of a firm to take out a new option", "investment propensity"]
definition: The initial foray into a new technological area is characterized as a real option, which creates a somewhat proprietary opportunity for the investing firm to make later decisions, such as to further exploit or to exit the area. The dependent variable is the propensity of a firm to take out a new option.

name: Power distance value
definition: PDV refers to the extent to which a national culture accepts hierarchy or equality as a norm of social life (Hofstede, 1980). PDV, as one aspect of national culture, affects how individuals make sense of and consequently behave in reaction to formal and informal hierarchical relationships.

name: Power distance value difference
authors_terms: ["PDV difference", "power distance value difference", "PDV divergence", "divergence in power distance value"]
definition: The divergence between the acquirer's and the target's power distance value. The authors model its effect as asymmetric: the two directions of divergence create two distinct types of conflicts that differ in how much they impede integration.

name: Long-term post-acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["long-term post-acquisition performance", "post-acquisition performance of acquirers", "Tobin's q"]
definition: Effective integration should translate into acquirers' improved operational performance, which can further translate into long-term value creation for acquirers' shareholders when the stock market assimilates the information about acquirers' value-creating activities.

name: Acquirer-target status difference
definition: The status difference between the acquirer and the target, which always exists but may vary in degree due to, for example, their size difference; greater status difference is likely to invoke greater feelings of superiority and inferiority from acquirer and target individuals respectively when they are sensitive to the acquirer-target hierarchy.

name: Business relatedness
definition: Business relatedness refers to resource or market similarity between acquirers and targets (King et al., 2004); the authors use it to capture at least partly the intensity of interactions during integration.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "an acquirer's acquisition experience in the country of the current target"]
definition: An acquirer's acquisition experience in the country of the current target; the number of acquisitions that an acquirer made in the current target's country in the past.

name: Multidivisional structure
definition: A categorical measure of structure was used to define U-form and M-form organizations along divisional lines. In order to form two distinct categories (U-form and M-form), the functional categories were classified as U-form firms and the three product divisional categories were classified as M-form firms.

name: Corporate diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "corporate diversification strategies", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification", "dominant business", "diversification"]
definition: The three diversification strategies examined are unrelated business, dominant business, related business. The classifications, each representing an increasing degree of diversification, are single business (95 percent or more of annual sales from one end product business), dominant business (70-94 percent), related business (less than 70 percent from one end product business and diversification primarily in concentrically related products) and unrelated business (less than 70 percent and diversification unrelated to the primary end product business).

name: Relative R&D investment
authors_terms: ["relative R&D investment", "relative R&D intensity", "R&D intensity", "R&D investment"]
definition: R&D intensity is the amount of research and development expenditures as a percentage of sales. In order to control for the industry effects, firm-level R&D intensity was divided by industry R&D intensity.

name: Market performance
definition: Market price of the firm's stock indicates the long-run performance of the firm on behalf of the stockholders; market return (also referred to as shareholders' return) is a financial performance measure. The financial performance measure used to test the tradeoff effects was the Treynor Index.

name: Divested unit performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the divested units", "performance of the spin-off divisions", "post-spin-off performance", "performance gains"]
definition: Our focus is on the performance of the spin-off divisions, specifically the change in performance from a pre-divestiture to a post-divestiture period. Abnormal returns in prior studies reflected gains expected to be achieved by the divesting firm, not the unit to be sold.

name: Relatedness between spin-off and parent
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "related subsidiaries", "unrelated subsidiaries", "closely related to the parent"]
definition: Relatedness here refers to joint activities, resource sharing or cross-market coordination established upon a high degree of similarity along both supply and demand dimensions between the spin-off unit and the rest of the parent firm. A subsidiary was considered to have been closely related to the parent if both sold to the same or very similar types of customers, or both engaged in the sale of similar lines of products or services, or both produced their products or services through the use of similar production technologies.

name: CEO organizational identification
authors_terms: ["CEO organizational identification", "organizational identification", "the degree to which the CEO's own identity and his/her perceptions of the organization's identity are tied together or overlap"]
definition: The degree to which the CEO's own identity and his/her perceptions of the organization's identity are tied together or overlap.

name: Tenor of press coverage
authors_terms: ["tenor of press coverage", "positive press about the firm", "positive firm press coverage", "tenor of firm press coverage"]
definition: The tenor of press coverage received by the firm, calculated as a coefficient of imbalance using the number of positive articles, the number of negative articles, and the volume of articles about the firm. A score of negative one indicates that all the articles are negative about a firm and a score of one indicates all positive coverage.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "level of firm performance", "positive firm performance", "favorable firm performance"]
definition: The level of firm performance measured with three indicators of financial performance: return on assets (ROA) for an accounting-based measure, and market-to-book value of equity and total stock returns as market-based measures.

name: CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO ownership", "CEO ownership of the firm", "CEO financial ownership"]
definition: The value of common shares owned by a CEO divided by total common stock.

name: Performance contingency of CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["performance contingency of CEO compensation", "firm-performance contingency of CEO compensation", "firm-performance contingent pay", "performance-contingent pay"]
definition: The total value of long-term incentives granted to the CEO in the particular year divided by total direct compensation, which includes annual salary, short-term bonus, and the value of long-term incentive grants.

name: Board independence
definition: Board independence is a complex construct and consequently we measured it using multiple indicators: the proportion of the board composed of outside directors not affiliated with the firm, whether the CEO and board chair positions are separate, the portion of outside directors whom the CEO considered to be personal friends, and outside director ownership.

name: Pressure-resistant institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["pressure-resistant institutional ownership", "institutional ownership of the firm", "institutional ownership"]
definition: The level of pressure-resistant institutional ownership, measured as the equity held by public pension funds, mutual funds, endowments and foundations, divided by the total amount of common stock.

name: Top management team prestige
definition: For the purposes of this paper, prestige is defined as the property of having status. Status is membership in an elite social circle such as the economic, military or political elites of American society.

name: Organizational bankruptcy
definition: The dependent variable in this study is nonpurposeful bankruptcy, i.e., the filing of a Chapter X and XI petition in the Federal bankruptcy courts when the filing was not a legal strategy to void onerous labor contracts, to fight hostile takeover attempts or to cope with major product or antitrust liability suits.

name: Political elite membership
authors_terms: ["membership in the political elite", "membership in political elites", "political eliteness", "political connections", "POLIT"]
definition: The degree of a top team's membership in political elites was measured by POLIT, which is the standardized sum of two standardized variables: (1) the percent of the top team who were former high government officials and (2) the percent of the top team who were formally partners in a big eight accounting firm or major law firm.

name: Military elite membership
definition: The degree of a top team's membership in the military elite was measured by MILT, which is the (standardized) percent of the top management team that held officer rank in any branch of the U.S. military.

name: Elite educational status
authors_terms: ["prestigious educational status", "elite educational backgrounds", "membership in elite educational circles", "EDUC"]
definition: EDUC is the standardized sum of three standardized variables: (1) percent of the top team who graduated from ivy league undergraduate schools or a small number of ivy league equivalent research institutions, (2) percent of the top team who attended a graduate level program in business, economics or law at an ivy or ivy equivalent university, and (3) the average education level of the top team.

name: Corporate board connections
authors_terms: ["board connections", "multiple board connections", "membership in webs of board directorates", "inner circle of the economic elite", "BOARDS"]
definition: BOARDS is the standardized sum of four standardized variables: (1) the number of corporate boards (other than his own firm) that the CEO sits on, (2) the number of officers in the top team who sit on corporate boards (other than their own firm), (3) the total number of corporate boards (other than their own firm) that the officers serve on, and (4) the number of officers in the top team who serve as trustees of nonprofit institutions.

name: Previous executive positions in other corporations
authors_terms: ["previous high level business experience based on formal titles", "previous employment as officers in other corporations", "PREVTITLES"]
definition: PREVTITLES is the (standardized) percent of the top team who were formerly officers (vice president and up) in another corporation.

name: Control-reducing threat
definition: An event was coded as a control-reducing threat when an aspect of the environment became more controlling (for instance, a regulatory body issued a new regulation harmful to the organization). The authors treat control-reducing threat versus control-enhancing opportunity as one of the two dimensions of threat and opportunity.

name: Control-enhancing opportunity
definition: An event was coded as a control-enhancing opportunity when an aspect of the environment became less controlling (for instance, the power of a regulatory body was lessened through legislation). It is the opposite pole of the control-reducing threat versus control-enhancing opportunity dimension.

name: Threat of likely loss
authors_terms: ["threat of likely loss", "likely loss", "likely losses", "threat of likely loss versus opportunity for likely gain"]
definition: An event was coded as a threat of likely loss when the organization reporting it stood to lose resources as a result of the event (such as a competitor launching a new product). The authors consider threat of likely loss versus opportunity for likely gain as a single dimension of threat and opportunity.

name: Opportunity for likely gain
authors_terms: ["opportunity for likely gain", "opportunities for likely gain", "likely gain", "likely gains"]
definition: An event was coded as an opportunity for likely gain when the organization stood to gain resources as a result of the event (such as a new market opening up for the organization). It is the opposite pole of the threat of likely loss versus opportunity for likely gain dimension.

name: Direction of organizational action
authors_terms: ["directionality of organizational actions", "externally directed actions", "internally directed actions", "direction-external or internal-of an organization's action"]
definition: An important dimension along which organizational actions can be differentiated is whether they are directed at the internal or the external environment of an organization. Externally directed actions are aimed more at modifying the environment, whereas internally directed actions are aimed more at adapting an organization to the pressures of the environment.

name: Strategic type
definition: Although Miles and Snow (1978) described four strategic types, the authors focus on two of them, prospectors (emphasizing product-market development) and defenders (emphasizing domain defense). Both types have a clearly focused strategy and capture the idea that organizations possess strategic momentum.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Available slack resources are slack resources that are immediately available to an organization to support initiatives. Unavailable slack resources are those embedded in the organization's cost structure or otherwise committed and thus not available for discretionary use.

name: Member overlap density
definition: Consistent with the organizational ecology literature, we define member overlap density as the number of online groups in a population that share members with a focal group, weighted by the degree of membership overlap between each pair of groups.

name: Group size
definition: Because online groups acquire resources through their active member base, we measured group size as the total number of its members.

name: Group age
definition: We measured group age as the number of years that have elapsed since a group's creation.

name: Membership growth
authors_terms: ["membership growth", "growth rate", "growth and decline in membership"]
definition: Because the expense of maintaining a virtual space is minimal, measures of growth and decline in membership are more generalizable indicators of the health of online groups than measures of online group 'deaths.'

name: Relative complementarity with the venture
definition: Firms participating in an IJV often possess different resource bases, and the IJV provides a means for the firms to combine their complementary assets; core to the argument is the notion that partner firms tend to have asymmetric complementarity with their joint venture. Asymmetry in the firms' complementarity with the IJV likely causes divergent valuations of the venture, leading one firm to value the venture more than the other does.

name: Relative IJV experience
definition: Given that a firm's learning capabilities develop from its prior IJV experience (Barkema et al., 1997), the partner with greater prior IJV experience is more likely to value the call option right highly and hold the option right. Firms with greater IJV experience will be better able to recognize and interpret cues of environmental change, since such firms may have developed greater capabilities or certain routines for monitoring the environment and analyzing the impact of environmental changes on the IJV.

name: Call option right
authors_terms: ["call option right", "explicit call option", "call option rights"]
definition: Also known as explicit call options, call option rights are contractual clauses conferring a firm in a JV the legal right to acquire equity stake from its partners (Kogut, 1991). Call option rights represent contingent control rights allowing the firm holding the right to gain greater control as the IJV evolves from its formation and such a need arises subsequently.

name: Initial equity ownership
authors_terms: ["initial equity stake", "majority equity ownership", "initial equity ownership", "greater initial equity position"]
definition: Lacking the option right to acquire additional interest and increase its equity stake in an IJV ex post, a firm can obtain greater control over the venture by negotiating for a larger initial equity ownership ex ante. Firms holding a larger initial equity stake may also find the call option right less valuable and thus may be more willing to give the option right to the partner.

name: CEO attention to the emerging technology
authors_terms: ["CEO attention toward the emerging technology", "attention to optics", "normalized optical words", "attention to the emerging technology"]
definition: The share of a CEO's cognitive effort devoted to the emerging optical technology; attention is the 'noticing, encoding, interpreting, and focusing of time and effort by organizational decisionmakers' and captures the presently evolving focus of a CEO's cognitive effort.

name: CEO attention to the existing technology
authors_terms: ["CEO attention to the existing technology", "normalized commtech words", "attention to existing technologies"]
definition: CEO attention to the specifics of the firm's existing, nonoptical communications technologies, which may indicate an overinvestment in the existing technological trajectory of the firm.

name: CEO attention to the affected industry
authors_terms: ["CEO attention to the affected industry", "normalized telecom words", "attention to the industry"]
definition: CEO attention to the industry affected by the technological change, reflecting awareness of competitive actions and dependence on the existing value network.

name: Organizational orientation toward the existing technology
authors_terms: ["organizational orientation toward the existing technology", "commtech patents/patents", "orientation toward existing technologies"]
definition: The firm's accumulated orientation toward the existing, nonoptical communications technologies; an organizational orientation toward a particular issue is the best organization-level corollary for attention because it captures the importance of that issue to the firm.

name: Organizational orientation toward the affected industry
authors_terms: ["organizational orientation toward the affected industry", "telecom sales/sales"]
definition: The firm's orientation toward the telecommunications industry; the notion captures the accumulation of investments in capabilities and complementary assets in a particular arena, so the higher the ratio of telecom sales the more focused and dependent the firm is on that industry.

name: Timing of entry into a new product market
authors_terms: ["timing of entry", "launch timing", "timing of entry into a new product market", "launch of optical product"]
definition: Heterogeneity in the timing of the firm's first entry into a new product market; the dependent variable is the launch timing of the firm's first commercial optical product, modelled as the likelihood of first introducing a product for the fiber-optics product market in a given year.

name: Policy-specific corruption
definition: Policy-specific corruption refers to corruption related to the enforcement of specific government regulations such as environmental regulations. Perceptions of policy-specific corruption usually arise from a firm's experiences with the enforcement of regulations and policies by specific government agencies.

name: General corruption
definition: General corruption refers to the public's belief that corruption cuts a wide swath across both the public and private sectors; it tends to be widespread and erodes trust not only in public but also in private institutions. Perceptions of general corruption are based on experiences with a range of transactions with different government agencies, levels of government, as well as with private sector entities.

name: Private management standard certification
authors_terms: ["certification", "private certification", "certification to private management standards", "ISO 14001 certification"]
definition: Firms can signal unobservable characteristics to external stakeholders by obtaining certification to private management standards. Obtaining certification requires firms to pass a third-party audit performed by a private auditing firm that verifies the firms' adherence to the requirements specified by the standard.

name: Technological overlap
authors_terms: ["technological overlap", "overlap in technological resources", "technological resource overlap"]
definition: A firm occupies a position in the technological space identified by the path-dependent nature of its upstream R&D investments across different technological knowledge areas, and this position constitutes the technological resource of the firm germane to its interactions within standards committees. The technological consideration of a firm depends upon the extent of overlap of its technological resource with that of other member firms.

name: Collaborative support during standards creation
authors_terms: ["collaborative support", "support during standards creation", "firm support", "interaction tone", "positivity index", "certainty index"]
definition: The support a firm exhibits during standards creation, captured in the interaction tone of its representatives' communications toward the committee. Higher scores indicate greater positivity, which suggests a more collaborative than competitive outlook, while lower scores indicate lower positivity, which suggests greater competitive tensions.

name: Breadth of complementary products
authors_terms: ["breadth of firm's complementary products", "breadth of complements", "breadth of prior investments in product complements"]
definition: Some firms deal with technological uncertainty by integrating technologies and providing a breadth of complementary products to offer a 'one-stop shop' system model. The higher the number of product categories a firm spans, the broader is the firm's array of complementary products.

name: Product-market competition
definition: Product competition is the extent of competition a firm experiences in the product-market space that it is incumbent in.

name: Heterogeneity in relational influence
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in relational influence", "heterogeneity of relational influence", "distribution of relational influence"]
definition: 'Relational influence' represents the extent of power or control that a particular firm has over other firms and is revealed by 'its location in the network of interorganizational relations.' The paper examines the heterogeneity (dispersion) of this influence across the member firms of a committee.

name: Heterogeneity in prior multiparty experience
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of prior multiparty experience", "heterogeneity in multiparty experience", "heterogeneity in multipartner alliance (MPA) experience"]
definition: The distribution of firms' negotiation experience - as obtained through prior exposure to the multiparty setting - across member firms. The heterogeneity of prior experiences of firms may be an antecedent to preventing deadlocks and ultimately achieving consensus.

name: Committee consensus
authors_terms: ["consensus", "level of consensus", "committee consensus on a ballot"]
definition: Consensus is revealed in the extent to which the group achieves agreement when voting to endorse proposed technological specifications. The level of consensus reflects the extent to which the group has been successful in working out differences prior to formal ratification.

name: Centralization of activities
authors_terms: ["organizational-level centralization of activities", "centralization of activities", "centralization of functional activities", "system-level centralization"]
definition: Firms centralize functional activities in the corporate headquarters to economize on synergies between divisions; the centralization of activities requires and leads to a greater harmonization of resource and information flows, and information becomes visible to the first-level modules when it is centralized in the system's global design.

name: Structural differentiation
authors_terms: ["degree of structural differentiation", "structurally differentiated divisions", "structural differentiation"]
definition: To varying extents, modules may be structurally differentiated into distinct nested modules (subunits), which reflects a module's direct span of control regarding the next lower level, and indicates that a task may be broken down into distinct subtasks that require some coordination through a first-level module.

name: Asymmetric division influence
authors_terms: ["asymmetric influence", "asymmetric division influence", "relative executive representation", "a division's relative visibility"]
definition: The degree of visibility of a module can vary in terms of how influential it is on the global design; a division's asymmetric influence captures the influence of a focal division's executive representation compared with the influence of all divisions, reflecting TMT representation as a means of visibility and influence in a company's decision making and course of strategy.

name: Proportion of subunit influence
authors_terms: ["proportion of subunit influence", "proportion of nested module influence", "proportion of submodule influence", "subunit power"]
definition: The proportion of a division's influence that resides with its nested subunits, capturing a division's internal asymmetry of sublevel to both top and sublevel titles; it is not a comparison of influence across divisions but a comparison of different loci of influence.

name: Structural recombination
definition: Structural recombination refers to design efforts that alter the existing structural boundaries of organizational modules by dissolving modules to merge into existing or to create newly formed ones; a first-level module is considered subject to structural recombination if it loses its identity as a first-level module in its own right and either becomes part of another module or is reorganized into one or multiple first-level modules.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of their member firms", "size-defined strategic groups"]
definition: Firm size is defined as the total monetary value of loans issued at the end of 1994. The authors use size, together with the parallelism between firm size and geographical spread, to delimit three size-defined strategic groups: large firms, which are national in scope; medium banks, which are regional in scope; and smaller banks, which are oriented toward a single local market.

name: Rivalry
definition: The authors argue that the degree of asymmetric rivalry within and between groups depends on the firm size, where size serves as a proxy for group interactions, and predict an asymmetric dominant-fringe behavior. A positive value of the conjectural variation reflects competition between firms, while a negative value reflects collusion, both in reference to the Cournot situation.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance in the loans market is captured by the relative margin (Lerner index). The authors chose this variable because oligopolistic competition models determine an equilibrium relationship between this relative margin and the structural and competitive conditions of the market, and because it is the best proxy for the social welfare loss suffered due to market power.

name: Service quality
definition: The authors propose an oligopolistic competition model wherein product differentiation is captured through service quality, which varies with the branch network and the service personnel in those branches. Service quality is a linear function that depends on the number of employees per branch and the number of branches per km2.

name: Performance relative to analyst forecasts
authors_terms: ["above target", "below target", "difference between the analyst forecast of earnings and actual reported earnings", "performance relative to analyst forecasts", "deviations of performance from analyst targets"]
definition: The difference between the analyst forecast of earnings and actual reported earnings, measured as the difference between the last analyst forecast of earnings before an earnings announcement and the announced earnings. The difference is split into two theoretical variables, one for earnings above the forecast and one for earnings below it.

name: Forecast guidance
definition: Managers can voluntarily issue predictions of their firm's future performance, termed 'forecast guidance'. Managers issuing forecast guidance signal confidence in their ability to predict and deliver future firm outcomes and absorb some of the uncertainty that analysts normally face.

name: Press releases
definition: Press releases cover a variety of topics with varying objectives; some simply provide routine information while others offer information that would not otherwise be public regarding the firm. The total number of press releases reasonably indicates a firm's level of effort in influencing analysts.

name: Conference calls
definition: In conference calls, the CEO or another senior manager participates in a conference call with the analysts who follow the firm. The calls give analysts time to discuss existing information with managers and demonstrate managers' personal commitment to attending to analysts' concerns.

name: Change in analyst forecasts
authors_terms: ["forecast change", "change in subsequent analyst forecasts", "change in the forecast"]
definition: The mean analyst earnings per share (EPS) as forecast for quarter t generated in quarter t-1, minus the mean analyst EPS as forecast for quarter t generated in quarter t-2. The immense majority of such changes (95%) are positive.

name: Level of investment in adoption processes
authors_terms: ["level of investment", "high levels of investment", "high investment", "Attainment of C-TPAT 'tier two/validation' (high investment)", "nominal investment"]
definition: The extent of monetary and resource commitment a firm makes in adopting C-TPAT processes, with high investment signified by attainment of the tier two/validation designation, which had a mandatory external assessment for validation of the firm's entire supply chain and required significantly higher monetary and resource commitments by the firm.

name: Adoption timing
authors_terms: ["timing of entry", "early adopters versus late adopters", "timing of C-TPAT processes adoption", "the later the adoption"]
definition: When a firm adopts C-TPAT processes, where early adopters are entering a weak institutional context with high information asymmetries and increased costs of doing business, while late adopters enter a stronger institutional context where relatively smaller information asymmetries prevail.

name: Speed of goods through customs
authors_terms: ["speed of goods through U.S. Customs", "speed through customs", "economic benefits in terms of speed through customs"]
definition: The impact of C-TPAT participation on the speed with which goods move through U.S. Customs, captured by changes in the number of CBP inspections, disruptions to the supply chain, lead time, and time and cost of getting cargo processed and released by CBP.

name: Competitiveness
definition: The relative importance of C-TPAT in making the respondent's company more competitive.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of the firms constituting the strategic group", "size of member firms", "size of its member firms"]
definition: Firm size is the size of the firms constituting a strategic group, defined by the total monetary value of loans issued at the end of each year of the analyzed period. The larger the firms are relative to the size of the market, the easier it is for them to collude; size is treated as more than a firm-level characteristic because it can affect group behavior through market power, efficiency, differentiation, and multimarket contact.

name: Within-group rivalry
definition: The degree of rivalry within a particular strategic group, which the authors argue depends on a variety of factors including firm size. It is measured at the group level through conjectural variations, that is, the expectations a firm has regarding its rivals' reactions to an initial change in its price.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of a firm in the loans market, measured by the relative margin between the loan interest rate and marginal cost. Differences in performance among strategic groups indicate that a firm's profitability is affected by the size of its competitors.

name: Target firm reputation
definition: A positive reputation indicates that an organization is highly esteemed, worthy or meritorious; it implies a good name and high regard. A partner with a positive reputation would be more desirable than one with a poor reputation.

name: Product and service quality reputation
authors_terms: ["product quality", "product reputation", "product/service quality", "product quality and innovation", "quality of product"]
definition: Product quality and innovation is one of the three components of a firm's reputation differentiated in this experiment. The manipulated description refers to the firm's reputation for value, quality products at a reasonable price, and for developing innovative products.

name: Management quality and integrity reputation
authors_terms: ["management integrity", "management reputation", "quality of management", "quality of its top managers and their integrity"]
definition: Management integrity is one of the three components of a firm's reputation differentiated in this experiment. The manipulated description refers to the quality of the top managers and their integrity, their concern for the community and responsiveness to environmental concerns.

name: Financial soundness reputation
authors_terms: ["financial reputation", "financial soundness", "financial soundness of Niche Manufacturing"]
definition: Financial soundness is one of the three components of a firm's reputation differentiated in this experiment. The manipulated description refers to the returns provided to investors and to efficient and effective use of corporate assets.

name: Joint venture decision
authors_terms: ["decision to engage in a joint venture", "alliance approval", "propensity to engage in a joint venture", "decision to proceed with the strategic alliance", "decision to form the venture"]
definition: The first question and principal dependent variable for analysis was a decision as to whether to form the venture or not.

name: Tolerance of ambiguity
definition: Tolerance of ambiguity refers to the tendency of an individual to view situations which are uncertain, potentially without solutions, and novel as desirable.

name: Locus of control
definition: Locus of control refers to an individual's beliefs that outcomes stem from internal or external factors. If a decision-maker is internal in his locus of control, he might be inclined to increase the domains and possible courses of action available to him.

name: Target firm position in the production chain
authors_terms: ["position in the production chain", "supplier or competitor", "conjugate alliances", "confederate alliances", "target firm's relationship"]
definition: The second component of our model concerns the target firm's position in the production chain, namely the potential differences between a supplier or competitor firm. Direct contacts and alliances with noncompeting firms (conjugate alliances) include long-term purchasing contracts and joint R&D projects, while direct contact and an alliance with a competitor is called a confederate alliance.

name: Prior entrants' failure experience
authors_terms: ["FDI failure experience before entry", "failure experience of earlier entrants", "prior FDI failure experience"]
definition: A cumulative count of failures of other Japanese subsidiaries in the target industry in China prior to a focal subsidiary's entry, excluding the parent firm's own failures. A subsidiary was considered failed if its operations had ceased or it had been formally dissolved.

name: Subsidiary survival
authors_terms: ["survival rate of a new entrant", "survival chances", "business survival"]
definition: The hazard rate for a Japanese subsidiary's cessation of its FDI activity in China; business failure (or survival) is used as a measure of the long-term performance of FDI and of learning outcomes in the context of failure-related experiences.

name: Causal heterogeneity of failures
authors_terms: ["overall heterogeneity across FDI failures", "causal heterogeneity", "heterogeneity in the causes of failures"]
definition: The level of heterogeneity in the perceived causes of prior entrants' failures, which determines how difficult it is for an observer to identify the key risks and primary causes. It is captured by heterogeneity in the size, ownership structure and location of failed entrants.

name: Parent host country experience
authors_terms: ["host country experience before entry", "parent host country experience"]
definition: A parent firm's prior direct operating experience in the host country, counted as its prior FDIs in China other than in the target industry, including both surviving and failed investments.

name: Ownership ties with failed investors
authors_terms: ["ownership ties with failed investors before entry", "ownership ties"]
definition: The number of jointly invested ventures a Japanese firm had created worldwide with other Japanese investors who had made failed investments in China, prior to launching a subsidiary in China.

name: Social outreach intensity
authors_terms: ["social outreach intensity", "poverty focus", "focus on high-need beneficiaries", "social mission pursuit"]
definition: The intensity of an MFO's social outreach is reflected in the poverty level of its clients: the very poor have a strong need for microfinance and arguably derive the most benefit from financial inclusion. It is measured as an MFO's poverty focus, i.e., the degree to which it focuses on serving clients who are more acutely poor.

name: Financial sustainability
definition: MFO operational self-sufficiency, calculated as operating revenue divided by the sum of financial expense, loan loss provision expense, and operating expenses; the variable excludes income not derived from an MFO's core business and is widely used by scholars and practitioners to reflect MFO financial sustainability.

name: Lending risk
definition: Lending risk is the value of loans over 30 days past due, divided by the value of an MFO's loan portfolio.

name: Operating efficiency
definition: Operating efficiency is an MFO's operating cost divided by its gross loan portfolio.

name: Intergroup discrimination
definition: The level of discrimination in a society, that is, a general pattern in which particular categories of people are subject to prejudicial and unjust treatment.

name: Market-supporting institutions
definition: Markets rest upon bundles of institutions that comprise the 'rules of the game' for economic activity in a society; key foundations include property rights, the rule of law, and regulatory regimes, which reduce information asymmetries, ease corruption, formalize exchange, and stabilize local currencies.

name: Microfinance business environment
definition: A variable created by the Economist Intelligence Unit to assess a nation's microfinance business environment, reflecting the quality of regulatory frameworks and practices as well as sector-specific institutions that support client protection, dispute resolution, and competition.

name: Professional management
definition: The index developed by Cobb et al. (2016), which combines MIX data about the quality of an MFO's financial reporting with data on its regulatory status (i.e., whether or not an MFO is regulated by a state banking authority): both measures are thought to reflect MFO management quality.

name: CEO outside directorships
authors_terms: ["CEO outside directorships", "CEO outside board service", "CEO directorships", "CEO outside board ties", "outside directorships", "CEO external directorate networks"]
definition: Outside directorships of the CEO of a source firm; by definition, outside directorships at least temporarily redirect executive attention to the interests of an outside organization. The authors' measure captures several latent dimensions of a CEO's directorship activity, such as the size of the CEO's network and breadth of environmental scan, information access (Fortune ranking), and prestige and status (size and performance of the outside firms).

name: Long-term firm performance
authors_terms: ["long-term firm performance", "subsequent performance", "long-term profitability", "source firm performance"]
definition: Long-term performance of the source firm, assessed with five-year averages of return on assets and return on sales; multiyear averages were used in an effort to mitigate concerns over potential variability in single-year returns.

name: Industry growth
definition: Growth directly affects the level of resources available to firms, as well as the degree of competitive uncertainty in an industry. In low-growth settings, few new customers enter the marketplace, rendering it difficult to achieve long-term objectives by simply tapping a fresh supply of new demand.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Concentration addresses heterogeneity in the size and profile of industry incumbents.
