At high levels of concentration—those approaching oligopoly—industries are populated by a small number of competitors each controlling a substantial portion of overall market share, whereas low-concentration industries approach fragmented markets containing heterogeneous sets of competitors.

name: Diversification
definition: A firm's diversification profile shapes the number of critical contingencies the firm and its leadership must negotiate as well as the core responsibilities of the CEO. As firms increasingly diversify, CEO focus shifts, becoming more financial—emphasizing allocation of capital and monitoring of performance over active management of individual businesses.

name: Language concreteness
definition: Language concreteness reflects the degree to which the words used in a message provide details and contextualization of information. Concrete language refers to descriptive words that provide specific information and entail context-specific, detailed descriptions of situations.

name: Investor reactions
authors_terms: ["investor reactions", "investors' reactions", "investor responses", "investors' assessments of firm value"]
definition: The importance of an event may be assessed by the security's price change during a period surrounding the event; this price change is called an abnormal return and is calculated as the difference between the observed return for a security and the predicted or normal return for the same security.

name: Earnings surprise
definition: A firm's earnings surprise is the unexpected deviation of the firm's performance from the consensus estimates of analysts. When the earnings surprise is negative, the negative deviation indicates that the firm fell short of expectations.

name: Financial risk profile
authors_terms: ["financial risk profile", "firm financial risk", "firms' financial risk profiles"]
definition: We measured each firm's financial risk profile using the firm's debt-to-equity ratio. When firms are highly leveraged (have a high debt-to-equity ratio), they have limited access to debt markets to fund strategic investments and must commit a large percentage of their cash flows to paying off debts.

name: Core relational stability
authors_terms: ["core relational stability", "RS C", "RSC", "social capital located in the core", "core social capital"]
definition: The relational stability of dyads among core organizational members, i.e. social capital located at the core of the intra-organizational task relationship network where task interdependence is at its maximum.

name: Peripheral relational stability
definition: The relational stability emerging from dyads that include at least one peripheral actor, i.e. social capital located outside the organizational core.

name: Relational stability
authors_terms: ["relational stability", "relational stability total", "RS TOT", "RSTOT", "stability of intra-organizational relationships"]
definition: The social capital imbued in the network of stable task relationships, defined as dyadic patterns of task interaction between organizational members; relational stability total captures the total effect of relational stability, irrespective of network location.

name: Human capital
definition: The knowledge, skills, and abilities of organizational members, whose utilization can be facilitated by stable ties between employees; in this setting it is captured by the players available to each team and their individual performance.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Organizational performance was measured as the percentage of games won during the regular season, following the most common practice among scholars studying organizational performance using sports data.

name: Newly public firm delisting
authors_terms: ["delisting", "delistings by newly public, VC-backed firms", "delisting of an IPO firm", "IPO firm delisting"]
definition: Our key independent variable is whether a firm is delisted within five years following its IPO, which reflects IPO firm failure. Delistings are those by the primary exchange on which a firm is traded with delisting codes between 500 and 587, which are associated with negative events such as firm bankruptcy and the firm's inability to maintain minimum listing requirements.

name: Venture capital firm reputation
authors_terms: ["VC reputation", "lead VC's subsequent reputation", "VC firm's reputation"]
definition: Reputation is an intangible asset based on broad public recognition of the quality of a firm's activities and outputs. Our dependent variable is the lead VC's reputation following a delisting event, where the lead VC is the VC who owned the greatest percentage of the company's stock at the time of its IPO.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: Underpricing, defined as the jump in stock price on the day a firm's stock begins trading on a public exchange, creates positive expectations about a newly public firm's promise.

name: Post-IPO firm performance
authors_terms: ["post-IPO firm performance", "performance in the years following its IPO", "post-IPO firm financial performance", "market performance"]
definition: How the firm performs after its IPO also plays a significant role: to the extent that stakeholders' expectations are met following an IPO, they are more likely to feel that the IPO firm has lived up to the promise signaled by the VC's endorsement. The newly public firm's post-IPO performance was operationalized in two ways: using the newly public firm's industry-adjusted ROA for each year following its IPO, and using the newly public firm's MTB ratio for each year following its IPO.

name: Post-IPO survival duration
authors_terms: ["post-IPO survival duration", "surviving years", "the time between the IPO and its delisting"]
definition: The longer newly public firms survive, the more likely stakeholders are to believe that VCs have fulfilled their expectations, that the signals from the VCs' endorsements were accurate, and that any eventual setbacks were due to reasons beyond what the VCs should be expected to predict or influence.

name: Professional endorsement
authors_terms: ["endorsement by top professional players", "professional endorsement", "product endorsement", "endorsements of top professional players", "endorsement by celebrities"]
definition: Its endorsement by prominent, high-status consumers could be construed as experience by proxy, particularly when the new product is as yet untested and surrounded by a good deal of causal ambiguity. The use of celebrities as spokespersons for a new product increases a communication's credibility.

name: Advertising
authors_terms: ["advertising", "advertisement pages", "advertising by innovator", "advertising by imitator", "aggregate advertising"]
definition: Other marketing tools, such as advertising, represent 'learning by education,' a top-down process. Through advertisements and other media coverage, consumers form a tentative hypothesis or a top-down belief about product quality and other features.

name: Competitor imitation
authors_terms: ["racket design replication by competitors", "competitors' launch of products imitating the innovation", "competitive contagion", "imitation", "mimetic isomorphism"]
definition: The dependent variable in this study is the number of new rackets with a particular design introduced by competitors of an innovating company. By excluding the innovator itself, we tease out imitation and thus capture an innovation's success as measured by competitors' replication.

name: Innovation quality
authors_terms: ["innovation quality", "quality of a racket design innovation", "playability"]
definition: To measure the quality of a racket design innovation, we use performance data collected from reviews published in World Tennis. One of the measures, 'playability,' was based on the judgment of test panelists who played with a racket for at least an hour and provided a score ranging from one to ten to indicate intrinsic quality.

name: Dyadic complementarity
definition: Complementarities between an incumbent technology firm and a new technology firm are the mutual strengths that allow each partner to compensate for the weaknesses of the other and to combine different competences along the value chain.

name: Dyadic similarity
authors_terms: ["similarities", "dyadic similarities", "technological similarity", "patent cross-citation", "patent common citation", "patenting propensity"]
definition: Similarities are the extent to which an incumbent and a new technology firm are alike in their technological base and in their overall orientation toward innovation, proxied by patent cross-citation rates, patent common citation rates and similarity in patenting propensity.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "alliance intensity", "the event of alliance formation", "the intensity of alliance activity"]
definition: The event of alliance formation between an old and a new technology firm is proxied by the probability of an alliance being formed in any possible dyad opportunity set between a pharmaceutical and a biotechnology firm; alliance intensity is the count of the total number of alliances formed within a dyad.

name: New technology firm age
authors_terms: ["Biotech Firm Age", "new technology firm age", "the age of the new technology firm"]
definition: The biotechnology firm's age since founding, used as a proxy for the new technology firm's legitimacy, power and credibility.

name: Corporate social responsibility activities
definition: An activity is socially responsible only if it furthers the social good, outstrips the firm's economic goals, and goes beyond the requirements of the law. Typical CSR activities include developing products that have social and environmental features, adopting production methods that reduce environmental impacts, employing human resource systems that care for employees and nurture labor relationships, investing in infrastructure development for local communities, and pursuing philanthropic initiatives.

name: Long-term orientation
definition: A firm's temporal orientation can range from being short to long; strategic decisions with a short-term orientation emphasize efficiency, whereas decisions with a long-term orientation emphasize effectiveness. New ventures whose strategic decisions have a long-term orientation, versus those with a short-term focus, emphasize long-term goals and strategies, resource allocation reflecting long-term considerations, basic research to build future competitive advantage, and building future competitive advantage.

name: Financial performance
definition: We measured financial performance through a nine-item, seven-point scale that was validated in prior research (Stam and Elfring, 2008). Respondents evaluated their firm's performance in the last year, where '1' means that the firm was much worse and '7' means that the firm was much better than major competitors.

name: Prior experience breadth
authors_terms: ["experience breadth", "breadth of a firm's prior product development experiences", "firm breadth", "focus", "focused prior experience", "breadth"]
definition: The breadth of the firm's experience, in terms of how closely related the various products that the firm has created are to one another. The focus or breadth of experience refers to the similarity or dissimilarity of the existing funds in the firm's portfolio, in terms of both the underlying knowledge and the processes needed to create a new fund.

name: Concurrent experience breadth
authors_terms: ["concurrent breadth", "breadth of a firm's concurrent product development activities", "breadth of new fund portfolio", "breadth of concurrent activity"]
definition: The breadth of product development activity undertaken concurrently, where the firm is simultaneously producing new products in multiple different niches. Capacity-constrained capabilities limit the ability of firms to engage in too many activities simultaneously.

name: Prior experience depth
authors_terms: ["experience depth", "depth of a firm's prior product development experiences", "firm's funds in category", "depth"]
definition: Depth refers to the volume of experience that the firm has within a particular niche, that is, the count of the firm's funds in the focal new category over its history.

name: Concurrent experience depth
authors_terms: ["concurrent depth", "depth of a firm's concurrent product development activities", "firm's new funds in same category"]
definition: The simultaneous creation of multiple new products in the same market niche. Depth of concurrent activity may increase new product quality by serving as a focusing mechanism for managerial attention and by enabling cross-project spillovers.

name: New product quality
authors_terms: ["new product quality", "product quality", "fund quality", "fund performance", "investment return of a fund"]
definition: New product quality is defined as the superiority of a newly created product along dimensions that create value for customers (as opposed to the firm). In the mutual fund setting, product quality is defined as a feature that benefits the customer-the financial return generated by the fund.

name: Niche familiarity
definition: A dummy noting whether the firm has ever created a new fund in the focal category, that is, whether the focal product is in a niche in which the firm has prior direct experience.

name: Community CSR participation
authors_terms: ["community CSR", "community engagement", "community initiatives", "participation in community CSR", "CSR participation"]
definition: Community CSR, also known as community initiatives or community engagement, refers to a type of CSR aimed at benefiting individuals and groups connected by geography, interaction, or identity.

name: Forecast accuracy
authors_terms: ["forecast accuracy", "accuracy of their earnings forecasts", "forecast performance"]
definition: The accuracy of the earnings forecasts issued by analysts covering local companies; improvements in forecast accuracy of local companies' earnings directly capture brokerages' acquisition and usage of local knowledge, and the authors measure it using negative forecast errors so that larger values indicate more accurate forecasts and better forecast performance.

name: Ground-level CSR activities
authors_terms: ["ground-level activities", "CSR with ground-level activities", "on-the-ground activities", "No ground-level activities"]
definition: Community CSR activities that feature substantial on-the-ground work, allowing participants to directly observe local conditions and interact with the local people; the authors coded ground-level activities to include providing on-site financial training, consultation or financial services for local businesses, establishing poverty alleviation workstations, and assigning stationed personnel.

name: Soft information importance
authors_terms: ["soft information importance", "importance of soft information", "soft information"]
definition: A variable describing whether being proximate to (as opposed to distant from) a company is important for accurately projecting its earnings, based on the assumption that soft information is more difficult to collect from a distance than hard information.

name: Reliance on the local market
authors_terms: ["% of local revenue", "percentage of local revenue", "local revenue"]
definition: The greater the revenue a company generates from the local market, the more its performance is contingent on local market conditions, making local knowledge more important for generating accurate forecasts.

name: Prior site visits
definition: A variable indicating that a brokerage had already conducted site visits to a company by the start of the TPA program in 2016.

name: Co-location of brokerage and company
definition: Forecasts made by brokerages on co-located companies, that is, when brokerages and companies are headquartered in the same province; analysts are familiar with their home province and are presumed to already possess abundant local knowledge of their brokerage headquarters' location.

name: Quantitative content in analyst reports
authors_terms: ["% of quantitative content", "quantitative content", "use of quantitative data"]
definition: The proportion of quantitative content in an analyst report, which serves as a proxy for easily codifiable, explicit information; the authors argue that because local knowledge is tacit, it cannot be easily conveyed through statistics, financial data, or other forms of quantitative information.

name: Upward-status asymmetry
definition: Upward-status asymmetries are those in which a lower-status lead brings in a higher-status follower.

name: Downward-status asymmetry
definition: Downward-status asymmetries are those in which a higher-status lead brings in a lower-status follower.

name: Venture performance trajectory
authors_terms: ["performance trajectory", "venture performance trajectory", "valuation trend", "trend in the portfolio company's valuation"]
definition: The performance trajectory of the syndicate is operationalized based on the trend in the portfolio company's valuation; the valuation change is the outcome of negotiations between new entrants and insiders with contradictory incentives and represents a relatively unbiased indicator of the change in the company's prospects since the previous round.

name: Market heat
definition: High public market valuations and a string of high-profile IPOs can trigger hot markets, i.e., a rush of investors and capital into some industries.

name: Tie formation
authors_terms: ["tie formation", "formation of status-asymmetric ties", "factual ties", "matching", "the likelihood of tie formation"]
definition: A factual observation is a tie that has actually formed, whereas counterfactual observations are plausible but ultimately unrealized ties between the lead and an alternative follower for the same investment round.

name: Status
definition: The measure draws on the idea that an actor's prominence is a function of their own centrality in the network, as well as the prominence of the actor's partners.

name: Geographic network balance
authors_terms: ["geographic network balance", "geographically balanced network", "network balance", "balanced geographic network", "second-order network efficiency"]
definition: The extent to which a venture's innovation development network is balanced between local and foreign network partners rather than focused on either alone. The authors describe it as 'second-order network efficiency by taking one minus an absolute difference in relative focus between local and foreign partners.'

name: Speed of new product internationalization
authors_terms: ["speed of internationalization", "new product internationalization speed", "speed of product internationalization", "internationalization speed"]
definition: The outcome variable is the hazard of exporting an innovation during the period of observation (1995-2005). To calculate the hazard of export the authors measure the number of years between 'Innovation prototype development year' and 'Export year.'

name: Innovation complexity
definition: Innovation complexity is defined by the number of components, component interfaces and subsystems in a product architecture. New product innovations vary in their level of complexity, or the variety and relatedness among product architectural design elements.

name: Industry clockspeed
definition: Originally introduced by Fine (1998), industry clockspeed refers to the rate of industry change based on the aggregate actions initiated by all incumbent firms. Hence, industry clockspeed takes into account actions at the product, process, and organizational levels.

name: Entrant size
definition: The size of the establishment entering the focal hotel's local market, measured as the room capacity added through entry in the zip code in the quarter in which entry occurred; in the case of multiple entrants this reflects the capacity of all entrants.

name: Entrant quality
definition: The relative magnitude of an entrant's resource endowment; a hotel is defined to be high quality if it operated in the Upscale, Upper Upscale, or Luxury segments, and upscale independents are also included as high quality.

name: Incumbent price
definition: The average daily price of an individual hotel room, known in industry terms as the average daily rate or ADR; the measure used is the hotel's average price over the particular quarter.

name: Experience with entry
definition: A count of the number of entries a particular hotel has faced since the beginning of the dataset with values ranging from zero to 11, capturing the experiential learning that lets incumbents recognize and respond to agglomeration-generating entrants.

name: Corporate social responsibility performance
authors_terms: ["firm CSR performance", "CSR performance", "firm CSR", "RKS rating", "CSR rating"]
definition: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is broadly recognized as a firm's initiatives to accomplish a range of economic, social, and environmental goals that create shared value for its stakeholders. The paper examines firms' CSR performance, measured with the RKS rating of their CSR reports.

name: Twelfth Five-Year Plan
authors_terms: ["Twelfth Five-Year Plan", "the plan", "national CSR initiative", "exogenous institutional pressure"]
definition: China's Twelfth Five-Year Plan significantly increased the importance of social criteria in facilitating national development. It constituted an exogenous institutional pressure for Chinese firms to engage in CSR.

name: Political contestability
authors_terms: ["political contestability", "provincial officials' political contestability", "provincial officials' past appointments"]
definition: We define 'political contestability' as provincial officials' credibility and capability of participating in the competition to the higher-level government positions. In the context of China, political contestability is often reflected in the officials' past appointments in similar government positions prior to their current posts.

name: Career horizon
authors_terms: ["career horizon", "provincial officials' career horizon", "years until retirement"]
definition: By 'career horizon,' we refer to the number of years until a provincial official's retirement. Provincial officials who are closer to retirement age have shorter career horizons, and those with more years left in their work have longer career horizons.

name: Political connections
authors_terms: ["political connections", "CEO's political connections", "CEO's connections to central government", "central ties"]
definition: Consistent with prior literature, we define 'political connections' as CEOs' current or previous formal appointments within the political party or to the central government. CEOs connected to the central government are typically appointed from within the political hierarchy.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Consistent with prior research on CEO tenure and firm CSR, we measured CEO tenure as the total number of years since the CEO took the position. Early on in their careers, CEOs face a higher threat of job terminations in their firms.

name: Local cohesion
definition: In an organization where cohesion is limited to neighborhoods, focal actors are densely connected to their neighbors, but sparsely connected to the rest of the organization; this is local cohesion. When the corresponding measure is high, all actors in the network are embedded in cohesive local neighborhoods.

name: Global cohesion
definition: Cohesion may be a characteristic of the global network, in which all members are embedded through cohesive ties. It is measured as the global degree of cohesion among all members of the network.

name: Innovation performance
definition: The innovative performance of each pharmaceutical firm is measured as the number of patents that led to new drugs, that is, patents that led to new product launches.

name: Family CEO leadership
authors_terms: ["family CEO", "family leadership", "presence of a family CEO", "family executive", "family CEO leadership"]
definition: Our independent variable is the presence of a family CEO, coded 1 if the CEO was a member of the controlling family and 0 otherwise. The familial nature of the CEO has been determined by surname affinity with that of the controlling family, as recorded in Chamber of Commerce filings.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: The dependent variable was return on assets (ROA)-net operating income before extraordinary items divided by total assets. ROA has been commonly used to assess top executive and family impact on firm performance.

name: Firm size
definition: In larger companies, firm size is an important indicator of administrative complexity. Firm size is measured as yearly revenues.

name: Family ownership concentration
authors_terms: ["ownership concentration", "Herfindahl ownership concentration", "concentration (family)", "family ownership is concentrated"]
definition: Herfindahl ownership concentration, measured according to the sum of squares of each family shareholder's percentage of shares held. A concentration index close to 1 indicates strong concentration (the maximum being 100 percent of shares in the hands of one shareholder).

name: Environmental segment homogeneity
definition: The more similar the interests of the various components of a certain environmental segment are, the more homogeneous that segment; and the more divergent the interests are, the more heterogeneous that segment.

name: Similarity of perceived effects on autonomy
authors_terms: ["affect the firm's autonomy in a similar way", "differentially affect the firm's freedom of action", "interrelationships between components"]
definition: The extent to which the components of an environmental segment are perceived to affect the firm's autonomy through the same means and therefore in a uniform way; in the analysis it is read from the weak monotonicity correlations between the perceived dependencies attaching to the components.

name: Perceived environmental dependency
authors_terms: ["environmental dependencies", "dependence", "dependencies on the environment", "influence on freedom of decision"]
definition: Dependence of an organization on forces in its environment, which may include not only the availability of inputs and the consumption of its output but also constraints on its operations; each one of the myriad of forces in the environment may decrease the organization's freedom of action.

name: Managerial autonomy
definition: The freedom of action and discretion of the organization and its managers, which environmental dependencies may decrease; managers are assumed to strive to increase or maintain their relative autonomy.

name: Tradeoff strategy
definition: A strategy in which pressures generated by one component of the environment are used as a means to reduce pressures by other components, so that dependence on one environmental force is used as leverage to reduce dependence on another.

name: Intensity and encompassing nature of environmental impacts
definition: The degree to which the impacts of the environment on the firm are intense and encompassing, as stated in the prediction about tradeoff strategy efficiency.

name: Beneficence
authors_terms: ["beneficence", "beneficent hospitals", "charity care", "indigent care", "medical education", "provision of unprofitable services"]
definition: Beneficent hospitals are hospitals that provide more charity care and medical education. Beneficence is measured as indigent care, the percentage of indigent patients for whose treatment the hospital received no compensation, and medical education, the number of residents per inpatient bed.

name: Regulatory enforcement leniency
authors_terms: ["leniency in prosecution", "leniency in regulatory enforcement", "regulatory leniency", "leniency in enforcement"]
definition: Regulators selectively decouple and exhibit leniency in prosecution for hospitals that fulfill the beneficence obligation. Under the FCA, the regulator has three ways of being lenient: do not initiate a prosecution, do not join a whistleblower, or join a whistleblower but make sure that the settlement amount is low.

name: Upcoding
authors_terms: ["upcoding", "mispricing", "coding into the Top DRG", "coding into a diagnosis-related group that yields higher reimbursement"]
definition: Upcoding is a technique that involves misclassifying a patient into a diagnosis-related group (DRG) that yields higher Medicare reimbursement. The DRG assigned by the hospital's medical coders at the time of discharge is the basis for reimbursement, and there is latitude in assigning a patient to one DRG versus another.

name: Successful intelligence
definition: Successful intelligence in the entrepreneurship context is the ability to succeed in new venture creation and growth. Sternberg (1997, 2004) explains that SI consists of practical intelligence (PI), analytical intelligence (AI), and creative intelligence (CI).

name: Practical intelligence
definition: Among the three components of SI, PI is an experience-based accumulation of skills, dispositions, tacit knowledge, and the ability to apply same to solve everyday problems (Sternberg et al. 1995a). PI has an implicit, unarticulated quality, and within specific domains, practical intelligence is the basis for expertise.

name: Analytical intelligence
definition: Sternberg (1997) referred to AI as the ability to learn, remember, and retrieve information quickly. It helps us to analyze and evaluate multiple and complex courses of action.

name: Creative intelligence
definition: CI is the ability to generate high-quality novel ideas that meet the needs of a task or context (Sternberg 2004). Those who have high CI challenge the status quo and seek alternative ways to solve problems and gain advantage from opportunities.

name: Entrepreneurial self-efficacy
definition: ESE is the extent to which individuals are confident in their ability to produce consistently high levels of performance in entrepreneur-specific tasks (Chen et al. 1998). High ESE reflects entrepreneurs' belief that they have the innovation, marketing, management, risk taking, and financial resources to succeed with new venture exploration, startup, and early growth.

name: Swift action
definition: Swift action concerns the time it takes to choose among possible improvement actions and to begin trial or revision improvement actions; participants were asked the approximate number of days 'it would take to choose from an array of possible improvement actions and to begin trial or revision improvement actions.'

name: Multiple improvement actions
definition: Taken together, we define MIA as change behaviors that involve repeated goal-driven revision and continuous searches for betterment. In the new venture context, MIA appears as actions toward goals that will involve new (or better) products, services, processes, or organizations.

name: New venture growth
definition: We study NVG because early-stage growth is an indicator of venture success. New Venture Growth (NVG) was measured with two items: (1) the compound annual sales growth rate from year-end 2001 to year-end 2005, and (2) the compound annual employment growth rate from year-end 2001 to year-end 2005.

name: Supply portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["supply portfolio concentration", "SPC", "concentration of outsourcing shares", "concentration in the firm's outsourcing portfolio"]
definition: Supply portfolio concentration (SPC) refers to the extent to which a firm apportions its outsourced activities or projects (of the same type) in a more or less concentrated manner among suppliers. High levels of SPC are indicated if most of the firm's outsourcing is to one or very few suppliers, whereas spreading the firm's outsourcing among a larger number of suppliers indicates low SPC.

name: Firm-specific knowledge
authors_terms: ["firm-specific knowledge", "firm specificity of knowledge work", "need for firm-specific knowledge"]
definition: The need for firm-specific knowledge arises when knowledge-based projects are closely related to a unique technology, organizational unit, or strategic niche that is specific to a firm, so that suppliers must invest in knowledge that is only valuable for servicing that firm. A higher percentage of backward self-citations implies that the firm's outsourced patents build to a greater extent on its own inventions than on technologies invented more broadly in the economy.

name: Interrelatedness of outsourced projects
authors_terms: ["interrelatedness", "interdependencies across outsourced projects", "complementarities across the entire set of transactions"]
definition: Interrelatedness refers to the extent to which a firm's outsourced patents are in connected (versus disconnected) subsets, and interrelated projects may have complementarities that need to be coordinated or scope economies from common knowledge inputs. This extends prior research on contemporaneous spillovers between transactions to complementarities across the entire set of transactions in the firm's portfolio.

name: Reliance on outsourcing
authors_terms: ["reliance on outsourcing", "the extent to which the firm uses—and thus relies on—outsourcing"]
definition: The extent to which the firm uses—and thus relies on—outsourcing relative to the total volume of its activity, controlling for the volume of outsourcing. As a firm increases its reliance on outsourcing across its entire portfolio of activity, it also increases its dependency on suppliers as a whole, making it more vulnerable to expropriation by suppliers.

name: Domain diversity
authors_terms: ["domain diversity", "domain diversity across the firm's portfolio of outsourced projects"]
definition: By domain diversity, we mean the extent to which a firm's outsourced projects are distributed across many and relatively unrelated knowledge or capability domains. Domain diversity in the firm's outsourced projects in turn requires diversity in its suppliers' capabilities.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: Technological dynamism refers to the pace of technological change in the domains where the firm's outsourcing takes place; if underlying technologies are highly dynamic, implying rapid changes in the knowledge needed to execute outsourced projects, there is a higher probability that knowledge-based capabilities currently employed for the firm's outsourced tasks may become obsolete. The growth rate of patents in a technological domain measures the pace of innovation, which adds rapidly to the prior art and thus increases dynamism in the knowledge needed to carry out patent prosecution work within that domain.

name: Centralization
definition: Centralization determines whether the locus of decision-making authority lies in the higher or lower levels of a hierarchical relationship. It measures the relative influence or control exercised by the headquarters and the organizational unit in relevant decision-making processes.

name: Social interaction
definition: Social interaction provides channels for information exchange among members of an organization. Greater use of such channels implies increased access to peer organizational units and their resources.

name: Intraorganizational knowledge sharing
authors_terms: ["intraorganizational knowledge sharing", "interunit knowledge sharing", "intrafirm knowledge sharing", "knowledge sharing"]
definition: The sharing of technology or know-how between organizational units within the firm, captured by the units from which a unit received technology or know-how and by the units that came to that unit for new knowledge or expertise.

name: Interunit competition
definition: Two dimensions of interunit competition were identified in this research: (1) internal resource competition and (2) external market competition. Internal resource competition refers to the extent to which two units obtain resources from the same source; external market competition refers to the extent to which two units offer similar products or services in the marketplace.

name: Occupational focus of contacts
authors_terms: ["occupational focus of the contacts", "occupationally focused contacts", "number of occupations in the network", "Herfindahl index of contacts"]
definition: In this paper, I concentrate on the occupational focus of the contacts in the network as the key dimension of network range. The primary measure of occupational focus of the contacts in this study was the Number_of_occupations_in_the_network of a job seeker, with more occupations in the network taken to indicate lower occupational focus of the contacts.

name: Relationship depth
authors_terms: ["relationship depth", "average relationship depth", "depth of the relationship"]
definition: How deep a relationship is has to do with how affectively close, from an emotional intensity point of view, the ego feels relative to the contact.

name: Interaction frequency
definition: Time spent in the relationship has to do primarily with how often the parties interact, an indicator that is in turn related to how the two parties know each other and in what social contexts they interact.

name: Number of job types applied for
authors_terms: ["number of job types applied for", "types of jobs for which to apply", "job types pursued"]
definition: The efforts made in this stage result in a preliminary set of job types that the job seeker intends to pursue, which will be further refined subsequently as job seekers and recruiters engage in iterative decision making. For analyses pertaining to the selection of job types for which to apply (the first stage of the job search process), the dependent variable is Number_of_job_types_applied_for.

name: Interviews obtained
authors_terms: ["total number of interviews obtained", "number of interviews", "interviews obtained"]
definition: Once a job type description was entered, a follow-up question asked for the number of interviews and the number of offers received in the respective job type. For analyses pertaining to interviews obtained, the dependent variables are the Total_number_of_interviews_obtained and the Herfindahl_index_of_interviews.

name: Concentration of interviews across job types
authors_terms: ["Herfindahl index of interviews", "concentration of interviews across occupations"]
definition: The Herfindahl_index_of_interviews captures the extent to which the interviews obtained are concentrated in one or more job types and was used to investigate in more depth the effects of the contacts' occupational focus on job search success at the interviews stage.

name: Job offers obtained
definition: Following the interviews, the company will decide to either extend a job offer to the applicant or reject the applicant. For analyses of the offers obtained, the dependent variable is the Number_of_offers_obtained.

name: Specialist form identity
authors_terms: ["specialist form identity", "specialist organization", "specialist agency", "employment in specialist", "specialism"]
definition: A specialist is an organization with a sharp and focused identity whose limited-scope offerings are typically craft-produced on a small scale and tailored to specific tastes. The widespread image of specialists is of small, informally organized, nonhierarchical firms whose focused identities command strong appeal.

name: Voluntary turnover
definition: Individual voluntary turnover (or external mobility) took the value of 1 when an individual moved from one firm to another within the advertising industry in Korea, and 0 otherwise.

name: Promotion waiting time
authors_terms: ["promotion clock", "promotion waiting time", "waiting time to promotion", "time elapsed since last promotion"]
definition: The promotion clock is a duration variable counting the waiting time (in years) until promotion in the current firm; this 'clock' started with an individual's entry in the firm and was reset to zero each time he experienced a promotion or transitioned to a job with a new agency.

name: Industry experience
definition: Extended industry tenure reflects work experience that is both more general and more diverse, and is measured as the years an employee had worked in the industry.

name: Managerial rank
definition: Employee rank is based on the conventional seven-level position system in Korea, ranging from deputy general manager and manager to CEO, chairperson, or president.

name: Educational prestige
definition: Educational prestige is measured as the reputation of an employee's educational institution contemporaneously, based on elite university credentials that elicit a shared understanding of where an individual belongs in the labor market.

name: Shareholder value orientation espousal
authors_terms: ["espousal of a shareholder value orientation", "shareholder value orientation espousal", "public self-presentation"]
definition: A company's public self-presentation of identification with a shareholder value orientation, captured by coding its annual reports for statements indicating espousal of a shareholder value orientation.

name: Shareholder value orientation implementation
authors_terms: ["implementation of a shareholder value orientation", "commensurate governance practices", "structural changes"]
definition: The firms' adoption of three specific governance practices that are considered consistent with a shareholder value orientation: 'value-based' management control systems, stock option plans for management, and internationally accepted accounting standards.

name: Ownership by espousing German banks
authors_terms: ["German bank ownership level (espousing)", "ownership by German banks that have espoused a shareholder value orientation"]
definition: Block ownership of a firm's voting shares by German banks that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation, as opposed to banks that have not.

name: Ownership by espousing German non-financial firms
authors_terms: ["German firm ownership (espousing)", "ownership by other German firms that have espoused a shareholder value orientation"]
definition: Block ownership of a firm's voting shares by German non-financial firms that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation.

name: Ownership by pro-business German government
authors_terms: ["German government ownership level (pro-business)", "ownership by pro-business German federal or state government"]
definition: Block ownership of a firm's voting shares by federal or state government entities controlled by the pro-business conservative party or a party-led coalition.

name: Ownership by later-generation family owners
authors_terms: ["family ownership level (3rd or later generation)", "ownership by German families beyond the second generation"]
definition: Block ownership of a firm's voting shares by families beyond the founder's and second generation, whose interests are argued to differ from those of the founding generation.

name: CEO educational background
definition: The chief executive officer's field of formal education, distinguishing training in economics or law from training in other areas such as the humanities or the sciences.

name: CEO age
authors_terms: ["CEO age", "age of the firm's chief executive officer"]
definition: The age of the firm's chief executive officer, which is argued to shape rigidity, resistance to change and exposure to the traditional German governance orientation.

name: Ownership by espousing corporate owners
definition: Ownership by corporate owners such as banks and other firms that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation, in contrast to non-corporate owners such as governments and families.

name: Managerial predisposition
definition: The predisposition of a firm's top executives toward a shareholder value orientation, as indicated by the CEO's age and educational background.

name: Stakeholder relations
authors_terms: ["stakeholder relations", "good stakeholder relations", "stakeholder relations (aggregate)", "relations with its nonfinancial stakeholders", "good relations with its various stakeholders"]
definition: The stakeholders in this study include employees, customers, suppliers, and the community at large; a firm's good relations with its various stakeholders can be a valuable resource that may lead to performance advantages for the firm. An aggregate measure of stakeholder relations was computed incorporating the community relations, diversity, employee relations, environment, and product dimensions of the KLD data.

name: Persistence of superior financial performance
authors_terms: ["persistence of superior financial performance", "persistence of superior profits", "sustain their performance advantage", "persistence of superior financial performance"]
definition: A positive β1 indicates that the above-normal profits earned by firms with good stakeholder relations have a greater persistence rate, that is, the profits dissipate more slowly rather than converging immediately to the industry average.

name: Persistence of inferior financial performance
authors_terms: ["persistence of inferior financial performance", "persistence of inferior profits", "move out of a disadvantageous position", "recover from poor performance"]
definition: A negative β1 indicates a lower profit persistence rate, that is, firms with good stakeholder relations move out of inferior financial performance more quickly; already established good stakeholder relations help a firm to more quickly move out of a disadvantageous position.

name: Founding of SRI funds
authors_terms: ["SRI founding", "founding of SRI funds", "SRI fund foundings", "rise of SRI funds", "number of newly started SRI funds per country year"]
definition: SRI is a hybrid form of investing that incorporates non-financial concerns—such as environmental, moral, and social—into investment decisions. Following most organizational analysis on new venture creations, the authors modeled founding of SRI funds as an event count: the number of newly started SRI funds per country year.

name: Prevalence of the financial logic
authors_terms: ["prevalence of the financial logic", "prevalence of finance", "financial logic prevalence", "prevalence of the financial logic in society"]
definition: The greater prevalence of the financial logic in a country increases the probability that financial values, norms, and ends will be taken for granted and externalized as objective facts, not only in the financial field but in society more broadly. The financial logic has seeped into each country's institutional fabric to a different depth.

name: Union density
definition: The presence of unions represents not only an institutional force but also a set of organized actors who own financial assets and determine how they are invested. In the case of unions, the logic prioritizes workers' welfare over the goal of profit maximization.

name: Christianity
definition: In the case of Christianity, the end is salvation and social justice. Christian churches ''played a pioneering role in the development of SRI globally,'' even in countries in which it was a minority religion.

name: Green party representation
authors_terms: ["green parties", "green political parties", "strength of green parties", "representation of green parties in government"]
definition: In the case of green parties, the goal is ecological and environmental sustainability rather than making as much money as possible. The strength of green political parties represents an institutional force that is both cultural (affecting ecological sustainability) and coercive (tapping the power of the state).

name: Patent race loss
authors_terms: ["lost patent race", "firms with a lost race", "After Lost Race", "a lost race"]
definition: An application that is submitted earlier gets accepted while the later ones are rejected (or abandoned). We label the earlier patent applicants that obtain patent rights as 'firms with a winning patent race' and the later applicants that receive patent rejections as 'firms with a lost patent race.'

name: Technological innovation
definition: We measure firms' technological innovation as the number of patent applications in a given year. This measure enables us to evaluate the innovation of both public and private firms.

name: Public listing status
definition: We first focus on a firm's public stock market listing status in evaluating shareholders' investment horizon. Unlike private firms, public firms are obligated to regularly disclose their accounting information to the public through quarterly reports.

name: Transient institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["transient institutional ownership", "transient institutional investors", "ratio of transient institutional ownership"]
definition: Transient institutional investors are institutional investors with a relatively short investment horizon, characterized by high portfolio turnover and diversified portfolio holdings, compared to others (e.g., pension funds or insurance companies; Bushee, 1998). These transient institutional investors hold relatively smaller equity positions across many firms and tend to trade more frequently compared to other institutional investors.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality, a governance structure where an individual simultaneously serves as both the CEO and Chairman of the Board (Krause et al., 2014).

name: Free-riding
definition: Partners' effort-withholding in a joint endeavor, that is, the extent to which an organization is withholding effort from the alliance. The authors stress that they are interested in free-riding as effort-withholding behavior in general, and thus not only limited to opportunistic cases.

name: Perceived alliance effectiveness
authors_terms: ["perceived alliance effectiveness", "perception of alliance effectiveness", "perceptions of alliance effectiveness", "perceived consortium effectiveness"]
definition: Partners' subjective evaluations of the extent to which the overall alliance is achieving its goals and those of its key stakeholders; in this setting, the extent to which partners perceive that a network performs up to its potential in accomplishing its goals.

name: Perceived peers' collaboration
definition: The intensity of collaboration partners perceive among their peers, where peers are defined as other organizations belonging to the focal organization's same institutional sector (universities, firms, or government agencies).

name: Shared migration cohort ties
authors_terms: ["shared migration cohort ties", "shared ecosystem migration ties", "shared migration ties", "migration cohort ecosystem ties", "ecosystem ties"]
definition: Inventors who share contemporaneous experience at incumbent firms create unique relationships between the new ventures to which they migrate. Ventures related through inventors' common prior experiences create what the authors term a 'migration cohort effect,' with organizations sharing practices and characteristics by virtue of drawing from the same incumbent sources of human capital.

name: Knowledge overlap
definition: Knowledge Overlap captures the extent to which the two firms in the dyad build on common technology areas in their patented inventions.

name: Market overlap
definition: Market Overlap captures the extent to which new ventures in our sample operated in the same product markets in the biotech industry.

name: Alliance formation
definition: Alliances measures collaborative or cooperative activity between dyad firms. Formal alliances offer a direct path for new firms to gain access to needed knowledge resources from their ecosystem counterparts.

name: Direct inventor migration
authors_terms: ["Inventor Migration", "direct inventor migration", "inventor moves", "direct exchange through inventor migration"]
definition: Inventor Migration measures the total count of inventor moves between the focal and alter firm in each observation year. It is another way in which firms can gain access to the resources they need, through the hiring of new inventors.

name: Knowledge quality
definition: Knowledge Quality reflects the importance of an innovation and is measured as the number of patent forward citations by external organizations within five years after its application. Higher-quality knowledge is associated with greater usage and future recombination.

name: Prior collaboration between inventors
authors_terms: ["Employee Incumbent Collaboration", "prior collaboration", "direct prior collaboration", "prior interactions between inventors"]
definition: Direct prior collaboration at the incumbent firm between inventors who migrate to different new ventures. Prior collaborations directly connect inventors of the two firms, demonstrated through the concurrent listing of one or more individuals from each of the two firms as inventors on parent firm patents.

name: Team migration
authors_terms: ["Team Migration from Incumbent", "comobility", "team migration", "group mobility", "cluster hiring"]
definition: Past literature has referred to this phenomenon variously as comobility, group mobility, cluster hiring, or team migration. Team Migration from Incumbent was measured as the total number of teams of two or more inventors who were observed to migrate from an incumbent to the new venture in the year of observation.

name: Performance-aspirations correlation
authors_terms: ["Performance-aspirations correlation", "correlation between performance relative to historical and social aspirations", "feedback clarity/ambiguity"]
definition: The variable Performance-aspirations correlation is measured as a five-quarters' rolling correlation between the focal firm's performance relative to historical and social aspirations. Positive correlations imply that the focal firm's performance is either declining or increasing relative not only to its rivals but also to its own past performance; negative correlations indicate that performance is increasing relative to one aspiration level but declining relative to the other.

name: Firm responsiveness
definition: Our dependent variable is New product introductions, measured as the number of new phones introduced during each quarter in a year. New product introductions exemplify an adaptive response to feedback, since they enable firms to improve their performance and increase the chances for survival.

name: M-form structure implementation
definition: Williamson (1975) proposed that the M-form is a unique structural framework that overcomes problems of both internal and strategic control that confront large multiproduct firms. Internal control improves as the information-processing requirements of the chief executive decrease, and the separation of overall strategic control from operating control in an M-form structure reduces strategic control problems.

name: Rate of return
authors_terms: ["rate of return", "return on assets (ROA)", "efficiency as measured by rate of return"]
definition: Efficiency as measured by rate of return; the central performance measure used in this study was a time series of return on assets (ROA). Tables of adjusted return on asset means by strategy type, before and after M-form implementation, were used for the hypothesis tests.

name: Total firm risk
authors_terms: ["total firm risk", "risk", "variability of return", "variability in rate of return", "standard deviation of ROA"]
definition: The measure of risk was variance in the ROA time series, or the standard deviation, in the 10 years before and the 10 years after implementation. As used in this study, accounting-determined risk measures are indicators of total firm risk.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: Galbraith and Nathanson (1979) traced the evolution of the M-form structure to three major categories of corporate diversification strategy: vertical integration, related business diversification, and unrelated business diversification. Each strategy involves a different economic objective.

name: Employee-experienced high-involvement work system
definition: A HIWS refers to a set of HRM practices that are designed to promote employee empowerment, collective collaboration, and relational coordination. In this study, the authors focus on employees' actual HIWS experiences rather than managerial reports of a HIWS.

name: Homogeneity of HIWS experiences
authors_terms: ["the homogeneity of HIWS experiences", "homogeneity of employees' HIWS experiences"]
definition: The homogeneity of employees' HIWS experiences captures the extent to which employees present low variability in their HIWS experiences in the focal workplace; it reflects employees' consensus regarding their general experiences of HIWSs.

name: Strategic importance of innovation
authors_terms: ["the strategic importance of innovation", "the strategic value that an organization attaches to innovation"]
definition: The extent to which an organization attaches strategic importance to innovation, used to probe the extent to which collective efforts are channeled toward innovation; measured with items reflecting the importance of innovation to the workplace business strategy.

name: Churn in human resources
authors_terms: ["the churn in human resources", "human resource flow"]
definition: The total quantitative flow of human resources into and out of the focal organization, which is a fundamental means for organizations to reshape collective interactions for innovative changes in adapting to the dynamic environment.

name: Innovation
definition: Innovation is defined as the intentional introduction and application of new ideas, processes, products, or procedures.

name: Trust for the general manager
authors_terms: ["employee trust for the general manager", "trust for a business unit's general manager", "GM Trust", "trust for the GM"]
definition: The willingness of a party (trustor) to be vulnerable to the actions of another party (trustee) based on the expectation that trustee will perform an action important to the trustor, regardless of the trustor's ability to monitor or control the trustee (Mayer et al., 1995).

name: Sales
definition: Financial success, for most profit-oriented firms, can be assessed both in terms of 'top-line' (e.g., sales) as well as 'bottom-line' (e.g., profitability) measures.

name: Net profit
definition: PROFIT is a measure of operating profitability calculated by subtracting total operating expenses (direct and indirect) from gross revenue. It reflects the efficiency of the restaurant and the manager's ability to increase sales while controlling variable costs.

name: Employee turnover
definition: In the restaurant industry the turnover rate among employees can be an important indicator of organizational success. High levels of turnover are common in this industry, due in part to the low wages and the unpredictable work hours.

name: Perceived ability of the general manager
definition: Ability has been defined as that group of skills and attributes which enables a party to have influence within some specific situation.

name: Perceived benevolence of the general manager
definition: The trust literature describes benevolence as the extent to which the trustor perceives that the trustee intends to do good to the trustor in the relationship. Benevolence represents a positive personal orientation of the trustee to the trustor.

name: Perceived integrity of the general manager
definition: An employee's perception of the GM's integrity involves the employee's belief that the GM adheres to a set of principles that the employee finds acceptable. Such factors as consistency, a reputation for honesty, and fairness all contribute to the employee's perception of GM integrity.

name: Partner human-capital leveraging
authors_terms: ["human-capital leveraging", "partner human-capital leveraging", "leverage ratio", "leveraging expert human resources"]
definition: A human-capital deployment strategy in which partners with a high level of expert knowledge work with a team of associate professionals, delegating less complex work to less experienced employees; the degree to which a firm leverages its partners is measured as the leverage ratio, the number of associates a firm employs per partner at a point in time.

name: Service diversification
authors_terms: ["service diversification", "diversification into new practice areas", "diversification strategy"]
definition: Given the highly specialized nature of legal practice areas, which is reflected by lifetime specialization in one or a few legal practice area(s) and departmentalization in law firms, a firm's participation in more than one area of legal practice area is regarded as service diversification.

name: Geographical diversification
definition: Geographical diversification can be a value-creating strategy for professional service firms because their typical clients such as Fortune 500 firms are geographically diversified and need service in multiple locations; it is measured by the Herfindahl index where p is the percentage of professionals in each local office.

name: Lateral hiring of associates
authors_terms: ["lateral hiring", "ratio of lateral hiring for associates", "lateral hiring ratio for associates", "human-capital development strategy"]
definition: Human-capital development strategy reflects the extent to which a firm relies on internal development of human capital vs. acquiring human capital through lateral hiring of professionals from other firms.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Firm profitability as the dependent variable is measured by annual profit dollars per partner; because partners are residual claimants in the law firm, this measure of performance is similar to the return on equity ratio.

name: Corporate environmental legitimacy
definition: Extending Suchman's (1995: 574) definition of legitimacy, we defined corporate environmental legitimacy as the generalized perception or assumption that a firm's corporate environmental performance is desirable, proper, or appropriate.

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: 'Unsystematic risk' reflects the variability in a firm's stock price associated with events that primarily affect only that firm. A firm's unsystematic risk is generally measured through the unexplained portion, or error term, of the expected returns for a stock after the firm's systematic risk has been accounted for.

name: Disclosure of environmental liabilities
authors_terms: ["disclosure of environmental liabilities", "voluntarily disclosing environmental liabilities"]
definition: A defensive impression management tactic in which the firm voluntarily discloses information about its own environmental liabilities; at the time of an environmental infraction the extent of the firm's liability is often unclear, which gives the firm flexibility about what to report and when.

name: Expression of environmental commitment
definition: To manage impressions, a firm can convey information regarding changes to its products or processes that demonstrate its commitment to the natural environment; this represents an accommodative impression management tactic.

name: Product diversification growth
authors_terms: ["product diversification growth", "growth along the product dimension", "Δ product scope"]
definition: The dependent variables capture growth in product and international diversification. Product diversification growth (Δ PD) was calculated as (Noncore business sales t+4 - Noncore business sales t)/Total sales t).

name: International diversification growth
authors_terms: ["international diversification growth", "growth along the international dimension", "Δ international scope"]
definition: International diversification growth (Δ ID) was calculated as (Foreign sales t+4 - Foreign sales t)/Total sales t). These measures reflect growth along the product and international dimensions over a four-year period.

name: Prior diversification experience
authors_terms: ["prior diversification experience", "diversification experience", "levels of diversification experience"]
definition: We created four subsamples based on a firm's levels of product and international diversification in the first year it enters our sample. These initial levels of diversification capture a firm's prior experience in product and international diversification.

name: Product diversification experience
authors_terms: ["product diversification experience", "prior product diversification experience", "initial product diversification level"]
definition: Experience in product diversification involves the accumulation of multiindustry-specific upstream resources capabilities, which are typically geographically fungible and more likely to be leveraged in subsequent diversification. The initial level of product diversification in the first year a firm enters the sample captures its prior experience with product diversification.

name: International diversification experience
authors_terms: ["international diversification experience", "prior international diversification experience", "initial international diversification level"]
definition: Diversification experience involves the accumulation of specialized resources and capabilities that are specific to particular settings. The initial level of international diversification in the first year a firm enters the sample captures its prior experience with international diversification.

name: Attention to own experience
authors_terms: ["attention to own experience", "relative attention to the own experience reference point", "attention to its own experience", "w1it"]
definition: We merge own prior aspiration and own prior performance into a single own experience reference point. The amount of relative attention is represented by the weights of these reference points in the adaptive aspiration formula; the larger the weight of a reference point, the more relative attention it receives, and the more sensitive the organization is to that reference point.

name: Attention to the political reference point
authors_terms: ["attention to the political reference point", "relative attention to the political reference point", "attention to the political reference group", "w2it"]
definition: The amount of relative attention is represented by the weights of these reference points in the adaptive aspiration formula, and the larger the weight of a reference point, the more relative attention it receives. The political reference point is the performance of sister divisions, and w2 = γ3 measures the attention allocated to it.

name: Attention to the economic reference point
authors_terms: ["attention to the economic reference point", "relative attention to the economic reference point", "attention to the economic reference group", "w3it"]
definition: The amount of relative attention is represented by the weights of these reference points in the adaptive aspiration formula. The economic reference point is the performance of external market rivals, and w3 = γ4 measures the attention allocated to it.

name: Political reference point
authors_terms: ["political reference point", "PR", "publisher average performance", "political reference group"]
definition: This results in a second social reference group for each division, the political reference group consisting of sister divisions, and the associated political reference point representing the performance of sister divisions.

name: Economic reference point
authors_terms: ["economic reference point", "ER", "category average performance", "economic reference group"]
definition: Extant empirical studies have largely assumed an entire population of external marketplace competitors as the reference group, which we call the economic reference group, and the mean or median performance of this reference group as the social reference point, which we call the economic reference point.

name: Consistent feedback above both social reference points
authors_terms: ["consistent feedback above both social reference points", "consistent feedback above", "cell 1", "consistent above"]
definition: Consistent feedback from social comparisons includes two cases. First is when comparisons with both economic and political reference points indicate that the focal division outperforms these two reference points, which we term consistent feedback above both social reference points.

name: Consistent feedback below both social reference points
authors_terms: ["consistent feedback below both social reference points", "consistent feedback below", "cell 4", "consistent below"]
definition: The other case is when the focal division underperforms both reference points, which we term consistent feedback below both social reference points.

name: Inconsistent feedback below the political reference point
authors_terms: ["below political reference point", "cell 2", "below publisher average", "inconsistent social feedback"]
definition: Inconsistent social feedback occurs when a division of a multidivisional firm outperforms the economic reference point yet underperforms the political reference point, or vice versa.

name: Inconsistent feedback below the economic reference point
authors_terms: ["below economic reference point", "cell 3", "below category average", "inconsistent social feedback"]
definition: Inconsistent social feedback occurs when a division of a multidivisional firm outperforms the economic reference point yet underperforms the political reference point, or vice versa.

name: Strong ties
definition: Tie strength is defined by Granovetter as a combination of the amount of time, the emotional intensity, the intimacy and the reciprocal services that characterize the tie. For interorganizational horizontal alliances the authors measure tie strength by the frequency of interaction between partners and their level of resource commitment to the relationship.

name: Weak ties
definition: Granovetter argues that weak ties are conduits across which an actor can access novel information, and they are more likely than strong ties to be local bridges to distant others possessing unique information. In this study weak ties are alliances that require a substantially smaller resource commitment and are closer in nature to an arm's length transaction.

name: Ego network density
definition: Local density examines the interconnectedness of relationships among a focal firm's direct partners. In an egocentric network it is usual to disregard the focal agent and his or her direct contacts, concentrating only on the links which exist among these contacts.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was operationalized as return on assets (ROA).

name: Exploitation and exploration environment
authors_terms: ["exploitation/exploration environments", "environments demanding relatively high investments in exploration", "environmental uncertainty", "industry context"]
definition: Firms facing a high degree of environmental uncertainty will need to invest more in exploring new opportunities and innovations than firms facing stable environments in which they can allocate more resources to exploit existing technologies. The authors examine firms (and their networks) in two industries exhibiting different degrees of environmental uncertainty in order to investigate embeddedness effects across contexts requiring different mixes of exploration and exploitation.

name: Organizational dissolution
authors_terms: ["organizational dissolution", "dissolution", "exit from the market", "risk of organizational dissolution"]
definition: Following Boone et al. (2000) and Phillips (2002), the authors define dissolution as exit from the market, without distinguishing between bankruptcy and merger or acquisition; it encompasses the case in which a firm disappears because its owners are no longer listed in the Certified Professional Accountant (CPA) directories and the case of dissolution by acquisition or merger.

name: Collective interfirm mobility of key members
definition: The authors define a group as consisting of two or more partners who leave their employer and wind up working together for another firm, whether an incumbent or a start-up. They argue that collective departure is more conducive to holistic replication of routines because preexisting systems of coordinated roles can be maintained.

name: Joint experience of departing members
authors_terms: ["average joint experience", "average number of years that the departing members spent together", "joint experience of departing members"]
definition: The accumulation of a common mind-set is subject to time compression diseconomies because compliance with or attachment to certain routines depends on the amount of time spent together. The measure is the average number of years that the departing members spent together before their exit.

name: Destination firm type
authors_terms: ["type of destination: incumbent or a newly founded organization", "newly founded firm", "incumbent firm", "start-up"]
definition: The classification of the destination firm as an established (incumbent) or an entrepreneurial (newly founded) organization. Incumbents exhibit an array of routines that become imprinted early on and therefore resist the import of extramural routines, whereas in newly founded firms no truce is under threat and replication faces no internal resistance.

name: Destination co-location
authors_terms: ["location of destination: same province or different province", "co-located competitors", "within/outside province"]
definition: Whether or not the source and the destination firms are co-located, that is, whether the migrating members move to a competitor located in the same province as the source firm or in a different one. When actors share the same context, existing patterns of interaction become geographically embedded, and replication of routines is more likely to succeed.

name: Imitation
authors_terms: ["imitation", "entry of an imitative product", "release of an imitative product"]
definition: The release of a competing product derived from the original; the launch of an imitative product represents an attention-triggering event, which spills over to the original.

name: Horizontal imitation
definition: When an imitative product is horizontally differentiated with respect to its original counterpart, it appeals to a slightly different set of consumers and consumer needs, but its quality and price are comparable with the original.

name: Vertically superior imitation
definition: When the imitative product is vertically differentiated with respect to the original, the imitative product offers a different price-quality trade-off compared to the original product, but they target the same set of consumers - that is, consumers with similar tastes. When a vertically differentiated imitative product offers a better price-quality trade-off, then consumers overwhelmingly prefer that imitative product.

name: Product awareness
definition: We measured product awareness based on the number of views that a product page received. Product views are counted when a user navigates to the page of a particular product.

name: Product demand
definition: We measured product demand based on the number of times a product was printed (that is, a user downloaded the design file and printed it). Even though products may be freely available, the printing of products is an indicator of product demand.

name: Original product popularity
authors_terms: ["well-known product", "ex-ante popularity of the original product", "how well-known a product is"]
definition: How well-known the original product is when the imitative product is released. When an original product is already well-known and a larger fraction of consumers are already aware of it, the marginal increase in awareness of the original product would be weaker.

name: Horizontal diversification
definition: Diversification is assumed to be exogenous but rational: "firms only diversify if they expect synergies to be greater than incremental costs" (P80). In this setting, taxicab fleets diversified into the limousine market during the early 1990s following entry deregulation (P107).

name: Outsourcing
definition: The authors assume that "firms outsource, or vertically disintegrate, when the costs of integration exceed the costs of using markets or long-term contracts to govern a transaction" (P16). Outsourcing shifts decision rights and employees outside the firm, relaxing monitoring, influence and social comparison costs (P93).

name: Task differentiation
authors_terms: ["task diversity", "task differentiation", "task differentiation between taxicabs and limousines"]
definition: Task diversity is "the variation in a firm's physical or intellectual production processes" (P96). The authors measure it with local market population density, because in dense urban markets taxicabs and limousines follow different processes to locate and service rides while in less urban markets limousines are essentially taxicabs painted black (P124).

name: Common ownership
authors_terms: ["common ownership", "common institutional ownership", "common owners", "common institutional owners", "CIO"]
definition: We consider common owners as investors that simultaneously own shares in two or more firms in the same industry. It is a structural property of an investor's holdings, not a particular type of investor.

name: Long-term common ownership
authors_terms: ["long-term common owners", "long-term common ownership", "dedicated CIO", "quasi-index CIO"]
definition: We define long-term common owners as those with stable portfolios that hold positions in companies for long periods of time. Using the classification of Bushee (1998), prior studies classify long-term investors as dedicated and quasi-index institutional investors, both of which have long holding periods.

name: Short-term common ownership
definition: We consider long-term investors as those Bushee classifies as dedicated and quasi-index and short-term investors as those classified as transient.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR refers to the voluntary integration of social and environmental practices in a firm's operations. Firms that embrace CSR commit to internalizing social and environmental concerns, for instance, by developing practices and policies to curb climate change or enhance social equality.

name: CSR strengths
definition: We also separate this measure into strengths (CSR strengths) and concerns (CSR concerns) by taking the sum of the respective indices across the six categories.

name: CSR concerns
definition: We also separate this measure into strengths (CSR strengths) and concerns (CSR concerns) by taking the sum of the respective indices across the six categories.

name: Financially material CSR
definition: Financially material CSR ('material CSR') refers to CSR issues that are most value-relevant for firm financial performance. The financial materiality of a CSR issue depends on how central it is to the industry.

name: Financially immaterial CSR
definition: Financially immaterial CSR ('immaterial CSR') refers to CSR issues that are unlikely to produce financial value.

name: Stakeholder sensitive industry
definition: We refer to these as stakeholder sensitive industries and theorize that they manifest in two distinct ways: industries where stakeholder trust and corporate reputation are most valuable for business, and industries where regulators respond strongly to errant behaviors.

name: Domestic mindset breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth", "breadth of domestic mindsets", "broad mindsets", "relational or horizontal complexity"]
