definition: Breadth, also called relational or horizontal complexity, reflects diversity and heterogeneity of viewpoints embedded in a mindset. Broad mindsets accommodate multiple and varied dominant logics and world views.

name: Domestic mindset depth
authors_terms: ["depth", "depth of domestic mindsets", "depth-oriented mindsets", "cognitive or vertical complexity"]
definition: Depth, also referred to as cognitive or vertical complexity, represents the level of expertise, sophistication, and specialization within a single dominant logic.

name: Early international performance
definition: The international performance of a firm's first international activities. In the internationalization literature, the commonly accepted goals include efficiency, market growth, and risk reduction.

name: International industry conditions
authors_terms: ["international industry conditions", "global industry conditions", "global integration-local adaptation", "global industries", "multidomestic industries", "transnational industries"]
definition: We use the integration-responsiveness (IR) framework to classify international industries into global, multidomestic, and transnational. Global industries have standardized and uniform markets with a high potential for economies of scale; multidomestic industries have diverse and fragmented markets that offer few opportunities for economies of scale; transnational industries offer opportunities for global integration in some areas but require local responsiveness in others.

name: Ease of knowledge transfer
definition: Knowledge transfer represents a cost to the source of knowledge, in terms of time and effort spent helping others to understand the source's knowledge. The dependent variable in this study is the ease of knowledge transfer from a source to a recipient, assessed by the source.

name: Common knowledge
definition: The knowledge that two individuals have in common, which can stem from formal training inside or outside of an organization, from shared social characteristics, or from common areas of expertise inside the organization. It is easier for knowledge to transfer from the source to a recipient when the source and the recipient have knowledge in common.

name: Tie strength
definition: The strength of an interpersonal connection, which affects how easily knowledge is transferred; respondents indicated the intensity of their connection with each contact in terms of emotional closeness and communication frequency.

name: Knowledge codifiability
definition: Codifiability represents "the degree to which knowledge can be encoded." Tacitness is the degree to which knowledge is difficult to codify (e.g., in writing) or articulate.

name: Social cohesion
definition: Cohesion refers to the extent to which a relationship is surrounded by strong third-party connections. Network density measures the presence of strong third-party ties around a connection.

name: Network range
definition: Network range is the prevalence of ties that cross institutional, organizational, or social boundaries (Burt, 1992: 148-149). Range measures the distribution of connections across different areas of expertise.

name: Board political ideology
authors_terms: ["board political ideology", "board conservatism", "board ideology", "the board's ideological central tendency"]
definition: Directors' political ideologies, specifically the board-level average of how conservative or liberal directors are; the authors view board ideology as the board's ideological central tendency, so that a board's decisions represent the pooled outcome of directors' ideological preferences.

name: Compensation committee political ideology
authors_terms: ["compensation committee conservatism", "board conservatism (compensation committee)", "the prevailing ideology of the compensation committee"]
definition: The prevailing political ideology of the directors serving on the compensation committee, the group of independent directors explicitly responsible for designing and recommending a pay plan to the rest of the board.

name: Non-committee director political ideology
authors_terms: ["board conservatism (other directors)", "the conservatism level of the remainder of the board"]
definition: The conservatism level of the remainder of the board, i.e., the directors who do not serve on the compensation committee.

name: CEO pay
authors_terms: ["CEO pay", "CEO annual pay", "overall CEO pay", "total ex ante amount of compensation"]
definition: TDC1 reflects the total value of all salary, bonus, restricted stock grants, option grants, performance share grants, and other income paid to a CEO in a given year t.

name: Recent financial performance
authors_terms: ["recent financial performance", "recent performance", "recent accounting performance", "recent market performance"]
definition: Recent financial performance was assessed using two common measures of accounting and market performance, namely return on assets and total shareholder return.

name: Israeli state
authors_terms: ["Israeli state", "establishment of the Israeli state", "formation of the State of Israel", "state formation"]
definition: Following Rueschemeyer and Evans, the authors define the state as "a set of organizations invested with the authority to make binding decisions for people and organizations juridically located in a particular territory and to implement these decisions using, if necessary, force." The state is an organizational actor that supplies institutions which smooth exchange.

name: Federation membership
definition: "We use the term federation to describe such a corporate actor" - a corporate actor given the right to regulate, which can establish rules of exchange and punish violators. The Histadrut's direct influence over the coops ran through the Merkaz Hakooperatzia (Cooperative Center); membership in the Merkaz was voluntary for coops and provided automatic membership in the Histadrut and access to its services.

name: Organizational failure
authors_terms: ["coop failure", "failure rate of coops", "hazard rate of failure"]
definition: "We modeled coop failure using r(t), the instantaneous risk of failing. This hazard rate of failure is defined as the limiting probability of a failure between t and t + Δt, given that the coop was operating at t."

name: Bank population growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the bank population", "bank density", "commercial banks"]
definition: Banks are key resource suppliers throughout the economic system and are described as "ideal-type representatives of capitalist ideology, in contrast to the socialism of the coops."

name: Credit cooperative population growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the credit cooperative population", "credit-cooperative density", "credit cooperatives"]
definition: "Credit cooperatives are cooperative financial institutions, the socialist analogs of banks." In Israel they emphasized supporting cooperative organizations and the little man and helping borrowers neglected by commercial banks.

name: Kibbutz population growth
definition: "Kibbutzim have been the economic and ideological leaders of the Israeli cooperative sector." They played an important role in the Israeli economy and in Israeli politics.

name: Fleet safety
authors_terms: ["fleet safety", "fleet accident rate", "hull-loss rate", "media tenor", "safety goal variables"]
definition: Fleet safety is the safety goal variable in this study and is measured with both objective and subjective indicators: the airline-specific fleet accident rate, which 'represents the average hull-loss risk of all aircraft in the focal airline's fleet that year,' and the net media tenor of the models in the fleet, taken as representing the degree to which the focal aircraft is perceived positively.

name: Profitability relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["ROA relative to aspirations", "ROA - AL", "ROA below AL", "profitability goal", "return on assets (ROA)"]
definition: Profitability performance is captured as return on assets relative to an aspiration level calculated as the weighted average of a social aspiration level (industry mean) and a historical aspiration level (exponentially discounted past ROA). The main purpose of the profitability goal variable is to distinguish firms with high and low profitability to test Hypotheses 2a and 2b.

name: Airplane sales
definition: Airline fleet changes as measured via Airplane sales, which is a count of the aircraft sold in the focal year.

name: Airplane purchases
definition: Airline fleet changes as measured via Airplane buys, which is a count of the aircraft bought in the focal year.

name: Foreign-based competition
authors_terms: ["foreign-based competition", "core industry import penetration", "import penetration", "foreign competition"]
definition: Foreign competition in the form of imports we label foreign-based competition. Foreign-based competition can be both stronger in its effects and more disruptive than domestic-based competition, and it can therefore have significantly greater economic and competitive ramifications for a country's domestic markets.

name: Level of firm diversification
authors_terms: ["level of firm diversification", "level of diversification", "extent of diversification"]
definition: The level of firm diversification is the extent of a firm's diversity across its activities, measured by three of the most commonly used measures of portfolio diversity: total entropy, the Herfindahl index, and the number of SIC business segments. The measures are calculated using annual data on a firm's sales in each of its 4-digit SIC business segments.

name: Resource-based relatedness
authors_terms: ["resource-based relatedness", "resource-based relatedness among the businesses within a firm's portfolio", "portfolio interrelationships"]
definition: Critical to the construct of resource-based relatedness is the ability to capture underlying economies of scope that determine the strategic interrelationships among businesses. It captures portfolio relatedness based on patterns of technology flows among manufacturing industries and does not rely on the hierarchical nature of the SIC system.

name: Core industry attractiveness
authors_terms: ["economic attractiveness of the core industry", "attractiveness of a firm's core business industry", "core industry growth", "core industry profitability"]
definition: The economic attractiveness of a firm's core industry is operationalized using two measures: industry growth and industry profitability. A core business located in a more attractive industry provides the firm with more favorable economic structural attributes that can provide greater profit potential.

name: Core business profitability
definition: Core business profitability reflects the financial profitability of the firm's core business and is measured as the ratio of operating profit to revenues in the firm's 4-digit SIC core business.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured as the firm's return on assets (ROA). ROA is a widely employed measure of performance and has been shown to be related to a variety of other indicators of a firm's financial performance.

name: Income growth uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty of income growth", "income growth uncertainty", "uncertainty of employee income growth", "income uncertainty"]
definition: Managers commonly anticipate changes in future income based on their previous experience; major variation of income growth within a firm in the past implies that managers cannot easily predict future changes, making future income growth uncertain. Uncertainty of income growth implies that it is difficult for the manager to predict future income.

name: Degree of monitoring
definition: The degree of monitoring within a firm, which is an important form of organizational control when tasks carried out by managers cannot be completely defined or evaluated. A larger distance between headquarters and branches increases the difficulty of carrying out inspections.

name: Middle manager involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement of middle managers in allocation", "greater involvement of middle managers in the allocation process", "middle managers are more involved in ATM allocations than in branch allocations"]
definition: The extent to which middle managers, rather than senior executives, participate in decisions about the allocation of a resource. Greater involvement of middle managers in the allocation process increases information asymmetry because senior decision makers typically have limited information about activity conducted at lower levels of the organization.

name: Resource allocation
authors_terms: ["resource allocation", "allocation of resources", "increased allocation of resources"]
definition: Resource allocation within a firm can be conceptualized as a process in which a principal procures information from managers (agents) and then allocates resources to these managers. Allocation of resources to a manager can increase the manager's visibility within the firm.

name: Conditions for increasing allocation
authors_terms: ["favorable conditions", "moderately favorable conditions", "highly favorable conditions", "unfavorable conditions"]
definition: Combinations of income growth uncertainty and degree of monitoring that create favorable or unfavorable conditions for managers to increase allocation of resources within firms. A combination of low uncertainty with high monitoring creates the most unfavorable condition, a combination of high uncertainty with low monitoring creates the most favorable condition, and combining high uncertainty with high monitoring or low uncertainty with low monitoring creates moderately favorable conditions.

name: Managerial net benefits from allocation
authors_terms: ["net benefits for managers", "net benefits of increasing allocation", "personal benefits"]
definition: The net benefits for managers will be higher when an increased allocation improves managerial visibility but also poses only limited risks of loss when allocations fail to yield intended results for the firm. Managers are likely to derive lower benefits for individual action in state-owned banks compared to privately owned banks.

name: Slack resources
definition: The amount of capital banks possess to absorb losses before turning insolvent; higher capital adequacy ratio implies that a bank has more slack.

name: New firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance of new firms", "firm performance", "new firm performance"]
definition: The performance of new firms is assessed with two dependent variables. Survival is the most commonly used dependent variable in studies assessing the performance of new firms, measured as the age of the firm at failure or at the end of the sample (or observation) window; the authors also tested all of their hypotheses using the natural logarithm of sales as an additional dependent variable.

name: Horizontal employee kin ties
authors_terms: ["horizontal employee kin ties", "Horizontal employee kin (ratio)", "horizontal employee kin"]
definition: Kin ties between employees at the same hierarchical level; in new firms, kin ties between employees can significantly alter the overall proportion of kin ties, and the continuous measure is the ratio of the number of such kin to the number of employees.

name: Vertical founder-employee kin ties
authors_terms: ["vertical founder - employee kin ties", "Vertical founder - employee kin"]
definition: Kin ties between a founder and an initial employee; the continuous measure is the ratio of the number of such kin to the number of all initial members (founders and employees) of the new firm.

name: Horizontal founder kin ties
definition: Kin ties between founders; the continuous measure is the ratio of the number of such kin to the number of founders.

name: Explicit rejection of a submitted idea
definition: An explicit rejection is an organization's notification to a newcomer that a submitted idea has not been selected for implementation, delivered by changing the idea's status so that the newcomer is informed and the idea is publicly labeled as rejected. It can be given with or without an additional explanation.

name: Explanation accompanying a rejection
definition: A rejection with an explanation provides more information than the outcome of the organization's decision, explaining why an idea was rejected. It signals to newcomers that the organization is interested not only in their ideas but also in developing relationships with them.

name: Content match between idea and rejection explanation
authors_terms: ["match in terms of informational content", "content match", "First idea rejected - explanation matches idea content"]
definition: The degree to which the explanation accompanying a rejection matches a newcomer's first idea in terms of informational content, i.e., whether the explanation indicates that the organization is focused on the same issues as the contributor. Such a match signals to newcomers that the organization is focused on the same kinds of issues.

name: Linguistic style match between idea and rejection explanation
authors_terms: ["match in terms of linguistic style", "linguistic style match", "First idea rejected - explanation matches idea style"]
definition: The degree to which the explanation accompanying a rejection is written in the same linguistic style as the newcomer's first idea. The shared usage of the same linguistic style signals a match and may make newcomers feel a bond even when their ideas are rejected.

name: Continued interaction with the organization
authors_terms: ["continued interaction", "willingness to continue to interact", "willingness to submit further ideas"]
definition: Whether a newcomer continues to interact with an organization, that is, whether a newcomer ever contributes a second idea to the organization. Newcomers' willingness to continue to interact is the outcome that the feedback they receive is argued to affect.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity defines the degree to which the assets in an exchange are more valuable in their current application than in their next best use. In semiconductor production the most relevant specific assets are the specialized reporting structures, information systems, and technical dialogue required to achieve coordination and adaptation between product design and manufacturing activities.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty refers to the degree to which unanticipated environmental changes alter the conditions underlying an exchange. The measure is designed to capture managers' perceptions regarding unanticipated shifts in the demand for a specific type of semiconductor device.

name: Fabrication experience
authors_terms: ["fabrication experience", "production experience", "experience using the relevant process technology"]
definition: Production experience provides learning opportunities that enhance a firm's production capabilities; such experientially derived capabilities improve subsequent production along a given trajectory in terms of both efficiency and technical performance. As a result, production experience is likely to enhance the likelihood that a firm will choose internal governance along a given technological trajectory.

name: Sourcing experience
definition: Greater sourcing experience also helps build dyad- and market-level capabilities that may enhance a firm's ability to engage in a successful sourcing partnership. Greater sourcing experience is likely to aid in the development of organizational routines that allow firms to efficiently collaborate with a broad array of partners.

name: Product-market diversification
definition: The variable is designed to measure the extent to which a firm is able to hedge against demand uncertainty and technological obsolescence by switching the use of its existing production technology across product-markets. Product-market diversification also imparts the firm with a portfolio of valuable options.

name: Vertical integration
definition: The governance outcome is whether a firm chooses to fabricate a particular product within the firm or through a contractual (alternate sourcing) relationship. The unit of analysis is the production decision, observed as a make (1) or buy (0) choice.

name: State ownership
definition: Shares held by government agencies and large state-owned enterprises. The authors state that higher remaining levels of state ownership indicate a more persistent state socialism institutional logic still existing in the firm.

name: Legal-person ownership
definition: Shares owned by a limited set of private-sector actors - typically large block holders with a long-term strategic interest in the firm. The authors state that the depth of the market capitalism logic's penetration and the power of its proponent coalition are reflected by the firm's number of legal-person shares outstanding.

name: Directors' state experience
authors_terms: ["proportion of directors with state experience", "board members with state experience", "directors with state experience"]
definition: Board members who have worked for the state in any capacity, currently or previously; the authors state that it is probably safe to view directors with state experience as being more influenced by the logic of state socialism than other directors.

name: Directors' stock ownership
authors_terms: ["proportion of directors owning stock", "proportion of board members who own stock in the firm"]
definition: The share of board members who hold stock in the focal firm. The authors state that stock market participation indicates acceptance of the market capitalism logic and that shareholding board members are its most reliable supporters.

name: Market-oriented acquisitions
definition: Market-oriented acquisitions are defined as acquisitions initiated by the firm. Their targets were firms believed to be capable of providing economic returns to the acquirer, and hence they are not motivated by state objectives, though they may still be done by partially-privatized SOEs.

name: Cumulative abnormal return
definition: The cumulative abnormal return around an M&A announcement, computed using the CAPM method over short event windows around the announcement day. Stock market returns represent the market's assessment of changes in firm value, so they also reflect whether investors believe that a firm's actions are beneficial.

name: Time period of transition
definition: In late twentieth-century China, the power of both institutional logics changed over time as market capitalism became more accepted and more ingrained in the national economy. The authors examine whether the effects differ between an 'early' and a 'later' time period.

name: State socialism coalition power
definition: Power of the coalition advocating state socialism; proxied by state ownership and directors with state experience.

name: Market capitalism coalition power
definition: Power of the coalition advocating market capitalism; proxied by legal-person ownership and directors owning stock.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissism is a multidimensional, multifaceted, and multicontextual concept that is sometimes identified as a personality disorder in psychiatry, but is examined as a personality characteristic that varies across individuals in much of the social psychology and organizational behavior literature. Narcissists possess an extreme need for self-enhancement, which manifests in grandiose self-promotion, unrealistic optimism, and self-entitlement.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is assessed with market-based measures: the one-year buy-hold return from the start of the crisis captures performance immediately after the crisis, while cumulative yearly unsystematic returns capture the effects of strategic actions over the postcrisis period. Cumulative effects of CEO actions on yearly unsystematic returns (8 quarters prior to start of crises and 12 quarters after start of crises) should be assessed over time to test Hypothesis 2.

name: Response to competitive entry
definition: In this study the responses of firms are measured by their change in price after an entry has occurred in one of their markets. Each type of response is included in the study: do nothing, defend, counterattack, and total war.

name: Market dependency
definition: Market dependency is the degree to which a firm is dependent on any particular market (Karnani and Wernerfelt, 1985; Porter, 1985).

name: Barriers to entry
definition: If entry barriers into the market are high, such as significant brand loyalties or economies of scale, then the defend strategy should be chosen. High entry barriers imply that it would be relatively expensive for the attacking firm to overcome the barriers in the first place.

name: Synergy
definition: Synergy is the ability of a firm to capitalize on its multimarket setting (Ansoff, 1965). High synergy motivates a firm to defend that market.

name: Sustainable capacity
authors_terms: ["sustainable capacity", "sustainable capacity to maintain its response"]
definition: Sustainable capacity is the ability of a firm to participate in a competitive action, such as a price cut or redeployment of resources, initiated by a new competitor (Edwards, 1955). In this study sustainable capacity is measured as the physical and financial capacity of an airline (Fruhan, 1972).

name: Stock market perception of firm riskiness
authors_terms: ["stock market's perception of firm riskiness", "riskiness", "stock beta"]
definition: Another measure, Value Line's stock beta for 1984, is employed to measure the stock market's perception of riskiness for each firm.

name: Bilateral communication
definition: The first dimension of procedural justice is the extent to which bilateral communication exists between managers of head offices and subsidiary units involved in global strategic decision making.

name: Ability to refute
definition: The second dimension of procedural justice is the extent to which subsidiary units can legitimately challenge and refute the strategic views of head office managers.

name: Local familiarity
definition: The third dimension of procedural justice is the extent to which head office managers are well informed and familiar with the local conditions of subsidiary units.

name: Provision of an account
authors_terms: ["provision of an account", "explanation for the final decisions of the head office"]
definition: The fourth dimension of procedural justice is the extent to which subsidiary units are provided a full account for the final strategic decisions of the head office.

name: Consistency of decision making procedures
definition: The last dimension of procedural justice is the extent to which head offices do not discriminate but apply consistent decision making procedures across subsidiary units.

name: Global learning
definition: Global learning refers to the extent to which the creation, adoption, and diffusion of knowledge and expertise occurs within and across the nodes of the multinational's global network of operations.

name: Balancing global efficiency and local responsiveness
authors_terms: ["balancing global efficiency and local responsiveness", "balancing of global and local perspectives", "balancing global and local"]
definition: Perhaps the global strategic objective receiving the most attention in the literature is the need for multinationals to strike a balance between global efficiency and local responsiveness in their global strategies.

name: Global strategic renewal
definition: The global strategic objective of strategic renewal refers to the multinational's ability to overcome the tendency toward the mere replication of past successful strategic moves and hence toward strategic complacency despite new conditions and changes in the global environment.

name: Rapid global strategic decision making
authors_terms: ["rapid global strategic decision making", "rapid global decision making", "speed of strategic decision making"]
definition: This high velocity of environmental change has placed a premium on rapid global strategic decision making, pushing this to the forefront of multinationals' global strategic objectives.

name: Corporate activism
authors_terms: ["corporate activism", "advocacy giving", "corporate advocacy giving", "Giving by a focal firm"]
definition: Corporate advocacy giving is a channel whereby firms take a stand on sociopolitical issues by donating to advocacy nonprofits. Unlike traditional corporate social responsibility, corporate activism targets issues characterized by ideological contention.

name: Ideological opponents' activism
authors_terms: ["giving by ideological opponents", "activism of ideological opponents", "ideological opponents' activism"]
definition: The giving from firms whose employees hold dissimilar ideology to a focal firm is used as a proxy for the giving from the firm's ideological opponents, promoting an opposing stance to what its employees will value. Giving by Ideological Opponents is defined as red competitors' giving for a focal blue firm versus blue competitors' giving for a focal red firm.

name: Other competitors' activism
definition: Giving by Other Competitors tracks donation from other industry competitors who are not firm i's ideological opponents. This variable serves as an empirical counterpart against which the effect of the main regressor, Giving by Ideological Opponents, is evaluated.

name: Ideological homogeneity
definition: The literature on corporate political ideology shows how firms often develop distinctive and homogeneous ideological preferences in their workforce. Ideological Homogeneity is measured as the inverse of the standard deviation of ideological preferences among a focal firm's employees who made campaign contributions during the study period.

name: Ideological gap
definition: Ideological Gap is measured as the absolute difference between the ideology of a focal firm's employees and the average ideology of all other corporate donors that gave to that nonprofit throughout the study period.

name: Firm ideological position
definition: This measure is calculated as the average ideological score of the firm's employees (CFScore in Bonica's DIME database) who made campaign contributions during my study period. Firms with positive ideological scores are categorized as conservative (red firms), whereas those with negative scores are categorized as liberal (blue firms).

name: Alliance governance
authors_terms: ["alliance governance", "governance structure", "hierarchical governance", "more hierarchical governance forms", "governance form"]
definition: Alliance governance modes are defined along a market-hierarchy continuum: with increased uncertainty about partner opportunism, the control provided by hierarchical governance forms (e.g., equity joint ventures) is preferred to market-based forms (e.g., licensing). Under TCE, governance forms are efficient when they minimize the combined costs of opportunism and administration arising from uncertainty and asset specificity.

name: Asset co-specialization
definition: Asset co-specialization is mutual investment by partners in activities and structures that facilitate information and knowledge exchange between individuals. We view co-specialization agreements as quasi-organizational structures where partners transfer know-how, develop relational contacts, and exchange information.

name: Partner uncertainty
definition: We focus on partner and task uncertainty as forms of behavioral uncertainty. Partner uncertainty decreases as partners gain mutual experience, reducing the need for the costly monitoring and control of hierarchical governance.

name: Task uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty also arises in task requirements, especially in knowledge-intensive industries such as biotechnology where emerging and highly specialized technologies make it difficult to monitor and evaluate a partner's capabilities and contributions. As task uncertainty rises, so do contracting costs, thus increasing the relative efficiency of more hierarchical governance forms.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Many biotechnology alliances reflect structural uncertainty, when for example novel combinations of technologies and lagged development of complementary related technologies can make a potential technology application irrelevant within a new and rapidly changing technological system. Based on prior work showing systematic differences in volatility among these three sub-fields we examined each alliance for its technology focus.

name: TMT gender faultline strength
authors_terms: ["gender faultline strength", "TMT gender-faultline strength", "relationship-related faultline strength"]
definition: We define the strength of relationship faultlines as the extent to which social identity subgroups are strongly formed based on a focal relationship-related attribute (e.g., gender, age, or educational level). A faultline-strength score indicates the degree to which TMT members could be arranged into potential subgroups based on the focal attribute (e.g., gender).

name: TMT age faultline strength
authors_terms: ["age faultline strength", "TMT age-faultline strength", "relationship-related faultline strength"]
definition: We define the strength of relationship faultlines as the extent to which social identity subgroups are strongly formed based on a focal relationship-related attribute (e.g., gender, age, or educational level). A faultline-strength score indicates the degree to which TMT members could be arranged into potential subgroups based on the focal attribute.

name: TMT educational-level faultline strength
authors_terms: ["educational level faultline strength", "TMT educational-level faultline strength", "relationship-related faultline strength"]
definition: We define the strength of relationship faultlines as the extent to which social identity subgroups are strongly formed based on a focal relationship-related attribute (e.g., gender, age, or educational level). A faultline-strength score indicates the degree to which TMT members could be arranged into potential subgroups based on the focal attribute.

name: TMT functional-background faultline strength
authors_terms: ["functional background faultline strength", "TMT functional-background faultline strength", "task-related faultline strength"]
definition: We define the strength of task-related faultlines as the extent to which knowledge-based subgroups are strongly formed based on a focal task-related attribute (e.g., functional background or tenure). A faultline-strength score indicates the degree to which TMT members could be arranged into potential subgroups based on the focal attribute.

name: TMT tenure faultline strength
authors_terms: ["tenure faultline strength", "TMT tenure-faultline strength", "task-related faultline strength"]
definition: We define the strength of task-related faultlines as the extent to which knowledge-based subgroups are strongly formed based on a focal task-related attribute (e.g., functional background or tenure). A faultline-strength score indicates the degree to which TMT members could be arranged into potential subgroups based on the focal attribute.

name: Strategic change
definition: Our focal strategic-decision variable is strategic change, which we define as change in a firm's strategic direction via reallocating its resources along multiple strategic components. Strategic change measures the extent to which a firm's financial resource allocation to important strategic components changes over time.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism, defined as the rate of unpredicted change within a focal company's industry. Environmental dynamism represents the magnitude and frequency of environmental change, as well as irregularity in patterns of environmental change.

name: Market pioneering
definition: To avoid any confusion, a pioneer was defined in the questionnaire as 'a firm that is the first to introduce a new product/brand into its primary markets.'

name: Pioneering performance advantage
authors_terms: ["pioneering performance advantages", "pioneering performance", "market performance", "market share and profits"]
definition: Pioneering Performance Advantages have commonly been described in the literature as increased market share and profits (e.g., Robinson and Fornell, 1985; Robinson et al., 1992). These scale items were designed to measure perceptions regarding the pioneering firm's market share and profitability.

name: Pioneering post-entry risk
authors_terms: ["pioneering risks after market entry", "post-entry risks", "pioneering risk"]
definition: Pioneering Risks After Market Entry are measured using a set of scale items based on the major categories of post-market-entry pioneering risks described in the literature (Lieberman and Montgomery, 1988; Robinson, 1988; Huff and Robinson, 1994): competitive free-riding and loss of initial advantage due to declining product quality, product line breadth, and cost advantage.

name: Pioneering cost advantage
authors_terms: ["cost advantages of pioneering", "cost advantages", "pioneering cost advantages"]
definition: From the literature we developed several scale items to capture the competitor-centered advantages of lower production costs, better access to labor and to experienced managers, better access to raw material supplies, and better choice of location (Robinson and Fornell, 1985; Robinson, 1988; Lieberman and Montgomery, 1988).

name: Pioneering differentiation advantage
authors_terms: ["differentiation advantages of pioneering", "differentiation advantages", "pioneering differentiation advantages"]
definition: By establishing a strong brand image with its customers or positioning itself as the high-quality provider, the pioneer obtains a differentiation advantage that may be difficult for competitors to overtake, permitting the pioneer to charge higher prices over the long term.

name: Industry sector
definition: Service products differ from manufactured goods in several ways: intangibility, simultaneous production and consumption, heterogeneity of service offering, and perishability (e.g., Zeithaml, Parasuraman, and Berry, 1985). Thus, we can expect that managers in service and manufacturing firms will perceive pioneering advantages and sustainability differently.

name: National region
authors_terms: ["Western managers", "Asian Pacific managers", "Western countries", "Asian Pacific countries", "Western and Asian Pacific business environments"]
definition: Western countries tend to be more short-term-oriented and individualistic, Asian Pacific nations long-term-oriented and collectivistic (Hofstede, 1994). In addition to cultural dimensions, government policies can also influence the perceived advantage of a pioneering strategy.

name: Triadic closure
authors_terms: ["triadic closure", "likelihood of closure", "LP evaluator-VC evaluatee tie formation", "LP-VC match"]
definition: Triadic closure is defined as the tendency of actors sharing ties with the same actor to disproportionately form and maintain ties among themselves. In this study it is the likelihood that the evaluator LP forms a direct investment tie with the evaluatee VC.

name: Collaboration failure
authors_terms: ["failure between the intermediary and the evaluatee", "failed collaborations", "failed indirect ties"]
definition: Failure of the collaboration is often assessed either as poor competence of or poor fit with the partner and reduces the likelihood of a repeat tie. In this setting a failure is a bankruptcy or a liquidation of the portfolio company in which the VC pair co-invested.

name: Collaboration success
definition: Portfolio companies are managed toward a successful liquidity event, either an initial public offering (IPO) that can allow the sale of the VC's shares on the open market or an acquisition by an established industry player.

name: Intermediary-evaluatee similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity of the offerings", "industry specialization overlap", "industry overlap", "similarity"]
definition: The similarity of the type of offerings the intermediary and the evaluatee provide, which determines whether the evaluator could drop the relationship with the intermediary and still receive substantively similar offerings from the evaluatee. VCs that are similar in terms of investment profile tend to compete for the same narrow sliver of an LP's assets.

name: Relative attractiveness of the evaluatee
authors_terms: ["relative attractiveness", "relative reputation", "higher reputation of the evaluatee relative to the intermediary"]
definition: Relative attractiveness concerns the expected quality of an exchange partner's offerings. Because quality is unobservable before an exchange, actors can use the prospective exchange partner's reputation, based in part on its track record of performance, as a signal of the future quality of its offerings.

name: Foreign venture longevity
authors_terms: ["longevity", "longevity of foreign ventures", "longevity of foreign entry", "venture persistence"]
definition: Longevity was defined as the number of years that the venture persisted, as evidenced by the firm's annual reports.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Both practice and theory (Hofstede, 1980) suggest that some cultures are more distant than others. Globalizing firms adjust to foreign cultures and are more likely to fail whenever the acculturation involved is more demanding.

name: Prior foreign expansion experience
authors_terms: ["foreign experience", "prior foreign expansion experiences", "foreign expansion experiences", "previous foreign entry experience"]
definition: Firms that expand abroad are likely to acquire knowledge about foreign sites, including foreign culture, institutional characteristics, and other site-specific knowledge. In this paper, the complementary hypothesis will be tested, that foreign experience increases the longevity of ventures.

name: Prior experience in the host country
authors_terms: ["previous expansions of the firm in the same host country", "learning effects within countries", "LHOSTEXP"]
definition: LHOSTEXP is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in the same host country. When starting a new venture, firms are expected to benefit more from previous expansion experiences in the same country, rather than from experiences in other countries.

name: Prior experience in the host country's cultural block
authors_terms: ["previous expansions in other countries in the same cultural block", "learning effects within culture blocks", "LHOSTBLOCK"]
definition: LHOSTBLOCK is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in other countries in the same cultural block as the host country.

name: Prior experience in culturally closer blocks
authors_terms: ["previous expansions in cultural blocks that were closer to the home country", "LNEARBLOCK"]
definition: LNEARBLOCK is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in cultural blocks that were closer to the home country than the cultural block to which the host country belongs.

name: Double layered acculturation
definition: Firms entering through WOSs or through JVs may both face cultural barriers, but the barriers need not be the same. When firms engage in JVs, their calibration to a foreign national culture involves 'double layered acculturation,' and a firm engaged in foreign acquisitions has to accommodate both the target firm's national and corporate cultures.

name: Quantity of innovation
authors_terms: ["quantity of innovation", "number of patents", "quantity of patents"]
definition: Defined as the total number of patents generated by firms in a given year; the authors contrast this quantifiable outcome with the novelty of innovation.

name: Novelty of innovation
authors_terms: ["proportion of novel patents", "novelty of innovation", "proportion of novel innovation"]
definition: Defined as the proportion of novel patents among all the patents produced by the focal firm in the given year; a patent is regarded as novel if it involves the first occurrence of a new combination of patent classes compared with all the patents that have ever been granted by the SIPO until the observation year.

name: Incentive alignment
authors_terms: ["incentive alignment", "alignment of agents' private interests with firm value", "proportion of board share"]
definition: The degree to which agents' private interests are aligned with firm value: when agents are given greater private incentives in accordance with firm value, they have a greater personal stake in preserving or enhancing firm value.

name: Monitoring
definition: The degree of monitoring performed by the principal over the actions of agents; through closer monitoring and supervision a principal is more likely to detect and correct the agents' actions of gaming the metrics.

name: Public governance quality
authors_terms: ["quality of public governance", "government quality", "quality of government"]
definition: In the Weberian tradition, high-quality governments are characterized by a modern legal rational public governance system bounded by impersonal rules, relying on hierarchy and meritocracy, and refraining from extracting from citizens.

name: Adoption of quantifying innovation metrics
authors_terms: ["metrics that rely on quantifying innovation outcomes", "quantifiable outcomes", "post-policy"]
definition: The state's adoption of evaluation metrics characterized by heavy reliance on directly measurable outcomes of the quantity of patents and minimum specifications regarding the evaluation of patent novelty; the authors use the post-policy period (2007 onward) as a good indicator of the adoption of these metrics.

name: Product exploration
definition: Within the product domain, product exploration emphasizes developing new products, technologies, and product capabilities. Product exploration can lead to architectural innovations that change linkages between subsystems or discontinuous innovations that change the product's core subsystem.

name: Product exploitation
definition: Within the product domain, product exploitation emphasizes increasing returns from existing product capabilities. Exploitation emphasizes the refinement and incremental extension of existing product and market capabilities.

name: Market exploration
definition: Within the marketing domain, market exploration emphasizes marketing programs that attract new customers; market exploration targets new customers outside of the currently served market.

name: Market exploitation
definition: Within the marketing domain, market exploitation emphasizes marketing programs designed to retain and increase purchases from current customers.

name: Revenue performance
authors_terms: ["revenue performance", "ticket revenue", "ticket revenue per available seat"]
definition: Revenue performance, which provides the purest measure of market response to an organization's strategic emphases—that is, whether exploration and exploitation activities effectively motivate current and new customers to purchase the firm's product offerings.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was operationalized as the organization's lagged budget size. Larger firms are argued to have the resources, capabilities, and experience necessary to successfully manage the complexity of within-function ambidexterity.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age was operationalized as FYs 2003-2005 minus the theater's founding date, so that age varied across the three-year time frame. Older firms are argued to possess the experience, knowledge, and extended time frame required to implement and benefit from contextual systems and processes.

name: Product ambidexterity
definition: Within functional domains, product ambidexterity simultaneously explores new product capabilities and exploits current product capabilities.

name: Market ambidexterity
definition: Within functional domains, market ambidexterity simultaneously explores new customer markets and exploits current customers.

name: Global market diversification
authors_terms: ["global market diversification (GMD)", "international market diversification", "global market diversity", "global market dispersion"]
definition: Global market diversification (GMD) reflects the extent of the global market dispersion of a firm's operations, that is, the dispersion of a firm's operations across global market areas.

name: Related product diversification
authors_terms: ["related diversification", "related diversifiers", "global related diversification (GRD)", "product diversification strategy", "unrelated diversifiers"]
definition: Unrelated diversifiers have been defined as firms that diversify predominantly across industries, while related diversifiers have been defined as firms that diversify predominantly within industries; global related diversification (GRD) reflects the extent of global diversification across business segments within the industry segments of a firm.

name: Profit growth
definition: We use profit growth rather than the profitability level itself as the profitability measure; using longitudinal data (improvement over firms' starting profitability levels, i.e. change in profitability over the time period of a study) rather than cross-sectional data (absolute levels of profitability) may better reflect the profitability impact of specific diversification strategies.

name: Profit stability
definition: Profit performance includes not only profitability but also profit stability, since a diversification strategy with a favorable return may not be managerially acceptable due to its risk; the instability measure does not confound stable growth or stable decline with variability and assesses instability independent of the absolute level of OPM(ROA).

name: Organizational attention
definition: We treated an organization's assignment of the status selected to a suggestion as attention from the organization. Attention cannot be paid to all elicited suggestions because the attention span of organizations is limited.

name: Crowding
definition: If organizations are successful in eliciting distant knowledge, they are exposed to numerous suggestions - a state we refer to as crowding. We recorded how many suggestions were at risk (i.e., had not yet experienced a status change) in calendar week t.

name: Content distance
definition: We define content distance as the extent to which the content of a suggestion diverges from the content of suggestions to which an organization has previously paid attention. Content distance thus constitutes the reverse of similarity, in that two suggestions are distant if there is little (or no) similarity between their contents.

name: Structural distance
definition: We define structural distance as the extent to which a focal suggestion lacks links to other suggestions via the support of external contributors. Two suggestions are structurally distant if no (or only a few) external contributors support both of them.

name: Personal distance
definition: We define personal distance as the extent to which the external contributor of a suggestion has previously received attention from the organization. A suggestion can thus be personally distant either because the external contributor has not made any suggestions in the past or because the organization has not paid attention to past suggestions.

name: Firm technological innovation
authors_terms: ["technological innovation", "technological innovations by the firm", "firm innovation", "R&D spending", "R&D productivity"]
definition: The study measures technological innovation as the change in two stock variables of firm knowledge-R&D spending and R&D productivity.

name: Rival technological innovation
authors_terms: ["technological innovation by rivals", "rival innovation", "rival R&D", "innovation by rivals"]
definition: Successful innovations by rival firms will strengthen the competition the focal firm faces and bring new knowledge to light, which alters the rents available to the focal firm.

name: Scope changing acquisitions
definition: Noncore acquisitions are defined by comparing the primary four-digit SIC code of the acquirer and the target as given in SDC-an acquisition is deemed noncore if the target is in a different SIC code from the acquirer.

name: Scope changing divestments
definition: The study uses two dependent variables-a count of acquisitions undertaken by a firm in a given year and a count of divestments undertaken by a firm in a given year. A similar procedure is followed for noncore divestments.

name: Investible resources
definition: I define investible resources to be the resources that are available to the firm to pursue new business opportunities at a point in time. These resources are assumed to be fungible/semi-fungible as well as congestible.

name: Competitive interaction with rivals
authors_terms: ["the nature of competitive interaction", "competitive strategy measure (CSM)", "complementary or a substitute relationship", "substitute relation", "complementary relationship"]
definition: Prior work suggests that a firm can have either a complementary or a substitute relationship with its competitors (Bulow, Geanokoplos, and Klemperer, 1985; Sundaram, John, and John, 1996), depending on whether aggressive moves by competitors cause firm returns to increase (complementors) or decrease (substitutes).

name: Time period
authors_terms: ["two time periods", "10-year period", "1987 and 1996", "as compared to 10 years ago"]
definition: All data were collected at two time periods, 1987 (1988 Fortune 500 firms) and 1996 (1997 Fortune 500 firms).

name: Women's board representation
authors_terms: ["women serving on Fortune 500 company boards", "women's representation on corporate boards", "women on their board of directors", "women's board seats"]
definition: The number of women serving on the board of directors of the focal Fortune 500 firm at both time periods.

name: Women's CEO representation
authors_terms: ["women serving as CEO", "female CEOs", "women as CEOs"]
definition: The number of women serving as CEO of the Fortune 500 firm at both time periods.

name: Women's inside director representation
authors_terms: ["women serving as inside directors", "female inside directors", "women's participation as inside corporate directors"]
definition: Consistent with past research, an inside director is defined as a member of firm management also serving on the board of directors; the study records the number of women serving as inside directors at both time periods.

name: Women's outside corporate director representation
authors_terms: ["women serving as outside directors with corporate backgrounds", "female outside directors with corporate backgrounds", "women with corporate backgrounds"]
definition: Women serving on the board who have corporate professional backgrounds, as compared to noncorporate backgrounds; a female director who serves as chief financial officer of another Fortune 500 firm, for example, would be a director with a corporate background.

name: Women's affiliated director representation
authors_terms: ["women serving as affiliated directors", "affiliated (6b) directors", "female outside board members with a 6(b) designation"]
definition: Affiliated (6b) directors capture directors with professional (and personal) ties to the firm or firm management; relying on the SEC 6(b) guidelines, the study includes those directors employed by firms providing services to the focal firm (e.g., legal counsel, consultant, accountant).

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Companies operating in Denmark that are owned by a foreign multinational parent, as opposed to domestically owned companies; the study samples only subsidiaries in which a single foreign corporation holds more than 50 percent of the stock.

name: Company survival
definition: The continued operation of a company as an independent unit; the exit event is not synonymous with liquidation or death but includes exit by merger into a larger entity if the company disappears as an independent unit.

name: Foreign subsidiary density
authors_terms: ["number of foreign companies operating at time of entry", "number of foreign subsidiaries", "local density", "competition intensity"]
definition: The number of foreign companies operating in the host market at the time of entry, which the authors treat as a measure of local density and competition among foreign subsidiaries.

name: Process management activities
authors_terms: ["process management", "process management activities", "extent of process management activities", "process management practices"]
definition: Process management practices are the shared underlying component of a series of quality-related initiatives, including total quality management (TQM), the Malcolm Baldrige Award criteria, ISO 9000, and Six Sigma programs. Process management techniques comprise three main activities: mapping or documenting routines, subjecting routines to process improvement aimed at incremental change, and adherence to routines through the adoption of standardized best practices.

name: Exploitative innovation
authors_terms: ["exploitative innovation", "exploitation", "exploitative patents", "innovations that leverage a firm's existing knowledge"]
definition: Exploitation involves local search that builds on a firm's existing technological capabilities, and exploitative innovations involve improvements in existing components and architectures and build on the existing technological trajectory. Innovation is increasingly exploitative the more deeply anchored it is in existing firm knowledge.

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: Exploration involves more distant search for new capabilities, and exploratory innovation involves a shift to a different technological trajectory. Innovation is increasingly exploratory the more it departs from knowledge used in prior innovation efforts.

name: Exploitation's share of innovation
authors_terms: ["exploitation's share of innovation", "share of innovations that are highly exploitative", "ratio of exploitative innovations to total innovation"]
definition: The share of innovations that are highly exploitative, i.e., the ratio of exploitative innovation to total innovation for a firm. The authors argue that organizations adopting process management activities will favor exploitative innovation at the expense of exploration, a shift toward an increasing share of exploitative innovations.

name: Private ownership
authors_terms: ["private control", "privately controlled firms", "private versus state ownership"]
definition: Privately controlled firms, a relatively new organizational form in China, lack legitimacy in the economy and the society and therefore have stronger incentives to compensate by cultivating their relationships with the government. The authors argue that SOEs have the most political legitimacy and therefore the least need to use activities such as CSR reporting to seek preferred status and associated resources from the government.

name: CSR report issuance
definition: CSR report is a dummy variable equal to 1 if the focal firm has issued a CSR report in a given year, and it is 0 otherwise. The authors describe issuing a CSR report as primarily a symbolic act by which firms respond to government signals.

name: CSR reporting substantiveness
authors_terms: ["CSR reporting substantiveness", "substantive CSR reporting", "substance of CSR activities"]
definition: CSR reporting substantiveness is an overall rating of CSR activities as portrayed in the report. It is meant to determine the extent to which the reports are purely symbolic exercises or indicative of substantive CSR activities.

name: Political council membership
authors_terms: ["CEO NPC/CPPCC membership", "members of national political councils", "connections to national congresses"]
definition: Corporate executives may be members of political councils such as the National People's Congress (NPC), the only legislative body in China, or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), an advisory board for the Chinese government. The NPC and CPPCC are often collectively referred as the 'Two Meetings,' signifying their status as the two most important political councils in China and the key means for business leaders to participate in the government.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age is the number of years since the firm was established. The authors argue that older firms have a greater 'socialist imprint' than younger firms and are less likely to pursue recent trends and management ideas that are inconsistent with their operating ideologies.

name: Financial resources
definition: Financial resources were captured by two variables: firm ROA, the return on assets calculated as net income over total assets, and slack resources, calculated as the sum of cash flow from a firm's operating, financing, and investing activities scaled by total assets. The authors argue that if the purpose of CSR and CSR reporting is to gain legitimacy from the government, then both higher-performing firms and those with more slack resources would be more likely to mobilize those resources to issue CSR reports.

name: Bureaucratic embeddedness
definition: In China, executives can hold government positions; for example, they can be heads of governmental departments and bureaus. Such bureaucratic connections have been shown to confer greater access to resources or material benefit than do the more symbolic connections to national congresses, and they also expose a firm to greater government monitoring.

name: Regional government institutional development
authors_terms: ["regional institutional development", "regional government institutional development", "regional development"]
definition: During the reform period, there have been significant variations across China in the extent to which regional governments have seized the opportunity to use market mechanisms to develop the local economy, enhance fiscal health, and, correspondingly, enhance development of regional government institutions. Governments in developed regions have accumulated significant financial resources and have introduced more advanced management techniques, making them more likely to have not only the resources but also the expertise to monitor corporate activities.

name: Navy Industrial Fund procedures
authors_terms: ["Navy Industrial Fund (NIF) procedures", "NIF procedures", "industrial funding procedures", "NIF"]
definition: The Navy Industrial Fund version involves a working capital procedure where customers pay for services provided by industrial funded activities. Starting in 1984 the NIF procedures were imposed on the NARDACs; all nontactical information system support provided to customers became reimbursable and customers were billed for services provided.

name: Life-cycle requirement order
definition: At the end of 1988 the Secretary of Navy issued Notice 5236 requiring Navy customers to first approach the NARDAC for projects exceeding $150,000 life cycle costs; if the NARDAC could not perform the requested service then a customer was provided a waiver, and could seek help elsewhere. Essentially it gave one strategic group (NARDACs) a 'first right of refusal.'

name: Civilian provider contracting
definition: The percentages of information services received from four sources (NARDACs, civilian providers, other Navy providers, and in-house operations). Essentially a Navy customer was classified as a mixed provider user if over 25 percent of its nontactical information requirements were met by the private-sector.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["vertical integration strategies", "in-house operations", "in-house vertical integration", "vertically integrate"]
definition: One strategy, vertical integration, always represents a potential alternative to the market solution of customer groups contracting with seller groups. If over 75 percent of a customer's information requirements were done in-house, the customer was considered to be vertically integrated.

name: Customer size
definition: The size of the Navy customer; the hypothesis distinguishes large Navy customers, whose projects exceed the $150,000 life-cycle threshold, from small Navy customers. In the logistic models size was measured by the customer's response to the question of whether their projects are typically under or over $150,000.

name: Technical sophistication
definition: One of nine strategic dimensions, along with product quality, quality of everyday service, quality of long-term support, timeliness of service, marketing effort, product line variety, familiarity with customer needs, and price of product, on which customers evaluated their principal NARDAC. The private-sector strategic group is described as emphasizing technical sophistication in its own strategy.

name: Product relatedness
authors_terms: ["product relatedness", "related diversification", "relatedness of products between parent firms and their ventures"]
definition: Product relatedness is the extent to which a firm's different lines of business or industries are linked. Product relatedness is hence highest when an IJV maintains a related linkage with both parents (bilateral relatedness), medium when it has a quasi-related linkage with one parent (unilateral relatedness), and lowest when it is unrelated to both parents.

name: IJV performance
definition: This study measures IJV performance by IJV managers' satisfaction with profitability, sales, competitive position, and overall performance.

name: Resource complementarity
definition: Resource complementarity was measured by an average of a respondent's assessment, on a 7-point Likert scale, to the extent to which one parent's contributed resources are complementary to those contributed by the other parent. The greater the resource complementarity between foreign and local parents, the greater the operational synergies resulting from related diversification.

name: Goal incongruity
definition: This study defines goal incongruity as the extent to which foreign and local parents have different strategic objectives about operations and evolutions of the IJV.

name: Structural opportunity
definition: Consequently, structural opportunities are manifested typically in an industry's sales growth, profit growth, and output growth. The growth variance across industries reflects the differences in market demand as well as the outcome of different government policies regulating different industries.

name: Institutional deterrence
definition: Institutional deterrence involves various kinds of interference and intervention from either central or local governments and their administrative agencies. Institutional deterrence increases along the sequence of encouraged technology-intensive industries, encouraged nontechnology-intensive industries, newly opened industries, and restricted industries.

name: Decision load of the formal authority holder
authors_terms: ["number of FAH's decisions", "information overload", "information processing overload", "number of decisions that a single individual is responsible for"]
definition: Increasing the number of decisions that need to be taken by one individual leads to less time and attention devoted to each decision; the risk of information overload is greater if a large number of decisions rest within the authority of a single individual.

name: Knowledge specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization of knowledge required for decision making", "specialized knowledge", "required knowledge specialization"]
definition: Decisions made in a large organization often require heterogeneous knowledge, and some decisions rely on specific knowledge, which involves specialized knowledge that is often tacit and is difficult and costly to transfer among people.

name: Knowledge-expertise match
authors_terms: ["knowledge-expertise match", "match of the FAH's expertise with the knowledge domain required for decision making", "colocation of authority and knowledge"]
definition: A scenario in which the person with authority also has the relevant knowledge needed to complete a task is an example of 'colocation' of authority and knowledge.

name: Authority split
authors_terms: ["authority split between the FAH and the RAH", "split of decision authority", "formal and real authority"]
definition: Firms approach the delegation trade-off by allocating formal authority, i.e., the right to decide, and real authority, i.e., an effective control over decisions, over particular decision tasks to selected employees located within the firm's hierarchy. When the FAH is also the RAH, the task decision authority is kept unified within one actor.

name: Delegation span
definition: We define the number of organizational levels between the FAH and the RAH as the delegation span. It determines the length of the path through which information travels between actors involved in decision making.

name: Family firm status
definition: Family firms are firms in which 'the person who established or acquired the firm or their families or descendants possess 25 percent of the decision-making rights.' Family firms have both economic and noneconomic goals and are willing to sacrifice economic gains in order to preserve noneconomic utility.

name: IPO underpricing
definition: IPO underpricing, i.e., the stock price increase on the first day of trading, represents the discount to a fair value at which a firm's shares are sold.

name: Managerial stock ownership
definition: Stock ownership by top managers ties their wealth directly to the firm's long-term value and motivates them to take more risks, because managerial stock ownership elicits variance-increasing strategies by allowing managers to focus on the upside potential of outcome variance.

name: Board monitoring
authors_terms: ["board monitoring", "nonexecutive directors' stock ownership", "outside directors' stock ownership", "monitoring by outside directors"]
definition: Board monitoring is an alternative governance mechanism to managerial incentives that mitigates agency problems in alliance partner choice; when nonexecutive directors own a higher amount of stock, they will promote alliance partner decisions that align with shareholder interests, that is, distant and existing alliance partners over new close partners.

name: Alliance partner network distance
authors_terms: ["alliance partner network distance", "partner network distance", "partner distance", "network distance"]
definition: Alliance partner network distance is captured by the shortest alternative path to a partner firm at the time period prior to alliance formation, and distinguishes three types of partners: existing ties (zero network distance), close partners (one-step distant, the focal firm's partner's partner), and distant partners (greater than one-step distant, with no mutual partner between the focal firm and the partner).

name: High-resource incumbents
definition: Hotels affiliated with nationally known branded chains in the upscale tier, which possess demand-heightening resources built up through advertising and branding and are most likely to enjoy the resources that attract customers to an area and that can spill over to other firms.

name: Low-resource incumbents
definition: Hotels that lack the demand-heightening resources of upscale branded hotels; the authors group branded economy hotels and non-branded hotels as low-resource firms that have fewer resources to attract customers on their own.

name: Entry by high-resource firms
authors_terms: ["location decisions of branded upscale hotels", "market entry"]
definition: The choice of a zip-code market made by an entering hotel affiliated with an upscale brand, analyzed as a discrete choice among the many markets possibly considered for each new hotel.

name: Entry by low-resource firms
authors_terms: ["location decisions of branded economy hotels", "location decisions of unbranded hotels", "market entry"]
definition: The choice of a zip-code market made by an entering branded economy or non-branded hotel, analyzed as a discrete choice among the many markets possibly considered for each new hotel.

name: External managerial hiring
authors_terms: ["external managerial hiring", "external hiring of managers", "External mgr. hiring"]
definition: The practice of filling managerial positions from outside the company rather than from within the firm; the authors create a dummy variable equal to one if managerial positions are reported as usually being filled 'from outside the company' as opposed to within the firm, with the added condition that at least one manager is hired in the same year if the practice changed from the prior year.

name: External hiring of high-skilled nonmanagerial employees
authors_terms: ["external hiring of high-skilled nonmanagerial employees", "external hiring of professionals", "External prof. hiring", "external professional hiring"]
definition: The practice of filling high-skilled nonmanagerial positions (defined in the survey as 'professionals,' whose 'duties would normally require at least an undergraduate university degree or the equivalent') from outside the company rather than from within the firm, measured by the same procedure as external managerial hiring.

name: Decision authority allocated to managers
authors_terms: ["ManagerControl", "allocation of decision authority to managers", "fraction of tasks allocated to managers"]
definition: To measure the allocation of decision authority to managers, the authors calculate the fraction of tasks allocated to either work supervisors or senior managers within the organization, based on the survey question of who normally makes decisions with respect to a set of operating activities.

name: Decision authority allocated to nonmanagerial employees
authors_terms: ["NonmanagerControl", "allocation of decision authority to nonmanagerial employees", "fraction of tasks allocated to nonmanagerial employees"]
definition: The authors measure the allocation of authority to nonmanagerial employees by calculating their fraction of allocated tasks, using the same survey question on who normally makes decisions about operating activities.

name: Strategic importance of workplace reorganization
authors_terms: ["strategic importance of workplace reorganization", "workplace reorg. strategic priority", "strategic priority of workplace reorganization"]
definition: The relative importance of 'reorganizing the work process' to the workplace's general business strategy, as rated by respondents on a Likert scale of importance.

name: Strategic importance of new product development
authors_terms: ["strategic importance of new product development", "new prod/svc dev. strategic priority"]
definition: The relative importance of 'developing new products/services' to the workplace's general business strategy, as rated by respondents on a Likert scale of importance.

name: Workplace reorganization
definition: Workplace reorganizations refer to changes in the organization of work for production, including work practices within the firm (Frost, 2000).

name: Product innovation
definition: New products or services are defined as differing 'significantly in character or intended use from previously produced goods or services.' To measure the novelty of innovations, the survey subsequently asks whether the innovation is the first in its local market, in Canada, or in the world.

name: Hiring rate
authors_terms: ["hiring rate", "managerial and professional hiring rate", "hiring rate for managers and professionals"]
definition: Hiring rate, or the ratio of new hires over incumbent employees, represents the relative amount of new KSAOs brought by newcomers.

name: Hiring rate change
authors_terms: ["hiring rate change", "hiring rate change in these positions", "hiring rate change for managers and professionals"]
definition: Hiring rate change reflects the relative newness of the KSAOs that the organization has acquired from newcomers. In essence, an increase in hiring rate indicates that the organization has greater access to newness over time, while a decrease suggests that the organization's access to novel knowledge and skills is diminishing.

name: Hiring rate dispersion
authors_terms: ["hiring rate dispersion", "hiring rate dispersion for these positions"]
definition: We use hiring rate dispersion, defined as the extent to which an organization hires continuously and evenly across time, to study this temporal characteristic of recruitment.

name: Collaborative work practices
definition: CWPs are plans and programs used by organizations to engage and facilitate employees' interaction and cooperation. Examples of CWPs include employee suggestion programs, self-directed work groups, and information-sharing practices.

name: Organizational innovation
definition: Organizational innovation includes 'a new good or a new quality of a good; a new method of production; a new market; a new source of supply; or a new organizational structure.' In the measure, new goods or services differ significantly in character or intended use from previously produced goods or services, and new processes include new methods of goods production or service delivery, whereas improvements refer to significant enhancements or upgrades to the performance of existing products or processes.

name: Complementor development rate
authors_terms: ["development rates", "rates of new complementary development", "new complementary development", "complementor development"]
definition: We infer variation in the intensity of complementor incentives to invest in development from changes in rates of new complementary development, focusing on the natural logarithm of (1 + ) the number of new mods generated for a given platform in a given month.

name: Platform usage
definition: We measure platform usage as the natural logarithm of the total number of minutes played for all mods for a given game engine platform in a given month (lnPlayerUsage). This and other platform variables were readily observable by all platform participants at the time, as they were publicly reported by C-Sport.net.

name: Number of complementors
authors_terms: ["numbers of complementors", "lnNumComplementors", "size of the complementor side of the platform", "the crowd"]
definition: The number of complementors in this context is almost precisely the same as the number of complementary mods generated because most individual complementors developed only one mod during the sample period. We therefore measure the size of the complementor side of the platform as the cumulative release of mods over time (lnNumComplementors).

name: Vertical merger
definition: The authors selected only those mergers where the two firms had a clear buyer-seller relationship before the merger, and were therefore classified by the FTC as vertical. The paper frames the merger as vertical integration executed by merger.

name: Change in systematic risk
definition: Systematic risk represents the sensitivity of a firm's returns to the aggregate returns of the marketplace, and accounts for about 20-30 percent of the total variation in a firm's returns. The regression equation yields an estimate of beta, the systematic risk of firm i, since this beta coefficient is the covariance of the return to a firm with the return to the market portfolio.

name: Integrator industry market power
authors_terms: ["market power", "level of competition", "industry 4-firm concentration ratio", "ICR", "market asymmetry"]
