definition: The market power of a firm vis-a-vis its vertical channels will depend in part on the level of competition in the firm's industry, and that level relative to the level of competition in its adjacent industries.

name: Target industry market power
authors_terms: ["target's industry concentration ratio", "TCR", "level of competition of the adjacent selling firm's industry"]
definition: The level of competition in the industry of the vertically adjacent stage from which the target comes, which the authors describe as one of the two adjacent industry stages whose market power may affect the risk outcome of a vertical merger.

name: Industry growth rate
authors_terms: ["growth rate of the integrator's industry", "industry growth", "life cycle stage", "IGRTH"]
definition: The rate of sales growth in the integrator's industry, which the authors use to characterize industry life cycle stages: an embryonic stage in which industry sales grow at annual rates in excess of 10%, a growth stage in which industry growth falls between 5% and 10%, and a transition to maturity with a slow annual rate of growth in sales, less than 5%.

name: Prior interactions
authors_terms: ["prior interactions", "repeated interactions", "relationship history", "history of prior interactions"]
definition: The number of times buyer and supplier had done business prior to the focal transaction; about half the transactions in the data involved a history of at least some prior interactions.

name: Technical clause detail
authors_terms: ["technical detail", "detail with which technical clauses are specified", "technical clauses"]
definition: Technical clauses specify the requirements of the product or service being procured, such as the desired performance and functions; technical detail is the extent to which technical specifications of the product or service being procured are specified in the contract.

name: Legal clause detail
authors_terms: ["legal detail", "detail with which legal clauses are specified", "legal clauses"]
definition: Legal clauses specify the legal terms of trade, penalties, and dispute-resolution processes rather than the specifics of the goods and services being transacted; legal detail is the extent to which legal clauses are specified in a contract.

name: Expertise in the technical domain
authors_terms: ["IT expertise", "expertise in the technical domain", "relevant expertise", "expertise in the product domain"]
definition: Possession of expertise relevant to the domain of the products/services being procured, which can significantly leverage learning rates; it is captured by whether the procuring firm had any employees with expertise in IT.

name: CEO successor origin
authors_terms: ["choice of CEO successor", "successor origin", "outside CEO succession", "inside CEO succession", "interim CEO succession"]
definition: The type of successor a firm selects as a replacement CEO; different types of successors (outsiders, insiders, and interims) convey different messages to investors. An outsider is appointment of an executive from another firm, an insider is succession by another company executive, and an interim is appointment of a temporary CEO 'while the firm searches for a permanent replacement.'

name: Investor perceptions of CEO succession
definition: Investors' perceptions about each type of CEO succession, measured as their likelihood of buying, selling, or holding the firm's stock based solely on the limited information provided in the scenario.

name: Integrity failure
definition: A specific situation wherein the firm's motives, honesty, and/or character fall short. Examples include incidents such as financial fraud, withholding important negative information about new products, or tax evasion.

name: Competence failure
definition: Specific situations where a firm falls short of technically proficient performance. Examples include making an ill-advised acquisition, not anticipating a foreseeable environmental shock that harms the firm, or lax internal procedures that create the need for a product recall.

name: Installed base composition
authors_terms: ["installed base composition", "changing composition of the platform's user base", "composition of the installed base", "composition of the potential pool of game adopters"]
definition: By definition, a game launched very early in a platform's life cycle will be facing a pool of potential adopters composed only of early platform adopters. By contrast, a game launched toward the tail-end of a platform's life cycle will be launching to a mixed pool of early and late platform adopters.

name: Complement sales
definition: Complement sales is operationalized as the video game's platform-specific lifetime unit sales (using sales revenue produces similar results).

name: Complement novelty
definition: Novel video games are those games that are based on an entirely new, or original, IP. Similar to newly launched platforms, novel complements are shrouded by uncertainty, thus imposing valuation ambiguities.

name: Alliance formation
definition: An alliance is established when two or more organizations mutually see collaboration as beneficial, so organizational goals and external opportunities jointly determine alliance formation.

name: Market complementarity
definition: Firms seek alliances when each firm has access to markets not possessed by the other, a condition the authors term 'market complementarity.'

name: Resource compatibility
definition: Compatibility gives match quality through similarities—capabilities can be combined to create value because they are similar or share a standard interface. In network technologies, compatibility is gained through the use of similar resources, so that the cost and output are made homogeneous regardless of which organization performs the task.

name: Isolate status
definition: Alliance networks contain already-networked firms that have entered into alliances, but an industry will also contain isolate firms, which have no alliances.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm growth through investment in production asset is a function of managerial choice and financial constraints and can reveal the intention behind alliances.

name: Firm failure
definition: The analysis of firm exit measured whether a firm was no longer seen in any liner market and thus had failed, been acquired, or exited liner shipping.

name: Financial performance
definition: Firm survival and financial performance are functions of market success and costs and can reveal the effectiveness of alliances.

name: Prior production experience
definition: Experience with producing cars; the authors argue that experience increases levels of organizational knowledge, and some of this knowledge is likely to be reflected in improvements in local error detection, better product design, or improved organizational processes that will reduce the incidence of errors.

name: Prior voluntary recalls
authors_terms: ["voluntary recalls", "recalls initiated by the automaker", "voluntary recall experience"]
definition: Decisions to recall and remedy safety defects on new vehicles that are made voluntarily by automakers prior to any involvement by NHTSA, through their own tests, inspection procedures and information-gathering systems.

name: Prior involuntary recalls
definition: Recalls initiated by the NHTSA rather than the automaker, after problems come to the agency's attention through vehicle owners, other government agencies, or the NHTSA's own testing of new vehicles.

name: Prior recall experience
authors_terms: ["prior recalls", "prior voluntary and involuntary recalls", "recalls, whatever their type"]
definition: The automaker's own experience with recall events; learning theories suggest that recalls themselves will stimulate organizational learning and change because a recall can be seen as a case of failure to meet aspirations.

name: Relative proportion of voluntary recalls
authors_terms: ["proportion of voluntary recalls", "relative proportion of voluntary to involuntary recalls"]
definition: The share of an automaker's cumulative recalls over the prior three years that were voluntary rather than involuntary; the authors argue that the relative proportion of voluntary to involuntary recalls may matter more for attention and salience than the absolute number of either.

name: Generalism
definition: Generalist firms are those that depend on a wide range of environmental resources; they are more complex because their larger resource space and broader range of products for customers mean that they have to deal with a wider range of issues than specialists.

name: Depth of learning processes
definition: The depth of analysis and knowledge retention that follows a recall; mandated events may induce a defensive response and shallow compliance that is unlikely to result in knowledge that penetrates the organization's routines and practices. Longer technical reports reflect deeper underlying learning processes than shorter technical reports.

name: Subsequent severe recalls
authors_terms: ["severe recalls", "annual number of severe recalls", "subsequent recall rate"]
definition: The annual number of severe recalls for each automaker, where severity is judged against the NHTSA criteria and severe recalls are those representing a significant hazard.

name: Subsequent severe voluntary recalls
definition: The annual number of severe recalls of the automaker's products that were initiated voluntarily by the automaker rather than by NHTSA.

name: Subsequent severe involuntary recalls
definition: The annual number of severe recalls of the automaker's products that were mandated by NHTSA rather than initiated by the automaker.

name: Managerial capabilities
definition: Managerial capabilities involve bodies of processes that span multiple areas or departments to coordinate, integrate, and direct firm activities. Managerial capabilities transcend other organizational capabilities and unify organizational activity into a cohesive system.

name: Functional capabilities
definition: Functional capabilities are discrete processes within particular areas or departments in a firm. They are more localized than managerial capabilities because they embody the specific abilities and knowledge that relate to day-to-day firm activities.

name: Exit mode
authors_terms: ["exit by acquisition", "exit by dissolution", "mode of exit", "form of exit"]
definition: At the firm level, both dissolution and acquisition are forms of selection out of a population: a firm ceases to exist as an independent entity. At the level of organizational capabilities, however, the two types of exit contrast with each other, the first being a selective outcome and the second being an adaptive outcome.

name: Firm age
definition: Because capabilities develop over time, older firms tend to possess larger stocks of organizational capabilities than younger firms. Learning and storing the knowledge embodied in organizational capabilities necessitates the passage of time because the learning process requires repetition and experimentation.

name: Firm size
definition: A capabilities perspective suggests that larger firms tend to have greater stocks of valuable embedded organizational capabilities as a result of the social and interactive aspects of organizational learning. Larger size indicates the potential presence of firm-specific learning mechanisms with value for the continued development and improvement of organizational capabilities.

name: Radical manufacturing technology adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of radical manufacturing technologies", "adoption likelihood", "the decision to adopt major manufacturing technologies"]
definition: 'Radical manufacturing technologies' are manufacturing tools and technologies that have the potential to redefine an industry through the disruption of existing competitive advantages, reducing the leverage of established firms and creating opportunities for the entry of new competitors. The authors highlight the notion of potential in this definition: radical manufacturing technologies may represent discontinuous innovation and quantum change in the way things are produced, but only implementation and competitive reaction can ultimately determine whether they are financially superior to existing technologies.

name: Firm survival
definition: At the firm level, the authors take the perspective of Mitchell (1994) and define failure as the exit of a company from the relevant product market, whether the business is dissolved or sold to another company. Firm survival is the avoidance of an exit from the product market.

name: Adoption timing
definition: The point in time at which a firm adopts a radical manufacturing technology, captured by the number of years elapsed since each technology was first adopted. Research on technology diffusion suggests that new technologies experience a diffusion process, with performance and survival advantages for earlier adopters.

name: Adoption timing relative to the diffusion inflection point
authors_terms: ["adopting prior to the point of inflection", "adopting radical manufacturing technologies prior to the point of maximum penetration", "adoption prior to t*"]
definition: Whether or not a firm adopted each technology prior to t*, the point of maximum penetration (inflection point) of the estimated Bass diffusion curve for each technology.

name: Adoption magnitude
authors_terms: ["adoption magnitude effect", "cumulative technology adoption", "bundling", "greater numbers of radical manufacturing technologies"]
definition: Magnitude refers to the variety of technologies in the manufacturing technology portfolio of each firm and is captured by whether a firm had adopted any one kind of technology, any two, any three, or any four. The authors refer to this technology strategy as the 'adoption magnitude effect.'

name: Technology bundles
definition: While individual technologies may each have a discrete value-added effect on the firm, certain technology combinations may exhibit an amplifying benefit effect; in a more complex form, technology ladders may exist in which new technologies build upon in-use technologies to produce firm advantage.

name: Firm-specific knowledge resources
authors_terms: ["firm-specific knowledge resources", "firm-specific knowledge", "firm-specific knowledge assets", "firm-specificity of knowledge resources"]
definition: If a firm pursues new knowledge close to its existing knowledge base and with specific applications to its own business setting, the firm is likely to develop firm-specific knowledge, which is more useful to the firm and has less applicability across firm boundaries. Firm-specific knowledge often results from a search for, and accumulation of, new solutions that build upon a firm's established knowledge base.

name: Employee stock ownership
authors_terms: ["employee stock ownership", "employee equity ownership", "employee ownership", "economic-based governance mechanism"]
definition: An economic-based employee governance mechanism intended to secure employees' economic gains against ex post value appropriation. Such equity ownership provides key employees greater power to bargain ex post over the economic rents generated from the deployment of firm-specific knowledge assets.

name: Firm-employee relationships
definition: A relationship-based governance mechanism that focuses on fostering trust between the firm and its employees. When employees consistently receive favorable treatment from their firm, they are likely to develop a sense of trust that the firm will not take advantage of their vulnerability ex post and thus are more likely to reciprocate the favorable treatment by engaging in firm-specific human capital investments.

name: Firm economic performance
definition: Although firm-specific knowledge resources are a potential source of a firm's superior economic performance, the firm's actual economic performance may diverge substantially from its potential. The governance of key employees who actually deploy and utilize a firm's resources moderates the de facto economic rents generated by the firm.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was proxied by the natural logarithm of the total number of employees in a firm.

name: Negative environmental information
authors_terms: ["negative news", "negative environmental information", "negative information revealed", "lack of governance mechanisms", "actions taken to reduce GHG emissions"]
definition: Negative news, from the perspective of the CDP, is firms failing to implement the desired actions to respond to and combat climate change. The measures are coded to reflect a failure to implement specific governance mechanisms or actions to reduce GHG emissions.

name: Linguistic obfuscation
definition: Linguistic obfuscation is presenting information in a way that is difficult to understand by virtue of the structure of the linguistic presentation, and is an anticipatory impression management tactic. Obfuscation is a structure of writing that obscures the information revealed and thereby confuses, distracts, or perplexes readers.

name: Disclosure completeness
authors_terms: ["disclosure completeness", "extent of disclosure", "disclosure score", "more complete disclosures"]
definition: CDP provides an assessment of the completeness of each survey response with the disclosure score, a rating between 0 and 100 that assesses the comprehensiveness of the respondent's answers to each of the survey questions.

name: Prior environmental reputation
authors_terms: ["prior environmental reputation", "domain-specific reputation", "good prior environmental reputation", "prior year performance score"]
definition: The prior year performance score rating of the firm is based entirely on the performance criteria dictated by the CDP and thus captures the firm's reputation vis-a-vis the CDP. In this context, firm reputation vis-a-vis the CDP represents the firm's domain-specific reputation.

name: Environmental performance rating
definition: CDP summarizes the survey responses of each firm with a performance score, a letter grade from A to E intended to summarize the reported actions to improve the environmental performance of the firm. It is an indication of the level of action taken by the company to manage its impacts, not a comprehensive metric of how low-carbon or green the company is.

name: Institutional complexity
definition: Organizations face institutional complexity whenever they are confronted with incompatible prescriptions from constituents holding different institutional logics, 'making it unclear how an organization can maintain its legitimacy.' The authors distinguish three levels of institutional complexity (low, moderate, and high) based on the support or opposition of powerful external constituents and organization members.

name: Powerful external constituent support
authors_terms: ["support of a powerful external constituent", "parental support", "powerful external constituents", "support of powerful constituents"]
definition: Powerful external constituents are 'constituents on whom the decision maker's organization especially depends for resources or legitimacy (Oliver, 1991; Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978), including exchange partners with whom the firm shares mutual commitments.' Parents are a key source of legitimacy in this sector, as they judge whether childcare centers provide 'good' care and guidance for children.

name: Organizational member support
definition: Organization members are the employees who typically must implement a new practice; 'employees are unlikely to accept practices that undermine their professional interests and identities,' and their lack of support is salient to decision makers as it may indicate an identity conflict for the organization.

name: Delay of intended compliance
authors_terms: ["delay of intended compliance", "delay of compliance", "delays in intended compliance"]
definition: The delay of intended compliance with the new law: when respondents would comply with the new law, changing their practices and installing the technology, given that inspection and enforcement would begin in five years.

name: Response to coercive institutional pressure
definition: 'Accommodative responses (those responses that were focused on moving themselves and/or others in the field toward acceptance of the practice)' and 'resistant responses (those responses that were focused on enabling the decision maker to resist the institutional pressure)'; delaying involved waiting to see how the situation unfolded.

name: Skilled employees
authors_terms: ["skilled employees", "qualified personnel", "employees with more than a secondary education"]
definition: To be able to invest in R&D, a firm has to have internal knowledge resources in the form of qualified personnel that can undertake the R&D and generate new knowledge; employees need skills to be able to understand not only how to use the technology but also why to use it.

name: Free cash flow
authors_terms: ["free cash flow", "financial resources in excess of those needed for current operations"]
definition: To be able to invest in formal R&D, a firm needs to have financial resources in excess of those needed for current operations; a firm that has limited free cash flow does not have discretionary funds to invest in R&D and will be more likely to never invest.

name: Tight relationship with customers
authors_terms: ["tight relationship with customers", "tight relationships with customers", "tight relationship with the customer"]
definition: Tight relationships with customers provide the firm with ideas on the needs of customers as well as where and how it can innovate its products. A tight relationship with the customer is needed to facilitate the development of trust and exchange of information.

name: Tight relationship with suppliers
authors_terms: ["tight relationship with suppliers", "tight relationships with suppliers"]
definition: Tight relationships with suppliers give the firm ideas on the development and integration of inputs into updated processes and new products. The firm that has a tight relationship with suppliers can develop the trusting relationships that facilitate the transfer not only of inputs but also of the technology and knowledge associated with these inputs.

name: Tight relationship with a parent firm
authors_terms: ["tight relationship with a parent firm", "tight relationship with the parent firm", "tight relationship with a parent company"]
definition: Tight relationships with parent companies provide the firm with ideas on new technologies. A firm that belongs to another company can rely on the parent firm for resources, not only managerial and financial but also technological.

name: Frequency of formal R&D investments
authors_terms: ["frequency of R&D investments", "frequency of formal R&D investments", "frequency of investing in R&D"]
definition: In terms of the frequency of investments in R&D, a firm has three main strategies open to it: always invest in R&D, never invest in R&D, and sometimes invest in R&D, with the last type further split into starting, stopping, and varying investing. This frequency is measured via a classification of firms by the frequency of their R&D expenditures during the period for which we have data, 1990-2002.

name: Mobile money platform penetration
authors_terms: ["mobile money platform penetration", "mobile money penetration", "penetration of mobile money platforms"]
definition: Mobile money platforms are digital multisided platforms that provide financial services through a mobile phone interface and enable unbanked customers to transact using their mobile phones without requiring a linked bank account, credit card, or the internet. The study identifies a source of variation in national policies that was plausibly exogenous to individual borrowers but increased the penetration of mobile money platforms.

name: Access to credit from formal financial institutions
authors_terms: ["access to credit from formal financial institutions", "access to credit", "borrowed from a formal financial institution"]
definition: Access to credit among end users from formal financial institutions, such as banks, credit unions, and MFIs. The main dependent variable is a binary variable coding for whether a respondent borrowed from a formal financial institution as applicable in the country where the survey was conducted.

name: Mobile money account ownership
authors_terms: ["mobile money usage", "mobile money accounts", "active mobile account", "has mobile money"]
definition: Whether respondents have a mobile money account; the authors report respondents' increase in mobile money usage after the regulatory reforms.

name: Employee approval of CEO leadership
authors_terms: ["employee approval of CEO leadership", "employee approval of the CEO", "employee approval", "employees' approval of CEOs' leadership"]
definition: The level of approval that a firm's employees express toward their CEO's leadership; employees can exhibit three responses to CEOs, including acceptance, indifference, or rejection. When a CEO receives a higher level of approval from employees, it signals that employees are confident in the CEO's leadership and are supportive of the CEO's strategies.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: CEO dismissal is the ultimate sanction that a board uses to discipline a CEO when its assessment of the CEO's leadership turns out to be unsatisfactory.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Firm financial performance is the most salient and relevant factor that boards use in deciding to retain or dismiss CEOs. Although firm financial performance is also affected by macro-economic conditions and industry trends that are beyond the CEOs' control, boards can make a more informed assessment by comparing their firms' financial performance to that of other firms in the same industry.

name: Analyst recommendation negativity
authors_terms: ["analyst recommendations", "security analysts' recommendations", "negative analyst recommendations", "negative recommendations"]
definition: Stock recommendations issued by security analysts, who are widely recognized as legitimate external experts who are qualified to assess a firm and its leadership, and which boards tend to utilize in CEO dismissal decisions. Security analysts are known to make more optimistically biased recommendations.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "power in the CEO's relationship with the board of directors"]
definition: The CEO's power in his or her relationship with the board of directors; prior research suggests that CEOs can influence board decisions by either controlling the information that is presented to boards or influencing how boards interpret that information.

name: Prior exits
authors_terms: ["Prior exits", "observed prior exits", "prior firm exits from the VC industry"]
definition: Prior exits represents the number of VC firms that exited at time t−1, were located in the same geographical state as the focal VC firm, and had the same investment focus as given by VentureXpert (early-stage, late-stage, or balanced).

name: Prior entries
authors_terms: ["Prior entries", "observed prior entries", "prior firm entries into the VC industry"]
definition: Prior entries is a count of all VC firms that entered the VC market at time t−1 and shared the geographical state and investment focus of the focal firm.

name: Firm uncertainty
authors_terms: ["firm uncertainty", "firm performance volatility", "Firm volatility", "uncertainty resulting from a firm's performance volatility"]
definition: Uncertainty that results from volatile firm performance is idiosyncratic and therefore uniquely affects that firm's decision making; we refer to this type as firm uncertainty.

name: Market uncertainty
authors_terms: ["market uncertainty", "market volatility", "Market volatility", "uncertainty resulting from market volatility"]
definition: Uncertainty that results from market volatility is common to all firms and therefore affects their decision making to the same degree; this type is market uncertainty.

name: Inference uncertainty
authors_terms: ["inference uncertainty", "information inconsistency", "Information inconsistency", "inconsistency in inferred information"]
definition: A third type of uncertainty stems not from volatility but rather from others' actions revealing inconsistent information, which inhibits the focal firm from updating its private information; we refer to this as inference uncertainty.

name: Firm exit
definition: Our focus is on exit of the firm itself (i.e., firm disbandment).

name: Executive compensation program
authors_terms: ["compensation program", "compensation programs", "executive compensation", "incentive program", "incentive plans", "compensation package"]
definition: The compensation program of the SBU manager, which the authors treat as an important mediating mechanism between the wishes of a firm's owners and the strategic behavior of that firm's management, and which is made up of salary, bonus and equity-based incentives and the objectives to which incentive pay is tied.

name: Marketing expenditures
authors_terms: ["marketing-oriented expenditures", "marketing expenditures", "overall marketing expenditures", "advertising expenditures", "expenditures on sales personnel"]
definition: Marketing-oriented expenditures of the SBU, whose benefits the authors argue are much shorter-lived and whose returns have a smaller variance than those of R&D expenditures.

name: R&D and innovation activity
definition: R&D expenditures, defined as expenditures designed to discover new knowledge, or new uses of current knowledge, not directly related to a firm's existing, market-ready product or design, together with their likely derivatives such as new product introduction and technological advances.

name: Product-line diversification
authors_terms: ["product-line diversification", "product diversification", "degree of product line diversification", "product breadth"]
definition: Diversification of the SBU's product line, which the authors argue allows a manager to hedge against divisional 'bankruptcy' and to smooth out divisional revenues and profits.

name: Investment in capital equipment
authors_terms: ["investment in capital equipment", "capital equipment expenditures", "capital investment"]
definition: Investment in capital equipment, which is typically considered a commitment to a project exceeding the current time period and is accounted for under GAAP as a fixed cost to be expensed over several periods.

name: Employee training expenditures
authors_terms: ["employee training expenditures", "employee training", "investment in employee training"]
definition: Expenditures on employee training, which a manager with a long-term perspective will typically make since the present value of the future cash flows associated with a well-trained employee base will likely exceed the current training cost.

name: Centralization of management decisions
authors_terms: ["centralization of management decisions", "MGMT CENT", "centralization of non-R&D decisions"]
definition: Concentration of management decision rights, the opposite of delegation (when the right to make decisions and evaluate activities is not concentrated); the authors' MGMT CENT factor combines the centralization of capital investment, budgeting, management personnel, and pricing/marketing decisions.

name: Centralization of R&D decisions
authors_terms: ["centralization of R&D decisions", "R&D CENT", "centralization of R&D-related decisions"]
definition: Concentration of R&D-related decision rights; the authors' R&D CENT factor combines the centralization of R&D investment, direction of R&D effort, and R&D personnel decisions.

name: Formality of procedures
definition: Formality is the presence of rules and procedures that influence decision-making behavior, examined relevant to the level in the hierarchy.

name: SBU size
definition: Size of the strategic business unit, obtained in terms of number of employees.

name: Internalization of value chain activities
authors_terms: ["internalization", "boundary choice", "internal development", "internalize a value chain activity"]
definition: Following Capron and Mitchell (2009), we define the boundary choice for a value chain activity as the decision to undertake it either through internal development (within firm boundaries) or external development (partnering with another firm through joint venture, licensing or strategic alliances, or outsourcing).

name: Enduring transaction hazards
definition: Transaction hazards are the costs incurred if an activity is carried out externally, and some sources of these costs, particularly as they relate to other types of uncertainty (e.g., demand and environmental, systemic technology shocks) and transaction frequency, may endure throughout an industry's life. The influence of enduring transaction costs (e.g., uncertainty and transaction frequency) is independent of industry evolution.

name: Entry timing
authors_terms: ["entry year", "transient transaction hazards", "late entrant", "timing of entry"]
definition: Entry year is defined as the year in which a firm started bioethanol production, and the timing of entry into the industry is an important determinant of the magnitude of transaction hazards an entrant experiences. Transient transaction hazards are those associated with asset specificity and technological uncertainty, whose relative importance declines as industries evolve.

name: Pre-entry activity-level experience
authors_terms: ["pre-entry activity-level experience", "pre-entry experience in an activity", "activity-level pre-entry experience"]
definition: We define a firm's pre-entry activity-level experience as experience accrued by the firm, or the founder(s) of a start-up, that is related to a particular value chain activity and gained prior to entry in the focal industry. Pre-entry activity-level experience is thus the possession of resources and capabilities related to that value chain activity.

name: Diversifying entrant
authors_terms: ["diversifying entrant", "integrative capabilities", "firm-level integrative capabilities", "pre-entry integrative capabilities"]
definition: Prior research has defined diversifying entrants as preexisting firms that enter a focal industry and start-ups as firms that are born in the focal industry context. By virtue of having existed in another industry prior to entry into a new one, diversifying entrants possess integrative capabilities relatively lacking in start-ups; firm-level or integrative pre-entry capabilities are defined as present in diversifying entrants.

name: Semantic autonomy
authors_terms: ["semantic autonomy", "autonomous subsidiary names", "a stock of autonomous subsidiary names"]
definition: Semantic autonomy is one of two ways of naming a subsidiary, whereby a completely new name is used to enact an autonomous identity; autonomous subsidiary names are woven out of previously unconnected semantic elements, and autonomy is instantiated when there is not a single word overlapping between the names of the parent and its subsidiary.

name: Semantic seeding
authors_terms: ["semantic seeding", "seeded subsidiary names", "a stock of seeded subsidiary names", "seeding moves"]
definition: Semantic seeding is the other way of naming a subsidiary, whereby the parent's name is retained at least partially to leverage its existing identity; seeding occurs when there is at least one word shared between the names of the parent and its subsidiary.

name: Creativity evaluations
definition: The gatekeepers' evaluation of a fashion house's creativity, grounded in their perception of symbolic novelty and commercial appropriateness; the Journal du Textile rankings are built from industrial buyers' creativity points assigned for the houses' showcased main collections.

name: Visibility
definition: Firm visibility is a concept closely related to the institutionalist definition of reputation: 'being known . . . irrespective of judgment or evaluation'; in this study media coverage is used as a measure of visibility because media selectively organize public attention around producers and products.

name: Media co-appearance with autonomous subsidiary names
authors_terms: ["autonomy co-appearance", "the parent's media co-appearance with its autonomous subsidiary names", "parent-subsidiary co-appearance in media"]
definition: When a subsidiary name frequently appears together with the parent's name in the media, it reinforces the gatekeepers' cognitive association of the new and old names, so that unaffiliated subsidiary names stop being surprising to onlookers and may as well be perceived as seeded names with a built-in link to the parent.

name: Time since last semantic move
authors_terms: ["time since last autonomy move", "time since last seeding move", "semantic continuity", "timing of a new semantic move"]
definition: The timing of a new semantic move is the extent of semantic continuity that comes before it, that is, the time elapsed since the parent's last semantic move of the same type or since the parent's founding if no such move has been made before.

name: Knowledge sharing
authors_terms: ["knowledge sharing", "sharing knowledge", "knowledge-sharing behavior", "the act of providing an answer"]
definition: Knowledge-sharing behavior is the act of providing an answer to other participants in the online knowledge community. The authors consider that knowledge was shared if participant i posted at least one reply to participant j's question k.

name: Categorical similarity
definition: By categorical similarity, the authors mean that participants belong to the same category; the two categories they investigate are geographic location and hierarchical status. Categorical similarity is comembership in categories, and membership in these categories provides diffuse information about what individuals are likely to know.

name: Expertise similarity
definition: By expertise similarity, the authors mean the extent to which participants' expertise about technical matters addressed in the community is similar. Expertise similarity provides fine-grained information about what individuals know.

name: Provider experience
authors_terms: ["provider experience", "a knowledge provider's experience", "experience in the online knowledge community", "knowledge-provider experience"]
definition: A knowledge provider gains more experience in the system each time he or she posts or answers a question. The measure should capture knowledge provider i's cumulative number of opportunities to observe other participants' knowledge-sharing activities.

name: Seeker visibility
definition: Seeker visibility captures the number of answers a seeker has provided to the online knowledge community. These answers provide information about the areas in which a seeker has expertise—about what he or she knows.

name: Product resource requirements
authors_terms: ["resource requirements created by the envisioned product", "project resource requirements", "product resource requirements"]
definition: The authors claim that product characteristics determine the scale and scope of resources needed to develop, produce, and commercialize the envisioned product; firms will be more likely to form horizontal alliances for more complex projects requiring greater and broader sets of difficult-to-trade resources.

name: Production experience
authors_terms: ["production experience", "firm production experience", "firm's production experience in a product domain"]
definition: The more firms have, in the past, launched products in the same domain, the more likely they are to have built relevant production capabilities by developing and codifying activity-specific know-how and by investing in assets redeployable to new products in the same domain.

name: Horizontal alliance experience
authors_terms: ["horizontal alliance experience", "past alliance experience", "firms' horizontal alliance experience in the considered product domain"]
definition: Having collaborated in the past enables firms to assess the trustworthiness of potential partners, better select with whom to collaborate, and reduce monitoring costs; thanks to their collaborative know-how, firms are capable of better managing day-to-day cooperation.

name: Product expansion mode
authors_terms: ["alliance", "make or ally choice", "expansion mode", "product expansion through horizontal alliances"]
definition: The authors define autonomous product expansion as a firm's independent decision to launch a new product and to fully bear the risks and rewards associated with such a decision; product expansion through horizontal alliances, in contrast, involves sharing product definition, risks, and returns with firms competing in the same business domain.

name: Inertia
authors_terms: ["inertia", "repetitive momentum", "number of past ties", "number of previous relationships", "momentum effect"]
definition: We view alliance selection decisions within an inertia framework and suggest that the inertia of previous alliance selection routines, independent of the information advantage gained from experiencing past partners' behaviors, drives selection decisions. As a firm engages in repeated alliances with a particular partner, this choice increasingly becomes a standardized response to the problem of alliance partner selection.

name: Reciprocity
definition: Reciprocity has been defined as a pattern of exchanges in which one partner receives a benefit from another partner in return for a benefit given previously to that partner. The extent to which a partner has engaged in reciprocity or reciprocal behavior in past ties is an indicator of its reliability.

name: Past alliance performance
authors_terms: ["alliance performance", "partnership outcomes", "past partnership outcomes", "performance level of past alliances"]
definition: We argue that firms deal with this uncertainty by considering the performance outcomes of past ties and choosing partners associated with favorable outcomes. A firm's previous success with a given partner produces a bias toward this partner when the focal firm evaluates new alliance opportunities.

name: Partner industry experience
authors_terms: ["experience", "bank j's industry experience", "experience in alliance context"]
definition: Partner selection is partly determined by the specific context, requirements, and purpose of an alliance, because firms seek partners with the appropriate expertise. Past partners possessing experience relevant to the objectives of a new alliance context are viewed as more capable and are more likely to be chosen in future alliances.

name: Partner selection
authors_terms: ["partner selection", "probability of a lead manager bank selecting each of its past partners", "alliance formation"]
definition: The dependent variable, partner selection, was a dichotomous measure recording whether bank i entered into an alliance with bank j for an IPO event.

name: Systematic risk
definition: That part of variation in return caused by economy-wide disturbances affecting all investments; it is the variation in an investment's return associated with the economy-wide or market return, and businesses with high betas need to compensate for additional risk by showing higher average rates of return.

name: Unsystematic risk
authors_terms: ["unsystematic risk", "unsystematic return", "standard error of the residual"]
definition: Variation in return not associated with economy-wide conditions; in this study it is estimated as the standard error of the residual from the accounting-beta equation.

name: Return on investment
definition: The return on investment of a business unit, used as the relevant measure of accounting return and as the dependent variable in explaining differences in profitability; its earnings numerator is a consequence of investment decisions made in the past, while its assets denominator also influences future earnings.

name: Preexisting interorganizational trust
definition: Broadly defined, interorganizational trust is an organization's expectation that another firm will not act opportunistically. The authors focus on dyadic preexisting interorganizational trust, the level of trust that existed prior to a dyad's current exchange.

name: Governance mode formality
authors_terms: ["governance mode", "mode of governance", "buy, ally, and make", "market, hybrid, and hierarchy", "less formal modes of governance"]
definition: The authors examine the three prototypical governance choices for dyadic exchanges, buy, ally and make, which Williamson (1991) called market, hybrid and hierarchy. In the buy mode an organization procures an input from another using simple contracts; in the ally mode one organization enters a formal arrangement with another using a complex (yet incomplete) contract; in the make mode one organizational unit procures from another unit that is part of the same broader organization.

name: Exchange performance
definition: Governance costs have a critical impact on expected exchange performance because performance levels increase when governance costs are lower, all else held equal. Because firms keep archival figures on the economic performance of exchanges confidential, the authors based their Performance measure on questions concerning assembler satisfaction.

name: Interorganizational conflict
definition: An empirically derived construct formed from the three performance questions that loaded onto a second factor; higher levels of this construct equate to higher levels of conflict. The authors consider it a potentially ambiguous measure of performance because it cannot differentiate between functional and dysfunctional conflict.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "Supplier Asset Specificity", "Assembler Asset Specificity", "Breadth", "cospecialized investments"]
definition: The degree to which dyad partners had made cospecialized investments, i.e., the level of asset specificity in an exchange. Williamson's 'main locomotive', asset specificity is the transaction attribute the authors focus on, suppressing uncertainty and frequency.

name: Embedding of challengers' power
authors_terms: ["embedding challengers' power in formal structures", "formal power possessed by challengers", "formalization of faculty councils"]
definition: Embedding of challengers' power refers to challengers securing their power and interests by establishing their interests as a formal structure of the organization after an initial victory over incumbents; once a certain interest or power is established as a formal structure, it tends to endure by allowing little opportunity for modification.

name: Persistence of role-committed incumbents
authors_terms: ["persistence of role-committed incumbents", "persistence of actors who are committed to the political role of the incumbents", "role commitment on the incumbents' side"]
definition: The organizational role as a structural property exists independent of specific actors who occupy and play that role, and the persistence of role-committed incumbents refers to formerly powerful incumbents surviving as a cohesive group with a considerable amount of political power and as institutional agents highly committed to the incumbent role after the challengers' initial victory.

name: Contentious countermovement tactics
authors_terms: ["contentious countermovement tactics by incumbents", "countermovement by incumbents", "contentious repression tactics"]
definition: A countermovement is 'a movement that makes contrary claims simultaneously to those of the original movement'; it is the incumbents' attempt to resist or subvert the change initiated by the challengers, and contentious countermovement tactics are repression tactics that bring about open confrontation with challengers.

name: Hybrid practice adoption
authors_terms: ["hybrid practice", "hybrid system", "adoption of a hybrid practice", "hybridization"]
definition: The label 'hybrid' is used in this paper to denote an organizational practice that distinctly differs from any existing pure practices, yet still retains the key (core) features of two or more of the existing pure practices; the 'hybrid' was defined as a system in which a university president was selected by the simultaneous participation of both professors and boards of trustees or government agents.

name: Power source match
definition: We define power source match as a syndicate member having both ownership and status advantage over another member.

name: Ownership-dominated power source mismatch
definition: We define ownership-dominated power source mismatch as a member's ownership advantage over another one being greater than the latter's status advantage.

name: Status-dominated power source mismatch
definition: We define status-dominated power source mismatch as a member's ownership advantage over another one being less than the latter's status advantage.

name: Effectiveness of VC syndication
authors_terms: ["the effectiveness of VC syndication", "effectiveness of interorganizational relations"]
definition: VC firms help new ventures to earn capital gains from the ventures' successful exit, which is a major indicator of the effectiveness of VC investment; the authors use time-to-IPO or mergers and acquisitions (M&A) as a proxy for the effectiveness of VC syndication.

name: Familiarity
definition: Familiarity stems from prior collaboration among syndicate members; in contrast to the relationship between new collaborators, repeated interactions contain greater trust and more stable role expectations.

name: Entrepreneurial performance
definition: Entrepreneurial performance (i.e., the performance of the portfolio company) may moderate the interactive effect of power source match and status-dominated power source mismatch; patents represent a major form of intellectual property for venture-backed portfolio companies and a key indicator of their performance.

name: Ownership
definition: Ownership is a source of legitimate power, because it involves the assertion of a legitimate right to take or retain the possession of an object and the acknowledgement of the rightfulness of this claim by others; it is the 'means of possessing a resource and therefore controlling it.'

name: Status
definition: Status refers to an actor's prestige, which reflects the worth of the actor. Status is a source of referent power, in that a low-status actor desires to be associated with a higher-status one and is willing to assume attitudes or beliefs held by the latter.

name: Shared cluster location
authors_terms: ["shared cluster location", "common cluster location", "sharing a cluster location", "shared cluster transactions"]
definition: Shared cluster location refers to transactions in which both exchange partners are located in the same geographic cluster of semiconductor firms. The authors emphasize that the importance of being in a shared cluster extends beyond the mere fact of increased proximity between any two particular firms, resting instead on the cluster-wide interactions, shared understandings, and social relationships that reduce information asymmetry.

name: Choice of acquisition over alliance
authors_terms: ["choice of acquisition over alliance", "acquisition versus alliance decision", "organizational governance choice", "comparative governance choice"]
definition: The comparative governance choice of how to organize a given transaction, specifically whether a particular transaction is structured as an acquisition or as an alliance. The authors argue that the choice between an alliance and acquisition is among the most important decisions a firm makes concerning its corporate development.

name: Technological distance
authors_terms: ["tech distance", "technological distance", "dissimilarity in the exchange partners' technological resources"]
definition: The similarity or dissimilarity of the exchange partners' technological resources, calculated from their patent portfolios. The authors argue that the relatedness of exchange partners is a key source of information asymmetry, because similar resources allow each partner to evaluate the other efficiently.

name: Knowledge stocks
authors_terms: ["total patents", "technical knowledge stocks", "knowledge stocks", "combined knowledge stocks"]
definition: The amount of the exchange partners' knowledge-based resources, measured as a logged sum of the parties' citation-weighted patents over the most recent five years. The authors argue that information asymmetry grows as the exchange partners' combined knowledge stocks increase.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: The geographic closeness of the two exchange partners, calculated from firm zip codes. The authors argue that information spillovers within clusters attenuate with distance, so information about nearby firms is most conspicuous and readily absorbed.

name: Problem structure
definition: Problem structure represents the level of understanding of the K interactions among N knowledge sets for a given problem. Given this level of understanding, problems vary on a continuum from relatively ill structured (poorly defined initial states and ambiguous problem-solving approaches) to relatively well structured (well-defined initial states and explicit problem-solving approaches).

name: Technological area experience
authors_terms: ["technological area experience", "TA experience", "therapeutic area experience", "prior therapeutic area experience"]
definition: Prior therapeutic area experience: because clinical approaches vary by the therapeutic characteristics of drug compounds, prior therapeutic area experience is an important determinant of development performance, and as firms gain therapeutic area experience they develop expertise and problem-solving approaches that can be drawn on in similar and subsequent development efforts.

name: Development organization mode
authors_terms: ["internal development", "insourced development", "outsourced development", "organization of drug development activity"]
definition: The variable internal development indicates whether the drug compound was insourced (coded 1) by the pharmaceutical firm or outsourced (coded 0) in part or in total to CROs. Insourcing offers control and coordination that support knowledge development and transfer, whereas outsourcing relies on market-based incentives and specialized expertise.

name: Drug development completion speed
authors_terms: ["drug development completion time", "technological development completion speed", "time-to-market", "IND time"]
definition: Whereas prior authors examine drug development success, this paper's data allow it to examine drug development completion time, i.e., the calendar time drug compounds are under clinical trials, measured as the logged calendar time between IND submission and NDA submission.

name: Mergers and acquisitions
authors_terms: ["mergers and acquisitions (M&As)", "ownership change", "plant that is destined to be sold", "plants that are sold", "partial acquisition", "full acquisition"]
definition: Ownership changes in which plants or firms are sold. A partial acquisition occurs when a firm purchases one or several plants from another company, whereas in a full acquisition it purchases a firm consisting of multiple divisions and numerous establishments.

name: Employee compensation
definition: When matching is efficient and workers are well sorted, they are paid on the basis of their productivity; a bad match arises when workers are overcompensated relative to comparable employees in the same industry and role.

name: Plant employment
definition: The labor input of the establishment; employment and output are the plant-level outcomes used, together with capital and materials, to assess what happens to establishments after an ownership change.

name: Earnings growth
definition: The change in a worker's earnings over time; the authors argue that the quality of the match is reflected in a worker's earnings, so departing employees should experience higher earnings growth.

name: Employee job change
authors_terms: ["employees changing jobs", "departing employees", "employee destinations", "employment status change"]
definition: Employees who change jobs in the aftermath of an M&A, either by moving to another establishment or by ceasing employment, as opposed to employees who remain in the same establishment.

name: Workforce quality
authors_terms: ["average worker quality", "quality of the workforce", "skill upgrading", "quality of human capital"]
definition: The average quality of the workforce of a plant, which the authors argue rises through 'skill upgrading' and an increase in the firm's demand for educated workers after an ownership change.

name: Plant productivity
definition: Total factor productivity of a plant, assessed from data on output and inputs, that is, capital, labor, and materials.

name: Firm performance
definition: For each acquiring firm the authors have two indicators of performance, profit (value-added per employee) and market share.

name: Acquisition scope
definition: The distinction between a partial acquisition, in which a firm purchases one or several plants from another company, and a full acquisition, in which it purchases a firm consisting of multiple divisions and numerous establishments.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["entry", "de novo entry", "de novo start-ups", "aggregate entry", "entry rate"]
definition: The authors define entry as a new commercial banking institution that comes into existence by way of a new charter, which restricts the sample to de novo entry by entrepreneurs. They study the amount of entry: how individuals' decisions combined with market conditions affect the amount of entry in a market.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: One of two distinct sources of uncertainty in entrepreneurial ventures: uncertainty regarding market demand. In the model the discount rate is decomposed into a risk-free component and a risk premium reflecting market volatility (demand uncertainty), and in the empirical work risk is approximated by variability in demand.

name: Ability uncertainty
definition: The second distinct source of uncertainty in entrepreneurial ventures: entrepreneurs know the performance distribution within a market but are uncertain about where they lie within that distribution. Overconfidence is modeled as A times ability (cost) dispersion, where the degree of ambiguity is captured by that dispersion.

name: Failure rate
definition: The failure rate represents the entrepreneur's ex ante probability of drawing a value for marginal cost above the cutoff. The authors adopt the FDIC definition of failure as the sum of 'forced mergers' and FDIC 'paid outs,' and measure the failure rate as the ratio of the number of these failures over the number of incumbents.

name: Mean survivor cost
authors_terms: ["mean survivor cost", "mean cost of surviving firms", "mean cost of the survivor pool"]
definition: The mean cost of surviving firms, those for whom marginal cost is at or below the cutoff. In the empirical work the survivor pool is the set of firms that have remained in the industry for three years, and the mean of the transformed cost inefficiency of that pool characterizes the market cost distribution.

name: Opportunity cost
definition: Entry occurs when the expected profit stream exceeds the entrepreneur's opportunity cost, which comprises the sunk cost of entry K plus the foregone wage stream from the best employment alternative W.

name: Positional embeddedness
authors_terms: ["positional embeddedness", "combined network centrality", "combined centrality at founding", "network centrality"]
definition: Positional embeddedness relates to the extent to which organizations occupy a central position in a network structure. Firms in central network positions have greater scope than noncentral firms for collecting and disseminating information.

name: Relational embeddedness
authors_terms: ["relational embeddedness", "prior direct ties", "direct ties at founding", "repeated ties"]
definition: Relational embeddedness refers to the presence of prior direct ties between two firms, which enable the exchange of information about each other's capabilities and reliability, enhance mutual trust and, in turn, mitigate the hazard of joint venture dissolution.

name: Structural embeddedness
authors_terms: ["structural embeddedness", "common partners", "common partners in previous year"]
definition: Structural embeddedness refers to partners that collaborating firms have in common. The partners common to two organizations encompass the set of direct ties common to both of them.

name: Positional asymmetry
authors_terms: ["positional asymmetry", "positionally asymmetric dyads at founding", "reputational imbalance", "positional imbalance"]
definition: Reputational imbalance arises when partners occupy different status brackets-that is, when one partner belongs to a high-status group while the other is a member of a low-status group. The positional imbalance between a central and a peripheral actor creates power imbalance between them.

name: Competitive overlap
authors_terms: ["competitive overlap", "resource and market overlap", "resource similarity and market commonality"]
definition: Firms exhibit high propensity to engage in mutual competitive behavior when they have a high degree of similarity in both the resources that they possess and the markets where they operate. Competitive overlap captures the potential for competitive interactions between partners.

name: Unplanned joint venture dissolution
authors_terms: ["unplanned joint venture dissolution", "hazard of unplanned dissolution", "unplanned dissolution"]
definition: We focus explicitly on unplanned joint venture dissolutions that occur because of problems arising during the course of the alliances. Although dissolution represents only one form of alliance performance, it usually reflects a business failure or irresolvable conflict between partners.

name: Regional similarity
authors_terms: ["regional similarity", "regional similarity between VCs and company founders"]
definition: Actors drawn from the same region (as proxied by their regional language) are likely to share the same taken-for-granted cultural assumptions and values. Since there is no pecking order among regions in this setting, regional similarity is more properly understood as a nominal attribute.

name: Caste similarity
authors_terms: ["caste similarity", "caste similarity between VCs and company founders"]
definition: The authors adopt the view of caste as practiced in contemporary Indian society, conceptualizing it as a nominal attribute consisting of the following five distinctive caste groups: priests, warriors, merchants, peasants, and untouchables.

name: Premoney valuation
definition: Premoney valuation is the postmoney valuation minus the investment amount. A higher valuation (either pre- or postmoney) implies a higher price from the VC's point of view since the equity stake is lower for a given investment amount.

name: Downside risk protection
authors_terms: ["downside risk protection", "downside risk protection aspect of pricing"]
definition: Bengtsson and Sensoy (2011) combine these individual contractual terms to conceptualize downside risk protection as the extent to which VCs possess a more debt-like claim on the company's cash flows.

name: Financial returns
definition: We measured the return earned by the VC firm in the investments (cumulated over funding rounds) it made in the focal portfolio company; a key strength of our study is that we measure the internal rate of return (IRR) earned by VC firms when investing into a focal company.

name: Investment stage
definition: By 'investment stage' we mean the timing of the venture capital investment into companies. Because of uncertainty, VCs typically stage investments in sequential rounds of financing, and subjective uncertainty likely decreases over funding rounds.

name: Industry newness to the VC firm
authors_terms: ["entering new industry", "market niche where it has little prior investment history"]
definition: Per deal we also measured the extent to which an industry is new for the VC firm(s). When they have a deep knowledge of the particular product market of the focal company, VCs are better able to understand the opportunities and challenges of building a valuable company, which reduces their subjective uncertainty.

name: Structural holes
definition: A firm can obtain important performance advantages when it exploits the brokerage opportunities created by the absence of ties among its partners. The more network partners-otherwise not connected to one another-are linked to the focal firm through bridging ties, the more structural holes this firm spans.

name: Firm scope of experience
definition: Organizational scope is defined as the number of markets in which a firm operates, and represents firms' capacity to absorb heterogeneous information; a firm that has maintained a wide scope of operations over time is termed 'wide-scope experience'. An investment advisor has wide-scope experience when it historically has provided services to customers that compete in different industries or originate from different countries.

name: Historic multimarket contact
definition: An increase in multimarket overlap between firms is associated with an increase in cooperation between them. Learning how to forbear in an open network with partners overlapping in different markets requires MMC experience from the focal firm, and a variable that adequately reflects firms' ability to prevent partners' noncooperation needs to capture the history of the firm's MMC with its network partners.

name: Firm centrality
definition: The bargaining power of firms is represented in their position in the overall social structure; more central firms have better access to information about business opportunities that circulates in their industry. Firms at the periphery of the social structure lack access to information about opportunities circulating in the industry, so their bargaining power is lower.

name: Firm performance
definition: The market share of investment banks is used as an indicator of their performance; the higher the market share of an investment bank, the greater are the fees that this bank earns from its M&A advisory business compared with its competition.

name: Stigma intensity
authors_terms: ["stigma intensity", "intensity of categorical stigma", "intensity of stigma"]
definition: The intensity of stakeholder disapproval targeting a category, which the authors label stigma intensity; disapproval can vary from quiet disapprobation to vocal condemnation and involve anything from a few isolated social actors to the plurality of an audience.

name: Media exposure
authors_terms: ["media exposure", "media coverage", "exposure of the stigmatized category in the media"]
definition: The exposure of the stigmatized category in the media; in a mass society the function of public exposure is institutionalized in the mass media of communication, and higher levels of coverage are associated with higher issue salience.

name: Extent of categorical membership
authors_terms: ["extent of membership in a stigmatized category", "extent of membership", "categorical membership"]
definition: Following Vergne (2012), membership in a stigmatized category is conceptualized as the relative extent to which an organization engages in activities pertaining to that category.

name: Disengagement from a stigmatized category
definition: A substantive response to disapproval whereby organizations reduce or withdraw their involvement in stigmatized activities, addressing stigma at its source rather than through cosmetic coping strategies.

name: Independent noncore director representation
authors_terms: ["outside noncore directors", "independent noncore directors", "number of outside noncore directors"]
definition: Outside or independent noncore directors are those who have no formal ties with the focal firm other than their board service, are not former executives of the firm, nor are currently executives of other public or large private firms.

name: Executive entrenchment
definition: According to Weisbach (1988, p. 435), 'Managerial entrenchment occurs when managers gain so much power that they are able to use the firm to further their own interests rather than the interests of shareholders.' Following Bebchuk et al. (2009), the authors assess the level of managerial control of the firm by examining the number of governance provisions that corporate boards adopt to provide incumbent executives protection from removal or the consequences of removal.

name: Corporate elite network embeddedness
authors_terms: ["outside noncore director embeddedness", "embeddedness of independent noncore directors in the network of corporate elites"]
definition: The embeddedness of outside noncore directors in the corporate elite network is computed using the mean number of ties the outside noncore directors of each firm have with other directors in the network of interlocking directorates among S&P 500 firms. A tie between two directors exists when both directors are present on the same corporate board of an S&P 500 firm.

name: Board tenure
authors_terms: ["outside noncore director tenure", "length of service of independent noncore directors"]
definition: The tenure of outside noncore directors for each firm is computed as the mean tenure among outside noncore directors that serve on a firm's board.

name: Independent noncore director equity ownership
authors_terms: ["outside noncore director equity ownership value", "equity ownership of independent noncore directors"]
definition: The equity ownership of outside noncore directors is measured by first extracting the number of shares owned by these directors and then multiplying these values by the year-end stock price.

name: Independent CEO director equity ownership
authors_terms: ["independent CEO director equity ownership value", "equity holdings by independent CEO directors"]
definition: The equity ownership of independent CEO directors is measured by first extracting the number of shares owned by these directors and then multiplying these values by the year-end stock price.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is computed as a firm's industry-adjusted return on equity. The authors first express a firm's ROE as net income over shareholders' equity and then deduct the industry ROE to arrive at a firm's performance relative to its rivals.

name: CEO organizational identification
definition: The degree to which a CEO's self-identity is intertwined with the identity of his/her organization, or the degree to which the CEO defines him-/herself in terms of the attributes of the organization. The authors argue that the fundamental nature of organizational identification is not different for CEOs.

name: CEO pay-performance decoupling
authors_terms: ["decoupling of firm performance from CEO cash compensation", "decoupling of CEO compensation from recent firm performance", "decoupling of high CEO pay from firm performance"]
definition: When high levels of CEO pay bear no significant relationship to firm performance, agency costs are more unequivocally present; the authors focus on the decoupling of CEO compensation from recent firm performance, that is, a weak relationship between CEO cash compensation and firm performance, as a more unambiguous representation of agency costs.

name: CEO perquisite-performance decoupling
authors_terms: ["decoupling of firm performance from CEO personal use of corporate aircraft", "decoupling of generous perquisites from firm performance", "decoupling of prior year performance from current year aircraft use"]
definition: The decoupling of generous perquisites from firm performance is a clear and straightforward instance of corporate policy entailing agency costs; the authors focus on the decoupling of CEO personal use of corporate aircraft from firm performance, rather than perquisite use itself, as a more unambiguous representation of agency costs.

name: Board independence
definition: Independence of a firm's board from management, measured as a composite of four indicators: the portion of the board composed of outside directors, separation of the CEO and board chair positions, the portion of outside directors who were personal friends of the CEO, and outside director stock ownership.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured with three indicators: return on assets (ROA), an accounting-based measure, and the market-to-book value of equity and total stock returns, two market-based measures.

name: Objective return on assets
authors_terms: ["after tax return on total assets", "objective measures of return on assets", "OBJATROA"]
definition: 'After tax return on total assets' is commonly viewed as one operational measure of the efficiency of a firm with regard to the profitable use of its total asset base.

name: Subjective return on assets
authors_terms: ["firm after tax return on total assets", "subjective measures of return on assets", "SUBATROA"]
definition: Members of a firm's TMT provided (subjective) perceptions of their firm's improvement (or decline) in return on assets relative to 'similar' firms in their industry over a 5 year time period, responding to an item that compared their firm to firms of similar sales volume in their industry and region.

name: Objective sales growth
authors_terms: ["growth in sales", "total sales", "objective measures of sales growth", "OBJSALES"]
definition: 'Growth in sales' provides a second measure of economic performance that reflects 'how well an organization relates to their environment' by successfully expanding their 'product market scope'.

name: Subjective sales growth
authors_terms: ["firm total sales growth performance/success", "subjective measures of sales growth", "SUBSALES"]
definition: Members of a firm's TMT provided (subjective) perceptions of their firm's improvement (or decline) in sales relative to 'similar' firms in their industry over a 5 year time period, responding to an item that compared their firm to firms of similar sales volume in their industry and region.

name: Global organizational performance
authors_terms: ["global measures of organizational performance", "global measures of performance", "overall firm performance", "OVERPERF", "SUBJCEOP"]
definition: Two measures of what may be considered overall or 'global' organizational performance: the TMTs' assessment of overall firm performance relative to peer firms and the CEO's assessment of the percentage of ideal or optimal performance the firm is achieving.

name: Economic performance
authors_terms: ["economic indicators of OP", "economic performance", "economic measures of performance"]
definition: The economic dimensions of organizational performance; two popular measures related to economic aspects of OP, return on assets and growth in sales, were used in this study.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The event study method was employed to estimate cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) that served as our dependent variable.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["independent outside board members", "independent outside board membership", "independent outside directors"]
definition: We refer to 'independent' outside directors as those who neither have business ties to the enterprise on whose board they serve, nor are they employed in an occupation that might cause them to seek to ingratiate themselves to firm management.

name: Blockholder board ownership
authors_terms: ["blockholder board member ownership", "blockholder board membership", "outside blockholder directors"]
definition: Blockholder board member ownership was estimated by first identifying all outside board members who either directly owned 5 percent or more of the acquiring firm's shares or represented an organization that did so.

name: Outside director ownership
authors_terms: ["board member ownership", "outside board member ownership", "equity holdings by outside board members"]
definition: Acquiring firm board member ownership was defined as the log form of the dollar value of outside board member ownership (exclusive of blockholder board member ownership).

name: Target-industry expertise
authors_terms: ["board member expertise of the target firm industry", "outside board members with target industry experience", "experience relevant to the target firm's industry"]
definition: In order for an outside board member to have been classified as having expertise related to the industry of the target firm, the board member must have been a manager or a board member of a firm in the same industry, as defined by the target firm's primary three-digit SIC code.

name: CEO acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["outside board members with experience as CEOs of acquiring firms", "CEO board members with acquisition experience", "board members who are CEOs with acquisition experience"]
definition: For a board member to qualify as a CEO with acquisition experience, he/she must have been the CEO of a publicly traded firm that completed an acquisition representing at least 10 percent of the acquiring firm's market capitalization within the 5 years preceding the focal acquisition.

name: Board service acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["outside board members with acquisition experience as directors of acquiring firms", "board member acquisition experience", "directors with prior acquisition experience as board members of other firms"]
definition: For a director to be recognized as having acquisition experience, he/she must have been a member of another board that presided over a major acquisition (representing at least 10% of the acquiring firm's market capitalization) during the 5 years prior to the focal acquisition.

name: Market entry into a nascent industry
definition: A firm's market entry is measured using a binary variable equal to 1 if a firm commercialized a transgenic crop for the first time in a given year. This measure is created by confirming sales of transgenic crops that are approved for commercial release based on the USDA coordinated framework for regulation of plant biotechnology.

name: Related technical capabilities
definition: Related technical capabilities are defined as a firm's expertise in similar and foundational, but not core, technology areas. Drawing on them may enable a firm's new technology development efforts by providing a broader repertoire of knowledge components, a scientific base, and higher levels of absorptive capacity.

name: Core technical capabilities
definition: Technical capabilities refer to a firm's expertise in the technology or scientific discipline of the focal industry. Expertise in agricultural biotechnology, that is, knowledge of gene sequences and methods of genetic transformation of plants, is considered to be the core technical capabilities.

name: Integrative capabilities
definition: Integrative capabilities refer to a firm's ability to integrate and link activities, capabilities, and objectives in a repeated and reliable manner. Integrative capabilities consist of a set of routines and mechanisms that underpin effective coordination, such as ongoing communication, common ground, and a supporting formal structure.

name: Complementary assets
authors_terms: ["complementary assets", "specialized complementary assets", "protected plant varieties", "elite varieties"]
