definition: Complementary assets refer to downstream market-related factors such as manufacturing facilities, distribution channels, and complementary technologies that not only are crucial for commercial success but also influential in shaping the direction of innovative activities. In this article, specialized complementary assets denote assets that have a narrow set of applications in a limited number of industries; high-quality crop varieties referred to as elite varieties or germplasm are considered specialized complementary assets used as platforms for genetic modification.

name: Legacy spinoff
definition: A spinoff of a firm's original line of business; legacy businesses are defined as the original business in which a firm operated at the time of its founding. Non-legacy spinoffs remove units other than a firm's legacy business and are not expected to have the same effect.

name: Analyst coverage termination
definition: Analysts who were covering the divesting firm prior to the spinoff announcement and terminate their coverage of it once the spinoff is announced, relative to analysts who continue their coverage unchanged.

name: Analyst coverage initiation
definition: Analysts who are not yet covering the divesting firm and start covering it after the spinoff is announced, relative to analysts who continue their coverage from the pre-announcement period.

name: Analyst forecast accuracy
definition: The accuracy of the earnings forecasts analysts produce about the divesting firms, the quality of analysts' research that the paper measures; higher EPS Forecast Errors indicate that an analyst is less accurate in his forecast, as the gap between forecasted and actual earnings is larger.

name: Platform owner entry
authors_terms: ["Amazon's entry", "direct entry", "compete with a complementor", "enter the product spaces"]
definition: After partnering with third-party sellers for a while, Amazon decides whether or not to enter the product market and sell to consumers directly in the second stage.

name: Product success
definition: If Amazon's entry is motivated by capturing profits from popular products, we expect Amazon to pick those with low rankings (that is, high demand) and high ratings.

name: Platform-specific investment
authors_terms: ["platform-specific investment", "Amazon-specific investment", "effort to grow", "seller effort to grow", "answers provided by sellers"]
definition: Some third-party products may require more investments to grow on Amazon. For example, Amazon consumers may have many questions about these products before they make purchase decisions.

name: Product price
definition: For each product not offered by Amazon, the authors obtain price (Price) from the default page Amazon displays when users search for a product.

name: Shipping cost
definition: For each product not offered by Amazon, the authors obtain shipping cost (Shipping) from the default page Amazon displays when users search for a product.

name: Platform fulfillment service use
authors_terms: ["Fulfillment by Amazon", "FBA", "Amazon's fulfillment service", "Amazon's distribution service"]
definition: In 2006 Amazon initiated a service called Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA), whereby third-party sellers ship inventory to Amazon and pay for storage, weight handling, and pick-and-pack operations. Amazon manages storage, order fulfillment, and customer service as well as other back-end operations for these products, which also qualify for its free shipping programs.

name: Number of product sellers
authors_terms: ["NumSellers", "number of third-party sellers that offer the product", "number of sellers that offer a particular product"]
definition: The total number of sellers that offer the product in new condition (NumSellers).

name: Seller rating
definition: The seller's rating, computed as the average of all ratings received for past transactions; SellerRating captures sellers' service quality (including whether products matched sellers' descriptions and whether sellers responded to inquiries in a timely manner).

name: Seller product portfolio
authors_terms: ["NumProdBySeller", "total number of products offered on Amazon by each third-party seller", "seller size"]
definition: The total number of products offered on Amazon by each third-party seller (NumProdBySeller), gathered in both rounds.

name: Product offering termination
authors_terms: ["StopOffer", "ceases to offer a product", "turnover rate for third-party sellers' product offerings"]
definition: We create a dummy, StopOffer, which is assigned a value of 1 if the seller ceases to offer a product in the second round, and 0 otherwise.

name: Product diversification
definition: A multiniche company sells in at least two of the nine niches. Diversified firms, or diversifiers, can move fungible, non-scale-free resources across product niches, as well as over time, by leveraging intertemporal economies of scope.

name: Sales growth
definition: Our dependent variable is Sales Growth, so it indicates an increase or decrease in sales at time t + 1 in country j in niche k for a particular brand z (Sales Growtht+1 = Salest+1/Salest). Sales offer a good proxy for strategic decisions by diversified firms.

name: Buyer concentration
definition: Buyer concentration is the concentration of the downstream retail industry: with fewer buyers, only a small number of organizations gather information about all available offers and customers' tastes, and the resulting information asymmetries grant those buyers relevant advantages. Greater buyer concentration increases the costs related to recognition and disclosure for each single-niche seller.

name: Specialized competition
authors_terms: ["Specialized Competition", "competition from single-niche firms", "competition among the single-niche firms", "specializers"]
definition: Competition by single-niche companies in a market: competition among more fragmented specializers likely increases transaction costs for changing contracts, because each heterogeneous, fragmented specializer owns unique information, which creates asymmetries.

name: Adverse demand shock
authors_terms: ["Tax Alcohol", "tax change", "tax increase", "demand shock", "exogenous demand variation"]
definition: Tax changes by these countries reduced demand for alcoholic beverages and might have prompted diversifiers to reallocate some of their resources from alcoholic to other beverage niches. A tax increase likely increases the product price, so, independent of firm strategies, it can reduce demand, especially among price-sensitive customers.

name: Resource redeployment
definition: Diversified firms can move these non-scale-free resources across product niches, as well as over time, by leveraging intertemporal economies of scope. Redeployment tends to be more prevalent when competition from single-niche firms is greater and downstream retail industries are more concentrated.

name: Multi-business firm membership
authors_terms: ["multi-business firms", "multi-business firm segments", "businesses within multi-business firms", "diversified firms"]
definition: Firms that operate more than one business, whose businesses are compared with single-business firms in the same industry and of the same size; single-business firms have no opportunity for internal resource redeployment among existing businesses and serve as an ideal control group.

name: Revenue expansion
definition: The positive part of a business's revenue growth, capturing how aggressively a business expands revenues relative to single-business firms.

name: Revenue retrenchment
definition: The negative part of a business's revenue growth, capturing how aggressively a business contracts revenues relative to single-business firms; there is no theory or evidence around why businesses of multi-business firms might retrench revenues more aggressively.

name: Variance in revenue growth
authors_terms: ["variance in revenue growth", "standard deviation in revenue growth"]
definition: The dispersion of a business's revenue growth, which businesses within multi-business firms are expected to show more of than single-business firms because they both expand and retrench revenues more aggressively.

name: Segment resource similarity
authors_terms: ["segment resource similarity", "resource similarity", "human and tangible resources being more similar"]
definition: An inverse proxy for adjustment costs within a multi-business firm, which should better enable revenue expansion and retrenchment; it has a higher value if the resources a segment requires might be usefully deployed in the firm's other segments.

name: Opportunity diversity
authors_terms: ["opportunity diversity", "firm opportunity diversity", "opportunity variance in the portfolio"]
definition: The variance in opportunities across the segments of a firm's portfolio, which raises the inducements to redeploy resources; opportunities are approximated by the average Tobin's q ratio among single-business firms in the segment's industry.

name: Segment illiquidity
definition: The degree to which the resources a business competes with are illiquid, which raises the relative advantage of internal redeployment; prior work is used to approximate a segment's illiquidity as the inverse of total industry long-term debt divided by total industry assets.

name: Value-added through resource redeployment
definition: The extent to which firms over- or under-pursue revenues relative to investment opportunities in their segments' industries and also to the firm's own investment opportunities; firms that expand into more attractive segments and retrench from less attractive segments create more value-added with their redeployment activities.

name: Software patents
definition: A firm's preexisting stock of granted software patents, that is, legal titles protecting software algorithms. The authors state that 'In the software industry, a patent usually protects an algorithm, that is, a series of step-by-step procedures that are necessary to perform a task.'

name: Software trademarks
definition: A firm's preexisting stock of live trademarks protecting software products; trademarks are combinations of words, phrases, symbols, or designs that identify and distinguish the source of the goods or services.

name: Hardware trademarks
definition: A firm's preexisting stock of live trademarks protecting hardware products and the marketing investments, reputation for quality, brand names, and distribution channels attached to them.

name: Hardware patents
definition: A firm's preexisting stock of granted patents protecting hardware technology.

name: OSS product commercialization
authors_terms: ["build OSS into its commercial software products", "number of OSS product releases", "number of new OSS products"]
definition: The efforts a firm makes to build open source software into its commercial software products, captured by the number of new OSS products (or new versions of already launched OSS products) it announces.

name: Misaligned perception of competition
definition: The case in which collaborating partners are misaligned in how they perceive each other: one firm (ego) does not perceive its partner (alter) as a competitor, while alter does perceive ego as a competitor.

name: Mutual perception of competition
definition: The case in which partners are aligned in perceiving each other as competitors; expectations for such collaborations tend to be low and are likely to be met.

name: Collaboration renewal
definition: Whether an announced collaboration between two firms in a given year follows a collaboration between the same two firms in the previous year; because renewal requires agreement by both partners, non-renewal can result from one partner's unmet expectations.

name: Ego's perception of a third party as competitor
authors_terms: ["third party perceived competitor", "ego perceives a third party in the collaboration as a competitor"]
definition: A triadic collaboration in which ego perceives the third party in the collaboration as a competitor, which the authors theorize changes ego's expectations for the collaboration to be consistent with an arm's-length relationship.

name: Third party's prior misaligned collaboration with alter
authors_terms: ["third party alter experience", "third party ... previously in a perceptually misaligned collaboration with alter"]
definition: A triadic collaboration in which the third party was previously in a misaligned collaboration with alter in which alter perceived the third party as a competitor but the third party did not perceive alter as a competitor, so that the third party held a perceptually equivalent position as that of ego to alter.

name: Collaboration performance relative to expectations
authors_terms: ["collaboration performance relative to expectations", "failure to meet expectations: collaboration performance"]
definition: Whether a collaboration meets the performance expectations partners held for it; expected collaboration performance is captured by jointly announced products and actual collaboration performance by actually released products, and the two are compared.

name: Litigation between collaboration partners
definition: The authors proxied for a partner's failure to meet behavior expectations via litigation: behavior far outside the boundaries of one partner's expectations in a negative way, especially if related to resource misappropriation, may prompt a lawsuit.

name: Equity-based CEO compensation
definition: Equity-based compensation is the number of newly issued shares awarded to the CEO; the authors interpret it more broadly as all contingent compensation, i.e. all equity-based awards such as restricted stocks, stock options and stock appreciation rights, and all discretionary compensation including bonuses and other compensation.

name: Fixed CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["fixed salary", "base salary", "fixed compensation", "non-performance-based compensation", "fixed cash compensation"]
definition: Fixed cash compensation paid to the manager in Period 1, i.e. the non-performance-related part of the pay package.

name: Largest shareholder ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership of the largest outside shareholder", "largest shareholder's ownership", "fraction of the firm held by the largest external shareholder", "ownership of the largest stockholder"]
definition: The share-ownership stake of the firm's largest shareholder, which determines whether that shareholder can profitably pose a takeover threat to managerial control. The authors distinguish the case where the largest holder is a non-CEO outside shareholder from the case where the largest stockholder is the CEO.

name: Board ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership of the BOD", "share-ownership of the BOD", "director ownership", "compensation committee's ownership"]
definition: The share-ownership of the Board of Directors (specifically of the representative director J who negotiates compensation with the CEO). In the empirical analysis director ownership is approximated by the ownership of the compensation committee, which is composed of outside directors and is usually given primary discretion in setting CEO compensation.

name: Default risk
authors_terms: ["default risk", "default probability", "bankruptcy risk", "probability of financial distress"]
definition: The ex ante probability of financial distress of the firm, which induces greater monitoring of the CEO from the self-preserving BOD.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm, which in the model is proportional to the number of shares outstanding; large firm size deters takeovers and provides the CEO greater leeway in compensation design.

name: Costs of displacing the CEO
authors_terms: ["costs of displacing the CEO", "costs of CEO displacement", "takeover-related transactions costs", "CEO entrenchment"]
definition: The costs of displacing the CEO, including takeover-related transaction costs and factors that increase CEO entrenchment; in the empirical analysis CEO duality serves as a proxy for high costs of displacing the CEO.

name: CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO's ownership", "CEO's stock ownership", "share-ownership of the CEO"]
definition: The CEO's (initial) shareholding in the firm. The authors show that the effect of the CEO's ownership on his compensation is theoretically ambiguous, in contrast to the usual conjecture of a positive relationship between the two.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: The investment opportunity set of the firm, which affects the marginal productivity of managerial effort and also makes the firm more attractive for takeovers, thereby impacting compensation in a complex way.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The firm's debt obligations; the authors use the firm's debt-equity ratio to represent the debt obligations of the firm.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["stock and accounting returns", "current and past economic performance of the firm", "firm's profits"]
definition: The firm's current and past economic performance; both stock and accounting returns can be jointly used as a proxy for the firm's profits.

name: Academic founder
authors_terms: ["academic startup", "academic founder", "startup with an academic founder", "academic scientist"]
definition: Academic startups refer to startups founded by academic scientists from a university. A founder is classified as an academic founder if their former employer was a university.

name: Within-industry employee founder
definition: Within-industry employee startups refer to startups founded by prior employees of a firm in the same industry. A founder is classified as a within-industry employee founder if their former employer was a medical device firm.

name: Markets for technology
authors_terms: ["markets for technology", "participation in markets for technology", "patent reassignment"]
definition: Startups can pursue markets for technology by selling the rights to their inventions to interested actors. The measure identifies whether a startup participates in the seller-side of markets for technology.

name: Markets for product
authors_terms: ["markets for product", "participation in markets for product"]
definition: Startups can pursue markets for product by selling their innovations to customers. The FDA approval of medical devices indicates that the device can begin commercial sales.

name: Markets for pioneering products
definition: Pioneering products refer to products that offer novel functionality or applications not previously available to customers.

name: Exposure to academic technology transfer
authors_terms: ["prior exposure to academic technology transfer", "exposure to academic technology transfer"]
definition: Among academic startups, the combined knowledge profile emerges when their founders have prior exposure to academic technology transfer, defined as exposure to university-based mechanisms that facilitate the translation of scientific knowledge into commercial applications.

name: Applied scientific and technical roles
authors_terms: ["applied scientific and technical roles", "science and technology position", "involvement in inventor teams"]
definition: Employment contexts that require scientific reasoning or advanced technical expertise expose founders to applied scientific principles; such exposure may arise through job roles in scientific and technical functions, where task requirements engage with scientific mechanisms, discovery, and experimentation, or from participation in inventor teams involved in patenting activities.

name: Former employer size
authors_terms: ["former employer size", "small firm", "small tech former employer", "young employer"]
definition: Heterogeneity among within-industry employee startups arising from the size of their founders' former employers, because the small size of former employers matters for the knowledge profiles that employees carry into their startups; measured as small versus large (and young versus old) former employers.

name: Social relationship strength
authors_terms: ["social relationships", "stronger social relationship", "weak and strong social relationships"]
definition: Strong social relationships between the source and the recipient increase the source's ER; two R&D scientists enjoying a strong social relationship will trust each other, regard each other as friends, and be more likely to share the other's social network. In describing strong social relationships, R&D scientists referred to time (how long they had known the individual and frequency of interaction) and affect (feelings of friendship, closeness, and trust) and whether the individual belonged to their social network.

name: Competition between source and recipient
definition: Interfirm competition tends to be high when firms produce similar products and compete for the same customers; intergroup competition tends to be high when project-groups within the same firm compete directly for limited project funding. The concepts of interfirm and intergroup competition are for our purposes equivalent since they affect the source's ER in the same way.

name: Firm boundaries
authors_terms: ["firm boundaries", "within or across firm boundaries", "organizational boundaries", "same organizational hierarchy"]
definition: Existing research assumes that know-how transfer inside a firm differs from know-how transfer across firm boundaries. When the prospective source and recipient are members of the same organization's hierarchy, the source has a heightened ER, and behaviors within a hierarchy can be monitored and controlled in ways that behaviors spanning between hierarchies cannot.

name: Know-how transfer effort
authors_terms: ["effort related to know-how transfer", "know-how transfer effort", "know-how transfer behavior"]
definition: When an R&D scientist (source) receives a request for know-how, she must decide whether to fulfill the request and what effort she will make in responding; effort depends on the time, details, and quality of information the source provides to the recipient and it is not simply a yes/no decision.

name: General resource complementarity
definition: The dyadic construct that captures resource complementarity operationalized as the diversity in the resource endowments or market niches of the dyad's members; in this conceptualization the resource complementarity of two potential partners grows with the size of their resource endowments and decreases with their overlap.

name: General resource imbalance
definition: A dyadic construct capturing the potential for asymmetric stores of resources to create a bargaining power imbalance, assessed without restricting the assessment to any particular resource except financing, which is not considered a crucial source of bargaining power.

name: Task resource depth complementarity
definition: The degree to which two firms cover a particular task's resource needs along the depth dimension of same-type resources, fulfilling four criteria: relevance, filling resource gaps, a lack of self-sufficiency, and minimal resource overlap.

name: Task resource scope complementarity
definition: The fit of two firms based on the different task resources they possess; the variable logically increases with the number of nonoverlapping task resources the firms possess.

name: Task resource depth imbalance
definition: Imbalance in stores of same-type task resources, defined as the inequality in the resource endowments of depth complementary resources held by two partners.

name: Task resource scope imbalance
definition: Imbalance in stores of different-type task resources, defined as the imbalance in scope of complementary task resources.

name: Tie formation
authors_terms: ["tie formation", "establish an alliance with one another"]
definition: The presence or absence of the j1-j2 link in construction project z, that is, the probability that lead firm j1 makes an invitation to partner firm j2 to form an alliance for project z and that j2 accepts.

name: Broad experimentation
authors_terms: ["broad experimentation", "multiple initial certifications", "Pattern 1", "multiple Phase I and no Phase II"]
definition: This form of experimentation occurs when a venture initially certifies multiple projects, each of which remains unproven, as none of these projects has yet to receive follow-on certification. Such certifications reflect experimentation with more, rather than fewer, knowledge domains as a means of unearthing the failures or inadequacies in the original project.

name: Targeted experimentation
authors_terms: ["targeted experimentation", "follow-on certification", "Pattern 2", "only one Phase I and one Phase II"]
definition: This form of experimentation occurs when a venture's initially certified project demonstrates adequate progress to garner follow-on certification. Such certifications reflect experimentation that arguably hones in, rather than expands, possible knowledge domains.

name: Breakthrough experimentation
authors_terms: ["breakthrough experimentation", "Pattern 3", "multiple Phase I and any Phase II"]
definition: In this form of experimentation, a venture's broad experimentation shows proof-of-concept in that one or more of their initially certified projects receive follow-on certification. These forms of certification reflect experimentation with more, rather than fewer, knowledge domains; yet, unlike broad experimentation, this form of experimentation realizes its potential.

name: Venture performance
definition: Annual sales is the dependent variable and a standard measure of market-based venture performance. Besides being salient for capturing value as perceived by prospective customers, most early-stage ventures are prerevenue, so sales is a conservative estimate of performance.

name: State SBIR/STTR matching program
authors_terms: ["State Match", "state program", "Phase I noncompetitive matching program"]
definition: A portion of state administrators have relied on the federal SBIR/STTR program to identify eligible ventures - Phase I recipients - as noncompetitive recipients of the State Match program. Prior work shows that the federal Phase I signals technical merit, whereas the State Match signals commercial merit.

name: Professional investment fund ownership
authors_terms: ["professional investment funds", "ownership by professional investment funds", "professional investment fund ownership", "ownership by professional investment management funds"]
definition: Professional investment funds are a major group of pressure-resistant institutional investors whose holdings turn over frequently; one estimate is that the average holding period is about one year for over 80 percent of the shares held by these funds, largely because fund managers' compensation is frequently based on quarterly evaluation of portfolio sizes and net asset values.

name: Pension fund ownership
authors_terms: ["pension funds", "ownership by pension funds", "pension fund ownership"]
definition: Pension funds, another pressure-resistant group, tend to emphasize yields over longer time horizons than professional investment funds and usually follow a buy-and-hold strategy; their managers also have stringent fiduciary responsibilities.

name: International diversification
definition: International diversification involves the complex allocation of multiple resources (including, for instance, financial and human capital). Prior studies on international diversification have recommended the use of multiple measures to improve validity.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["outside directors", "independent outside directors", "outside directors ratio", "ratio of independent outside directors on a board"]
definition: Independent outside directors, who are not employed by a firm and do not have an affiliation with its management, are considered important for controlling agency costs, because they can be more effective in aligning the interests of owners and managers.

name: Inside director incentives
authors_terms: ["inside directors", "inside director incentives", "inside directors' stock options", "inside director equity"]
definition: Inside directors are members of a firm's board of directors who were current firm employees. Inside director incentives were measured by inside director equity as a percentage of total equity and the value of inside directors' stock options.

name: Technological opportunity
definition: Technological opportunity is the degree to which a firm's market or industry demands or accepts product innovation.

name: Geographic diversification into resource-poorer host countries
authors_terms: ["geographic diversification into resource-poorer (R-P) host countries", "geographic diversification of NMNEs into R-P host countries as compared to the home country", "index of geographic diversification into R-P host countries"]
definition: The authors classify MNE host countries that are less or more developed than the home country in terms of strategic factor markets: resource-poorer (R-P) versus resource-richer (R-R) host countries. They argue that in the early stages of geographic diversification into R-P host countries relative to the home country, NMNEs will likely exhibit increased firm profitability.

name: Geographic diversification into resource-richer host countries
authors_terms: ["geographic diversification into resource-richer (R-R) host countries", "geographic diversification of NMNEs into R-R host countries as compared to the home country", "index of geographic diversification into R-R host countries"]
definition: The authors classify MNE host countries that are less or more developed than the home country in terms of strategic factor markets: resource-poorer (R-P) versus resource-richer (R-R) host countries. They argue that NMNEs choosing to expand into R-R host countries as compared to the home country in the early stages of geographic diversification will likely exhibit decreasing firm profitability.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Because firm profitability is a multidimensional construct (Venkatraman and Ramanujam, 1986), we measured it as the principal component of return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), and return on invested capital (ROIC). The study used firm profitability as the dependent variable.

name: Corporate legal affairs department influence
authors_terms: ["influence of corporate legal affairs department", "corporate legal affairs departments' influence on facility decisions", "influence of the corporate legal department"]
definition: Charged with assuring companies' legitimacy and 'license to operate,' legal affairs departments are typically the primary channel for pressures from constituents in their organizations' nonmarket environments. The more influence legal affairs departments have over facility managers regarding environmental issues, the more they will be able to convey the importance of such institutional pressures.

name: Corporate marketing department influence
authors_terms: ["influence of corporate marketing department", "corporate marketing departments' influence on facility decisions", "influence of the corporate marketing department"]
definition: Marketing departments, being responsible for orienting firms' products and services to meet and anticipate customer demands, focus on identifying factors that can provide competitive differentiation, and are often acutely aware of industry trends and competitors' positioning. The greater a corporate marketing department's influence over facility-level environmental management decisions, the more able it will be to convey the importance of pressures exerted by constituents in the facility's market environment.

name: Receptivity to nonmarket pressure
authors_terms: ["receptivity to nonmarket pressure", "facility's receptivity to pressures from nonmarket constituents", "receptivity of facility managers to pressures from nonmarket constituents"]
definition: Hypotheses 1 and 2 predict the extent to which facility managers are receptive to pressures from nonmarket and market constituents. To measure this, we asked survey respondents to indicate the extent to which various external groups influenced their facilities to improve environmental performance.

name: Receptivity to market pressure
authors_terms: ["receptivity to market pressure", "facility's receptivity to pressures from market constituents", "receptivity of facility managers to pressures from market constituents"]
definition: Hypotheses 1 and 2 predict the extent to which facility managers are receptive to pressures from nonmarket and market constituents. To measure this, we asked survey respondents to indicate the extent to which various external groups influenced their facilities to improve environmental performance.

name: ISO 14001 adoption
authors_terms: ["ISO 14001 implementation status", "adoption of ISO 14001", "adopting the ISO 14001 international environmental management standard"]
definition: Issued by the International Organization for Standardization, this international standard characterizes the essential elements of an EMS and provides a framework for organizations seeking to reduce their environmental impacts beyond regulatory requirements. ISO 14001 does not require any particular environmental performance level or improvement rate other than a commitment to comply with applicable regulations.

name: Participation in government-initiated voluntary environmental programs
authors_terms: ["government voluntary program participation", "participation in government-initiated voluntary environmental programs"]
definition: Government-initiated voluntary programs are collaborative arrangements between firms and regulators whereby firms voluntarily commit to actions that might improve their environmental performance. These programs are designed by policy makers to associate private benefits with the voluntary provision of public goods.

name: Community income
definition: The economic status of a local community, represented by residents' income level. Consumers' income influences a firm's category spanning by directly affecting their purchasing power and overall market demand.

name: Community education
authors_terms: ["degree of education", "education level", "proportion of the population aged over 25 who have at least a bachelor's degree"]
definition: The social status of a local community, represented by residents' education level and influencing their perception of categorical boundaries. Education is an important indicator of one's social status and influences one's perception of categorical boundaries.

name: Variety-enhancing spanning
definition: An extent to which an organization, or an entity, has membership in multiple market categories. It is related to decisions about an organization's boundaries and concerns the niche width the firm appeals to.

name: Atypicality-enhancing spanning
definition: An extent by which an organization fuses elements from disparate market categories to create hybridized offerings. Because the properties of the product violate existing categorical expectations, it may be more difficult to understand and thus deemed less legitimate.

name: Consumer preference for variety
definition: Consumers' stated likelihood of trying a restaurant that offers multiple categories of food, used as the survey outcome for the variety mechanism.

name: Consumer preference for atypicality
definition: Consumers' stated likelihood of trying a restaurant that offers atypical dishes from the category it belongs to, used as the survey outcome for the atypicality mechanism.

name: Openness to diversity
definition: One of the four groups of attributes of cultural omnivores measured in the survey. The authors describe the openness of elite omnivores as ranging from a passive tolerance of different forms to an active desire to discover new and challenging items.

name: Preference for novelty
definition: One of the four groups of attributes of cultural omnivores measured in the survey, capturing the inclination to seek intellectual stimulation and novel ideas.

name: Reliance on own evaluation criteria
definition: One of the four groups of attributes of cultural omnivores measured in the survey, capturing the extent to which individuals exert agency and make a conscious self-driven decision rather than relying on others.

name: Risk-taking propensity
definition: One of the four groups of attributes of cultural omnivores measured in the survey, capturing propensity to take risks involved in exploring unfamiliar offerings.

name: Relationship life-cycle stage
authors_terms: ["relationship phase", "relationship stage", "stage of cooperative development", "phase of the relationship"]
definition: DSO posited that relationships develop through a fixed order of phases: awareness, exploration, expansion (build-up), commitment (maturity), and then decline, perhaps ending in dissolution. Participants sense their stage and can indicate it readily.

name: Goal congruence
definition: The extent to which the parties have sorted out their priorities (long versus short term, market share versus growth, volume versus profit) so that their goals are congruent; it cannot be achieved by fiat or contract and must grow organically via interaction, negotiation, and sense-making.

name: Information exchange norms
authors_terms: ["information exchange norms", "a norm of frank and copious communication"]
definition: A norm of frank and copious communication between the parties; information exchange norms govern how parties handle issues that arise and how they share critical information, and holding back is costly and risky for the relationship.

name: Relationship harmony
definition: The extent to which firms learn to confront and resolve their conflicts so that relationship harmony increases steadily to maturity; discontent and disagreement may then set in to drive decline and dissolution.

name: Overall dependence
definition: One party is dependent when the other offers valued benefits that are difficult to obtain elsewhere. The overall dependence of the firms is the sum of the reseller's dependence on the supplier and the supplier's dependence on the reseller.

name: Idiosyncratic time investments
definition: Assets one side creates that are idiosyncratic, that is, customized to the relationship and difficult to redeploy without significant loss of productive value; idiosyncratic time investments are the time-based form of such one-sided investments.

name: Idiosyncratic adaptation investments
authors_terms: ["idiosyncratic adaptation investments", "idiosyncratic adaptation investments of existing routines by one side"]
definition: One side's investments adapting existing routines to the relationship, which are idiosyncratic in that they are difficult to redeploy without significant loss of productive value.

name: Bilateral idiosyncratic investments
definition: Investments in assets tailored to the relationship made by both sides; such bilateral idiosyncratic investments function as credible commitments, giving each side a reason to operate in good faith to maintain the relationship.

name: Trust in the manufacturer
authors_terms: ["the organization's trust in the other organization", "reseller's trust in the manufacturer"]
definition: Willingness to be vulnerable under conditions of risk and interdependence; the mainstream view, which DSO and RV share, holds that trust must be earned and builds slowly from experience.

name: Willingness to take risk
authors_terms: ["willingness to take risk", "willingness to take risks"]
definition: The parties become increasingly willing to take risks on each other's behalf, confident that risks will turn into better performance.

name: Outcomes given comparison level of alternatives
definition: An assessment of partner attractiveness on critical performance outcomes compared to what another partner might provide.

name: Consideration of alternative partners
authors_terms: ["the inverse of the number of seriously considered alternative partners", "number of seriously considered alternatives"]
definition: The number of alternative partners the organization has seriously considered; as relationships develop, organizations are expected to become less willing to work with other firms, which reverses itself as an organization seeks to leave the relationship.

name: Relationship performance
authors_terms: ["overall performance evaluation", "reseller overall performance evaluation", "relationship performance"]
definition: Proxied as the reseller's overall evaluation of the supplier's performance; for the reseller to rate the relationship as an excellent performer, the relationship must have grown the pie and the reseller must have received enough of this value to consider the relationship a success from its own standpoint.

name: Trust in the sales representative
authors_terms: ["reseller's trust in the salesrep", "reseller trust in the sales representative", "trust in the salesperson"]
definition: The reseller's trust in the individual sales representative, not the role; by demonstrating benevolence, honest communications, and extrarole efforts, the sales representative gains the customer's trust and satisfaction.

name: Regressive relationship movement
definition: Regression occurs when a relationship steps back one phase, or when it dissolves, then restarts. DSO considered such paths aberrant and perilous, emphasizing psychological scars and heavy costs that prevent recovery.

name: Downstream firm exit rate
authors_terms: ["exit rate", "organizational mortality rates of downstream firms", "failure rates"]
definition: The rate at which downstream (laser printer) firms leave the industry. Printer firm j exits the laser printer industry when it ceases to ship all products in the industry.

name: Upstream supplier density
authors_terms: ["EngineDensity", "density of core upstream firms", "population density of core upstream industry"]
definition: The population density of core upstream industry k at time t. Core upstream industries provide components that promote substantial variety in the downstream population and allow downstream organizations to achieve a higher differentiation or lower cost position relative to the competition.

name: Nonintegrated upstream supplier density
definition: One of the three decomposed density terms: the density of nonintegrated upstream firms in core industry k, i.e. independent suppliers that sell their components on the open market.

name: Partially integrated upstream supplier density
authors_terms: ["density of partially integrated upstream suppliers", "EngineSell&UseDensity", "tapered integration"]
definition: One of the three decomposed density terms: the density of partially integrated upstream firms in core industry k, i.e. suppliers that sell some of their components on the open market and some to their downstream divisions.

name: Fully integrated upstream supplier density
authors_terms: ["density of vertically integrated upstream firms", "EngineUseAllDensity", "captive suppliers"]
definition: One of the three decomposed density terms: the density of fully integrated upstream firms in core industry k, i.e. vertically integrated suppliers whose engine production is entirely consumed by a downstream division.

name: Downstream population density
authors_terms: ["PrinterDensity", "density of laser printer firms", "downstream population density"]
definition: The downstream population density at time t, i.e. the number of laser printer firms operating.

name: Fully integrated rival density
definition: The density of downstream rivals that are vertically integrated into core supplier industries, i.e. laser printer firms that use only in-house engines.

name: Partially integrated rival density
definition: The density of downstream rivals that are partially integrated into core supplier industries, i.e. laser printer firms that use both in-house and purchased engines.

name: Nonintegrated rival density
definition: The density of downstream rivals that are not integrated into core supplier industries, i.e. laser printer firms that buy all of their laser engines.

name: Focal firm vertical integration
authors_terms: ["own level of integration", "vertically integrated into core supplier industries", "in-house engine production"]
definition: The focal downstream firm's own level of integration into core supplier industries. The authors compare nonintegrated firms with firms that have any positive level of integration, i.e. those making at least some of their engines in-house.

name: Supplier concentration
definition: Instead, supplier concentration refers to the focal firm's choice about how many suppliers to contract with in a market structure that is reasonably fragmented and how to distribute work among those chosen.

name: Supplier stability
definition: Another aspect of a supplier portfolio relates to its longitudinal design, in particular the extent of repeated transactions with suppliers over time.

name: Supplier capability breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of supplier capabilities", "supplier capabilities", "scope of capabilities", "capability scope"]
definition: A third aspect of supplier portfolio design is the breadth of supplier capabilities. In competitive markets with many suppliers, firms can choose between suppliers with a broad or narrow scope of capabilities.

name: Insourcing
definition: The extent to which plural-sourcing focal firms rely on insourcing in the make-and-buy balance.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["product diversification", "product diversification strategy", "narrow spectrum diversification", "broad spectrum diversification"]
definition: Following Wood (1971), both narrow spectrum diversification and broad spectrum diversification were used: narrow spectrum diversification is the number of 4-digit SIC segments in which a firm operates; broad spectrum diversification is the number of 2-digit SIC segments in which a firm operates.

name: International diversification
authors_terms: ["international diversification", "international diversification strategy", "number of countries", "number of regions"]
definition: Two measures capture the extent of dispersion of the firm's activities into different countries and regions: the number of countries in which a firm has foreign subsidiaries and the number of regions in which a firm has foreign subsidiaries. The number of regions is an indicator of international diversification across heterogeneous regions or 'unrelated international geographic diversification'.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Return on assets (ROA) was employed as a measure of firm profitability. ROA is considered an accounting-based indicator and superior to ROE, which is affected by capital structure as well as operational efficiency.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth was measured as annual percentage change in sales. Growth is described as a key strategic goal of Japanese firms.

name: Power-dependence position in the keiretsu
authors_terms: ["power in the keiretsu", "power-dependence relationships", "power dependence", "keiretsu member firms with strong power", "keiretsu member firms with weak power"]
definition: Power fundamentally resides in the dependence of one actor on another, and asymmetric dependence between two actors in an exchange relation constitutes the essence of the concept of power dependence; the characteristics of relations reflect a member's dependence level (or its power) in the keiretsu. Keiretsu member firms with presidents' council membership and low levels of dependence on keiretsu equity and directors are in a strong power position, whereas firms with high intragroup shareholdings and many directors from other group members are strongly dependent and weakly positioned.

name: Activist investor ownership
authors_terms: ["activist ownership", "ownership by activist investors who have not yet targeted a firm for activism", "level of ownership by activist investors"]
definition: An ' activist investor ' is an institution with a stated intent to bring about material change within one or more companies in its portfolio of holdings. Our independent variable was the level of ownership by activist investors who have not yet targeted a firm for activism.

name: Corporate restructuring
definition: Scholars often investigate these four actions - divestitures, spin- or sell-offs, downsizing, and reorganization - together as restructuring, or refocusing, activities.

name: Growth activity
definition: Actions such as business expansion, new product development, acquisitions, and strategic alliances constitute different forms of growth activity that managers facing activist investors might limit or reduce with a view toward keeping potential activist behavior at bay.

name: Constitutional constraints on shareholder control
authors_terms: ["constitutional constraints on shareholder control", "constitutional limit provisions", "constitutional limits on shareholder control"]
definition: These constraints are firm-level structural characteristics that limit the control shareholders, including activist investors, could potentially have over firms.

name: Transactional institutional ownership
definition: Following work that classifies institutional investors based on their trading behavior, we define ' transactional institutional investors ' mainly by what they do not do, rather than what they do. Specifically, they do not engage in relational governance.

name: Specialized complementary assets
authors_terms: ["complementary assets", "complementary resources", "specialized complementary assets", "stock of complementary assets"]
definition: Teece (1986) defined complementary assets as the resources that a firm needs to commercialize an innovation successfully and classifies them into generic and specialized; specialized complementary assets are difficult for newcomers to replicate and keep their value in the next technological stage.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is measured through EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization) divided by the total revenues of the firm in its market; this is a country-specific profitability measure.

name: Market-supporting institutions
definition: Strong market-supporting institutions are those that 'support the voluntary exchange underpinning an effective market mechanism,' while weak ones are those that 'fail to ensure effective markets or even undermine markets'; they are the economic rules of formal institutions and concern the protection of property rights.

name: Political instability
definition: Previous research has identified political instability or political risk with the likelihood that the government changes the regulation and policies of the market; a market is characterized by political instability when politicians can arbitrarily take decisions that change the rules of the game in a market.

name: CEO compensation
definition: To measure our dependent variable CEO pay, we take the natural logarithm of total CEO compensation reported in the annual report, which includes salary, bonus, commission and all other benefits.

name: Family CEO status
definition: We operationalize family CEO as an indicator variable that is set to 1 when the CEO is drawn from the controlling family - termed promoter in Indian parlance - and 0 otherwise (i.e., a professional CEO).

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "financial return on assets (ROA), adjusted by industry median ROA", "industry-median adjusted ROA", "ROA"]
definition: The financial return on assets (ROA), adjusted by industry median ROA, is our measure of focal firm performance. We first defined industry boundaries using the National Industrial Classification (NIC) to identify which three-digit industry the focal firm belonged to.

name: Structural holes
authors_terms: ["structural holes", "team's external network structure", "external network structure", "network constraint", "non-redundant ties"]
definition: Non-redundant contacts are disconnected in some way—either directly, in the sense that they are unacquainted with each other, or indirectly, in the sense that they are connected to a nonoverlapping set of contacts. When the entrepreneurial team as a whole spans many structural holes (i.e., bridging many non-redundant contacts), it is more likely to enjoy superior access to a broad array of resources.

name: Venture growth performance
authors_terms: ["venture performance", "venture growth", "percentage change in sales revenues"]
definition: Venture performance is operationalized as the percentage change in sales revenues in the previous year; growth is an important performance outcome because it confers ventures with economies of scale, increased power, the ability to withstand environmental jolts, and eventually, likely greater profits.

name: Strategic consensus
definition: Strategic consensus is the extent to which team members agree on what the strategy and goals of the business ought to be.

name: Team cohesion
definition: Cohesion is the extent of interpersonal attraction within the group.

name: Functional diversity
definition: In entrepreneurial teams, functional diversity reflects completeness of skills required, and more functional diversity in this context implies a better match between task requirement and member skills.

name: Skill relatedness
definition: The degree to which two industries' production processes draw upon similar skills, quantified for each pair of industries by the extent to which their cross-industry labor flows exceed a well-defined baseline. If the index equals one the industries are unrelated, values over one indicate skill relatedness whereas values under one indicate relative skill dissimilarity.

name: Cross-industry labor flows
definition: Cross-industry labor flows occur if individuals leave firms in one industry to start new jobs in another. Because human capital is only partly fungible, such flows should be stronger among industries whose human capital is more interchangeable.

name: Diversification target choice
definition: The industry that a firm selects as the target of a diversification move, a move being defined as one that occurs from the firm's core industry to the industry in which the firm sets up a new plant.

name: Classification-based relatedness
definition: Relatedness measured from the structure of standardized industrial classification systems; classification-based relatedness is defined as the number of initial digits that industries have in common.

name: Value chain relatedness
definition: Relatedness arising from vertical linkages along the value chain, measured by the relative importance of industry j as a buyer or supplier of industry i's goods and services, based on commodity flows.

name: Portfolio skill relatedness
authors_terms: ["number of related industries in the portfolio", "skill-combination component"]
definition: The extent to which a potential target industry is related not just to a firm's core activity but to the firm's full range of activities, measured as the number of industries in the firm's portfolio that are skill related to the target.

name: Bridging tie formation
authors_terms: ["new bridging ties", "number of new bridging ties", "entering into bridging ties", "formation of new bridging ties"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the total count of new bridging ties formed by the focal firm at time t + 1. In contrast to a local tie, which connects firms within a network community, a bridging tie runs between network communities.

name: Bridging ties
definition: Bridging ties are theorized and modeled as ties that interconnect residents of distinct network communities, rather than simply ties between two otherwise unconnected actors. In contrast to a local tie, which connects firms within a network community, a bridging tie runs between network communities.

name: Local ties
authors_terms: ["current local ties", "local ties", "within-community ties", "local (within-community) network ties"]
definition: Local ties connect firms within the same network community; proximate search and homophilous attachment induce firms to stay within their familiar neighborhoods and form local (within-community) network ties.

name: Partners' bridging tie formation
authors_terms: ["bridging ties by dependent firms", "new bridging ties formed by the firm's partners"]
definition: We captured the value-distribution incentives of a firm at time t + 1 using the log-transformed count of new bridging ties formed by the firm's partners at time t. The variable bridging ties by dependent firms reflects value-distribution incentives for the firm to reinstitute the dependence status quo by forming new bridging ties.

name: Structural opportunity for bridging
authors_terms: ["opportunity to form bridging ties", "potential bridging partners", "structural opportunity for bridging", "opportunity for bridging"]
definition: A firm's opportunity to form a bridge is reflected in the number of available bridging partners, that is, firms residing in network communities different from the focal firm's and thus capable of forming a bridging tie. It is essential to look at how opportunities are distributed for encountering a bridging contact relative to encountering a local contact.

name: Succeeding a star CEO
authors_terms: ["following a star CEO", "succeeding a star CEO", "prior CEO was a star CEO", "previous CEO being a star CEO"]
definition: CEOs who are exalted by the media as 'star CEOs' are those singled out for their managerial acumen and treated as the primary causal agent of a firm's excellent performance; succeeding such an individual is the referent against which the new CEO is evaluated.

name: Succeeding the founder
authors_terms: ["replacing the founder", "succeeding the founder of a company", "follows the founder of an organization"]
definition: When a founder steps down, board members have an extreme, specific referent other in an ambiguous situation, because the founder shaped the firm, is revered by the board, and possesses unique skills.

name: Prior CEO experience
authors_terms: ["prior CEO experience", "previous CEO experience", "previously served as a CEO"]
definition: A general characteristic that may prime the early evaluation of a CEO is whether or not he or she has previously served as a CEO, which serves as a cue that the individual has prior applicable experience.

name: Stock market reaction to CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction to the appointment of a CEO", "initial stock market reaction", "stock market reaction to a CEO's succession announcement"]
definition: The stock market reaction to the appointment of a CEO is an objective piece of evidence regarding the degree to which shareholders endorse or repudiate a given CEO's appointment.

name: Change in CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["changes in the newly appointed CEO's compensation", "changes in CEO pay", "change in compensation"]
definition: CEO compensation is one of the two primary mechanisms boards use as outcomes of the CEO evaluation process, and the change in compensation between a CEO's first and second year captures the early-stage evaluation.

name: Early CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["early CEO dismissal", "likelihood of a CEO being dismissed early in his or her tenure", "early CEO dismissal (within two years)"]
definition: Whether the CEO continues his or her tenure with the firm is the second primary mechanism boards use as an outcome of the CEO evaluation process; early dismissal is a CEO turnover within two years of tenure that the coders judged involuntary.

name: Nature of executive succession
authors_terms: ["nature of executive succession", "non-routine executive succession", "routine executive succession", "non-routine succession", "executive dismissal"]
definition: A 'routine' succession is characterized by the president stepping down and taking on the position of kaicho (chairman of the board). When the departing president does not become the kaicho, it represents a significant departure from the customary succession process and constitutes a non-routine succession event, meaning the departing executive is completely removed from any further involvement in the affairs of the company.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["post-succession strategic change", "strategic change", "change in core business size"]
definition: At the corporate level, strategic change refers to changes in the scope of the firm. The measure captures both growth and decline in the importance of the firm's core business, which is the largest business in terms of the company's sales and thus represents the dominant strategic focus of the firm.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "financial performance", "industry-adjusted ROA", "change in ROA", "stock return"]
definition: Firm performance was measured using three different measures of performance: industry adjusted return on assets (ROA), change in ROA, and stock return. Prior research holds that poor prior performance tends to increase the probability of non-routine executive succession and influences the probability that strategic change will occur after succession.

name: Prior president duality
definition: One indicator of executive power is duality - where the chief executive also holds the position of board chair. In Japanese companies without a kaicho, the president holds the 'informal' position of board chair, and in such situations the president has considerable power since there is no executive ranked higher and no one who provides oversight or advice.

name: Referral network closure
authors_terms: ["referral network closure", "closure of the prior referral network", "closure", "structural hole constraint", "network constraint"]
definition: Closure describes the extent to which an individual's contacts are themselves connected to one another. In the focal partner's referral network, high values indicate few structural holes and therefore greater closure, while low values indicate less closure.

name: Interunit client sharing
definition: Interunit client sharing is client sharing between members of different combining organizations. When the partners sharing clients are in different legacy firms, this constitutes interunit client sharing.

name: Intraunit client sharing
definition: Intraunit client sharing is sharing clients with colleagues within one's own legacy unit. It is observed when the partners sharing clients are in the same legacy firm.

name: Intraunit tie cutting
authors_terms: ["cutting prior intraunit sharing ties", "intraunit tie cutting", "cutting of prior client-sharing ties"]
definition: Cutting prior intraunit sharing ties is a separate but related dimension of client-sharing behavior: the count of former unique partners in the focal partner's own legacy firm with whom he or she no longer shares clients during the three years following the acquisition.

name: Workplace change
definition: Major workplace change refers to changes experienced by members of some units after the acquisition event, identified by adoption of new information technology, billing, and accounting systems; change in headquarters location; change in the dominant coalition; and change in the organization's name.

name: Revenue generation
definition: Revenue generation is measured as the total number of billable hours charged to clients for which the focal partner has responsibility. The relationship between billed hours and revenues is nearly linear.

name: Human capital development
authors_terms: ["human capital development", "perceptions of partners' human capital development"]
definition: Human capital development refers to the development of workers' skills and knowledge through formal and informal training. In this setting it is measured through associates' upward evaluations of partners' training and development efforts.

name: Human capital retention
definition: Human capital retention is based on subordinate retention and is calculated as the percentage of associates with whom each partner worked who remained in the firm during the subsequent three years.

name: Industry-level uncertainty
definition: The presence of industry-level exogenous uncertainty means that there is an upside potential as well as a downside risk associated with the project. The authors focus on sources of industry-level uncertainty that can be attributed to shifts in the public market.

name: Portfolio focus
authors_terms: ["portfolio focus", "portfolio focus in a project's industry", "portfolio focus within a strategic domain"]
definition: Portfolio focus is defined as the dispersion of the firm's investment across projects in the same industry, reflecting the level of redundancy that each project on expectation adds to the firm's portfolio of investment projects.

name: Portfolio diversity
authors_terms: ["portfolio diversity", "portfolio diversity across multiple domains", "portfolio diversity across industries"]
definition: Portfolio diversity is defined as the dispersion of the firm's investment projects among different industries, reflecting the degree of spread of the firm's portfolio across industries.

name: Propensity to withdraw
definition: The propensity to withdraw is the hazard that a VC withdraws its investment in a venture in the current round conditional on the fact that the VC has invested in the previous round.

name: Supplier exchange hazards
authors_terms: ["exchange hazards", "supplier's exchange hazards", "focal firm exchange hazards (supplier)"]
definition: Following transaction cost theory, the hazards of exchange are derived from nontransferable asset-specific investments and environmental uncertainty; the authors define exchange hazards as the combination of asset specificity and uncertainty, rather than either asset specificity or uncertainty alone. This construct captures the exchange hazards faced by the supplier, i.e., the supplier's own relationship-specific investments and the uncertainty of the transaction environment.

name: Buyer exchange hazards
authors_terms: ["exchange hazards", "buyer's exchange hazards", "focal firm exchange hazards (buyer)"]
definition: Following transaction cost theory, the hazards of exchange are derived from nontransferable asset-specific investments and environmental uncertainty; the authors define exchange hazards as the combination of asset specificity and uncertainty, rather than either asset specificity or uncertainty alone. This construct captures the exchange hazards faced by the buyer, i.e., the buyer's own relationship-specific investments and the uncertainty of the transaction environment.

name: Trust in the buyer
authors_terms: ["trust", "Trust in the Buyer Organization", "supplier representative's trust in the buyer organization"]
definition: Trust is defined as the expectation that another organization can be relied upon to fulfill its obligations, will behave in a predictable manner, and will act and negotiate fairly when the possibility for opportunism is present; strictly speaking it is the perceived trustworthiness aspect of overall trust that is considered. The authors view trust as the degree to which the counterpart (buyer or supplier organization) is perceived by the boundary spanner (purchasing manager or supplier representative) to be reliable, predictable, and fair.

name: Trust in the supplier
authors_terms: ["trust", "Trust in the Supplier Organization", "purchasing manager's trust in the supplier organization"]
definition: Trust is defined as the expectation that another organization can be relied upon to fulfill its obligations, will behave in a predictable manner, and will act and negotiate fairly when the possibility for opportunism is present; strictly speaking it is the perceived trustworthiness aspect of overall trust that is considered. The authors view trust as the degree to which the counterpart (buyer or supplier organization) is perceived by the boundary spanner (purchasing manager or supplier representative) to be reliable, predictable, and fair.

name: Power imbalance
authors_terms: ["power imbalance", "degree of power imbalance", "ratio of supplier to buyer asset specificity"]
definition: Power imbalance explicitly recognizes the relative degree of divergence (correspondence) between the two parties' investments in relationship-specific assets. It consists of two mechanisms that combine to influence judgments about the trustworthiness of a counterpart: a threat of opportunism (stemming from a party's own exchange hazards) and a situation of mutual hostages (stemming from the counterpart's exchange hazards).

name: Star mobility
definition: The extent to which a star's performance is transferable across organizations, examined through the analyst's movement across firms. The independent variable of interest is the analyst's mobility, which is one if a ranked analyst switched to another sell-side research department and zero if he or she did not move during the year.

name: Analyst performance
authors_terms: ["analyst's performance", "Institutional Investor ranking", "Rank t+1", "performance of ranked analysts"]
definition: The dependent variable in this study is the analyst's performance, operationalized as rank in the Institutional Investor All-America Research Team poll, Rank t+1.

name: Firm capabilities
authors_terms: ["firm capability", "capabilities", "bulge-bracket", "moving to a weaker firm", "moving to a better firm", "moving to a comparable firm"]
definition: A firm's systems and practices, such as promotion criteria, resource allocation and managerial practices, can affect individual performance; capability differences between origin and destination firms could therefore produce a performance decline independent of firm-specific human capital. For each job change the authors determine whether the destination firm had lesser, equivalent, or better capabilities relative to the originating firm by using the bulge-bracket distinction.

name: Team movement
authors_terms: ["moving in teams", "team moves", "Coworker move", "lift outs", "moving solo", "moving with a team of colleagues"]
definition: Analysts may move to a new firm alone or with a team of colleagues; such a team can consist of other security analysts who cover complementary sectors, junior and senior research analysts, institutional salespeople, or traders who specialize in the same sector. A team move obviates the need for a star to get acquainted with new colleagues or to establish shared objectives, mutual accountability, or group norms.

name: Star hiring
authors_terms: ["hiring a star", "hiring star analysts", "hiring announcements", "the hiring firm"]
definition: A firm that succeeds in hiring a star can be viewed as the highest bidder in the labor market. When the firm that possesses an informational advantage fails to make a counteroffer, the hiring firm is likely to have made an offer that exceeds the value the new employee will generate.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: Stock-market movement is a well-established proxy for the value created or lost for a given firm in reaction to a specific event, and is used here to assess whether acquiring firms gain or lose value when they hire a star analyst.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["TMT heterogeneity", "heterogeneity", "demographic diversity", "TMT educational heterogeneity", "TMT functional/background heterogeneity", "TMT tenure heterogeneity"]
definition: The relative heterogeneity or diversity among top management team members' demographic characteristics; the authors coded educational background, functional background and team tenure heterogeneity 'to gauge the breadth of their demographic differences'.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured as return on assets (ROA), 'a widely used measure of accounting performance', averaged over the two years following the measurement of TMT characteristics.

name: Internationalization
definition: International strategy, defined as 'the degree to which a firm depends on foreign markets for revenues and owned-factors of production'; it is the authors' reference point for the complexity a top management team must manage.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["TMT average tenure", "average tenure", "TMT median tenure", "short-tenured top management teams", "long-tenured top management teams"]
definition: The time team members have spent working together on the top team, as indicated by average tenure; the authors use it to capture the top team's social context.

name: Reflexive learning
definition: Exploitation that occurs inside teams is called reflexive learning and involves considering different members' perspectives on current or changing conditions, evaluating ideas, and explicitly discussing ways to improve processes and strategies.

name: Vicarious learning
definition: Exploitation outside of teams is called vicarious learning and involves drawing on others' experiences to learn about key aspects of a project.

name: Contextual learning
definition: When exploration occurs outside a team, it is called contextual learning, which involves gathering information from the environment to learn about competitors, discover technology trends, or identify customer needs that stimulate new insights for a project.

name: Experimental learning
definition: When exploration occurs inside a team, it is called experimental learning, which involves brainstorming, building prototypes, drawing sketches, and running tests to help teams discover new ideas that lead to more-creative solutions to problems.

name: Coordination quality
definition: High-quality coordination helps teams integrate interdependent tasks to reach a common goal and relies on three conditions: accountability, predictability, and a shared understanding of project goals and strategies.

name: Team performance
authors_terms: ["team performance", "innovation project performance", "performance for team projects"]
definition: The overall performance of the innovation project team, rated in terms of the efficiency of team operations, the quality of its work, and the team's ability to meet project goals.

name: Rhythm of team learning
authors_terms: ["rhythm", "positive rhythm of team learning", "rhythm of learning activities"]
definition: A positive rhythm of team learning arises when dissonant learning activities are separated across teamwork episodes, creating a rise and resolution of tension over time that provides a feeling of stability and direction in a project and improves overall performance.

name: Attention focusing
definition: Attention focusing captures the tendency of participants to allocate attention repeatedly to the same issues, following a logic of familiarity.

name: Attention reinforcing
authors_terms: ["attention reinforcing", "logic of popularity", "popular problems", "popularity of problems"]
definition: Attention reinforcing captures the tendency of participants to allocate attention to problems that already attracted a high degree of attention, following a logic of popularity.

name: Participant activity
definition: The level of activity of organizational participants, that is, active people are people who pay attention to many items; the authors operationalize it as cumulative attention, the overall volume of a participant's past attention allocation to the project.

name: Attention mixing
definition: Attention mixing captures the interaction between the activity of participants and the popularity of problems so that a disassortative mixing effect indicates that participants that are more active are less attracted by popular problems, following a logic of devaluation.

name: Attention clustering
definition: Attention clustering captures the tendency of participants to extend their attention to future problems located in the vicinity of current problems, following a logic of proximity.

name: Attention allocation
definition: An attention allocation event linking participant i to problem m at time t is recorded whenever participant i modifies a field in (touches) the bug report associated with problem m.

name: Layoff announcement following an M&A
definition: Our dependent variable (LAYOFF) is a dummy variable coded as 1 for firms that announced layoffs associated with the mergers and 0 for firms that did not announce a merger-induced layoff.

name: Relatedness of merging firms' businesses
definition: Relatedness of the businesses of the firms involved in the M&As was measured in two ways. Clearly, when similar firms combine, there should be more opportunities for the combined firm to realize operational synergies by eliminating redundant activities than when dissimilar firms combine.

name: Cross-border acquisition
definition: Cross-border is coded as 1 if the acquiring and acquired firms listed different countries as their headquarters. Since the acquired firms are all domestic, this measure is 1 if the acquiring firm is non-U.S. and 0 if it is headquartered in the United States.

name: Target firm preacquisition financial performance
authors_terms: ["acquired firm financial performance", "TARGET ROIC", "return on invested capital", "target firm preacquisition performance"]
definition: Acquired firm financial performance was measured as return on invested capital the year before the M&A (TARGET ROIC). We expect, then, that the performance of acquired firms is inversely related to the likelihood that layoffs follow the acquisition.

name: Target firm preacquisition operating efficiency
authors_terms: ["operating efficiency", "labor efficiency", "TARGET REVENUE PER EMPLOYEE", "revenue per employee"]
definition: Operational efficiency of the target firm prior to the transaction was measured as revenue per employee (TARGET REVENUE PER EMPLOYEE). Operating efficiency can be signaled by a firm's relative labor efficiency.

name: Debt financing of the acquisition
definition: In order to test Hypothesis 5 we used a variable (SFB-BORROWING) from the SDC (Security Data Corp) data base of mergers and acquisitions. This variable is coded as 1 if the transaction is financed with borrowing.

name: CEO power
definition: A CEO's influence over new director selection decisions, which remains significant although it varies across companies; the authors examine it through five widely used indicators of power.

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissism is viewed as a personality dimension for the general population, and narcissistic CEOs are those with an inflated self-view who seek to have that self-view continuously reinforced.

name: Similarity to the CEO in narcissistic tendency
authors_terms: ["new director's similarity to the CEO in narcissistic tendency", "similarity in narcissism", "similarity in narcissistic tendency"]
definition: The extent to which a new director's narcissistic tendency resembles the focal CEO's; CEOs may assume that similarity in narcissistic tendency reflects similarity in preferred strategic approaches and hence reduces the uncertainty that a new director will not support their leadership.

name: Prior experience with similarly narcissistic CEOs
authors_terms: ["new director's prior experience with other similarly narcissistic CEOs", "prior experience with other CEOs who are similar to the focal CEO in narcissistic tendency"]
definition: A new director's prior ties to other CEOs whose narcissistic tendencies are similar to the focal CEO's, which suggest that the director has been generally accepted by other similar CEOs and hence should be acceptable to the focal CEO.
