name: Demographic difference from the CEO
authors_terms: ["new director's demographic difference from the CEO", "demographic difference from CEO"]
definition: The extent to which a new director differs from the focal CEO along salient demographic dimensions, which the authors argue makes the CEO rely more heavily on the director's similarity in narcissism and prior experience with similarly narcissistic CEOs.

name: Risk-taking spending
definition: CEOs' risk-taking decisions can be studied by examining the firm's major forms of risk-taking spending, namely expenditure on mergers and acquisitions, research and development, and advertising.

name: Production-dominant variety
definition: Variety is production-dominant if the increase in production costs associated with increased variety outweighs the increase in market mediation costs. In bicycles, the authors consider materials variety to be production-dominant.

name: Mediation-dominant variety
definition: Variety is mediation-dominant if the increase in mediation costs associated with increased variety outweighs the increase in production costs. In bicycles, the authors consider color variety, and also geometry/size and component variety, to be mediation-dominant.

name: Scale-efficient production
authors_terms: ["scale-efficient production", "scale efficient", "degree of scale in production"]
definition: We define scale efficient production as production using a facility over 600,000 units per year. Independent studies of scale within the industry suggest that plants reach minimum efficient scale between 150,000-200,000 units of annual production for one basic frame material.

name: Production location relative to target market
authors_terms: ["location", "Local", "Distant", "distance of production from target market", "localized production"]
definition: Supply chain structure is characterized in part by the distance of production facilities from a target market; geographic distance creates longer replenishment lead times and forecast horizons, which increase exposure to demand uncertainty. A firm is local if production for a process is located within North America and distant if over 50% of production for that process is located outside North America.

name: Match between product variety and supply chain structure
definition: This theory implies that there are coherent matches between product variety and supply chain structure. A firm is classified as matching an attribute when its variety level with respect to that attribute and its supply chain structure fall in one of the two quadrants predicted by the theory.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use two financial measures-return on assets and return on sales-to examine the hypothesis that firm performance is associated with matching variety and location. Both measures capture the cost and revenue benefits associated with matching variety and supply chain structure.

name: Proportion of banking experts
authors_terms: ["proportion of banking expert directors", "proportion of banking experts", "banking expert directors"]
definition: The proportion of those directors whose primary professional experience is within the focal firm's industry and who are thus seen as possessing a high degree of competence in that domain; in this setting, the directors whose biographical records indicated banking experience before joining the board.

name: Proportion of real estate experts
authors_terms: ["proportion of real estate experts", "proportion of real estate expert directors", "directors who are experts in the real estate domain"]
definition: The proportion of directors whose biographical records indicated a background in the real estate domain (e.g., in real estate development and construction); typical profiles included owners or top executives of real estate development and real estate investment companies.

name: Bank failure
definition: In our empirical definition, a bank failure occurs when the FDIC intervenes in response to a bank's inability to satisfy its depository obligations. Such intervention involves either liquidating the bank or acting as a broker between the focal bank and an acquiring bank that assumes its depository liability.

name: Asset growth
authors_terms: ["asset growth", "rate of asset growth", "rapid asset growth", "fast asset growth"]
definition: A bank's rate of asset growth, which involves new lending and leaves the bank operating in uncharted market territory, often facing decisions about previously unknown borrowers, lending areas, and sources of loans.

name: Non-standard real estate lending
authors_terms: ["non-standard real estate lending", "non-standard real estate loans", "involvement in non-standard real estate lending"]
definition: Lending markets that involve nonstandard real estate loans, that is, loans for real estate other than ordinary family residential properties; such loans include land, construction and development loans, farm loans, large multifamily residential loans, and other commercial real estate loans.

name: Number of locally-based banks
authors_terms: ["number of locally-based banks", "number of direct competitors", "number of locally-based banks in the same geographic area"]
definition: The time-variant count of banks based in the focal bank's county; interviewees indicated that the direct competitors of a local bank are other local banks in the same area.

name: Firm reputation
definition: We define a firm's reputation as the extent to which there is broad public recognition that it produces high-quality outputs. The management literature broadly coalesces around reputation as stakeholders' collective perception of a firm based on the quality of its track record.

name: Market heat
definition: Market heat is the extent of increased market activity relative to recent history, generally driven by an influx of interest from resource providers. It is thus an increase in the supply of resources available in the broad market.

name: Recent firm successes
definition: The second form of resource mobilization opportunity we consider is when firms have experienced recent successes. In contrast to market heat, recent successes represent firm-level resource mobilization opportunities.

name: Resource mobilization
definition: By resource mobilization, we refer to firms assembling tangible and intangible assets for better pursuing focal opportunities.

name: Saliency of social movement activism
authors_terms: ["saliency of SMO activism", "movement saliency", "clean energy SMO participation", "SMO activism"]
definition: The saliency of a movement, which depends on the visibility and size of the movement and the resources it allocates, and which intensifies the pressures that firms perceive. The authors measure movement saliency through measures that capture indirect pressures arising from SMO activism.

name: Competitor actions aligned with movement demands
authors_terms: ["competitor actions", "competitor actions in accordance with social movement pressures", "competitor adoption", "cumulative competitor wind power activity"]
definition: Competitor practices that increasingly align with a movement's goals, which may raise the perceived stakes and act as a source of pressure that motivates firm action.

name: Market dependence
definition: The concept of market dependence, which defines the relative contribution of a market to a firm's overall performance (e.g., revenue). As a firm's market dependence increases, the stakes are higher and the motivation to defend its position is greater.

name: Firm response to social movement pressures
authors_terms: ["firm response", "firm response to social movement pressures", "wind energy integration"]
definition: Whether an electric utility adopts new wind power in a state, that is, whether it builds a new wind farm or commits to buying wind power from a new wind farm in response to the environmental social movement.

name: Female representation in top management
authors_terms: ["female representation in top management", "female representation", "women in top management"]
definition: The presence of women among the managers reported for a firm's top management team; the authors operationalize it with a dummy variable, female representation, which takes the value 1 (0) if any (none) of the managers reported in ExecuComp for a given firm in a given year is female.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors' primary measure is Tobin's q, defined as the ratio of the market value of a firm's assets to their replacement value; the idea is that better firms create more economic value from a given quantity of assets.

name: Innovation intensity
authors_terms: ["innovation intensity", "firm's strategy is focused on innovation"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's strategy is focused on innovation, measured as the ratio of research and development (R&D) expense to assets from the prior year.

name: Input stigma
authors_terms: ["input stigma", "chemical stigma", "level of stigma of a firm's inputs", "stigmatization of a firm's inputs"]
definition: A stigma emerges as a visible label that evokes a collective perception that the use of a certain input is 'deeply flawed or discredited'. Such public stigmatization translates into strong pressures that come from stakeholders, such as customers, social movement organizations, and investors.

name: Input use
authors_terms: ["input use", "change in chemical use", "extent to which the firm uses that input", "use of stigmatized inputs"]
definition: Firms have two options: they can either keep using the same stigmatized input (resist) or remove it and use a more legitimate one instead (concede). The paper examines whether and how much a firm changes its use of an input that has become stigmatized.

name: Firm performance
definition: The economic performance of the firm, which using stigmatized inputs threatens directly through costs imposed on targeted firms and indirectly through reputational spillovers, and which is captured with the firm's return on assets.

name: Input overlap
authors_terms: ["input overlap", "chemical overlap", "overlap among production units", "high input overlap", "low input overlap"]
definition: The degree to which the stigmatized input is used across a firm's business units rather than in one single business unit; a firm using a stigmatized input across multiple business units has high input overlap.

name: Upper echelon affiliations
authors_terms: ["upper echelon affiliations", "upper echelon's affiliations with prominent organizations"]
definition: We propose that upper echelon members' affiliations with prominent organizations can affect the perceived legitimacy of a young firm in the eyes of external parties. Different types of upper echelon affiliations are theorized to assuage different types of legitimacy concerns.

name: Upper echelon upstream affiliations
authors_terms: ["upper echelon upstream affiliations", "prominent upstream affiliations", "upstream affiliations"]
definition: Upstream affiliations in the biotechnology industry derive from upper echelon members' employment affiliations with prominent organizations such as research institutions, think tanks, and/or universities. Such affiliations are symbolic of the firm's rank and membership in the scientific profession and can redress legitimacy concerns regarding technological viability.

name: Upper echelon horizontal affiliations
authors_terms: ["upper echelon horizontal affiliations", "prominent horizontal affiliations", "horizontal affiliations"]
definition: An upper echelon's horizontal affiliations in the biotechnology industry derive from upper echelon members' employment and board affiliations with prominent organizations in the industry. Such affiliations symbolize the firm's experience in the industry hierarchy, assuaging concerns regarding the firm's ability to compete effectively.

name: Upper echelon downstream affiliations
authors_terms: ["upper echelon downstream affiliations", "prominent downstream affiliations", "downstream affiliations"]
definition: In biotechnology, an upper echelon's downstream affiliations derive from team members' affiliations with prominent pharmaceutical and/or healthcare companies. Such affiliations are symbolic of the firm's membership position in biotechnology product markets, allaying concerns that the firm will be able to bring its products to the marketplace.

name: Upper echelon range of affiliations
authors_terms: ["range of upper echelon affiliations", "range of affiliations", "upper echelon range of affiliations"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's upper echelon has prominent affiliations across all three categories—upstream, horizontal, and downstream. The authors argue that symbols in each area complement one another and that a firm with coverage across all three types of affiliations should have an advantage in securing interorganizational endorsements.

name: Underwriter prestige
authors_terms: ["investment bank prestige", "underwriter prestige", "prestige of the investment bank", "prestige of a firm's lead underwriter"]
definition: The prestige of the lead investment bank that endorses a young firm at its IPO. Investment bank prestige was measured using an index developed by Carter and Manaster (1990) and then updated by Carter et al. (1998), with scores from 0 (lowest prestige) to 9 (highest prestige).

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: In the biotechnology industry, one of the major sources of uncertainty concerns a firm's scientific technology. Technological uncertainty is high when a biotechnology firm has products that are in early stages of development.

name: Strategic decision comprehensiveness
definition: In this study, we defined decision comprehensiveness as the extent to which a project team is exhaustive and inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions in developing a new product. It captures the extent to which the project team searches for information with a wide lens and considers multiple approaches, multiple courses of action, and multiple decision criteria in evaluating and selecting alternative courses of action.

name: New product performance
authors_terms: ["new product performance", "subjective new product performance", "sales growth", "market performance"]
definition: Informants rated a new product's degree of success relative to those of competitors' products on sales growth, market share growth, growth in profit, and return on investment. Sales growth is widely considered as the key indicator of the market acceptance of a new venture's products.

name: New product quality
definition: New product quality refers to the perceived superiority of a new product in terms of its reliability and customer satisfaction compared with other alternatives.

name: Technology uncertainty
definition: Technology uncertainty refers to the perceived speed of change and unpredictability of technology in a firm's principal industry. It is characterized by short product development cycles and fast technological obsolescence.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: Demand uncertainty refers to the perceived speed of change and unpredictability of customers' product preferences and demands as well as the emergence of new customer segments.

name: Product introduction delay
authors_terms: ["product introduction delays", "delays in product introductions", "delays in new product introductions", "product delay announcements"]
definition: Firms announcing that the introduction of a product has already been delayed or will be delayed relative to the planned introduction date.

name: Return on assets
authors_terms: ["ROA", "return on assets", "abnormal ROA", "change in the level of ROA"]
definition: Operating income divided by the average of beginning and ending period book value of assets, where operating income is sales less the cost of goods sold and selling, general, and administration expenses.

name: Sales over assets
definition: Sales divided by total assets; one of the components through which product introduction delays are linked to ROA.

name: Return on sales
definition: One minus the ratio of the cost of goods sold plus selling, general, and administration expenses to sales.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the sample firm; the authors argue that smaller firms are more likely to be focused and critically dependent on bringing a few key products to market in a timely manner, and have less resources and flexibility to absorb the negative consequences of delays.

name: Industry financial attractiveness
authors_terms: ["industry financial performance (or attractiveness)", "industry size", "industry median ROA"]
definition: The financial attractiveness of the industry in which the firm operates; the authors use industry size and the median ROA of the industry as proxies for it.

name: Firm relative profitability
authors_terms: ["industry-adjusted performance (IADPER)", "the firm's ROA relative to its industry", "more profitable the firm"]
definition: The sample firm's industry-adjusted performance, measured as its ROA in year -2 minus the median ROA of its industry in year -2.

name: Loss-making status
authors_terms: ["firms making losses", "loss-making firms", "firms with negative ROA", "NROA"]
definition: Whether the sample firm's ROA in the base year is positive (profitable firm) or negative (loss-making firm), captured by the indicator variables PROA and NROA.

name: Abiding behavior
definition: Actions that comply with the socially approved goal but exhibit a lower level of procedural commitment refer to abiding behavior; although these behaviors comply with expectations of environmental friendliness, they do not demonstrate strong adherence to the procedural aspect of the social norm and therefore do not contribute to reinforcing it.

name: Strengthening behavior
definition: Actions that both comply with the socially approved goal and exhibit a high level of commitment toward the procedures reflect strengthening behavior; by conforming to both dimensions of the norm, these behaviors contribute to strengthening it.

name: Targeting behavior
definition: Actions that do not comply with the socially approved goal but display a high level of procedural commitment are targeting behaviors; these behaviors fall short of the social expectation of environmental friendliness, but the high level of commitment shows that the firm explicitly acknowledges the disjunction between its current actions and what is expected from it as a margin of progress.

name: Finessing behavior
definition: Actions that fail to comply with the social expectations and exhibit low levels of procedural commitment are labeled finessing behaviors; for these behaviors, conformity to the norm of environmental transparency persists at a low level but the disjunction between the firm's actual and expected actions is hidden from scrutiny.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Reputation refers to the perceptions by a firm's audience about the firm's ability to provide value compared with its peers and rivals; reputation formation is defined as 'a signaling process, in which the strategic choices of firms send signals to observers and observers use these signals to form impressions of these firms.'

name: Prior reputation
authors_terms: ["prior reputation", "prior reputation score", "prior reputation ranking", "prior overall reputation"]
definition: Audiences tend to use prior reputation as a baseline from which to interpret and assess a firm's actions, and reputation-granting audiences may be willing to rely on the firm's prior reputation to assess the quality of its disclosures; prior reputation may thus be an important moderator of the reputation-granting process.

name: Second-order competitive overlap
definition: Potential partners often serve a firm's competitors, as the partner's expertise is sought by firms with similar needs, creating second-order competitive overlap for the focal firm. The paper uses the term competitive overlap for second-order competitive overlap in market networks.

name: Partner choice
authors_terms: ["law firm choice", "expert partner choice", "partner selection", "partner choice"]
definition: Law firm choice is binary, denoting whether or not the client–patent-law firm pair has been observed, thereby indicating a realized choice. For each patent, this variable takes on the value one when the law firm was chosen to work on the patent and zero for the matched law firm that was not chosen.

name: Prior ties between client and partner
definition: The authors identify whether a prior relationship exists between the patenting firm and the law firm. This variable helps distinguish initial interactions from those in which the client has first-hand, prior experience with the law firm.

name: Technology area age
authors_terms: ["technology age", "age of the technology area", "industry maturity"]
definition: Technology age is measured as the average age of patents in the same two-digit USPC category, capturing the maturity of the technology area in which the patent is filed.

name: Technology relatedness
authors_terms: ["technology similarity", "relatedness to the firm's existing technology", "relatedness of the technology"]
definition: Technology similarity is a measure of a patent's proximity to a client's prior work. To construct the measure, the authors calculate the Jensen–Shannon distance to the 10 closest patent applications of the same client over the past 3 years and normalize this measure (0–1) within each client; values closer to 0 represent distant technologies, while values closer to 1 represent similar patents.

name: Organizational failure
definition: The dependent variable is organizational failure: organizations are coded 1 if they failed during the time period studied and 0 otherwise. Failures include completed bankruptcies, completed liquidations, closures based on company request, and merger or acquisition of organizations at risk of bankruptcy.

name: Organizational independence
authors_terms: ["organizational independence", "organizational structure", "independent organizations", "subsidiary organizations", "degree of independence"]
definition: A key strategic characteristic of organizations is their degree of independence, especially with regard to whether they are tied to a parent organization or not. Organizational independence affects the autonomy an organization has in making 'its own decision about the use and allocation of its internal resources without reference or regard to the demands of potential linkage partners'.

name: Financial slack
definition: Slack refers specifically to financial resource availability in excess of resource demands. Financial slack is measured as the difference between current assets and current liabilities and describes short-term resource accessibility, indicating whether a firm is keeping excess resources that are not put into productive use or fueling growth that may include short-term deficits.

name: Employees
definition: Employees are one of the four key observable organizational resources considered; a greater number of employees allows organizations to acquire information faster.

name: Fixed assets
definition: Fixed assets are nonliquid assets required for operations and include facilities, equipment, and real property.

name: Equity
definition: Equity is the owner's reported equity in the business (total assets minus total liabilities). Subsidiaries receive equity primarily from parents with the expectation that it will be applied toward the predefined strategic objectives of the larger organization.

name: Environmental jolt
definition: Environmental jolts are 'transient perturbations whose occurrences are difficult to foresee and whose impacts on organizations are disruptive and potentially inimical'. The authors define the jolt period as the severe economic downturn occurring from 2001 through 2002.

name: Peer recognition
authors_terms: ["peer recognition", "peer evaluation", "symbolic capital granted by peers"]
definition: Peer recognition is the social endorsement granted by peers and a key resource for cultural organizations; within a field it is a direct indicator of an actor's legitimacy and embeddedness, and peers consecrate actors who deviate the least from normative expectations.

name: Salience of ties with extraneous stakeholders
authors_terms: ["salience of the ties with the extraneous stakeholder group", "salience of the relationship with corporate donors", "number of corporate donors"]
definition: Salience is operationalized as the number of corporate donors that a theater has in a given year, as this is the most noticeable feature of the ties with this group of stakeholders.

name: Breadth of the stakeholder relationship
authors_terms: ["breadth of the relationship", "breadth of involvement", "type of collaboration"]
definition: This is what we call the breadth of the relationship: it represents the scope of activities in which the donor can be involved.

name: Depth of the stakeholder relationship
authors_terms: ["depth of the relationship", "longevity of involvement", "longevity of the relationship with a donor"]
definition: This is the depth of the relationship: it captures how much the organization is accustomed to the stakeholder's influence.

name: Valence of the stakeholder relationship
definition: We define it as valence of the relationship, or the degree of taint of the relationship in the eyes of another key stakeholder group.

name: Market position
definition: A target market position is the description of needs, accessibility, or variety of products and services a firm desires to serve. The authors inductively identified three types of market positions in IC&SP service: package specialists, document specialists, and full-line service couriers.

name: Idiosyncratic IT resources
authors_terms: ["idiosyncratic IT", "idiosyncratic resources in IT", "degree of idiosyncrasy", "asset specificity"]
definition: By type of resource we mean the degree to which each resource or capability is idiosyncratic. This measure is the level of asset specificity familiar to transaction cost economists. The authors' resource profile consists of the idiosyncrasy of IT resources in domestic trucking, international air carriage, and foreign trucking.

name: Vertical integration
definition: The existence of any equity relationship between freight forwarder and transportation segment is classified as vertically integrated. The absence of an equity relation is classified as contracting out.

name: Delivery time
authors_terms: ["delivery time", "delivery speed", "elapsed delivery time", "net delivery time"]
definition: Interviews with shippers indicate that delivery reliability and delivery speed are the primary product attributes for differentiating IC&SP service and that these two product attributes go hand in hand. The authors collected information on parcel pick-up time at the place of origin and on parcel drop-off time at the destination and computed net delivery time in days.

name: Strong ties
definition: Strong ties refer to the level of trust, reciprocity, and proximity of interaction that characterize the portfolio of ties among the participants in a project alliance; such strength of ties reflects the level of relational embeddedness and cohesiveness among alliance partners at the project level.

name: Bridging ties
definition: A bridging tie is defined as a tie that spans a structural hole; a defining characteristic of bridging ties is nonredundancy, i.e., the connected actors are heterogeneous in their backgrounds, experiences, knowledge, and skills.

name: Knowledge integration
definition: We define knowledge integration as the process of jointly applying specialized knowledge held by various alliance partners at the project level.

name: Alliance ambidexterity
definition: We conceptualize alliance performance as the capacity to simultaneously exhibit alignment with alliance objectives and adaptiveness to changes in the environment; or what Gibson and Birkinshaw (2004) label as ambidexterity. Drawing on this thinking, we use alliance ambidexterity to assess alliance performance at the project level.

name: Media-rival common institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["media-rival common ownership", "Media-rival CIO", "media-rival common institutional ownership"]
definition: We define media-rival common ownership as the condition in which an institutional investor owns a blockholding stake (at least 5 percent of outstanding shares) in both a media company and at least one of a focal firm's industry rivals. Taking a different view, we defined common ownership as cases in which an investor owns one firm in the media industry and another firm in a non-media industry.

name: Media coverage negativity
authors_terms: ["Media coverage negativity", "negativity of a focal firm's media coverage", "media coverage negativity"]
definition: Our dependent variable captures the sentiment of a firm's media coverage as reported by a media outlet. Since the annual ESS average captures coverage positivity, we subtracted the score from 100 to measure a firm's Media coverage negativity by a media outlet, and we scaled the score by 100 so that the score ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate more negative media coverage.

name: Firm-rival product similarity
definition: Market overlap, in terms of both product similarity and geographic overlap, influences the intra-industry rivalry between two firms and its intensity and saliency. A high level of product similarity or geographic overlap between two industry peers indicates that these companies compete more directly for the same customers and business, which creates intense and recognizable rivalries.

name: Firm-rival geographic market overlap
authors_terms: ["geographic market overlap", "geographic overlap", "Firm-rival geographic market overlap"]
definition: Market overlap, in terms of both product similarity and geographic overlap, influences the intra-industry rivalry between two firms and its intensity and saliency. We computed the geographic market overlap ratio between a focal firm and each rival with Media-rival CIO, calculated as the number of states where both firms compete divided by the total number of states where the focal firm competes.

name: Investment horizon
definition: A focal characteristic that shapes an institutional investor's relationship with a portfolio firm is its investment horizon, defined as the average length of time an investor holds on to a firm's stock. Institutional investors with long investment horizons have more power to influence the coverage decisions of media executives.

name: Media CEO equity compensation
definition: The economic incentives that executives can use to please their investors vary considerably. We measured CEO equity compensation of media companies by obtaining compensation data from ExecuComp.

name: Tenure-based voting rights adoption
definition: TVRs increase owners' voting rights if the owners hold their shares for a minimum vesting period, leaving cash flow rights unaffected. In the Italian setting, TVRs grant double voting rights to any shares held by the same shareholder for at least 2 years after registration.

name: Family firm status
definition: The authors define a family firm as one where the family owner exercises influence over the firm's affairs. Empirically, they use a family control indicator equal to 1 if one or more family members hold 25% or more of issued equity and 0 otherwise.

name: Corporate investment
definition: An aggregate measure of investment (Investment) equal to the sum of capital expenditure, R&D expenditure, and acquisitions, scaled by lagged total assets.

name: Family control fragility
authors_terms: ["fragility of family control", "fragile family firm", "dominant family firm"]
definition: Fragile family firm is equal to 1 when family ownership is lower than 50% (family control is fragile); dominant family firm is equal to 1 when family ownership is greater than or equal to 50% (family control is dominant). The authors focus on the fragility of family control because constraints on new investment are likely more binding when family control is fragile.

name: Leisure time invention
authors_terms: ["leisure time invention", "leisure time insight", "incidence of leisure time invention"]
definition: Leisure time invention refers to invention where the main underlying idea occurs while the employee is away from the workplace. The paper focuses on the incidence of employee leisure time invention, i.e., whether the idea for the invention occurred during leisure time rather than work time.

name: Nature of the technical problem
authors_terms: ["conceptually based problems", "science-based problems", "heuristic problem search", "algorithmic problem search"]
definition: We refer to technical problems encountered in areas where design is important (for example, consumer goods) as conceptually based problems and to technical problems related more on algorithmic discovery as science-based problems. Conceptually based technical problems, for which the path to the solution is not clear, are contrasted with science-based problems that largely require the addition of new experimental knowledge through reiterative application of known methods.

name: Importance of strong ties
authors_terms: ["interactions with others (strong ties)", "strong ties", "interactions with people who work in the same organization"]
definition: The strength of an interpersonal tie is defined as a 'combination of the amount of time, the emotional intensity, the intimacy (mutual confiding), and the reciprocal service'. Interactions with people who work in the same organization are used as a proxy for strong ties in a work-related network.

name: Importance of weak ties
authors_terms: ["interactions with others (weak ties)", "weak ties", "people from outside the organization"]
definition: Interactions with people from outside the organization serve as a proxy for weak ties in the inventor's network; these people outside the organization include friends and family and other people not related to the daily work of the inventors whom they will typically meet during their leisure time.

name: R&D project size
authors_terms: ["R&D project size", "size of the associated R&D project"]
definition: To measure the R&D project size, we used the total labor input needed as a proxy. Large R&D projects involve substantial resource investments in people, materials, equipment, and working capital, plus extensive input coordination.

name: Coinventors from other organizations
definition: A dummy variable took the value of 1 in cases where coinventors from organizations other than the respondent's organization were involved in the project leading to the invention. This variable was included because coinventors from other organizations, who also form a proxy for weak ties, were explicitly excluded from the two variables describing interactions with other people.

name: Task overlap
definition: The overlap of the task content of different jobs, measured by the cosine similarity of the jobs' duties and responsibilities text; it is bounded between 0 and 1, where 1 represents complete overlap.

name: Task coordination
definition: Jobs whose descriptions include words that emphasize explicit coordination; job descriptions that have more such words in them should entail more coordination with other jobs. Interdependence for these jobs inheres in the explicit act of coordination: liaising, consulting, interacting, and so on.

name: Job death
definition: Job death is the removal of a specific bundling of tasks, even if some or all of the tasks are still performed. A job is defined as being 'dead' when the formal position is no longer occupied in any future period.

name: Neighbor job death
authors_terms: ["neighbor death", "deaths of jobs with which the focal job is technically interdependent"]
definition: The number of a job's five nearest neighbors, based on the task similarity measure, that died in the previous year.

name: Organizational subunit closure
authors_terms: ["closure of the organizational subunits", "number of units closed"]
definition: Subunits are the organizational locations in which employees work, such as academic departments, centers, institutes, medical facilities and physical maintenance plants; a subunit is coded as closed when any employees in that subunit disappear from later years.

name: Expatriate ability to transfer knowledge
authors_terms: ["expatriate ability", "ability to transfer", "expatriate ability to transfer knowledge to a subsidiary"]
definition: In this study, expatriate ability refers to the knowledge, skills, and experience needed to solve difficulties in transferring knowledge.

name: Expatriate motivation to transfer knowledge
authors_terms: ["expatriate motivation", "motivation to transfer", "expatriate motivation to transfer knowledge to a subsidiary"]
definition: Expatriate motivation refers to the willingness to devote time and to persist in solving difficulties in transferring knowledge.

name: Expatriate opportunity seeking to transfer knowledge
authors_terms: ["expatriate opportunity seeking", "opportunity seeking to transfer knowledge"]
definition: In this study, expatriate opportunity seeking refers to the search and utilization of resources and opportunities through social relationships to solve difficulties in transferring knowledge.

name: Knowledge received by subsidiary
authors_terms: ["knowledge received by subsidiary", "knowledge received by the subsidiary", "knowledge received"]
definition: One indicator of knowledge transfer success is the amount of knowledge received by a subsidiary from expatriates, which, as we argue, is influenced by expatriate competencies in transferring knowledge. The knowledge transfer process includes both transmission (by expatriates, in this study) and receipt (by subsidiaries) of knowledge.

name: Subsidiary absorptive capacity
definition: Absorptive capacity includes four components: (1) identifying and recognizing external knowledge, (2) processing and understanding it, (3) combining it with existing knowledge, and (4) applying the new knowledge to commercial ends. Subsidiary absorptive capacity represents a potential that can be brought to bear upon external new knowledge; it does not refer to actual knowledge received and applied by the subsidiary.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: We obtained two objective subsidiary performance measures—return on investment (ROI) and return on equity (ROE) for fiscal year 2009-10—from the FAME and TEJ databases. This gave a one-year time lag with the measures of expatriate competencies, subsidiary absorptive capacity, and knowledge received by subsidiary.

name: Network effect strength
authors_terms: ["direct (same side) network effects", "stronger network effects", "strengthening of network effects"]
definition: One of the most prominent characteristics of digital industries is the presence of demand-side economies of scale or 'direct network effects' (Shapiro, Carl, & Varian, 1998), where the value of a product increases based on the number of users.

name: Freemium strategy
definition: Freemium refers to the strategy of companies offering a basic version of a product at zero price alongside a full premium paid version.

name: Leader-follower revenue gap
authors_terms: ["difference in the revenues between the market leader and the followers", "revenue gap between the leader and the follower", "relative revenues of market leaders and followers"]
definition: To do so, we calculate the difference in revenues between the market leader and the follower. We do this with the difference between the log-transformed revenues of the market leader and the follower.

name: Market position
definition: We define the market leader as the firm with the highest sales revenue in a particular market category and the follower (second-ranked) as the firm with the second-highest sales revenue in that market category.

name: Product revenue
definition: The main outcome variable constitutes the daily product revenues of the market leader and the follower, specifically ln ( Total Daily Revenues c , t , r + 1 ) for each category ( c ), day ( t ), and rank ( r ) corresponding to 1 or 2 for the market leader and the follower, respectively.

name: Managerial discretion
authors_terms: ["managerial discretion", "latitude of managerial action", "latitude of action"]
definition: Managerial discretion is defined as 'latitude of managerial action,' or the extent to which CEOs are able to influence the actions and outcomes of their firm. Discretion is a joint product of stakeholder open-mindedness about executive actions and stakeholder inability to block objectionable actions.

name: Individualism
definition: Societies characterized by individualistic values will provide broader zones of acceptance for executives and will tend to permit individual initiative and tolerate unilateral decision making, whereas collectivistic societies, characterized by norms of consensus and compromise, grant less discretion.

name: Uncertainty tolerance
definition: Some societies have a relatively high tolerance for quantum actions, means-ends ambiguity, and unpredictability; societies with greater tolerance for unpredictable actions, and the uncertainty associated with those actions, will provide broader zones of acceptance for executives.

name: Power distance
definition: Power distance, as typically identified in cultural values research, refers to acceptance of inequality in general and is thus broader than simply the power of executive leaders, but is suggestive of the status of leadership in a society.

name: Cultural looseness
definition: Cultural tightness is defined as 'the strength of social norms and the degree of sanctioning within societies'; tightness reflects the extent to which norms are widely shared within a society and the extent to which transgressions will lead to repercussions, whereas loose cultures have weak norm enforcement and more ambiguous standards of behavior.

name: Ownership dispersion
definition: Countries differ greatly in the degree to which their public corporations are closely held by few investors vs. widely held by many investors; concentrated ownership provides shareholders with both the incentive and means to impose their interests on managers.

name: Common-law legal origin
definition: The collective work on law and finance focuses on the fundamental distinction between the common-law tradition, derived from English law, and the civil-law tradition, derived from Roman law; in common-law countries the rights of property owners are privileged over those of other stakeholders.

name: Employer flexibility
definition: Executives have flexibility to the extent they are legally allowed to easily alter the composition and deployment of their employee populations; executives lack flexibility when employee-employer relations are heavily determined by historical agreements, legislation, and other nonmarket factors.

name: CEO effects on firm performance
authors_terms: ["CEO effects on firm performance", "CEO-attributable variance in firm performance", "variance in firm performance attributable to CEOs"]
definition: If CEOs have considerable discretion, if they have the leeway to take idiosyncratic and bold actions, then the effects of CEOs on company outcomes will be more pronounced; the measure of 'CEO effect' for a given performance indicator is the variance for the CEO-level term divided by total firm variance in a country.

name: Shock distance
definition: We define shock distance as the distance from a manager's structural position (i.e., his or her subgroup) to the locus of direct impact of a given shock.

name: Capability perception
definition: Capability perceptions are defined as the extent to which each manager perceives his or her firm as having the resources and capabilities to successfully address the shock. Differentiated capability perceptions reflect differentiated cause-effect understandings or mental models about resources and capabilities.

name: Opportunity interpretation
definition: Managers interpret exogenous shocks by paying attention to salient categories or aspects, including whether the shock presents an opportunity versus a threat. Opportunity (threat) interpretation was measured using three items related to 'gain (loss) implications,' 'positive (negative) event,' and 'opportunity (threat).'

name: Threat interpretation
definition: Managers interpret exogenous shocks by paying attention to salient categories or aspects, including whether the shock presents an opportunity versus a threat. Opportunity (threat) interpretation was measured using three items related to 'gain (loss) implications,' 'positive (negative) event,' and 'opportunity (threat).'

name: Domain-specific experience
definition: We refer in this paper to managerial experience relating to the domain (industry) associated with the focal shock as domain-specific experience. Within a diversified firm, it is likely that different managers will have specific experience relating to different industries in which the firm operates.

name: Director depth/breadth expertise
authors_terms: ["director depth/breadth", "deep/broad expertise", "deep/broad director", "depth and breadth of prior experiences"]
definition: Depth reflects time spent as an executive in a company, industry, or with a unique strategy dominantly employed by these companies. Breadth reflects the number of different companies, industries, and unique strategies.

name: Nondirectional strategic change
authors_terms: ["nondirectional strategic change", "strategic change (in terms of magnitude)"]
definition: We define nondirectional strategic change as the extent to which - upon the addition of a new outside director - a firm moves strategic emphases scores for each of the seven generic strategies.

name: Directional strategic change
authors_terms: ["directional strategic change", "strategic change in the direction of his or her strategic experiences"]
definition: We define directional strategic change as the extent to which - upon the addition of a new outside director - a firm moves strategic emphasis directionally toward the strategic emphasis of that director.

name: Board turnover
definition: We define board turnover as the number of directors leaving the board during the year divided by the total number of board members at the beginning of the year.

name: Board tenure heterogeneity
definition: We calculate board tenure heterogeneity as the variance of member tenures on the board, divided by the mean of tenures.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Vertical integration offers a firm greater control over its innovation process and greater opportunities to accumulate knowledge about components and architectures, but it requires large capital investments and a broad set of technological capabilities.

name: Time to market
authors_terms: ["time to market", "time-to-market performance", "timing of the commercialization"]
definition: Our measure of firm performance is based on a firm's timing of the commercialization of a new DRAM generation, a key driver of competitive advantage in this industry.

name: Component knowledge
authors_terms: ["knowledge of the external component", "knowledge of outsourced components", "component knowledge", "mask knowledge", "resist knowledge", "knowledge integration"]
definition: This stream considers the possibility that firms may invest in knowledge integration by developing knowledge of externally produced components.

name: Architectural innovation
definition: Other product innovations are enabled by changes in components as well as changes in the links and the interactions among them.

name: Middle managers' championing alternatives
authors_terms: ["championing alternatives", "championing alternative strategies by selling them to senior management", "upward strategic influence", "upward influence"]
definition: One of the two adaptive strategy implementation behaviors; middle managers' upward influence, i.e., championing alternative strategies by selling them to senior management, as part of their upward and downward influence to propose, accommodate, and embrace adjustments in planned functional level strategies at the business unit level to fit with operational situations.

name: Middle managers' facilitating adaptability
authors_terms: ["facilitating adaptability", "facilitating adaptability on the frontline", "downward strategic influence", "downward influence"]
definition: One of the two adaptive strategy implementation behaviors; middle managers' downward influence, i.e., facilitating adaptability on the frontline, as part of their upward and downward influence to propose, accommodate, and embrace adjustments in planned functional level strategies at the business unit level to fit with operational situations.

name: Business unit performance
definition: A formative construct based on objective performance measures attained from the company's records and aggregated to the sales district level, which allow for between-unit comparability and reflect the market's response to middle managers' strategic adaptation implementation behaviors.

name: Reputational social capital
authors_terms: ["reputational social capital", "middle managers' reputational social capital in the advice network at the management level"]
definition: Middle managers' reputational social capital in the advice network at the management level, which captures their prestige of being knowledgeable in the circles of senior managers and peer middle managers.

name: Informational social capital
authors_terms: ["informational social capital", "middle managers' informational social capital in their regional advice network"]
definition: Middle managers' informational social capital in their regional advice network, which captures the extent to which they have access to information external to their regional network; middle managers gain nonredundant informational social capital from the social ties they hold with people outside their regional networks.

name: Business unit network size
authors_terms: ["middle managers' business unit network size", "middle manager's business unit network size", "middle manager's direct reports"]
definition: Middle managers' span of control; network size is the number of subordinates who report directly to a leader, here the sales representatives who directly report to a specific middle manager.

name: Senior managers' regional network size
authors_terms: ["senior managers' regional network size", "senior manager's regional network size", "senior manager's direct reports"]
definition: Senior managers' regional network size, which captures their span of control; network size is the number of subordinates who report directly to a leader, here the middle managers who report to a sales director.

name: Intrinsic speed capabilities
definition: By intrinsic speed capabilities, we mean firms' ability to execute investment projects faster than competitors at the same cost. They are conceptualized as the ability of the firm to complete investment projects faster than the industry average.

name: Entry timing
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "later market entry time", "late entry", "early entry"]
definition: The timing of a firm's entry into a new market, where the possession of speed capabilities should result in a later market entry time, ceteris paribus. Entry Timing are dummies indicating entry during the early (P = 1) or late (P = 2) regime of a new market opportunity.

name: Usage specificity
definition: We define irreversible investments as usage-specific investments that are useful for little else than their original intended purpose—or that have financially unattractive alternative applications. Gasification facilities are usage specific, whereas liquefaction facilities are usage flexible since the LNG output from liquefaction can be diverted and sold in other markets.

name: Entry performance
definition: The profitability from entry, whose variation across firms for the same strategic action is assessed through the stock market reaction to the announcement of entry, which reflects the discounted value of the action.

name: Prior adoption by smaller organizations
authors_terms: ["smaller adopters", "adoption by a smaller organization", "Smaller Adopter", "Number Smaller Adopters", "Bayesian Inference", "smaller initial adopters"]
definition: Adoption of a practice by an organization that is smaller than the focal organization; because observers expect smaller adopters to benefit less, their adoption provides particularly convincing evidence about the size threshold at which adoption becomes profitable.

name: Prior adoption by larger organizations
authors_terms: ["larger adopters", "Larger Adopter", "Number Larger Adopters", "adoption by a larger organization"]
definition: Adoption of a practice by an organization that is larger than the focal organization; larger organizations are thought to have more impact because observers expect them to have greater resources for identifying valuable practices and thus to make more profitable adoption decisions.

name: Adoption of ISO 9000
definition: Certification with the ISO 9000 quality management standard, which allows organizations credibly to communicate to their customers attributes of their quality management system and to ascertain that organizations have adopted a set of standardized practices for quality management.

name: Local adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption in the focal organization's locale", "local adopters", "Adopter in MSA", "Number Adopters in MSA"]
definition: Adoption of the same practice by organizations located in spatial proximity to the focal organization; local adopters can provide detailed information about the circumstance and the rationale of adoption, thereby enabling observers to assess the value of adoption for their own organization.

name: Corporate size
authors_terms: ["Corporate Size", "size of the corporation to which the focal organization belongs", "corporate information-gathering resources"]
definition: The size of the corporation to which the focal organization belongs; organizational size provides a suitable proxy for information-gathering ability and activity because size is closely related to investments in specialized knowledge activities.

name: Distinctiveness of complement portfolio
authors_terms: ["Distinctiveness", "distinctiveness", "distinctive positioning", "distinctiveness of a platform's complement portfolio"]
definition: Following previous research on platform competition, we thus focus on positioning at the level of complement portfolios and conceptualize distinctiveness as the degree to which a platform's complement portfolio deviates from the market's average complement portfolio. Low Distinctiveness thus indicates that a platform's MOOC portfolio closely mimics the market's average (i.e., prototypical) MOOC portfolio (in terms of its subject genres) and high Distinctiveness indicates that the MOOC portfolio substantially deviates from the average MOOC portfolio.

name: High-status complementors
definition: High-status complementors represents a platform's share of complementors that exhibits a high organizational status. Affiliation with high-status complementors - that is, complementors that are members of the high-status group in their organizational field - can provide an important source of legitimacy of platforms because it implies a positive legitimacy judgment.

name: User growth
definition: Our subsequent theorizing thus focuses on user growth as a critically important performance outcome in platform markets. Our dependent variable aims to capture each platform's number of users in a given month.

name: Group-level excess control
definition: Excess control is defined as the excessive control rights acquired by controlling shareholders through the use of cross holding and pyramids. At the group level, this is the gap between board control rights and ownership aggregated across the whole business group.

name: Firm-level excess control
definition: This study measured the gap between board control rights and ownership to represent the excess control rights of ultimate controllers at the firm level, with board control rights defined as the percentage of board seats held by the ultimate controllers.

name: Group performance
definition: Performance refers to financial, objective measures; two common profitability ratios were used simultaneously to measure different dimensions of performance, with return on equity as the primary proxy for shareholder wealth at the group level.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance refers to financial, objective measures; return on equity is used as the primary proxy for shareholder wealth and return on assets as the secondary proxy of the overall efficiency of asset allocations of an affiliated firm.

name: Family control of business group
definition: A fundamental aspect of a family-controlled business group is that family members are involved simultaneously in the ownership, control, and management of the grouping, in contrast to other types of business groups where there is separation of these roles.

name: Professional management governance of business group
definition: Business groups that are governed by professional managers, in which control and decision making are largely detached from family-manager ownership, lead to changes in the ways that major and minor shareholders interact.

name: Market share
definition: Market share is the share of the served market accounted for by the business. At the business level, market share, as much as profitability, serves as a key index of performance.

name: Business-level risk
definition: Risk is the chance of injury, damage or loss; in organization research the concept is gauged by the dispersion in the rate of return and is most commonly represented by the variance or standard deviation around a mean level of return. The study uses three measures of business-level risk: ROI variation, share instability and the difference between growth in price and growth in cost.

name: Business-level conduct
definition: Conduct variables describe the product positioning of the business relative to its competitors and the functional areas of marketing, production, research and development and financial management. They are controllable by managers at the business level.

name: Relative product quality
definition: Product quality enhances the reputation and customer loyalty enjoyed by the business, enabling it to better maintain its market shares, price premiums, sales and profitability.

name: Relative product breadth
definition: A broad product line allows for substitution within the product line, enabling businesses to stabilize shares and revenues.

name: Relative price
definition: High prices may indicate pricing umbrellas which will attract challenges by competitors, or they may reflect market power protected by strong entry barriers, weak competitors and bargaining power over buyers.

name: Advertising and promotion
definition: Advertising and promotion enable businesses to differentiate products from competitors; successful differentiation builds customer loyalty and reduces brand switching.

name: Sales force expenses
definition: An active sales force enables a business to maintain close contact with distributors and to provide services or technical assistance to customers, reducing brand switching.

name: New product emphasis
definition: New products stimulate customer interest and enable the firm to protect its share position, but new product introduction is often characterized by substantial investments in working capital and fixed assets.

name: Product research and development
definition: Product R&D supports the generation of new products.

name: Process research and development
definition: Process R&D enables the business to better maintain or achieve production efficiency, resulting in lower costs.

name: Net fixed asset intensity
definition: Capital-intensive processes impose high fixed costs which cannot be deferred during business downturns, but they may support a high volume-high share competitive strategy which enables the business to derive the lowest cost.

name: Forward vertical integration
definition: The degree of forward integration of the business relative to its three largest competitors, which increases the firm's control over sales, distribution and promotion.

name: Backward vertical integration
definition: The degree of backward integration of the business relative to its three largest competitors, which reduces the firm's dependence on suppliers and lowers material and transaction costs in the input markets.

name: Value added
definition: Value added is listed among the manufacturing conduct variables of the business; the study's variable table relates it to total manufacturing and distribution expenses and cost of goods sold.

name: Receivables to revenue
definition: Average receivables net of allowances for bad debt, expressed relative to net revenues; higher levels may represent a strategy of providing customers access to financing.

name: Inventory to revenue
definition: Average finished goods inventory net of reserves for losses, expressed relative to revenues; higher levels may represent a strategy of providing customers quick delivery or may be the outcome of poor management practices.

name: Use of external labor arrangements
authors_terms: ["use of external labor arrangements", "external labor arrangement use", "externalization"]
definition: The dependent variable was defined according to whether a position offered an "explicit or implicit contract for long-term employment"; positions labeled as limited-duration direct hires, as hires from temporary help services, or as contract work hires were categorized as external labor arrangements.

name: Likelihood of repetition
authors_terms: ["likelihood of repetition", "certainty about repetition", "uncertainty concerning the likelihood of repetition"]
definition: If a transaction is a decision to fill a given job opening by using either external labor or employment, a central consideration is how likely a firm is to need a person in that position in the future. Likelihood of repetition entails more than the duration of the relationship; it also relates to the parties' ability to confidently predict the duration of the need.

name: Firm-specific skills
definition: It is the distinction between transferable and firm-specific skills that is critical to the governance decision. Examples of "idiosyncratic" skills include the ability to accommodate to various on-the-job idiosyncracies—equipment, process, and communication idiosyncracies for instance—that only experience can create.

name: Uncertainty of performance
authors_terms: ["uncertainty of performance", "performance that is difficult to assess", "ability to assess performance"]
definition: With respect to employment, "uncertainty is the ease with which the productivity of human assets can be evaluated" (Williamson, 1981: 564). When the performance of the worker is difficult to assess, the firm has an interest in internalizing the transaction within a traditional long-term employment relationship.

name: Core position in the informal knowledge-sharing network
authors_terms: ["core position in the informal intraorganizational knowledge-sharing network", "coreness informal", "core of the informal network", "informal core positions"]
definition: The indicator variable core position in the informal knowledge-sharing network takes a value of 1 if the focal individual is structurally located at the core of the informal knowledge-sharing network and 0 if located in the periphery of that network.

name: Formal core position
authors_terms: ["affiliation with a core organizational unit", "coreness formal", "formal core positions", "affiliation to a core organizational unit", "core laboratories"]
definition: There is a general consensus that a core organizational component is (a) highly interdependent on other organizational units, and (b) highly influential toward the future development of other organizational units. The formal core/periphery structure refers to the core or peripheral position of distinct organizational units - in our case, R&D laboratories.

name: Tie distribution across the core and periphery
definition: We used an E-I index as an indicator of each individual's knowledge-sharing tie distribution across the core and the periphery of the network. This index measures the extent to which an individual's ties span different organizational subgroups.

name: Incremental innovation productivity
authors_terms: ["innovation productivity", "productivity of incremental innovation", "incremental innovations", "number of technological improvements to products"]
definition: Incremental innovations are characterized by relatively minor changes in technology and are 'associated with recombination that consists of combining improved components that are already connected within a technological domain'. We measure innovation productivity as the number of technological improvements to products contributed by each individual in our sample.

name: Generous giving
authors_terms: ["generous giving", "the quantitative aspect of giving", "charitable giving"]
definition: Corporate philanthropy programs characterized by the amount of giving, where some firms stand out by donating considerably large amounts to charitable causes.

name: Innovative giving
authors_terms: ["innovative giving", "the qualitative aspect of giving", "innovativeness of their giving activities"]
definition: Corporate philanthropy programs that are carefully designed to be more innovative and aimed at promoting self-sufficiency among the recipients, associated with considerable effort and/or positive long-term social impacts on the recipients.

name: Firm value
definition: The firm's share price, which represents the present value of expected net future benefits and costs.

name: Sin firm
authors_terms: ["sin firms", "firms providing sinful products or services", "triumvirate of sin"]
definition: Firms whose products or services are collectively known as the 'triumvirate of sin,' i.e., alcohol, tobacco, and gaming.

name: Firm life-cycle stage
definition: The life-cycle stage that the firm is in, which serves as an information cue facilitating stakeholder assessment of firm sincerity when engaging in corporate philanthropy programs; classified into Growth, Mature and Shakeout stages.

name: Previous sale price relative to round number
authors_terms: ["previous sales prices that straddle round numbers", "previous sale price being above a $10,000 threshold", "position of previous sales prices relative to round number reference points"]
definition: Instead of comparing round prices with precise prices, we examine whether discontinuities can arise because round numbers influence perceptions of value in meaningful ways, such that previous prices that fall just below round number reference points yield disproportionately lower subsequent valuations than numbers that are at or above the threshold.

name: Listing price
authors_terms: ["original list price", "initial listing price", "estimated listing price", "estimated list prices"]
definition: The original list price is set by the seller and listing agent. After setting the original list price, home sellers and listing agents may adjust the price upward or downward depending on consumer interest in the home.

name: Sales price
definition: The final sales price reflects the agreed-on final sales price by home buyers and sellers, although additional concessions can be made through closing costs to homebuyers by sellers, which are not reflected in the final sales price.

name: Listing agent experience
definition: The experience level of the agent listing the home; the authors reason that experienced agents' exposure to many properties and anchors could diminish the influence of any one particular anchor on judgments of value, and that listing agent experience is likely to be helpful in setting the initial listing price.

name: Buyer agent experience
definition: The experience level of the agent representing the buyer; exposure to more anchors and more developed pricing processes may lead experienced listing and buyer agents to move more off of anchors established by counterparts' offers within the negotiation.

name: Perceived likelihood of high-quality attributes
authors_terms: ["likelihood that characteristics would be present", "perceived likelihood of high-quality attributes in housing"]
definition: Participants indicated how likely they thought it was that each of seven listed characteristics would be present at houses at a new price point, using sliding scales.

name: Used car market experience
authors_terms: ["familiarity with used car prices", "number of cars purchased", "number of cars sold"]
definition: Participants' reported familiarity with used car prices and the numbers of cars they had purchased and sold; the authors expected that people who purchased or sold cars somewhat frequently would be less susceptible to the anchoring effect than people who did not.

name: General alliance experience
definition: Allying across a portfolio of partners leads to general alliance experience obtained from the breadth of a firm's alliance activity. More broadly, general alliance experience reflected the breadth of a firm's knowledge search when it attempted to improve alliance performance.

name: Partner-specific alliance experience
definition: A portion of the knowledge and skills that accumulate from repeated allying over time may also be partner-specific; it is learning to manage alliances by accumulating experience within a dyadic relationship, through recurring alliances with a single partner.

name: Joint R&D project performance
authors_terms: ["project success", "joint R&D project success", "alliance performance", "collaborative R&D project performance"]
definition: We considered a collaborative drug development project successful if its product completed the regulatory drug approval processes imposed by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and/or by the European Medicines Evaluation Agency (EMEA) and subsequently received endorsement for sale. The dependent variable, project success, was binary, with 1 indicating successful completion of a new drug development project resulting in an FDA- and/or EMEA-approved, marketable new drug.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Defining specificity as 'the loss of value of a firm asset when it is used by outsiders', we can consider 'complementary' or 'cospecialized' assets as synonymous with 'specific' assets to the extent that the former concepts reflect gains of value when assets are owned and deployed by a single and distinctive decision unit.

name: Resource opacity
definition: An opaque asset is one that, due to its nature or to the firm's actions, eludes its imitation by impeding the leakage of any related information to outsiders.

name: Financial leverage
definition: We have considered two traditional measures of financial leverage. LEVB is the ratio of the book value of total debt with explicit cost-long-term and short-term debt-to the book value of total debt plus the book value of total equity (Titman and Wessels, 1988). LEVM is the analogous ratio when using the market value of total equity (Balakrishnan and Fox, 1993).

name: Internalization of strategic resource accumulation
authors_terms: ["internalization level", "internalization of the accumulation process", "internal accumulation", "vertical integration"]
definition: Thus, it is reasonable to infer that internal accumulation of strategic resources reflects higher levels of specific investment than subcontracted activities or external acquisition.

name: Business planning document submission
authors_terms: ["planning documents", "business plans", "executive summaries", "private placement memoranda", "D DOCS", "BUS PLAN", "EXEC SUM"]
definition: Communications about planning activities are encoded in objects such as business plans, executive summaries, and similar types of documents.

name: Planning document completeness
authors_terms: ["plan completeness", "structural conformity", "conformity to document conventions", "PLAN COMPLETE"]
definition: The authors identified whether any of eight elements or their equivalents were in the plan: a description of the product/process, a description of the target market/industry analysis, the value proposition, the firm's competitive advantage, the business stage, a description of the team, the marketing plan, financials and the revenue model.

name: Prior equity funding disclosure
authors_terms: ["prior non-VC external private equity funding", "reporting prior equity funding", "D ANGEL"]
definition: Knowing that a third party has vetted a particular funding request and deemed it worthy of investment is a potential cue.

name: Prior equity funding amount
authors_terms: ["amounts of funding", "amount of private equity", "ANGEL AMOUNT"]
definition: Conditional on funding, a higher amount of funding would represent a stronger endorsement.

name: Financing request articulation
authors_terms: ["articulate financing requests", "inclusion of the requested funding amount", "D AMOUNT REQ"]
definition: Ventures associated with planning documents and related communications that articulate financing requests are more likely to receive VC funding.

name: Financing amount requested
definition: The amount requested was extracted either from the planning documents or from communications between the focal venture capitalist and the requesting firm.

name: Management team information disclosure
authors_terms: ["reference team information", "inclusion of team information", "D MGMT TEAM"]
definition: Ventures associated with business planning documents that reference team information are more likely to receive funding.

name: Management team size
definition: The total number of named executives listed in the business planning documents, excluding individuals associated solely with the board of directors or other advisory roles.

name: Team role specialization
definition: The number of management team members divided by the number of roles filled; a low number indicates less specialization.

name: Organizational completeness
definition: The number of managerial roles reported in the planning documents out of 17; a higher score reflects higher team completeness.

name: Educational human capital disclosure
authors_terms: ["prior educational human capital attainment", "including information about educational attainment", "D EDU"]
definition: Ventures associated with business planning documents that refer to prior educational human capital attainment are more likely to receive VC funding.

name: Advanced degrees
authors_terms: ["advanced degrees", "level of attainment", "D BACH", "D MBA", "D MASTTECH"]
definition: Conditional on reporting educational attainment, plans with team members who report advanced degrees are more likely to receive VC funding.

name: Entrepreneurial experience disclosure
authors_terms: ["prior entrepreneurial experience", "including information on start-up experience", "D ENTREP EXP"]
definition: Ventures associated with business planning documents that refer to the prior entrepreneurial experience of founding team members are more likely to receive funding.

name: Prior entrepreneurial experience
definition: ENTREP EXP was calculated as the total number of past claimed start-up experiences.

name: Professional experience disclosure
authors_terms: ["prior professional business experience", "including information about prior work experience", "D PRIOR COS"]
definition: Ventures associated with business planning documents that refer to the prior professional business experience of founding team members are more likely to receive funding.

name: Prior professional experience
authors_terms: ["prior professional business experience", "number of prior companies", "NB PRIOR COS"]
definition: The authors coded the total reported number of companies at which management team members worked prior to the venture described in the request.

name: Entrepreneurial prominence
definition: ENTREP PROMINENCE is measured as the relative frequency that a former employer appears in the dataset.

name: Venture capital funding acquisition
authors_terms: ["VC funding", "VC acquisition", "acquisition of desired funding", "funding outcomes"]
definition: The authors used archival methods to establish whether or not the venture succeeded in raising the funds sought in the solicitation.

name: Reported earnings relative to consensus forecasts
authors_terms: ["low reported earnings", "negative earnings surprise", "(Low) reported corporate earnings vs. forecasts", "reported corporate earnings that are low relative to consensus forecasts"]
definition: A firm's reported earnings are typically measured against the earnings that were forecasted by security analysts. When reported earnings are below analysts' consensus forecast (routinely measured as the median forecast), it is deemed a 'negative earnings surprise'.

name: CEO ingratiation toward journalists
definition: Ingratiation is comprised of assertive social influence tactics that enable individuals to gain favor with another person, and includes three types of ingratiatory behavior: flattery or 'other enhancement', opinion conformity, and favor rendering.

name: Negativity of journalist reporting
authors_terms: ["negative reporting", "negative journalist reports", "negative statements about the firm", "negativity of journalist reports"]
definition: Journalist statements referring to a company or CEO in the sample are coded as positive, negative, or neutral, and each negative statement is coded as (i) firm performance, (ii) the firm's leadership, including the CEO, or (iii) the firm's strategy.

name: Journalist's access to the CEO
authors_terms: ["journalist's ability to communicate with the CEO", "ability to communicate with the CEO", "communication access"]
definition: Losing direct communication with the CEO is likely to be aversive to most journalists and would constitute a meaningful form of retaliation in response to negative journalist coverage; journalists rely on communication with executives to obtain information and quotations for their stories.

name: Awareness of others' loss of CEO access
authors_terms: ["awareness of another journalist's inability to communicate with the CEO", "awareness of others' inability to communicate with the CEO"]
definition: A survey scale assesses whether journalists were aware of an instance in which another journalist had lost the ability to communicate with a CEO after issuing negative statements about the CEO's firm.

name: Accumulated own failures
authors_terms: ["one's own accumulated failures", "individuals' own accumulated failures", "surgeon's own accumulated failures", "own failures", "failures"]
definition: Failures have been defined as undesired performance outcomes that deviate from expected organizational goals. Following the literature on learning from failures, we measured surgeon's own accumulated failures in a focal hospital as the number of patient deaths experienced by a surgeon in a focal hospital up to period t.

name: Individual learning from failures
