definition: Failure learning has been defined as 'the process by which individuals, groups, or organizations identify error or failure events, analyze such events to find their causes, and search for and implement solutions to prevent similar errors or failures in the future'. Following prior literature, we measured learning from failures as an increase in a surgeon's performance in the period after experiencing patient deaths.

name: Perceived ability to learn
authors_terms: ["perceived ability to learn", "perceived abilities to learn", "higher perceived abilities to learn", "ability to learn"]
definition: The ability to learn is an individual's capacity to understand causes of failures and to find/implement solutions to prevent future failures. Individuals with higher perceived abilities to learn are those who regard themselves to be better than others at understanding the causes of their own failures and finding and implementing solutions to prevent them in the future.

name: Departmental power
definition: The power associated with organizational subunits. Because departmental power is not directly observable, it must be inferred from measurable power determinants and consequences.

name: Position power
definition: The legitimate authority vested in an employee solely because of the position held in an organization's hierarchy.

name: Favorable job evaluation outcomes
authors_terms: ["favorable job evaluation outcomes", "job evaluation outcomes", "job evaluation successes"]
definition: The resources a department obtains through job evaluation: the number of its new positions and position upgrades that were authorized at the requested pay grade levels. The dependent variables reflect the total number of a department's yearly successes in the official job evaluation process.

name: Visibility
definition: Visibility attracts the attention of the public, regulatory bodies, and the media as well as interest groups and thus leads to a greater burden of accountability and institutional conformity expectations, making organizations more susceptible to environmental and interest group pressures.

name: Vulnerability to interest group pressure
definition: Vulnerability to pressures varies to the degree with which an organization's operations expose it to negative attention or make it appear culpable or complicit in a disfavored activity, and such vulnerability also makes organizations more prone to disruption of resource flows.

name: Dynamic capability
definition: Some capabilities, called dynamic capabilities, enable firms to more efficiently alter their resource configurations when faced with unexpected environmental pressures; they center on skills and information and involve new or innovative means of competing and/or dealing with environmental disruptions.

name: Nondynamic capability
definition: Such nondynamic capabilities involve the procedures, routines, systems, and management techniques used by an organization and enable it to operate effectively in environments that are predictable and relatively stable.

name: Urgency
definition: The urgency assessment is the perceived cost of nonresponse to an issue; the higher the level of urgency, the more important it is for the organization to respond quickly and decisively.

name: Manageability
definition: The manageability assessment concerns whether or not the firm possesses the means needed to effectively respond to a specific set of pressures; it reflects the degree of optimism, positive valence, and confidence that decision makers have with regard to a particular set of circumstances.

name: Accommodation to interest group pressure
definition: The extent to which a firm accommodates the wishes of secondary stakeholders such as special interest groups; higher scores represented greater accommodation and acquiescence, which can range from total defiance to complete accommodation.

name: Strategic consensus
authors_terms: ["strategic consensus", "TMT consensus", "consensus on organizational goals", "consensus on means", "TMT agreement"]
definition: Agreement among an organization's top managers around strategic directions. The authors measure it as TMT consensus on organizational goals and consensus on means, with low strategic consensus reflecting differing TMT views as to preferable rather than actual objectives and strategies.

name: Demographic homogeneity
definition: The degree to which the members of a top management team are demographically similar. The authors developed an aggregate measure of demographic homogeneity based on Blau's index of heterogeneity across 12 demographic variables, subtracted from a positive constant.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: The extent to which a firm's industry environment is dynamic rather than stable, posited to moderate the relationship between TMT consensus and firm-level performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm-level performance, assessed in this study through TMT members' subjective, self-report assessments because outside, objective measures were largely unavailable.

name: Interdependence
definition: Interdependence is a central concept in the theory of organization design and refers to the property that says that the value of performing one activity depends on how another activity is performed. In technology acquisitions, the activities underlying the technological capabilities of the target and acquirer are highly interdependent when they cannot be used in combination without significant adjustments being made to one or both.

name: Structural integration
definition: Structural integration (distinct from postmerger integration in general) refers to the combination of formerly distinct organizational units into the same organizational unit following an acquisition. It results in the location within common organizational boundaries of related activities originating in the target and acquiring firms, the alternative being structural separation.

name: Common ground
definition: Common ground is knowledge that is shared and known to be shared. Clark defines common ground between two people as 'the sum of their mutual, common or joint knowledge, beliefs and suppositions'.

name: Product line exception adoption
authors_terms: ["product line exception", "PLE", "adoption of the product line exception"]
definition: Under the PLE, a successor continuing to market a product line previously sold by the predecessor would be liable for tort-based product defect claims (for instance, personal injury) arising from products and services related to that product line sold by the seller before the acquisition. Courts in several states expanded the traditional exceptions to the successor non-liability doctrine by adopting the PLE.

name: Acquisition
definition: We define an establishment as being acquired (Acquired) when the firm identifier of an establishment in the current year is different from that in the preceding year. Selling the business as a continuing operation to a potential buyer is one of the two main ways for sellers to exit a business.

name: Closure
definition: We define an establishment closure dummy (Closed) in a given year as 1 when the establishment identifier exists in the current year but does not appear in any future year, and 0 otherwise. Closing a business is done by disposing of its assets.

name: Entry
definition: We compute the entry rate by dividing the number of new establishments for each state-industry-year cell by the total number of establishments for that cell in the previous period.

name: Certification
definition: We define certification as a process in which a central institutional actor with authority or status formally acknowledges that a venture meets a particular standard. In this setting certification is a commission certification from FERC, which acknowledged through a letter on official FERC letterhead that the planned generator was congruent with PURPA regulations.

name: Operational start-up
authors_terms: ["operational start-up", "from plan to plant", "transition from planned venture to operational start-up", "reaching operational start-up"]
definition: The transition from planned venture to operational start-up, in which a venture assembles the human and physical resources necessary to begin operations; operational start-up requires both human and physical investment and infrastructure.

name: Sector legitimacy
authors_terms: ["sector legitimacy", "legitimacy of a new sector", "legitimacy of an organizational form", "sector-level legitimating processes", "institutional legitimating processes"]
definition: The legitimacy of an organizational form or sector as a whole, which comprises cognitive legitimacy, or the degree to which knowledge about an organizational form is widespread, and sociopolitical legitimacy, which refers to the extent to which key stakeholders, opinion leaders, government officials, and the general public accept a new organizational form as appropriate and right.

name: Legal endorsement of a sector
authors_terms: ["legal endorsement", "Supreme Court ruling", "legal sanctioning", "legal standing", "regulative legitimacy"]
definition: Legitimacy that flows directly from the legal system: legitimate organizations are those established by and operating in accordance with legal or quasi-legal requirements. In this context legal endorsement is the resolution of the legal uncertainty surrounding a new sector.

name: Positive media coverage
definition: Positive evaluations of a new sector serve as evidence of the sector's viability and thus reduce perceptions of sector risk; positive articles emphasized opportunities and growth within the new sector.

name: Negative media coverage
definition: Popular media that criticize the new sector or highlight its risks and the negative experiences of current entrepreneurs in that sector will reduce the ability of subsequent entrepreneurs to acquire the resources necessary to reach operational start-up; negative articles focused on the problems associated with the sector.

name: Recent sector operational start-ups
authors_terms: ["recent operational start-ups", "recent operational startups", "number of visible start-ups", "recent transitions to operational start-up"]
definition: Recent organizational successes in a sector that increase both the cognitive and sociopolitical legitimacy of the sector; the authors argue that recent start-ups are likely to have a bigger impact than those established many years prior.

name: Recent unsuccessful ventures
authors_terms: ["recent unsuccessful ventures", "recent unsuccessful entrepreneurial activity", "unsuccessful ventures", "failures to start up"]
definition: When entrepreneurs in a sector declare their intention to commence operations but fail to do so, they hurt the credibility of the sector as a whole; failures to start up signal problems with technology, labor, and capital, thereby raising skepticism at large.

name: Venture capitalist backing
authors_terms: ["venture capitalist backing", "VC backing", "venture financing", "backed by a VC"]
definition: The presence of venture capital financing prior to the IPO. VCs are a very powerful governance mechanism since they are (1) risk-seeking, (2) actively participate in and monitor management and strategy setting, and (3) have a significant amount of experience in risk-taking.

name: Top management team stock ownership
authors_terms: ["top management team stock ownership", "TMT stock ownership", "ownership by top managers", "TMT ownership prior to IPO"]
definition: Direct stock ownership by members of the top management team, which aligns the interests of agents and principals by offering contractual rewards to management for increases in shareholder wealth and is held to increase managerial risk-taking.

name: Firm internationalization
definition: The degree to which a high-technology IPO firm is willing to accept the risk associated with international sales, that is, the risks inherent in maintaining and increasing a high-tech IPO firm's international presence. It is measured as the ratio of foreign sales to total sales.

name: Top management team international experience
authors_terms: ["TMT international experience", "TMT international work experience", "TMT international education", "members of the TMT have international experience"]
definition: The prior experience of top management team members with international markets, captured as the number of TMT members with international work experience and international education. Experience can make an activity appear more reasonable by reducing an individual's subjective perceptions of the risks involved.

name: Outside board member international experience
authors_terms: ["board international experience", "outside board members have international experience", "board international work experience", "board international education"]
definition: The international experience of nonexecutive board members, which may serve as a substitute for TMT international experience and allows the board to be more adamant in encouraging international risk-taking by the TMT and to more effectively monitor such risk-taking.

name: Venture capitalist board member international experience
authors_terms: ["venture capitalist board member international experience", "the venture capitalist is represented by a board member with international experience", "VC director international experience"]
definition: Having a venture capitalist represented on the board by an appointee who possesses prior international work or education experience, so that the VC can judge the success or failure of similar scenarios and keep the venture from making professional mistakes.

name: Affiliated directors on compensation committee
authors_terms: ["affiliated directors", "proportion of affiliated directors on a compensation committee", "captured directors"]
definition: Nonmanagement directors who maintained some form of personal and/or professional relationship with a firm, its subsidiaries, or its management (SEC regulation 14A, item 6b). Nonmanagement directors with such relationships may be more likely to be subject to managerial influence.

name: Interdependent directors on compensation committee
authors_terms: ["interdependent directors", "proportion of interdependent directors on a compensation committee", "board interdependence"]
definition: Nonmanagement directors who had been appointed during the tenure of a focal firm's incumbent CEO.

name: CEO directors on compensation committee
authors_terms: ["CEO directors", "proportion of CEOs on a compensation committee", "the proportion of CEOs serving on a compensation committee"]
definition: The CEOs of other firms serving on a focal firm's compensation committee, excluding the focal firm's own CEO; corporate CEOs tend to be a relatively homogeneous, cohesive collection of individuals who may support peer CEOs in board decisions.

name: CEO compensation level
authors_terms: ["absolute level of CEO compensation", "absolute pay levels", "absolute pay measures"]
definition: The absolute level of CEO compensation. Three measures of CEO compensation were included in these analyses: noncontingent pay (salary and other annual cash compensation), contingent pay (stock options, bonuses, and long-term incentive plans), and the combination of noncontingent and contingent pay (total pay).

name: Change in CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["change in CEO compensation", "change in compensation", "change measures"]
definition: The change in compensation from one year to the next; models relying on change in compensation rely on the difference in the logarithmic values for the two years involved.

name: Compensation contingency
authors_terms: ["pay mix", "compensation contingency", "ratio of contingent to total pay", "noncontingent, as compared to contingent, CEO compensation"]
definition: The mix of contingent and noncontingent compensation in the CEO's package: compensation containing a high proportion of salary and other cash compensation (noncontingent pay) is much less risky for managers than compensation containing a high proportion of bonuses and long-term incentives, or contingent pay.

name: New bank founding rate
authors_terms: ["local founding rate", "founding rate of new banks", "number of foundings per community-year", "new bank foundings"]
definition: The rate at which new banks are created in a community, modeled as an event count of the number of foundings per community-year.

name: Bank acquisitions in a community
authors_terms: ["acquisitions in MSA", "acquisition activity", "local banks are acquired"]
definition: Recent bank acquisition activity in a community; the total number of acquisitions in an MSA is divided into acquisitions by local firms and acquisitions by out-of-town firms.

name: Acquisitions by local banks
authors_terms: ["acquisitions in MSA by local banks", "acquisitions by other local firms"]
definition: Acquisitions in a community made by firms local to that community, which would likely adhere to the same community logic as the firms they were acquiring.

name: Acquisitions by out-of-town banks
authors_terms: ["acquisitions in MSA by out-of-town banks", "acquisitions by out-of-town firms", "acquisitions by outsider banks"]
definition: Acquisitions in a community made by firms from outside that community, firms that represent a more national logic of geographic diversification.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["market concentration of a local community", "four-firm concentration ratio"]
definition: The concentration of a local banking market, measured as the percentage of bank deposits in each MSA held by the four largest firms in the MSA.

name: Presence of generalist banks
definition: The presence in a community of banks engaged in substantial efforts in the major banking businesses of retail, commercial, and real estate, which are able to leverage greater market reach and profits.

name: Bank professionals
authors_terms: ["number of bank professionals", "local bank professionals", "banking professionals"]
definition: Banking professionals, an elite subset of whom are the executives that create new banks, whose human and relational capital is portable and enables mobility and the creation of organizational alternatives.

name: Combined network centrality
definition: The joint embeddedness of the two firms in a dyad, captured by the centrality of each firm in the network formed by prior alliances. Higher centrality scores correspond to higher levels of embeddedness.

name: Network centrality asymmetry
authors_terms: ["dyad asymmetry", "centrality asymmetry", "socially asymmetric dyad", "asymmetry in the network centrality", "social asymmetry"]
definition: Asymmetry in structural position between two firms, which is likely to translate into asymmetry in negotiating power when they form an alliance.

name: Minority ownership position
authors_terms: ["minority ownership position", "minority position", "minority ownership", "acceptance of a minority position"]
definition: The holding of a minority equity share, that is, less than half of the equity, in a joint venture with a more central partner. Poorly embedded firms will often offer favorable terms of trade to entice central allies into an exchange relation.

name: Majority ownership position in joint ventures
authors_terms: ["majority ownership", "majority ownership position", "control structure of the alliance"]
definition: The holding of a majority ownership position in a joint venture, by which a firm is able to influence the activities of the alliance and to protect itself from the hazards inherent in interfirm collaboration.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "formation of an alliance", "formation of a technology-related alliance", "formation of interorganizational ties"]
definition: The formation of an alliance between two firms in a given year; the unit of analysis is the dyad.

name: Overconfidence
definition: Overplacement, the type of overconfidence on which we focus in this paper, is a relative assessment bias. It refers to an erroneous belief in one's performance or abilities compared with a reference group.

name: Market entry
definition: The decision to enter a competitive game or market, proxied in the experiment by the willingness to enter (willingness to bet). The indifference value elicited through a bisection method is called the 'willingness to bet' (WTB): for any fixed amount offered higher than the WTB, the participant would prefer to take the amount and not enter the game.

name: Attitude toward ambiguity
authors_terms: ["attitude toward ambiguity", "ambiguity attitude", "ambiguity seeking", "positive attitude toward ambiguity"]
definition: Attitude toward ambiguity (or ambiguity attitude) denotes a positive, negative, or neutral preference for unknown (compared with known) distributions over events. It captures the difference between behavior under unknown probabilities and behavior under known probabilities (risk).

name: Source of ambiguity
authors_terms: ["source of ambiguity", "internal source of ambiguity", "skill-based games", "chance-based games"]
definition: Chance-based games refer to risky gambles in which the outcomes depend on realizations of the world that are independent from the actions or the skills of the focal individual. By contrast, skill-based games are settings in which outcomes are based on factors that remain (at least partially) under the control and are believed to be affected by actions of the focal individual or firm.

name: Collective enterprise presence
authors_terms: ["collective enterprises", "collectively owned bicycle manufacturers", "Collective bicycle manufacturers", "presence of collective enterprises"]
definition: Collective enterprises were officially public organizations, under the control of the state, and research has characterized collective enterprises as an intermediate entity between private and state enterprises.

name: State enterprise presence
authors_terms: ["state enterprises", "state-owned bicycle manufacturers", "State bicycle manufacturers", "presence of state enterprises"]
definition: Of the three types of organizations, state enterprises were by far the largest; their scale and their institutional proximity to the locus of regulation also made them the most overwhelmingly bureaucratic type of organization in Chinese society.

name: Private enterprise presence
authors_terms: ["private enterprises", "Private bicycle manufacturers", "presence of private enterprises"]
definition: Private enterprises were entirely independent from the government and were also overwhelmingly the smallest and least bureaucratic of the three types of organizations during the economic transition.

name: Private startup founding rate
authors_terms: ["local founding rates of private startups", "likelihood of a private bicycle manufacturer being founded", "local entrepreneurial founding rates", "founding rates of private entrepreneurs"]
definition: Each cell represents an area at risk of a founding event occurring, and the analysis models the likelihood of a private bicycle manufacturer being founded in a given cell-month.

name: Startup size
definition: In our founding rate analysis, we split private startups into large, medium, and small sizes based on terciles of registered capital. For the purposes of entering entrepreneurship on a smaller scale, such as self-employment, managerial experience becomes less important.

name: Distant recombination
authors_terms: ["distant recombination", "distant recombination of domain knowledge", "distant recombination of knowledge", "cross-domain exploration"]
definition: Distant recombination is the integration of knowledge from outside the focal domain of an innovation. Given this definition, distant recombination can be viewed as a cross-domain connection that incorporates knowledge from a source domain into the focal domain.

name: Local recombination
authors_terms: ["local recombination", "local recombination of domain knowledge", "within-domain exploitation"]
definition: Local recombination is recombination occurring within the focal domain. Conceptually, local citations correspond to within-domain exploitation, whereas distant citations reflect cross-domain exploration.

name: Market valuation of firm patents
authors_terms: ["Market valuation", "market valuation of firm patents", "market valuations of firm inventions"]
definition: The market valuation of firm patents is the logged value of the market-based measure developed by Kogan et al. (2017), derived from an event study analyzing abnormal stock returns over a three-day window following patent grant announcements. Essentially, it quantifies the short-term financial return following the patent grant announcement.

name: Domain insularity
authors_terms: ["domain insularity", "insularity of a focal domain", "insular domains"]
definition: Because of their distinct historical trajectories and subject matters, some domains rarely incorporate knowledge from other domains and are thus more 'insular' than others. Domain insularity is the proportion of within-class backward citations of all the patents in a class over the previous five years.

name: Domain generality
authors_terms: ["domain generality", "generality of patent class", "general domains", "specific domains"]
definition: Knowledge from some source domains has been integrated across a wide range of technologies, whereas the applications of other domains are more specific and concentrated in a small number of areas. To capture the extent to which a domain may add value across a wide range of areas, the authors extended the generality measure proposed by Trajtenberg et al. (1997) to the domain level.

name: Inter-domain connection strength
authors_terms: ["connection strength", "inter-domain connectivity", "strongly connected domains", "weakly connected domains"]
definition: Some domain pairs have been connected more frequently through prior recombinations than others, resulting in varying degrees of inter-domain connectivity. Connection strength is a Jaccard-coefficient-based measure that quantifies the underlying dependence of a focal domain on a source domain.

name: Technological domain
definition: Technological domains are groups of technological components focused on common subject matters and codified in classification systems, and, more broadly, a subset of knowledge domains. Domains reflect the specialization of knowledge and solutions and serve as the basis of categorization and evaluation.

name: Market resource variation
authors_terms: ["resource variation", "market resource variation", "resource variability", "environmental variation", "amplitude, frequency, and unpredictability of change"]
definition: We focus here on the variation in resources available to firms as a source of uncertainty, with the resource of interest being the demand for the product or service under consideration. We consider the dimensions of amplitude, frequency, and unpredictability of resource variation.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entry", "entry", "investment in a market", "commences facilities-based traffic"]
definition: In this industry we define market entry as the decision to commence IMT service between the United States and a foreign market. Commencing IMT service to a market represents a change in an organization's domain.

name: Firm entry experience
authors_terms: ["firm entry experience", "entry experience", "experience with prior market entries"]
definition: We argue that increasing experience with market entry increases a firm's ability to assess market resource variation in prospective markets. We measure firm entry experience by the count of the number of other markets a firm has previously entered, and we update this count annually.

name: Focal market familiarity
definition: In addition to experience gained through entry to other markets, firms can also make initial forays into a focal market and gain direct experience with that market. This direct involvement, which we call focal market familiarity, increases the information that the firm has about that market and allows the firm to assess the market with more accurate information.

name: Customer experiential diversity
authors_terms: ["experientially diverse customers", "customer diversity in organizational experiences", "diversity in prior organizational experiences", "customers with diverse organizational experiences", "experiential diversity"]
definition: Our first independent variable is the extent to which a dispensary's customers have had prior experience with diverse types of dispensaries in the market, as reflected in their reviewing histories on Weedmaps. A customer is regarded as more diverse in organizational experiences if the firms s/he reviewed were highly dissimilar from one another in terms of the preference dimensions referenced in their self-descriptions at the time of review.

name: Congruence with market preferences
authors_terms: ["congruence with market preferences", "dispensary congruence with market preferences", "congruence between a firm's market-positioning claims and the preferences held by consumers in its market"]
definition: A higher congruence score indicates that a dispensary's self-description mentions dimensions that customers reflect on more in their review text (irrespective of whether customers mention them in positive or negative ways in their reviews).

name: Market preference change
authors_terms: ["rate of change in customer preferences", "changing market preferences", "market preference change", "changing demand landscapes"]
definition: Our next i.v. is the rate of change in customer preferences within a dispensary's geographical market.

name: Organizational survival
authors_terms: ["hazard of survival", "hazard of continued listing", "continued listing on Weedmaps"]
definition: We used a proxy for survival - a dispensary's continued listing on Weedmaps. This is only a rough proxy, since a dispensary could discontinue listing on Weedmaps because it finds the cost of listing to exceed perceived benefits.

name: New customer attraction
authors_terms: ["new customers a dispensary attracts", "monthly count of new customers", "count of new reviewers"]
definition: To measure the new customers a dispensary attracts, we calculated the monthly count of Weedmaps users who post a review of each focal dispensary for the first time.

name: Appeal to new customers
authors_terms: ["appeals to them", "appeal to new customers", "monthly average rating, new customers"]
definition: We measured a dispensary's appeal to new customers based on new customers' numerical rating of each dispensary on a scale of one to five stars.

name: CEO immigrant background
authors_terms: ["immigrant CEO", "CEOs' immigrant background", "appointment of an immigrant CEO", "first-generation immigrant CEO", "immigrant CEO's homeland country"]
definition: CEO immigrant background is a geography-related characteristic reflecting where CEOs originally came from. A first-generation immigrant CEO refers to a CEO who was born in a foreign country and immigrated to the United States later; CEOs who were born in a foreign country but had US citizen parents at birth are not considered immigrants.

name: CSI incidents in the homeland country
authors_terms: ["CSI incidents in the homeland country", "CSI incidents disclosed in the immigrant CEO's homeland country", "corporate social irresponsibility (CSI) incidents"]
definition: CSI incidents are adverse environmental, social, and governance events such as environmental pollution, human rights violations, and governance fraud; unlike CSR information, CSI information is typically created by external stakeholders and distributed in the media. The dependent variable captures the number of a focal firm's adverse ESG incidents publicly disclosed in the homeland country in a given year, weighted by the severity of the incidents.

name: Age at immigration
authors_terms: ["adult immigrant", "immigrated as an adult rather than as a child", "length of residence in their homelands"]
definition: Immigrant CEOs who spent a longer time in their homeland countries and immigrated as adults, rather than as children, tend to have stronger psychological attachment to and social capital in their countries of origin. Length of residence is positively associated with place attachment as it enables individuals to incorporate more place-based memories, preferences, and meanings into their self-identity.

name: Firm sustainability rating
definition: A firm's sustainability rating reflects the extent to which the firm has achieved sustainable development in social and environmental dimensions. Higher ratings give CEOs established knowledge, experience, and resources to prevent irresponsible behaviors and create stronger reputational incentives to avoid CSI.

name: Homeland-country press freedom
definition: A country's press freedom reflects the extent to which local stakeholders can independently express and spread information and perspectives. A free press makes it easier for stakeholders to access relevant information about firms and makes it more difficult for firms to conceal or suppress negative information.

name: Capital market development
definition: We recognize this duality and conceptualize capital market development in terms of both access to capital and quality of governance. Strong governance contributes to environmental pressures on firms and facilitates access to external resources, influencing the incentives and support for firm restructuring.

name: Firm restructuring
definition: Restructuring is the deliberate modification of a firm's strategy, structure, resources, or operations to improve alignment with an altered external or internal environment.

name: Financial restructuring
definition: Financial restructuring refers to changes in a firm's capital structure.

name: Portfolio restructuring
definition: Portfolio restructuring refers to significant changes in a firm's mix of assets or its scope of business.

name: Organizational restructuring
definition: Organizational restructuring refers to changes in structure, ownership, management, and employment.

name: Economic shock
definition: An economic shock is a substantial and unanticipated change in the macroeconomic environment whose impact spreads beyond specific industries to disrupt multiple sectors of an economy simultaneously (Reinhart and Rogoff 2009).

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["group affiliate", "business group affiliation", "business group affiliated firms", "business group membership"]
definition: Business groups comprise legally independent firms linked through a variety of financial and administrative ties, whose affiliates gain from internal resource sharing within the group and from privileged access to external resources.

name: Firm age
definition: The independent variable, age, is measured by calculating the number of years between the firms' founding year and the year of its entry into the generic market. Older firms are argued to be more constrained by their existing knowledge and by inertia than younger firms.

name: Technology similarity
authors_terms: ["technology similarity", "level of match with technology", "match with existing technology", "fit between new entries and prior firm knowledge in technology"]
definition: The level of match with technology, measured as the weighted number of prior products with the same technology as the new entry. A greater number of products using the same technology as the newly chosen product indicates a higher fit between new entries and prior firm knowledge in technology.

name: Market similarity
authors_terms: ["market similarity", "level of match with existing markets", "match with existing markets", "fit between new entries and prior firm knowledge in market"]
definition: The dependent variable, the level of match with existing markets, is measured by the weighted number of prior products in the same therapeutic area as the new entry. A greater number of products using the same market as the newly chosen product indicates a higher fit between new entries and prior firm market knowledge.

name: Managerial reputation
definition: We conceptualize managerial reputation as a perceptual judgment of the manager's overall role performance, as assessed by a specific audience. Our use of the term 'managerial reputation' should be taken to refer to evaluations of the collective management of the firm.

name: Poison pill adoption
definition: The practice we specifically focus on is that of the poison pill, a controversial takeover defense that arose in the mid-1980s in response to a wave of hostile takeovers. A poison pill is intended to make a firm an unattractive takeover target by granting shareholders of a target firm the right to buy shares of the newly formed entity at a deeply discounted price in the event of a hostile takeover not approved by the board.

name: Media coverage
authors_terms: ["media coverage", "media coverage of poison pill", "media visibility"]
definition: Media coverage is important because it can affect whether managers' actions come to the attention of evaluators, as well as the meanings that evaluators attach to those actions.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: The authors consider how the reputational penalty that managers bear for use of a poison pill is affected by their firm's financial performance. Firm performance is measured as profitability, the return on book assets in the relevant year.

name: Prior adoptions
definition: The final contextual factor the authors consider is the extent to which poison pills have been adopted by similar firms. Prior adoptions is the cumulative total of firms in the sample that had adopted a poison pill.

name: Evaluating audience
definition: These groups represent distinct audiences that may interpret the same questionable practice in different ways and apply different reputational penalties. In the empirical study the authors focus on two key evaluating audiences: stock analysts and peer executives.

name: Historical slave trade exposure
authors_terms: ["slave exports", "slave extraction", "log (slave exports / land area)", "historical slave trade", "traumatic shocks"]
definition: The African slave trade is treated as a traumatic historical shock: 'a devastating traumatic shock to hundreds of kingdoms, confederacies, and distinct ethnic groups.' It is measured as country-level slave exports, the logged number of slaves divided by geographic area.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: One of the most important dimensions of ownership structure is its concentration; concentrated ownership comes in many forms, and the most highly concentrated firms have one or a majority owner with a controlling interest.

name: Institutional strength
definition: Formal institutions are codified rules that include constitutions, laws, property rights, and contracts; they establish the ease and efficiency of doing business, with weak and corrupt institutions inhibiting foreign investment and business development both historically and in the modern era.

name: Social capital
definition: Social capital represents how embeddedness within groups and networks benefits individual actors, or facilitates the provision of socially valuable activities through cooperation and individual contribution; it is facilitated by interpersonal trust within groups, networks, and broader society.

name: Manufacturing sector
definition: A sector in which investment capital is crucial for growth and productivity, and where capital investment requirements have grown substantially as technological advances raised the capital equipment to production labor ratio.

name: Quiet giving
authors_terms: ["quiet giving", "strategic silence", "remain silent about their charitable donations", "remain quiet about giving"]
definition: The authors consider quiet giving as a form of strategic silence; firms that engage in giving and issue CSR reports but omit their information on CSR reports are quiet givers. Quiet giving equals one if the firm does not include giving information in its CSR report in a certain year and zero otherwise.

name: Employee mistreatment
authors_terms: ["Mistreatment of employees", "mistreating their employees", "underpaying employees", "underpaid employees"]
definition: A firm gains pragmatic legitimacy among employees by satisfying their basic financial needs, typically through reasonable compensation; employees form pay expectations by comparing their compensation to that of employees at other firms. Mistreatment of employees is measured based on comparisons with other firms in the same industry, where a high value suggests that the firm offers less competitive compensation.

name: Investor mistreatment
definition: A firm achieves pragmatic legitimacy among investors when it provides a return that meets or exceeds investor expectations, and investors generally look at the performance of similar firms to determine their expected returns. Investor mistreatment is measured via industry-level comparison, with a larger value showing that the firm pays below-average dividends among industry peers.

name: Employee long-term orientation
authors_terms: ["employee long-term orientation", "long-term orientation of employees", "R&D expenditures", "R&D expenditure"]
definition: R&D expenditures are often associated with a long-term orientation among firms and their employees because firms are unlikely to obtain payoffs from R&D investments in the immediate future. Employees of high-R&D firms are more willing to sacrifice low pay in the short term for greater payoffs in the long run.

name: Investor long-term orientation
authors_terms: ["investor long-term orientation", "long-term orientation of investors", "institutional shareholding", "institutional investors"]
definition: Investors with long-term orientations are more concerned about preserving equity value in the long run and less concerned about low or no dividend payouts. Institutional investors are known for their long-term orientation, especially compared with small, dispersed investors.

name: Organizational atypicality
definition: Typical hedge funds hold assets and employ trading strategies similar to the average or 'centroid' fund (Litov, Moreton, and Zenger, 2012) in the category to which they claim membership. Atypical funds deviate from that average.

name: Deliberate names
definition: We define deliberate names to be those that explicitly include the moniker of the market category to which the organization claims membership in the organization's name itself.

name: Difficulty of assessing organizational quality
authors_terms: ["quality is more difficult to assess", "uncertainty", "search and information costs", "when quality is ambiguous and information costs are high"]
definition: We further expect that uncertainty, manifested in higher search and information costs, will moderate the association between organizational atypicality and deliberate naming. Like status, identity signals such as deliberate versus nondeliberate names should be more important when quality is ambiguous and information costs are high.

name: Fund growth
definition: We model fund growth using fund size, measured as assets under management, as our dependent variable and lagged fund size as an independent variable. Coefficient estimates on all additional covariates thus amount to predictors of change in fund size.

name: Organizational failure
definition: The paper analyzes the likelihood of fund failure, studied during the recent financial crisis, when the hedge fund industry experienced a significant contraction. By focusing attention on 2008 and 2009, the authors help to ensure that many of the liquidation events present in the data were the result of investor flight as opposed to manager choice or fund performance.

name: Exploitation
definition: At the individual level, exploitation is defined as behavior that optimizes performance in the current task. Exploitation aims at optimizing the performance of a certain task and is associated with high-level engagement, selection, refinement, choice, production, and efficiency.

name: Exploration
definition: Exploration entails disengaging from the current task to enable experimentation, flexibility, discovery, and innovation; in the neuroscientific literature exploration has been defined as the behavior leading to 'disengagement from the current task and the search for alternative behaviors'.

name: Attentional control
authors_terms: ["attentional control", "cognitive and attentional control", "attentional-control regions", "attention control"]
definition: Attentional control is the ability to refocus attention and select actions in relation to internal goals; it refers to a separate, higher level, 'executive' branch of the attentional system that focuses attention on selected aspects of the environment.

name: Reward-related brain activation
authors_terms: ["reward-related brain regions", "mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic circuit", "reward processing", "reward anticipation"]
definition: A circuit involved in the assessment of rewards (gains) and punishments (costs) that lead to behavioral adjustments via reward-based learning; this mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic circuit is formed by the ventral midbrain, ventral striatum, nucleus accumbens and ventro medial prefrontal cortex.

name: Decision-making performance
definition: Decision-making performance is defined as the reward individuals obtain as a consequence of their decision.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence describes the capacity of the environment to support organizations in the marketplace (Dess and Beard, 1984; Yasai-Ardekani, 1989). Munificence, or resource availability, has been operationalized in terms of the industry's growth rate.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration (i.e., power) describes the number and the size distribution of firms competing against each other in an industry. The degree of environmental uncertainty is affected by the extent of realized or potential collusion that results from the number and size distribution of firms in the industry (Scherer, 1980).

name: Technological change
definition: Technological change creates environmental uncertainty, because it redefines competition as technologically superior firms displace firms with outdated technologies (Schumpeter, 1934). Technological shifts in the environment generate uncertainty because they increase firm-level competition as technologically superior firms attempt to displace firms with outmoded technologies.

name: Voluntary export restraints
authors_terms: ["voluntary restraint", "'voluntary restraints'", "voluntary export trade agreement", "trade restraints"]
definition: Threatened with possible trade sanctions by the U.S.A., the Japanese machine tool manufacturers voluntarily agreed to restrict their exports to the U.S.A. beginning in 1986 to avoid trade friction and high tariffs. Such restraints curtailed the ability of Japanese firms to export to U.S. markets, thereby reducing the munificence experienced by firms in the industry.

name: Competitive interdependence
definition: Competitive interdependence highlights the interrelations between the focal organization and its environment. Greater penetration of the domestic market by foreign imports indicates greater interdependence between domestic players and foreign firms from other machine tool exporting countries.

name: Cost efficiency
definition: Cost efficiency measures the degree to which costs incurred per unit of output are low.

name: Asset parsimony
definition: Asset parsimony measures the degree to which assets deployed per unit of output are few.

name: Differentiation
definition: Differentiation measures the degree to which the product and its enhancements are perceived as unique (Porter, 1980).

name: Scale/scope
definition: Scale/scope measures the relative size and range of activities of a business within its industry.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is measured in terms of firm profitability and growth. We employ return on sales (ROS) to assess profitability; we also investigate a growth model, where growth in sales is the dependent variable.

name: Corporate silence
definition: The absence of a corporate statement on a contentious social issue; as the authors put it, silence is intended to convey neutrality: a company that stays silent on a contentious issue is not expressing support for or against an issue. The authors also stress that inaction is harder for stakeholders to notice, assess and respond to than action.

name: Consumer social media engagement
definition: Stakeholder responses measured as social media engagement, which the authors treat as a proxy for customer support. They operationalize two measures of stakeholder response: follower growth and consumer liking.

name: Peer corporate activism
authors_terms: ["peer corporate activism", "peer activism", "rival BLM intensity", "competitors' BLM support"]
definition: The extent to which a focal firm's close competitors take a stand and engage in corporate activism on the social issue. When peers take a stand, silence becomes much more visible and it becomes easier for stakeholders to notice and assess the meaning of silence as a deliberate choice.

name: Market niche
authors_terms: ["market niche", "narrow market niche", "niche market", "mass-market firms", "mass market"]
definition: The breadth of the audience a firm serves: niche market firms appeal to a narrower audience with little overlap with customers of firms practicing mass-market strategies, whereas mass-market companies have more stakeholders watching them. Questionable behavior by narrow-niche companies attracts less attention, enabling them to escape stakeholder oversight.

name: Issue salience
authors_terms: ["issue salience", "salience of a social issue", "highly salient social issue"]
definition: Following Mohliver et al., the salience of a social issue captures both its pervasiveness and its valence, which refers to the number of stakeholders who care about the issue and the intensity of their concern. For highly salient issues stakeholders pay more attention to corporate behavior on the issue and are more likely to expect activism from companies.

name: Shareholder activism
definition: Shareholder activism is characterized by competence-based concerns rooted in market logic and entails well-defined and relatively predictable consequences. Through such activism, shareholders can express dissatisfaction and implement formal interventions aimed at transforming corporate strategy, including approaches to social issue engagement.

name: Social disapproval
definition: Social disapproval is defined as the social constituents' general enmity toward a firm that reflects their intuitive negative perceptions. It is featured by integrity-based concerns, thus leading to negative and diffused social judgment with relatively unpredictable consequences.

name: Materiality of social issue engagement
authors_terms: ["materiality of social issue engagement", "relative emphasis on material social issues over immaterial ones"]
definition: A high materiality of social issue engagement indicates that a firm prioritizes addressing social issues that are integral to the firm's core business operations (i.e., material social issues) and are often aligned with shareholder preferences, as opposed to social issues that are peripheral to its core business operations (i.e., immaterial social issues).

name: IR officer engagement
definition: IR officers are responsible for conveying a firm's vision, strategy, and value proposition to the investment community. They play a crucial role in facilitating communication and promoting transparency, which enhances the firm's reputation and credibility in financial markets; the authors use their attendance at earnings conference calls as an indicator of the level of engagement within firms.

name: Number of social welfare nonprofits
authors_terms: ["number of social welfare nonprofits", "social welfare nonprofits"]
definition: Social welfare nonprofits, as key institutional actors, play a pivotal role in upholding the interests of marginalized groups and addressing a wide range of social issues spanning healthcare, crime, housing, environment, civil rights, and gender equality.

name: SASB standards promulgation
definition: SASB aims to establish standards across various ESG topics that facilitate communication between firms and investors by advocating for firm engagement in social issues identified as financially material. The SASB guidelines were rolled out in a staggered manner across different industries between 2013 and 2016.

name: Board chair heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["board chair effect", "chair effect", "individual heterogeneity among board chairs", "individual differences among board chairs"]
definition: Individual differences among board chairs; the board chair effect is the share of variance in firm performance explained by those differences, which prior U.S. evidence put at 9.2% of variance in firm performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: The outcome whose variance the paper decomposes across year, industry, firm, CEO and board chair effects; following prior research on the CEO effect and board chair effect, the authors use ROA as the measure of firm performance.

name: Latitude of objectives
definition: 'The range of organizational outcomes managers believe they are able to target' (Parker et al., 2019, pp. 15-16); a firm has greater latitude of objectives to the extent that it can choose its objectives from a wider set of stakeholder priorities.

name: Political competition
definition: Supply-side competition is political rivalry between an elected official and a potential replacement that is based on being elected and re-elected. Politicians facing less political competition may be re-elected with relative ease, and consequently, serve multiple terms in office.

name: Ridesharing ban
definition: A city officially or unofficially (but de facto) banned ridesharing platforms, rather than accommodating their entry. Some cities became hostile to ridesharing entry (going so far as to ban them), while other cities accommodated ridesharing platforms.

name: City population
definition: We collect the population size of each city in the year prior to Uber's entry. We expect cities with a larger population to have institutional arrangements that mitigate such asymmetric information and put mayors in check even if they face less political competition, all else being equal.

name: Unemployment rate
authors_terms: ["Unemployment rate", "higher unemployment rate", "local labor market conditions"]
definition: The unemployment rate of each city in the year prior to Uber's entry. The benefit of having ridesharing platforms looms larger in cities with higher unemployment rates because they may help ease local labor market conditions with more - and potentially even better - employment options.

name: Market entry timing
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "timing of market entry", "year in which production began"]
definition: The timing of market entry is the time at which an MNC operation started production in China. The authors categorize entry into three time periods: those that started production prior to 1988; those that started in 1988, 1989 and 1990; and those that started in 1991, 1992 and 1993.

name: Mode of market entry
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "mode of market entry", "entry mode"]
definition: Three modes of entry are common in China: equity joint ventures (EJVs), wholly foreign-owned subsidiaries, and cooperative operations. Cooperative operations refer to arrangements that the local and foreign firms work together on a non-equity basis, such as contract manufacturing.

name: Market focus
authors_terms: ["market focus", "local market focus", "export focus", "export oriented focus"]
definition: Some foreign MNCs may focus on selling their products locally (i.e., local market focus) while others may concentrate on exporting what they produce to outside China (i.e., export oriented focus). A high proportion of sales in China vis-a-vis that of export indicates a local market focus.

name: Location advantages
definition: China has implemented a spectrum of prioritized locations across the country that offer various conveniences and incentives for foreign firms, thus increasing the likelihood that foreign MNCs would be profitable in China.

name: Profitability
definition: The dependent measure is the level of profitability of MNC operations in China. It is an ordinal measure of net profit.

name: Survival of MNC operations
definition: The dependent variable in the second-year analysis is whether the MNC operation continued its business or closed down in 1993.

name: Workplace democracy
authors_terms: ["workplace democracy", "worker cooperative", "democratic firm", "worker cooperative structure", "democratic organization"]
definition: Workplace democracy is defined as an organizational form where ownership and decision rights are widely and evenly distributed among a plurality of workers, and members are socialized to communitarian and collectivist norms. It is a mode of economic organization that widely and evenly distributes ownership and governance rights among workers.

name: Knowledge intensity
authors_terms: ["knowledge intensity", "knowledge intensive industries", "knowledge-intensive sectors", "high knowledge intensity industry"]
definition: Knowledge intensive industries are those in which a greater proportion of economic value is realized through the production of novelty and innovation as opposed to economies of scale, and whose most valuable asset is the novel and specialized knowledge held by knowledge workers. Industries are classified as knowledge intensive when at least one third of their employees hold tertiary degrees.

name: Firm productivity
definition: The market value produced by the firm, which the paper models with a translog production function that accounts for inputs of labor and capital. Value added (VA) is total revenue minus intermediary consumption of firm i in year t.

name: Intrafirm wage inequality
authors_terms: ["intra firm wage inequality", "pay inequality", "intraorganizational wage inequality", "pay dispersion", "wage dispersion"]
definition: The dispersion of pay within the workplace, which prior work consistently finds to be more condensed in democratic firms. Intra firm pay inequality is a key determinant of societal income inequality.

name: Performance below aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below aspiration", "Perf < Asp", "performance decreases below the aspiration level", "performance declines below the aspiration level"]
definition: Perf < Asp captures the difference between performance and aspiration when performance is below aspiration, and 0 otherwise. Firm performance was measured by return on assets, and the aspiration level was a weighted average of historical, social, and group aspiration.

name: Performance above aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance above aspiration", "Perf > Asp", "performance increases above the aspiration level"]
definition: Perf > Asp captures the difference between performance and aspiration when performance is above aspiration, and 0 otherwise. Firm performance was measured by return on assets, and the aspiration level was a weighted average of historical, social, and group aspiration.

name: Political slack
definition: Building on these ideas, we define political slack as a dominant coalition's cumulative payments to the firm's stakeholders that exceed what is necessary to maintain their approval.

name: Family CEO succession
definition: CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories: family succession equals 3 if the incumbent was replaced by a member of the family.

name: Retention of incumbent CEO
authors_terms: ["retention", "retaining the incumbent family CEO", "retaining the incumbent CEO"]
definition: CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories: retention equals 0 if the firm's incumbent CEO was retained in the focal year.

name: Insider professional CEO succession
definition: CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories: insider succession equals 1 if the incumbent was replaced by an insider who was not a member of the controlling family.

name: Outsider professional CEO succession
definition: CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories: outsider succession equals 2 if the incumbent was replaced by a professional, nonfamily manager who did not meet the insider criterion.

name: Transgenerational family CEO succession
definition: Transgenerational family succession indicates that the incoming family CEO was from a younger family generation than the most recent family CEO. To test H5, family succession was divided into transgenerational family succession and other types of family succession.

name: Incumbent CEO origin
authors_terms: ["origin of the incumbent CEOs", "incumbent CEO was an outsider", "incumbent CEO was a family member", "incumbent CEO from family coalition"]
definition: Models are divided by the origin of the incumbent CEOs: columns are the estimation results for observations in which the incumbent CEOs were outsiders, and other columns are the results for observations in which the incumbent CEOs were family members.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: Environmental volatility is defined as the rate and magnitude of change in the business environment (Dess & Beard, 1984; Duncan, 1972).

name: Top management locus of attention
authors_terms: ["locus of attention", "top-manager", "corporate versus plant level", "high-level management"]
definition: Organizational structure determines where attention resides - that is, the locus of attention; since the internal structure of an organization shapes decision-makers' perceptions and expectations, the distribution of attention varies according to hierarchical position.

name: Attention to social aspiration
definition: Coefficient α1 captures a firm's attention to current rival performance; when managers allocate more attention to current external cues, they set future aspirations by weighing social aspirations over self-referent historical aspirations.

name: Attention to prior historical aspiration
definition: Historical aspirations capture the self-referent aspirations influenced only by past internal cues; the attention rule weighs prior historical aspiration (α2) and past performance (1 - α2).

name: Social aspirations
definition: Social aspirations are the performance of others, that is, the current external cues a firm uses in forming its aspiration level; they were computed as the mean waste level across firms in the same industry using the same chemicals that same year.

name: Prior historical aspirations
definition: Prior historical aspirations denote waste levels set as goals for a given chemical in the previous year.

name: Past performance
definition: Past performance represents actual prior-year waste levels for that same chemical.

name: Disclosure of negative organizational outcomes
authors_terms: ["disclosure of negative organizational outcomes", "concealment of negative organizational outcomes", "concealment strategy", "negativity of president's letters", "number of negative words", "percentage of negative words"]
definition: Officers' revelation of negative organizational outcomes in the president's letter contained in the annual report to shareholders. Controlling for the number of words in a letter, the authors considered a letter more negative the more negative words it contained.

name: Financial performance
definition: An organization's financial performance, which provides a rough measure of possible negative outcomes besetting it and which the Securities and Exchange Commission requires officers to disclose in audited financial statements.

name: Change in financial performance
authors_terms: ["change in financial performance", "change in performance", "change in return on assets", "decline in the financial performance of a corporation"]
definition: The change in a corporation's financial performance from one year to the next; high performers in a given year tend to have experienced sharp performance increases in the previous year, low performers, sharp decreases, and average performers, minor changes.

name: Outside directors
definition: Directors who are not corporate officers; they should be more motivated than insiders to limit concealment, though they are probably less able to detect it, by virtue of the fact that they are not themselves managing the corporation and are therefore less knowledgeable about what managers may be concealing.

name: Shareholding by outside directors
authors_terms: ["shareholding by outside directors", "share ownership by outside directors", "percentage of shares held by outsiders"]
definition: The equity stake of directors who are not corporate officers; agency theorists generally assume that giving outside directors an equity stake in a firm aligns their interests with those of other shareholders.

name: Shareholding by top officers
authors_terms: ["shareholding by top officers", "percentage of shares held by officers", "managerial ownership", "equity ownership by officers"]
definition: The proportion of a corporation's shares held by its top officers. Agency theorists are divided over how such ownership motivates officers: the convergence-of-interest hypothesis suggests that making officers shareholders aligns them with other shareholders, whereas the management entrenchment hypothesis suggests that shareholding by officers allows them to dominate a board.

name: Owner control
definition: The 5 percent convention distinguishes owner-controlled firms, in which at least one nonofficer shareholder controls over 5 percent of shares, from management-controlled firms that have no dominant shareholders.

name: Institutional investor ownership
authors_terms: ["proportion of a corporation's total shares held by institutional investors", "percentage of shares held by institutional shareholders", "institutional shareownership"]
definition: The proportion of a corporation's total shares held by institutional investors. Myopic investor theory suggests that institutional fund managers have a short-term focus and high risk aversion and therefore react to the slightest hint of negative organizational outcomes by selling the organization's stock.

name: Institutional investor control
authors_terms: ["institutional investor control", "institutional investor-controlled corporations", "dominant institutional shareholders"]
definition: The presence of at least one institutional shareholder who is not an officer and holds more than 5 percent of an organization's shares.

name: Nondominant institutional investor ownership
authors_terms: ["nondominant institutional shareholders", "percentage of shares held by nondominant institutional investors"]
definition: Nondominant institutional shareholders (those owning less than 5 percent of a company's shares) can move in and out of stocks easily and should behave as myopic investor theory suggests, reacting to the slightest hint of negative outcomes by selling an organization's stocks.

name: Qualified audit opinion
definition: When accountants find that they must discuss nonadherence to accounting standards in certain aspects of a company's financial statements, they issue a 'qualified' opinion; under these circumstances, what the organization reports comes under greater scrutiny by shareholders and other constituents.

name: Subsequent selling of stock by top officers
authors_terms: ["subsequent selling of the corporation's stock by its top officers", "sale of shares by corporate officers", "number of officers selling shares", "value of shares sold by officers"]
definition: Officers who use a communication strategy intentionally, in order to prop up the value of their company's shares, will also tend to sell their shares in the short term, in order to avoid a loss when negative organizational outcomes are disclosed.

name: Venture capital backing
definition: Whether the focal entrepreneurial firm received funding from a venture capitalist during its first 10 years of existence; the indicator assumes a value of 1 when the firm received such funding, and 0 otherwise.

name: Strategic alliance formation
definition: Strategic alliances are tools through which firms access capital, knowledge, new markets, and share risks, and alliance formation is captured by whether the focal firm entered into at least one alliance during the first 10 years since founding.

name: VC prominence
definition: A VC's standing relative to other VCs based on the number of entrepreneurial firms in which it invested over five-year intervals; a VC is coded as prominent if its five-year investment count is greater than the count of the VC sitting at the 75th percentile of the overall distribution during the same period.

name: VC IPO experience
authors_terms: ["IPO experience", "experience with taking firms public", "VCs' IPO experience"]
definition: The number of firms a VC has taken public, coded relative to other VCs: IPO experience is computed if the number of firms taken public is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for that variable.

name: VC industry diversification
definition: The number of three-digit SIC codes in which a VC has invested, computed as an experience if that number is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for the variable.

name: VC geographic diversification
definition: The number of ZIP codes in which a VC has invested, computed as an experience if that number is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for the variable.

name: Elite founders
definition: We define elite individuals as those people with greater human capital, such as intelligence, education, and work experience, and greater social capital, such as connections to resource providers and high-status others.

name: Bankruptcy reform
authors_terms: ["bankruptcy reform", "lenient bankruptcy reform", "lenient bankruptcy regulation", "post reform"]
definition: An institutional change that lowers barriers to failure via more lenient bankruptcy regulation, what we term 'bankruptcy reform'. In Japan, the 2003 reforms made the Japanese bankruptcy process more lenient by both enabling the earlier 2000 reforms to take effect (notably by blocking the power of the courts) and by adding further protections and simplifications to the bankruptcy process.

name: Bankruptcy
definition: An individual's decision to enter bankruptcy can be thought of as the choice between the cost and benefits of operating a marginally performing firm versus the cost and benefits to the best alternative employment minus bankruptcy costs.

name: Firm founding
authors_terms: ["founding", "founding of a venture", "start a firm", "founding firms"]
definition: The decision to start a firm depends on whether the returns to entrepreneurship (i.e., starting a firm) are higher than the returns to wage employment alternatives.

name: New firm growth
definition: We assess venture growth using the compound annual sales growth rate since founding; sales growth is particularly germane to venture performance because it captures how quickly a firm gains traction with customers.

name: Hedge fund investor activism
authors_terms: ["hedge fund activism", "hedge fund investor activism", "activist hedge funds", "post-attack period"]
definition: Activist hedge funds typically take a non-controlling stake in the targeted company and then present their activist demands, hoping to persuade other shareholders or management to back their proposals; such activism is very disruptive for the targeted firm's employees.

name: Departure of valuable employees
authors_terms: ["departure of valuable employees", "departure of key employees", "employee departure", "loss of human capital", "employee stock option cancellations"]
definition: The unwanted loss of human capital in targeted firms, that is, the departure of the firm's most valuable employees, who may proactively leave a firm targeted by hedge fund activists to avoid uncertainty and potential adverse consequences for their jobs and careers.

name: Firm performance
definition: Tobin's q captures the market value of a firm relative to its total assets and directly reflects the value brought to shareholders by hedge fund activists.

name: Market differentiation
authors_terms: ["market differentiation", "differentiation within the social production space", "competitive position", "service niche overlap", "service competition"]
definition: The population-endogenous aspects correspond to market differentiation and overlap among organizations within a particular population.

name: Organizational adaptation
authors_terms: ["adaptation", "adaptive market differentiation", "ability to adapt", "strategic repositioning", "favorable movement"]
definition: Adaptation involves favorable movement initiated by the focal organization itself; the authors define it to be the improvement of an organization's fitness over what it would have been if the organization was structurally inert.

name: Organizational survival
definition: Survival chances refer to the probability that an organization remains in the population; exit events included bankruptcies and acquisitions by other hospitals, but excluded entry into multihospital systems.

name: Organizational change
authors_terms: ["service changes", "changes in core technologies or marketing strategies", "process of organizational change"]
definition: Modifications of core product and service lines, which can occur fairly regularly, without introducing excessive disruption.

name: Population density
definition: Local population densities are calculated with a variable-radius approach which scales market regions based on consumer concentration, and reflect the number of organizations occupying a focal organization's competitive niche.

name: Organizational size
definition: With respect to size, the authors employed the most common measure used in hospital economies-of-scale studies, which has been the number of patient beds.

name: Service portfolio scope
definition: Complexity is held to be tantamount to the scope of an organization's operation, as proxied by the size of its product/service portfolio; when the scope of operations is large the organization is a generalist, and adaptive movement within the social production space is enhanced.

name: Organizational age
definition: While young organizations are thought to be reasonably amenable to change due to a lack of well-defined routines and roles, structural inertia tends to set in with age.

name: For-profit ownership
definition: If we take the tax status of organizations to be an indication of their missions, one might expect for-profits (utilitarian organizations) to be more active in adapting to the requirements of market environments than NPOs (purposive organizations).

name: Seconded employee status
definition: Seconded employees are academics who are at the NSF on loan from their home institutions for a limited period and who are still active researchers; they are a contemporary example of the Simmelian stranger who comes today and stays tomorrow to import new qualities into the group.

name: Interaction with a seconded employee
authors_terms: ["permanent employees who interact with a seconded employee", "Seconded employee in program"]
definition: Permanent employees who interact with a seconded employee are those whose program hosted at least one seconded employee in the year the grant was awarded; secondees are co-located with permanent employees, share knowledge and networks, and are approached as objective and trustworthy confidants.

name: Novelty of selected ideas
definition: Novelty arises from recombining existing knowledge in unprecedented and unconventional ways, so that grants are more novel the more they deviate from existing knowledge.

name: Negative media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage", "negative media sentiment", "negative media attention"]
definition: Because the tone of media coverage provides a signal regarding the quality of the managers and directors currently leading a firm, negative coverage may lead to negative stigma or threaten those individuals' reputations.

name: Star analyst downgrades
authors_terms: ["star analyst downgrades", "star downgrades", "stock downgrades by star analysts"]
definition: Downgrades are a potentially stigmatizing event reflecting a discrete negative change in an analyst's evaluation of a focal firm; downgrades by star analysts will represent a greater threat to directors' reputations relative to those of non-star analysts.

name: Director exit
definition: One manifestation of directors acting to maintain their reputations will be their decisions to leave or remain on a particular board in response to a reputational threat.

name: Director status
definition: Even directors of large corporations vary in terms of their relative standing, or status, and status represents a form of social evaluation that may alter the degree to which a director internalizes a reputational threat.

name: Board chair position
authors_terms: ["board chair position", "chairing the board", "serving as chair of the board", "chairman"]
definition: Whether a director chairs the board; the board chair position is seen as the most influential position on the board.

name: Director tenure
definition: The number of years a director has served on a given board, which may influence how the director responds to negative external attention.

name: Age at international entry
authors_terms: ["age at entry", "age of a firm at first international sales", "age at the point when it first initiates international sales", "time to internationalize"]
definition: The time lag between the founding of a firm and its initiation of international operations, measured as the time in years between a firm's founding and its first international sales.

name: Knowledge intensity
definition: The extent to which a firm depends on the knowledge inherent in its activities and outputs as a source of competitive advantage.

name: Imitability of core technology
authors_terms: ["imitability", "imitability of a high-technology firm's technology", "core technology"]
definition: The ease with which a firm's technology can be learned or replicated by outsiders.

name: International sales growth
authors_terms: ["international sales growth", "growth in international sales", "subsequent international growth"]
definition: Growth in sales revenue derived from exports and from other international operations.

name: Degree of internationalization
authors_terms: ["degree of internationalization", "international sales as a percentage of total sales", "change in degree of internationalization"]
definition: International sales as a percentage of total sales, the most commonly used proxy for the degree of internationalization of a firm; change in it indicates how rapidly a firm internationalizes once the process has been started.

name: Total sales growth
definition: Growth in total sales, examined in order to understand the overall impact of growth in international sales.

name: Structural integration
