definition: Structural integration—as opposed to structural separation—is a fundamental design choice about the structural form of a combined organization; either a target firm is absorbed into the acquirer and loses its distinctive identity as an organizational unit, or it is preserved as a distinct organizational entity within the merged firm. As a formal design choice concerning the grouping of organizational units, structural integration precedes decisions about the use of linking mechanisms between organizational units.

name: Innovation outcomes
authors_terms: ["innovation outcomes", "hazard of new-product introduction", "innovation process performance"]
definition: We measured innovation outcomes as the hazard (instantaneous probability) of an acquirer launching a new product after an acquisition that has incorporated the acquired firm's technology. Since the theoretical antecedents are organizational, the authors focus on innovation process performance—the speed and productivity of product development.

name: Target prior product launch
authors_terms: ["target prior product", "launched products prior to their acquisition", "not yet launched their initial products"]
definition: Whether a target firm had introduced at least one product prior to acquisition. When acquired firms have not yet launched their initial products, they are in a stage that emphasizes exploration.

name: Post-acquisition innovation order
definition: Whether a product introduction is the first innovation after acquisition or a subsequent innovation; the initial innovation after an acquisition defines a new technological paradigm that shapes further innovations.

name: Search depth
definition: Search depth is defined as the degree to which search revisits a firm's prior knowledge. The variable search depth describes accumulation of search experience with the same knowledge elements.

name: Search scope
authors_terms: ["search scope", "search with high scope", "scope of search"]
definition: Search scope is defined as the degree of new knowledge that is explored, that is, the degree to which search entails the exploration of new knowledge.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["new product introduction", "new product innovation", "number of new products"]
definition: In this study, a new product introduction was defined as any change in a product's design. New product innovation is defined as the number of new products a firm introduces.

name: Communication vagueness
definition: Vague language is defined as the use of linguistic means to make communication less precise in meaning and impossible to paraphrase precisely. Vagueness refers to the use of linguistic means to make the meaning of communication nonspecific and imprecise.

name: Market profitability
definition: The desirability of a market to potential entrants, often gauged by its current profitability as a signal of future profits. The authors measured market attractiveness as the average profitability over a firm's portfolio of markets.

name: Prevalence of potential entrants
authors_terms: ["potential entrants", "prevalence of potential entrants", "number of potential entrants"]
definition: Potential entrants refers to rivals who are not yet present in the focal firm's market but have resources similar to those of incumbents. The prevalence of potential entrants captures the number of such rivals well-positioned to enter the market.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entry", "likelihood of entry", "likelihood of market entry"]
definition: Entering a new market is a major strategic decision that involves commitment of significant resources and incurrence of costs that sometimes cannot be recovered. The paper examines the likelihood of entry by potential entrants.

name: Average incumbent size
authors_terms: ["average incumbent size", "average size of incumbent firms"]
definition: The average size of incumbents plays a significant role in determining how much attention potential entrants devote to a market. It is captured by the average of all incumbents' total number of employees, weighted by market share.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["market concentration", "level of concentration in a market", "concentration rate"]
definition: The level of concentration in a targeted market, measured by using the Herfindahl index to calculate the sum of the square of the market shares of incumbent firms in a market.

name: Organizational identification
definition: Organizational identification denotes the extent to which members perceive themselves as subordinate parts of the organization; its emphasis is on the act of classifying oneself as an organizational member, and it can be thought of as a continuous concept ranging from low to high.

name: Subjective certainty
definition: 'Subjective certainty' can be formally defined as the strength of belief in the quality of one's judgments.

name: Attention to environmental stimuli
authors_terms: ["attention", "attention to environmental stimuli", "attention to the environment"]
definition: Attention can be captured by considering the time allocated to processing information from a source, and it involves the allocation of cognitive resources in working memory to incoming schema-inconsistent stimuli.

name: Resistance to environmental pressures
definition: Staying with one's previous choice (rather than changing it in response to a competing group's response) is used as a measure of resistance to environmental pressures, the dependent variable in this research.

name: Normative organizational identity
authors_terms: ["normative identity", "normative organizational identity", "utilitarian identity", "organizational identity content", "identity type"]
definition: Organizational identity content pertains to the central, enduring, and distinct attributes of the organization and can be represented by relevant ideal types, such as a normative and a utilitarian organizational identity. A normative identity underscores traditions, symbols, and values of altruism, and members tend to emphasize the authenticity and expressive value of their outputs.

name: Contract rent
definition: A central component of the economics approach to bribery is short-term financial incentive, referred to as 'rent' in the corruption literature. The rent indicates how large the gap is between the market price and the OFFP price.

name: Bribe payments
definition: The dependent variable, bribe, is the percentage of surcharges paid in contract value; surcharges were illicit payments requested by Iraq in violation of UN sanctions.

name: Ownership structure
definition: In explaining variability associated with managerial incentives to bribe, we focus on types of ownership structures where managers have differing equity stakes: state-owned enterprises (SOEs), privately held, publicly traded, and partially state-owned companies.

name: OECD Anti-Bribery Convention implementation
authors_terms: ["OECD Anti-Bribery Convention", "implementation of the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention"]
definition: We capture the illegality of cross-border bribes in the home country through its implementation of the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. Implementation indicates that it is a criminal offense in the home country to bribe a foreign public official.

name: Judicial system quality
authors_terms: ["legal environment", "quality of judicial systems", "legal origin, common law vs. civil law systems"]
definition: Legal systems are an important part of corruption detection and deterrence. The literature on law and finance indicates that common law legal systems put more weight on court decisions and are associated with more independent judiciaries, more secure property rights, and better contract enforcement than civil law systems.

name: Perceived corruption
authors_terms: ["perceived corruption", "Corruption Perception Index", "CPI", "social norms related to corruption"]
definition: We include 'perceived corruption' using Transparency International's Corruption Perception Index (CPI below) as a summary measure to capture 'social norms related to corruption'. National institutional environments influence corruption.

name: Network density
authors_terms: ["network structure", "ego density", "CBU network density", "density of the CBU network"]
definition: Ego density measures the number of links among the contacts in the network as a proportion of the maximum possible number of connections, not including the links with the ego (actor) who is the focal point of the network.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "level of development of a country's institutional environment", "institutional environment"]
definition: In foreign investments, certainty, stability, and trust are reflected in the institutional environment a firm faces in different country markets. Countries were assessed as having more or less developed institutional environments by creating an institutional development score for each country.

name: Operating margin
definition: Return on sales, or operating margin, has been considered a superior measure of performance in the global business environment because foreign affiliates must focus on ongoing business.

name: Direct profit-generating contacts
authors_terms: ["direct profit-generating (DPG) contacts", "DPG contacts", "network composition", "percentage of DPG contacts"]
definition: We suggest, therefore, that when the performance measurement is the CBU's operating margin, the most important contacts will be direct profit-generating (DPG) contacts such as customers, customer intermediaries, and suppliers.

name: Service customization
definition: Many high-contact services involve customization, which requires operational flexibility to accommodate each customer's unique and changing needs. Customization by its very nature requires frequent changes to the service delivery process.

name: Tacit content and interdependence of tasks
authors_terms: ["task characteristics", "tacit contents of tasks", "analyzability and interdependence", "tacit knowledge"]
definition: The tacit contents of the tasks related to a service offering and their analyzability and interdependence, captured indirectly through five survey variables (Q3-Q7). The authors argue that services involving less analyzable and interdependent tasks that rely on tacit knowledge are more likely to keep back-office activities in-house.

name: Demand volume
definition: The demand volume for the services offered by a process. High volume typically is associated with mature/standard services and multiple available suppliers, and high-volume demand offers the benefits of economies of scale to back-office operations.

name: In-house sourcing of back-office operations
authors_terms: ["in-house sourcing", "in-house back-office operations", "keeping back-office operations in-house", "outsourcing"]
definition: Whether a process maintains its primary back-office activities in-house or relies on an external supplier; respondents were asked whether their primary supplier of information, services, and/or materials is internal or external to the company.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: A corporation's actions intended to benefit society directly and itself indirectly rather than the other way around; a company taking action to benefit the greater good in any way is pursuing CSP.

name: Innovation
definition: As new ideas enter the market, companies that cling to the old are likely to be destroyed, while companies that introduce new ideas to the market may find themselves prospering.

name: Industry differentiation
authors_terms: ["differentiation within an industry", "industry differentiation", "level of differentiation in the industry", "level of differentiation in a firm's industry"]
definition: Some industries lend themselves to higher levels of differentiation than others, and competition in a highly-differentiated industry is unlikely to be price-based and, thus, is likely to be profitable for all concerned.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: The profitability of the firm with respect to the total set of resources, or assets, under its control.

name: Opportunism
definition: Opportunism is behavior by economic agents that involves "self-interest-seeking with guile"; for an organizational advantage to be considered a result of opportunism, "the strategic manipulation of information or misrepresentation of intentions" must have occurred.

name: Dependence on supplier
authors_terms: ["dealer dependence on a primary supplier", "dependence on that supplier", "dependence for critical services"]
definition: Although the degree of dependence on a supplier will vary across dealers, in general dealers' dependence on a major supplier will be substantially higher than the supplier's dependence on any one dealer. The dependence of dealers on their primary suppliers is likely to vary, depending on such factors as the number and availability of alternative suppliers and the internal strengths of a dealer.

name: Supplier control over dealer decisions
authors_terms: ["supplier control over dealer decisions", "control of dealer decisions", "control over decisions", "formalization", "centralization"]
definition: The second aspect of power proposed as related to dealer opportunism is a primary supplier's control over dealers' decisions, which could include those related to broad dealer policies or to daily operations. Suppliers have at least the capacity to exert control over some dealer decisions and thus constrain dealer autonomy, whether through formalization (rules and procedures) or centralization (direct involvement by a supplier's management).

name: Retrenchment
authors_terms: ["retrenchment", "asset retrenchment", "cost retrenchment", "reduction in firm assets and/or costs"]
definition: Retrenchment is defined as a reduction in firm assets and/or costs. Whether a firm was retrenching was determined by evaluating whether the firm reduced assets or costs within three years of its year of steepest performance decline.

name: Absolute financial performance
authors_terms: ["absolute performance", "actual performance", "actual level of financial performance", "ROI"]
definition: The authors argue that the performance gains of retrenching firms may not represent more successful turnaround attempts in terms of the actual level of financial performance attained. They hold that the absolute performance level of retrenching firms during their turnaround attempts is not significantly greater than that of nonretrenching firms.

name: Performance change
definition: The performance gain of a turnaround attempt is measured as the total change or difference in firm performance from the year of the firm's biggest performance drop until the firm either turned around or the industry average turnaround time had passed.

name: Business relatedness
definition: Business relatedness was treated in terms of managerial perceptions, separating business attributes as such from the way these attributes were perceived by individual managers. Each respondent was asked to rate the 16 attributes in terms of degree of relatedness between the two business units that most clearly manifested the main core competence of the firm.

name: High business relatedness
definition: The High relatedness cluster is characterized by significantly high similarities on all variables as confirmed by Sheffe tests, except for the brand variables and market knowledge. As business relatedness is so high, these firms to a great extent assume the character of single-business firms.

name: Technology relatedness
definition: The Technology relatedness cluster appears as a cluster built on the technology relatedness of business units. In comparison with the other clusters, these firms emphasize similarities between business units as regards product features.

name: Customer relatedness
definition: The Customer relatedness cluster represents business relatedness based on customer similarities, as similarities are particularly obvious as regards end customer types of the two businesses. On the contrary, the four variables of the product technology factor demonstrate low similarities.

name: Low business relatedness
definition: The firms in the Low relatedness cluster show low similarities on all variables, except for the brand and market knowledge variables, and this was confirmed by Sheffe test. A reasonable interpretation of the low similarities between businesses is that to a high degree they are unrelated.

name: Corporate profitability
definition: Corporate profitability was used as an indicator of corporate performance in the study. The measure chosen was objective accounting-based corporate performance, since market values and similar external measures are generally more distant from internal firm activities.

name: Specialized role adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of specialized roles", "adoption of OB nurses", "OB nurse adoption", "introduction of OB nurses", "introduction of a specialized role"]
definition: Specialized roles are formal positions oriented toward serving a defined set of client needs; they codify expertise into formal positions with defined scopes of practice, making expertise more legible and creating recognizable categories that simplify allocation decisions. Roles formalize specialization by bundling a set of expected behaviors and responsibilities into a recognized position in the organizational structure.

name: Professional-client matching
definition: Professional-client matching is the alignment between a professional's expertise and the specific needs of a client or case. It is the allocative outcome of the task allocation process.

name: Client demand
definition: Client demand is the volume of work organizations face; high client demand provides the volume needed to sustain finer-grained role differentiation, and larger volumes of work allow organizations to sustain narrower scopes of practice without underutilizing professionals.

name: Workflow predictability
definition: Workflow predictability is the extent to which client needs and task demands can be anticipated in advance; it enhances organizations' ability to plan and assign work based on expertise rather than availability.

name: Organizational experience
definition: Organizational experience refers to the accumulated exposure professionals gain from repeatedly working within the same organization's workflows, routines, and systems. Such experience embeds system-specific knowledge that complements technical expertise.

name: Client complexity
definition: Client Complexity is a clinically meaningful summary of maternal and pregnancy risks that captures the predicted probability of C-section delivery; it serves as a proxy for the risk level associated with each birth.

name: Provider risk specialization
definition: Provider's Risk Specialization is defined as the cumulative average Client Complexity of all patients previously attended by the provider; higher values indicate a historical focus on more complex cases, whereas lower values indicate a specialization in less complex cases.

name: Maternal and newborn outcomes
definition: The authors explore whether improved matching is associated with better maternal and newborn outcomes, and treat this analysis as evidence on the relevance of professional-client matching for clinical performance.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: The shareholding of foreign institutional investors, who are predominantly institutional investors from the U.S. and the U.K. and who lack means to gain benefit other than stock returns from their investment, and hence are assumed to follow shareholder logic.

name: Executive elite university education
definition: Educational background used to gauge the human capital and talent of managers, measured as the proportion of executives or directors who graduated from prestigious Japanese universities. A top management team with more graduates from elite Japanese universities indicates higher human capital.

name: Executive pay inequality
authors_terms: ["Pay inequality", "pay inequality between top managers and average employees", "deviant pay scheme"]
definition: The pay inequality between top managers and average employees in a firm, which is not aligned with Japanese egalitarian norms and therefore indicates a deviant practice that may attract close attention.

name: Sales growth
definition: The annual growth rate in total sales; high sales growth indicates promising market demand and future growth opportunities, whereas slow growth makes it difficult for managers to serve the interests of domestic stakeholders.

name: Adoption of executive stock option pay
authors_terms: ["adoption of stock option pay for executives", "stock option pay", "stock option plan"]
definition: The adoption of stock option pay for executives, a practice that links executive compensation to the future stock price and therefore provides financial incentives for managers to increase the stock price that serves shareholders' interests.

name: Top actor performance
authors_terms: ["top actor performance", "coach performance", "top actor's performance", "performance of the top actor"]
definition: The performance of the firm or its top actors, or perceptions of such performance, that influences outcomes following a violation. Coach performance captures the extent to which a coach is performing better or worse than the team can reasonably expect given the past decade of the team's performance.

name: Severity gap
authors_terms: ["severity gap", "divergence between perceived and objective severity"]
definition: The extent to which perceived violation severity deviates from objective violation severity. A positive severity gap is one in which perceived violation severity exceeds objective severity, and a negative severity gap is one in which the objective violation severity exceeds perceptions of it.

name: Dismissal
definition: An internal outcome imposed by governance arbiters affiliated with the organization, reflecting whether the head coach remained with the team, departed voluntarily, or was dismissed following a violation.

name: Equivalent or better position
authors_terms: ["equivalent or better position", "labor market prospects", "securing an equivalent or better position"]
definition: The external labor market outcome for a top actor who departed, reflecting whether the coach accepted a head coach position at a team of similar or higher caliber or a job as an athletic director.

name: R&D investment
definition: In specifying the model, R&D investments are considered to include both a productive component, which influences a firm's mean sales, and a risk abatement component, which influences the variability (and conversely the reliability) of sales.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family firms are defined by a family's ownership and control of a firm and a vision for how the firm will benefit the family, potentially across generations.

name: Sales variability
authors_terms: ["variability of sales", "variance of sales", "intrafirm variability in sales", "reliability of sales"]
definition: The risk abatement function is specified to capture the influence of its components on the variance of the dependent variable rather than its mean; the risk abatement model accounts for the effects of inputs on mean intrafirm sales and intrafirm variability in sales.

name: Sales
definition: We use sales as the dependent variable since it is proximal output of R&D and captures the tradeoff between growth and risk that influence R&D investment decisions; since the sales variable is not normally distributed, we use the natural logarithm of yearly sales at time t.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance above aspirations", "performance below aspirations", "aspiration levels", "historic aspirations", "social aspirations"]
definition: We assume that negative (positive) discrepancies between a firm's performance and either its historical performance or the performance of competitors are likely to cause decision makers to believe that current performance is below (above) aspirations.

name: Managerial attention to a new business model
authors_terms: ["Distributed Attention", "senior managerial attention toward a new business model", "managerial attention to that new opportunity", "attention to the emerging business model", "attention to a focal issue"]
definition: We explore how managerial attention to issues beyond a given new opportunity may moderate the relationship between managerial attention to that new opportunity (in this case, an emerging business model) and the organization's subsequent actions (namely, investments in the emerging opportunity). Senior managerial attention toward industry change is an important predictor of firms' responses to such change.

name: Attention to a directly conflicting issue
authors_terms: ["Centralized Attention", "senior managerial attention to a directly conflicting issue", "attention to the legacy business model", "attention to a competing issue"]
definition: Attention spread across two (or more) conflicting issues creates tension between divergent pathways that limits decision making at the intrapersonal level and creates confusion at the organizational level. Attentional allocation toward conflicting issues may reflect indecision at the managerial level.

name: Breadth of strategic attention
definition: Second, more generally, managers pay attention to a wide variety of issues beyond the focal issue, and the breadth of senior managerial attention across an array of strategic issues directly or indirectly associated with an organization's strategic agenda will play a key role in shaping the attentional context. We use this measure as we wish to capture the full range of orthogonal issues rather than attention to specific issues.

name: Organizational size
definition: Drawing on the literature on organizational adaption to industry change, we argue that organizational size is a key driver of the attentional capacity of a firm. Larger firms can divide the attention of individual actors between various strategic issues, allowing larger firms to better pursue multiple opportunities simultaneously.

name: Organizational investments in the new business model
authors_terms: ["Investment", "organizational investments associated with that model", "investments consistent with a distributed electricity generation model"]
definition: By investments, we focus on the number of these investments a firm makes in a specific time period (e.g., one year) rather than the value of these investments. We collect data on firms' announcements regarding investments in the distributed electricity generation model from Capital IQ.

name: Family dominance
authors_terms: ["family dominance", "family domination", "family-dominated business groups", "family control", "family ownership"]
definition: We used two variables to operationalize family dominance in a business group: family ownership and family control. Family control is institutionalized as a corporate governance model in which family members expect to control day-to-day activities, as well as key strategies of the firm, so that they can maintain the family assets for future generations.

name: Unrelated acquisition
authors_terms: ["unrelated acquisition", "enter unrelated industries", "number of unrelated industries entered", "unrelated industries entered"]
definition: The unrelated industries entered were those distinct two-digit industries that were present in a business group's industrial portfolio at t+1 but not at t. Unrelated acquisition is one of the acquisitions and divestitures through which business groups develop a new configuration of the lines of business.

name: Unrelated divestiture
authors_terms: ["divestment", "divestiture", "exit unrelated industries", "number of unrelated industries exited", "unrelated industries exited"]
definition: The unrelated industries exited were those distinct two-digit industries that were present in a business group's industrial portfolio at t but not at t+1. Family-dominated business groups are predicted to be less likely to exit unrelated industries than groups less dominated by families.

name: Foreign investment from shareholder-based countries
authors_terms: ["shareholder-based foreign investment", "shareholder-based foreign countries", "U.S./U.K. industrial investment", "investment from shareholder-based foreign countries"]
definition: In the shareholder model, shareholding is a vehicle for investment, and therefore short-term return on investment-or profitability-is the most important concern for investors. Foreign investors from countries with shareholder-based models are likely to bring their home governance models and associated corporate strategies to emerging economies.

name: Foreign investment from stakeholder-based countries
authors_terms: ["stakeholder-based foreign investment", "stakeholder-based foreign countries", "Japanese industrial investment", "investment from stakeholder-based foreign countries"]
definition: In the stakeholder model, shareholding is a means by which stakeholders maintain long-term relationships; therefore, the goal of balancing the needs of multiple stakeholders (such as core workers, the government, banks, and suppliers) is central to management.

name: Political connections of boards
authors_terms: ["politically connected boards", "politically connected directors", "political connections", "politically connected outside directors"]
definition: A politically connected board has at least one director who was a former politician, including a member of parliament, a minister, or any other top appointed government bureaucrat or officer in a state-owned enterprise. An outside director with political connections is one who was formerly a government officer or member of the Chinese People's Congress or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference at county and above levels.

name: Top executive compensation
authors_terms: ["top executive pay", "top executive compensation", "top executive cash pay", "executive remuneration"]
definition: Top executive pay was measured by salaries and bonuses and was calculated as the logarithm of average cash pay for the three highest-paid executives at year 2000 prices.

name: Pay dispersion
definition: Pay dispersion refers to the amount of difference (inequality) in pay created by a firm's pay structure; pay compression is the extent to which this difference is reduced.

name: Firm performance
definition: ROS is used to measure firm performance. This variable is included in our estimation equations in order to test the moderating effect of political connections on the relationship between executive pay and firm performance.

name: Corporate social responsibility strengths
definition: Total CSR strengths (totstr it) is the equally weighted sum of KLD's positive screens, classified as 'strengths' for firm i in year t adjusted by the mean of strengths averaged across all firms in the sample in year t to take into account firm entry into the KLD panel. The authors argue that CSR and CSiR (corporate social irresponsibility) are two theoretically separate and distinct constructs and treat the strategic choice to engage in positive CSR as the construct of interest.

name: Investment recommendation optimism
definition: We use the consensus (i.e., mean) investment recommendation (Mean analysts' recommendation) for each firm i in the month of March of year t as the dependent variable of our empirical specifications. The I/B/E/S scale is inverted so that more favorable recommendations take a higher value.

name: Analyst experience
authors_terms: ["analyst experience", "years of firm-specific experience", "total number of years that the focal analyst has followed the focal firm"]
definition: We regard analyst experience as a key variable for understanding the heterogeneity across the analyst population in terms of their perceptions and associated investment recommendations; based on the full sample, we calculate analyst experience as the total number of years that the focal analyst has followed the focal firm.

name: Brokerage house status
authors_terms: ["brokerage house status", "Mean house size", "mean House size", "larger brokerage houses"]
definition: We follow Hong and Kubik (2003) in approximating brokerage house status by the mean House size constructed as the average number of analysts working at the focal brokerage house in any given year. Higher-status (equivalently larger) brokerage houses are, on average, more likely to switch behavior and conform to the emerging stakeholder focus.

name: Institutional logic shift
authors_terms: ["shift in institutional logics", "emergence of a stakeholder orientation", "weakening of the agency logic", "stakeholder logic", "over time"]
definition: We adopt a social constructionist view of financial markets and explore how the weakening of the prevalent agency logic, due to the emergence of a stakeholder orientation, is associated with a shift in the way analysts respond to CSR ratings over a 15-year time horizon. Subsequently, we argue for a gradual weakening of this agency-based institutional logic through the emergence of a stakeholder orientation.

name: State nondiscrimination laws
authors_terms: ["number of state nondiscrimination laws", "state laws forbidding discrimination based on sexual orientation", "state legal environments"]
definition: State-level laws forbidding discrimination based on sexual orientation, which the authors treat as a coercive mechanism that guides organizations' practices. Such laws emphasized equal treatment but did not provide specific scope and guidelines as to how such equal treatment should be achieved.

name: Adoptions by industry peers
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of adoptions in the same industry", "adoptions by other corporations in the same industry", "adoptions by similar others"]
definition: The cumulative number of adoptions by other corporations within the same industry, which the authors posit is an important boundary of social proximity for the mimetic mechanism because each industry has its own sociocultural expectations associated with sexual orientation.

name: Adoptions by same-state peers
authors_terms: ["cumulative number of adoptions in the same state", "adoptions by corporations with headquarters in the same state", "adoptions by similar others"]
definition: The cumulative number of adoptions by corporations with headquarters in the same state, which the authors posit is an important boundary of social proximity because state legislative systems and societal attitudes toward lesbians and gay men differ between states.

name: Overall tenor in press coverage
authors_terms: ["overall tenor in press coverage", "overall tenor in press coverage on the benefits", "press coverage of the benefits"]
definition: The overall tenor of press coverage of same-sex partner health benefits, which the authors treat as a source of the normative mechanism and as an indicator of the evolution of societal attitudes and beliefs toward the institution of equal treatment.

name: Same-sex partner health benefits adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of same-sex partner health benefits", "benefits adoption", "rate of benefits adoption"]
definition: The adoption rate of same-sex partner health benefits by a corporation when it was at risk of adoption in a given year; the practice manifests the institution of equal treatment for lesbian and gay employees.

name: Policy stability
definition: Institutional features such as independent regulatory or judicial bodies and veto players provide assurances that the rules of the business game when initial project policies were set will have near-term persistence; in states where these features provide weaker assurances, project risk increases for private investors. Policy_Stability assesses the ease of changing policies relevant to private coinvestors and reflects the number of relevant veto holders in a state's national polity.

name: State ownership
definition: State ownership is the equity participation of the state in an investment project. State ownership in such projects signals the possibility of interference with the profit-oriented goals of private coinvestors under existing policies defined by state laws and regulations as well as more specific contract terms.

name: Minority state ownership
authors_terms: ["minority state ownership", "Minority_State_Ownership", "noncontrolling minority equity stakes", "substantial but noncontrolling state ownership"]
definition: To be net risk reducing, state ownership can be neither trivial (0%), and thus incredible as assurance to private coinvestors against near-term change in initial policies, nor controlling (>50%), and thus credible but potentially interfering with private coinvestor aims under those same initial policies. We assume that noncontrolling minority equity stakes by states signal to private coinvestors maintenance of initial policies.

name: Investment risk
definition: Investment_Risk is measured as the percentage of equity funding the project, that is, initial equity divided by the sum of equity plus debt multiplied by 100. Capital structure at the announcement date is used as a forward-looking indicator of the likelihood of loss from project term renegotiation, holdup, or expropriation.

name: Consideration for employee morale and welfare
authors_terms: ["consideration for employees", "consideration for employee morale and welfare", "consideration for employees' morale and welfare"]
definition: Downsizing practices that display consideration for employees' morale and welfare, including working to increase survivors' sense of job security and marketability, preserving the dignity of terminated employees, carefully explaining the reasons behind downsizing decisions, communicating more extensively with employees during the downsizing process, and counseling survivors throughout the process.

name: Advance notice of layoffs
definition: The extent to which downsizing organizations provide employees with advance notice of layoffs, considered as the time between the announcement of downsizing and notice about which employees will be laid off and between that notice and actual separation.

name: Financial benefits to laid-off employees
authors_terms: ["financial benefits", "provision of valuable economic benefits to laid-off workers"]
definition: Financial benefits that organizations extend to terminated employees beyond their legal obligations, commonly severance pay and the extension of health insurance coverage (COBRA) beyond the legally required minimum.

name: Planned work redesign
authors_terms: ["planned work redesign", "planned redesign of work", "work redesign"]
definition: Downsizing carried out as part of a larger plan for organizational design, in which systematic analyses of jobs in the organization accompany layoffs and attention is paid both to specific jobs and to broader organizational structures.

name: Post-downsizing performance
authors_terms: ["post-downsizing performance", "performance following the implementation of a downsizing program"]
definition: Organizational performance following the implementation of a downsizing program, assessed in two ways: human resource managers' perceptions of the overall success of the hospital's downsizing efforts, and cash margin as a bottom-line measure of organizational effectiveness.

name: Board representation by the investor
authors_terms: ["board representation", "board seat", "board membership", "representation on the investee's board", "board-level monitoring"]
definition: Whether the investing partner secures membership on the board of the investee firm in a minority equity partnership; the board of the investee firm is the highest level at which partners can interface with each other to manage strategic interdependencies and information flows between them.

name: Technology overlap between partners
authors_terms: ["investee technology overlap", "overlap of the partners' technological resources", "technology overlap", "overlap in patent portfolios"]
definition: The extent to which the investor's knowledge stock matches with the knowledge stock of the investee partner, captured as the overlap of the partners' technological resources in patent classifications.

name: Investor competing alliances
authors_terms: ["investor competing alliances", "the investor's collaborative agreements with potential competitors to the investee partner", "competitive collaborations"]
definition: Collaborative agreements that the investor maintains with other firms that already compete with, or can become potential competitors of, the investee partner, which provide a source of misappropriation risk because interorganizational relationships serve as conduits for the transfer of information and knowledge.

name: Investee knowledge value in overlapping technologies
authors_terms: ["investee knowledge value (overlap tech.)", "value of the investee partner's knowledge", "investee knowledge value"]
definition: The value of the investee partner's knowledge in the technological areas where the investor is active, reflecting the potential benefits that follow from exploiting the spillovers and therefore the investor's incentive to misappropriate.

name: Acquisition announcement
definition: For each quarter in our data set, we operationalized acquisition announcements as a dichotomous variable reflecting whether or not a firm announced at least one majority (51 percent or greater) acquisition investment (0 = 'no,' 1 = 'yes') worth at least $1 million in value (if reported) in that quarter.

name: CEO stock option exercise
authors_terms: ["options exercised", "exercising stock options", "cash out stock options", "CEO stock option exercise behavior"]
definition: Once stock options vest, CEOs may choose, largely at their discretion, to continue to hold those exercisable options or exercise and sell them to capture the accrued value; CEOs can manage their equity-based holdings by cashing out stock options.

name: CEO stock sales
definition: CEO stock holdings represent real, accessible current wealth that exhibits both upside and downside potential, and CEOs can manage their equity-based holdings by cashing out stock options and selling stock; when CEOs expect positive returns, they tend to retain their holdings to accrue future equity gains.

name: CEO stock option grants
authors_terms: ["options granted", "grant CEO stock options", "CEO stock option awards"]
definition: When CEOs' interests appear misaligned with those of shareholders, directors often opt to better align those interests by tying CEOs' wealth even more tightly to that of shareholders, through additional CEO stock option awards.

name: Acquisition announcement market performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition announcement performance", "market reactions to acquisition announcements", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "announcement CARs"]
definition: A firm's market performance (share price performance) reflects investors' perceptions of future firm value. Announcement CARs reflect investors' present expectations about future value of combined firms (i.e., bidders plus targets).

name: Preemptive power of patents
authors_terms: ["preemptive power", "preemptive power of a target firm's patent portfolio", "preemptive patents", "preemptive patenting"]
definition: The preemptive power of a target firm's patent portfolio is a source of value besides the value created by combining complementary resources, because it allows acquirers to secure market exclusion and their freedom to operate in R&D and hence to capture value from innovation activities. The patent portfolio associated with a firm's knowledge base serves as an indicator not only of a firm's technological capabilities but also of its preemptive power.

name: Acquisition price
authors_terms: ["price paid by the acquirer for the target firm", "acquisition price", "price p(T)"]
definition: The price p(T) approximates the value of the target when it is combined with the bidding firm; in this regard, the price reflects the acquiring firm's expectations of resource complementarity. Under the condition of resource competition, the price is a proxy for an acquirer's 'willingness to pay' and reflects its expectations for future value creation and capture.

name: Acquirer technology intensity
authors_terms: ["technology intensity of the acquirer", "acquiring firm's technology intensity", "acquirer's technology intensity"]
definition: Firms with higher technology intensity can be characterized by a higher number of patents employed in relation to their total assets. Value creation in technology-intensive firms relies on technological innovation and these firms have relatively large sunk R&D investments that they seek to protect.

name: Preemptive patent relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness between the acquirer's and the target's technology portfolios", "relatedness to the target firm's patents", "Relatedness A-cited/XY-cited patents"]
definition: The value captured by the acquirer is likely to increase monotonically with the relatedness to the target firm's patents; the value the acquirer may capture by combining its own knowledge base with the preemptive power of the patents held by the target firm is highest if the technology and patent portfolios are highly related or even largely overlapping in technology space. The measure captures the extent to which two firms develop technology in the same classes and is applied to the target's patents cited as preemptive (XY-type) and to the acquirer's patents cited as contributing to the state of the art (A-type).

name: Positive headquarters attention
definition: The extent to which a parent company recognizes and gives credit to a subsidiary for its contribution to the MNE as a whole. The authors conceptualize it as a meta-construct consisting of three interrelated and reinforcing dimensions: relative, supportive, and visible attention.

name: Local market strategic significance
authors_terms: ["strategic significance of a local market", "local market strategic significance", "importance of the local market"]
definition: This dimension reflects the perception that the particular market in which a subsidiary operates is critical to the performance of its parent MNE.

name: Subsidiary strength within the MNE network
authors_terms: ["subsidiary strength within an MNE network", "strength of a subsidiary within MNE network", "strength of the subsidiary operations within the MNE network"]
definition: The extent to which a subsidiary undertakes activities upon which sister subsidiaries depend.

name: Subsidiary initiative taking
definition: The conscious and deliberate actions of subsidiary managers in their marketplace, which are voluntary (not formally required by headquarters) and change-oriented (aimed at improving a subsidiary's status and perceived significance in a corporate system).

name: Profile building
definition: The broad set of efforts undertaken by subsidiary managers to improve their image, credibility, and reputation within their parent MNE, consisting of the subsidiary's track record, its commitment to the parent company, and the impression management efforts of subsidiary managers.

name: Geographic distance
definition: The physical separation between a subsidiary and its corporate headquarters, which means that headquarters executives understand the subsidiaries furthest away less well than the closer ones and are more likely to fall back on simple heuristics to evaluate them.

name: Downstream competence
authors_terms: ["downstream competence", "subsidiary downstream competence", "competence confined to the downstream part of the value chain"]
definition: A unit responsible for activities mostly confined to product sales, service, and/or marketing, in contrast to a subsidiary with an upstream competence, such as manufacturing, R&D, or strategic support services.

name: Homophilous interorganizational ties
authors_terms: ["homophilous interorganizational ties to industry peers", "homophilous relationships with industry peers", "alliances with industry peers", "homophilous ties"]
definition: Homophily is defined as the tendency to associate with similar others and to trust their advice; in this study homophilous relationships are the links incumbents establish with other incumbent firms in the same industry, which share similarities in organizational forms, knowledge, experiences, and mental frameworks.

name: Heterophilous interorganizational ties
authors_terms: ["heterophilous interorganizational ties with VCs", "heterophilous relationships", "coinvestment ties with VC firms"]
definition: By forming heterophilous interorganizational relationships, an incumbent may be able to gain access to more diverse information and diverging viewpoints that can help to reshape attention patterns within the incumbent; the study focuses on one specific set of such relationships, those incumbents form by coinvesting with VCs when making CVC investments in start-ups.

name: Alliance partner status
authors_terms: ["partner status in homophilous ties", "status of partners in homophilous interorganizational ties", "status of partners in homophilous ties"]
definition: The status of a player in an industry can be defined as the position it occupies in the social hierarchy; contrary to a firm's reputation, status is a reflection of the patterns of relations and affiliations in which a firm is engaged, and high-status firms are incumbents that have developed a central position in the social network of an industry over time.

name: VC partner status
authors_terms: ["status of partners in heterophilous interorganizational ties", "status of the partners in heterophilous ties", "status of the other VC investors with whom an incumbent coinvests"]
definition: In heterophilous relationships, the status of the partner plays a critical role in alleviating uncertainty about the quality of information; for CVC investments coinvested with VCs, the status of the other VC investors with whom an incumbent coinvests is critical, and VCs who coinvest with the incumbent usually have well-established track records on which to form status assessments.

name: Timeliness of top management attention
authors_terms: ["the timing of the formal attention to major discontinuities by an incumbent's top management", "timely attention to technological discontinuities", "the time when top management formally paid attention to the Internet", "time-to-attention"]
definition: The primary dependent variable was the timing of the formal attention to major discontinuities by an incumbent's top management, measured as the time between January 1989 and the time of a company's first mention of the technological discontinuity in its corporate documents.

name: Entry
definition: Entry occurs when at least one new rival magazine enters the market in which an incumbent magazine competes in the current year. Only new magazines introduced by rival publishers are considered new entrants, so entry is defined specific to each incumbent magazine.

name: Subscription price
authors_terms: ["per-issue price for a 1-year subscription", "incumbent price", "incumbent prices"]
definition: The price of a magazine subscription, measured as the log of the per-issue price for a 1-year subscription, which is the listed price for a 1-year subscription divided by the number of issues.

name: Incumbent age
authors_terms: ["incumbent's age (time in the market)", "incumbent age", "the incumbent's time in the market", "newer incumbents", "older incumbents"]
definition: The incumbent's time in the market, measured as the logarithm of the number of years since the magazine was founded (since it entered the market).

name: Corporate scope
authors_terms: ["corporate scope", "multi-market incumbents", "number of markets in which it sells magazines", "multi-market incumbency"]
definition: The number of markets in which the incumbent's publisher competes; the authors argue that by fighting entry in one market a multi-market incumbent can build a reputation for fighting entry that may deter entry in its other markets.

name: Market concentration
definition: The concentration of the market in which the incumbent competes, measured by a Herfindahl index. The threat posed by entry is argued to be greater in more concentrated markets.

name: Firm diversification
definition: The dependent variable in this study measures the supplier's business scope, which in this case is the scope of patent legal services across different technological domains.

name: Client diversification
authors_terms: ["Client Diversification", "clients' diversification", "diversification by clients", "diversification in the outsourcing needs of a supplier firm's existing clients"]
definition: Client diversification is the aggregated scope of all patent prosecution work outsourced by the set of clients in a focal supplier's portfolio in a particular year, adjusted for the extent to which clients' business scope overlaps with or is different from the supplier's business scope. Client diversification must combine both a change in the scope of business outsourced and a shift away from the focal supplier's own business scope.

name: Client-specific knowledge
definition: Detailed knowledge about a supplier's clients' business priorities and idiosyncrasies, unique technologies, and organizational structures and processes, which may create efficiencies in learning and problem solving. Because the work of patent law firms is essentially to create strong ownership claims in technology space for their clients, it is imperative that they understand the relevant technical knowledge that their clients' patents are building on.

name: Relational client commitment
definition: Prior research suggests that clients can provide credible signals of their relational commitment by allocating greater shares of outsourced work to the supplier, a costly action that makes it difficult to switch business to other suppliers and thus conveys positive expectations of relationship continuity to the supplier.

name: Relative demand opportunity
authors_terms: ["Relative Demand Opportunity", "relative demand opportunity", "relative demand opportunities"]
definition: The difference between growth in the market segments (IPCs) that a supplier's clients are active in and growth in the market segments that the supplier itself operates in; the difference in growth rates between the supplier's current market segments and its clients' (outsourced) market segments provides a measure of the relative opportunity offered by following clients into new areas.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspiration level", "performance compared with aspiration level", "performance relative to the historical aspiration level", "performance relative to social aspiration levels", "performance feedback"]
definition: Performance is calculated as return on assets (ROA), and the aspiration level is subtracted from it; the authors use either a historical aspiration level, the weighted average of past performance with most of the weight (0.9) assigned to the most recent ROA, or a social aspiration level, the average ROA of all other firms in the same industry.

name: Potential state coalition
authors_terms: ["potential state coalition", "stateness", "stateness factor", "stateness ASW", "potential dominant coalition"]
definition: The strength of a coalition is jointly determined by the number of members, their commitment, and their status within the board. While the actual coalition in each case is uncertain, potential coalitions can be predicted by examining the size of subgroups with shared experience that are likely to engage in coalition building, as well as the size of subgroups that are not already committed and hence can be recruited.

name: Board state experience
authors_terms: ["state experience", "directors with state experience", "proportion of board members with state experience"]
definition: Directors who have experience working or are still working for state agencies are quite common in listed firms in China; the state socialism experience makes them familiar with the actions of seeking state opinion and state help.

name: Board market experience
authors_terms: ["market experience", "directors with market experience", "proportion of board members with market experience"]
definition: Directors with market-related work experience and education are familiar with evaluating opportunities in the market and taking risk in order to increase firm value, and they see themselves as part of a corporate governance and management system that preserves shareholder rights.

name: Market orientation of acquisitions
authors_terms: ["market-oriented acquisitions", "type of acquisition", "nature of acquisition", "market orientation", "market-oriented actions"]
definition: Each acquisition target can be categorized by how distant it is from the usual state versus market actions, and hence what type of board member would see it as a more proximate option of change. The three main types of acquisition target follow the order from the least market-oriented to the most, and market-oriented acquisitions are further distinguished by level of market orientation.

name: State bank borrowing
authors_terms: ["state-bank loan", "loans from state-owned banks", "loans from state banks", "state-related actions"]
definition: Whether the firm chooses to borrow from state banks, which the authors use as an indicator of the firm choosing state-related actions; directors with state experience know that state-owned banks can act as a buffer for firms that are seeking to solve problems.

name: Pre-acquisition social interactions
definition: Social interactions between the management of two merging companies in the months preceding the acquisition announcement, measured by the frequency of intercompany visits between the two merging companies. Smartphone geolocational data are used to capture the frequency of these interactions.

name: Acquirer acquisition returns
authors_terms: ["the acquirer's abnormal returns from the acquisition", "acquirer's CAR", "acquirer's returns"]
definition: The returns the acquirer obtains from an acquisition, measured with the abnormal returns on the acquirer's stock at the acquisition announcement, which capture investors' expectations about the profitability of the acquisition.

name: Bids from alternative bidders
authors_terms: ["later bids", "the number of bids the target receives from other bidders after the announcement of the focal acquisition"]
definition: The number of bids the target receives from other bidders after the announcement of the focal acquisition, used because the timing of the target management's solicitation of alternative acquirers is not observable.

name: Target value appropriation relative to acquirer
authors_terms: ["the target's abnormal returns from the acquisition relative to those of the acquirer", "difference in gains between merging companies", "target's value appropriation vis-à-vis the acquirer", "target's abnormal returns relative to those of the acquirer"]
definition: The share of deal value appropriated by the target relative to the acquirer, measured as the difference in weighted abnormal gains between the two merging companies. The acquirer's gains can increase because the transaction creates more synergistic value or because the acquirer appropriates more value vis-à-vis the target.

name: Target management ownership
authors_terms: ["target management ownership", "the share of the target owned by the target's management"]
definition: The share of the target owned by the target's management, broadly defined as executives and directors. The greater the share of the management ownership of the target, the more the target's management internalizes the trade-off between the gains from selling the company and the benefit of establishing a one-to-one negotiation with a trusted acquirer.

name: Total value created by the acquisition
authors_terms: ["total CAR", "total abnormal gains of the two merging companies", "total value created by the acquisition"]
definition: The total abnormal gains of the two merging companies combined, used to verify whether intercompany visits affect the total value created by the deal in addition to the two parties' value appropriation.

name: Guanxi with business community
authors_terms: ["guanxi with the business community", "interfirm guanxi", "guanxi networks with competitive forces", "horizontal networks"]
definition: Interfirm guanxi specifically refer to cross-organizational connections among managers. Guanxi with the business community consists of horizontal connections with buyers, suppliers, and competitors.

name: Guanxi with government authorities
authors_terms: ["guanxi with government authorities", "guanxi with government officials", "vertical networks"]
definition: Guanxi with government authorities refer to personal relationships between firm managers and government officials. It includes vertical connections with political governments, industrial departments, and other regulatory authorities such as taxation bureaus, banks, and commercial administration bureaus.

name: Nonstate ownership
definition: Ownership structure distinguishes state-owned, collectively owned, and privately owned firms; private and collective firms, as nonstate-owned firms, are much more institutionally independent than state-owned firms.

name: Regional openness
definition: There are wide variations in the level of economic development and the stage of economic reform across regions, especially between the open and nonopen economic regions; open areas maintain more Western-style business facilities and a Western cultural atmosphere.

name: Market-oriented strategy
definition: The strategic orientation toward market effectiveness continually searches for market opportunities and experiments with emerging trends and technologies; market-oriented firms concentrate on scanning, identifying, and capitalizing on emerging market opportunities.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is an important attribute that shapes behaviors and decisions in a firm; as size increases, so do the bureaucratic structures, thus making it difficult to have a personal, entrepreneurial style of management.

name: Technological skills
definition: Technological skills are important for organizational competence; they allow for the development of new products and processes and for the potential to adapt to changing market dynamics.

name: Managerial capabilities
definition: Managerial skills are important for building organizational competence; they are difficult to imitate because they are scarce, specialized, and tacitly embedded within the firm.

name: Organizational age
definition: Organizational history is an important determinant of legitimacy, strategic behaviors, and guanxi cultivation. Organizational age reflects institutionalized managerial attitudes and beliefs.

name: Sales growth
definition: Performance is defined according to financial measures during the most recent 3 years, one of which is sales growth, which the authors treat as market expansion.

name: Profit growth
definition: Performance is defined according to financial measures during the most recent 3 years, one of which is net profit growth.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "tenure", "years a chief executive had been in office", "time in office"]
definition: CEO tenure was measured by counting the years a chief executive had been in office. It paces two simultaneous yet countervailing processes, one adaptive and one maladaptive.

name: Firm performance
definition: In this paper, performance refers to organizational outcomes, which are influenced both by CEOs and by factors outside their control. To assess firm performance, we examined three annual measures of profitability.

name: Industry dynamism
authors_terms: ["industry dynamism", "environmental dynamism", "dynamism of the external environment", "dynamic industry", "stable industry"]
definition: A stable industry is one in which customer preferences, technologies, and competitive dynamics change little. Prior research suggests that the factors affecting environmental dynamism include degrees of innovation, technological change, supply instability, competitive rivalry, and market growth.

name: Technology resource breadth
authors_terms: ["technology resource breadth", "breadth of technological resources", "breadth of the firm's patent portfolio", "technological resources"]
definition: Technological resources are defined as the firm's repository of technological knowledge and technological competencies (Miller, 2004). The breadth of a firm's patent portfolio is utilized as the indicator of the firm's breadth of technological resources.

name: Deviant competitive actions
authors_terms: ["deviant competitive actions", "competitive deviance", "nonconformity", "action repertoire dissimilarity", "attack heterogeneity"]
definition: Competitive deviance or nonconformity reflects the degree to which a firm's actions differ markedly from industry norms and emphasize a novel mix or sequence of actions not available to competitors (Miller and Chen, 1996). Deviant competitive actions capture the extent to which a firm's portfolio of actions for a given year differed from those of its competitors.

name: TMT heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["TMT heterogeneity", "top management team heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of the TMT"]
definition: TMT heterogeneity refers to the degree to which TMT members differ (Carpenter, Geletkanycz, and Sanders, 2004). TMT heterogeneity addresses diversity in top management demographics and is calculated for each management team member's age, tenure, and functional background.

name: TMT faultline strength
definition: Lau and Murnighan (1998) use the concept of faultlines to characterize the hypothetical lines that split a group into subgroups based on multiple demographic attributes; these faultlines reflect potential schisms within a team. The strength of a faultline depends on the number of salient attributes team members can use in categorizations, how clearly aligned those attributes are across the team members, and the number of potential subgroups that can be formed.

name: Firm performance
definition: A market-based measure of performance is necessary because all benefits of technological resources and competitive actions might not be evident in accounting performance at a specific time; market-based measures such as Tobin's q capture both short-term and long-term performance.

name: Business similarity
authors_terms: ["business similarity", "similarity between two firms", "resource similarity", "business relatedness", "product relatedness"]
definition: Similarities in products, markets, and technologies between two firms, generally referred to as the level of business relatedness. In this paper the authors focus on product relatedness at the categorization level of four-digit NAICS codes.

name: Business complementarity
definition: The extent to which two firms' resources are different, yet interdependent and mutually supportive.

name: Combined alliance capability
authors_terms: ["combined alliance capabilities of two firms", "combined alliance capability", "alliance capability"]
definition: Relational capability refers to a firm's ability to interact with and manage other firms in interfirm relationships; alliance capability is the ability of a firm to deal with its partners in an alliance. The combined alliance capability of two firms is the stock of this capability held by both firms.

name: Combined acquisition capability
authors_terms: ["combined acquisition capabilities of two firms", "combined acquisition capability", "acquisition capability"]
definition: Acquisition capability is the ability of a firm to deal with its transaction partners in an acquisition; it is one of the two types of a firm's relational capabilities. The combined acquisition capability of two firms is the stock of this capability held by both firms.

name: Partner-specific knowledge in alliances
authors_terms: ["partner-specific knowledge of two firms in alliances", "partner-specific knowledge"]
definition: Partner-specific knowledge is embedded in social relationships and characterized by trust between two firms, and its value is maximized when two firms continue the relationship by conducting more transactions in the future. Partner-specific knowledge in alliances is the partner-specific knowledge two firms develop through repeated alliance transactions with each other.

name: Partner-specific knowledge in acquisitions
authors_terms: ["partner-specific knowledge of two firms in acquisitions", "partner-specific knowledge"]
definition: Partner-specific knowledge is embedded in social relationships and characterized by trust between two firms, and its value is maximized when two firms continue the relationship by conducting more transactions in the future. Partner-specific knowledge in acquisitions is the partner-specific knowledge two firms develop through repeated acquisition transactions with each other.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["an alliance formation between two firms", "the likelihood of an alliance formation"]
definition: An alliance is a shorter-term plan of cooperation, typically based on certain specific joint projects, and it does not require two firms to integrate their operations fully. The outcome is the likelihood that an alliance is formed between two specific firms.

name: Acquisition occurrence
authors_terms: ["an acquisition occurrence between two firms", "the likelihood of an acquisition occurrence"]
definition: An acquisition is a longer-term plan for two firms to come together, typically requiring two firms (or an acquiring firm and the acquired division of the target firm) to fully integrate their operations. The outcome is the likelihood that an acquisition occurs between two specific firms.

name: CEO early-life disaster experience
authors_terms: ["CEO early-life disaster experience", "CEO disaster experience", "early-life disaster experience", "CEO disaster experience early in life"]
definition: We describe how the CEO's exposure to traumatic events (events exacting an extreme cognitive and emotional toll) in early-life is reflected in their firm's corporate social performance. We define CEO disaster experience as an indicator variable equal to ' 1 ' if a disaster event occurred at least once in the county where the CEO lived between the ages of 5 and 15 years and ' 0 ' otherwise.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: Corporate social performance encompasses engaging in behavior that benefits stakeholders and refraining from behavior that harms stakeholders (responsible and irresponsible corporate social behavior, respectively).

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Corporate social performance encompasses engaging in behavior that benefits stakeholders ... (responsible ... corporate social behavior).

name: Corporate social irresponsibility
definition: Corporate social performance encompasses ... refraining from behavior that harms stakeholders (... irresponsible corporate social behavior). Socially irresponsible corporate behavior has a larger impact on stakeholder assessments and lessens the stakeholder relationship benefits firms derive from engaging in responsible behavior.

name: CEO age at disaster
authors_terms: ["CEO age at the time of the disaster", "CEO disaster age 5_10", "CEO age at time of traumatic experience"]
definition: Early-life is also a period of rapid psychological development ... Consistent with the expectation that sensitivity to environmental imprints declines with maturation, traumatic events experienced earlier in early-life are found to have a more enduring influence.

name: Disaster severity
authors_terms: ["disaster severity", "severity of the disaster", "severity of the traumatic experience"]
definition: As psychological growth following a traumatic event increases with the stress induced by the event, the level of post-traumatic growth that people experience is thought to be positively correlated with the severity of the event.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: Ownership of common shares by the CEO, which strengthens the link between firm performance and the CEO's individual wealth and thereby aligns the CEO's financial interests with those of shareholders.

name: Performance-contingent CEO compensation
definition: Compensation mechanisms such as stock options, restricted stock, and performance shares that link firm performance to CEO employment income and are typically designed to motivate executives to improve firm financial and stock market performance over an extended time horizon.

name: Board monitoring of CEO
authors_terms: ["board monitoring", "board monitoring of the CEO", "board performance monitoring"]
definition: Intense director scrutiny of the CEO's strategic decision making and of the performance consequences of those decisions, reflected in demands for justifications and explanations, constructive criticism of management-proposed initiatives, and sanctioning of managers whose strategic choices have negative performance effects.

name: Outside directors' prior executive experience
authors_terms: ["executive experience of outside directors", "director executive experience", "prior executive experience"]
definition: The extent to which outside directors have served as top executives at other firms, which provides them with relevant knowledge and expertise for monitoring strategic decision making and evaluating CEO performance.

name: External advice seeking from nonfriends and dissimilar others
authors_terms: ["advice seeking directed toward executives of other firms with whom he or she does not share either a friendship tie or a common functional background", "CEO external advice networks", "advice-seeking interactions"]
definition: The extent to which a CEO solicits strategic advice from executives at other firms who are not personal friends and who have a functional background different from the CEO's, contacts that provide exposure to novel points of view on strategic issues.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "market-to-book value of equity", "return on assets"]
definition: Focal firm performance, measured with an accounting-based measure (return on assets) and a market-based measure (market-to-book value of equity), both adjusted for industry differences.

name: Change in R&D investment
authors_terms: ["change in R&D investment", "change in R&D", "one-period change in R&D investment", "R&D investment"]
definition: Firms adjust R&D investment levels on the basis of expected payoffs derived from uncertainty-reducing information. The dependent variable was one-period change in R&D investment.

name: New product awards
authors_terms: ["new product awards", "product awards", "awards", "count of new product awards"]
definition: New product awards provide market signals that influence R&D investment incentives in technically intensive industries. Awards that trade publishers bestow on new products signal impending market acceptance of a firm's products and indicate the quality of the research activities that underlie the firm's product family.

name: Network centrality
authors_terms: ["centrality", "network centrality", "eigenvector centrality", "centrality in an interfirm alliance network"]
definition: Central firms can mediate the flows of information between all other pairs of members in the network. Eigenvector centrality weights partners by their own centrality, whereas betweenness and closeness centrality treat all ties equally.

name: Partner awards
authors_terms: ["partner awards", "partners' awards", "product awards a firm's alliance partners receive", "number of awards that a firm's partners received"]
definition: New product awards to partners offer information about partners' capabilities that will have both positive and negative effects on a firm's investment incentives.

name: Technical proximity
authors_terms: ["technical proximity", "technical proximity of a firm and its partners", "cross-citation ratio"]
definition: Greater technical proximity implies greater likelihood that the firms are investing in related products, whether substitutes or complements. The greater the cross-citation ratio, the higher the technical proximity of firm i and firm j.

name: Capabilities relative to partners
authors_terms: ["capabilities relative to its partners", "relative capabilities", "ratio of partners' awards to a focal firm's awards"]
definition: The higher the ratio of partners' awards, the greater is the focal firm's loss of attractiveness relative to other firms with which the firm's partners might form alliances.

name: IPO success
definition: IPO success is a financial indicator of the issuing firm's performance, calculated from the firm's net proceeds from the offering, its pre-money market valuation, and its 90-day and 180-day market valuations after the IPO.

name: Equity market uncertainty
authors_terms: ["equity market uncertainty", "equity index", "equity market index", "hot/cold equity markets"]
definition: How favorable or unfavorable the market is for equity offerings is one critical aspect of uncertainty for investors; the measure ranges from low to high or from cold to hot (unfavorable to favorable).

name: Venture capital prominence
authors_terms: ["VC prominence", "endorsement by a prestigious VC", "ties to prominent venture capital firms", "prominent VC partnerships"]
definition: A firm's partnership with a reputable VC should signal both the present and future quality of a young firm, providing financial resources and expertise that serve as important signals of new venture quality.

name: Underwriter prestige
authors_terms: ["underwriter prestige", "endorsement by a prestigious underwriter", "prestigious underwriter", "lead investment bank"]
definition: Prior studies have established a clear role for underwriter reputation in IPOs; firms with prestigious underwriters are more likely to have successful IPOs.

name: Strategic alliances with prominent partners
authors_terms: ["strategic alliances", "downstream alliances", "prominent strategic alliances", "alliances with prominent pharmaceutical/health care organizations"]
definition: Strategic alliances are partnerships with major pharmaceutical and health care companies that engage in downstream activities and so have significant marketing and sales expertise as well as financial capital that can support the firm through its lengthy product development process.

name: Knowledge-sharing clique involvement
authors_terms: ["knowledge-sharing clique", "K clique", "knowledge-sharing embedded relationships", "instrumental embedded relationships"]
definition: A knowledge-sharing clique is a triadic clique in the scientific knowledge-sharing network, in which the parties are strongly and reciprocally connected to one another through ties of scientific knowledge sharing. Within such a clique individuals are willing to share more knowledge and to share knowledge that is unique or more relevant.

name: Friendship clique involvement
authors_terms: ["friendship clique", "F clique", "friendship embedded relationships", "affective embedded relationships"]
