definition: A friendship clique is a triadic clique in the friendship network, in which the parties are strongly and reciprocally connected to one another through friendship ties. It is a highly trustworthy environment where individuals can expose their ideas and obtain sensitive or strategic information.

name: Individual innovative performance
authors_terms: ["innovative productivity", "innovative performance", "ability to generate innovations", "patent applications"]
definition: The objective outcome of the innovation process at the individual level, captured through the number of patent applications obtained by inventors.

name: Geographic expansion of production
authors_terms: ["geographic expansion", "geographical expansion", "expand production geographically", "expanding their supply chains"]
definition: A fundamental operational strategy that firms can employ to meet increased demand is through expanding their supply chains (i.e., moving production to new locations or outsourcing production in other ways that can undermine an established connection to a place of origin).

name: Perceived authenticity
definition: Authenticity is conferred when a product's connection to some external referent resonates with consumers and validates an implied claim about the product; this is akin to what Lehman et al. (2019) refer to as 'Authenticity as Connection.'

name: Product appreciation
definition: The paper's ultimate dependent variable: participants were asked to rate how pleased they would expect that a cigar aficionado would be to receive the type of cigar described.

name: Provenance-based authenticity claim
definition: Provenance-based connections represent a spaciotemporal connection to the origin or source of production for a product. Provenance-based claims forward location of origin as the primary source of authenticity.

name: Symbolism-based authenticity claim
definition: A symbolism-based connection can be understood as a stylized link to an individual, whereby that individual stands for and symbolizes a remembered past or idealized reality; it need not be physical or spaciotemporal in nature, and it is not an origin-based claim.

name: Transference-based authenticity claim
definition: Transference-based claims represent another type of spaciotemporal connection, but instead of focusing on the origin of an entity, its authenticity is derived from a connection to another person, place, or entity that might engender value; authenticity is conferred because this other relevant person or entity simply came into physical contact with the product.

name: R&D search intensity
authors_terms: ["search intensity", "R&D search intensity", "R&D intensity", "technological search effort"]
definition: Search is defined here as an activity by which firms place bets on possible future opportunities. The search intensity variable measures the magnitude of the technological search effort.

name: Performance below aspiration
authors_terms: ["distance of past performance below aspiration", "unsatisfactory performance feedback gap", "past performance vis-a-vis aspiration level"]
definition: Problemistic search is triggered when organizations fail to attain their aspiration-the minimal outcome that would be deemed satisfactory by the decision maker. Firms increase R&D investment to search for alternatives when performance falls below aspiration.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack search is stimulated by the firm's slack resources-excess inputs such as underutilized capacity, facilities, or labor and financial reserves like working capital or borrowing capacity. Slack relaxes the managers' control of R&D projects and encourages experimentation and exploration.

name: Expected performance below target
authors_terms: ["expected distance by which performance will fall below target", "expected underperforming gap", "performance prospect", "performance expectation"]
definition: Performance expectation reflects a forward-looking cognitive image because it takes into consideration the future environment and choices of actions and their payoffs. The comparison of firms' expected performance with their target or goal simplifies the interpretation of the future world and serves as a guideline for subsequent organizational decisions, and search is expected to increase when firms anticipate a shortfall below their performance target.

name: Expected performance above target
authors_terms: ["expected distance by which performance will exceed target", "expected outperforming gap", "positive prospect", "performance prospect"]
definition: The comparison of firms' expected performance with their target or goal simplifies the interpretation of the future world and serves as a guideline for subsequent organizational decisions. Search is likely to decrease when firms are expected to outperform their target level, because they do not have an incentive (increased performance) to justify taking on risk.

name: Indispensability in client projects
definition: An agent is indispensable when the underlying assets have no effect on the marginal productivity of the other parties' investments without the indispensable partner—the agent's human capital is critical for the project outcome.

name: Innovation capability
authors_terms: ["capabilities to innovate", "innovation capabilities", "knowledge-creation activities", "service development activities"]
definition: Service providers that invest highly in service development activities are more likely to have accumulated innovation capabilities that enable them to make unique intellectual contributions in client relationships.

name: Bargaining power
definition: Ownership shares and control rights in collaborative arrangements may reflect the bargaining power of the partners rather than the importance of their contributions. According to Aghion and Tirole (1994), the chief source of this type of inefficiency is differences in bargaining power.

name: Retained control rights to intellectual assets
authors_terms: ["control rights to intellectual assets", "retaining control rights", "output control rights to client", "control rights"]
definition: The allocation of rights to control knowledge assets created or used in a supply relationship between two firms. The two aspects studied are output control rights to client and partial exclusivity restrictions regarding supply to the client's competitors.

name: Service innovation
definition: Innovation output is measured by whether the firm has launched new or significantly improved services. Control rights allocation influences the performance of the supply relationship and the partners themselves through its effect on incentives to invest in innovation.

name: Service improvement
definition: Improvements are arguably more incremental service developments than are new service introductions, which require a successful departure from existing service activities and competencies.

name: New service introduction
definition: New service introductions require a successful departure from existing service activities and competencies.

name: Military service
authors_terms: ["ex-military CEO", "military background", "CEOs' military background", "service in the military", "military service", "ex-military CEOs"]
definition: Service of the CEO in any of the branches of the U.S. military (Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard), including the reserves. The authors argue that a military background reflects a certain character that, in turn, influences the CEO's decisions.

name: Fraudulent financial reporting
authors_terms: ["fraudulent financial reporting", "financial fraud", "fraudulent reporting", "cook the books"]
definition: Fraudulent financial reporting captures accounting-rule violations such as manipulation of records, omission of relevant information from financial statements, misapplication of accounting principles, or misappropriation of assets; it refers to a presentation of financial statements that do not conform to U.S. GAAP and has to be committed intentionally, which means that others are purposely misled.

name: Stock option backdating
authors_terms: ["backdating", "backdating of stock options", "option backdating", "stock option backdating"]
definition: Backdating is an opportunistic practice related to the timing of stock option grants: options are labeled backdated if the grant date of the stock option is a date in the recent past on which the stock price was lower than on the day of the actual compensation decision.

name: Vertical wage dispersion
authors_terms: ["vertical wage dispersion", "vertical dispersion", "vertical variance in pay", "vertical pay dispersion", "wage dispersion across levels"]
definition: Pay variance may be vertical, when wages vary across organizational levels; vertical dispersion reflects the internal and external worth of jobs, and organizational policies on the relative value of jobs.

name: Horizontal wage dispersion
authors_terms: ["horizontal wage dispersion", "horizontal dispersion", "horizontal variance in pay", "horizontal pay dispersion", "wage dispersion within levels"]
definition: Horizontal wage dispersion arises when wages vary within an organizational level, reflecting differences across individuals holding same-level jobs (i.e., in qualifications, performance, or political connections). Same-level dispersion is not tied to career ladders; it aims to sort out high performers from average and lower performers.

name: External mobility
definition: Our key dependent variable is an external move, defined as an instance of an employee's change of jobs across organizations.

name: Pay position within the firm
authors_terms: ["pay position", "individual pay position", "top earners", "bottom earners", "top wage earners", "bottom wage earners"]
definition: Employees are top (bottom) wage earners when they rank above (below) the 90th (10th) percentile of the distribution of the absolute wage within their firm in any given year. We compute separate measures to indicate top and bottom earners within vertical and horizontal wage distributions.

name: Business risk
authors_terms: ["business risk", "business, or unsystematic, risk", "firm-specific business risk"]
definition: Business risk is the component of total risk about which stockholders are indifferent because it is diversifiable; it reflects the variation in a stock's return ascribable to firm-specific forces.

name: Firm value
definition: The market value of a firm is the expected net present value of future cash flows; it is measured as Tobin's q, the ratio of the market value of a firm's equity and debt to the replacement cost of the firm's assets.

name: Cash flow
definition: The expected level of cash flows that a firm's asset base can generate; the cash-flow motive holds that low business risk allows firms to acquire inputs cheaply or to operate efficiently, so that lower business risk is associated with higher cash flows.

name: Rate of return
authors_terms: ["rate of return", "rates of return", "equilibrium stock returns", "market return", "Jensen's alpha"]
definition: The return investors require on a firm's stock; assuming capital market equilibrium, lower business risk translates into a lower market return on the stocks of firms.

name: Technological dynamism
definition: The technological dynamism of an industry reflects the extent to which resident firms emphasize investments in research and development (R&D), estimated with an index of industry-level R&D intensity. Technologically dynamic industries should exhibit higher levels of RDI because their competitive dynamics are largely driven by innovation and technological change.

name: Ego network openness
authors_terms: ["open ego networks", "closed ego networks", "propensity to form more-open ego networks", "ego-network constraint", "constraint change"]
definition: Pursuing a closed ego network entails forming ties to partners that are connected to one another, while pursuing an open ego network involves forming ties to partners that are not connected. The two behaviors are distinguished by Burt's measure of ego-network constraint, which increases as ego's contacts become more connected to one another and decreases as they become more separated.

name: Network connectedness
definition: Network connectedness reflects the extent to which network actors can reach one another via network ties. High network connectedness indicates that most firms can access one another via a network path of some length, while low connectedness indicates that most firms are structurally isolated from one another.

name: Network community structure
definition: Community structure captures the distribution (rather than existence) of network ties throughout the network. Strong community structure signals that the distribution of ties is uneven and that the network is characterized by the presence of many relatively small groups (or communities) of densely interconnected firms, whereas weak community structure suggests a more homogenous distribution of ties.

name: High-performance work system
authors_terms: ["high-performance work system (HPWS)", "HPWS", "HPWS utilization", "use of an HPWS"]
definition: An HPWS has been defined as a configuration of coherent practices designed to enhance employees' skills, motivation, and participation in order to improve the value of their collective contributions.

name: HPWS internal consistency
authors_terms: ["HPWS internal consistency", "internal consistency", "internal consistency in the implementation"]
definition: Internal consistency refers to the relative uniformity in the intensity of implementation across HR practices within an HR system. In the present context it is focus on internal consistency in the intensity of implementation across the AMO domains of HR practices.

name: Market entry timing mode
authors_terms: ["market entry timing mode", "entry timing mode", "market entry timing", "entry timing"]
definition: Market entry timing represents the staging element of an innovative strategy, wherein organizations decide upon timing of entry into markets with their products. An organization may choose to be either a first mover, a fast follower, or a fence sitter.

name: Product sales
definition: We focus on product sales as a proximal indicator of organizational performance. We expect that the differential effects of vertical fit in an HPWS with respect to different entry timing modes will be manifested in the product sales revenues of the organization.

name: Financial performance
definition: Profitability is the ultimate performance measure of an HPWS in this context. Financial performance is measured as a ratio of operating profit to average total assets (ROA).

name: Peer regulation stringency
authors_terms: ["peer regulation", "regulations faced by peer firms in external jurisdictions", "PEER_REGULATION", "the RPS face by peers"]
definition: Peers are defined as firms that operate in common output markets but face differing policy obligations. Peer regulation is the average RPS faced by all other IOUs that operate in the same state(s) as a focal firm, excluding the RPS that they commonly face; where a peer is a multistate utility its RPS objective is measured as the most stringent policy it faces across its multiple states.

name: Neighboring jurisdiction regulation stringency
definition: The stringency of RPS policies in states contiguous to where a focal firm operates, coded as the average RPS objective of the contiguous states where the focal firm does not have any operations.

name: Environmental performance
authors_terms: ["environmental performance", "renewable power", "more stringent operating practices", "PERCENT_RENEWABLES", "total renewable power distributed to the end consumer"]
definition: The authors state that their predictions concern firms' environmental performance, which is a function of both what an IOU generates and what it sources from independent power producers. It is measured as the share of total power sold by the IOU from wind, solar, hydroelectric, biomass, and geothermal generating sources.

name: Industry velocity
authors_terms: ["industry velocity", "industry clockspeed", "high- and low-velocity conditions", "high-velocity conditions", "low-velocity conditions"]
definition: These changes in aggregate actions represent the velocity of an industry: The rate of new products, processes, and competitive changes. Industry clockspeed reflects rates of change in an industry and is made up of product, process, and organizational clockspeeds.

name: Social network homogeneity
authors_terms: ["network homogeneity", "homogeneity in social networks", "membership homogeneity", "resource access homogeneity"]
definition: We then identified network homogeneity by two key elements of networks—membership and resource access. A high coefficient of variation suggests that firms focus on developing ties with a single or few constituents, and therefore reflects high network homogeneity.

name: Social network tie strength
authors_terms: ["network strength", "strength of social network ties", "strong networks", "weak network ties"]
definition: Strong networks, reflecting high frequency and extended history of ties with a social actor, increase trust and commitment among constituents and promote detailed exchange of information. The higher the average network age and frequency of networks with the same member firms, the stronger the network.

name: Adaptive environmental assumptions
definition: Low-velocity firms are likely to assume that their environments are concrete and measurable; they therefore tend to collect detailed information to use in developing 'correct' assumptions of their environments. We refer to such assumptions about the environment as adaptive.

name: Enactive environmental assumptions
definition: Firms in high-velocity industries are likely to create their own environments by consistently searching for new ideas and experimenting beyond existing areas. We refer to such assumptions about the environment as enactive.

name: Collective strategy frame complexity
definition: Complexity reflects the breadth and range of the common stock of knowledge that firms accumulate about their environments, rules of competition, and actions. High complexity allows firms to construct their environments broadly by addressing a wider range of stimuli and by considering a wide repertoire of strategic actions.

name: Collective strategy frame consensus
definition: We defined consensus as the percentage of concepts and links between concepts that were present in the strategy frames of all the member firms in the core group.

name: Pattern of change in collective strategy frames
authors_terms: ["pattern of change", "pattern of evolution", "medium-scope changes", "radical changes", "incremental changes"]
definition: We further propose that the collective assumptions and social networks create distinct patterns of evolution in collective strategy frames, and we focus on three facets of evolution identified in the literature—pattern, magnitude, and timing. The pattern, magnitude, and timing of changes in collective strategy frames affect how and when firms collectively change their actions.

name: Magnitude of change in collective strategy frames
authors_terms: ["magnitude of changes in the collective strategy frames", "magnitude of change"]
definition: The magnitude of changes in the causal maps is represented by the level of change in the core concepts in the maps. Core concepts in a strategy frame represent central concepts that have a significant depth of meaning to strategic decision makers.

name: Performance decline
definition: We classified negative yearly changes in the three performance variables in which the standard error values were outside the 95% confidence interval, as assessed by ACF, as performance decline periods. We classified other years as stable performance periods.

name: Aggregate actions
authors_terms: ["aggregate actions", "changes in aggregate actions", "frequency of changes in aggregate actions"]
definition: These changes in the collective strategy frames drive the aggregate actions of member firms in the form of changes in product, process, and organization. Figure 2(b) shows the frequency of aggregate product changes (new products introduced), process changes (new processes introduced), and organizational changes (e.g., mergers, acquisitions, divestiture, capital expansions in the form of new machinery, and factories) undertaken by the aircraft and semiconductor groups.

name: Alliance benefits
authors_terms: ["alliance benefits", "benefits from membership in a multipartner alliance", "benefits to partners", "private benefits"]
definition: Multipartner alliances in technology-driven industries offer various benefits to partners with respect to both their product development and marketing efforts. To capture different aspects of alliance benefits, the authors consider three measures: productivity, market success, and market exposure.

name: Productivity
definition: The multipartner alliance's contribution to the product development efforts of each partner, measured as the partner's number of certified products standardized by the duration of the partner's membership in the alliance.

name: Market success
definition: The extent to which partners succeeded with the products that they introduced or marketed in the Wi-Fi market, capturing product quality and customer acceptance.

name: Market exposure
definition: Multipartner alliances offer legitimacy and reputation benefits beyond those directly related to products and services; market exposure captures these broader benefits.

name: Internal involvement in a multipartner alliance
definition: Internal involvement refers to the extent to which partners engage in organizational activities of a focal multipartner alliance.

name: External involvement in competing multipartner alliances
definition: External involvement pertains to the extent to which partners also participate in competing multipartner alliances.

name: Timing of entry into a multipartner alliance
authors_terms: ["timing of entry", "timing of alliance entry", "order of entry"]
definition: The authors define the timing of alliance entry in terms of the order in which partners join a multipartner alliance; an entry is early when it occurred before the majority of partners entered the multipartner alliance.

name: Earnings management
definition: Earnings management refers to the use of accounting techniques to produce a desired earnings figure, and one commonly adopted tool is accruals management, earnings components that are not reflected in current cash flows. The measure is based on total accruals, the greater values of which indicate that earnings quality is poor.

name: Performance relative to analyst expectations
authors_terms: ["meeting analyst expectations", "failure to meet analyst expectations", "earnings miss", "meeting or beating earnings expectations"]
definition: Each quarter, corporate earnings should meet or beat securities analysts' consensus forecasts, the average earnings forecast among analysts who cover a firm. Firms that miss earnings expectations, even by small margins, are likely to suffer severe drops in their stock prices while those meeting them typically enjoy substantial price appreciations.

name: Analyst earnings expectations
definition: The consensus forecast is the mean of forecasts made by analysts just before quarterly earnings' actual announcement. Their earnings forecasts have emerged as the single most important yardstick against which the performance of both firms and managers is gauged.

name: Cumulative success in meeting expectations
authors_terms: ["consecutive number of times a firm met analyst expectations", "cumulative", "past successes in meeting expectations"]
definition: Building on insights that current performance is compared with prior performance, the authors propose that analysts evaluate firms cumulatively such that each time they manage to meet analyst expectations, analysts raise the bar on future expectations.

name: Peer success in meeting expectations
authors_terms: ["density of a focal firm's industry peers that met analyst expectations", "comparative", "peer successes in meeting expectations"]
definition: Analysts are likely to adjust performance expectations about a focal firm according to how well or poorly its industry peers have done, so that evaluation of the focal firm may also be formed comparatively, relative to the performance of its industry peers.

name: Stock market reaction to earnings announcements
authors_terms: ["stock market penalties", "cumulative excess returns", "market reactions", "stock market valuation"]
definition: Firms that miss earnings expectations, even by small margins, are likely to suffer severe drops in their stock prices while those meeting them typically enjoy substantial price appreciations; these positive and negative market reactions are independent of firms' absolute performance.

name: Noncore asset divestiture
definition: Divestiture of noncore businesses is a quick, assured measure that managers can take to enhance shareholder value, and it helps firms display conformity to the precept of focusing on core competencies. Divested assets were considered noncore if they were not in the same four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code of the focal firm.

name: Quality affirmative action programs
authors_terms: ["high-quality affirmative action programs", "quality affirmative action programs", "high-quality voluntary affirmative action programs", "Exemplary Voluntary Efforts Award"]
definition: For the purpose of our study, we viewed high-quality affirmative action programs as a proxy for the effective management of diverse human resources. Current voluntary affirmative action initiatives instituted by corporations actively promote the employment of individuals who are members of traditional minority groups when those individuals possess the qualifications necessary for a job.

name: Discriminatory practices
authors_terms: ["discriminatory organizational practices", "discriminatory practices", "found guilty of discrimination", "discrimination settlements"]
definition: Our other premise was that discriminatory organizational practices are harmful and have negative economic consequences. Discriminatory practices are only a dimension of the ineffective management of diversity.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock price changes", "stock returns", "excess return", "stock price valuations"]
definition: The expected return is subtracted from the actual return to obtain the excess return. If a significant excess return occurs in response to an announcement, it suggests that the announcement will have either net costs or net benefits for the corporation concerned.

name: Spousal team
definition: The spousal team variable refers to a firm that is owned and managed by a spousal couple. A spousal couple is defined as a couple that is married, has a registered partnership, or lives together with children.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["firm growth", "growth rate", "change in number of employees"]
definition: We measured firm growth as change in number of employees; the growth rate for each firm i in point t is the logarithmic difference in employees from the previous year. The logarithm of the growth variable corrects for the skewed distribution, resulting in a normal distribution.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age was measured as the number of years a firm existed since its inception. The variable was truncated over 20 years because the exact founding year could only be determined from 1987 onward.

name: Number of owners
definition: We calculated this variable as the total number of owners for each firm in each year.

name: Heterogeneity in team industry experience
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in team industry experience", "heterogeneity in the team industry experience"]
definition: Heterogeneity in industry experience implies that team members have different points of view regarding how to operate the business. It was measured as the coefficient of variation for the number of years of industry experience within the entrepreneurial team, where years of industry experience denotes the number of years of work experience a team member has gained in the same industry as the firm he or she is currently involved in.

name: Technological recency
authors_terms: ["technological recency", "recency of technological inputs", "recency of factor inputs", "recency of the knowledge inputs", "recency of knowledge inputs", "technological input age", "input age"]
definition: The recency (i.e., age) of the knowledge inputs that an invention builds upon. Recent or nascent technologies are at the forefront of technological progress and define the technology frontier, whereas mature technologies have been in existence for some time and their characteristics are relatively well understood.

name: Inventive value
authors_terms: ["inventive value", "financial value of the invention", "financial performance", "financial returns to the innovation", "stock return"]
definition: The financial value of an invention, assessed as the response of the financial markets to a firm's new inventions. Because the price of a security represents market expectations of the discounted value of the firm's future cash flows, relating a measure to stock return provides insights into market expectations of the long-term value prospects of the invention.

name: Users in technical roles
authors_terms: ["user-inventors", "users in technical roles", "physician-inventors", "users as inventors (technical role)"]
definition: Inventors are expected to generate variety - that is, to find novel and different solutions to the firm's technology and customer problems. Because inventors are expected to generate a variety of solutions in their role, user-inventors can assist innovation by exposing the firm to a broad range of relevant user problems and solutions.

name: Users in executive roles
authors_terms: ["user-executives", "users in executive roles", "users as members of the executive team"]
definition: A young firm's executives mediate between the organization's technical core, which generates ideas for products, and the customers who buy them. Executive roles thus center on selecting from a variety of technical solutions a few feasible alternatives for the organization to implement.

name: Users in the CEO role
definition: The CEO is the most senior, and likely the most central and influential, single role in a young firm's executive team, dealing with the most diverse cognitive load and with the most time pressure to converge on a single path for the organization to follow.

name: Users in board roles
definition: Venture boards help firms as they generate a variety of ideas for innovation, and participate in the selection of relevant ideas to execute. Boards thus add variety to the firm's in-house expertise of spotting technology and market opportunities and recognizing product voids in the current market.

name: Product innovation
definition: Following Laursen (2011), we measured innovation using yearly counts of product approvals for each sample firm. Product approvals are an appropriate measure of commercial innovation because FDA approval is mandatory for any surgical instrument to be sold in the United States, and it demonstrates feasibility, effectiveness, and innovativeness of the product concept.

name: Collaborative integration
authors_terms: ["collaborative integration", "degree of integration", "integrated intraorganizational network", "integration of a firm's internal collaboration network"]
definition: By integration, we mean the degree to which the intraorganizational network consists of one interconnected component, providing inventors with opportunities for reciprocal knowledge exchange and 'continual re-definition of individual tasks through interaction with others'. Conversely, a lack of integration occurs when the intraorganizational network is fragmented across multiple unconnected groups and inventors, resulting in fewer opportunities for knowledge exchange and joint problem solving.

name: Knowledge diversity
authors_terms: ["knowledge diversity", "diversity of a firm's technological knowledge base", "degree of diversity of a firm's knowledge base"]
definition: The degree to which the specialized knowledge held by the firm's inventors is dispersed across different technological areas or, conversely, concentrated in a few areas. Knowledge diversity encumbers the exchange of recombination-related knowledge because when a firm's knowledge base is diverse, cognitive barriers arise that make it more difficult for inventors to understand each other and solve problems together.

name: Recombinant creation
authors_terms: ["recombinant creation", "innovation through recombinant creation", "creating new technological combinations"]
definition: Firms may vary in their ability to envision and create combinations using technologies that they have never combined before—what we call recombinant creation. Reflecting its capability-broadening nature, recombinant creation results in a widened repertoire of technological combinations.

name: Recombinant reuse
authors_terms: ["recombinant reuse", "innovation through recombinant reuse", "reusing known technological combinations"]
definition: Some firms may be more innovative than others because they have developed an ability to refine and reuse systematically known technological combinations to solve new problems and develop new applications—what we call recombinant reuse. Innovation through recombinant reuse is a 'capability deepening' exercise in which new technologies are derived by delving deeper into a firm's existing repertoire of combinations.

name: Expressive voting dissent
authors_terms: ["expressive voting dissent", "discharge dissent", "expressive dissent voting", "expressive voting dissent"]
definition: Prior research has conceived such voting, in which the instrumental decision-making function of shareholder voting is decoupled from its expressive use in voicing discontent with firm leadership, as expressive voting dissent (Sauerwald et al. 2016), and has documented its widespread use as a public communication channel with management (Yermack 2010).

name: CEO dismissal
definition: We consider a CEO turnover to be a dismissal when it was either: (a) announced as such (fired, agreed to step down, at the request of the board), (b) when the CEO stepped down immediately after a supervisory board or shareholder meeting, without a designated successor, or (c) when news coverage before the turnover mentions performance-related concerns with executive leadership (Wiersema and Zhang 2011).

name: Independent board chair
authors_terms: ["independent chair", "independent chair of the board", "independent board chairs"]
definition: The variable is coded 2 for a board chair who is 'independent from the company and its Management Board or any controlling shareholder' (Kodex 2022) (i.e., independent chair). We consider a chair to be independent when the chair has no personal (family ties or close associates) or professional (employment or advisory) relationship with a company stakeholder (e.g., management, shareholder, customer, or supplier).

name: Family board chair
definition: The variable is coded 1 (i.e., family chair) whenever the supervisory board chair is a member of the family with an ownership stake in the firm. Being the face of the family in the firm, family chairs identify with both the firm and the family, which likely engenders an understanding of their role in the firm as stewards of the legitimacy of both.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: We code institutional ownership by aggregating the percentage of a firm's shares owned by institutional investors (i.e., investors that invest on behalf of other investors) in a firm-year.

name: Family ownership
definition: We code family ownership by adding all ownership percentages held by the founding family or individual family members. This ownership percentage is calculated using the percentage of voting shares of total shares outstanding (Villalonga and Amit 2006).

name: Organizational failures
definition: Broadly defined, failures are deviations from expected and desired goals and are frequently operationalized as accidents or similar events; in this setting the failure events are accidents experienced by a pipeline operator in the focal year.

name: Prior organizational failures
authors_terms: ["past failures", "failure experience", "count of total accidents in the previous three years"]
definition: The accumulated experience of failure in an organization's past. The argument put forth by prior scholars is that failure spurs learning by prompting an organizational search for new ways of doing things in order to avoid the recurrence of failures.

name: Failures from human error
authors_terms: ["failures resulting from human error", "accidents by human error", "failures attributed to human error", "incorrect operation"]
definition: Failures for which the identified primary cause is human error, as opposed to some other factor. In this setting, an accident is coded as resulting from human error if the primary cause recorded on the accident report is 'incorrect operation'.

name: Failures from other causes
authors_terms: ["failures resulting from other causes", "accidents by other causes", "failures attributed to causes other than human error"]
definition: Failures for which the identified primary cause is not human error; organizational members attribute causality to some other situational, technical, or environmental factor.

name: Prior failures from human error
authors_terms: ["past failures resulting from human error", "failures resulting from human error in the past", "count of accidents by human error from t-3 to t-1"]
definition: The organization's accumulated experience of failures attributed to human error in prior periods; such failures are argued to elicit a greater allocation of attentional resources and to result in a subsequent decrease in the likelihood of failures resulting from human error.

name: Prior failures from other causes
authors_terms: ["past failures resulting from other causes", "count of accidents by other causes from t-3 to t-1"]
definition: The organization's accumulated experience of failures attributed to causes other than human error in prior periods; such failures act as weak cues that attract less organizational attention and tend to produce weaker learning outcomes.

name: Code-preserving changes
definition: We define code-preserving changes as a variation in a firm's product range that preserves the social code within which the firm positions its offering. A code-preserving change is any variation that conforms to the rules of conduct representative of the social form within which the organization is nested.

name: Code-violating changes
definition: By contrast, a code-violating change corresponds to a variation in the product range that breaks with past signals and embraces a rival social code. A code-violating change is any variation that violates the rules of conduct representative of the social form.

name: Code-preserving changes relative to peers
authors_terms: ["Code-preserving changes relative to peers", "code-preserving changes relative to peers"]
definition: For relative changes vis-a-vis peers, every year we calculated the difference between a chef's number of changes and the average of competitors' changes. We defined competitors as the chefs belonging to the same region with the same evaluations (same number of stars).

name: Code-violating changes relative to peers
authors_terms: ["Code-violating changes relative to peers", "code-violating changes relative to peers"]
definition: What matters is not only the absolute number of code-preserving and code-violating changes undertaken by a focal organization, but also whether they exceed the average number of such changes initiated by competitors. We called these variables 'Code-preserving changes relative to peers' and 'Code-violating changes relative to peers'.

name: External evaluation
definition: Our dependent variable, external evaluation, was defined as the number of stars received by a chef in the Guide Michelin each year. External evaluation can have three values: 1, 2, or 3.

name: Restaurant age
definition: Restaurant age is the logged number of years the organization was in existence after being given a star.

name: Prior evaluation
authors_terms: ["Lagged evaluation", "prior evaluations", "past evaluations", "lagged reputation", "evaluations received in the past"]
definition: Lagged evaluation is the number of stars obtained by the restaurant at t - 1. The more favorable the evaluation from critics received in the past, the higher is the organization's status.

name: Voluntary restatement of earnings
authors_terms: ["voluntary disclosure of wrongdoing", "voluntary restatement of earnings", "coming forward", "voluntary restaters"]
definition: 'Voluntary restatements were deemed to occur when a firm proactively announced that it was restating earnings without prodding from the SEC.' The authors relate voluntary disclosure of wrongdoing to the voluntary restatements in their sample, which are 'indicative of intentional, manipulative, or fraudulent behavior.'

name: Performance leader restatement
definition: The extent to which firms that previously voluntarily restated earnings held leadership positions in the industry in terms of performance; leaders can be viewed in terms of performance and size.

name: Size leader restatement
definition: The extent to which firms that previously voluntarily restated earnings held leadership positions in the industry in terms of size; leaders can be viewed in terms of performance and size.

name: Peer voluntary restatements
authors_terms: ["peer restaters", "number of previous voluntary restaters in the industry", "informal peer forces"]
definition: 'Peer disclosure of wrongdoing is operationalized as the number of previous voluntarily restatements by firms in a given industry.'

name: Shared auditor network tie
definition: Intermediaries connect firms indirectly, serve as transporters of information, and can facilitate diffusion of ideal behaviors; in this research network connections are operationalized using a shared auditor.

name: Formal regulatory forces
authors_terms: ["formal regulatory forces", "formal sanctions", "formal legal sanctions", "forced restaters"]
definition: Formal, regulatory pressures to conform to industry and societal standards; deterrence theory states that firms comply with the law out of fear of punishment. Such forces are measured as the count of firms in a given industry that were previously forced to restate by the SEC in the prior year.

name: Informal social forces
definition: Informal forces work through social norms and practices, encouraging voluntary compliance; informal pressures to disclose prior wrongdoing may arise from the actions of industry leaders and peers and through network connections.

name: Firm status
definition: 'Status represents a firm's perceived quality vis-à-vis its peers (Podolny 1993) or the amount of "honor or esteem" accorded to a firm.'

name: Entry barrier reduction
authors_terms: ["SARE", "System of Rapid Business Opening", "reduction in entry barriers", "lower entry barriers", "policy change"]
definition: A policy change in Mexico that reduced entry barriers to entrepreneurship: SARE cut the average business registration time from 30.1 to 1.4 days, reduced office visits from 4.2 to 1, and lowered the number of required procedures from 7.9 to 2.7, with a staggered rollout beginning in May 2002.

name: Patriarchy logic
definition: An institutional logic that defines the norms, values, beliefs, and practices that prescribe gender-appropriate roles and behaviors for men and women in society. From a normative standpoint it views women primarily as caregivers and men as breadwinners; in cognitive terms it holds that men align more naturally with the public and economic sphere and women with the private and domestic one.

name: Gender gap in entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["gender gap in entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial gap between men and women", "gender disparities in entrepreneurship", "gender gap"]
definition: The entrepreneurial gap between men and women following a policy change, that is, the differential effect of the policy on women compared with men in entering entrepreneurship.

name: Business ownership
authors_terms: ["Entrepreneurship", "registered business owner", "owner of a business", "entry into entrepreneurship"]
definition: An entrepreneur is an individual registered as the owner of a business, and the authors focus on ownership as their primary outcome to be consistent with past literature and the legal, social, and economic benefits that ownership provides.

name: Unpaid work in a family member's business
authors_terms: ["unpaid work in a family member's business", "unpaid work", "unpaid worker in a family member's business"]
definition: Working for a family member's business without pay in a given quarter. It specifically measures unpaid work in a family member's business and does not include other forms of family labor such as housework or childcare.

name: Gender
definition: A dummy variable indicating whether an individual stated that they were a woman.

name: Domestic market position
authors_terms: ["firm's domestic market share", "domestic market position", "market share in Japan"]
definition: We classified firms into four groups: those with market shares smaller than 5 percent, with market shares between 5 and 10 percent, with market shares between 10 and 20 percent, and with market shares greater than 20 percent, respectively. The latter group we consider dominant firms; firms with market shares within the 10-20 percent range are considered competitive but non-dominant firms.

name: Industry world market position
authors_terms: ["Japan industry's world market share", "position of Japanese industry in the world market", "global competitiveness of Japanese industry"]
definition: We measure the global competitiveness of Japanese industry (Hypothesis 2) by the world market share of Japanese firms. Based on the information available, Japanese industry's world market share could be classified as low (< 25 percent), intermediate (25-75 percent), or dominant (> 75 percent).

name: Loose oligopoly
definition: We followed Shepherd (1997) in defining a loose oligopoly as an industry with a Herfindahl index greater than 1000 and smaller than 1800. Loose oligopoly is a dummy variable that takes the value 1 for such industries and tests Hypothesis 3.

name: Technology intensity
definition: Technology intensity (Hypothesis 4) is measured as the number of patents in the 5-year period 1989-93 granted to the firm or its subsidiaries by the U.S. patent office, per 1 billion yen of turnover.

name: Global plant configuration
definition: We distinguish three major foreign plant configurations: (1) Asia-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in Asia only); (2) West-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in the United States and/or the European Union but not in Asia); (3) global configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in all regions).

name: West-bound plant configuration
definition: We distinguish three major foreign plant configurations: (1) Asia-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in Asia only); (2) West-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in the United States and/or the European Union but not in Asia); (3) global configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in all regions).

name: Asia-bound plant configuration
definition: We distinguish three major foreign plant configurations: (1) Asia-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in Asia only); (2) West-bound configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in the United States and/or the European Union but not in Asia); (3) global configurations (foreign manufacturing investment in all regions).

name: Foreign investment decision
authors_terms: ["decision to invest abroad", "foreign investment decision", "internationalization decision"]
definition: We model the probability that a certain plant configuration is chosen as the product of (1) the probability to invest abroad and (2) the probability that the plant configuration is chosen conditional on a positive internationalization decision.

name: Strategic reorientation
definition: We define strategic reorientation as a change in business strategy coupled with change in other key organizational dimensions. Thus, a change in business strategy is a necessary but not sufficient condition for strategic reorientation.

name: Past performance
authors_terms: ["past performance", "past performance relative to the industry average", "return on assets"]
definition: An organization's past performance provides feedback about the relative effectiveness of an organization's chosen strategy. Managers are assumed to compare their performance to a relevant reference point or target level of performance.

name: Environmental awareness
authors_terms: ["environmental awareness", "awareness of environmental changes", "awareness of environmental contingencies"]
definition: The more managers are aware of changes in their environmental context, the more likely they are to make strategic reorientations. Managers were coded as being aware of environmental contingencies if they indicated explicitly that they had observed or were predicting a specific change in their organization's environment.

name: External attribution bias
authors_terms: ["external attribution bias", "attributional bias", "external attributions for poor performance outcomes"]
definition: Managers' attributions for the organization's previous performance may be biased, such that poor performance outcomes are attributed to external events and good performance outcomes are attributed to the organization's strategy. The external attribution bias was coded as present when a company made external attributions rather than internal attributions for poor performance outcomes.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["top management team heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of a top management team with respect to functional backgrounds"]
definition: The heterogeneity of a top management team is likely to influence strategy formulation through its effect on the diversity of perspectives brought to bear on strategic questions, where a diversity of perspectives can create disagreements and equivocal experiences that result in more extensive discussion of strategic options and more learning opportunities.

name: CEO turnover
definition: A change in the CEO was coded when the CEO or President changed within the given time period.

name: Top management team turnover
authors_terms: ["top management team turnover", "top management team change"]
definition: Individuals were considered members of the top management team when they were listed as an executive officer; change in the top management team was measured as a percentage variable.

name: Environmental turbulence
authors_terms: ["turbulence of environmental context", "volatile or turbulent environments", "industry context"]
definition: The likelihood of strategic reorientation is expected to vary across industry contexts, with such change being more common in turbulent environments than in stable ones. The furniture industry represents a stable environment and computer software represents a turbulent environment.

name: Formal control structure
authors_terms: ["formal hierarchy", "formal hierarchical control structure", "hierarchical control structure"]
definition: Formal hierarchy refers to explicitly established layers of authority that create a vertical differentiation of power. It is the 'explicit' rank order of individuals, delineating the extent to which an organization is characterized by a vertical division of labor, such as between supervisors and subordinates.

name: Informal hierarchy
definition: Informal hierarchy has been defined as the 'unofficial stratification among members of a social system . . . which emerge[s] from social interaction and become[s] persistent over time through repeated social processes.' Informal hierarchy is the 'implicit' rather than 'explicit' rank order of individuals within an organization or group.

name: Collective psychological ownership
definition: Collective psychological ownership occurs when individuals within a group share the feeling that the target of ownership is 'ours,' which in turn determines guidelines for action around those objects.

name: Intragroup conflict
definition: This measure gauges conflict-related behavior among group members during decision-making and operational activities. Conflict stems from the process of collective decision making, in which members often have heterogeneous opinions regarding appropriate action, and also occurs when members fail to contribute equally.

name: Export sales
authors_terms: ["export sales", "absolute amount of export sales", "export performance"]
definition: The export sales of a company in millions of yen in year t. The authors present the absolute amount of export sales as one of two firm-level measures of export performance.

name: Export ratio
authors_terms: ["export ratio", "EXPORT%", "relative share of exports in the total sales of a firm"]
definition: (Export sales)/(Total sales) in percent in year t. It is the relative share of exports in the total sales of a firm and serves as the second firm-level measure of export performance.

name: R&D expenditures
definition: R&D spending of a company in millions of yen in 1983.

name: R&D intensity
definition: (R&D83)/(Total sales in 1983), i.e. the firm's R&D percentage of sales.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: Industry average R&D percentage compiled by Statistics Bureau, Management and Coordination Agency, Japan (1985) in 1983.

name: Firm size
definition: Total assets value of a company in millions of yen in 1983.

name: Domestic market leadership
definition: A LEADER is identified on the basis of the firm's relative size in the industry: if a company is a leading firm in an industry, it is assigned a 1; otherwise, it is assigned a 0. We include a dummy variable (LEADER) to analyze whether the industry leader's export behavior is different from that of smaller firms.

name: Domestic sales
definition: The domestic sales of a company in millions of yen in year t.

name: Frequency-based cross-border bandwagons of FDI
authors_terms: ["frequency-based cross-border bandwagons of FDI", "frequency mechanism", "frequency-based bandwagons of FDI"]
definition: The increases in the number (i.e., frequency) of FDI entries into a host country by industry peers from other home countries create both institutional and competitive bandwagon pressures for prospective investors and drive their new entries into the same industry in the host country. In a host country of emerging economy, increases in the frequency of early foreign entries in an industry by investors from other home countries impose both competitive and institutional bandwagon pressures, driving new foreign entries by firms from a different home country.

name: Cohesion-based cross-border bandwagons of FDI
authors_terms: ["cohesion-based cross-border bandwagons of FDI", "cohesion mechanism", "firm-country cohesion mechanism", "international networks of FDI"]
definition: A new firm-country cohesion mechanism in driving cross-border bandwagons of FDI: a firm's international networks of FDI. This new cohesion mechanism via international networks of FDI enables foreign firms to better access the information sourced from other foreign countries (i.e., the second origin) regarding these countries' outbound FDI entries into a host country of interest, so that prospective foreign investors can better sense cross-border bandwagon pressures of FDI to drive their own entries into the country.

name: Foreign market entry
authors_terms: ["Entry into a host country", "new entries into China", "FDI entries into China"]
definition: The dependent variable, Entryijt, is a dummy variable which equals 1 if Japanese firm i invested in China in relevant industry j in year t, and 0 otherwise. An industry is defined as relevant for a focal firm when it is one of the listed industries of the firm, or one in which the firm had previously invested in other countries.

name: Information voids
authors_terms: ["information voids", "host country information voids", "the extent of information voids"]
definition: Institutional voids are often accompanied by information voids - the absence of credible and readily available information about the local investment climate. Information voids in a host country of emerging economy would limit the provision of public information on early FDI entries, and the provided information would also be low in value regarding FDI bandwagons.

name: Knowledge-based resources
authors_terms: ["knowledge-based resources", "bundle of knowledge-based resources", "procedural knowledge", "market knowledge", "technological knowledge"]
definition: Whereas knowledge-based resources are the ways in which firms combine and transform these tangible input resources. Following Gupta and Govindarajan (2000), the authors focus on procedural knowledge, i.e. knowing the procedures for how to do things, which arises from experience with similar situations, with market and technological knowledge as two strands of procedural knowledge applicable to discovering and exploiting opportunities.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: EO refers to a firm's strategic orientation, capturing specific entrepreneurial aspects of decision-making styles, methods, and practices. EO is a combination of three dimensions: innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors ascribe to the view that performance is multidimensional and that performance comparisons with competitors reveal important information; respondents compared the development of their own firm over the past 3 years relative to their two most important competitors for 10 different dimensions of performance.

name: Market opportunity count
authors_terms: ["number of additional market opportunities", "number of market opportunities identified prior to market entry", "market opportunity count"]
definition: The number of alternative market opportunities entrepreneurs considered prior to the first market entry, i.e. the additional market opportunities identified before the first entry.

name: Market opportunity variety
authors_terms: ["variety of market opportunities", "opportunity variety", "variety of the venture's pre-entry opportunity set", "strategic variety of opportunities"]
definition: The variety of the venture's pre-entry market opportunity set, capturing how distant from one another the market opportunities identified prior to first entry are.

name: Founding team industry experience
authors_terms: ["founding team industry experience", "team industry experience", "number of different industries represented in the founding team's experience", "internal knowledge breadth"]
definition: The founding teams' preexisting industry knowledge, that is, the number of different industries in which the founding team had gathered experience prior to new firm creation.

name: External knowledge sourcing breadth
authors_terms: ["external knowledge sourcing relationships", "external knowledge sourcing breadth", "number of different external knowledge relationships tapped", "external knowledge sources"]
definition: The number of different knowledge sourcing relationships (suppliers, financiers, consultants, etc.) that founders may tap in their external search for market opportunities.

name: Technological experience
definition: Experience that provides founders with the ability to assimilate market-related knowledge in technology-to-market linking and to recognize how their technological resources can be employed to cater to more distant market opportunities.

name: Firm diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification after the initial market entry", "subsequent firm diversification", "likelihood of subsequent diversification"]
definition: Whether the venture diversified during its early-stage development, that is, within five years after the initial entry.

name: Strategic asset ownership
authors_terms: ["strategic asset ownership", "ownership rights", "strategic asset owners", "subsidiary ownership rights", "strategic asset ownership rights"]
definition: Ownership rights are all remaining rights not granted to the nonowners, namely, the control and income rights to the asset (Grossman & Hart, 1986). The business units or subsidiaries with strategic asset ownership rights (ownership rights) have both the right to income from the strategic asset and the right to control it.

name: Technological innovation output
authors_terms: ["technological innovation", "innovation output", "innovation quantity", "innovation quality", "technological innovation output"]
definition: Technological innovation, defined as the generation of a new product, service, or production process technology (Damanpour, 1991), is an important source of value creation.

name: Innovation opportunity
definition: R&D tax subsidies affect R&D opportunity by reducing the cost of undertaking R&D projects. I use R&D tax subsidies as a measure of innovation opportunity (Hall & Van Reenen, 2000).

name: Host-country relative technological advantage
authors_terms: ["host-country RTA", "host-country relative technological advantage", "relative technological advantage", "RTA"]
definition: Host-country RTA is operationalized using the revealed technological advantage index from the OECD, which represents the country-industry's technological specialization (Almeida, 1996). For each subsidiary, host-country RTA is measured as the host country-industry revealed technological advantage index minus the average value of the MNE's locations.

name: Income shielding potential
definition: MNEs also have an incentive to locate strategic asset ownership rights in income shielding locations to reduce taxes. Income shielding potential is operationalized using a binary indicator for whether the subsidiary is located in a Tax Haven as classified by Dharmapala and Hines (2009).

name: Procedural justice
definition: The extent to which the acquirer makes an effort to assure fairness of procedures and processes in decision making. This justice type incorporates both the acquirer's tendency of providing process control and giving voice to the acquired unit during the integration process.

name: Informational justice
definition: The extent to which the acquirer makes an effort to justify decisions and procedures. Informational justice reflects the extent to which information is communicated across former firm boundaries and the soundness of explanations provided about the M&A decision-making process.

name: Post-deal value creation
definition: Value creation following the acquisition, assessed as changes in the combined firm's performance. Perceptual measures of post-deal value creation resolve into two factors: market position (sales growth, market share, and innovation/research and development) and financial return (profitability and stock price).

name: Abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns from JV internalization", "cumulative abnormal returns", "CAR", "shareholder wealth effects of JV partner buyouts", "firm valuation effects of JV termination"]
definition: The parent firm performance effects of JV termination were measured using event study methodology; the technique captures the parent firm's stock price change surrounding the JV buyout announcement after adjusting for general stock market movements and the firm's systematic risk.

name: R&D intensity
definition: Firms with significant technological know-how can best leverage it within the firm rather than across markets in order to avoid hold-up problems or misappropriation by others. Intangible resources are theorized to be subject to exchange hazards and coordination difficulties and therefore affect the firm's governance decisions and efficiency.

name: Advertising intensity
authors_terms: ["advertising intensity", "marketing know-how and goodwill", "advertising expense-to-sales ratio", "brand-name capital"]
definition: Parent firms' intangible resources subject to exchange hazards and coordination difficulties extend beyond technological know-how to include marketing know-how and goodwill resources; firms will prefer greater control over subsidiaries to reduce problems with free-riding on a brand name that the firm has developed through its advertising investments.

name: Cultural distance
definition: As the cultural distance between the parent firm's home country and the subsidiary's host country increases, transaction costs can increase because of higher information needs as well as administrative costs from encoding and decoding gaps in languages.

name: International experience
definition: Firms inexperienced in international settings face difficulties in overcoming internal uncertainty, monitoring operations, and instituting appropriate organizational controls. As firms gain international experience, the relative costs of internal organization decrease.

name: Political risk
authors_terms: ["political risk", "political turmoil risk", "financial transfer risk", "investment restriction risk"]
definition: Teece (1986) identifies political risk in particular as an important environmental factor affecting the relative efficiency of alternative governance structures: whereas wholly-owned subsidiaries involve a direct connection between the MNC and the host government, and this in turn increases the likelihood of hold-up after the firm has made sunk investments, firms using JVs are less susceptible to political risk because the local partner acts as a buffer.

name: Course of action
authors_terms: ["continue prior action course", "change prior action course", "continuing (rather than changing) the course of action", "continuing-changing actions"]
definition: The directions of the actions that occurred in each event were coded according to whether they represented an expansion (addition, elaboration, reinforcement), contraction (subtraction, reduction, de-emphasize), modification (revision, shift, correction), or continuation (in current direction) of the course of action underway on the topic. In the analysis these four types of actions were grouped into continue prior action (continuation and expansion) and change prior action (contraction and modification).

name: Outcome assessment
authors_terms: ["positive or negative outcomes", "in-process innovation outcomes", "positive minus negative outcomes", "outcome assessments"]
definition: When events occurred that provided evidence of results, they were coded as representing either positive (good news or successful accomplishment), negative (bad news or instances of failure or mistakes), and mixed (neutral or ambiguous news or results indicating elements of both success and failure). Outcomes include both tangible results of action courses and completion of planned targets, as well as less tangible value judgments about the success or failure of an innovation's activities by key resource controllers and innovation managers.

name: Resource controller intervention
authors_terms: ["interventions by resource controllers", "interventions by outside resource controllers", "external interventions", "investor interventions"]
definition: When a resource controller was behaviorally involved in an event, it was coded as such; external investors or top management resource controllers may intervene in the assessment process and thereby modify the course of action being taken by the entrepreneurial unit.

name: Goal and outcome criteria shifts
authors_terms: ["shifts in goals or outcome criteria", "outcome criteria shifts", "goal/criteria shifts", "shifts in outcome criteria"]
definition: When a resource controller or TAP SBU manager stated a goal or an outcome criterion for judging TAP's success that was different from the past, it was coded as a shift. Repeated interview responses were tabulated to identify the in-process outcome criteria used and how they changed over time.

name: External context events
definition: When an event involved a change in technology, structure, or activity occurring external (but reported as relevant) to the TAP SBU, it was coded as a contextual event. Thus, context includes events that occurred in the larger environment (such as events in other organizations, the industry, or the FDA regulatory agency).

name: Competitive intensity
definition: Barnett (1997) defines competitive intensity at the firm level, as the effect that a firm has on other firms' survival chances. This definition suggests that firms within an industry compete differently depending on their resources and their competitive efforts.

name: Interfirm collaboration
definition: I define collaboration as voluntary cooperation between firms involving exchange, sharing, or codevelopment of products, technologies, or services (Gulati, 1998).

name: Industry technology intensity
authors_terms: ["industry technology intensity", "technology intensity", "technology intensive industries", "technological environments"]
definition: An industry's technology intensity is defined as the ratio of research and development (R&D) expenditure and indirect technology flows during the R&D processes to output (Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), 1997). More technology intensive industries are characterized by significantly greater technological opportunities, more demands for multiple technological developments, and higher speed of technological changes (Nelson and Winter, 1982; Dosi, 1988).

name: Firm growth
definition: Following prior research (Podolny, Stuart, and Hannan, 1996; Stuart, 2000), I model firm growth as ... [formula]. The first difference of log sales is estimated using ordinary least square regression for the tests on firm growth.

name: Zero based budgeting
authors_terms: ["zero based budgeting (ZBB)", "ZBB model", "ZBB planning model", "ZBB budgeting model"]
definition: A budgeting model that uses existing operations and projects only to describe the initial budget areas to be considered: it forces the manager to rank order or weight operational areas or projects in order of importance to the effectiveness of the unit, establishing a rank ordered list of operational areas from a review of unit requirements and projected demands.

name: Traditional incremental budgeting
definition: A budgeting model in which the previous costs associated with operations and projects form the historical base on which the new budget is built; the largest budget allocation is typically given to operations that historically accounted for the largest part of the budget.

name: Service importance-level alignment
authors_terms: ["the correlation between the importance and level of services offered", "synchronizing the importance of a specific service with the level of that service which is provided"]
definition: The correspondence between the importance of a specific service to the user and the level of that service provided by the computing centre: the more important a service is to the user, the greater is the level of that service that should be provided.

name: Attitudes toward instructional computing support
authors_terms: ["attitudes toward the computing centre's support of instructional activities", "user attitudes towards computing service efforts"]
definition: Faculty users' evaluation of the computing services available to support their instructional activities, used to judge the quality of the services provided from the user's perspective.

name: Attitudes toward research computing support
authors_terms: ["attitudes toward the computing centre's support of research activities", "user attitudes towards computing service efforts"]
definition: Faculty users' evaluation of the computing services available to support their research activities, used to judge the quality of the services provided from the user's perspective.

name: Unit effectiveness
definition: The performance of the organizational unit, measured as the level of objective accomplishment; the effectiveness of the budgeting model is evaluated in terms of its contribution to improving, over time, the computing function's support of instructional and research programmes.

name: Integration of budgeting into planning
authors_terms: ["the integration of budget generation into a general planning framework", "integrated planning framework", "the inclusion of budget generation in the operational planning process"]
definition: The inclusion of budget generation as an integral part of the unit's overall planning process, which comprises the four planning activities of anticipation, determination, formulation and assessment.

name: Planning effectiveness
authors_terms: ["the quality of the planning effort", "improved effectiveness"]
definition: The quality of the planning effort, which the authors propose is improved when budget generation is integrated into a general planning framework.

name: Modification flexibility
authors_terms: ["strategic flexibility, measured in terms of modification", "modification", "flexibility in modifying the terms of the alliance agreement"]
definition: Modification refers to the ability of partners to adjust their behaviors or the terms of the agreement in response to changes in the environment or to the needs of their partners.

name: Exit flexibility
authors_terms: ["strategic flexibility, measured in terms of exit", "exit", "flexibility to exit the alliance relationship"]
definition: The second type of strategic flexibility is the relative ease of exit from an alliance in which the partner is no longer satisfied or that no longer meets the partner's needs.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity refers to the nature of the transferability of assets from one use to another. "Specific assets are those whose value is less if switched to alternative transactions and consequently whose value is not fully salvageable if the relation breaks down."

name: Balanced asset specificity
definition: Balanced asset specificity refers to the extent to which each partner has contributed equal levels of specific assets to the alliance.

name: Hostages
definition: Hostage arrangements refer to the existence of other current relationships between the partners to the focal alliance.

name: Trust
definition: Trust is defined as a state of mind, an expectation held by one trading partner about another, that the other will behave in a predictable and mutually acceptable manner; the authors characterize trust as a construct based on three components - dependability, predictability, and faith.

name: Dependence
definition: Using the definition of dependence suggested by Pfeffer and Salancik (1978), the measure of power/dependence is composed of three elements: (1) the influence in the use of the resource, (2) the absence of alternatives, both current and potential, and (3) the importance of the resource being obtained.

name: Previous relationships
definition: A reputation for trustworthiness can be established either through previous relationships or alliances or over time as the length of the attachment between the partners increases.

name: Attachment
definition: Attachment refers to the prior history of a particular exchange relationship; in operative terms, attachment refers to the length of the current relationship.

name: Communication
authors_terms: ["communication", "quality of communication", "level and quality of communication"]
definition: Communication can be defined broadly as the formal as well as informal sharing of meaningful and timely information between firms.

name: Shared values
definition: Shared values refers to the extent that partners to an exchange have common beliefs regarding the importance of the motives for transacting as well as the goals and objectives of the exchange.

name: Product-market overlap
definition: An inverse proxy for asymmetric information, measured by the degree to which the product markets of the foreign firm and the Chinese firm overlap; the greater the overlap between the exchange partners' product markets, the less the amount of information asymmetry between the partners.

name: Hard-to-value intangible assets
authors_terms: ["Hard-to-value intangible assets", "intangible assets that are hard to value", "hard-to-value intangible resources"]
definition: The degree to which the Chinese firm possesses intangible assets that are difficult for the foreign firm to value. Such assets are not only difficult to observe, but their value is partly firm specific as well as imperfectly related to financial metrics or other indexes.

name: IJV attractiveness
authors_terms: ["IJV attractiveness", "attractiveness of a joint venture", "assessments of IJV opportunities"]
definition: Executives' assessment of the attractiveness of an investment opportunity as a joint venture.

name: Acquisition attractiveness
authors_terms: ["Acquisition attractiveness", "attractiveness of an acquisition", "assessments of international acquisition opportunities"]
definition: Executives' assessment of the attractiveness of an investment opportunity as an acquisition.

name: Preference for IJVs over acquisitions
authors_terms: ["preferences for IJVs over acquisitions", "preference for IJV vs. acquisition", "governance preferences"]
definition: Executives' preference for a joint venture over an acquisition for a particular investment opportunity and exchange partner, i.e., whether they view an IJV more favorably relative to an acquisition.

name: Familiarity with partner resources
authors_terms: ["Familiarity with Chinese business' resources", "familiarity with the local firm's resources and capabilities"]
definition: The foreign firm's familiarity and knowledge of the Chinese firm's resources and capabilities.

name: Reputable affiliations
definition: The extent to which the foreign firm would consider the Chinese firm's affiliated organizations reputable.

name: Political embeddedness
definition: Becoming politically embedded means having state bureaucrats serve as company executives or directors, which literally embeds political actors in economic institutions. It is a common form of business-state tie in China.

name: Market development
definition: Market development is the extent to which labor and capital are allocated through markets rather than by the state, measured by the proportions of labor and of fixed-asset investment in non-state-owned firms.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured as net return on net assets (ROA), a measure that is comparable across industries and across firms operating on different scales.

name: Industry competition
definition: Industry competition varies across industries; in highly concentrated industries the small number of dominant firms increases the likelihood of collusion, which reduces competition and uncertainty. The authors measure it with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of concentration, an inverse measure of competition.

name: Firm size
