definition: Compared with smaller firms, larger firms have more resources, more power to negotiate better terms and greater economies of scale, as well as greater visibility, legitimacy and status.

name: Access to bank loans
definition: Access to bank loans is the ability of firms to borrow from banks; in China during the study period banks were firmly under state control and many firms had limited access to bank loans from state-owned and state-controlled banks.

name: Related-party loans
definition: Related-party transactions are exchanges of information, funds, goods or services among business-group members that allow controlling shareholders to pull resources out of the listed firms in which they have partial ownership and transfer them to non-listed firms in which they have full ownership. The authors focus on related-party loans and loan guarantees made by listed firms to other business-group members.

name: Short-termism
definition: We will use 'short-termism' throughout the remainder of the paper to indicate a preference for actions in the near term that have detrimental consequences for the long term. The authors note that for Laverty (1996: 826) short-termism is about 'decisions and outcomes that pursue a course of action that is best for the short-term but suboptimal over the long run.'

name: Hierarchical contagion
authors_terms: ["hierarchical contagion", "hierarchical influence", "contagion", "the short-term bias exhibited by the immediate superior"]
definition: Hierarchical contagion begins with senior management short-termism, driven by belief in market myopia, and proceeds by transmitting this imperative down through the management levels below the most senior. Belief in the imperative of short-termism must cascade through the firm, and such a process may be achieved through hierarchical contagion.

name: Hierarchical level
definition: If capital markets are to exercise the influence that has been attributed to them, the degree of short-termism exhibited by managers may be related to level; senior managers must deal with stock market myopia, perceived or actual, while middle-level managers may be sufficiently removed from the influence of stock markets to be able to focus on actions that improve long-term performance.

name: Importance of accounting information
authors_terms: ["importance that is attached to accounting information", "accounting information", "budgetary and nonfinancial measures", "lean media"]
definition: It is not accounting information per se that influences behavior, it is the importance that is attached to accounting information, as one of a number of possible communication channels, that conditions behavior. Accounting information thus impacts the behavior of decision makers as one of a number of possible communication channels, which in turn reflect norms, values and principles of action, or rules of the game.

name: Role ambiguity
definition: Role ambiguity is the difference between the information a person needs to fulfill a role and the information available. Role ambiguity is a source of stress because it 'frustrates the human need for clarity or structure in the environment', and those who experience it may seek more certain outcomes in order to regain a gratifying role experience.

name: Work group short-termism
authors_terms: ["other group members' short-termism", "median short-term behavior for the group", "work groups", "conformity"]
definition: The interpersonal transmission of attitudes, opinions, and behaviors among individuals of a defined group leads to the establishment of social norms, which then act to influence the behavior of group members. Managers who shared a hierarchical superior were defined formally as members of a given work group.

name: Function and business unit socialization
authors_terms: ["social experiences within the particular function or business unit", "situationally derived socialization processes", "business unit affiliation", "strategic business unit (SBU)"]
definition: The individual is thus likely to develop, over time, a mode of behavior that is consistent with the particular procedures, attitudes, goals, and standards of a profession, function, or SBU. In effect, short-termism may be socially legitimized as an accepted form of institutional behavior.

name: Extent of recombination
definition: The degree to which incumbents in a focal category perform recombinant activities and collectively signal multicategory positioning. The higher the extent of recombination, the lower the distinction between the focal category and other categories in the eyes of potential entrants.

name: Mode of recombination
authors_terms: ["mode of recombination", "diverse mode of recombination", "recurrent mode of recombination"]
definition: The degree to which incumbents attempt a variety of scattered combinations (i.e., diverse mode) at the expense of reiterating them (i.e., recurrent mode). The more diverse the mode of recombination, the greater the difference among category incumbents appears to potential entrants.

name: Category status
definition: We define category status as the rank ordering that a category matures thanks to the acts of deference granted by third parties (Perrow 1961). Category status acts as a 'stabilizing force' that attenuates the market uncertainty evoked by recombinant activities and reassures potential entrants about investing in that region of the market.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entries", "number of market entries", "volume of investments", "organizational entries", "number of record labels entered"]
definition: To assess the collective propensity of potential entrants to invest in a given category, we constructed two dependent variables: the volume of investments that a category attracts and the count of the record labels entered in a focal style.

name: Target company top management turnover
authors_terms: ["target company top management turnover", "top management turnover", "target company's top management turnover rate"]
definition: The cumulative percentage of the target company's top management team that turned over at each of 5 years after the date of the merger or acquisition.

name: Merger and acquisition relatedness
authors_terms: ["type of merger or acquisition", "related merger or acquisition", "unrelated merger or acquisition"]
definition: Horizontal, vertical, product extension, and market extension mergers and acquisitions are all coded as related; unrelated conglomerate mergers and acquisitions are coded as unrelated.

name: Parent-target asset size difference
authors_terms: ["asset size difference", "size difference between the parent and target"]
definition: The difference between the logarithm of the parent's assets and the target's assets at the time of the merger or acquisition.

name: Previous merger and acquisition interest
authors_terms: ["previous merger and acquisition interest", "previous takeover interest"]
definition: If any mention was made in the Wall Street Journal during the course of the merger or acquisition negotiations that the target company had received previous takeover interest from another company, it was recorded.

name: Acquirer's approach
definition: Wall Street Journal articles were coded to portray whether the buyer approached the target's managers with a merger proposal or bypassed these managers and approached the target's shareholders directly with a tender offer.

name: Number of counteroffers
definition: The number of counteroffers made by the buyer was seen as evidence of positional bargaining. In 22 percent of the negotiations captured in this sample the future parent company was forced to make one or more counter-offers before the final price was agreed upon.

name: Negotiation duration
authors_terms: ["amount of time required to negotiate a deal", "days to settlement"]
definition: For each merger and acquisition the number of days was recorded between the time the names of the buyer and the target company were first linked in the Wall Street Journal, and the time the formal agreement of the merger or acquisition was established.

name: Buyer's assurance of management retention
authors_terms: ["assurance of management retention", "public assurance of top management retention"]
definition: Occasionally, the buyer issues a public statement during the course of the merger or acquisition negotiations assuring the managers of the target company that they will retain their jobs following an agreement.

name: Negotiation hostility
authors_terms: ["press characterization", "hostile, rather than friendly, merger or acquisition negotiations"]
definition: In this research the negotiations were coded as friendly, neutral, or hostile based upon the characterization of the negotiations in the Wall Street Journal.

name: Method of payment
definition: The method of payment was reported in the Statistical Report on Mergers and Acquisitions, 1979 for each of the mergers and acquisitions.

name: Premium paid for the target company
authors_terms: ["premium paid", "premium paid for the target company"]
definition: Typically, a buyer pays some premium over the average market value of the target company's stock.

name: Takeover resistance
authors_terms: ["takeover resistance", "resistance to a takeover attempt", "non-auction-inducing resistance", "non-auction-generating opposition"]
definition: Only non-auction-generating opposition to a takeover bid was considered resistance; takeover resistance that generates an auction, wherein the target firm is sold to the highest bidder, was not counted as resistance. Only firms that contested tender offers in a manner that did not result in auctions were considered to be resisting.

name: CEO golden parachute existence
authors_terms: ["golden parachute existence", "golden parachute", "existence of a CEO's golden parachute"]
definition: Golden parachutes are designed to protect managers' deferred compensation against the threat of a dismissal or a change in compensation resulting from a takeover and to resolve short-term conflict by providing side payments to executives who are adversely affected by a change in control.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: When managers own a substantial portion of a firm's equity, their personal wealth is tied to that of their shareholders; therefore, the ownership of a firm's stock can align top management's incentives with those of their shareholders. CEOs' stock ownership enables them to share in the premium when takeovers occur.

name: CEO age
definition: Age and length of tenure are the characteristics most relevant to a potential change in control because they affect not only the CEOs' general attitude toward change and their commitment to their firms, but also their need for financial and career security. A CEO's age may play an important part in his or her strategic choices.

name: CEO tenure
definition: As the durations of CEOs' tenures increase, so does their ability to influence board decisions. A long-standing CEO not only has more power to prevent undesired change than a new CEO, but also has a greater commitment to maintaining a firm's status quo.

name: CEO humility
definition: Humble individuals avoid arrogant and self-contemptuous behaviors, are deeply self-aware, and are fully aware of their abilities and limitations. Humble CEOs show low self-focus, recognize others' strengths and contributions, accept others' feedback and ideas, and own up to personal weaknesses or mistakes.

name: Analysts' EPS expectations
authors_terms: ["analysts' EPS expectations", "analysts' forecasted EPS", "analysts' expectations", "analysts' consensus forecast"]
definition: Financial analysts shape market expectations for firms by developing public forecasts of firms' expected future quarterly or annual earnings. The authors operationalize analysts' EPS expectations as the I/B/E/S last analysts' consensus forecast for the focal firm's EPS for the year, scaled by the year-end firm's stock price.

name: Actual EPS relative to analysts' expectations
authors_terms: ["actual EPS relative to analysts' expectations", "actual EPS relative to analyst's expectations", "ARAE", "earnings relative to analysts' expectations", "performance above market expectation"]
definition: Measured as the difference between a firm's reported EPS for a fiscal period and the I/B/E/S last consensus forecast for the period issued for the firm, scaled by the end-of-period stock price for the firm. The authors describe this as the firm's performance above market expectation.

name: Market performance
definition: The authors utilize three alternative measures of firms' market performance: abnormal returns (AR), Tobin's Q (TQ), and Total Shareholder Returns (TSR). TQ and TSR are measured for time t + 1 because the comparison between actual EPS and analysts' expectations is typically announced after the end of the year.

name: Operational performance
definition: The authors refer to the other side of the comparison between actual EPS performance and expectations as actual operational performance. They note theoretical reasons to expect that humble CEOs will have mixed or neutral effects on actual organizational performance.

name: Investor reaction to financial restatement
authors_terms: ["investor reaction to irregular financial restatements", "investor reaction to restatement", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)"]
definition: Investor reaction to a restatement at time t is operationalized as the CAR of the restating firm in the five-day window [t-2, t+2]; negative CAR indicate the penalty imposed by investors.

name: Frequency of alliance announcements
authors_terms: ["frequency of alliance announcements", "salience of alliance announcements"]
definition: The frequency of alliance announcements is the number of alliance announcements that a firm made discounted by the time (in months) between the alliance announcement and the restatement.

name: Extremity of alliance announcements
authors_terms: ["extremity of alliance announcements", "magnitude of investors' positive expectations"]
definition: The extremity of alliance announcements was measured as the magnitude of investor reaction: the sum of the CARs in the five-day period around a firm's alliance announcements, discounted by the time (in months) between the alliance announcement and the restatement.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was operationalized as the log-transformed total assets of the firm as reported in the quarter before the financial restatement.

name: Firm diversification
definition: The level of a firm's diversification was captured by the count of different industry segments in which a firm had a presence.

name: Product branding status
authors_terms: ["product branding status", "branding status of a product", "private branding", "private label", "manufacturer branding", "manufacturer brand"]
definition: Through private branding, retailers outsource a product from an unaffiliated supplier, put a private label or the store name on the product, and make all necessary investment to market it to consumers. I used a zero-vs.-one dummy variable to capture product branding status, where one represents that a product bears a private label, and zero represents that it carries a manufacturer brand.

name: Retailer commitment to product marketing
authors_terms: ["retailer commitment to product marketing", "commitment to product marketing", "marketing commitment", "retailer commitment"]
definition: Retailers make a marketing commitment to a product in two major ways, by advertising it through mass media and by promoting it at their stores. Under private (vs. manufacturer) branding, retailers are more likely to optimize their commitment to product marketing, that is, to maximize the gains (or minimize the losses) in the reputation of a product that carries a private label (vs. a manufacturer brand).

name: Barriers to private branding
definition: Private branding will not be efficient unless the savings on the costs of solving brand specificity are big enough to compensate the extra efforts that retailers must make to overcome all potential barriers to private branding. I collected four variables to measure the barriers faced by the retailer in extending a private label to an outsourced product.

name: Earnings pressure
definition: The gap between the firm's future performance and the analyst consensus earnings estimate, termed 'earnings pressure' because of the pressure it places on managers to seek to improve earnings in order to meet performance targets. It represents a forward-looking rather than backward-looking aspirational level of firm performance.

name: Extent of corporate downsizing
definition: Corporate downsizing refers to a permanent reduction in the firm's workforce with the aim to cut a firm's costs and improve its overall performance. It constitutes a major strategic decision that not only affects firm size but usually comes with changes in the firm's structure and operations.

name: Institutional investor stock ownership
definition: Institutional investors such as mutual funds, pension funds, or insurance companies are important and sophisticated investors of the firm; they are committed to a long-term investment outlook and are less likely to sell their shareholdings if the firm faces a short-term performance shortfall.

name: CEO power
definition: CEOs with greater power are less likely to suffer from the adverse consequences of missing performance targets, as they have been shown to be less likely to be dismissed for poor performance. CEO power is measured with CEO tenure, CEO duality, and CEO stock ownership.

name: Analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["analyst coverage", "high analyst coverage", "extent of analyst coverage"]
definition: While the majority of publicly traded firms have analyst coverage, the number of analysts that cover a firm varies considerably; extensive analyst coverage creates visibility and attracts investors and draws greater investor attention and scrutiny.

name: Firm financial condition
authors_terms: ["firm financial condition", "poor financial conditions", "less favorable firm financial conditions"]
definition: Firms with poor financial conditions face greater scrutiny by investors and shareholder activists who seek to discipline poorly performing managers, and poor firm performance is a major predictor of CEO dismissal.

name: Home country bribery
authors_terms: ["home country bribery", "bribe amounts paid to government officials in the home country", "firms' bribe amounts in the home country", "total bribery in the home country"]
definition: From this perspective, bribery is a process whereby government officials sell public resources and services to individuals and firms. Public services are therefore disproportionally allocated between bribers and nonbribers.

name: Export intensity
definition: Following Hundley and Jacobson (1998) and Filatotchev et al. (2001), we measured exports using export intensity or the ratio of a firm's foreign sales over total sales.

name: Interaction with customers
authors_terms: ["interaction with customers", "involvement of customers in innovation activities", "customer interaction"]
definition: This construct mirrors the extent to which the focal firm involves customers in its innovation activities. Together, the responses indicate the degree of involvement of customers in innovation activities.

name: Delegation of responsibility
definition: Delegation reflects the extent to which responsibilities and decision rights are delegated to employees. The first item captures delegation of responsibility toward the individual, whereas the second item refers to delegation at team/group level.

name: Knowledge incentives
authors_terms: ["knowledge incentives", "incentives for acquiring and sharing knowledge"]
definition: This construct measures to what extent employees' salaries are associated with acquiring knowledge and knowledge sharing.

name: Internal communication
authors_terms: ["internal communication", "communication within the firm", "communication in the vertical and horizontal dimensions"]
definition: This construct reflects communication within the firm, across the lateral as well as hierarchical dimensions.

name: Innovation performance
authors_terms: ["innovation performance", "innovation capacity", "innovation performance relative to competitors"]
definition: Managers were asked to indicate the performance of the focal firm compared with competitors on the following two dimensions: (1) innovation capacity and (2) profitability. The argument for including profitability to measure innovation performance is that the Schumpeterian notion of innovation pertains not only to the capacity to introduce 'new combinations' but also to the economic significance of those new products.

name: Diversification mode choice
definition: Once a firm decides to pursue a wholly owned venture, it must decide whether to acquire an existing venture or create a new (greenfield start-up) venture; this is referred to in the scholarly literature as diversification mode choice.

name: Relative investment size
authors_terms: ["relative investment size", "relative size of the investment", "relative size"]
definition: Relative investment size is the size of the new investment relative to the size of the firm, measured as the total number of employees of the subsidiary divided by the total workforce of the parent.

name: Technological intensity
definition: Technological intensity is the percent of sales devoted to research and development.

name: Multinational experience
definition: Multinational experience was determined by making use of the export ratio of each Japanese parent; more experienced firms have well-established domestic organizational routines which they expect to transfer abroad.

name: Market growth
definition: Market growth represents the profit potential of a host market and was represented by two five year growth averages (1983-1987 and 1988-1992) for each industry.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance indicates the difference in culture between a home country and each individual target country.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: Uncertainty avoidance is a measure of a firm's willingness to accept managerial or organizational uncertainty and was taken from Hofstede (1980); the more uncertainty avoiding a culture tends to be, the less attractive is the acquisition mode.

name: Firm diversity
definition: Firm diversity was determined by means of the Kompass UCS codes; the more codes a company had, the more diversified a company was assumed to be.

name: Product relatedness
definition: Product relatedness was determined by comparing the product codes of the subsidiary with those of the parent.

name: Technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["specialized technology knowledge", "Pure tech education", "Pure tech skill", "technological competencies", "technical capabilities"]
definition: The technological competencies of the founding team, coded from founders' STEM qualifications and from technology skill clusters reported on LinkedIn. Ventures are classified as pure tech by education if founders had only STEM degrees or a combination of STEM and nonbusiness degrees, and by skill if at least one founder holds a STEM degree or specializes in technology skills, provided no founder has a business background.

name: Business knowledge
definition: The business competencies of the founding team, coded from founders' business qualifications (business administration and law) and from business skill clusters reported on LinkedIn. Ventures with at least one founder possessing a business background are classified as business education companies, and a startup is classified as Business skill when any founder possessed business education or specialized in business skills.

name: Accelerator seed investment
definition: Seed investors specialized in training programs that offer business education and mentorship alongside limited financial resources. Crunchbase defines accelerators as investors who provide a set amount of seed equity to young startups in exchange for capital and mentorship, bringing a cohort of startups through an on-site program of three to four months.

name: Startup-investor matching
definition: The sorting of startups and seed investors into pairs, which the authors model as a bilateral, rational decision-making process in which both parties assess mutual fit. In market equilibrium it is impossible to generate more value by switching partners.

name: Startup value creation
authors_terms: ["value creation", "value-adding effect", "startup value", "joint value creation", "incremental funding"]
definition: The value generated by a startup-seed investor pairing, captured ex post by the amount of funding the startup subsequently raises. Accelerators add value through training and mentorship whereas primarily financial investors add value through capital.

name: Technology novelty
authors_terms: ["nature of the new technology", "nature of the product technology", "evolved technology", "novel technology"]
definition: New technology is defined as new artifact, new knowledge, or a combination of both, that meets the same functional need as an existing technology, which makes it possible to classify new technology in terms of its relative similarity to the existing technology. An evolved technology has a new artifact that is based on advances in existing knowledge, while a novel technology also has a new artifact but is based on a new knowledge base that represents a completely new way of meeting a functional need.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["nature of market", "dispersed market", "concentrated market", "type of market"]
definition: Dispersed markets have a large number of potential buyers with access to many information sources about the performance of products, and individual consumers make their purchase decisions by evaluating products on well-established criteria. Concentrated markets, on the other hand, have a small set of purchasing agents who negotiate evaluation criteria, which are then used for assessing the performance of a product.

name: Technical strategy
definition: A technical strategy is defined as a pattern of sequences of actions undertaken by firms, where the sequences predominantly deal with changes in technology specifications, followed by evaluation of the technology on existing criteria of evaluation.

name: Institutional strategy
definition: An institutional strategy is defined as a pattern of sequences of actions undertaken by firms, where the sequences predominantly deal with changes in criteria used to evaluate the technology followed by evaluation of the technology on newly developed criteria of evaluation.

name: Market success
authors_terms: ["success", "market success", "acceptance of a firm's product technology in the market"]
definition: In this study, success is measured by the acceptance of a firm's product technology in the market relative to all other competing product technologies.

name: Functional importance
authors_terms: ["functional importance", "functional importance mix", "relative strategic importance of functional areas", "strategic importance of functional areas", "functional importance scores"]
definition: For the purposes of this study, strategic importance refers to the impact on strategy implementation and effective achievement of a firm's grand strategy. The 'functional importance mix' is a surrogate for the functional structure of the firm.

name: Company performance
definition: Most policy researchers use some form of a financial measure as a performance criterion. Although there is no one commonly used financial criterion for company success, an examination of the literature does provide evidence of commonality.

name: Grand strategy
authors_terms: ["grand strategy", "type of grand strategy", "master strategy", "corporate strategy", "primary strategy"]
definition: Grand strategy was defined as a corporation's major plan of action for achieving the sales and earnings goals for the firm as a whole (rather than a product, division or market segment).

name: Industry type
definition: Industry type was measured using four normative classifications of industrial firms: consumer durable goods manufacturers, consumer nondurable goods manufacturers, capital goods manufacturers, and producer goods manufacturers.

name: Transaction dependence
authors_terms: ["transaction dependence of the bidder industry on the target industry", "interindustry transaction patterns", "industry constraint", "resource dependence"]
definition: The sales and purchases that an organization transacts with other organizations in a particular industry are one basic type of interdependency, crucial to the extent that the proportion of the organization's total sales or purchases transacted with that industry is high. Network measures of transaction dependence assess the degree of resource dependence by simultaneously accounting for the pattern of interindustry transactions an industry is subject to and the ability of buying and selling industries to force disadvantageous prices on firms in that industry by virtue of their concentration.

name: Interindustry mergers
definition: The dependent variable—interindustry mergers—was operationalized as the proportion of the total number of mergers of industry i that were with industry j between 1948 and 1969, where i and j represent one of the industries studied.

name: Antitrust enforcement
authors_terms: ["Celler-Kefauver Act enforcement", "period of strict antitrust enforcement", "antitrust legislation and actions"]
definition: It was the years between 1962 and 1974 that were the most difficult ones for firms contemplating vertical or horizontal merger to reduce their transaction dependence on firms in other industries. Research by Fligstein (1990) identified the years between 1962 and 1974 as the period of most intense Celler-Kefauver enforcement.

name: Past reliance on mergers
authors_terms: ["past reliance by firms in an industry on mergers to reduce transaction dependence", "strength of the resource dependence effect in panel period t - 1", "established industry patterns of response"]
definition: When firms consider merger to reduce transaction dependence, they will be more likely to engage in this strategy to the extent that they and other firms in the industry have traditionally done so.

name: Bidder industry concentration
authors_terms: ["bidder industry concentration", "concentration of the industry itself", "highly concentrated industries"]
definition: Structural autonomy is higher in more highly concentrated industries because of the advantages of oligopoly. These advantages increase the profit potential of firms in concentrated industries, making them more vulnerable to larger losses (relative to firms in less concentrated industries) when they are dependent on firms in other industries to buy their outputs and sell them inputs.

name: Time period
definition: Pfeffer's study focused on the relationship between interindustry transactions and mergers in a single time period. As such, he was unable to examine his basic hypothesis in any longitudinal manner, and especially whether the strength of the resource dependence effect varies over time.

name: IT investment
definition: The amount of annual IT investment includes hardware, software, and costs concerning maintenance, personnel, and training. This measure covers all major components of corporate IT spending.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured by ROA, the ratio of net income to the year-end book value of total assets. In this study, we examine both current period ROA and future ROA, defined as the two-year average ROA subsequent to IT investment.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "the presence of outside directors on the corporate board", "proportion of outside directors", "BIND"]
definition: Board independence is the presence of outside directors on the corporate board; an outsider majority board is associated with high independence, while an insider majority board is associated with low independence.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign ownership", "the share of foreign investment in a firm's common stock", "percentage of common stock owned by foreign investors", "FOR"]
definition: Foreign ownership is the share of foreign investment in a firm's common stock. For Taiwanese firms, foreign affiliation also gives domestic firms relatively easy access to superior technical, managerial, and financial resources.

name: Industry competitiveness
definition: The industrial organization literature commonly uses industry concentration as a proxy for industry competitiveness. We measure industry competitiveness by the four-firm concentration ratio (CR4) for each firm, which equals the percentage of total sales in the firm's industry sector accounted for by the four largest firms in the same sector; CR4 is negatively related to industry competitiveness.

name: Firm size
definition: We use total assets to measure firm size and classify our sample into small and large companies. Small firms are affiliated with 'resource poverty' in deploying IT while large firms have more expertise in deploying technologies.

name: Initial CEO human capital
authors_terms: ["CEO human capital", "initial level of CEO human capital", "Initial CEO HC Index", "initial CEO HC"]
definition: A CEO's human capital refers to his/her managerial skills gained from both education and experience. In this study the initial level of CEO human capital is the level of the CEO in office when the firm receives its first round of VC funding.

name: Lead VC-firm distance
authors_terms: ["lead VC-firm distance", "distance between a firm and its lead VC", "geographic distance", "geographic proximity"]
definition: The geographic distance between the VC and the portfolio firm, which affects the cost and thus the feasibility of the VC's direct monitoring in the firm; both monitoring cost and information cost decrease as VC-portfolio firm distance decreases.

name: CEO change before IPO
authors_terms: ["CEO change", "CEO change before IPO", "CEO Change dummy"]
definition: A firm changed CEO between receiving the first round of VC investment and IPO.

name: IPO valuation
definition: IPO valuation is measured by Tobin's Q, which is equal to the market value of the assets over its book value, and captures investors' perception of the IPO firm's current and expected profitability.

name: Feasibility of VC direct monitoring
authors_terms: ["directly monitoring", "direct monitoring", "onsite direct monitoring", "feasibility of direct monitoring"]
definition: Directly monitoring refers to VCs' onsite involvement with their portfolio firms. The authors propose that whether a VC changes CEO depends upon the extent to which its direct monitoring in the firm is feasible, and that a VC is more likely to change CEO in a portfolio firm if its direct monitoring of the firm is less feasible.

name: Strategic uncertainty
definition: Strategic uncertainty perception, defined as the combination of environmental uncertainty perception and sector importance, is considered the chief determinant of environmental scanning behavior. In essence, strategic uncertainty reflects the strategic value of environmental information for organizational performance.

name: Environmental sector layer
definition: The environment can be conceptualized as having several sectors that exist in two layers. The first, or closest to the organization layer is the task environment, which directly impacts business strategy; the second, or outer layer is the general environment, which refers to sectors that affect organizations indirectly.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: Perceived environmental uncertainty is the difference between the amount of information required to perform the task and the amount of information which has already been obtained. In practice, perceived environmental uncertainty exists when decision-makers do not feel confident that they understand what the major events or trends in an environment are, or when they feel unable to accurately assign probabilities to the likelihood that particular events and/or changes will occur.

name: Perceived sector importance
definition: Information from important sectors of the environment may become a source of competitive advantage. In a sector of high importance, external events are also perceived to be directly linked to operational performance.

name: Scanning frequency
definition: Scanning frequency is the number of times managers receive data about the environment (Hambrick, 1981).

name: Personal scanning
definition: Personal sources refer to direct human contact. Personal communications are content rich and enable managers to detect weak signals.

name: Impersonal scanning
definition: Impersonal sources are written, and include formal reports, newspapers, survey results, and the output of management information systems. Impersonal sources are appropriate when environmental events are discrete and analyzable.

name: External scanning
definition: External sources include direct contacts with government officials and politicians, discussions with managers from other companies, trade magazines, and attendance of association meetings.

name: Internal scanning
definition: Internal modes pertain to reports, memos, or discussions with internal managers and employees about the external environment.

name: Bank-firm relationship duration
authors_terms: ["duration of a bank-firm relationship", "duration of the bank-firm relationship", "duration of the bank-firm tie", "the log of the number of years of the longest relationship"]
definition: Previous research suggests that the duration of a relationship is an indicator of the degree to which commercial transactions become embedded in social attachments. The longer a relationship lasts, the greater the opportunities for bonds of trust to form and for reciprocity to develop.

name: Bank-firm relationship multiplexity
authors_terms: ["multiplexity", "degree of multiplexity in the bank-firm relationship", "multiplexity of the bank-firm relationship"]
definition: Multiplexity is another indicator of the degree of embeddedness. In banking, multiplexity increases when commercial exchanges between the bank and firm include both business transactions (e.g., cash box services, wire transfers) and private exchanges (i.e., personal accounts and advice).

name: Bank network size
authors_terms: ["size of a firm's bank network", "bank network size", "size of the firm's banking network", "network size"]
definition: A third measure of embeddedness is the dispersion or concentration of an actor's network of ties, and a common proxy for this measure is the size of the firm's banking network. Large networks are likely to be associated with arm's length bank-firm interfaces because they draw resources away from relationship building.

name: Early trade credit discount taking
authors_terms: ["the percentage of early-payment discounts on trade credit taken by the firm", "proportion of early trade credit discounts taken by the firm", "early-payment trade credit discounts", "percent of cash discounts offered for the payment of trade credit before the due date that were taken by the firm"]
definition: Trade credit permits a firm to acquire goods from a supplier and pay for them at a later date, with typically three payment options: paying early, on time, or late. A supplier can offer trade-credit discounts for paying before the due date (like a loan).

name: Late trade credit payment penalties
authors_terms: ["the percentage of late-payment penalties on trade credit incurred by the firm", "proportion of late payment penalties on trade credit incurred by the firm", "late-payment penalties", "percentage of case penalties incurred for the payment of trade credit made after the due date"]
definition: Trade credit permits a firm to acquire goods from a supplier and pay for them at a later date, with typically three payment options: paying early, on time, or late. A supplier can offer penalties for paying after the due date (like a credit card).

name: Senior headquarters manager involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement of senior headquarters managers", "involvement of senior managers from headquarters"]
definition: We assessed the involvement of senior headquarters managers by measuring the number of senior managers from headquarters involved in the problem-solving project. Specifically, we counted the number of headquarters managers listed in the name generator who were higher in the hierarchy than the project leader (i.e., senior).

name: Senior subsidiary manager involvement
authors_terms: ["involvement of senior subsidiary managers", "involvement of senior managers from the subsidiary", "involvement of senior managers from the same subsidiary"]
definition: The involvement of senior subsidiary managers was measured using the same procedure as the one with senior headquarters managers. Senior subsidiary managers may be involved for reasons similar to those of senior headquarters managers, including their diverse knowledge and perspective as well as information on complementary assets and activities.

name: Solution effectiveness
definition: When solutions are effective at addressing the problems, current products, services, or organizational practices of firms are extended or modified in beneficial ways. Our holistic conceptualization of solution effectiveness requires a measure that is useful across problems, firms, and industries.

name: Problem locus
definition: A distinction can be made between non-routine problems that have an external locus (i.e., problems primarily related to products and services) or an internal locus (i.e., problems primarily related to processes; Bertrand & Mol, 2013; Leiponen & Helfat, 2010). This distinction is important because problem locus influences the types of knowledge necessary to solve problems.

name: Certification contest victories
authors_terms: ["victories", "cumulative victories", "victories in certification contests", "number of cumulative victories", "Log of accumulated victories"]
definition: Rao proposed that certification contests, or 'yardstick competition[s] in which performances are ranked,' helped legitimate organizations; victories in such contests are 'small, fortuitous events that create a reputation' because of the taken for granted axiom that winners are 'better' than losers.

name: Firm exit rate
definition: We measured Firm exit as cessation of operations and we did not define mergers as exits.

name: Startup status
definition: Startups face more uncertainty and higher external liabilities of newness, so 'victories in contests are likely to improve the reputation of startup organizations to a greater extent than those of lateral entries.' The authors created a Startup variable to account for de novo organizations, which were expected to have a higher exit rate.

name: Reputation
definition: The greater is their reputation, as stated in Hypothesis 1; greater cumulative certification contest victories are said to produce greater organizational reputation.

name: Planning process sophistication
authors_terms: ["planning process sophistication", "sophistication of planning", "level of planning sophistication", "planning sophistication", "levels of planning sophistication"]
definition: A content analysis of the literature on planning practices of small and entrepreneurial firms reveals eight distinct components that constitute their planning process: objective setting; environmental analysis; SWOT analysis; strategy formulation; financial projections; functional budgets; operating performance measures; and control and corrective procedures. Based on these eight components, four distinct levels of sophistication in the strategic planning process were identified: structured strategic plans, structured operational plans, intuitive plans and unstructured plans.

name: Financial performance
definition: The accurate description of performance is essential to measuring success within organizations. Financial performance data that served as dependent variables were: (1) revenue growth, (2) entrepreneurial compensation growth, and (3) labor expense/revenue ratio growth.

name: Firm age
definition: Firms are classified by whether they have been established less than or equal to 9 years ago (young) or more than 9 years (older). The cut-off was based on SEFA board member recommendations, and the average age of subjects' firms was 15.2 years.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["size of firm", "firm size", "large firms", "smaller firms", "gross revenue"]
definition: Firms were classified as small if annual revenue was less than or equal to $400,000 and as large if gross revenue exceeded $400,000. The selection of the size cut-off was based on SEFA board member recommendations.

name: Length of planning history
authors_terms: ["length of planning history", "planning history", "long planning histories", "short planning histories"]
definition: Length of planning history distinguishes opportunistic entrepreneurs' firms with long planning histories (more than 5 years) from those with short planning histories. It takes time, expertise and experience to develop and implement a sophisticated strategic planning system within an organization, and firms with long planning histories have gone through at least two iterations of the planning process.

name: Opportunistic entrepreneurial orientation
authors_terms: ["opportunistic entrepreneur", "opportunistic entrepreneurs' firms", "entrepreneurial type", "type of entrepreneur", "entrepreneurial orientation"]
definition: Smith (1967), in an earlier typology, identified an entrepreneurial type (opportunistic) who perceives and reacts to a broad range of environmental impacts, exhibits breadth in education and training, has high social awareness and high social involvement, is flexible and confident in his/her ability to deal with economic and social environments, and exhibits an awareness and orientation toward the future. The opportunistic entrepreneur plans for growth.

name: CEO promotion focus
definition: A promotion focus sensitizes people to the presence and absence of positive stimuli (i.e., gains and nongains) and directs their attention toward opportunities for accomplishment and growth. A promotion focus involves acting in ways that attempt to maximize gains and minimize nongains.

name: CEO prevention focus
definition: A prevention focus sensitizes people to the presence and absence of negative stimuli (i.e., losses and non-losses) and the importance of safety, responsibility, and security. Rather than maximizing gains and minimizing non-gains, a prevention focus is geared toward minimizing losses and maximizing nonlosses.

name: Stock option grants
definition: A stock option is 'an option granted to an employee by an employer giving the employee the right to purchase a share of the firm's stock within a specified period of time, for a fixed price.' Stock options are a valuable compensation tool because they provide an upside potential with a limit on downside wealth risk.

name: Number of acquisitions
definition: Number of acquisitions is one of two variables capturing distinct and important parts of the firm's acquisition behavior; a CEO can significantly change the firm's resource allocation and strategic position through multiple small acquisitions.

name: Value of acquisitions
definition: Value of acquisitions is one of two variables capturing distinct and important parts of the firm's acquisition behavior; a CEO can significantly change the firm's resource allocation and strategic position through one large acquisition.

name: Firm investment horizon
definition: At the firm level, we define investment horizon as the ex ante average expected useful life of a firm's investments. This is measured using depreciation data that reflect upfront expectations about the productive life of capital investments.

name: Firm performance
definition: The study's dependent variable is firm performance, defined as return on assets (ROA).

name: Capital patience
definition: The second explanatory variable is capital patience, which cannot be measured directly but has been equated with observable data on trading frequency. The authors expect firm performance to be strongest when the firm's investment horizon most closely aligns with investors demonstrating capital patience by holding ownership in the firm's stock for long periods of time.

name: Related diversification
definition: DR is defined as related diversification arising out of operating segments within an industry group. The greater DR, the greater the extent of related diversification.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: DU is defined as unrelated diversification between industry groups. The greater DU, the greater the extent of unrelated diversification.

name: Firm performance
definition: Since our arguments focus upon the efficiency effects of achieving a fit between strategy and structure, it is appropriate to measure economic benefits by the efficiency of resource use within a firm. This is best captured by a measure of profitability.

name: Decentralization
authors_terms: ["decentralization", "centralization", "decentralization dimension", "decentralization of operating and strategic decisions"]
definition: Decentralization is the degree to which decisions are decentralized to divisions or centralized at the corporate office. Responsibility for operating and strategic decisions may be decentralized to divisions or retained by the corporate office.

name: Interdivisional integration
definition: Integration is the degree of integration between divisions. Coordination between divisions requires integrating mechanisms to achieve lateral communication between divisions.

name: Integration complexity
definition: The complexity of integrating mechanisms is the number of different mechanisms used to achieve integration between divisions, ranging from program or project managers to formal group structures.

name: Breadth of control
authors_terms: ["breadth of control", "breadth of control dimension", "control criteria", "subjective and objective nonfinancial criteria"]
definition: Breadth of control is the extent to which the corporate office relied on comprehensive subjective and objective nonfinancial criteria when evaluating divisional performance and deciding how to allocate capital within the firm.

name: Incentive system basis
authors_terms: ["incentive systems", "incentive schemes", "profit bonus schemes", "incentive schemes based on corporate profitability", "incentive schemes based on divisional profitability"]
definition: The basis of the incentive system is whether the firm based its incentive systems for divisional managers, at least in part, on corporate profitability, or whether incentives for divisional managers exclusively emphasized divisional profitability.

name: Customer volunteer engagement
authors_terms: ["customer volunteer engagement", "volunteering engagement", "volunteer engagement", "level of engagement in the volunteering activity", "task absorption"]
definition: The extent to which customers are fully involved and immersed in the volunteering experience; the authors argue that a customer's perception of the company will depend on the nature of this engagement.

name: Corporate reputation
authors_terms: ["corporate reputation", "company reputation", "perceptions of corporate reputation", "perception of the brewery's reputation"]
definition: Stakeholders' favorable impressions of an organization based on positive expectations about the firm's outcomes and behaviors that are relevant to the given stakeholder's group.

name: Emotional contagion
definition: A customer's positive emotions from the volunteering experience transfer to others who did not attend the event during their conversations, and the recipient subconsciously mirrors and internalizes those emotions, attaching them to the same target.

name: Company patronage
definition: Customers' behavioral support for the company in the form of continued patronage - repeat customer attendance and on-site support for the company.

name: Product purchases
definition: Customers' behavioral support for the company in the form of product purchases - the discretionary acquisition of company products from third-party vendors.

name: Transactive memory system
definition: A collective memory system for encoding, storing, retrieving, and communicating group knowledge, consisting of both an initial TMS structure-an organized store of knowledge contained within members' memories-and a set of transactive processes that members use to encode, store, and retrieve that knowledge.

name: Task performance
definition: Assembly accuracy on the task for which the TMS first developed, measured as the number of assembly operations done correctly.

name: Learning transfer
definition: Learning transfer is defined as occurring when knowledge acquired in one situation affects learning or performance in other situations; the extent to which groups transferred learning across tasks was measured in terms of transfer-task performance.

name: Abstract knowledge of the task domain
authors_terms: ["abstract knowledge", "abstract, generalized knowledge about the underlying principles relevant to the domain", "abstract, generalized understanding of the underlying principles"]
definition: An abstract, generalized understanding of the underlying principles common to the tasks, based on knowledge about the task and how the group might solve the problem.

name: Expertise stability
authors_terms: ["expertise stability", "perceived expertise remained stable across tasks"]
definition: The extent to which members' perceived expertise remained stable across tasks, derived from the number of times members agreed about each member's expertise, both within and between tasks.

name: Priced technology prevalence
definition: Priced technologies are defined as those technologies that must be paid for to be used. In many markets in this context, priced technologies may include MobileApps distributed by both commercial producers and noncommercial producers.

name: Free technology prevalence
definition: Free technologies are defined as technologies that can be used without paying a fee. Free technologies may include MobileApps distributed by both commercial and noncommercial producers.

name: Priced technology revenue
authors_terms: ["Monthly Revenue", "revenue earned from an individual priced technology", "unit sales"]
definition: Monthly Revenue is computed as the natural log of revenue for each priced MobileApp per month.

name: Free technology downloads
authors_terms: ["Monthly Downloads", "downloads of an individual free technology"]
definition: Monthly Downloads is computed as the natural log of downloads for each free MobileApp per month.

name: Indirect ties to competitors
authors_terms: ["indirect ties to competitors", "indirect competitive ties", "indirect ties via intermediaries"]
definition: Ties that arise when a firm and its competitors are connected through a shared intermediary organization; unlike direct ties, into which firms enter purposefully, indirect ties form at the shared intermediary's discretion.

name: Innovation
definition: We define 'innovation' as a process that begins with a new idea or novel invention and 'results in the introduction of a new product, process, or service to the marketplace.'

name: Tie formation sequence with shared investor
authors_terms: ["earliest shared VC tie", "sequence of tie formation", "first among their competitors to form ties with shared investors"]
definition: The order in which a focal firm, relative to its competitors, formed its ties with a shared investor; a focal firm that received funding from VC investors before these same investors made any subsequent investments in the focal firm's competitors.

name: Relative commitment from shared investor
authors_terms: ["relative commitment from shared VC", "tie commitment", "relative commitment"]
definition: We conceptualize 'tie commitment' in terms of the frequency and intensity of resources bestowed (Guler, 2007); tie commitment signifies the extent to which a given partner is favored, preferred, or valued by the shared intermediary.

name: Relative geographic distance to shared investor
definition: The geographic distance between a firm and a shared investor relative to that of its competitors, calculated as the distance between the center of each firm's zip code and that of each of its investors.

name: Investor status
definition: 'Status' refers to social deference, embodied in and influenced by a firm's pattern of affiliations; a firm's status is only loosely coupled with its past behaviors.

name: Investor reputation
definition: 'Reputation' arises directly from examining a firm's past actions (as distinct from its affiliations) to infer its skills and knowledge.

name: Family centrality
definition: Family ties are defined as a woman's connections with her family members, centrality in this network being family network centrality. Family and kinship networks include nuclear and extended family members.

name: Community centrality
definition: Community ties are defined as social and informal interactions among adult women in the village, with centrality in this network being community network centrality. Family ties are not considered part of community ties.

name: Ties to men in power
authors_terms: ["ties to men in power", "men in power"]
definition: Ties to men in power are defined as relationships with men who are political leaders, officials in industrial bureaus, officials in regulatory bodies of commercial administration, officials in legal institutions, and officials in state-owned banks located within a particular village; ties to family members are excluded from this network.

name: ICT use
definition: For women in the 10 intervention villages, ICT use was assessed as the total number of hours each participant used the ICT kiosks for in each year of the study; ICT use was set to zero for the participants in the control group villages.

name: Entrepreneurial activity
definition: Entrepreneurial activity was coded 1 if a woman started a new business venture in a particular year, and 0 otherwise; specifically, a 1 was entered if a woman had an operational business.

name: Entrepreneurial profit
definition: Entrepreneurial profit is the revenue generated in a specific year from entrepreneurial ventures, obtained each year via the interviews and cross-validated with the businesses' government or bank filings where available.

name: Time
definition: Time was coded from 1 to 7, in keeping with the year of data collection; most variables were measured each year, with the exception of ICT use, which was aggregated each year.

name: Other-regarding values
definition: Schwartz (1992) describes the tension between self-enhancement (power and achievement values) and self-transcendence (benevolence and universalism) as one of the key guiding principles in peoples' lives; Agle, Mitchell, and Sonnenfeld (1999) have further elaborated this tension as a continuum ranging from self-regarding (the self-enhancement values) to other-regarding (the self-transcendence values).

name: Utilitarian identity
definition: Organizational identity is defined as the members' shared perceptions about their organization's central, distinctive, and enduring qualities. Albert and Whetten (1985) conceptualize organizational identification in terms of two competing identities: a normative system, emphasizing traditions and symbols, internalization of an ideology, and altruism; and a utilitarian system, characterized by economic rationality, maximization of profits, and self-interest.

name: Slack resources
definition: Slack resources represent extra resources available to the organization that enable managers to change their focus of attention. Firms without slack resources will focus in first instance on short-term goals forcing managers to improve allocation efficiency, while firms with abundant slack resources will be more likely to use it as a buffer that can redirect the attention of managers to other goals.

name: Firm performance
definition: Scholars consider performance as one of the most important contextual variables to affect attention allocation; managers use performance as a means of assessing managerial effectiveness. High firm performance relaxes the focus of attention on activities associated with short-term performance, which allows firms to divert attention from economic goals to social goals.

name: Relative attention to social goals
authors_terms: ["relative attention to social goals", "attention allocation", "relative attention to social goals"]
definition: The ethical and philanthropic perspective is defined as 'the actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm, required by law.' The variable ranges between 0 and 40 with 0 being full attention to economic goals and 40 being full attention to social goals.

name: Media attacks on the focal firm
authors_terms: ["media attacks on focal firm", "media attacks on the focal organization", "media attacks"]
definition: Our main independent variable, media attacks, captures on a yearly basis the media attacks conveyed by multiple international newspapers against arms producers. A media attack publicly imposes onto a firm a vilifying label that signals an alleged violation of norms.

name: Media attacks on industry peers
definition: Thus, media attacks on peers represents the total number of articles attacking any firm in the industry but the focal firm.

name: Peer subcategory similarity
authors_terms: ["proximate peers", "similar peers", "distant peers", "industry subcategories", "subcategory structure", "segmentation of the global arms industry"]
definition: A distant peer is defined as a firm that has no direct product category overlap with the focal firm. ... By contrast, a proximate peer has at least one overlapping segment with the focal firm.

name: Asset divestment from the arms industry
authors_terms: ["asset divestment", "asset divestment from the arms industry", "divestment"]
definition: Our dependent variable, asset divestment from the arms industry (hereafter, asset divestment), captures a focal firm's decision to dissociate from the arms industry by divesting assets from the industry. We argue that asset divestment from the stigmatized industry signals to expert journalists, investors, and the public that the firm is determined to streamline its activities, refocus on more acceptable pursuits, and manage its long-term reputation.

name: Parent control
definition: Parent control is defined as the influence exercised by a partner over IJV operations (Schaan, 1983; Geringer and Hebert, 1989), and is used by parent firms to align IJV activities and performance with their own venturing objectives.

name: Output control
definition: Output control focuses on the outcomes of IJVs. To exercise output control, parent firms specify explicit outcome requirements, measure the achievement of such requirements, and exert rewards or penalties accordingly.

name: Process control
definition: Process control regulates the activities of IJV operations. To exercise process control, parent firms specify the behaviors and processes in which the IJV must engage, and monitor the implementation of such activities.

name: Social control
definition: Social control influences the IJV through social interactions, which facilitate shared values and common understanding between parent firms and the IJV.

name: Property-based resource contribution
definition: Property-based resources are well-defined assets, to which owners have clear property rights, such as financial capital, physical assets, patents, and brands.

name: Knowledge-based resource contribution
definition: Knowledge-based resources refer to a firm's intangible know-how and skills, such as technological and managerial expertise.

name: Venture importance
authors_terms: ["venture importance", "IJV importance", "importance of an IJV to its parent"]
definition: Venture importance refers to the importance of an IJV to its foreign or local parent.

name: Goal incongruence
definition: Goal incongruence measures differences between foreign and local parent objectives.

name: Parent resource contribution
definition: Parent resource contribution refers to the overall resources a parent firm contributes to an IJV, encompassing both property-based and knowledge-based resources.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "corporate strategic change", "change in corporate strategy", "product-market change"]
definition: Decisions about the products and markets firms compete in, that is, the range of products a firm competes in. It was operationally defined as the absolute percentage of annual change in degree of diversification across the 20 product-markets of the semiconductor industry.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of an organization is one of the clearest indicators of the viability of its strategy and an important predictor of whether it will change the markets it competes in; it was measured as industry-adjusted average growth over two years.

name: Chief executive succession
definition: Change in a firm's chief executive; when chief executive succession occurs, a new individual with new skills and perspectives takes charge of an organization. Succession was measured from t - 1 to t and was dummy-coded as 1 when a succession event occurred.

name: Chief executive tenure
definition: The length of time a chief executive has been in the job; measured as the number of years a firm's current chief executive had held the job at time t.

name: Top management team tenure
authors_terms: ["top management tenure", "top management team tenure", "team tenure"]
definition: The organizational tenure of a firm's top management team, whose members are the individuals reporting directly to a firm's chief executive; team tenure was measured by taking the average of the aggregate tenure of all top managers.

name: Top management team tenure diversity
authors_terms: ["top management tenure diversity", "top management team heterogeneity", "top management team homogeneity", "tenure diversity"]
definition: The homogeneity or heterogeneity of the distribution of organizational tenure within a top management team; it is not only the absolute level of a team's tenure but also the homogeneity of the tenure distribution that leads to a propensity to maintain the status quo.

name: HRM inducements and investments
authors_terms: ["HRM inducements and investments", "inducements and investments", "HRM inducement and investment index"]
definition: Certain HRM practices (e.g., training, pay level, benefits level, job security, and procedural justice) reflect higher levels of inducements and investments offered to employees. From an employer's perspective, HRM inducements and investments represent a sustained commitment to workers and an attempt to build deep pools of human capital.

name: HRM expectation-enhancing practices
definition: Certain HRM practices reflect higher levels of employer expectations about employee performance levels. Individual pay-for-performance systems, employee monitoring, and formal performance appraisals are examples of such practices.

name: Good-performer quit rate
definition: The voluntary turnover (quit) rate of employees who perform well, which the authors treat as dysfunctional turnover.

name: Poor-performer quit rate
definition: The voluntary turnover (quit) rate of employees who perform poorly, which the authors treat as functional turnover.

name: Public politics
definition: The act of leveraging the state or its agencies to effect policy change. In this study, public political tactics are captured by climate change activists serving as witnesses in U.S. Senate or House of Representatives hearings on climate change.

name: Private politics
definition: Collective interactions between parties attempting to advance their interests that do not rely on the law, public order, or the state. Private political tactics include consumer boycotts, protests, and blockades.

name: Internal practice adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of internal practices", "CO2 EOR injection", "CO2-injection technology", "practice adoption"]
definition: The adoption of firm practices that attempt to address movement demands; in this study, the internally focused practice is CO2 EOR injection.

name: Affiliation seeking
authors_terms: ["affiliation seeking", "affiliating with associations", "membership in movement-aligned associations"]
definition: Firms' seeking affiliation with prominent associations that seek to address movement concerns, signaling that the firm has aligned itself with movement demands.

name: Press release framing
authors_terms: ["press releases", "framing of movement concerns and firm actions via press releases", "framing activities"]
definition: Firms' use of press releases to frame the movement's issues and their own actions in ways that protect their image and reputation.

name: CDE prior M&A experience
authors_terms: ["CDE M&A Experience", "CDEs' prior M&A experience", "M&A experience of the CDE"]
definition: CDE M&A Experience is defined as the total number of announced deals that the CDE has done in prior jobs in corporate development or M&A functions before starting the current job.

name: M&A performance
definition: M&A performance is measured as Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CARs) to firms' stock prices at the time of deal announcement, providing an immediate and direct assessment of firms' strategic decisions.

name: CEO prior M&A experience
definition: CEO M&A Experience is defined as the number of announced deals the CEO has done before starting their current job, either in corporate development, prior CEO roles, or as specifically stated in their job descriptions.

name: Firm prior M&A experience
authors_terms: ["Firm M&A Experience", "the firm's prior M&A experience"]
definition: Following prior studies on firm-level M&A learning, the authors measure Firm M&A Experience as the log of the total announced deals prior to the current year.

name: Relative CEO M&A experience
authors_terms: ["CEO Has More M&A Experience", "CEO-CDE M&A Experience Gap"]
definition: To test H2, the authors create two measures for contexts where the CEO has more M&A experience than the CDE: a binary indicator, CEO Has More M&A Experience, that equals one when CEO M&A Experience is greater than CDE M&A Experience, and a continuous variable, CEO-CDE M&A Experience Gap, capturing the difference in deal counts when the CEO has more experience.

name: CDE similar deal experience
authors_terms: ["CDE Similar M&A Experience", "CDEs' prior experience with similar deals"]
definition: The authors construct seven alternative measures of CDE, CEO, and firm experiences based on the similarity between prior deals and the focal deal, and calculate CDE, CEO, and Firm Similar M&A Experience as the count of prior deals sharing each characteristic with the focal target.

name: CDE career diversity
authors_terms: ["CDE Career Diversity", "diversity of CDEs' prior career experiences"]
definition: CDE Career Diversity is calculated as one minus the Herfindahl index based on the proportion of years spent in different firms (Models 1-3) or different job functions (Models 4-6) before starting the current role.

name: Product line length
authors_terms: ["product line length", "product count", "number of products in line"]
definition: Following Bayus and Putsis (1999), I refer to the count of products that a firm offers at a given time as product line length. Measuring breadth via product line length ignores distinctions between products, but produces a measure of how much a firm tries to tailor its offerings to fine-grained consumer preferences.

name: Product line complexity
definition: Conceptually, it captures the degree to which the product line draws on different knowledge bases or the diversity of routines required to produce the product line.

name: Product line overlap
authors_terms: ["product line overlap", "overlap", "mean overlap with other firms"]
definition: A firm's product line defines the customers that it is attempting to attract, and the degree to which those customers are similar to those sought by other firms in its markets determines the overlap between that firm and its rivals. For new entrants, the effect of overlap between firms' product lines is to increase the degree to which they draw on the same resources and therefore reduce each other's life chances.

name: Firm failure
authors_terms: ["probability of failure", "failure", "exit from the bicycle industry", "dissolution"]
definition: The dependent variable is the firm's exit from the bicycle industry. Acquisitions are treated as right censored, as exit by acquisition is fundamentally different from exit by dissolution.

name: Complementor scale
definition: Complementors that are larger in scale (i.e., offer more content) are more likely to draw attention than smaller complementors; off-platform, scale reflects a larger consumer base.

name: Complementor scope
definition: Complementors that are broader in scope offer less specialized content that spans multiple categories, so they enjoy attention spillovers across multiple product categories and do not disproportionately lose attention in any specific category.

name: Removal from news aggregators
authors_terms: ["being removed from news aggregators", "being delisted from a news aggregator platform", "struck off", "platform removal"]
definition: Being delisted (struck off) a news aggregator platform: how the web traffic of delisted outlets is affected compared with the traffic of outlets whose content remained on the aggregators.

name: Web traffic
definition: An outlet's number of visits per month, where a visit is defined as an entire user session on the outlet's own web page rather than its content on the news aggregator.

name: Open-ended communication
definition: Communication behaviours that do not revolve closely around an existing artifact and therefore have, by definition, fewer artifact-based constraints; this communication is informal as it tends to be spontaneous, interactive, and rich. On the SF.net platform, open-ended communication is typical of forums.

name: Artifact-based communication
definition: Artifact-based communication refers to the 'epistemic machinery' that supports ongoing communication, including not only the actual means of communication but also the artifacts around which communication revolves. Such artifacts enable and constrain communication, and in the FOSS context they are existing lines of formal code, communicated through patch files, bug reports, feature requests, and support requests submitted to tracker systems.

name: Project launching
authors_terms: ["project launching", "projects launched", "launching a new project", "project-launching behavior"]
definition: Members of the FOSS community can formulate new problems by launching a new project; the initiator designs the problem architecture, formulates the problem, and outlines the first steps toward solving it. Project launching manifests that an overarching problem and a problem architecture have been formulated.

name: Project joining
definition: Other community members may join a project around a formulated problem and work on subproblems; members who join a project adopt a second-tier role within an existing team in which many routines, roles, tasks, and cognitive structures are predefined. An individual who joins typically joins a more or less well-defined subproblem within the architecture.

name: Risk
authors_terms: ["risk", "total risk", "variance of ROE", "variance of returns", "accounting-based measures of risk"]
definition: For each period, the authors calculated the variance of ROE as an accounting-based measure of firm risk. Total risk, or variance of returns, was evaluated rather than systematic risk (beta).

name: Firm return
authors_terms: ["return", "average ROE", "return on equity (ROE)", "accounting-based measures of firm return"]
definition: For each period, the authors calculated the average ROE as an accounting-based measure of firm return.

name: Target return level
authors_terms: ["target return level", "target level", "reference point", "industry's median return on equity (ROE)", "overall median ROE"]
definition: Because evidence indicates firms adjust financial ratios toward industry-wide averages, an average performance (return) level was taken as an appropriate proxy for a given firm's target or reference level: the industry's median ROE for within-industry analyses and the overall median ROE across industries.

name: Executive job anxiety
definition: Job anxiety, which we define as the general level of worry experienced in connection with one's job over time.

name: Social buffering
definition: The degree to which top executives appoint decision-making teams whom they perceive as providing a supportive inner circle, which we refer to as social buffering.

name: Strategic risk taking
definition: The level of risk that top executives are willing to accept in their firms' strategies; operationally the perception of firm risk associated with a given strategic decision.

name: Perceived gain/loss context
definition: We conceptualize decision context as a continuum reflecting the extent to which an executive frames his or her overall situation at a given time as generally favorable (i.e., gain context) or unfavorable (i.e., loss context) relative to a reference point.

name: Cumulative experience
definition: We followed the learning-curve tradition by cumulating all prior IVF cases that occurred since clinic i started offering IVF treatment until but not including the focal year. The natural log is used as the independent variable in keeping with the learning-curve literature.

name: Experience accumulation time
authors_terms: ["experience accumulation time", "time taken to accumulate experience", "clinic age", "time compression"]
definition: We measured this relationship by interacting cumulative experience amassed by a firm with the firm's age in years, which is the time it took to accumulate that level of experience. Firm age (Ageit-1) is the number of years since clinic i started offering IVF treatment as reported to HFEA until but not including the focal year.

name: Clinic performance
authors_terms: ["desirable performance outcomes", "clinic capabilities", "live birth events", "successful treatments"]
definition: We measured clinic capabilities as the natural log of number of live-birth events (or successful treatments) for a clinic in a given year. We controlled for the natural log of the total number of treatments (i.e., IVF cycles) administered in that clinic-year in the RHS.

name: Task complexity
definition: To test Hypothesis 2, we measured task complexity as the proportion of female patients above age 35 whom the clinic treated during the focal year. Since the chance of success through IVF decreases sharply after the age of 35, treating older women represents a challenge for clinics.

name: Integrator presence
