definition: In our data, some clinics had a defined integrator role fulfilled by either a nurse or a physician, who had the responsibility of shepherding a patient across the multiple specialists and ensuring transfer of all vital information about the patient across the several IVF treatment stages. Organizations employ integrators in order to facilitate coordination between interdependent individuals.

name: Generativity
definition: The ecosystem's capacity to produce new output through unfiltered contributions from broad and varied audiences, or the capacity to produce unprompted change driven by large, varied, and uncoordinated audiences.

name: User satisfaction
definition: How well a given game title satisfies users' preferences and expectations about product use and, thus, consumption utility, that is, how much gamers enjoy it; it reflects how a game's elements such as game-play mechanics, graphics, sound, user interface, narrative content, and software-hardware integration interact to create the consumption experience.

name: Platform maturity
authors_terms: ["platform maturity", "maturity stage", "late maturity stage", "early maturity stage"]
definition: The evolutionary stage of a console's life cycle; the late maturity stage is defined as titles launched from the end of the fourth year on, and the early maturity stage as titles launched during the first year of a console's life.

name: Cross-platform competition
definition: The intensity of competition among rival platform systems, which influences the extent to which a complementor cospecializes in a focal ecosystem and aligns to that ecosystem's shared objectives.

name: Variance in user satisfaction
authors_terms: ["variance in user satisfaction", "dispersion in user satisfaction", "variance of user satisfaction", "undesirable variance"]
definition: The dispersion of user satisfaction from complement consumption in the system, reflecting the coexistence of first- and second-rate complements and the information asymmetry that prevents consumers from distinguishing between them ex ante.

name: Complementor identification with focal ecosystem
definition: The extent to which complementors identify with the focal ecosystem.

name: Black faculty
definition: Because organizations may seek recognition for their diversity-related achievements, we adopted an observer-selection approach, which involves racial classification by perceivers. Due to the low representation of some underrepresented groups, as well as several unique features associated with Asian or Asian American faculty in particular, we restricted our primary analyses to examining differences between Black and White faculty.

name: Joint appointment
definition: A joint appointment is considered a formal one when each participating department contributes a portion of an individual's compensation. We argue that the disproportionate use of joint appointment among underrepresented groups instantiates the previously theorized paradox of diversity achievement: lack of adjustment for these unique costs in performance evaluation constitutes a significant discrepancy between allocation and valuation.

name: Attrition
definition: We expect that misalignment between allocation in the matching process and valuation in the evaluation process can overexpose individuals to a set of unique costs that negatively affect their career advancement, consequently increasing their likelihood of voluntary and involuntary attrition. Employees who experience a misalignment between the scope of allocation and the scope of evaluation have a higher likelihood of attrition.

name: Research productivity
authors_terms: ["research productivity", "productivity as research scholars", "rate of publication"]
definition: We followed the convention in the literature and measured research productivity by using article counts. The sum burdens of joint appointment may constitute substantial hurdles that handicap individuals' research productivity.

name: Use of technical consultants
authors_terms: ["technical consultants", "winemaking consultants", "use of winemaking consultants", "use of technical consultants"]
definition: Technical consultants are specialists that rely on a deep expertise in activities such as engineering, information technology, or manufacturing, in contrast to management consultants who work in generic areas of management expertise. Firms essentially hire technical consultants to benefit from their knowledge, in particular their 'best practices.'

name: Relative product quality
definition: Performance is best understood as relative rather than absolute, and the tasting scores used in the study are relative rather than absolute measures of wine quality: critics taste 'en primeur' wines against each other in order to assess the quality of the wine vis-a-vis its peers and to determine its relative value.

name: Extremeness of relative product quality
authors_terms: ["extremeness of relative product quality", "extreme quality ratings", "big failures", "big successes"]
definition: The extremeness of relative product quality refers to the likelihood of extremely low performance ('big failures') or extremely high performance ('big successes') relative to other wines. It is operationalized as a wine's absolute deviation from the average tasting score across all wines in the sample in a given year.

name: Relative resource quality
definition: Consistent with Holcomb et al. (2009), 'resource quality' is defined as the value creation potential of a resource. In the Bordeaux wine industry the terroir is the main productive resource, and its quality is assessed relative to other Bordeaux wineries.

name: Prior alliance experience
authors_terms: ["prior alliance experience", "prior experience", "alliance experience", "prior alliance participation"]
definition: Participation in alliances before the focal alliance. Via prior alliance experience, allying firms can develop means to assess alliance performance, judge how best to communicate with partners, and develop other metrics that provide guidance for other decisions such as alliance contract structure.

name: Firm collaborative benefits
definition: The benefits a firm obtains from its collaborations, which the authors measure through the firm's post-alliance innovative performance (patenting) since alliance outcomes can only be measured via the partner firms.

name: Alliance uncertainty and complexity
authors_terms: ["uncertainty", "complexity", "alliance characteristics", "uncertainty or complexity of alliance activities"]
definition: The extent to which alliance activities are characterized by greater complexity or uncertainty, such as when partner contributions and outcomes cannot be well specified in advance. The probability of selecting an equity joint venture captures the degree of uncertainty or complexity of alliance activities.

name: Service climate
authors_terms: ["service climate", "employee perceptions of the practices, procedures, and behaviors ... with regard to customer service and customer service quality"]
definition: Service climate is defined as employee perceptions of the practices, procedures, and behaviors that are expected, supported, and rewarded with regard to customer service and customer service quality. The authors describe it as a team-embodied, socially complex organizational resource that is intangible in character.

name: Managerial IT knowledge
authors_terms: ["managerial information technology knowledge", "managerial IT knowledge", "managerial IT skills", "shared knowledge between line and IT managers"]
definition: It is the overlapping pool of shared knowledge (the knowledge that the IT manager possesses about the business process, and the knowledge that the line manager possesses about the potential opportunities to apply IT to improve process performance) and common understanding regarding how IT may be used to improve the process that represents the construct of managerial IT knowledge. It is described as an important capability that is intangible in character.

name: Technology resources
authors_terms: ["technology resources in customer service", "technology resources", "information technology applications"]
definition: Technology resources are process-specific ITs that are used to support specific processes; they refer to the set of well-known computing technologies in an industry that are available from factor markets and understood to have a positive impact on the performance of specific processes. They are valuable physical capital resources that are tangible in character.

name: Investment in customer service
authors_terms: ["investments in customer service", "total investment in the customer service business process", "investment in customer service"]
definition: One possible determinant of the performance of the customer service process is simply the investment in this process; in general, the greater this investment, the higher the expected quality of this process. Such investments are very tangible.

name: Customer service process performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the customer service process", "customer service performance", "customer service quality", "effectiveness of business processes"]
definition: Performance of the customer service process is the key dependent variable in this study. The authors note that customer service is a very broad concept and that there is no perfect measure of customer service performance, so multiple measures were used.

name: Firm performance
definition: Most quantitative tests of resource-based theory correlate measures of resources and capabilities with some measure of firm performance, a highly aggregated dependent variable. A firm's overall performance depends on, among other things, the net effect of its business processes on the firm's position in the market place.

name: Inventive collaboration with product users
authors_terms: ["inventive collaborations with product users", "physician collaboration", "physician coinvention", "firm-physician inventive collaborations", "coinvented patents"]
definition: It is this type of inventive collaboration, where the company is listed as the assignee and a physician appears as an inventor on the patent, that we examine in our paper. Our primary independent variables of interest are firm-physician inventive collaborations in the current and prior year, which we proxy for with the count of patents assigned to the firm that are coinvented with a physician in a firm-year observation, where the year is the application year.

name: Innovative performance
definition: We constructed a firm-year count of the number of FDA-approvals (NumInnov) based on the CDRH data. To date the innovations, we used the year that the application was received by the FDA.

name: Radical innovation
definition: Radical innovation in contrast is based on a different set of engineering and scientific principles and often opens up whole new markets and potential applications. The most novel devices, for which no equivalent device exists, undergo the much more rigorous premarket approval (PMA) process, which involves animal testing and human clinical trials.

name: Incremental innovation
definition: Incremental innovation introduces relatively minor changes to the existing product, exploits the potential of the established design, and often reinforces the dominance of established firms. Devices approved through the 510(k) process are thus intended to be incremental and are often modifications to existing products.

name: Technology area age
authors_terms: ["age of the technology area", "technology class age", "newer technology areas", "established technology areas"]
definition: We used establishment dates at the primary and subclass level to determine the technology-class age of each patent as equal to the application year of the patent less the establishment date of the class to which it is currently assigned.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Diversification is the corporate strategy of pursuing economic rents by leveraging competencies to sell goods and services in multiple markets. The authors expected product and international diversification to have similar effects, as both entail entering new markets and both can generate sales growth and impact profitability.

name: Transactional ownership
definition: The authors describe foreign owners as transactional because they obtain returns solely from their shareholdings and lack other relationships with the firms in which they have ownership positions. They differ from domestic owners in having dispersed holdings, no business relationships with the owned firms, and frequent trading of shares.

name: Relational ownership
definition: The authors label domestic owners relational because they are long-term owners with complex performance goals; they do not just seek financial gains from their shareholdings but also have other business and reciprocal relationships with those firms that yield benefits.

name: Shareholder profit
definition: Following prior research, the authors label the rent appropriated by shareholders as profit. They measure shareholder profit with Tobin's Q, the ratio of a firm's market value to the replacement cost of its assets.

name: Sales growth
definition: The authors' theory suggests that relational owners may benefit as a focal firm's revenues increase, and they model firm growth accordingly, assessing it with the natural logarithm of year-over-year change in sales.

name: Employment growth
authors_terms: ["employment growth", "growth in employment", "growth in the workforce"]
definition: The authors argue that both rank-and-file employees and executives may benefit from growth in the workforce, and that relational owners support diversification as a prime vehicle for driving such growth and for avoiding layoffs by finding new roles for redundant employees.

name: Managerial compensation
definition: An argument in prior agency research is that growth, which diversification generally produces, may allow managers to capture value through higher salaries, and that increases in diversification may justify higher salaries because they raise the complexity of managerial tasks.

name: Generic human capital
definition: Human capital resources that are 'transferable across a variety of firms.' Generic human capital is expected to be valuable and potentially rare; in this study it is operationalized as a unit's aggregate of basic personality and cognitive ability.

name: Unit-specific human capital
definition: Human capital resources that are tied to a particular unit and have little relevance to other units; it accrues through on-the-job training and experience, so that knowledge of a job, other employees, and customers becomes increasingly embedded and tacit.

name: Unit service performance behavior
definition: The collective service behavior manifested by employees in a unit (e.g., efficiency, quality); it is operationalized as customer perceptions of the unit's service performance.

name: Unit effectiveness
definition: The consequences of unit service performance behavior (e.g., sales); the authors define unit effectiveness in terms of unit financial success and operationalize it through two indexes commonly used to reflect productivity and profitability in the service sector.

name: Public protest
definition: Protests against contentious firm practices act as external cues for regulators about social opposition to firm practices. The variable Protests is based on the count of reported protest events within the geographic vicinity of a firm's nuclear power plant generating unit(s).

name: Regulated rate of return
authors_terms: ["Rate of Return", "regulated financial rate of return", "ROR", "regulatory outcomes in nontargeted domains"]
definition: Our dependent variable, Rate of Return, is the percentage financial return a firm is permitted to earn on its assets as determined by the state PUC during a regulatory rate review. The ROR is a publicly visible and widely salient regulatory decision.

name: Government ideological alignment with activists
authors_terms: ["Democratic Governor and Legislature", "dominant political ideology of elected political institutions", "ideological alignment between executive and legislative branches of government"]
definition: Top-down political pressure is more effective when there is ideological alignment between legislative and executive branches of government. Under a politically aligned government, regulators are likely to be especially attuned to elected politicians' responses to activist protests, recognizing the greater risk of straying too far from political views of the public interest.

name: Regulator ideological alignment with activists
authors_terms: ["Democratic Regulator", "regulator political ideology", "ideological alignment between regulators and activists"]
definition: Regulators can have ideological orientations that inform their decision making on regulatory issues. Ideological biases that favor a particular stakeholder group can enter regulatory decisions because regulators possess discretion when weighing up competing stakeholder interests.

name: Firm reputation with regulators
authors_terms: ["firm's reputation with the regulatory agency", "prior reputation with an industry regulator", "reputational standing with the regulator", "Performance in Prior Rate Review"]
definition: Firms in regulated industries develop reputations with regulators for operating in a manner that is consistent with the public interest based on a history of repeated firm-regulator interactions over time, during which regulators learn about a firm's organizational culture and decision-making processes.

name: Prior accommodation of activist demands
authors_terms: ["prior accommodation of activist demands", "history of accommodating activist demands", "prior receptiveness to activist organizations' demands", "Nuclear Units Cancelled"]
definition: The ability of firms to defuse conflict and to reach agreement or compromise can signal that their business operates in the public interest and that they value cooperative relationships with external stakeholders. A track record of working productively with social movement organizations enables firms to develop a reputation for being a 'good corporate citizen' that responds to reasonable social concerns.

name: Interdisciplinary research
definition: Research that ''integrates perspectives, information, data, techniques, tools, concepts, and/or theories from two or more disciplines'' (National Academies of Science, National Academy of Engineering, and Institute of Medicine, 2005: 188). The authors measure it at the paper level as the variety, balance, and cognitive distance of the subject categories of a paper's references.

name: Research productivity
definition: The number of articles a scientist publishes; the authors rely on ''the total number of articles published in WoS journals from the beginning of a scholar's career-the year he or she first published-until 2005.''

name: Scholarly visibility
definition: In academe, positive reception is typically gauged via citations: ''A scientist's citation count gives a good indication of his or her visibility in the scientific community, and for this reason it is factored into promotion and tenure decisions.''

name: Variability in visibility
authors_terms: ["variability in citations", "variability in visibility", "variance of citations", "higher variance in reception"]
definition: The dispersion of the citations a scientist's work receives; the authors expect ''interdisciplinary work to have greater variability in citations'' and test this with the standard deviation of each scientist's citations.

name: Field-level interdisciplinarity
authors_terms: ["field IDR", "field-level interdisciplinarity", "intellectual context", "trend in field IDR"]
definition: The interdisciplinary nature and dynamism of a scientist's primary field: ''Interdisciplinarity varies across fields,'' and fields also change over time and at different rates.

name: Collaborative stakeholder engagement
authors_terms: ["collaborative engagement", "collaborative engagements", "community policing practices", "collaborative stakeholder engagement"]
definition: ''Collaborative engagement' refers specifically to organizational partnerships with dispersed stakeholder groups, such as customers, communities, advocacy groups, or other parties, to pursue or accomplish shared goals.',' These engagements could be formal or informal and are distinct from collaborations with consolidated exchange partners such as peer organizations or suppliers.

name: Information received from external stakeholders
authors_terms: ["volume of relevant information received from participants and observers", "volume of information received from external stakeholders", "information received from external stakeholders", "calls for service"]
definition: The volume of relevant information received from participants and observers, both from direct participants such as involved individuals and community groups and from third-party observers; in this setting, members of the general public provide information about crime events, emergencies, and other service issues directly to law enforcement agencies through 9-1-1 call systems.

name: Organizational problems
authors_terms: ["organizational problems", "organizational problems involving community members", "problems", "crime rate"]
definition: Problems and performance declines that prompt decision makers to mobilize resources and scan their environments for corrective solutions, and which involve the external stakeholders holding relevant information; in this setting the crime rate within an agency's jurisdiction is a clear and salient organizational problem involving community members.

name: Stakeholder power
definition: Law enforcement agencies are subject to varying degrees of formal and informal external oversight and governance from policymakers and legislators, judicial systems, advocacy organizations, and citizens, with greater governance and oversight leading agencies to operate less autonomously and therefore signifying increased stakeholder power.

name: Controversial practices
authors_terms: ["controversial practices", "controversy", "nonlethal patrol gear", "use of force complaints"]
definition: Organizational practices that outside observers have already deemed controversial, so that stakeholders may object to the organization's tactics, approach, or plans; the authors employ two different variables to separately proxy for distinct aspects of controversy in this setting.

name: Availability of automating research technology
authors_terms: ["automating research technology", "automating technology", "IT-based technology", "research technology", "the Kinect shock"]
definition: Throughout this paper, we use the terms automating technology, IT-based technology, and research technology and similar variants interchangeably to refer to IT-based devices (including both software and hardware) that are used in the process of research and that automate certain research tasks, for example, data-collection tasks and data-analysis tasks. Kinect suddenly and dramatically made available a research technology that automates certain motion-sensing research tasks.

name: Research productivity
authors_terms: ["rate of research output", "rate of knowledge output", "research productivity", "productivity"]
definition: Counts of academic publications and citations are established (though imperfect) measures of research output. We use these to evaluate the impact of Kinect on researchers' rate of knowledge output (i.e., productivity).

name: Research project portfolio composition
authors_terms: ["composition of research project types", "type of knowledge output", "type of knowledge produced", "portfolio of project types"]
definition: We distinguish between two concepts capturing changes in researches' portfolios of project types: (1) the extent to which the portfolio of researcher i is concentrated or diverse at time t (Diversificationit) and (2) the extent to which the portfolio of researcher i involves topics that are closer or further from each other in ideas space at time t - 1 versus t (Trajectoryit).

name: Research diversification
definition: We define diversification as the breadth of a researcher's portfolio of projects at one point in time t.

name: Research trajectory
definition: We define trajectory as the distance in knowledge space between a researcher's portfolio of projects at times t - 1 and t.

name: Research area expertise
authors_terms: ["within-area researchers", "outside-area researchers", "specialized human capital", "treated researchers", "involvement in motion-sensing"]
definition: We distinguish between two types of researchers: those who had previously worked in the research area where the tasks affected by the automating research technology reside, whom we call within-area researchers, and those who had not previously worked in the area, whom we describe as outside-area researchers.

name: Cultural diversity in management
authors_terms: ["cultural diversity in management", "cultural heterogeneity in management", "racial and gender heterogeneity in management", "racial diversity in management", "gender diversity in management"]
definition: Cultural diversity encompasses differences in visible characteristics such as race and gender; the authors assessed the racial and gender heterogeneity of each bank's management group, using Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity to develop measures of racial and gender diversity in management.

name: Firm performance
definition: Productivity, an intermediate output measure, is an important performance indicator in a bank; return on equity is the bottom-line measure of financial performance and a preferred measure of a bank's financial performance and overall viability.

name: Innovativeness
definition: Innovativeness reflects the propensity of a firm to actively support new ideas, novelty, experimentation, and creative solutions in pursuit of a competitive advantage.

name: Risk taking
definition: The risk-taking dimension of strategic posture is a firm's propensity to take business-related chances with regard to strategic actions in the face of uncertainty.

name: Proactiveness
definition: Proactiveness is its propensity to take the initiative to compete aggressively with other firms.

name: Governance structure
authors_terms: ["governance structure", "franchised vs. company-owned governance structures", "franchised and company-owned arrangements"]
definition: We define governance structure as an organization design that incorporates systems of decision making, operational control, and incentives.

name: Strategy complexity
authors_terms: ["strategy complexity", "more complex strategy (i.e., RBD)", "mixed strategy", "strategic choice"]
definition: An important dimension upon which a strategy can be characterized is whether it is relatively simple vs. more complex; i.e., the degree to which it entails mixed goals, strategic activity, and different views.

name: Store performance
definition: The main dependent variable in our study is store performance. Most research on the performance of franchising focuses on chain performance ... We shifted attention to individual stores' financial performance and measured performance specifically in terms of percent change in store sales from time t - 1 to t.

name: TMT acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["TMT acquisition experience", "top management team's experience with acquisitions", "top management acquisition experience", "TMT's average experience with acquisitions"]
definition: The acquisition experience accumulated by the top management team: how long each team member had been on the TMT and how many acquisitions had been made during that period, added across team members and divided by team size.

name: Acquisition success
definition: We define acquisition success by whether the acquisition was subsequently retained, i.e., successful (coded as '0'), or divested, i.e., unsuccessful (coded as '1').

name: Acquisition frequency
authors_terms: ["number of acquisitions per year", "frequency of acquisitions", "rate of acquiring", "pace of acquisitions"]
definition: The frequency of acquisitions was measured by the number of acquisitions made by each company in each year. An acquisition is defined as the takeover of an existing company or of any of its business units.

name: TMT tenure diversity
authors_terms: ["TMT tenure diversity", "top team tenure diversity", "diversity in a TMT's tenure"]
definition: TMT tenure is the number of years an individual has served on the top executive team. Tenure diversity was computed in the conventional way using the coefficient of variation.

name: TMT educational diversity
authors_terms: ["TMT educational diversity", "top team educational diversity", "diversity in a TMT's education", "diversity in educational background and training"]
definition: Diversity in the type of education was computed in a conventional fashion using Blau's heterogeneity index, calculated as the reverse of the Herfindahl-Hirshman homogeneity index. The managers' dominant educational tracks were identified from their titles.

name: Firm strategic risk
authors_terms: ["firm strategic risk", "strategic risk taking", "strategic risk investments", "strategic risk actions"]
definition: We gauge this alignment by examining the link between CEO compensation and strategic risk taking by the firm, as reflected in three strategic actions involving risk: research and development (R&D) expenditures, capital investments, and the use of long-term debt. Increases in these actions reflect the degree to which CEOs invest in uncertain, but potentially valuable, strategic actions that may augment shareholder wealth.

name: Value of exercisable stock options
authors_terms: ["value of exercisable options", "accumulated value of exercisable stock options", "exercisable options held"]
definition: A stock option is a contract in which executives are granted the right, but not the obligation, to purchase a specific number of shares of firm stock, for a predetermined price, within a specified future time range. Vesting confers the right of ownership over the accumulated option value, giving holders the opportunity to capture this value at their discretion; a stock option is 'in the money' when the current stock price underlying the option is above the exercise price.

name: Value of unexercisable stock options
authors_terms: ["value of unexercisable options", "accumulated value of unexercisable stock options", "unexercisable options held"]
definition: Unexercisable options are de facto promises of future wealth that are inaccessible and depend on the movement of the underlying stock and the holder's continued association with the granting firm.

name: Value of restricted stock
authors_terms: ["value of restricted stock", "restricted stock holdings", "accumulated value of restricted stock"]
definition: In the case of restricted stock grants, a predetermined number of actual shares of stock are granted to the holders, generally without an exercise price. Whereas at granting at-the-money stock options have no accumulated value until they move into-the-money, restricted stock contains accumulated value immediately upon award.

name: Proportion of cash-based pay
authors_terms: ["proportion of cash-based pay", "proportion of cash-based compensation", "cash-based pay", "cash-based compensation"]
definition: We include two measures of cash forms of pay: base salary and annual cash bonus awards. These measures are combined into a measure of total cash compensation that is then divided by total compensation to produce a variable that represents the proportion of cash-based pay in the CEO's pay package; cash-based pay is argued to provide some protection from the vagaries of uncontrollable events that can threaten the accumulated value of equity-based pay elements.

name: Stock option reloading and repricing
definition: In addition to adjusting the relative mix of pay in a CEO's pay package a priori, boards often adjust compensation contracts ex post by replacing expired or exercised options with new stock options (known as reloading) and by lowering the exercise price of underwater stock options (known as repricing).

name: Historical stock price volatility
authors_terms: ["historical stock price volatility", "stock price volatility", "historical volatility"]
definition: Volatility reflects the variability in the market value of the stock underlying equity-based pay. Historical stock price volatility is the variance in firm stock price calculated over the prior 60-month period using daily closing prices.

name: Culture of competitiveness
definition: The 'degree to which [supply] chains are predisposed to detect and fill gaps between what the market desires and what is currently offered' (Hult et al., 2002: 577); it is an unobservable latent factor reflected in three orientations—innovativeness, entrepreneurial, and learning.

name: Knowledge development
definition: A phenomenon wherein actions lead to knowledge acquisition, information distribution, shared meaning, and achieved memory in the supply chain.

name: Market turbulence
definition: The rate of change in the composition of customers and their preferences.

name: Cycle time performance
authors_terms: ["cycle time performance", "order fulfillment cycle time", "cycle time", "CT"]
definition: The length of time between taking an order and delivery of the needed product to the customer; cycle time is a key metric for directly assessing supply chain functioning.

name: Learning orientation
definition: Members' values associated with the generation of new insights that have the potential to shape supply chain activities.

name: Innovativeness orientation
definition: Supply chain members' values associated with new idea generation (i.e., members' openness to new ideas).

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: The chain members' values associated with the pursuit of new market opportunities and the renewal of existing areas of supply chain activities.

name: Knowledge acquisition
definition: The process by which entities, such as organizations or supply chains, obtain wisdom.

name: Information distribution
definition: The process by which information from different sources is shared; in supply chains this sharing occurs throughout the chain, including its various nodes and members.

name: Shared meaning
definition: The process by which members develop common understandings about data and events, which is needed to harness collective action in supply chains.

name: Achieved memory
definition: The amount of knowledge, experience, and familiarity with the supply chain process, its operations, and behaviors; it serves as the mechanism by which knowledge is stored for future strategic use.

name: Street protests over noneconomic issues
authors_terms: ["street protest", "street protests over noneconomic issues", "mass incidents", "environmental protection and human rights protests"]
definition: The authors developed four categories of nonviolent street protests in China: economic security, environmental protection, human rights, and land use. They focus specifically on noneconomic protests, using the total counts of environmental protection and human rights protests in a city.

name: New venture founding
authors_terms: ["founding of new ventures", "new venture founding", "founding of new ventures at time t", "urban entrepreneurship"]
definition: Newly founded ventures, which have been recently registered as small and micro domestic firms, are typically private and entrepreneurial organizations in China; the authors aggregate the count of newly founded ventures within a city as the proxy for the founding of new ventures at time t.

name: Business loan increase
authors_terms: ["business loan increase", "relaxed business loan policies", "expansion of business loans", "loans of balance"]
definition: Among the most immediate tools at the disposal of local governments in developing economies are changes to business loan policies. An increase in loans of balance, in and of itself, reflects the motivation and ability of local government officials to provide business resources.

name: Regulatory reforms
authors_terms: ["regulatory reforms", "regulatory reforms that reduce business operating costs"]
definition: Regulatory reforms are defined as actions aiming to lower operating costs and eliminate unnecessary barriers to competition, innovation, and growth; such regulatory reforms can substantially affect entrepreneurial activities.

name: Political position prospects
authors_terms: ["political position prospect", "political position prospects", "career prospects", "political opportunity structure"]
definition: The authors define this as a mayor's perception of their job security and potential for career advancement. Political position prospects refer to the extent to which political leaders believe their current standing supports continued career advancement.

name: Middle-ground approaches
definition: A middle-ground approach lies between purely symbolic gestures and targeted policies that directly tackle protesters' demands. It involves enacting broadly popular, noncontroversial policies that are orthogonal to activists' specific claims but appeal to a wider public, thereby defusing or redirecting the momentum of protests.

name: Treatment unit type
authors_terms: ["unit type", "hybrids", "hybrid units", "drug abuse treatment units", "mental health treatment units"]
definition: Types of treatment settings: units founded and funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse that did not provide mental health services (drug abuse treatment units), units located in mental health centers and specializing in drug abuse treatment services (hybrids), and units located in community mental health centers that predominantly provided mental health services (mental health treatment units).

name: Reliance on professionals
authors_terms: ["reliance on professionals", "hiring professionals", "professional degrees or credentials"]
definition: A hiring practice: the extent to which a unit relied on professional degrees or credentials as a criterion in hiring staff members.

name: Reliance on ex-addicts
authors_terms: ["reliance on ex-addicts", "hiring ex-addicts", "personal history of substance abuse problems"]
definition: A hiring practice: the extent to which a unit relied on a personal history of substance abuse problems as a criterion in hiring staff members.

name: Emphasis on complete abstinence
authors_terms: ["sobriety goal", "complete abstinence from drug use", "complete abstinence from alcohol or drugs", "abstinence as a treatment goal"]
definition: The importance in treatment plans for clients of sobriety or complete abstinence from drug use. In the AA model that dominates the drug abuse sector, alcohol and drug abuse are believed to be diseases that can be treated only when clients abstain completely from abused substances.

name: Routine use of DSM-III
definition: A central rational myth in the mental health sector is that professionals should diagnose clients using psychological tests or classification systems such as the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of the American Psychiatric Association (third edition), referred to as DSM-III.

name: Proportion of drug abuse clients
authors_terms: ["percentage of drug abuse clients", "client mix", "client composition"]
definition: The percentage of clients served by a unit in the last 12 months whose primary problem was labeled as drug abuse. The greater the percentage of drug abuse clients that a hybrid serves, the less isomorphic it is with mental health treatment organizations.

name: Unit size and age
authors_terms: ["unit age", "size", "large, old hybrid units", "total number of full-time employee equivalents"]
definition: Two structural features of hybrid units: unit age, established from data provided by unit directors, and size, measured as the total number of full-time employee equivalents in 1984. Hannan and Freeman proposed that large, old organizations are less likely than small, new units to change core features such as goals and technologies.

name: Isomorphism with the mental health sector
authors_terms: ["isomorphism", "isomorphic with the mental health sector", "isomorphism of hybrid units with the mental health sector", "conformity"]
definition: Conformity of a hybrid unit to the beliefs and practices traditional in the mental health sector; the rational myths of that sector prescribe isomorphism in three core features: client characteristics, technologies and goals, and personnel training and socialization.

name: Parent resource support
authors_terms: ["resource support", "parent's resource support", "support from parent organizations"]
definition: The extent to which a hybrid receives resources from its parent organization, including funds for operating and payroll expenses, staff, supplies, equipment, and office space. Parent organizations have resources to coerce or induce subunits to conform to parents' beliefs and practices.

name: Parent social-psychological support
authors_terms: ["social-psychological support", "accepted by the community mental health center"]
definition: The extent to which a hybrid unit and its staff members are accepted by the community mental health center (their parent organization).

name: Mental health licenses
definition: The number of the three primary mental health licenses a unit holds; licenses or accreditations legitimize a hybrid in the mental health sector.

name: Mental health financial sources
authors_terms: ["number of mental health financial sources", "mental health sector financial sources"]
definition: The number of central mental health sector sources from which a unit received money in fiscal year 1984.

name: Financial support from mental health sources
authors_terms: ["total mental health financial support", "financial support from mental health sources outside the parent organization"]
definition: The total amount of financial support a hybrid receives from mental health sources other than its parent organization, computed from the percent of the unit's total operating budget for fiscal year 1984 that came from each central mental health source.

name: Private equity placement
definition: Private equity placements are not registered with the Securities Exchange Commission and have resale restrictions, so they can only be purchased by 'certified' investors. It is illiquidity, created by a resale restriction of up to 2 years under Rule 144, that primarily distinguishes the public and private equity markets.

name: Seasoned public offering
authors_terms: ["seasoned public offering", "public offering", "seasoned public equity offering"]
definition: Seasoned public offerings are public equity offerings completed subsequent to a firm's initial public offering, the public-market alternative to private equity placements for public firms. In the presence of information asymmetry, a negative stock price reaction accompanies public offerings, because they signal managers' belief that the market price is high relative to true value.

name: Short-term abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["short-term abnormal returns", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal return", "prediction errors"]
definition: Abnormal returns are measured as the difference between a firm's actual stock price for any given day and its predicted stock price, derived from regressions involving a market portfolio; when the changes in the firm price diverge from predicted changes, it can be assumed that new information about the firm has been revealed. A firm's abnormal return on the most recent private equity placement represents the degree to which there was information asymmetry prior to the private equity placement.

name: Financial capital acquisition
authors_terms: ["rate of financing", "attract subsequent financial capital", "financial resources"]
definition: The rate at which a firm initiates financing events, namely private equity placements or (seasoned) public offerings. The rate summarizes the information on the intervals of time between successive events, with higher values of the rate corresponding to shorter times between events.

name: Research partner acquisition
definition: The rate at which a firm initiates research alliance events. The rate summarizes the information on the intervals of time between successive events, with higher values of the rate corresponding to shorter times between events.

name: Commercial partner acquisition
definition: The rate at which a firm initiates commercial alliance events. The rate summarizes the information on the intervals of time between successive events, with higher values of the rate corresponding to shorter times between events.

name: Time since last private placement
authors_terms: ["private placement clock", "time since the last private equity placement", "recency of the private placement"]
definition: The elapsed time since a firm's last private equity placement. The authors argue that the longer it has been since the last private equity placement, the more information asymmetry about the firm, and that a lack of a private placement over an extended period of time can be interpreted as a negative signal.

name: Number of prior private equity placements
authors_terms: ["private placement count", "more prior private equity placements", "multiple private placements"]
definition: The cumulative number of private equity placements a firm has initiated prior to an event. The authors contend that with each private placement firms learn how to recruit private investors and convey information more effectively through the due diligence process, and that firms able to disseminate multiple signals allow the receiving firms to cross-validate their interpretation of firm valuation.

name: Academia-industry collaboration
definition: Collaboration between academic scientists and an industry partner on a research project; in the data, a paper reporting a simultaneous discovery that is a collaborative work between academia and industry rather than an academia-only paper.

name: Follow-on scientific publications
authors_terms: ["follow-on publications", "follow-on academic publications", "main author's follow-on papers", "contribution to open science"]
definition: We define follow-on research output of a scientist as the count of scientific papers that list the scientist as an author and cite her initial paper reporting the simultaneous discovery.

name: Follow-on patents
definition: The follow-on patenting efforts are measured as the count of patents that cite the original discovery (in their nonpatent references) and list the main scientist behind the discovery as an inventor.

name: Commercial potential of a research project
definition: We use the total count of patents that have cited any of the twin papers reporting a simultaneous discovery as a proxy for the commercial potential of that discovery. We then categorize discoveries that are above the median in commercial potential as discoveries with high commercial potential.

name: Industry partner experience
authors_terms: ["experience level of industry partners", "established companies", "industry partner is established"]
definition: To identify whether a company partner was established or not, we use the age of the company partner at the time of each discovery. Companies with more than 10 years of experience at the time of collaboration are categorized as established.

name: Acquirer returns
authors_terms: ["acquirer cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "acquirer returns", "stock market returns", "acquirer performance"]
definition: The abnormal return represents the cumulative difference between a company's observed return and its expected return, during a specific period surrounding the date of the firm's divestiture announcement.

name: Acquisition of divested assets
definition: In contrast to acquisitions of stand-alone firms, they involve the absorption of segments, units, or groups of tangible or intangible assets rather than the full acquisition of a complete entity.

name: Increase in asset relatedness
authors_terms: ["increase in asset relatedness", "improved asset fit", "increase in asset fit", "asset relatedness"]
definition: An acquirer is expected to extract higher synergistic value from the assets for sale if the specific assets are more closely related to the acquirer's operations than to the seller's operations.

name: Seller distress
authors_terms: ["seller distress", "financial distress of the seller", "financial distress of the selling parent firm"]
definition: Financially constrained sellers may be forced to conduct 'fire sales' at significant discounts from the asset value in order to raise the liquidity needed to cover upcoming debt payments. Thus, the bargaining power of a financially constrained seller is significantly lower compared to that of a proactive seller that is not financially constrained.

name: Strength of knowledge protection
authors_terms: ["strength of IP protection", "strength of knowledge protection", "degree of IP protection", "strength of protection", "degree of protection"]
definition: The strength of the legal protection a patent confers against imitation, measured by the breadth of the patent: the more times a given patent is considered an XY-type reference in the search reports of the patents citing it, the more breadth it is likely to have, which confers stronger protection to the patented knowledge. Measures are built at the inventor level based on the XY-type citations received by an inventor's patent portfolio filed with the participating firm up to the alliance announcement year.

name: Inventor allocation to collaboration
authors_terms: ["allocation of inventors", "assignment of R&D workers to collaboration", "inventor allocation decisions", "alliance staffing", "assignment of R&D employees to external collaborations"]
definition: Whether an inventor is allocated to a collaboration in which her firm participates; the assumption is that the selection of the inventors deputed to the collaboration can also be used to address the misappropriation concerns faced by the firm. Inventors participating in alliances are identified by detecting the authors of the patent applications that presumably stem from the collaboration and who can be identified as employees of the participating firms.

name: Product market competition
definition: This variable captures whether the allied firms are direct product-market competitors. We consider them as such if they share the same four-digit SIC code.

name: Technology overlap
definition: A proxy for the overlap in technology portfolios between partner firms, based on the distribution of the firms' patent applications across technology classes (IPC four-digit classes) during the 5 years prior to alliance formation. The construct takes values that range from zero to one, with a higher value indicating a higher degree of overlap.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["scope", "vertical scope of an alliance", "broad scope", "narrow scope"]
definition: The vertical scope of an alliance, distinguishing whether an alliance involves R&D activities exclusively, that is, the alliance has a narrow scope, or it includes manufacturing and/or marketing in addition to collaborative R&D, that is, the alliance has a broad scope.

name: Position in an acquisition wave
authors_terms: ["position of the acquisition in an acquisition wave", "position in a wave", "wave position", "position in wave", "acquisition order within a wave", "position within a wave"]
definition: To calculate an acquisition's relative position within a wave, we divided its ordinal position by the number of acquisitions that occurred in the overall wave. The authors argue that firms are more likely to experience performance benefits when acting early but negative returns when acting later in an acquisition wave.

name: Acquisition returns
authors_terms: ["acquisition returns", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "acquirer shareholder returns", "acquisition performance"]
definition: This price change is called an abnormal return and is calculated as the difference between the observed return for a security and the predicted, or normal return for the same security. Thus, the impact of an event on a firm is measured by the portion of the firm's returns that is unanticipated by an economic model of anticipated, or normal, returns.

name: Industry munificence
definition: We measured munificence using the regression coefficients for each of the regressions noted above divided by the mean value of industry sales. This measure provides an indication of the degree of growth or decline within an industry over the measured period.

name: Industry stability
authors_terms: ["industry stability", "stability/dynamism", "degree of stability in an industry environment", "market dynamism", "degree of market dynamism"]
definition: We then divided the standard error of the regression coefficient for each industry by the mean value of industry sales. This value is a measure of stability/dynamism. To have a high score on the scale indicate stability, we then subtracted this value from 1.

name: Serial acquisition
authors_terms: ["serial acquirer", "degree to which an acquiring firm is a serial acquirer", "serial pattern", "serial acquirers"]
definition: We measured the degree to which an acquisition was part of a serial pattern undertaken by an acquiring firm by calculating the number of acquisitions a firm participated in throughout an acquisition wave and dividing this value by the total number of acquisitions within a wave. Researchers have argued and found evidence that some firms undertake acquisitions on a regular basis, as part of their core business routines.

name: Stock financing
authors_terms: ["stock consideration", "type of financing used", "stock-based acquisitions", "form of consideration offered", "type of financing"]
definition: We measured the form of consideration offered as a percentage of the acquisition price paid in the acquirer's common stock. Cash financing is often seen as a signal that a firm has great confidence in an acquisition and may possess asymmetric information.

name: CEO-board chair separation
authors_terms: ["CEO-board chair separation", "separation of the CEO and board chair roles", "separation"]
definition: Separation of the CEO and board chair roles occurs when a firm that combines the two roles in one individual moves to a separate leadership structure in which the roles are held by two different individuals.

name: Apprentice separation
definition: This is the apprentice separation, in which a sitting CEO-board chair relinquishes the chief executive title but effectively remains chair, in violation of agency theorists' assumption of independence.

name: Departure separation
definition: In the second type, departure separations, firms separate the roles by replacing a CEO-board chair with two different individuals.

name: Demotion separation
definition: Removal of the board chair title from a sitting CEO, what we term a demotion, involves only a governance change; the CEO necessarily loses a position of authority he or she previously enjoyed.

name: Current firm performance
definition: We measured firm performance in two ways. We calculated stock return as the holding period return on a company's stock from beginning to end of a calendar year. We also measured performance in terms of the mean composite analyst rating of the company's stock in a given year.

name: Future firm performance
definition: Firm performance after a separation, measured in the same two ways as performance at the time of separation: stock return as the holding period return on the company's stock over a calendar year and the mean composite analyst rating of the company's stock in a given year.

name: CEO-board chair combination
definition: The likelihood that a firm comes full circle and recombines the leadership roles following a separation, that is, a switch from a separate leadership structure in the previous year to a combined leadership structure in the present year.

name: Organizational political ideology
definition: Defined as the ''prevailing beliefs among organizational members about how the social world operates, including convictions about what outcomes are desirable and how they should be achieved''; the concept refers to the idea that many organizations-even for-profit firms-can be usefully placed on an axis ranging from conservatism to liberalism.

name: Community political ideology
authors_terms: ["community ideology", "community liberalism", "ideology of the community environment"]
definition: Communities tend to embody widely varying political values, and communities can be thought of as distinct stakeholders for the firm, with the capacity to reward or punish an organization based on its members' ideologically infused perceptions of the appropriateness of organizational conduct.

name: Industry political ideology
authors_terms: ["industry ideology", "industry liberalism", "baseline ideological leaning of their industry"]
definition: The baseline ideological leaning of an industry-the extent to which firms in the industry are collectively liberal or conservative leaning-which decision makers are aware of and reflect in conceptualizing the uniqueness of their own firm in relation to industry peers.

name: Spatial proximity of employees to headquarters
authors_terms: ["employees' spatial proximity", "organizational members' spatial proximity to decision makers", "spatial proximity", "spatial proximity versus dispersion"]
definition: The extent to which organizational members are co-located with the headquarters where executives and staff functions tend to be based, as opposed to being distributed across multiple, geographically distant locales.

name: Concessions to activists' demands
authors_terms: ["concessions", "concede to activists' demands", "corporate openness to social activism"]
definition: A firm's decision to enact changes in line with activists' demands or goals, coded when a media article clearly mentions corporate agreement to activists' demands following a protest.

name: Organizational niche
definition: Organizational niches characterize the different resource requirements and productive capacities of individual organizations in a population. Populations can be seen as comprised of multiple organizational niches in a multidimensional resource space.

name: Organizational niche overlap density
definition: We define a property of every organizational niche, the overlap density, which measures the potential for competition faced by all organizations in that organizational niche. Overlap density gives information about the effective number of organizations that compete for the underlying resources.

name: Organizational niche nonoverlap density
definition: Nonoverlap density gives information about the effective number of organizations whose resource requirements do not overlap with those in the focal organizational niche. Overlap density and nonoverlap density help disaggregate the competitive and noncompetitive parts of population density for a focal organizational niche with respect to the underlying resources.

name: Organizational niche density
definition: The first part, organizational niche density refers to the number of DCCs that occupy the same organizational niche.

name: Partial overlap density
definition: The second part, partial overlap density refers to the aggregate of the organizational niche overlaps with DCCs that occupy different organizational niches.

name: Zero overlap density
definition: The first part, zero overlap density, refers to the number of DCCs occupying organizational niches that do not overlap with the focal organizational niche.

name: Partial nonoverlap density
definition: The second part, partial nonoverlap density, refers to the aggregate of the organizational niche nonoverlaps with DCCs that occupy different, but partially overlapped, organizational niches.

name: Organizational founding rate
authors_terms: ["founding rate", "DCC founding rate", "organizational founding", "number of DCC foundings"]
definition: The dependent variables in the study are the yearly number of DCC foundings that occurred at four levels of disaggregation. Because the dependent variables are count measures, the authors estimate the number of organizational foundings expected to occur within an interval of time.

name: Category typicality
definition: A product's similarity to its category peers (its 'category typicality') therefore captures its level of differentiation within its competitive space. Throughout the empirical analysis, the author uses 'genre typicality' to refer to the film-specific operationalization of 'category typicality'.

name: Conspicuous differentiation
definition: Borrowing is conspicuous when it involves features that strongly evoke the alternative category. The main independent variable captures the degree to which the differentiating features of a product are typical to a genre other than the product's labeled genres; the author refers to this as the product's conspicuous differentiation.

name: Audience evaluation
definition: The outcome variable of interest is IMDb Rating, which captures aggregate audience evaluation. It is an appropriate metric of product appeal because the proposed mechanisms are thought to affect consumer assessment of product appeal, which audience rating most closely approximates.

name: Evoked genre density
authors_terms: ["evoked-genre density", "density of the evoked genre", "density of the alternative category"]
definition: The author computes the evoked-genre density as the proportion of films in the sample belonging to the differentiation-evoked genre, within the time period that the focal film was released.

name: Incentive-based compensation
authors_terms: ["incentive pay", "incentive mix", "incentive-based reward strategy", "incentive rewards", "incentive-based compensation strategy", "variable pay", "incentives"]
definition: Pay strategy is conceptualized in terms of pay mix, the relative importance of variable (incentive) and fixed (salary, fringe benefits) components of the compensation package; incentive pay is the variable component of that package. Far from a fixed expense, it is paid when financial or other strategic objectives have been reached.

name: Fixed compensation
authors_terms: ["fixed pay", "fixed compensation costs", "salary and fringe benefits", "fixed pay components", "base compensation"]
definition: The fixed component of the compensation package, made up of salary and fringe benefits, which mature firms emphasize through a formal job evaluation process. It is the counterpart of the variable, incentive component in the authors' pay mix concept.

name: Stage in the product life cycle
authors_terms: ["stage in the product life cycle", "stage in the life cycle", "stage", "growth stage", "mature stage"]
definition: The stage of a company or business unit's products in the product life cycle, designated by respondents as either the growth stage (sales growing at 20 percent or more annually in real terms; technology and competitive structure still changing) or the mature stage (products or services familiar to the vast majority of prospective users; technology and competitive structure reasonably stable).

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["company or business unit size", "scale", "size of the firm", "organizational size"]
definition: Company or business unit size was measured as annual sales revenues.

name: High tech industry
authors_terms: ["high tech", "high tech firms", "traditional firms", "non-high tech companies", "industry traits"]
definition: A company or business unit was defined as high tech if its annual research and development budget is 5 percent or more of its sales revenues, which is the Massachusetts High Technology Council definition of a high tech firm.

name: Pay effectiveness
authors_terms: ["pay effectiveness", "effectiveness of the compensation system", "pay system effectiveness"]
definition: Pay effectiveness was conceptualized in terms of the extent to which the compensation system contributes to the achievement of organizational goals.

name: Financial accounting regulation
authors_terms: ["financial accounting regulation", "the 1970 and 1983 changes in financial accounting regulation", "law changes", "demand regulation", "regulatory years"]
definition: Between 1967 and 1990 four key regulatory measures were implemented; the authors group the four regulatory measures into demand regulation (measures 2 and 4) and supply regulation (measures 1 and 3), the demand regulation consisting of the 1970 and 1983 changes in financial accounting regulation.

name: Demand for audit services
authors_terms: ["demand for audit services", "forced demand for audit services", "changes in the size of the audit market"]
definition: There are two proxies for demand for audit services: first, the number of annual accounts disclosed by public companies, private companies and cooperatives; and, second, the number of professionals.

name: Degree of concentration
definition: As regards supply-side imperfections, a key issue is concentration; high degrees of concentration are a well-established manifestation of product market imperfection, though high degrees of concentration alone are indicative of, but not sufficient evidence for, imperfect product market competition.

name: Nonpartner-to-partner ratio
authors_terms: ["the ratio of RA employees plus independent RAs to RA partners", "nonpartner-to-partner ratio", "the ratio (average annual change in the number of RA employees)/(average annual change in the number of RA partners)"]
definition: Hypothesis 2 requires the variable 'number of auditors' to be differentiated according to the auditors' status in the firm, so the data set distinguishes employees, independent practitioners and partners; for professional services this ratio is considered to be a rough estimate of the profits available for partners, with lower ratios indicating greater profits.

name: Rent appropriation by RA partners
authors_terms: ["rent appropriation", "RA partners were able to appropriate the associated rent", "income of RA partners"]
definition: Basically, Conjectures 1 and 2, like Hypothesis 2, predict that a group within the industry—the partners of large audit firms—can exploit a sustainable competitive advantage.

name: Audit market group structure
authors_terms: ["dual market structure", "two segments", "leading segment of large firms and a follower niche of small firms", "the composition of the leading segment", "top ranking of audit firms"]
definition: Conventional wisdom in the accounting literature suggests that audit markets are characterized by a dual market structure—with a leading Big Four, Big Five or Big Eight versus a large number of small following firms; the stability of the Big Five for audit firms, in terms of size and market share, is striking.

name: Environmental commitment
definition: What a company is actually doing or has done with reference to environmental issues can describe its commitment to the natural environment. Firms were classified into four environmental profiles: reactive, defensive, accommodative, and proactive.

name: Perceived importance of regulatory stakeholders
definition: Regulatory stakeholders include governments, which make environmental regulations; trade associations, which collect information regarding both current and pending legislation; informal networks, which are important sources of technological information; and a given firm's competitors.

name: Perceived importance of community stakeholders
definition: The third group, community stakeholders, includes community groups, environmental organizations, and other potential lobbies. These stakeholders can mobilize public opinion in favor of or against a corporation's environmental performance.

name: Perceived importance of organizational stakeholders
definition: The second group, organizational stakeholders, includes those who are directly related to an organization and have the ability to impact its bottom line directly. This stakeholder group includes customers, suppliers, employees, and shareholders.

name: Perceived importance of the media
definition: The fourth stakeholder group is the media. The media can influence society's perception of a company, especially when environmental crises occur, and their influence derives from the information they convey about a company.

name: Foreign R&D hires
authors_terms: ["newly hired foreign R&D workers", "foreign R&D hires", "share new foreign R&D hires"]
definition: Foreign workers are defined as those workers who immigrated to Denmark when they were at least 21 years old to guarantee that they obtained at least part of their higher education abroad. R&D workers are considered new hires only in their first year of employment at the firm.

name: Native R&D hires
authors_terms: ["newly hired native R&D workers", "newly hired native R&D hires", "share new native R&D hires"]
definition: Native R&D workers are the R&D workers in a firm who are not foreign workers. R&D workers are considered new hires only in their first year of employment at the firm, whereas R&D workers after their first year of employment are categorized as incumbents.

name: Incumbent R&D workers
authors_terms: ["incumbent R&D workers", "R&D incumbents", "firm's incumbent R&D workforce"]
definition: R&D workers after their first year of employment at the firm are categorized as incumbents; the stock of a firm's R&D workers therefore constitutes native R&D hires, foreign R&D hires, and R&D incumbents.

name: Firm-level exploration
definition: We define exploration as technology development situated in technology domains that are novel to the firm. This literature defines exploration as the outcome of a search process that requires firms to go beyond their established knowledge base.

name: International coinventor scope
definition: We define international coinventor scope as the natural logarithm of one plus the total number of EPO patents applied for by firm i over the five years prior to year t that were developed with the involvement of coinventors residing in distinct foreign countries. We use it as a proxy for the international search orientation of the firm.

name: Organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure", "median organizational tenure of a firm's incumbent R&D workforce"]
definition: We construct a measure whereby we take the natural logarithm of the median tenure of all incumbent R&D workers, both Danish and non-Danish, employed at firm i in year t. The log-transformation is justified by the fact that the untransformed value of this variable is strongly skewed to the right.

name: Home-country technology alignment
authors_terms: ["direction of exploration", "the technology domains of specialization of the home countries", "technological specialization of the foreign R&D hires' home countries"]
definition: First, we look at the direction of exploration and examine whether there is a relationship between the technology domains in which a firm patents and the technological specialization of the foreign R&D hires' home countries. The direction of exploration is measured with the revealed technology advantage (RTA), which captures the relative yearly intensity of patenting activity in a given technology compared with the rest of the world.

name: Knowledge sourcing from home countries
authors_terms: ["knowledge sourcing", "backward citations", "draw on knowledge produced in these foreign R&D hires' home countries"]
definition: Second, we look at knowledge sourcing and analyze whether firms increasingly draw on knowledge produced in the home countries of their foreign R&D hires. To identify the knowledge that firms build on, we utilize the backward citations of the patents filed by these firms.

name: CEO certification of financial statements
authors_terms: ["CEO certification", "certification of the firm's financial statements", "certification of the firm's financial statements by the CEO"]
definition: The major purpose of certification is to narrow the legal loophole between a company's financial statements and its senior executives' personal responsibilities; thus enhancing the quality of a company's financial disclosures. In this study's data, all companies but two filed CEO and CFO certifications on the same day.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "stock market response to CEO certification", "market value of the firm"]
definition: The stock market response to CEO certification is measured with the abnormal stock returns, or the cumulative difference between a company's observed return and its expected return, during a specific period surrounding the actual filing date of CEO certification.

name: CEO shareholdings
definition: CEO shareholdings are the proportion of a firm's outstanding shares owned by the CEO.

name: CEO external directorships
authors_terms: ["CEO external directorships", "the number of external directorships"]
definition: CEO external directorships refer to the number of external boards of directors (other than the focal firm's board) on which a CEO is serving.

name: CEO tenure
definition: CEO tenure is the number of years a CEO had been in office.

name: CEO association with prior financial restatement
authors_terms: ["CEO associated with the firm's prior restatement", "CEO not associated with the firm's prior restatement", "a CEO's association and nonassociation with his/her company's prior financial restatement"]
definition: A CEO's reputation is damaged when he/she is associated with the company's prior financial restatement - that is, the company filed a restatement in the prior three years and the filing of the restatement occurred during the CEO's tenure. A CEO who is appointed after the company has restated their earnings is not associated with the firm's prior financial restatement and is not stigmatized or discredited.

name: Knowledge sharing
definition: A firm shares knowledge by making its scientific and technological knowledge public. This paper considers only the sharing of explicit knowledge, which can be transferred through detailed documentation, and not tacit knowledge.

name: Quantity of knowledge shared
authors_terms: ["quantity of knowledge", "quantity of knowledge shared", "sharing a large quantity of knowledge"]
definition: One of two related dimensions of a knowledge-sharing strategy: the quantity of knowledge each firm shared with its innovation system, reflected in the number of journal articles published and papers presented at technical conferences.

name: Relevance of knowledge shared
authors_terms: ["relevance of knowledge", "high-quality, relevant knowledge", "relevance of knowledge shared"]
definition: One of two related dimensions of a knowledge-sharing strategy: the relevance of the knowledge each firm shared, where firms that published only well-established, scrubbed or obscure knowledge should rarely be cited by external organizations.

name: Innovative performance
definition: A firm's innovative performance refers to its ability to develop and hold intellectual property protection over a technology that is demanded by large commercial markets. It reflects the value of an innovation itself, rather than a firm's skills at manufacturing and marketing the resulting commercial product.

name: Managerial political power
authors_terms: ["managerial political power", "managers' political power", "JY's political power", "negative (positive) ruling on JY", "legal shocks on JY"]
definition: We define political power as managers' ability to impose their preferences in the strategic decision-making process by exercising influence through observable actions within their formal authority as well as more covert actions using informal power.

name: Samsung Electronics stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["share price of Samsung Electronics", "SEC's share price", "abnormal return", "stock returns"]
definition: As a forward-looking measure, share prices are uniquely advantageous to tracking fluctuations in managerial political power and its value that do not involve immediate or visible resource reallocation and instead center on more favorable future allocations.

name: Hotel Shilla stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["share price of Hotel Shilla", "HTS's share price", "abnormal return", "stock returns"]
definition: As a forward-looking measure, share prices are uniquely advantageous to tracking fluctuations in managerial political power and its value that do not involve immediate or visible resource reallocation and instead center on more favorable future allocations.

name: Inter-affiliate transactions
authors_terms: ["inter-affiliate transactions", "affiliate revenue growth", "affiliate revenue to payment ratio", "transfer pricing"]
definition: Negotiating more favorable trade terms (or transfer pricing) redistributes revenues and profits without affecting (short-term) investments.

name: Scrutiny of external stakeholders
definition: Attention and oversight from outside parties such as investors, analysts, regulators, and the public that can monitor and discipline managerial behavior.

name: Financial slack
definition: The availability of excess financial resources that can buffer an organization from resource constraints.

name: Organizational hiring patterns
authors_terms: ["organizational hiring pattern", "hiring pattern", "sources of an employer's TMT hires"]
definition: An organization's hiring pattern was defined as the sources of an employer's TMT hires in 1990-94. Each data point for a dyad represented the number of TMT members at employer i who came directly from source j.

name: Interfirm network ties
definition: Interfirm social network ties, such as board interlocks (the ties that exist when two organizations have directors in common), influence firm hiring behavior; network ties were represented as the number of individuals from a source that sat on the employer's board of directors or vice versa.

name: Frequency-based imitation
definition: With frequency-based imitation, organizations 'imitate actions that have been taken by large numbers of other organizations.' The greater the number of firms that hire TMT members from a specific organization, the more decision makers from other firms will perceive that organization as a legitimate source for their own TMT hires.

name: Size-based imitation
definition: Trait-based imitation refers to organizations' selective imitation of practices that some subset of firms with certain traits have used. Firms are most likely to imitate the actions of large organizations, whose behaviors are seen as legitimate.

name: Outcome-based imitation
definition: According to the logic of outcome-based imitation, decision makers will mimic the practices that they believe have produced positive outcomes for other firms; it can be viewed as a form of vicarious learning on the part of an imitating organization.

name: Transition stage
authors_terms: ["stage of transition", "stages of transition", "staged model of transition", "T2", "T3"]
