definition: The authors temporally bracket environmental changes during transition into two smaller segments: those between T1 and T2, as studied by Tan and Litschert (1994), and those between T2 and T3, which is the focus of this study.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: One of the environmental dimensions examined in the Chinese electronics industry; hostility can be interpreted as the impact of the environment on the firm.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: One of the environmental dimensions examined in the Chinese electronics industry; dynamism refers to the change in competitive environment.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: One of the environmental dimensions examined in the Chinese electronics industry; complexity can be understood as the predictability of the competitive environment.

name: Futurity orientation
authors_terms: ["futurity", "futurity orientation", "willingness to commit to future growth"]
definition: The futurity dimension measures the willingness to sacrifice short-term gain and to commit resources for long-term growth.

name: Proactiveness
authors_terms: ["proactiveness", "proactive and innovative orientation", "proactive and innovative strategies"]
definition: A strategic orientation measured by the willingness to make aggressive, proactive, and innovative strategic moves.

name: Risk taking
definition: A strategic orientation reflecting the firm's willingness to take risk; the authors list it among the strategic orientations as risk affinity.

name: Analysis orientation
definition: One of the five strategic orientation variables; together with defensiveness the authors call analyses one of the two relatively conservative orientations.

name: Defensiveness
definition: One of the two relatively conservative strategic orientations, alongside analyses; state-owned enterprises at the beginning of the 1990s generally preferred a defensive strategy.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance as reported by top managers; the authors note that top decision-makers in China have the most knowledge about strategic management processes, environmental conditions, and real performance associated with their respective firms.

name: Firm founding time
authors_terms: ["Time", "firm founding time", "stage of firm founding time", "stage during transition in which firms were founded"]
definition: The stage of the transition in which a firm was founded, used to categorize firms into two stages; those founded before 1990 were coded as 0, and those founded after 1990 were coded 1. The authors propose the stage of firm founding time as a moderating factor.

name: Firm strategic adaptation
definition: Strategy defined as a patterned stream of decisions which focuses on resource allocations in an attempt to reach a market position consistent with a firm's environment.

name: Host country corruption
definition: Corruption creates public and/or private additional nonmarket business costs that, depending on the type of FDI, may create a less attractive climate for investment. Additional costs resulting from corruption reduce the size of the potential market, thus lowering overall market attractiveness.

name: Market attractiveness
definition: What makes a market more attractive is determined in part by the motivation or purpose for the FDI. Lower costs, stability, and accessibility to labor/raw materials are what make country-level markets attractive for resource-seeking investment, whereas for market-seeking investment the size and wealth of an economy are what make country-level markets attractive.

name: Market-seeking FDI
definition: Market-seeking FDI involves investing in a host country market in order to directly serve that market with local production and distribution rather than through exporting.

name: Resource-seeking FDI
definition: Resource-seeking FDI involves investing in a host country market in order to achieve cost-minimization motives by obtaining resources either too costly to obtain or unavailable in the home market. Resource-seeking FDI is divided into two categories, raw materials-seeking and labor-seeking investment.

name: Value creation in acquisitions
definition: The concept of value creation is synonymous with that of synergy. Synergy exists in an acquisition when the value of the combined entity exceeds the sum of the values of the two combining firms.

name: Acquisition relatedness
authors_terms: ["related acquisitions", "unrelated acquisitions", "degree of relatedness of the combining firms", "acquisition strategy"]
definition: In our analysis, acquisition strategies are classified according to the degree of relatedness of the combining firms. Based on the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) classification, related acquisitions comprise nonconglomerate horizontal and vertical acquisitions and conglomerate product extension and market extension acquisitions, while unrelated acquisitions are 'pure' conglomerates.

name: New operating decisions
authors_terms: ["change in operating decisions", "new operating decisions", "changes in the operating decision"]
definition: Where value creation is associated with a change in operating decisions (defined broadly to include production, marketing, research and development, personnel, etc., decisions), the underlying economic motivation for the change could be cost economies arising from economies of scope, economies of scale, or improved management techniques. Alternatively, it could be increased market power in input or output markets.

name: New financing decisions
definition: The potential for value creation from a change in financing decisions is based on the coinsurance argument of Lewellen (1971) and Higgins and Schall (1975). The realization of this potential increase in value requires an increase in leverage after the acquisition.

name: Financial diversification
definition: Value may also be created by the mere fact of combination with no change in strategic decisions, as a result of financial diversification. Combining two firms in the presence of capital market imperfections such as costly information or indivisibility of financial assets can reduce required return without affecting expected cash flows, if the returns of the merging firms are imperfectly correlated.

name: Value of partner's resources
authors_terms: ["value of resources possessed by the partner", "value of the latter's resources", "value of the partner's resources", "the partner's resources", "Tobin's q of the firm with more valuable resources"]
definition: The value of the intangible resources possessed by a firm, including its knowledge, resources and skills, and capabilities; the higher the Tobin's q, the more valuable the intangible resources possessed by a firm. The authors use 'more valuable resources' and 'less valuable resources' to refer to the relative rent generating potential of the resources of the two partners.

name: Difference in wealth gains between partners
authors_terms: ["difference in wealth gains", "difference in abnormal returns", "difference in gains", "differential gains"]
definition: The difference between the wealth gains experienced by the two partners within a joint venture; in the paper it is the difference in cumulative abnormal returns between the firm with less valuable resources and the firm with more valuable resources.

name: Size of the firm with less valuable resources
authors_terms: ["size of the firm with less valuable resources", "larger", "bargaining power"]
definition: The size of the partner that brings less valuable resources to the JV. The authors argue that another dimension likely to influence a firm's bargaining power is its size, because larger firms may enjoy greater bargaining power in a JV due to their reputation in various markets and their financial resources.

name: Diversity of the knowledge base
authors_terms: ["diversity in its knowledge base", "diversity of the low-q firm", "product diversity"]
definition: A critical determinant of a firm's absorptive capacity is diversity in its knowledge base; diversity increases the probability that the firm possesses prior related knowledge with respect to a partner's specialized skills, thereby enhancing absorptive capacity.

name: JV capabilities
definition: A partner's accumulated experience and capabilities with respect to operating joint ventures, which may enable it to strike the right balance between divulging knowledge and protecting it from appropriation and to formulate better JV contracts.

name: Entrant aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["perceived aggressiveness", "perceived aggressiveness of the entrant", "competitive aggressiveness"]
definition: A trait-like characteristic of the entrant that captures its propensity to (re-) act in certain ways in the future; managers tend to view competitive actions in which the ratio of incumbent cost to entrant benefit is high, or when the entrant shows willingness to sacrifice profits to beat competitors, as signals of competitive aggressiveness.

name: Entrant commitment
definition: An action sends a signal of commitment when the receiver believes the sender will 'stick to its market action' - in this case, the market entry; like aggressiveness it is a trait-like concept referring to the entrant's longer-term behavioral intentions.

name: Perceived entry consequence
definition: The inferred, but not realized, consequences of the entry, capturing managers' beliefs about the potential loss in sales and market share due to the new market entry - if the incumbent does not respond.

name: Incumbent price response
authors_terms: ["incumbent firm's price response", "price response", "price reaction", "competitive response along the price dimension"]
definition: The competitive response the incumbent firm's manager decides along the price dimension of the competitive repertoire, indicated as the new price for the incumbent's brand; lower (higher) prices indicate stronger (weaker) incumbent firm responses.

name: Entrant product innovativeness
definition: The entrant's relative product innovativeness, manipulated as similar (the competitor's product did not offer more benefits than the incumbent's product) or superior (the entrant's product offered an improved screwing mechanism and slipping protection as additional benefits).

name: Customer price sensitivity
definition: Customers' price sensitivity in the market for specialized screws, manipulated as low ('price is a minor determinant for consumers when buying a specialized screw') or high ('price is a major determinant for consumers when buying a specialized screw').

name: Incumbent market share
definition: The incumbent's market share before market entry, manipulated as low or high ('Your company currently has a small [large] share of the market for specialized screws').

name: Alliance governance form
authors_terms: ["alliance form", "organizational form of strategic alliances", "governance mode", "organizational form"]
definition: The organizational form of an alliance, distinguished into equity joint ventures, non-equity bilateral collaborations and non-equity unilateral (i.e., quasi-market) agreements.

name: Technological similarity of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["SIMILAR CAPABILITIES", "similarity of partners' technological specialization", "overlap of partners' knowledge base", "technological proximity", "technological overlap"]
definition: An index that proxies the extent of overlapping of partners' knowledge base; SIMILAR CAPABILITIES reflects the capacity of alliance partners to absorb each other's knowledge.

name: Technological component of the alliance
authors_terms: ["TECH", "technological alliances", "a collaboration involves a technological component"]
definition: Whether a collaboration involves a technological component, that is R&D, design, engineering and/or knowledge transfer, as opposed to concentrating on production and/or commercial activities.

name: Interunit executive redeployment
definition: The dependent variable of this study is realized redeployment. It indicates whether executive redeployment occurs or not, coded as one for realized cases, that is, a destination affiliate to which a focal executive is redeployed, and zero for unrealized cases, that is, potential destination affiliates to which a focal executive could be redeployed but was not.

name: Destination unit performance
definition: We measure a potential destination affiliate performance using return on asset (ROA), wherein executives' turnaround experience can be applicable. Since our argument in the hypothesis concerns affiliate performance relative to the group, we use group-adjusted ROA by subtracting the group average from the focal affiliate's ROA.

name: Turnaround experience
definition: Turnaround is operationalized as when an affiliate's ROA, defined by net income to total assets, turns from negative to positive one year to the next. When an executive worked in an affiliate at the time of a turnaround, she likely dealt with the turnaround situation and accumulated relevant turnaround experience.

name: Competitive experience
definition: We measure an executive's competitive experience based on the profitability of those affiliates exceeding those of rivals in the same industry, since the ultimate outcome of winning competition against rivals will result in superior financial performance.

name: International expansion experience
definition: We measure an executive's international expansion experience as the logged number of foreign direct investments (FDIs) made by affiliates during her career in the business group. When an executive has worked in an affiliate with extensive foreign operations, she was likely exposed to international management.

name: Industry concentration
definition: We measure the industry-level, time-varying variable of destination affiliate industry concentration to capture the intensity of product market competition faced by each potential destination affiliate.

name: Destination unit internationalization
definition: We measure the destination affiliate internationalization of a potential destination affiliate by the logged number of foreign direct investments by the affiliate.

name: Unit age
definition: We therefore measure destination affiliate age as the number of years since the affiliate's founding, and interact it with two unit-generic human capital of executives to test Hypothesis 2.

name: Corporate control unit experience
authors_terms: ["group control unit experience", "control unit experience", "corporate control unit experience"]
definition: We define an executive's group control unit experience with a dichotomous variable capturing whether she has worked in an affiliate that functions as a de facto holding company, often the peak of a pyramidal ownership structure.

name: Interunit coordination experience
definition: We measure executives' interunit coordination experience as the number of affiliates where they have worked as directors.

name: Hierarchy of authority
authors_terms: ["hierarchy of authority", "hierarchy", "hierarchy of authority in the organization structure"]
definition: Hierarchy of authority reflects the degree of managerial oversight (i.e., supervisor presence and approval) necessary to go about one's job and is closely related to vertical authority (layers of sequential authority or formal rank).

name: Idea generation performance
authors_terms: ["idea generation", "idea generation tasks", "performance on idea generation tasks", "generation of ideas"]
definition: The idea generation stage at the beginning of the innovation process often involves a complex problem that cannot be solved with extant organizational devices (e.g., routines, standard operating procedures, or technology), and thus requires the generation of novel alternatives.

name: Idea selection performance
authors_terms: ["idea selection", "selection performance", "performance on idea selection tasks", "selection of ideas"]
definition: Idea selection is the phase of the innovation process in which agents select among the ideas that were generated and evaluated, and the authors note that prior empirical findings indicate that selection of high-quality ideas is a challenging task.

name: Self-promotion bias
authors_terms: ["a bias toward promoting the selection of one's own ideas", "self-promotion bias", "the tendency to promote/select one's own ideas", "egocentric discounting of advice"]
definition: Behavioral decision making research on advice taking has found that there is a robust tendency for people to egocentrically favor their own initial ideas and undervalue the advice or ideas of others, often leading to impaired decision quality.

name: Problem structure
definition: Problems can be characterized along a continuum from ill structured to well structured. Well-structured problems are those with well-defined initial states and known elements, explicit approaches for solving, and accepted end states or solutions, while ill-structured problems have either poorly defined initial states or indefinite problem-solving approaches.

name: Problem complexity
definition: Problems can also be characterized according to their complexity, defined as the number of issues, functions, or variables involved and the degree of relationship among these properties. Complex problems have high intransparency and significant connectivity between variables, whereas simple problems are composed of fewer knowledge sets that interact in more predictable ways.

name: Organizational mode
definition: Market modes of organization offer high-powered incentives, decentralized control, and mechanisms that allow individual actors to exploit and enhance their own specialized knowledge, whereas hierarchies rely on firm-specific languages, communication codes, and information channels, combined with low-powered incentives and dispute resolution mechanisms, that encourage knowledge sharing and promote coordination.

name: Problem-solving performance
authors_terms: ["problem-solving performance", "solution search", "problem-solving speed", "problem-solving quality", "technological development performance"]
definition: The paper uses two measures of problem-solving performance in technological development: the time from the start of process development to achievement of the first yielding product, which captures efficiencies in solving problems, and the quality of the manufacturing process, which captures the quality of solutions.

name: Scale economies
definition: Because technological development entails significant experimentation and trial and error, large firms are able to conduct more experiments in more diverse technological areas, develop more and different solution-search approaches, and spread important inputs over a larger base of development activity; beyond a certain point escalating coordination and agency costs lead to diseconomies of scale.

name: Scope economies
definition: Economies of scope are present if cost savings or performance benefits are realized when two or more activities are conducted jointly in comparison to when those activities are conducted separately. Knowledge developed and accumulated in one R&D activity can be transferred to other R&D activities at little cost, but with significant performance benefits.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm's operations and sales are spread across multiple business segments; the authors measure it with the widely used entropy measure based on the share of each segment in the firm's total sales.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured by return on assets (ROA); ROA with a 1-year lag is used as the measure of firm performance for the test of Hypothesis 1.

name: Change in firm performance
authors_terms: ["change in performance", "log of next period ROA", "performance declines"]
definition: The change in firm performance between periods; for Hypotheses 2 and 3 the authors use the log of next period ROA as the measure of change in performance.

name: Institutional development
definition: The degree of market and institutional development of an economy; the potential returns from diversification decrease with market and institutional development, because gains from diversification often relate to market failure.

name: Economy-wide shock
definition: An economy-wide economic shock is a broad, major, sudden, and unanticipated change in the economic environment; such shocks tend to be systemic and radical, creating discontinuities that disrupt firms, industries, markets and economies.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Affiliation of a legally independent firm with a business group, a network of legally independent firms linked by a set of formal and informal ties that coordinate their actions.

name: Common affiliations with a court's judges
authors_terms: ["potential common affiliations", "common educational and professional affiliations", "shared educational and professional affiliations"]
definition: Potential common affiliations capture the affiliations between the plaintiff-side lawyers and all judges of a given court. Common educational and professional affiliations connecting company lawyers and judicial arbiters provide opportunities for companies to influence judicial discretion.

name: Realized common affiliations with the presiding judge
authors_terms: ["realized common affiliations", "realized contemporaneous affiliations", "realized clerkship affiliations", "realized JD contemporaneous affiliations"]
definition: When a case is filed, common affiliations are only potential, and they become realized when the presiding judge is announced. Realized common affiliations capture the affiliations between plaintiff-side lawyers and the presiding judge only.

name: Unrealized common affiliations with non-presiding judges
authors_terms: ["unrealized common affiliations", "unrealized contemporaneous affiliations", "unrealized clerkship affiliations"]
definition: Unrealized common affiliations refer to potential affiliations between the plaintiff-side lawyers and all non-presiding judges of the focal court. They remain unrealized because the desired presiding judge is not assigned to the case.

name: Choice of legal venue
authors_terms: ["choice of venue", "venue shopping", "court selection", "selection of jurisdictions"]
definition: Corporate plaintiffs' practice of choosing favorable legal venues in which to initiate legal proceedings, often referred to as ''venue shopping.'' Because plaintiffs have almost complete control over the court in which a case will be heard, companies can seek a favorable legal venue to pursue private advantage.

name: Plaintiff's win
definition: The plaintiff's outcome following the termination of the case; the paper's second dependent variable captures the plaintiff's outcome following the termination of the case and the private advantage that accrues to the company.

name: Message tailoring
definition: The process by which social structures create opportunities for tailoring messages to a given alter: actors leverage intimate observations and private, often tacit knowledge to adapt the flow and content of the message to the evaluator. Tailoring arguments to the audience's preferred styles, interests, and values results in more persuasive messages.

name: Legal team human capital
definition: Human capital--both general and task-specific--varies across employees, and it is unlikely that social affiliations with key evaluators will perfectly coincide with the required human capital for the work at hand. If a team is composed based on social affiliations with key evaluators, it may shortchange the requisite human capital, and human capital is essential for team performance.

name: Activist directorship
authors_terms: ["activist director", "activist directors", "activist-sponsored directors", "activist-nominated directors", "appointment of an activist director"]
definition: Activist directors, meaning directors who were nominated by activist investors, are shareholders who are forcing their way into boardrooms by nominating their own directors in activist campaigns. With a board seat, activist investors gain a unique internal position from which to impose their interests onto corporate agendas.

name: Reported stakeholder harm
authors_terms: ["reports of stakeholder harm", "reported stakeholder harm", "stakeholder harm"]
definition: We investigate the influence activist directors have on reports of stakeholder harm, by which we mean a belief or perception that stakeholders may have been adversely affected, directly or indirectly, by the firm's behavior. Stakeholder harm often manifests when executives shift their organizational priorities away from the interests of stakeholders, and external audiences take note.

name: Organizational size
definition: A firm can be considered small in two different but related ways—in terms of sheer organizational size or in terms of its industry market share. In the context of this study, "small" and "large" indicate relative rather than absolute size.

name: Propensity for action
definition: Propensity for action, a firm's tendency to initiate competitive attacks.

name: Action execution speed
definition: Action execution speed, the length of time required to implement an action.

name: Action visibility
definition: Visibility indicates the amount of information available about a competitive move, whether action or response. Action visibility was defined as the average amount of information available about a competitive action that a firm initiated.

name: Responsiveness
definition: Responsiveness, a firm's tendency to move against competitors' attacks; responsiveness involves being adaptive to competitors' challenges.

name: Response announcement speed
definition: Response announcement speed, the length of time used to prepare and announce a response.

name: Response execution speed
definition: Response execution speed, the length of time required to implement an announced response.

name: Response visibility
definition: Response visibility was defined as the average amount of information available about a response and was measured by the number of lines Aviation Daily devoted to reporting this response.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Because of the general desirability of assessing performance with a multidimensional measure, the high interrelationships between the individual measures, and the similarity of the results obtained from using each of these measures, we assessed organizational performance using an index composed of two market-related and two profit-related performance measures.

name: Merger relatedness
definition: Concentric mergers, involving firms that produce similar products in different geographical regions (i.e. market concentric) or non-competing products that share similar production and/or marketing technologies (i.e. product concentric), are strategically analogous to related mergers. Conglomerate mergers involve firms that have dissimilar products and markets, and therefore are strategically analogous to unrelated mergers.

name: Change in systematic risk
authors_terms: ["changes in systematic risk", "systematic risk difference score", "shift in systematic risk", "merger event-induced changes in systematic risk", "risk shift"]
definition: Systematic risk represents the sensitivity (covariability) of a firm's returns to the aggregate returns of the marketplace. Merger event-induced changes in systematic risk were computed by subtracting each bidding firm's pre-merger estimate of beta from its post-merger estimate.

name: Short interest
definition: Short sellers borrow and re-sell the firm's stock with an obligation to buy it back, and they benefit when the firm's stock price declines. The independent variable is the level of short interest, which the authors measure as a percentage of the firm's total shareholdings.

name: Number of growth actions
authors_terms: ["number of growth actions", "number of growth actions", "growth activity", "growth actions"]
definition: Growth actions extend firms' portfolios of products, assets, and resources, and include expanding existing businesses, developing new products internally, acquiring the assets of another firm, or partnering with others to expand into new product or geographic arenas. The number of growth actions counts the total number of actions a firm announced throughout the year.

name: Diversity of growth actions
authors_terms: ["diversity of growth actions", "diverse repertoires", "mix of growth actions"]
definition: Firms that use a wide, and balanced, range of growth modes have diverse repertoires, whereas those that concentrate on fewer types have less diverse repertoires. The diversity of growth actions measures the extent to which firms are engaging in a broad range of actions.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: Absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990) is a measure of the firm's ability to exploit external knowledge (Tsai, 2001). When firms have high levels of absorptive capacity, they are able to acquire and assimilate information, and use it to gain competitive advantage.

name: Board centrality
definition: Firms that are central in the interlocking directorate have particularly robust access to, and ability to understand, external information. Board centrality is measured as the number of directors' total connections, normalized by the number of directors on the board.

name: Financial slack
definition: Researchers working in finance have developed a measure of financial constraints, which is the opposite of financial slack, called the KZ index. A firm with high (low) financial constraints has low (high) financial slack.

name: News sentiment
definition: Scholars often consider the extent to which news sentiment about the firm is positive or negative. RavenPack ascribes a news sentiment score based on language used in the news reports, incorporating commentaries and editorials about firms surrounding their action announcements.

name: Category contrast
authors_terms: ["category contrast", "patent class contrast", "contrast of a patent class", "class contrast"]
definition: Contrast is the extent to which a category contains unique and distinctive information that sets it apart from neighboring categories. A patent class exhibits high category contrast if most of the patents categorized therein belong only to that class, while a class is low-contrast if its categorical boundaries are unclear and many of the patents categorized therein are also categorized in other classes.

name: Patent citations
authors_terms: ["patent citations", "patent impact", "yearly citation count", "forward citations", "total citations received"]
definition: The number of citations a patent receives from future patents, which the authors measure yearly based on the citations a patent receives from patents applied for in a given year. The impact of an invention depends at least in part on how easy it is for potential users to find it as they search for relevant prior knowledge.

name: Classification-based search
definition: A search query that relies on patent classifications rather than searching for prior art without the aid of patent classifications, for example by keywords; 'ccls' stands for current classification in the examination search platform.

name: Initial search within primary class
authors_terms: ["First searched class is same as patent's primary class", "start their prior art search"]
definition: Whether, upon receiving a patent application, the examiner starts by searching for prior art within the patent's primary class itself rather than in other classes.

name: Within-class search scope
authors_terms: ["Proportion of classes searched that are the same as the patent's primary class", "scope of prior art search"]
definition: The extent to which an examiner focuses her search within the boundaries of the patent class or, conversely, broadens the scope of her search across patent classes.

name: Search effort
definition: The amount of search conducted by examiners, measured as the count of search queries they execute in a particular search session.

name: Search precision
definition: How on target examiners' search queries are, measured as the average number of 'hits' generated by a search query.

name: Extension strategy
definition: Firms may reasonably choose an extension strategy, or try to improve the incumbent technology in hopes that a potential performance increase will delay or forestall substitution. Incumbents that invested most of their product portfolio (more than 90%) in standard carburetors at the end of the emergence period (1982) were categorized as having chosen an extension strategy.

name: Bridging strategy
definition: Firms may also adopt a bridging strategy of recombining elements of incumbent and threatening technologies into intergenerational hybrids. Firms were categorized as having a bridging strategy otherwise than the extension classification, that is, when they did not devote more than 90% of their product portfolio to standard carburetors at the end of the emergence period.

name: Incumbent technology performance improvement
authors_terms: ["rate of incumbent technology product performance improvement", "annual MPG growth", "incumbent product performance"]
definition: The rate of incumbent technology product performance improvement is the annual growth in the product performance of the incumbent carburetor technology, estimated as annual MPG growth of car models equipped with standard carburetors and compared with the rate of incumbent product performance improvement before the arrival of EFI.

name: Hybrid product performance improvement
authors_terms: ["rate of hybrid product performance improvement", "hybrid carburetor performance"]
definition: The rate of hybrid product performance improvement is the annual growth in the performance of intergenerational hybrid products; the hybrid carburetor here bolts the electronic feedback fuel system introduced by EFI onto the carburetor architecture as a module replacing the old mechanical controls.

name: Timing of technology substitution
authors_terms: ["timing of technology substitution", "delay in EFI adoption", "substitution pace"]
definition: Improved incumbent product performance can delay the point at which one technology becomes a legitimate substitute for another. The paper estimates this delay by fitting a Fisher-Pry diffusion function to early EFI counts and comparing the predicted diffusion with realized EFI penetration.

name: Fuel delivery technology
authors_terms: ["standard carburetor", "hybrid carburetor", "electronic feedback fuel system controls"]
definition: A car model's fuel delivery technology is indicated by whether it has a standard carburetor or a hybrid carburetor, the latter identified by the presence of EFI-derived feedback fuel system controls in a car's carburetor.

name: Adaptation to the threatening technology
authors_terms: ["adapt to the threatening technology", "transition to EFI", "survival"]
definition: Adaptation to the threatening technology describes firms that move to the threatening technology generation after a substitution occurs, resulting in survival, acquisition, or failure.

name: Niche retreat
authors_terms: ["retreat to a market niche", "niche continuance", "niche retreat"]
definition: Retreat to a market niche describes firms focused on extending the incumbent technology that continue to produce it for market niches in which incumbent technologies retain an advantage, resulting in failure, continuance in a niche market for incumbent technology, or late adoption of threatening technology.

name: Consensus on company objectives
authors_terms: ["consensus on company objectives", "consensus on objectives", "consensus on goals", "agreement on ends"]
definition: Consensus or 'shared perspectives' among the members of a firm's top management team regarding the relative importance of the objectives (ends) of what the firm's strategy actually is; the lower the dispersion of responses to the objective items within a given TMT, the higher the level of consensus. The authors treat the terms ends, goals and objectives as synonymous.

name: Consensus on competitive methods
authors_terms: ["consensus on competitive methods", "consensus on means", "consensus on methods"]
definition: Consensus or 'shared perspectives' among the members of a firm's top management team regarding the relative importance of the competitive methods (means) the firm uses; the lower the dispersion of responses to the methods items within a given TMT, the higher the level of consensus. The authors treat the terms means and methods as synonymous.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The study uses what the authors call 'self-reported objective' and 'subjective' measures of organizational performance: sales growth, after-tax return on total assets, and overall or 'global' assessments of firm performance.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "performance–aspiration gap below aspirations", "performance shortfall"]
definition: The performance–aspiration gap is defined as the difference between performance and aspiration level for each focal fund. Performance below aspirations equals zero for all observations in which the performance of the focal fund is greater than its aspirations; for all other observations, it equals the difference between the fund's performance and its aspirations.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["change", "changes to current strategy", "annual turnover ratio", "change in the mutual fund's investment holdings"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the annual turnover ratio, which captures the overall change in the mutual fund's investment holdings during a given time period.

name: Experience level
definition: We measure fund managers' experience level by calculating the prior work experience of all fund managers in a mutual fund and averaging them across all managers; their prior work experience is the difference in months between when they started their career and the focal fund's annual report month in a given year.

name: Experience specialization
definition: Similar to Teodoridis et al. (2019), we define specialized experience as deep experience in a particular knowledge domain and general experience as broad experience across multiple knowledge domains.

name: Position within the business group hierarchy
definition: A central entity within a business group, referred to as an 'apex' firm, undertakes control and coordination activities. The apex firm is the top corporate owner within the group, and corporations placed lower in the chain of ownership are non-apex firms.

name: Symbolic CSR
definition: Symbolic_CSR captures any reporting, claims, or disclosures about CSR, including best practices, for example, Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) guidelines.

name: Substantive CSR
definition: Substantive_CSR captures the substantive actions related to socially responsible corporate policies and programs such as the use of renewable energy and investment in employee training and career development.

name: Equity ownership
definition: To capture the equity relationship between apex and non-apex firms, the authors computed equity ownership as the extent of control rights. It is the total (direct and indirect) ultimate ownership percentage of the apex firm over its subsidiaries and of the ultimate controlling shareholder of the non-apex firms.

name: Umbrella branding
definition: 'Umbrella branding' (Montgomery & Wernerfelt, 1992) is whereby an apex firm extends its name or a recognizable derivative thereof to non-apex firms (Ingram, 1996: 199).

name: CSR decoupling
definition: Decoupling characterizes a behavior whereby an organization seeks to gain legitimacy by adopting a facade of acquiescence to widely held societal norms while making minimal commensurate changes to internal practices. The authors define decoupling as the absolute value of the difference between Symbolic_CSR and lagged Substantive_CSR.

name: Market valuation
definition: TobinsQ is calculated as the ratio of the sum of market capitalization and total liabilities to total assets, for each firm in each year in our sample.

name: Acquirer dividend reputation
authors_terms: ["acquirer's dividend reputation", "dividend reputation", "strength of the acquirer's dividend reputation"]
definition: Those firms that consistently pay out dividends develop a dividend reputation. Once a firm initiates a dividend payment, it implicitly commits to maintaining or increasing it in the future, because failure to do so is punished by investors.

name: Acquirer growth reputation
definition: Those firms that consistently deliver growth over time develop a growth reputation. When a firm has a growth reputation, investors are particularly sensitive to potential declines in future growth prospects and evaluate the firm's actions based on their likely impact on future growth.

name: Target growth reputation
authors_terms: ["target's growth reputation", "target firm's growth reputation", "growth reputation of the target firm"]
definition: The organizational capabilities of the target firm, as reflected in its reputation for value creation. The growth reputation of a target may signal to investors that the acquirer intends to shift its strategic priorities from increasing dividend payments to accelerating growth.

name: Investor reactions to acquisitions
definition: CAR represent unanticipated returns to a stock resulting from a certain event—in this case an acquisition. We measured our dependent variable using cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) associated with an acquisition announcement and used the standard event study methodology.

name: Dividend framing
definition: Dividend framing refers to providing information in an acquisition announcement regarding how the acquisition is intended to enhance current and future dividend payments.

name: Growth framing
definition: Growth framing refers to providing information in an acquisition announcement regarding how the acquisition is intended to accelerate future growth, for example, by expanding innovation capabilities, disrupting current markets or exploring new markets.

name: Excess entry
definition: The collective outcome in which more players enter a market than its capacity can accommodate; the authors contrast it with under-entry. Statistical explanations hold that random errors can produce a collective outcome of excess entry (or under-entry), while psychological explanations claim entry errors are biased systematically toward excess entry.

name: Entrepreneurial market
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial market", "entrepreneurial markets", "small markets with uncertain capacity", "small markets with risky demand"]
definition: Markets that are small and risky: the authors defined entrepreneurial markets as small markets in which market capacity is probabilistic rather than certain, i.e., the combination of small market size and uncertain capacity.

name: Unbiased statistical errors
authors_terms: ["unbiased statistical errors", "random errors", "statistical errors", "unbiased errors", "fallible judgment"]
definition: Errors in forecasts of market opportunities that are correct on average but dispersed randomly; unbiased errors produce random dispersion around a zero mean, and statistical explanations argue that such errors can produce a collective outcome of excess entry (or under-entry).

name: Entry decision bias
definition: The claim that new market entry does not follow a random process but is biased systematically to produce more excess entry (and less under-entry) than in an unbiased random model.

name: Overconfidence
definition: Confidence measured as the difference between players' entry decisions when uninformed about their relative abilities and their entry decisions when partially informed about their relative abilities; the authors say it corresponds closely with the psychological construct of overconfidence, that is, construing information to support an over-belief in one's prospects for success.

name: Market entry
definition: The decision whether or not to enter a market in a given round; subjects were told that they would play rounds of the game deciding in each round whether or not to enter a market, with payoffs determined by their quiz performance and by market capacity.

name: Market capacity
definition: The number of entrants a market can accommodate, denoted c; market size c varied from round to round, and in each round the c 'best' entrants based on quiz scores received payoffs.

name: Market volatility
definition: Whether market capacity is known with certainty or subject to risk: in the 'known' condition c was fixed, whereas in the 'risky' condition c had expected values with realized values uniformly distributed across three outcomes, and players knew the distribution of possible capacities.

name: Direct ties
definition: We define a direct tie as a personal relationship between a decision maker and the party about whom the decision is being made.

name: Indirect ties
definition: We define an indirect tie as a relationship between two individuals who are not directly connected but through whom a connection can be made through a social network of each party's direct ties.

name: Reputation
definition: Reputation is defined as information about an individual's past performance.

name: Investment decision
authors_terms: ["investment decision", "venture finance decision", "decision whether or not to finance a new venture"]
definition: We seek to examine empirically the effect of variation in the direct and indirect ties across investor-entrepreneur dyads, at the time the entrepreneur seeks seed-stage financing, on the investor's decision whether or not to finance a new venture. The dependent variable was a binary variable of one if the investment was made and zero if the investment was not made.

name: CEO stock option pay
authors_terms: ["CEO stock option pay", "stock options", "option pay", "CEO option pay"]
definition: Stock options give the recipient the right to purchase company shares at a predetermined price over a specified period of time; the CEO benefits from future increases in the share price, but neither gains nor loses if the share price goes down.

name: Product safety problems
definition: The incidence of unsafe products released into the marketplace; the authors focus on product recalls as indicators of product safety problems, as a recall is a clear sign that a firm's product poses a danger to consumer safety.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The number of years since the executive became CEO. CEO tenure is thought to shape how CEOs perceive and act upon their environments, with a general tendency toward conservatism as executives advance in their tenures.

name: CEO founder status
definition: Whether the CEO was listed as the founder of the firm. Founder-CEOs are motivated primarily by an intrinsic need to see their firm succeed, rather than by the potential for large payouts such as those provided by stock options.

name: Resource provider reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation", "player reputation", "team reputation", "average reputation of players on the team"]
definition: Reputation is defined as an attribute-specific assessment, an "expectation of future behavior that is directly based on past demonstrations of that behavior." Because the authors consider firms in their efforts to acquire high-quality resources, the relevant attribute used to define reputation is the quality of resources provided by an actor.

name: Resource provider status
authors_terms: ["status", "player status", "team status", "average status of players on the team"]
definition: Status is based on the relative position of an actor in a hierarchical order and is not necessarily tightly coupled to past behaviors. It is an intangible asset that signals to potential customers the actor's prestige or esteem accorded to them by the positions they occupy in a social structure.

name: Product quality
authors_terms: ["product quality", "team product quality", "season performance", "team performance", "team's athletic performance on the court"]
definition: One of the two organizational goals examined is the quality of the products produced by the organization. The authors used performance in a season as the measure of a team's product quality.

name: Revenues
definition: The second organizational goal examined is the revenues generated by the organization's products. The authors used the teams' ticket income in a season as their measure of team revenues.

name: Product quality relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["product quality relative to aspirations", "performance relative to aspirations on the quality of its products"]
definition: Teams' historical aspiration level for product quality, defined as a moving average of past product quality, with an updating parameter that weights the relevance of recent performance information. The final measure subtracts a team's past product quality (product quality in the previous season) from its historic aspiration level for product quality in the previous season.

name: Revenues relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["revenues relative to aspirations", "performance relative to aspirations on revenues"]
definition: A team's aspiration level for revenues, measured as historical aspirations, a moving average of past revenues constructed in the same way as for product quality aspirations. The final measure subtracts a team's past revenues (from the previous season) from its historic aspiration level for revenues in the previous season.

name: Recruitment preference for reputation over status
authors_terms: ["preference for high-reputation/high-status resource providers", "preference for reputation over status", "preference for status over reputation"]
definition: The relative preference shown in a team's recruitment of new players between resource providers who are of high reputation but not high status and resource providers who are of high status but not high reputation, relative to equal preference for the two.

name: Price paid to resource providers
authors_terms: ["price paid by the organization", "the price paid for a resource", "player salary", "salary"]
definition: The price the organization pays to obtain resources from a resource provider. In this setting it is the yearly salary of a player.

name: Asset restructuring
definition: Restructuring commonly involves 'a sequence of acquisitions and divestitures to develop a new configuration of the lines of business' (Bowman and Singh, 1993: 6). Asset restructuring is treated as a strategic response by firms to changes in their environment, assessed through acquisitions, divestitures and the importance of each.

name: Change in country development
authors_terms: ["change in country development", "change in a country's HDI"]
definition: Changes in country development are among the most important environmental changes because they lead to critical opportunities and threats. Factors related to country development include Gross Domestic Product, development of human capital, level of inflation, level of employment, and life expectancy, and country development tends to be associated with increased governance by market forces leading to more efficient resource allocation.

name: Competitive change
definition: The entry of new competitors increases the level of competition and can reduce profit margins in an industry. Competition might intensify because of the diversity of strategies by firms in an industry, a shift in the power balance of players, and changes in market demand.

name: Deregulation
authors_terms: ["deregulation", "reduction of government involvement", "changes in government regulations"]
definition: The level of government regulation is a tool to control excessive risk-taking at the firm level: when an economy is highly regulated, organizations are faced with limited discretion in their business decisions. Governments of French civil law countries have substantially decreased their economic involvement in recent years, which increases the decision-making discretion of firms, improves the efficiency of governance mechanisms, and reduces barriers to trade and investment.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are generally composed of legally independent firms that are bound by formal and informal ties to take coordinated actions. These groups often serve as organizational substitutes for imperfections in capital, labor, and product markets, and group affiliation can provide firms access to substantial tangible and intangible resources that are typically unavailable to independent firms.

name: Ecosystem emergence challenge
definition: The extent to which technology bottlenecks elsewhere in the system constrain the new technology's realized performance from matching its potential performance.

name: Ecosystem extension opportunity
definition: The extent to which improvements elsewhere in the system enhance the realized performance attainable with the old technology system.

name: Pace of technology substitution
authors_terms: ["pace of substitution", "pace of technology substitution", "time to market dominance", "years to market dominance"]
definition: The speed with which a new technology generation substitutes the old generation, measured as the number of years from the year the new generation was commercialized to the year its annual market share surpassed that of the old generation. Market dominance is defined as the first year in which the new generation exceeds the annual market share of the old (previously dominant) generation.

name: Mergers and acquisitions
definition: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and organic growth are two commonly used strategies for firms to achieve horizontal growth, i.e., increase their size within a single business. M&A are more likely to generate greater bargaining power because horizontal mergers not only increase the size of the firm-which organic growth also achieves-but also directly reduce the number of competitors.

name: Organic growth
definition: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and organic growth are two commonly used strategies for firms to achieve horizontal growth, i.e., increase their size within a single business. When growing organically, a firm more freely chooses how, when and where to locate its growth activities, thus creating a more optimal array of resources and assets.

name: Bargaining power
authors_terms: ["bargaining power", "economic clout at the firm level"]
definition: Bargaining power measures the economic clout at the firm level and is positively associated with size, in particular relative size versus competitors, suppliers and customers. Bargaining power is related to the concept of market power; the latter being an industry level concept, while the former is a firm level concept.

name: Operating efficiency
definition: Increases in size also help create scale economies and hence lead to improved operating efficiency. A firm enjoys higher operating efficiency if its operating cost/sales ratio is lower.

name: Firm performance
definition: We also measure overall firm performance (i.e., profitability) by two variables, ROA (Return on Assets) and Operating Profit (operating profit as a percentage of sales).

name: Shareholder litigation risk
authors_terms: ["shareholder litigation risk", "litigation risk", "perceived shareholder litigation risk", "risk of shareholder litigation"]
definition: Shareholder litigation risk can function as a governance mechanism, as it makes salient for managers that their actions are monitored and that mismanagement will have negative consequences. The adoption of a UD law is an exogenous source of variation in firms' shareholder litigation risk, lowering the perceived level of that risk.

name: Engagement in stakeholder initiatives
authors_terms: ["engagement in stakeholder initiatives", "stakeholder initiatives", "stakeholder-focused efforts", "stakeholder engagement"]
definition: We measure engagement in stakeholder initiatives as the sum of the total strengths across items in the five categories that are highly relevant to stakeholder initiatives from the MSCI KLD STATS database: environment, community, human rights, diversity, and employee relations.

name: Outside director ownership
authors_terms: ["outside director ownership", "equity ownership by outside directors", "equity stakes held by outside directors"]
definition: Hypothesis 2 tests the moderation effect of outside director ownership. Our outside director ownership moderator is operationalized as a ratio of total shares owned by outside directors over total shares outstanding.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated institutional ownership", "dedicated institutional investors", "dedicated institutional owners"]
definition: Dedicated institutional investors are known for having a more focused investment strategy and a relatively longer-term time horizon. Because of their concentrated and persistent engagement with the firm, dedicated institutional investors have more private and comprehensive information about the firm and are able to actively monitor and influence firm strategic decisions.

name: Shareholder governance provisions
authors_terms: ["shareholder governance provisions", "strength of shareholder governance provisions", "shareholder governance"]
definition: Shareholder governance provisions represent a governance system established to monitor firm management and safeguard shareholder rights. Strong shareholder governance provisions lead to more regulated and more closely monitored managerial decisions and greater job security concerns for managers.

name: Corruption
authors_terms: ["corruption", "perceived level of corruption", "perceived corruption", "Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI)"]
definition: The authors employ the definition developed by Getz and Volkema (2001: 9): 'the abuse of public roles and resources for private benefit or the misuse of office for nonofficial ends.' In the context of this paper corruption is referred to in the general sense, as a comprehensive term for the myriad forms of corrupt activities that occur on a global scale.

name: Change in foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["change in FDI", "rate of change in FDI", "FDI change", "linear change in FDI", "V-shaped change in FDI", "U-shaped change in FDI", "developmental speed"]
definition: The study is dynamic in that it focuses on change in, rather than level of, FDI; change in FDI is operationalized as linear, V-shaped and U-shaped forms of the year-to-year rate of change of FDI into a country, and is described as capturing the construct of developmental speed.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: One of Hofstede's national culture dimensions, which the authors select because they consider it, along with masculinity, one of the dimensions of culture most relevant to change.

name: Masculinity
definition: Hofstede's cultural dimension in which the masculine values of assertiveness, aggressiveness, and materialism tend to associate with a higher degree of corruption than do feminine values, which tend to be more social.

name: Post-formation governance changes
authors_terms: ["post-formation governance changes", "ex post governance changes", "governance changes", "alliance adaptation"]
definition: Ex post changes in an alliance's governance, comprising significant contract alterations, major changes in the board or committee overseeing the alliance, and the introduction or formalization of monitoring mechanisms.

name: Technological experience
authors_terms: ["technological experience", "experience with alliances on similar product areas", "alliance experience for similar technological subjects"]
definition: The firm's previous experience with alliances on similar product areas, measured as the number of prior agreements with any partner on similar subjects.

name: Partner-specific experience
authors_terms: ["partner experience", "partner-specific alliance experience", "prior experience with alliances with the partner"]
definition: The firm's previous experience with the same partner as in the focal alliance, measured as the number of prior agreements with that partner.

name: General collaborative experience
authors_terms: ["collaborative experience", "alliance experience in general", "general collaborative experience"]
definition: The firm's general alliance experience, measured as the number of prior agreements with any partner on any subject.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["alliance scope", "scope of the alliance", "scope of the joint activity"]
definition: The number of project activities encompassed by the alliance, i.e., the breadth of the joint activity performed in collaboration.

name: Division of labor
definition: The degree to which parent firms' alliance responsibilities are complementary rather than overlapping, based on how responsibility for each individual project activity is allocated between the collaborators.

name: Alliance relevance
authors_terms: ["alliance relevance", "relevance of the alliance", "salience of the alliance"]
definition: The salience of the alliance for the overall business of the parent firm, described in terms of the amount of available resources committed.

name: Technical capability
definition: Technical capability enables a firm to develop new technology; more generally, higher technical capability lowers the cost of internally developing technology.

name: Marketing capability
definition: Superior marketing ability should lower the cost of marketing effort, and marketing and technology are complements: the marginal payoff of technology is greater if the firm also has greater marketing ability.

name: External technology supply
authors_terms: ["supply of external technology", "supply of technology", "technology supply", "markets for technology", "extent of supply in markets for technology"]
definition: The extent of supply in markets for technology, namely the ability of potential entrants to obtain the required technology inexpensively and easily. The price of external technology depends on competition among technology suppliers, so having more suppliers results in a lower price of external technology.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use two measures of performance, the first of which is failure, defined as exit from all submarkets in the ISM in which the focal start-up may have operated. We term a firm as having failed if it ceases to exist or if it enters a 'distress sale.'

name: Relative performance
definition: We define industry performance as the aggregated performance of all firms that operate in the industry. The relative performance is the gap between firm performance and the average industry performance among industries in which the firm operates.

name: Human resource profile dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["human resource profile (HRP) dissimilarity", "human resource dissimilarity", "human profile dissimilarity", "human resource similarity", "knowledge applicability"]
definition: The dissimilarity between the human resource profile of a focal industry and that of the other industries in which the firm operates, where the profile is the percentage of managerial, engineering, scientific, and marketing human resources in an industry and the distance between two industries is measured by the absolute difference in those percentages.

name: Market entry
definition: Entry into a new market, observed as entry into a new three-digit SIC industry (extensive search) or as entry into a new four-digit SIC in a three-digit SIC industry in which the firm is already operating (intensive search).

name: Extensive search
definition: Extensive search is entry into a new three-digit SIC industry in which the firm did not previously operate, described by the authors as entry into an unrelated field requiring search along a new knowledge dimension.

name: Intensive search
definition: Intensive search is entry into a new four-digit SIC in a three-digit SIC industry in which the firm is currently operating, described by the authors as entry into a related business area.

name: Market exit
definition: The divestiture of a line of business that no longer matches the firm's capabilities; the models estimate the likelihood of exit from all markets in which a firm operates.

name: Extensiveness of previous search
authors_terms: ["extensiveness of a firm's previous search activity", "extensive/intensive ratio"]
definition: As defined by Chang (1996), this variable is the ratio of the number of extensive search entries to the number of total entries in the previous period.

name: Accumulation of extensive search
definition: The accumulation of extensive search until time t - 1, which the authors predict to be negatively related to initiating extensive search in the next time period.

name: Middle East operations
authors_terms: ["operations in the Middle East", "controlled operations in the Middle East", "presence in the Middle East"]
definition: Firms are defined as controlling operations in the Middle East if the International Directory of Corporate Affiliations indicates that they operate a division, subsidiary, affiliate, or joint venture in the region.

name: Intangible assets
definition: Assets that tend to be knowledge based or intangible in nature and include superior production skills, patents, marketing abilities, and managerial skills. R&D intensity captures technological or production intangible assets whereas advertising intensity measures marketing intangible assets.

name: Firm size
definition: Larger firms, with greater scale and scope, can realize greater value when they gain access to location-specific advantages and often have greater internal resources that allow them to undertake foreign direct investment.

name: Foreign sales intensity
authors_terms: ["proportion of foreign sales to total firm sales", "sales from foreign sources", "more multinational firms"]
definition: Firms that derive a large proportion of sales from foreign sources have more experience handling the difficulties associated with doing business internationally and are better suited to manage the complexities of operating in the Middle East.

name: Profitability
definition: Profitable firms might have more resources to apply to international expansion, and in order to compensate for the risks of operating in the region, multinationals with operations in the Middle East might earn higher returns.

name: Misrepresentation of patient health status
authors_terms: ["misrepresentation", "patient misrepresentation", "strategic misrepresentation", "strategic manipulation of patient health status", "risky, unethical strategies", "unethical behavior"]
definition: This article proposes that unethical behavior can be considered a particular type of strategic risk-taking, and defines risky, unethical strategies as strategies that pursue strategic risk in the form of unethical behavior. These are identified in the liver transplant market as centers moving patients to the top of the waiting list through strategic manipulation of patient health status.

name: Entrant misrepresentation in the market
authors_terms: ["Entrant misrepresenting in OPO", "entrants that had begun misrepresenting patient status"]
definition: The variable, Entrant misrepresenting in OPO, measuring the count of the number of entrants that had begun misrepresenting patient status in a previous year for a given OPO, was created for each year.

name: New entrant status
definition: Any center that entered during the analysis time frame is identified as an entrant. Any center that entered after 1990 was considered an entrant unless they were the first center in a given OPO.

name: Market entry
definition: Entry is a dummy variable at the transplant center level where entry equals 1 in the year of the first liver transplant and 0 for the previous years. When firms enter the market, it is a forward-looking decision.

name: Transplant volume
authors_terms: ["number of transplants a center performs", "center volume", "Δ Volume"]
definition: The baseline performance metric that misrepresenting patient status could improve is the number of transplants a center performs.

name: Organizational survival
authors_terms: ["survival", "survival rates", "exit", "exit hazard", "exit probability", "forced out of the market"]
definition: Any year with no volume in the following year is considered an exit year, so exit is assumed to occur at the end of the year. Exit events are captured through the end of the data set and classified as right censored at that time.

name: Chart performance
definition: We measure it by chart position, which is the position on the Billboard chart that a certain label, song, artist, or genre reaches in a specific week (demand analysis) or month (information shock and supply analysis).

name: Portfolio novelty
authors_terms: ["portfolio novelty", "novelty of the offerings in a firm's portfolio"]
definition: Portfolio novelty is the novelty of the offerings in a firm's portfolio; it is measured as the average novelty of all the songs that a firm produces in a month.

name: Across-niche proliferation
definition: Across-niche proliferation is the extension of a firm's offerings in different submarkets to reduce the distance between a consumer's product ideal and the attributes of one of the products offered.

name: Within-niche proliferation
definition: Within-niche proliferation consists in increasing the quantity of products that an incumbent offers in its own niche to offer more choice to variety-seeking consumers.

name: Experience breadth
definition: Experience breadth is 'how closely related the various products that the firm has created are to one another'. Broad experience arises from serving submarkets that are distant from each other and that require the development of diverse knowledge.

name: Information regime change
authors_terms: ["change", "changes in information regimes", "Billboard chart change", "information regime change induced by streaming"]
definition: A new regime provides incumbents with novel and updated information about demand preferences and competitive dynamics. Thus, changes in information regimes represent a shock to the structure of information shared by a community.

name: Song novelty
definition: A song novelty is the Mahalanobis distance of the song from the centroid of a product space built from the attributes of all the songs produced in the previous 12 months in the song's genre.

name: Artist newness
definition: Emerging artist is a dummy variable that takes on value 1 if an artist has not had a single appearing in the top 50 of 'The Hot 100' chart nor an album in the top 50 of the 'Billboard 200' chart before the focal month.

name: Genre mainstreamness
definition: Mainstream is a dummy that takes on value 1 if the genre is mainstream according to Discogs.

name: Chart entry
definition: Entry is a dummy that takes a value of 1 if the artist i enters the chart in week t, and 0 otherwise.

name: R&D investment
authors_terms: ["RESEARCH INVESTMENT", "investments in the R&D process", "level of R&D investment", "size of the R&D investment"]
definition: Investments in the R&D process equal the total monetary cost, in Euros, of the research that led to the patent, before the date of application.

name: Regional absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["REGION ABSORPTIVE CAPACITY", "absorptive capacity of neighboring organizations", "absorptive capacity of organizations in the geographic location", "absorptive capacity of colocated firms"]
definition: As a proxy of the absorptive capacity of neighboring organizations in a specific technology space, the authors compute the number of patents classified in the same ISI-INPI-OST technological class of the focal patent, invented in the same NUTS3 region, for every year between 1978 and the year in which the inventor applied for the focal patent.

name: Relative external knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["external vs. internal knowledge sources", "External vs. Internal", "use of external (cf. internal) knowledge sourcing", "internal vs. external knowledge sourcing"]
definition: The ratio indicates the relative importance of external versus internal knowledge interactions during the research that led to the patent; it correlates well with the simple ratio of the use of internal and external knowledge sources and approaches zero if it derives from the intense use of both resources or a small difference.

name: Fear of imitation
authors_terms: ["FEAR OF IMITATION", "fear of imitation", "fear of imitation as a reason to patent"]
definition: The fear of imitation variable reported by the inventors in the survey indicates the importance of protecting an invention from imitation as a reason to patent; it is independent of the two factors that form the interaction term and enables a mediation test.

name: Forward self-citations
definition: The number of self-citations, that is, later patents by the same applicant citing the focal patent, in the five years following the application year, after controlling for total forward citations in the same period.

name: Firm failure
definition: The dependent variable, organizational failure, is coded as the year in which a firm was no longer listed in The Red Books. The authors use organizational survival as a measure of competitive advantage because it can provide an accurate measure particularly when a firm's assets are primarily knowledge based.

name: Top executive departure to a competing firm
authors_terms: ["interfirm executive mobility", "top executive departure", "top executive departure flag", "total top executive exits to competing firms"]
definition: The departure of a top executive to a competing firm, that is, mobility of an executive from the focal firm to another firm in the same industry. The authors focus on top executives who depart and join a competing firm rather than on all turnover.

name: Top executive entry from a competing firm
authors_terms: ["top executive entry", "top executive entry flag", "total top executive entry from competing firms", "gaining a top executive from a competitor"]
definition: The recruitment of a top executive from a competing firm, which is the bidirectionally opposite side of interfirm executive mobility. Recruited top executives bring knowledge that their new employers can utilize to improve firm performance.

name: Internal routine role executive departure
authors_terms: ["internal routine role executive departure", "administrative top executive departure", "production top executive departure"]
definition: The departures of production and administrative executives were categorized as internal routine role executive departure. These two executive roles were grouped together because the primary task of their positions is to manage firm operations that the authors classify as internal since they are not centered on direct contact with the external client.

name: External exchange role executive departure
authors_terms: ["external exchange role executive departure", "account top executive departure", "creative top executive departure", "media top executive departure"]
definition: The departures of creative, account, and media top executives were included in the category of external exchange role executive departure. The three positions were grouped into this category because their functional responsibilities require the most regular interactions with clients and the top executives are primarily tasked with managing the client exchange relationship.

name: Prior experience
definition: Experience refers to the cumulative number of patients treated with IVF by the organization. Experience was measured by cumulating all the prior cases that involved one or more IVF cycles using the patient's own fresh eggs.

name: Success rate
authors_terms: ["success rate", "clinic success rate", "live-birth rate", "overt success rate"]
definition: 'Success' in this business (IVF clinics) is very clearly defined: an IVF treatment that results in a birth is a success; otherwise, it is a failure. Hence, the measure of an organization's success rate is the proportion of live births among the patients receiving IVF treatment; the primary dependent variable is the success rate in standard cases, defined as the live-birth rate in the IVF patient group aged 35 and under involving the use of the patient's own fresh eggs.

name: Difficulty of patient mix
authors_terms: ["difficult cases", "difficult patients", "poor prognosis patients", "complex cases", "challenging cases", "difficulty in a clinic's patient mix"]
definition: To measure the level of difficulty in a clinic's patient mix, we identified three factors that IVF practitioners regard as relevant dimensions for assessing the complexity of a case: patients over 35 years old, patients that failed to conceive with previous IVF treatment, and patients who produce very few eggs. All three categories are considered to represent more difficult cases with relatively poor prognoses.

name: Hosting high-ranking government officials
authors_terms: ["hosting visits of senior-level central government officials", "Host firm", "hosting site visits of government officials"]
definition: The practice of firms hosting visits of senior-level central government officials, which the authors argue represents an emergent CPA strategy flowing from pre-existing relationships between the firm's managers and government officials.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock market reactions", "Cumulative abnormal return (CAR)", "abnormal market returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Cumulative abnormal returns for the portfolio between (0, +1) are calculated by summing abnormal returns, where abnormal returns are residuals from the standard market model, estimated using daily stock returns and daily total-value-weighted congregated market returns.

name: Prior financial performance
definition: The firm's profitability prior to the visit; the authors measure it as return on assets (ROA) lagged one year prior to the visit.

name: Private ownership
definition: Privately controlled firms are those controlled by nongovernment entities, Chinese citizens, or foreign investors, in contrast to state-owned enterprises.

name: Top managers' political connections
authors_terms: ["Top managers' political connections", "Percentage of top managers with political connections", "TMT political connections"]
definition: Top managers of Chinese companies who have direct personal connections to government officials through their prior experience of working in government organizations.

name: Provincial institutional development
authors_terms: ["Institutional development", "Institutional development of the province", "quality of local institutions"]
definition: The quality of local institutions, which plays an important role in the scope and cost of transactions and varies substantially across regions within China.

name: Strategic interdependence
authors_terms: ["the degree of strategic interdependence", "strategic interdependence (SI)", "strategic interdependence (SIND)"]
definition: We define the degree of strategic interdependence between any two organizations such as the JV and its parent to be a function of the importance and extent of shared resources.

name: Environmental uncertainty
