definition: We define the degree of environmental uncertainty to be associated with the complexity and volatility of environmental elements including customers, suppliers, competitors, regulatory groups, and technological conditions (Bourgeois, 1980). The degree of environmental uncertainty is a function of both the extent and the importance to the organization of changes in different elements of its task environment.

name: Integrative mechanisms
authors_terms: ["integrative mechanisms", "the use and/or complexity of integrative mechanisms", "COORD"]
definition: Integrative mechanisms such as direct contact between executives of the parent and the JV, liaison personnel, temporary task forces, etc.; their information-processing capacity increases as they increase in complexity from direct contact (the least complex) to permanent teams (the most complex).

name: Internal role of the JV board
authors_terms: ["the internal role of the JV board", "internal role of board members", "INROL"]
definition: The internal role involves monitoring and evaluating the organization's executives, and approving and coordinating the JV's strategic plans and actions with the objectives of the parents.

name: External role of the JV board
authors_terms: ["the external role of the JV board", "external role of board members", "EXROL"]
definition: The external role involves activities to manage the linkage between the JV and its external environment, i.e., facilitating the government, legal, and other public relations of the JV.

name: Socialization of JV managers
authors_terms: ["socialization", "the extent of socialization of JV managers", "control by socialization", "SOCAL"]
definition: The rotation of managers from one organization into another creates a new kind of control—control by socialization. Participation in executive training sessions and seminars conducted by the parent is another possible model of socializing JV managers.

name: Incentive compensation mix
authors_terms: ["incentive compensation based on a mix of JV plus parent performance", "the relative influence of parent performance on bonus determination", "INMIX"]
definition: The bonus for JV managers can be based on the parent's performance or the JV's performance or some combination of the two. Compensation arrangements with appropriate incentive plans can reduce the threat of JV managers taking actions contrary to the parent's interests.

name: Parent representation on the JV board
authors_terms: ["the proportion of JV board members representing that parent", "board structure", "RBOD"]
definition: The presence of their representative members provides each parent with both explicit control and implicit control. Board members can exercise explicit control by exercising their veto power and can also have implicit influence by their participation and influence in strategic deliberations and the decision-making process.

name: Parent staffing of JV top management
authors_terms: ["staffing", "the proportion of parent managers in the JV top management", "representatives from the parent"]
definition: To staff the JV's top management positions, managers may be selected from the parents' managerial pool or may be recruited from the 'external' labor market. Whether key management positions of the JV are staffed by parent company managers is an important feature of control structure.

name: Relative emphasis on the monitoring role
authors_terms: ["global framing", "relative emphasis of monitoring over resource-providing role", "Relative Emphasis of Monitoring Role", "cultural entrepreneurship"]
definition: The main dependent variable in our study is the degree of cultural entrepreneurship, as captured by the global framing of the independent director roles revealed in the director biographies of U.S.-listed Chinese companies. We define global framing as a mechanism of cultural entrepreneurship in corporate governance in which the foreign-listed firms tailor their narratives targeted to host country investors.

name: Board education in Anglo-American countries
authors_terms: ["Board Education in Anglo-American Countries", "overseas education of board members", "educational experiences in Anglo-American countries"]
definition: For individual director's education, we considered all undergraduate and higher levels of education that the individual director received in an Anglo-American country such as the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, or Australia. Foreign education in non-Anglo-American countries, such as the former Soviet Union, Japan, Germany, and France, was coded as zero.

name: Board interlock to Anglo-American companies
authors_terms: ["Board Interlock to Anglo-American Companies", "interlock linkages", "board interlock ties"]
definition: Board interlocks with foreign companies were counted as the number of interlock ties with Anglo-American companies, that is, the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, as indicated in the biography and BvD filing and then aggregated at the company level.

name: Foreign institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["Foreign Institutional Ownership", "ownership by foreigners", "global institutional owners"]
definition: We used Foreign Institutional Ownership to code the share ownership percentages of non-Chinese institutional shareholders (5% block shareholders) in the focal company. The nationality of foreign institutional owners included the United States and other offshore incorporation countries, such as the Cayman Islands and the British Virgin Islands.

name: Local business history
authors_terms: ["Local Business History", "cultural imprinting in the home country"]
definition: We first coded Local Business History as a continuous variable indicating the number of years since the local incorporation year of the firm, obtained from the 20F and BvD database. We believe that the local business history in China is an important indicator of this cultural imprinting, constraining U.S.-listed Chinese companies' global framing.

name: Connection to the state
authors_terms: ["Connection to the State", "director ties to the state", "politically connected directors"]
definition: Following prior research (Wang 2015), we also coded Connection to the State as a continuous variable after counting the total number of positions directors hold in the Chinese government, state-regulating authorities, or national committees such as the People's Congress (CPC) and the People's Political Consultative Conference.

name: Investor recognition in the host country
authors_terms: ["Investor Recognition", "investor recognition in the host country"]
definition: We examine how global framing relates to investor recognition in the host country, which we define as the acquisition of financial resources and endorsement of future business prospects at the host market.

name: Ownership dispersion
authors_terms: ["Ownership Dispersion", "independent director's capacity for monitoring in China"]
definition: We measured Ownership Dispersion, which is based on the stock ownership report in the sample company's 20F filing as the remaining stock ownership excluding the top three majority stock owners. Higher degrees of ownership dispersion under the principal-principal conflict indicate the fragmentation among the minority shareholders and uninterrupted power of the majority shareholders, which constrains the capacity of an independent director's monitoring task.

name: Advanced manufacturing technology
definition: AMT refers to a family of technologies that lie at the intersection of computer science and manufacturing engineering. We view AMT not as an isolated phenomenon restricted to production, but as the gradual penetration of computer technology into all the functions of manufacturing organizations, both production and support.

name: Computerization
definition: Computerization refers to the application of computer technologies in individual functions (e.g., CAD, CNC).

name: Computer integration
definition: Computer integration refers to applications that integrate transactions between functions (e.g., programs to download CAD data and create CNC machining programs).

name: Integration sophistication
definition: Sophistication of computer integration refers to the mode of data exchange; more sophisticated forms of integration will involve data exchange requiring less human intervention.

name: Structural differentiation
definition: There are three aspects of structural differentiation. Vertical differentiation (LEVELS) is defined simply as the number of hierarchical levels in the organization. Horizontal differentiation (SPECIAL) is defined in terms of functional specification, that is, the number of functional task areas in which there is at least one full-time specialist. Job specialization (JOB) is defined simply as the number of job titles in the organization.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization (FORMAL) is defined as the extensiveness of written rules and procedures.

name: Decentralization of decision making
authors_terms: ["decentralization", "decentralization of resource allocation", "decentralization of system design"]
definition: Resource allocation (DENRSCE) refers to capital spending and operating expense decisions. System design (DENSDSN) deals with decisions about new equipment, and creation or termination of jobs or departments. In each case, the lower in the organization these decisions are made, the more decentralized is the organization.

name: Professionalization
definition: Professionalization (PROF) was operationalized as the proportion of employees who occupy jobs that require a college degree.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["internal forms of governance", "internalize", "integration", "market forms of governance", "subcontracting", "governance decision", "governance choice"]
definition: Whether Compustar governs a particular transaction internally or elects to use an external subcontractor. The prescription from transaction cost economics is that firms should internalize transactions when contractual hazards are present and favor the market when such hazards are absent.

name: Contractual hazards
definition: The nature and extent of contractual hazards with which transactional exchange is imbued, which TCE treats as the key determinants of integration. The extent of such hazards is shaped by the degree of asset specificity, appropriability, or observability in an exchange.

name: Hold-up hazards
definition: Hazards that arise when assets are specific to a transaction and suppliers may act opportunistically to extract excessive rents from customers. Contracting costs can be so severe that the customer will prefer to internalize the transaction and perform the activity itself rather than be subject to potential ex post hold-up.

name: Observability hazards
definition: The observability of the outcomes of transactional exchange is an important exchange hazard. When the quality of output is difficult to observe and measure ex post, using market-based contracts to govern transactions can be problematic because it is unclear how to gauge, and thereby reward, quality.

name: Appropriability hazards
definition: Appropriability refers to contracting hazards that expose valuable intellectual property to expropriation. Such an exchange leads to the possibility that a partner firm will expropriate valuable knowledge, denying the originating firm sole rights to a rent-generating asset.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities are defined as superior ability to create a good or service that meets a customer's requirements for functionality, quality, and cost and schedule. The authors argue that, with transaction characteristics held constant, firms will outsource transactions when technological capabilities are weak, and govern transactions internally when technological capabilities are strong.

name: Contender successor
definition: Contender successors are inside executives who are promoted to CEO positions after the dismissals of their predecessors. An inside succession following a CEO's dismissal reflects a successful internal power contest against the CEO, and the successor is a contending executive who has won the support and approval of the board of directors.

name: Follower successor
definition: Follower successors are inside executives who are promoted to CEO positions following the ordinary retirements of their predecessors. Because successors who follow a CEO's ordinary retirement are often expected to continue and follow their predecessors' strategies, we refer to them as followers.

name: Outsider successor
definition: Outsider successors are most often selected in periods of poor firm performance and when directors cannot locate a competent successor within their firms. Outsiders come to new CEO positions from other organizations.

name: Postsuccession senior executive turnover
definition: We propose that senior executive turnover following CEO succession reflects top management team dynamics and that its impact on firm performance will be moderated by successor type. Senior executive turnover influences top management team composition and may have a significant impact on strategic decision making and firm performance.

name: Postsuccession operational performance
authors_terms: ["postsuccession operational performance", "postsuccession firm operational performance", "firm operational performance", "return on assets", "ROA"]
definition: Accounting measures reflect the current operational performance of a firm, while market measures indicate investors' perceptions of the firm's future performance potential. Our study focused on firms' operational performance rather than market valuation.

name: Departing CEO tenure
definition: The length of a departing CEO's tenure is another important component of the succession context and reflects the frequency of CEO succession at a firm. Departing CEO tenure influences postsuccession operational performance through organizational inertia and the disruption surrounding CEO succession.

name: Employee earnings
authors_terms: ["employee earnings", "annual earnings", "earnings", "able to generate value", "high earners"]
definition: All forms of taxable compensation that an employee received in a given calendar year; including salary, bonuses, and other reported income. The authors treat earnings as highly correlated with the employee's ability to generate value for the employer.

name: Employee mobility
definition: A dummy variable coded 1 if an employee's dominant employer changed since the previous year and 0 otherwise; a dominant employer is the one at which the employee earned the most during the year.

name: Employee entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["employee entrepreneurship", "moves to spin-outs", "exit to spin-out", "join spin-outs", "spin-out"]
definition: A move in which an employee leaves to join a spin-out; a spin-out is defined as a start-up founded by a former employee of an established firm within the same industry. It is measured as a move in which the employee's dominant employer changed and the new employer appeared in the data for the first time in that year.

name: Employee mobility to established firms
authors_terms: ["moves to established firms", "mobility to established firms", "leaving to established firms"]
definition: Employees who leave a firm to join another established firm rather than founding a new venture; the authors count the number of unique individuals who leave a firm to join another established firm in each measurement year and the four years prior to it.

name: Source firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "source firm performance", "revenues per employee", "revenue per employee"]
definition: The dependent variable for testing Hypotheses 3 and 4, firm performance, is measured as revenues per employee.

name: Sales growth
definition: The firm's growth in sales. The authors measure it as the compound growth rate in sales for firm J in year T.

name: Firm performance
definition: Strategic management researchers generally measure performance using either accounting profitability or returns to stockholders. We use both as each presents its own set of problems.

name: Free cash flow
definition: Free Cash Flow (FCF, undistributed cash flow in excess of that needed for positive net present value (NPV) projects). Internally generated cash in excess of positive NPV projects allows managers to pursue personal goals without having to go to the bond or equity markets.

name: Cash flow
definition: Defining Total Cash Flow as both normal cash flow (for firms with good investment prospects) and FCF (for firms with poor investment prospects).

name: Strong governance
authors_terms: ["strong governance", "governance controls", "governance mechanisms", "strong stockholder governance", "weak corporate governance"]
definition: Weak corporate governance, the second condition identified by agency theory, refers to a lack of mechanisms to align managerial decisions with shareholders' interests. Strong stockholder governance forces managers to invest FCF wisely or to return it to the stockholders.

name: Input control
definition: Input control can be considered a form of resource allocation because it regulates the antecedent conditions of performance. In the case of R&D professionals, it can be used to create the type of "knowledge environment" desired by firms by manipulating the degree and variety of core knowledge, skills, experiences, and attitudes displayed on the job.

name: Behavior control
definition: Behavior control consists of monitoring ongoing employee activities and behaviors and regulating how work gets done. Structural control, also referred to as bureaucratic or behavior control, regulates activities and behaviors and is most often implemented in the form of rules and procedures.

name: Output control
definition: Output control regulates outcomes and results as opposed to the means by which outcomes are achieved. In applying output control, firms define the dimensions of desired results, measure how well output aligns with the set standards, and provide respective rewards and punishment for success and failure in goal attainment.

name: Scientific diversity
definition: Scientific diversity was assessed as the extent to which different scientific specialties were represented in the R&D program. The number of specific scientific specialties represented in each R&D laboratory was used to measure scientific diversity.

name: Professionalization
definition: Professionalization was assessed as the propensity of R&D personnel to seek contact with professional colleagues and exposure to information external to the organization.

name: Centralization
definition: Centralization was assessed as the extent to which decision-making authority was at lower levels of the R&D laboratory hierarchy. Centralization of decision-making narrows channels of communication.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization was assessed as the extent to which rules governing behavior were precisely and explicitly formulated. Formalization through rules and procedures governing the approach taken in problem solving restricts scientists' ability to deal effectively with the high level of uncertainty inherent in the drug research process.

name: Frequency of performance appraisals
authors_terms: ["frequency of performance appraisals", "monitoring function of behavior control"]
definition: Frequency of performance appraisals was assessed as the extent to which behavior was measured and evaluated. Frequent monitoring can interfere with research activities and may reduce the likelihood that R&D professionals will pursue nonroutine and radical changes that involve higher probabilities of failure.

name: Goal specificity
definition: Goal specificity was assessed as the extent to which goals were explicit, clearly defined, and provided unambiguous criteria for selecting among alternatives.

name: Emphasis on output
definition: A more general measure captured the extent to which the quantity of outcomes was emphasized in performance appraisals and rewards. Organizations that emphasize quantity of output may inadvertently emphasize projects with shorter time horizons.

name: Emphasis on professional output
authors_terms: ["professional emphasis on output", "emphasis on professional output"]
definition: There was a measure that examined whether professional forms of output was emphasized. In most university and many corporate research laboratories, presentations and published papers are the primary outputs of research.

name: Rewards and recognition
definition: Rewards and recognition were assessed as the extent to which R&D professionals received public recognition for outstanding achievements.

name: Incremental innovation
definition: Incremental innovations represent minor changes to existing technology involving small advances based on an established foundation of knowledge. Following FDA criteria, drug enhancements involve combinations of existing drugs, new dosage forms, new indications, and formula changes, and would be considered incremental innovations.

name: Radical innovation
authors_terms: ["radical innovation", "new drugs", "new drug innovation", "new chemical entities (NCEs)"]
definition: Radical innovations represent major changes in technology involving the discovery of new knowledge, substantial technical risk, time, and cost. New Chemical Entities (NCEs) are totally new drugs which, in most cases, represent significant therapeutic advances, and these new drugs would be considered radical innovations.

name: Presence of a separate COO/president
definition: A top leadership structure in which a firm has an officer other than the CEO who holds the title of president or COO or both. The authors note that there can be two separate roles of a COO/president: one representing an heir apparent in training for the CEO position and the other representing a co-leader delegated with internal operating authority.

name: Magnitude of strategic change
definition: The extent to which a firm changed its resource allocations in key strategy dimensions; because the sample consisted of non-diversified firms, six strategy dimensions were used to create a composite measure.

name: Prior firm performance
authors_terms: ["prior firm performance", "firm performance", "low firm performance", "high firm performance"]
definition: Firm performance in the period preceding the focal year, operationalized as return on assets adjusted for industry differences. Low firm performance suggests that a CEO's competencies are not aligned with environmental conditions, while high firm performance suggests they are well aligned.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: CEO dismissal, in which a CEO leaves office against his or her will, is very disruptive to organizations and normally does not happen except under unusual conditions.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality occurs when the same person holds both the CEO and board chairperson positions in a corporation. The authors describe duality as a double-edged sword: it can entrench a CEO, or it can establish a unity of command at the top of the firm.

name: Board vigilance
definition: Vigilant boards are defined as boards that have the motivation and incentive to effectively monitor and discipline CEOs; they tend to be composed of a large group of independent, outside directors who often own sizable portions of the firm's stock.

name: Informal CEO power
authors_terms: ["informal CEO power", "informal power of a CEO", "informal power"]
definition: Informal CEO power derives from sources of influence that do not directly depend upon a CEO's formal position in an organization. CEOs may acquire informal power through such means as developing prestigious contacts with other organizations, managing critical organizational problems, engendering loyalty within their organizations, and co-opting boards of directors.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured by return on assets (ROA), a common indicator of short-term performance, calculated as net income divided by total assets. Boards of directors monitor firm profitability as an important indicator of how well CEOs are performing.

name: Economic integration
definition: Economic integration is defined as the extent to which respective resources pooled by alliance members and subsequent operations utilizing those resources have been effectively combined in an alliance's value chain system such that if one party withdraws, the alliance will not be able to survive and the other parties will suffer great loss.

name: Interparty trust
definition: Interparty trust engenders economic and social binding that sustains existing relationships. It reflects relationship investments made during the alliance's life and often increases with the duration and reciprocity of the relationship.

name: Joint governance
definition: Joint governance is purposefully and collectively designed to guide, monitor, and oversee an alliance's operations in pursuit of a maximum joint payoff. It is bilateral, and aims to increase an alliance's success or collective gains through harmonized group monitoring of overall operations as well as through specific functions that are critical to achieving the goals set forth by alliance members.

name: Procedural justice
definition: Procedural justice concerns the extent to which the alliance's decisionmaking process and procedures that impact each party's gains and interests are impartial and fair as perceived by the boundary spanners (senior alliance executives) representing each party.

name: Alliance profitability
definition: Profitability was defined as an average of ROI over the three-year period (2000-2002) examined. While profitability mirrors the achievement of financial returns, stability indicates, at least partially, the achievement of structural efficiency in a volatile environment.

name: Alliance stability
definition: Given that a majority of alliance population in this study remain in their operational phase and have not reached their restructuring stage, stability (i.e., the opposite of variability) is defined as how stable the major operating results have been over the years.

name: Shared team experience
authors_terms: ["shared team experience", "shared organizational experience", "average shared team experience", "cumulative experience", "shared experience"]
definition: The cumulative experience that members of a team have playing with each other; the authors argue it is a reasonable proxy for the value of the stock of tacit knowledge held in the collective mind of a team.

name: Tacit knowledge
authors_terms: ["tacit knowledge", "collectively held tacit knowledge", "team-based tacit knowledge", "group-level tacit knowledge"]
definition: Tacit knowledge is knowledge that is not codified. If it could be codified, then it would no longer be tacit knowledge; it would have become explicit knowledge. Group knowledge is stored in a collective mind and is difficult-to-articulate and socially diffused knowledge.

name: Team performance
definition: For a sports team, a competitive advantage is related to winning, and teams that win more than they lose, and continue to do so for an extended period of time, have a sustained competitive advantage.

name: Coaching experience
authors_terms: ["coaching experience", "coaching experience with the same team", "coaching tenure", "coach's tenure"]
definition: A variable that captured how long a coach had been with the team at the end of the season; it represents years of coaching experience with the team. The authors caution that it is merely the amount of time spent with a specific team and is not a measure of a coach's quality.

name: Tenure heterogeneity
definition: The dispersion of organizational experience among team members; the authors argue that although shared organizational experience is important, it is also important that team members are exposed to new perspectives and ideas.

name: Director demographic minority status
authors_terms: ["minority director", "demographic minority status", "female or ethnic minority", "demographic minority"]
definition: A director's demographic 'minority' status (i.e., female or ethnic minority), which the authors analyze for its effect on the ex post settling-up process in the director labor market; in the empirical tests the independent variable minority director was set equal to 1 for female directors and those who belonged to an ethnic minority, and 0 for White male directors.

name: Reputational penalties
authors_terms: ["reputational penalties", "net loss of outside directorships", "labor market penalties", "ex post settling-up outcomes"]
definition: The professional cost borne by fraud-tainted directors in the labor market, i.e., a 'net loss' of outside directorships after misconduct is uncovered, which includes the forfeiture of existing outside directorships and gaining fewer new outside directorships at nonfraudulent firms.

name: Media discourse on board diversity
authors_terms: ["media discourse on board diversity", "media discourse promoting board diversity", "media coverage emphasizing the importance of diversity in the boardroom"]
definition: Variation in the prevailing media coverage that reflects and reinforces the preference for board diversity; increases in such discourse would likely amplify the reputational immunity of fraud-tainted minority directors.

name: Board diversity
authors_terms: ["board diversity", "no. of minority directors at nonfraudulent firm", "level of board diversity"]
definition: The degree to which a board includes female and ethnic minority directors; the perceived marginal benefit of the diversity conferred by a minority director depends on the number of minority directors already serving on the board.

name: Managerial ability
definition: We define managerial ability as the knowledge, skills, and experience, which is often tacit, residing with and utilized by managers. From a strategic perspective, managerial ability derives from two main sources: domain expertise and resource expertise.

name: Resource productivity
definition: One important indicator of the potential value that managers create from their resources is the level of resource productivity, which refers to the net benefits achieved from resource management. Productivity increases when managerial actions produce greater utility with the same inputs or produce the same utility with fewer inputs.

name: Resource quality
definition: We define resource quality as the value-creating potential of a resource, which contributes to the extent to which a firm can develop and implement strategies that improve performance.

name: Resource synchronization
definition: Synchronization involves the integration and balancing of interdependent bundles to ensure that activities reinforce and align with the firm's strategic and competitive context. A firm with many resource combinations that reinforce each other has a high degree of synchronization.

name: Organizational performance
definition: In measuring performance, we operationalized organizational performance as team winning percentage within each season. Specifically, we used the ratio of games won to total games played during the regular season.

name: Firm status inconsistency
definition: Status inconsistency refers to the extent to which the different business units within a firm occupy differently ranked status positions.

name: Firm status
definition: Status refers to the hierarchical position an actor occupies in a social system. We operationalize status by the amount of public attention and recognition firms received for a given level of quality and performance.

name: Status inconsistency decreasing divestitures
authors_terms: ["status inconsistency decreasing divestitures", "divestitures that decrease status inconsistency", "divestitures that reduce status inconsistency"]
definition: We coded four types of divestitures: status inconsistency decreasing divestitures (coded 4), status inconsistency neutral divestitures (coded 3), no divestitures (coded 2), and status inconsistency increasing divestitures (coded 1).

name: Segment status inconsistency
definition: To test our segment-level hypotheses, we construct segment status inconsistency as the amount of weight a segment adds to the status inconsistency of its firm.

name: Firm relatedness
definition: We measure the firm-level relatedness, firm prevalence, as the sales-weighted average of segment relatedness. Firm prevalence reflects the extent to which a firm's segments are interrelated with each other.

name: Segment relatedness
definition: We first use the matrix formula developed by Teece et al. (1994) to measure the asymmetric interindustry relatedness between any two industries each year and then compute a segment's prevalence score in a firm, as its mean relatedness to all other segments in the firm.

name: Segment divestiture
definition: We estimate the likelihood of a segment being divested in year t, conditional on the segment not having been divested in prior years. The dependent variable in the discrete-time event history model is the hazard rate of divestiture.

name: Character questioning causal accounts
authors_terms: ["character questioning causal account", "character questioning causal accounts", "causal accounts"]
definition: Causal accounts serve as statements made to explain unexpected behavior and provide a causal reason for why the event occurred; causal accounts are likely to be most damaging when they call into question the integrity of an executive, indicating a lack of character.

name: Reemployment as a CEO
authors_terms: ["Rehired as a CEO", "reemployed as a CEO", "regain employment as a CEO", "reemployment as a CEO"]
definition: The dependent variable, Rehired as a CEO, is a binary measure of whether the dismissed executive regained employment as a CEO of any firm.

name: Reputational capital
definition: An executive's reputation is the 'collective judgment of observers regarding the quality or capabilities of a focal actor within a specific domain that is earned over time'. Reputational capital signals that others positively evaluate the executive.

name: Social capital
definition: Social capital refers to the ability of individuals to extract resources from relationships and to resources available through relationships and ties that individuals can use to enhance their positions.

name: Genetic factors
definition: By genetic factors, we mean those factors that are encoded in DNA and transmitted biologically. Genes increase the probability that people will engage in entrepreneurial activity; the authors argue they imply probabilistic propensities rather than hard-wired patterns of behavior.

name: Propensity to engage in entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["the tendency of people to engage in entrepreneurial activity", "the propensity of people to become entrepreneurs", "entrepreneurial activity", "entrepreneurship"]
definition: The research literature does not agree on the definition of entrepreneurship. Given these differences, the authors seek convergent validity for their argument by examining several different operationalizations common in the literature: self-employment, starting a new business, being an owner-operator of a company, and engaging in the firm start-up process.

name: Shared environment
definition: Shared environmental effects are the environmental factors that people in the same family have in common. The shared (or common) environment refers to environmental factors that make family members similar, capturing the extent to which being raised together makes relatives similar.

name: Nonshared environment
definition: Nonshared environmental effects are the environmental effects that are unique to an individual, i.e., environmental influences that contribute to differences between family members. The nonshared environmental influences, which are uncorrelated across siblings, capture the extent to which idiosyncratic experiences make relatives different.

name: Attitudes toward entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["attitudes toward entrepreneurship", "attitudes toward entrepreneurship as a career"]
definition: To identify the mechanism through which genetic factors operate, the authors also examined the respondents' attitudes toward entrepreneurship through a Likert scale item that asked them to indicate, on a scale from one (a very good career) to five (a very bad career), their view of entrepreneurship as a career.

name: Offshoring complexity
definition: Offshoring complexity is defined as a combination of configuration and task complexity. While task complexity resides within the actual implementation, configuration complexity occurs as a result of new interdependencies between countries, activities, and people.

name: Configuration complexity
definition: Configuration complexity refers to complexity in terms of the interdependencies in the organizational configuration, and encompasses the structural, operational, and social layers of the organizational configuration.

name: Task complexity
definition: Task complexity relates to the complexity of the individual offshoring implementations; characteristics such as the task's degree of standardized versus tacit knowledge flows, inexact means-ends connections, and the number and interdependence of subtasks influence it.

name: Cost-estimation error
definition: Hidden costs are ex ante unaccounted for, which is why they materialize ex post as a discrepancy between expected and realized costs. Cost-estimation error is the difference between the cost savings expected from the offshoring project and the achieved cost savings.

name: Organizational design orientation
authors_terms: ["organizational design orientation", "strategic orientation toward organizational design", "design orientation"]
definition: The degree to which offshoring strategies involve a strong orientation toward the overall system of structures and processes, rather than the mere relocation of particular tasks for resource-seeking reasons.

name: Offshoring experience
definition: Firms with prior offshoring experience are more likely to have accumulated organizational system knowledge and will therefore be comparatively better in estimating the costs of offshoring associated with complexity. It is measured as the time between the launch of the first offshoring project by the focal firm and the initiation of the focal implementation.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "dual structure", "dual CEO", "board leadership structure", "independent board leadership"]
definition: A board leadership structure in which 'the CEO wears two hats-one as CEO of the firm, the other as chairperson of the board of directors'; the alternative, an independence structure, describes the case in which different individuals serve in these capacities.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["corporate financial performance", "corporate performance", "return on investment", "ROI", "return on equity", "ROE", "profit margin", "accounting returns"]
definition: The authors rely on multiple indices of corporate financial performance - return on equity (ROE), return on investment (ROI), and profit margin - noting that 'the number of corporate performance measures that could serve as dependent variables is almost infinite.' The measures chosen are 'so-called accounting returns.'

name: Strategic alliance partner knowledge complementarity
definition: Knowledge complementarity occurs when two firms have nonoverlapping or different knowledge bases that might be combined and integrated to create value that did not exist in either firm before the alliance; more knowledge complementarity occurs when partners contribute different knowledge sets in areas such as customer relationships, marketing, R&D, industrial design, engineering, or information technology.

name: New product innovativeness
definition: New product innovativeness refers to the extent to which a new product differs from competing alternatives in a way that is meaningful to customers.

name: Process interdependence
definition: Process interdependence refers to the extent to which completing a new product development task depends on interactions between alliance partners during the various stages of the development process.

name: Process complexity
definition: Process complexity refers to the extent to which the NPD process is technically complicated and requires the broad involvement of different functions.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism refers to the perceived degree of change and unpredictability of the market environment.

name: Expropriation risk
definition: Expropriation risk refers to the extent to which firms' competitive behaviors appear opportunistic or unfair in the industry, which leads to expropriation hazards.

name: Technology leadership
definition: Firms that pioneer the introduction of new technology generations. The authors measure a firm's technology leadership as the time of its entry into a new technology generation relative to its rivals.

name: Component innovation challenge
authors_terms: ["component challenge", "technological challenges in components", "challenges in components"]
definition: The outputs of upstream suppliers serve as inputs to the focal actor; such inputs, which are bundled by the focal actor into its product, are components. The magnitude of a challenge is characterized by the extent to which it requires changes to the current approach to problem solving, so component challenges are the innovation challenges that suppliers must overcome for the focal firm to produce its offer.

name: Complement innovation challenge
authors_terms: ["complement challenge", "technological challenges in complements", "challenges in complements"]
definition: A customer may need to bundle other offers alongside the focal actor's product in order to utilize it; such offers, bundled downstream by the customer, are complements. Greater complement innovation challenges result in delays in the availability of the complement as complementors struggle to overcome their own technology hurdles.

name: Vertical integration
definition: A governance strategy to manage interdependence in the ecosystem; in this setting the variable takes a value of one if the firm produced its own lens component in a given technology generation and zero otherwise.

name: Technology maturity
definition: The number of years that have lapsed since the first commercial sale of a tool in the given technology generation, where the first year of commercial sales is coded as one.

name: Generation market share
authors_terms: ["generation share", "market share in a given technology generation", "firm performance in new technology generations"]
definition: Our dependent variable, generation share, is a firm's market share in a given technology generation in a given year. Industry participants and observers regularly use market share in a generation as a measure of firm success.

name: Acquired firm status
definition: The paper distinguishes inventors from acquired firms from inventors at two control groups: inventors from similar but nonacquired firms and inventors from the acquiring firms. In the regressions, the variable acquired takes a value of 1 for inventors from the acquired firms and 0 otherwise.

name: Postacquisition innovation productivity
definition: The innovation productivity of each inventor was measured using patent data. The dependent variable was the number of successful patent applications filed by an inventor in a given year after acquisition while working for the acquiring firm, observed for five years after an acquisition.

name: Routines overlap
definition: We refer to a firm's routines as its 'higher-order organizing principles' (Kogut & Zander, 1996) and 'knowledge-processing systems' (Lane & Lubatkin, 1998), as determined by the organization's structure, communication channels, and task interdependencies. Similarity in the routines acquired and acquiring firms use to coordinate activities should aid the postacquisition innovation productivity of inventors from the acquired firms.

name: Skills overlap
authors_terms: ["skills overlap", "overlap in skills", "degree of overlap in the skills"]
definition: We consider skills to be the aggregate technical knowledge of the inventors in a firm that manifests itself through research outputs such as patented innovations. Skills overlap is the degree of overlap between the granted and cited patents of an acquired firm and those of its acquiring firm, prior to the acquisition.

name: Acquired firm size relative to acquirer
authors_terms: ["relative size", "size of an acquired firm relative to its acquiring firm", "relative firm size"]
definition: Both agency (Holmstrom, 1989) and property rights (Aghion & Tirole, 1994) theories suggest that small firms are better in creating effort-inducing incentives for their R&D employees, so that the greater the size of a target firm relative to an acquirer, the less the reduction in employee incentives.

name: Contract specificity
authors_terms: ["contract specificity", "specificity of the contract governing the focal context", "highly detailed and specific contracts"]
definition: Throughout this paper, we use the term 'contract specificity' to mean specificity of the contract governing the focal context. Highly detailed and specific contracts 'contain more extensive provisions about the work to be performed, more specific objectives, more explicit monitoring mechanisms, and more highly prescribed penalties for work that does not meet standards or is performed late or over budget' than less detailed and specific contracts.

name: In-context trust
authors_terms: ["in-context trust", "competence-based trust", "confidence the partner will carry out its obligations in that particular context"]
definition: When firms experience consistently reliable performance from a partner, they begin to perceive in-context trust, which reflects confidence the partner will carry out its obligations in that particular context. In this paper trust refers to competence-based trust, positive beliefs about a partner's competency or ability to carry out obligations.

name: Out-of-context trust
authors_terms: ["out-of-context trust", "confidence that a partner will carry out its obligations outside the focal context"]
definition: Out-of-context trust is confidence that a partner will carry out its obligations outside the focal context; since it may not spread to other dimensions of the relationship, it is not likely to be pertinent to contracts those partners craft to govern other exchanges.

name: In-context distrust
definition: Distrust arises from a perception of incongruence between a focal organization's values and those of its partner, and it portends general suspicion that a partner will behave opportunistically. Distrust developed in one context (i.e., in-context distrust) will, at a minimum, increase specificity of the contract governing that context.

name: Out-of-context distrust
authors_terms: ["out-of-context distrust", "distrust that has developed in other exchange contexts of the IOR"]
definition: Because distrust is rooted in value incongruence it more readily generalizes across contexts of the relationship; distrust that has developed in other exchange contexts of the IOR (i.e., out-of-context distrust) will also positively influence contract specificity.

name: Regulatory change
definition: The institutional changes of interest are predominantly regulatory changes that make entrepreneurship a more attractive opportunity through either reducing risks or lowering the requirements needed to engage in such activity.

name: Cognitive support from institutional carriers
authors_terms: ["institutional carriers that can provide cognitive support", "cognitive support", "cognitive institutional carriers"]
definition: Institutional carriers bridge differences across sectors through developing shared knowledge sources that can cognitively support regulatory change. They can narrow the knowledge gaps that can hinder the development of shared understanding (i.e., cognitive basis) around a regulatory change by helping better demonstrate the market relevance of public sector science to potential entrepreneurs in the private sector.

name: Normative support from institutional carriers
authors_terms: ["institutional carriers that can provide normative support", "normative support"]
definition: When institutional carriers can span sectors that could not coordinate otherwise, they can help facilitate the development of agreed upon standards around acceptable business forms, practices, and outputs. Such facilitation helps provide normative support for regulatory change.

name: High-tech founding
definition: Founding as an outcome was the key objective of KIP and is one of the most immediately observable outcomes when institutional systems are reformed to encourage novel activity; all firms founded in the sample were tabulated for each province-year.

name: Local technological development
definition: Locales with less technological development are locales in which entities with technological breakthroughs may not yet adequately exist; before high-tech ventures can be conceived, the locale must first have an adequate knowledge base.

name: Local market development
definition: Locales with more nascent market development likely lack consensus around market standards, so the challenge is how to build the norms that guide how markets leverage knowledge into high-growth entrepreneurship.

name: Local legal development
definition: Less legal development suggests these locales lack formal protections for intellectual property as well as for consumer and producer rights.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence refers to the ability or capacity of the environment to permit organizational growth. Munificence captures the extent to which the environment can provide sustained growth.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Environmental instability refers to the rate of unpredictable change or turnover in those environmental factors pertinent to strategic decision-making. It is defined as the rate of change in factors relevant to strategic decision-making.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity pertains to the heterogeneity in and range of environmental factors that need to be considered in strategic decision-making. For large multi-business firms it can best be conceptualized by the heterogeneity of activities pursued by the firm, given a broad array of product-market environments.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was measured using a three-year average of the firm's Return on Assets (ROA) relative to the industry for the time period 1977-80. ROA is one of the most commonly used accounting based performance measures in the strategy literature.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in the firm's diversification strategy"]
definition: Corporate strategy within large, multibusiness organizations reflects diversification decisions on the mix and emphasis of businesses within the corporate portfolio. Strategic change was operationalized by using change in the firm's diversification strategy from 1977 to 1980.

name: Demographic heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["demographic heterogeneity", "top team demographic heterogeneity", "team demographic heterogeneity"]
definition: An individual's demographic characteristics are indicators of that person's underlying experiences, training, cognitive orientation, attitudes, and perspectives. The two demographic heterogeneity variables selected, reflecting both cohort and cognitive issues, allow a broad assessment of the demographic heterogeneity construct.

name: Top management team turnover
authors_terms: ["top management team turnover", "team turnover", "turnover within the top management team", "top team turnover"]
definition: Turnover within the top management team is defined as the proportion of team members in 1980 who were no longer with the firm in 1983 and were less than 65 years of age in 1983.

name: R&D lab investment
authors_terms: ["R&D lab investment", "lab investment", "R&D laboratory expenditure", "R&D investment"]
definition: Our dependent variable is a firm's R&D lab investment in a given year (in crore, which is equal to 10,000,000 rupees) as reported in DSIR's Annual Report. Free riding has been defined as the ability of a firm to lower its R&D investments by appropriating other firms' investments via inward knowledge spillovers.

name: Domestic intra-industry specialization
authors_terms: ["domestic intra-industry specialization", "same-industry domestic R&D labs", "domestic labs from their industry"]
definition: Our variable of interest is based on the number of domestic R&D labs in the same industry in the same metropolitan area, which comes from the Directory of Recognized In-House R&D Units. This variable captures the degree of industry agglomeration in a metropolitan area; an industry is considered agglomerated in a geographic area to the extent that the concentration of firms in it is higher than what a random distribution across the country would predict.

name: Foreign intra-industry specialization
authors_terms: ["foreign intra-industry specialization", "same-industry foreign R&D labs", "foreign labs from their industry"]
definition: To examine how the presence of foreign-owned labs in a metropolitan area influences R&D lab investment, we create a measure similar to the previous one but for foreign intra-industry specialization (ISFre). We identify foreign firms using Prowess and Internet searches.

name: Domestic interindustry specialization
authors_terms: ["domestic cross-industry specialization", "domestic interindustry specialization", "domestic labs in other industries"]
definition: To account for the presence of domestic R&D labs from industries other than the focal industry of an R&D lab in a metropolitan area, we use domestic cross-industry specialization (CSDrs). A higher value indicates a greater diversity of domestic labs across industries in a particular metropolitan area.

name: Foreign interindustry specialization
authors_terms: ["foreign cross-industry specialization", "foreign interindustry specialization", "foreign labs in other industries"]
definition: To account for the effect of the presence of foreign R&D labs from other industries in a metropolitan area, we use foreign cross-industry specialization (CSFre).

name: Organizational risk
definition: March and Shapira (1992) portrayed risk as performance variability, and strategic management and organization theorists have often depicted risk as volatility of financial performance. The authors used the standard deviation of return on assets as their measure of realized risk.

name: Proximity to bankruptcy
authors_terms: ["proximity to bankruptcy", "distance from bankruptcy", "bankruptcy risk", "Altman's Z", "threat of bankruptcy"]
definition: The degree to which a firm is threatened by bankruptcy, proxied by Altman's (1983) discriminant function measure of bankruptcy risk; the lower the Z, the higher the likelihood of bankruptcy.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspirations", "attainment discrepancy", "distance below aspiration level", "distance above aspiration level", "aspiration levels"]
definition: Managers not focused on survival consider their organizations' positions relative to their aspiration levels, where aspirations are based on the firm's own past performance and on the experiences of reference firms. The difference between performance and aspirations is referred to as attainment discrepancy.

name: Performance-based incentive plans
definition: We focused on the change of incentive plans from those that weakly link short-term individualized contributions with remuneration (e.g., seniority-based pay) to those that tightly link them (i.e., performance-based incentive plans). The renewed plans evaluate individuals' short-term performance based on the achievement of quantifiable outputs relative to targets and recognize individuals' respective contributions.

name: Network closure
authors_terms: ["closed networks", "network constraints", "closed networks with fewer structural holes", "structural holes"]
definition: We focused on whether individuals build closed networks, dense structures with many common third-party ties, or open networks with more structural holes (Burt, 1992). Network constraints capture the extent to which the focal individual i concentrates resources within an interconnected group.

name: Alter expertise similarity
authors_terms: ["similar expertise", "homogeneous networks", "alters' expertise dissimilarity", "knowledge similarity", "networks consisting of alters having similar or dissimilar expertise"]
definition: The content of networks refers to the types of expertise that egos can obtain via network ties with alters (Reagans, Singh, & Krishnan, 2015). Specifically, we focused on whether individuals build networks consisting of alters having similar or dissimilar expertise.

name: Network size
definition: The size of networks refers to the number of alters in an ego's network (Paruchuri, 2010).

name: R&D investment
authors_terms: ["R&D investment", "R&D intensity", "investment in knowledge-based assets", "R&D spending"]
definition: Investment in R&D is one way to maintain a stock of useful knowledge assets, as it generates knowledge-based advantages specialized to a firm's operations. The firm-specific nature of R&D impedes imitation, as it has an important tacit element that is difficult for outsiders to replicate.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Both market-based (Firm value) and accounting-based measures of financial performance (Return on assets) were employed. Stock performance and accounting returns are determined after various stakeholders have had an opportunity to extract above-market returns for their contributions.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Ownership concentration was represented by a dummy variable set equal to '1' when the percentage of shares held by the three largest shareholders is above the sample median. Greater concentration represents more power for the large owners and consequently more influence over strategic decisions.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: Managerial discretion, defined as a manager's latitude of action (Hambrick and Finkelstein, 1987), is generally considered critical in firms relying on knowledge-based assets. TMT equity ownership and CEO duality measure managerial discretion.

name: Regional institutional development
definition: Regional institutional development was captured by the NERI indices based on data from Chinese statistical yearbooks, reports from the administrations of industry and commerce, and surveys. The credit market index and the legal environment index were combined into a composite index, Regional institutional development.

name: Network centrality
definition: Closeness centrality is the focal firm's shortest (geodesic) distance to all other firms within the network. A more central location means that focal firms enjoy greater proximity to all other firms.

name: Ego network density
authors_terms: ["density", "ego network density", "density level of the firm's ego network"]
definition: This measure is the number of actual ties among the focal firm's partners, divided by the total number of potential ties among partners. It is known as ego network density in social network studies, in which it provides a measure of the cohesiveness of subgroups that enables information flows and mutual influence through direct and indirect ties in the ego networks.

name: Repeated partnerships
authors_terms: ["number of partners with repeated ties", "repeated partnerships", "repeated alliances", "strong ties"]
definition: This variable equals the number of direct partners with which a firm had established more than one technology alliance; the number of repeated partners for each firm-year observation derives from the accumulated alliance data.

name: Innovation performance
definition: To measure a firm's innovation performance, this study uses the count of product awards conferred by trade publishers on new products. Award counts also offer a success indicator of the market acceptance of new products by early adopters.

name: R&D investment
definition: A firm's annual R&D expenses indicate the extent of resources committed to maintain and develop new and existing products. This variable therefore proxies a firm's resource position.

name: CEO underpayment
definition: A condition in which the CEO's actual total pay was less than his or her predicted total pay, where predicted pay comes from a CEO wage equation representing the going rate of the executive labor market.

name: CEO overpayment
definition: A condition in which the CEO's actual total pay was greater than his or her predicted total pay, where predicted pay comes from a CEO wage equation representing the going rate of the executive labor market.

name: Change in firm size
authors_terms: ["change in firm size", "firm growth", "increases in firm size"]
definition: Change in firm size is calculated as (size t - size t - 1)/size t - 1, where firm size is a composite index represented by the single factor resulting from a principal components analysis of the natural log of firm sales and the natural log of the number of employees.

name: Voluntary CEO withdrawal
definition: A CEO who resigns the position but retains a director position has likely voluntarily withdrawn from being the CEO; retaining a director position does not represent dismissal.

name: Change in firm profitability
authors_terms: ["change in firm profitability", "change in firm ROA", "increases in firm profits"]
definition: Change in firm profitability is calculated as (ROA t - ROA t - 1)/ROA t - 1, where ROA is the firm's net income divided by total assets for each year.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Managerial capitalist theory suggests that the separation of firm ownership from firm control is the essential factor that affords CEOs discretion, with CEOs in manager-controlled firms having more leeway to pursue managerial objectives than CEOs of owner-controlled firms. Ownership structure is measured with a five percent equity-holding threshold that sorts organizations into manager-controlled, owner-managed (the CEO is the dominant stockholder), and owner-controlled categories.

name: Strength set
authors_terms: ["strength set", "capability strengths", "capability strength set", "set of strengths"]
definition: A set of capabilities whose relative value is above parity with rivals; a capability that is above parity represents a strength for those firms and the degree of strength increases as its relative value continues to increase beyond parity. Firms are conceptualized as bundles of capabilities, so capabilities individually identified as strengths form sets of capability strengths.

name: Weakness set
authors_terms: ["weakness set", "capability weaknesses", "capability weakness set", "set of weaknesses"]
definition: A weakness exists when a capability's relative value is below parity with rivals, and the degree of weakness increases as its relative value continues to decline further below parity. In total, when the value of a firm's capability is below parity, it is a weakness and the disadvantage associated with that weakness increases as its value decreases.

name: Relative performance
definition: The empirical correlate of competitive advantage; because the theory pertained to competitive advantage, a relative construct, the authors used a relative performance measure based on firm value-added centered within industries.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence refers to 'the scarcity or abundance of critical resources needed by (one or more) firms operating within an environment' (Castrogiovanni, 1991: 542).

name: Prior performance
definition: Higher prior performance provides an asymmetric source of firm-specific resources with which to enhance the firm's set of strengths and/or reduce its set of weaknesses; it is proxied by the firm's return on assets for the year of the first survey.

name: Strength set change
authors_terms: ["strength set change", "change in firms' strength sets over time"]
definition: The difference between the strength set at the time of the second survey and the strength set at the time of the first survey.

name: Weakness set change
authors_terms: ["weakness set change", "change in firms' weakness sets over time"]
definition: The difference between the weakness set at the time of the second survey and the weakness set at the time of the first survey.

name: CEO rewards
definition: The rewards paid to a firm's chief executive officer, which shareholders weigh against firm performance. An agency loss manifests when CEO rewards are high in the face of poor firm performance.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of the firm, which shareholders must examine to determine whether the CEO has earned his or her pay. In this study it is captured as shareholder return relative to a reference benchmark.

name: Shareholder vote to approve CEO pay
authors_terms: ["probability of approval", "vote to approve CEO pay", "say-on-pay vote", "approval"]
definition: The probability that a shareholder votes to approve, rather than reject, the compensation of the CEO in the scenario presented.

name: Agency-normative assessment
definition: The extent to which shareholders judge CEO pay to be justified, given firm performance. It reflects the degree to which shareholders believe CEO pay conforms to the normative prescriptions of agency theory.

name: Firm exit
definition: The variable that interests us is the time elapsed between the moment a firm is created and the moment it exits. Our indicator variable is a dummy that takes the value 1 if the firm exits in that year, and 0 otherwise.

name: Immigrant ownership
definition: We define a firm as immigrant-owned if all of its owners are immigrants. Immigrant is thus a dummy variable taking the value 1 for such firms, and 0 otherwise.

name: Institutional distance between home and host country
definition: Both formal and informal institutions create differences in the LOF that immigrants from different countries are confronted with. Formal institutions include property rights, constitutions, and laws, while informal institutions consist of sanctions, taboos, customs, traditions, and codes of conduct.

name: Host country work experience
authors_terms: ["host country work experience", "local labor market experience", "experience in the host country"]
definition: The work experience of immigrants in the host country helps to dissipate the LOF of individuals and helps them to integrate into the host economy. Local labor market experience is measured by the years that an individual was in the host country labor market before creating a particular firm.

name: National community size
authors_terms: ["Community size", "size of the national community", "size of the community"]
definition: The size of the community is relevant because larger communities can provide more diversified sources of resources and markets that can economically sustain firms from their co-members. Our measure of Community size is the absolute number of people sharing the same nationality that works in firms located in the same county (concelho) as the firm.

name: Female board representation
authors_terms: ["female representation on a board of directors", "female board representation", "women on corporate boards", "gender diversity on boards"]
definition: Whether a firm's board of directors includes at least one woman; the central research question concerned differentiating firms with female representation from those without it.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["organizational size", "firm size", "larger and more visible organizations"]
definition: The size of the organization, which determines its visibility to the public and the societal pressure it faces to conform to expectations for gender diversity.

name: Industry female employment base
authors_terms: ["industry female employment", "industry labor force", "industries with greater female employment bases", "degree of dependence on females in the labor pool"]
definition: The share of women in an industry's employment base, reflecting how much the industry depends on females in the labor pool.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: The firm's corporate strategy in terms of the number of product-market environments in which it operates, which shapes its scope of environmental dependencies.

name: Links to firms with female directors
authors_terms: ["network effects", "outside female director links", "linkages to other boards with women directors"]
definition: The number of linkages a firm has through its directors to other firms whose boards include women directors.

name: Responsiveness to accreditation standards
authors_terms: ["responsiveness to the new accreditation standards", "responsiveness of an unaccredited business school to the change in AACSB accreditation standards", "responsiveness to change in AACSB accreditation standards"]
definition: The authors use the term "responsiveness of an unaccredited business school to the change in AACSB accreditation standards" to describe the extent to which a previously unaccredited school engaged in the steps of seeking accreditation. A school's representatives typically take several steps when seeking accreditation: possible attendance at a workshop on the new accreditation standards, conducting internal fact finding about the feasibility of accreditation, entering precandidacy, filing a letter of intent to seek accreditation, and hosting a final accreditation site visit.

name: Share of business students
authors_terms: ["higher percentages of business students in a college or university", "percentage of business students", "large proportion of business students"]
definition: The potential economic value of accreditation is related to the number of resource providers who value it, and is therefore higher for schools with a large proportion of business students than for schools with only a small proportion of business students. The greater the potential economic resources to be derived from accreditation, the more likely a school is to seek it.

name: Share of out-of-state students
authors_terms: ["percentage of out-of-state students", "higher proportions of out-of-state students in a college or university"]
definition: The percentage of out-of-state students is an important indicator of a school's dependence on a geographically broad pool of students who are likely to use accreditation in their decision making; the higher it is, the more the school draws on a national rather than a local population of prospective students.

name: Tuition level
authors_terms: ["higher levels of tuition at a college or university", "annual tuition"]
definition: Schools are likely to experience strong pressures for accreditation when they depend on students who desire a prestigious (and typically costly) education, and conformance to AACSB standards is likely to increase costs and therefore tuition. The authors describe schools with higher tuition as operating in a high-prestige, high-cost market niche.

name: Admissions selectivity
authors_terms: ["selectivity in a college or university's admissions", "selectivity", "rejection rate"]
definition: The authors argue that schools depending on students who desire a prestigious (and typically costly) education and a select group of peers are likely to experience strong pressures for accreditation. Selectivity is assessed by the rate at which applicants are rejected.

name: Dean's prior experience at an accredited school
authors_terms: ["prior employment of an unaccredited business school's dean (or of the head of a business department) in an accredited business school", "dean experienced in accredited school", "dean's prior employment by an accredited school"]
definition: Deans of unaccredited schools who have had prior experience at an accredited business school may be familiar with the benefits of accreditation and may encourage their current schools to seek accreditation; deans are particularly likely to serve as agents of diffusion of accreditation practices.

name: AACSB membership
authors_terms: ["membership in the AACSB", "member of AACSB", "belong to the AACSB"]
definition: Unaccredited schools that belong to the AACSB are likely to be exposed to substantial information about how to seek accreditation and are also likely to be subject to social pressures to become accredited.

name: Number of accreditations held by other units
authors_terms: ["higher numbers of accreditations held by other units in a college or university", "number of accreditations"]
definition: The number of accreditations held by other units in a college or university may indicate both local norms about accreditation and the existence of coercive pressure from the central administration to become accredited.

name: Public control
definition: The authors argue that private organizations are more like market organizations and public organizations are more like nonmarket organizations, and that conformity to institutionalized practices is more consistent with the mission and goals of public organizations than those of private organizations.

name: Corporate political investments
authors_terms: ["corporate political investments", "CPI", "political investments", "corporate political activity", "lobbying and campaigns"]
definition: Firms invest in lobbying, PAC contributions, soft money contributions (legal until 2003), and contributions to 527 groups.

name: Cumulative corporate political investments
definition: Cumulative CPI is the firm's cumulative spending on PAC, lobbying, soft money, and 527 groups across sample years. The measure reflects the current year's CPI plus the previous years' CPI.

name: Board political service
authors_terms: ["board political service", "political service", "personal service", "politically tied directors", "former public officials serving as directors"]
definition: A form of CPA that may add value to a firm is the hiring of former public officials as directors, a practice that has been termed 'personal service' (Hillman et al., 1999), we call it here 'political service.'

name: Industry regulation
definition: Regulation, the limitations on firm behaviors placed by governments (i.e., via regulatory agencies), has long been cited as an impetus for CPA.

name: Corporate financial performance
authors_terms: ["corporate financial performance", "firm financial performance", "market value", "market performance", "return on sales", "ROS", "accounting performance"]
definition: We use two complementary measures of firm performance: (1) market value (dollar value of firms' equity at the end of the firm's calendar year); and (2) ROS (net income before extraordinary items to total revenue).

name: Executive home country
definition: The authors argue that executives' strategic orientations are affected by their cultural heritage, national policies and institutions, and that executives from different countries will therefore exhibit differences in their use of objective information in making decisions.

name: Emphasis on objective decision criteria
authors_terms: ["criteria used in strategic decisions", "objective criteria", "decision criteria"]
definition: Objective criteria employed by executives to evaluate the attractiveness of target firms in strategic decisions; the criteria were developed from a survey of the literature and recommendations from academic 'experts'.

name: Industry attractiveness
definition: Attractiveness of the target firm's industry as one of the objective criteria on which executives evaluate the merits of an acquisition opportunity.

name: Emphasis on growth criteria
authors_terms: ["objective criteria associated with growth", "sales and market share", "growth"]
definition: Weight that executives place on the objective criteria associated with growth, namely sales and market share, when making strategic decisions.

name: Emphasis on profitability criteria
authors_terms: ["objective criteria that focus on returns or profitability", "ROI, stock price, discounted cash flow, and projected demand"]
definition: Weight that executives place on the objective criteria that focus on returns or profitability (ROI, stock price, discounted cash flow and projected demand) when making strategic decisions.

name: Emphasis on manufacturing and R&D capabilities
authors_terms: ["objective criteria associated with manufacturing and R&D capabilities", "manufacturing ability", "R&D ability"]
definition: Weight that executives place on the objective criteria associated with manufacturing and R&D capabilities when making strategic decisions.

name: Emphasis on managerial capabilities
authors_terms: ["objective criteria representing managerial capabilities", "management talent", "managerial capabilities"]
definition: Weight that executives place on the objective criteria representing managerial capabilities when making strategic decisions; the authors argue that the individualistic heritage of U.S. executives makes them sensitive to managerial capabilities.

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence is the 'overestimation of one's actual ability, performance, level of control, or chance for success.' The authors focus on overconfidence rather than hubris because their theorizing does not require the 'pride' aspect of hubris.

name: Board expertise
authors_terms: ["board expertise", "heterogeneous expertise with breakthrough innovations", "board expertise with breakthrough innovations"]
definition: Board expertise reflects directors' knowledge and understanding of a specific domain gained through their experiences. The authors focus on directors' heterogeneous expertise with breakthrough innovations, gained through their experiences at other firms that previously conducted these innovations.

name: Board power
definition: Board relative power is the ability of boards to influence and constrain the decision-making of CEOs by blocking or even sanctioning their actions; board power may stem from multiple sources, including structural or ownership power.

name: Breakthrough innovation
definition: Breakthrough innovations represent a subset of innovations that replace existing technologies and thus serve as the basis for new technological paradigms; they refer to the most valuable types of innovations (i.e., reflected in the top 1% of the most cited patents) and enable firms to shape the competitive landscape.

name: De novo entry
authors_terms: ["de novo entry", "entry by de novo (entrepreneurial) firms", "De Novo Entrants", "entrepreneurial entrants"]
definition: De novo firms are entrepreneurial start-ups; their identity is often highly aligned with the emerging industry, and their attention and resources are dedicated only to the emerging market. Following prior work that designates new firms to be those 6-8 years old, firms founded after 1994 are treated as new entrants.

name: De alio entry
authors_terms: ["de alio entry", "entry by de alio (diversifying incumbent) firms", "De Alio Entrants", "diversifying incumbents"]
