definition: Diversifying incumbents are 'firms that already existed before entering the focal industry' (Ganco and Agarwal, 2009: 229). De alio firm identity is primarily derived from activities outside the focal market.

name: Economic conditions
definition: For de novo firms, the economic munificence of an emerging industry is a critical consideration; for de alio firms, positive economic conditions represent opportunity for diversification and reduce the uncertainty of entering new markets.

name: Regulatory policies
definition: The state may issue regulatory policies that mandate or forbid the use of specific products; such policies mandating the adoption of an industry's products create regulative legitimacy for the industry.

name: Economic incentive policies
definition: As an alternative to regulatory mandates, the state can influence entry through providing economic incentive policies, such as tax breaks, for adoption of products and services.

name: Collective action
definition: Social movements are 'organized collective endeavors to solve social problems' and are often enacted through social movement organizations, which are 'complex, or formal, organizations which identify their goals with the preferences of a social movement or a countermovement and attempt to implement those goals.'

name: Environmental social norms
authors_terms: ["social norms", "environmental social norms", "social norm of environmentalism"]
definition: Social norms are defined as the unwritten rules of conduct of a group (Elster, 1989); the authors define the sociocultural environment as the beliefs and attitudes that actors in a region hold toward the moral correctness of specific activities, aligned with Scott's normative pillar of legitimacy.

name: Defensive response
definition: A response set composed exclusively of defensive actions, which are attempts, made after the loss of two or more employees to the same firm, to decrease the effectiveness of future hiring attempts by both that firm and others without directly, negatively impacting the hiring firm.

name: Defensive-retaliatory response
definition: A response set that combines defensive and retaliatory actions. A retaliatory action involves threatening or harming a rival in reaction to its hiring actions and is explicitly directed at the firm that hired the former employees; a purely retaliatory response is unlikely to be observed.

name: Product-market overlap
definition: The greater the similarity of the markets in which firms compete, the greater the rivalry between the firms. Product-market competitors are defined as firms selling similar goods and services serving similar functions to similar users.

name: Nonlocal labor market status
authors_terms: ["nonlocal labor market status", "nonlocal labor market competitor", "nonlabor market competitor"]
definition: Nonlocal labor market competitors were defined as the set of firms more than 90 minutes away by car from the focal firm. Competitors for talent located outside of a target firm's local labor market present a unique threat.

name: Value of human capital
authors_terms: ["value of targeted human capital", "value of human capital", "human capital value"]
definition: The greater the value-creating capability of the employees targeted by a labor market rival, the greater the threat to the target firm's value-creating capabilities. A key component of utility formulae is 'SDy,' the dollar value to an employing organization of a one-standard-deviation improvement in the job performance criterion of an individual in a certain job.

name: Transferability of human capital
definition: Human capital can be decomposed into that which is valuable to a specific employer and that which has value in the broader labor market, a continuum of usefulness Stevens (1994) dubbed 'transferability' and Trevor (2001) called 'movement capital.'

name: Formal internal labor market
authors_terms: ["formal ILM", "formal rules of insider succession", "internal labor markets for CEOs", "formal designation of executives as directors and as president, chief operating officer, or vice chairman"]
definition: An important aspect of the formalization of the succession process is the creation and reliance on internal labor markets (ILMs) for top management executives, including the CEO; this internal market for CEOs is characterized by promotion from within, the salience of formal job titles and career ladders, and a reliance on and rigidity of formal rules and procedures for decision making.

name: Prevalence of formal internal labor markets
authors_terms: ["proportion of years with ILM", "past prevalence of formal internal labor markets"]
definition: The effect of rules may increase with their use; the greater the prevalence of formal rules, the more these rules will become institutionalized and the greater their effect.

name: Insider CEO succession
definition: Employees of the company are coded as insiders if they had been employees of the company for at least two years prior to becoming CEO; outside members of the board of directors who were appointed as CEOs were not classified as insiders.

name: Outsider CEO succession
definition: CEOs who had not been employees of the company for at least two years prior to becoming CEO are classified as outsiders; outsiders are sometimes appointed to the corporation for a short period of time in preparation for becoming CEOs.

name: Founder CEO
definition: CEOs of new companies were classified as founders. For founders, the power of the executive is more closely tied to his or her personal power and charismatic authority, rather than to the authority invested in the position, and no historical precedents of CEO succession are available.

name: Precedents of insider succession
authors_terms: ["past insiders", "past reliance on insider succession", "informal precedents of insider succession"]
definition: Past insiders is the category of past succession experience when all CEOs since 1950, other than the founder, were insiders; it measures reliance on informal rules of CEO succession.

name: Precedents of outsider succession
authors_terms: ["past outsiders", "past reliance on outsider succession", "informal precedents of outsider succession"]
definition: Past outsiders is the category of past succession experience when all CEOs since 1950, other than the founder, were outsiders; it measures reliance on informal rules of CEO succession.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age was calculated from the date given in Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors of the year of the firm's initial founding or incorporation; reliance on rules is expected to increase with the age of the organization.

name: CEO year of hire
definition: Historical effects on succession are best captured through the year of hire of the incumbent CEO: CEOs are affected by changing rules and expectations about CEO succession that were prevalent in the broader institutional context during the beginning of their tenure, and these rules are imprinted for the remainder of their tenure.

name: Firm performance
definition: Under theories of bounded rationality, reliance on rules, programs, and routines is contingent on favorable economic performance, and organizations will undertake failure-induced changes in rules when performance is poor; performance is measured as return on assets adjusted for industry average.

name: Founder tenure
authors_terms: ["founder tenure", "social and economic capital of founders"]
definition: The power of founders may increase from their social and economic capital, as measured by founder tenure.

name: CEO retirement age
authors_terms: ["retirement age", "CEOs facing retirement age", "late CEO departures"]
definition: Following Puffer and Weintrop (1991), retirement age is classified as 64 years old or over; the determinants of CEO succession and selection are argued to vary for CEOs facing retirement and for younger executives.

name: Proportion of outside directors
definition: The proportion of outside directors was estimated as the number of outside board members divided by the total number of directors; both agency theory and structural perspectives emphasize the relative roles of inside and outside directors in shaping the outcomes of corporate governance.

name: Strategic group membership
authors_terms: ["strategic group membership", "group membership", "membership within a particular group", "membership in a strategic group"]
definition: Strategic groups are bound by mobility barriers and contain firms that are similar to one another but different from those outside the group on key strategic dimensions. Sunk costs and differences in technology create differences in resource endowments and serve as mobility barriers that enable the existence of two separate groups.

name: Cointegration among member strategies
definition: The presence of cointegration among the strategy variables means that they display a long-run equilibrium-type relationship within the group, and do not stray far from this equilibrium. It suggests that within a group these strategies exhibit interdependence in the long run.

name: Equilibrium error
authors_terms: ["deviation from the long-run equilibrium", "equilibrium error", "departure from the group equilibrium", "deviation from equilibrium"]
definition: Members make adjustment to their strategies based on the anticipated and actual changes in strategies made by their peers, and their own departure from the group equilibrium. The behaviour of the equilibrium error (that is, Pa - Pb) is such that the error should revert to the mean.

name: Speed of adjustment
authors_terms: ["speed of adjustment parameter", "adjustment parameter", "error correction", "converging or diverging behavior"]
definition: Consider a situation in which the firm recognizes that its current size is above the equilibrium level. If the reaction by the firm is to reduce its size in the following periods, then the firm is converging back towards the equilibrium and this will produce a negative estimate of alpha; a positive alpha indicates that a firm is referencing its peers and yet diverges from the reference.

name: Cost efficiency
definition: 'Cost efficiency,' an important measure of a cost leadership approach (Porter, 1980), was assessed by calculating the ratio of cost of goods sold to total sales.

name: Capital expenditures
definition: 'Capital expenditures' and 'capital intensity' provide a measure of a firm's asset parsimony dimension (Hambrick, 1983); these two variables indicate a firm's commitment to employ technology to improve productivity and quality.

name: Capital intensity
definition: 'Capital expenditures' and 'capital intensity' provide a measure of a firm's asset parsimony dimension (Hambrick, 1983); these two variables indicate a firm's commitment to employ technology to improve productivity and quality.

name: Export intensity
definition: 'Exports' is operationalized as the percentage of foreign sales to total sales for the firm.

name: Firm size
definition: We assessed size as the number of employees on the firm's payroll for each year.

name: Violation type
authors_terms: ["violation type", "letter violations", "spirit violations", "letter versus spirit contract violations"]
definition: We define letter violations as the failure to fulfill a clear, documented expectation expressed in the contract, and we define spirit violations as the failure to fulfill an undocumented, yet still presumably tacitly agreed upon, expectation.

name: Perceived intentionality
definition: Perceptions of intentionality are the key mechanism the authors identify as driving potential differences in how letter versus spirit violations are interpreted; they are based on a variety of considerations, such as the surrounding context and inferences about the counterpart's actions and possible motives.

name: Trust
definition: Trusting intentions concern the violated party's willingness to make themselves vulnerable to their counterpart again in the presence of risk.

name: Initial trust
definition: The trust a party holds in a counterpart in a newly formed relationship before any violation occurs; the control perspective assumes initial trust may be quite low, whereas the coordination perspective assumes it is typically high.

name: Willingness to punish
definition: The violated party's behavioral response to a violation, reflecting the extent to which they sanction the violator by withholding resources or by taking legal action.

name: Contract complexity
definition: The comprehensiveness of a contract: increasing the comprehensiveness of contracts has the potential not only to improve clarity, but also to increase complexity, which may make it more difficult to understand what one needs to do in order to fulfill their responsibilities.

name: Alliance formation
definition: Alliance formation represents events in which an alliance did not exist between a pair of firms one year and existed the following year (l_ijt = 0 and l_ij,t+1 = 1). Because the dependent variable is symmetric for each pair of firms, the unit of analysis is the nondirectional dyad.

name: Alliance cospecialization
definition: Alliances differ on the intensity or strength of interorganizational dependence and, more particularly, on their levels of relation-specific investment (cospecialization) and sensitive knowledge sharing. Cospecialized alliances involve investments in partner-specific assets and activities and sharing of sensitive or proprietary knowledge, whereas nonspecialized alliances entail less mutual dependence and lower risk of leakage.

name: Rivals' cospecialized alliances with a potential partner
authors_terms: ["Rivals' cospecialized partner", "cospecialized alliances between rivals and potential partners"]
definition: Whether a potential partner already has cospecialized alliance relations with the rivals of the other potential partner, aggregated over all possible third parties and weighted by the percentage of total third-party revenues each third party accounts for.

name: Rivals' nonspecialized alliances with a potential partner
authors_terms: ["Rivals' nonspecialized partner", "nonspecialized alliances between rivals and potential partners"]
definition: Whether a potential partner already has nonspecialized alliance relations with the rivals of the other potential partner, aggregated over all possible third parties and weighted by the percentage of total third-party revenues each third party accounts for.

name: Cospecialized alliances among rivals
definition: Whether the respective rivals of two potential partners maintain cospecialized alliances, measured as the sum of the number of such alliances weighted by the competitive relations of those rival firms with the potential partners and by the combined revenues of both members of the rival alliances.

name: Nonspecialized alliances among rivals
definition: Whether the respective rivals of two potential partners maintain nonspecialized alliances, measured as the sum of the number of such alliances weighted by the competitive relations of those rival firms with the potential partners and by the combined revenues of both members of the rival alliances.

name: Common rivals
definition: Whether potential partners have competitive relations with third-party rivals that are more intense than the competitive relations with each other; the variable is the sum of the combined competitive ties to common rivals, provided those ties are greater than those linking the pair to each other, weighted by the revenues of those common rivals.

name: Nonprofit interlocks
authors_terms: ["nonprofit interlocks", "nonprofit board interlocks", "board interlocks with nonprofit organizations"]
definition: Nonprofit interlocks are corporate directors simultaneously sitting on the boards of nonprofit organizations. The measure focuses on the extent of a firm's board interlocks with nonprofit organizations.

name: Investment in intangible assets
authors_terms: ["investment in intangible assets", "Intangible Asset Investment", "intangible asset investment"]
definition: Examples of intangible assets include such valuable resources as firm reputation, brand image, and organizational knowledge; because of their firm-specificity and causal ambiguity they are considered one of the primary sources of competitive advantage. The authors examine two forms of investment in intangible assets for which data are publicly available: research and development intensity and advertising intensity.

name: Director power
definition: Power is 'the capacity of individual actors to exert their will' (Finkelstein, 1992: 506). A director who is powerful on the focal board has a greater capacity to exert his or her will on that board.

name: Industry mimetic pressures
authors_terms: ["mimetic pressures", "Industry Intangible Asset Investment", "mimetic pressures in the focal organization's field"]
definition: Organizations face constant mimetic pressure to conform to industry norms, with industry tendencies creating a potent mimetic force. Mimetic isomorphism occurs when an organization models its behavior or structure on other similar organizations as a way to reduce uncertainty in its environment.

name: Family ownership
authors_terms: ["family ownership", "family firms", "family influence", "minority family ownership", "majority family ownership"]
definition: We designate 'family firms' as businesses in which a single family has an ownership stake of at least five percent. Firms are then classified as non-family (less than 5 percent family ownership), family-minority interest (largest family ownership position at least 5 percent and no more than 50 percent) and family-majority interest (largest family ownership position 50 percent or higher).

name: New technology adoption
definition: These sources provide a suitable proxy by reporting the percentage of a firm's basic subscribers who choose to receive expanded basic service that increases the number of channels from around 13 to over 50. We use this percentage as the dependent variable, new technology adoption.

name: Performance improvements
definition: Cable operators were focused on revenue growth during the study period, so we have defined performance improvements as the year-to-year change in revenue for each firm.

name: Level of competition
definition: Conceptually, the threat of competition for cable companies therefore depends on the number of channels a potential cable subscriber could receive using a regular antenna. Markets with more free stations available to viewers posed a greater threat of competition to cable firms.

name: Sensegiving intensity
definition: Intensity is defined as the frequency with which an organization undertakes sensegiving activities.

name: Sensegiving diversity
definition: Sensegiving diversity is defined as the extent to which an organization uses different types of communications.

name: Industry media attention
authors_terms: ["industry media attention", "level of industry media attention", "attention from specialized industry media"]
definition: Attention from specialized industry media, which cater to smaller audiences with special interests and expertise and focus on the specifics of the technologies and organizations developing them; the authors measure it using articles categorized under 'Industry News.'

name: General media attention
authors_terms: ["general media attention", "level of general media attention", "attention from the general media"]
definition: Attention from general media outlets, which target the broadest audiences possible and seek high levels of circulation as they compete on the basis of scale; the authors measure it using articles categorized under 'Magazines and Journals' and 'Newspapers.'

name: Founders' start-up experience
definition: Founder's start-up experience is likely to alleviate journalists' concerns regarding the potential of a new organization because it indicates that the founders possess the general organizational knowledge needed to create and manage a viable organization.

name: TMT industry experience
authors_terms: ["TMT industry experience", "TMT members' industry experience", "top management team industry experience"]
definition: TMT industry experience indicates the possession of specialized technical knowledge and skills. Specifically, having worked for a major firm in the industry provides evidence that a TMT member possesses the relevant knowledge and skills to manage the new product development activities and to navigate the dynamic industry environment.

name: Level of VC funding
authors_terms: ["level of VC funding", "level of VC funding obtained", "VC funding obtained"]
definition: The level of VC funding obtained by each start-up was measured at the time of the first round of VC investment. Specifically, the authors used the total amount of investments made by all VCs participating in the first round of a focal start-up's funding, as reported in the VentureXpert database.

name: Causal ambiguity
authors_terms: ["causal ambiguity", "ambiguity about the causal structure", "level of causal ambiguity"]
definition: Ambiguity about the causal structure that relates control variables to performance outcomes, contingent on state and environmental variables; the level of causal ambiguity refers to the number of distributions that are not ruled out by one's knowledge of the situation.

name: Available financial resources
definition: A firm's liquid resources uncommitted to liabilities in the near future, reflecting the extent to which the sum of cash and marketable securities for the year covers current liability obligations.

name: Cost of a trial
authors_terms: ["costs of a trial", "sunk costs", "start-up cost of draws"]
definition: For each "draw" or "trial" resulting in firm performance, the decision maker incurs nonrecoverable sunk costs, such as the costs of learning about the domain, establishing a product identity and opening distribution channels.

name: Risk aversion
definition: The decision maker's aversion to high cost/high return trials, which leads him to engage in more trials of an incidental nature.

name: Experimental diversification
authors_terms: ["experimental diversification", "trials", "draws", "diversification rate", "rate of new business starts", "speed of diversification events"]
definition: Acts of diversification representing a firm's search for the most profitable use of its resources, modelled as the instantaneous rate of new business starts within existing firms.

name: Causal understanding
authors_terms: ["causal understanding", "general understanding of the firm's causal structure"]
definition: The decision maker's understanding of the causal structure of his firm, which he learns about with experience and which may be increased by the elimination of distributions from his causal map.

name: Firm age
definition: The time elapsed since the firm's inception, calculated from the month and year in which the firm was founded or, if that date was not provided, from the date of firm incorporation.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "sales revenue", "net income", "change in sales revenue", "change in net income", "total outcome of all prior draws", "outcome of the prior draw"]
definition: Firm performance measured in two types (revenues and net income) and in two forms (absolute levels and annual fluctuations); change in performance indicators and absolute levels of performance may both motivate firm responses.

name: Retention of a prior draw
authors_terms: ["keep a draw", "retain the draw", "keep decision", "multiple keeps"]
definition: The decision to keep a previously drawn business: as long as the immediate change in the firm's total profitability after the draw is positive, the decision maker will retain the draw, even when its incremental profitability is below his expectations.

name: Formal strategic planning
authors_terms: ["formal strategic planning", "strategic planning", "extent of formal planning", "comprehensiveness", "formality"]
definition: Formal strategic planning comprises the basic tools, techniques, and activities of formal planning, i.e., systematic intelligence-gathering, market research, SWOT analysis, portfolio analysis, mathematical and computer modeling, formal planning meetings, and written long-range plans. It is measured as the extent of formal planning.

name: Profitability
definition: The dependent variable, profitability over a 3 year period, was measured subjectively, but the convergent validity between subjective and objective measures was established.

name: Strategic planning dissemination
authors_terms: ["planning equilibrium", "planning disequilibrium", "strategic planning factor market imperfections", "dissemination of strategic planning"]
definition: In industries where strategic planning has become widely disseminated a condition approximating 'planning equilibrium' exists, while 'planning disequilibrium' industries are those where formal strategic planning is imperfectly disseminated because dissemination has been impeded, for example by a powerful nonplanning bias or tradition.

name: Agent commitment to the firm
authors_terms: ["agent commitment", "commitment", "attitudinal commitment", "organizational commitment", "commitment of the agent to the insurer"]
definition: We therefore define commitment on the basis of an individual's emotional attachment and sense of loyalty and obligation to an organization.

name: Relation-specific investments by the agent
authors_terms: ["idiosyncratic investments", "idiosyncratic investments by agents", "firm-specific investments", "relation-specific investments"]
definition: Idiosyncratic investments involve the deployment of resources in a relation-specific manner and have a tendency to promote unity and mutuality in the relationship.

name: Relation-specific investments by the firm in the agent
authors_terms: ["idiosyncratic investments by the firm", "insurer's idiosyncratic investments in the relationship", "firm-specific human capital"]
definition: In encouraging firm specificity, the firm may deploy its resources in a highly relation-specific manner as well, binding itself to the agent.

name: Generalized investments in human capital
authors_terms: ["generalized investments", "general investments", "general investments made by firms in the externalized employee", "general skill development"]
definition: General resources (e.g. general management skills and interpersonal skills), on the other hand, are deployable in various firms or contexts.

name: Agent performance for the insurer
authors_terms: ["agent performance for the insurer", "indicators of agent performance"]
definition: We will examine two general indicators of agent performance available to us in this context: a) the insurer's level of satisfaction with the agent (insurer-reported) and b) the insurer's expected future benefits from maintaining this agent (insurer-reported).

name: Accounting system
definition: An accounting system comprises 'the methods by which financial data about a firm or its activity are collected, processed, stored and/or distributed' (Bruns, 1968: 470).

name: Policies and procedures
authors_terms: ["policies and procedures", "clarity of policies and procedures", "written policies"]
definition: A company with clearer policies and procedures has clear divisions of responsibility, communications geared toward company-wide understanding of policies and procedures, a required management program that reinforces the importance of key policies, procedures and systems, and a company-wide program designed to identify, analyze, and address basic problems in the workplace.

name: Code of conduct
definition: A code of conduct is a policy or procedure that is specifically targeted to reduce unethical behavior.

name: Formal communication
definition: Communication can occur on a formal basis, with the intention to communicate about certain topics; these are often occasions arranged by the organization, for example a training event involving geographically dispersed employees, a job rotation program, or several employees whose job it is to compare divisions and transfer methods and practices throughout the organization.

name: Informal communication
definition: Communication can also be informal or ad hoc, outside of the company's express purpose, such as at a training event during a break or at a team meeting; lateral relations consist of joint work in teams, task forces and meetings.

name: Employee screening
definition: White-collar crime reduction should begin with the careful screening of potential employees; a potential employee's former employment, educational record, financial situation, and criminal record can all be checked, and such an exercise can reveal 'red flags'.

name: Employee contingent pay
authors_terms: ["employee contingent pay", "contingent pay for employees", "performance-based pay"]
definition: Mutual monitoring can be encouraged through gainsharing programs, and reward systems can be structured so that the acts of individuals in the group threaten all group members; the variable is focused on 'all employees,' not the CEO or top management team alone.

name: White-collar crime
definition: Crimes were identified from articles announcing economic crime within the firm; articles were eliminated if they did not discuss economic crime within the firm, dealt with an economic crime committed outside the United States or by a foreign firm within the United States, or discussed economic crime in private firms.

name: Exploration via internal organization
authors_terms: ["internal organization exploration", "exploration in the internal organization mode"]
definition: In the internal organization mode, a firm exploits by relying on its established knowledge to introduce refined versions of existing products or instead explores by introducing completely new products based on its new designs and recently developed knowledge.

name: Exploration via alliances
definition: Upstream alliances in the software industry entail moving beyond the firm's knowledge base and developing new products that integrate its partners' knowledge, thus representing exploration.

name: Exploration via acquisitions
definition: Acquiring a business that is less related to the firm's current business is indicative of exploration because it expands the scope of the firm's knowledge base and product offering.

name: Balance within a mode
authors_terms: ["balance within modes", "balancing exploration and exploitation within a mode of operation"]
definition: A firm that balances exploration and exploitation within a mode simultaneously relies on both types of routines, which induces organizational tension, complexity, and coordination challenges that can undermine performance.

name: Balance across modes
authors_terms: ["balance across modes", "balancing exploration and exploitation across modes of operation"]
definition: A firm that balances exploration and exploitation across distinct modes, i.e., explores in one mode while exploiting in another, can enjoy the complementary benefits of exploration and exploitation, thus improving productivity while ensuring adaptability.

name: Firm performance
definition: A function of market value that represents investors' ex ante expectations about a firm's future performance, thus capturing the outcomes of exploration and exploitation via alternative modes of operation.

name: Academic entrepreneur presence
definition: Scientists who were previously NIH-supported biomedical researchers at universities and other nonprofit research institutions and who subsequently served as the commercialization project leaders at an NIH SBIR firm.

name: Scientifically oriented human capital
authors_terms: ["scientifically oriented human capital", "research productivity", "scientifically oriented academic human capital", "scientific component of an academic scientist's human capital"]
definition: Human capital developed by scientists who focus on identifying, evaluating and exploiting scientific opportunities, reflected in their success at obtaining NIH research funding. This measure captures the degree to which the scientist is successful at engaging in 'large-scale' laboratory science because the NIH grant approval system acts as a peer review filter for scientific significance.

name: Commercially oriented human capital
authors_terms: ["commercially oriented human capital", "patent productivity", "commercial component of an academic scientist's human capital"]
definition: Human capital developed by scientists who put more emphasis on identifying, evaluating and exploring commercial opportunities, reflected in the patenting of their research portfolio. It captures the success of individual scientists at identifying and exploring commercial opportunities because the U.S. patent approval system acts as a filter for expected commercial potential.

name: Research task performance
authors_terms: ["research performance", "performance of research-oriented tasks", "successful completion of Phase I", "competence at research-oriented tasks"]
definition: The firm's success at research-oriented tasks, indicated by successfully completing Phase I of the SBIR program by winning a Phase II award, which shows that the firm is good at completing academic-style proof-of-concept studies.

name: Invention task performance
authors_terms: ["invention performance", "performance of invention-oriented tasks", "successful patenting", "competence at invention-oriented tasks"]
definition: The firm's success at invention-oriented tasks, indicated by successful patenting at the firm.

name: Exposure to war
definition: External threats can be general and commonly experienced across entities, or specific to a particular entity; exposure refers to the latter, that is, the extent to which an external threat is experienced proximally.

name: At-risk resources
definition: The value of an MNE's global portfolio in the host country that would be extremely hard to replace if damaged. The authors conceptualize at-risk resources as the value of a focal subsidiary in terms of its 'replacement options' within the MNE's portfolio of subsidiaries.

name: Resilience
definition: Resilience refers to the ability of entities to cope with external stressors and disturbances. Resilience to an external threat depends on (1) impact resistance and (2) recovery speed.

name: Foreign subsidiary exit rate
definition: The authors characterize vulnerability in terms of exit rate, that is, a foreign MNE's failure to survive in the host country. Closures and sell-offs of all Japanese equity ownership were treated as exits.

name: International technology resources
authors_terms: ["international technology resources", "access to international technology", "technology imports", "international technological know-how"]
definition: Technology imports include tangible resources, such as capital equipment and raw materials, and/or intangible resources, such as know-how and licensing in patented knowledge. Technology and capital form two critical gaps between firms from emerging markets and those from more developed markets.

name: International financial resources
authors_terms: ["international financial resources", "access to overseas capital", "international capital markets", "international finance resources"]
definition: Access to overseas capital, through listing firms in international stock exchanges, issues of American Depository Receipts (ADRs) or Global Depository Receipts (GDRs), and raising foreign currency debt, can therefore provide a second critical international input to facilitate product market internationalization.

name: Product market internationalization
authors_terms: ["product market internationalization", "foreign sales intensity", "internationalization of product markets", "degree of internationalization"]
definition: We measure the product market internationalization of a firm as the ratio of foreign sales to total sales, the most common measure of internationalization. Internationalization of resources and product markets constitutes an important component of organizational transformation for local firms in emerging economies.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["business group affiliation", "business group membership", "business group-affiliated firms"]
definition: Business groups have been defined as 'a set of firms which, though legally independent, are bound together by a constellation of formal and informal ties and are accustomed to taking coordinated action' (Khanna and Rivkin 2001, p. 47).

name: Postliberalization time clock
definition: To capture the dynamic effects of international technology and financial resource inputs on product market internationalization over the 10-year study period, we create a postliberalization time-clock variable. The time-clock variable assumes positive integer values of 1 to 10 corresponding to the 10 years of the data used in this study.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "economic performance", "financial measures of firm performance"]
definition: Following the lead of various studies that report that financial measures are highly correlated with other measures of performance (Chakravarthy 1986), we choose two commonly used financial measures of firm performance: return on sales and return on assets.

name: Resource allocation breadth
definition: By breadth, we mean the parallelization of innovation efforts, indicating a strategy of providing initial funding to several different projects.

name: Selectiveness
definition: Selectiveness refers to resource allocation decisions in later stages of project development, indicating a strategy of deliberate discrimination between projects that warrant further resource allocation and those that do not.

name: Innovative intent
definition: Innovative intent describes the overall ambition associated with the portfolio of product innovation efforts, ranging from only minor improvements to existing products to novel forays into new market segments.

name: Innovation performance
definition: Performance in product innovation is conceptualized as the extent to which a firm generates commercially successful new products, evidenced through revenue from new product sales in 2008.

name: Strategic orientation
definition: Accordingly, firms can be divided into prospectors, defenders, analyzers , and reactors based on their strategies. Most of the research on the fit of a firm's strategic orientation with its pay system design has used a simplified version of the Miles and Snow typology and focused on the differences between growth-oriented prospectors and efficiency-oriented defenders in relation to analyzers or reactors.

name: Horizontal pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["horizontal pay dispersion", "horizontal wage compression", "pay differentials horizontally"]
definition: One of the central choices regarding the overall pay system design is the extent to which individuals are paid based on differences in their ability, effort, and results.

name: Relative base pay
authors_terms: ["relative base pay", "base pay level", "salary market policy", "lead market pay policy", "market positioning", "pay level policy"]
definition: We asked the respondents whether the base pay of employees was below, at, or above market levels (Gerhart & Milkovich, 1990).

name: Vertical pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["vertical pay dispersion", "vertical pay compression", "differences in pay across hierarchical levels", "pay range"]
definition: In contrast to differences across individuals within an organizational level or job category ( horizontal pay dispersion), prior research has paid only limited attention to the effects of differences in pay across hierarchical levels ( vertical pay dispersion) in an organization (Shaw, 2014).

name: Firm performance
definition: We used two sources of data for firm performance. As the companies were randomly selected for the study from various industries, we utilized branch-specific percentile comparisons to categorize the profit margins of companies by using the archival database. We complemented this measure with productivity data, as financial performance measures might not always be optimal from the perspective of prospectors that may deliberately choose to sacrifice profitability at the expense of investments in the future.

name: Transactive memory
definition: A system for the shared division of cognitive labor with respect to encoding, storing, and retrieving knowledge from individual areas of expertise. As a collective property of teams, transactive memory is manifested in specialization, credibility, and coordination.

name: Firm performance
definition: Previous research suggests that capturing firm performance requires the use of multiple measures. Subjective, perceptual managerial assessments of performance are particularly useful for capturing broader dimensions of performance relative to direct competitors and have been shown to exhibit strong reliability and validity.

name: External tie strength
authors_terms: ["average strength of external ties", "strength of external ties", "TMT average strength of external ties", "external ties"]
definition: Defined as the average duration, frequency, and emotional intensity of external ties, the strength of a top management team's ties with external actors plays a large part in shaping their access to private and preferential market knowledge.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The level of dynamism, defined as the perceived speed and unpredictability of demand and technological change, imposes considerable cognitive challenges on top managers.

name: Autonomy over choosing team members
authors_terms: ["autonomy over choosing teams", "autonomy over choice of team members", "choosing collaborators", "Choose team"]
definition: A first dimension of autonomy is choosing team members, or the self-selection of collaboration partners.

name: Autonomy over choosing ideas
authors_terms: ["autonomy over choosing ideas", "autonomy over choice of ideas", "idea choice", "Choose idea"]
definition: A second dimension of autonomy enables people to self-select ideas or tasks to work on.

name: Entrepreneurial team performance
definition: Early-stage entrepreneurial team performance as captured by pitch deck evaluations. The pitch deck details a business proposal and is evaluated by practicing venture capitalists, business angels, and seasoned entrepreneurs.

name: Use of new knowledge
authors_terms: ["new knowledge", "company's use of new knowledge", "the more extensively a company's inventions build on new knowledge"]
definition: A company's use of knowledge components it has not previously used in its inventive activities, measured as citations to new patents as a percentage of the total number of distinct citations it made, excluding repeat citations and self-citations.

name: Brokerage firm coverage
authors_terms: ["brokerage firm coverage", "coverage by a brokerage firm", "the brokerage firm's decision to cover the focal company"]
definition: A brokerage firm's decision to cover a medical device company, assessed using brokerage firms' buy/sell recommendations and earnings forecasts. Coverage from a brokerage firm is a valuable form of recognition that can lower a company's cost of capital and increase its value.

name: Novelty of the company's new knowledge to the brokerage firm
authors_terms: ["share of the company's new knowledge that is new to the brokerage firm", "percentage of the company's new knowledge that has not previously been used by one of the other companies that the brokerage firm is covering"]
definition: The degree to which the company's new knowledge deviates from knowledge the brokerage firm has previously evaluated through its coverage of other companies.

name: Brokerage firm's exposure to the company's product markets
authors_terms: ["brokerage firm's exposure to the product markets in which a company commercializes its innovations", "brokerage firm's market exposure", "downstream exposure"]
definition: The exposure a brokerage firm gains, through evaluating the different companies it covers, to the downstream product markets in which companies are developing products.

name: Brokerage firm's coverage of companies using existing knowledge
authors_terms: ["brokerage firm's prior experience evaluating companies that use existing knowledge", "brokerage firm's coverage of companies that use existing knowledge"]
definition: A brokerage firm's prior experience covering companies that build more extensively on existing knowledge in their inventive activities, which shapes the evaluation routines it develops.

name: Brokerage firm's technological scope
authors_terms: ["technological scope", "brokerage firm's broad technological scope", "breadth of the brokerage firm's technological scope"]
definition: The range or scope of a brokerage firm's technological expertise, which it develops through its evaluation of different companies.

name: Alliance network size
authors_terms: ["alliance network at founding", "size of its alliance network", "more alliances", "alliance counts"]
definition: Hypothesis 1 proposes that a larger alliance network-or put differently, more alliances-should improve a startup's early performance; the founding network is the characteristics of a startup's initial configuration of alliances.

name: Alliance network efficiency
authors_terms: ["network efficiency", "network configuration efficiency", "efficient alliance configurations", "efficiency of its alliance network"]
definition: 'Efficient' alliance configurations are configurations that provide access to more diverse information and capabilities per alliance, and thus produce desired benefits with minimum costs of redundancy, conflict, and complexity; efficiency is defined as diversity of information and capabilities per alliance.

name: Alliances with potential rivals
authors_terms: ["alliances with potential rival BFs", "potential rival BF alliances", "rival partner BF"]
definition: Potential rival BFs are those operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the startup BF; such alliances are expected, on average, to adversely affect a startup's early performance.

name: Rival partners' relative scope
definition: The relative scope of allies' market domains captures the incentives each partner has to invest in learning and act competitively (versus cooperatively) within the alliance; a startup with a relatively narrower market domain than a given potential rival partner should generally face more severe intra-alliance competition in that alliance.

name: Rival partners' innovative capabilities
authors_terms: ["partner BFs' innovativeness", "innovative capabilities of potential rivals", "partners' technological competence", "partner quality"]
definition: Alliance benefits may also vary by partner quality-defined by skill level critical for competitive success in a particular market; high quality partners possess leading-edge technology and production capabilities, and alliances with the most skilled innovators are the most promising opportunities to learn new routines and acquire advanced technological knowhow.

name: Startup initial performance
definition: The paper examines multiple measures of performance including revenue growth, employment growth, R&D spending growth, and patenting success, gauging startup BFs' performance across dimensions that liability of newness and smallness arguments indicate are critical to early success: revenue generation, investment in innovation and innovative capabilities, success in recruiting human capital, and development of intellectual property.

name: Industry deregulation
definition: Deregulation of an industry represents a significant environmental shift for the firms in that industry and increases the level of managerial discretion. The new competitive environment after deregulation provides executives more strategic options and demands greater cognitive complexity and information-processing ability.

name: TMT compensation level
authors_terms: ["level of TMT compensation", "total compensation", "average total compensation", "total pay"]
definition: Total compensation was measured as the average total compensation each of the top five highest paid TMT members received, including base salary in cash, cash bonus, and long-term or deferred income.

name: Proportion of performance-based TMT pay
authors_terms: ["proportion of performance-based pay", "proportion of outcome-based compensation", "performance sensitivity of TMT compensation", "outcome-based TMT compensation"]
definition: Proportion of performance-based pay was measured by the average of the proportion of outcome-based compensation received by the top five highest paid TMT members, in which each member's proportion of outcome-based compensation was calculated as (total compensation - base salary)/total compensation.

name: Top management team turnover
authors_terms: ["TMT turnover", "magnitude of TMT turnover", "executive turnover", "magnitude of executive turnover"]
definition: In order to measure changes in the TMT, we included both executives who stepped down and newly hired executives. TMT turnover was calculated by summing the number of departed executives and the number of newly hired executives during each observation period as a percentage of the number of executives on the TMT at the beginning of that period.

name: Home country environmental munificence
authors_terms: ["home country environment", "environmental munificence", "more munificent home country environments", "less munificent home country environments"]
definition: The authors define munificence in terms of factors, the more tangible production factors, such as physical infrastructure, available to firms, and institutions, the less tangible forms of support, such as judiciary efficiency, that facilitate transactions. In focusing on the capacity of factors and institutions at the macro environmental level, they viewed environmental munificence as the availability of crucial factors and institutions in a home country environment.

name: Product diversification
definition: Product diversification refers to a firm's diversification into more than one product market.

name: Outbound international diversification
definition: Outbound international diversification refers to a firm's diversification into foreign environments, either alone or allied with other firms.

name: Inbound international diversification
definition: Inbound international diversification refers to a firm's international cooperative activities for improving its business operations or its competitiveness at home.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "return on assets (ROA)", "earnings before interest and taxes divided by assets (EBITOA)"]
definition: Firm performance was captured with accounting-based measures, return on assets (ROA) and earnings before interest and taxes divided by assets (EBITOA), which the authors used to facilitate comparison with most previous diversification studies.

name: Human expertise
authors_terms: ["human expertise", "human (expertise) resources", "human skills and expertise", "combinations of human expertise"]
definition: The term human expertise is used here to describe the types of knowledge, skills, ideas and experience possessed by individuals, teams or larger units (such as functional departments) in organizations. Human expertise can be viewed as the intersection of human resources and know-how resources.

name: Resource-related industry group
definition: Related Industry Groups (RIGs) are groups of industries related to one another in one or more ways; reflecting the special focus of this study, we divide the economy into Resource-Related Industry Groups (Resource-RIGs) identified by similarity in the required combinations of human expertise.

name: Related diversification
definition: To measure the extent of firm within-group diversification, the entropy measure of diversification was used. The less dispersed the firm's lines of business (industries) are across different Resource-Related Industry Groups, the higher is the related component of the entropy measure.

name: Total diversification
definition: The firm's total diversity across its lines of business, of which related (within-group) diversification forms a part; the authors report that firms pursue on average 43.4% related diversification (within Human Resource-RIGs) out of their total diversity.

name: Between-group diversification
definition: Diversification across different Resource-Related Industry Groups; note that the between-industry groups diversification is not identical to unrelated diversification because some of it may be related diversification not captured by similarity in human expertise (e.g., vertical integration to the trade sector, similarity in raw materials, or same distribution channels).

name: Organizational experience with natural disasters
authors_terms: ["organizational experience with natural disasters", "prior organizational experience with disasters", "experience with disasters", "experience with natural disasters"]
definition: Prior organizational experience with disasters that directly and negatively affected the firm can focus the mind and increase the likelihood of preparation.

name: Managerial perception of disaster risk
authors_terms: ["managerial perception of risk", "managerial perception of disaster risk", "managerial perceptions of risk", "managers' perceptions of natural disaster risk"]
definition: The authors adopt the definition of risk perception put forward by Slovic (1987, p. 280) who argues that risk perception is based on the judgments people make when they are asked to characterize and evaluate hazardous activities and disasters.

name: Organizational learning from others
authors_terms: ["organizational learning from others", "learning from other organizations", "managerial learning", "willingness to learn from others"]
definition: In addition to relying on their own experiences, managers try to learn from other organizations to gain new independent knowledge and insights.

name: Disaster preparedness
definition: Disaster preparedness is the acquisition of the skills and capabilities needed to reduce damage to a firm, to minimize disruption to the supply chain, and business activity more generally, and to save lives and protect employees.

name: Refugee hiring
authors_terms: ["newly hired refugees", "share of newly hired refugees", "refugee hiring"]
definition: The main explanatory variable is the share of newly hired refugees in the focal firm's total workforce in year t; refugees are explicitly identified by Statistics Denmark together with the issuance date of their residence permits, so they cannot be confused with regular immigrants or temporary asylum seekers.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Our dependent variable is firm profitability, which is equal to the gross profits in year t+1. It represents the difference between a firm's total revenue and the total costs arising from the consumption of goods, energy, wages, and subcontracting.

name: Job insecurity
authors_terms: ["job insecurity", "share of involuntary staff attrition", "involuntary turnover"]
definition: To test Hypothesis 2, we measure job insecurity in the firm as the share of workers in the firm who become unemployed in the following year (i.e., the share of involuntary staff attrition or turnover). The higher the value of either measure, the greater the job insecurity at the firm.

name: Work effort
definition: Refugees are willing to put a great deal of effort into their jobs to avoid an unfavorable job market. They often work long hours and tend to be flexible in shifts, staffing, vacation, and contract lengths.

name: Hourly wage
definition: Refugees are typically willing to accept low pay, which reduces the hiring firm's labor costs related to salaries. The authors report statistics for hourly wages of refugees and other foreign employees recruited by the firms in the sample, measured in the hiring year, when information asymmetries about these employees' productivity or quality are higher (i.e., entry wages).

name: Specialized experience
definition: Specialization is cumulative experience at a specific task; in this study it is the depth of experience an individual accumulates in a given software module.

name: Task variety
definition: Exposure to variety is experience that is dispersed across distinct tasks; the authors measure it as the number of distinct software modules an individual has worked on.

name: Experience portfolio concentration
authors_terms: ["Herfindahl-Hirschman Experience Index", "HHEI", "balance between specialization and exposure to variety"]
definition: An adaptation of the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index used to measure the relative dominance of specialization versus variety in an individual's experience portfolio and thus the degree of dispersion of the individual's exposure to variety.

name: Task newness
definition: Working on an unfamiliar module may be challenging no matter how experienced the individual is; individuals need time and effort to understand the code structure and domain of each module and its linkages to related modules.

name: Task resolution time
definition: The effort expended by an individual engineer employed in the software debugging operation to complete a maintenance task aimed at resolving a bug that is assigned to that individual at a certain point in time; shorter resolution times are treated as evidence of learning and higher productivity.

name: Workgroup member exit
definition: The exit of a member results in the loss of collective organizational memory and knowledge linkages within a group, and calls for task reallocation and workload realignment that impose new learning needs on the remaining members.

name: Workgroup member entry
authors_terms: ["new member entry", "entrance of a new member", "NEWENTRY"]
definition: New entrants to a workgroup need to learn about their tasks and about the communication patterns, cultural practices, and interindividual relationships that guide the working of the workgroup, which calls for extensive mentoring by existing members.

name: Specialized experience lost from workgroup
authors_terms: ["Degree of specialization lost", "SPLLOST", "degree of relevant specialized experience lost"]
definition: The degree of specialized experience related to a module that is lost from the workgroup when a member exits, relative to the focal maintenance task; the authors argue that not all individual exits are equal and that exits associated with a higher degree of lost specialized experience have a greater impact on the remaining members.

name: Variety experience lost from workgroup
authors_terms: ["Degree of variety lost", "VARLOST", "degree of variety experience lost"]
definition: The degree of variety experience lost from the workgroup when a member exits, computed by dividing the variety experience of the exiting individual by the combined variety experience of all individuals in the workgroup.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is captured by the firm's market share in the Canadian mutual fund industry, gathered for each firm in the industry as of December 31, 1998.

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: Innovativeness is the firm's tendency to lead the industry in creating and introducing new products or services and adopting new technology to enable new products or services, and has been identified as a key firm capability.

name: Alter innovativeness
authors_terms: ["alter innovativeness", "innovativeness of alters", "ties with innovative alters", "innovativeness of its contacts"]
definition: Alter Innovativeness is the average of the Overall Firm Innovativeness scores for all alters with which a focal firm is tied. The quality and value of the resources controlled or possessed by alters establish an upper bound to the value the focal firm can derive from its ties to the alter.

name: Access to structural holes
authors_terms: ["access to structural holes", "structural holes", "Hole Access", "bridging structural holes"]
definition: Firms occupying the favored network position of bridging structural holes-the gaps between firms otherwise disconnected in the network-are likely to perform better because of their superior access to information. Superior network position is defined as access to structural holes.

name: Network closure
definition: Coleman's notion of social capital as closure contends that actors benefit more from maintaining a network of dense ties; actors in a dense network are able to rely on norms and sanctions against opportunism and thereby freely share information amongst each other.

name: Network-enabled capabilities
definition: The authors refer to the augmentation of internal capabilities by beneficial network position as the firm's network-enabled capabilities, or the capability of an innovative firm to exploit a favorable network structural position.

name: External knowledge sources
authors_terms: ["external knowledge sources", "external sources of knowledge", "knowledge sources", "knowledge sourcing", "use of external knowledge sources"]
definition: Interactions with external holders of knowledge that control knowledge useful in the process of realizing strategic opportunities, such as technological service providers, process consultants, organization design consultants, or other outside parties. The paper captures the extent to which the firm has searched for knowledge and information from such sources beyond the opportunity recognition phase.

name: Opportunity exploitation
definition: The deployment of resources, actions, and investments to realize recognized opportunities. In the survey, exploitation is defined as those opportunities that had 'contributed to improve financial performance.'

name: Decentralization
definition: Decentralization refers to the distribution of decision-making authority in an organization, that is, the delegation of decision rights to lower organizational levels.

name: Coordination
definition: Organizational devices (e.g., cross-functional teams, liaison groups, and cross-divisional communication channels) that ensure the coordination and internal dissemination of the use of knowledge gained from external sources in opportunity exploitation.

name: Intervention type
definition: In attempting to shape how and what strategy will actually be implemented, middle managers can intervene in two ways, at two different stages in the decision-making process: taking a position on the alternatives being considered during the decision-making process, or resisting a decision after it has already been made.

name: Issue impact level
authors_terms: ["organizational level impact", "departmental level impact", "level of issue", "impact beyond the department"]
definition: Interventions were classified according to whether the issue over which the managers intervened had an impact that was confined to their department, or whether the impact went beyond the departmental level, i.e. organizational level.

name: Intervention success
definition: Actions were classified according to whether the intervention was perceived as successful or not, since respondents had been asked to report whether they had been successful or not.

name: Risk of organizational sanctions
authors_terms: ["risk of being sanctioned", "risk of organizational sanctions", "sanctions"]
definition: Self-interested intervention in organizational decision processes carries with it some risk of sanctions, if those in the organization who have the power to sanction (i.e. general management) see the intervention as inimical to the organization's interests. Resisting decisions after they are made carries higher risk of organizational sanctions than taking a position during the decision-making process.

name: Environmental innovation
definition: The development of products, processes, and services aimed at reducing environmental harm by using new methods for treating emissions, recycling or reusing waste, finding cleaner energy sources, and so on. It concerns the invention of new designs and the creation of novel products and processes to reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances.

name: Regulatory pressures
definition: Regulatory pressures are typically exerted by governments that ultimately have the power to recognize or deny the organization's existence in their jurisdiction. At the very least, noncompliance with regulations can be very costly to the firm given the government's superior power.

name: Normative pressures
definition: Normative influences typically come from professional organizations and other focal social actors, which define appropriate behavior and standards for group members. These norms, often implicit, are related to the issue of legitimacy.

name: Deficiency gap
definition: Firms with a greater deficiency gap are firms polluting relatively more than their peers; a firm's deficiency gap is the result of a combination of managerial decisions, consciously undertaken given the institutional context, and several other factors unrelated with the firm's environmental stance such as inertia, path-dependency, and bad luck.

name: Organizational slack
definition: 'Organizational slack is that cushion of actual or potential resources which allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for adjustment or to external pressures for change in policy, as well as to initiate changes in strategy with respect to the external environment' (Bourgeois, 1981: 30).

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "specificity of firm assets", "specific assets", "resource specificity"]
definition: Specificity of resources involves investments in durable, specialized assets that cannot be easily redeployed from existing uses and users except at a significant loss of productive value or at a deep discount.

name: Management faculty
definition: Management faculty are compared with two other populations: the pool of other business faculty, and then the broader pool of faculty from all disciplines.

name: Research productivity
definition: The level of research output of faculty; the authors compare 'research productivity norms' such as total articles published, articles in the last 2 years and hours per week spent on research, and model cumulative publications as a research outcome.

name: Particularism
authors_terms: ["particularism", "particularistic factors", "particularistic criteria", "prestige", "prestige of a faculty member's degree-granting institution"]
definition: Evaluations based on non-merit factors (e.g., pedigree, advisor reputation, social networks) are deemed 'particularistic'; in immature fields research outcomes are expected to be driven by particularistic criteria, measured here as the prestige of a faculty member's degree-granting institution.

name: Universalism
definition: Evaluation of a scientific contribution on the quality of ideas represents a universalistic standard; precocity and ability are universalistic predictors of research outcomes.

name: Research outcomes
definition: Research outcomes can be divided into primary (publications and citations) and secondary outcomes (hiring and job changes). Primary outcomes are the most appropriate level to test for universalistic and particularistic effects.

name: Citations
definition: Citations are the references accrued by an individual's published articles, reflecting the utilization of scientific knowledge; the authors constructed a cumulative count of citations accrued by an individual.

name: Citations per article
definition: Citations per article was the ratio of a person's cumulative citations to their total number of published articles.

name: Precocity
definition: Precocity has been defined as having had publications prior to completing the PhD.

name: Ability
definition: Author order provides an indicator of merit, with lead authorship indicating the greatest proportion of contribution; publication in a higher-quality journal is also likely to indicate the ability of an individual researcher.

name: Volume of media coverage
authors_terms: ["volume of media-provided information", "volume of media coverage", "exposure"]
definition: The degree of audience exposure to a firm through the media is a function of the volume of coverage a firm receives. Increasing volumes of media-provided information about an IPO firm facilitate favorable impression formation and legitimation.

name: Tenor of media coverage
authors_terms: ["tenor of media coverage", "positive tenor of media coverage", "framing"]
definition: The information that the media provide about a firm may affect the processes of impression formation and legitimation not only through the volume of the information, but also through its tenor, or its framing as positive or negative.

name: Underpricing
definition: On the first day they are traded, most stocks close at a price higher than their initial offering price—a phenomenon that finance scholars have labeled 'underpricing.' The greater the difference between the offering and the closing price, the more the stock is underpriced.

name: Turnover
definition: The turnover in the number of shares available on the first day a stock is traded. Turnover provides an indicator of the pent-up interest in, and demand for, the stock.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "corporate social engagement", "CSR practices", "socially responsible practices", "social responsible practices"]
definition: Attention to the interests of nonfinancial stakeholders (Freeman, 1984); CSR includes any corporate initiative pertaining to the firm's stakeholders - such as employees, customers, the environment, and the community at large - and hence is not limited to philanthropic initiatives.

name: Threat of knowledge leakage
authors_terms: ["threat of knowledge leakage", "threat of knowledge spillovers", "risk of knowledge leakage", "risk of knowledge spillovers", "threat of knowledge appropriation"]
definition: The risk that a firm's proprietary knowledge leaks to rivals when employees with valuable know-how leave to join competing firms or create new ventures, i.e., interfirm knowledge spillovers in which knowledge is created by one agent and used by another agent without proper compensation for the knowledge producer.

name: Knowledge workers' propensity to join a rival firm
authors_terms: ["propensity to join a rival firm", "less likely to ' walk '", "walking", "retain knowledge workers", "knowledge workers' decision to stay with the firm"]
definition: The likelihood that knowledge workers leave their current employer to join a rival firm; the authors argue that CSR decreases this propensity because it allows knowledge workers to derive intangible benefits and increases their appreciation of the current employer.

name: Knowledge workers' propensity to disclose valuable knowledge
authors_terms: ["propensity to disclose the firm's valuable knowledge", "less likely to ' talk '", "talking", "willingness to undermine their previous employer"]
definition: The likelihood that knowledge workers disclose their previous employer's valuable knowledge to a new employer after joining a rival firm, which the authors argue is reduced by the previous employer's CSR engagement through stronger identification with the firm and ethical decision-making.

name: Firm performance
definition: The firm's prior accounting performance, which the board interprets as a signal of whether a performance problem exists and whether a correction is needed.

name: Board independence
definition: The percentage of directors that are independent and not inside or affiliated directors (Dalton et al., 1998). Independent directors are assumed to be more vigilant monitors of managerial behavior and less tolerant of agency problems than are affiliated or inside directors.

name: CEO career horizon
definition: CEO career horizon is the amount of time remaining until a CEO reaches retirement age (Matta and Beamish, 2008); the relevant attribute of the CEO's age is how many years the board can expect the CEO to remain at the firm.

name: CEO-board chair separation type
authors_terms: ["CEO-board chair separation", "apprentice separation", "departure separation", "demotion separation", "types of CEO-board chair separation"]
definition: A CEO-board chair separation occurs when a firm reports a combined leadership structure in one year and a separate leadership structure in the following year. It can occur as one of three types: apprentice, departure, or demotion (Krause and Semadeni, 2013).

name: Industry foresight
definition: The authors refer to managers and entrepreneurs having superior industry foresight, that is, accurately forecasting industry opportunities and outcomes. "We operationalize industry foresight as an individual's forecasting accuracy, a measure of how accurate a given forecaster is with respect to all forecasters on a specific question."

name: Belief updating
definition: "we view the forecasting process through the perspective of learning in which individuals can update their beliefs based on new information by engaging in cognitive processes such as those of attention, perception, memory, and reasoning".

name: Bayesian belief updating
definition: "A Bayesian cognitive process is rooted in a systematic updating of one's beliefs over time that considers new information in conjunction with the prior beliefs, as specified by Bayes rule."

name: Uncertainty
definition: "managers can face significant uncertainty, which we define as the general unpredictability of the industry trajectory, while forming their initial beliefs".

name: Parent–unit industry relatedness
definition: Recent research focuses on relatedness in terms of the similarity of industries' human capital, hence we conceptualize industry relatedness as such. Parent-unit industry relatedness is the cosine similarity of two industry vectors in terms of human capital.

name: Parent-to-unit human capital redeployment
authors_terms: ["parent-to-unit (P→U) human capital redeployment", "P→U redeployment", "redeployment of employees from the parent to a business unit"]
definition: Human capital redeployment is the transfer of individual employees through internal labor markets between units of a multi-business firm. P→U is the redeployment of employees from the parent to a business unit.

name: Unit-to-parent human capital redeployment
authors_terms: ["unit-to-parent (U→P) human capital redeployment", "U→P redeployment", "redeployment of employees from a business unit to the parent"]
definition: Human capital redeployment is the transfer of individual employees through internal labor markets between units of a multi-business firm. U→P is the redeployment of employees from a business unit to the parent.

name: Human capital specialization
definition: Individuals' human capital varies in firm-specificity, which alters industry relatedness' effect on mobility. We differentiate between generalists - employees with a broader set of knowledge, not tied to a particular disciplinary domain, and specialists - employees with a narrower but deeper set of knowledge that is closely tied to a disciplinary domain.

name: Business unit closure
definition: Unit closure is largely reflected in the performance of business units, as developing, setting up, and staffing units is costly. Closure is a binary variable set to 1 for closure (i.e., the unit is officially closed, has filed for bankruptcy, dismisses all employees, or ceases to exist in the firm register) and 0 otherwise.

name: Unit performance
definition: Unit performance is operationalized as the natural logarithm of unit revenues in thousands of Norwegian kroner.

name: Local newspaper decline
authors_terms: ["local newspaper decline", "local newspaper declines", "post local newspaper declines"]
definition: Local newspapers have faced steep declines in circulation, staffing, and financial viability, resulting in widespread downsizing and closures across the United States; the data identify counties that experienced various forms of decline, including transitions to nondaily publications, mergers, and permanent closures.

name: CSR engagement
definition: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has become a core mechanism through which firms manage relationships with key stakeholders and sustain legitimacy in dynamic institutional environments; through CSR, firms demonstrate ethical conduct, community commitment, and environmental stewardship.

name: National newspaper coverage
definition: National outlets extend investigative scrutiny and amplify recognition at a broader scale; whereas national media such as The Wall Street Journal or The New York Times target broad, nationally oriented audiences, local newspapers prioritize community relationships and locally relevant business coverage.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: Financial analysts serve as oversight mechanisms by scrutinizing disclosures, flagging risks, and shaping investor perceptions; they also enhance visibility by featuring CSR in their reports, signaling to investors that these activities reflect long-term value creation.

name: Credit rating coverage
definition: Credit rating agencies provide episodic, certification-based oversight tied to firms' creditworthiness and financing conditions, and have increasingly incorporated CSR and related governance issues into their assessments.

name: Demographic heterogeneity change
authors_terms: ["demographic heterogeneity flow", "changes in heterogeneity", "diversity shifts", "increases in demographic heterogeneity"]
definition: A time-varying variable that measures the change in the value of the standard deviation of the local tenure of a team that can be attributed to partner mobility (i.e., new hires or departures). The authors argue that a drop in heterogeneity after a mobility event favors firm survival chances, whereas a surge in demographic diversity produces possible discord.

name: Team age
authors_terms: ["team age", "team age squared", "membership duration", "joint experience", "length of interaction"]
definition: Team age measures the average overlap in tenure among all the possible pairwise combinations of team members at time t - 1 (i.e., before the mobility event). It is a proxy for the members' social interaction over time, signalling how well ingrained their modus operandi has become.

name: Demographic overlap change
authors_terms: ["demographic overlap flow", "changes in demographic overlap", "changes in the compositional difference among top management teams"]
definition: Changes in the overlap computed from the average stock of provincial experience between the focal firm and its competitors located within the same province. The overlap measure varies over time as a result of the mobility of partners.

name: Organizational dissolution
authors_terms: ["organizational dissolution", "hazard of organizational dissolution", "risk of organizational failure", "market exit", "survival"]
definition: Organizational dissolution encompasses different types of exits, ranging from the case in which a firm disappeared because its owners were no longer listed in the Certified Professional Accountant directories, to the case of dissolution by acquisition or merger.
