The authors considered the last year of appearance on the Register of Accountants as the organization's year of dissolution.

name: Competitive intensity
authors_terms: ["competitive intensity", "interfirm competition", "severity of competition", "adverse market environment"]
definition: The severity of competition is proxied by mapping the strength of local competition on the geographical dimension and counting the number of firms dissolved within a given province in a given year. The authors argue that tight competitive conditions increase the struggle for limited resources, ultimately reinforcing its associated negative consequences.

name: User knowledge incorporation
authors_terms: ["corporate inventions that incorporate user knowledge", "user inventors", "physicians", "physician inventor", "input from product users"]
definition: In each case, we seek to contrast corporate inventions developed with input from product users from those developed without user input, which we will call 'traditional corporate inventions.' For the purposes of our analysis, we consider only patented inventions assigned to medical device companies, and of these assigned patents we consider those with at least one physician inventor to be a corporate invention that has incorporated the knowledge of a product user.

name: Invention importance
definition: The number of citations made to the focal patent by future follow-on patents (forward citations) reflects the contribution of the focal invention to future work and has been used as a measure of invention importance or impact in many prior studies.

name: Breadth of impact
authors_terms: ["breadth of impact", "breadth", "broader impact on future inventions", "generality"]
definition: The breadth of impact of a particular invention is the extent to which the knowledge contained therein is utilized in future work, spread across multiple technological domains.

name: Earliness in the product life cycle
authors_terms: ["position in the product life cycle", "beginning of the product life cycle", "earlier in the product life cycle", "proximity to the beginning of the product life cycle"]
definition: An invention near the beginning of a product life cycle is expected to have several characteristics: (1) It will not build on much prior art because it is distinct from what has come before, so few existing technologies are relevant to defining the scope of the new patented technology. (2) The prior art that it does build on will be more recent because it is substantially different from the older technologies. (3) It will be in a patent technology class that was formed more recently. (4) It will be utilized in a larger number of follow-on inventions developed in the industry as the life cycle unfolds.

name: Use of standardized development tools
authors_terms: ["standardized development tools", "middleware", "middleware components", "third-party development tools", "development tools", "toolkits"]
definition: Standardized development tools are a common form of enabling technology - foundational technologies that can form the basis for a variety of new products or innovations - found in software development. In the empirical analysis the comparison is between products developed by using these third-party development tools (i.e., game engines and physics engines) and those that do not use any third-party tools and therefore have to create their own functionality.

name: Product novelty
authors_terms: ["product novelty", "novelty of the products", "novelty score", "novelty frontier"]
definition: The specific meaning of a novel product in this case relates to how different or unique a product is from those that have come before, rather than being a determinant of the quality or value of an innovation.

name: Product commercial success
definition: The authors describe products that are more commercially successful as those with greater average sales.

name: Output growth
definition: We focus on growth in output, which basically captures the growth in the amount of electricity generated. Growth in output is calculated as percentage changes in annual output - that is, percentage changes in annual net generation for each electric utility.

name: Profitability
definition: We measure firm profits with net income. Net income represents managers' primary fiscal responsibility and reflects bottom-line performance.

name: Deregulation
definition: One circumstance under which shareholders become a markedly more salient stakeholder group is when a firm undergoes a change from governance by rate-of-return regulation on capital investment to governance by competition. Deregulation changes the scenario and exposes firms to greater uncertainty and risks, in particular with respect to rate of return.

name: External scrutiny
authors_terms: ["external scrutiny", "scrutiny from external stakeholders", "NGO and regulatory pressures", "regulatory scrutiny"]
definition: We expect that firms will be less likely to engage in greenwashing when external stakeholders such as regulators and environmental groups exert greater scrutiny over the firm's representations. If external scrutiny pressures firms to connect rhetoric and reality more closely, then scrutiny should moderate both incentives to greenwash and incentives to brownwash.

name: Investor pressure
authors_terms: ["investor pressure", "salience of shareholders", "pressure from shareholders", "shareholder salience"]
definition: We posit that as investor pressure intensifies, shareholders become the most salient stakeholder, thereby creating pressure to avoid disclosing information about social and environmental practices that could raise the firm's costs.

name: Deviation between reported and actual emissions reductions
authors_terms: ["deviation between reported and actual emissions reductions", "greenwashing", "brownwashing", "overreporting", "underreporting", "exaggeration", "undue modesty"]
definition: We focus on the accuracy with which a firm's reported emissions reductions correspond to the actual change in its greenhouse gas emissions. To do so, we compute the difference between reported and actual emissions reductions, normalized by the firm's level of reported reductions.

name: Economic performance
definition: Economic performance was defined as the composite of return on total assets, growth in net earnings, growth in earnings per share (EPS), improvement in profit margin (return on sales), and growth in capital averaged over the five years preceding data collection (1971-76).

name: Environmental volatility
definition: The authors focus on discontinuity, or volatility, as the key task environment attribute in the study, arguing that unpredictable discontinuities in an environment create the most risk and difficulty for effective strategy making. Volatility is measured through industry characteristics of product-market and technological change.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: This variable consisted of the total uncertainty score obtained with a version of Duncan's (1972) instrument, modified to reference strategic decisions rather than subunit decisions and to incorporate only components of an external task environment.

name: Perceptual acuity
authors_terms: ["congruence between perceived environmental uncertainty and volatility", "perceptual acuity", "match", "fit", "perceptual divergence"]
definition: The congruence, or fit, between a firm's true environmental volatility and its top management's perceived environmental uncertainty; the authors label the opposite pole perceptual divergence.

name: Perceived uncertainty diversity
authors_terms: ["homogeneity of perceived environmental uncertainty", "perceptual homogeneity", "PEU diversity", "perceptual disagreement", "diversity in perceptions"]
definition: The extent to which members of a top management team perceive their environment's uncertainty alike; the authors measure its reverse with a PEU diversity index computed by summing the five component standard deviations of team members' scores.

name: Goal diversity
authors_terms: ["goal consensus", "goal diversity", "goals diversity", "diversity in goals", "goal congruence"]
definition: The level of agreement or disagreement among top managers on the importance of corporate objectives; a goals diversity score was calculated by summing a team's standard deviation on each goal item.

name: Number of strategic goals
authors_terms: ["number of goals", "number of corporate goals", "number of strategic objectives"]
definition: The number of important corporate objectives a firm's top management attends to, inferred from managers' ratings of the importance of 12 possible corporate objectives.

name: CEO power
definition: Power is 'the capacity to alter others' states by providing or withholding resources and administering punishments.' CEO power is a multidimensional construct measured with an index of proxies based on both structural and ownership power.

name: Nonconforming reference group selection
authors_terms: ["nonconforming reference groups", "custom peer groups", "nonconforming peer group selection", "custom peer group selection"]
definition: Reference groups are 'sets of organizations, benchmarks, or indexes against which a focal organization is compared.' Nonconforming reference groups are reference groups chosen for publicly disclosed evaluations of performance that deviate from the normative standards held by audiences, such as custom peer groups.

name: Accountability pressures
definition: The extent to which CEOs are subject to accountability pressures, that is, to demands that make the evaluations of important audiences more salient. Research on accountability holds that feeling an obligation to explain or justify one's behavior to some significant others affects how individuals think and behave.

name: Salience of rewards
definition: The extent to which valued rewards are salient to CEOs, because the tendency to disregard norms of those who possess power derives in part from their orientation to pursue rewards. Attainable rewards activate approach-related processes, which increases attention to goals while decreasing powerholders' sensitivity to the evaluations of others.

name: Managerial risk taking
definition: 'Managerial risk' is defined as management's proactive strategic choices involving the allocation of resources. Strategic choices involve uncertainty because they promote change in organizations.

name: Organizational risk
definition: 'Organizational risk' is defined here as income stream uncertainty. Organizational risk is important to strategic management since income variation can have negative consequences for the firm as a whole as well as for its managers.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Complexity corresponds to industry size and describes the extent of competitive heterogeneity within an industry. Aldrich (1979) defined complexity as the amount of heterogeneity present in a firm's environment.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence describes an environment's ability to support sustained growth and is commonly associated with a market's growth in demand.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism describes environments typified by change that is difficult to predict. Dynamism identifies difficult-to-predict industry changes.

name: Attainment discrepancy
definition: Considered in tandem, the difference between one's aspirations (goals) and expectations (performance) results in an attainment discrepancy. A positive discrepancy is evidenced when performance is expected to fall below predetermined goals; risk taking is most likely in these cases.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
definition: High levels of heterogeneity in top management team (TMT) characteristics should promote managerial risk taking. Heterogeneous teams mitigate pressures to maintain the status quo, and diversity of perspectives increases the likelihood that more uncertain, risky, and non-routine strategies will be considered.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: Managerial ownership identifies the degree to which managers hold equity positions in their firms. Equity was defined as common stock held directly or indirectly (e.g., a family trust) for the executives' benefit, not including options to purchase additional shares in the future (i.e., stock option plans).

name: Slack resources
definition: We view slack as a measure of firm health such that adequate levels of slack provide insurance against unanticipated adverse economic shocks. Firms seek to preserve a level of slack and thus when slack resources fall, managers may increase efforts at raising resource levels through various risk-laden actions.

name: Industry rivalry
definition: Our final measurement model collapses complexity with munificence into a single construct called 'industry rivalry' that appears to be a function of life cycle effects. High levels of rivalry are common in fragmented industries characterized by rapid growth in sales.

name: CEO attention focus
authors_terms: ["CEOs' focus of attention", "attentional focus", "attention focus", "managerial attention", "CEOs' attention"]
definition: The strategic dimensions on which CEOs focus their attention when seeking to maximize their firm's competitive advantage; the approach measures the importance that the CEO attaches to particular resource and scope commitments in order to attain the firm's maximum efficiency over time.

name: Cognitive group membership
definition: Cognitive groups comprise firms within an industry with managers who possess similar or shared mental models of strategy; homogeneity of attention implies that CEOs recognize the same challenges, interpret them similarly, and agree upon the weights they assign to each aspect of their organizations.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measured performance using the ratio of accounting profits to total assets (ROA) and the average ROA between t and t + 5 for measuring long-run performance.

name: Knowledge diversification
authors_terms: ["individual-level diversification", "knowledge diversification", "level of knowledge diversification", "diversification of research portfolio areas", "diversification index"]
definition: We infer individual-level diversification from researchers' breadth of academic publications across knowledge areas. Individuals with the same amount of experience can have that experience either spread across multiple domains (wider breadth, shallower depth) or concentrated in one domain or a narrow set of domains (wider depth).

name: Exploration
authors_terms: ["exploration", "successful exploration", "propensity to integrate new knowledge from outside their domains of expertise", "engagement with Kinect", "Kinect author"]
definition: We define exploration as the process of integrating new external knowledge - that is outside of the individual's domains of knowledge - into successful knowledge creation.

name: High-impact research output
definition: We identify those Kinect publications that enter the ranks of the top 10% most-cited papers of all papers published in computer science, electrical engineering and electronics between 2011 and 2014, our 4 years of interest after Kinect's launch.

name: Breadth of knowledge combination
authors_terms: ["combining more categories of knowledge", "number of IEEE domains", "combination of keywords", "spread of these publications' keywords across IEEE domains"]
definition: We examine the number of IEEE domains the Kinect papers belong to as evidenced by the keywords used in each paper.

name: Academic employment
authors_terms: ["university affiliation", "academic researchers", "employer-type (academic vs. industry)", "researchers employed by universities"]
definition: We capture the affiliation of researchers, either in the public or private sector, based on the affiliation listed in the IEEE profile of researchers in the period before Kinect's launch.

name: Research age
definition: We capture age via how long a researcher has been active during the complete period of time we observe in our data (i.e., starting in 2001). Publication age is the number of years since a researcher's first publication.

name: National culture
definition: Hofstede (1991) identifies six dimensions of national cultures - power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term orientation, and indulgence - and demonstrates how these attributes influence individuals' behavior in social interactions and in the workplace.

name: Network prominence
authors_terms: ["network prominence", "prominent position", "prominence in the network", "prominent network position", "PROMIN"]
definition: Firms pursuing prominence in the alliance network seek to take advantage of network benefits arising out of two distinct mechanisms: prominence provides significantly more access to key and valuable information relative to those less prominent in the network, and affiliation-based benefits provide opportunities for the prominent firm to establish its competitive and strategic agenda as the defining norm in the industry/network.

name: Entrepreneurial position
definition: Firms pursuing an entrepreneurial position in the network seek to take advantage of the benefits arising out of both control and participation in resource diffusion between different and often unconnected groups in the network. In addition, firms in an entrepreneurial position benefit from information diversity because of their focus on partner diversity in designing their alliance network.

name: Firm performance
definition: We operationalized our dependent variable firm performance as Sales per employee in constant US dollars (PRODUCTIVITY). It also provides a measure of the efficiency of the firm's operation which has been the driving concern of many firms in the steel industry.

name: Environmental change
definition: We drew on an events-based classification scheme to operationalize environmental change. Industry events change the competitive dynamics, which forces firms to jockey for position in the network in order to acquire capabilities necessary to compete.

name: Firm strategy
definition: To specify the directional hypotheses for the interacting effect of firm strategy, we classified firm strategy in terms of the Miles and Snow typology; Miles and Snow (1978) distinguished between three types of firm strategies: Analyzer, Prospector, and Defender. Analyzers have been defined as 'a unique combination of the [p]rospector and [d]efender types' who service a firm's stable base of traditional products and customers while simultaneously locating new product and market opportunities that are closely related to its existing technological base.

name: Board independence
definition: Independent boards are expected to be more vigilant in monitoring firm strategies. Board independence is most often associated with a high level of outside director influence relative to inside director influence.

name: Corporate refocusing
definition: By the 1980s, the trend towards diversification was replaced by an increasing emphasis on corporate focus, or 'downscoping'. Under these circumstances, most firms would benefit the most from refocusing or reducing their levels of diversification.

name: Earnings guidance precision
authors_terms: ["forecast precision", "precision", "precision of firms' annual earnings guidance", "guidance precision"]
definition: We define precision as the spread with which a forecast is given. Within the earnings guidance context, precision refers to the range within which guidance is issued.

name: Earnings miss
authors_terms: ["earnings miss", "missed its earnings guidance in the prior year", "missing prior earnings expectations"]
definition: A robust result in the OIM literature is that leaders of organizations work to foster positive impressions after performance has not met expectations, including before, during, and after releasing a negative earnings surprise or 'earnings miss' - the extent to which actual earnings fall short of the forecast.

name: Below-industry-average performance
authors_terms: ["below-industry-average performance", "below-industry-average market performance", "underperforming relative to industry peers"]
definition: Another central condition of OIM arises when firms report below-industry-average performance. In these cases, investors could have generated superior returns by investing in competitor companies in the same industry.

name: Negative M&A announcement reaction
authors_terms: ["negative reaction to an M&A announcement", "negative market reaction to an M&A announcement", "negative reaction to an M&A"]
definition: CEOs can also greatly disappoint stakeholders and create the impression that they lack understanding and control after questionable mergers and acquisitions (M&As). In other words, such events raise questions about how well CEOs understand and can direct firm strategy and performance.

name: Upward earnings guidance
definition: This measures the degree (as a proportion) to which the focal guidance is higher than the previous year ' s EPS.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market ' s reaction", "abnormal return", "cumulative abnormal market adjusted returns"]
definition: As the dependent variable for Hypothesis 4, we use the cumulative abnormal market adjusted returns of a firm ' s share price based on a window of one day before the announcement until one day after the announcement.

name: Immigration uncertainty
definition: An additional type of uncertainty, beyond the uncertainty usually related to businesses' choices and processes, related to immigrant entrepreneurs' ability to stay in the host country for a prolonged period of time. It concerns their own and their conationals' immigration status, including that of potential immigrant customers, employees and suppliers.

name: Immigrant entrepreneurial entry
authors_terms: ["immigrant entrepreneurship", "immigrant entrepreneurial entry", "entry of new immigrant-founded firms", "entry decisions of immigrant entrepreneurs"]
definition: The establishment of new ventures in the host country by immigrant founders, which the paper compares across nationalities of founders.

name: Reliance on immigrant actors
authors_terms: ["reliance on immigrant actors", "dependence on immigrant actors", "reliance on other immigrant actors", "reliance on immigrant stakeholders"]
definition: The extent to which a firm depends on other immigrant actors in the host country, such as immigrant employees, suppliers and customers. The model assumes that the uncertainty an entrepreneur faces depends positively on this reliance, so firms that heavily depend on immigrant actors for their survival are more exposed to an uncertainty shock that threatens immigrants' legal status.

name: Venture quality
authors_terms: ["venture quality", "firm quality", "entrepreneurial quality", "quality of the firm"]
definition: The quality level of a venture at founding, drawn from a quality distribution, where a firm with higher quality has higher potential earnings and higher labour productivity. Higher-quality ventures are associated with higher growth potential and more global demand.

name: Seeking paid employment
authors_terms: ["looking for a job as employees", "seeking a job as employees", "looking to be paid employees"]
definition: The extent to which low-skilled individuals from a given country of origin in the United Kingdom are looking for paid employment rather than to be self-employed. The authors use the skill level of the workforce to proxy the quality of prospective entrants.

name: Seeking self-employment
authors_terms: ["seeking a job as self-employed", "looking to be self-employed"]
definition: The extent to which low-skilled individuals from a given country of origin in the United Kingdom are looking to be self-employed rather than to be paid employees.

name: High-growth start-up entry
definition: The incorporation of high-quality ventures, which the authors capture as ventures with an average annualized employment growth greater than 10% per year over a three-year period.

name: Development performance
authors_terms: ["development performance", "development time", "drug development project completion time", "technological performance"]
definition: The authors examine 'technological performance-defined as the speed with which CROs complete drug development projects for sponsoring pharmaceutical firms'. Time to complete is considered one of the most important performance measures for CROs, especially in consideration of the substantial competitive and financial costs associated with delay.

name: Firm size
definition: Development performance in knowledge-based activities such as R&D is most likely impacted positively by scale economies for several reasons. Greater size permits the undertaking of development on a larger scale; because development entails significant trial and error, larger firms are able to conduct more experiments in more diverse scientific and/or technological areas that guide problem solving in ways that smaller firms cannot.

name: Technological area diversity
authors_terms: ["technological area diversity", "therapeutic area scope", "TA Scope", "scope economies"]
definition: Economies of scope are present if cost savings or performance benefits are realized when two or more activities are conducted jointly in comparison to when these activities are conducted separately. Scope economies in development likely arise from knowledge spillovers: knowledge generated in a given technological area is not only informative, but also potentially beneficial to the development of other technological areas.

name: Technological area experience
definition: As CROs become more experienced in conducting drug development projects, they develop storehouses of knowledge that can be drawn upon for subsequent projects. As firms become more experienced in a particular therapeutic area, they acquire localized expertise and develop problem-solving strategies that can be drawn on in subsequent and similar efforts.

name: Government regulation
definition: Government regulation is a very important environmental condition for many managers; in a number of U.S. industries the federal government has historically restricted the level of competition by regulating prices, entry and exit. In regulated environments the link between strategy and performance is moderated by the regulatory agency, which buffers and protects the firm from market and competitive forces.

name: Environmental variation
definition: The transition from a regulated environment to a deregulated environment is a dramatic environmental change for a firm, and it provides a good setting for studying the dynamics of environmental variation and strategy.

name: Focused strategy
authors_terms: ["focused strategy", "unfocused strategy", "strategic focus", "focused versus unfocused strategy"]
definition: A focused strategy is defined as a pattern of firm behavior oriented toward one or two specific strategic dimensions; in contrast, an unfocused strategy is defined as a pattern of firm behavior in which no particular strategic dimension is emphasized.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "change in strategy", "changes in strategy", "strategic moves", "kinds of moves"]
definition: Firms that changed strategy can be identified by investigating those firms which were found in two different clusters, and firms clustered into the same strategic group at both pre- and post-periods did not change their strategy. There must be very dramatic change in strategy for the same firm to be clustered with some other firm as opposed to being clustered with itself.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "performance", "profitability", "return on investment", "return on total capitalization", "return on equity"]
definition: Railroads have strongly argued, and the Interstate Commerce Commission has accepted, that return on investment (ROI) is the single most important indicator of railroad performance; two related performance measures, return on total capitalization (ROTC) and return on equity (ROE), are used as well.

name: Large shareholder ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership structure", "large block shareholders", "percentage of stock owned by large shareholders", "percentage of shares held by large outside owners", "ownership concentration"]
definition: Agency theory assumes that the monitoring role of boards is best accomplished when ownership is concentrated in the hands of one or more large block shareholders because these shareholders have greater incentives to perform monitoring activities. In Study 2 the measure focuses exclusively on large outside shareholders.

name: Board vigilance
definition: Board vigilance refers to the ability and willingness of directors to monitor the activities of management and exercise legal authority over management.

name: Corporate strategy
authors_terms: ["managers' strategic behaviors", "strategic behavior of agents", "corporate strategy", "corporate diversification behaviors"]
definition: The strategic behaviors of managers, which in this paper are the type of acquisitions a firm makes and the level of a firm's diversification. Decisions regarding corporate strategy are argued not to create sharp conflicts of interests between managers and shareholders.

name: Acquisition type
authors_terms: ["type of acquisitions", "type of merger", "merger type", "merger relatedness"]
definition: The type of merger or acquisition a firm makes, classified by the relatedness of the merger. Study 1 uses the FTC large merger series categories (vertical, horizontal, product extension, market extension, pure conglomerate, plus an aggregated 'all conglomerates' category), while Study 2 ranks mergers from horizontal to unrelated using Rumelt's classification scheme.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["level of a firm's diversification", "level of diversification", "diversification strategy"]
definition: The level of a firm's diversification across businesses, captured by Rumelt's five-level classification of diversification strategies ranging from single business to unrelated business. Amihud and Lev's R-squared measure instead assumes that the more businesses a firm holds in its corporate portfolio, the more closely its returns will map to the all-market portfolio.

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: Risk specific to a particular investment, which shareholders can reduce to zero by holding diversified portfolios; the standard deviation of the error term of the market model reflects an estimate of the firm's unsystematic, or firm-specific, risk.

name: Shareholder returns
definition: The return to shareholders, measured as a 3-year average surrogate measure of Tobin's Q following the Fama and French (1993) definition, the ratio of market value to book value. Market-to-book is used because the higher the ratio, the higher the performance of the firm.

name: Structural complexity
authors_terms: ["structural complexity", "complex structures", "structural complexity of the organization"]
definition: Organizational structures refer to those objective properties of organizations per se that cannot be reduced to or deduced from properties of the organization's members. Structural complexity is indicated by higher levels of role specialization, horizontal differentiation, and vertical differentiation.

name: Role specialization
definition: The measure reflects the number of specialized roles across 16 functional areas.

name: Horizontal differentiation
definition: Horizontal differentiation was measured by the number of departments in the organization. A department was defined as any unit having at least two persons and two levels, the head of which reported to the mayor, the administrator, and/or an alderman.

name: Vertical differentiation
authors_terms: ["vertical differentiation", "number of levels in the hierarchy"]
definition: Vertical differentiation was measured by the number of levels in each department from the department head to the lowest level worker.

name: Task routinization
authors_terms: ["task routinization", "degree of task routinization", "routinization of task activities", "nonroutine tasks"]
definition: The degree to which the task activities of organizational members are routine; nonroutine tasks present individuals with ambiguous work situations in which organizational guidelines and controls often are lacking.

name: Boundary spanning
definition: Organizational members whose tasks require that they maintain greater contacts with outside groups to perform their functions.

name: Internal verbal communication
authors_terms: ["internal verbal communication", "internal communication", "rate of internal verbal communication"]
definition: The rate of internal verbal communication by organizational members, which facilitates the rapid diffusion of information throughout the organization about performance gaps and promotes a cross-fertilization of ideas about possible solutions.

name: Influence in work decisions
authors_terms: ["dispersion of influence", "influence in work decisions", "perceived influence"]
definition: The dispersion of influence among organizational members, measured as respondents' perceived influence over several facets of the work environment.

name: Hierarchical level
authors_terms: ["middle echelon", "lower echelon", "hierarchical level", "level in the organization"]
definition: The middle echelon department heads are responsible for translating policies devised by the upper echelon officials into effective service delivery programs, while their lower echelon subordinates directly supervise ongoing service delivery operations.

name: Proposals for innovation
authors_terms: ["reported proposals for innovations", "proposals for innovation", "proposal making", "proposals for change"]
definition: Organizational innovation has been conceptualized as a process consisting of a number of relatively distinct phases that involve the proposal for change and its later adoption and implementation. The present study focuses on the proposal phase, that is, propositions for change made by officials, regardless of whether or not they were accepted or put into practice.

name: Proposals for technical innovations
authors_terms: ["proposals for technical innovations", "proposals of technical innovations"]
definition: Propositions to change the technical equipment in the township administration, regardless of whether or not these propositions were accepted by the respondents' managers and whether or not they were put into practice.

name: Proposals for administrative innovations
authors_terms: ["proposals for administrative innovations", "proposals of administrative innovations"]
definition: Propositions made to a superior concerning changes in or modification in management methods, including techniques of leadership and other management techniques, regardless of whether these propositions were accepted or not by management and whether or not they were put into practice.

name: Parent technological knowledge transfers
authors_terms: ["parent technology transfers", "transfers of parent firm technological knowledge", "parent firm technology transfers", "royalty payments"]
definition: 'Technological knowledge' refers to a body of experience, contextual information, and techniques used in the design, development, production, and application of firm knowledge, and involves the practical application of firm knowledge. Subsidiaries that receive technology flows from their parent firm operations are receiving knowledge that was created elsewhere to be used in local production facilities.

name: Parent managerial knowledge transfers
authors_terms: ["parent expatriates", "transfers of parent firm managerial knowledge", "managerial knowledge transfers", "parent firm managerial transfers"]
definition: 'Managerial knowledge' includes the endowment of the managerial intellectual property or know-how of a firm, and its managerial and organizational practices and routines, and can play an important role in determining the productive efficiency of foreign operations. It covers aspects of the management of a firm, including strategic planning, decision making, human and financial resource management, and operations management.

name: Local knowledge investment
authors_terms: ["subsidiary R&D intensity", "investments in local knowledge", "local technology investments", "subsidiary expenditures on R&D"]
definition: Investments in local technological innovations, which may be needed if MNCs are to be competitive in these foreign markets, and which give firms access to know-how that can be used to increase performance in leading technology countries.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: Return on assets, used to measure subsidiary performance as an indicator of how profitable an operation is relative to its total assets.

name: New firm survival
definition: Our dependent variable is the survival time (in months) of the business (Brüderl et al. 1992, Delmar and Shane 2006). Respondents reported the month and year in which they commenced business activity, as well as the month and year in which the activity was terminated; a firm still alive at the time of the survey is recorded as right censored.

name: Early-stage business planning
definition: Early-stage business planning is the 'process by which the entrepreneur, in exploiting an opportunity, creates a vision of the future and develops the necessary objectives, resources, and procedures to achieve that vision' (Sexton and Bowman-Upton 1991, p. 118). Business plans are written prior to the launch of the new organization.

name: Product-line change
definition: Product-line change occurs when the founder adds, removes, or alters the products or service that he or she provides following the founding of the new firm. It occurs when the firm realizes that it would be more successful if it changed its product line.

name: Pre-entry knowledge of the business activity
authors_terms: ["pre-entry knowledge of the business activity", "pre-entry knowledge", "pre-entry business planning", "prior knowledge of the new business activity"]
definition: Pre-entry knowledge relevant to the new business activity can be obtained in a number of ways-for example, through prior work experience, education, and/or hobby or side activities. Pre-entry knowledge of the industry is argued to provide industry-specific information about the competitive landscape, profitable niches, customer preferences, supply chain issues, employment practices, industry rules and norms, etc.

name: Pre-entry management experience
definition: Pre-entry management experience indicates that founders had worked in a managerial capacity before they started the new firm (Bates 1990). Pre-entry management experience is argued to provide a variety of useful skills, such as greater functional (i.e., sales, marketing, finance) knowledge, greater skill in dealing with people and external actors (e.g., employees, customers, suppliers), and the ability to more effectively identify and allocate scarce resources.

name: Market specialization
definition: The degree of relatedness in firms' diversification strategy as manifest by the extent to which they concentrate their efforts by market type (consumer or industrial). The basic argument is that different types of markets require different sets of skills for success, so concentration allows for both economies of experience in key marketing and management skills, and for economies of scale in advertising, distribution and sales force, and should therefore lead to superior performance.

name: Diversification relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "constrained, linked and unrelated diversification", "related firms", "unrelated firms"]
definition: Business units are related 'when a common skill, resource, market or purpose applies to each' (Rumelt, 1974: 29). Rumelt used this concept to identify three broad types of diversification: constrained, linked and unrelated, where unrelated describes all other diversification strategies.

name: Financial performance
definition: The performance measures employed were return-on-capital (ROC) and sales growth for the 3-year period (1978-80) based on data from Value Line; multiple years were employed to minimize the unreliability associated with a single year.

name: Degree of diversification
authors_terms: ["extent of diversification", "specialization ratio", "corporate diversity", "dominant business", "diversified firms"]
definition: The proportion of a firm's revenues attributable to its largest single business, used to separate single, dominant and diversified firms; the overall extent of diversification is controlled by considering dominant and diversified firms separately.

name: Product-group concentration
definition: The proportion of a firm's revenues that are attributable to its largest product group, using the product group classification of consumer durables, consumer nondurables, industrial capital goods, components and raw or semi-finished materials, supplies or other consumable products, and services.

name: Equity joint venture partnership
authors_terms: ["equity joint venture", "JV", "joint venture partners", "equity-based joint venture agreement"]
definition: An alliance form in which the licensor and licensee are partners in a jointly owned but separate legal entity. The authors argue that this legal and administrative boundary enhances the range of control mechanisms available to the technology supplier relative to a license agreement directly connecting the two firms.

name: Cross-licensing agreement
definition: A contract-based technology-sharing agreement in which licensing is reciprocal. Moving from a unilateral to a cross-licensing agreement increases incentive alignment because of the reciprocal nature of the agreement: each partner risks forgoing access to the other's technology should they behave opportunistically.

name: Alliance-related technology building
authors_terms: ["alliance-related technology building", "related knowledge transfer", "related citations", "related technology building"]
definition: The extent to which the licensee builds on licensor technology in areas related to those of the focal licensing agreement, after initiation of the license.

name: Unrelated technology building
authors_terms: ["unrelated technology building", "unrelated knowledge flows", "knowledge leakage", "technology leakage", "unrelated citations"]
definition: The extent to which the licensee builds on licensor technology in areas unrelated to those of the focal license, after initiation of the license; the authors describe such flows as potentially harmful leakage of technology and intellectual property.

name: Speed of knowledge integration
authors_terms: ["speed of knowledge integration", "speed of technology transfer", "speed of knowledge transfer"]
definition: The speed with which the licensor's technology is incorporated into the licensee's subsequent inventions, indicated by the average citation lag, i.e., the lag between the time that a licensor's patents are granted and the time that they are cited in new patent applications by the licensee.

name: Breadth of knowledge transfer
definition: The extent to which changes in technology building under different alliance structures reflect symmetric changes in both related and unrelated technology areas or whether there are significant changes in the breadth of knowledge transfers.

name: New franchisor failure
definition: We define entry as occurring in the year that Entrepreneur Magazine indicated that the franchise system was established. We define failure as exit from Entrepreneur Magazine's listing, and nonreemergence in the listing at a later date.

name: Firm age
definition: Following institutional theory arguments about cognitive legitimacy, we test the effects of firm age and firm size on firm survival. Age is operationalized as the log of the number of years since firm incorporation.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "number of units in the chain"]
definition: Following institutional theory arguments about cognitive legitimacy, we test the effects of firm age and firm size on firm survival. Size is operationalized as the log of the number of units in the chain.

name: Media certification
definition: Following Rao (1994), we test the effects of media certification by operationalizing Entrepreneur Magazine's ranking of franchise systems. The ranking is based on a proprietary formula that incorporates the quantitative data that is reported in the magazine with the subjective assessment of the magazine's experts.

name: Company ownership of outlets
definition: We operationalize the relative emphasis of the franchise system on company ownership of outlets as Company, the percentage of total outlets that are company-owned.

name: Outlet capitalization
definition: We examine the interaction of Company X Capitalization (the amount of money needed to open an outlet). We also measure Capitalization Growth, the two-year change in the amount of capitalization necessary to open an outlet.

name: Termination-law legal environment
definition: Fourteen states ... have termination laws in which franchisors are required to show "good cause" to terminate franchisees before the expiration dates of their contracts. Termination was coded 1 if the franchise system was founded in a state in which franchisee termination laws exist and 0 otherwise.

name: Registration-law legal environment
definition: Sixteen states ... have laws which require franchise system registration with state authorities. Registration was coded 1 if the franchise system was founded in a state in which registration requirements exist and 0 otherwise.

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay dispersion", "dispersion in pay structures", "dispersed pay structures", "dispersion in pay"]
definition: Pay dispersion refers to the amount of difference (inequality) in pay created by a firm's pay structure. More dispersed pay structures concentrate pay among fewer employees at the top of the pay structure, thereby providing relatively rich rewards for these employees and relatively poor rewards for the rest.

name: Managerial tenure
definition: Tenure was computed from the recorded date of hiring and represents organizational, not job, tenure; average managerial tenure was computed for each firm and year.

name: Managerial turnover
definition: Turnover (coded as 1) was considered to have occurred if a manager left during the current year.

name: Investment opportunities
definition: The investment opportunity set, which captures the magnitude of an organization's options for growth, increases organizational uncertainty. For organizations with high investment opportunities, a significant proportion of organizational value is embedded in its future potential, and the realization of this potential is dependent on the decision making of high-performing managers.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Instability refers to the unpredictability and volatility of an organization's external environment.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Munificence refers to an environment's resource abundance. In munificent environments, organizations face relatively low levels of external threat.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: The diversification strategy pursued by an organization may also affect pay dispersion. Related diversifiers face greater interdependencies and require higher degrees of collaboration from managers as they attempt to share resources across divisions and business units; unrelated diversifiers avoid relationships across units and emphasize decentralization, autonomy, and strong performance incentives.

name: Overinvestment
definition: Overinvestment is defined as allocating high levels of capital to business units with relatively poor future growth prospects. It reflects inappropriate capital allocation due to a lack of fit between resource investment and deployment.

name: Underinvestment
definition: Underinvestment is defined as allocating low levels of capital to business units with strong future growth prospects, and it also reflects inappropriate capital allocation.

name: Business unit performance
authors_terms: ["business unit performance", "business unit ROA", "return on assets (ROA)"]
definition: When we use 'business unit performance,' we are focusing on the performance of individual business units. Business unit performance is measured as ROA and calculated as the ratio of operating income to assets.

name: Market fragmentation
definition: Market fragmentation (MF) is operationalized using the Herfindahl index and accounts for organizational environments exuding different degrees of competition based on the homogeneity and concentration of firms in that particular environment or industry.

name: Unrelated diversification
authors_terms: ["unrelated diversification", "degree of firm diversification unrelatedness", "unrelated firm diversification"]
definition: Unrelated diversification (DIV) measures the degree of unrelatedness among diversified firms. It is operationalized using the entropy measure of unrelated diversification.

name: Political and civil violence
authors_terms: ["political and civil violence", "civil and political violence", "violence", "political and civil unrest"]
definition: Environments characterized by high levels of political and civil violence are inherently unstable, difficult to predict, and uncertain. It is precisely the inability to anticipate where and against whom the violence will occur that causes high levels of uncertainty.

name: Incremental planning
definition: Incremental planning is concerned with reacting to environmental issues at the operational level. New firms that engage in incremental planning increase their probability of survival because such planning helps firms increase operational efficiency, adapt quickly to changes in the environment, and reduce costly mistakes.

name: Comprehensive planning
definition: Comprehensive planning entails proactively planning at the strategic level. Comprehensive planning is future oriented and often focused on making significant changes based on assumptions about trends and organizational needs; the process is characterized by exhaustiveness and inclusiveness when searching for information, analyzing it, and making detailed business plans.

name: New venture survival
definition: Our dependent variable is firm survival and our independent variables are political and civil violence and incremental and comprehensive business planning. The models estimate the probability that firm i will survive during the period t1 to t2.

name: Organizational politics in decision-making
definition: Within an organization, politics pertains primarily to 'the management of influence to obtain ends not sanctioned by the organization'. Adapting this to the context, the authors define partnership politics as the use of influence to pursue goals other than those agreed among all partners.

name: Procedural rationality in decision-making
definition: Procedural rationality refers to 'the extent to which the decision process involves the collection of information relevant to the decision and the reliance upon analysis of this information in making the choice'.

name: Total value created
definition: We refer to the sum of the positive or negative benefits that accrue to all partners as total value created in the partnership. In scale alliances, total value created results from the total cost reductions the partnership achieves.

name: Extra value appropriation
authors_terms: ["extra value appropriated", "extra value appropriation", "value appropriation", "extra value"]
definition: Any deviation results in at least one partner obtaining extra value appropriated, that is, benefits that exceed what could be expected given the partner's contribution to the alliance. In scale alliances, this results from the amount of costs the organization gets allocated relative to its contribution in the partnership.

name: Partnership-level politics
authors_terms: ["partnership-level politics", "PL-politics", "partnership's aggregate level of politics in decision-making"]
definition: The partnership's aggregate level of politics in decision-making, computed by summing the respective values of Organization-level Politics for the participating water authorities.

name: Partnership-level procedural rationality
authors_terms: ["partnership-level procedural rationality", "PL-rationality", "partnership's aggregate level of procedural rationality in decision-making"]
definition: The partnership's aggregate level of procedural rationality in decision-making, computed by summing the respective values of Organization-level Procedural Rationality for the participating water authorities.

name: Foreign subsidiary status
definition: A firm operating in the host country that has a foreign company as owner of some or all of its stock, i.e., a subsidiary of a foreign multinational enterprise competing in the same country as domestic firms.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovations", "number of new products", "number of product innovations", "innovativeness"]
definition: The number of new products introduced by the firm in the year, measured at the level of the firm operating in Spain.

name: R&D investment
definition: The ratio of total expenditures in R&D to sales, measured at the level of the domestic firm or subsidiary of a foreign MNE, not at the level of the parent firm.

name: Litigation
definition: All lawsuits involving conflict with franchisees are used; all represent attempts by the franchisor to terminate the agreement.

name: Tapered integration
authors_terms: ["tapered integration", "owned units", "franchisor-owned units", "owning some units while franchising others"]
definition: Tapered integration is defined as 'Some portion (but not all) of the firm's requirements for an input is supplied in-house or some portion of outputs is sold (consumed) in-house.' Tapered integration is an intermediate degree of vertical integration, between nonintegration and full integration.

name: Training program length
authors_terms: ["length of the franchisor's training program", "training", "weeks of training", "training weeks"]
definition: Training is likely to raise switching costs for the franchisee, because franchisees frequently rely on training to learn the specifics of the business and the industry and by increasing the system specific human capital the franchisee develops.

name: Franchisee prior industry experience
authors_terms: ["previous industry experience of the franchisee", "franchisee experience", "industry experience", "experience required"]
definition: A more experienced franchisee may have additional resources to bring to the franchise relationship, and also have more outside alternatives to operating the franchise, thus creating bargaining power for the franchisee.

name: Tying
authors_terms: ["tying", "percent tied", "tied products", "proportion of wholesale purchases by each franchisee that must be made from the franchisor"]
definition: The franchise contract frequently requires the franchisee to purchase specific inputs from the franchisor, termed tying.

name: Exclusive territory
definition: Some franchisors grant an exclusive territory, a geographic monopoly over a particular market area. Within an exclusive territory, no other unit (franchised or company-owned) can be opened without the franchisee's permission.

name: Shared caste affiliation
authors_terms: ["caste tie", "CEO-analyst caste tie", "same-caste tie", "traditional basis of affiliation"]
definition: A traditional institutional basis of affiliation in India: the caste system is defined as a status hierarchy of endogamous groups that individuals enter only by birth, and a CEO-analyst caste tie exists when the analyst and the CEO of the focal firm belong to the same caste category.

name: Shared regional language affiliation
definition: The other historically important institutional basis of affiliation in India is regional language; an individual's knowledge and use of regional language is a strong signal of regional identity in contemporary India, and a CEO-analyst language tie exists when both are proficient in the same Indian language.

name: Shared university affiliation
authors_terms: ["school tie", "CEO-analyst school tie", "shared university alumni membership", "contemporary basis of affiliation"]
definition: A contemporary basis of affiliation: whether the CEO and the analyst were affiliated to the same educational institution, based on the notion that higher educational institutions act as important social sieves by structuring opportunities for individuals to interact and form relationships.

name: Analyst forecast accuracy
authors_terms: ["forecast accuracy", "analysts' earnings forecast accuracy", "EPS forecast accuracy"]
definition: Analysts' forecast accuracy is defined as the difference between analysts' forecasted EPS and actual EPS of the focal firm; higher scores denote greater accuracy because the normalized absolute forecast error is multiplied by -1.

name: CEO generational cohort
definition: CEOs who completed their university education and entered the workforce after the introduction of the 1991 economic reforms are the postreform generation, which the authors argue is differentially imprinted compared with CEOs already in the workforce under the earlier, prereform regime.

name: Western MNC organizational form
authors_terms: ["MNC firm", "Indian subsidiary of a Western MNC", "Western multinational corporation"]
definition: A locally listed Indian subsidiary of a Western multinational corporation; Western MNCs are carriers of organizational arrangements based on impersonal rules and arm's-length exchange, and their subsidiaries foster an organizational climate in which economic exchange involving particularistic ties is more likely to be avoided.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are stable social structures of legally independent firms that are linked by dense formal and informal network ties and accustomed to taking coordinated action; the practices of a BG create a climate in which particularistic ties are a natural way through which to conduct economic exchange.

name: Earliness of entry
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "entry era", "earlier entrants", "early entry", "timing of entry"]
definition: The timing with which a firm enters its industry, framed in terms of how early or late that entry occurs. The authors predict that earlier entry into an industry decreases a firm's chances of developing a product based upon the dominant design; in measurement, entry era is constructed so that higher values indicate that the firm entered earlier.

name: Technological distance at founding
authors_terms: ["founding technology", "technological distance", "proximate technology", "distant technology", "technology at founding"]
definition: The distance between the product technology a firm is founded with and the product generation that eventually becomes the industry's dominant design. The design most technologically proximate to the pneumatic safety bicycle, in terms of having the most similar subsystems, was the solid-tire safety bicycle, while firms founded as ordinary or high-wheel safety producers are treated as founded with distant technologies.

name: Exploration
definition: Exploration with a variety of technologies or product configurations, which gives firms a wider base of knowledge from which to draw on as the industry evolves. Exploration typically involves changes in individual subsystems or in the ways in which these subsystems are brought together to create a particular product.

name: Transition to the dominant design
authors_terms: ["transition to the dominant design", "make the transition", "introduce a product based upon the dominant design", "transition to pneumatic safety production"]
definition: The firm's transition from production of one of the early bicycle forms to the pneumatic safety bicycle, the design that became the industry's dominant design.

name: Organizational mortality
authors_terms: ["firm survival", "failure", "exit from the bicycle industry", "mortality rate"]
definition: The event of a firm's exit from the bicycle industry, used to examine the relative organizational mortality of earlier versus later entrants.

name: Supplier performance
authors_terms: ["supplier performance", "price performance", "conformance to the buyer's target price", "meeting the target price of the organization"]
definition: Price performance is defined in terms of conformance to the buyer's target price for an input. The buyer's perception of the supplier's price performance combines its achievement of the initial target price and its accommodation of subsequent price changes.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "supplier asset specificity", "supplier asset uniqueness", "specialized assets"]
definition: Asset specificity is measured as the uniqueness of the supplier's technical labor skills and manufacturing equipment for producing the product delivered to the assembly division. Unique assets enable suppliers to appropriate quasi-rents in the contracting process.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["governance structure", "INOUT", "in-house component divisions", "market suppliers", "whether it is in the market or in-house"]
definition: This variable is a dummy variable, coded 0 if the part is produced by an in-house component division, and 1 if it is produced by a market supplier.

name: Volume uncertainty
definition: Studies of manufacturing firms have frequently proposed that adaptation problems in supply relationships are caused by uncertainty regarding volume requirements; these problems should increase with asset specificity since low asset specificity reduces the organization's switching costs.

name: Supplier production advantage
authors_terms: ["supplier production advantage", "production cost advantage", "scale advantage", "production efficiency"]
definition: The production efficiency of the supplier should predict supplier performance: suppliers may vary in their cost structures and lower efficiency inhibits the supplier's ability to meet an aggressive target price.

name: Age of input technology
authors_terms: ["age of technology", "age of the design technology", "age of the manufacturing process", "newer technology"]
definition: The age of the design technology of the input and of the manufacturing process used to produce it; supplier asset specificity may be determined by an organization's choice of an advanced design or technology.

name: Supplier proprietary technology
authors_terms: ["supplier proprietary technology", "proprietary technology", "technology which is proprietary to the supplier"]
definition: An organization may choose a technology which is proprietary to the supplier; when the supplier owns the technology the organization trades off the expected loss of not following against the higher transaction costs of managing the relationship, or gives up some of the expected gain from leading.

name: Early supplier involvement
authors_terms: ["early supplier involvement", "the stage at which the organization brings a supplier into the design-to-production process"]
definition: The stage at which the supplier is brought into the organization's process of designing and producing its product. This process begins with technology development, proceeds through product conceptualization, a design stage and building of prototypes, and ends at full scale production.

name: Ideological distance
definition: The distance between the prevailing ideological identity of a candidate location and the ideology of the firm's existing operations in the same business unit. Firms avoid opening new facilities in ideologically distant areas.

name: Location choice
authors_terms: ["location choice", "firm location", "the likelihood that county is selected"]
definition: Where to locate new facilities is a key strategic decision for firms; the dependent variable records which county a firm selects when it creates a new establishment relative to the risk set of counties it could have chosen.

name: Knowledge intensity
definition: The extent to which knowledge directly drives value creation and competitiveness in an industry; knowledge is a more significant contributor to performance in industries in which patents are more prevalent.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["firm age", "young, newly formed firms", "young firms", "more mature organizations"]
definition: The maturity of the organization; young firms have fewer formalized and entrenched structures, routines, and organizational identities than mature firms, which have established organizing principles and formal structures.

name: Affective polarization
definition: Negative attitudes, animus and dislike toward members of the other ideological identity group, measured at the level of society.

name: Board turnover
definition: Changes in board membership, which the authors note can have both positive and negative consequences for firms; consistent with the academic literature they use the term board turnover, while recognizing that it can have both positive and negative consequences. They operationalize it as the exit of outside directors from the board.

name: Board tenure overlap
definition: The extent to which directors on a board vary in how long they have served, which determines whether tenure can serve as a basis for sorting directors in the local status hierarchy. The authors measure it as the average of the pairwise overlaps in board service among directors, a measure of common historical experience.

name: Board expertise overlap
definition: The degree to which directors on a board possess similar professional expertise; when expertise overlaps it ceases to be a differentiating factor on which directors can establish distinct spheres of influence.

name: Global status homogeneity
authors_terms: ["global status homogeneity", "board global status homogeneity", "status homogeneity"]
definition: The extent to which a board's directors share the same standing in the global status order, which is based on affiliations with high-status institutions, such as degrees from prestigious universities and executive or director positions at high-status companies, that are not coupled with service on the focal board.

name: Technological relatedness
definition: The extent to which an NBF and a pharmaceutical firm rely on similar knowledge bases, that is, possess knowledge in similar technological domains, which provides the pharmaceutical firm with absorptive capacity toward the NBF's know-how.

name: Development experience
definition: The pharmaceutical firm's prior experience in developing new drugs for a given therapeutic area, which provides the know-how required to transform the NBF's knowledge into a successful new drug.

name: Therapeutic area diversity
definition: The extent to which a pharmaceutical firm has experience in developing new drugs for multiple therapeutic areas, which gives it opportunities to transform and exploit any absorbed knowledge into a marketable drug serving alternative therapeutic markets.

name: Knowledge applicability breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of NBF knowledge applicability", "breadth of knowledge applicability"]
definition: The potential degree of applicability across therapeutic domains of the active ingredient that arose from the NBF's knowledge base.

name: R&D alliance formation
authors_terms: ["likelihood that the NBF will establish an R&D alliance", "likelihood of R&D alliance formation", "alliance formation"]
definition: Whether a given NBF-pharmaceutical firm dyad established an R&D alliance in the 2003-2007 time window.

name: Nonuniformity of power imbalances
authors_terms: ["nonuniformity of power imbalances", "nonuniformity: power imbalances", "distribution of power imbalances", "nonuniformity of power imbalances within the focal firm's alliance portfolio"]
definition: The extent to which the power imbalances between a focal firm and its portfolio partners are unevenly distributed across the portfolio, captured by the Theil index computed from the set of dyadic power imbalances. An index close to zero denotes that power imbalances between the focal firm and each of its partners are all similar, whereas an index close to one denotes that there exists a focal firm-partner dyad with a power imbalance significantly different from the remaining dyads.

name: Nonuniformity of mutual dependences
authors_terms: ["nonuniformity of mutual dependences", "nonuniformity: mutual dependences", "distribution of mutual dependences", "nonuniformity of mutual dependences within the focal firm's alliance portfolio"]
definition: The extent to which the focal firm's mutual dependences with its portfolio partners are unevenly distributed, captured by the Theil index computed from the set of dyadic mutual dependences. An index close to zero denotes that the focal firm's mutual dependences with its partners are uniform, whereas an index close to one denotes that the focal firm has strong mutual dependence with one partner but less so with the remaining partners.

name: Portfolio redundancy
authors_terms: ["redundancy within the portfolio", "redundancy among partners within the focal firm's alliance portfolio", "portfolio redundancy", "redundancy"]
definition: The extent to which the focal firm's alliance partners resemble one another, that is, the redundancy of the resources offered by different partners in the alliance portfolio. A value close to one means that the focal firm's partners in its portfolio are redundant (e.g., substitutable with each other in terms of resources that could potentially be exchanged), whereas a value close to zero means that the focal firm's partners are unique in terms of their resources.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of the focal firm, which the authors measure as Operating profitability, computed as the natural logarithm of the carrier's time t RevEx ratio, or ln(Operating revenue / Operating expense).

name: Negative coverage of firm leadership
authors_terms: ["negative coverage of firm leadership and strategy", "negative statements about the leadership or strategy of a firm", "negative reporting about firm leadership"]
definition: Negative statements by a journalist about the leadership or strategy of a firm; the authors identify them by coding each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample as negative, positive or neutral and then determining whether the statement referred to firm leadership or strategy.

name: Positive coverage of firm leadership
authors_terms: ["positive statements about firm leadership and strategy", "more positive coverage of firm leadership and strategy"]
definition: Positive statements about firm leadership and strategy that a journalist issues across the firms that they cover, coded from the journalists' articles in parallel with negative statements.

name: Friendship ties between CEOs
authors_terms: ["friendship ties", "personal friends", "friendship tie between focal CEO and alter"]
definition: A personal friendship relationship between two corporate leaders; the authors argue that people socially identify with their friends and that such ties are governed by norms of self-disclosure that motivate empathic responding.

name: Demographic similarity between CEOs
authors_terms: ["demographic similarity", "similarity on salient demographic attributes", "demographically similar"]
definition: Similarity between CEOs on four characteristics that have been shown to be salient among corporate leaders: functional background, race, gender, and age.

name: Social identification with the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["CEO social identification with the corporate elite", "socially identified with the corporate elite"]
definition: The extent to which people define themselves in terms of their membership in a social category; the corporate elite has generally been defined in the literature as CEOs of large corporations who hold multiple board seats.

name: Social distancing
definition: The reduced willingness of social actors to communicate - or otherwise interact - with another social actor or set of actors; it can occur at the ego-network level, wherein multiple social actors distance themselves from the focal actor.

name: Journalist career stage
authors_terms: ["career stage", "early, middle, and late career stage"]
definition: A psychological or subjectively defined construct: individuals who perceive that they are in a particular career stage tend to exhibit a prototypical set of cognitions and social behaviors.

name: Process innovation activity
authors_terms: ["innovation activity", "process innovation", "process technology innovation", "amount of innovation activity"]
definition: We define 'innovation' or more precisely, 'process innovation,' as the application of new materials, equipment, procedures, or knowledge that alters the cost and/or value of a product or service. Process technology innovations are defined as significant changes in the tools, devices, and knowledge that mediate between inputs and outputs.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is defined as the natural log of a firm's sales.

name: Own operating experience
authors_terms: ["own operating experience", "own production experience", "operating experience developed within a focal firm"]
definition: An organization's own operating experience helps it develop a deep, introspective understanding of the conditions associated with the use of technology and equipment; create enhanced-and often more robust-routines, and develop more efficacious incentive and coordination systems within a given investment trajectory.

name: Codevelopment partner operating experience
authors_terms: ["experience of codevelopment partners", "operating experience developed within a focal firm's codevelopment partners"]
definition: This study considers horizontal codevelopment alliances where a focal firm and its partner(s) work together to solve manufacturing process and production problems, typically through substantial personnel interactions. Such codevelopment alliances provide access to other firms' experiences and, in turn, may alter the focal firm's incentive and ability to innovate.

name: Outsourcing partner operating experience
authors_terms: ["experience of sourcing partners", "operating experience developed within a focal firm's outsourcing partners", "outsourcing partners"]
definition: In this study, sourcing partnerships represent arrangements where a focal firm provides cash and/or design license rights in exchange for technological development and/or production services from its partner(s). These pay for service agreements that approximate arm's-length contracts in which the transacting parties specify the terms of trade and the repercussions for noncompliance.

name: Board gender diversity
definition: Because prior experiences and cognitions may vary as a function of demographics (Milliken and Martins 1996, Robinson and Dechant 1997), gender diversity on the board of directors should translate into a diversity of perspectives in the group.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "prior performance", "low firm performance", "prior accounting performance"]
definition: Firm performance was operationalized as accounting-based performance because our theory is based on strategic leaders' responses to past and present performance and because historically scholars have suggested that prior accounting performance rather than prior market performance is preferred when studying the adaptive effects of performance on the firm's current actions.

name: Strategic change
definition: Strategic change is a firm's response to the recognized need to change and adapt to the environment. Strategic change has been described as the 'content of strategy, i.e., the specifics of what was decided in terms of goals, scope, and/or competitive strategy, and in terms of the process of strategy-making'.

name: Structural power
definition: Structural power is rooted in formal position and hierarchical authority and indicates the human capital required for the job. Structural power within the organization's hierarchy is visible (Brass and Burkhardt 1993) and has been found to be a major determinant of power (Hambrick 1981).

name: Prestige power
definition: Finally, prestige power develops from one's institutional environment based on personal prestige or status, reputation, and perceptions of influence (Finkelstein 1992). Prestige power may develop as a result of having a position on one or more boards, serving on influential committees, or having attended elite educational institutions (Daily and Johnson 1997, Finkelstein 1992), suggesting a certain level of knowledge and connections.

name: Expert power
definition: Expert power develops when an executive exhibits keen judgment while managing an uncertain environment (Finkelstein 1992). Expert power can develop as a result of having exposure to many different functional areas and a breadth of assignments (Bunderson 2003, Daily and Johnson 1997, Van der Vegt and Bunderson 2005) as well as through organizational tenure or years of experience, indicating the task and job knowledge of the director (Bunderson 2003, Combs et al. 2007, Finkelstein and Mooney 2003).

name: Ownership power
definition: Ownership power is linked to equity ownership as well as founder status (Daily and Johnson 1997). Ownership power ensues when an executive can represent the will of the shareholders.

name: Nuclear unit cancellation
authors_terms: ["decision to cancel a previously proposed nuclear unit", "canceled units", "cancellation of a nearby nuclear unit", "victories for activists"]
definition: Canceled units are those proposed units that were later abandoned and never reached the operational stage; proposed units are those formally announced by an electric utility and approved by the NRC, regardless of whether construction has begun. A cancellation is treated as a victory for activists and a critical event.

name: Nuclear unit completion
authors_terms: ["decision to complete a previously proposed new nuclear unit", "completed units", "completion of a nuclear unit", "defeats for activists"]
definition: Completed units are those reactors that were eventually connected to the grid and began operating. The decision to complete is treated as a defeat for activists.

name: Antinuclear protest activity
definition: Protest events opposing nuclear power, identified in the protest database as those including the claim 'Antinuclear (Power) Movement.' The dependent variable for Hypotheses 1 and 2 is a count of antinuclear protests in year t within the focal county.

name: Unrelated protest activity
authors_terms: ["unrelated protest activity", "protests not targeting nuclear power", "mobilization towards other causes", "protest spillovers"]
definition: Protests taking place within the county that do not report claim 0200, i.e., protest activity on themes unrelated to nuclear power.

name: Technological resource breadth
authors_terms: ["technological resources", "breadth of technological resources", "technological resource breadth", "breadth of a firm's patent portfolio"]
