definition: 'Technological resources' refers to the firm's repository of technological knowledge and technological competencies, which include the ability to design and develop new products and processes. The authors focus on the breadth of technological resources, defined as the scope of the firm's knowledge related to technological advancement.

name: Competitive repertoire complexity
authors_terms: ["competitive complexity", "complexity of a firm's competitive behavior", "competitive repertoire complexity"]
definition: A firm whose strategic activities are characterized by competitive simplicity focuses exclusively on a very limited set of actions relative to its competitors; competitive complexity is its inverse. A firm with competitive complexity has a more varied repertoire of actions than most rivals, where no single action dominates in frequency of engagement.

name: Competitive repertoire deviance
authors_terms: ["competitive deviance", "deviance of a firm's competitive behavior", "competitive repertoire deviance"]
definition: Competitive deviance is a 'nonconformist' action repertoire. It reflects the degree to which a firm's actions differ markedly from industry norms, and may arise from emphasizing a novel mix or sequence of actions seldom used by competitors.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors measured performance as a firm's rate of return on assets (ROA), measured across three separate periods because technological resources and competitive actions may not immediately affect performance.

name: Competitor use of a strategic component
authors_terms: ["Prior opponents' use of hero", "recent opponents' hero choices", "incidence"]
definition: The frequency with which a competitor employs a practice; prior research identifies observational learning as the key mechanism underlying imitation, in that how frequently a firm's decision-makers observe others employing a practice (i.e., incidence) affects the likelihood that the firm will imitate it.

name: Component-level imitation
authors_terms: ["component-level imitation", "imitation of a competitor's choice about a strategic component", "imitation"]
definition: A team's likelihood of imitating its competitors' choices about different strategy components - hero choices for different roles. An organization is more likely to imitate a competitor's choice about a component if the component interacts with others similarly at the two organizations.

name: Interdependence asymmetry
authors_terms: ["Interdependence difference", "mismatch in interdependence structures", "asymmetry in interdependencies", "interdependence mismatch"]
definition: Two components are interdependent when the value of choices made about one varies depending on choices made about the other. The measure captures differences between the stable pattern of interdependence linking the focal role to the other roles in the focal organization and the pattern characterizing role-equivalent players in the opponents' teams.

name: Communication among decision-makers
definition: The extent of communication between team members, captured by the number of pings per minute a team's players used during a match. Effective communication allows decision-makers to resolve uncertainty about how a choice regarding one part of the organization could impact other parts.

name: Collaborative experience among decision-makers
definition: The level of familiarity among teammates, computed as the number of games they have played together on the same team. Familiarity among decision-makers resulting from repeated collaboration facilitates a better understanding of how different decision areas relate to one another and of how decisions in one area impact others.

name: Generalist skills
authors_terms: ["generalist skills", "generalist skills (MBA)", "broad strategic business knowledge and leadership skills", "'strategic' CFO", "MBA"]
definition: CFO specialists are defined as those possessing deep expertise in the accounting functional area, while generalist CFOs, defined as those who earned an MBA degree, fulfill the need of a 'strategic' CFO because the MBA degree imparts a broader, strategic knowledge-base.

name: MBA program quality
authors_terms: ["elite MBA", "elite 'strategic' CFOs", "quality of the MBA program", "MBA-Top25"]
definition: Compared to all other CFOs, those with an elite MBA degree will be more scarce as they will typically have superior talent and cognitive abilities, as well as a more sophisticated knowledge-base. In addition, elite CFOs bring along a valuable social network.

name: Accounting expertise
definition: CFO specialists are defined as those possessing deep expertise in the accounting functional area.

name: Non-MBA master's degree
definition: Because firms use relevance of education as a signal of managerial ability for the position, CFOs with non-MBA master's degrees, even those obtained from elite institutions, will not see any compensation premium.

name: CFO compensation
definition: The dependent variable, CFO Pay, is measured as the natural logarithm of total compensation (in 2008 dollars), including salary, bonus, options granted, restricted stock and other pay for the first full year the executive was in the CFO position.

name: Salary compensation
definition: We also examine the determinants of salary and equity based incentives separately by employing the following two dependent variables: (1) the natural logarithm of salary compensation and (2) the natural logarithm of (1 + equity-based compensation), both measured in 2008 dollars.

name: Equity-based compensation
definition: Equity-based pay is computed as the value of option grants and the restricted stock owned by the CFO.

name: Service adaptability
definition: Service adaptability involves the degree to which a firm alters its service output according to the desires of customers. It refers to a firm's ability to alter its service offering to meet the specific needs of customers.

name: Service focus
authors_terms: ["service focus", "breadth of an overall service offering", "service firm output specialization"]
definition: Service focus refers to the breadth of an overall service offering. Firms can offer a narrow focus, specializing in a specific type of service, or a broad array of services.

name: Customer coproduction
definition: Customer coproduction refers to the extent to which customers help produce a service offering. It is the time and effort a customer must expend to obtain a service; as customers are required to expend greater effort to get the service, their level of coproduction increases.

name: Service production complexity
definition: The complexity of service production refers to the level of coordination present in an entire service delivery process. It is a specific form of coordination that is affected by the number of processes required to produce the service as well as by the dependency among these processes.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors treat firm performance as multidimensional, combining return on equity, return on investment and top managers' perceptions of performance into a single overall composite of firm performance.

name: Strategic positioning
definition: According to the positioning view of strategy, firms undertake strategic positions in order to differentiate themselves from existing and potential competitors along dimensions that are of importance to customers. Three key differentiating mechanisms, or strategic positioning variables, for service firms are service adaptability, service focus, and customer coproduction.

name: Task requirements
definition: Heterogeneity across organizations in the difficulty of tasks they perform for their customers, which can shape the organization-specific value an innovation represents and the timing of adoption. Case Mix Index, the measure used here, represents the average clinical complexity of patients that a focal hospital has treated in a given year.

name: Competitor adoption of innovation
authors_terms: ["Competitor Adopters", "competing adopters", "adoption by competitors", "competitor adoption", "prior adoption by competitors"]
definition: Prior adoption of a focal innovation by competing organizations, which can accelerate a focal organization's investment through knowledge spillovers or delay it by reducing the value the organization can capture and increasing the opportunity cost of adoption. The authors measure it as a count of competing hospitals within a focal health service area that had adopted robotic surgery prior to the focal year.

name: Timing of adoption
authors_terms: ["timing of adoption", "hazard of adoption", "timing of investing in the focal technology", "hazard of investing"]
definition: The timing of a focal organization's investment in the focal technology, examined as the hazard of robotic surgery adoption in the models.

name: Supplier capabilities obsolescence
authors_terms: ["Supplier capabilities obsolescence", "obsolescence of a RISC microprocessor supplier's capabilities", "suppliers' capabilities are rendered obsolete"]
definition: Obsolescence of a RISC microprocessor supplier's capabilities is measured by whether the RISC supplier had been a CISC supplier before or was a new entrant in the RISC market. The rationale here is that firms which supplied this old technology are more embedded in the systems, routines and procedures of CISC than new entrants.

name: Supplier switching
definition: In adopting RISC, a workstation maker may switch from its supplier of CISC microprocessors to a new entrant supplier. The variable assumes the value of 1 if the firm switched suppliers and 0 otherwise.

name: Backward vertical integration into CISC
authors_terms: ["Backward vertical integration into CISC", "vertically integrated backwards", "vertically integrated into CISC"]
definition: Backward vertical integration into CISC captures the fact that the tacit relations that a firm may have cultivated with its in-house CISC suppliers can now become a handicap in evaluating RISC chip makers and establishing new relations with them. It is measured by whether the workstation maker was vertically integrated into CISC microprocessor design and development before adopting RISC or not.

name: Customer capabilities obsolescence
authors_terms: ["Customer capabilities obsolescence", "customers' capabilities are rendered obsolete", "customer capabilities obsolescence"]
definition: Customer capabilities obsolescence is measured by whether customers have to change from the operating system that they used with their CISC workstations to a new incompatible one when they buy RISC workstations. A new operating system is not only competence destroying to customers who must learn how to use it; often it also means that customers may not be able to use the applications programs that they had accumulated with the old operating system.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "workstation revenue market share", "dollar market share", "revenue market share"]
definition: The dependent variable is a firm's performance in developing and marketing a RISC workstation. This is measured by dollar market share for each workstation for each year that the product is in the market in the period studied, from 1988 to 1992.

name: Noncompete incidence
authors_terms: ["incidence of noncompetes", "noncompete incidence", "State-Industry Noncompete Incidence", "incidence of enforceable noncompetes"]
definition: The incidence of noncompetes is the fraction of workers constrained in a labor market; it is measured as the proportion of individuals bound by a noncompete in each state-industry.

name: Noncompete enforceability
definition: Enforceability is the extent to which courts will enforce the constraints. To become a legally binding constraint on an individual's mobility, noncompetes must be agreed on contractually and must be held up in court.

name: Job offers
definition: Job offers are a revealed indicator of the underlying recruitment, search, and bargaining factors because they represent a culmination of the recruitment, search, and bargaining processes.

name: Employee mobility
definition: Tenure reflects a lack of prior mobility (i.e., if a worker has stayed a long time at his or her job, it is because that worker has not had a mobility event).

name: Wages
definition: Wage outcomes are determined by preferences, the expected productivity of the potential match, and rent sharing by firms with workers; the authors use the worker's logged hourly wage in wage regressions.

name: Supplier performance
authors_terms: ["supplier performance", "supplier profitability", "supplier's return on sales from the OEM's business"]
definition: By supplier performance, we refer to the supplier's returns from conducting business with a specific OEM customer, and therefore the explanatory (governance) variables are also specific to the chosen customer.

name: Asset specificity
definition: The term TSI refers to durable investments undertaken by the supplier to support the unique transaction with an OEM customer, wherein such assets have little alternate use.

name: Buyer dependence
authors_terms: ["buyer dependence", "OEM dependence", "buyer's credible commitment", "black-box parts design", "supplier replacement time"]
definition: The customer's dependence on technological or product design, or both, serves as a credible hostage because it guarantees steady demand realizations. Credibility is also rooted in the inability of the OEM customer to switch suppliers easily.

name: Information exchange
authors_terms: ["information exchange", "information sharing by the supplier", "sharing of production information", "sharing of cost information"]
definition: Suppliers need to share their process and cost information for the success of JIT exchange, and yet getting the suppliers to share the information has proved elusive to OEMs. Information sharing by the supplier is measured by two variables: the extent to which the supplier provides details of its production process to the OEM customer, and whether any cost information is shared by the supplier.

name: Cost-plus pricing
definition: The use of rate of return or cost-plus pricing arrangements between buyers and suppliers is pervasive in many industries. The high incidence of cost-plus pricing (or a variant of it; namely, base price plus escalation (BPE)) provisions in LTCs protects supplier interests in that it guarantees a specific rate of return on investment.

name: Target pricing
definition: Buyers commonly set a target sales price for a new model and arrive at the targeted price for each part in a 'market-price minus' manner using VA results. Under the target-pricing regime, buyers typically expect the suppliers to achieve gradual cost reductions through investments in cost-reducing equipment, processes, and through experience curve effects.

name: Expected relationship length
authors_terms: ["expectation of the relationship's future length", "expectation of the length of the relationship", "longevity of association"]
definition: Expectation of the duration of the relationship is measured by a ranked categorial variable with four categories: (1) less than a year, (2) between one and four years, (3) between five and ten years, and (4) more than ten years.

name: Volume stability
authors_terms: ["volume stability", "production stability", "production-schedule sharing and minimal schedule alterations"]
definition: For the supplier to reduce its lot size, customer-delivery schedules must be stable at least for the duration of the supplier's lead time. Volume stability has been measured in terms of the percentage of production schedules that remain unaltered.

name: Contract duration
definition: Contract duration (CONT_DUR) is measured in terms of the number of months for which the parties (supplier and OEM) write a contract.

name: Quantity provisions
authors_terms: ["quantity agreement", "ex ante purchase quantity provisions", "quantity-take requirement"]
definition: Along with contract duration, it is not uncommon to find ex ante purchase quantity provisions in supply contracts. Quantity agreement has been measured as the percentage of customer's requirements to be met by the contract.

name: Progressive corporate activism
authors_terms: ["progressive corporate activism", "progressive activism", "corporate sociopolitical activism", "participation in letter-signing campaigns"]
definition: Public firms proactively taking progressive social and political stands in solidarity with other companies around potentially controversial causes that are seemingly unrelated to their core business functions or products.

name: CEO political ideology
authors_terms: ["CEO political ideology", "CEO ideology", "CEO's ideology", "the CEO's own ideological preferences"]
definition: A relatively consistent and stable reflection of the CEO's values that serves as an indicator of the policies a CEO may choose or an action they may take.

name: TMT political ideology
definition: The political ideology of the top management team, which upper echelons theory suggests shapes the firm's political strategy and which represents a broader coalition of interests than the CEO alone.

name: Employee political ideology
authors_terms: ["Employee political ideology", "employee ideology", "ideology of a firm's employees", "employee political ideology"]
definition: The collective political ideology of an organization's employees; the authors distinguish it from the overall organizational political ideology, which includes CEO and TMT ideology.

name: CEO-employee liberal ideological alignment
authors_terms: ["CEO-Employee liberal alignment", "CEO-Employee liberal political alignment", "liberal alignment between the CEO and employee ideology"]
definition: Ideological alignment occurs when the upper echelon and the firm's employees share a set of overlapping political values; the liberal form means both the CEO and employees fall on the liberal end of the political ideology scale.

name: TMT-employee liberal ideological alignment
authors_terms: ["TMT-Employee liberal alignment", "TMT-employee ideological alignment", "liberal alignment between top management and employee ideology"]
definition: Ideological alignment occurs when the upper echelon and the firm's employees share a set of overlapping political values; the liberal form means both the TMT and employees fall on the liberal end of the political ideology scale.

name: CEO conscientiousness
definition: Conscientious individuals are cautious, deliberate, and intolerant of ambiguity (Bono and Judge, 2004; Costa and McCrae, 1996). They have a need to control their environment (Costa and McCrae, 1988).

name: CEO emotional stability
definition: Emotional stability reflects the ability of individuals to adjust their emotional state to varied situational demands and to remain calm, level headed, and self-confident in stressful situations (McCrae and Costa, 1997).

name: CEO extraversion
definition: The principal component of extraversion is dominance or surgency (Goldberg, 1990; Judge and Bono, 2000; Trapnell and Wiggins, 1990), which makes extraverts assertive, influential, talkative, and forceful in communicating their opinions (Costa and McCrae, 1996; Judge et al., 2002).

name: CEO agreeableness
definition: Agreeable individuals are altruistic, empathetic, kind, cooperative, trusting, gentle, and modest. They value social affiliation with others (Bono and Judge, 2004).

name: CEO openness to experience
definition: Openness to experience promotes unusual thought processes, divergent thinking, and risk taking (McCrae and Costa, 1987).

name: Initiation of strategic change
definition: Initiation of strategic change, defined as discrete changes in the content and scope of a firm's existing strategies in response to environmental changes, subsumes initial activities where 'the knowledge of the need to change is built and a decision to make a change is made' (Dutton and Duncan, 1987: 108).

name: Implementation of strategic change
authors_terms: ["implementation of strategic change", "effective implementation", "strategic change implementation"]
definition: Effective implementation refers to changes in structures, processes, and incentive systems undertaken to support and carry out initiated strategic changes (Dutton and Duncan, 1987; Greiner and Bhambri, 1989). Strategic change implementation entails supportive changes in structures, processes, communication, and incentive systems to carry out and complete the initiated strategic changes (Dutton and Duncan, 1987; Greiner and Bhambri, 1989; Huy, 2002, 2011; Nutt, 1987; Rajagopalan and Spreitzer, 1997).

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "performance effects of strategic change implementation"]
definition: Because most SMEs are privately held, they do not publicly disclose their financial data, so we used the average performance ratings of the CEO and the top executive on a six-item scale adapted from Brouthers, Brouthers, and Werner (2003)-sales growth, net earnings growth, return on capital, market share, return on assets, and return on sales.

name: Licensing manager experience
authors_terms: ["licensing manager experience", "LME", "experience of the licensing manager"]
definition: We created the licensing manager experience (LME) variable by counting the number of prior contracts that were negotiated and signed by the focal licensing manager at the time of invention licensing. Experienced licensing managers generate value through improved selection of promising inventions and better matching with capable partners.

name: Commercial success
authors_terms: ["commercial success", "commercial success of the licensed invention", "licensing revenue", "income earned by an invention"]
definition: The first dependent variable - commercial success - is the licensing revenue earned by the TTO from an invention.

name: Upfront fixed-fee payment
definition: Almost all university licensing agreements contain some combination of an upfront fixed-fee payment and a royalty rate to balance these concerns. Licensing firms pay a fixed-fee payment to the TTO upon licensing the invention and royalties based on sales.

name: Royalty rate
definition: The royalty rate is a percentage of annual sales based on the licensed invention.

name: Science intensity
authors_terms: ["science intensity", "science-intensive inventions", "inventions heavily dependent on academic science"]
definition: The science intensity of an invention was based on the proportion of the number of backward citations to academic scientific articles - out of the total number of backward citations (academic articles plus other patents) - in the invention's patent.

name: Inventor experience
definition: Inventor experience is measured by the average number of prior disclosed inventions among inventors. Inventors experienced in licensing are knowledgeable about working with industry and their commercialization capabilities.

name: Patent scope
definition: Patent scope was created based on 'the number of sub-classes into which the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) assigns the patent' (Lerner, 1994: 320).

name: Resource allocation flow
authors_terms: ["resource-allocation flow across business segments", "reallocation of financial capital expenditures across business units", "capital reallocation", "reallocation flexibility", "Deviation of Investment Ratio"]
definition: At a most basic level, capital reallocation capabilities are indicated by the degree to which a firm changes the amount of capital expended across its business units. The DIR measure captures the rigidity in the capital-allocation process: firms that commit to maintaining stable allocations over time have low DIR, and firms that actively reallocate capital across their business units have a high DIR.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "firm profitability", "industry-adjusted profitability", "industry-adjusted return on assets", "added value to allocation"]
definition: To measure firm performance, the authors decompose a firm's profitability, as measured by ROA, into industry and industry-adjusted profitability, and use industry-adjusted profitability as the dependent variable throughout the analysis. Their alternative measure of firm performance, AVA, measures the extent to which a firm is good at investing more (relative to the industry median) in businesses with higher future prospects (as proxied by Tobin's q) and less in businesses with lower future prospects.

name: CEO stock option pay
authors_terms: ["CEO stock options", "stock option pay", "percentage of stock option pay", "stock option incentives"]
definition: Stock options allow CEOs to participate in upside gains without limit, while providing a floor to avoid losses; they were, at the time, the single biggest element of CEO pay.

name: Investment magnitude
authors_terms: ["magnitude of investments", "size of the outlay", "the size of the bet", "investment spending"]
definition: The first element of risk taking is the size of the outlay, or the amount at stake; for CEOs, the magnitude of investment outlays they make.

name: Performance extremeness
definition: Option pay should lead to performance extremes, defined as wide deviations from neutral or moderate levels.

name: Performance asymmetry
authors_terms: ["performance asymmetry", "performance symmetry", "big losses and big gains"]
definition: The authors contrast extreme performance that is centered on zero and 'evenly divided between big wins and big losses' with the possibility that CEOs who are paid largely with stock options generate more big losses than big wins.

name: Task difficulty
authors_terms: ["quiz difficulty", "task difficulty", "difficulty of the task", "the difficulty of the test"]
definition: The perceived ease of a task derives from a combination of personal ability and task attributes. It can be influenced by variations in either perceived ability or task difficulty.

name: Market entry
authors_terms: ["market entry", "entry decisions", "the decision to enter", "entry rates"]
definition: Each of the game's four rounds involved a decision to either stay out of a new market or to commit resources to entering that market.

name: Self-focus
definition: The degree to which a participant's stated thoughts about an entry decision center on the participant and his or her own ability rather than on factors external to the participant, such as the market, competitors and risks.

name: Market capacity
authors_terms: ["market capacity", "capacity of the competition to reward entrants"]
definition: The market capacity manipulation varied the number of entrants the market could sustain profitably.

name: Estimated competitor entry
authors_terms: ["estimate of the number of other competitors who would enter the market", "estimates of numbers of competitors"]
definition: Participants' estimate of the number of other competitors who would enter the market in each round of the game.

name: Ability factors
definition: Ability factors included those related to the individual decision maker's assessment of his or her ability to successfully run the business, such as self-confidence in, or concerns about, his or her skills or experience.

name: Venture-internal factors
authors_terms: ["Internal factors", "factors internal to the new venture", "factors related to the business itself"]
definition: Internal factors were about the business itself. These included concerns about conflicts between partners, the projected costs and selling prices of products, the capital intensity of the business, or the decision maker's confidence or concerns about the opportunity or technology.

name: External environment factors
authors_terms: ["External factors", "factors outside the business that may affect the business"]
definition: External factors included those within the external environment of the business, such as competitors, the broader economy, or the government.

name: Compensation strategy orientation
authors_terms: ["compensation strategy", "composite pay strategy score", "comps", "algorithmic compensation pattern", "experiential compensation pattern", "strategic compensation patterns"]
definition: The algorithmic and experiential compensation patterns represent two extreme poles on a continuum, with most organizations falling somewhere between these two end poles. The algorithmic pattern relies on mechanistic, predetermined, standardized, repetitive procedures, while the experiential pattern relies on personal skills and attributes as a basis for pay, extensive risk sharing, sensitivity to market rather than internal equity concerns, and a decentralized administrative framework.

name: Firm performance
definition: A composite firm performance score was calculated for each firm consisting of the four measures discussed above, and this composite score was used to categorize firms into performance quartiles. Each of the performance measures (in standardized form) was weighed by its respective factor loading in the calculation of the performance composite.

name: Diversification extent
definition: The extent of diversification measure used in the study is the widely known scheme developed by Rumelt (1974) who operationalized it as the degree to which a firm derives its revenues from single, dominant, related or unrelated products.

name: Diversification process
definition: Process of diversification was measured in a manner similar to Kerr's (1985) study of managerial rewards, which in turn was based on earlier work by Pitts (1976) and Leontiades (1980). Respondents rated the extent to which the firm follows a 'steady state' or an 'evolutionary' diversification process.

name: Manufacturer-specific assets
authors_terms: ["manufacturer-specific assets", "manufacturer-specific investments", "manufacturer-specific knowledge", "specialized human assets", "specific knowledge necessary for a manufacturer's rep to carry out the selling function"]
definition: The most common transaction-specific capital in the context of a manufacturer-rep relationship is specialized human assets. The most prominent example is the specific knowledge necessary for a manufacturer's rep to carry out the selling function for a given manufacturer; it includes special-purpose knowledge, such as knowledge about a manufacturer's product line and specialized selling techniques, as well as investments in working relationships with the manufacturer.

name: Customer-specific assets
authors_terms: ["customer-specific assets", "customer-specific investments", "specific knowledge reps acquire about their own customer accounts"]
definition: In a manufacturer-rep relationship, a rep may also invest in specialized assets with its own customer accounts. These customer-specific investments can take the form of building close, personal relationships or employing other bonding actions with the accounts.

name: Likelihood of terminating the interorganizational relationship
authors_terms: ["likelihood of terminating the relationship", "intention to terminate", "likelihood of relationship termination", "likelihood of changing to a different manufacturer's representative", "likelihood of setting up a direct salesforce"]
definition: Manufacturers typically terminate the relationship with their reps in two ways: by changing to a different rep or by dispensing with the rep and setting up a direct salesforce. Our strategy was to first measure each of these 'intentions to terminate' separately and subsequently combine them into a final measure of the likelihood of terminating the relationship.

name: Length of prior relationship
authors_terms: ["length of prior relationship", "length of the manufacturer-rep relationship", "prior duration", "DYADAGE"]
definition: This construct is the length of prior relationship between the manufacturer and the rep organization in the selected sales district. Specifically, respondents were asked to provide their best estimate (in terms of days, weeks, months, years, or combinations thereof) as to how long their selected manufacturer's representative had been selling the manufacturer's products in the sales district.

name: Use of development-oriented collaborative relationships
definition: Cooperative agreements that involve in-licensing of products or components from other businesses and technology agreements such as joint R&D and joint development of product interfaces or product compatibility.

name: Use of marketing-oriented collaborative relationships
definition: Cooperative agreements that involve marketing or distribution by one business of partners' products and value-added relationships such as a software business reselling systems for a hardware business.

name: Number of collaborative relationships
definition: The cumulative number of interfirm agreements that a business had formed by the beginning of each record year.

name: Use of other interfirm relationships
definition: Out-licensing relationships in which technology is licensed to other businesses and agreements that could not be classified among the development-oriented or marketing-oriented categories.

name: Business survival
definition: Survival is framed as the likelihood that a business will survive in any given year; empirically the authors distinguish between firms that exit an industry by shutting down their businesses (business dissolution) and those that exit by selling their businesses to other firms (business divestiture).

name: Business dissolution
definition: Exit from the industry by shutting down the business, which the authors describe as an unequivocal sign of business failure.

name: Business divestiture
definition: Exit from the industry by selling the business to another firm, an event the authors describe as more ambiguous because it sometimes occurs when at least partially successful businesses are purchased by expanding firms.

name: Environmental shock
definition: Sudden and substantial changes in technology or market segmentation; in this industry the shock was the 1983 introduction of the Prospective Payment reimbursement system and the concurrent increase in selective contracting by third-party payers.

name: Independent commercialization approach
definition: A business with an independent approach carries out some development, production, and marketing functions itself and acquires other components through hands-off relationships with other organizations.

name: Added product scope per time period
authors_terms: ["added product scope per time period", "additional product scope", "added product scope", "product scope expansion"]
definition: The information processing requirements with which a TMT must contend are driven by added product scope per period of time and implicit in that are the number of new products, and how closely they are related to the firm's existing product portfolio, of all of the product expansion steps in that period.

name: Firm performance
definition: Our dependent variable is firm performance. We measured it using the firms' return on assets (ROA) at the end of the expansion period; it reflects the relative efficiency of the use of a firm's assets and the synergies gained through expansion.

name: Task-related faultline strength
definition: Task-related faultlines are based on acquired characteristics that serve as indicators of knowledge and perspectives relevant to particular tasks. In this study they are calculated along organizational tenure, educational specialization, and level of formal education.

name: Bio-demographic faultline strength
definition: Faultline strength based on bio-demographic characteristics, which are innate attributes that are immediately cognitively accessible, pervasive, and hardly alterable; in this study bio-demographic faultline strength is measured by age and nationality.

name: Gender pay gap
authors_terms: ["gender pay gap", "adjusted gender pay gap", "unadjusted gender pay gap"]
definition: The empirical regularity that women are paid less than men despite equivalent qualifications and job responsibilities; in a semilogarithmic wage regression the coefficient on the female indicator, if negative, measures how much the firm's female employees are underpaid.

name: Employee wages
definition: The pay an employee receives. The dependent variable of the wage regression is a weakly increasing concave function of employee wages, with log wages (yi equals ln wi) and untransformed wages as the two empirically relevant cases.

name: Differential influence
definition: A statistic, the differential influence of employee i with respect to the female indicator (DIiF), that is the change in the gender pay gap coefficient from a marginal increase in employee i's wages.

name: Employee gender
definition: If employee i is female, then the element of the female indicator vector is one and zero otherwise.

name: Pay-relevant observables
definition: Employee, job, and potentially performance characteristics that would legitimately affect pay, such as age, experience, education, merit rating, and job category.

name: Resemblance to men on observables
authors_terms: ["similar to men on observables", "resemble men on observables", "typify men on observables"]
definition: The degree to which an employee scores high (low) on observables that men tend to score high (low) on; female employees who resemble men on observables and the few male employees who strongly typify men on observables have high differential influence.

name: Pressure for gender pay equity
authors_terms: ["pressure for gender pay equity", "pressure to reduce its gender pay gap", "internal or external pressure"]
definition: Internal or external pressure on a firm to reduce its gender pay gap, part of a growing focus on corporate social responsibility among stakeholders.

name: Use of ethics codes in strategic decision-making
authors_terms: ["ethics code use", "use of ethics codes", "use of their firms' ethics codes in strategic decision-making", "incorporation of ethics codes into strategic decision-making"]
definition: In our study, the behavior or action of interest is the incorporation of ethics codes into strategic decision-making.

name: Felt stakeholder pressure
authors_terms: ["felt stakeholder pressure", "stakeholder pressure", "pressure felt from salient social referents or stakeholders", "subjective norm"]
definition: The first factor is the subjective norm or the pressure felt from salient social referents or stakeholders by the individual to pursue the course of action in question.

name: Pressure from market stakeholders
authors_terms: ["pressure from market stakeholders", "market stakeholder pressure", "market stakeholders"]
definition: Market stakeholders interact with the firm through some form of economic transaction and play an integral role in the firm's value chain.

name: Pressure from non-market stakeholders
authors_terms: ["pressure from non-market stakeholders", "non-market stakeholder pressure", "non-market stakeholders"]
definition: Non-market stakeholders are those who interact with the firm on a non-economic basis.

name: Perceived internal benefits of ethics codes
authors_terms: ["internal perceived benefits", "internal benefits", "create an ethical firm culture", "deter unethical behavior"]
definition: Ethics codes can have positive internal consequences, promoting a broad ethical culture or value system as well as deterring unethical individual behaviors.

name: Perceived external benefit of ethics codes
authors_terms: ["external perceived benefits", "promote a positive external image", "reputational benefits"]
definition: A second potential benefit of ethics codes use lies not so much in doing the right thing, but rather in promoting a positive external image of the firm, influencing the perceptions of the firm's stakeholders, and generating reputational returns.

name: Training in ethics code principles
authors_terms: ["training in ethics codes principles", "ethics training programs", "training", "education or training"]
definition: Training on the principles of ethics codes will provide an awareness and an understanding of how ethics codes might apply in various decision-making contexts.

name: Material financial restatement
definition: Material financial restatements are a function of significant accounting problems within firms and are identified by the U.S. General Accounting Office as resulting from 'aggressive' accounting practices, misuse of facts, oversight or misinterpretation of accounting rules, or fraud in firms. These are not routine financial restatements resulting from changes in accounting procedures or bookkeeping errors.

name: CEO turnover
definition: Departure of a firm's chief executive officer; given the event history data, individuals retaining their positions in a period were assigned a value of 0, and those who left were assigned a value of 1.

name: CFO turnover
definition: Departure of a firm's chief financial officer; given the event history data, individuals retaining their positions in a period were assigned a value of 0, and those who left were assigned a value of 1.

name: Outside director turnover
definition: Departure of an outside (nonmanagement) director from a firm's board; the director and audit committee data sets were each updated annually, as changes in directorships are typically reported only in annual proxy filings.

name: Audit committee turnover
definition: Departure of a member of the audit committee, the board committee tasked with oversight of corporate governance, financial reporting, internal control structure, and audit functions; a director may be removed from a committee without being removed from the board.

name: Restatement prompt source
definition: Restatements were prompted either internally (by a firm's officers or directors) or externally (by external auditors or the SEC). External prompting means the leadership of the firm has twice failed to either detect or disclose improper accounting practices.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["market reaction", "stock market reaction", "cumulative abnormal market-adjusted returns"]
definition: The market reaction to a restatement announcement, which serves as an indicator that a firm's social legitimacy is at particular risk; negative stock market reactions denote a more severe stigma attached to firms' leaders.

name: Value placed on research
authors_terms: ["research orientation", "value placed on research", "value respondents place on research"]
definition: The value respondents placed on research, assessed by asking them to rank a set of criteria according to how they would use them in determining the overall merit of a department.

name: Perceived criticality of support staff relative to faculty
authors_terms: ["perceived criticality of support staff relative to faculty", "perceived criticality of personnel resources", "criticality of support staff"]
definition: Following Salancik and Pfeffer (1974), the authors defined criticality for respondents as the degree to which a resource was needed to maintain their departments' effective operation; the dependent variable is the perceived criticality of support staff relative to faculty positions in times of scarcity.

name: Paradigm development of academic disciplines
definition: The development of the paradigms of respondents' academic disciplines, assessed in terms of the length of the longest chain of prerequisite courses in a discipline; prerequisite course chains constitute a localized indicator of paradigm development.

name: Cooperative exchange norms
authors_terms: ["exchange norms", "cooperative exchange norms", "relational exchange norms", "cooperative norms", "relational norms", "Norms"]
definition: Exchange norms are shared expectations of how transacting individuals will and should behave. The authors use the terms relational and cooperative exchange norms interchangeably to describe the set of norms that supports cooperative adaptation by stressing behaviors that preserve and continue the relationship.

name: Joint transaction-specific investments
authors_terms: ["joint transaction-specific investments", "joint-specific investments", "joint TSI", "bilateral specific investments"]
definition: Specific investments are those investments that are less productive if employed outside the relationship by alternate users or for alternative uses. Joint transaction-specific investments are the idiosyncratic investments made by both parties to the transaction.

name: Observability of effort
definition: Observability is the degree of transparency—the probability that noncooperative behavior will be discovered and subsequently punished. Increased observability strengthens the self-enforcing mechanism and thus makes it easier to elicit and sustain cooperative exchange norms.

name: Exchange performance
authors_terms: ["exchange performance", "evaluation of the other party's performance", "overall satisfaction with outcomes", "willingness to collaborate in the future"]
definition: Performance is a complex construct, often idiosyncratic to the firm and setting; success for one company may constitute failure for another. Because precise economic measures of exchange performance are generally unavailable, the authors use qualitative perceptual measures that capture the evaluation of the partner's performance over the course of the project.

name: Cooperative norm shortfall
authors_terms: ["Low", "unexpectedly low levels of cooperative norms", "underrealization of cooperative norms"]
definition: When realized norms fall below their expected levels, exchange performance, whether measured by economic outcome or perceptual measures, is likely to suffer. The shortfall is operationalized as the negative residuals from the first-stage norms equation, a continuous measure of the degree to which collaborations achieved unanticipated low levels of cooperative norms.

name: Cooperative norm excess
authors_terms: ["High", "unexpectedly high levels of cooperative norms", "overrealization of cooperative norms", "overshooting expectations"]
definition: Overrealization of cooperative norms is argued either not to affect exchange performance or to increase it. The excess is operationalized as the positive residuals from the first-stage norms equation, a continuous measure of the degree to which collaborations achieved unanticipated high levels of cooperative norms.

name: Foreign corporate ownership
definition: Ownership stakes held by foreign industrial corporations, which the authors characterize as concentrated-outside and strategic-foreign holdings. These holdings are primarily foreign collaborator holdings and involve substantial technical and managerial collaborations with Indian firms.

name: Foreign financial institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign financial institutional ownership", "foreign institutional investors (FORI)", "financial-foreign shareholders"]
definition: Ownership by foreign financial institutions whose decisions to buy and sell shares of domestic firms are made by fund managers, whose performance is measured by comparing their results with a stock market index and/or with competing institutions of a similar class.

name: Domestic corporate ownership
definition: Shares held by domestic (Indian) corporations, which the authors describe as among the largest group of blockholders in emerging countries and as the largest component of equity ownership in Indian listed firms; these blockholders usually have a long investment horizon.

name: Domestic financial institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["domestic financial institutional ownership", "domestic financial institutions (DOMI)", "financial-domestic shareholders"]
definition: Domestic financial institutions form a significant chunk of the total shareholding of Indian firms, and consist of development financial institutions, insurance companies, banks, and mutual funds, which are predominantly government owned.

name: Owner-manager ownership
authors_terms: ["ownership by owner managers", "directors and relatives (DIR)", "owner-manager holdings"]
definition: Owner managers have a strong incentive to manage their companies well and generate wealth as their fortunes are tied to the well-being of the company; beyond a particular threshold level of owner-manager holding, the positive alignment effects are likely to be mitigated by entrenchment effects.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Firms are usually classified as belonging to a group when there is common ownership and management by family members; each group has a controlling family that sets the overall strategic direction of the firm and regulates all financial transfers, and every firm within a group has a separate legal entity and its own unique set of shareholders.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured by two variables: ROA, defined as the operating earnings before interest, depreciation, and taxes over the book value of total assets, and the Q ratio, defined as the sum of the market value of equity and book value of debt divided by the book value of assets.

name: Family-friendly workplace practices
definition: Family-friendly workplace practices do not directly affect the workplace, but rather enhance the ability of employees to combine working and personal life; their first-order effect is to 'provide relief for non work concerns'.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors use 'performance' to indicate a firm's financial performance unless noted otherwise, and measure it in multiple ways, including labor productivity and return on capital employed.

name: Workforce skill level
authors_terms: ["skills", "skilled employees", "proportion of skilled employees", "proportion of employees with a university degree"]
definition: The share of a firm's workforce that is highly qualified; the literature on strategic human resource management emphasizes a highly qualified workforce as a factor for competitive advantage, and college-educated workers may be able to extract a larger part of the firm's quasi-rents.

name: Female employee representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of female employees", "percentage of female employees", "Female total"]
definition: The proportion of employees who are female; the authors argue that female employees may demand more favorable FFWP at their workplace, which makes it advantageous and/or necessary for a firm to provide them.

name: Female manager representation
authors_terms: ["proportion of female managers", "percentage of female managers", "Female mngrs"]
definition: The share of the management layer that is female; the authors argue that the female employees best placed to implement improvements in FFWP are managers, who are also in a better bargaining position to negotiate practices beneficial to their own well-being.

name: Quality of management practices
authors_terms: ["management practices", "good management practices", "quality of management practices", "management score", "Mgmt"]
definition: An index of good management practices such as better shop floor operations like lean manufacturing, sensible targets, and merit-based promotion procedures, which prior work has shown to be positively correlated with firm performance.

name: Product market competition
definition: External pressure on the firm originating from its exposure to foreign competition or from deregulation or other structural features of its primary market.

name: Work-life balance
definition: Work-life balance is considered an 'outcome' while FFWP are considered an 'input'; the measure is managers' perceptions of their own firm's work-life balance versus that of other firms in the industry.

name: Coexistence of integrated and specialized firms
authors_terms: ["coexistence of integrated and specialized firms", "coexistence of the two organizational forms", "persistence of integration in the face of specialization"]
definition: Many industries are characterized by the coexistence of both vertically integrated and specialized firms over extended periods of time; in the semiconductor industry integrated incumbents have continued to persist and coexist with the fabless entrants.

name: Systemic innovation
definition: Innovations requiring extensive coordination and communication across different stages of production. A patented innovation is considered systemic if it is categorized by both design and manufacturing classes, suggesting a strong coupling between the two distinct knowledge bases.

name: Autonomous innovation
definition: Innovations that can be introduced without significant adjustment or modification to other stages of production. A patented innovation is considered autonomous if it is categorized by either design-only or manufacturing-only classes.

name: External manufacturing sourcing
authors_terms: ["make-and-buy choice", "make and buy", "using external specialized foundry suppliers", "transacting with specialized firms in upstream markets"]
definition: Instead of viewing their transactional choices as either make (stay integrated) or buy (become specialized), integrated firms can view them as an opportunity to both make and buy, having their own in-house manufacturing as well as using external specialized foundry suppliers.

name: Intermediate market participation
authors_terms: ["participating in intermediate product markets", "intermediate markets", "offering their manufacturing services to fabless firms"]
definition: The emergence of specialized firms can provide integrated firms with an opportunity to participate in intermediate product markets by supplying an upstream good or service to external buyers in addition to internal consumption.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Firms that carry out design, manufacturing, and marketing activities in-house; in the semiconductor industry integrated incumbents, unlike specialized fabless firms, do not rely on external suppliers for manufacturing.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance measured as the firm's return on invested capital (ROIC), used to assess the performance difference between integrated and specialized firms.

name: Host country-industry attractiveness
authors_terms: ["attractiveness", "more attractive", "count of investment transactions", "U.S. investment abroad"]
definition: The authors test the attractiveness of country-industry attributes using a count-based measure of foreign investment—how many incremental investments are made a year in each of a multitude of different countries and their industries. They examine what country-industry attributes attract more investment: why certain industries in certain countries receive more investment.

name: Host country-industry knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["patent count-host", "host country-industry's knowledge stock", "knowledge stock size", "technical activity"]
definition: To indicate knowledge stock, the authors use patent counts; more patents indicate greater knowledge stock size. Catching up emphasizes relative position in knowledge stocks, so larger stocks in target country-industries are more attractive.

name: Home country-industry knowledge stock
definition: The knowledge stock of the focal home country-industry, measured as the U.S. industry-year patent stock. Relative position would be a linear combination of the host patent count and the home patent count—the host count less the home count scaled by the home count—but the authors instead include both component terms.

name: Technical similarity
authors_terms: ["technical similarity", "sourcing technical diversity", "dissimilarity of home and host country-industry knowledge stocks", "technical overlap"]
definition: The authors use the overlap in the distribution of patent stocks across patent classes between a host country-industry and the U.S. industry. Technical similarity is the extent that two countries' industry vectors overlap—the uncentered correlation between a pair of countries' industry technical stocks.

name: Zero technical overlap
authors_terms: ["technical similarity equal zero", "zero technical overlap", "no technical overlap"]
definition: Country-industry-years whose patent-class distribution does not overlap at all with the corresponding U.S. industry, i.e., technical similarity equal to zero. The authors note numerous country-industry-years have zero overlap and include a dummy to account for this zero similarity discontinuity.

name: Procedural justice
authors_terms: ["procedural justice", "procedural justice in multinationals' strategy-making process", "exercise of procedural justice"]
definition: Procedural justice is defined here as the extent to which the dynamics of a multinational corporation's strategy-making process are judged to be fair by the top managers of its subsidiaries.

name: Subsidiary top management compliance
definition: Subsidiary top management compliance is defined here as the extent to which subsidiary top managers carry out the corporate strategic decisions made for their national units.

name: Organizational commitment
definition: When individuals are committed to an organization, they identify with its goals and objectives and pursue them to the best of their ability (e.g., Mowday, Steers, & Porter, 1979).

name: Trust in head office management
definition: When subsidiary managers trust head office managers, they are confident that the intentions and actions of the head office are guided by subsidiary-level concerns as well as by a concern with maximizing corporate revenues.

name: Outcome satisfaction
definition: The extent to which subsidiary top managers are satisfied with the strategic decisions made for their national units; satisfaction with the content of the resulting strategy decisions and preference for another strategy decision for the national unit.

name: Industry globalness
definition: Global industries are defined as those in which the principal strategic requirements for success are maximizing global economies of scale and scope, standardizing the majority of a business's value-added chain activities around the globe, and deploying its worldwide network of resources against its global rivals. Multidomestic industries are defined as industries in which the principal strategic requirements for success are substantially customizing product offerings to local customer needs, adapting the marketing approach to the local market, and instituting competitive moves based essentially on the competitive dynamics in the local market.

name: Redeployment potential
authors_terms: ["redeployment potential", "portfolio venture", "portfolio entrepreneur", "resource redeployability", "redeployment option", "potential for worker redeployment"]
definition: A founder operating multiple businesses has several options to redeploy underutilized workers from one venture to another in case of failure; the potential for worker redeployment reduces the irreversibility of human capital investments. We measure redeployment potential with a dummy for any venture launched and operated by a portfolio entrepreneur.

name: Number of employees hired
authors_terms: ["staff", "number of staff", "number of employees", "number of new hires"]
definition: Our annual and monthly measures of staff are the venture's number of staff employed at the end of the year and the end of the month, respectively.

name: Skill transferability
authors_terms: ["skill transferability", "transferable skills", "cross-industry skill transferability", "skill transferability score"]
definition: The measure assigns a value between 0 and 1 to each occupation-industry pair based on the estimated job availability for the occupation outside the focal industry. The higher the value of the measure, the more likely the employee within a given occupation and industry is to have opportunities outside the focal industry.

name: Positive market signal
definition: We proxy for a positive market signal with firm-level lagged annual revenue; revenue is a frequent proxy for a positive market signal because sales increase when new ventures face greater market demand.

name: Labor market rigidity
authors_terms: ["labor market rigidity", "labor market flexibility", "labor reform", "Employment and Growth Agreement"]
definition: In a rigid labor market environment, terminating employees imposes a more significant financial burden on employers, such as procedural costs of severance payment and potential lawsuits. Following the Employment and Growth Agreement, labor market rigidity decreased because employers could leverage various government programs to hire and terminate more easily.

name: Control system
definition: The approach a superior uses to manage a business unit; in performance evaluation a signal from a worker is measured, evaluated, and rewarded, and that signal can be either the actions of an employee or the outcomes of those actions.

name: Output control
definition: One aspect of employee performance that can be measured is the outcome of an employee's behavior, and control on these outcomes results in output control.

name: Behavior control
definition: A form of control in which the signal measured is the actions of an employee; the superior monitors the employee's decisions and actions on an ongoing basis rather than focusing on the attainment of the desired targets.

name: Resource sharing
definition: The extent to which a focal SBU shares functional activities like marketing, manufacturing, and R&D with other SBUs within a firm.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Porter's (1980) framework containing two opposite types: the low-cost strategy and the differentiation strategy. An SBU pursuing an overall cost leadership strategy has as its dominant focus achieving low cost relative to competitors; a differentiation strategy has as its primary focus creating something that is perceived as unique through superior product features, customer service, brand image, and/or performance.

name: SBU effectiveness
definition: SBU effectiveness measured along several dimensions, with the relative importance of each dimension for the individual SBU used as weights to arrive at a measure of overall effectiveness, and measured by comparing actual performance and a priori expectations rather than on an absolute scale.

name: Vertical integration
definition: For a Champagne house, 'vertical integration' means purchasing vineyards within the region. Such backward integration - houses purchasing vineyards - openly challenges the established division of roles in the industry (into vine growing and winemaking).

name: Foreign diversification
authors_terms: ["foreign diversification", "foreign subsidiaries", "winemaking subsidiaries outside of France"]
definition: The third violation of established roles is for a house to produce (non-Champagne) sparkling wine in a foreign subsidiary; grape growers perceive this action as a threat to the distinctiveness of Champagne wines.

name: Vertical disintegration
definition: It occurs when a house produces Champagne for supermarket brands, which implies a transfer of branding, sales, and distribution to the retailer, leaving only the responsibility of production to the house; this action constitutes a vertical disintegration and a contraction of the house's role.

name: Traditionality
definition: Interviewees described traditional houses as old, family houses from traditional villages that focus on artisanal winemaking rather than company financials. Being traditional refers to a sense of history, and whether a firm is traditional is determined by not only whether it is new to the industry but also whether it has other observable characteristics that are considered typical for an organization of its kind.

name: Price paid for grapes
definition: The price that buyers are charged by the sellers for the grapes they purchase. In the interviews growers viewed prices as a way to punish deviations from the institutionalized status quo.

name: Informal legacy
authors_terms: ["informal legacy", "informal start", "past informal operations", "having operated informally"]
definition: Firms that initiate their operations in the informal economy, that is, without registering at the time of foundation, but later formalize by registering their enterprises, are compared with firms that registered from the outset. All firms in the sample were formally registered at the time of the survey; they differ only in the timing of registration.

name: Export propensity
authors_terms: ["exporting", "export propensity", "propensity to initiate exporting", "participation in export markets"]
definition: The propensity of a firm to export, that is, to sell its products or services to customers outside the country, which is a mode of foreign entry with relatively low levels of resource commitment and risk.

name: Employee mobility
definition: Employees switching firms, studied as mobility between firms. The authors exclude mobility events where the employee founds or joins a start-up firm, or works directly for a client.

name: Employee utilization
definition: Performance within a firm is in large part determined by the degree to which an organization is able to integrate and utilize the employee in its value creating activities. The level of employee utilization is measured in terms of revenue from lobbying activities an individual lobbyist has participated in.

name: Human capital resource similarity
definition: Human capital resource similarity between an employee and firm refers to the degree to which an employee's human capital resources overlap with the human capital resources embedded within a given firm. Fit in terms of similarity means an employee's general human capital resources supplement the general human capital resources of employees within the firm.

name: Human capital resource complementarity
definition: Complementarity fit in terms of human capital resources involves situations where an employee's human capital resources differ from the human capital resources possessed by a firm, but the differences are beneficial in that the employee's human capital resources address a limitation or void in terms of the firm's human capital resources.

name: Internal social capital transfer
definition: Internal social capital refers to relationships developed within a firm (e.g., coworkers). A hiring firm may be able to utilize the benefits of an external hire's prior investments in internal social capital if it can be retained when the employee switches firms; one way employees can retain the benefits of coworker relationships is to move as a group, i.e., comobility.

name: External social capital transfer
authors_terms: ["external social capital resources", "client relationships", "retained client ratio"]
definition: External social capital refers to relationships developed outside the firm with external constituents; the focus of the framework is external social capital in the form of client relationships. The value of these relationships depends on whether the clients choose to follow the employee if the employee switches firms.

name: Skill-based pay
authors_terms: ["skill-based pay", "skill-based pay program", "skillbased pay", "skill- or knowledge-based pay"]
definition: A skill-based pay system motivates skill acquisition and demands demonstration of competency; it rewards the work-related attributes (knowledge, skills, and abilities) of individuals rather than the attributes of the task.

name: Product quality
definition: An expected organizational outcome of a skillbased approach to pay is increased product quality.

name: Productivity
definition: In addition to increased quality, organizations expect an increase in long-term productivity from skill-based pay systems.

name: Labor cost
definition: A potential disadvantage of skill-based pay is its effect on labor cost. As an employee progresses through a pay structure, both the cost of the individual's labor and total labor cost may rise.

name: Block-holding activism
authors_terms: ["block-holding activism", "financially motivated block-holding activism", "block-holding activists", "block-holding shareholder activists"]
definition: We focus on financially motivated block-holding activism, which is defined as cases in which an investor acquires at least 5% equity ownership in a firm with the stated intent to influence management or corporate direction as disclosed in Schedule 13D filings.

name: Lobbying expenditures
definition: Lobbying expenditures equals the natural logarithm of one plus a firm's total lobbying expenditures in a year.

name: Board political expertise
authors_terms: ["political directors", "political director ratio", "board members' political expertise", "directors with political backgrounds"]
definition: These so-called political directors have experience navigating legislative processes, personal ties to regulators, and specialized knowledge of political institutions. Such experiences and connections have been found to increase the effectiveness of firms' lobbying activities by enhancing the value of lobbying spending.

name: Director bandwidth
authors_terms: ["director bandwidth", "director busyness", "busy political director ratio", "nonbusy political director ratio"]
definition: The concept of director bandwidth highlights that board effectiveness depends not only on directors' knowledge and experience but also, on the cognitive and temporal resources that they can dedicate to firm issues based on their busyness elsewhere.

name: Lobbying-active shareholder ownership
definition: When lobbying-active shareholders hold sizable positions in a firm, managers may infer that lobbying is endorsed and perceive that cutting lobbying expenditures in response to activism could agitate these otherwise supportive owners. Shareholder lobbying activity constitutes a particularly strong and observable signal of shareholder preferences.

name: Shareholder holding period
authors_terms: ["holding period", "long-term lobbying-active shareholder ownership", "short-term lobbying-active shareholder ownership", "long-term investors", "short holding periods"]
definition: An investor's holding period in a specific firm signals more than a general investment philosophy; it indicates accumulated firm-specific knowledge and a commitment to the firm's long-term value creation path.

name: Market leadership
authors_terms: ["market leaders", "market leadership", "market share", "market position", "high-market-share firms", "leading incumbents"]
definition: Market leadership is defined on the basis of market share, i.e. the share of total value shipped in an industry, and the highest-market-share firms are referred to as market leaders.

name: Business process innovation adoption
authors_terms: ["business process innovation", "e-business adoption", "e-buying", "e-selling", "ERP adoption", "Internet-based business practices"]
definition: Adoption of new business practices, in this study the adoption of particular Internet-based business practices; business process innovation is a type of innovation that often spans firm boundaries and has received limited academic attention relative to product and physical process innovation.

name: Information technology capabilities
authors_terms: ["IT capabilities", "IT-related capabilities", "IT sophistication", "intensive internal IT", "prior IT investments"]
definition: A firm that has historically invested in IT, hires employees with IT-related skills, and has an up-to-date infrastructure that integrates easily with next-generation technology will have significantly lower costs of selecting, adapting and implementing new IT-based business processes.

name: Customer IT sophistication
authors_terms: ["customer IT sophistication", "customers' capabilities", "IT savviness of customers", "customer IT capabilities"]
definition: The IT-related capabilities of the locations to which a plant ships its output, used as a proxy for the capabilities of the focal establishment's customers.

name: Product market competition
authors_terms: ["competitive pressure", "Lerner index", "low competition industry", "high competition industry"]
definition: The intensity of product market competition in the plant's primary industry, which the authors assume determines the scope that manufacturers have to demand complementary business process innovation from their business partners.

name: Business-to-consumer orientation
definition: Whether an e-selling transaction is likely to be primarily business-to-business or business-to-consumer, identified at the industry level as industries where 75% or more of the value is transferred to 'final use' by consumers.

name: Innovation novelty
authors_terms: ["innovation novelty", "innovative novelty", "degree of innovation novelty", "degree of innovative novelty"]
definition: Innovative novelty refers to the degree of the original recombination of knowledge components within an industry, a process of bringing together previously unconnected elements (Fleming 2001). Innovation novelty refers to a recombination of knowledge components that is new in a given industry.

name: Venture capital funding
definition: VCs play an important role in fostering the innovation of cash-strapped entrepreneurial ventures by providing financial support and serving as intermediaries for external resources. Venture capital funding is set to 1 when a new venture received VC funding and 0 otherwise.

name: CEO structural power
definition: One source of a CEO's power is structural power that is 'based on formal organizational structure and hierarchical authority,' commonly reflected in the number of titles a CEO holds (Finkelstein 1992, p. 508). A high degree of structural power on the part of the CEO reflects a more centralized decision-making process.

name: CEO expert power
definition: We define a CEO's expert power as power stemming from the CEO's technical expertise and experience, evidenced by the number of patents on which the CEO served as a coinventor.

name: Venture stage of life
authors_terms: ["venture's stage of life", "life stages of a new venture", "early-stage ventures", "late-stage ventures"]
definition: A venture's stage of life can be generally divided into early, middle, and late periods (Aldrich and Ruef 2006). It is a common practice to consider a firm's first five years as the early stage, because this is the period when firms suffer from the 'liability of newness,' meaning they are unknown and likely to fail.

name: Erratic strategic decisions
definition: Erratic strategic decisions refer to a manager's inconsistent judgments that can shape the direction of the firm.

name: Metacognitive experience
definition: Metacognitive experience refers to a person's conscious experiences that are cognitive and affective in nature. These experiences relate to believing that one knows how to think about a task in order to successfully accomplish that task.

name: Environmental hostility
authors_terms: ["environmental hostility", "hostility of the environmental context", "hostile environments"]
definition: By definition, hostile environments are dangerous and threatening.

name: Environmental dynamism
authors_terms: ["environmental dynamism", "dynamism of the environmental context", "dynamic environmental context"]
definition: An environmental context that is dynamic is one with a highly unpredictable and unstable rate of change and high levels of uncertainty about the state of the context, the means-ends relationships, and/or the outcomes of actions.

name: Market orientation
definition: The extent to which a firm engages in the generation, dissemination, and response to market intelligence pertaining to current and future customer needs, competitor strategies and actions, channel requirements and abilities, and the broader business environment. It is examined as a key market-based asset and a firm's 'know-what' knowledge resource.

name: Marketing capabilities
definition: The capabilities by which firms deploy their market orientation into target market(s), usually associated with the marketing function. Two interrelated marketing capability areas have been identified: capabilities concerning individual 'marketing mix' processes, such as product development and management, pricing, selling, marketing communications, and channel management, and capabilities concerned with the processes of marketing strategy development and execution.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured using two approaches: respondents' subjective assessments of their firm's profitability and market effectiveness, and, for a subset of firms, the average return on assets (ROA) over a two-year period.

name: Industry uncertainty
definition: Consistent with Amram and Kulatilaka (1999), the authors define uncertainty as the randomness of the external environment that cannot be altered by the actions of individual firms or managers. In the context of new market entry they are concerned with uncertainty as it relates to the potential cash flows associated with entering the target industry.

name: New industry entry
authors_terms: ["entry", "entry into a new industry", "probability of entry"]
definition: Entry is activity by an existing firm in an industry in which the firm had not reported involvement in the previous 2 years.

name: Irreversibility of investment
definition: Most investments are at least partially irreversible since they cannot be fully recovered and costlessly redeployed in the event of a negative shock. The value of the option to defer is influenced by the degree of irreversibility of the investment required for entry: as those investments become more irreversible, there is a higher opportunity cost associated with entering.

name: Growth options
authors_terms: ["growth options", "option to grow", "total value of growth opportunities"]
definition: The option to grow gains its value from the possibility that early investment will help the firm to develop a 'capability' that will allow it to take better advantage of future growth opportunities in the industry. Since managers have discretion over the exercise of growth options, their value escalates with uncertainty due to the asymmetry in their pay-off distribution.

name: Early mover advantages
definition: Entering earlier may better position the firm to build a technological advantage, develop brand recognition, or accrue any number of resources that may lower costs or increase revenues relative to later movers. When early entry conveys an increased ability to benefit from future growth opportunities, there are added incentives to move early in highly uncertain environments.

name: Change in past internal performance indicators
authors_terms: ["change in past internal performance indicators", "variation of production over the last 2 years", "Past-Prod", "past production growth"]
definition: A firm's past change in internal performance indicators, measured as the variation of production over the last 2 years. The authors argue that when extrapolating the future from the past, firms tend to ignore the 'regression toward the mean' phenomenon.

name: Forecast bias
authors_terms: ["forecast bias", "straight error", "direction of the error", "error direction"]
definition: The straight error, i.e., the difference between each firm's industry growth estimate (IGE) and the actual 1997 industry growth rate, which measures the forecast bias (i.e., the direction of the error).

name: Magnitude of forecast error
