authors_terms: ["magnitude of errors", "absolute error", "absolute value of straight errors", "forecasting accuracy"]
definition: The absolute value of straight errors, which measures the magnitude of the error (i.e., forecasting accuracy).

name: Organizational illusion of control
definition: The two principal sources of illusion of control are (1) perceived ability to influence the environment and (2) organizational self-perception. Illusion of control causes an inaccurate assessment of risks: the higher the perception of control, the higher the likelihood of underestimating risks.

name: Relative investments in dynamic resources
authors_terms: ["relative investments in dynamic resources", "dynamic resources", "relative investments in R&D", "RelativeR&D"]
definition: Investments in dynamic resources (like R&D, recruiting visible managers, and so forth), which are observable and relevant for actual control and are likely to underlie a positive assessment of the future; the more a firm spends on dynamic resources relative to its competitors, the more it is likely to positively bias its forecasts.

name: Organizational self-perception
definition: An extension of perceived self-efficacy to the organization; organizational self-perception concerns, for instance, a firm's advantages, alignment or environmental fit.

name: Organizational attention
definition: Where and how much relative to its competitors a firm focuses its attention impacts its forecasting ability; organizations must focus attention on external and internal sources of information.

name: Relative investments in market information
authors_terms: ["relative investments in market information", "investments in market information", "marketing expenditures", "Rel-Market-Info"]
definition: All sources of market information (e.g., trends in customers' needs and tastes, retailers' aspirations, and competitors' situations) contribute to a firm's forecasting ability; marketing expenditures characterize a firm's focused attention on its external environment.

name: Relative investments in employee capability
authors_terms: ["relative investments in employee capability", "investments in employee capability", "investments in education and training", "Rel-Educ-Invst"]
definition: To articulate and distribute internal information to its employees, a company must focus its attention on employee motivation and capability; a capable manager deciphers and distributes multiple pieces of information to the appropriate beneficiaries.

name: Descriptive social norms for diversity
authors_terms: ["descriptive social norms", "the average observed behavior of individuals or groups in a population"]
definition: Descriptive social norms - defined as the average observed behavior of individuals or groups in a population (Prentice & Miller, 1993) - exert a potent influence on decisions. In this paper the relevant norm is the average number of women (or underrepresented group members) in peer groups.

name: Scrutiny
authors_terms: ["scrutiny", "negative scrutiny", "obtrusive and critical attention paid to particular behaviors"]
definition: Scrutiny refers to obtrusive and critical attention paid to particular behaviors (Sutton & Galunic, 1996), and it can come from a variety of sources.

name: Group visibility
definition: We follow past research and use the term 'visibility' to describe how much attention individuals, groups, or organizations typically receive (Chiu & Sharfman, 2011), regardless of why they are receiving this attention.

name: Group diversity level
authors_terms: ["groups' diversity levels", "the number of women on each board", "the composition of U.S. corporate boards"]
definition: The composition of a group in terms of how many of its members come from an underrepresented population; in the field setting this is the number of female directors serving on a corporate board.

name: Group diversity relative to the descriptive social norm
authors_terms: ["surpassed the pertinent descriptive social norm for diversity", "having two or more women on a board", "met the descriptive social norm for gender diversity"]
definition: Whether a group has already reached or surpassed the descriptive social norm for diversity established by peers; the authors predict that groups are less likely to increase their diversity once they have already reached that norm.

name: Selection of underrepresented group members
authors_terms: ["group diversity decisions", "add new members from underrepresented populations", "adding members of underrepresented populations to groups", "diversity-related hiring decisions"]
definition: Decisions about adding members of underrepresented populations (e.g., women, racial minorities) to groups, examined in board member additions and in experimental selection tasks.

name: Relational embeddedness
authors_terms: ["relational cohesion", "prior ties", "prior alliance ties", "relational embeddedness", "relationship-level cohesion", "alliance ties", "arm's-length ties"]
definition: A structural source of trust is prior ties among alliance members: prior ties give alliance members experience with each other, possibly including experience with how they react to problems and conflicts, so they facilitate development of trust through learning and accommodation. Prior ties also create a structural incentive to avoid noncooperative behaviors.

name: Resource incompatibility
definition: Resource incompatibility occurs when the resources that alliance members possess are insufficiently interchangeable with those held by other alliance members to produce uniform output quality and quantity. It causes inconsistent quality of services and products and implies that some partners may offer more or better resources than others.

name: Triadic closure
authors_terms: ["triadic closure", "closed triads", "third-party ties", "common third-party ties", "structural embeddedness", "network cohesion"]
definition: Two unconnected firms are more likely to form a tie if both have ties with a common third firm, resulting in a prevalence of 'closed triads,' characterized by collaborative ties in all three member pairs. Relationships structurally embedded in triadic ties are expected to be 'sticky.'

name: Position power inequality
definition: Position power in networks derives from control of information and resources; it is the ability to cut partners off that makes the threat of withdrawal effective. Imbalance of power among allying partners is thus a key predictor of network-level friction.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact refers to a 'situation where firms compete against each other simultaneously in several markets'. The multimarket theory prediction is that the more contacts a firm has in other markets with its rivals in a given market, the less competitive pressure it receives from the rivals in that market.

name: Market overlap
definition: Market overlap increases with the number of rivals that a firm faces in each of its operating markets. Whereas mutual forbearance is a source of market stability, market overlap is a source of instability.

name: Alliance duration
definition: The time since an alliance was established; the authors argue that relational and structural cohesion is less predictive of withdrawal as the duration of an alliance increases, because the build-up of experiential cohesion lets alliances with low initial cohesion catch up.

name: Member withdrawal
definition: Member withdrawal from an alliance occurs when a member firm leaves an alliance while the other members continue to operate the route; unlike alliance formation, it can be the unilateral action of a member firm.

name: Tertius iungens orientation
definition: Following Obstfeld (2005), we define TI orientation as an individual strategic orientation toward introducing unconnected others or facilitating new coordination between previously connected actors. The author conceptualized TI orientation as individuals' strategic orientation toward connecting people in their social network.

name: Individual creative performance
definition: Creativity refers to the development of novel and useful ideas, which originate primarily from employees. Employee creativity is the starting point for organizational innovation.

name: Strategic decision comprehensiveness
definition: Fredrickson and Mitchell (1984, p. 402) defined strategic decision comprehensiveness as 'the extent to which an organization attempts to be exhaustive or inclusive in making and integrating strategic decisions.'

name: Strategic decision speed
definition: Strategic decision speed refers to the velocity of the strategic decision-making process from the initial moment at which possible courses of action are considered to the moment at which the commitment to act is made.

name: Stakeholder orientation
definition: Stakeholder orientation is defined as the extent to which a firm's management focuses attention on and integrates the interests of multiple stakeholders in its decision-making. It reflects the extent to which a firm takes the interests of its primary stakeholders into account.

name: Divestiture activity
definition: We conceptualize these transactions as a costly alternative to the negotiated resolution of conflicts among stakeholders within a firm's existing governance structure, albeit one that avoids the potentially even more costly liquidation of the firm. Divestitures can be costly in economic, social, psychological, and resource-based terms for stakeholders.

name: Divestiture mode
definition: The two most common modes of divestiture are spinoffs and selloffs. Spinoffs occur when a divesting firm issues shares in the divested business pro rata to its existing shareholders, resulting in the creation of a new, publicly traded company (the 'spinoff firm'); selloffs occur when a divesting firm sells the divested business to an acquiring firm.

name: Divested business relatedness
authors_terms: ["unrelated businesses", "related businesses", "unrelated to the divesting firm"]
definition: Related businesses are those for which the primary SIC code of the divested business overlaps with that of the divesting firm by at least three digits.

name: Geographic distance
definition: Proximate businesses are those for which the distance between the zipcodes of the divested business and the divesting firm's headquarters is less than the median distance in the sample (562 kilometers).

name: Alliance partnership
definition: One situation in which selloffs economize governance costs on both sides of the transaction is likely to occur is when the divesting and acquiring firms have a current or prior alliance relationship with one another. Alliance partners develop routines, trust, and relational capital from their experience working together.

name: Acquired unit origin
authors_terms: ["unit origin", "unit entry type", "origin of units", "internally developed and acquired units"]
definition: Origin captures how the unit came to enter the firm: whether the company created it internally, obtained it through acquisition, or derived it by recombining several existing units. 'Unit entry type' is 0 for internal units and 1 for acquired units.

name: Time until unit reconfiguration
authors_terms: ["time (in years) until a unit is reconfigured", "duration until unit reconfigured", "duration until reconfiguration"]
definition: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 1 is time (in years) until a unit is reconfigured, calculated as the period between when a unit enters a firm (either by internal development, acquisition, or recombination) and when it is reconfigured (recombined, divested, or dissolved).

name: Unit recombination
authors_terms: ["recombining", "unit recombination", "units that were recombined", "unit was previously recombined"]
definition: Recombining involves the interaction of more than one component: a unit losing its identity and melting into an existing unit, or several units losing their identity and forming a new unit altogether, while resources and activities are still retained by the organization.

name: Unit longevity
authors_terms: ["longevity of business units", "retention", "time (in years) until a unit is divested or shut down"]
definition: The dependent variable is time (in years) until a unit is divested or shut down (exiting the firm), calculated as the time between entry into the firm and when a unit and its activities are completely extracted from the firm. If a unit is recombined with other units it is not considered deleted from the firm; its resources and activities are still within the firm.

name: Interpersonal trust
definition: The extent of a boundary-spanning agent's trust in her counterpart in the partner organization; that is, the trust placed by the individual boundary spanner in her individual opposite member.

name: Interorganizational trust
definition: The extent of trust placed in the partner organization by the members of a focal organization. It describes the extent to which organizational members have a collectively-held trust orientation toward the partner firm.

name: Negotiation costs
authors_terms: ["costs of negotiation", "negotiating costs", "costs of negotiation between the partners to the exchange"]
definition: The costs involved in reaching mutually acceptable agreements, including the time and effort required to determine efficient courses of action and to settle on divisions of costs and benefits.

name: Conflict
authors_terms: ["conflict", "level of conflict in the exchange relationship"]
definition: Divergent goals and unforeseen contingencies in the parties' day-to-day relationship result in disagreements; the construct captures the degree of conflict between the two organizations and the level of conflict between the two boundary-spanning individuals.

name: Supplier performance
definition: The extent to which the supplier has fulfilled the buyer's requirements in terms of price, timeliness of delivery, input quality, and supplier flexibility.

name: HRM investment strategies
authors_terms: ["direct HRM investment strategies", "indirect HRM investment strategies", "inducements and investments", "investment-focused HRM strategy", "investments"]
definition: An investment-focused HRM strategy subsumes HRM practices that ensure a high-quality human capital pool. Inducements and investments in employees increase employees' expected outcomes, making a job more attractive.

name: Employer expectations
definition: HRM practices can also increase the expected contributions of employees. Such employer expectations and the HRM practices that promote them increase what employees must give to an organization.

name: Organizational staffing systems
authors_terms: ["staffing systems", "employee selection (staffing) systems", "staffing practices", "hiring and firing systems"]
definition: The attention an organization devotes to its employee selection (staffing) systems affects the quality of its hires. Two elements of staffing systems are particularly important: how selective the organization can be, or the selection ratio, and the validity of the organization's selection process.

name: Organizational monitoring systems
definition: To the extent that a bad hiring decision is made in the first place, the better the organization is able to monitor its employees, the more likely it is to have information about the quality of its hiring decisions. Employee monitoring provides organizations with better information about employees.

name: Voluntary turnover
definition: An instance of voluntary turnover, or a quit, reflects an employee's decision to leave an organization. In an organization with high quit rates, for various reasons employees find it more attractive to leave than to stay.

name: Involuntary turnover
definition: An instance of involuntary turnover, or a discharge, reflects an employer's decision to terminate the employment relationship. A termination reflects a bad hiring decision that must be corrected.

name: Pay level
definition: Primary and certainly the most visible among an organization's investments is its compensation and benefits package. High pay promotes retention since employees' self interest is maximized through staying.

name: Benefits package
definition: Investment in a good benefits package should achieve the same ends as does high pay—that is, it should reduce voluntary turnover.

name: Job stability
definition: In an era of corporate downsizing, mergers, and acquisitions, job stability is a critical manifestation of an investment strategy. As a critical investment, stability should enhance retention of employees.

name: Training
definition: An investment strategy is also reflected in the training opportunities for employees an organization offers. An organization may be able to correct selection problems by training employees in requisite skills.

name: Procedural justice
definition: When HRM systems ensure procedural justice (for example, through grievance or appeal procedures), the relative attractiveness of a workplace is enhanced and employees' propensity to leave is diminished.

name: Electronic monitoring
definition: Employee monitoring is an expectations-enhancing HRM practice. It can take different forms; close supervision, low span of supervisory control, and electronic monitoring are a few.

name: Time on the road
authors_terms: ["time on the road", "how often drivers are on the road"]
definition: In the trucking industry, a critical factor affecting expected contributions is how often drivers are on the road, or time on the road. A company that enables drivers to be home more often is placing lower demands on drivers than one that enables their being home less often.

name: Selection ratio
definition: The selection ratio addresses how choosy an organization is in hiring employees. It reflects how selective the organization can be.

name: Use of valid selection procedures
definition: The use of valid selection procedures should lead to fewer bad hires. The index represents the general validity of an organization's selection procedures rather than validity with respect to driving jobs specifically.

name: Performance appraisal
definition: Performance appraisals are ways for organizations to keep track of the value provided by each employee. Consequently, performance appraisals should be positively related to involuntary turnover.

name: Foreign government ownership
authors_terms: ["state-owned foreign firm", "foreign government ownership", "government ownership", "state ownership", "state-owned foreign firms"]
definition: Acquisitions by state-owned foreign firms are viewed as less acceptable, appropriate, or desirable by host-country stakeholders because these firms might serve their home governments' political interests, may be less efficient, and are difficult for local stakeholders to evaluate due to lack of transparency.

name: Acquisition completion
authors_terms: ["acquisition completion", "completion of a cross-border acquisition", "likelihood of acquisition completion", "completion of an acquisition"]
definition: Acquisition completion refers to whether an announced cross-border acquisition was completed after the public announcement of a takeover attempt by the foreign firm.

name: Acquisition duration
authors_terms: ["acquisition duration", "time lapse between the announcement and completion", "time to complete an acquisition"]
definition: Acquisition duration denotes the number of days for a foreign firm to complete an acquisition, calculated as the difference between the date when an acquisition was announced and the date when the acquisition was completed.

name: Target public status
authors_terms: ["target public status", "public status of target firms", "target firm's public status"]
definition: Whether the acquisition target is a publicly listed firm rather than a privately held firm; public firms 'depend on public opinion for legitimacy and resources' and are under constant monitoring by regulatory authorities, analysts, and investors.

name: Target R&D alliances
authors_terms: ["target R&D alliance", "R&D alliances of target firms", "target firm's R&D alliances"]
definition: The R&D alliances a target firm has formed in the United States prior to the focal acquisition announcement; firms with more R&D alliances are likely to be active innovators and to possess critical technologies and technical know-how.

name: Host-country experience
authors_terms: ["host-country alliance experience", "host-country acquisition experience", "alliance and acquisition experience in the host country", "host-country experience"]
definition: The alliance and acquisition experiences of state-owned foreign firms in the host country may enhance their legitimacy, thereby helping them overcome legitimacy barriers to acquisition.

name: Board committee overlap
authors_terms: ["board committee overlap", "linking pin directors", "linking pins", "intra-board interlocks"]
definition: We suggest a synchronization mechanism that can enable both increased access to explicit knowledge as well as transfers of tacit knowledge-the use of 'linking pins' (Likert, 1961)-which, through their concurrent appointments on the audit and compensation committees, facilitate instantaneous and timely knowledge transfer between the two committees.

name: New board committee overlap formation
authors_terms: ["Committee Overlap Appears", "board committee overlap formation", "new linking pins"]
definition: The 'Committee Overlap Appears' variable describes board contexts where there was no board committee overlap in year t - 1 but there was a board committee overlap in year t (coded as 1 = yes, 0 = no).

name: Board committee overlap dissolution
authors_terms: ["Committee Overlap Disappears", "dissolution of existing linking pins"]
definition: The 'Committee Overlap Disappears' variable describes board contexts where there was committee overlap in year t - 1, but no board committee overlap in year t (coded as 1 = yes, 0 = no).

name: Total executive compensation
authors_terms: ["total executive compensation", "total compensation", "level of total compensation"]
definition: In addition to total compensation (logged), we considered the following two ratios: (1) salary to total compensation to assess reliance on behavioral compensation; and (2) options to total compensation to assess the reliance on a particular type of outcomes based compensation (Eisenhardt, 1989).

name: Salary proportion of total compensation
authors_terms: ["salary as a proportion of total compensation", "salary to total compensation"]
definition: salary to total compensation to assess reliance on behavioral compensation

name: Options proportion of total compensation
authors_terms: ["options as a proportion of total compensation", "options to total compensation"]
definition: options to total compensation to assess the reliance on a particular type of outcomes based compensation (Eisenhardt, 1989)

name: Accounting conservatism
authors_terms: ["accounting conservatism", "conservatism in financial reporting", "less conservative accounting", "conservatism in accounting choices"]
definition: An important element of managerial accounting discretion is the extent of conservatism in financial reporting that results from higher verification standards for gain recognition, while reducing managerial ability to withhold information on expected losses. Put another way, accounting conservatism is a choice undertaken by management that results in timely recognition of losses, and thereby prevents the extended pursuit of negative net present value projects.

name: Eponymy
authors_terms: ["eponymy", "eponymous ventures", "dummy for eponymy", "naming the firm after the founder"]
definition: Eponymy means the founder affixes his or her own surname to the business name, which more strongly links the firm's reputation to the entrepreneur's personal reputation. Because eponymy is a choice, the willingness to create this stronger link is a signal of underlying quality.

name: Profitability
definition: Firm profitability as captured by return on assets. The variable ROA is EBIT divided by assets, and the authors describe ROA and sales growth as indicators of 'success'.

name: Sales growth
definition: Growth of the firm's sales. Growth is computed as ln(Sales_t / Sales_{t-1}), and the authors frame rapid scaling as the objective that typically requires attracting outside capital.

name: Regional financial development
definition: Financial development refers to the quality and quantity of a firm's local financial institutions. In more financially developed regions the expected benefits of seeking financing are higher because there are a greater number of financial intermediaries with deeper expertise.

name: Industry external finance dependence
authors_terms: ["external finance dependence", "external equity dependence", "industry external dependence"]
definition: External finance dependence is the ratio between capital expenditures minus cash flow from operations and capital expenditures; external equity dependence is the ratio between the net amount of equity issued and capital expenditures. The value of obtaining external financing should be higher for firms in industries that are more reliant on external finance.

name: Financier bandwidth
definition: Because due diligence investigations take time, effort and money, financiers cannot investigate every firm, but only a fraction of them; there is a capacity constraint that limits the fraction of firms that financiers can investigate. The authors operationalize the inverse of bandwidth as density: as the number of firms closer to a bank increases, the likelihood that the focal firm will attract financing decreases.

name: Supplier capability accumulation
definition: We define learning by supplying as the accumulation of technological and marketing capabilities resulting from a firm's experience as an OEM supplier.

name: Supply experience
authors_terms: ["duration and extent of supply activity", "supply time", "cumulative customers", "supply experience"]
definition: Our first set of independent variables measures the duration and extent of a focal firm's supply experience in the mobile telecom handset industry.

name: Customer capabilities
authors_terms: ["capabilities possessed by the customer(s)", "technological sophistication of customers", "customer patents", "market leaders"]
definition: To capture the extent to which a supplier's customers can provide a window on the technological frontier we include a variable CUSTOMER PATENTS... to capture the extent to which a supplier's customers provide a window on the marketing frontier, we include the count variable CUM. LEADERS.

name: Preexisting capabilities
definition: An OEM supplier's accumulation of capabilities will be positively related to the level of its own preexisting capabilities.

name: Supply relationship scope
definition: supply relationships that encompass design in addition to manufacturing (i.e. Original Design and Manufacturing or ODM relationships) should offer greater opportunities for supplier learning than manufacturing-only ('pure' OEM) relationships.

name: Customer type
definition: The coexistence of two distinct categories of mobile handset providers (branded producers and mobile telecom operators), both of whom source phones from OEM suppliers.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: Our primary measure of suppliers' technological capabilities is based on patent data. PATENTS is defined as the number of 'patent families' in successful telecom-related U.S. patent applications filed by supplier i, in year t.

name: Marketing capabilities
definition: For our analysis of marketing capabilities we construct two firm-level proxies. The first, OWN BRAND is an indicator variable marking the first introduction of one or more own-brand mobile handsets by supplier i. Our second proxy for market capabilities is BRANDED SALES, the total number of units of own-brand handsets sold by supplier i in year t.

name: Non-location-specific knowledge transfer to acquired firms
authors_terms: ["non-location-specific knowledge transfer", "N-LSKT to", "N-LSKT to foreign acquired firm"]
definition: Non-location-specific knowledge relates to firm-specific knowledge, such as expertise in management practice, product and process design and research and development. N-LSKT involves piecemeal replacements of acquired firms' capabilities, which may often disrupt acquired firms' power structures, elevating uncertainty, and ultimately affecting their performance negatively.

name: Acquired firm performance
definition: The foreign acquired firm's performance following the acquisition, gauged with four items covering profitability, market share, sales volume, and new product development.

name: Acquirer predeal success
authors_terms: ["acquirer's predeal success", "predeal success of the acquirer", "acquirers' predeal success"]
definition: An acquirer's success before the deal, measured as industry-adjusted average return on assets during the three years before the deal. Success increases a firm's reliance on preexisting capabilities without adaptation and limits responding to performance feedback.

name: Functional integration
definition: Functional integration refers to the extent to which the practices, policies, and structures concerning activities within a range of functional areas of acquired firms are combined with those of acquirers.

name: Strategic control
definition: Strategic control refers to the extent to which acquirers set performance goals and strategic plans of acquired firms, thereby providing broad guidelines and aligning acquired firms' strategic agendas within the acquirers.

name: Character reputation
authors_terms: ["character reputation", "character reputation for bad behavior", "general character reputation"]
definition: A general character reputation is 'collective judgements regarding a firm's incentive structures and behavioral tendencies based on observations of its prior actions.' A firm's character reputation for bad behavior speaks to its moral underpinnings - a pattern of behavior across a broad array of activities that is established over time.

name: Capability reputation
authors_terms: ["capability reputation", "capability reputation for bad behavior", "specific capability reputation"]
definition: A specific capability reputation is 'collective evaluations about the quality and performance characteristics of a particular firm.' A firm's capability reputation for bad behavior suggests the firm does a particular activity particularly badly - that is, it may be incompetent in relation to a specific area of operations but is not necessarily inherently bad.

name: Error magnitude
authors_terms: ["error magnitude", "magnitude", "magnitude of the error", "oil spill volume"]
definition: An obvious indicator of an error's seriousness is magnitude, which prior research has shown to correlate with an error's consequences, with smaller errors resulting in firm-specific consequences and larger errors affecting the media coverage of all firms in the industry.

name: Media coverage
authors_terms: ["media coverage", "media coverage of serious errors", "oil spill media coverage"]
definition: Media coverage, by which the authors mean newspaper articles about major oil spills by firms in the oil and gas industry.

name: Women in management
authors_terms: ["percentage of management positions filled by women", "percentage of management positions held by women", "women in management"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's management positions filled by women, where management includes only employees with regular supervisory responsibilities.

name: Emphasis on development and promotion procedures
authors_terms: ["emphasis on development and promotion procedures", "emphasis on development and promotion"]
definition: The extent to which an organization emphasizes procedures for the development, reward, and promotion of its employees, which the authors argue strengthens employees' ties to the company and increases the supply of women qualified for management jobs.

name: Women in nonmanagement positions
authors_terms: ["percentage of nonmanagement positions held by women", "percentage of nonmanagement jobs filled by women"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's nonmanagement positions held by women, which the authors treat as a structural dimension that increases interactions between managers and nonmanagement women.

name: Average management salary
authors_terms: ["average management salary", "average salary levels for an organization's managers"]
definition: The average salary level of an organization's managers.

name: Difficulty in attracting and retaining employees
authors_terms: ["difficulty in attracting and retaining employees", "difficulty in attracting and retaining qualified employees", "difficulty in attraction and retention of employees"]
definition: The extent to which an organization perceives difficulty in attracting and retaining nonmanagement and management employees.

name: Nonwhites in management
authors_terms: ["percentage of management positions held by nonwhites", "nonwhites in management", "percentage of management jobs filled by nonwhites"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's management positions held by nonwhites.

name: Annual management vacancies
authors_terms: ["annual management vacancies", "number of annual management vacancies"]
definition: The rate at which an organization must fill management jobs annually because of turnover among existing managers or growth in the number of management positions.

name: Professional and skilled employees
authors_terms: ["percentage of professional and skilled employees", "percentage of professional or skilled employees", "professional and skilled workers"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's employees who are in professional and skilled positions.

name: Organizational age
definition: How long an organization has been in business, which theories of structural inertia link to resistance to change.

name: Industry type
definition: The type of industry in which a firm operates, distinguishing manufacturing from nonmanufacturing workplaces.

name: Options-based strategy
definition: Options-based firms are those that invest in associates' future partnership potential, emphasizing making partners through mentoring, development, and promotion opportunities.

name: Starting salary
definition: The average starting salary paid to newly hired associates, determined directly from the data.

name: Mentoring
definition: The guidance, feedback, and knowledge about partnership provided to associates by partners, measured as a subscale of the American Lawyer Midlevel Associates Survey.

name: Developmental work experience
definition: Challenging work assignments and client contact that develop associates' professional skills, measured as a subscale of the ALMAS survey.

name: Office and support services
definition: Office space and support services provided to associates, measured as a subscale of the ALMAS survey.

name: Promotion percentage
definition: The ratio of the number of promoted associates to the number originally hired into each entering class.

name: Up-or-out strictness
definition: The ratio of the number of nonpromoted associates leaving a firm to the number of associates actually considered for partnership in each entering class.

name: Firm size
definition: The number of attorneys in the firm.

name: Leverage ratio
definition: The ratio of associates to partners in a firm, a prior HR strategy indicator.

name: Target billable hours
definition: The target number of hours associates are expected to bill.

name: Expected value of partnership
authors_terms: ["expected value of partnership", "expected value of future possible partnership"]
definition: The relative expected value of partnership, estimated as a firm's average profits per partner multiplied by the historical chances of making partner, divided by the partnership track.

name: Partnership track length
definition: The length of time until an associate is considered for partnership.

name: Partnership track variability
definition: Variation in the time until consideration for promotion to partner, calculated as the ratio of the track's range to its lower bound.

name: Intentions to stay
definition: Associates' reported intentions to remain with the firm.

name: Turnover
definition: The rate at which associates leave the firm, a bonding effectiveness outcome.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "revenues per lawyer", "profits per partner", "relative profitability"]
definition: Financial performance measured by revenues per lawyer, profits per partner, and a relative profitability index.

name: Career mobility practices
authors_terms: ["career mobility practices", "hiring, bonding and development, and promotional practices"]
definition: Overall HR strategies in professional service firms are reflected by internally consistent bundles of career mobility practices, including hiring, bonding and development, apprenticeship, frequency of promotion, and up-or-out rules, whose relative levels are logically related and mutually reinforcing.

name: Career-related outcomes
authors_terms: ["career-related outcomes", "prior HR strategy indicators", "bonding effectiveness outcomes"]
definition: All of these career mobility practices would be expected to correspond with career-related bonding effectiveness outcomes, and the corresponding prior HR strategy indicators include leverage ratios and target billable hours as well as firm size.

name: Resource redeployment
authors_terms: ["resource redeployment", "redeployment logic", "intratemporal variance", "Non-Scale Free Variance", "Non-Scale Free Niches"]
definition: With non-scale free resources, diversifiers create competitive advantage by fine-tuning their resource allocation across product niches according to their relative productivities, diverting resources from niches with decreasing returns to product niches with higher returns. Redeployment increases the portfolio's intrafirm variance more than sector variability inducements.

name: Sales growth
authors_terms: ["Sales Growth", "firm sales growth", "overall firm sales growth"]
definition: For each product niche in which a company competes, the authors computed the ratio of sales in a focal product niche over two consecutive years in a specific country (Sales Growth = Salest/Salest-1); values greater than 1 indicate sales growth, values less than 1 signal a sales decrease. In Analysis 2 the same ratio is measured at the firm level.

name: Value of scale free resources
authors_terms: ["Scale Free Value", "brand value", "value of scale free resources"]
definition: High value brands are more capable of generating one-stop-shop effects and apply more readily to extensions; logically, the greater the value of the scale free resource, the greater the value that its corresponding synergies should offer across lines of businesses.

name: Scale free resource sharing
authors_terms: ["scale free resource", "Dummy Scale Free", "Scale Free Niches", "same brand"]
definition: Because a scale free resource can be applied without exhaustion in different domains, each product niche links simultaneously to this common resource, which provides returns through synergies. The presence of a scale free resource is captured with a dummy that takes a value of 1 if, for two paired product niches, the firm uses the same brand.

name: Sales growth variance across scale free niches
definition: The standard deviation, at time t, of sales growth across all product niches linked by the same brand, divided by the number of scale free niches to address potential size effects.

name: Corporate-level planning
definition: The corporate level is responsible for planning which changes a company's business mix as, for example, when it diversifies into or exits from products or markets. It is planning re mergers, divestments and reorganizations, and for a diversified multibusiness firm shifting resources among businesses, or changing the mix of its businesses, corporate-level planning is indicated.

name: Business-level planning
definition: Business-level planning focuses on competitive planning for current business operating within defined industry boundaries. It was viewed as 'the process of determining the scope of a division's activities'.

name: Diversification
definition: The degree to which a firm operates in multiple different lines of business and markets beyond its primary or core business. Increasing diversification is the outcome of successive stages of development, with the final stage representing diversification into unrelated products.

name: Perceived identity-reputation discrepancy
definition: This discrepancy is the difference between the position assigned to the organization in the reputational rankings and the position implied by the organization's identity in the minds of its top managers. It represents an aspect of 'organizational identity threat,' whereby a valued aspect of organizational identity is threatened by an organizational image.

name: Extent of organizational change
definition: The extent of change undertaken by the organization in response to rankings; the measure is an index of change, computed as the sum of all changes undertaken by the school, with each change weighted by its rating for magnitude of change.

name: Perceived validity of rankings
definition: The validity of a measure is the extent to which it measures what it is supposed to measure. The authors note that factors such as the sources of information, evaluation criteria, and methodology used by rankings are important considerations in assessing their validity.

name: Perceived strategic impact of rankings
authors_terms: ["perceived strategic impact of the rankings", "perceived strategic impact"]
definition: Top managers' perceptions of the extent to which the rankings have a strategic impact on the welfare of their organization, based on the perceived effects of rankings on the perceptions and actions of key constituents such as customers and employees.

name: Strength of organizational identity
definition: The extent to which an organization's identity is 'widely shared and deeply held by organizational members.' Organizations with strong identities generally tend to discount negative feedback from their environment and to resist change in response to external feedback.

name: External orientation of organizational identity
authors_terms: ["external orientation of organizational identity", "external, market orientation"]
definition: An aspect of organizational identity whereby organizations define themselves based on economic, utilitarian concerns, rather than on ideological and value-based, normative concerns; the authors discuss the continuum from internal, normative orientation, to external, utilitarian orientation.

name: Vertical integration
definition: For each specialty trade activity the contractor must decide whether to rely on external subcontractors or to execute the task directly; 'to buy' implies using subcontractors and internalizing means performing the activity with the contractor's own procurement team.

name: Temporal specificity
authors_terms: ["temporal specificity", "transactional hazards caused by temporal specificity"]
definition: A particular type of specificity that arises in construction because the success of specialty trade activities, and of the project as a whole, depends on timely completion; it is a combination of switching costs, change orders, and costs of project delay.

name: Quality standards enforcement
authors_terms: ["enforcement of quality standards", "quality measurement", "measurement transaction costs"]
definition: Governmental regulations typically appoint specialized agents that are responsible for evaluating construction quality and certifying that this quality meets required standards before issuing permits; where such enforcement is weak, vertical integration is increasingly used as a mechanism to save 'measurement' transaction costs.

name: Institutional change
authors_terms: ["institutional change", "change in the 2006 Chilean subcontracting law", "change in the Chilean outsourcing law"]
definition: Changes in property rights that affect the definition of the available uses of a good or an asset, and thereby the transaction costs faced by economic actors; in this setting the 2006 Chilean subcontracting law increased the transaction costs of subcontracting.

name: Productive capabilities
definition: The concept of capability refers to the productive efficiency of the firm in executing its activities: a strong capability implies a high productivity, whereas a weak capability implies a low productivity.

name: Cartel longevity
definition: The longevity of the cartel was measured by the period between the cartel's formation date and its termination date. Longevity, or survival, is a basic goal for a business organization and directly measures organizational failure.

name: Variety of age-based experience
definition: In this paper, we study the different types of experience associated with the age of an organization, and focus on the variety of age-based experience between firms. This is the recombination property of diverse knowledge pools that is likely to benefit the group.

name: Separation in uncertainty avoidance
definition: We refer to uncertainty avoidance as the extent to which parties feel either uncomfortable or comfortable in novel, unknown, surprising, and unusual situations. Separation in uncertainty avoidance is minimal when all actors in a group share the same values and maximal when a group is composed of two extreme cliques polarized on opposite levels of tolerance for uncertainty.

name: Power disparity
definition: Disparity refers to the differences in the concentration of valued social assets or resources (such as differences in the possession of pay or power) among unit members, and is studied as dispersion along a hierarchical continuum. The disparity was studied through the various sizes of the firms, as this indicates diverging power between the firms involved in collective organizational misconduct.

name: Practice-specific career experience
authors_terms: ["practice-specific experience", "practice-specific career experience", "prior experience in independent venture capital (IVC) firms"]
definition: Practice-specific experience is prior career experience performing a practice. For CVC managers it is career experience in independent venture capital firms, which yields specific knowledge about the activities that comprise the practice and mental models of its accustomed goals and methods.

name: Organizational fit-specific career experience
authors_terms: ["organizational fit-specific experience", "firm-specific career experience", "fit-specific experience-organizational", "internal hires"]
definition: Organizational fit-specific experience is career experience in the adopting organization, which gives firm-specific knowledge of the cultural, political, and strategic context and internalized mental models that inform assessment of the fit between a practice and the organization.

name: Technical fit-specific career experience
definition: Technical fit-specific experience is career experience that enables assessment of the technical fit between a practice and the technologies already in use by an adopting organization, whether or not the experience was acquired within the adopting firm.

name: Practice variation in goal orientation
authors_terms: ["extent of variation in goal orientation", "goal orientation is modified", "goal orientation"]
definition: The extent to which the goals of an adopted practice are changed as the practice is translated into a new organization, ranging from the canonical financial goal orientation of the practice to a strategic goal orientation oriented to the adopting firm.

name: Practice variation in operational strategies
authors_terms: ["extent of variation in operational strategies", "operational strategies are modified", "CVC operational strategies"]
definition: The extent to which the operational methods of an adopted practice are changed as the practice is implemented in a new organization, in this setting the investment stage and the range of investment targets.

name: Mindful use of technologies
authors_terms: ["mindful use", "mindful use of technologies", "mindful use of healthcare information systems", "mindfulness with IT"]
definition: Mindful use is the timely utilization of technologies to facilitate ongoing collective alertness and response to customer and operational needs within the specific context and organizational systems; it is based on the five mindful processes of mindful organizing.

name: Adherence to specified routines
authors_terms: ["adherence to specified routines", "ASR", "specification of routines", "specified routines"]
definition: Specification of routines refers to organizing through the precise content, timing, and/or sequence of work practices to meet set standards based on successful procedures; adherence to specified routines can represent effortful accomplishment in producing consistent patterns of action.

name: Time-sensitive performance
definition: Measures with specific time requirements; time-sensitive performance is dependent on the timing of actions.

name: General performance
definition: Measures that do not have specific timing requirements; general performance does not rely on urgency in timing.

name: Information technology adoption
authors_terms: ["level of IT adoption", "IT adoption", "HIT adoption", "aggregate levels of IT"]
definition: The hospital's aggregate level of IT adoption, calculated as the proportion of 87 types of live and operational technologies; it serves as the contextual factor, or grouping variable, for the split-group analyses.

name: Corporate donation
definition: Corporate donation is a type of corporate social responsibility practice, the private provision of public goods that used to be foreign to China, where the government was the sole provider of public goods and social services. The authors view the substantial increase of corporate philanthropy in China as a notable institutional change.

name: Returnee directors
definition: Returnee directors are a firm's Chinese directors who have foreign experience; a Chinese director has foreign experience if he or she has studied or worked outside mainland China.

name: Returnee directors from high-donation countries
authors_terms: ["returnee directors from high-donation countries", "returnee directors with relevant exposure", "returnee directors with relevant experiences"]
definition: Returnee directors with experience in countries where the practices and values are more conducive to corporate donation, i.e., high-donation countries, have likely received more exposure to the institutional idea of corporate donation and are therefore more likely to employ it when they return.

name: Returnee directors from low-donation countries
definition: Returnee directors coming back from countries with World Giving Index scores equal to or below the median of all sample countries; local directors and returnee directors from low-donation countries are not exposed to the idea of corporate donation in the same way.

name: Foreign directors from high-donation countries
authors_terms: ["foreign directors from high-donation countries", "foreign directors with comparable exposure"]
definition: Foreign directors who are foreign nationals with experience in countries whose practices and values are conducive to corporate donation; they are immersed through primary socialization but are less embedded in the focal institution.

name: Foreign directors from low-donation countries
definition: Foreign directors who are foreign nationals coming from countries with low levels of charitable giving.

name: Overseas duration of returnee directors
authors_terms: ["average overseas duration of returnee directors from high-donation countries", "duration of staying abroad", "length abroad"]
definition: The longer the duration of staying abroad, the more likely returnee directors are to get exposed to relevant sources of institutional ideas.

name: Board interlocks
authors_terms: ["local board interlocks", "interorganizational embeddedness", "returnee directors from high-donation countries and on multiple boards"]
definition: Returnee directors achieve a higher level of embeddedness through interorganizational connections; board members who serve on multiple corporate boards often serve as information circuits for new practices and maintain higher levels of cohesion with other corporate elites.

name: Politically connected local directors
definition: Local directors who hold political titles such as membership of the National People's Congress, membership of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, or appointment as a Government Counselor. Politically connected directors have strong embeddedness in the home institution.

name: Field need for institutional solutions
authors_terms: ["field-level conditions", "per capita GDP", "field need for exposure", "low levels of economic development"]
definition: Poverty at the local level is a field condition that may enhance the need for institutional transposition by returnee directors; provincial-level economic development is measured by per capita GDP.

name: Institutionalization of corporate donation
definition: The level of institutionalization of corporate donation is higher after 2008, given increasing regulatory pressure from the Chinese government and the 2008 earthquake that triggered activism demanding corporate donations, so the need for embedded actors such as returnee directors to implement it may become less evident.

name: Feedback delay length
definition: Feedback delays, time delays between actions and the realization of steady-state outcomes, are an important feature of such transient dynamics, although other features of these transient dynamics may also matter for learning.

name: Outcome uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty is a rather broad construct, and this study focuses on outcome uncertainty: how an observed outcome may deviate from its expected value because of randomness in the outcome generation process or in measurement.

name: Quality of learning
definition: Our hypotheses relate to the quality of learning and heterogeneity in strategies and performance. Quality of learning can be manifest both in the performance of adopted strategies and in the content of those strategies.

name: Strategy and performance heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity in strategies and performance", "heterogeneity in outcomes"]
definition: We define four different measures to quantify different aspects of those outcomes and quantify heterogeneity in terms of variance of those measures.

name: Strategy coverage
definition: Strategy Coverage captures the breadth of search as measured by the standard deviations of Compensation and Work Structure over the 96 training periods; we add the Z-scores of these two components together for an overall measure of strategy coverage.

name: Persistence
definition: Persistence captures the mean number of evaluation periods (in quarters) that decision makers stay with each strategy to see its implications before making any changes.

name: Step length
definition: Step Length captures the length of exploration segments as measured by the average normalized Euclidian distance traveled in each exploratory move during the training rounds.

name: Partner power and scale
authors_terms: ["partners of comparable power and scale of operations", "large global partners", "powerful world-class partners", "small or medium-size firms with regional operations"]
definition: Partners whose position is comparable to that of GE because they operate on a similar scale; these are firms whose multinational scope suggests they could develop the resources and abilities to pose a formidable threat to GE's aspirations for global market leadership, in contrast to firms that are not in the same 'league' as GE.

name: Scope of collaboration
authors_terms: ["scope of its collaboration", "scope of the value-chain", "geographical and value chain collaboration", "scope of activities", "scope of the market"]
definition: Each joint venture was categorized along two dimensions of scope: (a) whether it was intended to serve global versus regional markets; and (b) whether it was designed to cover a broad versus narrow range of value-chain activities.

name: Alignment with dominant logic
authors_terms: ["depart from GE's dominant logic", "more consistent with the corporation's dominant logic"]
definition: Joint ventures that depart from GE's dominant logic, as opposed to joint ventures that are more consistent with the corporation's dominant logic; a departure is presumed when a business unit forms a broad based alliance with a large global partner.

name: Joint venture survival
authors_terms: ["early success or failure of the alliance", "terminated", "successfully made the transition from agreement to implementation", "premature termination of alliances"]
definition: Whether the joint venture successfully made the transition from agreement to implementation, rather than being terminated soon after it was announced.

name: High reputation
definition: 'High reputation' refers to the accumulation of high levels of public recognition of the quality of a firm's capabilities and outputs; it is best understood as an intangible asset based on broad public recognition of the high quality of a firm's capabilities and outputs.

name: Firm celebrity
definition: 'Celebrity' refers to 'a high level of public attention' focused on a firm combined with 'positive emotional responses from stakeholder audiences.' The combination of visibility and emotional resonance gives celebrity its distinctive properties and effects.

name: Positive material earnings surprise
authors_terms: ["positive surprise", "material positive earnings surprise", "positive material earnings surprise"]
definition: Earnings surprises are positive when the announced earnings exceed analysts' estimates. Material earnings surprises are those that deviate from consensus forecasts by more than a few cents or a significant percentage and are more consequential for firms and investors.

name: Negative material earnings surprise
definition: Earnings surprises are negative when the announced earnings fail to meet analysts' estimates. Material earnings surprises are those that deviate from consensus forecasts by more than a few cents or a significant percentage and are more consequential for firms and investors.

name: Investor reaction to positive earnings surprises
authors_terms: ["investors' reactions to positive earnings surprises", "positive investor reactions", "cumulative abnormal adjusted return"]
definition: To test Hypotheses 3a-3c and 4a-4c, the dependent variable was a firm's cumulative abnormal adjusted return (CAR) over the three-day (-1, +1) window surrounding the earnings surprise announcement; reputation and celebrity are argued to enhance investors' reactions to the positive earnings surprises of firms that possess these assets.

name: Investor reaction to negative earnings surprises
authors_terms: ["investors' reactions to negative earnings surprises", "negative investor reactions", "cumulative abnormal adjusted return"]
definition: Investors' reactions to negative earnings surprises are captured by the firm's cumulative abnormal adjusted return (CAR) over the three-day (-1, +1) window surrounding the earnings surprise announcement; the authors predict that high-reputation and celebrity firms will experience less negative responses to negative surprises than firms that do not possess these assets.

name: Behavioral integration
authors_terms: ["behavioral integration", "TMT behavioral integration", "metaconstruct of TMT process"]
definition: Behavioral integration is a metaconstruct intended to capture three key interrelated and reinforcing elements of TMT process, including a team's (1) level of collaborative behavior, (2) quantity and quality of information exchanged, and (3) emphasis on joint decision making. It captures 'the degree to which the group engages in mutual and collective interaction.'

name: CEO collectivistic orientation
definition: People with a collectivistic orientation subordinate personal interests to the goals of the larger group and emphasize sharing, cooperation, group harmony, and welfare; those who value individualism over collectivism tend to emphasize self-interest, self-sufficiency, control, and the pursuit of individual goals.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Measured by asking respondents to indicate the number of years they had been CEOs. Long-tenured CEOs are argued to have intimate and thorough knowledge of TMT members, including a great understanding of the competitive and political dynamics underlying team interactions.

name: Top management team diversity
authors_terms: ["TMT diversity", "team diversity", "demographic diversity", "goal preference diversity", "tenure diversity", "educational diversity", "functional diversity"]
definition: Top management team diversity, an index of the degree of similarity or dissimilarity of a team as a whole, has been captured in differing ways, for example as diversity in demographic characteristics such as team tenure, education, and functional background, or as diversity in preferences.

name: Top management team tenure
definition: Team tenure was measured as the average of the aggregate tenure of all team members.

name: Top management team size
definition: Team size was measured as the total number of individuals on a company's TMT, as reported by the CEO.

name: Strategic group as reference group
authors_terms: ["strategic group as a reference group", "reference point", "reference group", "benchmark", "group reference point"]
definition: The basic theoretical argument is that a particular strategic group (or the set of strategic groups in general) may act as a reference point for group members as they make competitive strategy decisions.

name: Strategic behavior
definition: A vector representing the firm's strategic actions in terms of key scope and resource commitments.

name: Mobility barriers
definition: While entry barriers are typically structural elements (exogenous), mobility barriers are partly structural but also endogenous. Mobility barriers theory explains why some strategic groups are able to achieve persistent performance advantages over other strategic groups.

name: Solution familiarity
authors_terms: ["Familiarity", "familiar solutions", "familiar technological solutions", "familiar mechanism of action"]
definition: Familiarity of a technological opportunity for an established firm is assessed by comparing its mechanism of action to those already applied by the firm to the same therapeutic problem in the prior 10 years; the mechanism of action is the biochemical mechanism through which the interactions between the drug and its target(s) result in a response.

name: Technology in-sourcing
definition: The selection of an external technological opportunity offered by a specialized technology firm to solve a problem area; modelled as whether or not a firm in-sourced a solution to a problem area.

name: Selection of novel technological solutions
authors_terms: ["Novel Technology In-Sourcing", "in-source a novel technological solution", "novel technological solutions"]
definition: In-sourcing of a technological solution that is novel to the firm's prior problem-solving attempts in the therapeutic area, as opposed to a familiar solution or no in-sourcing at all.

name: TMT attention
authors_terms: ["TMT attention", "top management attention", "focus of TMT", "TMT focus"]
definition: The key problem areas and agendas on which top management focuses their attention; when top managers devote more attention toward a particular problem area, this extra scrutiny makes R&D personnel active in the solution space more accountable, driving them to identify a broader range of solutions.

name: Unexpected failures
definition: Salient failures are attempts to which established firms had already committed substantial resources and time, but that ultimately failed to get launched on the market; such failures are relatively unexpected and provide salient feedback challenging the prevailing mental maps connecting problems and solutions.

name: Commitment to an acquisition target
authors_terms: ["commitment to an acquisition target", "commitment to acquiring a specific target", "managerial overcommitment", "overcommitment to a specific acquisition target"]
definition: During the acquisition process, managers may become committed to acquiring a specific target, regardless of benefit to the acquiring firm. Once committed, managers may continue to pursue the target, even in the face of negative information and opportunities for withdrawal.

name: Personal responsibility
authors_terms: ["personal responsibility", "personal responsibility for the decision to acquire the target", "personal responsibility for the decision to pursue a particular acquisition target"]
definition: We define personal responsibility as having personally made the decision to purchase an acquisition target. This definition is consistent with past research on overcommitment (Staw 1976).

name: Competition for the target
authors_terms: ["competition for an acquisition target", "competition for the target"]
definition: Competition is defined as whether other firms were interested in acquiring the target.

name: Public decision context
authors_terms: ["public decision context", "public or private decision context", "public awareness of acquisition decisions"]
definition: We define public decision context as having one's peers know about the decisions one makes. This could occur through many avenues including the business press and personal communication.

name: CEO equity ownership
authors_terms: ["value of managerial equity ownership", "value of CEO stock ownership", "managerial equity stakes", "CEO shareholdings"]
definition: The value of the common shares held by each firm's CEO, adjusted for inflation; actual dollar values are used rather than percentage of ownership because one percent of a very large firm is most likely a greater portion of a manager's wealth than one percent of a much smaller enterprise. As senior executives increase their equity stakes in the enterprise, their personal wealth portfolios become correspondingly less diversified.

name: CEO stock option holdings
authors_terms: ["value of CEO stock option holdings", "executive stock option holdings", "stock options", "option holdings"]
definition: The value of the stock options held by each firm's CEO. Stock ownership plans result in executives being exposed to upside as well as downside price movements, whereas stock options result in managers being exposed only to upside movements.

name: Firm risk taking
authors_terms: ["firm risk taking", "risk-reducing or risk-enhancing corporate strategies", "changes in firm risk"]
definition: The change in firm risk associated with a takeover, captured through the covariance of returns to the investors of the merging firms over the sixty-month period preceding the announcement. This variable captures the risk profile of an acquiring firm paired with a target.

name: Acquisition announcement performance
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns resulting from acquisition announcements", "acquisition performance", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: The risk-adjusted returns associated with acquisition announcements; cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) serve as the risk-adjusted measures for the returns associated with acquisition announcements.

name: Adoption of energy-savings initiatives
definition: The dependent variable in our analysis is an indicator variable that takes a value of 1 if a given recommendation was implemented, and is 0 otherwise.

name: Disruption to routines
definition: The process effects involve the disruption to the firm's routines and relationships that arise during the change effort. For the remainder of the paper, we use process effects and disruption interchangeably, as the process effects we focus on are disruptions to routines.

name: Implementation cost
definition: Cost represents all the implementation costs associated with equipment, installation, training, etc. of the energy saving initiative. Costs have a larger influence because they are more certain and experienced sooner than the benefits.

name: Environmental norms
authors_terms: ["environmental norms", "local environmental norms", "regional environmental norms", "institutional norms"]
definition: Local norms affect the degree to which people in a local area consider the environmental benefits of an action when making decisions. The influence of local norms may be especially important for decisions that involve social responsibility.

name: Prior local adopters
authors_terms: ["prior adopters local", "Prior Adopters Local", "local adopters", "local adoption"]
definition: Managers can more easily learn of an initiative's effectiveness from other local firms that have implemented it, and can gain a richer understanding of the initiative through such contacts. In addition, prior local implementations can convince a manager that a given practice is appropriate in their setting.

name: Prior non-local adopters
definition: Prior Adopters Non-Local is defined similarly to Prior Adopters Local but counts recommendations by other IACs.

name: Product scope
authors_terms: ["product scope", "scope of services", "product portfolio scope", "scope of products and services offered by a firm"]
definition: The scope of a firm's product portfolio within a single industry; the authors use the number of services provided by each hospital in a given year as the hospital's product scope.

name: Governance mode for complementary activities
authors_terms: ["integration mode", "integrated governance mode", "nonintegrated mode", "governance mode with respect to physicians", "governance mode with respect to complementary activities"]
definition: The mode by which a firm organizes the set of complementary activities that underlie its product offering, internalizing an activity through integration or using a nonintegrated mode; in this setting, hospitals either pursued an integrated mode by employing their own physicians or a nonintegrated mode by contracting with external physician practices.

name: Educational prestige
authors_terms: ["educational prestige", "educational prestige differential", "difference in educational prestige"]
definition: Educational prestige, or the esteem accorded an individual on the basis of his or her educational institution's perceived academic quality, probably influences both employment and interorganizational relationships. Individuals tend to work with others of similar educational prestige.

name: Co-employment
authors_terms: ["co-employment", "co-employment relationships", "employed by the same organization", "employed by the same firm"]
definition: Pairs of individuals who are employed by the same organization form co-employment relationships; in this sample 53,191 individual dyads were employed by the same firm in 2006, a co-employment rate of 0.16 percent.

name: Interorganizational relationship formation
definition: Interorganizational relationships are voluntary organizational commitments of resources to the pursuit of common objectives (Lincoln, Gerlach, and Takahashi, 1992). In this setting firms typically form syndicates of ''co-investors'' in order to pool information, diversify investment risk across a portfolio of investments, perform due diligence, and advise portfolio companies.

name: Shared prior educational affiliation
authors_terms: ["shared prior educational affiliations", "prior educational affiliation", "share a prior educational affiliation"]
definition: Shared educational backgrounds facilitate trusting interpersonal relationships that encourage both information exchange and interorganizational relationships. Individuals who attended the same institution but at different times may also share valuable information because their educational experiences imprint them with similar beliefs.

name: Shared prior employment affiliation
authors_terms: ["shared prior employment affiliations", "prior employment affiliation", "share a prior employment affiliation"]
definition: The prior employment affiliations of their employees signal the quality of organizations and their offerings and probably also provide access to information. Nearly 50 percent of individuals report a coworker as being among their closest friends, and coworkers constitute large portions of managers' core discussion networks.

name: Prior interorganizational relationships
definition: As two organizations form more and more relationships, the predominant source of information on each other will be that gathered from those relationships and not from employees' prior affiliations. The number of prior co-investments is the number of times over the previous five years that two firms invested in the same portfolio company.

name: Educational prestige differential
definition: For each individual-individual dyad, I then computed the educational prestige differential as the absolute value of the difference between the educational prestige scores assigned to individuals i and j.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: Absorptive capacity is a firm's ability to recognize the value of new, external information, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends, which supports its innovative capabilities. The greater the absorptive capacity of a firm, the lower the adjustment costs for imitating the architectural innovation shock.

name: Imitation speed
authors_terms: ["adoption timing", "imitation timing", "faster imitation", "imitate more quickly", "timing of imitation", "accelerate imitation"]
definition: The point in time at which an incumbent imitates the innovation shock; firms imitated this architectural innovation at different points in time - some quickly while others with substantial delay.

name: Opportunity costs of delayed imitation
authors_terms: ["opportunity costs", "opportunity costs associated with imitating slowly", "opportunity costs for imitating slowly", "OC"]
definition: In the early period of a new architectural innovation, opportunity costs for imitating slowly can be substantial if the innovator can quickly capture market share from an incumbent. Incumbents in head-to-head competition with Shimano that did not quickly imitate index-shifting faced high opportunity costs as they would quickly lose market share, revenue, and profits.

name: Vertical integration of component production
authors_terms: ["make versus buy", "sourcing decision", "vertical integration", "outsourcing", "make versus buy sourcing decision"]
definition: Whether a firm produces a component of its gear-shifting set internally (make) or sources it through the market (buy); derailleur firms could source other components either internally (make) or though the market (buy) and offer a complete gear shifting set to bicycle original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).

name: Component co-specialization
definition: Architectural innovations imply that the underlying components are linked together into a coherent whole such that a modification to one component has profound consequences for the design and integration with other components; such tight coupling represents a type of co-specialization.

name: Inventive experience in the extant technology
authors_terms: ["inventive experience with the extant technology", "inventive knowledge in the extant technology generation", "inventive knowledge in the old technology", "CarbPatents"]
definition: Inventive knowledge developed in the existing technology generation, evidenced by inventing in that regime, which the authors describe as 'higher-order' or 'dynamic' knowledge that may have greater flexibility and applicability to intergenerational hybrids than more operational knowledge. Because an organization has experience creating novel recombinations with the extant technology, it may be more likely to spot recombinations with the new technology, some of which may be higher performing.

name: Inventive experience in the threatening technology
authors_terms: ["inventive experience with the threatening technology", "inventive knowledge in the new technology", "EFIPatents"]
definition: Inventive knowledge developed in the threatening technology domain before entry into that domain. If organizations develop intimate knowledge about a new technology domain, organization members are more likely to recognize new knowledge that could be recombined with their existing knowledge, so such knowledge may be more likely to yield elements of the future technology that can be recombined with the extant technology.

name: Related inventive experience
definition: Inventive capabilities developed in related technical areas, described as generalized inventive experience (e.g., experience with the knowledge creation process) or related inventive experience (e.g., knowledge related in some way to the focal area) that increases the likelihood of recombining knowledge in the focal domain.

name: Intergenerational hybrid performance
authors_terms: ["performance of its intergenerational hybrid technology", "intergenerational hybrid performance", "performance of the hybrid", "HybridPerf"]
definition: The performance an organization extracts from its intergenerational hybrid technology; among a group of competitors producing a particular type of hybrid, higher-performing hybrids are likely to be correlated with investments and resulting knowledge. It is measured from the fuel economy performance of the car models housing the hybrid carburetors, relative to the hybrids of competitors.

name: Product performance in the new technology
authors_terms: ["product performance in the new technology", "relative EFI performance", "performance of a firm's EFI offerings"]
definition: The performance of an organization's products in the new technology generation after the technology discontinuity, assessed relative to other incumbents. Relative EFI performance to competitor firms is used because it controls for variation (e.g., gas prices, government regulation) that might cause industry-wide increases or decreases in EFI performance.

name: Director candidate social capital
authors_terms: ["social capital", "candidate social capital", "director candidates' social capital", "candidates' personal social capital"]
definition: Social capital grounded on candidates' personal ties with other business elites; grounded on directors' personal ties with other business elites, social capital allows the directors to leverage the commitments and goodwill accumulated through these personal ties to secure support from their elite contacts on behalf of the firms they serve.

name: Director candidate human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "candidate human capital", "director candidates' human capital"]
definition: Human capital grounded on the expertise and skills candidates accumulate through prior experience; built on the skills and expertise a director accumulates from prior experience, human capital depicts directors' capabilities to advise firms' strategic decisions.

name: Organizational social capital
