authors_terms: ["declining firms' organizational social capital", "organizational social capital", "declining firm social capital"]
definition: The goodwill and resources the firm can access through contacts with external stakeholders; built on the goodwill and mutual commitments embedded in the relations between a firm and its external stakeholders, organizational social capital determines the resources and support the firm can derive from these connected stakeholders.

name: Likelihood of joining a declining firm
authors_terms: ["joining a declining firm", "new director appointment in declining firms", "likelihood of joining a declining firm", "director appointment"]
definition: A candidate's appointment as a new outside director of a declining firm during the observation window of that firm's continuous decline.

name: External knowledge acquisition capability
authors_terms: ["external knowledge acquisition", "external knowledge acquisition capability", "breadth of external interactions", "breadth of external ties", "external AC capabilities"]
definition: External AC capabilities enable the team's acquisition of knowledge from the external environment; the larger the number of diverse external parties the team interacts with, the greater its capability to acquire external knowledge.

name: Problem-solving network centralization
authors_terms: ["internal knowledge integration", "internal knowledge integration capability", "problem-solving network centralization", "centralization", "internal AC capabilities"]
definition: Centralization is a configural construct that represents the extent to which a specific internal activity is predominantly channeled through one central team member or is shared equally among many. In the context of creative problem-solving interactions among team members, centralization indicates the extent to which the problem-solving process in the team is mainly routed through one (vs. many) central member who acts as a liaison in controlling or transferring the flow of solutions.

name: Team creativity
definition: Team creativity refers to the development of novel and useful products, processes, and services by a group of people who share the responsibility for common team objectives, and who are interdependent in the execution of these objectives.

name: Task complexity
definition: Task complexity is the extent to which a team's core tasks entail low routine, but high cognitive demand in terms of the number of information cues and activities making up the task, and the dynamic integration of distinct activities.

name: Information elaboration
definition: Information elaboration processes in the team are the extent to which members openly share diverse perspectives, elaborate on them, and constructively discuss and integrate inputs from each other in developing solutions.

name: Investment bank reputation
authors_terms: ["investment bank reputation", "underwriter reputation", "reputation of the lead investment bank", "backing by prominent underwriters", "reputable investment banks"]
definition: The reputation of the lead investment bank that took the target firm public. Prior research suggests that having a reputable underwriter is one of the most important signals of an IPO firm's quality.

name: Venture capitalist backing
authors_terms: ["venture capitalist backing", "VC backing", "backing by venture capitalists", "backing by VCs"]
definition: Whether or not the issuing firm was associated with a venture capitalist at the time of the IPO; the prediction focuses on the presence or absence of a venture capitalist at the time a firm goes public. Venture capitalists are selective in the businesses in which they invest.

name: Market entry mode
authors_terms: ["joint venture versus acquisition", "joint venture vs. M&A", "governance structure", "market entry mode", "joint venture vs. acquisition choice"]
definition: The governance choice between a joint venture and an acquisition as alternative market entry modes; one of the most important judgments a firm can make concerning its collaborative strategy.

name: Transaction occurrence
authors_terms: ["the likelihood that an IPO firm experiences either a joint venture or an acquisition", "whether or not the IPO firm experiences a deal", "the realization of joint venture or acquisition transactions"]
definition: Whether an IPO firm experiences a joint venture or an acquisition rather than neither, distinguishing IPO firms that were either partnered with or acquired from firms that did not experience such transactions.

name: Knowledge distance
authors_terms: ["knowledge distance", "knowledge bases dissimilar to the IPO firm's", "differences in the knowledge bases of exchange partners"]
definition: The euclidean distance between firms' industries based on their knowledge requirements, as proxied by their respective employment distributions; it captures how dissimilar the exchange partners' knowledge bases are.

name: Acquiring firm environmental capabilities
authors_terms: ["environmental capabilities", "firm relative waste generation", "clean firms", "dirty firms"]
definition: To create a firm-level measure of environmental capabilities, we take the average of the relative waste generation of the facilities owned by the acquiring firm. Firms are divided by the level of firm relative waste generation, designated as 'clean' if they generate less than the median amount of waste and 'dirty' otherwise.

name: Target facility environmental capabilities
definition: At the facility level, we measure environmental capabilities based on a facility's relative waste generation. Thus, we measure a facility's environmental capabilities as the deviance from the waste generation we would expect it to create given its size and industry.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: The geodesic distance in kilometers between each facility currently owned by a firm and each potential target; we use the average distance so that our distance measure captures the average distance between each given potential target and the plants owned by the acquirer firm.

name: Acquisition target choice
definition: We model the probability that a particular facility changes owners as a function of a set of firm and facility characteristics; we are interested in modeling the 'which one' decision, that is, the choice of which facility to acquire among a set of alternatives.

name: Scope of outsourcing
definition: Scope of outsourcing assesses both the range of services, and the extent to which each service is implemented by third party vendors; in the context of process outsourcing, that is, the external sourcing of new technologies to enhance or provide new business processes.

name: Efficiency in customer service delivery
definition: We adopt a context specific definition of efficiency as the extent to which the costs of servicing customers through traditional channels was reduced as a consequence of adopting an online banking channel.

name: Adaptability in customer service delivery
definition: Adaptability refers to the speed of response to customers' changing needs. Such response entails the reconfiguration of activities in a process of successive approximation to changing needs of customers as those activities relate to providing online services and their interfaces with existing processes.

name: Market-related absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["market-related absorptive capacity", "MRAC", "market-based conceptualization of absorptive capacity"]
definition: Analogous to R&D intensity, which has been used to measure a firm's ability to innovate by solving complex technological problems, market-related absorptive capacity captures a firm's ability to innovate by solving new and complex market-related problems.

name: Construal level
authors_terms: ["construal level", "construal levels", "low construal level", "high construal level"]
definition: Construal levels refer to the degree of abstraction in cognition, ranging from concrete and subordinate at low levels to abstract and superordinate at high levels. A high construal level is related to thinking in terms of categories rather than exemplars, wholes rather than parts, and ends rather than means.

name: Symptom count
definition: Symptom count is the number of symptoms individuals identify during problem framing. Symptoms are the information cues that signify a deviation from expectations, such as the failure to meet performance expectations.

name: Problem formulation comprehensiveness
definition: Comprehensiveness is the number of alternative, potentially relevant causes that collectively explain the identified, correlated symptoms. It is the criterion for evaluating strategic problem formulation.

name: Construal level shift
authors_terms: ["construal level shift", "shifting construal levels from low ... to high"]
definition: A construal level shift is the sequencing of a low construal level during problem framing and a high construal level during problem formulation. The model proposes that both concrete and abstract thinking are needed for comprehensive problem formulation, but at different stages.

name: Global dispersion
definition: A firm's global configuration refers to "how many sites an activity is performed in" (Porter 1986: p. 29). Because banks typically have only one currency trading room in a country, the number of rooms measures global dispersion.

name: Single-unit operation
definition: The Single-Unit variable is a dummy variable that indicates if the current operation is not globally dispersed. For single-unit operations, the logarithm of Number-of-Rooms is zero.

name: Information technology diffusion
authors_terms: ["the Reuters' Dealing System", "generic information technologies", "intrafirm diffusion", "industrywide diffusion", "proportion of rooms with the Reuters' Dealing System", "Post-1984"]
definition: Diffusion of a generic information technology—the Reuters' Dealing System, an electronic dealing and conversation system used for information exchange and deal execution—measured both as diffusion within the firm (the proportion of a bank's rooms with the system) and as industrywide diffusion (whether the period follows the system's widespread adoption).

name: Expansion of global scope
definition: The dependent variable of the expansion model is the instantaneous rate at which the FX operation adds rooms to its global configuration; expansion is duration-based, using the duration that a room has not been added since either the study's beginning or the prior expansion event.

name: Contraction of global scope
definition: The dependent variable of the contraction model is the instantaneous rate at which the FX operation deletes rooms from its global configuration; for single-room operations contraction is equivalent to withdrawing from market-making.

name: Net change in global scope
authors_terms: ["net change", "annual net change in the number of rooms"]
definition: Net change is operationalized as a continuous variable to represent the combined effects of expansion and contraction and to allow for multiple events in a single year. The zero-net-change point defines optimal global scope.

name: Corporate reputation perceived by the general public
authors_terms: ["corporate reputation as perceived by the general public", "reputation perceptions of the general public", "total (raw) reputation", "corporate reputation"]
definition: The reputation perceptions of the general public, which are influenced by each individual's self-serving interests and needs and play a key role in forming a firm's overall reputational profile. We advocate for a more balanced conceptualization of corporate reputation that captures people's perceptions of a firm's abilities ('competence') and their feelings about the firm ('likeability').

name: Financial reputation
authors_terms: ["financial reputation", "the part of reputation that results from previous financial performance"]
definition: The part of reputation perceptions that results from previous financial performance, isolated by decomposing reputation perceptions in a financial halo model ('financial reputation').

name: Nonfinancial reputation
definition: The residual part of reputation perceptions that remains once the financial halo effect has been isolated ('nonfinancial reputation'). Perceptions of nonfinancial aspects, such as product quality, workplace environment, emotional appeal, and social and environmental responsibility, contribute to a firm's nonfinancial reputational profile.

name: Future stock returns
authors_terms: ["future stock returns", "future stock market performances", "long-term stock market performances", "shareholder value"]
definition: Firms' future stock market performance, which captures more channels (beyond merely accounting profits) through which superior reputations may increase shareholder value. Long-term stock market performances need to be analyzed because capital markets tend to discount the value of intangible assets as long as the benefits do not materialize in earnings.

name: Corporate bankruptcy
definition: Corporate bankruptcy is not a discrete intervention but a late stage of a "protracted process of decline" and a "downward spiral".

name: CEO-board chairperson duality
authors_terms: ["CEO-board chairperson structure", "joint CEO-board chairperson structure", "duality", "dual structures"]
definition: Of concern is whether these offices are held by one person, a structure called duality. The same individual either did or did not simultaneously serve as a firm's CEO and board chairperson.

name: Director affiliation
authors_terms: ["affiliated directors", "proportion of affiliated directors", "outside directors", "board composition"]
definition: Corporate boards with large proportions of affiliated directors, then, are characterized by little independence from the firms' CEOs. Succinctly, although a given board might be composed of many outside directors, if they are affiliated as defined by SEC item 6b, they have close personal or professional ties with the corporation or its CEO.

name: Failure experience
authors_terms: ["failure experience", "prior organizational failure experience", "prior failed launches", "direct failure experience"]
definition: Prior experience of organizational failure, where aspirations dichotomize organizational performance such that decision makers define performance that falls below the aspiration level as failure.

name: Success experience
authors_terms: ["success experience", "prior organizational success experience", "prior successful launches", "direct success experience"]
definition: Prior experience of organizational success, where decision makers define performance that exceeds a relevant aspiration level as success.

name: Others' failure experience
authors_terms: ["others' failure experience", "others' prior organizational failure experience", "observation of others' failures", "vicarious experience"]
definition: Knowledge developed through observation of the experience of other organizations; there is significant empirical evidence that the likelihood of organizational failure decreases as the number of failures experienced by other, similar organizations increases.

name: Others' success experience
authors_terms: ["others' success experience", "others' prior organizational success experience", "observation of others' successes"]
definition: Knowledge developed through observation of other organizations' successes; observing others' successes may increase decision makers' confidence in the accuracy of knowledge held by their own organization and lead them to reduce search activities.

name: Experience with major failures
authors_terms: ["major failure", "complete failure experience", "experience with complete failures", "large failures"]
definition: Experience with failures whose magnitude is large, which organization members are unlikely to ignore because of their magnitude and visibility; operationalized in this study as complete failures, launches in which the launch vehicle did not properly perform the function for which it was designed.

name: Experience with minor failures
authors_terms: ["minor failure", "small failures", "partial failure experience", "experience with partial failures"]
definition: Experience with small failures, which do not have large negative consequences and which organization members may redefine as successes; operationalized in this study as partial failures, launches that reached orbit but significantly damaged the satellite, failed to obtain separation between the satellite and the launch vehicle, or deposited the satellite into the wrong orbit.

name: Others' major failure experience
definition: Other organizations' prior experience with complete (major) failures, indexed as the number of prior completely failed launches made by organizations in the sample other than the focal organization.

name: Others' minor failure experience
definition: Other organizations' prior experience with partial (minor) failures, indexed as the number of prior partially failed launches made by organizations in the sample other than the focal organization.

name: Launch failure
authors_terms: ["failed launch", "launch failure", "likelihood of future organizational failure", "future organizational failure"]
definition: Whether a given orbital launch attempt failed; partial failures were considered failures because the launch vehicles involved did not properly perform the function for which they were designed.

name: Transaction price
definition: The transaction price is the hourly price that the staffing firm charges the client firm for the worker's services.

name: Broker's share of transaction value
definition: The margin is the difference between the bill rate paid by the client and the pay rate received by the worker, retained by the staffing firm as payment for its services.

name: Broker-seller relationship duration
authors_terms: ["worker-Agency relationship duration", "months worked with agency", "length of the worker-Agency relationship"]
definition: The total time in months that the worker has previously spent working on projects for the Agency at the start of the current project.

name: Buyer-seller relationship duration
definition: The number of months previously spent on assignment with that specific client.

name: Individual service orientation
definition: The roots of unit service orientation lie at the individual level, because it is a multidimensional construct capturing individual differences in willingness to treat customers with respect and dignity, perceptiveness of customer wants, and ability to communicate effectively and manage impressions.

name: Unit service orientation
authors_terms: ["unit service orientation", "unit service orientation stock", "stock of unit service orientation"]
definition: We define unit service orientation as a unit's aggregate, collective willingness and ability to deliver high-quality service.

name: Flow of unit service orientation
authors_terms: ["flow of unit service orientation", "unit service orientation flows", "change in unit service orientation"]
definition: The flows of the resource are represented by the water coming into the tub through the faucet and out of the tub through the drain. Flows influence the stock of a resource and whether a critical mass is achieved and maintained.

name: Quality of unit service orientation flows
authors_terms: ["high-quality flows of unit service orientation", "low-quality flows of unit service orientation", "consistently high flows of unit service orientation"]
definition: Units with higher-quality flows of unit service orientation will have a stronger (nonlinear) relationship and thus better unit effectiveness.

name: Unit effectiveness
definition: We used store productivity, profit, and percentage of sales growth as operationalizations of unit effectiveness because they have theoretical importance and relevance to service contexts, and their use ensures our findings were not metric-specific.

name: Fit business units
definition: We label units that share one or more of a market segment's information dimensions as fit units in relationship to that market. With more fit units in relation to a market segment, a firm will gather and share more information relevant to that market.

name: Nonfit business units
definition: We define units that share no structural dimensions with a market segment as nonfit units. The existence of business units that do not share information dimensions with a given market segment makes it less likely that a firm will act on opportunities related to that segment.

name: Fit-fit horizontal links
authors_terms: ["horizontal links between a firm's fit units", "fit-fit links", "fit-unit links"]
definition: Horizontal links connect different business units. Links between units enable ongoing operations through information sharing and mutual adjustment of activities, and act as informal networks that transmit information regarding perceived opportunities and threats.

name: Fit-nonfit horizontal links
authors_terms: ["horizontal links between a firm's fit and nonfit units", "links between fit and nonfit units", "fit-non links"]
definition: Links between fit and nonfit units will also increase the likelihood that a firm enters a market segment. These links bring together information about a market segment with information from other parts of the environment.

name: Nonfit-nonfit horizontal links
authors_terms: ["horizontal links between a firm's nonfit units", "links between nonfit units", "non-non links"]
definition: Tight links among units that do not share characteristics of a market reinforce the individual tendencies of such units to avoid the new markets. Information sharing between nonfit units will amplify information from parts of the environment unrelated to a focal opportunity.

name: Corporate-fit unit vertical links
authors_terms: ["vertical links between the corporate level and a firm's fit units", "vertical fit links", "corporate-fit"]
definition: Vertical links involving fit units, that is, those between a business unit and the corporate offices of a firm, may also increase the likelihood of entry. Vertical links can carry information from business units to the top level of the organization.

name: Corporate-nonfit unit vertical links
authors_terms: ["vertical links between the corporate level and a firm's nonfit units", "vertical non links", "corporate-nonfit"]
definition: Links from nonfit units to the corporate level will lead to increased filtering of information relevant to a focal opportunity. Promotion paths between nonfit units and the corporate level of the firm are strong indications that a focal opportunity lies outside the awareness of managers.

name: Market entry
definition: We considered entry to have occurred if, in a given year, a firm offered a service that it had not offered in previous years. We defined a segment as opening for potential entry the first year that one of the firms began offering the service.

name: New product introduction performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["NPI below aspiration levels", "distance of new product introductions below aspiration levels", "distance below aspiration level NPI", "NPI performance below aspiration levels", "distance below aspiration levels"]
definition: The distance of firms' new product introduction (new drug approval) performance below their historical aspiration level. An aspiration level represents the smallest satisfactory outcome considered acceptable when determining whether firm performance is good enough.

name: Number of R&D alliances
authors_terms: ["number of R&D alliances", "R&D alliances", "number of active R&D alliances"]
definition: R&D alliances are the formal agreements between organizations who exchange, share, or co-develop R&D activities in the pursuit of a joint R&D objective. The construct is the number of such alliances a firm has.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack refers to the stock of excess resources available to an organization during a given planning cycle. In the context of NPI, slack includes available cash, underutilized R&D facilities, or labor such as research scientists with specialized expertise.

name: Cluster membership
authors_terms: ["cluster membership", "industrial clusters", "located in an industrial cluster"]
definition: Cluster membership is assessed with a dummy coding, with 1 = the firm is located in an industrial cluster and 0 = otherwise. Firms in the study were sampled from manufacturing and technology zones in Shanghai that the local authorities clearly define and closely monitor as clusters.

name: Exploitative product innovation
definition: Exploitative product innovations are incremental innovations that build on and reinforce current product knowledge to improve existing products.

name: Exploratory product innovation
definition: Exploratory innovation involves a shift to a different knowledge domain with the aim to adopt or create new processes and products. Exploratory product innovations are radical innovations that require new knowledge or departures from existing knowledge to create new products.

name: Network ties with suppliers
authors_terms: ["network ties with suppliers", "network ties with supplier firms", "managerial network ties with their suppliers"]
definition: Focal cluster firms' network ties with their suppliers in their clusters. Because interfirm network ties tend to enhance trust and interpersonal relationships between the firms, which help the firms comprehend hard-to-understand tacit knowledge that they might receive from each other, such ties help focal firms understand complex knowledge about alternative product designs and related manufacturing practices.

name: Network ties with buyers
authors_terms: ["network ties with buyers", "network ties with buyer firms", "managerial network ties with their buyers"]
definition: Focal cluster firms' network ties with their buyers in their clusters. Interfirm network ties tend to enhance trust and interpersonal relationships between the firms and hence help the firms comprehend hard-to-understand tacit knowledge that they might receive from each other, allowing them to comprehend the product and output-related knowledge that buyer firms offer.

name: Interpretive knowledge representation
authors_terms: ["interpretive knowledge representation", "interpretive knowledge", "figurative knowledge objects", "interpretive representations", "interpretive treatment"]
definition: Interpretive knowledge requires an interpretive activity of meaning creation; to allow for interpretation, figurative knowledge is often represented in a narrative or a story that is both concrete and abstract. Interpretive knowledge representations simultaneously capture the power of both abstract and concrete representations.

name: General knowledge representation
definition: Concrete knowledge representations provide particularities of context, and abstract representations provide generalities; knowledge is presented at a level of abstraction that transcends context to provide potential guidance in a wide range of situations. The general treatments emphasized abstract knowledge that was less contextualized but presented the ideas literally.

name: Particular knowledge representation
definition: Particular knowledge representations present concrete and unambiguous knowledge, i.e., highly contextualized ideas in a literal manner with higher concreteness.

name: Managerial decision-making outcome
authors_terms: ["managerial decision-making outcomes", "decision outcomes", "decision-making outcomes", "decision task performance"]
definition: A managerial decision has several different dimensions, including the depth and breadth of the ideas and analysis used and the perceived decision satisfaction. In the absence of an agreed-upon standard for judging a correct answer, decision outcomes were evaluated on multiple dimensions.

name: Prior relevant technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["in-house access to relevant prior technological knowledge", "prior relevant technological knowledge", "prior experience in using electrical motors, potentiometers, rectifiers, and modulators", "technologically preadapted"]
definition: In-house access to relevant prior technological knowledge, i.e., the knowledge of electrical and electronic circuitry, electrical motors, potentiometers, rectifiers, and modulators. It is prior experience in using electrical motors, potentiometers, rectifiers, and modulators in manufacturing other products.

name: Access to in-house users of the new product market
authors_terms: ["in-house users of robots in the new product market", "access to downstream in-house users for the new product market", "in-house user division", "market preadaptation"]
definition: The in-house user division—a division within the focal firm that is a potential user of the new product created by the radical technological change—can help exploration efforts with new information about demand conditions and the product performance features that customers are likely to value. Firms with such access assembled electronics, communication, and information technology-related products like computers, calculators, and other electrical and electronic gadgets prior to entering the new product market.

name: Proximity to the new product market performance frontier
authors_terms: ["proximity to the performance frontier of the new product market", "proximity to the product performance frontier in the new robotics product market", "repeatability ratio"]
definition: Since the customers in the new product market valued repeatability as the critical performance feature, the best repeatability in a new robot introduced in a year is treated as the performance frontier.

name: Proximity to the original product market performance frontier
authors_terms: ["proximity to the product performance frontier in the original robotics product market", "load capacity ratio"]
definition: Since the customers in the original pre-CNC robot product market valued load capacity as the critical performance feature, the maximum load capacity of a new robot introduced in a year is treated as the performance frontier.

name: Product portfolio focus on the new product market
authors_terms: ["proportion of products in a firm's portfolio targeted to the new product market", "product portfolios that are more focused towards the new product market"]
definition: The share of a firm's products that are targeted to the new product market, measured as the ratio of the number of products manufactured by a firm in a given year in new applications of assembly, electronics assembly, arc welding, and inspection to the total number of products manufactured by the firm in that year.

name: Supplier-perceived switching probability
authors_terms: ["suppliers' perceived probability of a switch", "perceived switching probability", "perceived probability of a switch", "probability of switch", "switching probability"]
definition: The dependent variable is the suppliers' perceived probability of a switch. The authors constructed proxies to represent the perceived probability of a switch by inverting the suppliers' perceptions of their future with their customer, and normalizing by the mean perception in the sample.

name: Current competitive factors
authors_terms: ["current competitive factors", "competitive factors", "Compt", "threat perceived by an incumbent supplier"]
definition: These variables, representing competitive factors, were related to the threat perceived by an incumbent supplier in terms of retaining its position. In the context of the classical 5-forces model, these threats are largely horizontal.

name: Transaction-specific assets
definition: In the close but adversarial model, the suppliers' investments in specific assets are not protected by trust; in fact, investments in specific assets create the possibility of hold-up by the buyer. The level of transaction-specific assets was measured in dollar terms.

name: Technological complexity of suppliers' output
authors_terms: ["technological complexity of suppliers' output", "technological complexity of the product", "technological factors"]
definition: These variables were related to the type of work outsourced. They were drawn to represent the implications of the literature indicating that in the cooperative model inputs of high and low technological complexity would tend to be outsourced, while under the close but adversarial model outsourcing would be limited to items of low technological complexity.

name: Product characteristics
definition: The close but adversarial model predicts that product type or importance should not affect the switching probability perceived by the supplier. These variables can also be considered to normalize for firm-specific characteristics, specifically supplier technology and the buyer's purchase frequency.

name: Trust
definition: The notion of trust used here is what Sako (1992) calls 'goodwill trust' and Korczynski (1996) calls 'high trust', i.e., mutual expectations of open commitment to each other, where commitment is defined as a willingness to do more than is formally expected.

name: Task complexity
definition: Task complexity is the extent to which a task draws on different knowledge sets and requires interdependence between actors for effective implementation. The authors define task complexity on two dimensions: the number of knowledge sets and their interrelatedness.

name: Integration of new activities
definition: Integration of new activities assesses the extent to which a firm organizes internally (i.e., inhouse personnel) versus outsources to implement Internet banking services.

name: Unit autonomy
definition: We define unit autonomy as the allocation of decision-making authority for task funding to the same unit as is held accountable for the task.

name: Lateral coordination
definition: We define lateral coordination as the extent to which an organization aligns its actions across units to complete a task.

name: Internal organization structure
definition: Internal structure reflects a firm's allocation of decision rights to subunits completing distinct jobs and the coordination among those subunits. At any point in time, a firm's structure has a certain degree of unit autonomy and lateral coordination.

name: Educational prestige
authors_terms: ["educational prestige", "prestige of educational background", "educational background", "educational pedigree"]
definition: Organizational members vary in both the level and quality of their education, and educational background becomes one of the most salient forms of individuating information available to an outside observer. The prestige of organizational members' educational backgrounds becomes a signal of the knowledge available within the firm and generates expectations of the firm's performance.

name: Executive race
definition: Race is a highly salient status characteristic that has a significant impact on the outcomes that individuals experience in organizations. Race is one of the diffuse status cues that provide generalized information about ability or performance across a wide array of activities.

name: External expectations of team performance
authors_terms: ["expectations of performance", "expected performance", "outsiders' assessments", "external perceptions", "outsiders' valuations"]
definition: Outsiders form early assessments of a team and its leader before team members have any opportunity to act; such assessments affect outsiders' psychological commitment and allocation of resources to the team. The authors operationalize expectations of performance by the valuation of the company's stock.

name: Preferential treatment in admissions
definition: A readily accessible explanation for the coupling of African American managers with prestigious educational backgrounds is that they have been the recipients of preferential selection in the college admissions process. If an educational institution does not explicitly refute preference in its admissions process, executives who come from that institution may be assumed to be the target of preferential treatment.

name: Foreign R&D entry mode
authors_terms: ["sponsored research", "collaborative research", "controlled research", "mode of foreign R&D activity"]
definition: I categorize the organizational choices for a firm that undertakes foreign R&D into three basic types, including sponsored research, collaborative research, and controlled research.

name: Sequence position of foreign R&D activity
authors_terms: ["sequence of entry", "sequence of sponsored, collaborative, and controlled research activities", "sequence of modes"]
definition: Firms are likely to establish at least one sponsored research activity first, followed by one or more collaborative projects which, in turn, are followed by a controlled research activity.

name: Scientific knowledge capabilities
authors_terms: ["scientific knowledge capabilities", "domestic research capability", "domestic research skills", "complementary technical skills"]
definition: I focus on two types of scientific knowledge capabilities: domestic research skills and complementary technical skills. Domestic research skills provide linkages to the traditional knowledge base of an industry, while complementary technical skills provide linkages to emerging technological opportunities.

name: Entry timing
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "timing of the firm's initial R&D activity"]
definition: The time that a firm first undertakes foreign R&D activities; I used the number of years after 1979 that a firm undertook its first foreign research activity as the entry timing variable.

name: Foreign market knowledge
authors_terms: ["foreign market knowledge", "preexisting knowledge of the foreign market", "foreign market presence"]
definition: Firms obtain foreign market knowledge by participating in the market through a sales subsidiary or export activity (Ronstadt, 1977). Such firms might perceive their specific market knowledge as lessening the barriers to foreign R&D.

name: Breadth of exchange possibilities
authors_terms: ["exchange possibilities", "narrower exchange possibilities", "broader exchange possibilities", "exchange capabilities", "breadth of their exchange possibilities"]
definition: The extent of an organization's access to exchange partners and to final markets. Resource endowments and exchange possibilities are typically not distributed equally in interorganizational communities, so dependence on a central organization with broader exchange capabilities and access to final markets is a problem for organizations with narrower exchange possibilities.

name: Supply ties
definition: Relations between organizations in which one organization is named as a supplier by another; a unit entry in the supply matrix indicates that the row organization is named as a supplier by the column organization.

name: Multiple customers
authors_terms: ["out-stars in the supply network", "multiple downstream customers", "supply more than one producer"]
definition: A local network structure in which a supplier is linked to multiple producers, that is, an out-star in the supply network.

name: Equity ties
authors_terms: ["equity arrangements", "equity relations", "equity ties", "ownership ties", "comembership in the same group"]
definition: Relations of joint ownership among organizations in the community. Ownership ties are reconstructed as symmetric because the core organizations are subsidiary production units of larger industrial groups, so the question was posed in terms of comembership in the same group rather than direct ownership.

name: Technology transfer ties
authors_terms: ["technology transfer", "activities of technology transfer", "technology exchange agreements"]
definition: Relations defined in terms of a joint involvement in product development and comanufacturing, and therefore inherently symmetric. As defined in the questionnaires, technology transfer represents a pragmatic mechanism that companies adopt to coordinate collaborative manufacturing processes.

name: Third-party ties
authors_terms: ["ties of the members of the dyad to third parties", "ties with third parties"]
definition: Other ties of the members of a dyad, that is, their ties to organizations outside the dyad, on whose presence the formation of the dyadic interorganizational tie is conditional.

name: Interorganizational ties
definition: Dyadic relations between organizations in an organizational community; the authors claim that their formation is subject to endogenous and exogenous processes.

name: Multiplexity
definition: The fact that organizations may be tied to one another in many possible ways, or interact in more than one context or domain.

name: Endogenous network processes
definition: Network-dependent processes of tie formation in which the status of a given tie is both dependent on and predictive of the status of neighboring network ties; the supply network is hypothesized to have a self-organizing character.

name: Strength of host country intellectual property regime
authors_terms: ["strength of the intellectual property regime (IPR)", "strength of the IPR at the host location", "weak IPR", "strong IPR"]
definition: The authors assume that a weak IPR at a host location implies that both its patent and trade secrecy laws are weak, so that an IP holder has very few legal remedies when its IP is expropriated.

name: Share of host inventors
authors_terms: ["share of host inventors", "Share", "proportion of host inventors", "involvement of host inventors"]
definition: The key dependent variable is the proportion of host inventors in a focal patent, measured as the number of inventors from the host location divided by the total number of inventors listed in the patent. The share of host country inventors (Share) is the number of host inventors divided by the total number of inventors in an R&D project.

name: R&D project end-use market
authors_terms: ["host R&D project", "home R&D project", "location for which the invention is relevant"]
definition: The authors refer to a project that is mainly relevant to the host location as a host R&D project and a project that is mainly relevant for the MNE's home market as a home R&D project.

name: Internetworking depth
definition: Internetworking Depth measured the extent that online communications and transactions are conducted between employees, customers, suppliers, and partners of established businesses, where both reach and richness were accounted for.

name: Business focus and specialization
authors_terms: ["Business Scope/Specialization", "business scope", "specialization", "narrowing of business scope and an increase in business specialization", "more focused and specialized"]
definition: The statements measured Business Scope/Specialization; strong agreement indicated a firm whose business scope was narrowing and specialization was deepening, with non-core activities being outsourced and lower value-added jobs being eliminated.

name: Internal hierarchy
definition: Statements three and four captured the effects on internal hierarchy, and strong agreement indicated a noticeable decrease in managerial levels, internal hierarchy, and bureaucracy.

name: External partnering
authors_terms: ["External Partnering", "external partnering", "external strategic partnerships/alliances/joint ventures", "external partnering behaviors"]
definition: Statements two and five measured partnering and alliance behaviors, where strong agreement indicated firms where in comparison to a few years ago many more external strategic partnerships/alliances/joint ventures were being entered into, and where mergers/acquisitions/disposals had also increased noticeably.

name: Environmental performance
definition: The environmental record of a firm as reflected in the scores given to sample firms by the Franklin Research and Development Corporation, based on criteria such as compliance records, expenditures, and other initiatives used to meet new demands, reduce waste, and support environmental protection organizations.

name: Profitability
definition: The economic performance of the firm, described by the authors as its bottom line and measured as a company's return on assets, "a generally accepted measure of firm performance."

name: Industry growth
authors_terms: ["industry growth", "the growth rate of an industry", "industry growth rate"]
definition: The growth of the industry in which the firm competes; the authors measure it as the average annual increase in sales for four years (1991 observations) or five years (1992 observations).

name: Unearned status gain
authors_terms: ["gain status because of a category addition", "gained All-Star status because of a category addition", "unearned status gains"]
definition: When actors receive status from a structural change, they gain an exogenous boost in visibility and credibility, and their actions and opinions become perceived as more valuable than before simply because of their inclusion among those designated as high status. Such gains may occur without changes in actors' quality.

name: Unearned status loss
authors_terms: ["lose status because of a category removal", "lost All-Star status because of a category removal", "unearned status losses"]
definition: If high-status actors lose status when their category is removed, their visibility is correspondingly reduced by the lack of recognition, and the quality of their actions and opinions might be questioned by the audience that attends to them. The removal of a category can affect actors' status without a corresponding change in their own actions.

name: Market impact
authors_terms: ["market impact", "impact in the market", "market power and the market relevance of their opinions and products", "investors' response"]
definition: By arbitrarily changing actors' status, category changes also play a role in shaping actors' market power and the market relevance of their opinions and products. The authors capture this as the market's reaction to analysts' forecast revisions, as evidenced by investors' response.

name: Forecast revision
definition: We defined forecast revision as the current quarter's forecast minus the prior forecast, deflated by the stock price 10 trading days before the release of the revised forecast. The variable takes positive values when the analyst revises an estimate upward and negative ones when he or she revises an estimate downward.

name: Distinctiveness of the entrepreneurial story
definition: Distinctiveness refers to the degree to which an entrepreneurial story deviates from a market category's prototypical story. Distinctiveness represents the degree to which the content of an entrepreneurial story deviates from the content of the market category's prototypical entrepreneurial story.

name: Contribution claims
definition: Contribution claims are claims that 'reflect the contribution the venture will make to the community and how it will provide value to the members of that community.' Contribution claims in entrepreneurial stories provide an additional source of normative legitimacy.

name: Market category familiarity
definition: Market category familiarity is the degree to which a market category is familiar to the general public. The familiarity of a market category tends to increase as a category emerges and grows.

name: Resource acquisition from crowdfunders
definition: The number of backers that pledge crowdfunding to a venture during its crowdfunding campaign. The number of backers consequently provides a suitable proxy for resource acquisition in this context because it reflects the acquisition of both financial and nonfinancial resources.

name: Risk of event stigma
authors_terms: ["risk of event stigma", "higher risk of event stigma", "event stigma", "High Stigma"]
definition: The risk of event stigma is the risk of stigmatization arising from stigmatizing characteristics of the adverse event, such as its perceived severity and controllability; stigma is not an inevitable outcome of an event.

name: Event severity
definition: The severity of an event is defined by the negative magnitude of its consequences.

name: Event controllability
definition: Controllability refers to the extent to which the cause of the event is perceived to be under the firm's control.

name: Media vilification
definition: Media vilification represents the media's reaction, which is shaped by conditions created by the risk of event stigma; the authors operationalize it as a rhetorical strategy and measure it by the extent of negative media coverage of an adverse event.

name: Unplanned alliance dissolution
authors_terms: ["unplanned alliance dissolution", "probability of unplanned alliance dissolution", "probability of alliance dissolution"]
definition: The dependent variable is the probability of unplanned alliance dissolution, coded as 0 for an ongoing alliance and 1 for an unplanned alliance dissolution.

name: Firm status
authors_terms: ["firm status", "status of the stricken firm", "prestige-based status"]
definition: Firm status can be defined as the prestige, recognition, and privilege derived from a firm's position in a hierarchical social structure, positions that are largely determined by the perceptions of others.

name: External corporate governance
definition: External corporate governance encompasses monitoring and control mechanisms by stakeholders like institutional investors, regulators, trade organizations, and government agencies.

name: Prior funding decision
authors_terms: ["prior funding decision", "prior proposal funded", "prior funding awarded"]
definition: Our main independent variable captures the funding decision made before the focal decision. We can measure the outcome of a prior funding decision either as a dichotomous variable - whether the prior proposal received funding - or as a continuous variable - the amount of funding awarded to the previous application.

name: Funding decision
authors_terms: ["funding decision", "share of requested funding awarded", "funding outcome"]
definition: A project application can be rejected, fully funded, or partially funded. Our dependent variable therefore measures the share of requested funding awarded.

name: Timing of the panel decision
definition: To test Hypothesis 2, we measured timing by a variable (order of assessment) capturing the order in which the project was assessed during the panel meeting. Thus, the longer a meeting lasts, the lower the attentiveness of panel members and therefore the likelier they become to draw on decision-making heuristics.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["Foreign firm", "foreign firms", "foreignness", "foreign MNEs", "U.S. subsidiaries of foreign MNEs"]
definition: Our first main explanatory variable is a binary variable of whether the client firm in each transaction is foreign (Foreign firm). Following Kim (2019), we designated a firm as foreign only if a foreign entity at the top of its ownership hierarchy-that is, a global ultimate owner-controlled the operations of the U.S. subsidiary.

name: Home-country autocracy
definition: A regime is autocratic (or dictatorial or authoritarian, terms used interchangeably in political science) if leadership is chosen by undemocratic means, that is, by means other than free and fair elections. The authors use a political-regime measure that captures the institutionalized authority patterns that characterize a country's position on a spectrum ranging from institutionalized democracy to autocracy.

name: Lobbying fee premium
authors_terms: ["lobbying fee", "lobbying fees", "fee premium", "lobbying fee premium", "pay-for-legitimacy fee"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the natural logarithm of the Lobbying fee in each transaction. The fee premium is the additional amount that lobbyists charge one type of client relative to another; the authors state that the fee premium that a lobbyist charges represents a pay-for-legitimacy fee.

name: Nationalistic issue context
authors_terms: ["U.S. nationalism", "nationalism", "nationalistic implications", "nationalist issues", "issue areas exhibiting nationalism"]
definition: Nationalism is defined in Barrington (1997: 714) as "the pursuit-through argument or other activity-of a set of rights for the self-defined members of the nation, including, at a minimum, territorial autonomy or sovereignty." The authors classified congressional issues by whether a foreign firm is likely to encounter U.S. nationalism during the sample period, and further classified industries by their import tariff, an administrative tool that sovereign states use to protect their national industries.

name: Client lobbying experience
authors_terms: ["Client experience", "client lobbying experience", "years of lobbying", "lobbying experience"]
definition: We used the number of years that a given firm lobbied during our sample period (Client experience) as a foundational construct for testing Hypothesis 4's claim that autocracy-associated stigma is an enduring source of the liability of foreignness in the nonmarket strategy context.

name: Innovativeness
definition: Irrespective of differences in definitions across disciplines, innovativeness is universally perceived as exploring something new that has not existed before. A firm's level of overall innovativeness manifests its capability to explore new possibilities.

name: Quality of products or services
authors_terms: ["quality", "Quality of Products or Services", "QUAL", "product or service quality"]
definition: Regardless of differences in definitions, quality is almost universally perceived as a dynamic threshold that a firm must meet to satisfy customers. A firm's level of product or service quality manifests its capability to exploit currently established certainties.

name: Growth performance
definition: We measured a firm's growth performance by the three compound annual growth rates of total assets, total revenues, and market capitalization from 1998 to 2000.

name: Profitability performance
definition: We measured a firm's profitability performance by three profitability ratios: ROA, ROE, and ROI. Because most of these measures tend to be strongly related to one another, all three profitability ratios were used as indicators of a firm's overall profitability performance.

name: Market value performance
definition: We measured a firm's market performance by two market-based measures of return: market-to-book ratio and Tobin's q ratio.

name: Trust in government
authors_terms: ["trust in institutions", "trust in the institutions of government", "trust in government", "generalized trust in institutions", "institutional trust"]
definition: Although there are many types of institutions that individuals may trust to varying degrees, our focus in this paper is on general trust in the institutions of government. This is distinct from trust in nongovernmental institutions such as the media.

name: Entrepreneurial intention
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial intent", "entrepreneurial intention", "probability of starting a business within 5 years", "change in the probability of starting a business within 5 years"]
definition: We measure entrepreneurial intent by asking each respondent the likelihood that he or she would start a business in 5 years. I ask them to choose a response from 0 to 100% in 10% increments.

name: University tier
authors_terms: ["top university", "top 7 university", "top 30 university", "university rankings", "tier of the university"]
definition: The tier of the university the student attends is associated with the quality of the human capital generated. Prior research indicates that talented, high human capital individuals from higher tier universities may be more sensitive to aspects of the institutional environment related to risks of failure and barriers to growth.

name: Field of study
definition: We examine all the major listed in the survey and categorize the majors into seven categories: Engineering/Science (STEM), Business, Law, Medicine, Education, Arts/Sports, and Humanities and Social Sciences.

name: Decision feedback
definition: The outcome, i.e. success or failure feedback, of an initial decision to commit resources to a course of action, which frequently influences subsequent decisions; escalation of commitment occurs in response to success/failure feedback on a previous decision (past event).

name: Perceived organizational slack
definition: 'that cushion of actual or potential resources which allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for change in policy, as well as to initiate changes in strategy with respect to the external environment'; perceived organizational slack is a major contributor to the current context within which the subsequent decision must be made (present conditions).

name: Decision frame
authors_terms: ["decision frame", "framing", "positive frame", "negative frame", "gain-oriented decision frame", "loss-oriented decision frame"]
definition: 'The basic premise of framing is that the way in which decisions are presented influences the risk preference and behavior of the decision-maker.' Decision frame concerns the psychological orientation of decision-makers regarding the prospects of future gains or losses (future outlook).

name: Reinvestment
authors_terms: ["reinvestment", "reinvestment levels", "subsequent reinvestment decision", "amount of money reinvested"]
definition: The subsequent investment of additional funds in the same division that had been selected to receive the initial funding; the dependent variable was the amount of money allocated by a decision team to a division that had received funding from this team in a prior decision.

name: Perceived current context
authors_terms: ["negative decision context", "positive decision context", "failure feedback and low perceived slack", "success feedback and high perceived slack", "perceived context for the upcoming decision", "perceived current context"]
definition: 'The constructs may coexist along a single continuum ranging from a negative to a positive perceived context for the upcoming decision.' The first dimension, perceived current context, is defined by the prevailing conditions within which the decision-maker and the organization are operating.

name: Digital piracy
definition: Digital piracy, the unauthorized copying and distribution of digital products. Piracy is the violation of digital copyright, through which a pirated version of a product can be obtained by consumers at a lower cost (often zero).

name: Product innovation
definition: Our conceptualization of innovation is based on whether developers are likely to create a revision or improvement on their existing products. We operationalize this by looking at whether an update is released for a particular product.

name: Incremental innovation
definition: We define incremental innovations as minor tweaks that are released in order to correct minor issues or account for incompatibility issues. These are often referred to as bug fixes.

name: Substantial innovation
definition: We define substantial innovations as feature updates or other major product revisions (such as a shift from Version 1.0 to Version 2.0) where the software application experiences a considerable improvement in quality or user experience.

name: New product development
authors_terms: ["new product development", "new product releases", "products launched", "count of product releases"]
definition: New product development is whether the piracy event led developers to develop new products rather than to update or revise existing products, measured as the number of products launched by a developer.

name: Product popularity
definition: Popularity of a product, captured through measures of popularity such as average daily downloads. Popular products are the well-known products that gain little consumer awareness from piracy.

name: Product age
authors_terms: ["product age", "age (or maturity) of a product", "product maturity"]
definition: The age, or maturity, of a product, which the authors argue may influence the types of revisions that are released.

name: High-involvement human resource practices
authors_terms: ["high-involvement human resource practices", "high-involvement practices", "high-involvement work systems", "high-involvement work index"]
definition: High-involvement systems generally include three dimensions: relatively high skill requirements; work designed so that employees have discretion and opportunity to use their skills in collaboration with other workers; and an incentive structure that enhances motivation and commitment. In this study they were conceptualized along three dimensions based on prior research: skill level, work design, and involvement-enhancing HR incentives.

name: Employee quit rates
authors_terms: ["employee quit rates", "quit rates", "average annual quit rate"]
definition: The average annual quit rate, measured so that quits exclude discharges, retirements, transfers, and promotions. High quit rates not only increase the costs of recruitment and selection but negatively affect sales growth because new employees face a learning curve.

name: Sales growth
definition: Sales growth is measured as the natural logarithm of the percent change in the value of sales to the particular customer base served by the center.

name: Customer segment served
definition: Establishments were dummy-coded as serving all customers in their market (universal centers) or as serving a particular segment (large business, small business, or residential). The mass market is comprised of two customer segments, residential consumers and small businesses, while large business customers are high-value-added customers that usually require the bundling of complex products.

name: Skill level
definition: The basic skill requirements of the customer service or sales job at each call center, based on the formal education and the training needed for a new employee to become proficient.

name: Work design
definition: The design of work to provide opportunities for individual discretion and ongoing learning through collaboration with other employees.

name: HR incentives
definition: HR incentives such as ongoing investment in training, employment security, high relative pay, and performance management systems that build trust.

name: Litigation ability
authors_terms: ["litigation ability", "IP litigation ability", "ability to litigate", "ability to defend against IP infringement litigation"]
definition: We define the 'litigation ability' as having means to both initiate an IP-related litigation and defend against IP-related lawsuits filed by other firms (i.e., be a plaintiff or defendant in a lawsuit). The abilities to initiate and defend against a lawsuit are often intertwined.

name: Technological diversification
authors_terms: ["technological diversification", "expansion into new technological domains", "New Domains", "New Domain"]
definition: Diversification via innovating in a new technological domain is a key mode of firm growth and a driver of performance of many modern firms. The main dependent variable, New Domains, proxies for the extent to which the firm expands into new technological domains.

name: Inventor utilization
definition: The first contingency variable, Inventor Utilization, captures the ease with which the firm can utilize its inventors who are active in other technology classes in developing innovations in the focal primary class j.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: The second contingency variable, Inventor Mobility, captures the extent to which inventors within a domain tend to move across firms.

name: IP litigation propensity
authors_terms: ["IP Lawsuits", "litigation propensity", "IP lawsuits filed by the firm"]
definition: For our empirical design to be effective, Law Firm Exit must reduce the firm's litigation ability. In this section, we provide evidence that law firm exit affects the firm's litigation ability by demonstrating its effect on IP lawsuits filed by the firm in the year of exit.

name: External EEO-AA intervention
authors_terms: ["EEO-AA intervention", "external intervention into an organization's personnel practices", "external intervention", "regulation by the OFCCP", "compliance reviews", "EEO-AA-related lawsuits"]
definition: External intervention into an organization's personnel practices resulting from EEO-AA law; change may be imposed upon organizations, as when the government mandates such change by law, or induced, as when government and other agencies make organizational change an eligibility requirement for funding.

name: Formalized HRM structures
authors_terms: ["formalized HRM structures", "formalization of an organization's HRM practices", "number of formalized HRM structures"]
definition: Formal rules, programs, positions, and procedures influencing personnel decision making in an organization. These structures are developed with the intention of improving the employment status of protected groups.

name: Identity-conscious HRM structures
definition: Structures that formally recognize the gender, race, national origin, or other protected identity of an individual. Identity-conscious structures imply that in addition to individual merit, demographic group identity is taken into consideration by the makers of organizational human resource decisions.

name: Identity-blind HRM structures
definition: Formalized HRM practices designed to ensure that the human resource decision-making process is the same for each individual, judging an individual on the basis of his or her achievements under a veil of ignorance as to group identification.

name: Employment status of women and people of color
authors_terms: ["employment status of women and people of color", "employment status of protected groups", "employment outcomes"]
definition: Six measures were developed to assess the employment status of women and people of color in an organization, covering the percentage of employees and the percentage of managers who were women and who were people of color and the highest level of management attained by women and people of color.

name: Top management EEO-AA support
authors_terms: ["top management's EEO-AA values", "commitment to EEO-AA values by top management", "management attitude", "top management support"]
definition: Top management's values and support with respect to EEO-AA, which the authors argue is critical to the effectiveness of an organization's EEO-AA program. The measure was coded so that a high value indicated stronger support of EEO-AA.

name: Pre-grant patent publication
authors_terms: ["patent publication", "pre-grant publication", "18-month publication", "public disclosure through patent publication", "invention disclosure"]
definition: Publication of patent applications by the patent office 18 months after their priority date; AIPA generally required inventors filing for patent protection in the United States on or after November 29, 2000 to publish their applications 18 months after their priority date rather than at patent grant.

name: Licensing after patent grant
authors_terms: ["licensing after patent grant", "licensing after the grant date", "wait until patent grant"]
definition: The occurrence of the licensing transaction after the patent grant date; before AIPA the inventor could either license after the application date or wait until the grant date.

name: Licensing after 18-month publication
authors_terms: ["licensing after 18 months", "licensing after the publication date", "licensing between 18 months and patent grant", "18-month effect"]
definition: Licensing that occurs after 18 months from the patent application date and before patent grant, the window created by AIPA's separation of publication from grant.

name: Licensing delay
definition: The number of months between the patent application date and the license date, an important variable that determines the rate at which ideas are commercialized.

name: Licensor for-profit status
definition: Whether the licensor is a for-profit entity rather than a nonprofit organization such as a university, hospital, or research institute; 68.6% of the sample's licensors are for-profit entities.

name: Licensor licensing experience
authors_terms: ["licensor's prior licensing experience", "number of prior licensor deals", "less-experienced licensors"]
definition: The licensor's experience as a seller in the market for ideas, measured as the number of deals the licensor has undertaken prior to the focal agreement.

name: Trading opportunities
authors_terms: ["trading opportunities", "potential licensing opportunities", "transactions in the market for ideas"]
definition: The opportunities for buyers and sellers to transact inventions in the market for ideas, which the authors argue patent publication augments by infusing more information into the market. They propose that public disclosure through a centralized, standardized, and verifiable repository helps sellers establish the credibility of their ideas and augment potential licensing opportunities.

name: Authenticity
definition: Authenticity can be defined as an attribution accorded by social agreement to certain objects, persons, or places-entities, in a general sense-about whether the entity is 'genuine' or 'real'. In the modern context it is frequently a social construction, so that it is ultimately not about facts per se but rather about interpretations regarding those facts.

name: Consumer value ratings
definition: The value of a product or service offered to a consumer can be regarded as the person's 'overall assessment of the utility of a product [or, brand, service, or experience] based on perceptions of what is received and what is given'. At its core, value is an assessment of what is given up for what is received.

name: Chain affiliation
definition: Chain-affiliated organizations are the most visible manifestation of chain ownership; chain restaurants are identified by the number of restaurants listed with the same name in the metropolitan area. Chains are expected to be regarded as inauthentic because they involve the routinized application of formulas of operation, usually in the interests of efficiency and a profit motive.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family businesses, those organizations owned and operated by identifiable community members, tend to be smaller in size, do not always appear to be profit maximizers, and often reflect the idiosyncrasies of their owners.

name: Niche width
definition: An organization's niche width can be defined relative to existing institutional categories. An organization can operate exclusively within a single existing category (specialist), within multiple existing categories at the same time (generalist, to a degree that can be measured and compared), or fall outside the scope of any existing institutional categories.

name: Home-host bilateral ties
authors_terms: ["bilateral ties between home and host nations", "ties", "home-host ties", "relative ties"]
definition: Bilateral ties between home and host nations, categorized along five dimensions: geographic ties, colonial ties, immigration ties, linguistic ties, and institutional ties. 'Similarly, here, we are suggesting that bilateral ties emanating from national geography and history also influence MNEs' foreign performance outcomes (not just their investment behavior).'

name: Firm-specific advantages
definition: A theory premised on firm heterogeneity emphasizes relative levels of firm-specific advantages (FSAs); using the term 'technology' to refer broadly to MNE capabilities, the authors treat superiority in these advantages as the driver of leadership when an MNE dominates a rival in the rival's own home market.

name: Relative performance of rival foreign MNEs
authors_terms: ["MNE leadership in Brazil", "foreign MNE leadership", "lead status", "lead in that focal host market"]
definition: Which of two rival foreign MNEs leads in the focal host market; the dependent variable was foreign MNE leadership in Brazil (coded based on MNE sales shares in Brazil).

name: Institutional investor activism
authors_terms: ["institutional investor activism", "shareholder activism by institutional investors", "institutional investor activists"]
definition: Institutional investor activists, including pension funds, mutual funds, and hedge funds, undertake activist campaigns, ranging from communication with management to lawsuits and takeover bids, mainly to seek financial gains. The study keeps the first activism event for each targeted firm and focuses on filings whose stated purpose pertains to concerns, disputes, or control.

name: Workplace injury and illness rate
authors_terms: ["total case rate", "TCR", "rate of employee injuries and illnesses", "workplace injury and illness", "workplace safety"]
definition: The dependent variable is computed as the number of work-related injuries and illnesses divided by the number of hours worked by all employees in a given establishment year. The authors argue that institutional investor activism may lower safety standards and increase employee workload, leading to a rise in the rate of workplace injuries and illnesses.

name: Institutional investor activist political ideology
authors_terms: ["institutional investor activist liberalism", "political ideology of institutional investor activists", "liberal institutional investor activists", "nonliberal institutional investor activists"]
definition: The political ideology of individuals refers to ingrained convictions and philosophies about how society should be governed, and it reflects fundamental beliefs and values about societal goals and how to achieve them. The authors contend that institutional investor activists with distinct political ideologies will impose heterogeneous influences on targeted companies.

name: Board political ideology
definition: The political ideology of board members shapes their attention to the interests of different stakeholders, and therefore affects the influence of institutional investor activism on the rate of workplace injuries and illnesses. Conservative-leaning boards are more likely to support cost-cutting and efficiency-enhancing measures, whereas liberal-leaning boards are more likely to safeguard employees' rights and interests.

name: Market value
definition: The market value of a firm is modeled as a function of the firm's tangible and intangible assets that jointly constitute the firm's total stock of resources; in the estimation, the dependent variable, measuring the firm's market value according to the market-value equation, is Log (Tobin's q).

name: Internal CSR actions
definition: Internal actions typically reflect inward-looking practices that involve real actions to develop organizational capabilities and to meet the expectations of those social actors upon which the organization depends for critical resources. The internal actions category includes corporate policy questions as well as several quantitative indicators of CSR implementation.

name: External CSR actions
definition: External actions typically reflect public and highly visible initiatives and patterns of communication that involve the undertaking of ceremonies to gain legitimacy, primarily through the seeking of public endorsement of the organization and its practices by outside audiences. The external actions category includes claims that firms make and disclosures they issue.

name: CSR resources accumulated from internal and external actions
authors_terms: ["CSR resources", "the sum of internal and external actions", "Sum/assets"]
definition: The stock of intangible CSR resources is more likely to be the result of prior internal actions in combination with current external actions; this combination of prior internal and current external actions describes valuable CSR intangible resources.

name: Gap between external and internal CSR actions
authors_terms: ["the gap between external and internal actions", "misalignment", "absolute value of the difference"]
definition: Even though both types of actions fall within the same overall organizational practice (i.e., CSR engagement), the extent to which a firm engages in one type of action may either exceed or fall behind the extent to which it engages in the other. Such a misalignment may occur for many reasons, but the gap this process generates may compel internal and external audiences, stakeholders, and especially the market to withdraw their support.

name: Entrepreneurial start-up
definition: We define a start-up as a firm founded one year prior to or subsequent to the execution date of a license to commercialize a technology within our sample.

name: Commercialization of licensed inventions
authors_terms: ["successfully commercialize", "likelihood of achieving commercial sales", "first commercial sale", "commercialized"]
definition: We characterize inventions within outcome (1) as those for which the firm has paid royalties to the university based on achieving product sales.

name: License termination
definition: Outcome (2) includes inventions for which the license was cancelled, thus signalling that the licensee has discontinued development and commercialization of the technology.

name: Returns to licensed inventions
authors_terms: ["level of returns to inventions", "realized economic returns", "university licensing revenues", "royalty payments", "earnings"]
definition: Because many firms in the sample are not public and do not report product-line sales or costs related to these sales, we are unable to observe economic returns for these licensees directly. We therefore proxy for economic returns by the royalty payments received by the university as specified in the licensing agreement.

name: Supplier monitoring
definition: Monitoring is defined as one party's (e.g., a buyer's) effort to verify another's (e.g., a supplier's) performance and compliance with a sourcing arrangement.

name: Solidarity norms
definition: Conceptually, a solidarity norm is defined as a bilateral expectation that the relationship itself is valued. Its general effect is to align parties' goals and foster mutual consent.

name: Concurrent sourcing
authors_terms: ["concurrent sourcing", "concurrent sourcing context", "sourcing context", "sourcing form", "sourcing mode", "concurrent vs. singular"]
definition: Firms often rely simultaneously on external sourcing and internal manufacturing for the same product; using a 'plural governance' or 'concurrent sourcing' strategy. Under concurrent sourcing the focal (external) supplier coexists with the buyer's internal supply source and the latter also plays the role of 'supplier'.

name: Supplier opportunism
definition: Contractor opportunism (toward the focal manufacturer) captures the manufacturer's perception of whether the contractor engages in 'self-interest seeking with guile' vis-a-vis the focal manufacturer.

name: Supplier performance
definition: Contractor performance (toward the focal manufacturer) measures the contractor's supply chain performance toward the focal manufacturer, including delivery cycle time, proportion of shipments delivered on-time, quality of deliveries, and responsiveness to requests for change.

name: FDA lobbying
definition: The Lobbying Disclosure Act (2 U.S.C. § 1601) defines lobbying as the provision of information to policy makers and agencies by individuals representing the firm interests.
