All corporate expenditures used to design and coordinate external speakers' interventions in scientific advisory committee hearings fall under the lobbying activities category.

name: IP protection
definition: The IP behind a new drug is usually more protected the more patents the firm has on that specific drug. The threat from imitators is strongly determined by the level of IP protection behind the firm's new product, in that IP rights are a powerful mechanism to prevent the entry of similar products.

name: Revision time
definition: Our first dependent variable is the time it took the FDA to complete the NDA revision process. It is important to note that our measure represents the opposite to review speed.

name: Drug scope
definition: We define a drug's scope by the number of diseases it can treat. The committee determines the drug's scope (i.e., conditions/subpopulations and interactions/contraindications).

name: Creator role
definition: In the prototypical structure of innovation, creators are expected to generate novel and useful ideas (variation) and managers decide which of these ideas to implement (selection). Creators focus on generating their own novel ideas, while managers focus on evaluating creators' ideas.

name: Creative forecasting accuracy
definition: Creative forecasting is the skill of predicting the outcomes of new ideas. Accuracy was scored as two types: estimation (accuracy in predicting the absolute success of any one idea) and placement (accuracy in ranking how successful a set of ideas will be compared with one another).

name: Idea novelty
definition: The degree to which the content of the video was unique from existing ideas, particularly in the circus arts domain but also in general. In Study 2 novelty was measured as the degree to which a product idea was novel, unique, or original.

name: Past success of own ideas
definition: The marketplace success achieved by creators' own ideas; to measure the past success of creators' videos, the number of views each video had prior to the study was recorded.

name: Idea quality
definition: Quality is defined as the audience appeal that is intrinsic to ideas themselves, rather than driven by external factors such as social influence, marketing, or opportunity structures.

name: Idea ownership
definition: Whether the idea being forecasted is the creator's own idea rather than someone else's. Creators may become entrenched in the content of their own ideas or come to identify strongly with their ideas, making it difficult for them to accurately predict how audiences will experience their ideas.

name: Audience success
definition: Measures of how much the audience likes, shares, and seeks out the performer(s) in a show are treated as central and face-valid dimensions of success with the audience; in Study 2 the audience's purchase intent was used to measure how successful a product idea would be with consumers.

name: Innovation output
definition: Innovation output, the dependent variable, is measured through the patenting frequency of firms, that is, the number of successful patent applications by a firm in a given year.

name: Absolute size of acquired knowledge base
authors_terms: ["absolute size of acquired knowledge base", "absolute size of the acquired knowledge base"]
definition: The size of the acquired knowledge base is the number of patents (i.e., knowledge elements) on the list prepared for each acquiring firm and year of the patents its acquisitions had obtained in the preceding 5 years, combined with the patents cited by them.

name: Relative size of acquired knowledge base
authors_terms: ["relative size of acquired knowledge base", "relative size of the acquired knowledge base"]
definition: The relative size of the knowledge base to be integrated is the size of the acquired knowledge base relative to the size of the acquiring firm's knowledge base; the larger this relative size, the more difficult recognition, assimilation and application of the acquired knowledge are likely to be.

name: Relatedness of acquired and acquiring knowledge bases
authors_terms: ["relatedness of acquired knowledge base", "relatedness of the acquired knowledge base", "relatedness of acquired and acquiring knowledge bases"]
definition: The third critical dimension in the unification of two knowledge bases is their relatedness; while the previous arguments concerned the magnitude of the acquired and acquiring knowledge bases the relatedness argument concerns the content of these knowledge bases.

name: Nontechnological acquisitions
definition: Acquisitions that did not meet either of the two criteria used to classify acquisitions as technological were coded as nontechnological acquisitions.

name: Inventor commingling
definition: We define inventor commingling as team-level integration through collaborative interactions, by which inventors from the acquired and acquiring entities interact, collaborate, and share both technological and organizational knowledge, performing joint research and development.

name: Structural integration
definition: We define structural integration as a formal design that groups organizational units within one administrative boundary. Structural integration often implies a long-term, irreversible change, dampening the target's decision-making autonomy.

name: Innovation output
authors_terms: ["innovation output", "innovation performance", "firm patent stock", "firm forward citation stock"]
definition: The acquired firm's innovation output is evidenced by its patenting records. The authors measure it as the firm's patent stock (innovation quantity) and as the forward citation stock of its patents (innovation quality).

name: Tenure of commingling acquirer inventors
authors_terms: ["tenure of commingling acquirer inventors", "long-tenured acquirer inventors", "short-tenured acquirer inventors"]
definition: As organizational knowledge is cumulative, path-dependent, and firm-specific, the ability of inventors to facilitate organizational knowledge transfer increases with their tenure length. The authors focus on the tenure of commingling-acquiring entity inventors with the acquirer, controlling for their overall experience.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Product segments were classified as unrelated if they did not contain the same first three digits of the SSIC codes. Unrelated diversification (DU) has a minimum value of zero; the higher the DU value, the greater the unrelatedness.

name: Related diversification
definition: Product segments were classified as related if they contained the same first three digits of the SSIC codes, indicating the segments belonged to the same industry subcategory. Related diversification (DR) has a minimum value of zero; the higher the DR value, the greater the relatedness.

name: Debt financing level
authors_terms: ["debt financing level", "firm leverage", "leverage", "level of debt financing"]
definition: Firm leverage, or the level of debt financing, was operationalized as the ratio of long-term debt to total capital. The authors treat the amount of debt firms assume as an element of their capital structure.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism is concerned with instability and volatility. The unpredictable, unsystematic, and uncertain changes that resulted from the Asian Financial Crisis characterize a dynamic environment, while the higher predictability, lower uncertainty, and lower volatility of the period leading up to 1997 represent a stable environment.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: Entropy measures the diversity of a firm's business with respect to the number and relative size of segments; separate entropy indices are computed for related and unrelated diversification.

name: Political pressure
authors_terms: ["political pressure", "pressure from elected legislatures", "regulatory agency pressure", "institutional pressure through political mechanisms"]
definition: Pressure that a firm faces from political and legislative actors and from regulatory agencies, which varies because firms face a complex set of state regulations. Firms subjected to greater levels of political pressure within the state in which they operated were expected to be more likely to join a voluntary agreement early.

name: Earliness of participation
authors_terms: ["early joiners", "late joiners", "early participants", "late participants", "early entrants", "timing of participation", "type of participant"]
definition: Early joiners enrolled in the program during the official ceremony organized in March 1995 by the DOE and participated in the design of the program; late participants enrolled at a later date, after the official ceremony, when the program was established and publicized outside of the industry, and did not participate in the initial setup and configuration of the program.

name: Trade association membership
authors_terms: ["trade association membership", "membership of the Edison Electric Institute", "links with the industry association", "industry trade association"]
definition: Membership in the industry trade association, which constitutes an industry network that provides a central forum for communication about political issues at stake and employs informal mechanisms to encourage compliance with its program requirements. Firms participating in the trade association are more informed about the impact of potential regulations and are more exposed to normative pressure exerted by their peers.

name: Firm visibility
definition: Visibility affects the level of social pressure to which a firm is subjected, because constituents of an institutional environment are more likely to take interest in an organization of which they are aware. More visible firms are more likely to be the target of activism and to participate in collective action.

name: Prior environmental investment
authors_terms: ["air pollution controls", "environmental efforts", "investment in environmental improvements", "greener firms"]
definition: Investments undertaken to reduce, prevent, or abate the adverse impact of a firm's activities on the environment before the initiation of a voluntary agreement. 'Greener' firms are ones that have already invested in reducing their environmental impact before the initiation of a related VA.

name: Participation in the voluntary agreement
definition: A firm's decision to enroll in the Climate Challenge program, in which each participating firm committed to reduce, avoid, or sequester greenhouse gas emissions, to annually report its activities and achievement, and to confer periodically with the DOE.

name: Substantive cooperation
definition: Participation in a voluntary agreement that is coupled with practical changes at the operational level, in which participating firms accomplish organizational or technological changes that improve their environmental performance. Substantive cooperation resulting in reductions in emissions was more likely with early entrants than with nonparticipants.

name: Symbolic cooperation
definition: Participation in a voluntary agreement without substantive implementation of the VA's requirements, in which firms decouple their practical actions from the formal organizational structures in which they participate. Symbolic cooperation signifies firms that participated in the VA but did not improve their environmental performance significantly more than nonparticipants.

name: Agrarian frame salience
authors_terms: ["agrarian frames", "similar frames", "frame bridging", "media attention to agrarian frames"]
definition: Agrarian frames are the similar frames promoted by farm associations that defined and promoted biodiesel as a renewable energy product made from virgin-oilseed feedstocks, emphasizing economic benefits to rural economies and energy independence.

name: Industry frame salience
authors_terms: ["industry frames", "dissimilar and compatible frames", "frame extension", "media attention to industry frames"]
definition: Industry frames are the dissimilar but compatible frames promoted by National Biodiesel Alliance members and other industry supporters that focused on increasing biodiesel consumption and extended market meaning to environmental and health benefits and to additional feedstocks without advocating any specific feedstock.

name: Environmental frame salience
authors_terms: ["environmental frames", "dissimilar and incompatible frames", "frame transformation", "media attention to environmental frames"]
definition: Environmental frames are the dissimilar and incompatible frames promoted by environmental organizations that argued recycled waste vegetable oil was the only sustainable option for biodiesel and sought to exclude and stigmatize oilseed feedstocks.

name: Oilseed venture foundings
definition: Oilseed entrants are organizations that entered the market and used technologies that produced biodiesel only from oilseed feedstocks, as promoted by farm associations.

name: Combination venture foundings
definition: Combination entrants are firms that entered the market and used technologies that produced biodiesel from a combination of oilseed, animal tallow, and WVO feedstocks.

name: WVO venture foundings
definition: WVO entrants are organizations that entered the market and used technologies that produced biodiesel only from waste vegetable oil feedstocks, which was the only feedstock deemed acceptable by environmental organizations.

name: Perceived exclusivity of market meaning
authors_terms: ["perceived exclusivity", "perceived exclusivity indicating that the market values only nonstigmatized frame elements"]
definition: The perception that emerges from the salience of dissimilar and incompatible frames, indicating that the market values only nonstigmatized frame elements.

name: Structural similarity
definition: Strategic reference point theory argues that because of mobility barriers between strategic groups, the most natural referents are those with similar structural variables because they face similar resource constraints. The authors propose that, in general, emulation decisions will tend not to stray outside of these major structural barriers.

name: Present image similarity
definition: Insider perceptions of how external constituencies view the organization is termed "construed external image". Present image refers to how members think others see the institution.

name: Desired future image similarity
authors_terms: ["desired future image", "future image", "similar desired future images"]
definition: Gioia and Thomas (1996) demonstrate that desired future image is also critical, especially if the intention is organizational change. Top managers narrowed their emulation choices to universities whose reputations were similar to their desired future image and whose attributes echoed valued characteristics of their aspired identity.

name: Organizational identity type similarity
definition: Organizational identity represents how members answer the question "what kind of organization is this?". When members perceive their organization's character to be oriented mainly toward economic issues, identity is deemed more "utilitarian"; when they perceive the organization's character to be defined mainly by ideological and value-based concerns, identity is deemed more "normative".

name: Identity strength similarity
definition: Identity strength refers to the degree to which members hold a set of beliefs about the organization, or the extent to which members perceive their organization's qualities and values to be distinct or special, regardless of the type of identity perceived.

name: Reputation similarity
definition: We adopt Elsbach and Glynn's (1996) definition of "strategic reputation:" an external audience's beliefs about the central and distinctive traits that give an organization a competitive advantage, particularly in incomplete information settings.

name: Interorganizational emulation
definition: We define interorganizational emulation as striving to equal or surpass a comparison organization or organizations on a set of strategic qualities or features.

name: Perceived environmental threat
definition: High perceived environmental threat was conceptualized as top managers' perceptions that the university's environment was high in dynamism, high in complexity, and low in munificence.

name: Perceived degree of strategic change
definition: Top managers reported the extent to which their universities had changed along four dimensions over the past five years. These dimensions were developed and refined through pretesting. They included the institution's mission, its major goals, its program offerings, and its funding sources.

name: Reputation difference of emulation target
authors_terms: ["difference in reputation between the emulating university and the emulated university", "upward comparison", "downward comparison"]
definition: We created a matrix representing the difference in reputation between the emulating university and the emulated university. The authors distinguish emulating higher reputation targets (upward comparison) from emulating schools whose reputations are lower than one's own (downward comparison).

name: Comparison granularity
definition: Elsbach and Kramer's (1996) qualitative results indicated that business schools under the highest external threat invoked more categorization attributions (both structural and identity-related) and categorized themselves in terms of smaller, more specialized groups. Schools with the lowest external threat categorized themselves into less specialized groups and used fewer bases of categorization.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: The dependent variable, the cumulative abnormal return of each sample firm for each event accumulated in the event window of length w; the abnormal returns are the differences between the realized daily return and the constant expected return given by the mean return of the stock computed in an estimation window of 100 days before the events.

name: NGO donations
definition: Gifts that the firm makes to support an NGO project. NGO donations constitute arms-length contributions, although they can form the basis for more interactive forms of collaboration.

name: Political donations
authors_terms: ["political donations", "donations to politicians", "campaign donations", "political campaign donations"]
definition: Gifts that the firm makes to support a political campaign. Political campaign donations are typically considered a type of legislative subsidy provided by firms, which can facilitate access to allied politicians but not provide control over them or their stance on political issues.

name: Political board ties
authors_terms: ["political board ties", "board ties to political actors", "politically connected board members"]
definition: Corporate board members with direct political connections that they can leverage for the firm's benefit.

name: NGO board ties
authors_terms: ["NGO board ties", "board ties to NGOs", "corporate representation on NGO boards"]
definition: Corporate representation on NGO boards, that is, corporate board members with NGO connections that they can leverage for the firm's benefit.

name: Number of peers
definition: Firms that collaborate with a shared partner have to compete for the resources of that partner, and the number of peers counts the other developers releasing games with the publisher in the same year as the focal developer.

name: Superiority of peers
definition: The superiority of peers is the average review score that all games of developers working with the publisher received in the focal year divided by the review score of the focal developer's game; the higher the score, the more superior the other developers in the publisher's portfolio.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is measured at the individual project level as a game's revenues and across all projects at the level of the year as the sum of the revenues of all games a developer released in the focal year.

name: Employee's personal success
definition: An employee's personal success is measured by the revenues of all games in which the employee participated in year t + 1; how much revenue a game generates is important to employees because their personal income depends on it and being affiliated with high-grossing games increases their chances to work on interesting games in the future.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "transaction-specific investments", "high asset specificity", "buyer asset specificity"]
definition: Transaction-specific investments are tied to a particular exchange relationship and of much lesser or no value in their second best uses. The resulting quasi-rents render a firm vulnerable to opportunistic behavior when it makes a transaction-specific investment.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: We specifically examine technological uncertainty, which describes difficulties in foreseeing the technological developments and requirements in the relationship.

name: Performance ambiguity
definition: Performance ambiguity describes a situation in which a company is unable to evaluate the quality of the good or service received from its exchange partner. It can occur because of difficulties in measurement or the nonseparability of effort across actors.

name: Contractual complexity
definition: Although contracts are a common feature in alliances, they vary considerably in their complexity. More complex contracts are able to specify each of these points in greater detail as well as address a wider range of potential contingencies.

name: Formal governance mechanisms
authors_terms: ["formal governance mechanisms", "high levels of formal governance mechanisms"]
definition: Depersonalized means of controlling and coordinating partner behavior and output in a relationship. Typical examples include budget plans, cost breakdown methods, and audit programs based on the evaluation of files, records, and reports.

name: Relational governance mechanisms
authors_terms: ["relational governance mechanisms", "high levels of relational governance mechanisms"]
definition: Relational governance mechanisms enhance the building of trust and social identification through the interaction of individuals from the partner organizations. Typical examples are regular meetings or the formation of steering committees, both of which are based on the interaction of specific people in the collaborating companies.

name: Opportunism
definition: Opportunism refers to 'self-interest seeking with guile' and can include 'lying, stealing, and cheating' as well as the 'incomplete or distorted disclosure of information . . . to mislead, distort, disguise, obfuscate, or otherwise confuse' the partner.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are sets of legally independent firms linked by formal and informal network ties. Indian BG-affiliated firms differ from unaffiliated firms in that they are subject to network governance as well as hierarchical authority.

name: External focus of attention in setting aspirations
authors_terms: ["focus of attention", "external focus of attention", "internal focus of attention", "attention"]
definition: we expect business group affiliates to be more externally focused than are unaffiliated firms, and to compare their performance with that of other firms within their industry or business group

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance against aspirations (P - A)", "performance feedback", "performance below the aspiration level"]
definition: We specify the aspiration level (A) as a mixture of external and internal (i.e., historical) influences (Cyert and March 1963, p. 123). Performance was measured through ROA, an important measure for managerial performance evaluation that is not affected by the financial leverage of the firm.

name: Market search intensity
definition: Organizational search in the market domain is conducted by adding products to obtain a wider market position or adding customers to get a deeper market penetration. Both forms of search involve greater resource use of marketing, sales, and promotion.

name: Internal technology search
authors_terms: ["internal technology search (R&D intensity)", "R&D search intensity", "R&D intensity"]
definition: This is because search through R&D can solve performance problems stemming from outdated product lines.

name: Business group size
authors_terms: ["business group size", "BG size", "large BG-affiliated firm", "small BG-affiliated firm"]
definition: We computed a business group's revenues during a year as the total of the revenues of its constituent affiliate firms.

name: Number of business groups managed
authors_terms: ["average number of businesses managed", "number of business groups managed", "number of businesses managed", "span of control"]
definition: the average number of businesses managed (a proxy for changes in administrative structure that reflect shifting attitudes toward governance efficiences and effective span of control)

name: Business relatedness
authors_terms: ["degree of business-relatedness", "average mix of businesses managed", "business relatedness"]
definition: the average mix of businesses managed (a proxy for changing attitudes toward economies of scope achieved through business relatedness)

name: Entry mode
definition: One of the crucial decisions when deciding to expand into a new market is the decision on whether to set up a new venture or to acquire an existing firm.

name: Human capital
definition: Human capital is directly related to the extent of the firm's ownership advantages, and is measured as the proportion of college graduates in the firm's work force.

name: Firm closure
definition: Foreign firm closure occurs where the foreign owned firm ceases its operations.

name: Foreign capital divestiture
definition: Foreign capital divestiture occurs where the firm continues to operate, but no longer with foreign capital participation.

name: Foreign ownership stake
definition: Joint ventures differ with respect to the degree of control exerted by the foreign party. Although the foreign share can vary in a continuous scale between 0 and 100, two thresholds are of particular importance; the first threshold distinguishes portfolio investments from joint ventures in a narrow sense, and the second distinguishes majority from minority joint ventures.

name: Limitation of liability
definition: The reason why there are several legal forms under which firms can operate is to allow for different limitations on the degree of liability incurred by firms' owners. While in unlimited liability firms the owners are personally accountable for the firm's debts, the liability of the owners of a limited liability firm is restricted to the value of their equity in the company.

name: Market attractiveness
authors_terms: ["economic attractiveness of a market", "market attractiveness", "market occupancy", "mean occupancy"]
definition: Mean occupancy rates reflect the strength of local market demand conditions. When demand is high relative to supply, market occupancy, market prices, and market profitability all tend to increase, suggesting that mean occupancy is a good indicator for the economic attractiveness of the market.

name: Entry
definition: In the traditional economic perspective, entry is expected to occur when incumbent firms are earning above-normal returns. A firm will enter a market when the expected discounted value of future profits exceeds entry costs.

name: Exit
definition: We consider only shutdowns as exits and not cases of sales to other owners or rebranding of hotels. We expect that firms will evaluate the net present value of continuing in business and that these estimates are informed by their recent performance.

name: Pricing
definition: In the economic view of competition within markets, prices and quantities sold are outcomes of the interplay of supply and demand. Holding supply constant, as demand increases, firms have the ability to charge higher prices.

name: Prior performance
definition: To capture responsiveness to recent performance, our primary independent variable is the establishment's occupancy level in the prior quarter; occupancy is a measure that is frequently used in the industry as a performance indicator.

name: Closely held status
definition: Closely held firms are firms in which there is a high degree of overlap in ownership and management, or firms that generally feature (i) a relatively small number of shareholders, (ii) a limited market for the shares of the firm, and (iii) active shareholder participation in the management of the firm.

name: Asset durability
authors_terms: ["asset durability", "asset durability of CAPX", "asset durability of new capital expenditures", "durability of the assets purchased"]
definition: Asset durability equals the expected useful life of a firm's equipment... asset durability refers to the expected longevity of the firm's annual flow of CAPX.

name: Historic temporal orientation
definition: A firm's historic temporal orientation... captures the same firm's aggregate duration for its entire asset base (not just newly acquired assets) compared to the average for its industry. Positive values of historic temporal orientation correspond to a firm having, on average, longer-lived assets than typical for the industry.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspirations", "the difference between attained performance and aspirations", "performance versus aspirations"]
definition: The first factor is a firm's performance relative to aspirations, which the BTOF establishes as critical to the framing of managerial decision making. We adopt a measure of aspirations as a weighted average of a social comparison-to performance of similar firms in an industry-and a self-referent historical aspiration.

name: Stock-based compensation
authors_terms: ["stock-based compensation", "stock-based incentive grants", "grants of stock-based incentives"]
definition: Stock-based compensation equals the proportion of total direct compensation (including salary, bonus, and stock compensation) that comprises restricted stock and the value of stock options granted (based on the Black-Scholes formula) in year t - 1.

name: Option exercisability
definition: The option exercisability variable equals the value of the top management team's stock options exercisable in year t - 1 divided by total compensation in t - 1.

name: Alliance type
authors_terms: ["cross-function alliance", "same-function alliance", "type of alliance", "alliance structure", "link alliances", "scale alliances"]
definition: we define a same-function alliance to be one where the ultimate value of the alliance output is an additive function of the inputs of the partnering firms, whereas in a cross-function alliance the value of the alliance is a multiplicative function of the investments of partnering firms.

name: Number of partners in the alliance
authors_terms: ["number of partners", "number of partnering firms", "alliance size", "n partners"]
definition: There are n partners in each alliance. The experiments vary two levels of alliance size (n = 2 or 4).

name: Collective investment in the alliance
definition: Denote the investment of partner j in alliance i by xij, and denote the collective investment in alliance i by Xi.

name: Individual partner investment
authors_terms: ["individual investment", "resource commitment", "resources committed by partnering firms", "investment of partner j", "xij"]
definition: Denote the investment of partner j in alliance i by xij (0 <= xij <= zij), where zij is some upper bound on investments for partner j.

name: Perceived alliance performance
authors_terms: ["likely performance of an alliance", "predicted performance", "perceived performance"]
definition: investigate managers' prevailing view on how the inputs of partnering firms are combined to determine the output of an alliance. After participants read one of the alliance scenarios, they were told that if both partners in the alliance were to contribute 100% effort, then the likely performance of the alliance would be 100%.

name: Dispersion in perceived alliance performance
authors_terms: ["variance in the perceived performance", "average within-person variance in the predicted performance"]
definition: we should observe more variance in the perceived performance of cross-function alliances compared to the performance of same-function alliances, where the variance is taken across all the different input levels.

name: Partner's resource input
authors_terms: ["inputs by the partnering firm", "effort contributed by the partner", "exogenously given effort level x2l"]
definition: we ask 40 respondents to indicate how much effort they will commit to a cross-function alliance as well as a same-function alliance for 15 different levels of inputs by the partnering firm.

name: Opportunity to learn from alliance partners
authors_terms: ["opportunity to learn", "opportunity for learning", "learning opportunities", "interpartner learning", "SLgamma"]
definition: Sometimes firms forge alliances so they can also learn from partnering firms. In these alliances, collaborators earn both private and common benefits, where the common benefits flow from the joint output of the alliance, and the private benefits accrue from a firm's ability to leverage its new knowledge outside the scope of the focal alliance. The parameter SLgamma > 0 is a measure of firm j's opportunity to learn from its partners.

name: Investment in competition outside focal alliance
definition: Investment made by the firm in the competition outside the scope of the focal alliance.

name: Total investment
definition: The firm's total investment across the focal alliance and the competition outside its scope.

name: Alliance type
definition: Link alliances, in contrast with scale alliances, aim at combining different and complementary skills and resources that each partner contributes. Scale alliances are alliances in which the partners contribute similar resources pertaining to the same stage or stages in the value-chain.

name: Alliance reorganization
definition: We define reorganization as a major change in the distribution of functional activities such as R&D, manufacturing, assembly, and marketing among the partner firms.

name: Alliance takeover
definition: Alliance takeover occurs when the alliance ends with one of the partners undertaking all previously collaborative activities itself. Takeovers include cases where one partner buys the joint venture and cases when one partner acquires the other partner.

name: Alliance continuation
definition: An alliance outcome in which alliances continue within their initial distribution of activities, without reorganization or takeover.

name: Alliance dissolution
definition: Dissolution signals that an alliance has failed or, at least, has outlived its purpose. The partners dissolve the alliance with no takeover or prior reorganization.

name: Alliance duration
authors_terms: ["alliance duration", "length of time that the alliance operates before the outcome occurs"]
definition: An alliance duration dependent variable that recorded the number of years between the formation of the alliance and the first of the four types of outcomes that took place.

name: Voluntary labor code adoption
authors_terms: ["voluntary labor code adoption", "labor code adoption", "code adoption", "GwG adoption", "adoption of the GwG labor code"]
definition: The primary distinction between the former non-voluntary labor code adoption and the latter voluntary one is based on the former involving coercion or pressure exerted by a stakeholder to adopt the code, whereas the latter is a discretionary choice of the adopters.

name: Employee withdrawal
definition: Job withdrawal, either temporarily through absenteeism or permanently through voluntary turnover, will decrease at plants voluntarily adopting a labor code.

name: Operational performance
definition: Operational outcomes such as quality, productivity, efficiency, and on-time delivery; the study measures operational performance with efficiency, productivity, defect rate, and on-time delivery.

name: Financial performance
definition: Improvements in financial performance for code adopters in the form of increases in sales volume and price.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Two separate aspects of performance were of interest: organizations' profit performance and the subjective estimates of their top executives about organizational performance. Performance above or below the satisficing level determines whether an organization is in the domain of gains or of losses.

name: Organizational slack
definition: A two-component concept of slack was proposed that made the distinction between absorbed slack, referring to slack absorbed as costs in organizations, and unabsorbed slack, referring to uncommitted liquid resources.

name: Decentralization of decision making
definition: In this research decentralization refers to the extent to which the chief executive of an organization delegated decision making authority in key areas to other top executives.

name: Risk taking in organizational decisions
definition: Risk refers to the uncertainty of the outcomes of an organization's resource commitments; risk taking was measured as the extent to which top executives rated their organizations as oriented towards risk taking as demonstrated by decisions such as reliance on innovation, debt-financing, heavy R&D, and high risk-high return investments.

name: Opportunity riskiness
authors_terms: ["opportunity riskiness", "industry-specific risk rating of the opportunity", "riskiness of the opportunity", "risk rating", "industry-specific risk"]
definition: Riskiness of the opportunity exploited, captured by the industry-specific credit risk rating of newly founded firms; risk ratings are used as a proxy for the likelihood of insolvency or the riskiness of an organization's resource commitments in a given industry. The measure captures the average risk (across all start-ups on the detailed five-digit industry level) that the founder faced when he/she created the firm, and in each of the following two years for firms that survived.

name: Managerial experience
authors_terms: ["managerial experience", "management experience", "knowledge of how to operate a business"]
definition: Managerial experience (knowledge of how to operate a business) is acquired by investing time observing, studying, and making business decisions and understanding organizational routines; such knowledge has a high tacit component and cannot be readily acquired by individuals lacking it.

name: Industry experience
definition: Industry experience grows out of an individual's prior experience in the industry of his/her newly founded firm; like managerial experience, industry experience is costly to build from scratch and cannot be readily obtained by founders who lack this endowment.

name: New firm performance
definition: Performance of the newly founded firm, measured as the total amount of revenues generated by the start-up firms; the achievement of sales signals that a firm founded by an unemployed person was successful in attracting customers and, more generally, in meeting market demand with its offerings.

name: Procedural justice
definition: This study defines procedural justice in the alliance context as the extent to which an alliance's strategic decisionmaking process and procedures are impartial and fair as perceived by this alliance's boundary spanners.

name: Operational outcome
definition: Cooperation outcomes are defined as alliance performance in financial return (i.e., profitability) and operational consequence (i.e., competitive strength in labor productivity, quality control, technology development, customer service, and managerial efficiency).

name: Financial outcome
definition: Cooperation outcomes are defined as alliance performance in financial return (i.e., profitability). Financial outcome was defined as return on investment (%), obtained from the first survey.

name: Interpersonal trust
definition: Trust is a psychological state comprising the intention to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations of the intentions or behavior of another. Research on alliance trust suggests trust is a multidimensional construct containing both cognitive and affective contents and both macro (interorganizational between two parties) and micro (interpersonal between boundary spanners) elements.

name: Interorganizational trust
definition: Trust is a psychological state comprising the intention to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations of the intentions or behavior of another. Research on alliance trust suggests trust is a multidimensional construct containing both cognitive and affective contents and both macro (interorganizational between two parties) and micro (interpersonal between boundary spanners) elements.

name: Cultural distance
definition: One prominent attribute of global strategic alliances is cultural distance between investing parties, and justice judgment and its roles are affected by cultural differences.

name: Governance form
authors_terms: ["governance form", "equity based", "non-equity based", "equity joint venture", "contractual agreement"]
definition: Governance form (equity based vs. non-equity based) moderates the justice-outcome relationship through the level of interparty binding.

name: Cooperation outcomes
definition: Cooperation outcomes are defined as alliance performance in financial return (i.e., profitability) and operational consequence (i.e., competitive strength in labor productivity, quality control, technology development, customer service, and managerial efficiency).

name: Recent peer coverage initiations
authors_terms: ["recent adoptions", "number of analysts initiating coverage in the previous year", "logged recent adoptions"]
definition: Recent adoptions were measured as the natural logarithm of the number of analysts initiating coverage in the previous year.

name: High-status peer coverage initiations
authors_terms: ["recent adoptions by high-status actors", "recent adoptions weighted by status", "logged recent adoptions weighted by status"]
definition: Recent adoptions by high-status actors were recent adoptions weighted by the status of the research department employing the analyst.

name: Earnings forecast overestimation
definition: An error was defined as an analyst's estimate of earnings per share of the focal firm being less accurate than the consensus estimate of all the other analysts following the firm. Model 3 examines the most reputation-threatening form of forecast error: large overestimates of firm earnings.

name: Coverage initiation
authors_terms: ["coverage initiation", "added coverage", "new coverage initiation", "initiation of coverage"]
definition: The initiation of coverage means that the research department employing the securities analyst has decided to adopt the focal organization as a subject for study and to allocate resources to its research. The authors distinguished coverage initiation (added coverage), when an analyst started issuing recommendations on a focal NASDAQ firm, and new coverage initiation, when an analyst added coverage of a firm when no other analyst in the same brokerage firm had dropped the firm.

name: Coverage abandonment
definition: An abandonment event was defined as an analyst stopping the issuing of an earnings estimate and recommendations for the focal NASDAQ firm.

name: Recent peer coverage abandonments
definition: Recent abandonments were measured as the natural logarithm of the number of analysts stopping coverage in the previous year.

name: High-status peer coverage abandonments
authors_terms: ["recent abandonments by high-status actors", "recent abandonments weighted by status"]
definition: Recent abandonments by high-status actors were measured using the same weights as for adoptions.

name: Firm performance
definition: The study uses survival time as the measure of firm performance, the length of time a firm in the industry offered products for sale.

name: Product introduction rate
authors_terms: ["product introduction rate", "rate of product introduction", "overall product introduction rate", "overall rate of product introduction"]
definition: With product life, the rate of product introduction characterizes a firm's product line management strategy, reflecting the rate at which products are replaced or renewed and the rate at which product lines are expanded.

name: Product life
authors_terms: ["product life", "average product life", "length of time each product is offered for sale"]
definition: The length of time each product is offered for sale; together with the speed of product development it characterizes a firm's product line management strategy.

name: Platform introduction rate
authors_terms: ["platform introduction rate", "rate of platform introduction", "rate of introduction of product platforms"]
definition: A platform is a base product that can be leveraged, perhaps successively, over a significant time period to produce a family of related derivative products; the platform introduction rate is the rate at which a firm introduces such products.

name: Derivative introduction rate
authors_terms: ["derivative introduction rate", "rate at which derivatives were generated from a platform", "larger numbers of derivatives per year of platform family life"]
definition: Derivative projects share most with previous products and their development requires only minor changes to existing products and/or processes; for each firm the rate at which derivatives were generated from a platform is calculated.

name: Family life in excess of product life
authors_terms: ["family life in excess of product life", "the difference between average family life and average product life", "the time by which platform life exceeded the life of the average of individual platform family members"]
definition: Family life is defined as the time from the introduction of the platform until the retirement of the last derivative product, and the construct is the time by which platform life exceeds the life of the average of individual platform family members.

name: Market tie dissolution
authors_terms: ["dissolution of advertiser-agency dyadic market ties", "dyadic market tie dissolution", "occurrence of tie dissolution"]
definition: The dissolution of advertiser-agency dyadic market ties that existed between an advertiser and an advertising agency. Dissolution was identified as occurring in calendar year t when an advertiser was listed as an agency's exchange partner, and an agency listed as an advertiser's advertising agency, in the respective Red Book directories in year t but not in year t + 1.

name: Advertiser executive exit
authors_terms: ["number of exits of advertiser executives", "number of advertiser executives who exit", "advertiser executives exiting"]
definition: Executives are defined as members of firms' top management teams. Exit was recorded as occurring in year t when an exchange manager or executive was listed as employed by a firm in year t but not in year t + 1.

name: Advertiser exchange manager exit
authors_terms: ["number of exits of advertiser marketing managers", "advertisers' marketing managers who exit", "advertiser exchange managers exiting"]
definition: Exchange managers are defined as managers who 'make decisions, act as points of contact between advertisers and agencies, and represent the expectations, interests, and ideas of one exchange partner to the other'. Exit was recorded as occurring in year t when an exchange manager or executive was listed as employed by a firm in year t but not in year t + 1.

name: Agency executive exit
authors_terms: ["number of exits of agency executives", "agency executives exiting"]
definition: Executives are defined as members of firms' top management teams. Exit was recorded as occurring in year t when an exchange manager or executive was listed as employed by a firm in year t but not in year t + 1.

name: Agency exchange manager exit
authors_terms: ["number of exits of agency account services managers", "number of exits of agency creative managers", "agency exchange managers who exit"]
definition: Exchange managers are defined as managers who 'make decisions, act as points of contact between advertisers and agencies, and represent the expectations, interests, and ideas of one exchange partner to the other'. Although the authors theorize agency exchange managers as a group, they cluster them into account service managers and creative managers because the work roles of agency exchange managers are highly differentiated by functional area.

name: Advertiser financial performance
authors_terms: ["advertiser performance", "advertiser growth", "change in log advertiser size"]
definition: Advertiser performance was determined as change in the logarithm of advertisers' gross revenue from time t to time t + 1. Year-to-year change in advertiser gross revenues is an appropriate measure of performance since a primary purpose of advertising is to increase revenues.

name: Market tie duration
authors_terms: ["tie duration", "duration of market ties", "number of continuous years the advertiser and agency reported working with each other"]
definition: Market tie duration was measured as the number of continuous years the advertiser and agency reported working with each other. Over the course of an exchange, firms create procedures, develop coordination mechanisms, and establish operating routines, so the longer the duration of a market tie the less fragile it becomes.

name: Institutional change in universities
definition: Project 985 was an educational reform funded and implemented by the government of the People's Republic of China that allocated additional research expenditures to a set of universities and attempted to institutionalize belief in the importance of innovation among university graduates.

name: Beliefs in the importance of intellectual property
authors_terms: ["beliefs regarding the importance of intellectual property", "beliefs regarding IP", "IP importance", "beliefs regarding innovation and IP"]
definition: Entrepreneurs' beliefs regarding the importance of intellectual property protection, which the authors treat as core to, and particularly indicative of, beliefs regarding innovation in the Chinese context.

name: Investment in technologically intensive activities
authors_terms: ["technologically intensive activities", "investment in technologically intensive activities", "R&D intensity", "innovation"]
definition: The degree to which firms invest in R&D and other technologically intensive activities; beliefs in innovation lead to an increased investment in technologically intensive activities.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of the entrepreneurial venture, measured by revenue, which the authors argue is an effective measure of performance for firms across industries because all firms ultimately need revenue for survival.

name: Specific investments
authors_terms: ["specific investments", "asset specificity", "physical asset specificity", "human asset specificity"]
definition: Specific investments, or asset specificity, are 'durable investments that are undertaken in support of particular transactions'; they create a lock-in situation since they have a lower value outside the relationship than inside.

name: Complementary resources
definition: The complementary resources scale captures the degree of complementarity between the resources that each partner contributes to the alliance. Alliances are used to gain access to other firms' valuable resources and to pool resources in order to realize synergies.

name: Strategic importance
definition: The strategic importance scale describes the strategic importance of the alliance for the future development of the firm, judged by how closely related the alliance is to fulfilling the strategic intent of the firm.

name: Change in alliance involvement
authors_terms: ["changes in alliance involvement", "an increase in alliance involvement"]
definition: Changes in alliance involvement measure growth or reduction in the scope of the alliance and whether the partners are more or less committed to the alliance. Building a long-lasting alliance requires the partners to gradually increase their involvement.

name: Change in alliance management
authors_terms: ["changes in the management responsible for the alliance", "management changes"]
definition: Changes in the management responsible for the alliance capture whether the same company representatives are responsible for the alliance in both companies or if a great turnover of personnel has occurred. Frequent changes in management may result in a cyclical trust-developing process.

name: Abrupt termination
definition: Abrupt termination, which is an operational measure, refers to termination before the end of the intended cooperation period.

name: Short-term performance
definition: Short-term performance is an effectiveness measure that captures goal fulfillment; it reflects the benefits to the partner firms in the early stages of the alliance.

name: Long-term performance
definition: Long-term performance is an effectiveness measure that captures goal fulfillment; it reflects benefits realized at later stages in the cooperation.

name: Service technology intensiveness
authors_terms: ["service technology", "intensiveness of the services provided", "intensive service technology", "extensive service technology", "intensiveness of agency-client contact"]
definition: An internal organizational measure of the intensiveness of services provided to clients; it reflects the extent to which organizational resources are devoted to any one client. Agencies with intensive technologies experience a higher cost per client served than agencies with relatively extensive services.

name: Interexecutive communication
definition: A measure of strategic level interaction between agencies based on personal contact and covering a variety of issues.

name: Joint program involvement
authors_terms: ["joint program involvement", "joint program activity", "interagency activity through joint programs"]
definition: A service-related linkage involving an agency's clients and professional staff, which tends to be more formal and more difficult to alter over a short time period than interexecutive communication.

name: Referrals from other organizations
authors_terms: ["referrals from other organizations", "referral inflows", "referrals from other agencies", "referral activity"]
definition: Clients that come to an agency as referrals from other agencies and related organizations, expressed as the proportion of the agency's total clients.

name: Referrals to other organizations
authors_terms: ["referrals to other organizations", "referral outflows", "referrals to other agencies", "referral activity"]
definition: Clients that an agency sends to other agencies and related organizations, expressed as the proportion of the agency's total clients.

name: Technology development mode
authors_terms: ["technology development mode", "internal R&D vs. alliances", "alliances to mutually develop technology", "internal development"]
definition: The mode used to develop a substantial innovation: internal development (vertical integration) or a technology alliance, defined as a partnership between two or more independent companies which seeks to leverage the resources and competencies of each in order to develop substantial innovations. Technology alliances thus represent an intermediate (nonmarket and bilateral) governance mechanism between internal development and market contracting.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Transaction-specific assets involve investments in human and physical capital that cannot be redeployed without losing productive value. In our research these transaction-specific assets will be assessed at the product category level.

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: Demand uncertainty concerns the fluctuation of demand and the unpredictability of demand. As measured, demand uncertainty assesses volatility, or the difficulty of predicting demand.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty refers to the probability of improvements in technology; i.e. to new generations of technology which might render obsolete the current technology development effort. We view this as an exogenous variable at the product category level with similar values for all relevant firms.

name: Ability to measure innovation performance
authors_terms: ["ability to measure innovation performance", "difficulty in measuring an innovation's performance", "performance measurement"]
definition: The specificity with which the performance of the innovation was established and monitored, since the outcome of technology development may take some time to materialize and it may be difficult to measure a technology development project on objective criteria.

name: Alliance experience
authors_terms: ["firm's experience with alliances", "alliance experience", "experience with alliances"]
definition: A firm with experience in technological alliances has learned the intricacies of dealing with partners in that context. The experience of the firm with alliances is determined by the number of alliances already established by the firm.

name: Past alliance success
definition: The extent to which previous alliances have been positive, evaluated on different criteria such as meeting objectives and market penetration levels achieved. Such learning should be reinforced in forming future alliances when the experience with previous alliances has been positive.

name: Market growth
definition: Higher growth markets will be more attractive investment alternatives and may favor internal technology development. This is a four-item scale assessing demand growth at the product category level with a coefficient alpha of 0.83.

name: Group proportion of high-status individuals
authors_terms: ["group percentage of stars", "individual global status", "high global status", "star analysts", "ranked analysts", "star"]
definition: The authors define individual status as 'the amount of respect, influence, and prominence' people enjoy in the eyes of others, and distinguish global status, a person's status ranking in a larger collective such as an industry or field, from local status within an embedded group. They focus on status that is global and explicit, and use the term 'star' throughout the paper to indicate an individual with high global status.

name: Expertise similarity
authors_terms: ["expertise similarity", "similarity in expertise", "overlapping areas of expertise", "heterogeneous expertise"]
definition: Expertise similarity is the extent to which group members possess overlapping areas of expertise; the authors assume that analysts within the same sector possess more similar expertise, on average, than analysts in different sectors. Higher scores on the measure represent more clustering within sectors and thus higher similarity in expertise.

name: Perceived group effectiveness
definition: The authors draw on Hackman's (2002, p. 23) definition of group effectiveness, whose first criterion holds that 'the productive output of the team ... meets or exceeds the standards of quantity, quality, and timeliness of the team's clients.' They study group effectiveness as perceived by the clients who use the group's output.

name: Outward foreign direct investment
authors_terms: ["outward foreign direct investment (OFDI)", "firm-level OFDI", "EMF OFDI", "OFDI activities", "outward FDI activity"]
definition: OFDI is an equity type investment to expand outside a firm's home country, resulting in the establishment of a foreign subsidiary in a host country. The dependent variable, firm-level OFDI, is a count of OFDI projects (i.e., foreign subsidiaries) established by a Chinese firm in a given year.

name: Symbiotic interdependence
definition: In our research context, symbiotic interdependence occurs when foreign and local suppliers or buyers are concentrated in the same geographic region. Symbiotic interdependence in a region increases resource exchanges between EMFs and foreign firms, thus enhancing their mutual dependence with each other for resources.

name: Competitive interdependence
definition: Competitive interdependence occurs when foreign and local firms operate within the same industry. A competitor effect occurs when local and foreign firms that provide similar products or services and require similar inputs depend on the same market for exchange.

name: Partner interdependence
definition: Partner interdependence occurs when foreign and local firms form joint ventures (JVs) in the emerging market. EMFs are more likely to face partner dependence uncertainty as the nonsubstitutability of the IJVs that the EMFs establish at home increases.

name: State ownership
definition: State ownership is a unique type of interdependence between the government and state-owned EMFs. The measure captures a Chinese firm's dependence on the government through ownership ties.

name: Competitors' new resource investments
authors_terms: ["competitors' new resource investments", "competitors' renewable investment", "competitors' investments", "competitors' resource strategies"]
definition: We capture competitors' new resource investments as competitors' efforts to reconfigure their resource portfolio by adding clean technologies. The variable captures the extent to which competing firms in the state have already invested in renewables.

name: New resource investment
authors_terms: ["a focal firm's new resource investment", "renewable investments", "renewable electricity generation investments"]
definition: A firm's new resource investment is the percentage of its MW operational from renewable resources relative to its total MW operational at time t + 1. Renewables comprise electricity generation from wind, sun, biomass, geothermal, and landfill gas.

name: Regulatory mandate
definition: Regulatory mandates are command-and-control policies that stipulate the use of certain technologies, fuels, processes, or forbid the use of specific inputs. RPSs set the target quantity of resources in a firm's portfolio that need to be clean electricity generation.

name: Knowledge distance from the established resource base
authors_terms: ["distance of the new resource investment to the old resource base", "more distant resources", "distant new resource investments"]
definition: More distant resources are defined as resources whose underlying scientific knowledge is further away from the industry's established resource base. As a result, uncertainty increases as the knowledge base of a new resource becomes more distant from a focal firm's established resource base.

name: Regulatory mandate establishment
authors_terms: ["the more established the mandate", "RPS yearly goals", "how established the mandate is"]
definition: A regulatory mandate becomes a more reliable guide for new resource investments as it becomes more established and uncertainty about its persistence declines. RPS yearly goals capture the minimum targeted percentage of renewables in a utility's electricity portfolio mix in a respective state with an RPS mandate and thus capture the extent to which a mandate has become established in a state.

name: Path length
authors_terms: ["path length", "decreased path length", "Inverse Path Length of LC", "inverse path length in LC"]
definition: Path length measures the social distance between any two inventors as the minimum number of collaborative links between them.

name: Clustering
definition: Clustering increases when two inventors are more likely to patent together, if both have patented with the same third inventor.

name: Size of largest connected component
authors_terms: ["size of a region's largest connected component", "size of LC", "network aggregation", "aggregation", "largest connected component"]
definition: To measure the extent of network aggregation, the authors calculated the proportion of inventors within each region who had a collaborative tie within the largest component in the region.

name: Regional patenting
authors_terms: ["future patenting", "subsequent patenting", "regional patent counts", "patenting in the region", "innovative productivity"]
definition: The models estimated the influence of small-world and largest component measures during moving five-year windows on the number of successful patent applications in the following year.

name: Small-world structure
definition: Small-world networks are defined as clusters of locally dense interaction connected via a few bridging ties.

name: CEO replacement
definition: The dependent variable in all hypotheses is CEO replacement, measured at two points in time, within both one and two years of the restatement, and operationalized as a binary variable with a value of 1 when the incumbent CEO is replaced within this time frame and 0 otherwise.

name: CEO-appointed directors
authors_terms: ["board members appointed by the CEO", "proportion of board appointed by CEO", "appointed board members", "appointed directors"]
definition: Board members appointed by the current CEO have been viewed in past research as loyal to the chief executive, with these loyalties and personal ties limiting their ability to act independently. Proportion of board appointed by CEO was the proportion of board members appointed after the focal CEO was elected to the chief executive position.

name: Inside directors
authors_terms: ["inside board members", "proportion of inside board members", "inside directors"]
definition: Proportion of inside board members was measured as the proportion of non-CEO board members who are also executives of the firm.

name: Financial misconduct
definition: The study examines financial misrepresentation that occurs when firms are found to have misrepresented their earnings and are subsequently required to restate their financial position, thereby acknowledging that financial misrepresentation has occurred.

name: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
definition: The purpose of SOX is to minimize the occurrence of financial fraud that might jeopardize the interests of investors. As a result, SOX has created greater clarity around expectations for honest and unbiased disclosure of the financial condition of the firm and expectations for sound and effective corporate monitoring and governance by the board of directors.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: Managerial discretion refers to the latitude of options top managers have in making strategic choices. Managerial discretion defines whether an organization's form and fate sit totally outside the control of its top managers, completely within their control, or, more typically, somewhere in between.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "executive pay", "total cash compensation", "long-term compensation"]
definition: There are two primary elements of CEO pay: total cash compensation and long-term, or deferred, income. In the spirit of the multi-indicator model of discretion, cash and long-term compensation were treated as two indicators of the broader construct CEO compensation.

name: Firm performance
definition: The extent to which the relationship between discretion and CEO pay is stronger in firms that are performing well than in firms with lower performance. Subsequent performance was defined as a firm's average return on equity for the years 1987-91.

name: Imitation
definition: The degree to which a firm introduces an offering based wholly or in part on an innovation by a competitor.

name: Competitor organizational innovativeness
authors_terms: ["competitor organizational innovativeness", "competitor's organizational innovativeness", "organizational innovativeness", "a competitor's history of introducing innovative offerings over time"]
definition: A firm-level construct defined as a competitor's history of introducing innovative offerings over time; it signals an innovation competency that overshadows the uncertainty of an innovative new offering.

name: Competitor offering relatedness
authors_terms: ["competitor offering relatedness", "competitor's offering relatedness", "relatedness of a competitor's offerings"]
definition: A firm-level construct defined as the collective similarity of the competitor's offerings; provision of closely related products or services may signal that the competitor has superior information about a particular market.

name: Competitor offering innovativeness
authors_terms: ["offering innovativeness", "innovativeness of a competitor's offering", "innovativeness of an offering"]
definition: The extent to which a new offering introduces concepts and ideas previously unknown to the market; it represents a signal of the degree of fit between the offering and the market's perception of its reasonableness.

name: Strategic convergence-divergence
definition: One organization strategically converges toward (diverges from) another when its strategic profile of resource-allocation decisions or strategic choices becomes more (less) similar to the others. It refers to the direction of change in strategic position vis-à-vis other firms, not to static strategic similarity.

name: Performance relative to aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspiration (PRA)", "performance relative to aspiration levels", "performance feedback"]
definition: Relative performance is defined as performance minus aspiration level. Following Cyert and March (1963) and Herriott et al. (1985), aspiration level is defined as a weighted function of the historical level of a firm's aspirations and average industrywide performance, i.e., social aspirations.

name: Target-focal firm performance gap
authors_terms: ["target firm's performance relative to a focal firm's performance (TPFP)", "TPFP = TP - FP", "firm relative performance (Pj - Pi)"]
definition: In dyadic relationships, the target's performance relative to a focal firm's performance (TPFP, i.e., TP - FP) is important in the judgment of how appropriate the target firm is for imitation. Target firm j's performance is measured in the same way as the performance of focal firm i, by ROA.

name: Production worker human capital market frictions
authors_terms: ["market frictions in the factor market for production worker human capital", "market frictions for player human capital", "free agency era", "changes in frictions"]
definition: Market traits that create imperfect competition in a factor market serve as 'imperfections' or 'frictions.' In the NFL, unrestricted free agency and a salary cap reduced frictions in the market for player human capital, making that market more competitive and dispersing player talent more widely across teams.

name: Managerial dismissal
definition: Termination of a team's head coach at the end of a given coach-season; given the organizational adaptation approach to sourcing managerial talent, more frequent dismissal and replacement become a fundamental indicator of intensified search for effective managers.

name: Current organizational performance
authors_terms: ["current firm performance", "current period organizational performance", "team record"]
definition: Organizational evaluators commonly assume that current period performance is a reasonable predictor of a manager's expected future performance, such that strong current performance motivates a more positive appraisal and managerial retention, while relatively weak performance encourages dismissal.

name: Competitive context
authors_terms: ["competitive context", "difficulty of the competitive context", "quality of opposition"]
definition: The quality of a team's opponents provides a measure of the degree of competitiveness a firm faces in a given season; evaluators may find a replacement manager more attractive in environments with strong competitors.

name: Production worker human capital
authors_terms: ["player human capital", "production worker human capital", "quality of the team's production human capital"]
definition: Production worker human capital allows the performance of the essential tasks of the firm's value creation process. In the NFL it takes the form of the 53 players who make up a team's roster during a season, whose knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics influence the outcomes of games.

name: Managerial reputation
definition: Evaluators regard a manager's reputational capital - reflective of past accomplishments - as an important input when setting expectations of potential future contributions to firm performance relative to replacements.

name: Managerial tenure
definition: The number of seasons that a coach has been in his current coaching spell as of an observed coach-season. Because firms initially observe managerial talent imperfectly, managers commonly enjoy a 'honeymoon period' before the chances of dismissal rise with tenure.

name: Type of diversification
authors_terms: ["type of diversification", "type of market", "type decision", "type of market entry"]
definition: We refer to these decisions as type of diversification, which we view as varying along a continuum ranging from related to unrelated (Chatterjee and Wernerfelt 1991).

name: Mode of expansion
authors_terms: ["mode of expansion", "mode of (market) expansion", "mode decision", "mode of entry"]
definition: We refer to these as decisions about the mode of (market) expansion, which we view as varying along a continuum ranging from internal purchase of the inputs to acquiring a firm that possesses the inputs.

name: Internal financial resources
authors_terms: ["internal funds", "internal financial resources", "availability of internal capital", "liquidity"]
definition: When firms face difficulty in communicating the intrinsic value of their diversification moves, they will use internal funds (Myers and Majluf 1984, Kochar and Hitt 1998). The standard measures for liquidity were used as a proxy for availability of internal capital.

name: External financial resources
authors_terms: ["external funds", "external financial resources", "ability to raise external capital"]
definition: Firms prefer to use external funds in related diversification since such funds can be obtained without the large risk premium that would result from high information asymmetry in unrelated diversification. Firms can use external funds either by raising the cash through secondary offerings or by using the currency implicit in the stock price to acquire the assets of another firm.

name: Knowledge-based resources
authors_terms: ["knowledge-based resources", "knowledge-based assets", "marketing and innovative skills", "research intensity", "advertising intensity"]
definition: Research suggests that knowledge-based resources are quite specific to related markets (Montgomery and Hariharan 1991, Teece 1982, Chatterjee and Wernerfelt 1991). However, knowledge-based resources are not specific to either internal (Teece 1982, Lemelin 1982) or acquisitive mode of expansion (Hennart and Park 1993).

name: Physical resources
definition: The basic argument is that it is less costly for firms possessing excess physical resources (such as plants and equipments) to move into industries that can easily use such resources rather than modify these resources for unrelated markets.

name: Market power
definition: Market power is a resource that can lead to increased profits. A firm may be able to take advantage of market power by being in a concentrated industry.

name: Market growth
authors_terms: ["growth of markets", "high growth markets", "sales growth rate", "growth"]
definition: Some researchers have suggested that high growth target markets should be entered by acquisition because the long lead time of internal expansion (Biggadike 1978, Hennart and Park 1993) will lead to an opportunity cost in high growth markets.

name: De novo entry
definition: Following prior literature, we define a firm as a de novo firm if it was founded in the wireless telecommunications industry, and as a diversifying firm if it operated in another industry prior to entering wireless telecommunications.

name: Strategic renewal capability
authors_terms: ["strategic renewal", "capability for strategic renewal", "renewal capability", "integrative knowledge"]
definition: Integrating knowledge and activities across the firm is essential for strategic renewal. Superior integrative knowledge and transformational experience provide diversifying firms with a better ability to deal with the impediments to growth, enabling strategic renewal as they transition to incumbency.

name: Firm growth
definition: Our central dependent variable, firm growth, is the increase in firm size, measured in total subscribers, over two consecutive periods.

name: Firm size
definition: Size is computed as the natural logarithm of subscribers for the focal firm in the prior year. Size increases the challenge of growth because new techniques and practices are required to maintain the management system in the face of larger scale.

name: Tenure in industry
definition: Firm tenure in industry is measured as the years a firm has been in operation in the wireless telecommunications industry, and equals the difference between time t and entry year. Tenure in the industry represents a growth challenge because historic industry-specific practices accumulate in an interdependent activity system.

name: Technological regime change
authors_terms: ["technology regime", "technological regime change", "change in technology regime", "entered in prior technology regime", "regime change"]
definition: A change in technology regime represents a discontinuous shock to the industry that demands new configurations of organizational and managerial resources. It is also a key context within which the dynamics between entrants and incumbents have been studied.

name: Technology-intensive industry
definition: TI industries are defined as those with average R&D expenditure-to-sales ratios in 1997 at least one standard deviation above the mean R&D expenditure-to-sales ratio for all industries in 1997.

name: Time
definition: The period of observation runs from 1978 to 1997; in the business-level models linear time trends are captured by a year counter, and in the industry dynamism models by dummies for four five-year panels (1978-1982, 1983-1987, 1988-1992, and 1993-1997).

name: Durability of abnormal business returns
authors_terms: ["durability of abnormal business returns", "performance persistence", "decay of abnormal returns", "performance instability"]
definition: The degree to which abnormally higher or lower business returns decay over time to the population mean. Increasing dynamic competition is argued to imply that abnormal returns decay more quickly and that superior performance is harder to sustain.

name: Market leadership
authors_terms: ["market leadership", "market leading businesses", "industry sales leadership", "market share leadership"]
definition: A key metric of business success in TI industries is the ability to attain and maintain a leading market share position; positive network effects, feedback mechanisms, and increasing returns to scale from market leadership are especially important in TI industries.

name: Business mortality
