definition: The likelihood that a business exits its industry. The authors argue that exit by unsuccessful businesses is a natural result of dynamic competition in TI industries and should increase in frequency if dynamic competition is itself increasing.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: The dynamism score captures volatility in the demand for industry products and services, an important outcome of the TI industry trends noted by researchers contending that dynamic competition increased since the 1980s.

name: VC withdrawal
authors_terms: ["VC withdrawal", "withdrawal of VC investment ties", "nonrepetition of ties", "tie discontinuation"]
definition: A venture lacking a repetition of ties by one of its existing VC investors, that is, a VC firm that invested in an earlier round does not participate in the follow-on round of financing. The authors note that when a VC firm stops investing in subsequent rounds it can retain its diluted equity in the venture or sell its equity in the secondary market.

name: Venture valuation
definition: The valuation of a privately held VC-funded venture, which is informed by investors' subjective assessment procedures and is to some extent negotiated based on the relative bargaining power of VCs and entrepreneurs. In this study it is the pre-money valuation of the venture in the second round of funding.

name: Venture development stage
authors_terms: ["Early stage", "development stage of the venture", "stage of the venture development"]
definition: The development stage of the venture in the second round, which affects the amount of information available to investors; uncertainty about a venture's prospects is reduced as the venture accumulates more resources and grows.

name: New joining investors
authors_terms: ["new joining VCs", "new VC investors", "outside round", "new joining investors"]
definition: Prospective investors who were not previously part of the syndicate and decide whether to join the focal follow-on round of financing. A round composed of already existing investors is an 'inside round', while an 'outside round' is one in which new VCs join.

name: VC status
definition: A sociological concept that captures differences in social rank that generate privilege or discrimination (not performance-based awards); status reflects the position of a firm in a social hierarchy based on patterns of affiliations with those firms central in market networks.

name: VC reputation
definition: An economic concept that captures differences in perceived or actual quality or merit that generate earned, performance-based rewards; reputation reflects expectations of a firm's future behavior based on observations of, or direct prior experience with, the firm.

name: Innovative environment
authors_terms: ["innovative environment", "external knowledge milieu", "aligned innovative environment", "partially aligned environment", "nonaligned environment"]
definition: We investigate how the external knowledge milieu of an entrant, conceptualized as its innovative environment, causes systematic variation in survival patterns. Two knowledge-related dimensions, technology regime and technology intensity, together determine the innovative environment facing an entrant, whose four states are the aligned, the nonaligned and the two partially aligned environments.

name: Technology regime
authors_terms: ["technology regime", "entrepreneurial regime", "routinized regime", "regimes of technological change"]
definition: Nelson and Winter (1982) distinguish between entrepreneurial and routinized technology regimes; during the initial entrepreneurial regime of an industry, the stock of industry-specific knowledge is low, and knowledge that is critical to innovation lies outside established incumbent routines, thus favoring entrants rather than incumbents, whereas in the routinized regime innovation is increasingly determined by accumulated stocks of internalized expertise. Here, we refer to periods in the knowledge history of industries as technology regimes.

name: Technology intensity
definition: We conceptualize technology intensity as the degree to which the industry invests in creative activities that increase the stock of scientific knowledge and its use in new applications. Technology intensity captures the investment in knowledge-producing activities in an industry.

name: Entry size
authors_terms: ["entry size", "firm size at the time of entry", "size or scale of entry", "small entrants", "large entrants"]
definition: We now turn to a key entry characteristic of a firm, the size or scale of entry, and posit that size may moderate the relationship between innovative environment and entrant survival.

name: Firm exit
definition: Our interest lies in being able to predict patterns of firm survival, which we define as continued operations in the focal industry. Our dependent variable, firm exit, is coded as 1 if a firm exited the focal industry in a given year, and 0 otherwise.

name: Organizational structure
definition: The five types of structure that appeared in the Stopford and Wells study, and are presently used to manage international operations: international divisions, worldwide product divisions, area divisions, matrix structures, and mixed structures.

name: Foreign product diversity
definition: Foreign product diversity was measured by the number of broad product lines a company offered for sale in two designated foreign countries. In order to be considered a separate broad product line, products had to have either a different manufacturing technology or different customers and end uses, or both.

name: Foreign sales
definition: The percentage of foreign sales was measured by the percentage of a company's sales occurring outside of the parent country.

name: Foreign manufacturing
authors_terms: ["percentage of foreign manufacturing", "size of foreign manufacturing", "foreign manufacturing"]
definition: The size or percentage of foreign manufacturing was operationalized as the percentage of foreign sales accounted for by foreign manufacturing rather than exports from the parent country.

name: Density at founding
authors_terms: ["density at founding", "population density at founding", "density at birth", "N0"]
definition: The number of organizations in the population at the time an organization was founded. The authors specify a nonmonotonic effect of population density at founding on the hazard of failure, with low-level increases building constitutive legitimacy and high-level increases intensifying competitive crowding.

name: Hazard of failure
authors_terms: ["hazard of failure", "failure hazard", "failure rate", "instantaneous rate of failure", "survival chances", "death rates"]
definition: The instantaneous rate of failure of an organization in the industry. The modeled event of interest is industry exit, which includes exit to another industry, firm failure, and industry exit for an unknown reason.

name: Organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure", "tenure in the industry", "industry tenure", "firm tenure"]
definition: Variation in organizational tenure (u) is represented as a stochastic piecewise-exponential function, and each record in the event history data corresponds to a single firm-year spell reflecting tenure in the automobile industry.

name: Industry age
definition: Industry age (t) was measured as the number of years elapsed since the inception of the industry in 1885.

name: Public support
authors_terms: ["public support", "public support for the war", "war support", "public support for contentious actions"]
definition: The prevalent views and preferences among the general public; in this study, support for the war with Iraq. The authors write that "public opinion - the prevalent views and preferences among the general public (Hobolt and Klemmemsen 2005) - may be a critical factor in influencing the disclosure of sensitive information by organizations facing controversy."

name: Disclosure of sensitive performance information
authors_terms: ["sensitive performance information", "release of information about sensitive performance indicators", "release of sensitive performance indicators", "combat metrics", "disclosure of sensitive performance information"]
definition: Performance information that, regardless of its valence, may attract scrutiny and may have potentially damaging effects on external support. The authors write that organizations avoid assessment "by not disclosing performance data that, regardless of its valence, may attract scrutiny and may have potentially damaging effects on external support. Here, we refer to this type of performance information as sensitive performance information."

name: Adversity
definition: A condition that raises concrete doubts regarding the consequences of controversial actions and thus increases perceptions of threat. "Adversity increases threat because it raises concrete doubts regarding the consequences of controversial actions, leading organizational members to anticipate that such actions will be more severely assessed than in other circumstances."

name: Spokespersons' power
authors_terms: ["power of spokespersons", "spokespersons' power", "power of organizational members"]
definition: The power organizational members possess within the organizational hierarchy, which the authors define as "asymmetric control over valued resources in social relations" (Magee and Galinsky 2008, p. 361).

name: Disclosure of progress performance information
authors_terms: ["progress performance indicators", "progress indicators", "reconstruction and rebuilding metrics", "alternate performance frames that emphasize progress", "frames that emphasize progress"]
definition: The release of information about developments that signal getting closer to a desirable end state; in this setting, reconstruction and rebuilding metrics. "They may, therefore, reduce transparency by using frames that emphasize progress - that is, developments that signal getting closer to a desirable end state."

name: Geographic munificence
authors_terms: ["munificence of a firm's geographic area", "geographic location", "location", "munificence of the local environment", "hot spot"]
definition: Environmental munificence is the extent to which the environment can sustain growth. A firm located in a geographic area with high munificence (a high concentration of similar firms, specialized suppliers, such as research universities, and a large pool of trained labor) will have access to knowledge flows which may be unavailable or difficult to attain by similar firms which are geographically isolated.

name: Strategic alliances
authors_terms: ["number of strategic alliances", "number of alliances", "alliances", "external linkages"]
definition: Second, we examine the impact of alliances as explicit mechanisms for creating the flow of knowledge into the firm. In the biotechnology industry, the drug discovery and development process is a complex and multidisciplinary process requiring new ventures to access a broad range of knowledge.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D expenditures", "commitment to research and development", "R&D spending"]
definition: Greater commitment to R&D should result in greater flows of new scientific information into the firm. The relative amount of expenditures on research and development has traditionally been used as an indicator of innovative activity in many industries.

name: Products in the research pipeline
authors_terms: ["products in the pipeline", "number of new drugs in a biotechnology company's research pipeline", "products in development", "pipeline"]
definition: Products in the pipeline represent accumulated stocks of organizational knowledge. The strength of a firm's 'pipeline' is considered an important indicator of a company's future cash flows.

name: Patents
definition: Patents may be considered as representative of stocks of organizational knowledge. They are physical, codifiable manifestations of innovative ideas, techniques, and products that embody the knowledge of one or several employees. Given the relative young age of the firms and their cash flow situation, we suggest that patent counts are an appropriate proxy for a biotechnology firm's stock of codifiable knowledge.

name: Scientific citations
authors_terms: ["firm citations", "citation analysis", "number of times the published papers of a firm's research team is cited"]
definition: It is our contention that the number of citations a firm's scientists have is a proxy for the stock of knowledge contained within the firm's scientific team. Firms with a higher level of citations have larger stock of basic scientific knowledge.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "market value", "value the market places on the firm"]
definition: The state of the firm and its knowledge base at the time at which it issues an IPO are the culmination of the actions of the entrepreneurs/managers of the firm since its inception. Therefore, the value placed on a newly public firm is the market's evaluation of the firm's performance over its lifetime.

name: Regional social capital in terms of social interaction
authors_terms: ["social capital-social interaction", "geographically localized social capital", "localized social capital", "regional social capital", "social interaction component of social capital", "localized social interaction", "structural social capital"]
definition: We define regional social capital as the localized norms and networks that enable people to act collectively within a region. We examine a key dimension of social capital-namely, the level of social interaction at the regional level.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "propensity to innovate", "likelihood of introducing product innovation"]
definition: The dependent variable for the first logit analysis is a dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm introduced a product innovation and 0 if it did not.

name: Internal R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity, a firm-level variable reflecting internal R&D efforts, measured by the percentage of sales revenue spent on R&D.

name: External R&D acquisition
authors_terms: ["external R&D acquisition", "externally acquired R&D", "external R&D", "outsourced R&D"]
definition: By externally acquired R&D, we mean R&D conducted by other than the acquiring firm, excluding the acquisition of technologies.

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay dispersion", "compensation dispersion", "top team pay dispersion", "dispersion in total compensation", "compensation dispersion among members of the CEO's top team"]
definition: The level of dispersion in the total compensation of the non-CEO members of the CEO's top team. To assess compensation dispersion the authors calculated the coefficient of variation (multiplied by 100 for ease of presentation) in the total compensation of the non-CEO top team members.

name: Common board membership
authors_terms: ["common board membership", "board membership", "proportion of the CEO's top team members who are also board members"]
definition: The extent to which members of the CEO's top team also serve on the board of directors, which increases social interaction and comparisons among those members. It was measured as the percentage of the CEO's top team who were on the board of directors.

name: Variation in stock ownership
authors_terms: ["variation in stock ownership", "variation in executives' stock ownership positions", "ownership dispersion", "variation in the number of shares of common stock owned"]
definition: The dispersion in the number of shares of common stock owned by each member of the CEO's top team. Similar current shareholdings are argued to promote more social comparisons, while significant variation categorizes executives in different groups and limits comparisons across groups.

name: Variation in unexercised stock options
authors_terms: ["variation in unexercised stock options", "variation in option portfolios", "variation in option holdings"]
definition: The dispersion across the CEO's top team members in the number of unexercised stock options still owned by each such executive, treated as a form of ownership (i.e., rights to future ownership).

name: Average organizational tenure
definition: The average organizational tenure of the members of the CEO's top team, which shapes social bonds, the likelihood of social comparisons, and expectations of similar pay. It was measured as the average organizational tenure (in years) of those executives.

name: Firm performance
definition: The economic performance of the firm. For the performance hypotheses the authors used firm return on assets (ROA) as their indicator of firm performance.

name: Stock price volatility
authors_terms: ["stock price volatility", "volatility in firm stock price"]
definition: The volatility of a firm's stock price, which by the Black-Scholes option pricing formula makes future stock options more valuable, so that volatility signals high levels of realized stock option gains in the future. It was measured using the modified Black-Scholes option pricing volatility parameter.

name: Excess pay dispersion
definition: The level of pay dispersion that exceeds what could be justified by characteristics of the industry, firm, or team; it is measured as the difference between the actual levels of pay dispersion and expected dispersion.

name: Expected pay dispersion
definition: The predicted level of pay dispersion for each firm generated by the fully specified model (with the control and independent variables) used in the first stage of the analysis.

name: Platform adoption
authors_terms: ["Platform Adoption", "adopting the platform", "adoption of a platform"]
definition: A developer adopts a platform when she uses the focal platform, that is, writes code that calls on a platform's API. The developer decision to adopt a platform is a nonrepeatable event.

name: Hackathon attendance
authors_terms: ["Hackathon Attendance", "attending a platform-sponsored hackathon", "attendance at a temporary gathering"]
definition: Our baseline independent variable indicates whether a developer attends a platform-sponsored hackathon. A developer participates by developing software at the hackathon; a developer is a prospective complementor for the sponsors who own platform ecosystems.

name: Local adoption rate
authors_terms: ["Local Adoption Rate", "proportion of attendees who are prior platform adopters"]
definition: The proportion of hackathon attendees who were already platform users prior to the hackathon, that is, the count of peer developers at a hackathon who have already adopted the platform divided by the total number of peer developers at the hackathon.

name: Platform use in award-winning projects
authors_terms: ["Winner Adoption", "award-winning project at the temporary gathering uses the platform as a component"]
definition: Whether a platform was used in a project that won an award at the hackathon attended by the focal developer, capturing successful outcomes that prospective adopters can observe.

name: Platform sponsorship of the gathering
definition: Whether the platform owner is a sponsor of the temporary gathering, that is, the platform's presence as a sponsor at the event the attendee takes part in.

name: Entrepreneurship training
definition: Structured training in three growth-catalyst tools relevant for formulating and executing innovation-led growth: business-model design, leveraging external networks, and building internal teams. The treatment format comprised interactive lecture sessions and workshops on these tools supplemented by personalized coaching in applying the tools to entrepreneurs' specific challenges.

name: Venture growth
definition: Our dependent variable of interest is venture growth, which we measure using sales revenue - widely used in prior research to measure venture growth.

name: Growth goal
definition: Growth goals are related to the size of the venture that the entrepreneur expects to achieve. Growth goals combine the aspirations of the entrepreneur (what the entrepreneur desires) with the understanding of the resources and constraints to arrive at a projection for the size of the new venture.

name: Refocusing
authors_terms: ["refocusing", "scope reduction", "corporate scope reduction", "removal of a business", "fund closures"]
definition: Refocusing is a reduction in a multi-business firm's scope by closing, selling, or spinning off one or more of its lines of business.

name: Operating performance
definition: The paper's dependent variable, operating performance, is the information ratio, computed by dividing a fund's excess returns by the amount of risk taken on by the fund, relative to market benchmarks.

name: Business relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "degree of relatedness", "pairwise correlation in excess returns"]
definition: Relatedness captures how intensively firms share resources and activities across funds. It is measured as the pairwise correlation in excess returns between every pair of funds in a firm with at least 12 months of contemporaneous returns.

name: Time since refocusing
definition: The duration of time over which refocusing costs persist.

name: Organizational dormancy
definition: Organizational dormancy is a temporary reduction in an organization's activity following the onset of a detrimental public policy that allows it to avoid unwanted radical adaptation and rejuvenate when a favorable policy returns. During dormancy organizations remain minimally active, insulating themselves while remaining able to resume their normal level of activity.

name: Political awareness
definition: Political awareness allows an organization to quickly anticipate and effectively respond to policy changes that affect them; adequate information about policy makers, their opponents, and the policy-making process is essential for organizations considering dormancy, and organizations differ in this firm-specific awareness.

name: Exposure to political pluralism
authors_terms: ["exposure to political pluralism", "exposure to politically plural states", "politically plural"]
definition: A politically plural state is one in which the state government had been formed by a political party that was different from the one controlling the national government. Organizations with a strong presence in politically pluralistic states face less government scrutiny and may employ greater decision-making discretion.

name: Organizational fitness
authors_terms: ["organizational fitness", "relative fitness", "fit with the prescriptions of a detrimental new public policy", "proportion of rural branches"]
definition: An organization's fitness must be defined with respect to a particular environment: an organization will be fit in an environment if it possesses the capabilities necessary to take advantage of that environment, and if it is less fit it has to undergo radical adaptation to gain that advantage.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack refers to uncommitted resources that a firm can deploy with discretion to manage unexpected contingencies. It is the analogue of fat storage for hibernating animals, providing alternate means to sustain the organization while its level of activity is reduced.

name: Financial performance
definition: Performance was quantified as return on assets (ROA), which represented the ratio of net income to total assets, because most banks in the sample were not listed on any Indian stock exchange and no market-based performance metric was available.

name: Expected acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["expected acquisition performance", "acquisition performance", "cumulative abnormal returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the expected acquisition performance of the acquirer. We use the event-study methodology to measure the expected performance as the abnormal returns that accrue to the acquirer upon the acquisition announcement.

name: Number of prior transactions with investment banks
authors_terms: ["number of prior transactions", "number of prior ties", "prior transactions with investment banks", "prior bank transactions", "ability/advisor", "ability/nonadvisor"]
definition: In sum, multiple prior transactions with investment banks improve the banks' acquisition-related information transfer ability, which in turn increases the probability of acquisition success by increasing the likelihood of better financial returns due to accumulated knowledge.

name: Concentration of prior transactions with investment banks
authors_terms: ["concentration of prior transactions", "concentration of ties", "relational concentration", "tie concentration", "exclusive relationships", "willingness/advisor", "willingness/nonadvisor"]
definition: This observation points to the importance of considering another characteristic of the acquirers' relational configuration with information intermediaries—the extent to which the acquirer's relationships are concentrated or dispersed. The concentration of the advising investment bank is operationalized as its market share in the acquirer's overall investment advisory business in the 10 years preceding the focal transaction.

name: Acquirer-target relatedness
definition: When the acquirer and target are unrelated, the potential for creating synergies is more tenuous (Anand and Singh, 1997; Balakrishnan, 1988; Singh and Montgomery, 1987), and the value of the investment bank's transaction-specific information becomes considerably greater.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firms' performance on five measures rated relative to the major competitors in their industry. The measures are growth in productivity, growth in sales and revenues, growth in net income/profits, return on assets, and return on sales.

name: Social networking relationships with politicians
authors_terms: ["social networking relationships with politicians", "networking relationships with politicians", "networking with politicians", "social networking relationships with political leaders"]
definition: Social capital developed by a firm's top management through personal and social networking relationships with government political leaders. In Ghana, politicians have significant influence and control over the award of major projects and contracts, and access to financial resources for business activities.

name: Social networking relationships with bureaucratic officials
authors_terms: ["social networking relationships with bureaucratic officials", "networking with bureaucratic officials", "networking relationships with bureaucrats"]
definition: Social capital developed by a firm's top management through personal and social networking relationships with government bureaucratic officials. Bureaucratic officials control the regulatory and licensing procedures such as providing certification and approval to newly manufactured products as meeting government standards.

name: Social networking relationships with community leaders
authors_terms: ["social networking relationships with community leaders", "networking with community leaders", "networking relationships with community leaders"]
definition: Social capital developed by a firm's top management through personal and social networking relationships with leaders in community organizations and institutions. Networking relationships with community leaders facilitate the firm's legitimacy and promote access to resources and information as the community leaders endorse the organization and its activities in their communities.

name: Firm-specific managerial experience
definition: The experiential knowledge that is preserved at the top management of firms; it allows a manager to accumulate tacit knowledge of the firm's resources and capabilities that could be leveraged to allocate resources efficiently and effectively for value creation. It was measured as the average top management tenure in a firm, i.e., the number of years that top managers have spent in a particular firm.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family owned firms are those whose respondents answered 'yes' to whether the business is a family owned firm and to whether family members controlled the business and were involved in the business as directors or employees; nonfamily firms answered 'no' to these questions.

name: Supply chain visibility
authors_terms: ["supply chain visibility", "conflict-free status", "conflictfree", "ability to determine whether their products are free of conflict minerals"]
definition: Gaining visibility into a firm's supply chain is a problem of epistemology: when can a firm say with reasonable certainty that there are no conflict minerals from the DRC in its products? Supply chain visibility is a question of an organization's ability and motivation.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["industrially diversified companies", "product diversification", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification", "total diversification"]
definition: The diversification literature has typically focused on three types of diversification: related, unrelated, and international. Companies engaging in unrelated or international diversification face more diverse and unfamiliar environments.

name: International diversification
definition: Recognizing that the breadth and depth of international diversification may have a separate influence on firm behavior, the authors employed separate measures for the two dimensions.

name: Supply chain complexity
definition: Supply chain complexity, represented as the number of suppliers, differentiation among those suppliers, and the level of interrelationship between them, affects the level of effort necessary to visualize a focal (or buyer) company's supply base. 'Supply chain complexity' is a new construct in management research, and the authors therefore created two measures to get at this construct.

name: Power over suppliers
definition: Firms that have more power over their suppliers can obtain more favorable terms and have more control over suppliers' decision making. A firm's power over its supplier increases when the firm accounts for a major part of the supplier's revenue, or when it is less costly to switch to alternative suppliers.

name: Visibility
definition: Companies with high visibility - i.e., those that receive high levels of public attention - are subject to greater levels of external pressures and demands.

name: Reputation
definition: Reputation, or the public recognition and social approval of an organization as well as perceptions about its quality, may function similarly to visibility in that highly reputed companies put in more effort to meet their stakeholders' expectations.

name: Voluntary CSR participation
authors_terms: ["voluntary CSR participation", "voluntarily participate in sustainability-related programs", "participated in CDP"]
definition: Companies voluntarily engage in CSR for a variety of reasons. By actively engaging in CSR programs that go beyond their own four walls, companies can develop ecologically related resources and capabilities to build long-term profit potentials.

name: Science similarity
authors_terms: ["science similarity", "scientific similarity", "similarities in the acquiring and acquired firms' science domains"]
definition: Science similarity between firms is the degree to which their scientific research focuses on the same narrowly defined areas of knowledge.

name: Technology similarity
definition: Technology similarity between firms is the degree to which their technological problem solving focuses on the same narrowly defined areas of knowledge.

name: Science complementarity
definition: Science complementarity between firms is the degree to which their scientific research focuses on different narrowly defined areas of knowledge within a broadly defined area of knowledge that they share.

name: Technology complementarity
definition: Technology complementarity between firms is the degree to which their technological problem solving focuses on different narrowly defined areas of knowledge within a broadly defined area of knowledge that they share.

name: Invention quantity
definition: Patent counts are a direct measure of invention quantity and are used extensively as an indicator of invention productivity.

name: Invention quality
definition: Patent citations are the extent to which a firm's patents are cited in subsequent patents; this measures invention quality because it reflects the ability of a set of patents to support future inventions by creating a 'ripple effect' to stimulate subsequent patents.

name: Invention novelty
definition: Invention novelty reflects the degree to which a firm's patent portfolio extends to a broad range of technology classes. The expansion of the range of technologies post M&A indicates that the firm has made some new discoveries outside its existing scope of technology and has taken some inventive risk.

name: X-efficiency
definition: X-efficiency describes 'all technical and allocative efficiencies of individual firms, as distinguished from scale and scope efficiencies.' Our dependent variable reflects how close a bank is to the efficient frontier (X-efficient perspective), rather than how far away it is from the frontier.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Foreign-owned banks represent banks in a particular host country with a parent's headquarters in a different country; host country banks represent banks that are headquartered in a particular host country.

name: Home country competitiveness
authors_terms: ["home country competitiveness", "financial system efficiency", "relative financial system efficiency"]
definition: The most direct application of this general principle in the global banking industry is competitiveness of a bank's home country financial system relative to that of the host country. As a proxy for the overall competitiveness of a country's financial system, we adopt Demirgüç-Kunt and Levine's (2000) measure of financial system efficiency.

name: Regulatory distance
definition: Regulatory difference is a dichotomous variable based on the home country regulatory environment of a foreign-owned bank relative to the regulatory environment of the host country in which it operates. We classify each host country's financial system based on whether banks engage in securities-related activities within the bank (low-regulation environment) or whether they are conducted in legally separate subsidiaries (high-regulation environment).

name: Financial system distance
authors_terms: ["financial system distance", "financial system similarity/dissimilarity", "financial system orientation"]
definition: Home and host countries may differ sharply regarding their financial system orientation, i.e., on whether industry relies for financing primarily on capital markets or banks. Foreign-owned banks with high/low financial system distance reflects similarity/dissimilarity between the home country's and host country's financial system.

name: U.S. ownership
authors_terms: ["U.S.-owned banks", "U.S. home country advantage", "U.S. home country disadvantage"]
definition: U.S.-owned banks represent a subgroup of foreign-owned banks. This group includes only U.S.-owned banks that operate in the sample host countries; U.S.-owned banks never refer to the banking activity within the United States, which has been excluded as a host country.

name: External pressure for board gender diversity
authors_terms: ["external pressure for greater board gender diversity", "external pressure for greater gender diversity", "external pressure"]
definition: The low presence of women on corporate boards has generated significant public interest and pressure for greater board gender diversity, and there have been constant external calls and pressure for firms to increase the presence of female directors.

name: Increase of female directors
authors_terms: ["increase of female directors", "increase in the number of female directors", "increase the number of female directors"]
definition: An increase in the number of female directors at the firm from the prior year, measured as a dummy variable coded 1 if there was such an increase and 0 otherwise.

name: Presence of multiple female directors
authors_terms: ["presence of multiple female directors", "presence of multiple women on the board", "presence of multiple female directors on the board"]
definition: The authors theorize the presence of multiple (i.e., more than one) female directors on the board to be a key factor that reduces the external pressure for a firm to increase board gender diversity.

name: Addition of board seats
authors_terms: ["addition of board seats", "increase through addition of board seats", "addition of a new board seat"]
definition: One of two means firms can use to increase the number of female directors: they increase the number of board seats to accommodate the addition of new female directors while keeping the number of male directors unchanged.

name: Major board committee membership
authors_terms: ["major committee membership", "membership on major board committees", "serve on major board committees"]
definition: Whether a newly added female director served on major board committees, such as the audit, compensation, nomination and governance committees.

name: Knowledge sharing among competitors
authors_terms: ["knowledge sharing", "Knowledge Sharing", "knowledge sharing among competitors", "detailed justification"]
definition: Detailed justifications, unlike simple justifications, offer valuable insights into an investment professional's thought process and analysis that supports a recommendation. The knowledge included in a detailed justification is much closer to firm-level strategic knowledge than what a simple justification conveys.

name: Buy-in uncertainty
definition: Buy-in uncertainty is the likelihood that key stakeholders will come to realize the value of a potential opportunity in a timely fashion. The authors define it as the likelihood not only that key stakeholders will come to realize that an opportunity is present, but also, conditional on recognizing it, that they will act on it (i.e., buy in) in a timely fashion.

name: Short-selling recommendation
definition: Short selling allows an investor who is pessimistic about the current price of a given stock (i.e., believes it to be overvalued) to borrow shares of a stock that they do not own, for a fee, and sell them back to the market; a short seller profits when a stock price decreases relative to when they borrowed the shares. Short Recommendation takes a value of 1 if the investment recommendation was to short sell the stock and a value of 0 if the recommendation was to buy and hold the stock.

name: Buy-in
definition: If the opportunity does not achieve a certain level of buy-in from key stakeholders - adopting it, endorsing it, or committing resources to it - it will fail. In most markets it is difficult to discern objective quality, and a significant factor predicting an opportunity's success is whether key stakeholders come to realize that a potential opportunity is valuable and subsequently buy in, by adopting, endorsing, or committing resources to it.

name: Flexible automation
definition: For the purposes of this research, FA involves the use of computers in both product design (Computer-aided Design) and manufacturing (Computer-aided Manufacturing-parts manufacturing and or assembly) activities. The critical factor in analyzing FA, however, is the extent of flexibility housed in a firm's technology in comparison to its competition.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Following these authors, we took the internal benefits of FA as given and concentrated on the overall indicators of organizational performance. Thus, for analyzing performance, we chose a growth measure and a profitability measure: growth in sales and return on investment (ROI).

name: Scope flexibility strategy
definition: The former involves competing on product variety and volume flexibility. Flexibility refers to the firm's intentions to compete in one or more markets based on product/volume mix and product innovation in a cost effective manner.

name: Speed flexibility strategy
definition: Two types of flexibility are defined and analyzed here: scope flexibility and speed or changeover flexibility. The former involves competing on product variety and volume flexibility and the latter, frequent new product introductions, speed in innovation, etc.

name: Quality leadership strategy
definition: Quality leadership refers to ance. (Our definition of quality is analogous to Hayes and Wheelwright's, 1979a and 1979b, that defines it as frequent enhancement to product features as opposed to product replicability). Improvements to design and performance through unique and multiple product attributes is the overriding priority.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: The manufacturing approach associated with this strategy involves long production runs with minimal or no change in product design. A firm that emphasizes product selling price, aggressive pursuit of scale economies, etc. as its competitive priorities would be considered to be pursuing this strategy (Dess and Davis, 1984).

name: Operations-environment cooperation
definition: a firm should employ a strategy of cooperation between its operations (R&D, engineering, manufacturing) on the one hand and the external constituents relevant to product and process development (suppliers, equipment vendors, scientific community) on the other.

name: Organic structure
definition: organizational structure is considered to fall within the mechanistic-organic continuum (Burns and Stalker, 1961). A structure is highly mechanistic or highly organic depending upon its inherent attributes.

name: Shopfloor personnel skill diversity
definition: shopfloor personnel should possess complementary skills in product design and production to effectively meet product and process contingencies, i.e., they should have a high degree of skill diversity. Following these discussions, three manufacturing structure variables were included for analysis here: the firm's intentions to strive for shopfloor personnel skills (specialized or diversified).

name: Design-manufacturing workflow integration
definition: the workflow between design and manufacturing should occur almost in parallel so as to be congruent with the system's integrative capabilities. Following these discussions, three manufacturing structure variables were included for analysis here: design-manufacturing workflow (sequential or parallel).

name: Project teams and workgroups
definition: Since coordination among various operational staff functions cannot be preplanned in a flexible manufacturing environment, informal mechanisms such as project teams and workgroups have to be frequently used to manage exceptions and residual interdepencies. Following these discussions, three manufacturing structure variables were included for analysis here: project teams and workgroups (rarely used or often used).

name: Organizational size
definition: The number of employees of an organization. By virtue of their size and visibility, large organizations are subject to much attention from the state, media, and professional groups and have a strong incentive to take actions to ensure their legitimacy.

name: Dependence on female employees
authors_terms: ["dependence of an organization on female employees", "percentage of female employees", "dependence on women"]
definition: The ability of working women to influence organizational policies regarding work and family is likely to be a function of the dependence of employers on female employees. The greater this dependence, the more responsive industry employers must be to the values and expectations of female employees regarding employer responsibility for helping them balance work and family demands.

name: Dependence on employees who are parents
authors_terms: ["dependence of an organization on employees who are parents", "percentage of working parents"]
definition: To the extent that an organization must depend on women specifically and on working parents in general, they become influential groups in motivating employer responses to pressures for child care services.

name: Institutional sector
definition: In the domain of work-family issues, congruence between institutional expectations and organizational goals is likely to be particularly strong for public sector organizations: federal, state, and local governments can use their power to authorize or legitimate policies and structures that other organizations within the public sector will adopt. By contrast, in the private sector conformity to institutional pressures may be precluded by organizational goals that give greater weight to technical and economic standards.

name: Diffusion of work-family benefits
authors_terms: ["diffusion of work-family benefits", "voluntary diffusion", "number of other organizations within an organization's sector adopting work-family benefits"]
definition: As similar organizations adopt norms and practices, they are increasingly legitimated throughout a given organizational field or sector. Early adopters become models for other organizations and reduce the uncertainty associated with a specific innovation, and organizations will increasingly incorporate those norms in an effort to enhance their legitimacy, secure critical resources, and remain competitive.

name: Environmental interconnectedness
authors_terms: ["interconnectedness", "pervasiveness of business, professional, and membership organizations"]
definition: Institutional environments are more likely to be interconnected when they contain many business, professional, and other membership organizations, such as political organizations and civic groups. These membership organizations provide a vehicle for the definition and promulgation of normative rules about organizational and professional behavior.

name: Perceived child care costs
authors_terms: ["perceived child care costs", "perceived cost of child care services", "expense and liability concerns"]
definition: Employers are resistant to adopting child care services because of their perceived cost in terms of both direct expenses and potential liability. These services represent a type of fixed cost that can be perceived as constraining organizations.

name: Perceived child care benefits
authors_terms: ["perceived child care benefits", "perceived benefits of child care services"]
definition: Researchers have pointed out that child care services benefit organizations in a variety of ways: enhancing the recruitment and retention of employees, lowering employee stress, improving employee morale, and increasing productivity.

name: Responsiveness to institutional pressures
authors_terms: ["level of responsiveness to institutional pressures", "employer involvement in work-family issues", "strategic responses to institutional pressures"]
definition: Employer responsiveness to institutional pressures for involvement in work-family issues is assessed through the adoption of child care services and options affording flexibility to employees. The discussion emphasizes two primary areas of employer involvement in work-family issues: the adoption of child care benefits and the adoption of benefits that enhance workplace flexibility.

name: Strength of institutional pressures
definition: Oliver (1991) defined institutional pressures in terms of five factors: cause, constituents, content, control, and context. The five institutional factors outlined by the author determine the strength of institutional pressures.

name: Acquiescence strategy
definition: Organizations that provided one child care benefit or more and one flexibility benefit or more were categorized as pursuing an acquiescence strategy in response to institutional pressures. Organizations may acquiesce and fully conform to institutional pressures and expectations.

name: Compromise strategy
definition: Organizations that offered only one major type of work-family benefit, either child care or flexibility, but provided multiple options within that area were categorized as pursuing a compromise strategy. These organizations do not fully meet institutional expectations about child care and workplace flexibility but do comply in a meaningful way to institutional norms.

name: Avoidance strategy
definition: Organizations that offered only one work-family benefit were defined as pursuing an avoidance strategy. Providing only one benefit can be viewed as a strategy that allows organizations to avoid both the financial and administrative costs associated with the provision of a more comprehensive set of work-family options.

name: Defiance strategy
definition: Not providing either child care or workplace flexibility benefits represents a dismissal or ignoring of institutional norms and values regarding employer responsiveness to work-family issues.

name: Social interaction centrality
authors_terms: ["social interaction", "social interaction ties", "structural dimension of social capital", "centrality of a business unit in interunit social interaction"]
definition: The structural dimension of social capital includes social interaction. The location of an actor's contacts in a social structure of interactions provides certain advantages for the actor.

name: Trustworthiness
definition: The relational dimension of social capital, in contrast, refers to assets that are rooted in these relationships, such as trust and trustworthiness. Trust is an attribute of a relationship, but trustworthiness is an attribute of an individual actor involved in the relationship.

name: Shared vision
authors_terms: ["shared vision", "cognitive dimension of social capital", "shared code or shared paradigm"]
definition: The third dimension of social capital, which Nahapiet and Ghoshal called the cognitive dimension, is embodied in attributes like a shared code or a shared paradigm that facilitates a common understanding of collective goals and proper ways of acting in a social system. A shared vision embodies the collective goals and aspirations of the members of an organization.

name: Resource exchange and combination
authors_terms: ["resource exchange and combination", "resource exchange/combination", "resource combination and exchange"]
definition: Following Schumpeter (1934), Moran and Ghoshal (1996) argued that new sources of value are generated through novel deployments of resources, especially through new ways of exchanging and combining resources. Since the exchanged resources are used in a context that contains existing resources, the resource combination process often takes place in conjunction with resource exchange.

name: Product innovation
definition: In this study, we focused on product innovation as both a dependent variable and a measure of value creation. In this study, only major product innovations were counted (minor product changes and product facelifts were excluded).

name: Venture capital funding
definition: Funding provided to technology-based start-ups by venture capital firms, which the authors describe as a financial intermediary funding entrepreneurial ventures; it is contrasted with external funding through the U.S. SBIR program.

name: Cooperative commercialization
authors_terms: ["cooperative commercialization strategies", "cooperative behavior", "cooperation", "cooperative activity", "strategic alliances and/or technology licensing"]
definition: Start-up cooperative commercialization strategies are here defined as pursuing strategic alliances and/or technology licensing.

name: VC reputation
authors_terms: ["VC reputation", "reputation of VCs", "higher reputation VCs", "more reputable VCs"]
definition: Prior VC performance can assist VCs in raising subsequent investment funds, and to the extent that IPOs are a highly visible measure of VC performance, attaining a track record in bringing start-ups to the public market can contribute to VC reputation.

name: Initial public offering
definition: An important marker for technology-based start-ups is the ability to raise funds through an IPO; IPOs can serve several functions such as allowing firms to raise working capital for business development, allowing equity holders to achieve liquidity, and introducing a currency through which acquisitions can be facilitated. IPOs are therefore examined as a measure of performance.

name: IPO underwriter reputation
authors_terms: ["investment bank underwriter reputation", "investment banker reputation", "IB reputation"]
definition: The reputation of the investment bank that underwrites a start-up's IPO, based on underwriter placement in tombstone announcements; IPO underwriter reputation is linked to less variance in IPO returns.

name: Competition from similar products
authors_terms: ["competition from rival products building on similar knowledge", "competition from similar antihypertensives", "rival products building on similar knowledge", "products building on similar knowledge"]
definition: Competition in a product market comes in two forms: products building on similar knowledge and products building on alternative knowledge bases. Competition from products building on similar knowledge creates pressure for a firm to deal with rivals' incremental product improvements.

name: Collaborative invention
definition: Collaborative invention allows a firm to draw on a greater number and diversity of knowledge components from its inventors, creating greater recombinant potential. Moreover, collaborative invention entails social interactions that enhance creativity and enable inventors to combine previously unconnected ideas, technologies, and processes.

name: Commercial abilities
definition: Abilities to commercialize inventions reside not only in tangible downstream assets, such as production and distribution systems, but also in intangible skills, such as the craft of managing the trial-and-error process in development phases, awareness of appropriate experimental settings for testing prototypes' feasibility, sense of the right market for product launch, and relationships with distribution networks.

name: Technical abilities
definition: This refers to a firm's abilities to rapidly create new products based on a particular knowledge. It includes how quickly a firm can figure out which and how knowledge components can be combined.

name: Knowledge spill-in
authors_terms: ["knowledge spill-in", "Knowledge flow", "knowledge flow from new ventures to incumbent firms"]
definition: A flow of knowledge from those organizations that employ their former employees; in this study it is the flow of patented knowledge from a focal new venture to a focal incumbent firm, indicated by a citation.

name: Spin-out relationship
authors_terms: ["spin-out", "outward inventor mobility-founder", "new ventures founded by former employees of the incumbent firm"]
definition: New ventures that are commonly referred to as spin-outs of their parent firms, are independent from their parents, and are founded by individuals who were previous employees of existing firms in the same industry. At the dyad level, a spin-out relationship exists when a founder of the new venture had been previously employed by the incumbent firm.

name: Non-founding employee mobility
authors_terms: ["outward inventor mobility-employee", "non-founding employees", "mobility of non-founding employees"]
definition: One route by which employees leave incumbent firms and join new ventures within the same industry is to become employees of already-existing new ventures; such non-founding employees are often required to sign nondisclosure agreements and have less discretion and incentive to share proprietary information than founders.

name: History of misappropriating intellectual property
authors_terms: ["history of misappropriation", "history of misappropriating the intellectual property of others", "history of patent infringement litigation"]
definition: An incumbent firm's history of misappropriating the knowledge of others, proxied by the cumulative count of unique patent infringement lawsuits that involved the incumbent as a defendant.

name: Corporate investor status
definition: CVC is the practice of minority equity investment by established firms in entrepreneurial ventures, that is, innovative companies that seek capital to continue operations. To the extent that IVCs are expert investors, they constitute an informed benchmark against which to contrast CVCs' behavior.

name: Investment stage
authors_terms: ["investment stage", "stage of development", "targeting ventures at specific stages of development"]
definition: The dependent variable, Investment stage, denotes the venture's stage of development at the time of the investment round. Because the level of uncertainty declines as a venture matures, higher values of Investment stage are associated with less risky investment.

name: Syndicate size
definition: The dependent variable, Syndicate size, is a count of the number of syndicate members who participate in a focal investment round. Investment syndicates are formed when two or more investors participate in the financing of a given venture.

name: CVC performance pay
definition: Overall, the majority of CVC managers receive fixed salary, and only a smaller number of programs reward managers for success. A small minority of programs offers CVC personnel high-powered incentives in the form of 'carried interest.'

name: Fund performance
definition: The dependent variable, Fund performance, is defined as the fraction of portfolio companies that have successfully exited via an IPO or M&A transaction by 2006. We measure the frequency of liquidity events (e.g., IPO, M&A) within an investor's portfolio.

name: Rivals' expansion
definition: We test for one manifestation of this, namely that experienced firms try to avoid investment bandwagons should they arise and invest when their rivals are either unable or unwilling to do so. To explore this, we need measures of the degree to which rivals invest simultaneously and indicators of experience.

name: Capacity expansion
authors_terms: ["capacity expansion", "incidence of capacity expansion", "expansion probability", "decision to add capacity"]
definition: Firms can expand capacity through three methods: adding a greenfield plant, de-bottlenecking an existing plant, or adding an incremental unit to existing plants. Limiting capacity expansion therefore to discrete additions of capacity, we operationalized the dependent variable, the incidence of capacity expansion, by a binary choice measure.

name: Stock of previous expansion decisions
authors_terms: ["stock of expansion decisions", "S DEC", "stock of previous decisions", "history of expanding"]
definition: To analyze this relationship, a stock variable was constructed, S DEC or the stock of expansion decisions, which accumulates the total number of expansion decisions that a firm made prior to the observation year. This cumulative measure is consistent with the operationalizations in the learning curve literature.

name: Stock of poor outcomes
authors_terms: ["stock of poor outcomes", "S PO", "stock of poor outcome experience", "track record of poor capacity expansion outcomes"]
definition: To obtain a measure of a firm's track record (or stock) of poor capacity expansion outcomes, the firm's poor outcomes were cumulated over time. This stock, S PO, was called the stock of poor outcomes.

name: Stock of rivals' poor outcomes
authors_terms: ["stock of rivals' poor outcomes", "S RPO", "industry-level learning", "rivals' aggregate track record of poor capacity expansion outcomes"]
definition: A measure was constructed that aggregates the stock of poor outcomes for each of the firm's rivals in its product-market. This variable, S RPO, or stock of rivals' poor outcomes, includes the rivals' poor outcomes both when the firm expanded and when it did not expand.

name: Forgetting
definition: For the last hypothesis, which concerns the possible declining effect of experience over time, a measure of forgetting (FOR) was developed. We therefore resorted to a simple measure that counts the number of years from the previous capacity expansion in the product-market.

name: Prior expansion experience
definition: Secondly, we employed the firm's original relative market share (ORMS) in 1975 as an indicator of its experience prior to 1975. However, the origins of these experiences are unknown as they could come from previous expansion decisions or the poor outcomes of those decisions.

name: Direct disadvantage
definition: When an organization's power exceeds its partner's based on their direct resource exchange relationship, the organization is in a position of relative power or power advantage. Direct disadvantage is simply the opposite of direct advantage.

name: Indirect disadvantage
definition: The indirect disadvantage of an actor relative to a partner can then be defined as the combination of the actor's direct disadvantages relative to intermediaries (i.e., common partners of both) and those intermediaries' direct disadvantages relative to the partner.

name: Motivation to gain two-step leverage
definition: The greater an organization's direct disadvantage relative to a partner and the greater the partner's direct disadvantage relative to a non-partner, the stronger the organization's motivation to acquire the non-partner to gain two-step leverage over the advantaged partner.

name: Total indirect disadvantage
definition: The total indirect disadvantage of an actor relative to all exchange partners reflects its overall inability to negotiate desirable exchange terms with partners. It is measured through the firm's business in industry i as the sum of this business's indirect disadvantages relative to all other industries.

name: Acquisition likelihood of exchange partners
definition: The likelihood that a firm would acquire businesses in industry j, measured as 1 if the firm conducted at least one acquisition in industry j between years t and t + 4, inclusive, and 0 otherwise.

name: Acquisition expenditure on exchange partners
definition: To measure a firm's acquisition expenditure in industry j, the authors first calculated the total deal value of all acquisitions the firm conducted in industry j in a given year divided by its total sales, and then used the average value of this ratio during years t to t + 4 as the final measure.

name: Acquisition likelihood of non-partners
definition: The likelihood that a firm would acquire businesses in a non-partner industry j, calculated in the same way as the likelihood of acquiring partners.

name: Acquisition expenditure on non-partners
definition: The expenditure a firm commits to acquiring non-partners in industry j, calculated in the same way as the expenditure on acquiring partners.

name: Financial performance
definition: Firm performance was measured by industry-adjusted return on assets (ROA), calculated as a firm's ROA in year t minus the average ROA of the firm's primary industry in the same year.

name: Exposure to a competitor's CEO award
authors_terms: ["competitor CEOs' postaward period", "postaward period", "witnessing the first CEO award", "not winning CEO awards"]
definition: This study examines how award-winning CEOs' competitors change their strategic decisions in the postaward period. The postaward period is the time after a competitor CEO witnessed the first CEO award, whereas the preaward period covers the years prior to witnessing the first CEO award (including award years).

name: Acquisition activity
definition: Following prior research, the authors use the number of acquisitions and the value of acquisitions to capture acquisition activities.

name: Product similarity
definition: Hoberg and Phillips (2016) apply a text-based analysis of firms' 10-K filings to determine product similarity between firms to estimate the degree of competitiveness between two firms. The firm-by-firm similarity measure is based on firm product descriptions.

name: Award-winning likelihood
authors_terms: ["likelihood of competitor CEOs' winning certification awards", "award-winning likelihood", "how close competitor CEOs are personally to winning CEO awards"]
definition: The second moderator is the likelihood of competitor CEOs' winning certification awards, which captures how close competitor CEOs were personally to winning CEO awards.

name: Stock market reaction to acquisitions
authors_terms: ["acquisition announcement returns", "stock market reactions", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)"]
definition: The authors use the event study methodology to measure acquisition announcement returns, computing cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), or the returns over the event window minus the normal returns, which represent the expected returns if the event had not taken place.

name: Intrafirm product outflows
authors_terms: ["intrafirm product outflows", "product outflows", "manufacturing outflows", "export ratio with parent", "export ratio with third country"]
definition: Intrafirm product outflows are goods sold to parent or third-country operations divided by total sales. They reflect competencies built over time and embedded in the local operation and are intended to capture those operations that have the highest product export ratios for the MNC.

name: Intrafirm product inflows
definition: Total product inflows are defined as goods sold from parent firm operations to the focal country operation divided by total sales. High product inflows signal that the operation does not have capabilities or abilities to create important parts or products themselves.

name: Technology diversity
authors_terms: ["technology diversity in the innovations", "diverse technology", "diverse knowledge", "new-to-the-MNC technology domains", "knowledge diversity"]
definition: To capture knowledge diversity in the innovations that are generated in foreign subsidiaries, the authors created a dependent variable that reflects the proportion of innovations that contain new technology domains (to all innovations generated in the foreign operation) in each year.

name: Knowledge diffusion
definition: To examine knowledge diffusion, the authors considered the countries to which a foreign-generated patent has been transferred, following prior studies that have used patent families to measure the international diffusion of technology across countries.

name: Relationship history
authors_terms: ["relationship history", "history of repeated exchange", "prior repeated exchange", "prior exchange", "relational capital"]
definition: A history of repeated exchange, i.e., a relationship history, with a supplier: the historic pattern of exchange between buyer and supplier, which prior literature argues creates a relational asset with latent value derived from elevated social connections, norms, trust, and simple expectations of exchange continuity.

name: Buyer willingness to pay
authors_terms: ["willingness to pay", "supplier selection", "likelihood a bidder wins", "value to the buyer"]
definition: The change in price that is required to offset a change in relationship history, holding all else constant; i.e., the value that the buyer can trade for a change in relationship history keeping its utility constant, which is the buyer's willingness to pay, revealed in its choice among bidding suppliers.

name: Technological change
definition: The degree to which the underlying technology required to manufacture the products procured in a bid event has changed rapidly over the past five years, used as a proxy for whether prior exchange was conducted under expectations of exchange continuity, i.e., the shadow of the future.

name: Common language
definition: Whether the supplier's headquarters is located in an English-speaking country; a shared language is argued to facilitate communication and interaction and thereby lower the costs of developing social connections.

name: Close proximity
definition: Whether the supplier's headquarters is located less than the median distance from the buyer's headquarters; physical proximity is argued to reduce the costs of engaging in social interactions and to increase the likelihood of social interactions.

name: Part complexity
definition: The complexity of the part or product to be supplied: whether the parts are difficult to manufacture, require extensive specialized skill, knowledge and experience, and become completely unusable under very small variations from production specifications.

name: Asset specificity
definition: The extent to which producing the parts requires the supplier to make substantial investments in tooling and equipment that are specific to the buyer, i.e., investments with limited or no application in alternative uses.

name: Demand variability
definition: The difficulty of predicting demand for a given part, reflected in a high level of month-to-month or season-to-season variance from the forecast demand for the parts.

name: Downsizing
definition: We defined downsizing as a decrease in the number of permanent employees (excluding contract and temporary workers) of 5 percent or more between year t-1 and year t.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "return on assets", "sales growth", "mounting years of poor performance"]
definition: The paper's hypotheses treat performance as measured by return on assets and sales growth, and the analyses also track mounting years of poor performance, i.e., the number of years in the previous five in which a firm experienced losses.

name: Profits per employee
authors_terms: ["profits per employee", "ratio of profits to employees"]
definition: A low ratio of profits to employees reflected a high degree of redundancy (Budros, 1997). Profits per employee is the deviation from industry mean of the ratio of a firm's operation profits to total employees.

name: Firm size
definition: It is difficult to dispute that in Japan, the larger a firm, the greater its legitimacy; large firms were well known, prestigious, believed to be good, stable employers, and were at the core of the Japanese political economy.

name: Firm age
definition: The older an organization in Japan, the more likely it had achieved a high level of legitimacy, and thus, the more it had to lose by deviant behavior.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Organizations also enhance their legitimacy through endorsements by regulatory bodies or associations (Ruef and Scott, 1998). In Japan in the 1990s, the annual rankings of firms put out by Recruit, a Japanese business publisher and recruiting agency, were among the most watched and publicized measures of firm reputation.

name: Wage level
definition: High levels of human capital are likely to be reflected in a firm's wage levels. A firm that paid higher than average wages was likely to have recruited employees from top universities and to have put them through rigorous, long-term training programs.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign ownership", "percentage of a firm's shares held by foreigners", "foreign share ownership"]
definition: Different actors in an organizational field may have different conceptions of legitimacy. While permanent employment was legitimate and appropriate to most Japanese investors, it was less so to foreigners, who were influenced by U.S.-style shareholder capitalism.

name: Population downsizing
definition: The concept of safety in numbers leads to the proposition that firms would follow the lead of other firms in the population: the more other firms downsized, the more likely any given firm was to downsize. Increasing downsizing across the population would have provided safety in numbers and reduced the risk that a firm was censured for its deviant behavior.

name: Liability of foreignness
definition: The additional costs and disadvantages foreign firms face in a host country due to their unfamiliarity with and lack of roots in a foreign environment.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Ownership is classified by whether a firm's registered headquarters are located outside Britain (foreign-owned) or in Britain (British-owned).

name: Firm-specific advantages
definition: Advantages based on the possession and use of certain intangible assets, such as patents, trademarks, and management skills, which enable the firm to reach high levels of technical or price efficiency.

name: Multinationality advantages
authors_terms: ["advantages of multinationality", "advantages of multinationality per se", "multinationality advantages"]
definition: Advantages that arise from multinationality per se, confined to multinational firms, and arising directly from the ability to benefit from the cross-border dimension of activities undertaken under common governance.

name: Home-based advantages
definition: Advantages that arise from a firm's favorable access to the resources of its home country.

name: Duration of foreign operation
authors_terms: ["duration of foreign operation", "length of operation", "duration of activity in the City"]
definition: The length of time a foreign firm has operated in the host country; it is operationalized by years since the establishment of the London office.

name: Cultural distance
authors_terms: ["cultural distance between the host and home countries", "cultural distance"]
definition: The differences in political, legal, socio-cultural, and economic institutions between the home and host countries.

name: Entry mode
definition: Entry mode distinguishes between entry via greenfield investment and entry via the acquisition of a previously independent local firm.

name: Organizational structure
authors_terms: ["organizational structure", "level of autonomy of the affiliates", "greater autonomy to affiliates"]
definition: The organizational structure, notably the level of autonomy of the affiliates and the extent of their integration within the MNE of which they are part.

name: Franchise association
definition: Franchisees operate establishments with the franchisor's organizational routines while independents operate without franchisor routines; franchisees serve as the treatment group and independents as the control group. The franchise dummy distinguishes the two organizational forms.

name: Establishment performance
definition: Total returns is the sum of net owner income plus royalties in a given year. It is the total annual return available to the set of stakeholders (franchisor plus franchisee in the case of franchise, owner in the case of independent firms).

name: Organizational routines
definition: Routines are the organizational equivalent of individuals' skills in that they provide capability for a smooth sequence of coordinated behavior. The specific combination of the used practices, together with other unidentified practices, is taken to be the organizational routine for a given establishment.

name: Knowledge of best practices
definition: Whether the entrepreneur is aware that industry experts recommend the practice (yes = 1, no = 0). Knowledge captures differences in independents' ability to obtain information not intended for release outside the franchise.

name: Agreement about the value of practices
authors_terms: ["agreement", "strength of agreement", "agreement with the value of practice"]
definition: How strongly, on a scale of 1-5, the entrepreneur agrees that the practice will lead to higher profits (strongly agree = 1). Agreement captures differences in interpreting the obtained information.

name: Franchisor requirement
definition: Whether the franchise requires the entrepreneur to follow the practice (yes = 1, no = 0). Requirement captures the threat of franchisor sanctions for failure to use a practice.

name: Acquisition relatedness
authors_terms: ["related acquisitions", "unrelated acquisitions", "the primary economic relationship between the acquiring and acquired companies"]
definition: The F.T.C. classified each acquisition according to the primary economic relationship between the acquiring and acquired companies. The report's five categories are described by the F.T.C. as mutually exclusive: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated.

name: Post-acquisition divestiture
definition: This study focuses on one consequence of the 1960s merger wave: the extent to which acquisitions made within this period were later resold. The 1982 status of the acquired units was determined and coded into categories of liquidated, sold and not sold.

name: Multi-project work
definition: A work arrangement in which employees work on multiple projects simultaneously.

name: Project performance
definition: In the NPD context, judgments of project performance are primarily based on timely completion and delivery to the market. The company in the study is embedded in an innovative environment in which speed to market (timeliness) is the primary performance variable.

name: Employee specialized experience
definition: The total experience cumulated within the project technological area prior to working on the current project. Two projects that belong to the same Program-Category combination proxy for the same project area, and the more time employees spend within the same Program-Category combination the more specialized experience is accumulated.

name: Project similarity
definition: Two projects are considered similar if they belong to the same market segment. As described in the project files, projects belonging to the same market segment share similar characteristics, such as resources, demands, and expectations.

name: Employee familiarity
definition: Familiarity for each employee is the number of familiar project members within the focal project. An employee is classified as familiar if they were currently working or had previously worked with the focal employee.

name: Innovative performance
definition: The dependent variable, the yearly innovative performance, operationalized as the number of successful patent applications filed during each year.

name: Corporate venture capital investments
definition: Many large corporations have initiated CVC programs that provide funding and related services to entrepreneurial firms in return for an equity stake; a key objective of these investments is accessing knowledge and learning from the start-ups.

name: Strategic alliances
definition: Alliances help companies increase their innovativeness by facilitating access to partners' knowledge and complementary resources as well as joint knowledge creation.

name: Joint ventures
definition: Joint ventures entail the creation of a jointly owned separate entity that may help overcome problems of opportunism and facilitate knowledge transfer.

name: Acquisitions
definition: Acquisitions provide a conduit for a corporation to absorb the knowledge base of another firm by completely integrating the acquired firm into its operations.

name: Venture relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness", "venture relatedness", "relatedness of ventures", "relatedness of external corporate ventures"]
definition: The relatedness between the focal company and its external partner, measured as a categorical variable based on the SIC code match between the venture and the focal firm.

name: External business development activities
authors_terms: ["external business development activities", "external corporate venturing", "external relationships", "external ventures"]
