definition: Activities through which firms access knowledge from external sources, examined as four distinct forms of external relationships: CVC investments, alliances, joint ventures, and acquisitions.

name: Employee turnover
definition: We calculate the turnover rate in a particular period as the number of employees who left a store during that period divided by the average number of employees working at the store during that period.

name: Process conformance
definition: Process conformance is the extent to which managers aim to reduce variation in store operations in accordance with a set of prescribed standards for task performance. At high-process-conformance stores, managers use discipline in implementing standardized policies and procedures, whereas at low-process-conformance stores, managers tolerate deviations from these standards.

name: Store operating performance
authors_terms: ["store performance", "operating performance", "store performance, as measured by customer service score and profit margin"]
definition: We examine turnover's effect on two measures of store performance. Our second performance measure, profit margin (operating income divided by sales), is an objective measure of financial performance.

name: New venture growth
authors_terms: ["new venture growth", "growth", "growth rates", "organic increases in firm size"]
definition: The paper studies growth, i.e., organic increases in firm size. Since firm size can be measured in terms of revenues as well as number of employees, growth is measured in terms of change in the number of agency employees and the change in the agency's gross billings, compared with the previous year.

name: Structural mimicry
authors_terms: ["structural mimicry", "mimicry of organizational structure", "conformity with accepted organizational structures"]
definition: New ventures looking for legitimacy tend to adopt the structures of established firms in their field; new agencies that adopt popular elements of rational structure, i.e., structures similar to those of established organizations, will be considered legitimate and more familiar and reliable. Structural mimicry (of titles) is a symbolic, legitimacy-enhancing act rather than a rational, efficiency-enhancing one.

name: Ceremonial mimicry
definition: New ventures may mimic the ceremonies of established organizations in their field in order to gain legitimacy; organizations acquire legitimacy by adopting external criteria of worth, including externally validated assessments of the value of certain organizational activities. Such ceremonial mimicry is part of the symbolic or impression management process.

name: Customer status
authors_terms: ["customer status", "high-status customers", "status of the agency's customers"]
definition: Status is a social-structural attribute that indicates an organization's position in the implicit hierarchy in a market, based on its quality relative to the perceived quality of others in the market, and status can be derived from the status of the organization's exchange partners. Since data on revenues of agency customers are not available, annual advertising expenditure is used as a measure of the status of the agency's customers, since firm revenues are highly correlated with advertising expenditures.

name: Performance below aspiration level
authors_terms: ["performance below the aspiration level", "ROA < aspiration", "performance shortfalls", "performance declines", "performance feedback"]
definition: The gap between performance and the aspiration level; aspiration levels represent the minimum levels required for performance to be perceived as satisfactory, and performance below these levels signals that the organization's routines or practices may not match the requirements of its environment.

name: Risk taking
definition: Risk is typically studied as organizational risk, measured through income stream variation, or as managerial risk taking, measured through resource allocations toward activities with uncertain outcomes; the study focuses on managerial risk taking, examined through capacity expansions and contractions.

name: Operating experience
definition: Knowledge accumulated through the repeated operation of the organization's activities; as organizations gain operating experience, this learning process appears to lower the likelihood of organizational failure by buffering activities in the firm from external instability and by providing repositories of knowledge and expertise for crisis management.

name: Organizational legitimacy
definition: Organizational legitimacy refers to general judgments that an organization's actions are acceptable or appropriate within some socially constructed set of norms, values, and beliefs. The present focus is on normative legitimacy, which reflects evaluations of appropriateness within some set of socially constructed norms and values relevant to constituents in the organization's institutional environment.

name: Organizational age
definition: The length of time since an organization's founding; structural inertia theory suggests that the aging process increases inertia and decreases organizational responsiveness to environmental change.

name: Local institutional quality
authors_terms: ["institutional quality", "quality of informal institutions", "seller's local institutional quality", "relative institutional quality"]
definition: The extent to which informal institutions support the efficiency of market transactions; throughout the article 'institutional quality' refers solely to the quality of informal institutions, comprising judicial efficiency and the lack of corruption and organized crime.

name: Legal status obligations and controls
authors_terms: ["legal status", "obligations and controls", "institutionally induced obligations and controls", "relative legal status"]
definition: Legal statuses embody the collection of rules imposed on sellers by a legislature and so convey information on the institutionally induced obligations and controls acting on sellers. Companies with a higher legal status are subject to stronger obligations and controls.

name: Buyer contact initiation
authors_terms: ["request for quotation", "buyer-seller contact", "likelihood of contacting a seller"]
definition: Requests for quotation are important contacts between industrial buyers and sellers because final orders generally occur only after a request for quotation has been submitted; unlike final orders they are not confounded by additional information conveyed by the pricing of products and services.

name: Role formalization in founding teams
definition: Role formalization in founding teams captures 'what one is asked to do' and refers to the identification and designation of particular functional roles and their assignment to specific individuals.

name: Functional specialization in founding teams
definition: Functional specialization in founding teams is defined as the concentration of the types of tasks assigned to any one founding team member.

name: Administrative intensity
definition: Administrative intensity is measured by the ratio of administrators to employees and is an important feature of organizational structure that reflects the degree of bureaucratization within an organization. In new ventures the authors suggest it is best captured by the ratio of the number of founding team members to employees.

name: Founding team size
definition: Founding team size was the number of executives in a firm; the authors argue that small founding teams lack the managerial and financial resources to allow founders to focus on only a few tasks.

name: New venture performance
definition: Because the firms were mostly private, market-based and accounting-based performance measures were not applicable; the authors used the moving average of revenue (in millions of dollars) in years t and t + 1 as their indicator of new venture performance.

name: Exploitation orientation
definition: Exploitation learning involves a local search that builds on a firm's existing knowledge. This article conceptualizes exploitation and exploration as two ends of a continuum rather than as two separate constructs.

name: Exploration orientation
definition: Exploration learning involves a more distant search for new knowledge. Exploration is closely related to variation, experimentation, discovery, and risk-taking behavior, and it places less emphasis on current strengths and evidences low conformity to current organizational practices and strategies.

name: Integrated knowledge leverage
definition: Acquirers exhibit integrated knowledge leverage when they combine acquired knowledge with their own existing knowledge. With integrated knowledge leverage, acquirers identify the complementarity between their own knowledge and the acquired knowledge of target firms, and use both as inputs in post-acquisition innovations.

name: Independent knowledge leverage
definition: Independent knowledge leverage occurs when acquirers generate new innovations with the use of acquired knowledge without relying on their own prior knowledge.

name: Acquisition rate
definition: The acquisition rate is the number of acquisitions that acquiring firms perform over a given time.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["alliance scope", "vertical alliance scope", "functional scope of alliances", "broad scope"]
definition: The set of activities partners specify as falling within the scope of the alliance, which determines the challenges partners are likely to encounter when they work together. The functional, or vertical, scope of alliances can vary considerably, ranging from a focused effort in a specific function (e.g., research) to a broad program that spans several parts of the value chain.

name: Reciprocal interdependence
definition: Reciprocal interdependence between partners indicates a highly contingent pattern of decisions and actions among units, which require more formalized forms of coordination to bring about mutual adjustment. It is the highest of the three types of interdependence identified by Thompson (1967) and represents an ascending order of the degree of dependency of one unit on others to complete the allocated task.

name: Dedicated investments
definition: The costs and risks of decision impasses are associated with the scale of financial investments dedicated to the partnership. An increase in project size can result in a concomitant increase in bilateral dependencies because the amount of capital committed to the alliance impacts not only the share of partners' resources associated with the alliance but also, the portion of their organizational value originating from the alliance.

name: Competitive intensity
definition: Competitive pressure on alliance partners increases if many rival firms work on similar technologies or try to find and offer solutions for the same problems. The pressures are particularly acute when partners are racing with other firms to develop new therapies and obtain regulatory approvals for products to earn monopoly rents.

name: Authority delegation
definition: Authority delegation means that the alliance partners endow the steering committee with decision-making authority as opposed to using the steering committee primarily as an information exchange interface.

name: Authority reversion
authors_terms: ["authority reversion", "reversion of authority", "final decision-making authority", "casting vote", "tiebreaking vote", "final say"]
definition: Authority reversion occurs if the partners choose to grant one of the parties final decision-making rights in case of a deadlock in the steering committee versus relying solely on third-party dispute resolution via arbitration or litigation.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: A cost-leadership strategy involves giving consumers value comparable to that of other products at a lower cost; it emphasizes having efficient-scale facilities and lower costs than major competitors.

name: Differentiation strategy
definition: Firms following a differentiation strategy aim at creating a product or service that customers see as unique, building customer loyalty and creating barriers to entry for newcomers.

name: Marketing standardization
definition: Marketing standardization was defined in this study as the degree to which an exporting firm used the same marketing programs in different foreign markets; it concerns the consistency of marketing programs and processes between domestic and foreign markets as well as across multiple markets.

name: Export diversification
definition: The number of foreign markets that an exporting firm targets is a strategic choice that can have important implications for the firm's overall export performance; export diversification is the geographical diversification of a firm's export operations.

name: Foreign market focus
authors_terms: ["foreign market focus", "developed country focus", "developing country focus"]
definition: A surrogate measure for environment, dichotomized into developed countries and developing countries, reflecting that compared to developing country markets, developed country markets are more competitive and more dynamic.

name: Export performance
definition: Export performance was measured through a four-item scale assessing the overall role of exports in the firms' sales growth, market shares, and competitive positions, as well as the profitability of export sales.

name: Firm-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["firm-specific HC", "firm-specific human capital", "relevant firm-specific human capital"]
definition: Firm-specific HC refers to knowledge and skills that are unique to a firm, such as knowledge about specific strategies, processes, and technologies of the firm; to ensure clarity the authors refer to the narrower subsets of human capital that matter specifically to a focal project as 'relevant' human capital.

name: Industry-specific human capital
authors_terms: ["industry-specific HC", "industry-specific human capital", "relevant industry-specific human capital"]
definition: Industry-specific HC refers to knowledge about the industry setting or domain in which a project is situated, and thus it is redeployable across the (limited) set of firms with projects in the same industry domain.

name: Occupational human capital
authors_terms: ["occupational HC", "occupational human capital", "internal staff", "internal staff size"]
definition: Occupational HC consists of the knowledge and skills required to perform work within a professional or functional area, and as a type of general HC, it is most easily transferred across industry and firm settings. The authors argue that one key factor impacting the firm's development of superior occupational HC is the size of its internal staff with training and credentials in the focal occupation.

name: Highly contested area
definition: One factor that may increase the cost of errors (and thus the value of occupational HC) is the extent to which the project is in an arena with extensive competitive actions by rivals, which the authors refer to as a 'highly contested' area. At the time of patenting, patents that are in a contested domain marked by previous litigation are themselves likely to be viewed as being at risk of litigation.

name: Outsourcing of knowledge work
definition: The paper studies the outsourcing of patent prosecution, which consists of activities related to filing and obtaining a patent from the USPTO; a project is treated as outsourced if a supplier was involved in it and internalized if not.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["firm age at time of bankruptcy", "age at failure", "age of the business at the time of bankruptcy", "firm age"]
definition: The dependent variable in our models is firm age at time of bankruptcy.

name: Causes of failure
authors_terms: ["determinants of failure", "causes of failure", "attributed causes of bankruptcy"]
definition: Rather than examining which firms exit in contrast to those that do not, we evaluate causes of failure among firms that exited the economy at different ages.

name: Deficiencies in resources and capabilities
authors_terms: ["deficiencies in resources and capabilities", "resource and capability deficiencies", "shortages of tangible assets and/or intangible assets"]
definition: We propose that young organizations are more likely to suffer from resource and capability deficiencies than are older firms. This is the essence of the liability of newness expressed in the language of the resource-based view.

name: Industry change
authors_terms: ["industry change", "industry competitive conditions", "industry turbulence and change", "changes in the competitive environment"]
definition: The derived factor variable serves as our proxy for the level of industry turbulence and change.

name: Deficiencies in general management skills
authors_terms: ["general management", "deficiencies in general management skills", "general managerial abilities"]
definition: Just as high-quality management can confer competitive advantage (Coff 1997, Castanias and Helfat 1991), so can deficiencies in general management skills pose a significant threat to firm survival.

name: Deficiencies in financial management skills
authors_terms: ["financial management", "deficiencies in financial management skills", "financial management resources and capabilities"]
definition: A two-item factor was used to test for the impact of financial management resources and capabilities within the failed organizations.

name: Deficiencies in market development skills
definition: Our final variable for market development (H3c) evaluated the impact of (a) pricing strategy, (b) product quality, and (c) the establishment of market position.

name: Customer co-production
definition: Customer co-production is the degree to which customers participate in the design and delivery of the service offering.

name: Customer contact
definition: Customer contact refers to the degree to which customers and employees interact with one another during the service production process.

name: Service customization
definition: Service customization refers to a firm's ability to alter service production in order to meet specific customer needs.

name: Human capital
definition: Human capital is the skills, knowledge, and expertise of employees. Organizations can increase their human capital levels through selection (hiring employees with high levels of education and expertise from the external labor market) and/or training (internal developmental activities of current employees).

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance was measured using two variables: return on equity (ROE) and return on investment (ROI).

name: CEO judgment policy
authors_terms: ["judgment policy", "judgment policies", "executive judgment", "judgment model", "CEO judgment policies"]
definition: Judgment is defined as an individual's understanding of relationships among objects. The mean parameters from the two judgment regressions represent each CEO's judgment policy regarding causal relationships among strategy, structure, the environment, and firm performance.

name: Contingency-consistent judgment policy
authors_terms: ["judgment policies that are consistent with normative contingency theory", "contingent thinking", "contingent judgments", "contingent and noncontingent thinking"]
definition: Some executives' judgment policies may match the prescriptions of contingency theory; other executives' judgments may be different from, or even counter to, the theory. Cluster 1 CEOs exhibit above average recognition of the bivariate contingencies and multivariate configurations suggested by contingency and configuration theories, and these thought patterns were labeled contingent.

name: Strategy-structure-environment fit
definition: The alignment among business-level strategy, organizational structure and the competitive environment; the important factor is the relationship of the variables to each other rather than to a single ideal profile. This is actually an index of misfit, so the total is made negative to convert to an index of fit.

name: Firm performance
definition: Each respondent was asked to rank his/her firm's performance compared to other similar firms on sales growth, after tax return on sales, after tax return on total assets, and overall performance/success, all for the previous five-year period.

name: Length of CEO experience
authors_terms: ["length of CEO experience", "industry tenure", "firm tenure", "tenure as CEO"]
definition: CEOs with longer and broader experience may be more likely to perceive accurately the contingent action-outcome relationships in their environment and, therefore, employ judgment policies consistent with normative contingency theory.

name: Breadth of CEO functional experience
authors_terms: ["breadth of CEO functional experience", "functional breadth", "breadth of functional experience"]
definition: Exposure to learning opportunities may be related to the length and breadth of the manager's experience. The questionnaire asked the CEO to report the functional areas in which the CEO had previous experience.

name: Strategy making process rationality
authors_terms: ["rationality in the strategy making process", "process rationality", "composite rationality", "rationality in strategy making"]
definition: Rationality in the strategy making process is represented by the degrees of scanning and analysis and the futurity of planning (Miller 1987) associated with strategy making in a firm.

name: Failure rate
authors_terms: ["failure rate", "fatal accident rate", "subsequent failure rates", "number of fatal accidents"]
definition: The focus of this paper is on how population-level learning from failures leads to reductions in subsequent organizational failure rates, and performance is defined in terms of airline accidents. Thus, the dependent variable in the analyses is a count of the number of accidents experienced by an airline in a particular country during a particular year.

name: Others' failure experience within the population
authors_terms: ["others' failure experience (within country)", "vicarious experience", "others' failure experience"]
definition: Others' failure experience (within country) was a count of the number of fatal accidents that had been experienced by all commercial airlines based in a focal airline's home country (excluding the focal airline itself).

name: Others' failure experience outside the population
definition: Others' failure experience (outside of country) was a count of the number of fatal accidents globally that had been experienced by all airlines based outside of the focal airline's home country.

name: Population-level actor monitoring strength
authors_terms: ["population-level actor strength", "monitoring strength", "monitoring by aviation regulators"]
definition: When population-level actors have greater monitoring strength, here referring to entities that are better able to monitor member organizations, investigate their failures, and communicate associated knowledge throughout the wider population. In populations of airlines, the most important population-level actors are the aviation regulators in their respective countries.

name: Compensating action
definition: The literature refers to this active managing of collective procedures and routines by population-level actors following failure as 'compensating action,' in the sense that population-level actors take actions to compensate for the weaknesses that allowed a failure to occur in the population.

name: Organizational population
definition: Population-level actors are social actors such as regulatory agencies, trade associations, and nongovernmental organizations that can influence the knowledge, information, and routines available to the entire set of organizations that make up an organizational population. Given the importance that national regulators play in the airline industry, populations of airlines were defined at the country level; that is, all airlines based in a particular country were considered to be members of the same population.

name: Corporate experience
authors_terms: ["corporate experience", "generalized corporate experience", "prior experience working at an established firm in the same industry"]
definition: Prior experience working at an established firm in the same industry, that is, corporate experience, which prior work has identified as an important differentiator in shaping startups' outcomes. The measure captures whether the entrepreneurs associated with a startup have previously worked in an established firm.

name: Corporate experience at the focal investor
authors_terms: ["corporate experience - investor", "prior experience working at the same established firm that is the corporate investor", "firm-specific human capital"]
definition: The special case of corporate experience in which that experience is accumulated at the specific established firm that is making the focal CVC investment. Firm-specific human capital originating in the focal corporate investor itself should strengthen the effects of corporate experience.

name: Technology-focused corporate experience
authors_terms: ["corporate experience - R&D", "technology focused corporate experience", "technology-focused corporate experience"]
definition: Corporate experience accrued in the parts of the established firm that are technology-focused, such as R&D, engineering, or product development, which house the technical knowledge that would be valuable to a startup.

name: Commercialization-focused corporate experience
authors_terms: ["corporate experience - Commercial", "commercially focused corporate experience", "market focused role"]
definition: Corporate experience accrued in the more commercially oriented parts of the organization, such as sales, marketing or business development, which control the complementary assets associated with translating technologies into commercial products.

name: Access to the corporate investor's technical knowledge
authors_terms: ["technical knowledge", "access to the corporate investor's technical knowledge", "technical knowledge flows", "knowledge flows to the startup"]
definition: Expertise on technological invention and refinement possessed by employees of the established firm, to which startups seek access via their CVC relationships. Startups face impediments in locating and accessing this expertise because it is spread over divisions and its holders have weak formal incentives to engage with startups.

name: Access to the corporate investor's downstream complementary assets
definition: The complementary assets required to translate an invention into a commercial product or application, which could include physical assets such as laboratories or factories; relationships with suppliers, customers, or regulators; and intellectual property such as licenses on production or delivery mechanisms.

name: Technology shock
authors_terms: ["technology shock", "technological shock", "technology shock index", "IT technology shock"]
definition: 'Technology shocks' are defined as technological changes that affect production outcomes through, for example, the invention of new production processes or the improvement of existing ones; the authors examine the rapid growth of the Internet in the early 1990s as such a shock.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "alliance activity", "firm-level alliance activity", "technology alliances", "technology collaboration agreements"]
definition: The authors count every publicly announced technology collaboration agreement (joint research and development agreements, cross-licensing agreements, and cross-technology transfer agreements) completed between any two or more organizations. Alliances are one of the ways firms respond to a technology shock, allowing them to pool scarce resources.

name: Network reach
definition: A measure that captures both the size of the network component within which a firm is embedded and the average path length of the firm to each other member in its component. Distance-weighted reach is the sum of the reciprocal distances to every organization that is reachable from a given firm.

name: Innovation outcomes
definition: Innovations as embodied in patents; patents provide a measure of novel invention that is externally validated through the patent examination process.

name: Internal sources of new experiences
authors_terms: ["internal sources of new experiences", "internal fluctuations", "unexpected performance fluctuations"]
definition: Sources of new experiences that might result from experimentation, risk taking, conflict, and chance within a knowledge domain.

name: External sources of new experiences
authors_terms: ["external sources of new experiences", "external innovation", "innovation in the industry surrounding a knowledge domain"]
definition: Sources of new experiences originating in an organization's external environment, including environmental turbulence, innovation in the surrounding industry, and regulatory changes; the focus is on changes in the external environment (outside the boundaries of the company) of a knowledge domain.

name: Uniqueness of experiences
authors_terms: ["uniqueness of experiences", "uniqueness of a unit's experiences", "unique focus of operations"]
definition: The degree to which a subunit's experiences are unique rather than redundant with those of its peers, that is, the degree to which the subunit is the only supplier of some knowledge; it depends to a large degree on the type of experiences the subunit is exposed to.

name: Knowledge codification
definition: Encoding of knowledge in forms that facilitate its transmission: through encoding, knowledge becomes decontextualized and articulated in routines, and codifying knowledge into explicit forms renders it more fluid and easier to disseminate.

name: Horizontal knowledge outflows
definition: Horizontal outflows carry knowledge from a subunit to peer subunits, defined as units reporting to the same supervising unit.

name: Vertical knowledge outflows
definition: Vertical outflows carry knowledge from a subunit to its supervising unit.

name: Horizontal knowledge inflows
authors_terms: ["horizontal inflows", "inflows of knowledge from peer units"]
definition: Knowledge inflows are the knowledge a subunit receives from other units; horizontal inflows come from peer units, that is, units reporting to the same supervising unit.

name: Vertical knowledge inflows
authors_terms: ["vertical inflows", "inflows of knowledge from supervising units"]
definition: Knowledge inflows are the knowledge a subunit receives from other units; vertical inflows come from the subunit's supervising unit.

name: Natural capital
authors_terms: ["natural capital", "wind speeds", "wind energy potential", "High Wind Energy Potential"]
definition: Defined as 'the stock that yields the flow of natural resources' (Daly, 1996: 80), natural capital exhibits properties that distinguish it from traditional notions of productive capital. In the case of wind energy it is not depleted as it is used.

name: Project economics
definition: A proxy for project economics considered two components: a measure of the value of the wind resource to utility grids (avoided cost) and the tax credits available to wind energy projects in California. As avoided costs rise or tax credits rise, the Project Economics Index also rises.

name: Wind energy project founding
authors_terms: ["founding of a wind energy project", "project foundings", "wind energy projects founded"]
definition: The date on which the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission received an application from a project's proponents was used to track the founding of a wind energy project; each application could be treated as the founding of a new organization.

name: Within-county founding activity
authors_terms: ["recent wind energy activity in the county", "wind energy projects founded in the prior 12 months", "geographic concentration"]
definition: Prior foundings of wind energy projects within the focal county; the authors argue that as more projects are proposed and built, informal networks emerge that promote information dissemination, trust and other benefits of geographic concentration.

name: Adjoining-county founding activity
authors_terms: ["wind energy projects founded in adjacent counties", "foundings in adjoining geographic subunits"]
definition: Wind energy project foundings in counties that adjoin the focal county; the authors argue that the social networks arising within a geographic subunit have diminished value outside it, so prior foundings should have no impact on foundings in adjoining geographic subunits.

name: Unemployment insurance expansion
authors_terms: ["unemployment insurance (UI) expansions", "expansions in UI benefit amounts", "increases in UI benefits", "ΔUI"]
definition: We focus on year-to-year changes in the maximum potential benefits, calculated as the product of the maximum benefit amount and the maximum duration.

name: Layoffs
definition: Changes in firm-level employment have three components: involuntary layoffs, voluntary exits ('quits'), and new hires. Throughout the discussion, we refer to 'layoffs' when presenting results based on decreases in firm-level employment.

name: Negative economic shock
authors_terms: ["negative economic shocks", "low firm performance", "industry-level negative shocks", "industry-level negative economic shocks"]
definition: We examine how UI expansions affect layoffs in response to negative economic shocks that reduce the demand for labor.

name: Managerial prosocial preferences
definition: People differ significantly in the strength of their prosociality and care for others; prosocial preferences can be both an innate trait that remains stable across time and situations and a state that is influenced by the situation or the desire to care for a specific group of people.

name: Managerial discretion
authors_terms: ["managerial discretion to act on them", "discretion to act on moral concerns", "shareholder and financial pressures", "financial and shareholder pressures", "weak governance", "financial slack", "financial constraints"]
definition: Managerial preferences do not translate to firm behaviors unless managers have the discretion to act on their preferences.

name: Negative attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["negative attainment discrepancy", "(Performance-aspiration level) t-1 < 0", "performance below aspiration level", "performance below aspiration"]
definition: The difference between actual performance and aspiration level is called the attainment discrepancy, which is considered negative if firm performance falls short of the level of aspiration. The aspiration level here is the firm's own performance history.

name: Positive attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["positive attainment discrepancy", "(Performance-aspiration level) t-1 > 0", "performance above aspiration level", "performance above aspiration"]
definition: The difference between actual performance and aspiration level is called the attainment discrepancy, which is considered positive if it rises above the level of aspiration. The aspiration level here is the firm's own performance history.

name: Entry into new markets
authors_terms: ["entry into new markets", "entry into new product markets and new countries", "expansion into new markets"]
definition: The dependent variable is Entry into new markets t (product and geographic). It is a binary indicator equal to one if the firm adds at least one new market during a time window, and zero otherwise.

name: Charitable giving rating recognition
authors_terms: ["initial positive rating", "rated as a charitable organization", "Generous Giving Strength", "charitable giving rating"]
definition: KLD gave an initial positive rating titled Generous Giving Strength to firms that had consistently given over 1.5 percent of trailing three-year net earnings before taxes or had otherwise been notably generous in their giving. Because KLD's decision to initially rate these firms was unrelated to prior firm behavior or performance and because firms had no influence on the decision to be rated, we maintain that these initial ratings constitute an exogenous shock.

name: Corporate philanthropy
authors_terms: ["corporate philanthropy", "philanthropic contributions", "charitable contributions", "charitable giving", "level of corporate philanthropic contributions"]
definition: We focus on corporate philanthropy, defined as a voluntary, nonreciprocal transfer of assets from the corporation to another entity, generally a private, nonprofit organization.

name: Analyst downgrades
definition: To evaluate analyst perceptions of firm financial performance, we collected data on downgrades in analyst recommendations from the I/B/E/S database.

name: Family ownership and control
authors_terms: ["family ownership", "family firm", "control and influence of a founding family"]
definition: On the other hand, family ownership and control within public firms is commonly perceived to be less efficient and associated with lower profitability, precisely because of concerns that concentrated ownership and control could lead families to exchange profits for nonpecuniary forms of consumption such as philanthropy at the expense of minority shareholders' wealth.

name: Local community prosocial norms
authors_terms: ["charitable communities", "charitable community", "prosocial norms", "local norms for giving", "tithing clubs"]
definition: Charitable communities are likely to have local institutions such as tithing clubs that reflect the underlying norms, values, and expectations that firms should engage in prosocial behaviors. These prosocial norms arguably help to instill a common shared belief that charitable giving is in a firm's long-term interest.

name: Perceived industry operational risk
authors_terms: ["perceived operational risk", "socially contested industry", "high-risk industries", "industry-specific risk profiles"]
definition: While the level of operational risk surely has a firm-specific component, it also differs significantly by industry. Thus an important prediction from this theoretical perspective is that the optimal level of CSR investment is higher for firms with higher industry-specific risk profiles.

name: Outside rookie executives
authors_terms: ["outside rookies", "rookie outside executives", "new outside rookies", "rookies from outside the firm"]
definition: Rookie outside executives-those new to top management and the firm-whom the authors propose are an important vehicle for incremental renewal because they bring new operational and functional knowledge and are more open to socialization and integration at the TMT level.

name: Rookie executives from inside the firm
authors_terms: ["rookie executives from inside the firm", "rookie insiders", "internal rookies", "rookies from inside the firm"]
definition: New TMT members who were middle managers within the focal firm prior to entering the TMT; rookies are executives without prior experience in a top management team.

name: Rookie executives from competitors
authors_terms: ["rookie executives from industry competitors", "rookies from competitors", "new rookie executives from competitors"]
definition: New TMT members who were middle managers of wireless competitors prior to entering the TMT; they represent an important source of interorganizational learning for the firm's TMT.

name: Rookie executives from outside the industry
authors_terms: ["rookie executives from outside the industry", "rookies from other industries", "rookie industry outsiders", "rookies from outside the industry"]
definition: New TMT members who were middle managers in industries other than wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT; their functional and operational knowledge from outside the industry becomes less relevant as industry-specific knowledge accumulates.

name: Outside seasoned executives
authors_terms: ["seasoned outsiders", "outside seasoned executives", "seasoned outside executives", "seasoned executives from outside the firm"]
definition: Executives with prior experience in a top management team who join the focal firm from outside it; the authors argue they bring a high-level strategic perspective but can be more disruptive to existing teams.

name: Seasoned executives from competitors
authors_terms: ["seasoned executives from industry competitors", "seasoned executives from competitors", "new seasoned executives from competitors"]
definition: New TMT members with prior top management team experience who were top managers of competitors in wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT.

name: Seasoned executives from outside the industry
authors_terms: ["seasoned executives from outside the industry", "seasoned outside industry executives", "seasoned industry outsiders"]
definition: New TMT members with prior top management team experience who were top managers in industries other than wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT; the authors find them more disruptive and difficult to integrate.

name: Firm growth
definition: We proxy for incremental renewal of the firm by its growth. Our central dependent variable is the increase in firm size, measured in total subscribers excluding those added through acquisitions in year t, between two consecutive years.

name: Existing TMT average team tenure
authors_terms: ["average team tenure of existing TMT members", "average tenure of the existing team", "team tenure"]
definition: Average team tenure of existing TMT members, following other upper echelons studies, is measured by the existing TMT members' average years of experience on the TMT of firm i in year t. The potential disruption from an outside executive will depend not just on the nature of the executive, but on the team that they join, and in particular, the longevity of that team.

name: Industry age
authors_terms: ["industry age", "stage of industry development", "industry life cycle"]
definition: Industry age is measured by the number of years since the first introduction of wireless communications service in the United States in 1983 in year t. The value of knowledge embodied in top executives will also vary over industry age, given that managerial talent includes general, firm-specific, and industry-specific skills.

name: Alliance learning process
authors_terms: ["alliance learning process", "learning process", "learning and knowledge accumulation process"]
definition: A process in which firms undertake deliberate efforts to learn, accumulate, and leverage alliance management know-how, involving articulation, codification, sharing, and internalization of alliance management know-how. It is directed toward helping a firm and its managers improve their partnering skills and thereby achieve greater alliance success.

name: Knowledge articulation
definition: The efforts of accessing and externalizing individually held knowledge into explicit knowledge, to the extent that it is possible, is referred to as 'articulation.' Articulated knowledge is easy to access and store, and hence it facilitates learning.

name: Knowledge codification
definition: Codification involves creating and using knowledge objects or resources such as alliance guidelines, checklists, or manuals to assist action or decision making in future alliance situations. It provides the content (know-what), the methodology (know-how), and even the rationale (know-why) for executing and managing alliance-related tasks.

name: Knowledge sharing
definition: Knowledge sharing involves exchanging and disseminating individually and organizationally held alliance management knowledge, which is both tacit and/or codified, through interpersonal interaction within the organization.

name: Knowledge internalization
definition: Knowledge internalization involves efforts to facilitate absorption of accumulated organizational level know-how by individuals; it places emphasis on the absorption of relevant knowledge by individual receivers and stresses 'learning how.'

name: Alliance function
definition: An alliance function is essentially a structural mechanism, in the form of a separate organizational unit or team of managers, responsible for managing and coordinating a firm's alliance activity, that provides several benefits to firms.

name: Firm-level alliance success
authors_terms: ["overall alliance success", "firm-level alliance success", "alliance success rate", "overall alliance performance"]
definition: A firm's success across its entire portfolio or set of alliances over a given time period, rather than the performance of any single alliance. Firms with greater alliance success are presumed to have alliance capability.

name: Staffing purity
definition: The extent to which a bank's branch-manager staffing is based on purity, demonstrated by the relative absence of prior transfers among its branch managers, i.e., the proportion of all active branch managers who were not hired from conventional banking.

name: Managerial transfer from conventional banking
authors_terms: ["managerial transfers", "transfers from conventional banking", "hiring a conventional banker to head a new branch", "controversial hiring choices"]
definition: Hiring a branch manager who has a professional background in conventional banking, i.e., came from conventional banking and had never worked in Islamic banking, to head a new branch.

name: Performance feedback
definition: Incentives to adapt that originate from the myopic learning of decision makers who dynamically adjust their strategies based on the extent to which past performance is below or above their aspiration levels.

name: Historical aspiration performance
authors_terms: ["historical aspiration performance", "performance feedback based on a comparison with an organization's own performance history", "historical aspiration performance ≥ 0", "historical aspiration performance < 0"]
definition: A bank's performance relative to its own historical aspiration level, computed as its return on assets in a given quarter minus its historical aspiration in that quarter.

name: Social aspiration performance
authors_terms: ["social aspiration performance", "social comparison with the performance of a peer group", "social aspiration performance ≥ 0", "social aspiration performance < 0"]
definition: A bank's performance relative to a social aspiration level set by the mean performance of a peer group, computed as a focal bank's performance minus its social aspiration level in that quarter.

name: Community conservatism
authors_terms: ["conservativeness in town", "the strength of Islamist ideology"]
definition: The strength of Islamist ideology in the town in which a new branch is opened, measured by the share of votes for conservative political parties with an Islamic message.

name: Community polarization
authors_terms: ["polarization in town", "liberal-religious polarization of the local community"]
definition: The liberal-religious polarization of the local community, an index based on the Gini coefficient that takes both the size of the political party bases and the ideological distance between the political parties into account.

name: Prior local mobility
authors_terms: ["prior mobility in town", "prior local mobility", "prior diffusion of transfers in the community"]
definition: The extent to which the focal town has previously been exposed to transfers of managers from conventional banking into Islamic banks.

name: Move timing
definition: Move timing represents the elapsed time between the date of a new product introduction and the date of each imitation. A first mover's new product introduction is given a value of 1, denoting the introduction takes place on day 1.

name: Move order
definition: Move order reflects the rank order position of new product moves starting with the first mover to the last imitation. The first mover is designated as order 1, the second mover is designated as order 2, and subsequent laggards are designated in the same manner.

name: Abnormal returns
authors_terms: ["shareholder wealth effects", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "standardized cumulative abnormal returns (SCARs)"]
definition: The shareholder wealth effect of a new product introduction or imitative response, measured as the cumulative abnormal return over a short event window around the announcement date.

name: New product imitation
definition: The first article that reported the introduction of a product that was the same or imitative of an already existing competitor's product was considered the first imitation; subsequent imitative responses were identified in the same manner.

name: Foreign bank density
authors_terms: ["density of foreign banks", "number of foreign banks", "foreign bank density"]
definition: Domestic or foreign bank density was measured as the number of domestic or foreign banks in each strategic group.

name: Domestic bank density
authors_terms: ["density of domestic banks", "number of domestic banks", "domestic bank density"]
definition: Domestic or foreign bank density was measured as the number of domestic or foreign banks in each strategic group.

name: Domestic bank entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rate of domestic banks", "domestic bank entry rate", "number of domestic bank entries"]
definition: The empirical analysis used the entry rate (the number of new bank entries each year) into each of the four strategic groups as the dependent variable. The entry rate was further refined into a foreign bank entry rate (number of foreign bank entries) and a domestic bank entry rate (number of domestic bank entries).

name: Foreign bank entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rate of foreign banks", "foreign bank entry rate", "number of foreign bank entries"]
definition: The empirical analysis used the entry rate (the number of new bank entries each year) into each of the four strategic groups as the dependent variable. The entry rate was further refined into a foreign bank entry rate (number of foreign bank entries) and a domestic bank entry rate (number of domestic bank entries).

name: Strategic group
definition: Strategic groups are collections of firms that are similar in terms of key strategic dimensions. Banks classified into the same strategic group can be considered as occupying the same market niche.

name: Business unit relatedness
definition: Relatedness refers to the degree to which business units support or complement each other's business activities, particularly marketing and production. It is the mechanism by which businesses capture synergies that can enhance their competitive advantage relative to competitors.

name: Marketing relatedness
definition: Market relatedness is one of the two primary types of relatedness, referring to common markets or distribution systems; it was captured using questions about the extent to which customers, sales force, and advertisement and promotion were shared with sister business units.

name: Production relatedness
definition: Production relatedness is the other primary type of relatedness, referring to common production integration; it was captured by questions about the extent to which business units shared plant and equipment, research and development efforts, or interdivisional product transfers.

name: Business unit managerial autonomy
definition: Autonomy was considered to represent the extent of authority business unit managers exercise in making major strategic decisions, such as entering new product markets or changing product lines.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Two measures of performance were used as the dependent variables, the business unit's 5-year average after-tax return on assets and growth of business unit sales over the same period. Measures of profitability and growth were chosen because they have been theorized as two of the primary dimensions of business performance.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "average after-tax return on assets", "ROA", "return on assets"]
definition: Profitability was measured as the business unit's 5-year average after-tax return on assets.

name: Sales growth
definition: Growth was measured as growth of business unit sales over the 5-year period.

name: Number of control-enhancing mechanisms
authors_terms: ["control-enhancing mechanisms", "CEMs", "number of CEMs", "number of control-enhancing mechanisms"]
definition: Founder-CEOs can implement control-enhancing mechanisms (CEMs), such as dual class shares, pyramid control structures and pact agreements, to disconnect ownership from voting rights. These mechanisms rely on creating a wedge between founder-CEO's ownership of two fundamental assets: voting rights and equity shares, and they may act together to amplify the wedge when used simultaneously.

name: Firm valuation at IPO
authors_terms: ["firm valuation at IPO", "firm market capitalization at IPO", "market capitalization at the end of the first trading day"]
definition: We measured firm valuation at IPO using the logarithm of market capitalization in million euros at the end of the first trading day, inflation adjusted to constant 1992 euros.

name: Post-IPO stock returns
authors_terms: ["post-IPO stock returns", "abnormal buy and hold returns", "ABHRs", "IPO firm performance over the long-run"]
definition: We captured IPO firm performance over the long-run using abnormal buy and hold returns. As ABHR measures what an investor earned over a long-term period it is more representative of shareholders' investment experience.

name: Local specialization of expertise
authors_terms: ["local specialization", "specialized expertise within local sites", "differentiated expertise structure", "domain expertise structure"]
definition: At the organizational level, a differentiated expertise structure is likely to unfold whereby each site has a group of experts who specialize in areas that are different from the experts at other sites. Each site will achieve congruence between the knowledge of its employees and the site's products and services.

name: Local market expertise requirements
authors_terms: ["requirements of the local market", "requirements for domain expertise across different sites", "requirements for expertise at each site"]
definition: The expertise areas that meet the requirements of the local market: site managers will tend to recruit professionals who have the expertise that their sites frequently require, so that each site employs professionals who specialize in the expertise areas that meet the requirements of the local market.

name: Methodological expertise match
authors_terms: ["matched methodological experts", "match of scarce methodological expertise", "methodological expertise"]
definition: Methodological expertise areas include training, program assessment and evaluation, surveys and measurements, statistical analysis, database construction and management, and interviewing and ethnomethodology. The match of methodological expertise is the number of methodological experts on a project whose expertise is mentioned in the project abstract as a requirement.

name: Domain expertise match
authors_terms: ["matched domain experts", "match of domain expertise", "domain expertise"]
definition: Domain expertise areas are the organization's key program areas such as education, children's mental health, early childhood, employment equity, health, individual and organizational performance, social marketing and communications, community development, and usability engineering. The match of domain expertise is the number of domain experts on a project whose expertise is mentioned in the project abstract as a requirement.

name: Cross-site connections
authors_terms: ["cross-site connections", "cross-site connections for matched experts", "cross-site connections for unmatched experts", "cross-site work history network"]
definition: If professionals join distant projects, they start developing relationships or cross-site connections with coworkers at distant sites. These cross-site connections, serving as information bridges across sites, can aid people's search for new projects and help those who want to advertise their knowledge and interest in new areas of work.

name: Project dispersion
authors_terms: ["dispersed (vs. local) project", "dispersed projects", "percentage of dispersed team members"]
definition: A project was defined as dispersed if at least one project member's home site differed from the site where the project was managed. Dispersion creates barriers to collaboration across sites through coordination problems and the pull of local ties.

name: Project net earnings
definition: We defined project net earnings as AIR itself did, that is, as the net of project revenue over project expenses, including all labor costs and overhead cost allocations.

name: TMT gender diversity
definition: We use gender diversity to indicate a continuous degree of gender variety in TMTs, with the highest degree capturing a gender balance - the equal representation of male and female members. Blau's index essentially captures the degree of gender balance in TMTs.

name: TMT psychological safety
definition: Adapting from Edmondson (1999), we refer to TMT psychological safety as the shared belief of TMT members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, such as openly raising controversial issues and challenging each other. It contains two intertwined interpersonal components, a relational component of mutual trust and support and a voice-raising component of interpersonal risk-taking.

name: Ambidextrous strategic orientation
definition: As 'the simultaneous pursuit of exploration and exploitation in firm strategic activities,' ASO is increasingly considered essential for sustainable firm performance. It denotes the simultaneous pursuit of exploitative and explorative strategies in firms.

name: Firm slack
definition: Firm slack - the firm resources that are 'unfettered, uncommitted, and therefore available for discretionary use.'

name: Return mobility
definition: The mobility of rural migrants back to their home villages and townships. The authors define return barriers as existing structures (composed of social, cultural, or policy factors) that prevent migrants from returning home for an extended period of time, and the Jiangsu policy change reduced these barriers.

name: Rural online business performance
definition: The performance of rural e-commerce businesses (REBs); the main dependent variable on business performance is a REB's monthly Sales.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: The knowledge transfer mechanism argues that returnees carry with them important knowledge in the form of technical skills and managerial know-how, and through interactions with locals, pass it down to the entrepreneurs and managers of REBs.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovation", "new product innovation", "number of distinct products"]
definition: Product innovation is measured as the number of distinct products a business displays; to the extent that an increase in the count of distinct product items constitutes an 'implementation of new ideas' over time within an e-commerce business, it can be construed as a form of innovation.

name: Demand spillover
definition: An influx of returnees to rural areas may create new demand for local products; the demand spillover mechanism proposes that returnees may generate new demand for products at local businesses and contribute to the performance benefits associated with return mobility.

name: Logistics review score
authors_terms: ["customer review scores for logistics", "logistics scores", "review scores for logistics/shipping"]
definition: Customer review scores for logistics/shipping, one of the three types of review scores (logistics, services, and product descriptions) that customers assign to a business and that are scored out of five.

name: De novo entry
authors_terms: ["de novo businesses", "de novo REBs", "new entrants", "incumbent businesses"]
definition: De novo businesses are new entrants, as opposed to established (incumbent) businesses. Because de novo businesses were founded, by definition, in the postperiod, the authors categorize all REBs registered before October 2013 as incumbent and those registered after that date as de novo.

name: Wage level
definition: Wage level is measured as the average wage of all employees in the urban parts of each prefecture (data from 2014), and it proxies returnees' financial endowments in each prefecture.

name: Entrepreneur gender
definition: Whether the business is led by a female entrepreneur; the authors report that fifty-one percent of the entrepreneurs are female, and female entrepreneurs in rural areas are likely hindered in their ability to access returnees.

name: Knowledge network centrality
authors_terms: ["knowledge network centrality", "centrality in the knowledge network", "knowledge network position", "centrality in a knowledge network"]
definition: Each node in a knowledge network of member firms in the standards committee represents a particular firm's technological knowledge base, and the ties between firms represent some convergence of their knowledge bases. A central firm's position represents the extent to which a firm's knowledge has been foundational amongst peer firms in the committee.

name: Commercialization network centrality
authors_terms: ["commercialization network centrality", "centrality in the commercialization network", "commercialization network position"]
definition: A firm's commercialization network position captures the pattern of its formal agreements to commercialize current technologies. Firms most central in these commercialization networks have maximized the utilization of complementary resources through extensive partnering with upstream and/or downstream firms.

name: Opposition to the standard
authors_terms: ["opposition to the standard", "firm's vote on a ballot measure", "rate of opposition"]
definition: Firms that are more likely to be disadvantaged by the standard will contest its passage, while firms that are more likely to benefit from it will exhibit support for its expeditious acceptance. The dependent variable records the firm's vote on a ballot measure, capturing its opposition to the standard.

name: Stewardship behavior
authors_terms: ["stewardship behavior", "stewardship conduct", "stewardship (vs. agency) conduct", "agency behavior", "composite stewardship index"]
definition: Stewardship and agency were argued to manifest in three closely interdependent facets of strategic behavior: investment, funding, and risk tolerance. For purposes of the analyses, agency behavior was assessed as the inverse of stewardship.

name: Number of family directors
definition: Family impact and the family agenda are expected to be determined in part by the number of directors on the board who are family members. On balance, the more such family members there are in the business, the more apt they are to identify with the family rather than the business.

name: Number of family officers
definition: The scope for interaction among family members in the business may be influenced by the number of family members working there, most truly when family members occupy important positions, including the number of executives who are family members.

name: Family vote dispersion
authors_terms: ["breadth of vote dispersion across the family", "dispersion of family control", "family vote dispersion", "Herfindahl index of family votes", "distribution of votes within the family"]
definition: Where vote control is spread across different family members, it is more likely that these parties will have to consult one another and agree to get things done. Thus, stewardship becomes less possible, and agency issues more likely, as family vote control dispersion increases.

name: Multiple family generations
authors_terms: ["multiple generations present", "multigenerational involvement", "involvement of later family generations", "multiple family generations present"]
definition: Generational involvement tends not only to increase the number of family members participating in the business, more importantly, it also signals the presence of emotionally charged and profound personal relationships among the parties. Self-serving family behavior therefore may become more common than stewardship.

name: Family vote control
authors_terms: ["family control", "level of family control", "percentage of votes controlled by the family", "family vote control"]
definition: Where a family controls only a very small fraction of the business, its influence is less apt to be evidenced by either stewardship or private benefit seeking as it has not the power to shape strategy. By contrast, where family control is overwhelming, there is more incentive to care for the business; the greatest propensity for self-interested behavior might exist in the midrange of family control.

name: Lone founder CEO
authors_terms: ["lone founder CEO", "founder CEO but no other family members in the business"]
definition: Founders of a business are the least susceptible to family influence, especially where there are no other family members present as major owners or officers of the firm.

name: Family founder CEO or chairman
authors_terms: ["family founder CEO", "family founder chairman", "founder presides as CEO or chairman"]
definition: Family founder CEOs, too, are apt to be somewhat resistant to family pressures to compromise the business, although the stewardship motivations of the founder may be mitigated by the presence of other family members who have significant influence in the firm but little day-to-day association with or attachment to it.

name: Later-generation family CEO or chairman
authors_terms: ["second and later generation family CEOs", "family CEO-later generation", "family chairman-later generation", "family CEOs or chairmen of second or later generations"]
definition: The parties most susceptible to family influence are those who owe their jobs to the family, are close personally to other family owners, and are there at the sufferance of the family. Second and later family generation CEOs often fit that description.

name: Total shareholder returns
definition: Performance was assessed as total shareholder returns, a measure that reflects both growth and profitability and provides the most complete picture of how well shareholders have done with their investment.

name: Ideator's bias
definition: Ideator's bias (valuation forecast bias) is that individuals err systematically (though unintentionally) when forecasting the value of their own ideas. The dependent variable is the relative difference between the ideator's value forecast at Stage 1 and the true idea value as verified by accounting at Stage 5; positive (negative) values indicate overvalued (undervalued) ideas and zero indicates a correct evaluation.

name: Organizational position
definition: Organizational position denotes whether an idea was generated by employees of low or high rank. Lower-level employees include frontline workers and their first- and second-level supervisors, whereas higher-level employees include all upper-rank individuals according to the firm's formal organizational structure.

name: Group membership
definition: Group membership concerns whether innovative effort is initiated by lone or by multiple collaborating ideators. The authors expect that more optimistic self-efficacy beliefs drawn from generating ideas collaboratively will increase the ideator's bias.

name: TMT underqualification
definition: TMT underqualification is a deficit of functional qualification with respect to the role structure of the TMT, which results when there are too few managers with requisite capabilities currently in the firm. With TMT underqualification, stated goals cannot be met with the qualifications and associated human capital currently in the team, indicating an underlying need for change.

name: TMT overqualification
definition: TMT overqualification is an excess of functional qualifications with respect to the role structures that exist within the TMT. With TMT overqualification, the TMT is currently fulfilling its formalized role requirements yet has extra qualifications, indicating an unrealized opportunity for change.

name: TMT hiring
definition: The authors examine hiring net of adding new roles, a TMT change they term capability reinforcement. TMT hiring is calculated as the sum of all top managers who appeared in month t but who were not employed by the firm in month t-1.

name: New TMT roles
definition: The addition of new roles net of hiring, a TMT change the authors term structural elaboration. New roles involve the addition of distinct tasks not previously identified in the role structure, and are counted when a job title appeared that had never before existed in the firm.

name: Firm development
definition: The authors assessed firm development by examining whether a firm had received venture capital funding or staged an initial public offering. An important contingency factor that may affect the relationship between TMT misfit and TMT change may be a new firm's stage of development, as indicated by whether it has achieved developmental milestones such as receiving venture capital financing or staging an initial public offering.

name: Breadth of foreign professional experience
authors_terms: ["breadth", "breadth of professional experiences abroad", "breadth of foreign professional experiences"]
definition: In essence, breadth involves exposure to a variety of inputs; for breadth of professional experiences abroad, we calculated the number of foreign countries in which individuals had worked.

name: Depth of foreign professional experience
authors_terms: ["depth", "depth of professional foreign experience", "depth of foreign professional experiences"]
definition: Depth of professional foreign experience can also provide individuals with requisite variety, because, the longer a person works in a foreign country, the more this person is exposed to diverse inputs, ideas, and concepts; for depth of professional experiences abroad, we calculated the number of years each director had worked abroad in their professional career.

name: Cultural distance of foreign professional experience
authors_terms: ["cultural distance", "cultural distance of an organizational leader's foreign professional experiences"]
definition: The cultural distance between one's home country (i.e., the country where one was socialized) and the foreign countries in which one is working may be an important determinant of whether individuals experience optimal levels of variation but also have the psychological resources to adapt to the new environment.

name: Creative innovations
authors_terms: ["creative innovations", "creativity ratings of their collections", "creative output"]
definition: Given the difficulty of disentangling creativity from innovation in such contexts, we label such organizational output in creative industries as 'creative innovations,' defined as the extent to which final, implemented products are novel and useful from the standpoint of relevant external audiences.

name: Business ownership change
definition: Businesses which change ownership from one firm to another; the findings focus on the acquired business as it moves from the seller's to the acquirer's portfolio. The acquisitions analysed occurred between 1980 and 1984.

name: Operational synergy
authors_terms: ["operational synergy", "predicted market share change from operational synergy", "predicted change in market share", "prediction of market share"]
definition: The net change in predicted market share that is due to changes in interrelationships from the acquisition, used to test hypotheses concerning change in operational synergy of acquired businesses. If these predictions are positive, it suggests that the intent of the acquisitions was to increase the potential for interrelationships between businesses and hence to achieve greater operational synergy in the acquirer's portfolio.

name: Competitive performance
authors_terms: ["competitive performance", "business unit competitive performance", "post-acquisition performance", "market share", "change in market share"]
definition: Competitive performance, as measured by market share in a four-digit SIC industry. Market share and change in market share are the only measures of business performance available at the level of disaggregation necessary for intraindustry analysis at the business level of the firm for all manufacturing industries.

name: Operational relatedness
authors_terms: ["interrelationships", "relatedness variables", "seven dimensions of relatedness", "shared resources and activities"]
definition: The opportunities to share resources or activities in the acquiring firm relative to the selling firm. Porter catalogues activities which can be shared between value chains of different business units and calls these interrelationships.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "performance of a focal firm", "firm's performance", "return on assets (ROA)"]
definition: The performance of the focal firm, which the authors argue generates prestige for its directors, because directors affiliated with firms perceived as highly successful benefit from the assumption that the firm's success is at least partly the result of their managerial acumen.

name: Media visibility
authors_terms: ["media visibility", "media coverage", "press coverage", "amount of media coverage", "level of press coverage"]
definition: The level of media coverage the firm generates: media coverage focuses the public's attention on particular actors, elevating both their familiarity and perceived importance in the public's mind by making them more cognitively available.

name: Director executive status
authors_terms: ["not currently a corporate executive", "nonexecutive directors", "individuals who come from outside the corporate ranks", "executive status"]
definition: Whether a director is currently a corporate executive at another firm. The authors argue that individuals who come from outside the corporate ranks, such as academics, attorneys, and physicians, as well as retired corporate executives, place more value on board appointments than executives of other large public firms.

name: Elite education credentials
authors_terms: ["elite education credentials", "elite education", "elite educational backgrounds", "attended an elite educational institution"]
definition: Whether the director attended an exclusive secondary school, which the authors treat as an indicator of elite social status. They argue that directors with elite educational backgrounds are more likely to identify with the elite, in-group aspects of board service.

name: Board leadership position
authors_terms: ["chairing key subcommittees", "serving as the chairperson of a board", "chairing key board committees", "audit committee chair", "compensation committee chair", "board chair"]
definition: Formal positions through which influence can be exercised on a board, including chairing key board committees such as the audit or compensation committee and serving as the chairperson of the board. Directors who hold these positions are more likely to personally identify with a company's successes and failures.

name: Active CEO status
authors_terms: ["currently serving as a CEO", "active CEO", "CEO of another company"]
definition: Whether the director is currently the chief executive officer of another company; serving as a CEO increases the director's sense of external pressure and level of busyness.

name: Directorships held
authors_terms: ["number of directorships held", "number of board appointments", "total number of board appointments held", "number of boards on which he or she sits"]
definition: A count of the total number of board appointments a director holds, which increases the director's personal workload and level of busyness.

name: Financial and reputational risk
authors_terms: ["director financial and reputational risk", "personal reputational risk", "personal financial risk", "shareholder lawsuits", "restated earnings"]
definition: The personal reputational and financial risk associated with a particular board appointment, which the authors measure with shareholder lawsuits and restated earnings. Association with visible signs of organizational malfeasance can tarnish an upper echelon member's reputation, and the threat of being sued and facing personal liability makes directors wary of continuing to serve.

name: Director exit
definition: A director's departure from a focal firm's board, which the authors argue is primarily voluntary or by mutual consent rather than involuntary.

name: Component design quality
authors_terms: ["component design quality", "design quality of the component", "CDQ", "output performance"]
definition: The design quality of the developed component (output performance), based on multiple items, including performance, costs, conformance quality, and structural and functional coordination with other components.

name: Integrated problem solving
authors_terms: ["early, integrated problem solving", "integrated problem-solving pattern", "integrated problem-solving process", "PSP"]
definition: The level of early, integrated problem-solving process with a supplier; the variable scores high when, for example, the supplier's initial price/cost estimate was examined very carefully by the automaker from the beginning of the project, and the automaker examined the supplier's manufacturing process and design for manufacturing at the earlier stage.

name: Communication frequency
definition: The frequency (in days per year) of mutual visits by the automaker's engineers and purchasing staff and the supplier's engineers and sales staff.

name: Engineers' knowledge
definition: The knowledge level of the automaker's engineers about the component, measured as the mean of two subcomponents: engineers' component-specific knowledge (EKN1) and architectural knowledge (EKN2).

name: Internal coordination
definition: The level of the automaker's internal coordination; it consists of three subcomponents: internal coordination within engineering departments (INC1), internal coordination between engineering and purchasing departments (INC2), and external consistency of the automaker's various engineering functions and purchasing department toward the supplier during the project (INC3).

name: Automaker ownership of supplier stock
definition: One dimension of inter-firm relations is the degree of an automaker's ownership of a supplier; in Japan, it is not uncommon for an automaker to own a certain portion of its supplier's stock.

name: Supplier sales dependency
authors_terms: ["supplier's sales dependency on an automaker", "S's sales dependency on A", "SLD"]
definition: Another dimension of inter-firm relations, the supplier's sales dependency on an automaker; when a supplier is highly dependent on an automaker in sales, the automaker may have power to ask more of the supplier's efforts in component development.

name: Systemwide organizational change
authors_terms: ["systemwide organizational change", "systemwide change", "systemic change", "full system change", "System 1", "comprehensive organizational change"]
