definition: Firms may align their adoption announcement with the notion of shareholder value by conveying that the adoption of a poison pill will increase shareholder value, that is, a focus on gains.

name: Shareholder value protection framing
authors_terms: ["shareholder value protection framing", "a focus on nonlosses", "nonlosses framing"]
definition: Firms may align their adoption announcement with the notion of shareholder value by conveying that the adoption of the pill ensures the protection of shareholder value, that is, a focus on nonlosses.

name: Dual CEO/chair framing
authors_terms: ["framing by a dual CEO/chair", "the framing of a poison pill adoption by a dual CEO/chair", "source credibility"]
definition: Source credibility has two main dimensions, expertise and trustworthiness; trustworthiness is likely to differ depending on whether the announcement is made by a CEO who is also the chair of the board, because investors are less likely to believe speakers when they are perceived to have situational incentives.

name: Speaker visibility
authors_terms: ["speaker visibility", "visibility of the CEO/chair", "visibility of a frame articulator"]
definition: For firms, visibility reflects the level of awareness and exposure that a firm receives from its stakeholders, in many cases as reflected in media coverage; the authors apply the same reasoning to the visibility of a frame articulator such as a CEO/chair.

name: Prior firm performance
definition: Prior performance measured by a firm's financial record is the reference point investors use, since investors strongly rely on trends and consistency such as a firm's prior performance in forming investment decisions.

name: Adoption prevalence
definition: The prevalence and momentum surrounding the adoption of organizational practices, captured here as the number of recent prior poison pill adoptions, which increases the availability of information about adoptions and investor attention.

name: Market expansion
definition: The dependent variable is market expansion, defined as the extent (how many) and the selection (in which markets) of opportunities actually pursued by competing firms. It is measured as the number of new branches opened in each year in each market by each bank.

name: Market attractiveness relative to reference point
authors_terms: ["market attractiveness relative to the market reference point", "market attractiveness relative to the reference point", "market attractiveness relative to the firm's reference point", "opportunity prospects"]
definition: Market attractiveness relative to the market reference point corresponds to the difference between each market's attractiveness level and the firm-specific market reference point. The opportunity prospects rule is focused on this difference, that is, the extent to which market attractiveness is greater or lower than the focal firm's market reference point.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Organizational slack has been defined as the discrepancy 'between the resources available to the organization and the payments required to maintain the coalition' or as a cushion of actual or potential resources that allows the organization to deal with internal or external pressures.

name: Performance relative to aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspirations", "performance feedback", "performance relative to the aspirations"]
definition: The performance feedback simplifying rule focuses on performance relative to aspirations, that is, the extent to which a focal firm's performance is greater or lower than its aspiration level. Performance feedback signals the existence of a problem when performance is below the firm's aspiration level and signals a fully satisfactory position when performance is above the firm's aspiration level.

name: Market attractiveness
definition: In market expansion decisions, we call this market-specific expected outcome the market attractiveness. Given the nature of the primary goal, the degree of attractiveness of a particular market should correspond to the extent by which an organizational move toward that market is expected to contribute to the focal firm's profit.

name: Market reference point
definition: We define the market reference point as the focal firm's current status quo against which the market attractiveness is compared. Status quo is a natural aspiration level and is consistent with the idea that firms use an improvement criterion (relative to the existing situation) to evaluate new alternatives.

name: Entrepreneurial human capital
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial human capital (EHC)", "EHC", "share of employees with prior entrepreneurial experience", "share of former entrepreneurs"]
definition: A set of abilities and skills that individuals acquire when starting and managing a new venture. We argue that EHC should enhance firm-level resilience.

name: New venture survival
definition: Survival can be argued to be the ultimate test of a firm's resilience capacity. We adhere to the definition of resilience as an organization's ability to maintain functions, identify opportunities, build up and utilize resources during and after crises, and respond to sudden adversities, ultimately surviving.

name: Crisis
definition: A crisis is defined following Pearson and Clair as 'a low probability, high-impact situation that is perceived by critical stakeholders to threaten the viability of the organization'. Here, we adopt a crisis-as-event perspective.

name: Length of entrepreneurial experience
authors_terms: ["length of entrepreneurial experience", "length of the entrepreneurial spell", "longer spells in entrepreneurship", "years of entrepreneurial experience"]
definition: Learning occurs, for example, through the length of entrepreneurial experience, which further augments entrepreneurial abilities. Simply remaining in business for longer indicates the ability to handle various business situations that have arisen over the years.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "organizational size", "number of employees", "smaller new ventures"]
definition: Organizational size is positively associated with the degree of specialization, routinization, and bureaucratization in firms, in contrast with smaller and younger firms where employees are more likely to be empowered with decision-making authority and delegated responsibilities.

name: Knowledge fit
definition: We define the correspondence between an employee's acquired knowledge and the knowledge requirements of their current employer as human capital fit. The hypothesis is that the relationship between EHC and survival is stronger in organizations with a better knowledge fit.

name: Intrinsic speed capabilities
authors_terms: ["intrinsic speed capabilities", "intrinsic firm speed capabilities", "intrinsic investment speed", "speed capabilities", "firm speed"]
definition: "a firm's intrinsic speed capability, which is the ability to complete an investment project faster than others given the same cost and conditions." The authors add that "Firms' intrinsic speed capabilities include any organizational factors that allow firms to develop investment projects more quickly than competitors."

name: Firm value
definition: The paper's outcome is firm j's performance at time t, which "is measured by Tobin's q, which is defined as the ratio of a firm's market value to replacement costs of tangible assets"; the authors note that Tobin's q is often used to capture the value of firms' intangibles and that intrinsic speed capabilities are an intangible asset.

name: Corporate governance
definition: "Corporate governance refers to designs that monitor and discipline managers so that they take actions in shareholders' interest." The authors state that better governance reduces the weight of suboptimal behavior in their speed proxy and that firms with better governance make more and better use of their intrinsic speed capabilities.

name: Cost of capital
authors_terms: ["cost of capital", "discount rate", "firm discount rates", "leverage", "external cost of capital"]
definition: The authors state that "intrinsic speed generates more value in firms with lower discount rates; a lower discount rate raises the valuation of a project's stream of revenues and thus the returns from speed." They also note that leverage directly affects unobserved heterogeneity in firm discount rates, as debt erodes firm value more for firms facing greater liquidity constraints and a higher external cost of capital, which typically also have a higher discount rate.

name: R&D efficacy
authors_terms: ["ability to benefit from innovation efforts", "R&D efficacy", "innovative efficacy", "R&D intensity", "ability to draw value from R&D investment"]
definition: The R&D variable "captures innovation effort; q will be higher the greater a firm's R&D efficacy." The authors argue that "To the extent that larger value created by R&D investments correlate with successful product or process innovation, more innovative firms should also benefit more from intrinsic speed capabilities."

name: Project development time
authors_terms: ["time-to-build", "project completion time", "development time", "time-to-build of a new production facility"]
definition: "T f , i , t is a discounted transformation of the time-to-build of a new production facility f in industry i at time t," and it is measured as the lag between the start and end dates of plant development reported in the Oil and Gas Journal.

name: Collaborative engagement with the scandalized industry
authors_terms: ["collaborative relationship with firms in an industry implicated in a scandal", "primarily collaborative interactions with oil and gas firms", "collaborative oil and gas repertoire", "collaborative treated SMOs"]
definition: Many firms now seek out collaborative relationships with activist organizations to assist their formulation and implementation of socially responsible reforms, allowing for the expansion of SMOs' collaborative repertoire for corporate engagement. In the analyses, SMOs that had primarily collaborative interactions with oil and gas firms are coded one for the treatment dummy collaborative treated and zero otherwise.

name: Contentious engagement with the scandalized industry
authors_terms: ["primarily contentious relationship to firms in an industry implicated in a scandal", "contentious interactions with oil and gas firms", "contentious oil and gas repertoire", "contentious treated SMOs"]
definition: Contentious tactics engage in a process of problematization: activists make disparaging claims about established firms (or other incumbents) to convince the public that a contested practice is harmful or improper. Contentious treated is a dummy coded one if the SMO had primarily contentious interactions with oil and gas firms and zero otherwise.

name: Public support
definition: Our proxy for public support is the amount of total contributions received by an SMO in a given year, a critical performance metric in this setting.

name: Industry scandal
definition: Scandals are surprising and adverse events that reveal illegitimate or deviant information about an actor. We focus on industry scandals when blame for a deviant act is attributable to some feature that is common across the industry.

name: Collaborative interactions with firms
authors_terms: ["number of collaborative interactions an SMO has with any firm", "collaborative interactions between SMOs and firms", "collaborative tactical repertoire"]
definition: We use the number of collaborative interactions an SMO has with any firm in our 500-firm sample as our dependent variable to investigate whether the scandal had a broad-reaching, chilling effect on SMOs' use of collaborative tactics.

name: Commitment to the status quo
authors_terms: ["commitment to the status quo", "CSQ", "Leadership CSQ", "Strategy CSQ", "executive commitment to the status quo"]
definition: A belief in the enduring correctness of current organizational strategies and profiles. The authors argue it derives both from the individual's preferences and from knowledge, and treat it as the missing psychological link in research on executive characteristics and organizational outcomes.

name: Organizational tenure
definition: How long the executive has been employed by the company. The authors note that organizational and industry tenure are highly related and even definitionally nested.

name: Industry tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure in the industry", "industry tenure", "additional tenure in the industry"]
definition: How long the executive has worked in the current industry. The authors argue the industry is a social setting in which events, trends and concepts are interpreted and shared.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["current performance", "current organizational performance", "current level of performance", "profitability"]
definition: The organization's current level of performance, taken as the respondent's subjective assessment of firm profitability; acceptable performance is argued to induce confidence in the status quo, while poor performance erodes it.

name: Industry discretion
definition: Executives differ significantly in how much discretion, or latitude of action, they possess; an executive's discretion emanates in part, and perhaps most fundamentally, from the environment.

name: Prior firm profitability
authors_terms: ["prior firm profitability", "pre-acquisition firm profitability", "industry-adjusted firm profitability", "firm profitability within its industry"]
definition: The acquiring firm's own profitability in the period before the acquisition, examined as industry-adjusted firm profitability by subtracting industry average profitability from absolute firm profitability.

name: Prior industry profitability
authors_terms: ["prior industry profitability", "pre-acquisition industry profitability", "industry average profitability"]
definition: The average profitability of the acquiring firm's primary industry before the acquisition; industry average profitability reflects the structural attractiveness of the industry.

name: Acquisition strategy
authors_terms: ["acquisition strategy", "related acquisition", "unrelated acquisition", "direction of acquisition", "choice between related and unrelated acquisitions"]
definition: The direction of diversification as an isolated event in which the firm adds to its existing businesses a related or unrelated business through acquisition.

name: Exporting flexibility
authors_terms: ["exporting flexibility", "flexibility afforded by firms' exporting investments", "flexibility of a firm's exporting investments"]
definition: The flexibility of a firm's exporting investments is seen in the extent to which the firm is able to sell its products abroad (i.e., export) to nonroutine and new international customers.

name: Multinational flexibility
authors_terms: ["multinational flexibility", "flexibility afforded by firms' foreign direct investments"]
definition: The firm's activities of shifting or switching its production or sales from one location to another, which reflect the ability of the firm to act flexibly. This flexibility stems from the ability derived from foreign direct investments to shift production from less beneficial markets to those that are more beneficial.

name: Firm value
definition: Tobin's q is a standardized measure of the value ascribed to a firm by investors; while the denominator represents the investment inputs in the firm, the numerator captures the value created by the firm with these inputs.

name: First-time board appointment
definition: We define first-time directors as individuals with no prior public company board experience listed in the BoardEx database. The appointment can take two forms: an inside appointment to the board of the firm where he or she serves as an executive, or an outside appointment to a different firm.

name: Inside directorship
definition: When an executive is chosen to join his or her home company's board, it is likely because the board perceives that he or she will be able to add value to board discussions. Inside directors consisted of executives promoted to the board at their employer, and received a score of '1' for the insider dummy.

name: Outside directorship
definition: Outside directorships, which occur when an executive serves on another company's board, will also be influential, but due to different theoretical mechanisms. Outside directors were those promoted to boards at companies other than their employers, and received a '1' for the outsider dummy.

name: Promotion to CEO
authors_terms: ["promotion to CEO", "attainment of a CEO position"]
definition: Promotion to CEO reflects whether the executive was promoted to CEO within the five-year window following t. Promotion to CEO was measured using a binary variable that took a value of '1' if promotion occurred that year and '0' otherwise.

name: Inside promotion to CEO
authors_terms: ["inside promotion", "internal promotion to CEO", "promotion to CEO within the firm"]
definition: Executives can either be promoted to CEO from within the company or from outside the company; the inside promotion variable took a value of '1' when the executive was promoted to CEO at his or her company.

name: Outside promotion to CEO
authors_terms: ["outside promotion", "external promotion to CEO", "promotion to CEO at outside firms"]
definition: Executives can either be promoted to CEO from within the company or from outside the company; the outside promotion variable took a value of '1' when the executive was promoted to CEO at a firm other than his or her employing firm in t-1.

name: Promotion in title
authors_terms: ["promotion in title", "promotion in title above his or her current position", "TMT promotion"]
definition: The dependent variable, promotion in title, captures whether the executive experienced a promotion in title above his or her current position. We use two levels of promotion: (1) promotion to either COO or CFO and (2) promotion to president.

name: Executive pay level
definition: Executive pay level was measured using the TDC1 variable in Execucomp, which includes the total value of an executive's salary, bonus, long-term incentive payouts, stock grants, option grants, and other income in a given year.

name: Lead manager selection
authors_terms: ["choice of lead manager", "lead manager", "becoming lead manager"]
definition: The dependent variable is firms' choice of lead manager. When firms issue securities, they typically choose a bank (lead manager) to organize and manage the underwriter syndicate, who then chooses the rest of the management group and underwriter syndicate members.

name: Commercial banking ties
authors_terms: ["commercial banking ties", "market ties in commercial banking", "market ties based in commercial banking"]
definition: Market ties in commercial banking are dyadic business relationships based on whether or not a given bank helped arrange syndicated loans for a firm in the previous five years.

name: Investment banking ties
authors_terms: ["investment banking ties", "market ties in investment banking", "market ties based in investment banking"]
definition: Market ties based in investment banking are present when a firm had used a given bank as a lead manager or co-lead manager on bond or stock issues or as a merger and acquisition advisor in the last five years.

name: Network status in commercial banking
authors_terms: ["commercial-banking status", "status based in commercial banking", "network status in commercial banking"]
definition: Status refers to the relative position a bank occupies in a given market based on its direct and indirect ties with other firms as compared with the positions that other firms occupy based on their direct and indirect ties. Commercial-banking status is calculated from a symmetric network of agent ties in which a cell denotes how many times two commercial banks worked together as managers of a loan syndicate.

name: Network status in investment banking
authors_terms: ["investment-banking status", "status based in investment banking", "network status in investment banking"]
definition: Status refers to the relative position a bank occupies in a given market based on its direct and indirect ties with other firms as compared with the positions that other firms occupy based on their direct and indirect ties. Investment-banking status is calculated from the asymmetrical network of lead-manager/co-lead-manager ties based in the bond market.

name: Bank market tenure
authors_terms: ["bank years in market", "years since market entry", "time in investment banking"]
definition: The number of years banks had been present in investment banking, measured as the number of years passed since they first obtained investment-banking approval from the Federal Reserve Board.

name: Firm market experience
authors_terms: ["firm market experience", "firms' investment banking experience", "market experience"]
definition: The firm's investment banking experience, measured as the number (natural logarithm) of times firms had used the markets for bonds, stocks, and mergers and acquisitions in the prior five years.

name: Voluntary corporate spin-off
definition: A spin-off divides the existing asset base of a corporation into two (or more) separate parts, and the current shareholders receive a pro rata distribution of separate equity claims on the assets of each new corporate entity. There is no exchange of cash or financial securities for assets, so the existing principal-agent relationship remains unchanged, and by focusing on voluntary spin-offs the authors examine the governance role of corporate restructuring absent any challenge from the external control market.

name: CEO origin
definition: The authors coded the CEO of the spun-off firm as an insider if he or she was employed in the combined firm in the prior year (also noting whether or not this person was the combined firm's CEO) and an outsider if he or she was not. There are two alternative views about who might be chosen to lead the spun-off firm: a promotion-based logic favoring an insider versus an external CEO labor market logic favoring an outsider.

name: Stock option compensation
definition: Top managers receive compensation in the form of executive stock options, and a spin-off allows the spun-off companies to take the opportunity presented by their separately traded equity claims to write performance-contingent options contracts for their new CEOs.

name: Performance-contingent compensation
definition: The authors refer to the first four pay measures (salary and bonus, thrift plan contributions, insurance payments, and other fringe benefits) as nonperformance-contingent compensation and the latter five measures as performance-contingent compensation, i.e., various equity-linked financial rewards.

name: Insider representation on the board
definition: Insiders are those members of the board whose full-time employment is with the corporation. The board cannot provide independent oversight unless outsiders hold a majority of seats on the board, and the authors hypothesize that a company that voluntarily restructures itself will staff a board with sufficient outsiders to deny the insiders majority control.

name: Executive outsider representation on the compensation committee
authors_terms: ["executive outside directors", "independent executive outside directors", "% executives on the committee"]
definition: Executive outsiders are top-level executives of other companies, and the authors argue that it is not enough to staff the compensation committee with outsiders because the type of outsider matters; they predict that compensation committees will be staffed with a controlling number of such independent executive outside directors.

name: Stock market reaction to the spin-off announcement
authors_terms: ["market's reaction to the spin-off announcement", "announcement effect", "abnormal return", "shareholder wealth effects"]
definition: The authors examine the shareholder wealth effects of voluntary corporate spin-offs by utilizing the market model to compute abnormal returns, and report the mean standardized cumulative prediction error over the 2-day announcement period.

name: Trade secret legal protection
authors_terms: ["trade secret protection", "trade secret legal protection", "strength of local trade-secrecy protection", "trade secret law", "protection of trade secrets"]
definition: Trade secret law defines the extent to which trade secrets are protected from misappropriation by establishing the scope of trade secret protection, the remedies available to the injured party, and the harshness of punishment for misappropriation. It is part of the legal appropriability regime, the extent to which the legal system protects and enforces property rights on intangible resources.

name: Firm market value
authors_terms: ["firm market value", "market value", "target's market value", "change in firm market value"]
definition: The change in the target firm's market value over the private equity holding period, measured by the buyout's internal rate of return, which captures the percentage change in the target firm's market value in any period.

name: Inter-firm mobility of knowledge workers
authors_terms: ["industry mobility", "mobility of knowledge workers", "inter-firm mobility of knowledge workers", "cross-firm mobility of knowledge workers"]
definition: The rate of inter-firm mobility of knowledge workers at year t sell in the industry in which the target company operates. Mobility is a crucial driver of knowledge leakages, and employee departures associated with the loss of relevant knowledge to established competitors or start-ups are an important challenge for any acquirer.

name: Resource-value uncertainty
authors_terms: ["resource-value uncertainty", "industry resource-value uncertainty", "uncertainty about the resource future value"]
definition: The degree to which an industry features high uncertainty about the value of its resources, so that past performance is an unreliable indicator of the target's future performance and it is unclear whether past performance reflects a sustainable competitive advantage or sheer luck. It is measured as industry uncertainty about the resource future value.

name: Risk of poor investments
authors_terms: ["poor investments risk", "risk of poor investments", "risk of making a poor- or 'lemon'-investment"]
definition: The classic 'lemons problem' in an industry, that is, a substantial risk for a buyer of incurring an extremely poor deal, which exacerbates the typical information asymmetries between buyers and sellers in the markets for corporate control.

name: Industry bystander status
authors_terms: ["industry bystander firms", "non-industry bystander firms", "event industry", "bystander firms in the same industry"]
definition: Bystander firms that are in the same industry category in which the financial misconduct is revealed, as compared to bystander firms that are not in the same industry as the perpetrator.

name: Market valuation
definition: Investors' valuation of firms, captured as the cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) of the sample firms surrounding the announcement of financial misconduct; the CAR is the sum over the event window of the abnormal daily returns of each particular firm.

name: Perpetrator firm familiarity
authors_terms: ["perpetrator firm familiarity", "investors' familiarity with the perpetrator firm", "perpetrator firm size", "familiarity with the misconduct firm"]
definition: Investors' familiarity with the misconduct firm; characteristics of the perpetrator firm that increase investors' familiarity with such firms make investors' generalizations of culpability to the industry category more potent.

name: Employee firings at the perpetrator
authors_terms: ["perpetrator employees fired", "employees of the perpetrator firm are fired", "employee firings"]
definition: A characteristic surrounding the misconduct event whereby employees of the perpetrator firm are fired for the misconduct, which ascribes blame for the misconduct to individuals and thus restricts the guilt of the perpetrator from being generalized to the industry category.

name: Government investigation of the perpetrator
authors_terms: ["government probe", "ongoing government investigation", "governmental probe of the perpetrator"]
definition: An ongoing government investigation at the perpetrator firm at the time of the announcement of the financial misconduct, which typically results in specific individuals within the firm being held responsible for the misconduct and thus facilitates attributions of blame.

name: Industry bystander firm familiarity
authors_terms: ["industry bystander firm familiarity", "investors' familiarity with industry bystander firms", "bystander firm size"]
definition: Investors' familiarity with the industry bystander firms; industry bystander firms that are familiar to investors are more readily categorized to the industry and thus more likely to be perceived as instantiating the generalized culpability.

name: Board vigilance
authors_terms: ["board vigilance", "vigilant boards", "independent directors", "proportion of independent directors"]
definition: The degree to which investors perceive that a vigilant board is overseeing the firm, signified by the presence of independent directors-those directors who are not part of management and do not have financial dealings with the firm.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "dual CEOs", "CEO is also the chair of the board of directors"]
definition: When the CEO is also the chair of the board of directors, which serves as the most unambiguous indication that the leadership of the CEO is complete and confers legitimacy in the eyes of stakeholders who expect strong leadership.

name: Performance above aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance above aspirations", "performance-aspiration gap (above aspirations)", "phone level-perf. above aspirations"]
definition: When product performance increases above the aspiration level, the product is likely to be retained by the organization, because success creates confidence in existing knowledge and biases decisions against changes.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "performance-aspiration gap (below aspirations)", "phone level-perf. below aspirations"]
definition: As product performance falls below aspiration levels, managers will continue to invest in existing products and culling will slow, but as the performance-aspiration gap gets sufficiently large, culling will accelerate; this implies a U-shaped relationship between performance below aspirations and rate of phaseout.

name: Performance relative to the survival threshold
definition: Managers see aspirations and survival as distinct from each other, and sufficient decreases in performance may be interpreted as a step closer to the depletion of solutions, so that attention shifts to a survival threshold and away from the aspiration level.

name: Centralization
definition: Centralization reflects the extent to which the locus of authority to make final decisions affecting the organization is concentrated at higher levels of the hierarchy. As a structural property of the firm, centralization reflects a variety of standard operating procedures, formal roles, communication channels, and informal interactions that emphasize vertical information flow.

name: Product phaseout
definition: The key event for the analysis is phaseout of a product from the German market, defined as the cessation of product shipments from the handset manufacturer to German retailers, not as the cessation of all retail sales.

name: CVC portfolio diversification
authors_terms: ["CVC portfolio diversification", "portfolio diversification", "diversification of a CVC portfolio", "portfolio configuration"]
definition: The diversification of a CVC portfolio concerns how its portfolio companies are spread across industries, and its portfolio effect is likely to be derived from knowledge transfer rather than from the sharing or combining of physical resources. The higher the portfolio HHI, the more diversified the portfolio, and a value of 0 indicates that all the portfolio companies in which the corporate investor has invested are in the same industry.

name: Firm value
definition: We capture the firm value for corporate investors by Tobin's Q—a firm's market valuation over the replacement costs of its tangible assets. Because Tobin's Q incorporates growth values of equity, it explicitly includes not only investor valuations of current operations but also investor expectations for future growth.

name: Financial constraints
definition: In reality, financial constraints may force corporate investors to prioritize their investment agendas and even to give up investment opportunities. Corporate investors need sufficient internal capital and/or financing ability for future capital to undertake such activity, and the reversed values of available slack (current ratio) and potential slack (debt-to-equity ratio) indicate the financial constraint that corporate investors face.

name: Option value
definition: For a CVC investment the option value is derived mainly from the strategic benefits that such investment creates for the corporate investor, and the value of the option portfolio is also influenced by the interactive effects of the underlying technologies or industries. The real options literature has suggested that constructing an option portfolio is a process of actively managing the risk structure for future portfolio value, and spreading of risk through diversification would typically adversely affect option values.

name: Target revision
authors_terms: ["change in budgeted sales", "target revision", "change in targets"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the change in budgeted sales for each period and each branch. The variable measures the increase or decrease in a branch's target relative to its previous year's target.

name: Performance deviation
definition: Performance feedback is defined as the deviation between actual performance and aspirations. We use last year's actual guided sales minus the targeted guided sales as our measure of past performance deviation.

name: Relative target setting
definition: RTS compares last year's expected performance for a particular branch with the actual average performance of the branches in its region. A positive RTS indicates a target (per employee) for the branch above its peers, whereas a negative value indicates a target (per employee) below peers.

name: Branch age
definition: A branch's age is the number of full years of operation. Branches that have been in operation for two to three years are described as young branches, and branches that have been in operation for more than three years are mature branches.

name: Unfavorable performance deviation
definition: Performance below aspirations (failures) has been argued to lead to more changes. The variable takes a value of one if last year's deviation was unfavorable.

name: Large performance deviation
definition: The magnitude of the deviation is informative about the likelihood of permanent versus transitory components of the deviation. The variable takes a value of one for the branch-year observations with a performance deviation value larger than the 87.5 percentile or smaller than the 12.5 percentile of the performance deviation distribution.

name: CEO transformational leadership
definition: Widely examined as a multifaceted meta-construct, transformational leadership consists of exhibition of four interdependent and mutually reinforcing attributes: charisma, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration.

name: TMT behavioral integration
definition: Behavioral integration refers to the degree to which a TMT engages in mutual and collective interaction. It is a meta-construct consisting of one social dimension (the level of the team's collaborative behavior) and two task dimensions (the team's quantity and quality of information exchanged and its emphasis on joint decision making).

name: TMT decentralization of responsibilities
definition: Decentralization of responsibilities refers to the degree of concentration of decision making in regard to task and operational activities within a TMT. The more responsibility over day-to-day tasks and tactical decisions a firm's CEO delegates to the members of its TMT, the more responsibilities are decentralized.

name: TMT risk propensity
authors_terms: ["risk propensity", "risk-taking propensity", "TMT shared preference for risky growth opportunities"]
definition: A TMT's shared preference for risky growth opportunities.

name: TMT long-term compensation
authors_terms: ["long-term compensation", "compensation based upon the long-term performance of the firm"]
definition: The extent to which a top management team's compensation is based upon the long-term performance of its firm.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
definition: Corporate entrepreneurship is defined by Zahra (1996) as the sum of a firm's product innovation, business venturing, and strategic renewal activities.

name: Codifiability
definition: "Codifiability" captures the degree to which knowledge can be encoded, even if the individual operator does not have the facility to understand it; software controlling machinery is a good example.

name: Teachability
definition: "Teachability" captures the extent to which workers can be trained in schools or on the job; it reflects the training of individual skills.

name: Complexity
definition: "Complexity" picks up the inherent variations in combining different kinds of competencies; knowledge, no matter the education of the worker, is simply more complex when it draws upon distinct and multiple kinds of competencies. We defined complexity as the number of distinctive skills, or competencies, embraced by an entity or activity.

name: System dependence
authors_terms: ["System Dependence", "perceived importance of system dependence", "dependence of a system"]
definition: "System Dependence" captures the degree to which a capability is dependent on many different (groups of) experienced people for its production.

name: Product observability
definition: "Product Observability" captures the degree to which capable competitors can copy the manufacturing capability, because they are able to manufacture the innovation once they have understood the functions of the product.

name: Technological competition
definition: The variable Parallel Development is measured by the count of competitors perceived as engaged in parallel efforts aimed at developing a similar product at the time of the innovations' release; the authors interpret it as a high level of "technological competition" and the fear of losing the technological edge to competitors.

name: Knowledge spillover among competitors
authors_terms: ["spillover of the manufacturing capability", "knowledge diffusion among competitors", "common manufacturing capability", "manufacturing knowledge common to a group of competitors"]
definition: The extent to which principal aspects of the manufacturing capability have spilled over the boundaries of the firm, that is, the extent to which important aspects of manufacturing capability spill over quickly and easily among firms. Imitation should be quicker in industries where important capabilities, whether embodied in individuals or in machines, are more accessible.

name: Continuous development
authors_terms: ["Continuous Development", "continuous improvement", "subsequent improvements of the innovation"]
definition: Continuous Development is constructed to capture the importance of subsequent improvements of the innovation through recombining current knowledge. Innovations at the time of introduction undergo a period of incremental improvement, and the ability of the innovating firm to improve the product should deter imitation.

name: Speed of capability transfer
authors_terms: ["time to transfer", "hazard rate of transfer", "probability of early transfer", "speed of transfer"]
definition: The rates by which manufacturing capabilities were transfered to new sites; these rates, when expressed as the probability of transfer or imitation conditional on no previous event, are called hazard rates.

name: Speed of imitation
authors_terms: ["time to imitation", "hazard of imitation", "risk of early imitation", "speed of imitation"]
definition: The rates by which innovations were imitated by competitors; these rates, when expressed as the probability of transfer or imitation conditional on no previous event, are called hazard rates.

name: CEO charisma
definition: A characteristic of individuals who 'by force of their personal abilities are capable of having profound and extraordinary effects on followers' who 'often exude confidence, dominance, a sense of purpose, and the ability to articulate a vision for followers to grasp.'

name: Strategic dynamism
definition: Engaging in strategic change (i.e., strategic dynamism) signals a departure from the existing state of affairs; strategic dynamism is a flow that reflects year-over-year changes in resource allocations.

name: Strategic nonconformity
authors_terms: ["strategic nonconformity", "nonconformist strategies", "strategic nonconformity (i.e., the extent to which the firm's strategy deviates from industry central tendencies)"]
definition: The extent to which the firm's strategy deviates from industry central tendencies; strategic nonconformity is a stock that represents the cumulative result of resource allocation decisions that deviate from industry norms.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR refers to the various practices and initiatives that firms undertake for the benefit of non-shareholder stakeholders; CSR emphasis is the extent to which the firm prioritizes a broad array of stakeholders.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Tenure, a moderator variable in our analyses, reflected the time since becoming CEO.

name: Scandal publicity
definition: The amount of publicity that transgressions receive; publicity turns misconduct - real or alleged - into scandals by unleashing externalities on members and making even oblivious individuals aware of what is going on in their organization.

name: Catholic membership
authors_terms: ["Catholic membership", "number of Catholics", "adherents to the Catholic Church"]
definition: Membership of the Catholic Church at the local level; members are 'individuals who, in return for a variety of inducements, make contributions to the organization' (Scott, 1981: 16).

name: Non-Catholic denominational membership
authors_terms: ["non-Catholic membership", "number of adherents to non-Catholic denominations"]
definition: Membership of the 16 non-Catholic Christian denominations in the study at the local level; these denominations belong to a conceptually distinct category within Christianity, shielded from the fallouts of the scandals by a longstanding categorical boundary.

name: Dissimilarity to the Catholic Church
definition: The absolute value of the difference in strictness between the focal denomination and the Catholic Church, which the authors label dissimilarity; it is assumed to be stable and not to vary over time.

name: Denominational strictness
definition: A denomination's position on a strictness continuum ranging from church-like to sect-like, based on the degree to which it emphasizes maintaining a separate and distinctive lifestyle or morality in personal and family life rather than affirming the current American mainline lifestyle.

name: Social entrenchment
authors_terms: ["social entrenchment", "structural cohesion", "connectedness in the board network", "cohesively nested firms"]
definition: This paper introduces the concept of 'social entrenchment' to describe how cohesive social network structures can support collective resources among embedded corporate actors. Social entrenchment is most pronounced within cohesive and tightly knit sections of the board interlock network, where managerialist behaviors are most robust.

name: Shareholder proposal targeting
authors_terms: ["proposal targeting", "targeted by activist investors", "the target of a shareholder proposal"]
definition: In the first analytic component the focal dependent variable is a dichotomous indicator of whether a firm was the target of at least one governance related shareholder proposal in a given year.

name: Targeting by financial outsiders
authors_terms: ["union and individual sponsored proposals", "financial outsiders", "union sponsored proposals", "individual sponsored proposals"]
definition: In contrast to most institutional investors, financial outsiders such as unions and individual investors lack the resources, institutional legitimacy, or backchannel access to engage in private negotiations with firms.

name: Targeting by institutional investors
authors_terms: ["pension sponsored proposals", "investment fund sponsored proposals", "institutional investors"]
definition: Large institutional investors, particularly those with long-term investment horizons and low portfolio turnover, such as many private pension funds, public pension funds, and some mutual funds, tend to engage in private bargaining with management and boards and are generally more reluctant to adopt public confrontational tactics.

name: Shareholder proposal implementation
authors_terms: ["proposal implementation", "implementation outcomes", "responsiveness to shareholder proposals", "responsiveness to investor activism"]
definition: In the second analytic component, the focal dependent variable is a dichotomous indicator capturing whether the firm implemented a proposal that passed a shareholder vote. Implementation is a useful indicator of managers' responsiveness to shareholders.

name: Time period
definition: Recent evidence indicates that the board network has become more fragmented in recent years, particularly since the mid-2000s. While social entrenchment decreased the likelihood of proposal implementation in the earlier period, it does not reduce implementation in the more recent period.

name: CEO effect
authors_terms: ["CEO effect", "proportion of variance in performance attributable to individual CEOs", "effects of individual chief executives on company outcomes"]
definition: The proportion of variance in performance that is attributable to CEOs (as opposed to contextual factors), or the degree to which company performance is traceable to CEOs as opposed to contextual factors.

name: Calendar period
definition: The study window is divided into three distinct 20-year periods: 1950-1969 (Period 1), 1970-1989 (Period 2), and 1990-2009 (Period 3).

name: Firm performance
definition: The outcome variable of the study, examined through three measures of firm performance: return on sales (ROS), return on assets (ROA), and market-to-book ratio (MTB).

name: Market space unconventionality
authors_terms: ["market space unconventionality", "degree of unconventionality", "market unconventionality", "unconventional market positioning", "unconventionality"]
definition: Pioneering ventures bring together existing market categories and recombine them to craft new market positions or even industries; the authors refer to such firms as unconventional ventures. The structural and cognitive nascency of the market position a firm seeks to occupy is not simply binary, but a matter of degree.

name: External interface role development
authors_terms: ["external interface roles", "external interface functions", "external interface role professionalization"]
definition: External interface roles include the marketing & sales as well as the customer development functions; they facilitate the firm's engagement with outside audiences and their locus of attention falls outside the firm's boundaries. Professionalization entails the elaboration of roles in key functional areas, and one of the two role elaboration processes is an adjustment to the organization's external interface function.

name: Internal process role development
authors_terms: ["internal process roles", "internal process functions", "internal process role professionalization"]
definition: Internal process roles facilitate the routinization, standardization, and control of internal activities, and their attention falls inside the firm boundaries. Examples of internal process roles include the accounting, human resources, and finance functions.

name: Developmental milestone attainment
authors_terms: ["number of milestones completed", "number of milestones passed", "developmental milestones"]
definition: Raising each subsequent round of venture capital funding represents a critical milestone in the venture's progress down a professionalization path that, in the rarest and most successful cases, culminates in an initial public offering. The number of milestones passed is measured based on the completion of venture capital rounds and/or an initial public offering.

name: Expropriation concerns
definition: Expropriation concerns create contracting difficulties because valuable intellectual property may be expropriated by another party without appropriate safeguards. The authors employ the term expropriation to focus on the potential for losing sole rights to a rent-generating asset.

name: Measurement cost
authors_terms: ["measurement costs", "cost to verify project quality", "cost of verifying project quality"]
definition: Measurement costs create a moral hazard by generating noise in the relationship between effort and outcome. Projects vary in the cost of determining quality after completion, and where a key dimension of output is difficult to measure an outcome-based contract is problematic.

name: Interdependence
definition: Interdependencies within or among projects give rise to a third type of contracting difficulty because they lead to bilateral dependency among firms involved with the project. Such a condition is consistent with Thompson's concept of reciprocal interdependence.

name: Employment relation
authors_terms: ["choice of employment relation", "mode", "insourcing", "outsourcing", "employees versus independent contractors"]
definition: The choice of whether to use independent contractors or employees can be viewed as a governance decision. The authors define Mode as a binary variable coded as 1 if the project was insourced and 0 if an independent contractor was involved in the project.

name: Project profitability
definition: Profitability is measured as a project's profit margin, expressed as a percentage, for each project; because some projects incurred losses, the margin can be negative.

name: Acquired employee status
authors_terms: ["acquired employees (AEs)", "hiring mode", "mode of hiring", "hired employees (HEs)", "acquired-in workforce"]
definition: AEs are defined to be employees of all acquired companies whose tenure crosses the month and year in which the acquisition of their employer transpired. Companies have two, broad modes to recruit talent: they can hire employees on the open labor market or they can acquire an incumbent organization with an established workforce.

name: Employee turnover
definition: Employee departure from the employer at which the employment spell began, where the risk of turnover commences at the point of organizational entry at acquisition or organic hire; turnover events are distributed in time and are right censored for all workforce-active individuals that have not moved employers at the end of the observation window.

name: Job rank
definition: The seniority ordering of job titles, created by using individuals' mobility from origin to destination job titles to create a seniority order of job titles.

name: Job function
definition: An individual's job role is defined based on their specific, listed job title; the hierarchy of distinct job roles is derived from the text LinkedIn members use to self-characterize their work roles.

name: Educational attainment
definition: The highest tertiary educational degree an individual has attained, categorized into three degree levels: bachelor's, master's, and doctoral.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact refers to two firms competing in more than one distinct market. The authors use the terms multimarket contact and market overlap interchangeably, though the latter can exist without the former.

name: Reciprocity of market contacts
authors_terms: ["reciprocity of market contacts", "reciprocal market contacts", "reciprocal contacts", "nonreciprocal market contacts", "spheres of influence"]
definition: The reciprocity of market contacts, in addition to mere contact across multiple markets, increases the costs of an initial attack and thus strengthens deterrence and mutual forbearance. Sharing footholds of small market shares in each other's important markets (i.e., reciprocity of market contacts) is an important factor that facilitates mutual forbearance.

name: Technology cooperation
authors_terms: ["technology cooperation", "technology cooperation agreement", "partner selection for technology cooperation"]
definition: The dependent variable in this study intends to capture a formation of technology cooperation between two firms in a dyad. Technology cooperation is known to be particularly prone to the hazard of partner opportunism due to the inherent uncertainty surrounding R&D.

name: Corporate risk taking
authors_terms: ["risk", "risk taking", "income stream uncertainty", "uncertainty of a company's income stream"]
definition: I defined risk as the uncertainty of a company's income stream. In this research, risk was measured as the ex ante uncertainty of a firm's earnings stream.

name: Corporate performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "future performance", "economic performance", "return on total assets", "return on equity", "return on sales"]
definition: Risk taking, aspirations, expectations, slack, future average industry performance, and past company performance were hypothesized to influence future company performance. All the analyses presented were executed using return on total assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS) as performance measures.

name: Industry performance
definition: Industry performance was the average ROA for firms with a given two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code.

name: Performance expectations
definition: Managers in firms have both levels of performance they aspire to (aspirations) and levels of performance they expect (expectations). Expectations were measured by the mean of the earnings forecasts produced by securities analysts.

name: Performance aspirations
definition: If expectations fall below aspirations, managers search for solutions that can raise expected performance to the aspiration level, and if they cannot find such solutions, they lower aspirations.

name: Organizational slack
definition: The system is buffered by slack—excess resources that a company can use to loosen the ties between environmental changes and the need for organizational responses.

name: Team failure
definition: Team failure is defined as the deviation from desired team outcomes. In the study setting, when the new product version fails to improve over the original, teams deem it a failure on that performance criterion.

name: Team status differentiation
definition: Status differentiation is defined as the relative concentration of status among team members. In teams with high status differentiation, respect and admiration are concentrated among a few members.

name: Individual status level
authors_terms: ["individual status level", "members' status level", "members' own status level", "status level"]
definition: Status in work teams is based on members' judgments about each other's instrumental social value, which reflects their expected contribution to team performance. Members differ in their own status level within the team.

name: Status uncertainty
definition: After team failures, team members may feel uncertain about their status within the group. While success reinforces members' sense of security with their current status, failure undermines such security and signals the possibility of status change.

name: Potential benefit to collective performance
authors_terms: ["potential benefit to collective performance", "perceived benefits to collective performance", "potential benefits for collective performance"]
definition: High-status individuals typically possess essential skills, task-related knowledge, resources, and valuable connections, so adding new, high-status members is an efficient way to inject the capabilities and resources needed to turn failure into success. The authors theorize that, in teams with low status differentiation, members focus on the potential benefits for collective performance of adding high-status members.

name: Potential cost to individual status
authors_terms: ["potential cost to individual status", "perceived costs to individual status", "potential costs to individual members' status"]
definition: Adding high-status members may threaten incumbent members' status within the team, as the new member likely has higher status than incumbent members. The authors theorize that, in teams with high status differentiation, status uncertainty leads to a focus on the potential costs to individual members' status of adding high-status members.

name: Willingness to add high-status members
authors_terms: ["members' willingness to add a high-status member", "willingness to add a high-status member", "willingness to invite a high-status member"]
definition: When team members focus on the collective performance benefits potential new members may provide, they will be more willing to seek to add these new members; when they focus on the potential costs to their own status, they will be less willing to do so.

name: Team decision to add a high-status member
authors_terms: ["team's willingness to add high-status members", "team decision to invite a high-status member", "high-status member addition", "addition of high-status members"]
definition: Team decision-making is not simply a summation of individual members' preferences, but rather a process in which the way all members form their preferences ultimately shapes the collective decision. The authors focus specifically on adding high-status members, the form of membership change that offers the clearest potential for performance improvement while posing the most salient threat to existing members' status.

name: Team performance
definition: Team performance is operationalized as the percentage of performance criteria that improve, i.e., the percentage of performance criteria in which the new product version outperforms the baseline in a performance episode.

name: Within-team benefit–willingness relationship strength
definition: The strength of the positive relationship between team members' perceived benefits to collective performance and their willingness to add a high-status member within a team. Higher values indicate a stronger positive within-team benefit–willingness relationship.

name: Within-team cost–willingness relationship strength
definition: The strength of the negative relationship between team members' perceived costs to individual status and their willingness to add a high-status member within a team. Higher values indicate a stronger negative within-team cost–willingness relationship, meaning a more negative slope.

name: Risk aversion
definition: Risk-averse individuals are defined as decision makers who prefer the alternative with lower risk given an expected return (or who demand a higher return for any given risk).

name: Government guanxi
authors_terms: ["guanxi activities with government officials", "government guanxi", "guanxi with government", "business-to-government transactions", "political connections"]
definition: Strategic utilization of personal relationships with government officials, administrators and bureaucrats as a means of achieving organizational goals, measured across political government, industrial authorities and other government authorities.

name: Business guanxi
authors_terms: ["guanxi activities with other business firm leaders", "business guanxi", "business-to-business guanxi", "interfirm relations"]
definition: Strategic reliance on personal relationships with other business firm leaders, i.e. the cultivation and utilization of ties with suppliers, customers and competitors in interfirm transactions.

name: Firm age
definition: The number of years since registration as a private firm; young firms are those in business for up to six years, and are assumed to face a liability of newness and high resource dependence.

name: Local market orientation
definition: The extent to which a firm sources supplies and sells products locally, i.e. within the same community; nonlocal suppliers and customers may be located in the same province but not the same locality, or in other provinces or overseas.

name: Firm performance
definition: Self-reported economic performance of the firm, measured by return on assets and sales growth over the corresponding three-year period.

name: Value chain segment
authors_terms: ["stages of the swine genetics industry", "vertical segment", "respondent group"]
definition: This market comprises a focal swine genetics company that maintains the germplasm stock and breeds for specific biophysical characteristics, its downstream customers—hog producers—who transform the genetic potential into a marketable product, and its intermediary customers—veterinarians—who act as medical and scientific consultants between them.

name: Value chain distance
authors_terms: ["distance between an industry participant and the TMT firm", "farther away a value chain customer is from the TMT", "distant from the TMT"]
definition: This suggests that the farther away a value chain customer is from the TMT, the greater the degree of heterogeneity in competitive beliefs. Because the hog producer is the swine genetics market's end customer, the hog producer should receive the greatest information feedback and thus face fewer problems of overconfidence; whereas, because the veterinarian is an intermediary user of swine genetics, the veterinarian's beliefs should yield a divergence that is less than that between the hog producer and the TMT.

name: Competitive attribute perceptions
authors_terms: ["beliefs/perceptions about competitive attributes", "salient attributes of competition", "key competitive attributes", "competitive beliefs"]
definition: The salient or key competitive attributes used to determine cluster groupings, describing a swine genetics firm's competitive characteristics. Cognitive strategic group research suggests organizations use only a few, but salient, attributes to classify firms.

name: Competitive groupings
authors_terms: ["beliefs/perceptions about competitive groupings", "competitive groupings", "cognitive maps", "cluster solutions", "strategic groups"]
definition: A classification heuristic or a cognitive map facilitates interpretation of the competitive environment by simplifying the 'complex cognitive problem of independently analyzing a larger number of competitors by grouping them.' However, by simplifying the competitive environment, cognitive maps lead to myopic interpretations that resist or ignore emerging competitive threats and thereby creating blind spots.

name: Monitoring leniency
definition: A private monitor licensed by the state may ignore or downplay observed violations and profit from side payments from the party it is charged with monitoring. Temporary adjustments and the use of substitute vehicles violate state laws and constitute lenient regulatory monitoring.

name: Profit opportunity from cross-selling
authors_terms: ["profit opportunity of cross-sold product", "profitable opportunities to cross-sell", "cross-selling opportunity", "profit opportunity"]
definition: The profit opportunity from extending leniency depends on the profitability and frequency of cross-sold transactions. The opportunity to cross-sell a large, high-margin product or service creates incentives for firms to exchange leniency for an implicit side payment of such purchases.

name: Moral hazard risk of cross-sold product
authors_terms: ["moral hazard risk", "risk of moral hazard", "quality deception"]
definition: Moral hazard risk arises from information asymmetry regarding the quality of the cross-sold product, which creates the possibility that the firm might misrepresent product quality to the customer. The monitored party faces greater moral hazard risk from cross-sold products and services when quality is unobservable ex ante and when transactions are infrequent.

name: Organizational scope
authors_terms: ["organizational scope", "firm scope", "scope of facility activities", "product scope"]
definition: All testing facilities in the sample are multiproduct/service establishments-gasoline retailers, car dealers, or service and repair shops-for which inspections are a secondary business line. The authors argue that a monitoring firm's portfolio of cross-sellable products and services is a primary predictor of leniency in the monitoring activity.

name: Subsidiary ownership
definition: Whereas an independent, single-location firm risks the loss of just its own monitoring license, a subsidiary of a multiunit or multilocation firm risks government sanctions that impose additional costs on the parent company and its other establishments. Managers of subsidiaries have weaker incentives to engage in leniency than do managers of independent firms.

name: Brand affiliation
definition: Branding affects the consequences of potential government sanctions because the actions of one branded establishment can draw regulatory attention to other establishments that share its brand. A branded establishment caught providing lenient monitoring might invite brandwide investigations by the state regulator.

name: Institutional protection from employment discrimination
authors_terms: ["institutional protection from employment discrimination", "antidiscrimination laws", "employment antidiscrimination institutions", "Employment Non-Discrimination Act (ENDA)"]
definition: Institutional protections put in place "to counter discrimination in how employers hire, promote, and fire workers" (P44); in this study, the state-level enactment of the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, "which shields workers from employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity" (P105).

name: Rate of entrepreneurial foundings
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial foundings", "rates of entrepreneurial foundings", "new-firm entry", "startup foundings"]
definition: The rate of new-venture creation; the authors measure entrepreneurial foundings as "the total number of new, stand-alone establishments in a given U.S. state and year" (P119).

name: Startup quality
definition: The average quality of the new ventures founded in a region; the authors argue that "the average quality of new ventures will increase, when institutional protection of minority workers intensifies" (P86).

name: Prevalence of protected minorities
authors_terms: ["protected minorities are more prevalent", "presence of the minority groups targeted by the antidiscrimination legislation", "state gay population", "LGBT population", "protected groups"]
definition: The presence of the minority groups targeted by the antidiscrimination legislation; the authors argue that employers "will be more likely to enact these policies in environments where the protected minorities are more prevalent" (P94).

name: Prevalence of employment discrimination litigation
authors_terms: ["litigation against employment discrimination", "state employment antidiscrimination litigation levels", "civil rights suits relating to jobs"]
definition: The extent to which protected groups "mobilize regulatory institutions - via legal complaints and grievances - to enforce their rights and benefits" (P101), measured as the prevalence of litigation against employment discrimination in a state.

name: Speed of integration
definition: We define speed of integration as the shortness of the time period needed to complete the intended integration of systems, structures, activities, and processes of the two companies.

name: M&A success
definition: Consistent with the existing literature we define M&A success as the merging firms' return on sales after the merger or acquisition compared to the merging firms' situation prior to the merger or acquisition.

name: Internal relatedness
definition: Relatedness refers to aspects outside the two organizations (external relatedness) as well as to aspects inside the two organizations (internal relatedness). Internal relatedness relates to such phenomena as strategy, culture, and premerger performance.

name: External relatedness of target markets
authors_terms: ["external relatedness with respect to target markets", "relatedness with respect to target markets"]
definition: External relatedness with respect to target markets captures the extent to which the merging firms' geographical markets and customers are similar.

name: External relatedness of market positioning
authors_terms: ["external relatedness with respect to market positioning", "relatedness with respect to market positioning"]
definition: External relatedness with respect to market positioning refers to the extent to which the merging firms offers are similar in terms of customer needs which they satisfy, quality, price positioning, etc.

name: Internal relatedness of strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["internal relatedness with respect to strategic orientation", "relatedness with respect to strategic orientation"]
definition: Our study focuses on the two firms' relatedness with respect to strategic orientation; we draw upon Porter's (1980) classical distinction between cost-oriented and differentiation-oriented strategies and measure three strategic orientations referred to as cost orientation, product orientation, and customer intimacy.

name: Internal relatedness of management style
authors_terms: ["internal relatedness with respect to management style", "relatedness with respect to management style", "relatedness of management styles"]
definition: Our study focuses on the two firms' relatedness with respect to management style, a component of organizational culture; the items describe management styles in terms of such dimensions as centralized/decentralized, short-term-oriented/long-term-oriented, and proactive/reactive.

name: Internal relatedness of performance
authors_terms: ["internal relatedness with respect to performance", "relatedness with respect to performance"]
definition: Our study focuses on the two firms' relatedness with respect to performance; internal relatedness with respect to performance is measured by means of two items related to the merging firms' return on sales and market share.

name: External relatedness
definition: Relatedness refers to aspects outside the two organizations; external relatedness captures the extent to which the merging firms are similar in external aspects such as target markets and market positioning.

name: Executive race
authors_terms: ["race", "Black executives", "White executives", "Black CEO appointments", "White CEO appointments", "Black TMT appointments", "White TMT appointments"]
definition: Race was coded based on observers' perception of the executives' race, rather than self-identification, because the phenomenon of interest is examined from the perspective of external observers (i.e., investors' perception). As such, similar to investors, we used all publicly available information and photos of the executives to code the race variable.

name: Executive position
authors_terms: ["top executive appointments", "CEO appointments", "TMT appointments", "top management team (TMT)"]
definition: The study examines announcements of top executive appointments (CEO, COO, CFO, President, Executive Vice President), and distinguishes CEO appointments from TMT appointments.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: The authors follow the Lee and James (2007) event study procedure: the sample consists of N firms with each firm displaying T returns (T = -240 + 1 returns for N x T observations), and following this procedure they compute cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) and obtain standard errors from the distribution across 500 iterations.

name: Firm insider status
authors_terms: ["firm insider", "promoted from within the company", "insider/outsider status"]
definition: Firm insider was coded as 1 if the executive was promoted from within the company and 0 if the executive is not promoted from within the company.

name: Product social performance
definition: Product social performance (PSP) is the extent to which the product-focused actions—the development and marketing of products or services—of a firm are consistent with its social responsibility obligations.

name: Environmental social performance
definition: Environmental social performance (ESP) is the degree to which a firm ensures that environmental concerns that arise either out of its business operations or otherwise are addressed.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "Tobin's Q", "market value of a firm"]
definition: Firm performance is assessed in the market value of a firm; the authors use Tobin's Q as a measure of firm performance. Compared to accounting-based measures, Tobin's Q is a forward-looking measure and reflects future profitability.

name: Information uncertainty
definition: Information uncertainty (IU) refers to the reliability of information signals about a firm. High IU implies that a firm's information in the past has not allowed stakeholders to assess its performance clearly.

name: Cross-border acquisition
definition: Cross-border expansion enables firms to access new knowledge from foreign sources and to then transfer that learning back home. Cross-border acquisitions are viewed as a means to access resources from distant markets-resources that are often embedded in local knowledge clusters-while acquiring the context-specific skills necessary to absorb the attendant new capabilities.

name: Labor productivity
definition: Our main dependent variable is firm-level labor productivity, a commonly used productivity metric that measures the internal efficiency with which an organization transforms inputs into outputs.

name: Host country competitiveness
authors_terms: ["country competitiveness", "more competitive countries (MCC)", "less competitive countries (LCC)", "target firm's host country is more competitive"]
definition: The level of country competitiveness is based on the overall rankings in the World Competitiveness Yearbook, which is determined by four different factors: economic performance, government efficiency, business efficiency, and infrastructure. The authors posit that acquiring a firm located in a more competitive country than the acquirer's home country will lead to more learning opportunities and also to fewer frictions (and lower risks) associated with the redeployment of such learning back home.

name: Domestic productivity-enhancing investment
authors_terms: ["contemporaneous domestic productivity-enhancing investments", "domestic productivity-enhancing investment", "Investment rate"]
definition: Investments in domestic productivity-enhancing activities made in conjunction with the acquisition. In order to reap the benefits of new organizational and managerial practices, it is often necessary to make complementary investments in equipment, machinery, buildings, and infrastructure.

name: Executive past temporal depth
definition: Temporal depth refers to the temporal distance (or time horizons) into the past and the future that executives typically consider when contemplating events that have happened or may happen. PTD captures how far back executives tend to go when considering past events.

name: Executive future temporal depth
definition: Temporal depth refers to the temporal distance (or time horizons) into the past and the future that executives typically consider when contemplating events that have happened or may happen. FTD is how far ahead executives tend to look when considering the future.

name: Industry velocity
definition: Industry velocity is the rate at which new opportunities emerge and disappear in an industry; it reflects the speed or rate at which new opportunities emerge and disappear.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: Competitive aggressiveness is defined as 'the propensity of a firm to directly and intensely challenge rivals in order to maintain or improve its market position.' It reflects the degree to which a firm engages intensely with its rivals through its competitive repertoires.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is captured with two accounting measures of profitability—return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA)—which the authors combine into a composite measure.

name: Rational-analytic thinking
definition: Conscious, logical, and effortful form of thinking. Rational-analytic thinking is effortful, conscious, and logical.

name: Intuitive thinking
definition: Experiential, unconscious, and associative form of thinking; intuitive thinking is unconscious, associative, affective, and experiential.

name: Identification of distant symptoms
authors_terms: ["identification of distant symptoms", "distant symptom identification", "Distant Symptoms", "distant symptoms"]
definition: Identifying often overlooked or hidden symptoms; distant symptoms tend to be implicit, experiential, and affective.

name: Novelty of problem formulation
definition: Novel formulations of strategically important problems are uncommon judgments or 'theories' on potential causes based on available symptoms of problems.

name: Time period
definition: Because the primary question is the change over time of the rate at which firms lose superior profitability positions, the only independent variable is time period.

name: Economic performance
definition: Two measures were used to operationalize economic performance: return on assets (ROA), an accounting measure, and Tobin's q (the ratio of firm market value to the replacement cost of its assets), a market measure, because some studies have shown results that vary between accounting and market measures.

name: Persistent superior economic performance
authors_terms: ["persistent superior economic performance (PSP)", "persistent superior performance", "periods of persistent superior economic performance", "superior economic performance"]
definition: Superior economic performance was operationalized as statistically significant above average economic performance (relative to other firms in the same industry for the firm-level analyses, and relative to all business units, or all industries, or all firms for the segment-level analyses) over a 5-year period. Persistent superior economic performance at the corporate level was operationalized as superior economic performance lasting for six or more windows (i.e., a 10-year period).

name: Concatenation of short-term competitive advantages
authors_terms: ["concatenating a series of short-term competitive advantages", "series of temporary advantages", "a series of short advantages that can be concatenated into competitive advantage over time"]
