definition: Sustained competitive advantage has become less a matter of finding and sustaining a single competitive advantage and more a case of finding a series of competitive advantages over time and concatenating them into a sustained competitive advantage. Because successful firms may concatenate advantages seamlessly, the authors look for the pattern of superior, then less than superior, then superior performance over time.

name: Industry technology intensity
definition: Porter argued that hypercompetitive effects are likely to be limited to high-technology industries. The authors distinguish 'high-tech' industries (SIC codes 357x, 365x, 3661, 3674, 481x, and 7372) from 'low-tech' industries (all other SIC codes).

name: Hypercompetition
definition: D'Aveni defines hypercompetition as 'an environment characterized by intense and rapid competitive moves, in which competitors must move quickly to build advantage and erode the advantage of their rivals'; D'Aveni argues that hypercompetition is making it more and more difficult for firms to maintain a competitive advantage.

name: Remote problem source
definition: Remote problems are the converse of proximate problems - those outside firms' geographic and institutional environments. Remote problem sources, such as national and supranational agencies, lie outside firms' direct geographic and institutional environments.

name: Proximate problem source
definition: We define proximate problems as problems arising within firms' geographic and institutional environments. Proximate problem sources, such as state and county agencies, lie within firms' direct range of geographic and institutional environments.

name: Search breadth
authors_terms: ["search breadth", "technological search breadth", "breadth of technological knowledge search"]
definition: As the outcome, we examine variation in the breadth of technological knowledge search. A greater number signifies search for a greater variety of renewable electricity technologies.

name: Technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities reflect the ability to generate a technological good. In this context, the key ability that distinguishes firms' technological search choices is renewable generating capacity.

name: Profitability
definition: Profits over and above those attributable to industry, market share, generic strategy, or strategic group membership; the authors argue that profitable alignments produce supernormal profits and thereby constitute a source of sustainable competitive advantage.

name: Internal structural fit
authors_terms: ["internal structural fit", "fit between organizational differentiation and integration", "internal consistency", "differentiation-integration fit"]
definition: Organizational performance is a function of the fit between an organization's structural differentiation and integration; high-performing firms employ structural integration only to the extent required by their structural differentiation.

name: Size-structure fit
authors_terms: ["size-structure fit", "fit between organizational size and structural formalization", "size-structure interaction"]
definition: The proposition that the size-formalization match has important performance consequences for organizations, larger organizations adopting more formal procedures.

name: Size-planning fit
authors_terms: ["size-planning fit", "fit between organizational size and formal planning comprehensiveness", "size-planning interaction"]
definition: Because increased size brings greater environmental demands and internal complexity, comprehensive, formal strategy-making processes are required in large organizations, whereas less comprehensive, informal strategy-making processes are sufficient in smaller ones.

name: Industry stability-structure fit
authors_terms: ["industry-structure fit", "fit between environmental stability and structural formalization", "environment-structure fit"]
definition: Different levels of environmental variation require different levels of structural formalization: formal, mechanistic structures are appropriate in stable environments, informal, organic structures are appropriate in unstable environments.

name: Industry stability-planning fit
authors_terms: ["industry-planning fit", "fit between environmental stability and formal planning comprehensiveness"]
definition: Different levels of environmental variation require different degrees of decision-making comprehensiveness, or strategic planning formality; matching strategy-making formalization to environmental variability is a critical organizational alignment skill.

name: CEO internal locus of control
authors_terms: ["CEO internal locus of control", "CEO locus of control"]
definition: A strong free-will orientation wherein CEOs believe they control organizational outcomes by their own designs, held to be the critical CEO attribute in producing appropriate organizational alignments, particularly within single-business firms.

name: Decomposed search
definition: The case in which firms experiment with and evaluate an alternative by producing a decomposed module, as opposed to the case in which firms experiment with and evaluate an alternative by producing a full-scale product (integrated search). In the music industry firms can evaluate the talent of a new artist by either producing an album (an integrated search) or producing a single (a decomposed search).

name: Number of new alternatives
authors_terms: ["number of new artists", "new-to-the-world artists", "Number_New_Artists", "experiment with more new alternatives"]
definition: The number of new alternatives (new-to-the-world artists) that a firm experiments with in a year, corresponding to the variation generation stage of search. The first dependent variable measures the number of new artists in music firm i at year t.

name: Omission errors in selection and retention
authors_terms: ["omission errors in giving a second chance", "miss out on promising alternatives", "Miss_Talented_Artist", "number of top 20% talented artists whom the firm missed out on after their first release"]
definition: A type of omission error in the selection and retention stages: missing out on promising alternatives after the first evaluation of those alternatives, i.e., not giving a second evaluation chance to a promising alternative.

name: Performance target
definition: If the evaluated performance of an alternative satisfies a performance target (i.e., a minimum performance criterion), the firm will select and retain the option for future use; otherwise, firms will search for other alternatives.

name: Planning process sophistication
authors_terms: ["planning sophistication", "planning process sophistication", "level of planning sophistication", "planning orientation"]
definition: Bracker and Pearson (1986) identified eight planning components and, based on these components, four distinct levels of planning sophistication in order to study its relationship with performance. These levels are unstructured, intuitive, structured operational and structured strategic planners.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: According to Smith (1967) entrepreneurship reflects a constellation of characteristics and behaviors, and these vary among all individuals, including small business owners. The end-points of Smith's continuum are characterized as opportunistic (OE) and craftsman (CE).

name: Firm size
definition: Firms in the sample were classified as large or small; the size split was based on a discussion with an industry expert. Large firms were those with more than $3 million gross revenue.

name: Planning history
authors_terms: ["prior planning history", "planning histories", "long planning histories", "short planning histories"]
definition: Planning histories were classified as long or short and were a function of prior research by Bracker and Pearson (1986). Firms with long planning histories were those with more than 5 years of planning.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "industry-specific financial business performance data", "growth in revenue", "net income growth", "present value growth of the firm", "CEO cash compensation growth"]
definition: The industry-specific financial performance data that served as dependent variables were growth in revenue, net income growth, present value (including book value, patents and goodwill) growth of the firm, and CEO cash compensation growth over the 5 year time frame.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: Firms were classified into categories based on observed patterns of relatedness in marketing, distribution, R&D, and production. Following Rumelt's principal finding that performance does not vary with the amount of diversity but rather with the type of diversity, the authors compressed the nine strategy categories into five nominal categories: single business, dominant vertical, constrained, linked, and conglomerate.

name: Relatedness of diversification
definition: Related and unrelated strategies are defined and tested two ways: a narrow definition, designed to maximize possible contrasts, defines 'related' as only constrained strategies and 'unrelated' as only unrelated strategies; a broader definition defines 'related' as both constrained and single business strategies, and 'unrelated' as both unrelated and linked strategies.

name: Shareholder value
definition: Shareholder value of a firm is a function of its financial return, given the level of its systematic risk, or the sensitivity of its returns to the aggregate returns of the market place. The study measures shareholder value as a two-dimensional construct, systematic risk and excess return.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Systematic risk refers to the sensitivity of a firm's returns to the market's expected returns. The beta coefficient is the covariance of the return to a firm with the return to the market portfolio, i.e. the slope coefficient of the market model.

name: Excess returns
definition: Excess return refers to the deviation of a firm's return from the market-expected return, estimated by the intercept term of the market model, or alpha. A positive alpha means that shareholders of that firm will earn a long-term return which is above the firm's required, or expected, rate of return, i.e. that shareholders are pricing a firm at a premium.

name: Market cycle
definition: A cycle was defined by the direction of movement in the stock market time-series composite as presented in Value Line. A bear cycle was represented by general downward movement lasting at least 6 months, a bull cycle represented a general upward movement of the same duration, and a stable cycle was represented by at least a 6 month period that showed no discernible movement.

name: Inaugural inclusion of a syndicate partner
authors_terms: ["Inaugural inclusion by lead firm", "inaugural inclusion", "inaugural inclusions of partner firms"]
definition: A lead firm's inclusion of a syndicate partner firm that the lead firm had not included in prior syndicates it had assembled. From the perspective of the focal lead firm, such inclusions are inaugural (i.e., first time) and signify the lead firm's initial acceptance of the venture capital firm into its circle of suitable partners.

name: Shared nationality
definition: Nationality is a fount of similarity and shared identity; firms of the same nationality are embedded in a common society with mutual history, language, and behaviors. These unambiguous group boundaries and ingroup commonalities create a basis for loyalty and trust.

name: Collaborative first move
authors_terms: ["collaborative first move", "Collaborative first move by prospective partner", "collaborative first-move opportunity"]
definition: A collaborative first move occurs when Firm A includes, for the first time, Firm B in an investment syndicate that it has assembled, and Firm B had not previously included Firm A in any investment syndicates that it had assembled.

name: Lead firm nationality
authors_terms: ["Lead firm nationality", "U.S. syndicate lead firms", "Chinese syndicate lead firms"]
definition: We used a dummy variable to indicate whether the focal lead venture capital firm of the focal investment syndicate was Chinese (0) or from the U.S. (1). The nationality of lead firms is tied to the societal values, individualistic or collectivist, in which they are embedded.

name: Board involvement in strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["board involvement", "board involvement in the strategic decision-making process", "board strategic role"]
definition: The overall level of participation of board members in making nonroutine, organization-wide resource allocation decisions that affect the long-term performance of an organization; this excludes strategic activities by senior managers acting purely as corporate officers rather than as board members.

name: Organizational age
definition: An organization's age is the number of years elapsed between its founding and the present.

name: Level of diversification
definition: An organization's level of diversification can be conceptualized as the extent to which it is simultaneously active in many distinct businesses.

name: Insider representation
definition: Insiders are board members who are current or former employees of a firm or who are otherwise closely affiliated with the firm; affiliated outsiders are counted as insiders because they may not possess the independence to act independently of a firm's management.

name: Board size
definition: Board size is simply the number of members a board has.

name: Financial performance
definition: The financial performance of organizations; the authors note that many issues influence financial performance, such as competitive intensity and organizational size, and they measured economic profitability relative to the primary industry.

name: Social interactions
authors_terms: ["social interactions", "intensity in social interactions", "intensity in relationships"]
definition: Social interactions are manifestations of the structural dimension of social capital, which describes the mere existence of connections between employees of the organizations.

name: Trust
authors_terms: ["trust", "obligations resulting from common norms and values"]
definition: Trust is a manifestation of the relational dimension of social capital and a governance structure that is based on social relationships between and among individuals (and organizations).

name: Innovation
definition: Innovation refers to the conversion of knowledge into new products, services, or processes to be introduced on the market (or the introduction of significant changes into existing ones); it is defined as new or significant changes in products, processes, or services.

name: Proportion of female managers
authors_terms: ["proportion of female managers", "proportion of women in an organization's management", "percentage of managers in each agency annually who were female", "sex composition of management"]
definition: The percentage of managers in each agency annually who were female; the theoretical range of the variable was from 0 to 1. On average, managers were employed in agencies with 35 percent female managers.

name: New management jobs filled by women
authors_terms: ["number of management jobs created and first filled by women", "number of women's new job titles", "new jobs filled by female managers"]
definition: Counts of the number of managerial jobs created in an advertising agency in a given year that are initially filled by women.

name: New management jobs filled by men
authors_terms: ["number of management jobs created and first filled by men", "number of men's new job titles", "new jobs filled by male managers"]
definition: Counts of the number of managerial jobs created in an advertising agency in a given year that are initially filled by men.

name: Management job creation
authors_terms: ["job creation", "organizational job creation", "number of new job titles", "creation of jobs"]
definition: Organization-level job creation occurs when a new administrative job title representing a distinct amalgamation of tasks appears in the organizational hierarchy. New jobs may be created as employees enter organizations but may also be assigned to incumbents.

name: Foreign subsidiary ownership mode
authors_terms: ["operating mode", "mode choice", "ownership conversion", "joint venture turned wholly owned subsidiary", "continuing joint venture", "wholly owned subsidiary"]
definition: The paper defines a firm as a joint venture when the foreign partner holds between 25 percent and 95 percent of the venture's equity, and a firm in which the foreign partner owns more than 95 percent of the venture's equity as a wholly owned subsidiary. The study compares converted wholly owned subsidiaries with continuing joint ventures.

name: Subsidiary financial performance
definition: We use return on assets (ROA), the most common measure of profitability, as our measure of financial performance. ROA is defined as net income divided by total assets.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: The study uses the U.S. industry-level average R&D intensity for each three-digit SIC industry code in order to create subsamples of relatively high/low levels of intangible assets like technology or brand. The primary reason for using U.S. firms' R&D intensity is to classify industries with exogenous information unaffected by the sample firms' strategic R&D investment decisions.

name: Industry advertising intensity
definition: The study uses the U.S. industry-level average advertising intensity for each three-digit SIC industry code in order to create subsamples of relatively high/low levels of intangible assets like technology or brand. The primary reason for using U.S. firms' advertising intensity is to classify industries with exogenous information unaffected by the sample firms' strategic advertising investment decisions.

name: Level of foreign ownership
definition: We control for the level of foreign ownership by including foreign share, which is the percentage share held by foreign parents, and its squared term. We expect that the likelihood of conversion to a wholly owned subsidiary will have an inverted U-shaped relationship with the level of foreign ownership, as a higher level of foreign ownership would obviate the need for conversion, while a lower level of foreign ownership would make conversion more challenging.

name: Intangible assets
authors_terms: ["intangible assets ratio", "intangible assets", "technology, brands, and trademarks"]
definition: Intangible assets ratio measures the relative importance of a firm's intangible assets, defined as intangible assets divided by total assets. The intangible assets item in a foreign subsidiary's balance sheet is a key indicator of the transfer of intangible assets from multinational parents to foreign subsidiaries.

name: Industry peers' fraud punishment
authors_terms: ["industry peers' fraud punishment", "fraud punishments of industry peers", "punishment of its industry peers for corporate financial fraud"]
definition: Fraud punishment cases levied by the regulatory authorities on the observing firm's industry peers; the authors treat these as modeling cues that 'signal information about consequences of violations to the observing firms in the same industry' and posit that 'an observing firm is less likely to commit financial fraud if the peers in its industry are caught and punished.'

name: Corporate financial fraud commitment
authors_terms: ["observing firm's fraud commitment", "corporate financial fraud", "fraud commitment", "future fraud commitment"]
definition: Corporate financial fraud includes occurrences in which the top management of a listed firm undertakes actions that materially mislead outside investors about the firm's financial information or misappropriate the firm's assets; the dependent variable captures the observing firm's fraud commitment.

name: Prominent firms' fraud punishment
authors_terms: ["prominent firms' fraud punishment", "fraud punishments of prominent firms"]
definition: An environmental cue given by the regulator's punishment of high-prominence firms, that is, 'the regulator's determination and willingness to punish targets that are high in prestige, power, and competencies, which have greater utilitarian value for observers.'

name: Law development
definition: The level of development of the legal institutions, including how well the law is formulated and enforced, which the authors argue substitutes for observational learning: 'the negative effect of industry peers' fraud punishment ... is weakened when the level of law development is higher.'

name: Model-observer status similarity
definition: Model-observer status similarity, that is, the similarity in status of the fraud firm and the observing firm, which 'plays a crucial moderating role in the social learning process' because greater similarity indicates that the experiences of the model are more relevant for the observer.

name: Related diversification
definition: One of the two components of diversification strategy, measured by the entropy measure developed by Palepu (1985). Since total diversification is the sum of unrelated and related components, the authors calculated related diversification (DR) by subtracting unrelated diversification (DU) from total diversification (DT).

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: One of the two components of diversification strategy taken from the entropy measure, calculated in the same fashion as total diversification but considering the sales of business segments in each two-digit SIC code.

name: Technological search scope
definition: Technological search scope refers to the degree to which a focal patent cites prior art from a variety of technological domains. Search scope is a continuum that varies from using technologies from the familiar fields on the one end to using technologies from unfamiliar domains on the other end, so that local search is characterized as narrow or focused, while distant search is broad.

name: Innovation output
definition: The dependent variable, innovation output, represents the degree to which a firm benefits from its R&D activities.

name: Interlocks with successful adopters
definition: Ties to successful adopters are count variables, measured as the total number of interlocks to firms in which subsidiary establishment in China has been clearly successful.

name: Interlocks with unsuccessful adopters
definition: Ties to unsuccessful adopters are count variables, measured as the total number of interlocks to firms in which subsidiary establishment in China has been clearly unsuccessful.

name: Interlocks with nonadopters
definition: We operationalized ties to nonadopters as a count variable of the total number of interlocks with firms that have not established a subsidiary in China.

name: Interlocks with core adopters
authors_terms: ["ties to core adopters", "adopting firms closer to the network core"]
definition: The next independent variable, ties to core adopters, captures the number of adopters that are closer to the core of the network than those to whom they are connected.

name: Subsidiary establishment in China
authors_terms: ["adoption of the strategy", "establishing a subsidiary in China", "expansion into China"]
definition: The dependent variable is the rate of transition from one state to another. In this case, the transition of interest is establishment of a subsidiary in China.

name: Information technology investment
authors_terms: ["IT investment", "industrywide IT investment", "IT intensity", "IT equipment per full-time employee"]
definition: IT investment, broadly defined, includes investments in both computers and telecommunications and in related hardware, software, and services. It is measured as the total value of IT equipment per full-time employee in an industry.

name: Loosely coupled organizational forms
authors_terms: ["loosely coupled organizational forms", "loose coupling", "loosely coupled relationships"]
definition: We view contingent workers and alliances to be two distinct means by which a firm can access expertise from outside of its normal boundaries. Firms can specialize in a few key activities while accessing other activities through relationships with outside parties.

name: Industry standards
definition: Industry standards are one mechanism that reduces the level of asset specificity between contracting partners. Standards may emerge through ad hoc market mechanisms (such as voluntarily adopted uniform employment policies and shared groupware platforms) or may be formally negotiated by industry trade associations or standards organizations.

name: Technological change
definition: Technological change is the speed in which the underlying technology supporting the value being offered by an industry varies.

name: Input diversity
authors_terms: ["input diversity", "diversity of inputs", "diversity in terms of inputs"]
definition: Industries vary in the general complexity of production. In some industries, production entails combining a wide range of different inputs; other industries have much simpler production processes.

name: Entrepreneurship program participation
authors_terms: ["program participation", "participation in the CES or STVP", "entrepreneurship training", "entrepreneurship education", "entrepreneurship programs"]
definition: Participation in Stanford University's two entrepreneurship initiatives, the Center for Entrepreneurial Studies (CES) at the Business School and the Stanford Technology Ventures Program (STVP) at the Engineering School, which offer courses and experiential learning in entrepreneurship.

name: Entrepreneurship rate
definition: The rate at which alumni become entrepreneurs. The authors measure entrepreneurship as the founding of any type of organization, for-profit or non-profit.

name: Startup performance
authors_terms: ["startup performance", "performance of the first startup", "firm performance", "quality of entrepreneurship"]
definition: The characteristics and performance of the entrepreneur's first startup after graduation, which the authors examine in terms of the time to first startup, probability of failure, survival as a private entity, exit through an IPO or M&A, number of employees, revenue, and patenting.

name: Target-to-acquirer resource transfer
authors_terms: ["transfer of the target's resources to the acquirer", "resource transfer from target to acquirer"]
definition: We use postacquisition resource transfer as a proxy for the resource contribution of the target and the acquirer. Resource transfer is defined as the extent to which merging firms use the other business's resources following the acquisition.

name: Acquirer-to-target resource transfer
authors_terms: ["transfer of the acquirer's resources to the target", "resource transfer from acquirer to target"]
definition: We use postacquisition resource transfer as a proxy for the resource contribution of the target and the acquirer. Resource transfer is defined as the extent to which merging firms use the other business's resources following the acquisition.

name: Bilateral resource transfer
authors_terms: ["bilateral resource transfer", "joint transfer of the acquirer's resources to the target and of the target's resources to the acquirer"]
definition: Bilateral resource transfer (to and from the target). Synergy is generated out of the joint participation of both parties.

name: Acquirer abnormal returns
definition: CAR i,k,l represents the cumulative abnormal return for the acquirer i, during the period k, l. The daily excess return of firm i is estimated using the market model.

name: Focus on core function
authors_terms: ["focus on core function", "focus on the core function"]
definition: Focus on core function captures the extent to which a firm's new app focuses on its core function relative to peripheral functions.

name: Peripheral function overlap
authors_terms: ["peripheral function overlap", "overlap in peripheral functions with successful products"]
definition: Peripheral function overlap captures the extent to which a firm's new app differentiates from or imitates existing successful apps sharing the same core function.

name: Overall customer dissatisfaction
definition: Overall customer dissatisfaction reflects the extent to which other existing products fall short of customer expectations. Higher dissatisfaction signals that current products do not adequately address customers' needs and preferences, indicating unmet market demand.

name: Customer evaluation heterogeneity
definition: Customer evaluation heterogeneity captures the extent to which customers agree or disagree about the value of other existing products. High heterogeneity suggests that existing products only satisfy a subset of the market and fail to appeal broadly.

name: Non-compete enforcement
definition: Non-competition contractual agreements (hereafter, non-competes) prevent employees from joining a competitor or forming a new company, and they significantly limit outbound mobility to competitors.

name: Breakthrough inventions
definition: Breakthroughs are extremely valuable inventions; greater riskiness in the outcome distribution fattens the right-hand tail of inventions' value distributions, increasing the likelihood of breakthroughs.

name: Invention failures
definition: Greater riskiness implies an increase in the mass of both tails of the distribution, so that a greater probability of breakthrough outliers is accompanied by a greater probability of dead ends and failures.

name: New technological areas
authors_terms: ["new technological areas", "novel technological areas", "new technological domain", "invention in new technological areas"]
definition: Firms can choose whether to undertake projects closely related to their preexisting knowledge base or pursue projects distant from their current technological know-how; the exploration of novel technological competences is usually riskier than the exploitation of existing know-how.

name: Encompassing technological change
definition: Encompassing changes involve radical alteration of core activities, regardless of the degree to which the changes also affect complementary activities.

name: Complementary technological change
definition: Complementary changes involve radical alteration of complementary activities that do not also involve radical alteration of core activities.

name: Incremental technological change
definition: Incremental changes involve incremental adjustments to core or complementary activities.

name: Equity-based interorganizational relationships
definition: External relationships include equity-based associations, such as joint ventures and direct investments. Equity-based relationships allow greater control of technology acquisition than do nonequity approaches, but also require longer-term financial and managerial commitment to the other party.

name: Nonequity interorganizational relationships
definition: External relationships include nonequity associations, such as technology licensing, technology exchanges, testing agreements, technology sharing agreements, and research contracts.

name: Internal R&D
definition: Internal R&D offers the potential to protect existing competencies and to develop new competencies within a business organization. For reasons stemming from both cost and difficulty, internal R&D is likely to be most effective when the new capabilities being developed relate to the organization's existing set of capabilities.

name: Competence-creating subsidiary mandate
definition: The competence-creating mandate is defined by the output responsibilities of the subsidiary, and so the mandate is measured independently of the R&D function. The authors distinguish subsidiaries whose functional scope includes product development or international market development from those limited to sales and service, assembly or manufacturing.

name: Subsidiary R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D/sales ratio", "level of R&D expenditure", "quantitative level of subsidiary R&D"]
definition: The knowledge generation associated with R&D is a bi-dimensional process, and what the authors assess is the quantitative level of subsidiary R&D. The level of R&D expenditure, and hence the R&D/sales ratio, is determined by locational, subsidiary-level and MNE group-level characteristics, with the binary subsidiary mandate variable providing an additive difference.

name: Locational quality
authors_terms: ["locational quality", "better-quality locations", "location in an area covered by government investment incentives", "Regional Selective Assistance (RSA)", "Assisted Areas", "supply-related development characteristics"]
definition: The characteristics and development potential of the location in which the subsidiary is sited, notably a good local infrastructure, a science base and a more skilled workforce. In the United Kingdom, government investment incentive programs provide an inverse measure of overall locational quality, since they are made available to firms locating in areas with a combination of low labor skills and high unemployment, poor infrastructure, and many other drawbacks.

name: Local demand
definition: The level of local sales (demand) in the location where the subsidiary is sited. The authors argue that the higher the level of local sales (demand) in a location, the more the incentive to undertake process improvements, as well as to differentiate output to bolster margins.

name: Demand variability
authors_terms: ["variability of demand", "variability in local demand", "fluctuations in demand", "variance of demand"]
definition: Substantial fluctuations in demand in a location, associated with higher variance in a subsidiary's rate of return, and so presenting a greater demand-side financial risk to the MNE.

name: Subsidiary strategic independence
authors_terms: ["strategic independence", "subsidiary strategic independence", "subsidiary autonomy", "degree of subsidiary autonomy"]
definition: The extent of the subsidiary's strategic independence from the rest of the MNE, emphasized in the subsidiary-level literature as the basis for forming favorable external network linkages in its own local environment. What matters is not strategic independence per se but the manner in which it is used by the subsidiary in the context of competence-creating mandates.

name: Subsidiary acquisition
authors_terms: ["being part of an acquired group", "acquired subsidiaries", "acquisition", "subsidiaries that were part of the acquired group"]
definition: Whether the subsidiary was part of a group that has been acquired by its current MNE group, as opposed to having been established within it. The authors argue that acquired subsidiaries conducting standard competence-exploiting R&D tasks replicated in the acquiring group are in a more vulnerable position, while acquired subsidiaries with competence-creating mandates are likelier to make a novel contribution and to retain resources for local R&D.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["Diversified", "product or business diversification", "diversification away from the main lines of business activity", "new line of business (LOB)"]
definition: The degree of product or business diversification required of the subsidiary, in particular whether it operates outside of the parent MNE's main line of business. Subsidiaries with competence-creating mandates that have to contend with a new line of business find themselves more tightly resource-constrained and have fewer resources available for the R&D function.

name: Parent MNE home country
authors_terms: ["U.S. parent", "Japanese parent", "nationality of ownership of the group", "home country dummy variables"]
definition: The nationality of ownership of the MNE group, which regulates the proportion of subsidiaries able to earn a competence-creating mandate because it governs the priority accorded to the technology sourcing motive in the group's international investment strategy. Groups originating from countries whose outward investment is of more recent vintage are likelier to assign a higher priority to technology sourcing.

name: Perceived intensity of state control
authors_terms: ["intensity of perceived control", "perceived intensity of state control", "state control", "managerial autonomy", "autonomy"]
definition: The variable to be explained - intensity of perceived control (i.e., the reverse of autonomy) - is measured on certain distinct dimensions related to strategic business-boundary issues, pricing decisions, and resource acquisition and mobilisation decisions.

name: Resource dependence on the state
authors_terms: ["resource dependence on the state", "dependence on the state for resources", "financial dependence", "resource dependence"]
definition: The managers of SOEs depend on the state for certain essential resources, i.e., financial resources, markets (e.g., sales to public sector), appointments. The state also receives resources from SOEs, but the exchange is asymmetric in terms of essentiality and substitutability of resources.

name: Political visibility
definition: The "political visibility" of an SOE can be defined as the range of organised groups or the general public directly affected by the decisions and performance of the SOE.

name: Enterprise size
definition: Large SOEs manage significant amounts of resources which affect many sectors of economic activity and a wide range of social or industrial interest groups. On the other hand, size is a source of power for an enterprise and can be used to expand its autonomy.

name: SOE performance
definition: Performance as a multidimensional concept is related to both operations efficiency and innovativeness. Good performance means more effort to achieve efficient utilisation of resources and decisions on the basis of economic and commercial, business-like criteria, while aspects of performance related to innovativeness and adaptability are particularly important for SOEs.

name: Intensity of competition
authors_terms: ["perceived intensity of competition", "intensity of domestic competition", "market competition", "competition"]
definition: SOEs which operate in competitive environments are expected to have more autonomy, in comparison to those not exposed in competition, because market competition forces them to apply commercial and economic criteria in decision making and favours the development of autonomy strategies.

name: Environmental unpredictability
definition: Another related dimension of the environment is its unpredictability or volatility; a high degree of environmental change and unpredictability would require a high volume of information for decision making. In the tests a measure of demand unpredictability was used, as perceived by SOE managers themselves.

name: Participation in international markets
authors_terms: ["participation in international markets", "internationalisation of its operations", "exposure to international competition", "operations abroad"]
definition: The authors refer to a variable of participation in international markets, i.e., SOEs involved in exports and operations abroad, which is contrasted with enterprises not selling in foreign markets or involved only through noncompetitive trade agreements.

name: International tribunal ruling outcome
authors_terms: ["legal ruling by an independent international tribunal", "tribunal ruling", "ISDS ruling", "ruling in favor of the state", "ruling against the state", "state-win", "state-loss", "neutral"]
definition: A legal ruling by an independent international arbitration tribunal adjudicating an investment dispute between a foreign firm and a sovereign state. A tribunal can decide in favor of the state (state-win), in favor of the investor (state-loss), or in favor of neither party (neutral).

name: Assessment of the domestic institutional environment
authors_terms: ["perception of the domestic institutional environment", "assessment of the institutional environment", "firms' assessment of courts/licensing/tax administration as a severe obstacle", "domestic firms' perception of their domestic investment climate"]
definition: A country's institutional environment encompasses a variety of administrative, regulative and legislative factors. The authors focus on three characteristics that are important constituents of the institutional environment and are critical to firms' operations: courts, licensing, and tax administration.

name: Collective political action
definition: Joining the ACFIC as a deputy represents a collective political action for private entrepreneurs because it is an association; as an entity, the association, and not its individual members, takes actions on behalf of all of its members.

name: Private political action
definition: Joining either the Congress or the Conference as a deputy represents a type of private political action for private entrepreneurs because deputies act individually to benefit their own interests.

name: Infrastructure development
authors_terms: ["quality of the physical and institutional infrastructure", "less-developed infrastructure", "institutional infrastructure", "physical infrastructure", "market-supporting institutions"]
definition: The countries with weak market-supporting institutions are also likely to be less economically developed and to possess insufficient or lower-quality infrastructure. Deficiencies in infrastructure refer to both shortages of 'hard' physical infrastructure and underdeveloped institutional infrastructure, such as weak checks and balances on regulatory power.

name: State power to redistribute resources
authors_terms: ["government's discretion in redistributing key economic resources", "redistribution opportunities", "the state has greater power to allocate resources", "constraints on redistribution"]
definition: Political decisions and public policies involving the redistribution of resources and wealth often represent 'zero-sum' games in which one firm's gain is another firm's loss. If the state has substantial control over a pool of essential economic resources, such as bank credit, then allocating more resources to one firm can only be accomplished by decreasing the resources allocated to other firms.

name: Alternative access to state actors
authors_terms: ["alternative access to state actors", "other channels to access state actors", "alternative methods of accessing state actors"]
definition: Firms with public ownership may have a greater opportunity to become acquainted with politicians and regulators, and firms that have formed political connections with key state actors through other means may also have better chances of achieving success when undertaking private political actions.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is shown to indicate an individual firm's valuation of collective goods, and larger firms are found to be more capable of overcoming the free-rider problem. A firm is designated as a 'larger firm' if its number of employees or level of sales exceeds the median value; otherwise, the firm is designated as a 'smaller firm.'

name: Corporate social performance
definition: CSP measures the level of firm engagement in a number of social, ethical, and legal issues and is a multidimensional concept covering firm response to a wide range of stakeholder demands related to the firm's operation. CSP is used as a measure of firm response to stakeholder demands and social issues.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Firms pursuing unrelated diversification have a presence across industries that are widely different, and as a result, they face more diverging stakeholder demands and social issues than firms pursuing related diversification.

name: Related diversification
definition: Related diversifiers face much more coherent stakeholder demands, and therefore remain focused on a relatively narrow range of social concerns; for example, the Coca-Cola Company, a firm pursuing related diversification, faces similar demands from environmental activist groups across its carbonated beverage, sports drink, and bottled water markets.

name: International diversification
definition: International diversification refers to a firm's expansion beyond its domestic market into other regions or countries.

name: Focus on short-term profit
authors_terms: ["firm focus on short-term profit", "focus on short-term profit maximization", "corporate-level, short-term profit orientation"]
definition: When a diversified firm has a strong focus on short-term profit maximization, it may reduce investment in items that do not immediately contribute to short-term profit. Since it is impossible to directly measure the level of a firm's focus on short-term profit maximization, the author relied on an actual short-term profit measure (return-on-equity) as a proxy of this corporate-level, short-term profit orientation.

name: Incentive compensation
authors_terms: ["incentive compensation", "incentive-based compensation", "the portion of an executive's total compensation that is linked to stock market performance"]
definition: The variable, incentive-based component of an executive's compensation package, which is the portion of total compensation that is linked to stock market performance. Following Jensen and Murphy (1990), incentive compensation is calculated as the difference between an executive's total compensation and the sum of his salary and bonus.

name: Stock market performance
definition: The stock market performance of the firm a manager oversees, to which his incentive-based pay is set to increase in proportion; incentive alignment is the correlation between incentive compensation and stock market performance.

name: Corporate spinoff
definition: A type of divestiture in which a 'parent firm' distributes shares in one of its businesses pro-rata to its shareholders, resulting in the creation of an independent, publicly-traded 'spinoff firm.'

name: Divisional managers to spinoff firm
authors_terms: ["Divisional Managers to Spinoff Firm", "one or more divisional managers of the spun-off subsidiary become spinoff firm managers"]
definition: The situation in which one or more divisional managers of the spun-off subsidiary become top managers of the spinoff firm after the deal.

name: Cross-subsidization
authors_terms: ["Cross-Subsidization", "the spun-off subsidiary performs better than the remaining businesses in its parent firm"]
definition: The practice whereby multi-business firms use the cash flows generated by their better-performing divisions to subsidize their worse-performing divisions, so that the spun-off division performs better than the parent firm's remaining businesses.

name: Relatedness of the spun-off subsidiary
authors_terms: ["Unrelated", "unrelated (rather than related) to the parent firm's primary operations", "relatedness"]
definition: Whether the spun-off subsidiary is unrelated to, rather than related to, the parent firm's primary operations; the spinoff is classified as unrelated when a division does not share a three-digit SIC code with its parent firm.

name: Corporate governance quality
authors_terms: ["governance quality", "quality of corporate governance", "quality of governance", "G-Index"]
definition: The quality of corporate governance within a firm, captured by Gompers et al.'s (2003) index of governance quality, in which higher values reflect worse corporate governance.

name: Stock market reaction to spinoffs
authors_terms: ["CAR", "cumulative abnormal returns", "the stock market's reaction to spinoff announcements", "shareholder value created by these deals"]
definition: The cumulative abnormal returns to spinoff announcements, generated using an event study that measures the shareholder value created by these deals.

name: Post-spinoff change in parent firm compensation
authors_terms: ["the post-spinoff change in compensation", "change in the ratio of parent firm CEO compensation to market capitalization", "the post-spinoff pay increase enjoyed by parent firm managers"]
definition: The change in parent firm managers' compensation following the completion of a spinoff, measured as the change in the ratio of parent firm CEO (and mean executive) compensation to market capitalization between the effective year of the spinoff and the year thereafter.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: The scope of the diversification strategies pursued by the organization, examined in terms of related, unrelated, and total diversification.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Diversification into product domains that are unrelated to the firm's existing businesses; the authors measure it with an entropy index (DU-E) computed from product-wise sales data.

name: Related diversification
definition: Diversification into product domains related to the firm's existing businesses; the authors measure it with an entropy index (DR-E) computed from product-wise sales data.

name: Total diversification
definition: The overall level of product diversification of the firm; the authors measure it with an entropy index (DT-E) computed from product-wise sales data.

name: Government shareholding
authors_terms: ["government shareholding", "proportion of organizational shareholding controlled by government agencies", "governmental agencies", "GOVT%"]
definition: The proportion of shares held by governmental agencies, a class of investor the authors categorize as pressure-indeterminate.

name: For-profit financial institution shareholding
definition: The proportion of ownership represented by for-profit financial institutions, characterized by the authors as pressure-resistant investors that actively monitor the firms they invest in.

name: Mutual fund shareholding
definition: The proportion of ownership controlled by mutual fund companies, which the authors classify as pressure-resistant investors driven by strong wealth maximization motives.

name: Foreign investor shareholding
definition: The proportion of shares held by foreign investors, primarily corporate bodies that are joint venture partners or technology collaborators, largely pressure-resistant in the authors' classification.

name: Bank shareholding
authors_terms: ["banks and banking companies (BNKING%)", "banks and insurance companies"]
definition: The proportion of shares held by banks and banking companies, classified by the authors as pressure-sensitive investors that depend on the firms they invest in for interest and fee income.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: We measured multi-industry overlaps across groups using a firm-in-market level ''sales-at-risk'' operationalization of multimarket contact and hence allowed the extent and influence of multimarket contact to vary by group and by market. Feinberg's (1985) sales-at-risk measure calculates the percentage of the sales of the focal group ''at risk'' of being exposed to multimarket rivals (more explicitly, the percentage of sales that comes from markets in which the group faces multimarket rivals).

name: Subsidiary discretion in investment decisions
authors_terms: ["subsidiary discretion in investment decisions", "latitude of action", "discretion in investment decisions"]
definition: Following Shen and Cho (2005; see also Hambrick and Finkelstein, 1987; Finkelstein, Hambrick, and Cannella, 2008), we focus on two principal dimensions of managerial discretion: latitude of action and latitude of objectives. Latitude of action refers to the range of strategic options managers have in pursuing outcomes demanded by stakeholders.

name: Subsidiary discretion in setting objectives
authors_terms: ["subsidiary discretion in setting its objectives", "latitude of objectives", "discretion in setting objectives"]
definition: The latitude of objectives in the context of headquarters-subsidiary relationships refers to the freedom subsidiaries have to pursue the objectives that are optimal for them rather than those desired by their parent firm.

name: Inflow of financial resources
authors_terms: ["inflow of financial resources", "intrafirm resource flows", "intrafirm financial resource flows", "financial resource inflows"]
definition: Following Billett and Mauer (2003) and Berger and Hann (2003), we measured whether a subsidiary received financial resources from its group (as opposed to operating only with its own available funds) by its capital expenditure in a given year in excess of its internally generated cash flows. Expenditures above internally generated cash flows demonstrate inflow of financial resources to a subsidiary because these expenditures could not have been made without additional funds.

name: Relative market share
definition: We first controlled for relative market share, which we measured by the log of the ratio of total sales of the group in the focal subsidiary's industry to the sales of the leading rival in that industry.

name: Industry growth
definition: Following Dess and Beard (1984), we calculated these variables from a log-linear growth model using corresponding industry production data from industry input-output tables for seven previous years. The slope of the linear growth model corresponds to the average annual percentage change in industry size and is our measure of industry growth.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: Competitive behavior is considered to be aggressive when it attracts customers away from competitors by offering them more value for their money. We focused on growth as the indicator of a subsidiary's competitive aggressiveness because growth, especially market share gains achieved at the expense of rivals, is inherently competitive.

name: Knowledge about other technologies in a domain
authors_terms: ["knowledge about other technologies", "knowledge about different technologies", "top medical publications about other mechanisms", "knowledge about other mechanisms"]
definition: Knowledge about other technologies that exist in the same domain of the focal innovation provides the context in which its regulatory review takes place, and the more knowledge there is about other technologies in the domain of an innovation, the more likely that regulatory agencies will bring that knowledge to shed light on its evaluation and accordingly confront greater diversity of evaluation criteria. The greater the amount of knowledge about other technologies in a domain that is available to regulatory agencies, the greater the chances that the associated understandings will bring to the attention of regulators issues that, although relevant to other technologies, might not be directly applicable to the focal innovation.

name: Regulatory review time
definition: The regulatory review time comprises the time elapsed between the submission of a new drug application (NDA) and its FDA approval. In line with prior empirical studies of FDA review times, the dependent variable captures the number of months elapsed between the submission of an NDA and its FDA approval.

name: Recent introduction of new technologies in a domain
authors_terms: ["the recent introduction of new technologies", "recent new mechanisms", "new mechanisms"]
definition: The more frequently that regulatory agencies confront the task of reviewing an innovation that draws on a new technology, the more likely that, in sifting through a greater diversity of considerations and sorting out evaluation incongruities, they become aware of limitations associated with such transfer of learning. The more that regulatory agencies review innovations based on a new technology and ponder about conflicting interpretations associated with different technologies, the more that they become aware of distinctions that these different technologies entail, which reduces evaluation incongruities in the review of subsequent innovations.

name: CEO stock options
authors_terms: ["CEO stock options", "value of a CEO's stock options", "average annual CEO stock options"]
definition: The value of stock option grants to a firm's CEO, measured as the average annual value of stock option grants made during the period 1996-99 and computed using the Black-Scholes methodology applied to individual stock option grants.

name: Fraudulent financial reporting
authors_terms: ["fraudulent financial reporting", "restatement under pressure", "intentional financial misreporting"]
definition: Intentional financial misreporting that artificially inflated a firm's results, operationalized as a downward restatement of financial results made under pressure from federal or state regulatory agencies.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality occurs when a single individual serves as both the CEO of a company and the chair of its board of directors.

name: Board of director stock options
authors_terms: ["board stock options", "board of director stock options", "equity pay for directors"]
definition: Stock option compensation received by members of a firm's board of directors, which may either align directors' interests with shareholders or compromise the board's monitoring function.

name: Relational embeddedness
definition: Exchange relationships that develop through a history of interactions that create value, as when firms benefit from familiarity, trust, or feelings of solidarity with exchange partners.

name: Relational uncertainty
definition: The nonstricken partner's doubts regarding the trustworthiness and commitment of the stricken partner and apprehension regarding current and future state of the relationship.

name: Partner commitment
authors_terms: ["partner commitment", "commitment to the transgressor", "innocent partner commitment"]
definition: The amount in dollars contributed by the firm to the focal politician's electoral campaign in each election cycle.

name: Hedging with a competitor
definition: Hedging provides a means to guard against potential loss by pursuing new alternatives without foregoing all of the upsides of prior commitments; in this context it is buying from or selling to an existing exchange partner's direct competitor.

name: Boomerang
definition: To restart an ended relationship after a temporal separation.

name: Ending commitment
definition: The choice to end commitments to a transgressing exchange partner after misconduct, measured as whether the firm did not contribute to the misconduct politician in the misconduct election cycle after having given to that candidate in the prior election.

name: CEO return
definition: CEO return is the degree to which a CEO's firm-based wealth changes in a given year (including fluctuations in accumulated stock and option holdings as well as annual cash compensation) expressed as a percentage of beginning wealth.

name: Shareholder return
definition: Shareholder return was calculated as the fiscal year return to shareholders, in percentage terms, including stock price appreciation and monthly dividend reinvestment.

name: CEO-shareholder financial alignment
definition: Financial alignment is the degree to which an agent's economic rewards covary with those of owners; the authors conceptualize and operationalize it as the empirical relationship between CEO return and shareholder return.

name: Future shareholder return
definition: Future shareholder return for period t was the shareholder return over the periods t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3.

name: Average future earnings
authors_terms: ["firm average future earnings", "future earnings", "average future earnings"]
definition: Future earnings for period t were the average earnings over the periods t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3, calculated as total net income before extraordinary items divided by 3.

name: CEO total firm-specific wealth
definition: The level of CEO firm-specific wealth was computed as the aggregate value at time t of a CEO's in-the-money options portfolio, restricted stock portfolio, and other equity portfolio, as well as net proceeds accumulated throughout the fiscal year from exercises and sales in those portfolios.

name: CEO return/shareholder return dollar ratio
authors_terms: ["CEO return/shareholder return dollar ratio", "CEO share", "dollar ratio"]
definition: This ratio was created by dividing the dollar value of a CEO's one-year return by the dollar value of one-year total shareholder return; it represents the relative changes in wealth level for the CEO relative to all shareholders and is interpretable in percentage terms.

name: Technological relatedness
authors_terms: ["technological relatedness", "interindustry technological relatedness", "technical relationship between two industries", "relatedness of activities"]
definition: Business units within a corporation are related to the extent they share some activity, resource, or set of skills; because technologies are specific to industries, diversification patterns should reflect interindustry technological relatedness.

name: National institutional configuration
authors_terms: ["configurations of national institutions", "institutional environment", "country-specific institutions", "institutions of corporate governance and control"]
definition: A configuration of national institutions of corporate governance and control, for example financial institutions (more or less developed capital markets), form of government intervention (dirigiste or laissez faire), corporate governance (e.g., the role of labor), and ownership (e.g., the prevalence of institutional investors).

name: Similarity of interindustry diversification patterns
authors_terms: ["similarity in the patterns of interindustry diversification", "common pattern of diversification across countries", "convergence in diversification patterns"]
definition: The extent to which the pattern of interindustry diversification - the pairs of industries linked through corporate diversification - is the same across countries; the technological hypothesis predicts such patterns should be similar, the institutional hypothesis that they should be dissimilar.

name: Interindustry diversification pattern
authors_terms: ["patterns of interindustry diversification", "interindustry pattern of diversification", "matrix of diversification across industries"]
definition: The pattern of diversification across industries within a country, that is, which originating industries diversify into which target industries; it is given by the interaction between originating and target industries after controlling for their expansiveness and attractiveness.

name: Industry expansiveness
definition: The contribution of an originating industry to diversification events, that is, the industry's tendency to diversify out into other industries.

name: Industry attractiveness
definition: The tendency of an industry to be a target for diversification, that is, the industry's tendency to attract entrants from other industries.

name: Knowledge specialization
definition: Specialists have experience and deep expertise in a narrowly defined domain of knowledge, while generalists tend to have a large amount of experience but spread across multiple related or unrelated knowledge domains. Conceptually, generalists and specialists constitute two ends of a continuum.

name: Creative performance
definition: The authors follow a literature using scientific publications to measure scientists' creative output, and use three variables to capture both the quantity and the quality of their output.

name: Pace of change in a knowledge domain
authors_terms: ["pace of change", "pace at which new knowledge components become available", "fast-paced knowledge domain", "slow-paced knowledge domain", "Soviet impact"]
definition: A specific characteristic of a knowledge domain, namely the pace at which new knowledge components become available in the domain, which varies substantially across knowledge domains and over time.

name: Collaboration
authors_terms: ["collaboration", "collaboration rate", "number of collaborators", "number of unique collaborators"]
definition: Access to complementary collaborators is an important and limited resource in academia, and the authors examine changes in the collaboration patterns of specialists and generalists as a mechanism reflecting competition for complementary resources.

name: Top management team nationality diversity
definition: A timely, yet under-researched aspect of TMT composition that captures the variety in institutionally embedded experiences of the team members. Nationality is a superordinate construct that encompasses the influences of both formal and informal institutionally embedded experiences on executive orientation and decision making.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable firm performance is operationalized as return on assets (ROA) at the end of each calendar year.

name: Top management team tenure
definition: TMT tenure is measured as the median of the tenures of all TMT members.

name: Firm internationalization
definition: Internationalization is the average of (1) foreign sales to total sales, (2) foreign assets to total assets, and (3) geographic dispersion of foreign sales.

name: Industry munificence
definition: Munificence refers to the extent to which the environment can support sustained growth.

name: Growth along the product dimension
authors_terms: ["growth along the product dimension", "product diversification", "ΔPD", "growth in noncore businesses"]
definition: The extent of growth along the product dimension: the amount of growth undertaken by the firm in noncore businesses over the 1993-1997 period. The measure captures entry into new markets as well as increasing presence in existing noncore businesses.

name: Growth along the international dimension
authors_terms: ["growth along the international dimension", "international diversification", "ΔID", "growth in foreign markets"]
definition: The extent of growth along the international dimension: the amount of growth undertaken by the firm in foreign markets over the 1993-1997 period. The measure captures entry into new markets as well as increasing presence in existing foreign markets.

name: Upstream vertical alliance activity
authors_terms: ["upstream vertical alliance (UVA) activity", "UVA", "upstream strategic alliance", "vertical alliance activity with suppliers"]
definition: A UVA is a continuing long-term relationship among parties in a supply chain. The relationship involves expected mutual benefits based on collaboration and significant contributions by parties of capital and knowledge.

name: SME performance
definition: The main outcome variables measure a focal firm's market share, return on assets (ROA), product quality, competitive position, customer service, and overall performance.

name: Self-selection characteristics
authors_terms: ["self-selection characteristics", "SME characteristics", "characteristics that influence the choice to engage in alliance activity"]
definition: The characteristics can be categorized into two main types: those that make an SME capable of engaging in alliance activity (e.g., slack resources); and those that increase the SME's desire to engage in UVAs (e.g., greater belief in mutual benefits).

name: Perceptions of UVA benefits
authors_terms: ["SME perceptions of UVA benefits", "perceived effect variables", "Perception"]
definition: These variables consist of the SME manager's perceptions of how well the UVA is helping with that SME's market share, profitability, product quality, costs, and customer service. The authors note that these are perceptions of how an activity affects performance rather than perceptions of performance.

name: Multinational corporation
definition: The MNC is viewed as an international network that creates, accesses, integrates, and applies knowledge in multiple locations, and it is the institutional arrangement whose cross-border knowledge-building performance is compared with alliances and markets.

name: Strategic alliance
definition: Alliances are the 'constellations of agreements characterized by the commitment of two or more firms to reach common goals entailing the pooling of their resources and activities' (Teece 1992, p. 19), and include joint ventures, equity arrangements, and marketing, design and fabrication agreements.

name: Market contract
definition: Markets are arms-length contracting between independent firms, in particular technology licensing agreements, which are the arrangement against which firms and alliances are compared.

name: Cross-border knowledge building
authors_terms: ["knowledge building", "cross-border knowledge building", "knowledge transfer and development", "knowledge creation"]
definition: Knowledge building refers to the joint processes of knowledge transfer and knowledge development, where managing knowledge involves not only its transfer but also its development through the combination of the transferred knowledge with the recipient's existing knowledge.

name: Successor origin
authors_terms: ["successor origin", "origin of the incoming chair", "outside vs. inside successors"]
definition: The origin of the incoming chair, distinguished as a family successor, a nonfamily inside successor, or an outside successor. A family successor is related to the controlling family through marriage or family ties; a nonfamily inside successor is a nonfamily executive who was currently an officer or a director of the focal firm; an outside successor was not an employee of the focal firm (or, for group members, of other affiliates in the same group).

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is captured by a firm's profitability, measured as return on assets (ROA) because ROA is a well-understood and widely used accounting measure of operational performance. The authors focus on the performance effect of succession on a firm's profitability rather than on market valuation.

name: Family ownership
definition: The percentage of shares owned by the controlling family, where the controlling family refers to the family with the largest shareholding in a firm's ownership structure. Family members own company shares either directly or through other public and private firms that are de facto under their control.

name: Business group affiliation
definition: Business groups are sets of legally independent firms bound together by multiple and stable interfirm ties ranging from formal economic arrangements such as equity crossholdings and interlocking directorates to informal social links based on family and friendship. Group membership was coded 1 only if a firm was a member of the top 100 business groups.

name: High technology industry
definition: Industries in which the institutional logic imported from Silicon Valley, valuing innovation, achievement and professional management, prevails; in this study high tech industries are defined as the electronic and computer sectors.

name: Foreign institutional ownership
definition: The percentage of shares owned by foreign institutional investors, most of whom are based in the United States or the United Kingdom and follow the institutional logic of shareholder-based governance.

name: Dual strategy
authors_terms: ["dual strategies", "high product diversity and high foreign sales", "high foreign sales and high product diversity"]
definition: The pursuit of the dual strategies of high product diversity and high foreign sales, which the authors say creates organizational problems. In this study it describes the type of firm sampled: those high in both diversity and dependence on foreign sales relative to other large U.S. multinationals.

name: Product diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity", "product diversity", "number of two digit SIC codes", "number of two digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes of operations"]
definition: The range of products a firm operates in, measured by the number of two digit Standard Industrial Classification codes of operations; seven or more SICs was the dividing point for high diversity.

name: Foreign sales dependence
authors_terms: ["foreign dependence", "foreign sales dependence", "dependence on foreign sales", "foreign sales as a percentage of total sales"]
definition: The extent to which a firm depends on foreign sales, measured as foreign sales as a percentage of total sales. Twenty per cent or more foreign sales was the dividing point for high foreign sales dependence.

name: Worldwide functional structure
definition: In a world-wide functional structure, top-level line executives have world-wide responsibility for separate functions, e.g. for manufacturing, sales, engineering.

name: Matrix structure
definition: The defining characteristic of a matrix organization is the simultaneous reporting by middle-level line executives to two or more bosses who do not themselves have exclusive line authority.

name: Global product structure
definition: In a world-wide product organization, top-level line executives are responsible for one or more worldwide businesses.

name: International division structure
definition: In an international division form of organization, two kinds of line executives report to the chief operating officer. All but one of these are managers of domestic activities, whereas the remaining executive is in charge of all the company's foreign business.

name: Area structure
definition: Executives reporting to the chief operating officer in an area organization are responsible for all company businesses within specific geographic regions of the world.

name: Research intensity
authors_terms: ["research intensity", "research and development as a percentage of sales", "R&D expenditures as a percentage of sales"]
definition: The authors' proxy of research intensity, measured by research and development as a percentage of sales.

name: Diversification mode
definition: Whether a firm has diversified into unrelated businesses primarily by acquisition or merger (conglomerate) rather than through internal development into related businesses (diversified non-conglomerate).

name: Examiner leniency
authors_terms: ["examiner leniency", "leniency", "examiner 'leniency'", "an examiner's prior decisions (past approval rate)"]
definition: An examiner's prior decisions (past approval rate), what has been termed as examiner 'leniency,' is a strong predictor of patent approval. Our main variable, examiner leniency, is calculated by taking the percentage of applications the examiner approved before the submission of the focal patent application.

name: Citation inclusion in the original IDS
authors_terms: ["citation is in the original IDS", "whether a particular citation was added by the firm in the original IDS or in subsequent IDS", "timing of citations", "strategic timing of citations"]
definition: Our dependent variable is whether a particular citation was added by the firm in the original IDS or in subsequent IDS. Since our argument is that firms knowingly delayed a citation for later in the process, we only look at citations that the firm already knew about.

name: Patent thickets
definition: Firms facing patent thickets - i.e., multiple patents owned by different firms. The firms that will benefit the most are those facing patent thickets - that is, large numbers of patents with overlapping claims owned by multiple players.

name: Strategic-stakes technologies
authors_terms: ["high strategic stakes technologies", "strategic stakes", "high strategic-stakes technologies"]
definition: Firms developing high 'strategic stakes' technologies - i.e., technologies that are central to the firm. Those developing high strategic stakes technologies - that is, central to the firm's innovation strategy.

name: Field litigiousness
authors_terms: ["field litigiousness", "level of litigation in a given field", "litigiousness"]
definition: The risk that a patent will be challenged and re-examined in court is not homogeneous across technological fields; while in certain fields property rights are frequently challenged and patent litigation is customary, there are other fields where this rarely happens, that is, certain fields are comparatively more litigious than others.

name: Star scientists
definition: In the pharmaceutical industry, star scientists provide critical connectivity to universities and other sources of upstream knowledge. Star scientists provide an incumbent firm with access to upstream knowledge not only through their own research but also by being part of a broader scientific community.

name: Upstream alliances
definition: Firms can enter into upstream alliances for the purpose of exploring for new opportunities. Upstream alliances tend to be primarily focused on generating new basic knowledge and are usually undertaken with universities and other research institutions.

name: Downstream alliances
definition: Downstream alliances are undertaken to exploit an existing capability and are often focused on generating knowledge that is more applied in nature (i.e., focused on leveraging production and marketing activities).

name: Innovative performance
definition: We view new product development as a process of discovering new knowledge with the intent of transforming and embodying it in a final product. Innovative performance is captured by two dependent variables that represent different knowledge stages along the innovative process: citation-weighted patents and new drugs in development.

name: Human resources
definition: Human resources have long been viewed as being essential to a venture's ability to survive and grow. Superior human resources can reduce outside stakeholder uncertainty.

name: Social resources
definition: Social capital theory was founded on the premise that a network provides value to its members by allowing them access to the social resources that are embedded within the network. Thus, it is advantageous for a venture to form many links with high-status (credible and competent) external partners who have a diverse set of experience.

name: Financial capital
authors_terms: ["financial capital", "financial capital accumulated during the growth stages prior to a venture's initial public offering"]
definition: Although ventures must accumulate financial capital during their pre-IPO growth stages to survive and to fund development, financial capital by itself is not a productive resource: having it does not ensure post-IPO commercial success.

name: Post-IPO performance
definition: Each of the two dependent measures captured a different dimension of market legitimacy—the ability of a venture to compete for customers and for limited resources in its chosen market niche—and thus each is particularly relevant to gauging early market success.

name: Franchise system size
definition: Prior research on franchising (e.g., Lafontaine 1992, Lafontaine and Slade 1997) has shown that franchise-system size is a major factor shifting the relative costs and benefits of policies to manage freeriding, signaling, screening, and hold-up.

name: Franchisor failure
definition: Franchisor failure was defined as delisting of the franchisor from the Sourcebook.

name: Share parameter
definition: Franchisors generally charge franchisees an ongoing royalty rate and an ongoing advertising fee, established as a percentage of gross sales. Prior research has shown that together these fees represent a share parameter that divide the revenue stream from an outlet between the franchisor and franchisee (Lafontaine 1992).

name: Centralized services
definition: Franchisors often centralize several activities in the franchise system. Franchisee free-riding is reduced by control of key inputs used by franchisees.

name: Training services
