definition: Franchisors often provide field training to their franchisees.

name: Communication services
definition: Franchisors often provide communication mechanisms in their franchise systems.

name: Contract term
definition: Franchisors must establish a term for the franchise agreement.

name: Subfranchising
definition: Under subfranchising, the franchisor does not franchise directly to outlet operators, but sells territories to subfranchisors who sell franchises to outlet operators.

name: Registration states operation
definition: Franchisors must decide whether or not to operate in states and Canadian provinces with registration requirements. These laws include registration with and/or scrutiny of the franchisor by state regulators.

name: IFA membership
authors_terms: ["membership in the IFA", "International Franchise Association", "Member IFA"]
definition: Franchisors must decide whether or not to join the International Franchise Association (IFA). Membership in the trade association requires the payment of dues, the allocation of time to association business, and the willingness to adhere to trade association standards.

name: Site-selection assistance
definition: Franchisors must decide whether or not to offer assistance to franchisees in selecting locations for their outlets. Site-selection assistance often includes assessment of traffic flows in particular locations, and the suitability of particular facilities for the franchise system's business.

name: Franchisee cash investment
authors_terms: ["cash investment", "franchisee cash investment", "high levels of cash investment"]
definition: Franchisors must decide how large a cash investment the franchisee must make to obtain working capital and pay for the costs of setting up the outlet.

name: Co-CEO power gap
authors_terms: ["power gap", "co-CEO power gap", "power gaps between co-CEOs", "co-CEO power gap construct"]
definition: A difference in power between the two co-CEOs arising from sources other than hierarchical position: 'any remaining power gap from other sources signifies that influence both within the co-CEO dyad and throughout the organization is, in practice, allocated more to one of the co-CEOs than to the other.' The authors note that 'a minimal remaining power gap between co-CEOs suggests they truly share their command as equals, whereas a wide power gap suggests that command is more unified than the co-CEO structure would appear to suggest.'

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors state: 'We measured firm performance using operating return-on-equity (ROE), calculated as operating income divided by the book value of shareholder equity' and note that 'ROE reflects actual profitability outcomes, and is thus a concurrent measure.'

name: Political campaign contributions
authors_terms: ["political campaign contributions", "campaign contributions", "financial contributions to political election campaigns"]
definition: The amount of monthly political campaign contributions made by an IOU or its parent company to state legislators and legislative candidates in the state in which the IOU operated. The authors focus on these financial contributions as their primary measure of nonmarket strategy.

name: Merger and acquisition event
authors_terms: ["merger and acquisition events", "M&A proposals", "proposed corporate merger", "merger and acquisition transaction"]
definition: Proposed corporate merger and acquisition transactions in the electric utility sector. Pending mergers must obtain the approval of state Public Utility Commissions, which have jurisdiction to approve or deny electric utility mergers.

name: Political party competition
definition: The intensity of competition between the political parties in a state legislature, gauged by the size of party majorities; when political party competition is fierce—as gauged by slim majorities in the legislature—the value of incremental votes for politicians increases.

name: Individual network coreness
definition: By coreness we refer here to the degree of closeness of each node to a core of densely connected nodes observable in the network. A core/periphery network structure is characterized by a cohesive subgroup of core actors and a set of peripheral actors that are loosely connected to the core.

name: Team coreness
definition: Team coreness captures the extent to which the team to which a professional belongs consists of members that are closer to the core or the periphery or a mixture of both.

name: Individual creative performance
definition: Creativity refers to the production of outcomes that reliably can be assessed as novel or valuable by expert observers, and the definition adopted focuses on the creative outcome or product rather than on the process or the person behind it. Creative performance is therefore indicated by the quality of the products or responses judged to be creative by appropriate observers.

name: Employee treatment
definition: Firms' treatment of their employees, where favorable treatment is costly behavior such as being more generous to employees than the law demands and serves as a credible commitment made by firms to not holding up their employees.

name: Cost of bank loans
authors_terms: ["cost of bank loans", "cost of loans", "loan spread"]
definition: The price banks charge borrowers for credit, measured as the drawn-all-in spread (interest rate) charged by the bank over the London Interbank Offered Rates for the drawn portion of the loan facility.

name: Long-term institutional ownership
definition: 'Dedicated' institutional investors with concentrated portfolios and extended investment horizons who have incentives to monitor firm actions.

name: Supplier trust
definition: The existence of dependent suppliers, who put themselves in a vulnerable position and rely on long-term and repeated relationships with a principal customer, which reveals their belief that customer firms will not act opportunistically.

name: Prior firm-bank relationship
authors_terms: ["prior firm-bank relation", "prior lending relationship", "prior relationship with their banks"]
definition: The strength of the prior relationship between the focal borrowing firm and the bank; prior history provides insight into the predictability of the borrower's behavior.

name: Bank social capital
definition: Social capital is 'features of social organization such as networks, norms, and social trust that facilitate coordination and cooperation for mutual benefit'; for banks, it is the level of social capital in the bank's home county, which reflects the banks' emphasis on social values.

name: Perceived firm intent
definition: Intent denotes the organization's behavioral intentions, particularly those to maintain positive relations with exchange partners; it is reflected in perceptions of a firm's integrity and benevolence.

name: Perceived firm quality
definition: Quality denotes 'the underlying, unobservable ability of the signaler to fulfill the needs or demands of an outsider observing the signal'; it is reflected in expectations of the firm's profitability.

name: Willingness to lend
authors_terms: ["willingness to lend", "willingness to extend a loan"]
definition: The scored likelihood that a lending professional would extend a loan to the firm described in a scenario, on a scale from one (very low) to five (very high).

name: Pre-entry licensing
definition: With pre-entry licensing, firms enter a new domain by initially contracting to manufacture and commercialize another firm's product. A licensee carries out only a subset of the tasks necessary to introduce a new product, while the licensor undertakes critical tasks such as technological development and product design.

name: Post-entry performance
definition: We measured post-entry success by cumulative unit sales of the first independent aircraft in the new domain. Sales volume has long been a key indicator of profitability in the aircraft industry owing to the high level of fixed costs required to initiate a program.

name: Contextual dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["contextual dissimilarity", "dissimilarity between the initial licensed product and the first independently developed product", "technical complexity increase"]
definition: The authors consider how the degree of dissimilarity between the contexts in which licensees accumulated experience and in which they undertake new activities will exacerbate the biases produced by causal ambiguity. Technical complexity increase records the magnitude of the difference in complexity between the product(s) that a firm introduced in its pre-entry licensing phase and its first independently developed product.

name: Digital inventive performance
authors_terms: ["inventive performance in the new generation", "digital inventive performance", "inventive performance in the new technology", "inventive performance in the new domain", "performance in the new generation"]
definition: The authors measure how well a firm invents in the new technological generation as the number of forward citations made to a firm's portfolio of digital imaging patents. Forward citation counts are used as the well-established metric to measure the inventive performance of firms.

name: Inventor bridges
definition: When inventors with experience in the old technology participate in new-technology development efforts, they are engaging in recombination within the mind of an individual; the authors label these individuals 'inventor bridges.' Bridging inventors bring their understanding of the old technology to development teams.

name: Technology bridges
definition: When new-technology developments build upon elements of old-technology knowledge, they form what the authors term a 'technology bridge.' Technology bridges are the result of organization-level processes in which specific old-technology knowledge is invoked in the creation of an invention.

name: Hybrid product bridges
definition: When firms combine old and new technology knowledge in a single product, they form what the authors call a 'hybrid product bridge.' During the transition period, some photography companies produced intergenerational hybrid products based on the APS, which combined digital components with analog film, cameras, and film processing.

name: Analog inventive performance
authors_terms: ["analog inventive performance", "inventive performance in the old technology", "analog inventive capability", "inventive performance in the old domain", "analog technical performance"]
definition: A firm's inventive performance in the old technological generation, based on the importance of a firm's patent portfolio in analog photography. The authors reason that the stronger a firm's inventive performance in the old domain, the more likely it will be able to leverage intergenerational bridges when moving to the new domain.

name: Intergenerational knowledge bridges
definition: The authors conceptualize 'intergenerational knowledge bridges' as special cases of recombination that are formed when firms build upon and integrate knowledge related to the old generation of technology to develop knowledge related to the new technology. They distinguish among intergenerational knowledge bridges at three levels of analysis - the individual inventor, the technology, and the product.

name: Academic entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["academic entrepreneurship", "engaging in entrepreneurship", "in entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial entry", "becoming an entrepreneur", "founding a venture"]
definition: Academic entrepreneurship is where academic scientists found a firm to commercialize their inventions or expertise. In this study an entrepreneur is an Imperial scientist who is a director of a for-profit company at the time of foundation and who is a 'person with significant control' of that company.

name: Exploration
definition: The authors characterize exploration as a search in new knowledge domains, a form of distant search in which scientists expand their search beyond their discipline; broad search equates to exploration, where agents transcend their local search space and access distant knowledge.

name: Research impact
authors_terms: ["research impact", "scientific impact", "impact of an individual's research"]
definition: Research impact is the worth the academic community attributes to a publication, captured by citations, which act as an indicator of the intellectual debt to a cited publication that citing authors are 'repaying'.

name: Interdisciplinary organizational ties
definition: Interdisciplinarity refers to the tendency of an individual to integrate perspectives, theories, information, and tools from two or more disciplines; in this study it is captured by article coauthorships with academics affiliated with other Imperial departments, i.e., the degree to which an academic is routinely exposed to scientific disciplines different from the individual's own.

name: Technological similarity
definition: This variable reflects the similarity between the technology classes of the original patent and the citing patent. Technological similarity will increase knowledge transparency and its ease of integration across cluster or national boundaries.

name: Recognized value of knowledge
authors_terms: ["recognized value", "recognized value of knowledge", "public value to the industry of the original patent", "higher publicly imputed value"]
definition: This variable represents the public value to the industry of the original patent, captured by total number of citations it received (not including self-citations) up to the application date of the particular citing patent. When a firm seeks external knowledge, it is likely to show greater intent for accessing knowledge that has higher publicly imputed value.

name: Originating firm innovativeness
authors_terms: ["originating firm innovativeness", "firm innovativeness", "innovative capability of the originating firm"]
definition: The innovative capability of the originating firm is a representation or signal of the potential usefulness of its intellectual output. Firm innovative capability may provide an important signal regarding firm status and consequently the quality of its knowledge.

name: Prior firm knowledge flows
authors_terms: ["prior firm knowledge flows", "prior knowledge flows between firms", "prior knowledge exchanges", "prior firm linkages"]
definition: This variable reflects the number of prior knowledge exchanges between the firms engaged in knowledge transfer. Knowledge previously accessed by one firm from another is likely to have been incorporated into its internal stock of knowledge, increasing the common base of knowledge between the two firms and building a greater absorptive capacity for each other's knowledge.

name: Geographic span of knowledge flow
authors_terms: ["knowledge flows across geographic boundaries", "flows within cluster, between clusters, and between countries", "citations between countries", "intracluster, intercluster, and international"]
definition: We compared the inventor locations of the original and citing patents and classified the flows as within cluster, between clusters, and between countries. We examine how characteristics of the knowledge transaction might reinforce or mitigate the effects of geographical relationships.

name: Process interdependence
definition: The intensity of interactions between the focal process and other processes, and the magnitude of cascading effects of process changes across its linked processes prior to transition. Interdependence between a focal activity and surrounding activities gives rise to the need to coordinate them.

name: Post-offshoring process performance
authors_terms: ["steady state performance of the process post offshoring", "post offshoring process performance", "process performance"]
definition: Following industry usage, the cost reductions and/or performance improvements that occur in the immediate aftermath of moving the process offshore; measured as the steady-state performance of the process post transition to the offshore location.

name: Investment in modularization
authors_terms: ["investment in modularization", "investment in modularizing offshored processes", "modularity strategy"]
definition: The effort spent in reengineering the process, simplifying linkages between processes, creating well-specified interfaces, and portioning the process such that cross-location interdependencies were minimized. The essence of the modularity strategy is to decompose a system of activities into subsystems such that activities within a module are highly interdependent with one another, but there are few dependencies between activities that are part of different modules.

name: Investment in ongoing communication
authors_terms: ["investment in ongoing communication", "investment in facilitating ongoing electronic communication", "ongoing communication"]
definition: Ongoing communication is typically the most intuitive and potent mechanism for dynamically updating and maintaining sufficient common ground necessary for coordination; the investment comprises the effort spent to create or adapt an IT network to enable distributed teams to communicate, to train in remote collaboration, and access to communication tools.

name: Investment in tacit coordination mechanisms
definition: Mechanisms that enable the formation and leverage of common ground without the need for direct, ongoing communication; they work by leveraging preexisting common ground and by building common ground through enhancing observability across actors of contexts, actions, and outcomes.

name: CEO turnover
definition: The authors state that when CEO turnovers occur, they tend to be overly disruptive for companies, and that a CEO departure may signal a breakdown of strategic decisions in the near future or missed business targets.

name: Rival abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["positive abnormal stock price reactions for intra-industry rivals", "positive intra-industry information effects", "buy-and-hold abnormal returns (BHARs) for intra-industry rivals"]
definition: The reactions of intra-industry rivals to a turnover announcement: the authors say 'These reactions are referred to as positive intra-industry information effects,' and that the temporal competitive advantage of rivals 'should be reflected in positive abnormal intra-industry valuation effects during the transition period.'

name: Forced CEO turnover
authors_terms: ["forced turnover", "turnover reason: Forced", "forced top management turnover"]
definition: The authors state that the information effect inherent in a CEO turnover announcement is more pronounced for forced than routine turnovers, because forced top management turnovers are often related to prior negative performance, are usually more disruptive than routine turnovers, and are often viewed as a potential sign of internal problems.

name: Return on assets
definition: The authors use accounting performance to complement the evidence from analyzing stock performance, choosing return on assets as the main proxy measure.

name: Investment
definition: The authors define investment as the amount of capital expenditures divided by lagged net property, plant, and equipment in order to control for a company's investment policy.

name: Depreciation
definition: The authors look at depreciation (log [EBITDA minus EBIT]) among the accounting measures used to observe the impact of implemented strategic initiatives.

name: Stakeholder elements of the task environment
authors_terms: ["stakeholder elements of the task environment", "elements related to stakeholder acceptance or support"]
definition: The extent to which grand challenge task environments include elements related to stakeholder acceptance or support, i.e., elements influenced by whether a solution depends on the acceptance or support of important stakeholders outside a search consortium.

name: Advocacy group involvement
authors_terms: ["advocacy group involvement", "involvement of advocacy groups", "advocacy group inclusion"]
definition: The inclusion of advocacy groups, i.e., organizations that synthesize and aggregate knowledge from stakeholders and represent stakeholder concerns, as partners in a search consortium.

name: Likelihood of receiving funding
authors_terms: ["likelihood of receiving funding", "likelihood of a consortium to receive funding", "likelihood of receiving funding for implementing a proposed solution"]
definition: The likelihood of a search consortium to receive funding for implementing its proposed solution to a grand challenge problem, which increases with the evaluation score assigned to its funding application by independent experts.

name: Technological knowledge dispersion
authors_terms: ["high technological dispersion", "knowledge dispersion", "dispersion of technological knowledge"]
definition: High technological dispersion in a search consortium describes a situation in which the members possess little overlapping technological expertise. There is, in other words, a high degree of differentiation because the organizations involved are specialized in different technological domains.

name: Lack of experience
authors_terms: ["lack of experience", "lack of prior experience of the consortium leader", "inexperienced consortia"]
definition: A setting in which the search consortium does not have experience with coordinated exploration in a particular grand challenge task environment; because the consortium leader is particularly visible to the evaluating body, consortia particularly lack experience when the leader is inexperienced.

name: Status loss
authors_terms: ["status loss", "loss in status", "status decline", "slip in rank", "drop in rank"]
definition: A school is treated as suffering status loss when it is currently (in year t) more than five ranks worse than its school-specific, time-invariant mean rank, after having previously ascended above that mean. The authors set the width of the boundary between perceived failure and success at ten ranks around the school's mean rank.

name: Status gain
definition: The mirror image of status loss: a school is treated as gaining status when it is currently (in year t) more than five ranks better than its school-specific mean rank, after having historically fallen beneath that mean. Entering status gain alongside status loss allows the authors to disentangle the effects of loss versus gain on future price.

name: Price
definition: The price a focal organization sets for its good, measured here as the school's tuition in year t+1. Following Leavitt's early distinction, the authors focus on price not simply as a 'sacrifice' for consumers but also as a 'symbol' used strategically by status-aspiring organizations.

name: Breadth of appeal
authors_terms: ["appeals broadly to disparate kinds of buyers", "breadth of appeal", "broad appeal", "betweenness centrality"]
definition: Breadth of appeal is associated with an organization residing near the core (and away from peripheral players) of its market, with connections extending to multiple groups, so that normally disparate or disagreeing parties reach consensus about it. In the authors' setting it is captured by a school's reach across diverse college applicants.

name: Rivals' prior prices
authors_terms: ["weighted peer tuition", "structurally equivalent rivals have previously charged high prices", "peers' past pricing decisions", "rivals' past prices"]
definition: The lagged prices charged by a focal producer's structurally equivalent peers, who are producers with similar relationships to the same third parties. Rivals' past prices shape the normative context in which a focal producer selects its own price, granting it greater latitude to charge more without transgressing norms of fairness.

name: Organizational status
definition: The authors view status as a mutable position in a tournament in which producers seek to rank favorably, rather than exclusively as a trait that buyers value. In their setting status is a school's position in the annual U.S. News ranking, a public, manufactured reflection of the prestige of colleges and universities.

name: Cyclical environmental change
definition: Cycles exist whenever key elements of the environment transition among a limited set of contexts over time. A great deal of environmental dynamism takes the form of cyclical change, in which one of a limited set of environmental conditions appears and then gives way to other conditions, only to later reappear.

name: Organizational learning
definition: The authors draw on research on organizational learning and knowledge transfer to investigate how cycles and specific cyclical conditions alter the connection between experience and performance. The traditional experiential learning model assumes a continuous learning process unaffected by changes in learning context.

name: Construction lending performance
definition: A key to success in construction lending is reducing the prevalence of poor outcomes or error rates that lead to lost opportunities, costs, and losses. Reducing losses from delinquent loans is an important performance outcome in the construction lending industry.

name: Cumulative lending experience
definition: We define experience for a given bank i in year t, Q i,t , as the accumulated sum of the banks' annual construction loan balances starting from the year a bank is first established.

name: Same-phase experience
authors_terms: ["experience, same phase (Q s)", "experience accumulated during the same phase as the current one", "experience gained in the same cyclical phase"]
definition: We divide aggregate lending experience Q into experience accumulated during the same phase as the current one, Q s , and experience accumulated during alternate phases, Q a . Which stock is same and which is alternate switches as the focal phase changes.

name: Alternate-phase experience
authors_terms: ["experience, alternate phase (Q a)", "experience accumulated during alternate phases", "experience gained in an alternate phase"]
definition: We divide aggregate lending experience Q into experience accumulated during the same phase as the current one, Q s , and experience accumulated during alternate phases, Q a . Which stock is same and which is alternate switches as the focal phase changes.

name: Same-phase experience intensity
authors_terms: ["intensity, same phase (n s)", "intensity of experience in the same cyclical phase", "experience intensity"]
definition: Intensity is defined as the amount of activity taking place, on average, within a period of time. We define experience intensity as a bank's average annual loan volume in a particular phase of the cycle up to the current date.

name: Alternate-phase experience intensity
authors_terms: ["intensity, alternate phase (n a)", "intensity of experience in alternate cyclical phases", "experience intensity"]
definition: Intensity is defined as the amount of activity taking place, on average, within a period of time. We define experience intensity as a bank's average annual loan volume in a particular phase of the cycle up to the current date.

name: Same-phase experience duration
authors_terms: ["duration, same phase (y s)", "duration of experience in the same cyclical phase", "duration"]
definition: We define duration as the average number of years a bank spent in one phase of the cycle before transitioning to the next phase; duration is the amount of time spent in a phase.

name: Alternate-phase experience duration
authors_terms: ["duration, alternate phase (y a)", "duration of experience in alternate cyclical phases", "duration"]
definition: We define duration as the average number of years a bank spent in one phase of the cycle before transitioning to the next phase; duration is the amount of time spent in a phase.

name: Cyclical transitions
authors_terms: ["transitions (t)", "transitions between phases", "experience making transitions across cyclical phases"]
definition: We define transitions (t) as the total number of times that a bank has experienced a change from one phase to another (i.e., both upturn to downturn and downturn to upturn).

name: Decentralization of marketing activities
authors_terms: ["decentralization of key marketing decisions and activities", "SBU control over environmental monitoring and marketing activities", "centralization of environmental monitoring activities (CNTEM)"]
definition: Decentralization of the key marketing decisions and activities central to an SBU's strategy, i.e. the SBU's control over environmental monitoring activities such as assessing trends and analyzing competitors, which are the activities expected to be most important to the Prospector.

name: Decentralization of operational activities
authors_terms: ["decentralization of decisions and activities associated with cost reductions", "centralization of operational activities (CNTO)", "SBU control over operational decisions and activities"]
definition: Decentralization of the operational decisions and activities associated with cost reductions, following the suggestion that the Defender's success is largely a function of its ability to control operational decisions and activities.

name: Decentralization of strategic planning
authors_terms: ["decentralization of the strategic decision making process", "control over the strategic decision making process", "centralization of the strategic planning process (CNTSP)"]
definition: Decentralization of the strategic decision making process, that is, SBU control over initiating the strategic planning process, formulating the strategic plan, granting final approval of the plan and providing market research, relative to corporate management.

name: SBU profitability
definition: Profitability of the SBU's 15 major inpatient and outpatient services: because profit margin data were unobtainable across the sample, general measures of profitability were used for each of the 15 services.

name: SBU market share
definition: Market share of the SBU for each of its 15 major inpatient and outpatient services, adjusted for the number of hospitals in its local market area.

name: SBU strategy
definition: SBU strategies were categorized using the widely recognized procedure developed by Miles and Snow (1978); conceptually, organizations are likely to exhibit a strategy that is more or less similar to one of the types, and the Analyzer's strategy is essentially a dual strategy.

name: Constitutional constraints on shareholder power
authors_terms: ["constitutional limit provisions", "constitutional constraints on shareholder power", "corporate governance provisions that impose constitutional constraints on shareholder power"]
definition: Corporate governance provisions that impose constitutional constraints on shareholder power; the key distinction from takeover contingencies is that the former require shareholders' approval whereas the latter do not.

name: Managerial misconduct
definition: Managerial misconduct involves the pursuit of illegal activity designed to extract personal wealth from the firm. This operationalization captures a wide range of managerial misconduct, including illegal insider trading, illegal stock option backdating, bribery, and financial manipulation.

name: Industry takeover intensity
definition: One observable scenario that makes shareholder influence especially salient to top managers is when they are surrounded by takeovers in their industry.

name: CEO duality
authors_terms: ["CEO duality", "CEO and board chair separation", "unity of command structure", "unified command structure"]
definition: One important factor that puts CEOs in a position of power where they are less vulnerable to the whims of external stakeholders is when they hold a unified command structure wherein they fill the positions of both CEO and Chair of the Board.

name: Protestant affiliation
definition: The religious denomination with which a nonprofit hospital is affiliated: all Catholic hospitals are members of the Caritas organization and all Protestant hospitals are members of Diakonisches Werk. The authors classified nonprofit hospitals into Protestant, Catholic, and other types by looking at the hospital denomination and affiliation provided in each BQS report.

name: Patient volume
definition: The number of patients treated by each hospital.

name: Total casemix
definition: The casemix of a hospital is the sum of its severity scores. Hence, it depends on both the severity and the number of cases.

name: Casemix index
definition: The average severity of cases treated in a hospital is measured by the casemix index (cmi), a concept frequently used in healthcare studies and corresponding to average revenues of a provider.

name: Total revenues
definition: The total revenues of a hospital, obtained by multiplying the variable casemix with the base rate (Basisfallwert).

name: Average revenue per patient
definition: The revenues per patient in each hospital, obtained by multiplying the casemix index by the base rate.

name: Academic affiliation
authors_terms: ["academic", "academic teaching hospital", "links to universities and other academic institutions"]
definition: Whether a hospital is a teaching hospital linked to a university. In the BQS quality reports hospitals had to fill in question A-5: 'Academic teaching hospital (yes/no)? If yes, linked to which university?'.

name: Physicians per patient
definition: The number of doctors and, respectively, of specialists per patient in each hospital.

name: Horizontal diversification
definition: The number of different medical fields in which a hospital is active, where fields are defined as the class of diagnosis at the one-digit level of the ICD-10 classification and a hospital is considered active in a field if it had at least one diagnosis per week in that field in the given year. In the model, a hospital with more treatment areas offers more diverse, less specialized treatments.

name: Competitive pressure
definition: The degree of competitiveness to which a provider is exposed. Empirically the authors use the geographical distance to the closest neighboring hospital, irrespective of the latter's ownership status, assuming that the smaller the geographic distance to the nearest hospital, the higher the competitive pressure.

name: Previous venture outcome
definition: The success or failure of the entrepreneur's previous venture: the previous venture is coded as a success if it is an ongoing firm (typically still owned by the entrepreneur but managed by friends or close family members), and a failure otherwise.

name: Industry change between ventures
authors_terms: ["D industry", "change industry between the previous and subsequent venture", "industry change", "changing industries between ventures"]
definition: Whether the self-reported industry of the subsequent venture differs from that of the previous venture; the Chinese government classifies firms into 11 industries.

name: Relatedness between ventures
definition: The relationship between the previous and the current venture, assessed over categories: the current company is the supplier, the distributor or consumer, does almost the same thing, is the complement, is the substitute, or has no relationship.

name: Strategy change between ventures
definition: The change in the founder's value-creation strategy, in terms of differentiation versus cost focus, from the previous to the current business.

name: Planning style change
definition: The change in the formality of the strategic planning process, from more proactive to more reactive, between the previous and the current venture.

name: Management style change
definition: The change in the degree of centralization versus decentralization in decision making between the previous and the current venture.

name: Subsequent venture performance
authors_terms: ["growth", "performance of the subsequent venture", "three-year growth rate"]
definition: The performance of the subsequent venture, measured as the three-year growth rate of the current venture across a variety of measures.

name: Analytic skill
definition: Analytic skill is the ability to reason through abstract problems, that is, the ability to solve abstract problems. In an organizational setting it could relate to technical know-how, domain-specific expertise, and problem-solving skills.

name: Strategic intelligence
definition: Strategic intelligence is the application of social cognition to gain strategic advantage: the ability to anticipate competitors' behavior—and preempt it. The higher the strategic intelligence, the better one can anticipate rival behavior, infer their likely strategies, and preempt them.

name: Performance in competition
definition: Performance in competition is the collective, macrolevel outcome that is not decided by any single actor; the authors measured it in a straightforward manner as profit from trading. In the experiment it is the profit a participant earns from dividends and trading in the market.

name: Problem-solving supplier strategy
authors_terms: ["problem-solvers", "PSs", "problem-solving supplier", "black box suppliers", "Quadrant III", "firms in the PS quadrant"]
definition: Quadrant III describes firms that employ both advanced technologies and collaborative methods to promote innovations in product design and manufacture. Firms in this quadrant compete primarily on their ability to continuously acquire and evolve new ways to solve process and product problems (Clark and Fujimoto's black box suppliers).

name: Collaboration
definition: The collaboration dimension ranges from spot market arm's-length transactions on the low end to long-term relational contracts. Long-term relations include such practices as certification, target pricing, incentive contracts, and interfirm concurrent engineering with both customers and suppliers.

name: Advanced manufacturing technology
authors_terms: ["technology", "technology dimension", "advanced technologies", "advanced manufacturing and design technologies"]
definition: The technology dimension ranges from firms that struggle to maintain routine manufacturing practices on the low end to firms that take advantage of advanced manufacturing and design technologies on the high end.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["larger", "size of the firm", "number of employees", "total sales", "sales volume"]
definition: Because PSs need to retain technical personnel to interact with their customers and to keep abreast of the latest technological developments, they will tend to have more employees, i.e., be of larger size; the authors also refer to greater sales volume as part of being larger.

name: Profitability
definition: Because the new collaborative approaches and active technology involvement encourage relational physical and human capital investments, problem-solvers should generate relational rents. Also, PSs have governance structures that provide formal and informal mechanisms that promote trust and reduce risk.

name: Export intensity
authors_terms: ["percentage of their sales in exports", "percentage of export sales", "export sales", "successful in global markets"]
definition: Given that problem-solving firms have developed intricate networks and have mastered advanced information technologies, they are likely to be more successful in global markets than firms in the other quadrants.

name: Wages
definition: Innovative firms require well-trained employees to continually improve products and processes; these workers with their firm-specific capital should be able to bargain for wages higher than those found on the spot market.

name: Audience-specific reputation
definition: Reputation that is attribute-specific (containing information about a specific set of attributes) and audience-specific (containing information that can be evaluated in terms of the expectations of a focal audience). The authors argue that a reputation that represents a specific set of attributes is more valuable to one audience than to another.

name: Reputation for artistic quality
authors_terms: ["reputation for artistic quality", "a reputation that indicates that an artist's work is of high artistic quality"]
definition: A reputation indicating that an artist's work is of high artistic quality; in this setting it is signalled by winning prestigious awards, which are conferred on the basis of perceived artistic quality rather than on commercial viability.

name: Reputation for commercial viability
authors_terms: ["reputation for commercial viability", "reputation that indicates the commercial viability of an artist's work"]
definition: A reputation indicating the commercial viability of an artist's work; in this setting it is signalled by an artist's appearance on the cover of prominent art magazines, which is treated as indicating the commercial value of the work.

name: Success with museums
definition: An artist's success with the museum audience, captured by obtaining an exhibition at a museum; in the art field, the ability to exhibit work at museums is an accepted indicator of an artist's success with that audience.

name: Success with galleries
definition: An artist's success with the gallery audience, captured by obtaining an exhibition at a gallery; in the art field, the ability to exhibit work at galleries is an accepted indicator of an artist's success with that audience.

name: Status
definition: Status is based on an actor's position in a social hierarchy that both reflects and influences how the actor is acknowledged by others. In this study it is measured as affiliation-based status: an artist's exhibitions at high-status museums or galleries.

name: Interaction with other audiences
authors_terms: ["interaction with other audiences", "interaction with another audience", "inter-audience interaction", "interaction with a different audience"]
definition: A particular actor might differ in the extent to which they engage with different audiences in the same field; the extent to which an actor interacts with other audiences provides a source of information to a focal audience beyond the actor's audience-specific reputation.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: It is standard to measure the unexpected return that results from an event, such as an acquisition. This unexpected return is sometimes called an abnormal return and is calculated as the difference between the actual stock return and the return that would be expected given the performance of the market.

name: Acquirer-target industry similarity
definition: Because acquisitions take place among firms in a variety of industries, the more similar the industrial environment of the acquirer and target, the greater the likelihood that situation similarity will be accentuated. Situation similarity may increase the potential for positive transfer because an acquirer from a similar industrial environment can apply relatively more appropriate behavior to the target.

name: Acquisition sequence
definition: The classic two-stage experiment in psychology translates straightforwardly to a first acquisition where skills are gained (training period) and a second acquisition where skills from the first acquisition may be inappropriately applied to the second acquisition (testing period).

name: Target-to-target industry similarity
definition: When a firm acquires two strategically similar targets in succession, there should be opportunities for positive transfer between targets; when the two targets are from different industrial environments, there is little potential for knowledge transfer.

name: Financial asset investment
authors_terms: ["financial investment", "investment in financial assets", "financial assets over total assets", "dependence on financial activities", "operation in financial activities", "financialization"]
definition: Firm's dependence on financial activities is measured as financial assets over total assets. The financial assets measure includes both long-term and short-term financial investments, such as mortgages, business and consumer loans, leases, certificates of deposit, commercial paper, and government and other marketable securities.

name: Corporate debt
definition: Firms' dependence on debt is measured with the common debt ratio formula: total liabilities over total assets.

name: Shareholder rewards
authors_terms: ["shareholder rewards", "rewards for shareholders", "rewards to shareholders", "income return to shareholders", "dividends and stock buybacks"]
definition: I use the sum of stock repurchases and dividends paid over total operating expense as a size-adjusted direct measure of income return to shareholders.

name: Employment growth
authors_terms: ["employment growth", "employment dynamics", "actual, domestic employment size", "total employment size"]
definition: The current analysis avoids these issues by examining actual, domestic employment size. All jobs are categorized into one of the three occupational groups in the following analysis.

name: Managerial and professional employment growth
definition: Professional and managerial employment is measured as total professional and managerial jobs. These positions tend to be at the upper level of the corporate hierarchy and feature high autonomy.

name: Production employment growth
definition: Production employment size is measured as the sum of technicians, crafts, operatives, and laborer jobs. This category consists of blue-collar, traditionally working-class positions that engage in industry-specific production.

name: Service employment growth
definition: Service employment size is measured as the sum of sales, clerical, and service jobs. Many of these positions require less formal skills and require fewer educational credentials.

name: Firm-specific skill requirements
authors_terms: ["firm-specific skills", "sensitivity to firm-specific skills", "need for firm-specific skills"]
definition: 'Firm-specific skills' are skills acquired through on-the-job learning in one organization that cannot be used in another organization. Prior experience within the firm should provide current employees with much higher levels of firm-specific skills than potential hires.

name: Performance variability
definition: Consistent with prior research, we define 'performance variability' as the extent of differences in performance among different incumbents within a job.

name: Grade ratio
definition: The proportion of workers eligible for promotion can be calculated from the ratio of workers at the lower level on the job ladder to the number of workers in the focal job, which Stewman and Konda (1983) refer to as the 'grade ratio.'

name: Internal mobility
definition: In internal mobility, the worker moves from a different job within the organization. Hiring, promoting, and transferring represent equivalent means by which organizations can fill jobs with employees.

name: Promotion
definition: Consistent with much prior work, we define a promotion as a move from a job that was in a lower hierarchical rank within the same organization. When workers are promoted, they move into a job with substantially higher skills demands and task complexity.

name: Lateral transfer
definition: In a transfer, a worker moves from a job that was at the same hierarchical level as the destination job, but within a different function or in a different part of the organization, usually (but not always) involving different tasks, responsibilities, or reporting relationships.

name: Cultural element popularity
authors_terms: ["element popularity", "popularity of cultural elements", "popularity of stylistic elements", "popularity"]
definition: We capture an element's popularity by counting the number of fashion houses that adopted it during the focal time period; we call this count variable element popularity. Thus, the number of occurrences of a stylistic element is the number of houses using it during a given season.

name: Structural embeddedness of a cultural element
authors_terms: ["structural embeddedness", "structural embeddedness of cultural element", "structural embeddedness of cultural elements"]
definition: We start with the embeddedness of elements with other elements, what we will call the 'structural embeddedness of cultural elements'. The structural embeddedness of cultural elements captures their overall associativity and legitimacy in a given institutional domain.

name: Visibility of cultural elements' carriers
definition: The former is about the prior exposure audiences have to different cultural elements and, critically, the differential attention given to organizations endorsing competing cultural elements. Here, visibility does not measure the deference paid to an organization - its status - but rather how much this organization is in the public eye.

name: Female business ownership
authors_terms: ["businesses headed by women", "gender of a business's owner-operator", "women entrepreneurs", "woman"]
definition: The gender of a business's owner-operator; the authors compare businesses owned and operated by women with those headed by men on the two dimensions of organizational performance.

name: Organizational survival
authors_terms: ["survival", "going out of business", "failure", "probability of its survival"]
definition: Organizational survival is a fundamental aspect of performance and a necessary condition for sustained business success. A company was defined as out of business at the time of the second or third wave of interviews if the telephone number used in the previous wave was no longer operative and no new, valid number could be found for the business.

name: Business success
definition: Success can be measured in a variety of ways: by accounting-based indicators of financial performance, such as returns on investment; by market-based indicators of financial performance, like market share; and by stakeholders' evaluations of performance. Growth in the logarithm of gross earnings during the study period was the authors' measure of success.

name: Organizational age
definition: A company's age in years since its founding. The relation between an organization's age and its survival and success illustrates the divergence of the two dimensions of performance.

name: Organizational size
definition: An organization's size was measured as the logarithm of the number of its full-time employees.

name: Industry size
authors_terms: ["size of an industry", "number of businesses with employees in a respondent's industry and county", "industry size"]
definition: The number of businesses with employees in a respondent's industry and county, lagged one year; these counts include firms of all sizes, both incorporated and unincorporated, in each industry and each of the 12 counties represented in the data set.

name: Industry growth
authors_terms: ["percentage of change in industry size", "change in industry size", "rate of change in industry size", "rapid changes in industrial populations"]
definition: The percentage of change in the number of businesses in Indiana in a respondent's industry, lagged one year.

name: Competitive intensity
authors_terms: ["competition", "extent of competition", "level of competition", "highly competitive markets"]
definition: Entrepreneurs' perceptions of the extent of competition in the product market in which their businesses operated and how much of a problem competition was for them.

name: Business experience
definition: The authors used two measures of experience: the number of years a respondent had been in an industry and whether or not he or she had been self-employed before acquiring the current business.

name: Business innovation
definition: Respondents' reports of which of the following six types of innovations they had engaged in during the two prior years: new products, new services, new advertising techniques, new management or organizational structures, physical changes, and other innovations.

name: Confidence in business ability
authors_terms: ["confidence", "how successful they were in business", "confidence in their business abilities"]
definition: Respondents' assessments of how successful they were in business, measured by summing responses to the statements 'I have a better idea about running my business than most of my competitors' and 'Compared to others, I feel I am very successful in my present business.'

name: Internal locus of control
authors_terms: ["internal locus of control", "locus of control", "feel that they can influence the performance of their business"]
definition: An indicator of internal locus of control, assessed through responses to the statement 'I feel that outcomes of my business ventures are largely influenced by my own efforts.'

name: CEO cognitive complexity
definition: Cognitive complexity, or the degree of differentiation and nuance in one's mental representations. Individuals high on cognitive complexity have highly differentiated and well-nuanced cognitive schemas that allow them to perceive multiple complementary perspectives when making decisions.

name: Firm performance
definition: Our dependent variable is firm performance, which we assess using return on assets (ROA).

name: Industry complexity
definition: Industry complexity is associated with increased heterogeneity in the number and variety of competitors, suppliers, and customers with which firms interact. Complexity refers to heterogeneity in the size and market power of industry participants, where greater heterogeneity represents more complex industry conditions.

name: Industry munificence
definition: Munificence relates to an industry's ability to support growth and stability of the firms operating within it. Munificence and dynamism respectively represent an industry's ability to support sustained growth and its degree of instability.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Dynamism reflects instability in an industry, for instance, via rapid technological change or frequent product introductions, breakthroughs in input markets, or regulatory change.

name: Worker mobility
definition: Investments in adoption efforts enable workers involved in those efforts to gain human capital through on-the-job learning that is valuable to other firms in the industry, thus increasing the risk of outward worker mobility. When workers of the adopting firm move to new employers, particularly in the same sector, they can apply their experiences to those firms.

name: Time to machine learning adoption
authors_terms: ["time to ML adoption", "time to adoption", "ML adoption", "adoption of ML", "adoption of machine learning"]
definition: In our model, the time at which a firm adopts ML is determined by when the benefits of adoption exceed the costs. Because adoption is observed only in 2018, when changes in mobility and other factors reduce the likelihood of adoption by 2018, the authors interpret this as an increase in the time to adoption.

name: Establishment size
definition: q ≥ 0 is size (e.g., establishment output). The net benefit of adopting ML is assumed to be increasing in size, and prior literature has shown that large establishments are more likely to have related technological complements and more mature processes that will increase the value of adopting enterprise software systems.

name: Industry benefits of machine learning adoption
authors_terms: ["benefits of adoption", "net benefits of ML", "industry-level net benefits to ML adoption", "industries where benefits of adoption are likely to be higher", "lead user industries", "predictive analytics adoption intensity"]
definition: The parameter b denotes the extent of net benefits that the technology offers for a given firm size. This may vary across industries; industries where the benefits are higher tend to adopt ML earlier and the effects of worker mobility will be magnified in such industries.

name: Location size
definition: The parameter θ allows for potential differences across regions in labor market thickness that can affect the ease with which local employer-worker matches can be made. In large regions, thicker labor markets mean that it will be easier to find workers with the requisite skills elsewhere, and the costs of replacing departing workers will be lower.

name: Local large same-industry establishments
authors_terms: ["number of large establishments in the same industry-location", "large establishments in the same four-digit SIC code and in the same MSA", "large establishments in the same industry-location"]
definition: The authors examine heterogeneity in their effects based on the number of large (more than 100 employees) establishments in the same four-digit SIC code and in the same MSA. Because employer-worker matching is easiest for worker movements within the same industry, and because NCA laws restrict worker movement within the same industry, the effects of NCA enforceability will be strongest in locations with many large establishments in the same industry.

name: Planning system classification
authors_terms: ["planning classification", "planning continuum", "planning system", "planning openness", "planning horizon", "strategic planning"]
definition: Rhyne (1981, 1985) developed a continuum of corporate-level planning systems based on the level of their 'openness' and the length of their planning 'horizon'. Five points on the continuum were identified: short-term forecasting, budgeting, annual planning, long-range planning and strategic planning.

name: Long-term shareholder return
authors_terms: ["10-year total return to investors", "10-year total return to stockholders", "long-term financial performance", "relative return", "absolute 10-year total return to investors"]
definition: Since strategic management theory prescribes a long-term perspective, it is appropriate to use a long-term performance measure to evaluate company performance; calculating the return relative to the industry should largely eliminate differences in industry profitability, the effects of the level of economic activity, exogenous shocks to particular industries and changes in investor attitudes. Such a measure was found in the 10-year total return to investors relative to the industry.

name: Short-term financial performance
authors_terms: ["short-term measures of performance", "1-year return on equity", "1-year total return to investors", "annual performance measures"]
definition: Short-term measures of performance such as the 1-year return on equity (absolute and relative) and the 1-year total return to investors (absolute and relative), which were investigated alongside the long-term measures in order to verify the expectation about them.

name: Emerging industry
definition: Emergent industries are characterized by high uncertainty and turbulence. New ventures in emerging industries face the same liabilities of newness that confront ventures everywhere, but they also face additional liabilities as emerging industry norms are less developed.

name: Conformance to discontinued certification
authors_terms: ["conform to a discontinued certification", "compliance with discontinued certifications", "certification relics", "certification relic"]
definition: We define discontinuation as a material easing of certification rules, requirements, and standards. Following prior studies noting the persistence of standards, we term this conformance to discontinued certifications as certification relics: they are 'certifications' in that they were at one point used to evaluate whether ventures conformed to accepted standards of behavior, and 'relics' in that certifications may still influence activity well beyond their discontinuation.

name: Elite founder
definition: An elite founder is just such a legitimating attribute. Prominent founders typically have considerable human and social resources from their education, work experience, and social capital, which decrease their ventures' needs for other legitimating attributes.

name: Unconventional founder
definition: While elite founders increase the legitimacy of a new venture in an emerging field, other attributes may decrease legitimacy. Unconventional founders are likely to have a particularly difficult legitimacy deficit to overcome.

name: Time since certification discontinuation
authors_terms: ["over time", "earlier years following a reform", "later years", "postreform period"]
definition: As a critical mass of firms adopts such practices, they become more socially accepted, reducing the legitimacy risks in adopting such practices. From this perspective, we would expect the persistence of discontinued certifications to wane over time as mimetic isomorphism increases the diffusion of new less stringent standards, thereby increasing their social acceptance.

name: Internal advice seeking capabilities
authors_terms: ["internal advice seeking capabilities", "internal advice seeking", "internal advice seeking behaviors"]
definition: Internal advice seeking refers to gathering knowledge and information within the firm; internal advice seeking allows managers to get a holistic view of the firm's resources, processes, and knowledge assets.

name: External advice seeking capabilities
authors_terms: ["external advice seeking capabilities", "external advice seeking", "external advice seeking behaviors"]
definition: While internal advice seeking refers to gathering knowledge and information within the firm, external advice seeking focuses on capturing information from formal and informal ties outside of the company.

name: Coordination flexibility capabilities
definition: Coordination flexibility pertains to the adjustment of a flexible operating environment that reduces rigid structures and inertia in routines. Such capabilities are closely related to the asset orchestration function of organizational dynamic capabilities.

name: Business model innovation
definition: Many scholars describe a business model as the architecture of a firm's underlying logic of how the value proposition is created, delivered, and captured. The process of innovating a firm's business model is strategic and operative in nature.

name: Organizational digitalization
authors_terms: ["organizational digitalization", "firm-level digitalization", "degree of digitalization at the firm level"]
definition: The extent of digitalization across eight functional areas in an organization as outlined by Porter (1985); the authors developed this new measure because a comprehensive measure of firm-level digitalization has not yet been introduced.

name: CEO compensation
definition: Executive compensation is total cash compensation, consisting of salary, bonus, and miscellaneous earnings such as fringe benefits reported in the proxy. The paper deals solely with cash compensation and its two major components, salary and bonus.

name: CEO salary
definition: Salary is one of the two major components of cash compensation. Since salaries are set at the beginning of a fiscal year, they will have no necessary relationship to performance for that period.

name: CEO bonus
definition: Bonus is one of the two major components of cash compensation; an element of cash compensation can reasonably be considered a performance-related reward, and many compensation agreements include such an incentive component.

name: Firm size
definition: There is substantial evidence that firm size is a major determinant of CEO pay. The rationale for this association is disputed, ranging from greater demands on CEOs, greater ability to pay, and more hierarchical layers in large firms.

name: Corporate profitability
definition: The effect of corporate performance, particularly profitability, on CEO pay has been widely explored, with results varying from nil to strongly positive associations. To ensure that profit rates (and not profit size) were considered, return on equity (ROE) was taken as the measure of performance.

name: Corporate complexity
definition: Even after controlling for corporate size, some CEOs have more complex and demanding jobs than others. Not only is diversity a form of complexity, but it also signifies greater discretion than is possessed by a CEO whose board, or who himself, is committed to only one industry.

name: General management experience
authors_terms: ["human capital", "CEO general management track", "experience in general management", "main career tracks have been in general management"]
definition: CEOs with long experience in general management tend to develop expertise of greater relevance to the top management task than, say, executives with primarily production or marketing experience. This superior training is expected to command a premium in the managerial labor market for CEOs.

name: CEO tenure
definition: One source of power that may be particularly relevant is managerial tenure, because some important bases of power require time to take effect.

name: CEO ownership
definition: Executives who own significant portions of their firms are likely to control not only operating decisions but board decisions as well. Such executives would thus be in a position to essentially set their own compensation.

name: CEO family ownership
authors_terms: ["CEO's family's holdings", "family shareholdings", "proportion of firm stock owned by the CEO's family"]
definition: The holdings of other members of the CEO's family may provide him power: the stronger the family's position in the firm, the stronger the executive's position.

name: Board vigilance
definition: When the board is composed of individuals who themselves hold a significant personal stake in the firm's actions, it is more likely to meet its vigilance role; under these conditions the board can be expected to exert tighter control over the CEO.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Following McEachern (1975), the sample was divided into three ownership classes: owner-managed, where stock ownership was concentrated among a firm's managers; management-controlled, where stock ownership was dispersed among many shareholders; and externally controlled, where stock ownership was concentrated among a limited number of non-managers.

name: Key success factor stability
authors_terms: ["key success factor stability", "stability of key success factors"]
definition: Key success factors are the requirements necessary for success within a particular industry. If these remain stable (i.e., requirements necessary for success are unlikely to change radically during industry development), early commitment is likely to provide a sustainable competitive position; if they are unstable, a new venture is likely to face a high degree of technical and demand uncertainty.

name: Timing of entry
definition: A pioneer enters a new industry first and a late follower enters an industry late in the industry's stage of development.

name: Lead time
definition: Lead time refers to the period of monopoly for the first entrant prior to competitors entering the industry.

name: Competitive rivalry
definition: Competitive rivalry refers to the level of competition among industry members during industry development.

name: Educational capability
definition: Educational capability refers to the amount of resources and skills available to overcome market ignorance through education.

name: Industry related competence
definition: Industry related competence refers to the level of experience and knowledge with the industry being entered, or a related industry.

name: Probability of survival
definition: Survival is defined as the probability that this venture will continue to participate in the market. In the study it is assessed using a ten-year time horizon.

name: Existing collaboration
definition: The number of current collaborative relationships between two firms is modeled as the number of joint partnerships firms i and j held in year t. Such relationships include joint research and development, coproduction, and co-marketing agreements.

name: Existing conflict
authors_terms: ["current conflictual relationships", "current conflictual ties", "active patent infringement and antitrust lawsuits"]
definition: The number of current conflictual relationships is modeled as the number of active patent infringement and antitrust lawsuits between firms i and j in year t. Patent infringement and antitrust lawsuits exemplify the conflictual side of the social structure.

name: Collaboration formation
authors_terms: ["new collaborative relationship", "future collaboration", "likelihood of entering into a new collaborative relationship"]
definition: The likelihood of entering into a new collaborative relationship is modeled with a binary measure that takes on 1 if firms i and j had entered into at least one partnership in year t+1, and 0 otherwise.

name: Conflict formation
authors_terms: ["new conflictual relationship", "future conflict", "likelihood of initiating a new conflictual relationship"]
definition: The likelihood of initiating a new conflictual relationship is modeled with a binary measure that takes on 1 if firms i and j had initiated at least one lawsuit against each other in year t+1, and 0 otherwise.

name: Shared collaborators
authors_terms: ["number of collaborative third parties", "third parties to which both firms hold collaborative ties", "common collaborator"]
definition: The number of collaborative third parties is the count of third parties to which firms i and j were both linked through collaborative relationships in year t.

name: Shared adversaries
authors_terms: ["number of conflictual third parties", "third parties to which both firms hold conflictual ties", "common adversary"]
definition: The number of conflictual third parties is the count of third parties to which firms i and j were both linked through conflictual relationships in year t.

name: Mixed third-party ties
authors_terms: ["number of mixed third parties", "third parties to which one firm holds a collaborative tie and the other, a conflictual tie", "asymmetric ties"]
definition: The number of mixed third parties is the count of third parties to which firms i and j were linked through relationships of different types in year t (a collaborative tie for i and a conflictual tie for j, or vice versa).

name: Network segregation
authors_terms: ["segregation of the global network", "network segregation", "segregation index"]
definition: Network segregation is the correlation between firms' participation in the collaborative segment (G1) and the conflictual segment (G2) of the dual network at the same time. A value of -1 indicates a highly segregated network with two completely nonoverlapping segments, while 1 describes a uniformly mixed network.

name: Focused internal knowledge development
authors_terms: ["focused, internal knowledge development", "focused, internal knowledge development activity"]
definition: Patents in technology classes in which the venture had filed a patent in the previous five years (t-1 to t-5), classified as internal knowledge development activity when the patent was assigned only to the focal firm.

name: Diversifying internal knowledge development
authors_terms: ["diversifying, internal knowledge development", "diversifying, internal knowledge development activity"]
definition: Patenting in technology classes in which patents were not filed in the previous five years, classified as internal knowledge development activity when the patent was assigned only to the focal firm.

name: Focused alliance-based knowledge development
authors_terms: ["focused, alliance-based knowledge development", "focused, alliance-based knowledge development activity"]
definition: Patents in technology classes the venture had patented in during the previous five years that were jointly assigned to the focal firm and at least one other firm.

name: Diversifying alliance-based knowledge development
authors_terms: ["diversifying, alliance-based knowledge development", "diversifying, alliance-based knowledge development activity"]
definition: Patents in technology classes in which the venture had not patented in the previous five years that were jointly assigned to the focal firm and at least one other firm.

name: Post-IPO firm performance
definition: The authors consider a set of longer-term and more robust measures of post-IPO performance, such as survival, RoA, and Tobin's q: 'We do so with multiple measures of performance-i.e., survival, return on assets (RoA), and Tobin's q.'

name: Perceiver organization status
authors_terms: ["respondent firm status", "respondent status", "status of a respondent's firm", "status of a perceiver's organization", "hierarchical position of a perceiver's own organization"]
definition: We measure the status of a respondent's firm as the average rating received by a firm from survey respondents in a given year. This is the same way that Vault's published prestige scores are computed.

name: Perceived status differences
authors_terms: ["perceived status difference", "status differences between firms", "perceived status differences between a given set of organizations"]
definition: We measure respondent r's perceived status difference between firms i and j as respondent r's rating of firm i minus respondent r's rating of firm j. Such perceptual discontinuities reflect two properties of a typical status hierarchy: the status differences perceived by audience members are typically large and correlated.

name: Correlation of status perceptions
authors_terms: ["correlation between respondent r and respondent s", "correlations between individuals' perceptions of firm status", "correlation in raw ratings", "correlation in residual ratings"]
definition: We measure the correlation between respondent r and respondent s using the Pearson correlation coefficient between the respondents' ratings of the same set of firms i.

name: Surgical resource quality
authors_terms: ["surgical resource quality", "productive resource quality", "resource quality", "risk-adjusted mortality rate"]
definition: The productive resources in this study are specialist surgeons working on care teams in a hospital, whose most valuable resource skill is performing a specialist surgical service with minimal patient mortality and postoperative complications. Surgical resource quality proxies for productive resource quality and is operationalized by risk-adjusting actual surgeon outcomes for preexisting patient risk, following Huckman and Pisano (2006).

name: Bundled resource deployment
authors_terms: ["bundled resource deployment", "bundled deployment", "bundled deployment capability", "unbundled deployment", "unbundled resource deployment"]
definition: The patient-by-patient decision on how to constitute the care team: is the operating surgeon simultaneously the attending physician (a 'bundled deployment') or are these two roles split and leadership distributed across two different physicians (an 'unbundled deployment') with one responsible for only the operative, technical part and the other responsible more globally for the entire team's end result.

name: Hospital performance
authors_terms: ["firm's total task performance", "hospital performance", "firm performance", "task performance"]
definition: Hospital performance metrics such as market share, quality, and cost containment are examined as effects on hospital performance. All firm performance metrics are calculated at hospital*quarter level and are chosen to best reflect the appropriate dependent variable (Ray, Barney, and Muhanna, 2004).

name: Post-IPO performance
definition: We examined the performance impact of governance configurations firms can adopt in their early, post-IPO years, so we employed a market-based performance measure in the form of 24-month holding period returns (HPRs) for the 24 months immediately following the IPOs.

name: Original TMT board control
authors_terms: ["original TMT member board control", "original TMT members control a firm's board", "original TMT member-controlled boards", "original TMT member board majority", "original TMT member-board members"]
definition: We predict that the presence of a board on which a majority of the members are members of the firm's original top management team enhances performance in the years immediately following an IPO.

name: Original TMT ownership
authors_terms: ["original TMT member-board member ownership", "original TMT member-board member common stock ownership", "original TMT member-board member stock ownership", "TMT common stock ownership"]
definition: Original TMT member-board member ownership was the combined percentage of shares outstanding held collectively by directors who were original TMT members. We included in the percentage of shares outstanding held by original TMT members-board members all 'in-the-money' options held at the time of their firm's IPO and exercisable during the subsequent two years.

name: Ownership dispersion
authors_terms: ["original TMT member-board member ownership dispersion", "ownership dispersion", "distribution of ownership among TMT members"]
definition: The value of ownership dispersion increases as ownership is spread more evenly across a given number of original TMT directors.

name: Advice and counsel business experts
authors_terms: ["'advice and counsel' business experts", "advice and counsel business expert board members", "business experts not representing large shareholders"]
definition: Business experts not representing large shareholders would be less compelled to emphasize decision control. Their primary benefit should be facilitating strategic decision making and helping management navigate post-IPO waters.

name: Monitoring business experts
authors_terms: ["'monitoring' business experts", "monitoring business expert board members", "business experts representing large shareholders"]
definition: Business experts representing large shareholders may emphasize monitoring in the agency sense and be less helpful in the early post-IPO years.

name: Support specialists
definition: Support specialists lack general management experience but may possess expertise and connections in various areas in which the firm may need aid in the future. Drawn from professional fields such as law, accounting, public relations, and investment banking, they may have valuable ties to key external environmental actors with whom the firm must deal.

name: Demand agglomeration benefit
definition: Collocated firms compete with each other for customers, but they may attract more customers by collocating versus locating separately because they offer customers lower prices and/or reduced search costs when choosing among differentiated products. For a pair of firms, firm A's agglomeration benefit is proportional to firm B's size divided by the sum of firm A's size plus firm B's size, the 'size-benefit relationship.'

name: Neighboring firm exit
authors_terms: ["the exit of a neighboring firm", "neighbor's exit", "HHGregg's exit"]
definition: The agglomeration benefit is contingent upon the presence of another firm: the entry of firm B creates an agglomeration benefit for firm A, and the exit of firm B eliminates the benefit.

name: Focal firm size
authors_terms: ["the focal firm's size", "store size", "establishment's physical size", "square footage"]
definition: An establishment's physical size, its footprint in square feet, is expected to be correlated with the establishment's number of customers and how much customers spend, and thus to proxy for the potential demand agglomeration benefit it generates for neighboring establishments. The larger firm A is, the smaller firm A's agglomeration benefit from a given firm B.

name: Distance between focal and exiting firm
