authors_terms: ["distance between the focal and the exiting firm", "store_Distance"]
definition: Greater distance between firms increases transportation costs, which reduces the likelihood that one firm's customers visit the other firm; all else equal, as the distance between any two firms increases, the likelihood and magnitude of expected agglomeration benefits decreases.

name: Relatedness in economic activity
definition: Different firms may be involved in different economic activities, which vary in the extent of relatedness, with economic activities that are more related likely generating more agglomeration benefits. For demand agglomeration, two establishments in the same economic activity draw more customers than two establishments in different economic activities because, as competitors, they have the incentive to lower their price and/or differentiate their offerings.

name: Remaining neighbors' size
definition: A firm in a neighborhood is affected by its pairing with all of its neighbors, so a focal firm's total effect is the summation of all the individual pairs' effects. The larger the neighbor (firm B) is, the greater the agglomeration benefit for the focal firm, so having larger neighbors diminishes the loss from one neighbor's exit.

name: Distance to remaining neighbors
definition: Each neighbor's contribution to the focal firm's agglomeration benefit is also governed by distance between the neighbor and the focal firm; neighbors that are geographically closer generate more agglomeration benefits, which diminishes the loss from one neighbor's exit.

name: Remaining neighbors' relatedness
authors_terms: ["relatedness in economic activity between the neighbor and the focal firm", "store_avgNbrRelatedness"]
definition: Each neighbor's contribution to the focal firm's agglomeration benefit is governed by relatedness in economic activity between the neighbor and the focal firm; neighbors in more related activities generate more agglomeration benefits, which diminishes the loss from one neighbor's exit.

name: Focal store survival
definition: As obtaining store-specific revenue data is infeasible, survival is the store performance measure: how HHGregg's exit affects the survival of neighboring stores.

name: New technology adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of new technology", "new technology adoption", "level of new technology adoption", "levels of new switching technology adopted", "level of adoption"]
definition: The level of new switching technology adopted by firms is the dependent variable and is measured by the percentage of electronic to total switches, ADOPT, of a firm at each point in time.

name: Physical network size
authors_terms: ["physical network size", "size of the physical network", "conversion effect", "absolute size of the network", "relative size of the physical network"]
definition: In such cases the absolute as well as the relative size of the physical network controlled by the firm is important. As the size of the physical network increases, the marginal costs of replacing and operating the installed base of switches gets progressively lower.

name: Density and variety of the user population
authors_terms: ["density and variety of the user population", "consumption effect", "user density and variety", "density and composition of customers in the network"]
definition: This effect exists when there is demand interdependence among customers. This effect is enhanced by the density and composition of customers in the network.

name: Imitation
definition: The imitative effect is noted when firms model their behavior after firms perceived to be similar. The effect is salient in industries where firms share a common infrastructure, such as railroads or telecommunications.

name: Corporate venture capital program adoption
authors_terms: ["CVC program adoption", "adoption of a corporate venture capital program", "likelihood of adoption by focal organization"]
definition: We define the adoption of a corporate venture capital program as occurring when an established corporation creates a structurally distinct entity dedicated to making external equity investments in a portfolio of high-potential young enterprises.

name: Geographic proximity to a venture capital cluster
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity to a VC population cluster", "geographic distance to VC clusters", "proximity to the originating population"]
definition: Geographic proximity to a VC population cluster affords a prospective IT adopter direct exposure to the innovation itself, in situ. It allows members to obtain first-hand knowledge about the VC model-the requisite skills, values, procedures, behaviors, and know-how involved.

name: Efficacy of venture capital investments
authors_terms: ["efficacy of the investments made by the VC population", "observed benefits of VC practices", "observing success in the originating population"]
definition: Evidence of beneficial consequences flowing from the innovation in its originating population: vivid and reliable evidence that an endemic innovation is paying off for firms in another population should persuade performance-oriented decision makers to consider adopting it themselves.

name: Popularity of the innovation
authors_terms: ["popularity of the innovation", "popularity among peers", "number of prior adopters"]
definition: An innovation's popularity within a population, manifested by the number of prior adopters in the population; increases in an innovation's popularity, as reflected in the extent to which it has already diffused within an organizational population, are positively related to within-population contagion.

name: Prominence of prior adopters
authors_terms: ["prominence of prior adopters", "prominence of similar adopters", "prior adoption among prominent IT firms"]
definition: Prospective adopters are especially likely to be influenced by the moves of more prestigious organizations within their population. Organization-level traits such as size and profitability are often used to infer social prominence.

name: Outcomes experienced by prior adopters
authors_terms: ["outcomes experienced by prior adopters", "efficacious outcomes experienced by IT firms that are prior adopters", "observing peers' success"]
definition: Beneficial results obtained by prior similar adopters will lead prospective adopters to anticipate similar results; the rate at which firms select ventures from their CVC portfolios as acquisitions is an indicator of the vitality of CVC programs.

name: Proximity to prior IT adopters
authors_terms: ["proximate prior adopters", "proximity to similar adopters", "proximity to prior adopters"]
definition: Spatial proximity to previously adopting population members, which is expected to speed an innovation's diffusion; the measure captures the availability of innovation-related information through observation of and interaction with industry peers.

name: Within-population contagion
authors_terms: ["within-population contagion", "adoption behavior of other IT firms", "within-population contagion influences"]
definition: Within-population contagion spreads a formerly endemic innovation from prior adopter to prospective adopter within a new organizational population.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "excess value", "Tobin's q", "value of the firm"]
definition: This article uses two market measures of firm value: excess value, defined as the degree to which a diversified firm's value exceeds that of a portfolio of single segment firms competing in the same industries, and the natural log of Tobin's q. Using Tobin's q is an improvement over accounting measures as it incorporates forward-looking market valuations.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Corporate diversification is the central independent variable in this article, which adopts a simple, discrete measure of the type of diversification in which a firm can engage-an indicator variable equal to one if the firm operates in multiple industries. A firm is considered nondiversified (i.e., focused) if it operates in a single four-digit SIC industry. It is considered diversified if it operates in more than one four-digit SIC industry.

name: Related diversification
definition: A firm is said to be engaging in related diversification when it exploits resources and capabilities across multiple different businesses simultaneously. Among diversified firms, a firm is considered a related diversifier if it has any two segments in the same two-digit SIC industry.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: Unrelated diversification refers to corporate diversification strategies that do not leverage economies of scope across multiple businesses. Firms are categorized as unrelated diversifiers if they do not have any two segments in the same two-digit SIC industry.

name: Expected value of diversification
authors_terms: ["expected value of diversification", "expected, long-term impact of diversification on performance", "firm-specific diversification coefficient"]
definition: The value V_it that the firm derives from diversification is influenced by the expected, long-term impact of diversification on performance, betaDi/(1 - rhoi). Under the assumption of rational, profit-maximizing behavior, firms that derive a larger benefit from diversification are more likely to diversify.

name: Sociopolitical reputation
authors_terms: ["sociopolitical reputation", "net social CSR", "perceived commitments to social CSR", "social CSR"]
definition: I develop a sociopolitical dimension of reputation that applies when public policy makers attempt to discriminate within the category of legitimate firms. Firms' noneconomic, social, and political characteristics and practices allow them to construct sociopolitical reputations, which then serve as differentiating heuristics for resource-dependent and cognitively limited policy makers.

name: Access to public policy makers
authors_terms: ["access", "access to public policy makers", "access to Congress", "appearances"]
definition: Firms can only influence public policy making if they first have access to public policy makers. Counting appearances before congressional committees is a common technique for measuring access to policy makers, and invitations to testify are a limited good that organizations compete over.

name: Democratic control of Congress
definition: The differing institutional logics underlying the two major political parties' ideologies suggest that partisan control will affect the relationship between sociopolitical reputation and access. Since Democrats are more skeptical of business and place a stronger emphasis on social responsibility, the effect of sociopolitical reputation on access will be elevated when Democrats have greater power within Congress as an organization.

name: PAC contributions
definition: Contributions made by each firm's associated PAC to congressional candidates; by providing funds that members need to run their reelection campaigns, interest groups are effectively buying access.

name: Lobbying expenditures
definition: Each firm's annual federal lobbying expenditures. Lobbying is best understood as the communication of information between interest groups and policy makers, providing a conduit through which a firm draws policy makers' attention to its sociopolitical reputation.

name: Social trust
definition: Social trust, also known as generalized trust, is the trust that people have in their fellow members of society in general. Bilateral trust refers to the amount of generalized trust that people from one country have in people from another country.

name: Foundational skill orientation
authors_terms: ["foundational versus advanced skills", "foundational and advanced skills", "foundational-advanced skills", "foundational score", "preference for foundational skills"]
definition: The more-foundational skills are those that provide a foundation upon which people can develop other skills, while the more-advanced skills are those that require more skills as prerequisites. Foundational and advanced skills constitute two ends of a continuum.

name: Credentials
definition: Many jobs require credentials such as degrees, certifications, and work experience. Jobs that require more credentials provide key information that could help reduce employers' uncertainty about candidates' intentions and career objectives.

name: Referrals
definition: Employers could encourage employees to refer qualified candidates for openings. Referred candidates provide additional information from their referees, potentially relying less on social trust.

name: JIT performance
definition: JIT performance can be measured by inventory turnover, cycle time, lead time, delivery performance, and other measures. JIT performance was measured by average cycle time (CT), which the authors describe as a standard measure of JIT performance.

name: Quality performance
definition: Quality performance measures include customers' perceptions of quality, defects in parts per million, and the percentage of units that pass final inspection without requiring rework. It was measured by a five-point Likert scale that asked managers to describe their own and their customers' perceptions of the quality of the goods produced by a plant, relative to competitors'.

name: Common infrastructure practices
definition: We include as infrastructure practices those activities that have been frequently cited in the relevant literature as supporting both JIT and TQM. These practices are divided into five dimensions: information feedback, plant environment, management support, supplier relationship, and workforce management.

name: Information feedback
definition: Information feedback provides a workforce with process and performance information to assist in decentralized management of the production process and variance minimization.

name: Plant environment
definition: Maintenance of a clean and well-organized plant environment facilitates quick changeover between products and an orderly approach to problem solving; the scale deals with the development of a neat, organized, and predictable workplace.

name: Management support
definition: Management support includes communication of strategy, development of a corporate culture, or the "social energy that drives—or fails to drive—the organization", and rewarding JIT and TQM efforts. Management support is critical because it provides direction and validation to JIT and TQM efforts.

name: Supplier relationship
definition: Infrastructure activities encouraging the development of a supplier relationship supportive of TQM and JIT include basing selection of suppliers on quality and time criteria rather than on cost criteria, establishment of long-term mutually supportive relationships, and frequent meetings between purchasers and suppliers to exchange technical, economic, and managerial information and services.

name: Workforce management
definition: Workforce management involves investments in the training and development, selection, and retention of employees. Thus, investments in workforce management increase the human capital of an organization, which has economic value to the firm.

name: Unique JIT practices
definition: JIT is based on the notion of eliminating waste through the simplification of manufacturing processes. Practices unique to JIT are divided into four dimensions: kanban, lot size reduction, setup time reduction, and JIT scheduling.

name: Kanban
definition: Kanban controls the movement of orders to a shop floor; because a kanban card must be attached to every container of parts, the amount of inventory on the shop floor is controlled by the number of cards permitted.

name: Lot size reduction practices
definition: Lot size reduction practices minimize inventory and increase flexibility.

name: Setup time reduction practices
definition: Setup time reduction practices have as their goal the reduction of the times required to change machines over to work on a group of different parts, which is an economic prerequisite to the use of smaller manufacturing lots.

name: JIT scheduling
definition: JIT scheduling activities include mixed model scheduling and scheduling daily production to match demand.

name: Unique TQM practices
definition: Total quality management (TQM) is an approach to improving the quality of goods and services, founded on continuous improvement of all processes, customer-driven quality, production without defects, focus on improvement of processes rather than criticism of people, and data-based decision making. Practices that are unique to TQM are divided into three dimensions: statistical process control, product design, and customer focus.

name: Statistical process control
definition: Statistical process control is the use of statistical process control charts to provide operators with feedback, allowing them to base their actions on the variability of the manufacturing process.

name: Product design for quality
definition: Product design for quality includes improving design characteristics through design for manufacturability and reliability engineering, interfunctional design efforts, and new product quality efforts, incorporating trial runs, extensive prototyping, and design modifications prior to release to manufacturing.

name: Customer focus
definition: Through customer focus, TQM practices are designed to better assess both customer needs and an organization's effectiveness in meeting them, in order to develop a match between them.

name: Local density
definition: Local density is defined as the number of firms vying for similar resources in a local environment. Density is a measure of the number of firms in a population (for example, an industry) vying for similar resources, and because firms in an industry often cluster in locations such as cities, density varies across geographic areas within a country.

name: Market experience
definition: Over time, liability of foreignness is expected to decline as a foreign subsidiary accumulates market knowledge regarding customer preferences, suppliers, and institutions; market experience enables the foreign subsidiary to make more informed decisions in the host country.

name: Strategic conformity
definition: Strategic conformity reflects the degree to which a firm's strategy corresponds to the average strategic profile of industry rivals.

name: Foreign subsidiary performance
definition: Foreign subsidiary performance is measured by the return on assets (ROA) of a foreign subsidiary for a current year; ROA is a commonly used measure of bank performance in both strategy and finance research.

name: Manager control
definition: Firms that are manager-controlled are those with diffused ownership; the managers of these firms may be abusive as their control is unlikely to be challenged by diffused stockholders. Firms without a significant external shareholder and without an owner-manager were classified as manager-controlled.

name: Owner control
definition: Owner-controlled firms have a significant shareholder who closely monitors the strategies of top managers, thereby limiting the ability of the top executives to engage in abusive behavior. Significant owners are defined as those with at least 5 percent of their firm's stock.

name: Owner-manager control
definition: Owner-manager-controlled firms, or corporations with significant owners as CEOs, have top managers who as owners may be motivated to undertake acquisitions that benefit the shareholders, but who as managers may have abusive tendencies. These individuals have significant financial investments in their organizations.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size (sales)", "sales", "size of the organization", "increases in size"]
definition: Firm size is measured via total sales; since acquisitions result in larger firm sizes, acquisitions of manager-controlled organizations are expected to result in increases in CEO compensation.

name: CEO rewards
authors_terms: ["CEO rewards", "executive rewards", "managerial rewards", "changes in top manager rewards", "compensation"]
definition: Changes in top manager rewards consisted of changes in total cash payments, deferred compensation, and the annual changes in the values of CEO stockholdings, adjusted for inflation. Total changes in inflation-adjusted rewards were measured for a 5-year period, beginning 2 years before the announcement of the acquisition and ending 2 years following the year of the announcement.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["excess returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "quality of acquisitions", "acquisition performance"]
definition: The effect of an acquisition announcement on corporate value is assessed as the excess returns accruing to shareholders. For the purpose of the study, quality of acquisitions is assessed in terms of cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) as measured by the event-study method.

name: Refining R&D knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["refining R&D capital stock", "refining R&D capital stock intensity", "stocks of knowledge from past refining R&D", "refining-based technological knowledge"]
definition: Refining-based technological knowledge within the firm, accumulated through past R&D on oil refining, which may produce economies of scope. Because a speculative technology has less of an accumulated knowledge base on which to draw, a firm conducting such R&D may rely heavily on knowledge acquired from R&D and operations in technologically related business applications such as refining.

name: Refinery assets
definition: A firm's accumulated refinery assets provide a rough measure of the extent of a firm's experience in utilizing established refinery technologies.

name: Other synfuels R&D knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["other synfuels R&D capital stock", "stocks of knowledge from past R&D on other synthetic fuels", "other synthetic fuels R&D"]
definition: Knowledge acquired via prior R&D on other synthetic fuels (oil shale and tar sands). R&D on the processing of synthetic fuels from oil shale and tar sands in part involves extensions of established refinery technology, and thus could have produced some knowledge useful for coal conversion.

name: Coal assets
authors_terms: ["coal-related asset intensity", "accumulated coal assets", "coal reserves", "coal assets"]
definition: For coal conversion, a key asset required for commercialization is coal. Such reserves included coal owned by some firms prior to the 1973-74 embargo, as well as new investments in coal reserves as energy prices rose.

name: Coal conversion R&D
authors_terms: ["coal gasification/liquefaction R&D", "coal conversion R&D", "coal gasification/liquefaction R&D intensity"]
definition: R&D on coal gasification and liquefaction, the technologies on which the firms spent a disproportionately large share of their alternative energy R&D and which have the potential to produce a natural gas substitute of pipeline quality or substitutes for traditional refined oil products.

name: Past coal conversion R&D
authors_terms: ["lagged coal conversion R&D", "past coal conversion R&D", "lagged dependent variable"]
definition: The amount of past coal conversion R&D may have influenced the amount of current R&D as a result of at least two factors: organizational learning and adjustment costs. Both imply that R&D may have a strong inertial component.

name: Financial resources
definition: Firms' financial resources may have affected the amount of coal conversion R&D; overall company profits or cash flows may affect the level of R&D activity if, for example, firms are unwilling to share information about proprietary technologies with external capital markets in order to obtain funds for R&D.

name: Other firms' coal conversion R&D
authors_terms: ["industry coal conversion R&D capital stock", "other firms' coal conversion R&D", "other firms' coal conversion R&D capital stock"]
definition: Lagged total FRS firm coal conversion R&D capital stock minus own-firm coal conversion R&D capital stock serves as a proxy for external knowledge spillovers and also perhaps for an effect of R&D rivalry.

name: Oil and gas recovery R&D knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["oil and gas recovery R&D capital stock intensity", "oil and gas recovery R&D capital stock"]
definition: The firm's R&D capital stock in oil and gas recovery, a knowledge area that coal gasification/liquefaction R&D does not have strong know-how linkages to.

name: Other R&D knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["other R&D capital stock intensity", "general expertise in conducting R&D", "remainder of the firm's R&D capital stock"]
definition: A firm's general expertise in conducting R&D, represented by the remainder of the firm's R&D capital stock, might provide complementary knowledge for coal conversion R&D, although it has less direct commonality of technical knowledge with coal conversion than R&D and operations which utilize refining technology.

name: Market valuation
definition: MVit refers to the market value of company i at time t. We calculate the market value of company i at time t (MVit) by multiplying the stock price times the number of common shares outstanding and adding company debt.

name: Resource valuation
authors_terms: ["resource valuation", "resource value", "intrinsic value of the gold mine", "objective valuation of the physical assets", "RVjit"]
definition: RVjit reflects the current valuation of mine j of company i at time t, evaluated with an industry standard resource valuation model that builds upon the Hotelling valuation principle. Our measure of resource value is, by contrast, a better estimate of these mining firms' replacement value of assets (i.e., the denominator in Tobin's Q ratio).

name: Stakeholder support
authors_terms: ["stakeholder conflict/cooperation", "stakeholder support", "stakeholder cooperation", "stakeholder engagement", "degree of conflict or cooperation with different social, political, and economic stakeholders"]
definition: Activities perceived by stakeholders as socially responsible build up political and social capital that enhances stakeholder cooperation and reduces stakeholder conflict. The resulting empirical prediction is that holding constant the objective value of a firm's assets, its market valuation increases with stakeholder support.

name: Policy credibility
authors_terms: ["policy credibility", "policy certainty", "credibility of the formal policy environment", "credibility of the national policy environment"]
definition: We also seek to adjust the resource valuation for the credibility of the formal license to operate. Where the current concession, taxation, or royalty agreements lack credibility, investors may apply a discount to the resource valuation irrespective of the degree of stakeholder conflict/cooperation under the premise that a future government could more readily alter policies in a manner inimical to investors.

name: Excess physical capacity
authors_terms: ["physical resources", "excess physical capacity", "excess plant and equipment"]
definition: Physical resources of a firm, such as plant and equipment, are characterized by fixed capacity. A firm would have a relatively lower backlog of orders during a period when it has excess capacity.

name: Intangible assets
definition: Intangible assets include brand names or innovative capability. Unlike physical assets, intangible assets tend to have 'softer' capacity constraints and usually accrue to a firm over time, residing in the human capital of the firm in the form of knowledge and expertise.

name: Internal funds
definition: The first class, internal funds, consists of liquidity at hand and unused debt capacity to borrow at normal rates.

name: Equity capital
authors_terms: ["equity capital", "external funds", "ability to raise external capital"]
definition: The second class, external funds, consists of new equity and possibly high-risk debts (such as junk bonds).

name: Relatedness of diversification
authors_terms: ["type of diversification", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification", "degree of relatedness"]
definition: Most recent literature considers the issue a matter of degree which is continuously variable. The phrase 'type of diversification' should be understood as degrees of relatedness which can vary continuously from horizontal to unrelated.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use the average return on assets (ROA) over the period 1984-86 to measure ex-post performance.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Foreign ownership, the independent variable, is the percent shares held by foreign investors obtained from the Japan Company Handbook. Foreign owners are typically portfolio investors who frequently buy and sell shares and hold diversified portfolios of small stakes in many firms.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: Tobin (1969) proposed the ratio of market value of capital to replacement value, termed Q, as a measure of the desirability of additional investment. Strategic investments are more beneficial when firms have the potential to benefit from such investment, i.e., when firms have growth opportunities than when growth opportunities are unavailable.

name: Strategic investment
definition: Ownership structure has implications for long-term strategic investments that are needed to build competencies and exploit growth opportunities to maximize long-term profitability. We test these competing perspectives by examining the effect of foreign ownership on two types of strategic investments-R&D and capital intensity-in Japanese corporations.

name: Deviation from performance benchmarks
definition: The authors suggest that uncertainty concerning firms' relative abilities is best approximated via deviations from performance benchmarks; performance is one of the most important indicators of the condition of a for-profit firm and any deviation from this yardstick signals uncertainty about the firm's condition.

name: Reference group adaptation
authors_terms: ["reference-group adaptations", "changes in the self-selected references", "reference group change"]
definition: The main dependent variable, reference-group adaptations, is a dummy variable that captures whether a focal hotel adjusted (i.e., discontinued an existing reference, adopted a new reference) its selected references in t0 relative to t-1.

name: Reference group similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity between references and the selecting hotel", "references with more similar characteristics", "relative same class", "same quality class"]
definition: Only a comparison with an organization with similar attributes (in the case of hotels, the most important attributes concern class affiliation such as luxury or economy) can provide diagnostic information; comparing oneself with an organization with unrelated attributes yields ambiguous results because performance differences tend to reflect the different attributes rather than differences in inherent ability.

name: Slack time
definition: Break weeks are periods when the opportunity cost of time is lower; they should be broadly interpreted as uninterrupted periods of time during which individuals do not need to attend to their regular tasks, but are allowed to experiment with new projects more freely.

name: Quantity of projects
authors_terms: ["quantity of ideas developed", "number of projects", "number of crowdfunding campaigns"]
definition: The outcome variable is the number of projects posted on the platform in city c during week t; the paper examines the quantity of ideas developed.

name: Project value
definition: The realized value of a project v depends on two factors: the idea's intrinsic quality q (i.e., its latent potential), and the amount of effort devoted to developing the project, e. Funds raised are used as a proxy for a project's commercial potential and revealed market demand.

name: Effort provision
definition: The amount of effort (or, equivalently, time in this context) devoted to developing a project, e; given any quality level, less effort is spent when time is more precious, and more effort is spent when the idea is better.

name: Project complexity
definition: Complex projects are those that require people with complementary skills and perspectives; two proxies are used, the number of unique skills listed and the number of unique skills divided by the size of the team.

name: Use of teams
definition: Projects may be carried out by teams because with multiple people sharing the workload a team can achieve more than a single person, and because complex projects may require people with complementary skills and perspectives.

name: Minimum effort requirement
authors_terms: ["minimum effort requirement", "posting requirement", "minimum amount of effort required"]
definition: The minimum amount of effort required to have a project accepted by the platform, represented in the model by e-bar; a change in this threshold corresponds to an organizational change targeted at reducing low-quality contributions.

name: Market orientation
definition: A market orientation is a behavioral culture, the principal features of which are actionable, that dictates how an organization's employees think and act; it represents behaviors required for the implementation of the marketing concept.

name: Marketing strategy orientation
definition: These elements comprise the strategy orientation that ultimately form policies and programs that facilitate implementation.

name: Competitive context
definition: Contextual variables are generally uncontrollable by any one firm and are considered to be external in respect to control.

name: Performance
definition: The outcome element of the behavior-action-outcome model, measured as return on investment in a coalignment perspective.

name: Coalignment
definition: This model is a holistic environment-strategy-performance coalignment conceptualization in that it considers the interrelationship among primary elements of market orientation, strategy elements, contextual variables, and organizational performance.

name: Firm-level characteristics
definition: The idea that a firm's attributes, possessions, and actions are driving forces behind performance has long been central to the strategy field. In the analysis, firm characteristics are modeled as latent factors.

name: Strategic group
definition: Strategic groups are naturally occurring subsets of firms that are more homogeneous in actions than is found across industry incumbents in general.

name: Industry
definition: Indirectly, industry membership affects performance through strategic perspectives and actions. More directly, performance appears to be impacted by industry traits such as complexity, rivalry, and regulatory changes.

name: Firm performance
definition: To capture the multidimensional nature of firm performance, we examine a short-term accounting measure (ROA), a market measure (Tobin's Q), and a measure of default risk or bankruptcy propensity (Altman's Z).

name: Entertainment agency status
authors_terms: ["agency status", "entertainment agency's status", "entertainment agency status", "producer's status", "producers' status"]
definition: Status is defined as the prestige accorded to social actors based on their hierarchical position, which reflects both their access to resources and the identity-based expectations of relevant audiences. High-status agencies are well-known among fans and the general public and have better access to resources such as foreign composers and choreographers.

name: Concept alignment with market-dominant concept
authors_terms: ["alignment between their idol group's concept category and the dominant concept category in the market", "similarity with market dominant concept", "concept similarity", "category alignment with market trends"]
definition: The alignment (similarity) between an idol group's new concept and the market-dominant concept, where the market-dominant concept is defined as the concept that appeared most frequently among the songs released 6 months before the focal song. Aligning an idol group's concept with the dominant trend can help attract a broader audience.

name: Concept category shift magnitude
authors_terms: ["magnitude of their idol group's category shift", "distance from idol group's previous concept", "radical shifts", "radical category shifts", "magnitude of concept change"]
definition: Radical shifts refer to changes that are significantly different from prior categories and involve actions that the idol group has not previously attempted. The paper measures the distance between the idol group's current concept and their previous concept.

name: Idol group gender
authors_terms: ["gender of the idol group", "idol group's gender", "gender of idol groups"]
definition: The gender of the idol group; the authors examine gender as an ingrained and pervasive social system that shapes audience expectations. Gender, as a form of ascribed status (as opposed to achieved status), can moderate the influence of achieved status.

name: Diversity climate
definition: Employees' shared perceptions about the extent to which their business unit values diversity by utilizing fair practices and socially integrating all personnel.

name: Service climate
definition: A climate referent that denotes employees' shared perceptions regarding the policies, practices, and behaviors rewarded in regard to customer service, signalling the importance placed upon providing high-quality service.

name: Minority representation
authors_terms: ["minority representation", "percentage of minority associates", "employee minority representation"]
definition: The percentage of nonwhite employees working in a store unit.

name: Female representation
definition: The percentage of female employees working in a store unit.

name: Customer satisfaction
definition: Customers' evaluations of their store experience, computed as the percentage of customers who indicated 'strongly agree' in response to an overall summary question about their satisfaction with their overall experience at the company.

name: Issues management structural development
authors_terms: ["issues management structural development", "issues management structures", "structural development", "issues management structure"]
definition: The five dimensions of issues management structural development were the formalization of issues management activities, the resources expended for issues management, committee use, and the integration of issues management activities into corporate planning and line activities.

name: Media exposure
authors_terms: ["issue-related media exposure", "firm-specific media exposure about issues", "issue-specific media exposure"]
definition: Exposure of a firm to issue-related articles in the news media; the authors treat the media as an institutional stakeholder creating both coercive and normative pressures for conformity to public expectations.

name: Interest group pressure
definition: Pressure from interest groups, which the authors argue play a critical role in elevating concern about issues to a level at which there is institutional pressure for corporations and many of which focus their attention and resources directly on regulating the behavior of corporations.

name: Crisis severity
definition: A crisis was defined for respondents as an accident, scandal, or catastrophe that resulted in loss of profits, injuries, loss of life, damage, loss of reputation, or tarnishing of image; crises create another form of institutional pressure, albeit an indirect one.

name: Organization size
definition: Because issues management is primarily an administrative or staff function, the size of a firm may influence the level of its development; large organizations have sufficient resources and scale that they can alter their contexts in a significant fashion.

name: Top management commitment
authors_terms: ["top management commitment", "top management commitment to issues", "commitment of top management"]
definition: A managerial characteristic, top management commitment to attend to the social and political environment, which the authors contend positively influences firms' adoption of issues management structures.

name: CEO compensation
definition: The dependent variable in our study is total CEO compensation, which consists of salary, bonuses, the value of restricted stock granted, the value of options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and other compensation.

name: Firm performance
definition: For our independent variable, firm performance, we use industry-adjusted stock returns. We use a market-based measure instead of other performance indicators for two reasons. First, boards are sensitive to firms' performance in the stock market because a decline in stock price can increase external pressure (e.g., investor activism). Second, CEO compensation has a stronger connection to market performance than accounting performance.

name: Corporate strategic investment
authors_terms: ["corporate-level strategic investments", "strategic investments", "corporate strategic investment intensity", "corporate-level spending"]
definition: One way CEOs affect firm performance is by making corporate-level strategic investments (or just 'strategic investments' for brevity), which refer to major investments designed to grow the firm. Most importantly, they require a significant commitment of the company's resources. They are also difficult to implement and reverse.

name: CEO prestige
definition: Scholars have looked at a variety of aspects of prestige, such as social status, education, and media attention. Others consider prestige in terms of ' superstar ' CEOs that have won media awards for their achievements, which is the approach we adopt in this study.

name: Board political conservatism
definition: Political ideologies describe how people will vote, but they also affect decisions in various nonpolitical domains. Scholars rely on where people fall on a liberalism-conservatism spectrum to capture political ideology. Those with liberal ideologies favor social justice and egalitarianism, whereas those with conservative ideologies emphasize free markets and individualism.

name: Group fear
authors_terms: ["group fear", "fear of losing more money", "fear of the financial consequences of failure", "fear of losing a lot of money"]
definition: We capture a specific dimension of fear of failure: fear of the financial consequences of failure (i.e., increasing monetary sum entrepreneurial teams risk by escalating their commitment).

name: Group hope
authors_terms: ["group hope", "hope of turning the situation around", "state hope"]
definition: Hope is an explicitly anticipatory emotion involving the feeling that an unfavorable situation can be improved in the future. We focus upon hope for the ultimate success of a venture, specifically for the positive financial consequences associated with overcoming a negative financial situation, including recuperating losses and ultimately making a profit.

name: Group engagement
definition: Group engagement is a state in which group members jointly invest personal energy, emotionally connect with their work, and commit their psychological presence through attention and absorption in a task.

name: Group friendship strength
authors_terms: ["group friendship strength", "friendship strength", "the closeness of the friendships among a team's members"]
definition: The authors focus on the closeness of the friendships among a team's members, which they treat as more inherently affective than broader social constructs such as strong ties and group cohesion and as important in determining group processes in entrepreneurial teams.

name: Escalation of commitment
authors_terms: ["escalation of commitment", "escalating commitment", "terminating a currently failing venture", "venture termination", "ceasing escalation of commitment", "quit"]
definition: Escalation of commitment to a currently failing venture, which the authors contrast with termination of that venture; it involves persistence in the face of mounting sunk costs, negative feedback, a continuous decision-making process, and the opportunity to withdraw at set decision points.

name: Prior mergers of the same type
authors_terms: ["prior mergers of the same type", "cumulative count of prior mergers", "prior merger activity"]
definition: A cumulative count of the mergers of a given type that a firm has completed; when a firm engages in an acquisition it develops competency in the process of making that type of acquisition, and each acquisition of the same type increases the likelihood of more acquisitions of that type.

name: Merger activity
authors_terms: ["merger activity", "merger rates", "instantaneous probability of a merger"]
definition: The occurrence of mergers by a firm, modeled as the instantaneous probability of a merger at time t given the state of the particular firm at time t. The marginal rates for all four types of mergers were estimated simultaneously.

name: Product market diversification
definition: A firm's current strategic position in terms of its choice of product/market domain, measured by Rumelt's classification of the extent to which revenues are spread over distinct businesses. A broad definition of domain should make managers more likely to engage in diversifying mergers.

name: Structural decentralization
definition: The extent to which the firm's administrative structure is decentralized, ranging from functional firms to holding companies. Contextual momentum means that a decentralized structure should lead to diversifying actions.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Ownership concentration was calculated as a Herfindhal-Hirschman index based on the retained ownership of listed blockholders in the prospectus for each firm, which, apart from VCs and BAs, also included founders, industry partners, non-founding directors, and others.

name: IPO firm performance
definition: The percent price premium [(offer price-book value per share)/offer price] assesses investor optimism about the future value of IPO firms and demonstrates the difference between the accounting and the market value.

name: Venture capital retained ownership
authors_terms: ["VC retained ownership", "VC ownership", "retained ownership of VCs"]
definition: Retained ownership of the venture capitalists is calculated as a percentage of the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO date; VCs are 'formal' private equity investors, typically general partners of a limited partnership or employees of a bank or other financial institution specializing in directing investments in new ventures.

name: Business angel retained ownership
authors_terms: ["BA retained ownership", "BA ownership", "retained ownership of BAs"]
definition: Retained ownership of business angels is calculated as a percentage of the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO date; BAs are wealthy, successful individuals who, in contrast to VCs, are longer-term investors and are their own principals.

name: Legal institutions
definition: Legal institutions help form 'the rules of the game in a society' and can vary significantly across nations, with common law countries offering the strongest legal protection of minority shareholders and French civil law countries the weakest investor protection.

name: Business planning
authors_terms: ["business planning", "business plan", "completed business plan", "business planning measure"]
definition: We define business planning as those efforts by firm founders to gather information about a business opportunity and to specify how that information will be used to create a new organization to exploit the opportunity. Following prior researchers, we include as part of business planning the processes of gathering and analyzing information, evaluating required tasks, identifying risks and strategy, projecting financial developments, and documenting these things in a written plan.

name: New venture disbanding
authors_terms: ["venture disbanding", "disbanding", "hazard of venture disbanding", "hazard of disbanding"]
definition: We define venture disbanding as the cessation of the venture by all members of the team pursuing it. We require the entire venture team to cease pursuit of the opportunity to define a venture as disbanded because the composition of venture teams often changes over time and the cessation of effort by the respondent does not necessarily indicate the disbanding of the venture.

name: Product development
definition: Product development, which we define as the creation of the product or service that the venture will sell.

name: Venture organizing activity
definition: Venture organizing activity, which we define as activities to establish the organization that will provide the new product or service. Venture organizing consists of those activities that establish the physical structure and organizational processes of a new firm (Bhave, 1994).

name: Foreign owner-manager
authors_terms: ["owner-manager", "foreign owner-manager", "foreign entrepreneur-manager", "foreign entrepreneurs who choose to manage their firms personally"]
definition: We determine that a firm has a foreign owner-manager when one of its foreign owners is also a CEO. The owner-manager variable is a dummy variable that equals 1 when a firm has an owner-manager and 0 when a firm has a hired CEO.

name: Firm performance
definition: Following prior research (e.g., Anderson and Reeb, 2003), we measure firm performance as the operating return on assets (OROA), i.e., the ratio of operating profit to the book value of assets.

name: Operating costs
definition: Owner-managers can increase firm profits by reducing operating costs, increasing the productivity of assets, or both. Foreign owner-managers are able to significantly reduce firms' operating costs.

name: Revenue
definition: In Table 4, we examine the impact of foreign owner-managers on the firm's operating costs and revenue. Our results suggest that foreign owner-managers are able to significantly reduce firms' operating costs but have no impact on revenue and revenue growth.

name: Revenue growth
definition: Owner-managers could also use extra profit to grow their firms at a higher rate. Our results suggest that foreign owner-managers are able to significantly reduce firms' operating costs but have no impact on revenue and revenue growth.

name: Distance between owner and firm
authors_terms: ["distance between the owner's home base and the firm", "ln (distance)", "distance"]
definition: We measure the natural logarithm of the distance between the city where the firm is located and the home country of the firm owners.

name: Regional unemployment rate
authors_terms: ["region unemployment rate", "regional unemployment rate", "local competition for resources"]
definition: The measure of annual regional unemployment rate comes from the Russian Statistical Services website. We expect that the ability to engage cost-efficient foreign resources would be more valuable when local competition for resources is high and less valuable when local competition is low.

name: Home-country management practices
authors_terms: ["management practices", "average management practice score", "average management score of companies in the home country"]
definition: We use a measure of management practices developed by Bloom and Van Reenen (2007). We calculate an average management practice score of firms in the entrepreneur's home country.

name: Political affinity
authors_terms: ["political affinity", "similarity of national interests in global affairs"]
definition: Political affinity is defined as the similarity of national interests in global affairs. Political affinity is high when national interests between countries align, and vice versa.

name: Initial acquisition premium
authors_terms: ["initial acquisition premium", "initial bid premium", "initial premium", "initial offer price"]
definition: The initial acquisition (or bid) premium refers to the difference between the price proposed for a target firm and the pre-acquisition market value. It offers insights into business decision-making; it accounts for the acquirer's anticipated bargaining position in its negotiations with the target firm.

name: Government fractionalization
definition: It captures the likelihood that 'two members of parliament-picked at random-from governing parties belong to different parties.' A high fractionalization index indicates that the government consists of a large number of small parties, while a low fractionalization index indicates that the government consists of a small number of strong parties, possibly only one party.

name: Bilateral economic dependence
authors_terms: ["economic dependence of the host on the home country", "trade dependence", "economic interdependencies"]
definition: The ability to take coercive action is likely to vary across home countries because the vulnerability of the host country to retaliatory behavior depends on the degree of economic dependence of the host on the home country. With a higher degree of economic dependence, host government intervention against the foreign acquirer should become more costly, and therefore, less likely.

name: Product value
definition: A measure of performance closely related to the development of new products: productvalue is a measure of product-level outcomes based on independent expert ratings of three categories of LCD products (televisions, monitors, and laptop screens) from 1987 to 2005.

name: Precommercialization patenting in the losing technology
authors_terms: ["PRE-1983 PLASMA PATENTS", "precommercialization patenting in the losing technology", "early plasma patenting"]
definition: The firm's knowledge-creation investment in the losing technology before the resolution of uncertainty, measured with a count of early (pre-1983) patents in the losing technology (plasma).

name: Precommercialization patenting in the winning technology
authors_terms: ["PRE-1983 LCD PATENTS", "precommercialization patenting in the winning technology", "early LCD investment"]
definition: The firm's knowledge-creation investment in the winning technology before the dominant design emerged, measured with a count of early (pre-1983) patents in the winning technology (LCD); every pre-1983 LCD patent was missing at least one element of the dominant design.

name: Late initiation of patenting
authors_terms: ["LATE PATENTER", "late initiation of patenting in either technology", "firms that wait until uncertainty is resolved"]
definition: Firms that wait until uncertainty is resolved and the dominant design has been crowned avoid inefficient decisions and reduce their risk, but lack the experience-driven resources and knowledge that earlier investors accumulate.

name: Corporate reputation
authors_terms: ["Fortune reputation ratings", "corporate reputation rankings", "Fortune reputation score", "reputation ranking"]
definition: Since the early 1980s Fortune has published yearly numerical corporate reputation scores, displayed in ranked order. The authors suggest that although Fortune refers to its list as ranking reputation, social dialogues and judgments affect the rankings, so the list captures both status, which is socially defined, and reputation, which is defined by both social and market-based characteristics.

name: Traditional financial performance
authors_terms: ["traditional financial indicator", "traditional financial variables", "traditional measures of financial performance", "traditional performance"]
definition: The most fundamental performance indicators for Fortune's rankings are revenue and income; at the time of the first survey in 1983 Fortune had already been running its Fortune 500 ranking for 30 years, based solely on firm revenue, and net income is another widely used measure of firm financial performance.

name: Emergent financial performance
authors_terms: ["newly emergent financial performance indicators", "emergent financial indicators", "emerging nontraditional measures of financial performance", "emergent financial variables"]
definition: Scholars and practitioners began to critique traditional income-based financial indicators, and two categories of performance measurement emerged as viable alternatives to GAAP earnings: 'pro forma' earnings and cash-based indicators. The authors' two emerging measures of financial performance are earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and free cash flow.

name: Corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility (CSR)", "social responsibility indicators", "overall CSR", "social performance", "CSR performance"]
definition: KLD provides ratings of firms' social, environmental, and governance practices that assist investors' or other stakeholders' decision making. The KLD data set is composed of 80 binary indicators covering seven major qualitative issues around CSR: community relations, corporate governance, diversity, employee relations, environment, human rights, and product.

name: Media attention
authors_terms: ["media attention", "media coverage", "weighted valence measure", "business press rhetoric"]
definition: Evaluators' reliance on a particular financial indicator is moderated by the level of business press rhetoric associated with that indicator: as the business press gives more attention to a financial metric, evaluators tend to give more weight to that indicator when assessing a firm's reputation. Article counts measure the volume of attention and media coverage valence measures the tenor of that attention.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign equity share", "foreign ownership", "foreign ownership level", "MNE ownership level", "foreign equity ownership"]
definition: The ownership level of the foreign partner in an IJV; ownership level has been shown to reflect each partner's control over the IJV as well as the likely level of collaboration between partners.

name: IJV productivity
definition: Productivity is typically expressed as the relationship between IJV output and IJV resource usage. The dependent variable is firm productivity normalized by the average productivity of the industry.

name: FDI legitimacy
definition: FDI legitimacy captures the extent to which foreign investment is well accepted by a variety of legitimating actors (e.g., government, supplier groups, and labor unions) in the host country.

name: Local market competition
definition: The intensity of competition facing IJVs in the local market; when the level of competition heightens, IJVs need to be more responsive to the needs of local consumers, suppliers, and governments in order to seize more market opportunities and alleviate competitive threats.

name: Regional economic development
definition: The level of economic development of the region in which an IJV is located, which varies from coastal to inland areas in China.

name: Subsidiary survival
authors_terms: ["survival rate of subsidiaries", "survival rate", "subsidiary mortality", "viability of a firm's later ventures"]
definition: The dependent variable in this type of analysis is the instantaneous rate of subsidiary dissolution, which is based on the information on whether or not an affiliate is still in existence and how long it has persisted. Consistent with our hypotheses, our tables report the survival rate of subsidiaries, which is the dissolution rate's logical converse.

name: Likelihood of acquisition
authors_terms: ["likelihood of acquisition", "propensity to acquire", "likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition"]
definition: The hypotheses concerning the effect of previous expansions on a firm's propensity to acquire or establish a greenfield were tested using binomial logit models. The dependent variable captured the likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition rather than a greenfield.

name: Likelihood of greenfield
authors_terms: ["likelihood of a greenfield", "propensity to establish a greenfield", "propensity to acquire or establish a greenfield"]
definition: A greenfield is defined as setting up a subsidiary from scratch, and for reasons of simplicity the authors follow existing literature in treating greenfields and acquisitions as dichotomous. The propensity to acquire or establish a greenfield was tested with the logit model whose dependent variable captured the likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition rather than a greenfield.

name: Preceding greenfields
definition: Measurement as the number of previous expansions of each type is consistent with our theory and hypotheses, which suggest that, for instance, the propensity to acquire increases with each successive greenfield. Thus, the number of times a certain way of organizing has been reinstalled through a new subsidiary is relevant.

name: Preceding acquisitions
definition: The number of a firm's previous acquisitions, counted from 1966 onwards and controlled for the number of greenfields during the same period; because the two variables are expected to have opposite effects, it is their proportion that determines a current subsidiary's chance of survival and a firm's preferences.

name: Preceding greenfields in familiar markets
authors_terms: ["greenfields in familiar markets", "preceding greenfields in familiar markets", "prior greenfields in familiar markets"]
definition: A new market was operationally defined as a new business, identified by the subsidiary's Standaard Bedrijfs Indeling (SBI) code, and as a new geographical market; greenfields in countries to which the firm had expanded before were coded as greenfields in familiar markets. If a subsidiary is established in a market that is already familiar to a firm, it can apply familiar ways of organizing and managing.

name: Preceding greenfields in new markets
authors_terms: ["greenfields in new markets", "preceding greenfields in new markets", "greenfields in unfamiliar markets"]
definition: Greenfields that were the first in an SBI code and greenfields that were the first in a country are greenfields in new markets. If the firm sets up ventures in new product or geographical markets, it is exploring new territory.

name: Preceding acquisitions in related domains
authors_terms: ["acquisitions in related domains", "preceding acquisitions in related domains", "prior acquisitions in related domains"]
definition: A preceding acquisition was coded as related if it was within two digits of the SBI code characterizing the acquiring firm's prior activities, and if it was in a country in which the firm had acquired earlier. Learning from acquisitions only takes place if knowledge, routines, skills, and people flow from the acquired firm to the acquiring company.

name: Preceding acquisitions in unrelated domains
authors_terms: ["acquisitions in unrelated domains", "preceding acquisitions in unrelated domains", "prior acquisitions in unrelated domains"]
definition: A preceding acquisition was coded as unrelated if the SBI code that characterized the acquisition differed from that for the acquiring firm's prior activities by at least two digits, and if it was in a new country (prior research has shown that acquisitions in new countries are particularly difficult because they require double-layered acculturation).

name: Product specialization
authors_terms: ["commodity-to-specialty products", "commodity-to-specialty products dimension", "offering specialty products", "specialty products", "commodity products"]
definition: Product type can be conceptualized as a dimension ranging from commodity products to specialty products. Specialty products are typically high margin, unique products that are often targeted toward a clearly identified high price segment, while commodity products are generally low margin, nonunique products.

name: Marketing intensity
authors_terms: ["marketing intensity", "intensity of a firm's marketing efforts", "emphasis on marketing activities"]
definition: Firms vary significantly in their emphasis on marketing activities, and the intensity of a firm's marketing efforts is recognized as a critical dimension of business strategy. Some firms view advertising as a primary and necessary revenue generating tool while others build their business strategy around other competitive tactics.

name: Cost leadership
definition: A firm can gain a competitive advantage through achieving the lowest cost structure in the industry without neglecting other important areas such as service and product quality. Possible tactics include finding ways to reduce production costs, achieving high capacity utilization, offering competitive low prices, and establishing efficient operations in raw materials procurement, internal production processes, and product distribution.

name: Product line breadth
authors_terms: ["product line breadth", "breadth of a firm's product line", "line breadth"]
definition: This dimension refers to the number and variety of items embodied in a company's product line.

name: Aggressive technological posture
definition: This dimension refers to the firm's preference for or propensity to use technology proactively in positioning itself. A firm that employs technology proactively aspires to be on the leading edge of technological change in the industry by building a reputation for being first in the industry to try new methods and technologies, being an industry leader in innovation efforts, and being an early industry entrant regarding innovation efforts.

name: Automation and process innovation
authors_terms: ["automation and process innovation", "automation", "automation and process innovation dimension"]
definition: This dimension of technology policy relates to the level of automation of plants and facilities, the adoption of the latest technology in production, and capital allocations for new equipment and machinery.

name: New product development
authors_terms: ["new product development", "product development activities", "new product development dimension"]
definition: This dimension refers to the intensity of a firm's product development activities. Companies that pursue intensive product development activities tend to surpass their counterparts in the number and rate of new product introductions.

name: Firm performance
definition: Company performance measured by return on sales (ROS), one of the most widely used measures of company performance at the SBU and single-business level of the analysis. Using an objective performance measure following the survey data collection allowed inferences regarding the effects of technology and strategy choices on company performance.

name: Technology policy
definition: Technology policy embodies the choices companies make about acquiring, developing and deploying technology to help reach the goals of their business strategy. As defined in this research, technology policy is the set of organizational decisions concerning aggressive technological posture, automation and process innovation, and new product development.

name: Business strategy configuration
authors_terms: ["business strategy clusters", "strategy configurations", "business strategy patterns", "strategic clusters", "business strategy cluster"]
definition: A firm's strategic choices form overall gestalts or patterns that combine these decisions. The study derives empirically valid clusters of firms with similar business strategies from the four business strategy scales.

name: Negative performance feedback
definition: Negative performance feedback exists when a firm's performance falls short of its aspiration level, which is informed by the firm's past performance and the performance of industry peers. It constitutes a powerful motivation for firms and their boards to initiate strategic changes.

name: Board expertise diversity
authors_terms: ["expertise diversity", "board expertise diversity", "diversity of expertise among the directors of the board"]
definition: Expertise revolves around the craft or knowledge of a person and is developed through experience in specific domains or relevant fields. Directors can develop expertise in functional roles, in industries, and in directorial roles through multiple board appointments; board expertise diversity is the level of diversity in directors' expertise along these dimensions.

name: Board ascriptive diversity
authors_terms: ["ascriptive diversity", "board ascriptive diversity", "diversity in ascriptive backgrounds"]
definition: Ascriptive backgrounds, such as gender and race/ethnicity, are visible and perceived to be fixed attributes. Board ascriptive diversity is the level of diversity in board members' ascriptive backgrounds.

name: Expertise minority chairs
definition: An expertise minority chair exists when a director whose expertise is dissimilar to the rest of the board occupies a committee chair position.

name: Ascriptive minority chairs
definition: Ascriptive minority chairs are committee chair positions occupied by ascriptive minority directors, such as women and racial minorities.

name: Accelerator participation
authors_terms: ["accelerator participation", "being accelerated", "participation in accelerators", "participate in an accelerator"]
definition: Startup accelerators are limited-duration, cohort-based entrepreneurial programs that offer founders resources to build entrepreneurial capabilities and expedite the pace of new venture development. The authors measured the effect of accelerator participation as a dummy variable indicating whether a venture participated in an accelerator.

name: Startup performance post acceleration
authors_terms: ["startup performance post acceleration", "venture outcomes", "venture performance post acceleration", "startup performance"]
definition: To provide a comprehensive evaluation of the effect of accelerator participation on venture outcomes, the authors considered several dependent variables that reflect different aspects of venture performance and scaling. They used a triangulation approach measuring six different outcomes, spanning capital raising, revenue scaling, and employment and wages paid.

name: Venture capital funding
authors_terms: ["ability to raise external capital", "funding", "raise venture capital (VC)", "external funding"]
definition: The authors evaluated a startup's ability to raise external capital using a binary measure, raised VC equity funding, which indicates whether a venture secured VC in the year following application to the accelerator program. They also measured the amount of VC equity funding raised and the planned VC equity raise.

name: Revenue scaling
definition: The authors measured ventures' ability to scale revenue as the sales revenue of the startup (in thousands of US$) for the year after the accelerator program application. This outcome is indicative of growth in a venture's customer or user base and the achievement of product-market fit.

name: Employment and wage scaling
authors_terms: ["employment and wages paid", "scale employment", "full-time employees", "wages paid to employees"]
definition: The authors measured the number of full-time employees of the startup (other than the cofounders) who worked for the venture for at least 40 h per week in the year following the accelerator program application. They also measured the value of wages paid in salaries to employees, which reflects the startups' ability to scale employment and to attract highly skilled employees and talent.

name: Cohort knowledge depth of peers
authors_terms: ["cohort knowledge depth", "knowledge depth of peers", "knowledge depth within cohorts"]
definition: Accelerators that lean toward greater depth over breadth of knowledge in their cohort selection often arise from an industry-specific strategy, which targets specific sectors; this depth enables founders to gain deep knowledge from vicarious learning and thereby exploit existing opportunities within those sectors. The authors measured the knowledge depth of peers as a continuous index for each cohort, created from three primary variables measuring the depth of peer knowledge.

name: Cohort knowledge breadth of peers
authors_terms: ["cohort knowledge breadth", "knowledge breadth of peers", "knowledge breadth within cohorts"]
definition: Accelerators adopting an industry-agnostic strategy typically have a breadth-oriented approach to cohort selection, which encourages founders to explore new opportunities. The authors measured the knowledge breadth of peers as a continuous index for each cohort, created from three primary variables measuring the breadth of peer knowledge.

name: Knowledge-building programming
definition: Accelerators aim to build founders' knowledge and capabilities through intensive knowledge-building programming, including but not limited to feedback from industry specialists and customers, pitching opportunities, and structured educational programming. The authors used five distinct measures that capture considerable variation in some of the most prevalent programming elements offered by accelerators in the analysis sample.

name: CEO international assignment experience
definition: International assignment experience has been defined as living and working in a foreign country for at least one year.

name: Top management team international assignment experience
authors_terms: ["top management team international assignment experience", "top team international assignment experience"]
definition: The years of international assignment experience reported by the other members of a company's top management team, excluding the CEO.

name: Global strategic posture
definition: Global posture refers to the degree to which a firm is dependent on foreign sales and production and to the geographical dispersion of this dependence.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is captured as return on assets, which indicates the efficiency with which a firm employs its current asset base, and as stock market returns, which indicate how effectively a firm is managing shareholder interests.

name: CEO total compensation
authors_terms: ["total CEO compensation", "total compensation", "CEO compensation level", "total pay"]
definition: CEO compensation level is measured as the logarithm of the total of all forms of compensation granted, with long-term forms of compensation valued at their present value as provided by a company in its proxy statement. The authors predict that boards will grant CEOs a higher proportion of firm performance, in the form of higher total pay, when they possess international assignment experience.

name: Geographic scope of knowledge acquisition
authors_terms: ["geographic scope", "geographic scope of knowledge acquisition", "number of countries"]
definition: The extent to which a firm acquires knowledge from multiple countries. The authors note that acquiring knowledge from multiple countries bears important strategic implications due largely to the differences across countries.

name: Innovation output
definition: The output of firms' innovation activity, measured in the extant literature as the number of forward citations a patent receives or the number of patents weighted by the number of forward citations.

name: Isolating mechanisms
authors_terms: ["isolating mechanisms", "degree of isolating mechanisms", "degree of isolation"]
definition: A set of barriers that impede flows of knowledge across firms; isolating mechanisms thus limit firm-level imitation and allow the focal firm to sustain competitive advantage. An effect of isolating mechanisms can be captured in the increase in time to imitation.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance of a firm, operationalized with return on assets (ROA) in its natural logarithm form (ln(1 + ROA)) as a measure of firms' profitability.

name: Problemistic search distance
definition: The distance between the text descriptions of a developer's first and second apps. A score of 0.00 indicates that the developer's first and second app text descriptions are identical and that the developer engaged in extremely local search; a score of 1.00 indicates that the descriptions do not share any common words and that the developer engaged in extremely nonlocal search.

name: Subsequent performance
authors_terms: ["app two installs", "subsequent performance", "second app performance", "second app installs"]
definition: The higher the app two installs, the higher a developer's post-search subsequent performance is assumed to be based on the presumption that the goal of the majority of app developers is to get as many installs as possible.

name: Past performance
authors_terms: ["app one installs", "past performance", "prior performance", "initial performance", "app one performance", "first app performance"]
definition: The number of installs a developer's first app had in the month it was first observed. The lower the installs of a developer's first app, the more negative the developer's initial performance feedback is assumed to be.

name: Replication accuracy
authors_terms: ["accuracy in the replication of the features of the original template", "inaccurate replication", "deviation from the franchisor template", "replication accuracy"]
definition: The authors refer to deviation from the franchisor template as inaccurate replication, and their replication hypothesis concerns accuracy in the replication of the features of the original template. They note that replication is maximally effective when only the necessary value creating facets of a template are identified and replicated, and no time or effort is devoted to the replication of deleterious or superfluous features.

name: Local adaptation
authors_terms: ["local adaptation", "adaptation of the template to fit local conditions", "adaptation of standard practices and procedures"]
definition: Adaptation of the template to fit local conditions; the adaptation perspective holds that environmental characteristics and the organization's internal system of activities must align closely if the organization is to survive and prosper. Under conditions of market heterogeneity, some degree of local adaptation is argued to be required to reflect the peculiarities of the local environments.

name: Unit failure hazard
authors_terms: ["hazard of failure", "likelihood of exit", "hazard of franchise unit exit", "unit exit"]
definition: The outlet-specific hazard of failure. Outlets are at risk of failure (exit) until the end of the observation period or until they have permanently closed down as indicated by the franchisor internal information system; ownership transfers are not considered exits as long as the same outlet operates at the same location within the same franchise system.

name: Accelerator admission
authors_terms: ["Accelerated", "admission to an accelerator program", "access to the accelerated environment", "formal offer of admission to the accelerator"]
definition: A formal admission process drives access to the accelerated environment provided by the accelerator; the authors capture whether a startup in the sample received a formal offer of admission to the accelerator and how close the startup was to the admission threshold.

name: Resource acquisition
authors_terms: ["resource acquisition", "resources acquired", "external financing and employees", "grow in resources"]
definition: The ability of an early-stage startup to move from an early stage of development focused on ideation to an execution phase during which firms must acquire resources to enter their market and grow; nearly all growth-oriented startups need both external financing and employees.

name: Colocation with the accelerator's ecosystem
