The authors state that the reallocation of patent ownership occurs when a firm with a presumably better use for a patent buys the patent from the original assignee.

name: Product-market overlap
definition: Product-market overlap implies that product-market similarity in which firms' offerings compete begets rivalry among the firms. It is the level of product-market overlap between a potential seller-buyer pair, which implies that the firms' offerings compete.

name: Technological capability
authors_terms: ["technological capability", "technological capability of the original assignee", "innovation capability"]
definition: We conceptualize technological capability in the markets for innovation as a firm's ability to generate economic return from a patent. The value of a patent is determined by the marginal productivity that the patent contributes to the firm's gains via technological utilization or risk mitigation.

name: Racial dissimilarity between CEOs
authors_terms: ["white source CEO and racial minority target CEO", "demographic differences", "in-group/out-group distinctions"]
definition: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the source CEO was white and the target CEO was a racial minority.

name: Gender dissimilarity between CEOs
authors_terms: ["male source CEO and female target CEO", "demographic differences"]
definition: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the source CEO was male and the target CEO was female.

name: Status in the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["status in the corporate elite", "relative status", "target CEO's status relative to source CEO's status"]
definition: Corporate executives who occupy high-status positions in the corporate elite are perceived to enjoy a variety of tangible and intangible privileges and benefits, including relatively high compensation and perquisites, greater influence over corporate policy where they serve as executive or director, and opportunities to serve in prestigious and influential positions outside the corporate sphere. The authors adopt the traditional definition of social status as a position in a social system that encompasses a collection of rights, privileges, and duties.

name: Internal performance attributions by CEOs
authors_terms: ["internal attributions", "internal performance attributions by CEOs", "derogatory performance attributions"]
definition: CEOs attribute low firm performance to internal factors such as mistakes in strategic decision making or weak leadership rather than external factors such as adverse conditions in the industry environment. The articulation of such negative performance attributions to third-party observers is referred to as derogatory performance attributions.

name: Internal performance attributions in journalists' reports
authors_terms: ["internal performance attributions in journalists' reports", "internal attributions by journalists"]
definition: The number of internal attributions by the focal journalist for low performance of the target CEO's firm over the two months following the period for which performance attributions by CEOs were measured.

name: Negative earnings surprise
authors_terms: ["negative earnings surprise", "earnings that are below the consensus forecasts of security analysts"]
definition: Earnings that are below the consensus forecasts of security analysts. In the primary analyses it is measured with a dichotomous indicator coded 1 if a firm's most recently reported quarterly earnings were below the median forecasted earnings for the same period among all analysts covering the firm, and 0 otherwise.

name: Racial similarity between journalist and CEO
authors_terms: ["journalist and target CEO both racial minorities", "demographic similarity between journalists and target CEOs"]
definition: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if both the journalist and target CEO were racial minorities.

name: Gender similarity between journalist and CEO
authors_terms: ["journalist and target CEO both women", "demographic similarity between journalists and target CEOs"]
definition: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if both the journalist and target CEO were women.

name: Malicious envy toward the target CEO
definition: Social psychologists characterize envy as an interpersonal emotion that can range from a relatively benign form to a more negative form; the more negative form, which Smith and colleagues characterize as a kind of 'resentment emotion', also says, 'I should have what you have.'

name: Dual networking
definition: We define dual networking as the extent to which the networks of two individuals are equivalent in terms of the connectedness to role sets but non-overlapping with respect to connectedness to specific individuals.

name: Innovation performance
definition: For both technologists and managers, the dependent variable in the study is the annual performance rating, allocated with a forced distribution across three rating categories. The assessment criteria focus on individual contributions to innovations, such as innovations that have led to revenue growth or cost reduction, or key technology or market learnings.

name: Shared technical expertise
definition: The extent to which a manager and technologist have shared technical expertise, defined as the fraction of expertise areas in which the technologist is at least fairly competent in which the manager partner is also at least fairly competent.

name: Organizational prominence
definition: In the context of this study, organizational prominence captures the status of managers and technologists in the eyes of their colleagues, as sources of advice or influence in the organization.

name: Open source community affiliation
authors_terms: ["OSS Community Affiliation", "affiliation with OSS communities", "community affiliation", "OSS commitment"]
definition: A developer's connection to the open source software community, measured by the proportion of a developer's applications where the source code was listed on an open source site before the launch of the App Store. Making code publicly available requires additional effort and may have disadvantages, so doing so is a good indication of open source affiliation.

name: Commercialization
definition: Innovations become revenue-generating goods and services through the process of commercialization. In the second study the dependent variable measures the choice to commercialize innovations through entrepreneurial action, by starting a business or working as an independent contractor.

name: Anticommercial attitudes
authors_terms: ["anticommercial attitudes", "a general disutility of profit seeking", "disutility of profits", "noneconomic negative utility of commercialization"]
definition: Individuals associated with some innovative communities may view economic motivation as undesirable, so that profit may produce a noneconomic negative utility. Anticommercial attitudes have played a large role in OSS communities in the past.

name: OSS developer self-identity
authors_terms: ["OSS Self-Identity", "self-identity", "self-identity as an OSS developer", "community-based OSS self-identity"]
definition: Self-identity is 'the extent to which performing [a] behavior is an important part of one's self concept' (Terry et al. 1999, p. 226), and is shaped by both personal and social factors. In settings like OSS, self-identity combines elements of the social and role, and this paper focuses on self-identity as an OSS developer compared with that of an entrepreneur.

name: Joint venture choice
authors_terms: ["choice between mergers/acquisitions and joint ventures", "mode of entry", "greenfield equity joint venture", "full acquisitions"]
definition: The focus of the empirical analysis is the choice made by Japanese investors into the United States between full acquisitions of U.S. firms and greenfield joint ventures between Japanese and American firms. Mode of entry is captured by a dummy variable which takes a value of 0 if the Japanese parent made an acquisition and 1 if it established a greenfield joint venture.

name: U.S. partner size
authors_terms: ["size of the U.S. partner", "large partner", "number of employees", "SIZE"]
definition: The American partner is defined as the firm which holds the assets which the Japanese investor needs; if the U.S. partner is small, it is likely that the assets desired by the Japanese investor make up 100 percent of the assets held by the U.S. firm. Acquisitions become problematic when the partner is large, but not divisionalized, because it is then difficult to separate desired from nondesired assets.

name: U.S. partner divisionalization
definition: If the target firm is large but divisionalized, it is possible for the Japanese investor to acquire only the division that owns the desired resources. Acquisitions will be chosen when the parents are small, or if they are large, when they are organized in divisions which can be acquired separately from the rest of the firm, i.e., when they are divisionalized.

name: Japanese investor's U.S. market experience
authors_terms: ["experience of the U.S. environment", "experience of the U.S. market", "JEXP", "previous experience of the American market"]
definition: The Japanese investor's experience of the U.S. market at the time entry was made. Japanese firms are likely to expect their postacquisition integration costs to be lower the longer they have been in the United States.

name: Product commonality between parent and subsidiary
authors_terms: ["COMMON", "same industry as the planned subsidiary", "manufacture one common product"]
definition: Because company cultures and administrative routines differ systematically across industries, postacquisition integration problems are expected to be lower for Japanese investors whose U.S. subsidiary manufactures the same product as they do.

name: Partner industry similarity
authors_terms: ["PARCOMMON", "Japanese and American partners are in a different industry", "partners are in the same industry"]
definition: The extent to which the U.S. and the Japanese firms have divergent information concerning the value of the assets of the U.S. target firm is proxied by whether the Japanese and the American partners were in the same industry, calculated by comparing the products manufactured by the Japanese investor and those manufactured by its U.S. partner.

name: U.S. industry concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration ratio of the U.S. industry entered", "CONCEN", "concentrated U.S. industries"]
definition: The concentration of the U.S. industry entered: U.S. antitrust authorities see horizontal joint ventures in a more positive light than full horizontal acquisitions, while one advantage of acquisitions is that they do not create additional capacity. The concentration ratio is measured by the Herfindahl index for each 4-digit SIC U.S. industry.

name: U.S. industry growth rate
authors_terms: ["rate of growth of the target market", "GROWTH", "growth of shipments of the U.S. industry entered", "GROWDEV"]
definition: The growth rate of the target U.S. industry: acquisitions are encouraged when the U.S. industry entered grows either very fast or very slowly, because then the opportunity cost of greenfield entry is high or because a greenfield entry would add capacity which would depress profits.

name: Board prestige
authors_terms: ["preexisting board prestige", "pre-existing board prestige", "board prestige", "existing board prestige"]
definition: Prestige is an actor's position in a hierarchical social order tied to the pattern of relations and affiliations in which the actor does and does not choose to engage. Board prestige was calculated as the aggregate number of continuing prestigious directors that served on a focal firm's board in a given year.

name: CEO prestige
definition: CEO prestige was operationalized in the same manner as director prestige: it was coded 1 if the CEO possessed any one of the three prestige credentials (educational, employment, or directorial prestige) and was coded 0 otherwise.

name: Prestigious director recruitment
authors_terms: ["recruitment of a prestigious director", "recruiting a prestigious director", "prestigious hire"]
definition: The dependent variable in this study was the recruitment of a prestigious director in a given year. Outside directors were considered prestigious if they possessed at least one of the following credentials: a degree from an elite educational institution, experience as an executive at the level of vice president or above at an S&P 500 company, or experience as an outside director in an S&P 500 firm.

name: New director prestige
authors_terms: ["the amount of director prestige", "how prestigious a new director is", "total prestige of the new director"]
definition: A count variable ranging from zero to three that captured the number of prestige credentials a new director possessed; this measure reflects how prestigious a new director is.

name: Board tenure
authors_terms: ["average board tenure", "the amount of time directors had worked together"]
definition: The amount of time directors had worked together, operationalized as the average tenure of board members, calculated by summing the number of years each individual served as a director on a focal firm's board and dividing the sum by the total number of directors on the board.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["structural and ownership power", "sources of a CEO's power", "sources of executive power"]
definition: While prestige is one source of a CEO's power, Finkelstein identified two additional sources of executive power: the structural features of an organization (i.e., structural power) and ownership (i.e., ownership power).

name: Structural power
definition: Structural power is derived from the formal organizational structures and hierarchical authority that provide a CEO with 'the legislative right' to exert influence.

name: Ownership power
definition: Ownership power derives from a CEO's direct ownership of stock and from being a company's founder.

name: Regulatory punctuation
definition: In this paper, we focus on regulatory punctuations: sudden and extensive shifts in state constraints on business operations. Regulatory punctuations alter both technical and institutional features of organizational environments.

name: Time since regulatory punctuation
authors_terms: ["regulatory punctuation time clock", "time since regulatory punctuation", "punctuation time clock"]
definition: A regulatory punctuation time clock captures effects that emerge as time passes; it equals zero up to and including 1982; it shifts to one in 1983 and rises by one each subsequent year.

name: Domain expansion
authors_terms: ["domain expansion", "domain change", "shifts in organizational domain", "scope of operations", "activity in new lines of business"]
definition: We measured domain expansion as the one-year change in scope of operations. Organizations expand their domains by moving into new lines of business.

name: CEO succession
authors_terms: ["CEO succession", "executive succession", "executive turnover", "rate of CEO succession"]
definition: Executive succession can impart new knowledge and skills that make it possible to cope with the dramatic shifts in critical contingencies that follow regulatory punctuations. Job mobility, including the turnover of top executives, is generally modelled as a semi-Markov process.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "financial performance", "short-term financial performance", "return on sales", "return on assets"]
definition: We used a fine-grained measure of performance (short-term financial performance) rather than the coarse-grained measure (survival) used in previous studies. For hospitals, performance was return on sales, which reflects both effectiveness (good choices about services to offer) and efficiency (low cost); for savings and loans, return on assets.

name: Electronic data interchange linkage
definition: The implementation of an electronic linkage between the supplier and a customer for procurement transactions; the empirical comparison is between customers with links to the supplier and a control group of customers which do not have the electronic linkage.

name: Customer-initiated EDI linkage
authors_terms: ["customer initiated EDI", "linkage initiated by a customer", "initiators of the system"]
definition: The identity of the initiator of the system: when the customer initiates the EDI link, the customer is keen to realize the full benefits of its investments in EDI through reduced transaction costs.

name: EDI linkage enhancement
authors_terms: ["enhanced EDI", "enhanced features of the electronic linkage", "advanced EDI linkage"]
definition: EDI enhancements include features such as establishing an integrated electronic link and capabilities for transmitting additional transaction sets; the supplier brings about fundamental changes in the 'procedural specificity' of the exchange process by altering the flows of content and the quality of information.

name: EDI order integration
definition: An integrated EDI link requires mapping between the customer's item identification code and the supplier's item code. Orders transmitted via integrated EDI are entered directly into the supplier's order-processing system without human intervention.

name: Electronic invoicing
definition: Electronic invoicing makes invoicing information available to the customer far earlier than manual invoicing, and the information content of the invoice is more accurate.

name: Delayed payment
authors_terms: ["delayed payments", "intensity of delayed customer payments", "timely payment"]
definition: The intensity of delayed customer payments. Delayed payments hurt both parties, and both the supplier and the customer have an incentive to decrease the percentage of orders that lead to delayed payments.

name: Order-processing errors
authors_terms: ["credit intensity", "credits arising from erroneous order processing", "probability of a credit order", "probability of rework"]
definition: The intensity of credits arising from erroneous order processing; an increase in the accuracy of the information is expected, and accuracy results in lower credits to the customer.

name: Strategic benefits
authors_terms: ["strategic benefits", "gains in sales volume", "business growth", "gains in business from customers"]
definition: We use gains in sales volume as the key measure of strategic benefit; the strategic impact is modeled as the business benefits generated by EDI through changes in the relationship between the trading partners.

name: EDI linkage duration
authors_terms: ["age of the EDI linkage", "length of time", "duration of the electronic connection"]
definition: The length of time for which EDI customers had an electronic linkage with the supplier; this classification of the EDI customers allowed us to ascertain whether the duration of the electronic connection affected the level of strategic benefits.

name: Interteam gender alignment
definition: Founder and mentor teams that are aligned on gender composition—in terms of being marked by either a matched presence or a matched absence of gender diversity—should facilitate participation from more investors than misaligned teams, those marked by the presence of gender diversity in one team but not in the other.

name: Intrateam gender diversity
definition: Gender diversity within a team, demarcated by the critical mass threshold of at least 30% of each gender required for representation to be substantive rather than symbolic or tokenized; gender-diverse teams have representation of 30.00% through 70.00% while male-dominated teams have not reached a threshold level of representation.

name: Founder team gender diversity
authors_terms: ["founder team gender diversity", "gender-diverse founder teams", "Founder Team Gender"]
definition: Whether the venture's founding team has reached the 30% gender diversity threshold, coded as one for gender-diverse founder teams with representation of 30.00% through 70.00% and zero for the remaining male-dominated founder teams that had not yet reached a threshold level of representation.

name: Mentor team gender diversity
authors_terms: ["mentor team gender diversity", "gender-diverse mentor teams", "Mentor Team Gender"]
definition: Whether the team of mentors assigned to the venture has reached the 30% gender diversity threshold, coded as one for gender-diverse mentor teams with representation of 30.00% through 70.00% and zero for the remaining male-dominated mentor teams that had not yet reached a threshold level of representation.

name: Number of participating investors
definition: How many investors were associated with each of the ventures, captured as Time 2 data on participating investor counts for each Techstars venture.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The dependent variable is firm profitability. It was measured through the firm's return on assets.

name: Foreign subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["foreign subsidiaries", "number of foreign subsidiaries", "foreign affiliates", "foreign operations"]
definition: Foreign subsidiaries were measured yearly as the number of foreign affiliates of the firm. Affiliates had to represent a 'physical' foreign presence, ranging from a sales office to production facilities.

name: Speed of international expansion
definition: 'Speed' indicates how many foreign expansions a firm undertakes in a certain period of time.

name: Product scope of international expansion
authors_terms: ["product scope", "product scope of the expansion process"]
definition: The dispersion of the internationalization process into different product markets, which we label the product scope of the expansion process.

name: Geographic scope of international expansion
authors_terms: ["geographic scope", "geographic scope of the expansion process", "geographic scope of a firm's expansion process"]
definition: The number of countries in which a firm established subsidiaries during its international expansion; expansion into multiple countries, i.e., the geographic scope of a firm's expansion process.

name: Irregularity of the expansion pattern
authors_terms: ["irregularity", "rhythm", "regularity of the expansion process", "irregular pace", "irregular expansion pattern"]
definition: The (simultaneous) regularity of the process, or the rhythm at which new subsidiaries are established; firms that expand in an irregular, ad hoc fashion alternate years of rapid expansion with long periods of inactivity.

name: Inside ownership
definition: Inside ownership was defined as the sum of the percentage of equity shares owned by family members identified as the controlling shareholders of a business group and by other nonfinancial affiliates in the same group, measured at time t.

name: Family portion of inside ownership
definition: Family portion denotes what portion of inside ownership was held directly by the family. Higher values of this variable reflect the greater cash flow rights direct ownership confers, given the same level of inside ownership.

name: Firm performance
definition: This study contained both accounting-based and stock-market-based measures for firm performance, since it is difficult to identify a single indicator for firm performance.

name: Fads and fashions
authors_terms: ["fads and fashions", "fads", "fashions", "social influence", "social conformity", "media attention", "media reports", "peer action", "adoption within an industry", "adoption within an MSA"]
definition: Fads and fashions are a powerful contextual force that affects organizational decision making through a process of social conformity. Because decision makers are unclear about the potential benefits and costs of an innovation, they are likely to rely on social information and adopt a choice that is perceived as desirable by others.

name: Interorganizational tie formation
authors_terms: ["network formation", "formation of interlocks", "formation of Internet interlocks", "tie formation", "new initiation"]
definition: The first dependent variable is the formation of Internet interlocks, which is specified as the number of a conventional firm's interlocking companies, newly added within a year, that lie within the Internet sector. A tie to an Internet company was counted as a new initiation only if one focal firm was not connected to that Internet company during the previous year.

name: Interorganizational tie dissolution
authors_terms: ["network dissolution", "dissolution of networks", "dissolution of Internet interlocks", "tie dissolution", "failure hazard"]
definition: An interlock tie was coded as dissolved in a year if two firms shared at least one common director or executive in the previous year but not in the year in question. Ties were also restricted to those that failed in one year and were not reconstituted within the next three years.

name: Prior direct contact
authors_terms: ["contact with the Internet sector in the previous year", "previous contact", "direct contact", "prior contact", "Internet tie (t-1)"]
definition: A conventional firm's direct contact with the Internet sector means that it had Internet interlocks in the previous year. Direct contact affords a flow of knowledge and experience that reduces reliance on social information in judging the quality of network partners.

name: Integrated manufacturing
definition: Integrated manufacturing involves the elimination of barriers between stages, functions, and goals of production to create a streamlined value-added system. Advanced technology, just-in-time, and total quality are the means by which it is achieved.

name: Advanced manufacturing technology
definition: Advanced manufacturing technology (AMT), the manufacturing subset of information technology, includes a variety of computerized technologies, such as computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) and process planning (CAPP).

name: Total quality management
definition: Total quality management (TQ) is characterized by a few basic principles—doing things right the first time, striving for continuous improvement, and fulfilling customer needs—as well as a number of associated practices.

name: Just-in-time inventory control
definition: Just-in-time inventory control (JIT) is a set of practices for reducing lead time and inventory; its name derives from the practice of receiving or producing each raw material or subcomponent just in time for it to be used in the next step of production.

name: Staffing selectivity
definition: Selective staffing was a 7-item scale measuring the extensiveness of a firm's selection process, as demonstrated, for instance, by the time and money spent and the number of people involved.

name: Training comprehensiveness
definition: Comprehensive training was an 8-item scale measuring the extensiveness of training and development opportunities, such as the frequency and variety of training, money spent, and the percentage of employees trained.

name: Developmental performance appraisal
definition: Developmental appraisal was a 9-item scale measuring whether performance appraisal was used for developing employees, as exemplified by diagnosing training needs, frequent feedback, problem solving, and discussing future issues.

name: External reward equity
definition: External equity is defined as the degree to which a firm pays employees the price they would command in the external labor market.

name: Individual reward equity
definition: Individual equity is defined as the degree to which employees are rewarded proportionately to their individual performance.

name: Product competitive strategy
authors_terms: ["product competitive strategy", "product strategy", "cost leadership versus differentiation", "Porter's generic strategies"]
definition: This study uses Porter's (1980) strategy framework to conceptualize a firm's product strategy, which identifies two generic ways in which a firm can gain a sustainable competitive advantage: 'cost leadership' and 'differentiation.' A cost leadership strategy focuses efforts on cost efficiency and is applied to relatively standardized, low-margin products, whereas a differentiation strategy emphasizes the perceived benefits of products and is applied to relatively unique, high-margin products.

name: Product uniqueness
definition: The first factor of product strategy, reflecting the product uniqueness dimension of a firm's differentiation strategy, captured by R&D propensity, advertising and administrative expenses to net sales, relative gross margin and the market to book ratio. The higher (lower) the factor score in this dimension, the greater (lesser) a firm's emphasis on differentiation.

name: Capital intensity
definition: The second factor of product strategy, reflecting the intensity of the capital asset investment to support the strategy, measured by new capital investment to sales and asset utilization. A higher (lower) factor score reflects a greater (lesser) emphasis on differentiation, and a smaller value of these variables is likely to be associated with firms pursuing a cost leadership strategy.

name: Purchasing management design
authors_terms: ["design of purchasing management", "organization design of purchasing management", "purchasing management design", "purchasing organization design"]
definition: The organization design characteristics of the purchasing management practices, examined in this study as the degree of decentralization and the span of (supply chain) coordination.

name: Purchasing decentralization
authors_terms: ["organization form", "degree of decentralization vs. centralization", "organizational structure", "DECNT"]
definition: The degree of decentralization versus centralization of the purchasing management function, used to proxy the extent of within-firm governance style, i.e., the degree of decentralization and flexibility in decision making. The first factor of purchasing organization design, with a higher (lower) score denoting greater decentralization (centralization).

name: Scope of purchasing coordination
definition: The extent of coordination of purchasing-related activities, with a higher (lower) score denoting more (less) extensive coordination. The second factor of purchasing organization design, measured by the number of other functions reporting to purchasing management and by the use of electronic data interchange.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Overall firm financial performance, measured as return on assets and calculated before interest and extraordinary events because a firm's financing policy and extraordinary events are outside of the scope of purchasing. Using return on assets combines both income and asset utilization measures and enables an examination of their joint effect on firm performance.

name: Purchasing operational efficiency
authors_terms: ["operational efficiency of the purchasing management function", "purchasing operational efficiency", "purchasing efficiency"]
definition: The operational efficiency of the purchasing management function, assessed by purchasing amount per dollar of purchasing operating expenses, purchase amount per employee, and inventory turnover; all three measures are commonly used for benchmarking operational efficiency of a purchasing organization.

name: Change rhythm
authors_terms: ["rhythm of change", "change rhythm", "regular change rhythm", "irregular change rhythm"]
definition: The rhythm of change is defined as the timing of multiple changes in a given period. A regular change rhythm implies that the intervals between changes are relatively equal in length; an irregular rhythm has different intervals between changes.

name: Change frequency
definition: The frequency of change is defined as the number of changes in a given period. In capturing the overall extent of change, change frequency does not measure change timing within a given period.

name: Long-term firm performance
authors_terms: ["long-term firm performance", "industry-adjusted annual return on equity", "ROE"]
definition: The study's focus is on the accumulated, long-term performance effect of an entire set of repeated changes, measured as industry-adjusted annual return on equity lagged three years from the end of the change period.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["group affiliation", "group-affiliated firms", "membership in a business group"]
definition: Business groups are defined as a network of legally independent firms, operating in diverse industries, with a common dominant owner, and coordinated through multiple formal and informal ties. Affiliation denotes a firm's membership in such a group.

name: Growth opportunities
definition: Since growth opportunities are typically unobservable, the authors follow prior academic research in using the Q ratio as a proxy variable to measure them. Anchored on Keynes' insight that a firm would invest only if the additional market value created from such investments is likely to exceed their cost, a high Q ratio indicates high growth opportunities.

name: Access to group diversity
authors_terms: ["access to diversity through the business group", "group product access"]
definition: The affiliate firm's access to diversity through the network of other affiliate firms in the business group; firms affiliated to business groups with a widely diversified portfolio have access to a greater number and variety of resources than affiliates of business groups with a less diversified portfolio.

name: Multi-entity character of the business group
definition: The organization of businesses as separate legal entities, with a separate governance structure for each affiliate firm; the higher the number of legal entities a business group has, for a given level of diversification, the greater the ability of its affiliate firm to sense and seize opportunities.

name: Pro-market reforms
definition: Emerging economies around the world are characterized by wide-ranging market-oriented reforms that reduce government intervention in an economy and improve the functioning of product and factor markets through changes in laws and regulations.

name: Learning goal orientation
definition: Individuals' disposition in 'seek[ing] to increase their competence, to understand or master something new'.

name: Civic virtue
definition: Employees' discretionary behaviors that are characterized by 'responsible and constructive involvement in the issues and governance of the organization'; it describes an employee's macro-level interest in, or commitment to, the organization as a whole.

name: Potential absorptive capacity
definition: Potential AC focuses on the acquiring and assimilation of new and external knowledge.

name: Realized absorptive capacity
definition: Realized AC focuses on transforming and exploiting the new and external knowledge that has been identified and assimilated.

name: Bank industry near-failure experience
authors_terms: ["near-failures of other banks", "industry bank near-failure experience", "bank industry near-failure experience", "industry-level bank near-failure experience"]
definition: We define one important variation of failure-related experience, near-failure, as occurring when a firm experiences impending failure but later recovers. We defined a near-failure as occurring when a bank received a below-average CAMEL rating for at least two consecutive quarters and then recovered from its low ratings.

name: Thrift industry near-failure experience
authors_terms: ["thrift industry near-failure experience", "industry thrift near-failure experience", "near-failures of thrifts"]
definition: Thrift near-failure experience variables were created using the same method described for banks; near-failure was defined as occurring when a bank received a below-average CAMEL rating for at least two consecutive quarters and then recovered from its low ratings.

name: Bank industry failure experience
authors_terms: ["bank industry failure experience", "industry bank failure experience", "failures of other banks"]
definition: Industry bank failure experience was defined as the discounted sum of the total number of bank failures that had occurred in bank i's state since the bank's founding and until the year before the bank was at risk of failure.

name: Thrift industry failure experience
authors_terms: ["thrift industry failure experience", "industry thrift failure experience", "failure experience among thrifts"]
definition: Thrift failure experience variables were created using the same method described for banks; prior studies have documented that the rampant failure of thrifts during the S&L crisis acted as a wake-up call to banks.

name: Bank failure rate
authors_terms: ["bank failure rate", "unobserved hazard rate for bank failure", "survival"]
definition: The dependent variable was the unobserved hazard rate for bank failure in the population of commercial banks chartered since 1984. Bank failure rate measures a special type of learning outcome and has been frequently used in empirical studies on organizational learning.

name: Environmental risk management
authors_terms: ["environmental risk management", "improved environmental performance", "environmental risk management indicator"]
definition: Strategic investments that reduce emissions and pollution and thereby mitigate the firm's risk of litigation from governmental regulators or nongovernmental stakeholders. The authors state that higher levels of environmental performance should be viewed as environmental risk management.

name: Cost of debt capital
definition: The cost of debt financing incurred by a firm is based on the assessment by the capital market of the default risk of the firm; the applicable interest rate.

name: Financial leverage
authors_terms: ["leverage", "financial leverage", "level of long-term debt standardized by market capitalization"]
definition: The firm's level of debt in its debt-equity financing mix; in the tests it is the firm's level of long-term debt standardized by market capitalization.

name: Tax advantage from debt financing
authors_terms: ["tax advantage (shield) from debt financing", "tax reduction associated with debt financing"]
definition: The amount of income a firm can shield from taxation through higher leverage; computed as the tax reduction associated with debt financing.

name: Cost of equity capital
definition: The return investors in the firm's shares expect as reflected in the stock price they are willing to pay relative to future expected cash flows.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Cov(rE, rM)/Var(rM) measures the firm's systematic risk; a reduction in the cost of equity financing by reducing the firm's systematic risk is manifested in a lowered equity beta.

name: Share ownership dispersion
definition: The dispersion of the firm's share ownership, indicated by the total number of shareholders: the higher the number of shareholders, the less concentrated the shares.

name: Institutional share ownership
authors_terms: ["percentage of institutional share owners", "institutional holders percentage"]
definition: The published percentage of institutional holders of the firm's shares at the close of 2002.

name: Weighted average cost of capital
authors_terms: ["weighted average cost of capital (WACC)", "total cost of capital", "cost of capital"]
definition: The firm's overall cost of capital, given by the weighted average of its cost of debt and equity capital.

name: Organizational life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["organizational life cycle", "stage of the organizational life cycle", "stage of organizational life cycle", "position in the organizational life cycle", "organizational life cycle status or location"]
definition: There is consensus that changes in an organization follow a predictable pattern that is characterized by discrete stages of development. The study dichotomizes the life cycle between initial development, defined as formulation and market acceptance or early growth, and later development, comprised of later growth and maturity or stability.

name: Competition
authors_terms: ["level of competition", "intense competition", "level of competitive intensity", "competitive intensity"]
definition: The effects of competition on the organization range from high determinism where organizations must adapt or fail to low determinism where organizations function autonomously. Organizations operate either in intensely competitive environments where other organizations labeled competitors will have a clear, decisive impact, or in environments where the number and impact of competitors is minimal yet viable given the market niche of the firm.

name: Problem perception
authors_terms: ["problems/concerns", "problem perception", "identified problems", "relative importance of identified problems", "frequency of mention"]
definition: Problems/concerns may be defined as issues that galvanize interest and direct attention in organizations because of envisioned consequences associated with action or inaction. The study concentrates on the precipitating circumstances defined as problems/concerns which characterize the environments of organizations.

name: Organizational task environment
definition: The domain of task environments is defined as consisting of competitors, customers, suppliers, and those regulatory bodies with whom an organization must interact and whose actions directly affect organizational goal attainment. The organizational life cycle described in terms of successive phases/stages and the extent of competition encountered act as independent variables that interact to form distinct decision situations with different mixes of dominant problems/concerns.

name: Firm-specificity of patent assets
authors_terms: ["firm-specificity", "Firm-specificity of patent assets", "firm-specificity of patent assets"]
definition: Firm-specificity refers to the degree to which the patent's value is tied to the original venture and the tacit knowledge of one or more of the inventors. The authors seek to capture the degree to which the value of the patent asset is tied to the original venture and the tacit knowledge of the inventors.

name: Patent market liquidity
definition: Market thickness, or 'liquidity,' refers to the intensity with which patents related to the focal startup's inventions are transacting in the secondary market. The authors also describe it as trading activity in the secondary market for patents in the sector and the issue years of the startup's patents.

name: Patent sale as a standalone asset
authors_terms: ["patent sale as a standalone asset", "patent sales as standalone assets", "standalone sale"]
definition: The authors distinguish between two modes of transfer: patent sales as standalone assets and 'co-mobility' in which patents move with an inventor to the purchasing organization. A patent is sold as a standalone asset when it is sold without one or more of the inventors on the focal patent co-moving to the purchasing organization.

name: Co-mobility with an inventor
authors_terms: ["co-mobility", "co-movement with an inventor", "co-mobility of the patent and the inventors"]
definition: The authors distinguish between two modes of transfer: patent sales as standalone assets and 'co-mobility' in which patents move with an inventor to the purchasing organization. Co-mobility is the mode in which the patent is sold and one or more of the inventors in the focal patent moves to the purchasing organization.

name: Patent not sold
authors_terms: ["patent not sold", "not sold", "failure to sell the patent"]
definition: The model predicts three outcomes for patents originating from failed startups: sold as standalone assets, co-mobility, and not sold. The authors note that under certain conditions the most plausible alternative to transferring patent assets through co-mobility is failure to sell the patent rather than sale as a standalone asset.

name: International asset dispersion
definition: The extent of MNE investment in foreign markets, that is, the extent to which the MNE's assets are spread across foreign countries. It is one of the two related, but distinct, components into which the traditional concept of geographic scope is parsed.

name: Country environment diversity
authors_terms: ["country environment diversity", "CED", "environment diversity", "diversity in the country environments"]
definition: The range in political, economic, and cultural differences among the MNE's foreign operations, defined more precisely as the variance of country-level conditions in which the MNE operates. It is the second of the two components of geographic scope.

name: Economic performance
definition: Economic performance is defined through several objective market-based figures rather than a single parameter such as profit, growth or market share, on the assertion that firms are strategic, rational actors that are fundamentally concerned with economic results.

name: Mutual dependence
definition: Scholars have decomposed the concept of interdependence into two dimensions: (1) mutual dependence (the sum of the dependencies of A on B and of B on A) and (2) power imbalance. Mutual dependence captures the extent to which resources are exchanged between firms.

name: Subunit divestiture hazard
authors_terms: ["subunit divestiture", "hazard of divestiture", "the hazard that an acquired subunit would be divested"]
definition: The dependent variable was the hazard that an acquired subunit would be divested within a certain year; the event was the divestiture of the subunit. Retaining or divesting an acquired subunit is an adaptive process in response to the dynamics of the mutual dependence.

name: Subunit acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["subunit acquisition activity", "subsequent acquisition activity", "subsequent interindustry acquisitions"]
definition: One way for a subunit to increase its power relative to its parent is to control the resources outside the parent-subunit relation by establishing second-tier businesses through interindustry acquisitions. Subunit acquisition activity is the three-year cumulative number of interindustry acquisitions completed by the subunit after it was acquired.

name: Subunit alliance formation
authors_terms: ["subunit alliance formation", "formation of subsequent joint ventures", "interindustry alliance activities"]
definition: To enhance their relative power, subunits are likely to absorb constraints through interindustry alliances (including joint ventures), especially when M&A strategies are not viable. Subunit alliance formation is the three-year cumulative number of interindustry alliances formed by the subunit after it was acquired.

name: Business unit performance
definition: Performance is a complex multidimensional construct that is influenced by both the level of analysis (e.g., functional vs. business strategy) and strategy type (e.g., Prospector vs. Defender). We focus on profitability and market performance (i.e., sales and market share effectiveness) because they are widely recognized as two of the most important indicators of financial performance.

name: Strategy type
authors_terms: ["Strategy Type", "Miles and Snow strategy types", "Prospector", "Analyzer", "Low Cost Defender", "Differentiated Defender"]
definition: Miles and Snow (1978) developed a comprehensive framework that addresses the alternative ways in which organizations define and approach their product-market domains (the entrepreneurial problem) and construct structures and processes (the administrative and technical problems) to achieve success in those domains. Prospectors continuously seek to locate and exploit new product and market opportunities while Defenders attempt to seal off a portion of the total market to create a stable set of products and customers.

name: Selling strategy
authors_terms: ["Selling Strategy", "relationship selling strategy", "transaction selling strategy", "Extendedness of Relationship"]
definition: Relationship selling is based on interdependence between sellers and buyers, sharing of critical information that is based on trust between the two parties, and longevity of the relationship that enables both parties to enjoy financial rewards from coordinated strategic investments. At the opposite end of the continuum of selling strategies is transaction selling, a discrete activity with the transaction being the near-term outcome of the selling effort.

name: Internalization of selling activities
authors_terms: ["Internalization of Selling Activities", "internal sales force", "contracting with an external sales force", "independent sales representatives"]
definition: A transaction occurs when a good or service is transferred across a separable interface, such as when a firm contracts with independent sales representatives to facilitate transactions. The alternative is for the firm to integrate forward and add the selling activity to its activities in product development and production.

name: Extent of supervision
authors_terms: ["Extent of Supervision/Autonomy", "extent of supervision", "supervisory control", "sales force supervision"]
definition: The extent of supervision required is concerned with the degree to which sales people are monitored and directed. Low supervision requirements imply that sales people are knowledgeable and are best able to determine the appropriate activities to achieve the firm's goals and/or that the importance of retaining an individual account is relatively low.

name: Salesperson control system
authors_terms: ["Salesperson Control System", "outcome-based control system", "behavior-based control system", "mixed control system"]
definition: Anderson and Oliver (1987) classified sales force control systems into two types: outcome-based and behavior-based. Outcome-based control focuses on the results that a salesperson achieves; behavior-based control systems ensure consistency of action by prescribing and monitoring the activities of the sales force.

name: Compensation system
authors_terms: ["Compensation", "incentive-oriented compensation system", "salary-based compensation system", "balanced compensation system"]
definition: Compensation systems span a spectrum from straight salary or 'fixed' to straight commission or 'incentive-based.' Between these two extremes lie hybrid systems that provide both a base salary and some form of commission or bonus as an incentive.

name: Technology and marketing intensity
definition: We argue that investments in technology and marketing will amplify managerial awareness since both of these investments will increase the degree to which a firm has an external and forward-looking focus.

name: Firm size
definition: We measured firm size as the logarithm of total assets of the acquirer one year prior to the merger announcement.

name: Firm diversification
authors_terms: ["acquirer diversification", "level of diversification", "level of diversification of the firm"]
definition: Firm diversification describes the diversity of business lines and/or product markets, with diversified firms having more complex structures than more focused firms.

name: Firm slack resources
authors_terms: ["slack resources", "financial slack", "unabsorbed slack", "unabsorbed acquirer financial slack"]
definition: Slack resources represent liquid resources that the firm can leverage to fund competitive action.

name: Prior firm performance
authors_terms: ["prior firm performance", "firm performance", "acquiring firm prior performance"]
definition: Prior firm performance was measured with the firm's return on assets (ROA) one year prior to the acquisition.

name: Timing of action in merger wave
authors_terms: ["timing of firm action within an acquisition wave", "position in the wave", "temporal action within the wave", "action timing", "acquisition position within the merger wave"]
definition: To calculate the timing of firm action within an acquisition wave, we calculated the number of days that each acquisition announcement occurred after the first acquisition in the wave. We then divided this by the total number of days in the wave.

name: CEO MBA education
definition: We argue that chief executives with MBAs will be more likely to perceive requests to voluntarily disclose the firm's environmental performance as a strategic opportunity than other business executives.

name: CEO legal education
definition: Lawyers are trained to protect their clients' interests and socialized to behave conservatively and minimize risk.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Research on the effects of tenure has consistently demonstrated an inverse relationship between the time in office and organizational change.

name: Voluntary environmental disclosure
authors_terms: ["voluntary disclosure", "environmental disclosure", "disclose voluntary environmental information", "environmental performance disclosure"]
definition: Here, we focus on requests made by shareholders for firms to increase the disclosure of their environmental performance. Furthermore, disclosure about environmental performance is, in most instances, done on a voluntarily basis and is, therefore, subject to managerial discretion.

name: Novel recombinant innovation
definition: Novel recombinant innovation includes both the combination of new technological components and new configurations of previously combined technological components. The dependent variable specifically reflects the extent to which the focal subunit applied for patents containing subclasses that were not likely to be combined with each other.

name: Corporate staff arrivals
authors_terms: ["corporate staff arrivals", "corporate arrivals", "new staff members joining the corporate office", "corporate newcomers"]
definition: Corporate arrivals were defined as total number of individuals who were absent from the corporate staff directory in year t − 1 but appeared in the corporate directory in year t.

name: Corporate staff departures
authors_terms: ["corporate staff departures", "corporate departures", "existing staff members departing the corporate office"]
definition: Corporate departures were defined as total staff members who were listed by the corporate staff directory in year t − 1 but were absent from the entire directory in year t.

name: Subunit member arrivals
authors_terms: ["subunit member arrivals", "subunit arrivals", "new members joining a subunit"]
definition: Subunit arrivals were defined as total number of subunit members who were absent from the directory of a subunit location i in year t − 1 but were listed by subunit i's directory in year t.

name: Subunit member departures
authors_terms: ["subunit member departures", "subunit departures", "staff members leaving a subunit"]
definition: Subunit departures were defined as all those who were listed by subunit i's directory in year t − 1 but were absent from the entire directory in year t.

name: Efficiency strategy
definition: Firms that offer only standard products must compete on organizational efficiency. Efficiency firms provide products of a prescribed quality at predictable levels of demand.

name: Flexibility strategy
definition: Flexibility refers to a firm's ability to provide made-to-order products that are unique to individual customers or groups of customers. Firms that offer only made-to-order products must compete on their flexibility to meet individual customer needs.

name: Mixed strategy
definition: Firms that offer both standard and made-to-order products must attempt to be both efficient and flexible, which requires a hybrid configuration of technology, structure, control systems, and labor.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent construct, firm performance, was captured using three measures: return on invested capital, return on equity, and return on assets.

name: Alliance use
authors_terms: ["alliance use", "use or nonuse of alliance relationships", "alliances", "alliance relationships"]
definition: Alliances are structured agreements that establish exchange relationships between cooperating firms but do not involve a freestanding, wholly owned organizational entity. The study characterizes firms by their use or nonuse of such relationships.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: The perceived inability of an organization's key manager or managers to accurately assess the external environment of the organization or the future changes that might occur in that environment. The authors propose that it is a multidimensional construct that can be characterized by the source of the uncertainty.

name: General uncertainty
definition: General uncertainty, or effect uncertainty as Milliken labeled it, encompasses a firm leader's perceived inability to assess what the nature of the impact of a future state of the environment or environmental change will be on the organization.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technological demand and volatility", "technological environment", "technological complexity and volatility"]
definition: The second source of perceived environmental uncertainty is the technological environment of a firm; technological complexity and volatility have been found to be associated with the formation of alliances, and it is the rapid pace of technological development and the associated high costs that underlie the motive to cooperate.

name: Predictability of customer demands and competitor actions
authors_terms: ["predictability of customers and competitors", "predictability of markets", "state uncertainty", "low predictability of customer demands and competitor actions"]
definition: State uncertainty, as Milliken labeled it, is the perceived inability to predict a particular component of the environment, such as the actions of competitors or the demands of customers; the less predictable a leader believes the market of his or her firm to be, the more likely alliance use becomes.

name: Demands for internationalization
definition: The fourth source of perceived uncertainty is growing demands for internationalization; often the only avenue for involvement in international trade is through alliance use. The items assess perceptions of the extent to which internationalization seemed needed for firm success.

name: Perceived potential for future growth and profits in the principal industry
authors_terms: ["potential for growth and profits", "future potential for growth and profits", "perceptions of a future potential for profit and growth"]
definition: The fifth source of uncertainty is key managers' lack of faith in their ability to assess the future potential for growth and profits in their firms' principal industries; firms often seek refuge in alliances when faced with mature, low-growth markets.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial orientation", "entrepreneurial orientation of a firm's key manager"]
definition: A firm whose management team has an entrepreneurial orientation is characterized by risk taking in the face of uncertainty, the extensiveness and frequency of product innovation and the related tendency toward technological leadership; it reflects an overall strategic orientation that has a significant impact on how organizational leaders interpret and respond to the firm's environment.

name: Individualism/collectivism
definition: Individualism/collectivism has emerged as the cultural dimension most often associated with cooperative behavior; people with individualistic orientations believe that the self is the basic unit of survival, value independence and self-sufficiency, give priority to personal goals, and place high value on self-direction, social justice, and equality, whereas people with collectivist orientations emphasize the importance of belonging to a stable, select in-group and value cooperation with the in-group.

name: Firm performance
definition: Family-firm performance is defined in terms of sales growth, which the authors argue is a more reliable measure of family-firm performance than income-based measures because privately held firms have incentive to minimize reported taxable income and no incentive to minimize reported sales.

name: Pay incentives to nonfamily agents
authors_terms: ["Nonfamily Pay Incentives", "pay incentives to nonfamily agents", "incentive compensation paid to nonfamily agents"]
definition: Pay incentives tie a portion of an agent's pay to a performance objective that can be effectively monitored, and the authors posit that privately held, family-managed firms should offer them to nonfamily agents to mitigate agency threats to their performance.

name: Pay incentives to family agents
authors_terms: ["Family Pay Incentives", "pay incentives to family agents"]
definition: Tying a portion of the family agent's wage to outcomes that can be effectively monitored and objectively assessed, like firm performance; the authors liken family agent pay incentives to parents making a portion of their children's allowance contingent upon completing certain chores.

name: Strategic planning
definition: Strategic planning is a tool for achieving good agency: it reduces information asymmetries within the firm, requires agents to systematically assess firm performance relative to internal and external benchmarks, promotes alignment of attitudes toward growth opportunities and risk, and promotes consensus on goals and strategies.

name: Board entrenchment
definition: Widely held firms reduce executive or board turnover (entrenchment) and increase board autonomy and vigilance with rules regarding CEO and board tenure and the appointment of outside directors; the authors anticipate that family dynamics, self-control and owner control make family-firm boards prone to entrenchment.

name: Disclosure of share transfer intentions
authors_terms: ["Transfer Intentions", "disclosure of the major shareholder's estate and share transfer intentions", "share transfer plans"]
definition: Family-firm CEOs have incentive to keep the specific conditions of their share transfer intentions private, and uncertainty regarding share transfer plans increases agency problems because the ambiguous promise of ownership and/or leadership locks hopeful heirs into a dependent relationship with the firm.

name: Governance practice configuration
authors_terms: ["configuration of good governance practices", "configurations of governance mechanisms", "governance profiles"]
definition: Firms may bundle some or all of the governance mechanisms highlighted in the first four hypotheses into an internally consistent set or configuration of governance practices that addresses the agency problems which typically arise in privately held, family-managed firms.

name: Relative exploration orientation
authors_terms: ["relative exploration orientation", "relative amount of exploration", "exploration versus exploitation orientation", "relative exploration"]
definition: The balance between exploration and exploitation becomes evident in the extent to which the firm emphasizes exploration activities over exploitation activities (hereafter 'relative exploration orientation'). A firm with a low relative exploration orientation conducts primarily exploitation activities, while a high relative exploration orientation suggests that the firm focuses mainly on exploration activities.

name: Financial performance
definition: Instead of using accounting-based measures of performance, we use the market-based measure of Tobin's Q as our dependent performance variable. Market value based measures such as Tobin's Q have the advantage of capturing short-term performance and long-term prospects.

name: Industry technological dynamism
definition: The moderating effects of environmental conditions on the relative exploration orientation-performance relationship are studied focusing on industry technological dynamism. We operationalize industry technological dynamism as industry R&D intensity.

name: Third-party ties
definition: Firms weave webs of relationships that extend beyond their own industries; though they may not interact directly, they have a variety of indirect relationships—third-party ties—through common clients, through shared suppliers and service providers, and through hiring one another's past employees. Third-party ties could influence both the choice of acquisition target and the performance of the combined firm after the merger.

name: Acquisition target choice
authors_terms: ["target choice", "selection of acquisition targets", "target selection", "the probability that an acquiring firm acquires a particular target firm"]
definition: The selection of acquisition targets represents precisely the type of transaction in which one would expect choices to depend strongly on interorganizational relationships. The authors set a binary dependent variable, acquisition, to one for the actual mergers (the cases) and to zero for the unrealized combinations (the controls).

name: Distance between acquirer and target
authors_terms: ["distance between the acquiring firm and potential targets", "geographic distance", "shared industries", "industry distance"]
definition: The relational mechanisms of exposure and information access should become increasingly important as acquirers consider businesses more distant from their own operations. The authors measured proximity of the acquirer to potential targets on two dimensions, industry focus (shared industries) and geographic location.

name: Post-merger performance
definition: Because CAR and ROA offered unattractive assessments in this setting, the authors focused their analysis on two types of operational measures of performance: client retention and billings per client. Client retention matters greatly to firm performance given that agencies typically have few major clients.

name: Board interlock tie
definition: Two firms, A and B, are coded as having an interlock tie when at least one officer or owner from firm A serves as an outside director at firm B, or vice versa; ties are directional and are created by individuals who are principally affiliated as officers or owners with the firms they connect.

name: Independent board control
authors_terms: ["board control", "independent board control", "independent monitoring and control"]
definition: Items in the control scale assessed key behavioral elements of board control that have been theorized to entail board independence from management, including the board's tendency to monitor and evaluate CEO decision making and performance and the frequency with which directors challenge the CEO's position on strategic issues, rather than deferring to the CEO's judgment.

name: CEO-board cooperation
definition: A form of board involvement in which boards enter closer working relationships with CEOs by providing advice and counsel at the CEO's request, working together with them to govern the firm rather than separately in a principal-agent relationship.

name: Third-party ties
definition: A top manager is exposed to second-hand information about an outside director on his or her board when the manager has a common appointment on another board with a third director who sits on that director's board; indirect interlock ties between the CEO and outside directors run through third-party directors.

name: Alliance formation
definition: The formation of a strategic alliance between two firms, where the authors focus on a subset of alliances known as joint ventures, which entail the creation of a separate legal entity in which the parent firms take equity.

name: Technological intensity
authors_terms: ["technological intensity", "R&D intensity", "ratio between R&D expenditures and sales", "R&D-to-sales ratio"]
definition: Technological intensity as measured by the ratio between R&D expenditures and sales for the product area of the alliance; a high R&D-to-sales ratio is likely to reflect high uncertainty.

name: Intent to conduct joint R&D
authors_terms: ["joint R&D", "intention to conduct joint R&D", "intent to conduct R&D", "decision to engage in joint R&D"]
definition: The intention of the parent firms to conduct research and development jointly within the alliance; in joint R&D the knowledge being exchanged is not yet fully embodied in designs and specifications but embedded in the experience and skills of people.

name: Parent firm size
definition: The size of the parent firms of an alliance, indicated by their consolidated total assets; very large organizations may be comparatively invulnerable, with abundant slack resources and multiple technical cores.

name: Interorganizational governance form
authors_terms: ["form of governance", "governance form", "form of alliance", "joint venture", "contractual agreements", "quasi-market", "quasi-hierarchy"]
definition: The governance mode chosen for a cooperative relationship, ranging from market-dominated contractual agreements, which do not involve shared equity, to hierarchically dominated joint ventures, which involve creating a new legal entity with shared equity.

name: Top management team industry experience
authors_terms: ["industry-specific experience", "TMT industry experience", "industry experience in the top management team", "top managers' industry experience"]
definition: As a critical form of managerial experience, industry-specific experience embeds the tacit knowledge of the opportunities, threats, competitive conditions, technology, and regulations specific to an industry, as well as goodwill with industry players such as buyers and suppliers. Managerial familiarity with technology and market conditions in a specific industry enables managers to detect emerging opportunities and new trends and to evaluate alternative paths of investment and growth.

name: Outside director industry experience
authors_terms: ["outside directors' industry experience", "industry experience among outside directors", "managerial industry experience of outside directors"]
definition: Tacit (experiential) knowledge of the focal firm's industry, technology, competition, and regulations is foundational to the human capital of outside directors. Outside directors with experience in the focal firm's industry can supplement managers' experience in making strategic decisions, and their previous experience in different firms in the focal industry increases the number of links with industry players and access to information and resource networks.

name: Liability of newness
authors_terms: ["liability of newness", "exposure to the liability of newness", "firm's exposure to the liability of newness", "firm age"]
definition: Liability of newness occurs when young firms lack resources, slack, and the legitimacy of older firms and struggle to develop business relationships with suppliers and customers. It is recognized as a major factor contributing to the disproportionately high rates of failure among venture firms.

name: International diversification
definition: International diversification may be defined as expansion across the borders of global regions and countries into different geographic locations, or markets. A firm's level of international diversification is reflected by the number of different markets in which it operates and their importance to the firm.

name: Product diversification
definition: Product diversification is expansion into product markets new to a firm.

name: Firm performance
definition: Three accounting-based measures were initially considered as possible indicators of firm performance: return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), and return on equity (ROE).

name: Firm innovation
definition: R&D intensity was used as a proxy for innovation. It has been found to be positively related to measures of innovative output such as patents and new product introductions.

name: Private insurance coverage
authors_terms: ["Private insurance", "higher-paying private insurance patients", "patient ability to pay", "primary payment method billed"]
definition: Private insurance patients are the higher-paying patient group in the authors' setting; prioritizing the financial goal means overproviding service to them relative to lower-paying Medicaid patients, who represent the baseline of service.

name: EMS service provision
authors_terms: ["service provision", "service provision differences", "procedures", "time with patient", "overprovision of service"]
definition: Service provision refers to the medical procedures EMS crews perform and the time they spend with patients. These variables measure key dimensions of EMS service provision that are associated with patient billable charges and agency financial performance.

name: Agency financial need
authors_terms: ["agency financial need", "agency financial pressure", "long-term financial pressures", "short-term financial need", "high revenue agency"]
definition: Agency financial need relates to the perceived importance of the agency's financial goal relative to the social goal on a call. It is captured by the agency's patient payer mix over the long term and by recent private insurance call volume over the short term.

name: Call acuity
definition: Call acuity shapes relative goal importance by altering the perceived downside risk of failing to achieve the social goal. In high-acuity cases, the potential cost of delay or suboptimal service could be lethal.

name: Nonprofit agency status
authors_terms: ["non-profit EMS agencies", "for-profit EMS agencies", "organization type", "profit orientation", "agency types"]
definition: Nonprofit agency status distinguishes nonprofit EMS agencies, including community, government, and fire agencies, from for-profit agencies, including private non-hospital agencies. It may shape baseline prioritization of competing financial and social goals.

name: Initial public offerings
authors_terms: ["initial public offerings", "IPOs", "local density of BT IPOs", "IPO concentration"]
definition: Initial public offerings are one of the two types of liquidity events the authors study. An IPO results in a company's equity trading on a public stock market, which enables high-level employees to sell their equity holdings; ownership stakes become liquid assets following the transition to public status.

name: Acquisitions of biotechnology firms
authors_terms: ["acquisitions", "local density of acquired BT firms", "acquisition concentration"]
definition: Acquisitions are the second category of liquidity events the authors study. In a typical acquisition a larger organization subsumes a smaller one, and the authors measure the acquired firm's market capitalization in constant (1995) dollars based on the price paid by the acquirer.

name: Interindustry acquisitions
authors_terms: ["interindustry acquisition concentration", "acquisitions of early-stage technology companies by demographically dissimilar firms", "cross-industry acquisitions", "biotech firms acquired by non-BT firms"]
definition: Acquisitions in which a biotech firm is acquired by a non-DBF (non-biotech) enterprise; the demographic distance between acquirer and target is defined as a difference in the core industries of the merging firms.

name: Intraindustry acquisitions
authors_terms: ["intraindustry acquisition concentration", "biotech firms acquired by other BT firms", "intrapopulation acquisitions"]
definition: Acquisitions in which one biotech firm acquires another, that is, transactions within the population.

name: Organizational founding rate
authors_terms: ["founding rate", "rate of new firm formation", "new venture creation rates", "rate of creation of new biotech firms", "local founding rate"]
definition: The rate at which new companies are created; the authors examine how the rate of creation of new biotech firms in relatively small geographic areas (metropolitan statistical areas) varies with the recent occurrence of liquidity events in the industry.

name: Non-compete covenant enforceability
authors_terms: ["enforceability of post-employment non-compete covenants", "non-compete covenants", "non-compete regime", "weak-legal-regime"]
definition: Post-employment non-compete covenants are agreements, typically signed when an employee joins a firm in a high-ranking technical or managerial position, that specify a post-employment period of time during which the employee is restricted from enlisting with a rival employer. State-level statutes and case law determine the extent to which employers may enforce these covenants.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR involves widely observable actions that can signal a firm's unobservable intentions and capabilities; specifically, CSR signals that firms have both the intention and the capability to act with a long-term vision and to take into account the interests of different stakeholders. CSR involves both policies, which signal intentions, and practices, which signal capabilities.

name: Hedge fund targeting
authors_terms: ["target", "hedge fund targeting", "targeted by an activist hedge fund"]
definition: The authors use hedge fund targeting as a proxy for reaction costs, creating a dichotomous variable 'target' that was equal to '1' if a firm had been targeted by an activist hedge fund in a given year and '0' otherwise. Activist hedge funds buy shares to influence the strategy of targeted firms within a relatively short period of time.

name: Industry CSR level
authors_terms: ["industry CSR", "a high level of CSR in an industry"]
definition: The average CSR score for all firms, excluding the focal firm, in an industry group classified according to two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes.

name: Financial communication vagueness
definition: When firms use approximations, express doubt, and make general rather than specific statements, financial communication is vague. Vague financial communication increases the information asymmetry between firms and their shareholders.

name: Wholesale deregulation
definition: Wholesale deregulation emphasizes competition at the electricity generation stage. In competitive wholesale electricity markets, the basis of competition is price because those generating units that have lower costs, and thus lower bids, earn the right to dispatch electricity to the transmission grid.

name: Retail deregulation
definition: Retail deregulation emphasizes competition on the retail side; under retail deregulation, customers are allowed to choose their own electricity suppliers instead of having default suppliers.

name: Entry into renewable generation
authors_terms: ["entry into the renewable generation market", "entry into the renewable generation business", "entry into renewables", "entry into the renewable electricity generation business"]
definition: Entry by investor-owned electric utilities into the renewable generation market; a dummy variable takes a value of 1 if the firm-year observation is an entry into renewable generation and 0 otherwise, focusing on nonhydro renewables such as solar, wind, biomass, geothermal, and waste-to-energy.

name: Fossil fuel combustion efficiency
authors_terms: ["more capable of using fossil fuels", "capabilities with respect to brown technologies", "heat rate", "combustion inefficiency"]
definition: Heat rate, measured as the ratio of heat input to electricity generated (Btu/kWh), represents how efficiently an electric generator uses heat energy from fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas in generating electricity. Lower heat rate means less input per unit of electricity generated, pointing to higher combustion efficiency.

name: Actual renewable demand
