definition: Actual renewable demand is proxied by the renewable fraction of the total electricity generation capacity at the state level. The authors contrast it with latent green demand expressed as environmental sensitivity or preference.

name: Managerial discretion
authors_terms: ["managerial discretion", "latitude of action", "latitude of managerial action"]
definition: Managerial discretion refers to latitude of managerial action (Hambrick and Finkelstein, 1987). Managerial discretion may encourage investment in green technologies because it allows managers to deal effectively with risks and uncertainties associated with the use of unfamiliar green technologies.

name: Presence of independent power producers
definition: The presence of independent power producers in the renewable generation market was measured using the ratio of independent power producers' renewable capacity to total renewable capacity at the state level. For investor-owned utilities, the presence of independent power producers is a basis for both competition and cooperation.

name: Previous investments in renewables
authors_terms: ["previous investments in renewables", "renewable generation dummy at the utility level", "prior experience in using green technologies"]
definition: Previous investments in renewables are indicated using a dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm has nonhydro renewable capacity in year t - 1, and takes 0 otherwise.

name: Share of renewables in the fuel mix portfolio
authors_terms: ["percentage of renewables in the fuel mix portfolio", "share of renewables", "percentage of renewable capacity", "changes in the share of renewables in fuel mix portfolio"]
definition: Fuel mix portfolio refers to the proportions of each fuel type used by a company to generate electricity. The share of renewables can be represented by the ratio of renewable capacity to total capacity.

name: CEO power over the board
authors_terms: ["CEO power over the board", "the CEO's power relative to the board", "relative CEO/board power"]
definition: The CEO's power relative to the board of directors, which the authors argue helps determine whether firms decouple formally adopted policies from practice; it is captured by the CEO's relative tenure, board cooptation, board leadership structure, and director stock ownership.

name: Buyback program decoupling
authors_terms: ["decoupling of its buyback program from practice", "decoupling of stock buyback programs from practice", "the extent of repurchase plan implementation"]
definition: Repurchase plans specify the number of shares targeted for repurchase but not exactly when the purchase will occur, so management can formally adopt a program and then actually purchase only a small fraction of that amount or none at all; decoupling is the separation of formally stated plans from actual financial practices.

name: Buyback decoupling at tied firms
authors_terms: ["decoupling of stock buyback programs at tied-to firms", "decoupling of buyback programs at tied-to firms"]
definition: The extent of decoupling of stock buyback programs from practice at other firms to which the focal firm is connected by an interlock tie, measured for one-step (directional and non-directional) and two-step ties through the board of a financial institution.

name: Incentive plan decoupling at tied firms
authors_terms: ["decoupling of LTIPs at tied-to firms", "decoupling of CEO incentive plans (LTIPs) from practice at other firms"]
definition: The extent of decoupling of long-term incentive plans (LTIPs) from practice at other firms to which the focal firm is connected by an interlock tie; LTIPs were adopted ostensibly to improve the relationship between CEO pay and firm performance, yet a large portion of these plans were not actually implemented.

name: Prior buyback decoupling
authors_terms: ["prior decoupling of buyback programs", "prior decoupling of stock buyback programs from practice"]
definition: A firm's own prior experience with decoupling the formal adoption of a buyback program from practice, i.e., the extent to which shares were not actually repurchased under plans adopted previously.

name: Prior incentive plan decoupling
authors_terms: ["prior decoupling of LTIPs", "prior decoupling of CEO incentive plans (LTIPs) from practice"]
definition: A firm's own prior experience with decoupling an adopted long-term incentive plan from practice, i.e., the extent to which shares reserved under a previously adopted LTIP were not actually granted.

name: Creative performance
authors_terms: ["creative performance", "organizational creative performance", "creativity of fashion collections"]
definition: An organization enjoys superior creative performance when it consistently generates novel and useful products or services. To buyers, creativity is a combination of the novelty of a collection as well as their assessment of the probability that this collection will actually get sold in stores.

name: Mobility to foreign competitors
authors_terms: ["Foreign Mobility Out-Degree", "losing employees to foreign competitors", "mobility to foreign competitors", "employee mobility to foreign competitors"]
definition: Following Godart et al. (2014), we computed Foreign Mobility Out-Degree as the number of houses across different countries to which the focal fashion house becomes connected through designers' outward mobility.

name: Mobility to domestic competitors
authors_terms: ["Domestic Mobility Out-Degree", "within-country mobility", "mobility to domestic competitors"]
definition: We computed a Domestic Mobility Out-Degree as the number of houses within the same country to which the focal fashion house is connected through outward mobility of its past designers in a given six-year period.

name: Mobility to higher-status competitors
authors_terms: ["Higher-Status Mobility Out-Degree", "losing employees to higher-status competitors", "mobility to higher-status competitors"]
definition: The number of competitors belonging to the higher-status group to which a fashion house lost designers in the relevant window; status groups were identified by computing scores corresponding to the 33rd and 66th percentiles of status in a given year. For instance, a focal fashion house located in the medium-status group that lost designers to two houses located in the higher-status group would have a Higher-Status Mobility Out-Degree equal to two.

name: Mobility to same-status competitors
authors_terms: ["Same-Status Mobility Out-Degree", "mobility to same-status competitors", "same-status competitors that hire the focal firm's employees"]
definition: The number of competitors belonging to the same-status group to which a fashion house lost designers in the relevant window, with status groups identified from the 33rd and 66th percentiles of the status distribution in a given year. For instance, a medium-status house that lost designers to one house located in the same-status group would have a Same-Status Mobility Out-Degree equal to one.

name: Mobility to lower-status competitors
authors_terms: ["Lower-Status Mobility Out-Degree", "losing employees to lower-status competitors", "mobility to lower-status competitors"]
definition: The number of competitors belonging to the lower-status group to which a fashion house lost designers in the relevant window, with status groups identified from the 33rd and 66th percentiles of the status distribution in a given year. For instance, a medium-status house that lost designers to three houses located in the lower-status group would have a Lower-Status Mobility Out-Degree equal to three.

name: Industry product differentiation
definition: One of the three industry structure characteristics on which the authors focus; industries which are highly differentiated tend to offer more avenues for competition than industries which are less differentiated and provide multiple ways in which firms can choose to create and maintain competitive advantage. It is operationalized as the degree of advertising intensity in the industry, defined as advertising expenses as a percentage of sales.

name: Industry growth rate
definition: The average annual growth rate in value of shipments in the 3 years preceding the year of succession. Industry growth rates influence the availability of opportunities for market expansion, new product introduction and overall levels of competitive variation.

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: The ratio of the industry's gross book value of assets to value of annual shipments. The greater the degree of capital intensity, the greater the emphasis on efficient asset management and cost control and the more firms are committed to a course of action.

name: CEO organizational tenure
definition: Organizational tenure of the CEO successor was measured as the number of years the CEO had served in the firm prior to the year of succession.

name: CEO age
definition: The CEO successor's age was measured as the number of years from the year of birth to the year of succession.

name: CEO educational level
definition: CEO educational level was measured on a 7-point scale based on the highest degree earned by the CEO.

name: Throughput functional background
definition: Functional backgrounds of newly selected CEOs were classified into 'throughput' or 'nonthroughput' categories; executives with dominant functional experience in production and operations, process R&D, and accounting were categorized as having 'throughput' functional backgrounds.

name: Postsuccession improvement in firm performance
authors_terms: ["postsuccession improvement in firm performance", "improvement in firm ROA"]
definition: Average relative firm ROA in the 3 years following succession minus average relative firm ROA in the 3 years prior to succession; the change in firm performance was used rather than an absolute measure because the change in performance can be more directly related to the succession event.

name: Common technology elements
authors_terms: ["incorporation of technology elements common with relevant complementary technologies", "COMPLEMENTARY", "incorporation of common technology elements", "identification and incorporation of technology elements common with the complementary technologies"]
definition: Technology choices during initial product design that are in common with the important complementary product technologies (not specific complementary products per se), which reduce the complexity of the technology linkages needed later for cross-product integration.

name: Product modularity
definition: Product modularity refers to the creation of a high degree of independence or 'loose coupling' between product components by standardizing component interface specifications.

name: Modularity decision criteria
authors_terms: ["use of product integration criteria for product modularity decisions", "modularity decision", "extent of CPI considerations in product modularity decisions"]
definition: The use of product integration criteria in deciding product modularity, broadly focused on the nature of data and function sharing needed for cross-product integration and on the nature of coupling between core product modules and other modules.

name: Product upgrade intensity
authors_terms: ["intensity of product upgrades", "intensity", "frequency of product upgrades"]
definition: The intensity or frequency of product upgrades in the initial years, i.e. the number of new versions of the product introduced by the firm.

name: Complementary product integration
authors_terms: ["complementary product integration", "CPI", "number of complementary product integrations", "number of CPI"]
definition: Integration of the focal product with relevant complementary products; the authors identify three types based on the nature and extent of coupling between the focal and complementary product: value-added internal (VI), add-on module (AM), and data interface (DI) integration.

name: Market seeking
definition: Market-seeking investment is undertaken in order to serve particular markets by local production and distribution, rather than by exporting from the home country or from a third country.

name: Resource seeking
definition: The resource-seeking motivation is driven by a need to access resources not available in the home countries of the investing firms, or available at higher costs than could be obtained in other locations.

name: Export seeking
definition: Export-seeking investment, that is, locating production overseas in order to serve a third market, is undertaken by firms seeking to lower production and transportation costs.

name: Efficiency seeking
definition: Efficiency-seeking investment is driven by the intention to spread value-adding activities geographically in order to take advantage of differences in the availability and cost of factor endowments in different countries.

name: Knowledge seeking
definition: Knowledge-seeking investment is driven by firms' needs to access complementary resources, notably various kinds of knowledge, in order to upgrade their own capabilities.

name: Oligopolistic reaction
definition: Firms often invest overseas on account of competitive pressures of various kinds, i.e., in reaction to competitors' actions, or as preemption to advance the firm's competitive position vis-à-vis its major competitors.

name: Industry information intensity
definition: In order to distinguish between industries that are high and low on information intensity, we used the investment in information and communication technology (ICT) in an industry.

name: Foreign direct investment
definition: FDI is the total capital flow, including capital flow between parents and affiliates, intercompany loans, and reinvested earnings.

name: CEO charismatic visions
authors_terms: ["CEO charismatic visions", "CCV", "CEO charismatic language", "CEO visionary language", "projection of charismatic language"]
definition: The projection in organizational discourse of the CEO's vision in charismatic language. Vision statements incorporate the leader's evaluation of the status quo, his/her formulation and articulation of organizational goals, and his/her projected means to achieve the goals, and charismatic visions present these elements with criticality of the status quo, morally and ideologically laden goals, and empowering means.

name: Favorability of analyst recommendations
authors_terms: ["favorability of individual analyst recommendations", "favorability of analyst recommendations", "favorability of recommendations"]
definition: The favorability of the stock recommendation issued by an individual analyst covering the firm, reflected in the likelihood that analysts categorize the CEO and firm as a 'product' worth supporting.

name: Uniformity of analyst recommendations
authors_terms: ["uniformity of recommendations", "uniformity of analyst recommendations", "uniformity of recommendations across all analysts following the firm"]
definition: The degree of agreement among the recommendations of all analysts following a given firm, so that 'differences of opinion are likely to be rare'.

name: Analyst EPS forecast error
authors_terms: ["analyst EPS forecast error", "analyst forecast error", "forecast errors", "analyst forecast accuracy (inverse)"]
definition: The error made by an individual analyst in forecasting the firm's earnings per share, i.e., the absolute average forecast error of the analyst following the firm for a fiscal year.

name: Industrial disasters
authors_terms: ["industrial disasters", "industrial disaster incidents", "industrial crises", "technological catastrophes", "technological disasters"]
definition: Industrial disasters refer to human-caused, tragic, and sudden breakdowns in industrial, technological, and organizational systems that cause major disruption and damage to natural and social environments.

name: Foreign subsidiary entry
authors_terms: ["MNC's WOS entry into a host country", "entry"]
definition: To measure an MNC's WOS entry into a host country, we used a binary variable, which equaled one when the MNC invested in a WOS in a country for the first time and zero otherwise.

name: Foreign subsidiary expansion
authors_terms: ["MNC's WOS expansion into a host country", "expansion"]
definition: To measure an MNC's WOS expansion into a host country, we used the number of WOS in the host country after entry; changes in investment (expansion or contraction) are measured in terms of the increase or decrease in the number of an MNC's WOS in a given host country.

name: Technological capability
definition: Technological capability refers to 'the skills - technical, managerial, and institutional - that allow productive enterprises to utilize equipment and technical information efficiently'.

name: Safety management capability
definition: Drawing on this work, we conceptualize safety management capability as a firm's ability to control and manage the safety of its operations through its varied organizational routines.

name: Philanthropic capability
definition: We argue that a firm's philanthropic capability can refer to its ability to strategically manage its long-term charitable giving activities.

name: Geographic distance
authors_terms: ["geographic distance", "geographic distance between China and a foreign country"]
definition: Geographic distance reflects physical remoteness and is associated with challenging transportation and communication links. It directly increases the costs of doing business abroad, especially spatial costs and unfamiliarity costs.

name: Cultural distance
authors_terms: ["cultural distance", "cultural distance between a firm's home country and another country"]
definition: Cultural distance between countries reflects differences in social norms, religions, languages, and ethnicities. As cultural distance between home and host countries increases, it becomes harder for firms to adapt their organizational practices to the host countries.

name: FDI location choice
authors_terms: ["FDI location choice", "FDI location choices", "location choice", "foreign location choice"]
definition: FDI location choices are made deliberately by firms for revenue growth and can have important performance implications; firms tend to evaluate their strengths and weaknesses carefully and choose locations best suited to their internal resources and capabilities.

name: Firm size
definition: A firm's size affects its ability to acquire and retain resources in its home markets. Larger firms can achieve a stronger organizational reputation and obtain greater legitimacy from stakeholders.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age is another fundamental firm attribute. Old and young firms have different structures, processes, and strategies.

name: State ownership
definition: State ownership has long been linked to inefficiency, and a major cause of the inefficiency is that firms with higher state ownership are more likely to subject to the soft budget constraint. SOEs do not include sovereign wealth funds in this study.

name: Legacy divestiture
authors_terms: ["legacy divestitures", "legacy divestiture", "sale or spinoff of a company's legacy business"]
definition: The empirical context in which this tension will be investigated in this paper is legacy divestitures, the sale or spinoff of a company's legacy business.

name: Operating performance
definition: The interdependent routines that link legacy businesses to these companies' remaining operations will be broken. This implies that the functioning of these companies will be disrupted, which should be reflected in reduced short-term operating performance for these firms.

name: Stock market performance
definition: Hypothesis 1 predicts that investors will respond favorably to announcements of legacy divestitures, such that the stock market performance of the divesting firms will exceed that of their comparable non-divesting peers.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO Tenure", "tenure of a company's CEO", "new or recently appointed CEOs", "long-tenured CEOs"]
definition: To test both of these hypotheses, CEO Tenure is defined as the number of years a CEO has overseen a firm.

name: Industrial relatedness
definition: I operationalize the concept of relatedness by constructing a continuous measure, Relatedness, which is defined as the percentage of a firm's total business units that share a three-digit SIC code with the firm's legacy business.

name: Mutual trade dependence
definition: Mutual trade dependence refers to a resource dependent environment in which firms based in different countries mutually depend on each other for critical resources through international trade (imports and exports). The authors define the trade dependence of country A on country B as A's total exports to and imports from B, and then define mutual trade dependence as the sum of the dependencies of A upon B and B upon A.

name: Additional alliance activities
authors_terms: ["additional alliance activities", "additional alliance activities of the foreign partner"]
definition: Once alliance A is formed by a foreign partner and a local partner in a given country, the additional formation of alliances B by the foreign partner with other firms in the same industry increases the foreign partner's power because it has proportionally reduced its dependence on the local partner in A. Additional alliances may be formed in the home country, the host country, or a third country but in the same industry as A.

name: Additional acquisition activities
authors_terms: ["additional acquisition activities", "additional acquisition activities of the foreign partner"]
definition: If a firm is able to replace the role of a given partner by acquiring other sources of comparable resources, the firm can increase its power, thereby reducing its dependence relative to any given partner. Because individual alliances are embedded in a firm's alliance portfolio, additional acquisitions allow the firm to restructure its portfolio by using the acquired units to replace an existing alliance.

name: Repeated partnership
definition: Repeated partnerships indicate enhanced mutual partner dependence; when a foreign partner and a local partner engage in more repeated partnerships, their mutual dependence is more likely enhanced. Repeated partnerships, which are nurtured by multiple resource commitments, may also discourage the local partner from jeopardizing its multiple exchange relationships with the foreign partner and hence make the foreign partner less substitutable.

name: Alliance survival
definition: Alliance survival or termination is viewed as a logical consequence of a firm's adaptive responses to the dynamics of both environmental and partner dependencies. The authors limit their interpretations to the survival of alliances that have no anticipated duration by the involved partners.

name: Employer involvement in eldercare
authors_terms: ["employer involvement in eldercare", "level of employer involvement in eldercare", "total number of available eldercare benefits"]
definition: Employers were asked to indicate whether they provided a range of 17 different eldercare benefits in three primary areas: education and referral, including seminars and in-house referral services; eldercare support services, such as employer-sponsored adult daycare and case management; and financial arrangements, such as flexible spending accounts and cash subsidies for eldercare services.

name: Issue visibility
authors_terms: ["issue visibility", "visibility of eldercare issues", "employer involvement with other organizations responding to work-family issues"]
definition: The visibility of eldercare issues is likely to be high when an employer is involved with other organizations that are actively responding to work-family issues. Connections between organizations provide relational channels through which information can be shared and norms and practices made more visible.

name: Proportion of female employees
authors_terms: ["proportion of female employees", "proportion of female employees in an organization"]
definition: The exposure of an organization to eldercare concerns will depend in a number of important respects on the demography of the workforce; I focus on two particularly relevant demographic considerations, the proportion of female employees in an organization and the age composition of employees.

name: Employee age composition
authors_terms: ["age composition of employees", "proportion of employees 40 years of age and older"]
definition: The age composition of employees may also significantly increase the exposure of an organization to eldercare issues. It is generally recognized that eldercare concerns are greatest for employees 40 years of age and older.

name: Employee eldercare needs assessment
authors_terms: ["direct assessment of employee eldercare needs", "organizational assessment"]
definition: Employer involvement in eldercare will be influenced by whether the eldercare concerns and needs of employees are translated into critical human resource issues. Methods of assessment such as employee surveys or focus groups are likely to influence the importance of employee eldercare concerns and motivate greater employer involvement in eldercare.

name: Scope of work-family benefits
authors_terms: ["scope of other employer-provided work-family benefits", "total number of other employer-provided work-family benefits", "organizational values regarding eldercare"]
definition: The availability of a broad range of other family benefits, such as childcare, alternative work schedules, and leave practices, does reflect in an important way organizational values regarding meeting the work-family needs of employees.

name: Proportion of professionals
authors_terms: ["proportion of professionals", "proportion of professionals in an organization", "bargaining power of the organizational workforce"]
definition: Milliken and colleagues noted that the interpretation of eldercare issues as important may depend on the bargaining power of employees within organizations; they suggested that when employees are skilled and highly mobile, their bargaining power is likely to be high. One group of employees who tend to be highly skilled and mobile are professionals.

name: Perceived importance of eldercare for productivity
authors_terms: ["perceived importance of eldercare in enhancing employee productivity", "perceived importance of eldercare benefits to employee productivity"]
definition: A critical determinant of the degree of attention given to eldercare issues is the effect of eldercare demands on employee and organizational performance. Employers who perceive eldercare as a means to minimize lost employee productivity are more likely to expand their involvement in eldercare.

name: Firm market entry
definition: A core strategic response to such change is market entry: firms reshape their activity portfolios by entering new markets in order to maintain a competitive advantage.

name: Organizational unit market entry
authors_terms: ["Focal Unit-market-year entry", "focal unit's entry into adjacent product markets", "focal unit entry"]
definition: An organizational unit is coded as entering a market in year t if it is awarded a contract in that market in year t, provided that neither the focal organizational unit nor any other organizational unit within the same firm has previously received a contract in that market during the observation window.

name: Divisionalization
definition: We examine this experience-entry link in the context of firm divisionalization, a structural feature of firms in which activities are partitioned into multiple operating units or legally distinct entities under a corporate umbrella.

name: Adjacent market experience
authors_terms: ["Firm adjacent product market experience", "adjacent-market experience", "adjacent market experience"]
definition: To establish a baseline for market entry, we first define Firm adjacent product market experience, which captures whether a firm has prior experience in markets adjacent to a potential new entry.

name: Focal unit adjacent market experience
authors_terms: ["Focal unit adjacent market experience", "experience residing in the focal organizational unit", "locally embedded experience"]
definition: Focal unit adjacent market experience equals 1 if the focal unit held contracts in markets adjacent to the focal market during the pre-shock period (1996-2000), and 0 otherwise. This variable captures experience embedded within the operating unit associated with the observed entry.

name: Sister unit adjacent market experience
authors_terms: ["Sister unit adjacent market experience", "experience residing in sister organizational units", "sister-unit experience"]
definition: Sister unit adjacent market experience equals 1 if at least one other unit within the same firm, excluding the focal unit, held pre-shock contracts in markets adjacent to the focal market. This construction isolates experience located elsewhere in the organization.

name: Shared customer
definition: Shared customer, an indicator equal to 1 when the focal unit and sister units with adjacent experience served at least one common customer prior to the shock, captures a customer-based organizational linkage.

name: External engagement
authors_terms: ["External engagement (political)", "corporate attention oriented toward external engagement", "political donations"]
definition: External engagement (political), measured as the firm's political donations in the prior year, proxies for the salience of corporate-level external engagement.

name: Headquarters value added
authors_terms: ["headquarters value added", "value added by headquarters", "parent value added", "value creation by headquarters"]
definition: 'Headquarters value added' is defined as a situation in which the headquarters' influence leads to a level of performance in the subsidiary that is better than the subsidiary could have achieved as an independent, standalone entity.

name: Headquarters embeddedness
authors_terms: ["headquarters embeddedness", "headquarters' local embeddedness", "headquarters embeddedness in the subsidiary's context", "headquarters embeddedness in the subsidiary's network"]
definition: Headquarters maintaining its own relationships with the subsidiary's external network partners, in addition to the subsidiary's relationships; the authors argue that headquarters embeddedness in the subsidiary's local network is one important method of gathering and processing information and that it is one visible manifestation of the headquarters' parenting strategy for a particular subsidiary.

name: Subsidiary external embeddedness
definition: Subsidiary external embeddedness is typically defined in terms of the extent to which a unit has developed close relationships with local external actors as opposed to arm's-length relationships.

name: Organizational status
definition: Status is the esteem accorded to a firm by virtue of position in a social structure. High-status firms are able to exercise greater control over the terms of their relations with lower-status partners.

name: Status difference
authors_terms: ["status difference", "status differences between merging firms", "relative status", "status gap"]
definition: The direction and magnitude of the status difference between acquiring and target firms. The acquiring firm is socially superior to its target when this variable is positive.

name: Acquirer status outcome
definition: How the status of a postmerger organization compares to that of the acquiring firm prior to the transaction. Whether favorable or unfavorable, this "status outcome" may well alter the acquirer's ability to retain clients or command premium prices.

name: National culture incongruence
definition: Incongruence in the national cultures of the merging firms, indicated by whether the merged firms are headquartered in different countries. This potential stems from the fact that organizational routines are rooted in distinct national cultures.

name: Organizational culture incongruence
definition: Organizational cultures are complex systems of shared beliefs and assumptions; the intent was not to fully characterize these systems, but rather to identify measures that would allow assessment of their overall congruence.

name: Shareholder rights protection
authors_terms: ["shareholder rights", "rights of shareholders", "antidirector rights index", "protection of shareholder rights"]
definition: The extent to which shareholders' rights are defined and protected by corporate law, specifically against the discretion of the incumbent management team. Shareholders' rights are defined and protected in different ways and to different extents depending on the legal tradition that provides the foundation for corporate law.

name: Worker rights protection
definition: The degree to which workers' rights are defined and protected, as reflected in a country's ratification of International Labour Organization labor standards. A better protection of workers' rights makes this stakeholder more powerful in the firm and militates against practices that have the potential of eroding their well-being.

name: Bank ownership rights
authors_terms: ["banks' rights", "banks' rights to own stock in non-financial firms", "protection of banking rights", "bank rights"]
definition: The extent to which legislation defines and protects banks' right to own stakes in nonfinancial firms, and hence their power in corporate governance; banks are more powerful actors in countries in which legislation defines and protects this right.

name: Hostile takeover activity
authors_terms: ["hostile takeover activity", "hostile takeover attempts", "hostile takeover bids", "number of announced hostile takeovers"]
definition: A hostile takeover is a corporate acquisition that is actively opposed by the target firm's incumbent management or board of directors. The level of hostile takeover activity differs greatly across countries.

name: Transition to entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurship", "transition to entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial entry", "founding a hedge fund"]
definition: The variable entrepreneurship is defined as an event whereby a mutual fund manager exits the parent company in the mutual fund industry to launch a hedge fund. The dependent variable is defined as an individual's transition to entrepreneurship and coded as 1 if an individual founded a hedge fund, and 0 otherwise.

name: University peer entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["peer entrepreneurship (university)", "university peers' past foundings", "past entrepreneurial behaviors of university peers"]
definition: For each focal fund manager, I identified his or her university peers - that is, fund managers who share an educational affiliation with the focal manager. To construct the measure of peer entrepreneurship, I counted the number of managers who shared a university affiliation with the focal manager and who founded a hedge fund.

name: Gender similarity
definition: A well-established principle of homophily posits that individuals interact with those similar to them with respect to gender. For each focal manager I counted other managers who fulfilled three conditions: (1) they are of the same gender as the focal manager, (2) they share a university affiliation with a focal manager, and (3) they launched a hedge fund.

name: Peer spatial distance
authors_terms: ["peer spatial distance", "peers' average distance", "geographic distance of university peers"]
definition: For each focal individual, I calculated the average distance between that individual and his or her university peers. The higher the value of this measure, the larger the average distance between the focal manager and his or her peers.

name: CEO political liberalism
authors_terms: ["CEO political liberalism", "CEO liberalism", "political liberalism of a company's CEO"]
definition: We measured each CEO's political liberalism by using individual political contributions data to examine the degree to which they financially supported the Democratic Party; scores close to 0 indicate intensely conservative CEOs and scores close to 1 indicate intensely liberal CEOs.

name: Compensation committee liberalism
authors_terms: ["Compensation committee liberalism", "compensation committee members' values", "political liberalism of a company's compensation committee"]
definition: For Compensation committee liberalism, we first collected 10 years of donation records for each compensation committee members and calculated their individual liberalism index. We then took the mean of the individual members' indices and used it as a measure for compensation committee liberalism.

name: Horizontal pay equality
definition: Horizontal pay equality measures pay dispersion among non-CEO executives.

name: Vertical pay equality
definition: vertical pay equality measures pay differentials between CEO and non-CEO executives.

name: Multiple scenario analysis
definition: A set of strategic planning techniques with a long history in strategic management; the basic idea behind using these techniques is to bound uncertainty in a range of plausible scenarios that managers can use to generate strategic options and evaluate their robustness. In the study, both reading pre-written scenarios and creating one's own scenarios are treated as multiple scenario analysis.

name: Strategic reorientation
authors_terms: ["strategic reorientation", "adaptive shifts in patterns of strategic choice"]
definition: Shifting patterns of strategic choice to new bases of alignment, i.e., adaptive shifts in patterns of strategic choice following fundamental change. In the study it is indicated by the adoption of a price cutting strategy after the environmental change.

name: Confidence in the previous strategy
authors_terms: ["confidence in the previous strategy", "confidence in a previously successful strategy", "confidence in the current strategy"]
definition: Decision makers' belief in the efficacy of a previously successful strategy; imagining alternative futures can bring to light plausible reasons why a strategy might fail and thereby reduce belief in the efficacy of a previously successful strategy.

name: Belief in a new strategy
authors_terms: ["belief in a new strategy", "belief in potential new strategies", "causal beliefs"]
definition: The belief that an alternative course of action can provide a credible model for achieving one's goals in the circumstances anticipated; mentally simulating the effects of alternatives is argued to foster belief in their viability.

name: Past performance
definition: The level of market share attained at the end of year six, that is, immediately prior to the experimental interventions; performance in the early rounds before the environmental change.

name: Evaluation accuracy
authors_terms: ["evaluation accuracy", "accuracy of entrepreneur evaluations", "evaluative accuracy", "perceptual accuracy"]
definition: The degree of an entrepreneur's evaluation accuracy, measured as the absolute difference between an entrepreneur's ratings of a VC and their actual quality based on the LPJ index. Accuracy in evaluations of quality from a firm's track record is neither automatic nor homogenous.

name: Entrepreneur network centrality
definition: An entrepreneur's centrality as their position in the broader VC industry network, which affords shorter paths to others within an industry so that information is relayed more accurately and rapidly.

name: Entrepreneur motivation
definition: The extent to which individuals are motivated to think carefully about what constitutes reliable information and to diligently search for such information.

name: VC track record
definition: The observable past behavior and outputs of a firm relative to its competitors; the authors refer to the LPJ index as measuring objective track records.

name: VC prominence
definition: Prominence, or the collective awareness and recognition that a firm has received, which is substantially driven by the choices of influential third parties and collective social dynamics at the field level.

name: Ownership control
definition: The owners and the controllers are one and the same, e.g., friends or family members, and the owners participate in the management of their company; in the contrasting case, the owners neither control nor manage the business but hire and delegate the management of the firm to professionals.

name: Organization structure
authors_terms: ["organization", "flat organization", "multilayer organization", "simple vs. multiple levels of principal-agent relationships"]
definition: Organization is characterized according to the nature of the principal-agent relationship: whether it is direct, i.e., the business has a flat organization, or indirect, i.e., the level of delegation of the owner is multiple and the firm has a multilayer organization.

name: Productive efficiency
definition: The DEA measure of productive efficiency is an estimate of the percentage of theoretically possible outputs obtained from a given level of inputs.

name: Geographic overlap
definition: Geographical overlap refers to the extent to which the business operations and activities [beyond the HQ] of the concerned firms overlap in different geographies. The formal or informal interactions that occur between these overlapping operations of the respective acquirer and target firms enable a wide array of information flow.

name: Acquisition pairing
definition: Acquisition pairing refers to the final consummation of an acquisition between two parties. The more information the acquiring firm successfully obtains for that particular target, the better evaluation the acquiring firm can perform, and the more likely acquisition pairing will occur.

name: Acquirer size
authors_terms: ["acquirer size", "acquiring firm size", "size of the acquiring firm"]
definition: We measure acquirer size as the natural logarithm of the acquirer's total assets. Big firms have more resources and connections to conduct due diligence on potential targets.

name: Acquirer geographic dispersion
authors_terms: ["acquirer geographic dispersion", "geographic dispersion of the acquiring firm"]
definition: By geographic dispersion, we mean the extent to which a firm's internal business activities are distributed across multiple geographic areas.

name: Geographic distance
definition: Geographic distance between the respective HQ of the two concerned firms. We calculate the actual miles between the acquirer's and target's HQ using the following formula.

name: Product dissimilarity
definition: Product similarity between firm i and firm j is measured by the multiplicative product of firm i and firm j's normalized N-vectors. The measure is continuous between 0 and 1, in which 1 represents high product similarity. We adopt the same approach to measure product similarity between acquirer–target firms in our study and then estimate 'product dissimilarity' for each observation by simply multiplying the similarity measure by -1.

name: Network technological diversity
authors_terms: ["network technological diversity", "alliance network technological diversity", "network diversity", "network-level technological diversity", "technological diversity in a firm's alliance network"]
definition: "I define alliance network technological diversity as the extent to which the technologies pursued by a firm's alliance partners are different from one another and from those of the focal firm."

name: Alliance network density
authors_terms: ["network density", "ego network density", "density of a firm's alliance network", "network closure"]
definition: "Ego network density was the percentage of all possible ties among an ego's alters that had been formed (Scott, 1991)." The authors discuss it as the extent to which a firm's alliance partners are densely interconnected.

name: Exploratory innovation
authors_terms: ["exploratory innovation", "exploratory innovation performance", "degree of exploratory innovation", "exploratory content of a firm's innovations"]
definition: "Exploratory innovation is the creation of technological knowledge by a firm that is novel relative to its existing knowledge stock (Benner & Tushman, 2002; Rosenkopf & Nerkar, 2001)." It embodies knowledge that differs from knowledge used by the firm in prior innovations and shows the firm has broadened its technical competence.

name: External network density
authors_terms: ["external network density", "density of the external network"]
definition: Network density is the extent to which a partner's contacts interact with one another; a high score on network density indicates that the partner's contacts are highly interconnected. Separate density scores were calculated for the external and internal networks.

name: Internal network density
authors_terms: ["internal network density", "density of the internal network"]
definition: Network density is the extent to which a partner's contacts interact with one another; a high score on network density indicates that the partner's contacts are highly interconnected. Separate density scores were calculated for the external and internal networks.

name: External contact heterogeneity
definition: The heterogeneity of contacts providing knowledge in the network. Although contact heterogeneity is not a direct measure of the knowledge shared in the ties, it is a good indicator of the potential for heterogeneous knowledge flows in the ties in the network.

name: Internal contact heterogeneity
definition: The heterogeneity of contacts providing knowledge in the network. Although contact heterogeneity is not a direct measure of the knowledge shared in the ties, it is a good indicator of the potential for heterogeneous knowledge flows in the ties in the network.

name: External tie informality
authors_terms: ["external tie informality", "informality of ties", "external informal ties"]
definition: Whether ties within the network are formal (i.e., associated with the manager's formal role in the firm) or informal (i.e., independent of the manager's role). Informality of relationships was measured by the resources partners used to build and maintain each relationship, some of which were independent of their formal role in the firm and some made available through their formal position.

name: Internal tie informality
authors_terms: ["internal tie informality", "informality of ties", "internal informal ties"]
definition: Whether ties within the network are formal (i.e., associated with the manager's formal role in the firm) or informal (i.e., independent of the manager's role). Informality of relationships was measured by the resources partners used to build and maintain each relationship, some of which were independent of their formal role in the firm and some made available through their formal position.

name: Individual-level ambidexterity
definition: Managers that do allocate resources evenly between exploration and exploitation are considered to be acting ambidextrously, or in other words, to be 'ambidextrous managers'. Ambidextrous behavior of senior managers comprises four dimensions: resource allocation, cross-fertilization of knowledge, resource mobilization, and new opportunity identification.

name: Governance form integrativeness
authors_terms: ["governance form", "integrativeness of governance form", "more integrative governance form", "degree of integration"]
definition: Acquisitions, alliances, and divestitures are strategic alternatives along a continuum of governance modes: acquisitions represent greater integration at one end of the continuum, while divestitures represent less integration at the other end. The choice to organize a particular transaction as one form rather than another is a choice along this continuum.

name: Focal firm technological resources
authors_terms: ["focal firm's technological resources", "technological knowledge capital", "R&D intensity", "technological resources"]
definition: Intangible, technological capital of the focal firm, which is particularly vulnerable to appropriation by partnering firms in alliances or in market exchanges and which may lead firms to choose more integrative forms of governance.

name: Focal firm marketing resources
authors_terms: ["focal firm's marketing resources", "marketing resources", "advertising intensity", "brand capital"]
definition: Marketing and brand capital of the focal firm, which cannot easily be shared across partners except through extensive internal coordination of activities, so that advertising-intensive firms may opt for greater integration.

name: Insider ownership
authors_terms: ["insider ownership", "large insider ownership", "equity ownership by insiders", "end-of-year % of common stock owned by insiders"]
definition: Ownership of the firm's common stock by insiders, which can align managerial incentives with those of other shareholders; beyond certain levels it may instead have an entrenchment effect.

name: Blockholder ownership
authors_terms: ["blockholder ownership", "large blockholders", "end-of-year % of common stock owned by blockholders"]
definition: Ownership of the firm's common stock by large blockholders, whose monitoring mitigates agency problems and prevents executives from empire building through excessive acquisitions.

name: Institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional ownership", "institutional blockholders", "end-of-year % of common stock owned by institutions"]
definition: Ownership of the firm's common stock by institutions, which are large blockholders that exercise a monitoring role over managers.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "a firm's acquisition capabilities", "experience with these governance forms"]
definition: Repeated prior experience with acquisitions, which builds acquisition capabilities; a firm's experience at managing a particular governance form makes the firm more inclined to choose the same form for future transactions.

name: Divestiture experience
definition: Repeated prior experience with divestitures; firms with experience in divestitures may be more effective at managing disintegration than firms without prior experience.

name: Alliance experience
definition: Repeated prior experience with alliances, which builds alliance capabilities that make firms more inclined to choose alliances for later transactions.

name: Firm diversification
authors_terms: ["prior diversification", "diversification level", "number of segments in different SIC codes"]
definition: The level of prior diversification of the firm, which reflects the applicability of resources across industries and the potential for economies of scope from different resource combinations.

name: Relatedness between focal and target firms
authors_terms: ["focal-target firm relatedness", "relatedness between the focal firm and the target (or partner) firm", "proximity in the SIC codes"]
definition: Similarity in the activities of the focal firm and the target or partner firm, proxied by proximity in their SIC codes; greater relatedness implies a lower cost of integration and lower information asymmetry between the parties.

name: Size balance
definition: The ratio of the sales of the smaller firm to the sales of the larger firm; the more balanced in size partners are, the more difficult it becomes for any of them to be digested by the other.

name: Prior alliances between focal and target firms
definition: The number of prior alliances between the focal firm and the target or partner firm, which reflects social embeddedness and the trust created by prior ties, and which may also create valuable options for subsequent deals.

name: Relatedness between firm and transaction
authors_terms: ["focal firm-transaction relatedness", "relatedness between the firm and the activity that is subject to the transaction", "proximity in the SIC codes of the focal firm and the deal"]
definition: Similarity between the activities subject to the transaction and the focal firm's established activities; firms are more likely to choose integrative governance forms when the activities subject to the transaction are similar to the firm's established activities.

name: Governance specialization
definition: The degree to which a firm has repeatedly engaged in deals of the current type; governance specialization captures whether a firm shows evidence of pursuing a program of acquisitions, alliances, or divestitures.

name: Recency of same-form governance experience
authors_terms: ["recency of same-form governance experience", "recency of experience", "deal recency"]
definition: The proximity in time between the deal that is the subject of the governance choice and the last deal of the same form undertaken by the firm.

name: Target firm technological resources
authors_terms: ["target (or partner) firm's technological resources", "target's technological resources"]
definition: Technological resources of the target or partner firm, which the focal firm may seek in order to complement its existing resource base when it diversifies and expands.

name: Target firm marketing resources
authors_terms: ["target (or partner) firm's marketing resources", "target's marketing resources"]
definition: Marketing resources of the target or partner firm, which the focal firm may seek in order to complement its existing resource base when it diversifies and expands.

name: Uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty", "variability in profits", "variance of the target (or partner) firm's return on assets"]
definition: Uncertainty in the relevant market, one of the two proxies used for high market transaction costs; uncertainty leads to hierarchical governance only in the presence of asset specificity.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "human asset specificity", "specificity of the asset or activity being exchanged"]
definition: The degree of specificity of the asset or activity being exchanged; the authors propose the percentage of employees in the focal firm's industry that are engineers as a measure of human asset specificity.

name: Internal organization costs
authors_terms: ["internal organization costs", "costs of internal organization", "cost of integrating the target firm's activities"]
definition: The costs of organizing activities within the firm, which the authors proxy with the number of managers as a percentage of employees in the target or partner firm's industry; the costs of market exchange matter only after netting out these costs.

name: Personal service
authors_terms: ["personal service", "linkage with the government", "link between a firm and the government"]
definition: Personal service is a corporate political strategy in which a member of a firm's top management team or board of directors serves in an appointed or elected political position. Getz (1993) argues that personal service by corporate leaders in official government posts has many potential political benefits for the corporation; executives may serve at the federal or state cabinet level, as elected politicians, in executive and administrative departments, or as consultants or members of special committees.

name: Firm value
definition: The change in the value of the firm resulting from the Presidential appointment or election, measured through event-study methodology so that any abnormal return for the companies from which the individuals left to serve in a political capacity would be an indication of firm-specific benefits.

name: Media reporting on appointment likelihood
authors_terms: ["leakage dates", "positive leakage dates", "negative leakage dates", "media coverage"]
definition: Leakage dates used were any dates that three major newspapers (Wall Street Journal, New York Times, Washington Post) announced the likely appointees for the positions. These leak dates were further broken down into two types: leak dates where the media coverage portrayed the eventual appointee as the 'likely' or 'favored' nominee, and leak dates where the media coverage portrayed an alternative candidate as the most likely or favored nominee.

name: Mobility barriers
definition: In the location-analogy model, the costs of relocation are determined by the height of the mobility barriers inherent in the strategic variables; strategy variables that are easily changed (price, advertising spending) carry low barriers while strategic assets built up over years of investment carry high barriers.

name: Strategic groups
authors_terms: ["strategic groups", "group structure", "competitive structures developed from the archival measures"]
definition: Strategic groups describe intraindustry structure, a level of analysis between the individual firm and the entire industry. If a group of firms has similar scope and resource deployments it has met the first or weakest condition for a strategic group; inherent in the definition is that firms in a given group are also following a similar strategy.

name: Cognitive communities
definition: Managers enact the environment in which they compete by interpreting events and identifying actors in the marketplace, and the resulting cognitive framework is used to guide strategic decisions; if managers rely on the same information to make sense of the market, they should form similar cognitive structures.

name: Networks of interacting firms
authors_terms: ["networks of interacting firms", "direct measures of competitors", "direct group assignments"]
definition: Competitive structures can be identified from direct measures of competitors, the basis of any network of firms being mutual recognition of competitors.

name: Hospital performance
definition: Hospital performance was characterized by multiple measures corresponding to financial, operating, and marketing performance.

name: Semi-strong definition of strategic groups
definition: If the firms also share common cognitive structures, in addition to similar scope and resource deployment, the semistrong definition of strategic groups is satisfied.

name: Semi-strong definition of cognitive communities
definition: We propose an intermediate semi-strong definition of cognitive communities. In addition to similar cognitive structures, we add the condition of mutual recognition of competitors.

name: Geographic boundedness of competition
authors_terms: ["geographically delimited competitive environment", "geographically bounded market", "local metropolitan statistical area"]
definition: In large urban areas, the competitive area for hospitals is confined primarily to the local metropolitan statistical area or MSA. Hospitals in the same MSA compete for patients, physicians, and other resources.

name: Japanese partner ownership share
authors_terms: ["combined Japanese ownership levels", "combined Japanese share", "Japanese ownership levels", "Japanese stake"]
definition: The combined equity stake held by the Japanese parent or parents in a U.S.-Japanese joint venture. When a venture had two or more Japanese partners, the stakes held by the Japanese firms were aggregated into a single Japanese share.

name: Change in Japanese partner ownership
authors_terms: ["change in status", "changes in ownership levels", "change in Japanese partner share"]
definition: Whether a U.S.-Japanese joint venture experienced a change in status between December 31, 1980 and December 31, 1989. Affiliates in which Japanese ownership goes down to zero are those which have been sold to their American partner, sold to a third party, have been liquidated or have gone bankrupt over the period.

name: Knowledge expropriation by the foreign partner
authors_terms: ["Trojan Horse", "expropriate the contribution of their American partner", "knowledge expropriation", "expropriate and buyout", "expropriate and sellout"]
definition: Value is appropriated in joint ventures when the venture is used to absorb the skills of the partner; the party that learns the fastest gets the upper hand in the venture and is able to renegotiate its terms in its favor. In the Trojan Horse view the Japanese parent uses the venture to learn the American partner's contribution and then buys out or liquidates the venture.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: Pursuing three dimensions of EO-proactiveness, risk taking, and innovativeness-could also increase variations in performance and possibly lead to failure; EO is a firm-level strategic orientation.

name: Potential absorptive capacity
definition: Potential absorptive capacity (PACAP), which entails acquiring and assimilating knowledge, enables firms to experiment by increasing variability in innovation outcomes.

name: Realized absorptive capacity
definition: Realized absorptive capacity (RACAP), which entails transforming and exploiting knowledge, helps firms effectively exploit opportunities resulting from increased variability.

name: Variability in innovation outcomes
authors_terms: ["variability in innovation outcomes", "variance in innovation outcomes", "variability in forward citations"]
definition: Variability in innovation outcomes refers to variations in the innovation outcomes of a firm's portfolio of innovation activities (e.g., variability in forward citations among all patents in a firm's portfolio is a proxy for variability in innovation outcomes).

name: Firm performance
definition: Drawing on organizational theory, if firms effectively manage variation through EO-as-experimentation, then such firms would realize increased growth over time (Burgelman, 1991). Indeed, EO is a growth orientation (Lumpkin and Dess, 1996).

name: CEO equity reduction
authors_terms: ["CEO equity reduction", "reduction in CEO equity holdings", "reduction of their equity holdings", "CEO equity reductions"]
definition: Equity holdings are subject to CEOs' discretion (through hold/sell decisions) and can be decoupled from firm risk through equity reductions. When the reduction variable equals one, CEOs sold more equity than those acquired through options exercise and firm grants, thereby reducing their equity position in the firm.

name: Variance of historical returns
authors_terms: ["variance of returns", "variance of historical returns", "total variance", "firm's variance of returns"]
definition: A firm's variance of returns is the total volatility of the firm's returns; it differs from downside risk measures as it symmetrically captures the downside and the upside potential of firm equity.

name: Unsystematic downside risk
authors_terms: ["unsystematic downside risk", "firm-specific downside risk", "root-lower partial moment (RLPM_MKT)"]
definition: Unsystematic downside risk is the risk of underperforming a target return due to firm-specific factors. As a measure of idiosyncratic risk, it reflects firm-specific downside risk that could be diversified away by holding the market portfolio.

name: Firm performance
definition: Stronger firm performance suggests higher expected returns and offers an indication of the gains from holding equity in the firm over time. It is measured with an accounting measure of firm performance, which complements the downside risk measures that rely on historical market returns.

name: Value of CEO equity holdings
authors_terms: ["value of CEO equity holdings", "value of equity holdings", "value of a CEO's equity holdings"]
definition: The value of the shares owned by the CEO, evaluated at market price at year end of 1997. A higher value of CEO equity holdings indicates significant wealth and positive performance history, and both should incite risk taking.

name: Institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "degree of market orientation", "level of institutional development"]
definition: At a country level, institutional development (also called degree of market orientation) generally refers to the level of adherence to free-market policies. Environments with a high level of institutional development are characterized by profit-driven incentive structures, rule of law, including strong intellectual property rights, regulatory frameworks that support market behavior, and high economic productivity.

name: Transition economy context
definition: We use the term the institutional context to characterize the historical path of an economic system. The institutional context difference that we examine is that of transition economies compared to nontransition, market-based economies; transition economies are defined as post-Soviet, formerly-controlled economies.

name: New product deployment
authors_terms: ["new product deployment", "probability that firms deploy new products"]
definition: We define new product deployment as the introduction into the marketplace of products that are new to the firm, although they are not necessarily new to the world (i.e., they may imitate existing products and thus have limited or no innovation in traditional terms).

name: Knowledge-based resources
definition: Our model includes two types of knowledge-based resources: R&D intensity, spending on research and development divided by sales revenue, and university education density, the percent of employees who have some university education.

name: Competitive pressure
authors_terms: ["competitive pressure", "competitive intensity", "pressure from domestic competitors", "pressure from foreign competitors"]
definition: Prior research addresses the level of pressure in the competitive environment and its relationship to new product introductions. The authors measure competitive pressure with survey ratings of the importance of pressure from domestic competitors and pressure from foreign competitors with respect to developing new products or services.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The premise is that firm profitability is determined not only by the structure of its own industry but also by the relative power of the firms and industries from which goods are purchased and sold. In the model it is measured by return on sales.

name: Relative firm power
authors_terms: ["relative firm power", "economic power", "firm power", "bargaining power", "power relationships"]
definition: Broadly speaking, economic power is simply the ability of a firm to influence prices, contracts, distribution privileges, and the like, which ultimately affect profitability. The basis for such power is grounded in the essentiality (or importance) of the function a firm performs in the production chain, either by product or service, and the exclusivity by which the firm performs that function.

name: Supplier concentration
authors_terms: ["%PUR SUPPL", "percentage of total purchases made from the business's three largest external suppliers"]
definition: The percentage of total purchases made from the business's three largest external suppliers. The higher this percentage, the more dependent and vulnerable a firm is with respect to these suppliers.

name: Supplier dependence on the firm
authors_terms: ["%REV SUPPL", "sales of the three largest suppliers to the business as a percentage of the suppliers' total revenues"]
definition: Measures the sales of the three largest suppliers to the business as a percentage of the suppliers' total revenues. The greater this percentage, the more essential the particular business appears to the supplier's livelihood.

name: Availability of alternative suppliers
authors_terms: ["SOURCE SUPPL", "availability of good alternative sources of supplies"]
definition: A three level variable (no; yes, but with difficulty; yes, with no difficulty) defining the availability of good alternative sources of supplies.

name: Customer concentration
authors_terms: ["CONC IMM CUST", "counter measure of customer concentration"]
definition: The proportion of the total number of immediate customers accounting for 50 per cent of the firm's total sales. As this proportion increases the power and authority of the immediate customer base, relative to the firm base, become more fragmented and diffused; in a sense the variable acts as a counter measure of customer concentration.

name: Number of immediate customers
authors_terms: ["NUM IMM CUST", "number of immediate customers served by the business"]
definition: The approximate number of immediate customers served by the business; the variable was recoded to fit into a linear system.

name: Importance of the product to immediate customers
authors_terms: ["IMP IMM CUST", "percentage of the typical immediate customer's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service"]
definition: The percentage of the typical immediate customer's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service. The importance of the product or service to buyers should reflect an ability by the firm to dictate advantageous price:cost conditions.

name: Importance of the product to end users
authors_terms: ["IMP END USER", "percentage of the typical user's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service"]
definition: The percentage of the typical user's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service. The importance of the product or service to the end user should act as an inducement for new competitor entry.

name: Auxiliary services to the end user
authors_terms: ["AUX SERV", "importance of installation, repair, customer service, and other auxiliary services provided to the end user"]
definition: A three level dummy variable measuring the importance of installation, repair, customer service, and other auxiliary services provided to the end user. If such auxiliary services are material in selling or distributing a product, they may provide a firm an opportunity to differentiate itself.

name: Relative breadth of the customer base
authors_terms: ["REL CUST NUM", "breadth of the firm's served market relative to the average of its leading competitors with respect to the number of customers"]
definition: Estimates the breadth of the firm's served market, relative to the average of its leading competitors, with respect to the number of customers.

name: Relative customer size
authors_terms: ["REL CUST SIZE", "breadth of the firm's served market relative to the average of its leading competitors with respect to size of customers"]
definition: Estimates the breadth of the firm's served market, relative to the average of its leading competitors, with respect to the size of customers.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The percentage of industry shipments that is accounted for by the shipments of the four largest firms in that four-digit SIC industry group; if the industry spans several SIC groups a weighted average using dollar shipments as weights is employed.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["SHARE", "firm share of concentration", "firm specific market power"]
definition: The firm's sales in the industry expressed as a percentage of the top four firms' annual sales; the variable assesses the authority and economic power of an individual firm, relative to its rivals.

name: Industry growth
definition: The average annual percentage change in the size, expressed in real dollars, of the industry group. High market growth is expected to induce new firms to join competition.

name: Product proprietary advantage
definition: A dummy variable, equal to one if the business benefits to a significant degree from patents, trade secrets, or other proprietary methods of production or operations; PROD PAT reflects benefits pertaining to products or services.

name: Process proprietary advantage
definition: A dummy variable, equal to one if the business benefits to a significant degree from patents, trade secrets, or other proprietary methods of production or operations; PROC PAT pertains to processes.

name: Competitor entry
definition: A dummy variable, equal to one if at least one new competitor entered the market and claimed a market share of five per cent or more during the previous four years.

name: Category label specificity
definition: The specificity of a category label is defined as the extent to which the information encoded by this label differs from the information encoded by its superordinate. Greater specificity means the subordinate label encodes, and has potential to convey, a greater amount of information relative to its superordinate.

name: Category label distinctiveness
definition: The distinctiveness of a category label is defined as the extent to which information encoded by this label differs from information encoded by other labels connected to the same superordinate. Differentiation between labels connected to the same superordinate depends on the kind of information these labels encode, rather than the amount.

name: Category label assignment
authors_terms: ["assignment", "probability of assignment", "label assignment", "category label's probability of assignment"]
definition: Our outcome of interest is a Discogs user's decision to assign a given style label to a single. This is a qualitative choice, which can be appropriately modeled by conditional logit regression.

name: Candidate filter availability
definition: In digital labor markets, filters can be automated and applied to large pools of applicants, typically as rigid, rule-based algorithms that automatically exclude candidates who do not meet predefined criteria. The key difference from an employer's mental rule is that with a filter in place all candidates who fail the filter criterion are automatically removed before the employer ever sees their profile, so no compensating characteristic can offset a disqualifying one.

name: Number of applicants interviewed
authors_terms: ["number of applicants employers interview", "number of workers screened", "applicants interviewed"]
definition: Because interviewing every applicant is prohibitively costly, employers must decide how many candidates to sample and whom to interview.

name: Applicant interview probability
authors_terms: ["interview probability", "probability of being interviewed", "mean interview probability"]
definition: The mean interview probability of an applicant, computed by machine learning algorithm score group and treatment status, where a higher algorithm score proxies higher unobservable candidate quality.

name: Candidate quality
authors_terms: ["candidate quality", "unobservable-to-the-employer candidate quality", "actual, unobservable applicant quality"]
definition: Employers can readily evaluate common preferred characteristics, but revealing more of an applicant's actual quality requires conducting costly interviews; high-quality applicants often derive their value from rare hard-to-observe traits and can be hard to distinguish from adequately credentialed, average-quality applicants prior to an interview.

name: Wage bid relative to own profile rate
authors_terms: ["wage bid", "submitted wage bid", "bid-to-profile wage ratio", "pricing themselves more aggressively"]
definition: Because profile wage rates are relatively stable across jobs while bids are job-specific, the ratio of bid to profile rate captures how aggressively a worker is pricing themselves for a particular job relative to their own stable baseline.

name: Job offer rejection
definition: After receiving an offer, workers can either accept or engage in back-and-forth negotiation until a contract is formed, or the offer is rejected.

name: Contracted wage
definition: While employers typically extend a job offer at the same wage as the applicant's original bid, about 16.7% of applicants are offered a wage that is different from their original bid; the final contracted wage is the wage at which a contract is formed after any negotiation.

name: Post-contract performance
definition: Outcomes capturing whether the hire worked out: whether the employer reported the contract as successful to the platform, and the public and private feedback scores the employer left for the hired worker.

name: Human resource planning
authors_terms: ["human resource planning sophistication", "investments in human resource planning", "HR planning index", "human resource planning"]
definition: Human resource planning is defined as analyzing an organization's human resource needs under changing conditions and developing the activities necessary to satisfy these needs (Walker, 1980).

name: Recruitment and selection practices
authors_terms: ["investments in hiring", "recruitment and selection practices", "hiring index", "extensive search", "intensive search"]
definition: Search at the extensive margin involves seeking out a greater number of potential applicants, while the search for information about potential employees at the intensive margin involves increasing the amount of information gathered about each applicant in the pool before making a hiring decision.

name: Employee development
authors_terms: ["investments in employee development", "employee development strategy index", "employee development", "development index"]
definition: A further human resource management policy decision involves the mechanism through which the firm actually realizes the potential of its people; namely its strategy for developing employees. In particular, the authors consider the provision of training by the employer and the utilization of promotion-from-within to fill vacancies.

name: Labor productivity
definition: Labor productivity has been defined by Samuelson and Nordhaus as 'total output divided by labor inputs' (1989: 980). Labor productivity taps the extent to which the human capital is delivering value to the firm.

name: Capital intensity
definition: Capital intensity was measured by the ratio of assets to total employees. Capital intensity is an important factor because capital and assets are often used to replace or leverage labor.

name: Vertical pay disparity
authors_terms: ["vertical pay disparity", "vertical disparities between executive levels", "vertical disparity in executive pay"]
definition: Vertical pay disparities exist when pay differs greatly between executive levels. The authors argue that such disparity arises from the firm's creation of an extreme succession tournament and from a hierarchy in which the social, informational, and status distances between levels are great.

name: Horizontal pay disparity
authors_terms: ["horizontal pay disparity", "horizontal disparities among peers at a given hierarchical level", "pay inequality among executive peers"]
definition: Horizontal pay disparity exists when pay differentials between executives within the same hierarchical level are great. The authors posit two major contributors to its emergence: executives within a level being perceived as having very different economic value to the organization, and a compensation structure designed to reward individual or subunit performance over group performance.

name: Overall pay disparity
authors_terms: ["overall pay disparity", "overall pay dispersion of the TMG", "overall TMG pay disparity"]
definition: An overall measure of pay disparity within the TMG necessarily encompasses both vertical and horizontal dimensions.

name: Technological intensiveness
definition: In our conception, technological intensiveness is an environmental characteristic; it refers to the degree of scientific activity and research-based innovation in an industry. Typically gauged by an industry's R&D/sales ratio, technological intensiveness is characteristic of the computer, biomedical, aerospace, and scientific equipment industries, among others.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["subsequent organizational performance", "firm performance", "corporate performance", "subsequent corporate performance"]
