definition: The authors use two stock-market-based measures of company performance, which incorporate both current performance as well as the market's judgment about the firm's prospects: average relative market-to-book and average relative total shareholder returns. Both performance variables are adjusted for industry averages and focus on the two-year period following year t.

name: Entrant experience
authors_terms: ["stock of entrant experience", "∑ (Experience) Entrants", "aggregate experience of the entrant cohort"]
definition: A firm's stock of experience is represented as the number of years the firm has competed in the industry. The variable TE is the aggregate experience of the entrant cohort, summed over the rival entrant firms.

name: Incumbent postderegulation experience
definition: The aggregate postderegulation experience of the incumbent cohort, given by the number of years incumbent firms have competed in the industry after deregulation.

name: Incumbent prederegulation experience
authors_terms: ["∑ (Prederegulation Experience) Incumbents", "incumbent experience in the regulated era"]
definition: An incumbent firm's stock of prederegulation experience is defined as the number of years the incumbent firm competed in the industry before deregulation; the measure aggregates this stock across the incumbent cohort.

name: Organizational size
definition: Firm size is defined as the log of firm operating assets. In the aggregate, firm size is an indicator of firm position in Hannan's (1998) terms.

name: Exit hazard
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of exit", "exit rate", "instantaneous rate of exit"]
definition: The hazard rate is defined as the probability of a firm exiting the trucking industry in the interval (t, t+Δt) given the firm is operating at time t, estimated over the change in t.

name: Patriarchy in family and religion
authors_terms: ["patriarchy in the family/religion", "patriarchy in the family and religion", "patriarchy in the family, religion"]
definition: As an institutional logic, patriarchy comprises beliefs that prioritize male attributes and interests as well as practices that discriminate against women; the family and religion are sectors in which this influence is particularly relevant, conveying expectations about gender identity and domestic authority.

name: Gender equality in the professions
authors_terms: ["gender equality in professions", "greater gender equality in the professional sector", "patriarchy in the professions"]
definition: A nation's factor score for patriarchy in the professions, reverse-coded so that higher values indicate greater gender equality; it is based on the portion of women employed in professional and technical occupations and on female tertiary education enrollment.

name: Gender equality in the state
authors_terms: ["gender equality in state", "greater gender equality in the state sector", "patriarchy in state"]
definition: A nation's factor score for patriarchy in the state, reverse-coded so that higher values indicate greater gender equality; it is based on women's political representation and on the years since ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

name: Lending to women
authors_terms: ["lending to women", "number of women borrowers served", "outreach to women", "female borrowers", "female clients"]
definition: Reaching women is vital for any poverty-reduction initiative and a key facet of social outreach in microfinance; the authors measure it with the number of women borrowers served by an MFO.

name: Female employees
authors_terms: ["proportion of female employees", "female managers and loan officers", "female staff", "female loan officers"]
definition: The proportion of an MFO's employees who are women, comprising its managers and loan officers; employing women is theorized to make female outreach an organizational priority and to facilitate access to female borrowers.

name: Local funding
authors_terms: ["total amount of local funding received", "local funding", "local capital", "local financing"]
definition: Capital received by an MFO from local sources; while some local funding is from commercial lenders that aim to make a financial return on their investments, the majority is from public funders that have development goals and offer subsidized financing.

name: R&D pipeline similarity
authors_terms: ["R&D pipeline-to-R&D pipeline similarity", "similarity in R&D pipeline", "same-stage similarity"]
definition: Acquirers can make two broad resource comparisons when deciding whether to acquire a firm: the extent to which a target firm's resources overlap with its existing resources (similarity). Here the comparison is between the target firm's R&D pipeline and the acquirer's own R&D pipeline, i.e., the same stage of product development.

name: R&D pipeline complementarity
authors_terms: ["R&D pipeline-to-R&D pipeline complementarity", "complementarity between these resources"]
definition: Acquirers can make two broad resource comparisons when deciding whether to acquire a firm: the extent to which a target firm's resources add to its existing resources (complementarity). Here the comparison is between the target firm's R&D pipeline and the acquirer's own R&D pipeline, i.e., the same stage of product development.

name: R&D pipeline-to-product similarity
authors_terms: ["R&D pipeline-to-product similarity", "similarity in commercialized products to its own R&D pipeline", "across-stage resource comparisons"]
definition: A nonparallel or 'across-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's commercialized products overlap with the acquirer's own R&D pipeline (similarity).

name: R&D pipeline-to-product complementarity
definition: A nonparallel or 'across-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's commercialized products add to the acquirer's own R&D pipeline (complementarity).

name: Product-to-product similarity
definition: A parallel or 'same-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's commercialized products overlap with the acquirer's own commercialized products (similarity).

name: Product-to-product complementarity
definition: A parallel or 'same-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's commercialized products add to the acquirer's own commercialized products (complementarity).

name: Product-to-R&D pipeline similarity
authors_terms: ["Product-to-R&D pipeline similarity", "similarity between the target firm's R&D pipeline and its products", "across-stage resource comparisons"]
definition: A nonparallel or 'across-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's R&D pipeline overlaps with the acquirer's own commercialized products (similarity).

name: Product-to-R&D pipeline complementarity
authors_terms: ["Product-to-R&D pipeline complementarity", "complementary R&D pipeline to its own products"]
definition: A nonparallel or 'across-stage' resource comparison capturing the extent to which the target firm's R&D pipeline adds to the acquirer's own commercialized products (complementarity).

name: Target firm selection
authors_terms: ["target firm selection", "acquisition choice", "target firm choice", "likelihood of acquiring a target firm"]
definition: The choice of which potential target firm is acquired. 'Chosen target firms are those that are chosen for acquisition out of the consideration set of potential target firms.'

name: Strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["Miles and Snow's typology of strategies", "strategic orientation", "prospector, analyzer, and defender types", "self-typing"]
definition: Miles and Snow's (1978) typology divides organizations into prospector, defender, analyzer, and reactor types: a prospector frequently adds to and changes its products and services and consistently attempts to be first in the market, an analyzer maintains a relatively stable base of products and services while selectively moving into new areas with demonstrated promise, a defender offers a relatively stable set of services to defined markets and concentrates on operating efficiencies, and a reactor essentially lacks a consistent strategy. Because reactors are defined as lacking a consistent strategy, no a priori predictions can be made regarding their behavior and they were excluded from formal consideration in hypotheses and analyses.

name: New service and new market development emphasis
authors_terms: ["emphasis on new service and new market development", "new service-new market development", "overall emphasis on new services and markets"]
definition: The degree of emphasis an organization gives to new market and new service development activity, assessed for each of 15 specific service lines that include 5 core business services and 10 noncore (diversified) services.

name: Service diversification
authors_terms: ["number of diversified services offered", "diversified services", "services that are not part of their core business"]
definition: Diversified services are services that are not part of an organization's core business, selected from a 34-item services inventory involving such services as ambulatory care, geriatric care, health promotion, home health-extended care, outpatient diagnostic services, and service delivery alternatives such as health maintenance organizations and preferred provider organizations.

name: New diversified service initiation
authors_terms: ["number of diversified services started", "diversified services added in past two years", "initiated more diversified new services", "new services offered in most recent two years"]
definition: The number of diversified services an organization has initiated over a recent period, reflecting the rate at which new markets and new products are developed.

name: Service diversification ratio
authors_terms: ["ratio of diversified to nondiversified services", "ratio of outpatient to inpatient services offered"]
definition: The ratio of diversified to nondiversified services offered by an organization, measured as the ratio of outpatient to inpatient services offered.

name: High-technology service offerings
definition: The number of high-technology services offered, drawn from a list of 15 services ranging from intensive care units to nuclear magnetic resonance imaging and various organ and tissue transplant services.

name: Planned service diversification
authors_terms: ["number of new diversified services planned for the future", "planned diversified services"]
definition: The number of new diversified services an organization has planned for the future.

name: Share of services in high-growth areas
authors_terms: ["percentage of services in high-growth areas", "market growth potential", "overall portfolios of services"]
definition: The percentage of an organization's services that fall in high-growth areas, based on the perceived market growth potential of each of its service lines, examined as an overall portfolio of services.

name: Planning process formality
authors_terms: ["planning process formality", "planning formality", "formality of the planning process"]
definition: The formality of an organization's strategic planning process, covering agreement on goals, degree of formalization and discipline, degree of plan development, and the extent of department directors' and division heads' involvement in planning.

name: Planning innovativeness
authors_terms: ["planning innovativeness", "innovativeness of the plans developed", "innovativeness of plans"]
definition: The innovativeness of the plans an organization develops, expressed as the degree of innovativeness compared to past strategies and the degree of innovativeness compared with competitors.

name: Market research effort
authors_terms: ["market research", "market research efforts", "quality and importance of market research"]
definition: The perceived quality and importance of market research in an organization, reflecting the effort it devotes to monitoring external environmental conditions, trends, and events.

name: Innovative output
authors_terms: ["innovative output", "pharmaceutical patent output", "drug patent count", "patent output"]
definition: The dependent variable that we employ to measure the construct of innovative output is the count of U.S. drug patents granted to a firm in a given year, which we label DRUG PATENT COUNT.

name: Underlying technological capabilities
authors_terms: ["underlying technological capabilities", "underlying research capabilities", "existing research capabilities in the underlying technologies", "drug patent stock"]
definition: Firms with strong existing research activities in the underlying technologies will be better able to absorb and put to use the skills and technologies they are exposed to in their international R&D activities.

name: Complementary research capabilities
authors_terms: ["complementary research capabilities", "complementary technological capabilities", "fermentation patent stock", "research capabilities in complementary technologies"]
definition: Complementary capabilities are forms of know-how or technologies that might be used in conjunction with the underlying technologies to create new products (Teece, 1986).

name: International R&D activity
definition: We included the following types of activities in our definition of international R&D: sponsored, collaborative, and controlled (Penner-Hahn, 1998).

name: Social impact framing
definition: A frame that presents an entrepreneurial venture in light of its desirable impact on society; it 'emphasizes the social-environmental welfare benefits of a venture and its activities' and reveals itself through linguistic cues indicating how the venture 'makes the world a better place'.

name: Innovativeness framing
definition: A frame that emphasizes the innovativeness or disruptiveness of the entrepreneurial venture and offering.

name: Customer demand
definition: Attracting customer demand represents one of the most important performance objectives for new entrepreneurial ventures; it is inferred from the number of unique individuals that engage with a venture's platform in a given month.

name: Category salience
definition: The degree to which a market category receives collective attention from the general public; a continuous socio-cognitive property that can fluctuate over time and is conceptually independent of any consensus about the category's meaning.

name: Category crowdedness
definition: The degree of competitive intensity within the category, that is, the extent to which more organizations and offerings compete with each other in the market category.

name: Newcomer status
authors_terms: ["status of the newcomer", "newcomer's status", "high-status newcomer", "high-status inbound mobility", "star analyst", "star/runners-up"]
definition: Status is defined as the prestige accorded to actors 'because of the hierarchical positions they occupy in a social structure', or, put differently, as a superior rank in the social order that is only loosely coupled with quality. The paper applies this to the actor hired into the organization (the newcomer), whose status determines the intensity of the treatment to which incumbents are exposed.

name: Incumbent status
authors_terms: ["incumbent's status", "status of incumbents", "high-status incumbents", "low-status incumbents", "status of the incumbent analyst"]
definition: Status is defined as the prestige accorded to actors 'because of the hierarchical positions they occupy in a social structure', and the paper applies the same conceptualization and the same procedure to the analysts already employed by the hiring organization at the time of a hiring event.

name: Incumbent analyst performance
authors_terms: ["incumbents' performance", "performance of incumbent analysts", "recommendation profitability", "abnormal return of incumbents' stock recommendations", "incumbent portfolio performance"]
definition: The performance of a securities analyst is captured by the returns associated with his or her stock recommendations, i.e., the average abnormal return that would be obtained by following the analyst's investment recommendations in a given window. Analysts' performance is immediately revealed and constantly updated in this setting.

name: Relatedness of diversification
definition: Diversification represents the simultaneous operation of different businesses; the relationship between such businesses may be highly interrelated either through technology or markets at one extreme (related firms) or lack any meaningful relationship at the other extreme (unrelated firms). Whether the argument is based on technological or market relatedness, the performance potential appears to be higher for related than unrelated firms.

name: Internal diversification mode
authors_terms: ["diversification mode", "internal mode", "external mode", "internal diversification mode", "internal venturing"]
definition: The external diversification mode involves mergers and/or acquisitions, and the internal mode is reflected in internal venturing. The internal mode is a slow, methodological process, requiring several years for new ventures to be profitable, whereas mergers and acquisitions can be accomplished in a relatively short time.

name: Financial performance
definition: The performance measures used in this study are return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), return on invested capital (ROIC), and compound sales growth (CSG). The variables were selected because of their use as resource utilization measures and comparability with past diversification studies.

name: Combined diversification breadth and mode strategy
authors_terms: ["combined diversification breadth and mode", "combined dimensions", "combined dimensional strategy", "joint strategies"]
definition: The simultaneous consideration of both diversification breadth and mode; a two-by-two matrix provides a four-cell depiction of the combined elements (related-internal, related-external, unrelated-internal, unrelated-external). The combined classifications of diversification breadth and mode are more robust than either dimension alone, because the symbiosis in the decision-making process is recognized.

name: Outside director acquisition experience in the focal product market
authors_terms: ["outside directors' prior experience with acquisitions in the same product markets as a focal firm's acquisitions", "director experience with acquisitions in related markets", "outside directors' experience with acquisitions in the same industries or product markets in which a focal firm is making acquisitions"]
definition: Directors' prior involvement in acquisitions in the same industries or product markets in which the focal firm is currently pursuing acquisitions; the authors argue that outside directors 'will develop expert knowledge that can be usefully applied to enhance the quality of a focal firm's acquisition decisions to the extent that directors have been previously involved in pursuing acquisitions in the same industries or product markets in which the focal firm is currently pursuing acquisitions.'

name: Outside director experience with related acquisitions
authors_terms: ["outside directors' prior experience with related acquisitions", "directors' prior experience with decisions about related acquisitions", "experience with related acquisitions"]
definition: Directors' prior involvement in a relatively large number of related acquisitions in the past, either as firm executives or as outside directors at other companies, from which the authors expect them to develop expert knowledge in making related acquisitions.

name: Outside director experience with unrelated acquisitions
authors_terms: ["directors' experience with unrelated acquisitions", "directors' prior experience with decisions about unrelated acquisitions", "outside directors' experience with unrelated acquisitions"]
definition: Outside directors' prior involvement in a relatively large number of unrelated acquisitions in the past, from which they will develop expert knowledge in pursuing unrelated acquisitions.

name: Board independence from management
authors_terms: ["board independence", "board independence from management", "independence from management"]
definition: The degree to which a firm's board is independent from management, which the authors argue increases outside directors' willingness and ability to intervene in strategic decision making, including acquisition decisions.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["focal acquisition performance", "excess stock returns", "abnormal announcement returns", "excess returns"]
definition: Measured 'in terms of excess stock returns, or the difference between the acquiring firm's observed return and its expected return during a specified period of time surrounding the acquisition announcement.'

name: Business education and executive experience
authors_terms: ["four types of respondents", "CEO with business education", "CEO without business education", "MBA", "liberal arts graduate students"]
definition: Our research design permitted comparisons of cause maps between four types of individuals: (1) CEOs with both formal business education and top executive experience, (2) CEOs with top executive experience but without formal business education, (3) MBA students approaching the end of their business education but without top executive experience, and (4) liberal arts graduate students, lacking both business education and top executive experience.

name: Contingency thinking
definition: This variable reflects the degree to which the cause map of each respondent matches the overall alignment-performance relationships specified by business-level contingency theory. A respondent whose regression model shows large, positive parameters for each of the interaction terms has revealed a cause map that matches the prescriptions of business-level contingency theory.

name: Business-level strategy
authors_terms: ["business-level strategy", "low cost and differentiation strategies", "cost leadership strategy", "differentiation strategy"]
definition: Each respondent was provided with written definitions of low cost and differentiation strategies (Porter 1980). Differentiation strategies are said to be more likely to create sustainable competitive advantage in dynamic environments, while the efficiency-based competitive advantages following from cost leadership strategies are more likely to be achieved in stable environments.

name: Organization structure
authors_terms: ["mechanistic and organic structures", "Type A structure", "Type B structure"]
definition: Mechanistic and organic structures (Burns and Stalker 1961) were represented to the respondent as "Type A" and "Type B" structures respectively to avoid any negative connotations associated with the word "mechanistic". Implementation of differentiation strategies requires structures with decentralized decision making, relatively few formal controls, and little specialization of activities, while cost leadership strategies are most effectively implemented through more mechanistic structures that feature specialization of activities, formal controls, and centralized decision making.

name: External environment
definition: Respondents were provided with written definitions of dynamic and stable external environments (Duncan 1972). Dynamism in the environment encourages the development of organic structures, and stability in the environment encourages mechanistic structures.

name: EMS adoption costs
authors_terms: ["EMS adoption costs", "cost of EMS adoption", "EMS adoption expenditures"]
definition: The dependent variable, EMS adoption costs, was measured using facilities' self-reported expenditure data. These data included expenditures for the most common types of EMS adoption costs: staff time, consultants, travel and training, equipment, materials, corrective action, auditors and ISO 14001 certification.

name: Quality-based and inventory control management systems
authors_terms: ["quality-based and inventory control management systems", "quality-based management systems", "inventory control management systems", "continual improvement expertise"]
definition: A capability is considered complementary to EMS adoption if it facilitates the implementation process. Organizations' embedded expertise with complementary knowledge-based processes, such as quality-based and inventory control management systems, may assist the development of more advanced environmental management processes.

name: Pollution prevention practices
definition: An organization that has experience with pollution prevention reduces the waste it generates in the production process prior to recycling, treatment, or disposal. Pollution prevention activities were defined as any materials substitution, process changes, or other activities that minimized waste production.

name: Parent enterprise support
authors_terms: ["support from their parent enterprise", "parent organization support", "access to parent company resources"]
definition: Organizations that receive support from their parent enterprise are more likely to have fewer EMS adoption costs. Parent organizations may provide EMS adoption assistance in the form of financial support, technical support, or an EMS design template.

name: Government assistance
authors_terms: ["government assistance", "government-funded grants and technical assistance", "state-sponsored subsidies"]
definition: Government-funded grants and technical assistance are subsidies that encourage organizations to undertake actions which improve the welfare of society. Organizations that rely on government assistance may reduce their EMS adoption costs.

name: Consultant use
definition: Organizations that utilize external consultants do so in large part because they require outside assistance related to a specialized management concern. Organizations that rely on consultants are anticipated to increase their EMS adoption costs.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Ownership is a summative condition that includes the interests and constraints of respective owners and managers, as well as the abilities of these parties to obtain resources and factor markets such as capital, management, and technical talent.

name: Publicly traded ownership
authors_terms: ["publicly traded organizations", "publicly traded firms", "publicly traded facilities"]
definition: Publicly traded firms issue shares that are traded on stock exchanges, which increases the financial resources available to the firm through greater risk sharing among many owners, and enhances the firm's reputation and visibility.

name: Government ownership
definition: By contrast to the for-profit firm, the objective of government operations is to address public welfare. Government enterprises exist to ensure equal access to goods and services that cannot be acquired reliably through the private market.

name: Technological niche width
definition: The niche width of an organization refers to its variance in resource utilization, so organizations operating across a wide range of environmental resources possess a wide or broad niche and are classified as generalists. The authors defined technological niche width as the range of engine capacity in terms of horsepower across all models produced by each firm at any given point in time (a realized niche).

name: Distance from the market center
authors_terms: ["position", "niche position", "distance above market center (DAMC)", "distance below market center (DBMC)"]
definition: A firm's position or location in the niche can be described by the midpoint of its resource range; the market center covers the range of the niches of the four largest firms in the industry. Distance away from the market center is the difference between the midpoint of the focal firm's niche and the midpoint of the market center.

name: Niche-overlap density
definition: Niche overlap is the degree to which other firms also occupy the firm's niche range. Niche-overlap density is the number of other firms whose niches fall within at least some part of the range.

name: Small organizational size
definition: The authors regard very small size as reflecting specialism on one or more unobserved dimensions of specialism, and argue that very small firms are not engaged in scale competition. A size threshold was used to identify the subset of very small firms.

name: Market concentration
authors_terms: ["industry concentration (C4)", "market concentration", "consolidation level of a population"]
definition: The consolidation level of a population is regarded as part of the broader environment because, unlike niche-based variables, it is relatively immutable with respect to short-term firm movements and strategic actions. It is measured as the ratio of the annual production of the four largest firms to total industry output for that year.

name: Organizational mortality
authors_terms: ["hazard of mortality", "disbanding/exit hazard", "rate of disbanding/exit", "mortality rate"]
definition: Organizational life histories end in a variety of ways; because of the ambiguous meaning of mergers and acquisitions, the analysis is based on disbanding and exit to another industry. The outcome event of interest is disbanding/exit to another industry, defined to include events of unknown type, while firms known to have ended by other events were treated as noninformatively censored on the right.

name: Scale competition
definition: Scale economies exert their force in organizational evolution because of the worsened consequences likely experienced by small firms with relatively higher costs in competition with larger firms. This pressure is modeled by examining the size structure of the competitive environment faced by each scale competitor at any point in time.

name: TMT polychronicity
definition: We define top management team (TMT) polychronicity as the extent to which TMT members mutually prefer and tend to engage in multiple tasks simultaneously or intermittently instead of one at a time and believe that this is the best way of doing things (we adapted the definition by Bluedorn et al., 1999).

name: Strategic decision speed
definition: Strategic decision speed refers to the velocity with which organizations execute all aspects of the strategic decision process, from the initial consideration of alternative courses of action to the time a commitment to act is made (Eisenhardt, 1989).

name: Strategic decision comprehensiveness
definition: Strategic decision comprehensiveness refers to the extent to which an organization's executives systematically gather and process information from the external environment in making strategic decisions (Fredrickson, 1984). Firms that scan their environment for greater quantities of information or that analyze environmental information more extensively-for example, by employing quantitative analytic techniques to a greater degree-are considered more comprehensive (Forbes, 2007).

name: Financial performance
definition: Consistent with prior studies in a similar context (e.g., Murphy, Trailer, and Hill 1996; Robinson and McDougall, 2001) we selected two widely used performance measures: return on total assets (ROTA) as a measure of new venture efficiency, and return on sales (ROS) as a measure of new venture profitability.

name: Intra-industry populations
definition: We distinguish between "populations" which are at the species level of botanical categories and represent groupings of organizations with similar internal structure and processes and "families" which represent an industry level of analysis.

name: Markets served
definition: The market, or customers, of firms in the electronics industry comprises a large component of their niche. Hence, we identified a typology of markets (components, electric power, industrial, instruments, communications, retail/consumer, computer, government, and transportation) served by firms in the electronics industry.

name: Business competencies
definition: In addition to "markets served" as a key element of our elementary theory of organizational speciation, we proposed that organizational identity is also a composite of work place and organizational competencies that produce a competitive product or service. Given this rationale, we measured the business competencies each firm drew upon to serve each market (research & development/engineering, manufacturing/assembly, marketing, distribution, leasing).

name: Firm size
definition: The final component of our elementary theory of organizational differences included firm characteristics such as firm size, a concept extensively studied in the organizational literature (Starbuck 1965; Blau and Schoenherr 1971; Kimberly 1976).

name: Macro productivity
definition: Firm characteristics included macro productivity measures, e.g., sales per employee.

name: Organizational diversification
definition: Firm characteristics included organizational diversification as measured by Rumelt's (1974) specialization ratio.

name: Patent scope
authors_terms: ["scope of the patent", "invention patent scope", "scope of the invention's patent", "breadth of patent", "scope"]
definition: Patent scope defines the breadth of intellectual property protection. Broader patents protect inventions against imitation from a wider range of potentially competing inventions than narrower patents.

name: Pioneering nature of the invention
authors_terms: ["pioneering nature of the invention", "pioneering nature", "pioneering inventions", "pioneering"]
definition: A second characteristic of an invention that we consider is its pioneering nature, or the degree to which the invention opens up new technology domains.

name: Invention age
authors_terms: ["age of the invention", "age of the patent", "age of innovations", "age"]
definition: Finally, the age of the invention examines the balance between the passage of time necessary for the diffusion of an invention and the time remaining on patent protection.

name: Invention commercialization
authors_terms: ["invention commercialization", "commercialization of the invention", "likelihood of first sale", "first sale"]
definition: We operationalize the dependent variable, invention commercialization, as the achievement of first sale of a product or service that makes use of the invention. We measure this variable as the receipt of the first dollar of revenue by the licensing firm.

name: Buyer power
authors_terms: ["buyer power", "bargaining power of buyers", "high buyer power"]
definition: The bargaining power of buyers is one of the basic competitive forces comprising Porter's model. High levels of buyer power will limit a firm's ability to charge higher prices, as more powerful buyers will be able to demand price concessions from their suppliers.

name: Threat of substitution
authors_terms: ["threat of substitute products", "threat of substitution", "substitution threat", "threat of substitutes"]
definition: The threat of substitute products is one of the basic competitive forces comprising Porter's model. A high threat of substitution implies that an alternative product type offers a price or performance benefit and limits industry profitability.

name: Threat of new entry
authors_terms: ["threat of new entrants", "threat of entry", "threat of new firm entry", "entry threat"]
definition: The threat of new entrants is one of the basic competitive forces comprising Porter's model. The threat of entry by new firms is highest during the high growth phase of the product life cycle, as demand increases, new market segments emerge, and new entrants stake a claim in the emerging market.

name: Intensity of competitive rivalry
authors_terms: ["intensity of rivalry", "intensity of competitive rivalry", "competitive intensity", "rivalry between existing competitors"]
definition: Rivalry between existing competitors is one of the basic competitive forces comprising Porter's model. Competitive intensity is likely to be highest during maturity/late maturity stages of the product life cycle, as competition for selective demand intensifies and increasingly large sums are spent on incremental product innovations and communications programs.

name: Cost leadership strategy preference
definition: A strategy of seeking competitive advantage by becoming the lowest-cost producer for its target markets.

name: Differentiation strategy preference
definition: A strategy of seeking competitive advantage by distinguishing oneself from the competition through product offerings or marketing programs.

name: Focus strategy preference
definition: A strategy of seeking competitive advantage by targeting a narrowly defined market segment or niche, either through cost leadership or differentiation.

name: Differentiation or focus strategy preference
authors_terms: ["differentiation or focus competitive strategy", "differentiation or focus competitive strategies", "differentiation or focus strategy"]
definition: The authors group the differentiation and focus strategies together as the 'differentiation or focus' competitive strategies that U.S. managers are expected to prefer, in contrast to the cost-leadership strategy preferred by Japanese managers; results for the two strategies are reported jointly as cases of this combined category.

name: Country of origin
definition: The home country of the manager and firm (United States or Japan). Managers from different nations may use different criteria to select a competitive strategy, because they use different 'mental models', and culture-based differences in business environment affect managerial decision-making.

name: Interorganizational exchange
definition: Interorganizational exchange has multiple forms that vary by temporal duration, recurrence, and governance structure. The common element among forms of interorganizational exchange is the bilateral transfer of resources triggered by mutual decision of the exchange partners.

name: Organization-to-organization exchange ties
definition: Prior exchange ties between two organizations (organization-organization, henceforth denoted as 'OO'), excluding the experiences of their current leaders.

name: Leader-to-leader exchange ties
definition: Prior ties between leaders (leader-leader, 'LL'), that is, exchanges in which both current leaders were involved while not leading their current organizations.

name: Organization-to-leader exchange ties
definition: Prior exchange ties between an organization and the leader of the other organization (organization-leader, 'OL').

name: Organization ties shared with one leader
definition: Ties shared by both organizations and only one current leader (organization-organization-leader, 'OOL').

name: Leader ties shared with one organization
definition: Ties shared by only one organization but both current leaders (organization-leader-leader, 'OLL').

name: Fully shared ties
definition: Exchange ties shared by both organizations and both current leaders (organization-organization-leader-leader, 'OOLL').

name: Formal definition of avoided costs
authors_terms: ["formally defined avoided costs", "defined avoided costs", "formally defined avoided costs only"]
definition: Whether the state regulatory commission developed a formal, standardized definition of avoided costs, the price to be paid to a qualifying facility for power, based on the cost the utility avoided by purchasing that power. Without such a definition a wide range of avoided costs could be claimed, leaving the basis of payment unclear.

name: Approved standard contracts
definition: Whether the state regulatory commission authorized standardized contracts for utilities' purchases of power from qualifying facilities. Such standardized language reduces the transaction costs and uncertainties facing potential entrants by constraining the opportunistic latitude of the larger exchange partner.

name: Statewide QF industry association
authors_terms: ["statewide QF industry association", "statewide trade association representing QFs", "QF industry associations"]
definition: The presence of a statewide trade association representing qualifying facilities, which advances the interests of independent power production by consolidating the power and presence of QFs through intervention in regulatory hearings, lobbying of legislators, and other collective action.

name: Regulatory climate for utilities
definition: A summary rating of the regulatory climate facing utilities in a state, reflecting the preexisting, long-term relationship between regulated firms and their regulators; the categories run from below average to average to above average, in order of improving regulatory relations.

name: Qualifying facility founding rate
authors_terms: ["QF foundings", "founding rates of QF projects", "organizational foundings", "QF project foundings"]
definition: The number of new qualifying facility projects founded in a state in a year, recorded at the time the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission was notified that a proposed project was seeking QF status.

name: Market category leniency
authors_terms: ["leniency", "lenient market categories", "lenient categories", "leniency of the category", "leniency of the market category"]
definition: Lenient categories not only have fuzzy boundaries but also overlap with many different categories. Leniency is calculated by multiplying fuzziness of a market category by the number of distinct other categories with which it overlaps.

name: Market category entry
definition: Market category entry is the dependent variable used to test H1, H3, and H4. This is a binary variable that equals 1 if the organization enters the category from the dyad in the current year and 0 if it does not.

name: Market category exit
definition: Market category exit is the dependent variable used to test H2. This is a binary variable that equals 1 if the organization drops the category from the dyad in the current year and 0 if it does not.

name: Leniency of the organization's categories
authors_terms: ["leniency of the organization's categories", "average leniency of the organization's categories", "leniency of the organization's categories (weighted average)"]
definition: The leniency of an organization's categories is computed as a weighted average of the leniency of the categories the organization is in, weighted by its grade of membership in each category.

name: Venture capital funding
authors_terms: ["venture capital funding", "received VC funding", "having received venture capital funding"]
definition: A dummy variable that indicates whether the organization received venture capital funding in the previous year.

name: Category fuzziness
definition: A category is fuzzy if it has a high degree of overlap with at least one other category. The contrast of category A can be calculated as the average grade of membership of member organizations.

name: Across-niche product proliferation
authors_terms: ["across-niche product proliferation", "breadth", "niche width", "variegation", "intraindustry diversification", "across-niche product proliferation strategy", "APP"]
definition: Across-niche product proliferation (also referred to as breadth, niche width, variegation, or intraindustry diversification) arises when a firm increases the submarket niches in which it sells products; in this strategy, the firm sells products simultaneously in various submarket niches.

name: Within-niche product proliferation
definition: Within-niche product proliferation (i.e., depth or product versioning) implies that the firm augments the quantity of different variants that it sells in a single submarket niche.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance reflects the firm's ability to charge higher prices and increase its market shares, while also controlling for the underlying cost structure; it is defined as margins multiplied by the number of model units sold at time t for each brand i.

name: Product space complexity
authors_terms: ["complexity of the product space", "product space complexity", "complexity"]
definition: We refer to the level of complexity in product spaces as the degree of heterogeneity in the attributes of products marketed in a particular industry; a complex product space indicates heterogeneity in the product attributes marketed in a particular industry.

name: Market valuation
authors_terms: ["market valuation", "market capitalization", "firm market valuation", "firm market capitalization"]
definition: Our study examines how markets sort new firms in new industries by partitioning economic resources through market valuations. We measured market valuation as the firm's market capitalization.

name: Stock-based financial incentives
authors_terms: ["stock-based financial incentives", "stock-based incentives", "stock-based pay", "executive stock option pay", "executive stock ownership", "outside director stock ownership", "stock-based compensation"]
definition: Incentives like stock ownership and stock option pay require that executives and directors share in the risk of firm failure or success with shareholders. Information about stock-based incentives should affect investors' valuation and share pricing among new firms in emerging industries.

name: Blockholder ownership
definition: When a select number of investors own significant portions of the firms' outstanding shares (blockholders), much of the economic risk of failure is vested in the hands of a few. Blockholders, with their superior access to information and voting power, have the ability and incentives to vigilantly monitor top executives.

name: Institutional ownership
definition: Institutional owners employ professional analysts who are experts at screening and monitoring firm performance. To the extent that institutional money represents 'smart money,' market investors may view institutional ownership as an important endorsement of quality.

name: Venture capital ownership
authors_terms: ["venture capital ownership", "VC ownership", "venture capital backing", "venture capitalist funding"]
definition: One exchange relationship of firms completing IPOs that is likely to be interpreted as an uncertainty-reducing signal is the venture capital (VC) backing the firm has received. VC backing does not just provide access to resources during the early stages of development; its presence may cause outside investors to interpret funding from venture capitalists as a signal that other knowledgeable investors endorse the firm.

name: Venture capital equity sell-off
authors_terms: ["venture capital equity sold", "VC sell-off", "percentage of VC ownership liquidated", "proportion of equity sold by venture capitalists"]
definition: When venture capitalists sell significant portions of their prior investment, it may be interpreted negatively by outside investors. Selling large stakes in the firm may signal that the firm's value has peaked.

name: Board structure
authors_terms: ["board structure", "board outsiders", "proportion of board members who are outsiders", "board independence"]
definition: Boards of directors can reduce agency costs through vigilant oversight and can also add value by giving advice to top management. New firms with outsider-dominated boards are more likely to be priced at a premium than those that are dominated by insiders.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age, measured as the number of years since the firm was founded, because firms that have been in business longer have had more time to create value. Firms produce more objective data about their operations the longer they have been in operation.

name: Individual domain experience
authors_terms: ["individual experience", "individual domain experience", "domain-specific individual experience", "accumulated individual domain experience"]
definition: The domain-specific experience that individual scientists accumulate by learning by doing as they work in different technological domains. Each time a scientist creates a new patent using a technological category, he or she accumulates one unit of experience in that domain.

name: Team experience
authors_terms: ["team experience", "experience working together", "accumulated team experience", "relational experience"]
definition: The extent to which team members have experience working with each other in the past.

name: Firm experience
definition: The cumulative experience that a firm accumulates as it creates innovations. Each time a firm develops a new patent, it is considered to have accumulated one unit of experience.

name: Innovative productivity
authors_terms: ["innovative productivity", "inverse of unit labor requirement", "1/ULR", "productivity in innovation"]
definition: The inverse of the unit labor requirement of innovation, where the unit labor requirement is the time required to develop an innovation. Because innovative productivity increases as the time taken to develop an innovation decreases, the inverse of the unit labor requirement is a measure of innovative productivity.

name: Innovative capability
authors_terms: ["innovative capability", "the knowledge a firm uses to innovate", "the knowledge a firm uses to create new innovations"]
definition: Innovative capability is the knowledge a firm uses to create new innovations; the authors put forward the view that it accumulates by learning by doing, so that knowledge resulting from one innovation allows for quicker future innovations.

name: Strategic mission
definition: By definition, strategic mission (or portfolio strategy) signifies the nature of the SBU's intended trade-offs between market share growth and short term earnings/cash flow maximization.

name: Effectiveness at strategy implementation
definition: Effectiveness at strategy implementation was measured in the form of a comparison between actual performance and a priori expectations rather than on an absolute scale. It was assessed along a multiplicity of performance dimensions weighted in terms of their relative importance for the SBU.

name: Marketing/sales experience
authors_terms: ["experience in marketing/sales", "years of experience in marketing/sales", "marketing/sales experience"]
definition: The functional background of the SBU general manager, specifically the experience accumulated in the marketing/sales function. The authors argue that marketing/sales experience contributes to the development of skills at external industry analysis, which is important for build strategies.

name: Willingness to take risk
definition: The SBU general manager's willingness to take risk in the context of his/her job. The authors argue that to be effective, managers in charge of more uncertain task situations should be willing to take greater risks.

name: Tolerance for ambiguity
definition: The SBU general manager's tolerance for ambiguity. The authors argue that strategy implementation under conditions of greater uncertainty requires greater tolerance for ambiguity.

name: Knowledge breadth
definition: Our measures of knowledge scope and specialization are based on prior process patents. The variable Scope is the knowledge breadth or the number of unique subclasses (obtained from IPC codes) associated with the firm's patents filed by or granted to the firm over the 3 years prior to the post-TRIPS focal year.

name: Knowledge specialization
authors_terms: ["Specialization", "knowledge balance", "balance across technological knowledge assets", "degree of knowledge specialization", "lack of balance"]
definition: To measure the specialization or the balance of the knowledge base, we follow Hall, Jaffe, and Trajtenberg (2001) and Hall (2005), and create a Herfindahl index (HHI) based on the square of share of process patents filed in each subclass over the rolling 3-year periods. A high value of Specialization therefore is to be interpreted as the firm being unbalanced across its knowledge assets, and being focused on a narrower set of innovation routines.

name: New product innovation strategy
authors_terms: ["innovation-driven new product strategies", "product innovation", "product-based innovation", "new product strategy", "Percent Product"]
definition: Innovation-driven new product strategies: a move from process-based to product-based innovation. Firms that develop new drugs, create NCE or devise new methods of use through product innovations are able to obtain product patents to protect the new composition.

name: New generics process-based innovation strategy
authors_terms: ["new generics process-based innovation strategy", "new-generics strategy", "fast-entry into newly off-patent drugs"]
definition: New generics process-based innovation strategies: Fast-entry into newly off-patent drugs, a new-generics process innovation strategy. The strategy of entry into production of newly off-patent drugs redeploys a firm's previously developed process capabilities.

name: Old generics strategy
authors_terms: ["old generics strategies", "production of established generics", "reverse-engineering strategy"]
definition: Old generics strategies: Production of established generics through reverse-engineering activities. The final old generics strategy, reverse engineering of long off-patent drugs, mirrored a 'competitive' market where numerous firms had entered the market driving prices down to a 'normal' economic rent.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm financial performance", "change in income", "growth in income", "percent change in income"]
definition: We now examine firm financial performance following TRIPS by examining the association of change in income of Indian pharmaceutical firms with firm innovation strategy and knowledge capabilities. The outcome variable is the percentage of the change in income between the start and end of the time period.

name: Corporate diversity
definition: Diversity is the spread of a firm's activities across markets. This study also encompassed a broader concept of diversity than prior studies by considering both product and multinational diversity.

name: Product diversity
definition: We devised a quantitative index of product diversity (PDIV), a Herfindahl-type measure (Hirschman, 1964) based on the share of a firm's sales in each industry group.

name: Multinational diversity
definition: We devised an index of multinational diversity (MDIV), which measured diversity as the proportion of a firm's revenue derived from operations outside the United Kingdom.

name: Relatedness of diversification
definition: The relative costs and benefits of corporate diversity are likely to depend on how the different business activities of a firm are related to one another. The strategic-category approach has the advantage of taking into account the relatedness of a firm's activities as well as its breadth of diversity.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability", "firm profitability", "return on net assets (ROA)", "cash flow", "change in profitability"]
definition: We chose pre-tax return on net assets (ROA) as our primary measure of firm profitability. Our justification for using accounting return was, first, that managers and external analysts often use return on net assets as a measure of the effectiveness and efficiency of top management; second, the impact of corporate strategy on a firm's performance is more directly reflected in accounting profit than in stock price.

name: Diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification", "increases in diversity over time", "change in product diversity", "change in multinational diversity"]
definition: In contrast to earlier researchers who have used "diversification" and "diversity" synonymously, we used diversification to mean increases in diversity over time (i.e., change in PDIV and change in MDIV). We referred to reductions in diversity as "specialization."

name: CEO narcissism
definition: Narcissists have an inflated positive self-view that requires constant affirmation from others, and therefore they seek to be the center of attention. One key trait of narcissists is their strong need for social attention and applause - a trait not shared by hubristic individuals.

name: CEO hubris
definition: Hubris describes an individual's exaggerated self-confidence or pride as a result of both contextual stimuli and dispositional traits, and leads to 'the overestimation of one's actual ability, performance, level of control, or chance of success'. Hubristic individuals are not so concerned about what others think of them because they are overly confident about their own abilities.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Unlike other strategic decisions such as mergers and acquisitions (M&As) or R&D, which are more economic-oriented, CSR comprises both economic and social aspects. CSR has a dual nature that captures both economic instrumentality and social desirability.

name: Board-interlocked peer firms' CSR
authors_terms: ["interlocked peers' CSR engagement", "the CSR activities of board-interlocked peer firms", "the CSR activities of peer firms", "peer influence"]
definition: To measure interlocked peers' CSR engagement, we identified the list of interlocked firms in which a focal firm's CEO or directors held a board position in each firm-year, and for each interlocked firm we collected data on its CSR score and compared the score to that of the focal firm. The activities of interlocked firms provide a CEO with two types of informational cues.

name: Democratization of market mediation
authors_terms: ["democratization of market mediation", "democratization", "chart democratization", "Billboard's chart democratization experiment"]
definition: I argue that this power shift from intermediaries to consumers, who are typically far greater in number and more diverse, constitutes the democratization of market mediation. Due to consumers' inherent need for third-party valuation services, democratization usually results in diminishment rather than elimination of intermediary power.

name: Boundary spanning
definition: Boundary spanning, or the transfer and integration of knowledge, resources, and practices across social and technical boundaries. Product offerings that span market boundaries in this setting are often known as ''crossovers,'' a term referring to songs that cross genre boundaries.

name: Design scope
authors_terms: ["design scope", "Design Scope", "the design scope of the relationship", "design concept"]
definition: The design scope defines how problem solving is distributed between the partners. Supplier-manufacturer relationships can be distinguished on the basis of their design scope: they can be focused on the functional parameters definition, when suppliers are involved to define further a manufacturer's identified solution.

name: Level of task interdependency
authors_terms: ["level of task interdependency", "Level of Task Interdependency", "task interdependency"]
definition: The level of task interdependency focuses on the consequences of specific activities on other parts of the project. The higher the level of information that needs to be accessed to complete each individual task, the more individual task completion depends on others' actions and task interdependencies that arise.

name: Relationship efficiency
definition: Efficiency effects are the short-term efficiency-increasing outcomes of the relationship; six items were used to obtain a judgment of the supplier's performance in terms of measures of its "efficiency" (i.e., schedule deadline, cost objectives, quality levels, etc.).

name: Relationship learning
authors_terms: ["learning", "learning opportunities of the relationship", "Learning", "learning effects", "learning-enhancing effects"]
definition: Learning effects are the longer-term learning-enhancing outcomes of the relationship; one item assessed whether a project manager felt that his organization had learned something new from the interactions with the supplier, and the other asked to what extent solutions developed during the specific interaction were later used by the manufacturer in other projects.

name: Foreign owner-management
definition: We define an owner-manager as 'a CEO who owns at least 20 percent of firm shares,' based on the most conservative ownership threshold in the literature. The owner-manager variable equals 1 when any of the firm owners with at least 20 percent of the ownership stake is a firm CEO and 0 when a firm has a hired local CEO.

name: Operating costs
definition: Our dependent variable is the firm's cost-to-revenue ratio, that is, the sum of cost of goods sold and other operating expenses divided by operating revenue.

name: Hiring of foreign labor
definition: We expect that foreign entrepreneurs may be able to hire foreign labor from two sources: directly from abroad on sponsored visas and within local ethnic communities.

name: Access to foreign labor
authors_terms: ["superior access to foreign labor", "preferential access to foreign labor", "direct access to their home-country labor"]
definition: Foreign owner-managers typically have networks abroad and in local ethnic communities, with direct ties to foreign labor, whereas local managers lack access to those networks. The proposition is that for foreign owner-managers the advantage in hiring foreign labor is not purely informational, but includes superior access to foreign labor.

name: Industry labor intensity
definition: We measure industry labor intensity as the average labor intensity of all firms from that industry across all years of observation. As a proxy for the firm labor intensity, we use the number of employees per 1,000 rubles of assets.

name: Home-country GDP per capita
definition: Firms with owner-managers from countries with low gross domestic product (GDP) per capita should have greater benefits, since their native labor is less expensive.

name: Exposure to foreign-labor ban
definition: In 2007, Russia banned foreigners from working as sales people and cashiers in firms retailing liquor and pharmaceutical products and in firms operating in retail sales in markets and outside of stores. We call firms whose main activities were in the affected areas of retail an affected group.

name: Cash holdings
definition: Cash stock is recognized in the finance literature as stockpiled free cash flow because additions to cash reserves occur when managers accumulate free cash flow rather than spending it immediately through dividends or share repurchases. In this paper, cash stock is measured by cash and short-term investments divided by total assets.

name: Firm value
definition: Tobin's q is a well-established market-based measure suited to gauge the opportunity costs that shareholders must bear, in which the market value of the firm is divided by total assets.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured by the natural logarithm of the number of total employees; the number of employees is used rather than sales or total assets to avoid a spurious statistical relation with Tobin's q.

name: Economic globalization
definition: The exponential increase since World War II in cross-border flows of goods, services, money, people, information, and culture, accompanied by rising interdependence and mutual awareness among actors across the world. Globalization is a multidimensional construct referring to economic, political, and cultural features of global interconnectedness, of which the authors operationalize the economic dimension.

name: Market failure
authors_terms: ["market failure", "local credit market failure", "local credit market development", "credit market development"]
definition: The authors use the term market failure in a broad sense to refer to the presence of institutional voids in a country - that is, the relative absence of intermediaries to efficiently connect buyers and sellers. When the local credit market is poorly developed, there is likely to be unmet demand for banking services.

name: Religious polarization
definition: Religious polarization is the distributional property of a country's religious composition that is maximal when the Muslim and the non-Muslim populations are roughly equal in size, which increases the saliency of the ideologies underlying the oppositional banking logics and the value audiences attach to purity.

name: Constitutive legitimacy
definition: The taken-for-grantedness of the hybrid form, which grows as border crossing becomes more common: the diffusion of windows in geographically proximate countries signals to audiences that in similar environments windows are accepted to the point of being taken for granted, and this increased legitimacy is likely to spill over to the focal country.

name: Islamic window diffusion
authors_terms: ["diffusion of hybrids", "Islamic window formation", "window founding", "diffusion of windows"]
definition: Islamic windows appear when conventional banks enter the domain of Islamic banking by starting to sell Islamic banking services, and are examples of differentiated hybrids. The analysis models the hazard probability, that is, the conditional probability an Islamic window emerges at time t in a country, given that it has not emerged in the prior period.

name: Muslim population share
authors_terms: ["Muslims' ratio in the population", "Muslim ratio", "proportion of a country's population who are Muslim"]
definition: The moderating variable is the ratio of the Muslim population to the country's total population.

name: Manufacturing-based relatedness
definition: We defined two industries as loosely linked if one of the three categories of activities was the same, and as tightly linked if two or three categories of activities were the same. If none of the categories of activities were the same, then we described those two industries as manufacturing-unrelated.

name: Business unit performance
authors_terms: ["operating-level return on sales", "ROS", "business unit performance", "operating profitability"]
definition: Synergy is realized when two business units are more profitable or more competitive together than they would have been alone, reflected in superior operating profitability sustained over a multiyear period. We chose to measure performance as operating-level return on sales (ROS) over a 5-year period.

name: Intent to create synergy
authors_terms: ["intent to create synergy", "INTENT", "commitment to synergy creation"]
definition: In assessing coordination, we gathered information on evidence of managerial intent to create synergies (INTENT).

name: Resource and activity sharing
definition: In assessing coordination, we gathered information on evidence of actual resource and activity sharing (ACTION).

name: Administrative coordination mechanisms
authors_terms: ["administrative mechanisms for achieving coordination", "MECHANISMS", "administrative coordinating mechanisms"]
definition: In assessing coordination, we gathered information on evidence of use of administrative mechanisms to coordinate between the two related manufacturing organizations (MECHANISMS). More complex coordinating systems generally employ a combination of top-down controls, formal bureaucratic controls, structural changes to achieve interaction, and socialization methods.

name: Social affiliation
authors_terms: ["social affiliations", "social affiliation", "affiliation", "shared congregational affiliation", "ward or stake affiliation"]
definition: We define social affiliations as current shared memberships in formal social institutions (including churches, alumni organizations, corporations, clubs, charitable organizations, and schools) through which individuals interact and experience common identity, norms, and values. They are common memberships between individuals in formal social institutions.

name: Transaction value
authors_terms: ["transaction value", "higher-value transactions", "value of transactions", "home list price"]
definition: Higher-value transactions are especially important to professional performance, making competition to secure them especially intense; a high average transaction value indicates that a professional is capable of providing work of sufficient quality to justify the cost.

name: Transactions with social affiliates
authors_terms: ["transactions with affiliates", "affiliate transactions", "affiliate listings", "number of homes listed for affiliates to date"]
definition: Transactions in which a service professional lists for a client with whom he or she shares a social affiliation, in contrast to nonaffiliated transactions.

name: Transactions with nonaffiliates
authors_terms: ["nonaffiliate transactions", "nonaffiliate listings", "number of homes listed for nonaffiliates to date"]
definition: Transactions with clients with whom the professional shares no social affiliation.

name: Reputation for ability
definition: Reputation for ability accumulates over time as service professionals demonstrate high performance across multiple transactions; all else equal, a reputation for ability leads to increased access to valuable future transactions.

name: Firm reputation
authors_terms: ["firm-level reputation", "firm reputation", "high-reputation firms", "low-reputation firms", "major franchise brokerage"]
definition: Individual service professionals can often draw on firm-level reputation to improve transaction performance; firm reputation can provide significant information regarding professional ability, and professionals at high-reputation firms are typically judged to be of higher ability than those at lower-reputation firms.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: Entrepreneurship is defined as an agent starting a new brokerage that only employs one agent (i.e., themselves). In professional services the entrepreneurial decision reduces to whether the service professional believes that his or her reputation is strong enough to allow the potential new venture to grow and thrive.

name: Shooting range
authors_terms: ["shooting range", "shooting-range firms", "challenging yet attainable chance of achieving the $100 million revenue goal"]
definition: We define the shooting range as the revenue levels for which firms reaching $100 million revenue in the next year is challenging but attainable, so that firms switch their attention from an easier-to-reach goal based on historical and social reference points to the upward-striving $100 million revenue goal. The shooting range is the range of revenue in which the firm has a challenging yet achievable chance of crossing $100 million revenue in the following year.

name: Revenue growth
authors_terms: ["revenue growth", "revenue growth rate", "rate of revenue growth"]
definition: The firm's rate of revenue growth from year t to year t+1, which is the dependent variable in the tests of Hypothesis 1. The authors describe their variable of interest as the change in the revenue growth rate (i.e., essentially the second derivative, or acceleration, of an income statement item) rather than the level of earnings.

name: Firm investment
definition: Upward striving and the resulting need to accelerate growth are expected to lead to increased investment; the analyses examine three types of investments, the number of acquisitions, the number of employees (scaled by revenue), and the dollar amount of leasing (scaled by revenue).

name: Capital market visibility
definition: Firms' visibility with external resource providers increases when firms achieve the $100 million revenue threshold; the attention of these providers is a valuable resource that can provide tangible economic benefits, such as lower cost of capital and increased institutional investment.

name: Attainment of the $100 million revenue goal
authors_terms: ["Crossing $100 million", "crossing the $100 million revenue threshold", "achieving the $100 million revenue threshold"]
definition: An indicator for observations in which the firm's revenue crosses $100 million in the year; the authors examine whether attaining this threshold yields discontinuous increases in analyst coverage, media coverage, and institutional investment.

name: Number of institutional investors
definition: The number of institutional investors in the firm in year t+1, examined to show that an influx of new investors attracted by increased visibility drives the increase in institutional investment.

name: Number of block investors
definition: The number of block investors who hold more than 5% of the firm's outstanding shares in year t+1, for which no increase is expected because prior research finds that beating earnings thresholds has less effect on investors that are larger or that collect detailed information about and invest in a small number of firms.

name: Internal hire status
authors_terms: ["internal hire", "internal hire status", "external hire", "mode of job entry", "internal mobility"]
definition: Internal hire status is the dichotomous pathway by which a worker entered the current position (0 = external, 1 = internal). For salespeople an internal hire is a job transition from any nonsales job within or across stores, and the same definition is applied to department managers.

name: Worker performance
definition: A worker's objectively measured performance in the current position: for salespeople the logarithm of average sales per hour divided by the sales-per-hour target for that month, and for department managers the standardized EBITDA margin of the department they supervise.

name: Job tenure
definition: Job tenure is the consecutive monthly tenure of the person in the same job (e.g., commissioned sales or department manager jobs) and the same store; it is not reset when workers change from one commissioned sales role to another or from managing one department to another.

name: Turnover
definition: Workers' exit from their job; the authors model turnover, comprising both quits and terminations, as a competing risk with promotion, and contrast it with retention.

name: Promotion
definition: A move to a higher-ranking position: for salespeople a move to department manager in a given month, and for department managers a move to either the head store manager or district manager in a given fiscal year.

name: Rated career potential
definition: Subjective, explicitly forward-looking assessments of a manager's prospects for future career advancement and promotion, which the authors treat as an indicator of how raters subjectively interpret promotability as separate from objective performance.

name: Fundraising performance below the goal-based aspiration level
authors_terms: ["P < GAL", "fundraising performance below the goal-based aspiration level", "performance below goal-based aspiration levels"]
definition: The degree to which an entrepreneur's fundraising performance falls short of the entrepreneur's goal-based aspiration level, the predetermined fundraising goal that defines the amount of funds needed to develop and market the venture's product offering.

name: Fundraising performance below the social aspiration level
authors_terms: ["P < SAL", "fundraising performance below the social aspiration level", "performance below the social aspiration level"]
definition: The degree to which an entrepreneur's fundraising performance falls below the fundraising performance of the most-similar peer who sought funding for a video game on Kickstarter during the same time.

name: Deadline proximity
definition: The time remaining until the fundraising deadline during an underperforming fundraising attempt, with higher values indicating that the deadline is nearer.

name: Extent of change in product offering
authors_terms: ["extent of change in the product offering", "extent of change", "product-offering change"]
definition: The extent of substantive change in the product offering between two subsequent observations of a given campaign, where substantive changes involve an alteration of the look, feel, or technology of the video game as published on Kickstarter.

name: Board attention to monitoring
authors_terms: ["board's allocation of attention to monitoring", "attention to monitoring", "board monitoring percentage", "allocation of attention to monitoring"]
definition: Board members' attention is 'the noticing, encoding, interpreting, and focusing of time and effort' on a particular issue or issues; the allocation of attention to monitoring is that noticing, encoding, interpreting, and focusing of time and effort on the act of monitoring.

name: Deviation from prior performance
authors_terms: ["deviation from prior performance", "negative deviation from prior performance", "positive deviation from prior performance", "relative firm performance"]
definition: Deviation from prior performance is current performance compared with the average of the prior two years' performance; following prospect theory, this deviation from a reference level is coded as failure when performance is below the reference and success when above it.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO duality refers to instances in which the same person holds the titles of CEO and chairperson of the board of directors in a corporation.

name: Analyst performance
authors_terms: ["analyst performance", "individual performance", "ranked analysts' performance", "Institutional Investor ranking"]
definition: The analyst's performance, this study's dependent variable, is operationalized as rank in the Institutional Investor All-America Research Team poll, rank t+1.

name: Interfirm mobility
definition: Star analysts who leave one firm to join another are the 'movers,' compared with the 'stayers,' the star analysts who did not move, who serve as the control group. The paper also notes that when some of an employee's skills are firm-specific, changing jobs leads to a decline in performance until the employee develops skills specific to the new firm.

name: Exploration role
authors_terms: ["hired for exploration", "hiring for exploration", "explore", "initiate new activities", "initiate coverage of sectors that firms had not previously covered"]
definition: An analyst is hired for exploration when he or she is hired to begin coverage of a new sector not previously covered by the firm, i.e., when the hiring firm is exploring a new market and/or new 'product.'

name: Exploitation role
authors_terms: ["hired for exploitation", "hiring for exploitation", "exploit", "reinforce existing activities", "work in a sector already covered by the firm"]
definition: An analyst is hired for exploitation when he or she is hired to work in a sector already covered by the firm, adding quality or quantity to existing operations.

name: Team movement
authors_terms: ["lift outs", "moving with a team of colleagues", "moving with colleagues", "coworker move for exploitation/exploration", "group hire", "team movement"]
definition: The movement of work groups or teams from one company to another has been known as 'lift outs,' defined as the movement of more than one person simultaneously. The effect of moving with coworkers was tested by distinguishing analysts who switch to another sell-side research department solo from those who make such a move with a team of colleagues.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["value destruction", "value creation for the hiring firm", "share price", "abnormal returns", "stock-market reaction"]
definition: Stock-market movement is an established proxy for how much value is created or lost for a given firm in reaction to a specific event, here the announcement of a star analyst's hiring.

name: Star hiring
authors_terms: ["hiring a star", "hiring of a star analyst", "acquisition of 'stars'", "star analyst hirings", "hiring stars"]
