definition: The paper focuses on the practice of hiring individuals, typically star performers, away from a competitor to enhance or expand the hiring firm's capabilities.

name: Manufacturing strategy alignment and implementation
authors_terms: ["manufacturing strategy process", "well aligned and implemented manufacturing strategy", "alignment and implementation of a plant's manufacturing strategy"]
definition: We define manufacturing strategy to be a design or blueprint for the manufacturing function that frames the acquisition, development and elimination of manufacturing capabilities far into the future. A manufacturing strategy may be well aligned and implemented if it exhibits all or most of the dimensions described above, and is considered poorly aligned and implemented if it exhibits few of those characteristics.

name: Organizational culture
definition: Organizational culture has been used as an holistic construct that describes the complex set of knowledge structures which organization members use to perform tasks and generate social behavior. Organizational cultures exist on a continuum but are characterized here as hierarchically-oriented cultures, depending primarily on authority relationships for control of behavior, or clan-oriented cultures, relying mainly on shared values and beliefs.

name: Individualism-collectivism
definition: Hierarchical and clan cultures differ fundamentally in their beliefs about the role of the individual versus that of the group (Ouchi 1979). Hierarchical cultures are based on the premise that it is possible to define, control, and evaluate the contribution of individuals to the production process, while clan cultures emphasize group or collective contributions.

name: Power distance
definition: The power distance dimension describes the distribution of authority within the plant. Hofstede (1980) uses the term power distance to refer to the "practice of inequalities in the distribution of legitimate power and authority."

name: Cultural congruency
definition: Cultural congruency refers to homogeneity among various members and subgroups in the organization regarding central organizational assumptions (Saffold 1988). Clan cultures depend on shared values as a control mechanism and are expected to exhibit widely held and consistent beliefs regarding many aspects of organizational life.

name: Geographic distance
definition: By geographic distance, we mean distance in relevant units of space such as miles. Acquisition distance is the log of the miles between coordinates for the zip codes of the acquirer and target firm headquarters.

name: Acquisition match
authors_terms: ["acquisition match", "acquisition matches", "probability of an acquisition match"]
definition: We refer to the acquisition targets that firms select as acquisition matches. Testing the hypotheses involves modeling the probability that a firm acquires a particular target from a set of potential targets.

name: Business relatedness
definition: Unrelated acquisitions, such as General Electric's acquisition of NBC, are similar to venture capital investments, providing little scope of knowledge transfer or sharing of other resources. Related acquisitions provide firms with opportunities to benefit from economies of scale and scope, from operational synergies, and from improved competitive position.

name: Direct experience with distant search
definition: We expect that acquirers can improve their target selection capabilities through routine-based experiential learning (March and Simon 1958)—that is, learning by direct experience. This logic suggests that acquirers face weaker spatial influences in target selection as they gain direct experience in distant search, that is, after they have acquired prior targets involving substantial cumulative distance.

name: Contextual experience with distant markets
authors_terms: ["contextual experience", "contextual learning", "contextual knowledge", "prior acquisition in state"]
definition: Acquirers can accumulate contextual knowledge about distant markets that reduces the extent of information search that is necessary while searching for targets within those regions. Such findings reflect the effect of familiarity with the market and with firms operating in the market.

name: Vicarious experience
definition: Acquirers can utilize vicarious learning from secondary sources to help them gather information in unfamiliar contexts. We therefore predict that firms can at least partly overcome the constraints of distance by accessing information from parent and subsidiary organizations.

name: Organizational density
authors_terms: ["density", "density of brewers", "number of brewers per capita"]
definition: Past ecological studies examining competition between organizational populations have most often focused on density, or the number of organizations in an environment. Because the environment was examined at the state level, density was measured as the number of brewers per capita operating in each state for every year of the study.

name: Market concentration
definition: In a concentrated environment, a few brewers control a high proportion of the market. Measures of concentration provide detailed information about the relative share of the market specific organizations control.

name: Product demand
definition: For industrial organizations, level of resources is typically defined in terms of demand for their products. This study measured demand at the state level as the total consumption of beer for each state in each year.

name: Pricing regulation
definition: Price-posting laws restrict the number of temporary price cuts (or price promotions) that a brewer can engage in over the course of a year and their duration; they generally require brewers to file their prices with a state agency and to maintain prices at that level for three to six months.

name: Excise taxation
definition: State and federal excise taxes constitute the largest individual component in the price of beer; excise taxes are charged per volume, with a set amount collected per barrel of beer regardless of producer, so the proportionate effect of an increase is greater for low-priced beers than for high-priced beers.

name: Sales growth of national brewers
authors_terms: ["expansion or decline of national brewers", "increase sales", "growth of national brewers"]
definition: The dependent variable in the study was change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study. The hypotheses were posed in terms of the effects that each independent variable was expected to have on the expansion or decline of national brewers.

name: Sales growth of regional brewers
authors_terms: ["expansion or decline of regional brewers", "growth of regional brewers"]
definition: The dependent variable in the study was change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study.

name: Sales growth of local brewers
authors_terms: ["expansion or decline of local brewers", "growth of local brewers"]
definition: The dependent variable in the study was change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study.

name: R&D decentralization
authors_terms: ["R&D Decentralization", "decentralization of R&D", "decentralized R&D units", "centralization of R&D"]
definition: With respect to leadership, I distinguish between a single centralized R&D unit reporting to a single head manager and multiple, decentralized units, which have separate head managers at the same level in the organizational hierarchy. In developing my hypotheses, I will primarily focus on decentralization of R&D, noting that centralization of R&D has the opposite effect on knowledge flows and managerial incentives.

name: Invention novelty
definition: Consistent with prior studies, I portray novelty in terms of the knowledge that is recombined to create an invention. This variable measures the breadth of knowledge from which patents draw.

name: Invention quantity
definition: Beyond the novelty of inventions, another key outcome that is critical to firms is the quantity of inventions created. To measure the quantity of inventions (Quantity), the number of patent families in category (NACE2) 21 filed by firms annually is counted.

name: Progression into development
authors_terms: ["progression of inventions into development", "Development Conversion", "development outcomes"]
definition: Development is focused on converting an invention into a final product. The key dependent variable that I develop, Development Conversion, measures the proportion of drug candidates in a firm's pre-clinical portfolio moving into Phase 1 per year.

name: Proportion of novel inventions
authors_terms: ["proportion of novel inventions", "Proportion NCE", "proportion of novel inventions in a firm's portfolio"]
definition: The proportion of novel inventions in a firm's portfolio moderates the relationship between R&D decentralization and the progression of inventions into development. I develop the measure Proportion NCE that measures the proportion of a firm's preclinical development portfolio that are NCE.

name: Minority status on the board
authors_terms: ["minority status on the focal board", "minority status", "minority functional background", "minority industry background", "minority educational affiliation", "minority degree type", "minority race", "minority gender"]
definition: From the social psychological literature on minority influence, the term minority refers to an individual who has a salient attitude, belief, or social feature, such as a demographic characteristic, that is possessed by less than 50 percent of the group. Minority status is multidimensional, such that directors can have minority status on one dimension and majority status on another.

name: Director influence over board decision making
authors_terms: ["director influence on strategic decision making", "influence over decision making on the board", "director influence"]
definition: The dependent measure assesses director influence on strategic decision making by the board. Items in the director-influence scale assess the degree to which directors feel that they contribute to board discussions on strategic issues, as well as their overall perceived influence or impact on strategic decision making by the board.

name: Prior minority-role experience
authors_terms: ["prior experience in a minority role on other boards", "focal director experience, minority"]
definition: We measured a focal director's prior experience in a minority role on other boards as the total number of years the director has served on another board in a minority position for a given demographic characteristic, aggregated across all boards the director served on. This procedure yielded six indicators of minority experience on other boards, which were added together into a single, composite indicator.

name: Prior majority-role experience
authors_terms: ["prior experience in a majority role on other boards", "focal director experience, majority"]
definition: We also developed an analogous measure of a focal director's prior experience in a majority role on other boards, based on the number of years the director has served on other boards in a majority position.

name: Majority directors' prior minority-role experience
authors_terms: ["other majority directors' prior experience in a minority role", "majority director exper. as minority"]
definition: We measured other majority directors' prior experience in a minority role using the composite measure described above, averaged across majority directors.

name: Common board memberships
authors_terms: ["common board memberships", "common memberships on other boards"]
definition: We measured common board memberships between the focal director and other, majority directors as the number of other boards in the larger sample frame on which the focal director and another, majority director both held an appointment.

name: Third-party board ties
authors_terms: ["third-party board ties", "indirect board ties", "indirect, third-party ties to majority directors"]
definition: A third-party board tie exists between a minority director A and a majority director B when A sits on another board with a third director C, who also sits on a different board with B.

name: Negative publicity of recalls
authors_terms: ["negative publicity of recalls", "negative media publicity of recalls", "negative media coverage of a firm's product recalls"]
definition: Negative media coverage of a firm's product safety recalls, which the authors use as an external reputational cue signalling that the firm's actions in dealing with such recalls would be more important. It is measured as a count of negative articles on recalls for each manufacturer, reflecting both the negativity and the magnitude of coverage.

name: Negative publicity of recall-related lobbying
definition: Negative media coverage of a firm's lobbying on recall-related issues, built on the notion of lobbying visibility, which reflects the degree of awareness regarding lobbying and is measured by the news coverage on firm lobbying. It is the amount of negative media coverage of recall-related lobbying.

name: Recall-related lobbying
authors_terms: ["recall-related lobbying", "lobbying for recall-related issues", "lobbying for recalls"]
definition: Lobbying measured in terms of whether lobbying for recall and/or recall-related safety issues was documented in the quarterly lobbying report on behalf of the manufacturer, including lobbying that mentions the NHTSA, the governing agency for recalls, as the target agency.

name: Takeover protection
authors_terms: ["takeover protection", "increase in takeover protection", "takeover regime shift"]
definition: Governance provisions that protect managers from the threat of hostile takeover; in this study it is captured by the Delaware takeover regime shift, which exogenously increased takeover protection for Delaware-incorporated firms.

name: Firm-specific knowledge
authors_terms: ["firm-specific knowledge assets", "firm-specific knowledge", "level of firm-specific knowledge", "firm specificity in a firm's knowledge assets"]
definition: Knowledge assets whose value varies with firm settings and which cannot be transferred to other business settings without a significant loss in value; the extent to which a firm's new knowledge is built on its own knowledge base.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: The shareholding of all officers and directors, which aligns managers' interests with those of firm owners and gives them bargaining power over the rents from their specialized investments.

name: Top manager organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["organizational tenure of top managers", "managerial tenure", "CEO's organizational tenure", "tenure in a firm"]
definition: The number of years for which a top manager (the CEO) has joined the firm; a key source of specialized skills acquisition and commitment to the firm.

name: CEO stock option compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO stock option compensation", "CEO's stock option compensation", "stock option compensation to the CEO", "CEO's options"]
definition: Compensating the CEO with stock options is expected to make the CEO more willing to take risk because the CEO participates in the upside potential of risky decisions but not in their downside. The authors define the CEO's stock option compensation as the value of stock options that were granted to the CEO during a firm's fiscal year.

name: Outside director stock option compensation
authors_terms: ["outside directors' stock option compensation", "stock option compensation to outside directors", "directors' options"]
definition: Following the agency logic developed for CEO compensation, outside directors are viewed as self-interested agents who also have to be provided with incentives to align their interests with those of the shareholders; stock options should provide outside directors with incentives to increase their involvement in various board tasks, steering a firm's decision making toward higher risk taking.

name: Firm risk taking
authors_terms: ["firm-level risk", "risk taking", "firms' risk taking", "firm-level risk taking"]
definition: The paper's main dependent variable is firm-level risk. As its main measure the authors chose the ratio of a firm's book value of common equity to its market value, which has been shown to be a strong proxy for sensitivity to risk factors in returns.

name: Spatial connectedness
authors_terms: ["spatial connectedness", "physical connectedness", "enhanced spatial connectedness", "newly built bridges", "new bridges", "physical connectivity"]
definition: The extent to which spaces are not just proximate but are actually able to link people, ideas, resources, and knowledge together. New bridges, in particular, provide positive shocks to spatial connectedness in communities.

name: Startup founding rate
authors_terms: ["startup founding rates", "startup founding", "number of new startups", "new startups founded", "founding of new organizations"]
definition: The number of new startups (high-growth, high-potential ventures that receive angel or VC funding) founded in a CBSA in a year.

name: Founder entry rate
authors_terms: ["entry rate of founders into entrepreneurship", "founder entry rate", "more entry into entrepreneurship by potential (co)founders", "entry of prospective founders into entrepreneurship"]
definition: The rate at which potential (co)founders enter entrepreneurship in the local community, measured as the total number of startup founders in a CBSA in a year normalized by the existing number of startups in the CBSA.

name: Early-stage investors
authors_terms: ["early-stage investors", "number of early investors", "early investors", "early-stage financing"]
definition: The average number of early investors in the average startup founded, comprising angels and other individuals as the majority as well as some smaller seed/early VC funds, until the first round or earlier.

name: Recombination
definition: Recombination is a process of combining existing resources and business models in unique and novel ways; it can involve combining skills, methods, technologies, business models, and tacit knowledge to shake up the status quo within an industry.

name: Industry spanning
authors_terms: ["industry spanning", "spanning industry categories", "cross industry boundaries", "span more industry categories"]
definition: Recombination to create entirely new products and services that sit in the interstitial gaps between industries; here recombination is measured as industry spanning, the average number of industry categories spanned by startups.

name: Partner valuation
authors_terms: ["partner valuation", "target firm value", "value of the target", "subfield value", "valuation of growth opportunities", "firm valuation"]
definition: S corresponds to the partner value-including expected future cash flows from the existing business and the option value of future growth opportunities. In addition to the value of future growth opportunities, target value includes current expected cash flows and the value of current learning opportunities that can only be realized by committing additional resources to the partner.

name: External uncertainty
definition: In this paper the term 'uncertainty' refers to the unpredictability of the (internal or external) environment. The standard deviation of a stock market index represents uncertainty that is specific to the industry subfield and exogenous to the control of individual firms.

name: Proprietary buyout option
authors_terms: ["proprietary option", "how proprietary the option is", "proprietary buyout options", "exclusive partnerships"]
definition: Unlike financial options, however, the option to buy out the partner is generally not exclusive. It can be shared with other firms that also hold equity stakes in the target firm; when more than one established firm has an equity position in a single target firm, that option is shared.

name: Uniqueness of the growth option
authors_terms: ["growth options are more unique", "unique growth opportunities", "number of rivals", "technological preemption"]
definition: The threat of preemption may not merely reside at the level of the target firm, but may exist more broadly in the competitive space of the technical subfield. The greater the number of firms competing in a technical product area, the greater the likelihood that some other firm will develop a substitute technology that renders alternative technologies obsolete even before their development is completed.

name: Partner buyout
authors_terms: ["partner buyout", "buyout option", "additional equity purchases", "acquisition of a majority stake", "sequential equity commitments in partner firms"]
definition: Exercising the first stage-the buyout option-occurs when the firm makes further equity purchases granting a controlling interest in the partner. Buyouts may be either controlling-through acquiring a majority stake-or partial-through incremental equity purchases en route to a majority stake.

name: Knowledge breadth
definition: Knowledge breadth refers to the extent to which the firm's knowledge repository contains distinct and multiple domains. The breadth attribute captures the horizontal dimension of knowledge and heterogeneous knowledge content.

name: Knowledge depth
definition: Knowledge depth refers to the level of sophistication and complexity of knowledge in key fields. The depth attribute reflects a vertical dimension and unique, complex, within-field knowledge content.

name: Market knowledge acquisition
definition: Market knowledge acquisition is an external integration mechanism that facilitates the absorption of critical knowledge from external market sources. It captures the amount and extent of knowledge the firm has acquired from external parties, such as customers, competitors, and suppliers.

name: Knowledge sharing
definition: Knowledge sharing entails an internal integration mechanism, involving the dissemination and synthesis of individually and organizationally held knowledge through established processes and routines.

name: Radical innovation
definition: Radical innovation is the novel, unique, or state-of-the-art technological advance in a product category that significantly alters the consumption patterns in a market.

name: Regional firm population
authors_terms: ["count of all firms in a regional network", "number of firms already present in the same region", "intertemporal population of firms constituting a regional network", "count of all unrelated firms"]
definition: The intertemporal population of firms constituting a regional network. Count of all firms in a regional network adds a firm's own entries and entries by firms affiliated with the same group on top of the count of all unrelated firms, thus comprising all types of firms in a regional network.

name: Location choice
authors_terms: ["co-location", "likelihood of co-location", "location choice", "chance that a location will be chosen"]
definition: Our sample firm faces a set of location choices, each of which has different attributes. The model estimates how each attribute increases or decreases the chance that a location will be chosen rather than all other potential locations.

name: Firm's own prior entry
authors_terms: ["count of a firm's own prior entry", "a firm's own prior entries", "firm's own prior entry"]
definition: Count of a firm's own prior entry measured the number of a focal firm's own prior entries into each region up to the time of an entry event.

name: Business group affiliate prior entry
authors_terms: ["count of entry by firms within the same group", "entries by firms affiliated with the same group", "entry by the same group firms"]
definition: Count of entry by firms within the same group reflected the cumulative count of entries by firms associated with the same business groups in each region up to the time of each entry event. For firms with no group affiliation, this variable is coded as zero.

name: Same-nation firm prior entry
authors_terms: ["count of other Korean firms", "other Korean firms", "network externalities from other Korean firms"]
definition: Count of other Korean firms was measured as the number of Korean firms not associated with the same business groups that were operating in each region at the time of each entry.

name: Other foreign firm prior entry
authors_terms: ["count of other foreign firms", "other foreign firms", "count of other foreign firms in the same industry"]
definition: Count of other foreign firms and count of local firms were measured as the number of manufacturing operations of non-Korean multinationals and Chinese local firms, respectively, operating in each region at the time of each entry.

name: Local firm prior entry
authors_terms: ["count of local firms", "local firms", "local Chinese firms"]
definition: Count of other foreign firms and count of local firms were measured as the number of manufacturing operations of non-Korean multinationals and Chinese local firms, respectively, operating in each region at the time of each entry.

name: Willingness to cannibalize
definition: The extent to which a firm is prepared to reduce the actual or potential value of its investments in assets and organizational routines.

name: Constructive conflict
definition: Constructive conflict refers to the vigorous debate of ideas, beliefs, and assumptions by organization members.

name: Tolerance for failure
definition: The extent to which failure is seen within the firm as an opportunity to learn; in a failure-tolerant climate failure is regarded as the inevitable and even beneficial byproduct of reaching in new directions.

name: Environmental scanning
definition: The extent to which organization members devote their efforts to learning about events and trends in their organization's environment.

name: Resource slack
definition: Human and financial resources that are not consumed by the necessity of the continued daily operation of the firm, thus representing a reserve of resources in excess of what is needed for immediate continuation.

name: Second-order marketing competence
definition: A competence at explorative learning by exploring new markets, i.e. the firm's ability to identify and access new markets and to build new customer competences.

name: Second-order R&D competence
definition: A competence at explorative learning by exploring new technologies, i.e. the firm's ability to identify and incorporate new technologies and to build new technological competences.

name: Relatedness of restructured assets
authors_terms: ["relatedness of the restructured assets", "asset relatedness", "primary and related business assets", "secondary and unrelated business assets", "core business assets"]
definition: The relatedness of the restructured assets captures whether the assets exist within the restructuring firm's self-reported primary and related businesses or in the secondary and unrelated business lines. Assets in primary and related business lines reside within the firm's main business lines and create value by sharing and developing complementary interrelationships with other assets within the same groups.

name: Diversification strategy
definition: Diversification is 'the extent to which firms are simultaneously active in many distinct businesses.' It pertains to the 'scope of the firm in terms of the industries and markets in which it competes.'

name: Restructuring implementation alternative
definition: The implementation alternative is how the restructuring is conducted: a spin-off occurs when a firm 'distributes on a pro rata basis all the shares it owns in a subsidiary to its own shareholders,' while a sell-off arises when assets are sold from one firm to another in exchange for cash and/or securities.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction to the restructuring event", "stock market value", "cumulative abnormal return", "CAR"]
definition: Financial performance is considered from the perspective of the stock market reaction to the restructuring announcement, as investors' reactions provide a direct, clear, and immediate assessment of the expected financial returns associated with the restructuring event. It is measured by a cumulative abnormal return computed for the days surrounding the restructuring announcement.

name: Consumption of content
definition: The consumption of the information created by an open collaboration community, which the authors operationalize as the times the focal Wikipedia article was viewed in each month. Participants can both freely consume and contribute to the information created by the community, so every consumer is also a potential contributor.

name: Contributor activity
authors_terms: ["contributor activity", "number of contributors", "number of people who contribute", "distinct contributors"]
definition: The number of unique people who edit an article in a given month, excluding discussions around the construction of the pages such as comment and talk pages.

name: Content development
authors_terms: ["content development", "state of the content", "content state", "more developed content", "developed content"]
definition: The state of the content created by the community, which is determined by both active contributions and potential contributions. Since it is difficult to capture the development of content in a single variable, the authors use several measures of the content of a Wikipedia article.

name: Content age
definition: How long the content has existed; content age measures the opportunity consumers have had to contribute to the community, since the longer the content has existed the greater the likelihood that the people most interested in contributing will have done so.

name: Corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["corporate social performance", "CSP", "independently rated corporate social performance"]
definition: A construct that emphasizes a company's responsibilities to multiple stakeholders, such as employees and the community at large, in addition to its traditional responsibilities to economic shareholders. The authors conceptualized CSP as the set of socially responsible or irresponsible activities by firms.

name: Corporate reputation
definition: An organization's reputation as rated by prospective applicants on a five-point scale ranging from 1, 'very poor reputation,' to 5, 'very good reputation.'

name: Organizational attractiveness as an employer
authors_terms: ["attractiveness as an employer", "organizational attractiveness as an employer", "employer attractiveness"]
definition: The extent to which an organization is seen as an attractive employer by potential applicants, rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1, 'unattractive employer,' to 5, 'one of the most attractive employers.' The authors expect that CSP positively affects an organization's attractiveness as an employer because potential applicants will expect to experience positive outcomes, such as an enhanced self-concept.

name: Calculative trust
definition: With calculative trust, managers believe that the costs and benefits of complying with the business agreement will outweigh those associated with self-interested, opportunistic actions. It informs expectations by deliberately and rationally assessing forward-looking conditions: it requires calculations of benefits and costs, and hinges on the relative values of cheating (e.g., net costs of termination) and cooperation.

name: Relational trust
definition: Relational trust arises from social relationships when there are strong beliefs about the goodwill, honesty, and good faith efforts of others, which mitigate risk by aligning core values. It arises when social relations evolve to a state in which each partner can expect to act according to the other's preferences and priorities.

name: Supplier performance
definition: Supplier performance is the buyer's evaluation of the supplier's task performance in the focal exchange relationship.

name: Buyer asset specificity
definition: Buyer asset specificity means the buyer has invested in supplier-specific assets and risks sizable sunk costs if the exchange is terminated; it captures buyers' specific investments in product features, personnel, inventory and distribution, and capital equipment and tools to accommodate suppliers' needs.

name: Supply market uncertainty
definition: Supply market uncertainty refers to unpredictability in supply prices, vendor support, and the supplier's manufacturing technologies and product design; it concerns environmental changes in the supply market with respect to pricing, product features and specifications, vendor support services, technology, and product supply.

name: Behavioral uncertainty
definition: Behavioral uncertainty refers to the extent to which one party cannot effectively observe or evaluate the activities of the other party.

name: Foreign R&D lab investment
definition: Foreign subsidiaries whose main purpose is 'information gathering' or 'research and development'; the sample of R&D labs was limited to those that are creating new knowledge in their foreign R&D labs rather than adapting or exploiting knowledge from their home market.

name: Technological position
authors_terms: ["technologically leading firms", "technologically lagging firms", "global technology position", "domestic technology position", "technology position variables"]
definition: The relative technological position of the firm, leading or lagging, created using R&D intensity (R&D expenditures/Sales) and determined against two reference groups: global and domestic competitors. The leader/laggard categories refer to the technology position of the firm.

name: Market share position
authors_terms: ["dominant firms", "non-dominant firms", "non-dominant market share firms", "market share position", "domestic sales leader"]
definition: The dominant firm classification refers to the top firm in the industry in terms of sales, while non-dominant firms are those firms that are smaller than the largest firms in their industry and that do not have the same advantages or resources for retaliating and damaging challengers.

name: Congruence between resource and pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["congruence between resource and pay dispersions", "pay and resource dispersion congruence", "congruence between pay and resource dispersion"]
definition: Pay and resource dispersion congruence is when the dispersion in pay matches the dispersion in resource values; congruence between pay and resource value dispersions should reduce relative deprivation effects and consequently improve organizational performance.

name: Resource value dispersion
authors_terms: ["resource dispersion", "resource value dispersion", "dispersion of individuals' contributions to the performance of the organization"]
definition: The dispersion of individuals' contributions to the performance of the organization, that is, the dispersion of the value latent in the human resources that are part of an organization.

name: Pay dispersion
definition: The dispersion of individuals' total pay in the organization as reported by the organizations, including all actual pay to a player by a team in a year.

name: Overall resource value
authors_terms: ["overall resource value", "overall value of an organization's resources", "overall stock of resources"]
definition: The overall value of an organization's human resources, as specified by resource-based theorizing; organizations with more valuable employees are expected to perform favorably relative to organizations with less valuable employees.

name: Organizational pay level
definition: The level at which an organization pays its employees; according to efficiency wage theory, organizations that pay higher wages than competitors will experience increases in performance at the organizational level.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance was measured as the percentage of games each MLB organization won in a focal year.

name: Technology differentiation
authors_terms: ["tech differentiation", "technology differentiation", "uniqueness of a firm's technology portfolio", "uniqueness", "differentiation"]
definition: To assess the uniqueness or differentiation of firm i's technology portfolio in year t, we adopt the methodology of Arts et al. (2023) and compute technology differentiation. Firms with more unique and less overlapping technology portfolios compared to others in the technology space exhibit higher levels of technology differentiation.

name: Acquisition target probability
authors_terms: ["Target", "being a target", "probability of becoming an acquisition target", "probability of being targeted for acquisition", "acquisition target"]
definition: Hypothesis 1 formulates a baseline expectation by suggesting that the uniqueness of a firm's technology portfolio influences its probability of becoming an acquisition target, regardless of the characteristics of the acquirer or specifics of the deal.

name: M&A transaction pairing
definition: To study the M&A transaction probability between (pseudo) acquirers and (pseudo) targets, we follow Bena and Li (2014) and run a deal-level conditional logit model. Our outcome variable AcquirerTargetijmt equals one if firms i and j are the actual acquirer-target pair for deal m in year t, and zero in case of matched pseudo-acquirer-target pairs.

name: Product market overlap
authors_terms: ["prod similarity", "product similarity", "product market overlap", "product market rivalry", "close competitors in the product market"]
definition: Prod similarityijt is calculated for every pair of US public firms in each year as the overlap in the product descriptions found within the annual 10-K reports of firm i and firm j in year t.

name: Technological similarity
authors_terms: ["tech similarity", "technological similarity", "technological proximity", "closer in technology space"]
definition: For every pair of US public firms in each year, tech similarityijt is calculated as the cosine similarity between the technology portfolio of firm i and firm j in year t.

name: Client transfer
authors_terms: ["client transfer", "interfirm client transfer", "the likelihood a client follows the employee if the employee exits"]
definition: A client follows an employee who switches firms, so that employee mobility results in the interfirm transfer of the client relationship.

name: Employee-client repeated exchange
definition: The strength of a client's relationship with the exiting employee, examined as the degree to which the client and employee have engaged in repeated exchange, which generates economic and relational benefits that strengthen and embed the relationship.

name: Firm-client repeated exchange
definition: The strength of a client's relationship with the firm, examined as the degree to which the client and the firm have engaged in repeated exchange; the same employee(s) may or may not be involved in these interactions, so repeated exchange occurs distinctly at the individual and organizational levels.

name: Multiplexity
definition: Multiplexity broadly refers to situations in which two or more relationships simultaneously occur. The authors consider a client relationship to be multiplex if more than one employee works with the client, i.e. multiplexity exists with a single identity but multiple individual employee-client ties.

name: Specialization
definition: Specialists have highly specialized knowledge and expertise in a single area (high depth and low breadth), whereas generalists have a broader set of knowledge and expertise that touches upon a multitude of different areas (low depth and high breadth).

name: Diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification", "changes in diversification", "entropy index of diversification", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification"]
definition: Diversification was measured by the entropy index of diversification (Palepu, 1985), which can be broken down into an unrelated component (DU) and a related component (DR), such that DT=DR+DU. DR was defined as diversification arising out of operating in several segments within an industry group, whereas DU was defined as diversification across industry groups.

name: Opening diversification
authors_terms: ["opening diversification", "diversification at the beginning of that time period"]
definition: The firm's level of diversification at the beginning of the time period over which subsequent changes in diversification are measured. The change in a firm's diversification between two time periods is hypothesized to be a negative function of this opening diversification.

name: Firm risk
definition: We measure risk by a firm's asset beta. A firm's asset beta reflects its business risk (as opposed to its financial risk, which is captured by the equity beta); the asset beta is determined by the volatility of revenues and operating leverage.

name: Liquidity
definition: The current ratio is a standard measure of liquidity; ceteris paribus, the greater a firm's current ratio, the more diversification it is able to afford.

name: R&D intensity
definition: For firms in the pharmaceutical industry, R&D expenditures amount to approximately 9 percent of annual sales revenues. The measure used adjusts a firm's R&D-to-sales ratio for the extent to which the firm has diversified into industries with different R&D intensities.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: Advertising intensity in the pharmaceutical industry is high, amounting to 7 percent of annual sales revenues, on average, and is treated as placing competing claims with diversification on the funds a firm has available for investment.

name: Institutional holdings
definition: Institutional holdings are the percentage of a firm's stock held by institutions. The authors argue that institutions invest for the short term, so that increased institutional holdings are perceived by managers as exposing the firm to greater share price volatility and an increased risk of hostile takeover following a short-term decline in earnings.

name: Management holdings
definition: Management holdings capture the percentage of stock controlled directly and indirectly by managers. When a substantial block of stock is held by management, the risk of hostile takeover is significantly reduced, and managers also bear the wealth effects of their own actions.

name: Market to book value
definition: The ratio of a firm's market to book value gives an indication of how stockholders value a firm's assets; the lower this ratio, the greater the probability of a hostile takeover bid designed to replace current management.

name: Economic performance
authors_terms: ["economic performance", "profitability", "return on equity", "risk-adjusted market returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: The paper examines the effect of a change in diversification on economic performance, operationalized as a subsequent change in profitability measured by return on equity and as risk-adjusted market returns (abnormal returns) to stockholders.

name: Market share
definition: If we accept the view that market share is a proxy for the underlying efficiency of a firm (Demsetz, 1973), an increase in market share would be expected to have a positive impact on ROE. We used a weighted measure to compute market share, defined as the sum of a firm's market share in each four-digit SIC industry in which it was active, weighted by the proportion of total firm sales generated in that industry.

name: Leverage
definition: An increase in leverage will increase interest payments and reduce the funds available for distribution to stockholders, thereby reducing ROE. Leverage was measured by the debt to equity ratio, and the change in leverage was defined as debt to equity at the later date divided by debt to equity at the earlier date.

name: Social distancing
definition: Social distancing is a kind of informal ostracism that occurs in response to social deviance by individual members or minority subgroups of a larger group or society; individuals who experience distancing are not expelled from the group but are informally excluded to some degree from its work and from social interaction with other members.

name: Participation in elite-threatening actions
authors_terms: ["elite-threatening actions", "elite-threatening changes in corporate governance", "participation in elite-threatening actions", "participation in elite-threatening changes in corporate governance"]
definition: Actions that threaten the interests of top managers or diminish the social integrity of the corporate elite (which we term elite-threatening actions), operationalized as separation of the CEO and board-chair positions, creation of an independent board nominating committee, repeal of a poison pill, and dismissal of a CEO.

name: Director status in the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["director status in the corporate elite", "status in the corporate elite"]
definition: Status refers to individuals' social ranking or the esteem accorded to them in relation to other members of the corporate elite.

name: Interorganizational links
authors_terms: ["interorganizational links", "cooperative relationships among distinct but related organizations", "cooperative strategies"]
definition: Interorganizational links are "enduring transactions, flows, and linkages that occur among or between an organization and one or more organizations in its environment" (Oliver, 1990); the authors describe them as cooperative relationships among distinct but related organizations.

name: Structural links
definition: A fast-growing form of structural link in the hospital industry has been the multihospital system (MHS). An MHS is defined as two or more affiliated hospitals that are partially or fully owned, sponsored, or managed within a corporate framework, usually involving a governance structure that is legally distinct from the management structures of their member hospitals.

name: Administrative links
definition: One way in which hospitals link administratively is through management contracts, a strategy often used to access managerial and financial resources and organization-specific competencies owned by other hospitals. A management contract is a looser, more temporary form of governing cooperative behavior than a multihospital system.

name: Institutional links
definition: Hospitals are linked to their institutional environments through a variety of organizational mechanisms, including industry and trade associations, regional and national lobbying groups, and other industry-wide institutional associations, which are formed around various elements of common interest.

name: Resource links
authors_terms: ["resource links", "resource exchanges", "network resource and equity flows"]
definition: Hospitals often build various types of implicit resource-based networking relationships, both vertically and horizontally, and resource exchanges may occur regardless of any formal structures governing risk and reward sharing. The authors capture the variation in network exchange activity by examining the transactional intensity of resource exchanges between hospitals that are related by ownership, key personnel, or other types of informal arrangements.

name: Service innovation adoption
definition: Following the logic in Damanpour (1991), the authors defined an innovation in health care as a medical technology, structure, administrative system, or service that is relatively new to the overall industry and newly adopted by hospitals in a particular market area. They concentrated on service innovations: innovations that incorporate changes in the technology, design, or delivery of a particular service or bundle of services.

name: Interlocking political ties
definition: Interlocking political ties (hereafter, 'political ties') arise when current senior business leaders hold or previously held senior positions in key government or political organizations (hereafter, 'government organizations' or 'governments'), or when current senior politicians or government officials hold or previously held top positions in firms.

name: Local political ties
definition: Local ties are defined as those formed at sub-national levels of government such as provinces, states, and cities. Local political ties are likely to be based on greater interdependence and closer alignment of interests than central political ties.

name: Central political ties
definition: Central ties are defined as those formed at the federal or national levels of government. Central ties will often create less interdependence, interaction and alignment of interests because of the greater breadth of administrative, economic, political, and geographic responsibilities of central authorities.

name: Firm survival
definition: We define survival as a firm continuing to operate in its industry without shutting down. Survival is a fundamental indicator of firm performance because, when firms are dissolved, their routines and resources are destroyed or dispersed, indicating substantial failure of the organization.

name: Sales growth
definition: We use sales growth, i.e., increase in revenue, as our indicator of financial performance. We used sales growth as the indicator of financial performance, which we measured as percentage change in TV sales revenue (US$ billion) each year (Sales t / Sales t - 1).

name: Prior firm performance
definition: Two variables measured firms' prior performance, firm efficiency and prior sales growth. Firms that achieve stronger performance commonly possess stronger resources and capabilities, both because stronger resources often underlie superior performance, and because strong performance tends to generate greater resources and stronger capabilities.

name: Mental model accuracy
authors_terms: ["mental model accuracy", "accuracy of decision makers' mental models", "more accurate mental models", "accuracy of mental models of the business environment"]
definition: Each participant's mental model accuracy was the percentage of items on the knowledge test answered correctly; the possible scores range from 0 to 1, where a score of 1 indicates perfect knowledge of the tested aspects of causal structure and dynamic behavior of small sets of variables in the decision environment.

name: Deep structure accuracy
authors_terms: ["mental model accuracy of the deep structure", "deep structure accuracy", "accurate mental models of key principles of the deep structure"]
definition: Eleven items from the knowledge test involving questions about inferred causal relationships and dynamic behavior of small sets of variables assess participants' knowledge of the key principles of deep structure, and each participant's mental model accuracy of the deep structure was the percentage of these eleven items answered correctly.

name: Performance
definition: We measured performance by the cumulative profit at the end of the last decision trial for each of the nine trial blocks; because the potential achievable cumulative profit was different in the high and low complexity task conditions, we divided the raw performance scores by benchmarks for the high and low conditions.

name: Decision environment complexity
authors_terms: ["task complexity", "complexity of the decision environment", "decision environment complexity"]
definition: Two levels of task complexity were associated with either a monopoly market or a competitive market. Low complexity means there are fewer determinants to consider, fewer options, and the effects of decisions are immediate and more transparent; greater complexity involves time delays, nonlinearities, feedback effects, and stock accumulation processes.

name: Apps market competition
definition: Apps market competition refers to the actual as well as the potential competition that producers of applications would face in a given platform market. Competition among video game producers will be higher in the platform console market segment that is more crowded, i.e., the one in which a larger number of producers with similar market domains are vying for consumers' attention.

name: Apps exclusivity
definition: Apps exclusivity captures the extent to which a platform's complementary products are denied to its rivals- -i.e., developed for and sold only on the focal platform. The primary objective of exclusivity is to provide users with high quality applications they will be unable to obtain on other platforms.

name: Distinctive positioning
definition: We refer to this choice as distinctive positioning to stress the strategic challenge platforms face in their pursuit of market niches: namely, selecting how similar or dissimilar a portfolio of applications should be, relative to its rivals'. This variable measures the distinctiveness of platform positioning in terms of the distance between the focal platform's composition of games by genre and that offered by rival platforms.

name: Platform performance
definition: We use market share to measure platform performance. This is an important measure of firm performance in markets subject to network effects.

name: Clique size diversity
authors_terms: ["clique size diversity", "size diversity in a clique", "diversity in member size"]
definition: The extent to which the members of a clique differ in size, where bank size is defined as the inflation-adjusted dollar value of each bank's deals in that year. The authors computed it using the coefficient of variation, which they call the standard measure of diversity for continuous variables.

name: Size distance from clique
authors_terms: ["bank size distance", "a bank's size distance from the clique average", "distance in size from other clique members"]
definition: A bank's social distance (dissimilarity) in size from the other members of its clique, computed as the difference in size between a bank and all other banks belonging to the same clique. The authors describe it as measuring how unusual each member is in relation to the group.

name: Clique cohesion
authors_terms: ["clique cohesion", "density of ties in a clique", "clique's cohesion"]
definition: The density of ties in a clique: the actual number of syndicate ties among the banks within a clique relative to the total number of possible ties among the banks. Dense cliques create more value through cooperative exchanges than less dense cliques, because interconnectedness better enables members to monitor and sanction deviant behavior.

name: Embeddedness in clique
authors_terms: ["embeddedness of a firm in a clique", "bank cohesion", "bank contacts within a clique"]
definition: A firm's embeddedness in a clique, obtained by subtracting a bank's score for clique cohesion from its density of contacts within a clique, defined as the proportion of clique members to which the bank had syndicate ties. Deeply embedded clique members can rely more on reputation effects and collective sanctioning to promote cooperation.

name: Clique role diversity
authors_terms: ["clique role diversity", "role diversity in a clique", "diversity of roles"]
definition: The diversity of roles among a clique's members, where banks can serve one of two primary functions in an underwriting syndicate, the lead or the co-lead bank role, and specialize in each of these roles to varying degrees. Functionally integrated cliques comprised of a diverse mix of banks specializing in lead and co-lead roles are expected to be more stable.

name: Role distance from clique
authors_terms: ["bank role distance", "a bank's role distance from a clique", "distance of a firm's role from the roles of other clique members"]
definition: The distance between a focal bank's role and the roles of other clique members, based on bank lead role specialization, which is a bank's number of lead manager roles divided by the total number of syndicates in which it participated in each year.

name: Clique access to structural holes
authors_terms: ["clique structural holes", "a clique's access to structural holes"]
definition: A clique's access to structural holes, computed as the average number of structural holes spanned by a clique's members. Structural holes separate nonredundant sources of information and constitute opportunities to broker the flow of information among actors and control projects that bring network participants together from opposite sides of a hole.

name: Clique structural hole inequality
authors_terms: ["clique structural hole inequality", "inequality of access to structural holes for firms in a clique"]
definition: The inequality among a clique's members in the structural holes they span, measured with the gini index, which operationally defines inequality as the average gain in network effective size an organization could get if given the choice of trading places with a randomly drawn other organization. The resulting inequality gives disadvantaged members the greatest incentive to leave the clique.

name: Bank access to structural holes
authors_terms: ["bank structural hole distance", "a firm's access to structural holes in a clique", "the number of structural holes spanned by a bank"]
definition: A bank's access to structural holes relative to other members of its clique. The authors measured each bank's structural holes using Burt's network effective size and measured bank structural hole distance by subtracting clique structural holes from a bank's own structural holes.

name: Clique exit
authors_terms: ["clique exit", "exit from cliques", "exits of members from these cliques"]
definition: A bank exiting its clique. The authors distinguish voluntary exits, in which a firm decides to leave a clique and unilaterally terminates its ties to clique members, from involuntary exits, which occur either when clique members jointly organize to oust an unwanted firm or when a firm is simply unable to attract ties from other clique members.

name: Negative media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage", "negative media reports", "negative emotional words"]
definition: Media coverage tone that reflects social expectations and external evaluations of firms; negative media coverage highlights issues, including disagreement with a firm's activities.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "strategic change initiation", "extent of strategic change"]
definition: Discrete changes in the content and scope of a firm's existing strategies in response to environmental changes; the extent of change in a firm's strategy over time.

name: Novelty-centered business model design
definition: A novelty-centered BMD aims to find and adopt new approaches to economic transactions, fostering a logic of value creation through innovation by connecting previously unconnected parties and reorganizing the links between activities or by designing new activities, enabling firms to create novel value offerings.

name: Efficiency-centered business model design
definition: The efficiency-centered BMD aims less for innovation than for emulating other firms by imitating existing BMDs, but in a more efficient way; it aims to increase the activity system's efficiency by reducing the transaction costs for their participants.

name: TMT integrative complexity
definition: Integrative complexity is comprised of evaluative differentiation, which refers to 'the capacity and willingness to tolerate different points of view,' and conceptual integration, which is defined as the ability to 'generate linkages between points of view, to understand why people look at the same event in different ways, to confront trade-offs, and to appreciate interactive patterns of causation.' On the basis of evaluative differentiation and conceptual integration, people can be described on a continuum ranging from simple (having low integrative complexity) to complex (having high integrative complexity).

name: Decentralization of decision making
definition: Centralization occurs when decision-making power resides in the hands of a select few at the upper levels of an organization, whereas decentralization occurs when decision-making power involves individuals at various organizational levels. In other words, the more centralized the firm, the less top managers have delegated decision making.

name: Corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["corporate social performance", "net CSP", "overall corporate social performance"]
definition: We define corporate social performance as a componential model incorporating principles of corporate social responsibility, processes of corporate social responsiveness, and outcomes of corporate behavior (Wood, 1991). According to stakeholder theory, a firm achieves higher corporate social performance when it meets more stakeholder needs, whereas it attains lower corporate social performance when it meets fewer stakeholder needs.

name: Link alliance
definition: Scale alliances, in which the partners contribute similar resources for the same stage or stages in the value-chain, aim at producing economies of scale for those activities that firms carry out in collaboration. Link alliances, in contrast with scale alliances, aim at combining different skills and resources from each partner.

name: Change in relative competitive position
authors_terms: ["change in relative market share", "change in relative competitive position", "absolute variation in relative market share", "dRCP3, dRCP7 and dRCP10"]
definition: dRCP3, dRCP7 and dRCP10 record the absolute variation in relative market share 3, 7 and 10 years after the alliance was formed. Interpretation of the dRCP3, dRCP7, dRCP10 variables is straightforward—they correspond to the percent growth or decline in relative market share, 3, 7, and 10 years after alliance formation.

name: Severity of financial restatement
authors_terms: ["severity of restatement", "severity of the financial restatement", "severity of the firm's restatement"]
definition: The severity of the restatement is operationalized as the total decrease in net income of the focal firm following restatement divided by the firm revenue for the year prior to the restatement announcement.

name: Prior CEO experience
authors_terms: ["prior CEO experience", "successor CEO experience", "prior experience as a chief executive", "prior experience as CEOs"]
definition: Previous CEO experience may be seen as the most concrete evidence that a designated successor has the requisite background to help the firm restore its damaged reputation, and prior experience as a chief executive is the most relevant background for an individual being chosen for that position.

name: Turnaround experience
authors_terms: ["prior turnaround experience", "successor turnaround CEO experience", "turnaround experience"]
definition: Successor CEOs' experience in turnaround situations can increase outside observers' confidence in their ability to manage the aftermath of a financial restatement and restore the past prominence of a firm.

name: Elite education
authors_terms: ["elite educational background", "successor CEO elite education", "elite education", "elite degree"]
definition: A degree from an elite institution can be an indication of ability, and since employers cannot fully understand the overall quality of job candidates an elite educational background provides a proxy signal of quality.

name: Functional experience in finance or accounting
authors_terms: ["functional experience", "Successor CEO from Fin/Acct", "prior experience in accounting or finance", "background in finance or accounting"]
definition: Firms that experience the reputation-damaging event of a financial restatement may want to emphasize a renewed focus on unbiased and accurate financial reporting and may be more likely to select successors with qualifications and prior experience in the areas of accounting and finance.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: Stock market reactions to the naming of a successor CEO represent an objective indication of the extent to which shareholders endorse or repudiate the successor's appointment.

name: Analysts' reaction
authors_terms: ["analysts' reactions", "change in analysts' forecasts", "change in annual mean forecast made by analysts"]
definition: Favorable investment analyst reactions to a succession announcement should provide an important measure of the perceived success of the firm's intention to restore its reputation.

name: Positive media coverage
definition: The variable positive coverage was equal to the mean LIWC score for the positive tenor category from all articles about a sample firm.

name: Negative media coverage
definition: Since positive and negative tenors in coverage are distinct, we treated each positive and negative tenor in each article as a separate construct, and negative coverage was measured in the same way as positive coverage but for negative tenor.

name: Core technical performance
definition: The performance of the focal technology with respect to key technical attributes; technologies within an emerging industry differ in their core technical performance.

name: Availability of complementary assets in the ecosystem
authors_terms: ["availability of complementary assets", "complementary assets", "complementary assets availability"]
definition: Availability of complementary assets refers to the fact that the key assets required for commercialization of a given technology can be easily accessed through the markets with little modification.

name: Entrant technology choice
definition: Tied to a firm's entry into an emerging industry is the important decision as to the technology with which to enter that industry; entrants pursue distinct technological alternatives at entry.

name: Entrant type
authors_terms: ["diversifying entrants", "start-up entrants", "types of entrants", "entrants' pre-entry history"]
definition: Entrants could be established firms that are diversifying from their existing industries and redeploying their capabilities into the new industry or start-ups that are founded to participate in the new industry.

name: Relatedness of pre-entry capabilities
authors_terms: ["related pre-entry capabilities", "unrelated pre-entry capabilities", "pre-entry capabilities that were related or unrelated"]
definition: Diversifying entrants differ in the degree to which their capabilities match those required for technology commercialization in the new industry; the smaller the relatedness gap between the firm's pre-entry capabilities and those required for the technology's commercialization, the lower the firm's cost to adapt and redeploy its existing capabilities.

name: Relatedness of founder experience
authors_terms: ["related founder experience", "unrelated founder experience", "founders' prior experience"]
definition: Founders of start-ups differ in the extent that their prior experience facilitates technology commercialization in the new industry.

name: ACA health insurance reform
authors_terms: ["ACA reform", "the ACA", "Affordable Care Act reform", "treatment", "guaranteed issue regulations", "modified community rating regulations"]
definition: In 2010, the ACA health insurance reforms were enacted by the US Congress and signed into law to improve health insurance access for the US population through a range of regulations; two major provisions implemented on January 1, 2014 improved access to affordable individual health insurance. Henceforth, the authors use 'ACA reform' to refer to these two 2014 provisions.

name: Gender
definition: Female is the moderating variable in triple-difference models and is a binary indicator equal to 1 for women and 0 for men. Women are also argued to have greater demands for health insurance coverage and better plans than men.

name: STEM entrepreneurship
definition: STEM Entrepreneurship is set to 1 if an individual was self-employed and declared a STEM occupational code at the time of the survey and equals 0 otherwise.

name: Non-STEM entrepreneurship
definition: An indicator for self-employed individuals with non-STEM occupational codes.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: Consistent with prior work on entrepreneurial entry, the authors characterize entrepreneurship as self-employment status; this broad definition captures a range of entrepreneurial activities, including growth-oriented startups that are well funded, sole proprietorships or necessity-driven entrepreneurship, and bootstrapped unincorporated businesses.

name: Gender gap in STEM entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["gender gap in STEM entrepreneurship", "STEM entrepreneurial gender gap"]
definition: The coefficient of interest in the triple-difference regression represents the treatment effect difference between women and men - that is, the treatment effect on the gender gap in STEM entrepreneurship; a positive estimate suggests that the ACA reform encourages more women than men to enter entrepreneurship, indicating a reduced gender gap.

name: STEM occupational field
authors_terms: ["STEM occupational code", "STEM fields", "occupational field", "STEM (vs. non-STEM) fields"]
definition: Occupational codes are based on the 2018 census STEM, STEM-related, and non-STEM-related code list derived from the 2018 Standard Occupational Classification of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

name: Individual health insurance in own name
authors_terms: ["Direct-Purchase Insurance in Own Name", "direct-purchase insurance", "individual insurance in own name"]
definition: Direct-Purchase Insurance in Own Name equals 1 for individuals who were the policyholders of their recent health insurance plan that was purchased directly as an individual insurance plan (i.e., not related to current or past employment) and 0 otherwise.

name: Interlock network centrality
authors_terms: ["network centrality", "degree centrality", "centrality within the interlock director network", "interlock network centrality"]
definition: A firm's central position within corporate interlocks, where 'a firm can both independently and directly access a large number of other firms within the network.'

name: Interlock network structural holes
definition: A firm's position as a broker between otherwise unconnected firms (alters), brokering 'between otherwise unconnected firms known as alters.'

name: CEO compensation
definition: The annual cash compensation (salary and bonuses) that CEOs received between 2001 and 2006; it does not include long-term incentive plans such as stock options, and cash compensation is argued to be the closest match to the construct 'compensation' in China.

name: Compensation committee
definition: A visible formal structure for board control that signals that a firm's corporate control of CEO compensation is scrupulous; setting up a CC that 'in theory controls CEO compensation can be used as a symbolic management tool in China.'

name: Founder-based firm-specific experience
authors_terms: ["founder-based firm-specific experience", "founders' participation in the top management team", "founder-based firm-specific managerial experience", "ratio of the founders in the top management team"]
definition: In entrepreneurial firms, tacit knowledge of a firm's original purpose and initial capabilities is retained through founders, and because of historical knowledge and power, founder-based firm-specific managerial experience constitutes the foundation of a top management team's experience-based competence. The measure serves as a proxy for the level at which experiential knowledge of the original business model and the firm's capabilities are still preserved at the top management level.

name: Shared team-specific management experience
authors_terms: ["shared team-specific experience", "team-specific management experience", "shared team-specific management experience"]
definition: Shared team-specific experience refers to managers' decision-making and implementation experience and involves managers' collective knowledge of the skills, limitations, and idiosyncratic habits of team members. Rather than generic team experience, it concerns top management team members' shared managerial experience in making and implementing strategic decisions.

name: Industry-specific management experience
definition: Industry-specific managerial experience involves knowledge of the opportunities, threats, competitive conditions, and regulations specific to an industry, as well as goodwill with particular suppliers and customers. It includes the managerial knowledge of the opportunities, threats, competition, and technologies specific to an industry.

name: Rate of entrepreneurial growth
authors_terms: ["rate of entrepreneurial growth", "rate of sales growth", "rate of growth"]
definition: Firms that are engaged in new product and capability development are considered entrepreneurial, and the rate of entrepreneurial growth is measured as the annual rate of sales growth, a critical indicator of performance for entrepreneurial firms that are in a stage of product commercialization and growth. This indicator reflects a firm's ability to increase its sales relative to its previous sales through innovative medical technology products.

name: Downsizing approach
definition: Three downsizing, or selective resource reduction, approaches are evident in the literature: retrenchment, downscaling, and downscoping. The three approaches often involve similar resource reduction tactics (plant closings, layoffs, etc.), but they ultimately differ in their effect on the volume of firm output and the firm's boundaries, represented by the variety of its activities.

name: Recent firm investment
authors_terms: ["recent firm investment in capacity or products", "extent of recent capacity investment", "extent of recent product investment"]
definition: Recent firm investments in capacity or products limit a firm's ability to partially exit; e.g., downscale or downscope. The more recently the firm has invested in resources, the less depreciated the resource base, the higher the resale price or the write-off required to effect downsizing.

name: Firm investment in jointness
authors_terms: ["recent firm investment in capacity and products", "extent of recent firm investment in jointness", "joint investment in capacity and product introductions"]
definition: When concurrent investments improve line changeover speed or assure greater reliability of the finished goods, the firm may derive firm-unique advantages. Joint investment in capacity and product introductions is likely to provide a greater return from continued operation than from sale to another firm.

name: Recent competitor investment
authors_terms: ["recent competitor investment", "extent of recent competitor capacity investment", "extent of recent competitor product investment", "extent of competitor investment in jointness"]
definition: Competitor investments in absolute cost advantages, product differentiation, and economies of scale shrink the pool of acquirers for the resources of the downsizing firm. Competitors' investments also signal their belief in continued market viability.

name: Industry demand change
authors_terms: ["demand change", "change in industry demand", "declining industry demand"]
definition: When competitors investment slows or demand declines, some managers may decide to cash out resources early before competitors' unwanted resources depress salvage prices. Demand change was measured as a lagged 5-year average of annual demand changes in industry unit shipments of wheeled tractors (the dominant industry product).

name: Domain breadth
definition: One important business strategy component that influences a firm's resource investments and potentially influences its choice of downsizing approach is its domain breadth. Firms characterize themselves and their competitors as 'full-line' (broad) or 'short-line' (focused) manufacturers.

name: Nonredundancy in the advice network
definition: We define nonredundancy as the extent to which the contacts in a focal firm's advice network are not linked to one another.

name: Infrequency of interaction
definition: Infrequency of interaction refers to the rarity of interaction with the contacts in a firm's advice network; the variable measures the rarity of interaction with advisors in terms of the number of conversations per month.

name: Geographic dispersion in the advice network
definition: Geographic dispersion in the advice network is a proxy for face-to-face interaction among advisors. In our view, a dispersed advice network is comprised of contacts located far enough apart spatially to impede routine face-to-face interaction.

name: Participation in regional institutions
definition: This construct indicated the extent to which a firm used the services available from a regional industrial extension center. Participation in a regional institution is not a discrete event, but rather represents an ongoing opportunity for a small manufacturer to access information and ideas.

name: Acquisition of competitive capabilities
definition: 'Acquisition of competitive capabilities' refers to the process through which firms discover, internalize, and exploit industry-specific practices, methods, and techniques for achieving competitive advantage. We define competitive capabilities, following Amit and Schoemaker, as 'a firm's capacity to deploy resources ... using organizational processes' to achieve a strategic objective.

name: Experience depth
definition: Experience depth captures repeated, similar experiences over time and develops specialized knowledge that is mostly applicable to one niche only (i.e., non-fungible). Depth captures classic learning-by-doing, which leads to the ability to excel at doing the same task repeatedly.

name: Experience breadth
definition: Experience breadth captures experience across niches but within a single industry. Firms with greater breadth both have more experience with entering new niches over time, and have most likely structured their operations such that they share generalized resources and capabilities across niches.

name: New product performance
definition: Since the data are organized with one observation for each new game, the authors use revenue (in constant 1995 dollars) to measure performance. They focus on the total sales of a title released on a platform in its first 12 months post-release.

name: Technological transition
definition: Following Lawless and Anderson, the authors define a generational change as 'a major advance within a technology regime'; the most central aspects of generational changes are that they are discrete, happening quickly and being followed by a period of technological stability, and that they happen repeatedly over the lifecycle of the industry. The transition period covers the year of the first console's release in a new generation through the end of the year of the last console's release for that generation.

name: Industry evolution
definition: The evolution of industries is associated with a fundamental shift over time in the sources of learning and knowledge that drive innovative activity and performance; early in an industry's evolution an entrepreneurial regime drives innovation, and as the industry evolves uncertainty is reduced and innovation becomes more routinized and increasingly cumulative.

name: Income poverty
