definition: The greater the number of individuals who live in poverty, the greater the need for small loans; the level of income poverty in a country is argued to drive demand for microfinance.

name: State fragility
definition: State fragility is the degree to which 'state power is unable and/or unwilling to deliver core functions to the majority of its people: security, protection of property, basic public services, and essential infrastructure' (Engberg-Pedersen, Andersen, and Jung, 2008: 22). All states are fragile to a greater or lesser degree, allowing for a gradual transition from one type to another.

name: Commercial microfinance borrower growth
authors_terms: ["growth in commercial microfinance borrowers per capita", "commercial microfinance borrowers per thousand citizens", "growth of commercial microfinance", "grow its client base"]
definition: The number of borrowers registered to all commercial microfinance lenders in a particular country divided by the total population of that country, calculated for each country every year.

name: Commercial share of microfinance borrowers
authors_terms: ["relative growth in commercial, rather than nonprofit, microfinance borrowers", "proportion of all microfinance borrowers", "proportion for-profit"]
definition: The proportion of all microfinance borrowers in a particular country that are registered to for-profit lenders, calculated for each country every year.

name: Operating costs per loan
authors_terms: ["operating costs per loan", "total operating costs", "cost per loan"]
definition: The total operating costs a commercial microfinance lender incurs to make a single loan.

name: Commercial capital investment
authors_terms: ["commercial funding for the microfinance business model", "commercial investment", "flows of commercial capital into microfinance", "commercial capital"]
definition: Total capital invested into each country's microfinance sector that came from 'commercial' funders, defined as any organizations that MIX labels 'financial institutions' or 'funds'.

name: Pre-transition revolving door
authors_terms: ["revolving door pre-transition", "pre-transition revolving doors", "revolving door to in-house lobbying observed pre-transition", "revolving door to contract lobbying observed pre-transition"]
definition: Crucially, for both the pre-transition revolving door types, the regulator is still with the USDA and about to revolve out to a private sector role in a later period. As such, these two variables capture any potential skewing of regulatory outcomes because of the fact that regulators are looking to transition to corporate roles, either with the GE producers or with their retained lobbying firms.

name: Post-transition revolving door
authors_terms: ["revolving door post-transition", "revolving door to in-house lobbying observed post-transition", "revolving door to contract lobbying observed post-transition"]
definition: The revolving door to in-house lobbying observed post-transition takes the value of one for GE crop producers that have a former USDA regulator on their staff and zero otherwise. The revolving door to contract lobbying observed post-transition measures one if the focal firm has retained as their lobbyist at least one former USDA regulator and zero otherwise.

name: Regulatory approval speed
authors_terms: ["regulatory outcomes", "regulatory performance", "speed of regulatory approval", "time to regulatory approval", "regulatory process duration"]
definition: Our dependent variable is a measure of regulatory outcomes for GE crops. In terms of regulatory outcomes, two things matter to firms: gaining approval for their products and the speed of doing so.

name: Cognitive diversity
authors_terms: ["cognitive diversity", "overall cognitive diversity", "cognitive diversity among upper-echelon executives"]
definition: Cognitive diversity is defined in terms of differences in beliefs and preferences held by upper-echelon executives within a firm. More specifically, it refers to variation in beliefs concerning cause-effect relationships and variation in preferences concerning various goals for the organization.

name: Preference diversity
authors_terms: ["preference diversity", "diversity among executives concerning preferred goals for the firm"]
definition: Preference diversity is diversity among executives concerning preferred goals for the firm; it is one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity.

name: Belief diversity
authors_terms: ["belief diversity", "cause-effect belief diversity", "diversity among executives concerning the nature of cause-effect relationships"]
definition: Belief diversity is diversity among executives concerning the nature of cause-effect relationships; it is one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity.

name: Comprehensiveness of strategic decision-making
authors_terms: ["comprehensiveness", "comprehensiveness of strategic decision processes", "comprehensiveness of strategic decision-making"]
definition: Comprehensiveness is defined as the extent to which an upper-echelon executive group utilizes an extensive decision process when dealing with immediate opportunities and threats; it pertains to the absolute amount of investigatory activity rather than investigatory completeness per se.

name: Extensiveness of strategic planning
definition: Extensiveness of strategic planning is defined as the extent to which an upper-echelon executive group utilizes a substantial planning process to formulate long-term goals and strategies for the firm; it pertains to the absolute amount of activity rather than completeness per se.

name: Market-supporting institutions
definition: Institutions have an essential role in a market economy to support the effective functioning of the market mechanism, such that firms and individuals can engage in market transactions without incurring undue costs or risks. Institutional arrangements are considered 'strong' if they support the voluntary exchange underpinning an effective market mechanism, and 'weak' if they fail to ensure effective markets or even undermine markets.

name: Joint venture entry
definition: JVs and acquisitions both provide access to resources held by local firms, with JVs partially integrating selected local resources from a local partner. Foreign entrants in need of local resources may prefer the creation of a new entity in partnership with a local firm, with both partners contributing selected resources and sharing control.

name: Acquisition entry
definition: Acquisitions provide access to resources held by local firms by integrating the local firm in toto. Entry by acquisition is an entry mode that is particularly sensitive to the efficiency of markets, especially financial markets and the market for corporate control.

name: Greenfield entry
definition: A greenfield project does not directly access a local firm as a bundle of organizational resources, but allows the entrant to buy or contract for resource components available on local markets, such as real estate and labor.

name: Need for local resources
authors_terms: ["need to rely on local resources", "local resources required", "resource needs", "context-specific resources"]
definition: In emerging economies, investing firms usually require context-specific resources to achieve competitive advantages, such as networks and relationships with other firms, with agents in the distribution channels and with government authorities, and context-specific capabilities such as strategic and organizational flexibility. Foreign entrants that consider local resources to be important for their competitiveness may prefer to establish their operation with a local partner as a JV or through acquisition as opposed to greenfield.

name: Need for local intangible resources
authors_terms: ["intangible assets", "intangible resources", "intangible index", "need for intangible resources"]
definition: Local resources such as brands, business networks, distribution networks, managerial, innovation and marketing capabilities, networks with authorities, technological know-how and trade contacts. Information asymmetries, asset specificity and the costs of tacit knowledge are more relevant for intangible assets than for tangible assets, making them less suitable to market exchange.

name: Need for local tangible resources
authors_terms: ["tangible assets", "tangible resources", "tangible index", "need for local tangible resources"]
definition: Local resources such as buildings and real estate, equity, loans, machinery and equipment, patents, sales outlets and licenses, which can be acquired or accessed using market transactions more readily than intangible assets.

name: Price format
authors_terms: ["price format", "closed price", "closed-price format", "open price", "open-price format", "price terms"]
definition: At the contracting stage, M and S contractually agree on the governance - in our case, the price format - for the component being procured: they either specify the component's price upfront (a closed-price format) or agree to negotiate it ex post (an open-price format). Closed-price formats preclude renegotiation and hence pre-determine the division of trade surplus over the contract period, whereas under open-price formats the distribution of trade surplus is determined ex post.

name: Supplier's specific investment
definition: S can customize the component by making a relationship-specific investment - that is, undertaking effort to understand M's specific design, technology, and customer needs, and to produce the component accordingly. The measure denotes a broad spectrum of tangible and intangible investments undertaken by the supplier in resources, efforts, and training.

name: Importance of adaptation
definition: Measured by Interface complexity, which rates the complexity of the interface between the component and the end product; the more complex the interface among components, the more difficult it is to pre-specify all the architectural and technical interactions among them, so that when random events require the OEM to modify parts of such a complex system the focal supplier must also engage in unscheduled adaptation of its own component. Interface complexity is viewed as an exogenous feature of the buyer–supplier relationship.

name: Value of OEM's preexisting resources
authors_terms: ["value of M's preexisting resources", "OEM's preexisting resources", "OEM product strength", "preexisting resources"]
definition: The value of M's preexisting resources, ω, can be considered as an index of the OEM's differentiation in its end-product market at the time of contracting, which is independent of the relationship between M and S. It is measured by how strong the OEM's product is in terms of price premium, customer perception, and its competitive advantage compared to competitors' products, and hence constitutes a measure of the OEM's underlying preexisting resources and capabilities that a supplier may potentially appropriate.

name: Value add to the OEM's end product
authors_terms: ["value add", "value add to OEM's end product", "End-product enhancement"]
definition: The value add generated in the relationship, measured by the extent to which the procured component has helped to enhance the OEM's end-product performance and capture design and engineering synergies.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: CSR refers to firm activities 'that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law' (McWilliams and Siegel 2001, p. 117).

name: Newspaper conservatism
definition: The ideological leaning of a news organization toward conservatism, captured by the newspaper's endorsement of a Republican presidential candidate; such endorsements are made in an editorial by the newspaper's editorial board, which takes a clear position in favor of one presidential candidate over another.

name: CEO conservatism
definition: The ideological preferences of a firm's chief executive officer, proxied by individual political donations: 'the higher the CF score, the stronger the individual's conservatism' (Bonica 2014, 2016).

name: Stock market performance
authors_terms: ["stock market performance", "poor stock market performance", "strong stock market performance"]
definition: The economic returns a firm generates for its shareholders, as reflected in its stock market performance; conservatives are more likely to be concerned about the CSR activities of firms that fail to generate such returns.

name: Positive tone of news media coverage
authors_terms: ["positive tone of a firm's news media coverage", "positive tone", "news media coverage of firms"]
definition: The dependent variable is the positive tone of a firm's news media coverage, which the authors constructed by using the Loughran and McDonald (2011, 2014, 2016) dictionary.

name: Choice of status bracket
authors_terms: ["choice of status bracket", "choice of Big 4 auditor", "use of high-status auditors"]
definition: The choice of an auditor can be analyzed as a staged process in which firms first choose a particular status bracket and then decide which auditor to use within that bracket. We argue specifically that the accountability of a firm to external audiences affects the choice of auditor status bracket.

name: Choice of firm within status bracket
authors_terms: ["choice of firm within status bracket", "choice of auditor within a particular status bracket", "choice of a particular Big 4 auditor"]
definition: The choice of a partner within a status bracket requires a more detailed analysis of the specific resources provided by each potential partner and how well they match each firm's specific resource needs. Reputation allows assessment of the perceived quality of the individual attributes of firms within the same status bracket.

name: Accountability to institutional investors
authors_terms: ["accountability to institutional investors", "public pension fund ownership"]
definition: Accountability links individual actors to the social systems to which they are accountable by demanding that they explain and justify their decisions and behaviors to other actors. Firms that are more accountable to activist institutional investors, such as public pension funds, therefore have a greater incentive to promote trust in their financial statements.

name: Accountability to security analysts
authors_terms: ["accountability to security analysts", "security analyst coverage", "analyst coverage"]
definition: Security analysts act as information intermediaries between publicly traded firms and investors by eliciting information from management about corporate strategy and performance prospects. Firms that are covered by numerous security analysts therefore have a strong incentive to provide credible financial statements.

name: Accountability to major stock exchanges
authors_terms: ["accountability to major stock exchanges", "major stock exchange listing"]
definition: Some firms are traded on stock exchanges that have stricter regulations than other exchanges, and the comparative strictness of their governance requirements increased firms' incentive to use high-status auditors whose quality and independence were easy to justify. Listings on major stock exchanges also imply membership in an elite group of firms, which creates another incentive for choosing high-status auditors.

name: Auditor industry specialization
definition: An auditor acquires industry specialization by focusing on auditing firms within a few similar industries rather than spreading itself over many different ones, which enables it to develop industry-specific expertise and spread its training costs over more clients to achieve economies of scale.

name: Media coverage of audit failures
authors_terms: ["media coverage of an auditor's involvement in audit failures", "national audit failures", "local audit failures"]
definition: We argue therefore that media coverage of involvement in audit failures contributes to creating a negative reputation for business integrity for an auditor, thereby reducing the likelihood that other firms use the auditor. An audit failure is defined as the certification by an auditor of a financial statement with material omissions and/or misstatements.

name: Value creation for the high-q partner
authors_terms: ["value derived by the high Tobin's q firm", "HIVALUE", "value created for the HI group"]
definition: Value derived by the high Tobin's q firm (i.e., Tobin's q > partner's Tobin's q) over the [ - 1,0] period.

name: Value creation for the low-q partner
authors_terms: ["value derived by the low Tobin's q firm", "LOVALUE", "value created for the LO group"]
definition: Value derived by the low Tobin's q firm (i.e., Tobin's q < partner's Tobin's q) over the [ - 1,0] period.

name: Resource strength
authors_terms: ["strength of the resources", "strong resources", "Tobin's q", "value of the intangible resources"]
definition: Tobin's q is a measure of the value of the intangible resources possessed by a firm. The higher the Tobin's q, the higher the value of intangible resources.

name: Product market competition between partners
authors_terms: ["product market competition", "direct competitors", "closely related businesses", "degree of competition"]
definition: The extent of product market competition between firms in the dyad; JVs between relatively direct competitors show high incentives and ability to appropriate resources. The closer the SIC codes and the distance between the two partners, the more likely they will be direct competitors.

name: JV experience
authors_terms: ["JV experience", "prior experience with interfirm collaboration", "experience with JVs"]
definition: Another factor that may influence the behavior of firms within a JV is their prior experience with interfirm collaboration. Firms with experience in operating JVs are more likely to recognize the importance of devoting efforts toward common benefits and cooperative behavior in sustaining a mutually beneficial relationship from the outset.

name: Violent conflict
authors_terms: ["violent conflict", "incidents of violent conflicts", "violent conflict risk", "conflict incidents"]
definition: Violent conflict is defined here as the organized and sustained use of physical force that results in injury or death to persons and/or damage or destruction to property. It may include war, revolution, rebellion, insurgency, and sustained campaigns of violence or terrorism, but not petty crime.

name: Corporate-level experience
authors_terms: ["corporate-level experience", "corporate-level experience in violent conflict", "corporate-level knowledge"]
definition: Corporate-level experience is defined here as an MNC's experience across any of its wholly owned subsidiaries. For the purpose of our study it refers specifically to experience operating in countries where specific types of violent conflicts occurred.

name: Country-specific experience
authors_terms: ["country-specific experience", "country-specific experience with violent conflict", "country-specific knowledge"]
definition: Country-specific experience is defined here as MNC experience with specific types of violent conflicts in a particular host country.

name: Subsidiary-level investment
authors_terms: ["subsidiary-level investment", "subsidiary investment", "expansion", "number of wholly owned subsidiaries"]
definition: To measure MNC investments in a host country at the subsidiary-level we use the number of wholly owned subsidiaries hand-collected from annual reports of each sample firm. This figure is valuable because the establishment of a wholly owned subsidiary brings substantial responsibility, commitment, and higher risks to the MNC's headquarters.

name: Vertical integration into the old technology
authors_terms: ["vertical integration into CISC", "vertically integrated into the old technology", "vertically integrated into CISC technology"]
definition: A focal firm's having designed and produced a major component internally under the pre-existing technology, rather than obtaining it through arm's-length market transactions. The variable, vertical integration into CISC, designates whether or not a RISC workstation maker had been vertically integrated into designing CISC processors for workstations prior to its use of RISC.

name: Vertical integration into the new technology
authors_terms: ["vertical integration into RISC", "vertically integrated into the new technology"]
definition: A focal firm's designing and producing a major component internally under the technology that is new after the technological change, rather than obtaining it through arm's-length market transactions. Vertical integration into RISC designates whether or not a RISC workstation maker was vertically integrated into designing RISC processors.

name: Workstation development performance
authors_terms: ["performance of workstation makers in developing RISC workstations", "technical performance", "price-performance", "revenue market share"]
definition: The performance of workstation makers in developing RISC workstations, measured as the technical performance of the resulting workstation, the performance-to-price ratio of the workstation, and the revenue market share of the workstation maker.

name: Incumbent status
definition: An incumbent was a firm that developed and marketed CISC workstations before adopting RISC technology, and a new entrant was a firm that entered the workstation subfield using RISC technology.

name: Density between internal-local and internal-global ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the internal-local contacts and the internal-global contacts", "density between internal-local and internal-global ties", "density internal-local to internal-global"]
definition: The density of connections between the partner's colleagues in the local environment and those outside the local environment, calculated in the same way as the density within the categories of ties except that the total number of possible ties between the two groups is the multiplication of the number of nodes in each group.

name: Density between external-local and external-global ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the external-local contacts and the external-global contacts", "density between external-local and external-global ties"]
definition: The density of connections between a partner's local client contacts and client contacts outside the local environment, calculated like the other between-category densities.

name: Density between internal-local and external-local ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the internal-local contacts and the external-local contacts", "density internal-local to external-local"]
definition: The density of connections between the partner's colleagues in the local environment and contacts outside the firm in the same local environment.

name: Density between internal-global and external-local ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the internal-global contacts and the external-local contacts", "density internal-global to external-local"]
definition: The density of connections between the partner's colleagues outside the local environment and contacts outside the firm in the local environment.

name: Density between internal-local and external-global ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the internal-local contacts and the external-global contacts", "density internal-local to external-global"]
definition: The density of connections between the partner's colleagues in the local environment and client contacts outside the local environment.

name: Density between internal-global and external-global ties
authors_terms: ["density of connections between the internal-global contacts and the external-global contacts", "density internal-global to external-global"]
definition: The density of connections between the partner's colleagues outside the local environment and client contacts outside the local environment.

name: Innovation performance
definition: The dependent variable, innovation performance, was calculated by combining two measures from the performance evaluation survey: the partners' contribution to the firm in terms of new knowledge, and their ability to create new knowledge and expertise.

name: Large-firm employment
authors_terms: ["large-firm employment", "employment in large firms", "workers employed by large firms"]
definition: In the analyses we used as our measure of large-firm employment the log value of the number of workers in each state employed by firms with 10,000 or more workers nationally.

name: State income inequality
definition: The measure of income inequality used in this study is the Gini coefficient, which measures the extent to which the distribution of income deviates from a perfectly equal distribution.

name: Large-firm racial diversity
definition: Our examination of racial diversity's effect on the relationship between large-firm employment and income inequality is based on the conceptualization of diversity as ''variety'' (Harrison and Klein, 2007), with specific interest in the distribution of employees across distinct racial categories within firms.

name: Large-firm establishment dispersion
definition: One proxy for the physical and informational distance between workers in a firm is the extent to which large-firm employment is spread out across a larger number of establishments-that is, separate locations where the firm's business is conducted.

name: Acquiring platform market share
authors_terms: ["Rover's market share", "Rover market share", "market shares", "platform α's premerger market share", "n α"]
definition: Market shares are measured in terms of gross transaction volume (GTV, or the total amount paid by buyers for platform and seller revenues). The Rover market share in a zip code is defined using GTV, equal to Rover GTV divided by the sum of Rover and DogVacay GTV.

name: Buyer utility
authors_terms: ["buyers' utility", "buyer outcomes", "benefits of the merger", "consumer welfare"]
definition: The change in buyers' utility from the merger is proxied by outcomes such as match rates and the total number of transactions; the authors use outcomes that proxy for a buyer's utility: match rates, computed as the number of successful transactions in a given month and zip code divided by the number of posted requests, and total number of transactions in a month and zip code.

name: Platform differentiation
definition: The degree to which competing platforms differ in the ways buyers care about, so that removing the acquired platform reduces platform differentiation; the reduction in platform differentiation only negatively impacts switchers, and the authors attribute any difference in outcomes between Rover and DogVacay buyers in these symmetric markets to it.

name: Acquired platform buyer
definition: Buyers who, in the prior calendar year, had only engaged in booking inquiries on DogVacay, the acquired platform; in the model, switchers are buyers who migrate from platform β to α.

name: Multihoming
authors_terms: ["multihoming", "multihoming users", "propensity of users to join multiple platforms"]
definition: The propensity of users to join multiple platforms. The authors define a user as multihoming if they transact at least once on both platforms over the five years before the acquisition.

name: Technological similarity
authors_terms: ["technological similarity", "technological proximity", "Outsider - target TechProx", "text similarity in firms' patent portfolios"]
definition: TechProx is the text similarity between the patent portfolios of two firms in the year before the acquisition announcement. The key independent variable is the technological proximity between the outsider and the target company (Outsider - target TechProx), measured with the text similarity in firms' patent portfolios.

name: Abnormal returns
definition: For each outsider and acquisition announcement, I measure the cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) on the outsider's stock over a 5-day window centered on the acquisition announcement date (Brown & Warner, 1985). Abnormal returns are calculated as the residuals of a market model estimated over a period of 250 trading days ending 42 trading days before the deal announcement.

name: Industry effects
definition: Previous studies generally have found that the business unit explains roughly 32 to 44 percent of the variance in performance, the corporation explains two to 18 percent, and the industry explains four to 19 percent.

name: Corporate parent effects
authors_terms: ["corporate parent effects", "corporate parent level", "corporate effects", "corporation explains"]
definition: Previous studies generally have found that the business unit explains roughly 32 to 44 percent of the variance in performance, the corporation explains two to 18 percent, and the industry explains four to 19 percent.

name: Business-unit effects
authors_terms: ["business-unit effects", "business unit level", "business-unit effect", "business unit explains"]
definition: Previous studies generally have found that the business unit explains roughly 32 to 44 percent of the variance in performance, the corporation explains two to 18 percent, and the industry explains four to 19 percent.

name: Industry life cycle stage
authors_terms: ["industry life cycle", "life cycle stage", "growth, maturity, and decline"]
definition: Investigations of the industry life cycle often examine three main stages: growth, maturity, and decline (Miles et al., 1993).

name: Firm performance
definition: ROA is the most widely used metric of accounting profitability and the most common performance variable in variance decomposition studies (McGahan and Porter, 2002). ROA is obtained by dividing operating income by total assets.

name: Corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["corporate social performance", "CSP", "net KLD score", "social performance", "social responsibility"]
definition: CSP is a comprehensive concept, consisting of a variety of socially responsible behaviors (Carroll, 1979). KLD rates firms based on 13 individual social performance criteria, seven of which are key stakeholder attributes for which firms receive scores based on both their strengths and weaknesses, and six of which relate to whether or not the firm participates in socially 'controversial' business activities.

name: Corporate financial performance
definition: We test for the effects of CSP on CFP. Thus, following Waddock and Graves (1997), our dependent variable is the return on assets (ROA) for a given firm in a given year.

name: Stakeholder influence capacity
definition: Barnett (2007: 803) developed the concept of SIC, which he defined as 'the ability of a firm to identify, act on, and profit from opportunities to improve stakeholder relationships through CSR [corporate social responsibility].' Simply, SIC is a formalization of the basic logic that stakeholders view some firms as more credible than others and reward firms for their acts of social responsibility accordingly.

name: Strong indirect tie
definition: An indirect tie between an investor and a focal firm is a strong indirect tie when the investor was a limited partner (LP) of the focal firm's lead venture capital fund prior to the focal firm's IPO; such a tie is conducive to the transfer of private information.

name: Risk-adjusted return
definition: The event-time three-month holding risk-adjusted excess return to the focal firm's stock, where the investment period starts at the end of the calendar quarter of the focal firm's IPO date. Risk-adjusted return is the return above the expected return from an investment based on the investment's loadings on various risk factors.

name: Exogenous market uncertainty
authors_terms: ["exogenous market uncertainty", "exogenous market-level uncertainty", "market uncertainty", "exogenous uncertainty"]
definition: Uncertainty is the difficulty firms have in predicting the future, which comes from incomplete knowledge. Exogenous market-level uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be controlled by an economic actor; in this context it means lower precision in estimating the future fundamentals of companies and the associated future cash flows.

name: Information asymmetry
definition: Imperfect information about a particular focal firm can create substantial uncertainty in assessing its true value. The magnitude of both underpricing and overpricing might be higher when there is higher information asymmetry about the underlying value of a focal firm's stock.

name: Perceived strategic uncertainty
definition: Perceived environmental uncertainty is the absence of information about organizations, activities and events in the environment; it is the difference between available information and derived information. Uncertainty and importance together create what is defined as 'strategic uncertainty' for top managers.

name: Task environment sector
authors_terms: ["task environment", "sectors in the task environment", "task versus general environment"]
definition: The layer closest to the organization is the task environment which includes sectors that have direct transactions with the organization. The outer layer is called the general environment and refers to sectors that affect organizations indirectly.

name: Scanning frequency
definition: Research into manager scanning behavior suggests that frequency of scanning indicates amount of information obtained about the environment.

name: Personal information sources
definition: Personal sources refer to direct human contact as typified by face-to-face and telephone media.

name: Impersonal information sources
definition: Impersonal sources are written, analogous to the human versus documentary sources described by Kefalas and Schoderbek (1973).

name: External information sources
definition: External sources include personal tours, telephone discussions with peers in other companies, trade magazines, newspapers, information services, and attendance at association meetings.

name: Internal information sources
definition: Internal information pertains to data, reports, memos, or discussions with internal managers and employees about the external environment.

name: Company performance
definition: ROA = net income after taxes divided by total assets. ROA was averaged for three years, 1981 through 1983, to decrease the chance of a one-year aberration influencing results.

name: Social interaction
authors_terms: ["social interaction", "socially interactive collaboration", "social interaction between the partner firm and Lilly"]
definition: The level of social interaction between the expert alliance partner and the relative novice partner. More frequent and intense interaction builds trust and increases the flow of tacit information, and is also indicative of the novice firm's real time practice of collaboration within the alliance.

name: Internal collaboration
authors_terms: ["internal collaboration", "collaboration among the novice's internal scientists", "intraorganizational collaborative innovation", "intrafirm collaboration"]
definition: Collaboration among a firm's own internal scientists, observed as collaboration ties between the firm's inventors on its patent applications.

name: Building on partner technologies
authors_terms: ["backward citations of Lilly patents", "backward citation of Lilly patents", "building on Lilly technologies"]
definition: The extent to which a partner firm's post-alliance patent cites Lilly patents; inventors working on patents that cited Lilly patents were reasoned to be more likely to be directly involved in the Lilly alliance.

name: CEO political liberalism
authors_terms: ["political liberalism", "CEO political liberalism", "political ideology", "political conservatism vs. liberalism", "liberals", "conservatives"]
definition: CEOs' political ideologies are viewed as relatively stable and enduring personal inclinations, borne in the conservatism-liberalism dimension, that enter into their managerial actions. The authors characterize liberals as those who seek to advance social justice, economic equality, planned social change and controls over markets, whereas conservatives value individualism, property rights and free markets.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "advances in CSR", "CSR profile", "net CSR score"]
definition: Defined as ''actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law'' (McWilliams and Siegel, 2001: 117), CSR is an umbrella rubric for a variety of organizational practices that are intended to serve stakeholders beyond the firm's owners, including employees, customers, communities, and society at large. Scholars generally emphasize that managerial actions must be voluntary in order to be thought of as CSR.

name: CEO power relative to the board
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "CEO's power relative to the board", "CEO power index"]
definition: CEOs differ in their amounts of financial ownership of their firms relative to outside directors, which confers formal voting power as well as legitimacy; they differ in their structural power, as some serve as their companies' board chairs but others do not; and they differ in the degree to which their boards are vigilant and independent. This stream of literature suggests that CEOs' power will influence the degree to which their inclinations are reflected in a firm's decisions.

name: Recent financial performance
authors_terms: ["recent performance", "recent financial performance", "industry-adjusted MTB", "market-to-book value of common equity"]
definition: Prior research has reported a positive relationship between a company's recent financial performance and subsequent CSR initiatives, suggesting that companies tend to emphasize CSR to the extent they can financially afford to do so. The authors measure it as the market-to-book value of common equity minus the mean MTB for the industry.

name: Control provisions in a contract
authors_terms: ["control provisions", "control-oriented provisions", "control-related clauses", "the control function of contracts"]
definition: Provisions aimed primarily at exerting control, that is, at protecting a party against exploitation by a partner; the measure is defined as the number of control-related clauses in a contract.

name: Coordination provisions in a contract
authors_terms: ["coordination provisions", "coordination-oriented provisions", "coordination-related clauses", "the coordination function of contracts"]
definition: Coordination-oriented provisions in a contract are aimed at mitigating the risk that misunderstandings will disrupt collaboration among (presumably) well-intentioned parties; the measure is defined as the number of coordination-related clauses in a contract.

name: Goodwill-based trust
authors_terms: ["goodwill-based trust", "goodwill dimension of trust judgments", "perceptions of goodwill"]
definition: Perceptions of goodwill entail attributions regarding the intention of another party to behave in a trustworthy manner.

name: Competence-based trust
authors_terms: ["competence-based trust", "competence dimension of trust judgments", "perceptions of competence"]
definition: Perceptions of competence entail attributions regarding the other party's ability to behave or perform as expected.

name: Intent to continue the relationship
authors_terms: ["intent to continue", "willingness to continue the relationship", "continued collaboration", "relationship continuance"]
definition: We analyzed the intent of parties to continue a relationship after a dispute had been resolved; this measure provides a more direct measure of the consequences of trust than would be provided by some (eventual) financial measure of performance.

name: Transaction misalignment
definition: We measure a firm as 'misaligned' if it tends to produce standard engine types itself, and/or to source unique engine types from outside suppliers. By contrast, firms are 'aligned' if they tend to produce unique engines themselves, and/or to source standardized engines from outside suppliers.

name: Firm mortality
definition: The dependent variable we study is firm survival, measured by the instantaneous rate of firm failure.

name: Shakeout stage
definition: With the emergence of a dominant design, organizational mortality therefore increases, causing a net decline in the number of firms in the industry. The authors identify 1923 as marking both the emergence of the dominant design and the initiation of the final industry shakeout.

name: Firm size
definition: We also included the log of firm size (FIRM SIZE) measured by sales as an explanatory variable. In Klepper's model, larger firm size is associated with superior internal production capabilities.

name: Engine uniqueness
definition: Engine uniqueness is thus our proxy for asset specificity. Our assumption is that unique engines tend to require more transaction-specific investment on the part of the firm manufacturing the engine.

name: Technical exchanges
authors_terms: ["technical exchanges", "technical exchange", "technical communications", "exchanges of technical knowledge", "simple technical exchanges"]
definition: Small-scale exchanges of technical information between the buyer and the supplier, arising from ongoing mutual adjustment of their design and production operations. Technical communications pertain to the relatively narrow and simple informational resources necessary to handle engineering issues case by case.

name: Technology transfer
authors_terms: ["technology transfer", "transfer of higher-level technological capabilities", "higher-level technology transfer"]
definition: Scenarios where firms transfer, share, and/or deploy technology on their partner's behalf; it refers to concerted projects that allow one partner to access or replicate complete technological capabilities of the other partner, and involves higher-level, more complex knowledge than simple technical exchanges.

name: Link duration
authors_terms: ["link duration", "prior duration of a buyer-supplier relationship", "duration of the buyer-supplier link", "relationship duration"]
definition: The prior duration of a buyer-supplier relationship, i.e. the fact that the two firms have been doing business continuously for a given period of time. Link duration measures the amount of experience that the supplier and the buyer have in dealing with each other, the resulting routines being described as relation-specific assets.

name: Supplier performance improvement
authors_terms: ["supplier performance improvement", "a supplier's operational performance", "performance improvement"]
definition: The improvement in a supplier's operational performance over the last 2-3 years, where operational performance refers to the combination of product development efficiency, process improvements, quality conformity, and short lead time.

name: Focal individual's incentive change
authors_terms: ["focal individual's incentives change", "focal MD's incentives change", "a focal individual's incentives changing from pay-for-performance to fixed salary"]
definition: A focal individual's own incentives changing from pay-for-performance to fixed salary, that is, a change in A's compensation arising because A's own incentive contract changes.

name: Team incentive change
authors_terms: ["team's incentives change", "change in coworkers' incentives", "proportion of team members that have been changed from pay-for-performance to fixed salary"]
definition: The proportion of team members (in percentage terms) that have been changed from pay-for-performance to fixed salary; when all team members are still under the pay-for-performance system the variable takes a value 0, and when all team members are switched to fixed salary it takes a value of 100.

name: Production efforts
definition: In our empirical setting, production efforts refer to the sourcing of MDs' own suppliers and executing their own deals.

name: Outgoing collaboration
definition: Outgoing collaboration refers to sharing suppliers with peers so that peers could utilize those suppliers to perform better.

name: Incoming collaboration
authors_terms: ["incoming collaboration", "being helped by others", "collaboration received from coworkers"]
definition: The mirror image of outgoing collaboration is peers' effort toward helping the focal MD, or incoming collaboration.

name: Performer status relative to team
definition: Individuals whose productivity (measured by average revenue per day) before the change was higher than the average productivity of all team members, and those whose productivity before the change was lower than the average productivity of all team members.

name: Lead user attributes
definition: Lead users are individuals whose goal fulfillment is hampered by technological performance bottlenecks and who therefore expect significant benefits from technological advances in a given solution domain.

name: Technological probing
definition: Communication among users in online communities is organized around discussion 'threads': users open new discussion threads to signal and frame a new issue, problem, call for advice, or area of exploration. We characterize this activity as technological probing.

name: Community attention
definition: Attention signals that the individual's actions resonate with others in his/her user community and provides proof of widely experienced needs and emotional commitment to the eventual outcome, increasing individual's confidence that others will commit to a particular solution.

name: Community spanning
definition: We propose that community spanning, defined as participation in several communities, helps reduce market uncertainty and thus lower the threshold for entrepreneurial action.

name: Opportunity evaluation
definition: 'Opportunity evaluation' refers to his/her action of evaluating whether third-person opportunities represent feasible and desirable first-person opportunities for entrepreneurial action. We operationalize opportunity evaluation as business planning.

name: Entrepreneurial action
definition: We operationalize opportunity evaluation as business planning and entrepreneurial action as specific venture organizing and operating activities.

name: Largest institutional owner stake
authors_terms: ["largest institutional owner", "percentage of shares held by the largest institutional investor", "largest (blockholding) institutional investor"]
definition: The percentage of a firm's outstanding shares held by its single largest institutional owner. The authors argue that the largest institutional owner receives different treatment from management because of its financial commitment and 'may have access to superior information, as well as the greatest incentive to use it to trade profitably.'

name: Aggregate stake of other institutional owners
authors_terms: ["% held by all other institutions", "all other institutional owners", "percentage of shares held by all but the largest institutional owner"]
definition: The total percentage of a firm's outstanding shares owned by all institutional investors other than the largest institutional owner; in models that add the second largest owner, it is the total percentage owned by all institutions less the sum of the percentages owned by the largest and second largest institutional owners.

name: Perceived information risk
authors_terms: ["information risk", "perceived information risk", "bid-ask spread", "relative bid-ask spread"]
definition: The market maker's perception of the risk of trading with better informed investors, proxied by the bid-ask spread: 'the bid-ask spread proxies for the level of information the market maker believes the next trader has; all else being equal, wider (narrower) spreads mean the next trader probably has relatively more (less) information.'

name: Reciprocal multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contacts in which the roles of the rivals are reversed across markets; the most effective contacts should be those in which the focal-market challengers are leaders in the contact market. For a challenger in a focal market, reciprocal multimarket contact is the number of markets outside the focal market in which the challenger meets the focal-market leader and in which the focal-market challenger is the leader.

name: Nonreciprocal multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contacts that represent situations in which firms have the same role in the focal and contact markets. For a challenger in a focal market, nonreciprocal multimarket contact is the number of markets outside the focal market in which the challenger meets the focal-market leader and in which the focal-market challenger is also a challenger.

name: Competitive behavior intensity
authors_terms: ["intensity of competitive behavior", "competitive behavior", "intensity of rivalry"]
definition: The intensity of competitive behavior displayed by an airline-route, captured inversely by yields: firms behave competitively not just when they lower their yields, but also when they keep these yields low. Therefore, lower yields indicate more intense competitive behavior, and vice versa.

name: Market share
authors_terms: ["market share", "equilibrium market share", "sustainability of market position"]
definition: The market share of the airline-route, measured as the passengers transported by the airline-route divided by all passengers transported in the market. The analysis of sustainability is couched in terms of equilibrium market shares, which are not directly observable because observable changes in market share may not immediately reflect shifts in equilibrium market share.

name: Territorial interest
authors_terms: ["territorial interests", "asymmetric territorial interests", "strategic importance", "spheres of influence"]
definition: The strategic importance that a firm assigns to its position in a market. A leader is a firm which has strategically important interests in a market, while a challenger does not have important interests in that market. Market share dominance, market dependence and resource centrality are proposed as three general dimensions for delineating strategically important airline-routes.

name: Multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact", "multimarket competition", "multimarket contact between an MNC and its rivals"]
definition: The degree to which the same rivals meet each other in multiple markets; the measure counts the number of multimarket competitors that a focal firm encounters in a focal market, where the firms must meet in at least one market other than that focal one.

name: Competitive aggressiveness
definition: The propensity of a firm to directly and intensely challenge rivals in order to maintain or improve its market position.

name: Subsidiary ownership
authors_terms: ["extent of subsidiary ownership", "subsidiary ownership", "level of ownership", "degree of subsidiary ownership"]
definition: The extent to which a parent MNC owns a subsidiary, which determines how much the parent can coordinate the subsidiary's actions with the rest of the corporation and indicates how far the subsidiary emphasizes local responsiveness over global integration.

name: Home-host cultural distance
authors_terms: ["cultural distance", "cultural distance between a host country and an MNC's home country", "home-host cultural distance"]
definition: The cultural distance between a host country and an MNC's home country, which results in different organizational and administrative practices and employee expectations and makes communication and knowledge transfer between headquarters and subsidiary more difficult.

name: Local regulatory restrictions
authors_terms: ["local regulatory restrictions", "regulatory restrictions in the host country", "host country regulatory restrictions"]
definition: Government regulations that impose economic, political, or trade impediments affecting an MNC subsidiary's cost of doing business and hampering the flexibility of its operations.

name: Presence of local competitors
definition: Local competitors are firms whose production and sales are limited to a single country, their home country; the presence of such competitors in a host country is high when local firms hold a large share of that market.

name: Network closure
definition: Network closure describes a network that is small (ego has few key contacts), dense (ego's key contacts are strongly connected with each other), or hierarchical (contacts are connected indirectly through a central person). Network constraint is a summary measure of closure: it decreases toward zero with network size and increases with density and hierarchy.

name: Planning horizon
definition: The length of time in advance over which a business leader plans the strategic or organizational development of the firm. Temporal myopia is the associated pathology of a lack or neglect of long-run planning, described as a tendency to ignore the long run.

name: Business success
definition: Business success was measured by attributes that might be of personal interest to a self-made person in China during the period of rapid economic growth covered by the survey: a lot of money passes through their hands (annual sales), jobs are generated (total employment), and the company shows evidence of its technological sophistication by holding its own patents. The measure is a principal component analysis z score aggregating the value of annual sales, number of full-time employees, and number of patents at the time of the survey.

name: Project experience
definition: By experience, we mean an entrepreneurial firm's past exposure to the execution of tasks relevant to a given prediction. The main independent variable Project Experience measures an entrepreneur's total execution experience as her number of projects prior to her current project and of the same subtype.

name: Unforeseen interdependencies
definition: When the Project Complexity curve increases faster than the Learning curve, the entrepreneur ultimately faces an increasing number of Unforeseen Interdependencies that will be overlooked in the prediction process and impair strategic foresight. Unforeseen Interdependencies is the total number of updates posted by the entrepreneur during project execution, after the fundraising campaign has ended and before the product is delivered, that cite unforeseen interdependencies.

name: Project complexity
authors_terms: ["complexity", "Project Complexity", "total number of interdependencies", "number of features"]
definition: By complexity, we mean the full set of interdependencies that exist between the components (or tasks) in the execution of a particular strategy. Thus, the complexity of a given strategy is a function of the number of components and the dependencies between those components.

name: Timeline prediction accuracy
definition: Crowdfunding entrepreneurs make two important, and readily observable, predictions: product specification and delivery timeline, meaning the date they will deliver the product to customers. When inaccurate strategic foresight leads to unforeseen interdependencies that make it impractical to achieve both initial predictions, entrepreneurs can choose which prediction they will ultimately prioritize.

name: Delivery time
definition: Predicted Time is the time (in days) between the end of the fundraising campaign and the predicted delivery date. Actual Time is the time (in days) between the end of the fundraising campaign and the actual delivery date.

name: Cultural distance
definition: The scope and scale of these differences have been gauged in academic studies using the 'cultural distance' construct (Kogut and Singh, 1988).

name: Direction of investment flow
definition: Outward investment seeks a cooperative relationship in a foreign country in which the partner firm is operating. Cooperative domestic investment, on the other hand, seeks a cooperative relationship in the domestic market in which the focal firm is established.

name: Extent of control
authors_terms: ["level of control", "extent of control", "control modes", "tight control"]
definition: Here the level of control is defined as the extent of ownership involvement in a cooperative relationship (Erramilli and Rao, 1993).

name: External hiring
authors_terms: ["external hires", "externally hired", "external mobility", "mobility channel", "internally hired", "internal hires"]
definition: We considered individuals to be externally hired if they are hired from a different company (i.e., their immediate previous job spell is at a different firm). Likewise, individuals are internally hired if they move into the PM role from a different position within the company.

name: Intrapreneurship
authors_terms: ["intrapreneurship", "intrapreneurial activity", "intrapreneurial PM work", "intrapreneurial PM job spells"]
definition: Intrapreneurship is generally defined as entrepreneurship within existing organizations. The authors note that one of the most prominent definitions is 'corporate entrepreneurship' or entrepreneurship within existing organizations.

name: Employee turnover
definition: To measure company departure, we first recorded Post-PM Destination as one of three outcomes of the PM job spell: (1) company departure (the employee leaves the firm as a PM), (2) internal move (the employee remains in the firm but adopts a new job role), and (3) unknown because the employee still occupied the PM job role at the point of data collection.

name: Industry profitability
definition: The profitability of the principal industry in which the firm operates. This measure is a composite construct constructed from four profitability ratios listed in the Analyst's Guide.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["product diversification", "extent of product diversification", "extent of diversification", "product diversity"]
definition: The product diversification measure is an entropy measure based on Palepu (1985). The product diversification measure is defined by Palepu's (1985) entropy measure, in which PD is the extent of product diversification and P, is the proportion of sales made in industry i.

name: Technological assets
definition: Following Horst (1972), Grubaugh (1987), Kogut and Chang (1991), and other studies, a firm's possession of technological (marketing) assets was assessed using R&D (advertising) intensity.

name: Marketing assets
definition: Following Horst (1972), Grubaugh (1987), Kogut and Chang (1991), and other studies, a firm's possession of technological (marketing) assets was assessed using R&D (advertising) intensity.

name: Geographic scope
authors_terms: ["geographic scope", "multinationality", "international extent of a firm's operations"]
definition: Geographic scope, defined as the international extent of a firm's operations. The extent of geographic operations was measured by two counts: a count of the number of foreign direct investments the firm had made and a count of the number of countries in which FDI had occurred.

name: Corporate performance
definition: As in prior studies, we define corporate performance using accounting-based measures. From GlobalVantage we compiled data for three performance measures: return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS).

name: Innovation output
authors_terms: ["innovation output", "innovative output", "number of biopharmaceutical patents", "patents granted to a startup"]
definition: Our measure of innovation output is the number of patents granted to a startup up to 1989. Table 3 shows the distribution of startup innovation output, measured as U.S. patents granted, from before 1982 to 1988.

name: Interfirm cooperative relationships
definition: Established firms form cooperative agreements with startups to learn biotechnology techniques and lessen the threat they pose as a substitute for traditional product development. These relationships benefit startups which typically lack financial, marketing and distribution resources that established firms provide.

name: Startup size
definition: A startup's size should be related both to its number of relationships and to its innovation output. First, size measures the firm's capacity to form relationships.

name: Startup age
definition: Older startups have had more time for product development and therefore should have greater innovative output. Prior research has shown little or no association between startup age and the number of relationships.

name: Access to public equity markets
definition: The effect of raising equity through public offering is likely to have an effect on the number of a startup's relationships. But the sign of this effect is ambiguous.

name: Product diversity
definition: Biopharmaceutical startups may be able to take advantage of economies of scope in research and development (Teece, 1982). Technology platforms and trajectories (Dosi, 1982) in biotechnology are typically involved in a number of subfields.

name: Network position
definition: Drawing on Coleman's (1988) concept of social capital and Granovetter's (1985) concept of embeddedness, these studies argue that a startup's position in the network reflects a system-level constraint on partners to behave cooperatively. Increased partner cooperation releases resources for the establishment of new relationships.

name: Internal employment mode
authors_terms: ["internal employment mode", "internal mode of employment", "internal mode", "employment internalization"]
definition: The internal employment mode should be characterized by long-term or lifetime employment and promotion from within the organization, and is associated with the training and development of knowledge or skills, the socialization of employees, and an emphasis on loyalty to the organization.

name: Joint venture status
authors_terms: ["joint venture", "joint ventures with Chinese firms", "wholly owned firms", "wholly owned by an overseas investor"]
definition: Joint ventures are firms that MNEs set up with Chinese firms and that can be seen as part of their immediate relational networks; joint venture was tested as a dummy, with a joint venture coded as 1 and a firm wholly owned by an overseas investor coded as 0.

name: Japanese home country culture
authors_terms: ["home country culture of an MNE", "Japanese home country culture", "Japanese MNEs"]
definition: The home country culture of an MNE is also an important institutional factor that may influence the selection of an employment mode through the cultural-cognitive element of the institutionalization process.

name: Equipment/technology intensiveness
authors_terms: ["equipment/technology intensiveness", "equipment per employee", "invest heavily in production equipment"]
definition: Equipment/technology intensiveness is a strategic factor of the firm measured by the ratio of the value of the equipment to the total number of employees.

name: Industry environment
authors_terms: ["nature of competition", "industry environments", "character of the industry"]
definition: The character of the industry may also influence the selection of the employment mode; in some industries, such as electronics, firms face a rapid change in technology, which makes it difficult for them to obtain qualified human resources from outside.

name: Chinese institutional influence
authors_terms: ["Chinese institutional influence", "Chinese institution", "share of a firm that was controlled by the Chinese party"]
definition: Institutional pressure from the Chinese side, which in China includes the state and state-owned firms; it was tested by the share of a firm that was controlled by the Chinese party.

name: Firm performance
definition: The performance of each firm since 1996, reported as change since 1995 in the firm's profit (or productivity), market share, and the number of employees who have been disciplined or fired.

name: Presuccession organizational performance
definition: Presuccession performance indicates how well a large corporation has used its resources, given environmental constraints and opportunities. It is one of two aspects of the organizational context in which a succession occurs.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stockholder reaction", "stock market reaction", "cumulative abnormal returns", "abnormal returns"]
definition: Change in stockholder returns around the time of a CEO succession announcement was used as an indicator of the reaction to the event of an important constituency, the stockholders. Observations of abnormal movements in stock returns directly attributable to a succession announcement therefore estimate the extent to which the market expects a shift in an organization's future performance because of the change in leadership.

name: Initiating force
authors_terms: ["initiating force", "the force initiating a change in CEO", "initiating force driving a CEO's departure"]
definition: The force that impels a CEO to depart influences the extent to which the new CEO has discretion in affecting organizational outcomes, and it reflects the political process by which he or she is chosen; the initiating force indicates who controls the event. Four possible initiating forces can impel CEO successions in large corporations: custom, the departing CEO, the board of directors, and the death or health-related disability of a CEO.

name: Successor origin
authors_terms: ["successor origin", "origin of a new CEO", "inside successor", "outside successor"]
definition: The origin of a new CEO, which can be either inside or outside the organization experiencing succession. Previous organizational membership is a salient characteristic of an incoming CEO, and successor origin, a highly visible attribute, seems to convey the clearest signal among the messages implicit in successions.

name: Predecessor disposition
definition: A predecessor's disposition, or whether he or she stays with a firm or leaves. The disposition of former CEOs, whether they stay (usually as board members) or cut all ties with an organization, is an aspect of their departure.

name: National corporatism
definition: A multidimensional sociopolitical cooperative institution reflected in the concentration of a country's interest groups; more corporatist countries place an emphasis on coordination and inclusiveness among the society's stakeholders, with organized interest groups holding stable positions in society and formally participating in the formulation and implementation of economic policy.

name: Partner social value
definition: Partners' social value is reflected in their connectedness to other organizations in the industry and is measured by each partner's degree centrality; when a partner's degree centrality is higher, it has relationships with more firms in its industry, which suggests greater prominence in the industry network.

name: Partner technological value
authors_terms: ["partners' technological value", "technological value", "technological distance", "technological complementarity", "technological novelty"]
definition: Partners' technological value is reflected in the nonoverlapping nature of their technological profiles; because the 35 different patent subclasses represent distinct aspects of fuel cell technology development, greater technological distance between partners conveys the potential for accessing more novel and complementary technologies.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "alliance partner selection", "probability of alliance formation", "likelihood that two prospective partners will form an alliance"]
definition: Because both organizations must agree to partner with one another, alliance formation depends on decisions of both firms simultaneously assessing the suitability of one another within the set of all possible domestic dyads.

name: Knowledge acquisition
definition: The citing of a partner's patents is regarded as evidence that the focal firm has successfully internalized and built on the partner's knowledge base; private benefits occur when one firm acquires and internalizes its partner's knowledge for use outside of the alliance.

name: Knowledge inheritance
authors_terms: ["knowledge inheritance", "knowledge inheritance relative to that activity"]
definition: Such involuntary transfer of knowledge from parent firms to their spinoffs - commonly referred to as 'knowledge inheritance' - is thought to be an important source of spinoffs' capabilities. The underlying knowledge relevant to carrying out an activity in-house is more likely to be transmitted through the spinoff process when the parent firm also performs that activity internally.

name: Vertical integration of a key activity
authors_terms: ["vertical integration", "integration of a key activity", "engine integration", "key value chain activity"]
definition: A firm is expected to integrate a value chain activity that requires capabilities and resources that are uniquely complementary to its existing capability - resource profile, in order to avoid the transaction costs associated with accessing them through contracts. A key activity is an activity that enables the firm to create and capture substantial value.

name: Defensible strategic positioning
definition: Successful strategic positioning implies that a firm's product or service is unique in some way, whether in its features, cost of production, or some combination of features and costs. Our notion of 'establishing a defensible strategic position' is defined in terms of whether a given entrant was able to avoid competing in the lowest-price segment of the market following the introduction of the Model T.

name: Firm survival
definition: In addition, we created two alternative measures of firm survival. The first, Log Survival Years, is the log of the number of years the firm survived.

name: Knowledge utilization from alliance portfolios
authors_terms: ["knowledge utilization", "knowledge utilization from portfolio", "knowledge utilization outcome"]
definition: Knowledge utilization was measured as a citation-weighted patent count in the lagged five-year window following an observation year.

name: Technological diversity in the alliance portfolio
authors_terms: ["technological diversity", "technological diversity in a focal firm's alliance portfolio"]
definition: The technological diversity of a firm's alliance portfolio, measured over the pooled patents of all alliance partners, ranges from all partners concentrating their patents in one subclass to no overlap among partners' technologies, the latter indicating the greatest burden on the firm's latitudinal absorptive capacity.

name: Technological distance between the firm and its alliance portfolio
definition: The technological distance between each focal firm and its alliance portfolio is calculated as 1 - Pij, where Pij is Jaffe's (1986) measure of similarity between a firm and its alliance partners' pooled technological capabilities; it ranges from identical patenting, the lowest burden on the firm's longitudinal absorptive capacity, to nonoverlapping classes, the greatest technological distance and the most burden on longitudinal absorptive capacity.

name: CEO birth order
definition: Birth order is the 'relative rank of a child in terms of the age hierarchy among siblings in the family.' It captures early-life family experiences and is theorized to shape behavioral tendencies that persist into adulthood.

name: Strategic risk taking
definition: CEOs often make strategic decisions that involve risk - i.e., decisions that are highly uncertain and have a potential for negative returns. It was measured by aggregating three major outlays typically associated with uncertain and potentially negative returns: capital expenditures, R&D spending, and acquisitions.

name: Closest sibling age gap
authors_terms: ["closest sibling age gap", "age gap between a CEO and the closest-born sibling"]
definition: Closest sibling age gap is the number of years in age between an individual and his or her closest sibling. The authors theorize that it captures the extent of childhood sibling rivalry, which amplifies birth order-based niche differentiation.

name: CEO age
definition: A factor that may predict the extent to which sibling rivalry is recalled is age; research has suggested that age directly influences CEOs' strategic risking. The authors theorize instead that age moderates the effect of birth order because it impacts the recall of sibling rivalry and the emotional intensity associated with the recall.

name: Sibling CEO presence
authors_terms: ["presence of a sibling CEO", "sibling CEO", "having a sibling who is also a CEO"]
definition: For a CEO, having a sibling who also works as a CEO should promote greater sibling rivalry and thus amplify birth order's relationship with risk taking.

name: Market and entrepreneurship orientation combination
authors_terms: ["market/entrepreneurship orientation combination", "alignment between market and entrepreneurship orientations", "coalignment", "market/entrepreneurship orientation alignment"]
definition: Market and entrepreneurship orientation are arrayed on a continuum from low to high and firms are classified into a 2 x 2 matrix resulting in four distinct groups of firms: market/entrepreneurship oriented (ME), entrepreneurship oriented (EO), market oriented (MO), and conservative (CO) firms.

name: Market orientation
definition: Market orientation describes a firm's orientation toward the promotion and support for the collection, dissemination, and responsiveness to market intelligence to serve customer needs.

name: Entrepreneurship orientation
definition: An entrepreneurship orientation emphasizes aggressive product-market innovation, risky projects, and a proclivity to pioneer innovations that preempt the competition, and is distinguished by a high degree of innovativeness, risk-taking, and proactiveness.

name: New product performance
definition: New product performance describes the degree to which a new product is perceived to have achieved its market share, sales growth, customer use, and profit objectives.

name: Timing of market entry
definition: Timing of market entry refers to the firm's strategic choice as to whether to be "first to market," "early follower," "late follower," or "late entrant" with respect to new product introductions.

name: Product quality
definition: Product quality refers to the perceived superiority of the new product over the competition; it captures the competitive advantage of the new product in terms of cost saving, quality and performance.

name: Marketing synergy
definition: Marketing synergy refers to the extent to which the resources and skills required for a new product development project fit the current marketing resources and skills of the firm.

name: Proficiency of market launch
definition: Proficiency of market launch captures the effectiveness of the firm in commercializing its new products; it represents the firm's effort at getting customers to adopt its new product.

name: Management support for innovation
authors_terms: ["management support for innovation", "management involvement in product innovation", "importance given to innovation in human resource strategy"]
definition: Management support for innovation refers to the degree of support that top managers give to product innovation activities in the firm; it is indicated by two dimensions, direct acts of management involvement and encouragement of the new product project, and the importance that management gives to product innovation activities and experience in the firm's human resource strategy.

name: Environmental hostility
definition: Environmental hostility reflects the intensity of market competition, lack of marketable opportunities, and unfavorable, harsh business climates with the firm having little or no power to influence the environment.

name: Intensity of market competition
definition: Intensity of market competition was measured by items that tapped the perceived similarity of competitor offerings, price competition, and aggressiveness of the competitor's behavior, and is examined as one of two aspects of hostility.

name: SBU effectiveness
definition: The paper's dependent variable: managers' assessments of an SBU's performance measured as a comparison between actual performance and a priori expectations rather than on an absolute scale, assessed along several dimensions weighted by their relative importance for the SBU.

name: Strategic mission
definition: A build strategic mission implies a goal of increased market share, even at the expense of short-term earnings and cash flow; at the other extreme, a harvest strategic mission implies a goal of maximizing short-term earnings and cash flow, even at the expense of market share. For identifying an SBU's strategic mission, what is critical is the type of trade-off that would be made if one were necessary.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: Consistent with Porter's (1980) conceptualization, in this study competitive strategy signifies an SBU's intended basis for achieving a competitive advantage over other firms in an external product-market; the two generic bases are differentiation and low cost.

name: Openness in corporate-SBU relations
definition: Openness in corporate-SBU relations refers to the degree to which relations between SBUs' managers and their corporate superiors are open and informal and allow for spontaneous and open exchange of information and ideas.

name: Subjectivity in performance assessment
definition: A bonus award for any SBU's general manager can be determined on the basis of either a strict formula, such as a certain percentage of the SBU's operating profits, or a purely subjective assessment by corporate superiors, or some combination of the two; the study focuses on the subjective side of this mix for the purposes of bonus determination.

name: Corporate-SBU decentralization
definition: Decentralization refers to the degree of influence that an SBU's general manager has on the major decisions pertaining to the focal SBU relative to the influence of corporate superiors.

name: Position in an industry divestiture wave
authors_terms: ["position in an industry divestiture wave", "divestiture position in wave", "position in wave"]
definition: The position of a firm's divestiture relative to its industry peers, i.e., where in an industry divestiture wave the divestiture occurs; it conveys whether or not managers are imitating their industry peers or acting independently. Small values indicate divestitures that occur at the outset of a wave, and larger values indicate those at the end.

name: Divestiture announcement returns
authors_terms: ["divestiture announcement returns", "abnormal stock market returns", "stock market returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: The abnormal stock market returns associated with a firm's divestiture announcement; the abnormal return represents the cumulative difference between a company's observed return and its expected return during the event window surrounding the date of the firm's divestiture announcement.

name: Industry munificence
definition: Munificent industries are characterized by an abundance of resources, reduced resource dependencies, and greater opportunity for profitable firm growth; low-munificence industries are indicative of competition for resources wherein managers have fewer available resources at their disposal.

name: Industry dynamism
