definition: Industry dynamism indicates the extent to which a firm's environment exhibits unpredictable change and instability or uncertainty.

name: Technology stage of development
authors_terms: ["stage of development", "stage of a technology's development", "unproven technology", "proven technology", "technology's maturity"]
definition: When potential adopters are uncertain about a technology's advantages, a decision to adopt it is risky, and we refer to the technology as 'unproven'. By contrast, a technology has been 'proven' if its sponsor's performance claims have been publicly vetted, for instance through commercial deployment.

name: Peer-to-peer diffusion strategy
authors_terms: ["peer-to-peer diffusion strategy", "peer-to-peer contagion", "peer-to-peer ties", "peer-to-peer pattern", "simple contagion"]
definition: A simple contagion is passed on through singular contact between activated and unactivated nodes in a network; if a technology can diffuse via simple contagion, a sponsor can accelerate its diffusion by forming alliances sparsely throughout the network of potential adopters, so it does not need to form redundant ties with those actors.

name: Wide-bridge diffusion strategy
definition: Wide bridges are comprised of multiple local connections between activated and unactivated nodes in an adopter network. A sponsor can create the wide bridges required to activate complex contagions by building multiple indirect ties to potential adopters, emphasizing structurally redundant alliance ties over efficient ones.

name: Partner network centrality
definition: Centrality measures the number of connections each candidate partner has with other actors in the overall 2G-relevant network divided by the total number of possible connections in the network, i.e., normalized degree centrality. The more central a candidate partner's network position, the more visible and influential the candidate is with respect to technology diffusion.

name: Alliance partner selection
authors_terms: ["partner choices", "which (or, what type of) partners they choose", "alliance partner network", "choose particular alliance partners"]
definition: The choice of which (or, what type of) partners a sponsor chooses during technology battles, in contrast to scholarly study that has primarily investigated when sponsors seek partnerships. We suggest that in addition to the anticipated benefits of an economic exchange, sponsors will also consider potential partners' capacity to help diffuse their technologies.

name: CEO cognitive flexibility
definition: The authors adopt Martin and Rubin's (1995) definition of cognitive flexibility as a person's '(a) awareness that in any given situation there are options and alternatives available, (b) willingness to be flexible and adapt to the situation, and c) self-efficacy in being flexible'. They describe a CEO's level of cognitive flexibility as the tendency to adapt their thinking, emotions, and behaviors to changing conditions.

name: Information search effort
definition: Search effort refers to the extent to which CEOs allocate cognitive capacity to search processes relative to other tasks.

name: Information search persistence
definition: Search persistence refers to the duration over which attention is exerted to search for information.

name: Search for outside information
authors_terms: ["search for outside information", "outside information search", "search selection", "terrain distance"]
definition: Search selection refers to the sector of the operating environment the CEO directs her attention to, while search for outside information or terrain distance is a key component of search selection with important implications for firm innovative activities.

name: Organizational ambidexterity
definition: Organizational ambidexterity is a firm capability to pursue both exploratory and exploitative innovation. In the contextual perspective examined in this study, organizational ambidexterity refers to a firm's ability 'to simultaneously pursue both incremental and discontinuous innovation that results from hosting multiple contradictory structures, processes, and cultures within the same firm'.

name: User innovation
definition: The dependent variable is user innovation, which is discrete and constructed from whether users had developed modifications, add-ons, or extras to Propellerhead's products and whether these were 'new to the world' at the time they were developed.

name: Professional status
authors_terms: ["professional status", "professional or hobbyist", "hobbyist versus professional status", "professionals versus hobbyists"]
definition: The degree to which a user can be considered professional or hobbyist was measured by the user's income, derived from the use of computer-controlled music instruments. The authors use the notion of hobbyist to denote the fact that for these individuals, the development or use of the product in question is not their main source of income.

name: Peer recognition
authors_terms: ["peer recognition", "recognition from peers", "recognition from other community goers"]
definition: Users can easily signal their abilities to a large number of peers and may easily gain reputation this way; the question used is whether recognition from other community goers is a great reward.

name: Firm recognition
authors_terms: ["firm recognition", "recognition from the firm hosting the community", "recognition from Propellerhead"]
definition: Recognition by the firm hosting the community could take the form of, for example, the firm posting the innovation itself, or related information, or making a Web link to the innovation on its website; the question used is whether recognition from Propellerhead is a great reward.

name: Lead user attributes
authors_terms: ["lead user", "lead user attributes", "lead user characteristics", "leading-edge users"]
definition: Lead users are defined as users of a given product or service type who combine two characteristics: (a) they expect innovation-related benefits from a solution and are thereby motivated to innovate; and (b) they experience the need for a given innovation earlier than the majority of the target market. Innovators are likely to have lead user attributes that differentiate them from the remaining users in a population.

name: Same caste/religion CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["same caste/religion CEO hires", "within caste/religion hiring of professional CEOs", "'in-group' CEO hires", "same caste/religion as firm owners/chairpersons", "social proximity based on caste/religion"]
definition: We hypothesize the following for CEO hires, where same-caste/religion CEOs are those with same caste or religion as that of the owners/chairpersons of the hiring firm. The independent variable of interest was a dummy variable that indicated whether the CEO candidate belonged to the same caste/religion as the firm owners/chairpersons.

name: Information and trust reasons for hiring
definition: Similarity engenders trust and understanding and greater levels of social affiliation than would be expected among dissimilar individuals, and 'in-group' individuals are likely to be perceived as cooperative, honest, and trustworthy compared to 'out-group' individuals. Similarity in interests, shared values, and worldviews can facilitate communication leading to enhanced interactions than would be the case when individuals differ widely on these dimensions.

name: Taste-based preferences
definition: Taste-based preferences too predict the selection of in-group CEOs. In the process of exercising taste-based preferences, individuals may sacrifice quality, either consciously or unconsciously, for the opportunity to work with similar others, which maximizes their personal utility.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable was ROA (return on assets calculated as EBITDA over total assets) as a measure of firm value. The ROA of the year following CEO change was used in these firm performance regressions.

name: Insider CEO candidate
authors_terms: ["'insider' candidates", "'insiders' to the firm", "CEO candidate being an insider to the firm"]
definition: The bias in favor of same caste/religion is less in case of candidates who are 'insiders' to the firm, since information advantages are unlikely through same caste/religion hiring in case of 'insiders' who are already known to the firm. Information about directors helped in constructing the 'insider' candidates for CEO selection.

name: CEO candidate selection
authors_terms: ["Selected", "being selected as a CEO", "professional CEO appointments"]
definition: The dependent variable for the multivariate analyses for CEO hiring (H1 and H2) was whether the candidate was selected to be the CEO from the pool of potential candidates.

name: Coreness of firm names
definition: Coreness indicates the relative position of a firm on a continuous core/periphery spectrum. The core is a dense interconnected cluster; the periphery a set of nodes loosely connected to the core and each other.

name: Media visibility
definition: Extent (i.e., visibility) refers to the number of articles published about a firm or how often this firm is mentioned.

name: Negative media tone
definition: Tone refers to the valence of the coverage (i.e., how positive or negative it is). The higher the negative (positive) tone, the more the articles mentioning a firm contain negative (positive) words and expressions.

name: Realized auction price
authors_terms: ["realized prices of its outputs at auctions", "final realized auction Price (hammer price)", "auction prices"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the final realized auction Price (hammer price) at the watch level.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Weigelt and Camerer define the reputation of a firm as 'a set of attributes ascribed to a firm, inferred from the firm's past actions'; reputation is viewed as an intangible asset depending on 'the interpretations of multiple constituents about how firms create value in an industry.'

name: Total market actions
authors_terms: ["total number of market actions", "total number of firm actions", "total firm actions", "level of actions", "totality of a firm's actions"]
definition: Market actions are externally directed resource deployments that convey information about three fundamental aspects of the firm's strategy: strategic intent, strategic skills and capabilities, and market position. The total number of actions is the sum of the actions a firm takes in each action type category.

name: Action repertoire complexity
authors_terms: ["action repertoire complexity", "repertoire complexity", "complexity of the action repertoire", "firm repertoire complexity"]
definition: The diversity of types of actions that a firm takes defines its 'action repertoire complexity,' which differs from firm complexity or product line complexity; it describes the diversity of competitive actions and moves that a firm employs in its pursuit of competitive advantage over its rivals.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration, which describes the number of firms competing in an industry and their relative market presence, may be an important structural characteristic that influences firms' reputations both directly and indirectly. Highly concentrated industries are characterized by relatively few large players holding significant shares of the total market.

name: Total rival market actions
authors_terms: ["total number of rival market actions", "total rival actions", "total number of rival actions in the industry"]
definition: Rivals' actions are market signals that compete for the same stakeholder attention and favorable interpretations as the focal firm's actions; the total number of rival actions in the industry is the aggregate of the actions taken by rival firms.

name: Rival repertoire complexity
authors_terms: ["complexity of rivals' action repertoires", "rivals' repertoire complexity", "rival repertoire complexity"]
definition: When rivals employ complex action repertoires (i.e., they take actions of greater variety than the focal firm), they generate a greater variety of information to be attended to by stakeholders, posing additional demands on stakeholders' attention and comprehension.

name: Rival response lag
authors_terms: ["response lag", "rival action time lag", "lag between a focal firm's market actions and the actions of its rivals"]
definition: The amount of time that elapses between the action of a focal firm and a subsequent action of a rival, known as a 'response lag.' The lags between the actions of the focal firm and the actions of its rival provide stakeholders with information about the expected duration of the benefits the focal firm will obtain from its actions.

name: Repertoire similarity
authors_terms: ["repertoire similarity", "similarity between a focal firm's repertoire of market actions and the repertoire of its rivals"]
definition: The similarity of rivals' action repertoires to that of the focal firm affords stakeholders the possibility to assess the legitimacy of a firm's actions; it is operationalized as the difference between the proportion of actions of a given type for the focal firm and for its rivals.

name: Analyst coverage drop
authors_terms: ["a drop in analyst coverage", "a decrease in analyst coverage", "a drop in the number of analysts covering a firm", "reduction in analyst coverage"]
definition: We use a natural experiment based on brokerage house mergers and closures between 2001 and 2011 to test our predictions. Such events often lead to a drop in analyst coverage and are considered as exogenous shocks to deal with the endogeneity issues suffered by prior studies that examine the effect of analysts coverage directly.

name: Corporate social performance
definition: Corporate social performance (CSP) is a multidimensional concept covering a firm's response to a wide range of stakeholder demands and expectations.

name: Brokerage house size
definition: brokerage house size captures the degree of resources and support that analysts can obtain from their employer. Analysts working for larger brokerage houses have access to superior resources such as more general or firm-specific information, more administrative support, and better distribution networks.

name: Analyst experience
definition: Also, analysts' skills and knowledge improve with experience, so analysts with more general forecasting experience are better at analyzing financial statements and recognizing economic trends. In addition, analysts also acquire experience and skills relevant to the specific firms they follow which help them better understand the idiosyncrasies of a particular firm's information.

name: Analyst forecast accuracy
definition: Third, the quality of analysts and their influence on the market are also influenced by their past performance - past forecast accuracy. Studies suggest that there is a strong belief among investors that the accuracy of an analyst's past forecasts is a good indicator of his or her current recommendations.

name: Routine codification
definition: Deliberate learning in which a firm codifies its acquisition experience in manuals, checklists, and the like. These codified integration tools form the acquirer's zero-order routines, which specify how those on the front lines are to act in a given situation.

name: Risk management practices
definition: Practices aimed at identifying and managing deal-specific integration risks. These practices induce the first, or variation, stage of ad hoc problem solving, triggering those on the front lines to deviate from their firm's codified integration routines and to purposefully consider a variety of potential, ad hoc courses of action customized to a deal's unique features.

name: Tacit knowledge transfer practices
definition: Practices aimed specifically at reducing causal ambiguity by transferring tacit knowledge on acquisition integration to those within subunits currently integrating bolt-on deals. They go beyond what codified tools can offer by elevating understanding from the 'what' and the 'how' to the 'why'.

name: Relative acquisition size
authors_terms: ["relative acquisition size", "the size of the target relative to that of your company"]
definition: The size of a target relative to that of an acquirer, measured in terms of sales.

name: Level of integration
definition: The extent to which the separate functions and activities of the acquirer and the target were physically consolidated into one.

name: Acquisition integration performance
definition: The degree to which, according to a firm's own evaluation criteria, the integration of the focal acquisition was judged to have successfully realized the specific synergies projected for that acquisition.

name: Government ownership
definition: A government-owned investment vehicle structured like a VC firm is generally referred to as a government-sponsored VC (GVC) firm. Government involvement in GVC firms occurs through government ownership.

name: Political connections
authors_terms: ["connected VC firm", "connected VC", "personal political connections", "personal political ties"]
definition: A private VC firm that has personal connections to former or current government officials or princelings is known as a connected VC firm. This form of government involvement runs through personal political ties.

name: Risk-taking
definition: The financing stage of portfolio companies is a suitable proxy for the risk-taking decisions of VC firms; investment risk is highest in portfolio companies in the start-up stage and lowest in the mature stage.

name: Return on investment
definition: We used the annual ROI of VC firms to capture the returns from their investment portfolios. VC firms typically gain returns from their portfolio companies' successful exits through IPOs, mergers and acquisitions (M&As), and secondary sales.

name: Managerial tie utilization
definition: Managerial ties represent 'executives' boundary-spanning activities and their associated interactions with external entities'. In China, managers build ties not only with managers at other firms (i.e., business ties), but also with government officials (i.e., political ties).

name: Business ties
definition: Business ties involve three items that assess top managers' use of ties with managers of other firms (i.e., buyers, suppliers, and competitors).

name: Political ties
definition: Political ties contains three items examining top managers' use of connections with political leaders at various levels of government, officials in industrial bureaus, and officials in regulatory and supporting organizations during the past three years.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance entails a financial indicator: ROA in 2005.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["firm ownership", "foreign vs. domestic firms", "foreign firms", "domestic firms"]
definition: Because Sino-foreign joint ventures usually structure their operations and management in parallel with foreign partners, researchers tend to classify them together with wholly foreign-owned firms as foreign firms; the authors code firm ownership as a dummy variable, such that 0 = domestic firms and 1 = foreign firms (including both wholly foreign-owned and international joint ventures).

name: Competitive intensity
definition: Competitive intensity refers to the degree of competition that a firm faces in its industry. Increased intensity often is characterized by greater rivalry among incumbents, which can take the form of price wars, more advertising or product offerings, added services, and increased transactions.

name: Structural uncertainty
definition: Structural uncertainty is the extent to which the industry environment is volatile and fast changing, because it creates greater uncertainty about the actions of other economic actors, such as customers, competitors, suppliers, and regulators.

name: Structural similarity
authors_terms: ["structural similarity", "structural similarity between acquirer and target firms", "structural similarity index", "structural dissimilarity"]
definition: Structural similarity refers to the extent to which the two firms' organizational architectures, particularly the degree of modularity, align with one another.

name: Structural knowledge
authors_terms: ["structural knowledge", "managerial structural knowledge", "structural knowledge similarity", "manager-level structural similarity index"]
definition: We define structural knowledge as the executives' understanding of organizational structures or how they accomplish goals, including the organizational knowledge of coordination, politics, and relationships. It captures how tasks, workflows, and interdependencies are managed across units and is shaped by repeated exposure to organizational routines, governance systems, and social dynamics.

name: Target manager retention
authors_terms: ["target manager retention", "retention of target managers", "target TMT retention rate", "manager-level retention"]
definition: Managers still employed by the acquirer two years following deal completion were coded as retained, and managers no longer employed by the acquirer two years following deal completion were coded as not retained.

name: Organizational modularity
definition: Modularity in organizational structure is primarily determined by the degree of interdependence between units and often characterized by centralized decision making. Less modular organizations have a high level of interdependence among units and often centralize their decisions at the top of the hierarchy, whereas more modular organizations consist of semiautonomous units that are nearly decomposable with decision making often decentralized to the unit level.

name: Geographic distance
definition: We propose that geographic distance amplifies the value of structural similarity. Greater geographic distance makes it more difficult and costly for the acquirer to deploy their own managers to the target firm.

name: Acquisition integration approach
definition: Haspeslagh and Jemison (1991) identify four acquisition integration approaches: preservation, symbiosis, holding, and absorption. Among these, absorption-type acquisitions involve the deepest structural integration, implying a full consolidation, over time, of the operations, organization, and culture of both organizations.

name: Acquisition relatedness
definition: We measured technical knowledge relatedness between the target and the acquiring firms following the previous literature, which categorized related and unrelated acquisitions based on the primary two-digit SIC category.

name: Firm effects
definition: Firm-specific characteristics encapsulate firm resources, capital, technology and human resources, marketing, service, management, and production skills; firms have idiosyncratic skills generating endogenous efficiencies that enable them to become profitable, and firm effects are the share of profitability variance these firm-level factors explain.

name: Industry effects
definition: Industry-specific factors encapsulate features such as the industry concentration level, industry consolidation versus fragmentation, minimum capital requirements, or product differentiation; industry effects are the share of profitability variance explained by such industry-level factors.

name: Group effects
definition: Business groups are confederations of legally independent firms that are an especially important feature in emerging economies; group effects are the share of profitability variance explained by affiliation to such a business group.

name: Profitability variance
definition: A literature focuses on the decomposition of profitability variance so as to understand the magnitude of various effects; the authors evaluate the importance of firm effects versus industry effects versus group effects in explaining profitability variances.

name: Profitability
definition: Following the literature, the authors use return on assets (ROA) as the profitability measure and also use the operating profit margin, the ratio of profits before depreciation, interest, and tax to net sales (EBIDTA), as an alternative profit measure.

name: IP disclosure during standard setting
authors_terms: ["disclosure of IP during standard setting", "disclosure of SEPs", "disclosure of IP to SSOs", "IP disclosures"]
definition: Firms with intellectual property relevant to the standard formally disclose this IP to the SSOs, rendering the IP 'standard essential patents' (SEPs). Firms are required to disclose 'technically essential' IP, that is, ones which implementers of the standard cannot avoid infringing upon during implementation.

name: Returns from IP disclosure
authors_terms: ["returns from disclosure of IP during standard setting", "returns from disclosure of SEPs", "returns to the firm from disclosure", "returns from coordination"]
definition: The returns the firm generates for itself from its disclosure of IP during standard setting; the study examines these returns through the change in the firm's equity market valuation and through Tobin's Q.

name: Nondisclosed complementary components
definition: Two components are complementary when their joint value created in functioning together is larger than the sum of values they create in functioning individually. They are not 'technically essential' to the core technologies and are usually not disclosed as part of the standard.

name: Firm specificity of complementary components
authors_terms: ["firm specificity", "firm-specific complementary components", "firm specificity of the firm's nondisclosed complementary components"]
definition: A portfolio is firm specific when it contains components that are only complementary to the firm's own disclosed SEP and not to other firms' technologies in the same core technological area (as the SEP) that could have been the industry standard instead of the firm's core technologies.

name: Value of complementary components
authors_terms: ["value of the complementary components", "value of its nondisclosed complementary components", "value of the components"]
definition: The value of the firm's nondisclosed complementary components, which the authors examine as changes in the value of the components as measured by patent citations received over disclosure of SEPs. A patent's citations received (forward citations) are used as an indication of its value.

name: Ego network size
definition: Degree is the network theory name for ego network size. Degree as of 2000 was calculated as the count of direct competitor going concerns.

name: Ego network density
authors_terms: ["ego network density", "network density", "density", "interconnectedness of the ego network"]
definition: Density is measured as the percentage of possible competitive ties between members of the ego network that are actually realized.

name: Competitor diversity
authors_terms: ["competitor diversity", "diversity of competitors", "network diversity", "diversity of multimarket contact"]
definition: A network of diverse competitors should have different effects on product market entry than a network of similar competitors. The diversity of a focal firm's multimarket contact is measured as the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) of multimarket contact with the firm's direct competitors.

name: Product market entry
definition: Since each STC is issued to a single firm and specifies modifications not covered by its prior STCs, every STC represents an act of product market entry. Because an STC may apply to several aircraft types, it may represent simultaneous entry into several markets.

name: Timing of pollution-reducing investments
authors_terms: ["timing of investments", "timing of pollution-reducing investments", "timing of investments in new pollution-reducing technologies", "timing of investments in slow diffusion pollution-reducing process technologies"]
definition: Timing of investments in the new pollution-reducing technologies is proxied for by the number of years the firm has had investments in extended delignification vessels (1991 minus year of the first investment in an extended delignification vessel). A first mover firm in one of the new pollution-reducing technologies is argued to have an advantage over nonfirst movers.

name: Intensity of pollution-reducing investments
authors_terms: ["intensity of investments", "intensity of investments in pollution-reducing process technologies", "intensity of investment"]
definition: The higher the share of total investments represented by pollution-reducing investments, the more intense are the investments in the new technologies. Intensity of investments in new pollution-reducing technologies is proxied for by the percentage of the firm's total capacity that is capable of producing elemental or totally chlorine-free pulp.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["firm's financial performance", "firm performance", "net income growth", "profit growth"]
definition: Firm performance is proxied for by the percentage growth in real (1985) local currency net income from the mean for the period 1983-85 to the mean for the period 1989-91.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Trading rooms in banks that were substantially owned by individuals or firms from countries other than the country of the trading rooms' location, in contrast to local trading rooms, which were substantially owned by individuals or firms from the country of location.

name: Trading room profitability
definition: The performance of a trading room, indicated by profits per trader, which largely depend on the aggregate profits of its individual traders. A perceptual measure of room performance was also constructed from traders' ratings.

name: Liability of foreignness
authors_terms: ["liability of foreignness", "costs of doing business abroad"]
definition: The costs of doing business abroad that result in a competitive disadvantage for an MNE subunit, broadly defined as all additional costs a firm operating in a market overseas incurs that a local firm would not incur. Whatever its source, the liability of foreignness implies that foreign firms will have lower profitability than local firms, all else being equal.

name: Local isomorphism
definition: The tendency of MNE subunits to attend to the demands of their local, host country environments so that their organizational practices become similar, or isomorphic, to the practices of local firms. It is measured as the distance of a foreign room from the average value of a practice for the local rooms in the same city, the smaller the difference the greater the extent of local isomorphism.

name: Firm-specific advantage
definition: Resources or capabilities specific to the firm that a multinational brings to its foreign subunit, such as organizational or managerial capabilities embodied in organizational routines transferred from the parent. It is measured for each practice as the difference between the value of that practice for a foreign room and the value of that practice for its paired room in the home country.

name: Market control
definition: A mode of control under which an organization can simply reward each employee in direct proportion to his contribution, reflected in pay for performance, hiring experienced traders from the external labor market, and turnover among traders.

name: Bureaucratic microcontrols
definition: An aspect of bureaucratic control unique to the trading environment, involving firms' setting detailed limits on intraday and overnight open positions by currency and by trader in an attempt to micromanage speculation by individual traders.

name: Complementary human resources
authors_terms: ["Human resources", "Human resource set", "complementary human resources", "Human variables"]
definition: Human resources that may combine with ITs to produce competitive advantage through resource complementarity; the study investigates six potential complementary resources: open organization, open communications, organizational consensus, CEO commitment, organizational flexibility, and IT-strategy integration.

name: Complementary business resources
authors_terms: ["Business resources", "Business resource set", "complementary business resources", "Business variables"]
definition: Business resources that may combine with ITs to produce competitive advantage through resource complementarity; the study investigates supplier relationships, supplier-driven IT, IT training, business process design, team orientation, benchmarking, and IT planning.

name: Information technology resources
definition: Computer-based information systems, defined by Orlikowski and Gash as 'any form of computer-based information system, including mainframe as well as microcomputer applications.' In this study retail IT applications are divided into in-store ITs, which help administer store operations, and beyond-store ITs, which include everything else such as EDI and distribution-center or home-office systems.

name: IT performance
definition: Executives' perceptions about the impacts of IT on financial performance, measured with five survey items.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["Overall Performance", "Financial Performance", "overall company performance", "performance variance among firms"]
definition: A subjective measure of financial performance itself, consisting of questions about the firms' overall profitability and sales growth over the previous 3-year period.

name: Absorbed slack
authors_terms: ["absorbed slack", "absolute absorbed slack", "relative absorbed slack", "absorbed slack resources", "fat"]
definition: Downsizings aim to reduce 'absorbed' slack and transform it to 'available' slack through cost savings and increased cash flow. Available slack, such as retained earnings, is highly flexible and easily redeployed; in contrast, absorbed slack is not easily redeployed, as excess personnel are embedded in the organization through allocation to specific routines and tasks.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "post-downsizing performance", "performance changes following downsizings", "operating performance", "return on assets"]
definition: To assess post-downsizing performance, the authors used two related measures of a firm's operating performance, assessed in the 3 firm-years following the downsizing announcement.

name: Downsizing
definition: Downsizing is often defined as an intentional effort to permanently reduce personnel in order to improve organizational efficiency and/or effectiveness. Downsizings can be conceptualized as attempts to improve performance by reducing organizational slack.

name: Scope of downsizing
authors_terms: ["scope of the downsizing", "broad scope", "narrow scope", "broadly scoped downsizings", "narrowly scoped downsizings"]
definition: An important dimension of variation in firms' approaches to implementing downsizing is the range of organizational elements affected, which the authors refer to as the scope of the downsizing. Narrowly scoped downsizings focus almost exclusively on reducing personnel, whereas broadly scoped downsizings also pursue significant organizational redesign.

name: Timing of downsizing
definition: The authors consider whether firms do better if they initiate downsizing reactively—after performance has declined—or proactively, when performance has not declined.

name: Knowledge sharing
definition: Critical to the efficiency of knowledge production is the process of knowledge sharing between individuals possessing different types of knowledge. The study creates exogenous variation in opportunities for information-rich, face-to-face encounters between cross-disciplinary scientists.

name: Knowledge transfer
definition: Knowledge transfer involves the movement of facts, relationships, and insights from one setting to another, and becomes evident when the experience acquired by an individual, group or organization in one setting is applied in another setting.

name: Knowledge creation
definition: Knowledge creation refers to the generation of facts, relationships and insights to solve new problems. The emphasis on new knowledge is what distinguishes the process of knowledge transfer from creation.

name: Knowledge diffusion
definition: Knowledge diffusion refers to the process through which transferred or newly created knowledge is disseminated and used by other individuals, groups and organizations.

name: Field similarity
definition: Field specialties are developed through an individual's educational background, skills and training. Knowledge similarity describes the distance between the field specialties and intellectual specialties of two knowledge sharing partners.

name: Intellectual similarity
definition: In contrast, intellectual specialties are closely aligned to personal interests and passions that evolve over time. Individuals can have memberships in multiple intellectual specialties depending on their current pursuits and priorities.

name: Elemental collaboration
definition: We examine a specific type of tie persistence, namely the likelihood that an elemental collaboration persists into a complete knowledge product. In science, grant coapplications and copublications represent two essential but opposing ends of knowledge creation, from idea-generation to final output.

name: Target firm technology resources
authors_terms: ["target firm technology resources", "target firm R&D resources", "target firm R&D", "target R&D", "target firm's stock of R&D investments"]
definition: R&D is a recognized part of developing technology resources that are built over time through cumulative investments. Target firm R&D investments represent a primary motivation for acquisition activity.

name: Acquirer absorptive capacity
authors_terms: ["acquirer absorptive capacity", "acquiring firm absorptive capacity", "acquirer R&D", "acquiring firm R&D intensity", "relative R&D intensity"]
definition: An acquiring firm's 'absorptive capacity,' or its ability to recognize, assimilate, and convert new information to commercial ends, is critical. The capacity to recognize and exploit external technology is a function of a firm's R&D intensity that enables an acquiring firm to integrate a target firm's technology resources.

name: Acquirer marketing resources
authors_terms: ["acquiring firm marketing resources", "acquirer marketing resources", "acquirer marketing"]
definition: Advertising investments represent a key component of a firm's marketing resources. Marketing resources can play a critical role in a firm's ability to recognize and target customer needs and position products relative to competitors.

name: Post-acquisition firm performance
authors_terms: ["post-acquisition firm performance", "acquisition performance", "acquiring firm's abnormal return", "Jensen's alpha", "firm performance"]
definition: Jensen's alpha measures the average difference or abnormal return between competing investments. Positive values of Jensen's alpha indicate that an acquiring firm outperformed the market benchmark or S&P 500.

name: Local political connection
authors_terms: ["political connection", "City_PC", "connections with local politicians", "political connections in a candidate location"]
definition: A firm is considered to have political connections in a city if the city has at least one person in the current leadership position (party secretary or mayor) who used to be either the party secretary or the mayor of the city where the firm's headquarters is located after the firm became publicly listed. The presence of a firm's political connections in one location increases the expected benefits that the firm can obtain in that location.

name: Location choice
authors_terms: ["location choice", "Entry", "location choice decisions", "likelihood of choosing that location"]
definition: The dependent variable is an indicator of whether the listed firm established a new subsidiary in the candidate city in the given year, which the firm selects from a choice set of all candidate cities.

name: Local unemployment
definition: The city-level unemployment rate, measured as the proportion of unemployed citizens in the entire city population. Higher local unemployment pressures local politicians to find ways, including imposing costs on the firms they are able to influence, to alleviate such problems.

name: Position responsibility for local unemployment
authors_terms: ["political positions that come with primary responsibilities for resolving local unemployment issues", "responsibility in resolving local unemployment issues", "heterogeneity of political positions"]
definition: Some political positions carry a greater responsibility to resolve unemployment issues, and the politicians who hold more responsibility in resolving local unemployment issues are more likely to pressure their connected firms to overemploy compared with politicians holding less of such responsibility.

name: Ability to leverage higher-level political power
authors_terms: ["ability to leverage higher-level political power", "ability to leverage the power of higher-level governments", "leverage the political power of the central government", "TMT_ExCentral_Official"]
definition: If the firm can leverage the political power belonging to governments at a higher administrative level, particularly the central government, then the firm is more capable of resisting the demand made by local politicians to expend firm resources to help alleviate local unemployment conditions.

name: Business discussion network nonredundancy
authors_terms: ["nonredundancy in the academic's exoinstitutional business discussion network", "nonredundancy business", "nonredundancy in the business network"]
definition: Burt defines a structural hole as a relationship of nonredundancy between two contacts, meaning that contacts are not connected in any way and so can provide information benefits that are additive. Applied to the business discussion network, nonredundancy is the property that gives rise to opportunity enhancement, access to information and resources, timing, and referrals.

name: Social support network nonredundancy
authors_terms: ["nonredundancy in the academic's exoinstitutional social support network", "nonredundancy support", "nonredundancy in the social support network"]
definition: The authors believe that the presence of structural holes in exoinstitutional social support networks, which are more akin to 'black holes' as far as academic exodus is concerned, will not generate enough emotional closeness, support, and encouragement to induce an academic to leave the university.

name: Business discussion tie strength
definition: The strength of the tie combines closeness with the frequency of communication; the authors measure the weakness of the tie as the average of frequency and closeness scores in the business discussion network. Strong ties to nonredundant contacts are argued to be required if the academic is to access the information and resources needed.

name: Social support tie strength
definition: The probability of trust increases with the strength of these relationships, and strong ties in the social support network provide resources that counter social and psychological stress; strong ties to the cohesive social support contacts are required for the academic inventor to reap the full benefits of the network.

name: Academic exodus
definition: Every academic inventor is faced with a critical career choice: the inventor may leave the university to completely focus his or her energy in the firm, or may decide to remain in the university and may or may not accept a part-time position in the company. The authors define the former scenario as academic exodus and the latter as academic stasis.

name: Team-level nonredundancy
authors_terms: ["egocentric team-level nonredundancy measure", "team-level nonredundancy", "nonredundant contacts in the team's exoinstitutional business discussion network"]
definition: The egocentric team-level nonredundancy measure is treated as a configural unit property, since means are ambiguous and questionable representations of higher-level constructs; the authors propose an alternative formula to calculate the maximum number of indirect ties that could be reported by the team's members.

name: Spinout structure
authors_terms: ["orthodox spinout", "hybrid spinout", "technology spinout", "trichotomous categorization of university spinouts"]
definition: Nicolaou and Birley (2000) propose a trichotomous categorization of university spinouts into orthodox, hybrid, and technology spinouts. An orthodox spinout involves both the academic inventors and the technology spinning out from the institution; a hybrid spinout involves the technology spinning out and the academics retaining their university position but holding a directorship, membership of the scientific advisory board, or other part-time position; a technology spinout involves the technology spinning out but the academics maintaining no substantive connection with the newly established firm.

name: Contractual complexity
definition: The particular contractual provisions that firms incorporate into their collaborative agreements; the authors examine how such provisions bundle together and whether contractual complexity is a multidimensional or unidimensional construct.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Transaction-specific investments made by a firm in an alliance; when asset specificity is low, by definition resources can be readily deployed to other relationships or businesses, and partner identity and continuity therefore are not important.

name: Prior ties
authors_terms: ["prior ties", "prior alliances", "prior collaborative relationships", "repeat collaborators", "prior collaborative agreements"]
definition: Prior collaborative relationships between the two parties, measured as the number of prior alliances between the firms.

name: Time boundedness
definition: Whether or not parties put explicit time bounds on the collaborative agreement, i.e., whether the agreement was meant to last a definite length of time at the time the contract was signed, as opposed to a collaboration whose duration was open-ended.

name: Enforcement provisions
definition: Provisions that are concerned with confidentiality, proprietary information, alliance termination, arbitration, and lawsuits; they deal with concerns surrounding partners' knowledge, their behavior outside of the alliance, and severe breaches that would bring about termination or the need to pursue lawsuits or arbitration.

name: Coordination provisions
definition: The weaker, informational provisions that relate more directly to the monitoring and adaptation of the collaborative agreement, including rights of reports for relevant transactions, notification rights for departures to the agreement, and auditing rights.

name: Financial restatement
definition: Following prior research, the authors focus on material financial restatements, which are 'a function of significant accounting problems within firms.' Financial misrepresentation exemplifies a potential failure in governance and oversight.

name: Organizational status
definition: Organizational status reflects 'the position in a social hierarchy that results from accumulated acts of deference.' As such, status derives from a firm's network position and prominence of network connections.

name: Relative partner status
authors_terms: ["Focal Firm-Alter Difference in Status", "relative differences in firm status", "relative status"]
definition: The status of a potential interlock partner (alter firm) relative to the focal firm, i.e., the degree to which the alter firm is of higher status than the focal firm in the interlock network.

name: Board interlock tie formation
authors_terms: ["board interlock tie formation", "new interlock tie formation", "interlock formation", "tie formation"]
definition: A board interlock is formed when an individual affiliated with one firm is appointed to serve on another firm's board. Interlock formation is an outcome of the director selection process that reflects the socially embedded nature of corporate boards.

name: Board interlock tie dissolution
authors_terms: ["tie dissolution", "interlock dissolution", "disruption in interlock ties", "tie maintenance"]
definition: Interlock ties are dissolved as a result of individual-level director turnover, and to prevent spillover effects interlocking firms may initiate the dissolution of ties with offending firms.

name: Reciprocity
definition: Reciprocity captures the tendency of a firm with an existing incoming tie to reciprocate, forming an outgoing tie with the same counterpart firm.

name: Transitive closure
authors_terms: ["transitivity", "transitive closure", "transitive triplets", "a friend of a friend"]
definition: Transitive Closure captures the commonly reflected social process, 'a friend of a friend is my friend.' Firms may be more likely to seek interlocks with other firms currently tied to a common third party in the network.

name: Analyst recommendations
authors_terms: ["analyst recommendations", "average analyst recommendations", "positive analyst recommendations", "analyst recommendation"]
definition: Specifically, positive analyst recommendations (a 'buy' recommendation) suggest that the analyst believes that the current share price undervalues the firm's future fundamentals. In contrast, a negative analyst recommendation (a 'sell' recommendation) is issued if the analyst expects the firm's share price to underperform relative to the market.

name: Income-increasing earnings management
definition: We define income increasing earnings management as the use of judgment in financial reporting that leads to higher reported earnings in the focal accounting period. For shareholders, income increasing earnings management increases agency costs as it involves financial reporting decisions that mislead stakeholders, thereby exacerbating information asymmetry.

name: CEO extraversion
definition: Extraversion captures a broader group of traits, most of which relate to individuals' desires for interpersonal engagement.

name: CEO emotional stability
definition: Emotional stability broadly describes individuals' tendency to experience emotional stress in that emotionally stable individuals remain calm in difficult situations, are not as easily panicked, and are, thus, better able to adapt to new situations.

name: CEO agreeableness
definition: Agreeableness captures traits related to interpersonal behavior. Specifically, agreeableness describes individuals' attitudes toward others.

name: CEO conscientiousness
definition: Conscientiousness describes individuals' traits relating to their ability to succeed in a given task environment.

name: CEO openness
definition: Openness is positively correlated with environmental sensitivity, which is also referred to as sensory processing sensitivity. The Big Five personality traits are Extraversion (vs. Introversion), Emotional stability (vs. Neuroticism), Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to experience.

name: Stock-option backdating
definition: Stock-option backdating is the term used to describe misreporting the date of stock-option grants-reporting such grants without proper disclosure. Corporate executives engaging in this practice intentionally report an incorrect date of the stock-option grant on official documents audited by the firm's auditor and subsequently submitted to the SEC and investors.

name: Local auditor office backdating
authors_terms: ["backdating by proximate firms with the same auditor", "the frequency of adoption among firms served by the same local professional office", "the level of backdating at the local auditor office"]
definition: A variable that captures the proportion of backdating firms served by the auditor's local office: here i indicates the audit firm, backdatingizt is the number of backdating firms audited by auditor i in city z at time t, and Companiesizt is the total number of firms audited by auditor i in city z at time t.

name: Local peer backdating
authors_terms: ["backdating by proximate firms", "backdating neighbors", "peer effects on backdating"]
definition: Following established research on local diffusion, a variable that captures the proportion of backdating by proximate firms; here z is the city in which the focal organization's headquarters is located, t is the year of the grant award, Backdating denotes the firms that backdate their option grants, and Companies represents the city's population of public firms.

name: Uncertainty about practice appropriateness
authors_terms: ["uncertainty about the appropriateness of backdating", "high uncertainty", "reduced uncertainty", "legal ambiguity", "liminality"]
definition: These practices emerge in an institutional environment that is unclear about their label or moral standing, and uncertainty about the appropriateness of financial statement misrepresentations was sharply reduced by the July 2002 passage of Sarbanes-Oxley, although backdating was not specifically outlawed until it was publicly exposed in 2006.

name: Market overlap with arch incumbent
authors_terms: ["arch incumbent", "arch incumbency", "degree of market overlap", "percent of market overlap", "ArcInc"]
definition: For a de novo venture, the arch incumbent is the particular incumbent with whom it shares the most market or product overlap, and would potentially have the most to lose and therefore be the most motivated to launch an aggressive reaction. Market overlap is the percent of the venture's seat capacity that directly competes with a given incumbent in the same city-pair markets.

name: Venture survival
definition: The continued existence of a de novo venture in the industry after entry. Because schedules of defunct ventures showed no signs of intended route withdrawals, the probability of a de novo venture's post-entry exit, as witnessed by a lack of continued scheduled passenger air service, is used as the dependent variable and is treated as negative performance.

name: Inaugural capacity
authors_terms: ["inaugural capacity", "inaugural production capacity", "aggressive entry", "firm-wide capacity", "scale of entry"]
definition: The scale of a de novo venture's entry at inauguration, which signals the availability of resources and allows the venture to attain larger economies of scale earlier. Aggressive entry by a new venture is advocated as a means to increase survival odds.

name: Different market positioning
definition: Adopting a market position (low-cost, differentiated, or niche) that differs from that of the arch incumbent, which may signal the intention of a new venture to avoid poaching the most valued customers of its incumbents and hence increases the probability of entry forbearance.

name: CEO submissiveness
authors_terms: ["CEO submissiveness", "perceptions of CEO submissiveness", "submissive victims", "unassured-submissive interpersonal style"]
definition: Submissive victims possess characteristics others perceive as making them more unwilling or unable to respond to attacks. As a firm's CEO is perceived as more submissive, rivals are motivated to exploit the perception that the more submissive CEO will be less willing or able to respond and direct competitive attacks at that firm.

name: CEO provocativeness
definition: Provocative victims are attacked because their psychological, behavioral, and social characteristics manifest in ways perceived as threatening to the point that others are provoked to 'direct aggressive action against the perceived source.' Since CEOs who threaten rivals to a greater extent provoke more attacks on their firms as means of reprisal and behavior modification as well as to restore relative standing or security, provocativeness is expected to relate positively to attacks.

name: Competitive attacks
authors_terms: ["competitive attacks", "attacks on the CEO's firm", "competitive actions"]
definition: Competitive action is an 'externally directed, specific, and observable competitive move initiated by a firm.' Attacks are the four kinds of competitive action in which the focal firm or CEO is listed as a target: pricing attacks, product attacks, marketing attacks, and expansion attacks.

name: Partnering proactiveness
authors_terms: ["partnering proactiveness", "proactive portfolio formation", "proactive formation of alliance portfolios", "proactive alliance formation", "proactiveness"]
definition: We define partnering proactiveness as a firm's engagement in discovering and acting on new alliance opportunities ahead of competitors.

name: Relational governance
authors_terms: ["relational governance", "relational governance of the portfolio", "relational orientation"]
definition: We define relational governance as the extent to which an organization engages in behavioral routines that facilitate the development of informal self-enforcing safeguards in their relationships with various alliance partners in the portfolio.

name: Portfolio coordination
definition: Portfolio coordination comprises various organizational processes by which a focal firm engages in integrating and synchronizing activities, strategies, and knowledge flows across partners in their alliance network.

name: Alliance portfolio capital
definition: A firm's alliance portfolio capital is a critical source of competitive advantage, consisting as it does of an aggregate of interorganizational resources that are linked to a focal firm through their participation in a set of alliances. It captures the 'health/vigor' of a firm's alliances across the competitive strength of the portfolio as a group, the strength of relationships with individual partners, and the brand equity of the focal firm as a partner.

name: Alliance function
authors_terms: ["alliance function", "dedicated alliance function", "formalized alliance function", "formalized alliance program", "formal alliance program"]
definition: A dedicated alliance function is a centralized point of coordination, expressed as a separate and dedicated program that oversees the firm's alliances; respondents were asked whether their organization had a formal, dedicated program that was responsible for overseeing the firm's alliances.

name: Alliance portfolio diversity
authors_terms: ["portfolio diversity", "alliance diversity", "alliance portfolio diversity", "diversity of the portfolio"]
definition: A firm's alliance strategy as reflected in the composition of its alliance portfolio, i.e., whether it is focused narrowly on specific parts of the value chain or diffused across various activities. Portfolio diversity was operationalized as a variation of Blau's index, computed from the number of a firm's alliances in each of six value chain areas: new product development, research and development/technology, marketing/distribution, supplier, manufacturing, and customer.

name: Firm market performance
definition: For firm market performance, we adapted Venkatraman and Ramanujam's (1986) formative scale and measured four aspects, namely, market share, sales growth, market development, and product development.

name: Radical flank
authors_terms: ["radical flank", "existence of a radical flank", "combination of radical and moderate social movement tactics"]
definition: The existence of a radical flank, that is, the coexistence of both radical and moderate tactics by social movement activists. The radical flank variable is constructed as a dummy variable, coded as one to indicate the presence of both radical and moderate tactics during a facility's licensing process.

name: Regulatory discretion
definition: Regulatory agencies' freedom to interpret and implement public policies written by elected officials. Regulatory discretion stems from the institutional arrangements between elected officials and regulatory agencies.

name: Regulatory approval
definition: Our dependent variable is license approval of hydroelectric power facilities (one if approved, zero otherwise). After a license is approved, withdrawn, or denied, the case is dropped from the data set.

name: Entry timing
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "timing of entry", "entry lag", "order of entry"]
definition: This paper will focus on the first of those dimensions—the timing of a firm's entry into an emerging market. While the great majority of the research in this area has focused on the relationship between entry timing and subsequent firm performance, this paper will address a much less researched question: what factors determine when an existing firm enters a new market.

name: Research and development intensity
authors_terms: ["technological resources", "R&D intensity", "research and development intensity", "R&D expenditures/sales"]
definition: Technological resources refer to the commitment that a firm makes to research and development (Mahoney and Pandian, 1992).

name: Direct sales force
definition: The marketing resource that we will focus our attention on is the firm's investment in a direct sales force.

name: Internal financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources", "internal financial resources", "available cash and unused debt capacity"]
definition: We only expect internal financial resources (available cash and unused debt capacity) to influence timing of entry. Thus, it is likely that only financially secure firms will be able to afford the costs of early entry.

name: Commitment to threatened market
authors_terms: ["commitment to threatened market", "commitment to a threatened market", "presence in a threatened market"]
definition: The threat that a new product presents to a firm's current businesses should affect how long it waits before entering the new market. Additionally, firms with experience in a related business may have an easier time becoming early entrants since they already possess many of the necessary skills and capabilities needed to compete in the related field.

name: Firm size
definition: In this study, an organization's size refers to number of employees; this measure seems particularly relevant when considering influences upon the speed of decision making.

name: Firm diversity
definition: A value close to two for DW signifies a highly diversified firm with many unrelated businesses. A value close to zero signals the opposite.

name: First mover advantages
authors_terms: ["first mover advantages", "opportunities to build a first mover advantage", "first mover disadvantages"]
definition: Lieberman and Montgomery (1988) argue that first mover advantages arise from three sources: technological leadership (experience curve; patents and inimitable technology), the preemption of scarce assets, and switching costs.

name: Firm resources
definition: Firm resources form the building blocks of firm capabilities (Teece, Pisano, and Shuen, 1997), which are the basis for a firm's ability to compete against rivals. Chatterjee and Wernerfelt (1991) placed firm resources into three categories: physical, intangible, and financial.

name: Complementarity of partner distinctive competencies
authors_terms: ["complementarity", "potential complementarity", "complementarity of the distinctive competencies of the partners"]
definition: Complementarity is the extent to which the joint venture partners bring nonredundant distinctive competencies to the partnership. In this study it is operationalized as the combination of the distinctive competencies of the joint venture partners and reflects only potential complementarities based on partner selection.

name: Partner distinctive competence
authors_terms: ["distinctive competencies", "contributions in each functional area of distinctive competence"]
definition: Individual firms develop skills and resources that become their distinctive competencies in competing with other firms. The study rates the importance of each firm's contributions in 10 possible areas of distinctive competence in exploration and production.

name: Ownership and control
definition: Ownership/control concerns the question of which partner asserts the most influence or control and the degree of control asserted by each partner. The study examines control as comparative influence of the partners within each functional area rather than as a global shared-versus-dominant dichotomy.

name: Joint venture autonomy
definition: Joint venture autonomy is the degree of decision making latitude allowed to the joint venture management by the partners.

name: Joint venture performance
definition: Performance is conceptualized as the effectiveness of the joint venture in meeting the goals of the partner firms. It is measured on a number of dimensions using the partner firm managers' subjective assessments on a seven-point Likert scale.

name: Corporate parent density
authors_terms: ["parental density", "corporate parent density", "density of corporate parents with PC businesses"]
definition: Parental density is the number of corporate parents with PC businesses. Corporate parent density equaled the number of corporate parents whose PC businesses were alive in a given year.

name: Corporate parent mass
authors_terms: ["parental mass", "mass of corporate parents in their non-PC businesses"]
definition: Parental mass equals the sum of the sizes of multibusiness organizations, net of their PC businesses, that populate the environment of a specific PC firm. Mass attributes greater importance to the relatively larger firms whose size is thought to contribute to the legitimacy of a new industry.

name: Stand-alone density
definition: Stand-alone density equaled the number of freestanding PC businesses in a given year. If more stand-alones each generate greater rivalry, this rivalry will be reflected in standalone density.

name: Stand-alone mass
definition: Stand-alone mass equals the sum of the sizes of single-business PC firms that populate the environment of a focal PC maker. Larger stand-alones are expected to generate greater rivalry.

name: Corporate parent age
authors_terms: ["corporate parent age", "parent age", "age of a corporate parent"]
definition: Corporate parent age is the number of years since a corporate parent had been founded. Older parents are seen as more constrained by past practice and as imposing more resistance and bureaucratic delay on their children.

name: Business size
definition: The size of a child is a rough proxy for the stock of resources a child is able to build for itself; larger children have the slack to weather misfortunes without falling back on their parents and are less reliant on parents for access to financial credit.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Failure was defined as the death of an entire stand-alone business or the exit from the PC industry of a diversified corporation. A business was coded as failing in year t if it sold no PCs in year t + 1 and all subsequent years in the sample window.

name: Complementor alliance
authors_terms: ["complementor alliance", "alliance relationship with their complementors", "alliance form", "alliance mode"]
definition: An organizational form in which firms cooperate with their complementors through an alliance, a hybrid between markets and hierarchies that provides greater adaptability than markets while preserving greater incentives than hierarchies. Firms that have an alliance relationship with their complementors are expected to be better positioned to achieve the coordinated adaptation required to commercialize the new technology.

name: Complementor integration
authors_terms: ["complementor integration", "firms that integrate into the complementary activities", "hierarchy", "integrated organizational form", "Integrated Salary Model (ISM)"]
definition: A hierarchical organizational form in which complementors are integrated within the firm; in this study, an Integrated Salary Model (ISM) entails that hospitals use an integrated organizational form and employ their own physicians. Integration provides control and adaptation but imposes higher organizational costs from impaired incentives and bureaucratic distortions.

name: Alliance scope
authors_terms: ["alliance scope", "scope of the alliance", "scope of the activities that are carried out through the alliance relationship"]
definition: Alliance scope refers to the extent of activities that partners jointly carry out through the alliance as compared to their total set of activities.

name: Investment in a new technology
authors_terms: ["investment in a new technology", "hospital's decision to invest in new medical imaging technologies", "technology investment", "propensity to invest in a new technology"]
definition: The hospital's decision to invest in new medical imaging technologies, which have been key drivers of technical advances in the health care industry. Our dependent variable measures whether a hospital has invested in the new imaging technology in a given year.

name: Market context
authors_terms: ["market context", "dynamic market context", "perceived market environment", "environmental uncertainty and dynamism"]
definition: The perceived market environment facing the firm. Following Milliken (1990), the authors focused on perceptions and interpretations of specific changes in the industry environment and wrote seven items to assess market context, asking for the future probability of the event mentioned.

name: Customer and competitor change
definition: One of the three variables derived from the seven market context items, created after factor analysis suggested a three-factor solution for the environment items and labeled 'customer/competitor changes'.

name: Margin and volume pressure
definition: One of the three variables derived from the seven market context items after the factor analysis of the environment items, labeled 'margin/volume pressure'.

name: Internet channels
definition: One of the three variables derived from the seven market context items after the factor analysis of the environment items, labeled 'Internet channels', tapping the emergence of new Internet-based supplier and distribution channels.

name: Modular product architecture
authors_terms: ["modular product architecture", "modular product architectures", "product modularity", "modular products", "modularity", "product platforms"]
definition: Modular product architectures (or platforms) are created by decomposing a product design into relatively independent components and by specifying standard interfaces that define the inputs and outputs that flow between interacting components. Formally speaking, a modular architecture is one that minimizes interdependencies between modules performing different functions.

name: Strategic flexibility
definition: The concept of strategic flexibility broadly denotes firm abilities to respond to rapidly changing markets. In the context of product competition it can be operationalized as the number of product variations offered, the frequency of new model introductions, as well as the number of entirely new products introduced.

name: Model variety
definition: The total number of models/variants offered by the firm, one of the three indicators used to operationalize strategic flexibility.

name: Model introduction rate
authors_terms: ["model introduction rate", "new model introductions", "number of new models/variants introduced"]
definition: The total number of new models/variants introduced during 1998, one of the three indicators used to operationalize strategic flexibility.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["new product introductions", "new product introduction rate", "number of entirely new products introduced"]
definition: The number of entirely new products introduced during 1998, one of the three indicators used to operationalize strategic flexibility.

name: Firm performance
definition: Perceived performance was measured using three items developed by Powell and Dent-Micallef (1997); the authors note that subjective measures of performance have been widely used and that most studies find high convergent validity with objective measures such as publicly available accounting data.

name: Innovation climate
definition: Organizational climate is defined as the perceptions organization members share of fundamental elements of their organization; the authors focus on one element, the firm's orientation toward innovation, which they label innovation climate. A positive innovation climate exists where the development of new ideas is encouraged and rewarded and where there is a strongly shared mission among employees.

name: Entrepreneurial strategic intent
definition: Defined as the existence of plans for redesigning product development processes and for entering new or existing markets with new or existing technologies.

name: Modular organizational structure
definition: In capturing modular structure the authors included items about the existence of small, autonomous units and rotation of personnel between different product areas; modular organizational structures are described as one of the complementary organizational resources.

name: Modular work processes
definition: As indicators of modular process the authors used several items focusing on codification, standardization and reengineering of work processes, as well as items asking about knowledge management systems and knowledge transfer; modular work processes are described as one of the complementary organizational resources.

name: Legitimacy transfer
authors_terms: ["legitimacy transfer", "faux craft", "imitation of peripheral products by market-center organizations"]
definition: We conceptualize legitimacy transfer as the process whereby organizational forms borrow 'social acceptance from established forms and products with which they share a space of material and symbolic resources.'

name: Entry into the market center
authors_terms: ["craft entry", "entry of peripheral organizations into the market center", "peripheral entry"]
definition: Craft entry identifies the entry of craft breweries into the market center. Entry is considered to have occurred when a brewery's first product logs a sale in a given market.

name: Local identity
definition: A local identity embodies this collective past or heritage and helps consumers to form impressions about an organization's products, its history, and the ways in which they were produced. Ultimately, a local identity serves as a credible source of authenticity that facilitates growth for peripheral producers in the market center.

name: Product proliferator identity
definition: Additional research also identifies product proliferation as a salient code through which to convey distinctiveness and authenticity. A product proliferator identity serves to strengthen the link between an organization's internal identity and the broader collective identity, which can facilitate greater engagement of market-center consumers.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm sales is the dollar sales by craft brewery i in market j in year t; lagged sales are also controlled for on the right-hand side of the equation, so the dependent variable represents year-over-year sales growth of craft breweries.

name: Density of peripheral organizations in the market center
authors_terms: ["craft density", "density", "competition among peripheral organizations in the market center"]
definition: We also account for ... the density or count of the number of craft breweries in each market (Craft density), which represents a measure of competitive rivalry (and interaction term in H3 and H4).

name: Acquisition completion
authors_terms: ["M&A completion", "completion likelihood", "completion of an announced M&A", "completion of a focal M&A"]
definition: With regard to the public takeover phase, completion represents the most basic goal variable. We measured the dependent variable, M&A completion, by creating a dummy variable, which took on the value of 1 if an announced M&A was completed, and 0 otherwise.

name: Prior acquisition success experience
authors_terms: ["success experience", "prior aggregate success experience", "composite success experience", "completed deals"]
definition: Together this implies, first, that firms with past success in consummating M&As have routines in place that predispose them to complete a focal deal; second, that each success entails a strictly positive learning potential for improving performance due to the new information it conveys; and, third, that the contribution of each subsequent success to raising future completion likelihood decreases due to the self-limiting nature of learning from success.

name: Prior acquisition failure experience
authors_terms: ["failure experience", "prior aggregate failure experience", "composite failure experience", "abandoned deals"]
definition: Given the intention to complete an announced M&A, abandonment signals flaws in the routines that the bidding firm enacts during the public takeover stage. This failure experience induces 'problemistic search' for superior solutions.

name: Component modularity
authors_terms: ["component modularity", "modularity degree of component i", "modularity of sourced components"]
definition: Component modularity is the extent to which a component performs a few functions and is connected to other components by open standard interfaces. A perfect modular component performs only one function and has only open standard interfaces.

name: Organizational modularity
authors_terms: ["organizational modularity", "buyer-supplier information sharing", "degree of coupling between organizations"]
definition: Organizational modularity is related to the complexity, intensity, and frequency of information sharing between two organizations. This study captures the degree of coupling between organizations (organizational modularity) by analyzing the extent of the buyer-supplier information sharing as regards three key business processes: new product development, contract/price negotiation, and logistics, so that the degree of buyer-supplier information sharing is an inverse proxy for organizational modularity.

name: Component technological change
authors_terms: ["component technological change", "technological change", "rate of component technological change"]
definition: Refering to Henderson and Clark's (1990) definitions of incremental and modular innovation, the authors define component technological change as the rate of change of the product and process technologies underlying a given component within an existing product architecture.

name: CEO positional tenure
definition: CEO positional tenure was the CEO's number of years in office.

name: TMT risk-taking propensity
definition: The TMT's proclivity to engage in risky projects and preference for bold vs. cautious acts to achieve firm objectives.

name: Pursuit of entrepreneurial initiatives
authors_terms: ["the firm's pursuit of entrepreneurial initiatives", "entrepreneurial initiatives"]
definition: A three-dimensional metaconstruct made up of innovation, venturing, and renewal activities. Decisions are made to either modify or abandon established products, processes, and methods in favor of new ones based on a product or service vision for which markets do not yet exist and that may take years to generate a profit.

name: Firm performance relative to competitors
authors_terms: ["performance", "their firms' performance relative to that of their competitors'"]
definition: CEOs assessed their firms' performance relative to that of their competitors' on eight different dimensions (growth in sales, growth in market share, etc.).

name: Proportion of outlets franchised
