authors_terms: ["proportion of outlets franchised", "proportion franchised", "use of contractual forms of governance"]
definition: We use the proportion of outlets franchised in a given year as a measure of the use of contractual forms of governance, because franchisee outlets are operated by residual claimants and company-owned outlets are operated by salaried managers.

name: Franchising experience
authors_terms: ["franchising experience", "length of franchising experience", "firms that have franchised in the past"]
definition: Managers of firms that have franchised in the past are more experienced with that governance form and have developed capabilities that support franchising, and thus seek to grow their firms through franchising. Firms that have franchised in the past have developed a set of routines, capabilities, and cognitive schemata that are different from those of firms that have operated their own outlets.

name: Recent franchising experience
authors_terms: ["recent franchising experience", "recent use of franchising", "recent experiences"]
definition: Recent experiences of organizations are more prone to be repeated than temporally distant experiences and are more important in shaping current organizational decisions. Strategies and procedures used more recently are more 'cognitively available' to decision makers because memory decays over time.

name: Industry profitability
definition: Industry profitability was measured as the five-year average return on assets for the four-digit SIC industry in which the firm did the largest share of its business.

name: Organizational profitability
definition: Firm profitability is the difference between a firm's average return on assets and its industry's average return on assets during the five-year period.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry concentration is the degree to which an industry is dominated by a few companies.

name: Organization size
definition: Organization size is usually defined as the number of members in the organization, the organization's sales, gross revenues, or net profits, the organization's capacity to render services, or the quantity of assets held by the firm.

name: Structural complexity
definition: Structural complexity is the degree of spread and segmentation in an organization's structure, reflecting the combined effects of horizontal, vertical, and spatial differentiation.

name: Organizational decentralization
definition: Decentralization refers to the locus and dispersion of decision making in an organization.

name: Ethical climate
definition: Ethical climate is defined as the prevailing perceptions of typical organizational practices and procedures that have ethical content.

name: Corporate illegality
definition: Corporate illegality consists of actions (of omission or commission) by any individual or group within a business organization that violate an administrative, civil, or criminal law, and for which the organization is the primary intended beneficiary.

name: Divestiture of unrelated acquisition
definition: Acquisition success was defined in terms of whether the acquisition was divested (unsuccessful) or retained (successful), as few successful acquisitions are divested and fewer unsuccessful acquisitions are retained. The dependent variable was determined by tracking each acquisition over a 5-year period.

name: Cash flow contributions of the acquired unit
authors_terms: ["cash flow contributions", "contributions of cash", "cash flow from unit"]
definition: Contributions of cash were the total cash and monetary contributions transferred from the acquired firm to the acquirer. When the acquired company's cash flow contributions are low, the acquiring firm relies more heavily on raising resources through financial capital markets.

name: Debt capacity
definition: Postacquisition debt capacity is generally affected by the acquiring company's postacquisition debt-to-equity ratio: higher postacquisition debt for the acquiring firm means it has lower debt capacity. The acquirer's debt capacity was measured as the debt-to-equity ratio.

name: Current slack
definition: Slack has two dimensions that are relevant to internal resources: current slack, the amount of financial resources accessible to an organization in the short term (it is affected by the current ratio).

name: Potential slack
definition: Slack has two dimensions that are relevant to internal resources: potential slack, the amount of financial resources accessible in the long term (it is affected by the ratio of sales, general and administrative expenses to total sales, or SGA/sales).

name: Diversification strategy
definition: The internal control systems necessary to realize internal governance efficiencies from unrelated acquisitions can be represented by the acquiring firm's diversity profile. Diversity strategy was measured by using the concentric index of diversification (Caves et al., 1980), a continuous measure.

name: Relative size of acquired firm
authors_terms: ["relative size of the acquired firm", "acquired unit size", "size of the unrelated acquired firm (in relation to the acquiring firm)"]
definition: The relative size of the acquired firm was measured as the number of employees (logged) of that firm divided by the number of employees (logged) of the acquirer. Acquisitions of large unrelated companies are one method of satisfying managerial self-interests.

name: Variability in revenue streams
authors_terms: ["variability in revenue streams", "sales variability", "variability in the parent's sales"]
definition: Variability in revenue streams was measured as the difference in the standard deviation of the parent's sales before and after the acquisition of the unrelated business unit. When the parent firm's sales variability decreases after an unrelated acquisition, coinsurance increases and the acquisition is expected to be retained.

name: Change in cash flow contributions of the acquired unit
authors_terms: ["cash flow contributions over time", "change in cash flow"]
definition: The acquired unit's cash flow contributions over time, computed as the proportionate change in those contributions between the time of the acquisition and the time of divestiture (or the end of the five-year period if the acquisition had been retained). Changes for all variables (other than the sizes of the acquired firm) were calculated as (t2-t1)/t1, which allowed proportionate changes in the value of each variable to be determined.

name: Change in debt capacity
definition: The parent's debt capacity over time, computed as the proportionate change in the parent's debt-to-equity ratio between the time of the acquisition and the time of divestiture (or the end of the five-year period); a larger increase in the debt-to-equity ratio indicates a larger reduction in debt capacity.

name: Change in current slack
authors_terms: ["current ratio over time", "change in current ratio"]
definition: The parent's current slack over time, computed as the proportionate change in the parent's current ratio between the time of the acquisition and the time of divestiture (or the end of the five-year period).

name: Change in potential slack
definition: The parent's potential slack over time, computed as the proportionate change in the parent's ratio of sales, general and administrative expenses to sales between the time of the acquisition and the time of divestiture (or the end of the five-year period).

name: Performance relative to aspirations
definition: An attainment discrepancy occurs when performance deviates from aspirations, and may serve as an inducement for organizational search and risk-taking. Performance aspirations serve as reference points that help distinguish perceived failures and successes, and typically evolve over time as functions of a firm's own historical performance and the performance of comparable others.

name: Absorbed slack
definition: Absorbed slack, a particular form of organizational slack, refers to organizational capacity above and beyond what is required for a firm's day-to-day operations, such as excess facilities and personnel for research and development (R&D).

name: Equity ties to existing partners
authors_terms: ["equity ties", "equity commitment to existing partners", "%equity alliances"]
definition: Equity ties include joint ventures in which partners share equity in a newly created entity, and minority equity investments in which one or both partners make an investment in the other in exchange for equity. In contrast to purely contractual alliances, equity ties require alliance partners to make ex-ante investments, which increase their commitment to each other.

name: Firm-specific uncertainty
definition: Firm-specific uncertainty refers to ambiguity stemming from idiosyncratic sources regarding the expected outcomes of organizational actions.

name: Alliances with novel partners in existing resources
authors_terms: ["novel partners - existing resources", "alliances with novel partners focusing on existing resources"]
definition: The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving a novel partner and exclusively focusing on resources already accessible through the firm's existing alliance portfolio. A partner is novel in the sense that the firm had no active alliance(s) with that partner in its existing alliance portfolio.

name: Alliances with existing partners in new resources
authors_terms: ["existing partners - new resources", "alliances with existing partners focusing on new resources"]
definition: The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving at least one new resource, with a partner already in the firm's existing alliance portfolio. A resource is new if it was not already provided by an alliance in the firm's existing portfolio.

name: Alliances with novel partners in new resources
authors_terms: ["novel partners - new resources", "alliances with novel partners focusing on new resources"]
definition: The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving a novel partner and at least one new resource.

name: Innovation performance
definition: We measured innovation performance as a firm's number of successful patent applications in year t. Patents have the potential to protect competitive advantage in biotechnology because they offer effective intellectual property protection necessary for firms to bring new technologies to market.

name: Interstate tension
definition: We define interstate or geopolitical tension as a worsening of the relationship - from cooperative to less cooperative or more conflictual - between home and host countries, particularly when driven by media-reported events.

name: ESG performance
definition: The dependent variable is the annual ESG score of foreign MNEs' subsidiaries in a given host country (ESG score). Thus, the higher the ESG score, the more a foreign MNE's subsidiary engages in ESG activities in a host country.

name: Historical interstate conflict
definition: A type of collective memory relevant to the current context is a history of conflict (a stigmatized event deeply seeded in both societies) between two sovereign states. Particularly, a history of military and/or security conflicts, such as war in the past between two countries, is one of the main sources of negative perceptions and emotions toward another country.

name: Ongoing interstate conflict
definition: We argue that the main effect hypothesized above will not apply if an MNE's home and host countries are already experiencing ongoing conflict (e.g., a diplomatic crisis, armed/military conflict), a scope condition of the main effect.

name: Decision motive
definition: Decisions are characterized as being motivated by stimuli; Mintzberg and colleagues characterized strategic decisions as "ranging on a continuum from exploitation of opportunities to reaction to problems and crises."

name: Organizational performance level
definition: Strategic management and organization theory scholars have posited level of organizational performance as an influence on how strategic decisions are made. High levels of performance provide resources beyond what firms need to pay suppliers, attract employees, or otherwise engage in basic business, and those excess resources are called slack; poor performance does not generate excess resources and at its extreme does not even provide the minimum needed to stay in business.

name: Comprehensiveness of actions in the strategic decision process
definition: The items had served as indicators of how comprehensive organizations were in making and integrating strategic decisions; the earlier studies defined comprehensive actions as attempts to be exhaustive or inclusive.

name: Government dependence
authors_terms: ["government dependence", "government contract dependence", "dependence on governmental contracts", "dependence"]
definition: Government dependence is defined as the proportion of firm revenue that is sourced through government contracts. As the ratio of a firm's total sales from the government increases, the firm focuses more squarely on the needs of the government, to the detriment of alternative market opportunities.

name: Market performance
authors_terms: ["market performance", "market-based performance", "investors' perceptions of firm performance"]
definition: Market performance is measured with Tobin's Q because it is a forward-looking measure of a firm's future performance expectations and is used extensively to measure market perceptions. Tobin's Q 'reflects the market's valuation of the firm's future profit prospects.'

name: Firm investment
definition: Both capital investments and R&D expenditures are investments of current resources in anticipation of future benefits, which is analogous to our theorizing about firm investments.

name: Dependence scope
definition: Dependence scope, defined as the spread of dependence throughout the entity with which the dependence relationship resides.

name: Dependence supplementation
definition: Dependence supplementation, defined as the addition of new relationships within the prior dependence relationship; more specifically, supplementation is the addition of new contracts to a current dependence relationship.

name: Dependence stability
definition: Dependence stability, defined as the expected length of the dependence relationship.

name: Political connection to incumbent party
definition: Personal connections between a firm and the KMT in the pre-movement period, including formal ties developed through politicians serving in firms and the informal ties of blood and marital relations, friendships, classmates, and hometown relationships, and membership in the same social clubs.

name: Corporate philanthropy
authors_terms: ["philanthropic donation", "philanthropic donations", "corporate philanthropy", "charitable donations", "donations to public-welfare causes"]
definition: The prosocial pathway of making philanthropic donations to public-welfare causes, which helps firms build a positive corporate image and consolidate stakeholders' approval.

name: Political contestation
authors_terms: ["political contestation", "incumbent political elites lose control over the local government", "regime-affiliated candidates lose elections"]
definition: Local political contestation by opposition parties in elections, one of the main forces that shape regional democratic transitions: whether political figures of the old regime have lost their positions in local government.

name: NGO density
authors_terms: ["NGO density", "city-level per capita number of NGOs"]
definition: The city-level per capita number of NGOs, measuring local engagement in citizens' groups and indicating an increasing degree of social monitoring and a heightened risk for firms connected to the past authoritarian regime.

name: Anti-regime mass protest
authors_terms: ["anti-regime mass protests", "anti-government mass protests", "mass protests", "the Sunflower Movement"]
definition: Anti-government mass protests can expose the incumbent regime's past collusion and predict its future collapse, so they can signal transitional risks to politically connected firms.

name: Law firm growth
authors_terms: ["law firm growth", "growth rate", "adding associates", "adding one or more associates"]
definition: Our dependent variable is law firm growth, which we measure as a law firm adding associates in a given year. Because the ability to hire associates and grow is of vital importance to law firms, we focus on this activity as an outcome of value to law firms and one that is indicative of their success and competitiveness.

name: Contemporaneous bridging ties
definition: To represent contemporaneous ties, we coded, for each year t, the current affiliations of each lawyer and any movement of lawyers between firms that occurred only in the year t-1. The greater the extent to which partners' contemporaneous professional ties are bridging, the greater a law firm's growth rate.

name: Past bridging ties
definition: To represent past ties, we coded, for each year t, the current affiliation of each lawyer and any movement of lawyers between firms that occurred prior to t-1. The greater the extent to which partners' past professional ties are bridging, the greater a law firm's growth rate.

name: Imprinted bridging ties
definition: When a focal lawyer who was early in her career (i.e., first four years of legal practice) worked with one or more lawyers who were late in their careers (i.e., five years or more of legal practice), we identified the tie as imprinted. We coded, for each year t, the current affiliation of each lawyer and the movement of lawyers at any point in the past (i.e., t-1 and prior) who had been imprinted in the formative stage of their careers.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: A firm's financial performance is the primary metric by which its board assesses the CEO, and it is a major determinant of CEO dismissal and a key reference point for decision makers.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is a secondary objective on which CEOs should focus, involving the commitment of significant corporate resources (e.g., money, time, attention) to help address social and environmental problems; its value is contestable and open to interpretation by stakeholders because the overall impact of CSR on firms is often difficult to quantify.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Involuntary CEO turnover, coded following Shen and Cannella's (2002) method: dismissals are identified when CEOs were reported to have been fired or forced out, resigned immediately or unexpectedly due to poor performance, undisclosed personal reasons or a desire to pursue other interests, retired early amidst performance problems, or left before age 64 and also gave up their board seat.

name: Board-CEO cognitive conflict
authors_terms: ["board-CEO cognitive conflict", "cognitive conflict", "cognitive conflict with the CEO", "task-related disagreements"]
definition: Board-CEO cognitive conflict reflects the overall level of cognitive conflict between directors and the CEO; it has its origin at individual director's level of cognitive conflict with the CEO. Outside directors invariably bring views to the table that often differ from or run contrary to those of the CEO - a phenomenon commonly referred to as cognitive conflict.

name: Director monitoring
authors_terms: ["director monitoring", "directors' engagement in monitoring", "monitoring engagement", "monitoring of the CEO"]
definition: Directors' engagement in overseeing managerial decision-making (i.e., monitoring) has been seen as crucial for curbing managerial opportunism. In the survey it is captured by items that specifically reflect directors' monitoring behaviors, such as seeking information from top management for the purpose of evaluating the performance of top management, monitoring top management strategic decision-making, and being involved in formally evaluating top management.

name: Chair participative leadership
definition: These chair behaviors closely align with the concept of participative leadership, which has generally been defined as the active sharing of influence in decision-making by soliciting contributions and involves considering group members' suggestions and solving problems through consultation and joint discussion.

name: Board psychological safety climate
authors_terms: ["board psychological safety", "board psychological safety climate", "psychological safety"]
definition: This notion closely mirrors the construct of a psychological safety climate derived from group research, which has generally been defined as 'the sense of confidence that the team will not embarrass, reject or punish someone for speaking up,' thereby capturing the shared belief that group members respond constructively to the issues that are raised.

name: Categorical density
authors_terms: ["categorical density", "number of category members", "density of industry category members", "number of solar PV cell producers"]
definition: The yearly number of solar PV cell producers for each country in the dataset; as more firms participate in a new category, the cognitive acceptance of both the firms and the category is enhanced.

name: Industry coherence
definition: The degree to which the organizations forming a nascent industry are similar and coherent, measured as one minus the ratio of the number of producers with a contrasting identity over the total number of producers. Producers with a contrasting identity are those whose origins lie in the incumbent energy sector.

name: Rival sector concentration
authors_terms: ["rival sector concentration", "sector concentration", "concentration of rival interests", "concentration of incumbent interests"]
definition: The degree to which the market is monopolized by one industry (high concentration) or shared equitably among the industries comprising the sector (low concentration); for solar PV the rival industries are the conventional non-renewable energy sources that solar PV shares a market with.

name: Government policy support
authors_terms: ["government policy support", "feed-in tariff", "state support", "regulatory support", "policy support"]
definition: Regulatory support that generates protected market space for a new industry to flourish and grants socio-political legitimacy to that industry; in this setting a feed-in tariff, a support scheme offering long-term contracts whereby the government guarantees the purchase of renewable electricity fed into the grid at a particular price.

name: Controlling owner type
authors_terms: ["family firm", "family company", "lone-founder firm", "lone-founder-controlled firm", "regular public company", "family-controlled firm"]
definition: A family firm is one that is characterized by significant ownership by a single family and more than one family member (founder or descendants of founders) involved in the firm as officers and/or directors. A lone-founder firm is one characterized by the founder alone as a significant owner, officer, or director, with no other family members involved.

name: Interlock similarity
authors_terms: ["interlocks", "links to other family firms", "links to lone-founder firms", "links to regular public companies", "received interlocks", "neutral interlocks", "sent interlocks"]
definition: Lester and Cannella (2006) argued that family firms will seek out interlocks to other family firms because such firms share common interests and a common identity, and will therefore tend to affiliate with one another for common benefit.

name: Family firm experience
authors_terms: ["family experience", "family-firm experience", "outside director prior experience with the same type"]
definition: Executive or director experience with a family company, captured by the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other companies in the sample.

name: Lone-founder firm experience
definition: Executive or director experience with a lone-founder company, captured by the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other companies in the sample.

name: Outside director exit
definition: 'Director exit' represents the departure of an individual director from a given board.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated institutions", "dedicated institutional investors", "ownership by dedicated institutions"]
definition: 'Dedicated institutions' invest for the long term, and seek long-term value creation.

name: Foreign divestment
definition: Foreign divestment is a significant corporate-level decision that involves the sale of international subsidiaries, closure of foreign plants, and exit from foreign markets. The authors study the rate at which firms with investments in Burma divested their Burmese holdings.

name: Home country protest
authors_terms: ["Anti-Burma protest in the home country", "protest in country", "protest activity in the home country"]
definition: Protests, a form of social activism, in the home country should influence a firm's divestment decision; the movement against corporate financial ties to Burma targeted multinational corporations known to produce goods in Burma with protest demonstrations and boycotts.

name: Home country political freedom
authors_terms: ["Political freedom in the home country", "political freedom in country", "level of political freedom"]
definition: The general political conditions in the home country: in politically free and open countries, citizens can influence what their governments do and thus can have a voice in how governments regulate firms.

name: Home country transparency of public transactions
authors_terms: ["transparency in public transactions", "level of transparency (or lack of corruption)", "Transparency International Index"]
definition: The level of transparency (or lack of corruption) in a given country, i.e. the transparency of public transactions and of dealings with government officials. A high level of transparency in a firm's home country likely increases conflict between headquarters and subsidiary management in Burma.

name: Divestment by other firms
authors_terms: ["divestment activity of other firms", "divestment actions of other firms", "cumulative number of divesting firms"]
definition: Firms monitor what other firms are doing and often follow suit; in the heterogeneous diffusion model the susceptibility vector creates an interaction term between the cumulative number of divesting firms and the firm-level characteristic of interest.

name: Home country centrality in economic IGO network
authors_terms: ["centrality in the network of economic IGOs", "Country economic ties via IGOs", "home country centrality in economic IGO networks"]
definition: The centrality of a firm's home country in the network of economic intergovernmental organizations, based on the country's yearly mean number of economic ties to other countries via shared IGO memberships. Economic and social IGOs operate under different sets of norms, emphasizing economic growth and social welfare respectively.

name: Home country centrality in social IGO network
authors_terms: ["centrality in the network of social IGOs", "Country social ties via IGOs", "home country centrality in social IGO networks"]
definition: The centrality of a firm's home country in the network of social intergovernmental organizations, based on the country's yearly mean number of social ties to other countries via shared IGO memberships. Firms from home countries more central in social IGOs may be more sensitive to deteriorating social conditions in Burma.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured by the yearly logarithm of total sales. Because they employ more people and account for larger percentages of their countries' production, larger firms tend to gain high status and be regarded as examples of corporate success by other firms.

name: Firm internationalization
definition: A firm's level of internationalization captures two important motivations for international expansion: access to foreign markets and ownership of foreign operations. It is a composite of foreign sales as a percentage of total sales and foreign assets as a percentage of total assets.

name: Firm size similarity
definition: The similarity between a focal firm and prior divesting firms in firm size, measured by total sales.

name: Firm internationalization similarity
definition: The similarity between a focal firm and prior divesting firms in their level of internationalization, measured by foreign sales as a percentage of total sales and foreign assets as a percentage of total assets.

name: Prior organizational change
authors_terms: ["number of prior changes", "prior changes", "accumulated (i.e., prior) change events", "number of previous changes"]
definition: Change events can occur several times in the life course of the units under study and accumulate over time. Therefore, the change process can be considered as being dependent on the current number of accumulated (i.e., prior) change events.

name: Organizational change rate
authors_terms: ["change rate", "likelihood of a subsequent change", "probability of further change", "change propensity"]
definition: Change is conceptualized as the discrete modification of structural organizational elements. Research on the momentum of change deals with the analysis of discrete organizational change events, which are conceptualized as punctual incidents, and the rate of the change event is the dependent variable.

name: Agglomeration
authors_terms: ["collocation", "agglomeration", "local density", "degree of collocation", "economies of agglomeration", "industry cluster"]
definition: Firms engaged in the same business tend to be persistently collocated with one another in a small number of places, a phenomenon labeled 'economies of agglomeration'. The authors treat a Census Subdivision as a cluster of wineries and measure collocation as the number of wineries in a CSD in a given year, noting that the number of firms in a place (i.e., local density) serves as a proxy measure of agglomeration.

name: Firm founding rate
authors_terms: ["winery founding", "founding rate", "new winery establishments", "new entrants", "founding mechanism"]
definition: The founding mechanism drives geographic concentration of an industry when the founding rate of firms differs across places. Winery founding refers to the counts of new winery establishments in a CSD in a given year.

name: Firm survival
authors_terms: ["winery mortality", "survival mechanism", "firm survival", "mortality rate", "hazard rate at which a winery perishes"]
definition: The survival mechanism shapes the geographic concentration of an industry when the mortality rate of firms differs across places, because clustered firms obtain exclusive economic gains and thus survive longer. Winery mortality is the hazard rate at which a winery perishes.

name: Industry life cycle stage
definition: The ILC framework states that an industry has its own cycle of life, whose stages are distinguished by a discontinuous transformation of competitive dynamics at a particular time that separates the growth stage from the mature stage. The authors divide Ontario's wine production into a growth stage from 1865 to 1928 and a mature stage from 1929 to 1974.

name: M&A function
authors_terms: ["M&A function", "dedicated M&A function", "separate, dedicated organizational unit"]
definition: We assume that the creation of a separate, dedicated organizational unit—known as an M&A function—which is responsible for capturing prior experience, is important in enabling firms to gain, integrate, and disseminate their M&A process and management know-how. An M&A function can be found at the corporate level, business unit level, or both levels.

name: M&A capability
definition: An M&A capability builds on the articulation, codification, sharing, and internalization of knowledge. These four deliberate learning mechanisms are latent variables comprising several indicators.

name: M&A performance
definition: We followed Datta and Grant's (1990) and Capron's (1999) operationalization of M&A performance by using subjective evaluation criteria.

name: Articulation of M&A knowledge
authors_terms: ["articulation", "articulation of knowledge", "articulation of tacit knowledge", "articulation of M&A know-how"]
definition: The articulation of M&A know-how facilitates the ex post understanding of decisions made during prior M&A. The combination of debriefing sessions and a formalized review process requires managers to reflect on past activities and link their actions to the associated outcomes.

name: Codification of M&A knowledge
definition: Codification leads to a well-defined, repeatable process that enables a larger number of personnel to gain acquisition knowledge, thereby making the organization less dependent on individuals.

name: Sharing of M&A knowledge
definition: This ensures the dissemination of relevant knowledge to the right places within a firm and helps managers make sense of their M&A experience. Formal ways of transferring and sharing knowledge is conducted via committees, task forces, meetings, seminars, and retreats.

name: Internalization of M&A knowledge
definition: The internalization of acquisition knowledge focuses on the absorption of M&A knowledge. Internalized knowledge serves as a knowledge base from which managers can consolidate their knowledge regarding M&A.

name: Female occupancy of a top management position
authors_terms: ["Female", "a woman in a given top management position", "female top manager"]
definition: The dummy variable Female takes the value 1 if a given top management position in a given firm in a given year is occupied by a woman. A manager is coded as a woman if either ExecuComp coded the manager as a woman or the manager had the honorific 'Ms.'

name: Female occupancy of other top management team positions
authors_terms: ["Other woman", "another woman in a top management position", "gender spillovers"]
definition: For each observation, the dummy variable Other woman takes the value 1 if any of the other managers on the same top management team in the same year is also a woman and is otherwise 0.

name: Top management position category
definition: The taxonomy of job categories extends that of Helfat et al. (2006): chief executive officer, line officer (senior managers with profit-and-loss responsibility), professional (a manager with responsibility for a staff area), Ex CEO, and Miscellaneous, the omitted category. Where titles span categories the authors assign managers to the highest category in the hierarchy Chief executive officer > Line officer > Professional.

name: Foreign ownership of distilleries
authors_terms: ["foreign ownership", "number of foreign owners", "foreign corporations that own Scotch distilleries", "non-Scottish ownership"]
definition: The prevalence of foreign corporations among the owners of Scotch whisky distilleries, measured by the number of foreign owners based on the location of owners' headquarters. The authors propose that increasing foreign ownership sparks contestation of authenticity, which makes the resource space more complex.

name: Concentration of ownership by type
authors_terms: ["concentration of ownership by type", "concentration of distillery ownership by type of owner", "concentration by form of owner", "ownership-type concentration"]
definition: Concentration of distillery ownership in the hands of particular kinds of owners, in particular beverage groups and diversified firms. Concentrated distillery ownership by beverage groups and diversified firms makes product offerings more homogeneous and the authenticity of the category more contentious, which in turn opens up the resource space for new kinds of products.

name: Entry of focused distillery owners
authors_terms: ["hazard of entry of firms with the traditional form of distillery ownership", "focused entries", "entries of new independent owners", "new focused ownership"]
definition: Cases in which a new or existing distillery, not controlled by a focused owner, comes under the ownership of an owner whose only business is malt whisky production. These events include (1) building a new distillery, (2) acquiring a distillery that was previously owned by an owner with a more diverse set of industrial activities, or (3) taking a so-called 'mothballed' distillery back into production.

name: Grade of membership
authors_terms: ["grade of membership", "average grades of membership in whisky and malt whisky"]
definition: Each producer's grade of membership in the whisky category is calculated as the proportion of the articles that mention the firm that also mention whisky, and similarly the grade of membership in the malt whisky category as the proportion of all articles mentioning the producer that also mention malt whisky.

name: Electronic document quality
authors_terms: ["document quality", "electronic document quality", "quality of the codified knowledge", "quality of the knowledge contained in the electronic documents"]
definition: Content refers to the quality of the knowledge accessed by the task unit. Quality indicates the rigor, soundness, and insight of the knowledge conveyed by a document or person irrespective of the task at hand.

name: Document rework
definition: Adapting electronic documents that reside in the firm's knowledge management system for use in a new sales proposal often involves processing costs. This measure captured the amount of effort required to adapt the codified knowledge in the electronic documents to the team's proposal.

name: Time savings on task
definition: We consider efficiencies by examining the time saved by using knowledge from other parts of the firm, since time savings can make a critical difference to productivity levels within the firm as well as competitive performance in situations where earlier completion of a task is beneficial.

name: Advisor experience
authors_terms: ["advisor experience", "advisors' experience", "the experience that was needed for this particular proposal"]
definition: Teams that contacted more experienced colleagues to help them with their work were likely to receive higher-quality advice. Colleagues who have experience in areas related to a sales proposal can provide complementary expertise or analogous experiences that a team can draw on to generate ideas and identify possible avenues to pursue for viable solutions.

name: Advisor lack of effort
authors_terms: ["advisor lack of effort", "lack of effort", "lack of effort by colleagues advising the team"]
definition: The benefits available from colleagues' advice depend on the amount of effort those colleagues are willing to exert to help the team. Without their investment of effort, the advice offered by colleagues can be easily misinterpreted or applied inappropriately by the team.

name: Work quality
authors_terms: ["work quality", "quality of the sales proposal", "quality of the work output"]
definition: High work quality here refers to the extent to which the output of the task (e.g., a product, proposal or decision) meets or exceeds the expectations of those who receive or use it.

name: Signal of competence
authors_terms: ["signal of competence", "signaling of competencies", "ability to signal competence"]
definition: Through its work and interactions with others, a task unit provides a signal of its competence that may be only partially related to the inherent quality of its work, especially when it is difficult for outsiders to measure that quality directly.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: If firm A and firm B are different in observation (A1, B2), a job change may have occurred. The mobility rate is defined as the percentage of observations (A1, B2) in a time period for which firms A and B differ.

name: Spinoff spawning
definition: A firm was classified as a spinoff if its main founder previously worked for another semiconductor firm, and the last semiconductor firm where the main founder worked was designated as the spinoff's parent.

name: Neighboring firms' spinoff entry
authors_terms: ["number of spinoffs of other neighboring firms", "other recent entrants in firm A's region", "Number of SVEntrants"]
definition: the number of entrants in Silicon Valley in the five years prior to date 1 other than the firm itself and its spinoffs; this variable includes all entrants, not just spinoffs, in Silicon Valley, although nearly all the entrants there were spinoffs

name: Silicon Valley location
definition: The most notable of these regions is Silicon Valley, which was emerging as a significant player in semiconductors when our sample starts.

name: Initial hires from local firms
authors_terms: ["hires from other local firms", "hired a greater percentage of their inventors locally", "initial hires", "other Silicon Valley firms"]
definition: Our hypotheses concern the initial hires of spinoffs. To operationalize the idea of initial hires, we consider the hires of firms in their first five years.

name: Initial hires from the parent
authors_terms: ["hires from their parents", "hired a greater percentage of their inventors from their parents", "initial hires"]
definition: The first natural source for a spinoff to hire experienced inventors from is its parent.

name: Prior move from parent to spinoff
authors_terms: ["movers from parent to spinoff", "moved from parent to spinoff", "movers from a parent to one of its spinoffs"]
definition: An important reason why spinoffs hire inventors from their parent is because they are experts on the technology the spinoff developed. This implies that the fit between these workers' ability and the spinoffs' requirements will be very good.

name: Spinoff entry outside Silicon Valley
authors_terms: ["entry of spinoffs outside of Silicon Valley", "new entrants in other local areas", "recent entrants outside of firm A's region"]
definition: Spinoffs outside of Silicon Valley had fewer neighboring firms with the necessary competencies from which to hire inventors. As a result, one could expect spinoffs outside of Silicon Valley to rely more heavily on hiring inventors away from their parents.

name: Stakeholder orientation
definition: The degree to which a firm's management decides to focus its attention on stakeholders and integrate their interests and knowledge in its decision making. It comprises orientations toward employees, customers, suppliers, and local communities.

name: Long-term acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "long-term performance of the acquisition", "M&A performance"]
definition: The long-term performance of the acquisition, which the authors measure through the acquiring firm's Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CAR) over the 36 months following the acquisition.

name: Business relatedness
definition: Business relatedness, defined as the similarity in products and processes between the acquirer and the acquired firm.

name: Structural integration
definition: The situation where, following the closing of the deal, the acquired firm does not remain as a separate entity, but its resources and activities are retained and recombined with those of the acquiring firm.

name: Employee orientation
definition: Firms characterized by higher levels of employee orientation have developed routines and tools to evaluate their own workforce's characteristics, needs, and preferences; the literature has generally linked employee orientation with the notion of quality workforce relationships.

name: Customer orientation
definition: Customer orientation has often been associated with higher attention to client preferences or with the increased use of customer-sourced knowledge. It intensifies the involvement of customers in decisions related to products and brands.

name: Supplier orientation
definition: Supplier orientation has frequently been exemplified using the Japanese keiretsus system in which key suppliers are involved in decision and execution processes related to product development. The indicator assesses the firm's attitude (and behaviors) toward its suppliers.

name: Local community orientation
authors_terms: ["local community orientation", "community orientation", "orientation toward local communities"]
definition: Local community orientation has been associated with managers devoting greater attention to the institutional environment in which their firm is embedded as well as the use of communication and philanthropic initiatives.

name: Corporate social responsibility engagement
authors_terms: ["CSR engagement", "CSR participation", "CSR activity", "corporate social responsibility (CSR)", "substantial or noteworthy CSR"]
definition: Voluntary corporate actions designed to improve social conditions (Mackey, Mackey, and Barney, 2007), or corporate actions not required by law that attempt to further some social good and extend beyond the explicit transactional interests of the firm (McWilliams and Siegel, 2000). We use the simple term CSR engagement for CSR activity that is public knowledge and substantial enough to create a credible and reasonable declaration of unselfish intention.

name: Institutional CSR
definition: CSR activities that target the firm's secondary stakeholders, who lack both urgency and power to press their claims on the firm and are more likely to be viewed as voluntary acts of social beneficence providing evidence of an 'other-regarding' orientation.

name: Technical CSR
definition: CSR activities that target the firm's primary stakeholders, those who make legitimate claims on the firm and have both urgency and power to enforce those claims; such activities should produce exchange capital rather than moral capital.

name: Change in shareholder value
authors_terms: ["change in shareholder value", "abnormal return", "cumulative abnormal return (CAR)"]
definition: Change in shareholder value (our dependent variable) is the unexpected percentage change in the stock price surrounding the event, or the abnormal return. Our primary dependent variable is cumulative abnormal return, the cumulative abnormal stock return (as a percentage) accruing over the two-day event window.

name: Intangible assets
definition: Market-to-book has been shown in the literature to correlate strongly with Tobin's q, the theoretical standard for measuring intangible assets (Villalonga, 2004).

name: Firm size
definition: We collected data on firm size, measured as the natural logarithm of sales for the fiscal year before the event.

name: Negative social impacts
definition: Negative social impacts may arise from industry membership (e.g., tobacco, nuclear power, or gaming) or from a firm's own actions over time (e.g., the history of negative union relations at General Motors).

name: Competitively based negative event
definition: Negative events that occur when interpretations of acceptable competitive behavior and its boundaries are at issue; in these cases the other-regarding signal value of CSR activity should be irrelevant as the question does not turn on the other-regarding dispositions of the actors involved.

name: Stakeholder-based negative event
definition: Negative events that arise because the well-being of stakeholders is jeopardized in some way (such as product safety issues or health and safety violations in the workplace), where there is little ambiguity about the badness of the act but ambiguity about the underlying motivations of the actors involved.

name: Integrity-based negative event
definition: Negative events where the integrity or moral character of the firm is in question, including actions by management that violated well-accepted principles of ethical behavior, such as promise keeping, or resulted in the unfair treatment of employees or other key stakeholders.

name: Governance bundle
authors_terms: ["governance bundle", "governance bundles", "combinations of governance mechanisms", "constellations of governance mechanisms", "bundle of governance and contextual factors"]
definition: The authors argue that corporate governance mechanisms should not be considered in isolation from each other but should be looked at in 'bundles,' because mechanisms can be functionally equivalent; different combinations, or bundles, of governance mechanisms in foreign IPO firms may lead to similar investor perceptions of their value.

name: Board independence
definition: Board independence is used to approximate the extent of internal monitoring and monitoring by independent boards; independent (nonmanagement) directors are only those with no prior professional or personal ties to a firm or its management, and VC-related board members are not counted as independent directors.

name: CEO stock options
definition: Stock options are used as a proxy for executive incentives and represent incentive alignment between executives and shareholders; they have become an important element of CEOs' compensation packages because of the widespread belief that they are effective in aligning executive and shareholder interests.

name: Venture capital backing
authors_terms: ["venture capital backing", "VC backing", "monitoring by venture capital", "external monitoring"]
definition: Private equity investors, such as VCs, are identified in the literature as important external monitors in IPO firms, and VC backing indicates their presence among a firm's principal pre-IPO shareholders.

name: Home country legal protection for minority investors
authors_terms: ["strong home country investor protection", "strong home country legal protection", "home country legal protection", "minority investor protection"]
definition: From the US investor perspective, an especially relevant feature of foreign IPOs' home environments is the extent to which regulatory institutions protect minority investor rights, including establishing rules to hold managers accountable to shareholders, ensuring shareholder voting privilege, preventing self-dealing by managers, protecting creditors, and enforcing these rules in practice.

name: Investor perceptions of foreign IPO value
authors_terms: ["investor value perceptions", "investors' perceptions of foreign IPO value", "perceived value", "investor IPO valuations", "stock market evaluation", "price premium"]
definition: Investors' perceptions of a foreign IPO firm's value; price premium represents the potential value that investors perceive in an issuing firm's shares that exceeds their book value, and valuation assessments are an outcome of investors' perceptions of firms' legitimacy.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["poor firm performance", "poor financial performance", "firm financial performance", "ROA", "reverse-coded ROA"]
definition: Firm performance can effectively reflect the severity of the agency problem in a firm, and poorer performance can signal to shareholders a greater agency problem, making them more likely to attribute the underperformance to the CEO. It is assessed using prior ROA, calculated as operating return divided by total assets, with operating return indicated by EBITDA.

name: CEO turnover
definition: CEO turnover is defined as forced and voluntary CEO exits not due to sickness, death, retirements, or promotions; the study does not distinguish between forced and voluntary CEO turnovers.

name: Non-family ownership
authors_terms: ["non-family ownership", "non-family shareholders", "non-family shareholding", "ownership percentage of all the non-family shareholders"]
definition: To gauge the influence of non-family shareholders, the study focuses on the ownership percentage of all the non-family shareholders, who in Taiwan include the government and affiliated institutes, domestic and foreign individuals, domestic and foreign investment funds, domestic and foreign financial institutions, and related parties such as business groups.

name: Governance transparency
authors_terms: ["governance transparency", "weak governance transparency", "corporate governance transparency", "information disclosure"]
definition: Governance transparency refers to the extent to which firms choose to disclose their governance and management conditions through such channels as corporate annual reports, social media, and other outlets. In firms with high governance transparency the information asymmetry between investors and managers is often low.

name: Control rights-cash flow rights deviation
authors_terms: ["deviation between control rights and cash flow rights", "deviation between control and cash flow rights", "control-cash flow deviation", "deviation"]
definition: Control rights in a firm are the sum of direct and indirect voting rights held by the shareholder(s), whereas cash flow rights refer to the product of ownership in the intermediate companies along the ownership chain; the two can differ because corporations can issue different classes of shares that provide different control rights for given cash-flow rights.

name: Workplace context challenge
definition: Following Dill (1958) and Duncan (1972), the context of an organization encompasses every aspect of its external environment that influences the decision making, goal setting, and probability of goal attainment of its employees. Challenging workplace contexts are characterized by (1) high levels of uncertainty and (2) threats arising from external adversity.

name: Short-term career advancement
authors_terms: ["short-term career advancement", "promoted faster in the short term", "rate of career advancement"]
definition: The terms career advancement, progression, and growth are understood to signify vertical mobility within an organization, characterized by change in an individual's job description, responsibilities, and wages. Short-term career advancement is the speed of advancement in the initial years, observed as how many years it takes an individual to achieve a central posting.

name: Long-term career advancement
authors_terms: ["long-term career advancement", "faster career advancement in the long term", "average rate of promotion after reaching the center"]
definition: Early career deployment to challenging contexts is expected to have positive persistent effects on the speed of subsequent career advancement within the same organization via human-capital development.

name: Hierarchical level attained
authors_terms: ["higher levels on the organizational career ladder", "higher ultimate position in the organizational hierarchy", "upper echelons of the organization"]
definition: Individuals initially deployed to challenging workplace contexts are expected to attain a higher ultimate position in the organizational hierarchy; the reported test is the likelihood of attaining the rank of joint secretary, an entry point into the upper echelons of the administration.

name: Voluntary training-course participation
definition: The IAS provides officers the option to augment their managerial skills through annual training courses held in management institutes throughout India. This training is entirely voluntary, and officers may request or decline it; their voluntary participation signals motivation and ability as well as human-capital acquisition.

name: Static experience
authors_terms: ["static experience", "production and sales experience", "experience serving existing markets"]
definition: Static experience is gained from further elaboration of existing structures, positions, and strategies. It is the firm's experience producing and selling to existing markets.

name: Transformational experience
definition: Transformational experience is gained from changing existing structures, positions, and strategies, and is the firm's experience with major change.

name: Time since major organizational change
authors_terms: ["change clock", "time since it last underwent a major organizational change"]
definition: The time elapsed since the organization last underwent a major organizational change or reorganization, which theory suggests can reset the organization's inertial clock.

name: Entry into new market niches
definition: Entry is the probability that a firm will produce a drive in a new market niche (category) in the next year. A niche innovation occurs when new technology creates a new market opportunity but does not obsolete the capabilities of incumbent firms.

name: Future sales
definition: The sales the firm achieves in future years; the authors use a selection method to evaluate how entry affected the future sales of the company.

name: Frequency of organizational adjustments
authors_terms: ["organizational adjustments", "frequency of organizational adjustments", "adaptive organizational behavior", "adaptive organizational acts", "organizational adjustments as a direct response to actions by environmental groups"]
definition: The effects of environmental uncertainty and resource scarcity on an organization are a stream of adaptive organizational acts. Frequency of organizational adjustments was measured through a scale incorporating five categories of adjustments—procedural, personnel-related, process, structural, and strategic—arranged in ascending order of scope and cost.

name: Scope and cost of organizational adjustment
authors_terms: ["scope and cost", "ascending order of scope and cost", "breadth and cost"]
definition: Although simultaneous changes during periods of adaptation are possible, adaptational changes can differ greatly in breadth and cost. The five broad types of organizational adjustments are arranged in ascending order of scope and cost: procedural, personnel, process, structural, and strategic.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty refers to the extent to which organizational decision makers perceive unpredictable changes in their external environment.

name: Environmental resource scarcity
authors_terms: ["environmental resource scarcity", "resource scarcity", "resource availability or scarcity", "scarcity of environmental resources"]
definition: The use of resource availability or scarcity as an environmental variable flows from a resource dependence view of organizations that treats environments as arenas in which all compete for resources; adjustments are explained by disruptive resource instabilities and the inabilities of organizations to acquire and control critical and scarce resources.

name: Organic structure
definition: An organic structure, with its low degree of formality and high degree of information sharing and decentralization, enhances an organization's flexibility and ability to adapt to continual environmental change and uncertainty. Organic structures are characterized by participatory decision making, a decentralized hierarchy of authority, and few formalized procedures.

name: Interdepartmental consensus
authors_terms: ["consensus", "consensus between marketing and manufacturing groups", "interdepartmental consensus", "consensus between departments"]
definition: Consensus between marketing and manufacturing groups on key competitive strengths, company goals, and implementation actions. From this point on, high difference scores will be referred to as low consensus scores.

name: Marketplace performance reputation
authors_terms: ["marketplace performance reputation", "performance on order-winning dimensions of marketplace performance", "marketplace performance"]
definition: The performance attributes of interest are those that are the outcomes of the integrated pattern of marketing and manufacturing decisions and that serve to win orders in the marketplace: quality, delivery speed and reliability, product line uniqueness, price, and customer service.

name: Use of co-ordinating mechanisms
authors_terms: ["co-ordinating mechanisms", "mechanisms for co-ordinating between marketing and manufacturing", "frequency of use of mechanisms for co-ordinating", "integrating devices"]
definition: The measure of frequency of use was an attempt to capture the degree to which managers perceive that these types of co-ordinating mechanisms are relied on within their firms. The advocates of the different co-ordinating mechanisms believe that their use will increase co-ordination among interdependent groups.

name: Discrete productive tacit knowledge
authors_terms: ["discrete productive tacit knowledge", "discrete productive knowledge", "stand-alone knowledge of each individual player"]
definition: The application of the knowledge of an individual to the performance of a particular task or activity; the tacit knowledge that each individual draws upon to carry out particular tasks.

name: Discrete administrative tacit knowledge
authors_terms: ["discrete administrative tacit knowledge", "discrete administrative knowledge", "stand-alone knowledge of each individual manager"]
definition: The tacit knowledge that helps managers to extract the best-possible performance from subordinates, drawing upon their accumulated experience in using specific employees to accomplish particular outcomes.

name: Linked productive tacit knowledge
authors_terms: ["linked productive tacit knowledge", "linked productive knowledge", "connections between the knowledge of the players on a team"]
definition: The application of the knowledge of the larger group to the performance of the same task or activity; learning that allows various individuals to work together more effectively.

name: Linked administrative tacit knowledge
authors_terms: ["linked administrative tacit knowledge", "linked administrative knowledge", "connections between the knowledge of the manager and the players on a team"]
definition: The tacit knowledge that links the administrative knowledge of a manager with the productive knowledge of a particular set of players that he must manage, allowing managers to better understand and work with a particular set of employees.

name: Team performance
authors_terms: ["overall performance of a team", "winning percentage", "percentage of games won during the regular season"]
definition: The percentage of games won during the regular season, representing the degree to which a team has been successful over an entire season and generally comparable over different teams and across different time periods.

name: Knowledge codification
definition: Codification is the use of codified knowledge captured in written documents, such as manuals and rule books, to guide alliance activity. Firms rely on codified guidelines and tools to support alliance management in the different phases of the alliance process.

name: Strategic alliance portfolio performance
authors_terms: ["strategic alliance portfolio performance", "alliance portfolio performance", "alliance success", "alliance performance"]
definition: We define strategic alliance portfolio performance as the percentage of alliances in which the firm's goals were realized, assessed as the overall success rate of the firm's strategic alliances over the past five years.

name: Piece-rate use
authors_terms: ["use of piece wages", "piece wages", "piece rates", "adoption of piece rates"]
definition: A market-oriented labor practice that links pay to output. The use of incentive-based compensation schemes was prohibited following China's 1949 communist takeover, and beginning in 1978 firms were again allowed to use piece wages.

name: Worker support for managers
definition: The degree to which workers supported management; managers who had worker support were more able to adopt and implement innovative practices than those who were at odds with workers. An important indicator of worker support for managers was being elected by the workers.

name: Communist Party connections
definition: Managers who were members of the Communist Party were likely to be less market oriented than those who were not party members. The authors measured party connections as holding the secretary office because party secretaries generally have a higher degree of commitment to the Communist Party than ordinary members and thus tend to be more reluctant to use innovative, market-based strategies.

name: Market orientation
authors_terms: ["market orientation", "managers' orientation toward using market means of compensation"]
definition: The manager's orientation toward using market means of compensation rather than socialist means. Reforming the economic system forced managers to begin relying less on strategies such as cultivating bargaining position with superiors and more on profit maximization and improving competitive advantage.

name: Labor market development
authors_terms: ["labor market development", "market development", "poorly developed labor markets"]
definition: The degree to which labor markets were developed. In the early stages of reform in China markets were just beginning to develop, and because labor markets were just forming, labor surpluses and shortages plagued firms.

name: Simple exposure to peer adoption
definition: The degree to which a focal organization was exposed to other organizations using piece rates, captured by the simple number of other organizations using the practice. When a practice is new, it is likely that any imitation that does occur is frequency, or pure imitation, based.

name: Exposure to profitable peers' adoption
authors_terms: ["exposure to other organizations using piece rates profitably", "exposure weighted by profits", "targeted mimetic behavior"]
definition: Exposure to other organizations that used piece rates profitably. As time passed, simple imitation is likely to have been replaced by active imitation of successful (i.e., profitable) others, and organizations modeled themselves after others they perceived to be more legitimate or successful.

name: Benefit of prior piece-rate use
authors_terms: ["benefit of using piece rates", "benefits of past use", "past success with the practice"]
definition: An indicator of the degree to which the organization's profits differed from what would be expected by chance as a function of the use of piece rates in the prior time period. It can be interpreted as the benefit to financial performance of using piece wages.

name: Cost of alternative labor practices
authors_terms: ["cost of using alternative labor compensation strategies", "cost of alternatives", "cost of pluralism", "cost of using state workers"]
definition: An indicator of the degree to which profits differed from chance as a function of the continued employment of permanent, state-appointed workers in the prior time period. It can be interpreted as the cost of using state workers.

name: Stage of reform
authors_terms: ["early stages of reform", "later stages of reform", "as reform progresses"]
definition: The stage of China's economic reform at which adoption occurred. The authors argue that different combinations of influences are salient at different stages in the spread of a new practice, and they estimated separate equations for periods of reform.

name: Time-to-build
definition: The time it takes a firm to build and ramp up operations at a new manufacturing facility. Following Koeva (2000) and Pacheco-de-Almeida (2003), time-to-build is defined as the time it takes to complete a manufacturing facility.

name: Competitive rivalry
authors_terms: ["competitive rivalry", "rival plants with superior technology", "competition from rivals with superior technology"]
definition: When faced with competitors making large resource commitments to build similar (or more advanced) facilities, the focal firm has incentives to beat its competitors to market in order to preserve its position. The competitive pressures will be greater when more plants are scheduled to come online concurrently, and firms are likely to respond aggressively to plants with similar or superior technology.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Foreign direct investment occurs when a substantive operating investment is made in a foreign location. The standard used by academic researchers and governments is that foreign direct investment occurs when a firm takes an equity stake of at least 10% in a facility abroad.

name: Firm experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative firm experience", "domestic firm experience", "foreign firm experience", "experiential learning"]
definition: Experiential learning is a form of learning-by-doing that accrues as a firm repeatedly engages in an activity; in this context the relevant experience is that which accrues from prior deployments (e.g., building previous plants). Past deployments develop a 'discipline of practice' that creates more efficient replication routines.

name: Industry experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative industry experience", "industry-level experience", "learning from the industry's experience"]
definition: Learning based on industry-level experience refers to the insight that a firm gains as other firms 'do'-i.e., by encoding the experience of others within the industry.

name: Technology complexity
definition: Complexity increases with the number, variety, sophistication, and interactions among components, especially when the know-how represents an advance relative to the state of the art. Complex knowledge is difficult to understand, express, and replicate accurately.

name: Technical HRM effectiveness
authors_terms: ["technical HRM effectiveness", "technical human resource management effectiveness", "technical HRM activities"]
definition: Technical HRM effectiveness describes perceptions of how well the HRM function performed activities traditionally associated with personnel management, including recruitment, selection, training, performance appraisal, and compensation administration.

name: Strategic HRM effectiveness
authors_terms: ["strategic HRM effectiveness", "strategic human resource management effectiveness", "strategic HRM activities"]
definition: Strategic HRM effectiveness describes perceptions of how well the HRM function developed a firm's employees to support its business needs, including facilitating teamwork, communications, and involvement, enhancing quality, and developing talent to serve the business in the future.

name: Professional HRM capabilities
definition: Professional HRM capabilities describe expertise and skill relevant to performing excellently within a traditional HRM functional department. Items assess both capabilities important to managers in any function and capabilities that specifically insure that technical HR knowledge is both present and used within a firm.

name: Business-related capabilities
definition: Business-related capabilities describe the amount of business experience HRM staff members have had outside the functional specialty. These capabilities should facilitate the selection and implementation of HRM policies and practices that fit the unique characteristics of a firm, including its size, strategy, structure, and culture.

name: Firm performance
definition: The three indicators of firm performance used in this study were based on data taken from annual financial statements: employee productivity, the gross rate of return on assets, and Tobin's q.

name: Performance relative to internal aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to aspirations", "performance above social aspirations", "performance relative to internal aspirations", "high firm accounting performance relative to aspirations"]
definition: A firm's performance relative to the performance of its industry peers, which the authors label 'performance relative to internal aspirations'. It is defined as a spline function based on the difference between a firm's performance and the performance of a relevant comparison group, with accounting return on assets as the performance measure.

name: Stock price performance relative to external expectations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to external expectations", "stock price performance relative to expectations", "high firm stock price performance relative to expectations", "positive abnormal returns"]
definition: A firm's current market performance relative to its prior market performance, which the authors label 'performance relative to external expectations' and operationalize using abnormal returns, the difference between a firm's observed and expected stock market returns.

name: Firm prominence
definition: A firm's prominence reflects the degree to which external audiences are aware of its existence, as well as the extent to which they view it as relevant and salient.

name: Corporate illegality
definition: Corporate illegality is defined as an illegal act primarily meant to benefit a firm by potentially increasing revenues or decreasing costs. This definition expressly excludes illegal activities that are primarily meant to benefit the specific individual engaging in the act.

name: CEO liberalism
authors_terms: ["CEO political ideology", "CEO liberalism", "political liberalism of CEOs", "CEO ideology", "liberalism-conservatism"]
definition: An individual's political ideology reflects his or her core beliefs about the proper goals for society and how to achieve them. Liberals place emphasis on civil rights and associated social issues, including diversity, social justice, social change, and protecting the natural environment, whereas conservatives place more emphasis on individualism, respect for authority, stability, and the status quo.

name: Employee activism
definition: Employee activist groups may reflect the interests of members who share a common identity defined by race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, or disability. The formation of an LGBT employee group can be considered as an instance of activism because it demands that management either recognize or reject the legitimacy of employees' claims to self-identify in the workplace as LGBT people.

name: CEO power
definition: CEOs vary in how much power they possess, in ways that affect a wide range of outcomes, including CEO compensation and dismissal and strategic decision making. Powerful CEOs will be perceived by activists to be in a position to more readily acquiesce to activism, or, conversely, to resist it, according to their personal leanings.

name: Workplace conservatism
authors_terms: ["workplace conservatism", "organization-level climate", "workplace climate", "prevailing ideology of the overall employee population"]
definition: Perceptions of reprisal risk will be shaped in part by workplace climate or culture, including the prevailing ideology of the overall employee population. In a conservative workplace that is broadly antagonistic to the goals or identities of employee activists, risks of social reprisal will be seen as relatively great.

name: Social movement expansion
authors_terms: ["expansion of the movement", "phase of the social movement", "LGBT groups formed thus far", "movement expansion"]
definition: Social movements tend to have lifecycles, with attendant changes in uncertainty and taken-for-grantedness over time. Expansion is captured by the number of corporate LGBT groups formed thus far, reflecting the degree to which a social movement or a certain practice has diffused in a population.

name: CEO ideological contrast
authors_terms: ["liberal versus conservative difference between the successor and predecessor", "ideological contrast between a predecessor and a new CEO", "ideological contrast"]
definition: CEO succession represents a rare 'window in time' for activists, and the salience of this potential opportunity is heightened by any contrast between the ideologies of the departing and arriving CEOs. In instances of recent CEO succession, a greater liberal versus conservative difference between the successor and predecessor is expected to increase the likelihood of employee activism within the company.

name: Algorithmic recommendation tool adoption
authors_terms: ["algorithmic recommendation tools (ARTs)", "CDSS adoption", "adoption of CDSS", "adoption of ARTs", "algorithmic tool adoption"]
definition: ARTs are systems that use sophisticated computer programs to analyze databases and organizational inputs in order to produce an assessment or recommendation. Advanced CDSS, an early iteration of artificial intelligence tools used in organizational decision making, are the algorithmic recommendation tool studied here.

name: Experiential learning
authors_terms: ["experiential learning", "learning from experience", "slope of the learning curve"]
definition: Experiential learning is the improvement in organizational performance that results from accumulated experience, following a learning curve function. The authors measure experiential learning as the amount of performance improvement as a result of cumulative prior experience, that is, the slope of the learning curve.

name: Task difficulty
definition: Task difficulty often arises from complexity or interdependence of multiple elements in successful completion of a task. Difficult tasks may lack a single clear solution and instead require hybrid or novel solutions.

name: Task variety
definition: Task variety refers to the scope of activities required to carry out work.

name: Cumulative experience
definition: The cumulative number of patients treated by the focal ED, depreciated to incorporate the typical loss of experience over time and log transformed to take into account diminishing returns to accumulated experience. The relationship between an ED's cumulative experience and its clinical performance is the slope of its learning curve.

name: ED mortality
definition: The number of patients who expired in the ED divided by the total number of ED visits in each year, scaled by 100. A negative coefficient on this variable indicates higher clinical performance.

name: Product portfolio complexity
authors_terms: ["product portfolio complexity", "PPC", "complexity", "depth and breadth of product offerings"]
definition: Closs and colleagues (2008: 591) define PPC as the 'state of processing difficulty that results from a multiplicity of, and relatedness among, product architectural design elements.' Complexity is defined in the paper as the depth and breadth of product offerings, considered in relation to the portfolios of products offered by competitors within a firm's industry.

name: Firm performance
definition: Growth is argued to be a key measure of new venture performance; the authors employ a multidimensional measure that comprised sales growth, employee growth, and operating profit growth.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: The ability of a firm to recognize, assimilate, and apply external knowledge to commercial ends (Cohen and Levinthal, 1990; Zahra and George, 2002)-otherwise termed its absorptive capacity.

name: Ambidexterity
definition: Within the technological innovation context, ambidexterity refers to the simultaneous pursuit of exploitative and explorative activities; contextual ambidexterity relies on building a set of systems and processes that support such alignment.

name: Foreign institutional ownership
definition: FIO is the percentage of a U.S. firm's equity that is owned by foreign (non-U.S.) institutional investors. It is measured as the sum of the holdings of all institutional investors domiciled outside the United States, divided by the number of shares outstanding.

name: Corporate political spending
definition: Our dependent variable is CPS, which has two components. The first component is a firm's total annual lobbying expenditure ... The second component is firms' contributions to PACs.

name: Government-contract intensity
