definition: Firms with high government contract intensity are more dependent on the government since their financial performance is more significantly driven by the magnitude and renewal rate of their government contracts. It is a firm's revenue-weighted mean of the industry-level ratio of federal purchase payments to total revenues.

name: National-security industry
definition: Firms operating in national-security-related industries face more stringent governmental scrutiny; the classification is based on the list of four-digit SIC industries critical to national security in the 2008 CFIUS Annual Report to Congress.

name: Contributory role
definition: We use the term contributory role to refer to the extent to which the subsidiary has specialized resources that are recognized by the corporation as a whole.

name: Specialized resources
definition: Our preference is to use a less strict approach that requires the subsidiary's resources to be specialized, which we define as superior to those available elsewhere in the corporation. If the subsidiary's specialized resources are combined with other resources elsewhere in the MNC, we suggest that they then become part of the MNC's firm-specific advantage.

name: Subsidiary initiative
definition: Subsidiary initiative is defined as the entrepreneurial pursuit of international market opportunities to which the subsidiary can apply its specialized resources.

name: Subsidiary leadership
authors_terms: ["subsidiary leadership", "strong subsidiary leadership", "strength of top management"]
definition: The strength of subsidiary top management, whose championing and sponsoring efforts trigger the assignment of new international responsibilities or mandates to the subsidiary.

name: Entrepreneurial culture
definition: As defined here, initiatives are discrete cases of entrepreneurship; entrepreneurial culture is an organizational context in which certain behaviors, including initiative, are fostered.

name: Subsidiary autonomy
definition: One facet of the 'structural context' consisting of the subsidiary's relationship with the parent company; it refers to decision-making autonomy, i.e., whether certain decisions are made in the subsidiary, at the divisional level or at head office.

name: Parent-subsidiary communication
definition: High levels of parent-subsidiary communication, reflected in the frequency of communication between subsidiary and parent company.

name: Local competition
authors_terms: ["local competition", "competitiveness of the local market", "level of local competition"]
definition: We focused on the level of competitiveness in the local market. Competition drives the innovation process and the upgrading of capabilities.

name: Industry globalization
authors_terms: ["industry globalization", "global integration", "level of globalization of the industry"]
definition: At one end of the spectrum are 'pure global' industries (Porter, 1986) in which the subsidiary's activities are integrated with the rest of the corporate network. At the other end of the spectrum are 'multidomestic' industries in which competition in one national market is not substantially affected by competition in the next.

name: Competitive interaction group membership
definition: Firms are classified into groups using the patterns of competitive interaction of firms, defined as the exchange of competitive or cooperative moves (actions and responses) among firms in a market. The authors refer to this proposed approach as the formation of competitive interaction or industry groups, as distinct from past research on strategic groups.

name: Top management team heterogeneity
definition: Group heterogeneity refers to the amount of diversity found within the TMT. It is measured in four ways: (1) functional heterogeneity, (2) educational heterogeneity, (3) company tenure heterogeneity, and (4) age heterogeneity.

name: TMT heterogeneity deviation from group mean
authors_terms: ["Euclidean distance measure", "deviation of each firm's TMT characteristics from the dominant TMT characteristics", "deviation scores"]
definition: Euclidean distance measures identify the deviations of each firm's TMT characteristics from the dominant TMT characteristics for the competitive interaction group to which each firm belongs. The centroid of each group for heterogeneity variables, the mean vector, is used as the representative point of the group to calculate the distance.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance of each airline was measured by each firm's load factor. Load factor is defined as the proportion of an aircraft's seating capacity that is actually sold or used, determined by dividing revenue passenger miles by available seat miles.

name: Status inequality
definition: One fundamental distributional property of status hierarchies; substantively it reflects 'the concentration of status resources' and technically it refers to 'the average difference in status between any two pairs relative to the average status,' and thus is easily captured by the usual measure of inequality-the Gini coefficient.

name: Status position
definition: Status refers to the amount of deference that an organization receives from other market actors (e.g., competitors, consumers, industry analysts) regarding the quality of its products. Following previous research, the authors consider the status of a bowl as the deference that it receives from others regarding its quality or its capability in staging a successful annual bowl game.

name: Buyers' product choice
authors_terms: ["buyers' choice of products", "choice of products", "aggregated choices of an organization's product", "bowl stadium attendance"]
definition: The dependent variable proposed by the hypotheses is buyers' choice of organizations' products; each buyer's product choice can be aggregated to reflect how well the products of a target and a corresponding high-status referent fare in the market.

name: Product quality uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty about products", "uncertainty about product quality", "uncertainty about the quality of an organization's product", "ambiguity"]
definition: The precondition for the occurrence of assimilation and contrast effects: individuals feel ambiguous about a given property of a target, and when feeling uncertain about a target, individuals draw on a referent as a contextual cue for judgment. Although knowledge of whether a bowl game will be good is always uncertain before it is actually played, the track record of a bowl can help indicate the future quality of the bowl game.

name: Incumbent supplier status
authors_terms: ["supplier worked for buyer in the previous year", "already being a supplier", "current supplier base", "incumbent suppliers"]
definition: Suppliers that currently serve a buyer, i.e., that belong to the buyer's current supplier base. Because the knowledge a supplier acquires about a client is instrumental to serving that client, current suppliers are assumed to be more knowledgeable about a client than other suppliers.

name: Supplier selection for new needs
authors_terms: ["buyer choice of supplier for newly needed area", "being selected", "probability of selection"]
definition: The supplier a buyer chooses to fulfil an area of legal expertise the buyer has not previously required, identified by comparing the areas of legal advice buyers list from year to year.

name: Expertise advantage over relevant competitors
authors_terms: ["relative capability advantage", "number of areas with superior expertise relative to the set of competitors", "expertise advantage in relevant competitor set"]
definition: A supplier's level of expertise relative to that possessed by the competitors that comprise the narrower set that constitutes a credible threat given current relationships, i.e., the set of suppliers that currently serves the buyer.

name: Client-specific scope
definition: The cost savings and additional benefits that accrue to providing services to the same buyer in different areas. It differs from economies of scope as usually construed in that they arise only when different services are delivered to the same buyer.

name: Competitors' client-specific scope
definition: The extent of client-specific economies of scope generated by a focal supplier's competitors, which matters to the extent that it provides a client with strong alternatives; it is measured as the maximum number of areas in which a given competitor is selling services to a given client.

name: Relationship termination
definition: The end of a buyer-supplier relationship, observed when the relationship is no longer recorded the following year. The authors argue that a relationship in which either party is unable to capture sufficient value relative to alternative suppliers is more likely to be terminated, so termination proxies for insufficient value capture.

name: Supplier profitability
definition: The overall profitability of a supplier, measured as profit per equity partner, the analogue of return on equity in the context of a professional firm. Proposition 7 holds that profitability at the supplier level is positively related to the weighted average of added value measured at the dyadic buyer-supplier level.

name: Added value
definition: Added value in a competitive interaction is the amount of value creation that would be lost should a given player withdraw. It also represents the maximum amount of value a player can capture, and is a good indicator of the competition a firm faces; the added value of a supplier with a buyer is the difference between its value creation and the value creation ability of the next best alternative if the difference is greater than zero, and equal to zero otherwise.

name: Delta1R (excess value creation of current suppliers over outside suppliers)
definition: The excess value creation (client-specific knowledge) of suppliers in the buyer's current supplier base relative to suppliers outside this base.

name: Principle-based agreements
definition: A principle was defined as an agreement that is 'not based solely on a numerical definition of the quality to be delivered or the price to be paid … but [it] provides overarching, general guidelines for action.' Rules, by contrast, clearly state 'numerically a quality and the price to be paid for it.'

name: Nudge treatment
definition: A treatment in which the emergence of principles was exogenously stimulated by a nudge visible in the instructions and on the screen of the communication stage, telling participants that they did not yet know the exact situation in the second part of the study and that it might be helpful to think about general principles. The nudge did not add new information; it increased the salience of the upcoming change and suggested thinking about general principles.

name: Normative consensus
definition: We say that a pair exhibits normative consensus if the two parties agree on the price–quality combination ((pNB, qNB) = (pNS, qNS)) that their initial agreement implies in the new situation. If, in addition, they also both agree that the seller should choose the efficient quality of 10, we say that the pair reached efficient normative consensus.

name: Normative-behavioral consistency
definition: We say that a given party exhibits normative-behavioral consistency if that party acts in accordance with what that party thinks is implied by the initial agreement in the new situation. More specifically, the buyer exhibits normative-behavioral consistency if the buyer chooses the price that the buyer thinks the agreement indicates (p = pNB), and the seller exhibits normative-behavioral consistency if the seller chooses the quality that the seller thinks the agreement indicates (q = qNS).

name: Equilibration
definition: We use the term 'equilibration' to describe a situation in which a buyer–seller pair coordinates on a new price–quality combination that simultaneously meets the expectations of both parties. Specifically, a pair reaches equilibration if the buyer's chosen price (p) is equal to or larger than the seller's price expectation and the seller's chosen quality (q) is equal to or larger than the buyer's quality expectation.

name: Postshock performance
authors_terms: ["postshock performance", "performance after the shock", "performance after an exogenous change in the environment"]
definition: Performance after the shock is defined as the sum of profits earned by a buyer–seller pair in the repeated game after the environment changed. In the authors' setting, the seller's quality choice fully determines the overall performance of the relationship (i.e., joint profits).

name: Racial diversity
definition: We define racial diversity as the presence of employees from multiple racial categories in a firm as opposed to belonging to one category. That is, a firm is considered to be more racially diverse if people are equally distributed over all the different racial categories.

name: Intermediate firm performance
definition: We measured performance using two distinct measures: productivity—an intermediate output measure—and Tobin's q. Productivity reflects employee efforts disassociated from variations in product and capital markets.

name: Long-term firm performance
definition: Tobin's q, a commonly used measure of long-term profitability, reflects the market's perception of current and potential profitability.

name: Industry type
definition: The state and nature of competitive forces are particularly different for service-oriented vs. manufacturing-oriented firms, and human capital requirements are posited to be different for manufacturing and service firms.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence refers to the growth rates of an industry in which a firm operates. Environmental munificence positively relates to the range of strategy and available options for the firm.

name: Environmental instability
definition: Environmental instability refers to the rate of unpredictable change in environmental factors deemed relevant.

name: Current complementarities
definition: Firms coordinate within a structured network of existing relationships and resource flows; these connections reflect how firms have already managed interdependent product relationships to leverage complementarities between their resource bases. A firm's position in such complementarity networks gives it significant influence over strategic decisions, including the collective's choices during alignment deliberations.

name: Potential for future complementarities
definition: Firms that possess high potential for complementarities with many firms are likely to draw support from them; importantly, these are not existing but potential partners who could develop complementary technologies and products if the firm's proposals are adopted as part of the alignment structure. The potential for complementarities is rooted not only in the position of a firm in the ecosystem's value chain but also in the knowledge it has developed in complementary areas that surpass its existing products.

name: Comment centrality
authors_terms: ["comment centrality", "centrality of a firm's proposals", "core (central) proposals", "technical centrality"]
definition: An ecosystem's technical 'architecture' consists of modular components, some of which are more core (central) and others that are more peripheral; core components are interdependent with many other components, whereas peripheral components encapsulate relatively standalone functions. Comment centrality measures how central the firm's proposals are with respect to the ecosystem's technological components (functions) being shaped, computed as the position of each comment within the network of topics using a weighted degree measure.

name: Value capture
authors_terms: ["ability to capture value", "value capture", "asymmetric value capture", "standard-essential patent claims"]
definition: Value capture is the distribution of profits from a given rule; some firms will inevitably hold intellectual property (IP) claims that constrain adopters of the standard, and such IP ownership signals a broader risk, namely, that a firm's knowledge enables it to capture a disproportionate share of the ecosystem's value. Standard-essential patent claims indicate the ability of firms to capture future value from the emerging standard.

name: Shaping success
authors_terms: ["shaping success", "success at shaping the ecosystem", "shaping outcomes", "comment status"]
definition: Firms seek to 'shape'-that is, they seek to influence technical rules that govern how ecosystem components should work together. Given that authority is distributed, shaping is successful (i.e., proposed rules are adopted) only if it is accepted by other firms in the ecosystem.

name: Interim CEO succession
authors_terms: ["interim CEO succession", "interim CEO succession process", "the use of an interim CEO", "interim CEO", "acting CEO"]
definition: An interim CEO succession is a case where the title of chief executive officer is vacated by the incumbent and the board of directors has not announced a permanent successor, but instead designates a particular individual as 'interim CEO,' or 'acting CEO,' or 'CEO until a permanent successor is named.' The interim succession episode begins when the incumbent CEO formally departs the firm, and ends when the board officially agrees to employ an individual as the CEO and vests full power of the position in that individual.

name: Firm performance
definition: We measure firm performance in two different ways: encompassing accounting-based and market-based measures of performance. Accounting-based performance is the average quarterly return on assets (ROA); market-based performance is captured by the firm's Tobin's Q (TOBINQ).

name: Long-term firm survival
definition: Our analysis of firm survival captures the longer-term impact of this succession choice: whether the use of an interim CEO diminishes the firm's long-term chances of survival even after a permanent CEO is named.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Following prior research, we measured industry dynamism as the temporal variation in industry sales growth and employment growth at the four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code level.

name: Interim CEO duality
definition: The case where the chairman and the interim are the same person. This type of duality reflects higher levels of CEO power because it signals unambiguous decision-making authority at the top of the organization.

name: Perceived trustworthiness of the alliance partner
definition: Trustworthiness captures the degree to which an exchange partner is perceived not to exploit one's exchange vulnerabilities. It is conceptualized as a second-order construct reflected by three dimensions: ability, benevolence, and integrity.

name: Contractual safeguards
definition: Contractual safeguards can be defined as stipulations in a partnership agreement that inflict penalties for the omission of cooperative behaviors or commission of violating behaviors.

name: Clan culture
definition: Clan culture refers to the degree to which an organization's underlying values and assumptions emphasize collective goals, participation, and teamwork.

name: Familiarity
definition: Familiarity can be defined as the degree to which one party in an exchange relationship is knowledgeable of the characteristics of the other party.

name: Reputation
definition: Reputation is defined as the firm's favorable standing in the community that is based on its recognized achievements.

name: Firm performance
definition: Tobin's Q is a common market-based measure of firm performance; the appeal of this measure is that it incorporates current operations, potential growth opportunities, and future operating performance.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["board independence", "fraction of independent directors", "independent director influence"]
definition: Independent directors are individuals whose only business relationship to the firm is their directorship. Our primary measure of independent director influence is the number of independent directors divided by total board size (fraction of independent directors).

name: Founding-family ownership
definition: For this study, family firm refers to publicly traded firms in which the founding family continues to have an ownership stake or maintain board seats.

name: Relative family board representation
authors_terms: ["ratio of family directors to independent directors", "family board representation relative to independent directors", "family power", "family board control"]
definition: The family's influence relative to that of independent directors, measured as the ratio of board seats held by family members to board seats held by independent directors, and as whether family board control exceeds independent director control.

name: Affiliated director representation
authors_terms: ["affiliate directors", "affiliated directors", "fraction of affiliated directors on the board"]
definition: Affiliate directors are directors with potential or existing business relationships with the firm but are not full-time employees; consultants, lawyers, financiers, and investment bankers are examples of affiliate directors.

name: Family presence on the nominating committee
authors_terms: ["family presence on the nominating committee", "family members serving on the nominating committee", "family influence on the nominating committee"]
definition: The responsibility of developing a slate of directors for election by the firm's shareholders is delegated to a subcommittee of the board of directors, the nominating committee; founding families can play an important role in determining the overall structure of the board by exerting their influence through the firm's nominating committee.

name: Board control
definition: Board control was measured using Boyd's (1994) multi-indicator factor model. The indicators for this measure are CEO duality, ratio of insiders to total board members, director stock ownership, representation on the board by ownership groups, and director pay.

name: Corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["diversification", "level of diversification", "extent of diversification", "total diversification", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification"]
definition: While there are multiple measurement schemes available—including Rumelt's categories and SIC counts—the entropy measure (Palepu, 1985) has been reported to have superior reliability and validity. The entropy measure is particularly germane to our analysis, as it can be decomposed into unique elements—indicators of both related and unrelated diversification.

name: Measurement precision
definition: The number of indicators used to represent the constructs in a model: 'Hypothesis 2 stated that the relationship between control and diversification is stronger when using multiple vs. single indicators.' The authors argue that single indicators increase the likelihood of a Type II error and underestimate the magnitude of the relationship.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["business group affiliation", "BG affiliation", "BG dummy", "affiliation to a BG"]
definition: Diversified business groups control and coordinate two or more distinct legal firms through commonly held ownership stakes, often complemented by social ties; a firm's affiliation is whether it is owned by such a group. Following prior research, a firm's affiliation to a BG is operationalized using a simple dummy variable, which takes a value 1 if the firm is owned by a BG and 0 if it is not the case.

name: Capital market participation
authors_terms: ["market participation", "capital market participation", "active capital market participation"]
definition: BG-affiliated firms that participate in the capital markets (i.e., are listed and actively traded on a stock exchange) are potentially subject to capital market scrutiny in addition to the hierarchical control exercised through the controlling stake retained by the parent business group. It is measured as whether a firm is participating actively in the capital market and hence under market scrutiny or whether that is not the case, in any given year.

name: Capital market development
authors_terms: ["capital market development", "capital market efficiency", "capital market index", "quality of the capital markets"]
definition: The authors rely on the two widely considered indicators of capital market development-better investor protection, transparency, and enforcement-namely, (1) market capitalization of listed companies as a percentage of GDP, and (2) the domestic credit provided by the banking sector as a percentage of GDP. Effective market participation requires the capital markets to operate with some degree of informational efficiency.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors choose the most commonly used financial measure of firm performance that can be obtained for both listed and unlisted firms, namely, return on assets (ROA) adjusted for industry. They measure it as profit before interest and tax divided by total assets, adjusted for nonrecurring transactions, and subtract the average ROA for the firm's industry (at the two-digit level) from the firm's ROA.

name: Plant history
authors_terms: ["plant history", "conversion systems", "conversion plants", "start-up systems", "start-up plants", "history of top-down control and hierarchical authority"]
definition: This investigation studied the inertia which derives from an organization's history and its relationship to the control features of message patterns. This was done by comparing older operating plants that had traditional and mechanistic histories, but had converted to self-managing teams (hereafter, "conversion" systems), to other plants within the same company which had self-managing histories from their start-up (hereafter, "start-up" systems).

name: Plant manager style
authors_terms: ["plant manager style", "autocratic plant manager", "participative plant manager", "leadership style of the plant managers", "management style of the plant managers"]
definition: In addition, regardless of plant history, the organization also had participative and autocratic plant manages in both types of plants. The participative plant manager's style was aligned with the STS goals of the firm and should serve as a model for the participative patterns expected with an organic philosophy.

name: Participative communication
authors_terms: ["participative communication", "participative behaviors", "participative forms of behavior", "consultative communication", "question-answer", "discussion", "shared control"]
definition: In terms of the relational coding scheme, participative behaviors were defined as consultative communicative forms such as question / answer (1 1) and discussion (→→), but also subordinate attempts at shared control as revealed in an overall pattern of reciprocated one-upping by the subordinate (e.g., MTST).

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: Perceived environmental uncertainty was measured using three variables—the rate of change in the environment, degree of environmental complexity, and the degree to which the firm is dependent on the sector for important resources (importance) (PEU = Importance (Rate of change x Complexity)).

name: Environment sector
definition: The task environment is made up of factors external to the firm which exert great influence on its operations but on which the firm has little or no control; it consists of the competitor/industry, customer/market, and sources of resources sectors. The remote environment consists of the political/legal, economic, technological, and socio-cultural sectors.

name: Scanning frequency
authors_terms: ["scanning frequency", "frequency of scanning", "frequency of sector scanning"]
definition: The frequency of sector scanning and the degree to which the executives made it a point to stay abreast of information in each sector (degree of interest) were used to measure scanning.

name: Scanning interest
definition: The frequency of sector scanning and the degree to which the executives made it a point to stay abreast of information in each sector (degree of interest) were used to measure scanning.

name: External information source use
definition: This dependent variable was measured using external, internal, personal, and impersonal sources of information (Aguilar, 1967).

name: Internal information source use
definition: This dependent variable was measured using external, internal, personal, and impersonal sources of information (Aguilar, 1967).

name: Personal information source use
authors_terms: ["personal sources of information", "personal vs. impersonal sources"]
definition: This dependent variable was measured using external, internal, personal, and impersonal sources of information (Aguilar, 1967).

name: Impersonal information source use
definition: This dependent variable was measured using external, internal, personal, and impersonal sources of information (Aguilar, 1967).

name: Personal imprint strategy and structure
authors_terms: ["strategy and structure of personal imprints publishing", "personal imprints", "In N Imprints", "imprint-focus", "personal imprint lines"]
definition: Personal imprint publishing is an organizational form that recognizes the importance of personal and relational networks in developing new authors and manuscripts, and it emphasizes the professional autonomy of editors from the influences of management and the hierarchy. In publishing, the number of imprints in a firm is a measure of organization structure and differentiation that is parallel to the number of departments or divisions in an industrial firm, and is also a measure of editorial control in the firm and in the market.

name: Contractual distribution
authors_terms: ["distribution via contractual relations", "distribution contracts", "D Distribution Contract", "contracting of marketing"]
definition: A publishing organization (supplier) has a contract for distribution of its books by another separately owned distributor or publisher. These contracts do not involve equity ownership sharing arrangements between firms, but represent the outsourcing of expenses for services such as advertising, selling, and fulfillment that are payable as a percent of sales.

name: Resource competition
definition: Competition is treated as a constraint on the behavior of firms with consequences for acquisition. It is measured as a ratio of an annual count of potential competitors (all publishing organizations) to available resources (the number of college and university enrollments).

name: Risk of acquisition
definition: The risk of acquisition is the rate at which publishing organizations are acquired; event history analysis is used to examine the hazard rate of acquisition. Organizations were coded 1 only in the year of acquisition and 0 for every subsequent year in which acquisition did not occur.

name: Institutional logic
authors_terms: ["institutional logic", "editorial logic", "market logic", "institutional logics", "prevailing form of capitalism"]
definition: Institutional logics define the norms, values, and beliefs that structure the cognition of actors in organizations, and provide a collective understanding of how strategic interests and decisions are formulated. Two ideal types are identified in higher education publishing: an editorial logic, which prevailed during the 1960s and early 1970s, and a market logic, prevailing since the mid-1970s.

name: Open systems strategy
definition: A strategy through which a firm disseminates its technology and establishes a de facto standard by giving others access to its technical knowledge. The d20 license grants a perpetual, royalty-free, worldwide and non-exclusive right to use, modify, reproduce, and distribute on the market the open content of the sponsor's rules of play.

name: New entrant status
definition: Firms that arrive in the industry, as opposed to incumbents already present; the number of new entrants is one of the traditional elements of industry structure recognized by industrial economics.

name: Adoption of an open system
authors_terms: ["adopt an open system", "adoption of the d20 license", "technological system adopted", "support an open system"]
definition: A firm's decision to base its products on the open system rather than rely on its own proprietary technological system. Both incumbents and new entrants have strong incentives to adopt an open system once it has been introduced into the industry.

name: Average firm size
definition: The size of firms, measured by the number of employees, is one of the traditional elements of industry structure recognized by industrial economics. The authors compare the average size of companies in the industry before and after the diffusion of the open system.

name: Corporate philanthropic contributions
definition: charitable monetary donations-including donations in areas such as the arts, education, housing, health, social welfare, and the environment, among others, but excluding political contributions and commercial sponsorship.

name: Community mega-event
definition: Mega-events are large-scale cultural, political, athletic, and commercial events that attract significant media attention. The authors focus on three mega-events that are hosted at the community level: the Summer Olympics, the Super Bowl, and the Democratic and Republican presidential nominating conventions.

name: Natural disaster severity
authors_terms: ["natural disasters", "severity of damage", "major disasters", "small-scale disasters", "medium-scale disasters"]
definition: A natural disaster is a naturally occurring physical event with major unwanted consequences on a human population. The authors categorize disasters by the extent of economic damage, defining small-scale disasters as those with damages below $1 billion, medium-scale disasters as damages above $1 billion but below $5 billion, and major disasters as the top 25 percent of billion-dollar disasters, a definition that corresponds to a $5 billion minimum threshold.

name: Prior history of philanthropy
authors_terms: ["history of philanthropy", "prior history of large philanthropic contributions", "history of corporate generosity", "past contributions"]
definition: A company's prior history of philanthropy, that is, its level of past charitable contributions, which shapes the extent to which it faces public expectations and scrutiny regarding its giving.

name: Consumer orientation
definition: Firms that operate in industries in which the predominant customers are individual consumers rather than firms, such as consumer goods and personal services, in contrast to industries that produce primarily for industrial use, such as business services and capital goods.

name: Local intercorporate network cohesion
authors_terms: ["network cohesion among local corporations", "local network cohesion", "network cohesion among local firms", "cohesive interfirm networks"]
definition: A crucial feature of geographic communities is the extent to which their constituent members are connected by cohesive social networks that foster pressures toward conformity; cohesive interfirm networks in a community create normative environments for organizations.

name: Community economic strength
authors_terms: ["economic strength of the community", "local economy", "communities with a strong local economy"]
definition: The economic position of an urban community, which determines its dependence on corporations: communities with a weak local economy tend to provide benefits to corporations rather than coax contributions from them for community causes.

name: International market contraction
authors_terms: ["international contraction", "contraction of international market presence", "international market presence contraction", "contraction in international presence"]
definition: The contraction of international presence frees up multiple types of non-scale free resources - resources whose utilization in specific foreign markets is subject to significant opportunity costs in terms of their use in other parts of the corporation.

name: Business scope expansion
authors_terms: ["business presence expansion", "business scope expansion", "expansion into new business domains", "expansion of the business presence"]
definition: The expansion of the firm's presence in new business domains, which follows the contraction of international presence and is captured by changes in noncore segment sales. The expansion of the firm's presence in new business domains is not expected to occur concurrently with the contraction of its international market presence, but rather requires several time lags.

name: Availability of financial resources
authors_terms: ["financial resources", "non-scale free financial resources", "availability of financial resources", "internal capital market"]
definition: The liquid funds possessed by a firm are fully fungible in the sense that they can be readily applied in any geography or industry domain, but they are also non-scale free in the sense that they are fully absorbed by the activities in which they are invested.

name: Technological knowledge
authors_terms: ["technological knowledge", "scale free technological knowledge resources", "patent applications"]
definition: When expanding into new business domains, firms typically create new scale free resources, such as new technological knowledge. New technological knowledge that firms create while expanding into new business domains can serve as key scale free resources for expanding internationally.

name: International expansion
authors_terms: ["international expansion", "expansion of international presence", "resumed expansion into international markets"]
definition: In the long term, the new scale free resources reignite the expansion of the initially contracted international presence. Increased familiarity with new business domains may well allow firms to identify new opportunities in international markets, and thereby support renewed expansion of these firms into international markets.

name: Firm-employee relationship strength
authors_terms: ["firm-employee relationship", "FE relationships", "FE relationship strength", "strength of a firm's relationship with its employees"]
definition: We draw on the stakeholder literature to characterize the FE relationship as one that fosters secure work environments, long-term commitments, and trust. Strength of the relationship between a firm and its employees is measured in the KLD database using seven items.

name: Local search
definition: Local search is defined as the firm's utilization of knowledge in time t from its accumulated body of knowledge.

name: Distant search
definition: Distant search is defined as new additions to the firm's accumulated 5-year knowledge base in year t.

name: Business group market share
authors_terms: ["GroupShare", "group market share", "group share", "sector market share of business groups", "group dominance"]
definition: GroupShare is the ratio of total sales of firms that belonged to business groups within each sector to the sales of all firms in that sector during a particular year. Business groups are conglomerations of nominally independent firms that operate under common administrative and financial management and often are controlled by families.

name: Industry innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation", "TRCA", "relative technological specialization in patenting", "patent-based measure of innovation", "innovation performance"]
definition: The paper uses a patent-based measure of innovation: the dependent variable TRCA measures a sector's relative technological specialization in patenting, relative to the country's own total patents and to the overall distribution of patents in the United States.

name: Market-based innovation infrastructure
authors_terms: ["alternative sources of innovation infrastructure", "market-based innovation infrastructure", "market-based institutions"]
definition: The availability of market-based institutions that supply the infrastructure needed for innovation, such as venture capital, robust labor markets, external research facilities, multinational companies and complementary suppliers and distributors. When there are alternative institutions needed for innovation, the marginal benefits from group structure will be lower for every level of group share.

name: Technological opportunity
definition: Technological opportunity reflects how fertile a sector's technological environment is; it increases the possibilities for innovation, and when the technological environment is fertile the cost of developing new products declines, allowing independent players with good ideas to compete with the incumbents.

name: Importance of basic research
authors_terms: ["share of basic R&D", "BasicRD", "need for infrastructure", "importance of basic research"]
definition: The importance of basic research for innovation in an industry, capturing the need for access to costly innovation infrastructure to deal with the risks and uncertainty of basic research.

name: R&D intensity
definition: We use R&D intensity as a measure of innovation in the causality tests because it is more directly linked with the cost of R&D than patents are.

name: Micro-subsidiary control mechanisms
definition: The set of control mechanisms at the subsidiary level, comprising clinic autonomy (decentralization of decision making) and clinic-group interactions (interdependence and communications with headquarters).

name: Macro-corporate control mechanisms
definition: The set of corporate-level control mechanisms, comprising work standardization (formalization of policies and procedures) and headquarters-subsidiary integration (shared norms and culture), which apply uniformly across organizational subsidiaries.

name: Endogenous subsidiary performance
authors_terms: ["endogenous performance", "endogenous clinic performance change", "clinic efficiency change"]
definition: The component of subsidiary performance attributable to endogenous micro-subsidiary efforts; in the longitudinal analysis, the change in a clinic's performance with respect to its peers of the same clinic type.

name: Exogenous subsidiary performance
definition: The component of subsidiary performance attributable to exogenous macro-organizational policies; in the longitudinal analysis, the change in a clinic's performance with respect to all clinics in the sample.

name: Clinic autonomy
definition: The extent to which clinic employees (physicians, nurses, and staff) perceive that they exercise discretion or influence decisions about what work to perform, how work is performed, and the development of work policies or procedures.

name: Clinic-group interactions
definition: A measure of informal clinic-group relations tailored to individual clinics, defined as the degree of perceived interdependence and communications between individual clinics and group headquarters.

name: Work standardization
definition: Captures the combined effects of how group policy changes influenced the formalized structuring of work in clinics, dealing with the clarity, degree, number, and enabling of work rules and procedures.

name: Headquarters-subsidiary integration
definition: The perceived degree of headquarters-subsidiary integration, reflecting shared norms, culture, and integrative synergies between clinics and group headquarters.

name: Local environmental complexity
definition: The complexity of the local environment served by a clinic, operationalized as whether a clinic serves a broad (heterogeneous) or focused (homogeneous) mix of patients.

name: Clinic resources
definition: The size or number of employees of a clinic, chosen as the key input factor in the DEA model because labor costs account for approximately 80% of annual clinic operating costs.

name: Patient care performance
definition: A composite measure of patient care, the average of patient satisfaction, staff courtesy, and clinical quality care.

name: Business care performance
definition: A composite measure of business care, the average of clinic productivity (RVUs per provider) and clinic net income (net revenue per provider).

name: Cultural distance
definition: The distance between the national cultures of joint venture partners; the more culturally distant two firms are, the greater the differences in their organizational and administrative practices, employee expectations, and interpretation of and response to strategic issues.

name: Japanese partner nationality
authors_terms: ["U.S.-Japanese joint ventures", "Japanese-American joint ventures", "cross-border ventures with the Japanese"]
definition: Having a Japanese partner in a joint venture; the authors argue that values and institutions of Japanese culture, such as trust, long-term orientation, and concern for reputation, economize on transactions and make these ventures less likely to dissolve.

name: Strategic scope dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["strategic scope", "scope differential", "difference in product-market scopes", "breadth and scope"]
definition: The difference between partners in the breadth and scope of their strategic activities; diversified firms with broad product and market scope require different information-sharing and decision-making processes than single-business firms.

name: Partner size dissimilarity
definition: The difference in size between joint venture partners, which the authors argue leads to differences in corporate perspectives, value systems, and methods of aligning internal resources.

name: Partner age dissimilarity
definition: The difference in the organizational histories of the partners; an organization's history strongly influences the values and beliefs that develop over time, so partners of different ages experience conflict in coordinating activities.

name: Direct competition between partners
definition: Partnership between firms competing in the same market, where present friends can easily become future foes and goals are likely to be in direct conflict.

name: Operational overlap
definition: The extent to which the joint venture operates within the product-market scope of one or both partners, so that economic benefits from the collaboration tend to be minimal and less visible.

name: Technology transfer
authors_terms: ["technology transfer", "technology ventures", "exchange of technologically specific know-how"]
definition: A joint venture characterized by an exchange of technologically specific know-how that cannot easily be codified and requires intimate human contact for exchange, making partner firm-specific advantages appropriable.

name: Joint venture duration
authors_terms: ["duration of a joint venture", "dissolution", "joint venture survival", "longevity"]
definition: The length of time a joint venture persists; a fundamental premise is that a joint venture is not expected to last indefinitely, and instability can be signaled by unexpected termination through a dissolution, a sell-off, or an acquisition.

name: Platform-owner entry threat
authors_terms: ["platform-owner entry threat", "threat of Google's entry", "entry threat", "Under Entry Threat"]
definition: Under Entry Threatit equals 1 in the period during which app i faces an increased entry threat to its app category but does not face Google's actual entry, and 0 otherwise. To capture Google's entry threat to various mobile app markets, the authors look at instances in which Apple released its own apps on its iOS system but Google had not yet entered in the equivalent market on Android.

name: Platform-owner actual entry
definition: Under Actual Entryit equals 1 after Google actually enters and 0 otherwise. The authors use their empirical design to identify Google's threat of entry separately from its actual entry.

name: Innovation in affected markets
authors_terms: ["innovation efforts", "product refinements", "updates on affected apps", "new apps similar to those Google is about to release"]
definition: We define a complementor's innovation effort as the rate at which a complementor develops its products. Because the entry of the platform owner may take significant market share in the affected market, the benefits to complementors of continuing to work in that market are likely to be significantly reduced.

name: Innovation in unaffected markets
authors_terms: ["diverting innovation efforts to unaffected areas", "product expansions", "new apps unrelated to the entry threats"]
definition: As a result, complementors may accommodate platform-owner entry by diverting innovation efforts to unaffected areas. Innovation stimulated by platform-owner entry can take different forms, such as improving existing products (i.e., product refinements) or introducing brand-new products (i.e., product expansions).

name: App price
authors_terms: ["prices in the affected market segment", "price of app i", "increase their prices"]
definition: Our second dependent variable is the price of app i in month t. If an app's price changes within a given month, we use its price at the beginning of a month.

name: Product popularity
definition: We consider an app is popular if it had been ranked in the top 500 across all categories at any time prior to Google's entry threat.

name: Firm market value
definition: In our case, the dependent variable is derived from a market value equation in which market value is determined as the expected discounted future profits of the firm both due to tangible assets and intangible (knowledge) assets (Peters & Taylor, 2017).

name: Foreign R&D investment
authors_terms: ["Foreign R&D", "new cross-border R&D investments", "new R&D investments abroad", "new foreign R&D investments"]
definition: Foreign R&D (Hypothesis 1) is the count of new cross-border R&D investments in a year, or month, by the focal firm.

name: IP risk of foreign R&D
authors_terms: ["IP risk of Foreign R&D", "weak IPR protection", "weak IP protection", "IP risk"]
definition: IP risk of Foreign R&D (Hypothesis 2) is a weighted measure of the inverse of (effective) patent protection the firms are confronted with in the destination countries of their R&D investments.

name: Internal linkage strategy
authors_terms: ["(Internal) Linkage Strategy", "internal linkage strategy", "internal linkages", "cross-country inventor collaboration"]
definition: Following prior studies (e.g., Alcácer & Zhao, 2012; Belderbos & Somers, 2015), (Internal) Linkage Strategy is measured as the degree to which inventors based in different countries contribute to firms' patents (cross-country inventor collaboration), as identified from inventors' addresses.

name: Resource-capability combination value
definition: If a resource or capability yields the potential to enable a firm to reduce costs and/or respond to environmental opportunities and threats, it is valuable, and to the extent that a firm is able to effectively deploy such a resource or capability, it will attain a competitive advantage. The key to attaining a competitive advantage is the exploitation of a valuable resource-capability combination; the more valuable the firm's resource-capability combinations, the greater the advantage it will enjoy.

name: Resource-capability combination rareness
definition: Competitive advantage likely derives from the exploitation of resources and capabilities that are rare, or possessed by some number of firms in an industry that is small enough to prohibit perfect competition. Because resources and capabilities must be exploited in combination, rareness likely contributes to competitive advantage at the level of resource-capability combinations.

name: Competitive advantage
definition: A competitive advantage is generally conceptualized as the implementation of a strategy not currently being implemented by other firms that facilitates the reduction of costs, the exploitation of market opportunities, and/or the neutralization of competitive threats. A firm that has attained a competitive advantage has created more economic value (the difference between the perceived benefits of a resource-capability combination and the economic cost to exploit them) than its competitors.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is generally conceptualized as the rents a firm accrues as a result of the implementation of its strategies. Whereas competitive advantage refers to the economic value that has been created from the exploitation of a firm's resource-capability combinations, performance refers to the economic value that the firm has captured from their commercialization.

name: Corporate strategic refocusing
definition: The acquisition of related activities and the divestiture (e.g., the spinning off or shutting down of establishments or entire lines of business) of unrelated, peripheral businesses reflect a strategy of corporate refocusing. It entails the purposeful reduction in firm scope and the unequivocal negation of previous strategic decisions.

name: CEO power
definition: Power represents simply the ability to bring about a preferred or intended effect. CEO power was assessed using seven indicators developed by Finkelstein (1992): number of titles, compensation, stock ownership, family link to founders, functional expertise, elite education, and number of outside board memberships, which represent a relatively broad range of power bases.

name: Heir apparent experience
authors_terms: ["heir apparent experience", "experience as heir apparent", "time spent as president or COO"]
definition: Experience as heir apparent represents the extent to which a new CEO has been socialized to the CEO position by the predecessor, and is operationalized as the length of time, if any, the incoming CEO was in the position of president and/or COO in the organization prior to being appointed as the CEO.

name: Proximity to prominent high-status firms
authors_terms: ["Near PHSF Ads", "proximity to prominent high-status neighbors", "spatial proximity to high-status firms", "relative proximity"]
definition: Mere spatial proximity to other high-status firms - proximity in a visually observable space - prompts audiences to perceive associations between the focal firm and its high-status neighbors. The argument applies if these neighbors are prominent, that is, easily recognizable to general audiences.

name: Aspirational pricing
definition: A pricing strategy that signals a firm's status aspirations rather than actual selling prices; firms can set their listed prices to communicate their aspirational status. Such signaling of higher status through aspirational pricing needs to be acceptable by relevant audiences.

name: Status group
authors_terms: ["status group", "high-, middle-, and low-status fashion firms"]
definition: Fashion firms are classified into three status groups based on Bonacich's centrality measure from fashion-model sharing networks: high-status firms are those whose centrality measures are one standard deviation above the mean, low-status firms are those one standard deviation below the mean or not participating in fashion weeks, and middle-status firms include all the others.

name: Perceived status
definition: Proximity to other high-status firms influences status perceptions because external audiences simply assume that the focal firm belongs to the same status group as its proximate high-status counterparts. The experiment tests whether spatial proximity to prominent high-status firms changes how Vogue readers perceive the focal fashion firm.

name: Component modularity
authors_terms: ["component modularity", "degree of component modularity", "CM", "degree of coupling of product components"]
definition: The degree of component modularity is used as an inverse proxy for the degree of coupling of product architectures. CM refers to a specific product component and is close to 1 when the component implements one or few functions and most of its interfaces are open standard, and close to 0 when the component implements several functions and/or most of its interfaces are closed.

name: Product modularity
authors_terms: ["product modularity", "more modular product design", "higher levels of modularity across all of components", "modularity in product design"]
definition: The modularity of the firm's overall product design, i.e. the level of modularity that a firm achieves across all of its components, contrasted with the degree of coupling of a single product component.

name: Buyer-supplier information sharing
authors_terms: ["buyer-supplier information sharing", "information sharing", "degree of coupling between organizations", "IS"]
definition: The degree of coupling of organizational architectures, which depends on the extent to which the organizations involved in the design and production of the components that make a product communicate and exchange business and technological information, coordinating their decisions, actions, and efforts.

name: Supply relationship performance
definition: The performance of supply relationships is the degree of the OEM's satisfaction with its relationships with suppliers regarding component development, logistics, and price and contract negotiation; it is the purchasers' perception of supplier performance.

name: Operating cash flow
authors_terms: ["relative operating cash flow", "operating cash flow", "operating performance", "cash flow"]
definition: The variable equals the difference between an organization's operating cash flow and the sample mean operating cash flow for all MSOs in the same year. The authors focus on operating cash flow, which captures inflows and outflows of capital as they occur, rather than accounting measures of profit that amortize investments over their useful lives.

name: Long horizon investment
authors_terms: ["long horizon investments", "investment in long horizon projects", "long horizon projects", "long-term investments"]
definition: Investments that take a long period of time to pay off, featuring 'costs that reduce earnings today and benefits deferred into the future.'

name: Short horizon investment
definition: Extending an existing system to reach additional homes has a shorter payoff horizon: because the headend is already in place, revenue can be added from new subscribers as soon as the line is extended to their homes.

name: Firm age
definition: The number of years the organization has operated, measured in years and calculated only from 1972 onward because of regulatory changes that substantially alter the cable industry at the start of the study period.

name: Exercisable stock options
definition: When the option becomes exercisable, managers gain the discretion to choose whether to hold the option longer (i.e., up to 10 years) or cash it in and realize gains at any time.

name: Unexercisable stock options
authors_terms: ["unexercisable options", "options that are unexercisable until the future"]
definition: Because unexercisable options only have value in the future, they provide managers with an incentive to make longer horizon investments.

name: Degree of hierarchy
authors_terms: ["hierarchy", "degree of hierarchy", "hierarchy of the business unit", "steeper hierarchy", "corporate hierarchy", "layers of sequential authority"]
definition: Hierarchies are layers of sequential authority, introduced to solve the design problems of enabling coordination and fostering cooperation among employees. In most organizational settings hierarchies denote managers' rank ordering along a dimension of authority.

name: Propensity to pass information upward
authors_terms: ["propensity to pass information up", "vertical information flow", "passing information up", "business-wide relevance", "ideas passed up", "pass on ideas to their superiors"]
definition: The propensity of mid-level managers to pass information up the firm's line of command to their superiors. In the field data it is captured by the local mid-level manager's decision to declare an idea business-wide relevant and thereby kick it up to her superior.

name: Evaluation apprehension
authors_terms: ["evaluation apprehension", "fear of being assessed", "fear of negative feedback"]
definition: Evaluation apprehension refers to a term coined by Cottrell (1972), and is defined as the fear of being assessed. Evaluation apprehension inhibits knowledge sharing and may be the result of perceiving one's knowledge as inaccurate or as not valued, leading to unfavorable assessments.

name: Perceived lack of control
authors_terms: ["lack of control", "perceived lack of control", "lack of control over the final outcome"]
definition: Failure to control one's environment adversely affects a person's responsiveness to the outside world. Centralized decision making within a corporation, as is characteristic of hierarchical organizations, has been suggested as one factor that can induce a perceived lack of control in subordinate employees and lead to organizational silence.

name: Perceived cohesion among franchisees
authors_terms: ["cohesion among franchisees", "perceived cohesion", "perceptions of cohesion among franchisees"]
definition: For this study, we define cohesion as franchisees' inclinations to forge social bonds, help each other, and coordinate their efforts around the chain's tasks and objectives. Following a referent-shift consensus model, franchisees within a chain are assumed to share perceptions of the amount of cohesion in their chain.

name: Deviation from chain standards
authors_terms: ["deviation from standards", "deviation from chain standards", "deviating from standards"]
definition: Unauthorized deviation from a chain's standards occurs when franchisees use know-how other than that prescribed, deviating from the chain's standardized know-how and core format components; it is one of the two opportunistic behaviors particularly harmful to the efficiency and survival of franchise chains.

name: Information withholding
definition: Franchisees withholding information that would be useful to the franchise system; withholding information from a franchisor could prevent system-wide adaptations to changing markets, and franchisees who keep useful information to themselves are a threat.

name: Corporate venture capital investments
authors_terms: ["number of CVC investments", "number of corporate venture capital investments", "CVC investments", "corporate venture capital (CVC) investments"]
definition: CVC investments are defined as external equity investments made by established firms in privately held entrepreneurial start-ups (Gompers & Lerner, 1998).

name: Knowledge creation rate
authors_terms: ["rate of knowledge creation", "knowledge creation", "innovation performance", "patent count"]
definition: The rate of knowledge creation, the paper's dependent variable, was operationalized by the annual count of successful patent applications for firm i in year t.

name: Involvement with portfolio firms
authors_terms: ["involvement", "active involvement in investee firms", "involvement with portfolio firms", "degree of involvement with their portfolio firms"]
definition: Involvement refers to the extent to which corporate investors build relationships with their portfolio firms that go beyond just providing equity capital.

name: Technological knowledge diversity
authors_terms: ["technological knowledge diversity", "technological diversity", "diversity of prior knowledge", "knowledge breadth"]
definition: The authors focus on the heterogeneity (or diversity or breadth) of technological knowledge within the investor firm as a moderator of learning from CVC investments. It was measured by calculating the inverse concentration ratio of the distribution of a firm's patents over the primary technology classes to which they had been assigned.

name: Pre-entry use experience
definition: Pre-entry 'use experience' is defined as whether an entrant was a user in a context where a new product can fulfill needs. Before entering an industry, actors can accumulate use experience from activity in contexts that become potential users of a new product, regardless of a history of direct interaction with a new product.

name: Product portfolio usage breadth
authors_terms: ["portfolio usage breadth", "usage breadth", "product portfolio usage breadth"]
definition: Usage breadth is the extent to which products in a portfolio collectively span distinct customer segments. With low usage breadth portfolios, entrants target a single or small number of customer segments via one or few constituent products that closely overlap in the small number of targeted segments.

name: Product portfolio usage overlap
definition: Usage overlap is defined as the extent to which targeted customer segments of each of a firm's products overlap with its other products, separating high breadth portfolios built of segment-agnostic products targeting several segments from high breadth portfolios built of multiple products each catering to idiosyncratic needs in specific segments.

name: Entrant type
authors_terms: ["diversifying entrant", "startups", "diversifying entrants versus startups", "user diversifying entrants", "user startups"]
definition: Diversifying entrants come from other industries to a nascent industry, utilizing firm-level experiences from user industries. Startups draw on founder-level experiences as end users or employees in user industries.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D expenditures divided by total sales", "R&D", "R&D as a strategic asset"]
definition: R&D intensity, our primary independent variable, is the firm's R&D expenditures divided by total sales.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "positive abnormal returns", "negative abnormal returns", "stock price reactions"]
definition: We used standard event study methodology to measure abnormal returns. The premise is that price changes reflect investor expectations of changes in a firm's future performance based on new information; in this context, the new information is the revelation of insider trading.

name: Sociocultural distance
definition: Sociocultural distance, a "particularly potent form of internal uncertainty"; the more unfamiliar the multinational firm is with the values and operating methods of the foreign parent, the more it would tend to avoid high-equity entry modes.

name: International experience
definition: The parent firm's experience in international operations, indicated by a long tradition of international operations, many years of operating in foreign countries, and investing abroad as part of its strategy for many years.

name: Relatedness of strategic resources
authors_terms: ["relatedness of parent and IJV's rent-yielding strategic resources", "relatedness of strategic resources", "relatedness of core competencies", "STRATRES", "strategic resource similarity"]
definition: The relatedness of the rent-yielding strategic resources of the parent and the joint venture, that is, the degree to which the joint venture utilizes the skills and the technology contributed by the parent.

name: Relative resource contribution
authors_terms: ["relative contribution of resources to the venture by each partner", "relative resource contribution", "relative contribution of the parent", "RELCONT"]
definition: The parent firm's relative contribution is defined as the total of its contributions of resources minus the resource contributions of the other parent in each of several operational areas.

name: Bargaining power
authors_terms: ["bargaining power in the negotiation process", "relative bargaining power", "BARGPWER"]
definition: The relative bargaining positions of the parties determine the final outcome of the negotiations; bargaining power is defined as the ability to affect outcomes or to get things done, and it stems from control of critical resources.

name: Government restrictions on equity
authors_terms: ["regulation limiting equity share", "government restrictions", "legal requirements limiting equity share", "LAWS"]
definition: Government regulation of the ownership position; typically, government restrictions limit the equity share held by the foreign parent.

name: Equity share
definition: The equity share held by each of the parents, commonly used in the literature and a way of influencing strategic control over the joint venture, though conceptually distinct from control.

name: Control over specific activities
authors_terms: ["control over specific JV activities", "control over specific activities", "specialized control", "SCONTROL"]
definition: Control over specific operational activities of the joint venture; by bargaining to control specific areas of the IJV's activities to which it contributes key strategic resources, a parent firm can manage the effective application of its assets and skills.

name: Overall control
definition: Overall control of the IJV suggests that the parent, rather than focusing on its own contribution, is interested in controlling the strategic direction of the combined bundle of complementary strategic resources represented by the IJV itself.

name: Perceived joint venture performance
authors_terms: ["perceived performance of the JV", "performance satisfaction", "perceptions of performance", "PERFORM"]
definition: Performance of the joint venture as perceived by the foreign parent company, reflecting qualitative assessments of the venture from the perspective of the Norwegian parent.

name: Entry into new technological niches
authors_terms: ["branching", "entry into new technological niches", "expansion of a firm's capabilities by entering 'new to the firm' technological niches", "number of entries into new technological niches"]
definition: The expansion of a firm's capabilities by entering 'new to the firm' technological niches is termed branching. Branching is a count of the number of entries by a firm into 'new to the firm' niches measured at the patent main class level, consistent with Ahuja and Lampert (2001).

name: Firm age
definition: The relative benefit that accrues to the firm's branching activity systematically differs by the age at which the firm undertakes this capability expansion, traced to the tension between efficiencies in learning from cumulative output and the rigidities that occur with senescence. Firm age was measured as the number of years since incorporation.

name: Quantity of innovative output
definition: Quantity of innovative output is measured as the number of new patents applied for in two subsequent years (t + 1, t + 2). Use of patents to study firm-level innovativeness is common.

name: Technological impact
authors_terms: ["technological impact", "impact", "impact that this output has on the technology domain"]
definition: Technological impact is measured as the average number of citations, net of self-citations, received by patents filed by the firm in years t + 1 and t + 2 (citations received/count of patents) observed in five subsequent years (t + 2 to t + 6 and t + 3 to t + 7, respectively).

name: NPD motivation
authors_terms: ["unit-level NPD motivation", "NPD motivation", "employees' collective motivation for new product development (NPD)"]
definition: The collective motivation of the employees of an NPD unit to collaboratively share and recombine their knowledge and to take risks in order to operationalize new product designs.

name: NPD capability
definition: The collective cognitive ability of an NPD unit's employees to consistently and effectively coordinate their interactions and communications to combine specialized knowledge in order to create and introduce new products.

name: NPD performance
definition: Firms' performance in new product development, proxied by the revenue generated from new products.

name: Strategic orientation toward NPD
authors_terms: ["strategic orientation focusing on NPD", "strategic orientation toward NPD", "strategic orientation toward innovation"]
definition: A firm-level construct describing the organizational direction of the firm toward NPD; the authors treat it as a foundational antecedent to unit-level NPD motivation and capability.

name: Reward and recognition practices
authors_terms: ["reward and recognition practices emphasizing NPD", "rewards and recognition"]
definition: Reward and recognition practices tied to employees' participation in NPD activities and NPD performance, adopted within an NPD unit.

name: Staffing and training practices
authors_terms: ["staffing and training practices emphasizing NPD", "staff and training", "staffing and training"]
definition: A second-order construct that combines two sub-constructs: staffing practices and training practices related to NPD employees.

name: Board faultline strength
definition: Faultlines are hypothetical dividing lines that usually fracture a team into subgroups based on the alignment of multiple characteristics (Lau & Murnighan, 1998).

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance based on accounting returns, measured as 2-year average return on assets (ROA) after each observation.

name: CEO-minority director functional experience overlap
authors_terms: ["CEO overlapping personal range of functional experiences with demographic minority directors", "CEO overlap in personal range of functional experiences", "CEO-demographic minority directors' functional overlap"]
definition: Personal range of functional experiences refers to all functional experiences of CEOs and board members throughout their careers.

name: CEO-minority director tenure overlap
authors_terms: ["CEO overlapping tenure with demographic minorities", "CEO-demographic minority directors' tenure overlap"]
definition: Overlapping tenure of the CEO with the demographic minority directors is measured based on a variable of common historical experience for teams, developed by Carroll and Harrison (1998).

name: Demographic minority directors
definition: Demographic minorities (i.e., women and racial minorities) appointed to corporate boards.

name: Egocentric impression management tactics
definition: Impression management claims that try to convey a positive image of the focal organization by underscoring the low presence (or even absence) of certain negative attributes. In this context, they are claims that emphasize the absence or small amount of unhealthy nutrients in a focal food product.

name: Alter-centric impression management tactics
definition: Impression management claims that present an unfavorable image of a competing organization by pointing at the relatively greater presence of certain negative attributes in a competitor, inducing the target audience to benchmark the claimant against this other organization.

name: Nutrient contestation
definition: Stakeholder attacks that are attribute specific and apply to the market segment level, referring to the degree to which a negative attribute is attacked by hostile stakeholders such as the media. In this context, it is the yearly number of media articles attacking a food category for its amount of a specific unhealthy nutrient, namely sugar, salt, or fat.

name: Product sales
definition: Each UPC's annual sales in the U.S. territory in U.S. dollars, used to capture commercial performance and, indirectly, consumers' purchasing decisions and the effectiveness of impression management tactics.

name: Geographic dispersion of sales
authors_terms: ["geographic concentration", "geographic scope", "geographic sales concentration", "extent of a firm's operations outside its home location", "%Out-of-Province Sales", "outside-province sales"]
definition: The extent of a firm's nonlocal business operations, i.e., its geographic sales concentration. The authors argue that a firm's sales outside the home location is an important indicator of the geographic concentration of its business operations and serves as a first-order proxy of how 'local' the firm is in the eyes of the home-location government.

name: State expropriation hazards
authors_terms: ["state expropriation", "state expropriation hazards", "unauthorized levies (Tan Pai)", "political expropriation risk"]
definition: The infringement of firm property by the state and its agents; the authors focus on direct expropriation by the state without legal basis. Unauthorized levies (Tan Pai) are the primary means through which local governments expropriate privately held assets and typically consist of various 'fees' that are unlawfully charged to firms by local governments.

name: Political capital
definition: A firm's political capital can constrain state expropriation in general; favorable relationships with governments are understood to be critical to business development and growth. Political capital, such as favorable personal ties with local government officials, helps firms better align their interests with those of local government officials.

name: Institutional constraints on government extraction
authors_terms: ["institutional environment", "Province Refrainment from Extraction", "institutional constraints on government expropriation", "constraints on government extraction"]
definition: The hazards of state expropriation are not evenly distributed throughout all institutional environments: governments in some places are more constrained from extracting from firms than their counterparts in other locations. The measure captures the degree to which the government refrains from using discretion and power to extract revenue from businesses in a province.

name: Director dismissal
authors_terms: ["director departure from focal", "dismissal", "board dismisses a director", "remove a compromised colleague"]
definition: Our hypotheses address the likelihood that a director departed from a focal board following association with an incident of accounting fraud at a restating firm. A board translates this stigma into professional devaluation when its members decide to sever relationships with a director who has been compromised elsewhere.

name: Public pension fund ownership
authors_terms: ["public pension fund (PPF) investors", "PPF ownership of focal", "dependence on PPF investors"]
definition: Public pension funds (PPFs) have, on average, the largest equity holdings of any type of institution, giving them particularly strong incentives to monitor corporate decision making and performance. Firms are dependent on PPFs not only because they have a direct role in providing capital, but also because their activism can influence the perceptions of other resource providers.

name: Securities analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["securities analysts", "analyst coverage of focal", "coverage by securities analysts"]
definition: 'Sell-side' analysts are generally employed by independent research firms, brokerage firms, or full-service investment banks. Analysts provide regular forecasts of a firm's earnings and long-term growth, in addition to qualitative coverage about strategic, management, and industry developments.

name: Governance-rating agency coverage
authors_terms: ["independent governance-rating agencies", "governance-rating agency coverage of focal", "coverage by a governance-rating agency"]
definition: Independent governance-rating agencies are a third audience that monitors and assesses board governance decisions (e.g., The Corporate Library, RiskMetrics Group, GovernanceMetrics International).
