Governance-rating agencies compile and disperse a variety of data, including information related to a board's structure and functioning, the experience and qualification of individual directors, the board's executive compensation decisions, and its record of protecting shareholder rights.

name: Board human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital at focal", "board human capital", "board's human capital"]
definition: Directors' human capital is derived from position, training, and career history (Becker, 1964; Coleman, 1988), which constitute documented experience that signals valuable professional competencies. In the boardroom, prior top management and director experience is likely to be an especially valuable source of human capital.

name: Board social capital
authors_terms: ["social capital at focal", "board social capital", "board's social capital"]
definition: Social capital comes from directors' networks of relationships, the established connections that a board can leverage to help its firm succeed (Nahapiet & Ghoshal, 1998).

name: CSR-oriented shareholder unrest
definition: CSR-oriented unrest centers on advancing societal welfare by increasing engagement with CSR practices, such as reducing a firm's environmental footprint and improving employment practices. It is one of the two domains of shareholder unrest, the aggregate scale and gravity of shareholder dissatisfaction with company practices.

name: Wealth-oriented shareholder unrest
definition: Wealth-oriented shareholder unrest is aimed at enhancing the financial potential of the firm, with the ultimate goal of increasing shareholder wealth. Such unrest typically focuses on perceived shortcomings in corporate governance, such as board independence, as well as strategic matters, such as acquisitions, divestitures, and dividends.

name: CEO pay adjustment
authors_terms: ["CEO pay adjustment", "incumbent CEO pay change", "CEO pay change", "pay revision"]
definition: We measured CEO pay change as the percentage change in the CEO's annual compensation, from year t 2 1 to t. This measure indicates how pay changes are enacted by the board as described in firms' proxy statements, capturing the overall magnitude of compensation change year to year.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Dismissal is one of the two major ways that boards can sanction, or settle up, with their CEOs, through which the board removes the CEO. Departures were coded as dismissals by partitioning departure events on CEOs' age-based retirement proneness and carefully studying media reports.

name: CEO voluntary departure
definition: A voluntary departure is a case in which the CEO leaves the position willingly rather than being dismissed. Cases in which departures were preplanned, such as cases of long-announced and mandatory retirements, or induced by health, unexpected death, or family care, were excluded.

name: New CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["new CEO pay", "new CEO compensation", "compensation of a new CEO"]
definition: The compensation awarded to a new CEO in his or her first year; to offset the unappealing qualities of a position at a firm with shareholder unrest, the board will need to increase the attractiveness of the job by offering higher pay.

name: Exporting
definition: The export status of the firm captures whether the focal firm sold to foreign markets in a given year; export volume captures the volume of trade, since the intensity of knowledge spillovers across two countries is likely to covary with the intensity of trade.

name: Innovative productivity
definition: Our dependent variable is innovative productivity. We proxy for innovative productivity using a count of patent applications.

name: Technological capability
authors_terms: ["technological capabilities", "technological leader", "technological laggard", "relative R&D expenditures", "proximity to the technological frontier"]
definition: To identify whether a firm is a technological leader or laggard, we compare firms in these data to comparable others (in their industry) in the OECD on the basis of their R&D expenditures. Research suggests that relative R&D expenditures can proxy for a firm's technological capabilities.

name: Activist choice homophily
definition: In activist choice homophily, the basis of homophilic support is not merely dyadic similarity but rather perceptions of shared structural barriers stemming from a common group-level social identity and an underlying desire to help overcome them. It flows primarily from group-level interests rather than interpersonal mechanisms rooted in self-enhancement, functional considerations, or common thinking or taste.

name: Interpersonal choice homophily
definition: The generally understood form of homophily, which the authors refer to as ''interpersonal choice homophily,'' which invokes the adage that ''birds of a feather flock together.'' These potential sources of homophily are grouped under the single label of interpersonal choice homophily because they all operate through the dyadic identification of, and favorable inclination toward, those with common characteristics.

name: Founder gender
authors_terms: ["gender of the founder(s)", "female founder", "all-female team", "female creator"]
definition: The apparent gender of the founder or founders of a crowdfunding project, derived by visually analyzing and coding the apparent gender of each founder in each project. In the experiment, the only variation between the two founder conditions was the name and picture of the founder.

name: Project support
definition: Whether an individual chooses to support a particular founder by giving money to the project; in the experiment participants were told ''If you would like, you can donate some of the money to the project in order to help its chances of reaching its fundraising goal.''

name: Fundraising success
authors_terms: ["successfully funded", "successful funding raise", "achieving its fundraising goal"]
definition: A project's success, measured as a dummy variable that denotes that the project was successfully funded by meeting or exceeding the founder's fundraising goal. Kickstarter employs an ''all or nothing'' threshold, so the outcome quantifies whether a founder succeeded or failed to raise capital.

name: Backer gender composition
authors_terms: ["proportion of a project's backers who are female", "female backers", "female funders"]
definition: The proportion of a project's backers who are female (female backers/total backers), used to capture female funders supporting female founders.

name: Female representation in industry
authors_terms: ["industries in which they are underrepresented", "male-dominated industry", "female-typed categories", "gender distribution of backers and founders"]
definition: The gender distribution of backers and founders across industry categories: gaming and technology are predominantly male, film is more evenly weighted, and fashion and children's books include higher proportions of women as founders and funders.

name: Growth-oriented strategy
definition: In this study, we define a growth-oriented strategy as one that pursues high growth at the expense of profit.

name: Profit-oriented strategy
definition: We define a profit-oriented strategy as one that puts a higher emphasis on profit than growth.

name: Firm survival
definition: As a performance measure, survival is more fundamental than growth and profit since the first mandate of any firm is to survive. Firm survival is thus the ultimate measure of firm performance.

name: Non-scale free resources
definition: Non-scale free resources (e.g., human capital and superior management teams) are resources that are subject to opportunity costs and reduced rents when applied across multiple sectors, and are thus limited to one use or another versus those which a firm can allocate across broadly diversified markets or products. A critical non-scale free resource in emerging markets is the managerial attention of the top management team.

name: Exposure to growth-inducing stimulus
authors_terms: ["stimulus", "stimulus plan", "industries directly influenced by the stimulus plan", "growth-oriented economic policy"]
definition: Following the 2008 global financial crisis, China launched a stimulus plan of four trillion RMB to counter the external shock and regain economic growth, whose primary objective was to sustain high economic growth and create domestic demands across various industries. The authors create a variable to indicate whether a firm belongs to an industry directly influenced by the stimulus plan in 2008-2009.

name: Technological experience
authors_terms: ["technological experience", "experience in a platform technology", "experience in platform technologies", "experience in a subfield", "experiential acquisition of the firm's technological capability"]
definition: A firm accumulates experience by operating in one subfield that may serve as a platform in other subfields. Experience with a platform technology generates the organizational capability to compete in related fields, but it does not guarantee that a firm will, in fact, diversify or succeed.

name: Diversification into a new subfield
authors_terms: ["diversification", "diversification path", "entry into a subfield", "subsequent entries", "subsequent diversification"]
definition: Diversification is the outcome of temporally ordered decisions to adapt or acquire knowledge for exploitation in new markets. The event of diversification is the dependent variable to be related to a firm's technological experience.

name: Market growth
authors_terms: ["growth of the market", "growth of a subfield", "shipment growth", "growth of shipments", "market opportunity"]
definition: The munificence of the selection environment is indexed by two variables, density and growth of shipments. The growth of a subfield is measured by the yearly rate of change in shipment volumes; the timing of diversification is expected to depend on the favorability of market conditions.

name: Discrete semiconductor experience
authors_terms: ["experience in discrete devices", "experience with discrete semiconductors", "discrete semiconductor experience"]
definition: The firm's accumulated experience in discrete semiconductor devices, tested as a platform into the optoelectronics subfield. The authors report that experience with discrete semiconductors does not seem to be a significant factor in explaining entry into optoelectronics.

name: Gallium arsenide experience
authors_terms: ["gallium arsenide experience", "GaAs experience", "experience in GaAs devices"]
definition: The firm's accumulated experience in gallium arsenide devices, hypothesized to help firms enter the optoelectronics subfield. The authors state that the superior optical property of gallium arsenide in comparison with silicon serves as a platform into the optoelectronics subfield.

name: Divergent strategic behavior
authors_terms: ["divergent strategic behavior", "searching for and championing new initiatives", "search for new strategic initiatives beyond the boundaries of current strategy"]
definition: Managers' divergent strategic behavior involves facilitating search for new strategic initiatives and choosing which to champion to top management; we define it as searching for new strategic initiatives beyond the boundaries of current strategy.

name: Organizational historical aspiration discrepancy
authors_terms: ["historical aspirations", "organizational-level performance-aspiration discrepancy", "performance above-historical aspirations", "performance below-historical aspirations"]
definition: Historical aspiration levels are a unit's recent performance relative to its own past; for the MCOs in this study, historical aspirations are the MCO's performance in the previous year.

name: Organizational social aspiration discrepancy
authors_terms: ["social aspirations", "organizational-level performance-aspiration discrepancy", "performance above social aspirations", "performance below social aspirations"]
definition: Social aspiration levels are performance relative to that of other units; in this setting the comparison group is other MCOs rather than external competitors, so social aspirations are the average performance of all other MCOs.

name: Individual historical aspiration discrepancy
authors_terms: ["historical aspirations", "individual-level performance-aspiration discrepancy", "individual performance above historical aspirations", "individual performance below historical aspirations"]
definition: The historical performance-aspiration discrepancy is the difference between a manager's current and prior-year individual performance.

name: Individual social aspiration discrepancy
authors_terms: ["social aspirations", "individual-level performance-aspiration discrepancy", "individual performance above social aspirations", "individual performance below social aspirations"]
definition: The social performance-aspiration discrepancy is a manager's individual performance relative to the average performance of other colleagues at the same MCO.

name: Organizational identification
definition: Organizational identification is '[an] enduring state that reflects an individual's willingness to define him- or herself as a member of a particular organization'; it shapes goal preferences in terms of managers' interest in the larger entity.

name: Target CEO retention
authors_terms: ["target CEO retention", "retention", "retained by the acquiring firm"]
definition: The definition of retention is whether the target CEO is reported in any capacity (i.e., as an officer or director of the merged firm) in the acquirer's proxy statement in the year following merger completion.

name: Target firm performance
authors_terms: ["target firm performance", "preacquisition performance", "target preacquisition performance", "industry-adjusted ROA"]
definition: One direct way to characterize successful CEOs is to identify those that are effective in improving firm performance; we use measures of preacquisition performance of the target firm to characterize successful target CEOs. The measure is return on assets (ROA), defined as operating income divided by assets in t-1 and deviated from industry medians.

name: Target CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["target CEO compensation", "CEO pay", "total compensation", "higher-paid target CEOs"]
definition: Wages are a reasonable proxy for the marginal productivity of labor, whether the productivity is a result of greater effort by the employee, greater skill, or a combination of the two, and CEO compensation might be one indicator of the value of the human capital that the CEO brings to the target firm.

name: Target CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure in the position of CEO", "tenure in position", "tenure"]
definition: We use tenure in the position of CEO to represent the extent of the CEO's firm-specific skills or experience.

name: Managerial discretion provisions
authors_terms: ["governance provisions that protect managerial discretion", "managerial discretion", "acquirer managerial discretion", "governance provisions that maintain managerial discretion"]
definition: To the extent that governance provisions make it difficult for shareholders to overrule management and they are costly to change, such provisions will limit shareholder interference in the running of the company by top management. We expect that acquiring firms with governance provisions that protect managerial rights will be more able to credibly commit to maintaining managerial discretion.

name: Acquirer CEO ownership
authors_terms: ["fraction of stock held by the acquiring CEO", "CEO ownership", "acquirer CEO ownership", "large equity holdings"]
definition: Acquiring firms with CEOs that hold large equity stakes also may be able to make credible commitments; with large equity holdings, the acquiring CEO also has the control rights needed to make the commitment credible.

name: Regulatory institutional profile
definition: The regulatory component of an institutional environment 'reflects the existing laws and rules in a particular national environment that promote certain types of behaviors and restrict others' (Kostova, 1999: 314).

name: Cognitive institutional profile
definition: The cognitive component reflects the widely shared social knowledge and cognitive categories (for instance, schemata, stereotypes) used by the people in a given country that influence the way a particular phenomenon is categorized and interpreted.

name: Normative institutional profile
definition: The normative component reflects the values, beliefs, norms, and assumptions about human nature and human behavior held by the individuals in a given country.

name: Practice implementation
authors_terms: ["implementation", "subsidiary implementation of the quality management practice"]
definition: Implementation is expressed in the external and objective behaviors and the actions required, or implied, by the practice.

name: Practice internalization
definition: Internalization is that state in which the employees at the recipient unit view the practice as valuable for the unit and become committed to the practice.

name: Subsidiary dependence on parent
definition: Dependence of a subsidiary on headquarters is defined as the belief held by subsidiary managers that the subsidiary relies on, and is contingent on, the support of the parent organization for providing major resources, including technology, capital, and expertise.

name: Subsidiary trust in parent
definition: The trust of a foreign subsidiary in its parent organization is a common belief within the subsidiary that the parent: (1) makes good-faith efforts to behave in accordance with commitments, both explicit and implicit, (2) is honest in whatever discussions preceded such commitments, and (3) does not take excessive advantage of the subsidiary, even when the opportunity is available.

name: Subsidiary identification with parent
definition: Identification of the foreign subsidiary with the parent organization is defined as the degree to which subsidiary employees experience a state of attachment to the parent. They feel that they are part of the parent organization, belong to it, and partly derive their self-identities from this organizational membership.

name: Ceremonial adoption
definition: Formal adoption of a practice on the part of a recipient unit's employees for legitimacy reasons, without their believing in its real value for the organization. In the study, ceremonial adoption is defined as a relatively high level of implementation accompanied by a low level of internalization.

name: Firm status
definition: The status of an organization, defined by the hierarchical position it occupies in a social system, can be an asset or a liability in the context of organizational misconduct by decreasing or increasing the consequences of misconduct.

name: Multiple-actor scandal
definition: We use scandal in this paper to refer to multiple-actor scandals - that is, the disruptive publicity of a particular type of misconduct carried out by several different independent organizations, such as the 2006 options backdating scandal. Multiple-actor scandals imply a sudden spike in media attention to a particular type of misconduct (disruptive publicity) involving several different independent firms (multiple actors), with no individual firm dominating the media coverage (diffuse focus).

name: Labeling of misconduct
definition: Misconduct is understood as a property imposed on a behavior when a social control agent labels the focal behavior as misconduct; labeling of the focal act as misconduct is when a social control agent brings a formal charge of misconduct against a focal actor.

name: Top management team nationality diversity
definition: TMT nationality diversity refers to top management team members holding different nationalities; as executives are imprinted with the tacit norms and conventions specific to the countries in which they were born and raised, it is believed that TMT nationality diversity substantially boosts a TMT's human and social capital.

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["corporate entrepreneurship", "CE", "diversity of external knowledge sourcing strategies", "geographical and technological diversity of external knowledge sourcing strategies"]
definition: CE is 'the process through which firms innovate, create new businesses, and transform themselves by changing the business domain or key strategic processes'. It is operationalized as the diversity of external knowledge sourcing strategies, reflected in the geographical and technological heterogeneity of M&As, technology alliances and corporate venturing.

name: MNC innovation performance
definition: MNCs' innovation performance is measured by the number of patent applications of the firms in a given year; the patent application date is used as the first indication of new capabilities and invention.

name: TMT social stratification
authors_terms: ["TMT social stratification", "social stratification", "social stratification TMT", "vertical differentiation"]
definition: Social stratification among executives refers to power and status differences that may trigger nationality-based social categorization processes in TMTs. Socially stratified teams have elaborate social hierarchies associated with inequality in power, status, and privileges.

name: National power distance
definition: NPD is an important aspect of national culture and refers to the degree to which people accept that power in societies and organizations is distributed unequally. With regard to the work context, power distance proxies the extent to which power difference between power-holders and others is accepted, expected, and taken for granted.

name: Logic pluralism
authors_terms: ["logic pluralism", "organizational pluralism", "number of logics", "organizational logics", "logic plurality"]
definition: Organizational logics are thematic perceptual predispositions that have their roots in individuals' experiences and professional expertise and that guide an organization's interpretation of a new institutional practice. Logic pluralism is the number of distinct logics within an organization.

name: Organizational settlement
definition: We define negotiated settlements as temporally bound agreements on the meaning and legitimacy of an institutional practice or arrangement. Organizational settlement refers to an organization's agreement to a settlement, measured by its vote on whether developed draft content should move to the next development stage.

name: Embeddedness
definition: Embeddedness is an organization's participation in the social context within which it cognitively filters and frames a proposed institutional practice; it is operationalized in this study as an organization's voluntary decision to serve on or lead any of the committees involved in drafting the standard or overseeing the process.

name: Negotiation iteration
authors_terms: ["time", "iterations of negotiation", "two iterations", "rounds of proposed changes"]
definition: The two stages of the ISO 26000 development process at which proposed changes and votes were collected: the first draft and the final draft implementation standard. By collecting data at both stages in the process, the authors were able to assess the antecedents of settlement over time.

name: Imposing framing
definition: Actors used imposing frames through direct commands to alter the text, justifying change on the basis of the assumed (taken-for-granted) legitimacy of the organization proposing it.

name: Normative framing
definition: Participants made direct appeals to norms and rules as the basis for negotiating changes, using established norms as the basis for rhetoric promoting change as well as customary norms for reinforcing the status quo.

name: Supportive framing
definition: Rhetoric that encouraged drafters to retain the meaning of the text or used support of the existing text as a basis for proposing the addition of new text.

name: Nonparticipative framing
definition: A number of actors opted not to provide comments during the negotiation of the standard; the absence of comments was included as a category, speculating that failure to negotiate may be significant in and of itself.

name: Cognitive framing
definition: Cognitive negotiation frames reflected a thoughtful and considered cognitive orientation, in which organizations openly questioned or asked for the reconsideration or exploration of content and issues, often addressing the implications of the current text rather than providing a proposed change.

name: Relational mechanisms
definition: Relational mechanisms capture the dynamics of partners' behavior and interaction over the course of their alliance; the authors refer to the unified construct of relational mechanisms, which comprises mutual trust, relational embeddedness, and relational commitment.

name: Alliance performance
definition: Alliance performance refers to the extent to which an alliance met its objectives, increased revenues, improved quality, reduced time to market, generated new customers, products or projects, led to customer satisfaction, received favorable recognition, and could evolve into a long-term relationship.

name: Organizational differences
definition: We identified two dimensions of organizational differences whose intersection defines four relevant domains, namely management style, organizational responsiveness, internal task routines, and marketing routines.

name: Management style differences
definition: A firm's management style is defined by its unique managerial approach, control systems, decision-making style, and communication modes. Inherent differences in partners' management styles may hinder the relational mechanisms that support collaboration.

name: Organizational responsiveness differences
definition: Organizational responsiveness refers to a firm's reaction to external entities and events occurring in its environment.

name: Internal task routine differences
authors_terms: ["differences in internal task routines", "internal task routines"]
definition: Firms vary in how their employees perform ordinary tasks, manifested in the discretion that employees apply when carrying out routine duties and in the effort they exert, as well as in the emphasis placed on cooperation in carrying out tasks.

name: Marketing routine differences
definition: Firms differ in marketing routines, which are the procedures for learning about customer needs, devising plans for serving those needs and implementing such plans.

name: Recognition of organizational differences
definition: The implications of organizational differences may depend on the partners' willingness to recognize and reconcile their differences.

name: Negative own media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative own coverage", "negative media coverage", "negative coverage of the firm"]
definition: An increase in negative coverage means that the company's name is increasingly surrounded by negative words and phrases that are distinct from neutral or positive descriptions.

name: Positive own media coverage
authors_terms: ["positive own coverage", "positive media coverage", "positive coverage of the firm"]
definition: Positive coverage is different from the absence of negative coverage, because positive coverage is associated with specific words and phrases praising the firms that are distinct from a neutral tone.

name: Negative interlock media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative interlock coverage", "negative coverage of the company's interlock media coverage"]
definition: Indirect coverage is defined as media coverage of the firms' interlock partners; for the negative dimension the authors summed up the negative coverage scores of the companies to which the focal firm is connected through shared directors.

name: Positive interlock media coverage
authors_terms: ["positive interlock coverage", "positive coverage of interlock partners"]
definition: Indirect coverage is defined as media coverage of the firms' interlock partners; for the positive dimension the authors summed up the positive coverage scores of the companies to which the focal firm is connected through shared directors.

name: Board reform practice adoption
definition: Our dependent variable is a binary indicator that reflects firm adoption of governance practices in line with the logic of board reform.

name: CEO pay revision
authors_terms: ["annual CEO pay revision", "current CEO pay adjustment", "CEO pay adjustment", "pay revision", "current pay adjustment"]
definition: The central occasion for settling up is a board's yearly determination of how much to pay its CEO and, specifically, how much to increase or decrease the person's pay relative to the prior year's pay.

name: Current firm performance
authors_terms: ["current performance", "current company performance", "poor current performance", "current TSR", "poor current TSR", "current change in ROE", "poor current ROE"]
definition: Current performance provides the most up-to-date information about a CEO's abilities, particularly about his or her suitability to current business challenges. Our performance indicators were based on total shareholder return (TSR), a widely used measure of company market performance, and return on equity (ROE), a common measure of accounting performance.

name: Earlier performance
authors_terms: ["earlier performance", "earlier TSR", "earlier ROE", "CEO's earlier performance", "accumulated track record", "earlier record"]
definition: Earlier performance conveys meaningful information about a CEO's abilities-information that might not be fully reflected in strictly current performance. A CEO's accumulated track record provides a more complete picture of his or her ability than a narrow-window view of performance.

name: CEO over- and underpayment
authors_terms: ["over(under)payment", "over- or underpayment", "prior overpayment", "recent over(under)payment", "earlier over(under)payment", "earlier overpayment"]
definition: We conceptualize over- or underpayment as the difference between what the CEO was paid in years prior to the current year and what the CEO marketplace appeared to warrant as his or her pay over the same period. In this conception, which is consistent with prior research, marketplace norms for CEO pay are based on such factors as industry, company size, and firm performance.

name: CEO tenure
definition: Early in a CEO's tenure, a board has minimal information on which to base its assessment of the CEO's worth to the firm. With the passage of time, however, the board will develop a clearer picture of a CEO's talent, as evidenced by his or her cumulative performance over multiple years.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: Researchers interested in identifying CEO dismissals face the problem that many CEO firings are described by companies in neutral, often euphemistic, terms. Following others who have faced this challenge, we took multiple steps to control for, or set aside, CEO exits that were clearly not due to dismissal.

name: Product recall announcement
definition: Announcements that a firm is recalling a product; given that a recall is generally expensive to conduct, the firm's value is expected to be negatively affected.

name: Abnormal stock returns
authors_terms: ["abnormal stock returns", "abnormal returns", "mean cumulative prediction errors (MCPEs)", "shareholder wealth"]
definition: The stock market reaction to the announcement measured as mean cumulative prediction errors; stock price behavior is increasingly recognized as an important strategic variable.

name: Recall remedy
authors_terms: ["recalls that replace the product or return the purchase price", "repair or check of a product", "replacement recalls", "repair/check recalls"]
definition: Recalls can either be for product replacement or cost refund, or they can be to simply repair or examine a product.

name: Recall origin
definition: A government-ordered recall would include any recall specifically ordered by the federal or state government or one of their agencies. A voluntary recall is one coming specifically from the producer of the product.

name: Products taken off the market
authors_terms: ["products taken off the market", "problem products taken off the market", "products are taken off the market"]
definition: When products are taken off the market, the firm agrees to no longer sell the item, but no mention of recalling previously sold products is made.

name: Candidate gender
definition: The predictor variable was the gender of the respondent, coded as 1 = female or 0 = male. Women are seen as a poor fit for organizational leadership roles because the qualities stereotypically associated with femininity are viewed as irrelevant to or incompatible with the qualities desired of leaders.

name: Recruitment rejection
definition: We define rejection as occurring when an individual does not succeed in attaining the applied-for position and therefore examine gender differences in the responses to rejections occurring throughout the executive selection process.

name: Willingness to consider a previously rejecting firm
authors_terms: ["willingness to apply again", "willingness to consider a job opportunity from a firm that has rejected them in the past", "candidate declined to interview"]
definition: We examine men's and women's willingness to be considered for a job by an organization that has rejected them in the past. In the field data the outcome of interest is the candidate's decision at the very first stage of the process - whether the candidate agrees to proceed to a formal interview with the search firm - which is the nearest equivalent to applying for a job, our theoretical construct of interest.

name: Perceived procedural justice
definition: Individuals care a great deal about the perceived fairness of the procedures used to arrive at a selection decision - that is, procedural justice. Fair treatment is important because the procedures used to make decisions communicate identity-relevant information, including whether people are valued and belong in the particular group in which the treatment occurs.

name: Belonging uncertainty in executive domains
authors_terms: ["belonging uncertainty", "latent belonging uncertainty", "executive sense of belonging", "sense of belonging in executive domains"]
definition: Individuals who are members of negatively stereotyped groups in a domain frequently experience latent belonging uncertainty, a global uncertainty about whether they will be accepted or rejected in that context. Women executives' direct and vicarious experiences with negative gender stereotyping are likely to underlie a latent sense of uncertainty about whether they belong in the executive domain.

name: Past rejection
authors_terms: ["past rejections", "rejections", "rejected each other in the past"]
definition: Interactions between two market actors evaluating a transaction in which no match was made because one of the parties rejected the other. The authors state that there are two types of past rejections: rejecting and being rejected.

name: Prior rejection of the partner
authors_terms: ["rejecting", "if they had rejected this partner in the past", "previously rejected the other party"]
definition: The type of past rejection in which the focal actor is the party who declined to engage with the other; for these actors only information acquisition can operate, since they cannot have a negative emotional response to being rejected.

name: Prior rejection by the partner
authors_terms: ["being rejected", "if they had been rejected by this partner in the past", "previously rejected by the other party"]
definition: The type of past rejection in which the focal actor's candidacy or offer was declined by the other party. The authors argue that being the target of rejection can provoke negative affect, either fear of future rejection or anger.

name: Type of transaction considered
authors_terms: ["different types of transactions", "type of new job considerations", "job characteristics"]
definition: The kind of opportunity that the parties contemplate when they encounter each other again; the authors examine two characteristics (function and salary) of the jobs for which candidates are considered. Salary is associated with factors such as level of responsibility and firm characteristics that can vary within the same job function.

name: Future rejection of a potential partner
authors_terms: ["reject a potential partner", "future rejections", "candidate rejects search firm", "search firm rejects candidate"]
definition: Whether a party declines to engage in a potential transaction that is being actively considered; declining to interview represents, for either party, a decision not to pursue matters.

name: Covert corporate political activity
authors_terms: ["covert CPA", "covert political contributions", "independent political expenditures (IPEs)", "contributions to the Republican Governors' Public Policy Committee"]
definition: Unlimited independent political expenditures that corporations, using general treasury funds, can make directly or can fund through contributions to IPE-only committees or nonprofit entities formed under section 501(c) of the federal tax code that do not have to disclose their contributors.

name: Investor reaction
definition: Investor reactions are examined 'not … as completely accurate predictions of the longer-term performance implications …' but instead, 'as the collective opinions of investors regarding these implications, similar to an opinions survey'.

name: Industry regulation
definition: Regulated industries are those in which the government, including the states, has greater control over firm resources and prospects, so that the need to manage nonmarket environment uncertainty and to establish political connections is greater.

name: Prior campaign contributions
authors_terms: ["prior investment in financial nonmarket strategies", "financial nonmarket strategies", "campaign contributions", "PAC contributions"]
definition: Traditional financial nonmarket strategies, that is, the resources firms were previously allowed to employ in the electoral arena. PAC contributions are made by a PAC affiliated with a firm, with the firms' employees and shareholders as the source of the contributions, placing an upper limit on how much a PAC can raise, and thus, contribute.

name: Contention over political spending disclosure
authors_terms: ["prior firm-level contention over covert CPA", "shareholder resolution on political spending disclosure", "contention over CPA"]
definition: Activists and activist investors use tactics such as shareholder resolutions against firms to problematize practices they disagree with, decreasing the attractiveness of related investments.

name: Lateral transfers
authors_terms: ["lateral transfers", "lateral transfer rate", "cumulative transfer rate", "transfers", "job rotations"]
definition: Lateral transfers refer to alternative jobs that may involve different duties, titles, and locations but are at the same hierarchical (grade and pay) level (also called job rotations in some previous research) (Campion et al. 1994).

name: Job performance
authors_terms: ["job performance", "performance", "cumulative job performance", "cumulative average job performance"]
definition: In this organization, job performance reflects a given leader's mastery of a set of competencies, which were based on an extensive competency modeling study and are the same for each leadership level. Leader job performance was evaluated on a yearly basis on a scale of one to five (with five being the highest level of job performance).

name: Promotion
definition: Promotion decisions are vital to a pipeline as they directly affect the upward flow of leadership. Upon receiving these signals, leaders are promoted (i.e., their real options are exercised).

name: Improved operational effectiveness
definition: Improved operational effectiveness was measured using unit leader bonuses in U.S. dollars. In this organization, unit leaders' bonuses are based on approximately 50% performance evaluation rating and 50% changes (defined as improvements) in several objective indicators of their unit's productivity (e.g., increased sales, decreased costs) during that year.

name: Prominence of extrinsic rewards
authors_terms: ["extrinsic rewards", "increased prominence of extrinsic rewards", "extrinsic rewards focus", "customer awareness of producers' extrinsic rewards", "exposure to free agency"]
definition: Extrinsic rewards are the social (e.g., status, position) or material (e.g., monetary gains) rewards an actor receives for performance. The more clearly an audience can see that a producer is receiving extrinsic rewards for his performance, the more the audience will be concerned that the actor is incentivized to fake a performance merely to obtain those rewards.

name: Perceived producer inauthenticity
authors_terms: ["perceived player inauthenticity", "perceptions of inauthenticity", "perceptions that the producers or performers in a market are inauthentic"]
definition: Concerns about inauthenticity arise when social actors are perceived to be managing impressions by presenting a frontstage persona that is different from their backstage identity, the actor's true self. A clear presence of extrinsic rewards can push the audience's interpretation of an actor's motives toward extrinsic reward seeking and raise suspicion of such a gap.

name: Preference for traditional practices
authors_terms: ["preference for traditional ballpark features", "preference for traditional practices deemed authentic to a domain", "demand for authenticity", "traditional practices"]
definition: Traditional practices, those resurrected from the market's past, are valued as symbols of authenticity: they signal commitment to the market's origins and, when they highlight inferior and discarded technologies, signal indifference to extrinsic rewards. Increased concern about producers' inauthenticity tends to increase demand for such traditional practices.

name: Traditional ballpark style
definition: Ballparks coded as traditional are those built during the classic era (1909-1922) or the so-called retro era (1992-2006), which returned to traditional practices such as ornate brick exteriors, grass playing surfaces, and exposed steel girders or poles that obstruct views. Ballparks not built in these periods or lacking these features are coded as nontraditional.

name: Relative home attendance
authors_terms: ["difference in home and away capacity-controlled attendance per game, per year", "attendance"]
definition: The difference between the annual per game home and away attendance for each team, capacity controlled. Netting out away attendance from home attendance identifies the component of attendance that is specific to home games and home ballpark style.

name: Target company postacquisition top management turnover
authors_terms: ["target company top management turnover", "cumulative top management turnover", "annual turnover rates"]
definition: With the date of departure information provided by the survey responses, we were able to compute the cumulative percentage of the top management team that turned over at each of 5 years after the date of the merger or acquisition.

name: Parent company top management turnover
authors_terms: ["parent company top management turnover", "parent company cumulative turnover rate"]
definition: The names of each top manager in the parent and control companies were identified from each company's 10K or annual report. Their employment status was then tracked in these 10Ks or annual reports for 5 years from the point of initial observation.

name: Control company top management turnover
authors_terms: ["control companies' turnover rates", "normal rate", "control company turnover"]
definition: A control group of 75 companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity during the same time period was drawn from the Standard and Poor's Stock Guide. Their top management turnover rates were assessed by archival sources (e.g., 10K or annual reports).

name: Target company preacquisition top management turnover
authors_terms: ["preacquisition target company top management turnover", "preacquisition target company top management team turnover"]
definition: The preacquisition target company top management team turnover was assessed with archival data. The top managers were identified from each company's 10K or annual report 5 years prior to the merger or acquisition announcement date.

name: Parent company preacquisition stock performance
authors_terms: ["parent company performance", "parent company's preacquisition stock performance history", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: The abnormal return for any observation month was defined as the excess return on the company's common stock over that of the return on an equal weighted market index for that month. Cumulative abnormal returns were constructed to represent the company's performance throughout any period in the 5 years prior to the 2 months before a merger or acquisition announcement.

name: Target company preacquisition stock performance
authors_terms: ["target company's preacquisition stock performance", "preacquisition performance history", "cumulative abnormal returns"]
definition: The abnormal return for any observation month was defined as the excess return on the company's common stock over that of the return on an equal weighted market index for that month. Company performance was established by collecting the cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) for the target, parent, and control companies over a five-year period preceding the acquisition announcement.

name: Control company stock performance
definition: The abnormal return for any observation month was defined as the excess return on the company's common stock over that of the return on an equal weighted market index for that month. The company performance indices for the control companies were assessed over an equivalent time period.

name: Market reaction to the acquisition announcement
authors_terms: ["market reaction to the merger or acquisition", "market evaluation of the acquisition", "abnormal return on the day the acquisition was announced", "61-day cumulative abnormal return"]
definition: The market reaction to the merger or acquisition was assessed in two ways. First, we collected the target company's abnormal return for the day the acquisition was announced; with this in mind, we collected the cumulative abnormal returns for the period beginning 60 days before the merger announcement and ending with the announcement day itself.

name: Acquisition target status
authors_terms: ["target companies", "merged and acquired companies", "companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity"]
definition: The research sample was composed of a set of target companies, their parent companies, and a group of control companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity during the observation period. The sample of merged and acquired companies was drawn from the Statistical Report on Mergers and Acquisitions, 1979.

name: Network centrality
definition: Network centrality indicates the extent to which a person is 'in the thick of things'; central actors possess the range of contacts that enables them to facilitate smooth interactions across intraorganizational boundaries and the ability to disseminate information and ideas to many colleagues.

name: Structural holes
definition: Structural constraint is an inverse measure of the presence of structural holes in an actor's network; actors with low structural constraint have networks in which their contacts are not themselves connected-that is, they possess networks with many structural holes.

name: Cross-boundary integration
definition: A cross-boundary integrator is an individual who brings together people in her network from different parts of the organization; we define cross-boundary integration explicitly as communication activity that links two others from two different business units.

name: Corporate staff position
definition: Employees of the corporate headquarters (CHQ) and of the corporate sales force (CSF) are referred to as the 'corporate staff', in contrast with employees who are members of the 'line' organization (i.e., any of the 29 business units of the company).

name: Mobility into the corporate staff
authors_terms: ["line-to-CHQ switchers", "line-to-CSF switchers", "line-to-staff transition", "transitions from the line organization to a position in CHQ or CSF"]
definition: Transitions from the line organization to a position in the corporate headquarters or the corporate sales force; coupling communication network data with intervening mobility events allows the authors to attempt to disentangle person effects from role effects.

name: Mobility out of the corporate staff
authors_terms: ["CHQ-to-line switchers", "CSF-to-line switchers", "transitions from CHQ or CSF to a line role", "staff-line transition"]
definition: Transitions in which individuals leave the corporate headquarters or the corporate sales force and assume positions in the line organization.

name: Collaboration persistence
authors_terms: ["collaboration persistence", "persistence of collaboration", "tie durability", "durability of collaborative ties", "repeat collaboration"]
definition: The question the authors study is what drives some collaborations to persist and others to decay; persistence is observed as repeat collaboration, that is, whether a pair of coauthors keeps publishing together. The primary dependent variable is a dummy indicating whether a paper was published in year t that included both members of the dyad as coauthors.

name: Loss of a third party
authors_terms: ["death of k", "death of a third party", "passing of k", "loss of a helpful third party", "unexpected death"]
definition: The authors use the unexpected death of a third collaborator as a quasi-random loss that provides exogenous variation in the structure of a collaboration. The variable is coded as one for the years after the passing of k for the dyads in which k was the third party.

name: Third-party helpfulness
definition: Helpfulness consists of activities where the helper neither expects nor receives something in return from the receiver for the help. The authors measure the helpfulness of a third party k by the number of acknowledgments k received by the treatment time, treating acknowledgments as help given without formal coauthorship.

name: Third-party status
definition: Social status confers power and influence as well as visibility, credibility, and trust, and in the authors' context a scientist's status is derived from the number of papers published and the other scientists with whom one publishes. The authors use the eigenvector centrality of k as the key measure of status.

name: Pre-existing helpfulness of the dyad
authors_terms: ["pre-existing helpfulness", "prior helpfulness", "prior history of helpful behavior", "ij Prior Acknowledgments"]
definition: Groups vary in how helpful their members are: although many collaborations lack helpful behavior among members, others have a history of helpfulness in which trust, generosity, and reciprocal exchange are already present before the third party arrives. The authors measure it with the acknowledgments the two dyad members received before they began collaborating with k.

name: Coauthor helpfulness
authors_terms: ["helpfulness of i", "helpful coauthor", "the focal scientist's helpfulness", "become more helpful"]
definition: The helpfulness of an individual scientist, measured by the number of acknowledgments the scientist has received. The authors argue that helpfulness is contagious: each individual who has collaborated with a helpful third becomes more helpful through the experience of interacting with that third.

name: Outside options
authors_terms: ["outside options", "ecology of outside options", "outside options with higher complementarity than current partners"]
definition: The paper defines the ecology of outside options as the number of firms outside the current alliance that would afford greater complementarity, and predicts that alliance withdrawal is a joint outcome of the complementarity of the current partners and the ecology of outside options.

name: Alliance withdrawal
definition: Our dependent variable is member withdrawal from an alliance, coded as 1 when a given member of an alliance operating a route at time t is no longer part of the alliance operating the route in t + 1 and 0 otherwise.

name: Market complementarity
definition: Complementarity in alliances occurs when each firm has access to resources needed by but not possessed by the other, where resources are interpreted broadly to include not only financial and material assets but also intangible assets such as knowledge or market access. The authors measure complementarity through market presence, so two firms are complementary when each has access to markets in which the other has no or limited access.

name: Network renewal
definition: The key concern is whether the complementarity of the new alliance was previously unavailable. If two firms already have an alliance, they should be able to leverage the complementarity of each other's resources, and hence the incremental value of a new alliance is lower than that of alliances with a firm that offers an opportunity for network renewal.

name: Prior alliance ties
definition: when matching involves both observed and unobserved characteristics, it is likely that firms that had an alliance but withdrew discovered some mismatch that was not obvious from observable criteria. Hence, such firms should also be less promising outside options.

name: Structural embeddedness
definition: Structural embeddedness occurs when two firms both have ties to a common third firm. A firm that participates in alliances characterized by high structural embeddedness should make a poor outside option, the stability of its alliance relations translating into lower availability to new partners.

name: Rival alliance ties
authors_terms: ["alliances with a firm's rivals", "is in rival alliance", "rivalry"]
definition: Outside options with links to rivals of the focal firm are likely to value these alliances and consider the reaction of their alliance partners if they should establish an alliance with the focal firm, they are less likely to be available to form an alliance than a firm with no alliance relation with rivals of the focal firm.

name: Product variety
definition: Using the percentage of cargo delivered by each truck in each of the product categories, we compute a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) by summing the squares of the percentages of the five product categories; 1-HHI captures product variety.

name: Economies of scope
authors_terms: ["benefits per unit of resource", "economies of scope", "average drop size", "drop size"]
definition: Economies of scope arise when the cost of producing or selling two or more products jointly is less than the sum of their separate costs. The average drop size is a measure of economies of scope, that is, a direct result of the synergy attained by the product variety strategy.

name: Routine execution costs
authors_terms: ["routine execution cost", "frictions in routine execution", "costs of executing the routines"]
definition: An easy-to-miss but important cost of product variety, which we call a 'routine execution cost.' The force generating this type of cost is the friction that is introduced into the execution of operational routines by an increase in the variety of products.

name: Resource efficiency
authors_terms: ["efficiency of the resource being leveraged", "productivity", "delivered volume"]
definition: Delivered volume, a measurement of productivity, that is, the total number of 'equivalent boxes' that a truck successfully delivers to clients per month.

name: Product category dissimilarity
definition: Certain product categories are more alike in terms of product properties (size, shape, and weight), clients, and processes; the addition of less-related product categories impairs execution speed and decreases the usefulness of conserving cognitive resources.

name: Experiential learning
definition: We measure the accumulated volume of truck i up to month t - 1, which we consider Experiential Learning.

name: Social learning
definition: We measure the impact of social learning by computing an analogous variable considering the volume of the other trucks that operate in the same DC and for the same carrier as the focal truck.

name: Direct network effects
authors_terms: ["direct network effects", "Direct Network Effect", "product-level direct network effects", "complementor product-level network effects"]
definition: When products have positive direct network effects, the utility they create for any user will depend on whether they can create a sufficiently large installed base of users. In our context of the Apple App Store, some games may have direct network effects while others do not.

name: Selective promotion through awards
authors_terms: ["Editors' Choice award", "Award", "selective product promotions through awards", "product endorsement"]
definition: In the App Store, Apple promotes apps with an Editors' Choice award. Apps that receive the award will receive a visible badge that will appear under the name of the app for the app's lifespan.

name: Developer market share
definition: To measure Developer Market Share in category c, for each developer k, we take the summation of the daily revenue for a 3-month period, then divide this total by the total revenue proxy for apps in category c, and then lag the value by 1 month.

name: Market concentration
definition: We measure the Concentration for each category using the Herfindahl index on our revenue proxy across developers for a 3-month period and then lag the value by 1 month.

name: Challenger developer position
definition: To manage the potential threat of the dominant complementor the platform owner may promote a challenger. #2 Developer = 1 if the developer holds the second market share position in the category over the past 3 months, and similarly for #3 Developer and #4 Developer, while the omitted category is all non-top four developers.

name: Contentious challenges
authors_terms: ["contentious challenges", "total contentious challenges", "total activist challenges", "activist challenges"]
definition: Contentious challenges are captured through boycotts in which a company is named as a target. The authors use boycotts as a proxy for external activism because they are easily identifiable in media coverage and are one of the most common and effective contentious tactics used by anticorporate activists.

name: Successful contentious challenges
definition: Successful Contentious Challenges is a count variable indicating the total number of boycotts in the prior year in which activists were able to successfully coerce a concession from the targeted company.

name: Unsuccessful contentious challenges
definition: Unsuccessful Contentious Challenges is a count of the number of boycotts in the prior year in which activists were unable to successfully elicit a concession.

name: Corporate-sponsored activism
authors_terms: ["corporate-sponsored activism", "overt corporate-sponsored activism", "corporate-sponsored boycott", "sponsoring a social movement boycott"]
definition: Corporate-sponsored boycotts occur when firms openly align with contentious social activists to protest the problematic social practices of other companies, industries, or states. Firms engaging in overt corporate-sponsored activism adopt the tactics of insurgency, such as letter writing campaigns or issue advertising, to openly advocate for a particular social movement's cause.

name: Public approval
definition: A firm's reputation, defined as the level of general public approval of the firm, which affects how stakeholders interpret and respond to challenges levied at the organization. It is operationalized through a content analysis of media coverage about the firm.

name: Downsizing
definition: Downsizing is a planned reduction in a company's number of employees, undertaken to reduce headcount to some target level; the authors focus on layoffs as downsizing at its most severe and on the severity (i.e., magnitude) of the downsizing.

name: Voluntary turnover rate
definition: The critical employee behavior of voluntarily leaving the organization, measured at the organization level as the number of full-time voluntary leavers divided by the number of full-time employees from 12 months prior to the survey.

name: Organizational commitment
definition: An aggregated employee attitude that prior work identifies as both a downsizing consequence and a voluntary turnover antecedent; it is measured with two modified items from Mowday, Steers, and Porter's (1979) Organizational Commitment Questionnaire.

name: Procedural justice HR practices
authors_terms: ["procedural justice index", "HR practices likely to promote procedural justice perceptions"]
definition: An organization's commitment to providing employees with a formal process for addressing perceived injustices, indexed from HR practices that provide opportunities to appeal or challenge, to have concerns heard, and to correct past wrongs.

name: Job embeddedness HR practices
authors_terms: ["job embeddedness index", "HR practices likely to embed employees in their organization"]
definition: Job embeddedness is the level to which employees are bound in a social web (both on and off the job) that keeps them attached to their organization; the index is built from five practices that should yield perceptions along the fit and sacrifice dimensions of job embeddedness.

name: Career development HR practices
authors_terms: ["career development index", "HR practices likely to enhance career development"]
definition: HR practices likely to improve employees' ability to compete in the external job market via enhanced signaling or search capabilities, such as a career resource center, employee assessment, formal succession planning, and a transfer policy to support learning.

name: Project license openness
authors_terms: ["license type", "project license", "degree of openness of the project license", "highly open license", "open license", "closed license"]
definition: Each project is governed by a set of rules that define the terms of use of the software developed by its members and other participants. These terms of use are defined by the project license, which focuses mainly on the extent to which commercial use is allowed.

name: Project size
authors_terms: ["project size", "size of the project", "number of members"]
definition: The size of the project is defined by the number of developers registered as formal members, including the project manager.

name: Developer-oriented intended audience
definition: SourceForge identifies the intended audience for each registered software project in one of 19 groups. We aggregate these groups into five categories for the empirical analysis: Developers (programming tools), End Users, System Administrators, Mixed (of the preceding three), and Other.

name: Public resolution of contributions
authors_terms: ["public resolution", "visible contribution outcome", "reveals the outcome of the contribution"]
definition: We exploit information on whether the receiving project announces whether a contribution is accepted. After a developer makes a contribution, the project manager decides whether or not to accept it and to make the decision public on SourceForge.

name: Corporate sponsorship
definition: Projects are classified as having a corporate sponsor if they were initiated by a for-profit company, or if corporate involvement is present either directly or through offering a proprietary product that incorporates source code from the project.

name: Reciprocity
definition: We focus on reciprocity at the project level and define a contribution to project j in year t from a developer who is a member of project i as reciprocal if project i received a contribution from j prior to year t.

name: Source code contributions
definition: A contribution is defined as any contributed source code that aims to advance the software regardless of whether the project manager ultimately accepts the submission.

name: Project performance
definition: As our measure of project performance, we use the number of times the project has been downloaded. Project dissemination in open source is likely to be a main objective of project managers, and downloads are one strong indicator of project quality.

name: Intrinsic motivation
authors_terms: ["intrinsic motivation", "purely motivated developers", "open developers", "anonymous developers", "free-software ideology"]
definition: An individual is considered intrinsically motivated to act if he/she performs an activity for no apparent reward except the activity itself. We assume that developers reveal themselves as being intrinsically motivated if they are members only of projects that have open licenses.

name: Closed-license developer affiliation
definition: We define a developer as closed if all of the projects to which he/she belongs operate under closed licenses. We assume developers reveal a preference for extrinsic motivation if they belong only to projects with closed license types.

name: Reputation motivation
definition: Lerner and Tirole (2002) argue that developers improve their labor market prospects by signaling their quality through participation in open source projects. The second type of reputation gain is peer recognition, which is unrelated to labor market payoffs.

name: Strategic alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "strategic alliances", "alliance activity", "probabilities of alliance formation"]
definition: Strategic alliances are defined as ongoing cooperative relationships between independent firms, including relationships that involve exchange of equity and those that do not. The authors measure alliance formation in terms of whether or not a firm enters alliances as well as how frequently it does so.

name: Market demand change
authors_terms: ["market demand change", "market changes", "market demand growth", "market decline"]
definition: We used the yearly percentage of change in total semiconductor industry sales to measure changes in market demand. Compared to large firms, start-up firms are sensitive to yearly market fluctuations because they have more limited slack resources with which to buffer environmental changes.

name: Firm resources
definition: A firm's resources delimit the extent to which it implements its industry recipe; here, we define resources as a firm's fundamental financial, physical, and technological capital attributes, as they are shaped over time (Barney, 1991).

name: Technological resource diversity
definition: Dataquest specifies nine distinctive technological areas according to product categories; since these areas differ in technical concepts, product designs, and manufacturing systems, firms need different resources to produce each of these product types. Thus, the more technologies a firm has, the more diverse its technological resources are.

name: Manufacturing resources
definition: Manufacturing is an important resource dimension in the semiconductor industry because it is a primary determinant of the scope of business activities (Case, 1990). The lack of manufacturing resources also made it difficult for start-ups to 'second-source' (obtain alternative sources of) new technologies or products.

name: Financial resources
definition: For most start-up firms, venture capital is the primary source of financial resources. Given the limited availability of internal capital and costly operations, the survival of semiconductor start-ups often depends on the availability of external funding (Eisenhardt & Schoonhoven, 1996).

name: Exploration alliance formation
definition: Compared to other types of alliances, the essence of joint R&D is searching and experimenting to find new, uncertain, and risky alternatives that will produce future profits. This description fits the characteristics of exploration; therefore, we classified alliances with an R&D component as exploration alliances.

name: Exploitation alliance formation
definition: Other types of alliances are oriented toward exploiting existing resources to improve returns from present strategies and competencies, so they were classified as exploitation alliances.

name: Identification with the focal firm
authors_terms: ["director identification with the focal firm", "identification with the focal firm", "identification with the firm"]
definition: The strength of a government director's identification with the focal firm; when government directors strongly identify with the focal firm, they are likely to act in ways that benefit it, because effective governance is in the interests of the firm.

name: Identification with the government
authors_terms: ["director identification with the government", "identification with the government"]
definition: Given his or her affiliation with a government and/or its agencies, a government director tends to identify with the government to some extent; where one political party dominates political power and controls government institutions, government directors generally feature strong identification with the government due to the stability and consistency of the government's objectives and policy agenda.

name: Managerial monitoring
definition: Directors monitor managers' actions (e.g., decision making, strategy implementation and CEO succession) to ensure that management operates in the interest of shareholders, thus helping to resolve the agency problem.

name: Resource provision
definition: Directors help firms to manage their dependence on external institutions by providing advice and counseling, access to external resources and information, and legitimacy.

name: State ownership
definition: The dominance of state ownership was measured with a dummy variable to indicate whether the controlling shareholder of the firm is the state; in China state ownership has continued to play a dominant role since large-scale privatization.

name: Likelihood of litigation
definition: The probability that a dispute ends in a court-rendered judgment rather than being settled privately; the authors collapse arbitration, mediation, and negotiation into a single private dispute resolution category.

name: Technical complexity of the exchange
authors_terms: ["Technical complexity", "technical uncertainty", "technical complexity of the exchange"]
definition: Technical uncertainty is related to the complexity of the focal exchange; as technical complexity increases, technical glitches become more likely and it becomes increasingly difficult to demonstrate causal links between exchange partners' efforts and observed outcomes.

name: Predispute relationship duration
authors_terms: ["Predispute relationship duration", "elapsed duration of the exchange relationship", "shadow of the past", "history of prior exchange"]
definition: The elapsed duration of the exchange relationship at the time the dispute arises, equal to the time between the beginning of the exchange relationship and the date at which the dispute arose.

name: Cooperative norms
definition: Norms of cooperation emerging over the course of an exchange relationship, reflecting flexibility, participation, and solidarity in prior interactions between the partners; the authors argue the effect of elapsed duration on willingness to work things out is muted until and unless such norms develop.

name: Expected future duration of the exchange relationship
authors_terms: ["shadow of the future", "Time remaining", "expected future duration of the exchange relationship", "Open"]
definition: The shadow of the future: firms' expectation of continued profitable exchange, such that a longer expected time horizon over which future benefits are expected to accrue raises the benefits of continued cooperation.

name: Innovativeness of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["innovativeness of alliance partners", "technological capabilities of alliance partners", "technologically advanced alliance partners", "innovativeness-of-partners"]
definition: The summed innovativeness scores of a firm's alliance partners, where the innovativeness of a firm in a period is the proportion of prior art citations included in the universe of U.S. semiconductor patents applied for in that year that refer to patents assigned to that firm. Alliances with the most skilled innovators are treated as the most viable opportunities to learn new routines and acquire advanced technical know-how.

name: Size of alliance partners
authors_terms: ["revenues of alliance partners", "size of alliance partners", "combined sales volume of alliance partners", "sales of partners"]
definition: The combined semiconductor sales volume of a firm's alliance partners, size being operationalized as annual semiconductor sales volume. Large strategic partners are argued to be more valuable associates because they may provide access to extensive distribution channels, long-standing customer relations with influential end users, or a widely-adopted technology platform.

name: Innovation rate
definition: The rate at which an organization applies for new semiconductor patents, measured as a count of the number of new semiconductor patents applied for by each organization in the sample in each year of the analysis period.

name: Sales growth rate
authors_terms: ["rate of sales growth", "sales growth", "rate of revenue growth", "growth rate"]
definition: The rate of growth of a firm's semiconductor sales volume, chosen as the performance measure because the expected enhancement in reputation from gaining a highly regarded partner should manifest quickly in revenue increases from new customers.

name: Firm age
definition: The age of the firms in the sample, defined as the number of years since founding for dedicated semiconductor producers and as the number of years since entry into the industry for diversified producers.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of each firm", "focal firm size"]
definition: The size of each firm measured as its annual semiconductor sales; larger firms typically possess greater resources to invest in R&D.

name: Physical climate change exposure
authors_terms: ["physical climate change exposure", "climate change exposure", "climate exposure", "physical climate risk"]
definition: In this study, physical climate change exposure (henceforth, climate change exposure or climate exposure) refers to the assets and settings of firms that could be adversely affected by the physical effects of climate change. It is also called physical climate risk in some academic literature and in practice.

name: Climate change adaptation
authors_terms: ["climate change adaptation", "adaptation", "adaptation strategy", "adaptation breadth", "routine adaptation", "nonroutine adaptation"]
definition: Climate change adaptation (henceforth, adaptation) is the 'process of adjustment to actual or expected climate and its effects' (IPCC AR6, 2022, p. 1758) to reduce negative impacts and/or leverage positive ones. This article defines adaptation strategy as a combination of different adaptation measures in response to various types of climate exposure.

name: Perceived impact of climate change
definition: The perceived impact of climate change is defined as how companies perceive and interpret the magnitude of the impact of climate change on their business operation. Perceived impact of climate change refers to how companies perceive and interpret the magnitude of the impact of climate change on their business operation and performance.

name: ESG capabilities
authors_terms: ["ESG capabilities", "ESG", "environmental, social, and corporate governance capabilities"]
definition: In this study, I define ESG capabilities as firms' capabilities to integrate ESG concerns into their business models. They are intangible firm resources and capabilities with multiple uses and benefits.

name: Time horizon
definition: In this study, I define firms' time horizon as how far into the future firms consider events and risks when making decisions. Firms with longer time horizons focus more on the remote future, while those with shorter time horizons focus more on the present or near future.

name: Loss of star employees
authors_terms: ["star player exit", "star player loss", "losing star employees", "voluntary departure of a star player"]
definition: The unexpected voluntary departure of a star employee, that is, an employee with superior human capital; the authors define a star as a player listed in the top 5% of the league in player efficiency rating (PER).

name: Loss of non-star employees
authors_terms: ["non-star player exit", "non-star player loss", "losing non-star employees", "voluntary departure of a non-star player"]
definition: The unexpected voluntary departure of a non-star employee, that is, an employee with more ordinary human capital; even a non-star may be necessary to the effective functioning of interactions between roles in the organization's workflow.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The performance of the team, measured by its winning percentage within each season; winning percentage is the performance metric that players affect most directly, whereas financial performance is less relevant because the league operates jointly as a collective monopoly.

name: Workflow interdependence
definition: The way an organization's workflow arranges interdependence among roles: pooled interdependence is a workflow in which the performance of each role is relatively independent of the performance of all other roles, so that overall performance is additive, while reciprocal interdependence is a workflow in which the performance of any two roles can mutually affect each other, so that overall performance tends to be multiplicative.

name: External human capital acquisition capability
authors_terms: ["external acquisition capability", "external human capital acquisition", "external resource acquisition"]
definition: A team's success in identifying and recruiting new players whose individual performance will improve relative to that on their previous team; the external resource acquisition mechanism likely resides in an organization's recruitment processes.

name: Internal human capital development capability
authors_terms: ["internal development capability", "internal human capital development", "internal resource development"]
definition: A team's success in improving the individual performance of players who were already on the team; the internal resource development mechanism likely resides in an organization's training and development processes.

name: Entrepreneur gender
definition: Gender identification of speakers for attribution of all transcribed words, including those spoken by entrepreneur presenters and VC judges; the analyses distinguish startups led by female entrepreneurs from those led by male entrepreneurs.

name: Regulatory focus of investor questions
authors_terms: ["regulatory focus of investor questions", "promotion-focused questions", "prevention-focused questions", "predominant promotion focus"]
