definition: VC questions articulated with a promotion focus emphasize attaining growth-oriented gains that are facilitated by capital (e.g., how do you intend to acquire customers? what does your revenue forecast look like?), whereas those articulated with a prevention focus emphasize maintaining non-losses and not losing capital (e.g., what does customer retention look like? are you operating at breakeven?).

name: Regulatory focus of entrepreneur responses
authors_terms: ["regulatory focus of entrepreneur responses", "promotion-focused responses", "prevention-focused answers", "matching regulatory focus"]
definition: The promotion or prevention orientation expressed in the words entrepreneurs use when answering investor questions, matching or switching relative to the orientation of the question posed.

name: Venture funding
authors_terms: ["funds raised", "funding outcomes", "venture funding", "funds allocated", "natural log of funding"]
definition: In the field study, funds raised as the total U.S. dollar value of funding received by each of the startups across various funding rounds, including seed, angel, and venture-led rounds; in the experiment, the participant's allocation of a hypothetical pool of available funds to each venture.

name: Prevalence of prevention-focused questions
authors_terms: ["prevalence of prevention-focused questions", "number of prevention-focused questions", "prevention count", "degree of prevention focus"]
definition: The degree of prevention focus in the questions investors ask, captured by the number of prevention-focused questions that investors asked an entrepreneur.

name: Resource recombination
authors_terms: ["recombining existing resources", "valuable and difficult-to-imitate strategic actions that recombine existing resources", "new product introductions", "organic growth"]
definition: Value creation can occur by recombining existing resources and capabilities; recombining existing resources into new capabilities can be especially helpful in the internal development of new products. To reverse declining market performance the actions must, in addition, be valuable and difficult to imitate.

name: Resource acquisition
authors_terms: ["acquiring new resources", "mergers and acquisitions", "valuable and difficult-to-imitate acquisitions"]
definition: A common means of obtaining substantial new resources is through acquisition; strategic actions providing for the acquisition of significant amounts of new resources enable firms to alter substantially their existing capabilities and to pioneer new capabilities. These firms positively affect investor expectations by completing valuable and difficult-to-imitate acquisitions, thereby providing more immediate resource platforms to effect positive changes in performance.

name: Resource access
authors_terms: ["gaining access to new resources", "strategic alliances", "valuable and difficult-to-imitate strategic alliances"]
definition: Engaging in strategic alliances provides firms with access to, but not control of, additional resources from their partners that can help improve performance. For an alliance to help a declining firm exceed market expectations and create value, the combination of both partners' resources must be valuable and difficult to imitate, at least in the short term.

name: Performance relative to investor expectations
definition: A measure of value creation is a firm's ability to meet or exceed investors' performance expectations. Alpha is a continuous measure indicating the extent to which a firm has failed to meet, met, or exceeded investor expectations.

name: Repertoire conventionality
authors_terms: ["repertoire conventionality", "conventionality of the non-20th-century opera repertoire", "conventionality of their other repertoire choices"]
definition: Conventionality of the traditional operas in a repertoire, captured by the conventionality index, which is defined by the average number of times that each opera in a repertoire produced by the focal opera company has been produced by all the other opera companies in the population in a given period.

name: Unconventional repertoire choices
authors_terms: ["unconventional repertoire choices", "proportion of 20th-century opera", "modern operas", "unconventional operas"]
definition: Modern operas from the 20th century, characterized by a contemporary style of music and drama, are defined as unconventional operas, whereas traditional operas from before the 20th century, embracing baroque, classical, and romantic styles, are defined as conventional operas; 20th-century operas are those whose composers were born after 1880 and therefore had developed their adult musical style in the 20th century.

name: Audience divergence
authors_terms: ["audience divergence", "divergent audiences", "divergence of audiences", "divergent audience tastes"]
definition: A divergent audience is split between different tastes that follow a bimodal or U-shaped distribution, which implies that a firm would have to straddle relatively different positions at both peaks to engage most of the audience; divergent audiences are located toward opposite or nonadjacent ends of a continuum of audience tastes.

name: Within-category competitive pressure
authors_terms: ["within-category competition", "within-category competitive pressure", "competitive pressures from other opera companies"]
definition: The nature of competition refers to the extent to which competition is primarily between organizations in the same market category or between organizations in different market categories; within-category competition increases in regions with more opera companies and becomes more important there than in other regions.

name: Achieved status
definition: Ascribed status is defined as being 'assigned to individuals without reference to their innate differences or abilities' and achieved status as 'requiring special qualities' and 'open to individual achievement.' Achieved status is a 'delible', or 'reversible' dimension that allows for social mobility by means of 'performance or effort or volition.'

name: Ascribed status
definition: Ascribed status is 'assigned to individuals without reference to their innate differences or abilities' and is typically characterized as an 'indelible' or 'irreversible' dimension that is defined by an 'accident of birth.' It is not under an individual actor's control because it is given to him or her based on the status of the social group with which the actor shares some nominal characteristic inherited at birth, such as gender, race, or country of origin.

name: Conformity
definition: Conformity is the degree to which actors follow conventional practices in a field rather than deviating from them. In this setting, the authors assess the degree to which conductors showed conformity to what was established in the field by capturing the extent to which the repertoire played by a conductor leaned toward canonical composers versus more unconventional composers.

name: Hierarchical inconsistency
authors_terms: ["hierarchical inconsistency", "misaligned rank ordering", "inconsistency between formal and informal hierarchies"]
definition: Hierarchical inconsistency is defined as the misaligned rank ordering in the formal business and informal social hierarchies of the corporate elite.

name: Securities fraud
definition: Securities fraud refers to deceptive practices conducted by firms that violate laws or regulations enforced by securities regulators. These conducts include but are not limited to misrepresentation of financial reports, misappropriation of assets, insider trading, illegal share transaction, and illegal guarantee.

name: Formal power concentration
authors_terms: ["formal head's concentrated power in the formal hierarchy", "power concentration", "chair-CEO duality", "absolute formal authority"]
definition: Prior studies suggest that a business leader serving as both chair and CEO garners a higher level of power concentration and more unequivocal superiority in the formal hierarchy than leaders with only one of the two titles.

name: Unequivocal superiority in the informal hierarchy
authors_terms: ["informal head's unequivocal superiority in the informal hierarchy", "informal head with unquestionable superiority in the informal social hierarchy"]
definition: The superiority of the informal head is rooted in prevailing social norms and traditions, with repeated social interactions bolstering the deference order in the informal hierarchy.

name: Contestation among corporate elite
definition: To reinforce one's own superiority and erode the other's power and status, the two heads of formal and informal hierarchies may strive for dominance by overtly challenging each other's opinions and behaviors. Contestation among the heads enables mutual monitoring, the ability of peers to observe and control each other's actions.

name: CEO insider status
authors_terms: ["insider/outsider CEO", "insider versus outsider CEO", "promoted from within"]
definition: The organization can hire the type of CEO believed to be most likely to affect firm performance favorably, e.g. deciding between an insider (promoted from within the firm) versus outsider (brought in from outside the firm) CEO. The authors argue that the roots of this difference are not in the personal traits or attitudes of outsider versus insider CEOs, but in the features of the principal-agent relationship that characterizes CEO/Board relations.

name: CEO succession planning
authors_terms: ["CEO succession planning", "having a specific successor in mind", "specific successor in mind"]
definition: CEO succession planning concerns whether or not an incumbent CEO has a specific successor in mind. The authors argue that an incumbent CEO's having a specific successor in mind represents a strong positive signal about the firm's top management.

name: CEO compensation satisfaction
authors_terms: ["CEO satisfaction with total compensation", "satisfaction with his/her overall compensation", "satisfaction with overall compensation"]
definition: The satisfaction/performance relationship is most directly addressed by gauging the CEO's general satisfaction with his/her overall compensation, i.e. the extent to which a CEO is satisfied with his/her overall compensation and thus performs better.

name: Perceived personal wealth connection
authors_terms: ["perceived connection between personal financial wealth and firm wealth", "perceived connection between his/her personal wealth and the wealth of the firm"]
definition: The perceptions of the degree of connection between personal wealth and company wealth, as articulated by the CEOs themselves. From an economic perspective, the motivational effect of CEO compensation is unavoidably influenced by a CEO's personal wealth.

name: Perceived personal reputation connection
authors_terms: ["perceived connection between personal reputation as CEO and firm wealth", "perceived connection between firm performance and his/her reputation as CEO"]
definition: To the extent that the CEO perceives a stronger connection between firm performance and his/her reputation as CEO, s/he will be more motivated to maximize firm profits. This reputational incentive does not emerge directly from the CEO's compensation arrangement.

name: Firm performance
definition: The dependent variable of firm performance, taken from COMPUSTAT, was measured by average return on assets during the CEO's tenure.

name: New knowledge generation
authors_terms: ["knowledge generation in the new paradigm", "new knowledge generation", "new knowledge creation", "development of knowledge in the emerging biotech paradigm"]
definition: Patents by incumbent pharma firms in the new field of biotechnology seem to be an appropriate measure to capture new knowledge generation. To proxy the successful development of knowledge in the emerging biotech paradigm by pharmaceutical incumbents, the authors relied on the annual count of biotech patents assigned to the firms in the sample.

name: External knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["external knowledge sourcing", "external sourcing", "external capability sourcing modes", "knowledge-oriented alliances", "biotech-related acquisitions"]
definition: The authors collected detailed information about the external knowledge sourcing strategies that were undertaken by the pharmaceutical incumbents, focusing on two such external capability sourcing modes: knowledge-oriented alliances with sources of biotech knowledge (i.e., exploration alliances) and biotech-related acquisitions.

name: Internal knowledge recombinative potential
authors_terms: ["recombinatory potential", "potential for future knowledge recombination", "internal recombinative potential", "recombinative potential"]
definition: If a firm has an internal knowledge network with high clustering and average path length, then that firm has significant potential for internal future knowledge recombination. The authors measured each firm's recombinatory potential using two network metrics: average path length and degree of clustering.

name: Internal knowledge coordination costs
authors_terms: ["coordination costs", "internal coordination burden", "knowledge coordination costs", "high coordination burden"]
definition: If an incumbent firm generates knowledge in a new area and the firm already faces high internal knowledge production and coordination costs, then external knowledge sourcing strategies are less effective for new knowledge generation because they would simply add to the existing coordination burden. Coordination costs were measured with two different metrics: average ties per biotech patent and average ties per inventor.

name: Entry mode
authors_terms: ["entry mode", "mode of market entry", "de novo firm", "de alio firm", "de novo status"]
definition: An organization's mode of market entry: firms entering a market de novo (start-up) versus those entering de alio (diversification from another market). De novo firms (entrepreneurial start-ups) differ from de alio firms (entrants from another industry) in their entry conditions, their innovation behavior, and their market fates.

name: Product exit rate
authors_terms: ["product exit", "product's exit from the market", "rate of product exit", "product longevity"]
definition: The product-specific instantaneous rate of exit from the market: a product is considered to exit the market in year t if it is not shipped in year t + 1. The authors view this conversely as a product's longevity in the marketplace.

name: Firm tenure in the industry
authors_terms: ["tenure of the firm in the industry", "as a de novo firm ages in the industry", "start-up age"]
definition: The time that has elapsed since a firm was founded and entered the focal industry; the authors extend their argument by considering what happens as de novo firms age in the focal industry.

name: Multinationality
definition: Multinationality is measured as the number of host countries in which the Japanese firm operates manufacturing affiliates. Firms investing in a larger number of host countries are argued to be better positioned to exploit a broader set of growth opportunities present in these markets.

name: Value of growth options
authors_terms: ["value of growth options", "growth option value", "growth options"]
definition: The part of the market valuation of the firm that is attributable to future growth opportunities; growth options are discretionary future investment opportunities for the firm, having option-like features in that the firm has the right, but not the obligation, to decide in a future period whether or not to exploit the opportunities.

name: Market uncertainty in host countries
definition: Host countries' market uncertainty confronted by multinational firms is a most salient type of environmental uncertainty that shapes firms' value of growth options; the authors capture it as the volatility of a host country's economic growth.

name: Equity stake in foreign affiliates
definition: By assuming partial ownership in a joint venture rather than investing in a wholly owned venture, the firm is positioned to expand if market uncertainty is resolved favorably, while it can still hold on to its initial investment if favorable signals do not materialize. Equity Stake is calculated as the Japanese firm's average equity stake in its foreign affiliates.

name: Investment size in foreign affiliates
authors_terms: ["investment size", "size of investment", "size of the financial resources committed to the affiliates", "small investments"]
definition: One way the firm can commit resources incrementally to enhance its growth option value from multinational investment is to limit the size of investment in its foreign affiliates, reducing the scale of operations while preserving the potential to scale up later. Investment Size is a measure of financial resources invested in the foreign affiliate.

name: Country-level investment alignment
authors_terms: ["country-level investment alignment", "country-level investment alignment (country-level investment alignment)", "alignment within each country", "country-level alignment"]
definition: Alignment of investment strategies to each host country's environmental uncertainty improves the ''fit'' between investment strategy and uncertainty at the individual country level, and thus can be expected to enhance the value of growth options of the firm as a whole. An aligned configuration is one of relatively small investments (in terms of equity stake and size) in countries exhibiting relatively high uncertainty, or one of relatively large investments in countries exhibiting relatively low uncertainty.

name: Star performer turned manager
definition: An SPTM is a manager who had previously demonstrated star-level performance in an individual contributor role; the authors define an SPTM as a manager who had previously played in an NBA All-Star Game.

name: Organizational performance
definition: The performance of the organization, which the authors measure in their setting as whether the team wins a game, since the goal of winning games is universally shared, unambiguous, and objectively measured.

name: Visibility of manager expertise
authors_terms: ["accuracy of subordinates' perceptions of their manager's level of expertise", "geographic connection", "visibility", "salience"]
definition: The extent to which subordinates have observed a manager's prior star performance and therefore accurately perceive his level of expertise; the authors argue that role modeling requires visibility and that visibility is stronger when it is local (i.e., a hometown hero).

name: Morale building
definition: A social-level motivational influence mechanism: a leader's use of communications that emphasize the collective identity of the group and foster positive esprit de corps in order to motivate subordinates.

name: Manager influence over rewards and punishments
authors_terms: ["incentivizing", "manager's GM influence", "influence over the rewards and punishments"]
definition: The degree to which a manager can exercise discretion to allocate rewards and punishments to subordinates, or at least influence the incentive schemes that perform those allocations.

name: Subordinate experience level
authors_terms: ["experience level of subordinates", "novice players", "number of rookies"]
definition: How experienced the subordinates are; the authors argue that on-the-job training efforts are more relevant, and likely to produce larger skill improvements, when applied to less experienced learners than when applied to highly experienced learners, since skill development exhibits diminishing marginal returns.

name: Collaborative learning environment
authors_terms: ["collaborative learning environment", "trainer, mentor, or coach", "middle manager average tenure"]
definition: A social-level ability influence mechanism: a manager can only enlist the help of trainers, mentors, or coworkers for collaborative group learning if the organization actually has highly experienced employees available to serve in those roles.

name: Proprietary methods of organizing
definition: Organizing is the main tool managers use to improve subordinates' collective ability as a unit, and the authors focus on proprietary organizing methods, since only the most unique, proprietary, and difficult to replicate methods of organizing are likely to yield lasting advantages.

name: Customer firm-specific capabilities
authors_terms: ["customers' firm-specific capabilities", "customers' bank-specific online banking capabilities", "customers' online banking capabilities", "capability-based switching costs", "customers' capability-based switching costs"]
definition: Customers develop product capabilities and the ability to link product characteristics to product performance incrementally through learning-by-using. Such capabilities are likely to be firm specific and cannot be transferred perfectly to competitors' product offerings, so the investment required to learn new capabilities is a form of switching cost, which the authors term a capability-based switching cost.

name: Internal cross-selling capabilities
definition: In the traditional banking model the function of a bank is to accept deposits and use those funds to make loans, whereas banks following an aggressive strategy sell a wide gamut of complementary products and are more likely to have developed cross-selling capabilities. Such banks are more likely to collect information about customers' needs and wants, use it to anticipate and identify customers' complementary needs, and inform customers about the banks' products that will fulfill their needs in a timely manner.

name: Service income per account
authors_terms: ["service income per account", "noninterest income per account", "fee income or noninterest income per account", "noninterest income/account"]
definition: The noninterest income/account variable is the authors' proxy for service income per account; it is computed as a ratio of total noninterest income and the total number of deposit accounts. For banks, noninterest income is not net of expenses, and thus is more akin to 'revenue' than 'income.'

name: Operating expenses per account
authors_terms: ["operating expenses per account", "noninterest expenses per account", "noninterest expense/account"]
definition: Noninterest expenses/account is the authors' proxy for operating expenses per account; it is computed as a ratio of total noninterest expense for the period and the total number of deposit accounts. This figure reflects total expenditures for all the physical assets of the bank as well as total wages.

name: Noninterest profit per account
definition: The variable net noninterest income/account is the authors' proxy for banks' profit (i.e., noninterest income minus noninterest expense) for the period divided by the total number of accounts.

name: Overall profit per account
definition: Net income/account is the authors' proxy for banks' overall profit for the period divided by the total number of accounts. This measure of profitability goes beyond the narrower measure of net noninterest income/account since it encompasses all profits generated by the bank.

name: Strategy presentations
definition: These strategy presentations (sometimes called 'strategy updates,' 'strategy reviews,' and similar) involve discussions of firms' overall strategies. These strategy presentations are public rather than internal, and concern the future of the whole business, rather than announcements of specific events such as acquisitions, R&D projects, or joint ventures.

name: Stock price reaction
authors_terms: ["stock price responses", "cumulative abnormal returns", "CAR", "stock price reaction", "investor reactions"]
definition: In this study, we treat stock price responses as measures of how strategy presentations impress investors in the short term; we do not interpret stock price responses as necessarily effective measures of eventual economic returns.

name: New CEO status
authors_terms: ["new CEO", "new chief executive", "new CEOs' strategy presentations", "newly appointed CEOs"]
definition: We define a new CEO as someone who has been appointed to the role of Chief Executive in a given organization up to 200 days prior to carrying out his or her first strategy presentation.

name: Internal nonheir CEO origin
authors_terms: ["internal, nonheir apparent new CEOs", "insider nonheir apparent CEO"]
definition: We coded '1' if the new CEO presenting his or her strategy was appointed from inside the organization but was not an heir apparent, and '0' if otherwise.

name: External within-industry CEO origin
definition: We coded '1' if the new CEO presenting his or her strategy was appointed from outside the organization (but from inside their main industry), and '0' otherwise.

name: External outside-industry CEO origin
definition: We coded '1' if the new CEO presenting his or her strategy was appointed from outside the firm's main industry (and organization), and '0' otherwise, using the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code.

name: Board political capital
authors_terms: ["board political capital", "politically connected board", "political capital", "political directors"]
definition: At the board level, this is often termed 'board political capital' because it represents not only directors' human capital in terms of government knowledge and experience, but also their social capital or connections to government decision makers.

name: Blockholder rent appropriation
definition: We define 'principal - principal agency problems' as the conflicts between controlling blockholders and a large number of small shareholders over firm surplus and the associated opportunism on the part of blockholders of appropriating firm wealth. Such appropriation can take a variety of forms: aside from installing unqualified cronies in executive positions and pursuing projects that advance their private interests, blockholders can divert assets and cash flows away from publicly traded companies to parent firms or unlisted subsidiaries through self-dealing transactions.

name: Controlling blockholder identity
definition: In the Chinese context, dominant blockholders can be government or private entities.

name: Industry regulation
definition: The role of industry regulation has long been a factor in corporate political strategy and again is rooted in resource dependence theory. Since regulated firms are more dependent on government policy, firms in heavily regulated industries tend to engage in more political activities.

name: Subnational institutional environment
definition: Large economies, such as China, feature substantial heterogeneity in regional institutions. Although China is a unitary state with uniform legal and regulatory frameworks, laws and policies are open to interpretation and revision by local authorities.

name: Invention disclosure
authors_terms: ["invention disclosure", "disclosing innovations", "participation in technology transfer", "technology transfer activities", "disclosure filed"]
definition: The decision of individual faculty members to become entrepreneurial academics and engage in commercial activity with industry begins when an invention disclosure is filed with the university's TTO. Filing an invention disclosure is the initiating stage of the technology transfer process, and all of the subsequent measures of the university's progress toward this new organizational initiative depend on individual faculty disclosing their research results.

name: Technology transfer training imprinting
authors_terms: ["technology transfer culture of the institution where the faculty member received their graduate training", "protechnology transfer imprinting", "training effects", "graduate training incorporated technology transfer objectives"]
definition: In our context, the logic of imprinting implies that individuals trained at institutions where participation in technology transfer was actively practiced will be more likely to adopt these practices in their own careers. The intensity of a university's technology transfer culture can be proxied using the institution's patenting history.

name: Time since graduate training
authors_terms: ["years since last graduate degree", "experience years", "vintage of their last graduate degree"]
definition: The length of time an individual has been out of training is also likely to influence their disclosure decisions. The earlier an individual completed her training, the more likely she is to have been exposed to, and adopted, the traditional norms of science that do not favor disclosing.

name: Department chair technology transfer activity
authors_terms: ["chair discloses", "observed behavior of the chair", "leadership effects", "the chair is actively involved in technology transfer"]
definition: One signal that the chair is predisposed to consider technology transfer as a legitimate activity would be the observed behavior of the chair. If the chair is active in technology transfer as demonstrated by his or her prior disclosures, then he or she sends a signal that technology transfer is a valid activity.

name: Local cohort technology transfer activity
authors_terms: ["cohort disclosures", "local peers", "local peer effects", "percentage of faculty at the same rank within the department who disclosed"]
definition: We define an individual's cohort as those individuals of the same rank in the same department. The cohort effect is measured as the percentage of faculty at the same rank within the department who disclosed in the prior time period.

name: Formal organizational mandates
authors_terms: ["formal organizational mandates", "legal rules and authority", "organizational sanctions", "NIH guidelines"]
definition: It is possible that social pressure may induce only symbolic compliance: some individuals may comply with organizational initiatives simply to avoid sanctions. Our interviews suggest that symbolic individuals are more responsive to legal rules and authority; certainly, individuals with NIH grants may engage in symbolic compliance to conform to agency guidelines.

name: Depth of adoption
definition: The individual decision to disclose inventions indicates compliance with the university's technology transfer initiative, but this observed behavior may or may not indicate that the individual has adopted the new norms of behavior. Individuals who engage in symbolic compliance would be expected to disclose nominally, perhaps only once a period, whereas individuals who have undergone microemancipation would disclose frequently.

name: Collective teaching
definition: Collective teaching is a process in which members of the source organization collectively impart the knowledge, routines, and mindset of their organization to the individuals of the receiving organization.

name: Individual teaching
definition: The most common perception of teaching is that of individual teaching, in which the knowledge imparting activity is carried out by an individual source entity. Individual teaching is the teaching carried out by individual members of the source community in an independent manner.

name: Collective absorptive capacity
definition: Collective absorptive capacity is the communication and information structure as well as organizational culture characterized by collaboration and learning; it consists of both structural attributes that help to overcome the coordination challenges and cultural attributes that help to overcome the motivation challenges associated with absorbing and adopting new knowledge.

name: Individual absorptive capacity
definition: Individual absorptive capacity is the aggregation of the prior knowledge or experiences of the individual members of a recipient community, which account for the recognition, assimilation, and application of valuable external knowledge.

name: Collective knowledge
authors_terms: ["collective knowledge", "stock of collective knowledge", "improvement of the receiving organization's stock of collective knowledge"]
definition: Collective knowledge is the knowledge embedded among organizational members regarding how to coordinate, share, distribute, and recombine individual knowledge.

name: Individual knowledge
authors_terms: ["individual knowledge", "stock of individual knowledge", "improvement of its stock of individual knowledge"]
definition: The construct of individual knowledge in our study refers to the overall stock of individual knowledge of the organization.

name: Growth option value
definition: Our dependent variable is growth option value (GOV), which represents the portion of the firm's value that is attributable to growth options, consistent with prior research. Growth options tend to have a long-term, uncertain payoff structure and present asymmetric payoff structures to the firm.

name: Stock option holdings
definition: Stock option holdings allow managers to benefit from upward movements in the firm's stock price. In addition, because stock options provide managers with the right, but not the obligation, to purchase the firm's stock at a specified price, managers do not face downside risk to their wealth.

name: Managerial stock ownership
definition: The payoffs from stock ownership are longer term in nature, and such managerial payoffs have been shown to lead firms to undertake longer-term, uncertain investments. While stock ownership allows managers to profit from the upward movements of stock price, managerial wealth is also exposed to potential downward movements.

name: Short-term pay
definition: Short-term pay refers to the salary and bonuses paid to top managers. These two incentives are characterized by a short-term time orientation and exhibit relatively little variability.

name: Industry growth opportunities
definition: Growth option values of firms vary widely across industries, suggesting that larger sets of growth opportunities exist in some industries relative to others. Shared options refer to the collective growth opportunities that exist in an industry and that are potentially available to all firms in the industry.

name: Acquisition premium paid
definition: The acquisition premium paid is a reflection of management's overall perception of a deal's synergistic potential; premiums are major statements by acquiring managers of how much additional value they can extract from the target. It indicates the lower bound of management's estimate of a deal's synergistic potential.

name: Acquirer stock market return
authors_terms: ["investor reactions", "acquirer stock market returns", "stock market reaction", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: Investors' stock market reactions to acquisition announcements, operationalized as the conventional event-study measure of short-term cumulative abnormal returns. The CAR represents that part of the return that is unanticipated by a statistical or economic model of anticipated, normal returns.

name: Industry similarity
authors_terms: ["industry similarity", "industry similarity between the target firm and the acquiring firm"]
definition: Industry similarity between the two parties is used to study the performance effect of a key dimension of strategic fit. Industry similarity suggests considerable opportunity for synergy, thus signaling greater reliability of management's perception.

name: Payment method
definition: The payment method used by the acquirer is a prominent example of acquisition tactics, with stock payment unlike cash payment implying that any risk involved in the deal is shared with the target firm's investors.

name: Involvement of acquirer advisors
authors_terms: ["involvement of acquirer advisors", "advisor involvement", "extent of advisor involvement in the deal"]
definition: The degree to which the acquirer involves external advisors in the deal process; acquirers rely more heavily on advisors when faced with high levels of uncertainty, either because of the complexity of the acquisition or because of asymmetric information between the acquirer and the target.

name: Preexisting partial ownership position in the target
authors_terms: ["preexisting partial ownership position", "pre-existing partial ownership position in the target firm"]
definition: A partial ownership position held in the target before deciding whether to acquire it altogether; the target-specific knowledge gained through such a relationship is likely to enable the acquirer to more accurately assess the target's synergistic potential.

name: Use of acquisition defense tactics by the target
authors_terms: ["defense tactics", "acquisition defense tactics by the target firm", "antitakeover defense mechanisms"]
definition: Target firms' deployment of defense tactics such as poison pills, golden parachutes, and white knights in the face of an imminent takeover bid, thus signaling to investors that target managers and shareholders consider the proposed deal to have low synergistic potential.

name: Acquirer current performance
authors_terms: ["acquirer performance", "acquiring firm's current performance", "profitability in terms of return on assets"]
definition: The acquiring firm's current performance, described as a major determinant of hubris that, in combination with the free cash flow strong performance typically generates, often leads management to engage in empire building by undertaking riskier or less promising acquisitions.

name: Acquirer debt-to-equity ratio
authors_terms: ["acquirer debt-to-equity", "acquiring firm's current debt-to-equity ratio", "acquirer's capital structure"]
definition: The acquirer's capital structure, that is, the balance between its debt and equity. The higher the acquirer's debt relative to its equity, the less free cash flow it has available for new projects and the more management is motivated to take less risk by engaging only in promising acquisitions.

name: Acquirer acquisition experience
definition: The acquirer's prior experience with acquisitions, which can generally be expected to enhance management's effectiveness at undertaking acquisitions by enriching its understanding of target selection, deal negotiation, and the post-acquisition integration process.

name: Firm sales change relative to industry
authors_terms: ["trend performers", "static performers", "trend firms", "static firms", "growing firms", "declining firms"]
definition: We will refer to firms that have the same change in sales as their industry as trend performers (i.e. firms with increasing sales in an industry with increasing sales or firms with decreasing sales in an industry with decreasing sales) and to firms whose sales change little as 'static performers.'

name: Average accounting returns
authors_terms: ["average returns", "mean returns", "returns on equity", "returns on assets"]
definition: Returns are measured by return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA).

name: Variance of returns
definition: Risk is measured by variance in returns (ROE and ROA) and error variance of the regression of returns on time (see below). As discussed above, simple variance in returns does not distinguish between variation about a trend and the trend itself.

name: Error variance of returns around a time trend
authors_terms: ["mean sum of squared errors", "MSE", "error variance", "error terms", "variability around the trend"]
definition: Error terms (sum of squared errors) represent the variability (uncertainty) around the trend in returns.

name: Alliance network diversity
authors_terms: ["alliance network diversity", "diversity of an MNE's alliance network", "alliance portfolio diversity", "diversity of alliances"]
definition: Alliance network diversity refers to variance in partners' resources, capabilities, and industrial backgrounds; a firm's network becomes more diverse as its connections to other firms increase, although because firms often enter into repeated partnerships with the same firms, diversity is increased by the extent to which these relationships are separate or unique.

name: Economic performance
definition: Although it is widely recognized that firms pursue multidimensional goals, the mainstream view in strategy research is that firms are fundamentally concerned with economic results; in this study economic performance was defined by the same three well-accepted measures: return on assets, return on sales, and return on capital.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: Environmental munificence, the level of resources in a particular environment, critically affects both firm growth and survival.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction", "abnormal stock returns", "cumulative abnormal stock returns"]
definition: Stock market reactions measured as cumulative abnormal stock returns (CAR) during an event window of 3 days surrounding alliance announcements.

name: Alliance partner type
authors_terms: ["alliance partner", "alliances with e-commerce or bricks-and-mortar partners", "partner selection"]
definition: An important selection issue facing e-commerce firms is choosing between e-commerce and bricks-and-mortar partners because resource bundles of e-commerce and bricks-and-mortar firms differ.

name: Alliance type
definition: We classified e-commerce alliances into two types: marketing and technology.

name: Entry deregulation
authors_terms: ["entry deregulation", "reduction in barriers to entry", "lowering barriers to entry", "'On the Spot Firm' program", "entry deregulation reform"]
definition: An entry deregulation program—'On the Spot Firm' (Empresa na Hora)—which was enacted at different moments in time across different Portuguese regions ('concelhos,' or municipalities), determining a decrease in entry barriers in such regions. The reform reduced the barriers to startup entry by decreasing bureaucratic and financial burdens on those starting new ventures.

name: Entrepreneurial entry
definition: Entrepreneurship refers to launching a new business with employees to 'operate it from the owner-manager position' and is conceptually distinct from self-employment, which refers to 'initiating a sole proprietorship to sell one's own service or products'.

name: Employee gender
definition: Employees are distinguished by gender, with the main moderating variable being a dummy variable equal to '1' for female employees, and '0' for male employees; interacting this variable with the entry deregulation reform allows the authors to estimate the differential effect of the treatment for the female versus male employees.

name: Wage
definition: The monthly wage of the worker is constructed by adding up the following wage components: (a) base pay, or the gross amount of money paid in a given month to employees on a monthly basis for their normal hours of work; (b) regular payments (e.g., tenure-related payments); and (c) payment for extra work hours.

name: Managerial position
definition: A firm's hierarchy indicates whether an employee occupies a managerial position in the current firm, with records accounting for eight hierarchical levels based on the amount of autonomy individuals have in their jobs. An employee occupies a managerial position within an incumbent organization if she/he is a top or a middle manager.

name: CEO overpayment
definition: The extent to which a CEO's actual salary is higher than predicted: a positive residual from the CEO wage equation indicated that the CEO was overpaid because his actual salary was higher than his predicted salary.

name: CEO underpayment
definition: The extent to which a CEO's actual salary is lower than predicted; a negative residual indicated the CEO was underpaid, and the sign of the variable was reversed so that larger positive values were associated with greater underpayment.

name: Subordinate compensation
authors_terms: ["compensation of subordinates", "pay of subordinates", "employee wages", "salaries of those below them", "subordinate compensation"]
definition: The pay of managers at lower organizational levels than the CEO; compensation for the CEO and others in the sample was computed as the sum of base compensation and annual bonus.

name: CEO power
definition: The chief executive's structural power, which the authors argue may allow him to affect both his own pay and the wages of his subordinates; it was measured by whether the CEO also held the chair title.

name: Relative pay inequity with the CEO
authors_terms: ["relative internal inequity", "relative external inequity", "underpayment inequity relative to the CEO", "relative internal and external inequity"]
definition: The extent to which a manager's pay is unfavourable relative to the CEO: if the CEO's residual is larger than an employee's residual, it means that the CEO is overpaid relative to the employee and that the employee should feel inequity.

name: Manager turnover
definition: Exit of an individual from the company: individuals were recorded as exiting a company if they appeared in the survey for a given year but did not appear in the survey the following year.

name: Hierarchical level
authors_terms: ["hierarchical level", "levels in the organization", "Level 2 through Level 5"]
definition: The position of an executive in the organizational hierarchy: participating firms provided data for individuals in the top five levels of an organization, with the CEO as the only member of Level 1 and Level 5 including job titles such as division general managers.

name: Idiosyncratic risk taking
authors_terms: ["idiosyncratic risk", "risk taking", "excessive risk taking", "idiosyncratic risk taking"]
definition: Idiosyncratic risk is calculated as the standard deviation of excess returns, which is the residual risk a manager takes over and above the systematic market exposure a manager in an index fund would face.

name: Investment performance
definition: Excess returns are computed as the difference between raw returns and the benchmark risk-adjusted return predicted by this four-factor asset-pricing model. Performance is measured by the information ratio, which is equal to excess returns divided by idiosyncratic risk exposure.

name: Mutual fund to hedge fund transition
authors_terms: ["MF -> HF transition", "mutual fund to hedge fund transition", "transition to hedge funds"]
definition: Mutual fund managers who become hedge fund managers are transitioning to a related but different type of job with different investment strategies and compensation arrangements.

name: Mutual fund to mutual fund transition
authors_terms: ["MF -> MF transition", "mutual-fund-to-mutual-fund transition", "transition to a new mutual fund"]
definition: A mutual-fund-to-mutual-fund transition is a transition to a new mutual fund.

name: Learning on the job through experimentation
definition: Managers may engage in activities on the job that provide information about their fitness for an employment transition, and such activity is costly in the sense that it reduces their performance as employees. When both features are present, the authors say the employee is 'experimenting.'

name: Founding experience
definition: Entrepreneurship, or the act of leaving paid employment to start a new venture and exploit market opportunities, as a career choice. Our theory therefore pertains only to instances where individuals created new organizations, rather than to self-employment.

name: Candidate gender
authors_terms: ["Female Candidate", "Female", "gender of the applicant", "female ex-founders", "male ex-founders"]
definition: An applicant's gender, one of the demographic attributes that provide a likely additional source for stereotypes, and specifically for predictions regarding commitment and fit. Gender and racial stereotypes prove so influential that even identical experiences in an applicant's history can acquire differing significance or meaning, depending on the applicant's demographic attributes.

name: Employer evaluations at hiring
authors_terms: ["employers' evaluations", "interview request", "callback", "willingness to advance the candidate", "recommendation to hire", "willingness to recommend the applicant"]
definition: The employer's evaluation of a job candidate at the point of hire; these perceptual penalties function to reduce an employer's willingness to advance the candidate. The outcome of interest is whether the employer contacts the candidate (by phone or email) for a follow-up interview.

name: Perceived commitment and fit for wage work
authors_terms: ["fit", "commitment", "unfitness", "lack of commitment to wage work", "commitment and fit", "good fit for a more traditional/hierarchical organization"]
definition: Employers' beliefs that a candidate lacks fit and/or commitment to wage work, which the authors argue drive the founding discount; employers seek evidence of a cultural fit and willingness to commit to the future employer.

name: Perceived fit with the prior entrepreneurial job
authors_terms: ["good fit for their last job", "fit for recent job"]
definition: Respondents' assessment of whether the candidate was a good fit for their last job, that is, the job preceding the current job search, used to probe whether female ex-founders are seen as less fit for entrepreneurship.

name: Relatedness with the core business
authors_terms: ["relatedness of a segment", "relatedness of the core business", "forward vertical relatedness", "backward vertical relatedness", "forward complementarity", "backward complementarity", "internal and external transactions"]
definition: The four coefficients F, B, CF, and CB reflect the extent to which a segment shares various internal (F and B) and external transactions (CF and CB) with the core business. The very sharing of transactions with the core business is in itself a dimension of relatedness.

name: Relative core business size
authors_terms: ["relative core business size", "relative core size", "RELCORE", "size of the core business in the firm"]
definition: A relatively larger core business is likely to have greater power and influence in decision making than a core business that is not dominant in terms of size. Relative core business size is measured as core segment sales divided by total firm sales.

name: Segment productivity
definition: Segment productivity was measured as the sales of a segment less the sales of an average single-business firm in the same four-digit SIC code with comparable assets, normalized by firm size. Conceptually, it captures the extent to which the segment in the diversified firm is generating more or fewer sales, assuming the same asset turnover ratio of single-business firms.

name: Core business productivity
definition: Core business productivity is measured in a manner similar to segment productivity, and for every firm in the sample there is one core business productivity observation.

name: Firm value
definition: Firm value is measured by Tobin's Q, and the impact of core business productivity and segment productivity on firm value is examined with Tobin's Q measured at the firm level as the dependent variable.

name: Post spin-off market performance
authors_terms: ["market performance", "child firm post spin-off market performance", "shareholder return"]
definition: Market performance refers to shareholder return, calculated by compounding the daily returns to shareholders over each fiscal year and then standardized at the four-digit SIC code of the spin-off firm.

name: Parent ownership
authors_terms: ["continued substantial ownership by the parent firm", "ownership % held by parent", "block ownership", "ownership of the parent firm in the child"]
definition: The ownership of the parent firm in the child after the spin-off event; higher levels of ownership denote less autonomy for the child, and the variable represents the percentage of ownership retained by the parent post spin-off.

name: Parent board monitoring
authors_terms: ["board-level monitoring by a representative from the parent firm", "board oversight", "board representation", "oversight from the parent"]
definition: Oversight of the child firm through parent representation on the child's board; managers from the former parent are uniquely qualified to oversee the child due to their depth of knowledge about its operations.

name: Disproportionate parent monitoring
authors_terms: ["disproportionate monitoring by the parent firm", "too much parent monitoring"]
definition: Monitoring is considered to be disproportionately high when the parent firm retains both the chair of the child firm's board and at least one other regular board seat, representing a disproportionate amount of control concentrated in the hands of the parent firm.

name: Prior parent-child relationship
authors_terms: ["pre spin-off relationship of the child to the parent", "prior parent-child relationship"]
definition: The relationship between the parent and the child before the spin-off, classified by expert raters as unrelated, vertically integrated, or horizontally related.

name: Integrator structure
definition: Integrator roles are elements of the formal organizational structure that enable the coordination of efforts across specialized personnel within the organization. These formally mandated managerial roles are meant to enable coordination between (but have limited formal authority over) sets of specialized but interdependent actors.

name: Integrator structure type
definition: Integrator arrangements differ in the extent to which they can draw on the two ways in which an integrator functions: the exercise of informal authority and the provision of lateral communication channels. Doctor-integrators are generally known to exercise stronger informal authority than nurses, while nurse-integrators add a layer of informational richness and ease of communication with and about the patient that is superior to that of doctor-integrators.

name: Interdependence shift
authors_terms: ["interdependence shift", "shift in the pattern of interdependence"]
definition: Interdependence between agents in an organization exists when the optimal action of one agent is dependent on the actions of another. When this changes in a manner such that whether (and how) the agent's actions are interdependent is poorly understood, we say that an 'interdependence shift' has occurred.

name: Organizational performance
authors_terms: ["success rate", "operational performance", "rates of success", "births per patient"]
definition: The main measure of operational performance that allows for cross-clinic comparisons in IVF is the rate of success in each clinic. There is a well-established and widely agreed upon measure of success: the rates of success of IVF treatment at the clinic (i.e., births per patient).

name: Platform venture capital investment
definition: We refer to platform owners making equity investments in complementors as platform venture capital (PVC), clearly distinguishing it from the broader practice of CVC (Dushnitsky and Lenox 2005).

name: Product introduction
definition: The dependent variable in the complementor-subcategory-month data set is app introduction. It was coded as a dummy variable capturing a complementor's decision to introduce one or more apps in a subcategory in a given month.

name: Product withdrawal
definition: As such, we conceptualize product withdrawal decisions as forward-looking. That is, product withdrawal decisions do not merely depend on assessments of current performance and knowledge, but also on complementors' anticipations concerning the future.

name: Platform ecosystem experience
definition: Complementors with more products and a longer tenure in the platform ecosystem accumulate more knowledge faster. Stated another way, complementors vary in their stocks of platform-specific experience.

name: Exclusive platform focus
authors_terms: ["exclusive platform focus", "exclusive focus on the focal platform"]
definition: Some complementors choose to build their business exclusively on one platform, usually integrating their products tightly with this platform, while other complementors also engage in other business activities.

name: Reputation for IP toughness
authors_terms: ["reputation for IP toughness", "IP toughness", "litigiousness", "patent litigiousness", "reputation for toughness in patent enforcement"]
definition: Patent enforcement is therefore a particularly useful lever for firms seeking to build reputations for being tough about the unauthorized use of their proprietary technologies. The costliness of the activity has an important sorting function.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: Mobility is defined as the cumulative count of inventors hired from a given source firm by a recipient firm over the preceding five years, as measured by the application year of a mobile inventor's first patent at the recipient organization.

name: Knowledge spillovers
definition: The dependent variable is the count of citations made by patents of a recipient firm to patents of a source firm in a given year. More (fewer) such citations are interpreted as evidence of higher (lower) knowledge spillovers.

name: Entrepreneurial recipient firm
definition: Since these attributes tend to be highly correlated with one another, we refer to private/small/young firms collectively as 'entrepreneurial' and distinguish them from their more 'established' counterparts.

name: Entrepreneurial source firm
definition: Since these attributes tend to be highly correlated with one another, we refer to private/small/young firms collectively as 'entrepreneurial' and distinguish them from their more 'established' counterparts.

name: California-based source firm
definition: Finally, the dummy CA source firm is set to one if a firm has headquarters in California. Of the 129 source firms in the estimation sample, 80 are headquartered in California.

name: M-form adoption
authors_terms: ["M-form implementation", "M-form adoption", "M-form structure", "switch to the M-form", "M-form reorganization", "multidivisional structure"]
definition: Williamson (1975) proposes the M-form to be a unique structural framework that overcomes both internal control problems and strategic control problems confronting large multiproduct firms. The term M-form is reserved for those divisionalized firms in which the general office is engaged in periodic auditing and decision review and is actively involved in the internal resource allocation process.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["risk-adjusted equity returns", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "market reaction", "stockholder returns"]
definition: If market participants believe that the change to the M-form will increase future cash flows or decrease risk, then announcements of the reorganization will lead to stockholder returns greater than what would be expected in the absence of such announcements. If the announcement has information content then the market will adjust and result in returns different from those that are normally expected.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "related diversifiers", "unrelated diversifiers", "vertically integrated firms", "related diversification", "unrelated diversification", "vertical integration"]
definition: The firms were classified according to three major diversification strategies using Rumelt's (1974) methodology: vertically integrated firms, related diversifiers and unrelated diversifiers. Related diversification requires geometric increases in information processing, whereas vertical integration and unrelated diversification require less information processing as the span of control (number of divisions or SBUs) increases.

name: Long-term stock market performance
definition: The performance measures chosen for the long-term approach are the Sharpe and Treynor measures, calculated as the difference between each portfolio's measure and the market measure.

name: Internal social capital
authors_terms: ["internal social capital", "internal social capital among teachers", "social capital within each school"]
definition: Internal social capital is defined in terms of both the structure and the content of relationships among actors within a system; it comprises the relationships among individual members, specified as structural, relational and cognitive facets.

name: External social capital
definition: External social capital refers to the links between the organization and its external stakeholders, competitors, or partners.

name: Student achievement
definition: In the United States, school performance is increasingly assessed by examining student reading and mathematics achievement test scores, and the measures used are the percentage of students in the school attaining scores that meet or exceed state standards in mathematics and in reading.

name: Quality of instruction
definition: Our mediating variable is the level of quality of instruction provided in the school, generated as an average parent rating of instructional quality for each school.

name: Strategic action
authors_terms: ["strategic actions", "tactical actions", "type of action", "proportion of responses to strategic actions"]
definition: Strategic actions involve significant commitments of specific, distinctive resources and are difficult to implement and reverse. Tactical actions, on the other hand, are often designed to fine-tune strategy; they involve fewer and more general resources than strategic actions, are easier to implement, and are often more reversible.

name: External orientation
authors_terms: ["external orientation", "externality of orientation", "external orientation of the firm"]
definition: Miles and Snow (1978) characterized defenders as "internals" with a greater orientation toward efficiency and inner operations. In contrast, they describe prospectors as "externals" with a strong orientation toward environmental openness and change.

name: Structural complexity
definition: Structural complexity refers to the number of organizational levels and departments an organization has relative to total size.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Bourgeois defined slack as "that cushion of actual or potential resources which allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for adjustment or to external pressures for change in policy as well as to initiate changes in strategy with respect to the external environment."

name: Top management team education
authors_terms: ["education levels", "years of education", "highly educated managers", "management's years of education"]
definition: Education and experience levels relate to a manager's knowledge and skill base. Highly educated managers will conduct more exhaustive information searches than less educated managers, obtaining richer information with which to make response decisions.

name: Top management team experience
authors_terms: ["years of experience", "years of industry experience", "experienced managers", "management's years of experience"]
definition: Managers with many years of experience in a single industry will thus have a limited knowledge and skill base from which to make response decisions and will be more likely to engage in limited search when faced with a competitive action.

name: Response imitation
definition: One key dimension is response imitation, or the degree to which a response mimics an action.

name: Response likelihood
definition: Response likelihood was calculated by summing the number of times each airline responded to competitors' actions during a given year and dividing that figure by the number of times the firm had an opportunity to respond.

name: Response lag
definition: Response lag was measured by the amount of time it took a firm to respond to a competitor's action.

name: Response order
definition: Response order is the position in a temporal series of responses a firm occupies.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was measured in terms of net profit after taxes divided by total revenue. Profitability has been the dominant measure of performance in strategy research.

name: Endorsing beacon support
authors_terms: ["endorsing beacon", "Yale endowment's % VC allocation", "support for a sector"]
definition: An endorsing beacon is an organization that closely observes and monitors numerous sectors, actively supports a certain number of them (e.g., by investing in them), and is perceived as having exceptional insight into opportunities within sectors. An increase in an endorsing beacon's support for a sector is a credible signal of its viability and promise.

name: Demonstrating beacon outcome
definition: We have defined a demonstrating beacon as an enterprise whose exceptional outcome or event is viewed as a signal of its sector's attractiveness.

name: Venture-capital firm foundings
definition: Our dependent variable was an event count of the number of U.S. venture-capital foundings in each quarter.

name: New production subsidiary establishment
authors_terms: ["new subsidiary", "new production subsidiary", "establish a new production subsidiary", "network expansion", "expansion of international production networks"]
definition: This paper seeks to explain the decision to establish a new production subsidiary as a consequence of adverse environmental changes in the locations of the existing production network and to demonstrate that MNCs choose new locations that compensate for these deficiencies.

name: Labor cost growth
authors_terms: ["labor cost growth", "growth of labor costs", "rising labor costs", "wage growth"]
definition: To calculate labor cost growth, we use the real manufacturing wage index as a basis, which is the nominal wages index corrected for changes in purchasing power measured by the consumer price index. At an attained level of productivity, increasing labor costs erode the net present value C of the production network.

name: Uncertainty of labor costs
authors_terms: ["uncertainty of labor costs", "labor cost volatility", "volatility of wages", "uncertain wage developments"]
definition: Labor cost volatility leads to an extra discount on the cash flows that are going to be generated by the production sites and decreases the net present value C. The growth option value G of the international production network depends on the uncertainty of labor costs in its locations.

name: Diversity of labor cost developments
authors_terms: ["diversity of labor cost developments", "labor cost differentials", "heterogeneity of contemporary labor cost developments"]
definition: The variable diversity of labor cost developments shall reflect the heterogeneity of contemporary labor cost developments across the locations of the production network. The value of operational flexibility F depends on the diversity of labor cost developments in its locations.

name: Upper social class origins
authors_terms: ["upper social class origins", "upper social class background", "upper social class status", "upper social classes"]
definition: Having grown up with an abundance of resources, individuals from the upper social classes have experienced the benefit of a substantial safety net that provides not only economic security, but also - and perhaps more importantly - psychological security.

name: Lower social class origins
authors_terms: ["lower social class origins", "lower social class background", "lower social classes"]
definition: Having experienced the lowest level of resources and societal rank, executives of lower social class origins are familiar with circumstances characterized by regular uncertainty and lack of control.

name: Strategic risk taking
authors_terms: ["strategic risk taking", "firm risk taking", "managerial risk taking", "risk taking"]
definition: This approach is consistent with our focus on managerial risk taking, 'defined as management ' s proactive strategic choices involving the allocation of resources' (Palmer & Wiseman, 1999: 1038, emphasis original).

name: Elite education
authors_terms: ["elite education", "degree of elite education", "elite college education", "elite undergraduate institution"]
definition: Because our study focuses on the effects of early, formative life experiences, our index places a high importance on the elite status of undergraduate education as a key period of growth and self-discovery in the life of young adults.

name: General management functional background
authors_terms: ["general management functional background", "general management background", "intrapersonal functional diversity", "diverse functional background", "diverse managerial experience"]
definition: We focus on intrapersonal functional diversity, defined as 'breadth of functional experience within TMT members' (Cannella, Park, & Lee, 2008: 769, emphasis original); however, it should be noted that our focus is on the single most powerful executive - the CEO - rather than the entire TMT.

name: Protest activity
authors_terms: ["protest activity", "level of protest activity", "lagged protest activity", "protest events", "extraorganizational social mobilization"]
definition: The level of protest activity in a metropolitan area in the period before a union election, generated as a count of protest events in the relevant area in the five years preceding the year of the union election. A protest event is any type of activity that involves more than one person and is carried out with the explicit purpose of articulating a claim against (or expressing support for) a target.

name: Union vote share
authors_terms: ["union vote share", "vote share", "workers' support for unions", "votes for the union", "union support"]
definition: Workers' expressions of support for unions, operationalized as the votes that unions receive in representation elections; the vote share is calculated as the votes for the union over the votes cast.

name: Progressive protest activity
definition: Protest activity whose claims are politically progressive, such as protest in support of Civil Rights or against the Vietnam War. The authors built variables to track progressive protest activity by relying on the claims made by each protest as recorded in the DoCA dataset.

name: Civil Rights protest activity
authors_terms: ["Civil Rights protest actions", "Civil Rights-related protests", "Civil Rights protests", "lagged Civil Rights protests"]
definition: Protest activity around Civil Rights claims, which the authors argue should produce more osmotic mobilization into union organizing because the Civil Rights movement pressed for the elimination of employment discrimination.

name: Women's employment-related protest activity
definition: Protest activity by the women's movement around employment-related claims, such as equal pay and the removal of 'protective' legislation, which overlapped with what unions could help advance.

name: Union progressive track record
authors_terms: ["progressive unions", "more historically progressive unions", "unions' track records", "progressive records on racial integration", "political orientation"]
definition: How progressive a union's historical track record has been, for instance whether it supported black civil rights or opposed the Vietnam War or welcomed female members; the authors classified unions into progressive, neutral, and conservative subclasses.

name: Time period
authors_terms: ["earlier in the period", "later in the period", "years before 1982", "after 1981"]
definition: Whether an election falls earlier or later in the period studied; the authors treat the years before 1982 as earlier in these data for historical reasons, and break the data at 1981 when testing hypotheses 6 and 7.

name: Product diversification
authors_terms: ["product diversification strategy", "firm diversification level", "level of product diversity", "product diversity"]
definition: The level of product diversity of the firm, argued to vary as firms change strategy; product diversity ranges from single product, to vertical integration, to growth by internal diversification of related products and growth by acquisition of unrelated products.

name: Objectivity of performance criteria
authors_terms: ["performance criteria", "nature of the evaluation criteria", "objective criteria", "subjective criteria"]
definition: Subjective criteria are those such as personnel-related goals and coordination among same-level executives; objective goals are those which are more readily quantifiable, e.g. financial measures.

name: Bonus proportion of total compensation
authors_terms: ["proportion of executive pay received as an incentive or bonus", "proportion of bonus pay", "bonus as a proportion of pay", "incentive proportion"]
definition: The proportion of executive pay received as an incentive or bonus, measured by executives' estimates of the percentage they receive as base vs. bonus pay.

name: Bonus distribution method
authors_terms: ["method of bonus allocation", "method used to distribute the bonus pool", "bonus distribution method"]
definition: Two compensation variables were measured: proportion of executive pay received as an incentive or bonus and the method used to distribute the bonus pool, i.e. whether bonus distribution is based on a formula or on the judgement of evaluators.

name: Co-national immigrant community size
authors_terms: ["size of an immigrant community", "co-national immigrant community", "immigrants", "ln(immigrants)"]
definition: The stock of immigrants from the focal firm's home country residing in the host location. Access to the resources offered by an immigrant community is given preferentially to those who share the nationality or ethnicity of the population, such as firms owned by those from the same home country.

name: Firm profitability
definition: In line with prior studies, the authors use OROA as a firm performance measure, calculated by dividing earnings before interest and taxes by the book value of assets.

name: CEO nationality
authors_terms: ["immigrant CEO", "nationality of the CEO", "native (Russian) CEO", "immigrant manager", "top manager"]
definition: The nationality of the firm's top manager, an immigrant of the same nationality as the relevant community or a native (Russian, in this context) manager. The immigrant CEO could be a permanent resident or a manager on assignment from the parent firm, and is understood to be from the same country of origin as the focal firm's owner.

name: Foreign firm type
authors_terms: ["independent firm", "foreign independent firm", "MNC subsidiary", "co-national subsidiary", "type of firm"]
definition: A foreign independent firm is one owned by one or more individuals who are nationals of a country different from the one in which the firm operates. A foreign MNC subsidiary is one owned by a corporation headquartered in a country different from the one in which the firm operates.

name: Societal importance of networks
authors_terms: ["importance placed on networks and relationships", "importance of networks", "importance on network connections or luck"]
definition: The importance society places on networks and relationships for success in business and life, a local condition that creates an imperative to be embedded in a social community.

name: Xenophobia
definition: Local conditions under which natives distrust foreigners, i.e., locations with xenophobia, which make it particularly difficult for a foreign firm to become embedded within the native community.

name: Industry sector
definition: Firms operating in retail and services are more likely to sell their products locally and directly to consumers than firms operating in manufacturing; the need to interact directly with customers makes the national identity of the manager more important than in manufacturing.

name: MNC parent firm size
authors_terms: ["size of the MNC parents", "parent-firm size", "parent-firm employment"]
definition: MNCs vary in the availability of internal resources according to their size; subsidiaries of smaller MNC parent firms depend more on the local community for resources.

name: Initial sales performance
authors_terms: ["initial sales performance", "first-month unit sales", "prior sales performance", "sales rank"]
definition: Games' first-month unit sales, which account for a disproportionate share (more than 40%) of games' cumulative unit sales and thus are strongly indicative of overall market performance.

name: Selective promotion
definition: A key way a platform sponsor manages the value of its overall ecosystem is through selective promotion with which it nurtures the success of individual complements and manages end users' perception of the breadth and depth of the platform. In the console video game industry this takes the form of 'Best of' endorsements: video games chosen for endorsement are repackaged with the award figuring prominently and relaunched to the market.

name: Genre value
definition: The value of a product category, created by taking the percentage rank of all genres by total unit sales for each year and platform, where genres are first rank ordered by the sum of first-month unit sales of all games released in that genre, in that year, on that platform.

name: No prior hit in genre
authors_terms: ["no prior hit in genre", "no prior top-selling video game", "platform does not have a top-selling complement"]
definition: A dummy that takes the value of 1 if there is no top 20% ranked video game measured by first-month unit sales in the same genre and platform of a game under consideration, measured over a one-year rolling window prior to a game's release.

name: Platform exclusivity
definition: A complement is exclusive to a platform when it is launched only on the focal platform; complements can be exclusive because they are produced by the platform sponsor, because investments in cospecialization make it costly to work with multiple platforms, because of exclusivity agreements, or because a complement has not proven high quality or popular and is not sought by other platforms.

name: Complement quality
definition: The quality of an individual complementary good, which the authors check with Metacritic's reported Metascores; many video game publishers use Metascores as a proxy for quality, as is reflected by their contracts with game developers.

name: New complement releases
authors_terms: ["new game releases", "fewer new complements being released", "number of new games that are released"]
definition: The count of new games that are released within a particular genre per month on a platform; promoting during a period when fewer complements are being released lets the platform avoid competitive crowding and lessens cannibalization of newly released complements.

name: Product innovation
definition: The extent to which new ventures can successfully develop new products with superior quality and in a speedy manner for market penetration.

name: Ties with service intermediaries
authors_terms: ["ties with service intermediaries", "ties with multiple service intermediaries", "ties with service intermediaries (technology service firms, accounting and financial service firms, law firms, and talent search firms)"]
definition: Professional service organizations that provide firms with supporting services in areas such as accounting and finance, talent search, law, and technology services (e.g., technology commercialization and brokering).

name: Perceived industry growth
definition: The level of managers' perceived growth of their principal industry within the last three years.

name: Adoption of agency business for foreign firms
authors_terms: ["adoption of agency business for foreign firms", "agency business for foreign firms"]
