definition: The adoption of agency business for foreign firms, defined as a downstream alliance 'by which a firm markets and distributes a foreign firm's products and services' in their home country.

name: Export
definition: Whether or not a new venture exports reflects its market focus.

name: Knowledge flow
authors_terms: ["knowledge flow", "interfirm knowledge flow", "knowledge sharing", "access to knowledge (advice)"]
definition: Knowledge, modeled as advice flow, is transmitted between firm managers across ties. We measured interfirm knowledge flow in terms of access to knowledge (advice) by firm executives.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: We developed our variable geographic proximity using the location of each mutual fund company. We measured firms as located in the metropolitan area where its head office is located.

name: Institutional ties
definition: Institutional ties reflect the industry's governing structure; they are the ties formed by the industry trade association structure and arise incidentally to the firms involved, rather than purposefully by the firms or their executives.

name: Organizational ties
definition: Organizational ties operate at the firm level. They are direct ties between two organizations established for an instrumental purpose, for example equity holdings or alliances; in the mutual fund industry they exist when one firm manages one or more funds for another firm.

name: Friendship ties
definition: Friendships among firm executives operate at the individual level. They are established as a result of individual choices, and reflect liking between the individuals involved.

name: Structural holes
authors_terms: ["structural holes", "bridge ties", "structural holes bridged by project members", "past structural holes", "current structural holes"]
definition: A network rich in structural holes is one in which the different parts of the network are largely disconnected but bridged by a few nodes, which have the potential to act as brokers.

name: Internal network closure
authors_terms: ["network closure", "internal network closure", "closure", "past internal network closure", "current internal network closure"]
definition: Network closure refers to a pattern of dense, mutually interconnected ties among the members of a network. High closure implies that a project team is composed of highly mutually interconnected specialists who share meanings, trust, and routines.

name: Project network performance
definition: The size of the audience that watched a show, or its number of viewers, is fairly unanimously considered the measure of any TV production's performance.

name: Founder departure
definition: The study investigated firm and individual characteristics that influence the likelihood of departure among founders rather than the specific motivations (voluntary or not) of each founder. The dependent variable is the likelihood of a founder leaving a new venture.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size was measured quarterly as: (1) sales (using a logarithm) and (2) number of employees.

name: Firm age
definition: Firm age was measured as the number of quarters since a company's incorporation.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["firm growth", "new venture growth", "growth in size", "sales growth", "employee growth"]
definition: Beyond the absolute effects of size, the effects of change in size-firm growth-are also critically important determinants of founder departure. Firm growth was measured as both employee growth and sales growth.

name: Founder ownership
definition: Founder ownership was assessed as the proportion of total firm ownership held by the founders of a company.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Ownership concentration was the proportion of ownership held by the top four owners of a firm.

name: Board insiders
authors_terms: ["board insiders", "proportion of inside board members", "board composition", "inside directors"]
definition: Board insiders was the proportion of board members on who were employed by the firm. Founders of firms with higher proportions of inside directors may maintain more power and be less likely to depart.

name: R&D functional responsibility
definition: Research and development was coded as a dummy variable if the founder's primary responsibilities in the new venture were in research and development.

name: Industry experience
authors_terms: ["industry experience", "years of employment in the semiconductor industry"]
definition: Industry experience was a founder's number of years of employment in the semiconductor industry prior to founding the new venture.

name: Chief executive
definition: Chief executive was a dummy variable coded 1 for each founder who was the chief executive.

name: Organizational atypicality
authors_terms: ["organizational atypicality", "fund typicality versus atypicality", "atypical fund", "atypical organizations", "typical organizations"]
definition: Variations in the extent to which an organization conforms to the norms and expectations of a known organizational category. Atypical funds are 'funds that were members of a known market category but deviated from the prototypical fund in that category with respect to certain organizational features and trading strategies.'

name: Nonconforming referent selection
authors_terms: ["reference group selection", "strategic reference group selection", "referent selection", "nonconforming referents", "alternative referent"]
definition: The selection of the referent against which a focal organization is evaluated, where nonconforming referents are those that 'deviate from expected benchmarks.' Reference groups refer to 'sets of organizations, benchmarks, or indexes against which a focal organization is compared.'

name: Evaluator commitment
authors_terms: ["feelings of commitment", "commitment", "ex ante sentiment", "sense of attachment"]
definition: In ways comparable to the well-known endowment effect in psychology and behavioral economics (Kahneman et al. 1990), feelings of commitment reflect an evaluator's sense of attachment to an organization.

name: Fund performance
definition: The performance outcome of the organization being evaluated; at random, participants were assigned to one of five returns outcomes ranging from a high two-year net return of 27.23% to a low two-year net return of 4.67%.

name: Performance evaluation
authors_terms: ["performance evaluation", "Evaluation", "enhancing evaluations", "evaluations of the organization's performance"]
definition: Evaluators' assessment of an organization's performance; reference groups are important because they facilitate performance evaluation that in turn motivates subsequent action. Enhancing evaluations are evaluations that portray performance in a more positive light.

name: Past performance
definition: A series of past, positive performance outcomes. The authors note that 'when we use terms such as "success," "past success," or "history of success" in this article, we refer to a series of past, positive performance outcomes.'

name: Strategic persistence
authors_terms: ["strategic persistence", "persistence with past strategies", "persistence with old strategies", "persistence with the current strategy"]
definition: Following Finkelstein and Hambrick (1990), the authors define strategic persistence as the extent to which a firm's strategic profile remained stable over time, measured by the stability of financial and operational ratios that express the strategic position of a company.

name: Change in performance
authors_terms: ["change in performance after the environmental change", "reduction in performance", "performance decline"]
definition: Performance in the five years after the deregulation calculated with the same measure used for past performance, from which performance before deregulation was subtracted to compute a difference measure.

name: Satisfaction with performance
authors_terms: ["satisfaction", "satisfaction with performance", "satisfaction with the current level of performance"]
definition: When people succeed in attaining their objectives or values, they experience satisfaction, which the authors view, drawing on Locke and Latham (1990), as an affective response based on a subconscious value appraisal.

name: Confidence in current strategies
authors_terms: ["confidence in the effectiveness of the current strategies", "belief in current strategies", "beliefs in current strategies"]
definition: Following success, individuals develop beliefs regarding cause-effect relationships, including conclusions about what particular task strategies are effective in performance; successful individuals can become confident about the effectiveness of their actions and treat their beliefs about strategy-performance links as fact.

name: Self-efficacy
definition: In social cognitive theory, task-specific confidence is known as self-efficacy, the perception of one's capabilities to attain performance outcomes.

name: Goal level
definition: Previous research indicates that, following success, people tend to raise their goals, because individuals assume that they have learned from successful experiences and, as a result, perceive themselves as capable of additional improvement.

name: Amount of information sought
authors_terms: ["amount of information sought", "total information", "amount of information acquired", "information seeking"]
definition: The amount of information strategic decision makers acquire; individuals' motivation to seek information depends on the value they place on additional information, and noticing changes in an environment depends, in part, on the amount of information sought.

name: Information sought from favorable sources
authors_terms: ["favorable information", "information from favorable sources", "information acquired from favorable sources"]
definition: The amount of information sought from executives who had been supportive in the past.

name: Information sought from unfavorable sources
authors_terms: ["unfavorable information", "information from unfavorable sources", "information acquired from unfavorable sources"]
definition: The amount of information sought from executives who had been critical in the past.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "CEO/board power", "balance of power on the board"]
definition: The authors treat power as central to understanding the conflicts that occur between managers and boards, and describe CEO power as the inverse of board power. CEO power is treated as multidimensional, captured with an index of multiple measures.

name: Director power
definition: Director power reflects an individual's relative standing on the board as well as his or her value on the market for corporate directors.

name: Lead independent director appointment
authors_terms: ["lead independent director", "lead independent director appointment", "lead director"]
definition: The lead independent director is a compromise board leadership structure that preserves combined CEO and board chair positions while appointing an independent board member to a designated leadership position. It is described as a middle-of-the-road option between CEO duality and CEO–board chair separation.

name: CEO–board chair separation
authors_terms: ["separation of CEO and board chair positions", "CEO–board chair separation", "CEO–chair separation"]
definition: A board leadership structure in which the CEO and board chair positions are held by separate individuals; if the CEO and board chair are separate, the firm benefits from independent oversight but lacks clear hierarchical leadership. Separation captures whether another individual besides the CEO is appointed board chair.

name: Lead independent director selection
authors_terms: ["lead independent director appointment", "likelihood that the director is chosen as lead independent director", "chosen as lead independent director"]
definition: The choice of which independent director on the board is selected to serve in the lead independent director position, made once a board has decided to create the position.

name: Firm performance
definition: Following prior research in board leadership, the authors operationalize firm performance in a number of different ways.

name: Social capital
definition: Social capital is a means of enforcing norms of behavior among individual or corporate actors and thus acts as a constraint, as well as a resource. In a complex network, the degree of social capital available to a firm is determined by its position in the network structure.

name: Change in social capital
authors_terms: ["change in social capital", "increase in social capital", "increasing social capital"]
definition: The increase in the social capital available to a firm over a time period. The amount of social capital that can be increased by new relationships is related to the base amount, and if a group's contribution to network structure increases with new relationships, the authors assume that startups have chosen partners so that social capital is increased.

name: New cooperative relationships
authors_terms: ["new relationships", "relationships with new partners", "new startup relationships", "relationships with entering partners", "relationships with incumbent partners"]
definition: Network formation proceeds through the establishment of new relationships, building on the base of existing interfirm ties. Relationships are counted separately for partners entering the network and partners already in the network.

name: Presuccession performance context
definition: Previous research has suggested that the performance of an organization before a leader's replacement is an important contextual factor. In this study the performance context of firms at the time of the succession events was approximated by cumulating their excess returns over 200 trading days beginning 300 trading days before the first public announcement of the executive change.

name: Successor origin
definition: Previous research has supported the existence of a linkage between the origin of a successor and firm performance. An insider was designated as a successor who had at least five years of tenure with the firm in question and an outsider as a successor who had not been with the organization for more than one year before moving to the top.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: Capital market measures assess the influence of an event on a firm's security by estimating the normal, or expected, return to the stock in the absence of an event; the abnormal, or unexpected, return to the stock is the difference between its observed return and its expected return. Theoretically, abnormal returns represent an unbiased estimate of investors' evaluation of the changes in future earnings that they expect because of some firm-specific event, such as a change in leadership.

name: Slack resources
definition: Slack is potentially utilizable resources that can be diverted or redeployed for the achievement of organizational goals. Slack provides the cushion of actual or potential resources that allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal pressures for change in policy as well as to initiate changes in strategy.

name: High-discretion slack
definition: Slack resources at the high end of the continuum of managerial discretion: unabsorbed slack, which provides managers greater flexibility in their strategic options, with cash and receivables as examples of high-discretion financial resources.

name: Low-discretion slack
definition: Slack resources at the low end of the continuum of managerial discretion: absorbed slack, or excess costs in specialized assets, which provides less flexibility to managers and their strategic options, with debt, fixed assets, and excess capacity as examples.

name: Resource availability
definition: One of the two components of transient slack, capturing the resource availability side of the availability-demand distinction; resource availability was the permanent capital of a firm (i.e., owner's equity plus debt) less fixed assets and other noncurrent assets.

name: Resource demand
definition: One of the two components of transient slack, capturing the resource demand side of the availability-demand distinction; resource demand was an estimate of cash required (five days worth of sales) plus accounts receivable and inventory less accounts payable.

name: Financial performance
definition: The financial performance of the firm; performance was gross profit, calculated as revenues less the cost of goods sold, which the authors describe as a good indicator of profitability and as correlated with net income and with net worth.

name: Firm age
definition: Age is an important moderator of the effectiveness with which firms deploy resources; some firms are created with substantial resource endowments while others are disadvantaged at founding and are born out of scarcity. Firm age was measured as years since incorporation.

name: Industry complexity
definition: Industry complexity refers to the competition in an industry that stems from concentration, or the market share dominance of one or more firms.

name: Preference-decreased technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities that are well aligned with preshock demand conditions but that decline with respect to customer preferences postshock.

name: Preference-increased technological capabilities
definition: Technological capabilities that are less preferred by customers before the shock but that gain with respect to customer preferences postshock.

name: Customer relationship depth
authors_terms: ["repeated customer proportion", "customer-related capabilities", "downstream customer capabilities", "deeper customer relationships"]
definition: A firm's stock of customer-related capabilities is formed over time through its prior interactions with customers; deeper customer relationships are formed through repeated interactions with the same customer. It can be captured by the firm's repeated customer proportion, the proportion of existing customers with which the firm has repeated relationships within its overall portfolio of customers.

name: Extension-based adaptation
definition: A path in which firms modify and extend their existing technologies in a way that allows them to generate a better fit between their existing capabilities and the new demand environment.

name: Novelty-based adaptation
definition: A path in which a firm develops completely novel products and technologies that are well aligned with the new customer preferences.

name: Spinout status
definition: Spinouts are new firms founded by employees of established firms, especially in the same industry as their employer; incumbent new establishments are the new establishments of incumbent firms in their industries.

name: Parent financial resource availability
authors_terms: ["parent financial resource availability", "parent size", "greater financial resources"]
definition: Parents with greater financial resources are likely to have larger budgets; hence, such parents can choose more (and larger) projects for internal implementation.

name: Parent resource redeployment opportunities
authors_terms: ["parent firm resource redeployment opportunities", "parent number of industries", "resource redeployability", "redeployment opportunities"]
definition: Parent firms can redeploy resources from their new ventures to other parts of their operations if needed. This is especially true for diversified parents, as they have greater redeployment opportunities across industries.

name: Investment requirements
definition: Higher investment requirements increase the threshold of expected performance required to form a new venture (of any kind). Capital-intensive industries require large investments in physical capital, and industry capital intensity has been widely considered as an entry barrier.

name: New venture size
definition: Size is defined as the logarithm of the number of employees at the new venture.

name: New venture survival
definition: Survival is defined as a dummy indicating whether the new venture survived to a given age.

name: Connections with complementary technologies
authors_terms: ["complementary technologies", "connections with complementary technologies", "ecosystem-level complementary technologies"]
definition: An app's connections with complementary technologies is based on the number of complementary technologies that the focal app is connected to in the iPhone ecosystem, including complementary technologies provided by Apple and those provided by other firms participating in the iOS ecosystem.

name: Ecosystem-specific complementary technologies
definition: We consider a complementary technology to be specialized to an ecosystem if it is uniquely available to the innovations participating in the focal ecosystem and contributing to the focal value proposition. Ecosystem-specific complementary technologies are fine-tuned to the focal ecosystem's architecture and can generate unique complementarities in the ecosystem.

name: Ecosystem-generic complementary technologies
authors_terms: ["ecosystem-generic complementary technologies", "complementary technologies that are available across multiple ecosystems"]
definition: Some complementary technologies have broad applicability and can span multiple ecosystems, whereas others tend to be much more specific to an ecosystem; we refer to the former complementary technology as ecosystem-generic and the latter as ecosystem-specific complementary technology. A complementary technology is considered ecosystem-generic if it is also available in the Android ecosystem.

name: Architectural newness of the ecosystem
authors_terms: ["architectural newness", "architectural change", "new generations of the core module"]
definition: The evolution of core modules, such as the introduction of new generations, can also represent an instance of architectural newness within the ecosystem - it changes the interaction between modules while keeping the core design concepts and associated knowledge intact. The variable, architectural newness, is the number of months between the observation month and the month in which the latest generation of the iOS was launched.

name: Commercialization success
definition: We consider innovation as the commercialization (bringing to market) of invention(s), and commercialization success based on the economic outcomes of an innovation to the focal innovator. We measured the successful commercialization of innovation by examining whether the focal app made it to the Top 500 apps list by revenue.

name: Alliance partner overlap
authors_terms: ["spinout–parent alliance partner overlap", "alliance partner overlap", "partner overlap"]
definition: The degree to which employee spinouts and their parent firms have common alliance partners. The authors examine the antecedents of spinout–parent alliance partner overlap.

name: Technological cumulativeness
definition: The degree to which a spinout's new technologies build on its parent's technologies (the parent's technological lineage).

name: Product market overlap
definition: The degree to which an employee spinout competes in the same markets as its parent firm.

name: NPO channel
authors_terms: ["NPO channel", "NPO channeling", "channeling aid through NPOs", "channeling company aid through an NPO", "NPO mode"]
definition: A governance mode that involves donating aid to an international humanitarian organization that acts as the vehicle for allocating the aid to beneficiaries. The NPO assumes the role of managing the donation and ensuring that it reaches beneficiaries.

name: Magnitude of corporate disaster giving
authors_terms: ["magnitude of corporate disaster giving", "magnitude of company giving", "donation amount", "size of the donation", "disbursements of corporate aid"]
definition: The size of a firm's donation in response to a disaster, which depends on the perceived availability of alternative modes for aid allocation. This is the magnitude of corporate giving that each governance mode can deliver.

name: Local operations
authors_terms: ["local operations", "firms' local operations", "local market presence", "local presence", "local operations in the disaster-stricken country"]
definition: Whether a firm operated in the affected country at the time of disaster, that is, whether the firm has an affiliate in the focal country. Having a local market presence may help firms overcome the challenges of delivering aid by bringing their commercial assets and experience to bear.

name: Formal institutional development
authors_terms: ["formal institutional development", "institutional development", "level of national institutional development", "level of formal institutional development", "quality of national institutions"]
definition: The level of a disaster-stricken country's formal institutional development, i.e., the quality of its national institutions, which shapes the quality of formal institutions and resulting support systems for disaster response.

name: Organization status in the field
definition: Actors' position within the field of the NHS (i.e., center versus periphery), which is largely determined by the status of the organization to which they belong. In the NHS, PCTs are lower-status organizations compared with hospitals and administrative organizations.

name: Professional group status in the field
definition: Actors' position within the field of the NHS (i.e., center versus periphery), which is largely determined by the status of the professional group to which they belong. Two professional group statuses are represented in the NHS: physicians, who are of higher status, and other health-care professionals, who are of lower status.

name: Hierarchical position in the organization
authors_terms: ["hierarchical position", "position in the organizational hierarchy", "position in the organization"]
definition: Actors' position within their organization, which is largely dependent on their position in the organizational hierarchy; as actors get higher in the hierarchy, their access to resources, authority, and sense of power increase.

name: Divergence from institutionalized role division among organizations
authors_terms: ["changes that diverge from the institutionalized model of role division among organizations", "divergence from the institutionalized model of organizations' role division"]
definition: The degree to which a change project diverges from the institutionalized model of medical professionalism on the dimension of the institutionalized division of organizational roles, in which hospitals have traditionally dominated.

name: Divergence from institutionalized role division among professionals
authors_terms: ["changes that diverge from the institutionalized model of role division among professionals", "divergence from the institutionalized model of professionals' role division"]
definition: The degree to which a change project diverges from the institutionalized model of medical professionalism on the dimension of the institutionalized division of professional roles, in which physicians have traditionally dominated.

name: Inventor knowledge quality
authors_terms: ["quality", "quality of the inventor's set of knowledge", "quality of the inventor's work"]
definition: The contribution of an innovation to technological progress is referred to as its quality. High-quality innovations are backed by highly relevant scientific knowledge and have high expected economic value.

name: Knowledge complementarity
authors_terms: ["complementarity", "degree of complementarity of the inventor's know-how", "complementary knowledge"]
definition: An inventor's knowledge is complementary to that of other researchers if the former needs to be combined with the latter to develop its full potential value.

name: Core expertise
authors_terms: ["core expertise", "expertise in the firm's core areas", "Core"]
definition: The core of an innovative firm comprises technological areas typically associated with the firm's comparative advantage, in which innovative activity is especially intensive. Core expertise is the extent to which the inventor's patents fall within the firm's core areas.

name: Technological dominance
definition: An innovative firm has a dominant position in a technological field when it accounts for a high portion of the new technology created in that field.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: An employer shift by a change in the assignee of the patent in which the inventor appears; the inventor is observed in a sequence of discrete time points that correspond to his patent filings.

name: Order of entry
authors_terms: ["order of entry", "intra-market order of entry", "first entrant", "early follower", "later entrant"]
definition: The intra-market order of entry: order of entry takes a value of 1 for the first entrant to a market, 2 for an early follower (second or third entrant), and 3 for a later entrant (fourth entrant and up).

name: Market entry lag
definition: The time from product development, 1962, to the first-entry into a market, measured by the log of the time in years; negative coefficients denote earlier entry.

name: Market size
authors_terms: ["market size", "market need", "market reserves", "larger market needs and potentials"]
definition: Market size is measured by two indicators, population reflecting oil need (MARKET NEED), and expected offshore oil reserves from geophysical surveys reflecting potential oil exploration prospects (MARKET RESERVES).

name: Market development
definition: A country's literacy rate is used as an indicator of educational and infrastructural development (MARKET DEVELOPMENT).

name: Central planning
definition: Dealings with centrally planned economies often involve bureaucratic negotiations and extensive documentation, raising transfer costs and delaying market entry. Centralization also reduces sensitivity to new ideas which are filtered out in communication up the hierarchy.

name: Multinational incumbents
authors_terms: ["multinational incumbents", "incumbent MNCs", "market incumbents with rigs in more than one country"]
definition: Earlier entry should occur when there are many multinational incumbents, which can quickly enter with their internal transfer skills and ability to cross-subsidize entry with their overseas operations.

name: Simultaneous entry into multiple markets
authors_terms: ["simultaneous entry", "SIMULTANEOUS ENTRY", "multiple market entries", "multiple first entries"]
definition: Entry into multiple smaller markets in a single year, which can produce minimum scale economies and justifies entry earlier than if these potential markets had been evaluated and approached separately.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured by the number of rigs in an entrant's fleet at the time of entry.

name: Firm multinationality
definition: Multinational firm is a dummy variable equal to 1 if an entrant had rigs in more than one country at the time of entry, 0 otherwise.

name: Market incumbency
definition: Market incumbent is measured by a dummy variable equal to 1 if an entrant was an incumbent in the local market with other than semi-submersible rigs at the time of entry, 0 otherwise. Local market incumbents are more likely to be early followers and later entrants than first entrants.

name: Long-term market share
definition: Long-term market share is measured by the proportion of all semi-submersible rigs in a market operated by an entrant; an average market share of years 9 to 11 was used to control for market duration and annual market share instability.

name: Entrant survival
definition: Entrant life is the number of years between a firm's entry and withdrawal from a market; entrants surviving after 1984 were censored due to the end of the study period.

name: Early pioneer status
definition: The first three pioneers overall (Odeco, Sedco, and Santa Fe); EARLY PIONEER is a dummy variable set to 1 if an entrant was Odeco, Santa Fe, or Sedco, 0 otherwise.

name: Market localization pressures
definition: The extent to which markets experience growing pressures to localize operations, as referenced in the statement 'markets with growing localization pressures'.

name: CEO equity risk bearing
authors_terms: ["equity risk bearing", "CEO equity risk bearing", "equity wealth-at-risk"]
definition: Risk bearing is defined as the perceived wealth-at-risk of loss in the event of failed risk taking; equity risk bearing is the equity wealth component of their firm-specific wealth.

name: Strategic risk taking
authors_terms: ["strategic risk taking", "risk taking on behalf of the firm", "strategic risk decisions"]
definition: The risk the CEO takes on behalf of the firm is captured by a composite of long-term debt, R&D spending and capital expenditures; this variable is positively related to CEO strategic risk taking on behalf of the firm.

name: CEO conscientiousness
definition: Conscientiousness describes two important aspects of personality: achievement orientation and dependability. Conscientious individuals are seen as dependable, following established rules and obeying norms, making them reliable and responsible.

name: CEO neuroticism
definition: Neuroticism reflects the adaptability of individuals to different situational demands; more neurotic individuals are also described as less emotionally stable and less adaptable, meaning they are less likely to remain calm when having to adapt to new situations.

name: CEO extraversion
definition: Extraversion is grounded in the work by Eysenck (1973) who broadly conceptualize this personality dimension as a need for stimulation. Following this definition, Hogan (1986) suggests that extraversion captures individuals' ambition (reflected in traits such as surgency, excitement seeking, or assertiveness) and sociability.

name: CEO openness to experience
definition: Individuals that score high on openness to experience are best characterized as 'original, imaginative, having broad interests, and daring'. Open leaders are more receptive to new experiences such as new feelings, thoughts, perspectives, and ideas.

name: Product upgrading
definition: A particular form of innovation in which firms focus on the creation of new products of higher value by incrementally experimenting with new combinations of knowledge, materials, and natural resources.

name: Overall network embeddedness
definition: Ties to all alters, the count of a firm's ties to all the types of organizations and institutions mentioned above, captured the overall embeddedness of the firm, assuming homogeneity of alter types in knowledge resources afforded.

name: Ties to firms
definition: Degree centrality captures a focal firm's exposure to alters' knowledge and immediate influence by counting its total number of ties to other organizations and institutions; ties to firms counts the number of ties between the focal firm and firm alters such as wineries, independent grape growers, and technology suppliers.

name: Ties to government support institutions
authors_terms: ["ties to GSIs", "ties to government support institutions"]
definition: A government support institution is any institution that receives at least partial government funding, has government actors participating in its governance and program evaluation, and provides firms with specific services; ties to GSIs counts a focal firm's ties to such institutions.

name: Ties to associations, banks, cooperatives, and schools
authors_terms: ["ties to associations, banks, cooperatives, and schools", "ties to all alters except firms and GSIs"]
definition: The number of ties a focal firm has to nonfirm alters other than GSIs: associations (trade, peak level, etc.), banks, cooperatives, and schools (universities, technical schools, etc.). The authors expected that firms would not necessarily benefit from ties to organizations that offer limited knowledge resources and rather local professional relationships.

name: Ties to public-private institutions
definition: A subgroup of GSIs that are constituted with rules of empowered inclusion and multiparty governance, whereby participants representing the government and a variety of relevant stakeholder groups have rights and responsibilities in defining and evaluating industry support programs; their governance principles foster multiplex, cross-cutting ties among previously isolated public and private actors.

name: Ties to old government support institutions
definition: Old GSIs are all GSIs other than the public-private institutions, which predated them and differed in their governance, having governance centered in the state and bureaucracy and only ad hoc contact with a few elite groups.

name: Ties to firms with high network centrality
authors_terms: ["ties to top central firms", "ties to most central firms"]
definition: The total number of ties a focal firm has to firm alters that rank in the top decile of in-degree centrality, capturing the benefits a firm could obtain indirectly from being connected to alters with high centrality and therefore exposure to the influence and resources of a large number of network actors.

name: Ties to government support institutions with high network centrality
authors_terms: ["ties to top central GSIs", "ties to most central GSIs"]
definition: The total number of ties a focal firm has to GSI alters ranked in the top decile of in-degree centrality, capturing indirect exposure to the influence and resources of a large number of network actors.

name: Ties to firms with high geographic diversity
authors_terms: ["ties to top geographically diverse firms", "ties to most geographically diverse firms"]
definition: The total number of ties a focal firm has to firm alters ranked in the top decile on geographic diversity of their own connections, using geographic zones as proxies for different bodies of knowledge.

name: Ties to government support institutions with high geographic diversity
authors_terms: ["ties to top geographically diverse GSIs", "ties to most geographically diverse GSIs"]
definition: The total number of ties a focal firm has to GSI alters ranked in the top decile on geographic diversity of their own connections, using geographic zones as proxies for different bodies of knowledge.

name: IJV board involvement
authors_terms: ["IJV board involvement", "board involvement", "involvement by IJV boards"]
definition: We define IJV board involvement as the extent to which the board is engaged in controlling and coordinating an international joint venture's activities on behalf of the parent firms.

name: Partner market overlap
authors_terms: ["Market overlap", "overlap in the end markets of parent firms", "overlap in partners' markets served", "partner competition"]
definition: Overlap in the end markets of parent firms, i.e., the degree to which the firms operate in similar product markets, geographic markets, and customer segments. Such overlap is argued to create conflicting interests and a need to coordinate the venture's actions.

name: R&D activities
definition: Joint ventures that involve collaborative research and development activities, in which intangible assets such as R&D are exchanged and created and partners' rights and obligations are hard to delineate ex ante.

name: Cultural distance
definition: National cultural differences between parent firms, measured as the average distance between the parent firms' home countries based on an aggregate composite index of national culture dimensions.

name: Host-country environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["Environmental uncertainty in the host country", "environmental uncertainty"]
definition: Unpredictability of the host market in which an IJV is situated, characterized by changes in host government policies and regulations, customer demand, local supply conditions, and so forth, which make it difficult for boards to control and coordinate the venture.

name: Firm-specific uncertainty
definition: Firm-specific uncertainty can stem from a variety of sources, but the key underlying dimension is that these sources produce uncertainty that is unique and often internal to the firm. We propose that one key dimension underlying many uncertainty studies is the level of the uncertainty, i.e., whether it is firm specific or market based.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: If firm-specific uncertainty is largely internal, controllable, and unique, market uncertainty is external and shared across a set of firms. Market risk, because it is systematic, cannot be controlled and is independent of what happens at the firm level.

name: Network broadening
authors_terms: ["broadening", "broaden its alliance network", "broaden its interlock network"]
definition: Forming new relationships with new partners is a form of exploration, where firms expand their knowledge and access to resources through new network partners. The greater the uncertainty that a firm faces alone, the more likely that firm will broaden its set of ties by establishing ties with organizations that it has not had ties with in the past.

name: Network reinforcing
definition: Forming additional relationships with existing partners is a form of exploitation, where firms extend their existing knowledge base with existing partners. Reinforcing an existing network allows firms to strengthen, deepen, and exploit ties that already exist.

name: Network multiplexity
definition: Firms may add relationships of a different type with an existing partner, e.g., adding an alliance when an officer of that firm is already on the board. This latter form of reinforcing is analogous to the concept of relationship multiplexity in the network literature, where multiplexity is defined as two or more different types of relationships occurring together.

name: Governance mode
definition: In autonomous governance, firms undertake a business venture by incurring all costs and risks and concentrate all decision making authority; in collaborative governance, firms share costs, risks, and decision making authority with another firm or set of firms. We focus on horizontal collaboration, that is collaboration between two or more incumbents of the same industry.

name: Governance fit
definition: Governance fit refers to the extent to which the chosen governance mode is appropriate, given the focal firm's resource endowment and the venture's resource requirements, and accounting for exchange hazards.

name: Unit sales
definition: Unit Sales is the cumulative number of units produced over the life cycle of the aircraft.

name: Time-to-market
definition: Time-to-Market is the number of years between the prototype first flight and the first delivery of a production aircraft.

name: Price of the firm's product
authors_terms: ["exogenous increase in the price of the firm's product", "price", "exogenous shock to the price of the firm's product", "price per ton of ore mined"]
definition: A price per ton of ore mined, specific to each mine-year, which reflects the exogenous shock to the price of the output that each mine experienced during the period under study. It is computed by multiplying the average quantity of each mineral found per ton of rock mined by its international price.

name: Value appropriated by employees
authors_terms: ["value appropriated by employees", "value captured by employees", "average earnings", "employee compensation"]
definition: The value captured by employees, understood as the compensation they receive from the firm; an employee appropriates more value when she receives higher compensation for a similar amount of work. The difference between an employee's marginal product and his or her outside option defines a range that contains all the potentially acceptable payoffs, and the exact payoff depends on that range and bargaining ability.

name: Centralization of wage bargaining
definition: Collective action refers to the possibility of joint negotiations with employers; the wage bargaining process can be centralized (e.g., at the industry level) or conducted independently by each firm. A high value of wage decentralization implies a more decentralized negotiation process.

name: Flexibility of hiring and firing regulations
authors_terms: ["flexibility of hiring and firing", "regulations on hiring and firing"]
definition: Employment laws regulate the flexibility of hiring and firing policies; more flexibility favors easier hiring and dismissals, while less flexibility usually implies higher costs of hiring and firing, including higher severance payments and mandatory penalties. The variable measures the flexibility of companies to hire and to fire workers, where a higher value implies more flexibility.

name: Pay for performance
definition: Employment laws deal with the regulation of alternatives to standard labor contracts, one of which is the possibility of adjusting contracts to allow payments to vary according to the performance of the employee. A higher value of the pay and productivity variable implies that wages are more closely correlated with worker productivity.

name: State ownership
definition: SOEs are companies over which the state has significant control through full, majority, or significant minority ownership. The measure is a continuous variable where a higher value indicates more state ownership, computed as the total direct and indirect participation of a state in a mine.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Firms can have diluted or concentrated ownership, and large shareholders (usually associated with higher ownership concentration) have the power to monitor managers and influence them. A higher HHI value implies higher ownership concentration.

name: Knowledge creation
authors_terms: ["knowledge creation", "new knowledge creation", "level of knowledge created", "amount of knowledge created"]
definition: Knowledge creation involves the generation of facts, relationships, and insights that are new to the existing body of knowledge. Thus, new knowledge is not held by anyone prior to its creation and therefore is not subject to transfer.

name: Average tie strength
definition: Average tie strength captures the frequency of interactions between a knowledge worker and his or her direct exchange partners. Average tie strength derives from the amount of time spent and the emotional closeness of a relationship.

name: Ego network density
definition: Network density provides insights about the resources a researcher might obtain through exchange partners as well as potential constraints that the network might impose. In this context, a dense network is one in which many of a knowledge worker's direct exchange partners have direct ties to each other.

name: Negative earnings surprise
authors_terms: ["negative earnings surprise", "rival's negative earnings surprise", "rival negative earnings surprise"]
definition: Earnings surprises refer to deviations in a firm's realized earnings from security analysts' consensus estimates. A negative earnings surprise occurs when a publicly traded firm announces earnings less than the consensus forecast of security analysts.

name: Positive earnings surprise
definition: Positive earnings surprises occur when the earnings surpass estimates. Defined symmetrically to negative earnings surprises, the rival positive earnings surprise equals the absolute value of the difference between the rival firm's actual earnings and analysts' consensus estimates.

name: Competitive action intensity
authors_terms: ["competitive action intensity", "intensity of competitive actions", "firm action intensity", "intensity of tactical actions"]
definition: By competitive action intensity, we refer to the total volume of competitive actions a focal firm initiates against its rival in a given time period (Ferrier, Smith, & Grimm, 1999). Competitive action refers to externally directed, specific, and observable moves by a firm to enhance its competitive position.

name: Language complexity
authors_terms: ["complex language", "language complexity", "complexity of a rival's language", "rival complex language"]
definition: Complex language refers to the use of many different and connected words and sentences to make the content of the communication difficult to understand. It often includes the use of inflated vocabulary, excessive wordiness, and long-winded sentences with multiple subordinate clauses and prepositional phrases.

name: Language vagueness
authors_terms: ["vague language", "vagueness of a rival's language", "language vagueness", "rival vague language"]
definition: Vague language refers to the use of linguistic devices to make the meaning of communication nonspecific and imprecise. It includes, for example, the use of qualifiers before numbers (e.g., about, around, nearly) and the use of approximation terms (e.g., may, could be, perhaps).

name: Total quality management adoption
authors_terms: ["TQM", "Total Quality Management", "TQM firms", "TQM adoption", "quality program", "significant commitment to Total Quality Management"]
definition: TQM is an integrated management philosophy and set of practices that emphasizes, among other things, continuous improvement, meeting customers' requirements, reducing rework, longrange thinking, increased employee involvement and teamwork, process redesign, competitive benchmarking, team-based problem-solving, constant measurement of results, and closer relationships with suppliers.

name: Time since TQM adoption
authors_terms: ["years since adoption", "years since TQM adoption", "long-term TQM firms", "short-term TQM firms"]
definition: A central notion in TQM training and literature concerns the need to adopt longer time horizons, and the expectation that TQM programs will not produce short-term bottom-line results.

name: Industry
definition: The sector in which the firm competes; since TQM originally emerged from manufacturing environments, and because TQM remains more widely disseminated among manufacturers, manufacturing adopters are expected to outperform service adopters.

name: Firm performance
definition: Overall financial performance was measured subjectively, addressing profitability, sales growth, and overall financial performance. TQM performance was assessed separately and measures satisfaction with the TQM program.

name: Executive commitment
definition: Committed leadership: a near-evangelical, unwavering, long-term commitment by top managers to the philosophy, usually under a name something like Total Quality Management, Continuous Improvement (CI), or Quality Improvement (QI).

name: Adoption and communication of TQM
authors_terms: ["adoption and communication of TQM", "adopting the philosophy"]
definition: Adoption and communication of TQM: using tools like the mission statement, and themes or slogans.

name: Customer relationships
definition: Closer customer relationships: determining customers' (both inside and outside the firm) requirements, then meeting those requirements no matter what it takes.

name: Supplier relationships
definition: Closer supplier relationships: working closely and cooperatively with suppliers (often sole-sourcing key components), ensuring they provide inputs that conform to customers' end-use requirements.

name: Benchmarking
definition: Benchmarking: researching and observing best competitive practices.

name: Training
definition: Increased training: usually includes TQM principles, team skills, and problem-solving.

name: Open organization
definition: Open organization: lean staff, empowered work teams, open horizontal communications, and a relaxation of traditional hierarchy.

name: Employee empowerment
definition: Employee empowerment: increased employee involvement in design and planning, and greater autonomy in decision-making.

name: Zero-defects mentality
definition: Zero-defects mentality: a system in place to spot defects as they occur, rather than through inspection and rework.

name: Flexible manufacturing
definition: Flexible manufacturing (applicable only to manufacturers) can include just-in-time inventory, cellular manufacturing, design for manufacturability (DFM), statistical process control (SPC), and design of experiments (DOE).

name: Process improvement
definition: Process improvement: reduced waste and cycle times in all areas through crossdepartmental process analysis.

name: Measurement
definition: Measurement: goal-orientation and zeal for data, with constant performance measurement, often using statistical methods.

name: Value creation from alliance formation
authors_terms: ["the value a firm derives from a new horizontal alliance formation", "cumulative abnormal stock market return (CAR)", "value created on the alliance portfolio level"]
definition: To operationalize the dependent variable, that is, the cumulative abnormal stock market return (CAR), we followed a multi-country setting event study approach.

name: Network resource synergy potential
authors_terms: ["Network resource synergy potential", "the new alliance's potential to create synergistic combinations of new and existing network resources", "synergistic resource alignment"]
definition: A new alliance's potential to create value on the alliance portfolio level—that is, value above and beyond the value created by resource combinations on the single alliance level—is driven by the extent of the synergistic combinations between new network resources accessed through the new alliance and existing network resources accessed through alliances in the focal firm's alliance portfolio.

name: Partner resource substitutability
definition: A new alliance's potential to create resource combinations that substitute resource combinations of existing partners is a function of the extent to which a new alliance allows the focal firm to serve city-pair markets that are also served by existing partners and, thus, increases the market domain overlap between the two firms.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "R&D intensity (investments in R&D per sales dollar)"]
definition: R&D intensity is the proportion of sales revenues spent on R&D; it is measured as reported investments in R&D per sales dollar.

name: Market share improvement
authors_terms: ["% improvement in market share", "percentage change in market share", "increases in market share", "improvements in market share"]
definition: Changes (improvements) in market share for the principal product of the firm; percentage improvement in market share was found to be significantly correlated with market share in the major product group of the firm or unit.

name: Computerization of manufacturing
definition: Computerization of manufacturing was measured with a constructed summed scale consisting of answers from two items on the mailed questionnaire: the general level of automation in the plant and the highest level achieved. This measure was called CAM (computer-aided manufacturing) on the questionnaire although it covers cases of integrated, flexible manufacturing systems in the extreme.

name: Manufacturing agility
authors_terms: ["agility", "agility in manufacturing", "% change in agility", "increased manufacturing agility"]
definition: Agility in manufacturing was measured by the average of improvements (percentage) in five areas: speed of product development, on-time deliveries, customer service, manufacturing lead time, and delivery time. Agile firms can respond more quickly to market needs and can enhance the new product introduction process.

name: Distinctiveness
definition: Because distinctiveness entails deviation from the conventional, normal strategies in a category, the prototypical firm is often taken to be the most-average member of the category. Thus, distinctiveness predominantly entails differentiation vis-à-vis average positions.

name: Performance
definition: Revenues are an especially appropriate measure of performance in the creative industries, rather than an indicator of size, as these consist predominantly of small firms and freelancers.

name: Distinctiveness heterogeneity
definition: Distinctiveness heterogeneity, defined as the degree to which firms in a category cluster around a single position, captures the variation in the positions of firms, and represents how common distinctiveness is in the category.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: Concentrated ownership is a vestige of the historic stakeholder-value governance arrangements; in contrast to the United States, ownership among German firms is still very concentrated, and these large blockholders are generally composed of banks, other large companies, and founding families.

name: Stock-based incentive plan adoption
authors_terms: ["stock-based incentive plans", "stock-based incentives", "stock-based pay", "stock option plans"]
definition: Stock-based incentive pay is generally added on top of (not in place of) salary and bonus pay. Both stock option plans and phantom-stock incentive plans were coded as stock-based incentive plans.

name: Transparent accounting standard adoption
authors_terms: ["transparent accounting standards", "transparent accounting conventions", "IAS and GAAP accounting standards", "accounting change"]
definition: Both IAS and GAAP require significantly more disclosure than the traditional German HGB accounting rules and have fewer explicit accounting choices; IAS and GAAP are more investor-oriented than HGB accounting conventions.

name: Governance reform
authors_terms: ["governance reform", "corporate governance reform", "governance change", "adoption of governance reform"]
definition: The paper examines the voluntary adoption of corporate governance reform in firms embedded in a relationship-based governance system; the reforms studied are stock plan adoption and accounting change.

name: Corporate divestitures
definition: Divestitures represent a significant form of corporate restructuring and thus result in the reconfiguration of a firm's portfolio of businesses; the use of divestitures is one way that firms can reduce excess diversification.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "subsequent levels of firm performance", "market performance"]
definition: The authors use both market and accounting measures of performance, and all measures of performance are adjusted by industry so that performance is gauged relative to firms facing similar economic and competitive factors.

name: Business strategy similarity of tied-to firms
authors_terms: ["similarity in business strategy between tied-to firms and other firms in their industries", "change in business strategy similarity of tied-to firms", "imitation of business strategy at tied-to firms"]
definition: The extent to which the business strategy of a tied-to firm resembles the business strategies of the other firms in its industry, computed with a measure analogous to the focal-firm business strategy similarity measure and averaged across the focal firm's interlock partners.

name: Business strategy similarity of the focal firm
authors_terms: ["business strategy similarity", "intraindustry imitation", "change in business strategy similarity at the focal firm"]
definition: Intraindustry imitation is manifested by greater or lower strategic similarity between the focal firm and other firms in its industry, after controlling for common industry-level factors; similarity in business strategy was operationalized with a Euclidean distance measure based on key resource allocations across the primary functional areas of the firm.

name: Acquisition activity similarity of tied-to firms
authors_terms: ["similarity in acquisition activity between tied-to firms and other firms in their industries", "change in acquisition activity similarity of tied-to firms"]
definition: The extent to which the acquisition activity of a tied-to firm resembles the acquisition activity of the other firms in its industry, measured with measures that directly parallel the business strategy similarity measures and averaged across the focal firm's interlock partners.

name: Acquisition activity similarity of the focal firm
authors_terms: ["acquisition activity similarity", "change in acquisition activity similarity at the focal firm"]
definition: Similarity between the focal firm and other firms in its industry with respect to acquisition activity, measured with measures that directly parallel the business strategy similarity measures, separately for related and diversified acquisitions.

name: Compensation similarity of tied-to firms
authors_terms: ["compensation similarity between tied-to firms and other firms in their industries", "change in compensation similarity of tied-to firms"]
definition: The extent to which the performance-contingent compensation policy of a tied-to firm resembles that of the other firms in its industry, measured with measures that directly parallel the strategy similarity measures and averaged across the focal firm's interlock partners.

name: Compensation similarity of the focal firm
authors_terms: ["compensation similarity", "change in compensation similarity at the focal firm"]
definition: Similarity between the focal firm and other firms in its industry in the use of performance-contingent compensation, which is a central aspect of executive compensation policy and is measured as the relative use of long-term incentive compensation.

name: Mimetic decision process
authors_terms: ["mimetic script", "mimetic decision process", "imitation of competitors in the decision-making process"]
definition: A decision-making process that involves intraindustry imitation, i.e. the imitation of competitors: for example, obtaining information on policies at competitor firms, comparing those policies with the focal firm's policies, and planning changes to ensure that practices are in line with other firms in the industry. Survey items assessed the extent to which firms have adopted such a mimetic script (a sequence of steps that can lead to similarity to competitors) in different policy domains.

name: Cross-policy similarity of tied-to firms
authors_terms: ["greater similarity on a particular policy dimension between tied-to firms and other firms in their industries", "imitation of competitors on a particular policy dimension by tied-to firms"]
definition: The extent to which tied-to firms resemble the other firms in their industries in their imitation of competitors on a policy dimension (business strategy, acquisition activity, or executive compensation), i.e. similarity between tied-to firms and their industry competitors on that dimension.

name: Cross-policy similarity of the focal firm
authors_terms: ["greater similarity on different policy dimensions between the focal firm and other firms in its industry", "imitation by the focal firm on a different policy dimension"]
definition: The extent to which the focal firm resembles the other firms in its industry on policy dimensions different from the dimension on which its tied-to firms imitate their competitors, i.e. the focal firm's adoption of mimetic processes in multiple policy domains.

name: Ecological uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty caused by firms' dependence on natural resources and changing natural environmental conditions that can disrupt firms' access to those resources.

name: Natural-resource-intensive adaptation
definition: The adoption of practices that draw on resources directly from nature in response to natural stimuli that affect those or other natural resources.

name: Ecological mitigation
definition: Practices that address the underlying causes of natural environmental change and ecological uncertainty.

name: Environmental institutional pressures
definition: The regulatory, normative, and cultural pressures that shape how firms interpret and manage environmental issues.

name: Brand equity
definition: The value of a brand is reflected in brand equity, which is composed of brand awareness (brand recall and recognition) and brand image (favorable and unfavorable brand associations).

name: Human capital
authors_terms: ["human capital", "collective knowledge, skills, and abilities that reside with employees"]
definition: Increases in market performance and financial performance are also related to human capital (Huselid, 1995), which is the collective knowledge, skills, and abilities that reside with employees (Sirmon and Hitt, 2009).

name: Firm value
definition: We measure firm value, our dependent variable, using Tobin's q, cash flow, and cash flow volatility. We apply Tobin's q, cash flow, and cash flow volatility to gauge firm value.

name: Industry type
definition: We first classified industries using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) by referring to codes starting with 3 as manufacturing and services otherwise. Next, we subdivided services into retail (e.g., Best Buy) and services (e.g., US Airways), and we subdivided manufacturing industries into fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG; e.g., Coca-Cola) and consumer durables (e.g., Toyota) (Fischer et al., 2010).

name: Divestiture activity
definition: Business divestiture is the sale of all or part of an operating unit by an ongoing firm, and divestiture activity includes selling all (full divestiture) or portions of (partial divestiture) existing business units.

name: Full divestitures
definition: Full divestitures entail selling, liquidating, or spinning off a complete resource such as a unit or subsidiary of a given business segment.

name: Partial divestitures
definition: Partial divestitures include events where only a portion of the unit, a product line, or plant from an ongoing business unit were sold, liquidated, or spun off.

name: Negative performance gap
authors_terms: ["negative performance gap", "declining performance", "negative historical performance gap"]
definition: A negative performance gap occurs when a firm's performance is lower than that of relevant aspiration levels; it reflects decreasing performance and is measured as the absolute value of the historical aspiration gap when that gap is negative.

name: Positive performance gap
authors_terms: ["positive performance gap", "increasing performance", "positive historical performance gap"]
definition: A positive performance gap occurs when a firm's performance exceeds an aspiration level; it reflects increasing performance and is measured as the value of the historical aspiration gap when that gap is positive.

name: Performance level
authors_terms: ["current performance", "level of performance", "corporate return on assets", "Company ROA"]
definition: The firm's current level of corporate performance, measured as corporate return on assets (ROA); used as a main effect and to test the joint effects of performance level and historical aspiration gap.

name: Aspiration gap
authors_terms: ["aspiration gap", "aspiration gaps", "performance below a social aspiration level", "aspirations"]
definition: Decision makers evaluate outcomes based on historical or social reference points, commonly referred to as aspirations; facing an aspiration gap (being above or below a reference point) influences the intensity and choice of behaviors. It is coded from whether respondents say they are ahead of, level with, or behind the people they consider peers in their chosen field.

name: Collaboration preference
authors_terms: ["collaboration preference", "collaboration propensity", "propensity to collaborate", "preferences to form organizational partnerships"]
definition: The interest individuals express in forming organizational partnerships, measured as their rating of different collaboration scenarios.

name: Networking skills
definition: Self-assessed networking skills, captured by the mean of six items measuring self-assessments of networking skills; it is one dimension of relational capability.

name: Networking openness
definition: Openness to collaborating with network members one does not know well; the authors code every response on knowledge/preference that was above (below) the respective mean as 1 (0) and sum the number of times the actor preference was above the mean while the actor knowledge was below the mean.

name: Network awareness
definition: The authors conceptualize network awareness as how much an individual knows about other KTN members who are active in their focal technological domain.

name: Customer switching costs
authors_terms: ["customer switching costs", "switching costs", "reduction in customer switching costs"]
definition: The costs a customer incurs for changing firms; with high switching costs, customers are bound to buy the advanced version from the same firm that sold them the basic version. High customer switching costs generate a lock-in effect on customers and are treated by prior literature as a source of market power.

name: Basic version price
authors_terms: ["price of the basic version", "equilibrium price of the basic version", "ARPU Prepaid"]
definition: The price firms choose for the basic version of the product in the first period (pb), which they cannot change later. The basic version is a relatively inexpensive variation, with limited features, suitable for budget-constrained customers.

name: Advanced version price
definition: The price firms choose for the advanced version of the product in the second period (pa). The advanced version has more features and appeals to customers as their needs evolve over time.

name: Average market price
definition: The average market price over the two periods, that is, the sum of the equilibrium prices of the basic and advanced versions.

name: Firm profitability
definition: Firms' profitability from selling the basic and the advanced versions of the product; with symmetric constant marginal costs, an increase in the average price always translates into higher profits for firms.

name: Advanced version share
authors_terms: ["share of the advanced version", "share of customers purchasing the advanced version", "share of postpaid subscribers"]
definition: The proportion of customers purchasing the advanced version of the product in the second period.

name: Advanced version differentiation
authors_terms: ["(horizontal) product differentiation in the advanced version market", "differentiation in the advanced version market (Ta)"]
definition: The degree of (horizontal) product differentiation in the advanced version market (Ta), which the authors say is the main source of market power in location models such as Hotelling or Salop. The price effect of removing customer switching costs is larger the more the advanced version market is differentiated.

name: Branch sales performance
authors_terms: ["sales performance", "branch sales performance", "branch-level sales", "percent to goal"]
definition: Branch performance is based on branch-level sales, measured monthly. The actual measure is an index of how well the branch met its sales goal each month and represents the percentage of the branch sales goal that was achieved in a particular month.

name: Employee turnover event
definition: A turnover event occurs when an individual voluntarily or involuntarily leaves a unit; in this study, the term employee refers to workers who are not managers in a branch. The employee turnover event studied is the first employee turnover event during the sample period within each branch.

name: Manager turnover event
definition: Managers have the positional power to structure or revise work schedules, determine staffing levels, and influence collective states and processes, and they comprise the 'strategic core' of the unit. A manager turnover event is therefore the loss of an individual who is central to coordinating and structuring unit activities.

name: Branch interdependence
definition: Interdependence refers to coordination and synchronization of worker interactions; the more interaction required among members, the greater the (usually negative) consequences of turnover. It was measured as branch employees' perceptions that the people they work with cooperate to get the job done and help out when workload is high.

name: Recovery rate
definition: The rate of branch performance change after the turnover event is referred to as the recovery rate. The recovery rate estimates whether post-turnover performance is changing faster or slower than pre-turnover performance.

name: Compensation to minority shareholders
authors_terms: ["compensation", "compensation ratio", "compensation paid by controlling shareholders to minority shareholders", "value given to minority shareholders ex ante"]
definition: Each firm calculated and reported a 'compensation ratio' in its compensation agreement that must be agreed to by controlling and minority shareholders; a higher compensation ratio indicates greater compensation paid by controlling shareholders to minority shareholders.

name: Expected value of future business activities
authors_terms: ["expected returns from the firm's future business operations", "Tobin's Q", "expected value of future business opportunities", "expected value of the firm's business activities in the future"]
definition: Tobin's Q is commonly used to capture the expected value of future business opportunities; a higher Tobin's Q indicates that the firm expects to create higher value from future investments.

name: Financing constraints
definition: The K-Z Index is constructed from a model that predicts the probability that a firm becomes financially constrained based on debts (including bank loans), cash flow, market value, dividends, and cash holding, all scaled by total assets. A higher value of the K-Z Index indicates more severe overall financing constraints faced by the firm.

name: Controlling shareholders' ownership stake
authors_terms: ["ownership benefits", "ownership stake of controlling shareholders", "Nontradables", "proportion of nontradable shares"]
definition: The 'ownership benefits' are reflected in the percentages of shares owned by nontradable shareholders and by tradable shareholders; the ownership percentage determines the proportion of the firm's cash flow value to which each agent is legally entitled. Nontradables refers to the proportion of nontradable shares among all outstanding shares, which is a direct measure of controlling shareholders' ownership benefits.

name: Private benefits of control
authors_terms: ["private benefits", "ability of controlling shareholders to extract private benefits", "Control-cash gap", "private gains", "tunneling"]
definition: Private benefits refer to the 'tunneling' or the expropriation by controlling shareholders at the expense of minority shareholders; above and beyond their ownership gains, controlling shareholders obtain private benefits through tunneling, that is, by illegally expropriating firm value at the expense of minority shareholders.

name: Early-stage R&D disclosures
authors_terms: ["early-stage R&D disclosures", "total early-stage R&D disclosures", "voluntary public R&D disclosures", "voluntary public disclosures"]
definition: Voluntary public disclosures about a firm's independent R&D efforts that occurred between the inception of an R&D project and the initial discovery phase, before a firm began to develop and test new products or services. Total Early-Stage R&D Disclosures equal the sum of Early-Stage R&D Disclosures Excluding Alliances and Alliance Early-Stage R&D Disclosures.

name: Alliance early-stage R&D disclosures
authors_terms: ["alliance early-stage R&D disclosures", "R&D-alliance early-stage disclosures", "early-stage R&D alliance disclosures"]
definition: Early-stage R&D disclosures that involve the focal firm and one or more partners.

name: Voluntary executive turnover
authors_terms: ["voluntary executive turnover", "voluntary executive departures", "voluntary departures", "voluntary turnover"]
definition: Departures of executives at the level of director, vice president, or above that are classified as voluntary when press releases provide information about an executive's future employment and do not suggest he/she was fired, forced from his/her position, or departed because of unspecified policy differences.

name: Firm performance
definition: A highly visible quality signal that is readily available to hiring firms, namely the financial performance of the executive's firm. The authors note that existing studies report a negative relationship between firm performance and voluntary executive turnover.

name: Presence in the table wine market
authors_terms: ["presence in the table wine market", "table wine producer", "table wine mentions", "operating in the new table wine niche"]
definition: A winery's presence in the table wine niche, a niche the authors define as a product market: the opportunity to produce tart, low-alcohol table wines in the southern European manner rather than or in addition to the sweet dessert and fortified wines that had been the normal American fare since Prohibition.

name: Table wine production from founding
authors_terms: ["table wine production from founding", "wineries that began as table wine producers", "winery's presence in the table wine niche", "table wine producer from founding"]
definition: Wineries that may have been founded in the new niche with competencies and orientations that differed from those of existing wineries.

name: Diversification into the table wine niche
authors_terms: ["diversify into the table wine niche", "table wine production through later entry", "diversification"]
definition: Existing wineries taking the path of product diversification by initiating table wine production later in their histories, that is, modifying their production into the new niche.

name: Organizational mortality
authors_terms: ["failure rate", "mortality rate", "likelihood of failing", "instantaneous mortality rate"]
definition: The instantaneous mortality rate, the limiting probability of an organization failing at age t given that failure has not occurred before t.

name: Marketization
definition: The rules of the institutional setting determine the extent to which the enterprise is 'marketized' by fixing its position in respect of: enterprise autonomy; distance from the plan in respect of acquiring inputs, selling outputs, and pricing; the intensity of incentives; and the importance of profit. It is the variation in institutional setting, rather than ownership type per se, that is the key determinant of enterprise behavior.

name: Environmental munificence
definition: For environmental munificence a distinction was made between the immediate business environment, and the longer-term prospects determined by the technological environment. The environment has been characterized in terms of two broad constructs: marketization and munificence.

name: Emphasis on meeting customer needs
authors_terms: ["business strategies designed to meet customers' needs", "organizational strategies", "emphasis on meeting customer needs"]
definition: The second category of strategic action involves using 'organizational strategies' to secure revenues within the environments selected. In more marketized settings change in the direction of meeting customer needs is key.

name: Strategic trade-off
authors_terms: ["emphasizing some dimensions of strategy at the expense of others", "trade-off strategies", "trade-off of one strategic direction against another"]
definition: Superior performance on market economy criteria requires that firms direct their resources towards a limited set of strategic dimensions, in order to avoid becoming 'stuck in the middle'. Firms adopt business strategies that seek to meet customers' needs by emphasizing some dimensions of strategy at the expense of others.
