name: Performance on market economy criteria
authors_terms: ["performance on market economy criteria", "market economy criteria", "performance"]
definition: For more marketized firms, success or failure is reflected in market share, sales, growth, and profitability. Performance on market economy criteria was captured by following Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1986), with a broad measure covering both economic performance and operational success.

name: Target elite prestige
authors_terms: ["managerial prestige", "the target's managerial prestige", "target's outsider prestige", "the prestige of its entire top management team"]
definition: For the purposes of this paper, a firm's managerial prestige is the prestige of its entire top management team, operationalized as the number of its top managers with membership in or connections to the economic, social or political elites in America (adjusted for team size). Similar measures of prestige were computed for the targets' outside board members.

name: Bidder elite prestige
authors_terms: ["bidder's managerial prestige", "bidder's outsider prestige", "the bidder's prestige"]
definition: Similar measures of prestige were computed for the bidders' managers (inside board members) and outside board members, using the same seven elite-affiliation items divided by team size.

name: Target top management power
authors_terms: ["managerial power", "the target's managerial power", "managerial dominance over a target's board of directors"]
definition: For the purposes of this study, managerial power is defined as managerial dominance over a target's board of directors. The balance of power between insiders and outsiders determines who controls the firm.

name: Target resistance to tender offer
authors_terms: ["resistance", "cooperation", "the resistance or cooperation of the target", "hostility during a tender offer"]
definition: The main dependent variable in this study is a binary variable-the resistance or cooperation of the target. Cooperation refers to active cooperative behavior or, at a minimum, acceptance of the bid without active resistance by the target.

name: Bidder offer friendliness
authors_terms: ["friendly offers", "the friendliness (premium and type) of their offers", "premiums", "all cash offers", "mixed offers"]
definition: The authors also briefly consider bidder behavior by looking at the friendliness (premium and type) of their offers, where more friendly offers carry higher premiums and are all cash while less friendly offers carry lower premiums and are mixed offers comprised of cash plus securities.

name: Combinatory knowledge of direct contacts
authors_terms: ["value of combinatory knowledge among an inventor's direct contacts", "combinatory knowledge from direct contacts", "value of direct contacts' combinatory knowledge"]
definition: We define combinatory knowledge as the highly tacit ability and know-how to combine and reconfigure new knowledge. Combinatory knowledge is the knowledge and ability to combine and reconfigure knowledge from different technical areas into valuable innovations.

name: Combinatory knowledge of indirect contacts
authors_terms: ["value of combinatory knowledge available through indirect contacts", "value of indirect contacts' combinatory knowledge"]
definition: Combinatory knowledge is the knowledge and ability to combine and reconfigure knowledge from different technical areas into valuable innovations. An inventor's indirect contacts may also have valuable combinatory knowledge, but this knowledge may not be accessible to the focal inventor because of its tacitness.

name: Knowledge heterogeneity of direct contacts
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of knowledge available from those direct contacts", "direct contacts' knowledge heterogeneity"]
definition: Scholars have used the heterogeneity of knowledge in a social network to proxy for the availability of new knowledge in that network. Knowledge heterogeneity is measured as the diversity of unfamiliar technical classes in the prior patents of network contacts.

name: Knowledge heterogeneity of indirect contacts
authors_terms: ["knowledge heterogeneity among indirect contacts", "indirect contacts' knowledge heterogeneity"]
definition: It is likely that heterogeneous knowledge among indirect contacts does provide an indicator of the unfamiliar solutions available to the focal inventor through those contacts. Knowledge heterogeneity is measured as the diversity of unfamiliar technical classes in the prior patents of network contacts.

name: Innovative performance
authors_terms: ["innovative performance", "innovative performance of a patent", "forward citations"]
definition: Innovation is the process of creating and putting into use new knowledge that results in value creation for stakeholders. The key dependent variable in our study is the innovative performance of a patent, measured as the forward citations of the focal patent excluding self-citations.

name: Voting threshold
authors_terms: ["voting threshold", "aggregation structure's threshold", "aggregation structure's voting threshold"]
definition: The voting threshold, i.e., how many organizational members must vote yes to trigger an organizational investment.

name: Project support
definition: The degree to which organizational members support investments in uncertain alternatives, captured as the count of yes votes a participant casts; the authors describe the count-dependent variable as 'support of uncertain projects.'

name: Inferred information
definition: Information about project quality that voters infer from the organizational voting context, in particular from the pivotal vote constellation implied by the voting threshold.

name: Level of information
authors_terms: ["level of information", "level of private information", "private level of information"]
definition: Voters' private level of information, that is, whether they feel worse versus better informed relative to the other voters.

name: Perceived pivotality
authors_terms: ["perceived pivotality", "perceived probability of casting the pivotal vote"]
definition: The perceived likelihood of finding oneself in a constellation in which one's individual vote is going to make a difference for the joint team decision.

name: Environmental performance
definition: The study treats environmental performance as captured by two TRI-based measures, pollution prevention strategies and end-of-pipe pollution control: 'Of our two environmental performance measures, the first, pollution prevention strategies, has been traditionally measured as the difference between a predicted value and some actual pollution level' and 'Our second environmental performance measure was end-of-pipe pollution control.'

name: Pollution prevention
authors_terms: ["pollution prevention strategies", "pollution prevention", "pollution prevention success", "pollution prevention results"]
definition: 'In contrast, pollution prevention strategies minimize or eliminate the creation of toxic chemical agents during the various stages of production and thus require structural investments in new, cleaner technologies.'

name: End-of-pipe pollution control
definition: 'End-of-pipe technologies capture, treat, and dispose of pollutants and waste at the end of a manufacturing process.'

name: CEO total pay
definition: 'Our dependent variable for Hypotheses 1-3, CEO total pay, consisted of the sum of salary, bonus, and all long-term components of CEO pay (stock options, restricted stock, and other long-term compensation).'

name: Long-term pay
authors_terms: ["long-term pay", "total long-term pay", "long-term income", "long-term pay forms"]
definition: 'Long-term pay forms, like stock options, are explicit incentives, since their final value is contingent on future performance.'

name: Environmental governance
authors_terms: ["environmental governance", "environmental governance mechanisms", "environmental pay policy", "environmental committee"]
definition: 'To define this variable (see Hypotheses 3a and 3b), we analyzed the proxy statements each company issued over our time period to identify whether each firm had an environmental pay policy and an environmental committee within its board.'

name: Industry pollution position
authors_terms: ["industry pollution position", "industry pollution intensity", "presence in polluting industries"]
definition: 'we created an industry pollution position index that reflects the mix of sectors in which a firm operates and accounts for their pollution intensity.'

name: Formal intervention
definition: Formal interventions provide explicit instructions for the group to follow and help guide the discussion among members. A major effect of a formal intervention is to add a second agenda that is focused on improving some aspect of the knowledge integration process.

name: Targeted attention switching
authors_terms: ["attention switching", "targeted attention switches", "switches to the knowledge integration behavior targeted by the formal intervention"]
definition: An attention switch was coded every time the group departed from a discussion of the case to some other topic such as managing time; the switches were categorized into sharing information, questioning others, and managing time. Targeted switches are those in the category dictated by the formal intervention the group received.

name: Spillover attention switching
authors_terms: ["spillover", "spillover effects", "spillover activities", "attention switches to nontargeted process behaviors"]
definition: After a switch to consider the formal intervention, the heightened awareness of performance and of possibilities for changing the course for knowledge integration expands the focus of the group to improvements that go beyond the formal intervention; in other words, there are "spillover" effects that transcend the initial interruption. These are switches to other aspects of the knowledge integration process that were not targeted by the formal intervention.

name: Attention switch clustering
authors_terms: ["clusters", "clusters of attention switches", "organization of attention switches to knowledge integration behaviors into clusters"]
definition: These attention switches occur in close temporal proximity in what we term "clusters." Thus, these clusters of attention switches create focused time periods during which groups center their attention on improving their knowledge integration process.

name: Cluster size
authors_terms: ["number of attention switches in each interruption", "larger clusters", "number of attention switches that they include"]
definition: Larger clusters (i.e., more attention switches) are likely to be associated with more attention to different aspects of the knowledge integration process. Each interruption in all groups was coded according to the number of attention switches it included.

name: Aspects of the knowledge integration process considered
authors_terms: ["more aspects of the knowledge integration process", "number of different types of attention switches", "types of attention switches"]
definition: Larger clusters are associated with more attention to different aspects of the knowledge integration process, that is, with more different types of attention switches.

name: Group member participation
authors_terms: ["number of group members participating", "number of different people speaking", "participation by most or all group members"]
definition: More group members are probably participating in larger clusters because interruptions to a process tend to engage members, who are otherwise distracted, to bring their attention back to the group activity.

name: Suggestions for process improvement
authors_terms: ["specific suggestions for improving the knowledge integration process", "number of activities or paths to follow suggested", "suggestions for improving the process"]
definition: Larger clusters are associated with more fully engaged members who make more suggestions for improving the knowledge integration process, that is, more specific suggestions for improving that process being proposed.

name: Knowledge integration process change
authors_terms: ["change in the knowledge integration process", "change score", "changes in their work process"]
definition: The knowledge integration process involves the actions of group members by which they share their individual knowledge within the group and combine it to create new knowledge. Change in the knowledge integration process is the shift from the period prior to an interruption to the period following it.

name: Knowledge integration
definition: Knowledge integration is the outcome of the knowledge integration process, consisting of both the shared knowledge of individuals and the combined knowledge that emerges from their interactions. It is defined as several individuals combining their information to create new knowledge.

name: Incumbency status
definition: Firms are distinguished among incumbents and entrants based on whether a firm had been present in the anticancer drug market prior to 1983 (the start of the biotechnology revolution in that market), in which case it was an incumbent; otherwise the firm was classified as an entrant.

name: Pioneering in biopharmaceutical technology
definition: A firm was classified as a biopharmaceutical technology pioneer if it had a large-molecule drug that had been developed in house, had been approved in 1990 or earlier (irrespective of market application), and was the first drug with that active ingredient. Pioneers accrued the greatest expertise in this capability.

name: R&D performance in drug discovery
authors_terms: ["R&D performance", "performance in targeted anticancer drug discovery", "rate of production of patented molecules"]
definition: A dependent variable that measured R&D performance at the stage in the value chain of a firm in this market where competence destruction had taken place, namely, drug discovery.

name: Strategic value of a capability
authors_terms: ["strategic value", "comparative strategic value", "value added and ease of access"]
definition: The comparative strategic value of a capability is defined as value added and ease of access. Capabilities only constitute a source of competitive advantage when they are both value adding and inaccessible to competition.

name: Biopharmaceutical technology
definition: A nonmarket-specific R&D capability comprising knowledge originating with the invention of recombinant DNA technology, required for large-molecule but not for small-molecule targeted anticancer drug discovery.

name: Oncology research
authors_terms: ["oncology research", "market-specific R&D capability", "knowledge of the disease"]
definition: A market-specific R&D capability comprising knowledge of cancer as a disease, reusable from cytotoxic to both small- and large-molecule targeted drug discovery processes.

name: Home-country status
authors_terms: ["home-country status", "cross-border VC status", "Cross-border VC Status", "home country status", "status"]
definition: Status refers to a firm's rank in the social hierarchy, and is associated with esteem and prestige. Status is particularly valuable in markets as it provides a signal of a firm's quality.

name: Venture performance
definition: Because ventures in the sample are private and do not disclose financial statements, we measure performance by the occurrence of an IPO or an acquisition anywhere in the world.

name: Interconnectedness
definition: The interconnectedness of countries refers to the extent to which information, goods, and people move across national borders. Increased interactions between market participants in two countries create interdependence and mutual awareness by fostering information exchange.

name: Relative global position
definition: We develop the notion of relative global position to examine the standing of each country with respect to another within the broader world system. Relative global position seeks to measure how the cross-border VC firm's country stands in comparison to the venture's country.

name: CEO stock ownership
definition: For executives who own stock, the value of their shares changes in direct proportion to shareholder returns, both positively and negatively. Moreover, at any given time an executive's stock portfolio has currency: real and immediate value that can be exchanged for goods and services.

name: CEO stock option pay
authors_terms: ["CEO stock option pay", "stock option pay", "option pay", "stock options"]
definition: Like executives who own stock, those paid with options benefit along with shareholders when stock prices rise. However, in the event that the firm's stock price declines after the date of the stock option grant, executives experience no reduction in real wealth.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: Acquisitions are common investment choices that are, by their very nature, risky, and because acquisitions often fail they tend to result in subsequent divestitures. Acquisition activity is the number of acquisitions completed during a year.

name: Divestiture activity
definition: Divestitures have become an increasingly popular corporate restructuring tool, and they generally lead to an increase in shareholder value, although divestitures offer an opportunity to create value for shareholders they also bring with them the prospect for significant value erosion.

name: CEO position tenure
definition: Position tenure is the number of years an executive has held the CEO title at the firm; research suggests that position tenure is negatively associated with an executive's risk preferences.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance is a powerful factor that may affect executives' calculation of potential gains and losses from risky decisions, and it is measured as return on assets (ROA).

name: Prior brokerage
authors_terms: ["prior brokerage", "prior degree of brokerage", "degree of prior brokerage"]
definition: Following Shipilov et al. (2011), we consider brokerage a continuous variable. A firm with a higher degree of brokerage, for example, connects a greater number of unconnected others or spans more structural holes. The independent variable, prior brokerage, uses the same measure but applies to the prior network, established before the formation of the multipartner alliance.

name: Subsequent brokerage
authors_terms: ["subsequent brokerage", "subsequent degree of brokerage", "degree of brokerage in the subsequent network"]
definition: The dependent variable, subsequent brokerage, is a focal firm's degree of betweenness centrality in the subsequent network of new alliances among members of a multipartner alliance after the formation of this multipartner alliance.

name: Number of partners
authors_terms: ["number of partners", "number of partners of a multipartner alliance"]
definition: Number of partners is the total number of partners in a multipartner alliance, including the focal firm. As the number of partners increases, coordination becomes more important, because it is more difficult to maintain frequent interactions among partners in a big group.

name: Size heterogeneity among partners
authors_terms: ["size heterogeneity", "size heterogeneity among partners", "size disparity among partners"]
definition: Size heterogeneity refers to the distribution of firm sizes among a group of partner firms. Greater size heterogeneity means that partner firms vary significantly in their sizes, whereas a low level of heterogeneity means that partner firms are of similar sizes.

name: Density of prior alliances
authors_terms: ["density", "density of prior alliances", "density of partners' prior alliance network"]
definition: Density refers to the overall connectivity of members of a network, which we determine according to the prior alliance relationships among partners, before the formation of the multipartner alliance.

name: Task variety
definition: Jobs with a higher score are closer to an even mix of task types, while jobs with a lower score have a more homogenous set of tasks. As specialization increases, jobs become simpler with respect to their mix of tasks, and the entropy score decreases.

name: Coworkers' task variety
authors_terms: ["coworkers' task variety", "coworkers' average task variety", "task variety among coworkers"]
definition: A key determinant of job turf availability for a given worker is lower task variety among coworkers; the models include a control for the nodal worker's own task variety separately from coworkers' average task variety.

name: Job turf
definition: I use the term 'job turf' to capture the phenomenon in which a given worker performs tasks that are unique relative to those conducted by coworkers.

name: Worker earnings
definition: The dependent variable in the analysis is logged employee earnings, defined as gross salary payments to each individual employee and adjusted for inflation.

name: Competition between portfolio partners
authors_terms: ["Competition between P and PC s", "competition between a partner and other firms in the focal firm's alliance portfolio", "competition among partners"]
definition: Competition between the focal firm's partner P and the other firms in the focal firm's portfolio that operate in the same therapeutic areas. The authors' arguments do not require actual competition, but only that P perceives other portfolio partners to be competitors; references to competition between P and PC s include both actual and perceived competition.

name: Alliance termination
authors_terms: ["hazard of termination of the alliance between the focal firm and the partner", "termination of the F - P alliance", "alliance termination"]
definition: Termination of the alliance between the focal firm and the partner, modeled as a hazard. Termination is costly because of the difficulty of unravelling relationships, dismantling governance and coordinating structures, dealing with disruption, establishing replacement alliances, and mitigating negative reputation effects.

name: Equity investment in the alliance
authors_terms: ["equity investment", "equity investments in each alliance", "F ' s equity investment in F - P alliance"]
definition: Governance of an alliance in terms of equity investments: stronger governance can be achieved through the exchange or purchase of equity, which is associated with greater formalization through contractual agreement as well as the establishment of charters, routines, and mechanisms for coordinating exchange between partners.

name: Portfolio density
definition: Portfolio density measures the intensity of ties between partners and therefore indicates social cohesion in the focal firm's portfolio; a high-density portfolio has more ties among firms than a low-density portfolio.

name: Direct paths between partner and competitors
authors_terms: ["Direct paths", "direct paths between P and PC s", "direct paths between a focal firm ' s partner and the partner ' s competitors"]
definition: Direct ties linking the partner P and the other portfolio firms that compete with it, providing alternate conduits through which P's resources can be transferred to its competitors without the focal firm serving as a conduit.

name: Strategic similarity between focal firm and partner
authors_terms: ["Strategic similarity", "strategic similarity between F and P"]
definition: Strategic similarity refers to commonality in strategy, operational focus, technology, and challenges between the focal firm and its partner; it usually results from firms operating in the same industry or market segment, which creates overlapping leadership experiences, strategies, and resources.

name: Strategic planning intensity
authors_terms: ["strategic planning intensity", "planning intensity", "intensity with which banks engage in the strategic planning process"]
definition: For purposes of the present study, strategic planning intensity is defined as the relative emphasis placed on each component of the strategic planning process. Strategic planning is described as the process of using systematic criteria and rigorous investigation to formulate, implement, and control strategy, and formally document organizational expectations.

name: Managerial factors
authors_terms: ["managerial factors", "managerial determinants", "strategic planning expertise", "beliefs about planning-performance relationships"]
definition: Scales developed by Miller (1987) served as the model from which we derived the two observed variables, beliefs about planning-performance relationships and strategic planning expertise, used to measure the managerial factors latent variable.

name: Environmental factors
definition: This latent variable was also measured by two observed variables: perceived environmental complexity and environmental change.

name: Organizational factors
definition: Bank size and bank structural complexity were the two observed variables used to measure the organizational factors latent variable.

name: Financial performance
definition: In an attempt to derive a more comprehensive and unique picture of banks' financial situations, three measures were used for the financial performance latent variable.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Measures of multipoint competition capture the extent to which a firm's product-market scope, outside of a focal market, is similar to other firms already participating in that market. The authors treat it as a firm-in-market construct, so the extent to which multipoint competition is important can vary for each service market a firm could potentially enter.

name: Market entry
definition: Entry is the addition by a firm of a market it does not currently compete in; market entry becomes a critical action in defining a firm's competitive position vis-a-vis actual and potential rivals, and it is the dependent variable of the study.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The length of time a CEO has been in the position, which the authors link to the firm's propensity for undertaking strategic changes including entering new markets. They consider a CEO to be new if he or she had been on the job for less than three years, and contrast newer with longer-tenured CEOs.

name: Company ownership
definition: An outlet that is owned by the franchisor. In the first set of analyses company-owned outlets are contrasted with franchised outlets, with company owned set to 1.00.

name: Multi-outlet franchise ownership
definition: Franchising in which a franchisee owns multiple outlets. Multi-outlet franchises are contrasted with single-outlet franchises, with multi-outlet franchises set to 1.00.

name: Single-outlet franchise ownership
definition: An outlet owned by a franchisee who owns only that outlet; single-outlet franchisees can monitor closely by using their outlet or a nearby home as headquarters. The remaining outlets were coded as single-outlet franchisees.

name: Distance to franchisor headquarters
definition: The distance between an outlet and the franchisor's headquarters, calculated after each outlet's location address was converted to latitude and longitude coordinates.

name: Distance to owner headquarters
definition: The distance between an outlet and the headquarters of its owner. For company-owned outlets, distance to the franchisor's headquarters and distance to the owner's headquarters are the same because the owner is the franchisor.

name: Distance to nearest neighbor
definition: The distance in miles between each outlet and its nearest neighbor in the same chain within a maximum 60-mile radius.

name: Company-owned nearest neighbor
authors_terms: ["company-owned nearest neighbor", "having a company-owned nearest neighbor"]
definition: A coding of the focal outlet's nearest neighbor as being a company-owned outlet, as opposed to a multi-outlet-franchise nearest neighbor.

name: Multi-outlet franchise nearest neighbor
authors_terms: ["multi-outlet-franchise nearest neighbor", "having a multi-outlet franchise as the nearest neighbor"]
definition: A coding of the focal outlet's nearest neighbor as being an outlet of a multi-outlet franchise, as opposed to a company-owned nearest neighbor.

name: Market size
definition: Market size was measured based on the population of the county where the outlet was located, using the 2005 Census update.

name: Outlet size
definition: Outlet size was measured by the number of seats in each outlet as reported by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants.

name: Cognitive ability
definition: 'Cognitive ability' is the name given to describe the efficacy of a person's mental skills in understanding complex ideas, learning from experience, reasoning, and problem solving. The concept is closely related to 'analytical intelligence,' the ability to reason and solve problems involving new information without relying extensively on an explicit base of declarative knowledge.

name: Mean team cognitive ability
authors_terms: ["mean start-up team ability", "mean cognitive ability", "average ability", "teams' average test score"]
definition: The central location of the distribution of cognitive abilities within a team, summarized as the mean of team members' cognitive abilities.

name: Cognitive ability dispersion
authors_terms: ["ability dispersion", "diversity of cognitive abilities", "dispersion of abilities", "cognitive diversity", "coefficient of variation in test scores"]
definition: The dispersion (diversity) of cognitive abilities within a team, measured by the coefficient of variation in team members' test scores.

name: Start-up team performance
definition: The business performance of a start-up team, operationalized by four measures: sales, profits, a binary indicator for positive profits, and profits per share.

name: Problem load
authors_terms: ["number of all problems", "problem load", "new problems", "number of problems", "aggregate flow of new problems"]
definition: Problems are defined as the causes of airline accidents and incidents experienced by members of the U.S. airline industry and identified by the NTSB. With relatively stable attention capacity, the variation in the number of problems (or the problem load) can generate the variation in the competition for attention to problems.

name: Human factor problems
authors_terms: ["human factor problems", "human problems", "problems associated with human factors"]
definition: Problems associated primarily with human factors, such as pilot and crew errors. Pilot error, flight crew error, flight attendant error, ground crew error, air traffic controller error, inadequate group coordination, error of pilots on other airplanes, and passenger errors were categorized as problems associated with human factors.

name: Nonhuman factor problems
authors_terms: ["nonhuman factor problems", "nonhuman problems", "problems associated with nonhuman factors"]
definition: Problems associated primarily with nonhuman factors, such as engine failures. Equipment malfunction, maintenance error, manufacturer error, inadequate FAA supervision and procedures, inadequate airline supervision and procedures, inadequate weather assistance, improper maintenance of the runway, terrain conditions, and weather turbulences were categorized as nonhuman factor problems.

name: Rate of proposing rules
authors_terms: ["rate of proposing rules", "rule-proposing rate", "rate of proposing rules for a specific rule domain"]
definition: The dependent variables in this study are the rate of proposing and finalizing rules, meaning how fast the FAA proposes or finalizes a rule. From a learning perspective, the speed at which the FAA proposes or finalizes a rule reflects how the FAA allocates its attention.

name: Rate of finalizing rules
authors_terms: ["hazard rate of rule finalization", "rate of finalizing rules", "rate of rule finalization"]
definition: The hazard rate of rule finalization is the transition rate of a proposed rule being finalized; a rule enters into a risk set for estimation of the hazard rate at the time when it is proposed and exits the risk set until it is finalized or withdrawn. The rate of proposing and finalizing rules means how fast the FAA proposes or finalizes a rule.

name: Industry performance
authors_terms: ["industry performance", "average ROE of the airline industry", "industry's performance level"]
definition: The performance of the airline industry, which the agency evaluates economically during rulemaking processes; as government rules regulating industries are closely linked to industry performance, it is possible that the agency adjusts its rules based on industry performance feedback.

name: Rule complexity
authors_terms: ["complexity of rules", "rule complexity", "rules of low complexity", "rules of high complexity"]
definition: A rule can be more complex and thus difficult to finalize if it has more parties involved in the rulemaking process, has more comments given by different commentators, or covers more areas for consideration. This complexity can be both political and technical, with the former emphasizing the negotiation process among different rulemaking parties and the latter referring to the composition of rules.

name: External network size
authors_terms: ["external network size", "size of TMT external networks", "TMT external networks that are large in size"]
definition: Network size refers to the total number of contacts in a TMT's social network; larger networks comprise more ties. Networks differ in size, defined as number of contacts.

name: External network range
authors_terms: ["external network range", "broad in range", "range of external networks"]
definition: Network range refers to the diversity of contacts in a TMT's social network, measured as the number of different groups or actor categories a network accesses.

name: External network tie strength
authors_terms: ["strength of ties of external networks", "external strength of ties", "strong ties"]
definition: Strength of ties is a multifaceted construct consisting of interaction frequency, relationship duration, and the emotional intensity or closeness of a bond. Strong ties are those that are of long duration, exercised frequently, and emotionally close.

name: Internal network size
authors_terms: ["internal network size", "size of TMT internal networks", "TMT internal networks that are large in size"]
definition: Network size refers to the total number of contacts in a TMT's social network; larger networks comprise more ties. Networks differ in size, defined as number of contacts.

name: Internal network range
authors_terms: ["internal network range", "range of internal networks", "broad in range"]
definition: Network range refers to the diversity of contacts in a TMT's social network, measured as the number of different groups or actor categories a network accesses.

name: Internal network tie strength
authors_terms: ["strength of ties of internal networks", "internal strength of ties", "strong ties"]
definition: Strength of ties is a multifaceted construct consisting of interaction frequency, relationship duration, and the emotional intensity or closeness of a bond. Strong ties are those that are of long duration, exercised frequently, and emotionally close.

name: Network-building HR practices
authors_terms: ["network-building HR practices", "specific network-building HR practices", "networking-building HR practices"]
definition: We argued that specific network-building HR practices would include training, performance assessment, and rewards designed to help and encourage top managers to build relationships with external and internal actors. We generated eight items based on the theory used to develop Hypotheses 3 and 4.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "sales growth and stock performance", "one-year stock returns"]
definition: Sales growth is an indication of the extent to which customers value the ideas and products a firm is pursuing, and stock returns are an indication of the extent to which investors approve of the firm's actions. High-technology firms and analysts view these measures as leading indicators of performance for firms in high-technology industries.

name: Foreign acquirer
authors_terms: ["foreign acquisitions", "cross-border acquisitions", "acquisition by a non-U.S. firm", "non-U.S. acquirer"]
definition: The study contrasts U.S. firms acquired by non-U.S. firms with U.S. firms acquired by other U.S. firms; cross-border transactions represent about 25 percent of all acquisitions involving U.S. firms. Three theoretical perspectives suggest that top management turnover may be higher in foreign vs. purely domestic acquisitions.

name: Non-Anglo acquirer
authors_terms: ["'non-Anglo' foreign acquirer", "'Anglo' foreign acquirer", "non-Anglo countries", "Anglo countries"]
definition: Acquisitions of U.S. targets by firms headquartered in countries most culturally similar to the United States in language, religion, and historical development ('Anglo' countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia) most closely resemble purely domestic acquisitions. The authors argue that greater crossnational organizational and individual differences between U.S. and non-Anglo firms should lead to higher postacquisition turnover in non-Anglo acquisitions.

name: Japanese acquirer
definition: Increased acquisition activity in the United States by Japanese companies beginning in the mid-1980s and the reputation of Japanese companies for making heavy use of expatriates has fueled speculation that Japanese acquirers prefer to replace U.S. executives with Japanese managers.

name: Top management turnover
authors_terms: ["top management turnover", "postacquisition top management turnover", "cumulative top management turnover"]
definition: Each target firm's 'top management team' was defined by the list of managers and job titles provided to the Register or Million Dollar Directory by the reporting company. Turnover in each of the 5 years following the acquisition was calculated by dividing the number of managers employed by the target company in the year prior to the acquisition who departed the firm during the year in question by the total number of managers employed in the year prior to the acquisition.

name: Firm age
definition: Our key explanatory variable is firm age, measured as the number of years since the firm was founded or, nonparametrically, as a vector of categorical variables.

name: Diversification rate
authors_terms: ["diversification", "diversification rate", "new product introduction rate", "propensity to launch a new fund"]
definition: Diversification is the horizontal expansion of an established firm's scope via the introduction of new product offerings, and, consistent with the standard definition of diversified firms as multiproduct entities, hedge fund firms are considered diversified when they operate multiple distinct funds.

name: Ex ante performance
authors_terms: ["ex ante performance", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "track record", "average historical excess returns"]
definition: Exchange partners evaluate a firm's proposed change based, in part, on the ex ante performance of its legacy offerings, and investor returns capture the ex ante performance metric that external partners (e.g., investors) care about.

name: Ex post performance
authors_terms: ["ex post performance", "ex post returns", "ex post profitability", "excess returns", "information ratio", "firm performance"]
definition: Since it does not incorporate implementation costs, ex post performance is a good measure of project quality; investor returns as a measure of ex post performance always capture project quality in this setting, but can only be interpreted as a measure of profitability in the absence of implementation costs.

name: Analysts' recommendations
authors_terms: ["analysts' recommendations", "analysts' mean recommendations", "analysts' reactions", "negative recommendations from analysts"]
definition: Securities analysts assess the performance of firms and publish periodic reports that include forecasts of a firm's stock price and recommendations about whether to buy, hold, or sell the stock. Analysts' recommendations reflect their perceptions about how a firm's current actions and strategies will influence future stock value.

name: Strategic investments
definition: Future-oriented investment expenditures that reflect managerial decisions about strategic direction, captured by capital expenditures and R&D expenses, which are summed. Both capital expenditures and R&D expenses represent future-oriented technology investments.

name: Share repurchase announcements
authors_terms: ["share repurchase announcements", "stock repurchase", "value of repurchase announcements"]
definition: A stock repurchase or buyback entails an announcement by a firm that it will buy back its own shares at a price above the current market price. Announcements of share repurchases trigger increases in stock price and market value.

name: Radical technological change
definition: Radical technological change entails a shift to a new base of knowledge underlying the products in an industry that offers the potential for a superior price-performance trajectory, triggering a period of increased technological innovation and competition characterized by very high technological and market uncertainty.

name: Calculative human resource management practices
authors_terms: ["calculative human resource management practices", "calculative HRM practices", "calculative practices", "CALC", "hard model"]
definition: The hard model is rooted in a calculative approach aimed at ensuring that production activities are at all times efficiently supplied with the necessary input of human resources. Associated with this model are a range of efficiency-seeking devices aimed at ensuring that each employee's contribution to the firm is assessed and thereafter rewarded accordingly through individual performance appraisals and individually oriented reward systems.

name: Collaborative human resource management practices
authors_terms: ["collaborative human resource management practices", "collaborative HRM practices", "collaborative practices", "COLL", "soft model"]
definition: The "soft" model represents a collaborative approach to human resource management in that it has a distinctly more developmental or humanistic focus, often based on explicit statements about the value of the employees to the firm and ethical matters related to the employment relation. The collaborative emphasis is hence characterized by efforts to create and communicate a culture of partnership between employer and employee as well as among employees.

name: National embeddedness
definition: Cross-national dissimilarities in institutional structures are likely to create management practices that vary from country to country. The authors refer to this as the national embeddedness of firms and use country as the main regressor, represented by a set of five design variables with the United Kingdom as the reference category.

name: Industrial embeddedness
definition: Institutional theory also assumes that industries develop along particular trajectories characterized by distinct economic and organizational dynamics that distinguish them from other industries. Industry is the authors' second categorical regressor, represented by five design variables with manufacturing as the reference category.

name: Firm size
definition: Most studies of the relation between organizational size and structure indicate that size, in terms of the number of employees, tends to influence the methods used for controlling and coordinating employees. Lnsize, the natural logarithm of firm size, is the only continuous regressor in the analysis.

name: Influence of labor representative bodies
authors_terms: ["influence of labor representative bodies", "influential labor unions or similar employee bodies", "labor unions", "works councils"]
definition: Such autonomy requires that management's power not be curtailed by strong regulative pressure at the firm level in the form of laws and agreements or by influential labor unions or similar employee bodies.

name: Legislative pressure on firms
authors_terms: ["legislative pressure on firms", "labor law and collective agreements", "regulative pressure at the firm level"]
definition: Management's power must not be curtailed by strong regulative pressure at the firm level in the form of laws and agreements. The stronger the degree of legislative pressure on firms in the form of labor law and collective agreements, the lower the firms' general managerial autonomy.

name: Managerial autonomy
definition: The adoption of calculative practices requires that management possess substantial autonomy within the firm. In turn, such autonomy requires that management's power not be curtailed by strong regulative pressure at the firm level in the form of laws and agreements or by influential labor unions or similar employee bodies.

name: Role of the personnel function
authors_terms: ["role of the personnel function", "operative focus", "operatively oriented role", "personnel function"]
definition: The introduction of collaborative practices is highly dependent on the latitude for novel action enjoyed by personnel departments. The more operatively oriented the role of the personnel function is, the less frequently such practices will be implemented.

name: Labor-related regulation of firms
authors_terms: ["labor-related regulation of firms", "legislative regulations of firms' employment practices", "volume and detail of specific legislative regulations"]
definition: One major source of cross-national variation in collaborative practices is the volume and detail of specific legislative regulations of firms' employment practices. In countries where these are considerable, it can be expected that the amount of proactive behavior, in terms of efforts to introduce novel, sophisticated practices by personnel specialists, will be low.

name: Host country corruption level
authors_terms: ["host country corruption environment", "host country CPI", "institutionalization of corruption in the host country"]
definition: The institutionalization of corruption in the MNE subsidiary's host country corresponds with the prevalence of corruption in that country, as measured by Transparency International's CPI. The host country corruption environment was measured using the CPI, reversed and standardized so that higher numbers reflect more corrupt institutional environments.

name: Home country corruption level
authors_terms: ["home country corruption environment", "home country CPI", "institutionalization of corruption in the MNE's home country"]
definition: An MNE's home country corruption level was operationalized by the CPI score of its home country; CPI scores were reversed and standardized so that higher numbers reflect more corrupt environments. It captures the degree to which anticorruption norms have been institutionalized in the MNE's home institutional environment.

name: Home country participation in the OECD Convention
authors_terms: ["home country entry into force of the OECD convention", "home country participation in the OECD Convention", "Home OECD participation"]
definition: Participation of national governments in supranational efforts to reduce corruption levels worldwide, such as the OECD Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions, which calls for home countries to prosecute bribery of foreign officials as crimes.

name: Local corruption pressure
authors_terms: ["local pressure to engage in corrupt practices", "subsidiary's need to engage in bribery", "degree to which local corruption pressure poses an obstacle to performance", "pressure the MNE subsidiary will face to engage in corrupt practices such as bribery"]
definition: The propensity of local government officials to impose pressure on firms to make 'unofficial payments' (i.e., bribes) to get business done. The authors operationalize this dependent variable, local pressure to engage in corrupt practices, in two complementary ways in their two datasets.

name: Partial local ownership
definition: Taking on local partners, i.e., local firms or investors with partial stakes in the host country subsidiary. Firms with any local ownership were coded as '1' and those that were fully foreign owned were coded as '0.'

name: Local alliance partner
definition: Managers were asked to report the number of strategic alliances and joint ventures in which their firm had participated with Ghanaian-owned companies.

name: Localized decision making
authors_terms: ["localized decision making", "decentralized decision making", "local decision making", "localizing control"]
definition: Localizing control of operations, such as decentralizing decision making to the host country subsidiary. In the Ghana dataset, decentralized decision making was operationalized based on a three-item scale in which subsidiary managers were asked if strategic decisions were decentralized to the host country subsidiary.

name: Nationality of the managing director
authors_terms: ["nationality of managing director", "use of a local national to head the subsidiary", "Ghanaian managing director", "use of host country managers rather than home country nationals to head the subsidiary"]
definition: The nationality of the person heading the subsidiary, reflecting a strategy to localize control through the use of host country managers rather than home country nationals. In the Ghana dataset, this variable was coded as '1' when the managing director was Ghanaian and as '0' otherwise.

name: Localized control
definition: Firms engage in localization strategies in order to adapt to host country conditions; such strategies include taking on local partners and localizing control (e.g., decentralizing decision making to the host country subsidiary; using locals as managing directors). MNEs also make strategic decisions regarding the level of control and coordination that they impose from headquarters based on their needs for global integration versus local adaptation.

name: Regulatory discretion
definition: According to the political science literature, discretion is the flexibility formally granted, often through statutes and laws, to regulatory agency officials to interpret and implement public policies created by elected officials. Our central argument is that regulatory discretion-the formally granted flexibility of regulatory agency officers to interpret and implement public policies created by elected officials-can foster new entry in regulated markets.

name: New venture entry
definition: For this study, we define new ventures as de novo entrants: entrepreneurial startups originating in the hydroelectric power industry that have not previously received a license approval.

name: Time to license approval
authors_terms: ["regulatory approval", "license approval", "time to approval", "time to license approval", "approval time"]
definition: The dependent variable is license approval of hydroelectric facility projects (0 if not approved, 1 if approved). After an approval, withdrawal, or denial event, the permitting case is dropped from the data set.

name: Political competitiveness
authors_terms: ["political competitiveness", "competitiveness in the political market", "electoral competition"]
definition: We coded the political competitiveness as high if the margin of victory was less than 5 percent for gubernatorial elections. We extended this logic to legislative seats and coded the political competitiveness as high if the margin by which the dominant party in that chamber held a majority was less than 5 percent.

name: Divided political party control
authors_terms: ["divided political party control", "divided control", "political party control"]
definition: When the same political party controls the legislative and executive levels of government, political control is united; when the same party does not control them, political control is divided. This is coded as 1 if state government has divided control and 0 otherwise.

name: Firm age
definition: Studio age is the number of years since the studio has first released a game.

name: Firm-specific human capital tenure
authors_terms: ["studio tenure of lead team", "firm-specific employee tenure", "studio-specific tenure"]
definition: The studio-specific tenure for an employee who is part of any lead team is the number of years since that employee first appeared as being credited in any role in a game that was released by the focal studio.

name: Industry human capital tenure
authors_terms: ["industry tenure of lead team", "industry employee tenure", "tenure in industry"]
definition: The industry tenure for an employee who is part of a lead team is the number of years since that employee first appeared as being credited in any role in a game (regardless of the studio that developed that particular game).

name: Quality of exploitative innovations
authors_terms: ["quality of exploitative games", "quality of exploitative innovations", "better exploitative innovations"]
definition: We define exploitative games as games that are either part of sequels or games that use franchised content (i.e., non-original-content games). We measured the quality of exploitative games developed by a studio by using the average scores of the media reviews for these games.

name: Quality of explorative innovations
authors_terms: ["quality of exploratory games", "quality of explorative innovations", "better explorative innovations"]
definition: We categorize exploratory games as those that are neither parts of sequels nor use franchised content (i.e., original-content games). We measured the quality of exploratory games developed by a studio by using the average scores of the media reviews for these games.

name: Relative quality of explorative innovations
authors_terms: ["relative quality of exploratory games", "quality of explorative innovations, compared to exploitative innovations"]
definition: We measured the relative quality of a studio's exploratory games compared to exploitative games by using the average scores of the media reviews for the games in each category. Specifically, we subtracted the average score of the media reviews of non-original-content (i.e., exploitative) games released by the studio in a given year from the average score of the media reviews of original-content (i.e., exploratory) games released by the studio in that year.

name: Batting resource advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative resource advantage in batting skills", "comparative batting advantage", "batting skill"]
definition: Comparative advantage describes the strengths of resources relative to competitors rather than absolute strengths: the organization with the more valuable industry-specific skills holds the advantage. A comparative advantage in a unique industry-specific skill set embedded in an organization's human capital can contribute to the positive outcome of competitive engagements; in baseball the salient skill sets are batting, fielding, and pitching.

name: Pitching resource advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative resource advantage in pitching skills", "comparative pitching advantage", "pitching skill"]
definition: Comparative advantage describes the strengths of resources relative to competitors rather than absolute strengths, and a comparative advantage in an industry-specific skill set embedded in human capital can contribute to the positive outcome of competitive engagements. A comparative advantage in pitching reduces the likelihood of loss by decreasing the rival's ability to score.

name: Fielding resource advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative resource advantage in fielding skills", "comparative fielding advantage", "fielding skill"]
definition: Comparative advantage describes the strengths of resources relative to competitors rather than absolute strengths, and a comparative advantage in an industry-specific skill set embedded in human capital can contribute to the positive outcome of competitive engagements. A comparative advantage in fielding reduces the likelihood of loss by decreasing the rival's ability to score.

name: Batting management advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative managerial advantage in the bundling and deployment of batting skills", "batting management"]
definition: Bundling refers to the processes used to integrate resources in order to create capabilities, and leveraging involves the processes used to configure and deploy capabilities in a particular market context; in a specific competitive contest a firm is limited to managing existing resource stocks. A team's weighted average per indicator captures the effectiveness of the manager: positive differentials between the simple and weighted averages indicate the degree to which resources were successfully bundled and deployed.

name: Pitching management advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative managerial advantage in the bundling and deployment of pitching skills", "pitching management"]
definition: Bundling refers to the processes used to integrate resources in order to create capabilities and leveraging to the processes used to configure and deploy capabilities in a particular market context; during a specific competitive contest a firm is limited to managing existing resource stocks. Comparative managerial advantage is the differential between the simple and the weighted team average per indicator, where positive differentials indicate the degree to which resources were successfully bundled and deployed.

name: Fielding management advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative managerial advantage in the bundling and deployment of fielding skills", "fielding management"]
definition: Bundling refers to the processes used to integrate resources in order to create capabilities and leveraging to the processes used to configure and deploy capabilities in a particular market context; during a specific competitive contest a firm is limited to managing existing resource stocks. Comparative managerial advantage is the differential between the simple and the weighted team average per indicator, where positive differentials indicate the degree to which resources were successfully bundled and deployed.

name: Starting pitcher resource advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative resource advantage in the pitching skills of starters", "starting pitchers"]
definition: Subindices of pitching skill were created for starting and relief pitchers to assess Hypothesis 4. Starting pitchers were defined as the four pitchers on a team who had the most starts during the season, an operationalization capturing over 71 percent of the games started over the three seasons.

name: Relief pitcher resource advantage
authors_terms: ["comparative resource advantage in the pitching skills of relievers", "relief pitchers"]
definition: Subindices of pitching skill were created for starting and relief pitchers to assess Hypothesis 4. Relief pitchers were defined as all other pitchers on the team's roster.

name: Starting pitcher management advantage
authors_terms: ["management of starters", "management of starting pitching skills"]
definition: Starting pitchers have low deployment flexibility: they are deployed through a tightly fixed rotation and usually rest four to five days between deployments. Managers therefore have less discretion in the deployment of starting pitchers than they do in the use of relief pitchers, and a comparative managerial advantage in the bundling and deployment of starters' pitching skills is argued to have a smaller effect on competitive outcomes.

name: Relief pitcher management advantage
authors_terms: ["management of relievers", "management of relief pitching skills"]
definition: Relief pitchers offer a higher level of deployment flexibility: managers may deploy them readily, in many games for several innings, infrequently, or to only one batter. In view of this difference, the authors argue that the management of relief pitchers has a greater effect on competitive outcomes than the management of starting pitchers.

name: Batting skill parity
authors_terms: ["parity in batting skills", "degree of parity in the resources", "similar resources in batting"]
definition: Effective management is less important if the organization's comparative resource advantage is large, because the large differential in resources overwhelms the influence of managerial bundling and deployment. When rivals' resources approach parity, the outcomes of competitive engagements are determined more by resource management than by resources, so the relationship between management of resources and outcomes is moderated by the degree of parity in the resources held by the two competitors.

name: Pitching skill parity
authors_terms: ["parity in pitching skills", "similar resources in pitching"]
definition: Effective management is less important if the organization's comparative resource advantage is large, because the large differential in resources overwhelms the influence of managerial bundling and deployment. When rivals' resources approach parity, the outcomes of competitive engagements are determined more by resource management than by resources, so the relationship between management of resources and outcomes is moderated by the degree of parity in the resources held by the two competitors.

name: Fielding skill parity
authors_terms: ["parity in fielding skills", "similar resources in fielding"]
definition: Effective management is less important if the organization's comparative resource advantage is large, because the large differential in resources overwhelms the influence of managerial bundling and deployment. When rivals' resources approach parity, the outcomes of competitive engagements are determined more by resource management than by resources, so the relationship between management of resources and outcomes is moderated by the degree of parity in the resources held by the two competitors.

name: Competitive contest outcome
authors_terms: ["outcomes of competitive contests", "relative performance", "team A win percentage", "winning percentage in dyads"]
definition: The dependent variable is the relative performance of the teams in the dyadic competitive contests within each season. Measuring direct engagements between rivals allows the independent effects of resources and their management to be assessed, and isolating performance to the level of dyadic engagements is an important extension for resource-based logic.

name: Ethnic inventor composition of R&D headquarters
authors_terms: ["ethnic share of RDHQ", "ethnic inventor share of RDHQ", "ethnic invention at RDHQ", "ethnic workforce at RDHQ", "legacy ethnic composition of RDHQ"]
definition: The contemporaneous ethnicity of the inventive workforce in the firm's RDHQ; it is measured in the same way as the satellite outcome but using inventors located at RDHQ.

name: Ethnic inventor composition of satellite locations
authors_terms: ["ethnic share of inventors for the focal satellite location", "ethnic composition of inventors in satellite locations", "ethnic inventor share"]
definition: The observed ethnicity of the inventive workforce at the satellite aggregating over inventor-patents. It is the average share of the satellite's inventive workforce of neither Anglo-Saxon nor European ethnicity.

name: R&D centralization
definition: We measure R&D centralization as the firm's concentration of domestic inventive activity in the RDHQ. Our primary measure of centralization, labeled RDCentr, is the share of a firm's domestic patents in its RDHQ in the first period observed.

name: Intrafirm inventor mobility
authors_terms: ["intrafirm mobility", "career mobility", "rate of intrafirm career mobility to RDHQ", "inventor mobility"]
definition: Mobility is defined for inventors based upon whether they patent when working at RDHQ at least once during their career.

name: Cross-location inventor collaboration
authors_terms: ["cross-facility team collaboration", "team collaboration on patents between the satellite and RDHQ", "spatially distributed inventive teams", "rate of inventor collaboration over locations"]
definition: Cross-location inventive teams, measured as team collaboration on patents between the satellite location and the parent RDHQ.

name: Technology similarity between satellite and RDHQ
definition: Satellites have the same technology focus as RDHQ, defined using modal NBER subcategories of inventor-patents for the two locations.

name: Organizational reproduction
definition: Organizational reproduction speaks to persistence of features, long-standing or newly acquired, within and across locations, such as demographics and inequality.

name: Investor-centric contact selection
authors_terms: ["investor-centric contacts", "investor-centric search", "cognitive search cued by social proximity to targeted investors"]
definition: Selection of network contacts through cognitive search that brings investor-centric sub-sections of the average entrepreneur's personal network into salience, that is, contacts socially proximate to the targeted investor rather than to the focal entrepreneur.

name: Reciprocity persuasion tactic
definition: A promise of future reciprocity made to a selected network contact, which the authors expect to increase the contact's motivation to react favorably to the entrepreneur's referral request compared with baseline. It draws on social exchange theory's notion of reciprocal exchange, in which individuals contribute to an exchange without knowing when and to what extent the counterparty will reciprocate.

name: Monetary incentive persuasion tactic
definition: An unambiguous offer of monetary incentives by the entrepreneur to a selected network contact in return for the contact rendering assistance; the authors examine it as a specific type of negotiated exchange in which the precise terms of exchange are known before making it.

name: Successful referrals
definition: The count of successful referrals to panel investors that originated from a selected contact of the entrepreneur; a digital message is coded as a successful referral only if the investor informs the research team that the message that reached them came from a person whom the investor would respond to.

name: Gender diversity
authors_terms: ["gender diversity", "gender composition", "workforce gender composition", "a firm's overall gender diversity"]
definition: This study focuses on a firm's overall gender diversity rather than on diversity in small groups or in top management teams.

name: Normative legitimacy
definition: A practice gains normative legitimacy when it is accepted as appropriate and desirable based on norms and values that are widely shared in the larger society. It has both social and cognitive dimensions and is distinct from regulatory legitimacy.

name: Regulatory legitimacy
definition: Regulatory legitimacy refers to institutional processes based on monitoring, rule setting, and sanctioning. A practice gains regulatory legitimacy when regulators support it, usually through policies and standards.

name: Market valuation
authors_terms: ["market valuation", "future market valuation", "Tobin's Q", "investors' perceptions of a firm's future value"]
definition: Market valuation is the performance dimension determined by investors, capturing the market's perception of a firm's long-term value. It is measured in this study with Tobin's Q.

name: Firm revenue
definition: Firm revenue is the second dimension of firm performance examined, covering outcomes related to a firm's productivity and revenue. It is measured with return on assets, which measures actual return without taking into account stock market speculations.

name: Female entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["female entrepreneurs", "female-led ventures", "gender of the entrepreneur", "founder gender", "female founders"]
definition: Female entrepreneurs are the founders who pitch and seek capital for their ventures; in the field study this is captured by whether the entrepreneur completing the application was female (Female = 1, Male = 0), with the application to be completed by the founder or CEO.

name: Communicative abstraction
authors_terms: ["communicative abstraction", "speech abstraction", "level of abstraction", "abstract speech", "concrete speech", "abstractness", "concreteness"]
definition: An individual's communications can also be characterized in terms of their relative level of abstraction, i.e., whether they use more abstract language that captures the bigger picture or more concrete language that captures more specific details.

name: Long-term growth orientation
authors_terms: ["long-term growth orientation", "perceptions of long-term growth and scalability", "growth orientation", "long-term growth potential"]
definition: Long-term growth-oriented firms are startups that seek to scale and maintain rapid growth over time, distinguished from small businesses and low-growth firms in both their strategy to maximize profits through a long-term orientation on growth and scalability, and their reliance on venture funding to help them achieve this growth.

name: Likelihood of investment
definition: Investment likelihood is assessed based on a binary measure of whether the startup was one of the approximately 10% of startups that made it through the initial stage of funding consideration.

name: Supplier technical capabilities
authors_terms: ["technical capabilities", "technical capability of supplier", "supplier's technical capabilities", "capabilities"]
definition: The ability of a potential supplier to produce a component according to the desired specifications and schedule. Because capabilities are developed by carrying out related activities repeatedly and are difficult to articulate or transfer, potential suppliers have heterogeneous capabilities at any point in time.

name: Product modularity
definition: Modularity in product design implies that changes in one component of the product do not require changes in other parts of the product; modularity allows for information hiding, in which knowledge about the inner workings of one component need not be shared with the makers of other components.

name: Internal supply
definition: Organizing production around suppliers that are part of the same company as the buyer. Internal suppliers offer easier communication and lower risk of opportunism, through governance instruments such as managerial fiat, but dampen high-powered incentives and incur bureaucratic costs.

name: Prior buyer-supplier relationship
authors_terms: ["past relationship", "prior transactions", "manufacturer-supplier relationship", "prior relationships", "past transactions", "long-term suppliers"]
definition: The degree to which a manufacturer and a potential supplier have transacted in the past. Over extended interaction partners develop communication routines, a common language, and trust that eases governance, but long-term relationships may also incur the cost of diminished incentives.

name: Supplier selection
authors_terms: ["choice of supplier", "supplier selection", "selected that supplier", "CHOICE", "choosing a supplier"]
definition: For each innovation, the manufacturer chooses one supplier from the pool of all potential suppliers to work with in designing and producing the innovative component.

name: Multimarket contact in exploration
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact in exploration", "MMCexplore", "average MMCexplore", "multimarket contact explore"]
definition: An instance of multimarket contact in exploration (MMCexplore) occurs when firm i, an incumbent firm that is then researching new drugs in market m, and another firm j, that also conducts research in that market m (and is thus a rival in exploration), also meet in market n, where both also conduct research and development activities. It is measured as a count that sums the number of markets other than focal market m in which firms i and j also compete.

name: Multimarket contact in exploitation
authors_terms: ["multimarket contact in exploitation", "MMCexploit", "average MMCexploit", "multimarket contact exploit"]
definition: An instance of multimarket contact in exploitation (MMCexploit) occurs when firm i, an incumbent firm that is then selling drugs in market m, and another firm j, that also sells drugs in market m (and is thus a rival in exploitation), also meet in market n, where both also sell commercial products. It is measured as a count that sums the number of markets other than focal market m in which firms i and j also compete.

name: Explorative entry
authors_terms: ["explorative entry", "explorative activities in markets", "entry in exploration"]
definition: For exploration activities, entry is defined as the event of investing in research for a new-product technology that may or may not lead to a viable product in the future in a given market.

name: Explorative exit
definition: For exploration activities, exit is defined as the event of divesting from research for a new-product technology that may or may not lead to a viable product in the future in a given market.

name: Exploitative entry
definition: For exploitation activities, entry is defined as the event of starting sales activities of existing products in a given market.

name: Exploitative exit
definition: For exploitation activities, exit is defined as the event of ceasing sales activities of existing products in a given market.

name: Airbnb presence
authors_terms: ["Airbnb's entry", "the entry of Airbnb", "number of Airbnb listings", "Airbnb supply"]
definition: The entry of the Airbnb platform into a hotel's local market, measured by the county-month specific number of Airbnb listings; hotels with Airbnb in operation in the same county and time period are the treatment group.

name: Occupancy rate
authors_terms: ["occupancy rate", "occupancy rates of tourist hotels", "hotel demand"]
definition: The occupancy rate is the monthly average occupancy rate, defined as the ratio of the number of occupied rooms per month. After Airbnb's entry, hotel demand can be decreased if travelers decide to use Airbnb listings instead of hotels.

name: Room price
authors_terms: ["price", "hotel price", "daily room rate", "average hotel daily room rate"]
definition: The average daily room rate per night is the hotel price.

name: Investment in service quality
authors_terms: ["service quality", "investment in service quality", "quality response", "nonprice response strategy"]
definition: Service quality in lodging and food and beverage (F&B) are specified as the number of employees in the room department (housekeeping per room) and F&B department per guestroom, respectively. Since more human resources per guestroom imply a longer duration of service time and shorter customer waiting time, a larger value for these variables indicates better service quality.

name: Hotel quality
authors_terms: ["hotel quality", "high quality hotels", "low quality hotels", "five-star hotels", "three stars or fewer"]
definition: High quality hotels are those with five stars and low quality are those equal to or below three-stars in the ranking system of the Taiwan Tourism Bureau, which ranks tourist hotels based on their level of facilities, operation conditions and service quality.

name: Organizational resource endowments
authors_terms: ["resource endowments", "resources", "historical resource endowments and competencies", "accumulated stock of valuable resources", "distinctive competencies"]
definition: Scarce, valuable, and imperfectly imitable resources that are the only factors capable of creating sustained performance differences among competing firms, and which are accumulated through path-dependent historical processes of learning and asset accumulation. The authors focus on resources that have historically served as valuable mechanisms for differentiation and have provided organizations with the competencies necessary to successfully implement their strategies.

name: Reputation
definition: A college's renown, captured by the breadth of its national drawing power and the strength of its selectivity; colleges with esteemed reputations enjoy enduring advantages that cannot be readily imitated or competed away.

name: External support relationships
authors_terms: ["external support relationships", "philanthropic support", "social capital", "supportive external relationships"]
definition: Supportive external relationships with suppliers of financial resources and other production factors; measured as a college's philanthropic support from alumni, parents and other donors.

name: Human resources
definition: The quality of a college's faculty, an enduring resource that cannot be readily imitated or competed away.

name: Financial assets
definition: A college's financial resource endowment, defined literally as the annual market value of its endowment.

name: Cumulative organizational experience
definition: An organization's cumulative experience and learning, for which age is taken as an indicator: each additional year of an organization's continued survival necessarily reveals some significant evidence of increasing capability.

name: Student quality
definition: The ability of the students a college attracts; students are in an important sense inputs or raw materials, and those few colleges with access to exceptionally talented students enjoy a clear and enduring advantage over their peers.

name: Scale of operations
definition: The size of a college's operations, measured as its enrollment; included because of its prominent place in the evolutionary theories of Schumpeter and Nelson and Winter.

name: Scope of operations
definition: The breadth of a college's operations, measured as the total number of fields in which it granted undergraduate majors; included because of its prominent place in the evolutionary theories of Schumpeter and Nelson and Winter.

name: Strategic change
definition: A college's strategy is the percentage of degrees that it grants in non-liberal-arts fields in a given year; increases in this variable over time provide a particularly good indicator of strategic change, capturing the degree to which a liberal arts college has departed from its traditional and defining core strategy.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance is measured in terms of changes in a college's full-time-equivalent undergraduate enrollment, which provides a very clear indicator of the organization's fitness with its environment and is strongly correlated with financial performance measures such as operating margin.

name: Recombination
authors_terms: ["distant and diverse recombinations", "long-jump search", "wide recombination", "local search (narrow recombination)", "distant and diverse recombination", "technological distance", "technological diversity"]
definition: Long-jump search is recombination involving distant or diverse knowledge, where narrow recombination of similar knowledge can be seen as local search. Higher levels of the measures capture recombination (the tension view) and lower levels capture local search (the foundational view).

name: Cognitive novelty
definition: The formation of new topics in patent data can be seen as the emergence of novel ideas, and those patents that originate new topics can be thought of as cognitive breakthroughs. A topic-originating patent is an indicator of a truly novel idea.

name: Economic value
definition: An innovation may or may not turn out to be valuable in terms of generating economic returns for the owners of the invention.
