Breakthrough innovations have typically been measured by the number of forward citations, where higher numbers of citations indicate that a patent represents a breakthrough.

name: Downsizing
definition: The willingness of firms to take advantage of legislation that legitimated workforce downsizing as a response to market exigencies, indicated by reductions in a firm's permanent workforce.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "poor-performing Spanish firms", "high-performing firms", "Above Subsector Average EBIT Growth", "Above Subsector Average Sales Growth"]
definition: Performance judged relative to the average of the manufacturing subsector to which the firm belongs; poorer performing organizations are expected to be more receptive to change, whereas high-performing organizations are less likely to change.

name: Regional concentration
authors_terms: ["regional concentration", "regional dispersion", "regionally concentrated", "firms whose branches are concentrated in particular regions"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's branches are situated in particular regions rather than being dispersed across regions; regionally concentrated firms are expected to be the targeted recipients of community pressures.

name: Regional-national government
definition: A region governed by a party committed to a form of 'regional-nationalism' that champions the region's distinctiveness and pursues civic boosterism; the authors treat it as a signal of strong regional sentiment.

name: Regional government spending on industrial development
authors_terms: ["Regional Government Spending on Industrial Development", "high regional government spending on industrial development", "regional government invests heavily in industrial development"]
definition: High levels of regional government spending on industrial development, which indicate a regional stance that goes beyond the rhetoric of civic boosterism to purposeful commitment.

name: Regional salience of manufacturing sector
authors_terms: ["Regional Salience of Manufacturing Sector", "industries that provide high employment"]
definition: The salience of the manufacturing sector to the social and economic vitality of a region, indicated by the employment the sector provides; industries consequential to a region are monitored by the regional elite.

name: Firm size
definition: Organization size, used as an indicator of a firm's visibility: larger firms are highly visible and thus an especial target of regional pressures, and are more likely to be members of regional elites.

name: Family management
definition: A firm in which owners and their families are active in managing the firm, and which is therefore expected to be motivated by family values rather than only by market considerations.

name: Ethnic diversity
definition: Ethnic diversity refers to ethnic diversity of a community, which is fundamental to the way individuals identify themselves and develop communication boundaries; a high level of ethnic diversity in a community reduces social solidarity and social capital because it discourages reliance on other community members.

name: National origin diversity
definition: Diversity of national origin in a community; individuals in immigrant societies tend to display an attachment to their country of origin, as evidenced by patterns of individuals colocating with conationals, the use of their mother tongue, and the development of social clubs and informal activities delineated by national origin.

name: Religious diversity
definition: Religious diversity involves people congregating at regular intervals and hence has a strong influence on associational patterns and the spread of information; religion promotes intragroup trust but may discourage intergroup trust.

name: Economic inequality
definition: Inequality in wealth and income levels in a community; greater economic inequality is generally seen as leading to less intragroup trust and community participation, because individuals tend to develop distrust toward those in other economic classes.

name: Bank run
definition: Breakdowns in trust tended to occur between depositors and banks, leading to mass deposit withdrawals, often referred to as a bank run. Bank runs are typically measured using bank suspensions: banks faced with a bank run temporarily suspend deposit withdrawals, which is called suspension of convertibility.

name: Bank run contagion
definition: The influence of earlier bank runs elsewhere on the probability that a bank experiences a run; it is assumed that runs are less likely to influence distant communities than communities nearby, so the influence is distance weighted.

name: Board heterogeneity
definition: 'Heterogeneity' is defined as the extent to which actors form connections with others from quite different backgrounds. We argue that board heterogeneity provides a firm with access to a broad range of alliance opportunities.

name: Board multiplexity
definition: 'Multiplexity' is the extent to which actors are connected by more than one type of relationship. 'Multiplexity' is defined as two or more different relationships between the same actors.

name: Board centrality asymmetry
definition: We use the term 'asymmetry' rather than overlap because our theoretical attention is on the distribution and differences across ties rather than the density or overlap among the ties. When the structure of the network provides certain board members with more influence than others, there will be asymmetry in the network.

name: Outside director centrality dominance
authors_terms: ["outside-director asymmetry", "asymmetry with outside directors having dominance", "dominant outsider"]
definition: 'Outside-director asymmetry' is the difference in centrality between the top outsider and top investor board member when the outsider has higher centrality and is zero otherwise. When central outside board members dominate the board, the generic expertise of the outside board member will facilitate the sharing of information and the formation of diverse alliance portfolios.

name: Investor director centrality dominance
authors_terms: ["investor-director asymmetry", "investor board dominance", "asymmetry with investor board members having dominance"]
definition: 'Investor-director asymmetry' is the difference when the investor board member has higher centrality and is zero otherwise. When the asymmetry between outsider and investor board member centrality favors the investor board members, the firm will be slower to develop a diverse alliance portfolio.

name: Diverse alliance portfolio
definition: An 'alliance portfolio' is defined as a firm's collection of direct alliances with partners. Alliance portfolio diversity is defined as having multiple types of alliance partners.

name: Revenue milestone attainment
authors_terms: ["revenue milestones", "major revenue milestones", "attainment of important revenue milestones"]
definition: The second dependent variable is whether and when important revenue milestone events are reached. We code the year in which the firm obtains US$10 million, US$20 million, and US$50 million in annual revenues.

name: Director gender
definition: The focal independent variable is director gender (female = 1). Gender was identified by matching ISS director rosters with director biography profiles in the BoardEx database.

name: Multiboard holding
authors_terms: ["multiboard holding", "number of board seats", "multiple board appointments", "multiboard directors"]
definition: Holding concurrent board seats on multiple firms. The corporate 'inner-circle' is defined as the small group of elite directors who hold positions on multiple corporate boards; Useem (1984) defines inner-circle members as directors who hold two or more board appointments at U.S. public corporations.

name: Key committee chair
authors_terms: ["key committee chair position", "chairing key board committees", "key committee positions"]
definition: Whether the director held a key committee chair position; key committees include the audit committee, which oversees the firm's financial reporting, and the compensation committee, which oversees compensation of top executives. Chairing these committees affords directors greater influence in board processes.

name: Interorganizational network influence
definition: The transmission of corporate governance practices between firms connected by board interlocks, such that a focal firm adjusts its e-index score to match that of its network neighbors. The effect is estimated separately for interlocks mediated by male and female directors.

name: Corporate governance entrenchment
definition: A six-item index that captures the focal firm's corporate governance profile, and includes 1) poison-pills, 2) golden-parachutes, 3) staggered boards, 4) supermajority voting requirements, and limits on shareholder 5) by-law and 6) charter amendments. High scores indicate that managers are more entrenched, whereas low scores indicate more shareholder friendly governance.

name: Inequality in R&D expenditure within a segment
authors_terms: ["inequality in R&D expenditure", "R&D leadership", "kingpin's share of R&D expenditure"]
definition: Inequality in R&D expenditure is calculated using the kingpin's share of R&D expenditure relative to its segment's total R&D expenditure in each segment-year. High values mean there is a major inequality in technological investment among participating firms in a segment-year.

name: Inequality in value within a segment
authors_terms: ["inequality in value", "inequality of value", "kingpin's share of market capitalization"]
definition: Inequality in value is calculated using the kingpin's share of market capitalization relative to its segment's total market capitalization in each segment-year. High values for the kingpin's share mean there is a major inequality in value among participating firms in a segment-year.

name: Segment's share of value within the sector
authors_terms: ["segment's share of value", "share of total value", "percentage of market capitalization (segment to the sector)"]
definition: The dependent variable is the percentage of market capitalization (segment to the sector) for each NAICS code-year, that is, each segment's market capitalization divided by the total market capitalization of the entire sector for that year.

name: Value share of fringe firms in a segment
authors_terms: ["share of value to the other firms of that segment", "segment's share of value excluding that of the kingpin", "fringe firms"]
definition: The value share captured by the firms of a segment other than the kingpin, obtained by excluding the kingpin's market capitalization when calculating the segment's market capitalization so as to see how the fringe firms are affected over and above the kingpin.

name: Peer restatement event
authors_terms: ["peer restatement event", "financial restatement at a peer firm", "peer restatement", "peer restatement events"]
definition: Firms affected by a financial restatement at a peer firm, where peer firms are identified based on the presence of a shared director who is a member of both boards; the authors refer to the firms affected as focal firms and to the firms issuing the restatement as restating firms.

name: Audit-nomination multi-committee directors
definition: Directors who structurally link different board committees and are referred to as multi-committee directors (MCDs); audit-nomination MCDs are directors who are concurrent members of the board's audit committee and nomination committee, and their structural position allows them to be aware of the priorities and strategic considerations of multiple committees.

name: New director appointments
authors_terms: ["new director nominations", "# New directors", "appointing new directors"]
definition: New directors appointed to the board in a given year; the nomination committee's mandate of recruiting new directors can result in changes that are either substantive or merely symbolic, and director nominations can shift the capabilities of the board for years to come.

name: Prior board experience of new directors
authors_terms: ["prior board experience", "new directors w/ board exp.", "# New directors w/ board exp."]
definition: Newly appointed directors who possess prior board experience at a publicly traded firm; because such directors have been vetted by other firms, the focal firm is more likely to trust that they can effectively fulfill their responsibilities.

name: Prior audit committee experience of new directors
authors_terms: ["prior audit committee experience", "new directors w/ audit exp.", "# New directors w/ audit exp."]
definition: Newly appointed directors who possess prior experience on an audit committee on the board of a public firm; such directors have experience with another firm's financial reporting and thus a point of comparison for judging the focal firm's procedures.

name: Focal firm financial restatement
authors_terms: ["# Restatements", "financial restatements filed by the focal firm", "future financial restatements"]
definition: The total number of adverse financial restatements filed within each focal firm on an annual basis; adverse restatements are more likely to indicate overly aggressive accounting, operational and/or managerial problems and a corresponding governance failure.

name: Time
definition: The year of the event within the 60-year sample frame; the independent variable is a counter representing the year in the sample, from 1 to 60.

name: Absolute market reaction to unexpected CEO death
authors_terms: ["absolute (unsigned) market reactions", "absolute market reaction", "|CAR|", "mean |CAR|", "CAR standard deviation"]
definition: The overall magnitude or dispersion of market reactions-the size of the reactions, positive or negative, but without regard to the actual sign-to the deaths of CEOs.

name: Market reaction to unexpected CEO death
definition: The market reaction to an unexpected CEO death, computed as the actual market return minus the expected return generated by Eventus, cumulated over the event windows; the mean signed CAR is the average signed reaction to a CEO death.

name: Base pay level
authors_terms: ["base pay", "pay level", "base salary", "level of base pay"]
definition: Base salary is one of the three components of an individual's pay, along with short-term bonuses and long-term incentives; taken together, these three components determine the level of cash compensation.

name: Pay mix
authors_terms: ["pay mix", "extent of variable pay", "variable pay", "contingent pay", "ratio of bonus to base pay", "long-term incentive eligibility"]
definition: We measured pay mix, or the extent of variable pay, in terms of the relative amounts of short-term bonuses, long-term incentives, and base salary in an individuals' pay.

name: Human capital investment
authors_terms: ["human capital investment", "human capital", "years of education", "potential labor market experience", "length of firm tenure", "length of job tenure"]
definition: Human capital theory (Becker, 1975) identifies several employee attributes associated with lifetime earnings. Some of the most important of those attributes reflect investments in training, such as formal education and on-the-job training.

name: Job responsibility
authors_terms: ["level of job responsibility", "job level", "hierarchical level", "job characteristics"]
definition: The higher in an organizational hierarchy a job is the greater potential impact on organizational performance its incumbent is likely to have.

name: Organization membership
authors_terms: ["organizations", "organizational effects", "the organization an employee worked for", "a dummy variable for each firm"]
definition: Our approach was to take the increment in R2 occurring between Equations 1 and 2 as indicating the general organizational effect.

name: Industry
definition: Organizations in a particular industry "encounter similar constraints of technology, raw materials, product demand, and pricing" that provide a constraint on ability to pay.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["size", "firm sales", "unit sales", "total employees", "sales volume", "number of employees"]
definition: Specific organizational characteristics were size, measured as firm sales, business unit sales, and total employees.

name: Financial performance
definition: We defined ROA as net income divided by assets.

name: Stated pay level policy
authors_terms: ["self-reported pay level policy", "stated pay level policies", "target pay level"]
definition: We obtained that information from the survey question "How do you define your target pay level?" (below the median, at the median, between the median and the 75th percentile, at the 75th percentile, above the 75th percentile).

name: Attentional orientation toward earlier-stage exploration activities
authors_terms: ["attentional orientation", "orientation toward earlier stages of opportunity advancement", "degree of attention toward earlier-stage exploration activities", "attention toward earlier-stage exploration activities"]
definition: We adopt Cho and Hambrick's (2006) concept of attentional orientation, which in turn draws on Ocasio's (1997, 2011) work on attention, and apply it to a firm's degree of attention toward certain stages of opportunity advancement; ranging from a relatively higher degree of attention toward earlier-stage exploration activities and related evaluation decisions, to a relatively higher degree of attention toward later-stage exploitation activities and related evaluation decisions.

name: Speed of venture termination decisions
authors_terms: ["speed of venture termination decisions", "decision speed", "speed of terminating a venture", "speed of venture termination"]
definition: Decision speed is often thought of as 'how quickly organizations execute all aspects of the decision-making process' (Forbes, 2005: 355). Our measure of 'decision speed' captures the duration of time a mining venture spends in a stage before a decision is made to act on the venture.

name: Speed of venture advancement decisions
authors_terms: ["speed of venture advancement decisions", "decision speed", "speed of advancing a venture", "speed of venture advancement"]
definition: Decision speed is often thought of as 'how quickly organizations execute all aspects of the decision-making process' (Forbes, 2005: 355). Our measure of 'decision speed' captures the duration of time a mining venture spends in a stage before a decision is made to act on the venture.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: One critically important attribute of a venture's environment is the level of dynamism; that is, the degree of market change or volatility (Bakker & Knoben, 2015; Dess & Beard, 1984).

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance refers to the extent to which home and host country cultures are different.

name: Expatriate parent country national staffing
authors_terms: ["expatriate parent country national staffing", "expatriate staffing", "employment of expatriate parent country nationals", "use of expatriate parent country nationals"]
definition: Staffing subsidiaries with expatriate parent country nationals thus represents a cultural control strategy that simultaneously grants subsidiaries flexibility in choosing actual courses of action to achieve the parent's strategic objectives and ensures a high degree of compliance with commands from headquarters.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The performance of an overseas subsidiary; in this study it is captured by subsidiary labor productivity, measured as sales over the number of subsidiary employees.

name: Length of subsidiary operation
authors_terms: ["length of subsidiary operation", "years of operation", "number of years of operation", "longer operation"]
definition: The time a subsidiary has been operating in its host country; longer operation reduces agency costs, deepens local isomorphism, and therefore decreases reliance on expatriate parent country nationals in culturally distant locations.

name: Predecessor CEO retention as board chair
authors_terms: ["predecessor CEOs staying on as board chairs", "retention of the predecessor CEO as board chair", "predecessor - board chairs"]
definition: In this study, 'predecessor CEOs staying on as board chairs' referred to those staying on without an explicit departure plan; the presence of the predecessor as board chair challenges the principle of unified leadership and may lead to a potential power struggle between the predecessor CEO and the new CEO.

name: Stock market reaction to new CEO appointment
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction to the appointment of a new CEO", "negative stock market reaction to new CEO appointments", "cumulative abnormal return (CAR)"]
definition: Stock market reactions to new CEO appointments represent shareholders' collective assessment of whether a new CEO fits the job. A strong negative stock market reaction clearly reflects shareholders' concern about the new CEO.

name: New CEO early dismissal
authors_terms: ["CEO early dismissal", "early dismissal", "dismissal within three years of appointment"]
definition: 'CEO early dismissal' refers to a dismissal that occurs within three years of succession.

name: Public praise of predecessor CEO
authors_terms: ["public praise of predecessor CEO", "other-enhancement", "new CEO's public praise of their predecessor"]
definition: In the context of the present study, 'other-enhancement' refers to a new CEO's public praise of their predecessor who stays on as the board chair; it is a way of showing their recognition of the predecessor's achievements and contributions to the firm, and of affirming the retained predecessor's power in the firm.

name: Commitment to strategic continuity
definition: 'Opinion conformity' refers to the new CEO's commitment to strategic continuity (i.e., commitment to strategies that were adopted by their predecessor); such public commitment demonstrates the new CEO's willingness to inherit the predecessor's legacy and to recognize the latter's continued impact in the firm.

name: Self-centered expression
definition: In this study, we focus on new CEOs' self-promotion through self-centered expression; the use of first-person singular pronouns offers rich information about oneself and allows actors to draw attention to themselves.

name: Expression of confidence
definition: Actors who want to be seen as competent display their confidence more proactively; when new CEOs articulate their plans for future work in a more confident manner, they create an impression of a good person-job fit.

name: R&D search
definition: R&D search refers to the allocation of resources to R&D, which most studies have considered as a key behavioral consequence of performance feedback. Following earlier studies, the authors measured R&D search as the ratio of R&D spending to sales.

name: Inconsistent feedback
authors_terms: ["inconsistent feedback", "inconsistent performance feedback", "inconsistency between positive performance feedback and negative performance prospects"]
definition: When backward-looking feedback and forward-looking prospects are inconsistent, comparisons of current performance levels relative to those from the past and those foreseen in the future diverge systematically. In this study the configuration used is positive performance feedback combined with negative performance prospects, studied through the interaction of the two variables.

name: CEO structural power
definition: CEO structural power is based on formal organizational structure and hierarchical authority, and defines the interpersonal dynamics within TMTs.

name: CEO ownership power
definition: CEO ownership power is determined by the CEO's position in the principal-agent relationship, and indicates how the CEO interacts with the BOD and powerful shareholders.

name: CEO expert power
definition: CEO expert power is derived from the CEO's exposure and relationships with stakeholders within the firm's task environment, such as employees, suppliers, and customers.

name: CEO prestige power
definition: CEO prestige power is based on the CEO's reputation and standing within the firm's institutional environment.

name: Rational justification
definition: Rational justification can be defined as the use of rational appeals, data, analysis, and/or arguments to demonstrate the benefits of an initiative.

name: Use of formal authority
definition: Some groups may be in a position to accumulate hierarchical power either because they are launched on top management authority or because they manage to recruit powerful project sponsors, initiative leaders, or members of the team. Involvement and support by individuals with formal authority endows an initiative with hierarchical power.

name: Coalition building
definition: Coalition building represents behind-the-scenes efforts to develop relationships and secure cooperation from a wide variety of organizational actors.

name: Degree of exploration
definition: More exploratory initiatives are defined as innovative undertakings whose goals and methods are incompatible with the organization's existing knowledge base and capability. The degree of exploration is defined along a continuum rather than treating exploration and exploitation as orthogonal constructs.

name: Initiative performance
definition: As the proximate outcomes of group influence activity, therefore, the approval of internal stakeholders and the resources that result from such approval are appropriate indicators of initiative performance.

name: CEO career horizon
definition: Career horizon concerns relate mainly to the stage of the career of a CEO: the nearer a CEO is to retirement, the shorter is the career horizon. The variable was measured as the time to retirement for a CEO, calculated as 70 (retirement age and a few years of service on boards) minus the age of the CEO, so that the younger the CEO, the longer his or her career horizon.

name: Engagement in international acquisitions
definition: International acquisitions are equity-based modes of foreign market entry; compared to non-equity modes they entail more resource commitment, financial disbursement, structural adjustments, and control. Acquisitions are considered a form of risk taking and international acquisitions heighten the uncertainty about a firm's future income stream.

name: CEO equity holdings
definition: CEOs' equity holdings represent a significant amount of personal wealth and an endowed wealth, given equity is immediately available to possibly sell and use proceeds for consumption; their value is sensitive to the time left to hold them.

name: CEO in-the-money option holdings
authors_terms: ["in-the-money CEO option holdings", "unexercised in-the-money options", "option holdings"]
definition: As options become in-the-money (stock price exceeds grant price), a CEO's potential gain from option holdings becomes attainable rather than potential, and unexercised in-the-money options would then represent wealth that is available for consumption upon exercise (through income from their spread at exercise).

name: Franchised ownership
definition: The outlet's organizational form: whether the store is franchised or owned and operated by the franchisor. The franchisee keeps the remaining outlet profits, net of royalties paid to the franchisor.

name: Menu price
definition: The dependent variables are the (log) prices of the meals analyzed: Big Mac, Quarter Pounder, Double Quarter Pounder, Chicken McNuggets 6 pc., and Filet-O-Fish.

name: Repeat customer share
definition: Outlets that serve larger proportions of repeat customers face more salient reputational concerns, which attenuate their incentives to behave opportunistically. In outlets that serve few repeat patrons, such as outlets located near highways, franchisees do not have sufficient incentives to set low prices, because many of their patrons are unlikely to return.

name: Price advertising
definition: In running an advertising campaign, the franchisor determines the content of the campaign, specifically the prices advertised, whereas franchisees have the final say on whether to adopt the advertised prices at their outlets. Price advertising creates a reference price for customers, which they then compare with the actual prices they encounter.

name: Substitutability with advertised items
definition: The degree to which a nonadvertised item is a close substitute for the items advertised in the Dollar Menu campaign. The authors expect a low-price advertising campaign to induce franchisees to lower the prices of nonadvertised items that are close substitutes for the advertised items, and not to find similar effects for items without close substitutes in the advertised set.

name: Intangible assets
authors_terms: ["intangible assets", "intangible asset advantages", "advertising assets", "technological assets", "advertising intensity", "R&D intensity"]
definition: Intangible assets are the foundation of a firm's motivation to expand into new geographic markets and generate advantages in the home country that can be exploited in overseas markets. Caves (1996) defined an intangible asset as knowledge, technological or otherwise, that is unique to a firm, and it might also take the form of a trademark, patent, or brand.

name: Host country experience
authors_terms: ["host country experience", "investment history in the host country"]
definition: A firm's accumulated operational experience in the host country of a subsidiary, which contributes to the development of new knowledge and capabilities applicable to the local environment and thereby reduces the scope of the firm's competitive disadvantage. It was operationalized as the number of years of investment history a firm had in the host country.

name: Mode experience
authors_terms: ["mode experience", "experience with joint ventures", "joint venture experience"]
definition: A firm's accumulated investment experience with a particular entry mode: its investment history with joint ventures when the entry was a joint venture, or with wholly owned subsidiaries when it made an independent entry. Prior experience with the joint venture form can help a firm develop capabilities suited to successful management of joint ventures.

name: Foreign subsidiary survival
definition: The continued existence of the foreign subsidiary. Subsidiaries listed in earlier editions of the directory but not in the 1997 edition were treated as exits, and the exit definition includes exits by divestiture and dissolution.

name: Foreign subsidiary profitability
definition: A managerial assessment of subsidiary profitability in which the subsidiary's general manager classified the subsidiary's financial performance into one of three categories: loss, breakeven, or gain. It is an absolute assessment made without reference to other subsidiaries of the multinational.

name: Entry mode
authors_terms: ["entry mode", "joint venture", "wholly owned subsidiary", "local partner joint venture"]
definition: Whether the foreign subsidiary was established as a joint venture with a local partner or as a wholly owned subsidiary. A joint venture was an entry in which a Japanese firm and a local firm each held at least 5 percent of the subsidiary's equity; wholly owned subsidiaries had 95 percent or greater equity ownership by one firm. A local partner provides locally applicable skills and capabilities, reducing the subsidiary's dependence on the multinational's host country experience.

name: Team network density
authors_terms: ["network density", "density of a team's internal network", "density"]
definition: Network density is the average strength of the relationship between team members; it is minimized when no relationships exist between team members and maximized when all team members are connected by strong relationships. The authors calculate a team's network density as the average frequency of communication among the scientists on an R&D team.

name: Team network heterogeneity
definition: The authors define a team's network heterogeneity as the extent to which interaction on the team cuts across salient demographic categories. As they calculate it, a high level of network heterogeneity on a given team indicates that the fact that a given pair of team members entered the organization many years apart does not reduce their level of interaction.

name: Team productivity
definition: Team productivity is constructed from the answers team managers give to a question about how many of each of 11 written products and/or prototypes the team produced during the last three years. High scores on the variable indicate the extent to which a team has generated many papers, proposals, patents, and reports.

name: Socioemotional wealth endowment
authors_terms: ["SEW endowment", "socioemotional wealth", "family control and influence", "family control of firm equity and the board chairperson position"]
definition: The stock of affect-related value that the family has invested in the firm. The authors operationalize the SEW endowment (family control and influence) by combining family control of firm equity and the family occupying the board chairperson position, arguing that family control and influence are among the most important dimensions of SEW.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "performance below social aspirations", "performance below aspiration levels"]
definition: Firm performance before succession compared with other firms in the same industry, that is, performance that does not meet performance expectations. It captures the extent of the shortfall, since negative deviations from the industry average ROA are taken as absolute values while non-negative deviations are set to zero.

name: Successor birth order
definition: The birth order position of the incoming family leader within the nuclear family of the leaving leader, distinguishing the appointment of the firstborn child (primogeniture) from the appointment of a second- or subsequent-born offspring who breaks the primogeniture rule.

name: Post-succession firm performance
definition: The accounting performance of the firm after the leadership succession, measured with return on assets (ROA), which is computed as the ratio between operating income and total assets.

name: Family firm generational stage
authors_terms: ["founder successions", "non-founder successions", "second generation and later", "later-generation successions"]
definition: Whether the succession occurs while the leaving leader is the company founder or in a non-founder (second generation or later) succession; SEW preservation tendencies and the grooming of successors are argued to differ between these stages of a family firm's evolution.

name: Financial resource availability
authors_terms: ["financial resource availability", "firm financial resource availability", "financial resources", "self-generated funding"]
definition: Profitability and profit are direct measures of self-generated funding, a major supply of pecuniary resources and also represent a tangible indicator of the availability of resources to potentially fund social investments.

name: CSR expenditures
authors_terms: ["CSR", "corporate social responsibility", "CSR expenditures", "expenditures on CSR", "corporate socially-directed activity"]
definition: Our expenditure-related measure has the advantage of providing an objective, monetary quantification of a firm's CSR, as well as representing a substantive commitment of resources rather than the mere symbolic commitment associated with the making of verbal claims or CSR website reporting. GIPC data reflected monetary contributions by companies under six broad areas: health concerns, education, poverty alleviation, environmental concerns, issues relating to the socially vulnerable, and sports.

name: Employment protection
authors_terms: ["employment protection", "implied contract exception", "wrongful discharge laws", "employment-at-will doctrine"]
definition: Staggered adoptions of employment protection laws are exploited as a quasi-natural experiment that generates an exogenous decrease in the adjustment ability of firms located in adopting states. An implied contract exception becomes effective when an employer promises not to terminate a worker without just cause, decreasing the pace with which firms can reconfigure their human resources.

name: Competitive position
authors_terms: ["competitive position", "leader or laggard", "laggard position", "firm's position as a leader or laggard", "relative performance"]
definition: A firm's competitive position is whether the firm is a leader or a laggard relative to its industry benchmark. The authors rely on industry-adjusted return on assets (ROA) as the main measure of a firm's relative performance and competitive position.

name: Firm innovation
definition: As the creation and implementation of new ideas or products, innovation requires accessing and experimenting with diverse and novel resources. The authors examine both the quantity and, separately, the quality and novelty of firm innovation.

name: Innovation quality
authors_terms: ["quality", "number of citations received", "quality distribution of patents"]
definition: The authors use the number of citations received by a firm's patents to proxy for the quality of its innovation, in contrast to the quantity of innovation proxied by patent count.

name: Patent market value
definition: Kogan et al. (2017) measure a patent's market value based on three-day abnormal returns in response to news of its grant by the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

name: Patent novelty
definition: A patent is assessed to contain novel technology if it combines technology classes that have not been frequently combined before by other patents in the same USPTO technology class (three-digit nclass) in the past five years.

name: Technological search breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of technological search", "active patent classes", "number of distinct three-digit patent classes"]
definition: The count of distinct three-digit patent classes in which a firm files for patents each year proxies for the level of resource adjustment and experimentation based on the breadth of technological search rather than its direction.

name: Inventor turnover
definition: Each patent application contains information on the name of the inventor and its assignee, which permits examining firm-level adjustment in human resources. A 'new hire' is an inventor who produces his or her first patent at a given firm after producing at least one patent at a different firm in prior, and a 'fire' is an inventor who files for a patent at a different firm.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity is used as a direct proxy for the amount of effort at innovation, allowing the authors to distinguish between the inputs and the outputs of the innovation process.

name: Industry dynamism
authors_terms: ["industry dynamism", "mean reversion", "changes in a firm's position", "upward reversion"]
definition: Industry dynamism is examined as the likelihood of mean reversion whereby laggards catch up and overtake leaders, that is, the probability that firms change their position between leader and laggard.

name: Technological velocity of a sector
definition: Each four-digit SIC code is assigned as a high- or low-velocity sector based on the mean speed at which patents accumulate citations. The measure closely resembles the notion of a half-life and intends to capture the speed at which new technology is adopted.

name: Managerial overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence is the tendency of individuals to think that they are better than they truly are with respect to their abilities, judgments, or future prospects, and to underestimate risk. Following previous studies, we use overconfidence and optimism interchangeably.

name: Founder CEO status
definition: To determine whether a CEO is the founder or cofounder of a company, we utilize public information from multiple sources. Our main explanatory variable, Founder CEO, equals one for founder CEOs and zero for professional CEOs.

name: CEO issue ambivalence
authors_terms: ["ambivalence", "ambivalent evaluations", "evaluative ambivalence", "CEO's issue ambivalence", "ambivalent evaluation of a strategic issue"]
definition: Ambivalence describes an individual's experience of competing reactions toward an issue or object—for example, when a person simultaneously attaches positive and negative valence to an issue. It is the degree to which an issue is framed as simultaneously positive and negative.

name: Organizational action taking
authors_terms: ["action taking", "organizational action", "action in response", "likelihood of organizational action"]
definition: Action arises from search processes that match issues ('problems') to specific actions selected from the organization's 'solution space' of response routines; the paper predicts the likelihood that the organization will act in response to an issue.

name: Scope of action
authors_terms: ["scope of action", "scope of the action", "scope of action response"]
definition: The breadth of the overall response, which increases with the number of potential action responses considered and with the commitment to effectively implementing them.

name: Perceived riskiness of action
authors_terms: ["perceived riskiness", "riskiness of the action", "riskiness of action"]
definition: The CEO's perception of how much risk the actions taken in response to the issue contain for the firm; actions are perceived as riskier when experiential knowledge about the success of this type of action is rare.

name: Perceived novelty of action
definition: The CEO's perception of how new the actions taken in response to the issue are for the firm, ranging from continued existing activities to completely new activities.

name: Positive issue evaluation
definition: Positive evaluations are one of the two orthogonal dimensions of issue evaluation, associated with approach and promotion repertoires; the authors measured the degree to which the CEO evaluated the EU enlargement positively with two items.

name: Negative issue evaluation
definition: Negative evaluations are the second orthogonal dimension of issue evaluation, associated with withdrawal and prevention repertoires; the authors measured the degree to which the CEO evaluated the EU enlargement negatively with two items.

name: Reputational threat
authors_terms: ["reputational threat", "environmental shareholder activism", "environmental stakeholder activism", "environmental activism", "nonenvironmental shareholder activism", "nonenvironmental stakeholder activism"]
definition: Reputational threats can occur when stakeholders recognize organizational misdeeds and bring those actions to light in an effort to pressure the organization to rectify its actions or take responsibility for its transgressions. The authors focus on recent actions that threaten an organization's reputation for sustainability, evaluated as environmental shareholder resolutions and environmental protests, boycotts, or civil lawsuits.

name: Publicizing a certification
authors_terms: ["publicizing a certification", "publicize its certification status", "publicize its DJSI membership", "DJSI membership publicized", "strategic silence"]
definition: The managerial decision to publicly disclose membership in the DJSI, identified by any mention of DJSI membership in annual reports filed with the SEC, corporate social responsibility or sustainability reports, and corporate press releases.

name: Domain-specific organizational reputation
definition: A domain-specific evaluation made by certain actors, i.e., being known for something, rather than a global or generalized perception of favorability. Domain-specific reputation causes stakeholders to interpret actors' actions differently and to hold such actors to higher standards of accountability.

name: Certification legitimacy
definition: The degree to which the certification is recognized as a legitimate signal, which occurs as constituencies increasingly endorse, value, and discuss the certification so that it achieves legitimacy in the form of collective understanding and acceptance among audience members.

name: Information technology experience
authors_terms: ["accumulated experiences in computer and telecommunication areas", "cumulative experience, information technology", "prior experience in information technology", "experience in information technology", "learning by doing"]
definition: The main independent variables are the accumulation of experience in information technology and in interfirm linkages. Information technology in the banking sector consists of back-office automation and transactional-oriented technology.

name: Interfirm linkages
definition: Interfirm linkages include joint ventures, licensing or contracting the rights to use, produce or market certain products, systems or services without transferring the ownership rights, marketing agreements, R&D agreements and supply agreements. We distinguish two types of linkages; the first class contains various information technology firms, while other linkages are confined to the banking sector.

name: Capital investment experience
authors_terms: ["capital investments in systems and equipment", "investment expenditure in systems and equipment", "productivity index of systems and equipment", "learning by using"]
definition: A firm's capital investment history and its accrued performance reflect accumulated experience, which in turn reflects a propensity to allocate capital expenditures to new technologies such as video banking. The firm's experience in information technology is measured by two indicators: its investment expenditure in systems and equipment and a productivity efficiency index.

name: Video banking adoption
authors_terms: ["video banking services", "videotex adoption", "entering video banking", "the adoption event"]
definition: The empirical research in this study addresses the introduction of a specific new form of information technology: video banking services. This study centers on a dichotomous dependent variable: whether or not a firm employs the video-banking services.

name: Long-run financial performance of acquiring firms
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "long-run financial performance", "post-acquisition financial performance", "acquirer performance"]
definition: For the financial performance variable, two measures were used: accounting return on assets and market return.

name: Relative size of acquiree to acquirer
authors_terms: ["relative size", "relative size of acquiree to acquirer", "asset ratio"]
definition: The measure selected for the relative size analysis is the acquiree asset weighted mean as a percentage of the acquirer's assets at the end of the year prior to acquisition.

name: Acquisition rate
definition: The acquisition rate in terms of acquisition events over time is also believed to be a factor in the performance of an acquisition strategy. Two measures were used: the mean number of acquisitions per year and the mean number of acquisitions per year divided by 1976 assets.

name: Asset acquisition rate
definition: The measure used for asset acquisition rate, which reflects a combination of acquisition size and rate factors, is the percentage ratio of assets acquired in the study time period (1967-1976) to end-period (1976) assets.

name: Industry commonality between acquirer and acquiree
definition: Industry commonality between acquirer and acquirees was measured by the percentage of acquired assets which were of the same SIC code as the acquirer, analysed at the two-digit level.

name: Acquisition timing relative to the market cycle
authors_terms: ["acquisition timing", "market timing", "timing relative to the market cycle"]
definition: The measure used for the acquisition timing relative to the market cycle factor was based on the Standard and Poor 500 trend line; the acquisition timing measure is the ratio of the Standard and Poor 500 average value for the third month prior to the effective date of acquisitions to the Standard and Poor trend value for that month.

name: Type of consideration used in payment
authors_terms: ["type of consideration", "type consideration", "method of payment", "percentage cash acquisitions"]
definition: The type of consideration (cash or securities) used in payment. The measure used for the type of consideration factor was the percentage of asset acquisitions in dollars accomplished for cash.

name: Acquiree profitability prior to acquisition
authors_terms: ["acquiree profitability", "acquiree net income on assets prior to acquisition"]
definition: The acquiree profitability factor was measured by the acquiree net income after taxes as a percentage of the assets of the acquiree in the year prior to acquisition.

name: Price paid for acquisitions
definition: The price paid factor was measured by the acquiree net income after taxes in the year prior to acquisition as a percentage of the price paid; this reciprocal of the price paid to income stream was used in order to avoid a complex function involving extremely high positive and negative measure values.

name: Firm financial performance
authors_terms: ["poor firm performance", "firm performance", "industry-adjusted return on asset (ROA)", "ROA"]
definition: Our primary indicator of firm performance is industry-adjusted return on asset (ROA). ROA is equal to net income before extraordinary items divided by total assets for a given fiscal year.

name: CEO dismissal
definition: CEO dismissal takes 1 if CEOs forcibly discharged from the firm. We identified dismissals when CEOs were reported to depart as both CEO and board member before the age of 64 for reasons other than death, illness, acceptance of comparable positions at other organizations, or merger and acquisition.

name: Workforce downsizing
definition: Within the agency perspective, downsizing through layoffs is a normal practice, in which employees are regarded as costs to be cut. Agency logic is embodied in the practices of workforce downsizing and business refocusing - ones that are widely accepted as appropriate to generating economic returns for shareholders.

name: Business refocusing
definition: Another was refocusing the business through divestitures. Firms that were acquired were stripped into separate business units for sale; survivors voluntarily sold off noncore businesses to avoid takeover bids.

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Within the stakeholder perspective, CSR is perceived as a core business function that is vital to the firm's competitive success. In the post-Enron era, CSR has increasingly become a normal practice, in which it is viewed as a legitimate part of the firm's strategy.

name: Geographic distance
definition: The distance between two members' locations within the organizational forum. The authors transposed each senator's Chamber desk location into Cartesian space and used these coordinates to construct Chamber distance between two senators' desks with great precision.

name: Joint support
definition: Following other scholars, the authors consider bill cosponsorship to be a trace of the joint support between two senators, and use these cosponsorships to construct the pattern of joint support among U.S. senators.

name: Intraorganizational power
definition: Within an organization, the authors suggest that powerful individuals, those who have the ability to shape the allocation of organizational resources and attention, have a greater likelihood of being sought out. A senator's power is tightly correlated with his or her ability to control the legislative agenda, and, by tradition, this ability is primarily determined by seniority.

name: Election cycle
authors_terms: ["election cycle", "i and/or j in election cycle", "campaigning senators"]
definition: Within any given Congress, one out of three senators faces an impending election. Campaigning senators spend a greater amount of time in their home district, away from the Senate Chamber floor.

name: Market density
definition: The strength of competition is determined by the number of organizations participating in a given market (the organizational density), with many competitors giving stronger selection pressures. Market density is the number of stations in the market.

name: Unit organizational form
definition: Whether an organization is an independent unit organization or a component of a larger structure. Unit organizations are directly selected based on their fit to their environment, while organizations that are components of a larger structure are selected as a group.

name: Speed of aspiration-level updating
authors_terms: ["aspiration-level updating speed", "speed of aspiration-level adjustment", "aspiration-level adjustment speed", "slow adjustment of aspiration levels", "time perspective"]
definition: Aspiration levels can be updated with different speeds, depending on how quickly decision makers accommodate to performance that diverges from their aspiration level. A higher weight on the previous aspiration level relative to realized performance means slower updating.

name: Historical aspiration level
definition: An aspiration level formed from the organization's own past performance, where a decision maker makes a new aspiration level as a weighted average of the previous aspiration level and realized performance.

name: Design-based experimentation
definition: We refer to the first approach as design-based experimentation (DbE), emphasizing its focus on designing experiments to create an environment favorable to the entrepreneur's preferences.

name: Theory-based experimentation
definition: We label the second approach as theory-based experimentation (TbE) because it relies on a business theory tested with new information, akin to the scientific method.

name: Information acquisition
authors_terms: ["Information (cum)", "total amount of information collected", "amount of information"]
definition: We constructed variables to capture both the quantity and direction of information gathered by entrepreneurs. The total amount of information collected is calculated as the average of these four components.

name: Favorable information
definition: Favorable information is calculated as the product of information and its direction, which ranges from zero to one; zero represents negative information and one represents positive information.

name: Subjective belief of success
authors_terms: ["Belief p", "subjective belief of success", "estimated probability of success"]
definition: where p is the subjective belief of success based on the information accumulated up to that stage.

name: Project termination
definition: Termination is a dummy variable equal to one if entrepreneurs declared to abandon their project and zero otherwise.

name: Commitment to the idea
definition: Commitment is a dummy variable equal to one if four conditions are jointly satisfied for the two last rounds of data collection in a row; otherwise, it is equal to zero.

name: Revenue performance
definition: Cumulative revenue (in euros) accumulated by the start-up, measured at the latest data point collected for each start-up; the distribution is right-skewed as the majority of start-ups reported no revenue during the data-collection period.

name: Innovativeness of the business idea
definition: We asked entrepreneurs whether their business idea is based on a patent, providing a dummy variable equal to one if yes and zero otherwise.

name: Business model investment type
authors_terms: ["type of business model investment", "New Model", "investments in the new model", "investments in the existing model", "business model investment"]
definition: In this study, we focus on the problem of incumbents allocating their resources through investments in the existing and the new business models during the nascent period of industry change, and we explore how those strategic decisions impact their firms' valuations.

name: Firm value
definition: Firm value is a well-established forward-looking performance outcome for strategies whose payoffs are expected to accrue over time such as strategies related to R&D investments, acquisitions, and alliances. Theoretically, firm value also helps to isolate the effect of firms' investment decisions during the early stage of industry change when the emerging business model is still nascent, and there is a high degree of uncertainty with respect to its viability and industry dominance.

name: Existing model assets
authors_terms: ["assets that are specific to the existing model", "Existing Model Assets", "generation assets", "asset stocks"]
definition: Some assets such as retailers' physical stores are specific to the existing model and may not be readily deployed within the new business model. Such assets may be rendered obsolete if the new business model becomes dominant.

name: Market competition
definition: Incumbents have to manage a delicate balance between both business models, which may be especially challenging in more competitive environments such as those characterized by low barriers to entry and intense rivalry.

name: Alliance
authors_terms: ["Alliance", "alliances", "mode of investment (alliance versus in-house)", "investing via alliances"]
definition: Incumbents can pursue the new model on their own or through alliances. Alliances are likely to be with entrants or established firms from outside the focal industry, who can help incumbents gain access to new assets, capabilities, and even customers who may be more amenable to the new model.

name: Complementary technologies
authors_terms: ["complementary technologies", "technologies complementary to its focal technology", "complementary counterparts"]
definition: 'Complementary technologies' refers to the different technologies within an ecosystem where the value creation from one increases in the presence of the other. They are conceived as solutions to different, more narrowly defined modules of problems within a broader overarching problem.

name: Disclosure to standard setting organizations
definition: During standard setting, firms disclose their IP over technologies relevant to the standard in question. Their disclosure letters list components that are 'technically essential,' that is, ones where it is difficult for any firm to implement the standard without infringing on the IPs over them.

name: Technological area crowdedness
definition: The first contingency variable (Crowdedness) is the extent that technological areas in which the firm is involved, outside of the focal technology's area, are crowded with competitors.

name: SSO members' expropriation abilities
authors_terms: ["SSO Expropriation", "SSO members' abilities to expropriate others' technologies", "other firms with strong expropriation abilities that are active in the SSOs"]
definition: Not all firms, or in this case SSO members, can equivalently expropriate the focal firm's technologies; it depends on how quickly and effectively they can learn and absorb new knowledge. The measure captures the extent that there are other firms with strong expropriation abilities that are active in the SSOs that are relevant.

name: Secondary market thickening
authors_terms: ["thicken the secondary market", "thickening of the secondary market", "post craigslist entry", "entry of an intermediary"]
definition: Entry of a resale intermediary will 'thicken' the secondary market in the sense that it decreases search costs in that market, meaning that a customer who needs to resell a product will have an easier time locating a buyer. Craigslist is a platform for ticket resale, and therefore its entry into a county can indicate that the secondary market for tickets in the county has thickened.

name: Value appropriation
authors_terms: ["value appropriated", "appropriate more value", "distribution of economic rents", "mean price"]
definition: The value captured by firms in the primary market; prices are an important object of interest because, under certain conditions, they can be thought of as representing the value split between the seller and the customer on a given transaction. The authors' theory yields predictions about how the option value and cannibalization effects together affect the distribution of economic rents to firms in the primary market.

name: Product value and scarcity
definition: Temporal separation of the primary and secondary markets can arise when demand quickly outstrips supply, which might occur when a product is valuable and scarce. Firms selling valued products on the primary market can benefit from the option value effect of the thickening secondary market, and firms selling scarce products can avoid the cannibalization effect as they are likely to sell out their products before the secondary market starts to develop.

name: Quantity supplied
definition: The quantity a primary-market firm makes available; the authors argue that firms have incentives to engineer scarcity by limiting supply when secondary markets thicken, and that firms in their focal industry strategically manipulate supply in a manner that would increase the likelihood of selling out.

name: Propensity to sell out
authors_terms: ["sellout", "probability of selling out", "likely to sell out", "expected sellout"]
definition: The ex ante expectation that a show will sell out; prices were set as a function of the promoter and artists' expectations of how likely the show was to sell out, which the authors proxy with a predicted probability of selling out.

name: Reputation gap
definition: The reputation gap is the reputation differences between the focal seller and its matched competitor standardized by the reputation stock of both sellers. The authors argue that the ability of a reputable seller to command a price premium is driven by this gap rather than by the seller's absolute reputation stock.

name: Price premium
authors_terms: ["price premium", "P premium", "value added by Focal seller"]
definition: The price premium represents the difference in a customer's willingness to pay (i.e., her reservation price) for the product sold by Focal seller versus that for the product sold by Competitor. In this setting it corresponds to the value added by the Focal seller.

name: Seller reputation
definition: Reputation is defined as the 'representation of a company's past actions and future prospects that describes the firm's overall appeal to all of its key constituents when compared with other leading rivals.' It is measured as the difference between the number of positive and negative ratings for each selling party.

name: Cultural distance
authors_terms: ["cultural distance", "Kogut and Singh's (1988) cultural distance index"]
definition: The greater the aggregated differences in values between two countries, the greater the cultural distance (Kogut & Singh, 1988). It is used to estimate the magnitude of differences in sets of cultural values between countries.

name: Cultural tightness-looseness
authors_terms: ["tightness - looseness", "cultural tightness - looseness", "tightness of cultural norms"]
definition: Tightness - looseness is made up of two dimensions: 'how clear and pervasive norms are within societies' and 'how much tolerance there is for deviance from norms within societies'. Tight nations show strong norms, low levels of tolerance for deviant behaviors, and strong sanctioning; in loose nations, norms are weaker and deviant behavior is more tolerated.

name: Proportion of expatriate parent-country nationals
authors_terms: ["proportion of expatriate PCNs", "proportion of expatriate parent-country nationals"]
definition: Expatriate PCNs are individuals sent by MNE headquarters to foreign subsidiaries on a temporary basis for knowledge transfer, organizational development, or coordination and control. The dependent variable was the proportion of expatriate PCNs in a subsidiary, calculated by dividing the total number of expatriates by the total number of employees in a subsidiary.

name: Managers' educational affiliation ties
authors_terms: ["educational affiliation tie", "affiliation tie", "managers' ties", "practice leader ties", "Prac. leaders, same J.D., same time (dummy)", "Prac. leaders, same J.D. diff time (dummy)"]
definition: Affiliation ties develop when individuals have joint membership in the same social foci, where social foci are defined as psychological, legal, or physical entities around which joint activities are organized (Feld 1981); educational affiliation ties form when two individuals attend the same educational institution. The authors focus on educational affiliation ties that form when attorneys attended the same law school at the same time.

name: Interorganizational hiring
definition: Interorganizational labor mobility occurs when a hiring organization makes a job offer to a member of a different firm and that person accepts the offer. The authors measure it as the number of attorneys hired by one practice area from a rival practice area in a year.

name: Investment rate in physical capital
authors_terms: ["investment rate in physical capital", "investment rates", "investment conduct", "I/K"]
definition: I/K represents the gross flow of funds invested in fixed assets by a given firm in a given period, divided by the beginning of period stock of fixed assets. Investment excludes company acquisitions.

name: Tobin's Q
definition: Tobin's Q, the ratio of the market value of the firm to its current replacement value, is a positive determinant of investment; the more the market value of the firm exceeds its replacement costs, the greater the return to equity shareholders from further investment.

name: Internal cash flow
definition: Cashflow/K is the internal cash flow of the firm (funds from operations) normalized by the beginning-of-period capital stock. Internal cash flow rate is a second determinant of investment, beside Tobin's Q.

name: Coalitional firm governance
authors_terms: ["coalitional firms", "shareholder firms", "coalitional decision making", "bargaining power of labor"]
definition: In the United States actors have little long-term relationship with the firm and shareholders of common equity enjoy primacy in their claims on management, so U.S. corporations are characterized as shareholder firms, where investments are made primarily to maximize shareholder wealth. In Germany and Japan many external transactors are bound to the firm in long-term relationships and share control of strategic decisions, so German and Japanese corporations are characterized as coalitional firms, where investments are the outcome of a cooperative bargaining process among a broad array of constituencies.

name: Internal global environmental performance standards
authors_terms: ["level of internal global environmental performance standards", "level of minimum internal global environmental performance standards"]
definition: The level at which an MNC sets minimum worldwide environmental performance standards for all its operations; MNCs can thereby standardize the environmental impact of their operations across countries while allowing country subsidiaries to adapt policies, procedures, and technologies to local conditions.

name: Operational environmental policy standardization
authors_terms: ["global operational environmental policy standardization", "global standardization of operational environmental policies"]
definition: The extent to which an MNC standardizes its operational environmental policies globally, including environmental management practices, environmental control and auditing procedures, management incentives for environmental performance, and environmental technologies used in operations.

name: Environmental communication standardization
authors_terms: ["global environmental communication standardization", "global standardization of the content of its environmental communication"]
definition: The extent to which an MNC standardizes the content of its environmental communication globally, including the content of environmental messages in advertising and in communications to the public.

name: Government pressures
authors_terms: ["government pressures", "pressures by governments", "expectations about the international harmonization of environmental regulations"]
definition: Governments aim to control the environmental conduct of firms under their jurisdiction by imposing and enforcing environmental regulations, and rising international government cooperation contributes to harmonization of environmental regulations across countries; the construct captures management's expectations about this international harmonization.

name: Industry pressures
definition: Industry associations set industry norms for environmental conduct to protect the collective reputation of the industry, and industry pressures for environmental responsibility can also result from competitors' actions, because firms aim to enhance their legitimacy by imitating successful competitors.

name: Customer pressures
definition: As public concerns about environmental degradation rise, customers increasingly consider environmental factors in their purchasing decisions and assess MNCs' environmental responsibility on the basis of the companies' global environmental conduct.

name: Functional strategy standardization
authors_terms: ["global standardization of other functional strategies", "degree of global standardization of an MNC's functional strategies"]
definition: The degree of global standardization of an MNC's functional strategies outside environmental policy; environmental policies are closely integrated with other functional areas, so it is easier for MNCs with globally standardized strategies for other functions to standardize all of their environmental policy dimensions.

name: Subsidiary resource dependence
authors_terms: ["subsidiary dependence", "dependence of an MNC's subsidiaries on the rest of the company for resources"]
definition: The dependence of a subsidiary on the rest of an MNC for resources such as components, finished goods, funds, and technologies; such dependence is expected to reduce subsidiary resistance to the adoption of corporate environmental standards and policies and thus contribute to global standardization.

name: Network synergy
authors_terms: ["network synergy", "expected network synergy", "expected improvement in the acquirer's structural position"]
definition: The extent to which combining an acquirer's and a target's networks through node collapse results in a more favorable structural position for the combined firm. A network synergy is the net effect (benefits - costs) of collapsing the nodes of the acquirer and target plus inheriting the target's ties.

name: Structural hole synergy
authors_terms: ["structural hole synergies", "expected increase in access to structural holes", "change in constraint", "decline in constraint"]
definition: The expected increase in access to structural holes resulting from the combination of the acquirer's and target's networks, obtained either through access to novel, non-redundant ties or by eliminating preexisting, redundant ties. Declining constraint indicates an increase in access to structural holes.

name: Status synergy
authors_terms: ["status-based synergies", "expected increase in network status", "change in status", "change in eigenvector centrality"]
definition: The expected increase in network status resulting from the combination of the acquirer's and target's ties, indicated by an increase in eigenvector centrality. Because acquisitions always increase an acquirer's centrality if the target brings new ties, the comparison is against the increase that acquiring an alternative target would have produced.

name: Acquisition target selection
authors_terms: ["target choice", "acquisition target choice", "likelihood of selecting a target", "likelihood of acquisition"]
definition: The selection of a target firm by an acquirer out of the set of firms that could plausibly have been acquired instead. The dependent variable is coded as 1 if a firm i acquired target j, and 0 otherwise.

name: Common partners between acquirer and target
definition: The number of common partners between the acquirer and target pre-acquisition, which indicates redundant ties that a node collapse would eliminate.

name: Complementarity of new ties
authors_terms: ["complementary fit", "new ties that complement", "ties to universities", "university ties"]
definition: New ties gained from the target that complement the pre-acquisition network or capabilities of the acquirer, in contrast to new ties that merely add partners.

name: Acquirer technological diversification
authors_terms: ["acquirer technological diversification", "technologically diversified acquirers", "focused firms", "diversified strategies"]
definition: Whether the acquirer follows a focused strategy by working on one or a few therapeutic or technological areas or a diversified strategy by doing the opposite; diversified acquirers have a greater strategic need for networks rich in structural holes.

name: Acquiring ties to new partners
definition: The extent to which an acquisition target brings ties to partners that are new to the acquirer, regardless of whether those ties complement the acquirer's existing capabilities or network.

name: Aggregate process performance
authors_terms: ["aggregate process performance", "aggregate process efficiency", "aggregate process performance rank", "institutional aggregate process efficiency rank"]
definition: For each bank the individual process analyses are aggregated into an institutional aggregate process efficiency rank; the aggregation method determines the overall process performance score by combining tournament ranking techniques that accommodate missing data, as not every bank branch performed every process. We combine these individual ranks to establish an aggregate, or overall, process performance rank for each bank.

name: Process variation
definition: We define process variation as the variation in performance across the 11 individual process performance ranks for each bank. Specifically, we define process variation as the standard deviation for each bank across the set of up to 11 individual process performance rankings.

name: Financial performance
definition: We use Return On Assets (ROA) as our measure of performance because we believe it best captures the effect of internal process improvements on a firm's financial performance. The advantage of ROA is that it captures the efficiency of management's use of a firm's assets, independent of the firm's capital structure and size.

name: Going public
definition: An IPO is not simply a one-time financial transaction that provides a new source of capital. Instead, an IPO represents a broad transformation with longterm impact, not only on organizational structures, but also on organizational processes.

name: Overall innovative productivity
definition: Whereas overall innovative productivity reflects firms' current levels of commitment to innovation, innovation search strategies can be indicative of their future innovative prospects.

name: Exploratory search
authors_terms: ["exploratory search", "exploration", "proportion of innovation search that is exploratory"]
definition: To the extent that firms generate innovations by building on local, familiar knowledge, they are conducting exploitative search. When firms build on distant, unfamiliar knowledge, they are conducting exploratory search.

name: Flexibility increase
authors_terms: ["Flexibility increase", "increase in operational flexibility", "switching option value"]
definition: The core hypothesis testing variable, Flexibility increase, is the reduction in labor cost correlation in the foreign affiliate portfolio due to the addition of a potential host country to the portfolio. It captures the contribution an entry makes to the operational flexibility of the firm's manufacturing affiliate portfolio.

name: Foreign market entry
authors_terms: ["Market entry", "entry decisions", "propensity to establish a manufacturing affiliate"]
definition: The dependent variable is the hazard of a Japanese parent firm establishing a manufacturing affiliate in a host country. The decision of a focal firm to enter into a host country, Market entry, is a binary variable, which takes the value one when the firm enters a country, and zero otherwise.

name: Labor cost level dispersion increase
authors_terms: ["Labor cost level dispersion increase", "dispersion in labor cost levels", "labor cost level dispersion"]
definition: Labor cost level dispersion increase measures the increase in the dispersion of labor cost levels in the firm's portfolio of affiliates due to the addition of a new host country to the portfolio. Labor cost level dispersion in an affiliate portfolio is the standard deviation of labor cost levels of the host countries.

name: Product diversification
definition: Diversification takes into account both the number of industries in which a firm operates and the relatedness between the industries in terms of characteristics of the underlying resources. The greater the value of (unrelated) Diversification, the greater the difficulty and cost to shift production flexibly across countries.

name: Host country labor cost volatility
authors_terms: ["Host country labor cost volatility", "labor cost volatility in that host country"]
definition: Host country labor cost volatility is calculated as the standard deviation of labor cost over a five-year period (from t - 4 to t) for the focal country. A focal host country's labor cost volatility shapes switching option values and affects firms' decision to enter the country.

name: Organizational age
authors_terms: ["organizational age", "age of the work organization", "as organizations age"]
definition: The age of the individual's current work organization at a given point in time. The authors argue that as organizations age and grow they face pressures for formalization and rational bureaucracy, which change the entrepreneurial behavior of their members and founders.

name: Organizational size
authors_terms: ["organizational size", "size of the work organization", "as organizations grow"]
definition: The size of the individual's current work organization at a given point in time, measured in employees. The authors argue that as a social unit increases in size its members have less contact with outsiders and more homogeneous role relations.

name: Organizational role
authors_terms: ["organizational role", "founder role", "member role", "roles", "role in the organization"]
definition: The primary position an individual occupies in an organization, in particular whether the person is the organization's founder or a member (nonfounder). To measure organizational roles, the authors relied on answers to a survey question asking respondents to indicate their primary positions in their organizations; those who reported being in the founder role were coded as such and distinguished from members.

name: Transition to entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["transition to entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurship", "leaving to build a new organization", "foundings"]
definition: Entrepreneurship is the participation by an individual in the founding of a new organization; in the career history approach it is the transition from leaving one organization to founding another.

name: Centralization of procurement
