definition: Centralization is the concentration of decision-making, usually at the corporate level, whereas delegation grants decision-making authority to lower level employees. Here it is the choice of whether the materials procurement process is fully executed at the contractor's headquarters or delegated to the project level.

name: Vertical integration
definition: The firm boundaries decision: whether the contractor performs a specialty trade activity internally through an internal unit or buys it in the market using subcontractors.

name: Coordinated adaptation
authors_terms: ["coordinated adaptation", "hierarchically coordinated adaptation", "importance of coordination", "adaptation costs"]
definition: The management of interdependencies among activities, in which interdependencies must be optimized centrally to avoid inconsistent and nonsynergistic choices; centralization enhances coordinated adaptation at the expense of autonomous adaptation. Complexity and uncertainty increase the importance of coordination between procurement and specialty trades.

name: Agency costs
definition: Costs arising from asymmetric information and the impossibility of signing complete contracts between principals and agents, which create incentive misalignment; when agency concerns are important, centralization is more likely.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["local partners' affiliation with a business group", "local partner's affiliation to a business group", "group affiliation", "business group affiliates"]
definition: A business group is a set of legally independent firms bound together by a constellation of formal and informal ties; group-affiliated local partners possess resources and capabilities unlike those held by independent firms, and can help IJVs replace institutional voids, provide political capital, and bring project execution capability.

name: National business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["local partners' affiliation with a national business group", "local partner's affiliation to a national group", "nation-level groups"]
definition: With a national government's direct policy inducement and encouragement in their formation and development, nation-level business groups are often closely linked with the national government in their country; the 189 SASAC groups are considered China's 'national teams' and are leaders in their industries.

name: Regional business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["local partners' affiliation with a regional business group", "local partner's affiliation to a regional group", "region-level groups"]
definition: Region-level groups are embedded in a specific regional institutional environment and have stronger political connections with regional governments relative to independent firms and also as compared to national business groups; they have been formed primarily to promote regional economic growth and fiscal revenue.

name: FDI-restricted location
definition: During liberalization, specific areas in an emerging economy are favored for foreign investment activities; areas not among these designated FDI-open areas are FDI-restricted, have fewer investment and fiscal incentives, poorer infrastructural and institutional conditions, and larger institutional voids than FDI-open areas.

name: FDI-restricted industry
definition: Industries in which host country government policies restrict foreign ownership or encourage IJVs, so that a foreign firm is required to enter with a local partner; such industries have distorted market structures and heightened costs of doing business.

name: IJV performance
authors_terms: ["IJV performance", "survival likelihood", "IJV survival likelihood", "sales growth", "IJV sales growth"]
definition: IJV performance is captured by two outcomes the authors describe as critical to new ventures: the survival likelihood of the international joint venture and its sales growth.

name: Niche width
definition: Organizational ecologists define firms as specialists if they can only survive within a limited range of resources; generalists can draw sustenance from a wide range of resources—technologies, customers, employee skills, and other factors of production—to survive. One can therefore think of the organizational niche as the range of resource types and levels within which a particular firm can survive.

name: New product introduction rate
authors_terms: ["introduce new products", "product introductions", "proportion new products", "rate of product introductions"]
definition: The rate at which a firm brings new products to market, measured as the number of distinct new models divided by the total number of products offered by the firm. The authors note that 'the simple introduction rate of new products, however, does not completely explain the differences between generalists and specialists.'

name: Niche expansion
authors_terms: ["niche expansion", "products outside their existing niches", "products outside of the firm's existing niches", "niche-expanding products"]
definition: Product introductions that fall outside a firm's existing niche, i.e. products that require new resources or attract new customers. Operationally it is the number of products a firm introduces outside its existing niche divided by the total number of new products offered by the firm.

name: Technology adoption
authors_terms: ["adopt innovations", "technological expansions", "adoption of new technologies", "technological adoption"]
definition: Adoption of innovations that push the frontiers of current technology and product performance; the adoption of new technologies typically requires firms to develop new routines, to hire employees with new skills, and to court new customers.

name: Firm exit
definition: In both industries, an incumbent fails when it no longer offers products in that industry. Survival is used to assess organizational performance.

name: Mode of corporate diversification
authors_terms: ["mode of corporate diversification", "diversification strategy", "frequency of acquisition mode", "internal diversification", "acquisitive diversification", "mixed diversification strategies"]
definition: Of primary concern were the relative frequencies with which firms employed internal and external diversification strategies when they entered new businesses. Pitt's (1980) conceptualization of a continuum between purely internal and purely external strategies required that a measure of relative frequency be continuous and proportional.

name: Economic performance
definition: For each firm, economic performance between 1977 and 1981 was measured in four ways: by the average annual (1) growth in sales, (2) return on assets (ROA), (3) return on investments (ROI), and (4) return on equity (ROE). Averages were used to reduce variability in the data and to provide pictures of overall economic performance during the period.

name: Level of institutional development
authors_terms: ["institutional development", "level of institutional development", "the extent to which the economic, political, and social institutions in a host country are developed"]
definition: We define the level of institutional development as the extent to which the economic, political, and social institutions in a host country are developed and are favorable to foreign affiliates.

name: Level of foreign affiliate performance
authors_terms: ["level of foreign affiliate performance", "return on investment", "level of ROS"]
definition: The level of foreign affiliate performance represents the 'return' on an investment, and indicates the profitability of foreign affiliates in a host country.

name: Variation in foreign affiliate performance
authors_terms: ["variation in foreign affiliate performance", "risk of investment", "variation in ROS"]
definition: The variation in foreign affiliate performance within a host country represents the 'risk' of an investment, and indicates the extent to which the performance of foreign affiliates in a host country deviates from the host country mean.

name: Product line length
authors_terms: ["product line length", "product line action", "product line", "product line length (PROD)"]
definition: Product line length is measured by the number of product models. The authors use product line length and breadth interchangeably, consistent with prior research.

name: Past competitor product line action
authors_terms: ["past competitor product line action", "past competitor action", "past actions", "past competitor product line action (PCA)"]
definition: The total action of the major competitor(s) in product line or other marketing variable k in the period previous to t. The effect of past competitor actions on a firm's action in a marketing variable will be positive or negative, depending on whether the firm retaliates against or accommodates its competitors.

name: Anticipated competitor product line action
authors_terms: ["anticipated competitor product line action", "anticipated competitor action", "anticipated actions", "anticipated competitor product line action (ACA)"]
definition: The anticipated total action of the major competitor(s) in product line length or other marketing variable k in the period following t. Anticipated responses are a key determinant of new product introduction strategies.

name: Own product line demand elasticity
authors_terms: ["own product line demand elasticity", "own elasticity of demand", "clout (own demand elasticity)"]
definition: There are two components of competitive demand elasticity; namely, own elasticity of demand and cross-elasticity of demand. The own product line demand elasticity is a firm's clout, the elasticity of its own demand with respect to its own product line.

name: Cross-product-line demand elasticity
definition: Cross-elasticity of demand is the other component of competitive demand elasticity. The cross-product-line demand elasticity captures the effects of changes in competitors' product lines, including the market leader's, on the firm's demand, and is the firm's vulnerability.

name: Price action
definition: Price action (PRICE) is the firm's marketing action in price at time t. A firm's average price is based on the prices of its different product models weighted by their sales.

name: Distribution action
definition: Distribution action (DIST) is the firm's marketing action in distribution intensity or channel coverage at time t, that is, the weighted share of presence in the channels through which the products are sold.

name: Market leadership
definition: A market leader typically derives its dominance from selling a wide range of product models, while market followers are smaller firms that may not have adequate resources. HP was the market leader by a wide margin.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: New firms are classified as foreign or domestic using the data on equity held by nonresidents, firms having a foreign participation greater than 10 percent being classified as foreign owned. Foreign-owned firms typically have strong connections with other firms and must possess ownership advantages to compensate for their disadvantages in doing business abroad.

name: Workforce education
authors_terms: ["college graduates", "educational level of the workforce", "educated workforce", "human capital"]
definition: The level of education of a firm's workforce can be regarded as a measure (albeit imperfect) of ownership advantages. The propensity to develop firm-specific assets is measured by the share of college graduates among the firm's labor force.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["current size", "firm size", "number of persons in the firm", "employment"]
definition: Size was measured here by the number of persons in the firm. Current size should be a better predictor of exit than initial size, as the current size of firms includes information on the reaction of firms to their market success over time.

name: Firm growth
definition: An indirect measure of economic performance is used, such as the observed growth rate: firms which have experienced good outcomes will grow, while those which have bad times will contract, or ultimately exit. The fact that a firm has grown signals that it has been performing well and is optimistic about its success.

name: Limited liability
definition: Firms in our data set may operate under either limited or unlimited liability. Because the owners of limited liability firms are not accountable for the firm's debts, limited liability firms are argued to exit later than firms of unlimited liability.

name: Firm age
definition: In general, the probability of exit is expected to decline with the age of firms, a pattern widely established by research on new firm survival and attributed to the 'liability of newness' which characterizes the first years in business.

name: Probability of exit
definition: The hazard rate is defined as the probability that a firm exits during one particular period, given that it has survived until the beginning of that particular period. The left-hand side variable of the model is the logarithm of the hazard rate.

name: Ownership advantages
definition: Firms that go abroad must possess some type of asset that gives them some other sort of advantage, known in the theory of multinational enterprises as 'ownership advantages'; these include financial advantages, product differentiation and marketing advantages, and advantages accruing from economies of common governance or from the ability to exploit economies of scale at the plant level. The development of these firm-specific assets is largely dependent on the firms' ability to innovate and market their products, and is proxied in the empirical work by the educational level of the workforce.

name: Inventor structural centrality
authors_terms: ["structural centrality of an inventor in the intrafirm coinventing network", "centrality of an inventor in the intrafirm network", "inventor's structural centrality in the intrafirm network"]
definition: Inventors occupy a structurally central position in the intrafirm coinventing network when they form a large number of ties with other inventors who have coinventing ties with most others in the network (Bonacich 1987). These ties to central others put the focal inventor at the core of the intrafirm coinventing network.

name: Inventor impact
authors_terms: ["impact of an inventor on her firm's innovation activities", "impact of the firm's central inventors", "use of their knowledge in generating innovations of the firm"]
definition: One of the important dynamics in a firm's internal innovation activities is the impact that the firm's central inventors have on its innovation activities, for example, in the form of future innovations being built on their knowledge, as evidenced by citations to their knowledge. The dependent variable is the impact of an inventor on her firm's innovation activities.

name: Firm structural centrality
authors_terms: ["firm's centrality in the interfirm network", "firm's structural centrality in the interfirm network", "centrality firm"]
definition: As a firm becomes more structurally central in the interfirm network, it is connected to firms that are connected to most other firms. These multiple connections to other central firms generate large amounts of knowledge spillovers.

name: Firm span of structural holes
authors_terms: ["firm's span of structural holes in the interfirm network", "span of structural holes", "structural hole-spanning firm"]
definition: A firm spans structural holes when it connects those firms in the network that are not otherwise connected with one another (Burt 1992). A firm spans large structural holes if it is the only connection between large numbers of unconnected other firms.

name: TMT tenure heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["TMT tenure heterogeneity", "tenure heterogeneity", "TMT tenure heterogeneity", "tenure diversity"]
definition: Tenure heterogeneity, or the degree to which TMT members have spent widely varying amounts of time in their companies.

name: TMT member departures
definition: Departures was the number of members who left the TMT in year t. Such departures may be voluntary or involuntary, the former occurring because of members' own discomfort and the latter because of conflict and scapegoating in diverse groups.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance was measured using return on assets (ROA) in year t, or the ratio of net income to total assets (adjusted for operating leases; Ely, 1995).

name: Horizontal interdependence
definition: Horizontal interdependence is the degree to which roles are arranged such that the actions and effectiveness of peers affect each other.

name: Vertical interdependence
definition: Vertical interdependence refers to the degree to which members are peers, as opposed to hierarchically disparate.

name: Reward interdependence
definition: Reward interdependence is the degree to which members receive payoffs for firm (or group) performance rather than subunit or individual performance.

name: VC exit pressure
authors_terms: ["exit pressure", "VCs' exit pressure", "exit pressure faced by VCs on board", "exit pressure from VC directors"]
definition: VCs face increasing pressure to exit investments as their funds age. Their patience wanes as the fund ages and approaches the termination date.

name: Independent directors
definition: Independent directors are directors who are not venture managers/founders and do not represent investors.

name: IPO
definition: One of the four types of venture exit the authors measure; IPO tends to be limited to the most promising ventures.

name: High-value M&A
definition: M&As categorized by deal value; an M&A whose value is not lower than either the total amount raised or the latest valuation is a high-value M&A, and such exits can provide high returns for all shareholders.

name: Low-value M&A
definition: If an M&A value was lower than either the total amount raised or the latest valuation, it joined the category of low-value M&As, which fail to provide a good return for most shareholders.

name: Liquidation
definition: One of the four types of venture exit the authors measure; liquidations fail to provide a good return for most shareholders.

name: Internal agglomeration
authors_terms: ["internal agglomeration", "geographic clustering of business establishments owned by the same parent company", "internally agglomerated establishments", "firmMSA establishments"]
definition: Internal agglomeration is the geographic clustering of business establishments owned by the same parent company. In the study, internal agglomeration is clustering business establishments owned by the same parent firm in close geographical proximity.

name: Labor factor productivity
definition: LFP is measured as the establishment-level residual from a cross-sectional (year-by-year) regression of log sales on log payroll, and labor factor productivity is measured as the residual from a pooled OLS regression of log revenue on log payroll with year fixed effects.

name: Market-level productivity
authors_terms: ["MSA productivity", "market-level productivity", "average productivity of other establishments in the same market"]
definition: The average productivity of other establishments in the same market ('MSA productivity'); its inclusion controls for the effect of overall productivity changes in the focal establishment's market.

name: Geographic concentration of firm operations
authors_terms: ["All hotels in one MSA", "all of a firm's establishments are in the same market", "single market firm"]
definition: All hotels in one MSA, which is equal to one if the establishment is in a firm with all of its hotels in the same MSA in a particular year, and is zero otherwise; such firms are assumed to have their headquarters in that market and thus already low monitoring costs.

name: Change in internal agglomeration intensity
authors_terms: ["positive treatment", "negative treatment", "TREAT+", "TREAT-", "increasing intensity of internal agglomeration", "decreasing the intensity of internal agglomeration"]
definition: Positive treatment captures all the net benefits of internal agglomeration, including both contemporaneous and persistent effects; negative treatment only picks up a reduction in the net contemporaneous effects of internal agglomeration.

name: Liquidity
authors_terms: ["liquidity", "liquid assets", "cash held in reserve", "cash and equivalents"]
definition: Liquid assets refer to cash and equivalents that are fluidly exchanged in various markets. The authors use 'cash held in reserve' and 'liquid assets' interchangeably.

name: R&D intensity
definition: For each year, we calculated R&D intensity by dividing the firm's yearly R&D expenses by total assets in that same year. R&D intensity has frequently been used to gauge the fervor with which a firm pursues R&D and knowledge creation efforts.

name: Patent value
definition: Patents, weighted by their value, (hereafter 'patent value') should indicate a firm's inventive prowess, and should reduce capital costs as they inform external investors' about the abilities of the firm to successfully engage in the invention process, as well as the likelihood of achieving cash flows from the technology.

name: Exploitation alliances
definition: Exploitation alliances focus partners' efforts on deepening existing knowledge by improving established designs, products, and services to meet the needs of existing customers and markets.

name: Exploration alliances
definition: Exploration alliances focus more heavily on the development of new knowledge, and thus are likely to experience greater uncertainty and variation in outcomes.

name: Host-country experience
authors_terms: ["firm host-country experience", "own-firm experience", "own operating experience", "experience in a host country"]
definition: Cumulative years of experience that a firm has operating fabs within a given host country. Greater host-country experience helps to develop multinational expansion capabilities by reducing the overall liability of foreignness, and experienced firms draw on their own internal operating experience to assess a host country's environments rather than on the experience of others.

name: International experience
authors_terms: ["firm international experience", "international experience", "experience in other foreign countries"]
definition: Cumulative years of experience that a firm has operating fabs in other foreign countries outside its home country, capturing more general international expansion capabilities developed through a sequence of overseas investments.

name: Home-country experience
authors_terms: ["firm home-country experience", "firm's experience in its home country"]
definition: Cumulative years of experience that a firm has operating fabs in its home (origin) country.

name: Firm technological capability
authors_terms: ["firm technological capabilities", "technological sophistication", "technologically advanced firms", "technologically sophisticated firms"]
definition: The technological sophistication of a semiconductor firm's manufacturing facilities, measured relative to the leading edge in process linewidth for the products it manufactures. Firms in the industry vary in the degree to which they operate at or near the well-articulated technological frontier, and this capabilities difference is argued to influence their international expansion.

name: Political hazards
definition: A country whose political institutions fail to constrain policy makers from altering the status quo regime, thereby creating uncertainty over the future policy environment for domestic and foreign investors, is defined as being politically hazardous. The measure captures the extent to which a change in the preferences of any one actor can lead to a change in government policy.

name: Country technological environment
authors_terms: ["country technological environment", "country-level technological sophistication", "technologically sophisticated countries"]
definition: A country's innovative capacity, that is, its ability to produce and commercialize flows of innovation over the long term, reflected in the technological sophistication of the fabs located in the country. Multinational firms are argued to make foreign direct investments in host countries to source technological capabilities that are not resident, not cost-effectively available, or not available in adequate supply in their home countries.

name: Other foreign firms' host-country experience
authors_terms: ["foreign firms (different home country) host-country experience", "prior experience of other foreign firms", "other-foreign-firm experience"]
definition: The number of years of host-country fab operating experience accumulated by other foreign semiconductor firms whose home countries differ from the focal firm's home country, representing an external information source about the host country.

name: Same-home-country firms' host-country experience
authors_terms: ["foreign firms (same home country) host-country experience", "other producers from the same home country", "other-firm experience from the same home country"]
definition: The number of years of host-country fab operating experience accumulated by other foreign semiconductor firms that come from the same home country as the focal firm.

name: Domestic firms' host-country experience
definition: The number of years of host-country fab operating experience accumulated by domestic semiconductor firms resident in the host country.

name: Foreign investment
authors_terms: ["foreign investment", "foreign production facilities", "entry", "foreign investment by a semiconductor firm in a given country-year"]
definition: The construction of a new fab by a semiconductor firm in a host country outside its home country, which represents a significant capital expenditure commitment in both equipment and infrastructure development.

name: Retention of organizing patterns
authors_terms: ["retention", "retention activity", "retention intensity", "retention of a firm's existing organizing patterns"]
definition: Retention involves the preservation and subsequent dispersion of organizing patterns, previously adopted by a bank in certain subunits, across a bank's other subunits.

name: Intrafirm personnel inflow
authors_terms: ["intrafirm personnel inflow", "intrafirm inflow", "intrafirm personnel inflow event"]
definition: Intrafirm personnel inflows occur when individuals move within a firm's organizational boundaries; specifically, from one subunit to a peer subunit of the same parent firm. An intrafirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between two rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years.

name: Interfirm personnel inflow
authors_terms: ["interfirm personnel inflow", "interfirm inflow", "interfirm personnel inflow event"]
definition: Interfirm personnel inflows occur when individuals move to a subunit from a rival's subunit (e.g., across a firm's organizational boundaries). An interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves from a room of one parent bank into a room of a different parent bank over consecutive years.

name: Cross-border personnel inflow
definition: A cross-border personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving from one room into another room, and the rooms are located in different countries.

name: Local personnel inflow
definition: A local personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving from one room into another room and the rooms are located in the same country.

name: Cross-border intrafirm personnel inflow
definition: A cross-border intrafirm personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving between two trading rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in different countries. The authors reason that it combines the effects of cross-border inflow and intrafirm inflow.

name: Local intrafirm personnel inflow
definition: A local intrafirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between two trading rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in the same country. The authors reason that it combines the effects of intrafirm inflow and local inflow.

name: Cross-border interfirm personnel inflow
definition: A cross-border interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between the trading rooms of different parent banks over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in different countries. The authors reason that it combines the effects of interfirm inflow and cross-border inflow.

name: Local interfirm personnel inflow
definition: A local interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between the trading rooms of different parent banks over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in the same country.

name: Experience mix
authors_terms: ["experience mix", "mix of trader experience", "experience ratio", "organizational template"]
definition: The experience mix captures the diversity of the experiential knowledge base among traders in a room. A room's experience mix is the sum of the experience of the traders in that room.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility (CSR)", "CSR activities", "firm's CSR activities", "pro bono", "pro bono legal services", "pro bono activities"]
definition: Corporate social responsibility initiatives are defined as 'discretionary corporate activit[ies] intended to further social welfare' (Barnett, 2007: 795). In the empirical setting the primary CSR activity is pro bono legal services, the provision of free legal assistance to clients who cannot afford to pay for such services.

name: Occupation change
authors_terms: ["occupation change", "major occupation change", "occupation changes", "leaves the legal occupation"]
definition: A job change in which an employee changes occupations rather than moving to another firm within the same occupation. Individuals are likely to make occupation changes when they believe that the factors causing them dissatisfaction are occupation-related rather than firm-related.

name: New firm founding
authors_terms: ["founds a startup law firm", "founding a new firm", "the decision to found a new firm", "founds a new law firm"]
definition: The decision to found a new organization within the focal industry, which may reflect a preference for more meaningfulness as well as financial motives. The authors treat decisions to found a new firm as distinct from other employment transitions, including moves to a small but already established organization.

name: Mobility to established firms
authors_terms: ["leaves the firm for an established law firm", "joins established law firm", "moves to nonstartup law firms", "within-occupation mobility"]
definition: A move to an already established competitor while maintaining the current occupation. Movements within the occupation may be more likely to reflect motivations such as a desire to increase intra-professional status or compensation than a search for meaningfulness.

name: Overall employee turnover
authors_terms: ["overall turnover rates", "leaves the firm for any destination", "turnover", "employee departures"]
definition: Departure of an employee from the firm to any destination. The authors treat the turnover decision as containing mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive choices, of which overall turnover is the union of the departure destinations.

name: Mortality-related shock
authors_terms: ["mortality-related shock", "mortality-related shocks", "shock to the system", "the 9/11 terror attacks"]
definition: Shocks in the lives of employees cause them to reconsider the extent to which their jobs match their goals, desires, and preferences; shocks that enhance an individual's awareness of her own mortality may increase her desire for more meaningfulness on the job. The authors use the terror attacks of September 11, 2001 as a mortality-related shock for attorneys born in the NYC metro area.

name: Original search
definition: Original knowledge is that which a prior invention recombined for the first time, and ordinary knowledge is all other knowledge that is not original. 'Original search' is defined as search that targets original knowledge, regardless of where the search occurs.

name: Search boundary
authors_terms: ["search boundary", "search proximity", "local search", "boundary-spanning search", "locus of search"]
definition: The dimension of search boundary mainly concerns where to explore, whereas the dimension of search target concerns what to explore. On this dimension, search occurs either within or outside the local domain.

name: Path-breaking novelty
definition: A path-breaking novelty is an invention that breaks away from the existing path of technological progress by opening up a new path; it concerns the degree to which an invention is distinguished from existing knowledge.

name: High-impact breakthrough
definition: A high-impact breakthrough is an invention that provides an extremely useful basis for subsequent technology developments; it represents the extent of an invention's usefulness for subsequent inventions.

name: Exchange manager mobility
definition: When exchange managers move between firms in the same industry, they take with them critical human and social capital such as knowledge about the firm's routines and procedures and the client's trust and goodwill.

name: Market tie dissolution
definition: The termination of a relationship between a lobbyist and client; a relationship dissolution is defined as a market tie that existed in year t but not in any year between t + 1 and the end of the observation period (2009).

name: Relationship depth
definition: One of the key measures of an embedded relationship is the depth of the relationship, or the amount of time that each party spends engaged in actions specific to the connection.

name: Client load
definition: For an individual exchange manager, time is a critical constraining resource, and those with relatively large client loads are more likely to struggle with dedicating the desired amount of time to meet each client's specific needs.

name: Relationship focus
definition: The level of time and attention each client receives from its lobbyist in any year when compared with other clients; some high-focus exchange relationships receive an inordinately large share of an exchange manager's time, while other low-focus relationships receive an inordinately small share of time.

name: Relationship sharing
definition: Lobbyists are coded as working on a team when more than one lobbyist from the same firm is serving the same client in a focal year; the formation of multiplex ties encourages knowledge sharing within the firm and reduces the importance of the individual exchange manager.

name: Networking sponsorship services
definition: Sponsorship often provides opportunities for networking between new organizations and external resource providers via structured policies, programs, and initiatives. 'Networking efforts' refers to the extent to which sponsorship is aimed at connect new organizations with external resource providers.

name: Field-building sponsorship services
definition: Field-building efforts are aimed at connecting new organizations with similarly focused new organizations in emerging industries. A second way that sponsors increase new organizations' alignment and engagement with critical stakeholders is by connecting those organizations to other similar and new organizations within a field, to improve the opportunity for collaboration, knowledge sharing, and ultimately legitimacy for these emerging organizational communities.

name: Direct support sponsorship services
definition: 'Direct support' refers to the activities of sponsorship that involve direct transfer of knowledge, capital, and labor to new organizations. Sponsorship by way of direct support to new organizations can be provided in such a way that it bridges between them and their environments (e.g., via mentorship programs) or buffers resource dependencies for them (e.g., via subsidized back office support or real estate subsidies).

name: Geographic founding density
authors_terms: ["geographic founding density", "founding density", "density of competitors at founding"]
definition: The density of competitors at founding can have lasting effects on an organization's viability. Because most incubated organizations operate locally during and after incubation, we measured founding density as a count of the number of organizations in the same three-digit NAICS code at the county level in the organization's founding year.

name: Organizational exit
definition: Our dependent variable is organizational exit, which is a relevant measure of firm performance when firms are young (Geroski, 1995) and is central to the efforts of sponsorship (Hackett & Dilts, 2004). In our study, exits represent 7.7 percent of observations.

name: R&D consortia formation
authors_terms: ["formation of R&D consortia", "participation in R&D consortia", "rate of R&D consortia formation", "rate of participation"]
definition: In this study, the words 'formation of R&D consortia' and 'participation in R&D consortia' are used interchangeably because in this study we rarely observe incidents that firms participate in a consortium after it is formed, and so formation and participation are synonymous here.

name: Industry competition
definition: The degree of industry competition can be measured by market conduct or by market structure. Due to data constraints, the number of establishments in the three-digit industry classification is used as a proxy for the degree of industry competition.

name: Appropriability conditions
definition: Appropriability conditions are the means employed by firms to protect their profits due to invention and the success of those means.

name: R&D capabilities
definition: As a measure of a firm's R&D capabilities, we use the difference between a firm's R&D intensity (R&D expenditure/sales) and the R&D intensity of the industry to which the firm belongs.

name: Experience of past participation
authors_terms: ["experience of past participation", "experience of the participation in R&D consortia"]
definition: The experience of participation in past consortia can create a technological network through which a firm can gain access to technological resources of other firms.

name: Encounter with other firms in product markets
authors_terms: ["encounter with other firms in product markets", "product market network", "degree of diversification"]
definition: Contact with other firms in product markets constitutes a network through which the firm can obtain superior information on future consortia.

name: Firm age
definition: For the age of a firm, we use the number of years passed after the establishment of the firm.

name: Organizational political ideology
authors_terms: ["organizational political ideology", "organizational ideology", "organizational liberalism", "conservatism versus liberalism", "degree of liberalism"]
definition: 'Prevailing beliefs among organizational members about how the social world operates, including convictions about what outcomes are desirable and how they should be achieved' (adapted from Simons and Ingram, 1997). The authors characterize organizations' ideologies on the conservatism-versus-liberalism dimension.

name: Corporate social responsibility
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility", "CSR", "advances in CSR", "CSR profile", "advancement of CSR practices"]
definition: 'Actions that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law' (McWilliams and Siegel, 2001: 117). The authors operationalize CSR as three distinct outcomes: an omnibus measure of a firm's CSR profile, appointment of women to executive positions, and domestic partner benefits for gay and lesbian employees.

name: Industry prevalence of the CSR practice
authors_terms: ["prevalence of CSR practices in the firm's industry", "industry norms", "industry standards", "average industry CSR", "percent of female executives in industry", "prior adoption of benefits in industry"]
definition: The degree to which a given CSR practice is common among industry peer firms, which provides decision makers with normative guidance about CSR practices; when strong, industry isomorphic pressures 'provide a strong guide for behavior across all firms, leaving little opportunity for organizational ideology to exert its influence.'

name: Human capital intensity
authors_terms: ["human capital intensity", "human capital intensive firms", "knowledge workers"]
definition: 'The extent to which its production function is intensive in human capital inputs'; human capital intensive firms rely on knowledge workers, employees with high levels of education whose work involves using abstract information in nonroutine problem solving.

name: CEO organizational tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "CEO's tenure in the firm", "long organizational tenure"]
definition: The number of years a given CEO had worked in the firm; long tenure in an organization increases an individual's familiarity with the organization's belief system and provides more time for adjustment to it, socializing the CEO into the firm's prevailing ideology.

name: Prior exchange history
authors_terms: ["prior exchange history", "exchange history", "repeated exchange", "history of repeated exchange", "relationship history", "relational capital"]
definition: The prior history of repeated exchange between the buyer and a supplier, denoted h and valued as V(h). A history of repeated exchange generates a valuable asset that supports adaptation and problem solving and deters opportunistic behavior.

name: Rivals' exchange history
authors_terms: ["rivals with prior exchange history", "exchange histories of competing bidders", "magnitude of rival bidders' exchange history", "rivals' exchange histories"]
definition: The prior exchange histories that the competing bidders for an item possess with the buyer, captured by the log of the mean sales of j's rivals for item i and by the fraction of experienced j rivals for item i.

name: Supplier bid price
authors_terms: ["prices suppliers seek", "requested prices", "final bid offer", "bid prices", "premium over the lowest bid"]
definition: Bid prices represent suppliers' proposed division of value, including the value embedded in exchange history; the final bid offer by bidder j for item i is the product of the unit price offered by the bidder and the number of units that Buyco anticipates purchasing.

name: Prior contract wins
authors_terms: ["priorwin", "fraction of items bid upon and won", "fraction of the most recent CBE items won"]
definition: The share of items the bidder bid upon and won in the competitive bid event immediately preceding the one at hand, priorwin_jk, defined as the ratio of the number of contracts won by j in its kth CBE to the total number of items bid upon by j in that CBE.

name: Buyer supplier selection
authors_terms: ["buyer's awards", "buyer's choice of supplier", "supplier selection", "Buyco's decisions"]
definition: The buyer's choice of a single bidder from the menu of bidders and prices observed in a competitive bid event; measured as yij, which takes the value 1 if bidder j is awarded the contract for item i and 0 if j places a bid but does not win.

name: Symmetry of relational capital
authors_terms: ["symmetry of relational capital", "exchange history gap", "exchange history entropy", "concentration of relational capital", "asymmetry among suppliers"]
definition: The evenness with which relational capital is distributed among the buyer's suppliers, examined through the normalized difference between the two highest levels of exchange history among bidders and through an entropy measure of the distribution of relational capital across all bidders.

name: Consistency of exchange history valuation
authors_terms: ["consistent value assigned to this history over time", "stable weight on relational capital", "importance of exchange history", "weight placed on relational capital"]
definition: The stability over time of the value the buyer appears to assign to a supplier's history of exchange. Placing a consistent, unchanging value on relationship history over time makes it more likely that suppliers will develop bid strategies to appropriate relational rents.

name: Workforce racial diversity
definition: In keeping with prior research, we define racial diversity as the extent to which a firm's workforce is composed of employees from multiple racial groups rather than from one particular group.

name: Broad-based stock options
authors_terms: ["broad-based stock options", "use (versus nonuse) of broad-based stock options", "stock options granted to at least half the workforce"]
definition: Broad-based stock options (defined in this study as stock options granted to at least half the workforce, which is a widely used definition of 'broad-based') will effectively create reward interdependence that motivates employees to maximally achieve the collective performance targets of the company during the vesting period.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: We measured firm financial performance using operating profit divided by total assets (or operating ROA).

name: Voluntary turnover rate
definition: This variable was measured by the number of full-time employees who voluntarily left the company divided by the number of total full-time employees each year as reported by a management representative in the culture audit survey.

name: Individual affective commitment
definition: According to organizational commitment theory, employees develop affective commitment to their organization - defined as an emotional attachment to and involvement in the organization - when they are able to satisfy their individual needs for competence and accomplishment in their workplaces.

name: R&D search intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D search intensity", "search intensity", "R&D intensity", "R&D search investments"]
definition: Our dependent variable reflects firm-specific search expenditures adjusted for firm size. We used R&D expenditures divided by sales as a proxy for search intensity.

name: Attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["attainment discrepancy", "performance relative to aspirations", "distance of firms' past performance below aspirations", "distance of firms' past performance above aspirations"]
definition: Firms compare the difference between actual performance and aspirations, i.e., the 'attainment discrepancy' (Lant, 1992), and classify this gap as either favorable or unfavorable.

name: Distance from bankruptcy
authors_terms: ["distance from bankruptcy", "proximity to bankruptcy", "threat of bankruptcy", "Altman's Z"]
definition: We used Altman's (1983) Z as a measure of distance from bankruptcy. A lower Z value means a higher likelihood of bankruptcy.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Slack resources include excess inputs such as underutilized capacity and employees, as well as financial resources (Levinthal and March, 1981).

name: Institutionalized search
definition: Search may also be part of the ongoing activities of organizations; allocation of resources to R&D can become routinized, as when R&D expenditures are based on a fixed percentage of sales, or standard shares are allocated to basic research, risky projects, and incremental innovation. Greve (2003b: 54) referred to such ongoing search as institutionalized search.

name: Industry R&D search intensity
authors_terms: ["industry average R&D search intensity", "R&D search intensity of rivals", "Industry R&D/sales"]
definition: Firms within the same industry may perceive a common opportunity or threat that motivates similar search patterns and commitments to invest in innovation (Michael and Wall, 1986; Patel and Pavitt, 1997). Industry average R&D search intensity was computed by deleting the observation firm data (i.e., there are no own-firm effects on industry average R&D intensity).

name: IPO underpricing
definition: 'Underpricing' represents the difference between the first-day closing price and the offer price of an IPO stock. The dependent variable used in this study was underpricing, or first-day trading period returns.

name: Insider board representation
definition: The insider ratio was the number of firm officers serving as board members divided by the total number of board members. As the proportion of insiders serving on a board increases, their ability to monitor grows.

name: Insider equity ownership
authors_terms: ["insider equity", "percentage of equity owned by inside directors"]
definition: The percentage of equity owned by inside directors was the total equity owned by insiders divided by the total equity of a new venture as reported in the prospectus.

name: Insider board experience
authors_terms: ["insider other boards", "board experience", "number of other boards on which insiders sit"]
definition: The number of other boards on which insiders sit was a count measure based on information directors are required to report in an IPO's prospectus. This operationalization provided a measure of the experience and information levels of inside directors.

name: Insider tenure
definition: Insider tenure was operationalized as the average tenure of all insider directors.

name: Insider age
definition: Insider age was the average age of all insiders on a board.

name: Venture capital ownership
definition: Venture capital ownership was the percentage of all pre-IPO ownership by venture capital firms.

name: Prior VC-underwriter ties
authors_terms: ["prior VC-underwriter ties", "previous ties between a venture capital firm and the underwriter", "prior link between the primary venture capitalist for an IPO firm and the IPO underwriter"]
definition: Prior VC-underwriter ties was operationalized as the existence of a prior link between the primary venture capitalist for an IPO firm and the IPO underwriter.

name: CEO overconfidence
definition: Overconfidence, which is defined as the tendency to overestimate one's own abilities, is one of the most ubiquitous cognitive biases of individuals. It is argued to operate through two distinct effects: a better-than-average effect and a miscalibration effect.

name: Real options investment
authors_terms: ["real options investment", "real options intensity", "firm investment in real options"]
definition: Real options investment is defined as investing relatively small amounts in promising reversible opportunities. Firm investment in real options is approximated by how sensitive a firm's value is to changes in firm-level uncertainty, which captures the firm's level of strategic flexibility to perform under uncertain environments.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: We define market uncertainty as the extent to which a CEO faces an unstable and unpredictable business environment.

name: Within-tier position
authors_terms: ["within-tier position", "position within a tier", "within-tier positioning", "top of tier", "bottom of tier", "positions within a tier"]
definition: An actor's rank position within a tiered hierarchy contains two important elements - the tier they are in (i.e., membership in a specific tier) and their position within that tier (i.e., within-tier position). The paper focuses on whether an organization is positioned at the top of a lower tier or at the bottom of a tier, i.e., near the tier cut-off points.

name: Level of competitive actions
authors_terms: ["level of competitive actions", "number of acquisitions", "size of acquisitions", "acquisition activities", "acquisition level"]
definition: To estimate variation in the amount of business groups' acquisition activities in testing Hypotheses 1a, 2a, and 3a, the authors adopted measures that are widely used in the literature: the number of acquisitions and the size of acquisitions.

name: Riskiness of competitive actions
authors_terms: ["riskiness of competitive actions", "risk of competitive actions", "acquisition unrelatedness", "unrelated acquisitions"]
definition: Acquisitions can substantially vary in riskiness, and the authors used acquisition unrelatedness to capture the risk of competitive actions. In general, acquirers face greater risk if the targets are unrelated to their current businesses.

name: Asset growth of tier challenger
authors_terms: ["asset growth of tier challenger", "relative growth in total assets", "growth experienced by business groups at the top of the next lower tier"]
definition: The relative growth in total assets between the focal business group i and the business group j in the next rank; a positive value indicates that the business group at the top of the lower tier is growing faster than the business group at the bottom of the higher tier, whereas a negative value indicates the opposite.

name: Marketing cooperative arrangements
authors_terms: ["marketing cooperative arrangements", "marketing cooperative activities", "MKTCOOP", "external marketing arrangement"]
definition: Based on prior research, cooperative arrangements were defined as any of the following activities: Collaborative Arrangement—a noncontractual agreement between the new venture and another company to collaborate on certain functional activities; Licensing Arrangement—a contractual agreement by which the new venture is granted access to another company's functional resources through a license; Contractual Arrangement—a legally binding contractual agreement that allows the new venture to pay another company to perform certain functional activities; and Joint Venture—an independent third enterprise formed by the new venture with another firm to perform or develop certain functional activities.

name: R&D cooperative arrangements
authors_terms: ["R&D cooperative arrangements", "R&D cooperative activities", "R&DCOOP", "external R&D arrangement"]
definition: Based on prior research, cooperative arrangements were defined as any of the following activities: Collaborative Arrangement—a noncontractual agreement between the new venture and another company to collaborate on certain functional activities; Licensing Arrangement—a contractual agreement by which the new venture is granted access to another company's functional resources through a license; Contractual Arrangement—a legally binding contractual agreement that allows the new venture to pay another company to perform certain functional activities; and Joint Venture—an independent third enterprise formed by the new venture with another firm to perform or develop certain functional activities.

name: Manufacturing cooperative arrangements
authors_terms: ["manufacturing cooperative arrangements", "manufacturing cooperative activities", "MFGCOOP", "external manufacturing arrangement"]
definition: Based on prior research, cooperative arrangements were defined as any of the following activities: Collaborative Arrangement—a noncontractual agreement between the new venture and another company to collaborate on certain functional activities; Licensing Arrangement—a contractual agreement by which the new venture is granted access to another company's functional resources through a license; Contractual Arrangement—a legally binding contractual agreement that allows the new venture to pay another company to perform certain functional activities; and Joint Venture—an independent third enterprise formed by the new venture with another firm to perform or develop certain functional activities.

name: Marketing experience
definition: The first measure was intended to reflect the prior functional experience possessed by members of the management team in three functional areas: marketing, R&D, and manufacturing.

name: R&D experience
definition: The first measure was intended to reflect the prior functional experience possessed by members of the management team in three functional areas: marketing, R&D, and manufacturing.

name: Manufacturing experience
definition: The first measure was intended to reflect the prior functional experience possessed by members of the management team in three functional areas: marketing, R&D, and manufacturing.

name: Competitive strategy
authors_terms: ["competitive strategy", "marketing differentiation", "technical differentiation", "cost leadership", "Porter's strategic typology"]
definition: Porter's (1980) strategic typology, slightly modified, was used to classify the new venture's competitive strategy. Three basic types of competitive strategy were recognized: marketing differentiation, technical differentiation, and cost leadership.

name: New venture performance
definition: Average growth in sales (SALES) was adopted as the measure of performance since it has been suggested that sustained growth in revenues is often indicative of technical quality, market acceptance, and overall new venture success (Feeser and Willard, 1990).

name: Available slack
definition: Available slack (or x-efficiency) represents financial and other resources accumulated over time that are in excess of that required by the firm to operate efficiently and can fund strategic initiatives, such as adaptation or expansion via investment. It is a measure of resources held by the firm that can provide a buffer against economic turbulence, provide funds for adaptation or finance strategic investments.

name: Temporal orientation
definition: The CEO's preference for short- or long-term strategies. Because a CEO's temporal orientation when making investment choices cannot be measured directly, the paper uses the magnitude of investment in durable assets as a proxy for top management's temporal orientation, or investment horizon.

name: CEO current option wealth
definition: The accumulated cash value of options, or current wealth, reflects the potential losses to endowed wealth if risk taking is unsuccessful and the stock price falls. It is a useful heuristic for estimating current firm-specific wealth that is likely endowed in calculations of overall personal wealth.

name: CEO prospective option wealth
definition: Prospective wealth reflects future increases in wealth should strategic choices be successful as anticipated by optimistic and self-confident CEOs. It is an estimation of potential future additional wealth or potential gains to the value of stock options held by the CEO in their mixed gamble.

name: Firm skill demand
authors_terms: ["skill requirements of the firm's job posting", "high-skill requirements", "skill demand", "demand for high-skilled workers", "firm's skill demand"]
definition: Each firm demands an optimal number of skills xj, and the firm must hire workers with at least that number of skills to produce. The authors parameterize the skill requirements of a job posting as high or low skill using whether the role requires a college degree and the average number of skills listed in a firm's job postings.

name: Cost of outbound search
authors_terms: ["cost of outbound recruiting", "cost of searching for workers", "cost of finding workers", "worker visibility", "discoverability"]
definition: The exogenous cost of outbound search (σ) is the additional cost a firm faces for searching for candidates, which is determined in a competitive market where firms are price takers and can be considered the recruiter's time spent searching for suitable candidates, both online and offline. The authors parameterize it with indicators of whether the respondent is a frequent user of LinkedIn, a proxy for visibility, and with the share of workers in an MSA-Industry who frequently use LinkedIn.

name: Outbound recruiting
definition: Outbound recruiting is the hiring mechanism through which the firm uses its resources to find candidates and actively invite them to participate in the selection process, rather than posting a job and waiting for applicants to arrive (inbound recruiting). In the model, hj is the intensity of outbound recruiting chosen by firm j.

name: Local supply of skilled workers
authors_terms: ["Share of MSA-Industry workers who have a college degree", "share of college-educated workers"]
definition: The share of workers in an MSA-Industry labor market who have a college degree. When higher-skilled workers are fewer in number and so harder to find, firms should invest more in hunting for this relatively rarer talent.

name: Degree assortativity
definition: Degree assortativity refers to the tendency of nodes to attach to those with similar degree centrality ranks in a network. In an intra-firm network with high degree assortativity, central (peripheral) actors are more likely to establish collaborations with other central (peripheral) actors.

name: Invention quantity
authors_terms: ["quantity of inventive output", "quantity of inventions", "inventive output"]
definition: Invention quantity refers to the number of inventions produced.

name: Invention novelty
authors_terms: ["novelty of inventive output", "novelty of inventions", "average novelty"]
definition: We define novelty as the extent to which inventions include knowledge components that are unfamiliar to the inventors in a firm, regardless of whether they have been in existence elsewhere.

name: Invention impact
authors_terms: ["impact of inventive output", "average impact of inventive output", "impact"]
definition: Impact refers to the influence of those inventions on future work.

name: Structural recombination
authors_terms: ["degree of recombination", "structural recombination", "structural realignment", "business unit recombination"]
definition: A 'recombined' unit is any unit that has experienced a change in boundaries through some addition or deletion of activities and resources that have been moved within the firm. Structural recombination describes initiatives that firms undertake to reorient how they organize their existing resources and activities.

name: Industry growth
definition: As a common characteristic highlighted in studies of environmental change, munificence represents a strong and clear indicator of industry growth that can serve to signal that market conditions are abundant with opportunities for firms that adapt and capitalize on them.

name: Industry turbulence
definition: Environmental turbulence describes how rapidly the links between particular actions and key performance indicators can change. Dynamism has been commonly referred to as industry instability, unpredictability, or turbulence.

name: Reduction in industry turbulence
authors_terms: ["amount dynamism reduction", "reductions in industry turbulence", "decline in dynamism"]
definition: The change in industry turbulence, operationalized as the amount dynamism reduction: the difference between dynamism in an earlier period and dynamism in a latter period. As the level of environmental turbulence a firm faces begins to lessen, the authors argue that firms will engage in higher levels of structural recombination.

name: TMT turnover
definition: Managerial turbulence in the form of TMT turnover: as members enter and exit the TMT, both the expertise and the interpersonal dynamics of the group change, and changing preferences introduced by the loss or gain of members force TMTs to reformulate decision strategies.

name: TMT size growth
authors_terms: ["managerial turbulence", "TMT growth", "growth in top management team size", "amount increase in corporate team size"]
definition: Managerial turbulence in the form of TMT growth: as TMT size increases, the growing numbers of members tend to generate and actively consider a larger number and a more diverse set of issues, which retards the capacity of these collectives to build consensuses around potential sets of structural solutions.

name: Top management team demographic diversity
definition: Variability within the top management team on directly measurable attributes; the authors look at three aspects of demographic diversity: functional specialization, national origin, and age. Demographic variables are argued to be objective proxies for underlying cognitive variation.

name: Top management team cognitive diversity
authors_terms: ["cognitive diversity", "cognitive diversity exhibited in the team's decision-making processes", "variability concerning relatively unobservable attributes"]
definition: Cognitive diversity refers to variability concerning relatively unobservable attributes such as attitudes, values, and beliefs. The team-level coefficient of variation scores on six questionnaire items represented the measures of cognitive diversity.

name: Interpretative ambiguity
definition: Lack of clarity within the team concerning the degree to which team members share common attributions concerning, for example, organizational success and failure. Defined this way, interpretative ambiguity is a team-level construct.

name: Disagreement concerning basic team processes
authors_terms: ["team disagreement concerning basic team processes", "disagreement over basic team processes", "lack of team cohesion"]
definition: In some teams, members will tend to have differing perceptions of how such basic processes as decision making and task structuring are accomplished. An absence of agreement concerning basic team processes is evidence of lack of team cohesion.

name: Firm performance
definition: Because MARKSTRAT is a marketing simulation, the measures of performance relate to the results of decision making by the top management of the marketing department. The net marketing contribution was the basic measure of profitability and was defined as total revenues from sales minus expenses (cost of goods sold, research and development, inventory holding costs, etc.).

name: Contract explicitness
authors_terms: ["contract explicitness", "monitoring and intellectual property terms", "enforcement terms", "level of contract specification", "contract detail"]
definition: The detail with which the enforcement terms of a contract-the monitoring and intellectual property provisions-are explicitly specified. Formal monitoring and IP safeguards are used to guarantee that scientists transfer intended knowledge, that the sponsor is the priority recipient of knowledge generated, and that opportunism around IP appropriability is minimized.

name: Principal investigator contracting experience
authors_terms: ["PI-CO HISTORY", "experience contracting with a company", "prior partner-specific experience", "repeated interactions between scientists"]
definition: A count of the number of sponsored research agreements that the individual principal investigator has conducted with the same company prior to the current contract. As scientists gain contracting experience with an exchange partner, their focus of attention on knowledge creation supports the reduction of technical and behavioral uncertainty and the emergence of operational routines.

name: University-company contracting experience
authors_terms: ["UNIV-CO HISTORY", "contracting experience between parties in the university-company dyad", "repeated ties between the university and company", "contracting experience across a university-company dyad"]
definition: The contracting experience between parties in the university-company dyad, measured via the log of the number of previous sponsored research interactions between these two parties. For contract administrators these repeated ties are more representative of an accumulation of knowledge related to contract design and relationship-specific administrative routines than of uncertainty reduction.

name: Task innovation
definition: We define task innovation as the tasks that require service suppliers to create new methods or ideas to fulfill the buyer's requirements (i.e., production of new knowledge to meet a buyer's need). Innovative tasks differ in that they fall on the radical to incremental innovation continuum.

name: Exchange hazards
definition: We identified three types of contractual hazards present in the IT services industry: measurement cost, proprietary technology, and interdependency. Hazard denotes the number of exchange hazards each contract contains.

name: Payment mechanism
authors_terms: ["payment mechanism", "Payment method", "payment structure", "hybrid payment structure (T&M with a cap)", "T&M contract", "fixed-fee contract"]
definition: Fixed-fee contracts involve Compustar completing a well-defined project for a fixed price; time and materials (T&M) contracts involve the buyer paying Compustar an hourly (or possibly daily) rate until the job is done. Hybrid is a combination of two (i.e., T&M with a cap).

name: Description of requirements
authors_terms: ["Description of Requirements (DR)", "detailed description of the requirements"]
definition: The description of requirements concerns the detail the contract provides on the roles of each party and on deliverables; it was coded on a Likert-type scale ranging from 1 to 7, in which 1 indicates that the contract contains very few details about the DR on roles and deliverables, and 7 indicates the presence of an extensive description of the roles and/or deliverables.

name: Contingency planning
definition: Contingency planning tends to specify processes to follow in the event of issues that may arise and can be framed in a more promotion-focused way while still safeguarding against exchange hazards. Types of contingency planning observed in the sample examined in this paper include dealing with schedule adjustments, additional buyer requirements, and possible challenges encountered by the supplier.

name: Home country institutional environment
definition: Institutions are shared, collective understandings or rules of conduct reflected in laws, rules, governance mechanisms, and capital markets, which help to define observed patterns of market exchange.

name: Partner technological capabilities
definition: Firms in transition economies need current technology to compete in global markets. These firms often lack the knowledge and capabilities to develop or employ sophisticated manufacturing or product technologies; thus, they seek alliance partners with technological capabilities.

name: Partner managerial capabilities
definition: Managerial capabilities and decision-making processes are often not well developed in emerging-market firms. Managers in firms that have operated in centrally planned economies generally lack the understanding of free markets and rarely have the skills to help their firms compete effectively in such markets.

name: Partner intangible assets
definition: Obtaining alliance partners with strong positive reputations can confer legitimacy on the focal firm and lend additional prestige in the marketplace. Thus, reputational capital also represents an important intangible asset that Chinese firms seek to acquire.

name: Partner complementary capabilities
definition: Hitt et al. (2000) also found that emerging market firms placed a priority on specialized and complementary skills in selecting alliance partners. The complementarity between partners' capabilities is even more critical in unstable and uncertain environments such as in Russia.

name: Partner unique capabilities
definition: A focus on achieving longer-term growth allows Chinese managers to seek partners with unique capabilities. Unique capabilities are more difficult to learn because of their exclusivity and a lack of absorptive capacity of partner firms.

name: Partner prior alliance experience
definition: Previous alliance experience can contribute to the success of current alliances. The knowledge gained from prior experience should help the firm more effectively manage future alliances.

name: Partner attractiveness
authors_terms: ["partner attractiveness", "attractiveness of the firm as an alliance partner", "probability of recommending an alliance with the firm"]
definition: Executives rated each of the 30 potential partners described in the cases on a seven-point Likert-type scale on (1) the attractiveness of the firm as an alliance partner and (2) the probability of recommending an alliance with the firm. We averaged these two items to form the dependent variable.

name: Chain financial performance
authors_terms: ["chain performance", "financial performance of franchise chains", "financial performance"]
definition: The financial performance of franchise chains. The author notes that a chain may survive and even grow rapidly without reaching profitability, and measures chain performance with profitability ratios.

name: Brand name value
definition: A brand name is one of the two resources that make up the franchise package. The more valuable the brand name, the more opportunistic franchisees will benefit from providing a lower-quality product or service than customers typically associate with that brand name.

name: Business practices tacitness
authors_terms: ["business practices tacitness", "tacit business practices", "business practices tacitness", "tacit knowledge base"]
definition: In the franchising context, business practices are 'knowledge about how to manage day-to-day activities, improve efficiency, and promote products and services'; tacit knowledge is neither codified nor articulated, so tacit business practices are not fully articulated and their transfer requires up close observation, demonstration, and hands-on experience.

name: Proportion of franchised outlets
authors_terms: ["proportion of franchised outlets", "reliance on franchising", "extent to which chains franchise or company-own their outlets"]
definition: An important feature of most franchise chains is that they simultaneously use franchised and company-owned outlets; the proportion of franchised outlets captures how much of a chain's distribution is franchised rather than company-owned.

name: Service-type franchising
definition: In retail-type chains, chain operators can easily guarantee quality because they supply products to outlet managers. It is comparatively more difficult for chain operators to guarantee quality in service-type chains.

name: Lobbying breadth
definition: The extent of government activities or entities firms attempt to influence via lobbying, which the authors refer to as lobbying breadth, capturing heterogeneity in firms' lobbying expenditure allocation strategies.

name: Political connectedness
definition: Political connectedness is defined as the ability to access and influence government officials through prior relationships. The authors argue that the number of relationships with government officials relates to the benefits the firm receives.

name: Government contract value
authors_terms: ["government contracts", "firm government contract value", "government contract values"]
definition: Government contracts was measured as the logarithm of the total value of all contracts between the focal company and the U.S. federal government throughout the year, a directly visible benefit of lobbying that is observable across a wide swath of industries.

name: Firm performance
definition: Firm performance was measured as Tobin's Q, calculated as market value of the firm divided by total assets, capturing less directly observable benefits that nonetheless benefit firms' bottom line.

name: Competitive repertoire complexity
definition: We view complexity as encompassing the diversity, change, and newness of a firms' competitive action repertoire. Scholars have conceptualized competitive complexity in subtly different ways, but these depictions share the common trait that complexity involves a firm's diversity of competitive actions.

name: Short-term firm performance
definition: We operationalized short-term performance as return on assets (ROA) expressed as a percentage at the end of the focal year under investigation.

name: Performance trend
authors_terms: ["performance trend", "firms' performance trend over time", "firms' performance trend"]
definition: We operationalized firms' performance trend over time as the slope of the regression of ROA over three years, beginning with the focal year of analysis. Individual firm growth trends allowed us to observe the trajectory of firm performance, providing more detail about firm-level changes than simple averages or snapshots of performance.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
definition: Dedicated investors maintain concentrated shareholdings in a small number of firms for a long time and do not trade based on short-term earnings (Bushee, 2001). Dedicated institutional investors are sometimes called 'relational investors' because they engage with their agents and are active in establishing competitive strategies.

name: Transient institutional ownership
definition: Transient institutional investors are the opposite. They hold shares in a diverse range of firms, frequently trade in and out of stocks, and are keenly aware of earnings reports.

name: CEO-TMT pay gap
definition: Tournament theory suggests that the pay gap between the CEO and TMT is a particularly potent motivator of executive action (Lazear and Rosen, 1981). CEO-TMT pay gap measures tournament incentives among top managers.

name: Environmental strategy proactiveness
authors_terms: ["environmental strategy", "level of proactiveness of environmental strategies", "environmental management strategies", "green strategies"]
definition: The paper classifies firms according to their environmental management practices, building on Hart's resource-based framework, into three empirically significant strategies: reactive, pollution prevention and environmental leadership. Shifts between stages require simultaneous investments in several linked resource domains.

name: Regulatory stakeholder importance
authors_terms: ["regulatory pressures", "regulatory stakeholders", "government regulators", "national (and regional) governments", "local public agencies"]
definition: The perceived importance attached to government regulators at the national (and subnational) and local levels, in terms of their impact on decisions related to environmental management.

name: Primary stakeholder importance
definition: The primary stakeholders refer to employees, suppliers, customers, and public agencies engaged in formal relationships with the organization; in the hypothesis development regulators are excluded from this group.

name: Secondary stakeholder importance
definition: The secondary stakeholder groups include actors such as the media and special interest groups, not engaged in formal transactions with the organization; in this study they include industry rivals, international agreements, ENGOs and the media.

name: Local standards-based certification organizations
authors_terms: ["local standards-based certification organizations", "local SBCOs", "local organizations", "localized organizations"]
definition: Localized or local organizations operate at the state or city level and have no formal affiliations with other organizations. Local collective action organizations can serve as 'problem-solving structures' that exhibit flexibility and context-sensitive responsiveness to emergent problems and concerns.

name: Federated standards-based certification organizations
definition: The term 'federated' refers to organizations that have a national headquarters and multiple state-level subunits or chapters. What distinguishes federations from other interorganizational forms is the partitioning of control between affiliates and a headquarters.

name: Regulatory content innovation
definition: Content innovation captures provisions in a state law that have not been previously included in any other state legislation.

name: Regulatory content variation
