definition: Content variation is the degree to which a state's law deviates from the mean similarity score for all states that have previously passed a law.

name: Regulatory content elaboration
definition: Content elaboration refers to the refinement or expansion of existing legal structure that occurs via formal legislative amendment or through bureaucratic rule processes.

name: Pressure-resistant institutional ownership
definition: Pressure-resistant institutions do not have business relationships with firms and, accordingly, do not face conflicts with their investor relationship. These institutions, such as public pension funds, mutual funds, and endowments and foundations, can intervene in corporate governance without fear of retribution from corporate managers.

name: Pressure-sensitive institutional ownership
definition: Institutional investors with business relationships with firms in which they might invest include banks, insurance companies, and nonbank trusts. These investors are susceptible to influence exercised by firm managers and are termed pressure-sensitive.

name: Pressure-indeterminate institutional ownership
definition: A third category, pressure-indeterminate institutions, includes those whose relationships with the firms they invest in cannot be clearly defined. They are investors such as corporate pension funds, brokerage houses, and investment counselors, whose motives and actions could not be clearly defined.

name: CEO compensation level
authors_terms: ["level of CEO compensation", "level of compensation", "level of CEO pay"]
definition: The level of compensation was the sum of total salary, bonus, and long-term compensation (grants of restricted stock, stock options, stock appreciation rights, and performance plans) in a year.

name: Proportion of long-term incentives in total compensation
definition: The proportion of long-term incentives was the ratio of long-term compensation to total compensation. The compensation mix, or the proportion of long-term incentives in a compensation contract, may serve to align the interests of managers with those of shareholders by rewarding CEOs only if shareholder returns are enhanced.

name: Unrelated diversification
authors_terms: ["unrelated diversification", "change in unrelated diversification", "unrelated diversification index (DU)"]
definition: Unrelated diversification arises from the businesses in different 2-digit industry groups. Unrelated diversification must rely on financial synergies for value increases.

name: Related diversification
authors_terms: ["related diversification", "change in related diversification", "related diversification index (DR)"]
definition: Related diversification is defined as the diversification resulting from businesses in 4-digit segments within a 2-digit industry group (based on SIC code). Related diversification facilitates the sharing of activities and the transfer of skills across businesses to increase firm value.

name: Debt financing
authors_terms: ["type of financing", "proportion of new debt financing", "debt financing", "long-term debt issued"]
definition: Type of financing for diversification was measured by the long-term debt issued in 1982 as a proportion of total new financing in that year. This measure represents the funds required to finance diversification moves beyond available retained earnings.

name: Public financing
authors_terms: ["source of financing", "proportion of public financing", "public sources of funds"]
definition: Firms can obtain financial resources from private or public sources of funds. The amount of public financing as a proportion of total new financing in 1982 was used as the measure of the source of financing.

name: Mode of entry
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "direct entry", "direct entries", "internal development", "acquisitive entry"]
definition: Differences may arise due to the mode of entry (i.e., diversification via acquisitions versus through direct entry). Firms can enter new businesses by acquiring an existing firm, or through direct entries (internal development).

name: Rival firm dissolution
authors_terms: ["dissolution of a rival firm", "rival firm dissolution", "rival dissolution", "rival failure", "unexpected death of a rival solo practitioner", "rival solo practitioner dies unexpectedly"]
definition: The dissolution of a rival firm, which may release resources such as clients, employees and physical assets. In this study it is operationalized through the unexpected deaths of solo-practicing attorneys, which effectively dissolve their firms and create a source of rival dissolution that should be unrelated to conditions in the economic environment.

name: New firm founding
authors_terms: ["founds new firm", "firm founding", "founding of new firms", "new firm formation", "founds a new organization"]
definition: The creation of a new law firm by an attorney, identified when the attorney appears in a newly created law firm within 3 years of her exit from her current law firm without appearing in another organization and is a 'name partner' in that new firm.

name: Shared educational affiliations with powerful members of the firm
authors_terms: ["shared educational affiliations with powerful members of the firm", "law school ties to partners", "shared law school affiliations", "social ties"]
definition: The extent to which an attorney shares educational affiliations, such as a degree from the same educational institution, with powerful members of the firm. Individuals who lack such shared affiliations likely face higher barriers to value capture because powerful individuals have many reasons to give preferential treatment to those with whom they share school ties.

name: Competition for promotion
definition: The intensity of competition that associates face with each other for promotion into the firm's partnership. When individuals face more competition, their odds of obtaining a promotion and its attendant rewards decrease, so the value of remaining in the current job may decline.

name: Firm knowledge intensity
definition: Following Peters and Taylor (2017), we calculate the industry-average knowledge capital intensity, defined as the accumulated sum of past spending on research and development.

name: Employee skill level
definition: Skill Level is the central measure for benchmarking pay within and across firms, and it is a standardized cardinal measure of skill that ranges from level 1 to level 22. It is not equivalent to hierarchical level inside an organization; it varies within hierarchical levels and occupations with the tasks required, and it is intended as a reference level within which pay can be compared within and across firms.

name: Internal pay orientation
authors_terms: ["internal pay orientation", "internal pay sensitivity", "internal pay alignment", "internal pay benchmark", "internal benchmarking"]
definition: The sensitivity of employee pay to the internal pay benchmark, which is defined as average compensation of employees within the same firm and same skill level but drawn from different functions.

name: Market pay orientation
authors_terms: ["market pay orientation", "market pay sensitivity", "market pay benchmark", "market benchmarking"]
definition: The sensitivity of employee pay to the market pay benchmark, defined as the average pay of workers at other firms in the same occupation, skill level, and region.

name: Complex problem-solving intensity
definition: An index of complex problem-solving intensity estimated as the average of scores across three job components: practical/technical know-how, problem-solving thinking environment, and problem-solving thinking challenge. Complex problems require novel integration of diverse knowledge in ways that are difficult to specify ex ante.

name: Collaboration intensity
definition: A collaboration index that includes the average of scores for communicating know-how, planning know-how, account freedom, and account area.

name: Employee pay
definition: Our dependent variable is Employee Pay, a log of cash compensation (the sum of the base salary and cash bonuses) of the focal employee.

name: Innovation outcomes
authors_terms: ["innovation outcomes", "innovation performance", "patent and publication counts", "breakthrough innovations"]
definition: Innovation quantity (patent and publication counts), quality (citations), and breakthrough innovations, used to analyze how internal pay sensitivity predicts innovation outcomes.

name: Component constraint
definition: Constraint components are the component(s) that pose the greatest bottleneck to improving system performance. The constraint component in each year was identified from product reviews of the PC system.

name: Allocation of inventive effort
authors_terms: ["allocation of inventive effort", "inventive effort", "R&D effort", "relative allocation of inventive effort"]
definition: I employed patent count data to construct a measure of allocation of inventive effort. First, I obtained patent counts based on patent application dates for each firm year across all the patent classes that constitute the five components. I then computed the ratio of patents in a particular component to the total patents across all components for each firm year, to capture the relative allocation of inventive effort to a particular component.

name: Slack component firm
definition: C-firms (Fc) are firms that compete in the product market of a component that is a constraint in the current period, and S-firms (Fs) are firms that compete in the product market of slack components.

name: Slack component knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["firm slack knowledge stock", "R&D stock in the slack component", "sunk R&D investments in slack components", "stock of firm knowledge in the slack component"]
definition: I created a stock of firm knowledge in the slack component by cumulating the firm stock of patents in the primary slack component. Firms with the greatest sunk investments in slack component R&D are likely to face the greatest incentive to invest in resolving the constraint.

name: Organizational commitment to employees
authors_terms: ["organizational commitment to employees (OCE)", "commitment to employees", "commitment to its employees' well-being", "OCE"]
definition: An organization's commitment to its employees (OCE) may be reflected in its care for employee wellbeing and satisfaction, in the fairness and compassion of its rewards, and in its investment in competence development and compensation.

name: Financial performance
definition: Financial performance was measured using ROA, which the authors note has been the most widely used measure to date in strategy research and applies with equal relevance to each of the industries studied.

name: Cost leadership
definition: A Porter positioning strategy assessed by the dedication, that is the intensity and thoroughness, with which it is pursued; its elements include ongoing programs to reduce operation costs, efficient inventory management procedures, just-in-time manufacture, and related economizing techniques.

name: Marketing differentiation
definition: One of two kinds of differentiation strategies the firm may pursue; it was assessed by the use of advertising, the promotion of brand identification, and attractive design or packaging.

name: Innovative differentiation
definition: One of two kinds of differentiation strategies the firm may pursue; it was assessed by new product development, product R&D, the creation of state-of-the-art products, and the continual refinement of product lines.

name: Dedicated positioning strategy
authors_terms: ["dedicated positioning strategy", "positioning strategy", "dedication (intensity and thoroughness) of strategy"]
definition: Porter argued that positioning strategies can only be effective if they are pursued with dedication, that is, with thoroughness and intensity. The authors assessed a firm's positioning strategy according to the dedication, that is the intensity and thoroughness, with which it pursued cost leadership or differentiation.

name: Value of source unit's knowledge stock
authors_terms: ["value of the source unit's knowledge stock", "value of knowledge stock", "value of a subsidiary's knowledge stock", "value of the knowledge possessed by the source unit"]
definition: The greater the value of a subsidiary's knowledge stock for the rest of the MNC, the greater would be its attractiveness for other units. The authors visualize the knowledge stock of any subsidiary as composed of both duplicative as well as nonduplicative knowledge, with non-duplicative knowledge that is relevant for the rest of the global network being what makes it valuable to other units.

name: Motivational disposition to share knowledge
authors_terms: ["motivational disposition of the source unit", "motivational disposition of a subsidiary to share its knowledge with other units", "motivational disposition to share knowledge"]
definition: The disposition of the source unit to share its knowledge with other units within the MNC. The authors operationalize it in terms of the subsidiary vs. corporate (nodal vs. network) focus of the incentive system for the subsidiary president, arguing that factors enhancing this disposition counterbalance 'hoarding' tendencies.

name: Existence and richness of transmission channels
authors_terms: ["existence and richness of transmission channels", "richness of transmission channels", "transmission channels"]
definition: The existence and richness of transmission channels linking a subsidiary to other units within the MNC. Beyond mere existence, the most notable property is the richness/bandwidth of communication links, as captured in aspects such as informality, openness, and density of communications.

name: Motivational disposition to acquire knowledge
authors_terms: ["motivational disposition of the target unit", "motivational disposition to acquire knowledge", "motivational disposition of a subsidiary to seek/accept knowledge from other units"]
definition: A subsidiary's motivational disposition to acquire/accept knowledge from other units within the enterprise, which the authors argue is a function of incentives that increase subsidiary managers' eagerness to learn, the relative paucity of the subsidiary's knowledge stock, and/or coercive pressures from corporate headquarters.

name: Absorptive capacity of the target unit
authors_terms: ["absorptive capacity", "capacity of a subsidiary to absorb incoming knowledge"]
definition: The target unit's 'ability to recognize the value of new information, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends'. Absorptive capacity may differ across organizations because of the extent of prior related knowledge and the extent of inter-unit homophily of the receiving unit vis-a-vis the sending unit.

name: Knowledge outflows to peer subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["knowledge outflows to peer subsidiaries", "KO-S", "provides knowledge and skills to sister subsidiaries"]
definition: The transfer of largely procedural types of knowledge (know-how, e.g., product designs, distribution know-how) from a focal subsidiary to peer subsidiaries, measured as the extent to which the subsidiary 'provides knowledge and skills to sister subsidiaries'.

name: Knowledge outflows to the parent corporation
authors_terms: ["knowledge outflows to the parent corporation", "KO-P", "provides knowledge and skills to parent corporation"]
definition: The transfer of largely procedural types of knowledge (know-how) from a focal subsidiary to the parent corporation, measured as the extent to which the subsidiary 'provides knowledge and skills to parent corporation'.

name: Knowledge inflows from peer subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["knowledge inflows from peer subsidiaries", "KI-S", "receives knowledge and skills from sister subsidiaries"]
definition: The extent to which a focal subsidiary receives largely procedural types of knowledge (know-how) from peer subsidiaries, measured as the extent to which the subsidiary 'receives knowledge and skills from sister subsidiaries'.

name: Knowledge inflows from the parent corporation
authors_terms: ["knowledge inflows from the parent corporation", "KI-P", "receives knowledge and skills from the parent corporation"]
definition: The extent to which a focal subsidiary receives largely procedural types of knowledge (know-how) from the parent corporation, measured as the extent to which the subsidiary 'receives knowledge and skills from the parent corporation'.

name: Local component interdependence
authors_terms: ["local component interdependence", "local interdependence", "Change in Local Interdependence"]
definition: A firm has a high density of local component interdependence if it uses a set of integrated components where changes to one component require changes in others; low local interdependence means that a firm's set of components is relatively independent.

name: Concentration within ecosystem clusters
authors_terms: ["concentration within clusters", "Change in Concentration within Clusters", "concentration in a particular ecosystem cluster"]
definition: Ecosystems can contain clusters, that is, groups of components that are more tightly interdependent internally as compared with their external interdependence, such as 'technology stacks' in the software space. An acquisition increases concentration within clusters when the acquirer's components and the target's component are located in the same cluster.

name: Component centrality
authors_terms: ["component centralities", "Change in Component Centralities", "centrality", "central ecosystem position"]
definition: Some components can be more central in a network of interdependencies than others. These components are interdependent with a large set of other components which are, in turn, interdependent with many others.

name: Acquisition target choice
definition: We run a conditional logistic regression with a binary dependent variable (target choiceij) set to one for the actual targets and to zero for the potential targets of unrealized acquisitions.

name: Knowledge sourcing from CV spinouts
authors_terms: ["CV spinouts", "citing its own CV spinouts", "citations to the focal firm's CV spinouts", "CV spinouts' unfamiliar components"]
definition: Following Chesbrough (2003), I define CV spinouts as employee ventures that benefit from the support of the originating organization. CV spinout incubation in the parent and parent-CV spinout organizational imprinting let parents learn from the ventures they have spawned.

name: Knowledge sourcing from employee spinouts
definition: Following Agarwal et al. (2004), I refer to employee spinouts as employee ventures that originated independently, such that they receive no formal support from their parent.

name: Knowledge sourcing from CVC ventures
authors_terms: ["CVC investments", "CVC portfolio ventures", "CVC portfolio firms", "CVC ventures"]
definition: Corporate venture capital (CVC) investments are corporate backing of ventures that did not originate with corporate research.

name: Knowledge sourcing from alliances
definition: Following Rosenkopf and Almeida (2003), I assume that all alliances offer the potential for interorganizational learning.

name: Patent quality
authors_terms: ["patent quality", "patent quality index", "invention quality", "quality of the firm's invention"]
definition: Following their approach, I measure the quality of the firm's invention by a weighted index of the number of claims awarded to the patent, forward citations that the patent received in the five years after its granting, and the number of backward citations that the patent made to prior patents.

name: Parent-specific technological expertise
authors_terms: ["parent-specific technological expertise", "parent experts", "outbound mobility of parent's experts", "expertise with the parent firm's core technological areas"]
definition: In line with prior research on knowledge workers' mobility, I assessed the extent to which exiting inventors hold expertise on the parent's knowledge, routines, and procedures by matching their technological expertise (prior mobility) with the area of technological expertise of the parent.

name: Unfamiliar knowledge components
definition: Recombinations from previously unused, unfamiliar sets of knowledge components are less desirable, because they involve substantial outcome and procedural uncertainty. Subclassifications assigned to a patent by the USPTO proxy for knowledge components recombined in the focal patent.

name: Accumulated experience
definition: We measure Accumulated Experience as the number of franchises awarded in each specific origin- and host-country group prior to the focal decision date.

name: Long-run performance
definition: The long-term performance of a given franchisee is measured as the Daily Transaction Volume that a franchisee had on February 3, 2015. We infer learning from the rate at which franchise quality (as indicated by the long-run performance of each franchise) improved as selection experience accumulated in each market.

name: Pace of decision making
definition: One of the key attributes that shape the learning process is pace. We measure Pace as a moving average of days between the three decisions prior to the focal decision.

name: Variance in decision outcomes
authors_terms: ["variance", "performance variance", "variance in decision outcomes", "variance in franchisee revenues"]
definition: We examine how variance in the prior decisions' outcome (as indicated by variance in franchisee revenues) interacts with accumulated experience to shape the curvilinear experience-performance relationship. We use the same approach as for pace to compute Performance Variance, and measure it as the moving average of the Daily Transaction Volume for the three decisions prior to the focal decision.

name: Individual-level exploration
definition: Individual-level exploration refers to individuals' activities related to the creation of new knowledge. In this setting, exploration is related to acquiring or creating new knowledge to introduce novel products.

name: Spatial proximity to previously separated peers
authors_terms: ["increased spatial proximity to previously separated peers", "being moved closer to previously separated peers", "spatial design", "workspace reconfiguration"]
definition: The change in organization design that moves individuals' workspaces closer to those of previously separated peers, giving them direct access to and interaction with those peers' different knowledge and skills. It was measured as whether a focal individual was moved into a common workspace with previously separated peers, rather than as the actual dyadic distance.

name: Prior organizational experience
definition: The amount of prior experience an individual has acquired within the organization, which approximates the level of capability the individual has to recognize the value of new external information, assimilate it, and apply it to novel and useful ends.

name: Ties with previously separated peers
definition: Close and regularly used relationships through which information can flow across spatial boundaries between individuals situated in separate workspaces; in this context such a tie was defined based on whether the individuals joined the company together and were therefore part of the same cohort.

name: Inventor specialization
definition: Inventor specialization refers to the extent that the firm's inventors are individually focused on particular technological areas. The firm with a collection of technological specialists likely has greater knowledge depth, whereas the firm with technological generalists likely has greater knowledge breadth.

name: Scope of technologies
definition: Scope of technologies refers to how widely the individual technology can potentially be applied. It is an ex ante concept, as the firm often cannot perfectly predict the technology's eventual uses, and it is inextricably tied to the technology's scope of novelty.

name: Stakeholder management
definition: SM deals with the degree to which organizations move beyond their own needs and legal requirements to satisfy the needs of their various non-shareholding stakeholders such as employees, suppliers, customers, and individuals in the community whose primary benefit derived from the company is not from its shareholder returns.

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation levels", "CEO compensation", "categories of CEO compensation"]
definition: CEO compensation levels as captured by the different categories of CEO compensation, including salary, bonus, stock options granted value, and total compensation.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "firm financial performance", "return on assets", "total returns to shareholders"]
definition: Financial performance is measured using return on assets (following Berman et al., 1999) and total returns to shareholders, drawn from the Compustat database for the year prior to the CEO compensation measure.

name: Pipeline depth
authors_terms: ["pipeline hiring", "pipeline recruiting", "preceding players", "pipeline depth", "the number of preceding hires from the same source organization"]
definition: Pipeline hiring is repeatedly hiring individuals from the same external source organization. The number of individuals from the source who have joined the hiring firm can be described analogously as increased flow through or deepening of the pipeline; the authors count the players from the same source that preceded each player into the focal FBS team within the previous 4 years.

name: Pre-entry human capital
authors_terms: ["pre-entry human capital", "pre-entry quality", "human capital", "quality of a new joiner's pre-entry human capital"]
definition: Human capital here is the potential for future performance that is tracked and rated by third parties for players while they play in high school. The dependent variable was pre-entry human capital, measured by a third-party rating of each recruit's potential as an FBS player.

name: Post-entry performance
authors_terms: ["subsequent performance", "postentry performance", "player performance", "college career performance", "average number of games started"]
definition: The authors measure player performance with a count variable: the average number of games started per year in his college career. Teams generally play a schedule of 12 games per season and have strong incentives to start the best performing players and update these selections over time, such that the number of starts is a useful indicator of individual performance.

name: Performance turnaround
definition: To be considered successful in turning around, a firm must (1) have at least two years of increasing ROA after the two declining years of ROA, and (2) have achieved and maintained positive ROA by at least the sixth year after the base year before decline started.

name: New product introductions
definition: A firm can change its strategy autonomously by recombining existing resources and capabilities into new product offerings; such offerings provide the firm with a means to more effectively leverage its current resources and capabilities, and to create more value for its existing customers as well as to attract new ones.

name: Strategic alliances
definition: When a firm's current resource base is not adequate to engineer a change in strategy, it can acquire new resources and capabilities externally through acquisitions and strategic alliances, which provide an expeditious means of accessing and leveraging resources necessary for strategic repositioning but not currently owned by the firm.

name: Acquisitions
definition: When a firm's current resource base is not adequate to engineer a change in strategy, it can acquire new resources and capabilities externally through acquisitions and strategic alliances, which provide an expeditious means of accessing and leveraging resources necessary for strategic repositioning but not currently owned by the firm.

name: Layoffs
definition: Cost retrenchment refers to the wholesale reduction in costs, especially labor costs. Layoffs are defined as the wholesale reductions in employees.

name: Asset reduction
definition: Asset reduction involves the elimination of an entire business or other hard assets such as plants or facilities; asset reduction occurred when a firm sold or closed any of its physical assets.

name: Product withdrawal
definition: Product withdrawal occurred when a firm closed or sold product lines.

name: Extramural R&D
authors_terms: ["extramural R&D", "R&D outsourcing", "external technology sourcing", "external knowledge sourcing", "external technology sourcing influences firm innovativeness"]
definition: Extramural R&D is research that is purchased and involves payments to research collaborators. It includes all R&D expenditures incurred outside the focal unit of analysis.

name: Innovation performance
authors_terms: ["innovation performance", "firm innovativeness", "innovativeness", "innovativeness of the firm's product(s)"]
definition: Innovation performance due to new-to-market products measures the share of turnover in 2006 from products that were new to the firm's market and were introduced by the firm during 2004-2006.

name: Employee retention
authors_terms: ["employee retention strategies", "employee retention mechanisms", "retention of key employees", "incentive structures that induce employees to stay"]
definition: Creation of incentive structures that induce employees to stay and reduce flows of tacit knowledge and skills; companies try to lock in their most valuable employees with pay packages weighted toward deferred compensation to increase employees' exit costs.

name: Secrecy
definition: Creation of organizational structures that enhance secrecy and prevent explicit knowledge theft; since the value of a trade secret is predicated on the cost and effort of maintaining the secret, the onus is on the firm to create a culture of confidentiality.

name: Knowledge complexity
definition: Creation of knowledge structures embodied in complex technology and products that make imitation more difficult. Knowledge architectures can be simple and comprise only a few elements, or complex and involve a larger number of elements requiring more sophisticated interaction.

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: The authors define an entrepreneurial orientation as the processes, structures, and behaviors of firms that are characterized by innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk taking, and they view it as the simultaneous exhibition of these three dimensions.

name: New venture performance
definition: Previous research suggests that capturing the multidimensionality of new venture performance requires the use of multiple measures, so the study employs both self-reported measures of ten dimensions of performance relative to competitors and, for a subsample, sales growth as an objective measure.

name: Intraindustry network centrality
definition: We define network centrality as the degree to which a firm has quick and independent access to other firms in a particular industry network through the fewest possible links. Network centrality refers to a firm's position in the entire pattern of ties comprising a network and indicates the firm's structural proximity to all other firms in the network.

name: Range of extraindustry bridging ties
authors_terms: ["bridging ties", "range of bridging ties", "extraindustry bridging ties"]
definition: Range of bridging ties is defined as the extent to which a firm maintains ties beyond the focal industry network to organizations from other fields.

name: Founders' human capital
definition: Founders' prior work experiences may indicate differences in skills and credentials; the authors measure it as an equally weighted composite of industry experience, start-up experience, and managerial experience obtained prior to founding the current venture.

name: Predisposition to public employment
authors_terms: ["predisposition to public employment", "public sector predisposition effect", "predisposition for public employment", "predispositional effect"]
definition: People enter the public sector because they prefer job security, organizational stability, and free time, seek different rewards from their jobs than people entering private sector jobs, and are comfortable with working on low variety tasks in hierarchies and stratified environments; because these behavioral tendencies are generally held to be paradoxical to the dispositional determinants of entrepreneurship, it can be hypothesized that public employees are nonentrepreneurial.

name: Public sector employment
definition: Public organizations embody all the core features of a bureaucratic system, including specialization, centralization, formalization, and an overemphasis on tenure and norms of impersonality, consistency, and objectivity, and public managers strive to build a civil service culture that defines the attributes of a good public employee.

name: Public sector tenure
authors_terms: ["public sector tenure", "tenure in public employment", "length of public sector employment"]
definition: Tenure captures adaptation to the organization and selection by the internal labor market, and the effects of organizational dynamics, e.g., bureaucratic construction of the individual and accumulation of cospecialized human capital, tend to be amplified by length of public employment and to bind individuals to the public sector.

name: Transition to entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["transition to entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial exit", "hazard of entrepreneurship", "entry into entrepreneurship"]
definition: Based on the person-year work history, entry into entrepreneurship is treated as a transition, and because the authors model the occurrence of the first transition, succeeding observations are deleted once the individual has become an entrepreneur for the first time. The dependent variable is the hazard rate of entrepreneurship from the time the individual leaves full-time education.

name: Black employees
definition: Given our focus on Black respondents, we construct two dummy variables: one for Black respondents and one for respondents of other races excluding White. Thus, White respondents are the reference group in our models.

name: Intrapreneurship
authors_terms: ["intrapreneurship", "internal ventures", "internal venture", "intrapreneurial entry", "new venture for your employer"]
definition: Individuals can also seize new market opportunities through intrapreneurship: initiating and operating new ventures as employees within established firms. Intrapreneurs are workers who act entrepreneurially within the context of an organization's broader opportunity structure, seeking new opportunities, mobilizing resources, building the founding team, and managing the daily operations of the business.

name: Entrepreneurship
definition: Apart from starting and managing independent ventures, individuals can also seize new market opportunities through intrapreneurship; the data indicate whether individuals pursued the new business as an independent startup (i.e., entrepreneurship) or on behalf of an employer organization (i.e., intrapreneurship).

name: New venture financial performance
definition: Researchers concur that an important indicator of venture performance is financial performance. We thus compute two measures for new ventures' financial performance: (1) whether a new venture has earned revenue and (2) whether a new venture has been profitable.

name: Racial discrimination
authors_terms: ["discrimination", "racial discrimination", "high-discriminatory states", "no fair housing laws before 1968"]
definition: State-level variation in institutions and norms can have a profound effect on racial minorities' entrepreneurship; we therefore focus on state-level discrimination to examine the moderating effect of discriminatory behavior.

name: Educational credentials
definition: Educational credentials represent a frequent quality signal that can offset the disadvantages racial minorities face in the market by providing information about their abilities and competencies.

name: Business growth aspirations
authors_terms: ["aspirations to grow their business", "high growth orientation", "expected employment size"]
definition: A direct corollary of our theory is the expectation that Black employees may hold greater aspirations to grow their business when acting as intrapreneurs than entrepreneurs.

name: Ownership position
authors_terms: ["ownership strategy", "ownership position", "level of ownership", "percent equity holding", "equity position"]
definition: In this analysis, ownership strategy is defined as the choice concerning the degree of ownership (percent equity holding) taken when a foreign investment is made. The amount of equity ownership is equated with the amount of control that a firm could exert over its subsidiary's operations.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "specificity of assets", "proprietary content", "proprietary nature of the parent's assets"]
definition: The specificity, or proprietary nature, of the Japanese parent's assets, measured as the degree of proprietary content in the firm's technological and marketing assets. A basic tenet of transaction cost theory is that as asset specificity increases, the greater will be the hazards associated with market-based exchange and the greater the incentives to internalize the transaction.

name: Complementary assets
authors_terms: ["complementary assets", "market imperfections for complementary assets", "need to acquire new assets", "requirements for complementary assets"]
definition: Assets required by the foreign firm upon investment in the host country, which can include knowledge of markets, tacit technology, distribution systems, and other intermediate inputs. Firms are motivated to structure foreign entries as joint ventures, and to take lower equity positions, when faced with the need to acquire complementary assets that cannot be obtained efficiently in factor markets.

name: Host country risk
authors_terms: ["host country risk", "host country political and economic risk", "political and economic risk"]
definition: Host country political and economic risk is the aspect of the institutional environment that has received the most attention in conceptual and empirical studies of entry mode choice; in more externally uncertain and volatile environments firms are argued to be better off utilizing low control and ownership modes.

name: Host country restrictiveness
authors_terms: ["host country restrictiveness", "legal restrictions on foreign equity participation", "restrictions on foreign ownership", "legal limits on foreign equity participation"]
definition: The effect of host country restrictions on foreign and local ownership: government policies can effectively influence foreign ownership levels, and legal and political constraints in the host country may bring about local ownership, even where TC theory does not predict the existence of joint ventures.

name: Intellectual property protection
authors_terms: ["intellectual property protection", "property rights protection", "protection of property rights"]
definition: Effective property rights protection ensures that the owner of an asset has discretion over the uses to which the asset is put and is able to appropriate returns from the asset. Where property rights protection is weaker, the cost of contracting and the cost of using a hybrid such as a joint venture increases because of the increased risk of leakage or unwanted dissemination of proprietary technological and marketing assets.

name: International experience
definition: When firms make international investments, specific knowledge of the host country is gained as is more general knowledge of conducting international operations. Firms with more experience in a host country have developed organizational capabilities suited to that country, and are able to make greater commitments to foreign investments.

name: Exchange hazards
definition: Transaction cost economics scholars commonly point to three categories of exchange hazards that necessitate contractual safeguards (or vertical integration): asset specificity, measurement difficulty, and uncertainty.

name: Asset specificity
definition: Asset specificity emerges when sourcing relationships require significant relationship-specific investments in physical and/or human assets. Firm-specific assets were defined by human assets, physical assets, and company-specific routines and knowledge that were not redeployable to alternative uses.

name: Measurement difficulty
authors_terms: ["measurement difficulty", "difficulty in measuring the performance", "difficult performance measurement"]
definition: Difficulty in measuring the performance of exchange partners also generates market hazards. When performance is difficult to measure, parties have incentives to limit their efforts toward fulfilling the agreement.

name: Technological change
definition: Uncertainty, a third hazard, also challenges an exchange by requiring the parties to adapt to problems raised from unforeseeable changes. In this study, we focus on uncertainty arising from rapidly changing technology.

name: Contractual complexity
definition: Formal contracts represent promises or obligations to perform particular actions in the future. The more complex is the contract, the greater is the specification of promises, obligations, and processes for dispute resolution.

name: Relational governance
definition: Governance emerges from the values and agreed-upon processes found in social relationships. For such relationally-governed exchanges, the enforcement of obligations, promises, and expectations occurs through social processes that promote norms of flexibility, solidarity, and information exchange.

name: Exchange performance
authors_terms: ["exchange performance", "overall satisfaction with exchange performance", "satisfaction with exchange performance"]
definition: To incorporate both production and governance efficiency, we examine overall satisfaction with exchange performance, rather than governance costs. The underlying logic of our composite measure is that satisfaction is a focal consequence of a working partnership.

name: Relationship longevity
authors_terms: ["longevity of relationship", "duration of time that the two parties have worked with one another", "previous business relations"]
definition: A key determinant of relational governance is the duration of time that the two parties have worked with one another because a history of trade is necessary for the development of relational norms.

name: IS budget
authors_terms: ["IS budget", "size of the operating budget for IS", "IS resources"]
definition: We use measures of the firm's IS budget and the IS director's experience as identifying instruments in the contractual complexity equation. We expect that firms with greater IS resources will develop more customized contracts.

name: IS managerial experience
authors_terms: ["tenure", "experience of the IS director", "IS director's experience", "top managers' experience in IS"]
definition: In our study, top managers' experience in IS proxies for firm knowledge about outsourcing. We use measures of the firm's IS budget and the IS director's experience as identifying instruments in the contractual complexity equation.

name: Choice situation
authors_terms: ["choice situation", "minimum choice situation", "differentiated choice situation", "maximum choice situation", "incremental choice situation"]
definition: By dichotomizing the levels of strategic choice and environmental determinism, four choice situations are identified: minimum choice, differentiated choice, maximum choice, and incremental choice.

name: Strategic choice
definition: Levels of strategic choice refer to the power of the organization over its environment.

name: Environmental determinism
definition: Environmental determinism reflects the power of the environment over the organization.

name: Generic strategy
definition: The generic strategies (Porter, 1980) prevalent in different choice situations; muddlers, or firms exhibiting no coherent strategy, should dominate incremental choice situations.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Performance is reflected in a set of financial and operating indicators that the industry experts considered useful in discriminating between the high and low performing hospitals in the state.

name: Specialization
definition: Specialization allows individuals to develop deep skills and expertise in a specific area (Becker, 1962; Parsons, 1972; Rosen, 1983), and creates a clarity of identity (Leung, 2014; Zuckerman et al., 2003), which acts as a signal of quality in labor markets. The advantage to generalization stems from the need for coordination and communication, and bridging across distinct domains of knowledge.

name: Upstream relational capital
authors_terms: ["upstream relational capital", "upstream relational assets", "political connections", "changes in upstream relational capital", "shocks to upstream relational capital", "loss of power", "gain of power", "loss of connection", "gain of chair"]
definition: Relationships with upstream suppliers help enhance firms' product and service offerings by increasing diversity of knowledge base and access to resources (Hoetker, 2005; Mayer & Nickerson, 2005). Thus, prior connections through work experience to current policymakers constitute an important source of upstream relational capital. Political connections are key upstream relational assets, and their value varies based on position and power.

name: Lobbying revenue
definition: The main dependent variable of interest is the natural log of a lobbyist's Lobbying revenue reported in semi-annual lobbying disclosure reports. Lobbying revenue is calculated by aggregating the dollar amount of lobbying contracts each lobbyist is involved in each time period.

name: Perceived environmental pressure from stakeholders
authors_terms: ["environmental pressure from each stakeholder group perceived by managers", "perceived pressures from green stakeholders", "stakeholders' environmental pressure perceived by managers", "environmental demands from stakeholders"]
definition: The variables reflect the environmental pressure from each stakeholder group perceived by managers. Managers perceive only one dimension of stakeholders' demand for environmental protection, rather than different demands coming from different stakeholder groups.

name: Environmental proactivity
authors_terms: ["degree of proactivity", "environmental proactivity", "proactivity of the environmental response", "proactivity of environmental response patterns"]
definition: Patterns of environmental response differ in their degree of proactivity, that is, in their tendency to anticipate needs (related to environmental protection) and introduce changes voluntarily rather than as a reaction to environmental requirements and demands. Each pattern represents a specific and internally consistent configuration of both the scope of environmental objectives and the allocation of internal resources to achieve them.

name: Location knowledge spillover intensity
authors_terms: ["Location knowledge spillover intensity", "Location spillover intensity", "knowledge spillover intensity", "intensity of knowledge spillovers"]
definition: High intensity of knowledge spillovers in the location of the firm conducting the R&D activity elevates the hazard of diffusion of valuable knowledge in the region. The threat of leakage and diffusion of sensitive information and experimental outcomes within the local region can negatively affect the value of the technological opportunities partners are jointly pursuing or discovering during the partnership.

name: Location R&D rivalry intensity
authors_terms: ["Location R&D rivalry intensity", "R&D rivalry intensity", "local R&D competition", "regional R&D rivalry"]
definition: The intensity of R&D competition in the region of the R&D firm, reflecting whether research grants are concentrated among a few organizations in a region (lower rivalry) or whether many organizations in the region compete for these grants. More intense local R&D competition increases the magnitude of the threat from spillovers to the local economy.

name: Location sector employment density
authors_terms: ["Location sector employment intensity", "Location sector employment density", "sector employment intensity", "dense industry employment"]
definition: As the density of the individuals who belong to an industrial sector increases, individual actors face more opportunities to establish contact with others who share similar occupational and industry backgrounds, which aids in the development of informal relationships. Spatial proximity of individuals with common career or personal interests and backgrounds serves as an important antecedent to the formation, growth, and stability of local social networks in a region.

name: Location professional community density
authors_terms: ["Location professional community density", "professional community density", "strength of professional organizations", "intensity of membership in a professional body"]
definition: The intensity of membership in a professional body in a given location can indicate strength of the community in the region that shares common pursuits and actions guided by a common set of standards. A location with dense affiliation to a professional body can promote a web of thick institution-based relationships and increase the benefits from mutual interaction.

name: Formal governance provisions
authors_terms: ["detailed formalized governance provisions", "formal governance mechanisms", "formal contractual safeguards", "contract adaptation, monitoring, and enforcement safeguards"]
definition: Private mechanisms in the form of an array of rules, processes, and managerial interfaces for monitoring and decision making that facilitate ex post adaptation and safeguard execution by reducing the scope of defection from cooperative behavior. These contractual provisions can describe in detail the specific procedures to be followed for managing ongoing interactions, resolving emergent conflict, or terminating the relationship.

name: Task system decentralization
definition: Task system decentralization denotes the extent to which a carrier's task system contains few tasks that receive large resource flows from, and send large resource flows to, another task or tasks. A decentralized task system contains few task bottlenecks that disproportionally account for the resource flows or that 'stand between' other tasks in the task system.

name: Task system complexity
definition: Task system complexity captures the extent to which a task system contains long cycles before returning to the beginning of the cycle of tasks. Task system complexity represents how tasks interconnect with one another within the task system, specifically, how they follow other tasks in the system.

name: Resource fungibility
definition: Fungibility is 'an attribute of a resource that facilitates its application to different organizational and market settings'. In this context, resource fungibility denotes the extent to which a carrier uses its aircraft type in tasks of various distances.

name: Resource slack
definition: Resource slack refers to aircraft not out for maintenance or repairs, not already assigned to an activity within the task system, and not being used in a task; in essence, the resource is available to the firm for use. More generally, 'Slack is potentially utilizable resources that can be diverted or redeployed for the achievement of organizational goals'.

name: Firm performance
definition: A key task system (i.e., firm) performance metric in this industry is departure OTP, computed as the proportion of departures that actually departed within 15 min of the carrier's scheduled departure time. The authors focus on task system completion as a relevant measure of firm performance.

name: Figurative language in pitching
definition: With the protocol used, 'figurative' language is defined as the use of a word or expression (as single lexical units) that does not literally apply to the topic that was spoken about in the context of the speech. In their hypotheses the authors gloss a high level of figurative language as the frequent use of personal anecdotes, analogies, and metaphors throughout a pitch.

name: Hand gesturing in pitching
definition: Gestures are movements of hands and arms that co-occur with speech. The authors distinguish beat gestures, which mark the rhythm of an entrepreneur's speech and provide emphasis, from gestures used in an ideational manner, which symbolize abstract ideas associated with the business or demonstrate the features of a product or a service in use.

name: Mental imagery evoked in viewers
definition: Mental imagery is the mental imagery experienced by viewers of a pitch as evoked by the entrepreneur's gestures; viewers who see and understand a speaker's gestures are triggered to mentally simulate, through mental imagery, the underlying perceptual and motor processes for themselves.

name: Propensity to invest
definition: The authors view the investment decision as a staged process in which, after seeing pitches, investors decide whether or not to pursue the opportunity further, involving finding out more about the business or market and the entrepreneur in order to inform their decision to invest. Propensity to invest combines investment intentions with the likelihood of investing.

name: Affective passion displayed by the presenter
definition: 'Affective passion' refers to the display of emotions, enthusiasm, and energy in bodily movements, gestures, and speech during a pitch.

name: Preparedness of the presenter
definition: 'Cognitive passion' - which Chen et al. (2009) termed 'preparedness' - concerns the substance and understanding of the business idea that entrepreneurs communicate through the content of their pitch.

name: Cash holdings
definition: Cash is the most liquid and common form of available slack, which provides high discretion to managers to deploy quickly for adaptation, but can also be easily appropriated by stakeholders. It is defined as the ratio of cash and short-term investments to the book value of total assets.

name: Firm performance
definition: Market-based measures of firm performance are better able to capture the costs and benefits to shareholders of holding cash. Tobin's q denotes the market value of a firm's assets relative to replacement costs, and is proxied by the market-to-book ratio.

name: Industry competition
definition: Cash enables firms in highly competitive industries to adapt to the environmental turbulence and rapid pace of change typical of such industries, and provides a buffer that can absorb the impact of competitor activities. Managers of firms operating in competitive industries are under immense pressure to maximize efficiency.

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: R&D-intensive industries such as aerospace, computers, consumer electronics, and pharmaceuticals are often characterized by uncertainty, complexity, rapid pace of technological change, and a focus on innovation. It is defined as the mean R&D intensity of all firms in the focal industry.

name: Industry growth
definition: Firms operating in high-growth industries generally have numerous attractive investment opportunities, and often make strategic investments that take advantage of these opportunities. High-growth industries may also be characterized by uncertainties about when, in what sequence, or to what extent future growth opportunities will arise.

name: Corporate governance
definition: Corporate governance mechanisms are 'the formal structures, informal structures, and processes' that provide oversight or facilitate incentive alignment. Managerial tendencies toward appropriation of cash will be exacerbated if these mechanisms are weak.

name: Diversification
definition: High levels of diversification raise goal conflicts, bring about power imbalances, and make it easier to conceal value appropriation. Diversification also increases the complexity of a firm's operations and exacerbates the information asymmetry between management and stakeholders.

name: Corporate opacity
definition: In general, higher corporate opacity (i.e., lower corporate transparency) makes external market scrutiny of managerial decisions difficult, and may exacerbate agency problems if insiders such as managers or other opportunistic stakeholders take advantage of their preferential access to information to obtain private benefits of control.

name: Retail deregulation
definition: The formal adoption of retail deregulation policy in a given state, which the authors treat as an important threshold that is tractable and consistent across states.

name: Environmental sensitivity
authors_terms: ["environmental sensitivity", "environmental sensitivity of the population", "environmental sentiment", "demand for environmental quality"]
definition: The environmental sensitivity of the citizens of the state in which the firm operates, which the authors argue reflects demand for environmental quality in the state.

name: Coal generation
authors_terms: ["percentage of generation from coal", "coal generation", "dependence on coal", "investments in coal generation"]
definition: The percentage of electricity generated by coal; coal-fired generation benefits from generations-long path dependencies that have refined plant designs and operations.

name: Productive efficiency
definition: Productive efficiency refers to how, in relation to its peers, a firm can obtain maximum output with given inputs.

name: Environmental differentiation
authors_terms: ["environmental differentiation", "green power", "differentiation strategy", "increase in renewable generation"]
definition: Compared to conventional products, environmental differentiation consists of offering products that provide greater environmental benefits, or that impose smaller environmental costs; in this setting it takes the form of differentiating by offering power produced using less environmentally harmful methods.

name: Cultural differences
authors_terms: ["cultural differences", "perceived cultural differences", "perceptions of cultural differences", "cultural difference measure"]
definition: The authors examine whether the perceptions of differences between the cultures of the top management teams of merging firms of similar strategic fit have an effect on shareholder value. Differences in organizational cultures may have an important impact on the financial success of a related merger, and therefore on the value of the acquiring firm's common equity.

name: Tolerance for multiculturalism
authors_terms: ["tolerance of multiculturalism", "cultural tolerance", "the buyer's tolerance for multiculturalism"]
definition: The degree to which the buying firm values cultural diversity and is willing to tolerate and encourage it; the more the buyer tolerates multiculturalism, the less likely it is for the buyer to expect the acquired firm to conform to its own goals, strategies, and administrative practices.

name: Shareholder value
authors_terms: ["shareholder value", "change in shareholder value", "shareholder gains", "abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: Abnormal returns represent the firm's returns in excess of its expected market returns, and are interpreted as the reevaluation by the capital market of the firm's future profitability based on the information released in the merger announcement.

name: Positive affective traits
definition: Stable individual differences in the long-term tendencies to experience positive affects such as excitement and enthusiasm. Processing strategies conditioned by positive affects are described as simple and intuitive, but also favoring creativity, the search for novel information, and nonconservative behavior and decisions.

name: Negative affective traits
definition: Stable individual differences in the long-term tendencies to experience negative affects such as distress and irritability. Negative affects prompt careful, error avoiding, and conservative behavior and decisions.

name: Strategic conformity
definition: The degree to which a focal firm looks and behaves like the modal (or typical) firm in its industry.

name: Performance conformity
authors_terms: ["typical performance", "'typical' performance by the firm", "performance conformity", "performance deviation"]
definition: Performance that is below or above the average for the industry over a period of time; performance deviations at separate points in time cumulate into risk. The measures of typical performance were calculated like those of strategic conformity.

name: Ownership concentration
definition: The extent to which a firm's stock is held by large owners. The authors describe large shareholders (or blockholders) as owners of 5 percent or more of a firm's equity who have more at stake and, hence, a greater incentive to gather information about firm investments, and they note that concentrated ownership creates liquidity problems for shareholders.

name: R&D investment
definition: R&D expenditures are specific types of investments, in that their outcomes are neither immediate nor certain; investment in R&D is crucial for both the survival and growth of firms, and decisions regarding the magnitude and allocation of R&D expenditures are at the discretion of management.

name: National context
definition: The distinctive national ownership and governance environments that the authors compare: the United States, characterized as an agency environment with atomistic shareholders and a market for corporate control, and Japan, characterized as a stewardship environment with concentrated, relationship-based and relatively illiquid ownership.

name: Institutional pension fund ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional pension (public) fund ownership", "pension fund ownership", "public pension funds", "pension fund managers"]
definition: Institutional owners were classified as either (1) pension funds, (2) professional investment management funds (mutual funds, banks, investment banks), or (3) foundations, universities, and churches, which were not used in the analysis owing to their noted lack of activism.

name: Professional investment fund ownership
authors_terms: ["professional investment fund manager ownership", "professional investment management fund ownership", "investment manager funds", "professional investment funds"]
definition: Institutional owners were classified as either (1) pension funds, (2) professional investment management funds (mutual funds, banks, investment banks), or (3) foundations, universities, and churches, which were not used in the analysis owing to their noted lack of activism.

name: Internal innovation
authors_terms: ["internal innovation", "internal innovation (R&D intensity and new product announcements)", "internal innovation strategies", "internal new product development"]
definition: For instance, we include basic innovation and entrepreneurial activities internal to a firm, such as investments in R&D and new product introductions. Internal innovation was defined with two variables measuring different aspects of the construct: (1) firm R&D intensity, and (2) new product intensity.

name: External innovation
authors_terms: ["external innovation", "external innovation through acquisition", "external (acquired) innovation", "acquisition of innovation"]
definition: We also focus on the acquisition of businesses that provide new products, processes, or markets. External innovation was composed of three items from the survey: (1) external acquisition of new products, (2) external acquisitions to develop new processes, and (3) external acquisitions to build new markets.

name: Inside director ownership and incentives
authors_terms: ["inside director incentives and ownership", "inside board member ownership and incentives", "inside director equity and stock options", "inside director incentives"]
definition: Two indicators, collected for 1991, concerned inside directors, defined as directors who were current firm employees: (1) equity and (2) stock option valuation.

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["degree of representation (director ratio and ownership) of independent outside board members", "outside directors", "independent outside directors", "outside director representation"]
definition: There were also two indicators, collected for 1991, for independent outside directors, defined as those who had no affiliation with the firm on whose board they sat, except as directors: (1) outside director ratio and (2) outside director equity.

name: Associational diversity
authors_terms: ["associational diversity", "form diversity", "diversity of voluntary associations", "form-diversity of voluntary associations", "voluntary association diversity"]
definition: Organizational form comprises a mapping of the organization's activities to the structure of relationships and legal constraints under which those activities must be carried out. The author refers to the diversity of these voluntary associational forms both as associational diversity and form diversity.

name: Foundings of local human services organizations
authors_terms: ["founding rate of local human services organizations", "number of foundings of human services organizations", "local social entrepreneurship", "foundings of local (non-branch, secular) human services organizations"]
definition: The dependent variable is the number of human service organizations founded in a geographic community in any year. The author studies the founding rate of local non-branch, non-religious human service organizations as a measure of local social entrepreneurship.

name: Natural disaster shock
definition: Natural disasters are temporally exogenous shocks to the community's resources and relationships. A disaster shock is represented as a dummy variable set to 1 if there was a disaster declaration in a particular county in that year.

name: Disaster novelty
authors_terms: ["novelty", "unexpectedness", "more unexpected (more novel) disaster", "lower-probability natural disaster event"]
definition: Different places have differing propensities for particular kinds of disaster, and so some disaster shocks can be more novel or unexpected for a community. Novelty or unexpectedness of any disaster event is calculated as the ex-ante probability of the disaster being of a particular kind given a disaster (of any kind) has happened, based on the proportion of past disasters of the focal kind among all disaster events in the previous 30 years in the county.

name: Disaster complexity
authors_terms: ["multiple kinds of natural disasters", "multiple kinds of disaster in a county-year", "complexity of the disaster-imposed conditions", "number of kinds of disaster incident to the community"]
definition: What is undoubtedly rare is to have the same geographic community experience multiple natural disasters, either simultaneously or in the space of a few months. A source of complexity of the disaster-imposed conditions is the number of kinds of disaster incident to the community.

name: Prior shared experience extensiveness
authors_terms: ["prior shared experience (PSE)", "PSE extensiveness", "extensiveness of shared industry-specific experience"]
definition: PSE means that some or all of the founding team members worked together before they founded their new venture. PSE therefore varies in 'extensiveness,' which increases as the proportion of members within the team have longer shared industry-specific experience.

name: New firm performance
definition: New bank performance is measured with return on assets (ROA), a concise and valuable summary statistic of bank performance. Expressed as net income as a percentage of assets, ROA indicates a bank's ability to earn profit on its assets, and reflects how effectively a bank deploys its assets.

name: Current shared experience
authors_terms: ["current shared experience", "shared team-specific experience", "shared operating experience"]
definition: Once the entire team begins working together to lead the new firm, members develop a joint history; their 'shared team-specific experience' reflects accumulated knowledge about one another's 'skills, limitations, and idiosyncratic habits'. Team-specific experience represents increasing levels of familiarity in the team, which supports effective collaboration and interaction.

name: PSE task environment mismatch
definition: When the industry task environment of the new firm is materially different from where PSE was developed, we call it PSE task environment mismatch. PSE benefits are attenuated if the experience leads to inaccurate priorities and strategies.

name: PSE temporal gap
definition: A temporal gap between when PSE was obtained and the new firm was founded can affect accuracy; it is the gap, if any, between the last year in which members worked together and the year the new bank was established. Overall, temporal gaps lower PSE accuracy.

name: Firm climate risk
authors_terms: ["firm climate risk", "firm-specific climate risk", "perceived climate risk", "real climate risk", "physical climate risk"]
definition: A firm's specific exposure to physical climate risk: "We estimate firm-level physical risk from climate change based on managerial evaluation and firms' exposure to climate hazard events." It is estimated "from managerial evaluation of physical climate change exposure and firms' vulnerability to real climate disasters."

name: Bank loan term stringency
authors_terms: ["bank loan terms", "loan contracting terms", "stringent loan contracting terms", "stringent loan terms"]
definition: "Economically, higher loan spread, requiring collateral assets, and more covenants indicate more stringent loan contracting terms, which increase borrowing firms' funding cost and related constraints from lending banks."

name: Climate strategy integration
authors_terms: ["Business Strategy", "integrating climate change into business strategy", "climate risk consideration in business strategy"]
definition: Whether the firm integrates climate change into its overall business strategy, that is, into its grand strategic plan.

name: Board-level climate governance
authors_terms: ["Board-Level Governance", "board that takes direct responsibility for climate change issues", "board-level governance"]
definition: Whether the highest level of direct responsibility for climate change issues in the firm is with the board of directors.

name: Climate risk management process
authors_terms: ["Risk-Managing Process", "risk management process specifically for climate change"]
definition: Whether the firm has set up a specific climate change risk management process or climate risk is integrated into a multi-disciplinary company-wide risk management system.

name: Climate change opportunities
authors_terms: ["Climate Opportunity", "business opportunities from climate change", "climate change-induced opportunities"]
definition: Whether the firm possesses potential opportunities related to climate change, such as opportunities arising from changes in physical conditions, product and technology advances, or changes in customer preferences.

name: Climate policy involvement
authors_terms: ["Policymaking Involvement", "activities that influence public policy on climate change"]
definition: Whether the firm engages in activities that could directly influence public policies on climate change.

name: Operational performance
definition: The borrowing firm's operational performance, proxied by one-year ahead return on assets and one-year ahead cash flow from operations.

name: Default probability
definition: The likelihood that the borrowing firm's loan defaults, measured by the probability of default estimated following Bharath and Shumway (2008).

name: CEO MBA education
definition: MBA education should have a strong influence on CEOs' strategic orientation; it provides a unique experience that is temporally restricted, geographically separated, and intellectually intense, and its influence endures long after graduation.

name: Diversifying acquisition activity
authors_terms: ["diversifying acquisitions", "rate of diversifying acquisitions", "diversifying acquisition activity"]
definition: Acquisitions are regarded as diversifying ones when the acquiring firm's industry differs from that of the acquired firm or asset at the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) level.

name: Board monitoring
authors_terms: ["board monitoring", "monitoring by the board of directors", "monitoring by outsider-dominated boards"]
definition: The primary internal monitoring mechanism is the board of directors, whose fundamental role is to represent shareholders' interests; monitoring by boards, especially those dominated by independent, outside directors, can reduce top managers' opportunistic behavior.

name: Blockholder monitoring
authors_terms: ["external monitoring of top managers by investors", "monitoring by blockholding institutional investors", "blockholder monitoring"]
definition: Institutional investors often play the role of external monitors; in particular, those who own a significant portion of a firm's stock have both the power and incentive to closely monitor top managers.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "a CEO's power in the firm"]
definition: A CEO's power in the firm should have the opposite effect on managerial discretion; everything else being equal, powerful CEOs should enjoy greater decision-making autonomy in their firms.

name: Technology in-licensing
definition: Licensing-in is a mechanism firms use to absorb externally developed technologies and integrate them into their internal knowledge; it can be seen as a technology outsourcing strategy and an alternative to in-house research and development (R&D).

name: Time to invention
authors_terms: ["time to invention", "speed of invention", "invention speed", "time to invention (transition)"]
definition: The time that elapses before a firm introduces a new invention following an onset of risk, measured in months from the license date to the application date of the first patent filed after the signing of the license agreement.

name: Grant-back clause
definition: A grant-back clause, sometimes included in license agreements, obliges licensees to grant the licensor the rights on future advances or improvements to the licensed technology developed during the term of the agreement.

name: Technological unfamiliarity
definition: In a licensing context, knowledge relatedness refers to 'familiarity' with a technology, defined by the degree to which knowledge of the technology exists within the company, not necessarily embodied in its products; unfamiliar technologies are more difficult to assimilate and to recombine with in-house technology.

name: Top management team
definition: Our focus is the knowledge structures of organizations' top-team or dominant coalition who share a common understanding of their firm's overall strategy. While individual members need not have identical knowledge, nor equal influence on its development, we assume that it is broadly shared and reflects a form of consensus among this group.

name: Strategic attention
authors_terms: ["attention", "attentional focus", "what top teams pay attention to", "strategic themes attended to"]
definition: Following D'Aveni and MacMillan (1990: 640) we define attention as 'allocating information-processing capacity (receiving, cognitive processing, disseminating) to environmental stimuli over time,' which is close in meaning to the everyday phrase 'paying attention to.'

name: Strategic knowledge structure
definition: Walsh (1995: 281) defined the knowledge structure concept as 'a mental template that individuals impose on an informational environment to give it form and meaning.' Knowledge structures order an information environment in a way that enables subsequent interpretation and action, are built on past experience, and represent organized knowledge about a given concept or type of stimulus.

name: Cognitive strategic group
definition: Porac, Thomas, and Badden-Fuller (1989) described cognitive strategic groups as groups of companies whose top managers hold similar or shared mental models of strategy within their industry. The similarity to Porter's definition is obvious.

name: Industry
definition: The top-level Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) includes 10 sectors; we excluded Telecommunications and Utilities owing to the small numbers of firms, leaving eight industry sectors in the analysis.

name: Financial performance
definition: Given that we were investigating a multi-industry sample, we employed three widely applicable measures of financial performance: ROE, ROA, and PER.

name: Financial performance
definition: Performance was measured by return on assets before tax and exceptional items. Return on assets remains the most widely used performance measure in the strategy literature.

name: Related-constrained diversification
definition: Theory particularly favors related-constrained diversification: these diversifiers have the advantage over related-linked diversifiers because they are able to exploit synergistic and knowledge advantages over denser networks of internal relationships. Rumelt (1974) describes related-constrained diversifiers as having tightly clustered relationships between all businesses in their portfolio.

name: Related-linked diversification
definition: Rumelt (1974) describes relatedlinked diversifiers as having a series of limited relationships between businesses. Hoskisson and Johnson (1992) describe relatedlinked diversification as a 'between' form of diversification, lacking either the managerial simplicity of unrelated diversification or the focus advantages of related-constrained diversification.

name: Unrelated diversification
definition: One of Rumelt's four diversification types. Related diversifiers are said to be superior to unrelated diversifiers because of operational synergies in marketing and technology and the transferability of knowledge across allied businesses.

name: Undiversified strategy
definition: The authors combine Rumelt's (1974) single and dominant business strategies into a single 'undiversified' category.

name: National context
definition: The three European countries differ markedly in institutional structures. The United Kingdom is closest to the American model in terms of corporate governance and market for corporate control, Germany furthest away, and France somewhere in between.

name: Time period
definition: The study compares two time periods, 1983-93 being a period in which these European economies experienced substantial change in the direction to more efficient external markets, with privatization, deregulation, and European integration.

name: Domestic commercial performance
authors_terms: ["domestic commercial performance", "commercial performance", "domestic commercial success", "domestic box office"]
definition: Commercial success implies that a cultural product is popular with mainstream audiences and therefore in high demand.
