Domestic commercial performance functions, first and foremost, as a readily available quality screen that allows foreign distributors to select and market popular and, therefore, seemingly promising films for distribution in their own countries.

name: Artistic acclaim
authors_terms: ["artistic acclaim", "Cannes, Berlin, or Venice", "film festival participation", "artistic quality"]
definition: Artistic acclaim implies artistic approval by expert audiences such as critics and industry peers. Artistic acclaim achieved through film awards and festival participation is a different type of market signal that allows screening on artistic quality rather than popularity alone.

name: Cultural distance
definition: The perceived foreignness of a film depends on the 'cultural distance' between film audiences in domestic and foreign markets, defined broadly as the extent to which audiences in different countries are culturally similar or different.

name: Domestic distribution type
authors_terms: ["major or independent domestic distribution", "distribution type", "major distribution", "independent distribution"]
definition: The distinction between major and independent distribution captures an important source of heterogeneity for both domestic and foreign distributors based on product specialization rather than cultural distance. 'Major distribution' referred originally to widely distributed films with a broad appeal and originating inside the Hollywood studio system, whereas 'independent distribution' referred to narrowly distributed films with a narrow appeal originating outside the Hollywood studio system.

name: Foreign distribution type
authors_terms: ["major or independent foreign distribution", "distribution type", "major distribution", "independent distribution"]
definition: The distinction between major and independent distribution captures an important source of heterogeneity for both domestic and foreign distributors based on product specialization rather than cultural distance. Foreign audiences observe whether foreign films use major or independent distribution in their own markets.

name: Export likelihood
authors_terms: ["likelihood of export", "likelihood of film export", "export likelihood"]
definition: Our dependent variables are the unobserved likelihood of export and the subsequent, observed commercial performance (box office) in foreign markets. Export likelihood captures the expectations of foreign distributors about the potential demand from film audiences in foreign markets.

name: Foreign commercial performance
authors_terms: ["foreign commercial performance", "foreign box office success", "foreign market performance", "foreign commercial performance (box office)"]
definition: Foreign commercial performance measures the actual demand for the film by foreign film audiences.

name: Same-NPI-mode experience
authors_terms: ["same-NPI-mode experience", "internal development experience", "joint development experience", "licensing experience", "experience"]
definition: How a firm may benefit from launching a new product using the same NPI mode it has used in the past (hereafter referred to as same-NPI-mode experience). We captured it by counting the number of times a firm has used a mode since its entry into a particular area of business.

name: New product introduction performance
definition: Our dependent variable is NPI performance, which we assessed by the cumulative unit sales of each aircraft. Sales volume is therefore a key measure of the performance of any fighter, helicopter, jet, or turboprop.

name: New product introduction mode
definition: We focus on three governance modes commonly used by firms to introduce new products: internal development, joint development, and licensing. When using internal development, a firm takes on technology development, prototype design, tooling development, product manufacturing, and sales on its own; in a joint development, more than one firm shares these tasks; when a firm chooses licensing, it contractually acquires the right to manufacture and sell a product that was initially produced by another firm.

name: Technological complexity
definition: The conceptualization and manufacture of technologically complex products often pose fundamental problems that call for a higher level of cognitive effort. As is common in studies of the aircraft industry, we estimated an aircraft's technological complexity by the logarithm of its maximum speed, range, and takeoff weight.

name: Speed of experiential learning
authors_terms: ["speed of experiential learning", "speed of learning", "marginal performance benefit of experience"]
definition: The speed of learning, defined as the magnitude of the marginal performance benefits of experience. It is higher when firms carry out activities that allow them to develop ex post a clearer understanding of cause-effect relationships.

name: Experience threshold
authors_terms: ["experience threshold", "level of experience at which benefits plateau"]
definition: The experience threshold, the level of experience at which those benefits plateau. It is higher when firms carry out activities involving tasks that are sufficiently related to provide learning synergies between them.

name: Strategic similarity
authors_terms: ["strategic similarity", "strategic similarities between target and bidder firms", "similarity in strategic characteristics", "strategic dissimilarity"]
definition: If two firms exhibit very similar resource allocation patterns as measured across a variety of strategically relevant characteristics (e.g., risk propensity, marketing, efficiency), they can be considered to be strategically similar. The strategic characteristics (risk propensity, marketing emphasis, operational efficiency) are treated as a collective construct because a firm's strategic posture is depicted as a composite of key strategic attributes.

name: Postmerger performance change
authors_terms: ["change in performance following the merger", "postmerger performance", "performance change following the merger"]
definition: Ex ante performance was derived as the revenue-weighted mean of the ROA of both a target and a bidder firm over a three-year period preceding their merger, and ex post profitability of the bidder was computed similarly for the three years after. Change in performance following the merger was the difference between premerger and postmerger performance.

name: Market reaction to antitakeover provisions
authors_terms: ["market reactions to antitakeover provisions", "stockholder wealth", "stock price reaction", "cumulative average abnormal returns (CARs)"]
definition: The dependent variable is the market reactions or the cumulative average abnormal returns (CARs) earned by shareholders accompanying the adoption of antitakeover provisions. The abnormal return, estimated using the standard event study methodology extensively used in financial economics, is the difference between the observed return and the normal return as predicted by the capital asset pricing model (CAPM).

name: Outside director representation
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of outsiders", "outside directors", "outside board members", "greater outsider representation", "outsider-dominated boards"]
definition: Board composition involves the mix of inside directors (those employed by the organization in other capacities) and outside directors. Greater outsider representation is often advocated since outside directors are likely to be more objective in monitoring management actions than inside directors.

name: CEO-chairperson duality
authors_terms: ["board leadership structure", "board leadership", "separation of the CEO and chairperson positions", "boards chaired by the CEO", "combined CEO-chairperson"]
definition: The holding of the chairperson of the board and CEO positions by one individual versus their separation: 'when the CEO and chairperson positions are held by one individual, the board's ability to function effectively as a governance mechanism is severely curbed.'

name: Societal integration
authors_terms: ["integration", "the integration index", "Chinese Culture Connection's (1987) integration index"]
definition: Integration includes questions that discuss trustworthiness, harmony with others, tolerance of others, solidarity with others, and noncompetitiveness—in other words, interpersonal trust.

name: Power distance
authors_terms: ["power distance", "power distance index", "Hofstede's (1980) power distance scale"]
definition: The dimension of power distance, which represents the extent to which the members of a society expect power to be distributed equally in organizations and institutions, also represents societal trust; power distant societies exhibit low interpersonal trust and a great need for controls on the behavior of individuals.

name: Perceived transaction costs
definition: National differences in levels of trust impact perceptions of transactions costs and thereby influence the desirability of internalization and the choice of foreign market entry mode.

name: Preference for licensing over direct foreign investment
authors_terms: ["preference for licensing over direct foreign investment", "the choice between licensing and direct foreign investment", "preference for direct foreign investment over licensing", "the choice of foreign market entry mode"]
definition: The dependent variable is the ratio of royalties earned from licensing to unaffiliated foreigners over sales revenues from subsidiaries, which expresses the tendency of American firms to license their products relative to their tendency to engage in direct foreign investment.

name: Pooled R&D activities
authors_terms: ["pooled R&D activities", "pooling of R&D", "resource pooling", "scale alliances"]
definition: Alliances in which R&D activities are pooled (scale) to create new knowledge or capabilities by jointly building on the target firm's technological resources, versus those in which they are not pooled (link). The inclusion of pooled R&D activities describes a situation in which the parties are coinvolved at the same stage of the innovation process.

name: Equity in alliance governance
definition: The governance structure of the alliance, specifically whether the alliance included a minority equity investment or was purely contractual. The equity/nonequity decision sets the overarching framework under which all subsequent governance activities will occur.

name: Target firm alliance experience
authors_terms: ["target firm's alliance experience", "alliance experience of the target firm", "target's alliance experience"]
definition: Alliance experience provides learning across multiple stages of the alliance process, including selecting collaborators, negotiating terms and conditions, monitoring and managing the collaboration, and recognizing the optimal time to terminate a collaboration; as a target firm accumulates this experience it develops expertise in crafting contractual terms that mitigate unintended knowledge leakage and misappropriation.

name: Client firm alliance experience
authors_terms: ["client firm's alliance experience", "alliance experience of the client firm", "client's alliance experience"]
definition: Experience that lets a client firm develop a network of relationships from past collaborations that become a source of flexibility in monitoring and capturing new technological or business opportunities, and makes it more skilled in identifying when and how to terminate a collaboration.

name: Alliance experience asymmetry
authors_terms: ["asymmetry in alliance experience", "asymmetric alliance experience", "relative alliance experience"]
definition: The situation in which the partners have substantially asymmetric alliance experience, in which one firm has extensive alliance experience and the other has little experience, maximizing the gap between the versatility of the two firms vis-a-vis governance structure.

name: Decision-maker role
authors_terms: ["decision-maker role", "decision-making role", "decision-maker roles", "percentage of time in a decision-making role"]
definition: Within the context of creativity and innovation, the decision-maker role is a role defined by the responsibility for allocating or withholding resources for ideas; it is defined as being responsible for resourcing or funding ideas.

name: Economic mindset
definition: A cognitive tendency to prioritize concerns at the heart of economics, including accuracy, rationality, and self-interest.

name: Social approval cues
authors_terms: ["social approval cues", "social approval", "low social approval", "high social approval"]
definition: Indicators that others endorse, support, or favorably view an idea, item, or action.

name: Creativity assessment
definition: An idea is defined by scholars as creative to the extent that it is judged both novel and useful relative to domain knowledge; participants assessed how creative and innovative they thought an idea was.

name: Usefulness assessment
definition: Participants assessed idea usefulness, specifically how practical, feasible, and useful the idea was.

name: Industry hypercompetition
definition: We build on these studies and define hypercompetitiveness of the software industry as the changes in performance rank orders of independent software vendors in their respective product markets.

name: Performance rank
definition: We measure hypercompetitiveness of the software industry with annual changes in the performance rank orders of ISVs. We use ISVs' market shares to operationalize performance.

name: Product portfolio complementarity
authors_terms: ["complementarity within an ISV's existing product portfolio", "Complementarity within N existing", "Complementarity within N entry", "Complementarity within N exit"]
definition: Two software products are defined to be complementary when changes in activity levels of one of the products (e.g., sales, functionality, and ease of use) affect marginal returns to changes in the activity levels of the other software product as well. We compute the extent of complementarities within an ISV i's existing product portfolio at time t by taking a weighted sum of all pairwise complementarity scores in the portfolio.

name: Industry complementarity position
authors_terms: ["industry position of an ISV's product portfolio", "Industry position of N existing", "Industry position of N entry", "Industry position of N exit"]
definition: We conceptualize the industry position of an ISV's product portfolio in terms of the complementarity relationships of the products inside the ISV's portfolio with all other product markets in the industry. As the ISV's products develop stronger complementarity relationships with the other product markets in the industry, the firm's product portfolio occupies a more central complementarity position in the industry.

name: Resource reconfiguration capability
authors_terms: ["dynamic resource reconfiguration capability", "Resource reconfiguration in N existing"]
definition: We measure an ISV i's dynamic resource reconfiguration capability by computing the extent to which it is able make resource reallocations inside its product portfolio at time (t) in response to the changing complementarity relationships among product markets in the industry from (t - 1) to (t). If a firm increases (decreases) its time (t) resource allocations to product markets whose complementarities have strengthened (weakened) from (t - 1) to (t), we consider it a coherent response.

name: Political networking
definition: We define political networking as the extent to which managers cultivate relationships with government officials. Managers' ties with government officials represent a unique type of managerial resource in China's transition economy.

name: Functional experience
definition: We define functional experience as managers' working experience in various functional areas, including sales/marketing, R&D/engineering, manufacturing, finance, and administration.

name: New venture performance
definition: The respondent was asked to rate his or her venture's performance relative to its principal competitors over the last 3 years on return on investment, return on sales, profit growth, return on assets, overall efficiency of operations, sales growth, market share growth, and cash flow from operations.

name: State ownership
definition: In a transition economy state-owned ventures are founded by the government or its agencies and have great legitimacy and government protection, whereas non-state-owned ventures lack legitimacy and government protection and are in a relatively weak position in the institutional environment.

name: Dysfunctional competition
definition: It specifically refers to the extent to which the competition in a firm's environment is opportunistic, unfair, or even unlawful.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["environmental uncertainty", "product-market uncertainty at a divisional level", "increasing uncertainty in local markets", "uncertainty in local markets"]
definition: Environmental uncertainty is the degree to which future states of the world cannot be anticipated and accurately predicted. For multidivisional firms, an important dimension of uncertainty concerns complexity, change, and competition in local or divisional markets.

name: Centralization of decision-making authority
authors_terms: ["centralization", "centralization of decision making", "decision-making authority", "locus of decision making", "control practices"]
definition: Centralization is the concentration of authority and decision making in an organizational structure; as applied to multidivisional organizations, decision-making authority can vary on a continuum ranging from complete decentralization, with decisions made exclusively by local hospital managements or boards, to complete centralization, with decisions made exclusively by corporate management or boards.

name: Management accountability and control decisions
definition: Decisions affecting the behavior of divisional management, either indirectly through the selection or appointment of managers and board members or directly through the evaluation of management performance.

name: Resource allocation decisions
definition: Decisions about the transfer, sale, pledging, or purchase of the assets of a corporation or its divisions.

name: Operating policy decisions
definition: Decisions affecting the operating policies of the divisions of a corporation in their local markets, including decisions affecting changes in hospital bylaws, granting medical staff privileges to admitting physicians, and hospitals' operating and capital budget processes.

name: Local strategy decisions
definition: Decisions affecting divisions' competitive positioning in local markets through planning, diversification, and service and product mix, such as the formation of new companies, strategy formulation at a hospital level, and hospital service additions and deletions.

name: Initial control strategy
authors_terms: ["initial control strategy", "initial decision-making practices", "existing control practices", "initial centralization"]
definition: Initial control strategy was a system's 1983 score for overall centralization and the four subcategories of centralization. Systems whose decision-making practices are extremely centralized will be more likely to undergo change in their decision-making practices in response to increasing uncertainty in their environment.

name: Organizational size
definition: The size of a multihospital system was measured as the number of hospitals it owned, leased, or sponsored.

name: Organizational age
definition: Age was measured as the number of years a system had been incorporated as of 1983.

name: Geographic dispersion
definition: The measure of dispersion was intended to reflect geopolitical disparities in hospitals' operating environments as well as the approximate physical distances among hospitals operating in a given system, and was based on the number of states in which a system operated hospitals.

name: System ownership and control
authors_terms: ["system ownership", "ownership and control", "ownership or control of a multidivisional organization"]
definition: Ownership or control of a multidivisional organization was used as a proxy for institutionalization in organizational environments; ownership was measured with four categories: ownership by a state or local government, investors, a secular not-for-profit entity, or a religious entity.

name: Structural alignment
authors_terms: ["structural alignment", "cognitive process of structural alignment", "similarity comparison", "alignment processes"]
definition: Structural alignment is a cognitive tool that people use to compare things-and to draw implications from the comparison; alignment proceeds at two distinct levels, one centered on the superficial features and the other on structural relationships.

name: Alignment of superficial features
authors_terms: ["alignment of superficial features", "superficial features", "superficial alignment", "superficial characteristics"]
definition: Superficial features relate to the basic 'parts' of a mental representation, along with their attributes and characteristics.

name: Alignment of structural relationships
authors_terms: ["alignment of structural relationships", "structural relationships", "structural reasoning", "first-order relationships", "higher-order relationships"]
definition: Structural relationships refer to the links that unite different superficial features within a mental representation; first-order relationships consist of one-to-one functional relationships between superficial features, whereas higher-order relationships include more abstract 'relationships between relationships,' such as causal chains, goal statements, and conditional rules.

name: Prior knowledge
authors_terms: ["prior knowledge", "prior knowledge of markets", "levels of prior knowledge"]
definition: Prior knowledge provides a basis from which to interpret-and use-new information; because the distribution of knowledge in society is not uniform, prior knowledge helps to explain why some individuals are able to recognize particular opportunities that others simply fail to see.

name: Opportunity recognition
authors_terms: ["opportunity recognition", "the process of recognizing opportunities", "recognizing opportunities"]
definition: We define the process of recognizing opportunities as efforts to make sense of signals of change (e.g., new information about new conditions) to form beliefs regarding whether or not enacting a course of action to address this change could lead to net benefits.

name: Voice mail availability
authors_terms: ["voice mail", "access to voice mail", "voice mail capability", "voice mail regions", "sales regions having access to voice mail"]
definition: Voice mail is one of a class of store-and-forward communication technologies that have been shown to reduce communication barriers associated with time zone differences, geography, partner-unavailability, and social/organizational status; field representatives having access to voice mail were provided a voice mail telephone number which dealership personnel could call and leave verbal messages.

name: Dealership sales performance
authors_terms: ["dealership sales performance", "sales performance", "number of new trucks sold by each dealership"]
definition: Dealership sales performance is determined by the number of new trucks sold by each dealership, the outcome whose improvement characterizes greater effectiveness in the interorganizational relationship.

name: Verbal communication media use
definition: Verbal media, such as face-to-face and telephone, facilitate the rich communication exchanges required to resolve technical ambiguities arising in negotiating with end-consumers regarding, for example, customized product orders or service contracts.

name: Written communication media use
definition: Written media, such as printed documents and facsimile, are necessary in this interorganizational service context to confirm and expedite the handling of special customer requests.

name: Satisfaction with dyadic partner interaction
authors_terms: ["satisfaction with the dyadic interactions", "satisfaction with dyadic partner interaction", "satisfaction with the quality of interaction with the dyadic partner", "interaction satisfaction"]
definition: The extent to which each dyadic partner is satisfied with the other partner's interactions provides a transaction-specific evaluation of the quality of the service being provided by the dyad.

name: Intraorganizational network cohesion
definition: A high level of cohesion implies that an inventor has a tightly knit ego-network of collaborators within the firm, where direct and indirect contacts are also linked to one another. An inventor's ego network constraint measures the extent to which an inventor is embedded in a single group of interconnected colleagues, or brokers between weakly connected groups.

name: Geographic proximity to headquarters
authors_terms: ["Geographic distance", "Geographical distance", "geographical proximity", "colocation", "geographic distance between headquarters and R&D laboratories"]
definition: The geographic distance between inventors and the key decision makers located at the company headquarters. Geographical proximity engenders face-to-face interactions, which are crucial for effective information transfer and interpretation, reducing information asymmetry and fostering alignment of divergent representations.

name: Commission error
definition: A commission error occurs when an organization pursues a low-quality technological opportunity that should have objectively been rejected.

name: Omission error
definition: An omission error arises when an organization rejects a high-quality technological opportunity that should have objectively been pursued.

name: Regulatory monitoring costs
authors_terms: ["regulatory monitoring costs", "regulatory transaction costs", "monitoring costs", "regulatory commission expenses"]
definition: Within the relational contracting framework, regulatory transaction costs (herein referred to as monitoring costs) include all expenditures associated with planning for possible contingencies, adapting to unforseen circumstances, and compromising on renewed problems. For our purposes, we take these costs to vary with the costs associated with regulatory hearings, audits, and reviews.

name: Diversification
definition: In this industry, diversification constitutes moves into new businesses that typically are not regulated, because they lack monopolistic properties. Diversification by utilities represents a response to the impossibility of integrating the troublesome exchange partner, since it expands their domain to include new businesses that typically are not regulated.

name: Backward integration
definition: To measure the extent of backward integration, we sum up equity in all subsidiaries engaged in the location, procurement, and trasportation of natural gas to the electric utility and its gas distribution affiliates. Diversification and backward integration are mutually exclusive categories (i.e. one is not a subset of the other).

name: Activity load
authors_terms: ["activity load", "heavier activity load", "level of activity load"]
definition: The number of investments the private equity firm handled concurrently with the focal investment; managing a heavier activity load means managing a high level of simultaneous activity, which saturates decision makers' limited attention capacity.

name: Focal activity performance
authors_terms: ["performance of the focal activity", "performance of each single investment", "buyout performance"]
definition: The performance of an individual strategic activity, measured at the buyout level as the internal rate of return earned by investors from the acquisition of the company until it is sold.

name: Experience stock
authors_terms: ["stock of prior experience", "stock of accumulated experience", "experience stock"]
definition: The stock of prior experience accumulated in the execution of prior activities; the authors argue that experience accumulation leads firms to form routines, which frees decision makers' attention for other activities.

name: Experience homogeneity
definition: The extent to which a firm's accumulated experience was concentrated in specific industries, i.e., how homogeneous the array of past strategic activities is.

name: Experience pacing
authors_terms: ["experience pacing", "pacing", "pace at which experience is accumulated"]
definition: The mean temporal interval between one decision and the following decision in the process of accumulating experience.

name: Past success
definition: The level of success achieved by the organization in its prior activities, which the authors argue increases satisficing, negative transfer and overconfidence.

name: Divisionalization
definition: The degree of divisionalization represents the extent to which internal transactions are governed by hierarchy rather than semi-autonomous bargaining, and therefore the extent to which decisions concerning the overall directions of technology development activity are centralized.

name: Technological diversification
authors_terms: ["technological diversification", "R&D diversification", "technological diversity", "technical diversity", "range of R&D activities"]
definition: Technological diversity is defined as the range of R&D activities in which the firm is engaged, regardless of their location relative to the firm's principal business.

name: Technological progressiveness
authors_terms: ["technologically progressive firms", "less technologically progressive firms", "nonprogressive firms", "rates of technical progress"]
definition: The authors distinguish firms according to the rates of technical progress in the industries and market segments in which they operate; firms in which corporate-level management cannot be considered to give substantial weight to technology strategy because of slow rates of technical progress are less technologically progressive, since they are not explicitly attempting to capture gains from coordination of R&D in complementary technical areas, given the fewer technological opportunities.

name: Task performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "total moves to treasure", "total time to treasure", "moves to solution"]
definition: Performance was measured by two indicators: (1) the total number of moves a player carried out, equivalent to the number of rooms she has visited, and (2) the total amount of time (in seconds) she used to find the treasure in each trial.

name: Cumulative experience
definition: In the learning curve equation, X is the cumulative number of periods or units through time; in this study it is the number of trials a player or simulated organization has accumulated.

name: Learning rate
definition: The rate at which performance improves with experience, estimated as the exponent b of the power law learning curve. The standard measure of learning is also expressed as the progress ratio, indicating the percentage of previous performance reached whenever there is a doubling of output or experience.

name: Depth of credit assignment
authors_terms: ["depth of credit assignment", "depth of credit propagation", "deeper credit assignment"]
definition: A more generalized version of the credit assignment model explores the depth of credit propagation by including a parameter that specifies the number of preceding state-action pairs to which credit is assigned. As this parameter increases, credit is assigned more deeply.

name: Proximity to the solution
authors_terms: ["states closer to the solution", "proximity to the treasure", "one-step neighbors"]
definition: The physical closeness of a state (room) to the goal (treasure); the rooms that are physically proximate to the treasure represent important subgoals, allowing the problem to be broken down to smaller, intermediate steps.

name: Subgoal recognition
authors_terms: ["gradual recognition of important stepping stones", "recognition of subgoals", "valuation of rooms", "perceived proximity to the treasure"]
definition: The learning mechanism in the credit assignment model is the gradual recognition of important stepping stones to the goal; subjects' recognition of important subgoals cascades from rooms close to the solution to those further away.

name: Environmental change
authors_terms: ["a new environment", "environmental change", "change of the treasure", "new regime"]
definition: A change in the task environment: the location of the treasure was changed to a room four steps away from the original room for the last 20 trials, requiring subjects to substantially redraw their mental map.

name: Profit persistence
definition: The B estimate (the persistence parameter) indicates the rate at which abnormal profits converge upon long-run levels. More generally, the higher is B, the more persistent are the abnormal profit outcomes.

name: Long-run profit rate
definition: An indicator of the long-run rate of return (πlr) may be obtained by setting πlr equal to α/(1-B). When πlr is not significantly different from zero, high and low profits converge upon normal levels in the long run.

name: Profitability
definition: πit is the relative profitability of firm i in year t: πit = (πit - πavg)/πavg, where πit is the profit rate of firm i in year t and πavg is the average profit rate earned across all firms. ROA is defined as the ratio of net income to total assets.

name: Innovative propensity
definition: Firms with relatively high innovative propensities should derive a greater proportion of their sales from innovative products. New pharmaceutical products range from being highly innovative at one extreme to highly imitative at the other.

name: Competition intensity
authors_terms: ["competition intensity", "intensity of competition faced by a product", "low competition", "ability to avoid competition"]
definition: The intensity of competition faced by a new product over time is operationalized with reference to the average market share change over its term on the market. Firms with greater average slope estimates (for their innovative products) are better at avoiding competition.

name: Status
authors_terms: ["status", "organizational status", "social standing", "position in a social hierarchy"]
definition: Status is broadly understood as the position in a social hierarchy that results from accumulated acts of deference, and a firm's status is influenced by the status of the entities with whom the firm affiliates. It is a socially constructed asset that can generate privilege or discrimination and is used to signal quality when uncertainty is high.

name: Reputation
definition: A firm's reputation is best understood as broad public recognition of the quality of a firm's activities and outputs, capturing the perceived predictability of a firm based on past performance and behaviors and the extent to which these perceptions are widely known and shared.

name: Firm age
definition: VC firm age was calculated as the focal year minus the year a VC firm raised its first fund. During its early years a firm has little standing in its industry's social hierarchy, and as it ages its capabilities and history of relationships become better known and its relative standing in the status order stabilizes.

name: Blockbuster deals
authors_terms: ["blockbuster deals", "blockbuster IPOs", "big hits", "blockbuster initial public offerings"]
definition: In the VC firm context, blockbuster deals are initial public offerings that experience high levels of underpricing, the percentage change in the value of the stock on the first day it trades on the public market. Such highly visible, positive events create a buzz about the start-up and let the funding VCs grandstand.

name: Board diversity
definition: The effectiveness of the resource and strategy functions of a board is associated with board diversity measured in terms of such factors as board leadership structure, the number of outside directors, and the number of outside directorships ('interlocks') each individual board member holds in other organizations. The measurement of board diversity may include, in addition to membership of webs of board directorships, elements of director prestige such as membership of political elites and present or former partnerships in an accounting, law, or management consultancy firm.

name: Executives' experience
definition: We defined executives' experience as the management positions and board memberships held over the last 5 years before the IPO, which derive from the career histories of the CEO and other executive directors of the young firm.

name: Executive share ownership
authors_terms: ["share ownership of executive directors", "executive share ownership", "retained share ownership by IPO executives", "ESHAR"]
definition: Board interests were measured in terms of the percentage of the total number of ordinary shares retained by executive and nonexecutive board members after the IPO, as reported in the listing prospectus; by retaining equity, executive directors send positive signals to outside investors.

name: Nonexecutive share ownership
authors_terms: ["share ownership of nonexecutive directors", "nonexecutive share ownership", "nonexecutive directors' equity", "NESHAR"]
definition: Providing nonexecutive directors with an ownership stake in the firm may be a clear signal to outside investors that the young firm not only complies with the principles of 'good corporate governance', but also creates the incentives for nonexecutive directors to take an active role in the decision-making process.

name: Underpricing
definition: Underpricing in IPOs, i.e., the difference between a stock's offering price and the closing price on the first day the stock is offered for trading, is the norm and represents a direct transfer of wealth from the original owners to outside investors.

name: Prior entrepreneurial experience of coworkers
authors_terms: ["peer entrepreneurial experience", "prior entrepreneurial experiences among workplace peers", "career experiences of peers", "former entrepreneurs", "entrepreneurial peers"]
definition: The prior history of entrepreneurship among an individual's coworkers. The authors argue that working with former entrepreneurs may influence an individual's decision to start a business, and measure this experience as the prior entrepreneurial experience of the focal individual's peers.

name: Entry into entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["entry into entrepreneurship", "transition to entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial entry", "individual rates of entrepreneurship", "become an entrepreneur"]
definition: The transition from paid employment into entrepreneurship, i.e., founding a business with or without employees; the authors pool all types of entrepreneurial entry into a single transition.

name: Exposure to entrepreneurship outside the workplace
authors_terms: ["exposure to entrepreneurship in other aspects of their lives", "self-employed parents", "parental self-employment", "more entrepreneurial region"]
definition: Factors outside the workplace that expose an individual to entrepreneurship and that are known to increase entrepreneurial opportunities and motivation, examined here as parental self-employment and the level of entrepreneurship in the region where the individual works.

name: Ownership control imbalance
authors_terms: ["ownership control imbalance", "imbalance in ownership control", "imbalance of ownership"]
definition: Ownership control refers to the residual rights to making decisions regarding an asset's use that is not contractually given to another party; it is the legitimate authority that a firm has over its assets. For an IJV, this control is manifested by the percentage of capital that each partner invests in the venture.

name: Management control imbalance
authors_terms: ["management control imbalance", "imbalance in management control", "imbalance of management control"]
definition: Management control is the observable pattern of decision-making power. It may derive from informal control mechanisms including contractual arrangements, management teams, and the implementation of management systems from one partner, which may extract decision-making power apart from that derived from ownership.

name: Parental conflict
authors_terms: ["parental conflict", "conflict between the parents", "level of conflict between the parents"]
definition: Conflict between the parents of the IJV, including mistrust between the parents, conflicting goals of parents, and conflict over the original agreement.

name: Technical parent support
authors_terms: ["technical support", "technological support", "support in terms of technical know-how"]
definition: Technical support provided by the foreign parent includes process and product technology, that is, the degree to which the IJV received product- and manufacturing-related technology from the foreign parent.

name: Managerial parent support
authors_terms: ["managerial support", "managerial know-how", "support in terms of managerial skills"]
definition: Managerial support provided by the foreign parent entails administrative know-how, managerial expertise, and marketing direction, that is, the extent the IJV received sales, managerial, administrative, and emotional support from the foreign parent.

name: IJV learning
authors_terms: ["IJV learning", "learning by the IJV", "learning from the foreign parent"]
definition: Learning is the mechanism by which IJV technological and managerial capabilities are internalized through the support of the foreign parent, appraised as the extent to which the venture had learned technological expertise, marketing expertise, product development, managerial techniques, and manufacturing processes.

name: IJV survival
definition: Whether the international joint venture remained operational as an IJV at the time of the second survey, coded as a dichotomous variable (0 = dissolved, 1 = survived).

name: Bilateral idiosyncratic investments
definition: Bilateral idiosyncratic investments occur when a buyer and supplier both make idiosyncratic investments into the relationship. These investments may be tangible (e.g., a manufacturing facility, a specific tool, die, or machine), or intangible (e.g., tacit knowledge, a specific technology, or capability).

name: Goal congruence
definition: Goal congruence is the extent to which firms perceive the possibility of achieving compatible, if not identical, objectives. It is a latent sociological mechanism that motivates specific behaviors in an exchange.

name: Interpersonal trust
definition: Trust is the willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party based on the expectation that the other will perform a particular action important to the trustor, irrespective of the ability to monitor or control that other party. It occurs between two people who function as principal players on behalf of the buyer and the supplier.

name: Ex post opportunism
definition: Opportunism is self-interest seeking with guile. In practice, it involves (i) distortion of information, including overt behaviors such as lying, cheating and stealing, as well as more subtle behaviors such as misrepresenting information by not fully disclosing, and (ii) reneging on explicit or implicit commitments such as shirking, or failing to fulfill promises and obligations. Our focus is on opportunism after the transaction is underway (ex post opportunism).

name: Exchange outcomes
definition: Exchange offers many benefits, including economically significant outcomes and expectations of relationship continuity. We examine four short- and long-term economic and strategic outcomes: evaluations of the counterpart's performance, the achievement of competitive advantages, joint profit performance, and expectations of relationship continuity.

name: Counterpart performance evaluation
authors_terms: ["evaluation of the counterpart's performance", "evaluations of the counterpart's performance"]
definition: The firm's evaluation of the counterpart's performance is an economically significant short-term outcome. This is an individual outcome, reflecting the view of the focal firm alone; it is a holistic representation, entailing a rough comparison of benefits against costs, and a positive evaluation justifies involvement in a collaboration.

name: Competitive advantages
definition: Competitive advantages are strategic benefits gained over competing firms, such as superior access to resources, decreased supply and inventory costs, or the development of unique process technologies. They are long-term and accrue to the dyad, thereby enabling the firms to compete more effectively in the marketplace.

name: Joint profit performance
definition: Joint profit performance results from joint efforts in exchange. It is not merely a summation of the two firms' individually realizable profits, but instead indexes financial outcomes that result from the interdependence of effort and investments that reside within the dyad.

name: Relationship continuity expectations
authors_terms: ["expectations of relationship continuity", "continuity expectations", "expectations of relational continuity"]
definition: The firm's expectation of relationship continuity reflects the focal firm's perspective of the long-term viability of the relationship. When a firm expects that the relationship will continue into the future, it is more willing to engage in processes and make investments that will enhance the relationship into the long run.

name: Firm age
definition: As organizations age, they become inert to change and the gap between their knowledge and capabilities and the environment increases. A time varying measure of firm age is operationalized as the time elapsed in years since a firm first applied for a patent.

name: Core change to organizational knowledge
authors_terms: ["core change to their knowledge", "core change to organizational knowledge", "core change", "change to an organization's knowledge"]
definition: Core knowledge is represented as a subset of all organizational knowledge, comprised of the top 5 technologies in which an organization possesses expertise. A core change to areas of organizational expertise takes place when there is a change in the composition of this group of technologies.

name: Number of hires
authors_terms: ["number of hires", "number of new hires", "people they hire"]
definition: The greater the number of hires in an organization, the more is the disruption to encased learning and routine. It is a count of the number of hires in an organization in the two years prior to the application date of a patent divided by the number of scientists present in the firm.

name: Hire distant knowledge
authors_terms: ["hire distant knowledge", "hiring people with distant knowledge", "distant knowledge"]
definition: This captures the extent to which the knowledge hires possess is new to the organization. Hire knowledge distance may be computed by subtracting hire knowledge similarity from 1.

name: Hire experience
definition: For each hired scientist, experience is the number of patents that the scientist had already worked on prior to the application date of the focal patent. Hire experience is the average of the experience of all new hires that a firm recruited in the two years preceding the application date of a given patent.

name: Functional heterogeneity
definition: Functional heterogeneity is one of the demographic measures included in team structure; the Blau (1977) heterogeneity index was determined to be the best measure of it. Functional categories used for both industries were finance and accounting, production and operations, research and development, special services, marketing, and general management.

name: Variation in team tenure
definition: Functional heterogeneity and variation in tenure were both used for the heterogeneity measures of team structure. Variation in tenure was assessed with the coefficient of variation, calculated by using all the executives active on the team year by year.

name: Team fluctuation
definition: Keck and Tushman's term "fluctuation" is used here to refer to the entries and exits of team members. Team structure includes demographic measures such as functional heterogeneity, average team tenure, variation in team tenure, member fluctuation, and hierarchy (stratification).

name: Team stratification
definition: Stratification, or the differences in rank among individual members of a team, is an important property of team structure. The distribution of individuals among titles or ranks is a convenient way to think of stratification (number of levels and relative size of each) in the top management team.

name: Mean team tenure
definition: The mean team tenure was simply the average of the individual members' tenures on the team. Team structure includes average team tenure among its demographic measures.

name: Financial performance
definition: Change in return on assets (ROA) was the most appropriate measure of financial performance for both industries in the study. ROA growth was calculated over two years and represented growth from time t through t + 2.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: External environments that do not require constant scanning, vigilance, and response were labeled as stable. External environments that do require such activity were labeled as turbulent.

name: Foreign product/service diversity
definition: One of the two dimensions along which most researchers have viewed MNC strategy. Most researchers have operationalized product/service diversity as the number of two digit SIC codes in which the MNC participates.

name: Foreign market involvement
authors_terms: ["foreign market involvement", "extent of foreign involvement", "foreign sales as a percentage of total sales"]
definition: The second dimension of MNC strategy. Consistent with prior research, the extent of foreign market involvement was operationalized as the percentage of total sales or revenue earned from foreign operations.

name: MNC organization structure
authors_terms: ["MNC structure", "organization structure", "worldwide functional structure", "international division structure", "worldwide product/service division structure", "geographic region structure", "matrix structure", "mixed structure"]
definition: The MNC structure was worldwide functional if executives were responsible for particular functions globally; international division if one executive was responsible for all international operations while others at the same level were responsible for particular functions or product/service lines; multidivisional if executives were responsible for particular product/service lines globally; and geographic region or area if executives were responsible for all functions and product/service lines for particular regions.

name: Strategy-structure fit
definition: A good fit is found between the strategy and structure of the MNC when the information processing demand of its strategy is met by the information processing capacity of its structure. Firms which are able to achieve a fit between their strategy and structure can create a significant competitive advantage.

name: Economic performance
definition: The economic performance of the MNCs, measured by Return on Assets (ROA); ROA, by definition, reflects the firm's relative efficiency in the utilization of its assets.

name: MNC sector
definition: MNCs which have derived more than 50 percent of their sales from manufacturing and/or mining are defined as manufacturing MNCs. Similarly, MNCs which have more than 50 percent of their revenues from non-manufacturing and/or non-mining operating businesses are defined as service MNCs.

name: Ownership structure
definition: Ownership structure is defined by the distribution of equity holdings. When equity holdings in a large firm are widely dispersed, principals have less influence over management and the board of directors, which, though formally charged with representing the owners, is in fact controlled by management.

name: Managerial pay level
authors_terms: ["pay-level policy", "levels of management pay", "base pay", "base and bonus"]
definition: The first is the pay-level policy, which determines whether a firm will pay above, meet, or pay below the current market wage level. Firms make decisions as to whether they should pay above, meet, or pay below prevailing labor market rates.

name: Change in managerial pay
authors_terms: ["change in base and bonus", "changes in managerial pay", "changes in pay"]
definition: Change in base and bonus, measured by the average base and bonus in year t minus the average base and bonus in year t - 1, all divided by average base and bonus in year t - 1 for all surveyed managers for all years available.

name: Change in financial performance
definition: Financial performance is a composite index constructed from standardized values of return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE). Change variables were calculated for year t as the variable in year t minus the variable in year t - 1, all divided by the variable in year t - 1, for all years available.

name: Change in firm size
definition: Organizational size is a composite index constructed from a factor analysis of the standardized values of assets, sales, and number of employees. Change variables were calculated for year t as the variable in year t minus the variable in year t - 1, all divided by the variable in year t - 1, for all years available.

name: Long-term incentive eligibility
authors_terms: ["percentage of managers eligible for long-term performance incentives", "long-term performance incentives", "long-term incentives"]
definition: Pay can be linked to firm performance through long-term or short-term incentives. Short-term incentives do not shift as much risk to managers as long-term incentives, since long-term goals may be less clear and more uncertain.

name: Bonus eligibility
authors_terms: ["percentage of employees eligible for bonus", "percentage of the workforce eligible for bonuses", "bonus-eligible employees"]
definition: Two questions about compensation strategy that reflect pay risk are (1) what proportion of total pay should be placed at risk through incentives, and (2) what proportion of the workforce should be eligible for bonuses.

name: Bonus share of managerial pay
authors_terms: ["bonus to base and bonus ratio", "percentage of bonus to base and bonus", "percentage of employees eligible for bonuses"]
definition: Two questions about compensation strategy that reflect pay risk are (1) what proportion of total pay should be placed at risk through incentives, and (2) what proportion of the workforce should be eligible for bonuses.

name: Firm-level competitive activity
authors_terms: ["firm-level competitive activity", "competitive firm activity", "firm activity", "competitive actions"]
definition: Firm-level competitive activity is defined as the total number of competitive actions a firm takes in a given year; the authors consider it to include product introductions and announcements, as well as marketing and promotion campaigns (including price cuts).

name: Industry-level rivalry
definition: We define the level of competitive activity in the industry (industry-level rivalry) as the aggregation of firm-level competitive activity minus the competitive activity of the focal firm. When the number of competitive actions between all firms in the industry is high, rivalry will be intense.

name: Firm-level cooperative mechanisms
definition: We define firm-level cooperative mechanisms to be formal interfirm agreements including equity purchases, mergers, technology licenses, and participation in trade associations and technology consortia. That definition focuses on the linkages between organizations over which flow communication and resources.

name: Industry-level cooperation
authors_terms: ["industry-level cooperation", "industry-level cooperative mechanisms", "cooperative mechanisms in the industry"]
definition: We define the level of cooperative mechanisms in the industry (industry-level cooperation) as simply the aggregation of firm-level cooperative mechanisms minus those of the focal firm. That is, when the number of cooperative mechanisms involving firms in an industry is high, the level of industry cooperation will tend to be high.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "firm-level performance", "return on assets", "return on sales"]
definition: We used two commonly accepted financial measures of firm performance, return on sales and return on assets.

name: Volatility
definition: Volatility refers to the rate and unpredictability of change in an environment over time, which create uncertainty about future conditions.

name: Ambiguity
definition: Ambiguity refers to the degree of uncertainty inherent in perceptions of the environmental state irrespective of its change over time. Ambiguity is less about an uncertain future as about uncertainty about present and past experience.

name: Supplier opportunism
definition: Williamson (1985) defined opportunism as self-interest seeking of a strategic (i.e., secretive, deceptive, or guileful) nature undertaken to redirect profits from vulnerable partners.

name: Governance regime
authors_terms: ["governance regime", "fixed-price contracts", "negotiable price contracts", "formal contracting", "relational contracting"]
definition: The key differentiating feature between the two modes is that contractual forms offer strong recourse to court-ordered remedies and attempt to eliminate ex post negotiations, whereas relational forms do not. Governance regime was measured by the type of development agreement used in a relationship, categorized into the fixed-price contract and negotiable price contract regimes.

name: Prior exchange history
authors_terms: ["prior history", "prior exchange history", "prior history of the exchange", "shadow of the past"]
definition: The shadow of the past: trust is built incrementally over time through prior interaction and experiences, forming a social institution that supports trust. Consistent with previous work, the authors use prior history of the exchange to assess the degree of shadow of the past.

name: Expectation of continuity
authors_terms: ["expectation of continuity", "expectations of continuity", "shadow of the future"]
definition: An expectation of continued interaction, the shadow of the future, which is necessary to promote cooperation and perceptions of trust. The authors use the expectation of continuity as their measure of the shadow of the future.

name: Interorganizational trust
definition: An exchange partner's expectation that the other party can be relied on, will behave as predicted, and will act fairly.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "specialized assets", "reciprocal investments in specialized assets"]
definition: Transaction-specific assets that are not redeployable to alternative uses. Because the conceptual logic emphasizes reciprocal investments, it is operationalized as parties' dependence in the relationship and switching costs to alternative partners.

name: Uncertainty
definition: Unanticipated changes in circumstances surrounding the product exchange in the marketplace.

name: TQM implementation
definition: TQM primarily focuses on increasing efficiencies and improving processes, particularly when implemented in manufacturing organizations.

name: Cost leadership orientation
authors_terms: ["cost leadership", "cost leadership activity system orientation", "cost leadership strategic orientation"]
definition: Cost leadership is a high efficiency strategic orientation where organizations achieve competitive advantage by eliminating waste in the production and/or service delivery process.

name: Differentiation orientation
definition: Conversely, activity systems with a differentiation strategic orientation focus on enhancing the value of a product or service through innovation and responsiveness to customer preferences.

name: Organizational performance
definition: We measured the dependent variable performance as operating margin, calculated as operating revenues minus operating expenditures divided by operating revenues.

name: Scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making
authors_terms: ["scientific approach", "scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making", "scientific method", "intervention"]
definition: Treated startups were taught in each of the four steps of the process to frame, identify, and validate the problem; formulate falsifiable hypotheses; and test them in a rigorous fashion (using data and experiments), including defining valid and reliable metrics and establishing clear thresholds for concluding whether a hypothesis is corroborated or not.

name: Startup exit
definition: A binary variable that takes the value zero until the firm exits (abandons the program and ceases the startup), one in the time period in which the firm drops out, and a missing value thereafter. All firms that exit from our sample had not yet made heavy investments in their company; they are firms that abandon their idea before they commit to developing it, that is genuine exits and not failures.

name: Pivot to a new business idea
authors_terms: ["pivot", "major change to its business model", "major changes"]
definition: In the panel regressions, this is a binary variable that takes the value one in the exact time period in which the firm made a major change to its business model and zero whenever the firm does not pivot. A change is defined as major by analyzing whether the entrepreneur moved from the original idea to another idea that changed the core value proposition of the product or service offered or its target customers.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance is captured by the firm's revenue and by early signals of performance: the acquisition or activation of customers are standard performance measures that account for early signals of performance, and the acquisition or activation of customers represents early signals of future monetary returns.

name: Star inventor departure
authors_terms: ["star exit", "star departure", "star inventor departure", "departure of a star"]
definition: Star exit was calculated by tracking the patenting activities of stars across different firms; the star exit dummy variable equals one for firm i in year t if a star inventor stops patenting for firm i in year t and subsequently patents in another firm.

name: Firm innovation performance
authors_terms: ["firm's innovation performance", "firm performance", "firms' innovative performance", "citation-weighted innovation productivity"]
definition: We measured innovation performance using the cumulative number of forward citations to patents granted to each firm and to all coinventors from the firm in the three years immediately following the star's departure.

name: Coinventor innovation performance
authors_terms: ["coinventors' innovation performance", "coinventors' performance", "coinventor productivity", "performance of the remaining coinventors"]
definition: The remaining coinventors often experience a decline in productivity following a star's departure; we measured innovation performance using the cumulative number of forward citations to patents granted to all coinventors from the firm in the three years immediately following the star's departure.

name: Coinventor mobility
definition: For coinventors' mobility, we measured the number of coinventors who also exited their firms within two years of the departure of stars.

name: Star search breadth
authors_terms: ["search breadth", "star search breadth", "scope of innovation activities"]
definition: Search breadth refers to whether inventors recombine multiple knowledge domains.

name: Star search depth
definition: Search depth involves whether inventors focus on familiar domains wherein they have extensive experience.

name: Positional embeddedness
definition: Positional embeddedness is defined as the degree to which actors occupy a central position within a network.

name: Structural embeddedness
authors_terms: ["structural embeddedness", "coinventor network density", "density of the network of stars' coinventors"]
definition: Structural embeddedness is the degree of direct and indirect ties among the coinventors and often measured as network density.

name: Prior acquisition market reaction
authors_terms: ["prior stock market reaction to a prior acquisition", "prior abnormal market gains/losses", "prior abnormal dollar returns", "absolute prior dollar abnormal return", "prior market reactions"]
definition: The prior abnormal market gains/losses experienced by the acquirer at the time of the previous acquisition announcement, measured as the dollar value of abnormal returns obtained by multiplying the market capitalization with the percentage abnormal returns surrounding the prior acquisition announcement.

name: Target risk
authors_terms: ["risk associated with the current acquisition", "target stock volatility", "Target Risk", "risk associated with a subsequent acquisition"]
definition: The risk of the current acquisition, measured using target stock volatility, calculated as the standard deviation of the daily returns of the target from 275 to 30 days prior to the earliest acquisition announcement date. The higher the stock volatility of the target, the more idiosyncratic its resources, which enhances both ex-ante risks such as valuation and ex-post risks such as post merger integration.

name: Technological performance
authors_terms: ["innovation rate", "rate of innovation", "technological performance", "maximum areal density", "highest areal density"]
definition: Rates of innovation for hard disk drive producers, specifically a firm's highest areal density in any of its form factors in a given year. Improvement in areal density is the central technological metric in the evolution of the industry and will be the measure of innovation.

name: Having a spin-off
definition: A spin-off is defined as occurring when one or more employees from an incumbent hard drive producer establish a new disk drive company; spin-offs are new ventures created by former employees of an existing firm in the same industry.

name: Technological sophistication of the spin-off
authors_terms: ["technologically successful spin-offs", "average technology of the spin-off", "spin-off frontier ratio", "technological frontier"]
definition: The proximity of the focal firm's spin-off to the technological frontier, called the average technology of the spin-off and calculated as the spin-off's maximum areal density in a given year divided by the highest areal density in the industry in that year.

name: Time since the spin-off
definition: The amount of time in years that has lapsed since the progenitor has had that spin-off; if a hard drive producer had more than one spin-off, the spin-off clock was reset to zero and began counting until its next spin-off.

name: Business unit performance
authors_terms: ["business unit performance", "business segment performance", "business performance", "business unit relative performance stratum"]
definition: The relative performance of a business unit, expressed as one of three statistically significantly different and ordinally ranked performance strata: superior performers, modal performers, and inferior performers. For each time period the authors coded the business unit relative performance stratum.

name: Corporate performance
authors_terms: ["corporate effects", "corporate factors", "corporate-level relative performance stratum", "corporate performance"]
definition: The relative performance of the corporation that a business unit belongs to, expressed as the corporate-level relative performance stratum for that corporation.

name: Industry performance
authors_terms: ["industry effects", "industry factors", "industry-level relative performance stratum", "industry performance"]
definition: The relative performance of the primary industry in which a business unit operates, expressed as the industry-level relative performance stratum for that industry.

name: Persistence of superior performance
authors_terms: ["persistence of superior performance", "persistence of profitability", "persistence of performance"]
definition: The tendency of entities to remain in the superior performance strata, estimated as the hazard of exiting the superior performance strata. Higher hazard rates would be associated with lesser persistence, and vice versa.

name: Differences in management styles
authors_terms: ["differences in management styles", "differences in management style", "differences in top management styles", "differences in top management style"]
definition: Management style has been described as an element of the managerial or the subjective culture of an organization. It has been conceptualized as comprising a number of factors, including the management group's attitude towards risk, their decision-making approach, and preferred control and communication patterns.

name: Differences in reward and evaluation systems
authors_terms: ["differences in reward and evaluation systems", "differences in the reward and evaluation systems", "differences in reward and evaluations systems"]
definition: The reward and evaluation system is widely regarded as one of the most important components of the organizational form; such systems define the terms of exchange between individuals and the organization and do vary significantly across organizations. Differences exist along a number of factors, including factors related to the evaluation criteria such as the time period over which the process is focused, indices used to measure performance, and the type of performance indicator used, as well as the form and administration of compensation.

name: Post-acquisition integration
authors_terms: ["post-acquisition integration", "postacquisition integration", "extent of post-acquisition integration", "level of post-acquisition integration"]
definition: The need for post-acquisition integration of operations in an acquisition is primarily bounded by its objectives, and the primary objective in post-acquisition integration of operations is to make more effective use of existing capabilities. It is the extent to which the operations of the acquiring and acquired firms are integrated along manufacturing/R&D and marketing activities.

name: Acquisition performance
definition: Acquisition performance is the extent to which the acquisition was able to achieve prior expectations in terms of its impact on the performance of the acquiring firm, assessed along five performance criteria, namely ROI, EPS, stock price, cash flow, and sales growth.

name: Minority member status
authors_terms: ["status of minority players", "highest status of minority players", "high-status minority member"]
definition: By a high-status minority member, we mean a minority member who receives a relatively high level of respect, admiration, and prominence from other members: a 'star' baseball player in the team, a respected professor in the department, and a prominent lawyer in the office. Status is fundamentally embedded in the context, so the authors measured the highest level of status minority players had within their team.

name: Minority hiring
authors_terms: ["number of minority players added to the team", "minority hires in one year", "future efforts to increase diversity"]
definition: The dependent measure was each team's annual hiring outcome: how many more or fewer minority players were added to the team each season. In the experiment, the analogous dependent variable was the future effort to increase diversity, measured as the extent to which the company should invest its resources to hire more female executives.

name: Role prototypicality
definition: A role prototype is a set of attributes that are culturally transmitted and collectively shared to make up what a specific occupational role should look or behave like; role prototypes often involve race or gender, so a role can be more or less prototypical for a minority member occupying it.

name: Group membership
definition: Individuals quickly categorize others into a specific social group (e.g., Black, woman) and make inferences based on the group membership, and organizational decision makers may also base their decisions on subgroup categorizations. The authors propose that the effect of a minority member's status is stronger when the member belongs to the same minority subgroup as the candidate.

name: Functional breadth
authors_terms: ["functional breadth", "functional generalism", "broad functional experience", "experience with multiple job functions"]
definition: The degree to which an artist's credited skills were concentrated in a single job function; past research equates entrepreneurial skill with a broad functional background, or experience with multiple job functions.

name: Market breadth
authors_terms: ["market breadth", "breadth of market experience", "market experience", "multiple genres"]
definition: The degree to which an artist holds membership in multiple genres; a lower score indicates a narrower market experience (i.e., greater concentration).

name: Entrepreneurial entry
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurship", "entrepreneurial entry", "transition to entrepreneurship", "founding a new organization by an individual"]
definition: Entrepreneurial entry is an indicator variable that captures whether an artist launched a new, independent record label in a given year, so that the definition of ''entrepreneurship'' for this study involves the founding of an intra-industry spinoff.

name: Status
definition: An artist's status in the music industry; commercial success and critical acclaim are used to measure it, and status provides evidence of ability and clarity of identity otherwise acquired through specialized experience.

name: Functional typicality
authors_terms: ["typicality", "functional typicality", "more typical set of job functions", "typical combination"]
definition: The frequency with which any functional profile appeared across all observations, with a higher score indicating greater typicality of an artist's set of experiences.

name: Audience receptivity
definition: An audience's receptiveness to evidence of breadth, proxied for with income and education.

name: Media coverage
definition: The main independent variable of interest is the amount of media coverage of city i in year t. Media coverage of a place should increase its visibility and attract the attention of a great number of potential foreign investors.

name: Foreign entry
authors_terms: ["foreign entry", "number of entering foreign firms", "number of foreign entrants", "foreign entrants"]
definition: The dependent variable is the number of foreign firms that entered industry j in city i in year t. Only first-time foreign entries are included; a firm is foreign if 100 percent of its shares are owned by foreign shareholders.

name: Private information about the host country
authors_terms: ["private information", "private information about a host country", "background knowledge"]
definition: Prior research suggests that firms have richer background knowledge and greater access to private information about geographically and socially proximate locations relative to more distant ones. Firms with more abundant private information about a host country will pay less attention to the arguably less superior media coverage.

name: Amount of technical contribution
authors_terms: ["amount of technical contribution", "number of software packages maintained", "quantity of a developer's contribution"]
definition: To measure each developer's amount of technical contribution, we collected data from the project's bug-tracking database on the number of software packages a developer maintained in 2002.

name: Impact of technical contribution
authors_terms: ["impact of technical contribution", "popularity of the packages he or she maintained", "number of people that used these packages"]
definition: To measure the impact of technical contribution for each developer, we measured the popularity of the packages he or she maintained.

name: Online discussion participation
authors_terms: ["participates in online discussions", "online communication", "number of e-mail postings", "projectwide online communication"]
definition: To measure projectwide online communication, we focused on one list, 'debian-devel,' to which all developers subscribe. We downloaded all the postings to this list and measured each developer's number of e-mail postings as a first proxy for organization-building activity.

name: Face-to-face interaction
authors_terms: ["degree centrality", "the more people in the community one meets face to face", "face-to-face meetings", "number of other developers the focal developer had met face-to-face"]
definition: The other variable we used to measure a developer's involvement in the organizational life of the community was his or her degree centrality, a count of the number of other community members the developer had met as of January 1, 2003.

name: Leadership team membership
authors_terms: ["becomes a leader", "leadership team", "membership in the leadership team", "leadership team membership"]
definition: In measuring our dependent variable, we considered not only the position of project leader, but the community's full leadership team, which also includes the project secretary, software release coordinator, developer accounts manager, and members of the technical committee.

name: Bureaucratic basis of authority
authors_terms: ["bureaucratic basis of authority", "positional authority", "formal positional authority", "legal-rational basis of authority"]
definition: Positional authority is rooted in a defined role, decoupled from a person's individual characteristics; it separates the personal from the official and provides a legal-rational basis of authority. In a bureaucratic system, a legal and rationally based positional authority decouples the authority of a person from that of his or her position.

name: Democratic mechanisms
authors_terms: ["democratic mechanisms", "democratic rule", "democratic means", "directly democratic mode of governance"]
definition: However, democratic rule is reinforced by (1) requiring leaders to defer to the community, (2) granting leaders limited authority over technical matters, (3) allowing members to recall the leader's authority, and (4) creating a source of countervailing power. The four mechanisms described above limited the reach of bureaucratic rule by reinforcing democratic rule by community members as a whole.

name: Centralization
authors_terms: ["hierarchy", "polyarchy", "centralized decision making", "decentralized decision making", "organizational structure", "structural configuration", "coordinated polyarchy", "organizational context"]
definition: The hierarchy features centralized decision making and represents a bureaucracy-oriented organization, whereas the polyarchy features decentralized decision making and represents a market-like organization. In the hierarchy both evaluators must accept a project before the organization commits to it, whereas in the polyarchy both evaluators must reject a project before the organization passes on the opportunity.

name: Reservation level
