authors_terms: ["reservation level", "reservation levels of their screening functions", "bias", "aggregate bias", "conservative", "permissive"]
definition: The bias is measured relative to the projects for which the individual is indifferent, which is conveniently represented by a reservation level on net value, that is, the perfect screener has a reservation level of zero, whereas the biased screener has a nonzero reservation level. More generally, bias is a technical concept, defined in terms of a deviation from the best estimate of a threshold above which an organization's net gains are positive.

name: Discrimination capability
authors_terms: ["discrimination level", "discrimination", "discriminating capability", "sharpness of screening", "slope of the screening function"]
definition: The discrimination level captures sensitivity to changes in project value, which is represented by the slope of the screening function, for example, the perfect screener approaches infinite discrimination ability. Discriminating capability is defined as the screening function's slope (a higher value of the slope parameter implies higher screening capability).

name: Accuracy
definition: Accuracy, the fraction of decisions that are correct, captures both bias and noisy discrimination.

name: Alliance partners' market power
authors_terms: ["partners' market power", "nonsubstitutable partners", "critical partners", "share of resources controlled by alliance partners", "partner substitutability", "market power of alliance partners"]
definition: The extent to which a focal firm's alliance partners control large shares of the resources needed by the firm, which makes those partners difficult to replace. For organization i, partner j is substitutable insofar as there are other potential or current partners k that have resources comparable to those of j.

name: Alliance network density
authors_terms: ["network density", "density of alliances among the organization's partners", "density of connections among a firm's alliance partners"]
definition: Network density captures the presence (or absence) of ties among a firm's alliance partners and was calculated as the ratio between the observed and the maximum possible number of alliances for a given number of partners. It is treated as an adequate measure of both the absence of structural holes in an alliance network and of its closure.

name: Organizational profitability
authors_terms: ["organizational profitability", "return on invested capital (ROI)", "return on assets (ROA)", "the return an organization obtains from its alliance network"]
definition: The economic value an organization produces in a given year, captured with two closely related measures, return on invested capital (ROI) and return on assets (ROA). ROI is considered one of the most reliable measures of the economic value an organization produces in a given year.

name: Availability of pharmaceutical funding
definition: For early-stage projects, there is a scarcity of financing in comparison to the number of early-stage projects brought to the alliance market; in early-stage alliances pharmaceutical firms comprise the scarcer group, and the degree of relative scarcity is driven by the availability of pharmaceutical funding.

name: Availability of late-stage R&D projects
authors_terms: ["availability of late-stage projects", "availability of late-stage R&D projects"]
definition: In late-stage alliances biotechnology firms comprise the scarcer group, and the availability of late-stage projects drives relative scarcity: there is a scarcity of late-stage projects in comparison to the pharmaceutical firms willing to take them on.

name: Availability of public funding for biotechnology projects
authors_terms: ["availability of public funding for biotechnology projects", "previous IPO"]
definition: As R&D projects advance into later stages, initial information problems are alleviated and biotechnology firms are better able to attract public investors; when public funding is more available, fewer biotechnology firms will bring late-stage projects to the alliance market, thus increasing relative scarcity.

name: Superior biotechnology patent portfolio
definition: A biotechnology firm's patent portfolio is considered to be an independent observable indicator of its research capabilities and intellectual property pool, and the larger an R&D firm's patent portfolio relative to those of other paired firms, the more valuable it is perceived to be.

name: Superior biotechnology project experience
authors_terms: ["previous experience with R&D projects", "superior biotech project experience"]
definition: Another factor that pharmaceutical firms value highly is a biotechnology company's previous experience with R&D projects; R&D firms that have validated their core technologies in previous projects typically stand a greater chance of discovering valuable new drugs than firms that have not.

name: Superior pharmaceutical late-stage project experience
authors_terms: ["previous experience with late-stage R&D projects", "superior pharma late-project experience"]
definition: Pharmaceutical firms that have been involved in more late-stage projects in the past are more valuable late-stage partners, building up complementary assets necessary for carrying out large-scale clinical trials, relationships with regulatory authorities, and manufacturing, detailing and distribution capabilities.

name: Superior pharmaceutical absorptive capacity
definition: Pharmaceutical firms with superior absorptive capacity are better able to recognize the value of new knowledge, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends, and thus display superior complementarity in late-stage research projects.

name: Biotechnology firm's need for external funding
definition: A biotechnology firm's bargaining ability is influenced by how badly it needs external financing; most biotechnology firms have negative cash flows, and those that are more desperate for external funding have a weaker ability to bargain over PS control rights relative to their partner.

name: Pharmaceutical new product pipeline health
authors_terms: ["health of each pharmaceutical firm's pipeline", "pharma pipeline score"]
definition: A pharmaceutical firm's bargaining ability is influenced by the health of its product pipeline; pharmaceutical firms with static or deteriorating product pipelines are more desperate for promising R&D projects, and thus less able to extract value from their partner.

name: Pharmaceutical firm's alliance portfolio size
definition: Pharmaceutical firms are usually involved in several concurrent alliances that provide them with multiple options for developing profitable drugs, so the larger a pharmaceutical firm's alliance portfolio, the less dependent it is on any one alliance.

name: Share of pie-splitting control rights won by the pharmaceutical firm
authors_terms: ["pharmaPS percentage", "percentage of PS control rights", "share of PS control rights"]
definition: PS control rights confer ownership and control over activities and intermediate outputs that directly affect the allocation of portions of the overall value to be created by an alliance, and the measure captures the amount won by each partner relative to the size of the pool; since the share of PS control rights won by a partner is considered, a pharmaceutical firm's gain is its biotechnology partner's loss and vice versa.

name: Practice prevalence
authors_terms: ["practice prevalence", "number of past RMs", "number of past adopters", "RM prevalence"]
definition: The cumulative number of past adopters of a practice; the authors argue that growing prevalence increases awareness of the practice and its perceived value among potential adopters while also raising concern among third-party evaluators.

name: Practice diffusion
authors_terms: ["subsequent diffusion of RMs", "number of new RMs", "diffusion of RMs"]
definition: The subsequent adoption of a practice, modeled as the count of new adopters per unit of time; numerous diffusion studies typically estimate a Poisson (or negative binomial) regression in which the dependent variable is the count of new adopters per unit of time.

name: Proportion of lower-status adopters
authors_terms: ["lower-status adopters", "% of past lower-status RMs", "proportion of lower-status firms", "past adopters' status"]
definition: RM adopters were deemed lower status if they hired trivially small auditing firms with fewer than five partners and 10 professional staff members; RM status with respect to their accounting quality was reliant on their auditors.

name: Negative media coverage
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage", "negative articles", "media coverage of RMs"]
definition: Media coverage serves as a critical supplier of knowledge about new corporate practices and as a social arbiter making evaluative judgments of organizations and their practices; the authors measure the negative tenor as the weekly count of media articles depicting RMs negatively.

name: Stock market valuation
authors_terms: ["stock market returns", "stock market valuations", "negative stock market returns"]
definition: Stock markets represent a key third-party evaluator of RMs; the authors measure how the stock market evaluated RMs via the weekly abnormal stock market returns of each RM and an equally weighted portfolio of those returns.

name: Product variety
definition: Product variety is the range of products a unit offers, evaluated along dimensions such as brand, content, flavor, and packaging (material and size) but with numerous options along each dimension. It is measured using the number of brands carried by the DC and the number of SKUs carried by the DC.

name: Sourcing complexity
authors_terms: ["sourcing complexity", "number of sourcing and shipment relationships", "sourcing relationships"]
definition: Sourcing complexity is the complexity that pertains to inter-unit sourcing networks; the complexity of such a system can be measured using the number of linkages, or the number of sourcing and shipment relationships, in the system.

name: Coordination performance
definition: Coordination performance is the extent to which units' tasks are synchronized; failure to communicate and appraise interactions, or to correct decision errors, causes delays and a poor synchronization of tasks, such as a mismatch between supply and demand, which can result in a stockout where a customer order is not completely fulfilled due to insufficient supply.

name: Sourcing hub status
definition: A hierarchical sourcing structure is one in which a few hubs receive consolidated shipments from plants, and then forward them along to non-hub DCs. As a locus of interdependent relationships between plants and DCs, a hub may experience worsened performance due to the additional coordination burden.

name: Sourcing through a hub
definition: A DC sources through a hub when it receives a product through a hub, which consolidates shipments from plants and forwards them to downstream DCs; potential congestions at the hub worsen coordination performance for the DCs that source through it.

name: Era-based initial environmental conditions
authors_terms: ["era-based initial environmental conditions", "era-based initial conditions", "competitive era", "cooperative era", "competitive economy era"]
definition: The two socioeconomic eras in which ancestral founders began their entrepreneurial activity. The first era, which ended in 1977, comprises the formative years of the Israeli state and is referred to as the cooperative era, marked by a distinct ideology that elevated the collective above individual interests; the second era, which started in 1977, is the competitive economy era, marked by political upheaval, a shift toward a neoliberal economy, and substantial growth of the private sector.

name: Entrepreneurial proclivity of the first generation
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial proclivity of the founding parents", "entrepreneurial proclivity of the ancestral founders", "entrepreneurial proclivity of the first generation"]
definition: 'Entrepreneurial proclivity' is defined as the founder's predisposition to found new start-ups, and is manifested in the number of start-ups founded by this individual.

name: Entrepreneurial proclivity of the second generation
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial proclivity of the second generation", "second generation's entrepreneurial proclivity"]
definition: 'Entrepreneurial proclivity' is defined as the founder's predisposition to found new start-ups, and is manifested in the number of start-ups founded by this individual.

name: Entrepreneurial proclivity of the third generation
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial proclivity of the third generation", "third generation's entrepreneurial proclivity"]
definition: 'Entrepreneurial proclivity' is defined as the founder's predisposition to found new start-ups, and is manifested in the number of start-ups founded by this individual.

name: Entrepreneurial tenure gap
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial tenure gap", "entrepreneurial tenure", "temporal gap in entrepreneurial experience"]
definition: A temporal gap in entrepreneurial experience between the founder (parent) and the organizational members (progeny) with whom the founder interacts. The greater the entrepreneurial tenure of the founding parent, the greater the gap relative to his or her employees.

name: Female partner representation
authors_terms: ["female partner representation", "female representation in the senior rank", "number of female partners", "gender diversity in the focal firm"]
definition: Our dependent variable, Female Partner Representation, is a count of the number of female partners listed as employed by a focal law firm i in year t. A change in the firm's number of female partners can be directly interpreted as a change in the firm's gender diversity.

name: Gender diversity in rivals' buyers
authors_terms: ["gender diversity in rivals' buyers", "gender diversity in the executive level of rivals' buyers", "gender diversity in the executive ranks of potential buyers"]
definition: Gender Diversity in Rivals' Buyers is the weighted and averaged percentage of female executives in the buyers that bought legal services from a focal firm's competitors but not the focal firm in year t.

name: Gender diversity in rivals
authors_terms: ["gender diversity in rivals", "gender diversity in the partnership ranks of rival law firms", "percentage of female partners in the competitors of the focal firm"]
definition: Gender Diversity in Rivals is measured as the rivalry-weighted average percentage of female partners in the competitors of the focal firm.

name: Racial diversity in focal firm
authors_terms: ["racial diversity in focal firm", "racial diversity", "racial diversity in its partnership rank"]
definition: Racial Diversity in Focal Firm ('Racial Diversity') is computed as the percentage of partners in focal firm i in year t that are not identified as 'white.'

name: Relative standing
authors_terms: ["relative standing", "relative standing in a partner's portfolio", "relative standing in an affiliation portfolio"]
definition: Relative standing refers to how the venture ranks among other ventures in the partner's portfolio with respect to expected returns. It captures the importance of each venture with respect to other ventures in a partner's portfolio.

name: Venture exit performance
definition: One of the most well-accepted indicators of partnership benefits (value-added) in the VC literature is the venture's exit performance, because the multiplex of activities performed and resources provided by VC firms are inextricably linked to the possibility of a successful exit. Conventional measures of performance are not available for private biotechnology ventures since most ventures do not have marketable products and may be years away from a stable revenue stream.

name: Partner portfolio size
authors_terms: ["VC portfolio size", "partners' portfolio size", "size of the partner's portfolio"]
definition: The size of the partner's portfolio of affiliations, i.e., the number of ventures in the partner's portfolio competing for resources.

name: Partner status
definition: Status derives value from exclusivity and may 'leak' if a high-status partner becomes associated with lower-quality ventures; high-status partners are likely to be more discriminating than the average partner in extending endorsement benefits to the ventures in their portfolios.

name: Fraudulent financial reporting
authors_terms: ["fraud", "financial fraud", "fraudulent reporting", "profit manipulation", "financial data manipulation", "cooking the books"]
definition: Our analysis does not rely on the actions of regulatory agencies; rather, we directly observe instances of financial data manipulation by collecting and comparing two sets of financial books that are required to be identical under Chinese law. We consider incentive-compatible, discrepant reporting across the two sets of books to be evidence of financial fraud.

name: Political connection
definition: We define an indicator variable, Political Connection, which denotes that one or more company founders, (1) previously worked in the Chinese government, or (2) once held membership in the People's Congress (PC) or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC).

name: Organizational equity ownership
authors_terms: ["organizational equity holder", "organizational equity owners", "organizational equity holders (OEH)", "outside organizational equity holders", "organizational investors"]
definition: Young companies are heterogeneous in their ownership structures. In particular, some companies have only individual owners, whereas others have organizational equity holders, such as venture capital investors, universities, and other corporations.

name: Venture capital backing
definition: Second, Venture Capital Investor is 1 if one or more of the organizational equity holders is listed as a VC firm by the State Development Planning Council and has a profile on the website of China's premier VC/PE information provider, Zero2IPO.

name: Innovation grant receipt
definition: Innofund is modeled after the U.S. Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program: It was specifically created to overcome a 'market failure' by supporting innovative and commercially appealing projects at an early stage of development. The Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) administers Innofund.

name: Corporate venture capital backing
definition: Large incumbent corporations can undertake equity investments in innovative ventures similar to independent VCs. The activity is often managed by a corporate venture capital program that seeks a mix of financial returns as well as strategic gains, usually in the form of a window on technology.

name: Innovation output
definition: The paper studies both patent and publication outcomes of ventures, which affords a holistic understanding of the impact on the innovativeness of biotechnology ventures. Academic publications are often associated with scientific, or basic, research, whereas patents are often associated with applied, or commercially orientated, research.

name: Geographic proximity to corporate investor
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity", "CVC accessibility", "accessibility to its corporate investor", "co-location"]
definition: During the discovery stage, access to corporate R&D personnel and laboratories plays an important role, and these complementary assets are unique to corporate venture capital investors. The closer a venture is to corporate R&D facilities, the greater its opportunity to benefit from it; proximity to corporate R&D facilities facilitates access to corporate labs.

name: FDA approval applicability
authors_terms: ["FDA approval applicable", "subjected to FDA approval", "applicability of corporate FDA regulatory know-how", "regulatory approval"]
definition: A critical hurdle to innovation, once scientific viability has been established, is oversight by the FDA, which is necessary to sell new prescription or non-prescription drugs in the United States. To win FDA approval, one has to demonstrate safety and effectiveness in the drug's proposed use, adequacy of manufacturing methods to assure the drug's strength and quality, and appropriateness of the proposed labeling.

name: EJV entry
authors_terms: ["EJV adoption", "EJV rejection", "EJV formation", "rise and decline of EJV"]
definition: The dependent construct is the formation of an international equity joint venture in China, where each EJV includes one Chinese and one foreign partner. It is modelled as the hazard of EJV formation over time in the rise and in the decline period, with an increased number of EJV rejections read from the decline-period results.

name: Home-country industry peer EJV adoption
authors_terms: ["Number of EJVs (home country)", "prior EJV adoption by industry peers in the same home-country", "prior EJV rejection by industry peers in the same home-country"]
definition: The number of equity joint venture adoptions by foreign firms based in the same home-country industry, used as the measure of mimetic entry through the home-country industry reference group, since firms in the same home-country industry are viewed as belonging to the same field and tend to imitate one another's practices.

name: Host-country industry peer EJV adoption
authors_terms: ["Number of EJVs (host country)", "prior EJV adoption by industry peers in the same host country", "prior EJV rejection by industry peers in the same host country"]
definition: The number of equity joint venture adoptions by foreign firms based in the same host-country industry, used as the measure of mimetic entry through the host-country industry reference group, where strategic isomorphism among rivals in non-restricted industries is argued to occur because competitors in the same host-country industry monitor one another.

name: Home-country industry M&A adoption
authors_terms: ["Number of M&As (home country)", "emergence of M&A entry strategy in the same home-country industry"]
definition: The number of merger and acquisition adoptions by foreign firms based in the same home-country industry, representing the emergence and development of the competing M&A entry strategy inside that reference group.

name: Host-country industry M&A adoption
authors_terms: ["Number of M&As (host country)", "development of M&A entry strategy in the same host-country industry"]
definition: The number of merger and acquisition adoptions by foreign firms based in the same host-country industry, representing the spread of the competing M&A entry strategy within the host-country organizational field.

name: Labor productivity
definition: Labor productivity, i.e., output per worker. In the empirical implementation, labor productivity is calculated as the ratio of total sales to the total number of employees.

name: ICT investment
authors_terms: ["ICT investment", "ICT capital", "information and communication technologies investment"]
definition: ICT capital is one of the input factors of the production technology and is proxied by ICT investment; proxying ICT capital by ICT investment does not appear to be a severe shortcoming because ICT depreciates extremely quickly.

name: Non-ICT capital
definition: Non-ICT capital is one of the input factors of the production technology and is measured as investment in physical capital.

name: Labor input
definition: Labor is one of the input factors in the production technology; the analysis uses information on total employment taken from the 24th wave of the SSBS.

name: Workplace reorganization
authors_terms: ["workplace reorganization", "organizational change", "changes in human resources practices", "enhancement of group work", "flattening of hierarchies"]
definition: In this paper, two forms of organizational change are considered: enhancement of group work and flattening of hierarchies. Both are closely related to what Bresnahan et al. (2002) term 'decentralized workplace organization,' meaning that the authority of individuals and teams is enhanced.

name: Performance
definition: The performance of a firm in a new technical subfield, which each hypothesis is stated in terms of generally but which is tested for both market share and survival. The authors note that there are many types of performance, some of which may involve trade-offs.

name: Overall entry order
authors_terms: ["first clock", "overall rank order of entry", "entry order relative to all participants"]
definition: The entry clock that records all entries to a technical subfield and influences firms that enter without benefit of a strong set of specialized assets. It is measured as an entrant's overall rank order of entry, relative to all entrants.

name: Incumbent entry order
authors_terms: ["second clock", "incumbent rank order of entry", "entry order relative to other incumbents"]
definition: The second entry clock, which records the entry of entrants that do possess the specialized assets, measured as an industry incumbent's rank order of entry relative to other incumbents.

name: Incumbent status
authors_terms: ["industry incumbents", "industry newcomers", "entrant type", "the distinction between incumbents and newcomers"]
definition: The distinction between incumbents and newcomers depends on the possession of complementary assets, to which a new good is specialized, that retain their value from one product generation to the next. Industry newcomers lack the breadth of supporting capabilities possessed by incumbents.

name: Market share
definition: The average market share within a technical subfield of the imaging industry attained during a firm's first 4 years of participation in the subfield.

name: Survival
definition: Survival was defined as a spell equal to the number of years that an entrant to a technical subfield manufactured imaging systems, with a minimum of 1 year for firms that entered and exited during the same calendar year.

name: Family ownership control
definition: Whether the family is the largest shareholder of the firm; in this study, family firms are defined as those where the family is the largest shareholder.

name: Family strategic control
definition: Whether a family member (i.e., a member of the controlling owner's family) serves as chairman of the board, the most powerful executive position, charged with overall goal setting and strategic decision making.

name: Family operational control
definition: Whether a family member serves as the general manager, the second most powerful executive position, responsible for managing day-to-day business operations and administration.

name: Pattern of family control
authors_terms: ["pattern of family control", "patterns of family control", "types of firms", "family firms"]
definition: The configuration of family control across ownership, strategy, and operations. The authors separate family firms with ownership control alone (Type 1), family firms with strategic control but not operational control (Type 2a), family firms with operational control but not strategic control (Type 2b), family firms with complete management control (Type 3), and nonfamily firms (Type 4).

name: Firm performance
definition: The operational performance of firms, measured by industry-adjusted return on assets because the authors' argument concerns how family control affects the efficiency of a firm's internal operations.

name: Strength of market institutions
authors_terms: ["market institutions", "institutional void", "institutions with relatively strong market institutional development", "industries with weaker market institutions", "industries with stronger market institutions"]
definition: The development of market-supporting institutions such as market intermediaries and legal protection of shareholders; an institutional void is the lack of such institutions, and their development is uneven across industries, coded from foreign investment, analyst following, and appointment of independent directors.

name: Independent directors
definition: Members of the board who are brought in from outside the company and whose only tie to the company is their directorship; they have no managerial authority and relatively less influence than executives.

name: Board gender diversity reform
authors_terms: ["board gender diversity reform", "board gender diversity reforms", "major board gender diversity reform"]
definition: Many countries have implemented board gender diversity reforms through legislative measures or by amending governance codes to include gender diversity guidelines on board appointments. These reforms represent a significant regulatory intervention in corporate governance, as corporate boards play a crucial role in monitoring and advising corporate strategic decisions.

name: Firm innovation
definition: The study uses patent counts and patent citations to capture the quantity and quality of innovation output, respectively, using the patent application year instead of the grant year to better capture the actual invention date.

name: Female board representation
definition: The number of female directors who are present on the board but not involved in the major board committees serves as a proxy for representation, as such directors' influence is primarily exercised through broader board discussions. This mechanism is primarily concerned with achieving numerical targets for female representation.

name: Female board empowerment
definition: Female directors serving as chairs or members of the major committees provide a proxy for empowerment, as these committees operate with greater efficiency and speed than full boards because of their defined purposes, smaller size, and domain expertise, and such positions allow female directors to exert significant influence on firm outcomes.

name: Reform approach
definition: Rule-based reforms are established through legislation (legal authority) without allowing firms to explain noncompliance, whereas comply-or-explain reforms are either governance codes that recommend adherence while allowing firms to justify departures from recommendations or legislated requirements that permit firms to explain instances of noncompliance.

name: Prereform gender institutions
definition: The effect of board gender diversity reforms on firm innovation varies with prereform gender-related institutions, which establish the baseline level of gender inequality and may impose constraints on the supply of qualified female directors.

name: Payment mode
definition: According to Gaughan (2007), the payment mode refers to the decision of the acquiring firm concerning the cash, stock, or the mix of both that will be used to purchase the target.

name: Control premium
definition: The control premium is 'a value in excess of the market value of a company that is paid for the right to control and proportionately enjoy the profits of the business'.

name: Long-term incentive plan implementation
definition: LTIPs include such incentive vehicles as stock purchase plans, phantom stock plans, restricted stock awards, and performance units/shares, but exclude stock option plans and related stock appreciation rights. Implementation is coded as whether or not an acquirer announced in its proxy statements the adoption of a new attribute of executive compensation contracts.

name: Compensation protection device implementation
authors_terms: ["compensation protection devices", "employment agreement", "severance provision", "golden parachute clause"]
definition: Given that the employment agreement, severance provision, and golden parachute clause have the common feature of protecting executives from unforeseeable events, these three contractual attributes can be included in the group of compensation protection devices.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "market-based and accounting-based measures of firm performance", "RET", "ROA"]
definition: In line with previous research, the authors included both market-based and accounting-based measures of firm performance, as both of them may influence the adoption of specific attributes of executive compensation contracts in the context of M&A activities.

name: Corporate size
definition: Corporate size has long been recognized as the most significant factor explaining executive compensation, and the natural logarithm of total sales was retained as its measure.

name: Post-acquisition period
definition: The post-M&A period accounts for the four years following the transaction completion, including the base year of acquisition completion.

name: Nationalism
definition: Nationalism decrees that the society itself should have reasonable control over its economic choices and should minimize its vulnerability to outside currents and crisis. Nationalism, the ideology of the nation state, plays a critical part in the functioning of the economic system of much of the world.

name: Internationalism
definition: An internationalist orientation, in which the nation state would not be regarded as the sole unit; it does not presuppose the abandonment of a nationalist ideology but advances in addition an internationalist orientation, because the two orientations are perceived by the individual as furnishing compatible solutions to different ends.

name: Economic ideology
definition: An individual's economic ideology manifested through his attitude toward private big business and economic concentration, as well as his preference for a specific property modality (i.e. private vs. collective).

name: Confidence
definition: The self-confidence of particular elites, their reading of where their own nation stands vis-a-vis other nations and collectives; the confidence scale assessed Arab elite perception of their ability to influence the global economic system, specifically perception of power and leverage vis-a-vis the multinationals as well as the oil consuming industrial countries.

name: Satisfaction in direct personal contact
authors_terms: ["satisfaction in direct personal contact", "satisfaction of personal objectives through contact"]
definition: An individual's attitude toward an object is influenced through positive or negative experiences resulting from the interaction process with that object; satisfaction of personal objectives through contact with multinational firms.

name: Attitude toward multinational firms
authors_terms: ["attitude toward multinational firms", "overall attitude toward multinational firms"]
definition: The overall attitude of Arab elites toward multinational firms, which is the dependent variable of the study.

name: Contact with multinational firms
authors_terms: ["direct personal contact", "frequency of direct personal contact"]
definition: The personal contact questions were intended to measure the frequency of direct personal contact between the elites and multinational firms.

name: Response strategy accommodativeness
authors_terms: ["accommodativeness", "more accommodative response strategy", "response strategy", "less accommodative strategy"]
definition: Response strategies range along a continuum of accommodativeness, defined by the degree to which the firm accepts responsibility for the violation. More accommodative strategies attempt to manage the reputational damage from a violation by proactively accepting responsibility, and may include apologies, expressions of regret, and promises of action; less accommodative strategies attempt to avoid reputational damage by reducing a firm's perceived association with the violation, and may include excuses, justifications, and denials.

name: Capability reputation
definition: Capability reputation is based on a firm's ability to consistently deliver value over time. A firm's capability reputation reflects its ability to consistently deliver value to stakeholders.

name: Character reputation
definition: Character reputation is based on a firm's consistent demonstration of integrity and trustworthiness in its interactions with stakeholders.

name: Violation type
definition: Some violations might be perceived as accidents or mistakes, and thus signal a lapse in capability; in contrast, other violations might be perceived as intentional misdeeds, and thus signal a lapse in character.

name: National animosity
definition: We focus on conflict among nations, defined as divergence of interests and opposing actions. Animosity is 'hostility of mind tending to break out into action, active hatred or enmity,' which becomes part of the parties' societal beliefs and cultures, passed from generation to generation.

name: Cross-border alliance formation
authors_terms: ["formation of alliances", "firm-level cross-border alliances", "number of alliances in a nation-dyad"]
definition: The formation of firm-level cross-border alliances between firms from two nations in a dyad; the authors argue that firms' decision to form alliances is strongly influenced by the existence of antagonism between nation-dyads.

name: Proportion of equity alliances
authors_terms: ["proportion of equity alliances", "equity alliances", "cross-border equity alliances"]
definition: Equity alliances are higher-commitment, more clearly defined structures with direct implications for learning; the proportion of equity alliances in year t is calculated by dividing the number of cross-border firm-level equity alliances by the total number of alliances in a nation-dyad.

name: Proportion of nonequity alliances
definition: The proportion of nonequity alliances in a nation-dyad, calculated similarly to the proportion of equity alliances by dividing the number of nonequity alliances by the total number of alliances.

name: Dissimilarity in prior conflict ties
authors_terms: ["dissimilarity in the degree of prior conflicting relationships", "conflict network measure of dissimilarity in degree of conflict relationships of i versus j"]
definition: The dissimilarity in the degree of prior conflicting relationships of nation i versus j with other nations in a network over the years 1918-87, computed as the Euclidian distance between them; if the dissimilarity measure in a dyad is zero, then the two nodes are structurally identical.

name: Reputation for one-sided antagonism
authors_terms: ["one-sided antagonism", "antagonistic reputation", "reputation for antagonism", "total number of one-sided conflicts initiated by i and j with other nations in network in previous year"]
definition: The cumulative antagonism in a nation-dyad, measured by adding up the total number of conflicts for nations i and j in which at least one of the two nations was classified as the initiator in a conflict with a third nation outside of the dyad, excluding the conflicts in this dyad.

name: Learning to contract through prior alliance experience
authors_terms: ["learning to contract", "prior equity alliance experience", "contracting capabilities"]
definition: Firms' experiences in contracting may mitigate the effects of animosity as they learn not only about a particular governance mechanism but also about how to operate in certain environments; firms learn from their prior contracting experiences and over time develop contracting capabilities.

name: Breakthrough invention
definition: A breakthrough invention resolves several core challenges of knowledge couplings and achieves novel knowledge recombination with superior functionality. Breakthrough inventions are important technological advances that achieve novel knowledge recombination of superior functionality.

name: Problem complexity
definition: Problem complexity refers to the overall level of interdependence, or coupling, among the knowledge components potentially relevant to an invention problem.

name: Prior search breadth
authors_terms: ["prior search breadth", "search breadth", "broad search experience", "broad, past search experience"]
definition: Research indicates that inventors' past search experience is a major contributor to their existing knowledge. In particular, broad search experience in the past allows inventors to observe knowledge coupling attempts and their performance implications across a wide range of relevant knowledge domains.

name: Experimentation
definition: Engaging in experimentation effectively exposes inventors to new knowledge. Through an active trial-and-error process, inventors learn about previously neglected or misconceived knowledge couplings in unfamiliar contexts.

name: Adaptive innovation
authors_terms: ["adaptive innovation", "Adaptation of HQ Technology", "adaptation of headquarters technology", "innovation that is adaptive in nature"]
definition: Adaptive subsidiary innovation builds directly upon the existing knowledge base of the parent firm; adaptive technical activities are exploitation oriented in the sense that they are directed at capitalizing upon the firm's existing knowledge base. A citation to a prior headquarters patent indicates that the subsidiary's invention builds directly upon headquarters' technology while at the same time making a nontrivial advancement over that technology.

name: Technical leadership
authors_terms: ["Technical Leadership", "leadership position of the subsidiary in a particular technical field", "center of technical expertise", "technical capability of the subsidiary"]
definition: The capability of a subsidiary in a particular technical field, and in particular its position as a center of technical expertise within the firm, measured by the subsidiary's share of total company patents in the technical field of the citing patent. The authors argue that the strength of the subsidiary's technical capabilities relative to the other units in the firm is one factor predicting whether its innovation builds upon home or host country ideas.

name: Home country technological advantage
authors_terms: ["Home Country Advantage", "home country technological advantage", "revealed technological advantage", "RTA"]
definition: The extent to which a location specializes in a particular technical field, captured by indexes of 'revealed technological advantage'; scores greater than unity indicate that the location has a disproportionate position (relative to its position in other technical fields) of the world's patents in a particular technical field. Home country advantage means that the subsidiary's home country has an RTA greater than one in the field of the citing patent.

name: Host location technological advantage
authors_terms: ["Host Country Advantage", "Host State Advantage", "host country technological advantage", "local technological advantage"]
definition: Locational technological advantage of the host environment, measured by revealed technological advantage at the level of the United States and at the level of the subsidiary's host state. Host State Advantage is a proxy for patterns of local technological specialization, i.e., within the subsidiary's immediate geographic locale, which may be more relevant to knowledge generation and assimilation than aggregate country-level indicators.

name: Innovation scale
authors_terms: ["Innovation Scale", "innovation scale of the subsidiary", "scale of the unit's technical effort"]
definition: A count-based measure of the subsidiary's total technical resources across all technical fields, used as a proxy for the scale of the unit's technical effort; the authors argue that subsidiaries with greater innovation scale may be more likely to access and utilize local sources of knowledge.

name: Subsidiary age
authors_terms: ["Subsidiary Age", "subsidiary's tenure in the host country", "older subsidiaries"]
definition: The subsidiary's tenure in the host country, used to capture how established the subsidiary is: older, more established subsidiaries are argued to be more likely to have gained a reputation for cooperative behavior and hence access to local sources of knowledge than their younger counterparts.

name: Parent technical presence in host country
authors_terms: ["Parent Presence in Host", "parent firm's technical presence in the host country", "parent firm's technical presence"]
definition: The overall size of the parent company's technical presence in the host country, based on the total number of patents issued to all U.S.-based units belonging to the company; the reputation of the parent firm as an 'insider' in local technical circles is argued to shape a subsidiary's capacity to gain access to local knowledge-sharing networks.

name: Home country knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["Home Country Citation", "home country source", "technical ideas originating in the home country", "citing patents originating in the home base of the parent firm"]
definition: Whether the technical ideas a subsidiary's innovation draws upon - the prior patents it cites - originate in the home base of the firm, i.e., in the parent firm's home country. The authors focus on the conditions under which subsidiary inventions cite prior patents originating in the home base of the firm.

name: Host country knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["Host Country Citation", "host country sources", "technical ideas originating in the host country", "local (host country) environment"]
definition: Whether the cited invention was developed by inventors in the host country, i.e., anywhere in the United States, so that the subsidiary's innovation draws upon sources of knowledge located in its local (host country) environment.

name: Host state knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["Host State Citation", "host state sources", "technical ideas originating in the host state"]
definition: Whether the cited invention was developed by inventors in the U.S. state in which the subsidiary is based, the 'host state'. This finer-grained measure captures knowledge sourcing within the subsidiary's immediate geographic locale, which the authors argue may be more relevant to knowledge generation and assimilation than aggregate country-level indicators.

name: Spin-off status
definition: Spin-offs are organizations in which the controlling packet of stock (51% or more) was owned by one individual extant organization, and their founders came from the ranks of former state suppliers and state agencies; startups were created by economic outsiders from research institutes, universities or Party youth organizations.

name: Founding network density
authors_terms: ["social density", "founding network density", "density", "extent of overlap of social ties"]
definition: The density, or extent of overlap of social ties in the founding groups, was measured as a proportion of the number of asymmetrical ties between market organizers; it is the social density, or extent of previous ties, among founders.

name: Founder educational specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization", "educational diversity", "network educational diversity", "concentration in certain fields"]
definition: A second structural feature related to shared past professional relationships is a common or specialized educational background among the founders, measured as the concentration of founders in certain educational fields.

name: Founding group size
authors_terms: ["size of the founding teams", "number of founders", "org komitet"]
definition: The founding group is formalized in Soviet culture as the 'org komitet,' or organizing committee, the members of which constitute the founding network of the exchange.

name: Client-base organizational concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration of the client-base", "diversity of the client-base", "specialized client-base", "member-firm type concentration", "member-firm industry concentration"]
definition: The diversity of the client-base is a Herfindahl index of concentration applied to the placement of client firms in one of seven categories, and the diversity of industry is the analogous index over ten industry categories; both range from 0 (complete diversity) to 1 (uniformity).

name: Client profit motive
definition: The prominence of the profit motive among the clients of an exchange, as against commitment to past traditions and partners; clients of startup exchanges were described as committed less to past traditions than to profitable arbitrage.

name: Expectation of secure transactions
authors_terms: ["expectation of secure transactions", "reliability with which trades are actualized"]
definition: Clients' expectation that transactions will be actualized reliably, grounded in familiarity and repeated exchange, which supports trust and control and allows firms sharing the same set of partners to exert normative pressure against malfeasance.

name: Trading volume
definition: The average monthly trading volume of an exchange, used together with the number of sales as a measure of market performance in lieu of ROI and other standard measures of profitability.

name: Price variability
definition: Variability in prices paid for one unit of the same product, measured as a coefficient of variation.

name: Marketing-related acquisition strategy
definition: This acquisition strategy involves firms with an established competence in marketing, often specializing in branded consumer products, which these firms exploit by acquiring companies whose products are sold in the same or similar manner, distributed through the same or similar channels, and use the same or similar forms of advertising and promotion.

name: Conglomerate acquisition strategy
definition: This acquisition strategy involves firms without an industry-specific competence to limit them to acquiring in certain industries. These firms acquire companies in areas unrelated to their main business, and there are no marketing or technological commonalities between the acquiror's main business and the acquired firm.

name: Technology-related acquisition strategy
definition: This acquisition strategy involves firms which supplement an already established distinctive competence in some product technology or manufacturing process by acquiring firms with the same, or similar, production techniques or product technology.

name: Market position
definition: Market position refers to: (1) the nature of a firm's market, as characterized by market structure variables; and (2) a firm's position within its market, as characterized by market share. It is used to refer to the attractiveness of the industries in which a firm produces output and the competitive position a firm holds in its industries.

name: Change in market position
authors_terms: ["change variables", "changes in market position", "change in the market position variables"]
definition: The change in the market position variables between 1965 and 1979, used to assess whether there were significant differences between strategies in terms of changes in market position during the research period.

name: Acquisitive growth
definition: Growth through mergers and acquisitions, which, unlike internal development, may be associated with either related or unrelated diversification.

name: Hierarchical management
definition: Hierarchical managers in the broad sense, including a set of individuals together fulfilling the function, perform two distinct roles: an administrative role that enforces operational routines to achieve operational efficiency, and an entrepreneurial/legislative role that executes metaroutines to adapt the operational routines to changing environments. In this study the franchisor is used as a proxy for a hierarchical manager and the franchisee as a proxy for a profit center within a firm.

name: Compliance with operational routine
definition: The administrative role is the enforcement of operational routines to achieve operational efficiency. The administrative practices are ones that have been part of the operations manual since the earliest available edition, and for each practice owners were asked how often it was executed.

name: Adoption of franchisor innovation
definition: The metaroutine is the higher-order process that modifies the operational routine in response to changes in the environment. The entrepreneurial practices are outputs of the franchisor's metaroutine rather than elements of the metaroutine itself, and are ones that have been added to the routine in the last two editions of the operations manual, i.e., since 1990.

name: Establishment performance
definition: The primary performance metric is total returns, the sum of net owner income and royalties (the recurring franchise fee). Sales output is also examined, because enterprise size may enter the owners' utility function and because franchisor royalties are based on a percentage of sales.

name: Niche overlap in the specialist home market
authors_terms: ["niche overlap in the specialist PSF's home market", "degree of niche overlap in the home market", "intensity of competition in specialist p's home market"]
definition: A high level of niche overlap occurs when two organizations seek to gain access to the same resources and are substitutes in the marketplace. Specialists in urban areas with a higher number of cardiologists per capita have a higher degree of niche overlap because they face higher levels of competition for referrals from local generalists.

name: Number of rivals allied with the generalist
authors_terms: ["number of rivals", "number of existing VCC relationships that a rural hospital has with rivals", "number of rivals already involved with the same generalist"]
definition: The value of this variable in a given time period is determined by the number of VCCs involving a given rural hospital and rival cardiology practices in the immediate prior year. It captures the extent to which a generalist PSF is already linked to rival specialist PSFs.

name: Proximity of rival specialists
authors_terms: ["proximity of rival specialists", "distance to nearest rival", "proximity of generalist q to the closest rival"]
definition: The proximity of rivals to generalist PSFs influences the geographic scope of a specialist PSF's realized niche. A generalist PSF located very close to a rival is much more likely to enter into a future referral alliance with that rival.

name: Referral alliance involvement
authors_terms: ["VCC involvement", "involvement in a referral alliance", "involvement of a cardiology specialty practice in a VCC"]
definition: The involvement of a cardiology specialty practice in a VCC with a rural hospital in a given year. Because of frequent reviews, the status of these referral alliances can change from year to year.

name: Total resources committed to a referral alliance portfolio
authors_terms: ["total resources", "overall level of resources a specialist PSF commits to its portfolio of referral alliances"]
definition: The total resources that a specialist PSF dedicates to all of its referral alliances with rural hospitals.

name: Alliance-specific resource commitment
authors_terms: ["alliance-specific resources", "level of resources committed to a given referral alliance", "resources a specialist PSF commits to a referral alliance"]
definition: The level of resources committed to a given referral alliance by the specialist PSF. These visits reflect significant, nontransferable, nonrecoverable investments by the cardiologists in the specific referral alliance.

name: Rivals' resource commitment to the generalist
authors_terms: ["commitment by rivals", "level of resources committed by rivals to the same generalist", "total number of monthly visits by rivals to rural hospital q"]
definition: The level of resources committed by rivals to the same generalist. To secure a larger proportion of a generalist's referrals, a specialist PSF may have to allocate more resources to a generalist PSF that enjoys high levels of resources from its rivals.

name: Legislative competition
definition: Interparty legislative competition is defined as competition between political parties in legislative bodies, or more generally as competition between opposing factions of policymakers within legislative bodies. It is conceptually and empirically distinct from electoral competition, that is, competition in the selection process of policy-makers.

name: Young firm mortality
authors_terms: ["young firm mortality", "young firm exit rate", "ratio of young firm exit", "young firm exit"]
definition: Young firm mortality refers to the death of firms that are five years old or younger. The authors consider two measures of young firm mortality, both of which focus exclusively on firm death and do not include voluntary firm movement.

name: Incentives and subsidies to incumbent firms
authors_terms: ["incentives and subsidies offered to incumbent firms", "subsidies and incentives to incumbent firms", "firm-specific incentives and subsidies"]
definition: State and local business incentives and subsidies granted to incumbent firms, used to examine how the institutional environment changes with respect to incumbents as legislative competition increases.

name: Breakthrough innovation
authors_terms: ["rate of breakthrough innovation", "breakthrough innovation", "breakthrough patents", "highly cited or impactful patents"]
definition: Following prior research, we measured a firm's rate of breakthrough innovation as the number of highly cited or impactful patents it was granted per year.

name: Portfolio resource diversity
authors_terms: ["portfolio resource diversity", "diversity of portfolio resources", "technological diversity of portfolio resources", "portfolio tech. resource diversity"]
definition: Diversity of portfolio resources refers to the mix or variety of technological resources held by portfolio partners. Breadth of portfolio resources helps a focal firm engage in a greater degree of exploration.

name: Portfolio resource quality
authors_terms: ["portfolio resource quality", "portfolio resource quality", "quality of portfolio resources"]
definition: Quality refers to the reliability of portfolio partners' technological resources. Portfolio resource quality is high when partners have high volume of resources and when other firms have lent credibility to those resources by building on them.

name: Internal technological diversity
authors_terms: ["internal technological diversity", "diversity of internal technological resources", "internal tech. diversity"]
definition: Diversity of internal technological resources refers to the breadth or range of technologies possessed by a focal firm (Patel & Pavitt, 1997).

name: Internal technological strength
authors_terms: ["technological strength", "technological strength of a focal firm", "internal strength", "technological strength (t - 1)"]
definition: Technological strength refers to the internal resource competence of a focal firm relative to that of other firms in its industry. A firm's technological strength is high if it has traditionally generated more technological innovations than others.

name: Portfolio leverage intensity
authors_terms: ["portfolio leverage intensity", "portfolio leverage", "portfolio resource leverage intensity"]
definition: Use of some partners' technological resources by a focal firm implies that it has been able to partly overcome its motivational and attitudinal barriers and is already capable of acquiring and leveraging external resources. We name this capability portfolio leverage. We defined portfolio leverage intensity as the extent to which a firm leveraged its partners' resources, measuring this variable as the proportion of portfolio quality resources that a firm leveraged.

name: Firm bankruptcy
definition: Corporate bankruptcy is binary. All members of the experimental group filed bankruptcy over the period; none of the members of the matched control group did so.

name: CEO duality
definition: CEO/board chair structure addresses whether the CEO concurrently serves as board chairperson (duality) or otherwise.

name: Proportion of independent directors
authors_terms: ["% independent directors", "proportions of independent directors", "proportion of independent directors"]
definition: For board composition the authors rely on the independent/interdependent director distinction; directors are coded as 'independent' if they are members of the board traditionally classified as outside directors, and were appointed to the board prior to the current CEO's appointment. The proportion measure is this count expressed as a proportion of the board.

name: Number of independent directors
authors_terms: ["absolute number of independent directors", "# independent directors"]
definition: The last governance variable is simply the absolute number of independent directors.

name: Innovative productivity
definition: The innovative output of a firm, measured as new chemical entities (NCEs); the authors read innovative productivity from the proportionality between R&D expenditure and the number of NCEs, so that 'firms with larger R&D budgets have, on the average, produced fewer NCEs per dollar than firms with smaller budgets.'

name: R&D expenditure
authors_terms: ["R&D expenditures", "R&D effort", "size of the R&D effort", "R&D spending", "R&D budget"]
definition: The size of the R&D effort, for which 'R&D expenditures were taken from COMPUSTAT for the period 1969-87'; the level of the firm's research and development budget.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "size of the firm", "number of employees"]
definition: 'As a measure of firm size we used number of employees... The total firm employee count (as opposed to count of employees in the 2834 line of business) was used since we were interested in the full effect of firm size regardless of lines of business in which the firm participated.'

name: Local multihospital system membership
definition: Multihospital systems consist of two or more physically separate hospitals sharing common ownership. The authors define a local system as comprising three or more community hospitals in the same geographic market sharing common ownership.

name: High tech service offerings
definition: Six of the eleven hospital services examined, including magnetic resonance imaging, open heart surgery, radioisotope therapy, cardiac catheterization, therapeutic radiology, and neonatology, are likely to be associated with economies of scale, both because they require substantial fixed investments and because they may have learning curves.

name: High touch service offerings
definition: Some services are not generally associated with a high degree of technological sophistication; the authors define HIGH TOUCH to be the sum total of deliveries, alternate birthing, pediatrics, substance abuse, and home care. Unlike high tech services, there is less theory to predict the provision of high touch services.

name: Average total cost
authors_terms: ["average total costs", "COST", "costs per admission", "ADJUSTED COST", "total cost"]
definition: Costs per admission (COST), examined as one of two indicators of efficiency, calculated so as to control for hospital level differences in case mix and market level differences in total costs.

name: Administrative cost
authors_terms: ["ADMIN COST", "administrative costs", "administration and overhead costs", "ADJUSTED ADMIN COST"]
definition: Administration and overhead costs, which account for about 30 percent of total expenses for the typical hospital in the sample; the authors examine administrative costs as a percentage of total costs as a second indicator of efficiency.

name: Price-cost margin
definition: The average price-cost margin obtained from privately insured patients, measured by the Lerner index, which equals (price-cost)/price, where unit prices (net of insurer discounts) and unit costs are estimated for major hospital cost centers and aggregated for a fixed market basket.

name: Systemness
definition: The homogeneity of strategic intent across the subunits of a firm, which the strategy literature refers to as 'systemness'. The authors believe systemness will be evidenced by reduced variation with respect to firm characteristics such as organizational structure, product mix, or marketing strategies/pricing.

name: Profitability
definition: Operating margin (OPMARGIN), defined as net operating revenue divided by net operating expense, used rather than asset based profitability measures because the latter are difficult to measure and interpret for nonprofit institutions.

name: Subsidiary profitability
definition: The profitability of the unregulated ventures of regulated firms, measured at the business-unit level by return on equity: the equity invested in each subsidiary and the equity earned on it.

name: Regulatory intensity
authors_terms: ["regulatory intensity", "monitoring intensity of regulatory bodies", "regulatory oversight"]
definition: Regulation is not an either/or condition, but varies in intensity depending on the relative activity of the state's commission; some firms are continually involved in regulatory procedures while others are given a relatively 'long leash'.

name: Size of subsidiary relative to parent
authors_terms: ["size relative to parent", "relative size of a subsidiary compared to its parent"]
definition: The size of the subsidiary relative to the parent company; monitoring of subsidiary managers is argued to be less intensive the smaller the size of the subsidiary relative to the parent.

name: Multidivisional structure
definition: The multidivisional form separates business units into independent profit centers and thereby accentuates their differentiation, serving to reduce 'bureaucratic distortions' and to relay information to higher echelons more accurately.

name: Relatedness of subsidiary to parent business
definition: Diversification into fields that are related to one another, in which the skills and know-how of the parent company can be brought to bear on the subsidiary, improving performance.

name: Subsidiary age
definition: The lifetime of a subsidiary, computed from its birth date to its termination or censoring in the study period.

name: Subsidiary death rate
definition: The rate of death of subsidiaries across time; death was defined to include not only dissolution of these enterprises, but also those whose operations were sold to other companies.

name: Ends specificity
definition: The specificity of the major, higher level purposes, mission, goals or objectives set by organizations. Low specificity scores indicate ends typical of the Incremental Model, while high specificity scores denote ends characteristic of the Synoptic Model, reflected in many precisely quantified, formally documented, time-limited ends ranging from a statement of firm mission to specific market share/sales growth targets.

name: Means specificity
definition: The specificity of the patterns of action which marshal/allocate organizational resources into postures that, once implemented, increase the probability of attaining organizational ends. Specific means are formally documented, detailed action plans and programs used to direct firm action and measure timely performance against plan, while unspecific means are broad and unstructured, acting as loose guides only.

name: Planning flexibility
definition: A Guttman type scale measuring how often a firm's ends or means are changed or altered. The authors acknowledge that though they label the construct planning flexibility they are really measuring the change in or alteration of plans, and that they obtain only average measures of flexibility across the ends and means involved.

name: Firm performance
definition: Two subjective perceptual measures of performance were developed: Overall Firm Performance (OFP), which captured overall firm performance data relative to competitive peers and firm market share change over the past 5-10 years (an externally anchored performance measure), and Planning Performance (PP), which captured the planning performance of respondent firms (an internally anchored performance measure evaluating planning capabilities and effectiveness).

name: Environmental stability
definition: The stability of the firm's industry or business environment as self-categorized by respondents, ranging from a mature, stable industry in which trends can generally be forecasted to young, highly unstable industries with rapid change and high uncertainty. Because of the multi-industry, multinational nature of the sample, objective indicators of environmental stability were inappropriate and respondents self-selected the environment that most closely described their firm's industry/business environment.

name: Planning duration
definition: The period of time a firm had been conducting the planning, reported by respondents in one of five categories ranging from less than one year to more than 15 years.

name: Lower-cost production opportunities
definition: Foreign investment opportunities that provide access to cheaper input costs, including labor and raw materials, and thus allow firms to relocate value chain activities and reallocate firm resources. The authors argue that efficiency-seeking investments in lower-cost production subsidiaries abroad are likely to involve trade-offs across geographic markets and result in divestment of existing, higher-cost home-country activities.

name: New market opportunities
definition: Foreign subsidiary investments motivated by firms seeking new geographic markets for their existing products, which can extend the application of a firm's resources and capabilities to additional markets. The authors argue that because of constraints on managerial time and attention, such investments can also involve trade-offs in resource uses across markets.

name: Home-country divestment
authors_terms: ["divestment", "divestment of home-country operations", "home-country subsidiary divestment", "home-country activities"]
definition: The number of subsidiaries a firm divests in each year in its home market. Subsidiary closures in the United States can represent either exit from a business line, if a firm closes all subsidiaries listed under a division, or contraction in activities in a business line in a firm's home market.

name: Product diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm operates across multiple business segments; the measure takes into consideration both the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each of the segments in the total sales of the firm.

name: Foreign expansion
authors_terms: ["foreign expansion", "extent of international activities", "levels of foreign investment activity", "extent of international investment", "international expansion"]
definition: The extent of a firm's international subsidiary investment activity, captured by a firm's total number of foreign subsidiaries. The authors argue that firms with higher levels of foreign expansion are more likely to face capacity-constrained resources and to need to reallocate resources across product and geographic markets.

name: Scenario construction
authors_terms: ["multiple scenarios", "scenario construction", "scenario building", "scenario method", "multiple scenario development"]
definition: Scenarios are defined as 'focused descriptions of fundamentally different futures presented in coherent script-like or narrative fashion,' and the method decomposes a complex future into discrete states while presenting uncertainty across rather than within models.

name: Extreme scenario consideration
authors_terms: ["forced scenarios", "extreme scenarios", "the more extreme scenario condition", "high and low scenarios"]
definition: Forced or extreme scenarios place all positive outcomes of key uncertainties in one scenario and all negative outcomes in the other, testing the possibility that scenario analysis highlights particular combinations of outcomes as unlikely or implausible.

name: Subjective confidence range
definition: A subjective range around a point estimate that accords each best estimate an upper and a lower bound, so that one is highly confident the actual outcome will fall within that range; the ranges concern strategic variables involving significant stakes and complexity.

name: Perceived probability of conjunctive events
definition: The subjective probability subjects assign to a conjunctive outcome, i.e. one in which both of two elemental events occur; statistically such conjunctive events are never deemed more likely than either the probability of A or B occurring alone.

name: Perceived probability of single events
definition: The subjective probability subjects assign to each elemental (single) event, against which the probability of the corresponding conjunction is compared.

name: Consistency of belief systems
authors_terms: ["inconsistencies in subjects' belief systems", "internal consistency", "internally consistent", "consistency index"]
definition: The internal statistical coherence of a subject's belief system, assessed by whether the subjective correlations among five strategic uncertainties satisfy the mathematical bounds on partial correlations, i.e. yield positive-definite correlation matrices.

name: Subjective correlations
definition: A subject's assessment, ranging from -1 to +1, of how two strategic uncertainties are related; each subject provided an entire 5 by 5 matrix of such correlations.

name: Acquisition of corporate subsidiary
authors_terms: ["being acquired", "acquisition", "ownership change", "change in the ownership control", "station sold"]
definition: Acquisitions—changes in the ownership control of a firm or business unit—provide a means by which firms can accumulate resources and market power. The study measures acquisitions with a dichotomous variable that indicates the legal transfer of more than 50 percent of the station's equity.

name: Innovation adoption
definition: Innovation adoption—a firm's integration of an externally invented technology—represents an important form of vicarious learning. The dependent variable is a binary indicator of HD Radio adoption by a station in a given quarter.

name: Geographically proximate peer adoption
authors_terms: ["geographically proximate adoptions", "adoptions by other stations in the same geographic market", "same geographic market"]
definition: Geographic proximity strengthens the influences of information-transfer mechanisms by enabling interpersonal relations, and adoptions by geographically proximate industry participants are a primary referent group for mimetic adoption.

name: Corporate sibling adoption
authors_terms: ["corporate sibling adoptions", "corporately related adoption", "same corporate parent"]
definition: Social and legal structures link corporate proximity to the increased likelihood of mimetic adoption, and cooperative incentives motivate subsidiaries that are controlled by the same corporate parent to share knowledge about adopting new innovations.

name: Similar product peer adoption
definition: When firms or subsidiaries offer similar products, they can trigger mechanisms that promote mimetic innovation adoption.

name: Acquisition exposure
authors_terms: ["tie exposed to acquisition", "alliances exposed to acquisitions", "exposed to an acquisition event"]
definition: The treatment condition of interest: whether an alliance was exposed to an acquisition event, in contrast to alliances that were not exposed to an acquisition event.

name: Alliance termination
definition: The dissolution of an alliance-based relational asset following an acquisition, i.e., the acquirer discards, through sale or termination, a subset of its post-acquisition portfolio of resources.

name: Stress on acquirer's alliance management capacity
authors_terms: ["stress on the acquirer's alliance management capacity", "stress on acquirer's alliance capacity", "acquirer's alliance capability", "alliance management capacity"]
definition: The acquirer's alliance capability is its capacity to manage its portfolio of interfirm relationships; stress on this capacity arises from the proportional increase in the alliance portfolio that the acquirer must manage after inheriting the target's alliances.

name: Alliance inheritance
authors_terms: ["inherited alliances", "alliances inherited from the target firm", "target's alliance", "preexisting alliances", "inheritance effect"]
definition: The distinction between the post-acquisition vulnerability of alliances formed by the acquirer before the acquisition (i.e., preexisting alliances) and those that the acquirer obtains from the target firm after the acquisition (i.e., inherited alliances).

name: Common partners
definition: The connections between an inherited alliance partner and the acquiring firm's preexisting alliance partners.

name: Unique partners
definition: The connections between an inherited alliance partner and firms that do not have prior ties to either the acquirer or the target firm.

name: Divestiture type
definition: We investigate two of the most common types of these divestitures: spinoffs and buyouts. A spinoff occurs when a corporation distributes pro rate the shares of a subsidiary to the parent firm shareholders, thus creating a publicly-traded company to continue the operations of the division or subsidiary; a management buyout occurs when a corporation sells a subsidiary to an investor group that includes the managers of that organization, thus creating a private company set up to continue the operations of the division or subsidiary.

name: Strategic emphasis
definition: We define strategic emphasis as the relative amount of resources that a divestiture invests on R&D over marketing (Mizik and Jacobson, 2003). R&D investments have highly uncertain payoffs; marketing investments produce more certain, immediate payoffs (Steenkamp and Fang, 2011).

name: Radicalness of new products
definition: We use two ten-point scales, available from the authors, to measure the extent to which a new product (1) incorporates a substantially different core technology (adapted from Sood and Tellis, 2005) and (2) provides substantially higher customer benefits (based on Chandy and Tellis, 2000). While marketing investments provide valuable insights into market needs, these insights are likely to lead to incremental innovations.

name: Profitability
definition: We use profits to measure performance, and specifically return on asset (ROA).

name: Acquisition premium
definition: Acquisition premium is commonly defined as the acquirer's bid minus the target's preannouncement market value divided by the target's pre-announcement market value. In order to reduce the effect of distracting events without excluding the stock market's pre-announcement anticipation, this paper examines the announcement-day premium.

name: R&D capital
authors_terms: ["R&D capital", "R&D investments", "R&D investment-to-market ratio", "4-year accumulated R&D divided by target market value"]
definition: The information asymmetry is expected to increase the more a target firm has accumulated R&D capital and the higher its R&D growth rate. In this paper, the R&D investment was scaled by dividing it by the target's pre-acquisition market value.

name: R&D growth rate
definition: R&D growth rate is measured as the growth of the target firm's R&D 4 years prior to the acquisition. The information asymmetry is expected to increase the more a target firm has accumulated R&D capital and the higher its R&D growth rate.

name: Target market-to-book ratio
definition: The market-to-book ratio corresponds to the number of times that a firm's market value is higher than its book substance value. A target firm's market-to-book ratio is determined consistent with previous research by dividing target pre-acquisition market value by its book value of equity.

name: Stock market reaction
