authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns", "market reaction of an acquisition", "stock market reaction", "abnormal returns"]
definition: A market model was created for each acquiring firm's stock and used to determine the expected returns for a chosen acquisition time period. Differences from the model were regarded as abnormal returns for acquirer shareholders, which were then summed up over a chosen window to form the eventual cumulative abnormal returns for the period of observation for each acquirer.

name: Network closure
definition: Closure is the extent to which a firm's contacts are themselves connected (Coleman, 1988, 1990); as a source of social capital it facilitates sanctions and norms of reciprocity and affects the quality of information by maintaining the trustworthiness of others. More constraint means more network closure.

name: Relational embeddedness
authors_terms: ["relational embeddedness", "repeated interactions with direct contacts", "alliance-per-partner ratio"]
definition: The second mechanism through which quality of information operates; repeated interactions with direct contacts enhance information quality because information exchange in ongoing relationships is enriched with fine-grained detail and because repeated interactions create a common language between the partners. Having multiple ties per direct contact is associated with more reliable communication channels and higher information quality.

name: Network configuration change
authors_terms: ["changes in a firm's network configuration over time", "temporal changes in network configuration", "configuration lock-in"]
definition: Relational embeddedness may lead to lock-in effects because repeated interactions with direct contacts constrain a firm's flexibility in changing its network configuration over time; existing network configurations may inhibit the creation of new ties, and thus diminish the benefits of network resources in the long run.

name: Brokerage opportunities
definition: Brokerage (building bridges that link between cohesive groups otherwise disconnected) is a mechanism through which information quantity increases. Occupying the position at the crossroads of social relations increases the efficiency of information diffusion through early access to more information sources.

name: Network size
authors_terms: ["number of alliance partners", "count of alliance partners", "network size", "number of direct ties"]
definition: The number of alliance partners a firm has. As the number of direct ties increases, network costs may outweigh the benefits derived from network resources, turning social capital into social liability; as the size of the network grows, adding network partners may result in diminishing returns or even negative effects.

name: Compositional heterogeneity
definition: A mechanism by which the diversity in network resources affects the timing of market entry, based on the diversity of alliance partners' operational context. The authors distinguish partners that are horizontally linked (competitors active in the same market segment or industry) from those that are vertically linked (suppliers, customers, and complementors active in different industries and/or stages of the value chain).

name: Rate of entry into an emerging product market
authors_terms: ["rate of entry into an emerging product market", "timing of market entry", "timing of entry"]
definition: The speed with which firms enter a newly developed market, modelled as the rate of entry: the dependent variable is the amount of time elapsed between the emergence of the networking switches market and a firm's entry event, or censoring. Firms enter a marketplace earlier if they can resolve the technological and market uncertainties sooner.

name: Density of firms in the market
authors_terms: ["density", "the count of firms operating in the market", "the number of firms already entered"]
definition: The count of firms operating in the market, used as a proxy for the level of legitimation and competition in the emerging product market. At low levels of density, growth in firm count serves primarily to legitimate a population's goals and chosen form; at high levels of density, increases in density strengthen competition far more than legitimation.

name: Corporate risk
definition: Building on previous studies which conceptualize risk as variation of return, the variance of ROA across the 5-year period 1977-81 is chosen as the measure of corporate risk.

name: Industry risk
authors_terms: ["industry risk", "IRK", "weighted industry risk (WIRK)", "risk of its product markets", "industry-specific risk"]
definition: This study used the relative variation of four-digit industry demand as a surrogate for industry risk (IRK).

name: Firm size
definition: SIZE is the logarithm of mean assets of firm i over the 5-year period 1977-81.

name: Number of businesses
definition: For each firm, the total number count of three-digit SIC industries is the number of businesses.

name: Corporate return
definition: The measure of corporate return is the mean value of return on assets (ROA) over the 5-year period 1977-81.

name: Industry profitability
authors_terms: ["industry profitability", "mean industry profitability (MIP)", "weighted industry return (WIRN)", "return of its product markets"]
definition: Since no return on investment or return on assets data are available at the four-digit SIC industry code level in the Census and the Survey data, surrogates are used; the industry profitability measure used in this study is the price-cost margin. For a firm, the mean industry profitability (MIP) of each industry it operates in is weighted by the fraction of the firm's total net sales generated from that industry, giving the weighted industry return (WIRN).

name: Generic diversification strategy
definition: Rumelt used the degree of relatedness among businesses in a diversified firm to classify highly diversified firms into a number of categories, including related constrained (RC), related-linked (RL), and unrelated businesses (UR). There are three categories in the sample: related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated strategies.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: Diversification is represented by the level of product diversity and of geographic diversity: the authors use the Herfindahl index as a continuous measure of product diversity and a continuous measure of geographic diversity, namely the ratio of international sales to the total corporate sales.

name: Pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["pay dispersion", "pay distribution", "pay distributions", "dispersion in pay", "spread of pay", "wage differential"]
definition: A hierarchical pay distribution is one in which a greater proportion of pay is concentrated in relatively few levels, jobs, or individuals near the top of the distribution, so pay is more widely dispersed and less equal across pay levels; a compressed pay distribution is one in which pay is less dispersed and is spread more equally across jobs or individuals. The focus of this study was on the spread of pay, or differences in actual pay, not on the number of pay levels.

name: Position in pay dispersion
authors_terms: ["position in a pay dispersion", "rank of a player's pay"]
definition: An employee's position in a pay dispersion, operationalized as the rank of a player's pay on his team (rank of highest-paid player = 1); a lower value indicates a higher position in the dispersion.

name: Individual performance
definition: For players, performance metrics were taken directly from the literature on baseball statistics: three measures for nonpitchers—adjusted batting runs, fielding runs, and total player rating—and three for pitchers: adjusted earned run average, pitching runs, and total pitcher rating. All of these measures are commonly used by professional baseball teams to judge player performance.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Two primary groups of performance goals are pursued by owners of professional sports teams: on-field performance and financial performance. It is possible for owners to pursue higher financial performance at the expense of on-field performance, and vice versa.

name: Matrix management adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of matrix management", "adoption of unit management", "matrix adoption"]
definition: Adoption by a hospital of the matrix program called unit management, defined as the presence of unit managers, administrators, or coordinators in hospital inpatient units.

name: Matrix management abandonment
definition: Discontinuation by a hospital of a matrix program it had previously adopted; the survey asked administrators whether they had discontinued unit management and in what years.

name: Task diversity
authors_terms: ["task diversity", "organizational diversity", "domain diversity", "horizontal differentiation", "diversity of clients", "diversity of functions"]
definition: Organizational diversity, measured as the breadth of a firm's domain and horizontal differentiation; information-processing requirements are influenced by it, since diversity increases the number of decision-making points and causes coordination problems.

name: Organizational size
definition: Increased scale raises coordination requirements both directly, through raising the number of relationships in an organization, and indirectly, through increasing differentiation.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Following Cyert and March (1963), slack is the income remaining after an organization has covered the costs necessary to sustain operations.

name: Sociometric centrality
definition: The degree to which a hospital occupied a central and prestigious position in a local hospital network, measured by the academic reputation and visibility of the medical school with which it was affiliated; dominant organizations in central sociometric positions tend to be early adopters.

name: Professional media reports
authors_terms: ["published reports", "professional media", "reports", "transmission of information about matrix management"]
definition: The transmission of information about matrix management, measured as the number of reports of matrix programs appearing each year in health administration research and trade journals.

name: Cumulative force of adoption
authors_terms: ["cumulative force of adoption", "cumulative level of adoption", "regional force of adoption", "local force of adoption"]
definition: The cumulative level of prior adoption of matrix management by organizations in regional and local networks, which legitimated the innovation and increased pressure on other organizations to follow suit.

name: Cumulative force of abandonment
authors_terms: ["cumulative force of abandonment", "cumulative level of program terminations", "regional force of abandonment", "local force of abandonment"]
definition: Program abandonment may occur as institutional support for a program wanes, as the cumulative level of program terminations increases in local or regional networks.

name: Local acceptance of matrix management
authors_terms: ["local acceptance", "degree of local acceptance", "acceptance group", "cumulative experience with matrix management"]
definition: The assumed degree of local acceptance and normative approval of the matrix program, taken to increase with the collective experience with the program in a local network.

name: High-prestige prior adoption in local network
definition: Adoption of matrix management by organizations with high visibility and prestige in local networks, which is expected to influence organizations of lower prestige to follow suit.

name: Entrepreneurial strategy making
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurial strategy making", "ESM", "Entrepreneurial SMP", "entrepreneurial strategy-making process", "entrepreneurial orientation", "entrepreneurial posture"]
definition: Entrepreneurial strategy making is a distinctive strategy-making mode that combines features of a command mode—bold, directive, opportunity-seeking style—with aspects of the generative mode—risk taking and experimentation. It is a strategy-making process characterized by experimentation, innovativeness, risk taking, and proactive assertiveness.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["sales growth", "profitability and return on investment", "overall company performance"]
definition: Executives assessed their organization's performance over the past five years relative to competitors on three indices: sales growth, profitability and return on investment, and overall company performance.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Unpredictability and dynamism are considered to be 'the key components of the overarching construct of uncertainty', so the dynamism and unpredictability variables were combined into a composite index of environmental uncertainty.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: Environmental heterogeneity is treated as a facet of the firm's competitive environment assessed through managerial perceptions, and is measured with three items relating to customer buying habits, competition, and technological requirements.

name: Cost leadership strategy
definition: A cost leadership strategy suggests an internal orientation whereby a firm concentrates on product efficiencies and cost control in order to be the lowest cost producer relative to competitors.

name: Marketing differentiation strategy
definition: Marketing differentiation is characterized by extensive advertising, image management, and intensive marketing such as offering attractive features, convenience, and service guarantees.

name: Innovative differentiation strategy
definition: Innovative differentiation is characterized by creativity in product development, original applications of new technologies, up-to-date innovations, and quality design.

name: Participative strategy-making process
definition: The participative SMP factor includes variables such as 'business planning involves everyone in the organization' and consensus and cooperation across departments and functional areas that are clearly indicative of a participative management style.

name: Adaptive strategy-making process
definition: The adaptive SMP factor suggests an external orientation focused on adapting to customer needs, and responding to cues and feedback from the environment.

name: Simplistic strategy-making process
definition: The simplistic SMP factor includes several variables that indicate a well-established but limited strategy-making process, corresponding to the emphasis on a routine way of conducting business or narrow focus on a dominant element of strategy.

name: Hypercompetition
definition: With hypercompetition, assumptions of market stability are replaced by notions of inherent instability and change. Hypercompetition increases the frequency of decision making and consequently decreases the stability of markets and business performance over time.

name: Business performance stability
authors_terms: ["business performance stability", "stability of business performance", "stability in performance across the population over time"]
definition: The persistence of business performance patterns across a population of businesses over time. Under hypercompetition businesses have more opportunities to deviate from their current performance trend, both positively and negatively, than those in more stable environments.

name: Durability of abnormal business returns
authors_terms: ["durability of abnormal business returns", "durability of abnormal business profitability", "rate of decay of abnormal business returns"]
definition: The degree to which abnormally high or low business returns persist rather than dissipate over time, regressing to mean levels as a consequence of competitive pressures. A hypercompetitive shift should increase the rate of decay of abnormal business returns.

name: Business mortality
authors_terms: ["business mortality", "business mortality (exit from industries)", "exit from an industry"]
definition: The disappearance (exit) of a business from an industry. Organizations that are not well adapted to their environment and have seen the value of their resources depleted are more likely to be selected out.

name: Market stability
definition: The stability of markets and industries over time. Hypercompetition is argued to decrease the stability of markets and business performance over time.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Dynamism reflects the degree to which there is unpredictable change or volatility in an industry.

name: Industry munificence
definition: Munificence reflects the degree to which an industry may support sustained growth.

name: Speed of scaling
authors_terms: ["speed of scaling", "knowledge transfer", "spatial replication of routines", "replicating routines across space", "scaling (opening new outlets in which required routines are replicated)"]
definition: Knowledge transfer to new outlets, that is, replicating a chain's value-creating standard set of required routines in new outlets. We measured Speed of Scaling as the number of outlets an area unit opened in their area in a given month.

name: Nonadherence to required routines
authors_terms: ["nonadherence to required routines", "lack of adherence to required routines", "knowledge retention", "temporal replication of routines", "adherence to required routines"]
definition: Our dependent variable is the extent to which individual outlets do not comply with the set of required routines of the franchise chain (Nonadherence to Required Routines). Knowledge retention, that is, ensuring continued adherence to required routines in existing outlets over time, is fundamental to the operation of a chain organization.

name: Adherence-related failure experience
authors_terms: ["adherence-related failure experience", "area unit experience with adherence-related failures", "experience with adherence-related failures of outlets"]
definition: The experience that an area unit has with adherence-related failures of outlets under its purview. In the literature on learning from failures, failure experience is typically measured as the cumulative number of failures experienced by a focal organization over its lifetime or within a given period; we followed that approach focusing on outlet failures, that is, permanent closures of outlets.

name: Irregular rhythm of scaling
authors_terms: ["irregular rhythm of scaling", "area unit experience with an irregular rhythm of scaling", "pacing (rhythm) of its scaling"]
definition: An irregular rhythm of scaling implies that an area unit's speed of scaling has been more irregular, that is, more heterogeneous, variable over time, in the past.

name: Outlet operating experience
authors_terms: ["outlet operating experience", "outlet-level learning from operating experience", "operating experience of the outlets under its supervision"]
definition: A third kind of experience that may affect an area unit's management of dual demands (knowledge transfer and knowledge retention) is the operating experience of the outlets under its supervision. We measured Outlet Operating Experience as the number of months an outlet had been in operation.

name: Volume of associative rhetoric
definition: The volume of associative rhetoric is the amount of media rhetoric that associates an emerging market with a firm's existing markets, representing the popularization of the new logics through exposure. 'The volume of associative rhetoric is related to exposure, which increases familiarity and liking of the association between new and existing logics' (P29).

name: Tenor of associative rhetoric
authors_terms: ["tenor of associative rhetoric", "tenor", "positive versus negative tenor"]
definition: The positive (negative) tenor of associative rhetoric provides public expressions of approval (disapproval) of the association between new logics and existing logics. It is the relative proportion of associative rhetoric that is framed positively versus negatively.

name: Source of associative rhetoric
definition: The source is whether the association between the origin market(s) and the destination market stems from firms or from journalists/analysts. 'Although the media create an interpretive context, the information presented in the media can be gathered from diverse sources, such as journalists, analysts, and firms' (P33).

name: Focus of associative rhetoric
authors_terms: ["focus of associative rhetoric", "focus", "generalization versus specific cases"]
definition: Associative rhetoric can appear in contexts with different foci, ranging from a general focus, where broad trends and general principles are reported, through a more specific focus, where the actions of several firms are reported, to a highly specific focus, where the actions of one or two firms are reported.

name: Timing of entry into an emerging market
authors_terms: ["timing of entry", "hazard rate of entry", "decision to enter an emerging market", "rate of entry"]
definition: The timing of a firm's diversification into a newly emerging market, modeled as the hazard rate of entry: the rate at which firms that are at risk enter the destination market in a given year.

name: Superior economic performance
authors_terms: ["superior economic performance", "statistically significantly above-average performance", "above-average performance"]
definition: Rather than make any such assumption, this research will start with the less restrictive definition of statistically significantly above-average performance relative to a reference set of comparable firms (in this research, an industry). Superior economic performance was operationalized as statistically significant above-average (relative to the industry or reference set) economic performance over a five-year period.

name: Persistent superior economic performance
authors_terms: ["persistent superior economic performance", "sustained superior economic performance", "PSP"]
definition: Persistent superior economic performance is defined here as statistically significant above-average performance relative to a reference set (such as an industry) that persists over a long-term period of calendar time (such as ten years or more). Sustained superior economic performance was operationalized as superior economic performance that lasted six or more consecutive windows (i.e., ten years).

name: Industry concentration
definition: Industry four-firm concentration ratio was operationalized by dividing the combined total revenues of the four largest firms in each industry by the total revenues of all firms in the industry. Both the SCP IO paradigm and evolutionary economics predict that sustained competitive advantage will be associated with industry concentration and firm market share, so that a few large firms will be the beneficiaries of sustained competitive advantage.

name: Market share
definition: Market share was operationalized as the ratio of each firm's total revenues to the total revenues of all firms in the industry.

name: Stability of superior performance group membership
authors_terms: ["stable in membership over time", "stability of group membership"]
definition: One of the assumptions of strategic group theory is that the strategic groups have predictive validity, i.e., firms in a strategic group have equivalent performance. If the firms demonstrating persistent superior economic performance, which form a group with equivalent performance, are in fact a strategic group, then the presence of mobility barriers should make this group relatively stable, since other firms cannot readily change their strategies in order to enter the strategic group.

name: Personal attachment
definition: In the context of an ICV, personal attachment represents the degree to which boundary spanners (resident board members and senior venture managers) from each party are socially bound through having developed interpersonal relationships and interpersonal learning.

name: Tenure overlap
authors_terms: ["tenure overlap between boundary spanners", "overlap in tenure"]
definition: The tenure overlap between boundary spanners determines the amount of time during which personal attachment is established; it is the number of years foreign and local boundary spanners have worked together within the venture in their boundary-spanning positions.

name: Educational difference
definition: The educational level of a boundary spanner reflects the potential knowledge he or she can offer to another boundary spanner as well as his or her ability to learn and absorb skills; the smaller the educational differences (in terms of years of schooling) between boundary spanners, the higher the probability that they will be able to share knowledge with one another.

name: Goal congruity
authors_terms: ["goal congruity between ICV partner firms", "goal congruity", "goal congruence"]
definition: The congruity of the goals set by an ICV's parents before it commences operations affects the extent to which partner firms will behave cooperatively or opportunistically during operations.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance between partner firms is a particularly potent form of internal uncertainty for ICVs because it implies differences in managerial values, mind-sets, and norms.

name: Market disturbance
definition: Market disturbance is the extent to which the industrial environment and related market structure are volatile and variable.

name: Regulatory deterrence
definition: Regulatory deterrence is the extent to which business operations are hampered and deterred by administrative regulations imposed by a host government.

name: ICV performance
definition: Performance was defined by two measures: the subjective construct, process performance, and the objective measure, return on investment (ROI).

name: Investment in internal R&D
definition: Level of investment in R&D, or 'R&D intensity,' is commonly operationalized as R&D expenditures expressed as a percentage of sales. Internal R&D was defined as biotechnology R&D conducted in-house by the firm, at either the corporate or the divisional level.

name: Technological breadth
authors_terms: ["breadth of the firm's internal R&D activities", "breadth of a firm's expertise in biotechnology", "technological breadth", "BREADTH"]
definition: A basic premise of the absorptive capacity construct is that firms need to manage the diversity of their knowledge structures; the possession of diverse and different knowledge structures enhances the organization's potential for innovation by providing an opportunity to make novel linkages and associations. Breadth of a firm's expertise in biotechnology was measured by counting the number of biotechnologies the firm reported using.

name: Variety of technology sourcing linkages
authors_terms: ["number of different types of technology sourcing linkages", "variety of types of linkages", "TYPE"]
definition: The number of different types of technology sourcing linkages pursued by the firm. Because different types of linkages are used to access different kinds of knowledge, firms need to pursue multiple types of linkages to build the absorptive capacity needed to generate new technical outputs.

name: Technical output
authors_terms: ["technical output", "biotechnology patents", "biotechnology products", "reputation for possessing expertise in biotechnology", "PAT", "PROD", "REP"]
definition: Technical output is multidimensional; the study employs three measures of technical output: the number of patents that the firm holds based on new technologies, the number of products based on the new technologies that the firm has on the market or under review by regulatory agencies, and the firm's reputation for possessing expertise in the new technologies.

name: Use of R&D contracts
definition: A contract whereby the firm paid an external firm to provide research services; the measure counts the number of times the firm used research contracts.

name: Use of licenses
definition: A licensing agreement which involved fixed payments and/or royalty payments in return for access to an external firm's technology; the measure counts the number of licenses the firm used.

name: Acquisition activity
definition: The acquisition of a firm that already possesses expertise in a new technology, described as a speedier means of building internal capabilities than establishing a green-field R&D unit; the measure counts the number of acquisitions undertaken.

name: Joint venture activity
definition: A joint venture is defined as a new venture created by the equity contributions of two or more partners; the measure counts the number of joint ventures formed.

name: Minority equity investment activity
authors_terms: ["number of minority equity investments", "minority equity investments", "ME"]
definition: Minority equity investments in other commercial firms provide an efficient way to access basic knowledge and monitor technological developments in areas in which the firm is unwilling or unable to develop its own internal capabilities; the measure counts the number of minority equity investments made.

name: Social environmental disruption
authors_terms: ["social environmental disruptions", "social disruptions", "environmental disruptions", "environmental changes", "refugee influx", "Syrian refugee crisis"]
definition: Social disruptions within a society can result from revolutions, population and demographic shifts, natural disasters, and cultural changes. The authors examine the Syrian refugee influx into Jordan as such a disruption.

name: Family funding partner logic
definition: A guiding institutional logic carried by family funding partners that emphasizes relational ties, loyalty, and reciprocity. Ventures funded by family likely carry a family logic.

name: Market funding partner logic
definition: A guiding institutional logic carried by bank funding partners that prioritizes efficiency, profit maximization, and formalized processes. Ventures funded by banks may be more likely to carry a market logic.

name: Venture failure
definition: Failure of a venture within its first 2 years. Entrepreneurship studies show that failure rates are highest within a business's first 2 years and decrease substantially after that infancy stage.

name: Business group affiliation
authors_terms: ["group affiliation", "group membership", "belong to the same group", "group brethren"]
definition: The paper treats groups as socially constructed: groups are 'arrived at by an unspoken consensus among societal actors' and can assume a taken-for-granted nature. The authors rely on the regulatory record of which firms belong to which group, in which a group is a set of companies whose property, management, administration, or credit relationships suggest that their decisions are guided by a shared interest.

name: Visible interfirm ties
definition: Ties between firms that a researcher can observe. The authors stress that many types of ties may be visible to the actors who help to socially construct group boundaries but invisible to the observer, so any particular study observes only a subset of the ties that exist.

name: Family connections
definition: Among field-based studies of business groups, no type of tie has received greater attention than family connections. Family relationships are placed uppermost in the hierarchy of ties that might be associated with goal congruence, and family involvement introduces a stable institution that guarantees repeated social contact among the individuals in a group.

name: Common ownership
definition: The involvement of the same individuals, not just members of the same family, holding major stakes in a group's constituent firms. Ownership overlap promotes both alignment of interests and flow of information between firms, and it may be highly visible to network actors.

name: Director interlocks
definition: An individual may be involved in multiple companies not only through ownership stakes but also through board positions. Whether conveying information or promoting alignment, director interlocks may be especially prominent signifiers of group borders.

name: Direct equity holdings
authors_terms: ["direct equity holdings", "direct equity interlocks", "direct equity ties", "direct equity holding"]
definition: Groups of firms that trade with one another regularly may hold equity stakes in each other to reduce the hazards of trade. Direct equity interlocks may arise not only to support exchange among existing firms but also to nurture new ventures, with established companies taking ownership stakes in start-ups.

name: Indirect equity holdings
authors_terms: ["indirect equity holdings", "indirect equity ties", "indirect holdings", "indirect equity interlocks"]
definition: Indirect equity ties are the building blocks of pyramids: Firm A has a stake in Firm C not directly, but through an equity position in Firm B, which in turn owns part of C. Indirect ties may promote alignment between connected firms, but they are usually represented as allowing powerful individuals to control chains of companies with miniscule equity stakes.

name: Hiring directors
authors_terms: ["hiring directors", "directors who help hire a CEO", "directors who appointed the CEO", "number of hiring directors"]
definition: Directors who were present during a CEO's hiring, whom the authors refer to as 'hiring directors' for simplicity of exposition. In the archival data they are measured as the number of directors who were serving on the board when the CEO was hired.

name: Choice-supportive bias
definition: Choice-supportive bias is the unwitting tendency to misremember prior choices such that favorable aspects are exaggerated, and unfavorable aspects are downplayed. Psychologists use the term to describe the cognitive process that occurs following decision-making whereby individuals misremember decisions to convince themselves of the decision's correctness.

name: Change in CEO pay
authors_terms: ["change in CEO pay", "change in pay", "year-over-year change in pay", "CEO excess pay"]
definition: Annual CEO excess pay is calculated as the residuals from the regression of CEO total pay on important determinants of CEO total pay; CEOs with positive residuals enjoy pay that exceeds predictions based on these objective factors, whereas CEOs with negative residuals are paid less than predicted. Change in pay is operationalized as the year-to-year change in these excess pay figures.

name: CEO dismissal
authors_terms: ["CEO dismissal", "likelihood of CEO dismissal", "probability of CEO dismissal"]
definition: CEO dismissal is measured with a 0/1 indicator equaling 1 when the CEO was replaced. The measure captures cases where the CEO was under the age of 65, did not remain on the board, was fired or forced to resign, left due to poor performance, left immediately or unexpectedly for nonhealth reasons, or retired early in the face of negative performance.

name: Board experience
definition: Individuals accumulate knowledge through experience, which ultimately shapes their cognitive frameworks, and boards with greater experience have a richer array of knowledge structures and perspectives to apply to issues under discussion. The authors measure it as the total number of years of board service across all boards other than a focal firm's board among the firms' independent and affiliated directors over the 5 years prior to the focal year.

name: Husband's chaebol
authors_terms: ["husband's chaebol", "a business group owned by a husband's family", "the chaebol owned by the husband's family"]
definition: The business group owned by the husband's family in a marriage between two chaebol owner-families; under the Confucian tradition the husband's family holds the privileged position in the marriage tie.

name: Wife's chaebol
authors_terms: ["wife's chaebol", "a business group owned by a wife's family", "the wife's family's business group"]
definition: The business group owned by the wife's family in a marriage between two chaebol owner-families; it must repay the favour of the marriage by supporting the husband's chaebol.

name: Market entry
definition: Entry by a chaebol into a market, defined at the level of 4-digit SIC codes, in which the partner chaebol is present.

name: Market exit
definition: Exit by a chaebol from a market, defined at the level of 4-digit SIC codes, in which both chaebols are present.

name: Chaebol performance
authors_terms: ["the chaebol's performance", "the personal wealth of chaebols' owner-CEOs", "wealth rank"]
definition: The personal wealth of the owner-CEOs is highly linked to the overall financial performance of the chaebol, hence it represents a reasonable proxy for the chaebol's performance.

name: Marriage tie between chaebol owner-families
definition: Such marriage relationships represent multiplex ties that comprise both personal and business domains as bases for interaction; the formation of a marriage tie opens a reliable communication channel between two business groups.

name: Communist ideology
authors_terms: ["communist ideology", "mayor's communist ideology", "stronger communist ideology", "ideological imprint"]
definition: Before 1978, the communist party of China strongly adhered to the orthodox Marxist-Leninist doctrine, indicating that mayors joining the party during this period were imprinted with a strong communist ideology. Such an imprint would shape their perceptions of the private business sector through the lens of class struggle, preventing them from understanding and appreciating the new role of private entrepreneurs during the subsequent economic reform era.

name: Private firms' political appointment
authors_terms: ["political appointment", "private firms' political appointment", "private firms' political participation", "deputyship"]
definition: Following the literature, we identified political appointment as having a top executive serving as a deputy in the PC or PPCC at the city level or above in a given year.

name: Youthful Cultural Revolution experience
authors_terms: ["mayor's Cultural Revolution experiences", "Cultural Revolution cohort", "experienced the Cultural Revolution at a young age"]
definition: To investigate this process, we consider that exposure to the Cultural Revolution (1966 - 1976) at a young age is an important early life experience that may lead to a stronger communist ideological imprint.

name: Regional communist legacy
definition: An important historical difference between provinces is that they vary in the timing and conditions of formally establishing the communist regime, which has led to different regional communist legacies. These institutional arrangements, both physical and cultural, continue to influence the beliefs, values, and behaviors of organizations and individuals in those regions.

name: Local economic development
authors_terms: ["economic development level", "city GDP", "higher contemporary economic development"]
definition: Economic development level was measured by the focal city ' s gross domestic product (GDP) in a given year.

name: Firm restructuring
definition: Restructuring here refers to the reduction of internal markets that occurs when a firm spins off, carves out or otherwise divests its divisions.

name: Extent of firm restructuring
authors_terms: ["extent of restructuring", "extent of firm dismemberment", "break-up of the original firm", "number of restructured units from original firm"]
definition: It is further argued that greater disruption will be caused in internal markets when the original firm divests more divisions and subsidiaries. It takes into account the extent to which the original firm was restructured or broken up.

name: Firm value
authors_terms: ["firm value", "share value", "value of the firm", "measures of value"]
definition: Firm value is assessed through the valuation of shares in voucher privatization, where 'the relative value of shares for different firms can be assessed by examining the number of shares demanded (as a percentage of those supplied) during the privatization process', and through the share price set in the first RMS auction.

name: Bank ownership
definition: With weak external capital markets, banks were the primary sources of capital. Banks may also be considered to be superior monitors: they may provide a substitute source of up-close monitoring that otherwise would have been obtained by divisions within an internal market.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign ownership", "foreign firm ownership", "level of foreign ownership"]
definition: Foreigners could be an excellent replacement for the technical know-how embedded in the former internal market of the restructured firm. Furthermore, as external members of the board of directors, foreigners could be expected to exercise authority more effectively and provide the monitoring lost in the disruption of the internal market.

name: Managerial ownership
definition: Managerial ownership in the restructured firm can help align the interests of managers with that of other shareholders. Thus, in lieu of internal market monitoring, managerial ownership can motivate, through self-interest, to undertake actions that will benefit all shareholders.

name: Government ownership
definition: Restructured firms with significant governmental connections would be able to reduce some of the risks of relying on still evolving external markets. Government connections would likely give such firms an edge in anticipating the nature of laws still to be passed, influencing policy-makers towards favorable legislation, as well as advantageous treatment in courts.

name: Investment fund ownership
authors_terms: ["investment fund ownership", "fund ownership", "ownership of investment funds"]
definition: Through the bidding process associated with the voucher scheme, these investment funds obtained ownership stakes, and as a result directorships on the boards, of many Czech firms. As relatively sophisticated investors, these funds too represent a valuable alternative monitoring mechanism to that lost by the restructured firms.

name: Network centrality
definition: An actor's location in a social network captures the structural dimension of social capital; an organizational unit that is centrally located in the interunit network is likely to have privileged access to critical resources and is highly visible and a major channel of information for other units.

name: Trustworthiness
authors_terms: ["trustworthiness", "relational dimension of social capital", "reputation for trustworthiness"]
definition: Trustworthiness is an attribute of an individual actor that signals to other parties its willingness to forego short-term outcomes obtainable through opportunistic behaviors; an organizational unit's reputation for trustworthiness is mainly determined by other units' perceptions and evaluations of the unit's integrity and reliability in interunit exchange.

name: Strategic relatedness
authors_terms: ["strategic relatedness", "strategic similarity", "relatedness at the strategic rather than the operational level"]
definition: Strategic relatedness characterizes the extent to which two organizational units are strategically similar and pinpoints the opportunity for sharing strategic resources between the two units. Two organizational units are considered strategically similar when they value the same kinds of strategic assets.

name: New interunit linkage creation
authors_terms: ["new linkage creation", "rate of new linkage creation", "creation of new interunit linkages", "intraorganizational linkages for resource exchange"]
definition: Intraorganizational linkages for resource exchange involve transfer and sharing of resources or knowledge among organizational units; the event of interest here is the creation of a new strategic linkage between an existing unit and the new unit, and the rate of new linkage creation is the hazard of such an event given that it has not yet occurred.

name: Boycott targeting
authors_terms: ["boycott treatment", "targeted by social protests", "boycotts", "targeted by social movement boycotts"]
definition: We use boycotts as a proxy for social protest because they are a relatively common contentious tactic that provoke a meaningful reputational threat for their targets. We test our hypotheses with a unique, self-constructed database that allows us to track the refunded political campaign contributions, congressional committee hearing appearances, and federal procurement contracts of public companies that are the targets of social movement boycotts.

name: Refunded campaign contributions
authors_terms: ["proportion of refunded contributions", "proportion of refunded PAC contributions", "proportion refunded PAC donations", "proportion of political contributions refunded"]
definition: The proportion of all contributions dispersed from a firm's affiliated PACs that were reported as refunded in a given quarter, indicating that they were rejected by the recipient politicians.

name: Congressional hearing appearances
authors_terms: ["appearances in congressional hearings", "invited congressional appearances", "invited appearances before congressional committee hearings", "invited corporate testimony in congressional hearings"]
definition: A more direct and commonly used indicator of a firm's access to policymakers and the policymaking process is the number of times politicians invite the company to provide testimony in congressional committee meetings. We collected data on firms' invited appearances before congressional committee hearings using ProQuest's Congressional Hearings data archives, searching for each treated and matched firm and hand-collecting and aggregating the number of times that a representative of a given firm testified in congressional hearings in a given quarter.

name: Government procurement contracts
authors_terms: ["awarded government contracts", "count of awarded government contracts", "federal procurement contracts"]
definition: We collected data on government procurement contracts awarded to each firm using the Federal Procurement Data System, wherein the federal government keeps archives of all procurement contracts, searchable by contractor (assigned party) and date. As each individual contract represents a unique associative tie, we summed the total number of unique assigned contracts by quarter in constructing our measure of the count of government contracts awarded to each sampled firm.

name: Media attention
authors_terms: ["media attention", "amount of media attention attracted by the boycott", "media attention garnered by the boycott"]
definition: Past research has shown that social movements generating more media attention represent greater threats to their targets. Media attention legitimizes activists' challenges and assists activists in mobilizing broad audience support.

name: Issue salience
authors_terms: ["issue salience", "salience of the issue advocated by activists", "salience of the boycotters' claims"]
definition: In political science, the concept of salience refers to the extent to which an issue is paramount in the public's mind or perceived as being of chief importance (Taylor and Fiske, 1978). Social movement theory suggests that activists primarily use contentious tactics to 'problematize' a given issue for the public.

name: Firm status
authors_terms: ["field status", "corporate status", "status of the targeted firm"]
definition: Firms with higher status within their field hierarchy benefit from more 'subjective standing' than do their peer organizations, from which they derive more-robust reputations, prestige, and power. As a proxy for corporate status, we used Fortune magazine's annual 'Most Admired Companies' index, a ranking of corporate prestige based on surveys of the executives of an organization's peer firms.

name: Modular search
definition: Search for better ways to carry out the tasks fulfilled by different specialists, which the author calls ''modular search''; it is one of the two levels of organizational search in a complex system and may be recognized by attending to direct cues about the viability of solutions to specialists' tasks.

name: Systemic search
definition: Search for better ways to integrate the work of the specialists performing different tasks, which the author calls ''systemic search''; searching systemically for new collective processes requires making sense of causal paths involving lateral and vertical interdependencies.

name: Exogenous shock with indirect systemic impact
authors_terms: ["change with indirect systemic impact", "game updates", "exogenous shock"]
definition: Environmental change whose direct impact is contained within specialized tasks but which, through lateral and vertical interdependencies among choices, indirectly affects the viability of an organization's systemic processes. The author captured it through an indicator variable equal to one if the game happened within two months of a game update that affected only the abilities of heroes.

name: Lateral communication
definition: Communication among specialists performing different tasks, which facilitates the emergence of rich shared representations of their task environment; members responsible for different tasks are more likely to understand how they depend on each other in contributing to systemic processes if they communicate frequently as they implement these processes.

name: Reliance on a formal coordinator
definition: Reliance on a formally designated coordinator or integrator who is responsible for facilitating coordination and shared understandings among specialized interdependent actors. Coordinators may form richer representations of task interdependencies than other members and may facilitate other members' sensemaking efforts.

name: Co-national immigrant concentration
authors_terms: ["immigrant concentration", "co-national immigrant concentration", "concentration of same-nationality immigrants", "concentration of co-national immigrants", "presence of same-country immigrants"]
definition: The variable immigrant concentration captures the percentage of the total population of state s born in home country c. This measure is consistent with the notion that immigrant clusters comprising a larger proportion of a total population will have greater influence, knowledge, and legitimacy.

name: Foreign location choice
authors_terms: ["location choice", "probability of entry", "likelihood of co-national firms having a subsidiary in that location", "where firms will establish foreign operations"]
definition: Within this realm of activity, where to establish foreign operations is a crucial decision with profound performance consequences.

name: Subsidiary survival
authors_terms: ["subsidiary survival", "probability of a subsidiary's survival", "survival", "prospects of survival for a foreign subsidiary"]
definition: A key outcome for firms expanding abroad is the ability to survive in the face of inherent disadvantages of newness and foreignness. The presence of these demand or supply benefits will increase the prospects of survival for a foreign subsidiary by increasing revenues or reducing costs.

name: Host-country experience
authors_terms: ["prior experience", "country-specific experience", "experience in the host country", "prior U.S. experience", "experience in the U.S."]
definition: Accumulated experience helps the firm develop country-specific knowledge and operational routines that alter the benefits of obtaining these from external sources—such as immigrants—because the firm develops an internal repository of local know-how.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The notion that the geographic clustering of industries has certain advantages has become generally accepted. The interactions among these specialized firms, workers, and suppliers leads to a proliferation of ideas that gives rise to knowledge spillovers.

name: Knowledge intensity of operations
definition: Firms with highly knowledge-intensive operations should receive a greater benefit from co-locating with immigrants than firms with less knowledge-intensive operations. High-technology industries are known to be knowledge intensive because the underlying assets most important to success are the proprietary know-how embodied in patents, trade secrets, or trademarks and—even more importantly—in tacit knowledge residing in employees' minds or in intangible organizational routines.

name: Withholding influence from regulators
definition: Stakeholders with power over critical resources use a direct strategy to withhold resources from the focal firm unless it adopts certain practices; regulators can deny a forestry company licence to operate on Crown lands unless it adopts certain sustainable practices. With the introduction of directors' and officers' liability for infringement of pollution laws, regulators have become the most important stakeholders in driving pollution control practices.

name: Withholding influence from social and ecological stakeholders
authors_terms: ["withholding influences from social and ecological stakeholders", "withholding stakeholder influence strategies"]
definition: Social and ecological stakeholders such as environmental NGOs, local communities and wildlife protection groups influence firms directly, or indirectly via the firm's economic stakeholders, by withholding legitimacy, disrupting operations, lobbying regulators and participating in environmental assessment proceedings.

name: Usage influence from customers
authors_terms: ["usage influences from customers", "usage influences from major customers"]
definition: Under high resource interdependence, stakeholders use a direct strategy to influence the firm's usage of resources so that their objectives are accommodated; in the forestry industry major customers have worked with supplier forestry companies to implement certification standards and more sustainable timber-harvesting practices.

name: Usage influence from economic stakeholders
authors_terms: ["usage influences from economic stakeholders", "usage influence strategies"]
definition: Economic stakeholders exercise usage influence strategies through their resource interdependence with the focal firm, pressing for information, certification and changes in products and processes; these strategies include customer demands for information and certification, employee suggestions and information via task forces and trade conferences.

name: External stakeholder influence
definition: Managers' perceptions of the importance of stakeholder influences on the firm, comprising both the withholding influence strategies of stakeholders who withhold resources and the usage influence strategies of stakeholders who direct the firm's use of resources.

name: Pollution control
definition: The earliest phase of corporate sustainability performance focused on end-of-pipe pollution control, including installing equipment for the capture of toxic emissions, treatment of chemical effluents before discharging them into water bodies, detoxification of wastes prior to disposal, making wastes biodegradable, and clean-up of contaminated sites.

name: Eco-efficiency
definition: Eco-efficiency involves the changing of processes and products to reduce wastes at source, reducing the use of energy and materials, water conservation, and greater fuel efficiency.

name: Recirculation
authors_terms: ["recirculation", "improving the recirculation of inputs and outputs"]
definition: Improving recirculation involves the reduction of the ratio of virgin to recycled material use in each succeeding time period; paper and wood mills reuse process waste, develop by-products from internal wastes, and improve recycling.

name: Eco-design
definition: Firms make more fundamental design changes in their products and processes by reducing or eliminating packaging, making products more durable and easy to disassemble and reuse, examining the life cycle environmental impacts of their products, services and operations, and eliminating harmful and toxic chemicals.

name: Ecosystem stewardship
definition: Ecosystem stewardship involves the firm taking responsibility for the environmental and social impacts of its operations on the carrying capacity of ecosystems and the societal/cultural heritage of local communities and social groups; in forestry operations it involves sustainable harvesting to meet the ultimate objective of no net loss of genetic, species, or ecosystem diversity.

name: Business redefinition
definition: Sustainable business models involve business redefinition that visualizes a business future with no negative impacts on the environment and social equity, redefining the forest products business in terms of the consumer functionalities delivered.

name: Strategic change
authors_terms: ["strategic change", "service additions", "service divestitures", "changes in the breadth of products or services", "changes in product and service domains"]
definition: Following Ginsberg (1988), we adopted a definition of strategic change that emphasizes changes in product and service domains. Through both adding and divesting new products and services, organizations alter their domains.

name: Ownership change
authors_terms: ["ownership change", "changes in a hospital's ownership", "fundamental transfers of control", "changes in ownership involving the transfer of control"]
definition: We determined changes in ownership involving the transfer of control from one individual, group, or organization to another individual, group, or organization. Each ownership change can alter the strategic decision-making context in a hospital by shifting power and control.

name: Board turnover
authors_terms: ["turnover on a hospital's board of directors", "board composition changes", "turnover among directors"]
definition: We computed the proportion of new members on a board of directors as a result of turnover from one year to the next. The turnover measure may in part reflect changes due to the expiration of terms of service.

name: Outside board representation
authors_terms: ["increase in outsiders", "proportion of outside board members", "outsider representation", "change in the proportion of inside members"]
definition: Of particular importance are changes in board composition and structure that alter the mix of inside and outside board members. Outside board members are more likely than insiders to act in a manner representative of stockholder interests.

name: CEO succession
definition: CEO successions were coded for each year in the study. Because we lacked data on the origins of new CEOs, we were not able to distinguish between internal and external succession.

name: Market competition
authors_terms: ["degree of competition in its market environment", "market competition", "change in hospital bed capacity"]
definition: In general, excess capacity in a market increases competition (Harrigan, 1983). Growth in bed capacity puts pressure on hospitals to use facilities and services efficiently.

name: Medicare Prospective Payment System implementation
definition: the implementation of the Medicare Prospective Payment System (PPS) in 1983, a change in legislation that established ceiling rates on specific medical procedures, thus shifting the burden of cost control to hospitals.

name: Hospital occupancy
authors_terms: ["declines in hospital occupancy", "changes in hospital occupancy", "change in occupancy"]
definition: We expected changes in competition, governmental funding of health care, and variations in hospital performance associated with changes in hospital occupancy to exert direct effects on strategic change in hospitals.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "asset specificity of supplementary services", "specific assets"]
definition: Asset specificity refers to investments made in specific (nonmarketable) resources. Consistent with Erramilli and Rao's suggestion, this study defined idiosyncratic services as those that require a high level of professional skills, major investments and training, and specialized know-how.

name: Capital intensity
definition: Capital intensity is the level of investments on fixed assets to generate sales revenue (Erramilli and Rao, 1993; Kim and Lyn, 1987). The level of capital intensity can range from extremely low to extremely high in different service industries.

name: Inseparability
definition: Inseparability 'forces the buyer into intimate contact with the production process' (Carman and Langeard, 1980: 8) and requires close buyer-seller interactions. It was defined as the degree of which production and consumption of core (supplementary) services would occur simultaneously.

name: Uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty was a construct proposed by Williamson (1979) in TCA. The demand uncertainty of core (supplementary) services was assessed using a 5-point scale.

name: Transaction frequency
definition: Transaction frequency relates to the frequency with which transactions involved in sourcing the same service recur. Transaction frequency of core (supplementary) services was defined as the frequency with which transactions involved in sourcing the same core (supplementary) services recurred (Williamson, 1985).

name: Internal global sourcing of supplementary services
authors_terms: ["internal global sourcing of supplementary services", "extent of global sourcing of supplementary services", "internal sourcing of supplementary services"]
definition: The extent of global sourcing of supplementary services was measured as a percentage of total value of supplementary services that were procured inside the corporate system on a global basis (both from domestic and foreign sources). As the focus is on internal sourcing, the term 'internal' is dropped to reduce repetition.

name: Internal domestic sourcing of supplementary services
authors_terms: ["internal domestic sourcing of supplementary services", "extent of domestic sourcing of supplementary services"]
definition: The extent of internal domestic sourcing of supplementary services was measured as a percentage of total value of supplementary services that were procured from domestic suppliers inside the corporate system.

name: Internal global sourcing of core services
authors_terms: ["extent of global sourcing of core services", "internal global sourcing of core services"]
definition: The extent of global sourcing of core services was measured as a percentage of total value of core services that were procured inside the corporate system on a global basis (both from domestic and foreign sources).

name: Internal domestic sourcing of core services
authors_terms: ["extent of domestic sourcing of core services", "internal domestic sourcing of core services"]
definition: The extent of internal domestic sourcing of core services was measured as a percentage of total value of core services that were procured from domestic suppliers inside the corporate system.

name: Foreign sourcing of supplementary services
definition: 'Foreign sourcing' means procuring from overseas suppliers (e.g., a U.S.-based service firm procures services from a supplier in Ireland). Due to the unique characteristics of services, the extent of foreign sourcing of supplementary services is related to a service's market performance.

name: Market performance
definition: Roth and Morrison (1990) suggested that a firm may pursue both the strategic and financial dimensions of market performance as the objectives of its business operation. Based on their recommendation, in this study, market performance consisted of two composite measures: strategic market performance and financial market performance.

name: Geographic dispersion
authors_terms: ["geographic dispersion", "degree of geographic dispersion", "geographically dispersed team"]
definition: A geographically dispersed team is defined as a group of people 'with a common purpose who carry out interdependent tasks across locations and time' (Cramton 2001, p. 346). Conceptually speaking, geographic dispersion is perceived to be on a 'continuum,' as a team that spans multiple countries is more dispersed than one whose participants are located in the same country, region, or city (Gibson and Gibbs 2006, p. 456).

name: Innovative novelty
definition: Novelty refers to an original recombination of knowledge components within an industry, a process of bringing together previously unconnected elements or of 'developing novel ways of combining elements previously associated' (Nahapiet and Ghoshal 1998, p. 248). Novelty refers to a recombination of knowledge components that is original in a given industry, meaning it has not been done in the industry before (Ahuja and Katila 2001).

name: Relational strength
definition: Relational strength, which refers to the frequency of prior collaboration among members, facilitates the development of familiarity (Espinosa et al. 2007), trust (Uzzi and Lancaster 2003), shared understanding (Cramton 2001), and social support for initiative taking (Amabile 1988, Edmondson 1999). Relational strength, as reflected by the frequency and intensity of prior knowledge-related collaboration among scientists, complements the continual access of geographically dispersed team members to diverse knowledge and perspectives.

name: Status asymmetry
authors_terms: ["status asymmetry", "status asymmetries", "social hierarchy among team members"]
definition: Status asymmetries, or social hierarchy among team members, encompass the extent to which social influence is concentrated in a small number of members or distributed more evenly among team members (Kehoe and Tzabbar 2014, Tzabbar 2009).

name: Technical specialized knowledge
authors_terms: ["technical specialized knowledge", "use of technical specialized knowledge in the firm", "knowledge conditions of firms", "specialized knowledge"]
definition: We define the technical specialized knowledge of an individual as scarce technical skills and accumulated contextual knowledge that are derived from education and life experiences such as work, intellectual endeavors, and the pursuit of specific business opportunities.

name: Founder selling of secondary shares
authors_terms: ["founder selling", "founders selling secondary shares at IPO", "one or more founders will be observed selling secondary shares at IPO"]
definition: Whereas capital paid for primary shares is paid directly to the company for corporate uses, capital paid for secondary shares flows directly to the private owners who are selling the secondary shares, thereby permitting them to divest all or part of their holdings in the venture.

name: VC selling of secondary shares
authors_terms: ["VC selling", "venture capitalist selling", "VCs selling secondary shares at IPO"]
definition: Whereas capital paid for primary shares is paid directly to the company for corporate uses, capital paid for secondary shares flows directly to the private owners who are selling the secondary shares, thereby permitting them to divest all or part of their holdings in the venture.

name: Secondary shares in the IPO
authors_terms: ["secondary shares", "any secondary shares", "use of secondary shares in IPOs"]
definition: The IPO provides founders and VCs with an opportunity to diversify their holdings by creating a public market for ownership stakes in the venture, or by enabling them to sell equity to new investors during the IPO through secondary shares.

name: Market acceptance of outputs
authors_terms: ["sales", "greater market acceptance of their outputs", "sales revenues"]
definition: One key objective characteristic of the market acceptance of the products of a new venture is reliable information that the primary product or service is being successfully sold. As firms demonstrate greater market acceptance of their goods and services, public investors are likely to be able to more accurately develop an assessment of firm value independent of the signals provided by private owners.

name: Inventor patenting experience
definition: Through repeated interactions, inventors gain experience with the patenting process. Prolific inventors garner extensive experience with the patenting process by developing patentable inventions on a regular basis.

name: Performance below aspirations
authors_terms: ["performance below aspirations", "firm performance below aspirations", "performance below aspirational levels"]
definition: The performance aspirations of profit-seeking firms are generally established through a comparison with competitors in the same industry. Performing below aspirations is typically viewed by individuals as a loss situation.

name: Failure to disclose known relevant prior art
authors_terms: ["failure to disclose known relevant prior art", "failure to disclose relevant prior art known to them", "failure of inventors to disclose relevant prior art", "nondisclosure of known relevant prior art"]
definition: By not disclosing known relevant prior art, inventors and their firms may be granted patents and claims they would not have otherwise been awarded. Applicants are legally bound to disclose prior art known to them which is relevant to the invention they are seeking to protect.

name: Outsourced legal counsel
definition: While some patent applications are represented by in-house legal counsel, others are done so through outside legal counsel. When inventors and legal counsel reside within the same organization, their levels of interaction are greater than if they were employed by separate organizations linked by an outsourcing agreement.

name: Supplier sanction adoption
authors_terms: ["supplier sanctions", "supplier-sanction practice", "adoption of supplier sanctions", "practice adoption"]
definition: The sanctions consisted of terminating apparel-licensing contracts with Russell until the violations were resolved. Our dependent variable is the date on which each college or university in our sample applied sanctions on Russell by terminating and agreeing not to renew its licensing contract without the firm ceding to the specified activist demands.

name: Independent adoptions
authors_terms: ["independent adoptions", "independent sanction adoptions", "adoptions that were not associated with any visible signs of activism"]
definition: We constructed this variable to indicate the schools that did not experience any activist tactics but still adopted the practice. The absence of activism was confirmed from interviews with activists and administrators.

name: Disruption-linked adoptions
authors_terms: ["disruption-linked adoptions", "adoptions coupled with disruption-based tactics", "adoptions under duress"]
definition: This time-varying variable reflects the count of prior adoptions within a school's network that were coupled with disruption-based tactics (included in the propensity vector).

name: Evidence-linked adoptions
authors_terms: ["evidence-linked adoptions", "adoptions coupled with evidence-based tactics", "adoptions linked to evidence-based tactics"]
definition: This time-varying variable reflects the count of prior adoptions within a school's network that were coupled with evidence-based tactics (included in the propensity vector).

name: Consonant commitment
authors_terms: ["consonant commitment", "consonant commitments", "prior commitments that are consonant with the controversial practice"]
definition: Consonant commitments may take the form of earlier official proclamations regarding the organization's values, goals, or interests, which now implicate the organization's behavior in relation to the controversial practice. Our measure of consonant commitment is based on organizational participation in a private regulatory initiative involving the Fair Labor Association (FLA) Code of Conduct at the time of the Russell campaign.

name: Proximal disruption
authors_terms: ["proximal disruption", "proximal disruptions", "disruptive protests in an organization's proximal environment"]
definition: The second source of issue salience involves disruptive protests that occur in an organization's proximal environment. Our measure of proximal disruption in the network reflects the time-varying count of peers within the focal school's network that had experienced disruptive tactics, irrespective of those peer schools' response to the practice.

name: Activist group presence
definition: We coded whether each school had a USAS chapter at the start of the study time window. These data were obtained from a USAS website and triangulated with information from media reports and key informants associated with the movement.

name: Disruption-based tactics
definition: We categorized tactics as disruption-based if they were intended to influence organizational decision makers by disrupting organizational routines; examples include holding large gatherings outside the university president's office, occupying and shutting down administrative buildings, and holding picketing demonstrations at retail apparel stores on or near campus.

name: Evidence-based tactics
definition: A common form of non-disruptive tactic is an evidence-based tactic: the provision of information and/or material evidence to enhance the credibility of activists and the practices they seek to bring about. We considered these tactics to be evidence-based because activists clearly intended them to influence organizational decision makers by strengthening the evidentiary basis for the ongoing claim of harm caused by the existing organizational procurement policies.

name: Equity collaboration
authors_terms: ["equity collaborations", "equity-based collaborations", "equity linkages", "minority investment or joint venture", "transitional governance"]
definition: The equity linkages include both classic joint ventures, where two or more parties create a separate, jointly owned entity; and direct minority investments, where one party takes an equity position of less than 50 percent of its partner. Equity collaborations are particularly useful when confronted by technological uncertainty because they provide an option to defer internal development or acquisition of a target firm or venture.

name: Partner dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["dissimilar partners", "dissimilarity between partners", "information asymmetry between partners", "partners whose primary business operations are dissimilar"]
definition: There are basically two types of firms participating in commercial biotechnology: established firms having a core business outside of biotechnology (generally from chemical, pharmaceutical, and agricultural industries), and firms dedicated to biotechnology. Since biotechnology and established firms have different areas of expertise, there is an increased likelihood of information asymmetry, and the potential for opportunistic behavior between such firms is greater than when transactions involve firms of like kind.

name: Technology value of technical subfield
authors_terms: ["technology value", "growth potential of technical subfield", "subfields with greater value"]
definition: Technical subfields may vary in rates of growth and their ability to provide platforms on future growth opportunities. We broadly define this as the subfield's technology value.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Technological uncertainty is meant to capture the exogenous uncertainty specific to the technical subfield; it is defined as being exogenous to the firm or transaction, and present in industries undergoing technological change.

name: Number of rivals
authors_terms: ["number of rivals", "number of rival firms", "fewer rivals in a technological domain"]
definition: To represent the number of rival firms, we use the number of biotechnology firms with R&D programs in subfield m at time t.

name: Asset specificity
definition: R&D expense has been widely used to proxy the degree of proprietary content and to represent the level of human and dedicated capital specific to a transaction. Given higher levels of asset specificity greater degrees of integration will be favored.

name: Resource similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity between product categories", "similarity of resources", "target category similarity", "previous exit-target category similarity", "previous entry-target category similarity"]
definition: The more attributes two product categories share, the more similar those categories' technological characteristics are and the easier resources can be redeployed between them. The measure captures the similarity of technological resources required by the businesses rather than only the similarity of businesses.

name: Entry
definition: Entering a new business means releasing a first product family in a product category in which the firm did not previously participate; entry requires a big commitment of resources and is less flexible and less reversible than deepening.

name: Deepening
authors_terms: ["deepening", "temporary resource redeployment into an incumbent business"]
definition: Deepening captures temporary resource redeployment into an incumbent business, measured as the introduction of new product families in a business in which the firm is already active.

name: Retrenchment
authors_terms: ["retrenchment", "temporary resource redeployment out of an incumbent business"]
definition: Retrenchment captures temporary resource redeployment out of an incumbent business without incurring exit; resources can be redeployed back to the originator later.

name: Exit
definition: Exit is a complete withdrawal: the firm stops producing new product families in a product category from time t until the end of the observation time period.

name: Resource characteristics
definition: Anand et al. (2016) classify four characteristics of resources that condition possible resource redeployment: (1) fungibility, (2) scale-free nature, (3) decomposability, and (4) tradability. Resources common to both fabless and IDM firms are in general more fungible, scalable, and decomposable than resources specific to IDMs.

name: Adoption of a new market position
authors_terms: ["mimetic adoption of market positions", "adoption of a new format", "market position adoption", "entry into a new market position"]
definition: This paper argues that organizations use other organizations as reference groups when abandoning their market position, so an organization abandoning its market position is likely to adopt an existing rather than create a new position. Mimetic adoption of new market positions is an important type of strategic change under high uncertainty because it allows firms to explore new niches in the market with less risk and innovation effort than developing new market positions on their own.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: It seems likely that market positions also are more easily observable for organizations nearby, leading to contagion within a region. Organizational decision-makers tend to be more aware of the strategies of nearby competitors because personal observation and communication are stronger mediators of information over small distances.

name: Market size similarity
authors_terms: ["market size", "similarity of market size", "difference in market size"]
definition: The relevance of a particular adoption to the decision faced by a particular manager then depends on the similarity of market size. Managers economize on the information they collect and use, and are likely to be strongly influenced by easily judged relevance criteria, hence market size is used as a way to organize information about the industry.

name: Common corporate ownership
