definition: Consensus in evaluation criteria for a nascent technology is conceptualized as the extent to which technology experts - academic and industry scientists with domain-specific knowledge of the technology - use similar criteria to compare different technology solutions in the field.

name: Investment in a firm
authors_terms: ["investment", "investment intention", "investment amount", "willingness to invest in firms"]
definition: Investment refers to investors' willingness to provide funds to a firm in a nascent technology field; the authors argue that both perceptions of a firm's technological competence and others' positive evaluations of the firm should encourage individuals to invest in the firm.

name: Perceived technological competence
authors_terms: ["perceived technological competence", "perceived technology competence", "perceptions of a firm's technological competence", "propriety perceptions", "propriety beliefs"]
definition: Investors' perception of the technological competence of a firm in a nascent sector - that the firm's technological solutions are more capable and reliable. The authors note that this is referred to as propriety perceptions in Bitektine and Haack (2015) and Haack et al. (2020).

name: Prediction of others' positive evaluation
authors_terms: ["prediction of others' positive evaluation", "predictions of others' positive evaluations of the firm", "consensus perceptions", "consensus beliefs"]
definition: Investors' confidence that their peers will also hold a positive view of the focal firm, referred to as consensus perceptions in Haack et al. (2020).

name: Executive narcissism
definition: From a cognitive perspective, narcissists define themselves in a grandiose way; they have inflated self-views and think they are special and unique, and they tend to overestimate their intelligence, competence, and achievements.

name: Inter-unit knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["inter-unit knowledge transfer", "knowledge transfer to the focal unit from other units", "receptivity to external knowledge", "inter-organizational knowledge transfer"]
definition: Inter-unit knowledge transfer - that is, knowledge transfer among different business units or subsidiaries inside a multi-unit firm.

name: Environmental complexity
definition: Environmental complexity describes the heterogeneity of environmental factors with which organizations have to contend.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Environmental dynamism indicates the rate of unpredictable change and the degree of instability in an organization's external environment, which can pose significant challenges to corporate executives.

name: Perceived inter-unit competition
authors_terms: ["perceived inter-unit competition", "perceived competition with other units", "inter-unit competition"]
definition: Unit heads' perceptions of competition with other units in the corporation, which the authors describe as competing for status, performance evaluation, and resources in the corporation.

name: Physician supply
authors_terms: ["change in the number of physicians per capita in a county", "supply of physicians", "availability of physicians"]
definition: When the supply of physicians in a local environment is decreasing per capita, it is likely that hospitals will view attracting physicians as an important activity and that physicians will have more influence and power than they might otherwise. Change in the supply of physicians referring patients is an important and potentially limiting contingency for a hospital.

name: Hospital bed supply
authors_terms: ["change in the number of beds per capita in a county", "supply of hospital beds per capita", "beds per capita"]
definition: The supply of available hospital beds relative to the size of the population served offers some indication of the level of competition among hospitals for patients. An important concern for many hospitals in recent years has been an oversupply of hospital beds, which has often resulted in greatly increased competition among hospitals for patients.

name: HMO prevalence
authors_terms: ["change in the number of health maintenance organizations per capita in a county", "number of HMOs per capita"]
definition: The recent proliferation of HMOs, which provide comprehensive health care that is often less expensive to patients and employers than that provided by hospitals, also represents an important competitive threat to the viability of traditional hospitals.

name: Change in hospital payment
authors_terms: ["change in hospital payment", "Prospective Payment System (PPS)", "introduction of the Prospective Payment System"]
definition: A very important change in the health care environment that occurred during the period of this study was the implementation of the Prospective Payment System (PPS) within Medicare. Uniform and limited rates for various medical services and procedures, identified as diagnosis-related groups, were established, and hospitals became more responsible for cost control.

name: Physician board representation
authors_terms: ["proportions of physicians on their boards", "proportion of board members that are physicians", "representation of physicians on hospital boards"]
definition: Change in the composition of the hospitals' boards of directors was examined in terms of changes in the representation of three groups predicted to provide links to different environmental segments: physicians, hospital executives, and business executives.

name: Business executive board representation
authors_terms: ["proportions of business executives on their boards", "business executives"]
definition: Business professionals and individuals from financial or banking institutions may be able to offer help in both managing cost-cutting programs and providing additional sources of capital.

name: Hospital executive board representation
authors_terms: ["proportions of hospital executives on their boards", "hospital executives"]
definition: As the administrative staffs of hospitals have gained importance for helping hospitals cope with cost control pressures, they gained power.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Measuring hospital performance is potentially problematic given the differences in orientation toward profits; two measures were used to assess performance, profitability and level of occupancy. Zucker (1987) noted that occupancy rate is the most common measure of performance in hospital research.

name: Environmental change
authors_terms: ["environmental change", "changes in their environments", "environmental contingencies", "changing environmental conditions"]
definition: The conceptual literature on organizational change and adaptation has generally assumed that environmental change leads to organizational change, and this study attempted to clarify the role that performance plays in moderating the relationship between environmental change and organizational change.

name: Organizational change
authors_terms: ["organizational change", "modifying organizational characteristics", "changes in board composition", "changes in the composition of boards of directors"]
definition: Change in the composition of boards of directors was examined as a dependent variable reflecting organizational attempts to deal with changing external contingencies, examined as an ongoing process of adjustment to changing environmental demands rather than as a static relationship between organization and environment.

name: Provision of advice and information to the CEO
authors_terms: ["provision of advice and information", "providing advice and information to management", "advice and information giving", "advice giving", "providing input or advice on strategic issues"]
definition: Outside directors contribute to effective corporate governance by providing advice and information to management on strategic issues, for instance by serving as a kind of consultant or sounding board to management during the strategic decision making process and by furnishing information about the plans and practices of other firms.

name: Monitoring and control behavior
authors_terms: ["monitoring and control behavior", "decision control", "monitoring and control of management decision making"]
definition: Outside directors engage in decision control on behalf of shareholders when they monitor and regulate management decision making and evaluate management performance, which includes soliciting information about the progress of executives in implementing corporate strategies and ratifying, blocking, or forcing changes in management initiatives.

name: Ingratiation
definition: Ingratiation can be conceived of as a set of interpersonal influence tactics that function to 'enhance one's interpersonal attractiveness' and ultimately 'gain favor' with another individual, and comprises three specific behaviors: flattery or other-enhancing communications; acts of opinion conformity; and favor rendering.

name: Demographic minority status
definition: Status of a director as a member of a demographic minority, that is, as an ethnic minority or a woman; the authors note that ethnic minorities and women constitute a small portion of all corporate directors and an even smaller portion of CEO or nominating committee positions.

name: Additional board appointments
authors_terms: ["board appointment", "additional board appointments", "further board appointments", "board seats"]
definition: Whether a focal director receives an appointment as an outside director of the board of a particular firm where another director served on the nominating committee or as CEO; directors acquire such appointments through referrals from fellow outside directors who serve in key roles on other boards.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth", "growth rate", "employee growth", "relative growth rate in employees"]
definition: In this study, the authors conceptualize growth as a strategic choice that entrepreneurs make to accomplish other performance goals, such as profitability and survival. They measure the growth of a firm as the relative growth rate in employees from year t-1 to year t-2.

name: Firm failure
definition: The authors used firm survival/failure, the most universal measure of performance, which furthermore is a prerequisite for most other performance measures. Failure was coded as 1 if the firm ceased to exist in a given year and as 0 otherwise; technically, failure was identified when a firm stopped having employees or stopped filing a tax return.

name: Agglomeration
definition: The phenomenon of geographic agglomeration is defined here as concentration of economic activity within an industry in geographic space. Agglomeration economies result from the combination of several micromechanisms, classified into supply-side and demand-side benefits.

name: Local market concentration
authors_terms: ["local market concentration", "local level of market concentration", "local structure of competition", "market concentration"]
definition: As an indicator of the competitive structure of local markets, the authors used the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index calculated at the local level. Low HHI levels indicate that the local market is composed of a large number of small competitors, whereas high HHI levels (concentrated markets) indicate that the local market consists of fewer, relatively large firms.

name: Passive ownership
definition: Franchised outlets owned by passive investors who hire managers to operate the outlet, so that the outlets are not run by owner-operators and the beneficial effects of residual claimancy are lost.

name: Franchisee cash investment
definition: The size of the franchisee's cash investment in a franchised outlet, which serves as a quality signal to reduce the franchisee adverse selection problem.

name: Franchisee experience requirement
authors_terms: ["franchisee experience", "requiring franchisees to have prior experience"]
definition: A requirement that franchisees have prior experience, used as a quality signal since potential franchisees with experience are more likely to have knowledge of local markets and management skills.

name: Royalty rate
definition: The ongoing royalty the franchisor receives, which gives the franchisor an incentive not to default on his monitoring obligations and is seen by potential franchisees as a measure of the franchisor's incentive to develop and uphold system assets.

name: Geographic concentration
definition: The geographic concentration of the franchise system; monitoring costs increase with the geographic distance between the principal and the agent, so the more geographically concentrated its franchise system, the more the firm is able to economize on agency costs.

name: Franchise concept complexity
authors_terms: ["complexity", "the complexity of the task to be transferred to the agent"]
definition: The complexity of the task to be transferred to the agent, which increases monitoring costs and makes it more difficult and costly for the principal to specify the agent's required behavior under all contingencies.

name: Master franchising
definition: Master franchise agreements grant the rights of development to an individual whose purpose is to recruit, train, and oversee the operations of individual franchisees in the area.

name: Contract length
authors_terms: ["length of contract", "length of the agreement", "term of the agreement"]
definition: The term of the agreement between the franchisor and the franchisee; increasing the term reduces the incentive for the agent to engage in misdirected effort.

name: Total investment
authors_terms: ["total investment", "franchisee's initial investment in franchisor specific assets"]
definition: The amount franchisees must invest to create a franchise outlet, including franchisor-specific investments in materials, signs, or building designs, which are worth more in the system than outside and therefore generate quasi-rents.

name: Franchise system failure
authors_terms: ["failure", "exit from franchising", "cessation of franchising", "new franchisor failure"]
definition: Exit from franchising is the dependent variable; cessation of franchising and firm failure are statistically indistinguishable in this sample.

name: Star employee absence
authors_terms: ["a star's temporary absence", "absence of a star", "absence phase"]
definition: A star's absence decreases organizational performance by removing her individual contributions and unique skills, and undermining routines built around those skills.

name: Organizational performance
definition: For our main analyses on the effects of a star's absence and return on team performance (H1 and H2), and for the absence duration effect (H3), the dependent variable is a win-loss dummy, W. This measure has strong linkages to a team's goal of winning the league title and a player's goal of contributing to winning.

name: Star absence duration
definition: A short absence provides insufficient time to learn, while a long absence might make absence-phase routines less flexible and thereby harder to re-incorporate the star.

name: Organizational routines
definition: Our theory builds on the perspective that organizational learning is accomplished through changes in routines, conceived as patterns of interactions among individuals.

name: Star employee
definition: The emphasis on individual human capital is particularly salient in work that examines star performers, who are considered to make disproportionate individual contributions to their organizations.

name: Structural recombination
definition: We refer to these changes as structural recombinations, meaning changes in business units as their resources and market activities are reorganized by merging units together, generally through the absorption of one unit into another unit or the formation of a new business unit by combining existing units.

name: Firm innovation
definition: Innovation, or the creation of new knowledge, is central to the role of organizations; the authors' dependent variable for all hypotheses is firm innovation in a period, measured through the quality of the firm's patented innovation.

name: Knowledge coherence
authors_terms: ["knowledge coherence", "KnowledgeCoherence", "relatedness between a firm's patents", "knowledge relatedness"]
definition: The extent of relatedness between a firm's existing knowledge resources, which the authors argue determines the potential for intraorganizational knowledge recombination following structural recombination. In effect, the knowledge coherence measure calculates the average relatedness of each patent of the firm to all of the firm's other patents, where relatedness is based on the extent to which patents in the two classes cite each other in the population of all patents.

name: Path dependence
definition: Firms may be subject to path dependence; i.e., they may fail to respond adequately to changing conditions on account of established routines, processes, and mental models. Such path dependence may constrain innovation potential, limiting the extent to which the firm is able to absorb new or external knowledge and limiting the scope of its search for new innovations.

name: Knowledge quality
authors_terms: ["knowledge quality", "KnowledgeQuality", "quality of the firm's existing knowledge resources", "high-quality knowledge resources"]
definition: The quality of the firm's existing knowledge resources, measured as the average number of citations a firm's patents have received per patent relative to other patents in the same year and patent class; values greater than 1 imply that the firm's patents are, on average, of higher quality than those of other firms, whereas a value less than 1 implies that they are of lower quality.

name: Automatic information processing
definition: Automatic processing was described as unintentional, involuntary, effortless, autonomous, and occurring outside of awareness. Processing that is relatively effortless, comparatively fast, and largely autonomous of conscious awareness is near the automatic pole.

name: Controlled information processing
definition: Controlled processing was described as flexible, within an individual's intentional control, effortful, active, constrained by short-term attentional resources and motivated or strategic. Comparatively effortful, extended, and intentional processing is near the controlled pole.

name: Environmental turbulence
authors_terms: ["environmental turbulence", "environmental dynamism", "rate and amount of environmental change"]
definition: One dimension that captures a potentially important effect on mental models is the rate and amount of environmental change, or environmental turbulence.

name: Construct diversity
authors_terms: ["greater diversity in the constructs managers contemplate", "construct diversity", "heterogeneity of constructs"]
definition: Across the collectivity of managers, cognitive maps became less consensual as the environment became more turbulent. This divergence was manifested through the inclusion of a progressively more extensive range of constructs in each successive study.

name: Number of constructs per manager
authors_terms: ["total number of constructs", "number of constructs per individual", "mean number of dimensions per informant", "number of dimensions"]
definition: The total number of constructs assessed by any one manager. Human information processing is easily overloaded and only a finite number of constructs can be included in a mental model.

name: Cognitive control capabilities
definition: The supervisory cognitive mechanisms through which individuals monitor and control their own attention and cognitive processes; they are the mindful abilities behind decision making and are used for purposefully paying attention, planning, organizing, forecasting, strategizing, abstracting, drawing analogies, and trying to overcome routinized behaviors.

name: Routinization propensity
definition: 'The individual tendency to develop and enact a behavioral repertoire that provides standard solutions (routines) for problems involving choice'; it encompasses the repetition and execution of standard patterns of behavior while excluding coordinated and interdependent actions.

name: Decision-making performance
definition: The performance achieved in the strategic decision-making task, measured as cumulative profit over eight simulated years; to achieve high performance the participant needs to balance financial goals against the need to innovate, capitalize on new product/market opportunities, and guard against disruptive technologies.

name: Spillover knowledge pool
authors_terms: ["spillover knowledge pool", "firm-specific pool of related external knowledge"]
definition: We refer to this firm-specific pool of related external knowledge as the originating firm's spillover knowledge pool. An originator's spillover knowledge pool represents all external knowledge components that have been linked directly to its knowledge by recipient firms through spillover.

name: Spillover knowledge pool size
authors_terms: ["pool size", "size of a firm's spillover knowledge pool"]
definition: As the spillover knowledge pool of an originating firm grows larger in terms of knowledge components, the number of future recombinatorial opportunities associated with the firm's knowledge base increases. Larger spillover knowledge pools provide greater potential for an originating firm to learn vicariously from the recombinatorial activity of other firms.

name: Spillover knowledge pool similarity
definition: Similarity refers to the extent to which the knowledge in a firm's spillover knowledge pool is located in the domains in which the originating firm has expertise. The similarity of the knowledge in the spillover knowledge pool to the originating firm's existing knowledge influences the extent to which the vicarious learning opportunities associated with the knowledge pool are valuable and accessible to the originator.

name: Knowledge integration
authors_terms: ["knowledge integration", "the extent to which the firm's subsequent innovations build on knowledge from its spillover knowledge pool"]
definition: The extent to which the innovative output of an originating firm built on the knowledge from its spillover knowledge pool. The extent to which a firm uses elements of knowledge (e.g., patents) contained in its spillover knowledge pool reflects that it is searching and exploiting this knowledge pool.

name: Innovative output
definition: Learning from the spillover knowledge pool is also evident in a firm's rate of innovation. An originating firm expands and refines its search routines by learning from its spillover knowledge pool, and larger pools lead to higher levels of innovative output, all else being equal.

name: Industry profitability
definition: The influence of industry membership is represented by average industry return on assets; the measure of industry profitability is a weighted average of the profitability of all of the industries in which the sample firms participated.

name: Extent of diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm operates across industries, assessed by an entropy measure. This continuous measure uses Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes to identify and evaluate the extent of diversification.

name: R&D expenditures
definition: Spending directed at the development of new product and process technologies; the authors treat R&D spending and capital investment as the factors underscored by studies of business effectiveness.

name: Capital investment
definition: Capital investments are required so that firms can exploit new technologies and bring promising product innovations to market or implement cost-reducing production processes.

name: Business-unit effectiveness
definition: The performance of a firm's business units relative to their rivals, such that the businesses achieve "the greatest output for the least input"; it is assessed by a weighted average of the operating margins of each firm's business units adjusted for industry membership.

name: Equity-based governance structure
authors_terms: ["equity-based governance", "equity-based governance structure", "equity-based structures", "equity governance structure"]
definition: An equity-based governance structure is a well-known mechanism to encourage knowledge exchange and reduce partners' knowledge leakage concerns in R&D alliances.

name: Multilateral alliance
definition: A multilateral alliance is a single cooperative arrangement involving three or more partner firms; the authors follow the literature and define the multilateral alliance as a single cooperative arrangement involving at least three firms.

name: Net-based trilateral alliance
authors_terms: ["net-based trilateral R&D alliance", "net-based exchange relationship", "net-based trilateral alliance", "net-based", "net"]
definition: A net-based exchange relationship refers to the setting in which individual parties give to the group as a whole and derive benefits directly from the group. Therefore, a net-based trilateral R&D alliance involves partner firms that pool their resources allocated to R&D activities and benefit from the innovations derived from the collective contributions of all partner firms.

name: Alliance scope
definition: The scope of R&D alliances can vary from exclusive R&D activities to comprehensive value creation efforts that begin with R&D activities and end with customer sales and support.

name: Alliance duration
definition: Given the complexities of alliance performance, the authors focus on alliance duration to proxy alliance performance, and alliance duration/termination has often been used to proxy alliance performance in strategic management research.

name: Governance alignment
definition: Alignment takes the value of 1 if the governance structure is as predicted and 0 if the governance structure diverges from the predicted.

name: Entrepreneurial role
authors_terms: ["role (lead entrepreneur versus potential cofounder)", "lead entrepreneurs", "potential cofounders", "role"]
definition: Lead entrepreneurs are individuals who have a venture idea and then form a team; potential cofounders are individuals who are evaluating whether to join a lead entrepreneur.

name: Construal level
authors_terms: ["construal level", "lower construal level", "higher construal level", "low-level construal"]
definition: Individuals' mental representations of a target (people, objects, events) can be characterized on a continuum of concreteness to abstractness; objects that are closer and more proximal elicit a lower construal level, whereas more psychologically distant objects are often seen in broader and more abstract ways.

name: Utilitarian motives
definition: Utilitarian motives are the extent to which individuals are driven by the practical benefits associated with a decision.

name: Resource seeking
authors_terms: ["resource seeking strategy", "resource seeking", "resource seeking behavior", "preference for resources"]
definition: In the resource seeking strategy, team members select each other using pragmatic, instrumental, and functional considerations, with a particular focus on the resources needed for the venture to thrive.

name: Interpersonal attraction
definition: The interpersonal attraction strategy suggests that team members select each other with social fit serving as the utmost consideration.

name: Hybrid tie formation
definition: A hybrid strategy is one in which the ties formed between the lead entrepreneur and potential cofounders are both rich in resources as well as interpersonal attraction.

name: Interpersonal communication
authors_terms: ["interpersonally oriented communication topics", "lead entrepreneur interpersonal communication", "interpersonal content", "interpersonal communication"]
definition: The extent to which lead entrepreneurs discussed nonventure related topics, such as hobbies, shared group memberships, personal background, and common friends.

name: Resource-oriented communication
definition: The extent to which lead entrepreneurs discussed venture-related topics, such as aspects of the venture and its development, as well as the professional experience or educational qualifications of either the lead entrepreneur or potential cofounder.

name: Family ownership
definition: Family-controlled firms, in which the goals and risk-taking appetite of controlling families are different from minority shareholders. The non-economic values that controlling families aim to protect and nurture comprise the family's emotional bond and its generational continuity, secrecy from scrutiny, and exceptional managerial discretion and influence over the business.

name: Patent licensing
definition: Commercial exploitation of a patent through licensing or selling it to another party, which subjects the licensor to dependence on the licensee for the financial success of the technology and limits the licensor's control over the trajectory of the technology. The variable takes value 1 if the patent was licensed or sold and 0 otherwise.

name: Internal patent commercialization
definition: Commercial exploitation of a patent within the firm, which grants the owner more control over the technological and financial returns of the innovation than licensing. The variable takes value 1 if the patent was internally commercialized and 0 otherwise.

name: Inclusionary hierarchy technological shift
authors_terms: ["technological shift in the inclusionary product hierarchy", "inclusionary hierarchy dominant design", "dominant design in the inclusionary product hierarchy"]
definition: A technological shift in the inclusionary (controlled) product hierarchy of a complex product. In automobile emissions control systems a dominant product-level design in the inclusionary product hierarchy emerged in 1981: an architecture described as a 'catalyst-based three-way catalytic converter' (TWC).

name: Digital control hierarchy technological shift
authors_terms: ["technological shift in the digital control hierarchy", "digital control hierarchy technology-shift period", "architectural innovation in the digital control hierarchy"]
definition: A technological shift in the digital control hierarchy of a complex product. In automobile emissions control systems this came in 1994 with the advanced onboard diagnostic electronic control module (OBD); the module's main functions were to monitor all emissions-related devices mounted on a vehicle.

name: Component innovation
definition: Component innovation involves changes to technologies within individual components or subsystems. The patents that capture the identifiable physical part of the product represent component innovation.

name: Architectural innovation
definition: Architectural innovation involves changes to schemes for organizing among individual components or subsystems in the context of broader systems. Patents that address the interfacial problems among components and how the components can be linked together into a whole system were coded as architectural innovation.

name: Firm type in the supply chain
definition: The firms in a supply chain of a given complex product are characterized in terms of two broad categories: OEMs and suppliers. The OEMs are large industrial firms that act as assemblers, integrators, and marketers that bridge customers and the supply chain, whereas suppliers provide components to OEMs.

name: Anticipation of social interaction
authors_terms: ["anticipation of social interaction with alter", "anticipating interacting with the alter"]
definition: The extent to which a focal director anticipates social interaction with an alter.

name: Relative social status in the corporate elite
authors_terms: ["alter's relative social status in the corporate elite", "relative social status", "status in the corporate elite"]
definition: An individual director (alter) has high or low status (i) relative to other directors at large (i.e., reflecting the director's position in the status hierarchy of the corporate elite), and (ii) relative to the focal director.

name: Demographic dissimilarity
definition: The extent to which a director is relatively dissimilar from the focal individual on salient demographic characteristics (functional background, age, gender, ethnicity, and primary industry of employment).

name: Reflection on shared characteristics
authors_terms: ["reflection on characteristics held in common with alter", "reflecting on personal and social characteristics held in common"]
definition: Reflecting on personal and social characteristics that one shares in common with another director.

name: Reflection on non-shared characteristics
authors_terms: ["reflection on characteristics not shared with alter", "thoughts about characteristics not shared"]
definition: Reflecting on characteristics of the alter that the focal director does not share.

name: Self-regulated cognition
definition: Self-regulated social cognition, or cognition about another person that regulates one's feelings or attitudes about him or her in preparation for social interaction.

name: Expressions of liking and admiration
authors_terms: ["expressions of liking and admiration", "expressions of liking for alter", "expressions of admiration for alter", "ingratiation", "ingratiatory behavior"]
definition: Interpersonal behaviors that serve to enhance one's interpersonal attractiveness to another person, including flattery, or expressions of admiration and respect more generally, as well as verbal and non-verbal expressions of liking.

name: Recommendation for a board appointment
authors_terms: ["recommendation for a board appointment", "recommendations for board appointments"]
definition: One way to favor a focal person is to recommend him or her for a board appointment at another firm, in particular by the director who serves on the nominating committee of that board.

name: Peer firm CEO charisma
authors_terms: ["CEO charisma", "charisma of peer firms' CEOs", "charismatic CEOs"]
definition: One of the two universally recognized prototypical leader categorizations: the characteristics and behaviors that comprise charismatic leadership are universally seen as contributing to outstanding leadership and are universally endorsed as positive, so focal firms view the strategic actions of charismatic peer CEOs as effective.

name: Peer firm CEO narcissism
authors_terms: ["CEO narcissism", "narcissism of peer firms' CEOs", "narcissistic CEOs"]
definition: A negative leader categorization: narcissism involves the leader characteristics and behaviors that have been found to be a prototype of ineffective leadership, so observers view strategic actions of peer firms led by narcissistic CEOs as ineffective.

name: Peer firms' recent strategic behaviors
authors_terms: ["peer firms' strategic behaviors", "recent strategic actions by peer firms", "peer firms' recent behaviors"]
definition: The recent strategic actions of firms in the same industry (peer firms), which serve as the behaviors that focal firms may imitate when decision makers face means-ends ambiguity. They are the average of the peer firms' actions in a given strategic domain over recent years, aggregated at the level of each focal-firm observation.

name: Interorganizational imitation
authors_terms: ["interorganizational imitation", "focal firms' behaviors", "focal firm's emulation", "focal firm's actions"]
definition: Imitation occurs as an information-based contagion that operates through social comparison processes as a means of reducing uncertainty; the focal firm's subsequent strategic behavior in a given domain is the outcome in which its imitation of its peer firms is observed.

name: Industry dynamism
definition: Dynamic industries are characterized by ambiguous, uncertain, and volatile conditions in which means-ends linkages are poorly understood, which increases the difficulty managers have in discerning what constitutes effective managerial action.

name: Focal firm prior strategic experience
authors_terms: ["focal firm prior strategic experience", "prior experience in a given strategic domain", "prior experiences with the strategic practice"]
definition: The focal firm's own prior experiences with the strategic practice in question, which reduce its decision makers' uncertainty about the practice and thus lessen the need for sensemaking based on peer firms' actions.

name: Ivy League selection
authors_terms: ["Ivy League school", "Ivy League education", "Ivy degree", "Ivy League human capital selection", "graduates of Ivy League schools"]
definition: A type of human capital that is relatively rare and highly selected: graduates of Ivy League schools with stringent admissions policies, schools that are among the most selective in the world. The binary variable reflects whether or not the CEO either possessed an Ivy League degree or had gained admission to an Ivy League school.

name: Firm market valuation
definition: Tobin's Q reflects the evaluation by the market of all of the information about a company available to investors and, as such, is a better measure of performance than profit-based indexes such as return on assets. It also reflects investors' evaluations of the prospects of the company.

name: Degree level
authors_terms: ["degree level", "Master and above", "Bachelor and below", "Ivy undergraduate as opposed to graduate degrees", "undergraduate versus graduate training"]
definition: Education varies in the types of students it selects, and hence their suitability to the task of outstanding general management. Undergraduate programs at Ivy schools select for general intelligence and past achievements, academic and nonacademic alike, while graduate programs base selection for admission more on general cognitive intelligence and competency within a specialized field of knowledge.

name: CEO age
authors_terms: ["executive age", "CEO age", "earlier in CEO careers", "younger CEOs"]
definition: Less-seasoned CEOs may have to rely more on their natural talent and education as they often lack the reputation, connections, and political clout accruing to older executives. The authors measured CEO age to capture where in the career the observation falls.

name: Firm size
definition: CEOs have more discretion to influence a company more quickly and more profoundly in smaller firms, where there are fewer administrative levels to remove them from direct command and less bureaucracy to slow them down. By contrast, larger firms have been shown to be more bureaucratic, rule bound, and thus more sluggish to adapt.

name: Graduation year
authors_terms: ["year of graduation", "era of graduation", "1960 year of graduation", "Ivy cohort"]
definition: Up until about 1960, Ivy League schools based admission in part on the social connections and wealth of the parents of their applicants. Beginning in the 1960s, however, admission criteria at the Ivy schools became more reliant upon applicants' intelligence and achievement.

name: Multipoint contact
definition: An analyst's multipoint contact captures the extent to which an analyst covering a stock jointly with other analysts also covers other stocks jointly with those analysts, and is specific to a particular analyst-stock pair. Higher values indicate a greater proportional stock coverage overlap between a focal analyst and his/her alters on a given stock (and thus a greater potential for mutual forbearance on the focal stock).

name: Analyst boldness
authors_terms: ["bold earnings estimates", "bold estimates", "analyst positive boldness", "analyst negative boldness", "boldness"]
definition: A bold estimate for a given stock is one that is beyond a band set by the mean and standard deviation of preceding estimates for that stock. Boldness is a qualitative distinction: estimates differ from the current mean, or consensus, estimate for a stock by more than 1.5 standard deviations; bold estimates are competitive actions that threaten rivals.

name: Accuracy of bold earnings estimates
authors_terms: ["accuracy of bold estimates", "accurate positive boldness", "accurate negative boldness", "accuracy"]
definition: Accurate positive boldness is defined for estimates that have positive boldness and are closer to actual earnings than the analyst consensus; accurate negative boldness is analogously defined for estimates that have negative boldness and are closer to actual earnings than the analyst consensus.

name: Analyst status
definition: Status is a signal that participants can use to reduce uncertainty about performance, since status is correlated with quality, and higher status gives greater credibility in the eyes of audiences. A primary determinant of analyst status is Institutional Investor's annual ranking, the All-American Research Team (the 'All-Stars'), and analysts listed there are considered to be of higher status than those who are not.

name: Competitive parity
definition: Competitive parity is a situation in which no actor possesses an overwhelming competitive advantage because all actors have equal access to resources that yield competitive advantage. Regulation Fair Disclosure, enacted in October 2000, prohibited companies from disclosing material information privately to preferred analysts and investors, thereby removing preferential access to idiosyncratic information as a source of competitive advantage.

name: Vague language
definition: Vagueness in language is defined as an effect caused by a speaker in which the information received lacks the expected precision. Semantic vagueness, or vagueness in expression, is the trait of giving a statement that lacks precision and specificity as well as expressing approximation rather than certainty and clarity.

name: Rhetoric-oriented human capital
authors_terms: ["rhetorical human capital", "rhetoric-oriented human capital", "rhetoric-oriented skills", "rhetorical founders"]
definition: Founders with unique skills in using language, which the authors call rhetorical human capital, are able to engage in vagueness in expression relatively more effectively. Individuals with education or professional experience relevant to the effective use of rhetoric are trained to understand appropriate word choice and sentence structure.

name: Investor interest
authors_terms: ["investor interest", "formal indication of interest from the judges"]
definition: The dependent variable is a binary variable that takes the value of zero if the firm does not receive a formal indication of interest from the judges and a value of one if it does. The binary measure captures the general construct of investor interest in response to the focal pitch, allowing a tight connection between the pitch and the outcome because investors decide whether to advance the start-up immediately following the pitch.

name: Transactional leadership
definition: A transactional leader is one who operates within an existing system or culture (as opposed to trying to change them) by: (1) attempting to satisfy the current needs of followers by focusing on exchanges and contingent reward behavior and (2) paying close attention to deviations, mistakes, or irregularities and taking action to make corrections.

name: Charismatic leadership
definition: We defined charisma as a relationship between an individual (leader) and one or more followers based on leader behaviors combined with favorable attributions on the part of followers. Key behaviors on the part of the leader include articulating a vision and sense of mission, showing determination, and communicating high performance expectations.

name: Perceived environmental uncertainty
definition: According to Milliken (1987), uncertainty can be defined in terms of an individual's perceived inability to understand the direction in which an environment might be changing, the potential impact of those changes on that individual's organization, and whether or not particular responses to the environment might be successful.

name: Organizational performance
definition: We measured organizational performance as net profit margin (NPM), computed as net income divided by net sales. The industry-adjusted measure of NPM was obtained by subtracting the average industry (two-digit Standard Industrial Classification [SIC] code) NPM from a firm's own net profit margin.

name: CEO initial contract duration
authors_terms: ["CEO initial contract duration", "Initial Duration", "initial fixed-term contract duration", "duration of a CEO's initial contract"]
definition: The duration in years of a new CEO's initial employment contract. The authors focus on new CEOs' initial contracts because these contracts create uncertainty with CEOs about the possibility of contract renewal, given the greater information asymmetry between these new CEOs and the board.

name: Number of corporate acquisitions
authors_terms: ["No. of Acquisitions", "number of corporate acquisitions", "corporate acquisitions"]
definition: The number of corporate acquisitions conducted during the initial contract period. Corporate acquisitions have the advantage of facilitating quick resource commitment, reconfiguration and organizational growth, and M&As facilitate quick resource acquisition as they enable firms to bundle resources, acquire knowledge, enter new markets, and grow quickly.

name: Acquisition target ownership status
authors_terms: ["private targets", "Private Target %", "private rather than public targets"]
definition: The acquisition of a public firm generally requires a long negotiation period and faces more bidder competition and a higher premium; therefore, such transactions are more complex than the acquisitions of private firms. Acquiring a private firm is more straightforward and faces less bidder competition.

name: Acquisition target divestiture status
authors_terms: ["divested business units", "Divested Target %", "divested rather than nondivested"]
definition: A divesting firm is more likely to sell a business unit when the marginal cost of owning and operating that business exceeds the marginal benefit. From the acquirer's perspective, acquiring a divested business unit is relatively straightforward because such units offer attractive, quick acquisition opportunities and are often easier and cheaper to negotiate.

name: Acquisition target business relatedness
definition: In an unrelated acquisition, the target operates in an industry other than that of the acquirer, and the acquirer and target usually have very different resources and capabilities, products, and markets. In a related acquisition, the acquirer and target are typically more similar in terms of their resources, technology, location, and capabilities.

name: Acquisition deal size
authors_terms: ["Deal Size", "M&A deal size", "Small vs. Large M&A Deals"]
definition: Larger deals may be more time-consuming and challenging to complete. Smaller deals typically require fewer resources, have shorter timelines, and involve less complexity and uncertainty, which can reduce the risk of failure.

name: Acquisition payment method
authors_terms: ["Cash PMT %", "cash payment percentage", "Cash vs. Equity Payment Method"]
definition: M&A transactions typically involve two main payment methods: equity and cash, and acquirers may choose all equity, all cash, or mixed payments. Relative to an equity swap arrangement that involves a long period of negotiating a share exchange price, a cash payment is more straightforward and takes less time to settle.

name: Fixed-price contract value
definition: Fixed-price contracts, where contractors bear financial risk and must deliver within predetermined budgets, create strong incentives for cost control and efficiency.

name: Cost-plus contract value
definition: Cost-plus contracts shift financial risk to the resource provider, creating different oversight challenges. These contracts are typically used for high-uncertainty projects with evolving requirements, where flexibility is essential but oversight complexity increases.

name: Discretionary oversight intensity
definition: We measured discretionary oversight intensity as the number of selective inspections a firm underwent each year by OSHA.

name: Contract duration
definition: The length of a contract shapes the dynamics of monitoring and compliance, because different contract lengths imply varying levels of scrutiny and stability.

name: Negative media coverage of labor issues
authors_terms: ["negative media coverage of labor issues", "media coverage of labor issues"]
definition: We constructed a measure of negative media coverage related to labor issues as identified by RepRisk, including forced labor, child labor, restrictions on freedom of association and collective bargaining, employment discrimination, occupational health and safety violations, and poor working conditions.

name: CEO past focus
definition: One dimension of temporal focus, defined as the extent to which people characteristically devote their attention to perceptions of the past; a strong past focus is associated with reflection on the past and repeated use of past memories in decision making.

name: CEO present focus
definition: One dimension of temporal focus, defined as the extent to which people characteristically devote their attention to perceptions of the present; individuals with a strong present focus possess a 'here and now' orientation and emphasize the current time frame in decision making.

name: CEO future focus
definition: One dimension of temporal focus, defined as the extent to which people characteristically devote their attention to perceptions of the future; future focus is associated with thinking primarily about what the future holds and with envisioning of future events.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The rate and unpredictability of change in environmental variables; it is also described as the rate and unpredictability of change in a specific environmental domain.

name: Rate of new product introduction
definition: New product introduction is described as the primary mechanism through which firms adapt to changing environmental conditions, gain competitive advantages, and achieve superior performance, and involves the core tasks of detection of new product ideas and their development into launched products; rate of NPI is the rate at which firms introduce new products.

name: Level of organizational adaptation
authors_terms: ["adaptation", "high-level of adaptation", "low-level of adaptation", "adaptive states", "adaptation value"]
definition: Adaptation is a general term that describes a period of gradual, long-continued, and incremental change in response to environmental conditions. One method of measuring adaptation is the extent to which an organization is able to initiate strategic change; Ginsberg (1988) defined strategic change and adaptation using a measure that emphasized changes in product and service domains.

name: Organizational structure
definition: An organization with a high-level of adaptation has structural characteristics of flexibility and decentralization, similar to organic structure, while an organization with a low level of adaptation has the structural characteristics of tight control and centralization, analogous to a mechanistic structure. Hage's (1965) instrument measuring organic and mechanistic structures includes two items for each of four variables: formalization, stratification, complexity, and centralization.

name: Strategy type
authors_terms: ["prospector strategy", "defender strategy", "analyzer strategy", "reactor strategy", "Miles and Snow's (1978) strategy typology"]
definition: Organizations having different levels of adaptation utilize different strategies to match their structural arrangements: organizations with a high-level of adaptation exhibit a prospector strategy and organic structure while organizations with a low-level of adaptation adopt a defender strategy and a mechanistic structure.

name: Strategy-structure fit
definition: Chakravarthy (1982) argued that organizations with an optimal strategy-structure match would have a superior performance when compared to other organizations in the same adaptive state. Chakravarthy conceptualized that organizations in each adaptive state would have specific strategy and structure alignments which yield certain performances.

name: Firm performance
definition: Three performance measures, used in consort, provide a 'snapshot' of the financial condition of a particular savings and loan. These three ratios measure value, profitability, and risk: the value ratio determines net worth, the profitability ratio measures profitability using total assets rather than owner's equity, and the risk ratio measures the extent to which assets have been repossessed.

name: Stock market value growth
authors_terms: ["growth in stock market value", "mean growth in firm stock market value", "changes in stock market value", "ln(grow(SMV))"]
definition: The two main effects in this study concern changes in firm stock market values due to escalating industry rivalry, analysed as industry means and intra-industry variances for changes in the stock market value of firms in the industry.

name: Intra-industry variance in performance
authors_terms: ["intra-industry variance in firm performance", "within-industry variance", "variance in the growth of firm stock market values"]
definition: The within-industry variance in performance around the industry mean value-rivalry relationship; the authors argue that as firms' experiences diverge under dynamic competition, this variance increases.

name: Dynamic resourcefulness of an industry
authors_terms: ["dynamic resourcefulness", "dynamic resourcefulness of an industry", "hypercompetitive industries"]
definition: The dynamic resourcefulness of an industry is the ease with which new strategic assets can be created, or the innate propensity of an industry to create new strategic assets. It is the contingency factor that determines whether competition in an industry is essentially static or dynamic.

name: Secular time trend
definition: A steady, almost linear increase in the dynamic resourcefulness of many U.S. industries during the 1958 to 1991 span of the study; a simple linear time trend interacted with key variables is used as a proxy for the general intertemporal increase.

name: Industry shipment growth
authors_terms: ["changes in industry shipments", "growth in industry shipments", "escalations in shipments", "ln(grow(Shipments))"]
definition: Changes in industry unit sales, one of the core independent variables of the study, which drive industry cashflows and signal escalating challenge from rivalry. Growth in demand facilitates new technologies and firms and rewards innovation.

name: Industry price growth
authors_terms: ["changes in industry prices", "growth in industry prices", "wholesale price index", "ln(grow(Price))"]
definition: Changes in industry prices; a reduction of industry prices ceteris paribus implies escalating industry challenge and signals greater competition, while price increases reflect the shared, static side of competition.

name: Unit cost of goods sold growth
authors_terms: ["changes in unit cost of goods sold", "rivalry in unit-CGS", "ln(grow(Unit-CGS))"]
definition: Industry changes in unit cost of goods sold, one of the core independent variables of the study that drive industry cashflows; increases of unit costs ceteris paribus signal greater competition and challenge.

name: Unit SGA cost growth
authors_terms: ["increased rivalry in unit-SGA expenses", "unit selling, general, and administrative expenses", "ln(grow(Unit-SGA))"]
definition: Changes in unit selling, general, and administrative expense. SGA aggregates the marketing and R&D expenses that are the most important firm-specific instruments of rivalry, and is the instrument most likely to be associated with the creation of new strategic assets.

name: Firm-specific human capital
definition: Becker (1962) distinguishes two types of human capital: general (equally valuable to all firms) and specific (most valuable to a specific firm). Controlling for the former, our analysis focuses on the latter, which we refer to as firm-specific human capital (FSHC).

name: Productivity
definition: As a form of human capital, FSHC should lead to higher productivity, as previous research suggests (Hatch and Dyer, 2004). Table 2 shows how FSHC affects managers' productivity, measured by the average daily value and number of loans sold.

name: Incentive gaming
definition: We define 'gaming' to be the manipulation by the agent of performance measures that are imperfectly correlated with value creation.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Productive effects of FSHC will move the branch's observed profits closer to the theoretical benchmark, while agency cost effects will move them farther away. Our general approach therefore resembles the theoretical 'lost profits' analysis in Anton and Yao (2007), and we will refer to the distance from the benchmark as 'lost profits.'

name: Elapsed time
definition: Time measured in months elapsed since the introduction of the new incentive regime.

name: Contextual distinctiveness
authors_terms: ["contextual distinctiveness", "regional contextual distinctiveness", "industry contextual distinctiveness", "a category's contextual distinctiveness"]
definition: The degree to which a particular subordinate category offers its members technical, material, and/or symbolic resources to distinguish themselves from organizations that are not members of the subordinate category yet belong to the same basic category.

name: Category promotion
authors_terms: ["category promotion", "category text promotion", "category image promotion", "promotional forbearance"]
definition: Members' efforts to champion the labels or cultural artifacts signifying the category.

name: Subordinate category peer group size
authors_terms: ["regional category peers", "industry category peers", "subordinate category peer group", "subordinate category members within a region", "subordinate category membership"]
definition: The subordinate category's size and consequent familiarity within these respective contexts. As the collective presence of organizations associated with a subordinate category grows, it constitutes a cultural resource that affords members of that collective greater discretion to deviate from other conventions or pressures of conformity that might be imposed by the wider basic categories.

name: Knowledge principles
definition: Principles, conversely, provide a fundamental, primary, or general law or truth to guide individuals. A principle may be a list of best practices, key questions, or cause-and-effect associations that provide a theoretical explanation for why they might be useful as a general guideline for other projects.

name: Knowledge templates
definition: Templates provide a pattern or a model for other individuals to copy. A template might be a project prototype or how to document that walks a project manager through the steps needed to successfully replicate a project.

name: Cost efficiency
definition: The M&E Unit also determines the cost efficiency of projects. In doing so, they evaluate the degree to which the project deviates from the schedule and allocated resources.

name: Customer responsiveness
definition: This measure was determined by the degree to which the customer's specific goals and objectives were met by the consulting project.

name: Individual experience
definition: To assess individual experience, we examined each manager's project-specific training, experience within the country, and industry experience.

name: Geographic distance
definition: Geographic distance was coded as the log of the miles from headquarters to the project's country office.

name: Institutional distance
definition: Institutional distance captures the difference between the institutional environments of two countries (Kostova, 1999). It is based on regulative, normative, and cognitive pillars of the institutional environment.

name: Distance from the knowledge source
authors_terms: ["geographically and institutionally distant from the knowledge source", "distance"]
definition: Firm-level factors such as geographic, firm, and institutional distance make managers more or less likely to be able to reuse knowledge in a new context.

name: CEO humility
definition: An attribute grounded in a transcendent self-view that recognizes oneself as bounded and limited, yet capable and responsible for improvement. It comprises two essential dimensions: the intrapersonal dimension of recognizing one's own weaknesses and limitations and the interpersonal dimension of appreciating the strengths and contributions of others.

name: Corporate social irresponsibility occurrence
definition: CSIR is 'the set of corporate actions that negatively affect an identifiable social stakeholder's legitimate claims.' The authors focus on legal irresponsibility, i.e., violating (1) criminal, civil, or administrative laws or (2) industry or professional codes.

name: Post-CSIR corrective actions
definition: Corrective actions taken after CSIR occurrence to mitigate damages or improve management, such as organizational restructuring and policy or practice changes that are intended to improve management and prevent future CSIR.

name: Industry CSIR incidence
authors_terms: ["high-CSIR industries", "industries with a high number of CSIR incidents", "industry peer CSIR incidents"]
definition: Industries with a high number of CSIR incidents ('high-CSIR industries') represent a context where the need for stakeholder interest protection is strong and information regarding CSIR prevention and correction is readily available. The measure counts CSIR incidents reported in the past three years in a given (two-digit) industry, excluding the focal firms.

name: TMT minority representation
authors_terms: ["TMT minority ratio", "ratio of female and racial minority members in TMT"]
definition: The ratio of female and racial minority members in the TMT. Female and racial minority members represent stakeholder groups fighting for equality and inclusion, and their unique life experiences offer valuable perspectives concerning customers, employees, and suppliers.

name: Adoption timing
authors_terms: ["early adoption", "early adopters", "later adopters", "adoption period", "time of adoption"]
definition: The point in the diffusion process at which a hospital begins using TQM. The authors argue that early adoption is associated with opportunity framing and motivations to achieve gains, both economic and social, while later adoption is associated with threat framing and motivations to avoid losses.

name: Economic gain motivation
authors_terms: ["economic gains", "motivations to achieve economic gains", "perceived opportunity of achieving economic gains", "efficiency motivations"]
definition: Adoption reasons that relate to TQM as an opportunity for achieving gains in performance and internal functioning; the authors followed previous research in broadly defining efficiency as relating to improving organizational performance and internal functioning.

name: Social gain motivation
authors_terms: ["social gains", "perceived opportunity of achieving social gains", "achieving social gains"]
definition: The prospect of achieving social gains in the eyes of other constituencies, such as being perceived as a market leader, maintaining high status vis-a-vis competitors, and earning the esteem of peers.

name: Economic loss motivation
authors_terms: ["economic losses", "perceived threat of incurring economic losses", "threat of economic losses", "avoiding economic losses"]
definition: Adoption reasons relating to the avoidance of competitive disadvantage, such as loss of market share and competition from other hospitals or HMOs; later adopters are theorized to frame the diffusing practice as a threat of incurring economic losses.

name: Social loss motivation
authors_terms: ["social losses", "perceived threat of incurring social losses", "avoiding social losses"]
definition: A view of TQM adoption as a way to avoid social losses, indicated by the importance a hospital attached to the influence of the JCAHO, which exerted considerable coercive pressure on hospitals; failing to conform raises the prospect of social sanctions for being out of step with what has become legitimate and standard.

name: Extent of practice implementation
authors_terms: ["extent of practice implementation", "extent of TQM implementation", "implementation efforts", "extent of implementation"]
definition: How extensively TQM was implemented in a hospital overall, how far training in TQM had progressed, and how many different aspects of TQM were integrated within the various departments of the hospital.

name: Entry collaboration
authors_terms: ["entry collaboration", "collaborative relationships when they enter an industry", "entry relationships"]
definition: Collaborative relationships that a business forms when it enters an industry, involving substantial ongoing interaction between legally autonomous organizations. The entry collaboration variables record whether a business had formed at least one collaborative relationship by the end of its first full calendar year of participation in the industry.

name: Post-entry collaboration
definition: Collaborative relationships that businesses form after entering an industry; like entry collaboration, post-entry collaboration provides access to capabilities and legitimacy that would be difficult, costly, and time consuming to develop independently.

name: Initial sales level
definition: Sales during the first full year of operation in the industry.

name: Initial sales growth
definition: Growth during the years immediately following the first full year, which the authors measure as percentage sales growth during the second, third, and fourth years.

name: Business sales
definition: Business managers commonly focus on sales levels and growth as key performance metrics, both because higher sales may lead to higher profitability and because firms frequently value higher sales independent of profitability. Higher sales might both cause collaboration and result from collaboration.

name: Ongoing sales growth
definition: Ongoing sales growth following entry is important, as growth demonstrates that the firm continues to be a successful competitor. Operating efficiencies that result from collaboration may reinforce existing sales levels and lead to greater sales for the collaborating businesses.

name: Past collaboration experience
authors_terms: ["Cumulative Partnerships", "past collaboration", "collaborative links a business has formed in the past"]
definition: The number of collaborative links a business has formed in the past, which is likely to influence the formation of new collaborations, because businesses with partnerships become embedded in an industry network and develop competence in forming and managing alliances.

name: Core/periphery position
authors_terms: ["core/periphery position", "position in the core/periphery structure", "position on a core/periphery continuum", "core/periphery structure", "coreness"]
definition: A network has a core/periphery structure if it has a core of individuals who are densely tied to each other and a periphery whose members have more relationships to core members than to each other. A person's position can range on a continuum from core to peripheral.

name: Spanning multiple external communities
authors_terms: ["spanning multiple external communities", "boundary spanning", "external boundary spanning", "spanning community boundaries", "cosmopolitans"]
definition: Communities have permeable boundaries because little prevents individuals from being members of multiple communities, and we refer to people spanning community boundaries as cosmopolitans. We argue that the extent to which people span multiple communities affects whether they are innovative because easy access to many sources of diverse knowledge from external communities provides increased opportunities for recombination.

name: Individual innovation
definition: In user communities the 'market' is not necessarily someone buying a product or service but an idea or artifact that is being used by peers in the community, so individuals are thus innovative if peers perceive them as contributing something novel. Following Amabile, a product or response is deemed creative to the extent that appropriate observers independently agree it is creative.

name: Physician power
authors_terms: ["physician power", "power of physicians", "physician influence", "intraorganizational power of physicians"]
definition: Power derived from the ability of individuals or groups to solve important organizational problems that may be linked to resource dependencies and other critical strategic contingencies, or structurally from one's position in an organization. Physician power may derive from the importance of physicians as a strategic contingency for the hospital.

name: Managerial power
definition: Power resting on the strategic contingencies facing management and on the formal authority held by management; as competitive pressures in the environment become a critical strategic contingency for a hospital, managers assume a more central and powerful role in determining how hospitals respond.

name: Medical service contracting
authors_terms: ["service contracting", "medical service contracting", "contracting of medical services", "proportion of medical services contracted"]
definition: The percentage of services contracted by the hospital. The CHFC distinguishes between services that are directly organized and staffed by the hospital and those that are provided on a contractual basis and staffed by the contractor.

name: Prospective Payment System
definition: The introduction of the Prospective Payment System (PPS) in 1983 shifted the hospital payment structure from reimbursement based on cost to one based on predetermined rates for specific medical procedures, significantly increasing competition among hospitals by intensifying pressure on hospitals to contain costs and find new sources of revenues.

name: Resource transferability
definition: A form of resource relatedness interpreted as the absence of limitations or barriers to making use of established firm resources and capabilities for building up the required resources in the new segment; when such commonality is high, a straightforward transfer of established firm resources to the new segment is possible (relatively low costs of transfer).

name: Resource complementarity
definition: The value that can be created by the unique combination and integration of the firm's current resources and capabilities with target segment resources in day-to-day operations. It consists of commonality between the established business and the new target segment activity in terms of durable operational synergies, and strategic relatedness in terms of a difficult-to-match competitive advantage (uniqueness of synergies).

name: Entry by internal development
authors_terms: ["entry by internal development", "internal development", "entry mode choice"]
definition: Entry mode choice is defined as a decision on the mode of gaining access to resources that are required in a newly entered business segment, but not already available to a firm; the focal alternative is entry by internal development rather than entry in collaboration with an external partner.

name: Investment intensity of target segment
authors_terms: ["investment intensity of target segment", "investment intensity of segment", "investment intensity of the target segment"]
definition: A target segment characteristic: business segments differ in the volume of initial investments required for developing the tangible and intangible assets needed in the entry phase.

name: Partner trustworthiness
authors_terms: ["partner trustworthiness", "perceived trustworthiness of the (potential) collaboration partner"]
definition: The perceived trustworthiness of the potential collaboration partner, based on the partner's fairness and consideration in negotiations about the collaboration, certainty that the partner would be reliable and keep any promises made, and absence of worry that the partner might take advantage of the firm's dependency.

name: Partner competence
authors_terms: ["partner competence", "confidence in the competence of the (potential) collaboration partner"]
definition: The focal company's perception at the time of the decision of whether the (potential) collaboration partner had the relevant competencies to develop and/or deliver the resources or capabilities required to perform the collaborative activity successfully.

name: Information asymmetry
authors_terms: ["information asymmetry", "information asymmetry benefits", "information asymmetry between buyers and sellers"]
definition: Generally, the sellers of services have more information than buyers do about the true quality of their services. This information asymmetry leads to "moral hazard" for sellers, giving them an incentive to exert less than complete effort in delivering services.

name: Economies of scope
definition: Economies of scope arise when the joint cost of producing two or more outputs is less than the sum of the costs of producing each output by itself.

name: Service characteristics
authors_terms: ["service characteristics", "search services", "experience services", "search and experience qualities"]
definition: The extent of information asymmetry varies with the characteristics of a service, which can be examined by differentiating services in terms of the mix of three attributes: search, experience, and credence qualities. It is sufficient here to only distinguish search services--those dominated by qualities that buyers can determine before consumption--from experience and credence services, whose dominant qualities are only ascertainable after consumption or are not ascertainable.

name: Firm performance
definition: Industry- and systematic risk-adjusted return on equity (ROE), the industry-adjusted market-to-book value of equity, and Jensen's alpha were the performance measures.

name: Subsidiary-level investment
authors_terms: ["MNC subsidiary-level investment", "investment at the subsidiary level", "subsidiary-level investment", "number of a firm's subsidiaries in a country"]
definition: Throughout the paper we use the terms MNC subsidiary-level investment and investment at the subsidiary level to refer to the presence of European MNCs' subsidiaries in a particular host country. The change in subsidiary-level investment is the MNC's response to disaster(s) and reflects an increase or decrease in the number of subsidiaries in a host country.

name: Country governance quality
authors_terms: ["governance quality", "quality of governance", "country governance", "host country governance", "quality of host country governance"]
definition: The quality of governance and the strength of the institutions in a country are assumed to have a significant impact on the ability and willingness of governments to respond to disasters within their borders.

name: Major disasters
definition: A wide variety of disasters can befall businesses in their normal course of operations. Three major categories include terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and technological disasters.

name: Terrorist activity
definition: The first category of risks, terrorist attacks, has been defined as the use of violence or the threat of violence to attain political or ideological goals and the willingness to attack noncombatants.

name: Natural disasters
definition: Natural disasters, also called 'acts of God,' comprise the second category of disasters. Examples include, but are not limited to, droughts, earthquakes, epidemics, extreme temperatures, floods, insect infestations, mudslides, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, and wild fires.

name: Technological disasters
definition: The third category of disasters involves technological disasters. Although modern technologies have led to dramatic improvements in labor productivity during recent decades, breakdowns of technological systems, or accidents associated with the processing, storage, and transportation of explosive or toxic chemicals, radioisotopes, and other hazardous materials have the potential to cause massive loss of life and property.

name: Geographic distance
definition: Geographic proximity reduces the cost of both information acquisition and opportunity appraisal, which are key for the success of collaboration, and it is known from prior research to enable parties to collude without leaving a trace of discoverable culpability. The authors examine the geographic proximity between grant officials and resource-seeking firms as one of the factors shaping their likelihood to collude.

name: Irregular awards
definition: Irregular awards are allocated to firms whose rule-complying merits would not have earned them such access. The authors conceptualize irregular awards as the outcome of public-private collusion in which grant officials deliberately misallocate state funding to illicitly advance certain firms' interests.

name: External bureaucratic oversight
authors_terms: ["oversight and monitoring from an external and competing bureaucratic agency", "inter-agency checks and balances", "external scrutiny", "inter-ministry rivalry", "indigenous innovation"]
definition: Institutional arrangements such as judicial review, the launch of an independent commission, and shared leadership (i.e., two or more ministries being tasked with handling a common program) bring forth the kind of oversight that may induce government bureaucrats to adhere to role expectations and codes of conduct. Such constraints can be particularly binding when bureaucrats in one state agency must secure approval for overall budget funding from a distinct, external state agency.

name: Direct state intermediary
authors_terms: ["intermediary state agency", "direct intermediary", "direct STM subsidiaries", "intermediary agencies", "venue of application"]
definition: Central agencies often rely on intermediary (and typically subordinate) agencies to interact with policy targets for program promotion and implementation. Among all the intermediaries, only the provincial STCs interact with the Z-center on a routine basis, and other intermediary officials have much fewer opportunities to interact and build personal relationships with the Y-program.

name: State ownership
authors_terms: ["state ownership", "state-affiliated equity owners", "state affiliation through equity ownership", "shared identity"]
definition: The authors expect a firm's state-capture capability to vary across ownership types and that those with state-affiliated equity owners are well positioned to collude with grant officials. A state ownership dummy measures whether a firm has state-affiliated equity owners such as the state-owned assets administration commission, public research institute, and government bureau and public organization.

name: Grant size
definition: Grant winners receive around 65.7-131.4 thousand US dollars (2007 value) from the central government, with local governments providing a 50%-100% match. In cases where grant officials collude with an entrepreneur through rule-violation means, they may as well have incentives to help secure a larger grant rather than a typical one.

name: Firm valuation
authors_terms: ["firm valuation", "market valuation", "market value of the company's equity"]
