definition: Firm valuation is the market value of the company's equity. In practice this is of great interest to entrepreneurs because their economic returns hinge on how the markets value their firms.

name: Exploration alliances
definition: Exploration alliances are formed to seek and generate new knowledge and technologies, focusing on upstream activities of the value chain such as drug discovery and development.

name: Exploitation alliances
definition: Exploitation alliances are formed to leverage complementary assets between alliance partners, focusing on downstream activities of the value chain such as manufacturing and marketing.

name: Equity-based alliance governance
authors_terms: ["formal governance", "equity alliances", "equity-based structure", "equity governance", "number of equity-based exploration alliances", "number of equity-based exploitation alliances"]
definition: Formal governance refers to the legal delineation of rights and obligations between alliance partners within an exchange agreement. Equity alliances refer to structures that involve equity ownership such as equity transfers or the creation of a new entity, and are considered to present a higher level of hierarchical control than nonequity alliances.

name: Nonequity-based alliance governance
authors_terms: ["nonequity alliances", "nonequity governance structure", "nonequity-based structure", "number of nonequity-based exploration alliances", "number of nonequity-based exploitation alliances"]
definition: Nonequity alliances refer to contractual agreements that do not involve any equity ownership changes. The authors contend that a nonequity governance structure is more desirable than an equity structure for small firms forming exploitation alliances with large firms.

name: Relational governance
definition: Relational governance entails the informal enforcement of obligations, promises, and expectations following the values and agreed-on processes in social relationships. It is an informal governance mechanism created through trust and shared value that may serve as an alternative interorganizational governance structure in alliance relationships.

name: Outbound mobility
authors_terms: ["outbound mobility", "outbound mobility tie", "loss of an employee"]
definition: The loss of an employee to another firm, which the authors term 'outbound mobility' and which generates a communication channel between the two firms.

name: Knowledge transfer
authors_terms: ["knowledge transfer", "reverse transfer of knowledge", "draws upon the new employer's knowledge", "citation"]
definition: Knowledge transfer occurs when an organization is affected by the experience of other organizations; patent citations are records that allow the authors to track when a firm draws on another firm's knowledge stock.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: Geographic proximity is likely to proxy for a host of mechanisms that may facilitate knowledge spillovers, of which mobility is one; an outbound mobility event within a geographic region is more likely to create a duplicative channel because of the multiplicity of channels already available within a region.

name: Activist-impelled divestiture
authors_terms: ["activist-impelled divestitures", "divestitures that are impelled by activist investors", "divestitures undertaken at the behest of activist investors"]
definition: Divestitures that activist investors demand in their campaigns and that managers may not have undertaken of their own accord; activist-impelled divestitures represent only those deals with the highest positive value-creation potential, as activist investors seek to generate significant investment returns but must also be cognizant of campaign costs and the need to maximize the likelihood of success.

name: Shareholder value
authors_terms: ["shareholder value", "stock market performance", "stock market response", "shareholder returns"]
definition: The stock market response to activist-impelled and manager-led divestitures, measured in two ways: investors' immediate reaction to divestiture announcements and longer-term buy-and-hold returns calculated by compounding the divesting firms' market-adjusted monthly stock market returns following the completion dates of their divestitures.

name: International expansion
definition: The study examined the effects of international expansion, as measured by international diversity and mode of market entry, on a firm's technological learning.

name: International diversity
definition: International diversity denotes a firm's increased reliance on foreign markets as a means of growth and financial performance improvement. It refers to the scope of a firm's foreign operations.

name: Use of high-control entry modes
authors_terms: ["high-control modes of international market entry", "high-control entry modes", "high-control transactions", "foreign direct investment (FDI)"]
definition: High-control international entry modes typically require closeness to a market and its customers and involve deep stakeholder involvement, in contrast to low-control transactions that require few interactions with markets, suppliers, and customers.

name: Use of low-control entry modes
definition: In contrast to the high-control transactions characteristic of foreign direct investment, some low-control transactions (for instance, exporting, licensing) require few interactions with markets, suppliers, and customers.

name: Breadth of technological learning
definition: Breadth denotes the multiple areas in which a venture learns new technological skills.

name: Depth of technological learning
definition: Depth refers to a venture's mastery of new knowledge, evidenced by an ability to draw new conclusions and find new links among diverse knowledge bases.

name: Speed of technological learning
definition: Speed of technological learning describes how rapidly the venture acquires new insights and skills.

name: Knowledge integration
definition: In this study the authors emphasized formal integration, defined as the process by which managers inventory, synthesize, and use the knowledge they have gained from their firm's international expansion.

name: New venture performance
authors_terms: ["new venture performance", "new venture firm performance", "return on equity (ROE)", "sales growth"]
definition: The importance of profitability and growth as key outcomes of new venture international operations has been noted; two performance measures were selected, sales growth and return on equity (ROE).

name: Lead partner departure
authors_terms: ["lead partner exit", "departure of the client lead partner", "partner exit"]
definition: The exit of the partner who serves as the client lead partner, the partner who interprets and anticipates the client's needs and forms connections inside the firm with lawyers holding relevant knowledge, and who plays an important role coordinating this knowledge.

name: Client relationship performance
authors_terms: ["client relationship performance", "performance of the client relationship", "billable hours"]
definition: Billable hours is a key measure of the performance of each client relationship for the law firm; the authors operationalized client relationship performance using the total billable hours charged to each client in a given year.

name: Domain heterogeneity
definition: The heterogeneity of expertise in the knowledge network, i.e., heterogeneity in the domains of expertise that are applied to the client relationship; the authors measured it as a count of different departments (knowledge domains) represented in the team billing the client each year.

name: Geographic heterogeneity
definition: Heterogeneity in the geographic reach of the knowledge network, calculated as a count of the different city office locations of the lawyers in each client knowledge network each year.

name: Expert knowledge
definition: The extent to which the knowledge network includes expert knowledge. Experts are considered among the best in their fields and consequently are afforded power and status within the firm and industry.

name: Network cohesion
definition: Cohesion in a knowledge network arises from the density of connections existing among the members of the network. It is associated with trust, enhanced information sharing, and enforceability of norms.

name: Network closure
authors_terms: ["network closure", "structural closure", "degree of structural closure", "structural holes", "ego network constraint"]
definition: The degree of structural closure in a network, defined as the extent to which an actor's network contacts are connected to one another. A high degree of structural closure creates a cohesive network of tightly linked social actors, and a low degree of structural closure creates a network with 'structural holes' and brokerage potential.

name: Divergence from the institutional status quo
authors_terms: ["divergence from the institutional status quo", "divergent organizational change", "change divergence", "degree of divergence"]
definition: The extent to which an organizational change breaks with existing institutions in a field of activity. Changes that diverge from the status quo, hereafter referred to as divergent organizational changes, are particularly challenging to implement because they require change agents to persuade other organization members to adopt practices that break with the norms of their institutional environment.

name: Change adoption
authors_terms: ["change adoption", "level of adoption", "adoption of organizational changes", "change implementation"]
definition: The degree to which a change initiative is actually adopted, that is, the probability that a change initiative will actually modify organizational functioning.

name: Racial diversity
authors_terms: ["racial diversity", "racial diversity within a community", "racial diversity within each school district"]
definition: The racial diversity of a community, which the authors measure from the racial composition of students enrolled in the district's schools rather than all residents in the district.

name: Community support for public schools
authors_terms: ["support for public service organizations", "local support for public schools", "community support for public schools"]
definition: A community's financial support for its local public schools, captured by per-pupil school spending from local sources and by the per-pupil voter-approved bond amount issued by the school district.

name: Community inclusion
definition: The extent to which different demographic groups within a community engage and participate in activities with each other, including the extent to which members of different groups live in propinquity or have contact with each other, form bridging social ties, or feel generally trusting of others in the community.

name: Shared values
definition: The extent to which members of different racial groups in a community share the same values, measured by how similar members of different races in the community are in their political ideologies.

name: Organizational representativeness
definition: The extent to which public service organizations are representative, that is, whether different groups receive services from the same organizations or not.

name: Board gender diversity
authors_terms: ["gender diversity on boards", "gender diversity on a board", "proportion of female directors", "Female Director Ratio", "presence of women on boards"]
definition: Female Director Ratio (the proportion of female directors on the board) is the measure of gender diversity on a board; the authors note that the maximum percentage of women on boards in China is 50%.

name: Securities fraud
authors_terms: ["fraud", "securities fraud", "violation of a regulation or fraud", "frequency of fraud", "likelihood of fraud"]
definition: Securities fraud refers to violations of securities regulations such as asset fabrication, embezzlement, share price manipulation, and illegal guarantees; the authors study both its frequency and its severity.

name: Stock market reaction to fraud announcements
authors_terms: ["abnormal share price reaction", "abnormal returns", "negative investor reaction", "share price reaction to corporate fraud", "severity of fraud"]
definition: The authors study the consequences of committing fraud in terms of abnormal share price reaction, because abnormal share price reactions are a direct measure of the public's perception of the severity of fraud.

name: Industry gender composition
definition: Different industries require different degrees of masculinity to achieve success; the authors classify an industry with more than 50% female employees as a 'female-dominated industry' and the remainder as male-dominated industries.

name: Female chairperson
definition: The chairperson is the head of the board of directors; Female Chairperson is a dummy variable that takes a value of '1' if the firm is led by a female chairperson, and '0' otherwise.

name: Female general manager
definition: The general manager is the president of the corporation, hired by the board of directors; Female General Manager is a dummy variable that takes the value of '1' if the firm is led by a female general manager, and '0' otherwise.

name: Within-agency multiplexity
definition: A relationship is multiplex if a single agency maintains multiple ties to the same client firm; that is, within-agency multiplex ties. Each tie corresponds to a separate client account acquired via separate pitching processes.

name: Across-agency multiplexity
definition: A relationship is multiplex when the agency is tied to a client that has a tie to another agency in the same holding company as the focal agency; that is, across-agency multiplex ties. The measure is best understood as multiplex tie density, or the extent to which a given dyad is embedded in the number of across-agency multiplex ties possible.

name: Executive departures
authors_terms: ["executive departures", "proportion of agency executives departing", "proportion of executive departures"]
definition: Executive departures are measured as the proportion of agency executives leaving the agency annually. 'Departure' is defined as the absence of an executive name listed by the agency in the previous year from the agency's REDBOOKS entry in the current year.

name: Client tie dissolution
authors_terms: ["client relationship dissolution", "tie dissolution", "dissolution of an agency-client tie"]
definition: The main dependent variable is a dichotomous variable set to one if the agency-client tie dissolved in that year. A tie is coded as 'dissolved' the first year the advertising firm no longer lists the client account in its REDBOOKS record.

name: Non-competitive ties
definition: The extent of competition among agencies in across-agency multiplex ties was measured as the proportion of non-competitive ties and constructed by counting the number of across-agency multiplex ties involving agencies in the same network divided by the count of all across-agency multiplex ties surrounding the agency-client dyad. Agencies in the same network are incentivized to cooperate, or, at a minimum, they are not allowed to compete with one another, in contrast to agencies in different networks.

name: Breadth of innovation objectives
authors_terms: ["breadth of innovation objectives", "innovation objectives", "breadth in objectives", "breadth of objectives"]
definition: Firms' pursuit of innovation activities is likely to have different objectives that may range from product-related goals, for example, develop a new product, to process-related goals, for example, reduce labor costs.

name: Breadth of knowledge sources
authors_terms: ["breadth of knowledge sources", "knowledge sources", "breadth in sources", "breadth of sources"]
definition: Firms in performing their innovation activities may also seek information from different sources such as customers and supply chain partners.

name: Innovation performance
authors_terms: ["innovation performance", "innovation success", "percent sales from new products", "% sales from new products", "percent of product sales revenues from innovation"]
definition: Leiponen and Helfat (2010) used two variables as indicators of innovation performance. First, they used a binary variable (0, 1) that indicated 'whether the firm introduced any technological innovations (product as well as process)'; second, they used a variable that measured the percent of firm revenues from the 'sale of technologically new products'.

name: Corporate philanthropic contributions
definition: The total dollar amount of corporate philanthropy, which the authors manually recorded from the National Directory of Corporate Giving in the years matching the sample; the variable was log-transformed to reduce highly skewed values.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The length of a CEO's time in office. Early on, CEOs are highly attuned to their external environments and relatively more likely to adapt to them; as time goes on, CEOs become 'stale in the saddle' and tend to conform to the strategies of peer companies.

name: Board network centrality
authors_terms: ["board centrality", "director degree centrality", "centrality in the director interlock network", "degree centrality of board members"]
definition: The centrality of a firm's board in the director interlock network; the degree centrality of board members is calculated from the network of shared directors among the boards of all public firms in 1997 and 2002.

name: Board size
definition: The number of directors on the corporation's board. Large boards are argued to have more difficulty coordinating activities and may be more vulnerable to fractures and the emergence of special interests.

name: Gender composition of senior management
authors_terms: ["percentage women senior managers", "presence of women senior managers", "women senior managers", "gender composition of the senior executive team"]
definition: The gender composition of the senior executive team. The authors predict that the combination of individual differences and gendered roles will lead corporations with more women senior managers to be more generous.

name: Gender composition of the board of directors
authors_terms: ["percentage of women directors", "proportion of female board members", "women directors", "more women on the board"]
definition: The presence of women at the director level. Female directors may be more likely to be from nonprofit backgrounds, which would give them greater awareness of and exposure to corporate philanthropy ideas.

name: Corporate foundation size
authors_terms: ["foundation assets", "size of the corporate foundation", "greater corporate foundation assets", "corporate foundation structure"]
definition: The corporate foundation is a legally separate entity created to manage the parent corporation's philanthropy. The size of the foundation reflects structural differentiation and overall power within the organization, and larger corporate foundations tend to be more structurally differentiated from the rest of the firm.

name: Spawning
authors_terms: ["spawn", "spawned venture", "spin-off", "prior employment at an incumbent firm"]
definition: Entrepreneurship in which former employees of incumbent firms found entrepreneurial ventures in the same industry; here a spawn is an individual who at some point in his career worked at a large medical device (or life sciences) firm before becoming an entrepreneur.

name: Time to funding
definition: The time to funding variable is calculated by taking the difference (in days) between the first reported round of outside funding in VentureOne and the founding date for the company.

name: Entrepreneurial performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "pre-money (private) valuations", "successful commercialization of a product", "FDA approval"]
definition: Performance of private entrepreneurial firms, which is difficult to measure; the authors use pre-money (private) valuations at the last round of venture capital financing and the successful commercialization of a product as proxies for performance.

name: Technical knowledge inheritance
authors_terms: ["technical knowledge inheritance", "technological spillovers", "knowledge inheritance", "cites to parent"]
definition: The extent to which spawns incorporate technical knowledge from the parent firm, traced here by analyzing citations from spawn patents to the parent firm's patents as a measure of technological spillovers from parent to spawn.

name: Technological relatedness to the parent
authors_terms: ["related", "Spawn Related", "parent's top three patent classes", "same patent classes"]
definition: Whether a spawned venture patents in the same technology area as its parent firm, judged by whether the majority of the spawn's patents fall in one of the parent firm's top three patent classes.

name: Input usage
authors_terms: ["input usage", "usage of that input", "firm's usage of that input", "usage of the toxic chemical"]
definition: The degree to which a nonresponsible firm handles the chemicals involved in an accident, normalized by these chemicals' toxicity. Some firms may use large amounts of a given input, whereas others may make negligible use of the same input.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["cumulative abnormal returns (CARs)", "market discount", "decline in market value", "abnormal returns"]
definition: A nonresponsible firm's cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) following each accident, calculated with the standard event study methodology. An increase in investors' expectations that an accident will occur at a given firm is likely to lead to a discount of that firm's market value.

name: Input-level regulatory sanctions
authors_terms: ["input-level regulatory sanctions", "ex ante input-level regulatory sanctions", "regulatory sanctions"]
definition: Fines and penalties imposed by the regulatory agencies on input users that fail to meet existing requirements for regulated inputs.

name: Input-level association
definition: Any institution, code, agreement, or commitment that coordinates communication actions of users of the same input. An ILA's mission is to inform consumers and investors about the real risks of specific inputs, as well as to explain how firms are effectively handling these inputs within their internal processes.

name: Input-portfolio similarity
authors_terms: ["input-portfolio similarity", "input portfolio", "input-portfolio similarity between the responsible and the nonresponsible firms"]
definition: The degree to which the responsible facility and the nonresponsible firm's facilities used a similar portfolio of toxic chemicals (other than that involved in the accident) in the year before the accident. A firm's broader input portfolio is an attribute that investors may take to be informative about the firm's underlying technology.

name: Geographic proximity
authors_terms: ["geographic proximity", "geographic location", "geographic proximity between the responsible and the nonresponsible firms"]
definition: The proximity between the responsible firm and the nonresponsible firm, calculated from the distance between the facility of the responsible firm where the accident took place and the facilities of the nonresponsible firms. Investors will take geographic proximity as informative of the degree of similarity between (unobservable) security practices at the responsible and nonresponsible firms.

name: TMT sociobehavioral integration
authors_terms: ["TMT sociobehavioral integration", "sociobehavioral integration", "TMT integration", "top management team sociobehavioral integration"]
definition: TMT sociobehavioral integration reflects how well senior executives of a firm work together, both socially and as a team. Our conceptualization, which includes both social and behavioral components of team integration, is a refinement of this construct.

name: Hypercompetitive environment
definition: We define the intensity of a hypercompetitive environment as the degree of volatility in basic areas such as customer demands and production methods in the industry in which a firm competes. Hypercompetition concerns a degree of uncertainty that 'produces deficits in the information needed to identify and understand cause-and-effect relationships'.

name: Action aggressiveness
definition: Action aggressiveness reflects how a firm engages rivals in a hypercompetitive environment. It is a firm-level construct that characterizes a firm's tendency to initiate actions and the firm's agility in doing so.

name: Firm performance
definition: We used two widely accepted measures of financial performance: profit margin and return on equity (ROE). Profit margin is defined as operating profit divided by operating revenue, while ROE is defined as net profit divided by equity.

name: Performance variation
authors_terms: ["variation in firm performance", "intraindustry variation in firm performance", "volatility over time"]
definition: Firm performance is highly volatile as temporary advantages are exploited and then dissipate, and one strategic oversight could force a firm to concede its leadership position to opponents. Specifically, we expect to observe greater intraindustry variation in firm performance for industries within a hypercompetitive context, as well as greater volatility over time.

name: Home country stakeholder pressure
authors_terms: ["home country's stakeholder pressure on MNE's HQ", "stakeholder pressure at the HQ level", "home country's stakeholder pressure"]
definition: Through a process of institutional isomorphism, stakeholders exert pressure on an organization by assessing its conformity to their own and diverse value systems, existing rules and laws, and shared social knowledge and cognitive categories. We therefore measured stakeholder pressure through a wide range of controversies that an MNE had faced in its relationships with its stakeholders.

name: Transfer of CSiR practices
authors_terms: ["transfer of CSiR practices", "transfer of corporate socially irresponsible practices", "transfer of socially irresponsible practices"]
definition: A subsidiary's underreaction to a shock affecting the subsidiary's industry is seen as evidence of intragroup transactions. CSR underreaction thus provides evidence of the transfer of CSiR practices between an HQ and that subsidiary.

name: Interlocked minority ownership
authors_terms: ["interlocked, minority-owned subsidiary", "interlocked, minority-owned subsidiaries", "loosely affiliated to an MNE but controlled by HQ through board interlocks"]
definition: An interlocked, minority-owned subsidiary is, therefore, a subsidiary in which the HQ of a focal MNE held a stake between 5 and 10 percent and at least one HQ executive served on the subsidiary's board.

name: Institutional control
authors_terms: ["institutional control", "regulatory and/or civil society control", "regulatory pressure", "civil society pressure"]
definition: Institutional control, which we define as the set of processes through which pressure for conformity is imposed on organizations. Oliver (1991) identified legal coercion as a critical process; government regulations shape organizational behavior through force, persuasion, or direct imposition.

name: Risk taking
definition: On the fourth down, the conservative choice is to punt the ball so that the opposing team begins its attack from as far away as possible, while the risky choice is to go for it, that is, to attempt to win the necessary yards for a new first down.

name: Performance shortfall
authors_terms: ["negative attainment discrepancy", "performance below the aspiration level", "below aspirations", "shortfall"]
definition: The magnitude by which organizational performance falls short of the aspiration level (negative attainment discrepancy). From an organizational perspective, when performance is below aspirations, decision makers focus on achieving gains to amend the shortfall, and the more so the larger the attainment discrepancy.

name: Performance surplus
authors_terms: ["positive attainment discrepancy", "performance above the aspiration level", "above aspirations", "overperforming"]
definition: The magnitude by which organizational performance exceeds the aspiration level (positive attainment discrepancy). When organizations are slightly overperforming, decision makers focus on avoiding losses and turn to the likelihood of losses as the key diagnostic attribute.

name: Deadline proximity
authors_terms: ["deadline proximity", "proximity to performance evaluation", "the farther away the performance evaluation is", "remaining time"]
definition: Deadline proximity captures the time to performance evaluation and is a dimension of within-period performance feedback. The final evaluation occurs at the end of the performance period, and organizational rewards and punishments are linked to achieving goals at that point.

name: Magnitude of outcomes
authors_terms: ["magnitude of outcomes", "magnitude of potential losses/gains", "magnitude of gains and losses", "Yard line"]
definition: The intrinsic attribute capturing how large the potential gains and losses of an alternative are; the magnitude and likelihood of outcomes capture the extent to which the alternative is expected to make the decision maker better off. In the NFL setting the expected points scored or received when starting a new play are a direct function of the field position, so the yard line captures the magnitude of outcomes.

name: Likelihood of outcomes
authors_terms: ["likelihood of outcomes", "likelihood of adverse/positive outcomes", "likelihood of losses", "likelihood of gains", "Yards to go for first down"]
definition: The intrinsic attribute capturing decision makers' estimates of the probability of the outcomes of an alternative. In the NFL setting the fewer the yards left for a first down, the more likely the team is to succeed in its attempt, so the yards left capture the likelihood of outcomes.

name: Asset specificity
authors_terms: ["asset specificity", "business process asset specificity", "human asset specificity", "procedural asset specificity", "transaction-specific assets"]
definition: Given our focus on a service industry as a research context, rather than considering physical asset specificity, we develop the concept of business process asset specificity—which incorporates components of both human asset specificity and procedural asset specificity. Procedural asset specificity refers to the degree a firm's workflows and processes are customized in line with the requirements of the exchange partner, while human asset specificity deals with the degree to which skills, knowledge and experience of a firm's personnel are specific to the requirements of dealing with another firm in a vertical relationship.

name: Behavioral uncertainty
definition: In an exchange context, the relevant form of uncertainty is 'behavioral uncertainty' (Williamson, 1985), which could be viewed as a subset of Koopmans' (1957) 'secondary uncertainty.' Behavioral uncertainty arises from the difficulty in predicting the actions of the other party in the relationship, in view of the potential for opportunistic behavior and since bounded rationality precludes the writing of complete contingent contracts.

name: Reciprocal investments
definition: Reciprocal investments (or reciprocal asset specificity) refer to transaction-specific investments by the other party to the exchange and are akin to being a mirror image of asset specificity. Reciprocal assets may tend to moderate opportunism by serving as 'hostages' in an exchange (Williamson, 1985).

name: Trust
definition: In behavioral terms, trust reflects 'the extent to which negotiations are fair and commitments are upheld' (Anderson and Narus, 1990) and one party's belief that its requirements will be fulfilled through future actions undertaken by the other party (Anderson and Weitz, 1989). Our focus in this research is on trust as a property of the interorganizational dyad, and is primarily sociological in nature.

name: Vertical quasi-integration
definition: We define vertical quasi-integration as a 'close relationship which is based primarily upon the [firm's] dependence for a significant proportion of its total business upon a particular [firm]' (Blois, 1972: 267). Blois asserts that a relationship of this type involves an interdependence between the two firms such that it 'can be considered as a type of vertical integration without the legal form'.

name: Joint action
definition: Joint action reflects a move toward closer relationships which 'involves the parties carrying out the focal activities in a cooperative or coordinated way' (Heide and John, 1990: 25). It is viewed as governance process since it comprises a set of decision process mechanisms that determine the terms of exchange between the members of the dyad.

name: Board demographic diversity
authors_terms: ["board demographic diversity", "demographic diversity", "gender diversity", "racial diversity", "nationality diversity"]
definition: Following social psychological research on social categorization, we assess board demographic diversity using three characteristics of directors: (1) gender diversity, (2) racial diversity, and (3) nationality diversity. Gender, race, and nationality are categorical variables and thus, require that we operationalize diversity in terms of attribute variety.

name: Governance problems
definition: Based on prior research, our study considers two types of problems that can attract the attention of activist hedge funds: governance and performance problems. Governance problems raise concerns among shareholder activists about mismanagement and the potential for managers to undertake self-serving actions at the expense of shareholders.

name: Performance problems
definition: The second type of problem is performance problems, which we measure as a firm's stock-market performance relative to that of its industry peers. Performance problems can attract the attention of shareholder activists, who tend to target firms with lower financial performance in hopes of initiating strategic and operational changes.

name: Hedge fund activism targeting
authors_terms: ["hedge fund activism", "targeted by an activist hedge fund", "likelihood of being targeted"]
definition: Our focal dependent variable for Hypotheses 1(a) and 1(b) identifies instances where firms are targets of hedge fund activism. Hedge fund activism equals one for firm-years associated with hedge fund activism and zero otherwise.

name: Targeting by dedicated activist hedge funds
authors_terms: ["dedicated activist hedge funds", "dedicated hedge fund targeting"]
definition: According to Insightia, dedicated activist hedge funds are hedge funds 'who proactively and systematically identify' promising companies to target and for 'whom activist investments typically form a significant majority of their investment portfolios'. Nondedicated activist hedge funds, by contrast, rely more significantly on nonactivist investment strategies (e.g., long-short strategies) to derive their portfolio returns and thus, target firms more irregularly.

name: Firm response time to activist campaigns
definition: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 3(a) is the firms' response time, which is measured as the number of days that have lapsed between the announcement date of a hedge fund campaign and the date the firm responds to the activist with a formal decision of how to proceed. The longer a board takes to deliberate and respond to an activist, the longer the firms' response time and the higher the value.

name: Target acquiescence to activist campaigns
definition: By acquiescence, we refer to firms' tendencies to undertake activities that are likely to benefit activist hedge funds by increasing the share price in the short term. Acquiescent firms will undertake actions that aim to improve shareholder value in the aftermath of hedge fund activism.

name: Favorable host country currency change
authors_terms: ["favorable change in its host country currency", "positive change in the exchange rate", "depreciating value of the host country currency", "depreciation"]
definition: Here, a favorable change means that the host country currency of an MNC subsidiary is depreciated relative to other host countries' currencies, and the MNC subsidiary can therefore produce at a lower cost. Meanwhile, an unfavorable change indicates that the host country currency of an MNC subsidiary is appreciated relative to other host countries' currencies, and the MNC subsidiary will have higher production costs.

name: Subsidiary production change
authors_terms: ["change in production of a subsidiary", "percentage change in sales volume", "change in sales (or output) of a subsidiary", "Delta1 Pit"]
definition: In order to measure the production change of a subsidiary, we use the sales volume of the subsidiary. This sales information allows the examination of how production output in one subsidiary is related to the activities of subsidiaries in other host countries within the same MNC network.

name: Peer subsidiary production change
authors_terms: ["change in production of other subsidiaries in the same MNC", "percentage change in production of all other peer subsidiaries in the same MNC", "change in the level of intra-MNC production shifts", "Delta1 P-it"]
definition: In order to examine production shifts among foreign subsidiaries of the same MNC relating to Hypothesis 2, we include changes in the level of intra-MNC production shifts for the MNC's other subsidiaries. We measure this variable by subtracting the sales volume of a subsidiary from the total sales volume of its parent MNC, then computing the annual percentage change in sales volume for the remaining subsidiaries.

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: In order to test Hypothesis 3 which posits a positive impact of production increase on subsidiary performance, we measure subsidiary performance using return on assets (ROA).

name: Organizational disaster
authors_terms: ["disaster", "fatal accident", "fatal coal-mining accident", "fatal accident propensity", "fatal accident rate"]
definition: For the purposes of this study, I define a disaster as a coal-mining accident that results in one or more fatalities. This definition of disaster coincides with the most severe category in MSHA's own accident classification system (fatal accidents).

name: Minor accident experience
authors_terms: ["prior organizational experience with minor accidents", "minor accident experience", "direct minor accident experience"]
definition: The independent variables of interest in this study are counts of the numbers of disasters and minor accidents previously experienced by a focal mine, or by all other mines. Minor accidents are defined here as reportable mining accidents that did not result in permanent disability or death.

name: Disaster experience
authors_terms: ["prior disaster experience", "prior organizational experience with disaster", "direct fatal accident experience"]
definition: The independent variables of interest in this study are counts of the numbers of disasters and minor accidents previously experienced by a focal mine, or by all other mines.

name: Vicarious disaster experience
authors_terms: ["prior disaster experience at other organizations", "vicarious disaster experience", "others' fatal accident experience", "vicarious fatal accident experience"]
definition: Studies of organizational learning curves also document vicarious learning from experience, such that performance at a focal organization improves as a result of experience at other related or similar organizations. The independent variables of interest in this study are counts of the numbers of disasters and minor accidents previously experienced by a focal mine, or by all other mines.

name: Powerful stakeholder approval requests
authors_terms: ["powerful stakeholder requests", "farm association approval requests", "approval requests from powerful stakeholders"]
definition: Following the convention of defining power in terms of degree of dependence, we suggest that the most powerful stakeholders are those that have the greatest sway in affecting the lawmakers who oversee and determine an agency's resources, autonomy, and responsibility. As such, we consider farm associations that represent organized farmers to be the most powerful stakeholders of the USDA.

name: Peer agency assessments
authors_terms: ["peer agency memorandum", "FDA consultation", "positive memorandum from a peer agency"]
definition: During product review, an agency may look to peer agencies that it believes to possess pertinent evaluative abilities that can effectively identify sources of environmental hazards. Thus, by providing credible information and procedures to help the USDA better evaluate products' risks, an FDA consultation can serve as a shield against threats to procedural legitimacy.

name: Regulatory approval
authors_terms: ["GMO approval", "product approval", "rate of petition approval by the USDA"]
definition: Our dependent variable is GMO approval events by the USDA. We employed an event-history analysis to investigate the effects of stakeholder and peer agency product assessments on the rate of petition approval by the USDA.

name: Congressional electoral competitiveness
definition: Congressional electoral competitiveness is a measure of the closeness of political races between candidates.

name: GMO protests
definition: A protest is a form of public action that calls for the involvement of previously uninterested audiences in fostering change among organizations.

name: Foreign company
definition: Foreign biotechnology firms that develop GMOs in their home countries and then petition the USDA for approval in the United States may face unfavorable decisions, particularly if they develop and test their products under different regulatory supervision and decision procedures than those of the United States.

name: Technological novelty
definition: Genetically modified organisms characterized by novel components and technologies, such as new transgenic procedures, are at greater risk in regulatory review processes.

name: Target acquisition returns
authors_terms: ["target's returns from the deal", "target's returns", "cumulative abnormal returns (CAR)", "target's CAR"]
definition: The price offered by the acquirer to take over the target relative to the target's standalone value determines the target's returns and therefore how the synergistic gains created by the acquisition are allocated between the two merging companies.

name: Travel time to distant latent acquirers
authors_terms: ["time(target-DLAs)", "travel time between the target and its DLAs", "travel time to the DLAs"]
definition: The key independent variable is the average travel time between the focal target and its DLAs (labeled time(target-DLAs)) when the deal is announced. In the main analysis, DLAs are defined as the latent acquirers that are located more than 300 miles from the focal target.

name: Travel time to distant latent targets
authors_terms: ["time(acquirer-DLTs)", "travel time between the acquirer and its DLTs", "travel time to the DLTs"]
definition: The key independent variable is the average travel time between the focal acquirer and its DLTs (labeled time(acquirer-DLTs)) when the deal is announced. DLTs are defined as the latent targets that are located more than 300 miles from the focal acquirer.

name: Number of competing bids
authors_terms: ["number of competing bids", "number of competing bidders"]
definition: The number of competing bids for the target following the first bid. In the sample of this study, only 4.6% of the deals have observed competing bids.

name: Prior related experience
authors_terms: ["prior related experience", "prior related work experience", "prior occupational experience", "prior industry experience"]
definition: Prior related jobs, i.e., those comprised of similar work activities, should provide portable experience in that they impart knowledge and skill that a worker can transfer and apply to a new job. Consistent with previous studies, we focus on prior experience that is related through industry or occupation, as these are two important sources of task-relevant knowledge and skill.

name: Task-relevant knowledge and skill
authors_terms: ["task-relevant knowledge and skill", "knowledge and skill", "job knowledge", "competencies"]
definition: Task-relevant knowledge can result from work experience, but it is not the only outcome. The authors operationalize it with an archival rating of employees' most recent job competency evaluation; because the ratings are generated by the organization as part of its normal operation, they represent knowledge and skill that is valued by InsurCo specifically.

name: Job performance
definition: Performance is measured using the organization's annual performance review ratings, which summarize how well the worker has met the requirements of the job into a single score ranging from the best rating of 'clearly exceeds' to the worst rating of 'development needs.'

name: Firm experience
definition: We use firm tenure to represent work experience within the firm. It is the most common way that researchers have studied the effects of experience on performance.

name: Shareholder proposal activism
definition: Activism through shareholder proposals is a mechanism by which shareholders who desire changes in CSP attempt to influence managerial decisions: "Shareholder proposals formally and visibly signal discontent over CSP issues."

name: Corporate social performance
definition: Shareholder proposals are often used by activist investors such as social groups, individuals, churches, and large pension funds to direct attention, raise awareness, and challenge corporations to improve their 'corporate social performance' (CSP).

name: Managerial responsiveness to investor activism
definition: When faced with an activist shareholder proposal, firms have an option to challenge it and exclude it from the proxy, include it on the proxy for shareholder vote but oppose it, or settle prior to proxy inclusion. Each option varies in terms of its responsiveness to activist shareholders.

name: Stakeholder salience
definition: Stakeholder saliency is determined by the stakeholder's power to influence the firm, the legitimacy of the stakeholder's relationship with the firm, and the urgency of the stakeholder's claim on the firm.

name: Preceding acquisition premium
authors_terms: ["market's preceding acquisition premium", "preceding acquisition premium", "preceding deal premium", "the anchor"]
definition: The premium paid by another firm that made the acquisition directly preceding the focal deal in a given country and target industry (established by four-digit SIC code), which was calculated like the focal premium.

name: Focal acquisition premium
definition: Focal acquisition premium was calculated as the percentage difference between the offer price and the target firm's stock price four weeks before deal announcement.

name: Recency of the preceding acquisition
definition: Recency was calculated by number of days between the preceding and focal deal, then reversed so that higher values corresponded to more recent preceding deals. Information about more recent events is more readily available, making more recent events more salient.

name: Deal size similarity
authors_terms: ["deal size similarity", "size similarity", "similarity in deal size"]
definition: Deal size similarity reflected the percentage difference between the deal values of the preceding and focal deals, taken as an absolute value and reversed so that larger values indicated more similar deal sizes. Similarity in deal size increases decision makers' belief that their focal deal is like the anchor deal.

name: International acquisition
definition: International acquirers face considerably greater uncertainty than domestic acquirers due to cultural, economic, and institutional differences across countries, liabilities of foreignness, and more information asymmetry between firms located in different countries.

name: Related acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["related acquisition experience", "acquisition experience in the focal market", "task-related acquisition experience"]
definition: For related acquisition experience, the authors counted completed acquisitions that the firm made in the focal target industry prior to the acquisition, so it should capture related instead of unrelated experience. Task-related acquisition experience allows decision makers to transfer specific lessons to the focal deal.

name: Acquisition rate
authors_terms: ["acquisition rate", "number of deals in a short period prior to a focal deal"]
definition: Higher acquisition rates, i.e., the number of deals in a short period prior to a focal deal, constrain decision makers' time to set a premium. Acquisition rate was measured by counting the average number of acquisitions in the two years prior to the focal deal.

name: Cross-border connection facilitation
authors_terms: ["facilitate connections", "facilitate cross-border connections", "share international connections", "broker connections", "facilitate the formation of cross-border connections"]
definition: A migrant's enabling of members of their multiple networks to form connections, that is, facilitating connections among non-migrants in their home country organization and individuals in their host country. The authors examine this as a brokerage mechanism through which migrants enable the transfer of knowledge and resources across borders without direct involvement.

name: Home country gender parity
authors_terms: ["gender parity", "home country gender parity", "high-gender-parity home country"]
definition: Countries with high levels of gender parity are those with high levels of female education, health, and labor force or economic outcomes, and gender parity of a country has been found to correlate with opportunities for women and expectations of roles for men and women. In low-gender-parity countries the authors expect greater persistence of traditional gender roles and greater barriers to women obtaining optimal positions.

name: Host country gender parity
authors_terms: ["host country gender parity", "high-gender-parity host country", "gender parity level in the host country"]
definition: The gender parity level in the host country of the female migrant, which the authors expect reflects the extent to which women are supported in network facilitation and is correlated with the extent to which they connect home and host country individuals.

name: CEO change
authors_terms: ["CEO change", "CEO succession", "CEO turnover", "managerial succession", "leadership succession", "announcement of a CEO change"]
definition: This study intendedly focuses only on top leadership changes in large corporations, and it examines the stock market reaction to announced changes in CEO leadership.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["stock market reaction", "market reaction", "market value of the firm", "cumulative average residual", "abnormal return"]
definition: The cross-sectional responses to a CEO change are relatively pure aggregations of investors' perceptions of the future performance of the firm, and these daily perceptions, when analyzed longitudinally, provide a strong surrogate for actual economic performance.

name: Systematic risk
definition: Previous capital markets research strongly suggests a direct relationship between production/investment decisions and a firm's systematic risk, i.e. beta. In the longitudinal test the dependent variable is no longer the daily price change resulting from market reactions, but rather the shift in a firm's beta after a CEO succession.

name: Successor origin
authors_terms: ["successor origin", "insider and outsider successions", "insider versus outsider successor distinction"]
definition: Successor origin uses the traditional outsider versus insider successor distinction; each CEO change was recorded as having an insider, outsider, or unannounced successor.

name: Multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact (MMC), which is essentially the extent of market overlap between two firms, has been shown to affect the intensity of rivalry or multimarket competition. It is the degree to which pairs of rival firms compete across different product categories.

name: Knowledge protection
authors_terms: ["protect its knowledge-based resources", "knowledge protection", "protecting knowledge", "patent litigation"]
definition: Firms can use different mechanisms to protect their knowledge-based resources, such as secrecy, lead time, complementary assets, and patents, and may have to take competitive actions against rivals by initiating patent litigation in order to protect their knowledge.

name: Technological quality of knowledge
authors_terms: ["technological quality of the focal firm's knowledge-based resources", "technological quality", "forward patent citations"]
definition: Prior literature has shown that a firm's forward patent citations capture the technological quality of its knowledge; the technological quality of a firm's knowledge-based resources enhances the value of a firm's innovations and increases its shareholder value.

name: Rival's ability to protect knowledge
authors_terms: ["rival firm's ability to protect its knowledge-based resources", "rival's ability to protect its knowledge", "ability to retaliate"]
definition: The rival firm's ability to protect its knowledge-based resources, since rival firms that have initiated patent litigation have demonstrated the ability to protect their knowledge-based resources.

name: Junior stock exchanges
authors_terms: ["junior stock exchanges", "new growth exchanges", "new junior exchanges", "new IPO exchanges"]
definition: Junior stock exchanges are one example of institutional intermediaries, an increasingly common prescription in emerging economies to facilitate flows of financial capital to new firms. Their general purpose is to benefit small firms that could not otherwise raise capital on public exchanges because they lacked the required size, growth, profitability, or stability, and most are restricted by rules or norms to technology firms.

name: Technology firm
definition: A new venture is a technology firm if the focal firm is engaged in a technical business. The authors note that this coding reflects only the classification of a firm into an industry category and is not reflective of the firm's innovativeness or other technical qualities.

name: Initial capital
definition: Initial capitalization is measured as the log value of the opening capital account when the firm was founded, in thousands of constant 2009 yen. The authors select initial capital to represent the commitment of financial resources that providers and stakeholders make to the firm at its outset.

name: New firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth", "pre-IPO growth", "compound annual growth rate of sales revenue"]
definition: Pre-IPO growth is assessed using the compound annual growth rate of sales revenue since founding. The authors use a standard compound annual growth rate calculation that takes the nth root of the total percentage growth rate, where n is the number of years in the period considered.

name: Reputation
definition: Reputation is determined by the value or quality of one's previous actions. In this study context, reputational signals correspond to the research achievements of a scientist (i.e., publications and citations).

name: Status
definition: Status is a 'socially constructed, intersubjectively agreed-upon and accepted ordering or ranking of individuals, groups, organizations, or activities in a social system.' In this study context, status signals correspond to the prestige of the university from which the scientist graduated, independent of his/her research and publication achievements.

name: Alliance formation
authors_terms: ["alliance formation", "likelihood of an alliance being formed"]
definition: The likelihood that an incumbent and a newly created firm will form an alliance; the first dependent variable, used for comparability to prior alliance research.

name: Alliance timing
authors_terms: ["alliance timing", "timing of the alliance", "timing of formation", "stage at signing", "stage in the commercialization process"]
definition: The stage in the commercialization process in which the alliance is formed; the earlier the stage in which an alliance is formed, the greater the uncertainty regarding the product's commercial prospects.

name: Science distance
definition: Science distance in an invention is the distance between multiple knowledge domains on which the invention is based. It captures the breadth of knowledge domains that are combined in an invention.

name: Prior licensing experience
definition: Prior licensing experience is the licensing record of an inventor team's members; licensing experience provides higher levels of shared knowledge between an inventor team and a licensee firm, enabling them to more clearly explain the technology and tailor their knowledge transfer efforts to the needs of the licensee firm.

name: Prior collaboration experience
authors_terms: ["prior collaboration experience", "prior joint work experience", "prior collaborative ties", "density of prior collaborations"]
definition: Prior joint work experience is used as a proxy for preexisting stocks of common ground that can be leveraged in the coordination situation. Prior collaboration experience alleviates within-team coordination costs by enabling participants to generate shared mental models.

name: Licensing likelihood
definition: The hazard (likelihood) of licensing of an invention, i.e., the likelihood that a given invention will be licensed.

name: Experiencing privatization
authors_terms: ["privatization", "experiencing privatization", "privatized SOEs", "privatized from an existing state-owned or collectively owned firm"]
definition: We explore the latter possibility in the context of privatization in China by considering privatization as a harm-inflicting firm action. Because privatization was a nationwide policy, privatized SOEs and their leaders were less likely to be perceived as irresponsible when laying off workers.

name: Corporate philanthropy
definition: Following prior studies in the Chinese context, we measured corporate philanthropy using charitable contributions. The 2006 and 2008 surveys asked firms to report the amount of their charitable contributions since their registration as private firms.

name: Layoffs during privatization
authors_terms: ["privatization with layoffs", "layoffs", "the privatization of an SOE resulted in more layoffs"]
definition: The privatization of SOEs created harm because of layoffs. The scale of layoffs varied across SOEs due to their particular conditions at the time.

name: Province unemployment rate
authors_terms: ["province unemployment rate", "unemployment rate", "higher rate of unemployment at the time of privatization"]
definition: Layoffs could inflict even greater harm in areas already stricken by unemployment. Because the surveys asked about firms' postal codes, we measured the unemployment rate in the province where a privatized SOE was located in the year before its registration as private.

name: Leader involvement in privatization
authors_terms: ["involvement in privatization", "owner involved in privatization", "the leader of a privatized SOE was involved in the privatization"]
definition: Involvement in the planning and execution of privatization is likely to cause firm leaders to feel at least partially responsible for the resulting harm inflicted on laid-off workers and their families. As a result, they are more likely to feel guilty and engage in corporate philanthropy as a form of restitution.

name: Confucian influence
definition: Confucian values have three elements, with ren emphasizing benevolence to or compassion for others, yi representing the principle of moral rightness, and li specifying many concrete norms for social relationships. These three values together promote good deeds and discourage harmful acts toward others.

name: Leader tenure in the SOE
authors_terms: ["owner SOE tenure", "tenure in the SOE", "longer tenure in the SOE"]
definition: The longer firm leaders worked for their SOEs, the stronger their social ties with workers. This reasoning suggests that firm leaders' tenure in their SOEs was likely to intensify the feeling of guilt aroused by privatization.

name: Guilt
definition: nei jiu is personal guilt aroused by one's own action that violates the deservedness of, or fails to uphold an obligation to, another person, and it is always felt toward another person. Guilt, by bringing out an other-oriented focus, draws one further away from the self but closer to harmed others.

name: Philanthropic intention
authors_terms: ["philanthropic intention", "charitable intention", "intention to engage in philanthropy"]
definition: The subjects answered questions about their intention to engage in philanthropy after their firm's financial conditions improved. In Study 3, we conducted a vignette experiment to directly test the mediating effect of guilt between privatization and philanthropic intention.

name: Harm to laid-off workers
definition: The large-scale layoffs inflicted great harm on many individuals and their families. Layoffs can create serious physical and mental distress because it often takes a long time for those who have been laid off to find new jobs, and they experience significant wage cuts when reemployed.

name: Rating difference between competitors
authors_terms: ["comparative restaurant rating differential", "difference in i's and j's rating", "rating scale differential", "diff in i's and j's rating"]
definition: We created an overall restaurant rating based on the mean of a restaurant's food, décor, and service scores, and then calculated the difference between restaurant i's and j's rating in year t − 1. This is the performance consequence of a basic rating disparity, which captures potential quality differences between restaurants and the publicization and increased accessibility of these differences.

name: Sales disparity between competitors
authors_terms: ["relative disparity in sales", "difference in sales between restaurants i and j", "competitors' sales differentials", "comparative sales"]
definition: The outcome measure used in this study is the urban CPI-deflated difference in sales between restaurants i and j in year t. Our outcome variable thus represents yearly sales performance differences for private firms.

name: Availability of ratings information
authors_terms: ["availability of information concerning the rating difference", "accessibility of ratings information", "online restaurant rating platform entry/expansion period", "ease of access to ratings information"]
definition: The entry and expansion of online restaurant rating systems made it far easier for consumers to access ratings information. The biggest change to the industry over the past few decades has not been the content itself, but rather the expanded coverage of, and ease of access to, this content.

name: Tourist market segment
authors_terms: ["tourist-focused market segments", "both i and j located in a tourist area", "areas with a high concentration of tourists", "tourist-concentrated"]
definition: In the New York City restaurant market, tourists represent the prototypical consumer segment that has comparatively less local information and, thus, a greater need for ratings information. Local residents, by contrast, have other sources of information about restaurants—be it first-hand experience, word-of-mouth, or from coverage by local media sources—that make ratings information relatively less useful.

name: Price tier
authors_terms: ["most expensive price point", "highest price-tier ($$$$)", "high price segment", "expensive price-point"]
definition: Just as with the tourist segment (compared with locals), the relative value of ratings information should be greater for those consumers who are making particularly expensive dining decisions compared with those seeking less costly dining options. We should, therefore, expect to observe even greater sales performance implications from ratings information for firms serving the high price segment of the market.

name: Firm error
definition: We use the term 'error' to describe an event associated with a firm that carries adverse consequences. Managers in the chemical industry consider industrial accidents to be serious errors, so the authors used industrial accidents at chemical plants as the measure of error.

name: Peer firm stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["spillover harm", "spillover", "negative spillover", "industrywide harm", "harm to other firms"]
definition: Just as one firm's successes can 'spill over' to other firms, so too can its problems, so that firms with operations in the same industry suffer harm from an error at another firm. The authors measure the degree to which accidents 'harmed' other firms in the industry by evaluating the stock price movements of other firms with chemical operations following each accident.

name: Major industry crisis
definition: A major crisis can be a catalyst for shifts in stakeholder perceptions of an industry, causing stakeholders to update their beliefs about the reliability and accountability of other firms in the same industry. A major crisis alters perceptions of an industry, so that future problems within the industry carry the risk of more severe industrywide harm.

name: Industry self-regulatory institution
definition: Interest in self-regulatory institutions, whereby firms in an industry create and voluntarily abide by a set of governing rules. In many industrial settings antitrust laws forbid centralized industry bodies from controlling and sanctioning member firm behaviors, and so industry self-regulation tends to take the form of a private and decentralized institution.

name: Self-regulatory institution membership
authors_terms: ["ACC member", "Responsible Care member", "membership", "perpetrator in Responsible Care"]
definition: Membership in the parent association, the American Chemistry Council, assigned a value of 1 if the ACC listed the company as a member in a given year and 0 otherwise. From 1990 onward, participation in Responsible Care was a condition of membership in the ACC.

name: Acquisition performance
authors_terms: ["acquisition performance", "focal acquisition performance", "announcement returns", "immediate acquisition returns", "analysts' ratings"]
definition: The dependent variable, acquisition performance, is the level of wealth that acquirors generate from their focal acquisition. The article introduces multiple measures of acquisition performance: namely, announcement returns and analysts' ratings; while both measures estimate acquisition performance, they are conceptually distinct.

name: Similarity of prior acquisitions
authors_terms: ["similarity of prior acquisitions", "similarity of the businesses of prior acquisitions", "similarity of the business of prior acquisitions to each other"]
definition: Similarity of Prior Acquisitions measures the similarity of the business of prior acquisitions to each other. Prior acquisitions that are highly similar or dissimilar to one another will negatively relate to focal acquisition performance.

name: Small acquisition losses
authors_terms: ["small acquisition losses", "small losses", "small acquisition mistakes", "acquisition losses"]
definition: Small acquisition losses is the number of times a firm recorded an announcement loss of less than 3% as measured by the cumulative abnormal return methodology. Small losses from prior acquisitions promote learning and superior performance on subsequent acquisitions.

name: Timing of prior acquisitions
authors_terms: ["timing of prior acquisitions", "mean number of days between prior acquisitions", "intervals between acquisitions"]
definition: Timing of prior acquisitions is the mean number of days between prior acquisitions, excluding the focal acquisition.

name: Timing of focal acquisition
authors_terms: ["timing of focal acquisition", "the time elapsed between the focal acquisition and the one before it"]
definition: Timing of focal acquisition is the number of days between the focal acquisition and the one before it.

name: Acquisition experience
authors_terms: ["acquisition experience", "firm acquisition experience", "recent acquisitions undertaken by the firm"]
definition: Firm acquisition experience is the sum of recent acquisitions undertaken by the firm, from 1985 to the focal deal. Firms that made their first acquisition during the focal period (1990-1995) received an experience score of 0.

name: Fit with institutionalized professional norms
authors_terms: ["normfit", "fit with dominant norms", "product appropriateness", "fit with extant professional norms", "poor fit with extant professional norms"]
definition: The degree to which a product category accords with institutionalized professional norms of 'sound asset management' held by financial analysts. Index and SRI funds are considered contrary to these norms, while regional and industry funds are fully in line with extant norms of appropriate products.

name: Time to imitation
authors_terms: ["imitation lag", "lag times to imitation", "time to imitation", "speed to imitation", "slower imitators"]
definition: The lag from a first industry-pioneering adoption of a product category until another firm adopts that category. The analysis models the hazard of adoption, that is, the marginal likelihood of a firm adopting a product for the first time.

name: Ownership type
definition: The majority ownership of a mutual fund firm. The authors identify three ownership groups whose reasoning regarding challenging norms differed: privately held firms, union-held firms, and state-owned firms.

name: Analyst intensity
authors_terms: ["analyst intensity", "invested in financial analysts", "relative strength of the analyst collective", "core competences of mutual fund firms"]
definition: The degree to which a firm is invested in the professional group of financial analysts, which became regarded as the mutual fund firms' core competence and an important internal referent for the appropriateness of new product categories.

name: Environmental change
definition: Deregulation, on October 24, 1978, removed those regulatory controls and was a discontinuous environmental change that affected the industry's competitive environment.

name: Change in strategic orientation
authors_terms: ["change in strategic orientation", "core feature change", "change in core features"]
definition: Fundamental changes in product-market strategic orientation occur when organizations change from specialism to generalism, or broaden their niches, and when they change from generalism to specialism, or narrow their niches.

name: Organizational age
definition: The age of an airline was calculated by subtracting the time of founding from the time of any change in strategic orientation or failure.

name: Organizational size
definition: We used the natural logarithm of airline assets at the time of any change in strategic orientation or of failure as an indicator of the size of an airline.

name: Prior strategic change experience
authors_terms: ["cumulative changes in strategic orientation", "prior experience with such change", "cumulative change", "history of changes", "momentum"]
definition: These variables capture the cumulative number of changes in strategic orientation that each airline had experienced up to the time of a change or failure. When organizations repeat changes that they have experienced in the past, their change processes are said to have momentum.

name: Organizational failure
definition: Failure was defined as an organization's ceasing operations and disbanding or as its acquisition and merger into the operations of a new parent organization.

name: Voluntary turnover
definition: The rate at which employees quit voluntarily; the authors focus on voluntary turnover exclusively, not on the sum of quit and discharge rates, since the etiology and consequences of these phenomena vary.

name: Workforce performance
definition: Intermediate workforce performance measures, operationally defined as the organization-level outcomes of the behaviors (i.e., productivity and safety) of key employee groups.

name: HRM inducements and investments
authors_terms: ["HRM inducements and investments", "HRM index", "investments and inducements", "commitment systems"]
definition: HRM practices that ensure a high-quality human capital pool, termed investments, and those that enhance retention, termed inducements. Investment-oriented practices are those, like training, that directly contribute to human capital accumulations over time, and those, like job stability, that indirectly do so.

name: Financial performance
definition: The ultimate financial performance of organizations, measured in Study 2 by operating ratio and return on equity.

name: Industry self-categorization
authors_terms: ["industry self-categorization", "industry categories", "industry-based peers", "peers in primary SIC code"]
definition: We defined industry self-categorization as the number of companies in a peer group that had the same 2-digit SIC code as the board's own company. A board's performance comparison is assumed to be anchored in an industry category to the extent that its chosen peer group consists of many other firms from within the same 2-digit SIC category as the board's own company.

name: Peer discussion
definition: To test H2, we measured the amount of peer discussion by counting the number of sentences within the 'Report of the Compensation Committee' section of a company's 1993 proxy statement that contained any reference to peer companies.

name: Firm performance
definition: Company performance was operationalized using two indices: the log of the five-year total shareholder return on the company's stock for the period 1988-1992, and the average annual return on assets from 1988 through 1992. When performance comparisons place a firm in a negative position relative to industry peers, boards should seek broader comparisons.

name: Industry performance
authors_terms: ["industry performance", "performance of a firm's primary industry"]
definition: To measure industry performance, total annual return and market capitalization data were collected from COMPUSTAT on all firms for each 2-digit SIC code represented in our sample. The 1988-1992 five-year performance of each industry group was calculated using the method specified by the SEC in CFR 229.402.1 (1993).

name: CEO compensation
authors_terms: ["CEO compensation", "CEO salary", "CEO pay", "CEO annual pay", "long-term compensation"]
definition: We incorporated two major components of CEO compensation into our regression models: CEO annual pay, operationalized as the sum of a CEO's 1992 base salary and bonus, and long-term compensation, operationalized as the logged gain realized by the exercise of any stock options or restricted stock by the CEO in 1992.

name: Ownership power
authors_terms: ["ownership power", "owner power", "concentrated outside ownership", "powerful outside owners"]
definition: We operationalized owner power as whether there were any outsiders listed as significant shareholders, a significant shareholder being anyone who controls 5 percent or more of the company's outstanding common stock. Large investors are not easily manipulated by company persuasion campaigns, and concentrated ownership transfers power to shareholders.

name: Shareholder activism
definition: This variable was defined as the number of resolutions presented by shareholders that were to be voted on at the 1993 shareholder meeting, as listed in the company's 1993 proxy statement. Larger numbers of shareholder resolutions are indicative of greater levels of shareholder activism.

name: Peer-group performance
authors_terms: ["peer-group performance", "average peer-group performance", "5-yr. cum. peer group returns"]
definition: To test H5, we defined peer-group performance as the average five-year total shareholder return of all peer groups reported in the performance graph of a company's 1993 proxy statement. Our measure represents the value on 12/31/92 of $100 invested on 1/1/88 in the stock of the companies comprising a focal company's peer groups.

name: Charismatic leadership
authors_terms: ["charismatic leadership", "charisma", "charismatic CEO", "charismatic leader", "salience of charismatic leadership"]
definition: The term 'charismatic leadership' has been used to describe a subset of leaders who 'by the force of their personal abilities are capable of having profound and extraordinary effects on followers'. The charismatic leader is one who gains trust, affection, and willing obedience of employees and who can generate excitement and motivation among employees as they pursue organizational goals.

name: External financial support
authors_terms: ["external support for the organization", "financial support for the organization", "attractiveness of a company", "investment in a company's stock", "stock price appreciation", "willingness to invest money in a troubled firm"]
definition: Support from outside constituencies, such as suppliers, customers, and outside investors, that leaders can secure for the organization. In this study it is evidenced by investors' willingness to commit money to a company, either by paying increased prices for its stock or by allocating funds to its stock.

name: Economic conditions
definition: The general economic climate in which sampled firms were operating, measured both at the macro level and with a more industry-specific measure of the conditions facing firms in the sample.

name: Turnaround prospects
authors_terms: ["turnaround information", "business prospects", "information about a possible organizational turnaround", "information about Apple's future"]
definition: Information about the direction of an organization's prospects as it attempts a turnaround: positive forecasts combined with objective data about the current financial position make a turnaround clearly evident, while negative forecasts make the prospects more dubious.

name: Stock endowment
authors_terms: ["endowment", "endowment of stock", "prior commitment to the organization"]
definition: A prior commitment to the organization, such as an endowment of stock in the company, which is posited to make an individual particularly susceptible to charismatic influence.

name: Risk propensity
authors_terms: ["risk propensity", "risk propensities of followers", "propensity to assume risk", "risk-taking", "willingness to engage in risky behavior"]
definition: An individual's propensity for risk, which charismatic leaders may influence by leading followers to frame investment decisions in a less skeptical manner, resulting in a greater acceptance of risk.

name: Illegal corporate behavior
definition: We investigated only cases in which a firm's agents—managers or employees with authority to take action—knowingly engaged in illegal acts. These were violations in which the law assumed a firm acted with knowledge or intent and the courts ruled that the firm was guilty of illegal behavior.

name: Environmental munificence
