definition: An environment with scarce resources increases the uncertainty facing a firm, and managers will take action to reduce that uncertainty, including engaging in illegal activities when they experience difficulty acquiring the resources necessary for survival. An environment with scarce resources will exhibit little or no growth in value added since firms will attempt to operate as efficiently as possible.

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism incorporates characteristics of Aldrich's (1979) stability-instability and turbulence constructs. Dynamism involves both the degree of turnover characteristic of an industry and the interconnections among elements and organizations in a firm's environment.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: This aspect of complexity (Aldrich, 1979; Dess & Beard, 1984) refers to the degrees of similarity and diversity of the organizations and individuals in a firm's environment; high uncertainty and competitiveness are associated with a heterogeneous, or diverse, environment.

name: Financial performance
definition: Since the primary goal assumed to be guiding corporations is profitability, poor or declining financial performance has been one of the most frequently posited antecedents of corporate illegality. Poor performance pressures firms to find alternative sources of resources or to cut costs in ways that may not be legal.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["organization size", "large firm size", "large organization size", "number of employees"]
definition: Previous researchers have developed several measures of size, but its major aspects—sales, assets, and number of employees—are highly intercorrelated (Kimberly, 1976). We chose number of employees because it is the most common measure of size (Hall, 1987).

name: Organizational slack
authors_terms: ["organizational slack", "low organizational slack", "unabsorbed slack", "excess resources", "slack resources"]
definition: Organizational slack is the excess that remains once a firm has paid its various internal and external constituencies to maintain their cooperation. Firms with slack resources have more alternatives to illegal behavior than firms without slack.

name: Prior violations
authors_terms: ["prior violations", "history of prior violations", "history of violating the law", "prior convictions"]
definition: A history of prior violations of the law can indicate that a firm engages in a pattern of wrongdoing. Firms may become committed to illegal activities (Finney & Lesieur, 1982), resulting in repeated violations.

name: Industry membership
definition: The industry in which a firm operates may be related to the extent to which it engages in illegal behavior for at least two reasons: illegal behavior is more frequent in some industries than in others, and surveillance and legal enforcement is more strict in some industries than in others.

name: Type of violation
authors_terms: ["type of violation", "type of illegal behavior", "type of illegality"]
definition: It is possible that a particular type of violation may depend on particular antecedent conditions—one combination of antecedents may result in discrimination, another in product liability problems. The type of illegality in which a firm engages is a situational variable because it represents a characteristic of a specific situation.

name: Defined benefit pension utilization
authors_terms: ["DB utilization", "DB plan utilization", "DB pension utilization", "rates of DB participation"]
definition: DB utilization is measured as the log number of DB participants. The number of participants in a DB plan, controlling for the size of the firm, represents the extent to which a company relies on these plans to remunerate its entire workforce.

name: Passive financial investor ownership
authors_terms: ["passive financial share ownership", "passive finance investors", "passive financial investors"]
definition: Passive financial investors, which include mutual funds, insurance companies, and investment banks, are the most prevalent shareowner type of U.S. corporations today. These investors are considered passive because, though they can vary in the extent to which they engage with their investments, they typically do not engage directly in issues related to corporate governance.

name: Active financial investor ownership
authors_terms: ["active financial share ownership", "active finance investors", "active financial investors"]
definition: I refer to these investors as 'active' financial investors because they typically participate in the management and/or corporate governance of their investments. Included in this category are private equity firms, venture capital firms, hedge funds, and other private investors and groups known for taking an active role in management.

name: Dedicated institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["dedicated investors", "dedicated share ownership", "dedicated institutional share ownership"]
definition: Dedicated investors desire longer-term dividend income and capital appreciation, thereby providing more stable, longer-term share ownership. These investors acquire concentrated positions in a smaller number of firms, have extended investment horizons, and are characterized by large investments and low stock turnover.

name: Transient institutional ownership
authors_terms: ["transient investors", "transient share ownership", "transient financial share ownership"]
definition: Transient investors tend to acquire less-concentrated equity stakes in a large number of firms and have high portfolio turnover. A preference for short-term earnings, diversified holdings, and high portfolio turnover leads transient investors to devalue long-term firm strategies.

name: Firm unionization
definition: Employee power can be enhanced greatly when workers mobilize and act collectively. The primary means by which employees can do so is via unionization, which provides workers an institutionalized apparatus to exert influence on firms by engaging in or threatening strikes and slowdowns and expressing worker demands through collective bargaining.

name: Code-of-conduct violations
definition: We measure the extent to which factories adhere to codes of conduct as the number of violations in each audit, obtained from the social auditing firm's database. During an audit, the auditors code a common set of dichotomous indicators (violation or no violation) in each category.

name: Ongoing auditor-supplier relationship
definition: If auditors repeatedly inspect the same supplier, they are more likely to focus on the domains they highlighted previously and to align their perspectives with that of management, whereas a new audit team would bring a fresh set of eyes and focus on different issues, likely uncovering new violations.

name: Auditor team tenure
definition: Auditors' tenure on the job is associated with their level of professional knowledge, their place in the audit firm's organizational hierarchy, and their professional self-concept. We measure an auditor's experience as his or her years of service at the auditing firm based on data from the auditing firm's database.

name: Auditor professionalization
definition: Education and training are important sources of professional socialization that should impart to monitors both the skills to detect more violations and the sense of professional obligation to report violations to their principal.

name: Audit team gender composition
definition: Research has suggested that, even when constrained by bureaucratic rules and roles, men and women may perform their work 'somewhat differently.' This evidence suggests that supply chain auditors' gender will influence whether they detect and cite violations.

name: Audit team gender diversity
definition: We expect that mixed-gender audit teams will exhibit superior performance because they benefit from the complementarity of men's and women's different perceptual styles and from performance-enhancing interpersonal team dynamics.

name: Newness of external technology linkage
authors_terms: ["newness of a patent's external technology linkage", "newness of external technology linkage", "external technology linkage"]
definition: A patent's external technology linkage is defined as the patent's citations of prior patents owned by other firms. The newness of this linkage reflects how recently the cited external inventions were made, so that a higher value indicates that the focal patent cites newer patents of other firms.

name: Patent pledge likelihood
authors_terms: ["patent pledged", "likelihood that the patent will be used as loan collateral", "likelihood of the patent being pledged"]
definition: The likelihood that a specific patent offered by a borrowing firm passes the lender's due diligence check and is accepted and used as loan collateral. A 'security agreement' record indicates that a patent was pledged as loan collateral, and the lender typically has the final say on whether the patent offered by the borrower will be accepted.

name: Firm-specificity of patent assets
authors_terms: ["firm-specificity of borrowing firms' patent assets", "firm-specificity in a firm's patent assets"]
definition: A knowledge asset is considered specific to a firm if its value to the firm exceeds its second-best use value in an alternative business setting.

name: Technological domain specialization
authors_terms: ["a firm's specialization in a focal patent's technological domain", "firm's technology domain specialization"]
definition: A firm specializing in a technological domain puts greater effort and produces more patents in this domain relative to other domains, compared to other industry players. The construct compares a firm's focus on the focal technological domain versus the firm's focus on other domains.

name: Proportional representation of women among business owners
authors_terms: ["proportional representation", "local proportional representation of women among business owners", "proportional representation of female-owned businesses", "women's proportional representation among proprietorship owners"]
definition: The theory is based on proportional representation within geographic areas, defined as each area's female-owned proprietorship count divided by its total proprietorship count. The independent variable of interest is women's proportional representation among proprietorship owners in each zip code on January 1 of each yearly observation.

name: Relative survival duration of female-owned businesses
authors_terms: ["survival duration ratio of female- to male-owned businesses", "relative survival duration", "relative survivorship", "female/male owner hazard ratio"]
definition: The survival duration of female-owned businesses relative to that of male-owned businesses. The exponentiated coefficient is the hazard ratio, defined as the ratio of the estimated instantaneous hazard rate of female-owned to that of male-owned businesses.

name: Local bank presence
authors_terms: ["local bank presence", "presence of banks", "number of bank branches in a zip code"]
definition: Local banks are a source of financing for small firms, and small firms often are dependent on local bank branches, which are often given autonomy to adapt lending routines to local norms. The authors argue that an increase in local proportional representation should improve relative survival duration more when there are many banks.

name: Local customer presence
authors_terms: ["local customer presence", "customer presence in zip", "count of McDonald's"]
definition: The ability to attract customers is a key success factor for any business, and small businesses try to find locations within their area that are most likely to attract customers. Customer presence is proxied by the count of McDonald's in a zip code.

name: Local networking opportunities
definition: Social networks within a geographic area are a source of knowledge and information resources for small business owners. A high density of business owners among residents in a community increases these networking opportunities.

name: Absorptive capacity
definition: ACAP refers to 'a firm's ability to acquire, assimilate, transform, and exploit new knowledge' (Zahra and George, 2002).

name: Entrepreneurial orientation
definition: EO refers to the 'strategymaking practices, management philosophies, and firm-level behaviors that are entrepreneurial in nature' (Anderson, Covin, and Slevin, 2009: 220); EO captures an organizational decision-making posture favoring entrepreneurial activities, strategic decisions, and managerial philosophies.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: Financial performance is examined through growth, since 'growth is a key indicator of successful small firms and a central ambition of technology-based firms.'

name: Founder CEO
authors_terms: ["founder chief executive officer", "founder CEO", "founder-led firms", "active founders"]
definition: The chief executive officer is defined as the highest-level manager of the firm and included the role names CEO, chief executive officer, and President for this sample. Founder identity was collected by survey from firm agents, and the influence of the founder is tied, at least in part, to the identification of individuals as founders within the idiosyncratic firm management and ownership structure.

name: Inside board representation
authors_terms: ["percent board insiders", "percentage of inside members of the board of directors", "insider board control"]
definition: A ratio of the number of inside board members to total board members at IPO. An inside board member is defined as any member of the board of directors who was, or ever had been, a member of management, or was a member or descendent of the company founder's family or a representative or beneficiary of any legal entity set up in the founder's family's name.

name: CEO-chair duality
authors_terms: ["CEO/Chair duality", "dual roles of chief executive officer and chair of the board of directors"]
definition: Coded as 1 if one individual holds the positions of chief executive officer and chair of the board of directors simultaneously at IPO.

name: Corporate investor board representation
authors_terms: ["corporate investor board member", "outside corporate investor representatives on the board of directors"]
definition: A corporate investor firm is defined as any corporation owning a portion of the firm before public shares are sold. A corporate investor board member is a member of the firm board of directors who is identified as holding a seat on behalf of the corporate investor before public shares are sold.

name: Corporate equity ownership
definition: The percentage of firm ownership held by corporate investors before public shares are sold.

name: CEO equity ownership
definition: The percentage of firm ownership held by the CEO after public shares are sold.

name: Founder equity ownership
definition: The sum total of all founder equity as a percentage of firm ownership after completion of the IPO. This variable includes the influence of non-CEO founders in directing management structure.

name: Public equity released at IPO
authors_terms: ["percent public equity released", "percentage of the firm to sell", "percent of firm offered at IPO"]
definition: The percentage of firm ownership released for purchase at IPO. This number is operationalized as 100 percent less the percent share ownership of the top management team, including all members of the board of directors, after public shares are sold.

name: Price premium over book value
definition: One measure that has been applied to the assessment of investor optimism about the future value of firms at IPO is the percent price premium [(share price-book value per share)/share price]. This measure uses both accounting-based and stock price information in an effort to measure 'difficult to account for' assets of the firm.

name: CSR scope conformity
authors_terms: ["scope conformity", "CSR scope conformity", "conformity in CSR scope"]
definition: We defined scope conformity as the extent to which the focal firm's CSR portfolio resembled practices defined in the established guidelines; this mainly captured variation along the scope dimension of a firm's CSR practice.

name: CSR emphasis differentiation
authors_terms: ["emphasis differentiation", "CSR emphasis differentiation", "differentiation in CSR emphasis"]
definition: The second measure, emphasis differentiation, was defined as the extent to which a firm's pattern of CSR emphasis deviates from the common patterns of other firms in the same industry.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: We considered an analyst to be covering a firm in year t if that analyst has issued an annual earnings forecast for that firm's fiscal period ending in year t.

name: Analyst recommendation
definition: We used the mean investment recommendation for each firm i in year t as one of the dependent variables of our study. The dependent variable is the average of all investment recommendations published by the analysts that followed the firm.

name: Firm market value
definition: We used Tobin's q to measure each firm's market value, which was calculated as the sum of the market value of equity and book value of debt over the book value of total assets.

name: State ownership
definition: We constructed a dummy variable to indicate a firm's ownership type based on the status of the firm's ultimate controllers. Firms that are controlled by state asset-management agencies or other government agencies are regarded as SOEs; otherwise, they are regarded as nonstate owned.

name: Firm visibility
definition: Firm visibility was operationalized by a firm's advertising intensity. This variable was calculated as the ratio of selling and administrative expenses to sales. It captures a firm's willingness to spend on marketing and selling-related activities in an effort to differentiate itself from competitors.

name: High-status brokerage houses coverage
definition: High-status houses coverage is measured by the ratio of star houses to the total number of brokerage houses that cover a firm. If a brokerage house has analyst teams on the New Fortune Best Analyst list, we coded the brokerage house as a star house.

name: Earnings pressure
definition: Earnings pressure is used to account for the extent to which firm performance meets analysts' expectations. This variable is measured as the difference between analysts' consensus forecasts of a firm's earnings in year t and the firm's actual earnings for year t.

name: Relational capital
definition: Relational capital refers to the level of mutual trust, respect, and friendship that arises out of close interaction at the individual level between alliance partners; it resides upon close interaction at the personal level between alliance partners.

name: Integrative conflict management
authors_terms: ["conflict management", "integrative conflict management", "integrative process of conflict management"]
definition: Integrative conflict management entails joint management of conflict with mutual concern for 'win-win' for all concerned. It engenders a communication- and contact-intensive process of conflict management.

name: Learning from the alliance partner
authors_terms: ["learning", "learning from the alliance partner", "degree of learning achieved"]
definition: Learning in alliances refers to learning that involves the acquisition or internalization of some critical information, know-how, or capability possessed by the partner.

name: Protection of proprietary assets
authors_terms: ["protection of proprietary assets", "protecting core proprietary assets", "protection of core proprietary assets", "crown jewels"]
definition: Firms want to protect some of their own core proprietary capabilities from being unilaterally absorbed or appropriated by the partner, and to prevent the leakage of critical know-how between them.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Reputation-i.e., stakeholders' perceptions of a firm's ability to deliver value along key dimensions of performance. These perceptions are based on the firm's demonstrated ability to create value-a characteristic that distinguishes reputation from other related constructs, such as celebrity, status, and legitimacy.

name: Sector legitimation
authors_terms: ["sector legitimation", "legitimation of an emerging sector", "legitimation process"]
definition: Sector legitimation-defined as 'the process of social construction of legitimacy' (Bitektine, 2011: 152) that unfolds within a nascent domain-influences the 'collective structuration . . . of entire fields or sectors of organizational life.'

name: Likelihood to invest in an emerging sector
authors_terms: ["likelihood to invest in an emerging sector", "likelihood that it will invest in an emerging sector"]
definition: Whether a VC firm invests in at least one startup in an emerging sector; the variable takes a value of 1 if the focal VC firm invested in at least one clean energy startup and 0 otherwise.

name: Use of syndication
definition: Syndication is particularly relevant when investing in sectors in which the VC firm has less experience, because it reduces the investment risk that these firms take through sharing information and knowledge.

name: Use of later-stage investment
definition: Later-stage investment is appealing for VCs with less experience in a given technology or sector, because later-stage startups usually need less hands-on coaching and do not require specific technical expertise.

name: Level of commitment
authors_terms: ["level of commitment", "level of commitment", "low levels of commitment"]
definition: We conceptualize level of commitment as the total resources, time, and effort that a VC firm commits to a given sector, relative to its activity across all sectors in a period of time.

name: Acquisition foreshadowing
definition: We label that technique foreshadowing, meaning that the firm issues intentionally vague information about the possibility of future involvement in an activity or event that potentially is controversial. Foreshadowing entails releasing vague information about potential future strategic activity in advance of a detailed announcement of a strategic move.

name: Security analyst downgrades
authors_terms: ["analyst downgrades", "analysts downgrading their recommendation of the firm", "analysts downgrading", "analysts downgrading after the SEO"]
definition: Analyst downgrades count the number of analysts downgrading their recommendation of the firm; analyst downgrades are important as they are often associated with decreased market valuations, less access to capital markets, and a greater effect on trading than upgrades.

name: Analyst recommendation dispersion
authors_terms: ["analyst recommendation dispersion", "dispersion in analysts' stock recommendations", "recommendation dispersion", "analyst uncertainty about the firm"]
definition: The dispersion in analysts' stock recommendations for a firm represents a common operationalization of analyst uncertainty about a firm. Low levels of recommendation dispersion indicate that analysts are more certain about the firm's future performance, whereas high levels of dispersion suggest that analysts have less consensus about the prospects of a firm.

name: Acquisition announcement
authors_terms: ["acquisition announcement", "announced an acquisition", "likelihood of a subsequent acquisition", "acquisition announcement following an SEO"]
definition: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 3 is dichotomous, indicating whether a firm issuing an SEO subsequently announced an acquisition within the following year.

name: Firm profitability
definition: The performance level of the firm in the period before the succession; the choice of an internal versus an external CEO candidate is argued to be influenced by a firm's desire to achieve desired performance levels. It is measured as the average return-on-assets (ROA) in the 3 years prior to the succession event.

name: Firm growth
definition: Growth of the organization prior to the CEO succession, measured as the percentage change in total company sales over the three years preceding the CEO succession event.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["R&D intensity", "relative emphasis on R&D", "investment in R&D"]
definition: The firm's relative emphasis on research and development, reflecting a competitive strategy of innovation; it is measured as expenditure on R&D as a percentage of sales in the period preceding the CEO succession event.

name: CEO firm-specific experience
definition: The extent of firm-specific experience of the selected executive, captured by whether the new CEO comes from inside or outside the organization. CEOs having fewer than 5 years of organizational tenure at the time of succession were categorized as outsiders.

name: Technical functional background
authors_terms: ["functional background experience", "functional track experience", "technical backgrounds", "technical functional areas"]
definition: The selected CEO's primary functional track experience. Executives with primary functional background experience in engineering or research and development or manufacturing/production were categorized as having technical backgrounds.

name: CEO education level
definition: Educational background has been discussed by management researchers as indicating executives' knowledge and skill base, with attained education level equated to attributes such as cognitive ability and receptivity to innovation. Education level was calculated based on the highest degree earned by the selected CEO.

name: Focal insider code violation
authors_terms: ["focal insider code violation", "a focal insider to violate the same code", "derivative use", "adoption of derivatives"]
definition: The dependent behavior: adoption of a practice that violates the category's central codes. In this setting the authors take the use of derivative products as a code violation, because derivatives are considered inherently incompatible with sharia law and are understood to violate the principles of Islamic banking.

name: Insider-initiated code violation
authors_terms: ["insider-initiated code violation", "peer insider-initiated code violation", "Peer insider derivative use"]
definition: Code violation initiated by a fellow category insider - an instance where the code violator possesses an insider identity. Insiders are full-fledged Islamic banks, defined as those that were born in the Islamic finance category and are not owned by a conventional bank.

name: Outsider-initiated code violation
definition: Code violation introduced by an outsider member of the category. The authors define Islamic banks that are owned by conventional banks as outsiders (CB-owned Islamic banks), because they entered late and are majority owned by conventional banks.

name: Outsider code preservation
authors_terms: ["code preservation", "code-preserving behavior", "Outsider zakat payment", "outsider code preservation"]
definition: Public adherence to one category code while violating another; the authors take the giving of zakat as code preservation. Code preservation enables new entrants to appear more authentic and to assimilate into the category.

name: Concurrent sourcing
authors_terms: ["concurrent sourcing", "concurrently source", "tapered integration", "dual distribution", "plural governance mode"]
definition: Concurrent sourcing occurs when firms both make and buy some of their requirements for a component. The authors use the term 'concurrently source complementary components' to refer to cases in which a firm both makes and buys two or more complementary components.

name: Interfirm expertise
definition: The degree to which a firm and its potential suppliers each have skills relevant to a particular component and/or set of components.

name: Within-firm shared expertise
definition: Knowledge within a firm that spans two or more components, such as possessing a deep understanding of the scientific technology related to a family of goods.

name: Substantive ceremony participation
authors_terms: ["substantive ceremony participation", "substantive participation", "substantive ceremonial participation", "substantive ceremony actions"]
definition: Organizations that benefit from large, visible honors or awards presented during ceremonies are discussed as substantive ceremony participation, and successfully winning competitive market bids within the context of ceremonial events is interpreted as a positive substantive signal.

name: Symbolic ceremony participation
definition: Symbolic ceremony participation is participation in which organizations gain a status benefit based on symbolic actions that signal they are important marketplace participants to the collective set of market actors.

name: Status
definition: Status refers to the relative prominence of the social structural position a firm occupies in an interorganizational network based on the firm's overall centrality in comparison with other actors' centrality in the same social structure. Marketplace status represents the perceived differential positions (versus roles or quality) that actors hold in the overall structure of exchange relations within a market.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: For construction firms, performance is directly related to the ability to earn profits across multiple projects.

name: Vicarious learning
authors_terms: ["vicarious learning", "reliable vicarious learning", "an increase in the number of adverse event reports by that set of relevant others", "failure patterns between firms", "failure trajectories"]
definition: Vicarious learning is learning from the failure events of other firms, and the authors' null hypothesis is that there exist no similar failure patterns across firms. The measure of reliable vicarious learning between firms in period t-1 is the average interfirm correlation between a firm's failure trajectory and another firm's failure trajectory in the past.

name: Volume of others' failure experience
authors_terms: ["volume of adverse events from other medical device manufacturers", "volume of failure experience", "others' volume of experience", "volume of failure reports"]
definition: The volume of adverse events contributed by other medical device manufacturers; an increase in the volume of failure events could simply follow from an increase in device production volume, could signal that a firm has discovered new information, or could signal normal variation in failures.

name: Reporting delays
authors_terms: ["delays in adverse event reports", "reporting delays", "delays in disclosing its own adverse events"]
definition: Delays are an ambiguous signal: the FDA mandates that firms report adverse events within 30 days of learning of an incident, so reports that violate this mandate may signal unusual events that merit attention. A failure experience is not available to other firms until the report is filed.

name: Focal firm adverse event reports
authors_terms: ["the number of adverse events reported by a firm", "adverse event reports by that focal firm", "failure reports"]
definition: The primary dependent variable is the number of adverse events reported by a firm i from the current month (t). Unlike prior operationalizations of accident and incident rates, the measure is event based, so it is not scaled.

name: Analyst performance projections
authors_terms: ["analyst performance projections", "performance projections", "analysts' performance projections relative to expectations", "analysts' projections of firm performance", "analyst EPS projections", "5-year EPS growth projections"]
definition: Analysts' performance assessments of firms, which the authors refer to as performance projections; the benchmark against which managers compare these projected performance assessments is referred to as performance expectations. Analyst performance projections are captured using analysts' projections of the firm's EPS growth over the course of the coming 5 years.

name: Allocation deviation
authors_terms: ["allocation deviation", "deviation from a winner-picking capital allocation approach", "deviation from winner-picking"]
definition: Allocation deviation represents the extent to which managers depart from the winner-picking approach to capital allocation. Firms that allocate capital strictly proportional to divisional performance receive a score of 0, which represents pure winner-picking, and the value increases as managers allocate more capital to weaker-performing divisions.

name: Multidivisional relatedness
definition: Multidivisional relatedness captures the degree to which there is homogeneity in the divisional assets and outputs within the firm. Business units within a multidivisional firm often possess similar asset structures that create input and output overlaps between them, or what is referred to as asset complementarity between the divisions.

name: Asset durability
definition: Asset durability involves the temporal expectations of the equipment owned by the firm, such that firms with higher asset durability have more long-lasting assets that are expected to be capitalized over several years, and firms with lower asset durability are able to restructure their platforms more frequently owing to shorter-lived equipment.

name: Strategic group membership
definition: Strategic group membership is defined by similarities in those strategic actions intended to alter competitive advantage; the strategic actions of interest are business scope and resource commitments.

name: Risk position
definition: The risk position of a firm refers to the risk exposure of its strategic investments; the authors evaluate total risk rather than systematic risk.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance refers to the return realized by a firm's pharmaceutical operations; a return on sales measure was defined for the pharmaceutical operations of each firm.

name: Locally active corporate disaster aid
authors_terms: ["share of aid from locally active firms", "aid from locally active corporations", "corporate disaster giving", "locally active corporations", "share of corporate giving"]
definition: We define 'local presence' based on a company having an affiliate or subsidiary that creates products or performs services in a focal nation. We argue that aid will arrive more quickly, and a nation will recover more fully, when locally active firms account for a larger share of disaster aid.

name: Speed of aid provision
authors_terms: ["speed of aid provision", "the speed with which aid is provided to a disaster-affected nation", "speed of disaster relief"]
definition: Effective disaster responses are related not just to the quantity of aid, but also to the speed with which it arrives. We used the portion of total disaster aid provided in the four weeks following a disaster as a proxy for the speed of aid provision.

name: Disaster recovery
authors_terms: ["a nation's recovery from disaster", "long-term recovery", "disaster recovery"]
definition: We analyze a nation's recovery from disaster based on the annual growth rate of its Human Development Index (HDI) score, which is a measure of aggregate social welfare.

name: Related giving
authors_terms: ["related giving", "relatedness", "related aid", "giving that leverages firm-specific routines and resources"]
definition: We developed a measure of related giving that reflects the degree to which disaster aid leverages firm-specific routines or resources. Related giving is the dollar amount of in-kind donations that aligned with a firm's key business activities - that is, products, services, or activities that are relevant to the firm's market operation.

name: Profitability
authors_terms: ["pre-tax ROI", "ROI", "return", "performance", "low return market share leaders", "high return market leaders"]
definition: The study focuses on market share leaders that differ in profitability, and the results show that market share does not always translate into profitability, as evidenced by a sizeable number of leaders all earning a pre-tax ROI of less than 10 per cent.

name: Market stability
authors_terms: ["market stability", "stability or turbulence in the market", "market structure"]
definition: Market stability describes the degree of stability or turbulence in the market and covers variables such as life cycle stage, real market growth, product age, product and technological change, number of competitors, industry concentration, geographic location, proprietary products and processes, competitor entry and exit, value added/revenue, buyer and supplier concentration, and cost-price squeeze.

name: Non-price demand characteristics
definition: Products which require specific tailoring and auxiliary user services do not as easily lend themselves to a volume strategy where standardization is necessary, and these activities respond to demand characteristics which reduce the competitive advantage associated with scale economies often enjoyed by share leaders.

name: Organization commitments
definition: Because most businesses in the sample are divisions or SBUs of larger multi-product firms, the issue of organizational linkages arises; variables available for measuring these internal commitments were percentages of purchases from and sales to internal divisions and the degree of shared facilities, distribution channels and marketing programs.

name: Competitive strategy
definition: How a business competes directly determines its resulting performance; competitive behaviour such as pricing, advertising and new product activities, along with quality and R&D intensity, are the competitive strategy factors included to explain why some share leaders enjoy success and others do not.

name: CEO power
authors_terms: ["CEO power", "the power of the CEO on the board of directors"]
definition: The power of the CEO on the board of directors at a focal firm in a given year. The authors note that truly high CEO power results from the combination of contributing factors, and so they measure it as an aggregate of visible firm attributes.

name: Demand-side cultural power distance
authors_terms: ["demand-side cultural power distance", "DSCPD", "demand-side exposure to cultural power distance"]
definition: The firm's demand-side exposure to the cultural-cognitive institution of power distance, calculated as a sales-weighted average of the cultural power distance values of the countries from which the firm derives sales. Power distance at the level of a national culture refers to 'the extent to which a society accepts the fact that power in institutions and organizations is distributed unequally.'

name: Geographic concentration of sales
authors_terms: ["geographic concentration of the firm's product markets", "geographic concentration", "product market geographic concentration"]
definition: The extent to which a firm's customer base is geographically concentrated rather than spread across many countries. Firms are more dependent on their customers, and therefore in greater need of legitimation, when their customer base is geographically concentrated.

name: Cultural variance
authors_terms: ["cultural variance", "variance in demand-side cultural power distance", "variance in demand-side cultural power distance across the firm's geographic markets"]
definition: The degree to which the cultural-cognitive characteristics of a firm's geographic markets differ from one another, measured as the variance in demand-side cultural power distance across the countries in which the firm competes.

name: Industry bargaining power over customers
definition: The extent to which firms in an industry have bargaining power over their customers; greater bargaining power makes firms less dependent on their customers for resources and thus reduces the importance of demand-side legitimation.

name: Inventor mobility
definition: Mobile inventors are R&D scientists that currently work for one firm but were previously employed by a competing firm. In the analysis, inventor mobility is a dyad-year count of the number of inventors moving from competitor j to the focal firm i during the period t-5 to t-1.

name: Inventor firm-specific knowledge
authors_terms: ["firm-specific knowledge", "firm-specific knowledge held by mobile inventors", "knowledge stock of mobile inventors"]
definition: The stock of firm-specific knowledge about their prior firm's R&D activities and organizational beliefs that mobile inventors bring to the hiring firm; it is observed through their personal connections in their prior firm, i.e. the number of unique co-inventors on the patents that the inventor filed before the move.

name: Familiarity with a competitor's technological capabilities
authors_terms: ["familiarity", "firm's familiarity with that competitor's technological capabilities", "firm technological familiarity"]
definition: The extent to which the two firms cite the same pool of patents in their own patent filings, capturing to what extent the two firms draw upon the same knowledge resources in their own R&D activities.

name: Alliance formation
definition: Alliance formation is a process that starts with the identification of potential partners and subsequently involves bilateral negotiations on alliance purpose, structure, and the implementation of a potential collaboration. Development alliances are partnerships where firms interact to share knowledge and together develop a new technology, whereas transfer alliances are agreements where one firm passes its knowledge on a specific technology over to another company.

name: Partner industry diversity
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio partner industry diversity", "partner industry diversity", "industry diversity"]
definition: The degree of variance in the industry background of a firm's alliance partners, coded from partners in the same four-digit SIC code to partners sharing no SIC code. The authors note that alliances with firms from different industries can bring a host of benefits and costs.

name: Partner national diversity
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio partner national diversity", "partner national diversity", "national diversity"]
definition: The degree of variance in the national background of a firm's alliance partners. Cross-border partners bring differences in political economic systems, societal and cultural institutions, government policies, and national industry structures.

name: Partner organizational diversity
authors_terms: ["alliance portfolio partner organizational diversity", "partner organizational diversity", "organizational diversity"]
definition: The variance in the types of organizations with which the firm allies. Alliances can be formed between large multidivisional firms, between public and private firms, and between for-profit businesses and not-for-profit organizations such as universities and government agencies.

name: Functional diversity
definition: The range of value chain activities for which the firm uses alliances. Alliances can serve different functional purposes as firms employ marketing, manufacturing, and distribution alliances to broaden their market reach, enhance value creation, and further exploit core competencies.

name: Governance diversity
definition: The variety of structures with which the firm manages its alliances. Alliances can be structured as nonequity or various equity-ownership arrangements where different governance structures have different implications on level of commitment, degree of integration, and learning.

name: Firm performance
definition: Measured at the corporate level as the three-year average of net profit margin, which is useful for comparing corporate performance in the same industry.

name: Imitation time lag
definition: Imitation time lag was measured as the time difference in years between the FDA approval date of the innovator drug and the approval date of the imitator drug. Imitation timing is treated as a proxy for the underlying uncertainty about the imitator's product.

name: Product differentiation
authors_terms: ["product differentiation", "vertical differentiation", "horizontal differentiation", "difference in indications", "difference in side effects"]
definition: Product differentiation was measured using two variables—indications and side effects respectively offered by the imitator's product in comparison with the innovator. Product differentiation in the branded drug industry is along two dimensions: efficacy, seen from the number and nature of treatment indications for which the drug is approved, and safety, seen from the number and nature of side effects that the drug engenders.

name: Relative sales performance
authors_terms: ["beat innovator", "beating the innovator in sales", "likelihood of beating the innovator"]
definition: Each imitator drug for each year was coded zero if its sales rank was lower than that of the innovator and coded one if its sales rank was higher; in all cases, when the imitator beat the innovator, it also became the market share leader in the product class.

name: Ownership structure
authors_terms: ["ownership structure", "owner-controlled firms", "management-controlled firms", "owner-managed firms", "ownership dispersion", "ownership concentration"]
definition: Firms were classified as Manager-Controlled (MC), Owner-Controlled (OC) or Owner-Managed (OM): MC firms are those in which no individual or institution other than an employee benefit plan owns 5 percent or more of the firm's outstanding voting stock, OC firms are those in which at least 5 percent of the stock is in the hands of one individual or organization not involved in the actual management of the company, and OM firms are those in which at least 5 percent of the stock is in the hands of one individual who was involved in the actual management of the company.

name: Employee pay-performance sensitivity
definition: The extent to which changes in employee compensation levels are related to changes in financial performance; the authors argue that, in the aggregate, employee compensation will be more sensitive to firm performance in owner-controlled firms than in manager-controlled firms.

name: Employee pay-size sensitivity
authors_terms: ["pay/size sensitivity", "pay-size sensitivity", "linkage between pay increases and firm growth"]
definition: The extent to which changes in employee compensation levels are related to changes in firm size; the authors argue that linking compensation increases to firm growth involves lower risk sharing for employees and that MC managers are more likely to reward firm size.

name: Change in employee pay level
authors_terms: ["change in per capita pay level", "change in average pay level", "change in pay level"]
definition: Change in average compensation expense per employee from 1997 to 1998, which includes salaries, wages, pension costs, profit sharing, incentive compensation, payroll taxes, and other employee benefits, but excludes commissions.

name: Change in firm size
definition: Change in a composite of assets, sales, and number of employees, which were standardized and averaged to create the size variable.

name: Change in firm performance
authors_terms: ["change in performance", "change in return on assets (ROA)"]
definition: Change in return on assets (ROA), which has been frequently used as a measure of performance in compensation and governance research.

name: Rural location
definition: Our study focuses on a defining aspect of sellers' local environment: rural versus urban. Rurali measures whether a seller is located in a rural or an urban area.

name: Category focus
authors_terms: ["Category Focus", "category focus", "alignment with the new design"]
definition: Category focus indicates the level of category focus in a seller's product portfolio - that is, the extent to which sellers focus their resources toward building up a rich product line in one or a few categories. It is the response outcome used to gauge how aligned a seller's response is with the platform's design change.

name: Seller performance
definition: The dependent variable for Hypothesis (H2) is logged log(Sales). The normalized average monthly sales is the sum of all sales from a seller's top three grossing categories in a given month.

name: Time since the design change
authors_terms: ["Temporal Distance", "months from when the design change happened"]
definition: Temporal Distance indicates the number of months from when the design change happened (May 2013); for instance, observations from February 2013 would have temporal distance = -3, and observations from January 2014 would have temporal distance = 8.

name: Board independence
authors_terms: ["director independence", "proportion of independent directors", "percentage of independent directors", "independent directors", "independent outsiders"]
definition: Truly independent directors-those with no ties to a company-may be more effective in representing the interests of the organization's shareholders. Independent board members were those who appeared to have no ties to the corporation or whose board they sat.

name: Board leadership structure
definition: Leadership structure refers to whether one person or two people serve in the roles of chief executive officer (CEO) and board chairperson.

name: Independent director tenure
authors_terms: ["independent director tenure", "average length of the tenure of a board's independent outside directors", "average tenure of the independent directors"]
definition: Tenure data, measured as number of years served on a board, were collected from proxy statements on all independent directors; these data were aggregated and averaged for each firm.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "tenure of a firm's CEO", "length of CEO tenure"]
definition: The longer a CEO has been with a company, the more entrenched that person is likely to be; tenure data, measured as number of years served on a board, were collected from proxy statements on all independent directors and CEOs.

name: Inside director stock ownership
authors_terms: ["equity holdings of inside directors", "inside director ownership", "inside director stock ownership", "inside directors' equity holdings"]
definition: When insiders own a significant portion of a firm's stock, they have a strong incentive to enhance its value and act in ways that are in shareholders' best interests. We collected data on each board member's beneficial shares, which are common shares an individual owns or has voting control over and stock options exercisable in the very near future.

name: Independent director stock ownership
authors_terms: ["independent director ownership", "independent directors' equity holdings", "stock holdings of its independent directors"]
definition: Since ownership increases the personal stakes of directors in the companies on whose boards they sit, the interests of directors with significant holdings will be more closely aligned with those of shareholders.

name: Institutional stock ownership
authors_terms: ["institutional holdings", "institutional stock ownership", "institutional equity holdings", "institutional ownership"]
definition: One of the major trends in stock ownership over the past several decades has been an increase in the holdings of institutional investors. Institutions include pension funds, mutual funds, insurance companies, banks, endowments, and foundations.

name: Poison pill adoption
authors_terms: ["poison pill provision", "poison pill", "poison pill adoption", "takeover protection"]
definition: The term actually refers to a family of contingent securities that result in the assumption of unwanted financial obligations by an acquirer, dilution of the acquirer's equity holdings, or loss of the acquirer's voting rights if the issuing firm becomes a takeover target.

name: Stock of past inventions
authors_terms: ["stock of past inventions", "individual stock of past inventions", "stock of past inventions", "past invention records", "successful inventive experience"]
definition: STOCK_OF_PAST_INVENTIONS is the number of patents the inventor applied for in the past. Because this output-based measure of experience may also proxy for inventor ability, the authors include inventor fixed effects.

name: Inventive rate
authors_terms: ["rate of invention", "inventive rate", "rate of new invention generation", "INV_rate"]
definition: The rate at which an inventor produces a generic patented invention, one of the two components of the rate of breakthrough generation.

name: Breakthrough probability
authors_terms: ["probability of any invention being a breakthrough", "probability that a future invention is a breakthrough", "PROB_BKT"]
definition: The likelihood that any single invention an inventor generates is a breakthrough, i.e. an extremely valuable invention whose importance is reflected in the recognition it receives from the technological community.

name: Breakthrough rate
definition: The rate at which an inventor produces breakthroughs, jointly determined by the rate of invention and the probability of any invention being a breakthrough.

name: Centrally targeted R&D
authors_terms: ["centrally targeted R&D", "CENTRALLY_TARGETED_R&D", "managerial control over R&D target"]
definition: Firms establish a clear invention problem and ask inventors to find a solution, rather than letting inventors pursue the research paths they prefer. Control here is whether firms or corporate inventors decide on the topics and direction of research projects.

name: Internal-external orientation
authors_terms: ["internal/external orientation", "internal versus external orientations", "internal or external orientation", "insider versus outsider orientation"]
definition: The attitude of the individual toward factors affecting internal operating efficiency, relative to concern for the factors in the external environment, might more appropriately define the perspective and orientation of individual decision makers. The internal or inside-out approach is seen as being oriented toward efficiency in operations, whereas the external or outside-in approach orients the firm's strategy toward responding to factors existing in the firm's competitive environment.

name: Financial performance
authors_terms: ["financial measures of organizational performance", "financial measures of strategic performance", "financial performance", "corporate performance"]
definition: The relative success of the companies' strategies was measured through the use of eight generally accepted indices of bank performance, selected to represent three major strategic policy areas: profitability policy, credit policy and capitalization policy. A percentile ranking was computed for each bank on each performance measure as a reflection of the firm's relative success in comparison to a control group of the 70 other banks located in the state from which the sample was chosen.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty, the degree to which future states of the competitive environment cannot be anticipated or accurately predicted. The logic that environmental uncertainty can be represented as product-market uncertainty suggests a hypothesis linking diversification strategy and product-market uncertainty.

name: Diversification strategy
authors_terms: ["diversification strategy", "diversification strategy type", "corporate strategy type", "intermediate diversification", "related linked"]
definition: Diversification strategy refers to a company's number of business lines, the relations among the lines, and the relative importance of each line to the parent company. One way to describe a company's diversification strategy is by Rumelt's (1974) typology: dominant business, related constrained, related linked, and unrelated business.

name: Portfolio restructuring
definition: Portfolio restructuring has been defined as "a change in the firm's configuration of lines of business through acquisition and divestiture transactions". Portfolio restructuring is a two-sided process involving both acquisitions and divestitures.

name: Growth option value
authors_terms: ["Growth Option Value", "GOV", "growth option value", "value of growth options"]
definition: Growth options refer to the future growth opportunities of a firm, which often arise from its uncertain real investments. Growth option value is the proportion of firm value that can be attributable to future growth opportunities rather than assets in place.

name: Equity alliance formation
definition: Our dependent variable, Equity Alliance, denotes whether the IPO firm became the object of an equity alliance. In our specific context, such equity alliances are investments made in an IPO firm seeking an equity position of less than 50%.

name: Pre-IPO alliances
definition: One of the chief means through which an IPO firm can become visible is collaborative relationships leading up to its IPO. To measure the firm's number of pre-IPO alliances, we used SDC to count the number of alliances the firm had previously formed.

name: Investment bank reputation
authors_terms: ["Investment Bank Reputation", "investment bank reputation", "prominence of the investment bank"]
definition: The second variable used to interact with growth option value is the prominence of the investment bank that took a firm public; an IPO firm's association with its investment bank represents another type of interfirm relationship that is likely to have an important effect on the visibility of the firm.

name: Media coverage
definition: The third interaction variable is the coverage that an IPO firm receives in the media, and it is a proxy for the level of publicity during the IPO process. Knowledge about the IPO firm can also reach out to other firms from a broad range of industries or geographic markets through more diffuse, public channels, such as the media.

name: Visibility
authors_terms: ["visibility", "the visibility of the IPO firm", "visible to prospective partners"]
definition: Our central proposition, therefore, is that the formation of equity alliances with IPO firms will depend not only on the value of their growth options, but will also be conditioned by the degree to which such firms are visible to prospective partners. In the development of the hypotheses that follow, we suggest that visibility varies across IPO firms and that IPO firms can obtain visibility in different ways.

name: Intraorganizational divisional multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["intraorganizational divisional contact", "intraorganizational multimarket contact", "division's level of existing intraorganizational multimarket contact with a market's incumbent divisions"]
definition: The multimarket contact levels among a firm's own divisions, the primary concern being a headquarters' choice of a given division to receive a mandate to operate in a new market. The measures concern each franchisee's multimarket contact with same-firm franchisees.

name: Cross-organizational divisional multimarket contact
authors_terms: ["cross-organizational divisional contact", "cross-organizational multimarket contact", "divisional multimarket contact between its divisions and their counterparts in other firms"]
definition: Multimarket contact between a firm's divisions and their counterparts in other firms, that is, a division's level of existing multimarket contact with a market's incumbent divisions of other firms.

name: Mandate assignment
authors_terms: ["assignment of a mandate", "chosen to operate in that market", "probability that headquarters will choose the division to operate in that market"]
definition: A franchisor's assignment of a mandate for a new unit in a given market, which is a choice among the franchisees existing at the time and a new franchisee. The decision concerns which division will operate in a new market.

name: Same-firm dominance of market
authors_terms: ["same-firm dominance of market", "markets where a firm's own divisions dominate"]
definition: Markets in which the units of the firm's own divisions dominate, that is, where they outnumber the units of rivals. The binary variable is set equal to one if the number of units affiliated with the same franchisor within five miles of the new unit was greater than or equal to the number of other franchisors' units within five miles.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Markets with substantial uncertainty, operationalized as markets with declining per capita incomes, which are often those in which uncertainty regarding a unit's viability is high. The binary variable is set to one if per capita income had declined in the year the new unit was opened relative to its level two years previously.

name: Republican state political context
definition: We distinguish between an institutional context that is in line with the views of the platform of the Democratic Party ('blue') versus one in line with those of the Republican Party ('red'). The economic and societal norms in the blue states are more accurately characterized as those that support firms' commitments to employees, unions, the environment, and community issues than are such norms in the red states.

name: Shift toward Republican political context
authors_terms: ["Turned Red", "TurnedRed", "Turned Blue", "TurnedBlue", "recently shifted from Democratic to Republican"]
definition: While institutional context is likely to evolve gradually, election results serve as strong signals to investors that such changes are taking place. For example, a Republican victory in a formerly Democratic state signals a trajectory toward an institutional environment that is particularly advantageous for buyouts.

name: Level of buyout activity
authors_terms: ["buyout activity", "level of activity of leveraged buyouts", "BO Activity"]
definition: The dependent variable in our analysis of the local level of buyout activity is a count of all buyouts made in a given calendar year of companies located in any of the 50 states and Washington, D.C.

name: Buyout exit performance
authors_terms: ["exit success", "average performance of buyouts", "successful exit", "buyout success rate"]
definition: We also analyze the exit success of individual transactions; a successful exit is an initial public offering, secondary LBO, or trade sale observed within five calendar years following the investment date, while the other realization options are unrealized (censored, living-dead) and write-off.

name: Shareholder discontent with director monitoring
authors_terms: ["shareholder discontent with director monitoring", "shareholder discontent", "shareholder opposition", "votes withheld"]
definition: The authors develop shareholder discontent with director monitoring as a collective construct influenced by both firm- and director-level characteristics. When shareholders are discontented with director monitoring, they withhold votes for the candidates, signaling that they wish to alter existing corporate governance structures.

name: Firm performance
definition: In the realm of public trading, shareholders are arguably more interested in firm performance-both accounting and stock market measures-than any other issue. When firm performance is high, shareholders benefit from increased share prices and potentially increased dividends.

name: CEO compensation
definition: High levels of executive compensation may signal that the board is unwilling to carry a hard line on executive compensation, again suggestive of agency costs and ineffective monitoring; although CEO compensation may be viewed as a potential instrument for alleviating agency problems, it may also be viewed as part of the agency problem itself.

name: Board size
definition: Large boards are associated with poor group cohesiveness, an inability to initiate strategic change, poor communication, and a lack of control vis-a-vis the CEO; the lack of open boardroom discussion as board size increases is likely to enable CEOs to gain power over directors, thereby reducing director monitoring.

name: Affiliated director status
definition: Affiliated directors, those outside directors who have a history with the firm, including former employment, family ties, or other financial ties (e.g., customers, suppliers), are assumed to lack the independence needed to monitor management.

name: Director tenure
definition: Agency logic also suggests that when directors serve on boards for several years, their independence is compromised. Long tenure, for example, may enable firm management to co-opt directors, and directors who have served for extended periods may become stale in the saddle.

name: Director block ownership
definition: Directors who own a meaningful financial stake in the firm are likely motivated to monitor and discipline management; agency logic suggests that the interests of blockholder-directors are better aligned with shareholders and, therefore, these directors, as significant shareholders themselves, should be more effective at monitoring managers on behalf of all shareholders.

name: Number of outside board seats
authors_terms: ["number of board seats", "number of outside directorships", "number of public firm board seats"]
definition: Critics contend that when directors serve on multiple boards, the time they dedicate to any one firm is reduced and that directors on many boards can be overboarded so that their ability to monitor management is diminished because they have so many firms to serve in this capacity.

name: Occupational minority status
authors_terms: ["occupational minorities", "occupational minority", "white women and men and women of color", "nontraditional incumbents"]
definition: Taylor (2010) defines occupational minorities as members of an occupation that are numerical rarities. In this study, occupational minorities are defined as white women and men and women of color.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "firm financial performance", "struggling firms", "weak firm performance", "corporate performance"]
definition: Measures of firm financial performance fall into two primary categories: accounting-based and market-based measures; return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE) represent accounting-based measures and share price return represents a market-based measure.

name: CEO tenure
definition: The authors predict that the experience of token or solo status will reduce job success and satisfaction, resulting in higher turnover and shorter tenures for occupational minorities; tenure was reported in months.

name: Savior effect
authors_terms: ["savior effect", "replacement by white men CEOs", "transition of a traditional white male leader replacing an occupational minority CEO", "corporate saviors"]
definition: We predict that occupational minorities will be replaced by white men should firm performance struggle under their leadership, a process we term the savior effect. The dependent variable to test the savior effect is the transition of a traditional white male leader replacing an occupational minority CEO.

name: Network reach
definition: Network reach refers to the short-path lengths to other actors in a network. An actor's reach is the sum of the reciprocal distances that are reachable from that actor to every other actor in a network.

name: Span of structural holes
authors_terms: ["span of structural holes", "spanning of structural holes", "span the structural holes"]
definition: If an actor is the only bridge or connection between two groups of unconnected actors, the actor is defined as spanning a structural hole. Span of structural holes refers to the number of unconnected groups bridged by the focal inventor.

name: Depth of local search
authors_terms: ["depth of local search", "depth of organizational local search"]
definition: Depth of local search refers to the amount of organizational knowledge that is used in one's innovation activities. Inventors using more organizational knowledge in their innovation activities perform deeper local search than inventors using less organizational knowledge.

name: Breadth of local search
authors_terms: ["breadth of local search", "breadth of organizational local search"]
definition: Breadth of local search refers to the extent of different domains from which organizational knowledge is drawn; technological breadth (geographical breadth) of local search refers to the extent of technological classes (geographical locations) from which organizational knowledge is drawn.

name: Interorganizational learning rate
definition: We define learning as occurring only when a partner acquires knowledge, assimilates it, and exploits it in its operations (Zahra and George, 2002). In the study, knowledge flow is observed as patent cross-citations from a set of corporations and their partners.

name: Alliance duration
definition: We measured the duration from the beginning of the interorganizational relationship with the variable months, which received values from 1 to 48 across the first four years from the formation of the alliance.

name: Technological similarity
definition: Research has found that the similarity of technological areas (measured either in terms of patenting or product market domains) helps companies to acquire and exploit knowledge from one another. Technological similarity was measured by examining the overlap of a focal company's patents with those of its partner in terms of patent classes.

name: Technological focus
definition: Technological focus represents the diversity vs. focus of the firm's technological activities. Technological diversity is a firm-level measure that describes the degree to which the technological development in a firm is focused upon a narrow set of technologies or a broad range of technologies.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity, which is probably the most commonly used measure of firm-level absorptive capacity, captures the inputs into the R&D process as a share of total sales.

name: Trust
definition: One party's 'confidence in the goodwill' of an exchange partner (Ring and Van de Ven, 1994: 93). Trust is an attribute of an exchange relationship, rather than an attribute of a particular exchange party.

name: Opportunism
definition: Calculated efforts by an exchange agent 'to mislead, distort, disguise, obfuscate, or otherwise confuse' an exchange party (Williamson, 1985: 47). The study focuses on ex post opportunism, measured from the agent's point of view.

name: Relationalism
definition: The set of behaviors that support relational contracting, which refers to 'the extent to which an exchange relationship can be characterized as long-term-oriented, reciprocal, and extending beyond mere buying and selling' (Li and Dant, 1997: 202). As a latent construct, relationalism characterizes the set of behaviors that exchange parties exhibit in performing tasks, duties, or obligations.

name: Subjective performance
definition: Principal-agent performance evaluated according to the rational goal model, which views organizations as striving for efficiency and productivity, and measured relative to other similar agents of the principal.

name: Search in corporate partner's technological domains
authors_terms: ["startup's search in corporate partner's domains", "search for innovations in the technological domains of its corporate partner", "search shift"]
definition: The outcome in the hypotheses refers to the extent to which a startup searches for innovations in the technological domains of its partner.

name: Corporate investment relationship
definition: A relationship that occurs when an incumbent acquires a minority equity stake in a private and relatively new venture.

name: Post-investment period
authors_terms: ["Post", "postinvestment", "years after the year of formation of the investment relationship"]
definition: The years after the year of formation of the corporate investment relationship, distinguishing a startup's search postinvestment from its search prior to the investment.

name: Innovation radicalness
authors_terms: ["radicalness of a startup's innovations", "startup's patent originality", "patent originality"]
definition: The radicalness of a startup's innovations is operationalized based on the extent to which they result from search spanning the boundaries of various technological domains; radical innovations result from search with broader scope that combines knowledge from a greater diversity of technological domains.

name: Corporate partner's commercial success
authors_terms: ["corporate partner's commercial success", "corporate partner's best-selling drugs", "commercial success of a corporate partner"]
definition: The degree of commercial success of a startup's corporate partner, measured through the commercial success of its drugs, which reflects the presence of strong complementary assets that can help the startup make progress toward commercialization.

name: Relative sales goals
definition: The ratio of the monthly sales goal for one product category to the monthly sales goal for another product category, in the authors' experiment wine relative to spirits. The authors study relative sales and goals (i.e., ratios) because this allows them to avoid income effects in the analysis.

name: Relative sales
authors_terms: ["ratio of sales", "Sales Wine/Sales Spirits", "sales of wines relative to spirits"]
definition: The ratio of a salesperson's sales in one product category to her sales in another product category, used to capture how sales effort is allocated across the categories. The authors study relative sales and goals (i.e., ratios) because this allows them to avoid income effects in the analysis.

name: Goal ratcheting
definition: Incentive ratcheting can be defined as the practice of setting next period goals, piece rates or any other key incentive parameter based on current-period performance. In the model, the parameter captures how future goals are affected when sales exceed goals, that is, the extent of goal ratcheting in the goal updating process.

name: Salesperson tenure
definition: Worker tenure is measured in months by subtracting the month in which each salesperson signed a formal labor contract with CCU from the month t, the periods of the data set. New C.CCU salespersons have, on average, a one year period in which they are under evaluation and no formal long-term contract is signed, which explains why negative tenure exists in the data set.

name: Knowledge flow
authors_terms: ["external learning", "knowledge flows", "external knowledge acquisition", "likelihood of a citation", "draw upon the knowledge of another organization"]
definition: External learning is the acquisition of knowledge that resides beyond organizational boundaries; the paper focuses on external learning through knowledge flows across organizations. If patent A contains a reference to a preceding patent P as prior art, the knowledge documented in patent P was identified by the inventor/applicant of patent A.

name: Geographic distance
authors_terms: ["geographic distance", "geographic proximity", "distance between inventors on patent pairs in km"]
definition: The geographic distance measured in kilometers between two inventors, based on the place of residence listed in the patent document. If more than one inventor is listed on a patent application, the distance between the two inventors on the separate applications that are closest to each other is used.

name: Technological distance
definition: Patents are technologically distant when they are assigned to a different IPC4 technology class, i.e., when citation pairs share no IPC4 class.

name: Shared professional service firm
authors_terms: ["contracting the same service firm", "same law firm", "same patent law firm", "access to a patent law firm's knowledge repository"]
definition: A focal company is more likely to learn from the experience of another organization if that organization has already interacted with the focal company's PSF, so that the knowledge is included in the PSF's knowledge repository.

name: Strategic type conformity
authors_terms: ["strategic type", "degree to which an organization conforms to a given strategic type", "degree of conformity to the strategic type"]
definition: Miles and Snow proposed a typology of strategic types based, for the most part, on the organization's orientation toward product-market development, suggesting four strategic types: defenders, prospectors, analyzers and reactors. The study measures the degree to which a firm conforms to each of these types.

name: Strategy-making mode conformity
definition: Strategy-making is the process whereby strategies are consolidated. Mintzberg suggested three modes of strategy-making—the entrepreneurial, the adaptive and the planning—focusing mainly on the motives for decisions, who makes them, how alternatives are evaluated and the decisions' horizons. The study measures the degree to which a firm uses each mode.

name: Strategy-strategy-making fit
definition: Fit between strategy and strategy-making is conceptualized and defined as that particular configuration which will achieve completeness, and which will in turn result in higher performance. Strategy/strategy-making fit types are high conformity to the defender type and to the planning mode; high conformity to the prospector type and to the entrepreneurial mode; high conformity to the analyzer type and to the planning and the entrepreneurial modes; and low conformity to the reactor type and to the adaptive mode.

name: Firm performance
definition: Performance evaluation was based on seven indicators. Two indicators related to market share—retail market share at the end of the game (RMS), and accumulated last 6 months' sales (LSH); and five indicators related to profit—gross profit as a percentage of sales (GPP), profit as a percentage of sales (PSH), owners' equity (EQ), return on assets (RA), and stock price (SP).

name: Order of entry
authors_terms: ["order of entry", "first mover", "second mover", "follower", "copycat follower", "non-copycat follower", "late mover", "being first"]
definition: We focus our theorizing and empirical validation on situations where the first and later entrants introduce an organizational form that is distinct from prior organizational forms. The class of situations to which our theory applies has a defined scope, in which the audience recognizes a qualitative difference on various dimensions by which the new products or services are brought into the world.

name: Legitimation work
authors_terms: ["legitimation work", "costly and risky legitimation work", "legitimacy appropriation"]
definition: Securing legitimacy for a new organizational form requires a great deal of effort, which we term 'legitimation work.' In this paper, we focus on normative and sociopolitical legitimation work.

name: Perceived authenticity
definition: Firms are at an (dis)advantage when they are perceived to be true to (against) their claims, or, in other words, (in)authentic. There is good reason to expect perceived authenticity of a startup to reflect the validity to its claim to originality along three dimensions of value: originality per se, greater capability, and greater commitment.

name: Audience preference
authors_terms: ["audience preference", "consumer preference", "willingness to use", "willingness to recommend", "market selection", "audience selection", "preference for adoption", "relative discount"]
