definition: Such an advantage would be present if, even when the two firms sell identical products or services, prospective customers or 'the audience' prefer the first mover to the second mover because they perceive the first mover to be more authentic.

name: Extent of similarity
authors_terms: ["extent of similarity", "copycat", "copycat follower", "non-copycat follower", "cosmetic features", "substantive features"]
definition: In the 'copycat follower' condition, participants are given descriptions of two firms: a first mover and a follower firm that exhibits extensive similarities to the first mover, including both 'substantive' features and 'cosmetic' features. In the 'non-copycat follower' condition, we presented a follower that was similar to the first mover in terms of substantive features but does not show any evidence of cosmetic similarities.

name: Follower entry timing relative to legitimation
authors_terms: ["entry timing", "early follower", "late follower", "arrival after versus before legitimation work"]
definition: Insofar as followers are discounted as inauthentic based on the perception that they were not motivated by an original insight or vision but rather by the opportunity to appropriate the legitimacy attained by their predecessors' hard work, this perception should be mitigated by a follower's willingness to enter before legitimation work has been completed.

name: Perceived legitimacy
definition: One of the most well-established axioms in organizational theory is that a firm cannot thrive and survive unless it is regarded as 'desirable, proper, or appropriate within some socially constructed system of norms, values, beliefs and definitions' (Suchman 1995:574) by customers and others who provide resources to the organization.

name: State policymakers' political conservatism
authors_terms: ["state policymakers' conservatism", "stakeholder conservatism", "ideologically opposed stakeholders", "stakeholder opposition"]
definition: Because we analyzed adoptions of a practice that was overwhelmingly aligned with political liberalism, our conception of ideologically opposed stakeholders was operationalized as their degree of political conservatism; higher values on this spectrum reflected cases where the state policymakers were highly conservative and therefore, opposed to the practice in question, whereas lower values indicated cases where the state policymakers collectively leaned liberal and therefore, were less opposed to the practice of same-sex partner benefits.

name: Prior adoptions by proximal corporations
authors_terms: ["prior adoptions by proximal corporations", "corporate adoptions (same state)", "proximal corporate adoptions", "adoptions by for-profit business organizations"]
definition: We coded this variable to capture the adoption decisions of major for-profit corporations (i.e., Fortune 500 companies) headquartered in the same state where a given university is situated.

name: Prior adoptions by peer universities
authors_terms: ["peer adoptions (intercollegiate conference)", "prior adoptions by peer public universities"]
definition: We focused on prior adoptions by peer schools that are part of the same intercollegiate athletic conferences (e.g., Big 10 or Pacific 12) as the focal school. This approach approximated the phenomenological reality of how organizations conceptualize institutional equivalence in the higher-public-education sector.

name: Domestic partner benefits adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of domestic partner benefits", "adoption of same-sex domestic partner benefits"]
definition: For an organization, adopting domestic partner benefits meant extending the organization's existing family health insurance coverage from employees' married opposite-sex partners to also include employees' same-sex partners.

name: Market-based justification of adoption
authors_terms: ["market-based justifications", "market-based reasoning", "justifications rooted in the logic of market efficiency"]
definition: To test rhetorical effects, we track whether university communications about adoption decisions featured (liberal) social equity-based justifications or (conservative) market-based justifications rooted in the logic of organizational effectiveness.

name: Convergence in understanding
authors_terms: ["convergence", "convergence in understanding", "organizational convergence", "convergence on the importance of a unit's business activities", "convergence on the potential for a technology to support a unit's business activities"]
definition: Convergence reflects the existence of a consensual understanding, between technology providers and other organizational members, of both the nature of the organization's business activities and the importance of a focal technology in supporting these activities. It is the thread of coherence among an organization's members that enables the organization to interpret information as a system.

name: Communication channel richness
definition: Information richness refers to the potential for information being communicated through a channel to overcome different frames of reference held by communication partners or to clarify ambiguous issues such that joint understanding between the partners is enhanced.

name: Communication frequency
definition: Frequency of communication indicated the degree to which the technology providers and the business personnel had communication contact. It is the degree of contact in group or individual communication.

name: Information technology innovativeness
definition: For this research, an information technology innovation refers to administrative or operational ideas, practices, or objects perceived as new by an organizational unit and whose underlying basis lies with information technology.

name: Project performance
authors_terms: ["project performance", "performance outcome", "box office performance", "box office returns", "movie box office rating"]
definition: The performance outcome of a focal movie project, for which box office returns provided the primary source of movie revenue because the period predates merchandising, TV release and video release; the key project performance indicator (box office revenue) was widely accepted and easily available to industry members.

name: Future collaboration
authors_terms: ["future collaborations", "future project collaborations", "future collaborations between the same participants", "future collaborations with the same partners", "repeated collaboration"]
definition: Collaboration between the same project participants in a future project venture, captured as the number of repeated dyadic relationships between key project contributors during the four years after project completion.

name: Prior collaboration
authors_terms: ["prior collaborations", "prior collaborations between the same participants", "prior collaboration history", "previous collaborations"]
definition: Collaborations between the same key project participants that occurred before a focal project; the hypothesis focuses on whether there were previous collaborations between the same partners even before project A.

name: Project-type similarity
definition: Whether a focal project and a future project are of the same type; in this setting, whether prior and future movies were in color, a project type that introduced an important new technology requiring substantial adjustments of how participants performed their interdependent tasks.

name: Organizational power
authors_terms: ["organizational power", "organizational control", "institutional control over project participants", "power asymmetry", "nonintegrated studio", "integrated studio"]
definition: The ability of an organizational entity to control decisions and outcomes; in this context, relative control over project participants, where integrated studios maintained considerable control through long-term employment contracts (closed organizations) while nonintegrated studios could not block participants from joining future projects at other studios (open organizations).

name: Differential M&A experience
authors_terms: ["M&A experience difference", "differential experience", "differential M&A experience", "experience advantage", "differential experience of the target and the acquirer"]
definition: The asymmetry linked with negotiation outcomes is likely to come from the extra experience that the acquirer has relative to the target or vice versa (i.e., differential experience); the party with more previous M&A experience, whether it is the acquirer or the target, stands to obtain more of the value generated by the deal.

name: Value obtained by the acquirer
authors_terms: ["value obtained by the acquirer", "acquirer's value obtained", "value that the acquirer obtains", "amount of value obtained by the acquirer"]
definition: The value created by the acquirer can be calculated by multiplying its pre-announcement market value by the CARs to the acquirer during the event window. The authors use the absolute amount obtained by the acquirer as one of the two dependent variables.

name: Value obtained by the target
authors_terms: ["value obtained by the target", "target's value obtained", "value that the target obtains", "amount of value obtained by the target"]
definition: The target's value created can be calculated in an identical way using target-side pre-announcement market value and CARs. The authors use the absolute amount obtained by the target as the other dependent variable.

name: Target product-market scope
authors_terms: ["target product-market scope", "product-market scope of the target firm", "target firm's scope", "target's level of diversification"]
definition: The first important source of information asymmetry that we consider is the product-market scope of the target firm, which reflects the number of economic activities it performs-more precisely, the number of industries it operates in.

name: Friendly deal attitude
authors_terms: ["friendly deal attitude", "friendly deal", "whether the deal was friendly", "friendly attitude"]
definition: The severity of the information asymmetry issue also depends on whether the attitude of the target toward the acquirer is friendly, that is, whether the target firm's management and board of directors agree to the deal.

name: Founder power
authors_terms: ["power", "founders' power at IPO", "managerial power", "structural power", "ownership power", "expertise power", "prestige power", "power index"]
definition: In the context of top management, power refers to an actor's capacity to exert his or her will on organizational decisions and actions. Following Finkelstein (1992), the authors use four dimensions of managerial power: structural, ownership, expert, and prestige power.

name: Full exit
authors_terms: ["full exit", "fully exit", "full exit from the venture via IPO"]
definition: We operationalize a full exit as when a founder leaves the top management team and the board of directors and holds less than 3% ownership of the firm 24 months after the lock-up period. Since nobody can 'force' founders to sell their shares, full exits are, by definition, voluntary acts.

name: Managerial partial exit
definition: A founder can resign from his or her managerial position but keep ownership shares in the venture (i.e., a managerial partial exit). We operationalize a managerial partial exit as when a founder leaves the top management team and the board of directors but still holds 3%, or more, ownership in the venture 24 months after the lock-up period.

name: Financial partial exit
definition: A founder can sell his or her ownership shares in the venture but retain a managerial role (i.e., a financial partial exit). We operationalize a financial partial exit as when a founder sells all his or her shares but remains in the top management team and on the board of directors 24 months after the lock-up period.

name: Frustration
definition: Frustration is a negative emotional state caused by 'interference with goal attainment or goal-oriented activity'. In simple terms, frustration occurs when something or someone blocks one's efforts toward a desired goal.

name: Deregulation
definition: The process by which property rights associated with utilities' assets were redefined in the electric utility industry: exclusive franchise rights have been revoked and competitive market principles substituted in their place, so that parameters with low uncertainty in the regulated environment become parameters with high uncertainty in the deregulated environment.

name: Vertical integration
authors_terms: ["vertical integration", "level of vertical integration", "proportion of electricity generated", "governance structures"]
definition: A governance structure on a continuum from fully vertically integrated structures to market transactions; a vertically integrated utility owns its own generating plants, transmission system, and distribution lines to provide all aspects of electric service.

name: Productive efficiency
definition: The ability to obtain maximum output with given inputs.

name: Technologically related diversification
definition: TRD is a cross-citation measure designed to capture whether a firm's operating sectors exhibit significant technological interactions. This measure can only be calculated for diversified firms, defined as those that report sales in more than one SIC4 industry within a given year.

name: Stock market mispricing
authors_terms: ["stock market mispricing", "undervaluation", "under-valued by the stock market", "mispricing", "abnormal returns"]
definition: In this context of return predictability, such a finding suggests mispricing - specifically, an undervaluation if the predictable abnormal returns are positive. We interpret a positive alpha as evidence that the securities in the portfolio are undervalued given their level of risk.

name: Investors' attention
authors_terms: ["investors' attention", "investor attention", "attention from stock market participants"]
definition: For investors' attention, we follow Hirshleifer et al. (2018) and use the inverse of the ownership percentage by transient investors as our proxy. This approach is motivated by empirical studies that show the presence of transient investors leads to an emphasis on short-term performance and an underweighting of long-term prospects.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: For analyst coverage, we calculate the average monthly number of sell-side analysts' earnings-per-share (EPS) forecasts for the current fiscal year. Sell-side analysts, who work for brokerage houses, aim to reduce information asymmetry between firms and investors.

name: Technological familiarity
definition: We assess the complexity of the firm's disclosures by analyzing the wording of its granted patents, specifically focusing on the extent to which the language used is similar to that of other patents granted by the USPTO. The more standard (i.e., less novel) the language in the patent documents, the more familiar external parties should be with it.

name: Patent information disclosure
authors_terms: ["the American Inventors Protection Act (AIPA)", "Post AIPA", "Post-AIPA", "increased transparency following the American Inventor's Protection Act"]
definition: The AIPA required US patent applications filed after November 29, 2000, to be published 18 months after their priority date, with the earliest batch of information released on May 29, 2002. This reform accelerated the disclosure of information that would eventually be published in granted patent documents.

name: Patent time-to-grant
authors_terms: ["Time-to-Grant", "time lag between patent application and grant"]
definition: Our key independent variable for this test, Time-to-Grant, is calculated as the average time lag in months between patent application and publication for the period 1996-2000.

name: Business unit strategy
authors_terms: ["business unit strategy", "generic business unit strategy", "Miles and Snow's typology of prospector, defender, analyzer and reactor strategies", "prospector", "analyzer", "defender"]
definition: Miles and Snow's typology of business strategies distinguishes prospector, defender, analyzer and reactor business units; the three viable business unit strategies differ along a continuum in terms of entrepreneurial effort in the marketplace.

name: Interfunctional conflict
authors_terms: ["level of conflict between marketing and research and development", "level of conflict", "interfunctional conflict", "amount of interfunctional conflict"]
definition: The level of conflict between marketing and R&D personnel within a business unit, arising from resource and workflow interdependencies and from differences in short-term objectives and desires for autonomy, and reflected in how frequently the two groups disagree.

name: Formalization
definition: Formalization refers to the use of rules and standard operating procedures within an organization, which clarify each party's role and constrain dysfunctional behavior.

name: Avoidance conflict resolution
definition: One of four common mechanisms for resolving conflicts between functional departments, in which the parties ignore or avoid the issue.

name: Conciliatory conflict resolution
definition: One of four common mechanisms for resolving conflicts between functional departments, in which the parties smooth over conflicts.

name: Participatory conflict resolution
authors_terms: ["openly confronting issues", "participatory resolution", "participatory mechanisms", "working out a compromise between the parties involved"]
definition: One of four common mechanisms for resolving conflicts between functional departments, in which the parties openly confront issues and work out a compromise among themselves.

name: Hierarchical conflict resolution
authors_terms: ["resorting to higher authority", "hierarchical modes of conflict resolution", "hierarchical mechanisms"]
definition: One of four common mechanisms for resolving conflicts between functional departments, in which the conflict is passed to higher-level managers or authorities for resolution.

name: Attitudes toward conflict resolution
authors_terms: ["attitudes toward how well conflicts are resolved", "attitudes concerning how well interdepartmental conflicts are resolved", "perceived effectiveness of conflict resolution"]
definition: The attitudes of the members of the affected departments concerning how well their conflicts are being resolved, i.e. their satisfaction with the efficiency and effectiveness of the conflict resolution mechanisms being employed.

name: Perceived effectiveness of interdepartmental relations
authors_terms: ["perceived effectiveness of the interaction between marketing and R&D", "perceived effectiveness of the relationship between the marketing and R&D departments", "effectiveness of the interfunctional relationship"]
definition: The perceived effectiveness of the relationship between the marketing and R&D departments, reflecting the effectiveness of a department's performance on those tasks and objectives where it depends on workflow or resource inputs from the other functional area.

name: State ownership
definition: An acquirer was classified as an SOE if its immediate or ultimate owner was any level of the Chinese government. SOEs are generally more opaque than other types of firms.

name: Cross-border acquisition completion
authors_terms: ["deal completion", "completion of CBAs", "likelihood of deal completion", "completion rate"]
definition: The likelihood of completing a cross-border acquisition was the outcome of interest: the study investigated whether and how the opaqueness of an SOE affects its likelihood of completing a crossborder acquisition (CBA).

name: Opaqueness
definition: Opaqueness, or lack of transparency, is defined as the unavailability of credible firm-level information to stakeholders (Bushman, Piotroski, & Smith, 2004). Opaqueness can occur when a firm does not disclose or when the disclosed information cannot be validated or certified, for example, by reputable financial auditors.

name: Public listing
definition: Being publicly listed is costly and is a commitment to continuously providing a great deal of information (Stulz, 1999). Most stock exchanges require their listed firms to make many regular and irregular filings.

name: Foreign listing
authors_terms: ["Foreign-listed acquirer", "being listed on an exchange in a developed economy", "foreign listed"]
definition: By definition, exchanges in better-developed financial markets have stronger requirements and can enforce them more effectively (Karolyi, 2006; Stulz, 1999); listing in a developed economy is particularly credible because it is costly for lower-quality firms.

name: Auditor reputation
definition: An auditor's main duty is to guarantee the credibility of the information firms report. Accounting firms with better reputations have more to lose from poor auditing, and, therefore, are less likely to collude with their clients and fail to report problems they discover.

name: Precarious situations
authors_terms: ["precarious situations", "more precarious situations", "situational precariousness", "more precarious situation"]
definition: Situations with lower odds of success such that negative outcomes are more likely. It is a broad concept that applies to many forms of performance, settings, and events.

name: CEO hubris
definition: Individuals' tendency to overestimate their abilities. More hubristic individuals also have heightened beliefs that they can succeed regardless of challenges and are more inclined to resist negative information about a situation.

name: Committee chair home district
authors_terms: ["Trans Chair", "home district of the House Transportation Committee chair", "chair's district", "home airports"]
definition: We overlay airports on a congressional district map and find those located within the geographical boundaries of the chairs' districts. We construct a dichotomous treatment variable, Trans Chair, which takes a value of one if, for the given origin airport-carrier-year observation, the airport is in the home district of the current Transportation Committee chair.

name: Pork strategy
definition: We define market actions that primarily target politicians' public interests as pork strategies, which involve firms providing economic benefits by expanding their presence in the politicians' home districts.

name: Perk strategy
definition: We define market actions that primarily target politicians' private interests as perk strategies, which involve firms increasing the supply or quality of products or services valued by targeted politicians.

name: Policy inaction
authors_terms: ["policy inaction", "policy inactions", "inactions on formal policy changes"]
definition: Firms generally seek to avoid formal policy changes as they typically entail costly responses (i.e., most formal policy changes create regulatory burdens relative to the status quo). We posit that pork and perk strategies can be effective vehicles to prevent policy changes and maintain the status of quo.

name: Supplier knowledge acquisition efforts
authors_terms: ["supplier knowledge acquisition efforts", "knowledge acquisition efforts", "generic knowledge acquisition"]
definition: Suppliers who acquire collective production know-how out-compete those that do not. This acquisition of collective production know-how is defined as the implementation of a broader set of capabilities involving far-reaching organizational and technological adaptations inherent in advanced production systems (as opposed to the implementation of one or another specific technique).

name: Joint buyer-supplier knowledge acquisition efforts
authors_terms: ["joint buyer-supplier knowledge acquisition efforts", "joint knowledge acquisition efforts", "joint learning"]
definition: Joint buyer-supplier knowledge acquisition efforts are defined as the acquisition of collective or complex manufacturing know-how by suppliers where the focus buyer has direct participation in the process. Direct participation relates to buyers being involved in the supplier knowledge acquisition efforts either by 'teaching' and/or 'co-participating.'

name: Dyad-specific assets and capabilities
authors_terms: ["supplier dyad-specific assets and capabilities", "dyad-specific assets and capabilities", "specific assets and capabilities"]
definition: Our multi-item scale identifies the degree to which the supplier has invested in new or modified existing capabilities (e.g., order taking, production processes) and physical assets (e.g., production equipment, new facilities) primarily to serve the unique needs of this customer. One's specific assets and capabilities are known to have better fit with assets owned by the relationship partner.

name: Relational governance
authors_terms: ["buyer-supplier relational governance", "alliance relational governance mechanisms", "relational governance mechanisms"]
definition: Relational governance mechanisms are defined as 'informal agreements and unwritten codes of conduct that powerfully affect the behaviors of individuals within firms [and] . . . the behaviors of firms in their dealings with other firms'.

name: Redeployable performance
definition: For redeployable performance (the performance suppliers are usually able to replicate across customers) we used the respondents input for performance they achieved with an 'average' customer. The possession of newly learned capabilities enables suppliers to improve performance in general, across different contexts.

name: Relational performance
definition: By contrasting processes leading to a supplier's relational performance (the difference between its performance with a focus partner vis-`a-vis with its average partner base) with its redeployable performance . . . we attempt to integrate and advance the resource-based and relational views. This conceptualization is consistent with our definition of relational performance presented earlier as well as with the concept of 'relational rent' as presented in Dyer and Singh's (1998) relational view.

name: Abnormal returns to the parent firm
authors_terms: ["abnormal returns", "cumulative abnormal returns", "parent firm valuation effects", "shareholder wealth effects", "parent firm performance effects"]
definition: Firm i's abnormal return for a given day within the event period is the difference between the firm's actual return and the return predicted by the market model; cumulative abnormal returns accumulate these over the event period.

name: Inside ownership
authors_terms: ["inside ownership percentage", "parent firm's ownership structure", "inside ownership"]
definition: OWN is the percentage of stock held by U.S. parent firm i's officers and directors.

name: Free cash flow
authors_terms: ["free cash flow", "free cash flows", "internally available funds", "slack resources"]
definition: U.S. parent firm i's free cash flow, FCF, is estimated as income before extraordinary items plus depreciation and amortization less capital expenditures, which is then scaled by dividing by the parent firm's market value on the event date.

name: Leverage
definition: LEV is total liabilities divided by total assets for the U.S. parent firm.

name: Firm responsiveness to stakeholder requests
authors_terms: ["Saliency", "saliency of the stakeholder request", "firm response", "positive firm responses", "responds positively"]
definition: 'We assert that saliency arises out of the stakeholder-request-firm triplet. With such a conceptualization, we can measure saliency by action rather than preference. In other words, saliency is determined by the degree to which a firm positively responds to a specific stakeholder request. By 'positively', we mean that the firm acts in ways consistent with the stakeholder's request.'

name: Relative stakeholder power
definition: 'We define stakeholder power as the relative access to resources for the stakeholder group with respect to the firm being targeted.' The authors note that this definition 'emphasizes that stakeholder power is a two-way street' and is thus 'an attribute of a stakeholder-firm pair.'

name: Stakeholder group legitimacy
authors_terms: ["Group Legitimacy", "Stakeholder Legitimacy", "legitimacy of the stakeholder group"]
definition: Following Mitchell et al., legitimacy is 'a generalized perception or assumption that the actions of an entity are desirable, proper or appropriate within some socially constructed system of norms, values, beliefs, and definitions.' The authors measure the degree to which different types of stakeholder groups are perceived by the general public to be legitimate arbiters of environmental issues.

name: Request legitimacy
authors_terms: ["Request Legitimacy", "legitimacy of the stakeholder request", "legitimacy of the environmental issue"]
definition: 'We propose that legitimacy is granted not only to the stakeholder group, but also to the specific issues championed by the stakeholder.' The measure 'focus[es] on the legitimacy of the environmental issue at the center of a stakeholder request' - the degree to which the issue raised by the request is well accepted and well defined.

name: Request urgency
authors_terms: ["Request Urgency", "urgency of the stakeholder request", "immediacy of the request"]
definition: 'We propose that it is the urgency of the claim or request rather than the urgency of the stakeholder group that matters,' casting urgency 'in terms of whether an individual stakeholder claim or request is intended to stop or alter present, ongoing actions of the firm vs. altering future, planned actions.'

name: Technical marginality
authors_terms: ["technical marginality", "expertise distance", "problem-expertise distance", "distance between the solvers' field of expertise and the focal field of the problem"]
definition: Being distant in terms of technical expertise from the field of the problem, i.e., being in a different technical field. Because they are not closely affiliated with the problem field, marginal individuals are well positioned to possess perspectives and heuristics that are not present in the focal field context.

name: Social marginality
authors_terms: ["social marginality", "gender", "being a woman", "female solvers", "the 'outer circle' of the scientific establishment"]
definition: Being distant from the 'establishment' in one's own professional community; the authors proxy it by gender, arguing that women are more likely to be in the 'the outer circle' of the scientific establishment. Because individuals become socialized to the norms and beliefs of their fields, remaining at the margins offers those marginalized a different set of perspectives and heuristics than those at the core of the professional establishment.

name: Problem-solving success
authors_terms: ["successful solution generation", "problem-solving success", "solver winner", "winning solver", "developing a winning solution"]
definition: Generation of a solution that the problem holder firm declares meets its solution criteria and for which the solver is awarded the prize; firms declare problems solved or not solved after blind evaluation of submissions.

name: Decision to submit a solution
authors_terms: ["submit solution", "decision to exert effort and submit a solution", "self-selection to submit a solution"]
definition: The solver's decision to exert effort and submit a solution for evaluation upon getting the details of a problem.

name: New product introductions
authors_terms: ["number of new products", "new product introductions", "new product introduction"]
definition: New product introduction is an important measure of innovativeness, because it indicates the potential commercial significance of a firm's innovation activities. New product introduction is defined as the number of new products a firm introduces yearly.

name: Internal search age
authors_terms: ["average internal search age", "mean age of the internal knowledge searched", "average age of the knowledge a firm uses in its internal search"]
definition: Average search age is defined as the mean age of the knowledge used in a firm's yearly innovation search. This variable represents the average age of the knowledge a firm uses in its internal search; internal search consists of citations to the firm's own patents.

name: Competitor search age
authors_terms: ["average competitor search age", "mean age of the competitor knowledge searched"]
definition: This variable captures the average age of the competitor knowledge a firm uses in its search. A patent was defined as competitor knowledge if it belonged to any of the other 130 robotics companies in the sample.

name: External search age
authors_terms: ["average external search age", "mean age of the external knowledge searched"]
definition: This variable represents the average age of the external knowledge foundations used in search. External search age was the average age of cited patents that were not self- or competitor citations per firm year.

name: External search quantity
authors_terms: ["external search quantity", "search quantity", "number of external knowledge elements searched each year"]
definition: Search quantity is the number of external knowledge elements searched each year. This variable describes the intensity of external search efforts.

name: Internal search age diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of internal search age", "age variance of the internal knowledge searched"]
definition: Diversity of search age is defined as the degree of temporal heterogeneity in search, or the extent to which firms search a narrow or a broad age range of knowledge. This variable represents the diversity in the ages of the internal knowledge elements a firm searches.

name: Competitor search age diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of competitor search age", "age variance of the competitor knowledge searched"]
definition: This variable stands for the diversity in the ages of the competitor knowledge a firm uses in its search, measured as the variance in competitor search age in each firm-year.

name: External search age diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of external search age", "age variance of the external knowledge searched"]
definition: Capturing the diversity in the ages of the external knowledge used in search, this variable was measured as the variance in external search age in each firm-year.

name: Prior employment tie to an interlocking director
authors_terms: ["prior employment ties", "prior employment tie", "executive to interlocking director employment tie", "executive to interlocking director employment ties", "employment ties to interlocking directors", "shared prior employment"]
definition: Prior employment ties are conceptualized as preexisting interpersonal links between executives and interlocking directors from having previously worked at the same prior employer at the same time. Conceptualized this way, a prior employment tie reflects a form of a direct (or strong) tie that not only underlies executives' professional networks, but also provides directors with an intimate knowledge of the executive and that individual's quality as a manager.

name: Movement to an outside firm
authors_terms: ["movement to an outside firm", "movement to outside firms", "interfirm mobility"]
definition: The authors tracked employment histories in BoardEx for each exiting executive and coded the variable movement to an outside firm as '1' if the individual left the focal firm in t and became an executive of another public or private firm in t + 1, and '0' otherwise.

name: Movement to an interlocking firm
authors_terms: ["movement to an interlocking firm", "movement to a director's interlocking firm", "movement to the director's interlocking firm", "executive poaching"]
definition: Firms were classified as interlocking if one or more directors in the focal firm was either an executive or director in the new employing firm in t; movement to an interlocking firm was coded '1' if the executive left the focal firm and was listed as an executive in such a firm in t + 1, and '0' otherwise. A more direct binary measure at the executive-director dyad level captures movement to a specific director's interlocking firm.

name: Lead outsider position in the focal firm
authors_terms: ["lead outsider in focal firm", "lead outside director", "lead outsider on the focal firm's board", "independent chairperson of the board", "lead independent director"]
definition: Depending on the board's leadership structure, the lead outside director may either be an independent board chair or a lead independent director. In either of these positions, an outside director represents fellow board members and has primary responsibility for ensuring that the board executes its duties in ways that support the interests of the focal firm and its shareholders.

name: CEO position in the interlocking firm
authors_terms: ["CEO in interlocking firm", "CEO at the interlocking firm", "director who is also a CEO at an interlocking firm"]
definition: Some directors actively work as CEOs of other firms, so an individual can simultaneously serve as an outside board member in one firm and be the CEO at another firm. Such directors are likely to prioritize their primary role as a CEO when considering whether to use a prior employment tie to poach an executive.

name: Institutional stockholder control
authors_terms: ["institutional stockholder control", "institutional investors' stockholding", "institutional stock ownership", "institutional investment"]
definition: The size of institutional investors' stake in companies gives them two advantages: they can efficiently gather information required to vote more consistently in accordance with stockholders' economic interests, and they can efficiently organize and use their clout to influence managements' actions, including the prevention of antitakeover provisions.

name: Managerial stock ownership
authors_terms: ["managerial stock ownership", "managerial equity ownership", "managers' stockholding", "managerial stock holdings"]
definition: Managerial stock ownership is a means of aligning managers' and stockholders' interests and reducing agency problems: when managers own stock in a company, they essentially become stockholders and bear the wealth effects of their decisions. However, high levels of managerial equity ownership can result in accumulation of power and, consequently, entrenchment as well.

name: Antitakeover provision adoption
authors_terms: ["adoption of antitakeover provisions", "rate of adoption of antitakeover provisions", "adoption of antitakeover amendments", "antitakeover provisions", "takeover defenses"]
definition: Actions that mitigate the influence of the external market for corporate control, such as antitakeover provisions, are viewed by most observers as entrenchment strategies which are against stockholder interests. The basic premise of this study is that antitakeover provisions are entrenchment strategies that restrict the monitoring influence of the external market for corporate control.

name: Board composition
authors_terms: ["board composition", "proportion of outsiders on the board", "relative mix of insiders and outsiders"]
definition: Board composition relates to the mix of insiders and outsiders on the board. Insiders are employees of the firm, while outsiders are not employees of the organization.

name: Loyalty of outside board members
authors_terms: ["loyalty of outside board members", "outsiders' loyalty", "percentage of loyal outsiders"]
definition: Even if outsiders dominate a board, their loyalty to the current CEO is likely to influence their governance effectiveness. Outsiders' loyalty can depend on the incumbent CEO's influence on their appointment to the board, so outsiders appointed during the current CEO's tenure are likely to be more loyal to the CEO and incumbent management.

name: Outside director equity ownership
authors_terms: ["outsiders' stock ownership", "outside directors' equity ownership", "outside board members' stock ownership", "outsiders' shareholding"]
definition: Directors owning stock in the company are more likely to identify with stockholders' interests and actively participate in board decisions. Consequently, outside board members' stock ownership will increase their incentive to prevent the adoption of antitakeover provisions.

name: Unitary board leadership
definition: Corporate leadership is structured in two ways. Dual leadership occurs when different individuals serve as CEO and chairperson of the board, whereas unitary leadership exists when the same individual serves as both CEO and chairperson.

name: Board characteristics
authors_terms: ["board characteristics", "board attributes", "characteristics of corporate boards", "structure of corporate boards"]
definition: Past studies in the governance literature have used several board attributes as measurements of board independence: composition and leadership structure, tenure of board members, and outside board members' stock ownership.

name: Involvement of affected groups
definition: The relation of the project to the affected groups and, in particular, the priority groups placed on the project, their level of concern and awareness about the project, and value conflicts surrounding the project (a negative association), together with how well participants thought they understood the causation of the problem and how well they actually understood what caused the problem.

name: Quality of planning staff
authors_terms: ["Planning Staff", "experience, skill, and adequacy of numbers of planning staff"]
definition: The experience, skill, and adequacy of numbers of the planning staff.

name: Technological change
definition: The level of technology perceived to be needed, the level actually needed, and the extent to which the technology differed from current technology.

name: Time available
definition: How adequate the lead organization judged the staff and calendar time available.

name: Project impact and mandate
authors_terms: ["Impact/Required", "potential impact on organizational structures of affected groups"]
definition: The potential impact on the organizational structures of affected groups, whether the lead organization was required to undertake the project, the level of conflict over values, and (negatively) the stability of the political environment.

name: Environmental stability
authors_terms: ["Stability", "stability of the general political and economic environment"]
definition: Economic and political environmental stability and, somewhat, past success.

name: Prior coalitions
definition: The existence and stability of coalitions among affected organizations prior to the change effort.

name: Lead organization power
definition: The power of the lead organization and the adequacy of the money available, and (negatively) the potential impact on resources.

name: Communication
definition: Internal and external communication, the extent of search for solutions, and the number of groups involved in searching for solutions.

name: Forcing
authors_terms: ["Forcing", "the use of forcing as a conflict resolution strategy"]
definition: Projects that took longer than expected and in which the lead organization tried to force its views on other groups to resolve conflicts and did not use problem-solving.

name: Compromise
authors_terms: ["Compromise", "the use of compromise as a conflict resolution strategy"]
definition: Involving affected groups in identifying problems and solutions, using compromise as a conflict resolution strategy, and turnover.

name: Project success
definition: Overall goal achievement, satisfaction with the outcome, enhanced future problem-solving capacity, few deviations from success criteria, and little change from the project-as-approved to the project-as-implemented.

name: Learning from the project
authors_terms: ["Learning", "learning that would be useful in the future"]
definition: Learning that would be useful in the future, and fewer deviations from the success criteria of other involved organizations.

name: Environmental strategy
authors_terms: ["environmental strategy", "conformance versus voluntariness", "voluntary environmental strategy", "conformance environmental strategy"]
definition: Environmental strategy refers to "a pattern in action over time" intended to manage the interface between business and the natural environment, and here it refers to outcomes in the form of actions firms take for regulatory compliance and to those they take voluntarily to further reduce the environmental impacts of operations. The classification adopted is the continuum of conformance to voluntary, where conformance involves complying with regulations and adopting standard industry practices and a voluntary strategy is a consistent pattern of company actions taken to reduce environmental impact that go beyond regulations and standard practices.

name: Managerial interpretations of environmental issues
authors_terms: ["managerial interpretations of environmental issues as threats or opportunities", "threat interpretations", "opportunity interpretations", "threat-opportunity categorization of strategic issues"]
definition: Three attributes help explain managers' reactions to strategic issues as opportunities or threats: negative or positive emotional associations, loss or gain considerations, and a sense of the issues as uncontrollable or controllable. Categorizing issues as opportunities rather than as threats helps managers reduce the ambiguity and unpredictability surrounding environmental technologies and information and has been found to result in a more open search for solutions.

name: Legitimation of environmental issues in corporate identity
authors_terms: ["issue legitimation as an integral aspect of corporate identity", "legitimation of environmental issues as a part of corporate identity", "environmental concern as central to the company's identity"]
definition: When concern for the environment becomes an integral component of corporate identity, environmental issues become "harder to disown," which channels resources for action on these issues and provides political ammunition for justifying and legitimating further issue commitment. Environmental issues may be legitimated as an integral part of corporate identity on the basis of an internal economic focus or a broader corporate social responsibility focus.

name: Discretionary slack
definition: Discretion is latitude of managerial action, and slack is the "resource that enables an organization both to adjust to gross shifts in the external environment with minimal trauma, and to experiment with new postures in relation to that environment." Thus, discretionary slack is a manager-level variable that facilitates "certain types of strategic or creative behavior within an organization" and allows adjustment to changes in the external business environment.

name: Integration of environmental criteria into employee performance evaluation
authors_terms: ["integration of environmental criteria into employee performance evaluation systems", "integration of environmental performance criteria into control systems", "employee evaluation systems"]
definition: The extent to which a company integrates environmental performance criteria into its control systems, notably environmental performance criteria used as incentives and balanced with economic performance criteria. Balancing long-term, output-based environmental performance criteria with economic criteria in employee performance evaluation encourages managers to view environmental issues as opportunities for gain rather than as threats of loss.

name: Behavior control
definition: Within a bureaucratic framework, formal behavior control regulates the actions subordinates exhibit on the job. More generally, it structures the transformation process of work (Ouchi, 1977).

name: Output control
definition: Output control differs from behavior control in that superiors do not translate intentions into standardized operating procedures but instead set targets, such as financial results, for subordinates to pursue (Hill & Hoskisson, 1987).

name: Input control
authors_terms: ["input control", "clan control", "skill standardization", "ex ante control", "socialization control"]
definition: Input control regulates the antecedent conditions of performance—the knowledge, skills, abilities, values, and motives of employees; behavior control regulates the transformation process; and output control regulates results.

name: Knowledge of cause-effect relations
authors_terms: ["knowledge of cause-effect relations", "cause-effect knowledge", "cause/effect relations", "knowledge of the transformation process", "task programmability"]
definition: Thompson (1967: 85) argued that behavior control assumes managerial knowledge of "cause/effect relations," or the link between the actions subordinates take and the results they achieve. The measure captures the extent to which the relationship between subordinates' actions and outcomes can be predicted and observed.

name: Crystallization of standards of desirable performance
authors_terms: ["crystallization of standards of desirable performance", "crystallized standards", "standards of desirable performance", "outcome observability", "availability of output measures"]
definition: Crystallized standards require reliable and valid criteria that represent performance benefiting firm. Other authors have called this requirement "outcome observability" (Eisenhardt, 1985) and "availability of output measures" (Ouchi, 1977).

name: Product-market variation
definition: In this study, I conceived of strategic posture in terms of product-market variation, or the degree of breadth and change in a firm's products or markets (Hambrick, 1983; Snow & Hrebiniak, 1980).

name: Work flow integration
definition: Technology in general and work flow integration, the way work flows between units, in particular have a direct impact on the informational demands placed on superiors (e.g., Child, 1973; Perrow, 1967; Reeves & Woodward, 1970; Thompson, 1967). The measure covers Thompson's three types of work flow integration (independent, sequential, and reciprocal), which represent increasing levels of technological interdependence.

name: Firm size
definition: Child (1974) argued that firm size limits the capacity of executives to personally monitor the activities of subordinates. Firm size was defined as number of full time employees.

name: CEO-board friendship ties
authors_terms: ["CEO-board friendship ties", "friendship ties", "perceived friendship ties", "perceived friends"]
definition: Friendship is characterized as a prototypical personal relation that is normatively free of instrumental and calculative orientations, governed by communal norms whereby individuals are obligated to care for each other's welfare rather than to reciprocate benefits. Friendship ties between a CEO and outside directors imply trust, or the expectation of personal loyalty.

name: CEO-appointed outside directors
authors_terms: ["the portion of outside directors appointed after a given CEO's appointment", "portion of a firm's board appointed after its CEO", "subsequent board appointments"]
definition: The portion of a board appointed after a CEO is the number of outside directors appointed during a CEO's tenure divided by the total number of outside board members. Norms of reciprocity are argued to make such directors feel socially obligated to support the CEO responsible for nominating them.

name: Board monitoring
definition: The function of boards is to reduce agency costs resulting from the delegation of strategic decision making, or "decision management," to top executives by exercising "decision control," which involves monitoring managerial decision making and performance. Monitoring is one of the two distinct functions within the board's broader administrative role, along with the provision of advice and counsel.

name: Board advice and counsel
authors_terms: ["advice and counsel interactions", "board advice and counsel", "advisory interactions", "advice giving", "provision of advice and counsel"]
definition: Board advice and counsel complement board monitoring as a form of involvement: when involvement extends beyond control to include advisory interactions, directors participate in formulating strategic decisions as well as in evaluating them, so that boards influence each major phase of the decision-making process.

name: CEO incentive alignment
authors_terms: ["CEO incentive alignment", "incentive alignment", "financial incentive alignment", "CEO ownership", "long-term incentive plan compensation"]
definition: Incentive alignment motivates a CEO to use corporate resources to the advantage of shareholders; financial incentives are recognized by agency theorists as a partial substitute for monitoring activities, so that the need for monitoring declines as agent incentives are aligned more closely with the interests of principals.

name: Firm performance
definition: Two measures of firm performance were used: return on equity (an accounting-based measure) and the market-to-book value of equity (a market-based measure). The latter measure gauges a firm's effectiveness in creating value for shareholders by comparing its market value with the cost of capital contributed by shareholders.

name: Strategic noise
authors_terms: ["strategic noise", "noisy CEO succession event", "noisy CEO succession", "anticipatory obfuscation", "confounded CEO succession"]
definition: Strategic noise occurs when: (1) two or more important events are announced simultaneously; (2) the timing of announcements is under the control of the organization; and (3) announcements are neither intended to clarify nor are they causally related to the initial event. It is an anticipatory, preemptive, and obfuscatory form of impression management that is injected at the time a new CEO is announced.

name: Outgoing CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["tenure of the outgoing CEO", "outgoing CEO tenure", "CEO tenure"]
definition: The length of service of the outgoing CEO. The longer the tenure of an outgoing CEO, the less likely it is that members of that board have been involved in a CEO succession, and the more the CEO is identified with the firm, which exacerbates board uncertainty about shareholder reaction to a successor.

name: Outgoing CEO pay gap
authors_terms: ["pay gap between outgoing CEO and top managers", "gap in pay between the outgoing CEO and the rest of the top management team", "CEO-top management pay gap"]
definition: The pay of the CEO compared to other top managers, which is an indicator of the 'relative significance of the CEO in terms of abilities, contribution, or power' (Bebchuk, Cremers, and Peyer, 2006: 1), or the degree to which a CEO dominates a firm. As the pay gap grows, the new CEO simply has bigger shoes to fill.

name: Managerial discretion
definition: Managerial discretion is defined as the latitude for action or range of strategic options that executives have at their disposal. The greater the amount of discretion at a firm, the greater the amount of influence a CEO has on organizational outcomes.

name: Firm stock market performance
authors_terms: ["recent firm performance", "recent firm stock performance", "company market performance"]
definition: Firm performance as assessed by recent stock market returns; the measure consists of a firm's yearly stock returns assuming reinvestment of dividends. Stock market performance, more directly than accounting performance, captures assessments that inform how risky or uncertain a CEO succession may be in the minds of directors.

name: Prior CEO experience
authors_terms: ["previous experience as CEO", "prior CEO experience", "CEO experience"]
definition: Whether the newly appointed CEO has previously served as a CEO; previous CEO experience may signal to shareholders the ability to lead from day one, may legitimate the selection, and may mean the person is generally known and thus a less uncertain or less risky choice.

name: Incoming CEO age
authors_terms: ["incoming CEO age", "age of the incoming CEO"]
definition: The appointee's age at the time of appointment, an observable characteristic that may influence external perceptions of the qualifications of a new CEO; a young CEO may not be viewed as having the breadth and depth of experience of an older candidate.

name: Incoming CEO home firm reputation
authors_terms: ["reputation of an incoming CEO's home firm", "outside CEO home firm reputation"]
definition: Whether a person hired from outside the organization comes from a firm that has a strong, positive reputation; a key determinant of a candidate's legitimacy is the reputation of his or her firm, and experience in a firm held in high regard may be an important informational cue for investors.

name: Content knowledge
definition: Content knowledge refers to discrete knowledge about a concept or stimulus, which increases with experience. As entrepreneurs increase their cumulative experience with a specific strategy element they develop greater content knowledge about that element.

name: Structural knowledge
definition: Structural knowledge consists of knowledge about the relationships between different knowledge components and relates to the sequencing, association, or linkage between concepts or stimuli. Entrepreneurs develop greater structural knowledge about strategy elements through exposure to those elements in different contexts.

name: Knowledge recency
definition: The recency of an entrepreneur's specific knowledge acquisition affects the degree to which he or she can access that knowledge; knowledge decay occurs quite rapidly within the first few years, but then levels off over time.

name: Knowledge variety
authors_terms: ["knowledge variety", "variety of experience", "breadth of domain experience"]
definition: Entrepreneurs whose knowledge spans problem domains will have greater opportunity to recombine knowledge elements and derive solutions that deviate from past ways of doing things. Knowledge variety was measured using a count variable that tallied the number of product markets, geographic markets, or resources in which the founder had prior work experience.

name: Shared knowledge
definition: Experience-based knowledge that the entrepreneur and members of the founding team hold in common; teams tend to discuss shared more than unique experience, so shared experience will likely influence the decision outcome.

name: Unique knowledge
definition: Knowledge held uniquely by individual members of the founding team; team members who possess unique knowledge may be able to stimulate the decision making of other members and foster the consideration of new options.

name: Strategy element choice
authors_terms: ["strategy choices", "strategy elements", "product market choice", "geographic market choice", "resource choice", "customer scope"]
definition: The strategy choices examined include the product and geographic markets (i.e., customer scope) in which the new venture will compete and the form of physical resources that the new venture will choose to deliver a product or service within these markets. The three dependent variables are the choices made with respect to product market, geographic market, and resources.

name: Host-country policy dispute
authors_terms: ["dispute against host", "policy dispute", "dispute with a host government", "firm-specific policy behavior"]
definition: A policy dispute is a formal dispute between a firm and a foreign host government, identified through claims lodged by firms against governments at the World Bank's International Center for the Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). The authors focus on instances in which the government policy behavior that triggered the dispute was targeted directly and specifically at the firm(s) involved.

name: Same-region policy dispute
authors_terms: ["dispute against another country in host's region", "contagion effect", "intra-firm contagion process"]
definition: A firm's dispute with the government of one country is expected to affect its assessments in other countries that are politically, economically, and socially similar; the authors identify similar countries as those within the same political-geographic region.

name: Other firms' policy disputes
authors_terms: ["total disputes against host involving other firms", "number of disputes in which a firm is not directly involved", "spillover effect"]
definition: The number of disputes involving firm-specific policy behavior in which other firms, rather than the focal firm, are involved with the host country in the dyad.

name: Divestiture
definition: A divestiture takes place when a firm disposes of a business unit by offering it up for sale on the market.

name: Institutional barriers to entrepreneurship
authors_terms: ["institutional reforms", "institutional changes", "barriers to new firm entry", "barriers to firm growth", "barriers to exit", "reduced barriers to entry", "reduced barriers to growth", "reduced barriers to exit"]
definition: Obstacles to new firm entry comprise lengthy and costly procedures for obtaining operating permits and registering new firms. Barriers to firm growth include limits on firm growth, such as antitrust laws and laws restricting firm size, and barriers to exit comprise regulatory and government-imposed impediments to recovering from failure and losses.

name: Perceived benefits of accelerators
authors_terms: ["perceived benefits of accelerators", "perceived value of venture accelerators"]
definition: Entrepreneurs' perceived value of the resources and benefits that venture accelerators provide — network development, business skills development, and securing direct venture funding — for early-stage start-up development.

name: Probability of being selected
authors_terms: ["applicants' probability of being selected", "probability of being selected", "Pr(Selected)"]
definition: The probability that an applicant is admitted to the accelerator program of choice; the combination of more and more heterogeneous applicants lowers applicants' average probability of being selected.

name: Quality of accelerator cohorts
authors_terms: ["cohort quality", "quality of start-up cohorts", "quality of accelerated cohorts"]
definition: The quality of selected applicants into each accelerator in each application cycle, measured as the average log Revenue, log Employees, and log Patents for selected applicants.

name: Start-up applicant quality
definition: The quality of the start-ups that apply, probed through their traction at the time of applying, focused on three primary indicators: employees, revenue, and intellectual property.

name: Number of accelerator applicants
definition: The count of the total number of applicants to each accelerator, computed by summing the total number of applicants to each accelerator per year.

name: Applicant heterogeneity
definition: Applicants' industry and stage heterogeneity relative to the accelerator's previously admitted applicants, with 100 denoting high heterogeneity in terms of industry and stage of development relative to previously admitted applicants, and 0 denoting low heterogeneity.

name: Founding team education
definition: The combined education of members of the founding team listed on the application, using the sum of individuals' levels of education.

name: Founding team experience
authors_terms: ["Team Experience", "founders' years of previous work experience"]
definition: The total number of years of prior work experience of members of the founding team listed on the application, using the sum of founders' years of previous work experience.

name: Founding team gender composition
definition: Whether any of the members of the founding team of each start-up applicant were women.

name: Combination of political tactics
authors_terms: ["combine political tactics", "use multiple political tactics", "bundling", "combining tactics", "politically active firms combine tactics"]
definition: In this study, we argue that firms use multiple tactics in order to enter the political arena. Politically active firms often combine making PAC contributions, having Washington offices (inside lobbyists), and contracting with outside lobbyists.

name: Political action committee contributions
definition: PAC contributions to all congressional candidates in the 1991-92 and 1993-94 elections. A PAC is a legal mechanism that permits certain organizations to contribute money to politicians.

name: Inside lobbying
definition: The average number of staff members in each firm's Washington office from 1991 to 1994 (such staff are called inside lobbyists).

name: Outside lobbying
definition: The average number of outside lobbyists and political consultants retained by each firm from 1991 to 1994.

name: Industry concentration
definition: In concentrated industries, it is generally easier to organize political cooperation and to discourage individual firms from free riding, which results in a larger overall collective good and larger portions for individual firms.

name: Industry political rivalry
definition: For each political activity, we calculated the proportions of a firm's competitors within its three-digit SIC code that used PACs, inside lobbying, and outside lobbying during the years 1991-94. Although this measure, industry political rivalry, does not capture the strength of a particular firm within its industry, it does indicate for a target firm how many of its rivals engaged in each of the political activities of interest here.

name: Industry unionization
authors_terms: ["unionization", "industry unionization", "percentage of its workforce that was represented by unions"]
definition: For each industry, we measured unionization as the percentage of its workforce that was represented by unions, as measured by Curme, Hirsch, and McPherson (1990).

name: Congressional caucus representation
definition: Some of the informal congressional organizations called caucuses (Hammond, 1998) are organized around industries; examples include the Congressional Automotive Caucus, the Congressional Biotechnology Caucus, and the Congressional Steel Caucus.

name: Firm size
definition: The logarithm of a firm's sales, averaged over 1991-94, was calculated from COMPUSTAT data.

name: Free cash flow
definition: Free cash flow, averaged over 1991-94, was calculated as net income minus income taxes minus gross interest expense on long-term debt minus dividends paid on preferred stock minus dividends paid on common stock.

name: Government contract reliance
authors_terms: ["government contracts", "Department of Defense contracts", "proportion of total revenue from the federal government"]
definition: We measured government contracts as the log of the dollar amount of Department of Defense Primary Contracts and Department of Defense Research and Development Contracts, divided by firm's total sales, averaged over 1991-94.

name: Contextual ambidexterity
definition: Contextual ambidexterity is the behavioral capacity to simultaneously demonstrate alignment and adaptability across an entire business unit. It is a multidimensional construct, with alignment and adaptability each constituting a separate, but interrelated, nonsubstitutable element.

name: Alignment
definition: Alignment refers to coherence among all the patterns of activities in the business unit; they are working together toward the same goals.

name: Adaptability
definition: Adaptability refers to the capacity to reconfigure activities in the business unit quickly to meet changing demands in the task environment.

name: Organization context
definition: Broadly defined, organization context is the systems, processes, and beliefs that shape individual-level behaviors in an organization. It reflects a combination of the structural context, culture, and climate of a business unit and is considered an objective, higher-level attribute of the unit as a whole.

name: Performance management context
definition: One of these factors represents a combination of the items developed for discipline and stretch, and so we refer to this as 'performance management context.'

name: Social context
definition: The other factor represents a combination of the items developed for support and trust, so we refer to this factor as 'social context' to represent the content of the items in this construct.

name: Business-unit performance
definition: The dependent variable was measured with four items that required the senior and middle management respondents to reflect on performance over the last five years.

name: Idea radicalness
definition: A radical idea, as opposed to an incremental one, is an idea that departs substantially from prior ideas and practices, and therefore, typically requires access to new knowledge, skills, and competencies for successful development.

name: Team idea development
authors_terms: ["team idea development", "working with a team", "developing an idea with a team", "work with a team to develop the next idea"]
definition: We define team idea development as occurring when the idea generator collaborates with at least one other person on developing an idea.

name: Prior team idea development
authors_terms: ["prior team idea development", "prior team experience", "worked with a team to develop the prior idea"]
definition: Prior team idea development measures whether an idea generator worked with a team to develop the prior idea; the authors refer to prior team idea development when they previously worked with a team to develop an earlier idea.

name: Prior idea success
authors_terms: ["prior idea success", "prior success", "having developed a successful idea before"]
definition: Prior idea success means that a prior idea passed the second stage of the screening process.

name: Idea success
authors_terms: ["idea success", "successful idea", "success of the second idea"]
definition: We classify a successful idea as one where an idea is selected after the second panel, and an unsuccessful idea as one where an idea is not accepted after either the first or second panel.

name: Political uncertainty in the host country
authors_terms: ["political uncertainty", "uncertainty about future government policies", "heightened political uncertainty right before national elections"]
definition: Political uncertainty is uncertainty about future government policies. The host government's economic policies (e.g., labor laws, exchange rate, corporate taxation) shape its business landscape and affect investment outcomes, so uncertainty over such policies can complicate the valuation of cross-border acquisitions.

name: Target's relative acquisition gains
authors_terms: ["Δ$CAR", "target firms' relative gains", "the fraction of the total acquisition gains that accrues to the target relative to the acquirer", "bargaining outcomes"]
definition: The fraction of the total acquisition gains that accrues to the target relative to the acquirer, calculated as the target's cumulative abnormal dollar returns minus the acquirer's cumulative abnormal dollar returns, scaled by the sum of the acquirer and target market values. It is based on stock price reaction to the announcement of a deal and reflects investors' expectations about the division of the acquisition gains.

name: Abnormal profit
authors_terms: ["abnormal profits", "abnormal ROS", "return on sales (ROS) minus the industry average ROS", "superior profits", "profit advantage"]
definition: The abnormal profit of firm i in period t, r it, is defined as the return on sales (ROS) for firm i in period t minus the industry average ROS. Firms with abnormal profits greater than zero are referenced as superior, or above average, performers and firms with abnormal profits less than zero as poor, or below average, performers.

name: Profit persistence
authors_terms: ["persistence", "convergence", "persistence rate", "persistence (convergence) of abnormal profits", "duration of an advantage"]
definition: Persistence is defined as the percentage of total abnormal profits in any period before t that remain in period t. A value greater than zero and less than 1 suggests the persistence of abnormal profits; a value less than zero and greater than (-1) indicates convergence.

name: Organizational cohort
definition: A cohort is a group of firms that enters an industry at roughly the same time or during the same era in an industry's history, where an era is defined by distinct historical, institutional, technological, and competitive conditions. Cohort effects thus explain part of the competitive heterogeneity in an industry.

name: Ambiguity
definition: Ambiguity exists whenever a situation spawns multiple, competing interpretations of what is going on and thereby produces a shock of confusion. This confusion can arise both because a given person can see multiple ways to interpret a situation and because different people may interpret the same situation differently.

name: Formal network tie
definition: Two people working in the same formal subunit, for example the same department, can be thought of as having a formal network tie that is independent of whatever personal connection they might have. Formal organization refers to the departmental affiliations, reporting relationships, and roles that prescribe behavior and interaction.

name: Semiformal network tie
authors_terms: ["semiformal network tie", "semiformal tie", "semiformal network contacts", "semiformal organization"]
definition: The closer two individuals are to each other in semiformal structure, based on the extent to which they participate together on many project teams, task forces, employee groups, and so forth, the more we can think of them as having a semiformal network tie. Semiformal organization consists of shared affiliations afforded but not necessarily mandated by participation in project teams, task forces, and employee groups.

name: Informal network tie
definition: People who do not have a formal or semiformal tie to one another but nevertheless have an interpersonal relationship can be thought of as having an informal network tie. Informal organization represents discretionary patterns of behavior and interaction.

name: Communication with formal-only contacts
authors_terms: ["communication with formal network contacts that do not have a significant semiformal component", "communication with formal network ties that do not have a significant semiformal component"]
definition: A formal tie with no, or a limited, semiformal component is one of three possible configurations of formal and semiformal ties between two colleagues. With respect to such ties, the focal actor will tend to know what the other knows but will deem what the other knows to be less valuable during periods of ambiguity relative to times of clarity, and will also perceive greater interpersonal cost in reaching out.

name: Communication with semiformal-only contacts
authors_terms: ["communication with semiformal network contacts that do not have a significant formal component", "communication with semiformal network ties that do not have a significant formal component"]
definition: A semiformal tie with no, or a limited, formal component is one of three possible configurations of formal and semiformal ties between two colleagues. The focal actor will be less likely to know what such a contact knows but will consider what that contact knows to be more valuable during periods of ambiguity relative to times of clarity.

name: Communication with informal contacts
authors_terms: ["communication with informal network contacts", "communication with informal network ties", "communication with informal ties"]
definition: People who do not have a formal or semiformal tie to one another but nevertheless have an interpersonal relationship can be thought of as having an informal network tie. The choice to initiate contact with informal network contacts is shaped by a similar set of considerations as the choice to interact with semiformal ties that do not have a significant formal component.

name: Religious diversity within Islam
authors_terms: ["religious diversity within Islam", "diversity within Islam", "internal diversity of Islam"]
definition: I focus on a key characteristic of Islam, its internal diversity. Islam is a diverse and decentralized belief system; it includes multiple denominations, such as Sunni and Shia, and each has a distinct set of organizing principles.

name: Founding rates of Islamic investment funds
authors_terms: ["founding rates", "entrepreneurial supply of Islamic investment funds", "product supply of Islamic funds"]
definition: I used founding rates to measure the entrepreneurial supply of Islamic investment funds in a country, and followed previous studies on new venture creations to model the founding of Islamic investment funds as the number of newly started Islamic investment funds per country year.

name: Investor demand for Islamic investment funds
authors_terms: ["assets managed by Islamic investment funds", "assets under management", "investor demand"]
definition: I used the logged assets under management as a measure of investor demand in the Islamic investment fund sector. This captures the amount of pooled savings from investors, and as Islamic investing is still highly domestic, it proxies for the demand for Islamic investment funds in a given country.

name: Market logic
definition: Market logic is rooted in global neoliberalism, and it serves to maximize individual liberty in the pursuit of economic wealth and advocates free-market approaches to the economy.

name: State logic
definition: State logic emphasize stability and development through laws and regulations.

name: Bribery relationship
definition: Bribery conceptualized as a relationship in which bribery transactions are repeated and firms may frequently interact with rent-seeking government officials. A bribery relationship consists of repeated bribery transactions, and bribery relationships between firms and government officials can go beyond just paying and receiving bribes.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm growth is measured using the rate of firms' sales growth, which is the most imminent and critical goal for firms and a performance measure universally applicable across industries and ultimately necessary for survival.

name: New product introduction
authors_terms: ["new product", "new products", "new product introduction", "firms with new products", "firms without new products"]
definition: Whether a firm introduces new products or services, used as a firm status that signals future potential and draws market attention. The authors use a dummy for firms that introduced new products or services and invested in research and development.

name: Pervasive corruption
definition: The extent to which corruption is established as taken-for-granted rules and norms, defined as 'the average firm's likelihood of encountering corruption in its normal interactions with state officials'.

name: Quality of governance
definition: The quality of governance, such as how effective and stable regulations, rules of law, and political status are in a country, which determines the country-level institutional environments where firms in bribery relationships are doing business. It is a more comprehensive country-wide institutional environment reflecting how much firms can depend on sound regulations and rules of laws that govern an entire country.

name: Perceived technological uncertainty
