definition: A second type of uncertainty is associated with technologies themselves and their commercial success. This uncertainty is due to the inherently unpredictable and dynamic nature of R&D activities.

name: Technology alliance use
authors_terms: ["technology alliance use", "use of technology alliances", "technology alliance formation", "pursuit of technology alliances"]
definition: Technology alliances occur when two or more firms contribute their technological expertise to achieve an agreed-upon innovation. These are not one-way transfers of know-how such as licensing agreements, one-time-only contracts, or equipment purchases, but rather, interdependent and ongoing relationships.

name: Use of equity ties
definition: One means of establishing an alliance with hierarchical characteristics is with equity ties—the investment of one partner in the other. A shared ownership structure deters opportunistic behavior and, in effect, decreases relational uncertainty by aligning the partners' interests.

name: Uncertainty avoidance
definition: Uncertainty avoidance is the "extent to which the members of a culture feel threatened by uncertain or unknown situations."

name: Masculinity
definition: Hofstede (1991) further distinguished among countries in terms of their masculinity, which refers to the overall "toughness" and competitiveness of a society.

name: Individualism
definition: As defined by Hofstede, individualism characterizes "societies in which the ties between individuals are loose: everyone is expected to look after himself or herself and his or her immediate family."

name: Exemplar similarity
authors_terms: ["exemplar similarity", "similarity to the exemplar", "similarity to category exemplars"]
definition: Exemplar similarity quantifies the degree to which a firm resembles exemplars in its industry.

name: Analyst coverage
definition: Analyst coverage refers to the number of analysts who actively follow a specific firm in a given year; it determines whether a firm is covered by an analyst, signaling the firm's legitimacy and facilitating the dissemination of information about the firm to the market.

name: Analyst recommendations
definition: In the second stage of evaluation, analysts assess the performance of covered firms and provide recommendations regarding whether to buy, hold, or sell its stock based on whether it appears under- or overvalued.

name: Category coherence
definition: Category coherence refers to the degree of resemblance and relational patterns among members within a category.

name: Category distinctiveness
definition: Category distinctiveness pertains to a category's relative position within the broader classification and meaning system, emphasizing its uniqueness and separation from other categories.

name: Exemplar typicality
definition: Exemplars can align with category prototypes, defined as the typical attributes of most firms within that category, or they can deviate from the category prototype; exemplar typicality captures how closely the exemplar corresponds to the category prototype.

name: Licensor core technology
authors_terms: ["licensor core technology", "closeness of the licensed technology to the core of the licensor's patent portfolio", "licensor's core technologies"]
definition: Consistent with the innovation literature, the authors consider the types of technologies in which the firm has accumulated substantial technological experience to have become the core technologies of the firm. The construct captures the degree of correspondence between the licensor's core technologies and the licensed technology, so that higher values indicate closer proximity of the licensed technology to the licensor's core patent portfolio.

name: Licensee core technology
authors_terms: ["licensee core technology", "closeness of the licensed technology to the core of the licensee's patent portfolio"]
definition: The same notion of core technologies applied to the licensee: the technologies in which the licensee has accumulated substantial technological experience. The construct captures the degree of correspondence between the licensee's core technologies and the licensed technology, computed separately for licensees.

name: Technological uncertainty
authors_terms: ["technological uncertainty", "uncertainty associated to the technology", "uncertain technology"]
definition: The authors' concept of technological uncertainty is intended to reflect the level of uncertainty related to future developments of the licensed technology and the consequent uncertain future application of the resulting invention.

name: Grant-back clause inclusion
definition: A grant-back clause 'requires the potential licensee to agree to grant back to the patentee [i.e., the licensor] rights to improvement patents developed by the licensee that relate to the original patent as partial consideration for the license rights' (Schmalbeck 1975, p. 733). The authors posit that the grant-back clause can be seen as a type of preclusive condition driving appropriability.

name: Direct ties to venture investors
authors_terms: ["direct ties", "direct tie to VC or angel investor", "pre-established relationships with venture investors"]
definition: A direct tie is present when at least one member of the founding team had a direct business or social relationship with a venture investor prior to the founding of the firm.

name: Indirect ties to venture investors
authors_terms: ["indirect ties", "indirect tie to VC or angel investor", "ties to third parties who are connected to venture investors"]
definition: A founding team has an indirect tie when at least one member had a business or social tie to a third party who had a direct tie with a venture capitalist or angel investor prior to the founding of the firm.

name: Venture capital funding
definition: Financing obtained from venture capital firms; the time-to-VC-funding regressions are limited to the first occurrence of financing from a VC firm, which the authors treat as the milestone of greatest significance.

name: Initial public offering
authors_terms: ["IPO", "initial public offering", "initial sale of securities on the public equity markets"]
definition: The most desirable type of liquidity event from the perspective of the owners of the firm is an initial sale of securities on the public equity markets.

name: New venture failure
definition: Firm failure is one of the three organizational transitions modelled, treated as a competing risk with the IPO; dissolutions and IPOs are described as lying at opposite ends of the performance continuum.

name: Founders' industry experience
authors_terms: ["industry experience", "previous experience in the industry of the start-up"]
definition: Founders with industry experience presumably have knowledge of effective strategies and customer preferences, as well as valuable contacts with customers, suppliers, and other industry participants.

name: Founders' start-up experience
definition: Start-up experience enhances entrepreneurs' understanding of how to staff and lead early-stage organizations, to develop new products, and to manage relationships with investors, employees, suppliers, and customers.

name: Patent stock
authors_terms: ["patent stock", "number of MIT patents licensed to the new venture at founding"]
definition: Patent stock designates the number of MIT patents that were licensed to the new venture at founding; many of the firms in the sample license more than one MIT-assigned patent.

name: Exclusive technology license
authors_terms: ["exclusive license", "exclusive right to use MIT technology in a particular field of use"]
definition: Exclusive license indicates whether the new venture has an exclusive right to use MIT technology in a particular field of use.

name: Inventor rank
authors_terms: ["highest university rank", "highest inventor rank", "highest rank of the MIT inventor"]
definition: As a proxy for the status and depth of knowledge of the MIT inventors who developed a licensed technology, the authors measure for each firm the highest university rank achieved by any member of the team of inventors that created the technology licensed by the firm.

name: Industry size
authors_terms: ["size of the industry", "size of industry, year of founding"]
definition: The size measure, obtained from the Census of Manufacturers, is the total value of shipments in the industry, measured in the year that the new venture is founded.

name: Patent effectiveness
authors_terms: ["patent effectiveness", "effectiveness of patents in industry", "strength of intellectual property protection"]
definition: The Levin et al. (1987) measure of patent effectiveness is obtained from a survey of R&D managers and gauges the extent to which patents are perceived to be successful at protecting intellectual property.

name: Organizational status
authors_terms: ["organizational status", "employer status", "status of the firm", "higher status firms"]
definition: Status is a dimension of social structure that ranks actors according to their relative social position or prestige. An organization's status may vary across different audiences; we focus on firms' status among workers, reflecting the respect accorded to them as employers.

name: Pay
definition: Tested using respondents' self-reports of their approximate annual earnings in their first year in each of the job spells that they reported; because of the skewed nature of the pay variable, the authors use natural logarithms.

name: Job rank
authors_terms: ["job rank", "rank", "vertical location of a job in the organizational hierarchy"]
definition: A job rank for each job, referring to the vertical location of a job in the organizational hierarchy, coded from the titles respondents reported within each job to create a consistent rank across the various different jobs.

name: Career experience
definition: Experience workers have accumulated later in their careers; the authors argue they would not expect high status firms to be able to hold down wages for more experienced workers, and that later in their career workers should be paid the full value created by their ability.

name: CEO deception
authors_terms: ["deception", "CEO deception", "deceptive CEOs", "a CEO's use of deception"]
definition: We focus on deception that is used to intentionally mislead stakeholders, or in other words, language that is indicative of fraud and malintent. Our focus is on deception regarded as dishonest, egregious, and often illegal.

name: History of deception
authors_terms: ["history of deception", "prior deception", "prior use of deception", "history of dishonesty"]
definition: The temporal component of the analyst–CEO relationship reflecting how much the CEO has used deception in the past. A history of dishonesty may exhaust deception's benefits as analysts stop justifying continuous positive evaluations.

name: Analyst reputation
definition: Institutional Investor's annual 'All-Star' analysts list recognizes those analysts with exceptional reputations in their respective industries. These All-Stars, known for their market influence, experience greater benefits including working at larger firms, higher compensation, and privileged access to firms and executives.

name: Analyst recommendations
definition: Analysts provide earnings forecasts and recommendations to investors by analyzing the financial health and potential growth of firms.

name: Family ownership
definition: The paper takes the nonfamily firm as its baseline and classifies a firm as family controlled when (a) a family holds more than 50% of the shares of the firm, and (b) at least two board members share the same last name.

name: Financial stewardship
definition: Financial stewardship, which we define as farsighted financial management of the firm.

name: Employee compensation
definition: We measured Compensation as total labor-related expenses in a given firm-year divided by the total number of hours worked in the same firm-year.

name: Employee training
authors_terms: ["off-site training", "investment in off-site training", "investment in employee training"]
definition: Off-site training initiatives are defined as courses or internships, characterized by a high degree of organization by a trainer or training institution, and must take place at a site separated from the workplace.

name: Dismissals
definition: We measured Dismissals as the number of employees (FTEs) who were dismissed by the firm during a given firm-year divided by the number of employees (FTEs) at the start of that firm-year.

name: Voluntary employee turnover
definition: We measured Voluntary turnover as the number of employees (FTEs) who voluntarily left the firm during a given firm-year divided by the number of employees (FTEs) at the start of that firm-year.

name: Labor productivity
definition: Labor productivity, defined as the ratio of firm outputs to labor inputs (Samuelson & Nordhaus, 1989), is a critical indicator of workforce performance.

name: Profitability
definition: The study uses price-cost margin (PCM) as an appropriate index of firm profitability, on which the impact of strategy and industry-level factors is tested. A high PCM value reflects the firm's ability to elevate price above costs and/or lessen average costs.

name: Competitive strategy type
authors_terms: ["hybrid strategies", "pure strategies", "'stuck-in-the-middle' strategy", "'no strategy' alternatives", "strategy types", "strategy combinations"]
definition: The study defines a model where a firm can 'select' any of the 27 possible combinations obtained by scoring low, medium, or high on each of the three generic strategy dimensions of (i) low cost, (ii) marketing, and (iii) technology-based differentiation. The remaining seven combinations collectively define a reference group ('no strategy') characterized by no clear or presumably unattractive strategy combinations.

name: Number of generic dimensions emphasized
authors_terms: ["the number of generic dimensions that are simultaneously emphasized", "number of generic strategy dimensions strongly emphasized", "number of strategy dimensions emphasized"]
definition: The number of generic strategy dimensions a firm distinctively emphasizes in its strategy mix; the authors argue that the more complex and 'multidimensional' the strategic profile of a firm, the more balanced and defensible its strategic position will be, and hence the higher its profitability.

name: Low cost strategy
definition: A generic strategy of low cost involves giving consumers value comparable to that offered by rivals at a lower cost, entailing that the firm is constantly improving its ability to produce at costs lower than the competition. It is one of the three generic strategy dimensions, and its inclusion as a primary component of a hybrid mix is expected to raise profitability.

name: Marketing differentiation
definition: One of the two central forms of differentiation Miller posited, based on marketing and aiming at creating a superior brand image.

name: Technology differentiation
definition: The form of differentiation founded on innovation and technology, the second of the two central forms of differentiation in Miller's modification of Porter's conceptualization.

name: Industry concentration
definition: Within the dominant SCP framework of IO research, industry structure, principally in the form of industry concentration and entry barriers, is assumed to be a key determinant of profitability. Industry concentration (structure) is expected to foster collusion (conduct) and hence monopoly pricing (performance).

name: Industry entry barriers
definition: Industry structural characteristics that insulate incumbent firms from potential entrants: unless there exist considerable barriers to entry, high profits will attract new entrants and hence the ability to collude will be undermined. They are represented using industry advertising intensity, cost efficiency, capital intensity and technology intensity.

name: Industry growth
definition: High industry growth is associated with environmental munificence, the latter signifying an environment with ample resources and opportunities for incumbent firms; environmental munificence is generally considered to exert a positive influence on firm profitability.

name: Lagged profitability
definition: Lagged profitability is included in the extended model as a proxy for firm resources and capabilities, since idiosyncratic firm qualities are largely 'unobservable' characteristics that defy objective measurement; it may also represent past industry circumstances.

name: Director CEO hiring experience
authors_terms: ["director CEO hiring experience", "board's cumulative experience with any CEO hiring decision", "experience with CEO succession", "all succession experience"]
definition: A board's cumulative experience with any CEO hiring decision, averaged across directors and carried forward from each director's prior CEO succession experiences at the focal board to the month before the focal CEO's start date.

name: CEO performance
definition: The CEO in context (CiC) performance measure is used as the proxy for the incoming CEO's performance and thus the board's capability for CEO selection, capturing the proportion of variance in firm performance explained by CEOs versus contextual factors.

name: Succession context similarity
authors_terms: ["similarity of the prior hiring experience", "domain-specific experience", "prior experience with voluntary CEO successions", "experience with hiring after an involuntary transition"]
definition: The extent to which a board's prior CEO hiring experiences occurred in situations similar to the focal firm in terms of whether the CEO succession was voluntary or involuntary, which the authors argue reduces superstitious learning.

name: Strategic similarity
authors_terms: ["strategic similarity", "firm-level strategic similarity", "industry strategic similarity", "domain-specific experience"]
definition: The average strategic similarity between a director's other board seats and the current board, measured as the difference between the strategic distinctiveness of the director's other board seats and the strategic distinctiveness of the focal firm, and separately as industry-level similarity in managerial discretion.

name: Breadth of strategic attention
authors_terms: ["breadth of strategic attention", "strategic breadth", "breadth of managerial strategic attention"]
definition: We define the breadth of strategic attention as both the number of strategic issues to which executives pay attention and the relative level of attention that executives give to each of these issues. It is the range of opportunities to which senior managers pay attention, and the relative frequency with which they do so.

name: Firm performance
definition: The authors measure the dependent variable, performance, based on firms' return on assets (ROA) using data from Compustat (winsorized at the 1% level).

name: Quantity of opportunities in the environment
definition: The quantity of available opportunities to which executives can pay attention; a market with a high quantity of available opportunities, such as an expanding market with munificent demand from customers, provides firms with many ways to capture value and enhance their performance. The authors estimate it with industry munificence, which provides a direct measure of industry growth and an indication of the capacity available within an industry.

name: Quality of opportunities in the environment
definition: The quality of the opportunities available in a given market, for which the authors focus on the profitability of opportunities because firms are focused primarily on maximizing this aspect. Average industry ROA provides an indication of the average profitability of the available opportunities within an industry at a point in time.

name: Effectiveness of capability usage
authors_terms: ["effectiveness of usage of a firm's capabilities", "current effectiveness of usage of a firm's capabilities", "lagged performance"]
definition: The recently demonstrated effectiveness of firms' capabilities to convert on market opportunities, i.e., the fit between a firm's capabilities and the opportunities it pursues, which is evident in the firm's recent financial performance. In determining whether a firm is effectively matching its capabilities to available opportunities, managers will primarily focus on their firms' recent performance.

name: Efficiency of resource usage
authors_terms: ["efficiency of usage of a firm's resources", "current efficiency of usage of a firm's resources", "current assets turnover"]
definition: The recent efficiency of a firm's utilization of its resources, such that the firm requires relatively limited additional effort or asset investment to generate revenue. Current assets turnover provides an indication of the efficiency of a firm's usage of its current assets such as cash.

name: Trait positive affect
definition: Trait positive affect is the degree to which a person is high in enthusiasm, energy, mental alertness, and determination. Trait PA is people's tendency toward pleasant emotional engagement with, or appraisal of, their environment.

name: Mean level trait positive affect
authors_terms: ["mean level trait positive affect", "mean level of a team's trait positive affect", "group-level trait positive affect", "mean trait PA level of TMT"]
definition: The average level of trait positive affect in a team, calculated as the average of the team members' trait PA scores, including the CEO. Almost all research examining group-composition effects related to affect has concentrated on the relationship between the mean level of affect and various group processes and outcomes.

name: Trait positive affect diversity
authors_terms: ["affective diversity", "trait positive affective diversity", "affective homogeneity", "affective heterogeneity", "affective fit", "similarity in trait positive affect"]
definition: Trait positive affective diversity is individual differences in positive affective personality. Affective diversity is a result of the cumulative affective fit or misfit among group members.

name: Interpersonal satisfaction
authors_terms: ["satisfaction with team interpersonal relations", "satisfaction with the interpersonal nature of their group experience", "interpersonal satisfaction with the TMT"]
definition: Affective diversity should influence individual levels of satisfaction with the group: the more similar a group member is to others in the group in positive affective personality, the more satisfied that group member should be with the group's interpersonal relations.

name: Perceived influence
authors_terms: ["perceptions of individual influence", "self-perceptions of influence", "perceived influence on TMT"]
definition: Being affectively similar to others is expected to produce a high self-perception of one's influence level in the group.

name: Group cooperation
definition: Affectively homogeneous groups should be more cooperative and have less conflict than affectively heterogeneous groups because of the greater feelings of familiarity, attraction, and trust that are engendered from affective similarity-attraction processes.

name: Group conflict
definition: The construct of conflict has often been divided into two areas, relationship conflict, pertaining to interpersonal incompatibility among team members, and task conflict, pertaining to disagreement about how the group tasks should be performed.

name: CEO participative decision making
authors_terms: ["participative leadership style", "CEO participative vs. autocratic decision-making style", "participativeness in decision-making style"]
definition: Leaders who feel similar to their teams trust their teams' perspectives to be similar to their own and will be more likely to give their teams greater decision-making power. The scale measured each CEO's degree of participativeness versus autocracy as rated by their top management teams.

name: Firm financial performance
definition: The variable used to measure financial performance was the logged annual market-adjusted return, averaged across each year that the entire top management team (including the CEO) worked together. Market-adjusted returns indicate the company's stock returns minus the return on a value-weighted market index.

name: CEO political ideology
authors_terms: ["CEO political ideology", "CEO liberalism", "CEO conservatism", "liberal-leaning CEOs", "conservative-leaning CEOs"]
definition: Political ideologies-deeply rooted values, beliefs, and preferences about the ideal goals for the society and convictions about how to achieve them-have been conceptualized across a conservatism-liberalism axis. It is defined as a ''set of beliefs about the proper order of society and how it can be achieved.''

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Firms' social engagement activities, which the authors describe as involving catering to the needs of multiple stakeholders and of society at large, furthering equality among varied demographic and socioeconomic groups, and mitigating the negative impact of firms' practices on the natural environment.

name: Corporate downsizing
definition: Downsizing involves an intended reduction in workforce personnel. The authors also describe it as a set of proactive, well-planned managerial actions intended to ''improve efficiency, productivity, and/or competitiveness.''

name: CEO narcissism
definition: A broad higher-order trait; narcissists exhibit grandiosity, arrogance, self-absorption, and entitlement, and are characterized by an extreme self-confidence and a sense of psychological entitlement.

name: CEO extraversion
definition: A broad higher-order trait; extraverted individuals tend to be high on sociability, gregariousness, talkativeness, and assertiveness, and the core component of extraversion, social dominance, makes extraverts assertive, influential, talkative, and forceful in communicating their opinions.

name: Structural differentiation
definition: Structural differentiation refers to 'the state of segmentation of the organizational system into subsystems, each of which tends to develop particular attributes in relation to the requirements posed by its relevant external environment.' It establishes differences across organizational units in terms of mindsets, time orientations, functions, and product/market domains.

name: Organizational ambidexterity
definition: Organizational ambidexterity refers to the routines and processes by which organizations mobilize, coordinate, and integrate dispersed exploratory and exploitative efforts, and allocate, reallocate, combine, and recombine resources and assets across differentiated units. Studies on ambidexterity consider exploration and exploitation to be orthogonal and refer to the simultaneous pursuit and combination of exploratory and exploitative innovation within organizations.

name: Senior team contingency rewards
definition: Contingency rewards, which reflect the degree to which benefits for individual team members depend on their team's outcome, are favorable to senior teams confronted with pressures for mutual adjustment. The measure refers to the extent to which senior management team incentives, such as bonuses and profit sharing, were tied to overall firm performance.

name: Senior team social integration
definition: Social integration is a multifaceted phenomenon that reflects the 'attraction to the group, satisfaction with other members of the group, and social interaction among the group members.' It captures the attraction to senior management members, satisfaction, and social interaction among team members.

name: Cross-functional interfaces
definition: Ambidextrous organizations may use cross-functional interfaces such as liaison personnel, task forces, and teams to enable knowledge exchange across exploratory and exploitative units. The measure captures the extent to which firms use cross-functional boundary-spanning integration mechanisms, such as cross-functional teams, projects, and liaison personnel.

name: Connectedness
definition: Connectedness concerns the overall pattern of a firm's social network in terms of density and facilitates knowledge exchange. It refers to the extent to which employees were networked to various levels of the hierarchy in their organization.

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: Exploratory innovations require new knowledge or departure from existing knowledge and the pursuit of new technological and customer competences. The measure captures the extent to which organizations depart from existing knowledge and pursue radical innovations for emerging customers or markets.

name: Exploitative innovation
definition: Exploitative innovations meet the needs of existing customers or markets and deepen existing knowledge by refining established technological and customer competences. The measure captures the extent to which organizations build on existing knowledge and pursue incremental innovations that meet the needs of existing customers.

name: Employee mobility barriers
authors_terms: ["employee mobility barriers", "mobility barriers", "higher-mobility barriers", "noncompete agreements (NCAs)", "inevitable disclosure doctrine (IDD)", "legal mobility barriers"]
definition: Two key legal barriers that limit the mobility of R&D employees: noncompete agreements are clauses in employment contracts that specify companies or technical fields in which employees pledge not to work for a period of time, whereas the inevitable disclosure doctrine is a legal doctrine that extends trade secrecy law to restrict an employee's ability to work for a rival firm if it would 'inevitably' disclose the former firm's trade secrets.

name: Internal inventor collaborativeness
authors_terms: ["collaborativeness in firms' innovation", "internal collaborativeness", "inventor collaborativeness", "collaborative innovation", "collaboration among inventors", "internal inventor collaboration"]
definition: The authors theorize that higher-mobility barriers would result in greater collaborativeness in a firm's innovation activities, operationalized using the number of coinventors in a firm's patents. As the number of coinventors who collaborate on patented innovation increases, the firm becomes more vulnerable to inventor mobility and knowledge spillovers to competing firms.

name: Knowledge complexity
authors_terms: ["knowledge complexity", "technological complexity", "complexity of knowledge", "complexity of knowledge embedded in a firm's technological innovation"]
definition: Knowledge is described as a recipe, which includes both the list of potential ingredients and the processes of combining them, and becomes more complex when it includes more elements that interact more richly. The complexity of knowledge embedded in a firm's technological innovation is a significant determinant of the difficulty of knowledge transfer.

name: Community income inequality
definition: Our dependent variable, community income inequality, was operationalized as the community's Gini index, the most widely used measure of inequality. A Gini value of 0 means that all households have equal income; a value of 1 means that only one household has all of the income, while all others have none (maximal inequality).

name: Welfare nonprofit density
authors_terms: ["welfare nonprofit density", "density of welfare-oriented nonprofit organizations", "welfare-oriented nonprofits"]
definition: Welfare nonprofit density was calculated as the Herfindahl index of the revenues of a community's welfare nonprofits, reversed to show density instead of concentration. Welfare nonprofits are tax-exempt organizations with the social mission of eradicating income inequality through the provision of products and services that significantly increase the economic well-being of individuals at the bottom of income distribution.

name: Elite nonprofit density
definition: Institutional scholars have categorized these nonprofits as elite-oriented given that their goals are better aligned with the interests of the upper classes. An extensive set of community nonprofits focuses on arts, culture, and education issues aimed at enhancing the local cultural context while preserving traditional values.

name: Government enforcement capability
definition: Governments have the capacity to establish and enforce rules and thus affect organizational behavior and performance. Local governments with greater enforcement capabilities are better able to signal the importance of local social services, help local organizations take advantage of federal policies aimed at helping low-income individuals, and develop effective partnerships with welfare service providers.

name: Weak social policy
authors_terms: ["weak social policy", "weak or ineffective government social policies", "weak government policies"]
definition: While strong government enforcement aligns with the mission of organizations addressing grand challenges, weak or ineffective government social policies can undermine organizations' effectiveness. Weaker social policies imply a significant reduction in the government services that form the backbone of the safety net in poor communities.

name: Union coverage
definition: Central among labor institutions are unions, which are important community actors that share with welfare nonprofits the goal of protecting and empowering an economically vulnerable category of individuals. Labor institutions provide important normative support for the action of nonprofit organizations, given their value congruence and moral alignment.

name: Financial institution presence
definition: A growing body of evidence suggests that local financial institutions are prominent community actors that have important effects on individual attitudes, including civic behavior and willingness to participate in civic initiatives. Financial presence was calculated as the percentage of firms in the community belonging to the finance and insurance sector.

name: Demographic heterogeneity
definition: There is general agreement among scholars that a critical characteristic of the community fabric in relation to social problems is its demographic heterogeneity, such as its racial and cultural diversity. We developed two proxies for demographic heterogeneity: racial diversity and national origin diversity.

name: Political ideology
definition: Political ideology is also a central pillar of the community fabric. Individuals who lean toward certain political ideologies are more likely to share a cognitive framework that strongly influences how they interpret and make sense of the world.

name: Location choice
definition: The decision of a new entrant about which available location to take; the unit of analysis is the entrant-by-location dyad, and the dependent variable is coded as 1 if the focal location was chosen and 0 otherwise.

name: Entrant collective identity
definition: The collective identity claimed by a new entrant. Whether a baker affiliates with a brand or remains unaffiliated captures the divide between traditionalists and modernists: traditionalists enter the market unaffiliated and maintain independence over their individual craftsmanship, while affiliated modernists value consistency and homogenization in breadmaking.

name: Prior occupant collective identity
definition: The collective identity claimed by the firm that previously occupied a location. Locations imprinted by a prior firm that claimed the same collective identity as that of a new entrant are ideally suited for new entrants to carry out assimilation, because when firms exit locations they leave local traces that other organizations can reaffirm.

name: Geographic proximity to traditionalist competitors
definition: The geographical closeness between a location in the risk set and the nearest incumbent traditionalist bakery; geographic proximity eases evaluative judgments and invites comparisons between collective identities, so new entrants can use it as a lever to express distinctiveness from a competing collective identity.

name: Geographic proximity to modernist competitors
definition: The geographical closeness between a location in the risk set and the nearest incumbent modernist bakery; geographic proximity eases evaluative judgments and invites comparisons between collective identities, so new entrants can use it as a lever to express distinctiveness from a competing collective identity.

name: Geographic proximity to same-identity incumbents
authors_terms: ["proximity to in-group members", "distance from another traditionalist", "distance from an existing traditionalist (modernist)"]
definition: The geographical closeness between a location in the risk set and an incumbent that claims the same collective identity as the new entrant. Because competition with similar members threatens the assimilation of a new entrant into a collective identity, the need for assimilation leads new entrants to favor locations not too close to others who claim the same collective identity.

name: Managerial delegation to a local agent
authors_terms: ["managerial delegation", "hiring an agent-manager", "delegate venture management to a local agent", "agent managed"]
definition: Whether the entrepreneur manages the new business himself or herself or instead delegates management to a local agent-manager. Empirically, a firm is defined as owner managed when the chief executive officer is also the owner, and firms where the CEO is not an owner are designated as agent managed.

name: Competition in the target market
authors_terms: ["expected level of competition", "level of competition", "local industry competition", "High Competition"]
definition: The expected intensity of competition in the target market in which the entrepreneur plans to compete. Where entry barriers are low and competition is intense, economic rents dissipate and little or no surplus remains for the owner to share with the agent, so self-enforcing agreements become unstable.

name: Revenue growth in the target market
definition: The expected future growth rate of returns to the venture, that is, growth in demand (revenues) in the target industry. A high growth rate raises the expected value of continued cooperation and reduces the incentives of either party to defect.

name: Intertemporal variability of returns
definition: The expected intertemporal variability of returns in the target market. High uncertainty and intertemporal variation in returns increase the likelihood of unforeseen and extreme events, making it harder to link agents' efforts to outcomes and increasing the short-run gains from reneging.

name: Agent-managers' outside employment options
authors_terms: ["outside employment options", "outside employment options of potential agent-managers", "Employment"]
definition: The outside employment options available to potential agent-managers, equivalent to the supply of available agents in the local labor market. Relational contracts are predicted to be most effective when there is an excess supply of potential agents such that the outside employment options of current agents are limited.

name: Foreign ownership
definition: Whether the entrepreneurial firm is owned by foreign nationals rather than domestic (Russian) owners. Foreign entrepreneurial firms have individual owners who are foreign nationals; new subsidiaries of multinationals and other established foreign firms are excluded.

name: Density of the domestic entrepreneurial network
authors_terms: ["Domestic Density", "network density", "density of the local entrepreneurial network"]
definition: The density of the local network of domestic entrepreneurial firms, which the authors argue can provide third-party, reputation-based discipline of agent-managers. Because information flows most freely and reputation effects are strongest in dense networks of homogeneous actors, domestic firms' willingness to delegate is expected to increase with the number of other domestic entrepreneurs operating in the same geographic region.

name: Density of the coethnic entrepreneurial network
definition: A logged count of entrepreneurial firms in the region coming from the same home country as the focal firm, included to capture any potential benefits of the coethnic entrepreneurial network in facilitating enforcement of informal contracts with agent-managers.

name: Profitability
definition: Firm profitability, measured as operating return on assets (OROA), compared across foreign versus domestic and owner-managed versus agent-managed entrepreneurial firms over the first three years of operation.

name: CEO award
definition: CEO awards represent a positive status shift that provides formal recognition and certification of their accomplishments, status within their profession and industry, and entry into an exclusive group of 'superstar' CEOs.

name: Affiliation with an awarded CEO
authors_terms: ["director CEOs", "director CEOs affiliated with awarded CEOs", "affiliated with the awarded CEOs", "outside directors on the awarded CEOs' boards"]
definition: We shift focus to how awards affect director CEOs, defined as the outside directors on the awarded CEOs' boards who are CEOs themselves. From this set of affected directors, we use the subset of board directors who are simultaneously CEOs of S&P 1500 companies (director CEOs) as reported by ExecuComp.

name: CEO compensation
definition: Total direct compensation is the total amount of compensation paid to the CEO in a given year, including salary, bonuses, other annual compensation, the total value of restricted stock grants, the total value of stock options granted (using Black-Scholes), long-term incentive payouts, and all other miscellaneous forms of compensation.

name: Media attention
authors_terms: ["public attention", "media coverage", "articles in WSJ", "increase in WSJ articles"]
definition: The media act not only as intermediaries between corporations and the general public, but 'as a political force that scrutinizes corporations to inform the public.' Public media function as external monitors that reduce self-serving CEO behavior.

name: Security analyst coverage
definition: Security analysts act as intermediaries between corporations and potential investors, thus playing a similarly important role in corporate governance.

name: Performance relative to expectations
definition: Although a CEO may have won an award based on superior performance, the expectations to continue delivering superior performance and surpass themselves can be hard to meet going forward. Awarded CEOs may simply not be able to keep pace with ever-increasing expectations and, therefore, end up disappointing shareholders and other important stakeholders.

name: External CEO succession
authors_terms: ["external successors", "external CEO successors", "internal and external successors"]
definition: Internal successors are CEOs promoted from within the firm, all of whom have at least some firm-specific human capital; external successors are CEOs hired from outside the firm, all of whom lack firm-specific human capital. When a company hires an external successor, the new CEO lacks firm-specific skills.

name: External succession outside the industry
authors_terms: ["external successors from outside the industry", "outside-of-industry external successors", "external successors without industry work experience", "external successors who have only generic skills"]
definition: External successors from outside the industry lack both firm-specific and industry-specific human capital, and thus possess only generic skills. Their prior work experience is not in any of the industries in which the hiring firm operates.

name: External succession within the industry
authors_terms: ["external successors from within the industry", "within-industry successors", "external successors with industry work experience"]
definition: External successors from within the industry lack firm-specific human capital but possess industry-specific experience, having prior work experience in at least one of the industries in which the hiring firm conducted business.

name: Initial non-contingent compensation
authors_terms: ["initial non-contingent compensation", "initial salary and bonus", "salary plus bonus", "non-performance-contingent compensation"]
definition: Short-term compensation not contingent on firm performance, i.e., salary and nonperformance-based bonus. Our empirical analysis deals with initial CEO salary and bonus, because differential skill specificity of CEOs should most clearly affect this measure of compensation.

name: CEO hubris
definition: CEO hubris is generally defined as extreme self-confidence and pride. Prior research tends to treat the terms hubris and optimistic overconfidence as synonymous: both hubristic and optimistically overconfident individuals overestimate their capabilities and have a strong sense of self-sufficiency.

name: Socially responsible activities
authors_terms: ["CSR strength", "socially responsible activities", "good deeds", "positive aspect of CSR", "engagement in socially responsible activities"]
definition: The positive aspect of CSR refers to voluntary corporate actions designed to improve social conditions. The authors create a CSR Strength variable by summing the number of strengths across five KLD dimensions to measure the extent of a firm's participation in socially responsible activities.

name: Socially irresponsible activities
authors_terms: ["CSR concern", "socially irresponsible activities", "bad deeds", "negative aspect of CSR", "engagement in socially irresponsible activities"]
definition: Socially irresponsible activities pertain to 'the set of corporate actions that negatively affects an identifiable social stakeholder's legitimate claims in the long run.' The authors treat firms' engagement in socially irresponsible activities as another dimension of CSR, measured as the total number of concerns across the five KLD dimensions.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is a primary indicator of the volume of tangible and intangible resources a firm possesses, and larger firms have more resources at their disposal and are less dependent on stakeholders for resources and support.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Firm slack describes the excess resources a firm has to shield itself against environmental change and other external shocks. Increased slack facilitates experimentation and organizational change as such activities require a substantial input of resources.

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Market uncertainty measures the extent to which a firm's external environment is unstable and unpredictable. As market uncertainty intensifies, it becomes increasingly difficult for firms to deliver good performance because the market demands are more difficult to predict.

name: Market competition
definition: Market competition is likely to intensify with a lower industry concentration where there are more competitors in the market; when firms are confronted with a greater level of market competition, they depend more on various stakeholders for resources.

name: Success of knowledge set change
authors_terms: ["success of knowledge set change", "success of change"]
definition: The extent to which a firm is successful in changing a particular knowledge set such that the knowledge set (and the activities based on it) is better suited to meet the demands of the new, more market-oriented economic environment.

name: Socialist institutional imprinting
definition: The level of imprinting of the socialist institutional environment on a firm's knowledge set, where that environment comprises formal institutions such as laws and regulations formulated on socialist principles emphasizing the central role of the State and the collective, and informal institutions such as norms and customs emphasizing salary equality, working conditions, worker rights and job security.

name: Socialist market imprinting
definition: The level of imprinting of the socialist market environment on a firm's knowledge set; the socialist market environment is characterized by centrally determined product and process introductions, output quotas, guaranteed state purchase of output and government financial support, little competition, and little concern for quality, cost or productivity.

name: Search location
definition: Local search is defined as a search within formerly socialist countries (Lithuania, Russia, Poland), and distant search is defined as a search in traditionally free-market economies (Western Europe, Canada, United States).

name: Performance relative to analyst forecasts
authors_terms: ["performance relative to analyst forecast", "performance gap relative to analyst forecast", "performance to forecast", "performance relative to forecast"]
definition: The size of the performance gap relative to analyst forecast, calculated from the consensus of analysts' EPS forecasts: the absolute value of the difference between actual EPS and the EPS forecast divided by the EPS forecast. Compared with a dollar value-based difference measure, the ratio-based measure takes into account the difference in the size of analyst forecasts across firms and thus better reflects firm performance relative to analyst forecast.

name: Analyst coverage
authors_terms: ["analyst coverage", "security analyst coverage", "number of analysts who issued earnings forecasts"]
definition: Firms vary in the number of security analysts who track and issue earnings forecasts for them; firms that receive coverage from more security analysts generally receive a higher level of publicity, which makes them receive greater attention and scrutiny from investors.

name: R&D intensity
definition: R&D intensity is measured as the percentage of firm R&D expenses over sales during each fiscal year.

name: Career specialization
definition: At its core, specialization reflects a fundamental tradeoff between depth and breadth. Career specialization allows workers to develop deep skills and expertise and corresponding social networks in a focused work area, whereas career diversification leads workers to develop broader skills and expertise spread across multiple work areas.

name: Employment in congressional staffing
authors_terms: ["Employment in staffing", "employment", "secure employment", "likelihood of securing employment"]
definition: Our main dependent variable, Employment in staffing, takes the form of a dummy variable set to 1 if a staffer is employed as a congressional staffer in the year after an election (i.e., t+1) and 0 otherwise; it captures a staffer's ability to secure work within the congressional staffing industry or, inversely, the likelihood that a staffer exits congressional staffing after displacement.

name: Job category market thickness
authors_terms: ["Job category size", "thickness or market demand for a particular functional work area", "thicker market demand", "market thinness"]
definition: To capture the thickness or market demand for a particular functional work area, the authors create the variable Job category size, measured as the count of jobs at year t+1 that are categorized in the same functional job category as the focal staffer at the election year t.

name: Job displacement
definition: Involuntary separations (job displacement) are not an endogenous choice but, rather, reflect situations in which workers are thrust into the labor market, often abruptly and with limited time to plan, and hence must scramble to locate and secure work.

name: Abandonment of quarterly earnings guidance
definition: U.S. public companies' abandonment of quarterly earnings guidance (QEG), a voluntary financial disclosure in which companies provide forecasts of their forthcoming firm profitability for investors. The study examines the abandonment of institutionally supported practices, specifically quarterly earnings guidance abandonment by U.S. public companies.

name: Analyst coverage breadth
authors_terms: ["coverage breadth", "analyst coverage breadth", "lack of analyst coverage breadth"]
definition: Coverage breadth refers to the degree of market reporting or recognition provided by the intermediaries or the number of intermediaries covering the firm. Firms that lack coverage breadth become more dependent on intermediaries in the mediated market.

name: Analyst coverage depth
definition: Coverage depth is the length of the relationship between market intermediaries and the firm. This relationship forms the basis of market intermediaries' evaluation of the firm's current and future performance.

name: Peer nonprovision of quarterly earnings guidance
authors_terms: ["Nonprovision of QEG, Industry Peers", "observed lack of peer support", "peer support for the practice"]
definition: To capture the overall support for QEG among a firm's industry peers, the authors aggregated individual sample companies' nonprovision of QEG for a respective quarter, coding nonprovision dichotomously as 'one.' The measure includes the nonprovision of QEG by companies that had never adopted QEG.

name: Observed peer sanction against abandonment
authors_terms: ["Sanction Against QEG Abandonment, Industry Peers", "observed peer sanction against abandonment", "analyst punishment of QEG abandoners"]
definition: To measure the influence of observed peer punishment, the authors considered reductions in analyst coverage among firms that stopped providing QEG. When analyst coverage is taken away, it functions as an important source of punishment for firms.

name: Negative earnings surprise
definition: We followed prior studies and coded a negative earnings surprise as a quarterly event, in which a firm delivers financial performance (earnings per share) that is below the consensus analyst forecasts. The consensus forecast is the average of all quarterly earnings forecasts provided by the analysts who cover the firm.

name: Central information provision
definition: By 'information provision' the authors mean the transfer of practice-specific data from a central knowledge repository (e.g., a corporate R&D lab) to agents within the firm that make technology adoption decisions. Such information provision usually occurs through internal seminars, demonstrations, and promotional brochures.

name: Extent of practice adoption
authors_terms: ["PP Adoption", "extent of adoption", "adoption of pollution prevention practice"]
definition: The dependent variable for our analysis is the adoption of pollution prevention practice at the facility level. We coded this variable (PP Adoption) as a count variable to reflect the varying degree to which a facility may engage in pollution prevention.

name: Cumulative adoption by other facilities
definition: As the number of previous adopters increases, information about the existence and value of the practice increases. This is particularly true when adoption occurs within one's own industry segment.

name: Past negative environmental events
definition: Spills, lawsuits, fines, and regulatory violations are all significant events that shape a firm's information set. One type of local experience—unexpected events such as accidents or product failures—provides little information about implementing a new practice but can provide extensive information on its value.

name: Adoption of related practices
definition: Theories of absorptive capacity propose that prior related practices may inform the decision to adopt a new practice. The adoption of one practice may provide information about the value of similar practices.

name: Compensation for adoption
definition: We measure Compensate as the degree to which corporate environmental managers report that headquarters provides explicit rewards (or punishment) for adoption of (or failure to adopt) pollution prevention practices.

name: Technological capability
definition: Technological capability refers to a firm's ability to employ various technologies; it is developed over time and accumulated through the firm's past experience.

name: Strategic flexibility
definition: Strategic flexibility is the ability of a firm to reallocate and reconfigure its organizational resources, processes, and strategies to deal with environmental changes, and it depends jointly on resource flexibility and coordination flexibility.

name: Exploitation
definition: Exploitation is the use and refinement of existing knowledge and skills in product development.

name: Exploration
definition: Exploration refers to the search and pursuit of completely new knowledge and skills in product development.

name: Motherhood status
definition: Whether and when a woman has become a mother, measured from data on women's biological children as a time-varying indicator equal to 1 for all observation years after a woman had a child.

name: Motherhood wage penalty
authors_terms: ["motherhood wage penalty", "motherhood earnings penalty", "reduced earnings prospects", "reduced earnings opportunities", "wage penalty", "earnings penalty"]
definition: The reduced earnings prospects women face in wage employment following motherhood, resulting partly from demand-side employer discrimination based on motherhood status.

name: Entrepreneurship entry
authors_terms: ["entry into entrepreneurship", "transition from paid employment to entrepreneurship", "transition to entrepreneurship"]
definition: The action of leaving wage employment to strike out on one's own by either becoming self-employed or founding a new venture.

name: New-venture founding
authors_terms: ["new-venture founding", "founding a new venture", "founding a new organization", "new-business founding"]
definition: Launching an incorporated business with employees to operate it from the owner-manager position; incorporation is treated as the key distinction between founding an organization and becoming self-employed.

name: Self-employment
definition: Initiating a sole proprietorship in an unincorporated business to sell one's own services or products.

name: Managerial position
definition: Occupational positions coded as managerial, identified from the first digit of the standard occupation codes; managerial positions are considered the most conducive to skill acquisition.

name: Occupational earnings level
authors_terms: ["higher-paying occupations", "average earnings of an occupation", "average occupation earnings", "high-paying occupations"]
definition: The annual average earnings within each occupation in the sample, with occupation defined at the two-digit level.

name: Formal strategic human resource planning
authors_terms: ["human resource planning", "HRP", "formal strategic human resource planning", "strategic human resource planning", "formal human resource planning"]
definition: Human resource planning is a method of linking strategic organization objectives to human resource programs and policies; strategic human resource planning is viewed as an important component of functional-level strategic planning. Human resource planning is future-oriented and addresses two questions: what kinds of people will be needed to manage and operate the organization in the future, and what kinds of human resource policies and programs are needed to achieve human resource and organization objectives.

name: Organization performance
definition: Six performance measures are used in this study. All of these measures describe related, but distinct, characteristics important to profit-seeking organizations.

name: CEO positive affectivity
definition: CEOs' relatively stable, underlying tendency to experience positive moods and emotions. High-PA individuals tend to experience a higher level of positive emotions, such as enthusiasm, interest, and happiness.

name: CEO negative affectivity
definition: CEOs' relatively stable, underlying tendency to experience negative moods and emotions. High-NA individuals are more likely to experience a higher level of negative emotions, such as distress, dissatisfaction, and anxiety.

name: Corporate social responsibility engagement
authors_terms: ["corporate social responsibility (CSR)", "CSR engagement", "the firm's CSR engagement"]
definition: Corporate social responsibility refers to voluntary managerial actions 'that appear to further some social good, beyond the interests of the firm and that which is required by law'. The authors focus on proactive engagement in CSR efforts.

name: CEO social capital
definition: CEO social capital emerges from a CEO's social connections and interactions (e.g., educational connections, employment links, and joint memberships in social clubs).

name: Postentry performance
authors_terms: ["postentry performance", "postentry survival", "postentry growth in sales", "sales gain"]
definition: Postentry performance of entrants was evaluated as survival and as growth in sales, because the primary concerns of entrants are likely to be survival and long-term viability; growth reflects the degree to which the entrant has found acceptability in the entered markets.

name: Structural entry barriers
authors_terms: ["structural entry barriers", "sunk cost barriers", "sunk costs", "structural attributes of entered industry"]
definition: Structural entry barriers are conceptualized as sunk costs or irrecoverable investments that entrants must make in the entered industry to be competitive vis-a-vis incumbents; sunk costs are those necessary expenditures the entrant has to incur to begin operations and which are not fully recoverable in the short or intermediate term.

name: Mode of entry
authors_terms: ["mode of entry", "de novo entry", "acquisitive entry", "internal development", "acquisition"]
definition: Diversification by firms into unfamiliar product-markets is typically achieved by internal development of a new business from ground up, by acquisition of an existing business in the destination industry, or by some combination of these two basic approaches.

name: Scale of entry
authors_terms: ["scale of entry", "large-scale entry", "scale at which entry is made"]
definition: The scale at which entry is made, which while influenced by technological considerations determining minimum efficient scale is also a choice variable reflecting the parent firm's resource profile; large-scale entry is often associated with large capital investment and strong managerial commitment.

name: Seller concentration
definition: Incumbents' stake in the entered industry can be proxied by seller concentration, and high concentration inflates the potential for collusive behavior and coordinated retaliation among incumbents.

name: Product relatedness
definition: Relatedness between the entrant business and the rest of the businesses of the parent firm, reflecting the degree to which the parent has experience in managing activities that may be important for success in the new environment.

name: Industry technology
definition: Technology is one of the two industry characteristics examined; industries can be classified into three groups according to Thompson's (1967) typology, a classification that can be viewed as a continuum ranging from long-linked through mediating to intensive based on the amount of discretion required for production.

name: Industry growth
definition: Growth is the second industry characteristic examined; it influences the extent to which organizations attempt to strategically manage interdependencies and complexities, behaviors that are reflected in organizational culture, and in a high-growth industry many firms experience resource munificence.

name: Innovation
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture; organizations will certainly vary in their levels of innovation, but innovation remains a relevant dimension on which organizational cultures can be described.

name: Stability
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture; the cultures of firms in industries characterized by long-linked technologies should be characterized by high levels of stability, since tasks are repetitive and predictable.

name: People orientation
authors_terms: ["people orientation", "an orientation toward people", "respect for people", "respecting of people"]
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture, an orientation toward people; Hofstede and colleagues suggested that all service sector organizations will be more people oriented than outcome oriented.

name: Outcome orientation
authors_terms: ["outcome orientation", "an orientation toward outcomes or results", "outcome oriented"]
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture, an orientation toward outcomes or results.

name: Detail orientation
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture, attention to detail; firms in long-linked technology industries should show a strong detail orientation since only refinements to processes are required.

name: Team orientation
authors_terms: ["team orientation", "a collaborative or team orientation", "team oriented"]
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture, a collaborative or team orientation; ill-structured tasks are more likely to require that members collaborate to solve problems.

name: Easygoingness
definition: One of the seven dimensions of organizational culture, an emphasis on being easygoing; the authors view it as the opposite pole of the factor that O'Reilly and colleagues labelled aggressive.

name: Advocacy group work experience
authors_terms: ["advocacy group work experience", "advocacy group experience", "advocacy group related human capital"]
definition: Advocacy groups accumulate stakeholder knowledge, can voice concerns, and mobilize media, politics, or the general public. Employees of advocacy groups have access to these unique pools of knowledge from stakeholders and other sources.

name: Employee earnings
definition: Our dependent variable is gross annual income earned by the newly hired employees in the year t in which they are hired.

name: Proximity to the technological frontier
authors_terms: ["proximity to the technological frontier", "technological frontier", "technological distance"]
definition: A useful framework for expressing heterogeneity among innovative firms is to describe their innovation activities relative to the maximum of technological opportunity from the most advanced technologies that exists at a given point in time. This maximum level of technological opportunity is typically referred to as the technological frontier.

name: Occupational stakeholder interaction
authors_terms: ["occupations that interact with stakeholders", "stakeholder interaction occupation"]
definition: Employees of advocacy groups working in occupations dealing regularly with stakeholders, for example, patients, can much more convincingly signal that they have acquired an understanding of stakeholders.

name: Top management team membership
authors_terms: ["TMT member at previous employer", "top management of advocacy groups", "TMT membership"]
definition: We focus on the top management of advocacy groups, which has relatively more potential to transfer legitimacy from advocacy groups compared to the average advocacy group employee.

name: Analyst reputation
definition: Analyst reputation is based on specific attributes and is highly related to the audience's expectations (e.g., stock investors); the reputation is built upon forecast accuracy.

name: CEO reputation
definition: Shareholders view CEO reputation as an indicator of CEO competence, and star CEOs' firms build their reputation on sustained high-performance levels. Firm performance is the most common and necessary antecedent to a CEO developing a strong reputation, but a CEO's quality is only loosely coupled with firm performance, so CEO reputation is based upon a number of diverse attributes.

name: Firm reputation
definition: Firm reputation is most commonly measured using 'most admired' lists and so it encompasses a broad array of factors; the attributes upon which firm reputation is based have very little to do with a company's stock performance.

name: Stock market reaction
definition: Cumulative abnormal returns - the amount a stock moved within a particular window that is abnormal relative to other equities in the market - are a common measure for stock performance and have been used in prior reputation research.

name: Organizational restructuring
definition: Restructurings pursue alignment by changes in fundamental organizational design principles, that is, adding or subtracting structural axes or organizational layers. Restructurings imply pervasive change because they involve different reporting relationships throughout the organization.

name: Organizational reconfiguration
definition: Reconfigurations pursue alignment by adding, splitting, transferring, merging, or deleting of units without change to fundamental structural principles. Relative to restructuring, reconfigurations' direct effects are limited in scope, involving the specific units concerned.

name: Economic performance
definition: We use two performance measures: a forward-looking, stock market-based measure (Tobin's Q) and an accounting-based measure (return on assets).

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: Dynamism is the volatility of the rate of change of annual industry sales, that is, the standard error of the rate of change of annual industry sales.

name: Manager-worker separation
definition: When manager and worker are separated, i.e., their interaction is mediated by information and communication technologies. For each task, the authors code whether or not the task belongs to a project whose project manager operates from a different unit than the worker.

name: Worker performance
definition: The time it takes to process a given task is the main metric used by managers in the unit to quantitatively track workers' performance; task execution time therefore captures both worker speed and quality.

name: Technical task complexity
definition: Technical task complexity is measured as the count of the number of subtasks that have been assigned to the same worker within a project; when a manager is concerned that a worker may struggle in executing a technically complex task, the manager usually decomposes the task into smaller subtasks.

name: Coordinative task complexity
definition: Coordinative task complexity is greater when the task requires the worker to interact with and account for the actions of workers executing interdependent tasks.

name: Collocated peer expertise
authors_terms: ["collocated expertise", "experience in the worker's location", "collocated expert peers", "cumulated experience"]
definition: The extent to which the worker is collocated with peers who are experts in executing software maintenance tasks, captured as the cumulated total experience acquired by others in the worker's location at the moment of the assignment of the task.

name: Project team collocation
authors_terms: ["proportion of collocated project team", "proportion of collocated project team members", "collocated project team"]
definition: The extent to which the team members working on the same project are collocated with the focal worker.

name: Manager experience with the focal worker
authors_terms: ["same worker-manager experience", "manager-worker familiarity", "experience in supervising a focal worker"]
definition: The total number of tasks performed in the past by the focal worker under the supervision of the focal manager prior to the assignment of the focal task; it is essentially a measure of manager-worker familiarity.

name: Manager experience with other workers
definition: The total number of projects in which the manager has managed other workers than the focal one prior to the assignment of the focal task; it is essentially a measure of breadth of experience.

name: Market orientation culture
definition: The cultural approach defines MO as an aspect of corporate culture that places the highest priority on creating and maintaining superior customer value. The cultural element relates to a set of values and beliefs that put customer interests first, and thus represents more fundamental aspects of the organization.

name: Market orientation behavior
definition: The intelligence perspective views MO as 'the organizationwide generation of market intelligence pertaining to current and future customer needs, dissemination of the intelligence across departments, and organizationwide responsiveness to it'. Unit-level MO behavior serves as the organizing mechanism that enables firms to exploit the full potential of their MO culture.

name: Leadership quality
definition: To facilitate changes throughout the whole organization as required by the successful implementation of MO, leaders must possess the abilities to envision and energize. The measure of leadership quality includes five items that assess the envisioning and energizing qualities of firm leaders.

name: Employee job satisfaction
authors_terms: ["employee job satisfaction", "employee-level job satisfaction", "employee satisfaction", "aggregated employee satisfaction"]
definition: Employee satisfaction is focused on as an internal process factor through which MO affects performance. Satisfied employees are more devoted to their work and company, and aggregated employee satisfaction is expected to affect firm performance.

name: Product quality
definition: Following Zeithaml (1988), we view product quality as the extent to which a product or service meets customer needs. Following Zeithaml (1988), we measure product quality with three items that assess the degree to which a firm's products or services meet customer needs.

name: Firm performance
definition: Organization-level financial performance of the firm, assessed as subsequent firm performance with an objective indicator, return on assets (ROA).

name: Firm risk taking
definition: R&D intensity is used as a specific firm risk-taking behavior, because R&D investments involve highly uncertain activities that might result in negative firm outcomes; following the literature the authors assume that 'high investment in R&D is generally a high risk-high return strategy.'

name: Negative attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["negative attainment discrepancy", "negative discrepancy", "performance below the aspiration level"]
definition: Performance feedback is the firm's actual performance relative to a benchmark aspiration level; performance below the aspiration level (negative attainment discrepancy) is predicted to trigger problemistic search and increased risk taking, and firms in a loss domain might invest in risky activities because higher outcome variation may help turn around performance.

name: Positive attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["positive attainment discrepancy", "positive discrepancy", "performance above the aspiration level"]
definition: Performance above the aspiration level (positive attainment discrepancy) places decision makers in a gain domain; a positive context resulting from superior performance creates an anticipation of future gains that engenders risk reduction.

name: CEO stock option grants
authors_terms: ["values of CEO stock option grants", "CEO option grant", "stock option grants"]
definition: Stock option grants are call options that offer big potential wins but a low risk of losses, because those paid with options benefit along with shareholders when stock prices rise but experience no reduction in real wealth if the stock price declines after the grant date; the authors focus on at-the-money grants.

name: Outside director stock option grants
authors_terms: ["values of outside director stock option grants", "director option grant", "outside director options"]
definition: Equity-based incentives awarded to outside (nonmanagement) directors, who are believed to provide superior performance benefits to the firm as a result of their independence from firm management and who, unlike CEOs, are not reliant on the focal firm for their primary employment or concentrated compensation.

name: Likelihood of arm's-length resource exchange
authors_terms: ["likelihood of an arm's-length resource exchange", "likelihood of exchange"]
definition: The probability that two parties simultaneously divest and acquire resources with each other in a transactional manner without joint decision-making or long-term commitment.

name: Competitive overlap
definition: The degree to which potential resource exchange parties compete directly in the same market space.

name: Relational capital
definition: Mutual trust, friendship, and respect cultivated through personal connections at the individual level between organizational boundary spanners.

name: Resource bundle
definition: Exchanges involving multiple complementary resources traded together rather than as single items.

name: Relational rivalry
definition: A subjective competitive relationship with a specific opponent in which the psychological stake is heightened by a historical and ongoing narrative of intense animosity.

name: Discourse broadening
definition: A discursive strategy where entrepreneurs incorporate new or unshared interpretations in their responses to vocal discursive partners; it captures the extent to which entrepreneurs introduce meanings around their innovation that are distinctive from those of their vocal discursive partners.

name: Support from silent audiences
authors_terms: ["support from silent audiences", "upvotes", "support for their innovation from silent audiences"]
definition: The upvotes cast by platform users who observe the entrepreneur's conversation with discursive partners but do not participate in it, representing users' expressions of support for the innovation.

name: Similarity between discursive partners and silent audiences
authors_terms: ["similarity between discursive partners and silent audiences", "similarity between entrepreneurs' discursive partners and silent audiences"]
definition: The degree to which the interpretative lenses of entrepreneurs' discursive partners align with those of the potential base of silent audiences for a given innovation.

name: Negative customer reviews
definition: In the context of online marketplaces, the authors focus specifically on negative customer reviews as a particularly relevant form of expectation violation cues - salient pieces of information indicating that their offering appears to violate customers' expectations.

name: Category-switching
definition: Category-switching refers to a producer's deliberate decision to change the category with which they affiliate themselves or their offerings.

name: Category heterogeneity
definition: Category heterogeneity is defined as the degree of diversity in the features exhibited by members of a product category, an observable characteristic that reflects the extent to which a consensus about expected features exists.

name: Inter-category proximity
definition: Inter-category proximity is defined as the inverse of the distance between the previously chosen category and each alternative in the choice set.

name: Category choice
authors_terms: ["category choice", "category selection", "likelihood of selecting a given category"]
definition: A choice set including the category the producer chose (the realized outcome) and the categories they did not choose (non-realized outcomes), from which the conditional probability that a category was chosen is estimated.

name: CEO integrity
