authors_terms: ["perceived CEO prevention focus", "CEO prevention focus", "prevention-focused language", "high prevention-focused CEOs"]
definition: The extent to which investors perceive, from the CEO's regulatory-focused language, a vigilant approach toward minimal losses, risk reduction, and avoiding negative outcomes.

name: Distinctiveness from prior competitors
authors_terms: ["distinctiveness from prior competitors", "distinctiveness from history", "distinctiveness from the status quo", "distinctiveness from historical standards"]
definition: Distinctiveness is defined as a departure from an existing point of reference, and the most canonical reference point is the status quo, i.e., that which has been performed in the past. In this context the prior competitors are the historical standards of representational art.

name: Distinctiveness from current competitors
authors_terms: ["distinctiveness from current competitors", "distinctiveness from peers", "distinctiveness from contemporaries"]
definition: If history is the "sitting duck" of competitive positioning, industry peers present a moving target; audiences reward producers that are more different from peers (i.e., contemporary competitors).

name: Distinctiveness from past self
authors_terms: ["distinctiveness from past self", "distinctiveness from one's own past", "distinctiveness from their past selves", "distinctiveness from a producer's own past output"]
definition: An artist competes with their own self in the need to offer the market something that is distinct from their own past work, but not so distinct as to undermine their identity.

name: Exhibition opportunities
definition: Certifications are processes through which third-parties' public actions acknowledge that a producer or a product meets a particular standard; in this setting the certifying agent is the gallery or salon owner, who acts as a third-party certifier of artists by inviting them to exhibit their artworks.

name: Status in peer network
definition: A producer's position in the peer network signals the acceptance of their distinctiveness within the industry, and susceptibility to supply-side norms is a function of whether peers have normative control over an actor, which depends on the actor's status in the peer-to-peer relational network.

name: Market status
definition: What matters as a signal to the demand side of expected performance is the producer's position in the structure that connects producers to certifiers, which we call market status.

name: Volume uncertainty
definition: Volume uncertainty depends on the assessment of fluctuations in the demand for a component and the confidence placed in estimates of the demand.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty defined in terms of change in component specifications; technological change in component design requires retooling and recontracting with the supplier.

name: Supplier production cost advantage
authors_terms: ["supplier production cost advantage", "comparative production costs", "supplier production advantage"]
definition: The comparative cost of production between buyer and supplier, i.e., the extent to which substantial differences in manufacturing process and scale of operations between outside suppliers and the buyer favor the outside suppliers.

name: Supplier market competition
authors_terms: ["competitiveness of the supplier market", "market competition", "competition among suppliers"]
definition: The less specialized the buyer-supplier relationship as indicated by the number of potential suppliers and their competitiveness; the level of market competition was used to indicate asset specificity.

name: Buyer experience
authors_terms: ["buyer experience", "prior production experience", "experience a buyer has in producing a component"]
definition: The experience a buyer has gained in producing a component; in-house production knowledge due to on-the-job learning.

name: Make-or-buy decision
definition: Make-or-buy decisions determine the firm's level of vertical integration, since each decision specifies which operations the firm will engage in and which it will contract out to a supplier.

name: Patent effectiveness
authors_terms: ["patent effectiveness", "effectiveness of patents in a line of business", "effectiveness of patents"]
definition: The effectiveness of patents as a mechanism for capturing and protecting the competitive advantages of new or improved processes and products in a line of business; the effectiveness of patents varies significantly across technologies, and patents are less effective when they are unlikely to be held valid if challenged, cannot be enforced, can legally be invented around, or when licensing is required by court decisions or firms cross-license.

name: University invention licensing
authors_terms: ["likelihood of license", "hazard of first license", "licensing of university technology"]
definition: The licensing of a university invention, measured as the hazard that a patent assigned to the university is first licensed.

name: Noninventor licensee
authors_terms: ["noninventor licensee", "license to noninventors", "firm not founded by any of the inventors", "licensees were coded 'noninventor'"]
definition: Whether the entity that licenses a university invention is a firm that was not founded by any of the inventors listed on the patent.

name: Inventor licensee
authors_terms: ["inventor-licensee", "license to inventors", "patents licensed to inventor-founded firms"]
definition: Whether the license to a university invention is taken by a firm founded by one of the inventors, which the authors treat as inventor commercialization and entrepreneurship.

name: License termination
authors_terms: ["hazard of termination", "abandoned prior to commercialization", "license termination"]
definition: Termination of the license agreement's coverage for a patent after it has been licensed; technology licensing officers explain that licensees typically terminate licenses because they cannot make the technology work in a cost-effective manner, because their strategic plans change, because the company does not want to continue to pay license fees, or because the intellectual property is no longer useful.

name: Invention commercialization
definition: Commercialization of a licensed university invention occurs when a product or process using the licensed patent first generates revenues through sale to another company.

name: Royalties
definition: The dollar value of the nonequity royalty payments made to MIT from sales of products that employed licensed patents.

name: University prestige
definition: Buyers are influenced by an organization's general prestige; that is, the relative esteem in which an organization is held in an "ordered total system of differentiated evaluation" (Parsons 1951, p. 132). Institutional prestige increases the likelihood of exchange transactions through the halo effect, increased visibility, increased credibility, and buyer preferences to transact with more prestigious others.

name: Technology licensing rate
authors_terms: ["rate of technology licensing", "licensing rate", "annual count of new technology licensing and option agreements"]
definition: The dependent variable in our analysis was the annual count of new technology licensing and option agreements established by the university.

name: Interrater reliability of capability evaluations
definition: The degree of agreement between evaluations performed by corporate and subsidiary managers of the capabilities of organizational units.

name: Clarity of capability definition
definition: The extent to which the definition of the capability to be evaluated is clear and raters weigh various dimensions of performance in a similar way.

name: Ease of evaluation
definition: How easy each capability dimension was to evaluate.

name: Tacitness of capability
definition: The extent to which the underlying skill is tacit, i.e., difficult to describe, document and teach.

name: Corporate managers' knowledge of subsidiary capabilities
definition: How well corporate managers knew the capabilities of various subsidiaries.

name: Task experience
definition: The number of years that managers have spent in marketing in any firm, i.e., corporate managers' experience in the task to be evaluated.

name: Communication with headquarters
definition: How often subsidiary managers communicated with corporate managers face to face and by other means to discuss operations.

name: Market importance
definition: The strategic importance and competitive intensity of the markets in which each subsidiary operates.

name: Perceived profitability of subsidiaries
definition: The perceived profitability of subsidiaries, assessed relative to average.

name: Subsidiary age
definition: The number of years from the year in which the subsidiary was established to 1997.

name: Cultural distance
definition: The Euclidean distance from the subsidiary country to the multinational company's home country, i.e., Sweden, using Hofstede's four dimensions of national culture.

name: Global strategy
definition: The degree to which the market activities of the subsidiary are part of a global strategy, as opposed to responsiveness to national markets with autonomous local units.

name: Unit failure
authors_terms: ["failure", "unit failure", "likelihood of a unit's failure", "failure rate", "transition rate between active units and their failure"]
definition: The dependent variable is the transition rate between active units and their failure. The length of time is calculated by subtracting the founding date (or acquisition date by the current owner) from the exit date or from December 31, 1999 if the unit is still open for business.

name: Owner local congenital experience
authors_terms: ["Same Owner's Local Congenital Experience", "local congenital experience of the owner", "owner's local congenital experience"]
definition: The owner's congenital experience—experience of the owner at the time of the unit's founding—that was gained locally, where local means within the closest 25 units from the unit under observation.

name: Owner distant congenital experience
authors_terms: ["Same Owner's Distant Congenital Experience", "distant congenital experience of the owner", "owner's distant congenital experience"]
definition: The owner's congenital experience gained outside the closest 25 units from the unit under observation (but within Texas).

name: Franchisor local congenital experience
authors_terms: ["Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Local Congenital Experience", "franchisor's local congenital experience", "local congenital experience of other owners affiliated with the franchisor"]
definition: The congenital experience of the unit's franchisor gained locally, calculated from experience at units of other franchisees affiliated with the same franchisor and at company-owned units of that franchisor.

name: Franchisor distant congenital experience
authors_terms: ["Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Distant Congenital Experience", "franchisor's distant congenital experience", "distant congenital experience of the franchisor"]
definition: The congenital experience of the unit's franchisor gained outside the closest 25 units from the unit under observation (but within Texas).

name: Waste prevention
definition: Firms may reduce their emissions by preventing waste at the source, often referred to as source reduction or pollution prevention; waste prevention requires both conceptual and operational learning and its benefits are hard to observe.

name: Onsite waste treatment
definition: Firms may reduce their emissions by treating waste onsite; waste treatment activities often entail unexpected costs because such buffers reduce the information flowing to managers.

name: Offsite waste transfer
definition: Firms may reduce their emissions by transferring waste to a third party processor.

name: Waste generation
definition: The total toxic waste generated at a facility in a given year, calculated as the toxicity-weighted sum of all core chemicals released into the environment, treated onsite, and transferred offsite.

name: Total emissions
definition: The firm-level total pollution, the outcome of a firm's waste generation and its efforts to reduce this waste by prevention and treatment.

name: Financial performance
definition: We measure financial performance in two ways: return on assets (ROA) and Tobin's q.

name: Profitability
definition: The dependent variable is a measure, for each kibbutz in each year, of profitability (in thousands of 1958 Israeli Lira) per labor unit.

name: Federation experience
authors_terms: ["federation experience", "experience of others in their group"]
definition: The variable Federation experience, for kibbutz i in year T, is an accumulation over the life of kibbutz i of the labor units employed by the other kibbutzim that were members of its federation; the experience of kibbutz i is not included.

name: Nonfederation experience
authors_terms: ["nonfederation experience", "experience of others outside their group"]
definition: Nonfederation experience, for kibbutz i in year T, is an accumulation over the life of kibbutz i of the labor units employed by the other kibbutzim that were not members of its federation.

name: Own experience
authors_terms: ["own experience", "cumulative experience of the kibbutz in agriculture"]
definition: Own Experience for kibbutz i in year T is the cumulative labor units used by the kibbutz in its history since 1954 to the year preceding the observation.

name: Technology transfer experience
authors_terms: ["own technology transfer experience", "experience with technology transfer", "experience with traditional licensing", "prior experience in technology-transfer"]
definition: The university's own experience with technology transfer, arising from experience with traditional licensing and with industry-sponsored research. Hands-on experience seemed to expose previously unconsidered limits of traditional licensing and to create a willingness to experiment with alternative transfer mechanisms.

name: Equity involvement intensity
authors_terms: ["equity-based transfer mechanisms", "use of equity", "adoption of equity", "intensity of equity involvement", "equity share"]
definition: Equity positions in companies taken as payment for the use of university intellectual property, measured for this study as the intensity of a university's equity involvement. The dependent variable is the total number of a university's equity interests divided by the number of the university's active licenses for 1998.

name: Technology transfer office budgetary self-sufficiency
authors_terms: ["budgetary structure", "expectation that the technology transfer office should be self-supporting", "TTO self-sufficiency"]
definition: The budgetary expectation that the university's technology transfer office must be self-supporting. Transfer offices that are required to be self-supporting may rely on the immediate and certain revenues coming from the up-front fees of traditional licenses.

name: Technology transfer performance relative to cohort
authors_terms: ["relative technology transfer experience", "leading their cohort", "lagging their cohort", "experience relative to other institutions"]
definition: The university's technology transfer performance relative to a cohort of similar institutions, defined by status as a public or private institution and the presence or absence of a medical school. It is operationalized by comparing annual licensing revenue relative to the university's total research budget against the category average.

name: Current aspiration level
authors_terms: ["aspiration level", "current aspiration", "target for sales of certificates of deposit"]
definition: The aspiration level serves as a target for organizational performance. The current aspiration level is the aspiration level for the ith unit in the current period.

name: Previous aspiration level
authors_terms: ["previous aspiration level", "previous aspiration", "aspiration level in the previous period"]
definition: The aspiration level of the ith retail unit in the period (t-1); it serves as an anchor from which incremental changes in aspiration levels are made.

name: Attainment discrepancy
authors_terms: ["attainment discrepancy", "performance feedback", "actual performance relative to the previous aspiration level"]
definition: Actual performance relative to the previous aspiration level; the difference between performance and aspiration level in the previous period.

name: Social comparison
definition: A difference variable that provides a direct comparison of the performance of the focal entity with the performance of comparable entities (i.e., focal entity's performance minus the performance of comparable others).

name: Real exchange rate of the home currency
authors_terms: ["real exchange rate", "real exchange rate of the home currency", "real exchange rate between home country and foreign currency"]
definition: The real exchange rate between the home country and the foreign currency, defined as units of home country currency (say dollars) per unit of foreign currency (say yen). In the regressions the authors calculate the real exchange rate of the home currency so that an increase (decrease) in its value indicates an appreciation (depreciation) of the home currency with respect to the foreign currency.

name: Ownership mode of foreign production
authors_terms: ["choice of foreign production strategy (CFPS)", "ownership structure of production facilities", "production mode", "ownership mode", "mode of operations"]
definition: The firm chooses at any point in time among three modes: export (EXP), joint venture (JV), and wholly owned subsidiaries (WOS). The export mode supplies the foreign market from production facilities in the home country, the joint venture mode is an equity-based cooperative venture in which the firm shares ownership and investment with a local partner, and the wholly owned subsidiary is wholly owned and completely controlled by the firm, with production facilities in the foreign market.

name: Real exchange rate volatility
authors_terms: ["volatility of the real exchange rate", "exchange rate volatility", "variance parameter"]
definition: The volatility parameter of the real exchange rate process; the real exchange rate follows a geometric Brownian motion with drift, so future values are lognormally distributed with a variance that grows linearly with the time horizon. An increased volatility of exchange rates makes the switching option from any foreign investment alternative (i.e., WOS or JV) more valuable.

name: Switchover cost
definition: The switching costs model the required investments and managerial time commitment in developing production facilities, suppliers, and distribution network in the foreign market. Switching costs in the reverse direction model all relevant costs for closing down the foreign production facilities and reestablishing the exporting business, such as labor laws restricting worker layoffs, liquidating fixed assets, getting out of long-term contracts with local suppliers, and bureaucratic transactions in dissolving the subsidiary.

name: Foreign production investment flows
authors_terms: ["flows of WOS and JV", "growth rate of net outflow of WOS or JV", "WOS and JV flows"]
definition: The flows of investment financing the two local-production ownership modes; the growth rate of net outflow of WOS or JV is the dependent variable used to test whether mode-switching inertia dampens the response of these flows to the real exchange rate.

name: Total transaction cost per unit
definition: The total transaction cost per unit of foreign production mode; one of the two factors that jointly determine which WOS or JV mode is most profitable in the long run.

name: Design interface
authors_terms: ["design interface", "design interfaces", "component dependency", "interfaces between product components"]
definition: A design interface between component i and component j is defined as component i depending on component j for functionality, that is, component j either imposes geometry constraints or transfers forces, material, energy, and/or signals to component i for component i to function properly.

name: Team interaction
definition: Team interaction between design team i and design team j is defined as team i requesting technical information directly from team j during the detailed design phase of the development process.

name: Alignment of design interfaces and team interactions
authors_terms: ["alignment of design interfaces and team interactions", "misalignment", "aligned cases", "unmatched cases"]
definition: The correspondence between the design interface network of components and the communication network of design teams, such that the existence or absence of a design interface between two components corresponds to the existence or absence of technical interaction between the teams designing them.

name: Unmatched design interface
definition: Unmatched design interfaces correspond to design interfaces that are not addressed by direct team interactions.

name: Unmatched team interaction
definition: Unmatched team interactions correspond to communication between teams whose components do not explicitly share design interfaces.

name: Design interface strength
authors_terms: ["design interface strength", "strong design interfaces", "weak design interfaces"]
definition: Weak design interfaces are those which involve few types of design dependencies and have low impact upon the functionality of the other component, whereas strong design interfaces are those that involve several types of design dependencies and have high impact on the functionality of the other component.

name: Indirect team interaction
definition: Indirect team interactions are technical information flow that takes place between two teams through an intermediary design team.

name: Indirect design interface
definition: An indirect design interface is the indirect impact of component j over component i through an intermediary component k.

name: System modularity
definition: Modular systems are those whose design interfaces with other systems are clustered among a few physically adjacent systems, whereas integrative systems are those whose design interfaces span all, or most of, the systems that comprise the product due to their physically distributed or functionally integrative nature throughout the product.

name: Organizational and system boundaries
definition: System boundaries are established to cluster components so that a significantly larger proportion of design interfaces are within these boundaries; organizational boundaries are formed between design teams that belong to different groups of teams.

name: Situational misfit
definition: Situational misfits are performance diminishing situations among (between) situational factors in the multicontingency model; the situational fit involves the balance of the environmental conditions, the strategy, the management style, the climate, the size, and the technology.

name: Contingency misfit
definition: Contingency fit is a match between the organization structure and contingency factors that has a positive effect on performance, and a contingency misfit is the misalignment between the organization's situation and its organizational design (configuration, formalization, complexity, centralization).

name: Organizational misfit
definition: Misﬁts are misalignments, deviations, out-of-kilter situations, gaps, and undesired properties that need to be ﬁxed; a misfit is an organizational misalignment that diminishes performance, and a misfit may be situational, contingency, or both.

name: Return on assets
definition: ROA is one of the most widely used profitability ratios in organizational and strategic analyses; the performance measures in the study are ROA96 and ROA97, computed as profit divided by assets.

name: New product introductions
definition: New product activity is the number of new products a firm introduces in a year; a new product is any new, unique brand-CPU combination.

name: Profit rate
authors_terms: ["profit rate", "firm profit rate", "size-adjusted earnings", "return on assets (ROA)", "profitability"]
definition: Profit rate is a firm's profit rate (i.e., size-adjusted earnings), measured in the analysis as return on assets.

name: Profit-rate persistence
definition: The persistence of profit rate is the length of time that a firm's advantage or disadvantage in the market place exists, which is commonly captured by the time-series properties of profit rate.

name: Asset growth
authors_terms: ["asset growth", "growth of firm size", "firm size", "firm growth"]
definition: Firm size is the size of the firm (i.e., assets); growth of firm size is examined as reflected in asset growth.

name: Alliance ambidexterity
authors_terms: ["alliance ambidexterity", "ambidextrous formation of exploratory and exploitative alliances", "ambidextrous formation of alliances", "ambidexterity", "focused formation of either exploratory or exploitative alliances"]
definition: Ambidexterity is referred to as the simultaneous and balanced presence of both existing and new partners in a firm's alliance network. The authors focus on structure-based ambidexterity in alliance formation, contrasting an ambidextrous formation with a focused formation that either strengthens ties with existing partners or expands to new partners.

name: Firm performance
definition: We use net sales over current assets to measure Firm Performance because they capture the amount of resources being produced and exchanged as well as the amount of total resources a firm has. It shows how efficiently a firm uses its assets to generate sales, reflects the current profitability, and is widely used in the accounting and finance literature.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is treated as a commonly adopted proxy for firm resources, reflecting the extent of a firm's overall resource constraints. It has been conceptualized in various ways, with some emphasizing a firm's human resources such as number of employees and others emphasizing a firm's physical resources.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental Uncertainty refers to the volatility or difficult-to-predict discontinuities in a given industry. It is measured as the volatility of net sales of all firms in a four-digit SIC industry, where larger values of volatility indicate greater environmental uncertainty.

name: Firm centrality
definition: Firm Centrality is defined here as the extent to which a firm occupies a central position with strong ties to other network members. Centrality captures a firm's positional advantage and status within the network.

name: Structural holes
definition: Firms can derive benefits in a network by arbitraging resource and information flows between two otherwise disconnected actors in the network. To calculate a firm's structural holes, the authors first identified a firm's alliance partners and then counted how often any two of its alliance partners are not directly connected, which measures the number of structural holes that have been filled by the firm.

name: Network dynamics
authors_terms: ["network dynamics", "alliance event year", "early years of the network", "later years of the network", "stages of network development"]
definition: Given that alliance formation is a function of firms' past interactions, the authors posit that the performance implications will change at different stages of network development. The empirical study uses the observation year of alliance activity, whereas the simulation can model the age of the network over time.

name: Cumulative experience
definition: The cumulative activity level of the organizational unit; the learning curve expresses the decrease in average cost per unit when the cumulative production level increases.

name: Average cost
definition: The total costs of a region in a month divided by the traffic measure of that region in that month, i.e., average cost per mail item.

name: Temporary employees
authors_terms: ["temporary employees", "temporary workers", "employees with a temporary contract", "degree of temporary employees", "Flex"]
definition: Employees hired on temporary contracts, who are less socialized to the firm's organizational code and therefore more likely to experiment with existing work processes and to contribute new knowledge.

name: Product heterogeneity
authors_terms: ["product heterogeneity", "heterogeneity of products", "related variation in tasks", "product diversity", "Hetero"]
definition: The degree to which a region's mail volume is spread across the firm's seven product types; it captures the diversity in the experience of mailmen in related tasks.

name: Excess capacity
authors_terms: ["excess capacity", "free capacity", "strained capacity", "slack in resources", "excess resources", "Cap"]
definition: The degree to which an organizational unit has time and resources beyond those needed to execute its tasks; when capacity is strained, employees have little time to explore smarter ways of working.

name: On-time delivery
authors_terms: ["on-time delivery", "OTD", "delivering products within 24 hours at the right address"]
definition: The reliability of the work processes, i.e., the percentage of letters delivered on time at the right address; in this setting it is the most important performance dimension next to costs.

name: Learning rate
definition: The parameter -b in the learning curve equation AC = aK-b, giving the percentage of cost reduction when cumulative experience increases; from it the progress rate p = 2-b is computed as the reduction in average cost when cumulative production doubles.

name: Parent firm performance
authors_terms: ["better-performing firms", "the better the firm", "performance of parents", "heritage of spinoffs", "past performance of the parent firm"]
definition: The performance of an incumbent firm determines its spinoffs: "the better the firm then the greater its expected rate of spinoffs and the better the expected performance of its spinoffs." The total years of production is a conventional measure of a firm's overall performance whereas the production-leadership variables reflect the firm's performance at or just before year t.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["performance of firms", "firm performance", "firm survival", "hazard of exit", "total years they produced automobiles"]
definition: The metric of performance that can be constructed for all firms is the total years they produced automobiles. Accordingly, the analysis focuses on the determinants of the annual firm hazard of exit.

name: Spinoff rate
authors_terms: ["spinoff rate", "rate of spinoffs", "probability of a firm having one, two, or three spinoffs"]
definition: The annual rate at which automobile firms spawned spinoffs, estimated as the probability of a firm having one, two, or three spinoffs in each year t.

name: Spinoff origin
definition: Firms were classified as spinoffs if at least one of their founders had worked for or founded, or both, an automobile firm in Smith's list.

name: Pre-entry experience
authors_terms: ["experienced firms", "experienced entrepreneurs", "inexperienced firms", "pre-entry experience", "backgrounds of firms"]
definition: Entrants are classified by their backgrounds: all firms listed in Smith as producing another product prior to automobiles were classified as experienced firms; firms were classified as experienced entrepreneurs if at least one founder was the head of a named firm that was active or had recently been sold; the rest were lumped into a residual category of inexperienced firms.

name: Detroit-area location
authors_terms: ["Detroit area", "located in the Detroit area", "Detroit-area firms"]
definition: In addition to Detroit, the Detroit area was defined to include a set of locations in Michigan, all of which are within approximately 100 miles of Detroit.

name: Co-location with parent
authors_terms: ["located close to their parents", "locate close to their geographic roots", "located within 100 miles of their parents"]
definition: The theory takes on special significance when coupled with the tendency of firms to locate close to their geographic roots; for spinoffs, it implies they will locate close to their parents.

name: Firm age
authors_terms: ["years of production", "age of the firm", "middle aged"]
definition: The probability of a spinoff initially rises and then falls with the age of the firm, measured by the number of years of production of automobiles through year t.

name: Acquisition
authors_terms: ["acquisition", "acquired by another auto firm", "acquired by non-auto firms"]
definition: Any development that lowers the decision making influence of a more informed decision maker will increase the chance of a spinoff; one such development is an acquisition, which typically shifts decision making influence toward new owners.

name: Knowledge flow
authors_terms: ["knowledge flow", "knowledge flows", "knowledge diffusion", "probability of knowledge flow", "probability of citation"]
definition: Patent citations are used to measure knowledge flows: a citation leaves behind a trail of how an innovation potentially builds on existing knowledge. The estimated quantity is the probability that a patent K cites a patent k, i.e., the probability of knowledge flow between two innovations.

name: Geographic colocation
authors_terms: ["within same region", "same region", "geographic colocation", "geographic localization", "intraregional knowledge flows"]
definition: Knowledge flows are geographically localized, so knowledge flow is expected to be stronger within a region than between different regions. A patent's region is one of the 337 Metropolitan Statistical Areas or Primary Metropolitan Statistical Areas in the United States, as determined by the first inventor's address.

name: Firm boundary
authors_terms: ["within same firm", "intra firm knowledge flows", "firm boundaries", "same firm"]
definition: Knowledge diffuses more easily within a firm than between firms, i.e., more effectively than would be possible through a market-mediated mechanism. The analysis asks whether the probability of knowledge flow is greater within a firm than between different firms.

name: Social distance
authors_terms: ["social distance", "past collaboration", "common collaborator", "collaborators with ties", "indirect social link", "no social link", "collaborative tie", "interpersonal ties", "collaborative networks"]
definition: Social distance is defined as the minimum number of intermediaries needed to pass knowledge from the source team to the destination, i.e., the number of intermediate nodes on the minimum path (the geodesic) between any two nodes in the social proximity graph constructed from past patent collaborations.

name: Prior entrepreneurial experience
definition: One particularly important type of preexisting knowledge is the knowledge that has been acquired through prior entrepreneurial experience, because repeat founders can draw on high levels of task-specific knowledge and may have obtained special insights on the entrepreneurial process. Because prior entrepreneurial experience has many tacit components that are learned by doing, it provides a particular type of knowledge that cannot be acquired easily through other types of learning.

name: Market opportunity identification
authors_terms: ["market opportunity search", "preentry market opportunity search", "number of alternative market opportunities", "choice set of market opportunities", "market opportunity identification"]
definition: The identification of multiple market opportunities prior to first entry, i.e., the number of alternative market opportunities entrepreneurs considered for their technological competence prior to the first market entry, or the size of the choice set of such opportunities. The acquisition of knowledge on market opportunities is conceptualized as an organizational search problem in which boundedly rational founders search for alternatives until they identify one that is good enough.

name: New firm performance
definition: Annual sales revenues (in euros) achieved by the new venture in Year 1 and in Year 2 after the initial market entry were used as dependent variables. The achievement of sales revenues once a new firm has entered the market is important, because it shows financiers and other stakeholders that a firm's vision of the market is real ("proof of market") and that it can deliver on its vision.

name: Acquisition entry
definition: An acquisition takes place when one or more Japanese parent acquires an existing U.S. company, and a greenfield investment when one or more Japanese parents build a new plant.

name: R&D intensity
authors_terms: ["research and development intensity", "R&D/sales of parent", "RND", "technological intensity"]
definition: The Japanese parent's technological intensity is measured by its research and development expenditures as a percentage of its domestic sales (R&D) for the year preceding entry.

name: U.S. market experience
authors_terms: ["experience of the U.S. market", "U.S. experience of parent", "EXP"]
definition: A parent's experience of the U.S. market at the time entry was made (EXP) is measured by the number of years between a given entry and the establishment of the parent's first U.S. manufacturing subsidiary. How to operate in the U.S. market is learned as a by-product of doing business there.

name: Entry diversification
authors_terms: ["an entry which represents a diversification for a Japanese investor", "commonality of product between parent and subsidiary", "sameness of products between parent and subsidiary", "COMMON"]
definition: The commonality of product between parent and subsidiary (COMMON) is measured by a dummy variable equal to one if any one of the products produced by the affiliate matched those produced by the parent, and to zero otherwise. An entry which represents a diversification for a Japanese investor is one in which the parent manufactures in the U.S. a product which it does not produce in Japan.

name: Parent product diversification
authors_terms: ["degree of product diversification", "diversification ratio of parent", "DIV"]
definition: The degree of product diversification (DIV) of the Japanese parent is measured by a Herfindahl-Hirschman type index, using the sales breakdown of the Japanese parent the year before entry as published in the Japan Company Handbook.

name: Advertising intensity
definition: ADV is the ratio of media advertising expenditures to sales of the Japanese parent as listed in the company's Yukashoken Hokokusho. Advertising expenditures in Japan are used as a proxy for the investor's marketing skills.

name: Availability of acquisition bargains
authors_terms: ["Relative Value Index", "RVI", "bargains in the market for acquisitions"]
definition: Each year's Relative Value Index (RVI) is calculated to capture the availability of bargains in the market for acquisitions. The RVI is high when acquisitions of U.S. firms are relatively cheap for Japanese investors, i.e., when the dollar is weakening and U.S. stock prices are relatively low.

name: Target industry growth rate
authors_terms: ["rate of growth of demand in the target market", "growth of shipments of U.S. industry entered", "GROWTH", "GROWTHDEV"]
definition: GROWTH is equal to the average annual growth rate of shipments of the four-digit U.S. industry in the 5 years before entry. GROWTHDEV is the absolute value of GROWTH's deviation from its sample mean divided by its standard deviation.

name: Follower status
definition: We first identified the Japanese parent who was the first to enter any given four-digit SIC U.S. industry. We called that parent a leader, and all the subsequent entrants followers.

name: Target industry concentration
authors_terms: ["concentration ratio of U.S. industry entered", "Herfindahl-Hirschman index", "CON"]
definition: Concentration (CON) is measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman index for the 50 largest companies for each four-digit SIC U.S. industry (1982).

name: Endowment of human resources
authors_terms: ["parent's endowment of human resources", "excess supply of managers", "PSALG"]
definition: When employment grows faster than sales and PSALG is high, the firm has excess labor personnel resources, and does not need to obtain them through acquisitions (H12).

name: Relative size of the subsidiary
definition: The relative size of the subsidiary (RELSZ) is the ratio of the employment of the subsidiary over that of the parent.

name: Financial leverage
definition: We measure a firm's financial leverage (LEV) by the ratio of its long term debt to its market value, as reported in its Yukashoken Hokokusho.

name: Organizational experience
definition: By operating experience we mean the cumulative history of core operations (production or service provision) of the organization. For each hotel, the organizational experience variable equals the (discounted) number of room-years the hotel had accumulated between the time the hotel was founded and the current year.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: Failure was defined as the cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors. The hazard rate of a hotel failing is the probability of failure in the interval t, t + At given the hotel was still alive at time t.

name: Population experience
authors_terms: ["population experience", "vicarious experience", "experience of other organizations in the population"]
definition: The Manhattan hotel population's cumulative (discounted) operating experience, measured by the number of rooms offered by the entire population, between the current year and the time the focal hotel was founded.

name: Congenital population experience
authors_terms: ["congenital learning", "congenital population experience", "population experience at the time of organizational founding"]
definition: Huber (1991) refers to learning from population experience before the organization's founding as congenital learning. The variable is the Manhattan hotel population's cumulative (discounted) mass of organizations alive in the year before the focal organization's founding.

name: Local experience of related organizations
authors_terms: ["Chain's Manhattan experience", "local experience of related organizations"]
definition: A hotel chain's operating experience within Manhattan, measured as a function of the number of component hotels it operated in Manhattan during its history, separated into experience accumulated by the time a component joined the chain and experience accumulated afterwards.

name: Non-local experience of related organizations
authors_terms: ["Chain's Non-Manhattan experience", "non-local experience of related organizations"]
definition: A hotel chain's operating experience outside Manhattan, measured as a function of the number of component hotels it operated outside Manhattan during its history, again separated into initial and incremental components.

name: Source of innovation initiation
definition: Innovations are 'user initiated' when they are triggered by either a user's order or serious inquiries; they are 'innovator initiated' when innovative firms take initiatives and either respond to direct market pressure (passive) or deliberately search for new markets and techniques (active).

name: Local availability of related foreign products
authors_terms: ["local availability of related foreign products", "RFPs locally available"]
definition: Whether related foreign products (RFPs) are locally available from which local firms can learn and creatively imitate. Firms that have RFPs locally available can learn to a great extent from them, while firms without them have to look for different means.

name: Innovation pattern
authors_terms: ["patterns of innovation", "pattern of the innovation process", "innovation behavior"]
definition: The pattern of behavior that firms exhibit in the innovation process, covering variables related to idea generation, problem solving and implementation. The innovation pattern associated with these variables is likely to differ significantly by the four cell scheme.

name: Customer role in idea generation
authors_terms: ["customer's role in idea generation", "role of users in idea generation", "role of customers in idea generation"]
definition: The role played by customers as external agents in generating ideas for the innovation in the idea generation stage.

name: Customer role in problem solving
authors_terms: ["customer's role in problem solving", "role of customers in technical problem solving"]
definition: The role played by customers as external agents in the problem solving stage of the innovation.

name: Entrepreneur role in idea generation
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurs as key person in idea generation"]
definition: Whether the entrepreneur was the key person who contributed significantly to the initiation of the innovation.

name: Entrepreneur role in problem solving
authors_terms: ["entrepreneurs as key person in problem solving", "key technical role"]
definition: Whether the entrepreneur played the key technical role in the problem solving stage of the innovation.

name: Overseas observation of foreign suppliers
authors_terms: ["overseas observation", "use of overseas observation of foreign firms producing related products"]
definition: Use of visits to foreign producers abroad to examine their products and obtain catalogs and product specifications.

name: Domestic observation of related foreign products
definition: Observation within the country of local firms using related foreign products.

name: Assistance from local R&D institutes
authors_terms: ["assistance from local R&D institutes", "contribution of local R & D institute", "assistance of local R&D labs"]
definition: Assistance obtained from local research and development institutes in solving technical problems.

name: Usefulness of technical catalogs
authors_terms: ["usefulness of catalogs", "catalogs of related foreign products"]
definition: The use and benefit of catalogs of related foreign products collected from local agents or directly from foreign producers.

name: Degree of imitation
definition: The extent to which the innovation imitates a related foreign product.

name: Patentability of innovations
authors_terms: ["patentability of innovations", "firms obtained patents for NDIMs"]
definition: Whether the firm obtained a patent for its newly developed innovative machine.

name: Import substitution policy opportunity
authors_terms: ["import substitution policy", "opportunity opened by import substitution policy"]
definition: The opportunity for innovation opened by the government's import substitution policy.

name: Educational level of key technical person
definition: The educational level of the key technical person involved in the innovation project.

name: Position of key technical person
authors_terms: ["position of key technical person within the firm"]
definition: The position of the key technical person within the firm involved in the innovation project.

name: Competitive history
authors_terms: ["survived a history of competition", "historical competition", "exposure to competition", "competitive experience", "organization-years of competition"]
definition: The organization-years of competition to which an organization has been exposed historically in a market. Red Queen theory holds that organizations are more viable the more that they have survived a history of competition in that context.

name: Organizational failure rate
definition: The rate at which organizations fail (exit) in a market; in the model the failure rate of organization j is a function of its market tenure and of the historical competition it has faced.

name: Market entry rate
authors_terms: ["rate of entry into new markets", "rate at which the organization enters into new markets", "organizational expansion into other markets"]
definition: The rate at which organizations enter new markets; high estimates of the ability to change increase the rate at which the organization enters into new markets.

name: Functional-background diversity
authors_terms: ["functional-background (FB) diversity", "FB diversity", "functional background (FB)", "knowledge-based diversity", "diversity as variety"]
definition: Diversity in the functional categories in which team members gained the most experience during their career; a knowledge-based (variety) form of diversity whose asymmetric distribution of information is a precondition for effective TMT decision making.

name: Locus-of-control diversity
definition: Diversity in a deep-level personality trait, LOC, which refers to differences in a generalized belief in internal versus external control of reinforcement.

name: Collaborative behavior
definition: The degree to which a TMT acts as a real team with fruitful cooperation among executives.

name: Accurate information exchange
definition: A team process variable assessing the degree of accurate information sharing among TMT members.

name: Decentralized decision making
authors_terms: ["decentralized decision making", "decentralization of decision making", "decision-making decentralization"]
definition: The extent to which decision-making influence is broadly distributed over team members rather than concentrated in the CEO; a team process variable assessing the degree of decision sharing.

name: Firm performance
definition: Organizational effectiveness assessed with a standard accounting measure of profitability: return on sales, i.e., operating income divided by sales.

name: Firm profitability
authors_terms: ["profitability at the firm level", "return on invested capital", "firm performance"]
definition: Profitability at the firm level is measured by return on invested capital, defined as net income after tax plus interest divided by equity and long term debt; it represents the return to all employed resources.

name: Industry profitability
definition: Industry profitability is a weighted-average variable: the return on assets in each 3-digit market the firm sells in, weighted by the percentage of the firm's total sales in that market.

name: Industry growth
definition: Industry growth is a weighted-average variable: the annuity measure of shipment growth (in dollars) in each 4-digit market, weighted by the percentage of the firm's sales in that market.

name: Diversifier efficiency
definition: Firms with low Herfindahl scores are considered efficient diversifiers, and firms with high Herfindahl scores inefficient diversifiers; firms pursuing more related types of diversification (focusing on specific, related skills) have significantly lower Herfindahl scores than firms pursuing less related types of diversification.

name: Technological innovativeness
authors_terms: ["technological innovativeness", "technological sophistication", "technological novelty", "technological newness", "technological innovation", "new technology or first of a kind"]
definition: The technological sophistication of a firm's products, rated on the importance of three product attributes for competitive advantage: the product is based on new technology or is first of a kind, the product has special purpose and specifications, and the product is perceived to be technologically advanced because of the calibre of personnel in the firm.

name: Risk associated with use
authors_terms: ["risk associated with use", "risk associated with use of the product", "perceived risk associated with their use"]
definition: The risk associated with use of a product, assessed as the risk to the patient and the extent to which the product is invasive to the patient, estimated independently by a panel of medical experts.

name: FDA regulatory impact
authors_terms: ["impact of the FDA regulations", "impact of the FDA regulations on firm's operations and management decision-making", "expenses for the FDA interface"]
definition: The impact of U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulations on the firm's operations and management decision-making, and the out-of-pocket expenses precipitated by the requirements of the FDA interactions.

name: Economic performance
definition: The commercial success of the new firm; the authors argue that growth rate of sales alone is unreliable because it is biased towards fast growing young firms, and use average annual sales as the indicator of the firm's commercial success.

name: Initial capital
authors_terms: ["initial capital", "initial financing", "financial resources at founding", "initial financial inputs", "total initial capital"]
definition: The financial resources a firm mobilizes at its founding; the authors argue that only firms which mobilize adequate financial resources are able to benefit economically from their technological innovativeness, and that there is a minimal threshold financing below which the net contribution of technological innovation to economic success becomes negative.

name: Manpower flows
authors_terms: ["manpower flows", "interorganizational manpower flows", "positive gain manpower flows", "net manpower flows", "new blood"]
definition: Manpower flows were defined as the "movement of people across organization boundaries," and are proposed to be a significant alternative and complement to the information flows and boundary spanning line of research.

name: Radical innovation
authors_terms: ["radical innovation", "radical technological change", "radical (new to the industry) process innovations", "adoption of retort pouch technology", "sum of staged adoption behaviors"]
definition: In most cases, it appears, radical innovations involved the application of a new science, skill, or a discontinuous break from the past. The more novel, e.g., new to the world vs. new to a firm or industry, the more radical the innovation.

name: Incremental innovation
authors_terms: ["incremental innovation", "incremental process innovations", "introduction of new products"]
definition: There appear to be at least two ways of distinguishing between a radically new innovation in product or process and one that is not radical, say an incremental change. New products are assumed to be incremental in the food industry.

name: Innovation outcomes
definition: Innovative outcomes of an organization, i.e., offering new products and incorporating new processes.

name: Organizational structure
authors_terms: ["organizational structure", "differentiated structure", "centralization", "formalization", "complexity", "nonfood diversification", "concentration of technical specialists"]
definition: Organizations which are more decentralized, more complex, and more informalized would be more able to assimilate new innovating personnel. Indicators of organization structure included centralization, formalization and complexity from the Aston group, as well as diversification into nonfood markets and the presence of engineering or technical groups in the firm.

name: Slack resources
definition: Innovation is usually a drain on financial and human resources of an organization, so without slack resources that can be allocated to the innovation effort, little change is possible. Slack is defined as actual or potential resources, e.g., retained earnings or credit rating, sufficient to adopt a significant, new processing technology or offer a product that's the first of its kind.

name: Ability to influence formal standardization
authors_terms: ["ability to influence formal standardization", "standard-setting influence", "standardization impact", "influence formal standard setting", "standard-setting outcomes"]
definition: Firms' ability to shape the development of formal compatibility standards; for our purposes, individually submitted change requests provide information about the influence exerted by the members, and contributions to technical specification development are the other influence outcome examined.

name: External cooperative participation
authors_terms: ["participation in external consortia and alliances", "external cooperative technical organizations", "position in external cooperative networks"]
definition: Participation in cooperative technical organizations outside the focal SDO, such as industry consortia and private alliances; we argue that external consortia and alliances are venues, first, for learning, producing, and exchanging valuable technical knowledge, and, second, for advertising firms' own technological assets, aligning positions with peers, and signaling commitment to specific technologies in the formal SDO.

name: Consortium network connections
definition: A firm's connections to other firms formed through comembership in consortia, i.e., the unipartite projection of the bipartite affiliation network, where companies are connected to others if they are comembers.

name: Consortium memberships
definition: The number of consortia in which a firm is a member, i.e., the firm's degree in the bipartite affiliation network of companies and consortia.

name: Membership in consortia related to the focal SDO
authors_terms: ["related memberships", "institutionally related consortia", "consortia closely related to the focal SDO"]
definition: Memberships in consortia that are technologically or institutionally closely related to the formal SDO; consortia are institutionally related to 3GPP if they are its designated market representative partners or organizational partners.

name: Alliance partners
definition: The number of alliance partners a firm has among other 3GPP members; if the number of partners matters, then, from the standard-setting perspective, alliances act as a vehicle for lining up positions and gathering support for technical proposals.

name: Alliances
definition: The number of alliances a firm holds with other 3GPP members; the number of alliances would be a significant predictor of influence if alliances were most useful as venues for developing technical assets and expertise that matter in the standards-development work.

name: Work item committee connections
authors_terms: ["WI connections", "connections formed through specification development committees"]
definition: Connections to peers formed by participating in the work item committees through which new technical features are developed; these work item committees give rise to yet another affiliation network where companies' cooperative relations can be tracked.

name: Specification development committee contributions
authors_terms: ["WI committees", "contributions to specification development committees", "number of work item committees joined"]
definition: Firms' contributions to the development of technical features, measured by the number of work item committees the firm joins; a firm supports a work item by joining a committee of four or more companies.

name: Business strategy focus
authors_terms: ["focused strategies", "strategies that are more focused on a particular market segment", "strategy content"]
definition: Strategies that target a particular market segment, allowing the management group to develop an in-depth understanding of the customers' needs and providing the opportunity to build continuing relationships. Strategy content was operationalized over three key dimensions related to business strategy over which the managers had control: product mix, pricing, and internal operating efficiency.

name: Performance return
definition: The traditional conception of performance in strategic management research has been an accounting figure representing the firm's profit levels or a representative ratio such as return on investment.

name: Performance risk
definition: Variation in performance level. Because we cannot use ex post variation in return to explain ex ante risk taking, this study uses variation in return ex post as an indicator of the risk that exists.

name: Internal operating efficiency
definition: One of the three key dimensions related to business strategy over which the managers had control, along with product mix and pricing.

name: Decision centralization
definition: A greater degree of decision centralization would insure consistency in funds acquisition and allocation which would lead to both lower overall costs in a stable environment and more equitable treatment of customers.

name: Planning formalization
authors_terms: ["formalized strategic planning processes", "formality of a firm's planning activities"]
definition: The formality of a firm's planning activities.

name: Planning operationalization
definition: The extent to which aspects of the plan are operationalized and objectives are converted into measurable outcomes.

name: Environmental interaction amount
authors_terms: ["absolute levels of environmental interaction", "amount of environmental interaction"]
definition: The absolute amount of managers' interaction with their firm's environment; firms with greater absolute levels of environmental interaction are expected to experience higher returns and lower risks.

name: Environmental interaction type
authors_terms: ["type of environmental interaction", "boundary spanning roles", "customer contact", "information acquisition"]
definition: The actual segments of the environment with which the managers choose to interact; in this industry customer contact and information acquisition are the types hypothesized to be associated with better performance.

name: Departmental interdependence
definition: Departmental interdependence within a firm reflects the interaction of various organizational subunits in the performance of their duties.

name: Influence on strategic decisions
authors_terms: ["distribution of influence on strategic decisions", "influence on strategic decisions"]
definition: The distribution of influence on strategic decisions reflects the distribution of power among groups within the firm.

name: Withdrawal announcement
authors_terms: ["corporate announcements of withdrawal from South Africa", "the decision to withdraw", "public withdrawal announcements", "withdrawal announcement"]
definition: A firm's explicit decision to pull out of South Africa that was carried in the U.S. press; the event is treated as the independent variable in the study.

name: Stockholder wealth
authors_terms: ["stockholder wealth", "value of a firm's stock", "stock price", "value of the withdrawing firms' stock"]
definition: The value of a firm's stock, which reflects the present value of its expected future cash flows discounted by a risk-adjusted rate, so that any stock price change is related to changes in expected cash flows or risk.

name: Timing of withdrawal announcement
authors_terms: ["timing of the announcements", "earlier announcements", "later announcements", "early withdrawers", "late withdrawers"]
definition: Where in the debate over withdrawal a firm announced its exit; firms whose announcements appeared in 1986 or before are early withdrawers and those whose announcements appeared in 1987 or thereafter are late withdrawers.

name: Stage of growth
authors_terms: ["stage of growth", "stages of growth", "stage of growth model", "four stages of growth"]
definition: TBNVs are postulated to evolve through four discrete stages of growth—Conception and Development, Commercialization, Growth, and Stability—each characterized by a subset of dominant problems and by associated processes and structures.

name: Stage of growth progression
authors_terms: ["stage of growth progression", "progress according to stages of growth", "advance in stage", "mature over time"]
definition: The predicted pattern by which technology based new ventures mature over time, advancing one stage at a time from Conception and Development through Commercialization and Growth to Stability.

name: Firm size
definition: The total number of employees of the venture, reported by the CEO.

name: Firm age
definition: The age of the venture in years, reported by the CEO.

name: Sales growth rate
authors_terms: ["rate of sales growth", "percentage rate of growth in sales"]
definition: The current year's sales divided by the previous year's sales, calculated from the sales figures the CEOs reported.

name: Announcement effects of duality status changes
definition: The market's price reaction around the announcement date of changes in a firm's CEO duality status, measured as cumulative average excess returns.

name: Operating performance
definition: Accounting measures of performance including return on equity, return on assets, operating cash flow to total assets, and operating cash flow to sales.

name: Market value added
authors_terms: ["market value added (MVA)", "change in the industry-adjusted, standardized MVA ratio"]
definition: The market value of debt, preferred equity and common equity capitalization less the book value of a firm's entire capitalization, adjusted for past write-offs of capital.

name: CEO duality status
definition: A duality structure exists when the CEO and Chairperson of the Board are the same individual; nonduality implies that different individuals serve as the CEO and the chairperson.

name: Inside chairman
authors_terms: ["inside chairman", "Chairman of the Board was previously a member of the company's management team"]
definition: A dummy variable reflecting whether the Chairman of the Board was previously a member of the company's management team, likely exercising less independent control over managers.

name: Firm size
authors_terms: ["firm size", "natural log of average annual sales"]
definition: Firm size measured as the natural log of average annual sales between 1986 and 1991, controlling for size effects on MVA performance.

name: Capital structure
authors_terms: ["capital structure", "average annual total debt to total assets ratio"]
definition: The disciplining impact of capital structure, controlled using the average annual total debt to total assets ratio computed over the period 1986-91.

name: Dividend policy
definition: Dividend policy included as the average annual dividend payout ratio in the regressions, argued to be an effective controlling mechanism for agency problems.

name: Firm risk
definition: Firm risk measured by beta values, expected to be associated with greater returns for shareholders on average.

name: Insider ownership
definition: The proportion of inside ownership as reported in Value Line at the end of 1991, argued to positively impact value creation.

name: Conflict in decision making
definition: When the term "conflict" is used in this paper, it refers to conflictual behavior in the context of a particular decision.

name: Overall decision quality
authors_terms: ["overall quality", "quality of decisions", "quality of the decision"]
definition: From the adjectives which loaded most heavily on Factor 1, it seems to represent a judgment of overall quality and so was labeled "Overall Quality."

name: Clarity of the decision process
definition: Factor 2 represented the extent to which the decision process was understandable or comprehensible. It was labeled "Clarity."

name: Aversiveness of the decision process
definition: Factor 3 describes the extent to which the process was unpleasant, tense, and emotional. It was labeled "Aversiveness."

name: Organization type
definition: The sample was divided into for-profit and not-for-profit organizations.

name: Conformity to industry rule
authors_terms: ["conformity", "index of conformity", "index of observance", "observance of the industry rule", "conformity to industry practice", "degree of conformity to the industry rule"]
definition: The extent to which a sales district's observed choice of a rep or direct sales force conforms to the apparent industry rule (industry practice) as expressed by the estimated descriptive decision model. A low index of observance means the district is not observing industry practice (not conforming), while a high index means the opposite.

name: Selling efficiency
definition: The outcome of the rep/direct choice is the ratio of sales to the cost of running the sales force, i.e. selling efficiency. It is the level of sales/cost each sales force form attains under different selling situations.

name: Environmental unpredictability
authors_terms: ["environmental unpredictability", "environmental uncertainty", "level of environmental uncertainty", "unpredictable environments", "turbulence/instability"]
definition: A multi-item scale covering two sources of uncertainty: turbulence/instability, reflecting an environment that is complex, volatile, difficult to monitor, and difficult to forecast correctly, and venturing into the unknown (new products and new markets), which makes prediction inherently difficult for the firm.

name: Sales force integration
authors_terms: ["integrated or independent sales forces", "rep or direct", "the rep-direct choice", "going direct", "the decision whether to integrate the selling function"]
definition: Whether a firm should serve a given market with an integrated sales force, composed of employees, or an independent sales force, composed of businesses with whom the firm writes a contract. The integrated option is called a direct sales force, while the independent option is called a manufacturers' representative or sales agency.

name: CEO tenure
authors_terms: ["CEO tenure", "tenure of the CEO", "lengthy tenure", "long-tenured CEOs"]
definition: The length of time a CEO has been in office; the longer a CEO's tenure in office, the more likely it is that he or she will have the influence, autonomy and desire to resist external pressures for change.

name: Environment-structure match
authors_terms: ["match between environment and structure", "environment-structure match", "structural match"]
definition: The alignment between a firm's structure and its environment, defined by the normative criteria of the contingency literature: environmental uncertainty should be negatively related to centralization and positively related to formalization, specialization, technocratization and the use of liaison devices, and environmental heterogeneity should be positively related to specialization and liaison devices.

name: Environment-strategy match
authors_terms: ["match between environment and strategy", "environment-strategy match", "strategy match"]
definition: The alignment between a firm's strategy and its environment, defined by the relationships of Porter's generic strategies to the environment: differentiation positively related to environmental uncertainty, cost leadership negatively related to uncertainty, and focus strategies inversely related to market heterogeneity.

name: Financial performance
definition: The firm's financial results, assessed with quantitative indices of return on investment, growth in sales, growth in net income and profitability relative to competitors.

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: Environmental uncertainty refers to the degrees of change and unpredictability of customers, competitors and technologies.

name: Environmental heterogeneity
definition: Environmental heterogeneity reflects the range of differences in customer buying habits, competition, and required methods of production or service.

name: Centralization
definition: The concentration of authority within the organization; one of the primary dimensions of structure to have emerged empirically.

name: Formalization
definition: The formalization of positions and procedures; one of the primary dimensions of structure to have emerged empirically.

name: Specialization
definition: The specialization of tasks and roles within the organization; one of the primary dimensions of structure to have emerged empirically.

name: Technocratization
definition: The use and empowerment of highly skilled and well-trained technocrats; a technocratization aspect of structure stressed by Burns and Stalker, Hage and Aiken and Khandwalla.

name: Use of liaison devices
definition: The use of liaison devices to integrate the efforts of specialists; described as integration, one of the primary dimensions of structure to have emerged empirically.

name: Innovative differentiation
definition: A strategy of differentiation that strives to create a unique offering through product innovation and new product development; uncertain environments were said to warrant its expense and to benefit most from it.

name: Marketing differentiation
definition: A form of differentiation pursued through advertising, market segmentation and prestige pricing.

name: Cost leadership
definition: A strategy in which cost leaders produce standard products at the lowest possible cost, typically succeeding only in stable settings where they can develop standard, specialized routines.

name: Focus strategy
definition: Porter's third generic strategy, the concentration on a circumscribed group of customers that a firm is able to serve better than any of its competitors.

name: Concentration of ownership
definition: The extent to which shares are owned by one party; where ownership is concentrated, effective control of the firm generally lies with the owner-CEO or his powerful supporters.

name: Product line breadth
authors_terms: ["product line breadth", "PLB", "broader product line", "breadth of the product line"]
definition: The breadth of the business's product line as compared with its competition; the authors use the closest surrogate available in the data base and note that the product line breadth measure is subjective in nature.

name: Market share
definition: Percentage sales of the served market; one of the six endogenous variables of the model.

name: Relative price
definition: Average selling prices of the business relative to the average of its three leading competitors.

name: Direct costs
definition: Average direct costs of the business relative to the average of its three leading competitors.

name: Total inventory cost
definition: Average finished goods plus raw material plus work-in-process inventory as a percentage of net sales.

name: Manufacturing costs
definition: Total manufacturing expenses (direct plus overheads) as a percentage of net sales.

name: Profitability
definition: Net income as a percentage of average investment less book value.

name: Dependability
authors_terms: ["dependability", "D Score", "minimum acceptable level of dependability", "dependability of the debtor"]
definition: For the purposes of the model, "dependability" in the eyes of the creditors is defined as the combined level of a firm's managerial capital (i.e., prestige) and financial health (i.e., liquidity and leverage). A firm that falls below the dividing line is judged undependable because the combined risks of low liquidity, high leverage and nonprestigious managers are too high for the creditors.

name: Financial strength
definition: Liquidity and the inverse of leverage (labeled unused borrowing capacity) have been collapsed to one dimension, called financial strength, to present a simple two-dimensional picture that conveys the concept of a dividing line between survivors and bankrupts.

name: Managerial prestige
authors_terms: ["managerial prestige", "prestige of the top management team", "managerial capital (i.e., prestige)"]
definition: Creditors consider the top management's education level, eliteness or "pedigree", and board affiliations because these are factors which indicate that the managers are "decision experts" who are likely to be more capable and trustworthy. The prestige of the top management team was measured using a scale designed to capture both educational and board affiliations.

name: Organizational survival
definition: The paper argues that debtors with unprestigious top managers, low liquidity and high leverage signal that they will be undependable exchange partners; if a firm falls below the threshold level it has a higher probability of bankruptcy because creditors withdraw their financial support from the debtor, and bankruptcy can be viewed as the legal resolution of severe shareholder-creditor conflicts about the levels of financial and managerial assets that the debtor should maintain.

name: Salvage value of net fixed assets
authors_terms: ["net fixed assets", "salvage value of net fixed assets", "saleable (nonessential) assets"]
definition: A measure of saleable (nonessential) assets was not available, so net fixed assets was used as a proxy variable; the losses of creditors are limited by the salvage value of the property held by the debtor, so creditors may be willing to take greater risks when they are partially protected by the debtor's ability to self-cannibalize in the future.

name: Downsizing
definition: Self-cannibalization is the pre-bankruptcy liquidation of assets to generate cash to cover liabilities, a form of downsizing or phased exit from an industry; by freeing up cash to pay debts, it allows the creditors to be paid and to avoid recognizing any losses in the short run.

name: Firm growth
authors_terms: ["growth in the debtor's size", "growing size", "debt financed growth"]
definition: Growth in the debtor's size or evidence of a turnaround in costs or sales may also signal the possibility of improved financial strength and the ability to attract high prestige managers with higher salaries.

name: Turnaround in sales or costs
authors_terms: ["turnaround in sales or costs", "improving costs and sales", "turnaround in costs or sales"]
definition: A second survival strategy for undependable firms is to show evidence of improving dependability, which suggests that the debtor may be only temporarily undependable; growth in the debtor's size or evidence of a turnaround in costs or sales may also signal the possibility of improved financial strength.

name: Environmental shielding
authors_terms: ["environments that shield the firm from adverse competitive conditions", "environments that shield the firm from competition", "lack of competitive rivalry", "low threat of competitive entry", "power over the buyer", "power over buyers", "power over suppliers"]
definition: The firm's environment represented via a set of external forces previously postulated to affect a firm's profitability, i.e., supplier power, buyer power, competitive rivalry within the industry, and potential threat of entry into the industry. Higher values imply increasingly good competitive conditions that shield the firm from adverse competitive forces.

name: Average unit price
authors_terms: ["average unit price", "average annual unit price", "firm's average price"]
definition: The firm's average unit price, the price component of the accounting identity in which total revenue equals quantity times price.

name: Average unit cost
authors_terms: ["average unit cost", "average annual unit cost", "firm's average cost"]
definition: The firm's average unit cost, the cost component of the accounting identity in which total cost equals quantity times average cost.

name: Market position
authors_terms: ["market position", "lagged market position", "initial market share position"]
definition: Market position is defined as a firm's market share divided by the market share of its three biggest competitors, and is lagged one year in the model.

name: Change in market share
authors_terms: ["change in market share", "changes in market share", "change in dollar market share", "shifts in market share"]
definition: The increase or decrease in the firm's market share over the last year, i.e., what happens when a firm experiences shifts in market share.

name: Joint venture diffusion
