authors_terms: ["diffusion of joint venture", "adoption of joint venture", "first-time adoption of joint venture"]
definition: The first-time adoption of a joint venture by an organization, viewed as an administrative innovation representing a fundamental shift away from the established mode of conducting an economic activity, namely hierarchy versus market.

name: M-form structure diffusion
authors_terms: ["diffusion of M-form structure", "M-form structure as an administrative innovation"]
definition: The adoption of M-form (multidivisional) organizational structure, considered an administrative innovation that constitutes a fundamental structural response to organizational complexities brought about by strategies of internal growth.

name: Internal influence
definition: The internal-influence model purports that diffusion takes place solely through channels of communication within a specific community and is appropriate for testing the imitation hypothesis; the diffusion rate is contingent only on the interaction between prior adopters and potential adopters.

name: External influence
definition: The diffusion process in this model is driven only by information from a communication source external to the social system; the rate of diffusion at time t is dependent only on the potential number of adopters present in the social system at time t, so the imitation process is not recognized.

name: Product market signal
authors_terms: ["product market signal", "market cue", "signal that the valuation of the venture has increased", "unexpected growth in the product market"]
definition: A market cue indicating an increase in the venture's valuation; positive movements in the value of industry shipments signal improved investment opportunities and an increase in the value of the real option embedded in the venture.

name: Joint venture acquisition
authors_terms: ["acquisition", "termination by acquisition", "likelihood of an acquisition", "buy out the venture"]
definition: Termination of the venture by acquisition, in which one of the partners or a third party buys out the venture; the authors treat the timing of the acquisition as the timing of the exercise of the option to expand.

name: Joint venture dissolution
definition: Termination of the venture by dissolution, treated by the authors as a mode of termination distinct from acquisition and used to test whether managers react to downward market movements.

name: Industry concentration
definition: The four-firm concentration ratio at the four-digit SIC level, used as a proxy for industry maturity that promotes the use of joint ventures as vehicles of planned divestment.

name: Subsidiary autonomy
definition: We operationalize centralization by its obverse, subsidiary autonomy, and measure it as the relative influence exercised by the headquarters and the subsidiary in making the following decisions: (1) major reorganizations in the subsidiary involving creation or dissolution of departments, (2) career development plans for subsidiary managers, and (3) changes in product design.

name: Networking
definition: Informal relationships between managers are operationalized in terms of a second latent variable construct, networking. We operationalize networking through the following three indicators: (1) time spent in interunit (e.g. subsidiaries and headquarters) committees, teams, and task forces, (2) time spent in interunit meetings and conferences, and (3) time spent in the world headquarters, all measured in days, on the most recent annual basis.

name: Subsidiary-headquarters communication
definition: We define subsidiary-headquarters communication as the typical frequency of an individual national subsidiary senior manager's communication with his or her counterparts in the headquarters.

name: Intersubsidiary communication
definition: We define intersubsidiary communication as the aggregate typical frequency of an individual national subsidiary senior manager's communication with his or her counterparts in other national subsidiaries of the company.

name: Production relatedness
definition: By production similarity, the authors mean commonality in the physical characteristics of the products, raw materials, or manufacturing processes; SIC groupings are based only on such production or output similarity.

name: Marketing relatedness
authors_terms: ["marketing relatedness", "marketing-based relatedness", "related on the basis of marketing"]
definition: The drug-health products linkage, primarily marketing and to a lesser extent innovation in origin, is related on the basis of marketing to hospitals and physicians even though output-based SIC codes make the two appear unrelated.

name: Synergy
definition: By synergy, the authors mean super-additivity in valuation of business combinations; in simpler terms, synergy means that the valuation of a combination of business units exceeds the sum of valuations for stand alone units.

name: Corporate diversification
definition: The shares of sales of a firm in various industries are used to measure diversification because asset-based shares are unavailable before the mid-1970s.

name: Industry life cycle
definition: The phases of industry evolution over which the strategic importance of different points of the value chain shifts; the authors argue synergies between chemicals and pharmaceuticals declined over the industry life cycle as production declined in strategic importance.

name: Stock market value
authors_terms: ["capital market value", "stock market value of common equity", "constant dollar stock market value of common equity"]
definition: The constant dollar stock market value of common equity of the firm, denoted M, representing the numerator of Tobin's Q.

name: Innovative productivity
definition: The productivity of each pharmaceutical unit measured by the number of FDA-approved new drugs that were discovered; pharmaceutical innovation is described as the core strategic activity of firms in this industry.

name: Continuation-in-part filing
definition: The CIP includes a substantial portion or all of the parent application and adds matter not disclosed in that application, although the benefit of early priority is awarded only for the claims carried forward from the original application.

name: CAP and division filing
definition: The CAP discloses the identical invention claimed in the prior 'parent' nonprovisional application before that application was patented or abandoned; a division or divisional application occurs when an original application contains more than one independent invention and the other inventions disclosed in the parent application are pursued in new applications called divisions.

name: Patent intensity
definition: The patenting intensity of firms, calculated as annual log number of patents/M$ of annual R&D.

name: R&D intensity
definition: The R&D intensity of firms, log annual R&D expenditure in M$/1,000 employees.

name: Capital intensity
definition: The capital intensity of firms, log book value of plant, property, and equipment in M$/1,000 employees.

name: Technological importance of a patent
definition: Forward citations are used as indicators of the technological importance of patents, based on the argument that a higher number of citations to a patent in subsequent patents indicate that the invention in the cited patent influenced the development of a greater number of subsequent inventions.

name: Initial assessment of competitor's likely behavior
authors_terms: ["initial assessment of the competitor's likely behavior", "managers' initial expectations", "EXPECT CMOVE1 = $1", "subject's assessed subjective probability that the competitor's first bid would be $1"]
definition: In situations of strategic interdependence, one's initial assessment of the competitor's likely behavior is an important influence on managers' decisions; the variable used to represent it equals the assessed probability that the computer competitor's first bid will equal $1.00.

name: Cooperation
authors_terms: ["cooperation by the subjects", "cooperative choices", "$1.00 bids", "SMOVE", "the manager's choice of a $1.00 bid"]
definition: The dependent variable is a binary variable indicating the managers' bid on a round of the simulation; cooperative choices ($1.00 bids) are assigned a value of 1 and noncooperative choices ($.95 bids) are assigned a 0.

name: Competitor moves
authors_terms: ["moves", "competitor's moves", "competitor's behavior", "observations of the pricing decisions made by the competitor", "CMOVE(t-1)"]
definition: Moves are the observable behavioral signal from the competitor. Because the competitor follows a strict tit-for-tat strategy and the only behavioral options are a cooperative move or a competitive move, the effect of a move is interpreted as the effect of a cooperative move versus a competitive move.

name: Cooperative messages
authors_terms: ["cooperative messages", "messages that imply (truthfully) that the competitor's next move will be cooperative", "$1 MESSAGE(t-1)"]
definition: Messages that imply (truthfully) that the competitor's next move will be cooperative; $1 MESSAGE(t-1) equals 1 if a message suggesting that Moxy would bid $1.00 next time was sent last period.

name: Competitive messages
authors_terms: ["competitive messages", "messages that imply (truthfully) an upcoming competitive move by the competitor", "$.95 MESSAGE(t-1)"]
definition: Messages that imply (truthfully) an upcoming competitive move by the competitor; $.95 MESSAGE(t-1) equals 1 if Moxy sent a message indicating that it was about to bid $.95.

name: Round in the simulation
authors_terms: ["ROUND", "round in the simulation", "repeated moves", "over the course of the simulation"]
definition: ROUND is a continuous variable corresponding to the particular round in the simulation for which the manager's move is observed. Repeated interactions are used because subsequent encounters provide the opportunity for learning, i.e., for sense to be made of signals.

name: Competitive impact
definition: Competitive impact reflects the pervasiveness of an action's effect on competitors; it is concerned with how many competitors are affected by an action and thus may respond to it.

name: Attack intensity
definition: Attack intensity reflects the degree to which the markets of a given competitor are threatened by an action; it focuses on the effect of the move on an individual competitor and on the strategic importance to that competitor of the affected market.

name: Implementation requirement
definition: Implementation requirement is defined as the degree of effort an initiating firm requires to execute an action, as reflected by the amount of time spent preparing to execute that action.

name: Type of action
definition: Action type is dichotomized as strategic or tactical; an action was considered strategic if it involved significant investment in fixed assets and/or people/structure, and tactical if it did not involve significant commitments of fixed assets and had little long-term impact on the firm making the move.

name: Number of responses
definition: Number of responses is the total number of competitors who actually respond to an action.

name: Response lag
definition: Response lag is defined as the length of time a competitor takes to respond to an initiator's competitive action.

name: Standards endorsement
authors_terms: ["endorsement of a standard", "published standards", "standards-track RFCs", "technology endorsement", "authorship of successful Internet standards"]
definition: Endorsement of a firm's technology standard by the open standards community; published standards are documents that have undergone peer review within a working group and have generated consensus in both the working group and the community in general.

name: Open development
definition: Openly developing the startup's technology within the community by engaging external actors, which exposes the firm to helpful comments and criticism; the process of writing and developing a standard, whether or not it is ultimately endorsed.

name: Conference attendance
authors_terms: ["physical attendance at community meetings", "conference attendance", "attending physical meetings of the community"]
definition: Simple physical attendance by startup employees at the community's meetings, as opposed to electronic monitoring or developing technology.

name: Community leadership
authors_terms: ["community leadership", "working group chairs", "employment of a community leader", "leadership positions"]
definition: Employment of a community leader, defined in the IETF as leading a working group or serving as an area chair.

name: Liquidity event
definition: Defined as the announcement of an IPO or acquisition; the authors assume that all these venture-funded firms desire an IPO or acquisition.

name: Product architecture centrality
authors_terms: ["centrality in a product architecture network", "centrality of a subsystem", "subsystem centrality", "degree centrality"]
definition: The position of a subsystem in the product architecture network, where subsystems are nodes and interfaces between subsystems are links; a subsystem with many physical and functional interfaces has high centrality. The centrality of a subsystem can serve as a proxy for complexity, because more interfaces imply more design issues.

name: Coordination deficit
authors_terms: ["coordination deficit", "mismatches between product architecture and organizational coordination", "misalignment of the design organization and the product architecture"]
definition: A metric that quantifies mismatches between product architecture and organizational structure, computed from the product architecture and organizational coordination networks. It includes only links where the architectural connection is stronger than the coordination connection, to capture undercoverage of subsystem linkages.

name: Quality problems
authors_terms: ["quality problems", "warranty claims", "warranty incidents", "IPTV (incidents per thousand vehicle)"]
definition: The quality problems observed in a subsystem of the final product, measured by warranty claims reported in the field. Warranty claims data were aggregated from roughly 17,000 unique problem codes up to the subsystem level, and IPTV (incidents per thousand vehicle) was used as the measure of quality.

name: ICJV innovativeness
definition: Innovation is "the generation, acceptance, and implementation of new ideas, processes, products, or services . . . for the first time within an organizational setting" (V. Thompson 1965, p. 5); the study focuses on managerial innovation in the ICJV unit, defined as new organized primary care services instituted by the unit.

name: Environmental competition
authors_terms: ["environmental competition", "market competition", "the level of market competition which the organization faces"]
definition: Characteristics of the organization's environment that act as a source of information and constraint; measured as the degree of competition the ICJV faces relative to local primary care physicians and organized services sponsored by local community health agencies.

name: Environmental resource scarcity
definition: The environment being "lean in needed resources" (Miles 1980, 229); the level of discretionary resources potentially available to support new services.

name: Sponsoring organization's innovation orientation
authors_terms: ["sponsoring organization's innovation orientation", "organization's orientation to innovation", "the degree to which the sponsoring organization engages in innovative behavior"]
definition: An ICJV's orientation to activities such as innovation may be linked to the orientation held by the pre-existing, sponsoring organization; a generally innovative sponsor is likely to be more receptive to and supportive of innovative activities by the ICJV.

name: Sponsoring organization's prior venturing experience
authors_terms: ["prior venturing experience", "the degree to which the sponsor is experienced at managing relationships similar to the ICJV"]
definition: The specific prior venturing experience of the sponsoring organization with relationships similar to the ICJV; inexperienced sponsors tend to dominate and overly shelter the new organization, whereas more experienced joint venture partners recognize the need for semi-autonomy.

name: Age diversity
authors_terms: ["age diversity", "the degree of age diversity among organizational members", "individual diversity"]
definition: The degree of age diversity among the individual members of the ICJV unit; in ICJVs comprised of a mix of young and old professionals, agreement regarding which innovative services to provide may be difficult to achieve.

name: Integrative participation
authors_terms: ["integrative participation", "integration", "the extent to which the ICJV unit participates in integrative activities with the sponsor"]
definition: The degree of connectedness between the sponsoring organization and the ICJV unit, manifested in the position of a liaison or integrator, and the ICJV's representation in the top-level decision making processes of the sponsoring organization.

name: Organizational slack
definition: Bourgeois's (1981, 30) definition: "that cushion of actual or potential resources which allows an organization to adapt successfully to internal . . . or . . . external pressures for change . . . as well as to initiate changes in strategy with respect to the external environment"; slack can free up resources necessary for creative behavior.

name: ICJV unit autonomy
definition: The extent to which the ICJV unit was free to determine its own policies with respect to marketing, budgeting, and physician personnel.

name: Organizational inauthenticity
definition: I adopt the general meaning of the term, which describes whether an actor is considered genuine and acts in accordance with their true character. An actor is considered authentic if they act in accordance with these expectations.

name: Perceived product quality
authors_terms: ["perceptions of quality", "perception of quality", "perceived product quality"]
definition: The first component of the total utility an audience member derives from an object is the physical aspects of the object, which I refer to as the consumer's "perception of quality." The perceptions of quality variable captures the evaluator's perception of the physical object after experiencing it.

name: Symbolic value
definition: A symbolic object is what the good represents, and symbolic goods are distinct from the physical object and often allow audiences to demonstrate their social standing or personal characteristics. The total utility an audience member derives from an object can be broken down into the physical aspects of the object and the nonphysical or symbolic value of the object.

name: Overall product rating
authors_terms: ["overall rating", "overall product ratings", "overall impression of the beer"]
definition: The overall rating dimension has no objective criteria. It is simply a measure of how well the consumer "liked" the product.

name: Formal IP protection
authors_terms: ["IP protection", "formal IPR", "intellectual property rights (IPR)", "formal appropriability mechanisms"]
definition: Formal appropriability mechanisms such as patents and copyrights are a means of deterring entry by the platform owner because strong appropriability mechanisms increase the cost to the platform owner of entering the complementary market and expectations of legal infringements may deter imitation ex ante.

name: Downstream capabilities
authors_terms: ["downstream capabilities", "downstream complementary capabilities", "complementary capabilities", "brand capital", "marketing capabilities"]
definition: Downstream capabilities are the manufacturing, marketing, or other capabilities required to commercialize an innovation; they are hard to acquire through the market on competitive terms and may therefore be rare and difficult to imitate, and they reduce the potential losses in the ISV's markets in case of an ex post squeeze.

name: Platform partnership
authors_terms: ["platform partnership", "partnership with the software platform owner", "joining the platform", "becoming certified by SAP"]
definition: Entry is measured by an independent software vendor's (ISV's) decision to become certified by a platform owner and produce applications compatible with the platform; the entry decision is essentially one to produce an application for (or to join) the platform at a particular time.

name: Market growth
definition: When the ISV's target markets present higher growth opportunities, incentives to enter are higher, leading to an increase in the likelihood of entry. We construct two variables measuring the growth prospects of each ISV based on alternative ways of characterizing growth.

name: Public API adoption
authors_terms: ["public API adoption", "API adoption", "implementing APIs", "public APIs", "adopting public APIs"]
definition: An API is a set of routines, protocols, and tools that standardizes building software applications compatible with an associated program or database, and it is the public APIs, ones that can be accessed without permission by third parties, that are essential to an inverted firm.

name: Firm market value
definition: Firms' financial performance, including market capitalization, is measured from Compustat quarterly data and is used as the log of market value of the firm.

name: API network centrality
authors_terms: ["API network centrality", "network centrality", "betweenness centrality", "API network position", "network importance"]
definition: Each node corresponds to a firm's API and each link connects a firm's APIs via third-party applications; betweenness centrality calculates the share of shortest paths between nodes in the network that pass through a given node, degree sums a node's connections, and effective network size captures nonredundant connections that each node provides.

name: Data breach risk
authors_terms: ["data breach", "breach events", "risk of data breach", "hack events", "leaky API"]
definition: A data breach is a recorded event in which a firm's data are exposed, with PRC categories distinguishing theft of physical storage media, paper documents and stationary devices, insider breaches, unintended disclosures, and incidents of hacking or malware leading to the data breach.

name: External value creation
authors_terms: ["external value creation", "external mechanisms", "third-party value creation", "inverted firm hypothesis", "firm inversion"]
definition: By external mechanisms, we mean the inverted firm hypothesis: third-party value creation that expands the boundaries of the firm.

name: Internal value creation
authors_terms: ["internal value creation", "internal mechanisms", "internal productivity effects", "private value creation"]
definition: By internal mechanisms, we mean private value creation that does not expand the boundaries of the firm.

name: Algorithmic skills
definition: Algorithmic literacy refers to a worker's capacity not only to operate technical tools but also to interpret algorithmic outputs, assess their reliability, and integrate them into decision-making; the empirical analyses focus on algorithmic skills, the measurable subset of literacy reflected in the demonstrable ability to use tools such as machine learning and data science algorithms, predictive software, generative AI systems, and AI-powered analytics platforms.

name: Domain expertise
definition: Domain expertise refers to the knowledge required to work in a specialized field such as nursing, sales, marketing, or accounting.

name: Decision-making responsibility
definition: DMK indicates levels of decision-making needed in that occupation; the importance of decision making for an occupation is retrieved from the O*NET database.

name: Ease of learning algorithmic tools
authors_terms: ["easy to learn", "EASYLEARN", "no-code tools", "barriers to acquiring algorithmic skills"]
definition: EASYLEARN is an indicator of whether the skill is related to a "no-code" technology; the barriers to using many tools are falling as vendors compete to speed adoption of their products in the workplace.

name: Decentralization of algorithmic skills among domain experts
authors_terms: ["decentralization of algorithmic skills", "dispersion of algorithmic skills", "φALG"]
definition: For organization i in year t, an aggregate measure of the dispersion of algorithmic skills across occupational groups that are highest in both their domain knowledge and decision-making requirements (φALG); firms in which employees in these occupations have more algorithmic skills have larger φALG values.

name: Firm investment in algorithms
authors_terms: ["ALG IT", "investment in algorithms", "algorithmic investments", "AI and data science investments"]
definition: Investments in aggregate IT or its subcategories (i.e., ALG_IT, IT, DS_IT, AI_IT) are computed as the quantity of relevant skills in the firms' IT workforce in a given year; the "stock" of skills in a technological area can be interpreted as the intensity of investment in that domain.

name: Firm investment in information technology
definition: A measure of the firm's aggregate IT investment, constructed in the same way as the algorithmic investment measures from the quantity of relevant skills in the firms' IT workforce in a given year.

name: Market value
definition: Total market value represents the total worth of a firm as assessed by the financial markets.

name: Corporate risk tolerance
authors_terms: ["risk tolerance", "ex ante corporate risk tolerance", "risk propensity", "ex ante risk tolerance", "risk tolerance ratio (RTR)"]
definition: Risk tolerance is defined as the inverse of the risk aversion coefficient, c, in the exponential utility function; it characterizes the firm's ex ante risk propensity, where a positive c implies risk-averse behavior, a negative c risk-seeking behavior, and c approaching 0 risk-neutral behavior.

name: Firm size
definition: For oil companies, an appropriate measure of firm size is the Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Net Cash Flows (SMCF), a measure of the value of the firm's oil and gas reserves that represents the 'wealth' of the oil and gas exploration business unit.

name: Firm performance
authors_terms: ["firm performance", "ex post returns", "return on E&P assets (ROA)", "economic performance"]
definition: Ex post return is measured in terms of return on total exploration and production assets (ROA), where income for purposes of the return calculation is defined as earnings before interest but after taxes.

name: Ex post risk
definition: Risk is an ex ante concept, but in empirical work on organizational performance it is generally measured after the event (ex post) through such measures as the variance of returns; the authors also use an ordinal risk measure defined in terms of a loss in strategic position.

name: Acquisition premium
authors_terms: ["acquisition premium", "premium paid by the acquiring firm", "premium"]
definition: A premium is the percentage difference between the trading price of the target's stock before the announcement of the acquisition and the price per share paid by the acquiring firm. It is the decision of how much to pay when acquiring another company.

name: Prior premiums paid by interlock partners
authors_terms: ["prior premiums paid by their interlock partners", "interlock partner premium", "average premium paid by those tied-to firms"]
definition: The average premium paid by those firms on whose boards the inside and outside directors of the acquiring firm sat, during the three years before the date of the acquiring firm's transaction.

name: Target valuation uncertainty
definition: The uncertainty surrounding the value of an acquisition target: when there is general disagreement about the value of a target, the managers of the acquiring firm should be more likely to turn to others for information and to respond to any information gained. It is operationalized as the variance of opinion about the value of the target.

name: Number of investment banking firms used
authors_terms: ["number of investment banking firms used by the acquiror", "# Acquiror IBankers", "investment banker relationship count"]
definition: The number of investment banking firms used by the acquiror on a given acquisition transaction.

name: Premiums paid by other clients of the same investment banker
authors_terms: ["own IBanker premium", "prior premiums paid by other acquirors using the same investment banking firm", "premiums paid by other firms on transactions involving that same investment banking firm"]
definition: The average premium paid on all transactions involving the investment banking firm used by the acquiror during the prior three years; if multiple investment bankers were used, these premiums were averaged.

name: Premiums paid by clients of other investment bankers
authors_terms: ["other IBanker premium", "prior premiums paid by acquirors using different investment banking firms", "premiums paid on prior transactions involving investment bankers not used by the acquiror"]
definition: The average premium paid during the prior three years on all transactions involving investment banking firms not used by the acquiror.

name: Organizational mortality
definition: Exit of a carrier from the population by failure; the authors categorize as failed only those carriers that disappear from the ICC's Form M population and never return (through 1989).

name: Large motor carrier density
authors_terms: ["Large Density", "large carrier density", "density of large carriers"]
definition: Organizational survival rates are affected by two forces—legitimation and competition—each of which is in turn a function of population density. Large carriers are the Class 1 and 2 firms with revenues exceeding $1 million that are the focus of the study.

name: Small motor carrier density
authors_terms: ["Small Density", "small carrier density", "density of small carriers"]
definition: The number of small (Class 3, revenues below $1 million) motor carriers operating in the population; the motor carriers that entered after regulatory reform have tended to be small firms.

name: Age at deregulation
definition: An age clock that freezes in 1980, the year of deregulation: for the years 1981 through 1989, AgeAtD retains its value from 1980 and it is set to 0 for carriers that were not born before 1980.

name: Post-deregulation age
definition: Age clocks for firms existing in 1980 and for firms that are born after 1980, respectively; each begins with the first year of a carrier's existence after 1980 and captures the effects of age (or experience) in the deregulated environment.

name: Transactional alignment
definition: The extent to which a motor carrier's use of company drivers rather than owner-operators conforms to transaction cost predictions; TCE prescribes that organizations should internalize transactions characterized by high levels of asset specificity and contract through the market for transactions characterized by generic assets.

name: Leverage
definition: The extent to which firms rely on debt to finance their assets; the authors employ debt and equity to construct the leverage variable, in the form debt/(debt + equity) so that Leverage ranges from zero to one.

name: LTL carriage share
definition: Less-than-truckload carriage involves the movement of shipments of under 10,000 pounds, typically using a hub-and-spoke system and specialized breakbulk facilities; LTL carriage tends to require a comparatively greater investment in idiosyncratic or illiquid assets than does truckload carriage.

name: Profitability
definition: The authors rely on measures of current profitability—return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA)—as second-best proxies for expected profitability, the theoretical construct that economic theory treats as the primary driver of organizational mortality.

name: Organizational level
definition: The executive's position in the corporate hierarchy, into which the authors allocated each executive director after identifying his or her job title/role.

name: Executive compensation
definition: The pay received by an executive. The authors use three measures: total cash compensation, incentive compensation (long-term incentive awards), and total compensation, the sum of the two.

name: Tournament prize
authors_terms: ["tournament prize", "the prize or gap", "the prize for becoming CEO", "wage gap"]
definition: The prize for winning the tournament to become CEO, measured as the gap between CEO pay and the median pay received by the non-CEO executive team.

name: Number of contestants
authors_terms: ["number of competitors", "number of contestants", "number of executives", "number of directors in the executive team"]
definition: The number of participants competing for the CEO position, i.e. the size of the executive team.

name: Executive wage dispersion
authors_terms: ["wage dispersion", "pay dispersion", "pay variation", "executive wage dispersion", "coefficient of variation of executive team compensation"]
definition: The variation in wages within the executive team; the authors argue a relatively large prize, i.e. a gap or variation in wages, is required to motivate employees.

name: Corporate performance
definition: The firm's financial performance, measured in the performance determination equations as return on assets and total shareholder return.

name: Founding market stage
definition: Each market was typed as emergent, growth, or mature for each year in the study. Emergent markets were new and had less than $100 million in sales (adjusted to 1988 dollars); growth markets had at least $100 million in annual sales and an average annual growth rate of at least 20 percent; mature markets were also at least $100 million markets, but grew less than 20 percent annually.

name: Competitive concentration
definition: Competitive concentration was measured by the four-firm concentration ratio obtained from market-research data, the ratio of sales of the four largest competitors in the market to the total sales in the market. It reflects the competitive power of the established firms.

name: Technical innovation
authors_terms: ["technical innovation", "technical innovation of firm strategy", "micron line width", "technical innovation (3-item scale)"]
definition: The most relevant difference in strategy across technology-based ventures is the degree of technical innovation within the core technology of the firm; some firms compete by using highly innovative technologies that require extensive new knowledge creation and/or technology synthesis, while others compete by offering a less innovative technology.

name: Previous joint work experience
authors_terms: ["joint experience", "previous joint work experience", "past joint work experience"]
definition: Prior joint work experience is the extent to which founding executives had worked with another founding executive for at least six months prior to founding the company.

name: Founding team size
definition: The founding team size was measured as the number of individuals who were designated by the company respondents as founders and who worked full time for the firm in executive positions at its inception.

name: Heterogeneity of industry experience
authors_terms: ["heterogeneity of industry experience", "variation in the industry experience"]
definition: The variation across the founding team in the number of years of semiconductor-industry experience of its members.

name: Founding top-management team
authors_terms: ["founding top-management team", "top-management team", "strong top-management team", "weak top-management team"]
definition: The founding top-management team was defined as those individuals who were founders of the firm and who worked full time for the firm in executive-level positions at the time of founding.

name: Firm growth
definition: Firm growth was measured as the difference in sales in each year of life through 1988 relative to sales at founding; since sales at founding were 0 for all firms, the measure of growth in any year reduced simply to the sales in that year.

name: Fragmentation of external technology markets
authors_terms: ["fragmented external rights", "fragmentation index", "fragmented markets for technology", "widely distributed technologies", "diffuse entitlements"]
definition: Firms patent more aggressively than otherwise expected when rights to complementary patents (i.e., ones that would likely be infringed if the firm manufactures or sells its products without a license) are widely distributed among outside entities.

name: Patenting aggressiveness
authors_terms: ["patent more aggressively", "incentives to patent", "patent acquisition strategies", "propensity to patent", "patenting behavior"]
definition: First, if fragmented rights to patents render ex ante contracting less feasible, we should expect firms that draw on widely distributed technologies to patent more aggressively (controlling for other determinants of patenting) than firms that face more concentrated external markets for technology.

name: Capital intensity
authors_terms: ["capital-intensity", "investments in technology-specific assets", "sunk investments in manufacturing facilities", "assets that are costly to redeploy"]
definition: Expropriation risks are higher for firms with assets that are costly to redeploy to alternative uses or users (in line with traditional transactions cost reasoning).

name: Legal appropriability regime
authors_terms: ["strengthened legal appropriability regime", "propatent shift", "legal enforcement regime", "strength and enforceability of patent rights"]
definition: Important changes in the U.S. legal environment during the 1980s effectively strengthened the rights of patent owners in the United States, notably the 1982 creation of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which is widely credited with tilting the judicial treatment of patent rights more in favor of the patentee.

name: Leadtime
definition: Increasing leadtime, or the time between entries, should enhance first-mover advantages; it is the length of time the first-mover has a temporary monopoly versus a later entrant.

name: Order of market entry
definition: The first variable measures order of market entry. When the first entrant has an advantage over the second, it should have an even greater advantage over the third.

name: Years of competitive rivalry
definition: The competitive rivalry stage is measured by the number of years the pioneer and the later entrant have both been in the market.

name: Relative market share
definition: The dependent variable is a later entrant's market share relative to the pioneer's share (relative market share).

name: Market start period
authors_terms: ["markets started from 1960 to 1974", "markets started earlier", "markets pioneered from 1876 to 1956"]
definition: To test this dynamic change, the data are split into two groups: markets pioneered from 1876 to 1956 and those pioneered from 1960 to 1974.

name: Computer capital
authors_terms: ["COMPUTER CAPITAL", "computer capital stock", "market value of central processors"]
definition: The variable for COMPUTER CAPITAL was obtained by adding the "market value of central processors" to an estimate of the value of PCs and terminals, which was computed by multiplying the weighted average value for PCs and terminals by the number of PCs and terminals.

name: IS staff labor
definition: IS STAFF was computed by multiplying the IS Budget figure from the IDC survey by the "percentage of the IS budget devoted to labor expenses", and deflating this figure.

name: Firm output
definition: The variables for IS STAFF, NON-IS LABOR AND EXPENSE, and OUTPUT were computed by multiplying the relevant quantity from the IDG survey or Compustat by an appropriate government price deflator.

name: Non-computer capital
definition: Total capital for each firm was computed from book value of capital stock, adjusted for inflation by assuming that all investment was made at a calculated average age (total depreciation/current depreciation) of the capital stock. From this total capital figure, we subtract the deflated value of COMPUTER CAPITAL to get NON-COMPUTER CAPITAL.

name: Other labor and expenses
authors_terms: ["NON-IS LABOR AND EXPENSE", "OTHER LABOR AND EXPENSES"]
definition: NON-IS LABOR AND EXPENSE was computed by deflating total expense and subtracting deflated IS STAFF from this value. Thus, all the expenses of a firm are allocated to either IS STAFF or NON-IS LABOR AND EXPENSE.

name: Market influence
definition: The extent to which a bank is called by other banks for quotes, which represents an opportunity for the bank to influence market prices; it can also be viewed as akin to market share in this industry.

name: Extensiveness of out-ties
authors_terms: ["extensiveness of out-ties", "firm centrality", "degree centrality as applied to out-ties"]
definition: The extensiveness of a bank's out-ties, which is Freeman's degree centrality as applied to out-ties, is the number of banks called by the focal bank and is a result of proactive behavior by the bank and thus serves as a firm capability.

name: Maintenance of multiple weak ties
authors_terms: ["maintenance of multiple weak ties", "multiple weak ties"]
definition: A network use pattern in which a bank seeks information from a wide network but concentrates most of its information seeking among only a few players, thereby maintaining an extensive web of weak ties through infrequent contact with a large number of other banks.

name: Bridging of structural holes
authors_terms: ["bridging structural holes", "bridging of structural holes", "probability of bridging structural holes"]
definition: A structural hole is a missing tie between two actors who are not otherwise connected; the actor bridging the structural hole has connections to each of these otherwise unconnected actors and thereby serves as a conduit between them.

name: Global scope
definition: Global scope, as mentioned earlier, is the extent to which the focal bank is global in the reach of its information network.

name: Responsiveness
definition: Responsiveness in general refers to the quickness with which firms respond to environmental signals; in our formulation, responsiveness is concerned with the ability of the firm to make quick assessments of a rapidly changing information environment.

name: Product-process development integration
authors_terms: ["product-process development integration", "design-manufacturing integration", "functionally integrated product-process development regimen", "integration of functions"]
definition: The manifestation of focus (strategy) and discipline (tactics) is defined as product-process development integration in this study. It is that set of focused, disciplined, rigorous practices designed to concentrate efforts on evolving concepts to market introduction.

name: Benchmarking on design practices
definition: Benchmarking was measured by the answer to one "yes-no" question: "Do you benchmark (make visits to other firms and gauge their practices because of their known good reputation) in Design Approaches?" Benchmarking on the practices of development for new products is contrasted to performance outcome.

name: Concentration of specialists
authors_terms: ["concentration of specialists", "concentration of engineering specialists", "degreed design engineers", "degreed manufacturing engineers"]
definition: The resource selected was concentration of specialists (Hage 1980, Ettlie et al. 1984) which has been shown to be relatively important in innovation introduction and is relatively nonseparable from the firm. It was measured by documenting two proportions, the percentage of degreed design engineers and the percentage of degreed manufacturing engineers.

name: Organizational performance
definition: Sales per employee, obtained from the Dun & Bradstreet Corporate Directory which lists employees and sales for 1990, is used as a proxy for overall performance.

name: Product development time
definition: Product life-cycle and the development time for the last major product were both estimated by respondents. Development time averaged three years.

name: Internal market
definition: Internal markets consist of the set of exchanges between a buying profit center, a large assembly division, and its supplying profit centers. The corporation creates the internal market by decentralizing price determination and trading rights to each division, and trading profit centers jointly determine price through negotiations.

name: Renegotiation costs
definition: Incomplete contracts and imperfect markets create bargaining costs: renegotiation costs, including the costly delays to reach a new agreement, occur as the two parties bargain over the size of the price adjustment.

name: Product cost disclosure
authors_terms: ["product cost disclosure", "disclosure of private cost information", "supplier openness"]
definition: The degree of supplier openness about manufacturing costs and cost structure is used as a proxy for the level of disclosed detail. Supplier cost disclosure is one outcome of the implementation of cost reduction practices.

name: Repeat purchase incentives
authors_terms: ["repeat purchase incentives", "probability of repeat business", "repeat business"]
definition: Repeat purchase incentives encourage internal or external suppliers to disclose product cost information or to facilitate price renegotiations, since buyers can punish noncooperative suppliers by failing to renew business. The relevant horizon is the time period from the part's first use to its replacement with a design in which the part is no longer used.

name: Asymmetric product cost information
definition: Asymmetric information settings exist when one party has access to information that the other party lacks. In this study, asymmetric information settings exist when supplier prices do not have comparable market prices.

name: Asset uniqueness
definition: Suppliers have almost no bargaining power when assets are standard, because buyers can easily find alternative sources of supplies. However, when a supplier's assets are unique to the buyer's product, both the buyer and supplier incur costs from premature termination.

name: Investments in architectural design
definition: The resources allocated to architectural design activities, relative to those allocated to development and test activities, reflecting the emphasis given to resolving the potentially conflicting objectives of maximizing product performance and facilitating process flexibility.

name: Early market feedback
authors_terms: ["early market feedback", "earlier feedback on a product's system-level performance"]
definition: The extent to which feedback on product performance from customers is obtained early in a project, captured as the percentage of product functionality developed at the first prototype and first beta release.

name: Early technical feedback
definition: The extent to which feedback on how modules in the design interact is obtained early, captured as the percentage of product functionality developed at the first system integration.

name: Generational experience
definition: Experience that comes from having previously worked on multiple different project generations, differentiating it from the context-specific form of experience whose value is subject to obsolescence in uncertain and dynamic environments.

name: Product quality
definition: The overall quality of products relative to other competitive products which targeted similar customer needs at the time the product was launched, defined as a combination of product features, technical performance, and reliability.

name: Propensity to franchise internationally
definition: The organizational choice between two polar control modes for the creation and delivery of services: in a corporate equity arrangement the parent firm wholly owns and manages the service unit or relies on a joint venture, whereas in a franchise arrangement the owner of a service concept contracts with an unrelated party to use a specific business formatted service concept under the franchisor's trademark.

name: Monitoring costs
definition: Unit managers must be directly monitored by field staff to ensure that managers are performing in line with agreed upon standards, which is a costly administrative burden to the principal; in an international setting such monitoring costs are increased by geographical and cultural distance.

name: Geographical distance
definition: Geographical distance is due to the localized nature of most business formatted services which creates a network of many service outlets that are physically far removed from corporate headquarters; the problem of incomplete information regarding agent behavior is exacerbated by a decentralized service delivery system whose geographical scope extends beyond national boundaries.

name: Cultural distance
definition: Cultural distance stems from the added difficulty of managing a service business in a foreign cultural environment which is significantly different from the principal's domestic environment; the transferability of the service concept and its management system becomes a function of the cultural distance between the foreign and domestic culture.

name: International experience
authors_terms: ["international experience", "international experience effect", "experience accumulated by the international service firm"]
definition: As the service firm gains international experience, it develops a knowledge base about the management of international business thereby becoming more confident about engaging in long-term international franchising; it is proxied by the cumulative number of years of the service firm's overall foreign involvement.

name: Brand name asset specificity
authors_terms: ["brand name asset specificity", "reputation specific assets", "reputation specificity", "advertising intensity"]
definition: Brand name is perhaps the most important intangible asset to protect against potential hazard since service companies cannot depend upon patented proprietary technology or processes as a protection against close substitutes; what is important to the success of the service firm and what its agents must uphold are the intangible assets of reputation and brand name.

name: Host country environmental uncertainty
definition: International service firms must deal also with the uncertainties and risks embodied in the contextual environment of the host country; this research decomposes such environmental risk into political and currency dimensions.

name: Political risk
authors_terms: ["political risk", "political turmoil", "restrictions on investment", "transfer of funds"]
definition: Political risk arises when contextual uncertainty is high and is defined by unexpected changes in government policies from a "friendly" to a "hostile" attitude; it captures the impact of political change and policy restrictiveness in the host country's system of laws and regulations vis-a-vis foreign-owned or franchised business entities.

name: Currency risk
definition: Currency risk arises from fluctuating exchange rates between the principal's (reference) currency and the agent's (local) currency which may result in lost income for the international service firm.

name: Environmental change
definition: The interplay between the magnitude of change and the number of sectors involved characterizes the extent of change and complexity of environmental conditions to be confronted. Two composite measures of environmental change are developed, one for the task environment and another for the general environment.

name: Organizational size
definition: Size here refers to the logarithm of the number of people employed.

name: Technological inflexibility
definition: Those operations technologies with less flexibility often involve highly automated, specialized equipment that limit the range and variability of output, and thus they are highly vulnerable to downturns in demand and disruptions in supply of critical inputs.

name: Low-cost orientation
definition: Some organizations choose to compete by offering low prices based on low costs, whereas some other organizations compete by differentiating their products in ways that enable them to charge higher prices. Organizations that pursue a low-cost oriented strategy tend to be more vulnerable to environmental changes than organizations that pursue other strategies because cost-based advantages may be more readily replicated than advantages based on product or market differentiation.

name: Scanning scope
authors_terms: ["scanning scope", "scope of scanning", "scope of environmental scanning", "wider scope of scanning"]
definition: Scanning scope and scanning frequency refer to the number of different environmental sectors that a system monitors and the frequency with which they are monitored.

name: Scanning frequency
authors_terms: ["scanning frequency", "frequency of environmental scanning", "frequency of scanning"]
definition: Scanning scope and scanning frequency refer to the number of different environmental sectors that a system monitors and the frequency with which they are monitored.

name: TMT scanning responsibility
authors_terms: ["top management scanning responsibility", "TMT scanning responsibility", "top management's responsibility for scanning", "TMT scanning"]
definition: Top management scanning responsibility refers to the number of environmental sectors for which top management assumes the responsibility for scanning.

name: Scanning system effectiveness
authors_terms: ["scanning system effectiveness", "effective scanning systems", "ineffective scanning systems", "system effectiveness"]
definition: A scanning system can be considered effective if it generates awareness of environmental conditions, knowledge about the organization's strengths and weaknesses, and an awareness of existing or impending problems. However, only those scanning systems that are aligned with the requirements of organizational context would be expected to be effective.

name: Technological innovativeness
definition: In this paper, we define the extent to which a firm creates technologies which are technologically significant as the firm's level of technological innovativeness.

name: Joint venture agreements
definition: Joint ventures are defined as new operating entities resulting from the combination of complementary resources by distinct firms which share ownership and control for the venture (Harrigan 1985).

name: Licensing agreements
definition: Licensing agreements occur when one firm sells the rights to use that firm's technology to another firm.

name: Marketing agreements
definition: Marketing agreements are defined as partnerships where one firm takes responsibility for the marketing and/or distribution of another firm's products/technologies.

name: Research and development agreements
definition: Research and development agreements have been argued to be different from the other agreements since although there is a transfer of tacit technological knowledge from a technologically innovative firm to its partner, the technologically innovative firm is also in a position to access tacit technological knowledge about its partner's innovations.

name: Pattern of partnership agreements
definition: We use the term "pattern" to mean a firm's relative number of agreements of one type versus another.

name: Component familiarity
authors_terms: ["component familiarity", "recombination of familiar components", "familiarity with components"]
definition: Component familiarity proxies inventors' familiarity with components, based on the average degree to which the components have been recently and frequently used. Understanding and knowledge increase with use; the greater the use of a component, the greater the knowledge of and familiarity with it.

name: Combination familiarity
definition: Combination familiarity proxies inventors' familiarity with the combination, based on the degree to which the combination has been recently and frequently used. As with knowledge about individual components, knowledge about combination relationships increases with frequency of use and decreases since last use.

name: Cumulative combination usage
authors_terms: ["cumulative combination usage", "cumulative use of a combination"]
definition: The cumulative usage measures how many times since 1790 a particular combination of subclasses has been used.

name: Invention usefulness
authors_terms: ["invention's usefulness", "usefulness of inventive efforts", "technological importance and value"]
definition: An invention's usefulness or importance is measured as the number of prior art citations that it receives from subsequent patents.

name: Inventive uncertainty
definition: Incorporation of familiar components should decrease inventive uncertainty and, hence, the variability of outcomes. Variables that decrease the dispersion parameter will decrease the variability and hence the uncertainty of inventive outcomes.

name: Product development structure
authors_terms: ["concentrated new product development structure", "distributed new product development structure", "product development structure"]
definition: A concentrated structure locates all product designers in one facility to facilitate cross-product learning, whereas a distributed structure disperses the new product development effort among multiple manufacturing locations, allowing close interaction with local customers and production engineers.

name: Time to prototype
definition: The time for a new product to progress from conception (marked by the entry date of an engineering file) to the time when the first customer-ready prototype is released.

name: Time to volume production
authors_terms: ["Time to Volume Production (VTIME)", "time to volume production"]
definition: The time from the date on which the first customer-ready prototype is released to the date on which accumulated shipments exceed 2000 units.

name: Number of customers
definition: The number of individual customers who expressed intent to buy the product.

name: Number of concurrent prototype projects
authors_terms: ["Number of Prototype Projects (PPROD)", "number of concurrent prototypes", "number of concurrent new product developments"]
definition: The number of concurrent projects being prototyped simultaneously in any quarter.

name: Number of concurrent volume production projects
definition: The number of concurrent projects going to volume production during the period of time when a particular new product is being taken to volume production.

name: Engineering expenditures
definition: The engineering expenditures for new product development and process design (excluding engineering to maintain ongoing production), representing the investment made by a company for product development effort.

name: Joint venture failure
definition: The authors focus on the causes of joint venture failure as opposed to instability, which in general includes not only failures, but also acquisitions of the operation by one of its partners. Failure is taken to be dissolution or spin-off to third parties, both of which represent a strategic setback for the original partners vis-a-vis their initial hopes.

name: Competition between joint venture partners
authors_terms: ["direct competitors", "joint venture between direct competitors", "competition between partners"]
definition: We expect joint ventures to have a higher failure rate when their partners are direct competitors. The potential for appropriability in a joint venture setting clearly is higher when the partners are direct competitors.

name: Partner contribution interdependence
authors_terms: ["interdependence between the partners", "integrative joint ventures", "sequential joint ventures"]
definition: A key variable in joint venture outcomes is the pattern of interdependence between the partners, of which two basic forms can be identified. In sequential joint ventures contributions are not integrated but lie on a sequential path, whereas in integrative joint ventures the partners' contributions represent a pooling of their talents.

name: Interfirm collaboration experience
authors_terms: ["experience in interfirm collaboration", "previous joint ventures", "prior experience with interfirm collaboration"]
definition: A firm with experience in interfirm relationships is likely to be considered trustworthy, since once labelled an opportunist it becomes difficult for a firm to pursue and maintain interfirm transaction relationships in the future with other firms.

name: Concurrent ties between partners
definition: A firm may also be judged as less opportunistic when it and its partners have other, ongoing, agreements. A joint venture is less likely to fail when partners have simultaneous agreements, and multiple ties can also facilitate retaliatory action by providing several contact points with the offending party.

name: Number of joint venture partners
authors_terms: ["number of parties in a joint venture", "number of partners", "number of participants"]
definition: The numbers of partners to an agreement can affect coordination costs and managerial complexity: as the number of participants increases, the chances escalate that there will be ex post disagreements about the original aims and statutes of the contract, transaction costs to monitor contractual terms increase, and so does the chance that a dysfunctional pairing will undermine the venture.

name: Joint venture age
definition: The management of joint ventures is an ongoing task, and there is reason to expect a specific, nonmonotonic pattern of failure rates across the venture's age. The failure rate is expected to rise with time initially and then to decline as the organization, momentum and legitimacy of the venture become established and initial reservations recede.

name: Institutional balance
authors_terms: ["balance", "state of balance", "balanced institutional environments", "balanced social control network", "imbalance"]
definition: Balance is defined as the establishment of ideological consensus and harmonious working relations among legislatures, publics, regulatory agencies, and professional associations. It emerges in particular domains of activity as the social control network develops ideological consensus and coordinated working relations, whereas imbalance emerges when consensus and cooperation are not achieved or are lost.

name: Adoption of administrative structures
definition: A district was judged to have adopted a structure in a given domain when it listed an administrative officer with a job title relevant to the type of work done in a domain. Diffusion is the period in which local school districts adopt newly institutionalized service units.

name: Retention of administrative structures
definition: Retention is the persistence of a structure once adopted; it is measured as the proportion of instances in which a personnel-type position observed in any district was observed in that same district five and ten years later. The authors state that retention of structures is itself problematic and that structures, once spawned, do not inevitably persist.

name: Organizational size and complexity
definition: A count of the total number of occupational titles listed by a district in a given time period, used as a proxy for organizational size, although the authors note it is more accurately a reflection of district complexity.

name: Input uncertainty
authors_terms: ["input uncertainty", "uncertainty characterizing a particular element of an organization's task environment"]
definition: Input uncertainty refers to uncertainty about the overall composition of patient inputs, such as the number of patients in various conditions. It is expressed as a function of the number of choices or alternatives in a given situation and of the probability of various alternatives occurring.

name: Programmed means of coordination
authors_terms: ["programmed means of coordination", "programmed coordination", "rules", "scheduled meetings", "authority arrangements"]
definition: In programmed coordination, the activities of organization members are dictated by plans, programs, and relationships specified in advance by the organization. Programmed means of achieving coordination used in this study are rules, scheduled meetings, and authority arrangements.

name: Nonprogrammed means of coordination
authors_terms: ["nonprogrammed means of coordination", "nonprogrammed coordination", "autonomy of the staff", "policies of the units", "mutual adjustment"]
definition: In nonprogrammed coordination, activities are not specified in advance by the organization, but rather are worked out on the spot by organization members; the organization only specifies desired ends. The nonprogrammed means of coordination studied here include autonomy of organization members, general policies of the units, and mutual adjustment among the members involved.

name: Clinical efficiency
authors_terms: ["clinical efficiency", "promptness of care", "quality of nursing care", "quality of medical care", "organizational effectiveness criteria"]
definition: Clinical efficiency involves the quality of care and of staff performance from a patient's entry into an emergency unit to the patient's exit from the unit. It represents how a patient is handled along an emergency unit's input-transformation-output work cycle.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["environmental uncertainty", "uncertainty", "volatility of price", "market volatility", "volatility of the market"]
definition: Uncertainty occurs because the future value of the things to be exchanged (goods and services) may not be determined precisely or may not be achieved after an agreement is made. In this study, environmental uncertainty is defined in terms of the volatility of prices in the market, which directly reflects the predictability of the future value of a commodity.

name: Secondary working rule changes
authors_terms: ["secondary working rules", "secondary rules and regulations", "secondary rulemaking", "changes in secondary rules", "margin changes"]
definition: Any interorganizational organization developed to allow stable and predictable exchanges will develop two rulemaking processes: secondary rulemaking, which defines the conditions of transaction, and primary rulemaking, which maintains its authority to enforce them. Secondary rules and regulations relate to specific commodities; they specify trading conditions and conditions for storage and delivery, and margin changes in each commodity constitute a separate category within secondary working rules.

name: Primary working rule changes
authors_terms: ["primary working rules", "primary rules and regulations", "primary rulemaking", "changes in primary rules"]
definition: Primary rulemaking maintains the authority of the interorganizational organization to enforce its rules. Primary rules and regulations for the CBT deal with issues of governance, the conditions under which a member enters into transactions, and where, when, and what kind of market transactions can take place.

name: Volume of transactions
definition: Volume is the total contracts traded in each month for each commodity. Total monthly volume and open interest in each commodity are measures of present and possible futures transactions and indicate the degree of economic activity and the amount of interest in commodity contracts.

name: Organizational sanctions
definition: Sanctions and punishments of the members by the CBT were measured in two categories: the number of reprimands and the number of suspension orders issued by the CBT in a given month.

name: Environmental diversity
definition: The range of an organization's environmental activities, here estimated by the economic and demographic characteristics of the county in which the bank resided: population size, income level, and distribution of the labor force between industry and agriculture.

name: Environmental volatility
definition: The rate of change among an organization's environmental activities; here measured by comparing the relative change in the level of unemployment in the county of each bank to national unemployment levels.

name: Environmental uncertainty
authors_terms: ["uncertainty of the environment", "environmental uncertainty", "uncertainty arising from environmental conditions"]
definition: Uncertainty relating to environmental conditions, such as diversity and volatility, which act upon an organization to create uncertain outcomes.

name: Repayment probability
authors_terms: ["probability of repayment", "repayment probabilities assigned loan applications", "probability of success"]
definition: The probability that a given loan applicant will repay the bank's loan, which loan officers predict and which is the outcome relevant to the loan decision.

name: Decision entropy
definition: A derived measure of the theoretical uncertainty of the loan officer's decision, estimated from the individual probability estimates for each case.

name: Perceived uncertainty
authors_terms: ["perceived uncertainty", "uncertainty that decision makers report", "the uncertainty experienced for particular decisions"]
definition: The uncertainty of each loan decision as reported by decision makers, estimated by asking respondents to judge how certain or uncertain they were about their probability estimates that the loan would be repaid.

name: Routine information collection
authors_terms: ["routine information collected", "information gathered as normal procedure", "information that the banks normally collected"]
definition: Information gathered as part of the normal procedures for handling a group of decisions, which is expected to reflect environmental conditions of some duration and to be embodied in the permanent information system of the organization.

name: Decision-specific information gathering
authors_terms: ["new information required for decision", "additional information required", "additional items of information which would be desired"]
definition: The additional information a loan officer would require before making a decision on a particular loan application, beyond the information requested on the application form.

name: Formalization of decision procedures
authors_terms: ["routine and formal procedures", "formalization level of loan decisions", "general structural characteristics of decision making"]
definition: The general structural characteristics of a bank's loan decision making, including the authority structure, the routine information collected, the method of evaluating credit applications, the amount of loan authorization allowed, and the specifications contained in the written loan policy.

name: Flexibility of decision procedures
authors_terms: ["flexibility", "more flexible and changeable procedures", "judgmental forms of decision making"]
definition: The ability to shift from permanent procedures to temporary and flexible procedures; high volatility is expected to result in less formal, more variant use of information, which allows more subjective interpretations and more judgmental decision making.

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: The degree of task uncertainty is the contingent variable on which turn alternative organizational and subunit structures; our indicators of technology measured variation in the workflow of the operating room and, hence, uncertainty.

name: Destandardization
authors_terms: ["destandardization", "standardization of rules and procedures", "rules and programs"]
definition: There should be less standardization of rules and procedures as uncertainty increases; "destandardization" can be substituted for "less standardization" to simplify the wording.

name: Decentralization of decision making
authors_terms: ["decentralization", "decentralization of decision making", "centralization of decision making"]
definition: As uncertainty increases, increased participation in decision making must be exercised by the workforce; this can be accomplished by increasing the amount of discretion exercised by employees at lower levels of the organization.

name: Professionalization
definition: To increase the probability that employees will select the appropriate behavior, organizations substitute craft or professional training of the workforce for lower levels of training and skill, referred to as professionalization, or selection of responsible workers who have the appropriate skills and attitudes.

name: Organizational effectiveness
definition: We defined effectiveness as an organization's ability to create acceptable outcomes and actions; consistent with the definition, we measured the outcomes of surgical care.

name: Organizational resources
definition: Greater resources appear to allow for implementation of the relations between uncertainty and structure believed to be necessary for effectiveness or, in Galbraith's terms, to allow for the relative costs of various structural designs.

name: Organizational structure
definition: The level of organizational structure, encompassing the degree of destandardization, decentralization, and professionalization; each structural characteristic has an optimal value conditional on technological uncertainty.

name: Interorganizational cooperation
definition: Networking among organizations, here defined as the formation of cooperative relationships, can be based as much on particularistic criteria, such as the personal networks of organizational leaders and status targeting, as on strict cost-benefit calculations in terms of resource procurement.

name: Overlapping organizational memberships
authors_terms: ["overlapping memberships", "joint organizational memberships", "common organizational memberships", "personal connections in the neighborhood"]
definition: Personal connections with other organizational leaders through overlapping local organizational memberships.

name: Leader status group similarity
authors_terms: ["similar status group affiliations", "common status group affiliations", "similar racial, religious, or educational backgrounds", "lesser social distance"]
definition: Leaders would seek out those who they believe are at a lesser social distance, i.e., who have a common ethnic, religious, or educational background, even though they may not know these individuals personally.

name: Environmental turbulence
authors_terms: ["environmental turbulence", "turbulent neighborhood environments", "less turbulent neighborhood environments", "turbulence", "placidity"]
definition: The turbulence or placidity of an organization's neighborhood environment, described along three dimensions focused on the clientele of the organizations: stability and instability, homogeneity and heterogeneity, and richness and leanness.

name: Leader local residence
authors_terms: ["leader's residence", "residence of leaders", "leaders who live in a neighborhood", "local leaders", "outside organizational leaders"]
definition: Residence was measured by whether the leader of the organization resided in the neighborhood or outside the neighborhood.

name: Power within the top management team
definition: The extent to which an executive has power over the full array of strategic decisions that an organization faces.

name: Involvement in output functions
definition: An executive's functional area partly determines how well situated he or she is to cope with critical contingencies; output functions are marketing and product/service development.

name: Involvement in throughput functions
definition: Throughput functions are accounting/finance, process improvement and operations, the functional areas situated to cope with efficiency and cost-control contingencies.

name: Output scanning
definition: Scanning is the process of learning about events and trends in the organization's environment and is a form of coping by information; output scanning covers external product/market trends or events.

name: Throughput scanning
definition: Scanning is the process of learning about events and trends in the organization's environment and is a form of coping by information; throughput scanning covers external developments bearing on the processing or delivery of products/services.

name: Business strategy type
definition: Strategy is used in the descriptive sense to mean a pattern in a stream of important decisions; Prospectors compete primarily by new product/market development while Defenders maintain a position by low prices, service, quality or delivery.

name: Organizational birth frequency
authors_terms: ["organizational birth frequency", "birth frequency", "birth rates", "birth activity", "creation of new organizations"]
definition: The frequency with which new organizations are created in an industry within an urban area. Births were determined by comparing entries from one year with those of the following year, and only genuinely new ventures were counted.

name: Urban dominance
definition: Urban dominance has two interrelated meanings: it refers both to cities as centers of important activities and to cities as hubs in an interurban network.

name: Urban size
definition: Urban size is treated as a very important predictor of organizational birth activity, measured by the number of people in the metropolitan area.

name: Urban differentiation
definition: A city is differentiated to the extent that its elements (i.e., individuals or organizations) belong to different and overlapping or nonoverlapping segments.

name: Domestic immigration
definition: The percentage of the 1970 SMSA population who resided in 1965 outside the 1970 SMSA.

name: Foreign immigration
definition: The percentage of SMSA individuals who had immigrated from abroad into the SMSA.

name: Economic volatility
definition: Urban change that reflects unpatterned variability in social or economic behavior; frequent and major departures from the trendline of industrial employment reflect instability.

name: Industry size
definition: The size of the relevant organizational population, which can be viewed as the pool of potential entrepreneurs from which the founders of new organizations are primarily recruited.

name: Industry size distribution
authors_terms: ["size distribution", "concentration", "concentration of organizational populations", "market concentration ratio"]
definition: Size distribution, as measured by the market concentration ratio, signals the difficulty that new firms will have in entering a market; concentration is high when a disproportionately small number of organizations dominate the market.

name: Urban resource richness
authors_terms: ["richness", "availability of resources", "price and accessibility of these resources", "generic resources", "sustenance"]
definition: The availability and cost of economic and social resources for which every firm or population of firms competes, including investment capital, energy, scientists, engineers and other types of labor, as well as the presence of colleges and universities.

name: Unit redundancy in R&D
definition: We followed the approach of Birkinshaw and Lingblad (2005) to conceptualize redundancy at the unit level, which captures the extent to which a specific unit's R&D overlaps with that of other units. This acknowledges that units differ in their exposure to redundancy-induced competition.

name: Firm-specific value of innovations
