definition: The value of a unit's innovations to the firm. Greater redundancy is argued to increase the firm-specific value of the unit's R&D projects because it raises the amount and diversity of relevant knowledge available and gives the unit greater incentives to align its R&D with the firm's needs.

name: Project termination
definition: The failure to renew a patent reflects a deliberate portfolio management strategy employed by firms to free resources by identifying and terminating patents whose future value to the firm is less than its maintenance cost.

name: Organizational proximity
definition: The unit's relative organizational proximity is defined as the closeness of a unit to the firm's headquarters. A unit's proximity can have many dimensions, including hierarchical and geographical nearness.

name: R&D centralization
authors_terms: ["centralization", "R&D centralization", "centralization of a firm's R&D management"]
definition: Corporate managers' control over resource allocation and decision-making in R&D activities is greater in firms with centralized R&D management.,

name: Inventive breadth
definition: Inventors can accumulate knowledge as either specialists or generalists based on the breadth of their inventive activity; generalists accumulate and possess diversified knowledge in a broader array of domains.

name: Inventor brokerage
definition: Brokers connect those who are otherwise unconnected, or in network parlance, bridge “structural holes”; they have a broader reach within the network and are able to locate and access knowledge that is widely distributed in different parts of the network.

name: Inventor redeployment
definition: Redeployed is an indicator variable that captures redeployment to an ethylene unit from any non-ethylene business unit.

name: Source-unit resource slack
definition: Slack refers to excess capacity of resources that can be utilized at another activity. If the source unit has excess resources, the opportunity cost of losing such resources will be lower, as they can be more easily substituted by remaining resources.

name: Source-unit knowledge interdependence
authors_terms: ["knowledge interdependence", "interdependence", "knowledge interdependence in the source unit"]
definition: Interdependence refers to interactions between components of a system such that the value of a particular component depends on the value of others.

name: Centralized patent reassignment
definition: Whether an acquired patent is reassigned from the target to the acquirer (i.e., centralized) or remains with the newly acquired unit (i.e., decentralized), reflecting the locus of resource control within the corporate structure.

name: Technological versatility
definition: The variety of services a resource offers; for a patent, the variety of technological knowledge it embodies, observed through the variety of technological areas the patent draws on in its inventive step.

name: Product-market versatility
definition: The extent to which a patent bears potential for applications in various therapeutic areas, the medical specialties recognized by the FDA for device classification.

name: Technological diversity
definition: The acquirer's degree of diversity in technological domains, reflecting its capacity to integrate knowledge and envision new technological opportunities through recombination.

name: Product-market diversity
definition: The acquirer's degree of diversity in product-market domains, reflecting its commercialization competencies to envisage valuable product-market opportunities.

name: Worker redeployment
definition: We define worker redeployment as the hiring of a worker who held a position at another mill belonging to the same business group within the previous year.

name: Labor market thickness
authors_terms: ["labor market thickness", "thickness in frontier", "thickness in initial market", "labor market thickness in the frontier"]
definition: Labor market thickness, and thus the probability of hiring a high-skill worker, differs across markets; while some markets are "thick" and abound with high-skill labor, others are "thin" and have few workers with suitable skills. Labor market thickness is higher when more of a municipality's workers are employed in industries that are more highly related to sugar processing.

name: Output sensitivity to worker skill
authors_terms: ["sensitivity of output to worker skill", "occupations in which output is more sensitive to worker skill", "marginal productivity with respect to skill", "resource heterogeneity"]
definition: The magnitude of resource heterogeneity—the degree to which variation in resource quality impacts firm output. For human capital resources, heterogeneity can manifest as variations in the degree to which worker skill impacts firm performance outcomes: in some jobs, marginal productivity with respect to skill is low, while in others, small differences in skill have large effects on outcomes.

name: Land quality
authors_terms: ["land quality", "quality of the complementary resource", "quality of a second input (land)"]
definition: Land is the complementary input whose quality may vary across markets; the authors examine how the importance of worker skill varies with the quality of a second input (land), and predict opposite-signed effects of the quality of the complementary resource in the initial market and in the new market.

name: Human capital quality
authors_terms: ["higher quality resources", "higher levels of human capital", "skill", "worker skill"]
definition: Redeployed workers are compared with workers hired in external markets on their experience, educational attainment, and wages (as a proxy for skill) to see whether they are more skilled.

name: Mill size
definition: The scale of a mill's operations, measured by the log number of workers; the analysis examines whether business group mills are larger than standalone mills and whether redeployment in the opening year is related to later size.

name: Performance outcome favorability
authors_terms: ["favorable or unfavorable outcomes", "success or failure of the performance", "type of outcome", "nature of the outcome"]
definition: Any explicit statement of improvement over past years or an absolute high level of performance in sales, profits, or costs was coded as a favorable outcome, with statements of the opposite sort coded as unfavorable outcomes.

name: Locus of causality
authors_terms: ["locus of causality", "internal versus external attributions", "self-serving attributions"]
definition: Locus of causality can be internal or external. A cause is internal if it resides in the individual or organization whose behavior is being examined, and external if it resides elsewhere in the environment.

name: Causal stability
authors_terms: ["causal stability", "stability of the cause", "stable or unstable causes"]
definition: A cause is stable if it persists over time; it is unstable if it does not.

name: Causal controllability
authors_terms: ["controllability of the cause", "controllable or uncontrollable causes"]
definition: A cause is controllable if the individual or organization whose behavior is being examined has it within its power to change that cause; it is uncontrollable if that individual or organization cannot do anything about it.

name: Economic context
definition: Since it was critical to several of the hypotheses to examine performance in both a good year and a bad year, a year of each type was chosen by examining indices of economic activity such as the Gross National Product (GNP) and stock market indices; 1972 was chosen as a good year and 1974 as a bad year.

name: Performance relative to expectations
authors_terms: ["performance relative to expectations", "expected or unexpected outcomes", "worse than expected", "better than expected"]
definition: The percentage change from 1971 to 1972 and from 1973 to 1974 was calculated for each company. Then the companies were ranked on this index, within industry, for 1972 and 1974. Within each year for each industry, the companies were split into thirds; the lowest third was considered to have worse than expected performance in that year, the middle third to have expected levels of performance, and the top third to have better than expected performance.

name: Amount of causal reasoning
authors_terms: ["amount of causal reasoning", "number of lines of attributions", "relative number of lines of attributions", "frequency and amount of causal reasoning"]
definition: To measure the amount of causal reasoning, coders recorded the number of attributions, the total number of lines devoted to attributions, and the total number of lines in each letter.

name: Project network embeddedness
authors_terms: ["network embeddedness of a project", "project embeddedness", "project network embeddedness"]
definition: The architecture of a project's network ties, made up of three subconstructs: structural, junctional, and positional embeddedness. Higher values on the subconstructs imply greater embeddedness and social capital.

name: Project manager network embeddedness
authors_terms: ["network embeddedness of a project manager", "project manager embeddedness", "project manager network embeddedness"]
definition: The architecture of the network ties of the project manager, made up of three subconstructs: structural, junctional, and positional embeddedness. Higher values on the subconstructs imply greater embeddedness and social capital.

name: Technical project success
definition: The technical achievements of an open source software project, which together with market indicators form the criteria for project success. The authors treat the number of CVS commits as an indicator of successful technical refinement.

name: Commercial project success
definition: Indicators of market or commercial success of an open source project, which together with technical achievements form the criteria for project success. The authors assess it with the number of downloads over the life span of a project, a market-based measure of popularity.

name: Project age
authors_terms: ["project age", "number of months since the inception of the project", "AGE"]
definition: The number of months since the inception of the project, which signals the stage of the project life cycle. The authors use it to control for project age because CVS commits and downloads are likely to increase with the age of a project.

name: Number of page views
definition: The number of page views of the project, which the authors say directly signals the general interest level in the project and its market potential.

name: AI capability
definition: The authors define AI as advanced computing power for making predictive actions using machine learning techniques. To measure the extent to which a startup can utilize AI resources in research and development, they measure a startup's AI capability by combining AI-related job posts, original social media posts, and news reports about a firm into a single measure and taking the first principal component.

name: Discovery-oriented AI
definition: Discovery-oriented AI focuses on uncovering new areas of innovation by analyzing large data sets to reveal hidden patterns, trends, and generate hypotheses. This type of AI is instrumental in identifying product directions, validating market demand, and increasing certainty about the correctness of the objective function.

name: Optimization-oriented AI
definition: Optimization-oriented AI is designed to refine, automate, and optimize existing processes, products, and strategies where the objective function is already established. This type of AI leverages advanced techniques to enhance efficiency and performance.

name: Lean startup method
definition: The lean startup method is one of the most well-known methodologies for developing new products, used widely in both early-stage and mature firms. Instead of relying on business plans or entrepreneurial insights, it emphasizes validating ideas in the marketplace and iteratively improving products based on feedback.

name: Prototyping
definition: Prototyping focuses on developing minimum viable products (MVPs) to gather consumer insights and address uncertainties before a product launch. It typically involves qualitative methods, such as interviews or surveys, to collect contextual market insights.

name: Controlled experimentation
definition: Controlled experimentation involves systematically testing and refining specific features of established products to optimize performance. It leverages digital traces generated by existing products to process large data sets using statistical methods.

name: Product innovation
authors_terms: ["product innovations", "number of product innovations", "new products", "product development outcomes"]
definition: New product development involves activities that begin with identifying a market opportunity and culminate in creating a product or service that meets market needs. For software companies the authors measure the number of new products using the number of software copyrights a company applies for each year, and for physical product companies they use the number of product trademarks.

name: First-release products
definition: First releases are defined as new products for the company. All V1.0 software is treated as the first release of the firm, and a trademark is treated as a first release if it contains at least one new subclass in comparison with the company's existing trademarks, as it suggests the company is expanding to a new market niche.

name: Iterative-release products
definition: Iterative releases are defined as new versions of existing products. Software version numbers after V1.0 are treated as iterative release versions of an existing product, and trademarks that contain no new subclass relative to the company's existing trademarks are treated as iterative releases.

name: Product development time
authors_terms: ["Average Completion Time", "product development speed", "completion time", "development time"]
definition: By taking the average number of days between two first-release products and two versions of the same product, the authors calculate average completion time for first-release products and average completion time for iterative-release products for each company in each year as a proxy for product development speed.

name: Environmental performance
authors_terms: ["environmental performance", "strong environmental performance", "weak environmental performance", "environmental performance awards", "environmental crises"]
definition: Environmental performance measures how successful a firm is in reducing and minimizing its impact on the environment, often relative to some industry average or peer group.

name: Stock market reaction
authors_terms: ["financial performance", "market valuation", "change in market valuation", "cumulative abnormal return", "market reaction", "abnormal return"]
definition: The stock (equity) return or market valuation is used as the measure of firm financial performance: the market's assessment of firm value and its expected performance are reflected in the equity value of the firm, relative to other market assets of comparable risk (Capital Asset Pricing Model).

name: Industry environmental cleanliness
authors_terms: ["environmental cleanliness", "pollution intensity", "historically clean industries", "dirty industries", "historically dirty industries"]
definition: Industries differ in the level of interaction between the firm and the natural environment (pollution intensity) and are thereby viewed as environmentally clean or dirty; the proportion of capital expenditures on pollution abatement equipment is used to approximate the environmental cleanliness of different industries in the manufacturing sector (SIC 20 to 39).

name: Time
definition: Time is entered as a centered date variable to reduce collinearity and is used to assess whether the market's reaction to indicators of strong environmental performance has changed over the sample period.

name: Firm speed
definition: The speed in which firms execute their operations. In this setting it is the focal driller's intrinsic speed, isolating firm-specific deviations in drilling rates from systematic project-level factors.

name: Environmental accidents
definition: High-impact events with severe consequences for the responsible party and the planet; highly visible and consequential organizational failures that are difficult to disguise or downplay and that distinguish them from other measures of environmental performance such as emissions or waste.

name: Automation technology
definition: Involving standardized, tireless machines to take over routine, error-prone manual work performed by workers.

name: Labor market thickness
definition: Labor market thickness reflects the depth of the available worker pool relative to demand.

name: RegRoom access
authors_terms: ["RegRoom", "access to the RegRoom", "treatment", "invited to participate in the RegRoom"]
definition: The RegRoom is an online institutional intermediary staffed by experts who explain to participating MSMEs the exact public-interest purposes of a draft regulation and help them craft clear, constructive, public-interest-oriented comments before submission to the state's formal online consultation system.

name: Perceived consultation process legitimacy
authors_terms: ["quality of the consultation process", "firms' views of the N&C process quality", "legitimacy of the government's public consultation process"]
definition: Firms' evaluations of the quality of government agencies' consultative process in the notice and comment system.

name: State regulatory legitimacy
authors_terms: ["the state's regulatory legitimacy", "government regulatory legitimacy", "perceptions of state legitimacy"]
definition: Firms' perceptions that the government and its regulatory apparatus are legitimate, i.e., that its actions are desirable, proper, or appropriate within a system of norms, values, beliefs, and definitions.

name: Understanding of the draft regulation
authors_terms: ["firms' understanding of the focal draft", "understanding of the regulation"]
definition: The extent to which a respondent reports understanding the content of the draft regulation under consultation.

name: Expected government comprehension of comments
authors_terms: ["government understanding of submitted comments", "expectations that government officials understand comment"]
definition: Firms' beliefs that the responsible government department fully understands the content of the comments the firm submitted.

name: Expected government use of comments
authors_terms: ["government will use submitted comments", "expectations that government officials use the comment in revision"]
definition: Firms' beliefs that the responsible government department will use their submitted comments to make changes to the draft regulation.

name: Regulatory comment submission
authors_terms: ["submitting a comment to the online platform", "likelihood of comment submissions"]
definition: Whether the firm submitted a comment on the focal draft to the online notice and comment platform.

name: Quality of regulatory comments
definition: External legal experts' evaluations of submitted comments on relevance to the regulation under consideration, comprehensibility, and feasibility of government action based on the comment.

name: Intermediary focus on legitimacy restoration
authors_terms: ["the primary goal of institutional intermediaries", "improve legitimacy perceptions", "legitimacy certification", "legitimacy enhancement"]
definition: The primary goal pursued by institutional intermediaries seeking to overcome the legitimacy–co-creation paradox when governed actors' perceptions of authorities' legitimacy are below a minimum level, namely to improve those legitimacy perceptions.

name: Intermediary focus on capability building
authors_terms: ["building actors' previously neglected co-creation capabilities", "capability enhancement", "capacity building"]
definition: The primary goal to which institutional intermediaries seeking to overcome the legitimacy–co-creation paradox can shift once governed actors' perceptions of authorities' legitimacy exceed a minimum threshold, namely building those actors' previously neglected co-creation capabilities.

name: Firm divisionalization
definition: Firms organized around separable business units with identifiable financial accountability, as opposed to non-divisionalized firms that do not generate such separable business-unit performance records. Divisionalized firms are composed of business units, such as divisions or subsidiaries, each operating as a profit center with its own revenues, costs, and bottom line.

name: Manager gender
definition: Whether the manager is a woman manager; because the theory concerns how evaluators respond to managers they perceive as women or men, inferred perceived gender is the relevant empirical construct.

name: P&L accountability experience
authors_terms: ["prior P&L-accountable experience", "head of subsidiary experience", "P&L-accountable experience", "subsidiary-head experience"]
definition: Experience heading a role that carries responsibility for the financial outcomes of an identifiable operating unit, such as division heads, subsidiary heads, and other managers with direct P&L accountability, whose performance can be observed and evaluated more directly than that of managers in functionally interdependent roles.

name: Relative unit performance
authors_terms: ["relative unit performance", "unit-level financial performance relative to within-firm peers", "relative performance"]
definition: How well a unit performs compared to peer units within the same divisionalized firm, capturing the yardstick-comparison logic in which the performance of the manager's associated unit is evaluated relative to comparable units within the same organization.

name: Internal CEO promotion
definition: Whether a manager ascends to the CEO position of a parent company in a given year, provided that in the preceding year the individual did not hold the CEO position at the parent company.

name: Collaboration with advocacy groups
authors_terms: ["collaboration with advocacy groups", "innovation collaborations with advocacy groups", "advocacy group collaborations"]
definition: Formal collaborative innovation relationships between firms and advocacy groups, that is, interest groups or non-profit organizations that operate separately from government, depend on voluntary involvement, and pursue objectives serving the public or community.

name: Adoption of innovations
authors_terms: ["adoption of innovations", "innovation sales", "adoption of firm innovations"]
definition: The adoption of innovations is the "decision to make full use of an innovation as the best course of action available" (Rogers, 1962: 71), an inherently social process shaped by interactions, networks, and signals among potential adopters.

name: Product-centric negative media coverage
definition: Media reports criticizing a firm for corporate social irresponsibility whose descriptions explicitly mention products, services, or product-related terms as the focal object of criticism.

name: Industry-level variation in corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["industry-level variation in corporate social performance", "variation in corporate social performance"]
definition: The dispersion of corporate social performance across firms within an industry, indicating that norms regarding socially appropriate corporate behavior are ambiguous or contested.

name: Category erraticism
definition: Category erraticism describes the degree of incoherence in the sequence of horizontal categories that firms enter over time, operationalized as the average perceived socio-cognitive distance between consecutive categories in a firm's category path.

name: Upward status mobility
definition: Status mobility is simply the magnitude of change in a VC's status over a given time interval.

name: Audience concern about category commitment
definition: Commitment refers to the dedication to a particular course of action over time. Concerns about commitment center on whether a firm will reliably deploy its efforts and attention to meet the expectations of exchange partners.

name: Audience concern about category capability
definition: Capability refers to the ability to perform the activities required by that course of action. Concerns about capability center on whether the firm can do so effectively given its accumulated experience and resources.

name: Status
definition: Status, defined by the vertical position a firm occupies in its industry, functions as a signal of quality.

name: Experience
definition: VC Experience in year t is the logged number of companies in which the VC invested until year t.

name: Modularity
definition: Modularity thus refers to the extent to which a product's architecture consists of loosely coupled modules with distinct functionalities.

name: Component compatibility
definition: The ease with which an extracted module or component can be ported into a different product depends on its compatibility with the receiving product; at the product level this is how widely a product's constituent parts are used across different product contexts.

name: Esthetic product variants
definition: Esthetic variations in either color, size, material, or appearance, for example, "white," "queen," "patterned," "ash," or "stainless steel," but they are the same product, offering no new functions or functionalities.

name: Visual simplicity
definition: Visual simplicity, that is, the absence of ornamental, decorative, or functionally signaling features, determines whether these material properties become perceptually accessible to users.

name: New functions
definition: Function is the specific purpose the product serves in a given context; one kind of exaptation leverages a product's existing functionalities to deliver new functions.

name: New functionalities
definition: Functionality is the set of physical interactions an artifact affords; another kind of exaptation identifies new functionalities.

name: Speed performance
authors_terms: ["speed performance", "firm speed", "faster drilling", "speed performance of the firm"]
definition: The speed performance realized in a given project; in this setting, it is the average feet drilled per day for a well site, so that a higher value denotes faster speed.

name: Partnering
authors_terms: ["partnering", "alliances", "partnership project", "partnering versus going it alone", "alliance versus the autonomous alternative"]
definition: Whether the focal driller enters into a partnership with another driller for the given well project rather than going it alone; a partner firm may be able to provide needed capabilities and resources to the focal firm via the partnership.

name: Intrinsic speed capabilities
authors_terms: ["intrinsic speed capabilities", "intrinsic firm speed capabilities", "slowness", "firm slowness", "intrinsically slow firm", "intrinsically fast firm"]
definition: The ability of firms to execute investment projects or operations faster than competitors at the same cost; a firm skillset that captures firms' abilities to execute investment projects faster than competitors at the same cost.

name: Collaborative experience
authors_terms: ["collaborative experience", "partnering experience", "collaborative capabilities", "absorptive capacity through collaborative experience", "alliance experience"]
definition: The accumulated experience of managing alliances, which has been shown to develop collaborative capabilities in firms that enable them to more effectively process and digest information during the collaboration process.

name: Interlock content type
authors_terms: ["interlock Content Type", "directional interlocks", "nondirectional interlocks", "directional interlock content"]
definition: The types of interlocks composing a tie. Directional interlocks are created by persons principally affiliated with one of the firms linked; nondirectional interlocks are created by persons not principally affiliated with either of the firms linked.

name: Interlock intensity
definition: The number of interlocks of which a tie consists, distinguishing ties composed of only one interlock (single-interlock ties) from ties composed of more than one interlock (multiple-interlock ties).

name: Interlock break type
definition: Whether the interlock whose elimination disrupted a tie was directional or nondirectional, evaluated for ties that included at least one directional and one nondirectional interlock.

name: Connective continuity
authors_terms: ["connective continuity", "reconstitution", "maintenance", "rates of reconstitution", "rates of maintenance or reconstitution"]
definition: Whether a tie that has been accidentally disrupted or broken is continued: connective continuity is evaluated by whether tied firms create a new interlock or maintain an already existing interlock between the same firms, and it is a necessary but not sufficient condition for labeling a tie a vehicle of formal coordination.

name: Interlock direction
authors_terms: ["directional continuity", "direction of a tie's interlock", "sending partner", "receiving partner"]
definition: Among firms linked by directional interlocks, the corporation that elects a principally affiliated director of another firm to its board is the receiving partner to the link, and the other firm is the sending partner.

name: Directional continuity
definition: Whether a broken tie that consists of a directional interlock, when continued, is continued in the same direction as the original tie.

name: MNC macro-structure
definition: Four types of macro-structure commonly used by MNC's are considered: worldwide functional divisions, international divisions, geographical regions, and worldwide product divisions. Each type of structure is seen as facilitating certain types of information processing between the subunits of the organization, in this case the parent and foreign subsidiaries, while at the same time restricting others.

name: Foreign product diversity
definition: As product diversity increases, there is an increase in both market diversity (environmental complexity) and manufacturing and technical diversity (technological complexity), and with it a greater need for tactical and strategic information processing for product matters.

name: Product modification differences across subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["product modification differences among subsidiaries", "product modification differences across foreign subsidiaries", "product modification"]
definition: The degree to which products are locally modified or differ from one foreign subsidiary to another specifies yet another type of product complexity or heterogeneity.

name: Product change
definition: High rates of product change require that an MNC have the ability to transfer new technology as well as the ability to reformulate product strategy on a frequent basis.

name: Size of foreign operations
authors_terms: ["size of foreign operations", "percentage of foreign sales"]
definition: As the relative size of foreign operations increases, the opportunities for increased integration either across subsidiaries or between foreign and domestic operations increases, and so does the requirement for product-related information-processing capacity.

name: Size of foreign manufacturing
authors_terms: ["size of foreign manufacturing", "level of foreign manufacturing"]
definition: A company's foreign operations can be split into the percentage of foreign sales exported from the parent and the percentage manufactured by the foreign subsidiaries; exports from the parent create interdependencies that increase the requirement for product-related information processing between parent and subsidiary.

name: Number of foreign subsidiaries
definition: As the number of foreign subsidiaries increases, requirements for all four types of information-processing capacities at the parent level will increase.

name: Outside ownership in foreign subsidiaries
authors_terms: ["extent of outside ownership", "outside ownership", "level of outside ownership in foreign subsidiaries"]
definition: Significant outside ownership in foreign subsidiaries places additional constraints on the way the subsidiaries can be managed, since outside owners will oppose decisions that reduce subsidiary profits for the sake of maximizing total company profits.

name: Extent of foreign acquisitions
authors_terms: ["extent of acquisitions", "extent of foreign acquisitions", "foreign acquisitions"]
definition: Most acquisitions are themselves multifunctional organizations containing subunits that already possess some kind of organizational structure and information-processing system; structures that can absorb a foreign acquisition while leaving that system intact should accommodate a higher rate of growth by acquisition.

name: Complexity of construction type
authors_terms: ["complexity", "type of construction", "complexity of the type of construction"]
definition: Complexity is in part determined by the number of functions performed by the structure; buildings that must perform either a variety of functions or some highly specialized functions will require many high-skill specialties in their construction.

name: Project size
definition: Size of the project: the larger the building the greater the opportunity for applying the principles of task simplification to achieve labor efficiencies, and larger projects require more labor and materials and are more costly.

name: Market extent
definition: By Stigler's thesis, a sufficiently large market is required before some task specialties can be performed by independent firms to achieve economies of scale; market extent was taken to be indicated by urbanization, measured as the percentage of population living in Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas.

name: Subcontracting
definition: The practice of general contractors subcontracting portions of a project to special trade contractors; subcontracting in the construction industry is a response to uncertainty arising from complexity, given bounded rationality of the firm.

name: Workload variability
definition: Construction is subject to variability in the volume of work and the product mix; the variability measure used was the month of greatest employment of construction workers divided by the month of lowest employment.

name: Bureaucratization
definition: Bureaucratic administration implies having the planning of the work process centralized in the administrative component of the firm and is further characterized by a finely adjusted and stable communications structure and a high proportion of continuously functioning clerks.

name: Budget allocation
authors_terms: ["relative number of projects approved", "relative number of words approved", "larger allocation", "total allocation", "size of allocation"]
definition: The dependent variable in each hypothesis is the relative number of projects (i.e., words) approved for each type of manager by the budget officers.

name: Manager profitability
definition: Average profitability is one of the three attributes characterizing the simulated managers, high or low; high profit managers were designed, on the average, to propose projects which were actually twice as profitable as those proposed by low profit managers.

name: Attempted influence
authors_terms: ["attempted influence", "attempts at influence", "influence attempts", "high influence managers", "low influence managers"]
definition: Attempts at influence describe the attempts by managers to classify some or all of their projects as 'urgent' or 'very high quality', descriptions intended to reflect the desirability of the particular manager's projects relative to any other manager's projects.

name: Estimation accuracy
authors_terms: ["estimation accuracy", "accurate estimators", "biased estimators", "deliberate estimation bias", "estimation bias"]
definition: Estimation accuracy is an attribute of the simulated managers, accurate or biased; the second form of political behavior discussed is deliberate bias in the estimation of costs and benefits.

name: Compensation policy
authors_terms: ["sales compensation", "salary versus commission", "type of compensation", "compensation policy", "performance-contingent pay"]
definition: The purpose of this study was to explore when firms use salary compensation and when they use compensation with a substantial commission component; retailers choose between salary plans in which salespeople's pay is more or less assured and commission plans in which a substantial portion of pay depends on individual sales performance.

name: Job programmability
definition: Programmed jobs are ones in which behaviors can be precisely defined. In retail selling, a highly programmed job is one that consists primarily of cashiering, whereas a job with low programming requires extensive personal selling and behaviors that are much more difficult to evaluate.

name: Span of control
definition: Span of control is the size of the space supervised and the number of employees supervised in that space. When their span of control is low, store managers can maintain close supervision and have good information upon which to evaluate employee behavior.

name: Outcome uncertainty
definition: Outcomes are only partially a function of behaviors; government policies, economic climate, competitors' actions, the weather, and other factors may intervene to cause variations in outcomes, and such uncertainty introduces not only inability to plan but also financial risk. The measures tap the volatility dimension of uncertainty, the dimension most germane to the risk implications of agency theory.

name: Store chain age
authors_terms: ["age of a store chain", "age of a store", "age"]
definition: Age captures a range of qualitative factors (e.g., managerial philosophy, union power) related to changes in an institutional environment over time; older stores are more likely to use commissions and newer ones are more likely to use salaries.

name: Merchandise category
definition: The segment of retailing defined by the merchandise a store sells; stores were typed according to their designated line of merchandise, and one such segment, shoe stores, is a tradition in which commissions remain the traditional form of compensation.

name: Average purchase size
definition: The average size of a purchase at the store. Selling high-priced merchandise by commission is a tradition that has its roots in early department stores, in which the highest commission tiers were associated with the highest-priced merchandise.

name: Decision-making approach
authors_terms: ["dialectical inquiry", "devil's advocacy", "consensus approach", "decision-making approach", "programmed conflict approaches"]
definition: The approaches to group strategic decision making compared in the study: dialectical inquiry, devil's advocacy, and consensus. In dialectical inquiry and devil's advocacy, decisional conflict is incorporated through formalized debate between two subgroups of the group.

name: Decision quality
authors_terms: ["group performance", "quality of decisions", "quality of recommendations", "validity of assumptions", "importance of assumptions"]
definition: The quality of a group's final recommendations and supporting assumptions, assessed through the number, validity, and importance of its assumptions and the quality of its recommendations.

name: Group members' reactions to their group
authors_terms: ["group members' reactions", "members' reactions to their groups", "satisfaction with the group", "acceptance of group decisions"]
definition: Members' affective reactions to the decision-making experience, including their satisfaction and desire to continue working with their group and their acceptance of the group's assumptions and recommendations.

name: Critical evaluation
authors_terms: ["critical evaluation", "critical reevaluation", "reevaluate their own assumptions and recommendations"]
definition: The extent to which group conditions had led members to reevaluate their own assumptions and recommendations.

name: Meeting time
authors_terms: ["meeting duration", "meeting time", "time required to make decisions"]
definition: The number of minutes elapsed from the moment the experimenter left a group's workroom until the experimenter received the group's final assumptions and recommendations.

name: Experience with a decision-making approach
definition: Repeated use of a decision-making approach: each group remained intact and used the same decision-making approach for the second case as for the first.

name: Organizational effectiveness
definition: Organizational effectiveness is multidimensional; it was assessed along five distinct dimensions adapted from Quinn and Rohrbaugh's (1983) model of organizational effectiveness: resource acquisition, efficiency, human relations, quality, and costs.

name: Design configuration
definition: An organization's design configuration is characterized by design factors: the key coordinating mechanism, the key part of the organization, the type and degree of centralization, and secondary bureaucratic characteristics such as formalization, specialization, and hierarchy.

name: Contextual configuration
definition: Multiple factors define the contextual configurations, including an organization's age and size and attributes of its environment and technology.

name: Design-context alignment
authors_terms: ["correct pairing between its design and contextual configuration", "correct design-context pairing"]
definition: The correct pairing between an organization's design configuration and the contextual configuration that is appropriate for it.

name: Ideal types fit
definition: Ideal types fit is high to the extent that an organization's design is similar to the design of any one of the ideal types identified in the theory.

name: Contingent ideal types fit
authors_terms: ["contingent ideal types fit", "contingent ideal types model"]
definition: In the contingent ideal types model, an organization's design is contingent on its context; the organization must mimic the one ideal type that is most congruent with the contingencies facing it.

name: Contingent hybrid types fit
authors_terms: ["contingent hybrid types fit", "contingent hybrid types model"]
definition: The contingent hybrid types model retains the assumption that a set of contingencies constrains the forms that an organization can adopt and remain effective but adds the possibility of hybridization of the ideal types to form effective hybrid types; the one hybrid type that an organization must adopt is determined by the unique contingencies that the organization faces.

name: Hybrid types fit
definition: The hybrid types model implies that many different effective hybrid combinations can arise from the congruence between a constructed environment and a chosen organizational configuration; an organization is free to mimic any hybrid of the initial ideal types and remain effective.

name: Composite configurational fit
authors_terms: ["simultaneous processes", "ideal types, contingent ideal types, and contingent hybrid types fit"]
definition: The possibility that the different models of configurational fit represent simultaneous rather than mutually exclusive processes, so that they should be used together to predict organizational effectiveness.

name: Change in employment
authors_terms: ["change in employment", "employment-change", "changes in employment", "employment downsizing", "employment upsizing"]
definition: The primary variable of interest in this study was change in employment from one year to the next, as reported in the COMPUSTAT database, calculated as the ratio of the number of employees in the event year to the number in the prior year. Firms were further grouped into employment downsizers, stable employers, and upsizers according to whether employment fell by more than 5 percent, stayed within plus or minus 5 percent, or rose by more than 5 percent.

name: Profitability
definition: A standard measure of the financial performance of a firm is return on assets (ROA), measured as operating income before depreciation, interest, and taxes divided by total assets. If the policy of adjusting a company's workforce is successful, it should increase the productivity of employees and reduce costs, resulting in an increase in the profitability of the firm, as measured by ROA.

name: Total return on common stock
authors_terms: ["total return on common stock", "return on common stock", "stock returns", "stock performance"]
definition: The return to the stockholders surrounding the change in employment was equal to the dividend yield plus price appreciation in each one-year period. The authors describe stock performance as the ultimate performance measure from the shareholders' point of view.

name: Investment management fund ownership
authors_terms: ["investment management funds", "mutual funds and investment bankers", "institutional holdings by mutual funds and investment bankers"]
definition: Mutual funds and investment bank managers' primary objective is a high current return because of their own reward systems, which emphasize quarterly performance.

name: Pension fund ownership
authors_terms: ["public pension funds", "pension funds", "institutional holdings by pension funds"]
definition: Pension fund managers may monitor management closely and press for needed changes (exercise "voice") because they cannot exit by selling large blocks of stock.

name: Top management team equity
authors_terms: ["top management team equity", "top management equity", "managerial equity holdings"]
definition: High managerial equity holdings should bond managerial actions to shareholder interests; top management equity is the percentage of firm equity owned by a firm's top management team.

name: Outside director representation
definition: Outside director representation is the number of directors with no personal or professional relationship to a firm, other than their membership on its board, divided by board size.

name: People dimension of corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["people dimension", "people dimension of CSP", "people dimension of GSP"]
definition: The community, women and minorities, and employee relations grouping, which we hereafter call the people dimension, relates to the contributions firms make to communities, to their hiring of women and minorities, and to their treatment of employees.

name: Product quality dimension of corporate social performance
authors_terms: ["product quality dimension", "product quality dimension of CSP", "product quality dimension of GSP"]
definition: The product quality and environment dimension—hereafter, the product quality dimension—relates to product and service quality and to a firm's stance toward the natural environment.

name: Power imbalance
definition: Power imbalance captures the difference in the power of each actor over the other. Formally, this construct can be defined as the difference between two actors' dependencies, or the ratio of the power of the more powerful actor to that of the less powerful actor.

name: Mutual dependence
definition: The second dimension of dyadic power, mutual dependence, captures the existence of bilateral dependencies in the dyad, regardless of whether the two actors' dependencies are balanced or imbalanced. Formally, this measure can be defined as the sum, or the average of actor i's dependence on actor j and actor j's dependence on actor i.

name: Dependence
definition: An actor i is dependent upon actor j in proportion to i's need for resources that j can provide and in inverse proportion to the availability of alternative actors capable of providing the same resources to i.

name: Constraint absorption
definition: Absorbing constraint entails giving the rights to control the resources that create dependencies to the dependent actor. Organizations can absorb constraint completely through mergers and acquisitions.

name: CEO succession
definition: Replacement of the chief executive officer; the authors treat CEO succession as a mechanism for organizational learning that alters the top team's demography and, in turn, the team's ability to attend to and deal with environmental conditions.

name: Executive team change
definition: Change in the senior executive team, defined as all individuals who report directly to the CEO; the scope of executive team change triggers different learning modes within the firm, with changes limited to either CEO succession or executive team change triggering incremental change in the system.

name: Executive team entry
definition: The number of executives reporting to the CEO who were not on the team in the previous year.

name: Executive team exit
definition: The number of executives who were listed the prior year but not in the current year.

name: Strategic reorientation
definition: Reorientations are discontinuities in the life of a firm, system-wide organization changes involving concurrent shifts in strategy, structure, power, and control mechanisms; during reorientations organizations shift to fundamentally different operating modes rather than incrementally improving existing organizing modes.

name: Organizational performance change
authors_terms: ["performance change", "subsequent organizational performance", "relative change in ROA"]
definition: The relative change in return on assets from the time of organizational change until two years later, adjusted by industry change in ROA to control for year effects.

name: Environmental turbulence
definition: Turbulence driven by environmental events such as technological jolts, regulatory action, or war; it was coded as a binary variable where 1 indicates turbulence during and subsequent to the event.

name: Organizational performance crisis
definition: Organizational turbulence arising from the firm's own performance; performance crisis was determined by examining the firm's ROA level over three successive years, and if ROA decreased two years in succession a dummy variable representing performance crisis was coded as 1.

name: Foreign ownership
authors_terms: ["foreign subsidiaries in the U.S.A.", "foreign (non-U.S.) semiconductor firm", "foreign firms"]
definition: Firms from outside the U.S.A. that have subsidiaries engaged in design or fabrication activity in the U.S.A.; the paper contrasts their patents with those of matched U.S. (domestic) firms.

name: Local knowledge sourcing
authors_terms: ["learning", "local knowledge", "localization of knowledge flows", "knowledge building patterns"]
definition: The extent to which the technological knowledge used in a firm's innovation (the patents it cites) originates in the same geographic location (U.S. region or country) as the innovation itself.

name: Local knowledge contribution
definition: The extent to which the knowledge embodied in a firm's patents is used by other firms located in the same geographic location, measured by the geographic location of the patents that cite the firm's patents.

name: Home country technological weakness
definition: A country's relative technological position in a particular semiconductor technology, computed with the Revealed Technological Advantage indicator; an RTA of less than 1 indicates relative weakness and greater than 1 indicates relative strength.

name: Firm status
definition: Status is a reflection of the importance of the firm among other stakeholders in the network. We measure status using eigenvector centrality based on the premise that the status of a node in a network is a function of the statuses of the nodes with whom it interacts.

name: Stakeholder status
definition: We compute the status of each stakeholder j at time t in the same manner as firm status. To effect a comparison between our two status measures, we measure a given stakeholder’s status as their percentile rank in status among all the stakeholders for that mine.

name: Stakeholder cooperation
definition: Our dependent variables, cooperation and conflict, are the monthly averages of the Goldstein scores representing all events initiated by a given stakeholder toward the firm that are cooperative (i.e., ≥10 on the conflict-cooperation scale).

name: Stakeholder conflict
definition: Our dependent variables, cooperation and conflict, are the monthly averages of the Goldstein scores representing all events initiated by a given stakeholder toward the firm that are conflictual (i.e., <10 on the conflict-cooperation scale).

name: Access to structural holes
authors_terms: ["firm access to structural holes", "ability to span structural holes", "firm structural hole efficiency", "structural holes"]
definition: Structural holes are defined as network positions that bridge nonredundant actors within the network thereby enabling actors occupying these network gaps to gain brokerage advantages via access to and control of diverse and possibly unique information.

name: Degree centrality
authors_terms: ["firm degree centrality", "stakeholder degree centrality", "firm centrality", "stakeholder centrality", "degree centrality"]
definition: We measure the simple count of media reports in which a firm or a stakeholder appears in a given year.

name: Rule of law
definition: The rule of law is a subjective rating of the “extent to which citizens have confidence in and abide by the rules of the society.”

name: Disruptive technology adoption
authors_terms: ["potentially disruptive technology", "disruptive technology", "pioneer", "early adopter of disruptive technology"]
definition: Technologies that are initially less compatible with incumbent products and processes because they perform poorly on dimensions currently valued by the majority of consumers, but that have a trajectory of improvement and may eventually outperform existing technologies on those dimensions; adopting such technologies is used as a measure of increased uncertainty regarding commercialization value.

name: Dynamic commercialization strategy
authors_terms: ["dynamic technology commercialization strategy (TCS)", "two-stage commercialization strategy", "switching from compete to cooperate", "compete -> cooperate"]
definition: A strategy in which the entrant first competes with incumbents in the product market to establish the value of its technology and later switches to cooperating with them through licensing, acquisition or both.

name: Experience requirement length
definition: The length requirement is the time an individual must be employed in a public accounting firm to receive certification. Length is the time that an accountant must be employed to fulfill the requirements.

name: Narrow focus of experience requirement
authors_terms: ["focus", "focus requirement", "breadth of focus", "narrowly focused experience requirement", "broadly focused experience requirement"]
definition: The extent to which the experience requirement restricts the types of experience that count toward certification. A narrowly focused experience requirement demands a restrictive set of audit experiences, whereas a broadly focused experience requirement allows a wide range of experience, including nonaudit and nonpublic-accounting experience, to be used for certification.

name: Audit specialization
definition: The type of work an accountant does, ranging from auditing to tax, consulting, and other nonaudit activities. The third dichotomy, specialization, separates audit from nonaudit experience.

name: Employee resignation
definition: Exit from the firm that is employee driven; the authors analyzed resignation rather than termination or placement because it is employee driven.

name: Timing of resignation hazard shift
definition: Hazard shifts are sudden changes in hazard rates, the instantaneous probability of exiting. The authors expected requirement length to position the hazard shift at different times.

name: Magnitude of resignation hazard shift
definition: The size of the change in the resignation transition rate around fulfillment of the certification experience requirement. A lower transition rate prior to and a higher rate after employees' fulfillment of the experience requirement demonstrates a hazard shift; a greater difference between the two periods shows a larger hazard shift.

name: Assessed risk
authors_terms: ["assessed risk", "risk rating", "risk rating scale", "riskiness of a decision"]
definition: By risk, the bank meant the likelihood of default by the borrower, measured on a seven-point scale based on a comprehensive, subjective evaluation of the borrower. In essence, the risk rating reflected the lender's perceptions of the degree to which there was a risk that the borrower would not repay the loan.

name: Expected return
authors_terms: ["expected returns", "interest rate returns", "risk-adjusted expected returns", "risk-adjusted returns", "expected return on assets"]
definition: The bank used two measures of expected returns: the interest rate charged a borrower relative to the prime interest rate and the return on assets expected for that borrower, after adjustment for the administrative and default risk costs that the bank associated with different levels of borrower risk, termed risk-adjusted expected returns.

name: Change in assessed risk
authors_terms: ["upgrades and downgrades in risk ratings", "changes in assessed risk", "changed risk rating", "upgraded and downgraded borrowers"]
definition: When the relative riskiness of a borrower changes, decision makers should be slow to adjust their pricing of a loan to match the change in the risk the borrower presents. Indicator variables measured whether the risk rating for a borrower had changed since the last annual review.

name: Number of exchange relations
authors_terms: ["number of relations", "number of direct ties", "number of direct exchange partners", "number of direct exchange relationships", "number of relationships"]
definition: The number of relations for a given scientist-year was the sum of that scientist's coauthors during the previous five years. The number of direct ties a researcher maintains provides insight into the redundancy of knowledge resources he or she is exposed to in the research process.

name: Strength of exchange relations
authors_terms: ["strength of relations", "strength of relationships", "strength of direct ties", "relationship strength"]
definition: The strength of relations reflected the number of interactions and, therefore, how well a given scientist knew his or her research partners. The frequency of interactions during a relationship is an important index of the time and effort that the partners have invested in one another.

name: Knowledge creation
definition: We define new knowledge as discoveries about phenomena that were not known previously. In our study, new knowledge is something that does not exist anywhere before it is discovered and published by research scientists.

name: Pro-environmental values
authors_terms: ["pro-environmental values", "respect for nature", "values that underlie respect for the natural environment", "sustainable development values"]
definition: Values related to the natural environment, specifically respect for nature, defined as 'prudence in the management of all living species and natural resources' to ensure they are 'preserved and passed on to our descendants'; values are 'an enduring belief that a specific mode of conduct or end-state of existence is personally or socially preferable to an opposite or converse mode of conduct or end-state of existence'.

name: Weight assigned to harm to the natural environment
authors_terms: ["weight assigned to a specified harm to the natural environment", "weight assigned to harm to the natural environment in the assessment of opportunity attractiveness", "weight assigned to specified harm in individuals' assessments of the attractiveness of acting on an opportunity"]
definition: The emphasis entrepreneurs place on information about a specified harm to the natural environment generated by an opportunity when assessing that opportunity's attractiveness; as moral disengagement operates, pro-environmental values have a reduced impact on this weight.

name: Entrepreneurial self-efficacy
definition: The strength of a person's belief that he or she is capable of performing the tasks required to create and successfully manage his or her own business.

name: Perceived industry munificence
definition: Industry munificence is the 'scarcity or abundance of critical resources needed by (one or more) firms operating within an environment'; the authors focus on entrepreneurs' perceptions of this munificence as a belief of personal agency.

name: Vision imagery
definition: We hereafter refer to image-based words only as they are used in a leader's vision of the future, and vision imagery as the concrete representations of the future that are triggered by image-based words in a vision.

name: Number of values
definition: Values represent desired end-states as well as guiding principles that provide a sense of purpose by capturing which day-to-day behaviors are important and desirable; the authors examine the number of values, because it represents the number of discrete concepts that can be used to derive meaning.

name: Shared ultimate goal
authors_terms: ["shared ultimate goal", "shared sense of purpose", "shared representation of the ultimate goal", "shared purpose"]
definition: A shared sense of purpose, which is achieved when multiple employees possess the same understanding of the purpose of work; an ultimate goal represents what leaders consider to be the final level of goal achievement for an organization at a given time.

name: Coordination
definition: Organizational members who share the same understanding of the long term are likely to collectively adopt a 'global focus' rather than a purely 'local focus', aligning their responsibilities with those of others; enhanced coordination improves performance quality because it leads the skills and responsibilities of different individuals to better fit the task at hand.

name: Performance quality
definition: The quality of a product design or the effectiveness of a service.

name: Individual creativity
definition: Creativity consists of the generation of ideas, products, or services that are judged to be novel and useful by external observers.

name: Knowledge depth
definition: Knowledge depth is the degree to which an individual is knowledgeable about a specific domain.

name: Knowledge breadth
definition: Knowledge breadth is the degree to which an individual's knowledge covers multiple domains; it represents the diversity of an individual's knowledge, know-how, and experiences.

name: Career age
definition: Career age is defined as the amount of time one has spent in a given field.

name: Network openness
definition: Network constraint measures the extent to which an artist's network was closed, increasing with few contacts, contacts strongly connected to one another, or contacts connected indirectly through the same other person. To ease interpretation, the authors operationalized their independent variable as 1 − constraint, so that high scores reflect openness and low scores reflect closure.

name: Content heterogeneity
definition: Content heterogeneity was measured in terms of how similar an episode's content was compared to other episodes the artist had worked on, using content categories describing story type, setting, incarnation of the Doctor, and type of alien foe.

name: Network stability
definition: We define 'network stability' as the degree to which individuals maintain their existing ties or add new ones.

name: Creativity
definition: Creativity is the generation of novel and appropriate outcomes, assessed following the consensual assessment technique: a product has to be judged as creative by appropriate expert observers belonging to the field.

name: Late handoffs
definition: Late handoffs occur when the implementer is handed a mature idea after someone else drives the generation and elaboration stages, meaning the implementer only drives the implementation stage.

name: Creativity of final products
authors_terms: ["creativity", "creative final products", "creativity of their final products"]
definition: To be deemed creative, ideas or final products must be judged as both novel and useful; ideas must be implemented successfully to become creative final products.

name: Psychological ownership
definition: Psychological ownership is the state in which individuals feel as though the target of ownership (material or immaterial in nature) or a piece of it is 'theirs' (Pierce et al., 2001: 299).

name: Product coherence
definition: We define 'product coherence' as the degree to which the different parts or elements of the product work well together as a whole.

name: Concreteness orientation
authors_terms: ["concrete orientation", "concrete (vs. abstract) orientation", "CEO concreteness/abstraction", "dispositional concreteness", "abstract orientation"]
definition: A pattern of thought and speech residing on a continuum ranging from leaders with an abstract orientation at one pole, leaders with a concrete orientation at the other pole, and various gradations in between; concrete thought and speech use words that paint a picture of perceivable reality rather than words that are abstract.

name: Organizational hierarchy
definition: Hierarchies are stronger when there are clearer distinctions between employees in terms of authority, reflected in more layers of management and greater concentration of authority.

name: Organizational change
definition: Change through both growth and reduction, and change that is both internally generated (building from within) and externally obtained (buying from without).

name: Attention toward large-scale goals
authors_terms: ["attention toward large-scale goals", "attention to large-scale goals", "large-scale goals"]
definition: Attention to goals that are both long term and broad in scope, as opposed to short-term, narrowly defined problems.

name: Inside-out network sequencing
definition: The practice by which individuals elaborating novel ideas mobilize feedback and support from their inner-circle ties before their outer-circle ones. It is presented as a continuum: at the high end individuals expose their ideas gradually from their inner circle to their outer circle; at the low end they adopt an outside-in approach or an all-in-one mobilization approach.

name: Individual innovation performance
definition: An individual's ability to develop 'good ideas', assessed by the organization's annual performance review system on the basis of contributions to innovations that generate revenue or reduce costs for the organization, or that offer significant promise of doing so further down the line.

name: Unsupportive work environment
authors_terms: ["less supportive work environments", "less supportive innovation contexts", "work contexts that are more hostile to innovation", "unsupportive work contexts"]
definition: Work contexts that restrict the support that individuals receive - or perceive that they receive - for their innovation efforts, in contrast to 'safe spaces' where innovation is celebrated and encouraged. Four characteristics are delineated: emphasis on accountability rather than autonomy, leaders' lack of support for innovation, lack of organizational slack, and reluctance to cannibalize existing assets.

name: Image-based cues
definition: Cues conveyed through the images influencers post; image-based competence cues are before and after images and self-portraits, and image-based warmth cues are group images and personal life images.

name: Word-based cues
definition: Cues conveyed through the words influencers use in their posts and replies; word-based competence cues are analytic words in posts and replies plus first-person singular pronouns, and word-based warmth cues are positive affect words in posts and replies plus other-inclusive pronouns.

name: Competence cues
definition: 'the competence dimension reflects traits that are related to perceived ability, including intelligence, skill, creativity and efficacy.'

name: Warmth cues
definition: 'the warmth dimension captures traits that are related to perceived intent, including friendliness, helpfulness, sincerity, trustworthiness and morality.'

name: Number of followers
definition: Following an influencer requires only the time and effort needed to click the 'follow' option; it is the lower-level engagement behavior, and the authors operationalize an influencer's ability to attract followers as the number of followers the influencer had at the end of each month.

name: Positive interactions
definition: Positive interaction reflects greater engagement than following because the follower takes the time and effort to reply to or comment on the influencer's posts, and it is measured by counting the number of positive affect words used by others in the comments portion of the influencer's posts.

name: Joiner gender
authors_terms: ["job seeker's gender", "job seeker gender", "joiner gender", "participant gender"]
definition: Job seeker's gender, coded as man (0) or woman (1); in Study 1 it was coded algorithmically from job seekers' first names and in Study 2 it was self-reported.

name: Interest in applying
definition: A joiner's interest in applying for a startup job; in the field study it captured whether a job seeker indicated interest in a viewed job posting, and in the experiment it was measured with Highhouse et al.'s (2003) application intentions scale.

name: Startup gender composition
authors_terms: ["gender composition of the company", "proportion of women in a startup", "startup gender composition", "organizational gender composition"]
definition: The proportion of men and women employed by the startup, representing a startup's track record in hiring and retaining men and women; reported by startups on each of their job advertisements.

name: Diversity debt signal
authors_terms: ["diversity debt", "diversity debt signal", "startups signaling diversity debt"]
definition: A startup's initially skewed gender composition - no or only a token representation of women - that endures through growth and demands costly engagement with diversity at scale; signaled to job seekers as an extreme gender imbalance.

name: Identity threat concerns
definition: A set of psychological concerns pertaining to the value of one's identity in a setting, typically involving worries about the prospect of being singled out, disrespected, stereotyped, marginalized, or mistreated.

name: Investor reactions
definition: Investor reactions are captured with the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) over the three-day (−1, +1) period surrounding the earnings announcement, which the authors use to capture investor reactions to earnings surprises.

name: Predictive expectancy violation
authors_terms: ["predictive expectation", "predictive expectancy violation", "material earnings surprise", "positive material earnings surprise", "negative material earnings surprise"]
definition: A violation of predictive expectations would entail the observed behavior not matching the behavior that was predicted to occur, for example whether a firm's earnings came in above or below what investors predicted.

name: Prescriptive expectancy violation based on past performance
authors_terms: ["prescriptive expectancy violation (past performance)", "prescriptive expectation based on past performance", "past performance"]
definition: A violation of prescriptive expectations entails the observed behavior not matching normative guidance regarding what is considered appropriate behavior. The authors argue that the belief that performance is only "acceptable" when it meets or exceeds prior performance is likely to be part of the normative beliefs of most individuals, including investors, so that comparison with the firm's past performance serves as a prescriptive expectation.

name: Prescriptive expectancy violation based on peer comparison
authors_terms: ["prescriptive expectancy violation (peer comparison)", "prescriptive expectation based on peer comparison", "peer comparisons"]
definition: A violation of prescriptive expectations entails the observed behavior not matching normative guidance regarding what is considered appropriate behavior. The performance of peers—that is, the idea that the firm should meet or beat the performance of its peers—is likely to act as another prescriptive expectation.

name: Prospective expectancy violation
definition: Prospective expectations are defined as the current expected value, to the stakeholder, of future interactions with the individual or firm; a violation of prospective expectations occurs if the observed behavior resulted in an updating of the prospective expectation held prior to witnessing the behavior.

name: Professionally ambiguous attributions
definition: When used as a label, "creative differences" acts as a professionally ambiguous attribution, which the authors define as the strategic use of vague language to publicly obscure behavioral causes of ostensibly negative professional outcomes. They describe it as a form of strategic ambiguity used to provide vague justifications within the profession.

name: Access to future projects
authors_terms: ["access to future projects", "future work opportunities", "future project opportunities"]
definition: The work opportunities a director obtains on subsequent projects; the authors' dual operationalization captures both the financial scale of directors' future projects and the frequency of their employment, providing an assessment of their sustained work opportunities.

name: Film box-office performance
authors_terms: ["box office", "U.S. domestic gross box office", "global box office"]
definition: The success of a feature film, commonly measured by its box-office revenues, which reflect audience preference and the success of those receiving them.

name: Professional relationships
authors_terms: ["professional relationships", "(dis)continuation of professional relationships", "major distributor involvement"]
definition: The authors use the (dis)continuation of professional relationships as a proxy of reputational change caused by reputational spillovers, focused on relationships with major studios because work with major studios is coveted.

name: Prior collaborator status
authors_terms: ["previous collaborator status", "status of prior collaborators", "high-status collaborators"]
definition: The status of the collaborators previously involved in a focal individual's project. High-status individuals are magnets for attention and have more influence and power, so they are able to violate professional norms without exposure to the same sanctions.

name: Prior interorganizational mobility
authors_terms: ["prior interorganizational moves", "prior mobility", "number of prior moves"]
definition: We assessed prior interorganizational moves as the number of times a fund manager changed hedge fund employers between their entry into the industry and their final mobility event.

name: Post-mobility performance decline
authors_terms: ["performance decline", "magnitude of newcomers' performance decline", "immediate performance shift following mobility event"]
definition: The coefficient for mobility reflects the immediate change in an individual's performance in the period mobility occurs (i.e., a shift in the intercept associated with the mobility event), such that a negative (positive) coefficient reflects an immediate decrease (increase) in performance following mobility.

name: Time to performance recovery
authors_terms: ["time required to achieve performance recovery", "time to performance recovery"]
definition: Recovery takes the value of 0 up to and including the observation period in which the mobility event occurs, and then takes the value of 1 in the period immediately following the mobility event, increasing by one in each subsequent observation period thereafter. The authors test recovery hypotheses based on a comparison of the number of months it takes managers to recover to pre-mobility performance levels, rather than the rate of performance recovery.

name: Unfamiliar geographic context
authors_terms: ["unfamiliar move", "moving to a firm located outside a hub in which they have previously worked"]
definition: We measured unfamiliar move using a dummy variable set equal to 1 when a manager moves to a firm located outside a hub in which they have previously worked, 0 otherwise.

name: Key employee shared tenure
definition: We first calculated shared dyadic tenure for each dyad of incumbent managers in the firm—or the number of years of overlapping tenure shared between each pair of managers. We then computed the mean shared dyadic tenure across all managers, reflecting the average shared tenure among all incumbent managers at the firm.

name: Role collaboration requirement
authors_terms: ["centrality of collaboration to a fund manager's new role", "comanaged fund", "requirements for collaboration with other organizational members"]
definition: To capture the centrality of collaboration to a fund manager's new role (as specified in Hypothesis 4), we created a dummy variable set equal to 1 for managers whose primary fund is a comanaged fund, 0 otherwise. Whereas in all other funds a single fund manager has sole discretion and responsibility for investment decisions, in comanaged funds investment decisions are made jointly with at least one other fund manager.

name: Residual performance
definition: Residual performance reflects the extent to which a manager's fund performs above (as indicated by a positive residual value) or below (as indicated by a negative residual value) its expected performance based on the above-noted firm- and fund-level factors.

name: Angel investment received
authors_terms: ["investment received from angels", "angel funding", "VC + angel funding"]
definition: Receiving funding from individual angel investors (as opposed to only venture capital); in the archival data this is a dummy variable equal to 1 if the focal entrepreneur's ventures had received an angel investment as of year t.

name: Transition to angel investing
authors_terms: ["becoming an angel investor", "entry into angel investment", "pay-it-forward behavior", "founder-to-funder transition"]
definition: The transition of venture-backed entrepreneurs to angel investing—that is, their first angel investment; the dependent variable in all models is the hazard of entry into angel investment.

name: Educational ties
authors_terms: ["same-school angels", "shared educational backgrounds", "attended the same educational institution"]
definition: Shared educational background between the entrepreneur and the angel investor, one of the three forms of structural embeddedness the authors examine; angels coded as same-school if they attended the same higher education institution as the entrepreneur.

name: Professional ties
authors_terms: ["same-company angels", "shared professional background", "worked for the same company"]
definition: Shared workplace background between the entrepreneur and the angel investor, one of the three forms of structural embeddedness the authors examine; angels coded as same-company if they worked at the same company as the entrepreneur.

name: Geographic proximity
