authors_terms: ["same-location angels", "located in the same community", "geographically proximate", "investing locally"]
definition: Geographic embeddedness between the entrepreneur and the angel investor, one of the three forms of structural embeddedness the authors examine; angels coded as same-location if Crunchbase listed them in the same metropolitan area as the entrepreneur.

name: Gratitude
definition: The emotional experience of gratitude for help received as a founder and the broader prosocial motivation it engenders; measured as the extent to which the investment decision was a function of feeling grateful for help received as a founder and a desire to give back to entrepreneurs.

name: Reputation concerns
definition: The rewarding reputation mechanism, in which A helping B leads C to help A based on A's reputation for generosity; measured as the extent to which the decision was influenced by being seen as someone who supports entrepreneurs and by enhancing one's standing among peers.

name: Investment target embeddedness
authors_terms: ["embeddedness of potential investment targets", "embedded founder", "shared school tie"]
definition: The embeddedness of the potential investment target, that is, whether the founder seeking investment shares an embedded tie (a school tie) with the focal entrepreneur.

name: Tertius iungens orientation
authors_terms: ["tertius iungens orientation", "tertius iungens strategy", "tertius iungens activity"]
definition: A strategic, behavioral orientation toward connecting people in one's social network by either introducing disconnected individuals or facilitating new coordination between connected individuals.

name: Structural holes
definition: A structural hole exists between two acquaintances in an individual's network if the acquaintances share a tie with the individual but are not connected to each other. Density, the ratio of existing ties between those in a subject's network out of all possible ties, is often seen as a general proxy for structural holes, and constraint captures the extent of an individual's dependence on the others in his or her network as well as his or her access to novel, non-redundant information.

name: Technical knowledge
definition: Familiarity with the respondent's area of functional expertise, measured through comfort in addressing the more advanced technical issues in that area.

name: Social knowledge
definition: Broad access to current and often unofficial information about the activity in various areas surrounding the G5's development, which served as a conduit for unfiltered intelligence about individual and departmental issues and interests.

name: Individual stock of knowledge
authors_terms: ["accumulated technical and social knowledge", "individual stock of knowledge"]
definition: An accumulated stock of individual knowledge, which is important to innovation both as a resource to draw upon directly as well as the basis for assimilating new knowledge; time in the firm and formal education are treated as measures of it.

name: Innovation involvement
definition: A respondent's highest level of participation in a change to the G5 product or process, using a scale of five categories of innovation involvement.

name: Collaborative brokerage
definition: A broker occupies the sole intermediate position between others, such that others can interact only through the broker. Brokerage involves direct ties to collaborators who themselves do not have direct ties to each other.

name: Cohesion
definition: Cohesion occurs when individuals have dense and overlapping ties with each other; a cohesive social structure is one in which most people have direct ties to each of the others in the network.

name: Generative creativity
definition: The assemblage of new combinations; if creativity is restricted to an initial insight, generative creativity is increased by exposure to a wide variety of ideas and components that have not already been combined.

name: Focal inventor's breadth of experience
definition: The breadth of an inventor's personal information and experience, including diverse experiences, ideas, media, technologies, and processes brought to future collaborations.

name: Collaborators' breadth of experience
definition: Collaborators' greater breadth of experience confers a marginal benefit to the focal actor because they bring nonredundant information and broader backgrounds to the collective effort.

name: Multiple organization experience
definition: Individuals who have worked in a variety of organizations bring a greater diversity of ideas, perspectives, assumptions, creative techniques, and other relationships to the collaboration.

name: Collaborators' external ties
definition: A focal person benefits from his or her collaborators' external collaborations, which provide social access to recent, salient, and non-redundant information.

name: Future use of new combinations
authors_terms: ["uses of the combination", "future use", "use of new combinations", "creative success"]
definition: Creative success is best measured by its reception; the uses variable counts how many times other inventors used the focal inventor's new combinations.

name: Organizational design
definition: The paper studies the two polar extreme of decentralized resource allocation commonly found in the organizational design literature: price-direction in which transfer pricing is used by a central agent to coordinate resource allocation, and resource-direction in which rationing is used to effect coordination.

name: Decision-making performance
authors_terms: ["performance", "organizational payoff", "overall contribution of the final proposal", "contribution of the final proposal"]
definition: Comparative managerial performance of the subjects as central coordinating agents, measured by organizational payoff, i.e. the aggregate dollar contribution from the colleges to the university.

name: Decision time pressure
authors_terms: ["decision time pressure", "time pressure", "low time pressure", "high time pressure"]
definition: The maximum decision time allowed to the subject in each planning iteration. Low time pressure meant the subjects had a maximum of five minute to make a decision in each iteration.

name: Decision agent
definition: Who performs the central coordination task: the human subject as central agent, or the decomposition algorithm applied to the same problem. The performance of the Dantzig-Wolfe algorithm for subsequent iterations is indicated in Figure 4.

name: Market research information availability
authors_terms: ["information manipulation", "presence of information", "additional information", "the information presented"]
definition: The manipulated provision of a particular set of market research information: each team either had to or could not purchase four market research studies (Consumer Survey, Semantic Scale, Perceptual Mapping, Advertising Experiment) in a given period.

name: Marketing-mix decisions
definition: The set of discrete yet interrelated marketing-mix decisions each team makes in a period, involving the allocation of the marketing budget across advertising, sales force, R&D, price, positioning and number of brands marketed.

name: Net marketing contribution
definition: Cumulative gross contribution across all brands (i.e., revenues minus cost of goods sold minus brand specific inventory holding and advertising costs) minus R&D, sales force and marketing research expenses.

name: Competitors' receipt of information
authors_terms: ["number of competitors ... who received the information", "INFCMP", "INFO2"]
definition: The number of competitors in a team's industry who received the manipulated information in a given period.

name: Advertising expenditure
definition: The dollars spent on advertising across all brands by a team in a period.

name: Sales force expenditure
definition: The dollars spent on the sales force by a team in a period.

name: New product R&D expenditure
definition: The dollars spent on R&D to develop new products by a team in a period.

name: Product improvement R&D expenditure
definition: The dollars spent on R&D to improve existing products by a team in a period.

name: Price
definition: The average price charged by a team for the brands it marketed in a period.

name: Product repositioning
definition: Each firm begins a period with its brands at specified spatial coordinates in a two-dimensional perceptual map and can decide either to leave a brand's coordinates unchanged or provide new coordinates as perceptual objectives; repositioning activity is the amount of movement so undertaken.

name: Number of brands marketed
definition: The number of different brands a team markets in a period, with a maximum of five imposed by the simulation.

name: Investment allocation behavior
authors_terms: ["investment allocations", "allocations of units", "allocation path", "observed investment behavior"]
definition: The number of the 400 experimental units a subject chooses to allocate in each of the ten decision rounds; the sequence of these choices is the subject's allocation path and represents how investment input is spread over time.

name: Myopia in investment decisions
definition: Subject A is more myopic than subject B if F_A(t) > F_B(t) for rounds t = 1,...,10, where F_A(t) and F_B(t) are the cumulative amount of units allocated by subjects A and B by round t. A larger cumulative allocation early in the horizon means greater myopia.

name: Long-term bonus scheme
authors_terms: ["long-term bonus scheme", "long-term compensation contract", "moving average bonus"]
definition: A compensation scheme that ties an agent's compensation to long-term (usually 3-4 years) organizational performance. In Corporation X's contract the long-term bonus is a function of the arithmetic mean of profit over the past four periods.

name: Discount-rate-inducing compensation scheme
authors_terms: ["magnifier", "alternative long-term compensation contract", "compensation contract that induces behavior consistent with lower discount rates"]
definition: A compensation contract that magnifies or inflates compensation in later periods so that profits earned later become relatively more valuable, thereby altering the manager's perceived tradeoff between short- and long-term performance. In the experiment this is done by multiplying output in any round by a number called the magnifier before applying the multiplier.

name: Lone inventorship
authors_terms: ["lone inventor", "individual inventor", "isolated inventor", "working alone", "single inventor", "socially isolated"]
definition: A lone inventor is socially isolated and either does not work with coinventors in a team, does not work for an organization, or both. The authors measure the team dimension with an indicator distinguishing a single inventor from a team of two or more.

name: Organization affiliation
authors_terms: ["organization affiliation", "assigned", "working within an organization", "unaffiliated inventor", "garage inventor"]
definition: Whether the patent originated within an organization rather than outside the boundaries of any organization. The authors argue that a single inventor working within an organization is less isolated than an unaffiliated inventor, because firms act as social communities that extend teams in the creation of new knowledge.

name: Invention impact
authors_terms: ["impact", "citation impact", "ultimate success of a new idea", "success of an invention"]
definition: The authors define the ultimate success of a new idea as its impact on future inventions, and follow the tradition of using the extent to which a specific patent is cited by future patents as the measure of that impact.

name: Breakthrough invention
definition: Inventions at the far right tail of the distribution of creative outcomes. Breakthrough inventions are defined using an indicator set to 1 if and only if a patent is in the top 5% in terms of frequency of future citations received, compared with patents of the same application year and technology class.

name: Invention failure
authors_terms: ["particularly poor outcomes", "particularly bad outcomes", "low impact inventions", "failures", "poor ideas"]
definition: Inventions at the far left tail of the distribution of creative outcomes; particularly poor outcomes are defined using an indicator set to 1 if and only if a patent receives no citations.

name: Diversity of technical experience
authors_terms: ["experience diversity", "diversity of experience", "diversity of past technological experiences", "diversity of technical experience"]
definition: The diversity of past technological experience of the members of a collaborative team, defined as the number of distinct technology classes the inventor or inventors have patented in before, assuming that knowledge of more technical areas offers a greater diversity of ideas available for recombination or criticism.

name: External collaboration network size
authors_terms: ["network size", "extended social network", "external collaboration networks", "indirect collaborators", "supporting team members"]
definition: The size of the extended collaborative network of the team members, i.e., people who work with one or more team members on another project but are not part of the immediate effort; defined as the number of unique inventors at a social distance of not more than two from the focal inventor(s).

name: Technological recombination breadth
authors_terms: ["technological recombination breadth", "breadth of technological recombinations", "breadth of the inventor's technological recombination activities"]
definition: The breadth of the inventor's activities in recombining technological knowledge, measured from the technological classification of the prior art referenced in the examiner's search reports rather than from the classification of the focal patent.

name: Field of education
authors_terms: ["field of study", "educational background in science or in engineering"]
definition: Inventors with a science degree are those educated in the natural sciences, such as astronomy, biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, atmospheric science, oceanography, and materials science; inventors with an engineering degree are those educated in domains such as chemical, civil, electrical, mechanical, and computer engineering.

name: Educational attainment
definition: The attained level of formal education of the inventor, which is reflective of an individual's cognitive ability and knowledge structures and is captured here by whether the inventor holds a doctoral degree.

name: Temporal distance to education
authors_terms: ["years since final educational degree", "temporal distance to his education"]
definition: The number of years that have passed since the inventor completed his education, i.e. the time over which his educational knowledge may become obsolete.

name: Research ability
definition: People differ in their abilities to learn extant knowledge and develop new innovations, either because of innate differences in intelligence or prior investments in knowledge; scientists are differentiated by ability and a taste for nonpecuniary returns.

name: Taste for nonpecuniary returns
authors_terms: ["taste for nonpecuniary returns", "taste for science", "nonpecuniary returns", "nonmonetary returns"]
definition: The characterization of the scientist's preferences or 'taste for science' independent of ability, which reflects attitudes toward open science, freedom of research topics, and intellectual challenge and is informed in the socialization process when receiving scientific education.

name: Research domain
authors_terms: ["basic versus applied science", "type of research", "research type", "basic (applied) research"]
definition: A scientist's career is defined by a combination of the type of research she conducts (basic or applied) and the type of institution she works in (academia or industry); respondents who reported basic (applied) research as their primary job activity are identified as such.

name: Institutional setting
definition: The two institutional settings, academia and industry, seek scientists for different reasons, are governed by different norms and incentive structures, and differ in the relative emphasis on basic and applied science.

name: Earnings profile
definition: Because scientists are paid according to the current level of their human capital, their current earnings are Yit, and survey respondents report their annualized salary, excluding bonuses, overtime or other additional compensation; differences in research ability and preferences for nonpecuniary returns are associated with the evolution of average earnings for each career path.

name: Initial earnings
definition: Because the initial level of human capital is assumed to be the same for all scientists, the average initial earnings of academic basic scientists are lower than those of academic applied scientists.

name: Earnings growth
authors_terms: ["slope of the earnings profile", "earnings profile", "earnings trajectories"]
definition: Under positive sorting, basic scientists in academia invest more in human capital at early stages of their life cycle, making the earnings profile of basic scientists in academia steeper than that of applied scientists in academia; the expected value of the slope of the earnings profile is higher for basic than for applied scientists in academia and similar for basic and applied scientists in industry.

name: Past success in generating implemented ideas
authors_terms: ["past success", "past success in generating implemented ideas"]
definition: The cumulative number of implemented ideas proposed by individual i that were known to be implemented before day t, constructed based on implementation dates rather than submission dates.

name: Idea implementation
authors_terms: ["implemented idea", "idea the organization finds valuable enough to implement", "quality ideas"]
definition: Ideas that an organization does not already offer (new ideas) and considers valuable enough to implement; whether or not an idea is actually implemented is the key success outcome considered in the study.

name: Idea diversity
authors_terms: ["diverse ideas", "ideas that differ from their previous implemented ideas"]
definition: Ideas proposed by an individual that are not in the same categories as their prior implemented ideas, i.e., ideas that differ from their previous implemented ideas.

name: Commenting diversity
authors_terms: ["diversity of past commenting activity", "diversity of their past comments on others' ideas"]
definition: Diversity of an individual's previous activity in commenting on the ideas of other community members, defined using an entropy measure over the idea categories.

name: Analogous market origin
authors_terms: ["analogous market", "market origin", "problem solvers from analogous markets", "analogous market problem solvers"]
definition: A market that is analogously related with the focal target market in terms of sharing similar relational characteristics of the problem, i.e., markets with similar relational characteristics (such as similar problems or customer needs) but no or only few similar product attributes.

name: Novelty of idea
definition: The extent to which a new product idea or problem solution is original and thus new in light of current market offerings.

name: Usefulness of idea
definition: The extent to which an idea can be directly converted to a product that generates immediate benefits for a potentially large number of users.

name: Valence of other reviewers' scores
authors_terms: ["treatment score valence", "valenced treatment scores", "negative information", "positive information", "critical scores"]
definition: The direction of the treatment scores relative to the evaluator's own original score. Treatment score valence was coded as a categorical variable indicating whether the treatment scores from the other reviewers were strictly lower than the evaluator's original score, strictly higher than the evaluator's original score, or within the same range as the evaluator's original score.

name: Evaluation score change
definition: The main dependent variable measures the difference between the updated score (after exposure to the treatment scores) and the original score.

name: Associative stigma
definition: Scandals contaminate not only the implicated transgressor but also others with whom the transgressor associates; this phenomenon is commonly referred to as courtesy stigma or stigma by association. Workers stigmatized by association are employees tainted by connection to a manager or workplace tie involved in misconduct.

name: Domain of managerial misconduct
authors_terms: ["domain of the scandal", "professional versus personal domain", "professional transgressions", "personal transgressions"]
definition: Professional transgressions are misconduct occurring primarily within the professional domain initiated by work-related intentions and producing work-related consequences; personal transgressions are misconduct occurring primarily in the personal domain initiated by nonwork-related intentions and producing nonwork-related consequences. The two domains exist on a continuum rather than as a strict dichotomy.

name: Sorting into stigmatized organizations
authors_terms: ["sorting", "sorting of stigmatized workers into stigmatized organizations", "Newly Hired by Employer w/ Scandal"]
definition: Stigmatized workers who remain in an industry should be more likely to find employment in organizations relatively more supportive or less punitive toward their underlying source of stigma, producing sorting of stigmatized workers into stigmatized organizations.

name: Employment in a stigma-free organization
authors_terms: ["Newly Hired by Employer w/o Scandal", "joining a nonstigmatized employer", "joining a stigma-free employer"]
definition: Joining an employer that is free of a history of managerial misconduct, one of the competing career outcomes the authors jointly explore.

name: Industry exit
definition: A staffer is no longer employed as a congressional staffer in the year following the focal year and is not rehired within three years.

name: Stigma apprehension
definition: The concern about being devalued, socially rejected, or discriminated against; when workers or firms recognize their associative stigma and experience stigma apprehension they become more tolerant and less penalizing of counterparts who also bear stigmatizing marks.

name: Hiring intention
definition: An employer's stated likelihood of hiring the applicant being evaluated.

name: Job acceptance intention
definition: A worker's stated likelihood of accepting a job offer from a prospective employer.

name: Perceived accountability
definition: The perceived responsibility or culpability of employees of the firm for the scandal.

name: Risk of future contamination
definition: The perceived risk that associating with a stigmatized counterpart could contaminate one's own reputation.

name: New product success
authors_terms: ["product success", "success of a product", "market success", "market performance"]
definition: A failure is (1) a product that was totally rejected by the market and ceased to exist, or (2) a product that failed in market tests, resulting in a decision to abort its introduction. Only products that generated substantial positive financial results were defined as successes.

name: Template affiliation
definition: The five basic templates in the evolution of products are Attribute Dependency, Component Control, Replacement, Displacement and Division; they define regularities that can be inferred from product-based trends. In the present study the templates are classified into the attribute dependency template (variable manipulations) and four component templates that manipulate the components.

name: Need and solution spotting
definition: Need spotting is when need identification precedes product (form) development; solution spotting is when a form is identified and the inventor searches for a suitable need (use), or both the need and a solution are identified concurrently.

name: Mental invention
definition: Mental invention is when, according to the inventor's report, the idea is based on a decision to innovate and on internal cognitive process rather than on external market stimulus.

name: Trend following
definition: Following a trend is when a product is developed to follow a market trend in a different class of products.

name: Newness to the market
definition: Newness to the market classifies how new a product is to the market; because people were already using soap bars to wash their hair before the introduction of shampoo, shampoo was classified as a new, but not radically new, product.

name: Newness to the firm
definition: Newness to the firm captures how new the product is to the firm; in the context of a specific product, newness to the firm may lead to failure, and the fact that the first shampoo was introduced by a soap manufacturer suggests that it was not very new to the firm.

name: Technology change
authors_terms: ["changes in technology", "level of required technology change", "technological change"]
definition: Changes in technology are measured in relation to existing technologies in the field and to the changes required in the firm's technology to manufacture the product; the level of required technology change is classified into three groups: minor, moderate, and major.

name: Early analysis determinants
definition: Early determinants consist of idea-based information: the idea itself and the circumstances of its emergence. They allow for evaluation of the product idea at the earliest stage of all, the stage of conception.

name: Process choice
authors_terms: ["process choice", "process-focused", "product-focused", "production process", "job shop", "batch shop", "production line", "continuous flow shop"]
definition: A pivotal decision for the operations function. Process choice ranges from process-focused job shops producing low-volume, customized products to product-focused continuous flow shops producing high-volume, highly standardized products.

name: Product plans
authors_terms: ["product plans", "product customization", "customization", "degree of product customization", "demand characteristics"]
definition: Product plans determine the degree of product customization and volume that process choice should accommodate.

name: Competitive priorities
definition: The operations function translates business strategy into competitive priorities such as flexibility, quality, cost, and time; innovativeness is sometimes included as a fifth priority grouping. Manufacturing firms place stronger emphasis on those priorities that characterize their distinctive competence.

name: Quality priority
definition: Factor 1, labeled QUALITY. Four variables dealing with quality have high loadings on this factor; two deal with quality level and the physical aspects of product, and the other two connote consistent quality, relating to the ability to conform to specifications and customer perceptions of quality.

name: Cost priority
definition: Factor 3, labeled cost (COST), is composed of product cost and product price.

name: Time priority
definition: Factor 2, labeled time (TIME), is made up of delivery time and dependability on delivery.

name: Product flexibility priority
definition: Factor 4, named product flexibility (PFLEX), corresponds to the ability to customize and respond to the unique needs of customers; it primarily captures the customization dimension of product flexibility.

name: Development speed priority
definition: Factor 5, called development speed (DVSPEED), deals with the speed of introducing new products; it connotes the priority that the literature has labeled innovativeness.

name: Volume flexibility priority
definition: Factor 6, called volume flexibility (VFLEX), deals with the ability to adjust capacity rapidly.

name: Manufacturing performance
definition: The overall performance of operations is measured in two ways: a plant's performance relative to corporate performance criteria, and the performance of the operations function relative to plants owned by other companies in the same industry.

name: Product-process matrix position
authors_terms: ["on-diagonal", "off-diagonal", "positions on or close to the diagonal", "extreme off-diagonal positions"]
definition: The product-process matrix divides process choices and product plans into four categories each. Cells to the immediate right or left of the main diagonal are considered 'on-diagonal'; positions farther away from the diagonal are 'off-diagonal'.

name: Network centrality
definition: Centrality in an exchange network, computed as an organization's distance from the centroid of the reachability matrix; a basic postulate of power theories is that network centrality enhances power because the ability to control valued resources increases as a function of proximity to the core of a system of transactions.

name: Referral centrality
authors_terms: ["referral centrality", "centrality in the referral network", "referral network centrality"]
definition: Relative centrality in the client referral network: more central organizations are those having the greatest number of referral ties to other organizations and the shortest reachability paths in their indirect ties to peripheral organizations.

name: Attributed influence
definition: The extent to which an organization is named by other network members as particularly influential in shaping the formation of policies related to employment and training activities.

name: Joint program strategy
definition: A strategy of jointly planning and implementing programs or activities with other organizations; while a joint program results in a certain loss of autonomy, it gives an organization access to more resources and increases the possibilities for referral exchange.

name: Strategic communication
authors_terms: ["strategic formal and informal communication linkages", "communication strategies", "formal communication", "informal communication"]
definition: Strategic formal and informal communication linkages with other organizations, including formal transmittal of written correspondence, brochures and program announcements and interpersonal exchanges between organization representatives.

name: Advisory board strategy
authors_terms: ["advisory board", "advisory council or board of directors", "cooptation"]
definition: The placement of administrators from other organizations on an advisory council or board of directors, a form of cooptation that is expected to increase an organization's visibility and legitimacy.

name: Client difficulty
definition: The number of problems of the typical client served by an agency; clients with more problems are more difficult and costly to serve successfully.

name: External administration
authors_terms: ["external administration", "state or federal organizations", "locally administered organizations"]
definition: Whether an organization is administered by a state or federal body rather than locally; locally administered organizations are expected to be more responsive to local conditions.

name: Organization size
authors_terms: ["organization size", "staff size", "number of services offered", "extent of services"]
definition: The scale of an organization's operations, measured by the number of staff members and the number of services offered.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: The physical proximity of an organization to other organizations in the community network, which facilitates communication between staff members and reduces the referral costs borne by clients.

name: Ideological conformity
authors_terms: ["ideological conformity", "ideology", "ideologies dissimilar to the ideologies of other network organizations"]
definition: The similarity of an organization's ideology to the ideologies of other network organizations; organizations with ideologies that deviate sharply from the norm are expected to be located on the periphery of the referral network.

name: Mandated ties
definition: Relationships with other organizations that are mandated by law or court order rather than chosen by the organization.

name: Interpersonal ties
definition: Ties between staff members of different organizations, distinguished into social ties, such as club memberships, attending the same schools, or growing up together, and work ties, such as transfer of persons from one agency to another.

name: Abnormal stock returns
definition: A return that differs from the expected, or normal, return based on the portfolio's historical relationship with the general market; for individual firms, abnormal returns were cumulated over a 12-day window and standardized.

name: Past profit growth
authors_terms: ["past rate of profit growth", "change in income"]
definition: A firm's past rate of profit growth, measured as the percentage change in a firm's net income over the two years preceding the relevant legislation.

name: Financial leverage
definition: The extent to which a firm's capital structure is made up of debt, measured as the ratio of total liabilities to total assets.

name: Firm size
definition: The size of the firm, measured as a firm's net sales.

name: Cost containment legislation
authors_terms: ["health care cost containment policy", "cost containment legislation", "adverse legislative event"]
definition: National legislation intended to control health care costs, first through direct regulation and later by using market competition as the driving force for cost control.

name: Customer orientation
definition: A bank's customer orientation involves behaviors such as providing services and products that fit customers' specific needs.

name: Manager interface continuity
definition: Manager interface continuity refers to the degree that banks maintain personnel stability over time in interacting with small firms and handling their accounts.

name: Relational trust
definition: Relational trust refers to a 'trustor's' confident belief that a 'trustee' will act beneficially because the trustee cares about the trustor's welfare.

name: Likelihood of switching banks
authors_terms: ["customer likelihood of switching", "likelihood of switching banks", "likelihood of switching", "propensity to switch banks"]
definition: The likelihood of switching is viewed as an indication of the intention to terminate or continue a business relation.

name: Alter content homogeneity
authors_terms: ["content homogeneity among past alters", "homogeneity of current alters' content", "alter content homogeneity"]
definition: The similarity of the symbolic and aesthetic characteristics of the creative output ('content') of the focal team's alters; a TV production team's content is the essential symbolic and aesthetic characteristics of its creative output.

name: Structural holes
definition: Structural holes are present in an actor's network of relationships when the focal actor (or 'ego') is tied to others ('alters') who are not themselves connected.

name: Status
authors_terms: ["status", "status of the focal team", "status derived from past alter performance"]
definition: The status of a focal actor derives from the performance of the alters with whom it is affiliated; a signal of high status is particularly valuable when market uncertainty is high.

name: Centrality
definition: The prominence of the team in purely network terms, measured as the Freeman degree centrality of the focal team in the network of past ties.

name: Team cohesion
definition: Past team cohesion refers to the extent to which members of the current organization or team have worked together in the past; it is the density of relations among the members of a team.

name: Team performance
definition: Performance in this industry is the eventual commercial success of the production; the share of viewers that watched a show is considered the most crucial performance indicator of any TV production.

name: Contract type
definition: Contracts in offshore software development can be broadly classified into two categories: fixed-price contracts, which include a fixed fee negotiated before the start of the project and in which the vendor bears the major part of the risk, and time-and-materials contracts, in which the vendor contracts out his services at a certain rate and the client bears the cost of over-runs.

name: Requirements uncertainty
definition: The uncertainty surrounding the requirements of a software project; software development is an inherently uncertain process and requirements uncertainty, along with project size, characterizes risk in a software project.

name: Project size
definition: The size of the project, captured through project effort; large projects, like projects with greater requirements uncertainty, pose greater risks and task uncertainty.

name: Risk of availability of trained personnel
authors_terms: ["resource shortage", "risk of availability of trained personnel", "risk of getting and retaining trained personnel"]
definition: The perceived risk that trained personnel will not be available to work on a project, given that the lack of trained software engineers and high attrition are major problems in Indian software companies.

name: Client MIS experience
definition: The client's knowledge and experience in managing software development through its own MIS department, which reduces the risk for the vendor and increases the client's bargaining power by providing an alternative to keep development in-house.

name: Client experience with outsourcing
definition: The client's prior experience in handling offshore outsourcing contracts, which allows it to specify contractual terms more precisely and mitigates task uncertainty from the vendor's point of view.

name: Client reputation
definition: The reputation of the client, an indicator of bargaining power that increases the client's bargaining power and can be leveraged during the contracting process.

name: Future business potential
definition: The possibility of future business with the client, an indicator of bargaining power that can increase the client's bargaining power.

name: Client size
authors_terms: ["client size", "larger clients", "relative size of the parties"]
definition: The size of the client relative to the vendor, which strongly increases the client's bargaining power and signals to the vendor a strong possibility of future business.

name: Project importance to the client
authors_terms: ["project importance to the client", "importance of the project to the client"]
definition: The importance of the project to the client; the more important the project is to the client, the less the client will use her bargaining power.

name: Competition in the offshore software market
definition: Competition from alternative developers in the client's country and from other vendors in the vendor's country; the presence of competition provides the client with an alternative and thereby reduces the vendor's bargaining power.

name: Prior projects with the client
authors_terms: ["number of projects completed by the vendor for the client", "number of prior projects", "repeat projects"]
definition: The number of projects the vendor has already completed for the same client; an established relationship creates transaction costs of switching and a lock-in effect that increases the vendor's bargaining power.

name: Project profit
definition: Project profits are the net profits attributed to each project, calculated by subtracting all travel- and project-related costs from the total revenues attributable to the project, measured in Indian rupees.

name: Information available at contracting
authors_terms: ["information variables", "information set at the time of contracting", "Ic variables"]
definition: The information available to the contracting parties during the contracting period, comprising the vendor-, client-, and project-related characteristics known at the time of choosing the contract.

name: Project duration
definition: The actual duration of the project, an ex post development factor susceptible to unforeseen circumstances such as rework that may have arisen during the development of the software.

name: Core team size
definition: The core number of programmers that were assigned to the development team during the development of the project; the actual number of people working on a project changes over time but the core team personnel remain on the project.

name: Employee turnover
definition: Employee turnover in the project team during the project life cycle, which the authors expect to significantly impact the profits of the vendor.

name: Relationship present discounted value
authors_terms: ["PDV", "preshock PDV", "relationship's PDV", "maximum reneging temptation", "network adaptation cost", "Cnorm"]
definition: The maximum reneging temptation in a relational contract—namely, a regional airline's cost of adaptation in the worst case scenario in which bad weather strikes all the routes it operates for the major. If the relational contract's incentive constraint is binding, this maximum reneging temptation equals the relationship's unobservable PDV.

name: Route outsourcing survival
definition: Whether a major airline continued to outsource a given route to the same regional partner after the 2008 financial crisis, as opposed to restructuring the relational contract by reducing the portfolio of routes outsourced to that partner.

name: Host country environmental pollution
authors_terms: ["host country environmental pollution", "environmental pollution in that country", "pollution in host countries"]
definition: Host country environmental pollution captures a host country's pollution levels in air, water, and land-three domains that are considered most important by the Environmental Protection Agency. It is measured as 100 minus the average of a country's Climate Change (PCC) and Environmental Health (HLT) scores, such that higher values correspond to worse environmental pollution.

name: MNC investment
authors_terms: ["MNC investment", "foreign investment", "investment in a host country"]
definition: Our dependent variable, MNC investment, refers to an MNC's investment in a host country in a given year. It is measured as the number of an MNC's subsidiaries in a host country in a year because the establishment of a subsidiary represents a substantial commitment of the MNC to the host country.

name: Skilled labor market depth
authors_terms: ["skilled labor market depth", "deeper market for skilled labor"]
definition: A host country's skilled labor market depth refers to the availability, size, and quality of the pool of skilled workers within that country.

name: Rail transport network
definition: A host country's rail transport network reflects the distribution capacity of its railway infrastructure.

name: Labor-intensive industries
definition: Labor-intensive industries refer to industries that require a large amount of human labor to produce goods or services. These industries are highly dependent on the labor market for human resources.

name: Consumer goods industries
definition: Consumer goods industries are industries that produce and sell products or services to individual consumers for personal consumption, rather than to industrial buyers for further production or resale.

name: Bribery
definition: Payments made by firms to government officials 'to get things done'; the survey asks what percentage of total annual sales firms like the respondent pay in informal payments to public officials. The authors study bribery as a key type of corruption.

name: Investment in fixed assets
definition: Money spent by the firm for the purchase of machinery and equipment, which the authors treat as the backbone of long-term growth in firms.

name: Financial constraint
definition: Whether access to finance is an obstacle to the current operations of the establishment, taken from the survey question 'To what degree is Access to Finance an obstacle to the current operations of this establishment?'

name: Firm efficiency
definition: The ability of a firm to reap returns from its investments in fixed assets; in the analysis it is proxied by exports, because exporting firms exhibit significantly higher productivity than nonexporting ones.

name: Long-term orientation
definition: The temporal preferences of a firm: firms with a short-term orientation overvalue present profits and discount future profits, whereas long-term-oriented firms invest in assets and capability development.

name: Vertical integration
definition: Before the integration, each CP had owned a 30–40 percent shareholding stake in its anchor bottlers; the rest of the shares were publicly traded. After the integration, both CPs established wholly owned subsidiaries that bought out all the shares in the bottlers.

name: Noncarbonated products
definition: NonCSDs are noncarbonated soft drinks, the healthier product category that the concentrate producers expanded into away from traditional carbonated soft drinks (CSDs).

name: Stockouts
definition: Stockouts happen when customer orders are not completely fulfilled. Stockouts occur when a DC cannot deliver an entire order to a given retail outlet, and unfilled demand is not backordered.

name: Inventory
definition: Inventorysit is inventory (in days of sales) of SKU s carried by DC i in period t. The Bottler tries to retain four weeks of forecasted demand in inventory at the beginning of every four-week period, though actual inventory varies both across product categories and over time.

name: Sales forecast level
definition: Sales forecasts_levelsit is the ratio between actual and forecasted sales. It is also called the AF ratio, a standard measure of forecasting accuracy in operations management, and it reflects the bias in sales forecasts.

name: Sales forecast noise
definition: Sales forecasts_noisesit is the standard deviation in weekly AF ratios. It reflects the noise in sales forecasts.

name: Mode of job entry
authors_terms: ["route of entry", "mode of job entry", "internal mobility", "external hiring", "mode of entry", "internal movers", "external hires"]
definition: Workers can enter similar jobs—as defined by criteria such as functional roles, reporting relationships, and hierarchical rank—through either internal mobility or external hiring, and internal mobility itself can take the form of promotion, lateral transfer, or a combined promotion and transfer.

name: Job performance
definition: Performance is captured with three indicators from the firm's annual performance evaluations: contribution, competence, and performance rank, a forced ranking intended to reflect both performance and overall value to the organization.

name: Externally observable indicators of ability
authors_terms: ["externally observable indicators of ability", "observable indicators of ability", "observable ability", "externally observable attributes", "observable characteristics"]
definition: Some correlates of performance, such as a worker's education and the jobs he or she has held, are 'externally observable,' in that they can be observed by all potential employers, unlike externally unobservable attributes that can only be assessed by the current employer.

name: Compensation
definition: Employees were paid a salary and an annual bonus that was based on both individual and firm performance; bonuses represented 38 percent of pay, on average, and rose as high as 98 percent.

name: Rate of subsequent promotion
definition: Promotions occur among those workers who are able to demonstrate the skills necessary to be promoted to the next level, and more rapid promotions occur among those who are performing well ahead of expectations.

name: Involuntary exit rate
definition: Involuntary exit (both for cause and as part of downsizing) tends to occur among workers performing well below the average.

name: Voluntary exit rate
definition: A further form of worker mobility is voluntary exit; prior research suggests that such exit can be affected by a poor match between workers and their job or organization, as well as by underlying individual propensities to leave jobs.

name: Manager partisanship
authors_terms: ["Share of managers Democratic", "manager partisanship", "managers' political affiliations", "share of managers registered as Democrats"]
definition: The political partisanship of the managers of a firm, measured as the share of managers at firms registered as Democrats. The authors describe it as their measure of manager partisanship based on party registration and primary voting.

name: Hourly pay
definition: The inflation-adjusted log of reported base pay for the subset of Glassdoor pay reports that reported their pay hourly. It does not include additional sources of income, such as tips and bonuses.

name: Position in the earnings distribution
authors_terms: ["the earnings distribution", "distribution of earnings", "the bottom third of the distribution"]
definition: A worker's location in the overall U.S. earnings distribution, approximated by combining hourly, monthly, and salaried pay reports converted to annual-equivalent pay and weighting them to the occupation-industry distribution of jobs.

name: Inferred worker partisanship
definition: Workers' likely partisan affiliation, which managers infer from observable characteristics of the workforce such as gender and occupation, because managers rarely have direct knowledge of workers' partisan affiliations. Democratic and Republican coalitions are dissimilar across many demographic and social characteristics.

name: Fifteen-dollar hourly wage
authors_terms: ["$15 wages", "paying workers $15 per hour", "$15 an hour"]
definition: Payment of exactly $15 per hour, a threshold that has been the focus of much progressive organizing, including the Fight for $15 movement.

name: State minimum-wage increase
authors_terms: ["state-level minimum wage increases", "minimum wage changes", "minimum-wage increases"]
definition: A policy context coded 1 if the state in which a worker was employed had increased its minimum wage by more than 50 cents the previous year.

name: Manager position
authors_terms: ["senior managers", "managers based at headquarters", "human resource managers", "operations managers", "local managers", "front-line managers"]
definition: The location and functional position of managers within the organization, differentiating managers based at headquarters from local managers and senior managers, HR professionals, and operations managers from one another, to capture whether they could influence organizational wage-setting policies.

name: Manager-employee co-partisanship
authors_terms: ["Same party", "Different party", "No party", "partisan alignment of managers and employees"]
definition: The relative partisanship of a manager and an employee: Same party indicates that the manager and employee both identify with the same political party, Different party indicates they identify with different political parties, and No party indicates that the employee's résumé does not reveal partisanship.

name: Assignment to a high-wage position
definition: Whether a manager assigns a hypothetical new employee to the higher-paid of two otherwise equivalent positions.

name: Location choice
definition: The location within the United States that a first-time foreign entrant chooses, modeled as a choice of one economic area from the set of potential locations.

name: Location technological activity
definition: The amount of knowledge-generating activity present in a location; greater knowledge generating activity and the larger associated knowledge stocks increase the potential for and amount of spillovers.

name: Academic technological activity
definition: Patenting by academic institutions, one of the public sources that produce knowledge that is more basic and less appropriable.

name: Industrial technological activity
definition: Patenting by private firms, a private source that produces knowledge that is less basic and more appropriable.

name: Government technological activity
definition: Patenting by government agencies, a public source producing basic, less appropriable knowledge such as federal laboratories' work on basic science, space exploration and defense-related technologies.

name: Firm technical capability
authors_terms: ["technical capabilities", "technological capabilities", "R&D intensity", "technically leading firms", "technically lagging firms", "leaders", "laggards"]
definition: The main source of heterogeneity among potential receivers, their relative technical capabilities, which determine their ability to absorb knowledge and give rise to strategic concerns about inadvertent outward spillovers.

name: Prefounding social tie to a prominent incumbent
authors_terms: ["prefounding friendship tie", "prefounding social tie", "friendship tie to Inniskillin", "network progeny"]
definition: Our main independent variable indicates the presence of a prefounding friendship tie with one of the founders of Inniskillin. Prefounding professional friends were defined as individuals that founders 'liked and whom he/she would have felt very comfortable asking for advice or a favor' prior to starting their wineries.

name: Product price
authors_terms: ["average retail price", "ice wine prices", "valuations (and therefore prices)"]
definition: We focus attention on one market outcome that is clearly relevant for new firms—product prices. With expected benefits on the production and consumption sides of the market, the valuations (and therefore prices) of products made by an entrant improve in the presence of a prefounding social tie to a prominent industry incumbent.

name: Geographic distance from prominent incumbent
definition: We used Google Maps to determine the driving distance separating each winery pair and then recorded the distance from the focal winery to Inniskillin.

name: Chairperson sent-down youth experience
definition: Whether the chairperson of a securities company was sent down to rural areas as a 'sent-down youth' (SDY) during China's Cultural Revolution. The authors argue this formative experience instilled a strong work ethic in the face of adversity.

name: Earnings forecast accuracy
authors_terms: ["forecast accuracy", "accuracy of earnings forecasts", "Forecast_Accuracy", "relative forecast accuracy"]
definition: The relative accuracy of an analyst's earnings forecast—how precise a given forecast is compared with the average forecast error of all analysts covering the same firm for the same future fiscal year.

name: Analyst site visits
definition: The number of site visits conducted by the focal securities analyst to the focal covered listed firm during the focal year, an effort-intensive activity for gathering firm-specific information.

name: Work ethic
authors_terms: ["work ethic", "strong work ethic in the face of adversity"]
definition: A commitment to exert greater effort to achieve goals despite adversity.

name: Engagement with open source communities
authors_terms: ["engagement with OSCs", "EngagementWithOSC", "engagement with open source communities", "engagement with external repositories"]
definition: For the purpose of this study, we define engagement with OSCs as actively participating in the collaborative open source ecosystem where software, tools, or projects are developed openly and transparently. Specifically, this entails interacting with external repositories that the focal startup does not directly control.

name: Startup funding
authors_terms: ["raised funds", "likelihood of being funded", "raising a first financing round", "funding milestones"]
definition: We focus on a startup's first round, as this is a fundamental funding milestone. Indeed, investors participating in this round typically provide the necessary network for raising subsequent rounds.

name: Innovation
authors_terms: ["innovation", "product launches", "launching of new technology products", "commercialization of invention"]
definition: We follow the classic Schumpeterian definition of innovation—commercialization of invention—and use product launches as the closest available proxy in our analysis.

name: Technology novelty
authors_terms: ["technology novelty", "novelty of a startup's technology", "Novelty", "novel technologies"]
definition: We measure novelty by whether the combination of a startup's industry group keywords at the startup's founding year is relatively new. That is, less than three years should have passed since a keyword combination first appeared on Crunchbase.

name: Market competition
definition: To operationalize the level of competition in each technology space, we count the number of startups active in a given year-quarter and with the same industry group keywords as the focal one. The market in which a focal startup operates is thus considered competitive if the number of startups possessing the same technology keyword combination is greater than the 90th percentile.

name: Internal repository engagement
definition: In contrast to external repositories, we define internal repositories as those that originate from and are held by the focal firm. In other words, the focal organization created these and can determine what happens to the original source code.

name: Adaptive–innovative cognitive style
definition: Individuals' position along the adaption–innovation continuum: at one end, adaptors have an innate propensity for idea-implementation tasks, focus on doing things better, and seek solutions within the perimeter of existing paradigms; at the opposite end, innovators are innately skilled at idea creation, turn around information through repeated cognitive re-framings, and come up with ideas that break away from established practice.

name: Bridging relations across structural holes
authors_terms: ["bridging relations", "bridging ties", "bridging relationships across structural holes", "brokering networks", "constraint"]
definition: Relations that span structural holes: to build bridging relations, one has to engage in sustained interactions with colleagues with whom one has neither a direct connection (i.e., prior history or familiarity) nor an indirect connection via shared group membership or third-party ties.

name: Innovative performance
definition: Employees' ability to generate and implement new ideas that contribute value to the organization, evaluated through supervisors' ratings of their subordinates.

name: Exposure to a networking intervention
definition: The treatment consisted of a full day of executive education designed to encourage the formation of bridging relations with colleagues across the organization, leveraging knowledge acquisition and joint problem-solving activities with potential bridges.

name: Organizational disruption
definition: Following Zhang's (2021) definition, we conceptualize disruptive events as those that induce punctuated changes in an organization's day-to-day operations over a relatively short period.

name: Tie formation
definition: The creation of new connections in a network; uncertainty stimulates tie formation, as individuals seek new connections to access diverse perspectives and novel information.

name: Tie maintenance
definition: Tie maintenance—that is, the preservation of existing relationships.

name: Dyad gender composition
definition: In physician-level analyses, gender indicates whether a physician is a woman or a man; in dyadic analyses, gender is categorized as all-women, all-men, or mixed-gender.

name: Network-based resources
definition: The total number of shared patients captures a physician's total volume of network-based resources.

name: Tie embeddedness
definition: This variable aligns with Granovetter's theory (1973) that individuals embedded in close-knit communities with higher mutual trust, cooperation, and similarity represent strong ties. Conversely, a dyad connecting disconnected groups and having fewer mutual contacts constitutes weak ties.

name: Same-gender tie maintenance
authors_terms: ["same-gender maintained", "maintained same-gender ties", "maintained ties with other women"]
definition: The variables same-gender maintained and different-gender maintained are counts of the total number of ties that persisted with same- and different-gender contacts, respectively, between 2005 and 2007.

name: Same-gender tie formation
definition: Same-gender formed and different-gender formed are measurements of the number of same- and different-gender relationships initiated in 2007.

name: Different-gender tie maintenance
definition: The variables same-gender maintained and different-gender maintained are counts of the total number of ties that persisted with same- and different-gender contacts, respectively, between 2005 and 2007.

name: Different-gender tie formation
definition: Same-gender formed and different-gender formed are measurements of the number of same- and different-gender relationships initiated in 2007.

name: Scientific specialization
authors_terms: ["specialization", "knowledge specialization", "specialization of scientific experience", "specialization of a scientist's knowledge portfolio"]
definition: The degree to which the set of experiences that people have moved through over time are similar to one another rather than more varied; the authors focus on whether people acquire deep, specialized expertise by continually working within closely related fields or acquire more generalist experience through working in a broader set of areas.

name: Promotion within scientific roles
authors_terms: ["promotion within scientific roles", "promotions within scientific ranks", "promotion within the scientific ranks"]
definition: Promotion is usually defined as a move to a job in a higher hierarchical rank. Jobs of rank 3 or below (titles such as scientist, senior scientist, principal scientist, fellow) are coded as scientific jobs.

name: Promotion to first managerial role
authors_terms: ["transition to the first managerial job", "promotion to the first managerial position", "promotions from scientist to manager"]
definition: The move of a scientist into a first managerial job: at rank 4 a job is managerial if it includes 'manager' or 'associate director' in the title, and all jobs of rank 5 ('director') or above are managerial jobs.

name: Promotion within managerial roles
definition: An upward change in rank among jobs coded as managerial, examined within the subsample of observations that have already attained managerial status.

name: Pipeline orientation
definition: We define the pipeline orientation of a job as the extent to which realized promotions out of that source job feed into a narrow set of destination jobs. Jobs with high pipeline orientation advance people repeatedly into a small number of destination jobs, while jobs with low pipeline orientation promote people into a broad range of destination jobs.

name: Task content breadth
authors_terms: ["task content breadth", "narrower task content", "narrow set of tasks"]
definition: The narrower the set of tasks that a job involves, the narrower the set of roles to which job incumbents will likely advance. A job with narrow task content is one that is described with words that appear in few other job descriptions, while a job with broad task content is described with words that tend to appear in many other job descriptions.

name: Function size
definition: Jobs within organizations are often grouped into higher-level categories, such as occupational groups or functions and subfunctions, which group jobs with broadly similar task content. Jobs located in smaller functional specializations have fewer other roles to move into.

name: Organizational distribution
definition: One possible determinant of cohesion is the distribution of the role across different organizational units, such as departments or divisions; some roles may be highly concentrated within a few organizational units while others are distributed across a broad range of units.

name: Promotion rate
authors_terms: ["promotion rate", "rate of promotion", "promotion likelihood", "speed of advancement"]
definition: We define a promotion as a move into a job in a higher pay grade. The promotion rate is the rate at which employees are promoted out of a job.

name: Job recruiting breadth
authors_terms: ["job recruiting breadth", "breadth of jobs that the focal job recruits from"]
definition: The diversity of roles that people entering the focal source job are promoted from.

name: Promotion typicality
definition: Move typicality describes whether a given move follows a well-established path, often defined in terms of the frequency with which that move takes place within a broader population. For a given promotion out of source job i into destination job j, promotion typicality is the proportion of all promotions out of source job i during our entire observation period that ended up in destination job j.

name: Career diversity
authors_terms: ["career diversity", "diverse career history", "diversity of prior experience"]
definition: Prior work experience in a diverse set of job functions, measured independently of the sequence of positions held; it reflects the content rather than the order of a career.

name: Career atypicality
authors_terms: ["Misfit", "career atypicality", "atypical career trajectories", "organizational misfits", "deviation from prototypical career trajectories"]
definition: The degree to which an individual's career sequence departs from the prototypical career trajectories in the organization; organizational misfits are people whose career paths are atypical for the organization.

name: Brokerage
definition: A broker is one who connects people and groups that are otherwise disconnected in the informal network structure, that is, one who spans structural holes in the social fabric of an organization. Brokerage therefore involves communication across specific group boundaries that are rarely crossed.

name: Bridging tie
definition: The dyad-level analog of brokerage: communication within a dyad that spanned significant organizational distance that made their communication improbable.

name: Prior co-employment
definition: The number of months prior to the terminal period in which two people were both assigned to the same job function (or subfunction, office location, or business unit); it indicates that two people are likely to know each other.

name: Common third parties
definition: The number of unique individuals who communicated with both members of a dyad, capturing embeddedness in mutual acquaintances and the indirect ties through which people can find friends of friends.

name: Mutiny hazard
definition: The event in the empirical setup is an act of mutiny, construed under the military-legislative definition of the Mutiny Act as a collective action by serving members of the military to overthrow or resist lawful authority, to disobey and subvert discipline, or to cooperate with such forces. Regiments exit the risk set once they mutiny.

name: Time elapsed since a religious festival
authors_terms: ["days since a religious festival", "festival clock", "religious festivals as free spaces", "elapsed time since a religious festival"]
definition: Religious festivals involving communal gatherings, processions and public rituals were the free spaces that primed emotion, fostered shared identity and created collective empowerment for disobedience. A clock was constructed that was set to 0 on the day of a festival and then ticked upward in increments of 1 with the passage of each day, resetting to zero at the next festival.

name: Distance from place of recruitment
authors_terms: ["distance from place of recruitment", "community ties", "closeness to the place of recruitment", "kinship networks and neighborhood ties"]
definition: Each regiment was typically recruited almost entirely from a particular district, town or set of villages, and the closer a regiment was stationed to those places the greater was its interaction with civilian kith and kin. Distance from the place of recruitment therefore measures the strength of community ties available as an additional means of mobilization.

name: Oppositional symbols
authors_terms: ["oppositional symbols", "presence of Christian missions", "oppositional identity", "oppositional consciousness"]
definition: The presence of antagonists is essential for articulating grievances, arousing emotion and mobilizing identity for collective action; in the Bengal Army the presence of Christian missions championing Christianity would have activated the Hindu and Muslim identities of soldiers. Christian missions are therefore treated as an additional source of identity salience and oppositional consciousness for discontented soldiers.

name: Size of British presence
authors_terms: ["size of British presence", "strength of British presence", "local British presence"]
definition: When regiments were located in stations with a larger British presence, it could serve as a deterrent to mutiny or it could trigger greater emotional reactions; the strength of British presence is used to test whether festivals operated as purely affective mechanisms rather than a mix of affective and informational ones.

name: Racial diversity
definition: The extent of racial diversity (social heterogeneity) in each county in each year, constructed from the reported shares of the county population in different racial groups.

name: Income inequality
definition: The extent of income inequality (economic heterogeneity) in each county, capturing dispersion across the entire household income distribution.

name: Effectiveness of local civic action
authors_terms: ["effectiveness of local civic action", "campaign effectiveness", "funds raised"]
definition: Local civic action comprises events in which community residents work together to raise awareness, funds, and other resources to support specific issues; its effectiveness in this study is the amount of money collected in each community's TOT-UNICEF campaigns.

name: Promoting organization type
authors_terms: ["promoting organization type", "schools, churches, and clubs", "promoter organization"]
definition: TOT-UNICEF campaigns are organized by individuals typically working under the auspices of three types of local organizations; the types differ in whether participation is mandated or voluntary, with public schools subject to non-voluntary participation and churches and clubs based on voluntary selection.

name: Network isolation
definition: Isolation is a state in which a physician has no professional ties; the authors operationalize it as a position that is distinct in character from being connected to the network. The idea that isolation begets the drifting of norms from those of the broader society has been central to sociological theory.

name: Network size
definition: Degree centrality is the total number of ties a physician has to other physicians; the authors describe it as the number of professional connections a physician has through which updated information and norms can be transmitted.

name: Network cohesion
definition: Cohesion, how connected network members are to each other, influences the speed and accuracy of information transmission and promotes social learning. It is measured by local transitivity, the likelihood that any two colleagues with whom a physician formed a tie are also connected to each other.

name: Liminal prescribing
definition: Liminal practices are systematic departures from societal norms, rules, or laws that perpetrators correctly perceive as morally and legally ambiguous. In this setting, liminal prescribing is counting the number of patients prescribed benzodiazepines for durations that clearly exceed the guidelines but who do not exhibit prescription-fill patterns consistent with misuse or abuse.

name: Deviant prescribing
definition: Deviance is the act of knowingly breaking with societal norms or laws in ways that carry punishment for those caught doing so. Deviant prescribing is construed as routinely prescribing to patients with prescription-fill patterns consistent with misuse or abuse.

name: Years since medical training
definition: Number of years since the physician finished medical training; higher values indicate earlier completion of training (older cohort).

name: Friendship with employees in the hiring organization
definition: Friendships are close, interpersonal relationships comprised of sentimentality and obligation; they are affective relationships that are voluntary in nature and are formed and maintained for their own sake.

name: Job offer receipt
authors_terms: ["offer", "job offers", "receiving a full-time postgraduate job offer"]
definition: The offer variable records whether the intern received a full-time postgraduate job offer from the internship employer.

name: Geographic proximity
definition: Propinquity concerns whether the intern completed an internship in the same state as the university he or she was attending, rather than being forced to move from a greater distance.

name: Loan officer individual relational style consistency
authors_terms: ["individually consistent relational style", "individually (internally) consistent relational styles", "within-loan-officer consistency", "intra-loan officer consistency"]
definition: SL and LL styles are regarded as consistent and distinct relational styles guided by principles that subsume scripts that 'hang together' in a logical fashion. By contrast, loan officers exhibiting a mixed style engage in practices that incorporate elements of both SL and LL styles—practices that often do not hang together in a logically complementary manner.

name: Between-loan-officer relational style consistency
authors_terms: ["along consistent relational styles", "between-actor consistency", "inter-loan officer consistency"]
definition: consistency in the individual styles employed by successive individuals

name: Transition from individually inconsistent to individually consistent relational style
authors_terms: ["inconsistent to consistent", "moving from a mixed to a consistent style"]
definition: moving from a within-actor individually inconsistent style to an individually consistent style (Mt → SLt+1 or Mt → LLt+1), which denotes that the original loan officer employed an inconsistent relational style whereas the subsequent one employed a consistent one—either letter or spirit of the law.

name: Loan officer change
authors_terms: ["change in loan officer", "changed officer", "broken tie", "loan officer change"]
definition: cases when a client was transferred to a different loan officer

name: Missed loan payment
authors_terms: ["miss a payment contrary to contractual terms", "missed payment", "delinquency", "breach of contract"]
definition: dummy-coded outcome measures that evidence breach of contract: the first denotes that the borrower missed one payment or more in breach of contract during the life of the loan.

name: Relational style
authors_terms: ["relational styles", "letter of the law (LL)", "spirit of the law (SL)", "mixed"]
definition: the specific manner in which social actors in given roles interact and relate to other social actors in given roles

name: Deadline penalty
definition: Deadlines are defined as periodically occurring checkpoints when the agent faces a penalty for having incomplete tasks. This penalty is usually imposed directly by the principal—for instance, as negative performance evaluations, fewer unbilled hours, or loss of business—but it can also be indirect, such as peer pressure associated with not meeting deadlines.

name: Clustering of task completions
authors_terms: ["clustering of task completions", "clustering of workflows", "month-end clustering"]
definition: In the presence of a deadline penalty, there is clustering of task completions at the period-end deadline. The authors also refer to this as clustering of patent-filing workflows at monthends.

name: Task complexity
definition: Complexity is a scalar characteristic such that, all else equal, the benefits of filing are higher, and the costs of filing to both principals and agents, including the cost of errors, are higher for more complex applications. Under the model assumptions, task duration is longer for more complex jobs.

name: Work quality
definition: Work quality of a patent application is measured using two types of measures: (i) errors and additional work needed during the patent prosecution process, called work-process-based measures, and (ii) the quality of outcomes associated with the application, called work-outcome-based measures.

name: Firm size
definition: Firm size is measured as the number of patents (or applications) belonging to firm j that were applied in year t.

name: Pace of technological innovation
authors_terms: ["pace of technological innovation", "speed of innovation", "speed of technology change", "technology cycle time"]
definition: Technologies vary in the speed of innovation; some technologies change slowly, while others change rapidly. Technology cycle time, the mean time gap between a patent application and its backward citations, is used to represent the speed of technological changes in a field.

name: Gender
definition: The candidate's gender, contrasted as professionally trained women versus professionally trained men; the authors code Female as dichotomous based on admissions office records.

name: Tryout
definition: Tryouts are a type of employment practice whereby organizational decision makers observe candidates in their milieu prior to making long-term hiring and salary decisions. Tryouts take the form of internships for professionals.

name: Initial salary offer
definition: By 'initial salary,' we mean the salary that the candidate would be paid if employment commenced.

name: Relative managerial expertise
definition: For the Japanese retailer, expertise is measured by a manager's total work experience on each task; for the Chilean producer, by total work experience on each product category. Relative expertise is the ratio of the two, and in the model the manager's knowledge about a task is an additive function of her expertise in that task and the attention she devotes to it.

name: Relative attention allocation
definition: Each manager reports her working hours and self-rated effort intensity on each of the two tasks or product categories, and ratios of these measures between the two tasks or products are constructed. In the longitudinal analysis the ratio of sales volumes across product categories is used as a proxy of allocation of attention.

name: Attention capacity
definition: Cognitive capacity - or how much rationality is bounded - may very well vary across situations; depending on the work environment, family demands, and personal circumstances, managerial cognitive capacity may be abundant or scarce, varying between individuals as well as within individuals over time. The allocation of managerial attention crucially depends on the degree of attention capacity.

name: Latent cognitive dissimilarity
authors_terms: ["latent cognition", "latent cognitive similarity or dissimilarity", "latent cognitive differences", "cognitive dissimilarity", "schemas"]
definition: Latent cognition refers to schemas, the semantic associations through which people understand and develop their point of view on a focal issue; because these schemas are not directly accessible to others, they are latent.
